units.la: IEsus Christus heri, hodie & in secula idem est; & qualis Heri fuerit, hactenus dictum est. 1. Qualis Hodie, in plenitudine temporum, sit, deinceps dicendum. Ordo dicendorum. 2. Persona Jesu Christi definitur. 3. Filii Dei in carnem adventus in Veteri & Novo Testamento testatissimus est. 4. Filius Dei, ceu λόγος, caro factus; 5. & Deus in carne manifestatus est. 6. Jesus Christus secundum carnem ex Semine Davidis; secundum Spiritum sanctitatis definitus in potentia Filius Dei est. 7. Nebulæ S. Pauli testimonio huic obductæ discutiuntur. 8. Spiritus Jehovæ super Christo Evangelium prædicante fuit. 9. Is ipse, qui in forma Dei fuit, formam servi assumpsit. 10. In Christo omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter habitat. 11. Princeps salutis Christus similiter, ut pueri ejus, carnis & sanguinis particeps factus, semen Abrahæ assumpsit. 12. Mosis & Prophetarum incarnationem Christi prædicentium testimonia. 13. Veritas incarnationis, seu duarum naturarum, Divinæ & Humanæ in una persona Christi existentium, ex collectione testimoniorum præcedentium concluditur. 14. Christus verus Deus, & verus homo est. 15. & Deus Patri, & Homo nobis consubstantialis est. 16. Divinam naturam per æternam generationem à Deo Patre: Humanam per conceptionem ex Spiritu S. ex B. Virgine Maria accepit. 17. Maria ex tribu Juda, familia Davidis orta, statu Virgo, sed desponsata Virgo, & perpetua Virgo fuit. 18. Ab Angelo salutatur κεχαριτωμένη. 19. Jesum ex Virgine nasciturum, Esaj. VII.14. prædictum est. 20. Παρθενογένεια Vaticinii ab Hebræis detorti refellitur. 21. Jeremiæ de fœmina marem circumdante vaticinium. 22. Blasphemiæ Judæorum adversus nativitatem Jesu ex Virgine retunduntur. 23. Natus est Jesus ex Virgine per conceptionem ex Spiritu S. non exclusa operatione Patris & Filii. 24. Spiritui S. superventio super Virginem: Virtuti Altissimi ejusdem obumbratio tribuitur. 25. Formatio naturæ Christi humanæ in utero matris explicatur, & Socinianorum, propter eam à Spiritu S. peractam Christum Spiritus Sancti Filium fingentium, error perstringitur. 26. Objectiones eorundem elisæ. 27. Christus
units.tr: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. What he was yesterday has been discussed so far. 1. What he is today, in the fullness of time, must be discussed next. The order of the topics. 2. The person of Jesus Christ is defined. 3. The coming of the Son of God in the flesh is most clearly attested in the Old and New Testaments. 4. The Son of God, as the Word [λόγος, logos], was made flesh. 5. God was manifested in the flesh. 6. Jesus Christ, according to the flesh, is from the seed of David; according to the Spirit of holiness, he is defined as the Son of God in power. 7. The clouds that have been cast over this by the testimony of St. Paul are dispelled. 8. The Spirit of Jehovah was upon Christ as he preached the Gospel. 9. He who was in the form of God took the form of a servant. 10. In Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily. 11. Christ, the Prince of salvation, likewise, since his children were partakers of flesh and blood, took on the seed of Abraham. 12. The testimonies of Moses and the Prophets, which foretold the incarnation of Christ. 13. The truth of the incarnation, that is, of the two natures, divine and human, existing in the one person of Christ, is concluded from the collection of the preceding testimonies. 14. Christ is true God and true man. 15. He is God, consubstantial with the Father, and man, consubstantial with us. 16. He received the divine nature by eternal generation from God the Father; the human nature he received by conception from the Holy Spirit, from the Blessed Virgin Mary. 17. Mary, sprung from the tribe of Judah and the family of David, was a virgin in her condition, a betrothed virgin, and a perpetual virgin. 18. By the angel she is greeted as "highly favoured" [κεχαριτωμένη, kecharitomene]. 19. That Jesus would be born of a virgin was foretold in Isaiah VII.14. 20. The Hebrews' distortion of the prophecy concerning "virgin-birth" [Παρθενογένεια, parthenogeneia] is refuted. 21. Jeremiah's prophecy about a woman encompassing a man. 22. The blasphemies of the Jews against the birth of Jesus from a virgin are repulsed. 23. Jesus was born of a virgin through conception by the Holy Spirit, the operation of the Father and the Son not being excluded. 24. The coming of the Holy Spirit upon the Virgin; the overshadowing of the Most High's power is ascribed to the same. 25. The formation of Christ's human nature in the mother's womb is explained, and the error of the Socinians is censured, who, because the Holy Spirit accomplished this, imagine that Christ is a son of the Holy Spirit. 26. Their objections are overthrown. 27. Christ was formed out of the substance of Mary's flesh and blood, and was begotten from her and in her.

units.la: a ex substantia carnis & sanguinis Mariae formata, & ex ea, atque in ea genitus est. 28. Fanaticorum, de carne Christi non ex substantia matris decerpta, sed aliunde formata, deliria, & argumenta ad partes vocantur. 29. Originem humanam carnis Christi ex Adamo per Abrahamum & Davidem, ejusdem genealogia comprobat; quae duplex, altera a Matthaeo, altera a Luca, utraque generationis carnalis, non regenerationis spiritualis, texitur. 30. Fanaticorum & aliorum exceptio, quod Matthaeus non Mariae, sed Josephi genealogiam executus sit, eliditur. 31. Conciliatio genealogiae utriusque apud Matthaeum & Lucam pertextae instituitur. 32. Formatio Christi in utero matris non in momento, sed temporis successu peracta est. 33. Christus in utero matris a Spiritu S. sanctificatus est, ut labis omnis expers nasceretur. 34. Ejusdem anima rationalis a Deo creata est. 35. Filius Dei humanam naturam in unitatem personae suae assumpsit. 36. Assumptionem illam unio duarum naturarum in una persona Christi sequitur. 37. Modus unionis hypostaticae mysterio plenus est. 38. Unionis rerum diversarum species a Veteribus, Athanasio inprimis & Bernhardo, collectae. 39. Synodica Fidei in Concilio Chalcedonensi de unione naturarum in Christo expositio duplex approbatur; una κατ' ἀρσιν. 40. Altera κατὰ θέσιν; unio videlicet personalis, & quodammodo etiam essentialis & naturalis Veteribus dicta, oppositè ad unionem accidentalem Nestorii. 41. Ex unione personali naturarum in Christo etiam communio, seu communicatio quaedam oritur, eaque vel non-mutua, vel mutua. Non-mutua est communicatio humanae naturae facta, eaque tum Gratiae eminentiae; 42. tum Gratiarum habitualium, quae supra dona omnibus creaturis aliis a Deo collata eminent. 43. Perfectio Gratiarum illarum quo ad numeros, gradus & operationes sub initium demum exaltationis coepit. Sapientia ejus ita indies proficiente, ut tamen ab ignoratione rerum quarundam innoxia natura ejus humana immunis non fuerit. 44. Etiam corpus ejus impassibilitatis, subtilitatis, levitatis & invisibilitatis in statu exinanitionis expers fuisse, adversus Docetas, Pontificios, alios aestruitur. 45. Mutua communicatio est in persona, eaque triplex, idiomatum, officii & operationum. Idiomatum communicatio definitur. 46. & amplius explicatur. 47. Communicatio ea respectu personae realis, respectu naturarum verbalis est. 48. Communio officii & honoris explicatur. 49. Ex ea communio operationum, seu apotelesmatum resultat, quae fusius exponitur. 50. Unionis naturarum in persona manifestatio facta est in ejusdem nativitate, in qua & tempus & modus pariendi ordinarius fuit, cum Maria & consveto post conceptionem tempore, & referatis uteri claustris Christum pepererit. 51. Natalis annus Christi licet in Verbo Dei definitus non sit, tamen nec plane incertus est, & characteres quosdam in Verbo Dei expressos habet. 52. Alia ratio est natalis dei Christi, qui ex Verbo Dei accurate definiri, deficientibus characteribus similibus, non potest. 53. Circa mysterium incarnationis Christi errores innumeri Ecclesiam infestam semper habuerunt, neque id mirandum est. 54. Haeretici personam Christi oppugnantes vel Θεομάχοι, in loco recensiti, sunt; 55. vel Χριστομάχοι, quorum Veterum & recentiorum in quatuor classes tributorum historia fusius edisseritur. 56. Eorundem argumenta Veritati incarnationis Christi oppósita diluuntur. 57. Errantium circa communicationem idiomatum perplexitas attingitur. 58. Subsistentia τὸ λόγος nec proprie humanitati Christi communicata est; nec quatenus communicata est, idiomatum communicationem naturae humanae factam probat. 59. Idiomata Divina humanae naturae communicata non esse argumentis ponderosis probatur. 60. Inprimis natura Christi humana non est omnipraesens. 61. Nec omniscia, vel omnipotens. 62. Argumentis adversantium fit satis. 63. Dissensus Protestantium circa communicationem idiomatum momentum expenditur. 64.
units.tr: 28. The ravings of the fanatics, who hold that the flesh of Christ was not taken from the substance of his mother but formed from elsewhere, and their arguments, are summoned to the field. 29. His human origin in the flesh from Adam, through Abraham and David, is proved by his genealogy; this is twofold, one given by Matthew, the other by Luke, and both are woven in terms of carnal generation, not spiritual regeneration. 30. The objection of the fanatics and others, that Matthew followed the genealogy not of Mary but of Joseph, is refuted. 31. The reconciliation of the two genealogies, as woven by Matthew and Luke, is set out. 32. The formation of Christ in the mother's womb was accomplished not in a moment but by the progress of time. 33. Christ was sanctified in his mother's womb by the Holy Spirit, so that he might be born free of all stain. 34. His rational soul was created by God. 35. The Son of God assumed human nature into the unity of his person. 36. That assumption is followed by the union of the two natures in the one person of Christ. 37. The manner of the hypostatic union is full of mystery. 38. Examples of the union of diverse things, collected by the ancients, above all by Athanasius and Bernard. 39. The synodical exposition of the Council of Chalcedon concerning the union of the natures in Christ is approved in a twofold form: one by way of "lifting up" [κατ' ἀρσιν, kat' arsin]; 40. the other by way of "setting down" [κατὰ θέσιν, kata thesin]; namely, the personal union, which the ancients also called in some sense essential and natural, set against the accidental union of Nestorius. 41. From the personal union of the natures in Christ there also arises a certain communion, or communication, and this is either non-mutual or mutual. The non-mutual communication is that made to the human nature, and this consists both (42) in the eminence of grace and in the habitual gifts of grace, which stand out above the gifts conferred by God on all other creatures. 43. The perfection of those gifts, as to their measure, degrees and operations, began only at the beginning of his exaltation; his wisdom so advanced day by day that yet his human nature was not free from ignorance of certain things, which was not harmful. 44. Against the Docetists, the Papists and others, it is maintained that his body also was without impassibility, subtlety, lightness and invisibility in the state of humiliation. 45. The mutual communication is in the person, and it is threefold: of idioms, of office, and of operations. The communication of idioms is defined. 46. and is further explained. 47. This communication is, with respect to the real person, real; with respect to the natures, verbal. 48. The communion of office and honour is explained. 49. From this there results the communion of operations, or "apotelesmata", which is set out more fully. 50. The union of the natures in the person was made manifest at his birth, in which both the time and the manner of the ordinary delivery were observed: Mary, at the usual time after conception, and with the closed womb opened, brought forth Christ. 51. Although the year of Christ's birth is not defined in the Word of God, yet it is not wholly uncertain, and it has certain marks expressed in the Word of God. 52. The birth-day of Christ is another matter, which cannot be precisely defined from the Word of God, since similar marks are lacking. 53. Countless errors concerning the mystery of Christ's incarnation have always troubled the Church, and this is no cause for wonder. 54. Heretics who attack the person of Christ are listed in the place as "God-fighters" [Θεομάχοι, theomachoi]; 55. or "Christ-fighters" [Χριστομάχοι, christomachoi], whose history, divided into four classes, ancient and recent, is set out more fully. 56. Their arguments opposed to the truth of Christ's incarnation are answered. 57. The perplexity of those who err concerning the communication of idioms is touched upon. 58. The subsistence of the Word [τὸ λόγος] was not properly communicated to the humanity of Christ, nor, insofar as it was communicated, does it prove a communication of idioms made to the human nature. 59. That the divine idioms were not communicated to the human nature is proved by weighty arguments. 60. Above all, the human nature of Christ is not omnipresent. 61. Nor is it omniscient or omnipotent. 62. Enough is done for the arguments of the opposing side. 63. The weight of the disagreement among the Protestants concerning the communication of idioms is weighed. 64.

units.la: ESUS CHRISTUS heri & hodie ἀυτὸς Idem est, & in secula, Hebr. XIII. 8.
units.tr: JESUS CHRIST, yesterday and today, is the same, and for ever, Heb. 13:8.

units.la: I. Esus Christus heri & hodie ἀυτὸς Idem est, & in secula, Hebr. XIII. 8. Nam & Jesus est Christus, Unctus a Deo, ut sit Salvator, Sospitator Generis humani; & non est Alius, לא אלה Non Deus, quem non noverint Patres, novitius, e propinquo, quem non timuerint Patres, Deut. XXXII. 17. sed Αυτὸς idem הוא אלהים Ipse, Idem Deus, ibid. IV. 35. εἷς Θεὸς unus Deus, qui justificabit circumcisionem ex fide, & praeputium ex fide. Rom. III. 30. Gal. III. 20. utpote qui, ceu Jehova, non mutatur, Mal. III. 6. Ut aliquando in eum, ut Salvatorem & Redemptorem credi; aliquando in eum non credi debeat. Nam Idem est χθὲς heri, non quemadmodum solemus dicere, χθὲς ἡ πρὸ χθές, χθὲς ἡ πρὸ πέντε Heri vel Pridie natus, novellum Numen & Salvator, factus talis in procedente novissima nativitate sua, & Evangelii praedicatione, uti hostes Majestatis Christi blasphemant, quia continuatus licet, unus tamen praedicandi ille actus fuit, qui proin non sub χθὲς Heri, sed sub σήμερον Hodie comprehenditur: & alias sufficiebat dicere, Eundem esse in seculum: denique consequens non foret, variis doctrinis non debere nos circumAcumagi, si demum coepto Evangelio Christus existere, atque sic à non esse ad esse mutari coepisset; sed omni æternitate & tempore praecedente: Σήμερον Hodie, præsenti tempore, quo Evangelii prædicatio coepta continuabatur, & εἰς τὸς αἰῶνας in secula, in æternum. Inde nempe constare poterat, Christum perpetuò Eundem esse, non mutari, adeóque nec convenire fidelibus, ut doctrinam de eo mutent, hoc est, uti v. 9. sequitur, & ex immutabilitate Christi, objecti fidei, velut causa colligitur, doctrinis variis & peregrinis circumagantur. Convenit cum verbis Apostoli explicatio nominis יהוה ὁ ὤν, ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, Qui est, Qui erat, & Qui venturus est, Apoc.I.8.
units.tr: I. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and for ever, Heb. 13:8. For Jesus is Christ, anointed by God, so that he may be the Saviour and Preserver of the human race. He is not another, [לא אלה] "not God," a novelty recently come from nearby, whom the Fathers did not know and did not fear (Deut. 32:17). He is rather [αὐτὸς] the same, [הוא אלהים] "he himself, the same God" (ibid. 4:35), [εἷς Θεὸς] "one God, who will justify the circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith" (Rom. 3:30; Gal. 3:20). He does not change, like Jehovah (Mal. 3:6). It is not that at one time he must be believed in as Saviour and Redeemer, and at another time must not be believed in. For he is the same [χθὲς], "yesterday," not in the sense we commonly use: "yesterday or the day before," "yesterday or five days ago," "born yesterday or the day before," a newly made God and Saviour, become such in the course of his latest nativity and the preaching of the Gospel, as the enemies of the majesty of Christ blaspheme. Although that preaching was continuous, it was nonetheless one single action, and so it is comprehended not under "yesterday" but under "today" [σήμερον]. Otherwise it would have been enough to say that he is the same for ever. Nor would it follow from this that we should not be swayed about by various doctrines, if Christ had only begun to exist when the Gospel began, and so had begun to change from not-being to being. He exists instead through all eternity and before all time. "Today" [σήμερον] means the present time, in which the preaching of the Gospel began and continues; "for ever" [εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας] means in eternity. From this it can indeed be established that Christ is perpetually the same and does not change. It therefore does not befit believers to change their doctrine about him, that is, as v. 9 goes on to say. From the immutability of Christ, the object of faith, it is rightly inferred as a cause that they should not be carried about by various and strange doctrines. The explanation of the name יהוה as ὁ ὤν, ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, "who is, who was, and who is to come" (Rev. 1:8), agrees with the words of the Apostle.

units.la: II. Vidimus hactenus, qualis fuerit Jesus Christus χθὲς Heri, ab æterno, πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου ante jactum fundamentum mundi, in consilio illo Dei, quo in Christo nos elegit, Ephes.I.4. & ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου inde à jacto mundi fundamento, Apoc.XIII.8. quando in Paradiso revelatus, ut semen Mulieris promissus, sed tempore præstituto demum in carne manifestandus fuit, ad quod tempus usque ἐπαγγελία Promissio duravit. Pergimus nunc ad decantatum illud Σήμερον Hodie, seu πληρωμα τῆς χρόνου Plenitudinem illam temporis, quo Deus emisit Filium suum, nascentem ex muliere, & se subjicientem Legi, ut eos qui sub Lege erant, emptos redimeret, ut adoptionem filiorum acciperemus, Gal.IV.4.5. Haec enim illa οἰκονομία τῆς πληρώματος τῶν καιρῶν oeconomia plenitudinis temporum est, qua Deus statuit ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι τὰ πάντα ἐν Χριστῷ recapitulare, seu in unam summam confundere omnia in Christo, sive quæ sunt in Cœlis, sive quæ sunt in terra. Ephes.I.10. Cumq; in hac demum Oeconomia Plenitudinis temporum Divinæ Sapientiæ placuerit, Filium suum in carnem mittere, per eum hactenus affecta perficere & consummare, & merito suo Gloriam in altissimis Deo, terræ Pacem, & hominibus Dei εὐδοκίας Beneplacitum (Luc.II.14.) in solidum restituere; prius quàm œconomiam Fœderis Gratiæ sub Evangelio exponere instituimus, Jesu Christi, Filii Dei, in carne manifestati Personam, eique connexam Vitæ, mortis, resurrectionis, ascensionis in altum, & sessionis ad dextram Dei historiam, ac demum Ejusdem Mediatorium munus, vividioribus Verbi Dei, cujus hæc Doctrina centrum, scopus & medulla est, coloribus exhibere, ipsomet Jesu Christo duce & auspice, conabimur.
units.tr: II. So far we have seen what Jesus Christ was yesterday, from eternity, "before the foundation of the world" [πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου], in that counsel of God by which he chose us in Christ (Eph. 1:4), and "from the foundation of the world" [ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου] (Rev. 13:8). He was revealed in Paradise, promised as the seed of the woman, but was to be manifested in the flesh only at the appointed time, until which the promise [ἐπαγγελία] remained in force. We now come to that much-discussed "today" [σήμερον], or "the fullness of time" [πληρωμα τῆς χρόνου], in which God sent forth his Son, born of a woman and made subject to the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive the adoption of sons (Gal. 4:4–5). This is that "economy of the fullness of times" [οἰκονομία τῆς πληρώματος τῶν καιρῶν], in which God decided to "sum up" [ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι] all things in Christ, that is, to bring all things together into one sum in Christ, whether in heaven or on earth (Eph. 1:10). Since in this economy of the fullness of times it pleased divine Wisdom to send his Son into the flesh, so that through him he might perfect and complete what had been begun, and by his merit restore fully the glory of God in the highest, peace on earth, and the good pleasure [εὐδοκία] of God among men (Luke 2:14), we shall attempt, with Jesus Christ himself as our guide and patron, to set out in more vivid colours the person of Jesus Christ, the Son of God manifested in the flesh. Before we begin to explain the economy of the covenant of grace under the Gospel, we shall also present the history connected with him: his life, death, resurrection, ascension on high, and sitting at the right hand of God; and finally his mediatorial office. This doctrine is the centre, aim and marrow of the Word of God, and we shall present it in the living colours of that Word.

units.la: III. Est autem Jesus Christus Filius Dei in tempore caro factus, seu, ex Matre Maria Virgine per conceptionem ex Spiritu S. natus Θεάνθρωπος, Messias, Salvator & Mediator humani generis, S. Patribus promissus, ab iisdem expectatus, cujus nativitatem, vitam, mortem, resurrectionem, ascensionem in Cœlum sancti Evangelistæ describunt; cujus verbum in hunc usque diem in mundo prædicatum, eundem mundum sibi subjicit; quem denique è Cœlo reducem expectamus, futurum judicem mortuorum & viventium. De nominibus Jesu & Christi infra, ubi de ejusdem officio dicturi sumus. Id verò ante omnia firmissimis argumentorum ponderibus præstituendum est; Jesum Christum esse Θεάνθρωπον, Deum & Hominem in eadem persona, quod μέγα Στήριον μυστήριον magnum pietatis mysterium S.Paulus I.Tim.III,16. appellat. Et prius quidem καινὸς hujus δόξης Principalis & summæ Veritatis ac mysterii τὸ ὅτι, deinceps verò, ubi de Officio Christi acturi sumus, ejusdem τὸ διότι seu causam explicatam demonstratamque dabimus.
units.tr: III. Jesus Christ is the Son of God, made flesh in time; that is, born of the Virgin Mary, his mother, by conception from the Holy Spirit. He is the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], the Messiah, the Saviour and Mediator of the human race, promised to the holy Fathers and expected by them. The holy Evangelists describe his nativity, life, death, resurrection and ascension into heaven. His word, preached in the world to this day, subjects that same world to himself, and we await him to return from heaven as the future judge of the living and the dead. We shall speak of the names Jesus and Christ below, where we treat of his office. But above all this must be established by the weightiest arguments: that Jesus Christ is the God-man, God and man in one person. St. Paul calls this "the great mystery of godliness" [μέγα τὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον] (1 Tim. 3:16). First we shall set out the "that" [τὸ ὅτι] of this principal truth and of the mystery, which is the foremost point; then, when we come to treat of the office of Christ, we shall give its "why" [τὸ διότι], that is, its explained and demonstrated cause.

units.la: IV. Filium igitur Dei ex Cœlo à Patre missum advenisse, descendisse in terram, visitasse homines, in carne apparuisse, carnem factum, in carne manifestatum esse, & similia, scripturæ V. & N.T. magno consensu testantur. De Missione Filii sic ipse Filius Jehova exercituum, loquitur: Appropinquate ad me, audite hoc לא מראש בסתר דברתי Non à capite, seu principio in occulto locutus sum. A tempore, quo id exititit, ibi eram ועתה אדני יהוה שלחני ורוחו Et nunc Dominus Jehova misit me, & Spiritus ejus, vel Spiritum ejus, Esaj.XLVIII.16. Ubi de se loquens Filius Dei Jehova exercituum (v.2.) duo tempora distinguit. Prius, quo inde à principio locutus est non in occulto; adeóque palam, ceu λόγος sermo, qui in principio fuit apud Deum, Joh.I.1. Posterius, quo nunc in plenitudine temporum à Deo missus est, & Ipse & Spiritus ejus, Spiritus gratiæ & precum effusus in omnem carnem. Inde est vox ἀποστόλης & ἐξαποστάλης missionis. Οὐκ ἀπέστειλε. Non misit Deus Filium suum in mundum, ut judicaret mundum, ibid.III.17. Ὃν ἀπέστειλε Quem misit Deus, loquitur verba Dei, ibid. v.34. ἐξαπέστειλε misit Deus Filium suum, nascentem ex muliere, Gal.IV.4. Quæ missio non simpliciter deputationem, vel excitationem ad officium aliquod, qualis fuit Johannis ἀπεσταλμένος missi ante Christum, Joh.III.28. sed κατ' ἐξοχὴν dationem & missionem ἐκ τῶν ἄνω ex superioribus notat. Qui ἄνωθεν desuper venit, supra omnes est. Qui est ex terra, ex terra loquitur. Qui ex Cœlo venit, supra omnes est, ibid.31. Ubi Christum inter & Johannem Baptistam, omnésque alios Prophetas & Mosen ipsum, quorum nemo ex Cœlo venit; vel locutus est, antithesis statuitur. Unde sic missus puer natus nobis, filius datus nobis Esaj.IX.6. dicitur. Et sic missus est, ut ex Cœlo descendisse dicatur. עליתָ למרום Ascendisti in altum, & gifti prædam, &c. Psalm.LXVIII.19. Unde sic Apostolus argumentatur: Τὸ δὲ ἀνέβη, τί ἐστιν εἰ μὴ ὅτι καὶ κατέβη πρῶτον εἰς τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς. Illud autem, Ascendit, quid est, nisi quòd & descendit prius in inferiores partes terræ? Qui descendit, ipse est, & is, qui ascendit supra omnes Cœlos, ut omnia impleat; Ephes.IV.9.10. Haud equidem in omni ascendente verum est; quòd qui ascendit, prius descenderit, quia etiam Moses ascendit in montem, qui ex eo prius non descenderat. Sed Christus, quia ascendit, prius descendit, quia est ἐκ τῶν ἄνω desuper Joh.III.13. 31. VIII.23. Et id ipsum ex verbis Davidis intelligitur, qui ascendentem v.8.9.12. vocat אלהים Deum & אדני Dominum. Neque vel ascensus ex monte in Cœlum, unde prius Jehova descendit, vel ascensus Christi post Baptismum in Cœlum, & ex eodem descensus intelligitur, quorum illud Grotius, hoc Socinianí pertendunt. Non ille, quia Psalmus v.7. loquitur de Deo, ut vecto in campestribus in pulchritudinem nominis sui, cujus beneficia, & nominatim אכא מפשרות exercitus magnus evangelizantium v.10. 11.12. & fuga Regum, v.13. & locus habitationis latior quàm vel mons Sinai; vel terra Canaan fuit, v.16.17.18. destribitur, utpote in quo Deus habitare לשכת in seculum dicitur, currus Dei, myriades millium iteratorum, quas inter etiam v.19. סוררים rebelles, gentes ad Deum adductæ. Non posterius, quia sic etiam Moses, qui cum Deo Israelis in monte fuit, verba hæc sua facere posset; & Apostolus ex eo, quòd ascendit in altum, colligit, prius eum descendisse, quia videlicet erat ex Cœlo; non ascendisse prius & posterius descendisse, quasi æquè ut reliqui ex terra fuisset. Davidem secutus Solomon ascendentem, adeóque prius descendentem diserte Filium Dei vocat: Quis, inquit, ascendit in Cœlum, & descendit, &c? Quod est nomen ejus, & nomen Filii ejus, si noris? Prov.XXX.4. Accedit, quòd Jehova visitare Filium hominis, & homines, dictus est. Quid est homo, quòd memor es ipsius: & Filius hominis, quòd visitas ipsum? Et fecisti eum paulò inferiorem infra Deum, Psal.VIII. v.6. Quam מקרה επισκοπην Visitationem esse Dei, hominis formam induentis, ut homini in carne innotescat, satis inde constat, quia nulla alia visitatio facit, ut sit בן אדם Filius hominis, qui parvo tempore minor factus Angelis & Diis nominatis, gloria & honore coronari posset, & is Filius hominis Dominus omnium operum Dei sit, & ingens sit nomen Dei in tota terra, ibid. v.6.7. 10 Quo cum convenit vaticinium Mich.VII. 4. Venit יום מצפיך dies speculatorum tuorum. Visitatio tua venit nunc: nec non illud Zachariæ: 'Επεσκέψατο Visitavit & fecit redemptionem populo suo, Luc.I.68. Visitavit nos Germen ex alto, ib. v.78. Eodem facit 'Επιφάνεια apparitio Christi in carne. Nam visitavit nos Germen ex alto, επιφάνει ut appareat iis, qui in tenebris sunt, ibid. v.78.79. Gratia nunc manifestata est nobis διὰ τῆς Ἐπιφανείας per apparitionem Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi, 2.Tim.I.10. De qua sic Prophetæ: Revelabitur gloria Jehovæ, & videbit omnis caro, quod os Domini sit locutum, Esaj XL.5. Oculo in oculum vident, cùm Jehova reducit Sionem, ibid.LII.8. Unde Christus vocatur Sol justitiæ, Malach.IV.2. & Lux, Esaj.IX.2, XLII.6. Joh. I.4. quia Solis instar orientis subitò mundo illuxit.
units.tr: IV. Therefore the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments testify with great agreement that the Son of God came down from heaven, sent by the Father; descended to earth, visited men, appeared in the flesh, was made flesh, and was manifested in the flesh, and similar things. The Son himself, Jehovah of hosts, speaks of his own sending in this way: "Come near to me, hear this: I have not spoken in secret from the beginning [לא מראש בסתר דברתי]; from the time that it came to be I was there. And now the Lord Jehovah has sent me, and his Spirit [ועתה אדני יהוה שלחני ורוחו]" (Isa. 48:16). Here the Son of God, Jehovah of hosts (v. 2), speaking of himself, distinguishes two times. The first is that in which he has spoken from the beginning not in secret, but openly, as the Word [λόγος] which was in the beginning with God (John 1:1). The second is that in which, now in the fullness of time, he has been sent by God, both he and his Spirit, the Spirit of grace and supplication poured out upon all flesh. Hence come the words ἀποστολή and ἐξαπόστολή, "sending." "God did not send [οὐκ ἀπέστειλε] his Son into the world to judge the world" (John 3:17). "Whom God sent [Ὃν ἀπέστειλε]" speaks the words of God (ibid. v. 34). "God sent forth [ἐξαπέστειλε] his Son, born of a woman" (Gal. 4:4). This sending does not simply denote an appointment or stirring up to some office, such as that of John, the one sent [ἀπεσταλμένος] before Christ (John 3:28); it denotes par excellence the giving and sending from the things above [ἐκ τῶν ἄνω]. "He who comes from above [ἄνωθεν] is above all. He who is of the earth is of the earth and speaks of the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all" (ibid. v. 31). Here an antithesis is set up between Christ and John the Baptist, and all the other prophets, and Moses himself, none of whom came from heaven or spoke as he did. From this he is called the child born to us, the son given to us, who was sent (Isa. 9:6). And so he was sent that he is said to have come down from heaven. "You have ascended on high, and have taken captivity captive," etc. (Ps. 68:19). Hence the Apostle argues thus: "Now that he ascended, what does it mean but that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same as he who ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things" (Eph. 4:9–10). It is not indeed true of every ascending person that, because he ascended, he had first descended; for Moses also ascended the mountain, and had not first come down from it. But Christ, because he ascended, first descended, because he is "from above" [ἐκ τῶν ἄνω] (John 3:13, 31; 8:23). The same is understood from the words of David, who calls the one ascending "God" [אלהים] and "Lord" [אדני] (Ps. 68:8, 9, 12). Nor is the ascent here understood either as an ascent from a mountain into heaven, whence Jehovah had first descended, or as Christ's ascent into heaven after baptism, with a descent from there; the former is maintained by Grotius, the latter by the Socinians. Not the former, because the psalm (v. 7) speaks of God as one who is carried in the plains, to the beauty of his name; it describes his benefits and, by name, the great army of those who bring good tidings (v. 10–12), the flight of kings (v. 13), and a dwelling place wider than either Mount Sinai or the land of Canaan (v. 16–18), since God is said to dwell there for ever, the chariot of God, myriads of repeated thousands, among whom also (v. 19) the rebellious [סוררים], the nations brought to God. Nor the latter, because in that case Moses also, who was with the God of Israel on the mountain, could have made these words his own. And the Apostle infers from his ascending on high that he had first descended, because he was clearly from heaven; not that he had first ascended and afterwards descended, as if he had been from the earth like the rest. Following David, Solomon also plainly calls the Son of God the one who ascended, and therefore first descended: "Who," he says, "has ascended into heaven and descended, etc.? What is his name, and the name of his Son, if you know?" (Prov. 30:4). Moreover, Jehovah is said to visit the Son of man and men. "What is man, that you are mindful of him; and the son of man, that you visit him? And you have made him a little lower than God" (Ps. 8:6). That this visitation [ἐπισκοπή] of God, who puts on the form of man so as to make himself known to man in the flesh, is indeed a visitation of God is sufficiently clear from this: no other visitation makes the son of man, who, made a little less than the angels and the gods so called, could be crowned with glory and honour, and this son of man is Lord of all the works of God, and the name of God is great in all the earth (ibid. v. 6–7, 10). With this agrees the prophecy of Micah: "The day of your watchmen [יום מצפיך] has come; your visitation is now at hand" (Mic. 7:4), and that of Zechariah: "He visited and wrought redemption for his people" (Luke 1:68); "The Dayspring from on high has visited us" (ibid. v. 78). The appearance [ἐπιφάνεια] of Christ in the flesh amounts to the same thing: "The Dayspring from on high has visited us, to appear to those who sit in darkness" (ibid. v. 78–79). "The grace now manifested to us through the appearing [διὰ τῆς ἐπιφανείας] of our Saviour Jesus Christ" (2 Tim. 1:10). Of this the prophet says: "The glory of Jehovah shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see that the mouth of the Lord has spoken" (Isa. 40:5); "They see eye to eye when Jehovah brings back Zion" (ibid. 52:8). Hence Christ is called the Sun of righteousness (Mal. 4:2) and Light (Isa. 9:2; 42:6; John 1:4), because, like the sun rising, he suddenly shone upon the world.

units.la: V. Clarè inprimis Scriptura & Sermonem carnem factum; & Deum in carne manifestatum esse testatur. Ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο Sermo caro factus est, inquit S. Johannes Cap.I. 14. Sermonem Filium Dei, & quidem ab æterno existentem esse, supra demonstravimus, causam insuper reddentes, cur λόγος Sermonis nomine veniat. Cùm igitur sermo ille in principio creationis, imò ab æterno extiterit, in tempore etiam σὰρξ caro factus est, hoc est, σάρκα καὶ αἷμα carnem & sanguinem participavit, Hebr.II.14. se ipsum exinanivit, formam servi assumens, in similitudine hominum factus, Phil.II.7. Caro igitur est ἀνθρώπου humanitas Christi, qui ortus est secundum carnem (seu secundum id, quo homo fuit) ex semine Davidis, Rom.I.3. Non enim quævis caro intelligitur, sed viva, & quidem humana, quæ spiritum humanum hospitem & rectorem habet. Unde idem אמר ירוה Germen Jehovæ, & פרי הארץ fructus terræ appellatur, Esaj.IV.2. Talis ergo caro factus est Sermo, non per τροπὴν conversionem, seu mutationem in carnem; sed per carnis assumptionem, & in eadem habitationem. Statim enim sequitur: Καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν, & habitavit, seu, habitare coepit in nobis; hoc est, sic caro factus est, ut in nobis habitaret; sive in habitaculo & tabernaculo suo inter nos versaretur, oculis videretur, auribus audiretur, & manibus palparetur, velut carnis & sanguinis nostri particeps, Hebr.II.14. 1.Joh.I.1. Neque omnino in verbis illis S. Johannis, λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, vel λόγος humanitatem notat Christi, vel ἐγένετο vertendum est, fuit, non factus est: vel caro sic assumpta infirmitates humanas & miseram in mundo conditionem Christi significat, ut sensus sit, Christum ἄλλον ἄνθρωπον nudum hominem ex B. Virgine Maria natum, humanis infirmitatibus & miseriis in mundo obnoxium fuisse. Quomodo impiè verba S. Johannis hæretici detorquent. Nam Sermonem quidem Christi Divinitatem notare, in loco asseruimus. Cúmque Deus fuerit, non fuisse, sed factum esse carnem, sequitur; quia Deus non est caro, sed fieri caro per ejus πρόσληψιν potest. Neque etiam verbum γίνομαι pro εἰμί accipi, vel copulæ munere fungi solet. Ineptum certè foret dicere: ἐν σαρκὶ ἐγένετο ὁ Θεός. Cúmque S. Johannes de λόγῳ loquens septies usus fuerit voce ἦν erat, fuit, nulla ratio est, cur, à loquendi suo genere subitò deflectens, diceret, λόγος ἐγένετο, & non potius ἦν, si hæc æquipollerent. Aliàs enim, quicquid ante de Sermone dixerat, de carne etiam dici deberet, Velut quòd caro sit Deus, v.1. quòd per eam omnia facta sint, v.3. &c. Filius certè Dei dictus γεννηθεὶς ἐκ γυναικὸς Gal.IV.4. 'Ἐκ σπέρματος Δαυὶδ, Rom.I.3. non fuisse, sed factus esse ex muliere, Semine Davidis, hoc est, assumpsisse Semen Abrahæ. Hebr.II.16. intelligitur. Denique σάρξ Caro non infirmitatem & conditionem carnis, quæ accidens est, sed substantiam ipsam carnis notat, quia in Christo non tantùm carnis imbecillitas & conditio, sed etiam substantia est; neque quisquam eum, qui in carnis imbecillitatem incidit, carnem factum dixit; & misera conditio carnem, ceu subjectum suum supponit, atque eo ipso, quòd caro ei tribuitur, etiam carnis substantia ei tribui intelligitur; unde S. Petrus 1.Pet.III.18.IV.1. Christum θανατωθέντα σαρκὶ mortificatum, passum carne dixit. Denique cùm prius factus caro dicatur, quàm habitasse inter nos dicitur; illi habitationi inter nos ἐσκήνωσεν illam σαρκὸς postponunt, carnem interpretati eas miserias, quæ mortem Christi proximè antecesserunt.
units.tr: V. Scripture above all clearly teaches that the Word was made flesh and that God was manifested in the flesh. "The Word was made flesh," says St. John, ch. 1.14 [ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο]. We have already shown that the Word, the Son of God, existed from eternity, and we have also given the reason why the Word is so called. Since that Word existed at the beginning of creation, indeed from eternity, in time he also was made flesh, that is, he partook of flesh and blood [σάρκα καὶ αἷμα], Heb. 2.14. He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, Phil. 2.7. Therefore the flesh is the humanity of Christ, who was born according to the flesh (that is, according to that in which he was man) of the seed of David, Rom. 1.3. For the word does not mean any flesh whatever, but living flesh, and indeed human flesh, which has a human spirit as its inhabitant and ruler. Hence the same flesh is called the Branch of Jehovah [צמח יהוה] and the fruit of the earth [פרי הארץ], Isa. 4.2. Such flesh, then, the Word became, not by a change or conversion into flesh, but by assuming flesh and dwelling in it. For there immediately follows: and dwelt [καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν], that is, he began to dwell among us. That is, he became flesh so that he might dwell among us, or move among us in his own habitation and tabernacle, be seen by our eyes, heard by our ears, and handled by our hands, as a partaker of our flesh and blood, Heb. 2.14; 1 John 1.1. Nor, in those words of St. John, the Word was made flesh [λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο], can either the word "Word" signify the humanity of Christ, or became [ἐγένετο] be rendered was, not was made. Or else flesh so assumed signifies the human infirmities and the wretched condition of Christ in the world, so that the sense is that Christ, a mere man born of the Blessed Virgin Mary, was subject to human infirmities and miseries in the world. This is how heretics impiously twist the words of St. John. For we have shown in the proper place that the "Word" does indeed signify the Divinity of Christ. And since he was God, it follows that he did not merely become flesh, but was made flesh; for God is not flesh, but can become flesh by his assumption of it. Nor is the verb γίνομαι [to become] usually taken for εἰμί [to be] or made to serve as a copula. It would certainly be absurd to say: God became in the flesh [ἐν σαρκὶ ἐγένετο ὁ Θεός]. And since St. John, speaking of the Word, uses the word ἦν [was] seven times, there is no reason why, suddenly departing from his manner of speaking, he should say "became" and not rather "was", if these meant the same. Otherwise, whatever he had said before about the Word ought also to be said about the flesh: for example, that the flesh is God, v. 1, and that all things were made through it, v. 3, and so on. Certainly the Son of God, said to be born of a woman, Gal. 4.4, and of the seed of David, Rom. 1.3, is understood not to have been woman or seed of David, but to have been made so, that is, to have assumed the seed of Abraham, Heb. 2.16. Finally, flesh [σάρξ] signifies not the weakness and condition of the flesh, which is an accident, but the very substance of flesh; because in Christ there is not only the weakness and condition of the flesh but also its substance; and no one has ever said that he who falls into the weakness of the flesh has become flesh. A wretched condition presupposes flesh as its subject, and by the very fact that flesh is attributed to him, the substance of flesh is understood to be attributed to him too. Hence St. Peter says that Christ, put to death in the flesh, suffered in the flesh, 1 Pet. 3.18; 4.1. Finally, since he is said to have first been made flesh before he is said to have dwelt among us, those who interpret the flesh as the miseries which immediately preceded the death of Christ place that "dwelling" [ἐσκήνωσεν] after the flesh, as if it came later.

units.la: VI. Accedit, quòd Christus non tantùm caro factus, sed etiam Θεὸς ἐν σαρκὶ φανερωθεὶς Deus in carne manifestatus 1.Tim.III.16. dicitur. Nam quòd vocem Θεὸς Interpretes, Latinus & Syrus, omiserunt, & à Nestorio suppletam Grotius divinat, nil moramur, quia omnes ferè codices Græci impressi & scripti, & Græci Patres, atque ipse etiam Chrysostomus, Nestorio antiquior, eam retinent; & non mysterium, sed Deus, Christus in carne manifestatus est. quod iidem Patres Latini, qui vocem eam omittunt, agnoscunt. Forte in codice aliquo, erasò nomine Θεὸς, scriptum est ὃς, quod etiam per pronomen quòd reddi potest. Unde Syrus habet quòd manifestatus fit, (Christus Deus vivens, v.13. 1 r.) in carne &c. Illum manifestatum in carne Apostolus dixit, qui prædicatus est in gentibus, susceptus in gloriam, qui Deus, Christus est. Sicut olim Deus ἐφανερώθη manifestatus visus est vel AbrahaAbrahamo, vel in tabernaculo & Templo inter Cherubinos, Genef.XVII.1. XVIII.1. Exod. XXV.18.22. XXIX.43. Levit.XVI.2. ita in tempore manifestatus est in carne, quando in ea, velut Templo suo, habitare coepit. Sicut etiam homo, qui spiritus est, habitat in corpore, quod ipsius σκηνῶ tabernaculum 2.Cor.V.1. appellatur, & in quo videtur, auditur, cognoscitur: ita Filius Dei in carne sua, velut tabernaculo, manifestatus est, ut tanquam Dei & hominis Filius videri, audiri, cognosci posset. Ad φανέρωσιν prolin illam pertinuit, ut ipse Filius Dei sibi, & Pater ipsi faceret corpus, & quidem humanum, humano spiritu motum, & in eo agens & patiens conspiceretur, loquens audiretur, & ipse potentiam Divinitatis & obedientiam humanitatis cognoscendam praberet. Neque difficilius fuit Filio Dei sic in carne manifestari, sibi facere corpus & instrumentum sermonis, & ex eo loqui, agere, in eo pati &c. quam sibi formare vocem, qua loquatur, cum saepius locutus ad homines dicatur. Nam & vox humana aeque res corporea est, atque structura omnium membrorum humani corporis. Si autem Deus sibi corpus assumere potest, etiam spiritum humanum sibi creare potest, ut hominis actiones ederet. Sic ergo φανερᾶσθαι est manifestari in ὁρᾳνῷ ἐνυπο-στάτῳ; quod sibi ipse fecit ad agendum humana, & loquendum Verba Dei, & patiendum ea, quae Mediatoris sunt. Idem ergo verba Apostoli valent, ac si dixisset; Deus Abrahami, Isaci & Jacobi; Sanctificator Israelis; Justitia peccatoris; Salvator hominum apparuit in carne. Haec veritas secundum pietatem est, sive prima & principalis pars μυστήριον τῆς εὐσεβείας mysterii pietatis, magni, seu leti valde (Psalm.CXIX.96.) qua sublata totum mysterium pietatis tollitur; & eidem mysterium impietatis substituitur, quale illud hostium Divinitatis Christi est, quod S. Paulus voce Θεὸς (si omnino γνῶσι sit) personam Dei Patris intellexerit; utpote cujus voluntas manifestata fuerit in carne, id est, in infirmitate Christi & Apostolorum; cum tamen nuspiam Pater, semper Christus apparuisse, habitasse, manifestatus esse in carne dicatur; neque uspiam vox σαρκὸς absolute posita Christi & Apostolorum infirmitatem significet; neque manifestatio voluntatis Dei per ministerium infirmorum hominum grande illud mysterium pietatis absolvat, cum sub V. T. saepe eo modo se manifestaverit; & Deus Pater ἀναλημφθεὶς susceptus in gloriam dici non possit, quia gloria nunquam caruit, neque, sicuti Christus, ipse quoque exinanitus, humiliatus, & post ἐπὶ πρῶτον sublatus (Act.I.9.) ἀνεφέρετο sursum latus (Luc.XXIV.51.) ἀνελήφθη sursum susceptus (Act.X.16. Luc.IX.51.) est.
units.tr: VI. Moreover, Christ is said not only to have been made flesh but also to be God manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. 3.16 [Θεὸς ἐν σαρκὶ φανερωθεὶς]. As for the Latin and Syriac translators having omitted the word "God", and Grotius guessing that it was supplied by Nestorius, we need not dwell on it, since almost all printed and written Greek codices, the Greek Fathers, and even Chrysostom himself, who is older than Nestorius, retain it. And it was not a mystery, but God, who was manifested in the flesh, as the same Latin Fathers, who omit that word, acknowledge. Perhaps in some codex, after the name Θεὸς was erased, ὃς was written, which can also be rendered by the pronoun who. Hence the Syriac has that was manifested (Christ, living God, v. 13, 1r) in the flesh, etc. He whom the Apostle says was manifested in the flesh, was preached among the Gentiles, received up into glory, is God, Christ. As God was once manifested [ἐφανερώθη] to Abraham, or seen in the tabernacle and Temple between the cherubim, Gen. 17.1; 18.1; Exod. 25.18, 22; 29.43; Lev. 16.2, so in time he was manifested in the flesh, when he began to dwell in it as in his own Temple. Just as a man, who is a spirit, dwells in a body, which is called his tabernacle [σκηνῶ], 2 Cor. 5.1, and in which he is seen, heard, and known, so the Son of God was manifested in his flesh, as in a tabernacle, so that as the Son of God and of man he might be seen, heard, and known. The purpose of this manifestation [φανέρωσιν] was that the Son of God himself might make for himself, and the Father for him, a body, and indeed a human body moved by a human spirit, in which he might be seen acting and suffering, heard speaking, and might present the power of his Divinity and the obedience of his humanity to be recognised. Nor was it more difficult for the Son of God to be thus manifested in the flesh, to make for himself a body and an instrument of speech, and from it to speak, act, and suffer in it, than to form for himself a voice with which to speak, since he is often said to have spoken to men. For the human voice is equally a corporeal thing, as is the structure of all the members of the human body. But if God can take to himself a body, he can also create for himself a human spirit, to perform the actions of a man. Thus to be manifested [φανερᾶσθαι] is to be manifested in an organ hypostatically united [manifestari in ὁρᾳνῷ ἐνυπο-στάτῳ], which he made for himself to act as a man, and to speak the words of God, and to suffer those things which belong to the Mediator. So the words of the Apostle have the same force as if he had said: The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; the Sanctifier of Israel; the Righteousness of the sinner; the Saviour of men, appeared in the flesh. This is the truth according to godliness, that is, the first and principal part of the mystery of godliness [μυστήριον τῆς εὐσεβείας], great, or exceedingly joyful (Ps. 119.96). If this is taken away, the whole mystery of godliness is removed, and the mystery of impiety is substituted in its place, such as that of the enemies of the Divinity of Christ, who, if the word God [Θεὸς] is retained at all, understand by it the person of God the Father, since his will was manifested in the flesh, that is, in the infirmity of Christ and the Apostles. Yet nowhere is it said that the Father, but always that Christ, appeared, dwelt, or was manifested in the flesh. Nor does the word flesh [σαρκὸς], used absolutely, anywhere signify the infirmity of Christ and the Apostles. Nor does the manifestation of the will of God through the ministry of weak men complete that great mystery of godliness, since under the Old Testament he had often manifested himself in that way. And God the Father cannot be said to have been received up into glory, because he never lacked glory; nor, like Christ, who was himself emptied and humbled and afterwards taken up [ἐπὶ πρῶτον] on high (Acts 1.9), was he carried up [ἀνεφέρετο] on high (Luke 24.51), or taken up [ἀνελήφθη] on high (Acts 10.16; Luke 9.51).

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Testimoniorum plurimorum instar sit illud S. Pauli, quo testatur, Evangelium Dei, ad quod separatus fuit, esse περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ de Filio ejus (Dei) Jesu Christo Domino nostro, qui factus est ex semine Davidis secundum carnem, & definitus Filius Dei in potentia secundum Spiritum Sanctitatis ex resurrectione ex mortuis, Rom.I.1.2.3. In eadem proin persona Filii Dei est & caro ex semine Davidis; & Spiritus sanctitatis seu spiritualis natura Dei, secundum quam definitè, solitarie, cum exclusione omnium aliorum Christus denotatus, compellatus, vocatus est Filius Dei, ᾧ ὁρισθεὶς υἱὸς Θεοῦ definitus, singulariter a Deo denotatus, judex vivorum & mortuorum, Act.X.42. & quidem ἐν δυνάμει in potentia, secundum potentissimam, validissimam & maxime propriam vocabuli Filii significationem, ut non sit Filius λεγόμενος, sed ὁρισθεὶς Rom.VIII.32. cum omni potentia, (Esaj.IX.5.XI.2.) seu efficacia voluntatis, qua vivificat, quos vult, & similiter operatur, ut Pater, Joh.V.19.21.26. X.28.29. Hebr.I.3. denique cum potentia & jure eo, ut sit Christus, Sacerdos, Dominus & Rex populi Dei; & Propheta verba Dei loquens; cui soli, ut haereditas & peculium donari potuimus. Cujus definitionis Filii in potentia tali argumentum ostensivum est resurrectio Christi ex mortuis, qua & Pater ipsum resuscitavit, ut justificator ejus, Esaj.L.8. & meriti ejus acceptator, ibid.XLIX.8. & ipse Templum corporis sui Divina potentia erexit, Joh.II.19.
units.tr: Let this saying of St. Paul stand for many testimonies. He declares that the gospel of God, to which he was set apart, concerns [περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ] his (God's) Son Jesus Christ our Lord, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, and was declared the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by the resurrection from the dead (Rom. 1:1–3). In the same person of the Son of God there is therefore both the flesh from the seed of David and the Spirit of holiness, that is, the spiritual nature of God. According to this nature Christ is definitely, solely, and with the exclusion of all others, designated, addressed and called "Son of God" [ᾧ ὁρισθεὶς υἱὸς Θεοῦ], that is, defined and singularly designated by God, "judge of the living and the dead" (Acts 10:42). He is so indeed in power [ἐν δυνάμει], according to the most powerful, most effective and most proper sense of the word "Son", so that he is not merely called Son [λεγόμενος] but declared Son [ὁρισθεὶς] (Rom. 8:32). He has all power (Isa. 9:5; 11:2), that is, the efficacious will by which he quickens whom he wills, and works in the same way as the Father (John 5:19, 21, 26; 10:28, 29; Heb. 1:3). Finally, he has power and that right by which he is Christ, Priest, Lord and King of the people of God, and Prophet speaking the words of God; to him alone we could be given as inheritance and special possession. The proof of this definition of the Son in power is the resurrection of Christ from the dead, by which the Father also raised him up, as his justifier (Isa. 50:8) and the acceptor of his merit (ibid. 49:8), and by which he himself raised up the temple of his body by divine power (John 2:19).

units.la: VIII. Clarissimo dicto huic nequicquam haeretici, Enjedinus inprimis, nebulas offundunt, tricantes videlicet, πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης Spiritum Dei, quo Christus homo sanctificatus, & in Filii Dei dignitatem sublatus sit, intelligi. Sed aliud videlicet esse πνεῦμα ἁγιασμοῦ Spiritum sanctificationis, aliud πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης Spiritum sanctitatis, jam diximus. Illud Spiritum, quo aliud sanctificatur: hoc Spiritum, qui ipse sanctus, imo sanctitas est, significat; & eum quidem, qui ὁρίζει definite notat Filium Dei in omni potentia, per quem Christus se ipsum obtulit, & ex mortuis suscitavit, quae resuscitatio sui ipsius est non causa, sed ὁρισμὸς definitio, declaratio Filiationis Dei. Quod vero iidem & pios omnes duplicem generationem, unam ex Deo, alteram ex carne habere: & Judaeos quoque duas nativitates, unam ex Abrahamo, alteram ex Diabolo habuisse; cum tamen nec illi, nec hi in eadem persona diversas naturas habuerint, tricantur, nihil ad rem praesentem facit. Aliud enim est nasci & Filium dici secundum carnem & secundum Spiritum: aliud nasci ex carne & Spiritu; ex Abrahamo & Diabolo. Illud diversas ejusdem personae naturas: hoc ejusdem naturae diversa nascendi principia notat. Nam quod etiam Isacus natus dicitur ἐκ πνεῦμα secundum Spiritum, sensum eum habet, quod natus, seu renatus fuerit vi spiritus parentes effoetos foecundante, & quod acceperit Spiritum Patris, qui ipsum sanctificavit, ut fides Abrahami in ipso habitaret. Sicut fides Loidis & Eunices in Timotheo habitavit, 2.Timoth.I.5. Tum nascendi modus utrobique variat. Nam nativitas piorum ex carne pure naturalis, Christi secundum carnem supernaturalis: illorum nativitas ex Spiritu est ἀναγέννησις; haec secundum Spiritum sanctitatis naturalis & aeterna Filii Dei generatio est. Praeterea Judaeorum nativitas ex Abrahamo propriè; ex Diabolo improprie talis fuit; posterior naturae non diversae a priori, sed ejusdem depravatio. Christi autem secundum Spiritum Sanctitatis Filii Dei definiti natura ab ea, quae secundum carnem est, diversa plane est.
units.tr: VIII. The heretics, Enjedinus above all, try in vain to becloud this most clear saying, quibbling that "Spirit of holiness" [πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης] should be understood as the Spirit of God, by whom Christ as man was sanctified and raised to the dignity of Son of God. But we have already said that the Spirit of sanctification [πνεῦμα ἁγιασμοῦ] is one thing and the Spirit of holiness [πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης] another. The former signifies the Spirit by whom something else is sanctified; the latter signifies the Spirit who is himself holy, indeed holiness itself, and who definitely marks out the Son of God in all power, through whom Christ offered himself and rose from the dead. That resurrection is not the cause of his sonship but its definition [ὁρισμός], the declaration of the Sonship of God. As for their trifling that the same men, and all the pious, have a twofold generation, one from God and the other from flesh, and that the Jews also had two births, one from Abraham and the other from the Devil: this has nothing to do with the present matter, since neither the pious nor the Jews had diverse natures in the same person. For it is one thing to be born and called Son "according to the flesh and according to the Spirit," and another to be born of flesh and Spirit, or of Abraham and the Devil. The former denotes diverse natures of one and the same person; the latter denotes diverse principles of birth within one and the same nature. For the statement that Isaac too was born "according to the Spirit" [κατὰ πνεῦμα] means that he was born, or reborn, by the power of the Spirit, who made his worn-out parents fruitful, and that he received the Spirit of the Father, who sanctified him so that Abraham's faith dwelt in him, just as the faith of Lois and Eunice dwelt in Timothy (2 Tim. 1:5). Moreover, the mode of birth differs on each side. The birth of the pious from flesh is purely natural, while Christ's birth according to the flesh is supernatural. Their birth from the Spirit is regeneration [ἀναγέννησις]; but the birth according to the Spirit of holiness is the natural and eternal generation of the Son of God. Furthermore, the Jews' birth from Abraham was properly so called, while their birth from the Devil was so only improperly; the latter is not a different nature from the former but its corruption. But the nature of Christ, the Son of God defined according to the Spirit of holiness, is plainly different from that which is according to the flesh.

units.la: IX. Etiam Spiritus Jehovae dicitur fuisse super Christo Evangelium praedicante. רוח אדני ... Spiritus Domini Jehovae est super me, quia unxit me Jehova ad Evangelium nuntiandum mansuetis, misit me ad obligandum confractos corde, ad praedicandum abductis in captivitatem libertatem, & vinctis acutum visum; ad praedicandum annum acceptaacceptationis Jehovæ, Esaj.LXI.1,2. Luc.IV.18. Ubi alia natura est Spiritus Domini Jehovæ, alia prædicando loquentis, seu evangelizantis, super quo Spiritus Domini Jehovæ fuit: & utraque illa natura in eadem persona subsistens inducitur; quia evangelizans inducitur ille, super quo Spiritus Domini Jehovæ fuit. Neque enim iis verbis Spiritum tantùm Patris, sed etiam Spiritum Filii intelligi liquet, tum quia vocatur Spiritus Domini Jehovæ, hoc est, Spiritus, cujus est populus, qui habet hæreditatem & peculium in mundo; quod jus constat esse à redemptione, quæ Filii est: tum quia Unctio ejus, sive effusio Spiritus S. & operatio virtutum, qua demonstratus est Evangelii Nuntiis, & missio ad fanandum fractos corde, profertur velut argumentum demonstrans, quòd Spiritus Domini Jehovæ super eo sit; non eo certè modo, quo super Prophetas loquentes fuit, sed augustiori longè & ἀκαφορῶ πρὸς, pro magnitudine & gloria finis atque operis, ad quod missus est; atque ita, ut effusio Spiritus S. in nomine ejus, & opera per ipsum facta, eum demonstrent nuntium esse Evangelii, & eum, super quo est Spiritus Dei. Alia quoque Deitatem Christi Evangelium prædicantis arguunt. Cujusmodi sunt, quòd is, qui primus annum beneplaciti prædicavit ad recreandum mansuetos, non potuit esse unus de mansuetis lugentibus & corde contritis: quódque idem ille Evangelista, super quo fuit Spiritus Domini Jehovæ, de se ipso sic v.8. loquitur: Quia ego Dominus, diligens judicium, & odio habeo raptum in holocausto, & dabo opera pretium illorum in veritate, & fœdus seculi pangam illis. Quæ verba cohærent cum v.7. uti causalis quia ostendit: versus autem 7. cum præcedentibus, adeóque etiam cum v.1. in quo Evangelista ille dicit; Spiritum Domini Jehovæ supra se esse.
units.tr: IX. The Spirit of Jehovah is also said to have been upon Christ as he preached the gospel: "The Spirit of the Lord Jehovah [רוח אדני] is upon me, because Jehovah has anointed me to preach the gospel to the meek; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound, to proclaim the acceptable year of Jehovah" (Isa. 61:1, 2; Luke 4:18). Here the Spirit of the Lord Jehovah is one nature, and the one who speaks, that is, who preaches the gospel, upon whom the Spirit of the Lord Jehovah rested, is another nature; and both natures are introduced as subsisting in the same person, because he who preaches is the very one upon whom the Spirit of the Lord Jehovah rested. For it is clear that by these words we are to understand not only the Spirit of the Father but also the Spirit of the Son. This is so, first, because he is called the Spirit of the Lord Jehovah, that is, the Spirit whose people are, and who has an inheritance and a special possession in the world; and it is agreed that this right comes from the redemption, which belongs to the Son. Second, his anointing, that is, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit and the working of miracles by which he was shown to be the messenger of the gospel, and his mission to heal the brokenhearted, are set forth as proof that the Spirit of the Lord Jehovah is upon him. Not indeed in the same way as he was upon the prophets who spoke, but in a far more exalted manner, in proportion to the greatness and glory of the end and work for which he was sent. And so the outpouring of the Holy Spirit in his name, and the works done through him, show that he is the messenger of the gospel and that the Spirit of God is upon him. Other things also prove the deity of Christ as the preacher of the gospel. Among them: he who first proclaimed the acceptable year of the Lord to refresh the meek could not be one of the meek who mourn and are contrite in heart; and the same evangelist, upon whom the Spirit of the Lord Jehovah rested, speaks of himself in verse 8 thus: "For I, the Lord, love judgment, I hate robbery in the burnt offering; I will faithfully give them their due reward, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them." These words cohere with verse 7, as the causal "for" shows; and verse 7 coheres with what goes before, and so also with verse 1, in which this evangelist says, "The Spirit of the Lord Jehovah is upon me."

units.la: X. Præterea S. Paulus Jesum Christum in forma Dei existentem rapinam non duxisse, esse instar Dei, sed se ipsum exinanivisse μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν, formâ servi acceptâ in similitudine hominum factum, inventum esse habitu ut homo, testatur Phil.II.6.7.8. Qui ergo fuit in forma Dei, & instar Dei, is formam servi accepit, & in similitudine hominum factus est, & inventus est habitu, ut homo, hoc est, in tali servi forma, non ut Deus, sed ut homo abjectus, & vermis, Psalm. XXII.7. Cujus loci insignis detorsionem impiam supra Loc.IV.§ 8.excussimus.
units.tr: X. Moreover, St. Paul testifies that Jesus Christ, existing in the form of God, did not regard being equal to God as a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant [μορφὴν δούλου λαβών], made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man (Phil. 2:6–8). Therefore he who was in the form of God and equal to God took the form of a servant, was made in the likeness of men, and was found in appearance as a man. That is, he was in such a servant's form, not as God, but as a lowly man and a "worm" (Ps. 22:7). We have already rejected the impious distortion of this notable passage above, in Locus IV, §8.

units.la: XI. Insuper Christus homo Templum & domicilium quoddam est Numinis & Deitatis plenissimæ in se hospitantis. Nam placuit Deo in ipso Christo, capite corporis Ecclesiæ, habitare omnem plenitudinem, Coloss.I.19. Clarius: In ipso (Christo Jesu) omnis plenitudo Deitatis habitat corporaliter, ibid. cap.II.9. Promisit Deus Israeli in fœdere, quòd ei & Semini ejus futurus sit in Deum Gen.XVII.7. Hoc fieri Deum nobis in Christo habitat secundum plenitudinem; & quidem corporaliter, non secundum umbram (v.17.) uti olim in Propitiatorio habitavit; & perfectissimè, quasi diceret, secundum omnem mensuram, longitudinem, latitudinem & profunditatem, quomodo Ephes.III.18.19. dicitur, nos ἐς πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ complete in omne completum Dei, per καταλαβέσθαι & μῆκος, & πλάτος, & ὕψος, & βάθος per comprehensionem longitudinis, latitudinis, altitudinis & profunditatis. Quod eas mensuras habet, id corpus proprie; & quod omnem rei mensuram habet, adeóque omnibus numeris perfectum est, σῶμα corpus, hoc est, rerum soliditas per similitudinem & improprie vocatur, quomodo σωματικῶς Græcis sæpe solidare significat. Etiam σωματικῶς subsistentialiter vel essentialiter nonnulli reddunt; dialecto Hebraica, qua גוף & corpus & subsistentiam seu essentiam (quomodo גוף corpus diei ipsum diem, Gen.VII.13. Exod.XII.17. &c. גוף corpus perfectionis, ipsam perfectionem Job.XXI.23. notat) imo imitatione Dialecti illius etiam σῶμα corpus essentiam rei (Rom.VI.6.VII.24. Col.I.18. coll. cum Ephes.I.22.) significat: Alii personaliter per Synecdochen speciei q.d. non per efficaciam vel assistentiam meram, sed per unionem hypostaticam: Nam Græcis σῶμα etiam personam significare, ex Thucydide & Demosthene probant. Verè ergo Christus & σωματικῶς, & πληρωματικῶς est Θεὸς Deus, & Christus homo in se hospitantem θεῖον φύσιν Divinam naturam habet. Nemo enim nobis fit in Deum, sicut in ipso fiamus πεπληρωμένοι completi (v.10.) atque adeò ipse sit omnia in nobis Col.III.11. nisi qui Deus est in veritate. Ac licet etiam fideles quivis sint Templum Dei, in quibus Deus habitat; in nemine tamen eorum tanta & inusitata cum emphasi Omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter habitare dicitur. Nam quòd Enjedinus pro Θεότητος Deitatis, legit θειότητος Divinitatis, desperatam audaciam prodit, dum & lectionem sacram adulteratur, & frivola adeò crisi Christi Deitatem oppugnat. Similis audacia est Schlichtingii, omnem illam plenitudinem Deitatis de notitia voluntatis Dei, quæ in Christo sit, explicantis, ut Deitatis nomine ea, quæ Deum authorem habent, & ad salutem nostram pertinent, per metonymiam causæ, intelligantur. Nam si mera creatura Christus est, ejusdem notitiæ Dei, quæ Deitatis πληρωμα plenitudinem comprehendat, capax non est. Et quis unquam Deitatem dixit id, quod Deum authorem habet; hoc est, Deum, imò Deitatem ipsam, quod Deus non est? Mendax hæc metonymia est. Sed ideo in Christo, non in ullo homine, philosopho, traditore (v.8.) omnia cognoscimus, quia is verus Deus est, & eo cognito verus Deus cognoscitur, & is in sinu Patris est, Johan.I.vers.18. ceu Filius Dei plenitudinem Deitatis habens, solus Patrem novit, Matth. XI.vers.27. Aliud est, quod S. Paulus Ephes. III.19. etiam fideles cognoscentes charitatem Christi, quæ cognitionem excedit, πληρωθῆτε εἰς πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ compleri usque ad omnem plenitudinem Dei, dixit. Nam πλήρωμα ibi passive usurpatur, ut & cap.IV.13. hoc sensu, quòd Deus fideles impleat, ut in iis sit omnia I.Cor.XV.28. Nam & in hac vita Christus τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν omnia in omnibus est, Coloss.III.11. quatenus tollit discrimen populorum, & ea, quæ discrimen illud fecerunt; & in nobis regnat, & per meritum & efficaciam ejus causa est omnium, quæ sunt novitatis, in cognitione, fide, amore Christi, & obedientiæ ejus imitatione consistentis. Denique nique & frivola est ejusdem Schlichtingii argutatio, quòd locus hic Christum ab omni plenitudine Deitatis tanquam continens à contento, & habitatum ab habitante distinguat, nec Deus ille unus pars esse potuerit, qui cum homine, parte altera Christum componeret, atque sic Deus tanquam pars in Christo, tanquam toto habitaret. Non enim à toto Christo, sed à Christo homine omnem plenitudinem Deitatis distinguit; & distinguit, non ut partem, vel δεχόμενον contentum, sed ut Regem à Palatio, Dominum Templi à Templo, sic tamen, ut in eo non παροικεῖν ad tempus, ceu πάροικος advena in diversorio morari, sed κατοικεῖν habitare, ut in fixa & stabili sua sede, non ei inclusus, nec ab ea exclusus dicatur.
units.tr: XI. Moreover, Christ as man is a certain temple and dwelling-place of the Deity, which dwells in him in all its fullness. For it pleased God that in Christ himself, the head of the body of the Church, all fullness should dwell, Col. 1:19. More plainly: in him (Christ Jesus) all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, ibid. 2:9. God promised Israel in the covenant that he would be God to him and to his seed, Gen. 17:7. This being God to us is in Christ, in whom he dwells according to the fullness; and indeed bodily, not according to the shadow (v. 17), as he once dwelt in the mercy-seat; and most perfectly, as if to say, according to every measure, length, breadth and depth, as Eph. 3:18-19 says that we are filled unto all the fullness of God [eis pan to plērōma tou Theou], to comprehend [katalabesthai] length [mēkos], breadth [platos], height [hypsos] and depth [bathos], that is, by comprehending length, breadth, height and depth. That which has these measures is properly a body; and what has every measure of a thing, and is thus perfect in every respect, is figuratively and improperly called body [sōma], that is, the solidity of a thing, just as bodily [sōmatikōs] often means solidly among the Greeks. Some also render bodily [sōmatikōs] as subsistentially or essentially, in the Hebrew idiom, in which gûph [גוף] means both body and subsistence or essence (as gûph [גוף] means the day itself in Gen. 7:13 and Exod. 12:17 etc., and gûph [גוף] means perfection itself in Job 21:23); indeed, by imitation of that idiom even body [sōma] signifies the essence of a thing (Rom. 6:6, 7:24; Col. 1:18, compared with Eph. 1:22). Others render it personally, by synecdoche of the species, as if to say: not by mere efficacy or assistance, but by a hypostatic union. For they prove from Thucydides and Demosthenes that body [sōma] among the Greeks also signifies a person. Therefore Christ is truly God both bodily [sōmatikōs] and fully [plērōmatikōs], and Christ, as man, has the divine nature [theion physin] dwelling in him. For no one becomes God to us, so that in him we are made complete [peplērōmenoi] (v. 10), and so that he himself is all things in us, Col. 3:11, unless he is God in truth. And although every faithful person is a temple of God in whom God dwells, yet of none of them is it said with such emphasis and unusual force that all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily. For Enjedinus, who reads divinity [theiotētos] for Godhead [theotētos], betrays a desperate audacity, since he both corrupts the sacred text and assails the Deity of Christ by such frivolous criticism. Schlichting shows a similar audacity, explaining all that fullness of the Godhead as the knowledge of God's will which is in Christ, so that by metonymy of cause the things which have God as their author and pertain to our salvation are understood under the name of Godhead. For if Christ is a mere creature, he is not capable of that knowledge of God which comprehends the fullness [plērōma] of the Godhead. And who has ever called by the name of Godhead what has God as its author; that is, God himself, or indeed the Godhead itself, which is not God? This metonymy is false. But we know all things in Christ, and not in any man, philosopher or traitor (v. 8), because he is true God, and by knowing him the true God is known; and he is in the bosom of the Father, John 1:18, as the Son of God, having the fullness of the Godhead, and alone knows the Father, Matt. 11:27. It is another matter that St. Paul, in Eph. 3:19, says that the faithful, knowing the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, are to be filled unto all the fullness of God [eis pan to plērōma tou Theou]. For fullness [plērōma] is used there in the passive sense, as also in ch. 4:13, in the sense that God fills the faithful, so that God may be all in them, 1 Cor. 15:28. For even in this life Christ is all things in all [ta panta en pasin], Col. 3:11, inasmuch as he removes the distinction between peoples and the things which made that distinction; and he reigns in us, and by his merit and efficacy is the cause of all that belongs to newness, consisting in the knowledge of Christ, faith, love, and the imitation of his obedience. Finally, Schlichting's quibble is also frivolous, that this passage distinguishes Christ from all fullness of the Godhead as the container from the contained, and the dweller from the dwelling, and that that one God could not be a part, who together with a man as the other part would make up Christ, so that God would dwell in Christ as a part in a whole. For it distinguishes not Christ as a whole, but Christ the man from all the fullness of the Godhead; and it distinguishes him not as a part, nor as the receiving [dechomenon] container, but as a king from his palace, or the lord of the temple from the temple; yet in such a way that he is said not to sojourn [paroikein] for a time, like a stranger [paroikos] lodging in an inn, but to dwell [katoikein] as in his fixed and stable seat, neither enclosed in it nor excluded from it.

units.la: XII. Denique non minùs emphaticè S. Paulus Hebr.II.14.15.16. mysterium illud pandit. Quia nempe pueri illi, quos Deus Christo redimendos dedit, communem carnem & sanguinem habent; etiam Princeps salutis (v.10.) sanctificans omnes, qui sanctificantur (v.11.) ὁ ἁγιάζων inquit Apostolus, μετέσχε τῶν αὐτῶν similiter particeps factus est eorundem, carnis & sanguinis v.14. Quæ incarnationem Christi palam comprobant. Nam is, de quo sermo est, & Princeps salutis est, atque ὁ ἁγιάζων sanctificans, Sanctificator, Vindex Israelis, adeóque Filius Dei, priùs quàm homo: & particeps carnis & sanguinis æquè ac pueri. Claram veritatem offuscare nequicquem Schlichtingius nititur, tricatus scilicet, sic quoque Christianos incarnari debere, quia Christus iis similis dicitur, & verbum κοινωνῆσαι, quod de Christianis dicitur, participationis actum magis, quàm μετέχω significet. Nam similitudo Christum inter & pueros ejus non in incarnatione, vel assumptione carnis & sanguinis, sed in carnis & sanguinis habitatione ponitur. Nam κοινωνεῖν Apostolo significat, commune aliquid habere: μετέχειν vero, commune aliquid habere coepit. Illud naturæ communionem, hoc simul etiam novæ personæ statum notat. Pueri κεκοινωνήκασι communem carnem & sanguinem habuerunt: Christus μετέσχε particeps factus est, sive cum illis carnem & sanguinem habuit singulari dignatione. Licèt ergo pueri incarnari non debuerint, non tamen Christus eorum salutis Princeps & Pontifex esse non potuit, quia nisi φανερωθῆναι ἐν σαρκὶ manifestatus in carne Princeps salutis, Sanctificator & Pontifex puerorum esse non potuisset, cùm salvatio & sanctificatio sit Dei. Hactenus igitur Christum inter & pueros differentia statui debuit. Manifesta porrò προεψημένως est, quòd carnis & sanguinis participatio passiones Christi & fidelium, de quibus v.10. loquitur, significet, quia κοινωνῶν & μετέχειν σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος passiones carnis & sanguinis præsedit, & multi carnem & sanguinem participantes non patiuntur. Sed clarius v.16. Οὐ δήπου, inquit, Ἀγγέλων ἐπιλαμβάνεται, ἀλλὰ σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ ἐπιλαμβάνεται. Non uspiam (in loco aliquo S. Scripturæ) Angelos apprehendit, sed semen Abrahæ apprehendit. Nam quia talis ἐπιλήπτωρ vindex seminis Abrahæ fuit Christus, ideo frater, particeps ejusdem carnis & sanguinis esse debuit. Quomodo sub Lege גאל Ἀγχιστεύς vindex proximus frater fuit, cui alterius & bona & mala communia erant, cui conveniebat hæreditatem defuncti adire, semen ei excitare, & sanguinem illius requirere. Hanc vocem גאל Græca ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι, ἐπιλήπτωρ optimè exprimit. Nam rei suæ vindicationem Græcis ἐπίληψιν dici; ex Platone Budæus docet. Christus certè גאל קדוש ישראל Assertor sanctus Israelis, Esaj.XLI.14. appellatur. Quid autem sit גואל Vindicis, Assertoris, elegantì formula Deus ipse indicat, dicens: Ne metuas; גאלתיך קראתי בשמך לי אתה Asserui te, nuncupavi nomen tuum, ibid.XLIII.1. Apostolus ergo citatis verbis ibid.VIII.18. Pueri, quos dedit mihi Dominus, dationem puerorum ejusmodi esse docet, ex qua consequitur, ut is, cui pueri dati sunt, debuerit eos, ceu גואל Ἀγχιστεύς, suos dicere, eorum causam suam facere, & secundum legem, ad recuperandum alienatos, satisfacere. Si igitur debuit esse ἁγχιστεύς, ut lege eos petat, & pro iis ad satisfaciendum se sistat, necesse erat, ut idem illud haberet, quod pueri & nati habebant, puta carnem & sanguinem, seu σπέρμα Ἀβραὰμ Semen Abrahæ. Nam quòd Paulus dicit, Semen Abrahæ ἐπιλαμβάνεται apprehendit, in præsenti, non ἐπελάβετο in præterito, usitata enallage temporis dictum satis apparet; & causam etiam hanc habet, quia effectus apprehensionis in iis, quos fratres suos Christus frater vindicat, & manu velut injecta אחז vel תפש apprehendit, continuus est. Neque proin idem est ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι apprehendere v.16. quod βοηθεῖν opitulari iis, qui tentantur v.18. sed apprehendentis finis est, opitulari. Ut enim justè, rectè, decorè & ordine Semini Abrahæ auxiliari, opitulari Christus posset, consecutus est agendo & faciendo id, quod ἐπιλήπτωρ vindicem decuit, ut sibi datos, velut à se emptos ex servitute & malo, tanquàm Dominus & hæres eorum, liberaret.
units.tr: XII. Finally, St. Paul no less emphatically unfolds that mystery in Heb. 2:14-16. For those children whom God gave to Christ to redeem have a common flesh and blood; and the Prince of salvation (v. 10), who sanctifies all who are sanctified (v. 11), ho hagiazōn, the Apostle says, likewise partook [metesche tōn autōn] of the same flesh and blood (v. 14). These words plainly prove the incarnation of Christ. For he of whom the discourse is, is both the Prince of salvation and the sanctifier [ho hagiazōn], the Sanctifier and Avenger of Israel, and so the Son of God before he was man; and he partook of flesh and blood just as the children did. Schlichting strives in vain to obscure this clear truth, pleading, of course, that Christians too ought in this way to be incarnate, because Christ is said to be like them, and that the word koinōnēsai, which is said of Christians, signifies the act of participating more than metechō does. For the likeness between Christ and his children lies not in incarnation, or the assumption of flesh and blood, but in the indwelling of flesh and blood. For koinōnein signifies to the Apostle to have something in common; but metechein signifies to begin to have something in common. The former denotes communion of nature, the latter at the same time the state of a new person. The children have shared [kekoinōnēkasi], that is, had a common flesh and blood; Christ partook [metesche], that is, became a partaker, or had flesh and blood with them by singular condescension. Therefore, although the children ought not to be incarnate, Christ could not fail to be the Prince of their salvation and their High Priest, because unless he had been manifested in the flesh [phanerōthēnai en sarki], the Prince of salvation, Sanctifier and High Priest could not have been of the children, since salvation and sanctification belong to God. Thus a difference must be established between Christ and the children. Moreover, it is plain in a prior sense that the participation in flesh and blood signifies the sufferings of Christ and of the faithful, of which v. 10 speaks, because sharing [koinōnein] and partaking [metechein] of flesh and blood precede the sufferings of flesh and blood, and many who share flesh and blood do not suffer. But v. 16 speaks more clearly: Ou dēpou, he says, Angelōn epilambanetai, alla spermatos Abraam epilambanetai [Οὐ δήπου Ἀγγέλων ἐπιλαμβάνεται, ἀλλὰ σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ ἐπιλαμβάνεται]. Nowhere (in any place of Holy Scripture) does he take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham. For because Christ was such a deliverer [epilēptōr], the avenger of the seed of Abraham, he therefore had to be a brother, a partaker of the same flesh and blood. So under the Law the go'el [גאל] or agchisteus [ἀγχιστεύς] was the avenger, the nearest kinsman, to whom both the goods and the ills of another were common, to whom it belonged to take up the inheritance of the deceased, to raise up seed for him, and to require his blood. The Greek epilambanesthai and epilēptōr express this Hebrew word [גאל] very well. For Budaeus teaches from Plato that the vindication of one's own right is called epilēpsis among the Greeks. Christ is certainly called the holy go'el of Israel [גאל קדוש ישראל], the holy Asserter of Israel, Isa. 41:14. What the go'el [גואל], the Vindicator or Asserter, is, God himself indicates in an elegant formula, saying: Fear not; I have redeemed you, I have called you by your name, you are mine [גאלתיך קראתי בשמך לי אתה], ibid. 43:1. The Apostol, then, by the words cited from ch. 8:18, the children whom the Lord has given me, teaches that the giving of such children is of such a kind that he to whom the children were given ought, as go'el [גואל] or agchisteus, to call them his own, to make their cause his own, and to satisfy the law in order to recover those who had been alienated.
