If therefore he was to be the agchisteus, to claim them by law and to present himself to make satisfaction for them, it was necessary that he should have the same thing which the children and those born had, namely flesh and blood, or the seed of Abraham. For that Paul says the seed of Abraham takes hold [epilambanetai] in the present, not took hold [epelabeto] in the past, is sufficiently clear as a customary change of tense; and it has this cause as well, that the effect of the seizing, in those whom Christ as brother vindicates, and with his hand as it were laid upon them, seizes [ach] or takes [tpsh], is continuous. Nor is epilambanesthai, to take hold of, in v. 16, the same as boēthein, to help those who are tempted, in v. 18; rather, the aim of taking hold is to help. For Christ could help and succour the seed of Abraham justly, rightly, fittingly and in order, by doing and accomplishing what became a deliverer [epilēptōr] and avenger, so that he might free those given to him, as though bought by himself out of servitude and evil, as their Lord and heir.

units.la: XIII. Pleni sunt libri V.T. Vaticiniis & Typis Incarnationem hanc præsagientibus & figurantibus.
units.tr: XIII. The books of the Old Testament are full of prophecies and types foreshadowing and figuring this Incarnation.

units.la: Nam Semen Mulieris serpentis caput contriturum, Genes.III.15. in quo omnes gentes benedicendæ erant, ibid.XII.3.XXII.18.coll. cum Esaj.XLV.25. LXV.16. Angelus Assertor, Gen.XLVIII.16. Pastor & Lapis Israelis, ib.XLIX.24. Angelus Jehova, in cujus medio est nomen Jehovæ, habitans in rubo, Exod.III.2. 4.6. XXIII.20 &c. Deut.XXXIII.16. Deus Israel, sub cujus pedibus erat later Saphiri, Exod.XXIV.10. Esaj.VI.1. Ezech.I.26. Ille in medio Israelis habitaturus, & eidem in Deum futurus, Levit.XXVI. 12. Σκηνωσις habitatio Jehovæ in tabernaculi Propitiatorio inter Cherubinos, nec non Gloria, seu Thronus Dei in igne & nube, Exod.XXIV.16. XL.33.34. Levit.XVI.2. Num.VII.89. IX.15. Psal. XCIX.1. &c. Jehova in columna nubis ambulans cum populo, & ex igne ac nube cum eodem loquens, Num.XIV.14.Deut.V.4. Manna, panis ex Cœlo datus, Exod.XVI.4.14. Num.XI.7. Psalm. LXXVIII.24. Præco Legis fidei de Cœlo descensurus, & è morte reditururus, Deut.XXX.11.12.13. Rupes Salutis, cui magnitudo danda fuit ex Cœlo & terra, quam ipsam tamen Israel בנו ceu stultam, vel ceu cadaver tractaturus erat, Deut.XXXII.4. 12.15.18. Semen Davidis, Templum Nomini Dei, non materiale duntaxat, sed & verum erecturum, cujus Regnum finem habere non debuit, 2 Sam.VII.13.14. Vermis & non vir, opprobrium hominis & contemptus populi, narraturus nomen fratribus suis, idémque, Jehova, Rex dominaturus gentibus,&c. Psal.XXII.7.8.23.29. Servus Dei, cui
units.tr: For the Seed of the Woman was to bruise the serpent's head, Gen. 3.15, the Seed in whom all nations were to be blessed, ibid. 12.3; 22.18, compared with Isa. 45.25; 65.16. He is the Angel the Assertor, Gen. 48.16; the Shepherd and Stone of Israel, ibid. 49.24; the Angel of Jehovah, in whose midst is the name of Jehovah, dwelling in the bush, Exod. 3.2, 4, 6; 23.20, etc.; Deut. 33.16. He is the God of Israel, under whose feet was a pavement of sapphire stone, Exod. 24.10; Isa. 6.1; Ezek. 1.26. He is the one who was to dwell in the midst of Israel and be their God in the future, Lev. 26.12. He is the tabernacling (σκηνωσις), the dwelling of Jehovah in the mercy-seat of the tabernacle between the cherubim, and also the glory or throne of God in fire and cloud, Exod. 24.16; 40.33-34; Lev. 16.2; Num. 7.89; 9.15; Ps. 99.1, etc. He is Jehovah walking with the people in a pillar of cloud and speaking with them out of fire and cloud, Num. 14.14; Deut. 5.4. He is the manna, the bread given from heaven, Exod. 16.4, 14; Num. 11.7; Ps. 78.24. He is the herald of the law of faith, who was to descend from heaven and return from death, Deut. 30.11-13. He is the Rock of salvation, to whom greatness was to be given from heaven and earth; yet Israel was to treat him as foolish, or as one whose sons were not his own, Deut. 32.4, 12, 15, 18. He is the Seed of David, the Temple of the Name of God, to raise up a temple that is not only material but true, whose kingdom was never to have an end, 2 Sam. 7.13-14. He is the worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the contempt of the people, who was to declare the name to his brothers; and the same is Jehovah, the King who would rule the nations, etc., Ps. 22.7-8, 23, 29. He is the Servant of God, to whom the ears were to be bored, who was to come to do the will of God, ibid. 40.7-9.

units.la: Mos. & Prophetarum Incarnationem Christi prædicentium testimonia. cui perfodiendæ aures, venturus, ut faceret voluntatem Dei, ibid.XL.7.8.9. [Hebrew] Germen Jehovæ & fructus terræ, Esaj.IV.2. Ex Virgine nasciturus, & Immanuelis nomine nuncupandus, ibid. VII.14.15. Filius idem & [Hebrew] puer, cujus nomen [Hebrew] Admirabilis &c. ibid. cap.IX.6. Lapis in Sione ædificandus &c. in quo qui credit, non confunditur, cap.XXVIII.16. Mare desiccans & Cœlum caligine induens, & simul corpus suum dans percutientibus, & genas vellentibus, cap.L.2.3.6. Idem Angelus faciei, Salvator populi, & veniens de Edom, rubeas vestes habens de Bozra, cap.LXIII.1.9. Davidi suscitandum [Hebrew] Germen justum, regnaturus Rex & [Hebrew] Jehova justitia nostra, Jerem.XXIII.5.6. XXXIII.15.16. Jehova & David Rex, suscitandus populo, sponsurus & approximaturus Jehovæ, ib. c.xxx. 9.21.22. Filius hominis, sedens in throno Gloriæ, Ezech.I.26. Gloria Dei descendens desuper, seu de Cœlo, quod supra Cherub erat, ad limen Templi, & rursus, à limine Templi se levans & super Cherubim ascendens, ibid.X.4.17.18. Dominator Israelis, ex Bethlehem egressurus, cujus egressus à principio, à diebus seculi, Mich. V.2. Domus Davidis, seu Semen Davidis, futurus [Hebrew] ut Deus, ut Angelus Jehovæ coram ipsis, Zach.XII.8. Venturus ad Templum suum, Dominus & Angelus fœderis. Malach.III.1. &c. hic, inquam, graphicè adeò & toties prædictus, figuratus, imò vivis coloribus depictus Jesus Christus, in carne manifestatus, est.
units.tr: The testimonies of Moses and the Prophets foretelling the Incarnation of Christ. He is the Branch of Jehovah and the fruit of the land, Isa. 4.2. He is to be born of a virgin and named Immanuel, ibid. 7.14-15. He is the same Son and child, whose name is Wonderful etc., ibid. ch. 9.6. He is the stone to be laid in Zion, etc., in whom whoever believes shall not be confounded, ch. 28.16. He is the one who dries up the sea and clothes the heavens in darkness, and at the same time gives his body to those who strike him and to those who pluck his cheeks, ch. 50.2-3, 6. He is the same Angel of his face, the Savior of the people, who comes from Edom with red garments from Bozrah, ch. 63.1, 9. He is the righteous Branch to be raised up to David, the King who shall reign, and Jehovah our righteousness, Jer. 23.5-6; 33.15-16. He is Jehovah and David the King, to be raised up for the people, who shall betroth and draw near to Jehovah, ibid. ch. 30.9, 21-22. He is the Son of Man, sitting on the throne of glory, Ezek. 1.26. He is the glory of God descending from above, or from heaven, which was above the cherub, to the threshold of the temple, and again rising from the threshold of the temple and ascending above the cherubim, ibid. 10.4, 17-18. He is the ruler of Israel, who is to come forth from Bethlehem, whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting, Mic. 5.2. He is the house of David, or the Seed of David, who was to be as God, as the Angel of Jehovah before them, Zech. 12.8. He is the Lord and Angel of the covenant who is coming to his temple, Mal. 3.1, etc. Here, I say, is Jesus Christ, so vividly and so often foretold and figured, indeed painted in lively colours, now made manifest in the flesh.

units.la: XIV. Cùm ergo Filius Dei à Patre missus in terram descenderit, Filium hominis, & humanum genus visitaverit, in carne apparuerit, caro factus, & in carne manifestatus; Secundum carnem ex semine Davidis, secundum Spiritum sanctitatis definitus Filius Dei in potentia ex resurrectione mortuorum; super quo fuit Spiritus Domini Jehovæ, unctus ad Evangelium nuntiandum mansuetis; in quo omnis plenitudo Deitatis habitavit, & qui Princeps salutis, sanctificator, similiter ut pueri participes factus carnis & sanguinis, semen Abrahæ apprehendit; manifestum est, in eadem Jesu Christi persona esse duas naturas, Divinam & Humanam; illam Filii Dei, hanc Filii hominis; utramque non separatam, sed in eadem persona distinctam, & sic unitam, ut in eadem [Greek] persona existant, & per subsistentiam Filii Dei carnem in unitatem personæ suæ assumentis subsistant.
units.tr: XIV. Therefore, since the Son of God, sent by the Father, has come down to earth, visited the Son of Man and the human race, appeared in the flesh, been made flesh and been manifested in the flesh; according to the flesh born of the seed of David, but declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by the resurrection from the dead; upon whom was the Spirit of the Lord Jehovah, anointed to preach the gospel to the meek; in whom all the fullness of the Deity dwells, and who, as the Prince of salvation and sanctifier, was made a partaker likewise of flesh and blood like the children, and took hold of the seed of Abraham: it is evident that in the one person of Jesus Christ there are two natures, the Divine and the Human; the former of the Son of God, the latter of the Son of Man; both not separated, but distinguished within the same person, and so united that they exist in the same person and subsist, through the subsistence of the Son of God who assumed the flesh into the unity of his person.

units.la: Nam qui à Patre missus è Cœlo in terram descendit, Filium Hominis & homines visitavit, in carne apparuit, caro factus, & in carne manifestatus est, secundum carnem ex semine Davidis genitus, secundum omnem Divinitatis plenitudinem in Christo homine habitat, & semen Abrahæ assumpsit; is iisdem locis, quibus talis describitur, & Jehova exercituum Esaj. XLVIII.2. & Filius Dei Prov.XXX.4. Luc.I.35. Joh.III.17. Gal.IV.4. Hebr.V.8. Filius Dei in potentia secundum Spiritum sanctitatis definitus, Rom.I.3.4. & λόγος Sermo, qui in principio fuit, per quem omnia facta sunt, Joh.I.1.3. & Θεὸς Deus, 1.Tim.III.16. habens omnem plenitudinem Deitatis, Col.II.9. Princeps salutis & Sanctificator, Hebr.II.10.11. appellatur, adeóque verus Deus, Deus ille Abrahami, Isaci & Jacobi est. Nam Filium Dei, Sermonem, Sermonem ὁμοούσιον esse Deo Patri, supra etiam demonstra-
units.tr: For he who, sent from the Father, came down from heaven to earth, visited the Son of Man and men, appeared in the flesh, was made flesh and was manifested in the flesh, was born according to the flesh of the seed of David, dwells in Christ the man according to all the fullness of the Deity, and took up the seed of Abraham, is the same who is described in the same places as Jehovah of hosts, Isa. 48.2, and as the Son of God, Prov. 30.4; Luke 1.35; John 3.17; Gal. 4.4; Heb. 5.8; the Son of God declared in power according to the Spirit of holiness, Rom. 1.3-4; and the Word (λόγος), who was in the beginning, through whom all things were made, John 1.1, 3; and God (Θεὸς), 1 Tim. 3.16, having all the fullness of the Deity, Col. 2.9, and is called the Prince of salvation and Sanctifier, Heb. 2.10-11; and therefore he is the true God, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. For we have shown above that the Son of God, the Word, is homoousios with God the Father [ὁμοούσιον].

units.la: vimus. Hæc ergo Divina natura in Christo habitans appellatur & Θεότης Deitas secundum omnem plenitudinem suam Col.II.9. Spiritus, qualis Dei est, 1.Cor.XV.45. 1.Pet.III.18.19. πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης Spiritus Sanctitatis Rom.I.4. μορφὴ Θεοῦ Forma Dei, Phil.II.6. Cùm tamen Filius Dei, Deus & ipse, è Cœlo descenderit in terram, ut ibi habitaret; & Filium Hominis visitaverit; & in carne apparuerit; & caro factus, in eadem manifestatus fuerit; & secundum carnem ex semine Davidis fuerit; & in ipso velut Templo omnis plenitudo Deitatis habitet; & Princeps salutis carnis & sanguinis puerorum similiter particeps factus fuerit, atque Semen Abrahæ apprehenderit: in eadem persona carnem, seu ἀνθρωπότητα humanitatem, Filium hominis, Semen Davidis & Abrahæ σκηνὴν tabernaculum, & Templum Divinitatis, carnem & sanguinem existere & subsistere consequitur, τῆς ἰδέας δόξαν.
units.tr: Therefore this Divine nature dwelling in Christ is called also the Deity (Θεότης), according to all its fullness, Col. 2.9; the Spirit such as God is, 1 Cor. 15.45; 1 Pet. 3.18-19; the Spirit of holiness [πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης], Rom. 1.4; the form of God [μορφὴ Θεοῦ], Phil. 2.6. Since, however, the Son of God, himself God, has come down from heaven to earth to dwell there; and has visited the Son of Man; and has appeared in the flesh; and, made flesh, was manifested in it; and was according to the flesh of the seed of David; and in him, as in a temple, all the fullness of the Deity dwells; and the Prince of salvation was likewise made a partaker of the flesh and blood of the children, and took hold of the seed of Abraham: it follows that in the same person there exist and subsist the flesh, or humanity (ἀνθρωπότης), the Son of Man, the Seed of David and Abraham, the tabernacle (σκηνὴ) and temple of the Divinity, flesh and blood, the glory of its form [τῆς ἰδέας δόξαν].

units.la: XV. De Deitate, seu Divina natura Christi Filii Dei dedita opera in loco egimus. Humanæ naturæ ejus veritatem insuper alia convincunt; inprimis quòd & humanæ naturæ partes essentiales, corpus & animam, & partium earum proprietates tum essentiales, tum naturales; & earundem infirmitates & defectus passim Christo tribuuntur. Nam & verum corpus humanum, non φανταζόμενον habet, quia phantasticum corpus à se removens Christus, post resurrectionem etiam carnem & ossa se habere protestatur, Luc.XXIV.39. atque ὁμοίως μετέχει similiter particeps factus est carnis & sanguinis, sicut & pueri, adeóque carnis & sanguinis humani, Hebr. II.14. & vera anima rationali præditus est. Nam ψυχὴ anima ejus fuit περίλυπος tristis usque ad mortem, Matth. XXVI.38. & ἐνεβριμήσατο τῷ πνεύματι infremuit spiritu, Joh.XI.33. atque moriens πνεῦμα spiritum suum commendavit in manus Patris, Luc.XXIII.46. ubi nec ψυχὴ anima, nec πνεῦμα spiritus Deitatem Christi notat. Non illa, quia περίλυπος esse Deitas non potest. Non hic quia Deitas commendatione humana in manus Patris, à quo nunquam exulat, & à cujus Deitate non distinguitur, haud indiget. Eidem proprietates tum essentiales, tum naturales animæ & corporis competunt. Animæ proprietates essentiales sunt spiritualitas, intelligentia, voluntas. Atqui πνευματικὸν spiritus fui à Divinitate distincti ipse Christus Luc. XXIII.46. meminit: & profecisse σοφίᾳ sapientia ibid.II.52. dicitur, & suum ipse ἰδίαν voluntatem à Patris voluntate distinguit, dicens: πλὴν οὐχ ὡς ἐγὼ θέλω, ἀλλ' ὡς σύ. Attamen non sicut ego volo, sed sicut tu, Matth.XXVI.39. Naturales quoque utriusque proprietates mutabiles utique & animæ & corpori Christi attribuuntur. Animæ, cùm profecisse sapientia dicitur, Luc.II.52. cùm in Cœlo ejus sapientia nullam ἀτελεσμὸν habeat. Corpori, quod non eandem agilitatem & gloriam in terra habuit, quam nunc in Cœlo habet, Matth.XIV.26.27. XVII.2. Phil.III.21. Denique nec infirmitatibus & defectibus humanæ naturæ caruit. Licet enim singulorum individuorum defectus, cujusmodi lepra, cœcitas, &c. sunt, non habuerit; at habuit tamen totius naturæ, quatenus illa per peccatum corrupta est. Sed sine peccato tamen. Nam & spiritu περίλυπος tristis factus fuit Matth. XXVI.38. infremuit Greek commovit se ipsum, miseratus humanam miseriam, quòd tam Greek essent, dolentes propter jacturam hujus vitæ, & non cogitantes de meliore, Joh.XI.33. coepit Greek expavescere & tristari, Marc.XIV.33. ira & indignationis signa edidit; Flagellis numularios ex templo exigens, Joh.II.15. & corpore Greek in Greek itinere, ibid.IV.6. & sudavit sicut grumos sanguinis, Luc.XXII.44. Greek lachrymatus est, videns Lazarum mortuum, Joh.XI.35. Greek ploravit super Hierosolyma, Luc.XIX.41.
units.tr: XV. We have treated the Deity, or divine nature, of Christ the Son of God in its own place, on purpose. The truth of his human nature is further proved by other arguments: first, because the essential parts of human nature, body and soul, and their properties, both essential and natural, as well as their infirmities and defects, are everywhere attributed to Christ. For he has a true human body, not an imaginary one, since Christ, removing from himself the notion of a phantasmal body, even after the resurrection declares that he has flesh and bones, Luke 24.39; and he likewise partook of flesh and blood, like the children, and thus of human flesh and blood, Heb. 2.14; and he is endowed with a true rational soul. For his soul was sorrowful unto death [περίλυπος], Matt. 26.38, and he groaned in spirit [ἐνεβριμήσατο τῷ πνεύματι], John 11.33, and dying he commended his spirit [πνεῦμα] into the hands of the Father, Luke 23.46; where neither soul [ψυχὴ] nor spirit [πνεῦμα] denotes the Deity of Christ. Not the former, because the Deity cannot be sorrowful; not the latter, because the Deity has no need of commending itself into the hands of the Father, from whom it never departs, and from whose Deity it is not distinguished. The same person possesses both essential and natural properties of soul and body. The essential properties of the soul are spirituality, understanding and will. Christ himself mentions his own spirit [πνευματικὸν] as distinct from the Divinity, Luke 23.46; and he is said to have grown in wisdom [σοφίᾳ], Luke 2.52; and he distinguishes his own will [ἰδίαν] from the will of the Father, saying: Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt [πλὴν οὐχ ὡς ἐγὼ θέλω, ἀλλ' ὡς σύ], Matt. 26.39. The natural properties of each are also attributed to the soul and body of Christ, which are certainly mutable. To the soul, since he is said to have grown in wisdom, Luke 2.52, whereas in heaven his wisdom has no perfection [ἀτελεσμὸν]. To the body, which on earth did not have the same agility and glory that it now has in heaven, Matt. 14.26-27; 17.2; Phil. 3.21. Finally, he was not free from the infirmities and defects of human nature. For although he did not have the defects of single individuals, such as leprosy, blindness, etc., yet he did have those of the whole nature, insofar as it has been corrupted by sin, but nonetheless without sin. For he became sorrowful in spirit, Matt. 26.38; he groaned, moving himself, pitying human misery, since men were grieving over the loss of this life and not thinking of a better one, John 11.33; he began to be amazed and distressed, Mark 14.33; he gave signs of anger and indignation, driving the money-changers out of the temple with a whip, John 2.15; he was weary in body on the journey, John 4.6; he sweated as drops of blood, Luke 22.44; he wept, seeing Lazarus dead, John 11.35; he wept over Jerusalem, Luke 19.41.

units.la: XVI. Sicut proin Christus secundum Divinam naturam Deo Patri suo Greek est: ita secundum Humanam nobis Greek est, Greek in Greek factus in similitudine hominum, sicut quoad Divinitatem est Greek instar Dei, & Greek in forma Dei, Phil.II.6.7. Greek per omnia assimilatus fratribus, Hebr.II.17. Sanctificator enim ille, cui semen Abrahæ vindicandum Deus dedit, non tantùm frater esse, sed etiam mori, adeóque in omnibus fratribus suis assimilari & tentari debuit, quia Sacerdos & fidelis & misericors esse debuit. Neque enim illa Greek similitudo tantùm in qualitate est, uti quidem Philosophi Greek simile in qualitate constituunt, & sic à Greek identitate distinguunt; (quem stylum Scriptura non imitatur, in qua etiam Jobus dicens: Hebrew Hebrew similis factus sum pulveri & cineri, cap.xxx.19. non ad solam qualitatem, sed substantiam etiam respicit, quia quæ sub eodem genere sunt, similitudine idem sunt, & propterea idem nomen habent) sed tum in substantia, qua sic similis factus est pueris, ut eorundem carnem & sanguinem participaverit, Hebr.II.14. tum in quantitate, qualitate, actionibus, quia Greek habitu inventus fuit Greek ut homo, quoad formam servi nihil amplius quàm homo (non Greek instar Dei, non Hebrew Vir, homo spectabilis, Psalm.XXII.7.) Phil.II.8. Unde homo 1.Tim. II.5. Rom.V.15. Filius hominis Joh.III.13. Filius Davidis, Matth.XXII.42. alibique passim appellatur.
units.tr: XVI. Just as Christ is, according to his divine nature, equal with God his Father, so according to his human nature he is inferior to us, having been emptied and made in the likeness of men, just as in respect of his deity he is in the form of God, equal with God (Phil. 2:6-7), and in all things made like his brethren (Heb. 2:17). For that Sanctifier, to whom God gave the seed of Abraham to be claimed, had to be not only a brother but also to die, and so to be made like his brethren in all things and to be tempted, because he had to be a priest who was faithful and merciful. For that likeness is not merely one of quality, as the philosophers define "similar in quality" and so distinguish it from "identical"; Scripture does not follow that usage, in which Job also says, "I have become like dust and ashes" (Job 30:19), looking not only to quality but also to substance, because things that fall under the same genus are alike and therefore share the same name. Rather, the likeness is in substance, since he was made like the children so as to share their flesh and blood (Heb. 2:14); and also in quantity, quality and actions, since he was found in the appearance of a man, and in the form of a servant was nothing more than a man (not like God, not a mighty man, a conspicuous man, Ps. 22:7) (Phil. 2:8). Hence he is called "the man" (1 Tim. 2:5; Rom. 5:15), "the Son of man" (John 3:13), "the Son of David" (Matt. 22:42), and so throughout.

units.la: XVII. Divinam naturam Jesum Christum à Patre per æternam generationem habere, supra firmavimus. Humanam verò ex matre Maria Virgine, per conceptionem ex Spiritu S.habet. Dissimilis enim generationis naturæ Christi humanæ, & reliquorum hominum ratio est. Cùm enim hi ex sanguinibus, ex voluntate seu cupidine carnis, ex voluntate viri (Joh.I.13.) nascantur; illa sine carnis & viri cupidine, ex matre Virgine manente, virtute Spiritus S. concepta & nata est. Personam enim planè extraordinariam, quæ Deus & Homo, idémque purus & labis omnis expers. Deitatis ipsius Templum esset, extraordinaria & singulari planè genitura edi oportuit. Quis dabit Hebrew purum ex impuro? Ne unus quidem, Job. XIV.4. Quod ex carne gignitur, caro est, Joh.III.6. Quicquid enim communi ordine ex patre & matre nascitur, sub maledictione nascitur. At Christus debuit esse Greek impollutus.Hebr. VII.26. Execratio quidem, sed non natus talis, verùm Greek factus pro nobis, Gal.III.13. XVIII. Mater Jesu Christi B.Virgo Maria, communi ortu nata, gente & tribu Judæa, ex familia Davidis orta, statu virgo, sed desponsata fuit. Nam in Adamo, æquè ac omnes alii meri homines, peccavit, Rom.V.12. adeóque imputato ei peccato Adami sine labe etiam inhærente ei nasci non potuit. De quo plura Loc X.56.diximus. Tum ex Judæis salus est, Joh.IV.22. Horum sunt promissiones, & Patres, ex quibus est Christus, quod ad carnem attinet, Rom.IX.4.5. Sicut etiam Christus, Schiloh promissus, est ex tribu Juda, Genes.XLIX.10. & Greek manifestum est, quòd ex Juda exortus sit Dominus noster, Hebr.VII.14. ita ex eadem tribu mater ejus fuerit oportet, cùm carnem suam à sola matre, non à Patre, quippe Greek fine patre, (ibid.3.) habuerit. Sed & ex familia Davidis ortum similem ob rationem traxisse arguitur, quia Davidi Deus promisit, fore ut è visceribus ejus prodeat Semen, cujus Regnum in seculum usque stabiliturus sit, 2.Sam.VII.12. &c. Quæ promissio toties iterata est per Prophetas, ut Christus inde non tantùm Hebrew Semen & Hebrew Germen Davidis, sed etiam Hebrew David, quasi gentile hoc nomen esset, appelletur, Jerem.XXX.9. Ezech.XXXIV.24. XXXVII.24. Neque illud obstat, quòd Elizabetha, quæ fuit Greek ex filiabus Aaronis Luc.I.5. Greek cognata Mariæ ibid.v.36. vocatur, quia cognatio eas inter ex matre ex tribu Judæ oriunda intercedere potuit. Statu Virginem fuisse, historia sacra testatur. Nam Angelus Gabriel missus dicitur in urbem Nazareth Greek ad Virginem, cujus nomen erat Maria, ibid.v.26.27. Cui cùm conceptionem & nativitatem Jesu ex ea futuram annuntiasset, obstupescens illa quæsivit: Greek Quomodo hoc erit, siquidem virum non cognosco, ibid.v.34. Quæ verba vel dubitantis sunt, uti Chrysostomus opinatus est; vel, quod alii rectiùs censent, actionitæ, & cùm promissionem de Virgine partura, & exempla Patrum, qui per congressum cum uxoribus suis semen promissionis acceperunt, consideraret; de modo interrogantis, Virgo an nupta paritura esset, cùm virum nondum cognoscat, hoc est, cum nullo viro consuetudinem habeat. Nam & vox Hebraica Hebrew sæpissime hunc significatum habet; & Græca Greek apud exoticos etiam, Plutarchum imprimis, ut ex eo Xylander notavit; denique etiam Latina cognoscere apud authores probè Latinos, Ovidium, Statium, Cæsarem, Tacitum &c. Greek seu concubitus notionem habet, quia rem naturæ lege operiendam verecunda quadam verborum tralatione protegere placuit. Nuspiam enim familiaris adeò & intima notitia est, quàm cùm vir pro viro, fœmina pro fœmina, uxor pro uxore cognoscitur. Quòd verò Veteres non pauci, & eosdem secuti Monachi, verba illa Mariæ sic interpretantur, quasi propositum vel votum æternæ virginitatis, sive à se, sive à parentibus ejus, juxta narrationem illam, seu potiùs somnium ex eburnea porta, quod nomine Greek nuncupatum indicasset; oppidò falluntur, quia voto sive proprio, sive alieno constricta Josepho nupturam se non spopondisset. Nam jam tum Virgo fuit, sed Greek Josepho desponsata, Matth.I.18. cum quo συνελθεῖν conveniendi propositum eam habuisse, ibidem innuitur. Desponsari autem Virginem sanctissimam Deus voluit, ne aut Filius, ceu spurius, in congregationem non admittendus (Deut. XXIII.2.) in muneris sui administratione impediretur; vel Mariae, ceu adulterae, juxta legem, Levit. XX. 10. capitale crimen intentaretur. Qui Virginem ἐπίxληρον fuisse ex Epiphanio asserunt, eos à ratione destitui, supra ostendimus. Etiam ἀεὶ παρθένον semper Virginem fuisse Ecclesia credit. Nam ante, & in partu virginem fuisse, credere fides in Jesum Christum sine peccato natum jubet. Etiam post partum illibatum Virginitatis florem retinuisse, piè Ecclesia credit, licèt fidei in Christum nihil interfit. Sed probabilibus conjecturis tamen res isthaec adversus Helvidium & complices pridem decisa est, quam in rem multa post Hieronymum, aliósque Veteres viri πολυμαθεῖς Rivetus Apol B.V.M. lib.I.15. & novissimè Bynaeus de Nat. J.C. lib.I.2.6. &c. dixerunt; & nos quoque in loco diximus.
units.tr: XVII. We have shown above that Jesus Christ has his divine nature from the Father by eternal generation. His human nature, however, he has from his mother Mary, a virgin, by conception through the Holy Spirit. For the manner of generation of Christ's human nature is unlike that of other men. For while these are born of blood, of the will of the flesh, and of the will of a man (John 1:13), that nature was conceived and born without the desire of the flesh or of a man, the virgin mother remaining a virgin, by the power of the Holy Spirit. For a person altogether extraordinary, who is God and man and at the same time pure and free of every stain, and who was to be the temple of the Deity itself, had to be brought forth by a wholly extraordinary and singular birth. "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?" Not one (Job 14:4). "What is born of the flesh is flesh" (John 3:6). For whatever is born in the common order from father and mother is born under a curse. But Christ had to be undefiled (Heb. 7:26). Indeed he was accursed, yet not born such, but made a curse for us (Gal. 3:13). XVIII. The mother of Jesus Christ, the blessed Virgin Mary, was born by ordinary birth, of the Jewish people and tribe, sprung from the family of David, a virgin in her state, but betrothed. For in Adam, as all other mere men, she sinned (Rom. 5:12), and so, since the sin of Adam was imputed to her, she could not be born without the stain of inherent sin. We have said more on this in Loc. X, §56. "Salvation is of the Jews" (John 4:22). To them belong the promises and the fathers, from whom Christ came according to the flesh (Rom. 9:4-5). Just as Christ, promised as Shiloh, is of the tribe of Judah (Gen. 49:10), and it is plain that our Lord sprang out of Judah (Heb. 7:14), so his mother must have been of the same tribe, since he had his flesh from his mother alone, not from a father, indeed without father (ibid., 3). But it is argued that for a similar reason she also drew her descent from the family of David, since God promised David that a seed would come forth from his bowels, whose kingdom he would establish for ever (2 Sam. 7:12, etc.). This promise was repeated so often through the prophets that Christ is called from it not only "the seed" and "the branch" of David, but even "David" himself, as if that were a gentile name (Jer. 30:9; Ezek. 34:24; 37:24). Nor does it stand in the way that Elizabeth, who was of the daughters of Aaron (Luke 1:5), is called a kinswoman of Mary (ibid., 36), since kinship could exist between them through a mother who was of the tribe of Judah. That she was a virgin in her state, sacred history attests. For the angel Gabriel is said to have been sent to the city of Nazareth to a virgin, whose name was Mary (ibid., 26-27). When he had announced to her that the conception and birth of Jesus would come from her, she, astonished, asked: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" (ibid., 34). These words are either those of one in doubt, as Chrysostom supposed, or, as others more rightly judge, those of one reflecting upon the promise about a virgin who would bear, and upon the examples of the Fathers who received the seed of promise through intercourse with their wives; so the question concerns the manner: whether the virgin would bear as a married woman, since she does not yet know a man, that is, has no intercourse with any man. For the Hebrew word has this meaning very often; and the Greek word also among foreign writers, Plutarch above all, as Xylander noted from him; and finally the Latin cognoscere, among thoroughly Latin authors, Ovid, Statius, Caesar, Tacitus, etc., has the sense of intercourse, since it has pleased people to cover a matter to be concealed by nature's law with a modest turn of words. For nowhere is familiar and intimate knowledge greater than when man is known by man, woman by woman, wife by husband. But that not a few of the ancients, and the monks who followed them, interpret those words of Mary as if they expressed a purpose or vow of perpetual virginity, either made by herself or by her parents, according to that narrative, or rather dream, of the ivory gate, which indicated that she was named by that name, is greatly mistaken, because she, bound by a vow, whether her own or another's, would not have promised to marry Joseph. For she was already a virgin, but betrothed to Joseph (Matt. 1:18), with whom she had the purpose of coming together, as is implied in the same place. But God willed that the most holy virgin should be betrothed, lest the Son, as a bastard not to be admitted into the congregation (Deut. 23:2), should be hindered in the administration of his office, or lest a capital charge should be brought against Mary as an adulteress, according to the law (Lev. 20:10). Those who assert, from Epiphanius, that she was a heiress (epiklēros), we have shown above to be destitute of reason. The Church also believes that she was ever a virgin (aei parthenos). For faith in Jesus Christ, born without sin, bids us believe she was a virgin before, in and at the birth. The Church also devoutly believes that after the birth she kept the unbroken flower of virginity, although this makes no difference to faith in Christ. Yet this matter was long ago settled against Helvidius and his companions by probable conjectures, on which many after Jerome and other learned ancients (polymathes) have written, namely Rivetus in his Apology for the Blessed Virgin, Book I, ch. 15, and most recently Bynaeus, On the Nature of Jesus Christ, Book I, ch. 2, 6, etc.; and we also have said something on it in our place.

units.la: XIX. Talem ergo Virginem prae aliis ejusdem gentis, Tribus, familiae, status, mulieribus Deus elegit, non ob dignitatem Virginis, sed ob dignationem suam. Unde Angelus sic eam compellat; χαῖρε κεχαριτωμένη, salve vel potius gaude (exprimitur sic Formula salutantis לך שלום Pax tibi) gratiam consecuta; vel, uti statim Angelus explicat, χάριν εὑρες παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ gratiam invenisti apud Deum, Luc. I.28.30. Ulus etiam voce χάριτὴν gratia prosequi, cumulare est S. Paulus Ephes. I.6. & voce κεχαριτωμένος Siracides cap. XVIII.17. Ecce sermo pluris est quam donum. Et utraque apud virum κεχαριτωμένον. Planè ut falli constet Angelum Canonium, Bezam & Glassium, quibus visum est, Lucam verbum hoc fabricatum esse, ut vocem vel Syriacam, רחמיתא quae gratiosissimam, acceptissimam significat: vel Hebraicam נרצה quae δεκτὴ, ἀποδεκτὸν notat, exprimeret. Quanquam verisimile est, Lucam vocem aliquam vel Syriacam vel Hebraicam, puta רחמיתא, uti Gatakero, Grotio, vel מחננת, uti Capello, vel חסידה, quae gratia donatam significat, uti Fullero visum est, respexisse. De quo quicquid fiat, parum commodè Gratia plenam Latinus reddit, cùm aliud sit κεχαριτωμένον gratia cumulatus, aliud πλήρης χάριτος gratia plenus, qualis solus Christus fuit, Joh. I.14. Sed insulsè inprimis gratia plenam Mariolatrae gratia inhaerente plenam interpretantur, quasi fons, causa, datrix gratiae, gratis diligens, benefaciens, sive largiens intelligatur. Nam si etiam gratia plenam appellare liceret, hoc unum significaretur, quòd Deus gratiam suam coelestem in Mariam profuderit, ut sancta Christi Mater & Θεοτόκος evaderet. Incredibilis enim & inusitata gratia est, quòd Deus virginem illam inter omnes mulieres elegit, ex qua mundi Servator nasceretur. Unde mox Angelus ἐξηγητικῶς subjicit indicium favoris & benignitatis Divinae. ὁ Κύριος μετὰ σοῦ Dominus tecum, benedicta inter mulieres, Luc. I.28.
units.tr: XIX. God therefore chose such a virgin above other women of the same people, tribe, family and state, not on account of the virgin's dignity but on account of his own condescension. Hence the angel addresses her thus: "Hail [chaire kechāritōmenē], rejoice, or rather be glad, highly favoured" (the formula of greeting, Peace be to you, is expressed in Hebrew by "Shalom lekha"), or, as the angel explains at once, "You have found favour with God" (Luke 1:28, 30). For Paul also uses the word grace to mean to bestow grace abundantly (Eph. 1:6), and Sirach uses the word kechāritōmenos (Ecclus 18:17): "Behold, a word is more than a gift." And both are said to a man who is kechāritōmenos. This plainly shows that Calvin, Beza and Glassius are mistaken, who thought that Luke invented the word to express either the Syriac word that means most gracious and most acceptable, or the Hebrew word that means acceptable, received. Yet it is likely that Luke had regard to some Syriac or Hebrew word, such as rechemitha, as Gataker and Grotius suppose, or mechannenet as Cappel suggests, or chasidah, which means one endowed with grace, as Fuller judged. Whatever the truth on this, the Latin translation full of grace renders it poorly, since kechāritōmenos, endowed with grace, is one thing and plērēs charitos, full of grace, is another, such as Christ alone was (John 1:14). But the Mariolaters especially interpret full of grace foolishly, as if it meant full of inherent grace, as if she were understood to be the fountain, cause or giver of grace, lavishly loving, doing good, or bestowing. For if it were permissible to call her full of grace in that sense, only this would be signified: that God poured out his heavenly grace upon Mary, so that she might become the holy Mother of Christ and Theotokos. For it is an incredible and unusual grace that God chose that virgin above all women, from whom the Saviour of the world would be born. Hence the angel at once adds, by way of explanation, the sign of divine favour and goodwill: "The Lord is with you; blessed are you among women" (Luke 1:28).

units.la: XX. Ex Virgine nasciturum esse Jesum, vetera etiam vaticinia praesagiverunt. Nam a Maria Virgine natus est Jesus, ut impleretur, quod dictum est a Domino per Prophetam dicentem; ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει, καὶ παξ-
units.tr: XX. The ancient prophecies also foretold that Jesus would be born of a Virgin. For Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary, so that what the Lord had spoken through the Prophet might be fulfilled, saying: "Behold, the virgin shall have a child in her womb, and..." [ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει, καὶ παξ-]

units.la: Ex Virgine nasciturum E-saj. VII.14. praedictum est. dunt, nil moramur, quia Judæi & apostatæ suæ hypothesi inservire, quàm veritati litare maluerunt. Potior est LXX. Interpretum, Judæorum quidem, sed fidelium adhuc, authoritas, qui παρθένον Virginem reddiderunt. De hac Virgine Jesajas dicit: עלמה הרה וילדה Virgo concipit (ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχει in utero habet, fert) & parit filium, quæ ita junguntur, ut nonnisi eodem tempore & esse Virgo & uterum ferre dicatur. Si enim diversum tempus virginitatis & uteri ferendi indicasset, non עלמה Virginem, sed נערה vel omnino אישה appellasset, uti quævis fœmina imprægnata uterum ferre, parere filium &c. intelligitur. Inprimis si accentus addatur, & cum iono aliquo expressius pronuntietur; Ecce Virgo uterum gerit; dubitari non poterit, quin utrumque conjunctim dicatur. Et in hoc Signum, miraculum & evidens opus Dei est; quale non est, si puella aliqua nubere & uterum ferre dicatur. Hunc sensum Matthæus ostendit, & eventus atque analogia Scripturarum, inprimis S. Paulus, Pontificem secundum ordinem Melchisedeci ἀπάτωρ sine patre esse innuens, demonstrant. Neque illud obstat, quòd in præsenti הרה concipit, dicitur, cùm sexcentos post annos Maria uterum tulerit; quia Prophetiæ omnes futura propter certitudinem per præsentia vel participia explicent. De futuro autem sermonem esse, liquet ex verbis Prophetæ יתן Dabit Dominus vobis signum, v.14. Unde Græci habent: ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται, in utero feret. De Filii hujus virginis nomine sic Propheta: וקראת & vocabit vel Virgo mater, vel quivis alius, cui partus hujus historia proponetur, nomen ejus עמנו אל Nobiscum Deus; hoc est, Deus populum suum visitans, in carne manifestatus, datus Filius, idémque Deus confirmaturus thronum Davidis, & Princeps pacis, Esaj.IX.6.7. Omnium hostium consilia frustraturus, quia עמנו אל Nobiscum Deus, ibid. VIII.10. Nil obstat, quòd Angelus ei nomen proprium Jesus, non Immanuel imposuit, & communiter Jesu, non Immanuelis nomine venit; quia Immanuelis nomen cum nomine proprio Jesu virtute & significatione convenit, atque hoc explicat; adeóque diverso vocabulo, sed eundem sensum habente, exprimi debuit. Quomodo Israel proprium gentis nomen per Lo-Ammi, Lo-Ruchamah, Chephziba &c. & Hierosolyma per Jehova Schammah, Jehova Nissi, &c. explicatur.
units.tr: That the one born of a Virgin was foretold: Isa. VII.14. We need not linger over the Jews and apostates, who preferred to serve their own hypothesis rather than to sacrifice to the truth. The authority of the Seventy Interpreters is greater. They were Jews, but still faithful, and they rendered παρθένος as Virgin. Of this Virgin Isaiah says: "a young woman [עלמה] is with child and bears" [עלמה הרה וילדה], that is, she conceives (in the Greek, ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχει, she has in her womb, she bears) and gives birth to a son. These two things are joined together so that it is said that she is at the same time a virgin and carrying a child in her womb. For if the prophet had meant a different time for her virginity and for her bearing a child, he would not have called her virgin (עלמה) but a young wife (נערה) or simply a woman (אישה), as any pregnant woman is understood to bear and give birth to a son. Especially if the emphasis is placed on the words and they are pronounced more expressively with a certain intonation, Behold, a virgin bears a child, there can be no doubt that both are meant together. And in this the sign is a miracle and a plain work of God, which it would not be if some girl were said to marry and become pregnant. Matthew shows this sense, and the outcome and the analogy of the Scriptures, especially St Paul, who indicates that the priest after the order of Melchizedek was ἀπάτωρ, without father, demonstrate it. Nor does it stand in the way that the word הרה, conceives, is in the present tense, although Mary bore the child six hundred years later. For all prophecies express future things by the present or participles, for the sake of certainty. That the speech concerns the future is clear from the Prophet's words יתן, The Lord himself shall give you a sign, v. 14. Hence the Greeks have ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται, she shall take into the womb. The Prophet speaks thus of the name of this Virgin's son: וקראת, she shall call, either the Virgin mother or whoever else the story of this birth is set before, his name עמנו אל, God with us; that is, God visiting his people, manifested in the flesh, a Son given, and the same is God who will establish the throne of David and the Prince of peace, Isa. IX.6, 7. He will frustrate the counsels of all enemies, because עמנו אל, God is with us, ibid. VIII.10. It is no objection that the angel gave him the proper name Jesus, not Immanuel, and that he generally came under the name of Jesus, not of Immanuel; for the name Immanuel agrees in power and meaning with the proper name Jesus and explains it, and so it had to be expressed by a different word having the same sense. Just as Israel, the proper name of the people, is explained by Lo-Ammi, Lo-Ruchamah, Chephziba, etc., and Jerusalem by Jehovah Shammah, Jehovah Nissi, etc.

units.la: XXI. Hæc cùm ita sint, falsò Judæi hanc עלמה vel Regis Achazi uxorem, sive Ezechiæ matrem, sive aliam, vel Prophetæ uxorem, adeóque Filium Immanuelem unum ex his uxoribus filium explicant. Ut signum intelligatur vel nomen infanti impositum, memoriale, ne Prophetia hæc ex ore ipsorum obliteretur; vel salvatio ipsa, quæ ἀνσημασίαι sunt. Nam Ezechias jam tum natus fuit; quia natus viginti quinque annos Rex factus, & Achaz summùm sedecim annos regnavit. Tum Propheta promiserat signum ex alto & ex imo; quale merum memoriale, vel salvatio ipsa esse non potuit. Quærebatur enim signum Verbo Prophetæ de futuris prædicentis fidem faciens. Præterea ridiculum fuisset, magno hiatu incipere: Deus vobis dabit signum, & addere Ecce; ac tum subitò subsidere, & dicere: Ecce Filia tua, vel uxor mea, gravida est, quod tu nescis; & erit nomen ejus Immanuel. Atqui nec filia Achazi, vel uxor Prophetæ gravida dici עלמה potuit: nec Immanuelis nomen vel omen filio alterutrius competiit, vel impositum est: nec sic signum aliquod fuit, quod Deus dederit: nec sic in verbis Prophetæ quicquam fuisset, quo fides populi circa cætera omnia prædicta confirmaretur: nec מלא רחב ארץ plenitudo latitudinis terræ Canaan, quæ cap.VIII.8. Emmanuelis esse dicitur, ullius hominis, certè non filii Prophetæ, vel Achazi &c. alia quapiam, quàm Ezechiæ matre, sed solius Dei, Filii Dei fuit, qui terram illam selegit, in qua hominibus appareret, & Templum suum haberet; unde εἰς τὰ ἴδια in propria sua venisse, Joh.I.11. ceu ארץ כל Dominus totius terræ, Psalm.XCVII.5. dicitur. Hoc enim maximè modo Signum illud cap.VII.14. datum ad consolationem fidelium applicavit, tum eum, qui vocandus est Immanuel, verum Regem populi esse, & ex toto mundo sibi terram Judæ, ut peculium suum, & ad quam venturus erat, selegisse; ut metuendum non fuerit, ne thronus Achazi concuteretur, & hæreditas alienaretur: tum omnes futuras calamitates accipiendas esse, tanquam paternas castigationes Dei, cùm noverint, Filio datum esse Israelem in peculium, & plagas omnes inde provenire, quòd eum contemneret; Denique Deum Filii sui Emmanuelis, jugiter pro populo intercedentis, rationem habiturum, & plagas in benedictionem conversurum.
units.tr: XXI. These things being so, the Jews wrongly explain this עלמה as the wife of King Ahaz, or the mother of Hezekiah, or some other woman, or the prophet's wife, and so explain the son Immanuel as one of these wives' sons, so that the sign is understood as a memorial name given to the infant, lest this prophecy be erased from their mouths; or as deliverance itself, which are ἀνσημασίαι. For Hezekiah had already been born by then, since he was born twenty-five years before becoming king, and Ahaz reigned sixteen years at most. Then the prophet had promised a sign from on high and from the depths, which could not be a mere memorial or deliverance itself. For what was sought was a sign that would make the people believe the word of the prophet who foretold the future. Moreover, it would have been ridiculous to begin with a great gap, The Lord will give you a sign, and to add Behold, and then suddenly to subside and say: Behold, your daughter or my wife is pregnant, which you do not know; and his name will be Immanuel. Yet neither Ahaz's daughter nor the prophet's wife could be called עלמה while pregnant, nor could the name or omen Immanuel belong to or be given to a son of either of them; nor would it then have been any sign that God had given; nor would anything in the prophet's words have confirmed the people's faith concerning all the other things foretold; nor could the מלא רחב ארץ, the fullness of the breadth of the land of Canaan, which in chapter VIII.8 is called Immanuel's, belong to any man, certainly not to the prophet's son or to Ahaz etc., nor to any other woman than Hezekiah's mother; but it belonged to God alone, the Son of God, who chose that land in which he would appear to men and have his temple. Hence he is said to have come εἰς τὰ ἴδια, to his own things, John I.11, and, as the Lord of the whole earth, כל ארץ, Ps. XCVII.5. For in this very way the sign given in chapter VII.14 was applied for the comfort of the faithful: that he who is to be called Immanuel is the true King of the people, and has chosen the land of Judah out of the whole world as his own possession, to which he was to come; so that there was no need to fear that the throne of Ahaz would be shaken and the inheritance alienated; and that all future calamities were to be received as the fatherly chastisements of God, since they knew that Israel had been given to the Son as his possession, and that all the plagues arose from the fact that they despised him. Finally, God would take account of his Son Immanuel, who continually intercedes for the people, and would turn the plagues into blessings.

units.la: XXII. Cum Esajæ Vaticinio convenit illud Jeremiæ: Quò usque circumduces te, Filia aversa? Nam creavit Jehova novum in terra. נקבה תסובב גבר Fœmina circumdat masculum Jerem.XXXI.22. Compellantur Judæi apostatæ, ἀποστάσεις subductionis, fugæ à Christo, filii, Hebr.X.39. monentúrque de repenitus nova, prodigiosa, à sæculo non audita, sed expectata tamen à patribus, qua facta ad plenam convictionem Judæorum certum est, venisse salutare Domini, & Jehovam populo suo in Deum factum esse. Quæ res est puerperium virginis, quo נקבה fœmina (nil nisi γυναικα fœmina, non uxor, adeóque Virgo, quia vox illa simpliciter sexum fœmineum, sicut גבר alterum sexum notat) תסובב גבר circumdat virum, hoc est, υἱὸν ἄρρενα filium marem (Apoc.XII.5.) in utero feret. Nam circumdatio illa non per amplexum, sed per conceptionem facta est, quippe opus solius Dei, & non voluntaria operatio hominis. Quæ explicatio cùm verbis Prophetæ, scopo sermonis, & eventui consentanea sit, & sine hoc argumento revocatio Judæorum à suo errore inefficax sit, à Judæis rejici nullatenus potest. Nam & ipsi Hebræi veteres in Berefith Rabba §89. & Midrasch tillim in Psalm.2:7. locum hunc de Virgine & Messia interpretantur.
units.tr: XXII. The prophecy of Jeremiah agrees with that of Isaiah: "How long will you go about, O backsliding daughter? For the Lord has created a new thing in the earth: a woman shall compass a man" (נקבה תסובב גבר), Jer. XXXI.22. The apostate Jews are addressed, the backsliders, withdrawing from Christ, the sons of Heb. X.39, and are warned of a new, prodigious thing, not heard of in the age, but nevertheless expected by the fathers; and this having happened, it is certain for the full conviction of the Jews that the salvation of the Lord has come, and that Jehovah has become God to his people. This event is the childbirth of the virgin, in which the נקבה, the woman (nothing but γυνή, woman, not wife, and therefore a virgin, because that word simply denotes the female sex, as גבר denotes the other sex), תסובב גבר, compasses a man, that is, will bear υἱὸν ἄρρενα, a male son (Rev. XII.5), in the womb. For that compassing was done not by embrace but by conception, being the work of God alone and not a voluntary operation of man. Since this explanation agrees with the Prophet's words, with the purpose of the discourse, and with the event, and without this argument the recall of the Jews from their error is ineffective, it cannot by any means be rejected by the Jews. For the ancient Hebrews themselves, in Bereshith Rabba §89 and Midrash Tehillim on Ps. 2:7, also interpret this passage of the Virgin and the Messiah.

units.la: XXIII. Hæc cùm ita sint, tolerandæ non sunt eorundem Judæorum adversus B. Virginem, & de ea narrationem Evangelistarum blasphemiæ, quas inprimis author Nizzachon, & liber piacularis תולדות ישו eructant. Nam Jesum non ex Virgine illibata, sed ex concubitu adulterino Stadæ cum Maria, uxore Pandiræ, (unde & Stadæ & Pandiræ filium blasphemo ore appellant) natum esse; & Esajæ verba pro partu Virgineo alienissimo sensu Matthæum citat. citasse, cum res adeo ab aevo Achazi remota ejus animum nutantem confirmare non potuerit, & alia obstent, inprimis etiam illud quod a muliere natus purus non est, Job.XV.14. & Josephus Mariae ἀνὴρ maritus (Matth.I.19.) appellatur; & alia ejusmodi ex libris illis scelestissimis a Celeb. Wagenseilio producta, virulentissime blasphemant. Sed illibatus Iesu & Mariae honos, nequaquam ab infensissimis hostibus laceratus, perstat. Veteres quidem Gentiles & Judaeos Jesum Pantheris filium appellasse, eo quod Jacobo Josephi patri, simul & ipsi Josepho, nomen Pantheris haesisset, Epiphanius, haeres.88. prodidit, & Doctiss. Vossius de Geneal. J.C. cap.5: 1.2. conjectat, simulque Panther non nomen, sed cognomen Josephi & majorum ejus fuisse, asserit. Sed haec ἀδηλα sunt, & ex Epiphanii & Damasceni discrepantibus narratiunculis hausta, & ipsis Hebraeorum commentis adversantia, fidem nullam merentur. Inventum a Judaeis Pantheris nomen fuisse, ut adultero supposittitio nomen ne deesset, merito o πανυ Wagenseilius ariolatur. Sed calumniam ipsam, de nato ex adultera Jesu multa alia discutiunt. velut, quod nullis fide dignis testibus id comprobatum est: quod infamis mulier inter consanguineos, infensos inprimis Filio Scribas & Pharisaeos, tuto habitare non potuisset: quod Jesus ipse, si Mamser ejusmodi fuisset, ad sacra solennia & congregationem admissus non fuisset: quod a nemine, ac ne subornatis quidem falsis illis adversus Jesum testibus infame facinus vel Mariae, vel Jesu exprobratum legere est: quod Evangelistae & Apostoli adversus rei palam editae notitiam, superstitibus etiam pervulgati facinoris testibus, mirabilem Jesu ortum, commenti non fuisset, nec eum ad Davidem, maximum illum Regem, retulisset. Quae vero adversus S. Matthaeum, vaticinium Jesajae partui Virgineo applicantem, iidem objiciunt, pleraque supra diluimus. Frivolum plane etiam illud est, quod res adeo ab aevo Achazi remota, ejusdem animum prostratum erigere non potuerit, cum tralatitium sit, signa ad rem promissam confirmandam non semper praesentia, sed consequentia etiam & futura, sed certitudine maxima, & Divina promissione suffulta, adhiberi. Quomodo etiam Mosi, Exod.III.12. signum, ex quo de missione ejus constaret, post exitum populi demum consecutum, datum fuisse legitur. Hoc tibi, inquit Deus, erit signum, quod ego misi te, quando populum eduxeris ex Aegypto; servietis Deo in monte hoc. Insanum vero & illud est, quod verba Eliphazi: Quid est אנוש homo deploratus, ut jus illi sit, & ut justus sit ילד אישה natus muliere, Job.XV.14. eo trahunt, ut Jesum, ex muliere sine viro natum γαληνον putentur. quasi ad rem fecerit ibi, ubi Eliphaz omnes mortales, ipsumque adeo etiam Jobum, ex aequo injustos pronuntiat, in solum Jesum longissimo post tempore in dias mundi oras prodituram crimen detorquere. ילד אישה natum muliere dixit Eliphaz, obvia periphrasi, quemvis communi forte a muliere, sed non sine voluntate Viri, natum, quia mulier, non vir parit; & proxime ex muliere, non viro, homo nascitur. Denique Josephum ἀνδρα Virum Mariae S.Matth.cap.I.19. dixit, sed non συνελθειν, verum sponsum. Un-
units.tr: XXIII. These things being so, the blasphemies of the same Jews against the Blessed Virgin, and against the Evangelists' account of her, must not be tolerated; these the author of the Nizzachon and the expiatory book תולדות ישו especially belch forth. For they say that Jesus was born not of an undefiled Virgin but of an adulterous union of Stada with Mary, the wife of Pandera (whence they also call him with blasphemous mouth the son of Stada and Pandera), and that Matthew cited the words of Isaiah for a virgin birth in a sense most alien, since a thing so remote from the age of Ahaz could not confirm his wavering mind; and other objections, especially that a man born of woman is not pure, Job XV.14, and that Joseph is called Mary's ἀνήρ, husband (Matt. I.19), and other such things produced from those most wicked books by the renowned Wagenseil, they blaspheme most virulently. But the untarnished honour of Jesus and Mary, by no means torn by the most hostile enemies, stands firm. Epiphanius, in heresy 88, reports that the ancient Gentiles and Jews called Jesus the son of Panthera, because the name Panthera had stuck to Jacob, the father of Joseph, and also to Joseph himself; and the most learned Vossius, in De Genealogia Jesu Christi ch. 5, conjectures and asserts that Panther was not the name but the surname of Joseph and his ancestors. But these are uncertain matters, drawn from the discrepant little tales of Epiphanius and Damascene, and opposed even to the fictions of the Hebrews themselves, and deserve no credence. That the name Panthera was invented by the Jews so that the supposititious adulterer should not lack a name, Wagenseil rightly and most absurdly guesses. But many other things refute the calumny itself, that Jesus was born of an adulterous woman: such as that this has not been proved by any trustworthy witnesses; that an infamous woman could not have lived safely among her relatives, who were hostile especially to her Son, the Scribes and Pharisees; that Jesus himself, if he had been a mamzer of this kind, would not have been admitted to the solemn festivals and the congregation; that no one, not even the false witnesses suborned against Jesus, is read to have reproached either Mary or Jesus with an infamous deed; that the Evangelists and Apostles, if they had been inventing a wondrous birth of Jesus against the knowledge of a deed openly made known, with witnesses of the notorious deed still living and widely known, would not have traced him to David, that greatest King. As for the objections which the same men raise against St Matthew for applying Isaiah's prophecy to the virgin birth, we have for the most part answered them above. It is also quite frivolous that a thing so remote from the age of Ahaz could not raise up his prostrate mind, since it is commonplace that signs are used to confirm a promised matter, not always present but also following and future, yet supported by the greatest certainty and divine promise. Likewise we read that the sign to Moses, Exod. III.12, by which his mission would be established, was given only after the people had gone out. This shall be the sign to you, says God, that I have sent you, when you have brought the people out of Egypt; you shall serve God on this mountain. Insane too is the way they twist the words of Eliphaz, What is man (אנוש), the forlorn one, that he should be righteous, and that he who is born of a woman (ילד אישה) should be just? Job XV.14, so as to think that Jesus, born of a woman without a man, is γαληνός, mild, as if it had any bearing there, where Eliphaz equally pronounces all mortals unjust, Job himself included, to turn a crime onto Jesus alone, which would come to light in the farthest corners of the world after a very long time. Eliphaz said ילד אישה, born of a woman, by a common periphrasis, meaning anyone born of a woman, perhaps, but not without the will of a man, since a woman, not a man, bears; and by a closer figure man is born of a woman, not of a man. Finally, the Evangelist in Matt. I.19 called Joseph Mary's ἀνήρ, husband, but did not say συνελθεῖν, but betrothed, and of Mary, μνηστευθεῖσα, betrothed to him, in v. 18.

units.la: de Maria μνηστευθεισα desponsata ei v.18. dicitur.
units.tr: Of Mary it is said that she was betrothed [μνηστευθεῖσα] to him, v. 18.

units.la: XXIV. Virgo cum fuerit Maria, & Virgo incognita cum parere Jesum debuerit, nihil in eo negotio operae voluntati viri fuit.
units.tr: XXIV. Since Mary was a virgin, and a virgin unknown to man when she was to bear Jesus, the will of a husband had no part in that affair.

units.la: Ideo Angelus Gabriel mysterium, quo Virgo, quae virum non cognovit, paritura fit, Mariae fiscitanti sic explicat: Πνευμα αγιον επελευσεται επι σε, και δυναμις υψιστου επισκιασει σοι. Διο και το γεννωμενον αγιον, κληθησεται υιος Θεου. Spiritus S. veniet super te, & Virtus Altissimi inumbrabit te. Propterea etiam quod ex te nascitur sanctum, vocabitur Filius Dei, Luc.I.35. Praedictioni eventus respondit. Nam Maria ... inventa est in utero ferre ex Spiritu S. Matth.I.18. Et Josepho, metuenti ... assumere Mariam gravidam, Angelus dixit: Ne metue assumere Mariam uxorem tuam. Nam quod in ea genitum est ex Spiritu S. est, ib. v.20. Ubi Spiritus nomine Veteres, Justinus Apol.2. Tertullianus contr.Jud. cap.13. & adv. Prax. cap.26. Ambrosius ad Rom. I.4. Gregorius Nyssenus in diem Nat. Christi, Filium Dei, ceu carnis suae λατομον lapicidam, uti Gregorius Nyss. appellat, intelligunt. Rectius alii Spiritum Patris intelligunt.
units.tr: Therefore the angel Gabriel explains the mystery, by which the virgin who has not known a man is to conceive, to Mary when she asks how this can be: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore also the holy thing that is born shall be called the Son of God [Πνευμα αγιον επελευσεται επι σε, και δυναμις υψιστου επισκιασει σοι. Διο και το γεννωμενον αγιον, κληθησεται υιος Θεου]," Luke 1:35. He answers her with the event foretold. For Mary is found to be with child by the Holy Spirit, Matt. 1:18. And when Joseph was fearful to take Mary as his wife while she was pregnant, the angel said: "Do not fear to take Mary your wife. For what has been begotten in her is of the Holy Spirit," ib. v. 20. Here the Fathers understand by "Spirit" the Son of God, as the stonecutter [λατομον] of his own flesh, as Gregory of Nyssa calls him: Justin, Apol. 2; Tertullian, against the Jews, ch. 13, and against Praxeas, ch. 26; Ambrose on Romans 1:4; Gregory of Nyssa in his sermon on the Nativity of Christ. More correctly, others understand the Spirit of the Father.

units.la: Licet enim & Patri & Filio Spiritus, seu Deitas spiritualis tribuatur; & Filius etiam domicilii sui sacratissimi architectum gesserit, tamen in S. Scriptura Spiritus S. nomine fere Patris & Filii Spiritus, seu tertia S.S. Trinitatis persona venit. Neque tamen a διαταξεως hac peculiarem operationem etiam Patris & Filii excludi, sequentia illa; Et Virtus Altissimi (omnibus personis communis) inumbrabit te; arguunt. Nam & Deus Pater aptavit Filio corpus, Hebr.X.5. eumque misit in similitudine carnis peccati, Rom.VIII.3. & ipse quoque Filius assumpsit μορφην δουλου formam servi, Phil.II.7. sibique בנה את היכל aedificavit Templum, Zach. VI.13. Ad omnes igitur personas, quamvis distincta ratione, pertinet promissio: Quia ecce lapis ille, quem dedi coram Jehova, super quem unum erunt septem oculi; en ego ... coelabo coelaturam ejus, dixit Jehova exercituum, auferamque iniquitatem ipsius terrae in die uno, ibid. III.9. Haud inconcinne Scholastici similitudine trium puellarum, uni ex numero suo vestem parantium, induentium, & coronam imponentium rem explicant. Ante illos S. Augustinus Serm.3.de Temp. In cithara, inquit, tria sunt, ars, manus, chorda; & tamen unus sonus auditur: Ars dictat; manus tangit, chorda resonat. tria pariter operantur; sed sola chorda personat, quod audiatur; nec ars, nec manus sonum reddunt, sed ea cum chorda pariter operantur. Sonum sola chorda excutit. Carnem solus Christus excepit: Operatio in tribus constat. Sed quomodo ad solam chordam pertinet soni redditio: sic pertinet ad Christum solum carnis susceptio.
units.tr: For although the Spirit, or spiritual Deity, is ascribed both to the Father and to the Son, and although the Son too was the architect of his own most holy dwelling, nevertheless in Holy Scripture the name Holy Spirit usually stands for the Spirit of the Father and the Son, that is, for the third person of the Holy Trinity. Nor does this arrangement exclude a special operation of the Father and the Son as well, which is shown by the following words: And the power of the Most High (common to all persons) will overshadow you. For God the Father also prepared a body for the Son, Heb. 10.5, and sent him in the likeness of sinful flesh, Rom. 8.3; and the Son himself took the form of a servant [μορφὴν δούλου], Phil. 2.7, and built the temple [בנה את היכל], Zech. 6.13. The promise therefore applies to all the persons, though in distinct respects: For behold the stone that I have laid before Joshua; upon one stone shall be seven eyes; behold, I will engrave its inscription, says the LORD of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day, ibid. 3.9. The Scholastics explain the matter well enough by the likeness of three maidens, one of whom prepares a garment, another puts it on, and a third places a crown upon it. Before them St. Augustine, in Sermon 3 on the Time, says: "In a lyre there are three things: the art, the hand, and the string, and yet only one sound is heard. The art directs, the hand touches, the string resounds. The three work together, but only the string sounds, so that it may be heard. Neither the art nor the hand produces the sound, but they work together with the string. The string alone sends out the sound. Christ alone took on the flesh. The operation consists of three, but just as the producing of sound belongs to the string alone, so the taking up of the flesh belongs to Christ alone."

units.la: XXV. Spiritui S. επιλεσις superventio super B.Virginem: Virtuti Altissimi το επισκιασθεν inumbratio ejusdem ab Angelo tribuitur.
units.tr: XXV. The coming upon of the Holy Spirit upon the Blessed Virgin (ἐπέλευσις, superventio), and the overshadowing of her by the Virtue of the Most High (τὸ ἐπισκιασθέν, inumbratio), are both ascribed to the same work by the angel.

units.la: Spiritus S. inquit, superveniet super te, hoc est, veniet ex Coelo; Veniet super te; Veniet magno cum molimine; in te efficaciter operabitur, & id denique sataget, ut quod ex te nascetur, purum & omnibus modis sanctum, Filius Dei nuncupari tupari possit. Virtuti vero Altissimi τὸ ἐπονιάζειν inumbratio tributa, viris doctis vocem שכך, quam ἐπονιάζειν Graeci reddunt, repraesentare videtur. Ita David: Ala sua כאברתו יסך לך ἐπονιάσει σι (ita Graeci) obumbrabit te, Psalm. XC I.4. & CXL.8. Jehova, Domine, robur salutis meae; סכתה ἐπονιασεως obumbrasti super caput meum. Eandem vocem שכך quae tuendi, tegendi, obtegendi (uti etiam umbra tuetur, tegit) notionem habet, David de ea operatione Dei, qua Deus efficit, ut foetus in utero exsistat, & secure lateat, usurpat Psalm. CXXXIX. 13. תסכני בבטן אמי occultasti & velut sub umbra protexisti me in utero matris meae; hoc est, Fecisti me existere in latebris uteri: Texisti me & fecisti in utero, ut nascerer, qui natus sum: Formationis meae architectus &c. Plane sicut in Genesi rerum omnium Spiritus Dei dicitur רחפת incubasse aquis, sicut gallina ovis incubat, eadem fovet, protegit & enitITur, Genes.I.2. Unde etiam Syrus Interpres τὸ ἐπονιάζειν reddit נצ protegendi notione. Sic ergo Virtus Altissimi B. Virginem inumbravit, quia omnipotente & efficacissima operatione ejus effectum est, ut in utero ejus foetus, ex substantia B. Virginis decerptus, existeret, in eodem foveretur, ad maturitatem provueheretur, velut umbra ejus adversus injurias quasvis imminentes protegeretur, & ipsa denique B. Mariae Virginitas detrimentum prorsus nullum pateretur. Etiam ad naturae operationem allusum videri potest. Nam quae loca nimio calori expositia sunt, arida, sterilia sunt. Umbra vero humiditatem generat, conservat; & temperata humiditas cuncta profert. Quo pacto verbum ἐπονιάζειν obumbrandi etiam foecundandi notionem habet. Possunt enim ex phrases explicari in omni significandi potestate, quam secundum Scripturas habent. Tametsi vero reliqui etiam homines operatione efficacissima Spiritus S.& Virtute Altissimi inumbrante concipiuntur, juxta illud Psaltis: Tu occultaveras me in utero matris mee. Confitebor Tibi כי נוראות נפליתי משיך quia tremendis modis separatus sum. Mirabilia sunt Opera tua. Factus sum in occulto רקמתי Varie contextus sum (phrygionici operis ad instar) in imis terrae, Psalm.CXXXIX.13. tamen non idem in Christo & aliis hominibus concipiendi modus est. Hi enim simul Spiritus S. & Altissimi virtute ac potentia, simul e semine viri concipiuntur: Christus vero sine semine viri. Illi ex parte in Spiritu Sathanae, quia quotquot ex Adamo descendunt, maledictioni obnoxii & irae filii sunt: Hic ex Spiritu S. in solidum. Ideo accedente licet ad reliquorum hominum conceptionem Virtute Dei, ipsi tamen carnales relinquuntur, quia organon, Vir ex Adamo progenitus, quo homo concipitur, naturā suā carnale est. At in Christi conceptione organon totum sanctum & coeleste est, nimirum Spiritus sanctificans. Unde quod ex Maria natum est, sicut sanctum & coeleste est, ita verè Filius Dei est & vocatur.
units.tr: "The Holy Spirit," he says, "will come upon you, that is, will come from heaven. He will come upon you: he will come with great effort, he will work efficaciously in you, and finally he will take care that what is born of you, pure and holy in every way, may be called the Son of God." The overshadowing ascribed to the Virtue of the Most High (τὸ ἐπισκιάζειν, inumbratio) seems to represent, for learned men, the Hebrew word שכך, which the Greeks render ἐπισκιάζειν. So David: "His wing" [כאברתו] "will cover [יסך] you" (ἐπισκιάσει σοι, as the Greeks have it), "will overshadow you," Ps. 91.4, and 140.8: "LORD, the Lord, the strength of my salvation, you have covered [סככת] my head in the day of battle" (ἐπισκιάσεως). David uses the same verb שכך, which has the sense of protecting, sheltering and covering (as shade also protects and covers), of that operation of God by which he brings about that the embryo exists in the womb and lies hidden securely, in Ps. 139.13: You have hidden me [תסכני] in the womb of my mother, and as if under a shadow you have sheltered me in the womb of my mother; that is, you made me exist in the hiding-place of the womb; you covered me and formed me in the womb, so that I might be born; you were the architect of my formation, etc. In the same way, in Genesis, the Spirit of God is said to be brooding [רחפת] over the waters, as a hen broods over an egg, warming it, protecting it, and striving over it, Gen. 1.2. Hence also the Syriac interpreter renders τὸ ἐπισκιάζειν with the sense of protecting [נצ]. So then the Virtue of the Most High overshadowed the Blessed Virgin, because by his almighty and most efficacious operation it came about that the embryo, taken from the substance of the Blessed Virgin, came into being in her womb, was nourished there, and was brought to maturity, sheltered by her as by a shadow against any injuries that threatened, and finally because the virginity of the Blessed Mary itself suffered no harm at all. The phrase may also be taken as alluding to the operation of nature: places exposed to excessive heat are dry and barren, but shade produces and preserves moisture, and moderate moisture brings forth everything. In this way the verb ἐπισκιάζειν, to overshadow, also carries the sense of making fruitful. These phrases can be explained in the full range of meaning that they have according to the Scriptures. Yet although other human beings too are conceived by the most efficacious operation of the Holy Spirit and the overshadowing power of the Most High, according to that saying of the Psalmist: You had hidden me in the womb of my mother. I will praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made [כי נוראות נפליתי], wonderful are your works; I was made in secret [רקמתי], intricately wrought (like embroidery) in the depths of the earth, Ps. 139.13 (the mode of conception is still not the same in Christ as in other men). For these are conceived at once by the Holy Spirit and the Virtue and power of the Most High, and at the same time from the seed of a man; but Christ was conceived without the seed of a man. The others are conceived partly in the spirit of Satan, since all who descend from Adam are liable to the curse and are children of wrath; but Christ was conceived wholly of the Holy Spirit. So although the conception of other men also takes place by the Virtue of God, they are nevertheless left carnal, because the instrument by which a man is conceived, the man descended from Adam, is by its own nature carnal. But in the conception of Christ the whole instrument is holy and heavenly, namely the sanctifying Spirit. Hence what was born of Mary is as holy and heavenly as it is, and so truly is and is called the Son of God.

units.la: XXVI. Conceptionis Christi ex Spiritu S. tres actus sunt: Formatio naturae humanae, ejusdem sanctificatio, & in personam Filii Dei assumptio.
units.tr: XXVI. The conception of Christ from the Holy Spirit has three acts: the formation of human nature, its sanctification, and its assumption into the person of the Son of God.

units.la: Formatio Naturae humanae est, qua illa virtute Spiritus S. absque interventu viri, ex sanguine & substantia Virginis Mariae formata est,
units.tr: The formation of human nature is the act by which, through the power of the Holy Spirit and without the intervention of a man, it was formed from the blood and substance of the Virgin Mary.

units.la: Qua in διακόνου Spiritus S. non supplevit vicem Patris, id agendo, quod in generatione naturali pater agere solet; hoc est, Mariam foecundando, substantiam quandam creando, eamque in uterum B. Virginis immittendo, ita ut ex massa illa creata & semine Virginis Christus conceptus genitusque dicatur. qui foedus & blasphemus Socinianorum & Fanaticorum error est, eo etiam impietatis procedentium, ut Spiritum S. parentem Christi, & propter ejusmodi conceptionem Christum Filium Dei esse & vocari blasphement. Atqui Christus secundum naturam humanam ἀπάτωρ Patris expers est, Hebr.VII.3. & Josephus ejus pater vομιζόμενος putatitius fuit, Luc.III.23. Genuinus vero Christi pater non alius, quam secundum Divinitatem ejus est, Pater videlicet ille, à quo est πᾶσα πατριὰ ἐν οὐρανοῖς καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς omnis paternitas in Coelo & in terra. Ephes.III.15. à quo etiam ὑπόστασις subsistentia Spiritus S. est ἄλλος alius, Joh.XIV.16. & qui ab ipso Filio mittitur, procedit, donatur, ibid.XV.26. Patrem vero à Filio mitti, procedere, donari quam insolens est? Praeterea Scriptura omnem carnem Christi, quam is in persona sua habet, non aliunde quam à B. Virgine derivat. Neque aliud uspiam Semen, quam Mulieris Genes.III.15. Abrahami, ibid.XXII.17.18. Jesse, Esaj.XI.1. Davidis, 2. Sam.VII.12. Psal.CXXXII. promittitur. Estque incarnatio communicatio carnis & sanguinis nostri, qua Christus factus est Filius hominis & frater noster, per omnia nobis similis, excepto peccato, Hebr.II.14--17. IV.15. Cum igitur nos ex mixto Coelesti & Humano semine nec concipiamur, nec nascamur, consequens est, nec Christum quo ad naturam humanam per omnia, excepto peccato, nobis similem, ex tali mixto semine progenitum esse. Denique neque actus Spiritus S. supervenientis & inumbrantis in Scriptura uspiam nisi de formatione naturae humanae ex Beata Virgine, ejusdem naturae sanctificatione, & cum Divina unione; nuspiam vero de creatione substantiae; ex qua aequè ac ex Maria humana Christi natura formata sit, declaratur.
units.tr: In this act the Holy Spirit did not take the place of a father, acting as a father normally does in natural generation: that is, fertilising Mary, creating some substance and introducing it into the womb of the Blessed Virgin, so that Christ is said to have been conceived and born from that created mass and the seed of the Virgin. This is the foul and blasphemous error of the Socinians and Fanatics, who go so far in impiety as to blaspheme that the Holy Spirit is the parent of Christ, and that Christ is and is called the Son of God on account of such a conception. Yet Christ according to human nature is without a father [ἀπάτωρ], Heb. 7:3, and Joseph, his supposed father [νομιζόμενος], was merely putative, Luke 3:23. The genuine Father of Christ is none other than the one according to his divinity, namely that Father from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, Eph. 3:15; from whom also the Holy Spirit has his subsistence as another [ἄλλος], John 14:16; and who is sent by the Son himself, proceeds, and is given, ibid. 15:26. But how unseemly it is to say that the Father is sent by the Son, proceeds, and is given! Moreover, Scripture derives all the flesh that Christ has in his person from nothing other than the Blessed Virgin. Nowhere is any other seed promised than the seed of the woman, Gen. 3:15; of Abraham, ibid. 22:17-18; of Jesse, Isa. 11:1; of David, 2 Sam. 7:12, Ps. 132. And the incarnation is the sharing of our flesh and blood, by which Christ became the Son of man and our brother, in all things like us, apart from sin, Heb. 2:14-17; 4:15. Since, therefore, we are neither conceived nor born from a mixed heavenly and human seed, it follows that Christ, as to his human nature, like us in all things apart from sin, was not born from such a mixed seed. Finally, nowhere in Scripture is the action of the Holy Spirit that came upon and overshadowed Mary declared to be anything other than the formation of human nature from the Blessed Virgin, the sanctification of that same nature, and its union with the divine; nowhere is it declared that a substance was created from which the human nature of Christ was formed just as much as from Mary.

units.la: XXVII. Frustra haeretici impudens commentum suum verbo ἐπονιάζειν inumbrandi, quasi talem materiae etiam virilis formationem ea voce pudice Scriptura denotaverit, incrustare satagunt.
units.tr: XXVII. In vain do the heretics labour to plaster their shameless invention onto the word overshadow [ἐπισκιάζειν], as if Scripture had chastely used that word to denote such a formation even of the male material.

units.la: Nam σπέλαιον illam scopus Angeli Mariae respondentis, partes responsi, & ejusdem Scripturae analogae declaratio abunde convincunt. Tota Spiritus S. operatio δημιουργικὴ, ἀγαθικὴ, πλεωνικὴ, non ἀσωμάτικὴ fuit. Rectè Justinus Apol.2. Τὸ πνεῦμα, inquit, ἐλθὸν ἐπὶ τὴν παρθένον, ἡ ἐπονιάσει σε Ὑψίστου σωσ-ρίας, ἀλλὰ Ὑψίστου δυνάμεως ἐγχωμένη χαρίσματι. Spiritus S. super virginem veniens, & eam inumbrans, non per concubitum, sed per potentiam eandem foecundavit. Neque errori favet, quod B. Virgo ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου ex Spiritu S. in utero ferre Matth.I.18. & quod in ea natum est, ex Spiritu S. esse ibid.v.20. testatur. Non enim, uti scite Basilius de Spiritu S. haereticos perstringit, ex aucupiis syllabarum haereses fabricare licet; inprimis cùm particula ἐκ non semper ὕλην materiam, sed non raro etiam pro ὑπὸ vel ὑπὲρ posita efficientem modo principalem, modo organicam nicam significet; & eadem latitudine, qua Hebraicum בן, cui ἐκ respondet, accipiatur. Ita enim etiam fideles ἐκ πνεύματος ex Spiritu & ἐκ Θεοῦ ex Deo generari Joh.III.5. 1.Joh.III.9. & infideles ἐκ πατρὸς ὁ διαβόλου ex Patre Diabolo esse Joh.VIII.44. Cain ἐκ πονηροῦ ex malo esse, 1.Joh.III.12. dicitur, ut innumera ejusmodi praeteream. Praeclarè Ambrosius de Spir. S.lib.II.5. Quod ex aliquo est, inquit, vel ex substantia ejus, vel ex potestate ejus est. Ex substantia; sicut Filius, qui ait: Ex ore Altissimi prodivi &c. Ex potestate autem, sicut illud est: Unus Deus Pater, ex quo omnia. Quomodo ergo in utero habuit Maria ex Spiritu S. Si quasi ex substantia, ergo Spiritus in carnem & ossa conversus fuit. Nam utique, si quasi ex operatione & potestate ejus Virgo concepit, quis neget Spiritum creatorem? Praeterea nec propter conceptionem Christi ex Spiritu S. idem Filius Dei fuit vel factus, sed κλητὸς vocatus, demonstratus est. Dixit enim Angelus: Spiritus S. superveniet super te, &c. Διὸ propterea quod ex te nascitur Sanctum, κληθήσεται vocabitur (non ἔσται erit, quia egressus ejus à diebus seculi fuerunt, Mich.V.2. & generatio ejus fuit initium viae Dei ante opera, seu molitiones Prov. VIII.22.) Filius Dei Luc.I.35. Nempe Spiritus S. ἐπελεύσεται superveniet, & Virtutis Altissimi ἐπισκιάσει obumbratio, ex qua Salvator conceptus est, certissimum τεκμήριον, argumentum & signum omni exceptione majus fuit, id quod ex Spiritu S. natum est, æternum Dei æterni Filium esse, quia hac ratione nemo alius nisi Messias, Immanuel (Esaj.VII.14.) nasci debuit, potuit.
units.tr: For the purpose of the Angel who answers Mary, the parts of his reply, and the analogous declaration of the same Scripture all clearly refute this. The whole operation of the Holy Spirit was creative, beneficent and powerful, not incorporeal. Justin rightly says in his Second Apology: The Spirit, coming upon the virgin and overshadowing her, impregnated her not through intercourse but through the same power. Nor does it favour the error that the Blessed Virgin is said to bear of the Holy Spirit [ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου] in the womb, Matt. 1:18, and that what was born in her is of the Holy Spirit, ibid. v. 20. For, as Basil wisely rebukes the heretics concerning the Holy Spirit, one may not manufacture heresies from quibbling over syllables; especially since the particle ek [ἐκ] does not always denote the material cause but is often put for hypo or hyper, and signifies now the principal, now the instrumental efficient cause; and it is taken with the same breadth as the Hebrew ben [בן], to which ek corresponds. Thus believers are said to be born of the Spirit [ἐκ πνεύματος] and of God [ἐκ Θεοῦ], John 3:5; 1 John 3:9, and unbelievers are said to be of their father the devil [ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς τοῦ διαβόλου], John 8:44, and Cain is said to be of the evil one [ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ], 1 John 3:12, not to mention countless similar instances. Ambrose splendidly says in On the Holy Spirit, Book 2: What is from something is either from its substance or from its power. From its substance, as the Son, who says: "I came forth from the mouth of the Most High," etc. From its power, as in: "One God the Father, from whom are all things."
