How then did Mary have in her womb of the Holy Spirit? If as from the substance, then the Spirit was turned into flesh and bones. But if the Virgin conceived as from his operation and power, who would deny that the Spirit is the Creator? Moreover, not even on account of the conception of Christ from the Holy Spirit was the same Son made or become the Son of God, but he was called and shown to be so. For the Angel said: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, etc. Therefore, because the holy one born of you shall be called [κληθήσεται] (not shall be, because his goings forth have been from the days of eternity, Mic. 5:2, and his generation was the beginning of the way of God before his works, or undertakings, Prov. 8:22), the Son of God, Luke 1:35. Indeed, the coming of the Holy Spirit upon her and the overshadowing of the power of the Most High, from which the Saviour was conceived, was a most certain token and sign, greater than any objection, that what was born of the Holy Spirit is the eternal Son of the eternal God, since in this way no one other than the Messiah, Immanuel (Isa. 7:14), ought to be born, or could be.

units.la: XXVIII. Formatio naturæ Christi humanæ Virtute Spiritus S. ex sanguine & substantia Virginis Mariæ facta est.
units.tr: XXVIII. The formation of Christ's human nature was accomplished by the power of the Holy Spirit from the blood and substance of the Virgin Mary.

units.la: Spiritus S. veniet super te, &c. Ideo τὸ ἐκ σὲ γεννώμενον ἅγιον, quod ex te (Maria) nascitur Sanctum, &c. Luc.I.35. Licèt enim verba illa ἐκ σὲ ex te in quindecim M.S. codicibus, quibus Stephanus usus est, & in nonnullis etiam exemplaribus Graecis & Latinis editis desint, ac proin etiam ab Erasmo obelo notata sint; eorum tamen γνησιότης suspecta esse non debet; cùm lectionem eam & Complutensis editio optima, Biblia Regia, & aliæ editiones habeant, & variæ lectiones à Valesio, Frakardo, aliis collectæ repræsentent; & Syrus, Arabs, Hieronymus, & Patres plerique Graeci & Latini retineant; inprimis Athanasius Epist. ad Epict. ubi eam adversus hæreticos urget, eò quòd Angelus non simpliciter dixerit, τὸ γεννώμενον ἐν σοι quod nascetur in te; sed τὸ γεννώμενον ἐκ σὲ quod nascetur ex te. Ad planiorem etiam sensum quàm maximè etiam apposita, & reliquis Scripturis analoga est. Nam Christus γεννώμενος ἐκ γυναικὸς factus ex muliere Gal.IV.4. & זרע אשה Semen Mulieris, Gen.III.15. quod in beato utero suo Maria gestavit, Luc.XI.27. appellatur. Neque aliam ob causam vocatur בן אדם Filius hominis, Psalm.VIII.5. Matth. XVI.27. Joh.V.27, &c. Licèt enim vox Filii hominis de quovis vulgari homine passim usurpetur, & proprie non aliud significet, quàm hic homo, uti Hebraei dicunt הא בר נשא hic homo, pro ego; tamen Christus κατ' ἐξοχὴν & ἀνθρώπου, בן אדם, ὁ υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου, Filius hominis appellatur, ad designandum singulare aliquod in specie Filiorum hominum individuum, quomodo cùm omnes homines sed men mulieris ילידי אשה nati ex muliere, (Job, XV.14.) omnes Davidis posteri ejusdem filii fuerint; tamen Christus nomine Seminis Mulieris & Filii Davidis, (Matth.I.1, IX.27, XV.22, XX.30, XXI.9.) singulariter venit.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, etc. Therefore the holy thing born of you (Mary), that is, that which is born of you, is holy, etc. Luke 1:35 [τὸ ἐκ σὲ γεννώμενον ἅγιον]. For although the words ex σὲ [ἐκ σὲ, "of you"] are absent from fifteen manuscripts used by Stephanus, and from some printed Greek and Latin copies, and so were marked with an obelus by Erasmus, their genuineness should not be doubted. The excellent Complutensian edition, the Royal Bible and other editions have this reading, the various readings collected by Valesius, Frakardus and others attest to it, and the Syriac, the Arabic, Jerome, and most of the Greek and Latin Fathers retain it. Above all Athanasius, in his letter to Epictetus, where he presses it against the heretics, because the angel did not simply say τὸ γεννώμενον ἐν σοι [what will be born in you], but τὸ γεννώμενον ἐκ σὲ [what will be born of you]. It also fits the plainer sense very well and is consistent with the other Scriptures. For Christ, made of a woman [γεννώμενος ἐκ γυναικός], Gal. 4:4, and the seed of the woman [זרע אשה], Gen. 3:15, which Mary bore in her blessed womb, is called so in Luke 11:27. Nor is he called the Son of man [בן אדם], Ps. 8:5, Matt. 16:27, John 5:27, etc., for any other reason. For although the expression Son of man is commonly used of any ordinary man and properly means nothing more than this man, as the Hebrews say [הא בר נשא], this man, for I, yet Christ is called the Son of man par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχήν], [בן אדם, ὁ υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου], to designate a particular individual among the sons of men. Thus, although all men are born of woman [ילידי אשה], Job 15:14, and all the posterity of David were sons of the same stock, yet Christ came in the singular under the name Seed of the Woman and Son of David, Matt. 1:1, 9:27, 15:22, 20:30, 21:9.

units.la: Unde etiam Hebraei Dan.VII.13. voce בר נשא Filii hominis Messiam intelligunt. R. Solomon Jarchi ad eum locum diserte: הוא מלך המשיח Ipse est Rex Messias. Etiam R. Abenezra, qui in loco Danielis Filium hominis populum Israelis interpretatur, refert sententiam R. ישועה cui בר נשא est המשיח Messias. Rabbi Gaon verò, inter Rabbinos illustris cumprimis, non tantùm Danielis locum illum, sed similes etiam aliios de Messia interpretatur. Quamvis autem nomen illud de Christo acceptum sit ἀνεπιφθονον, & humilitati atque κενώσει Christi maximè conveniat, plus tamen significat, nempe illum ילד natum, de quo Esaj.IX.6. dicitur. Puer natus est nobis, בן Filius datus est nobis; & Germen Davidis justum Jerem.XXIII.5. XXXIII.15. sed ejusmodi tamen natum, Germen, quod simul sit גאל ἱμαλλόω, cognatus hominum ad vindicandum eos; denique eum, quem sub nomine Seminis Deus Patribus promisit, Gal.III.16.
units.tr: Hence the Hebrews also understand the words Son of man [בר נשא] in Dan. 7:13 to mean the Messiah. R. Solomon Jarchi, on that passage, says plainly: He himself is King Messiah [הוא מלך המשיח]. R. Abenezra too, who in Daniel's passage interprets Son of man as the people of Israel, reports the opinion of R. Jeshua, for whom בר נשא is the Messiah [המשיח]. Rabbi Gaon, a most distinguished man among the rabbis, interprets not only that passage of Daniel but other similar passages of the Messiah. Although that name, applied to Christ, is free from envy and especially suits his humility and self-emptying [κένωσις], it nevertheless signifies more, namely the child born [ילד], of whom Isa. 9:6 says: A child is born to us, [בן] a son is given to us; and the righteous Branch of David, Jer. 23:5, 33:15. But such a born one and Branch is at the same time a [גאל], that is, a kinsman who redeems men and avenges them; finally, he whom God promised to the Fathers under the name Seed, Gal. 3:16.

units.la: XXIX. Valentinianorum veterum castra ingressi recentiores fanatici Christum carnem ex substantia Virginis Mariæ decerptam habere, pernegant; concordia admodum discorde, minimè consentientes, unde, ubi, quando originem suam caro Christi acceperit. in eo tamen concordes, quòd Christus non sit verus Hominis vel Mariæ filius, nec Maria ejus mater. Cùmque appellatio illa Filii hominis, similésque apertæ nimis, & minimè δυσνόητοι sint, illi spirituale aliquod Semen, sive ex Patris substantia, sive ex verbo æterno, sive ex Spiritu S. decisum, foris in uterum B. Virginis per Spiritum S. & fidem ejusdem B. Virginis illatum, atque sic Mariam matrem Christi spiritualem per fidem finxerunt. eò torquentes verba Elizabethæ de Mariâ: Μακαρία ἡ πιστεύσασα Beata quæ credidit, Luc.I.45. Sed detorsionem illam refutavit ipse Christus, fidem à gestatione in utero secernens. Nam ad mulieris verba illa: Beatus est uterus, qui te gestavit, & ubera, quæ te lactarunt, respondit: Quin potiùs beati sunt audientes verbum Dei, & illud custodientes, Luc.XI.27.28. Aliud igitur est verbum Dei audire, eique credere: aliud in utero gestare; quæ duo perperam fanatici illi miscent. Neque carnem Christi extra uterum Mariæ formatam, foris operâ Spiritus S. utero ejus illatam & inditam esse, comprobant loca, quæ docent, Christum superne è Coelo venisse, Joh.III.31. VIII.23. Eph.IV.8.9.10. exivisse à Patre Joh.XVI.27.28. esse panem, qui de Coelo descendit, & Dominum è Coelo ibid.VI.33.&c.1.Cor.XV.47. &c. Haec enim & similia loca non originem coelestem carnis Christi, sed personæ Divinæ exinanitionem, qua suppressis Coelestis Majestatis radiis in terra in utero Virginis carnem assumpsit, arguunt. Christus inprimis dicens: Ego sum panis vitæ, qui è Coelo descendit. Si quis comederit ex hoc pane, vivet in æternum. Et panis quem ego dabo, caro mea est, quam ego dabo pro vita mundi, Joh.VI.51. non carnem ex Coelo descendisse, sed eum panem, qui ex Coelo descendens, ad vitam comedi debet, etiam carnem factum esse, & in eo etiam carnem esse, ita ut ad vitam
units.tr: XXIX. The recent fanatics who have entered the camp of the ancient Valentinians deny outright that Christ has flesh taken from the substance of the Virgin Mary. They are very much at odds among themselves and do not agree on whence, where and when Christ's flesh received its origin; yet they agree on this, that Christ is not the true son of man, nor is Mary his mother. Since that designation Son of man, and similar expressions, are too plain and not at all obscure, they have imagined a certain spiritual seed, either separated from the substance of the Father, or from the eternal Word, or from the Holy Spirit, introduced from outside into the womb of the Blessed Virgin through the Holy Spirit and her faith, and so they have made Mary a spiritual mother of Christ through faith. They twist to this end Elizabeth's words about Mary: Blessed is she who believed [Μακαρία ἡ πιστεύσασα], Luke 1:45. But Christ himself refuted that twisting, separating faith from bearing in the womb. For to the woman's words, Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you, he replied: Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it, Luke 11:27–28. It is one thing to hear the word of God and believe it; it is another to carry it in the womb; these two things those fanatics wrongly mix. Nor do the passages which teach that Christ came down from heaven above, John 3:31, 8:23, Eph. 4:8–10, went out from the Father, John 16:27–28, is the bread which came down from heaven, and the Lord from heaven, ibid. 6:33, etc., 1 Cor. 15:47, etc., prove that his flesh was formed outside the womb of Mary, brought in from outside by the work of the Holy Spirit and placed in her womb. For these and similar passages point not to a heavenly origin of Christ's flesh but to the self-emptying of the Divine Person, by which, with the rays of his heavenly majesty laid aside, he took on flesh on earth in the womb of the Virgin. Christ especially, saying: I am the bread of life which came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread he will live forever. And the bread which I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world, John 6:51, does not say that the flesh came down from heaven, but that the bread which descends from heaven and must be eaten for life has also become flesh, and that flesh is in it, so that for life

units.la: Christus ex substantia carnis & sanguinis Mariæ formatus, & ex ea, atque in ea genitus est. vitam spiritualem totus Christus, Deus in carne manifestatus, Deus & homo pro nobis moritur, comedi debeat. Dupliciter enim ibi Christus se considerandum proponit, ut vivit & venit de Cœlo; hoc est, ut est Filius Dei æternus; & ut est caro, fructus terræ, & moritur. Nam carnem dare pro mundi vita, mori est. Secundum carnem igitur fructus terræ, uteri matris est, non de Cœlo descendit. Antithesis vero illa in verbis S. Pauli 1.Cor.XV.47. Primus homo ex terra, Secundus homo Dominus ex Cœlo; non simpliciter Christum ex terra & χοϊκὸν pulvereum non esse; sed vel non tantum esse ex terra, sicut primus homo fuit; sed simul Dominum ex Cœlo; vel non sic ex terra, non sic pulvereum esse, ut in pulverem cæterorum hominum more, qui pulvis sunt, & in pulverem revertuntur, Genes. III.19. redigi debeat, adeóque se ipsum adversus pulverem, & ex morte, corruptione vindicare non poslit, arguit. Est enim in verbis illis crypsis quædam, qua reticetur, quod maximè tamen urgetur, nimirum τὸ ἀδὲνές illud (v.43.) Adami ex terra terreni, qui post peccatum & maledictionem in mundum ingressam reverti in terram, ex qua sumptus est, debuit; neque ipse à morte & corruptione se ipsum vindicare, & supra primam animalis vitæ caducæ tandemque dissolvendæ conditionem assurgere potuit: cùm secundus Adamus non sic è terra vel pulvereus, sed Κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ Dominus ex Cœlo, qui in terram descendit, & in carne, sed nunquam in pulverem redigenda, vel penitus corrumpenda, se manifestavit, possit etiam carni suæ supra terrenam ejus originem & vitam animalem præstare è Cœlis vitam immortalem. quod primus Adamus non potuit. Verba porrò Angeli ad Josephum τὸ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν, quod in ipsa genitum est, ex Spiritu S. est, Matth. I. 20. originem carnis Christi ex substantia Virginis non tollunt, cùm Luc.I.35. etiam ἐκ ex illa natus, & Gal.IV.4. ex muliere factus dicatur: & in hoc ipso loco Codices quidam, Beza notante, ἐκ legant. Quin potius eam non obscurè confirmant, quia quod in Maria genitum est, extra eam genitum non est; & non aliunde, quàm ex ejus substantia genitum est, quia alibi fructus uteri ejus, & Filius Abrahami, Davidis, Mariæ appellatur. Quòd verò in universum omne Semen Mulierum hostes humanæ originis Christi negant, & ἀφιλόσοφον est, Medicorum scitis repugnans, & Scripturæ contrariatur, in qua & mulier vocatur זרע semen faciens, Levit.XII.2. coll. cum Genes.I.11.12. & Sara Divina benedictione fœcundata δύναμιν εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος virtutem ad ejaculationem seminis in locum suum accepisse Hebr.XI.11. dicitur.
units.tr: Christ was formed from the substance of the flesh and blood of Mary, and was begotten from her and in her. The whole Christ, God manifested in the flesh, God and man, dies for us, so that for life he must be eaten. For there Christ presents himself to be considered in two ways: as he lives and came down from heaven, that is, as the eternal Son of God; and as flesh, the fruit of the earth, who dies. For to give flesh for the life of the world is to die. Therefore, according to the flesh, he is the fruit of the earth, of his mother's womb, and did not come down from heaven. That antithesis in the words of St. Paul, 1 Cor. 15:47, The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven, does not simply deny that Christ is of the earth and earthy [χοϊκός, dusty]; rather it shows either that he is not only of the earth, as the first man was, but at the same time the Lord from heaven; or that he is not so of the earth, not so dusty, as to be reduced to dust in the manner of other men, who are dust and return to dust, Gen. 3:19, and so he could not defend himself against dust and corruption by death. For in those words there is a certain hidden meaning, which is passed over in silence yet is strongly implied: that the first Adam, earthy of the earth, after sin and the curse entered the world, had to return to the earth from which he was taken, nor could he rescue himself from death and corruption or rise above the first condition of a transient animal life, which must be dissolved; whereas the second Adam is not so of the earth or dusty, but the Lord from heaven [Κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ], who came down to earth and showed himself in flesh, yet flesh never to be reduced to dust or wholly corrupted, and so he is able to grant to his flesh, beyond its earthly origin and animal life, an immortal life from heaven, which the first Adam could not do. Moreover, the words of the angel to Joseph, what is begotten in her is of the Holy Spirit, Matt. 1:20, do not remove the origin of Christ's flesh from the substance of the Virgin, since in Luke 1:35 he is also said to be born of her [ἐκ], and in Gal. 4:4 made of a woman; and in this very passage some codices, as Beza notes, read ἐκ. Rather, they confirm it clearly, because what was begotten in Mary was not begotten outside her, and was begotten from nothing other than her substance, since elsewhere he is called the fruit of her womb and the Son of Abraham, of David, of Mary. But that all the seed of women universally is denied in the case of Christ's human origin is unphilosophical, contrary to the findings of physicians, and opposed to Scripture, in which even a woman is called seed-producing [זרע], Lev. 12:2, compared with Gen. 1:11–12, and Sarah, made fruitful by divine blessing, is said to have received power for the conception of seed [δύναμιν εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος], Heb. 11:11.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Originem verè humanam carnis Christi ejusdem Genealogia ab Abrahamo ad Josephum, virum Mariæ Matth.I.1--17. & à Josepho, cujus Filius Jesus ἐνομίζετο putabatur, ad Adamum usque Luc.III.23. f. pertexta comprobat. Nam quòd non generationis carnalis, sed regenerationis causa Genealogiam Christi ex Patribus Evangelistas arcessivisse, Fanatici regerunt, nulla ratione nititur. Imò Lucas patres omnes, & ex illis Christum censet in Adamo primo, ut capite & stirpe, cùm in causa regenerationis omnes in Christo, ut capite & stirpe illius συγγενὴς seu cognationis, quæ in Cœlis & in terra nominatur, Ephes.III.15. censeri debuerint. Ac licèt Matthæus initium genealogiæ Christi ab Abrahamo, credentium patre texuerit, non tamen id regenerationis causa factum est; quia in filiis Abrahæ, patribus Christi, ibi etiam Reges impii, Roboam, Achaz, Ammon &c. recensentur. Sed & diserte Scriptura Christum ex patribus, non secundum regenerationem, sed τὸ κατὰ σάρκα secundum carnem Act.II.30. Rom.I.3. IX.5. progenitum affirmat. Neque causa regenerationis, sed generationis factum est, quòd singulariter ex una Judæ, non ex aliis tribubus Israelis natus est, Hebr. VII.14. Neque prætereundum illud est, quòd Judæi infideles, à gratia & Christo rejecti, tamen in causa generationis rami ἐξ φύσιν naturales; at gentes per fidem jam Christo insitæ παρὰ φύσιν præter naturam Rom. XI.24. dicuntur.
units.tr: The genealogy of Christ's flesh, traced from Abraham through Joseph, the husband of Mary (Matth. 1.1–17), and from Joseph, who was supposed to be the son of Jesus [ἐνομίζετο], back to Adam (Luke 3.23 ff.), proves that his human origin was real. The Fanatics claim that the Evangelists traced Christ's descent from the Fathers for the sake of regeneration, not of natural generation, but this has no basis at all. Indeed, Luke counts all the fathers, and Christ among them, back to the first Adam as their head and stock, whereas in the cause of regeneration all believers ought to be reckoned in Christ as their head and stock, that is, as kinsfolk [συγγενὴς], a family named in heaven and on earth (Eph. 3.15). And although Matthew began the genealogy of Christ with Abraham, the father of believers, he did not do so for the sake of regeneration, since among the sons of Abraham, the fathers of Christ, he also lists wicked kings such as Rehoboam, Ahaz, Amon and others. Scripture also states plainly that Christ was descended from the fathers not according to regeneration but according to the flesh [τὸ κατὰ σάρκα] (Acts 2.30; Rom. 1.3; 9.5). Nor was it for the sake of regeneration but of generation that he was born of one tribe, Judah, and not of the other tribes of Israel (Heb. 7.14). Nor should we pass over the fact that the unbelieving Jews, rejected by grace and by Christ, are nonetheless called natural branches [ἐξ φύσεως] in the matter of generation, while the Gentiles, now grafted into Christ by faith, are said to be grafted contrary to nature [παρὰ φύσιν] (Rom. 11.24).

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Vanum porrò & illud est, quòd non Christi, vel Mariæ genealogiam texi, adeóque carnalem originem non Christi, sed Josephi, cujus Christus naturalis filius non fuit, ad patres referri iidem, Judæorum etiam crimine abrepti, objectant. Nam Lucas saltem Mariæ adeóque etiam Filii ejus genealogiam texit, & originem carnalem ad Adamum usque produxit. quod duplici indicio liquet. Prius præbet interjecta parenthesis illa, qua Lucas Josephum putativum, non verum Christi parentem fuisse innuit, his verbis constans: (ὡς ἐνομίζετο υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ ut existimabatur, seu, opinione Vulgi filius Josephi) revera autem, quod parenthesis illa subinnuit, ὢ ΗΛΙ filius, seu nepos ex filia Maria Heli, patre Mariæ, Luc.III.23. Posterius suppeditat deductio Genealogiæ usquè ad primum hominem Adamum, qua opus fuit, ut Christus illud primæ mulieri promissum Semen verum esse demonstretur. Ac licèt apud Matthæum genealogia naturaliter ad Josephum, non ad Mariam descendat; tangit tamen etiam Mariæ & Christi per Mariam cum ipso Josepho cognationem secundum carnem, non in solo Davide, sed etiam in Zorobabele & Salathiele Matth.I.12.coll.cum Luc.III.27.
units.tr: Equally empty is the objection, raised by the same men and by the Jews in their wickedness, that the genealogy traced is not that of Christ or of Mary, and that his carnal origin is therefore referred to the fathers through Joseph, of whom Christ was not the natural son. For Luke at least traces the genealogy of Mary, and therefore of her Son, and brings his carnal origin up to Adam. This is clear from two indications. The first is the parenthesis Luke inserts, implying that Joseph was the reputed, not the true, parent of Christ, in these words: (ὡς ἐνομίζετο υἱὸς Ἰωσήφ, as was supposed, that is, by common opinion the son of Joseph), while in fact, as the parenthesis hints, he was the son, or grandson through his daughter Mary, of Heli, Mary's father (Luke 3.23). The second is the tracing of the line back to the first man Adam, which was needed to show that Christ is the true Seed of the Woman promised to the first woman. And although in Matthew the genealogy naturally descends to Joseph and not to Mary, it nonetheless touches on the carnal kinship of Mary and Christ through Mary with Joseph himself, not only in David but also in Zerubbabel and Salathiel (Matth. 1.12, compared with Luke 3.27).

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Conciliationis porrò genealogiæ Christi apud Matthæum & Lucam variantis admodum rationem geminam pariter eruditi perhibent. Prior eorum est, qui S. Matthæum genealogiam Christi legalem, & Josephi naturalem ab Abrahamo ad Josephum descendentem, adeóque Josepho propriam: Lucam verò genealogiam Christi naturalem, à Josepho putativo patre, vel potiùs Heli, ejus socero, Mariæ verò parente, & Christi avo ad Adamum usque ascendentem, pertexere statuunt. Genealogiam verò Josephi naturalem, & Christi legalem à Matthæo contextam, genesin Christi ex Patribus, Abrahamo inprimis; satis probate iidem existimant, quia Josephus & Maria consanguinei fuerint, ut alterutrius genealogia contexta utriusque genealogiam contexi, credendum fuerit. Ideo enim Josephum & Mariam unâ censeri Bethlehemi, urbe Davidis, voluisse putant, quia utriusque eadem familia & cognatio fuerit, & Maria ceu Virgo ἐπίκληρος, fratribus destituta, juxta legem Num. XXXVI.7.8. &c. Josepho, ceu proximo cognato nupserit, Rationem, ob quam sic dedita
units.tr: Learned writers offer two main ways of reconciling the very different genealogies of Christ in Matthew and Luke. The first group holds that Matthew sets out Christ's legal genealogy, descending from Abraham to Joseph, which is Joseph's own by natural descent, while Luke sets out Christ's natural genealogy, ascending to Adam, from Joseph, who was his supposed father, or rather from Heli, Joseph's father-in-law, who was Mary's father and Christ's grandfather. They also think that the genealogy of Joseph's natural descent, and the legal genealogy of Christ, traced by Matthew from the fathers, above all Abraham, is well enough established, because Joseph and Mary were blood relatives, so that once the genealogy of one is set out, the genealogy of the other must be taken to be set out too. They think that Joseph and Mary are counted together at Bethlehem, the city of David, because both belonged to the same family and kindred, and that Mary, as an heiress (ἐπίκληρος) with no brothers, married Joseph, her nearest kinsman, in accordance with the law of Num. 36:7-8 etc. As for the reason why the evangelists deliberately chose to vary their accounts,

units.la: opera Evangelistæ variare voluerint,hanc iidem reddunt, quòd Matthæus Evangelium Hebraicè scripserit Hebræis, quibus de cognatione Josephi & Mariæ, & necessitate invicem nubendi juxta legem Num.XXXVI.7. &c. nec non de genealogia ex patre,non matre, juxta vulgatum Canonem: משפחת אם אין קריה משפחה Familia materna non vocanda est familia (Juchas. sol. 55.) derivanda,satis constiterit: Lucas verò suum Græcè orbi universo, Græcis inprimis, quibus de cognatione ista non liqueret, exaraverit. Cùm tamen conciliationis hæc ratio, à Doctiss. Gerhardo Johanne Vossio Dissert. de Genealogia Christi fusiùs exposita, gravibus admodum difficultatibus,à Judæis inprimis,prematur, & ἀδηλα non pauca contineat; magis se nobis probat conciliatio posterior,ab Hugone Broughthono inventa, & ab eodem adversus Judæos solidè defensa; quòd Matthæus Regiam, Lucas Humanam & naturalem Christi originem panderint. Promissus enim Christus est, & ut Semen Mulieris, & ut Filius Davidis; hoc est, ut Homo & ut Rex. In conscribenda igitur ejus genealogia utriusque ratio haberi cùm debuerit, genealogiam ejus ut Hominis & Seminis Mulieris ab Heli,cujus filia Maria,nepos Jesus fuit ad Adamum usque assurgentem; Lucas: ut Regis genealogiam à Familia Davidis Regia ad Josephum usque, qui tutelaris Christi pater, & Mariæ vir fuit, descendentem, Matthæus persequitur. Matthæi scopum fuisse, Regni Israelis successionem hæreditariam ad Christum usque, Davidis Regnum modo administrandi spiritualí perficientem demonstrare, liquet tum ex titulo γενέσεως generationis Jesu Christi, filii Davidis, filii Abrahami, cui,ceu capiti gentis,facta est promissio(Matth.I.1.)tum ex progressu genealogiæ, veluti cùm, ubi ad Davidem perventum est, bis βασιλέως Regis nomen (v.6.) exprimitur; & v.12. Jechonias dicitur genuisse Salathielem post captivitatem Babylonicam, quasi diceretur, ei natalium jure successionem in Regnum Jechoniæ competiisse; cùm contra Lucas,qui Christi,ut hominis, ex Adamo propagationem tradere instituit,Salathielis proavos v. 27.31. non à Solomone,e cujus posteris fuit Jechonias,sed,quasi deflectens à Regia dignitate,à Nathane derivet: tum denique, quia per Mariæ connubium cum Josepho,& nativitatem Christi ex Maria,Josepho nupta,jus Reghi à Josepho ad Christum non tam generationis, quàm connubii illius vi pervenit. Lucæ verò institutum fuisse, Genealogiam Christi Filii hominis, è Davide,quà homine, non quà Rege, nati describere, tum terminatio genealogiæ ad Adamum generis humani stirpem usque: tum recensio proavorum non Josephi, sed Mariæ, adeóque Christi, juxta verba Lucæ: ὢν ὡς ἐνομίζετο υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ, ὢν Ἡλί existens, ut putabatur, filius Joseph, (revera autem,non putatus, filius) Heli, cap.III.23. ubi verba, ὡς ἐνομίζετο, de Josepho solo dicta solum illum parentem Christi νομιζόμενον, Heli verò avum, & proavos reliquos ipsius & Mariæ genitores & majores naturales recenseri testantur. Mariam verò nominari,& Jesum filium Mariæ enuntiari nihil attinebat,quia ex præcedentibus satis id constitit,nec Lucæ scopus fuit,fœminas, sed viros potiùs, quorum filius Christus fuit, & quorum
units.tr: they give this: Matthew wrote his Gospel in Hebrew for Hebrews, among whom the kinship of Joseph and Mary, the necessity of their marrying within the family under the law of Num. 36:7 etc., and the principle that genealogy is traced through the father and not the mother, according to the accepted rule, "The maternal family is not to be called a family" [משפחת אם אין קריה משפחה] (Juchas. sol. 55), were well known. Luke, however, wrote his in Greek for the whole world, and above all for Greeks, among whom this kinship was not clear. Yet since this method of reconciliation, set out at greater length by the most learned Gerhard Johann Vossius in his dissertation On the Genealogy of Christ, is weighed down by serious difficulties, especially from the Jews, and contains not a few obscure points, the later reconciliation, discovered by Hugh Broughton and solidly defended by him against the Jews, commends itself to us more: that Matthew sets out the royal, and Luke the human and natural, origin of Christ. For Christ was promised both as the Seed of the Woman and as the Son of David; that is, as Man and as King. In writing his genealogy, therefore, both aspects had to be considered. Luke traces his genealogy as Man and Seed of the Woman, ascending from Heli, whose daughter Mary was and whose grandson Jesus was, up to Adam. Matthew follows his genealogy as King, descending from the royal house of David to Joseph, who was Christ's foster father and Mary's husband. That Matthew's aim was to show the hereditary succession of the kingdom of Israel up to Christ, who would fulfil the kingdom of David in a spiritual way, is clear both from the title "genealogy" (γενέσεως) of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham, to whom as head of the nation the promise was made (Matt. 1:1), and from the course of the genealogy. For example, when it reaches David, the title "king" (βασιλέως) is used twice (v. 6). And in v. 12 Jechoniah is said to have begotten Salathiel after the Babylonian captivity, as if to say that by right of birth the succession to Jechoniah's kingdom passed to Salathiel. Luke, by contrast, who sets out to trace Christ's descent as man from Adam, derives the ancestors of Salathiel (vv. 27, 31) not from Solomon, from whose descendants Jechoniah came, but, as if turning aside from royal dignity, from Nathan. Finally, the right to the kingdom passed from Joseph to Christ not so much by generation as by the force of that marriage, since through Mary's marriage to Joseph, and the birth of Christ from Mary, who was Joseph's wife, it came by that union. Luke's intention was to describe the genealogy of Christ, the Son of Man, born of David as man and not as king. This is shown by the ending of the genealogy at Adam, the stock of the human race, and by the listing of the ancestors not of Joseph but of Mary, and so of Christ, according to Luke's words: ὢν ὡς ἐνομίζετο υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ, ὢν Ἡλί ["being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, who was of Heli"] (Luke 3:23). Here the words ὡς ἐνομίζετο, said of Joseph alone, testify that only Joseph was supposed (νομιζόμενον) to be Christ's parent, while Heli and the remaining ancestors were the natural begetters and forefathers of both Mary and Christ. That Mary is not named, and that Jesus is not called the son of Mary, was unnecessary, because this was sufficiently established by what went before. Nor was it Luke's purpose to list women, but rather the men of whom Christ was the son, and of whom

units.la: nulla hactenus facta mentio est,recensere. Sed de conciliatione Evangelistarum quicquid fiat, Christum genus suum ab Adamo per Davidem Regem duxisse, ἀνεξαγώνιστον est; neque de eo ei controversia mota est; vel id scripturi Evangelistæ fuissent, nisi res vulgò nota & omnibus comperta fuisset; ne mox falsi convincerentur, & Evangelium simul universum in suspicionem adducerent. In Thalmude ipso,tractatu Sanhedrim cap.4. editionis Venetæ קרוב למלכות propinquus regno, hoc est, Regiæ prosapiæ homo dicitur.
units.tr: no mention has been made so far. But whatever the case with the reconciliation of the Evangelists, that Christ traced his descent from Adam through King David is beyond dispute, and no controversy has been raised about it. The Evangelists would hardly have written it unless the matter were commonly known and recognised by everyone, lest they be soon convicted of falsehood and at the same time bring the whole Gospel into suspicion. In the Talmud itself, tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 4, of the Venetian edition, a man of royal lineage is called קרוב למלכות ["near to the kingdom"], that is, a kinsman of the royal house.

units.la: XXXIII. Formatio naturæ humanæ Christi in utero B. Virginis per Spiritum. S. in momento an successu temporis successerit, ambigitur.
units.tr: XXXIII. The formation of Christ's human nature in the womb of the Blessed Virgin by the Holy Spirit: whether it took place in an instant or over the course of time is disputed.

units.la: Scholastici & orthodoxi etiam Theologi nonnulli præparationem materiæ, quæ fuit sanguis Virginis: formationem corporis ex tali materia jam præparata, & perfectionem seu incrementum ejusdem distinguunt. Et præparationem quidem æquè ac perfectionem temporis tractu & successu factam nulli dissitentur,illam, quia sanguis in locum conceptionis non in instanti, sed per motum fluere debuit: hanc, quia B. Virgo fœtum novem menses in utero gestavit,ut cresceret & maturesceret. Sed formationem in momento factam pertendunt. Parum equidem ejus rei definitio ad summam fidei facit. Nihilominus & Scripturæ, & existimationi Christi magis convenit eorum sententia, qui formationem etiam successu temporis factam asserunt. Scriptura enim conceptionis,gestationis & nativitatis actus distinctè recenset, iisque tempus ordinarium deputat, Luc.I.38.56.57. II.6. Sicut igitur gestatio, ita etiam formatio successiva fuit. Tempus enim novimestris gestationis hunc potissimùm in finem Deus constituit,ut fœtus sensim coalescere,formari, animari, crescere facilius posset. Si etiam corpus in utero Virginis,& extra eum certis incrementi gradibus provectum & perfectum est, ibid. II. 6.40.52. quorsum fingamus diversum accidisse in formatione,aut ejusdem gradus aboleamus? Exinanitionis etiam status Christum nobis similem fecit in omnibus, ne infirmitatibus quidem, sed solo peccato excepto, Phil.II. 6.7. Hebr.II.14--17. Quid nì ergo etiam in ordine assumptionis carnis? Neque id repugnat vel Prophetiæ, quæ Jerem. XXXI. 22. prædixit, Fœminam circumdaturam גבר virum, non, ut illi colligunt,embryonem; quia גבר ibi simpliciter marem notat, nec à Propheta tempus conceptionis potiùs,quàm peractæ mense circiter nono formationis, indigetatur: vel miraculosæ conceptioni Christi, cujus ratio non in momentanea naturæ humanæ secundum omnes partes productione, sed in eo consistit; quòd virgo absque viro, peccatrix absque peccato,homo Deum concepit; vel operationi Spiritus S. utpote quæ etiam in operibus Naturæ & gratiæ ab imperfectioribus ad perfectiora procedere solet: vel Christi Majestati, utpote qui formam servi, aliàsque naturæ infirmitates assumpsit, & in ipsa morte corpus exanime sibi unitum retinuit: vel denique B.Virginis ὑπερ-ρόχῃ, utpote quæ novem etiam mensibus fœtum, ut ad justam quantitatem proveheretur, gestavit.
units.tr: Scholastic and some orthodox theologians distinguish three things: the preparation of the matter, which was the Virgin's blood; the formation of the body from that matter once prepared; and the perfecting or growth of the body. Nobody denies that the preparation and the perfecting took place over a period of time and in succession: the preparation, because the blood had to flow into the place of conception not instantly but by motion; the perfecting, because the Blessed Virgin carried the fetus in her womb for nine months so that it might grow and mature. But they maintain that the formation took place in a moment. The definition of this point contributes little to the substance of faith. Nevertheless, the view of those who assert that the formation also took place over time agrees better both with Scripture and with what is fitting for Christ. For Scripture distinctly recounts the acts of conception, gestation and birth, and assigns to them their ordinary time (Luke 1:38, 56, 57; 2:6). Just as the gestation was successive, so the formation was successive too. For God appointed the nine months of gestation chiefly for this purpose: that the fetus might gradually coalesce, be formed, be animated and grow more easily. If the body was also advanced and perfected through certain degrees of growth both in the Virgin's womb and outside it (Luke 2:6, 40, 52), why should we imagine that something different happened in the formation, or abolish its stages? The state of humiliation also made Christ like us in all things, not excepting even infirmities, but sin alone excepted (Phil. 2:6-7; Heb. 2:14-17). Why, then, should it not be so also in the order of the assumption of flesh? Nor does this conflict with the prophecy of Jeremiah 31:22, which foretold that a woman would encompass a גבר (man). They take this to mean an embryo, but גבר there simply denotes a male, and the prophet does not point to the time of conception rather than to the formation, which was completed about the ninth month. Nor does it conflict with the miraculous conception of Christ, whose nature does not consist in the momentary production of human nature in all its parts, but in this: that a virgin without a man, a sinner without sin, conceived a man who is God. Nor does it conflict with the operation of the Holy Spirit, which in the works of nature and of grace is wont to proceed from the less perfect to the more perfect. Nor with the majesty of Christ, who took on the form of a servant and the other infirmities of nature, and who in death itself kept his lifeless body united to himself. Nor, finally, with the excellence [ὑπεροχή] of the Blessed Virgin, who likewise carried the fetus for nine months until it was brought to its due size.

units.la: XXXIV. Formationis naturæ humanæ ejusdem Sanctificatio comes fuit, in eo consistens, quòd eadem Spiritus S. virtute natura humana Christi ab omni labe peccati originalis segregata & præservata fuit.
units.tr: XXXIV. Sanctification accompanied the formation of that same human nature. It consisted in this: that by the power of the same Holy Spirit the human nature of Christ was set apart from, and preserved from, every stain of original sin.

units.la: Spiritus S. veniet super te, &c. Διὸ καὶ τὸ γεννώμενον ἅγιον, κληθήσεται υἱὸς Θεοῦ. Ideo quod nascetur ex te, Sanctum, Filius Dei vocabitur, Luc. I. 35. Spiritus S. proin super B. Virginem venientis, & eandem inumbrantis operatio id effecit, ut quod ex B. Virgine nasceretur, ἅγιον Sanctum esset. Alias enim, quod ex carne nascitur, caro est, Joh. III. 6. & טהור מטמא purum ex impuro nemo homo dare potis est, Job. XIV. 4. Atqui Pontifex talis nos decuit, qui esset ὅσιος, ἄκακος, sanctus, expers mali, &c. Hebr. VII. 26 tentandus per omnia ad similitudinem, sed absque peccato, ibid. IV. 15. Agnus ἄμωμος καὶ ἄσπιλος inculpatus & incontaminatus 1. Pet. I. 19. in quo esset δόξα beneplacitum Patris, Matth. III. 17. cujus victima pro salute populi sufficeret. Modus sanctificationis haud æquè explicatu facilis est.
units.tr: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you," etc. "Therefore the holy one who is born of you will be called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35). So the operation of the Holy Spirit, coming upon the Blessed Virgin and overshadowing her, brought it about that what was born of the Blessed Virgin would be holy [ἅγιον]. For otherwise what is born of the flesh is flesh (John 3:6), and "who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? No one" (Job 14:4) [טהור מטמא]. Yet such a high priest became us: one who was holy [ὅσιος], innocent [ἄκακος], sacred, free from evil, and so on (Heb. 7:26); tempted in all things as we are, but without sin (Heb. 4:15). He is the lamb without blemish and without spot [ἄμωμος καὶ ἄσπιλος], unblemished and uncontaminated (1 Pet. 1:19), in whom was the good pleasure of the Father [εὐδοκία] (Matt. 3:17), and whose sacrifice would suffice for the salvation of the people. The mode of sanctification is not equally easy to explain.

units.la: Mittimus commenta temeraria quorundam, cujusmodi sunt tum illud Galatini, qui Arc. Cath. Verit. lib. VII. 3, ex Rabbenu Hakkados asserens, partem quandam carnis Adami à lapsu præservatam esse, eandem mirabili ratione ad Virginem usque Mariam propagatam, atque ex eadem naturam Christi humanam efformatam esse statuit: tum Pontificiorum, quorum alii, Dominicani, inveterato dissidio, Mariam originali peccato infectam quidem, at mox ab ejus tum reatu, tum macula purgatam & sanctificatam; alii Franciscani & Jesuitæ eandem ab omni peccato præservatam, prolem etiam sanctam generasse nugantur.
units.tr: We set aside the rash inventions of some, such as that of Galatinus, who in Arcana Catholicae Veritatis book 7, chapter 3, citing Rabbenu Hakkados, asserts that a certain part of Adam's flesh was preserved from the fall, was propagated by a wondrous means down to the Virgin Mary, and that from it the human nature of Christ was formed. We also set aside the trifling of the Papists. Some of them, the Dominicans, in a long-standing dispute hold that Mary was indeed infected with original sin but was soon cleansed and sanctified from both its guilt and its stain. Others, the Franciscans and Jesuits, babble that she was preserved from all sin and also bore a holy offspring.

units.la: Quasi Spiritus S. superventus, inumbratio & sanctificatio necessaria fuisset, si B. Maria Christum generans omnis & maculæ & reatus expers fuisset. Sicut enim Adamus integer, si perstitisset, prolem sanctam, sine speciali Spiritus S. sanctificatione genuisset; ita B. Virgo, siquidem & ipsa integra & labis expers fuisset, Spiritus S. superventu & inumbratione nulla indiguisset. Rectius modum illum explicant, qui sanctificationis carnis Christi causam proximam & remotam distinguunt.
units.tr: It is as if the coming of the Holy Spirit, the overshadowing and the sanctification would have been necessary if the Blessed Virgin, who bore Christ, had been free of every stain and every guilt! For just as Adam, had he persisted, would have begotten a holy offspring without a special sanctification by the Holy Spirit, so the Blessed Virgin, if she herself had been whole and free of defilement, would have needed no coming and overshadowing of the Holy Spirit. Those explain the matter more correctly who distinguish the proximate and the remote cause of the sanctification of Christ's flesh.

units.la: Proxima est Spiritus S. qui non tantum semen Mariæ fœcundavit, sed etiam ab omni labe, qua, siquidem ordinariæ generationis instrumentum esse debuisset, maculatum pariter fuisset, segregavit & præservavit, uti ex Luc. I. 35. & Matth. I. 20. ubi causæ & effectus nexus attendi debet colligitur. Nam ut purus Christus nasceretur, totius Virginis sanctificatione, & à labe omni præservatione opus non fuit; cùm separati seminis, ex quo Deus in secula benedictus nasci debuit, sanctificatio suffecerit. Alias statuendum esset, ad præservationem ipsius Virginis à peccato, ejus quoque parentes à peccato præservari debuisse; & sic in infinitum. Sive autem semen illud, ex quo corpus Christi formatum est, ut à peccatrice decisum, sic peccato, saltem quoad dispositionem, infectum, & à Spiritu S. ab omni labe repurgatum fuit, uti nonnulli sustinent: sive peccati & labis omnis expers, adeóque similis libri alicujus, quoad scripturam impii, parti marginali, virgini, puræ, cui nihil inscriptum est, & quidvis inscribi poterit, fuit; quæ aliorum sententia minoribus difficultatibus obnoxia (cùm purificatio labis sine Mediatore nulla sit, & sui ipsius Mediator Christus non fuerit) & Scripturæ, quæ Pontificem nostrum κεχωρισμένον ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν separatum à peccatoribus (sicut margo talis à scriptura impia libri separari, & meliori, utiliori, sanctiori libro componendo destinari potest) exhibet, Hebr. VII. 26. congruentior est; salva immaculata Christi conceptio est.
units.tr: The proximate cause is the Holy Spirit, who not only fertilized the seed of Mary but also set it apart and preserved it from every stain which, had it been the instrument of ordinary generation, would equally have been defiled. This is gathered from Luke 1:35 and Matt. 1:20, where the connection of cause and effect must be noted. For in order that Christ be born pure, there was no need for the sanctification of the whole Virgin and her preservation from all stain, since the sanctification of the separated seed, from which the God who is blessed forever was to be born, was sufficient. Otherwise it would have to be held that, for the Virgin's own preservation from sin, her parents too must have been preserved from sin, and so on to infinity. Whether that seed from which the body of Christ was formed was cut off from a sinful woman and so was infected with sin, at least in its disposition, and was cleansed from stain by the Holy Spirit, as some maintain; or whether it was free of sin and stain, and so like the margin of some book, impious in its writing, a pure part, blank, on which nothing is written and anything may be written, as the view of others holds, which is subject to fewer difficulties (since purification from stain is nothing without a Mediator, and Christ was not his own Mediator), and which agrees more with Scripture, presenting our High Priest as separated from sinners [κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν] (just as such a margin can be separated from the impious writing of a book and destined to be filled with a better, more useful and holier text) (Heb. 7:26): in either case the immaculate conception of Christ stands safe.

units.la: Nam & quod à labe repurgatum miraculosè est, & quod labis omnis expers est, æquè purum, sanctum, defecatum, integrum est, & τὸ ἅγιον Sanctum illud ad totum Christum hominem pertinet, adeóque creationem animæ sanctæ, cui corpus obsequens, quale inprimis illud est, quod non ex voluntate viri & mulieris concipitur, pariter sanctum est, involvit. Remota verò sanctificationis, seu immaculatæ conceptionis ejusdem causa est Non-imputatio peccati Adamici. Cùm enim Christus, Adami licèt filius, & in Adami creati lumbis existens, in eo tamen, quatenus peccante, non fuerit, quia non pars aliqua fœderis operum ab Adamo repræsentata fuit, adeóque nec peccante Adamo peccare & ipse potuit; sed novi fœderis gratiæ Mediator (qualis esse in Adamo, & cum eo fœdus operum cum Deo contrahens, & fœdus in Adamo & cum Adamo violans, esse non potuit) destinatus est; peccatum Adami ipsi imputari nullatenus potuit. Sicut in lumbis Abrahami à Melchisedeco decimati etiam Christus fuit, nec tamen in Abrahamo decimatus est: ita in lumbis Adami etiam peccantis fuit, nec tamen in Adamo peccavit. Christus certè Adamo, ejusque posteris opponitur, ut author justitiæ & vitæ, ab ipsis peccatum & mortem auferens, ut ex Rom. V. 12. &c. 1. Cor. XV. 22. liquet; neque etiam Adami hæres naturalis (quales soli in eo peccarunt) utpote non ex sanguinibus, nec ex voluntate viri, sed ex Spiritu S. genitus fuit, adeóque nec seminali ordinaria generatione, nec κατ' ὁμοιωσιν ex Adamo procesisset.
units.tr: For both what is cleansed from stain miraculously and what is free of all stain are equally pure, holy, refined and whole. That "holy" [τὸ ἅγιον] pertains to the whole man Christ, and so involves the creation of a holy soul, to which the body, obedient to it, is likewise holy, especially that which is conceived not of the will of man and woman. Yet the remote cause of the sanctification, or immaculate conception, is the non-imputation of Adam's sin. For Christ, although a son of Adam and existing in the loins of the Adam who was created, was nevertheless not in him as he sinned, because he was not any part of the covenant of works represented by Adam, and so he could not sin even when Adam sinned. He was destined to be the Mediator of the new covenant of grace, which could not be the case with one who was in Adam and contracted the covenant of works with God along with him, violating the covenant in Adam and with Adam. Therefore the sin of Adam could in no way be imputed to him. Just as Christ was in the loins of Abraham when he was tithed by Melchizedek, yet was not tithed in Abraham, so he was in the loins of Adam even as Adam sinned, yet did not sin in Adam. Christ is certainly set over against Adam and his posterity, as the author of righteousness and life who removes sin and death from them, as is clear from Rom. 5:12 and following and 1 Cor. 15:22. Nor is he a natural heir of Adam (such as alone sinned in him), since he was begotten not of bloods, nor of the will of man, but of the Holy Spirit. Therefore he did not proceed from Adam either by ordinary seminal generation or by likeness [κατ' ὁμοίωσιν].

units.la: XXXV. Formatæ & sanctificatæ Naturæ Christi humanæ corporeæ, creatio Divina spiritus ejusdem incorporei, seu animæ rationalis, intellectu & voluntate constantis, accessit.
units.tr: XXXV. To the formed and sanctified corporeal human nature of Christ was added the divine creation of the incorporeal spirit of the same, that is, the rational soul, consisting of intellect and will.

units.la: Nam animam, qualis hominum est, Christo Scriptura tribuit. Tradidit in mortem animam suam, Esaj. LIII. 12. Venit datur animam suam ἀντὶ λύτρου, Matth. XX. 28. Animam pono pro ovibus meis, Joh. X. 11. Quæ locutiones synecdochicæ locum habere, nisi Christus animæ compos esset, non possent. Etiam in manus Patris spiritum suum commendavit, Luc. XXIII. 46. & animâ suâ ad mortem usque tristatus Matth. XXVI. 38. dicitur. Sed & Voluntatem Christo Scriptura tribuit, Joh. IV. 34. V. 30. VI. 38. Matth. XXVI. 39. Voluntas autem Intellectum supponit. Eadem verò animæ Christi, quæ animarum reliquarum humanarum, origo est, ἀμέσως Divina & Cœlestis, quia nullus spiritus, nedum sanctissimus ille, nullâque labe pollutus spiritus Christi, generatur, omnis à Deo immediatè creatur. Cùm tamen hominum reliquorum spiritus creetur à Deo non purus, non sanctus: Christi spiritus purus & sanctus, sicuti ipse à peccatoribus separatus, creatus est.
units.tr: For Scripture attributes to Christ a soul such as human beings have. He poured out his soul to death, Isa. 53:12. The Son of Man came to give his soul as a ransom [ἀντὶ λύτρου], Matt. 20:28. I lay down my soul for my sheep, John 10:11. These expressions are synecdochical, and they could not stand unless Christ possessed a soul. He also commended his spirit into the hands of the Father, Luke 23:46, and is said to have been sorrowful in his soul even unto death, Matt. 26:38. Scripture also attributes will to Christ, John 4:34; 5:30; 6:38; Matt. 26:39. Now will presupposes intellect. The origin of the soul of Christ is the same as that of the other human souls: it is immediately divine and heavenly. For no spirit is generated, much less that most holy spirit, polluted by no stain; every spirit is created immediately by God. Yet the spirits of other human beings are created by God not pure and not holy, whereas the spirit of Christ was created pure and holy, just as he himself was separated from sinners.

units.la: XXXVI. Restat Humanæ Naturæ in personam Filii Dei Assumptio; qua λόγῳ, Filius Dei, in ipso formationis & sanctificationis momento Naturam humanam propriæ ὑποστάσεως expertem in unitatem personæ suæ assumpsit, ut λόγῳ assumentis, & naturæ humanæ assumptæ una eademque sit ὑπόστασις, extra quam ipsa nec subsistit unquam, nec subsistere potest. Cùm enim unus tantùm sit Christus Gal.III.16. Unus Mediator 1.Tim.II.5. Unus Dominus, Ephes.IV.5. & in Christo per gratiam unionis Deus sit & dicatur homo, & vicissim; & passim de Christo homine prædicentur, quæ Dei sunt, & vicissim; una certè ὑπόστασις, persona subsistens una sit oportet. Vel Divina natura in humanam, vel humana in Divina subsistit. At Divinam in humana subsistere, & ab eadem sustentari, infinitæ ejus perfectioni contrariatur. Humana igitur per se ἀνυπόστατον est, & ἐνυπόστατον fit in λόγῳ, qui præexistens, imò ab æterno existens, in tempore accepit formam servi, Phil.II.7. & Semen Abrahæ ἐπιλαβὲς assumpsit, Hebr.II.16. tanquam Templum & organum suum. Unde ἀνθρώπινον ὄργανον humanum instrumentum, & προσλημμα assumptum vel adjunctum veteres appellant; illud ratione operationis, hoc ratione existentiæ, quia λόγῳ absque carne inde ab æterno existenti conjuncta est in tempore in unitate personæ, sicut dicitur: Corpus adaptasti mihi Hebr.X.5. coll. cum Phil.II.7. Hebr.II.16. Et assumptio hæc facta est non ad naturam, sed ad personam Filii. Unde non Deitas, sed λόγῳ sermo caro factus 1.Joh.I.14. Deus in carne manifestatus 1.Tim.III.16. dicitur, qui solus incarnatus est. Neque ideo vel Dei Filio humanam naturam assumenti aliquid accessit, quo perficeretur ipse, sed potius aliquid, quo perficeret ipse alios: vel humanæ naturæ aliquid decessit, quo sublato vel veritas, vel perfectio ejus detrimentum pateretur. Nam subsistentia propria nec ad veritatem naturæ humanæ pertinet, cùm hæc definitionem hominis, cujus essentia in materia, forma & proprietatibus humanis consistit, non ingrediatur; nec ad perfectionem, quia humana Christi natura etiam absque propria personalitate partibus essentialibus & integralibus omnibus, itémque proprietatibus humanis omnibus constat. Cùm tamen humana natura subsistat in λόγῳ ipso, cui personaliter unita est, satis apparet, nobiliùs longè, quàm ullam naturam humanam, eam subsistere. Quod Apostolus ipse innuit, Hebr.II.16. ostendens, humanam in Christo naturam longè supra Angelos exaltatam esse.
units.tr: XXXVI. There remains the assumption of human nature into the person of the Son of God. By this assumption the Word, the Son of God, at the very moment of formation and sanctification, took into the unity of his person a human nature lacking its own hypostasis [ὑπόστασις], so that the one hypostasis of the assuming Word and of the assumed human nature is the same, and outside it the human nature neither ever subsists nor can subsist. For since there is only one Christ, Gal. 3:16; one Mediator, 1 Tim. 2:5; one Lord, Eph. 4:5; and since in Christ, through the grace of union, God is and is called man, and vice versa; and since what belongs to God is predicated everywhere of Christ the man, and vice versa; there must surely be one hypostasis, one subsisting person. Either the divine nature subsists in the human, or the human subsists in the divine. But for the divine to subsist in the human, and to be sustained by it, is contrary to God's infinite perfection. Therefore the human nature is in itself anhypostatic [ἀνυπόστατον], and it becomes enhypostatic [ἐνυπόστατον] in the Word, who, existing before, indeed existing from eternity, in time took the form of a servant, Phil. 2:7, and took hold of the seed of Abraham, Heb. 2:16, as his temple and instrument. Hence the ancients call the human nature an instrument [ἀνθρώπινον ὄργανον] and an assumed or adjoined thing [προσλημμα]: the former with respect to operation, the latter with respect to existence, because the Word, existing from eternity without flesh, was in time joined to flesh in the unity of person, as it is said: "a body you have prepared for me," Heb. 10:5, compared with Phil. 2:7 and Heb. 2:16. This assumption was made not to the nature but to the person of the Son. Hence it is not the Deity but the Word [ὁ λόγος] that is said to have become flesh, John 1:14, and God to have been manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. 3:16; the Word alone was incarnate. Nor, on that account, did anything accrue to the Son of God in assuming human nature, by which he himself would be perfected; rather, something was added by which he might perfect others. Nor did anything depart from human nature, which, if removed, would suffer loss either of its truth or of its perfection. For personal subsistence belongs neither to the truth of human nature, since it does not enter into the definition of man, whose essence consists of matter, form and human properties; nor to its perfection, since the human nature of Christ, even without its own personality, consists of all its essential and integral parts and likewise all its human properties. Yet since the human nature subsists in the Word itself, to whom it is personally united, it sufficiently appears that it subsists in a far nobler way than any other human nature. The Apostle himself hints at this, Heb. 2:16, showing that the human nature in Christ has been exalted far above the angels.

units.la: XXXVII. Assumptionem Naturæ Christi Humanæ in unitatem personæ & λόγῳ sequitur Unio duarum Christi naturarum in persona eadem & λόγῳ. Quæ sacris scriptoribus λαβὴ τ μορφῆς δούλου acceptio formæ servi, Phil.II.7. κοινωνία σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος commu-nio carnis & sanguinis, Hebr.II.14. ἐπιλήψις assumptio vel apprehensio seminis Abrahæ, ibid.16. Patribus ἑνώσις, σάρκωσις, ἐνσάρκωσις, ἐνανθρώπησις, σὺν σαλπίς ἀνθρωπότητος εἰς τὸν Θεόν (ita Athanasius) appellatur. Eandem probant ex Virgine natus Emmanuel Jesaj.VII.14. Sermo caro factus Joh.I.14. Filius Dei factus ex semine Davidis secundum carnem, definitus Filius Dei in potentia, Rom.I.3.4. Deus in carne manifestatus 1.Tim.III.16. nec non modus loquendi de Christo, juxta quem de eodem Deus, Filius Dei, Homo, & Filius hominis prædicatur. Nam qui Deus est, idem sanguinem habet, Act.XX.28. qui Filius Dei unigenitus, idem Filius hominis primogenitus Joh.III.16. Matth.I.25. qui immortalis idem mortalis & mortuus, 1.Tim.VI.16. 1.Pet.III.18. qui æternus, ante Abrahamum existens, idem in plenitudine temporis ex muliere natus Mich.V.2. Joh.VIII.58. Gal.IV.4. qui è Cœlo descendens, idem simul in Cœlo existens, Joh.III.13. qui Dominus gloriæ, idem crucifixus 1.Cor.II.8. dicitur, quæ nisi in eadem persona Filii Dei Divina, & hominis humana natura unitis, constare non possunt.
units.tr: XXXVII. The union of the two natures of Christ in the same person and Word follows the assumption of the human nature into the unity of person and Word. The sacred writers call this union the taking [λαβὴ] of the form of a servant, Phil. 2:7; the communion [κοινωνία] of flesh and blood, Heb. 2:14; the assumption or apprehension [ἐπιλήψις] of the seed of Abraham, ibid. 16. The Fathers call it union [ἑνώσις], incarnation [σάρκωσις], enfleshment [ἐνσάρκωσις], becoming man [ἐνανθρώπησις], and the assumption of humanity into God (so Athanasius). The same is proved by: Emmanuel born of a virgin, Isa. 7:14; the Word made flesh, John 1:14; the Son of God made of the seed of David according to the flesh, and declared Son of God in power, Rom. 1:3, 4; God manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. 3:16; and also by the manner of speaking about Christ, according to which the same person is called God, Son of God, man, and Son of Man. For he who is God has blood, Acts 20:28; he who is the only-begotten Son of God is the same as the firstborn Son of Man, John 3:16, Matt. 1:25; he who is immortal is the same as the mortal one who died, 1 Tim. 6:16, 1 Pet. 3:18; he who is eternal, existing before Abraham, is the same who in the fullness of time was born of a woman, Mic. 5:2, John 8:58, Gal. 4:4; he who came down from heaven is the same who at the same time existed in heaven, John 3:13; the Lord of glory is the same who is said to have been crucified, 1 Cor. 2:8. These things cannot hold unless the divine nature of the Son of God and the human nature are united in the same person.

units.la: XXXVIII. Sed modus unionis personalis singularis planè & mysterio plenus est. Nam Christus est מלא Mirabilis Esaj.IX.6. & Dei in carne manifestatio ὁμολογουμένως μέγα μυστήριον extra controversiam ingens mysterium est 1.Tim.III.16. gloriosum quidem Deo, & magnitudini ejus consentaneum, sed tamen supra exspectationem hominum. Dum feceris נוראות terribilia, quæ לא נקוּ non exspectabamus, ירד Descendisti: coram te montes evilue-runt, Et à sæculo non audiverunt, non auscultarunt, Oculus non vidit Deum præter te, qui יעשה למחכה לו faceret (satisfaceret juxta promissa) præsto-lanti se, Esaj LXIV.3.4. 1.Cor.II.9. Id fatentur & credentes & non credentes. Tantum enim & tam mirabile mysterium est, ut animum inducere nolint, ut verum id esse, & non stultum credant. Quemadmodum שממו stupuerunt super te multi, adeò corrupta præ viro erat species ejus, etiam forma ejus præ filiis hominum. sic asperg. gentes multas, Esaj.LII.14.15. Videte ex gentibus & adspicite והתמהו תמהו & admiramini, admiramini. כי פעל פעל Nam molitionem molitur in diebus vestris, non credetis cùm narrabitur, Habac.I.5. Ideo Judæi & hæretici verba Scripturæ, Prophetiæ inprimis & promissionis, extenuare, enervare, quædam etiam eradere, quàm mysterii magnitudinem credere malunt. Licet enim non magis perceptu facile sit, quomodo Deus sibi vocem formet, ut ab hominibus audiatur; quàm quomodo Deus sibi linguam, faciem, oculos, manus & cætera membra, ut à nobis videatur, palpetur, & pro nobis victima fiat, formet: tamen quia id inusitatum, & maximæ συγκαταβάσεως (sine qua tamen mundus non subsisteret) est; ideo velut maximum mysterium & miraculum Scriptura prædicat, Deum videri oculo in oculum Esaj.LII.8. facie ad faciem Ezech.XX.35. vocem ejus audiri, Mich.VI.6.9. Deum stare in cœtu Dei, Psalm.LXXXII.1. Verbum vitæ manibus contrectari, 1.Joh.I.1. Rupem salutis indignè tractari, Deut.XXXII.15. fustibus percuti, Esaj.L.6. Germen Domini adigi ad respirandum, Malach.I.13. Deum resurgere, Zeph.III.8. & in altum ascendere, Psal.LXVIII.19.
units.tr: XXXVIII. But the manner of this singular personal union is wholly plain and full of mystery. For Christ is "Wonderful" [פלא], Isa. 9:6, and God manifested in the flesh is by common confession "a great mystery," 1 Tim. 3:16. It is a mystery beyond dispute, glorious indeed to God and consonant with his greatness, yet beyond human expectation: "When you did terrible things [נוראות] which we did not expect, you came down; the mountains melted before you. From of old they have not heard, nor given ear; the eye has not seen a God besides you, who acts (that is, fulfils his promises) for the one who waits for him," Isa. 64:3, 4; 1 Cor. 2:9. Believers and unbelievers alike confess this. The mystery is so great and so marvellous that men are unwilling to bring their minds to believe it true rather than foolish. Just as "many were astonished at you, so marred was his appearance beyond that of a man, and his form beyond that of the sons of men; so he will sprinkle many nations," Isa. 52:14, 15. "Look among the nations and see, and be astonished, be astonished [והתמהו תמהו]; for I am doing a work [פעל פעל] in your days which you will not believe when it is told," Hab. 1:5. Therefore the Jews and the heretics prefer to weaken and enervate the words of Scripture, especially of prophecy and promise, and even to erase some of them, rather than believe the greatness of the mystery. For although it is no easier to grasp how God forms a voice for himself so that it may be heard by men, than how he forms for himself a tongue, a face, eyes, hands and other members, so that he may be seen and touched by us and become a victim for us, nevertheless, because this is unusual and a matter of the greatest condescension (without which the world could not subsist), Scripture proclaims it as the greatest mystery and miracle: that God is seen eye to eye, Isa. 52:8; face to face, Ezek. 20:35; that his voice is heard, Mic. 6:6, 9; that God stands in the congregation of God, Ps. 82:1; that the Word of life is handled with the hands, 1 John 1:1; that the Rock of salvation is shamefully treated, Deut. 32:15; that he is struck with rods, Isa. 50:6; that the Branch of the Lord is driven to draw breath, Mal. 1:13; that God rises again, Zeph. 3:8; and ascends on high, Ps. 68:19.

units.la: XXXIX. Quod pii Veteres de Deo in universum dixerunt, melius sciri quid non sit, quàm quid sit: id de unione naturarum in una persona non minus rectè enunciatur. Athanasius tract. de desin. cap. ἑνώσεως quinque unionis species enumerat, συγχύσεως commixtivam, qualis est aquæ & vini: διαιρετικὴν divisivam, fivam.qualis est hominis ad hominem; αὐτολὼ relativum, qualis est auri ad aurum; Ἑνωλὼ positivam, ubi plura inter se componuntur; & ὑποστατικὼ personalem, cùm naturæ diversæ in persona uniuntur. Remotis quatuor prioribus quintam unioni naturarum vendicat. Damascenus Orth. Fid. lib. III. 3. diversos etiam unionis modos à Nestorianis confictos recensèt & refellit. Bernhardus lib. de consid. ad Eugen. octo unionis species distinguit: collectivam, cùm multi lapides unum acervum faciunt: constitutivam, cùm multa membra unum corpus fiunt, vel multæ partes unum totum constituunt: conjugativam cùm duo una caro fiunt: nativam, cùm anima & corpus hominem efficiunt: potestativam, cùm homo sibi semper unus, similis, non instabilis & à se diversus est: consentaneam, cùm per charitatem multorum unum cor, unus spiritus est: votivam, cùm anima omnibus votis Deo adhærens, unus cum eo spiritus est: & dignativam, qua limus noster à Dei Verbo in unam personam assumptus est. Rejectis prioribus postremam in unione naturarum Christi obtinere asseritur.
units.tr: XXXIX. What the godly ancients said of God in general, that it is better known what he is not than what he is, is no less rightly said of the union of the natures in one person. Athanasius, in his treatise on the Incarnation, enumerates five kinds of union: the mixing [συγχύσεως] kind, such as that of water and wine; the dividing [διαιρετικὴν] kind, such as that of one man to another; the relative kind, such as that of gold to gold; the positive kind, where several things are compounded together; and the personal kind, when diverse natures are united in one person. Setting aside the first four, he claims the fifth for the union of the natures. Damascene, in De Orthodoxa Fide, book III, chapter 3, also recounts and refutes the various modes of union devised by the Nestorians. Bernard, in On Consideration, to Eugenius, distinguishes eight species of union: the collective, when many stones make one heap; the constitutive, when many members make one body, or many parts constitute one whole; the conjugal, when two become one flesh; the natural, when soul and body make one man; the powerful, when a man is always one with himself, similar, not unstable, and not different from himself; the harmonious, when through charity many have one heart and one spirit; the votive, when the soul, adhering to God in all its vows, is one spirit with him; and the dignitative, by which our clay was assumed by the Word of God into one person. The former being rejected, the last is claimed to obtain in the union of the natures of Christ.

units.la: XL. Receptior verò & planior etiam est Synodica Fidei expositio in Concilio Chalcedonensi edita, & ex quinta ejus Actione excerpta, quæ sic habet: Docemus, unum & eundem Christum, Filium, Dominum, Unigenitum, in duabus naturis ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως, ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως γνωριζόμενον, οὐδαμῶς τῆς τῶν φύσεων διαφορᾶς ἀνῃρημένης, διὰ τὴν ἕνωσιν, σωζομένης δὲ μᾶλλον τὴν ἰδιότητα ἑκατέρας φύσεως, καὶ εἰς ἓν πρόσωπον καὶ μίαν ὑπόστασιν συντρέχουσης, οὐκ εἰς δύο πρόσωπα μεριζόμενον ἢ διαιρούμενον, ἀλλ' ἕνα καὶ τὸν αὐτὸν υἱὸν καὶ μονογενῆ Θεὸν λόγον, Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν, inconfuse, inconvertibiliter, indivulse & inseparabiliter manifestatum: haudquaquam differentia naturarum propter unionem sublata, sed magis utriusque naturæ in unam personam & unam hypostasin concurrentis, proprietate servata: non in duas personas bipartitum aut divisum, sed unum & eundem Filium Unigenitum Deum Verbum, Dominum Jesum Christum. Quæ Scripturis prorsus consonant. Nam unus Filius Dei Jesus Christus in duabus naturis manifestatus est tum ἀσυγχύτως inconfuse, sine crasi seu commixtione duarum naturarum in tertiam quampiam, quia post unionem etiam naturæ in persona distinguuntur, juxta Rom. I. 3.4. Filius Dei factus ex Semine Davidis secundum carnem, & definitus Filius Dei in potentia secundum Spiritum Sanctitatis, & I. Pet. III. 18. Mortificatus carne, vivificatus Spiritu: & passim etiam post resurrectionem, quando Christus non Deitatis duntaxat suæ luculenta documenta edidit; sed ipsam quoque carnis veritatem discipulis suis ad oculum demonstravit. Luc. XXIV. 39.40. Joh. X X. 20.27. tum ἀτρέπτως inconvertibiliter, citra conversionem vel naturæ Divinæ in Humanam, vel Humanæ in Divinam; qualis & Scripturæ repugnat, quæ Christum apprehendisse, vel assumpsisse semen Abrahæ, non in illud conversum esse, Hebr. II. 16. docet; & impossibilis est, quia multò minus Deus in creaturam, vel creatura in Deum, quàm homo in lapidem, vel vilissim converti potest; & planè ἄλογος, quia sic Christus nec Deus, nec homo, nec Patri, nec ma- tri ὁμοούσιος esset, sed tertium quid, sicut homo nec corpus nec anima, sed tertium quid ex corpore & anima constans est: tum ἀδιαιρέτως indivisè, absque naturarum divisione in duas personas seorsim subsistentes, quia Scriptura nobis unum Mediatorem, unum Dominum, unum Christum ostendit, I. Cor. VIII. 6. I. Tim. II. 5. & quod ex Maria natum est sanctum, Filius Dei vocatur, Luc. I. 35. & Deus sanguine suo Ecclesiam acquisivit, Act. XX. 28. & Judæi Dominum gloriæ crucifixisse I. Cor. II. 8. dicuntur; ut innumera hactenus aliata præteream; tum denique ἀχωρίστως inseparabiliter, quia tam insepar-abilis ea unio fuit, ut ne morte quidem soluta fuerit; quando idem, qui vitam in mortem dedit, eandem ex morte vindicavit, non in sepulchro reliquit, Psal. XVI. 10. Joh. X. 18. XLI. Unionis verò modum eadem Chalcedonensis Synodus ἐν δύο φύσεων in eo constituit, quòd servata utriusque naturæ proprietate, utraque natura ὡς ἐν πρόσωπον καὶ μίαν ὑπόστασιν in unam personam & unam hypostasin concurrit. Nam Verbum assumens carnem ante & post incarnationem erat Deus, & persona αὐτοπαλὴς ex seipsa perfecta, completa & integra; olim quidem nuda, postea verò carne vestita: non tamen, quòd caro accidentaliter per modum externi habitus λόγῳ supervenerit, & conjuncta sit; sicut homini vestitus accidentaliter & mutabiliter inforsecus adhæret. Nam in intimam & penitissimam ἕ λόγῳ ὑπόστασιν sic assumpta est caro, ut unio ejus cum λόγῳ verè, & multò magis, quàm unio corporis cum anima sit hypostatica, hoc est, eandem ipsa cum λόγῳ subsistentiam habeat. Unde Damascenus lib. III. 3. etiam ὁμοούσιον, ὑπέρων ἀληθῆ essentialem, hoc est, veram, oppositè ad unionem ἐν φυσικὴν, appellat. Etiam Maxentius ille, qui Monachorum Scytharum nomine duodecim capitula contra Papam Hormisdam consignavit, & alii Catholici Patres, uti cernere est Orat. I. Gregorii Nazianzeni, unionem illam ἐν φύσιν secundum naturam & naturalem dixerunt, anathema dissentientibus intonantes, non quòd duæ naturæ unam compositam naturam effecerint; sed quòd verè, non opinione tantùm vel specie, in una Filii Dei composita persona unitæ sint. Quam phrasin opponendam duxerunt fraudibus Nestorii, qui & ipse in Christo unionem καθ' ὑπόστασιν seu hypostaticam vel personalem confessus est, sed ita explicavit, ut diceret, personam humanam esse unitam personæ Divinæ, quæ jam non est unio hypostatica, seu καθ' ὑπόστασιν, sed duarum personarum consociatio, quæ ἐνωσις ἑνωσις relativa unio dicitur. Illi autem non talem, sed ὁμοιώδη & φυσικὸν subsistentialem & naturalem dixerunt, quia non subsistentiæ, sed subsistantiæ, essentiæ & naturæ unitæ sunt. Qui & ipsi tamen ὑποστατικὸν personalem dici orthodoxo sensu facile tulissent. Revera enim unio hæc naturarum in Christo non est vel nuda πρόσωπον, qualis inter duos asseres, vel nautam & navim est, quia ex ἀρχῆς tali nulla communicatio oritur, nec in ea mysterium aliquod obtinet: vel ὁμοιώσις essentialis: vel φυσικὴ naturalis, quatenus illa opponitur unioni non accidentali, vel apparenti, sed personali, quia quæ sic uniuntur, extra unionem non usque quaquaque perfecta sunt, & tertium aliquod constituunt; nec modum unionis, vel terminum ἑνωτικόν, à quo unio denominatur, & in quo unita conveniunt, id exprimit: vel σχέσις συμβεβηκὸς accidentalis, uti Scotus existimat, quia neutra natura accidens, substantiæ oppositum est, nec unio ejusmodi ὑπόστασιν ἀνύπαρκτον efficere potest, nec terminus ἑνωτικὸς naturarum in Christo accidens est; nec cùm à Patribus περίωσις, ab aliis adjunctum appellatur, accidentale illud, sed substantiale, & in intimam cum λόγῳ ὑπόστασιν assumptum intelligitur: vel σχετικὴ relativa, qualem Nestorius somniavit, quia naturæ non separatæ non nudam ad se invicem relationem habent, sicut personæ diversæ habere solent: non integralis, quia naturæ in Christo nec quantitativæ sunt, & homo de Deo, Deus de homine prædicatur: sed καθ' ὑπόστασιν, uti rectè Chalcedonenses definiunt, quia terminus ἑνωτικὸς est ἡ λόγος ὑπόστασις Sermonis subsistentia vel persona, in cujus unitatem ipse sermo carnem suscepit. Non quòd vel carni communicata sit ὑπόστασις, ut propriam, sed communicatam sic subsistentiam habeat, quod Nestorianam hæresin saperet; vel duæ naturæ, Divina & Humana, in tertiam aliquam hypostasin, ex Divina & Humana conflatam, & quæ partim à λόγῳ, partim à carne fit, coiverint, quia sicut naturæ non uniuntur in unam tertiam, ita nec personæ; & natura humana per se ἀνυπόστατος nihil ad τὸ esse ὑποστῆναι confert: sed quòd caro in λόγῳ solius persona subsistat, & à λόγῳ in æternum sustentetur, non ad extra, uti loquuntur, velut creatore, conservatore; sed ad intra, cujus sustentationis ut modus, sic terminus & fructus longè alius est; scilicet ut non sicut res creata in suo esse aut operari sustineatur, sed ut in λόγῳ ita subsistat, ut cum eo unam eandémque personam constituat. Neque naturarum infinitæ & finitæ, quæ proportionem nullam prorsus habent, inæqualitas obstat, quia unio illa non in naturarum exæquatione, sed in naturæ finitæ in infinita, Humanæ in Divina, vel potiùs carnis in Persona Filii Dei, salvis naturis, proprietatibus & operationibus, existentia indivisa consistit.
units.tr: XL. The exposition of the faith issued by the Council of Chalcedon, taken from its fifth session, is more widely received and clearer still. It reads as follows: "We teach that one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, Only-begotten, is to be acknowledged in two natures [ἐν δύο φύσεσιν], unconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably [ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως, ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως]. The difference of the natures is by no means taken away on account of the union; rather the property of each nature is preserved, and both concur into one person and one hypostasis. He is not parted or divided into two persons, but is one and the same Son, the Only-begotten God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ." These statements are wholly consonant with Scripture. For one Son of God, Jesus Christ, has been made manifest in two natures: unconfusedly [ἀσυγχύτως], without any mixture or blending of the two natures into a third, since even after the union the natures remain distinct in the one person, according to Rom. 1:3–4, "made of the seed of David according to the flesh, and declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness," and 1 Pet. 3:18, "put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit." And this is shown throughout, also after the resurrection, when Christ not only gave clear proofs of his deity but also showed his disciples the reality of his flesh before their eyes: Luke 24:39–40; John 20:20, 27. He is also unchangeably [ἀτρέπτως], without conversion either of the divine nature into the human or of the human into the divine. Such conversion is contrary to Scripture, which teaches that Christ laid hold of, or took on himself the seed of Abraham, and was not changed into it (Heb. 2:16). It is also impossible, since God can much less be converted into a creature, or a creature into God, than a man can be converted into a stone or the basest thing. It is also plainly absurd, for then Christ would be neither God nor man, neither consubstantial with the Father nor with the mother, but some third thing, just as man is neither body nor soul but a third thing made up of body and soul. He is also indivisibly [ἀδιαιρέτως], without division of the natures into two persons subsisting apart, since Scripture shows us one Mediator, one Lord, one Christ (1 Cor. 8:6; 1 Tim. 2:5), and what was born holy of Mary is called the Son of God (Luke 1:35), and God purchased the Church with his own blood (Acts 20:28), and the Jews are said to have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8). I pass over the countless other passages cited so far. Finally, he is inseparably [ἀχωρίστως], because that union was so inseparable that it was not even dissolved by death. The same one who gave his life into death took it back from death; he did not leave it in the grave (Ps. 16:10; John 10:18). XLI. The Council of Chalcedon itself fixes the mode of the union in two natures [ἐν δύο φύσεων] in this way: while the property of each nature is preserved, each nature concurs into one person and one hypostasis. For the Word, when he assumed flesh, was God both before and after the incarnation, and was a person self-sufficient, complete and whole in himself: once indeed bare, but afterwards clothed with flesh. Yet the flesh did not join itself to the Word accidentally, by way of an external garment, as clothing clings to a man from outside, changeable and accidental. Rather, the flesh was assumed into the innermost and most intimate hypostasis of the Word, so that its union with the Word is truly, and far more than the union of body with soul, hypostatic; that is, it has the same subsistence as the Word itself. Hence Damascene (Book III, ch. 3) also calls it consubstantial and, as it were, a true essential union, that is, a real one, as opposed to a natural union in one nature. Also Maxentius, who in the name of the Scythian monks drew up twelve chapters against Pope Hormisdas, and other Catholic Fathers, as may be seen in Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration I, called that union in one nature, according to nature and natural, thundering anathema on those who disagreed. They did not mean that the two natures made one compound nature, but that they were truly united, and not merely in opinion or appearance, in one composite person of the Son of God. They judged this phrase should be set against the tricks of Nestorius, who also confessed a union according to hypostasis, that is, hypostatic or personal, in Christ, but explained it so as to say that the human person was united to the divine person. That is no longer a hypostatic union, or one according to hypostasis, but a joining of two persons, which is called a relative union. The Fathers, however, did not call it such, but a union homoiōdē, and a natural and subsistential union, because natures, not subsistences, are united, that is, essences and natures. Yet even they could readily have allowed the term hypostatic or personal to be used in an orthodox sense. Indeed, this union of natures in Christ is neither a mere juxtaposition, such as there is between two planks, or between a sailor and his ship, since no communication arises from such a union at the start and it contains no mystery; nor an essential union [ὁμοίωσις], nor a natural union, in so far as that is opposed to a union that is not accidental or apparent but personal, since things so united are not perfect apart from the union and constitute some third thing, and that term does not express the mode of the union or the uniting term from which the union is named and in which the united things come together; nor an accidental union of accident, as Scotus thought, since neither nature is an accident opposed to substance, and a union of that kind cannot produce a non-existent hypostasis, nor is the uniting term of the natures in Christ an accident. Nor, when the Fathers call it perichōrēsis [περίωσις] and others call it an adjunct, is that adjunct to be understood as accidental, but as substantial and assumed into the innermost hypostasis of the Word. Nor is it a relative union, such as Nestorius dreamed of, since natures that are not separate do not have a bare relation to one another, as different persons usually do. Nor is it an integral union, since the natures in Christ are not quantitative, and man is predicated of God and God of man.
