Rather it is according to hypostasis, as the Chalcedonians rightly define, because the uniting term is the hypostasis of the Word, that is, the subsistence or person of the Word, into whose unity the Word itself took up the flesh. Not that a hypostasis was communicated to the flesh as its own, so that it would have a subsistence communicated to it, which would savour of the Nestorian heresy; nor that the two natures, divine and human, came together into some third hypostasis compounded of divine and human, which would be partly from the Word and partly from the flesh; for just as natures are not united into a third nature, neither are persons. A human nature, which is in itself without hypostasis, contributes nothing to its being to subsist. Rather, the flesh subsists in the person of the Word alone, and is sustained eternally by the Word, not ad extra, as they put it, as by a creator or preserver, but ad intra. The mode, the term and the fruit of this sustaining is quite different: namely, the flesh is not sustained in its being or operating as a created thing is, but subsists in the Word in such a way as to constitute one and the same person with him. Nor does the inequality of the infinite and finite natures, which have no proportion whatever, stand in the way, because that union does not consist in an equalising of the natures, but in the undivided existence of the finite nature in the infinite, the human in the divine, or rather of the flesh in the Person of the Son of God, the natures, properties and operations being preserved.

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: Ex unione hac etiam κοινωνία communio, seu potiùs communicatio quædam oritur. Quæ vel Non-mutua, vel Mutua est. Illa in Natura humana, hæc in persona ἡ Θεανθρώπου consistit. Illa est, qua λόγῳ Naturæ humanæ sibi unitæ Gratiam Eminentiæ, & Gratias Habituales liberaliter contulit. Gratia Eminentiæ est dignitas Naturæ Humanæ supra omnes creaturas, orta ex ejusdem unione cum natura Divina, per quam propria Filii Dei caro est. Quam dignitatem & ἰσοχὴν licèt propter œconomiæ necessitatem ad tempus occultaverit מסר inferior factus paulum infra Deos, seu Angelos Psalm. VIII.6. Hebr.II.7. tamen postea, gloria & decore coronatus, exeruit, & super omnes creaturas sese eminere demonstravit. Nam qui paululum infra Angelos fuit, non semper infra eos fuit, sed aliquando eosdem ἡ ἀξία dignitate & excellentia superare debuit.
units.tr: From this union there also arises a certain κοινωνία, or communion, or rather communication. This is either non-mutual or mutual. The former lies in the human nature, the latter in the person of the God-man (ἡ Θεανθρώπου). The former is that by which the Word freely bestowed on the human nature united to it the Gift of Eminence and the habitual gifts. The Gift of Eminence is the dignity of the human nature above all creatures, arising from its union with the divine nature, by which the flesh is the proper flesh of the Son of God. Although, for the necessity of the economy, he concealed this dignity and excellence for a time, having been made "a little lower than the gods," that is, than the angels (Ps. 8:6; Heb. 2:7), he afterwards, crowned with glory and honour, brought it forth and showed that he surpasses all creatures. For he who was "a little lower than the angels" was not always lower than them; at some point he was bound to surpass them in dignity [ἡ ἀξία] and excellence.

units.la: XLIII.
units.tr: XLIII.

units.la: Gratiæ Habituales sunt excellentes illæ dotes, quas λόγος humanæ naturæ contulit, & ei velut implantavit. Gratiæ vocantur, quia ex Gratia unionis indebitæ fluunt: Habituales, quia per modum ἕξεως habitus in anima Christi exi-stunt. Quas non vulgares esse, Christus ipse innuit, ajens: Non ἐκ μέτρου ex mensura (communi, vulgari, avara, quomodo tempore angustiarum quidam dicuntur comedere panem במשקל in pondere, & aquam bibere במשורה in mensura, Ezech.IV.16. sed liberaliter, ut Artaxerxes jussit Esræ dare Sal כתר non ad præscriptum, Esr.VII.22.) dat Deus Spiritum, Joh.III.34. nisi forte non de Spiritu sibi non ex mensura dato; sed de Spiritu non ex mensura fidelibus N.T. dato, hoc est, post missionem Christi, loquentis verba Dei, in carnem omnem, juxta prædictiones effusio, loquitur; quod series verborum, & omissa vox αὐτῷ ipsi, vel ἐμοὶ mihi innuere videtur. Cùm tamen Christus carnem assumpserit, sed sine peccato, 2.Cor.V.21. sine δόλῳ dolo, 1.Pet.II.22. sine defectu damnabili, vel, uti Damascenus loquitur, ἀπαλλήτῳ detestabili ullo, quippe propter conceptionem ex Spiritu S. ἁγίῳ Sanctus; caro ejus personæ ἡ λόγου unita intimè, nullo apud reliquas creaturas exemplo simili, fuerit; quin & Christus Spiritu Dei unctus fuerit משחרי supra consortes suos Psalm.XLV.8. Hebr. I.9. Gratias ejusmodi supra omnium creaturarum, sive Angelorum, sive hominum gratias & dona in eo eminere tum subjecti dignitate, tum partium graduumque perfectione, dubitari nequit. Non minùs enim dona carnis, quàm caro ipsa, sunt Filii Dei: & quæ in alijs sejuncta & imperfecta, in Christo conjuncta & perfecta sunt.
units.tr: The habitual gifts are those excellent endowments which the Word conferred on the human nature and, as it were, implanted in it. They are called gifts because they flow from the grace of the undeserved union, and habitual because they exist in the soul of Christ by way of a habit [ἕξις]. That these are not ordinary gifts Christ himself indicates when he says: "Not out of measure [ἐκ μέτρου] God gives the Spirit" (John 3:34). This is not a meagre, common, grudging measure, such as in times of scarcity some are said to eat bread [במשקל] by weight and drink water [במשורה] by measure (Ezek. 4:16); it is a liberal gift, as Artaxerxes ordered Ezra to give salt [כתר] without prescribed limit (Ezra 7:22). Unless perhaps the words are to be taken not of a Spirit given to himself by no measure, but of the Spirit given without measure to the faithful of the New Testament, that is, after the mission of Christ, who speaks the words of God, and the outpouring upon all flesh according to the predictions; the sequence of the words and the omission of the word αὐτῷ, "to him," or ἐμοί, "to me," seem to suggest this. Yet since Christ assumed flesh without sin (2 Cor. 5:21), without guile (1 Pet. 2:22), without any damnable defect, or, as Damascene puts it, without any detestable [ἀπαλλήτῳ] blemish, because of his conception from the Holy Spirit, who is Holy [ἁγίῳ]; and his flesh was intimately united to the person of the Word, with no similar example among the other creatures; and since Christ was anointed with the Spirit of God above his fellows [משחרי] (Ps. 45:8; Heb. 1:9), there can be no doubt that these gifts and graces are eminent in him above the graces and gifts of all creatures, whether angels or men, both in the dignity of the subject and in the perfection of its parts and degrees. For the gifts of the flesh are no less the Son of God's than the flesh itself; and what in others is separate and imperfect is in Christ joined and perfect.

units.la: XLIV.
units.tr: XLIV.

units.la: Sed perfectio tamen illa donorum quoad numeros, gradus & operationes omnes non in ipso statim unionis primordio, & durante exinanitionis statu, sed sub initium demum gloriæ & exaltationis cœpit; secus quàm gratiæ Eminentiæ. quod nequicquam Bellarminus & complices ejus inficiantur. Sicut nempe Divina natura in Christo comprimebat nonnihil & occultabat Majestatem suam in exinanitionis statu, ne eam, sicut in statu exaltationis factum, exereret: ita etiam in natura humana comprimebatur spiritus sapientiæ, ne statim in perfectione, sed paulatim pro ratione status Christi exerebatur. Sicut ergo Christus homo ἡ σοφία sapientia, ita aliis etiam virtutibus, ἀπροκόπτω proficiebat, Luc.II.52. Puerulus crescebat, & corroborabatur Spiritu, ἐπλήρωτο implebebatúrque (crescendo, proficiendo, nam ἐπληρώμενον junctum cum imperfecto ἐκέκτητο actum successivum notat) sapientia, ibid. v.40. Neque admittenda est Sophistice illa, quæ crescere, corroborari, proficere, pro videri crescere, corroborari, proficere positum fingit. quomodo etsi idem perseveret ardor Solis, crescere tamen dicitur, cùm à nobis vehementius sentitur: tum quia sic sapientia crevit, ut ætate creverat, at ætate ὄντως, non φαινομένως crevit: tum quia crescere Christus dictus est ætate, sapientia, gratia non apud homines duntaxat, sed etiam ἀπὸ Θεῷ apud Deum, v.52. tum quia quod semel crescere dictum, postea ἐπληρώθη impleri dicitur, quod non ad alienum sensum vel judicium, sed ad id, quod in re ipsa factum est, pertinet: tum quia Scriptura voce גדל, αὔξεσθαι, crescendi, de re, non de opinione homi-
units.tr: But that perfection of the gifts, as to their number, degrees and all operations, did not begin at the very outset of the union, nor during the state of emptying, but only at the beginning of glory and exaltation. It is otherwise with the grace of eminence, which Bellarminus and his companions deny in vain. For just as the divine nature in Christ held in check somewhat and concealed its majesty in the state of emptying, so that it did not display it as it did in the state of exaltation, so too the spirit of wisdom in the human nature was held in check, so that it was displayed not at once in perfection, but gradually, according to the manner of Christ's state. Therefore, just as Christ as man grew in wisdom [ἡ σοφία], so in other virtues too he advanced [προέκοπτεν], Luke 2:52: "The child grew [Puerulus crescebat], and was strengthened in spirit [corroborabatur Spiritu], and was filled [ἐπληροῦτο] and was being filled with wisdom" (the participle ἐπληρούμενον, joined with the imperfect ἐκέκτητο, denotes successive action), v. 40. Nor is that sophistical view to be admitted, which pretends that to grow, to be strengthened and to advance means only to seem to grow, be strengthened and advance. Just as the heat of the sun remains the same and yet is said to increase when it is felt more strongly by us, so here: first, because wisdom grew in the way that it had grown with age, and it grew with age in truth, not in appearance; second, because Christ is said to have grown in age, wisdom and grace not only before men but also before God [ἀπὸ Θεῷ], v. 52; third, because what was once said to grow is afterwards said to have been filled [ἐπληρώθη], which pertains not to an alien sense or judgment but to what was actually done in fact; fourth, because Scripture uses the word גדל [gadal], αὔξεσθαι [auxesthai], of the growing [crescendi] of the thing itself, not of the opinion of men.

units.la: Ex unione personali naturarum in Christo etiam communio, seu communicatio quædam sequitur; eáque vel non-mutua, vel mutua.
units.tr: From the personal union of the natures in Christ there also follows a certain communion, or communication; and this is either non-mutual or mutual.

units.la: Non-mutua est communicatio humanæ naturæ facta, eáque tum gratiæ eminentiæ.
units.tr: The non-mutual communication is that made to the human nature, and this comprises both the gift of eminence,

units.la: Tum Gratiarum Habitualium,
units.tr: and the habitual gifts.

units.la: Perfectio Gratiarum illarum, quoad numeros, gradus & operationes sub initium demum exaltationis capit. Sapientia ejus ita indies proficiente, ut amen ab ignoratione rerum quarundam innoxia natura ejus humana immunis non fuerit. hominum utitur. Velut de Jacobo & Esavo Genef.XXV.27. de Johanne Baptista Luc.I.80. &c. tum quia licebit pari ratione Christum nil nisi φαντασμα cum haereticis veteribus & recentioribus facere. Neque rectius Bellarminus incrementum isthoc sapientiae practice, hoc est, de experimento earum rerum, quas Christus antea theoretice cognoverit, intelligi jubet, quia qui experitur, quae ante theoretice perfecte cognovit, impleri sapientia dici non potest, neque sic phrasis uspiam usurpatur. Tum eadem ratione sapientia Christi etiam post resurrectionem crevit, & in Coelo crescit, quando non aequae, ut puer, sapientia crescere dici potuit, vel potest. Idem Christus e longinquo videns, ficum habere folia, accessit ad eam, visurus, ei αρα ἀρησει ἢ ἐν αὐτῇ an videlicet aliquid (βρωσιμον puta) in ea inveniret, Marc.XI.13. Ignoravit ergo, arbor illa fructum edulem haberet, nec ne. Hoc factum, non simulatum, ὀντως non δοκητως sacri Scriptores referunt, sine ullo simulationis, quam nonnulli heic Christo tribuunt, vestigio. Cui bono alias ille labor, deflexio ab intinere, ambulatio ad arborem, inquisitio, & quidem ei αρα an videlicet, vel, ut alii, forte aliquid haberet? Alias sine labore miraculum procederet, imo glisecere magis potuisset, si arborem a se remotam, sibi nihilominus cognitam, adeoque se Deum non tantum מקרוב ex propinquo, sed etiam מרחוק ex longinquo (Jerem. XXIII. 23.) esse demonstrasset. Quid vero multis? Etiam Filius diem judicii ignorasse Marc.XIII.32. dicitur. non κατ' ἀξιαν, ει κατ' ἀληθειαν secundum praxin, vel experientiam, non secundum notitiam, uti nonnulli ex Epiphanio φλυαρουσι. Quis enim quicquam potest ειδεναι μη κατ' αληθειαν? Perinde idem est, atque videre sine visu, amare sine amore. Qui novit κατ' αληθειαν, eum ειδεναι nosse necesse est. Nil huc facit exemplum Adami & Evae, qui post peccatum se nudos esse cognoverunt, utique κατ' αξιαν, sed ante peccatum non κατ' αληθειαν eo sensu sciverunt. Nesciverunt enim ante peccatum se ita nudos esse, ut erubescenda iis nuditas esset, sicut post peccatum. Nescivisse vero Filium Dei diem judicii, ut aliis diceret, audax verborum detorsio est, quae efficit, ut recte dicatur, etiam Patrem nescivisse, quia nec is cuiquam id revelare voluit, Act.I.7. Et tamen Patrem scivisse, Christus, os veritatis, dixit. Inauditum certe est, sine mendacio dicere: Nescio, id est, nolo dicere. Recte igitur Ambrosius in Luc.cap.XVII. Temporum finem non per naturam hominis, sed per naturam Dei novit. Neque etiam illud obstat, quod super Christo requievisse Spiritus sapientiae, Esaj.XI.2. Unctus is supra consortes, Psal.XLV.8. Unctus Spiritu S. & virtute, Act.X.38. accepisse Spiritum sine mensura Joh.III.34. dicitur. quia Esajas de unione hypostatica, efficiente, ut in Christo omnis plenitudo Deitatis habitaret, loquitur; & Spiritus sapientiae atque unctio in Christo homine sapientiam ponit, at incrementum ejusdem non tollit, sed adjuvat. Nam quae sapientia actu primo & intensive perfecta est, illam actu secundo, per extensionem ad nova objecta, augeri nihil prohibet. Spiritus porro ille sine mensura nec Christo tribuitur, nec mensuram omnem, sed tantum vulgarem, qualis in consortibus est, re-
units.tr: The perfection of those gifts, as to their numbers, degrees and operations, began only at the beginning of the exaltation. His wisdom so progressed day by day that his human nature nevertheless was not free from ignorance of certain things, which is harmless. (The text here is garbled in the scan; the sense is that the human nature of Christ was not immune from some ignorance, as with the examples of Jacob and Esau (Gen. 25:27) and John the Baptist (Luke 1:80), and that otherwise one would have to make Christ a mere appearance, as the ancient and recent heretics did.) Nor does Bellarmine rightly direct us to understand this increase of practical wisdom, that is, of the experience of those things which Christ had earlier known theoretically, because one who experiences what he previously knew perfectly in theory cannot be said to be filled with wisdom, and the phrase is not used in that way anywhere. By the same reasoning the wisdom of Christ grew even after the resurrection and grows in heaven, whereas it could not, and cannot, be said to grow in the same way as the wisdom of a child. Christ, seeing a fig tree from afar as having leaves, went to it, intending to see whether he might find anything on it (edible, namely) (Mark 11:13). Therefore he did not know whether the tree had edible fruit or not. The sacred writers report this as a real event, not a pretended one, truly and not in appearance, without any trace of the pretence some attribute to Christ here. For what purpose would that labour otherwise serve, the turning aside from the road, the walk to the tree, the inquiry, and indeed the inquiry whether it might have anything, or, as others say, perhaps something? Otherwise the miracle would have proceeded without effort, and indeed could have grown greater, if he had shown himself God by knowing the distant tree without going to it, and so being God not only from near [מקרוב] but also from afar [מרחוק] (Jer. 23:23). And to say more: the Son is also said not to know the day of judgement (Mark 13:32), not in worth [κατ' ἀξιαν] but in truth [κατ' ἀληθειαν], according to practice or experience, not according to knowledge, as some babble following Epiphanius. For who can know anything not in truth? It is just the same as to see without sight or to love without love. He who knows in truth must necessarily know. The example of Adam and Eve, who after sin knew themselves to be naked, does nothing to the point; they knew it in worth, but before sin they did not know it in truth, in that sense. For before sin they did not know that they were so naked that nakedness was shameful to them, as it became after sin. But to say that the Son of God did not know the day of judgement, in order to tell others, is a bold distortion of words, which would imply that one could rightly say the Father too did not know it, since he did not wish to reveal it to anyone (Acts 1:7). And yet Christ, the mouth of truth, said that the Father knew it. It is certainly unheard of to say without lying "I do not know," meaning "I will not tell." Therefore Ambrose rightly says on Luke 17: he knew the end of the times not through the nature of man but through the nature of God. Nor does it stand in the way that the Spirit of wisdom rested upon Christ (Isa. 11:2), that he was anointed above his fellows (Ps. 45:8), anointed with the Holy Spirit and power (Acts 10:38), and that he received the Spirit without measure (John 3:34). For Isaiah speaks of the hypostatic, effecting union, by which all the fullness of the Deity dwells in Christ; and the Spirit of wisdom and the anointing in Christ as man posit wisdom, but do not exclude its increase; indeed they help it. For nothing prevents wisdom which is perfect in first act and intensively from being increased in second act, by extension to new objects. Moreover, that Spirit without measure is attributed neither to Christ, nor is it all measure, but only the ordinary kind, such as is in his fellows, re-

units.la: movet. Etiam fidelibus N.T. competit Spiritus sine mensura, tali videlicet, qualem Deus Patribus admensus est; stillatim, non pleno alveo, flumine integro. Qui credit in me, sicut dicit Scriptura, flumina aquae vivae ex ventre ipsius fluent. Hoc autem dixit de Spiritu illo, quem accepturi erant credentes in eum, ibid.VII.38.39. De quo Spiritu fidelibus sine mensura dato Christum ibid.III.34. loqui verisimilius est.
units.tr: ...moves. Spirit without measure is also given to the faithful of the New Testament, namely of the same kind that God measured out to the Fathers: by drops, not in a full channel, not as a whole river. "He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" (John 7:38–39). He spoke this of that Spirit which believers in him were to receive. It is more probable that Christ also spoke, in John 3:34, of this Spirit, given to the faithful without measure.

units.la: XLV. De dotibus corporis Christi, impassibilitate, subtilitate, levitate, invisibilitate inprimis Veteres & recentiores disceptant. Et Passibilitas quidem sic a peccato est, ut tamen in vitio non sit. Proin corpus Christi ante Resurrectionem πασχοντος passibile fuit, at post resurrectionem απαθες impassibile est; ut nihil ei noxam vel dolorem afferre possit. Improbamus ergo tum veteres haereticos, qualescunque illi sint; tum Hilarium etiam, quibus persuasum fuit, ab ipso nativitatis momento Christi corpus nullis passionibus obnoxium fuisse: Docetas praecipue, qui in tota ista oeconomia Passionis Christi nihil non ludicrum, & ex composito gestum asserunt. Sed histrioniam hanc tota Scriptura, & fidei analogia refellit. Non habemus Pontificem, qui non possit compati cum infirmitatibus nostris, tentatus in omnibus similiter sine peccato, Hebr.IV.15. Subtilitas molem omnem corporis auferens, Christi corpori non competit, quia est contra naturam corporis, cujus est habere partes extra partes. Etiam quae subtilitas molem corporis humani minuit, in statu exinanitionis eidem corpori Christi non competiit, quia corpus nostro simile in omnibus, atque adeo nutritum iisdem cibis, ex quibus substantia non quanta augeri non potuisset; habuit. Post resurrectionem vero hac terrenae molis importunitate deposita corpus ejus longe subtilius factum concedimus: non tamen absolute subtile; quia non transiit in naturam Spiritus, sed quantitatem & extensionem retinuit, quin & tactui visuique obnoxium fuit. Nam quae de corpore Christi, dimensiones corporum, velut sepulchri, januarum clausarum penetrante Pontificii tradunt, nullius pretii sunt. Levitatis eadem, quae subtilitatis ratio est. Nam quod super aquas Christus ambulasse Matth. XIV.25.26. dicitur, non magis corpus Christi non ponderosum fuisse arguit, quam non ponderosum fuit corpus Petri, qui ibid.v.29. ἐπὶ τὰ ὕδατα super aquas ambulasse dicitur. Nempe etiam ponderosa aquis superstant, vel natura, ut lignum, vel arte, ut animantia. Facilimum Deo est sustentare corpus quodcunque grave, uti etiam Elizaei securim sustentavit. Forte etiam miraculum in aquis Divinitus solidatis fuit, uti Hieronymus, Theophylactus & alii arbitrantur. Denique nec Invisibilitas talis Christi corpori competit, ut oculis corporeis, recte ad visum dispositis, videri non possit; quia corpus Christi tum ante, tum post resurrectionem ἀόρατον visum esse, non per accidens, uti Angeli per alienas formas visi sunt, & Deus per effecta videtur, sed per se, satis ex I.Joh.I.1. Act.I.3. I.Cor.XV.5.6. liquet. Quod vero διὰ τῆς θύρας transiit per mediam turbam, Luc.IV.30. non invisibilitatem corporis ejus, sed securitatem populi arguit. Nam sine fuga, sine festinatione, tione, per medios hostes, gravi & lento gradu processit. Sed & ἀφανῶ non ἀοξῶ ibid. XXIV. 31. dicitur, eo sensu, quo Anacreon de hirundine dixit: χειμῶνι δ' ἡ ἀφανὴς ἡ Νάξου, ἡ ἐπὶ Μέμφιν, Hieme ēs invisibilis (non apparens) velapud Nilum, velapud Memphin.
units.tr: XLV. The ancient and more recent writers dispute chiefly the endowments of Christ's body: impassibility, subtlety, lightness and invisibility. Passibility is indeed tied to sin, yet is not itself a vice. Accordingly, Christ's body before the Resurrection was passible, being subject to suffering (πασχοντος), but after the Resurrection it is impassible (ἀπαθες), so that nothing can bring it harm or pain. We therefore reject both the ancient heretics, whoever they were, and also Hilary, who were persuaded that from the very moment of his birth Christ's body was subject to no sufferings. The Docetists especially, who assert that in the whole economy of Christ's Passion nothing was real, but everything was a play and a pretended act. But the whole of Scripture and the analogy of faith refute this stage-play: "We have not a high priest who cannot sympathise with our infirmities, but was tempted in all things as we are, yet without sin" (Heb. 4:15). Subtlety, which removes all bulk from a body, does not belong to Christ's body, because it is contrary to the nature of a body, which is to have parts outside parts. Nor did that subtlety which diminishes the bulk of a human body belong to the same body of Christ in the state of humiliation, because his body, like ours in every respect, and nourished by the same foods, had a substance that could not be increased without quantity; it had that. After the Resurrection, however, with this earthly burden of bulk laid aside, we grant that his body became far more subtle; yet not absolutely subtle, because it did not pass into the nature of spirit, but retained quantity and extension, and indeed was still open to touch and sight. For what the Papists teach about the body of Christ, that the dimensions of bodies, as of a sepulchre or of closed doors, were penetrated, is of no worth. The reasoning for lightness is the same as for subtlety. For that Christ is said to have walked "upon the waters" (Matt. 14:25–26) proves no more that Christ's body was not heavy than that Peter's body was not heavy, of whom it is said that he walked "upon the waters" (ἐπὶ τὰ ὕδατα) (ibid. v. 29). Indeed, even heavy things stand upon water, either by nature, like wood, or by art, like ships. It is very easy for God to sustain any heavy body whatever, as he also sustained Elisha's axe. Perhaps the miracle lay in waters Divinely made solid, as Jerome, Theophylact and others suppose. Finally, invisibility of such a kind as cannot be seen by bodily eyes properly placed for sight does not belong to Christ's body. For that Christ's body, both before and after the Resurrection, was invisible (ἀόρατον) and could be seen, not accidentally, as angels were seen in borrowed forms, and God is seen through his effects, but in itself, is clear enough from 1 John 1:1, Acts 1:3, 1 Cor. 15:5–6. That he passed "through the door" (διὰ τῆς θύρας) through the midst of the crowd (Luke 4:30) proves not the invisibility of his body but the safety of his person: for he went on without flight, without haste, through the midst of enemies, with a heavy and slow step. Moreover, in Luke 24:31 he is said to have become "unseen" (ἀφανῶς), not "unseen" in the sense of "invisible", but in the sense in which Anacreon spoke of the swallow: "in winter, the one unseen (not appearing), whether by Naxos or by Memphis" [χειμῶνι δ' ἡ ἀφανὴς ἡ Νάξου, ἡ ἐπὶ Μέμφιν].

units.la: XLVI. Mutua communio, seu communicatio est in Persona Christi; eaque triplex, tum idiomatum, tum officii, tum operationum.
units.tr: XLVI. There is a mutual communion, or communication, in the Person of Christ; and it is threefold: of idioms, of office, and of operations.

units.la: Communicatio idiomatum est, qua utriusque Naturæ proprietates Personæ communicantur. Veteres κοινωνίαν τῶν ὀνομάτων communionem nominum; recentiores κοινωνίαν τῶν ἰδιωμάτων communionem proprietatum, hoc est, sicut naturæ, ita etiam utriusque naturæ proprietatum essentialium communionem in persona, eámque consequentem prædicationem de persona vocant. Est enim communicatio idiomatum veritas tum denominationis personæ ab utraque natura, quippe utramque habentis, & per utramque agentis: tum prædicationis eorum, quæ utriusq; naturæ sunt, de persona ab alterutra, Divina vel Humana natura, denominata. Quam Veteres ... nominarunt, quisque ut sibi visum est, rem insusitatam, sed non inusitata prædicatione explicare conatus. Neque enim magis inusitata prædicatio est, cùm Filium Dei, Filium Hominis, vel Radicem Jessæ & Davidis, hoc est, eum, unde & Jesse & David originem habet, genus Davidis, vel natum ex Virgine Filium Dei & hominis prædicamus, quàm cùm eundem hominem φυσικῶν & χοικῶν, intelligentem, volentem, loquentem, ambulantem, morientem, & post mortem in sinum Abrahæ receptum: vel Gabrielem Angelum, Spiritum ministrantem, Mariæ locutum, & ab eadem visum prædicamus.
units.tr: The communication of idioms is that by which the properties of each nature are communicated to the Person. The ancients called it communion of names (κοινωνίαν τῶν ὀνομάτων); the more recent writers call it communion of properties (κοινωνίαν τῶν ἰδιωμάτων), that is, the communion, in the one person, of the essential properties of both natures, just as of the natures themselves, and the predication consequent upon it, which is made of the person. For the communication of idioms is the truth both of the denomination of the person from each nature, since he has both and acts through both, and of the predication of those things which belong to either nature, made of the person from one or other nature, the Divine or the Human. The Ancients named this ... each as seemed best to him, trying to explain an unusual matter by an unusual predication. For it is no more unusual to predicate of the Son of God, the Son of Man, or the Root of Jesse and David (that is, him from whom both Jesse and David have their origin), the Son of David, or the Son of God and man born of the Virgin, than to predicate of the same man that he is psychical and earthly [ψυχικῶν καὶ χοϊκῶν], understanding, willing, speaking, walking, dying, and after death received into the bosom of Abraham; or to say that the Angel Gabriel, a ministering spirit, spoke to Mary and was seen by her.

units.la: XLVII. Sed ut rem tot disputationum tricis & nebulis involutam, felicius evolvamus, notandum, nomina Christi alia personam absolutè significare, alia per se alterius naturæ propria esse. Prioris generis sunt, quæcunque per se utrique Naturæ communia sunt. Cujusmodi sunt nomina Jesu, Christi, Mediatoris, Redemptoris & similia, ab officio, cujus gratia Christus incarnatus est, petita. Posterioris vel abstracta, vel concreta sunt. Illa sunt substantiva, velut Θεότης Deitas, ἀνθρωπότης Humanitas, &c. Hæc Deus, Homo, Filius Dei, Filius Hominis. In his tribus Nominum ordinibus, qui primus est, nunquam nisi totam personam, qui tertius, nunquam nisi alterutram naturam; qui secundus, modò Personam, modò Naturam promiscuè designat. Et scripturis quidem abstracta rariora, semel tantùm Θεότης Deitas Col. II. 9. semel Θεότης Divinitas Rom. I. 20. At in Ecclesiæ usu frequentiora, propter hæreticos, inveniuntur. Idiomata porro appellantur, quæcunque naturis inter se comparando oppositis propria sunt. quomodo Divinæ æternitas, infinitas, omnipotentia: Humanæ mortalitas, localitas, visibilitas, & hujusmodi alia conveniunt. Hæc idiomata de uno eodémque Christo prædicantur, quia uni eidemque conveniunt, haud secus ac omne genus attributorum de suo subjecto prædicari solet, ut supra confirmavimus. Sed pro variis tamen nominibus prædicationis ratio variat. Et naturarum quidem nomina abstracta de se invicem non prædicantur. Neque enim recta prædicatio est; Deitas est Humanitas, & vicissim, quia abstracta non tam quid res sit, quàm rationem, qua id sit, significant, quomodo albedo non parietem album, sed rationem, propter quam paries albus est, significat. De se invicem ergo talia sine rerum inter se distinctarum essentiali & interna ratione confusa prædicari nullo modo possunt. Neque etiam unius naturæ nomen abstractum de alterius nomine concreto, vel vicissim rectè prædicatur. Quomodo Deitas esse homo, vel Humanitas Deus dici non potest, quia sic in Christo naturæ oppositæ distingui non possent; Velut si candor esset niger, per candorem paries albus à nigro distingui non posset. His remotis, sola naturarum nomina concreta de se invicem, propter unionem hypostaticam, prædicari possunt, quia sola hæc non præcisè formalitatem entis, sed ipsum ens, hoc est, formalitatem cum omnibus adjunctis & circumstantiis, quibus persona constituitur, & ab aliis distinguitur, significant. Ita qui Alexandrum Victorem Asiæ dicit, aliud quàm Victoriam Asiæ dicit; quia uno & eodem vocabulo illo designatur hominis individuum, Philippi Regis & Olympiadis filius, Rex Macedonum. Tam verè igitur Deus, hoc est, persona, in qua Deitas simul & humanitas est, ex Virgine natus dici potest: quàm verè Victor Asiæ ex Olympiade natus dicitur. Proin nec inusitata, nec ἄλογον vel absurda hæc locutio est. Hoc solum interest, quòd cùm Deus & Homo nomina sint naturarum, non tantùm per se & inter se disparatarum, sed etiam completarum & perfectarum, exemplum prædicationis simile nullum in rerum natura dari potest, ac ne hominis quidem, quia licèt constet anima & corpore, naturis duabus toto genere disparatis, tamen nemo animam corpus, vel corpus animam dixit, quia hæc nomina sunt naturarum incompletarum, quarum neutra ὑφισάμενον constituere potest: adeóque iis nominibus, quæ abstracta diximus, respondent. Si tamen ab iis concreta declines, similitudo constabit. Sic enim de Petro rectè dixeris: Hoc animal est rationale: & Hoc rationale est animal. Idiomatum porro nomina de naturarum nominibus abstractis nulla nisi sua de suis prædicantur, non de alienis aliena. Ita Deitas omnipotens, sed non passa; Humanitas corporea, mortalis, sed non æterna, dicitur. Abstracta enim cùm rationem essendi significent, hæ phrases significant, rationem idiomatum esse ejus naturæ, quæ nominatur. At qui nec ratio patiendi est in Deitate, nec ratio æternitatis in humanitate. Sed legitimè idiomata quæcunque de tota persona, utramque naturam comprehendente, prædicantur. Sicu-sitatissima est prædicatio: Homo est rationalis, visibilis, &c. ab altera hominis parte, quæ una cum opposita hominem constituit. Sed id dupliciter fit, prout persona vel communibus, vel propriis naturarum nominibus designatur. Priori modo Christus, Mediator mortuus & redivivus; posteriore Deus mortuus, homo omnipotens dicitur. Utraque phrases per κοινωνίαν ἰδιωμάτων significantur; sed posterioribus Damascenus peculiariter nomen ἀνθρωπότης, θεάνθρωπἀνθρώπους impositus. Utrisque inest tropus synecdoches; sed in ἀντιδόσει tropus geminatus, cùm non tantùm persona tota cognominatur ab idiomate alterutrius naturæ, sed etiam ipsa persona per alteram naturam significatur. Itaque non raro occurrunt hujusmodi phraseon limitationes sine explicatione, veluti cùm Christus dicitur mortificatus carne, 1.Pet. III.18. pro nobis passus carne, ibid.IV.1. Filius Dei factus ex Davide secundum carnem, Rom.1.3. Crucifixus ex infirmitate, 2.Cor.XIII.4. Hinc celeberrimus ille Canon, quem his verbis Justinus Martyr in Expositione fidei concepit: Cùm audiveris de eodem Filio (ἐναντίας φωνὰς) contrarias voces, distribue naturis sua quaeque dicta. si quid magnum est & Divinum, assignans Divinae naturae: si quid verò exiguum & humanum, humanae.
units.tr: XLVII. But in order to unfold more happily a matter entangled in the snares and mists of so many disputations, it must be noted that some names of Christ signify the person absolutely, while others belong to him by reason of one nature alone. Of the first kind are all those which are common to both natures in themselves. Such are the names Jesus, Christ, Mediator, Redeemer and similar ones, taken from the office for whose sake Christ was made flesh. Of the second kind some are abstract, others concrete. The abstract ones are substantives, such as Θεότης (Deity), ἀνθρωπότης (Humanity), etc. The concrete ones are God, Man, Son of God, Son of Man. Of these three orders of names, the first always designates only the whole person; the third always designates only one or other nature; the second designates now the Person and now the Nature indifferently. In Scripture the abstract names are rarer: Θεότης (Deity) occurs once, in Col. 2:9, and Θεότης (Divinity) once in Rom. 1:20. But in the usage of the Church they are more frequent, on account of the heretics. Moreover, those things are called idioms which belong to each nature when compared with the other opposed nature, such as eternity, infinity and omnipotence of the Divine, and mortality, locality, visibility and other such things of the Human. These idioms are predicated of one and the same Christ, because they belong to one and the same subject, just as every kind of attribute is customarily predicated of its subject, as we have confirmed above. Yet the manner of predication varies according to the different names. The abstract names of the natures are not predicated of each other. For it is not a right predication to say "Deity is Humanity" or the reverse, because abstract names signify not so much what a thing is as the reason by which it is so; just as "whiteness" signifies not a white wall but the reason on account of which the wall is white. Therefore such things cannot be predicated of each other in any way without confusing the essential and inner reason of things distinct from one another. Nor is the abstract name of one nature rightly predicated of the concrete name of the other, or the reverse. Thus Deity cannot be called "man", nor Humanity "God", because in that case the opposed natures in Christ could not be distinguished; as if whiteness were black, the white wall could not be distinguished from the black. These being set aside, only the concrete names of the natures can be predicated of each other, on account of the hypostatic union, because these alone signify not merely the formality of being, but being itself, that is, the formality with all the adjuncts and circumstances by which a person is constituted and distinguished from others. Thus he who says "Alexander the Conqueror of Asia" says something other than "the Victory of Asia"; because by that one word is designated the individual man, son of King Philip and Olympias, King of the Macedonians. Therefore it can be said just as truly that God, that is, the person in whom Deity and humanity are together, was born of the Virgin, as it is truly said that the Conqueror of Asia was born of Olympias. Hence this way of speaking is neither unusual, nor ἄλογον [unreasonable] nor absurd. Only this differs: since God and Man are names of natures not only disparate in themselves and with respect to each other, but also complete and perfect, no similar example of predication can be found in the nature of things, not even in the case of man. For although man consists of soul and body, two natures wholly disparate in kind, nobody has called the soul "body" or the body "soul", because these are names of incomplete natures, neither of which can constitute a subsistent (ὑφισάμενον [ὑφιστάμενον]); and so they correspond to the names which we called abstract. If, however, you decline from those to the concrete names, the similarity will hold. Thus you may rightly say of Peter: "This animal is rational", and "This rational thing is an animal". Moreover, the names of the idioms are predicated of the abstract names of the natures only as their own of their own, not as alien of alien. Thus Deity is called "omnipotent but not suffering", and Humanity "corporeal and mortal but not eternal". For since abstract names signify the reason of being, such phrases signify that the reason of the idioms is of that nature which is named. But there is no reason for suffering in Deity, nor a reason for eternity in humanity. Rather, all idioms are legitimately predicated of the whole person, comprehending both natures. The most common predication is: "Man is rational, visible," etc., from the other part of man, which together with the opposite constitutes man. This happens in two ways, according as the person is designated by the common or by the proper names of the natures. In the former way Christ is called "the Mediator who died and rose again"; in the latter, "God who died" and "man who is omnipotent". Both phrases are signified by the communion of idioms; but to the latter, John of Damascus gave the peculiar name "theanthropos" [θεάνθρωπος]. Both contain the trope of synecdoche; but in the antidosis [ἀντιδόσει] the trope is doubled, since not only is the whole person named from the idiom of one or other nature, but the person itself is also signified through the other nature. Hence there often occur, without explanation, limitations of such phrases, as when Christ is said to have been "put to death in the flesh" (1 Pet. 3:18), "to have suffered for us in the flesh" (ibid. 4:1), "to have been made the Son of God from the seed of David according to the flesh" (Rom. 1:3), "to have been crucified through weakness" (2 Cor. 13:4). Hence that celebrated canon, which Justin Martyr framed in these words in his Exposition of the Faith: "When you hear of the same Son contrary expressions (ἐναντίας φωνὰς), distribute to the natures what belongs to each. If something is great and Divine, assign it to the Divine nature; but if something is small and human, to the human nature."

units.la: XLVIII. Communicatio haec idiomatum respectu personae realis, respectu naturarum verbalis est.
units.tr: XLVIII. This communication of properties is real with respect to the person, but verbal with respect to the natures.

units.la: Realis est respectu Personae, quia persona utriusque naturae proprietates sibi vendicat. Cùm enim suae cuique naturae realiter insint proprietates, & toti personae utraque natura etiam insit, necesse est, toti personae realiter inesse proprietates utriusque naturae. Quemadmodum quia candor dentibus Æthiopis realiter inest, & dentes realiter insunt Æthiopi, etiam candor realiter Æthiopi inest; atque inde Æthiops albus dentes realiter dicitur. Respectu verò Naturarum non realis, sed verbalis est, quia una natura suas proprietates in aliam minimè transfert. Alias enim idiomata desinerent esse idiomata. Nam quod proprium est, commune dici nequit. Velut si Deitas realiter mortua esset, mors humanitatis propria esse desineret. Tum Deitatis attributa nihil aliud quàm Deitas sunt; quia non sicut corpus à pondere corporis; ita Deitas ab immensitate sua differt. Si igitur proprietates Deitatis Humanitati realiter communicarentur, ipsa Deitatis essentia ei communicaretur, neque amplius Humanitas, sed Deitas esset. Cùm ergo Deus mortuus, Homo omnipotens dicitur, vel personaliter, vel reduplicativè ita dicitur. Personaliter, quòd persona, quae Deus est, mortua sit; quae Homo est, omnipotens sit, quae realis & verissima praedicatio est. Reduplicativè, quòd homo, quatenus homo, omnipotens; Deus quatenus Deus, mortuus sit. quae praedicatio salsissima est. Unionem enim salvis naturarum proprietatibus factam esse, rectè Chalcedonensis confessio, uti supra vidimus, asseruit.
units.tr: It is real with respect to the Person, because the person claims for itself the properties of both natures. For since each nature really has its own properties, and both natures are really in the whole person, the properties of both natures must really belong to the whole person. Just as whiteness is really in an Ethiopian's teeth, and the teeth are really in the Ethiopian, so whiteness is really in the Ethiopian too, and so the Ethiopian is really called white-toothed. With respect to the natures, however, it is not real but verbal, because one nature does not transfer its properties into the other. Otherwise these properties would cease to be properties. For what is proper to one cannot be called common. For example, if the Deity were really dead, death would cease to be a property of the humanity. Again, the attributes of the Deity are nothing other than the Deity itself, since, unlike body and weight, the Deity does not differ from its immensity. If, then, the properties of the Deity were really communicated to the humanity, the very essence of the Deity would be communicated to it, and it would no longer be humanity but Deity. Therefore when God is said to have died, or Man to be almighty, this is said either personally or reduplicatively. It is said personally, because the person who is God has died, and the person who is man is almighty; this is a real and most true predication. It is said reduplicatively, because man, as man, is almighty, and God, as God, has died; this predication is most absurd. For the Chalcedonian confession rightly asserted, as we saw above, that the union was made with the properties of the natures preserved.

units.la: XLIX. Communio Officii & Honoris est, quòd Christus secundum utramque naturam Mediator est inter Deum & Homines. Unus Deus, unus Mediator Dei & Hominum, Homo Jesus Christus, 1.Tim.II.5. Mihi data est omnis potestas in Coelo & in terra, Matth.XXVIII.18. Potestatem dedit ei judicium faciendi, quia filius hominis est, Joh.V.27. Propterea Deus eum superexaltavit, & gratificatus ei est nomen super omne nomen, ut in nomine Jesu omne genu se flectat, Phil.II.9.10. Quam communionem tum συνπαθῆ Officii, ab utraque natura, & utriusque naturae operationibus dependentia, velut cùm sanguis Christi ab omnibus peccatis nos purificare, 1.Joh.I.7. Deus Ecclesiam proprio sanguine acquisivisse. Act.XX.28. dicitur: tum unitas cultus seu adorationis, quae propter officium Mediatorium ad Christum Θεάνθρωπον dirigitur, evincunt. L. Ex Officii Mediatorii communione Operationum Communio resultat. Nam Christi Θεανθρωπικὰς actiones & passiones Mediatoriae, quas Θεανθρωπικὰς Graeci appellant; & à persona & ab utraque ejus natura dependent. Sed recte Damascenus, qui eam solidè explicavit, lib. III.15. Ἰσὸν, inquit, ὡς ἄλλο ἐστιν ἐνέργεια, καὶ ἄλλο ἐνεργούμενον, καὶ ἄλλο ἐνέργημα, καὶ ἄλλο ὁ ἐνεργῶν. Sciendum est, quòd in his aliud sit operatio, aliud activum, seu operationis principium, aliud opus, aliud operans. Et ἐνέργεια operatio quidem est actio seu operatio utriusque naturae, Divinae & Humanae, efficax: ἐνεργητικὸν activum, seu principium actionis internum & formale utraque natura Christi: ἐνέργημα opus id, quod actione hac producitur, & συνπαθὲς seu perfectio ab utraque natura operis nomine venit: ἐνεργῶν operans tota persona Mediatoris. jus αὐθεντία & ἐξουσία in docendo. Hoc verò communio hæc operationum & operum singulare habet, quòd tam ipsæ ἐνέργειαι, quàm ἐνεργήματα Christi de eo passim in Scripturis non in concreto duntaxat, sed etiam in abstracto prædicantur. In concreto, velut cùm Scriptura dicit: Per unum hominem justi constituuntur multi, Rom.V.19. Deus redemit Ecclesiam, Act.XX.28. In abstracto cùm Christus dicit: Panis, quem ego dabo, caro mea est, quam ego dabo pro mundi vita, Joh.VI.51. Sanguis Jesu Christi, Filii Dei, purificat nos ab omni peccato, 1.Joh.I.7. Ipse est ἱλασμὸς propitiatio, seu sacrificium propitiatorium pro peccatis nostris, ibid.II.2. Nam & persona, & naturæ, opera illa, per ἐνέργειαν utrique naturæ competentem, producunt.
units.tr: XLIX. The communion of office and honour is that Christ, according to both natures, is Mediator between God and men: One God, one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, 1 Tim. 2:5. All power is given to me in heaven and on earth, Matt. 28:18. He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of man, John 5:27. Therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, Phil. 2:9–10. This communion, which depends on each nature and on the operations of each, is shown both by the sympathetic character of the office (as when the blood of Christ cleanses us from all sins, 1 John 1:7, and God is said to have acquired the Church with his own blood, Acts 20:28), and by the unity of the worship or adoration which, because of the mediatorial office, is directed to Christ the God-man. L. From the communion of the mediatorial office there follows a communion of operations. For the mediatorial actions and passions of Christ, which the Greeks call theanthropic [Θεανθρωπικὰς], depend on the person and on each of his natures. Damascene, who explained this soundly, says well (Book 3, ch. 15): "Know that in these things the operation [ἐνέργεια] is one thing, the thing operated [ἐνεργούμενον] another, the effect [ἐνέργημα] another, and the agent [ἐνεργῶν] another." That is: the operation is the efficacious action or working of both natures, divine and human; the active principle [ἐνεργητικὸν] is the internal and formal principle of action in each nature of Christ; the effect [ἐνέργημα] is the work produced by the action, and the sympathetic or perfected result is attributed to each nature under the name of the work; the agent [ἐνεργῶν] is the whole person of the Mediator, with the authority [αὐθεντία] and power [ἐξουσία] in teaching. This communion of operations and works has this peculiarity: the operations themselves [ἐνέργειαι] and the effects [ἐνεργήματα] of Christ are predicated of him throughout the Scriptures, not only in the concrete but also in the abstract. In the concrete, as when Scripture says: By the one man many shall be made righteous, Rom. 5:19, and God redeemed the Church, Acts 20:28. In the abstract, as when Christ says: The bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world, John 6:51; the blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from all sin, 1 John 1:7; He himself is the propitiation [ἱλασμὸς], that is, the propitiatory sacrifice, for our sins, ibid. 2:2. For both the person and the natures produce those works, through the operation [ἐνέργειαν] belonging to each nature.

units.la: LI. Unionis naturarum in Persona Christi manifestatio facta est in ejusdem Nativitate, cùm Virgo Maria expleto mensium ordinariorum spatio, Christum, Filium suum, Bethlehemi in lucem edidit.
units.tr: LI. The manifestation of the union of the natures in the person of Christ took place at his nativity, when the Virgin Mary, after the ordinary span of months had been completed, brought forth Christ her Son at Bethlehem.

units.la: Et tempus partus ordinarium fuisse, testatur Lucas, ajens, impletos fuisse dies ἡ ἡμέραι ut parerent, cap.II.6. & modus pariendi ordinarius fuit. Idem enim Lucas v.22. &c. docet, observatam circa infantem fuisse legem Exod.XIII.2. XXII.29. XXXIV.19. Num.III.13. VIII.16.17. de primogenitis uterum aperientibus, Deo sacrandis, jugulans quasi apocryphum illud commentum recentiorum Scholæ Pontificiæ sciolorum, qui decernere ausi sunt, Christum non νόμῳ κυήσεως, uti Nazianzenus loquitur, hoc est, more pariendi reliquorum hominum, educto per naturales meatus corpore, sed penetrante, instar radiorum Solis per vitreos cancellos, natum esse. Quod multeum dogma etiam Xavierium Indis suis propinasse, Historia ejus à Lud.de Dieu Latinè reddita testatur. Theophylacto contra visum est, Christum solum uterum matris aperuisse, cùm aliis matribus vir vulvam aperiat; adeóque legem in solo eo impletam esse. At impletam esse constat: in solo, non item. Accedit veri corporis humani Christi modus, qui cum hujus penetratione consistere non potest, quia à corpore separari non potest occupatio loci, qua differentia corpus à spiritu disparatur. Quòd verò Virginitatem cum fractis Virginis claustris consistere posse, iidem inficiantur, inconsiderate faciunt; quia Virginitas non ex integritate partium corporis, quæ per accidens multis modis violari potest; sed ex concubitus abstinentia definitur. Ut verè Virgo dicatur, quæ virum non cognovit. Rectè Tertullianus de carne Christi: Virgo, inquit, fuit, quantum à viro, non quantum à partu. Si nihil de Virginitate partus delibavit, quid claustrorum apertio delibare potuit? Hæc taceri poterant, nisi error adversantium gangrænam haberet.
units.tr: Luke testifies that the time of the birth was the ordinary one, saying that the days were fulfilled that she should be delivered (ch. 2:6), and the manner of birth was also ordinary. For Luke likewise teaches (2:22 etc.) that the law of Exodus 13:2, 22:29, 34:19, Numbers 3:13, 8:16–17, concerning the firstborn who open the womb and are to be consecrated to God, was observed with regard to the infant. In this he refutes that spurious fiction of the half-learned men of the recent Papist school, who have dared to decree that Christ was born not by the law of conception [νόμῳ κυήσεως], as Nazianzen puts it, that is, by the usual manner of other men, the body being brought forth through the natural passages, but by penetrating, like rays of the sun through glass lattices. The history of Xavier, translated into Latin by Ludovicus de Dieu, testifies that this very widely held dogma was also poured out to his Indians. Theophylact thought that Christ alone opened his mother's womb, whereas with other mothers a man opens the vulva; and so the law was fulfilled in him alone. But it is clear that it was fulfilled in him, not that it was fulfilled in him alone. Moreover, the mode of a true human body, which belongs to Christ, cannot be reconciled with such penetration, because the occupation of place cannot be separated from a body, and this is the difference by which body is distinguished from spirit. As for the claim of the same men that virginity can be compatible with a broken virginal enclosure, they are inconsiderate; for virginity is not defined by the integrity of the parts of the body, which may in many ways be violated by accident, but by abstinence from intercourse, so that she is truly called a virgin who has not known a man. Tertullian rightly said of the flesh of Christ: She was a virgin, he says, as far as concerns a man, not as far as concerns the birth. If nothing was taken from the virginity by the birth, how could the opening of the enclosure take anything from it? These things might be passed over in silence, were it not that the error of our opponents has a gangrene.

units.la: LII. Quoad tempus Nativitatis Christi, id ante omnia certa fide tenendum est, post Jesum ex Maria Virgine ante annos plus minus MDCXCIV. (quo ipsi hæc scribo) natum, non fuisse ultra cum Judæis infidelibus expectandum adventum Christi primum, quia jam tum coepit πλήρωμα ἡ καιρὸς plenitudo illa temporis, ultra quam prænuntiatus oraculis Propheticis temporis articulus Messiæ in carne exhibitionem differre non patiebatur. Ad muniendam porro hanc fidem necessaria est aliqua non nimis vaga determinatio anni natalis Christi, post quem alium Messiam Judæi frustra expectant; quia Messias advenisse credi non potest citra aliquam temporis epocham creditam, circa quam advenerit. Est autem hic commune quasi symbolum fidei Christianæ, Æra Dionysiana, authore Dionysio Exiguo, Abbate Romano edita; cujus annus MDCXCIV. currit. Quam Æram licèt biennio fere breviorem Chronologi emunctiorum narium asserant, tamen illa ab omnibus & singulis Christianis, quantumvis in sectas scissis, calculum valde ἀγχίθυρον habere creditur. Ut tantùm non hæc discors concordia sit, à Nativitate Christi currere jam Annum MDCXCIV vel MDCXCVI. Ad Theologiam verò & fidem Christianam à scandalo irreconciliabili discordiæ de tempore Nativitatis Christi vindicandam, minùs prudens esse videtur tractatio quæstionis de tempore adventus Christi, si quæras, quo Anno Mundi Christus natus sit. Sic enim, præter necessitatem Chronologiæ, dissensiones augentur, & qui accuratissimè de anno natali Christi consentiunt, dissentire videntur, ex eo fonte, quòd alibi, partim de anno natali Abrahami, partim de annis Regni Persici dissentiunt. Rectius longè faciunt, qui omnia mundi tempora principaliter ad Epocham Passionis Christi unanimi fere consensu, in æræ Dionysianæ annum XXXIII. incidentis, referunt, numeris annorum mundi, non à mundo condito, porro, sed ad mundum conditum, retro numeratis. De cætero non negligendi sunt characteres temporis, quos Scriptura ipsa exhibet, velut cùm Luc.III.1.2. &c. Johannes baptizasse apud Jordanem anno decimo quinto Principatus Tiberii Cæsaris &c. & eodem tempore Jesus ab eodem baptizatus fuisse ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα circiter annorum triginta, ibid. v.23. dicitur; cùm Christus Bethlehemi natus innuitur eo tempore, quo Augusto Imperatore, Cyrenæo, seu Quirino Procuratore Syriæ πρώτη ἀπογραφὴ descriptio Orbis prima (non sub Augusto, sub quo alia præcesserit, sed sub Quirino, primùm extra ordinem missio eo tempore, quo ἐπίτροπος præfectus Syriæ fuit Sentius Saturninus) facta est, ibid.II.1.2.4. Nisi forte πρώτη scribitur pro πρωτοπρόσωπον, ut sensus sit, descriptionem hanc factam esse priùs, quàm Syriæ Quirinus præsideret. Quæ sententia Georgii Harvarti, Chronol. c.241.242. prolixè asserta, & à Viris Doctissimis, Kepplero, Reinesio, inprimis Jacobo Perizonio, eximii & quondam mihi amicissimi parentis Filio dignissimo, recepta & defensa, omnem difficultatem tollit. Quibus ex ratione temporum mediocri studio digestis, & ipso etiam Josepho Judæo ad partes vocato, arduum non erit tempus Christi natale ad calculos Æræ Dionysianæ revocare, & simul obelo configere perfidiam recentiorum Judæorum, Evangelistas & Jesu nostri tempus in suspicionem adducentium, calido callidòque invento, quòd Jesus ex Josepho Pandera, anno sexcentesimo septuagesimo primo quarto ab orbe condito millenarii, in diebus Jannæi Regis, quem aliàs Alexandrum vocant, adeóque octoginta novem annis seriùs, quàm à Christianis creditur; natus fuerit. {y} Dei expressa haberet. fuerit. Uti inititio Stygii libri Toldos Jeschu dicitur; & in libro etiam Juchasin alibique habetur. Sed esse hoc mendacium a Diabolo, ad excaecandos & magis indurandos Judaeos, excogitatum, multa evincunt; velut quod id serae originis est, neque aliam quam magistralis traditionis hostium Jesu authoritatem habet: quod post centum & amplius annos demum Nazaraeorum, seu Christianorum nomen sub Cajo Caesare innotuit, & de discipulis illius Jesu Nazareni, qui sub Jannaeo fuerit, nec apud Josephum, nec in libris Thalmudicis vel apex extat: quod Josephus Antiq.lib.XVIII. 4. Jesum pro Christo habitum ad tempora Pilati refert, & ibid.lib.XX.8. fratrem ejus Jacobum jussu Annani Sadducaei sub Albino paulo ante bellum Judaicum lapidatum narrat: quod externus & nomini Christiano infensissimus hostis Tacitus A.XV.44. Christum Tiberio imperante per procuratorem Pontium Pilatum supplicio affectum scribit: quod si falsa essent, quae Evangelistae suo tempore de Jesu praedicarunt, Israelitae tot eo argumento, quod isthaec vidissent & audivissent, non credidissent, si nec vita ab iis, nec audita essent, quod in Thalmude, in Abodah Zarah sol.17. Rabbi Eliezer legispe ritus, cujus sunt capitula Eliezeris, qui ante excidium urbis anno circiter 85. natus est, cum uno ex discipulis Jesu, Jacobo collocutus inducitur. Conferri cum hisce merentur, quae Celeb. Wagenseilius Confut. libri Toldos Jeschu p. 20. veterem Jesum, qualis in Thalmude describitur, & novum, qualis in perditissimo libro Toldos Jeschu inducitur, comparans, scripsit. Qui etiam Sota cap.9. pag.1054. &c. dissertationem Samuelis Zevi, qua Jesum Nazarenum alium ab eo, qui in Thalmude memoratur, esse probare conatur, allegat, & cum aliis argumentis, tum testimonio etiam Abrahami Zachut in Juchasin, & Abenezra refellit.
units.tr: LII. As to the time of Christ's birth, this must above all be held with certain faith: Jesus, born of the Virgin Mary about 1694 years ago (as I write this), was not still to be awaited by the unbelieving Jews as their first coming of Christ, since already then πλήρωμα ἡ καιρὸς [the fullness of the time] had begun, beyond which the moment of time foretold by the prophetic oracles did not allow the manifestation of the Messiah in the flesh to be deferred. To fortify this faith, however, some not overly vague determination of the year of Christ's birth is necessary, after which the Jews vainly await another Messiah; for the Messiah cannot be believed to have come unless there is some believed epoch of time around which he came. Now the common, as it were, creed of the Christian faith here is the Dionysian Era, published by Dionysius Exiguus, a Roman abbot, whose year 1694 is now running. Although more acute chronologers assert that this Era is almost two years too long, nevertheless it is believed by all and each of the Christians, however split into sects, to have a reckoning ἀγχίθυρον [closely neighbouring]. So that, this discordant concord aside, from the birth of Christ the year 1694 or 1696 is now running. But for theology and the Christian faith to be vindicated from the irreconcilable scandal of discord about the time of Christ's birth, a treatment of the question of the time of Christ's coming seems less prudent if you ask in what year of the world Christ was born. For thus, beyond the necessity of chronology, dissensions are increased, and those who agree most exactly about the year of Christ's birth seem to disagree, from the source that elsewhere they differ partly about the birth year of Abraham and partly about the years of the Persian kingdom. Those do far better who refer all the times of the world principally to the epoch of Christ's Passion, which falls in the year 33 of the Dionysian Era, by an almost unanimous consensus, counting the years of the world not forward from the created world but backward to the created world. Moreover, the marks of time that Scripture itself provides must not be neglected, as when Luke 3:1, 2, etc. says that John baptized at the Jordan in the fifteenth year of the principate of Tiberius Caesar, etc., and that at the same time Jesus, baptized by him, was ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα [about thirty years old] (ibid. v. 23); when Christ is indicated as born at Bethlehem at the time when, under the Emperor Augustus, with Cyrenius, or Quirinus, as procurator of Syria, the πρώτη ἀπογραφὴ [first registration], the first enrolment of the world, was made (not under Augustus, under whom there was another earlier, but under Quirinus, the first sent outside the ordinary course, at the time when Sentius Saturninus was ἐπίτροπος [governor] of Syria), ibid. 2:1, 2, 4. Unless perhaps πρώτη is written for πρωτοπρόσωπον [the first person], so that the sense is that this registration was made before Quirinus presided over Syria. This opinion, expounded at length by Georg Horvath, Chronol. cc. 241, 242, and received and defended by the most learned men, Kepler, Reinesius, and above all Jacob Perizonius, most worthy son of that distinguished and once most dear parent of mine, removes every difficulty. With these matters of time arranged with moderate study, and with Josephus the Jew also brought into the argument, it will not be difficult to recall the birth of Christ to the reckoning of the Dionysian Era, and at the same time to pierce with the obelus the perfidy of recent Jews, who, with a hot and crafty invention, cast suspicion on the Evangelists and on the time of our Jesus, claiming that Jesus was born of Joseph Pandera in the year 671 of the fourth millennium from the founding of the world, in the days of King Jannaeus, whom elsewhere they call Alexander, and therefore eighty-nine years later than is believed by Christians. As is said at the beginning of the Stygian book Toldos Jeschu, and is also found in the book Juchasin and elsewhere. But many things prove that this is a lie invented by the Devil to blind and harden the Jews: for instance, that it is of late origin and has no authority beyond the magisterial tradition of the enemies of Jesus; that the name of the Nazarenes, or Christians, became known only after a hundred and more years, under Caius Caesar, and that of the disciples of that Jesus of Nazareth, who lived under Jannaeus, not even a trace survives either in Josephus or in the Talmudic books; that Josephus (Antiq. 18.4) refers to Jesus, regarded as Christ, as living in the times of Pilate, and (ibid. 20.8) relates that his brother James was stoned by order of Ananus the Sadducee under Albinus shortly before the Jewish war; that Tacitus, a foreign and most hostile enemy of the Christian name, writes (Ann. 15.44) that Christ was put to death under Tiberius by the procurator Pontius Pilate. If the things the Evangelists preached about Jesus in their own time were false, the Israelites would not have believed them on the ground that they had seen and heard these things, so many of them, if neither life nor hearing had been given them for this. Also, in the Talmud, in Abodah Zarah fol. 17, the rabbi Eliezer, the legalist, whose chapters are the Chapters of Eliezer, who was born about 85 years before the destruction of the city, is introduced in conversation with Jacob, one of the disciples of Jesus. Worthy to be compared with these are the things which the celebrated Wagenseil, in his Confutatio libri Toldos Jeschu, p. 20, wrote, comparing the old Jesus, as he is described in the Talmud, with the new Jesus, as he is introduced in the most wretched book Toldos Jeschu. He also, at Sota ch. 9, p. 1054 etc., cites the dissertation of Samuel Zevi, in which he tries to prove that the Jesus of Nazareth is other than the one mentioned in the Talmud, and refutes it both with other arguments and with the testimony of Abraham Zacuto in Juchasin, and of Abenezra.

units.la: LIII. Frustra esse videntur, qui etiam diem natalem Christi definiri posse autumant, quia deficiunt characteres chronologici authentici in Scriptura expresii, vel feriam septimanae, vel mensis diem indicantes. Imo ne quidem anni tempestas, sed sola nocturni temporis, quo natus Christus est, ne quidem expressa noctis vigilia Luc. II.8. indicatur. Nam quod die XXV. Decembris natum esse Romana Ecclesia ex antiquis tabulis censoriis, & publicis Romani Imperii Codicibus, a Senatorii generis hominibus, qui aut Christiani erant, aut postea facti sunt, inspectis & a Chrysostomo Serm. de Natali Christi allegatis definivit, consentientibus eidem Tileno, Montacutio Longio, aliis, temere factum vel eam ob causam, pronuntiamus, quia articulum fidei ... cudere non licet. Nec Chrysostomi narratio tanti est, ut ei articulus fidei superstrui possit. Inprimis cum ipse non tantum fassus sit, opinionem illam de die natali Christi ex tabulis Romanis eruto tantum decem annos ante habitam a se de die natali Christi orationem Constantinopolin venisse; sed etiam inepto argumento, ex summo Zachariae sacerdotio petito eandem confirmare tentaverit, quae latius Scaliger prosequitur; qui Christum non die XXV. Decembris, sed circa festum Scenopegiae natum esse, ex ratione ordinis Hieratici, sed non omni exceptione majore illa, probare conatur. Sicut ergo annus, ita dies etiam natalis Christi ex Scripturis, saltem ... designari nequit; credendumque adeo est, Deum annum, mensem vel diem natalem revelare nobis accurate pensi non habuisse, quia fides nostra ex tali determinatione non pendet, & ad eam latitudo quaedam temporis, quo Christus in carnem venire debuit, certa & ... ad fidem sufficit.
units.tr: LIII. They seem to be wrong who also claim that the day of Christ's birth can be defined, because the authentic chronological marks expressed in Scripture are lacking, which indicate either the day of the week or the day of the month. Indeed, not even the season of the year is indicated, but only the part of the night at which Christ was born, and not even an explicit night watch (Luke 2:8). For that Christ was born on 25 December, as the Roman Church defined from ancient censual tables and public codices of the Roman Empire, examined by men of senatorial rank who were either Christians or became so later, and as Chrysostom cites in his sermon on the Nativity of Christ, with the agreement of Tillemont, Montfaucon, Longueval and others, we pronounce to have been done rashly, or for this reason, that it is not permitted to coin an article of faith. Nor is Chrysostom's account of such weight that an article of faith can be built upon it. Especially since he himself not only confessed that this opinion about the birthday of Christ, drawn from Roman tables, had reached Constantinople only ten years after the oration on the birthday of Christ that he had delivered there, but also tried to confirm the same with an inept argument taken from the high priesthood of Zechariah, which Scaliger pursues at greater length; Scaliger tries to prove, from the order of the priestly courses, that Christ was born not on 25 December but about the feast of Tabernacles, yet by no means with an objection greater than that one. Therefore, just as the year, so also the day of Christ's birth cannot be designated from the Scriptures, at least not ... ; and it must be believed that God has not taken care to reveal to us exactly the year, month or day of his birth, because our faith does not depend on such a determination, and for faith a certain latitude of time within which Christ was to come into the flesh is sufficient, certain and ... .

units.la: LIV. Fuit mysterium incarnationis & Personae Jesu Christi, ex limpidis Scripturarum fontibus erutum.
units.tr: LIV. The mystery of the incarnation and of the Person of Jesus Christ has been drawn from the clear fountains of Scripture.

units.la: Circa illud errores innumeros Ecclesiam Christianam inde ab ejus initio mirum in modum vexasse, ne miremur. Praedictum enim est, futurum Jehovam in Sanctuarium (hominem manifestatum in medio Israelis ad sanctificandum eum) & in lapidem offensionis & petram scandali, duabus domibus Israelis, in laqueum & tendiculam habitanti Hierosolymae. Et impingent, inquit Deus, in ea plurimi, & cadent, & conterentur, irretientur & capientur, Esaj.VIII. 14. 15. Futurum enim erat, ut ipse compareret cum pueris, quos ipsi vindicandos & asserendos Dominus dederat, & sic fieret in signa & prodigia Israeli a Domino exercituum, qui habitat in Sion, ibid.v.18. Similiter Simeon de Christo nato prophetavit: Ecce hic jacet, situs est in casum & resurrectionem multorum in Israele, & in signum, cui contradicitur, &c. ut manifestentur ex multorum cordibus cogitationes, Luc.II.34.35. Atque ita plane evenit, quia Christus revelatus cum populo & Principibus ejus non tantum de justitia & officio, sed etiam de persona sua disceptare debuit. quod tota Evangelii & Ecclesiae historia docet. Ideo filiae Hierusalem, omnes de civitate sancta nuncupati, ad Sponsam Ecclesiam Christi, quae illas adjuravit, dicit: Quid est dilectus tuus prae dilecto? O pulchra inter mulieres: quid est dilectus tuus prae dilecto? quod ita nos adjurasti? Cant.V.9. q.d. Cupimus vehementer noscere, quis, qualis sit dilectus tuus, quae ejus persona, dignitas, officium, beneficia, proprietas, &c. quid habeat eximium prae dilecto eo, Christo, qui ab aliis nominatur, amandus ostenditur, ratiocinationibus humanis, & in imagine humana proponitur.
units.tr: That the Christian Church, from its very beginning, has been troubled in a remarkable way by countless errors about this matter should not surprise us. For it was foretold that Jehovah would become a sanctuary (a man made manifest in the midst of Israel to sanctify him), and a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence to the two houses of Israel, a snare and a trap to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. "And many among them," says God, "shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be snared and taken" (Isa. 8:14, 15). For he was to appear among the children whom the Lord had given to him to be defended and vindicated, and so he would become "for signs and wonders to Israel from the Lord of hosts, who dwells in Zion" (ibid. v. 18). Likewise Simeon prophesied about Christ when he was born: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be spoken against, etc., that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed" (Luke 2:34, 35). And so it clearly came about, because Christ, once revealed, had to dispute with the people and their leaders not only about his justice and office, but also about his person; the whole history of the Gospel and of the Church teaches this. Therefore the daughters of Jerusalem, all those called from the holy city, ask the Bride, the Church of Christ, who has adjured them: "What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you so adjure us?" (Song 5:9). That is to say: we earnestly wish to know who your beloved is, and what kind of person he is, what his dignity, office, benefits and properties are, and what there is in him that is outstanding above other beloveds, namely Christ, who is named by others, and who is shown to be worthy of love, but is presented through human reasonings and in a human image.

units.la: LV. Qui personam Christi oppugnarunt jam olim, & hodieque oppugnant, haeretici, vel Theomachi, vel Christomachi sunt. Utrorumque veterum historiam Theodoretus in Hermogenis Theomachorum, Jesu Divinitatem oppugnantium, Loc.I P.67. expositium. Omnes illi incarnationis veritatem seu manifestationem Dei in carne inficiati sunt, & inficiuntur. Paucis nunc etiam historiam Christomachorum, veterum & recentiorum, qui contra orthodoxam de Verbi incarnatione doctrinam belligerati sunt, pandamus.
units.tr: LV. Those who have assailed the person of Christ, both long ago and still today, are heretics, either Theomachi or Christomachi. Theodoret, in his account of Hermogenes, who attacked the divinity of Jesus, among the Theomachi, has set out the history of both. All of them have denied, and still deny, the truth of the incarnation, that is, the manifestation of God in the flesh. Now we shall briefly lay out the history of the Christomachi, ancient and recent, who have waged war against the orthodox doctrine of the incarnation of the Word.

units.la: LVI. Christomachorum igitur classes quatuor in universum sunt. Prima eorum, qui de natura & veritate carnis Christi errarunt. Eorum alii, Saturninus, Basilides, Cerdon, Marcion, &c. Christi carnem non veram, sed phantasticam cam esse, asserunt: alii, Apelles & sectatores eius, Christum aëream & sideream carnem, de sideribus & substantiis superioris mundi contextam habuisse, & in resurrectione & ascensu in Coelum singulis elementis, quae ex iis mutuatus sit, reddidisse, & in Coelo spiritum tantum retinuisse, nugati sunt: alii, Valentiniani, Gnostici, Heracleon, Ophitae Christum spirituale nescio quod corpus de Coelo detulisse per B. Virginem, ut aqua solet per fistulam transmeans, nec quicquam ex ea mutuans, delatum in Virginem transmeatorio, non generatorio more; per ipsam, non ex ipsa; non matrem, sed viam passum; & super talem Christum in Baptismatis Sacramento Soterem per effigiem columbae devolasse, delirarunt: alii carnem Christi animalem, & animam carnalem, adeoque carnem Christi esse animam factam, visibilem somniarunt, quos false Tertullianus de carne Christi cap. 10. &c. irrisit: alii, Apollinaristae, in Christi carne animam, saltem rationis participem fuisse negarunt; asserentes insuper, ipsam Domini carnem non ex B. Maria susceptam, sed ex Coelo in Virginem delapsam esse; quam Apollinaris nutabundus semper & dubius modo coaeternam Deo verbo, modo de Verbi Divinitate factam praedicavit; ajens, Verbi naturam esse discissam, & aliam ejus partem Deo haesisse, aliam in carnem transisse: alii, Manichaei, Priscillianistae, Servetus animam Christi ex Dei substantia natam; & quod Servetus addidit, carnem Christi ex Deitate, & tribus elementis factam esse, pertenderunt. Omnium illorum Christi carnem ἐπιφανιον statuentium, inprimis Valentinianorum haeresin recens Anabaptistae & Schwenkfeldius, fanatici alii incrustarunt. Secunda Χρηστομαχων classis eorum est, qui veritatem humanae naturae Christi agnoscentes, circa ejusdem naturae originem errarunt. Eorum alii, Carpocrates, Cerinthus, Ebion, Gnostici, Jesum & Christum dividentes, Jesum non ex Virgine Maria natum, sed ex semine Josephi hominem tantum genitum, & Christum in Baptismo Jesu supervenisse, & ab eodem in passione avolasse, blasphemarunt: alii Origenistae, Christum animam prius conditam, & in Coelo subsistentem corpori suo copulasse, finxerunt. Tertia classis eorum est, qui de humanitatis Christi veritate & origine cum orthodoxis consentientes, de persona Christi errarunt. Eorum alii cum Theodoto Byzantio, Theodoto haeretico, authore Melchisedecianorum, hominem Christum duntaxat ex Spiritu S. natum ex Virgine, & minorem Melchisedeco, propugnarunt; quorum haeresin Paulus Samosathenus Antiochiae, & Photinus Syrmii Episcopi, & longo post eos temporis intervallo Socinus interpolarunt: alii cum Nestorio, Episcopo Constantinopolitano, personam Divinam concedentes, ab humanitate eam separarunt, & pro uno Mediatore ἀνθρώπῳ duos Mediatores, duas personas introduxerunt; a Concilio Ephesino anathemate notati: alii cum Schismaticis trium capitulorum Theodoro Mopsuesteno, Iba &c. Nestorianorum reliquiis, alio licet schemate & fraude Patribus Chalcedonensibus facta, eandem Nestorii haeresin interpolarunt: alii cum Elipando, & Felice Urgelitano, Adoptionariis Christum secundum carnem esse Dei Patris Filium adoptivum sustinuerunt, atque eo nomine a Synodo Francofurtensi, a Carolo M. coacta, damnati sunt, sed, raro ab hominibus damnatorum exemplo, resipuerunt. Quarta denique Χρηστομαχων classis eorum est, qui de Persona Christi cum Catholicis consentientes, in explicanda unione naturarum ejusdem in una persona, a sanctorum sermonum hypotyposi descivERUNT. Horum in numero sunt Eutychiani, & Dioscoritae, Monophysitarum nomine infames; qui Eutyche, Archimandrita Constantinopolitano, & Dioscoro, Patriarcha Alexandrino authoribus, unam tantum in Christo post incarnationem naturam esse, contenderunt, & corpus ejusdem matri & nobis consubstantiale esse, pertinaciter negarunt: & a Synodo Generali quarta Chalcedone habita, anathemate percussi sunt: Acephali, sine capite dicti, quia sectae author in obscuro latuit, in Christo unam naturam cum Eutyche, & duas subsistentias cum Nestorio insanissime statuerunt: Aphtartodocitae, qui Juliano Halicarnasseo Episcopo, haeresi Eutychianae addicto, authore, corporis Christi ἀφθαρσίαν incorruptibilitatem asserentes, Severi Episcopi Antiochiae pariter Eutychiani, sed Christum corruptibilem agnoscentis, sectatores φθαρτολάτρας Corrupticolas appellarunt, ipsi vicissim φανταστῶν phantasiastarum convitio ab iisdem notati; quorum haeresi etiam Justinianus Imperator implicitus, ad eandem Episcopos vi inducere nequicquam, Anastasio Sinaita moliminibus ejus intercedente, conatus est: Agnoëtae, qui a Themistio Alexandrino Diacono authore, Themistiani etiam dicti, Christum quaedam ignorare professi, eundem Deum esse, & secundum Deitatem ea scire, cum Arianis negarunt, & cum Eutychianis naturam utramque Christi in tertiam, ignorantia quarundam rerum laborantem, coaluisse, definiverunt: Monothelitae, qui Cyro Alexandrino, & Sergio Constantinopolitano Episcopis authoribus, agnitis duabus in Christo naturis, ne Chalcedonensi Concilio repugnare viderentur, unam utriusque naturae voluntatem esse, constituerunt. Ad postremam hanc classem jure etiam Transsubstantiatores referimus, quia verbo licet unicum corpus Christi confessi, reapse tamen corpus ejus multiplicant, asserentes, illud integrum & totum simul pluribus in locis existere, imo totum & integrum Christum, sub panis specie, & sub quavis speciei parte, totum item sub vini specie, & sub ejus partibus existere. Taceo errorem eorum, qui corporis Christi ubiquitatem pertinaciter aequo propugnantes, seu scientes prudentes, seu inscii & imprudentes, naturarum & proprietatum Christi confusionem quandam inducunt. Christianorum circa Christum, personam & naturas ejus, labia adeo divisa fuisse & esse, pudendum equidem & lugendum est. Sed oportuit tamen Christum esse signum, cui contradicitur, ut manifestarentur multorum cogitationes, Luc. II, 35. & oportuit haereses esse, ut probi manifesti fierent, I. Cor. XI. 19.
units.tr: LVI. The Christomachi, then, fall in general into four classes. The first are those who erred concerning the nature and reality of Christ's flesh. Some of them, Saturninus, Basilides, Cerdon, Marcion and others, maintain that Christ's flesh was not real but phantasmal. Others, Apelles and his followers, babbled that Christ had an airy and starry flesh, woven from the stars and substances of the higher world; that in his resurrection and ascension into heaven he returned to each element what he had borrowed from it; and that in heaven he kept only spirit. Others, Valentiniani, Gnostici, Heracleon, Ophitae, raved that Christ brought down from heaven some spiritual body, I know not what, which passed through the Blessed Virgin as water passes through a pipe, borrowing nothing from her. It was carried into the Virgin by a passing, not a generating, manner; it came through her, not from her; he suffered as a way, not as a mother. They also held that over such a Christ, at the sacrament of baptism, the Saviour [Soterem] descended in the form of a dove. Others dreamed that Christ's flesh was animal and his flesh carnal, and so that Christ's flesh was a soul made visible. Tertullian mocked these men, falsely so called, in On the Flesh of Christ, ch. 10, etc. Others, Apollinaristae, denied that Christ's flesh had a soul, or at least a soul sharing in reason.
