They asserted moreover that the Lord's flesh was not taken from the Blessed Mary but came down from heaven into the Virgin. Apollinaris, always wavering and doubtful, sometimes taught that this flesh was coeternal with God the Word, and sometimes that it was made from the divinity of the Word, saying that the nature of the Word was split, one part clinging to God and another passing into the flesh. Others, Manichaei, Priscillianistae, Servetus, contended that the soul of Christ was born of the substance of God; and Servetus added that Christ's flesh was made from the Deity and three elements. Of all who held that Christ's flesh was of this heavenly kind, the Anabaptists and, recently, Schwenkfeld, along with other fanatics, have renewed especially the heresy of the Valentinians. The second class of the Christomachi are those who, acknowledging the true humanity of Christ, erred concerning the origin of that nature. Some of them, Carpocrates, Cerinthus, Ebion, Gnostici, dividing Jesus from Christ, blasphemed that Jesus was not born of the Virgin Mary but was merely a man begotten from the seed of Joseph, and that Christ came upon Jesus at his baptism and flew away from him at the passion. Others, Origenistae, feigned that Christ's soul had been created beforehand, subsisted in heaven, and was joined to his body. The third class are those who, agreeing with the orthodox about the reality and origin of Christ's humanity, erred concerning the person of Christ. Some of them, with Theodoto Byzantio, Theodotus the heretic, author of the Melchizedekians, maintained that Christ was only a man, born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin, and less than Melchizedek. Their heresy was renewed by Paulus Samosathenus at Antioch, by Photinus, bishop of Sirmium, and, after a long interval of time, by Socinus. Others, with Nestorio, bishop of Constantinople, granting a divine person, separated it from the humanity, and in place of one Mediator, a man [ἀνθρώπῳ], introduced two Mediators and two persons. He was marked with anathema by the Council of Ephesus. Others, with the Schismaticis trium capitulorum, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Ibas and others, remnants of the Nestorians, revived the same heresy of Nestorius under another form, and by a fraud practised on the Fathers of Chalcedon. Others, with Elipando, & Felice Urgelitano, the Adoptionists, maintained that Christ according to the flesh was an adopted Son of God the Father. On this account they were condemned by the Synod of Frankfurt, convened by Charlemagne; but, a rare thing among men thus condemned, they came to their senses. Finally, the fourth class of the Christomachi are those who, agreeing with the Catholics about the person of Christ, departed from the outline of the holy sayings in explaining the union of his natures in one person. Among these are the Eutychiani and Dioscoritae, notorious under the name of Monophysites. With Eutyche, archimandrite of Constantinople, and Dioscoro, patriarch of Alexandria, as their authors, they contended that after the incarnation there is only one nature in Christ, and stubbornly denied that his body is consubstantial with our mother and with us. They were struck with anathema by the fourth General Synod, held at Chalcedon. The Acephali, so called because the author of their sect lay hidden in obscurity, most madly maintained with Eutyches one nature in Christ, and with Nestorius two subsistences. The Aphtartodocitae, whose author was Juliano, bishop of Halicarnassus, addicted to the Eutychian heresy, asserted the incorruptibility [ἀφθαρσίαν] of Christ's body. The followers of Severi, bishop of Antioch, likewise Eutychian but acknowledging Christ as corruptible, called them Corrupticolas [φθαρτολάτρας], worshippers of the corruptible. In turn, those same men were marked by the Aphthartodocetae with the reproach of being phantasiastarum [φανταστῶν], phantasiasts. Justinian the Emperor, entangled in their heresy, tried in vain to force the bishops to adopt it, with Anastasius the Sinaite interceding for these efforts. The Agnoetae, who were also called Themistiani after their author Themistio, a deacon of Alexandria, professed that Christ was ignorant of certain things. With the Arians they denied that he was God and knew those things according to the Deity; and with the Eutychians they defined that the two natures of Christ had coalesced into a third nature, labouring under ignorance of certain matters. The Monothelitae, with Cyro, bishop of Alexandria, and Sergio, bishop of Constantinople, as their authors, acknowledged two natures in Christ, yet, so as not to seem to contradict the Council of Chalcedon, established that there is one will of both natures. To this last class we rightly also refer the Transsubstantiatores, because, although they confess in words one body of Christ, in fact they multiply his body. They assert that it exists whole and entire at the same time in many places; indeed that the whole and entire Christ exists under the species of bread and under any part of that species, and likewise the whole under the species of wine and under its parts. I pass over the error of those who stubbornly defend the ubiquity of Christ's body as equal to his divinity, and who, whether knowingly and wisely or unknowingly and unwisely, induce a certain confusion of Christ's natures and properties. It is indeed shameful and lamentable that the lips of Christians have been, and still are, so divided concerning Christ, his person and his natures. But it was necessary that Christ be "a sign which shall be spoken against, that the thoughts of many may be revealed," Luke 2:35, and it was necessary that there be heresies, "so that those who are approved may be made manifest," 1 Cor. 11:19.

units.la: LVII. Ficulnea plane sunt argumenta, quibus incarnationis veritatem, & duarum naturarum in persona Christi unionem Samosathefatheniani olim oppugnarunt, & hodiéque Sociniani oppugnant. Nam quæ contra Divinitatem Christi movent, supra excussimus. Finitæ & infinitæ naturæ unionem impossibilem esse, nequicquam iidem jactant, quia nulla finitum inter & infinitum sit proportio. Verùm minimè sic unio & conjunctio naturarum tantopere licèt disparatarum impeditur, quia illa non in exæquatione tali, qua sibi naturæ proportionatæ fiant, sed in naturæ finitæ in infinita existentia consistit. Etiam vocem Deus sibi facere, ut audiatur, linguam, faciem, oculos &c. sibi formare, ut ab homine videatur, palpetur, potuit. Cur ergo sibi humanam naturam, organon, in quo ab homine videretur, audiretur, palparetur, & pro hominibus morere-tur, formare, adaptare non potuisset? Ille, cujus thronus Cœlum, & terra scabellum est, qui Cœlum & terram implet; quem Cœli Cœlorum non capiunt, nihilominus in nube, igne tabernaculo, in templo habitavit; inter Cherubim sedit, & habitaturum se in populi medio, Levit.XXVI.12. promisit: & revera ἐσκήνωσεν habitavit, Joh.I.14. Qualis, amabò, inter augustum illum habitatorem & habitaculum, hospitem & hospitium proportio fuit? Et Christus quidem unus est, 1.Tim.II.5. Ephes.IV.5. At Deitas & Humanitas disparatæ, fateor, non unum quid sunt. Sed unum tamen in supposito illo extraordinario sunt Deus & Homo; quia Deus in unitatem personæ suæ humanitatem assumpsit; atque sic etiam Unus Christus est. Præterea Christus, quà homo, personalitate propria destitutus licèt, verus tamen & perfectus homo fuit. Verus, quia veritatem naturæ humanæ non ex personalitate, sed ex materia, forma & proprietatibus metimur. Unde aliter natura, aliter personalitas definitur. Perfectus, quia Personalitas non pars, sed terminus quasi naturæ est. quem quia in subsistentia non creata, verùm increata sortitur, eo ipso perfectior est, quàm si à λόγῳ separata seorsim exisseret. Cùm igitur S. Paulus ab ὁμοιότητι similitudine Christum inter & nos non aliud quàm peccatum excipit, Hebr. IV.15. de natura, non de persona & conditionibus individuantibus loquitur. Potest autem integra esse natura, quæ persona non est. uti integra est natura animæ humanæ, licèt persona non sit. Ideo S. Paulus similitudinem illam ibid. II.14. ad κοινωνίαν communionem carnis & sanguinis restringit. Licèt etiam Christus à Patre unctus, & Spiritu S. inde ab utero repletus fuerit, non tamen ideo τῷ λόγῳ, qui cùm Deus existimetur, unctione & donis alterius non indigeret, uniri non potuit. Nam nec alter ille, sive Deus Pater, sive Deus Spiritus S. à Filio essentiâ, sed solâ ἐνεργείᾳ differt, eóque, quicquid ita facit, id Filius, pro natura operationum ad extra, similiter facit: nec ὁ λόγος Deus unctione indiget absolutè, sed relatè tantùm, quoad munus Mediatorium, secundum dispositionem consilii Divini: nec donis Spiritus S. in natura Divina, sed tantùm in humana indiget. Neque etiam Christus ipse se Deum nunquàm nuncupavit, cùm Filium Dei unigenitum, unum cum Patre, parem ei proprietatibus, operationibus, gloriâ jam ante conditum mundum habitâ, diserte se professus fuerit; Joh.III.16. Matth.XVI.26.27. XXVI.64. Joh.V.18.19. X.28.29.30. XVII.5. Palam etiam facto se Deum haud raro demonstravit. Quòd verò non crebrius se Deum nuncupavit & demonstravit, inde est, quòd per exinanitionem gloriam Deitatis & radios Majestatis suæ in forma servi occultavit. Falsum quinetiam est, quòd Christus homo propter humanam naturam, Deus propter dominium & gloriam exaltationis, Act.II.36. Phil.II.9.10. vocetur, quia exaltatio Deitatis Christi argumentum, non ratio formalis est. Deus enim proprie vocatur, quia Deus Pater ab æterno Divinam ei essentiam per generationem communicavit. Quod dominium ejus & exaltatio demonstrant. Denique nec infinitas ἐν λόγῳ obstat, quò minùs carni suæ magis, quàm rebus omnibus aliis, quibus intimè præsens est, Act. XVII.27. uniatur, quia generalis ille præsentiæ Divinæ modus, qui ex necessitate naturæ ejus pendet, specialem, qui liberrima ipsius voluntate, & sapientissima dispositione nititur, non tollit. Nam etiam quodam modo in Cœlo est, quo in inferno non est, & vicissim. Sic, si magna parvis componere licet, per totum diaphanum radii solares diffunduntur, ut tamen singulari modo in speculi ardentis centro colligantur & uniantur.
units.tr: These arguments are indeed flimsy, the ones by which the Samosatenes and Photinians once attacked the truth of the incarnation and the union of the two natures in the person of Christ, and by which the Socinians still attack it today. What they urge against the divinity of Christ we have already examined above. They insist in vain that a union of finite and infinite nature is impossible, since there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite. But the union and conjunction of natures, however disparate, is by no means hindered in this way, because it does not consist in an equalising by which the natures are made proportionate to each other, but in the existence of the finite nature within the infinite. God could make a voice for himself so that it might be heard, and form for himself a tongue, a face, eyes and so on, so that he might be seen and touched by a man. Why then could he not form for himself a human nature, an organ in which he might be seen, heard and touched by men, and die for men, and fit and adapt it to himself? He whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth, who fills heaven and earth, whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain, nevertheless dwelt in the cloud, in the fire, in the tabernacle, in the temple; he sat between the cherubim, and promised that he would dwell habitaturum se in populi medio [in the midst of the people], Lev. 26.12; and indeed he ἐσκήνωσεν [dwelt], John 1.14. What, pray, was the proportion between that august inhabitant and his dwelling, between the guest and his lodging? Christ is indeed one, 1 Tim. 2.5; Eph. 4.5. But the Deity and the humanity, I grant, are disparate and are not one thing. Yet God and man are one in that extraordinary suppositum, because God took the humanity into the unity of his own person; and so Christ is also one. Moreover, Christ as man, though lacking a personality of his own, was nevertheless a true and perfect man. He was true, because we measure the truth of human nature not by personality but by matter, form and properties; hence nature and personality are defined in different ways. He was perfect, because personality is not a part of nature but, as it were, its terminus; and since the humanity has as its personality not a created but an uncreated subsistence, it is on that very account more perfect than if it had existed separately, apart from the Word. Therefore, when St. Paul excepts nothing between Christ and us except sin, in the likeness similitudine [ὁμοιότητι], Heb. 4.15, he speaks of nature, not of person and individuating conditions. A nature can be complete even though it is not a person, as the nature of a human soul is complete though it is not a person. For this reason St. Paul restricts that likeness to the communionem carnis [communion of flesh] and sanguinis [blood], Heb. 2.14. Although Christ was anointed by the Father and filled with the Holy Spirit from the womb, he could not on that account be united to the Word, who, since he is held to be God, had no need of anointing or of gifts from another. For neither is that other, whether God the Father or God the Holy Spirit, distinguished from the Son in essence but only in operation, and therefore whatever he does in this way, the Son likewise does, according to the nature of external operations; nor does the Word, God, need anointing absolutely, but only relatively, with respect to the mediatorial office, according to the disposition of the divine counsel; nor does he need the gifts of the Holy Spirit in the divine nature, but only in the human. Nor did Christ himself ever call himself God, since he openly professed himself the only-begotten Son of God, one with the Father, equal to him in properties, operations and glory possessed before the world was made; John 3.16; Matt. 16.26-27; 26.64; John 5.18-19; 10.28-30; 17.5. He also frequently showed himself to be God by his deeds. That he did not more often name and show himself as God comes from this, that through his emptying he hid the glory of his Deity and the rays of his majesty in the form of a servant. Nor is it true that Christ is called man on account of his human nature and God on account of his lordship and the glory of his exaltation, Acts 2.36; Phil. 2.9-10, because the exaltation is a proof of the Deity of Christ, not its formal reason. For he is properly called God because God the Father from eternity communicated to him the divine essence by generation; his lordship and exaltation demonstrate this. Finally, the infinity of the Word does not prevent him from being united to his flesh more than to all other things, in which he is intimately present, Acts 17.27, because that general mode of the divine presence, which depends on the necessity of his nature, does not abolish the special mode, which rests on his most free will and most wise disposition. For in a certain way he is in heaven in a way he is not in hell, and vice versa. So, if small things may be compared with great, the rays of the sun are spread through the whole transparent medium, yet are gathered and united in a singular way at the centre of a burning mirror.

units.la: LVIII. Qui circa idiomatum communicationem à sententia orthodoxa superiùs exposita diversi abeunt, & naturæ humanæ per unionem personalem communicatas esse essentiales Dei proprietates contendunt, ante omnia illi illibatam de unione naturarum in Christo, & modo unionis, in Chalcedonensi confessione definito, fidem se retinere profitentur. Movent tamen illi de communicatione idiomatum controversiam, quia sine ea ad sensum alienum detorta præsentiam corporis Christi in Cœna Domini corporalem propugnari non posse, perviderunt. Proin Eucharistica controversia hanc de Persona Christi, velut φαντασία & φαντασμα quoddam peperit. Sed nec omnes ἐν λόγῳ proprietates essentiales, saltem quoad actus secundi exercitium, carni communicatas esse, sed quasdam tantùm, puta ἐνεργητικὰς operativas, quales inprimis omniprælentiam, omniscientiam, omnipotentiam & vim vivificandi faciunt, plerique largiuntur; reliquas verò, infinitatem, immutabilitatem, æternitatem &c. nonnisi in actu primo. Ad modum communicationis explicandum ubi perveniunt, Divinam naturam non tantùm subsistentiam suam, sed etiam proprietates humanæ naturæ verè & realiter communicasse, ut propterea humana natura omniscia, omnipræsens, omnipotens &c. sit & dicatur; ita quidem asserunt, ut tamen cautionibus multis utantur. Eas Gerhardus Loc.IV. §267. his verbis constringit, 1. Unio, inquit, non est verbalis: Ergo nec communicatio, &c. 2. Unio non est essentialis; Ergo nec communicatio. 3. Quod unius naturæ in Christo proprium est, illud nunquam fit alterius naturæ proprium, sed idiomes est, & manet ἀχώριστος. Divina enim idiomata nec per ἐκπώσιν, nec per ἐκγονὴν in carnem assumtam, tanquam in aliud subjectum derivantur ac transfunduntur, sed manent ἐν λόγῳ propria. Unde etiam communicatio nec est, nec Errantium circa communicationem idiomatum perplexitas attingitur. nec dici potest essentialis. 4. Unio non est accidentalis, Ergo nec communicatio. Si Divina illa idiomata per accidens humanae naturae competerent, tum humanae naturae subjectivè inessent atque inhærerent. Id verò dici nequit, cùm Divina idiomata non sint accidentia, nec subjectivè alteri inhærere possint. 5. Unio non est naturalis. Ergo nec communicatio. Aliàs idiomata illa Divina φυσικῶς & naturaliter assumpta naturæ competerent. quod absit. 6. Unio est personalis. Ergo etiam communicatio. Ut enim assumpta natura in ipsam ὑπόστασιν per unionem personalem evecta est, ita quoque in κοινωνίᾳ ἰδιωμάτων illa ipsa evectione est assumpta. Divina Filii natura inter intimum ὑποστάσεως suæ complexum Divina idiomata retinet; assumendo autem naturam humanam in suam ὑπόστασιν, eandem quoque in κοινωνίαν ἰδιωμάτων suæ illius ὑποστάσεως assumit. Ac proinde humana natura Divinam Majestatem habet non à se originaliter, sed à λόγῳ; nec per se essentialiter, nec in se subjectivè, sed in λόγῳ, verè quidem & realiter, sed tamen hypostaticè ac personaliter. Hæc ab insigni communionis illius Theologo vel minùs bona fide, ac subdolè dicta sunt, vel parum à modo communicationis idiomatum orthodoxo dissident. Nam distinctionem sicut naturarum, ita etiam proprietatum in Christo sic asserunt, ut earundem in persona, non in natura communicatio realis constituatur, & Divina idiomata in humanam naturam vel transfusa esse, vel ei, sive essentialiter, sive naturaliter, sive accidentaliter inesse fortiter negetur. Quomodo verò cum modo illthoc communicationis idiomatum communicatio illa, secundum quam natura humana verè omnipræsens, omniscia, omnipotens &c. sit & dicatur, conciliari possit, ipsi certè viderint. Nos enim nulla ἀγχνοίᾳ nostra id videre possumus, & hoc unum judicamus, inconsultiùs assumpta præsentia corporali, & orali manducatione in Eucharistia ad has angustias viros cætera pios & magni nominis redactos esse, ut modum orthodoxum (ne in hæresεon antiquitus damnatarum scopulum impingerent) & rem heterodoxam (ne stipulare illud de præsentia corporis Christi in Eucharistia dogma, fundamento fidei rectè confesso & retento, malè superstructum, ipsimet comburerent) afferendo parum sibi ipsis constarent. Ex eadem perplexitate inter eosdem exortum est intestinum illud de Ubiquitate naturæ Christi humanæ bellum, dum alii Ubiquitatis dogma à Fabro Stapulensi primitus satum, à Luthero in contentionis adversus Zwvinglium fervore utcunque fotum, at mox abdicatum, à Brentio & Andrea obstetricantibus, dias in luminis auras prolatum, alii cum eodem Brentio mordicus & omnibus interdictis defensitant: alii cum inferioris Saxoniæ Theologis, Chemnitio, Hofmanno, &c. nec non Brunsuicensibus, inprimis Helmstadiensibus repudiant. Glisçere inprimis seculo nostro de eadem Suevos inter & Hassos acre certamen coepit, dum illi, Osiandro, & Thummio ducibus, universalem humano corpori ab omnibus locis & creaturis indistantiam & apud omnes creaturas & loca propinquitatem substantialem inde à primo conceptionis & unionis momento, & κτίσει & γεννήσει competere, ingenuè & rotundè (cùm præsentia corporalis Christi in Eucharistia id omnino exigere videatur) asseruerunt: hi, Menzero, & Feurbornio, Suevorum mirmillonibus & retiariis, humanam naturam in statu Christi exinanitionis omnipræsentem γένησιν fuisse pernegarunt, & in statu demum exaltationis factam esse contenderunt. Illi omnipræsentiæ fundamentum in unione hypostatica; hi in unione hypostatica, liberrima voluntate, & exaltatione, quarum prima effecerit, ut ubique esse posset, secunda, ut vellet, tertia, ut esset, collocarunt. Quæ non ideo commemoramus, quasi ex certaminibus illis delicias nobis faceremus, sed ut dogmatis novitii perplexitatem dissentientibus ad animum revocemus. Quo tamen non obstante, stat concordi eorum animo fixa sententia, quòd & subsistentia & proprietates Divinæ naturæ humanæ communicatæ sint. quam paucis refellere juvabit.
units.tr: LVIII. Those who depart from the orthodox doctrine of the communication of idioms set out above, and who contend that the essential properties of God have been communicated to the human nature through the personal union, first of all profess that they hold unimpaired the faith concerning the union of the natures in Christ and the mode of union defined in the Chalcedonian confession. Nevertheless they raise the controversy about the communication of idioms, because they have perceived that without it the corporeal presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper, distorted into a foreign sense, cannot be defended. Hence the Eucharistic controversy has given birth to this notion about the person of Christ, as a kind of phantasm and phantom. But most of them grant that not all the essential properties of the Word, at least as to the exercise of the second act, have been communicated to the flesh, but only certain ones, namely the operativas [operative] ones, such as above all omnipresence, omniscience, omnipotence and the power of giving life; the rest, infinity, immutability, eternity and so on, they grant only in the first act. When they come to explain the mode of communication, they assert that the divine nature has truly and really communicated to the human nature not only its subsistence but also its properties, so that the human nature is and is called omniscient, omnipresent, omnipotent and so on. They assert this indeed, but with many cautions. Gerhard, Loc. IV, §267, restricts these in the following words. (1) The union, he says, is not verbal; therefore neither is the communication. (2) The union is not essential; therefore neither is the communication. (3) What is proper to one nature in Christ never becomes the proper possession of the other nature, but remains an idiomes [idiom] and remains inseparable. For the divine idioms are not derived or transfused into the assumed flesh, as into another subject, either by an outflowing or by a begetting, but remain proper to the Word. Hence the communication is not essential. (4) The union is not accidental; therefore neither is the communication. For if those divine idioms belonged to the human nature by accident, they would inhere in and adhere to the human nature as a subject. This cannot be said, since the divine idioms are not accidents and cannot inhere subjectively in another. (5) The union is not natural; therefore neither is the communication. Otherwise those divine idioms would belong to the nature as naturally and physically assumed, which is far from the truth. (6) The union is personal; therefore so is the communication. For just as the assumed nature has been raised into the very hypostasis through the personal union, so also in the communion of idioms it has been assumed by that very elevation. The divine nature of the Son retains the divine idioms within the intimate complex of its hypostasis; and by assuming the human nature into its hypostasis, it also takes it into the communion of idioms of that same hypostasis. Accordingly the human nature has the divine majesty not from itself originally, but from the Word; not essentially through itself, nor subjectively in itself, but in the Word, truly indeed and really, yet hypostatically and personally. These things were said by that notable theologian of the communion either with less than good faith and deceitfully, or else they differ little from the orthodox mode of the communication of idioms. For they assert the distinction of the properties in Christ just as of the natures, so that a real communication is established in the person and not in the nature; and they strongly deny that the divine idioms have been transfused into the human nature or inhere in it, whether essentially, naturally or accidentally. How that communication, according to which the human nature is and is called truly omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent and so on, can be reconciled with this mode of communication, they themselves must certainly see. For we, by no effort of our own, can see this, and we judge this one thing: that men otherwise pious and of great name, by rashly assuming a corporeal presence and oral manducation in the Eucharist, have been reduced to such straits that, in affirming the orthodox mode (lest they strike upon the rock of heresies condemned of old) and a heterodox thing (lest they themselves burn the dogma of the presence of the body of Christ in the Eucharist, badly built upon the foundation of the faith rightly confessed and retained), they have been rather inconsistent with themselves. From the same perplexity there arose among the same men the internal war over the ubiquity of the human nature of Christ: while some defend the dogma of ubiquity, first sown by Faber Stapulensis, somehow nursed by Luther in the heat of his contention against Zwingli, but soon renounced, brought forth into the light of day by Brenz and Andreae acting as midwives, others with Brenz himself defend it stubbornly and with all prohibitions; others with the theologians of Lower Saxony, Chemnitz, Hofmann and so on, and also the Brunswick theologians, especially those of Helmstedt, reject it. Especially in our century a bitter contest over the same matter began to blaze up between the Swabians and the Hessians: the former, led by Osiander and Thummius, openly and frankly asserted that a universal indistance of the human body from all places and creatures, and a substantial nearness to all creatures and places, belongs to it from the first moment of conception and union, both by creation and by generation, since the bodily presence of Christ in the Eucharist seems altogether to demand this; the latter, Menzer and Feurborn, gladiators and net-fighters of the Swabians, denied that the human nature was omnipresent in the state of Christ's emptying and contended that it became so only in the state of exaltation. The former placed the foundation of omnipresence in the hypostatic union; the latter placed it in the hypostatic union together with the most free will and with exaltation, of which the first made it that he could be everywhere, the second that he would be, the third that he should be. We recall these things not as if we took delight in those contests, but so that we may bring to the minds of the disputants the perplexity of a novel dogma. Nevertheless, despite this, there stands in their united minds the fixed opinion that both the subsistence and the properties of the divine nature have been communicated to the human nature; this it will be helpful to refute in a few words.

units.la: LIX. Et Subsistentiam quidem
units.tr: LIX. And indeed we confess that the subsistence

units.la: naturæ humanæ communicatam esse, ultra fatemur, sed orthodoxo sensu. Nam ejusmodi subsistentiæ communicatio si facta dicatur, per quam humanitas Christi subsistentiam à λόγῳ subsistentia diversam, sed ab ea tamen, velut à causa pendentem, habeat, næ præceps hic ad Nestorianismum lapsus erit. Nam duæ sic subsistentiæ, duæ personæ erunt, una λόγῳ, altera carnis: illa efficiens, hæc effecta. à quo omnes, nisi fallor, vehementer abhorremus. Par ratio est, si communicatio subsistentiæ intelligatur de reali traditione ejusdem rei, diversis subjectis facta, ita ut λόγος suam hypostasin in carnem transfundat. Nam & sic duæ personæ essent, quia caro non minùs persona esset, quàm λόγος. Cùmque personalitas λόγῳ sit ejus æterna generatio à Patre, per quam ab æterno Filius subsistentiam, à Patris subsistentia distinctam, habuit, prorsus utique illa eatenus incommunicabilis est ulli creaturæ, ac ne ipsi quidem Deo Patri, quia aliàs Pater esse desineret, & Filius fieret. Non aliter ergo subsistentia λόγῳ carni communicata est, quàm quatenus illa semen Abrahæ, hoc est, carnem assumpsit, Hebr. 11. 16. hoc est, uniendo sibi carnem id effecit, ut caro per se ἀνυπόστατος fieret ἐνυπόστατος, non separatim, sed in λόγῳ existens vel subsistens, ut organon aliquod ad perficiendum opus redemptionis ei personaliter unitum; quæ communicatio rectiùs unio, quàm communicatio dicitur; & in Scripturis non tam hypostaseos communicatio, quàm λαβὴ μορφῆς δούλου acceptio formæ servi, Phil. 11. 7. ἐπιλήψις assumptio seminis Abrahæ, Hebr. 11. 16. appellatur. Quòd si ita carni hypostasin communicatam esse pertenderint, sicut idiomata naturæ communicata esse docent; jam sicut carnem propter communicationem idiomatum esse omniscian, omnipræsentem, &c. asserunt: ita iisdem asserendum foret, carnem hypostasin esse, vel hypostasin personalitatem habere, quæ si ab hypostasi λόγῳ distincta est, duæ personæ emergent; si eadem in λόγῳ & carne existens, velut utrique communis, ejus confusio inde oriatur.
units.tr: was communicated to the human nature as well, but only in an orthodox sense. For if it is said that such a communication of subsistence took place, by which the humanity of Christ would have a subsistence distinct from the subsistence of the Logos, yet still depending on it as on a cause, then here we would have fallen headlong into Nestorianism. For in this way there would be two subsistences and two persons: one of the Logos, the other of the flesh; the one effecting, the other effected. From this, unless I am mistaken, we all strongly shrink. The reasoning is the same if the communication of subsistence is understood as a real transfer of the same thing, made to different subjects, so that the Logos pours his own hypostasis into the flesh. For in that case too there would be two persons, since the flesh would be no less a person than the Logos. And since the personality of the Logos consists in his eternal generation from the Father, by which from eternity the Son has had a subsistence distinct from the subsistence of the Father, that is certainly altogether incommunicable to any creature, and not even to God the Father himself, because otherwise the Father would cease to be Father and the Son would come to be. Therefore the subsistence of the Logos was communicated to the flesh only insofar as he took hold of the seed of Abraham, that is, the flesh, Heb. 11. 16; that is, by uniting the flesh to himself he brought it about that the flesh, which was of itself without subsistence [anypostatos], became subsisting in another [enypostatos], not existing separately but existing or subsisting in the Logos, as some instrument personally united to him for carrying out the work of redemption. This communication is more correctly called a union than a communication; and in the Scriptures it is called not so much a communication of hypostasis as the taking of the form of a servant [lēmpsis morphēs doulou], Phil. 11. 7, and the assumption [epilēpsis] of the seed of Abraham, Heb. 11. 16. But if they insist that hypostasis has been communicated to the flesh in the same way as they teach that the properties of the natures are communicated, then just as, on account of the communication of properties, they assert that the flesh is omniscient, omnipresent, and so on, so they would have to assert that the flesh is a hypostasis, or has the personality of a hypostasis. If this is distinct from the hypostasis of the Logos, two persons emerge; if it is the same, existing in the Logos and in the flesh as common to both, confusion of the two natures arises from it.

units.la: LX. Dispar verò idiomatum Deitatis ratio est, quæ humanæ naturæ communicata esse, se, nec Scriptura, nec fidei analogia patitur. Scriptura enim de Christo loquens, inuspiam Divina idiomata, in specie & proprie sic dicta, humanae naturae tribuit; multò minus humana Divinae. Alias enim humanitatem Deificatam, & Deitatem ἀνθρώπινον nobis proponeret. Cùm enim idiomata Divina ipse Deus sint, & humana ab humanitate essentialiter non distinguantur, non posset non humanitas Deificari, si Deitatis idiomata ei communicarentur, nec Deitas non ἀνθρωπίζεσθαι, si humanitatis idiomata eidem tribuerentur. Ficulnea enim folia sunt, cùm Deitatem omnipotentem, omnipraesentem &c. denominari κατ' αὐτὸ & σὺνσὼς secundum se & essentialiter; at humanitatem κατ' ἄλλο, ὑποστατικῶς secundum aliud & personaliter, regerunt. Nam omnipotentem, omnipraesentem &c. esse, solius Dei est. Sicut autem non datur alius Deus κατ' αὐτὸ & σὺνσὼς secundum se & essentialiter, alius κατ' ἄλλο secundum aliud & personaliter: ita nec alius omnipotens, omnipraesens, &c. est secundum se, essentialiter; alius secundum aliud & personaliter. Planè enim uti illud secundum aliud, notionem Deitatis, sic etiam omnipotentiae, omnipraesentiae &c. notionem corrumpit. Neque personaliter omnipotens & omnipraesens esse potest, qui non idem talis est essentialiter, quia persona Divina essentiam Divinam supponit, neque ab ea separari potest. Si terminorum hae tricae pondus ullum haberent, orthodoxis argumentum pro Deitate Filii ex proprietatibus Divinis petitum peribit; quia similiter per aliud omnipotens, omnipraesens &c. dici poterit, qui secundum se & essentialiter Deus non est. Neque felicius evadunt, cùm μέθεξιν inter & συνδυασιν distinguentes, humanae naturae idiomata Divina communicata esse non κατ' μέθεξιν secundum participationem, ut subjectivè ei insint, sed κατ' συνδυασιν secundum & propter naturarum conjunctionem, pronunciant. Nulli enim propria communicantur, quin subjectivè ei insint. Tum communicatio κατ' συνδυασιν non inter naturas συνδεδυασμένας locum habet, sed ad personam, seu compositum ex naturis unitum, pertinet. Et eadem ratione naturam humanam κατ' συνδυασιν etiam Deum esse, cùm non minùs Deitas, quàm omnipotentia, omnipraesentia &c. communicata dicatur, consequens foret. Praeterea naturae Divinae idiomata humanae vel omnia, vel quaedam, vel nulla communicata sunt. Non omnia, quia aeternam, immensam, immutabilem esse, ne ipsi quidem dicere sustinent. Non quaedam, quia cùm omnes proprietates Dei realiter idem, & ipse Deus sint, separari non possunt. Ergo nulla communicata sunt. Quem ictum non declinant οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας, cùm communicatas esse omnes, quoad inhabitationem personalem Deitatis in humanitate, quasdam quoad praedicationem, nullas physicè & essentialiter statuunt. Distincti enim respectus illi sine fundamento confinguntur, & rem minimè expediunt. quia personalis inhabitatio Dei in carne non est communicatio, vel consequens unionis, sed ipsa unio; & personam ἐξ λόγου sicut cum natura humana, ita cum omnibus ejusdem proprietatibus unitam esse, ita ἀνεξαγωγιον est, ut tamen propterea tam non natura humana omnipotens & omnipraesens dici possit, quàm non Deus dici potest. Communicatio verò quoad praedicationem nec in omnibus, nec in quibusdam proprietatibus Divinis obinet, quia Scriptura nec omnes, nec quasdam de natura humana praedicat: nec praedicari ulla proprietas de natura verè & proprie potest, cui non insit. Inane etiam illud κρινσφύγειν est, cùm inter proprietates ἐνεργητικὰς operativas quae peculiaribus operationibus ad extra se proferunt, & non-ἐνεργητικὰς, per quas Divina natura non operatur, distinguentes, illas, velut omnipotentiam, omnipraesentiam, non has, velut infinitatem, aeternitatem &c. communicatas esse pertendunt. Nam ἐνεργητικά dicuntur alia, alia non, respectu effectorum & nostri, non in se; utpote inter quae respectu Dei propter summam essentiae simplicitatem nulla differentia est. De quocunque ergo una Dei proprietas sive ἐνεργητικὴ, sive non ἐνεργητικὴ praedicatur, de eo omnes praedicari necesse est. Si porro Divina natura humanae realiter uniri non potuit, nisi communicatis eidem proprietatibus suis; nec humana Divinae realiter uniri potuit, nisi proprietatibus suis huic communicatis. Ita natura Divina parem ob rationem finita, visibilis, mortalis &c. praedicari poterit. quod blasphemia non carere, omnes fatentur. Nam quod naturam Divinam immutabilem & perfectissimam nihil accipere vel pati posse; at humanam, cùm multis modis perfici possit, per & propter unionem Divinorum idiomatum communicatione longè perfectiorem reddi potuisse, dissentientes ratiocinantur, nodum non solvunt; tum quia sic idiomatum communicatio non ex unione personali, quatenus unio est, sed ex naturarum unitarum inaequalitate oritur: tum quia Scriptura veram idiomatum communicationem inter naturas & personam reciprocam testatur; personae non tantùm propter Divinitatem Divina, sed etiam propter humanitatem humana tribuens: tum quia naturae Christi humanae omnino perfectio major accedere potuit, sed finita illa, & cujus capax est, non infinita, cujus capax non est. Insuper etiam propria subjecto realiter diversa communicata propria esse desinunt, & communia evadunt. Quorum verò communis essentia non est, illorum nec propria communia esse possunt, quia propria quaevis ab essentia, ut causa proxima necessariò procedunt, nec eam unquam egrediuntur. Neque haec distinctione ἀσυνδυάζων & συνδεδυασμένων conciliari possunt. quasi in illis propria communicari non possint, in his possint; quia in subjectis συνδεδυασμένοις copulatis & unitis, in quibus unio salvis naturis & naturarum proprietatibus fit, id aequè obtinet. Similitudo porro animae corpori vitam, ignis ferro calorem & lucem communicantis planè ἀπεγοσιόνυσις est; quia nec anima rationalis vitam sibi propriam corpori communicat, & sensitiva ipsa corporis vita est: calor verò & lux in ferro, ignis effecta, non proprietates sunt, non ferro, quia tali, communicantur, sed unà cum subjecto suo uniuntur. Denique unio personalis naturarum in Christo salvis naturis ipsis & earum proprietatibus facta est. Nam & natura Divina planè immutabilis est, & persona Θεανθρώπῳ in S.Scriptura passim secundum naturas & earum proprietates in ea unitas limitatur. Atque id ipsum Chalcedonensis confessionis de unione ea formulæ ab omnibus non-hæreticis receptæ & professæ confirmant. Parum se dissentientes extricant, cùm & salvas proprietates, utpote non humanæ naturæ in se, vel ex se & naturæ suæ proprietate, sed in ὑπostasi & λόγῳ: & distinctas etiam, quia Divinæ naturæ ἰδίως & per naturam, humanæ per gratiam unionis manere asserunt. Si enim in sese non conveniunt naturæ humanæ, in concreto personæ conveniunt. Nulla proin communicatio vel prædicatio in abstracto est. Per gratiam vero unionis humanæ naturæ Divina idiomata competere, & ἀντιδιδόμενον plane, & ipsum ζωοποιοῦν est.
units.tr: LX. The case of the properties of the Deity is different, for neither Scripture nor the analogy of faith allows that these were communicated to the human nature. For Scripture, speaking of Christ, nowhere attributes the divine properties, taken specifically and strictly so called, to the human nature, much less the human to the divine. Otherwise it would set before us a deified humanity and a humanized [ἀνθρώπινον] Deity. For since the divine properties are God himself, and the human are not essentially distinct from the humanity, the humanity could not but be deified if the properties of the Deity were communicated to it, nor could the Deity avoid being humanized [ἀνθρωπίζεσθαι] if the properties of the humanity were attributed to it. These are fig-leaves, since they assert that the Deity is called omnipotent, omnipresent, and so on in itself [κατ' αὐτὸ] and essentially [σὺνσὼς], but the humanity in another way [κατ' ἄλλο] and hypostatically [ὑποστατικῶς], that is, according to another and personally. For to be omnipotent and omnipresent belongs to God alone. Just as there is no other God who is in himself [κατ' αὐτὸ] and essentially [σὺνσὼς], according to himself and essentially, and another who is in another way [κατ' ἄλλο], according to another and personally, so there is no other who is omnipotent, omnipresent, and so on, according to himself and essentially, and another according to another and personally. Clearly, just as the phrase "according to another" corrupts the notion of the Deity, so it corrupts the notion of omnipotence, omnipresence, and so on. Nor can one who is not essentially such be personally omnipotent and omnipresent, since a divine person presupposes the divine essence and cannot be separated from it. If these verbal subtleties had any weight, the argument for the Deity of the Son drawn by the orthodox from the divine properties would perish, since in the same way one could be called omnipotent and omnipresent through another, though he is not God in himself and essentially. Nor do they fare better when, distinguishing between participation [μέθεξιν] and conjunction [συνδυασιν], they pronounce that the divine properties were communicated to the human nature not by participation [κατ' μέθεξιν], so as to inhere in it as subjects, but by conjunction [κατ' συνδυασιν], according to and on account of the conjunction of the natures. For no properties are communicated without inhering in that to which they are communicated. Moreover, communication by conjunction does not take place between natures conjoined [συνδεδυασμένας], but pertains to the person, or the composite united from the natures. And by the same reasoning, the human nature would also be God by conjunction, since the Deity is said to be communicated no less than omnipotence, omnipresence, and so on, which would follow. Furthermore, either all, or some, or none of the properties of the divine nature were communicated to the human nature. Not all, since they cannot even bring themselves to say that it is eternal, immense, and immutable. Not some, since, as all the properties of God are really the same and are God himself, they cannot be separated. Therefore none were communicated. Those on the opposite side do not evade this blow, when they state that all were communicated as regards the personal indwelling of the Deity in the humanity, some as regards predication, and none physically and essentially. For those distinct respects are invented without foundation and do not help the matter at all, because the personal indwelling of God in the flesh is not a communication or a consequence of the union, but the union itself. That the person of the Word is united with the human nature, and with all its properties, is so inescapable that yet on that account the human nature cannot be called omnipotent and omnipresent, any more than it can be called God. The communication as regards predication holds neither for all nor for some of the divine properties, since Scripture predicates neither all nor some of these of the human nature, and no property can be truly and properly predicated of a nature in which it does not inhere. Equally empty is their evasion when, distinguishing between energetic [ἐνεργητικὰς] properties, which are operative and put forth particular operations outwards, and non-energetic [non-ἐνεργητικὰς] properties, through which the divine nature does not operate, they contend that the former, such as omnipotence and omnipresence, were communicated, but not the latter, such as infinity and eternity. For some things are called energetic and others not with respect to their effects and to us, not in themselves; since, with respect to God, on account of the supreme simplicity of his essence, there is no difference among them. Therefore, whatever divine property, whether energetic [ἐνεργητικὴ] or not energetic [non ἐνεργητικὴ], is predicated of anything, all the others must necessarily be predicated of it as well. Again, if the divine nature could not be really united with the human unless its own properties were communicated to it, then neither could the human be really united with the divine unless its properties were communicated to the divine. Thus, by the same reasoning, the divine nature could be predicated as finite, visible, mortal, and so on, which everyone admits is not free from blasphemy. For the dissenters argue that the divine nature, being immutable and most perfect, can receive or suffer nothing, but the human, since it can be perfected in many ways, could through and on account of the union be made far more perfect by the communication of the divine properties; yet they do not solve the knot. For, first, the communication of properties would then arise not from the personal union as such, but from the inequality of the united natures; second, because Scripture attests a true reciprocal communication of properties between the natures and the person, attributing to the person divine things on account of the Deity, and human things on account of the humanity; third, because a greater perfection could indeed be added to the human nature of Christ, but it would be finite, of the kind of which it is capable, and not infinite, of which it is not capable. Moreover, properties that are really different in their subjects cease to be proper when communicated and become common. But those of which there is no common essence cannot be common properties, since every property proceeds necessarily from its essence as its proximate cause, and never goes beyond it. Nor can these things be reconciled by the distinction between unconjoined [ἀσυνδυάζων] and conjoined [συνδεδυασμένων] natures, as if properties could not be communicated in the former but could be in the latter; for in conjoined subjects, which are joined and united, in which the union takes place with the natures and their properties preserved, this holds equally. Furthermore, the likeness of the soul giving life to the body, or fire giving heat and light to iron, is altogether inappropriate [ἀπεγοσιόνυσις]: for the rational soul does not communicate its own life to the body, and the sensitive soul is itself the life of the body; but heat and light in iron, effects of the fire, are not properties communicated to the iron as such, but are united with their subject. Finally, the personal union of the natures in Christ was effected with the natures themselves and their properties preserved. For the divine nature is altogether immutable, and the God-man [Θεανθρώπῳ] in Holy Scripture is everywhere limited to the natures and to the properties united in him, according to them. The Chalcedonian confession of this union, a formula received and professed by all non-heretics, confirms this very thing. The dissenters extricate themselves poorly, since they assert that the properties are preserved, as not belonging to the human nature in itself or from itself and by its own property, but in the hypostasis and the Word; and also that they remain distinct, since they affirm that the divine belongs to the divine nature properly [ἰδίως] and by nature, and the human to the human nature by the grace of union. For if the human nature does not agree with the divine in itself, it agrees with it in the concrete person. Therefore no communication or predication takes place in the abstract. But that the divine properties belong to the human nature by the grace of union is altogether a giving in return [ἀντιδιδόμενον] and a giving of life [ζωοποιοῦν].

units.la: LXI. Cùm tamen tota hæc de communicatione idiomatum disceptatio ab asserta corporis Christi in Eucharistia præsentia ortum habeat, de omnipræsentia, seu Ubiquitate naturæ Christi humanæ palmaria quæstio est. Eam nonnulli unionis hypostaticæ formam & differentiam specificam: alii mollius effectum & consequens dixere. Adversantium de ea contentionem jam vidimus. Sed omnes tamen judicatum & constitutum habent, Christum corpore suo in Eucharistia præsentem esse ἀδιαφόρως. quod si non omnipræsentiam, certè multipræsentiam à Pontificiis assertam, sed ab Augustanis repudiatam, requirit. Imò Jacobus Andreæ in Colloquio Maulbrunnensi; Quicunque, inquit, Majestatem Ubiquitatis carnis Christi nobiscum fateri non volunt; isti fundamentum præsentiæ corporis in Cœna negant. Omnipræsentiam vero naturæ Christi humanæ non una ratio infringit. Nam historia Evangelica clarissimè docet, humanam Christi naturam in utero B. Virginis conceptam, formatam, ex ea natam esse, adeóque in lucem prodiisse, in qua ante non erat; & hominem Christum tum ante, tum post resurrectionem de loco in locum migrasse, & ex terra in Cœlum ascendisse. Ante resurrectionem Christus se non fuisse Bethaniæ, cùm moreretur Lazarus, Joh.XI.15. profitetur; idem circuivit vicos in orbem, Marc.VI.6. 56. obambulavit passim, Act.X.38. Post resurrectionem nec in terra ambulans, nec supra eam evectus ubique fuit. In terra ambulans, Scio, inquiebat, vos Jesum crucifixum quærere. Non est hic, resurrexit enim; Adeste, videte locum, ubi jacebat Dominus; Matth.XXVIII.5.6. Videte manus meas & pedes meos. Ego ipse sum. Nam spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me habere videtis, Luc.XXIV.39. Per dies quadraginta ab iis conspectus, Act.I.3. Nec supra terram in Cœlum evectus ubique fuit. Pauperes, inquit, semper habetis vobiscum, me verò non semper habebitis, Matth.XXVI.11. Relinquo mundum & proficiscor ad Patrem. Joh.XVI.28. Non amplius sum (ero) in mundo: sed isti sunt in mundo. Ego ad te venio, ibid.XVII.11. Ideo ex mundo migravit, Act.I.9. & nunc in Cœlo degit. Ὃν δεῖ ἀποδέξασθαι, Quem oportet cœli suscipiant (non, quem oportet ipsum Cœlos suscipere, quia non corpus Christi locus Cœli est, sed Cœlum locus & thronus corporis Christi) usque ad tempus restitutionis omnium, ibid.III.21.
units.tr: LXI. Although this whole dispute about the communication of idioms arises from the asserted presence of Christ's body in the Eucharist, the chief question is the omnipresence, or ubiquity, of Christ's human nature. Some have called it the form of the hypostatic union and its specific difference; others have described it more mildly as an effect and consequence. We have already seen the contention of those who oppose it. But all of them hold it as settled and decided that Christ is present in the Eucharist with his body indifferently [ἀδιαφόρως]. If this is not omnipresence, it certainly requires multipresence, which the Papists assert but the Augustana men reject. Indeed Jacob Andreae, at the Colloquy of Maulbronn, said: "Those who are unwilling to confess with us the majesty of the ubiquity of Christ's flesh deny the foundation of the presence of the body in the Supper." Yet the omnipresence of Christ's human nature is opposed by more than one argument. For the Gospel history teaches very clearly that the human nature of Christ was conceived in the womb of the blessed Virgin, formed, and born of her, and so came into the light, in which it had not previously been; and that Christ as man moved from place to place, both before and after the resurrection, and ascended from the earth into heaven. Before the resurrection, Christ declared that he was not at Bethany when Lazarus died (John 11:15); he went around the villages in a circle (Mark 6:6, 56); he walked about here and there (Acts 10:38). After the resurrection he was not everywhere, neither walking on the earth nor lifted above it. While walking on the earth: "I know," he said, "that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen. Come, see the place where the Lord lay" (Matt. 28:5-6). "See my hands and my feet; it is I myself. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have" (Luke 24:39). He was seen by them for forty days (Acts 1:3). Nor, lifted above the earth into heaven, was he everywhere. "The poor you always have with you, but me you will not always have" (Matt. 26:11). "I leave the world and go to the Father" (John 16:28). "I am no longer (I will not be) in the world, but these are in the world. I come to you" (ibid. 17:11). Therefore he departed out of the world (Acts 1:9) and now dwells in heaven: "whom heaven must receive" [Ὃν δεῖ ἀποδέξασθαι] — "whom heaven must receive" (not "whom heaven itself must receive", because heaven is not the place of Christ's body; rather heaven is the place and throne of Christ's body) "until the time of the restitution of all things" (Acts 3:21).

units.la: Si esset in terra, ne Sacerdos quidem esset, Hebr. VIII.4. Sed consedit ad dextram throni Majestatis in Cœlis, ib.v.1. rediturus inde novissimo die. Videbunt Filium hominis, venientem in nubibus Cœli, Matth.XXIV.30. Dominus cum voce Archangeli descendet è Cœlo, 1.Thess.IV.16.17. Ex Cœlis expectamus Servatorem Dominum Jesum Christum, Phil.III.20. Quæ cuncta clarior a sunt, quàm ut ingeniosis præsentiæ circumscriptivæ & definitivæ, relictionis mundi quoad visibilem & localem hujus mundi, familiaremque suorum conversationem; & quoad præsentiam invisibilem & illocalem: præsentiæ vel absentiæ secundum naturam & unionem cum λόγῳ &c. distinctionibus, quarum opposita membra nullo Scripturarum præsidio nituntur, se offuscari patiantur. Nam corporis humani non alia quàm visibilis, localis, circumscriptiva præsentia est, & oppósita illi invisibilis definitiva, & illocalis spirituum est. Neque aliud vel revelatio, vel sana ratio docet. Simile σωφὸν φάσεμα ἐσὶ est, cùm Christi carnem in statu exinanitionis communicatam sibi Majestatem non exeruisse, sed localitati & aliis sæculi hujus conditionibus se subjecisse, asserunt. Nulla enim ratione solida id conficiunt. Et omnipræsentem esse actum, non potentiam notat, neque adeò omnipræsentia exeri vel inhiberi, dilatari vel coarctari potest. Localitas enim ex naturæ necessitate, non ex voluntatis libertate pendet. Quomodo igitur natus est, qui etiam extra uterum fuit, antea quàm nasceretur? Quomodo mortuus, cujus anima & corpus ubique præsens, separari non potuit? Quomodo sepultus, qui jam in sepulchro erat? Quomodo in Cœlum (& quidem terræ oppositum, Psalm, CXV.16. Esaj.LXVI.1. Matth.V.34.35.) ascendit, qui priùs ibi erat? Quomodo ad dextram Dei, & quidem in Cœlis, Ephes.I.20. in excelsis, Hebr.I.3. consedit, qui extra Cœlum est? Quomodo ad judicium descendet, qui ante judicium in terra est? Præterea corpus Christi in unione corporis humani naturam retinuit, vel non retinuit. Si non retinuit, corpus esse desiit. Sin retinuit, omnipræsens esse nequit, quia corpus humanum suis dimensionibus circumscriptum, non immensum: locale, visibile, palpabile est: & tale corpus Christi esse, Scriptura testis est, Luc.II.52. XXIV.39. Joh.XX.27. Habet equidem corpus Christi hyperphysica non pauca, respectu unionis personalis cum λόγῳ; sed illa naturam corporis physici non mutant, nec proprietates ejus abolent. Unio enim unitorum naturam neutiquam evertit. Denique cùm corpus Christi in quocunque statu finitum sit, simul omnipræsens esse non potest. Nam quod finitum est, & suis, & alienis terminis finitur. Contra quod ubique est, nec suis, nec alienis terminis finiri potest. Non satisfaciunt dissentientes, cùm idem & finitum esse, & ratione subsistentiæ personalis infinitæ à λόγῳ communicatæ, omnipræsens esse, decernunt. Cùm enim ne Divina quidem natura nisi per infinitatem ubique esse possit, quomodo humana absque infinitatis communicatione ubique esse poterit? Si tamen per subsistentiam personalem infinitam à Filio Dei communicatam humana natura ubique est, etiam ubique
units.tr: If he were on earth, he would not even be a priest (Heb. 8:4). But he sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens (Heb. 8:1), from which he will return on the last day. "They will see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven" (Matt. 24:30). "The Lord himself will descend from heaven with the voice of the archangel" (1 Thess. 4:16-17). "We look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, from heaven" (Phil. 3:20). All these things are too clear to be obscured by clever distinctions between circumscriptive and definitive presence, or between Christ's leaving the world as to its visible and local aspect and his familiar converse with his own, and his invisible and non-local presence, or presence and absence according to nature and union with the λόγος, and so on; the opposite members of these distinctions rest on no support from the Scriptures. For the presence of a human body is nothing other than visible, local, and circumscriptive; its opposite, invisible, definitive, and non-local, belongs to spirits. Neither revelation nor sound reason teaches anything else. It is similar to a subtle pretence [σοφὸν φάσμα] when they assert that Christ's flesh, in the state of humiliation, did not put forth the majesty communicated to it, but subjected itself to locality and the other conditions of this age. For they establish this by no solid reasoning. Omnipresence denotes an act, not a power, and omnipresence cannot be put forth or held back, expanded or contracted. For locality depends on the necessity of nature, not on the freedom of the will. How then was he born who was also outside the womb before he was born? How did he die, whose soul and body, being present everywhere, could not be separated? How was he buried, who was already in the sepulchre? How did he ascend into heaven (and indeed to that which is opposed to earth: Ps. 115:16; Isa. 66:1; Matt. 5:34-35), who was there before? How did he sit at the right hand of God, and indeed in the heavens (Eph. 1:20), in the heights (Heb. 1:3), if he is outside heaven? How will he descend to judgment, who is on earth before the judgment? Moreover, the body of Christ either retained the nature of a human body in its union, or it did not. If it did not, it has ceased to be a body. But if it retained it, it cannot be omnipresent, because a human body, circumscribed by its dimensions, is not immense; it is local, visible, and palpable. And Scripture bears witness that Christ's body was such: Luke 2:52; 24:39; John 20:27. Indeed Christ's body has not a few hyperphysical qualities with respect to its personal union with the λόγος; but these do not change the nature of a physical body or abolish its properties. For union by no means overturns the nature of the things united. Finally, since the body of Christ is finite in whatever state, it cannot be omnipresent at the same time. For what is finite is bounded both by its own limits and by foreign ones; but what is everywhere cannot be bounded either by its own or by foreign limits. Those who dissent are not satisfied when they decree that the same body is both finite and, by reason of the infinite personal subsistence communicated to it from the λόγος, omnipresent. For since even the divine nature can be everywhere only through infinity, how will the human nature be able to be everywhere without a communication of infinity? But if the human nature is everywhere through the infinite personal subsistence communicated by the Son of God, then it is everywhere also—

units.la: Imprimis natura Christi humana non est omnipræsens. ubique erit per infinitatem cum subsistentia personali communicatam. Et quomodo sic eadem natura finita & infinita esse, sive per unionem, sive absque ea, potest?
units.tr: First, the human nature of Christ is not omnipresent. It will be everywhere through the infinity communicated with personal subsistence. And how can the same nature be both finite and infinite, whether through union or apart from it?

units.la: LXII. Par ratio est cæterarum proprietatum, quas communicatas naturæ humanæ scisçunt. Nam omniscium non fuisse, vel esse, satis ex iis, quæ de ejus profectu, & nonnulla ἀγνοίᾳ supra diximus, liquet. Habuit quidem humanitas Divinum oraculum intimè & personaliter sibi unitum, τὸν λόγον, sed ei irradians liberè, non necessariò naturaliter. Intellectus finitus quomodo omniscientiæ, quæ infinita scientia est, capax esse potest? Cumque Christus noverit successivè, ab uno ad aliud discurrens, omniscius esse non potuit, quia omniscientia discursum tollit, & cui omnia nota sunt, is nil successivè cognoscit. Neque juvat omniscientiæ causam distinguere, ut, quæ, maximè in statu exaltationis, in actu est, omniscientiam in actu ponat, quæ verò successionis intervalla admittit, scientiam distinctis & successivis actibus obnoxiam reddat. Nam causa scientiæ Christi, quam illi communicationem & revelationem ᾗ λόγῳ faciunt, non est proprietas Dei essentialis. Ergo nec scientia Christo secundum humanam naturam communicata proprietas Dei essentialis est. Et si causa omniscientiæ semper in actu est, non potest causa illa esse assumptio carnis in λόγῳ, utpote quæ semel tantùm facta est, & ex quo facta est, semper manet. Præterea si causa omniscientiæ semper est & fuit in actu, ipsa quoque omniscientia semper, adeóque æquè in statu exinanitionis atque exaltationis in actu, eóque secundo, esse debuit. Accedit, quòd revelatio Dei, quæ est opus ad extra, humanæ Christi naturæ facta, ejusdem scientiam nonnisi successivè & per intervalla operari potuit. Et qualiscunque scientia Christi secundum naturam humanam, Dei effectum est. Nullum autem effectum Dei proprie dictum & ad extra, Deo æquale est. Sicut non omnipotens caro Christi est, quia Christus, quà homo, potentiorem se agnovit. Nam in passione se sustentari petiit, & multis modis Patri se commendavit; miracula editurus Patrem invocavit Joh.XI.41. Quæ ita κατ' οἰκονομίαν facta sunt, ut secundum naturam humanam aliter fieri non potuerint, adeóque secundum eam etiam ἀπλῶς facta sunt, quia secundum eam simpliciter auxilio & sustentatione Dei indiguit; & pro conservatione sui orare debuit.
units.tr: LXII. The same reasoning holds for the remaining properties which they say are communicated to human nature. For that he was not omniscient, or is not, is clear enough from what we said above about his progress and certain [states of] ignorance [ἀγνοίᾳ]. The humanity indeed had the divine Oracle, the λόγος, intimately and personally united to itself, but the λόγος shone upon it freely, not necessarily by nature. How can a finite intellect be capable of omniscience, which is infinite knowledge? And since Christ knew successively, passing from one thing to another, he could not have been omniscient, because omniscience excludes discursive reasoning, and one to whom all things are known in a single act knows nothing successively. Nor does it help to distinguish the cause of omniscience, so that what is in act especially in the state of exaltation posits omniscience in act, while what admits intervals of succession makes knowledge subject to distinct and successive acts. For the cause of Christ's knowledge, which they call a communication and revelation through the λόγος, is not an essential property of God. Therefore knowledge communicated to Christ according to human nature is not an essential property of God either. And if the cause of omniscience is always in act, that cause cannot be the assumption of flesh into the λόγος, since that happened only once and, from the time it happened, always remains. Moreover, if the cause of omniscience always is and always was in act, omniscience itself must also always have been in act, and so equally in the state of humiliation as in that of exaltation. Add to this that God's revelation, which is an external work made to the human nature of Christ, could operate its knowledge only successively and at intervals. And whatever knowledge Christ had according to human nature is an effect of God. But no effect of God, properly so called and external, is equal to God. Just as the flesh of Christ is not omnipotent, because Christ as man acknowledged himself to be weaker. For in his passion he sought to be sustained, and in many ways he commended himself to the Father; about to work miracles, he invoked the Father (John 11:41). These things were done according to the economy [κατ' οἰκονομίαν], so that they could not have been done otherwise according to human nature, and so according to that nature they were done absolutely [ἀπλῶς], because according to it he simply needed the help and support of God, and had to pray for his own preservation.

units.la: Tum humana Christi natura multis infirmitatibus obnoxia, passibilis fuit, passa est, & dotes innumeras unionis beneficio accepit. At qui omnipotens est, semper impassibilis, immortalis est, & infinitam potentiam habet, sive eam exerat, sive non. Præterea omnipotentia carnis vel eadem est cum omnipotentia Dei, vel diversa. Si diversa, duo erunt omnipotentes. Si eadem, erit etiam formale principium Divinarum operationum, quin & ipse Deus, quia quisquis eadem potentia operatur, qua pater, Deus est, Joh.V.19. &c. ᾿Αντιπόθος proin est dicere, omnipotentem esse non ex se, & proprietate essentiali, sed ex gratia unionis, quia omnipotentia nulla datur ex gratia, sed ex naturæ necessitate; & omnipotens Deus est. Deus autem non est ex gratia, sed per essentiam. Ideo passim apud Prophetas Deus ab iis, qui natura Dii non sunt, hoc argumento se disparat, quòd omnipotens omnia creaverit, conservet & gubernet. Excusatiùs errant, qui cum Rintelensibus nuperis naturæ humanæ non omnipotentiam, sed Divinam Majestatem & supremum Dominium, quod per omnipotentiam ᾗ λόγῳ, principii hypostatici sibi uniti, exerceat, vendicant; sed errant tamen, quia Divina Majestas & supremum Dominium solius Dei est, nec principio alio, quo exerceatur, indiget; & sic ὁ λόγος esset organon carnis, cùm contra caro sit organon Deitatis. Denique vis vivificandi & judicandi, cùm non proprietas Dei essentialis, sed opus θεανδρικὸν & apotelesma sit, utrique certè naturæ Christi competit, utraque faciente quod suum est; Divina, quod Divinum, humana, quod humanum est. Nec vis infinita, quæ in potestate vivificandi & judicandi gliscit, humanitatis; nec opera humana, quæ in eadem exercentur, Divinitatis proprie sunt. Aliás vitam habere in se ipso solius Patris & Filii est, Joh. V.26. & vita Dei ipsa viva & actuosa ejus essentia est; & si humana natura vim vivificam, qualis in Deitate est, habet, ἔχει ὁ Θεὸς vivens Deus pariter erit. Et quid tum ei factum est in morte Christi? An unà cum natura humana extincta est? At vita & vis vivifica Dei non magis, quàm ipse Deus extinguitur. An ante mortis tempus ab ea separata fuit? At sic unio personalis soluta fuisset. Nam quòd vitam naturalem, non supernaturalem, quæ ex unione pendet, extinctam esse, & in morte actus secundi vitæ hujus liberam abdicationem factam esse, excipiunt, minimè satisfacit, quia idem corpus in cruce pendens, in sepulchro jacens, mortuum propter vitæ naturalis privationem, & nihilominus propter vitæ supernaturalis communicationem vivum dicere, est corpus mortuum & non mortuum dicere; & vita Dei, adeóque vis ejus vivifica, viva & actuosa ejus essentia, purus actus, non potentia actui permixta est. Λόγος equidem potentiam & vim suam Divinam effectivè inhibuit, ut caro mori posset; at non humanitas, quæ talis potentiæ expers fuit.
units.tr: Then the human nature of Christ, subject to many infirmities, was passible, suffered, and received countless gifts through the benefit of the union. But he who is omnipotent is always impassible and immortal, and has infinite power, whether he exercises it or not. Moreover, the omnipotence of the flesh is either the same as the omnipotence of God or different. If it is different, there will be two omnipotent beings. If it is the same, it will also be the formal principle of the divine operations, and indeed God himself, since whoever operates by the same power as the Father is God (John 5:19, etc.). It is therefore absurd [ἀντιπόθος] to say that he is omnipotent not from himself and by essential property, but from the grace of the union, since omnipotence is given by no grace but by the necessity of nature, and the omnipotent one is God. But God is not from grace but by his essence. Therefore throughout the Prophets God distinguishes himself from those who are not gods by nature by this argument, that as the omnipotent one he created, preserves and governs all things. They err more excusably who, with the recent Rintelians, claim for human nature not omnipotence but divine majesty and supreme dominion, which it exercises through omnipotence in virtue of the Word, the hypostatic principle united to it. Yet they still err, because divine majesty and supreme dominion belong to God alone and need no other principle by which to be exercised; and so the Word would be the instrument of the flesh, whereas on the contrary the flesh is the instrument of the Deity. Finally, the power of quickening and judging, since it is not an essential property of God but a theandric work and effect, certainly belongs to both natures of Christ, each doing what is its own: the divine nature what is divine, the human nature what is human. Nor is the infinite power that lies in the authority to quicken and judge proper to the humanity, nor are the human works exercised in the same proper to the Deity. Otherwise, to have life in himself belongs only to the Father and the Son (John 5:26); and the life of God is his living and active essence itself. If the human nature had the quickening power that is in the Deity, then God would have it, and the living God would likewise be [affected]. And what then happened to him in the death of Christ? Was he extinguished together with the human nature? But the life and quickening power of God is no more extinguished than God himself. Was it separated from him before the time of death? But then the personal union would have been dissolved. For to say that the natural life, not the supernatural life which depends on the union, was extinguished, and that in death the second act of this life was freely laid aside, is not at all satisfactory. For to call the same body, hanging on the cross and lying in the tomb, dead because of the privation of natural life, and yet nonetheless living because of the communication of supernatural life, is to say that the body is dead and not dead. And the life of God, and therefore his quickening power, his living and active essence, is pure act, not power mixed with act. The Word indeed inhibited his power and divine might effectively, so that the flesh could die; but not the humanity, which had no share in such power.

units.la: LXIII. Non magnam speciem, & vim omnino nullam adversantium argumenta habent. De communicatione hypostaseos supra diximus. Qualiscunque ea est, idiomatum communicationem in natura factam non probat, quia subsistentia per se & in universum cum natura humana non pugnat, (nam homines meri per se subsistunt) at communicatio idiomatum Deitatis cum humanitate cum natura humana pugnat, non minùs quàm Deitas cum humanitate, creator cum creatura. Tam enim proprietates Divinæ soli Deo conveniunt, quàm ipsa Deitas. Neque etiam realis duarum naturarum in Christo unio communicationem idiomatum inter naturas infert, tum quia unio illa naturarum discrimen non tollit, sed ponit, cùm unita nisi in unione distincta dici non possint: tum quia aliás etiam Divina natura finita, mortalis, passa esset, & dici posset. quod cogitatu dictúque impium foret. Etiam a persona ad naturas ἀσυμβάλλους argumentatio est, quia persona equidem sicut naturam utramque,
units.tr: LXIII. The arguments of the opponents have no great appearance, and no force at all. We have spoken above of the communication of the hypostasis. Whatever kind of communication that is, it does not prove a communication of properties made in the nature, because subsistence in itself and in general does not clash with human nature (for mere men subsist in themselves), but the communication of the properties of the Deity with the humanity does clash with the human nature, no less than the Deity with the humanity, the Creator with the creature. For the divine properties belong to God alone, just as the Deity itself does. Nor does the real union of the two natures in Christ bring about a communication of properties between the natures, both because that union does not remove the distinction of the natures but posits it, since things united cannot be called united unless they are distinct in the union; and because otherwise the divine nature too would be finite, mortal and passible, and could be said to be so, which would be impious to think or say. Argument from the person to the natures that are incommunicable [ἀσυμβάλλους] is also invalid, because the person indeed claims the properties of both natures for itself, just as it has both natures; but a single nature cannot claim the properties of the individual person, and so also of the opposed nature, without the confusion [σύγχυσιν] of the natures. Therefore the passages usually opposed are unassailable [ἀνεγκλήτους]: Where two or three are gathered together...

units.la: Adversantium argumentis satis fit. que, ita proprietates utriusque naturæ sibi vendicat; sed natura una singulas personæ, adeoque etiam oppositæ naturæ proprietates citra naturarum συγχυσιν vendicare non potest. Ἀνεγκλητουσ igitur sunt, quæ opponi solent loca: Ubi duo vel tres congregati sunt in nomine meo, ibi sum in medio eorum, Matth.XVIII.20. Mihi data est omnis potestas in Cœlo & in terra, ibid.XXVIII.18. (ubi tamen potestas Mediatoria, apotelesmatis indolem habens, & certo sensu personæ secundum utramque naturam, quoad exercitium inprimis ejus, conveniens intelligitur.) Ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi, ib.v.20. In Christo habitat tota plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter, Col.II.9. aliaque eiusmodi; quæ de persona Christi loquuntur, & secundum alterutram naturam sensum determinatum habent. Neque etiam quæ Christo, qua Mediatori, & in œconomia Mediatoris, tribuuntur, idiomatum communicationem arguunt, sed apotelesmatum duntaxat, quæ toti personæ secundum utramque naturam competere, supra diximus & exposuimus. Huc pertinent loca: Mihi data est omnis potestas &c. Matth.XXVIII.18. Requiescit super eo Spiritus Jehovæ, spiritus sapientiæ & intelligentiæ, &c. Esaj.XI.2. Unus Deus, unus Mediator Dei & hominum, &c. 1.Tim.II.5. Potestatem ei fecit judicium faciendi, quia Filius hominis est, Joh.V.27. Qui descendit ipse est, qui etiam ascendit super omnes Cœlos, ut impleret omnia, Eph.IV.10. Propterea exaltavit eum Deus, &c. Phil.II.9.10. Panis quem dabo, est caro mea, quam dabo pro vita mundi, Joh.VI.51. Sanguis Jesu Christi purificat nos ab omni peccato, 1.Joh.I.7. Hæc naturæ etiam humanæ suo modo & sensu convenire indubitatum est: sed ut ei, ceu humanæ, non Divinæ, & propter participationem muneris Mediatorii convenire possunt. Opera enim, vel gloriæ Mediatoris, non proprietates Deitatis sunt. Præterea non ideo natura Christi humana à Divina separatur, vel utramque inter χωρισμα vel διαστημα intercedit, quia non amplius in terra est, ubi tamen natura ἡ λογος Divina est, utpote quæ Cœlum & terram implet. Cùm enim Divina natura ubique sit, etiam cum humana natura in Cœlo existente est, & eo quidem singulari modo, quo eam in utero B. Virginis in personæ suæ unitatem assumpsit, cum ea est, adeoque ab ea nullatenus separatur. Quod ii ipsi diversarum partium, qui ubiquitatem carnis negant, vel restrictam duntaxat ad statum exaltationis tuentur, agnoscant oportet. Est sanè caro in toto λογω, qui ubique est; at non iccirco ipsa quoque ubique est; quia in λογω omnipræsente est non per commensionem, extensionem in eo, vel exæquationem, qualis unio rerum infinitarum, si plures infinitas dari possibile esset, foret; sed per unionem rei manentis finitæ cum infinita, corporeæ cum spirituali, partibilis cum αμερι impartibili. Si enim caro, quia in omnipræsente subsistit, omnipræsens est, erit etiam æterna, infinita, quia in λογω pariter æterno & infinito subsistit. Est autem λογος extra carnem, quia non includitur, nec æquatur carni: & non extra carnem, quia ab ea non separatur. Et totus est in carne, licèt non inclusus carni: & totus extra carnem, sed ab ea non separatus, idque propter essentiæ suæ simplicitatem & infinitatem. Neque propterea λογος alicubi est non homo, si alicubi est, ubi homo non est; vel alicubi ἐνσαρκος, alibi ἀσαρκος, quia nullibi ab humanitate separatur. Paulus equidem simul in carne, & simul extra carnem esse non potuit, 2.Cor.XII.3: quia finitus: at potest λογος, quia infinitus. Alioquin nec simul in Cœlo & in terra esse posset, quia nec Paulus simul in Cœlo & in terra esse potest, πρωτον ψευδος est, quòd finitum & infinitum, compositum & simplex, creatura & creator, ceu paria comparantur, cùm maximè disparia sint. Par ferè fallacia est, cùm ex verbis S.Pauli, ajentis in Christo κατοικειν habitare plenitudinem Deitatis corporaliter Col.II.9. colligunt, λογος, si extra carnem esse potest, etiam extra domum suam κατοικειν habitare posse, & ibi habitare posse, ubi non est σωματικως corporaliter. quæ nimis crassa sunt. Non enim plenitudo omnis Deitatis extra domum suam habitat, quia nullibi ab ea separatur, licèt, ceu infinitus, ei non includatur: nec in carne, ceu Templo suo Deitatis plenitudo omnis non habitat corporaliter, quia alicubi Deitas est, ubi non est λογος. Non enim ibi σωμα carnem Christi, sed essentiam Deitatis ejus notat: & si carnem notaret, in ea λογος habitat, ibi etiam, ubi caro localiter non existit, quia non coëxistens licèt ubique cum carne, ab ea tamen non separatur. Gloriosa porro operatio humanæ naturæ Christi in iis etiam locis, in quibus localiter non existit, ejusdem omniprædsentiam non arguit, quia virtute meriti, nec non communi imperio & ministerio secundarum causarum, Angelorum inprimis & hominum, operari etiam ibi potest, ubi corporaliter præsens non est. Quomodo etiam Reges eas regni sui partes, à quibus corpore suo maximè dissiti sunt, regere possunt. Ita Christus ascendit ὑπερανω παντων τ ἐξουρανων supra omnes cœlos (aspectabiles, viam ad tertium Cœlum munientes) ut omnia impleret donis & ministerii delegatione, Ephes.IV.10.11. Accepit enim dona in hominibus, ibid. v.8. ex Psalm. LXVIII.19. quia impetravit merito suo, ut dona Spiritus S. Christo & Patre donante digna hominibus donarentur, imò ipse Christus, ceu caput, illa in corpore suo acciperet. Sicut meritum, ita impletio & donatio utriusque naturæ est; opus & apotelesma Mediatoris. uti supra innuimus. Ac multò minus etiam sessio Christi ad dextram Dei carnis omnipræsentiam infert, tum quia est dignitas officii, quod Christus in Cœlo, Regia sua, secundum utramque naturam, sed utrique naturæ convenienter, exercet, gloriosè dominando in medio inimicorum suorum, uti eam S.Paulus 1.Cor.XV.25. ex Psalmo CX.1. interpretatur: tum quia non ubique, sed in Cœlis ad dextram Dei sedet, & hujus rei gratia, relicta terra in Cœlum ascendit. Quem collocavit ad dextram ejus in cœlestibus, Eph.I.20. Talem habemus Pontificem, qui sedit in dextra throni magnificentiæ εν τοις ουρανοις in Cœlis, Hebr.VIII.1. Sed & Christus, quà homo, unctus est spiritu sapientiæ & intelligentiæ, spiritu consilii & fortitudinis, scientiæ & timoris Jehovæ &c. Esaj.XI.2. supra confortes suos, Psalm. XLV.8. Spiritum habens ἐκ ουκ μετρου non ex mensura (longè magis ipse, ceu caput, quàm Ecclesia, clesia, ejus corpus) Joh.III.34. quia natura ejus humana non equidem Divinis idiomatibus, sed spiritu sapientiæ, intelligentiæ, scientiæ donisque aliis sine numero & gradu communi, & conjunctis perfectis iis, cum disjuncta imperfecta, & ex donorum Christi ipsius plenitudine redundantia alii possideant, pollet. In mysterio Dei Patris & Christi, non proprie in humanitate Christi, omnes thesauros sapientiæ & cognitionis ἀπόκρυφας abscônditos, esse S.
