Paulus Col.II.3. docet, quia mysterium illud, seu Evangelium facit sapientes per fidem ad salutem, 2.Tim.III.15. & est veritas secundum pietatem, Tit.I.1. Est enim sapientia in adultis, 1.Cor.II.6. Non possunt tamen sic in Evangelio thesauri sapientiæ & cognitionis abscondi, quin iidem in toto Christo, qui in Evangelio prædicatur, adeoque etiam in humanitate, sed finito & creaturæ conveniente modo, lateant. Pertinere enim thesauri illi quodammodo possunt non ad idiomata communicata, sed ad charismata, perfectam omnium salutis mysteriorum cognitionem, & totam salutis rationem, quam Filius, quâ homo, à λόγῳ informatus, nobis revelavit. Quòd insuper Christo omnem ἐξουσίαν potestatem in Cœlo & in terra datam esse, ipsemet Matth.XXVIII.18. testatus est, de tota persona, & ejus non idiomate, sed apotelesmate intelligendum esse, jam dicere occupavimus. De cætero sicut ἐξουσία potestas non est δύναμις potentia: ita nec πᾶσα ἐξουσία omnis potestas, est πᾶσα δύναμις omnis potentia. Nam ἐξουσία rei faciendæ jus, authoritas, potestas: at δύναμις ejusdem faciendæ vis, facultas & potentia est. Quæ duo adeò distincta sunt, ut etiam separari possint. Hoc inprimis loco non potentiam, sed mandandi, judicandi authoritatem significari, sequentia: Euntes ergo, prædicate &c.v.19. h.e. potestate data vobis mando, ut prædicetis Evangelium; nec non illa: Qui crediderit, salvabitur, qui non crediderit, damnabitur, Marc. XVI.16. q.d. quia judicandi potestatem habeo, qui salvandi, qui damnandi sint, declaro; demonstrant. Idem loca similia Matth.VII.29. Marc.I.27. Joh.XVII.2. comparanti liquet. Ac licet Luc.IV.36. IX.1. ἐξουσία & δύναμις conjungantur, non tamen ut synonyma conjunguntur, sed ad significandum, quòd in Christo & Apostolis non tantùm jus & authoritas edendi miracula, sed etiam vis ac potentia fuerit. Accedit quòd πᾶσα ἐξουσία omnis potestas, apotelesma personale Mediatoris; at πᾶσα δύναμις omnipotentia proprietatis essentialis Dei; illa potestati superioris Dei, qui Jesum Dominum fecit, Act.II.36. & ejusdem pedibus omnia subjecit, 1.Cor.XV.27. subordinata; hæc nullius potestati subjecta est. Non ergo si Christus, quâ Mediator, secundum utramque naturam omnem potestatem in Cœlo & in terra, in Angelos & homines utrobique existentes, accepit, omnipotentiam essentialem Dei eidem datam esse consequitur: quia illa potestas omnis, non omnipotentia essentialis Dei, sed officii Regii pars, imò ipsum officium Regium Christi est, tam verè ei secundum utramque naturam competens, quàm verè secundum utramque naturam Rex est. Et potestas quidem illa Christo est δόσεως data, & in tempore data, sed non ideo soli naturæ humanæ, non etiam Divinæ
units.tr: Sufficient answer is given to the arguments of our opponents. The person claims for itself the properties of each nature in the same way, but a single nature cannot claim the properties of the individual person, and therefore not even the properties of the opposite nature, without confusion of the natures [συγχύσιν]. The passages usually brought against us are therefore blameless: Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them, Matt. 18.20. All power is given to me in heaven and on earth, ibid. 28.18 (where, however, the mediatorial power, having the character of an effect, is understood to belong to the person according to both natures, especially as regards its exercise). I am with you always, even to the end of the age, ibid. v. 20. In Christ dwells all the fullness of the Deity bodily, Col. 2.9; and others of this kind, which speak of the person of Christ and have a definite sense according to one or other nature. Nor do the things attributed to Christ as Mediator, and in the economy of the Mediator, prove a communication of properties, but only of effects, which, as we have said and explained above, belong to the whole person according to both natures. To this belong the passages: All power is given to me, etc., Matt. 28.18; The Spirit of Jehovah rests upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, etc., Isa. 11.2; One God, one Mediator between God and men, etc., 1 Tim. 2.5; He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of man, John 5.27; He who descended is the same who also ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things, Eph. 4.10; Therefore God exalted him, etc., Phil. 2.9-10; The bread which I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world, John 6.51; The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin, 1 John 1.7. It is beyond doubt that these things belong to the human nature too, in its own way and sense; but they belong to it as human, not as divine, and on account of its participation in the Mediatorial office. For the works or the glory of the Mediator are not properties of the Deity. Moreover, the human nature of Christ is not separated from the divine because he is no longer on earth, while the divine nature, the Logos, is present there, since it fills heaven and earth. For since the divine nature is everywhere, it is also with the human nature existing in heaven, and indeed in that singular manner by which it assumed that nature into unity of person in the womb of the blessed Virgin; so it is with it and is in no way separated from it. Those of the different parts who deny the ubiquity of the flesh, or confine it only to the state of exaltation, ought to acknowledge this. Certainly the flesh is in the whole Logos, who is everywhere; yet the flesh is not therefore also everywhere. For it is in the omnipresent Logos not by commensurate extension within it or by equalization, such as would be the union of infinite things, if several infinites could exist, but by the union of a remaining finite thing with the infinite, of the corporeal with the spiritual, of the divisible with the indivisible [ἀμερῆ]. For if the flesh, because it subsists in the omnipresent, is omnipresent, it will also be eternal and infinite, since it subsists in the Logos, who is equally eternal and infinite. The Logos is outside the flesh, because it is not enclosed by it nor made equal to it; and it is not outside the flesh, because it is not separated from it. It is wholly in the flesh, though not enclosed by the flesh; and wholly outside the flesh, yet not separated from it, and this on account of the simplicity and infinity of its essence. Nor is the Logos therefore somewhere not man, if it is somewhere where man is not; or somewhere incarnate and elsewhere non-incarnate, since it is nowhere separated from the humanity. Paul indeed could not be at once in the flesh and at once outside the flesh, 2 Cor. 12.3, because he is finite; but the Logos can, because it is infinite. Otherwise it could not be at once in heaven and on earth, since Paul himself cannot be at once in heaven and on earth. That is a first falsehood: finite and infinite, composite and simple, creature and creator are compared as if they were equal, when they are most unequal. A similar fallacy is involved when, from the words of St. Paul saying that in Christ the fullness of the Deity dwells [κατοικεῖν] bodily, Col. 2.9, they infer that the Logos, if it can be outside the flesh, can also dwell outside its own house, and can dwell where it is not bodily. These are too crude. For the whole fullness of the Deity does not dwell outside its own house, since it is nowhere separated from it, although, as infinite, it is not enclosed by it; nor does the whole fullness of the Deity dwell bodily in the flesh as in its temple, since the Deity is somewhere where the Logos is not. For the word "body" there does not denote the flesh of Christ but the essence of his Deity; and if it denoted the flesh, the Logos would dwell in it even there where the flesh does not exist locally, since, although it is everywhere with the flesh without co-existing, it is nevertheless not separated from it. Moreover, the glorious operation of the human nature of Christ, even in those places where it is not locally present, does not prove its omnipresence, since by virtue of merit, and also by the common command and ministry of secondary causes, especially of angels and men, it can act even where it is not bodily present; just as kings can rule those parts of their kingdom from which they are most distant in body. So Christ ascended above all the heavens [ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν οὐρανῶν] (the visible ones, paving the way to the third heaven), that he might fill all things with gifts and with the delegation of ministry, Eph. 4.10-11. For he received gifts among men, ibid. v. 8, from Psalm 68.19, because by his merit he obtained that the gifts of the Holy Spirit, worthy to be bestowed by Christ and the Father, should be given to men; indeed Christ himself, as head, would receive them in his body. As with merit, so the filling and the bestowal belong to both natures; it is the work and effect of the Mediator, as we hinted above. Much less does the sitting of Christ at the right hand of God imply the omnipresence of his flesh: first, because it is the dignity of the office which Christ exercises in heaven, his royal seat, according to both natures, but fittingly to each nature, gloriously ruling in the midst of his enemies, as St. Paul interprets it, 1 Cor. 15.25, from Psalm 110.1; and second, because he does not sit everywhere but in the heavens at the right hand of God, and for this reason, having left the earth, he ascended into heaven. Whom he set at his right hand in the heavenly places, Eph. 1.20. We have such a high priest, who sat at the right hand of the throne of majesty in the heavens [ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς], Heb. 8.1. But also Christ, as man, was anointed with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, of knowledge and of the fear of Jehovah, etc., Isa. 11.2; above his fellows, Psalm 45.8; having the Spirit not by measure [ἐκ οὐκ μέτρου] (much more so himself, as head, than the Church, his body), John 3.34; because his human nature is strong, not indeed by the divine properties, but by the spirit of wisdom, understanding, knowledge and other gifts without number or degree, common and joined, the perfect gifts with the imperfect, and others possess them by overflow from the fullness of the gifts of Christ himself. St. Paul teaches, Col. 2.3, that in the mystery of God the Father and of Christ, not properly in the humanity of Christ, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge [ἀπόκρυφοι] are hidden, because that mystery, or Gospel, makes wise unto salvation through faith, 2 Tim. 3.15, and is the truth which accords with godliness, Titus 1.1. For there is wisdom among the mature, 1 Cor. 2.6. Yet the treasures of wisdom and knowledge cannot be hidden in the Gospel without also lying hidden in the whole Christ who is preached in the Gospel, and so also in his humanity, but in a finite manner fitting a creature. For those treasures can in some sense pertain not to communicated properties but to gifts of grace: to the perfect knowledge of all the mysteries of salvation and the whole plan of salvation, which the Son, as man, informed by the Logos, has revealed to us. Moreover, that all power in heaven and on earth [ἐξουσία] has been given to Christ, Matt. 28.18 itself attests, and we have already undertaken to show that this must be understood of the whole person, and of an effect rather than a property. For the rest, just as power [ἐξουσία] is not might [δύναμις], so also all power is not all might. For ἐξουσία is the right, authority and power to do a thing, but δύναμις is the force, faculty and might to do the same. These two are so distinct that they can even be separated. In this passage not might but the authority to command and to judge is signified, as the following shows: Going therefore, preach, etc., v. 19, that is, by the power given to you I command you to preach the Gospel; and also He who believes will be saved, he who does not believe will be condemned, Mark 16.16, as if to say: because I have the power of judging, I declare who are to be saved and who condemned. This is clear when one compares similar passages, Matt. 7.29, Mark 1.27, John 17.2. And although Luke 4.36 and 9.1 join ἐξουσία and δύναμις, they are not joined as synonyms, but to signify that in Christ and the apostles there was not only the right and authority to work miracles, but also force and power. Moreover, all power is a personal effect of the Mediator, but all might, omnipotence, is an essential property of God; the former is subordinate to the power of the superior God, who made Jesus Lord, Acts 2.36, and subjected all things under his feet, 1 Cor. 15.27; the latter is subject to no power. Therefore, if Christ as Mediator received all power in heaven and on earth, over angels and men existing in both, according to both natures, it does not follow that the essential omnipotence of God was given to him; for that all power is not the essential omnipotence of God but a part of the royal office, indeed the royal office of Christ itself, belonging to him as truly according to both natures as he is truly King according to both natures. And that power was indeed given to Christ by gift, and given in time; but it was not therefore given to the human nature alone, and not also to the divine.

units.la: data, quia, juxta regulam Patrum, quod Christo in tempore datum est, secundum humanitatem, non secundum Divinitatem, cui nihil dari posset, datum intelligi debeat. Licet enim Deitati ratione essentiæ nihil dari posset (quo sensu Patres regulam eam intellexerunt, & adversus Antitrinitarios urserunt) at dari potuit ratione officii, ut illud de voluntate Patris suscieperet, & exequeretur. Habuit ille jam ante, quâ Deus, omnem potestatem. Sed ut gloriam Deitatis, occultatam in forma servi, à Patre accepit, Joh.XVII.1.5. ita & potestatem restitutam quasi recepit.
units.tr: given, because according to the rule of the Fathers, what was given to Christ in time must be understood as given according to his humanity, not according to his divinity, to which nothing could be given. For although nothing could be given to the Deity by reason of its essence (in which sense the Fathers understood that rule and pressed it against the Antitrinitarians), something could be given by reason of office, namely that he should take up and carry out what was the Father's will. He had already, as God, all power before. But just as he received from the Father the glory of the Deity hidden in the form of a servant (John 17:1, 5), so he is said to have received back the power, as it were restored.

units.la: LXIV. Sed hæc veritatis tuendæ, non schismatis alendi gratiâ à nobis disceptata sunto. Nam nec dissensus ille per se, & ab affectu um æstu summotus, tanti est, ut scindere Ecclesias in præcipua de Christi Persona doctrina consentientes posset vel debeat. Utrique enim veteris Ecclesiæ confessioni de Persona Christi in Synodo Chalcedonensi editæ, subscribimus. Nec dissentientes nobis Nestorianismi scabiem affricare jure possunt, quia eò doctrina nostra de Persona Christi velis & remis omnibus tendit, ut naturæ & earum proprietates nec separentur, nec confundantur: nec nos, Spiritu Christi, qui charitatis est, incalescentes, adversantibus moderationibus, & veritatis studio flagrantibus, Eutychianismi convitium facimus, eò quòd incautiùs communicationem idiomatum explicent. Nam consequentiarum nexum se non pervidere, quin potiùs naturarum & proprietatum distinctionem se agnoscere palam profitentur; & quàm profiteantur non perfunctorie, sed ἐν μυελῷ καρδίας, satis exquisitum illud studium, quo ita anxii modum communicationis explicant, ne ullatenus in doctrinam Ecclesiæ inprimis veteris orthodoxam arietet, adhibita inprimis phrasi de communicatione idiomatum non naturali, sed personali; testatur. Accedunt benignæ declarationes henoticæ in Colloquiis novissimis, Lipsiensi inprimis & Cassellensi, perhibitæ, quæ ad concordiam plenam viam patefacere possent, dummodo ne præsentiæ corporalis Christi in Eucharistia priùs asserta imprudenter, & ex mero contentionis æstu assumpta opinio obstaret. Quæ tamen opinio quamdiu durat, gangrænam quandam in doctrina de Persona Christi, non præcipua tamen & unicè salutari illa, sed apicibus quibusdam, nec ad fidei, nec ad pietatis summam facientibus, sed veritatis tamen, quæ ne minima quidem agnita abnegari, vel non seriò defendi debet, curam & studium, ut stipulæ illæ fundamento superstructæ veritatis & charitatis salutari incendio consumantur, exigentibus, facit. Cùm tamen plus hic precibus ἐκπυρώσεως quàm contentione intempestiva & intemperante inprimis, proficiatur, rogandus enixissimè Deus Veritatis & Pacis est, ut in iis, ad quæ pervenimus, eadem regula incedere, idem sentire pergentibus, revelet ea, in quibus aliter sentiunt; inprimis verò, ut affectuum intemperiem sanet, & charitatis, quæ patiens, benigna est, non perperam agit, non intumescit, non agit indecorè, non quærit ea, quæ sua sunt, non exacerbatur, non imputat malum, non gaudet injustitia, sed condelectatur veritate, 1.Cor.XIII.4. &c. Spiritu nos totos impleat.
units.tr: LXIV. But these matters have been debated by us for the sake of defending the truth, not for the sake of feeding schism. For that dissent, taken in itself and removed from passion and heat, is not so great that it could or should split churches that agree on the chief doctrine of Christ's Person. For we both subscribe to that ancient confession of the Church concerning the Person of Christ, set forth at the Council of Chalcedon. Nor can those who dissent from us justly rub the itch of Nestorianism upon us, since our doctrine of Christ's Person strives with every oar and sail to ensure that the natures and their properties are neither separated nor confused. Nor, glowing with the Spirit of Christ, who is the Spirit of love, do we, though moderation is opposed to us and we burn with zeal for truth, hurl the reproach of Eutychianism at them on the ground that they explain the communication of idioms too incautiously. For they openly profess that they do not fail to see the connection of consequences, but rather acknowledge the distinction of natures and properties; and that they profess this not perfunctorily but ἐν μυελῷ καρδίας [from the marrow of the heart]. The careful zeal with which they explain the mode of communication so anxiously, lest it in any way strike against the doctrine of the Church, especially the ancient orthodox doctrine, bears witness to this, not least because they employ the phrase about a communication of idioms that is not natural but personal. There are also the kindly henotic declarations put forward in the most recent colloquies, especially at Leipzig and Kassel, which could open a way to full concord, provided that the opinion asserted earlier, imprudently and taken up in the mere heat of contention, concerning the bodily presence of Christ in the Eucharist does not stand in the way. Yet as long as that opinion lasts, it produces a certain gangrene in the doctrine of Christ's Person. It is not the chief point, nor the one point that alone saves, but certain small points that contribute neither to the sum of faith nor of piety, yet still belong to the truth, which, even if it is least recognized, must not be denied or seriously defended in a half-hearted way. This demands care and effort that those stubbles, built upon the foundation, be consumed by the saving fire of truth and charity. Since, however, more is achieved here by prayers for purification than by untimely and especially intemperate contention, God, the God of Truth and Peace, must be earnestly entreated: that, for those who proceed by the same rule and think the same in what we have reached, he would reveal those things in which they think otherwise; and above all that he would heal the intemperance of their passions and fill us wholly with the Spirit of that charity which is patient, is kind, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, does not act unbecomingly, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not impute evil, does not rejoice in injustice, but rejoices together with the truth (1 Cor. 13:4 etc.).

units.tr: TOPIC EIGHTEEN, On the STATE OF JESUS CHRIST. A SUMMARY.

units.la: Personæ Jesu Christi ejusdem Status, Officio ejus exequendo singulariter accommodatus, accidit. qui duplex est, Exinanitionis & Exaltationis. 1. Status Exinanitionis definitur, & quatenus Deitas & Humanitas exinanita fuerit, explicatur. 2. Exinanitio Christi in ejus nativitate, non extrema passione cœpit. 3. Neque tamen exinanitio proprie in incarnatione Filii consistit. 4. Sed in eo potius, quòd non simpliciter homo, sed homo servus, & legi subjectus fuit. 5. Obedientia per exinanitionem à Christo suscepta non ea fuit, quam ut creatura debuit, & nunquam exuit; sed humilis & ærumnosa illa, quam ut Sponsor debuit, & legi sub conditione merendi præstitit. 6. Exinanitio & humiliatio Christi distinguuntur: illa in omni ejus vita usque ad mortem; hæc in novissimis passionibus emicuit. Privata vita ejus vulgaris fuit. 7. Infantiæ Christi memorabilia; Angelorum eum annuntiantium concentus, ejus circumcisio, præsentatio, elogium à Simeone ei perhibitum: Xenia eidem à Magis oblata, fuga & reditus, atque habitatio in Nazareth. 8. Profectus Jesu de infantia in pueritiam, in qua illud præcipuum, quòd Propheticum & Regium actum in Templo docens, & authoritatem muneris sui adversus parentes ipsos asserens, exercuit; missis cæteris, de pueritiæ ejus facinoribus, fabulis. 9. Exinanitionis voluntariæ in vita Christi privata characteres. 10 Vitæ Christi publicæ auspicia. 11. Baptismus Christi. 12. Ministerium Christi publicum trium & dimidii annorum, adeòque Paschatum quatuor spatio exactum est. 13. Historia primordiorum Ministerii Christi ad primum usque Pascha. 14. Historia Paschatis primi. 15. Historia Paschatis secundi. 16. Historia Paschatis tertii. 17. Historia Paschatis quarti emortualis. 18. Paschatis Coenæ δειπνον à Christo cum discipulis celebratæ tempus, & eidem succedanea lotio pedum discipulorum. 19. Passio emortualis Christi ab ejus in horto ἀγωνία initium cepit. 20. Christi in ἀγωνία illa ad Deum pro transferendo poculo precatio. 21. Ejusdem per Judam proditi traditio in manus Judæorum & gentilium. 22. Non tumultuariè Jesus occidi, sed in judicio damnari debuit. 23. Nec qualecunque, sed crucis supplicium sustinere, execrationis subeundæ ergo, debuit. 24. Crucifixionis illius historia. 25. Christo in cruce pendente alia mortem ejus præcesserunt: alia consecuta sunt. Quæ præcesserunt, alii alia Christo fecerunt. 26. Alia, eaque septuplicia à Christo in cruce dicta sunt. 27. Alia Deus Pater Christo glorificando fecit; tenebris universam terram, non Judæam solùm, immergens. 28. Mortem Christi in cruce pendentis consecuta sunt tum prodigia, velum Templi scissum & terræ motus; tum crurifragium latronum Christo mortuo superstitum: tum perfossio lateris Christi, ex quo sanguis & aqua fluxit. 29. Historia Sepulturæ Christi. 30. Ejusdem mysterium eruitur. 31. Descensus Christi ad Inferos explicatur. 32. Error eum localem animæ Christi ad limbum vel inferos, ad liberandos Patres ibi languentes, fingentium Pontificiorum perstringitur. 33. Non corpore duntaxat passus & mortuus est Christus, sed anima etiam mortem peccato debitam, cruciatus infernales, sustinuit. 34. Pontificiorum, passiones animæ Christi ad cruciatus animæ ejus sensitivæ detorquentium, elenchus. 35. Exaltationis Christi status alter exponitur. 36. Totus Christus communiter & indivisè, sed sed gemina, distincta & inconfusa significatione exaltatus est. 37. Christus exaltatus Nomen super omne nomen accepit, ut in ejus, ceu Jesu Christi & Domini, nomine omne genu se flecteret. 38. Nominis hujus Christo dati causa fuit ejus exinanitio & obedientia ad mortem crucis usque; 39. Non obstante eo, quòd Deus Pater Nomen ist-hoc Christo gratificatus dicitur. 40. Donatio Nominis supra omne nomen toti Personæ, & utrique naturæ, sed diversimode, facta est. 41. Exaltationis Christi gradus Primus fuit in resurrectione ejus ex mortuis. 42. Tempus resurrectionis Christi, ejusque mysterium. 43. In V. T. prædictum oraculo, & typo Jonæ tres dies & tres noctes in utero ceti latentis præumbratum est. Quo sensu Filius hominis tres dies & tres noctes in corde terræ extiterit? 44. Vis illa, qua Christus ex mortuis resuscitatus est, fuit potentia infinita Patris & Filii; cujus symbolum fuit terræ motus magnus, resurgente Christo factus; nec non Angelus saxum a monumento devolvens. 45. Per resurrectionem Christi redintegrata est unio animæ ejus cum corpore eodem quoad substantiam, quam ante habuit, sed reddito tamen gloriosó, spirituali & cœlesti. 46. Neque tamen gloria corporis Christi in terra commorantis consummata fuit. 47. Veritas resurrectionis Christi argumentis irrefragabilibus asseritur. 48. Infidelium adversus ejus veritatem & admirabilitatem objectiones solvuntur. 49. Ex morte resuscitatus Jesus iterum in orbem habitabilem intravit, & discipulis suis identidem apparens, eosdem in fide resurrectionis & Regni sui confirmavit. 50. Apparitionum Christi novem historia; quarum quatuor singulis & paucis factæ sunt. 51. Reliquæ factæ sunt pluribus; duæ in Judæa; 52. Duæ in Galilæa, quarum posteriore, eâque celeberrima in Galilæa, ubi Concilio plus quàm quingentorum coacto, resurrectionis Christi veritas documentis certissimis solennius patefacta & publicata est. 53. Novissima iterum in Judæa, in monte oliveti, & ea montis parte, ubi Bethania erat: ubi vale ultimo Apostolis dicto in Cœlum suscipitur. 54. Ascensio Christi in Cœlum, secundus Exaltationis gradus, & ἀνάληψις assumptio, seu sursum evectio à Patre facta, & ἀνάβασις ascensio, jure & potestate propria facta est 55. Ejus veritas & necessitas asseritur. 56. Fidem ejus non minuit, quòd hostibus coram non ascendit, & Apostoli eum in Cœlum intrantem non viderunt; quòdque alii etiam, inprimis Apollonius Thyanæus, ascensioni Christi à Gentilibus oppositus, in Cœlum ascendisse conficti sunt. 57. Ascensio Christi à Patre sublati argumentum justificationis ejus; & Filii respectu singularis planè fuit, quia jure & merito suo ascendit, quomodo ante ipsum nemo in Cœlum ascendit. 58. Cœlum, in quod Christus ascendit, supremum, idémque locus proprie dictus, ab aliis distinctus est. 59 Elenchus erroris, quòd Christus in Cœlum ascendens non præsentiam humanitatis, sed visibilem duntaxat modum præsentiæ terræ subduxerit, adeóque ascensio in Cœlum non loci, sed status mutatio fuerit. 60. Idem Christus in Cœlum ascendens captivam captivitatem duxit; & dona in hominibus accepit. 61. Tertius & supremus Exaltationis gradus est Sessio Christi ad dextram Dei, Psalm. CXI. prædicta. 62. Dextra symbolum potentiæ & honoris est, quia apud gentes moratiores omnes, Turcis exceptis, dextra honoratior habita est nequicquam repugnante Goropio Becano. Christo proin tributa Sessio ad dextram Dei summam ejus gloriam & potestatem merito obedientiæ acquisitam notat. 63. Scripturæ testimonia, quibus Sessio hæc explicatur, & summa Christi in Cœlo gloria & potestas confirmatur. 64. Sessio eadem in executione muneris triplicis, Prophetici, Sacerdotalis & Regii se ex æquo diffundit. 65. & Christo secundum utramque naturam competit; sic tamen, ut honor & potestas illa non noviter Christo toti collata, uti Socinus blasphemat; sed Christo secundum Deitatem noviter tantùm vindicata sit. 66. Etiam caro Christi ad dextram Dei sedet, non in suppositó duntaxat, uti Bellarminus fingit, sed in se. 67. Sessio carnis Christi ad dextram Dei consistit in perfectione excellente animæ & corporis ejusdem. 68. Socinianorum hæresis, quòd Christus ad dextram Dei confidens, exuto veteri, in quo resurrexit, corpore, novum induerit, refellitur. 69. Sessio carnis ad dextram Dei ejusdem omnipræsentiam non confirmat, sed potiùs evertit. 70. Socinianorum & Maldonati impia assertio, quòd Christus ad dextram Dei Patris confidens, eodem in administratione Regni honoratior fuerit, perstringitur. 71.
units.tr: The person of Jesus Christ has a state that belongs to him, singularly suited to the discharge of his office. It is twofold: of emptying and of exaltation. 1. The state of emptying is defined, and it is explained in what respect the deity and the humanity were emptied. 2. The emptying of Christ began at his birth, not at his final suffering. 3. Yet the emptying does not properly consist in the incarnation of the Son. 4. It lies rather in this, that he was not simply a man, but a man who was a servant and subject to the law. 5. The obedience that Christ rendered in his emptying was not the obedience he owed as a creature, which he never laid aside, but that humble and laborious obedience which he owed as Surety, and which he rendered under the law on the condition of meriting. 6. Emptying and humiliation are to be distinguished: the former runs through his whole life up to death, the latter shone forth in his last sufferings. His private life was ordinary. 7. Memorable events of Christ's infancy: the chorus of angels announcing him, his circumcision, his presentation, the testimony Simeon gave concerning him, the gifts the Magi offered him, the flight and return, and his dwelling in Nazareth. 8. The progress of Jesus from infancy into boyhood, in which the chief thing is that, teaching in the Temple, he exercised the prophetic and kingly act and asserted the authority of his office even against his own parents; the other stories about the deeds of his boyhood are set aside as fables. 9. The marks of voluntary emptying in the private life of Christ. 10. The beginnings of the public life of Christ. 11. The baptism of Christ. 12. The public ministry of Christ lasted three and a half years, and so spanned four Passovers. 13. The history of the beginnings of Christ's ministry up to the first Passover. 14. The history of the first Passover. 15. The history of the second Passover. 16. The history of the third Passover. 17. The history of the fourth Passover, the Passover of his death. 18. The time of the Lord's Supper celebrated by Christ with his disciples [δειπνον], and the washing of the disciples' feet which took its place. 19. The passion of Christ unto death began with his agony [ἀγωνία] in the garden. 20. The prayer Christ made to God in that agony, that the cup might be taken away. 21. His betrayal by Judas into the hands of the Jews and the Gentiles. 22. Jesus ought not to have been killed in a tumult, but condemned in judgment. 23. Nor ought he to have suffered any sort of punishment, but the punishment of the cross, for the sake of the curse he was to bear. 24. The history of that crucifixion. 25. While Christ hung on the cross, some things preceded his death and some followed it. Of the things that preceded, different people did different things to Christ. 26. Seven sayings, and not one or two, were spoken by Christ on the cross. 27. Other things God the Father did to glorify Christ, plunging the whole earth, and not Judea alone, into darkness. 28. Following the death of Christ on the cross came both prodigies, the veil of the Temple torn and an earthquake; and the breaking of the legs of the thieves who survived Christ, and the piercing of Christ's side, from which blood and water flowed. 29. The history of the burial of Christ. 30. The mystery of the same is drawn out. 31. The descent of Christ into hell is explained. 32. The error of the Papists is censured, who feign that the soul of Christ went locally to limbo or the lower regions, to free the fathers languishing there. 33. Christ suffered and died not only in body, but his soul also endured the death owed to sin and the torments of hell. 34. A refutation of those Papists who twist the sufferings of Christ's soul into torments of his sensitive soul. 35. The other state of Christ's exaltation is set forth. 36. Christ as a whole was exalted in common and undivided, but in a twofold, distinct and unconfused sense. 37. Christ, exalted, received the Name above every name, so that at the name of him, as Jesus Christ and Lord, every knee should bow. 38. The cause of this name given to Christ was his emptying and his obedience even unto the death of the cross. 39. Notwithstanding that God the Father is said to have granted this Name as a gift to Christ. 40. The gift of the Name above every name was made to the whole Person and to each nature, but in different ways. 41. The first step of Christ's exaltation was his resurrection from the dead. 42. The time of Christ's resurrection, and its mystery. 43. In the Old Testament it was foretold by oracle, and the type of Jonah foreshadowed, that the Son of man would be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, as Jonah was in the belly of the whale. In what sense did the Son of man remain three days and three nights in the heart of the earth? 44. The power by which Christ was raised from the dead was the infinite power of the Father and the Son; its symbol was the great earthquake made when Christ rose, and also the angel rolling the stone away from the tomb. 45. Through the resurrection of Christ the union of his soul with the same body, as to substance, which he had before, was restored; yet the body was returned glorious, spiritual and heavenly. 46. Nevertheless the glory of the body of Christ was not completed while he dwelt on earth. 47. The truth of Christ's resurrection is established by unanswerable arguments. 48. The objections of unbelievers against its truth and wonder are answered. 49. Jesus, raised from death, again entered the inhabited world, and appearing repeatedly to his disciples, confirmed them in the faith of his resurrection and of his kingdom. 50. The history of nine appearances of Christ; four of them were made to individuals and to a few. 51. The rest were made to many; two in Judea. 52. Two in Galilee, of which the latter, and that the most famous, was in Galilee, where, a council of more than five hundred having been gathered, the truth of the resurrection of Christ was more solemnly revealed and published with the most certain proofs. 53. The last again in Judea, on the Mount of Olives, on that part of the mount where Bethany was: there, after he had bidden the apostles farewell, he was taken up into heaven. 54. The ascension of Christ into heaven, the second step of exaltation, both the assumption [ἀνάληψις], that is, the lifting up on high done by the Father, and the ascent [ἀνάβασις], was done by his own right and power. 55. Its truth and necessity are established. 56. Its credibility is not diminished by the fact that he did not ascend in the sight of his enemies, and that the apostles did not see him entering heaven; nor by the fact that others also, above all Apollonius of Tyana, opposed by the Gentiles to the ascension of Christ, were invented to have ascended into heaven. 57. The ascension of Christ, taken up by the Father, is a proof of his justification; and with respect to the Son it was altogether singular, because he ascended by his own right and merit, in a way in which no one had ascended into heaven before him. 58. The heaven into which Christ ascended is the highest, and the same is a place properly so called, distinct from the others. 59. A refutation of the error that Christ, ascending into heaven, withdrew not his presence in his humanity but only the visible mode of his presence from the earth, so that the ascension into heaven was a change of state and not of place. 60. The same Christ, ascending into heaven, led captivity captive and received gifts for men. 61. The third and highest step of exaltation is the sitting of Christ at the right hand of God, foretold in Psalm CXI. 62. The right hand is the symbol of power and honour, because among all the more civilised nations, the Turks excepted, the right hand was held more honourable, though Goropius Becanus contends otherwise to no effect. Therefore the sitting at the right hand of God, attributed to Christ, signifies his supreme glory and power, acquired by the merit of his obedience. 63. The testimonies of Scripture by which this sitting is explained, and by which the supreme glory and power of Christ in heaven is confirmed. 64. The same sitting spreads itself equally into the execution of the threefold office, prophetic, priestly and kingly. 65. It belongs to Christ according to each nature; yet in such a way that that honour and power were not newly conferred on Christ as a whole, as the Socinian blasphemes, but were only newly claimed for Christ according to the deity. 66. Even the flesh of Christ sits at the right hand of God, not merely in the person, as Bellarmine feigns, but in itself. 67. The sitting of the flesh of Christ at the right hand of God consists in the excellent perfection of his soul and body. 68. The heresy of the Socinians, that Christ, sitting at the right hand of God, put off the old body in which he rose and put on a new one, is refuted. 69. The sitting of the flesh at the right hand of God does not confirm the omnipresence of the same, but rather overturns it. 70. The impious assertion of the Socinians and of Maldonatus, that Christ, sitting at the right hand of God the Father, was more honoured in the administration of the kingdom, is censured. 71.

units.la: I. Actenus de Persona Iesu Christi. Qui eidem accidit Status officio ejus singulari exequendo singulariter accommodatus, duplex est, Exinanitionis & Exaltationis. Qui utrumque status ejusdem etiam Iesu Christi historiam vitæ, mortis, sepulturæ, descensus ad inferos, resurrectionis, ascensionis in Cœlum, & sessionis ad dextram Dei complectitur. Annon oportebat isthæc pati Christum, & introire in gloriam suam? Luc. XXIV.26. Jesus Christus cum esset in forma Dei non duxit raptum esse instar Dei: sed se ipsum exinanivit, dum formam servi assumpsit; quando in similitudine hominis esse incepit. Et cum habitu inveniretur ut homo, humiliavit se ipse, dum obedientem se præstitit usque ad mortem; mortem autem crucis. Quamobrem Deus ipsum superexaltavit, & gratificatus ei est nomen super omne nomen; ut in nomine Jesu omne genu se flectat, supercœlestium & terrestrium, & eorum qui infra terram sunt, Phil.II.6--11.
units.tr: I. Thus far concerning the Person of Jesus Christ. The state that befell him, singularly suited to the carrying out of his singular office, is twofold: that of humiliation and that of exaltation. Each of these states embraces the history of Jesus Christ himself: his life, death, burial, descent into hell, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and sitting at the right hand of God. Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? Luke 24:26. Jesus Christ, though he was in the form of God, did not consider being equal with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, when he came to be in the likeness of men. And being found in human appearance, he humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God highly exalted him and graciously bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth. Phil. 2:6–11.

units.la: II. Status igitur Κένωσις Exinanitionis Christi est, quo Is, cum esset in forma Dei & ei proprium, non alienum esset, esse ἴσα Θεῷ instar Dei, se ipsum tamen exinanivit, in similitudine hominis formam servi accipiens, & dum sic habitu, ut homo inveniretur, se ipsum humiliavit, & obedientiam Deo præstitit usque ad mortem crucis. Ante omnia κένωσις est totius Christi, non Humanitatis duntaxat, sed etiam Deitatis. Nam is se exinanivit, qui erat in forma Dei, & tamen formam servi assumpsit, & ad tempus non fuit ἴσα Θεῷ instar Dei. qui Deus est. Neque tamen hoc respectu Deitatis exinanitio essentiæ, vel gloriæ ejus Divinæ μείωσις imminutio in se, sed respectu carnis sibi unitæ, & hominum duntaxat, fuit, utpote quibus coram, sub forma servi latens, gloriam suam, ne pleno jubare splenderet, ut olim in monte Sinai splenduit, & in ultimo judicio splendebit, ad tempus occultavit, & cohibuit, iis etiam in humanitate sibi unita receptis infirmitatibus & toleratis injuriis, quas solo nutu facile discutere potuisset. Quod œconomiæ, quam suscepit, ratio exegit; nullo Deitatis & perfectionis cum præjudicio, quia exinaniri Deus voluit, non quod rapinam duceret esse instar Dei, sed quod salutis nostræ eum sic exinaniri interfuit; & Divinitatem gravem ob causam salutis nostræ occultari, & non semper exeri, haud indignum Deo est. Tu אל מסתתר Deus se tegens, occultans, Deus Israelis Salvator, Esaj. XLV.15. quasi dicat: Tu te exhibuisti non ἴσα Θεῷ instar Dei, te ipsum κένωσις exinanivisti, factus es lapis scandali, ibid. VIII.14. Plane sic exinanitio Dei non fuit depositio potentiæ, sed assumptio infirmitatis in carne, & omissio, sive non usus illius Majestatis, qua si usus fuisset, nemo coram illo subsistitisset, nedum assumtæ carni noxam ullam intulisset. quomodo nec mori per causam salutis nostræ potuisset. Non obstante vero hac humilitate, & gloriosus fuit, & ut lux vera, luxit in tenebris, quemadmodum inde à monte Sinai, imò à Paradiso, in tenebris luxerat. Sed multò magis exinanitio facta est secundum humanam naturam, quæ in se exinaniri, servitutem novilli-mam subire, humiliari ad mortem usque potuit, debuit, & ita exinanita, humiliata est. ἩΛΑΤΛΩΣΕΝ αὐτὸν βεχ. Minorasti, minorem fecisti eum paulisper præ Diis, Psal.VIII.6. Hebr.II.7. hoc est, præ illo, qui verè Deus est, & præ iis, qui Dii dicuntur. quales etiam Angeli, imò & homines dominantes prioris seculi, quorum servus ad tempus fuit, Esaj. XLIX.7.
units.tr: II. The state of humiliation, the kenosis [κένωσις] of Christ, is therefore that by which he, though he was in the form of God, and this was proper to him and not foreign to him, to be equal to God [ἴσα Θεῷ], nevertheless emptied himself, taking the form of a servant in the likeness of men; and, being thus found in human appearance, he humbled himself and rendered obedience to God unto death on the cross. Above all, the kenosis belongs to the whole Christ, not only to his humanity but also to his deity. For he emptied himself who was in the form of God, and yet took the form of a servant, and for a time was not equal to God, who is God. Yet this emptying was not, with respect to the deity, a diminution [μείωσις] of his divine essence or glory in itself, but was with respect to the flesh united to him and to men only. For in their presence, lying hidden under the form of a servant, he concealed and restrained his glory for a time, so that it should not shine with full brightness, as once it shone on Mount Sinai and will shine at the last judgment. He also accepted, in the humanity united to him, infirmities and endured injuries which with a mere nod he could easily have dispelled. The arrangement of the economy he undertook required this, with no prejudice to the deity and its perfection. God willed to be emptied, not because he thought being equal to God a thing to be grasped, but because it was in the interest of our salvation that he be so emptied. And that the divinity, for a grave reason of our salvation, should be hidden and not always displayed, is not unworthy of God. You are a God who hides himself, the God of Israel, the Saviour, Isa. 45:15 [אל מסתתר]. As if to say: you did not show yourself as equal to God; you emptied yourself [κένωσις]; you became a stone of stumbling, ibid. 8:14. Clearly, then, the emptying of God was not a laying aside of power but an assumption of weakness in the flesh, and an omission, or non-use, of that majesty which, had it been used, no one could have stood before him, much less have done any harm to the assumed flesh; nor could he have died for the cause of our salvation. Yet despite this humility he was also glorious, and as the true light he shone in darkness, just as from Mount Sinai, indeed from Paradise, he had shone in darkness. But the emptying happened far more according to the human nature, which in itself could be emptied, could undergo the lowest servitude, could be humbled even to death, and which, being so emptied, was humbled. You have made him a little less [ἠλάττωσας] than God, Ps. 8:6; Heb. 2:7 [מְעַט מֵאֱלֹהִים]. That is, less than him who is truly God, and less than those who are called gods, such as angels, and indeed even the ruling men of the former age, whose servant for a time he was, Isa. 49:7.

units.la: III. Cœpit autem κένωσις hæc in nativitate Christi; secus quàm Sociniani perten-dunt, afferentes, formam Dei, statum Christi ante extremam passionem, & exinanitionem, tempus extremæ passionis notare. Atqui exinanitio sui refertur ad illud tempus, quo Christus cœpit esse in similitudine hominis, Phil.II.7. Tum exinaniri, & esse ἴσα Θεῷ instar Dei, opponuntur. Atqui inde à nativitate non fuit ἴσα Θεῷ instar Dei, hoc est, non ostendit Divinitatem, Majestatem & gloriam suam, uti ostendere potuisset, assumptam naturam ab omni infirmitate vindicando, si e re generis humani fuisset. Sed & exinanitio in eo constituitur, quòd incipiens esse in similitudine hominis, formam seu conditionem servi & hominis ad obedientiam obligati, assumpsit, cum esset Dominus gloriæ, & talem se gerere posset. Atqui ex muliere natus cœpit esse sub lege. Gal.IV.4. Fieri autem sub lege, est formam servi accipere. Præterea S.Paulus κένωσιν exinanitionem distinguit à ταπείνωσιν humiliatione, qua factus est obediens usque ad mortem crucis. In exinanitione est non esse instar Dei; cum inciperet esse in similitudine hominum, idque propter servitutem & obedientiam. In humiliatione vero plus est, nempe obedientem se præstare usque ad mortem, mortem vero crucis. Servitus obedientiam importat, sed ad τὸ δικαίωμα: humiliatio obedientiam μετὰ κατακρίσεως cum execratione ad δικαίωμα ex πολλῶν ἐκδεχομένων meritum justitiæ ex multis lapsibus, Rom.V.16. Sicut igitur humiliatio ad omnes passiones: ita exinanitio ad omnem subjectionem & obedientiam, quæ duravit per totum tempus apparitionis in carne, pertinet. Quinimo ipsa etiam ταπείνωσις à nativitate cœpit, quia non tantùm in morte, sed etiam in obedientia omni, quatenus illa cum tentationibus & passionibus conjuncta est, glisci t. Ideo dicitur μέχρι θανάτου usque ad mortem. q.d. in omni genere afflictionum, tentationum, passionum, tum etiam in morte. Denique exinanitio opponitur glorificationi consecutæ, quæ v. gr. ὑπερύψωσις superexaltatio vocatur. Omne ergo tempus illud, quo Christus non est exaltatus, adeóque etiam tempus conceptionis, nativitatis significat.
units.tr: III. This kenosis, however, began at the nativity of Christ, contrary to what the Socinians maintain, asserting that the form of God denotes the state of Christ before the final passion, and that the time of the final passion is the emptying. But the emptying of himself is referred to that time when Christ began to be in the likeness of man, Phil. 2:7. Then, to be emptied and to be equal to God are set in opposition. But from his nativity he was not equal to God, that is, he did not display his divinity, majesty and glory, as he could have done by shielding the assumed nature from every infirmity, had that been for the good of the human race. The emptying also consists in this: beginning to be in the likeness of man, he assumed the form or condition of a servant and of a man bound to obedience, though he was the Lord of glory and was able to bear such a role. But born of a woman, he began to be under the law, Gal. 4:4. To be made under the law, however, is to take the form of a servant. Moreover, St Paul distinguishes the kenosis, the emptying, from the tapeinosis, the humiliation, by which he became obedient unto death on the cross. In the emptying there is the not being equal to God, since he began to be in the likeness of men, and this on account of servitude and obedience. In the humiliation there is more, namely that he rendered himself obedient even to death, and the death of the cross. Servitude implies obedience, but obedience to a righteous requirement [δικαίωμα]; humiliation implies obedience under condemnation and curse, with respect to the righteous act [δικαίωμα] which, from many trespasses, brings the merit of righteousness, Rom. 5:16. Just as humiliation extends to all sufferings, so the emptying extends to all subjection and obedience, which lasted through the whole time of his appearance in the flesh. Indeed humiliation itself began from the nativity, because it grows not only in death but in all obedience, insofar as that is joined with temptations and sufferings. Hence it is said unto death, that is, in every kind of affliction, temptation and suffering, and then also in death itself. Finally, the emptying is opposed to the glorification that followed, which is called, for example, hyperhypsosis [ὑπερύψωσις], superexaltation. So all that time in which Christ was not exalted, and therefore also the time of his conception and nativity, is signified.

units.la: IV. Sed in nativitate, qua cœpit esse in similitudine hominis, imò & conceptione ipsa exinanitus Christus fuerit, non tamen exinanitio propriè in ἐνσαρκώσει, ἐνανθρώπησις in carnatione ejus consistit. Nam simpliciter homines fieri, in similitudine hominis esse, non est exinaniri, humiliari. Qui exinaniri debuit, homo esse debuit; sed non quisquis homo est, exinaniri debet. Nam etiam in statu exaltationis mansit homo; neque tamen vel exinanitus vel humiliatus amplius. Et exinanitus, minoratus est ΤΟΝ βεχ. paulisper, ad breve temtempus, Psal.VIII.6. Hebr.II.7. Sed homo fuit non paulisper, nec ad breve tempus; sed inde à nativitate semper fuit, est & erit. Potuit igitur esse homo, & non exinaniri, sed esse ἴσα Θεῷ instar Dei. Ideo S. Paulus Phil.II.7. eas phrases, γινέσθαι ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων esse in similitudine hominum, & μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν, formam servi accipere, habitu inveniri ut hominem, diligenter distinguit, innuens non prius, sed duo haec posteriora exinanitionem dicere. Poterat enim Filius Dei apparere similis hominibus in corpore humano, & non esse hominum frater, non servus, non ἐξ ἑνὸς ex uno cum peccatoribus, non Sponsor, Goel, Mediator, non obligari ad obedientiam legis, sic, ut obedientia illa esset conditio acquirendi vitam ex merito. Sicut nempe Deus olim in forma hominis apparuit Patribus: ita Filius Dei potuit & apparere in corpore, quod sibi vel ex terra, vel ex nihilo aptasset; & esse ἴσα Θεῷ instar Dei, non habitu repertus ut homo. Nam etiam nullo merito indigebat, ut, si vellet humanam naturam assumere, eam beatitudine & gloria, absque subjectione sub lege, facile implere posset. Tantum abest, ut oportuerit eum, sine alia, quàm incarnationis causa, subjici legi tali, quæ etiam peccatum accusat, & satisfactionem pro eo postulat. qualis fuit lex Mosis.
units.tr: IV. But in the nativity, by which he began to be in the likeness of man, indeed even in the conception itself, Christ was emptied; yet the emptying does not properly consist in the enfleshment [ἐνσάρκωσις], the incarnation [ἐνανθρώπησις]. For simply to become a man, to be in the likeness of men, is not to be emptied or humbled. He who was to be emptied had to be a man; but not everyone who is a man ought to be emptied. For even in the state of exaltation he remained a man, yet no longer emptied or humbled. And he who was emptied was made a little less [βραχύ], for a little while, Ps. 8:6; Heb. 2:7. But he was a man not for a little while, nor for a short time; from the nativity he always was, is, and will be a man. He could therefore have been a man without being emptied, and have been equal to God. So St Paul carefully distinguishes the phrases "to come to be in the likeness of men" and "to take the form of a servant, to be found in human appearance", indicating that the former does not speak of the emptying, while the latter two do. For the Son of God could have appeared like men in a human body without being a brother of men, not a servant, not one of the same stock [ἐξ ἑνὸς] with sinners, not a surety, redeemer or mediator, and not bound to obedience to the law, so that that obedience would be the condition of acquiring life by merit. Just as God once appeared to the Fathers in the form of a man, so the Son of God could also have appeared in a body which he had fashioned for himself either from the earth or from nothing, and have been equal to God, not found in human appearance. For he had no need of any merit, so that, if he willed to assume human nature, he could easily have filled it with blessedness and glory, apart from subjection under the law. So far is it from being necessary that he should, for no cause other than the incarnation, be subject to such a law, one which also accuses sin and demands satisfaction for it, such as the law of Moses was.

units.la: V. In eo ergo exinanitio Christi hominis consistit, quòd non simpliciter homo factus, sed ejusmodi homo factus est, ut μορφὴν δούλου formam servi habuerit, & σχήματι habitu, ut homo repertus fuerit. Hanc enim quasi definitionem exinanitionis S.Paulus Phil.II.7. 8. proponit, dicens: Se ipsum exinanivit, dum formam servi assumpsit, quando in similitudine hominis esse coepit; & cùm habitu inveniretur ut homo, se ipsum humiliavit. Verba enim illa, χωρὶς, hoc est, ὅτι ἐκένωσε ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων, cùm esset in similitudine hominum (non conjungenda cum κενώσει, sed cum λαβὼν) circumstantiam, tempus & subjectum κενώσεως, nempe hominem, quando is homo factus est: at μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν formam servi accipiens, & σχήματι ὡς ἄνθρωπος εὑρεθεὶς similitudine repertus ut homo, exinanitionis ejusdem formam & essentiam clarissimè significant. Formam autem servi accipere significat statum, conditionem, munus & nomen servi accipere cum ea natura, in quam servitus cadit. Id autem accipere cum natura non erat ei necessarium, qui erat Dominus & Filius, sed voluntarium, quia ei perinde ut servo voluntario aures Deus perforavit, Psal. XL.7. Potestatem habeo ponendi animam, Joh.X.18. Non enim suo nomine Filius sub lege natus est. Cùm dives esset, propter nos pauper factus est. 2.Cor.VIII.9. Habens ἀπολαύσαι χαρὰν λætitiam in promptu toleravit crucem, Hebr.XII.2. Cùm esset in forma Dei, exinanivit se, Phil.II.7. Sed id nobis utile, imò ad vitam & salutem nostram necessarium erat. Ideo hoc faciendo Filius Dei quodammodo nos sibi præstulit (hoc scilicet φρόνημα habens, ut non sua, sed aliorum spectaret, v.4.) hoc est, neglecto bono suo, quo ilico, in corpore suo, uti poterat, bonum nostrum quæsivit, corpus, quod sibi aptavit, non habens tantùm ut σχῆμα ta-
units.tr: V. In this, then, consists the exinanition of Christ as man: not that he was simply made man, but that he was made such a man that he had "the form of a servant" [μορφὴν δούλου] and was found "in fashion" [σχήματι] as a man. For St Paul gives this as something like a definition of the exinanition, Phil. 2:7-8, saying: "He emptied himself, when he took the form of a servant, when he began to be in the likeness of man; and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself." For those words, "that he emptied himself in the likeness of men" [ὅτι ἐκένωσε ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων], "when he was in the likeness of men" (not to be joined with "emptied" [κενώσει] but with "taking" [λαβὼν]), state the circumstance, the time and the subject of the emptying, namely the man, at the point when he became man. But "taking the form of a servant" [μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν] and "found in fashion as a man" [σχήματι ὡς ἄνθρωπος εὑρεθεὶς] very clearly express the form and essence of that same exinanition. To take the form of a servant means to take on the state, condition, office and name of a servant, together with that nature into which servitude falls. Yet for him who was Lord and Son, taking this on together with the nature was not necessary but voluntary, since God pierced his ears as those of a voluntary servant, Ps. 40:7. "I have power to lay down my life," John 10:18. For the Son was not born under the law in his own name. "Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor," 2 Cor. 8:9. "Having joy set before him [ἀπολαύσαι χαρὰν]," he endured the cross, Heb. 12:2. "Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself," Phil. 2:7. But this was useful for us, indeed necessary for our life and salvation. Therefore, by doing this, the Son of God in a certain way placed us before himself (having this mind [φρόνημα], namely not to look to his own things but to those of others, v. 4); that is, neglecting his own good, which he could at once have enjoyed in his own body, he sought our good, having taken a body which he fitted to himself, not only as a tabernacle [σχῆμα] to dwell in us,

units.la: bernaculum, ad habitandum in nobis, sed etiam ut servus factus sub legem, tanquam instrumentum præstandi pro nobis obedientiam legi, quæ violata à nobis non jam justitiam duntaxat ad vitam, sed etiam mortem exegit debitam. quæ nisi homo, & quidem homo servi, hoc est, legi Dei subjecti, formam accipiens præstare non potuisset. Hæc illa legalis Christi exinaniti servitus est, de qua Apostolus: Deus emisit Filium suum, genitum ex muliere, γενόμενον ὑπὸ νόμον factum sub lege, ut eos, qui sub lege sunt, redimeret. Gal.IV.4.ƒ. Quæ lex est tum operum, seu dilectionis Dei & proximi, cui ipse, ceu sponsor Testamenti subjectus est, ut obedientiæ legi huic præstitæ merito hæreditatem iis, qui in Testamento scripti sunt, hæredibus acquireret: tum etiam illa rituum, à Mose populo Israelis demandatorum, qua peccatum & reatum commemorante, Israelitæ ut debitores, compulsi sunt ad offerendas pro peccatis victimas, & purificationes obeundas. Unde עבד משלים servus dominantium (qui legis Divinæ executores constituti sunt) Esaj.XLIX.7. appellatur. Licèt enim Christus pro peccatis propriis victimam nunquam obtulerit, nec offerre necesse habuerit, quia non peccavit; tamen & oblationes atque purificationes in lege præscriptæ factæ sunt in ejus nativitate: & ipse circumcisus est: & à se sanatos sacerdotum examini subjecit, &, quod caput est, in se ut corpore & veritate omnes umbras & figuras implevit. Sic ille formam servi accepit; sic legi subjectus est; sed non ut sacerdotum & Principum quis, qui ipsi etiam sub lege erant, licèt illis fratres sui subjecti essent; verùm ut σχῆμα habitu repertus, ut homo (Phil.II.8.) non ἴσα Θεῷ instar Dei, sed ut quivis homo servilis alius, vilissimus de populo, utpote in quo nihil externum erat, quod à promiscuo etiam servili populo eum distingueret; non stola Pontificalis, non approximatio ad altare, non ingressus in Sanctum, vel Sanctum Sanctorum cum sanguine hirci, non sceptrum dominantis, non gladius, arcus, instrumenta belli. verbo, לא איש non vir, Psal.XXII.7. הרל איש deficiens viris, vel robore virili Esaj.LIII.3. non tantùm עבד יהוה Servus Jehovæ, ibid.XLII.1. sed etiam dominantium, XLIX.7. Lapis ab architectis reprobatus, Psal.CXVIII.22. qui etiam se ipse ἐταπείνωσε humiliavit, præstans obedientiam ad mortem usque crucis; qui κενώσεως exinanitionis ultimus gradus fuit.
units.tr: but also as one made a servant under the law, as an instrument for rendering obedience to the law on our behalf. The law, which we had violated, demanded not only righteousness for life but also the death that was due. Unless a man, and indeed a man of the servant form, that is, subject to the law of God, had taken this form, he could not have rendered it. This is that legal servitude of the exinanited Christ, of which the Apostle speaks: "God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, made under the law [γενόμενον ὑπὸ νόμον], that he might redeem those who are under the law," Gal. 4:4 ff. This law is the law of works, that is, of the love of God and neighbour, to which he himself, as surety of the covenant, was subject, so that by the merit of obedience rendered to this law he might acquire the inheritance for those who are written in the covenant as heirs. It is also the law of the rites, enjoined on the people of Israel by Moses, which, by recalling sin and guilt, compelled the Israelites as debtors to offer victims for sins and to undergo purifications. Hence he is called "servant of rulers" [עבד משלים], that is, servant of those who are appointed as executors of the divine law, Isa. 49:7. For although Christ never offered a victim for his own sins, nor had need to offer one, since he did not sin, nevertheless the offerings and purifications prescribed in the law were performed at his birth; he himself was circumcised, he submitted himself to the examination of the priests as one who was healed by himself, and, what is the chief thing, in himself, as body and truth, he fulfilled all shadows and figures. Thus he took the form of a servant; thus he was subject to the law; yet not as one of the priests or princes, who were themselves also under the law, though their brothers were subject to them; but he was found "in fashion" [σχῆμα], as a man (Phil. 2:8), not "equal to God" [ἴσα Θεῷ], but like any other servile man, the most lowly of the people, since in him there was nothing external which would distinguish him from the common servile people: not a priestly stole, not approach to the altar, not entry into the Holy Place or the Holy of Holies with the blood of goats, not the sceptre of a ruler, not the sword, bow or instruments of war. In short, he was "not a man" [לא איש], Ps. 22:7; "one lacking men, or manly strength" [הרל איש], Isa. 53:3; not only "Servant of Jehovah" [עבד יהוה], ibid. 42:1, but also "of rulers," 49:7; "the stone rejected by the builders," Ps. 118:22; who also "humbled himself" [ἐταπείνωσε], rendering obedience even to the death of the cross, which was the last step of the exinanition [κένωσις].

units.la: VI. Satis hinc apparet, exinanitionem illam Christi, formam servi, legi Dei subjecti; habitum hominis, in quo inventus est; humiliationem, obedientiam usque ad mortem crucis, Christo exinanito convenisse, non ut simpliciter homo, creatura, Dei creatoris legi obnoxia fuit: sed ut homo Sponsor, Mediator, Salvator populi sui à peccatis fuit. Nam omnes quidem Angeli & homines legi Dei creatoris obedire tenentur, eo ipso, quòd creaturæ sunt. Nam & Adamus integer & lapsus, & homines lapsi irregeniti & regeniti in terra, & Angeli, sancti homines in Cœlo voluntatem Dei facere, legi amoris Dei obedire tenentur. Fiat voluntas tua in cœlo, sicut in terra, Matth. VI.10. Imò ipse Filius Dei regnum Deo Patri tradens γίνητω subjicietur ei, qui ei omnia subjecit, 1. Cor.XV.28. Sed aliter homines in terra, nondum δικαιώματα factum justum, justitiam plenam, opus, causam & meritum justitiæ habentes: aliter Angeli, sancti in Cœlo, consummati, & δικαιώματα ejusmodi habentes, partâque jam gloria fruentes, Deo obediunt. Illi legi dilectionis Dei & proximi, ut conditioni vitam promerenti, & ut creaturæ vel integræ in se, vel lapsæ in alio; hi eidem, sed non sub conditione merendi, verùm beatitudine jam promerita fruentes, & Deum purè, sine conditione acquirendi demum per obedientiæ meritum gloriam diligentes: illi in stadio, hi in meta obedire tenentur. Prior, non posteriori modo Christus natus & exinanitus legi Dei, & obedientiæ ejusdem humili & ærumnosæ subjectus, formam servi accepit, & habitu ut homo, vulgaris, vilissimus, nondum consummatus vel glorificatus, inventus est; quia in carnem venit, non simpliciter, ut homo seu consummatus, seu non consummatus; sed ut Mediator & Sponsor Testamenti, qui non poterat sic fieri homo, quin esset sub lege; & cui, quia ex muliere natus est, & fratres habuit, juxta legem fratres diligere, & juxta sponsionem ac Testamentum Dei pro iis sese legi ad omnem justitiam faciendam & ad pœnam exemplarem, pacis nostræ causa, ferendam, atque sic nobis, quorum vice legi se subjecit, justitiam & salutem promerendam, se subjicere æquum justúmque fuit.
units.tr: VI. From this it is sufficiently clear that the exinanition of Christ, the form of a servant subject to the law of God, the habit of a man in which he was found, and the humiliation, obedience even to the death of the cross, belonged to Christ the exinanited, not in that he was simply a man, a creature bound to the law of God the Creator; but in that he was a man, the Surety, Mediator and Saviour of his people from their sins. For all angels and men are bound to obey the law of God the Creator, by the very fact that they are creatures. Both Adam in his integrity and fallen, and fallen men unregenerate and regenerate on earth, and the holy angels and men in heaven, are bound to do the will of God and to obey the law of God's love. "Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven," Matt. 6:10. Indeed the Son of God himself, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, "shall be subjected [γίνητω] to him who subjected all things to him," 1 Cor. 15:28. But men on earth, not yet made just [δικαιώματα], not yet having full righteousness, the work, cause and merit of righteousness, obey God in one way; the angels and the saints in heaven, consummated, having such righteousness, and already enjoying the glory obtained, obey God in another way. The former are bound to obey the law of love of God and neighbour as a condition of meriting life, and as creatures either whole in themselves or fallen in another; the latter are bound to obey the same law, not under the condition of merit, but already enjoying blessedness merited, and loving God purely, without the condition of finally acquiring glory by the merit of obedience: the former obey in the race, the latter at the goal. Christ, born and exinanited, was made subject to the law of God and to its humble and burdensome obedience in the former manner, not the latter. He took the form of a servant, and was found in the habit of a man, common and most lowly, not yet consummated or glorified. For he came into the flesh not simply as a man, whether consummated or not consummated; but as Mediator and Surety of the covenant, who could not become man without being under the law; and since he was born of a woman and had brothers, it was fitting and right for him, according to the law, to love his brothers, and, according to the promise and covenant of God, to subject himself to the law on their behalf, to fulfil all righteousness, and to bear the exemplary punishment for the sake of our peace, and thus to merit righteousness and salvation for us, on whose behalf he submitted himself to the law.

units.la: VII. Exinanitio Christi in omni ejus vita, qua legi Divinæ, ut Sponsor & Salvator Israelis, agendo & patiendo se subjecit; κένωσις vero seu Humiliatio ultimus exinanitionis & obedientiæ gradus, in ejus morte maximè conspicua fuit. Et vita quidem Christi privata vel publica fuit. Privata illa fuit, quam inde à nativitate ad baptismum usque, per annos ὡσεὶ τριάκοντα triginta circiter (Luc.III.23.) exegit. De qua parce satis Evangelistæ loquuntur, commemorantes nonnulla de ejus infantia & profectu. Infantiæ schema infantile fuit, quo habitus est, & egit ut infans. Unde βρέφος infans Luc. II.12.16. & παιδίον puerulus Matth. II.11.13.14.20.21. Luc.II.21.27.40. appellatur. Qui etiam fasciis involutus, ibid.7.12. in præsepi positus, v.7.12.16. in ulnis gestatus, ibid. v.28. uberibus lactatus, ibid.v.27. & butyro ac melle, perinde ut alius infans, nutritus, Esaj.VII.15. fuit. Ita ᾠμάτι habitu inventus est, ut quivis infans alius.
units.tr: VII. The exinanition of Christ was in his whole life, by which, acting and suffering, he subjected himself to the divine law as the Surety and Saviour of Israel; but the kenosis, or humiliation, the last step of exinanition and obedience, was most conspicuous in his death. And the life of Christ was either private or public. The private life was that which he spent from his birth until his baptism, for about thirty years [ὡσεὶ τριάκοντα] (Luke 3:23). The Evangelists speak of it sparingly enough, recording some things about his infancy and progress. His infancy had an infantile appearance, in which he was regarded and acted as an infant. Hence he is called "infant" [βρέφος], Luke 2:12, 16, and "little child" [παιδίον], Matt. 2:11, 13, 14, 20, 21; Luke 2:21, 27, 40. He was wrapped in swaddling clothes, ibid. 7, 12; placed in a manger, vv. 7, 12, 16; carried in arms, ibid. v. 28; suckled at the breast, ibid. v. 27; and, like any other infant, he was nourished with butter and honey, Isa. 7:15. Thus he was found in the likeness [ὁμοιώματι] of any other infant.

units.la: VIII. Circa eandem verò infantiam memorabilia quædam Evangelii prædicati incunabula sunt. Nam Bethlehemi recens natus ilico ab Angelis Pastoribus in agro noctu annunciatus est, concentu ab iisdem facto in hæc verba, Evangelii summam complexa: Δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις Θεῷ, καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς εἰρήνη, ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία. Gloria in excelsis Deo, & super terra pax, & in hominibus beneplacitum, Luc.II.8.9.14. Jesus enim ille, quem Angeli annunciaverant, Deo gloriam, terræ pacem, hominibus Dei εὐδοκίαν restituturus fuerat. Qui etiam ilico à Pastoribus Bethlehemum festinantibus visus & prædicatus est, ib.v.16.17. Octavo à nativitate die circumcisus est, & nomen Jesu, ante ab Angelo ei impositum, accepit, v.21. Circumcisio hæc authoramentum velut quoddam fuit subjectionis Christi sub lege. Testificor omni homini circumcisο, ὅτι ὀφειλέτης ἐστὶν ὅλον τὸν νόμον ποιῆσαι quòd debitor sit implendæ totius legis, Gal.V.3. Licèt enim non fuerit mortuus in præputio carnis (uti de nobis S.Paulus Col.II.13. loquitur) atque adeò circumcisione non eguerit; tamen quia sponsor fuit, reus debendi omnem obedientiam legis nostro loco, adeóque peccata nostra sua fecit, & à peccatis nostris, cùm per passiones consummatus esset, absolvi & justificari debuit, ideo & voluit, & propter nostram consolationem debuit circumcidi, ut in eo, ceu capite, facta circumcisio, testimonium esset partæ nobis, membris suis, circumcisionis ἀχειροποιήτῳ quæ non fit manu, atque ita in ipso circumcisi videremur. In quo circumcisi estis circumcisione non manufacta, ibid. v.11. hoc est, cujus circumcisio, ceu signum & sigillum vobis obsignat circumcisionem, quæ non fit manu, quæ circumcisio reatus in justificatione, peccati in sanctificatione, ceu spiritualis præputii resectio quædam & abolitio est. Unde sequitur, eos, qui in Christo sunt, verè circumcisos esse, tum spiritu, tum corpore, quia & conscientia eorum ab operibus mortuis purificata, & corpus aqua pura lotum est, Hebr. X.14.22.23. Nos enim sumus περιτομὴ circumcisio (perfecta) qui spiritu Deo servimus, & gloriamur in Jesu Christo, & non confidimus in carne, Phil.III.3. Sicut enim olim præputiati corde, etiam præputiati carne censebantur, Ezech. XLIV.7.9. ita etiam nunc, qui in Christo plenariè circumcisi sunt corde, etiam circumcisi carne habendi sunt. Si præputium τὰ δικαιώματα & νόμως statuta legis servat, nonne præputium illis pro circumcisione reputabitur? Rom.II.26. Cùm enim caput circumcisum est, etiam membra circumcisa reputantur; neque in membris circumcisio repeti potest, ne videatur per caput non ablatum esse id omne, quod auferendum erat. puta reatus peccati, conscientiæ accusatio, elementorum mundi servitus. Sicut verò circumcisus fuit Jesus, ita etiam impletis diebus καθαρισμοῦ purificationis Mariæ (cujus quoad Christum eadem, quæ circumcisionis, ratio fuit) Hierosolymæ in Templo, secundum legem de primogenitis, Domino præsentatus & consecratus fuit, Luc.II.22.23. Deinceps à Simeone & Anna Spiritu S. afflatis exceptus est, cum pia ἐξομολογήσει, aliorúmque piorum applausu, ibid. v.25. &c. Accesserunt mox Magi ex Oriente, indice & velut ἀστέρα stella, extra ordinem à Deo creata, ut perinde itineris dux esset, atque olim Israelitis columna nubis & ignis fuit; advenæ, qui accepto Hierosolymæ Sacerdotum & Scribarum, ab Herode turbato convocatorum responso, Bethlehemum profecti, illum, ut natum Christum Regem (χρηματισμῷ seu Divino oraculo, uti ex v.12. colligitur, de eo edocti) religiosè adorarunt, & xeniis etiam coluerunt, Matth.II.1–12. Post Magorum eorum abitum ab Herode ad necem, instituto horribili infanticidio, & oborta inde tristi eclipsi Evangelii de Christo exhibito, tantùm non in incunabulis suis extincti; quæsitus, velut novus Rex, monitu Angeli à parentibus in Ægyptum abreptus; atque inde, post Herodis
units.tr: VIII. The events around this infancy are also memorable as the cradle of the preached Gospel. For when he was born at Bethlehem, angels announced him at once to shepherds in the field by night, with a song from them in these words, which sums up the Gospel: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men" [Δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις Θεῷ, καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς εἰρήνη, ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία], Luke 2:8, 9, 14. For this Jesus, whom the angels had announced, was to restore to God glory, to earth peace, and to men God's good pleasure [εὐδοκία]. He was also at once seen and proclaimed by the shepherds, who hurried to Bethlehem, Luke 2:16, 17. On the eighth day after his birth he was circumcised and received the name Jesus, which the angel had given him earlier, Luke 2:21. This circumcision was, as it were, a kind of pledge of Christ's subjection to the law. "I testify again to every man who is circumcised that he is a debtor to keep the whole law" (Gal. 5:3). For although he had not died in the uncircumcision of the flesh (as Paul speaks of us, Col. 2:13), and so had no need of circumcision, nevertheless, because he was our surety, bound in our place to render all the obedience of the law, he made our sins his own, and having been brought to perfection through sufferings, he had to be absolved and justified from our sins. Therefore he both willed and, for our comfort, had to be circumcised, so that the circumcision made in him, as in the head, might be a testimony to the circumcision "not made with hands" [ἀχειροποιήτῳ] that is obtained for us, his members, and so that we might be seen to be circumcised in him. "In whom you are circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands" (ibid. v. 11). That is, his circumcision seals to you, as a sign and seal, the circumcision that is not made with hands; this circumcision is the removal and abolition of guilt in justification and of sin in sanctification, as a kind of cutting away of spiritual foreskin. Hence it follows that those who are in Christ are truly circumcised, both in spirit and in body, because their conscience is purified from dead works and their body is washed with pure water (Heb. 10:14, 22, 23). For "we are the circumcision" (perfect circumcision), who serve God in the spirit, glory in Jesus Christ, and do not trust in the flesh (Phil. 3:3). For just as of old those uncircumcised in heart were also reckoned uncircumcised in flesh (Ezek. 44:7, 9), so now too those who are fully circumcised in heart in Christ are also to be held circumcised in flesh. "If the uncircumcised keeps the righteousness [τὰ δικαιώματα] and the ordinances [νόμως] of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision?" (Rom. 2:26). For when the head is circumcised, the members too are reckoned circumcised; nor can circumcision be repeated in the members, lest it seem that through the head not all that was to be removed has been taken away, namely the guilt of sin, the accusation of conscience, the bondage to the elements of the world. But just as Jesus was circumcised, so also, when the days of Mary's purification [καθαρισμοῦ] were fulfilled (the reason for which, as far as Christ is concerned, was the same as for circumcision), he was presented to the Lord and consecrated in the Temple at Jerusalem, according to the law concerning the firstborn (Luke 2:22, 23). Afterwards he was received by Simeon and Anna, inspired by the Holy Spirit, with a pious confession [ἐξομολογήσει] and the applause of other godly people (ibid. v. 25, etc.). Soon after came the Magi from the East, with a star, [ἀστέρα], created by God outside the ordinary course of nature to be their guide on the journey, just as the pillar of cloud and fire was to the Israelites of old. These strangers, having received the answer of the priests and scribes at Jerusalem, who had been summoned by the troubled Herod, set out for Bethlehem. Instructed about him by a divine oracle (χρηματισμῷ), as is gathered from v. 12, they worshipped the newborn Christ, the King, with reverence and honoured him with gifts (Matt. 2:1–12). After the departure of these Magi, Herod, having instituted a horrible massacre of the infants, sought to kill him, and a sad eclipse arose from this, so that the Gospel of Christ, just revealed, was almost extinguished in its cradle. He was sought as a new king; on the warning of an angel, his parents carried him off into Egypt; and from there, after Herod's [death]...

units.la: Exinanitio & Humiliatio Christi distinguuntur; illa in omni ejus vita, usque ad mortem; hæc in novissimis passionibus eminentis. Privata vita est vulgaris fuit.
units.tr: The emptying and the humbling of Christ are distinguished: the former belongs to his whole life, up to death; the latter stands out in his final sufferings. His private life was that of an ordinary man.

units.la: Infantiæ Christi memorabilia, Angelorum eum annuntiantium concentus, ejus circumcisio, præsentatio à Simeone et perhibitum elogium, xenia eidem à Magis oblata, fuga & reditus atque habitatio in Nazareth. Herodis mortem, Dei jussu ex Ægypto redux, metu regnantis in Judæa Archelai, ab iisdem parentibus in Galilæam, Nazarethum abductus, ibique nutritus & educatus est, ibid. v.21. &c. Luc.II.39. IV.16. Unde Ναζωραῖος Nazareni nomen ei hæsit. Matth.II.23. non tam errore populi, locum nativitatis ejus ignorantis, quàm provido Numine, tum quia vocabulum נצרת Nazara forma Syra ambiguum, adeóque æquè furculum atque Nazareth significans, cogitationem etiam נצר surculi de radicibus Jesse crescentis Esaj.XI.1. & eidem gemini נסר Germinis ibid.IV.2. Jerem.XXXIII.15. Zach.III.8. VI.12. quorum utrumque Messiæ epitheton est, ingerere debuit: tum quia ibi Christus educari debuit, ubi conceptus, ceu ἀνατολὴ ἐκ ὕψους exortus ex alto germinare in utero matris debuit, Luc.I.26-78. II.4.
units.tr: Memorable events of Christ's infancy: the chorus of angels announcing him, his circumcision, his presentation and the testimony given him by Simeon, the gifts offered to him by the Magi, the flight, and the return and dwelling in Nazareth. After Herod's death, on returning from Egypt by God's command, and fearing Archelaus, who was reigning in Judea, his parents led him away into Galilee, to Nazareth, where he was nourished and brought up (ibid. v. 21, etc.; Luke 2:39; 4:16). Hence the name Nazarene [Ναζωραῖος] clung to him (Matt. 2:23). This came about not so much through the error of the people, who did not know the place of his birth, as by the providence of God. Both because the word נצרת (Nazara, in Syriac form) is ambiguous, meaning both a shoot and Nazareth alike, it was bound to suggest the thought of the shoot (נצר) growing from the roots of Jesse (Isa. 11:1), and also of the same kind of branch (נסר) of the Germ (Isa. 4:2; Jer. 33:15; Zech. 3:8; 6:12), both of which are titles of the Messiah. And because Christ had to be brought up in the place where, conceived as the rising from on high [ἀνατολὴ ἐκ ὕψους], he had to sprout in his mother's womb (Luke 1:26–78; 2:4).

units.la: IX. Profectus Jesu fuit de infantia in pueritiam, de quo sic Lucas: Puerulus crescebat, & corroborabatur Spiritu, implebatúrque sapientia, & Dei gratia erat super eum, Luc.II.40. De pueritia profecit in adolescentiam, in qua annos duodecim natus, radiante denuo post tristem eclipsin in fuga Christi factam Evangelii luce, luculentum specimen officii sui Prophetici & Regii exhibuit. Prophetici, quando in Festo Paschatis in Templo sedit, sacrorum magistris immixtus, eos audiens & interrogans, & interrogantibus cum stupore audientium respondens ib.v.46.47. Regii, quando parentibus eum anxiè nimis quærentibus, eos πυρρην- ... sic allocutus est: Quid est, quòd quærebatis me?
