An nescie-batis, ὅτι ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου (subintellige ...; veluti Syrus supplet ... in domo patris mei) δεῖ εἶναί με, oportere, ut sim in iis (rebus) quæ Patris mei sunt, v.49. q.d. Non vestrum erat, me tam anxiè quærere, quia sciebatis in iis, quæ Patris mei sunt, me esse oportere. Et parentes suspicit, & parentibus Patrem suum cœlestem præfert. Vix visis parentibus à stupente turba discedit; loquentes eos audit, interrogantibus respondet. quæ obsequium erga parentes probant. Sed Cœlestis Patris authoritatem præfert, cum παρρησίας parentibus terrestribus dicens: Quid est, quòd me quærebatis? An nescietis, oportere, ut sim in iis, quæ Patris mei sunt? Filius honorat Patrem. An ego cœlestem Patrem, ejus mandatum, voluntatem negligerem? Non enim in iis eram, quæ caro appetit, mundus fugerit, pueritia suadet, sed in iis, quæ Patris sunt; Patris gloriam, cujus gratia in mundum venit concernunt. Hic mihi adversus vos imperii, vobis obsequii gloria relicta est. Non percepe-runt tamen parentes filii mentem. Ideo cum iis Nazarethum rediit ὑποτασσόμενος αὐτοῖς obediens iis, ib.v.51. Cujus ὑποταγὴς specimen in eo etiam exhibuit, quòd ad Josephi parentis vitæ privatæ genus se applicavit. Quò pertinet ἐκφαυλισμὸς ille Judæorum: 'Οὐχ' οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ τέκτων. Nonne ipse est faber ille? Marc.VI.3. Nonne ipse est ille fabri filius? Matth.XIII.55. Justinus aratra & juga fecisse tradidit. Et quærentibus Juliani asseclis, ecquid fabri filius rerum gereret, scite à Christiano responsum est; Juliano feretrum fabricatur. Neque id κενώσεως Christi statu indignum fuit, quando eum habi-
units.tr: IX. Jesus advanced from infancy to boyhood, of which Luke writes thus: "The child grew and was strengthened in spirit, and was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him" (Luke 2:40). From boyhood he advanced into youth, and at twelve years of age, when the light of the Gospel, having shone again after the sad eclipse caused by Christ's flight, he gave a clear sample of his prophetic and royal office. His prophetic office: when at the Feast of the Passover he sat in the Temple, mingling with the teachers of sacred things, listening to them and questioning them, and answering those who questioned him to the amazement of those listening (ibid. v. 46, 47). His royal office: when his parents sought him too anxiously, he addressed them thus: "Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in the things of my Father [ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου]?" (the words "in the house" are to be understood, as the Syriac supplies them: "in the house of my Father"), v. 49; that is, "It was not for you to seek me so anxiously, since you knew that I must be in the things of my Father." He both regards his parents and prefers his heavenly Father to them. Scarcely had his parents appeared when he left the astonished crowd; he listens to them speaking and answers their questions, which proves his obedience to his parents. But he puts the authority of his heavenly Father first, speaking with freedom [παρρησίας] to his earthly parents: "Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be about my Father's business?" The son honours the Father. Would I neglect my heavenly Father, his command and his will? For I was not in those things which the flesh desires, which the world flees, which childhood urges, but in those which belong to the Father; they concern the glory of the Father, for whose sake he came into the world. Here the glory of command is left to me over you, and the glory of obedience to you. Yet his parents did not grasp the mind of the son. Therefore he went back with them to Nazareth, being subject [ὑποτασσόμενος] to them, obedient to them (ibid. v. 51). He also gave a sample of this subjection in that he adapted himself to the manner of private life of his parent Joseph. To this belongs that disparagement of the Jews: "Is not this the carpenter?" (Mark 6:3). "Is not this the son of the carpenter?" (Matt. 13:55). Justin reported that he made ploughs and yokes. And when the followers of Julian asked whether the son of the carpenter did any work, a Christian gave a witty answer: He makes a coffin for Julian. Nor was this unworthy of the state of Christ's emptying, since it was necessary that he be found as a man. Moreover, according to Hesiod's saying, "no work is a disgrace" [ἔργον οὐδὲν ὀνείδος]; no craft is shameful. This is especially so among the Hebrews, among whom it is well known that even the rich and the wise laboured at crafts. Thus from adolescence he advanced into youth, or manhood, and...

units.la: tu, ut hominem, reperiri necesse fuit. Præterquam quòd juxta Hesiodi illud, ἔργον οὐδὲν ὀνείδος, nullum opificium probrosum est. Apud Hebræos inprimis, apud quos etiam divites & sapientes opificiis insudasse constat. Ita exadolescentia in juventutem, seu virilem ætatem profecit, & ... proficiebat sapientia & statura, & gratia apud Deum & homines. Luc.II.52. Tametsi enim apocrypha sunt, quæ de adolescentia & vita omni privata Christi tenebriones novelli in suis de infantia Salvatoris libris, & ... Legendis (quo nomine Scripturæ, quæ ... Legenda Nehem.VIII.9. appellatur, somnia sua æquiparant) minimè legendis; nec non Xaverius Jesuita in Historia Christi Persicè scripta & fabulosis narrationibus fœdè collutulata tradiderunt: tamen totum illud vitæ privatæ curriculum per Mediatorii muneris sui tyrocinia, & subinde sparsos Divinitatis suæ radios, ab eo decursum esse, donec publica vocatione ἐξοδῷ expositus, devotus (Joh.XVII.4. Act.II.23.) fieret, dubitari nequit.
units.tr: ...it was necessary that he be found, as a man, in such a state. Besides, according to Hesiod's saying, "work is no disgrace" [ἔργον οὐδὲν ὀνείδος], no craft is shameful. This is especially so among the Hebrews, among whom it is well known that even the rich and the wise devoted themselves to manual labour. So he advanced from adolescence into youth, or manhood, and Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and men (Luke 2:52). For although the apocryphal books about the boyhood and private life of Christ, which the new young scoundrels have written in their books on the childhood of the Saviour, are by no means to be read (they put their own dreams on a level with that writing which in Nehemiah 8:9 is called Legenda, "the reading"), and although Xaverius the Jesuit, in his History of Christ written in Persian and foully smeared with fabulous narratives, has handed down similar things, yet it cannot be doubted that the whole course of his private life passed through the apprenticeship of his mediatorial office, with the rays of his Divinity breaking out from time to time, until he was made ready for his public calling and devoted himself to his departure [ἔξοδος] (John 17:4; Acts 2:23).

units.la: X. Non unus in vita Jesu privata exinanitionis voluntariæ ejusdem & satisfactionis pro nobis character conspicitur. Nam ἀνθρωπῳ licet, quàm primum tamen natus est, ilico formam servi assumpsit, Phil.II.6. & legi se subjecit, Gal.IV.4. Deus enim metus ejus fuit ... ab utero, Psal.XXII.10. Jehova ab utero vocavit me, de ventre matris meæ memoravit nomen meum. Et dixit mihi: Servus es tu Israelis, Esaj.XLIX.1.3. Tum paupertatem cum probro quodam & ignominia, cum subjectione sub parentibus, labore manuum tolerata, subiit. Vulpes foveas suas, & volucres cœli habitationes suas habent. Sed Filius hominis non habet, quò caput suum reclinet, Luc.IX.58. Cognoscite gratiam (consilium gratiæ ad nos redundantis) Domini nostri Jesu Christi, quòd propter vos pauper factus est, cùm dives esset, 2.Cor. VIII.9. Sed paupertatem subiit loco nostro, non πενίαν mendicitatem, quam in populo Dei obtinere lex vetuit: neque proprietates abdicavit: neque paupertatem cum indigentia non conjunctam coluit, ut mendicantibus Monachis nihil inde præsidii accedat. Accessit in illa ad laborem manuum sub parentibus subjectione demonstratio charitatis erga parentes. Qua incitante à miraculis saltem privatim, domi matris suæ, sublevandæ familiæ gratia, patrandis non abstinuisse eum, nonnulli ex Mariæ intercessione, Joh.II.3.5. & exemplo Eliæ apud viduam Sareptanam commorantis, ejusque paupertati miraculoso beneficio succurrentis, 1.Reg.XVII.7. &c. colligunt. Præterea metus mortis per omnem vitam, ex hostium persecutionibus, inde ab Herodis infanticidio, & certa ex unctionis ad munus Mediatorium conscientia, nec non patiens in silentio & spe expectatio vocationis Divinæ ad functionem muneris Mediatorii, non parum exercitum eum habuit. Denique in praxi pietatis quotidiana, & observantia Deo debita, in diebus carnis præstita, unctionis & προσευχάς suæ in domo cœlestis Patris sui, (Luc.II.49.) inde à puero sibi conscius, δεήσεις καὶ ἱκετηρίας deprecationes & supplicationes pro salute Ecclesiæ, cujus Rex & Servator natus erat, obtulit, Hebr. V.7. V.7. Nam eas ad omnes dies carnis Christi extendere nihil vetat, quia ex iis ὑπακοήν obedientiam v.8. didicisse dicitur.
units.tr: X. Not once only in the private life of Jesus can we see the character of his voluntary self-emptying and of his satisfaction for us. For as soon as he was born as a man [ἄνθρωπος], he at once took on the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6), and subjected himself to the law (Gal. 4:4). For you are my God from my mother's womb (Ps. 22:10), the LORD called me from the womb, from my mother's bowels he made mention of my name. And he said to me, You are my servant, Israel (Isa. 49:1, 3). Then he endured poverty with a certain disgrace and reproach, with subjection to his parents, and with toil of the hands. Foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58). Know the grace (the counsel of grace overflowing upon us) of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor (2 Cor. 8:9). But he underwent poverty in our place; not destitution [πενία] in the sense of beggary, which the law forbade among the people of God; nor did he renounce property; nor did he cultivate poverty apart from need, so that no support is gained from it for begging monks. In that poverty, his labour with his hands and his subjection to his parents was a demonstration of love towards his parents. Some gather from this, from John 2:3, 5, and from the example of Elijah dwelling with the widow of Sarepta and relieving her poverty by a miraculous benefit (1 Kings 17:7 etc.), that at least in private, in his mother's home, he did not refrain from performing miracles to relieve the family's need, at the prompting of Mary's intercession. Moreover, the fear of death throughout his whole life, arising from the persecutions of enemies, beginning with Herod's slaughter of the infants, and his sure consciousness of his anointing to the mediatorial office, together with his patient, silent and hopeful waiting for the divine call to the function of his mediatorial office, kept him not a little exercised. Finally, in his daily practice of piety, and in the observance owed to God, which he rendered in the days of his flesh, from boyhood on conscious of his anointing, he offered prayers and supplications [δεήσεις καὶ ἱκετηρίας] for the salvation of the Church, whose King and Saviour he had been born to be (Heb. 5:7). For nothing forbids extending these to all the days of Christ's flesh, since it is said that from them he learned obedience [ὑπακοή] (v. 8).

units.la: XI. Vitam publicam & Ministerium publicum Jesus annum agens tricesimum auspicatus est. Ipse autem Jesus ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τεσσαράκοντα circiter annorum triginta incipiens, hoc est, incepit ministerium publicum Luc.III.23. Nam ἤρχετο non cum ἦν ἐτῶν erat annorum &c. construi debet, quia insolens foret dicere, ἀρχόμενος ἐτῶν τεσσαράκοντα, sed scribendum fuerat, ἐτῶν τεσσαράκοντα incipio annum tricesimum, & illud ὡσεί abundaret. Neque incipiebat tum Christus annum tricesimum, sed poene compleverat. Sensus ergo est: Ipse Jesus post Johannem incipiens (ἀρξάμενος διδάσκειν, docere, Evangelium praedicare, v.18.) erat quasi annorum triginta. Non enim dicitur, καὶ ὁ Ἰησοῦς, sed αὐτὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς Ipse Jesus, cum emphasi Ipse, non amplius Johannes, ut innueretur distinctio Johannis ministri & prodromi prius praedicantis, & Jesu ipsius magistri in praeconio ei succedentis. Atque adeo ipsum Jejum incipere est oppositum praedicare per prodromum, & significat incipere praedicare immediate. Salus ἤρξατο λαλεῖν initium cepit praedicari per Dominum, puta immediate Hebr.II.3. Prius enim praedicaverat & baptizaverat Johannes. Sed Christo ab eodem baptizato, & mox Johanne Baptista sublato, αὐτὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἤρξατο ipse Jesus coepit evangelizare. Et tum fuisse ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν quasi annorum triginta, hoc est, egisse annum trigesimum, dicitur, juxta axioma Hebraeorum: יום ראשון שנה Dies primus anni reputatur pro isto anno. Ut frustra nonnulli verba Lucae hiulca quadam latitudine de anno tricesimo completo explicent.
units.tr: XI. Jesus began his public life and public ministry in his thirtieth year. Jesus himself, beginning at about thirty years of age [ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τεσσαράκοντα, about forty years], that is, he began his public ministry (Luke 3:23). For ἤρχετο ("began") ought not to be construed with ἦν ἐτῶν ("was of years"), since it would be unusual to say ἀρχόμενος ἐτῶν τεσσαράκοντα; it should rather have been written ἐτῶν τεσσαράκοντα I begin my fortieth year, and the word ὡσεί would then be superfluous. Nor was Christ then beginning his thirtieth year, but had almost completed it. The sense therefore is: Jesus himself, beginning after John (ἀρξάμενος διδάσκειν, to teach, to preach the Gospel, v. 18), was about thirty years old. For it is not said καὶ ὁ Ἰησοῦς ("and Jesus") but αὐτὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς, Jesus himself, with emphasis on himself: no longer John, so that the distinction is shown between John, the minister and forerunner who preached first, and Jesus himself, the master who succeeded him in the proclamation. Thus to begin preaching is the opposite of preaching through a forerunner, and means to begin preaching immediately. Salvation (Heb. 2:3), which began to be spoken [ἤρξατο λαλεῖν] to be declared by the Lord, that is, immediately, is what is meant. For John had preached and baptized before. But after Christ had been baptized by him, and John the Baptist soon removed, Jesus himself began [αὐτὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἤρξατο] to preach the gospel. And he is said to have been then about thirty years old, that is, in his thirtieth year, according to the Hebrew axiom: the first day of the year is reckoned as that year (יום ראשון שנה). So some vainly explain Luke's words, with a certain loose latitude, as referring to a completed thirtieth year.

units.la: XII. Praecessit initium Ministerii Christi ejusdem Baptismus, ceu quaedam ad ministerium ejus inauguratio. Nam advenit Jesus a Galilaea ad Jordanem ad Johannem, ἵνα βαπτισθῇ ὑπʼ αὐτοῦ, ut ab eo baptizaretur, Matth.III.13. Deprecante Johanne ministerium Jesu baptizandi his verbis: Necesse habeo, ut a te baptizer, & tu venis ad me, v.14. respondit ei Jesus: Ἄφες ἄρτι Sine nunc (in hoc oeconomiae, exinanitionis, servitutis meae statu) ἔτω γὰρ πρέπον ἐστὶν ἡμῖν πληρῶσαι πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην. Sic enim decet nos (te & me) implere omnem Justitiam; omne debitum, quod ex mandato Patris nobis incumbit. Sicut Christus venit tanquam διάκονος τῆς περιτομῆς minister circumcisionis, sic Judaeos assumens, ut in omnibus iis, circumcisis, assimilaretur, & legalibus eorundem institutis se subjiceret, Rom.XV.8. ita etiam Johannem, primum Regni Coelorum praeconem recognoscere, & ab eo signaculum justitiae & libertatis nobiscum recipere voluit, ut in omnibus se servum Dei, nec tantum servum, sed etiam caput Ecclesiae suae, quae omnia cum ipso communia habet, demonstraret. Si enim circumcisus esset, & baptizatus non esset, non omnem justitiam, omne debitum capitis, implevisset. Circumcisio enim sacramentum obligatorium est, quo, qui circumciditur, ad legem servandam se obligat, Gal.V.3. Baptismus justificatorium, quo libertas a legis servitute, absolutio a maledictione, & impetratio justitiae obsignatur. Si igitur circumcisus duntaxat, non etiam baptizatus esset, & ipse ad legem servandam, & Ecclesia ad circumcisionem suscipiendam obligaretur; manente quippe Sacramento, quo ipse Deus se obligaverat ad benedictionem praestandam per Semen. Nunc vero quia & circumcisus est, ad servitutem obeundam, & debitum Sponsoris praestandum: & peccata per obedientiam suam expiare incipiens (Joh.I.26–37.) & mox expiationem finiturus, Baptismi, libertatis & absolutionis a lege Sacramentum una nobiscum suscepit, omnem utique justitiam praestitit, & nos in ipso, ceu capite, circumcisi reputamur circumcisione, quae non fit manu, quae Baptismo ejus nobis obsignatur. Constat enim sic, quod & obligatio Seminis cesset, & nos in Christo, capite nostro, benedicti simus. Nam etiam ideo nobis Baptismum dedit, quia non tantum Christum perfectum Salvatorem nostrum declarari, sed etiam nobis, qui ad ipsum confugimus, communionem cum ipso obsignari oportuit. Ac licet Christus remissione peccatorum, quae in Baptismo obsignatur, non indiguerit, indiguit tamen obsignatione absolutionis a debito impetrandi Ecclesiae remissionem peccatorum, nec non potestate Ecclesiae remissionem peccatorum, regenerationem & Spiritum S. donandi. Sic ergo Johannes Jesum baptizavit. qui baptizatus ascendit statim ex aqua, vel ἀνέβη statim atque ascendit ex aqua; Et ecce aperti sunt ei (Johanni, cui visio ea Joh.I.33. promissa est, ipsique etiam Christo, qui vidit ἀνοιγομένους coelos Marc.I.10.) Coeli; & vidit Spiritum Dei descendentem ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν instar columbae (σωματικῶ εἴδει, ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν corporali specie sicut columbam Luc.III.22.) cum & descensus fuerit columbinus, sicut & Spiritus רוח alitis instar alas suas super pullis vibrans, Genes.I.2. & species corporea columbae, quae ἀκεραίως Matth.X.16. & יונה integritatis in amore symbolum est, fuerit) & venientem super ipsum. Et ecce vox e Coelis, dicens: Hic est filius ille meus, Dilectus ille, in quo acquiesco, Matth.III.16.17. Qui Baptismus insuper & augustissimae Triadis, & triplicis officii Christi Mediatorii clarissima effigies fuit. Nam & pater, e Coelo locutus, Filius Patris Filius Dilectus declaratus, Spiritus S. in columbae specie missus est; & Christus audiendus Propheta ἀκούειν benepla-citum Patri, ceu sacrificium boni odoris, offerens Sacerdos, Filius Rex perspicue ὀρίζειν definitur.
units.tr: XII. The beginning of Christ's ministry was preceded by his own baptism, as a kind of inauguration into his ministry. For Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, that he might be baptized by him (Matt. 3:13). When John objected to baptizing Jesus, saying, I have need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me? (v. 14), Jesus answered him: Let it be so now (Ἄφες ἄρτι, in this state of my economy, emptying and servitude), for thus it becomes us to fulfil all righteousness [ἔτω γὰρ πρέπον ἐστὶν ἡμῖν πληρῶσαι πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην]. For thus it becomes us (you and me) to fulfil all righteousness; every obligation which lies upon us by the Father's command. As Christ came as minister of the circumcision (Rom. 15:8) (διάκονος τῆς περιτομῆς), taking on the Jews so that in all those circumcised he might be made like them and submit himself to their legal institutions, so also he willed to acknowledge John, the first herald of the kingdom of heaven, and to receive from him with us the seal of righteousness and liberty, so that he might show himself in all things the servant of God, and not merely a servant but also the head of his Church, which has all things in common with him. For if he had been circumcised and not baptized, he would not have fulfilled all righteousness, every obligation of the head. For circumcision is a sacrament that binds (obligatorium est), by which he who is circumcised obliges himself to keep the law (Gal. 5:3). Baptism is that justifies (justificatorium), by which liberty from the servitude of the law, absolution from the curse and the attainment of righteousness are sealed. If therefore he had been circumcised only and not baptized, both he himself would be bound to keep the law, and the Church would be bound to receive circumcision; for the sacrament would remain in force by which God himself had bound himself to bestow the blessing through the Seed. But now, because he was both circumcised, to undertake the servitude and to render the debt of the Surety, and beginning to expiate sins by his obedience (John 1:26–37) and about to finish the expiation, he took up with us the sacrament of baptism, of liberty and absolution from the law; he certainly fulfilled all righteousness, and in him as our head we are reckoned circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands (Col. 2:11), which is sealed to us by his baptism. For thus it is established both that the obligation of the Seed ceases, and that we are blessed in Christ our head. For he also gave us baptism for this reason: that it was fitting not only that Christ should be declared our perfect Saviour, but also that communion with him should be sealed to us who flee to him. And although Christ had no need of forgiveness of sins, which is sealed in baptism, he did need the sealing of his absolution from the debt, so that he might obtain for the Church the forgiveness of sins, and also the power of the Church to forgive sins, to regenerate and to bestow the Holy Spirit. So John baptized Jesus, who went up straightway out of the water (ἀνέβη statim atque ascendit ex aqua); and behold, the heavens were opened to him (to John, to whom that vision was promised, John 1:33, and to Christ himself, who saw the heavens opened, Mark 1:10), and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove (ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν, in bodily form, as a dove, Luke 3:22), for the descent was dove-like, just as the Spirit (רוח) hovering like a bird spreading its wings over its young (Gen. 1:2), and the bodily appearance of the dove, which is a symbol of innocence (ἀκεραίως, Matt. 10:16) and of love (יונה), was present; and coming upon him. And behold a voice from heaven saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased (Matt. 3:16–17). This baptism was also a most clear image of the most august Trinity and of the threefold office of Christ the Mediator. For the Father, speaking from heaven, declared the Son to be his beloved Son; the Holy Spirit was sent in the form of a dove; and Christ, as priest offering his good pleasure to the Father like a sacrifice of sweet savour, is clearly defined as the Prophet to be heard (ἀκούειν), as the Son, and as King.

units.la: XIII. A Baptismo Jesu Publicam ejus vitam & Ministerium auspicandum esse, Scriptura testatur.
units.tr: XIII. Scripture testifies that Jesus' public life and ministry are to be dated from his baptism.

units.la: S. Petrus enim εἰσελθὼν καὶ ἐξελθὼν introitum & exitum Ministerii sic distinguit: Toto tempore, in quo ingressus & egressus inter nos est Dominus, incipiens a Johanne Baptismo usque ad illum diem, quo assumptus est a nobis, Act.I.21.22. Incipiens a Galilaea post Baptismum, quem praedicavit Johannes. quomodo unxerit Deus Jesum a Nazareth Spiritu S. & virtute; qui pertransiverit benefaciendo & sanando, quem occiderunt. &c. ib.X.37. &c. De spatio vero temporis, quod inde a Baptismo ad ascensionem usque in publico munere exegit, qui ad tempo-rum calculos sedent, non consentiunt. Pleriisque calculos juxta numerum Paschatum subducere
units.tr: St Peter distinguishes the entrance and exit [εἰσελθὼν καὶ ἐξελθὼν] of the ministry in this way: The whole time in which the Lord went in and out among us, beginning from John's baptism until the day on which he was taken up from us, Act.I.21.22. Beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John preached, how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power; who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed, whom they put to death, etc., ib.X.37, etc. As to the length of time that he spent in public office from his baptism until his ascension, those who work out chronologies do not agree. Most have thought fit to reckon the years by the number of Passovers that fell within the period.

units.la: Ministerium Christi publicum trium 1 & dimidii annorum, a debque Paschatum quatuor spatio exactum. ducere placuit. Mittimus traditionem ab Irenæo proditam, & S. Johannì authori tribuntam, plane ἀδηλον, quòd Christus anno trigesimo baptizatus, docere anno demum quadragesimo cœperit, & vitam circa annum quinquagesimum finiverit. Nostro tempore Theologi & Chronologi sententiarum divortiis distracti, alii quidem tempori Ministerii Christi publici tria, alii quatuor, alii cum Scaligero, Calvisio, Langio ex Canonibus Periodi Callipicæ, nec non medio motu Lunari quinque Paschata deputant. Qua de re sic habendum. Sicut olim Thucydides bellum Peloponnesiacum per æstates & hyemes descripsit: ita omnino hac in re paulò obscuriore intervalla quædam assumenda sunt, quibus totum illud tempus à Baptismo Christi ad ejusdem assumptionem usque perspicuè distingui posset. Intervallum illud per Paschata optimè dividitur. Quot verò Paschata à Baptismo Christi ad ejusdem ascensionem in Cœlum decurrerint, omnium optimè ex S. Johanne, qui de industria illa signasse videtur, colligi potest. Is autem quatuor, nec plura, nec pauciora memorat; Primum cap. II.13.23. ubi propinquo Paschate Christus Hierosolymam ascendisse dicitur: Secundum cap. V.1. ubi dicitur fuisse ἑορτὴ festum Judæorum, ad quod Hierosolymam ascendit Christus, quod Pascha fuisse colligitur ex verbis Christi præcedentibus: Nonne vos dicitis, quòd quatuor adhuc menses sunt, & messis sit, cap. IV.35. quæ cùm circa Thebeth seu Decembrem dicta sint (inde enim ad messem usque quatuor circiter menses fluunt) festum ei tempori proximum non aliud quàm Pascha esse potuit; quia in Palæstina messis hordeacea statim post Pascha inchoari, & triticea ante Pentecosten finiri solet: Tertium cap. VI.4. ubi ἐγγὺς τὸ πάσχα propinquum Pascha fuisse dicitur: Quartum cap.XI.55. XII.1.2. XIII.1. ὡ προσφατὸν, quo Christus verus agnus pro nobis mactatus est. Quòd verò Quintum, inter secundum & tertium a nobis recensitum, ex Matth.XII.1. Marc.II.23. Luc.VI.1. ubi fit mentio Jesu ἐν σαββάτῳ δευτεροπρώτῳ Sabbatho altero-primo per segetes ambulantis, Scaliger aliique elicere conantur, solidum non est, quia Sabbathum illud δευτεροπρώτου, Pascha consequens, illud ipsum intelligitur, quod Pascha Joh. V.1. commemoratum consecutum est, adeóque cum secundo à nobis definito convenit. Accedit, quòd Daniel.IX.27. in medio septimanæ ultimæ abolenda hostia & sacrificium dicitur, unde (non firma tamen ex loco Danielis consecutione, sed firma sententia) sumta est recepta opinio; quæ etiam in Theophili fragmentis extat; Christum in ministerio suo faciendo & docendo (Act.I.1.) consumpsisse annos tres cum dimidio, hoc est, dimidium à Baptismo usque ad Pascha anni XXX. & tres usque ad Pascha anni XXXIII. Cui sententiæ etiam exteras historias suffragari, alibi ex Eusebio ostendimus. Totidem annos XXXIII. David Hierosolymæ regnavit 2.Sam.V.5.
units.tr: Many have thought fit to measure the public ministry of Christ as a span of three and a half years, marked off by four Passovers. We set aside the tradition handed down by Irenaeus and attributed to the author John, which is plainly uncertain, that Christ was baptized in his thirtieth year, began to teach only in his fortieth, and ended his life around his fiftieth year. In our own time theologians and chronologers are divided by differing opinions: some assign three Passovers to the public ministry of Christ, others four, and others, with Scaliger, Calvisius and Lange, five, reckoning from the canons of the Callippic period and also the mean lunar motion. On this matter the position is as follows. Just as Thucydides once described the Peloponnesian War by summers and winters, so in this rather obscure matter certain intervals must be assumed, by which the whole time from the baptism of Christ to his taking up could be clearly divided. That interval is best divided by the Passovers. How many Passovers ran their course from the baptism of Christ to his ascension into heaven can best be gathered from St John, who seems to have marked them deliberately. He mentions four, neither more nor fewer. The first is at ch. II.13.23, where Christ is said to have gone up to Jerusalem when the Passover was near. The second is at ch. V.1, where it is said that there was a feast [ἑορτὴ] of the Jews, to which Christ went up to Jerusalem; that this feast was the Passover is inferred from Christ's preceding words, Do you not say that there are yet four months, and the harvest comes? ch. IV.35. Since these words were spoken around Thebeth, or December (for about four months run from then until harvest), the feast nearest to that time could be nothing other than the Passover, because in Palestine the barley harvest usually begins immediately after the Passover and the wheat harvest ends before Pentecost. The third is at ch. VI.4, where the Passover is said to have been near [ἐγγὺς τὸ πάσχα]. The fourth is at ch. XI.55, XII.1.2, XIII.1, the Passover [ὡ προσφατὸν] at which Christ, the true Lamb, was sacrificed for us. As for the fifth Passover, which we have counted between the second and the third, Scaliger and others try to derive it from Matt. XII.1, Mark II.23, Luke VI.1, where mention is made of Jesus walking through the grainfields on the second-first Sabbath [ἐν σαββάτῳ δευτεροπρώτῳ], but this is not sound, because that second-first Sabbath [δευτεροπρώτου], following the Passover, is understood to be the very one that followed the Passover mentioned in John 5.1, and so it agrees with the second Passover that we have fixed. Moreover, Daniel 9.27 says that in the middle of the last week the sacrifice and offering would be abolished; from this (though the sequence in Daniel is not a firm basis, the opinion itself is firm) the accepted opinion was drawn, which also appears in the fragments of Theophilus: that Christ, in performing and teaching his ministry (Acts 1.1), spent three and a half years, that is, half a year from his baptism until the Passover of the year 30, and three years until the Passover of the year 33. Other histories also support this view, as we have shown elsewhere from Eusebius. For the same thirty-three years David reigned in Jerusalem, 2 Sam. 5.5.

units.la: XIV. Longum esset ex historia Evangelii ἀναλυτικῶς repetere, quæ temporis hujus intervallo Jesus fecit & locutus est. Summa eorum capita ut delibemus, alia in primordio Ministerii sui, inde à Baptismo ad primum Pascha: alia Pascha tum supra enumeratorum tempo-ris fecit & locutus est. In Primordio Ministerii ante omnia ad ipsum Ministerium suum per tentationem, quam à Sathana in deserto sustinuit, se præparavit, Matth.IV.1–12. Marc.I.12.13. Luc.IV.1–14. Nam post Baptismum non in Cœlum, ad hauriendos Divinæ sapientiæ latices, uti Sociniani fingunt, ascendit, sed verius ad inferos descendit, hoc est, Spiritu Dei authore, in desertum secessit cum feris agitans, & jejunio per quadraginta dies exacto, cùm esuri-re inciperet, Sathanas ei suasor, ut ex lapidibus panes conficeret, extitit. Sed scuto verbi Dei, promittentis vitam non ex pane duntaxat, sed quolibet verbo ex ore Dei prodeunte, Deut.VIII.3. Tentatorem repulit.
units.tr: XIV. It would be long to repeat from the Gospel history, in an analytical way, what Jesus did and said during this interval of time. Let us touch on the main points: some occurred at the beginning of his ministry, from his baptism to the first Passover, and others at the Passovers of the time enumerated above. At the beginning of his ministry, Christ first prepared himself for that very ministry by the temptation which he endured from Satan in the desert, Matt. IV.1–12, Mark I.12.13, Luke IV.1–14. For after his baptism he did not ascend into heaven to draw from the springs of divine wisdom, as the Socinians imagine; rather, he descended, as it were, into the depths, that is, by the Spirit of God as author he withdrew into the desert, living among the wild beasts, and after a fast of forty days, when he began to hunger, Satan appeared as his tempter, urging him to make bread from stones. But with the shield of the word of God, which promises life not by bread alone but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God, Deut. VIII.3, he repulsed the tempter.

units.la: Sed mox eundem assumpsit in urbem sanctam, & in pinnaculo Templi statuit, non per aëra ex deserto eodem avectum, sed eodem Spiritu, quo in desertum abreptus fuerat, Sathanam, in angelum lucis se transformantem, & ad locum eum libenter comitantem; uti athleta, vel secutor retiarium suum, sectari solet. In hoc ἑπαγγέλλω, in quod per conclavia juxta Templum ipsum in summum educta, plana tecta, quæ per cochleas & porticus conscendi poterant, habentia, Sathana comite, enixus est, positus, se ipsum in terram præcipitare jubetur, auctoritate Dei ipsius, Psal.XCI.11. promittentis, quòd Angelico præsidio suos custoditurus sit. Verùm Christus temeritatem, non posito in viis, non vocato Divinitus ad se præcipitandum suadenti, validius longè scutum oppositum, mandatum Dei vetans, ne tentemus Dominum Deum nostrum, Deut.VI.16. Frustratione hac non acquiescens Sathanas, denuo Christum in sublimem montem seorsum abripit, & in eo ostensis ei, in idea forte oculis inspicienda (ut in tabulis geographicis artifices solent, & Diabolus per spectrum aliquod longè luculentius & magnificentius exhibere potuit) mundi Regnis & omni eorum gloria; perinde uti olim Deus Mosi in monte alto terram Canaan conspiciendam præbuit; forte etiam revocata ad ejusdem animum promissione de finibus terræ in possessionem, & gentibus in hæreditatem dandis, (Psal.II.8.) Regnorum illorum possessionem ei promisit hac lege, si adorare eum dignatus fuerit. Sed Christus tentatorem repulit gladio verbi Dei, præcipientis, Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & ei soli servies, Deut.VI.13. X.20. Ita ter victus infernalis serpens Jesum dimisit, secum haud dubiè reputans, eum legem Dei in medio sui habere, Psal.XL.9. & ne minima quidem cupiditate contra eam titillari, ibid.XVI.7. adeóque Semen illud Mulieris esse, à quo multùm capiti ejus timendum sit. Ex hoc tempore Jesus prodiit in publicum, incipiens in Galilæa prædicare & dicere: Resipiscite. Appropinquavit enim Regnum Cœlorum, Matth.IV.17. Inde discipulos vocavit, ib. IV.18–23. Marc.I.16–22. Luc.V.2. Joh.I.42. Etiam ποιεῖν facere incepit in Cana Galilææ, ubi nuptiis cùm adesset, matre petente importunius, sed horam suam observante Filio (ne in talibus eum admonitione indigere crederetur, & ut alias matris, alias Filii rationes & curas esse pateret) aquam in vinum commutavit, Joh. II.1–12. Hoc signorum Christi initium fuisse, & per illud manifestasse eum δόξαν αὐτοῦ gloriam præcel-
units.tr: But soon the same tempter took him into the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the Temple, not carried through the air from the desert, but by the same Spirit by whom he had been carried off into the desert. Satan, transforming himself into an angel of light and willingly accompanying him to that place, as a wrestler or pursuer usually follows his net-bearer, urged him to throw himself down from there, on the authority of God himself, Ps. XCI.11, who promises that he will guard his people with angelic protection. The pinnacle is the highest point of the Temple, reached through rooms beside the Temple itself, with flat roofs which could be climbed by stairs and colonnades; Satan was eager to lead him there as a companion. But Christ, with a far stronger shield, rejected this rashness, the suggestion that he should throw himself down when he was neither placed on the way nor called by God to do so: the command of God forbids it, You shall not tempt the Lord your God, Deut. VI.16. Satan, not satisfied with this failure, again carried Christ away to a high mountain apart, and there showed him, to be viewed perhaps in a picture before his eyes (as artists do on geographical maps, and as the Devil could display by some much clearer and more splendid appearance), the kingdoms of the world and all their glory, just as God once showed Moses the land of Canaan from a high mountain to be seen; perhaps he also recalled to his mind the promise concerning the bounds of the earth for possession and the nations for inheritance (Ps. II.8), and promised him the possession of those kingdoms on this condition, that he deign to worship him. But Christ repulsed the tempter with the sword of the word of God, which commands, You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone, Deut. VI.13, X.20. Thus the infernal serpent, thrice defeated, let Jesus go, no doubt reflecting in himself that he had the law of God in his heart, Ps. XL.9, and was not stirred by even the least desire against it, ib. XVI.7, and that this was therefore the Seed of the Woman, from whom he had much to fear for his head. From this time Jesus came forward in public, beginning to preach in Galilee and to say: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand, Matt. IV.17. From there he called his disciples, ib. IV.18–23, Mark I.16–22, Luke V.2, John I.42. He also began to do miracles [ποιεῖν] in Cana of Galilee, where, when he was present at a wedding and his mother pressed him too urgently, he, observing his own hour (so that he would not be thought in need of admonition in such matters, and so that it would be clear that the mother's concerns and the Son's were different), changed water into wine, John II.1–12. This was the beginning of Christ's signs, and through it he made manifest his glory [δόξαν αὐτοῦ], his excellence

units.la: {f} præcellentiæ & potentiæ suam (non alienam, ut Prophetæ rem magnam facientes) atque credidisse in eum discipulos, animas suas ei, ut veraci testi, Filio Dei à Deo misso, commisisse, nec de doctrina ejus dubitasse, v. 11. dicitur.
units.tr: and power, as his own (not borrowed, as the prophets did when performing great deeds), and it is said that the disciples believed in him, having committed their souls to him as to a true witness, the Son of God sent by God, and did not doubt his teaching, v. 11.

units.la: XV. Paschatis Primi historia iter Christi ex Galilæa in Judæam, & ex Judæa in Galilæam reditum, & quæ utrobique ille gessit, complectitur. Ascendit enim Christus Hierosolymam ad Pascha, ubi Templum purgavit, & miracula satis multa edidit, Joh. II. 13–f. per discipulos baptizavit, ibid. III. 22.26. cum Nicodemo de regeneratione per aquam & Spiritum commemorabile colloquium instituit, ibid. III. 1–22. Sed audita Johannis captivitate, Judæam reliquit, & in Galilæam rediit; & Samariam transiens cum muliere Samaritana de aqua vitæ & cultu vero Dei, ibid. IV. 1–32. Et cum discipulis suis de cibo suo & messe Evangelii v. 31–39. divinos sermones cædit; credentibus in eum Samaritanis pluribus, v. 39–43. In Galilæam ubi rediit, Regnum Cœlorum prædicare perrexit, Marc. I. 14. 15. Filium Regium sanavit, Joh. IV. 46–54. Nazarethi appellens Prophetam Esajam exponit, sed mox expellitur, Luc. IV. 16–30. inde moram in Capernaum trahens, Sabbatho docet, Matth. IV. 13–18. Marc. I. 21. 22. Luc. IV. 31.32. Spiritum immundum ejicit, Marc. I. 23–28. Luc. IV. 33–37. Socrum Simonis sanat, Matth. VIII. 14. 15. Marc. I. 29–32. Luc. IV. 38.39. allatos ad se undique ægrotos curat, Matth. VIII. 16. Marc. I. 32–35. Luc. IV. 40. 41. Capernaumo relicto Galilææ urbes obambulans, in Synagogis docet, & dæmonia ejicit, Marc. I. 39. Luc. IV. 44. ex navi Simonis turbam docet, ibid. V. 1–4. miraculosam piscium capturam instituens, Simonem Petrum, Jacobum, Andream piscatores hominum facit, & passim in Synagogis docet, Matth. IV. 18–25. Marc. I. 16–20. Luc. V. 1–12. Leprosum in urbe quadam sanat, confluentibus ad eum undique pluribus, Matth. VIII. 1–4. Marc. I. 40–45. Luc. V. 12-16. iterum Capernaumi docet, & Paralytico peccata remittit, Matth. IX. 1–8. Marc. II. 1–12. Luc. V. 18–26. apud mare turbam docet, Levin seu Matthæum vocat, Matth. IX. 9. Marc. II. 13. 14. Luc. V. 27.28. in ejusdem domo se & publicanos convivantes defendit, & non jejunantes vindicat, Matth. IX. 10–13. Marc. II. 15–22. Luc. V. 29–39. Sabbatho διὰ π̔ρο̄π̔ε̄ω̄τῶ̄ transiens per sata discipulos spicas vellentes defendit, Matth. XII. 1–8. Marc. II. 23–28. Luc. VI. 1–5.
units.tr: XV. The history of the First Passover covers Christ's journey from Galilee into Judea and his return from Judea to Galilee, and what he did on each journey. Christ went up to Jerusalem for the Passover, where he cleansed the Temple and worked many miracles (John 2:13–f.). He baptized through his disciples (ibid. 3:22, 26), and he held a memorable conversation with Nicodemus about regeneration by water and the Spirit (ibid. 3:1–22). But when he heard that John had been imprisoned, he left Judea and returned to Galilee. Passing through Samaria, he spoke with the Samaritan woman about the water of life and the true worship of God (ibid. 4:1–32). With his disciples he delivered divine discourses about his food and the harvest of the Gospel (vv. 31–39). Many Samaritans came to believe in him (vv. 39–43). On returning to Galilee, he continued to preach the Kingdom of Heaven (Mark 1:14, 15). He healed the royal official's son (John 4:46–54). At Nazareth he taught and expounded the prophet Isaiah, but he was soon driven out (Luke 4:16–30). From there he stayed at Capernaum, where he taught on the Sabbath (Matt. 4:13–18; Mark 1:21, 22; Luke 4:31, 32). He cast out an unclean spirit (Mark 1:23–28; Luke 4:33–37). He healed Simon's mother-in-law (Matt. 8:14, 15; Mark 1:29–32; Luke 4:38, 39). He healed the sick who were brought to him from everywhere (Matt. 8:16; Mark 1:32–35; Luke 4:40, 41). Leaving Capernaum, he went about the towns of Galilee, teaching in the synagogues and casting out demons (Mark 1:39; Luke 4:44). From Simon's boat he taught the crowd (ibid. 5:1–4). Through a miraculous catch of fish he made Simon Peter, James and Andrew fishers of men, and he taught in the synagogues everywhere (Matt. 4:18–25; Mark 1:16–20; Luke 5:1–12). He healed a leper in a certain town, while many came together to him from every side (Matt. 8:1–4; Mark 1:40–45; Luke 5:12–16). Again at Capernaum he taught, and he forgave the paralytic's sins (Matt. 9:1–8; Mark 2:1–12; Luke 5:18–26). By the sea he taught the crowd, and he called Levi, or Matthew (Matt. 9:9; Mark 2:13, 14; Luke 5:27, 28). In Matthew's house, while he was dining with himself and the tax collectors, he defended them and vindicated the fact that they did not fast (Matt. 9:10–13; Mark 2:15–22; Luke 5:29–39). Passing through the grainfields on the Sabbath [διὰ τῶν σπορίμων], he defended his disciples who plucked the heads of grain (Matt. 12:1–8; Mark 2:23–28; Luke 6:1–5).

units.la: XVI. Ad Secundum Pascha Hierosolymas ascendens (Joh. V. 1.) ibidem ad piscinam Bethesdæ ægrum 38. annorum sanat, & se, quòd Deum Patrem suum nuncupasset, accurate defendit, Joh. V. 1–47. in Synagoga alio Sabbatho docet, & aridam dextram sanat, Matth. XII. 9–14. Marc. III. 1–6. Luc. VI. 6–11. Inde insidiarum metu ad mare secedens, multos sanat, Matth. XII. 15–21. Marc. III. 7–12. in montem ascendens orat, & coram discipulis & turba Divinissimam in eodem monte concionem habet, Matth. V. VI. VII. Marc. III. 13–22. Luc. VI. 12–49. Varia inde loca denuo obambulans, Capernaumi centurionis servum sanat, Matth. VIII. 5–13. Luc. VII. 1–10. in Nain
units.tr: XVI. Going up to Jerusalem for the Second Passover (John 5:1), he healed there, at the pool of Bethesda, a sick man of thirty-eight years, and he carefully defended himself for having called God his Father (John 5:1–47). On another Sabbath he taught in a synagogue and healed a man's withered right hand (Matt. 12:9–14; Mark 3:1–6; Luke 6:6–11). Then, withdrawing to the sea for fear of plots, he healed many (Matt. 12:15–21; Mark 3:7–12). Going up a mountain, he prayed, and in the presence of the disciples and the crowd he delivered the most divine sermon on that same mountain (Matt. 5–7; Mark 3:13–22; Luke 6:12–49). From there he wandered again through various places. At Capernaum he healed the servant of a centurion (Matt. 8:5–13; Luke 7:1–10). At Nain

units.la: viduæ unigenitum resuscitat, ibid. II–17. in Simonis domo mulierem pedes ipsius lachrymis rigantem defendit, ibid. 36–48. Dæmoniacum sanans, se contra blasphemantes, quòd per Beelzebulem dæmonia ejiceret, defendit, Matth. XII. 22–37. Marc. III. 22–30. Signum petentibus negat in præsentiarum, & resurrectionem ex morte futuram ejus vice offert, Matth. XII. 38–45. mater, frater, soror quæ sit, ostendit, ibid. 46–50. Marc. III. 31–35. Luc. VIII. 19–22. in mari ex navigio parabolam seminantis, plurësque alias recitat, Matth. XIII. 1–53. Marc. IV. 1–34. Luc. VIII. 4–18. in ulteriorem ripam transiens mare tranquillat, ventos increpat, Matth. VIII. 18–27. Marc. IV. 35–41. Luc. VIII. 22–25. apud Gadarenos dæmonia ejicit, in porcos intrare finit, & inde Capernaum redit, Matth. VIII. 28–34. Marc. V. 1–20. Luc. VIII. 26–39. apud mare cùm esset, discipulis Johannis de jejunio respondet, filium Jairi resuscitat; hæmorrhoisan sanat, Matth. IX. 14–26. Marc. V. 21–43. Luc. VIII. 40. Inde secedens cæcis oculos aperit, dæmoniacum restituit, Matth. IX. 27–34. Urbes omnes obiens, docens, sanans, in urbem patriam redit, &c. ceu faber, ibi contemnitur, ibid. IX. 35. XIII. 54–58. Marc. VI. 1–6. commiseratus ibi turbam, messem magnam, operarios paucos, duodecim Apostolos cum mandatis ablegat, Matth. IX. 36–38. X. 1–42. Marc. VI. 7–11. Luc. IX. 1–5. qui obeuntes singulos Judææ vicos prædicant, sanant, Marc. VI. 12–16. Luc. IX. 6. quibus reversis, & Johannis audita morte discipulorumque fœctis, in desertum urbis Bethsaida cum discipulis abit, sequentibus ipsum turbis. Unde in montem subiens quinque panibus & duobus piscículis homines quinquies mille pascit, & volentibus eum Regem facere, discipulos intrare navim, & præire in ripam alteram, Capernaum versus, noctu super mare ambulat, in Gennesareth venit, ubi mox ægros allatos curat, Matth. XIV. 13. 14. Marc. VI. 31–56. Luc. IX. 10–17. Joh. VI. 1–22. ac demum Capernaumi in Synagoga de pane vitæ concionatur, & se eum esse asserit. ibid. v. 22–71.
units.tr: he raised the widow's only son (ibid. 11–17). In Simon's house he defended a woman who was wetting his feet with her tears (ibid. 36–48). Healing a demoniac, he defended himself against those who blasphemed, saying that he cast out demons by Beelzebul (Matt. 12:22–37; Mark 3:22–30). He refused a sign to those who asked for one at that time, and he offered in its place his resurrection from the dead in the future (Matt. 12:38–45). He showed who his mother, brother and sister are (ibid. 46–50; Mark 3:31–35; Luke 8:19–22). From a boat on the sea he recited the parable of the sower and several others (Matt. 13:1–53; Mark 4:1–34; Luke 8:4–18). Crossing to the farther shore, he calmed the sea and rebuked the winds (Matt. 8:18–27; Mark 4:35–41; Luke 8:22–25). Among the Gadarenes he cast out demons and allowed them to enter the swine, and from there he returned to Capernaum (Matt. 8:28–34; Mark 5:1–20; Luke 8:26–39). While he was by the sea, he answered John's disciples about fasting, raised the daughter of Jairus, and healed the woman with a flow of blood (Matt. 9:14–26; Mark 5:21–43; Luke 8:40). Withdrawing from there, he opened the eyes of the blind and restored a demoniac (Matt. 9:27–34). Going through all the towns, teaching and healing, he came to his native town, where, like a carpenter, he was despised (ibid. 9:35; 13:54–58; Mark 6:1–6). Moved with compassion there for the crowd, which was a great harvest with few workers, he sent out the twelve Apostles with their instructions (Matt. 9:36–38; 10:1–42; Mark 6:7–11; Luke 9:1–5). They went through each village of Judea, preaching and healing (Mark 6:12–16; Luke 9:6). When they returned, and after John's death had been heard of and the disciples had been informed, he went with his disciples into the desert near the town of Bethsaida, the crowds following him. From there he went up a mountain, and with five loaves and two small fish he fed five thousand people. When they wanted to make him king, he ordered the disciples to get into the boat and go ahead to the other shore, toward Capernaum. In the night he walked on the sea and came to Gennesaret, where he at once healed the sick who were brought to him (Matt. 14:13, 14; Mark 6:31–56; Luke 9:10–17; John 6:1–22). Finally, at Capernaum, in the synagogue, he preached about the bread of life and declared that he is that bread (ibid. vv. 22–71).

units.la: XVII. Ad Tertii Paschatis historiam plurescula referenda sunt.
units.tr: XVII. Several things must be related concerning the history of the third Passover.

units.la: Ante omnia enim Pharisæos discipulis suis, quòd illotis manibus panem comederent, exprobrantes, aboliti prætextu traditionum Divini mandati convincit, Matth. XV. 1–20. Marc. VII. 1–23. in confinia Tyri & Sidonis secedens, Syrophœnissæ ibi filiolam à dæmonio liberat, Matth. XV. 21–28. Marc. VII. 24–30. mox ad mare Galilææ veniens surdum restituit, ibid. VII. 31–39. ibi in montem ascendens plures sanat, Matth. XV. 29–32. in deserto turbam pascit, ibid. XV. 32–38. Marc. VIII. 1–9. hinc in partes Dalmanutha seu Magdala veniens, Matth. XV. 39. Marc. VIII. 11–14. & in ulteriorem ripam abiens à fermento Pharisæorum dehortatur, Matth. XVI. 5–12. Marc. VIII. 14–21. Bethsaidæ cæcum sanat, ib. 22–26. in vicis Cæsareæ Philippi Petri confessionem audit, mortem suam prædicit, &c. Matth. XVI. 13–28. Marc. VIII. 27–38. Luc. IX. 18–27. Post dies octo in monte sublimi transfiguratur, & sequente die de monte descendens, filium lunaticum à dæmonio libe-berainvaluit, ut ab Angelo è Coelo ἐνισχύεσθαι corroborari necesse habuerit, Luc. XXII. 43. non externa corpori remedia applicante, sed interna animo consolationum in tanto certamine fomenta adhibente, & ἔξοδος exitus ejus (uti Moses & Elias in monte ibid. IX. 30.31.) necessitatem, utilitatem, efficaciam, pretium enarrante.
units.tr: First of all, rebuking the Pharisees for eating bread with unwashed hands, which they blamed on his disciples, he refutes them by showing that they had set aside the command of God for the sake of their traditions (Matth. XV. 1–20; Marc. VII. 1–23). Withdrawing to the borders of Tyre and Sidon, he frees there the little daughter of the Syrophoenician woman from a demon (Matth. XV. 21–28; Marc. VII. 24–30). Soon coming to the sea of Galilee, he restores a deaf man (ibid. VII. 31–39). Going up into a mountain there, he heals many (Matth. XV. 29–32). In the desert he feeds the crowd (ibid. XV. 32–38; Marc. VIII. 1–9). From there, coming to the region of Dalmanutha or Magdala (Matth. XV. 39; Marc. VIII. 11–14), and crossing to the farther shore, he warns against the leaven of the Pharisees (Matth. XVI. 5–12; Marc. VIII. 14–21). At Bethsaida he heals a blind man (ibid. 22–26). In the villages of Caesarea Philippi he hears Peter's confession and foretells his own death, etc. (Matth. XVI. 13–28; Marc. VIII. 27–38; Luke IX. 18–27). After eight days he is transfigured on a high mountain. On the following day, coming down from the mountain, he frees a lunatic boy from a demon. In his agony he was so overcome that he needed to be strengthened by an angel from heaven [ἐνισχύεσθαι] (Luke XXII. 43), not applying outward remedies to his body, but administering inward comforts to his soul in so great a conflict. And, as Moses and Elijah did on the mountain (ibid. IX. 30–31), he spoke of his departure [ἔξοδος] and explained its necessity, its usefulness, its efficacy and its price.

units.la: XXI. Sed quò magis tenebrarum potestas omnis Christum pressit, hoc ille ἐκπνέσ-τερον intensius, vehementius, ardentiús precatus est, Luc. XXII. 44. Precationes & intercessiones ad eum, qui ex morte ipsum salvare poterat, cum clamore valido & lachrymis offerens, Hebr. V. 7. oravit positis genubus, Luc. XXII. 41. in faciem prolapsus, Matth. XXVI. 39. Marc. XIV. 35. ἐκ δευτέρου & ἐκ τρίτου bis terve Matth. XXVI. 39. 42. 44. non spiritu duntaxat, sed etiam voce. Oravit enim; Abba, Pater, omnia possibilia tibi: παρένεγκε τὸ ποτήριον ἀπ' ἐμοῦ τοῦτο. Transfer à me poculum hoc. ἀλλ' οὐ τί ἐγὼ θέλω, ἀλλὰ τί σύ. Sed non quod ego volo, verùm ut tu, Marc. XIV. 36. Pater mi, si possibile est, transeat à me ποτήριον τοῦτο poculum hoc. Sed non ut ego volo, verùm ut tu. Matth. XXVI. 39. Pater, si vis transferre à me poculum isthoc! sed non voluntas mea, sed tua fiat, Luc. XXII. 42. Poculum, quod à se transferri petit, non bonum & laetificum illud, de quo Psalm. XVI 5. יהוה כוסי Dominus poculum meum; sed malum, excandescentiæ, λαᾶες horroris, qui in ipsius anima per clarum intuitum iræ Dei; sive poenarum peccato debitarum, extitit. Cùm nihilominus hic iræ Divinæ sensus à nobis transire, at à Christo gustari, & non transire debuerit, nostra tamen, ad æstimationem sanctitatis Dei, quæ ad restitutionem imaginis Dei in nobis necessaria erat, intererat, non ignorare, quòd Christus in anima sua hunc dolorem & terrorem persenserit. Petere igitur, ut hic calix transeat, erat testari amaritudinem calicis, & spem repræsentandæ consolationis, & anhelationem ad illam. Tum grave Christo erat videre non tantùm, quòd & discipuli in ipso scandalizarentur, & exagitandi essent, quos proin πειρασμὸν tentationem deprecari Matth. XXVI. 41. jussit: sed etiam, quòd Ecclesia imposterum cribranda & ventilanda esset. Ut homo igitur, fratres suos diligens, cohorruit, & cupere se ostendit, ne in tantas dubitationes, perplexitates, cribrationes sui venirent. Ac licèt fieri non potuerit, quin scandala hæc evenirent, tamen intercessionis hujus fructus, consolatio electorum fuit. Sicut Petrus id ex oratione Christi impetravit, ne fides ejus deficeret. Quamvis etiam Christus non oraverit pro mundo, sed pro iis, quos Pater ipsi dedit: tamen quod decuit Mosen Exod. XXXII. 32. & Paulum Rom. IX. 1. ut pro fratribus anathema fieri cupientes, iis pereuntibus vehementer indolescerent, id decuit etiam Christum, legi dilectionis fratrum per omnia subjectum, ut plurimorum hominum, nominatim etiam fratrum secundum carnem, quorum nefariis manibus jam jam tollendus erat, interitu vehementer cruciaretur, & indolesceret. Ideo etiam casum Hierosolymæ deploravit, & propter incredulitatem hominum haud raro infremuit. Sed ut dilectio hæc justa secundum legem fuerit, petitio tamen conditionalis voluntati Dei, cujus τὸ ὠρισμένον definitum transfire non potuit, adstringi & subjici debuit. Cogitari verò etiam potest, multis modis tristitiam eam, & calicis πικρότητα augeri vel inde potuisse, quòd hæreditatis ex labore animæ consecuturæ amplitudo nondum plane humanitati ejus innotuit; ita ut ex hac anxietate & horrore, per ostensionem hæreditatis consequendæ à λόγῳ & ipso etiam Angelo corroborante factam, non parùm sublevari & recreari debuerit. Unde collecto animo sic se ipsum Christus erexit: Jehova pars (ferculum) portionis meæ, כוסי poculi mei. Tu tenuisti sortem meam. Funes mei ceciderunt in amœnis, etiam hæreditas, quæ decet me. Benedicam Jehovæ, qui consuluit mihi &c. Iccirco lætatur cor meum, & gaudet gloria mea, &c. Psal. XVI. 5.6.7.9. De cætero oratio isthæc Christi, qua calicem deprecatus est, non pugnavit vel cum fortitudine & constantia ejus, quasi infra Martyrum saltem constantiam subsidente, quia Martyres utcunque corpore afflicti animam à peccatorum per sanguinem Agni expiatorum mole liberam, serenamque habent; Christus contra omnia omnium salvandorum peccata in corpore suo supra lignum ferre, & corpore animáque infernales cruciatus, desertus à Deo, tolerare, Dei & Angelorum consortio destitui, tenebris Sathanæ, leoni rugienti, canibus, improborum coetui, cornibus monocerotum Psal. XXII. 17.20. &c. βεβρ-χνύ-π paulisper tradi debuit; vel cum sanctitate ejus, quasi consilio Dei repugnantia petiisset, quia sub conditione voluntatis Divinæ petiit, non gestiens vadimonium deserere, sed naturæ à malo tanto abhorrentis φρυγάς, nec non magnitudinem patientiæ in apricum proferre: vel cum sapientia ejusdem, impossibilia petere visi, quia sanctissimus homo extra se velut raptus, neque sibi praesens, & ingenti animæ perturbatione (Joh. XII. 27.) tentatus in omnibus secundum similitudinem, sed sine peccato, Hebr. IV. 15. ita loqui, & naturæ dolenti horrentique extortum, & velut anticipatum suspirium exprimere; & simul se promptè corrigere potuit. Sicut alibi: Serva me ex hac hora. Sed propterea veni in hanc horam, Joh. XII. 27. Quæ & ipsa passionis & infirmitatis pars quædam, sed ἀδιαλείπτως fuit.
units.tr: XXI. But the more the power of darkness pressed upon Christ, the more intensely, vehemently and fervently he prayed [ἐκπνέστερον] (Luke XXII. 44). Offering prayers and supplications to him who could save him from death, with strong crying and tears (Heb. V. 7), he prayed kneeling (Luke XXII. 41), falling on his face (Matth. XXVI. 39; Marc. XIV. 35), a second time and a third time [ἐκ δευτέρου, ἐκ τρίτου], twice or three times (Matth. XXVI. 39, 42, 44), not only in spirit but also with his voice. For he prayed: Abba, Father, all things are possible to you: take this cup away from me. [Transfer à me poculum hoc.] But not what I will, but what you (will) [ἀλλ' οὐ τί ἐγὼ θέλω, ἀλλὰ τί σύ]. Not what I will, but what you will, (Marc. XIV. 36). My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. But not as I will, but as you (will). (Matth. XXVI. 39). Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me! Yet not my will, but yours be done, (Luke XXII. 42). The cup which he asked to be taken from him was not that good and joyful cup of which Psalm XVI. 5 speaks, The Lord is my portion and my cup [כוסי]; it was the bitter cup of wrath, of horror, which arose in his soul through a clear sight of the anger of God, that is, of the punishments due to sin. Although this sense of divine wrath ought to pass over us but be tasted by Christ and not pass over him, yet it is not to be ignored by us that, for the esteem of the holiness of God, which was necessary for the restoration of the image of God in us, Christ felt this pain and terror in his soul. Therefore to ask that this cup pass away was to bear witness to the bitterness of the cup, and to the hope of representing comfort, and to longing for it. Then it was grievous to Christ to see not only that his disciples too would be scandalized in him and would have to be shaken, whom accordingly he commanded to pray against temptation [πειρασμόν] (Matth. XXVI. 41), but also that the Church would have to be sifted and winnowed in time to come. So, as a man loving his brothers, he shuddered and showed that he wished that they might not fall into such doubts, perplexities and sifting. And although it could not be that these scandals would occur, yet the fruit of this intercession was the comfort of the elect, just as Peter obtained from Christ's prayer that his faith would not fail. Although Christ did not pray for the world, but for those whom the Father gave him, yet what became Moses (Exod. XXXII. 32) and Paul (Rom. IX. 1), who wished to be made an anathema for their brothers and were deeply grieved when these perished, that became Christ too, who was subject in all things to the law of love for brothers. He was sorely tormented and grieved at the destruction of very many men, and especially of his brothers according to the flesh, by whose wicked hands he was soon to be removed. Therefore he also lamented the fall of Jerusalem, and on account of the unbelief of men he often groaned. But so that this love might be just according to the law, his conditional request nevertheless had to be bound and subjected to the will of God, whose appointed decree [τὸ ὠρισμένον] could not be passed over. It may also be thought that this sadness and the bitterness of the cup could have been increased in many ways by the fact that the greatness of the inheritance to be obtained from the labour of his soul was not yet fully known to his humanity; so that from this anxiety and horror he ought to have been not a little relieved and refreshed, by the showing of the inheritance to be obtained, made strong by the Word [λόγῳ] and by the angel himself. Whence, with his spirit gathered, Christ thus raised himself up: Jehovah is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup. You have held my lot. My cords have fallen in pleasant places; yes, I have a goodly heritage. I will bless Jehovah, who has given me counsel, etc. Therefore my heart rejoices and my glory is glad, etc. (Ps. XVI. 5, 6, 7, 9). Moreover, this prayer of Christ, in which he asked that the cup be removed, was not at odds either with his fortitude and constancy, as if it sank below at least the constancy of the martyrs, since the martyrs, however much they are afflicted in body, have a soul free and serene from the burden of sins expiated by the blood of the Lamb; whereas Christ had to bear upon his body upon the wood all the sins of all who were to be saved, and to endure in body and soul infernal torments, forsaken by God, deprived of fellowship with God and the angels, delivered for a little while into the darkness of Satan, to a roaring lion, to dogs, to the assembly of the wicked, to the horns of the unicorns (Ps. XXII. 17, 20, etc.). Nor was it at odds with his holiness, as if he had asked for something contrary to the counsel of God, since he asked under the condition of the divine will, not eager to desert his bond, but to bring to light the shrinking of his nature from so great an evil, as well as the greatness of his patience. Nor was it at odds with his wisdom, as if he seemed to ask for impossible things, since this most holy man, as if carried outside himself, not present to himself and tested in all things according to likeness, yet without sin (Heb. IV. 15), in a great perturbation of soul (John XII. 27), could speak thus and utter a sigh wrung from his suffering and shuddering nature, as if anticipating it; and at the same time he could promptly correct himself, as elsewhere: Save me from this hour. But for this cause I came to this hour (John XII. 27). This too was a certain part of his passion and weakness, but [ἀδιαλείπτως] unceasing.

units.la: XXII. Agone hoc in horto finito Jesus à Juda proditus traditur Judæis, juxta Prophetiam. אִישׁ שְׁלוֹמִי vir pacis meæ, cui considebam, & qui manducavit panem meum עָקַב הִגְדִּיל עָלַי magnificavit contra me calcem, calcibus me impetiit, Psal. XLI. 10. Quæ ἐκδοσις traditio sic in Scripturis explicatur, quasi ipse Christus Sacerdotibus se obtulerit, ut mercedem suam, & æstimationem sui, si vellent, penderent. Dicam ad eos, si bonum est in oculis vestris, afferte mercedem meam: sin autem, cessate. Appenderunt autem mercedem meam triginta argenteis, Zach. XI. 12. Sine ipsius enim scitu, gubernatione, industria, occasionem prudentem praebente, traditio ejusmodi fieri non potuit; quia nemo ipsi animam eripere potuit; sed ipse sponte eam, secundum mandatum Patris, ponere debuit, Joh. X. 18. Sic proditus à Juda, à monte olivarum progrediens, capitur, vincitur, dispersis discipulis ad domum Cajaphæ mittitur, Matth. XXVI. 47.57. Marc. XIV. 43. Ejusdem per Judam proditi traditio in manus Judæorum & gentilium.
units.tr: XXII. When this agony in the garden was over, Jesus was betrayed by Judas and handed over to the Jews, according to prophecy: The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted up his heel against me (Ps. XLI. 10). This handing over is explained in the Scriptures as if Christ himself offered himself to the priests, so that they might pay his wages and his valuation, if they wished. I said to them: If it is good in your eyes, give me my wages; but if not, refrain. So they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver (Zech. XI. 12). For without his knowledge, direction and diligence, providing a prudent occasion, such a betrayal could not have happened; because no one could take his soul from him, but he himself had to lay it down of his own accord, according to the command of the Father (John X. 18). Thus betrayed by Judas, going forward from the Mount of Olives, he is seized and bound, his disciples scattered, and he is sent to the house of Caiaphas (Matth. XXVI. 47, 57; Marc. XIV. 43). His betrayal by Judas was also a handing over into the hands of the Jews and the Gentiles.

units.la: XIV.43-53. Luc.XXII.47-54. Joh.XVIII.1-12. & ibidem accusatur, damnatur, illuditur, Matth.XXVI.57-f. Marc.XIV.53-f. Luc. XXII.54-66. Joh.XVIII.12-28. Captivitas pertinet ad עצר coarctationem, Esaj. LIII. 8. Elongasti מודעי notos meos (discipulos meos) a me. Fecisti me iis תועבות abominationes כלא ולא אנא Inclusus sum, & non exeo, Psal. LXXXVIII. 9. Ac ne Angeli quidem amplius ad eum corroborandum venerunt; sed traditus est consortio daemonum. Non fuit cum ipso איש vir, qui torcular calcaret. Esaj. LXIII.3. Circumdederunt eum vituli, tauri Basan. Leo rapiens & rugiens, canes עדת מרעים Coetus maleficorum, os leonis, cornua monocerotum, Psal. XXII. 13. 14. 17. 22. In Concilio inprimis matutino, postquam anquisitus, an Christus esset, minimè id inficiatus, imò Filium Dei se professus palam esset, de ipso conclamatur, & vinctus ad Pontium Pilatum mittitur, adeóque potestati gentium, כלבים Canum, ibid. 17. αμαρτωλων peccatorum, uti gentes ipse Christus, Matth. XXVI. 45. Marc. XIV. 41. Luc. XXIV. 7. appellavit, committitur. Pertinuit enim etiam ad signa temporum, ut pateretur Christus sub gentibus, quarum ditio fieri Judaea debuit, tributaria illi civitati, quae imperium habuit in Reges terrae, & in qua Christus crucifigi debuit, Apoc. XI. 8. Unde Christus non semel in Evangelio praedixit, fore ut tradatur in manus gentium, ab iis illudendus, flagellandus, crucifigendus, Matth. XX.19. Joh. XVIII. 32. &c. Praeterea traditio haec in manus immanes gentium testimonium fuit tum odii Judaeorum, חנם fine causa, Psal. LXIX. 5. quia cum potestatem non habentes occidendi, à profundendo sanguine abstinere potuerint, maluerunt eum peccatoribus tradere, quàm sinere, ut vivat: tum innocentiae Christi, quia Judaei crimen seditionis apud judicem probare non potuerunt: tum scortationis spiritualis Judaeorum, magis ad Capitolium, quàm ad montem domus Domini respicientium, & in Capitolio Deos Romanorum colentium, quia clamantes; Non habemus Regem nisi Caesarem, Joh. XIX. 12 15. Christum & Regnum Dei αποδοκιμασιν reprobarunt, Matth. XXI.42. Psal. CXVIII.22. & Romanis suum panem, aquam, linum, lanam, vinum, oleum imputarunt, non cognoscentes eum, qui omnia ei dederat. Hos. II.4.7.
units.tr: Mark 14:43-53; Luke 22:47-54; John 18:1-12. And there he is accused, condemned and mocked: Matth. 26:57ff.; Mark 14:53ff.; Luke 22:54-66; John 18:12-28. His captivity pertains to עצר [ʿātsar], restraint, Isa. 53:8. "Thou hast put far from me my acquaintances (my disciples)" [mōdaʿay]. "Thou hast made me an abomination to them" [tôʿēvōt]. "I am shut up and I cannot come out" [lō' ʾēṣā], Ps. 88:9. Nor did angels come any longer to strengthen him, but he was delivered into the company of demons. "There was no man [ʾîsh] with him who trod the winepress," Isa. 63:3. "Bulls of Bashan surrounded him, a roaring and ravening lion, dogs [kelābîm], an assembly [ʿădat] of evildoers [merēʿîm], the lion's mouth, the horns of the wild oxen," Ps. 22:13, 14, 17, 22. Above all, in the morning council, after he was asked whether he was the Christ, and he did not deny it but openly professed himself the Son of God, he was cried down concerning this, and bound and sent to Pontius Pilate. He was thus handed over to the power of the Gentiles, "dogs" (Ps. 22:17), and "sinners" [ἁμαρτωλῶν], as Christ himself called the Gentiles (Matth. 26:45; Mark 14:41; Luke 24:7). For it also belonged to the signs of the times that Christ should suffer under the Gentiles, under whose dominion Judea was to become tributary, that city which held power over the kings of the earth and in which Christ was to be crucified (Rev. 11:8). Hence Christ foretold more than once in the Gospel that he would be delivered into the hands of the Gentiles, to be mocked, scourged and crucified by them (Matth. 20:19; John 18:32, etc.). Moreover, this delivery into the hands of savage Gentiles was a witness both to the hatred of the Jews, "without cause" [ḥinnām] (Ps. 69:4), since, although they had no power to put him to death and could have refrained from shedding blood, they preferred to hand him over to sinners rather than let him live; and to the innocence of Christ, since the Jews could not prove before the judge the charge of sedition; and to the spiritual whoredom of the Jews, who looked more to the Capitol than to the mountain of the house of the Lord, and worshipped the gods of the Romans in the Capitol, for they cried out, "We have no king but Caesar" (John 19:12, 15). They rejected Christ and the kingdom of God [ἀποδοκιμασίαν] (Matth. 21:42; Ps. 118:22), and they ascribed to the Romans their bread, water, flax, wool, wine and oil, not knowing him who had given them all these things (Hos. 2:4, 7).

units.la: XXIII. Neque tamen Jesum in tumultu occidi, sed potius in judicio causam ejus discuti Sacerdotes & Pilatus ille Romanus, voluerunt. Non tantùm enim ex עצר coarctatione, sed etiam ממשפט ex judicio assumi debuit, Esaj. LIII.8. ut causa ejus publicè discussa liqueret, innocentem & justum pati pro nocentibus & injustis 1. Pet. III. 18. Et Sacerdotum quidem definitiva sententia ex ore improbi & imprudentis Pontificis Cajaphae, non ex se loquentis, sed prophetantis, pronuntiata fuit, praestare Judaeis, ut unus homo moriatur pro populo, & non tota gens pereat, Joh. XI. 50. Postea in aedibus Pilati falsae doctrinae, tributi negati, affectati Regni accusatus, in aedes Herodis Tetrarchae Galilaeae traductus, denuo ad Pilatum reductus, iterato accusatus, denudatus, flagellatus, coronatus, illusus, &, innocens licèt à Pilato palam de-
units.tr: XXIII. Yet Jesus was not put to death in a tumult; rather the priests and that Roman Pilate wished his cause to be examined in a judicial hearing. For he was to be taken not only from restraint [ʿātsar] but also from judgment [mimmishpat], Isa. 53:8, so that his cause might be publicly examined and it might be clear that the innocent and just one suffered for the guilty and unjust (1 Pet. 3:18). The definitive sentence of the priests was indeed pronounced from the mouth of the wicked and unwise high priest Caiaphas, who spoke not on his own but prophesied: that it was expedient for the Jews that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish (John 11:50). Afterwards, in the house of Pilate, he was accused of false teaching, of refusing tribute, and of aiming at a kingdom; he was led to the house of Herod, tetrarch of Galilee, then brought back again to Pilate, accused a second time, stripped, scourged, crowned with thorns, and mocked; and although he was openly declared innocent by Pilate,

units.la: claratus, ad mortem tamen crucis ab eodem condemnatus est, Matth. XXVII.2-31. Marc. XVI.1-20. Luc. XXIII.1-26. Joh. XVIII.28-40. XIX.1-16. Atque haec etiam Christi voluntas, & judicium Patris fuit, facientis, ut in ipsum incurreret peccatum omnium; & peccata sic in eum incurrentia, eorumque poenas ita abeo נשא exigentis, ut pro iis animam suam sacrificium poneret, Esaj. LIII.6. 7. 10. & solveret id, quod non rapuerat, Psal. LXIX. 5. In hoc enim judicio damnari debuit peccatum, quod actionem habebat ex lege ad mancipandum sibi hominem, eum morti dandum, & simul Diabolus imperium mortis habens judicatus & abolitus est, Joh. XII.31. XVI.11. Hebr. II. 14. Denique Deus sanctus sanctificatus est, & ut sanctificans, justificans, salvans impium, justificatus est, Esaj. V. 16. Rom. III.25.26. Verbo, Deus judicium exire ad justitiam Psal. XCIV.15. Esaj. XLII.3. voluit.
units.tr: he was nevertheless condemned by the same man to the death of the cross (Matth. 27:2-31; Mark 15:1-20; Luke 23:1-26; John 18:28-40; 19:1-16). And this was also the will of Christ and the judgment of the Father, who ordained that the sin of all should fall upon him; and the sins thus falling upon him, and their punishments, he bore [nāśāʾ] as one who exacts them, so that he might lay down his soul as a sacrifice for them (Isa. 53:6, 7, 10), and might restore what he had not taken away (Ps. 69:4). For in this judgment sin had to be condemned, which had a legal claim to enslave man and to deliver him to death; and at the same time the Devil, who held the power of death, was judged and abolished (John 12:31; 16:11; Heb. 2:14). Finally, God, being holy, was sanctified, and, as the one who sanctifies, justifies and saves the ungodly, he was justified (Isa. 5:16; Rom. 3:25, 26). In a word, God willed that judgment should go forth unto righteousness (Ps. 94:15; Isa. 42:3).

units.la: XXIV. Neque tamen qualecunque mortis supplicium, sed vilissimum, abjectissimum, turpissimum, & maximè dolorificum atque execrabile crucis ipsi decretum est. Obedire enim debuit usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, Phil. II.8. Quod supplicium & praedictum, & non sine causa, Deo moderante, delectum est. Nam & in deserto is, cujus aspectu salus & liberatio à morsu serpentis contigit, hoc est, Christus per serpentem aeneum in pertica suspensum figuratus est, Num. XXI.9. & Christus manus ac pedes suos fodiendos, ossa sua separata annumeranda, ad numerum spectanda & exhibenda esse Psal. XXII. 17.18. praedixit: & sepeliri debuit cum improbis, Esaj. LIII.9. Sepultura autem cum improbis à sepultura cum divitibus, & à sepultura asini distincta crucifixionem, genere pro specie posito, significat. Nec sine causa supplicium hoc, non aliud, delectum est, quia pro nobis morituris execratio pro nobis fieri, hoc est, execrationem legis peccatori obnuntiatam in se suscipere, & eandem morte sua finire, abolere debuit. At eadem lex execrationem esse eum, qui ex ligno pendet, & ante vesperam eundem ex ligno sepeliri, finitae maledictionis signum, jussit. Cum fuerit in aliquo judicium mortis, & interficiendus fuerit, & suspendes eum de ligno, non pernoctabit cadaver ejus in ligno, sed sepeliendo sepelies eum eo die, quia קללת אלהים תלוי maledictio Dei est suspensus, & non contaminabis terram tuam, quam Jehova Deus tuus tibi dat in haereditatem, Deut. XXI.22.23. Quae lex innuit, tum maledictionem seu sententiam, qua peccator à communione Dei & bonorum ejus removetur, & omnibus malis oneratur, per legem nondum factam fuisse irritam, sed valorem suum adhuc retinuisse: tum suspensionem ex ligno, cujus species est crucifixio, atrocissimum & acerbissimum supplicium esse; utpote quo Deus vim maledictionis ostendere voluit: tum neminem sive justum, sive injustum suspendi è ligno, nisi vi maledictionis, & propterea, quia lex postulat sanctificationem Dei, usque dum maledictio aboleatur: tum maledictionem quandoque aboleri & finiri debere, quia suspensi cadaver ex ligno tolli & sepeliri debuit: adeóque ut qui id facere omitterent, terram Dei in haereditatem datam polluant, & spem Israelis, quòd
units.tr: XXIV. Yet the death penalty decreed for him was not just any kind of death, but the most vile, abject and shameful, and the most painful and accursed, that of the cross. For he had to be obedient unto death, and the death of the cross (Phil. 2:8). This punishment was both foretold and chosen, not without cause, by God's providence. For in the wilderness that serpent whose sight brought salvation and deliverance from the bite of the serpent was a figure of Christ, who was lifted up on a pole (Num. 21:9). And Christ foretold that his hands and feet were to be pierced, and his bones were to be counted and looked upon and exhibited, in number (Ps. 22:17, 18). He was also to be buried with the wicked (Isa. 53:9); and burial with the wicked, distinguished from burial with the rich and from the burial of an ass, signifies crucifixion, the genus put for the species. Nor without reason was this punishment chosen rather than another, because for us who were to die a curse had to be made for us, that is, he had to take upon himself the curse of the law pronounced against the sinner, and to end and abolish it by his own death. The same law, however, declared that he who hangs on a tree is accursed, and ordered that he be buried in the tree on the same day before evening, as a sign that the curse was finished: "If there is in anyone a judgment of death, and he is to be put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his corpse shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him on that day, because 'he who hangs is accursed of God' [qilelat ʾĕlōhîm tālûy], and you shall not defile your land, which Jehovah your God gives you for an inheritance" (Deut. 21:22, 23). This law implies: first, that the curse or sentence by which the sinner is removed from communion with God and his good things, and is burdened with all evils, had not been annulled by the law not yet made, but still retained its force; second, that hanging on a tree, of which crucifixion is a kind, is the most atrocious and bitter punishment, since by it God wished to show the force of the curse; third, that no one, whether just or unjust, is hanged on a tree except by the force of the curse, and therefore, because the law demands the sanctification of God, the curse must be abolished; fourth, that the curse must at some time be abolished and ended, since the corpse of the hanged man had to be taken down from the tree and buried; and so those who neglected to do this would pollute the land given to God for an inheritance, and the hope of Israel, that

units.la: Non tumultuariè Jesus occidi, sed in judicio damnari debuit. beratum Patri restituit, Matth. XVII. 1-22. Marc. IX. 1-29. Luc. IX. 28-43. Capernaum veniens tributum pro se & Petro solvi jubet, Matth. XVII. 24-27. Litem inter discipulos de primatu obortam decidit, ibid. XVIII. 1-7. Marc. IX. 33-38. Luc. IX. 46-50. mox Hierosolymam ad festum tabernaculorum occultè ascendit, Joh. VII. 1-10. mittens ante se discipulos, qui progressi in viam Samaritanorum ab iis recepti non sunt, Luc. IX. 51-56. & discipulos LXX. ante faciem suam, binos in omnes urbes ablegat, ib. X. 1-16. turba eum quaerente in Templo docet, Joh. VII. 11-53. profectus mox in montem olearum, diluculo iterum in Templo docet, & mulierem adulteram damnare detrectat, ib. VIII. 1-59. caecum natum sanat, ib. IX. 1-41. concionatur de se Pastore & ovili suo ibid. X. 1-21. discipulos reversos excipit, Legis peritum de vita aeterna instruit, in domo Marthae divertit, Luc. X. 17-42. orare docet, daemonium ejicit, &c. ibid. XI. 1-f. à fermento Pharisaeorum dehortatur, ibid. XII. 1-f. de Galilaeis à Pilato male habitis accepto nuntio ad poenitentiam hortatur, ibid. XIII. 1-7. hydropicum Sabbatho sanat, parabolas de magna coena, homine turrim aedificaturo, ibid. XIV. 1-f. de ove perdita, drachma, filio prodigo, ib. XV. 1-f. de dispensatore dissipante ib. XVI. 1-14. proponit; contra offendicula, de vi fidei disserit, ib. XVII. 1-f. exemplo viduae jugiter orare docet, ib. XVIII. 1-15. se & Patrem unum esse docet, Joh. X. 22-39. in trajectum Jordanis abiens docet & sanat, Matth. XIX. 1, 2. Marc. X. 1. Joh. X. 40-f. Pharisaeis de divortio respondet, Matth. XIX. 3-12. Marc. X. 2-12. infantibus manus imponit, & divitem superbum tentat, Matth. XIX. 13-f. Marc. X. 13-21. Luc. XVIII. 15-30. Bethaniae Lazarum resuscitat, Joh. XI. 1-54. inde in urbem Ephraim abit, ibique habitat. Demum Hierosolymam ad ultimum & emortuale Pascha ascendens, maxima cum vigilantia & industria sanctissimis negotiis suis ad finem provehendis insudat. Nam in itinere ipso mortem suam discipulis praedicit, Matth. XX. 17-20. Marc. X. 32-35. Luc. XVIII. 31-34. filios Zebedaei de vero primatu instruit, Matth. XX. 20-28. Marc. X. 35-45.
