Zachaeum convertit, Luc. XIX. 1-10. duos caecos sanat, Matth. XX. 29-34. Marc. X. 46-52. parabolam de homine nobili peregre profecto narrat, Luc. XIX. 11-27. Bethaniae cum Lazaro ad mensam discumbens à Maria ungitur, Joh. XII. 1-11. Demum pullo ad montem olearum accersito, Regis instar, Hierosolymam vehitur, urbe visa plorat, eandem ingressus, ementes & vendentes Templo exigit, caecos, claudos sanat, Graecis de passione sua concionatur, in Bethaniam cum duodecim suis secedit, ubi cives sui in eum non credunt; inde discedens ficui foliis fructum mentitae imprecatur, atque iterum urbem ingressus vendentes ex Templo ejicit, Matth. XXI. 1-46. Marc. XI. 1-33. Luc. XIX. 28-f. Joh. XII. 11-48. Sacerdotibus de authoritate sua respondet, Luc. XX. 1-8. parabolam vineae agricolis elocatae narrat, Marc. XII. 1-12. Luc. XX. 9-19. parabolam nuptiarum edisserit; Herodianis de censu, Sadducaeis de resurrectione, Pharisaeo de
units.tr: Jesus was not to be put to death in a tumult, but condemned in a judicial hearing. He restored [the glory] to the Father (Matth. 17:1-22; Mark 9:1-29; Luke 9:28-43). Coming to Capernaum, he orders the tribute to be paid for himself and for Peter (Matth. 17:24-27). He settles a dispute about primacy that had arisen among the disciples (ibid. 18:1-7; Mark 9:33-38; Luke 9:46-50). Soon after he went up secretly to Jerusalem for the Feast of Tabernacles (John 7:1-10), sending before him disciples who, when they went on into a Samaritan road, were not received by them (Luke 9:51-56). He also sent off the seventy disciples before his face, two by two, into every city (ibid. 10:1-16). While the crowd sought him, he taught in the Temple (John 7:11-53). Setting out at once for the Mount of Olives, and at dawn again teaching in the Temple, he refused to condemn the adulterous woman (ibid. 8:1-59). He healed the man born blind (ibid. 9:1-41). He preached about himself as the Shepherd and his sheepfold (ibid. 10:1-21). He received the returning disciples, instructed a lawyer about eternal life, and lodged in the house of Martha (Luke 10:17-42). He taught them to pray, cast out a demon, etc. (ibid. 11:1ff.). He warned against the leaven of the Pharisees (ibid. 12:1ff.). When news came about the Galileans whom Pilate had ill-treated, he urged repentance (ibid. 13:1-7). He healed a man with dropsy on the Sabbath, and proposed the parables of the great supper, of the man building a tower (ibid. 14:1ff.), of the lost sheep, the drachma, and the prodigal son (ibid. 15:1ff.), of the squandering steward (ibid. 16:1-14). Against stumbling-blocks, he discoursed on the power of faith (ibid. 17:1ff.), and by the example of the widow taught them to pray without ceasing (ibid. 18:1-15). He taught that he and the Father are one (John 10:22-39). Going away beyond the Jordan he taught and healed (Matth. 19:1, 2; Mark 10:1; John 10:40ff.). He answered the Pharisees about divorce (Matth. 19:3-12; Mark 10:2-12). He laid hands on infants, and tested the proud rich man (Matth. 19:13ff.; Mark 10:13-21; Luke 18:15-30). At Bethany he raised Lazarus (John 11:1-54). Thence he went away to the city of Ephraim and dwelt there. At last he went up to Jerusalem for the final Passover, the Passover of his death, and with the greatest vigilance and diligence laboured to bring his most holy undertakings to their end. For on the way itself he foretold his death to the disciples (Matth. 20:17-20; Mark 10:32-35; Luke 18:31-34). He instructed the sons of Zebedee about true primacy (Matth. 20:20-28; Mark 10:35-45). He converted Zacchaeus (Luke 19:1-10). He healed two blind men (Matth. 20:29-34; Mark 10:46-52). He told the parable of the nobleman who went away into a far country (Luke 19:11-27). Reclining at table at Bethany with Lazarus, he was anointed by Mary (John 12:1-11). At last, having a colt brought to the Mount of Olives, he was carried to Jerusalem as a king; seeing the city, he wept; entering it, he drove out those who bought and sold from the Temple, healed the blind and the lame, preached to the Greeks about his passion, and withdrew with his twelve to Bethany, where his fellow-citizens did not believe in him. Departing thence, he cursed a fig tree which pretended fruit with its leaves, and entering the city again he cast out the sellers from the Temple (Matth. 21:1-46; Mark 11:1-33; Luke 19:28ff.; John 12:11-48). He answered the priests about his authority (Luke 20:1-8). He told the parable of the vineyard let out to husbandmen (Mark 12:1-12; Luke 20:9-19). He set forth the parable of the marriage feast; he answered the Herodians about the tax, the Sadducees about the resurrection, and a Pharisee about the great commandment (Matth. 22:1-45; Mark 12:1-38). He pronounced woe to the scribes and Pharisees, and foretold the destruction of the city (Matth. 23:1-39; Mark 12:38-41; Luke 20:45ff.). He commended the widow's offering (Mark 12:41-44; Luke 21:1-5). Going out of the Temple, he foretold the ruin of Jerusalem,

units.la: mandato magno respondet Matth. XXII. 1-45. Marc. XII. 1-38. Scribis, Pharisaeis vae & urbi excidium obnuntiat, Matth. XXIII. 1-39. Marc. XII. 38-41. Luc. XX. 45-f. viduae eleemosynam collaudat, Marc. XII. 41-44. Luc. XXI. 1-5. egressus è Templo Hierosolymae ruinam praedicit, Matth. XXIV. 1-51. Marc. XIII. 1-37. Luc. XXI. 5-10. Parabolam decem virginum, talentorum narrat, Matth. XXV. 1-f. proditionem, crucifixionem suam praedicit, Bethaniae in domo Simonis leprosi mulierem se ungentem defendit, Sathana ilico in Judam intrante ibid. XXVI. 1-17. Marc. XIV. 1-12. Luc. XXII. 1-13. Haec omnia mortis Christo proximè imminentis, poenarum hostium, & Regni ejusdem initiorum ac progressus certissima praesagia continent.
units.tr: He answers the great commandment (Matt. 22:1-45; Mark 12:1-38). He pronounces woes on the scribes and Pharisees and foretells the destruction of the city (Matt. 23:1-39; Mark 12:38-41; Luke 20:45-end). He commends the widow's offering (Mark 12:41-44; Luke 21:1-5). Leaving the Temple at Jerusalem, he foretells its ruin (Matt. 24:1-51; Mark 13:1-37; Luke 21:5-10). He tells the parable of the ten virgins and of the talents (Matt. 25:1-end). He foretells his betrayal and crucifixion. At Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, he defends the woman who anointed him, and at once Satan enters into Judas (ibid. 26:1-17; Mark 14:1-12; Luke 22:1-13). All these things contain the most certain foreshadowings of the death now close at hand, of the enemies' punishment, and of the beginnings and progress of his Kingdom.

units.la: XVIII. Successit enim his Pascha Quartum, idémque novissimum & πυρώσιμον, quo Agnus ille tollens peccata mundi pro nobis madari debuit.
units.tr: XVIII. For this was followed by the fourth Passover, and that the last and the fiery [πυρώσιμον] one, on which that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world had to be sacrificed for us.

units.la: Quae fuit illa ταπεινωσις humiliatio, qua se ipsum humilians obedivit Deo usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, Phil. II. 8. novissimus exinanitionis gradus, poltremo exinaniti ejus biduo potissimum exactus. Licet enim per totam vitam Christi ejusdem humilitas emicuit, juxta ejusdem vocem illam; Discite à me, quia mansuetus & ταπεινος τῇ καρδίᾳ humilis corde sum, Matth. XI. 29. & tota vita ejusdem nil nisi passio, tenuitas, status irrequietus, labor, fatigatio, fames, sitis, modus vivendi communis, non notabilis, qualis Johannis Baptistae fuit, metus hostium, eorundem subtetfugatio, fuit: tamen humiliatio extrema & τὰ πάθηματα passiones ejus κατ' ἐξοχὴν se in ultimo illo fatali biduo, morte ejus terminato, quo inprimis hora potestatis tenebrarum venit, Luc. XXII. 53. protulerunt. Debuit enim Jesus ταπεινωθῆναι humiliari, deprimi non obiter, sed ad mortem usque & illam crucis; quia accepit à Patre mandatum exponendi animam suam redemptionis pretium, Joh. X. 18. Matth. X. 28. Illi, qui in foedus populi datus est, conveniebat, ut animam suam poneret satisfactionis pretium, Esaj. LIII. 10. Neque enim populus Dei סגולה Sancti ejus cum eo foedus facere, nisi mediante sacrificio Psal. L. 5. & ejus quidem, quem dat Sacerdotem & Apostolum ὁμολογίας aštipulationis seu confessionis nostrae, Hebr. III. 1. potuerunt. Peccatum enim nisi morte peccatoris, vel vicarii ejus sponsoris expiari, nec sanctitas & justitia, ejusque ἀπόδειξις demonstratio in מופת Paradigmatica quadam poena, (Esaj. LIII. 4.) nec veracitas, Genes. II. 17. sivit. Non aliter Deus peccata remittens justificari & sanctificari potuit. Exaltabitur Jehova exercituum propter judicium, & Deus sanctificabitur propter justitiam, Esaj. V. 16. Cognoscent gentes, quod ego Jehova, בהקדשי בכם לעיניכם quum sanctificatus fuero in vobis, in oculis vestris, Ezech. XXXVI. 23. Justificamur gratis &c. per redemptionem, quae est in Christo Jesu; quem Deus praestituit placamentum per fidem in sanguine ejus ad demonstrationem justitiae, Rom. III. 24. 25. Nam Princeps salutis, mortem gustare pro omnibus, & hac ratione per passiones consummari debuit, Hebr. II. 9. 10. Unde S. Paulus parvo & magno testificatus tus est Χριστὸν παθητὸν Christum passibilem & passum esse, Act. XXVI. 22.23. & Judaei ipsi passim תמיד המשיח משיח passiones Messiae commemorant. Qui etiam conciliaturi cum Prophetiis gloriosum suum Messiam, diversum ab eo, Messiam alterum, Josephi filium, confinxerunt.
units.tr: What was that humiliation [ταπεινωσις humiliatio], by which he humbled himself and became obedient to God unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil. 2:8)? It was the final step of his self-emptying, carried out chiefly during the last two days of his emptying. For although his humility shone forth through the whole of Christ's life, according to his own words, Learn of me, for I am meek and lowly [ταπεινος τῇ καρδίᾳ] in heart (Matt. 11:29), and although his whole life was nothing but suffering, poverty, unsettled condition, toil, weariness, hunger, thirst, a common and unremarkable way of living such as John the Baptist's, and fear of his enemies and flight from them, yet his deepest humiliation and his sufferings [τὰ πάθηματα] in the preeminent sense [κατ' ἐξοχὴν] revealed themselves in that final, fatal two days, which ended in his death, and in which especially the hour of the power of darkness came (Luke 22:53). For Jesus had to be humbled, to be brought low not in passing but even unto death, and that the death of the cross; because he had received from the Father the commandment to lay down his soul as the price of redemption (John 10:18; Matt. 10:28). It was fitting for him who was given as covenant of the people that he should lay down his soul as the price of satisfaction (Isa. 53:10). For the people of God, his peculiar treasure [סגולה], could not make a covenant with him except through a sacrifice (Ps. 50:5), and indeed of him whom God gave as High Priest and Apostle of our confession [ὁμολογίας] or stipulation (Heb. 3:1). For sin could be expiated only by the death of the sinner or of his vicarious surety, and neither the holiness and righteousness of God, nor its demonstration [ἀπόδειξις] in a certain paradigmatic punishment [מופת] (Isa. 53:4), nor his truthfulness (Gen. 2:17), would have allowed otherwise. Nor could God, in remitting sins, be justified and sanctified in any other way. The LORD of hosts shall be exalted in judgment, and God that is holy shall be sanctified in righteousness (Isa. 5:16). The heathen shall know that I am the LORD, when I shall be sanctified in you before their eyes [behiqqadeshi bakem] (Ezek. 36:23). Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus; whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness (Rom. 3:24-25). For the Captain of salvation had to taste death for all, and in this way was to be made perfect through sufferings (Heb. 2:9-10). Hence St. Paul witnessed to both small and great that Christ was suffering and passible [Χριστὸν παθητὸν] (Acts 26:22-23). The Jews themselves also constantly recall the sufferings of the Messiah [תמיד המשיח משיח]. Wishing to reconcile the Prophets with their glorious Messiah, they even invented another Messiah, different from him, the son of Joseph.

units.la: XIX. Sed funestum & nefastum illud biduum, in quod passionum Christi τὸ ἀκρον incidit, penitius lustremus. Ante omnia cum discipulis suis Pascha typicum comedit, ipse mox, ceu Agnus Dei, Pascha nostrum verum, pro nobis mactandus. Noverat enim ὅτι ἐγγὺς ὁ καιρὸς quod prope sit tempus suum, Matth. XXVI. 18. Ideo cum suis Pascha comedere gestivit. Primo ergo Azymorum die accesserunt discipuli ad Jesum, dicentes: Ubi vis praeparemus Pascha tecum manducandum, &c. ibid. v. 17. &c. Venit dies azymorum, ἐν ᾗ ἔδει θύεσθαι τὸ πάσχα quo oportebat mactari pascha, &c. Luc. XXII. 7. 8. &c. Ubi Lucas non obscure Judaeos perstringit, non comedentes Pascha ἡμέρᾳ, ἐν ᾗ ἔδει die, quo oportuit. Christus celebravit die XIV. Nisan, quo oportuit. Sed Judaei sequente die, traditione sua tempus celebrandi Paschatis corrumpentes. Plane id Evangelista Johannes innuit, qui tum cap. XIII. 1. Christum δείπνον convivium celebrasse πρὸ ἑορτῆς & πάσχα ante festum Paschatis, à Judaeis celebratum dicit; tum cap. XVIII. 28. non intrasse Judaeos in praetorium, ne contaminarentur, sed ut comederent Pascha, significat, innuens, eo die, quo Christus damnatus est, nondum Judaeos Pascha (non utique victimam Paschalem sequentis Pascha magnum diei, quae nuspiam simpliciter Pascha appellatur; neque bovem, vel armentum Paschale, secundo die edi solitum, quia instauratio Paschatis per armentum Paschale nondum eo tempore apud Judaeos usitata fuit) comedisse, sed comedere demum destinasse: tum cap. XIX. 14. Parasceven Paschatis fuisse, cum diceret Pilatus: Ecce Rex vester, testatur; cum parasceve Festi & ipsum Festum simul esse non potuerint: tum ibid. v. 31. diem eum, quo Judaei Pascha celebrarunt, diem Sabbathi fuisse innuit, appellans μεγάλην ἡμέραν σαββάτου magnum diem Sabbathi; propter Festum in eundem incidens. Cum enim apud Judaeos diversimode Νουμηνία constitui sueverit, secundum calculum vel Astronomicum, in die συνοδὸς seu conjunctionis luminarium, vel secundum φάσιν seu apparentiam Lunae, certis testimoniis, & indictione Senatus probatam, religiosi bis Pascha comedere sueverunt, & XIV. & XV. die Nisan; illo propter legem & συνοδον, hoc propter traditionem & φάσιν. Tempore igitur Passionis Christi Calendas mensis Nisan a Senatu constitutas fuisse in die φάσεως postridie conjunctionis, atque inde evenisse, ut & Christus, & cum eo alii, die XIV. Nisan legitime Pascha comederent, juxta luminarium συνοδον, & alii Senatus definitioni attendentes die XV. Nisan illud comederent, atque legitime etiam se id facere posse persuasi essent, plane probabile fit. Sic ergo Christus Pascha a primoribus Judaeorum celebratum anticipavit, ut non propterea pane fermentato usus fuerit. qui Graecorum error est. Paschali Agno manducato memoriam sui, veri Agni, jam jam
units.tr: XIX. But let us examine more closely that gloomy and ill-omened two-day period in which the height of Christ's sufferings fell. First of all, he ate the typical Passover with his disciples, soon to be himself slain for us as the Lamb of God, our true Passover. For he knew that the time was near [ὅτι ἐγγὺς ὁ καιρὸς] (Matt. 26:18), and therefore he eagerly wished to eat the Passover with his own. So on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, "Where do you want us to prepare the Passover for you to eat?" (ibid. v. 17, etc.). "The day of Unleavened Bread came, on which the Passover had to be sacrificed [ἐν ᾗ ἔδει θύεσθαι τὸ πάσχα]" (Luke 22:7-8, etc.). Here Luke plainly censures the Jews for not eating the Passover on the day on which it ought to be eaten. Christ celebrated it on the fourteenth of Nisan, as it ought to be. But the Jews, corrupting the time of celebrating the Passover by their own tradition, did so on the following day. The Evangelist John clearly hints at this. He says that Christ celebrated a supper [δείπνον] before the feast, and before the Passover celebrated by the Jews (John 13:1). He also indicates that the Jews did not enter the praetorium to avoid defilement, but so that they might eat the Passover (John 18:28). This implies that on the day on which Christ was condemned, the Jews had not yet eaten the Passover; not indeed the Passover lamb of the following day, which is never simply called the Passover, nor the bullock or herd-animal eaten on the second day, since the renewal of the Passover by means of a paschal herd-animal was not yet customary among the Jews at that time. Rather, they had only then decided to eat it. Again, in John 19:14 he testifies that it was the Preparation of the Passover, when Pilate said, "Behold your King." The preparation of a festival and the festival itself could not be the same day. Again, in verse 31 of the same chapter he implies that the day on which the Jews celebrated the Passover was the Sabbath day, calling it a great day of the Sabbath [μεγάλην ἡμέραν σαββάτου], because the feast fell on that day. For since among the Jews the new moon has been fixed in different ways, either by astronomical calculation on the day of conjunction [συνοδὸς] of the luminaries, or according to the appearance [φάσιν] of the moon, as attested by certain witnesses and approved by a proclamation of the Senate, the pious used to eat the Passover twice, on the fourteenth and the fifteenth of Nisan: on the one, on account of the law and the conjunction, on the other, on account of tradition and the appearance. It is therefore quite probable that at the time of Christ's Passion the first day of the month Nisan, fixed by the Senate, fell on the day after the conjunction, on the day of the appearance. From this it came about that Christ and others legitimately ate the Passover on the fourteenth of Nisan, according to the conjunction of the luminaries, while others, following the decision of the Senate, ate it on the fifteenth of Nisan, being persuaded that they too could legitimately do so. So Christ anticipated the Passover celebrated by the leaders of the Jews, and therefore did not use leavened bread, which was an error of the Greeks. Having eaten the paschal lamb, he instituted, in the Eucharistic Supper, which is added to the Passover, a most devout remembrance of himself, the true Lamb, who was now just about to be slain (Matt. 26:26, etc.; Mark 14:22, etc.; Luke 22:19, etc.), of which more in its place.

units.la: mactandi, in Coena Eucharistica, Paschati succenturiata, religiosissimè recolendam instituit, Matth. XXVI. 26. &c. Marc. XIV. 22. &c. Luc. XXII. 29. &c. de quo in loco. Finita ea Jesus pedes discipulorum suorum abluit, Joh. XIII. 2. &c. significans, accepisse se potestatem purificandi, hoc est, justificandi & sanctificandi, quos velit. Homo enim per peccatum patris & suum impurus est, communione & sanctificatione Dei indignus; neque purus fieri poterit, nisi ab eo, qui peccatorem per justitiam suam lavare, sibi unire, justificare & sanctificare potest. Simul discipulos suos docere voluit, quam erga se invicem charitatem exercere debeant; ne alii aliis dominari contendant; Sed ut potius aliis in charitate serviant. Mox discipulos, praedictis fatis suis nimium moerentes, eximie consolatur ibid. XIV. 1-f. similitudinem vitis & palmitum, aliaque mysterio & consolatione plenissima recitat, ibid. XV. 1-27. adversus tristitiam variis promissionum ἡλα-κτηείοις eos demulcet & munit, ib. XVI. 1-f. & oratione divinissima gloriae suae revelationem, Apostolorum & credentium omnium salutem, & in mundo ἀφθαρσίαν Deo Patri suo, commendat, XVII. 1-f.
units.tr: When that was finished, Jesus washed the feet of his disciples (John 13:2, etc.), signifying that he had received the power to purify, that is, to justify and sanctify, whomever he wills. For man through the sin of his father and his own is unclean and unworthy of communion with God and of his sanctification, nor can he be made clean except by him who can wash the sinner by his righteousness, unite him to himself, justify and sanctify him. At the same time he wished to teach his disciples what love they ought to show to one another, so that they would not strive to lord it over one another, but would rather serve one another in love. Soon he greatly comforted his disciples, who were excessively grieved by his foretold fate, with the likeness of the vine and the branches, and recited other words full of mystery and consolation (ibid. 14:1-end; 15:1-27). He soothed and fortified them against sadness with various promises of comfort (ibid. 16:1-end), and in a most divine prayer he commended to God the Father the revelation of his glory, the salvation of the Apostles and of all believers, and their incorruptibility in the world (17:1-end).

units.la: XX. Passio ipsa emortualis subsecuta ab anxietate illa summa, quam in horto Gethsemane sustinuit, initium cepit. Assumpto enim Petro, & duobus filiis Zebedaei, quos olim in monte magnificentiae suae spectatores habuit, Matth. XVII 1.2. Pet. I. 16. coepit λυπεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν tristari & gravissime angi, Matth. XXVI. 37. imo & ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι expavescere, Marc. XIV. 33. esse ἐν ἀγωνίᾳ lucta, & interno quodam mentis certamine; imo etiam sudare sudorem ὥσπερ θρόμβους αἵματος grumorum instar sanguinis, non corpus duntaxat humectantium, sed fluvii instar in terram descendentium, Luc. XXII. 44. Sanguinem sudare vinum rubrum largius bibentes, tenuem & languidiorem sanguinem habentes, & a vipera, haemorrhois dicta, morsos ajunt. Sed nil tale in Christo, cui ardor precandi, & antiquus ille serpens, calcem ejus admordere jam incipiens, sudorem sanguineum spissum adeo expressit. In tanta enim anxietate in haec etiam verba erupit: ΠΕΡΙΛΥΠΟΣ ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου, undique tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem, Matth. XXVI. 38. Tristitiae, anxietatis, pavoris, sudoris hujus causa non fuit metus qualiscunque mortis naturalis, quam multi infideles contempserunt, fideles promiscuè sine horrore sustinuerunt, Martyres & Callinici ovantes exceperunt; Sed supernaturalis, quam peccata in eum ab irato & justo judice Deo impacta, totius mundi reatus, ira Dei, execratio Legis, Diaboli infestatio gravem nimiùm nimiùmque effecerunt. Hinc illae sanguineae lachrymae, hinc ille עמל נפש la-bor animae, cujus fructus esse שבע satietas debuit, Esaj. LIII. 11. Effusus sum ut aqua, sor meum factum est ut cera, liquefactum in medio viscerum, Psal. XXII. 15. Cor meum dereliquit me, XL. 13. Tuli אימות terrores tuos. Deficio. Super me transierunt הרונך excandescentia tua. Terrores tui consternarunt me. Circumdederunt me sicut aqua toto die, &c. ibid. LXXXVIII. 16. 17. 18. Adeò verò ἀγωνία & tristitia haec invaquòd abolenda sit execratio, abnegent. Ex quibus ad liquidum perducitur, auctorem benedictionis Christum, qui pro nobis κατάρα maledictio factus est, debuisse per suspensionem è ligno, &, cùm Romanis, à quibus damnatus est, non alia in usu fuerit, crucifixionem maledictionem portare & finire, ut justitiæ compotes fieremus. Causa igitur crucifixionis Christi equidem fuit, ut tam acerbo, horrendo, & contumeliosomortis genere insigni effectus maledictionis in ipso spectaretur, atque ita revera peccatum fieret. Sed bonum nostrum hoc est, quòd eum non tantùm maledictionem tulisse, sed etiam abstulisse, & benedictiones omnes nobis impetravisse novimus. Denique cùm crux servile Romanorum supplicium fuerit, Christus servi formam assumens, & contemptibilis in omnium oculis, cui nec forma, nec decor fuit, Esaj. LIII.2. servile supplicium sustinere dedignatus non est. Unde Lucianus in Palæstina crucifixum Christum falsè irrisit.
units.tr: XX. The death itself began with that extreme anguish which he endured in the garden of Gethsemane. For, taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, whom he had once had as witnesses of his glory on the mountain (Matt. 17:1-2; 2 Pet. 1:16), he began to be grieved and troubled [λυπεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν], to be very sorrowful and sorely distressed (Matt. 26:37); indeed also to be amazed [ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι], to be dismayed (Mark 14:33); to be in agony [ἐν ἀγωνίᾳ], wrestling in an inward conflict of mind; indeed even to sweat drops of blood [ὥσπερ θρόμβους αἵματος], like clots of blood, not merely wetting the body but falling to the ground in streams (Luke 22:44). They say that those who drink red wine too freely, having thin and weak blood, sweat blood and are bitten by a viper called the haemorrhois. But nothing of the kind was in Christ. The intensity of his prayer, together with that ancient serpent, now beginning to bite at his heel, forced out a thick, bloody sweat. For in such anguish he burst out with these words: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death" [ΠΕΡΙΛΥΠΟΣ ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου] (Matt. 26:38). The cause of this sorrow, anguish, dread and sweat was not the fear of any ordinary natural death, which many unbelievers have despised and believers have endured without horror, and which martyrs and the Callinici received with exultation. It was a supernatural dread, which the sins laid upon him by the angry and just Judge God, the guilt of the whole world, the wrath of God, the curse of the Law, and the assault of the Devil made exceedingly grievous. Hence those bloody tears, hence that "labour of the soul" [עמל נפש], whose fruit ought to have been "satisfaction" [שבע] (Isa. 53:11). "I am poured out like water, my heart is become like wax, melted in the midst of my bowels" (Ps. 22:15). "My heart has forsaken me" (Ps. 40:13). "I have borne your terrors [אימות]. I faint. Your fierce wrath [חרון] has passed over me. Your terrors have cut me off. They surround me like water all the day long," etc. (Ps. 88:16-18). So truly was this agony and sorrow intended to bring about the abolition of the curse, that they deny it. From these things it is made clear that Christ, the author of blessing, who was made a curse [κατάρα] for us, had to bear and end the curse, by hanging on a tree, so that we might be made partakers of righteousness. And since crucifixion was not in use among the Romans, by whom he was condemned, otherwise than as a punishment, the cause of his crucifixion was that in so cruel, horrible and shameful a kind of death the effect of the curse might be seen in him, and so he might in truth become sin. But we know that this is our good: he not only bore the curse but also took it away, and obtained for us all blessings. Finally, since the cross was the servile punishment of the Romans, Christ, taking the form of a servant, and despised in the eyes of all, who had neither form nor comeliness (Isa. 53:2), did not disdain to undergo a servile punishment. Hence Lucian rightly mocked the crucified Christ in Palestine.

units.la: Damnatus à Pontio Pilato Jesus præcedentium passionum animæ & corporis omnium colophonem sustinuit, verè vir dolorum, Esaj. LIII.3. Exuta tunica coccinea, propriisque vestibus indutus, reliæta forte capiti corona spinea, è prætorio deductus est, primùm quidem cruentis pallibus per urbem, deinde ex ea porro usque ad montem calvariæ militari manu per arduam viam trusus, quæ verbera, quas sannas perpessus sit, divinare licet. Propriam crucem bajulare coactus est, quia nec Judæi, quibus moriens in ligno maledictus censebatur, nec Romani, qui crucis gestationem ipsi cruciario injungere sueverunt, suppetias ferre dignati sunt. Unus Simon Cyrenæus, Pater Alexandri & Rufi, forte e discipulis Christi, quem milites ipsi ad ferendam Christi lassi, & ob flagellationem infirmi angariaverunt, sive solus, sive unà cum Christo humeros cruci supponens, opem tulit. Unà cum Christo abducti sunt duo λῃσταί, latrones, Luc. XXIII.32, atque ita ille defectoribus annumeratus est. Esaj. LIII.12. Ad Golgotha, seu calvariæ locum ubi perventum est, Jesus vini myrrhati cum felle mixti, sive ex consuetudine, sive potius malo animo (nam Judæi ad supplicia raptis vinum cum grano thuris propinarunt; hi pro vino acetum, pro thure benigni saporis amarorem myrrhæ) potus ei præbitus est, sed ob amarorem ab eo non gustatus. Inde vestibus suis exutus, nudatúsque totus, ne tectis quidem verendis partibus, uti plerisque veteribus visum est, in crucem actus est, die non Jovis, uti Chronologi nonnulli recentiores, sed Veneris, quippe parasceve Paschatis, seu Sabbathi magni (Joh. XIX. 14.31.) ejusque diei ὥρα ὡσεὶ ἕκτη hora quasi sexta, ibid. 14. Tum enim Pilatus consedit in tribunali, in loco, qui dicitur Lithostroton, Hebraicè Gabbatha. Cum quo non pugnat Marcus dicens Cap. XV.25. ἦν δὲ ὥρα τρίτη, καὶ ἐσταύρωσαν αὐτόν. Erat autem hora tertia & crucifixerunt eum. Hoc enim sibi vult, inde ab hora tertia id eos egisse, ut eum crucifigerent. Nisi forte vel Marcus per horam intellexit vigiliam seu quadrantem diei; vel Johannes per sextam
units.tr: Condemned by Pontius Pilate, Jesus underwent the culmination of all the previous sufferings of soul and body, truly a man of sorrows (Isa. 53:3). His scarlet robe was taken off, he was clothed in his own garments, and with a crown of thorns, perhaps still on his head, he was led out of the praetorium. First he was driven through the city in bloodied garments, and then from there up the steep road to the hill of Calvary, pushed on by a military hand. What blows and mockeries he suffered may be imagined. He was compelled to carry his own cross, since neither the Jews, who considered him cursed as one dying on a tree, nor the Romans, who were accustomed to impose the carrying of the cross on the condemned man himself, deigned to give help. Only Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, perhaps one of Christ's disciples, whom the soldiers forced to carry it because Christ was weary and weak from the scourging, gave aid, whether alone or by placing his shoulders under the cross together with Christ. Together with Christ two robbers [λῃσταί], thieves, were led away (Luke 23:32), and so he was counted among the transgressors (Isa. 53:12). When they reached the place of Golgotha, or the hill of the skull, Jesus was offered a drink of wine mingled with myrrh and gall, either by custom or rather with malicious intent (for the Jews gave wine with a grain of frankincense to those led to punishment; these gave vinegar in place of wine, and the bitterness of myrrh in place of the pleasant flavour of incense). He did not taste it because of its bitterness. Then, stripped of his garments and wholly naked, not even his private parts covered, as many of the ancients thought, he was nailed to the cross, on a day that was not Thursday, as some more recent chronologers hold, but Friday, namely the Preparation of the Passover, or the great Sabbath (John 19:14, 31), and at the hour "about the sixth hour" (ὥρα ὡσεὶ ἕκτη), John 19:14. For then Pilate sat down on the judgment seat, in the place called the Pavement, in Hebrew Gabbatha. Mark does not contradict this when he says in chapter 15:25: "And it was the third hour, and they crucified him" (ἦν δὲ ὥρα τρίτη, καὶ ἐσταύρωσαν αὐτόν). For this means that from the third hour they were busy with the crucifixion. Unless perhaps Mark understood the hour as a watch or quarter of the day, or John, by the sixth,

units.la: non Parasceves Judaicæ, sed Christianæ, quæ prima est Judaicæ, innuitque adeò, hora hac sexta Christum à Pilato pro tribunali damnatum, & inde Christum abductum demum hora tertia Judaica, seu nostra & Romanorum crucifixum esse. quæ posterior Augustini conciliatio est. Sed omnino hora sexta Judaica, & duodecima Romana, seu nostrae crucifixus videtur, quia Matthæus etiam cap. XXVII.45. scribit, à sexta hora ad nonam usque tenebras fuisse super totam terram. Eadem verò hora Christum crucifixum; & paulò post tenebras consecutas esse, verisimile est. Sed de tempore eo quicquid sit, certè Christus actus est in crucem, & quidem non improprie dictam, quaelis patibulum vel futura est; sed proprie dictam, Romanis eo tempore usitatam, & à patibulo & furca sic distinctam, quòd literam T referebat, sicut furca seu patibulum vetus literam Y nempe stipitis superius bifidi; & patibulum recentius Constantini M. literæ Græcanicæ Π. In veteri Romana clavis figi cruciarius solebat: in patibulo suspensus reste strangulatur. Componebatur ex duobus lignis, stipite arrectario, qui malo in navi respondebat; & ligno transverso antennæ malo navis alligatæ simili. Prior magnam partem obtegebatur corpore cruciarii, alteri brachia extenta alligabantur, vel affigebantur. Pedes cruciarii à terra tribus vel quatuor pedibus aberant. Sunt, qui corpori sustinendo medianum lignum, cui cruciarius insideret, & ὑποπέδιον seu suppedaneum lignum inserviisse putant. Sed iis opus fuisse alii negant, quia nervosæ adeò sunt hominis manus, ut periculum non sit, ne mole corporis rumpantur; inprimis ubi moris erat, cadavera de cruce tollere. Sed hæc antiquitatum ruspatoribus relinquamus.
units.tr: meant not the Jewish Preparation but the Christian one, which is the first of the Jewish one; and he implies that Christ was condemned by Pilate from the judgment seat at the sixth hour, and then led away and at last crucified at the third Jewish hour, that is, our and the Romans' hour. This is the later reconciliation of Augustine. But it seems altogether that Christ was crucified at the sixth Jewish hour, which is the twelfth Roman or our hour, because Matthew also writes in chapter 27:45 that from the sixth hour to the ninth there was darkness over the whole earth. It is likely that Christ was crucified at that same hour, and that the darkness followed shortly afterwards. But whatever the time, certainly Christ was put on the cross, and indeed not what is improperly called a cross, such as a stake or gibbet, but properly so called, the form then in use among the Romans, distinguished from a stake or fork in that it resembled the letter T, as the old fork or gibbet resembled the letter Y, namely a stake bifid at the top; and the later gibbet, of Constantine the Great, resembled the Greek letter Π. In the old Roman manner the condemned man was accustomed to be fixed with nails; on a gibbet he was strangled by a rope suspended. The cross was composed of two pieces of wood: an upright stake, which in a ship corresponded to the mast, and a transverse beam, like the yard tied to the mast of a ship. The upright part was largely covered by the body of the condemned man, and his outstretched arms were tied or nailed to the other. The feet of the condemned were three or four feet from the ground. Some think that a middle piece of wood, on which the condemned man might sit, or a footrest [ὑποπέδιον, suppedaneum], served to support the body. But others deny that these were needed, since human hands are so sinewy that there is no danger of their being torn by the weight of the body, especially where it was the custom to take the bodies down from the cross. But let us leave these matters to the antiquarians.

units.la: XXVI. Christo in cruce pendente ea contigerunt, quæ commemoranda inprimis sunt. Eorum alia mortem ejus antecesserunt, alia consecuta sunt. Quæ præcesserunt; alia alii Christo fecerunt: alia à Deo ad glorificandum Christum facta sunt. Quæ Christo alii fecerunt, ab inimico animo proiecta sunt. Eò quadruplex ignominia pertinet. Nam & cum eo crucifixi sunt duo latrones, imò in medio eorum Christus, seu facinorosior, Matth. XXVII.38. Marc. XV.28. Esaj. LIII.12. & Pilatus in tabula capiti ejus affixa scribi tribus linguis jussit causam supplicii, quòd Regnum apud Judæos affectasset, Joh. XIX.19. & milites vestes ejus, vivente & vidente eo forte, in partes quaternas; quia vestes Judæorum partes quatuor, diviserunt, non dissecta tamen tunica ἀπράφῳ inconsutili, ita dicta, quia non habuit ῥαφίδα, seu πρόσλω ἰστὸν bulam Matth. XXVII.35. Psal. XXII.19. & utrique Judæi pariter & gentiles præstereuntes, Sacerdotes, milites, latrones, vel unus saltem è latronibus (nam alter Christo enixè se commendavit) non uno modo eum subsannarunt, in eò conspirantes omnes, ut Salvator aliorum, Rex, Filius Dei; Christus, se ipsum salvet, & de cruce descendat, quasi de cruce descendenti creditum fuissent, qui ex morte resurgenti non crediderunt. Humanitatis speciem præbuisse videtur, qui clamante Christo, se sitire, accurrens sponspongiam aceto immersam calamo involvit, ut eo in sublime elevato, inde Christus liquorem exugeret, Matth.XXVII.48. Marc.XV.36. Joh. XIX.29. quo postremo loco spongiam hyssopo circumpositam fuisse dicitur, quia in summo calamo esse fasciculus hyssopi, & ei spongia imponi potuit. Factum id more castrensi Romanorum, quo honestiores etiam in acri siti & calore, acetum aquæ permixtum, cui posca nomen (à πίνω poto) biberunt. qui mos etiam obtinuisse apud morituros in cruce videtur, quia ibidem dicitur, vas aceto plenum fuisse ad manum. Jam olim de se Christus Psalm. LXIX.22. Dederunt in escam meam fel, & in siti mea propinarunt mihi acetum.
units.tr: XXVI. While Christ hung on the cross, things happened which deserve especially to be recorded. Some of them preceded his death, others followed it. Of those that preceded, some were done to Christ by others, and some were done by God to glorify Christ. Those done to Christ by others were carried out with hostile mind. To these belongs a fourfold ignominy. For two robbers were crucified with him, indeed Christ was in the midst of them, as if the more wicked one (Matt. 27:38; Mark 15:28; Isa. 53:12). Pilate ordered the cause of his punishment, that he had aspired to kingship among the Jews, to be written in three languages on a tablet affixed above his head (John 19:19). The soldiers, while he was perhaps still living and watching, divided his garments into four parts, since the garments of the Jews are divided into four parts; but they did not cut the tunic, which was seamless [ἄραφος], woven without seam, so called because it had no seam (Matt. 27:35; Ps. 22:19). And both the Jews and the Gentiles who passed by, priests, soldiers, robbers, or at least one of the robbers (for the other commended himself earnestly to Christ), mocked him in more than one way, all conspiring in this: "Saviour of others, King, Son of God; let him save himself and come down from the cross." As if they would have believed in him who was coming down from the cross, when they did not believe in him rising from death. He seems to have shown a kind of humanity, when Christ cried out that he was thirsty, one who ran up, dipped a sponge in vinegar and wrapped it around a reed, so that Christ might suck up the liquid when it was lifted high (Matt. 27:48; Mark 15:36; John 19:29). In the last passage it is said that the sponge was placed around a hyssop, because a bundle of hyssop was at the top of the reed and the sponge could be placed on it. This was done in the military manner of the Romans, by whom even the more respectable drank vinegar mixed with water in fierce thirst and heat, called posca (from πίνω, to drink). This custom also seems to have been in use among those about to die on the cross, since it is said there that a vessel full of vinegar was at hand. Long ago Christ himself said of himself: They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink (Ps. 69:22).

units.la: XXVII. A Christo in cruce dicta septuplicia sunt.
units.tr: XXVII. The seven sayings of Christ on the cross.

units.la: Nam & oravit pro inimicis: & latroni Paradisum promisit: & matrem allocutus, eandem Johanni commendavit: & se a Deo desertum questus est: & potum popo-scit, & eo sumpto consummationem omnium factam testatus est: & Domino spiritum suum commendavit. Pro inimicis crucifigentibus eum oravit his verbis: Πάτερ ἄφες αὐτοῖς· ου γὰρ οἴδασι τι ποιῶσι. Pater remitte iis. Non enim nescunt, quid faciant, Luc. XXIII.34. Ita non aperuit os suum adversus eos, qui contumeliis & violentia eum vexarunt; sed oravit pro defectoribus, Esaj.LIII.12. pulcherrima homologia & oratione testatus est bonam conscientiam & charitatem, per quam se pro ovibus perditis, quarum causa etiam cum infernalibus anxietatibus luctatus est, obtulit. Habuit enim etiam inter crucifigentes, quorum peccatum & ignorantiam in se suscepit, qui poenitentiam egerunt, Act.III.17. XIII.27. qui ipsi dati fuerunt, pro qualibus diserte oravit, Joh.XVII.9. Quomodo etiam Saul persecutor licet, ipsi datus, & misericordiam consecutus est, quia ἀγνοῶν ignorans peccavit I.Tim. I.13. Non defuerunt certe inter crucifigentes, qui nec Filium Dei, nec procuratorem salutis generis humani eum esse noverant, non subsannaturi alias, nedum crucifixuri eum. Ideo ceu verus Pontifex obtulit ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀγνοημάτων pro ignorantiis populi, Hebr.IX.7. & ejus exemplo pro hostibus suis ignorantibus Stephanus Act.VII.60. & Hieronymo lib. de Scriptor. Eccles. teste, Jacobus, frater Domini, praeceps datus de pinna Templi, orarunt; omnesque pro persequentibus nos orare, Luc.VI.28. jubemur. Latroni sic Christum, ceu Regem adoranti: Memor mei esto, cum veneris in Regnum tuum, his verbis Paradisum promisit: Amen dico tibi; hodie (non cum hoc dico, uti cavillantur nonnulli, quia eo die eum locutum esse, facto testatus est, ut verbis opus non fuerit) mecum eris in Paradiso, ibid.XXIII.42.43. Quibus verbis suum esse, Paradisum, Regnum (quod suis διέταξε disposuit, ibid. XXII.29.) dare, cui velit; & receptum se ilico iri in Paradisum, tertium Coelum, testatus est. Voluit enim, ut ubi ipse est, etiam sint illi, quos Pater illi dedit, Joh.XVII.24. Matrem suam unà cum Johanne, Maria Magdalena, Maria Salomæ, filia Cleopæ, ad crucem adstantem conspicatus, sic allocutus est: Γύναι Mulier (quod honoris nomen censeri potest, quia apud Hebræos אשה virtus) ...
units.tr: For he prayed for his enemies, promised Paradise to the thief, addressed his mother and commended her to John, complained that he had been forsaken by God, asked for a drink, and when he had taken it testified that all was accomplished, and commended his spirit to the Lord. He prayed for those who crucified him in these words: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing" [Πάτερ ἄφες αὐτοῖς· ου γὰρ οἴδασι τι ποιῶσι]. Father, forgive them. For they do not know what they do, Luke 23.34. Thus he did not open his mouth against those who vexed him with insults and violence, but he prayed for the transgressors, Isa. 53.12. With a most beautiful confession and prayer he showed his good conscience and charity, by which he offered himself for the lost sheep, on whose account he also struggled with infernal anguish. For among those who crucified him, whose sin and ignorance he took upon himself, there were some who repented, Acts 3.17; 13.27, and who were themselves given to him, for whom he expressly prayed, John 17.9. So also Saul, though a persecutor, was given to him and obtained mercy, because he sinned in ignorance, 1 Tim. 1.13. Certainly there were among those who crucified him some who did not know that he was the Son of God or the author of salvation for the human race, and who would not otherwise have mocked him, much less crucified him. Therefore, as a true High Priest, he offered for the ignorance of the people [ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀγνοημάτων], Heb. 9.7, and following his example Stephen prayed for his ignorant enemies, Acts 7.60; and, as Jerome testifies in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, James the brother of the Lord, thrown headlong from the pinnacle of the Temple, prayed too. And we are all commanded to pray for those who persecute us, Luke 6.28. To the thief, who addressed Christ as King, saying, "Remember me when you come into your kingdom," he promised Paradise in these words: Truly I say to you, today (not, as some sneer, because on that day he showed by the fact that he spoke, so that words were not needed) you will be with me in Paradise, ibid. 23.42, 43. By these words he testified that Paradise is his, and that the kingdom (which his Father has appointed to him, ibid. 22.29) is his to give to whomever he wills, and that the thief would at once be received into Paradise, the third heaven. For he willed that where he himself is, there also should be those whom the Father has given him, John 17.24. Seeing his mother standing by the cross together with John, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the wife of Clopas, he addressed them thus: "Woman" [Γύναι] (which may be counted a title of honour, since among the Hebrews אשה signifies strength and vigour, and in the Talmud signifies a matron, the mother of a family; and among the Greeks γυνή also signifies Lady [Κυρία]), "behold your son," meaning the disciple John; and to the disciple John: "behold your mother" [ἰδοὺ ἡ μήτηρ σου], whom I commend to your care, John 19.26, 27. From that hour he took her into his own [εἰς τὰ ἴδια], into his own home. Then especially we must think that the sword pierced the soul of Mary, when she saw her Son as a sign that would be spoken against and set for the fall (Luke 2.34, 35).

units.la: tem & strenuitatem, ac in Thalmude matronam, matrem familias notat: & apud Græcos γυνή etiam Κυρία notat) ecce filius tuus, discipulus Johannes; & Johannem discipulum: ἰδοὺ ἡ μήτηρ σου ecce mater tua, quam curæ tuæ commendo, Joh.XIX.26.27. Ex quo tempore eam εἰς τὰ ἴδια in propria, domum suam, recepit. Tum maximè gladius animam Mariæ transiisse putandus est, quando Filium suum σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον signum contradictum, & in scandalum datum (Luc.II.34.35.) spectavit. Post silentium aliquod φωνῇ μεγάλῃ voce magna se à Deo desertum his verbis queritur: אלי אלי למה שבקתני, ἠλί ἠλί λαμὰ σαβαχθανί, hoc est, Θεέ μου, Θεέ μου, ἵνατί με ἐγκατέλιπες; Deus mi, Deus mi, quare deseruisti me? Matth.XXVII.46. Marc.XV.34. Petita verba sunt ex Psal.XXII.2. pro עזבתני substituto verbo שבקתני. Hæc oratio אלי rugitus ab ipso Christo ibidem appellatur, propter τὸ πρὸς ἀνάπνευσιν. ..
units.tr: After a silence he cried with a loud voice [φωνῇ μεγάλῃ], complaining in these words that he was forsaken by God: אלי אלי למה שבקתני, ἠλί ἠλί λαμὰ σαβαχθανί, that is, Θεέ μου, Θεέ μου, ἵνατί με ἐγκατέλιπες; My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Matt. 27.46; Mark 15.34. The words are taken from Psalm 22.2, with the verb שבקתני substituted for עזבתני. This cry, אלי, is called by Christ himself a roar [rugitus] in the same place, because of the breath it required [propter τὸ πρὸς ἀνάπνευσιν].

units.la: Sed verba illa: Quare deseruisti me? sunt velut rugitus naturæ, pondus iræ Divinæ, & communionis Dei occultatæ sustinentis; proin summam infirmitatem, horrorem, dolorem, tristitiam animi significant.
units.tr: But those words, Why have you forsaken me?, are like the cry of nature, bearing the weight of divine wrath and of God's hidden withdrawal from communion; therefore they express the utmost weakness, horror, pain, and sadness of soul.

units.la: {a} Alia, eaque septuplicia à Christo in cruce dicta sunt. & quòd brevi ab quem sibi unitum intimè συναγωνίζεσθαι noverat, liberandus & gloria coronandus sit: tum quia in omnibus tentari similiter debuit, excepto peccato, Hebr.IV.15. cum desperatio peccatum sit: tum quia peccata non sua, sed aliena, sed absque peccato, luebat: tum quia per rugitum & querimoniam hanc non ergo Deum diffidentiam ullam, sed verum dolorem & cruciatum, quem in cruce sustinuit, exprimere voluit. Ac licèt etiam desertio hæc Christi ut damnati, & peccata nostra luentis fuerit, tamen cum desperatione conjuncta esse non debuit, quia pœna peccati, quam damnatus aliquis luit, desperationem essentialiter non includit, sed per accidens, cùm exantlari & finiri illa non potest. qualis est damnatorum eorum, qui meri homines sunt. Post hæc Jesus de siti quæstus dixit: Διψῶ sitio, Joh.XIX.28. In siti mea potarunt me aceto, Psal.LXIX.22. Voluit hæc profiteri, ut occasionem præbendi sibi aceti daret, præscius, quo potu se refecturi essent. Sumto aceto consummationem omnium factam testatus, dixit: Τετέλεσται consummatum est, Joh.XIX.30. significans, agonem Christi finitum, & impleta esse omnia, quæ ipsi ut Sponsori & Sacerdoti patienda erant, ut damnaretur peccatum, & justitia adduceretur, simulque Deus peccata condonans, & vitam æternam donans sanctificaretur. Mox igitur denuo φωνὴ μεγάλη κράξας, φωνήσας voce magna clamans, dixit: Pater, in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum, Matth.XXVII.50. Luc.XXIII.46. Quæ verba etiam Psal.XXXI.6. extant. Declamatis his verbis, παρέδωκε τὸ πνεῦμα reddidit spiritum, ibid. Matth.& Luc. Expirantis clamor ille, magnus virium naturæ ejus humanæ residuarum argumentum, ponere Christum spiritum suum, non ei ab aliis auferri (Joh.X.18.) probavit. Idque admiratus vehementer centurio dixit: Verè hic homo Filius Dei erat, Marc. XV.39. & omnis turba, quæ simul ad hoc spectaculum accesserat, spectans quæ facta fuerant, tundens pectora sua, revertebatur, Luc.XXIII.47. 48. Præter clamorem eum sponte ponentis animam argumentum etiam illud fuit, quòd crucifixi sæpe biduum, triduum supervixerunt; ac plurimum fame sola mortui sunt. Quibus verò lenta adeò morte defungi displicebat, iis crura fracta sunt. Quem morem etiam Judæi amplexi sunt, quia suspensos ante Solis occasum de ligno sublatos sepeliri oportuit. Sed Christus oravit Deum, ut eripiat animam suam à gladio & יחידתי unicam suam à manu canis, Psal. XXII.21. quia gladio occidi, vel crura sua à cane vel homine impuro frangi noluit. Ideo citius mortuus est.
units.tr: {a} Other sayings of Christ on the cross, seven in number, are also recorded. He said that he was to be delivered soon, since he knew that the one united to him most intimately was struggling together with him [συναγωνίζεσθαι], and crowned with glory; then, because he had to be tempted in all things like us, apart from sin, Heb. 4.15, since despair is sin; then because he bore the sins not his own but of others, and yet was without sin; then because by this cry and complaint he willed to express not any diffidence in God but the true pain and torment which he endured on the cross. And although this desertion of Christ was that of one condemned and paying for our sins, yet it ought not to have been joined with despair, because the punishment of sin which a condemned person suffers does not essentially include despair, but only by accident, when it cannot be endured and brought to an end. Such is the case of those condemned who are mere men. After this Jesus, complaining of thirst, said: I thirst [Διψῶ], John 19.28. "In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink," Psalm 69.22. He willed to declare this in order to give them an occasion of offering him vinegar, foreknowing with what drink they would refresh him. When he had taken the vinegar and testified that all was accomplished, he said: It is finished [Τετέλεσται], John 19.30, signifying that the contest of Christ was finished, and that all the things that had to be suffered by him as Surety and Priest were fulfilled, so that sin was condemned, righteousness was brought in, and God, forgiving sins and granting eternal life, was at the same time sanctified. Soon afterwards, therefore, crying again with a loud voice [φωνὴ μεγάλη κράξας, φωνήσας], he said: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit, Matt. 27.50; Luke 23.46. These words also occur in Psalm 31.6. Having uttered these words, he gave up the spirit [παρέδωκε τὸ πνεῦμα], ibid., Matthew and Luke. That loud cry of one dying, a proof of the strength still remaining in his human nature, showed that Christ laid down his spirit of his own accord and was not deprived of it by others (John 10.18). Greatly astonished at this, the centurion said: Truly this man was the Son of God, Mark 15.39; and the whole crowd that had gathered to see this spectacle, beholding what had been done, returned beating their breasts, Luke 23.47, 48. Besides that cry of one who lays down his life of his own will, there was also this proof: crucified men often survived two or three days, and most died of hunger alone. But for those to whom so slow a death was distasteful, their legs were broken. The Jews too adopted this custom, because bodies hanged had to be taken down from the wood and buried before sunset. But Christ prayed God to deliver his soul from the sword and his only one from the hand of the dog, Psalm 22.21, because he was unwilling to be killed by the sword, or to have his legs broken by a dog or an unclean man. Therefore he died more quickly.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Singulare quid etiam Deus Pater, Christo in cruce pendente, ad glorificandum Filium suum fecit. Nam cùm fuisset hora sexta, σκότος ἐγένετο ἐφ' ὅλην τὴν γῆν, tenebræ factæ sunt super universam terram, usque ad horam nonam, Marc.XV.33. Similiter Matthæus cap.XXVII.45. At Lucas: Ἦν ὡσεὶ ὥρα ἕκτη, Erat quasi hora sexta, & tenebræ factæ sunt, cap.XXIII.44. Ita enim prædictum est. Faciam occidere Solem in meridie, & tenebras inducam super terram, Amos.VIII.9 Sol mutabitur in tenebras, Joel.II.31. Epistola
units.tr: God the Father also did something singular while Christ hung on the cross, to glorify his Son. For when it was the sixth hour, "there was darkness over the whole earth" [σκότος ἐγένετο ἐφ' ὅλην τὴν γῆν], "and darkness fell over all the land until the ninth hour," Mark 15:33. Matthew 27:45 is similar. Luke says, "It was about the sixth hour" [Ἦν ὡσεὶ ὥρα ἕκτη], "and there was darkness," 23:44. For this had been foretold: "I will make the sun go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in broad daylight," Amos 8:9; "The sun shall be turned into darkness," Joel 2:31. Epistle

units.la: Dionysii Areopagitæ ad Polycarpum Apollophanem tenebras illas totum orbem obscuraße, & eas sibi & Aristophani Heliopoli in Ægypto visas esse, testis est. Quin & visa hac eclipsi dixisse Dionysium: ἢ τὸ θεῖον πάσχει, ἢ τῷ πάσχοντι συμπάσχει Aut Numen patitur, aut patienti compatitur, Suidas author est. Sed Dionysii Epistolæ dubiæ fidei cùm sint, nihil ex iis decidi potest. Nihilominus Tertullianus Apolog.c.21. commemorat, in Archivis Romanis prodigiosam hanc Solis eclipsin consignatam reperiri. Etiam Phlegon Olymp.Chron. lib.XIII. Olympiade CCII. ἐκλείψιν ἡλίου μεγίστην eclipsin Solis maximam, & terræ motum in Bithynia factum commemorat. Eandem autem à Phlegonte & Evangelistis historiam notari, indicio est, quòd utraque in eundem annum, eandem horam sextam incidit. Etiam Thallum Histor. lib.III. eandem eclipsin notasse, insignis temporum metator Africanus prodidit. Quin & novissima Sinensis historia Hadriani Gressonii, Sinenses in rerum suarum monumentis ad id ipsum tempus Solare deliquium contra naturæ ordinem adnotasse, testis est. Ut verè tenebras factas ἐφ' ὅλῳ γῆν super totam terram, Marcus dixerit. Nam de sola Judæa quomodo id intelligamus? De eo quicquid fit, prodigiosa omnino eclipsis fuit, quia tempore Paschatis, sive Luna XV. ἡ συζυγία, at XIV. ἡ φάσιν; quando plenilunium, & Luna ex adverso Solis, non inter Solem & homines interjecta erat, accidit. Accedit trium horarum mora, qualis in maxima etiam eclipsi naturali non obtinet. Neque tamen sic Luna ad Solem accurrit, vel Solem inter & terram constitit. quod nullis monumentis consignatum legitur; Sed verisimilius obscuratio ea ex retractione radiorum solarium, vel interpositis corporibus opacioribus contigit. Planè ita Deus obscurationem Solis justitiæ, & tempus ἐξουσίας τοῦ σκότους potestatis tenebrarum, Luc.XXII.53. nec non tum atrox Judæorum Jesum crucifigentium scelus, dignum à quo Sol intuendo se avertat, tum graves tenebras Judæis inde obventuras, adumbrare voluit.
units.tr: The letter of Dionysius the Areopagite to Polycarp Apollophanes testifies that those shadows covered the whole world, and that he and Aristophanes saw them at Heliopolis in Egypt. Indeed, on seeing this eclipse, Dionysius is said to have exclaimed, "Either the Deity suffers, or it suffers with the one who suffers" [ἢ τὸ θεῖον πάσχει, ἢ τῷ πάσχοντι συμπάσχει]; Suidas is the authority for this. But since the letters of Dionysius are of doubtful authenticity, nothing can be settled from them. Nevertheless Tertullian, Apology c. 21, records that this prodigious eclipse of the sun is found noted in the Roman archives. Phlegon also, in the Olympic Chronicle, book 13, in the 202nd Olympiad, records "the greatest eclipse of the sun" [ἐκλείψιν ἡλίου μεγίστην] and an earthquake that happened in Bithynia. That Phlegon and the Evangelists are recording the same history is shown by the fact that both fall in the same year and at the same sixth hour. That Thallus, in book 3 of his Histories, also noted the same eclipse was reported by Africanus, the distinguished chronologer. Indeed, the recent Chinese history of Hadrian Gresson testifies that the Chinese, in their records, noted a solar eclipse at this very time, contrary to the order of nature. So Mark could truly say that darkness came "over the whole earth" [ἐφ' ὅλῳ γῆν]. For how are we to understand this of Judaea alone? Whatever the case, it was certainly a prodigious eclipse, because it happened at the time of the Passover, on the fifteenth day of the moon [ἡ συζυγία], or rather the fourteenth [ἡ φάσιν], when the moon was full and opposite the sun, not interposed between the sun and men. There is also a delay of three hours, which does not occur even in a great natural eclipse. Nor did the moon rush to the sun or stand between the sun and the earth, which is not recorded in any monuments; rather the darkening more probably came from a withdrawal of the sun's rays, or from opaque bodies interposed. Thus God clearly wished to foreshadow the darkening of the sun of justice, and "the power of darkness" [ἐξουσίας τοῦ σκότους], Luke 22:53, as well as the atrocious crime of the Jews crucifying Jesus, which deserved that the sun turn away from looking on it, and the heavy darkness that would come upon the Jews as a result.

units.la: XXIX. Mortem Christi in cruce adhuc pendentis consecuta prodigia quædam sunt. Nam ante omnia velum Templi, quod adytum à Sancto separaverat, scissum est in duas partes à summo usque ad imum, Matth.XXVII.51. Marc. XV.38. Luc.XXIII.45. Cùm enim velum fuerit figura carnis Christi, per cujus fractionem seu mortem via ad Cœlum, seu accessus ad Deum cum libertate, cujus Cœli Sanctum Sanctorum figura erat, aperiri debuit: iccirco illud moriente Christo scindi debuit, & scissum est. Non potuit enim testimonium viæ ad Cœlum, seu accessus ad Deum cum libertate, nondum patefactæ, manere, cùm corpus Christi fractum, & aditus in Cœlum patefactus jam esset. Corpus autem Christi nondum fractum per velum figuratum fuit, quia quamdiu Christus sub Lege fuit, tandiu Ecclesia Deum tanquam Patrem in fiducia filiali, sine accusatione Legis, & servitutis onere adire non potuit; Hebr.IX.8-14. X.14-20. Sicut rupto velo Sanctum Sanctorum patuit, ita corpore Christi fracto rectà, sine ambagibus & involutis. cris,aditus ad Coelum patet. Alterum prodi-gium fuit, Terræmotus. Nam ἡ γῆ ἐσείσθη, καὶ αἱ πέτραι ἐσχίσθησαν Terra commota est, & petræ fissæ sunt, Matth. XXVII.51. Quod iræ Divinæ adversus scelus crucifigentium, & movendi propediem status & Regni Judaici indicium fuit. Commota est & contremuit terra, & fundamenta montium conturbata sunt, quia iratus est, Psal. XVIII.8. Rupta petra salutis, petræ etiam terræ ruptæ sunt. Addunt alii apertionem monumentorum. de qua statim: καὶ τὰ μνημεῖα ἀνεῳχθησαν, Et monumenta aperta sunt; & multa corpora sanctorum, qui dormierant, ἠγέρθη resurrexerunt, Matth.XXVII.52. Sed id contigit μετὰ τὴν ἔγερσιν post resurrectionem Christi v.53. quæ verba cum utroque versu connectenda sunt. Christus enim, ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων primitiæ dormientium fuit, 1.Cor.XV.20. Col.I.18. Mox Judæi Pilatum rogant, ut adfixis cruci crura frangerentur, & ad sepulturam illi tollerentur, non tam legem Dei Deut.XXI.23. vetantis,ne suspensi in ligno relinquerentur, caussati, quia sub Romanorum, qui corpora in cruce insepulta relinquere soliti sunt; potestate erant, quàm imminens Sabbathum præexentes, Joh.XIX.31. Nescieverunt Judæi, quid agerent, & nescientes operam dederunt, ut Scripturæ implerentur. Nescieverunt enim,jam suspensum esse in ligno, qui execratio fieri debuit, ut ad Israelem benedictio perveniret. Nesciverunt eum, qui maledictio factus erat ad abolitionem peccati, sepeliendum esse, quia jam in ipso maledictio, lex & ira interfecta erat, ne, si in cruce permaneret, peccatum nondum expiatum videretur; & ejus commemoratio in hominum oculis maneret. Milites, Pilato Judæorum postulatis annuente, venientes utriusque latronis superstitis crura fregerunt; sed Christi jam mortui non item. Accurrens unus ex militibus lancea Christi latus pupugit, καὶ ἐξῆλθεν αἷμα καὶ ὕδωρ & statim sanguis & aqua exivit, ibid. v.34. hoc est, sanguis cum sero, sive ex pericardio,quod aqua repletum est ad temperandum calorem cordis; sive ex thorace. Unde idem S.Johannes 1.Epist. V.6. elicit: Hic est, qui venit cum aqua & sanguine, Jesus Christus ille, non cum aqua tantum, sed cum aqua & sanguine, hoc est,cum puritate obedientiæ & cruentis passionibus, quibus omnes illi veteres βαπτισμοὶ ablutiones & purificationes per aquam, nec non cruentæ oblationes, & effusio sanguinis pecorum, antiquatæ sunt. Plaga in latere magna fuit, quia Joh.XX.25.27. cùm digitus ad implendum vestigium clavorum aptus innuatur, manus sola ad metiendum vestigium plagæ in latere idonea innuitur. Copiam igitur sanguinis ex latere effluxisse, vereq; Christum sanguinem suum effudisse,intelligitur. Ejus porro rei veritatem magnopere Johannes, ceu testis ἀληθής, confirmat, quia alios Evangelistas ejus rei oblitos observaverat, & interesse, ne id ignoraretur, reputaverat; quia ita impleri debuerunt prædicta: Os non conteretur ei, Agno,Christi typo, adeóque etiam antitypo Christo, Exod.XII.46. Num. IX,12. Οὐ συντρίβ, ὡς ἂν ἐξεκέντησαν, Asficient, quem transfixerint, Zach.XII.10. ubi Prophetia docet, Jesum, super quo,velut בכור unigenito &
units.tr: XXIX. Several prodigies followed the death of Christ while he still hung on the cross. First of all, the veil of the Temple, which separated the sanctuary from the Holy Place, "was torn in two from top to bottom," Matt. 27:51; Mark 15:38; Luke 23:45. For since the veil was a figure of the flesh of Christ, through whose breaking, that is his death, the way to heaven, or access to God with freedom, of which the Holy of Holies was a figure, ought to be opened, it therefore had to be torn when Christ died, and it was torn. For the testimony to the way to heaven, or to access to God with freedom, not yet revealed, could not remain, since the body of Christ was already broken and the entrance to heaven was opened. The body of Christ was not yet broken as the veil was a figure of it, because as long as Christ was under the Law, the Church could not approach God as Father with filial confidence, without the accusation of the Law and the burden of servitude; Heb. 9:8-14; 10:14-20. Just as the Holy of Holies lay open when the veil was torn, so when the body of Christ was broken, the entrance to heaven lies open directly, without ambiguities or veiled riddles. The second prodigy was an earthquake. For "the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split" [ἡ γῆ ἐσείσθη, καὶ αἱ πέτραι ἐσχίσθησαν], Matt. 27:51, which was a sign of divine wrath against the crime of the crucifiers, and of the coming shaking of the state and kingdom of the Jews. "The earth shook and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains were troubled, because he was angry," Ps. 18:8. The rock of salvation being broken, the rocks of the earth were also broken. Others add the opening of the tombs, which I shall come to at once: "and the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had slept rose" [καὶ τὰ μνημεῖα ἀνεῳχθησαν; ἠγέρθη], Matt. 27:52. But this happened "after the resurrection" [μετὰ τὴν ἔγερσιν] of Christ, v. 53, and these words must be joined to both verses. For Christ was "the firstfruits of those who had slept" [ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων], 1 Cor. 15:20; Col. 1:18. Soon afterwards the Jews asked Pilate that the legs of those fixed to the cross be broken and that they be taken down for burial. They pleaded not so much the law of God, Deut. 21:23, forbidding the hanged to be left on the tree, as the fact that they were under the power of the Romans, who were accustomed to leave bodies unburied on the cross, and that the Sabbath was at hand; John 19:31. The Jews did not know what they were doing, and in their ignorance they worked to fulfil the Scriptures. For they did not know that he who had to be cursed was already hanging on the tree, so that blessing might come to Israel. They did not know that he who had been made a curse for the abolition of sin had to be buried, since in him the curse, the Law and wrath were already destroyed; otherwise, if he remained on the cross, sin would seem not yet expiated, and his memory would remain in the eyes of men. The soldiers, when Pilate granted the request of the Jews, came and broke the legs of the robber who was still alive on each side; but they did not do so to Christ, who was already dead. One of the soldiers ran up and pierced Christ's side with a lance, "and immediately there came out blood and water" [καὶ ἐξῆλθεν αἷμα καὶ ὕδωρ], ibid. v. 34; that is, blood with serum, either from the pericardium, which is filled with water to temper the heat of the heart, or from the chest. Hence the same St John, 1 John 5:6, infers: "This is he who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ; not by water only, but by water and blood," that is, with the purity of obedience and with bloody sufferings, by which all those old baptisms [βαπτισμοὶ], ablutions and purifications by water, as well as the bloody offerings and the shedding of the blood of cattle, were abolished. The wound in the side was large, because at John 20:25, 27 the finger is pointed to as suited to filling the mark of the nails, while the hand alone is pointed to as suited to measuring the mark of the wound in the side. So it is understood that a copious flow of blood came from the side, and that Christ truly poured out his blood. Moreover, John, as a "true" witness [ἀληθής], greatly confirms the truth of this matter, because he had noticed that the other Evangelists had forgotten it, and he judged it important that it should not be ignored, since the things foretold had to be fulfilled in this way: "His bone shall not be broken," said of the lamb, the type of Christ, and so also of Christ the antitype, Exod. 12:46; Num. 9:12. "Ὀὐ συντρίβ..." [Οὐ συντρίβ...], "They shall look on him whom they pierced" [ὡς ἂν ἐξεκέντησαν], Zech. 12:10, where the prophecy teaches that Jesus, upon whom, as upon an only son and firstborn [בכור], ...

units.la: Primogenito plantum factum sint, transfigendum esse a populo, qui in eum creditur us erat. Ad quem locum etiam Rabbini ipsi, Jarchi, Abenezra, Kimchi veteres Rabbinos verba illa הביטו אלי &c. de Messia, sed filio Josephi (ne non contra veritatem luctari viderentur) interpretatos esse; notarunt.
units.tr: ...was to be pierced by the people who believed in him, and mourned as for a firstborn. On this passage the rabbis themselves, Jarchi, Abenezra and Kimchi, noted that the older rabbis interpreted those words "look upon me" [הביטו אלי] of the Messiah, but of the son of Joseph, so that they would not seem to fight against the truth.

units.la: XXX. Post hæc Christus è cruce sublatus & sepultus est. Sepeliverunt eum duo primcipes viri, Josephus Arimatheensis, vir nobilis, dives,Senator Hierosolymitanus, μαθητὴς Χριστοῦ discipulus Christi, sed κεκρυμμένος occultus propter metum Judæorum, Matth.XXVII.57. Marc.XV.43. Luc.XXIII.50. Joh.XIX.38. & Nicodemus ille, qui nocte ad Christum accesserat, ibid.III.1.2. & Christum adversus Pharisæos defenderat, ibid.VII.50. Prior ille & corpus de cruce depositit,ibid.XIX.38. & illud sindoni mundæ,quam hunc in finem mercatus erat,involvit: & ita involutum novo sepulchro ex petra excisio, & magno sumptu à se parato imposuit: & monumenti ostium lapide munivit, Matth.XXVII.59.60. Posterior ad condiendum cadaver attulit μίγμα σμύρνης καὶ ἀλόης mixturam myrrhæ & aloes, quasi libras centum, Joh.XIX.39. Ubi aloen non medicam, sed aromaticam,ad thymiamata vulgò usurpatam intelligi, rectè Salmasius docuit. Neque ex mixtura illa confectum est unguentum,quo ungeretur corpus Christi,quia eam in rem non centum librae necessariae fuissent, sed vel quatuor suffecissent; verùm ad condiendum Christi corpus illa adhibita est. Tanta verò copia aromatum Nicodemi & opulentiæ, & non exigui erga Christum affectus signum fuit. Nam cum magno aromatum cumulo magnatum corpora deponi sueverunt,uti ex sepultura Regis Asæ 2.Paralip. XVI.14. colligitur. Acceperunt ergo duo illi viri corpus Jesu (sub finem parasceves Sabbathi Joh.XIX.42. seu παρασκευὴ pridie Sabbathi Marc.XV.42.) & ligarunt illud ὀθονίοις μετὰ τῶν ἀρωμάτων linteis cum aromatibus,quemadmodum mos est Judæis ἐνταφιάζειν funerare, Joh.XIX.40. Mos enim Judæis pollingentibus, seu funera curantibus erat corpus lavare,ungere,condire, & linteis sepulchralibus involvere. Ablutionis & unctionis corporis Christi historia diserte non meminit. Ablutum tamen dubitari nequit. Præparata verò à mulieribus unguenta applicata Christo resurrectionem anticipante, non sunt, Luc.XXIII.56. XXIV.1.2. Sed linteis involutum fuit. Tria verò lintea adhiberi fuerunt; brevius, quod sudarium dictum est,& caput texit: longum,sindon, quo reliquum corpus nudum circumvolvebatur: & ὀθονία vel χειρία fascia, sive institæ, quibus sindon coërcebatur, & manus pedésque ligabantur. Cùm verò Evangelistæ, qui sindonis meminere, non nominent ὀθόνια sive χειρίας, hoc est linteamina seu fascias; & qui hæc expressere, de sindone taceant, credibile est, idem illos per sindonem & ὀθόνια signasse. Potuit enim esse ανδῶν seu ὀθόνη initio,prout emptum; & post discerpi, ut inde fierent ὀθόνια sive χειρία, quibus fasciatim corpus involveretur,& pars capiti tegendo sudarii nomine Joh.XX.6. pars colligando pectori, ventri & brachio utrique; pars femori ac pedibus inserviret. Quæ fusius Salmasius idem secunda de Cruce ad Bartholinum Epistola explicat. His à Josepho & Nicodemo ἐνταφιασταῖς funeratoribus curatis, corpus Christi non arcæ prius inclusum, & hinc sepulchro immissum, ut moribus nostris obtinet; sed ita uti erat, linteis involutum in sepulchro repositum est. Fuit autem solum, in quo monumentum hoc fuit, ὑπόπετρον, quomodo etiam Strabo lib.XVI. Hierosolymæ solum fuisse πετρῶδες καὶ ὑπόπετρον dixit. Talis fuit hortus Josephi, & in eodem monumentum, in quod Christus illatus est, λελατομημένον ἐκ πέτρας excisum ex petra, Marc.XV.46. seu ὁ ἐλατομημένον ἐν τῇ πέτρᾳ, quod Josephus excidi curavit in petra Matth.XXVII.60. Quæ conciliare non potest Salmasius, qui in Solinum pag.1209. Jesu sepulchrum cryptam fuisse in terra excavatam, lapide stratam, inædificatam, concameratam desuper, & foramine in medio fornice apertam, quod injecto extrinsecus lapide clauderetur, pertendit, & in horto eo, in quo Christi monumentum fuit, rupem ullam fuisse negat, sed subactam humum, qualem horti esse oportuit. Etiam duplex crypta fuit, una extima, tanquam aditus & vestibulum: altera intima, in qua Christi corpus reconditum fuit. Quæ veterum & recentiorum testificatio temere vellicari non potest, inprimis cùm demonstrationi Evangelicæ resurrectionis Christi accommodata sit. Ita repositum in sepulchro corpus Christi Occidentem facie respexisse putatur. Posthæc ingens saxum ori monumenti impositum est, Matth. ibid. Etiam mulieres, inprimis Maria Magdalena, & Maria altera, pollincturæ & sepulturæ curam suscepepunt. Nam à sepulchro domum reversæ ἀρώματα καὶ μύρα aromata & unguenta pararunt, eo animo, ut exacto sabbatho, pollinctura ergo reverterentur. Sed reversæ Christum, qui jam resurrexerat, in monumento non offenderunt, neque ei destinata officia præstiterunt, Luc.XXIII.56. XXIV.1.2.&c. Cum Christo etiam crucem, de qua pependerat, sepultam, hoc est, terra obrutam, ex more è Judæorum Libris Thalmudicis & Maimonide eruto, Viri docti, Morinus inprimis, & Constant. L'Empereur, conficere satagunt. Hæc instante Sabbatho contigerunt. Sed ubi Sabbathum magnum illuxit, principes Sacerdotum & Pharisæi, neglecta religione Sabbathi, Pilatum rogarunt, ut, quia Christus superstes tertia die se resurrecturum promiserat, sepulchro custodiam adderet, ne discipuli corpus ejus suffurando prædictioni fidem facere anniterentur; & error posterior priore periculosior evaderet, Matth.XXVII.62. &c. Impetrata à Pontio custodiendi, per Romanos etiam milites, sepulchri venia, lapidem sepulchri obsignarunt, & sepulchro milites illud custodituros apposuerunt, ibid.v.66.
units.tr: XXX. After these things, Christ was taken down from the cross and buried. Two leading men buried him: Joseph of Arimathea, a noble, wealthy member of the Jerusalem Senate, disciple of Christ [μαθητὴς Χριστοῦ] but secret [κεκρυμμένος] for fear of the Jews (Matt. 27:57; Mark 15:43; Luke 23:50; John 19:38); and that Nicodemus who had come to Christ by night (ibid. 3:1-2) and had defended Christ against the Pharisees (ibid. 7:50). The former also took the body down from the cross (ibid. 19:38) and wrapped it in clean linen, which he had bought for this purpose, and laid it in a new tomb hewn out of rock, prepared at his own great expense, and he closed the entrance of the tomb with a stone (Matt. 27:59-60). The latter brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes [μίγμα σμύρνης καὶ ἀλόης], about a hundred pounds (John 19:39). Salmasius rightly showed that the aloe here is not the medicinal kind but the aromatic kind, commonly used for incense. Nor was ointment made from that mixture with which the body of Christ was anointed, for a hundred pounds would not have been needed for that purpose; four pounds would have sufficed. Rather, that mixture was used to embalm the body of Christ. Such a great quantity of spices was a sign of Nicodemus's wealth and of no small affection towards Christ, for great quantities of spices were customarily laid with the bodies of great men, as is gathered from the burial of King Asa (2 Chron. 16:14). So those two men took the body of Jesus (at the end of the Preparation day, that is, on the eve of the Sabbath, John 19:42, or the Preparation, the day before the Sabbath, Mark 15:42), and they bound it with linen cloths along with the spices [ὀθονίοις μετὰ τῶν ἀρωμάτων], as the Jews are accustomed to prepare for burial [ἐνταφιάζειν], John 19:40. For it was the custom of the Jews, who were the undertakers or attended to funerals, to wash the body, anoint it, embalm it and wrap it in burial linens. The history of Christ's washing and anointing is not explicitly mentioned, yet it cannot be doubted that he was washed. The ointments prepared by the women were not applied to Christ, since he was anticipating the resurrection (Luke 23:56; 24:1-2). But he was wrapped in linens. Three kinds of linen were used: the shorter one, called sudarium, covered the head; the long one, sindon, in which the rest of the naked body was wrapped; and the ὀθονία or χειρία, that is, bands or strips, with which the sindon was bound and the hands and feet tied. Since the Evangelists who mention the sindon do not name the ὀθόνια or χειρία, that is, the linen wrappings or strips, and those who mention these are silent about the sindon, it is credible that they signified the same thing by sindon and ὀθόνια. For at first it could have been an ἀνδῶν or ὀθόνη (a single piece of cloth), as it was bought; and afterwards it was torn up so that ὀθόνια or χειρία might be made from it, by which the body was wrapped in strips, and one part served to cover the head under the name of sudarium (John 20:6), another to bind the breast, belly and each arm, another to serve the thighs and feet. Salmasius explains these matters more fully in his second letter On the Cross, addressed to Bartholinus. When these things had been attended to by Joseph and Nicodemus, as undertakers [ἐνταφιασταῖς], the body of Christ was not first enclosed in a chest, and then placed in the tomb, as is the custom among us; but it was laid in the tomb as it was, wrapped in linens. The ground in which this tomb lay was rocky below [ὑπόπετρον], as Strabo also said in book 16, that the ground at Jerusalem was rocky and stony below [πετρῶδες καὶ ὑπόπετρον]. Such was the garden of Joseph, and in it the tomb into which Christ was laid was hewn out of rock [λελατομημένον ἐκ πέτρας] (Mark 15:46), or, as Matthew says, which Joseph had had cut in the rock (Matt. 27:60). Salmasius cannot reconcile these, for in his commentary on Solinus, p. 1209, he maintains that Jesus's tomb was a crypt excavated in the earth, paved with stone, built up, vaulted above, and opened in the middle of the vault by an aperture, which was closed by a stone placed on it from outside; and he denies that there was any rock in that garden in which Christ's tomb was, but says there was levelled earth, such as a garden ought to have. There was also a double crypt: one outer, as an entrance and vestibule; the other inner, in which Christ's body was laid. This testimony of the ancients and moderns cannot be rashly challenged, especially since it is suited to the evangelical demonstration of Christ's resurrection. Thus the body of Christ, laid in the tomb, is thought to have faced west. Afterwards a huge stone was placed at the mouth of the tomb (Matt. ibid.). The women too, especially Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, undertook the care of the embalming and burial. For after returning home from the tomb they prepared spices and ointments [ἀρώματα καὶ μύρα], intending to return to embalm him once the Sabbath was over (Luke 23:56; 24:1-2, etc.). But when they returned, they did not find Christ, who had already risen, in the tomb, nor did they perform the duties intended for him. Learned men, especially Morinus and Constantin L'Empereur, labour to prove that the cross on which he had hung was also buried with Christ, that is, covered with earth, according to a custom drawn from the Jewish Talmudic books and Maimonides. These things happened as the Sabbath was approaching. But when the great Sabbath dawned, the chief priests and Pharisees, disregarding the religious observance of the Sabbath, asked Pilate that, since Christ, while alive, had promised that he would rise on the third day, a guard be added to the tomb, lest his disciples steal the body and strive to make the prediction seem true, and so the later error prove more dangerous than the former (Matt. 27:62ff.). Having obtained from Pontius permission to set guards, including Roman soldiers, they sealed the stone of the tomb and placed soldiers to guard it there (ibid. v. 66).

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Singula hæc prægrande mysterium habuerunt. Sepeliri Christus debuit, quia execratio tolli debuit, Deut.XXI.23. In ligno si relictus fuisset, extans adhuc peccatum & execratio mansisset, & commemorari simul debuisset. Accedunt alia argumenta, quòd sic Scripturæ impleri, veritas mortis Christi demonstrari, mors in ultimo arcis suæ angulo & asylo debel-
units.tr: Each of these events carried a great mystery. Christ had to be buried, because the curse had to be removed (Deut. 21:23). If he had been left hanging on the wood, sin and the curse would still have stood and would have had to be remembered together with him. There are further reasons: that the Scriptures might thereby be fulfilled, that the truth of Christ's death might be shown, that death might be defeated in its last corner and refuge, that our sins might be buried with Christ, that our graves might be sanctified,

units.la: lari, peccata nostra cum Christo sepeliri, sepulchra nostra sanctificari, & Sabbathum cæterasque legis ceremoniæ simul etiam, ut emeritæ & rude donatæ, tanquam cadaver in sepulchro, componi debuerunt. Unde Jesus Sabbathismum in sepulchro peregit. Debuit Jesus ab oculis hominum abscondi, & in terra publicè non amplius comparere, uti Manna post sextum diem in terra non apparuit. paratus enim erat cibus salutaris, & vitam æternam dans mundo.
