Sepelivit Christum Josephus dives, Senator, vir justus, discipulus Christi antehac occultus, sed tum in maximo pavore à metu liber; & eandem sepulturam impensis Nicodemus honoravit. Non enim tantum cum improbis in cruce ἀνασταυρωθῆναι pendere mortuus, & sepulturam habere, sed etiam cum divite in monumento ejus sepeliri debuit, Esaj.LIII.9. Etiam hi, Senatores cùm essent, mortuum Christum justificarunt, & in ejusdem ὀνειδισμῷ ignominia partem habere voluerunt. Hi Christum sepeliverunt sub finem Parasceves, seu pridie Sabbathi magni, in quod Pascha incidit, quomodo etiam Thalmud Sanhedr. sol.43. dicit: בערב פסח תלאוהו לישו in vespera Paschatis (pridie Paschatis) Jesum suspenderunt. Debuit enim in Sabbatho illo magno quiescere, & novæ quietis allatæ fidem facere. Sepulchrum ejus debuit esse & in petra, ne per occultos meatus & cuniculos inde extractum à discipulis corpus calumniari hostibus liceret: & novum, ne alienà virtute cadaveris ibi prius jacentis resuscitatus, vel alius ex eo resuscitatus fingi posset: & alienum, ut Christi exinaniti continua pauprtas, & quòd propter alios cuncta sustinuerit, cognosci posset. Sumptus magni in funerationem adhibiti probrum crucis ejus utcunque mitigarunt; & aromata copiosè adeò applicata ex morte & sepulchro Christi odorem bonæ fragrantiæ ad Deum & homines expirare, significarunt. Sed mulieres tamen parata à se aromata non applicarunt, quia corruptionem videre non debuit, Psal.XVI.10. Senatus populi custodiam apposuit, tanquam volens eum in sepulchro retinere. Ita adiit τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς inferiores partes terræ, cor terræ, ᾅδην infernum, Ephes.IV.9. Matth.XII.40. Act.II.31. Sed anima ejus in inferno relinqui non potuit, ibid. Quando enim corpus in inferno, seu intra superficiem terræ fuit, etiam anima, qua corpus vixit, seu sanguis mortuus, in inferno esse dicitur. Qua ratione etiam corpus mortuum שפש anima, Levit.XXLI. XXII.4. &c. appellatur.
units.tr: and that the Sabbath and the other ceremonies of the law, now fulfilled and given their discharge, should be laid in the tomb together with him, like a corpse. Hence Jesus kept the Sabbath in the grave. Jesus had to be hidden from the eyes of men and no longer appear publicly on earth, just as the manna did not appear on the earth after the sixth day, for the saving food was ready and was giving eternal life to the world. Joseph, a rich senator, a just man and a disciple of Christ, who had until then been secret but was now freed from fear in his great dread, buried Christ; and Nicodemus honoured the same burial with his expense. For Christ had to hang dead on the cross not only with the wicked, and receive a burial, but also had to be laid in a tomb with the rich man (Isa. 53:9). These men, being senators, also justified the dead Christ and wished to share in his disgrace. They buried Christ near the end of the Preparation, that is, on the day before the great Sabbath on which the Passover fell, just as the Talmud, Sanhedrin fol. 43, also says: "On the eve of the Passover (the day before the Passover) they hanged Jesus." For he had to rest on that great Sabbath and make it certain that a new rest had been brought. His tomb had to be in rock, so that the enemies could not slander that the body had been stolen out by hidden passages and tunnels; and new, so that it could not be pretended that he had been raised by the borrowed power of a corpse lying there before, or that someone else had been raised from it; and belonging to another, so that the continual poverty of the emptied Christ, and that he endured everything for the sake of others, might be recognised. The large expense of the funeral in some measure softened the disgrace of his cross; and the spices so abundantly applied signified that from the death and tomb of Christ there would breathe out a fragrance of good odour to God and men. Yet the women did not apply the spices they had prepared, because his body was not to see corruption (Ps. 16:10). The Senate set a guard over the people, as if wishing to keep him in the tomb. So he entered the lower parts of the earth, the heart of the earth, Hades (hell) (Eph. 4:9; Matt. 12:40; Acts 2:31). But his soul could not be left in hell (ibid.). For when the body was in hell, that is, below the surface of the earth, the soul too, by which the body lived, or the dead blood, is said to be in hell. For this reason also the dead body is called soul (Lev. 21:11; 22:4, etc.) [nephesh].

units.la: XXXII. In vulgari Symbolo, Apostolico dicto, sepulturam Descensus ad inferos sequitur. Verba sunt: Descendit ad inferos; vel juxta Symbolum Aquilejense, ad inferna. Græcus Codex in Benedictini apud Cantabrigienses Collegii Bibliotheca, Psalterio Græco Papæ Gregorii additus, sed multò Gregorio recentior, verba Latina reddidit καταβάντα εἰς τὰ κατώτατα. Sed in Symbolo veteri Romano & Orientali non comparuisse verba illa, Rufinus & Usferiani Codices testantur. Etiam Patres & Concilia vetera, Confessiones inprimis veteres plus quàm sexaginta, quæ in recensione Fidei & Symboli nullam descensus ad inferos mentionem sece-
units.tr: XXXII. In the common Symbol, called Apostolic, the burial is followed by the Descent into Hell. The words are: He descended into hell; or, according to the Aquileian Creed, into the lower regions. A Greek manuscript in the library of the Benedictine College at Cambridge, appended to the Greek Psalter of Pope Gregory but much later than Gregory, rendered the Latin words as [καταβάντα εἰς τὰ κατώτατα] "having descended into the lowest parts". But that those words did not appear in the old Roman and Eastern Creeds is attested by the codices of Rufinus and Ussher. The Fathers and the early Councils, and above all more than sixty of the earliest Confessions, which in reciting the Faith and the Creed made no mention of a descent to hell,

units.la: Ejusdem mysterium eruitur.
units.tr: The mystery of the same is brought out.

units.la: Descensus Christi ad inferos explicatur. fecerunt, Parkerus de Descensu ad inferos Lib.IV. § 25. recitat. Cujus etiam, ut & Doctiss. Lavateri nostratis, idem argumentum tractantis, sagacibus conjecturis effectum est, ut nemo paulo emunctiorum narium amplius dubitet, quin verba illa ex Symbolo Athanasiano margini Nicæni adscripta (uti Codex Biblicus M. S. Caroli M. Bibliothecæ nostræ Carolinæ illatus ejusdem rei testis est) in ipsius primo Nicæni, ac inde etiam in Apostolici Symboli textum irrepserint. Quæ haud illibenter retinemus, quia & S. Scripturæ analoga sunt, cum descendere in infernum debuerit, qui in inferno relinqui non debuit Psal.XVI.10. & concinnum in hac etiam συναφεια verborum sensum fundunt. ut non sine Numine Symbolum verborum illorum accessione, sero licet, crevisse videri posset. Nam vel proprium, vel analogicum sensum maximè significantem & Scripturis analogum habent. Proprie Christus in sepultura sua verè ad inferos descendit, cum inferi Hebræis שאול hoc est, locus, in quo, qui non videtur, quæri debet, Græcis ἅδης, quasi locus ἀΐδης, qui intus non videtur, Latinis infernus ab inferendo, vel quia infra terram est, proprie & κυέμως sepulchrum, seu התחתיות הארץ κατωτερω μέρη τῆς γῆς inferiores terræ partes, superioribus, in quibus homines vitali aura vescuntur, oppositas, Ephes.IV.9. significat. uti Parkerus & Lavaterus fusè probarunt. Attamen ex usu Scripturæ plus etiam descendere ad inferos significat, quàm sepulturam; cum sepultura actum sepeliendi, seu funerationem, descensus ad inferos statum seu perseverationem status illius sub dominio mortis, quo à morte absumptus aliquis videri potest, significet. Ita Christus proprie ad inferos descendit, quando non tantum sepultus est, sed etiam per triduum in sepulchro perseveravit, adeò ut sui à morte vel subacti & triumphati simulachrum exhibuerit. Unde S. Petrus Act. II.31. verba illa Psal.XVI.10. Non relinques animam meam לשאול εἰς ᾅδῃ in inferno, tum impleta interpretatur, cum Christus ex morte resurrexit. Unde statum illum, qui resurrectionem Christi proximè antecessit, adeóque triduanam in sepulchro commorationem, quam discipuli Emauntici, dicentes: Nos sperabamus fore, ut Israelem liberaret. Sed super omnia hæc tertius hodie dies agitur, ex quo hæc contigerunt, Luc.XXIV.21. in rei conclamatæ argumentum traxerunt; proprie esse illam καταβασιν εἰς ᾅδῃ descensum ad inferos, doctissimi quique ψυχῶς colligunt. Cui tanquam supremo humiliationis gradui Sessio ad dextram Dei, exaltationis supremus gradus opponitur. Analogicè verò, & simillitudine quadam, qua שאול ᾅδης, infernus etiam locum damnatorum significat, descensus ad inferos nomine etiam enervationem Christi in anima, חבלי שאול dolores inferni (2.Sam.XXII.6. Psal.XVIII.6. Matth. XVI.18. Luc.XVI.23.) hoc est, horribiles & infernales cruciatus & angores, quos Christi anima loco nostro sustinuit, quando super ipsum transiverunt חרוני iræ Dei, &c, בעותי φοβοι terrores ejus illum succiderunt, Psalm. LXXXVIII.17. insinuantur, non quòd illos post mortem, quando anima ejus in Paradiso & manu Patris fuit, sustinuerit; sed quia illos tum in tota vita, tum inprimis post coenam in ἀγωνία anxietate sua, quando inprimis calicem deprecatus est; & in cruce exanimavit, Matth. XXVI. 37.38. Luc.XXII.44. Qui metaphoricus ad inferos descensus etiam tenebrarum, seu eclipseos symbolo Matth.XXVII.44. repræsentatus videri potest. Convenit sensus ille analogicus verbis Petri: Prævidens locutus est de resurrectione Christi, ὅτι οὐ καταλείψῃ ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ εἰς ᾅδην, οὐδὲ ἡ σὰρξ αὐτοῦ εἶδε διαφθοράν, quòd non relinquetur anima ejus in inferno, nec caro ejus videbit corruptionem. Act.II.31. Ubi prius tmema de anima Christi in inferno non relinquenda; posterius de carne corruptionem non visura, distincte loquitur. Neque analogico huic sensui obstat ordo symboli, quo descensus ad inferos sepulturæ postponitur, cum tamen post mortem nihil anima Christi passa sit. Nam ordo ille articulorum non à tempore, sed à gradduum distinctione sumptus est. quasi diceretur: crucifixus, mortuus, sepultus est, denique, quod descensu ad inferos in Scripturis significatum est, etiam spiritualiter exanimavit. Mittimus crisin Doctiss. Brougthoni, qui illud καταβεβηκεν εἰς ᾅδης interpretatur media significatione vocis ᾅδης, pro statu invisibili animæ Christi à corpore separatæ, & in Cœlo existentis. quomodo in Macedonum Christianorum Oratione Dominica olim sic lectum est: Pater noster, non ὁ ἐν οὐρανοῖς, sed ὁ ἐν ᾅδῃ. Nusquam enim ille vocis ᾅδης sensus, saltem in Scripturis, occurrit.
units.tr: The descent of Christ into hell is explained. have set this aside. Parker recites it in On the Descent into Hell, book IV, §25. Through the shrewd conjectures of him and of our own most learned Lavater, who treated the same subject, it has been brought about that no one of even moderately keen nose any longer doubts that those words, written in the margin of the Nicene Creed from the Athanasian Creed (as the Biblical Codex of our Carolingian Library, brought in from Charlemagne's manuscripts, bears witness to the same thing), crept into the text of the first Nicene Creed and from there also into the Apostles' Creed. We retain them not unwillingly, because they are also in keeping with the analogy of Holy Scripture, since he who was not to be left in hell had to descend into hell (Ps. 16:10), and because in this connection they also pour out a harmonious sense of the words, so that the addition of those words to the Creed, though late, may seem to have grown up not without the divine will. For they have a sense either proper or analogical, which is most significant and agrees with the Scriptures. Properly, Christ truly descended into hell in his burial, since hell in Hebrew is she'ol, that is, the place in which what is not seen must be sought; in Greek hades, as if the place aidēs, which is not seen within; in Latin infernus, from inferendo, or because it is below the earth; properly and in a manner of speaking it signifies the tomb, or the lower parts of the earth (ta katōtera merē tēs gēs), opposed to the higher parts, in which men feed on the vital air (Eph. 4:9), as Parker and Lavater have argued at length. Yet by the usage of Scripture, to descend into hell signifies more than burial; for burial signifies the act of interring, or laying in the grave, while descent into hell signifies the state, or the continuance of that state under the dominion of death, in which one may appear to have been swallowed up by death. Thus Christ properly descended into hell not only when he was buried, but also when he remained in the tomb for three days, so that he displayed the image of one overcome and triumphed over by death. Hence St. Peter, Acts 2:31, interprets those words of Psalm 16:10, You will not leave my soul [lish'ol] in hell [eis hadēn], as fulfilled when Christ rose from death. Hence the learned all agree that the state which immediately preceded the resurrection of Christ, and therefore the three-day stay in the tomb, which the disciples on the road to Emmaus took as proof of a matter already despaired of, saying, "We had hoped that it was he who was going to redeem Israel. Yet besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened" (Luke 24:21), is properly that descent into hell (katabasis eis hadēn). To this supreme step of humiliation the Session at the right hand of God is opposed as the supreme step of exaltation. Analogically, however, and by a certain resemblance, since she'ol (hades, hell) also signifies the place of the damned, the descent into hell is also understood to mean the enervation of Christ in his soul, the pains of hell (2 Sam. 22:6; Ps. 18:5; Matt. 16:18; Luke 16:23), that is, the horrible and infernal torments and anguish which Christ's soul endured in our place, when the wrath of God passed over him [hărōnê], and his terrors [ba'ăthôthay] cut him down (Ps. 88:16). This is hinted at not because he suffered these after death, when his soul was in Paradise and in the Father's hand, but because he suffered them during his whole life, and above all afterward in the agony [agōnia] of his anxiety at supper, when he especially prayed that the cup might pass, and in the cross he expired (Matt. 26:37-38; Luke 22:44). This metaphorical descent into hell may also be seen as represented by the symbol of darkness or eclipse (Matt. 27:45). That analogical sense agrees with Peter's words: "Foreseeing, he spoke of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul would not be left in hell, nor would his flesh see corruption" (Acts 2:31). There he speaks distinctly, first of the soul of Christ not being left in hell, and afterward of the flesh not seeing corruption. Nor does the order of the Creed, in which the descent into hell is placed after the burial, stand in the way of this analogical sense, since after death the soul of Christ suffered nothing. For that order of the articles is taken not from time but from the distinction of steps, as if it were said: he was crucified, dead, buried; finally, what in Scripture is signified by descent into hell he also accomplished spiritually. We pass over the judgment of the most learned Broughton, who interprets katabebēken eis hadēs by a middle sense of the word hadēs, for the invisible state of the soul of Christ, separated from the body, and existing in heaven; as in the Lord's Prayer of the Macedonian Christians it was once read thus: "Our Father," not ho en ouranois (who art in heaven) but ho en hadē (who art in hell). For that sense of the word hadēs occurs nowhere, at least in Scripture.

units.la: XXXIII. Ex ordine articulorum Symboli, quo descensus ad inferos sepulturæ postponitur, fluxit error Pontificiorum, localem animæ Christi ad inferos, limbum cumprimis Patrum ex eodem liberandorum causa; descensum & κατάβασιν circumerrationem per triduum, quo corpus in sepulchro fuit, fingentium, discorde concordia, dum alii cum Durando Christum ad nullum locum aliter quàm per effectum, alii cum Thoma nonnisi ad limbum per realem præsentiam, per effectum autem ad omnia loca inferni descendisse asserunt. Bellarminus verò assertionem suam sola probabilitate commendat. At probabilitas est profectò &c. inquit. Caterum Limbus Utopia est; nec si quis exitteret, ad eum post mortem Christum descendisse, solus symboli ordo arbitrarius ille, humano ingenio contextus, imò hujus articuli respectu, casualis, & cujus arbitrarii licèt humani & casualis ordinis alium etiam sensum esse posse, supra ostendimus, evinceret. Præterea Christus nec corpore, nec anima localiter ad damnatorum infernum descendit. Non corpore, quia in sepulchro exanime & motus expers quievit. Non anima, quia in Paradiso & in manu Patris fuit, Luc.XXIII.43.46. Non enim in Paradisum receptus est secundum Divinitatem, quæ Paradiso non indiget, & nunquam extra eum fuit; inprimis cùm sic Christus se considerari voluerit, non ut Paradisi conditorem, Deum; sed ut Adamum secundum, Cœlesti Paradiso recipiendum, & jacturam, quam primus Adamus, Paradiso exclusus, fecerat, reparaturum. Nulla porro necessitas fuit descensus ad gehennam, quia Christus sine eo negotium suum cum inferno absolvere & expedire facilè potuit; imò etiam in cruce absolvit & expediit, quando clamavit: Τετέλεσται. Error locatum animæ Christi ad limbum vel inferos, ad liberandos Patres ibi languentes, fingentium Pontificium rum perstringitur. Τελεσθῆ consummatum est. Neque illam in Utopiam hanc profectionem Scriptura probat. Nam S. Paulus dicens: Ne dicas in corde tuo: Quis descendet in abyssum? hoc est Christum à mortuis revocare, Rom. X. 7. non Christum post mortem animam suam ad inferos penetrasse innuit: sed in abyssum descendisse, hoc est, mortis periculum adiisse & subiisse, licet ex morte redierit, significat. Pro eo Moses Deut. XXX. 13. habet עבר אל עבר הים transfire ultra mare, quod ænigma S. Paulus per καταβαίνειν εἰς τὸν ἄβυσσον descendere in abyssum, extricat, quia qui ultra mare transit, hoc est, mare totum inquisitionis causa ad omnem terminum ejus pererrat, præsentissimum mortis & interitus periculum adit, perinde ac is, qui in abyssum descendit, licet maris terminum assecutus ex abysso veluti redeat. Neque aliud per descensum in abyssum, quàm mortem & sepulturam Christi S. Paulus intellexit, quia ei opposuit ἀναγαγεῖν ἐκ νεκρῶν reducere ex mortuis. Atqui Deus ex morte reducens Christum, non eum ex inferno, sed ex statu mortis & sepulchro vindicavit. Neque etiam S. Petrus asserens, Christum, carne mortificatum, spiritu vero vivificatum, eodem spiritu profectum prædicasse τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασι spiritibus qui in carcere sunt, 1.Pet. III. 18.19. Christum, hoc est, animam ejus post mortem εἰς φυλακλῶ in carcerem (sive ille Limbus, sive alius medius locus, sive verius infernus intelligitur) localiter descendisse arguit, quia nec πνεῦμα spiritus, quo, seu à quo vivificatus dicitur, animam Christi, sed ejus Divinitatem, seu πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης Spiritum Sanctitatis, secundum quem ex morte Christum resuscitantem definitus est Filius Dei in potentia, Rom. I.4. significat, nec Christus prædicasse spiritibus infernalibus tum, cùm Spiritu vivificatus est, sed ποτὲ olim, seu ἐν ἡμέραις Nῶε in diebus Noë (v.20.) quando spiritus illi, qui S. Petri loquentis tempore in carcere erant, inobedientes se gesserunt, & longanimitatem Dei expectantis, cùm arca struereretur, frustrati sunt: nec spiritus in carcere sanctorum Patrum spiritus, quos in limbo illi collocant, sed ἀπειθεῖς inobedientes, inferno, ex quo non datur exitus, damnati intelliguntur: nec ullius ex φυλακὴ carcere illo liberationis mentio est. Nam quòd Christus profectus Spiritu prædicasse dicitur, non præconium liberationis, sed poenitentiæ agendæ notatur. Ita νεκροῖς ἐυηγγελίσθη mortuis Evangelium prædicatum est, 1.Pet. IV. 6. in sensu non compositò, sed divisò, hoc est, nunc mortuis, sed tempore Noæ viventibus. Denique descensum ad תחתיות הארץ κατωτέρω γῆς, שאול ᾅδην, Psal. XVI. 10. LXVIII. 19. Act. II. 27. Ephes. IV. 9. non localem animæ Christi ad gehennam, sed propriè corporis in sepulchrum, analogicè animæ ad passiones & agones suos descensum significare, jam fidem fecimus. Plura eandem in rem Loc. XI. 89. dicta repetere nihil attinet.
units.tr: XXXIII. From the order of the articles of the Creed, in which the descent into hell is placed after the burial, the error of the Papists arose: they imagine a local descent of Christ's soul into hell, into limbo, chiefly to free the Fathers from there. They also imagine a katabasis and a wandering about for three days, while his body lay in the tomb, and they do so in a discordant agreement. Some, with Durandus, assert that Christ descended to no place except by his effect; others, with Thomas, assert that he descended only to limbo by real presence, but to all places of hell by effect. Bellarmine commends his own assertion on probability alone: But probability is surely etc., he says. Moreover, limbo is a Utopia. Even if someone should exist, the arbitrary order of the Creed, devised by human ingenuity, would not prove that Christ descended to it after death. Indeed, with respect to this article, that order is accidental, and we have shown above that this arbitrary, human and accidental order can also have another sense. Furthermore, Christ descended locally to the infernal place of the damned neither in body nor in soul. Not in body, because in the tomb he rested lifeless and without motion. Not in soul, because it was in Paradise and in the Father's hand, Luke 23:43, 46. For he was not received into Paradise according to his Divinity, which has no need of Paradise and was never outside it, especially since Christ wished to be considered in this way: not as the Creator of Paradise, God, but as the second Adam, to be received into the heavenly Paradise and to repair the loss which the first Adam, excluded from Paradise, had caused. Nor was there any necessity for a descent into hell, since Christ could easily settle and complete his business with the underworld without it; indeed he did settle and complete it on the cross, when he cried out: Tetelestai [Τετέλεσται], "It is finished." The error of the Papists, who imagine that the soul of Christ went to limbo or the underworld to free the Fathers languishing there, is refuted by this word, Teletheis [Τελεσθῆ], "consummated." Nor does Scripture prove that this journey into utopia occurred. For when St Paul says: Do not say in your heart: Who will descend into the abyss? that is, to bring Christ back from the dead, Rom. 10:7, he does not hint that Christ's soul penetrated into the underworld after death, but signifies that he descended into the abyss, that is, that he faced and underwent the danger of death, even though he returned from death. For this Moses, Deut. 30:13, has 'avar 'el 'ever hayyam [עבר אל עבר הים], "to pass beyond the sea," which riddle St Paul unravels as katabainein eis ton abysson [καταβαίνειν εἰς τὸν ἄβυσσον], "to descend into the abyss," because he who crosses beyond the sea, that is, who wanders over the whole sea to every boundary of it for the sake of exploring, faces the most immediate danger of death and destruction, just as one who descends into the abyss, although he reaches the boundary of the sea, returns as if from the abyss. Nor did St Paul understand by the descent into the abyss anything other than the death and burial of Christ, because he opposed to it anagagein ek nekrōn [ἀναγαγεῖν ἐκ νεκρῶν], "to bring up from the dead." But God, when he brought Christ back from death, rescued him not from the underworld but from the state of death and the tomb. Nor does St Peter either, when he asserts that Christ, put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit, went and preached in the same Spirit to the spirits [τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασι] who are in prison, 1 Pet. 3:18–19, prove that Christ, that is, his soul after death, descended locally eis phylakēn [εἰς φυλακήν], into prison (whether that is understood as limbo, some other middle place, or more truly hell). For the pneuma, spirit, by which or in which he is said to have been made alive, signifies not the soul of Christ but his Divinity, or the pneuma hagiōsynēs [πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης], Spirit of holiness, according to which Christ was declared to be the Son of God in power, Rom. 1:4, when he raised himself from death. Nor did Christ preach to infernal spirits at the time when he was made alive by the Spirit, but pote [ποτὲ], at some time formerly, or en hēmerais Nōe [ἐν ἡμέραις Nῶε], in the days of Noah (v. 20), when those spirits, who at the time of St Peter's speaking were in prison, behaved disobediently, and, while the ark was being built, frustrated the patience of God who waited. The spirits in prison are not the spirits of the holy Fathers, whom they place in limbo, but are understood to be the apeitheis [ἀπειθεῖς], the disobedient, damned to hell, from which there is no exit; and there is no mention of any liberation from that prison. For the fact that Christ is said to have gone and preached in the Spirit does not denote a proclamation of liberation, but a call to repentance. So nekrois euēngelisthē [νεκροῖς ἐυηγγελίσθη], the gospel was preached to the dead, 1 Pet. 4:6, in a divided, not a compound, sense: that is, to those who are now dead, but who were living in the time of Noah. Finally, we have already shown that the descent to tachtiyyot ha'aretz [תחתיות הארץ], katōterō gēs [κατωτέρω γῆς], the lower parts of the earth, and Sheol [שאול], hadēn [ᾅδην], Ps. 16:10; 68:19; Acts 2:27; Eph. 4:9, signifies not a local descent of Christ's soul into hell, but properly the descent of his body into the tomb, and, by analogy, the descent of his soul into his sufferings and agonies. It is unnecessary to repeat what has been said on the same matter at Loc. XI, 89.

units.la: XXXIV. Ex his de Passionibus Christi universis in corpore & anima ejus, ad mortem usque crucis abundè liquet.
units.tr: XXXIV. From these things it is abundantly clear that all of Christ's sufferings, in body and in soul, extended even to the death of the cross.

units.la: Nam post cætera πκθήματα corpus ejus fractum, sanguis ejus effusus, adeóque verè ille mortuus est. Ad quam mortem corporis sanguinis, effusione testatam inprimis crucifixio comparata fuit, quia transverberatione, seu perfossione manuum & pedum, nec non aperto & perfosso latere, ex quo aqua & sanguis fluxit, peracta est. Quæ tamen sic violenta respectu hominum, naturalis respectu causarum fuit, ut voluntaria etiam fuerit respectu patientis, qui præter naturalem licet voluntatis suæ propensionem ea passus est, quæ naturali corporis constitutioni, indéque ortæ mentis proclivitati contrariabantur; spiritu tamen suo sponte libenterque, uti sponsorem decuit, passus fit, & lubens se invitum vicerit, atque illam naturæ imbecillitatem prolixa in hominis voluntate superaverit. Ecce venio, ut faciam voluntatem tuam, Psal. XL. 8.9. Zelus domus Domini consumpsit me, ibid. LXIX. 10. Nemo tollit vitam à me, sed ego pono vitam à me ipso, Joh. X. 18. Pro gaudio sibi proposito sustinuit crucem, Hebr. XII. 2. Neque corpus duntaxat mortem sustinuit, sed cruciatus graviores etiam, imò infernales, utpote peccato debitos, & sine quibus exantlatis liberatio nostra à potestate Diaboli & inferni non constitisset, anima ejus sustinuit, uti ea, quæ de agonibus ejus in horto & cruce diximus, comprobant.
units.tr: For, besides his other sufferings [παθήματα], his body was broken and his blood poured out, and so he truly died. The crucifixion was arranged chiefly to attest this death of the body by the shedding of blood, since it was carried out by piercing the hands and feet, and by the opened and pierced side, from which water and blood flowed. Yet this violence was violent with respect to men and natural with respect to the causes, and it was also voluntary with respect to the one who suffered. Although, beyond the natural inclination of his will, he endured things that were contrary to the natural constitution of the body and to the resulting disposition of the mind, he nevertheless suffered them of his own spirit, spontaneously and willingly, as a surety ought to do. He gladly conquered himself though unwilling, and by a prolonged exercise of the human will he overcame that weakness of nature. Behold, I come to do your will, Ps. 40:8-9. The zeal of your house has consumed me, ibid. 69:10. No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself, John 10:18. For the joy set before him he endured the cross, Heb. 12:2. Nor did his body alone undergo death, but his soul also underwent more severe torments, indeed infernal ones, as being owed to sin, and without his enduring these our deliverance from the power of the devil and of hell would not have been secured. This is confirmed by what we have said about his agonies in the garden and on the cross.

units.la: XXXV. Impiè hîc Pontificii nullas in Christo nisi corporales passiones agnoscunt; ideóque non patiuntur dici, animam Christi quicquam poenarum sustinuisse. Licet enim nonnulli saltem animam Christi rationalem suo modo in partem passionum admittant, sive per ἀσυλλήψιν assistentiam, sive per συμπάθειαν, sive per œconomiam, sive alia quapiam ratione; tamen eam ἰδίως proprie in se, & ex irae Dei sensu passam esse, omnes inficiantur; & animæ sensitivæ, seu inferiori, remota rationali & superiori, passiones omnes adscribunt. Verùm quas poenas peccati proprie dictas & essentiales meretur reus, eàdem haud dubiè Sponsor sustinuit, quia ea natura Sponsoris est, ut se in locum rei substituat, ac proinde sumatur tanquam reus. quod fieri nequit, si non obnoxius sit eidem cum reo damnationi. Ideo Scriptura dicit: Verè languores nostros ipse pertulit; & dolores nostros portavit, Ipse vulneratus est propter prævaricationes nostras, attritus propter iniquitates nostras, &c. Esaj. LIII. 4. 5. Atqui homines rei omnium confessione poenas non corporis duntaxat, sed etiam animæ rationalis merentur. Ergo eàdem sponsor sustinuit. Neque enim Redemptionis ratio tantùm a dignitate personæ pendet, ut jam vel minima poena, & uti loquuntur, unica sanguinis effusi guttula reparandis mille mundis sufficiat: sed etiam ab institutione Divina, quæ non sanguinis guttulam, sed integram mortem, ipsam inprimis maledictionem poposcit. Si enim sola circumcisione, in qua aliquot sanguinis guttæ effusæ sunt, redemptio perfecta est, quorsum crux ipsa? Per hanc tamen nos reconciliatos Scriptura Ephes. I. 16. dixit. Ideo Scriptura Christum tota anima, & omnibus ejus potentiis passum esse, testatur. Nam Christi animam tristantem, Matth. XXVI. 38. Marc. XIV. 34. cogitatione cruciatuum instantium turbatam, Joh. XII. 27. Voluntatem afflictam, Matth. XXVI. 39. testatur; & passiones internas animæ Christi, ceu sensum gravissimum irae Dei ac poenarum inferiorium pro generis humani peccatis.
units.tr: XXXV. Here the Papists impiously acknowledge no sufferings in Christ except bodily ones; therefore they do not allow it to be said that Christ's soul underwent any punishment. For although some at least admit Christ's rational soul in some way into a share of the sufferings, whether through ἀσυλλήψις [non-conception] assistance, or through συμπάθεια [sympathy], or through οἰκονομία [economy], or by some other manner, yet all of them deny that it suffered in itself, properly and of its own accord, from a sense of God's wrath. They ascribe all sufferings to the sensitive or lower soul, with the rational and higher soul set aside. But the punishments that the guilty person properly and essentially deserves for sin, the Surety undoubtedly underwent, because it is the nature of a surety to substitute himself in the place of the guilty and so to be reckoned as guilty. This cannot happen unless he is liable to the same condemnation as the guilty. Therefore Scripture says: Surely he has borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows. He was wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities, etc., Isa. 53:4-5. But all men, as all confess, deserve punishment not only of the body but also of the rational soul. Therefore the Surety underwent the same. For the manner of redemption depends not only on the dignity of the person, so that even the least punishment, and as they say, a single drop of spilt blood, would suffice to repair a thousand worlds; it depends also on the divine institution, which required not a drop of blood but the whole death, and above all the curse itself. For if redemption had been made complete by circumcision alone, in which some drops of blood were shed, why the cross itself? Yet Scripture says that through it we have been reconciled, Eph. 1:16. Therefore Scripture testifies that Christ suffered in his whole soul and in all its powers. For it testifies that Christ's soul was sorrowful, Matt. 26:38; Mark 14:34, troubled by the thought of impending torments, John 12:27, and his will was afflicted, Matt. 26:39. It testifies also to the inward sufferings of Christ's soul, as the most grievous sense of God's wrath and of the penalties of the lower sins, for the sins of the human race.

units.la: § 3 peccatis repræsentat. quod & Scripturæ aperta testimonia, & gradus ac partes passionum, velut horror & ἀδηλεια, pavor ingens, cum extrema dejectione & perturbatione conjunctus, Matth. XXVI.37. dolor, quo anima ejus ad mortem usque pressa fuit, ibid.v.38. lucta animæ & conscientiæ cum terroribus mortis æternæ, nondum aculeo suo spoliatæ; sed adhuc sævientis, Psal.XXII.2.3. LXIX.5.6. 1.Cor.XV.56. & causæ doloris ac horroris Christi, puta reputatio magnitudinis & gravitatis peccatorum totius mundi, quæ uni ipsi luenda incumbebant, Psal.LXIX.5.6. Joh.I.29. 1.Joh.II.2. & aspectus Dei summopere peccatis offensi, faciem misericordem occultantis, ipsum ad tempus deserentis, & nisi vindictam spirantis, Psalm. XXII.2.3. Esaj.LIII.5.&c. Gal.III.10.13. vehementer confirmant. Et pleraque hæc, cum ante crucem, & corporis passionem ullam accidenterint, non potuerunt non animam afficere. Quin & agones Christi ejusmodi describuntur, ut nullum illis æquale vel simile exemplum dari possit, cum dolores corporis illis supervenientes nulli fuerint, quin similes aliis, vel latronibus συνεσταυρωμένοις; & sæviores etiam longè Martyribus pluribus, inprimis illis, quos Nero Sarmentarios appellabat, & pro facibus in compitis statuebat; acciderint. Unde sequeretur, Christum iisdem, aut minoribus propositis doloribus, vehementius timuisse, longéque fuisse mollissimum mortalium & timidissimum. Non alia igitur tanti angoris causa, quàm Serpentis calcem ejus propter peccatum admordentis crudelissima tyrannis, & mortis imperium, quod adhuc dum ille obtinuerat, esse potuit. Fecit enim Deus, ut, qui non novit peccatum, fieret peccatum pro nobis, & hostia pro peccato nostro, 2.Cor.V.21. Neque illud obstat, quòd Christum ita timuisse voluntarie, non necessario Bellarminus objicit. Licet enim passiones voluntariè, non necessariò suscepta fuerint; tamen eædem ut φυσικὸν πάθος non voluntariæ sed naturales & violentæ fuerunt; perinde ut qui propter gangrænam membrum aliquod secari sustinent, sectionem volentes patiuntur; at inter secandum non jam voluntate, sed merè naturali necessitate dolent & timent. Quod in Christo inprimis precatio illa, qua & à removeri calicem, & fieri tamen non secundum voluntatem suam postulavit. Cùm enim voluntas non feratur nisi in bonum, ratio nulla patitur, ut dolorem vel timorem jam suscep-tum voluntarium dicamus, neque exemplum dari potest, quo quisquam quemquam voluntate timuisse constet. Et tribuitur quidem tota salus nostra morti & sanguini Christi, quia in ea facta est consummatio Sacerdotis; non soli tamen illi, sed etiam passionibus animæ אשם תשים נפשו Cùm posuerit animam suam pretium satisfactionis, videbit semen; מעמל נפשו propter laborem animæ suæ (obedientiam, amorem, compassionem, tristitiam, anxietatem, & ipsam mortem corporis, quæ sine dolore animæ exantlari non potuit) saturabitur, Esaj.LIII.10.11, animam meam pono pro ovibus meis, Joh.X.15. Cúmque sanguis Christi fusus fuerit cum sensu infinitæ iræ Dei adversus peccata, Psal.XXII.2.3. Hebr.V.7. &
units.tr: This also Scripture's clear testimonies and the degrees and parts of the sufferings strongly confirm: such as horror and ἀδηλία [anxiety], immense dread joined with extreme dejection and perturbation, Matt. 26:37; the grief by which his soul was pressed even unto death, ibid. v. 38; the struggle of the soul and conscience with the terrors of eternal death, not yet stripped of its sting but still raging, Ps. 22:2-3; 69:5-6; 1 Cor. 15:56; and the causes of Christ's grief and horror, namely the reckoning of the magnitude and gravity of the sins of the whole world, which were laid upon him alone to be paid for, Ps. 69:5-6; John 1:29; 1 John 2:2; and the sight of God, greatly offended by sins, hiding his merciful face, forsaking him for a time, and breathing nothing but vengeance, Ps. 22:2-3; Isa. 53:5, etc.; Gal. 3:10, 13. Since most of these arose before the cross and any bodily suffering, they could not but affect his soul. Indeed Christ's agonies are described in such a way that no equal or similar example can be given of them, since the bodily pains that came upon him were not unlike those of others, or of the thieves crucified with him, and in many Martyrs, especially those whom Nero called "torches" and set up as lights at the crossroads, they were even far more severe. From this it would follow that Christ feared more intensely under the same or lesser prospective pains, and was far the softest and most timid of mortals. Therefore there could be no other cause of so great anguish than the most cruel tyranny of the Serpent, who had bitten his heel on account of sin, and the dominion of death, which he still held. For God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, and a sacrifice for our sin, 2 Cor. 5:21. Nor does it stand in the way that Bellarmine objects that Christ feared voluntarily, not necessarily. For although the sufferings were undertaken voluntarily, not necessarily, yet as a φυσικὸν πάθος [natural passion] they were not voluntary but natural and violent. Just as those who submit to having a limb cut off on account of gangrene undergo the amputation willingly, yet during the cutting they grieve and fear not by will but by mere natural necessity. This applies especially to Christ in that prayer in which he asked that the cup be removed, and yet that it be done not according to his own will. For since the will is directed only to the good, no reason permits us to call a pain or fear already undergone voluntary, nor can an example be given of anyone who is known to have feared another by will. And indeed all our salvation is attributed to the death and blood of Christ, because in it the consummation of the Priest took place; yet not to that alone, but also to the sufferings of his soul, if you make his soul an offering for sin [אשם תשים נפשו], he shall see his seed; from the travail of his soul [מעמל נפשו] he shall be satisfied, Isa. 53:10-11 (by his obedience, love, compassion, sorrow, anxiety, and the death of his body itself, which could not be endured without the grief of his soul); I lay down my soul for my sheep, John 10:15. And since the blood of Christ was shed with a sense of God's infinite wrath against sins, Ps. 22:2-3; Heb. 5:7, and

units.la: XXXVI. Exinanitionis statum alter Exaltationis sequitur.
units.tr: XXXVI. The state of exinanition is followed by the state of exaltation.

units.la: Non enim Christus ἐνκατ-ᾶλαβή minorari, inferior fieri, formam servi sustinere in perpetuum debuit; sed ונפש בסגר ad parvum tempus, post quod exactum, gloria & honore coronandus fuit, Psal.VIII.6. Hebr.II.7. Debuit δικαιωθῆναι justificari, 1.Tim.III.16. Tergum meum percussoribus, & maxillas colaphizantibus dedi. Faciem meam non abscondi ab ignominia & sputo. Et Dominus Jehova auxiliabitur mihi; propterea non subterfugi perplexa; posui faciem meam instar silicis; קרוב מצדיק Prope est justificans me. Quis contendet mecum? Constiteramus unà: Quis adversarius meus? Accedat ad me. Ecce Dominus Jehova auxiliabitur mihi. Quis condemnabit me? Ecce omnes illi tanquam vestis antiquabuntur, tinea comedet illos, Esaj.L.6-9. Jam ut Filius, à Pontificibus & populo abnegatus, & Vas ac Mediator Testamenti (Hebr.VII.22.VIII.6.) consummatus est, ibid.II.10. Ut ἀρχηγὸς ζωῆς princeps vitæ, Act.III.15. non detineri à morte, sed ab ea vindicari, ibid.II.24. Vitam suis donare, regnare, seu potestatem obediendo acquisitam in Regno exercere, adeóque post passiones glorificari 1.Pet.I.11. publicè proponi, definitè Filius Dei & Princeps salutis denotari, compellari debuit; suffragante lege ipsa, quæ uti potentiam suam exercuerat adversus Sponsorem, execrationem factum; ita obedientiam ejus, ut Servi justi vita æterna & gloria humanitatis remunerari debuit. Proin glorificatio ejus personæ dignitatem obedientiæ, meritum, satisfactionis plenitudinem, justitiæ & Regni ejus jus consequitur. Hæc illa ὑψωσις, ἐξυψωσις exaltatio, superexaltatio, seu Christi ex statu humiliationis ignominioso in statum gloriosum, quem nunc in Cœlo obtinet, evectio & traductio est, contraria illi, qua in crucifixione ignominiosè ὑψωθεὶς exaltatus, ut serpens in ligno, Joh.III.14. VIII.28. XII.32.33. dicitur. Dextra Dei ὑψωθεὶς exaltatus est, Act.II.33. Deus Principem & Salvatorem ὑψωσε exaltavit dextra sua, ibid.V.31. Propterea Deus eum ὑπερυψωσεν superexaltavit, Phil.II.9. Quibus locis Exaltatio Deo, hoc est, Patri, & ejus dextræ, seu potentiæ tribuitur. Licet enim exaltationis illius efficientia sit à communi tribus Personis unica Divina omnipotentia, adeóque etiam ipsi Filio, Templum corporis sui excitanti, Joh.II.19. & similiter facienti, quæ Patrem facientem videt, ibid.V.19. ob communem, quam cum Patre & Spiritu S. habet, potentiam, jure asseratur: tamen Deo Patri in œconomia salutis appropriatur, quia jure & merito sententia Patris, ut judicis justificari debuit, Esaj.L.8. 1.Tim.III.16. In Christi enim gloria spectanda est non tantum potentia, per quam glorificatio ejus facta est, sed etiam gratia Dei & judicium sive demonstratio tum ejus, quod Deus nobis in Christo donavit: tum ejus, quod Christus secundum Legem consecutus est. Ad judicium referenda sunt verba Pauli: Διὸ Propterea superexaltavit eum Deus; Pater judex justificans. Ad gratiam verba, ἐχαρίσατο gratificatus est ei nomen super omne nomen, Phil.II.10. Ita Judicium & gratia in negotio salutis concurrunt. Justitia & judicium firmamentum. Gratia & veritas sunt ante faciem tuam, Psal.LXXXIX.15. Accedit, quod ut homo, ad Regnum Sacerdotale Mediatoris Divinitus vocari debuit, ut omnis mali species abesset, Hebr.V.4.
units.tr: For Christ ought not to be held down (ἐνκατ-ᾶλαβή), made lower, or to bear the form of a servant forever. Rather, his soul [was shut up] [ונפש בסגר] for a short time, and after that time was over he was to be crowned with glory and honour (Ps. 8:6; Heb. 2:7). He had to be justified (δικαιωθῆναι) (1 Tim. 3:16). I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair. I did not hide my face from shame and spitting. For the Lord GOD will help me, therefore I have not been confounded; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be ashamed. He is near who justifies me [קרוב מצדיק]. Who will contend with me? Let us stand together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord GOD will help me; who is he that shall condemn me? Lo, they all shall wax old like a garment; the moth shall eat them up. (Isa. 50:6-9). Now the Son, rejected by the priests and the people, has been completed as the Vessel and Mediator of the covenant (Heb. 7:22; 8:6), (Heb. 2:10). He was to be shown as the Prince of life (ἀρχηγὸς ζωῆς) (Acts 3:15), not to be held by death but to be freed from it (Acts 2:24). He was to give life to his own, to reign, or to exercise in his kingdom the power won by obedience, and so after his sufferings to be glorified (1 Pet. 1:11), to be publicly set forth, and to be definitely marked out as the Son of God and Prince of salvation. The law itself supported this: just as it had exercised its power against the Surety, making him a curse, so it had to reward his obedience with the eternal life and glory of a righteous servant in his humanity. Therefore the glorification of his person follows the dignity of his obedience, his merit, the fullness of his satisfaction, and the right of his justice and kingdom. This is that exaltation (ὑψωσις, ἐξυψωσις), or superexaltation, that is, the transfer and passage of Christ from the shameful state of humiliation to the glorious state which he now holds in heaven. It is the opposite of that exaltation by which he was lifted up in shame on the cross, as the serpent on the wood (John 3:14; 8:28; 12:32, 33). Being exalted (ὑψωθεὶς) at the right hand of God (Acts 2:33). God has exalted (ὑψωσε) his Prince and Saviour with his right hand (ibid. 5:31). Therefore God has super-exalted (ὑπερυψωσεν) him (Phil. 2:9). In these places exaltation is ascribed to God, that is, to the Father, and to his right hand or power. For although the efficient cause of that exaltation is the one divine omnipotence common to the three Persons, and so is rightly ascribed also to the Son himself, who raised up the temple of his body (John 2:19), and who does likewise what he sees the Father doing (ibid. 5:19), on account of the power he shares in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit, nevertheless in the economy of salvation it is appropriated to God the Father, because the sentence of the Father, as judge, had rightly and deservedly to justify him (Isa. 50:8; 1 Tim. 3:16). For in considering Christ's glory we must look not only at the power by which his glorification was effected, but also at the grace of God and the judgment, or demonstration, both of what God has given us in Christ and of what Christ obtained according to the law. Paul's words, Therefore God has superexalted him; the Father is the judge who justifies (Διὸ), are to be referred to the judgment. His words, he has graciously bestowed on him (ἐχαρίσατο) the name above every name (Phil. 2:10), are to be referred to grace. Thus judgment and grace concur in the business of salvation. Justice and judgment are the foundation; grace and truth go before your face (Ps. 89:15). Moreover, as man he had to be called by God to the priestly kingdom of the Mediator, so that every appearance of evil might be absent (Heb. 5:4).

units.la: XXXVII. Totus Christus exaltatus est communiter & indivise; sed gemina, distincta & inconfusa significatione; impropria secundum naturam Divinam, propria secundum humanam.
units.tr: XXXVII. The whole Christ was exalted in common and undivided; yet with a twofold, distinct and unconfused signification: improperly according to the divine nature, properly according to the human.

units.la: Divina enim natura ob beatitudinem immutabilem & infinitam, eminentissimam perfectionem, qua Deus verus & עליון Altissimus Psal.LXXXIX.28. XCVII.9. est, proprie exaltari, hoc est, altior fieri, in forma Dei; nunquam potuit, nec poterit. Potuit tamen exaltari impropriè, hoc est, altitudo ejus manifestari, apparere serenior in operationibus suis gloriosis potuit. Divinae proin naturae exaltatio est Majestatis ejusdem illustrissima patefactio, quae ex naturae humanae gloria, post perpessiones secuta, relucens plenissimo jubare radiat. Sicut autem exinanitio ejus secundum Divinitatem non in vera & propria naturae Divinae κατάβασιν descensione, sed in gratiosa συγκατάβασιν, qua formam servi assumpsit, & sub ejus velo gloriam & Majestatem suam ad tempus, raris & a plerisque neglectis scintillis ejus tum emicantibus, occultavit; constitit: sic ex adverso ejusdem exaltatio in depositione formae servi & tota plenitudine Deitatis ex carne in gloriam subvecta plenissimo fulgore emicantis, hoc est, quòd se gessit ἴσα Θεῷ instar Dei, conspicua fuit. Non ergo summum illud, ad quod sic exaltatus dicitur, fastigium noviter Christo datum, sed tantum ei, ut vero Deo Altissimo, vindicatum & in carne glorificata, rupto ejusdem velo, quod Divinitatis radios, quo minus se in ea exerant, ad tempus cohibuit, manifestatum est, juxta verba ipsius Christi: Glorifica me Pater, gloria illa, quam apud te habui, antequam mundus esset, Joh.XVII.5. Humanae naturae exaltatio in altitudinis, quam nunquam antehac habuit, acquisitione, & in statu humilis, vilis & abjecti supra modum cumulatissima, qualis in creaturam cadere potest, & gloriosa maxime commutatione consistit.
units.tr: For the divine nature, on account of its unchangeable and infinite blessedness and its most eminent perfection, by which it is the true God and עליון Most High (Ps. 89:28; 97:9), could never be exalted properly, that is, made higher, in the form of God, and never can be. Yet it could be exalted improperly, that is, its loftiness could be made manifest and it could appear more serene in its glorious operations. The exaltation of the divine nature is therefore the most illustrious disclosure of the same majesty, which, shining forth from the glory of the human nature that followed the sufferings, radiates with the fullest brilliance. Just as his exinanition according to the Godhead did not consist in a true and proper descent (κατάβασις) of the divine nature, but in a gracious condescension (συγκατάβασις), by which he assumed the form of a servant and for a time hid his glory and majesty under its veil, letting out only rare sparks, which many neglected, so on the other side his exaltation consisted in the laying aside of the form of a servant, and in the whole fullness of the Godhead carried up from the flesh into glory, shining with the fullest brightness. That is, he was made conspicuous in that he behaved ἴσα Θεῷ, as God. Therefore that highest dignity, to which he is said to be so exalted, was not newly given to Christ, but was claimed for him as the true and most high God, and it was made manifest in his glorified flesh when the veil was torn, the veil which had for a time restrained the rays of the Godhead from shining out in him, according to the words of Christ himself: Glorify me, Father, with the glory which I had with you before the world was (John 17:5). The exaltation of the human nature consists in its acquiring a height it never had before, and in a most glorious change from a state of humility, lowliness and abjection beyond measure, such as can befall a creature.

units.la: XXXVIII. Superexaltationem Christi, ejusdem exinanitioni & humiliationi usque ad mortem crucis oppositam S. Paulus in eo collocat, quòd Deus ei ἐχαρίσατο ὄνομα gratificatus est (vel gratum fecit dando) nomen illud, quod est super omne nomen, ut in nomine Jesu omne genu se flecteret supercoelestium & terrestrium, & eorum, qui sub terra sunt, & omnis lingua profiteatur, quod Dominus sit Jesus Christus, ad gloriam Patris, Phil.II.9.10.11. Ubi ὄνομα Nomen non tam magnam nominis fa- mam & celebritatem, quam Christo Scriptura etiam asserit, Psal.VIII.2. Esaj.XLI.6. XLIX.6. LII.15. LIII.12. quàm altitudinem & praecellentiam personae significat. Est enim ὄνομα διδόμενον ἐν ἀνθρώποις Nomen datum ei apud homines, in quo nos salvari oportet, Act.IV.12. Est nomen Ἰησοῦς Jesu, seu Jesu Christi Κυρίου Domini, uti Apostolus ipse definit. Quod verè ὄνομα ὑπὲρ πᾶν τὸ ὄνομα Nomen super omne Nomen, maximum & summum est. Ante eum, nominati alii sunt Reges, Filii, Sacerdotes, Mediatores, Pastores, Dii, Domini. Sed Christus est Rex & Dominus gloriae, 1.Cor.II.8. Solus potens, Rex regum, & Dominus dominantium, 1.Tim.VI.15. nactus nomen Filii διαφορώτερον praecellentius, quia ei dictum est: Tu es Filius meus, ego hodie genuite, Hebr.I.4. Psal.II.8. nominatus etiam Filius unigenitus, Joh.III.16. ἰδίου proprius, Rom.VIII.32. primogenitus Col.I.15.18. Sacerdos non gregarius aliquis, sed secundum ordinem Melchisedech, Psal.CX.4. Hebr.V.10. VI.20. VII.16.17. Sponsor & Mediator Testamenti melioris, aeterni, ibid.VII.22. VIII.6. XIII.20. Pastor ille bonus, Joh.X.14. ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ μέγας Pastor ille magnus, Hebr.XIII.20; Ἀρχιποίμην princeps Pastor, 1.Pet.V.4. אל Deus παντοκράτωρ omnipotens Esaj.IX.5. אלהים Deus absolutè, stans in coetu Dei, & inter Deos judicium agens, Psal.LXXXII.1. Deus Israelis, Esaj.XL.9. LII.7.10. imò יהוה Jehova, Esaj.XL.3.5. XLV.24.25. LII.8. φύσει Θεὸς natura Deus, Gal.IV.8. 2.Pet.I.4. quod ex oppositione 1.Cor.VIII.5.6. liquet. Nomen certè majus compellatione Deorum, quod nomen Angelis & Principibus populi datum est, non potest esse, nisi nomen Jehova. Nam is solus adorandus est, sicut ei, cui nomen super omne nomen datum est, omne genu se flectere debet; Psal.XCVII.7. Hebr.I.6. Ex comparatione igitur nominum Christi cum nominibus, quae Angelis & hominibus data sunt, quantum nomen super omne nomen Christo datum sit, facilè cognoscitur; nimirum simpliciter summum; & supra omne nomen, quod nominatur in seculo non praesenti duntaxat, sed etiam futuro, Ephes.I.21. Est enim ex Coelo, Dominus ex Coelo, ideòque ἐπάνω πάντων super omnes, Joh.III.31. 1.Cor.XV.47. Est super omne nomen cogitabile, adeòque ineffabile. Quod est Nomen ipsius, & Nomen Filii ejus, ut cognoscas? Prov.XXX.4. Accedit, quòd in nomine eo omne genu (eorum qui in Coelo, terra & infra terram sunt, hoc est, Angelorum, sanctorum Coelitum, velut Enochi, Eliae; in terra viventium, & sub terra in pulvere jacentium, qui secundum spiritum ἐπιγείων Coelestes sunt) se flectit (omnes adorant, gratias agunt, se subjiciunt, ut signatum per nomen signi intelligatur, & nonnulli etiam coram ipso judice, sententiam accipientes Rom.XIV.11. se incurvant) & omnis lingua confitetur, quòd Jesus Christus sit Dominus (omnis generis creaturae, quae loqui possunt, sive Angeli, sive homines; vel lingua & corde humili, cum voluntate Deo gratias agendi & gloriam dandi, velut homines ex omni gente & familia cum Deo foedus habentes; vel sola gloriae confessione, ut Angeli; vel ore saltem, licet non corde & integre, adeòque Deo mentiendo, velut ii, qui dicunt, Totus Christus communiter & indivise, sed gemina, distincta & inconfusa significatione exaltatus est. Christus exaltatus nomen super omne nomen accepit, ut in Jesu Christi & Domini nomine omne genu se flecteret. eunt, Domine, Domine, Matth. VII.21. vel inviti & dolentes in ultimo Judicio Jesum Christum Dominum confitentur) ad gloriam Dei Patris (ut is verus Deus, qui peccatoris Deus esse posset, & Pater Christi, in quo est Deus Abrahami & Seminis ejus, agnoscatur) Phil.II.10.11. Quæ verba posteriora ex Esaj.XLV.23. petita sunt. Ubi sic Deus: Per me juravi, ex ore meo justitia, verbum, quod non revertetur. Mihi se flectet omne genu, jurabit omnis lingua.
units.tr: XXXVIII. St. Paul places the superexaltation of Christ, set against his exinanition and humiliation even to the death of the cross, in this: that God gratified him with the name (ἐχαρίσατο ὄνομα), that is, made him a gift of grace by bestowing the name which is above every name, so that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord is Jesus Christ, to the glory of the Father (Phil. 2:9-11). Here name (ὄνομα) signifies not so much the great fame and renown of the name, which Scripture also ascribes to Christ (Ps. 8:2; Isa. 41:6; 49:6; 52:15; 53:12), as the height and pre-eminence of the person. For it is the name given to him among men, in which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). It is the name Jesus, or Jesus Christ, the Lord, as the Apostle himself defines it. This is truly the name above every name, the greatest and highest. Before him others were named kings, sons, priests, mediators, pastors, gods, lords. But Christ is the King and Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8), the only Potentate, the King of kings and Lord of lords (1 Tim. 6:15). He obtained the more excellent name of Son, because it was said to him: You are my Son, today I have begotten you (Heb. 1:4; Ps. 2:7); he is also named the only-begotten Son (John 3:16), his own (ἰδίου) (Rom. 8:32), the firstborn (Col. 1:15, 18). He is the priest not as some ordinary member, but according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. 110:4; Heb. 5:10; 6:20; 7:16, 17). He is the Surety and Mediator of the better, eternal covenant (ibid. 7:22; 8:6; 13:20). He is that good Shepherd (John 10:14), the great Shepherd (ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ μέγας) (Heb. 13:20), the Chief Shepherd (Ἀρχιποίμην) (1 Pet. 5:4). He is El (אל), God Almighty (παντοκράτωρ) (Isa. 9:5); Elohim (אלהים), God absolutely, standing in the assembly of God and judging among the gods (Ps. 82:1); the God of Israel (Isa. 40:9; 52:7, 10); and indeed Jehovah (יהוה) (Isa. 40:3, 5; 45:24, 25; 52:8); God by nature (φύσει Θεὸς) (Gal. 4:8; 2 Pet. 1:4), as is clear from the contrast in 1 Cor. 8:5, 6. Certainly no name greater than the appellation of gods, which is given to angels and princes of the people, can exist, except the name Jehovah. For he alone is to be adored, and to him to whom the name above every name has been given, every knee must bow (Ps. 97:7; Heb. 1:6). From the comparison, then, of the names of Christ with the names given to angels and men, it is easily recognised how great the name above every name given to Christ is: namely, simply the highest, and above every name that is named not only in the present age but also in the age to come (Eph. 1:21). For he is from heaven, the Lord from heaven, and therefore above all (ἐπάνω πάντων) (John 3:31; 1 Cor. 15:47). He is above every conceivable name, and therefore ineffable. What is his name, and the name of his Son, that you may know? (Prov. 30:4). Moreover, in that name every knee (of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth, that is, of angels, of the holy inhabitants of heaven, such as Enoch and Elijah; of the living on earth, and of those lying in the dust under the earth, who are heavenly according to the spirit, ἐπιγείων) bows (all adore, give thanks, subject themselves, as is understood by the sign named in the name; and some also, standing before the judge and receiving sentence, bow themselves, Rom. 14:11), and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord (every kind of creature that can speak, whether angels or men; either with a humble tongue and heart, with the will to give thanks to God and to give him glory, as men of every nation and family who have a covenant with God; or by confession of his glory alone, as angels do; or at least with the mouth, though not with the heart and wholly, and so lying to God, as those who say, Lord, Lord, Matt. 7:21; or unwillingly and sorrowfully confessing Jesus Christ as Lord at the last judgment) to the glory of God the Father (so that he may be acknowledged as the true God, who could be the God of the sinner, and as the Father of Christ, in whom is the God of Abraham and of his seed) (Phil. 2:10, 11). These last words are taken from Isa. 45:23, where God says: By myself I have sworn; from my mouth goes forth righteousness, a word that shall not return. To me every knee shall bow; every tongue shall swear.

units.la: XXXIX. Nomen isthoc supra omne Nomen, puta Jesu (Salvatoris) Christi (Messiæ, Uncti) Domini (Jehovæ facti populo suo in Deum, Regem, caput) Christo donatum, Phil.II.9. datum, Act.IV.12. hoc est, in plena vi, & emphasi vindicatum est post exinanitionem ad mortem usque crucis: ita ut exinanitio & humiliatio usque ad crucem præstita sit Altitudinis & gloriæ dati nominis illius causa. Licet enim Nominis supra omne nomen absolute nulla causa sit, quia summa Dei Majestas & præcellentia ipsa Deitas, cujus causa nulla datur, est: tamen relate ad id, ad quod se Nomen illud Salvatoris & Domini extendit, & propter quod Nomen illud Christo, à Deo Patre gratificante, dante assertum est, causam habere potest. puta opus aliquod œconomicum, quod meriti ad Altitudinem & Nomen illud habet. Quo pertinet particula Dio, Propterea superexaltavit eum, Phil.II.9. quæ sic rationalis est, ut simul causalis sit, quia rationem Altitudinis & Nominis ex causa ejusdem meritoria, obedientia ad mortem usque crucis arcessit. Nam & superexaltatio ea spontanea fuit, cum Christus sine raptu potuerit esse ἴσα Θεῷ ad instar Dei, & in forma Dei fuerit, adeoque Deus propter veritatem & manifestationem illius eum superexaltavit, cum veritatem abnegare, & non justificare Filium suum, à Principibus & populo abnegatum non potuerit: & Christus Deo Patri obedivit usque ad mortem crucis, justumque adeo servum se demonstravit, cui Deus justus judex non potuit non obedientiæ suæ præmium. & mercedem retribuere: & obedivit præcepto, quod Deus ei imposuit ex gratia non erga Filium, sed erga homines; juxta præceptum illud se ipsum exinaniens, formam servi accipiens, ex gratia Patris sub Lege factus, & gratia eadem Dei Patris mortem gustans pro omnibus, Hebr.II.9. & sensus, sententia ejus, propter quam se exinanivit (Phil.II.5.7.) frustra, sine operæ suæ pretio esse non potuit. Alias in vanum vim suam consumpsisset, & humiliatio ejus insipiens fuisset. Ideo Deus ipsi sortem suam sustentavit, Psal. XVI.5. & operæ suæ pretium retribuit. Ego dixi (ἀνθρώπινον) in vanum laboravi, in cassum & frustra vim meam consumpsi. Certe (hæc διόρθωσις est) judicium meum est apud Dominum, & operæ meæ pretium cum Deo meo, Esaj.XLIX.4. Sicut porro Christus ex pacto ab æterno cum Patre inito nobis vitam æternam promeruit: ita sibi Nomen super omne nomen Jesu, Salvatoris & Domini, adeoque simul populum, peculium, cujus Salvator Dominus esset, cujus salutem in hac vita curaret, & quem æterna gloria ornaret, promeruit. Dedit semetipsum pro nobis, ut nos liberaret ab omni injustitia, & purgaret sibi populum peculiarem, qui cum zelo bona opera prosequeretur, Tit.II.14. Neque potuit sibi mereri peculium, quin eo ipso dignitatem eam promereretur, ut peculii illius Jesus Salvator, Dominus, Rex & Caput esset.
units.tr: XXXIX. This name above every name, namely Jesus (Saviour), Christ (Messiah, the Anointed), Lord (Jehovah, made by his people God, King and Head), was given to Christ, Phil. 2:9, and granted, Acts 4:12. That is, it was vindicated in full power and emphasis after his self-emptying unto the death of the cross, so that the self-emptying and humiliation, even unto the cross, were undertaken for the sake of the height and glory of the name given to him. For although the name above every name has no cause absolutely, since the supreme majesty and pre-eminence of God, which is the Deity itself, has no cause, nevertheless relatively to that to which the name of Saviour and Lord extends, and on account of which that name was asserted to be given to Christ by God the Father bestowing it, it can have a cause: namely some economic work that has merit toward that height and name. To this belongs the particle "Dio" (therefore), in "Therefore God highly exalted him," Phil. 2:9. It is so rational that it is also causal, because it derives the reason for the height and the name from its meritorious cause, obedience unto the death of the cross. For that superexaltation was also voluntary, since Christ could have been "equal to God" [ἴσα Θεῷ] without robbery, and was in the form of God. God therefore exalted him on account of the truth and manifestation of this, since he could not deny the truth or fail to justify his Son, who had been denied by the princes and the people. Christ obeyed God the Father unto the death of the cross and so showed himself a just servant, to whom God, the just judge, could not but repay the wage of his obedience. He obeyed the precept that God laid upon him out of grace, not toward the Son but toward men. According to that precept he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, was made under the Law by the grace of the Father, and by the same grace of God the Father tasted death for everyone, Heb. 2:9. His purpose, for which he emptied himself (Phil. 2:5-7), could not be in vain or without the worth of his work; otherwise he would have spent his strength to no purpose, and his humiliation would have been foolish. Therefore God upheld his lot, Ps. 16:5, and repaid the worth of his work. "I said: I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing and to no purpose" (human speech). Surely (this is a correction) my judgment is with the Lord, and the worth of my work with my God, Isa. 49:4. Moreover, just as Christ merited eternal life for us by the covenant entered into with the Father from eternity, so he merited for himself the name above every name, Jesus, Saviour and Lord, and at the same time a people, a peculiar possession, whose Saviour and Lord he would be, whose salvation he would care for in this life, and whom he would adorn with eternal glory. He gave himself for us, that he might free us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself a peculiar people, zealous for good works, Titus 2:14. Nor could he have merited a peculiar people for himself without at the same time meriting the dignity by which Jesus would be their Saviour, Lord, King and Head.

units.la: XL. Neque illud obstat, quod & Deus Pater Christo Nomen illud supra omne nomen εχαρίσατο gratificatus est, vel donavit, Phil.II.9. & Deus ὑπερυψωσεν nullius rei indigus Act.XVII.25. nihil sibi acquirere, vel mereri dici potest. Præterquam enim quod χαρίζεσθαι non tantum gratificari, donare, sed etiam rem gratam, sive commeritam, sive immeritam facere, nec non largiri significat: etiam compellatio hominis Jesu, qua compellatus est Dominus, est consequens gratiæ tum illius, qua voluit Filium habere tabernaculum ex carne hostra, adeoque incarnari, cum mera gratia & Δόξα beneplacitum Dei fuerit, quod caro in unitatem Personæ assumpta est: tum illius etiam, qua eundem, ut vadem nostrum, & sic nostrum, propter nostram, non suam justitiam, ταπεινῶσαι humiliari voluit. Fuit igitur gratia respectu tum carnis Christi, in qua omnis plenitudo talis Dei habitare, & se gloriose manifestare, exerere voluit: tum Electorum, quorum gratia Deus Pater Christum in toto mundo nominavit, & nominari fecit nomine excellentissimo, quo nullum nomen majus est, nempe ut omnis lingua ei, ceu Domino, juret, & omne genu in nomine ejus se flectat; non respectu obedientiæ & consequentis superexaltationis. Non enim Deus Pater obedientiam Filii, ceu ἀνίσον inæqualem, & non satis τίμιον pretiosam ex gratia mera remuneratus est, sed tum ex pacto, tum ex condignitate obedientiæ operis, quod infinita potentia sua Christus operatus est. qua operatione plane id meruit, ut Nomen super omne nomen Salvatoris, & Domini acquireret, & simul populum, hæreditatem & Regnum suum haberet. Nihil proin sibi quà Deo proprie acquisivit, sed quicquid obedientia sua omni acquisivit, gloriæ, tum sibi quà Deo improprie per manifestationem Nominis sui & flexionem omnium genuum coram ipso: tum carni gloria, quam ante non habuit, coronatæ, cum Filio Dei, habente. Nomen super omne nomen, & illud simul exercenti, unitæ, ejusque in se ἐνέργειαν experienti: & πωτικα super creaturas reliquas omnes adeptæ, Psal.VIII. 6.7. tum electis, quorum saluti præcellentissimum illud Nomen Jesu & Domini unicè prodesse & velificari debuit. Sed plura etiam eam in rem Loc.XI.27-31. diximus.
units.tr: XL. Nor does it stand in the way that God the Father is also said to have graciously bestowed [ἐχαρίσατο] on Christ that name above every name, or to have given it, Phil. 2:9, or that God highly exalted [ὑπερύψωσεν] him, Acts 17:25, though he needs nothing, and so nothing can be said to be acquired or merited by God for himself. For apart from the fact that χαρίζεσθαι signifies not only to show favour, to give, but also to make a thing pleasing, whether merited or unmerited, and also to bestow freely, the very address of the man Jesus, by which he is addressed as Lord, follows from grace: both from that grace by which God willed the Son to have a tabernacle of our flesh, and so to be incarnate, since it was by sheer grace and the good pleasure of God that the flesh was assumed into the unity of the Person; and also from that grace by which he willed the same man to be humbled [ταπεινῶσαι] as our surety, and thus on account of our righteousness and not his own. There was therefore grace with respect both to the flesh of Christ, in which he willed all the fullness of such a God to dwell and to display and manifest himself gloriously, and to the elect, for whose sake God the Father named Christ in the whole world and caused him to be named with the most excellent name, than which there is none greater, namely that every tongue should swear to him as to Lord, and every knee bow in his name. It was not with respect to obedience and the consequent superexaltation. For God the Father did not reward the obedience of the Son, as unequal [ἀνίσον] and not sufficiently precious [τίμιον], out of mere grace; but both by covenant and by the condignity of the work of obedience, which Christ performed by his infinite power. By that work he plainly merited that he should acquire the name above every name of Saviour and Lord, and at the same time have a people, an inheritance and a kingdom. Therefore he acquired nothing for himself as God properly, but whatever he acquired by his obedience, he acquired of glory: for himself as God improperly, through the manifestation of his name and the bowing of every knee before him; and for the flesh, which before had no glory, now crowned, united with the Son of God who has the name above every name, and who exercises it at the same time, and experiences its energy in himself; and it obtained dominion [πωτικα] over all the remaining creatures, Ps. 8:6-7; and for the elect, for whose salvation that most excellent name of Jesus and Lord ought to benefit and profit alone. But we have said more on this matter at Loc. 11, 27-31.

units.la: XLI. Sicut superexaltatio, ita etiam Donatio Nominis supra omne Nomen toti Personæ Christi Dei & Hominis facta est. Tota enim Persona θεανθρώπως Jesus Christus, Dominus est; adeoque gloriam Nominis illius participat. Licet enim mera creatura Nomine eo supra omne nomen compellari non possit, adeoque humana Christi natura seorsim & simpliciter Nomen supra omne nomen non possideat, quia creaturæ cujuslibet nomen altius aliud habere potest, & nihil in creatura tam perfectum fieri potest, quin fieri perfectius possit, cum Dei volun-
units.tr: XLI. Just as the superexaltation, so also the bestowal of the name above every name was made to the whole Person of Christ, God and man. For the whole Person, Jesus Christ, is God-man [θεανθρώπως] and Lord, and so participates in the glory of that name. For although a mere creature cannot be addressed by that name above every name, and so the human nature of Christ, taken separately and simply, does not possess the name above every name, since any creature can have some other, higher name, and nothing in a creature can be made so perfect that it cannot be made more perfect, with the will of

units.la: Non obstante eo, quòd Deus Pater Nomen ipsi hoc Christo gratificatum dicitur. voluntate sit, quicquid est, & quantumcunque dignitatis accipiat, nihilominus finitum semper maneat: tamen Nominis illius supra omne nomen, puta Jesu, Christi, Domini mensuram nec Christus Deus sine homine, nec Christus homo sine Deo implet. Est enim in eo communio sicut officii, ita & gloriæ. Sed in gloriæ illius communione & πλεωσει utrique naturæ tribuendum est, quod suum est: Divinæ quod Divinum: Humanæ quod humanum est, cum communione alterius. Divina enim natura Nomen habet supra omne nomen creatum simpliciter, adeoque etiam supra nomen ipsius naturæ humanæ, quæ omnem gloriam & περιπρηματα sua à Divina habet: Humana vero non simpliciter Nomen super omne nomen creatum habet, quia & ipsa creatura est; & se ipsa altius nomen habere, vel ὑπάνω πάντων super omnia (Joh.III.31.) esse non potest; sed κατὰ τὴν super nomen & gloriam Angelorum & hominum. Ideo in nomine Jesu, hoc est, Personæ, quæ Jesus est, sic omne genu se flectit, ut tamen γονυπετία & adoratio illa non in carne, sed in persona carnem habente, & in eo, quod in persona Θεου Divinum summum & plane ἀπειρον est, terminetur.
units.tr: Notwithstanding that God the Father is said to have bestowed this name on Christ as a gift: whatever it is, and however much dignity he receives, it always remains finite, by the will of God. Yet neither Christ as God without man nor Christ as man without God fills the measure of that name above every name, namely Jesus, Christ, Lord. For there is a communion in him of office and likewise of glory. But in the communion of that glory, each nature must be credited with what is its own in the fullness of the other: the Divine with what is Divine, the human with what is human, with communion of the other. For the divine nature has a name above every created name simply, and so also above the name of the human nature itself, which has all its glory and honours from the Divine. The human nature, however, does not have a name above every created name simply, because it too is a creature; nor can it have a higher name by itself, or be above all (John 3:31); but it is above the name and glory of angels and men only in a relative sense. Therefore in the name of Jesus, that is, of the Person who is Jesus, every knee so bows that the kneeling and that adoration terminate not in the flesh but in the Person who has the flesh, and in that which, in the Person of God, is the supreme Divinity and entirely infinite.

units.la: XLII. Exaltationis Christi Gradus tres sunt, Resurrectio ex mortuis, Ascensio in Coelum, & Sessio ad dextram Patris, quorum postremus proprie & κατ' ἐξοχὴν dicta Exaltatio, vel superexaltatio est. Sed omnes tamen gradus totidem Christi gloriæ sunt. Spiritus Christi ante testificatus est passiones ei obventuras, καὶ τὰς μετὰ ταῦτα δόξας & glorias, quæ post eas, 1.Pet.I.11. XLIII. De tempore resurrectionis Christi confitemur in Symbolo: Tertia die resurrexit à mortuis. quod cum Christi prædictionibus, & Evangelii Historia convenit. Δεῖ τὴν τρίτην ἡμέραν ἐγερθῆναι. Oportet ipsum tertio die resurgere, Matth.XVI.21. Τῇ τρίτῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἀνασταται Tertia die resurget, Matth.XX.19. Parasceves Sabbathi, quæ Veneris dies erat, vespera sepulchro illatus, in eo quievit toto die Sabbathi, & ὀψὲ σαββάτων, τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ εἰς μίαν σαββάτων vespera Sabbathorum, quæ in primam sabbathorum diluscesebat, venit Maria Magdalena, & altera Maria ad sepulchrum ut spectarent. &c. Matth.XXVIII.1. Marcus dicit: διαγενομένου σαββάτου exacto sabbatho, & λίαν πρωΐ valde mane primæ Sabbathorum, cum Sol exoriretur, hoc est, vix exorto sole, cum primo sole, cap.XVI.1.2. Lucas, τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων, ὄρθρου βαθέως Prima sabbathorum profundo diluculo, cap.XXIV.1. Johannes: τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων πρωΐ, σκοτίας ἔτι οὔσης Prima Sabbathorum mane, cum adhuc essent tenebræ, cap.XX.1. Quod Matthæus dixit, ὀψὲ σαββάτων vesperâ Sabbathorum, id Hebræi dicerent במוצאי שבת in exitibus Sabbathi, vel, uti in Avodah Zarah appellatur במוצאי שבת in exitu Sabbathi; hoc est, tempore, quo Sabbathum exiverat, finitum fuerat, seu noctë tota Sabbathum sequente. Solebant enim Hebræi religionis gratia de die sequente profesto assumere ad festum, hoc est, Sabbathi sanctificationem ultra tempus Lege definitum longius protrahere. Idem Matthæus ἐπιφωσκουσαν εἰς μίαν diluescentem subintellige, νύκτα noctem, vel ὥρᾳ horam in primam sabbathorum, hoc est, diluculum primæ sabbathorum, seu initium primæ Sabbathorum dixit. Nam à mane ad mane Hebræi dies computabant; Licèt Sabbatha & festa à vespera inciperent. Resurrexit ergo Christus primo mane, seu diluculo diei primæ Sabbathorum, seu Κυριακὴς Dominicæ, sic dictæ ab Ecclesia ob resurrectionem Domini in diem eum incidentem, Apoc.I.10. Unde Thalmudici etiam יום נוצרים Diem Christianorum vocant. In Lege מחרת השבת postridie Sabbathi dicitur dies, quo in Paschate manipulus offerri debuit. In Paschate hoc πλεωπικῶ evenit, ut postridie Sabbathi esset secundus dies Festi, quo Christus resurrexit, ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων primitiæ resurgentium 1.Cor.XV.20. & apud discipulos suos, qui verum ejus Templum erant, apparuit, iisque lucem ac cibum paratum præstitit, quemadmodum manipulo oblato, cibus in agro omnibus paratus, & sanctificata omnia erant. XLIV. Tempus illud resurrectionis Christi in V.T. & Oraculo & typo præfinitum est. Oraculum extat Hos.VI.2. יחיינו vivificabit nos (caput & corpus) post biduum ביום השלישי יקמנו die tertia suscitabit nos, & vivemus in conspectu ejus. Ubi unâ cum consolatione, qua Ecclesia in spe propinquæ liberationis se erigit, bàsis consolationis, mysterium futuræ olim resurrectionis ex mortuis, cujus fides ex Psal.XVI. in Ecclesia decantata erat, indicatur: quia nudè de corpore Christi mystico verborum in Hosea sensus literalis non constaret. Typus fuit Jonas; ab ipso Christo sic explicatus; sicut Jonas in ceti utero fuit tres dies & tres noctes: ita Filius hominis erit in corde terræ tres dies & tres noctes, Matth.XII.40. Jon.II.1.2. Ubi ἡμέρας καὶ νύκτα dies & nox ponitur pro die civili, seu νυχθημέρῳ; quod Daniel.VIII.4. ערב בקר verspera mane dicitur, quomodo τρίτῃ νυχθημέρῳ in terræ corde Christus egit συνεδοχῶς; primum die Veneris, parte ejus extrema: secundum die Sabbathi toto: tertium initio diei Solis, adeoque parte quadam diei Solis. Ut necessum non sit vel cum Viro Doctissimo Wilhelmo Teelingio in Melet. Catech. dicere, Christum in corde terræ fuisse ex illo tempore, quotactus sensu iræ Divinæ ἐπεσεν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς procidit in terram, Marc.XIV.3 f. hoc est inde à nocte diei Jovis, qua proditus Christus, humi prostratus & velut in pulvere mortis poni cœpit, Psal. XXII.16. usque ad initium diei Solis; vel cum altero Chronologo percelebri Wilhelmo Langio, libro de Anno Christi, à communi sententia facere divortium, & passionem Domini in diem Jovis, non Veneris transferre. Non enim his assertionibus proprietatem verborum Christi sic tueri possunt, quin & ipsi saltem in ultimo die synecdochen agnoscere teneantur. Fabulam porro, non historiam Ambrosius de Interpell. lib.I:5. prodidit, asserens, tres dies & tres noctes Jesum inter mortuos fuisse, sed citius tamen, quàm trium dierum & noctium intervalla patiuntur, triduo & trinoctio à Sole abbreviato, ex mortuis resurrexisse. Aptius non-nihil alii tridui initium in hora illa, quia in cruce exaltatus, è terra viventium sublatus est: ex qua In V.T. prædictum Oraculo & typo Jonæ tres dies & tres noctes in utero ceti latentis præambulum est; Quo sensu Filius hominis tres dies & tres noctes in corde terræ existerit? qua hora ad resurrectionem usque ter visus Sol est, & ter fuerunt tenebræ miraculosis illis intervenientibus. Sed nihil attinet ἐνσήμων similibus calculum addere, cùm convenientius Scripturæ dicamus, Christum non mathematicè, sed πεχυλῶς, recepta vulgo catachresi synecdochica, supra explicata, locutum esse. Similis catachresis est in numerandis diebus azymorum, qui alibi septem, at Deut.XVI.8. sex definiuntur: nec non in locis Matth.XVII.1. & Luc. IX.28. Ubi Christus transfiguratus priore loco post dies sex, id posteriore post ὡσεὶ ὀκτὼ circiter octo dicitur. Facit huc traditio R. Eliezeris Ben Azariæ in Hierof. Schab. sol. 12. יום ולילה עונה ומקצת עונה ככולה Dies & nox constituunt totum; & pars totius est sicut totum. Sed nihil tamen vetat, quò minùs partim proprie, partim analogicè tria νυχθημερον integra sine synecdoche etiam explicentur; ut terminus à quo sit vespera Coenæ; terminus ad quem vespera diei solis, qua primùm discipuli recreati sunt, cùm hactenus Jesus in illorum cordibus veluti mortuus fuerit. Tanto enim spatio partim verè corpore suo fuit in corde terræ, partim analogicè, lucans cum potestate tenebrarum, & adhuc in discipulis suis mortuus. Ita inferiora terræ Psal.CXXXIX.15. fovea, status inter mortuos, sepulchrum, tenebræ, Psal.LXXXVIII. 5.6.7.19. analogicè dicuntur.
units.tr: XLII. Christ's exaltation has three stages: his resurrection from the dead, his ascension into heaven, and his sitting at the right hand of the Father.
