The last of these is properly and par excellence called the Exaltation, or superexaltation. Yet all the stages are equally marks of Christ's glory. The Spirit of Christ testified beforehand the sufferings that were to come upon him, and the glories that would follow them [καὶ τὰς μετὰ ταῦτα δόξας], 1 Pet. 1:11. XLIII. We confess in the Creed the time of Christ's resurrection: On the third day he rose from the dead. This agrees with Christ's predictions and with the history of the Gospel. He must rise on the third day [Δεῖ τὴν τρίτην ἡμέραν ἐγερθῆναι], Matt. 16:21. On the third day he will rise [Τῇ τρίτῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἀνασταται], Matt. 20:19. He was laid in the tomb on the evening of the Preparation, which was the Friday, and he rested in it the whole day of the Sabbath. Late on the Sabbath [ὀψὲ σαββάτων], as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week [τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ εἰς μίαν σαββάτων], that is, on the evening of the Sabbaths, which was dawning into the first of the Sabbaths, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to look at the sepulchre, etc., Matt. 28:1. Mark says: When the Sabbath was past [διαγενομένου σαββάτου], and very early [λίαν πρωΐ] on the first day of the Sabbaths, when the sun was rising, that is, scarcely after sunrise, at the first light, ch. 16:1-2. Luke says: on the first of the Sabbaths [τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων], at deep dawn [ὄρθρου βαθέως], ch. 24:1. John says: on the first of the Sabbaths [τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων] early in the morning, while it was still dark [σκοτίας ἔτι οὔσης], ch. 20:1. What Matthew called late on the Sabbath [ὀψὲ σαββάτων], the Hebrews would call at the going out of the Sabbath [במוצאי שבת], or, as it is named in Avodah Zarah, at the going out of the Sabbath [במוצאי שבת]; that is, the time when the Sabbath had gone out and was ended, or the whole night following the Sabbath. For the Hebrews, out of religious scruple, were accustomed to take on the following ordinary day as part of the festival, that is, to prolong the sanctification of the Sabbath beyond the time defined by the Law. Matthew likewise, by dawning into one [ἐπιφωσκουσαν εἰς μίαν], is to be understood as supplying night [νύκτα] or hour [ὥρᾳ]: he meant the dawn of the first of the Sabbaths, that is, the daybreak or beginning of the first of the Sabbaths. For the Hebrews counted their days from morning to morning, although Sabbaths and festivals began at evening. Christ therefore rose early in the morning, at the daybreak of the first day of the Sabbaths, that is, the Lord's Day (Κυριακή), so called by the Church because the Lord's resurrection fell on that day, Rev. 1:10. Hence the Talmudists also call it the day of the Christians [יום נוצרים]. In the Law, the day on which the sheaf had to be offered in the Passover is called the day after the Sabbath [מחרת השבת]. In this Passover it happened, by a fitting arrangement, that the second day of the feast, the day on which Christ rose, fell on the day after the Sabbath, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep [ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων], 1 Cor. 15:20. And he appeared to his disciples, who were his true Temple, and provided them with light and food, just as, when the sheaf was offered, food was prepared in the field for all, and everything was made holy. XLIV. That time of Christ's resurrection was fixed in the Old Testament both by oracle and by type. The oracle is in Hos. 6:2: He will revive us [יחיינו] (head and body) after two days; on the third day he will raise us up [ביום השלישי יקמנו], and we shall live in his sight. Here, together with the consolation by which the Church lifts herself up in hope of imminent deliverance, the basis of that consolation is indicated: the mystery of the future resurrection from the dead, whose faith had been sung in the Church from Ps. 16. For the literal sense of the words in Hosea did not clearly refer to the mystical body of Christ alone. The type was Jonah, explained thus by Christ himself: As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so the Son of man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights, Matt. 12:40; Jonah 2:1-2. Here day and night [ἡμέρας καὶ νύκτα] is used for a civil day, or a day and a night [νυχθημέρῳ). Compare Dan. 8:14, where evening and morning [ערב בקר] is spoken of. So Christ spent three days and nights [τρίτῃ νυχθημέρῳ] in the heart of the earth by synecdoche: the first on Friday, in its last part; the second on the whole Sabbath; the third at the beginning of Sunday, and so part of that day. Thus there is no need either, with the most learned Wilhelm Teelinck in his Melet. Catech., to say that Christ was in the heart of the earth from that time when, in the sense of divine wrath, he fell to the ground [ἐπεσεν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς], Mark 14:35, that is, from the night of Thursday, when Christ was betrayed and began to be laid prostrate on the ground and as if in the dust of death, Ps. 22:16, until the beginning of Sunday; nor, with the other very famous chronologer Wilhelm Lange, in his book on the year of Christ, to depart from the common opinion and move the passion of the Lord to Thursday rather than Friday. For by such assertions they cannot defend the proper sense of Christ's words; they too are bound at least on the last day to acknowledge a synecdoche. Ambrose, in De Interpellatione I.5, gives us a fable rather than a history, asserting that Jesus was among the dead for three days and three nights, but nevertheless rose from the dead sooner than the intervals of three days and nights allow, the triduum and trinoctium having been shortened by the Sun. Others have more aptly placed the beginning of the three days at that hour when, being lifted up on the cross, he was taken from the land of the living; from that hour the sign of Jonah, foretold in the Old Testament oracle and type, of three days and three nights lying hidden in the belly of the whale, was the prelude. In what sense, then, did the Son of man exist in the heart of the earth three days and three nights? From the hour of crucifixion until the resurrection the Sun was seen three times, and three times there was darkness, those miraculous events intervening. But it is pointless to add a reckoning of signs and equivalents to the similar reckonings; rather, we say more suitably to Scripture that Christ spoke not mathematically but roughly [πεχυλῶς], using the synecdochical catachresis commonly accepted and explained above. A similar catachresis occurs in counting the days of unleavened bread, which elsewhere are defined as seven but in Deut. 16:8 as six; and likewise in Matt. 17:1 and Luke 9:28, where Christ, transfigured, is said in the former place to be transfigured after six days, and in the latter after about eight days. The tradition of Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah in Jerusalem Shabbat, sol. 12, belongs here: Day and night make up a whole, and a part of a period is like the whole period; and a part of the whole is as the whole. Nevertheless nothing forbids that the three entire days and nights be explained partly properly and partly analogically, without synecdoche: the starting point being the evening of the Supper, and the end point the evening of Sunday, when the disciples were first refreshed, since until then Jesus had been as if dead in their hearts. For during so long a space he was partly truly in the heart of the earth in his body, and partly analogically, lying in the power of darkness and still dead in his disciples. So also the lower parts of the earth (Ps. 139:15), the pit, the state among the dead, the sepulchre, darkness (Ps. 88:5-7, 19) are spoken of analogically.

units.la: XLV. Vis illa, qua Christus resuscitatus est, fuit Potentia infinita, seu ἐνέργεια & κράτος τῆς ἰσχύος efficacitas roboris virium Dei, Ephes. I.19. eaque Filii & Patris. Filii, quia πνεῦμα ἀμωμονῆς Spiritu Sanctitatis suo, Rom.I.4. 1.Pet. III.18. eo videlicet, quo in diebus Noæ praedicatum ivit, ibid.v.19. resuscitatus est. Potestatem habeo ponendi animam, & potestatem habeo recipiendi eam, Joh.X.18. Solvite Templum hoc, & intra tres dies resuscitabo illud, ibid.II.19. quod dixisse eum de ναῷ & σώματος, Templo corporis sui mox v.21. additur. Excitavit enim suum, & ut בנה היכל יהוה structor templi Domini, Zach. VI.12. Domus Dei, Hebr.III.3-6. ut Spiritus vivificans, 1.Cor.XV.45. Ut vitam in se habens, Joh.V.26. Deus potens & Victor Esaj.IX. 7. qui tuba Dei & κελευσματι celeusmate mortuos vivificat, 1.Thess.IV.16. Patris eadem potentia fuit, cui inprimis Christi resuscitatio tribuitur. Nam Deus Domini nostri Jesu Christi, Pater gloriæ, efficacitatem roboris virium suarum exeruit in Christo, resuscitans eum ex mortuis, Ephes.I.17.19.20. Quem Deus (Pater) resuscitavit, solvens dolores mortis, Act.II.24. Hunc Jesum suscitavit Deus, ibid.v.32. Deus eum resuscitavit ex mortuis ib.IV.10. Cùm enim resurrectio Christi ex mortuis debuerit esse argumentum tum justificationis & absolutionis Christi: tum ὁρισμὸς definitionis illius, quòd sit Filius Dei, juxta vocem Dei Filium compellantis: Tu es Filius meus, ego hodie genuite, Psal.II. 7. tum judicii illius, quo in Filio redempti absolvuntur; iccirco ejus operationem Patri, qui judicis in oeconomia salutis vicem sustinet, ἰδιωματίζει appropriari decuit. Ideo resuscitatus est per gloriam Patris, Rom.VI.4. non tantum cum gloria ejus, sed exigente, & sic quasi operante gloria Patris, cujus intererat, ut Filius, idemque Sacerdos consummatus, justus, hæres resurget, & talis tum ostenderetur, tum crederetur, ut Deus nobis justitia fieri, in Filio, & in nobis glorificari posset. Unde etiam propter justificationem nostri resuscitatus, ibid.IV.15. dicitur. Facit huc miraculum, quòd circa resurrectionem Christi contigit. Nam σεισμὸς μέγας magnus motus terræ, Matth.XXVIII.2. factus est, uti videtur, circa tempus illud, quo mulieres adsepulchrum perrexerunt. Quod præsentis virtutis Divinæ symbolum fuit. Deus cùm egrederetur coram populo tuo, &c. Terra tremuit, &c. Psal. LXVIII.8-9. Etiam Angelus Domini descendens ex Cœlo adveniens, avolvit saxum ab ostio, & sedit super illud, Matth.XXVIII.2. Johannes δύο ἀγγέλους duos Angelos cap.XX.12. nominat; unum nempe, forma νεανίσκου juvenis & δεξιῶν ad dextram, uti Marcus cap.XVI. 5. loquitur: adeòque alterum à sinistris; quorum aliis uterque, aliis unus visus est. Ita Angelis quasi è Cœlo à Deo missis apparitoribus Jesus ex carcere evocari, & cum testimonio soluti ultimi quadrantis justificari & dimitti potuit. Quo maximè intuitu Apostolus δυνατὸν possibile fuisse, ut à morte detineretur, negat, Act.II.24.
units.tr: XLV. The power by which Christ was raised was infinite power, that is, the working [ἐνέργεια] and the might of the strength [κράτος τῆς ἰσχύος], the efficacy of the mighty strength of God (Eph. 1:19), and this belonged to the Son and to the Father. To the Son, because he was made alive in the Spirit of holiness [πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης] (Rom. 1:4), namely by that same Spirit by which he went and preached in the days of Noah (1 Pet. 3:18-19). I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again (John 10:18). Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19), which he said of the temple of his body, as is added at v. 21. For he raised up his own, and is the builder of the temple of the Lord (בנה היכל יהוה, Zech. 6:12); the house of God (Heb. 3:3-6); as the life-giving Spirit (1 Cor. 15:45); as having life in himself (John 5:26); the mighty God (Isa. 9:6), who with the trumpet of God and with a shout [κέλευσμα] quickens the dead (1 Thess. 4:16). The same power belonged to the Father, to whom Christ's resurrection is especially ascribed. For the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, exerted the working of the strength of his might in Christ, raising him from the dead (Eph. 1:17, 19-20). Whom God (the Father) raised up, loosing the pangs of death (Acts 2:24). This Jesus God raised up (ibid. v. 32). God raised him from the dead (ibid. 4:10). For since the resurrection of Christ from the dead was to be the proof both of the justification and absolution of Christ, and the definition of his being the Son of God, according to the voice of God addressing the Son: You are my Son, today I have begotten you (Ps. 2:7), and also of that judgment by which those redeemed in the Son are absolved, it was fitting that his working be appropriated to the Father, who in the economy of salvation takes the place of judge. Therefore he was raised through the glory of the Father (Rom. 6:4), not only with his glory, but as the glory of the Father required and, as it were, worked it, since it was for the Father's glory that the Son, the perfected priest, righteous and heir, should rise, and that he should be shown and believed to be such, so that God might become our righteousness in the Son and be glorified in us. Hence he is also said to be raised for our justification (ibid. 4:25). The miracle that occurred around Christ's resurrection points here: for a great earthquake [σεισμὸς μέγας] (Matt. 28:2) happened, as it seems, around the time when the women went toward the sepulchre. This was a symbol of the present divine power: When God went forth before your people, etc., the earth trembled, etc. (Ps. 68:8-9). Also an angel of the Lord, descending from heaven and coming, rolled the stone away from the door and sat upon it (Matt. 28:2). John names two angels [δύο ἀγγέλους] (ch. 20:12), one, namely, in the form of a young man, and at the right side, as Mark speaks (ch. 16:5), and so another on the left; each of them was seen by some, while by others only one was seen. Thus, as if the angels were sent from God as attendants, Jesus could be summoned out of prison, and, justified by the testimony of the last quarter-penny released, could be set free. It is with this especially in view that the Apostle denies that it was possible [δυνατὸν] for him to be held by death (Acts 2:24).

units.la: XLVI. Resuscitatus & vivificatus est Christus σαρκὶ carne, secundum carnem & corpus, 1.Pet.III.18. Unita cum eo postliminiò anima è Cœlo recepta. Nam Christus moriens animam suam, ceu depositum brevi repetendum, in manus Patris sui commendavit, Luc. XXIII.46. Idem verò: Ego, inquit, pono animam meam, & eam rursus assumam. Potestatem habeo eam ponendi; & potestatem habeo πάλιν λαβεῖν iterum assumendi eam, Joh.X.17.18. Licèt igitur per mortem ὁ λόγος à corpore separatus non fuerit, adeòque unio ejus cum corpore nulla instauratione indiguerit, cùm desierit tantùm ὁ λόγος per corpus, ut organon, operari; at de caetero etiam dum corpus in sepulchro jacuit, Christus sepultus dictus est: tamen per eam unio corporis cum anima soluta, restitui in integrum ab ipso λόγῳ debuit, & restituta etiam est. Resurrexit verò, & unitum est idem illud corpus, quod mortuum erat; manente ejus veritate naturali, ut haberet carnem & ossa, neque adeò spiritus esset, Luc.XXIV.39. & cùm hic esset, non esset simul alibi, Marc.XVI.6. Fuit tamen πνεῦματικὸν spirituale, 1.Cor.XV. 46. non quòd corpoream, visibilem, palpabilem, & suo loco mensurabilem naturam deposuerit, & in spiritum transfierit (ita enim corpus & frater noster esse desiisset, & duo spiritus finiti in eodem fuissent;) sed quia à spiritu ejus vivificante, (Rom.I.4. 1.Pet.III.18.) à corruptione vindicatum, in aeternam vitam vivificatum, in Coelo collocatum, factum est ἀφθαρτον, ἐν δόξῃ, ἐν δυνάμει, incorruptibile, in gloria, in potentia ibid.v.42.43. liberum ab omni necessitate terrenarum vitæ animalis functionum, Deo, spiritu, vitæ hujus animalis functiones compensante, plenum. Ubi Deus erit omnia in omnibus, ibid.v.28. ibi ipse quoque vita est in corporibus, sine cibo aliisve adjumentis; adeòque corpus spirituale est. Caro porro & sanguis, qui Regni Coelorum haereditatem adire non possunt, ibid.v.50. non utriusque veniar, sed mistum hoc est, carnis & sanguinis guinis ejusdem conditionem animalem, juxta quam ad corporis in perpetuo fluxu consistentis substantiam conservandam cibo & potu, à quo sanguis, & in eodem anima, sicut à sanguine caro est, indiget, significant. Sed in Regno gloriæ, quod κατ' ἐξοχὴν Regnum Dei appellatur, cum Deus erit omnia in omnibus, nullus corporis defectus, nullus partium fluxus ad φθορὰν corruptionem vergens, indigentia nulla locum habet; neque indigentia alterius causæ vitæ, vel alterius rei vivificantis, quàm spiritus, obtinebit, quia aliàs Deus non foret omnia in omnibus. Ac licèt carnis & sanguinis substantia ex elementis inter se natura contrariis constet, adeóque eatenus sua natura corruptioni semper obnoxia sit; tamen Deus temperamentum conservare, & unita continere suo spiritu, quæ ipse conjunxit, facilè potest. Neque obstat, quòd corpus non amplius ἐπίγειον terrestre, sed ἐπουράνιον cœleste est, 1.Cor.XV. 48.49. quia idem corpus,quod in terra fuit, potest esse in Cœlo; sed ita, ut Regno Dei dignum est. Regnum verò Dei, & caro & sanguis,vel corpus terrestre, non utique in substantia, sed in defectu opponuntur. Comparanda hisce sunt, quæ de corporis Christi dotibus plura Loc. XVII.45. diximus.
units.tr: XLVI. Christ was raised and quickened in the flesh, according to the flesh and the body (1 Pet. 3:18). His soul, received again from heaven, was united with him again. For in dying Christ committed his soul into the hands of his Father, as a deposit to be recovered shortly (Luke 23:46). And he said: "I lay down my life, and I take it up again. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again [πάλιν λαβεῖν]" (John 10:17-18). Therefore, although the Word was not separated from the body by death, so that its union with the body needed no restoration, since the Word ceased only to work through the body as its instrument, yet while the body lay in the tomb Christ was said to be buried. Nevertheless the union of the body with the soul, which had been dissolved, ought to be restored entirely by the Word himself, and it was restored. He rose, and the same body that had been dead was reunited with the soul, its natural truth remaining, so that he had flesh and bones and was not a spirit (Luke 24:39); and while he was here, he was not at the same time elsewhere (Mark 16:6). Yet he was spiritual [πνευματικὸν] (1 Cor. 15:46). This is not because he laid aside a corporeal, visible, tangible nature, measurable in place, and was changed into spirit (for then the body and our brother would have ceased to be, and two finite spirits would have been in one), but because, rescued from corruption by his life-giving Spirit (Rom. 1:4; 1 Pet. 3:18), quickened to eternal life and placed in heaven, he became incorruptible [ἀφθαρτον], in glory, in power (ibid. vv. 42-43), free from every necessity of the earthly, animal functions of life, and filled with God, the Spirit making up for those animal functions of this life. Where God will be all in all (ibid. v. 28), he himself is also life in the bodies, without food or other aids; and so the body is spiritual. Further, flesh and blood, which cannot inherit the kingdom of heaven (ibid. v. 50), signify not the one or the other alone, but a mixture, that is, the animal condition of that same flesh and blood, according to which the substance of the body, which is in constant flux, needs food and drink to preserve it. From food and drink blood comes, and in the blood the soul is, just as flesh comes from blood. But in the kingdom of glory, which is called pre-eminently "the Kingdom of God," when God will be all in all, there is no defect of the body, no flow of parts tending toward corruption [φθορὰν], and no need has a place; nor will any need obtain of any cause of life or any life-giving thing other than the Spirit, for otherwise God would not be all in all. And although the substance of flesh and blood consists of elements naturally contrary to one another, and so by its nature is always liable to corruption, yet God can easily preserve the mixture and hold together by his Spirit the things he has joined. Nor is it an objection that the body is no longer earthly [ἐπίγειον] but heavenly [ἐπουράνιον] (1 Cor. 15:48-49), because the same body that was on earth can be in heaven, but in such a way as is worthy of the Kingdom of God. Flesh and blood, or the earthly body, are opposed to the Kingdom of God not in substance but in defect. What we have said more fully about the endowments of Christ's body at Loc. XVII.45 should be compared with these points.

units.la: XLVII. Neque tamen gloria illa, quam Christus corpori suo per resurrectionem ex mortuis vivificato superinduit, ilico in terris consummata fuit; ut eodem sensu glorisum appellari possit, quo nunc supra cœlos evectum σῶμα δόξης corpus gloriosum (Phil.III. 21.) est. Licèt enim amplius mori Christus non potuerit, quippe à peccato justificatus,semel peccato mortuus, & nunc vivens Deo,(propter Dei vitam, voluntatem & gloriam) Rom.VI.7.9. 10. & resuscitatus à Patre ex mortuis νηκρῶν μέλλων ὑπογρέφειν εἰς διαφθορὰν non amplius reversurus in sepulchrum ad corruptionem, Act.XIII. 34. neque amplius pro peccato offerendus,Hebr. IX.26. X.18. nedum ita humiliandus, ut vel panis fiat, vel sub specie panis aliquod esse in terra, manu, stomacho, hominis etiam impii; imò muris habeat; & ibi destructionem patiatur,quæ Transsubstantiatorum ἀποπμάτα sunt: tamen glorificatio illa corporis Christi, facti immortalis & incorruptibilis, in resurrectione coepta,progressum in ascensione, apicem verò & coronidem demum in sessione ad dextram Dei in Cœlis sortita est. Quamdiu enim post resurrectionem in terris Christus agitavit, & cum charissimis suis conversatus est, discipulorum ejus infirmitati indulsit Deus, ut illa corporis gloria visibiliter non radiaret. Neque enim gloriam illam mortales inconnivis oculis intueri magis potuissent, quàm Israelitæ faciem Mosis potuerunt; 2.Cor.III.7. quantisper ille in terris morari, & resurrectionem suam multis πεκμηρίοις signis (Act.I.3.) comprobare voluit. Huic ergo liberæ & œconomicæ radiorum gloriæ suppressioni, non corporis Christi vel mortali conditioni,vel cibi indigentiæ tribuendum est, quòd Christus post resurrectionem,ut comederet, flagitavit τὸ ὀψάριον obsonium, vel aliquid εἰς τὸ φαγεῖν comedendum (Joh.XXI.5.) & quòd cum eo Apostoli post resurrectionem comederunt & biberunt, Act.X.41. Neque etiam illud de gloria corporis Christi delibat; quòd post resurrectionem vulnerum in manibus, pedibus, latere, vestigia & clavorum palpabiles & spectabiles typos habuit; Joh.XX.24.25. quia typi tales potius ad glorisam ex morte devicta triumphum pertinent.
units.tr: XLVII. Yet that glory which Christ, through the resurrection from the dead, put upon his body thus quickened did not at once reach its completion on earth, so that it could be called glorious in the same sense in which the body that is now raised above the heavens is "a glorious body" (Phil. 3:21). For although Christ could no longer die, having been justified from sin, once dead to sin and now living to God (by the life, will and glory of God) (Rom. 6:7, 9-10), and raised from the dead by the Father, about to return no more to the tomb for corruption (Acts 13:34), and no longer to be offered for sin (Heb. 9:26; 10:18), much less to be so humbled that he would become bread, or be in some form of bread in the earth, in the hand, in the stomach of a man, even of an impious man, or in the mouse's belly, and there suffer destruction, which are the excrements of the Transsubstantiators: nevertheless that glorification of the body of Christ, made immortal and incorruptible, begun in the resurrection, obtained its progress in the ascension and its summit and crown at last in the sitting at the right hand of God in the heavens. For while Christ moved about on earth after the resurrection and lived with his dearest ones, God indulged the weakness of his disciples, so that that glory of the body did not shine forth visibly. Indeed mortals could no more have gazed at that glory with unblinking eyes than the Israelites could look at the face of Moses (2 Cor. 3:7), for as long as he wished to remain on earth and to prove his resurrection by many proofs [πεκμηρίοις] (Acts 1:3). Therefore the fact that after the resurrection Christ asked for a fish [τὸ ὀψάριον] to eat, or something to eat [εἰς τὸ φαγεῖν] (John 21:5), and that the apostles ate and drank with him after the resurrection (Acts 10:41), must be ascribed not to the mortal condition of Christ's body nor to need of food, but to that partial suppression of the rays of glory which was for a purpose and arranged by his dispensation. Nor does it detract from the glory of Christ's body that after the resurrection he had palpable and visible marks of the wounds in his hands, feet and side, and of the nails (John 20:24-25), because such marks rather belong to the triumph of glory over conquered death.

units.la: XLVIII. Veritas resurrectionis Christi, articuli fidei maximè capitalis; argumentis indubitabilibus cognoscitur. Nam testimonia eorum, qui eum redivivum viderunt, & à se visum aliis prodiderunt, omni exceptione majora sunt. Nihil enim fingere, vel ex composito agere potuerunt.
units.tr: XLVIII. The truth of Christ's resurrection, the chief of the articles of faith, is known by indubitable arguments. For the testimonies of those who saw him alive again, and who reported to others what they had seen, are beyond all exception. They could not have invented anything or acted by prior agreement.

units.la: Nam & dissipati illi fuerunt; & mulieres primæ, quæ ad monumentum accurrerant; non fraudem faciendi, sed pollingendi simplice animo & studio, eam annunciarunt; & postquam idonea visi ejus testimonia extiterunt, subdubitarunt tamen, donec sæpe diúque multis unà visus est, de quibus apparitionibus post, & in solenni inprimis Concilio Galilææ, ubi plus quàm quingentis visus resurrectionis suæ fidem rerum documentis & publicè fecit, 1.Cor.XV.6. de quo post: & inter testes ejus etiam professus ante hostis & persecutor ejus Saulus fuit, & hi omnes tantum abest, ut ex testimonio illo quæstum facere instituerint,ut propter illud etiam plagas, injurias, mala concatenata libentes volentésque sustinuerint; imò morte sua testimonii sui veritatem obsignaverint. Tum ipsi hostes Jesu ejus sepulchro custodiam & sigillum apposuerunt; & qui illud custodiverunt, nec cadaver ostendere potuerunt,nec aliud ejus in locum cadaver substituere tentarunt; neque quod certò constet, vi illud ablatum esse, unquam questi sunt; neque ob male custoditum sepulchrum perinde ut custodes illi Petri Act.XII. 19. puniti sunt. Præterea debuit Christus tertia die resurgere κατὰ τὰς γραφὰς secundum Scripturas, 1.Cor.XV.4. puta Psal.XVI 10 Esaj. LIII.9. Jon.II.1. Matth.XII.40. &c. Atque id ipsum tempus fuit; quo Christus venire. & resuscitatus in mundo prædicari debuit. Planè autem juxta prædictionem Christus venit, locutus est, fecit, passus, prædicatus, creditus est eo tempore, quo oportuit, & quo omnia signa impleta fuerunt, & illustri modo אבן cœlatura lapidis illius unius, quem Deus Jehosuæ Sacerdoti & sociis ejus proposuit, & in quem septem oculi dirigi debuerunt; hoc est, omnes notæ, omnia signa, quibus ejus Nomen super omne nomen ipsi datum dignosci, Filius Dei, Ecclesiæ caput, Lapis fundamentalis demonstrari, & ut sigillum habens characterem, poni debuit;(Hagg.I.23.) manifestatæ sunt; Zach.III.9. Accedit, quòd Christum in Cœlum ascendisse, ad dextram Dei consedi-se, Spiritum S. in omnem carnem effudisse, & in medio hostium suorum hucusque dominari, satis constat. Quæ omnia nisi eodem ex morte resuscitato, & supra mortem ipsam regnante, succedere non potuissent. Neque exiguum hanc in rem momentum miracula multifaria, distributio donorum Spiritus S. judicia Dei adversus incredulos Judæos & gentes tum apertè Christo adversantes, tum eidem mentientes; patesacta; quibus Deus Evangelii & resurrectionis ChriChristi veritatem comprobavit, habent. Quin & S. Coena, quam Christus moriturus & resurrecturus instituit, & Baptismus, quem idem post resurrectionem injunxit; & dies Dominicus, quem Christus resurgendo dedicavit, & Apostoli in memoriam & honorem resurrectionis hujus celebrarunt; evidentia, & inde a Christo ad nostra usque tempora in Ecclesia perseverantia resurrectionis Christi monumenta, omnem dubitationis aleam superant. Cum enim re gesta nitantur, si res ea gesta firmiter probata non esset, a tot hominibus non stultis, & plerisque optantibus, ne id verum esset; sine armis, frustrato hominum furore, in mundo credita & recepta minime fuisset. Sed & caete—ra omnia argumenta, quibus fides Christiana, inprimis consummatio & justificatio Christi Salvatoris, & Fidei ac salutis nostrae principis, justitia, salus & vita nobis a Christo moriente parta, & a vivente collata, & nostra ex mortuis resurrectio, quae monimenta resurrectionis Christi, ceu ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων primitiarum eorum, qui obdormiverunt, resurrecturi (1. Cor. XV. 20.) unice insistunt; (ibid. 4-35.) confirmatur, veritatem resurrectionis ejusdem propalant. Denique etiam Josephus, Judaeus & ipse, in celeberrima illa de Jesu Christo θεῖον, quae Antiq. lib. XVIII. 4. extat, haec scripsit: Ἐφάνη δ᾽ αὐτοῖς τέτρω ἔχων ἡμέρας πάλιν ζῶν, τῶν θείων πνευμάτων τῶν περὶ αὐτὸν μυρίᾳ θαυμάσια. Post triduum enim redivivus ipsis apparuit, cum Divini Prophetae haec aliaque innumera de eo nuntiassent. Etiam vetustissimus & celeberrimus Judaeorum Doctor & princeps R. Jehuda Haccados, in libro R. Abrahami, qui גלי רזיא Revelans arcana, inscribitur, sic disserit: Post triduum vero anima Messiae ad corpus suum revertetur, & exibit ex illo lapide, in quo erat sepultus, sicut dictum est, Exod. XXXIII.21. Ecce locus est apud me, stabit super petram: Cumque transierit gloria mea, ponam te in foramine petrae. Qui liber a Galatino identidem citatus, diu eruditis suspectus fuit, donec magnus ille Wagenseilius Tel. Ignit. p. 221.222. suspicionem refellens, se illum MS. diversum licet ab eo, quem Galatinus supposuit, a Polono exule emptum, cum paucissimis Judaeorum, possidere testatus est. Quem publici juris ab eo fieri merito boni omnes desiderant, ut quibus in rebus ille fidei Christianae suffragetur, paulo certius, quam ex Galatini ostentatis fragmentis, dijudicari posset.
units.tr: For those men were scattered; and the women who first ran to the tomb did not announce it to deceive, but with a simple mind and zeal for telling the truth; and after his appearances had been reliable witnesses, they still doubted until he was seen often and for a long time by many together. Of these appearances more will be said later, and especially at the solemn gathering in Galilee, where he gave proof of his resurrection to more than five hundred at once, publicly and with sure evidence (1 Cor. 15:6), of which more later. Among his witnesses even Saul, his former enemy and persecutor, professed it. And all these men were so far from setting up a trade in that testimony that they willingly and gladly endured blows, injuries and a chain of evils because of it; indeed they sealed the truth of their testimony with their deaths. Moreover, Jesus' own enemies placed a guard and a seal on his tomb; and those who guarded it could neither show the corpse nor try to substitute another corpse in its place; nor did they ever complain that it had certainly been taken away by force, nor were they punished for a badly guarded tomb in the way that Peter's guards were punished (Acts 12:19). Besides, Christ had to rise on the third day according to the Scriptures [κατὰ τὰς γραφὰς] (1 Cor. 15:4), namely Psalm 16:10, Isaiah 53:9, Jonah 2:1, Matthew 12:40, and so on. And that was the very time in which Christ had to come, and be raised and preached in the world. Christ certainly came, spoke, acted, suffered, was preached and believed at the time when it was fitting and when all the signs were fulfilled, and in the illustrious manner of the engraving of that one stone [אבן], which God set before Joshua the priest and his companions, and on which seven eyes had to be directed (Zech. 3:9), that is, all the marks and all the signs by which his name, given to him above every name, is recognized, and by which he is shown to be the Son of God, the head of the Church, the foundation stone, and as one bearing the character of a seal, had to be placed (Hag. 2:23), were made manifest. Add to this that it is quite clear that Christ ascended into heaven, sat at the right hand of God, poured out the Holy Spirit on all flesh, and has ruled to this day in the midst of his enemies. None of this could have come about unless he had been raised from the dead and reigned above death itself. For this purpose the many kinds of miracles, the distribution of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the judgments of God against the unbelieving Jews and the nations, who both openly opposed Christ and lied against him, which are open to view, have no small weight; by these God confirmed the truth of the Gospel and of Christ's resurrection. Indeed the Holy Supper, which Christ instituted when he was about to die and rise, and the baptism, which he enjoined after the resurrection, and the Lord's Day, which Christ dedicated by rising and which the apostles celebrated in memory and honour of this resurrection, together with the evident monuments of Christ's resurrection, which have persisted in the Church from Christ down to our own times, overcome every chance of doubt. For since these rest on an event that actually happened, if that event had not been firmly proved, it would never have been believed and received in the world, without arms and with the rage of men frustrated, by so many men not foolish, and by most who wished that it were not true. But all the other arguments too, by which the Christian faith is confirmed, above all the completion and justification of Christ the Saviour, the prince of our faith and salvation, and the righteousness, salvation and life won for us by Christ dying and bestowed by him living, and our own resurrection from the dead, which rest solely on the monuments of Christ's resurrection, as the firstfruits [ἀπαρχὴ] of those who have fallen asleep [τῶν κεκοιμημένων], the firstfruits of those who are to rise (1 Cor. 15:20), and on the arguments that follow (ibid. vv. 4-35), all these establish and make clear the truth of that same resurrection. Finally, Josephus too, himself a Jew, in that famous passage about Jesus Christ, which stands in the Antiquities, book 18, chapter 4, wrote these words: "He appeared to them on the third day, alive again, since the divine prophets had foretold these and countless other wonders about him." Even the most ancient and most famous Jewish teacher and chief, Rabbi Jehuda Haccados, in the book of Rabbi Abraham entitled Revealing Mysteries [גלי רזיא], discourses thus: "After three days the soul of the Messiah will return to his body and will come out of that stone in which he was buried, as it is said (Exod. 33:21): 'Behold, there is a place with me; he shall stand upon the rock; and when my glory has passed by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock.'" This book, cited again and again by Galatinus, was long suspected by learned men, until the great Wagenseil, in his Tela Ignea, p. 221-222, refuting the suspicion, testified that he himself possesses that manuscript, though different from the one that Galatinus put forward, bought from a Polish exile along with a very few Jews. All good men rightly desire that it be published, so that by it we might judge, with greater certainty than from the fragments Galatinus displayed, in what respects it supports the Christian faith.

units.la: XLIX. Nihilominus testatissimae Resurrectionis Christi fidei Judaei infideles, quibus aes triplex circa pectus est, non pauca opponunt. Quorum tamen exiguum pondus sit, nullo negotio cognoscitur. Testis est Matthaeus, milites, sepulchri Christi custodes, edixisse, discipulos Christi, cum ipsi dormivissent, noctu venisse, & Christum ex sepulchro furtim abstulisse. Addit: Καὶ διεφημίσθη ὁ λόγος οὗτος παρὰ Ιουδαίοις μέχρι σήμερον. Et divulgatus est ille sermo apud Judaeos usque ad hodiernum diem, Matth. XXVIII.11-15. Sed salva res est, si Matthaeo fides constat. Is enim milites illos a Sacerdotibus ἀργυρίοις ἱκανοῖς nummis multis, ut talia spargerent, conductos v.12. testatur. Tum Jesu corpus positum est in sepulchro novo, in quo nullum antehac conditum fuit; ne, sic Hieronymus in Matth. XXVII.60. arguit, post resurrectionem, caeteris corporibus remanentibus, resurrexisse alius fingeretur. Etiam sepulchrum appositis custodibus ab hostibus obsignatum est, ob praedictionem Jesu, tertio die resurrectionem suam pollicitantis, ne ulla fraus sibi fieri posset. Eadem vero opera caverunt illi, ne factam sibi fraudem causari possent, postquam vere Christus resurrexisset. Qui cum jam revixerit, quomodo hostibus ejus de dolo malo actio vel exceptio competit? Haec enim sic Deus fieri voluit, ne quis doctrinam hanc de reditu Christi ad vitam labefactare posset. Quam facultatem non aliis duntaxat, sed sibi etiam hostes Christi praeciderunt. Quanto enim accuratius Christi corpus custoditum & reservatum est, tanto resurrectionis Christi virtus validius ostenditur. Tum nec latenter Jesus ex monumento penetravit; sed facto ingenti terrae motu, Angelo e Coelo descendente, & sepulchrum reserante, custodibus tantum non examinatis, & nonnullis etiam rem apud Sacerdotes testificantibus. Quae ab Evangelistis eo tempore, quo portentorum illorum oculati & auriti testes supererant, fingi nullo modo potuerunt. Discipulos insuper Christi dispersos, simplices, rudes, meticulosos, ad satellitum adventum, & ancillae vocem paulo ante trepidantes, tantum facinus ausos esse, & deceptis custodibus toti Synedrio os sublinere potuisse, quis animum, ut credat, induxerit? Quomodo etiam milites sopiti deprehendere per somnum corpus Jesu ab Apostolis fuisse subreptum? quomodo, quod insciis & incautis iis factum est, rescicere potuerunt? Sed & portenti hujus conscios fuisse multos, id evincit, quod Sanctos in corporibus redivivos in urbe sancta visos esse, idem Matthaeus cap. XXVII. 52.53. testatur. Neque tam male pudori suo is consuluit, ut stolidum adeo crasumque mendacium confingeret, quod unicuique refellere promptum fuisset. Sed cuniculis actis, & suffossa humo corpus Jesu subtractum esse, regerunt. Atqui non ita Pontifices existimarunt, qui dormientibus custodibus illud subreptum esse finxerunt. Si per cuniculos res acta est, etiam vigilantibus custodibus id fieri potuit, & ne quid de temporis angustiis dicam, quomodo cuniculi in solo ὑπόπετρω, rupe ferro excavata, seu monumento ex lapide excisio, quale Christi fuisse, supra ostendimus, agi potuerunt? Licet enim Josephus de Bello Jud. lib. I. 13. II. 17. VI. 30. VII. 20. narret, Hierosolymitanum solum, obsidente urbem Herode, & dein Tito, & in seditione Manahemi cuniculis perfossum esse; atque idem multo post a Salahadino urbem oppugnante factum Abulfarajus Histor. Orient. Dynast. 9. testetur; tamen Golgothae montis, & horti, cui sepulchrum Christi in rupe excisum inerat, diversam rationem fuisse, satis liquet. Nec satis otii, vel animi Apostolis fuisset, ut per durum silicem tam longos cuniculos agere possent. Manifesta insuper in rupe suffossa vestigia furti extitissent, quae nulla arte vel humo ingesta, vel infartis lapidibus & coementis celari ab Apostolis potuissent. & quae Judaeorum principes, omissa illa de sopore custodum calumnia, lumnia, ad fraudem detegendam haud dubiè divulgassent. Mittimus decantatas à Veteribus de Divinis quibusdam, uti crediderunt, viris ex morte ad vitam revocatis, historias, quibus revivíscentis Christi admirabilitatem minuere jam olim gentiles conati sunt. Aristeam, Proconnesium, Cleomedem, Hermotimum Clazomenium, Epimenidem, Romulum, Apollonium Thyanæum, alios Celsus apud Origenem, Contr. Celf. lib. III. obduxit. Complures etiam Plinius lib. II. 52. & Æneas Gazæus in Theophrasto memorarunt. Sed in exemplis illis ad incudem revocatis superstitionem, credulitatem incautæ plebis, impostturas hominum, & fallacias Sathanæ pridem apricati alii, paulò emunctiorum narium, sunt. Notum inprimis, quod de Aristea Proconnesio & Hermotimo Clazomenio fertur, quorum hic multis post obitum annis non semel revixisse dictus est; ille animam ad arbitrium ponere & recipere, quæ dum sejuncta esset à corpore, vagari soleret, & multa è longinquo cognoscere, rursumque induto corpore renuntiare; quoad hoc ab inimicis cremato, velut vagina amissa, cùm quò se reciperet, non haberet, penitus tandem abscessit. Sed talia citra interitum magicis artibus fieri Scriptores rerum Septentrionalium, & nuper demum doctissimus Schefferus Histor. Lapp. cap. II. nos docuere. Sed Jesus verè mortuus est, neque à Sathana resuscitatus est, quia Regni ejus intererat, ut in sepulchro computresceret, neque aliena, sed propria virtute resuscitatus est, & semel resuscitatus, morti non amplius obnoxius est, cùm nemo alius propria virtute resurrexerit, vel resuscitatus novam mortem non subierit. Ut ἴσα valde ἀνίσα nullo negotio deprehendantur.
units.tr: XLIX. Nevertheless, the unbelieving Jews, whose brows are as hard as bronze, raise not a few objections against the most firmly attested faith in Christ's Resurrection. How little weight these objections carry is easily recognised. Matthew is a witness that the soldiers who guarded Christ's tomb gave out that the disciples of Christ had come by night, while the guards were asleep, and had secretly stolen Christ away from the tomb. He adds: "And this saying was spread abroad among the Jews until this day" [Καὶ διεφημίσθη ὁ λόγος οὗτος παρὰ Ιουδαίοις μέχρι σήμερον]. And that story was spread among the Jews until this day, Matt. 28.11-15. But the matter is secure if Matthew's credibility stands. For he testifies that the soldiers were hired by the priests with "large sums of money" [ἀργυρίοις ἱκανοῖς] to spread such reports, v. 12. Then Jesus' body was laid in a new tomb, in which no one had been buried before, lest, as Jerome argues on Matt. 27.60, after the resurrection, while the other bodies remained, someone might pretend that another had risen. The tomb was also sealed by his enemies, with guards posted, because of Jesus' prediction that he would rise again on the third day, so that no fraud could be practised on them. By the same act they took care that they could not complain of a fraud done to them after Christ had truly risen. Since he had already come back to life, how could his enemies have a claim or a plea of deceit against him? God willed these things to happen so that no one could undermine this teaching about Christ's return to life. His enemies cut off this means not only for others but also for themselves. For the more carefully Christ's body was guarded and kept, the more powerfully the power of his resurrection is displayed. Nor did Jesus leave the tomb secretly; rather, a great earthquake occurred, an angel came down from heaven and rolled back the stone, while the guards were scarcely examined, and some of them even reported the matter to the priests. These events could in no way have been invented by the Evangelists at a time when eye and ear witnesses of those wonders were still alive. Who could be persuaded to believe that the scattered disciples of Christ, simple, rough, and timid, trembling a little earlier at the arrival of the soldiers and at the voice of a servant girl, dared such a deed, and were able, with the guards deceived, to smear the whole Sanhedrin in the face? Moreover, how could the soldiers, lulled to sleep, detect through sleep that the body of Jesus had been carried off by the apostles? How could they find out what was done while they were unaware and off their guard? But that many were witnesses of this wonder is proved by the fact that Matthew himself, in chapter 27.52-53, testifies that holy men were seen in the holy city, raised bodily from the dead. Nor did Matthew care so badly for his own reputation as to invent so foolish and gross a lie, one that could be refuted at once by anyone. The enemies, however, reply that the body of Jesus was taken away by digging tunnels and by tunnelling through the ground. Yet the priests did not think so, those who claimed it had been taken while the guards slept. If the thing was done through tunnels, it could also have been done while the guards were awake. And, to say nothing of the shortness of time, how could tunnels have been dug in the ground beneath the rock [ὑπόπετρω], that is, in a rock hewn out with iron, or in a tomb cut from stone, such as Christ's was, as we have shown above? For although Josephus, Jewish War 1.13; 2.17; 6.30; 7.20, relates that Jerusalem alone was pierced with tunnels when Herod besieged the city, and then Titus, and during the sedition of Manahem; and although Abulfaragius, Historia Orientalis, Dynastia 9, testifies that the same was done much later when Saladin attacked the city, it is nonetheless quite clear that the situation at Golgotha, and in the garden where Christ's tomb was cut into the rock, was different. Nor would the apostles have had enough leisure or courage to drive such long tunnels through hard flint. Moreover, clear traces of a theft would have been visible in the rock that had been dug through, and these could not have been hidden by the apostles, whether by any art or by earth heaped up, or by stones and mortar packed in. The chief priests of the Jews, setting aside that calumny about the guards' sleep, would certainly have made the fraud known in order to expose it. We pass over the much-praised stories of the Ancients about certain divine men, as they believed, who were called back from death to life, by which pagans already long ago tried to diminish the wonder of Christ's return to life. Celsus, cited by Origen, Against Celsus book 3, drew up a list of Aristeas, Proconnesius, Cleomedes, Hermotimus of Clazomenae, Epimenides, Romulus, Apollonius of Tyana, and others. Pliny, book 2 chapter 52, and Aeneas of Gaza in Theophrastus, have recorded many more. But other men, of a keener nose, have long since brought those examples back to the anvil and shown that they rest on superstition, the credulity of the unwary crowd, the impostures of men, and the deceits of Satan. Especially well known is what is told of Aristeas of Proconnesus and Hermotimus of Clazomenae. Of these, the latter is said to have come back to life more than once after many years of death; the former, to have been able at will to put his soul out and take it back, which used to wander while separated from the body, to know many things from afar, and then to report them, once again clothed in the body; until at last, when his enemies had burned his body, as if his sheath had been lost, he had nowhere to return to and at length departed altogether. But writers on northern affairs, and most recently the most learned Schefferus, in History of Lapland, chapter 2, have taught us that such things happen by magical arts without death. But Jesus truly died, and he was not raised by Satan, since it was not in the interest of his kingdom that he should rot in the tomb; he was raised not by another's power but by his own, and once raised he is no longer subject to death, since no one else has risen by his own power, or, once raised, has not undergone a new death. Thus things that are called equal [ἴσα] are very easily shown to be unequal [ἀνίσα].

units.la: L. Ex morte resuscitatus Jesus πάλιν iterum in orbem habitabilem intravit, Hebr.I.6. Sicut enim Sacerdos Leviticus ab altari non recta in Sanctum Sanctorum, sed in tabernaculum prius perrexit, ac demum inde in Sanctum Sanctorum: Sic Jesus verus Sacerdos ex cruce & morte non recta in Cœlum perrexit, sed ad tabernaculum prius, Ecclesiam fidelium suorum, jam reconciliatam & non amplius terreno altari affixam, illam luce, parato cibo & thure precum, quibus clamamus Abba, Pater, impleturus, invisit. Nam primò εἰσερχόμενος εἰς τὸν κόσμον intrans in mundum, dixit: Sacrificium & oblationem noluit, ibid.X.5. & minoratus est pauli-sper pro Angelis, ibid.II.7. At secundùm intrans non amplius minor Angelis, vel iis subjectus, sed prælatus fuit. Dictum enim ei est: Adorent eum omnes Angeli Dei, ibid.I.6. ex Psal.XCVII.7. Et dari ei coepit Nomen illud super omne Nomen, Phil.II.9. Ideo Christus ante mortem Apostolis dixit: Postquam resuscitatus fuero, προάξω ὑμᾶς εἰς Γαλιλαίαν, præibo vobis in Galilæam, Matth.XXVI.32. Marc.XIV.28. Et diu ante: Cùm irrigavero animam defessam, & omnem animam, quæ tabuerat, implevero. Propterea evigilavi, ויאראה & vidi (denuo vidi, visi, revisi mcos, utut mœstos, tamen mei cupidos, in amore mei constantes, & per Dei gratiam conservatos, de quibus v.20. dixerat: Viscera mea super ipso strepuerunt) וישנתי ערבה לי & somnus meus suavis mihi fuit, Jerem.XXXI.25,26. In hocEcclesiæ suæ tabernaculo priori Jesus quadraginta dierum moram cum suis exegit. Apostolis se, postquam passus est, exhibuit vivum cum multis certissimis τεκμηρίοις signis (qualia sunt, loqui, ambulare, edere, bibere, se conspiciendum, contrectandum præbere, vestigia corporis crucifixi ostendere) per dies quadraginta ab iis ὀπτανόμενος & conspectus, & loquens de iis, quæ ad Regnum Dei spectant, Act.I.3.
units.tr: L. Having been raised from death, Jesus entered the inhabited world again [πάλιν], Heb. 1.6. For just as the Levitical priest went from the altar not straight into the Holy of Holies, but first into the tabernacle, and only from there into the Holy of Holies, so Jesus, the true priest, after the cross and death, did not go straight into heaven, but first visited the tabernacle, the Church of his faithful, now reconciled and no longer fixed to the earthly altar, to fill it with light, with food prepared, and with the incense of prayers, by which we cry, Abba, Father. For first, when entering into the world [εἰσερχόμενος εἰς τὸν κόσμον], he said: "Sacrifice and offering you did not desire," Heb. 10.5; and he was made a little lower than the angels for a time, Heb. 2.7. But on his second entrance he was no longer lower than the angels, nor subject to them, but was exalted above them. For it was said to him: "Let all the angels of God worship him," Heb. 1.6, from Ps. 97.7. And there began to be given to him that name which is above every name, Phil. 2.9. Therefore, before his death, Christ said to the apostles: "After I have been raised, I will go before you [προάξω ὑμᾶς] into Galilee," Matt. 26.32; Mark 14.28. And long before: "When I have watered the weary soul and filled every soul that had pined away, therefore I have awakened and seen" [ויאראה], (I have seen again, I have visited again, my people, however sorrowful, yet longing for me, constant in my love, and preserved by the grace of God, concerning whom in v. 20 he had said: "My bowels have sounded for him") "and my sleep was sweet to me" [וישנתי ערבה לי], Jer. 31.25-26. In this earlier tabernacle of his Church, Jesus spent a space of forty days with his own. After he had suffered, he showed himself alive to the apostles with many most certain tokens [τεκμηρίοις] (such as speaking, walking, eating, drinking, offering himself to be seen and touched, and showing the marks of his crucified body), being seen by them [ὀπτανόμενος] over forty days and speaking to them of the things that pertain to the kingdom of God, Acts 1.3.

units.la: LII. Pertinent huc apparitiones Christi, charissimos suos revisentis. quas novem Evangelistæ describunt. Et quatuor quidem singulis, vel paucis, reliquæ pluribus factæ sunt. Inter eas, quæ singulis vel paucis factæ sunt, Prima facta est Mariæ Magdalenæ, Matth.XXVIII.9.10. Marc.XVI.9. Joh.XX.11. &c. Illa enim apud sepulchrum stans, plorans, & illud inspectans, vidit Angelos duos in albis sedentes, sed mox conversa retrorsum Jesum ipsum stantem vidit, at non agnovit, hortulanum esse rata. Ex quo quum scisecitata esset, an Jesum tulerit, & quò eum posuerit, Jesum audivit dicentem: Maria. Prius eam compellaverat, ceu ignotus ignotam: Mulier quid ploras? Joh.XX.15. Hostibus jam abactis, & triumphans, cum suis ludit & jocatur, & velut crescere tristitiam finit, ut lætitia abundantior evaderet. Sed non diu moratus, ut notam, & quam in corde suo gereret, compellat. Ad eum igitur conversa respondit: Ῥαββουνί, quod est Διδάσκαλε Magister. Ita depulsa omni nebula Solem justitiæ, sine labe ac sordibus peccatorum nostrorum, prima vidit, & subita lætitia impleta est. Sed noluit tamen Jesus ab ea tangi, eò quòd nondum ad Patrem suum ascendisset; quin potius eam ad fratres suos ocyus currere, & iis dicere: Ascendo ad Patrem meum, & Patrem vestrum, & Deum meum, & Deum vestrum, jussit, ibid.v.17. Noluit enim tempus otioso amplexu, quasi jam ad lætitiæ colophonem perventum esset, teri; majoris momenti & studii illud æstimans, ut quantocyus fratribus suis: (sic discipulos post resurrectionem appellat, juxta illa Psal.XXII.23: Narrabo fratribus meis nomen tuum) significaret, se non diu in terra cum iis futurum, imò in procinctu esse, ut ceu summus Sacerdos, ilico in cœlestę sacrarium pro iis ingrederetur, & locum iis apud Patrem & Deum suum & illorum pararet. Secunda apparitio facta est duobus discipulis Emauntem euntibus, Marc.XVI.12. Luc.XXIV.13. &c. Iis se manifestavit ἐν ἑτέρᾳ μορφῇ in alia forma, hoc est, non in ea forma, in qua hactenus cum iis versari solebat; sed cum nitore, claritate, vigore, in vultu alio, quàm cui assueverant, aut si quid aliud simile fuit, quod speciem ejus mutaret. Accesserunt nebulae ratiocinationum, quibus intenti erant, σκυθρωπῷ tetrico vultu disputantes de Regno Coelorum, & quid Christo in sepulchro non reperto amplius facto deinceps opus esset. Quibus rebus effectum est, ut Christum συμπορευόμενον itineris comitem, passiones ac glorias suas ex Mose, Prophetis & Psalmis fusissimè edisserentem, non agnoscerent tamen, donec inter benedicendum & frangendum panem oculi eorum; qui hactenus ἐκρατοῦντο retinebantur; aperti sunt, ut eum agnoscerent. Sed agnitus Jesus ilico ἐφανερώθη ἀπ' αὐτῶν ex eorum conspe- b j conspectu ablatus est: clanculum, non advertentibus iis, vel retentis, ut ante, eorum oculis, se subduxit, quia jam satis fides eorum confirmata erat, & aliorum fides confirmari similiter debuit. Tum invicem discipuli dixerunt: Οὐχὶ ἡ καρδία ἡμῶν κα ι ομένη ἦν ἐν ἡμῖν; Nonne cor nostrum ardebat in nobis in via, & dum Scripturas nobis aperiret? Luc.XXIV.32. Nam Spiritus Christi animos eorum incenderat, ut moveri se & commoveri ad assensum & amorem loquentis sentirent. Non probat enim se nobis Doctiff. Heinsius, qui κα ι ειν notione ןפב obbrutescendi interpretatur, quia Christi ipsius cum fidelibus suis loquentis suada, non ut obbrutescant, sed ut amore ipsius inardescant, efficit. Tertiò Christus ὤφθη Σίμωνι visus est Simoni Petro, ibid.v.34. 1.Cor.XV.5. Quartò Jacobo, ibid. v. 7. Quid illis locutus sit & fecerit Christus, Evangelistae tacent. Nam quae Ignatius Epistola ad Smyrnaeos, & Hieronymus ex Evangelio secundum Nazaraeos iis a Christo dicta commemorant, nullam fidem merentur.
units.tr: LII. To this belong the appearances of Christ when he visited his dearest ones, which the nine Evangelists describe. Four of them were made to single persons or to a few, and the rest to larger groups. Among those made to single persons or to a few, the first was to Mary Magdalene (Matth. 28:9, 10; Mark 16:9; John 20:11, etc.). She was standing outside the sepulchre weeping and peering into it, and saw two angels in white sitting there. Turning round at once, she saw Jesus himself standing, but did not recognise him, thinking him to be the gardener. When he asked her why she was weeping and whom she was seeking, and she asked whether he had carried Jesus away and where he had laid him, Jesus said to her, "Mary" (John 20:15). Before this, he had addressed her as a stranger addresses a stranger: "Woman, why are you weeping?" Now that the enemies were already routed and he was triumphant, he played and joked with his own and let their sadness grow, so that their joy would be the fuller. But he did not delay long; he addressed her by the name he held in his heart. She turned to him and replied, "Rabbouni," which is "Teacher" [Ῥαββουνί; Διδάσκαλε]. So, with every cloud dispelled, she saw first the Sun of Righteousness, free of the stain and filth of our sins, and was filled with sudden joy. Yet Jesus did not want her to touch him, because he had not yet ascended to his Father. Rather, he bade her run quickly to his brothers and tell them, "I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God" (ibid. v. 17). He did not want the time to be wasted in an idle embrace, as if the height of joy had already been reached. He judged it of greater weight and urgency that he should, as quickly as possible, tell his brothers (so he calls the disciples after the resurrection, in line with Psalm 22:23, "I will declare your name to my brothers") that he would not be with them on earth for long. Indeed, he was about to enter, like the High Priest, the heavenly sanctuary at once, and to prepare a place for them with his Father and his God. The second appearance was made to two disciples going to Emmaus (Mark 16:12; Luke 24:13, etc.). He revealed himself to them in another form [ἐν ἑτέρᾳ μορφῇ], that is, not in the form in which he had hitherto been accustomed to live with them, but with a brightness, radiance and vigour, and with a countenance other than they were used to, or with some other such difference as changed his appearance. Clouds of reasoning gathered over them, since they were engaged in discussion, with gloomy [σκυθρωπῷ] faces, about the Kingdom of Heaven and what would now be needed for Christ, since they had not found him in the sepulchre. The effect was that, although Christ walked with them as a companion on the road and expounded fully from Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms his sufferings and his glories, they did not recognise him. Only when, in the blessing and breaking of bread, their eyes, which had hitherto been held [ἐκρατοῦντο], were opened, did they know him. But as soon as he was recognised, he was taken from their sight [ἐφανερώθη ἀπ' αὐτῶν]: he withdrew secretly from their eyes, without their noticing, or without holding them as before, because their faith was now sufficiently confirmed, and the faith of others ought to be confirmed in the same way. Then the disciples said to one another: "Was not our heart burning within us?" [Οὐχὶ ἡ καρδία ἡμῶν καιομένη ἦν ἐν ἡμῖν;] "Was not our heart burning within us on the road, while he opened the Scriptures to us?" (Luke 24:32). For the Spirit of Christ had kindled their minds, so that they felt themselves moved and stirred to assent and love by the speaker. For the very learned Heinsius does not recommend himself to us when he takes καίειν in the sense of the Hebrew [בער] meaning to grow brutish, because the persuasive power of Christ himself speaking to his faithful does not make them brutish, but sets them aflame with love for him. Thirdly, Christ appeared to Simon [ὤφθη Σίμωνι], that is, to Simon Peter (ibid. v. 34; 1 Cor. 15:5). Fourthly, he appeared to James (ibid. v. 7). What Christ said and did to them the Evangelists are silent about. As for the things that Ignatius in his Epistle to the Smyrnaeans, and Jerome from the Gospel according to the Nazarenes, record as said to them by Christ, they deserve no credence.

units.la: LII. Apparitionum, quae pluribus factae sunt, duae in Judaea, duae in Galilaea, & una eaque novissima iterum in Judaea, contigerunt.
units.tr: LII. Of the appearances made to more than one person, two took place in Judaea, two in Galilee, and one last one again in Judaea.

units.la: In Judaea primò, adeòque post reliquas quatuor apparitiones supra memoratas Quintò Apostolis, uno Thoma absente, die Dominica post follis occasum, ὑστερον, uti Marcus habet, hoc est, non novissime, uti Vulgatus, vel posteremò, uti Beza & Syrus reddunt; sed postea, uti recte Erasmus, & Arabs (confer Matth.XXI.32. Joh. XIII. 36. Hebr. XII. 11.) Hierosolymae apparuit, Marc.XVI.14. Luc.XXIV.36.&c. Joh.XX.19-25. Venit ad eos ὀψὲ γιομένης cum jam serum esset, & θυρῶν κεκλεισμένων foribus clausis, ob metum Judaeorum, Joh.XX.19. sive ipse omnipotente virtute, sive alii fores ei advenienti & pulsanti referarunt. Sic stans in medio eorum ad eos dixit: Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν Pax vobis, seu voce Punica, Avete, Luc.XXIV.36. Vulgatus addit: Ego sum: nolite timere. Eadem Syrus & Arabs habent: sed Graeci codices non legunt: & male illa cum sequentibus cohaerent. Subito adventu attonitos & putantes, se πνεῦμα spiritum (spectrum, Diabolum) videre, alloquitur Christus: Τί τεταραγμένοι ἐστέ; quare conturbati estis, & quare ratiocinationes ascendunt in corda vestra? quasi scilicet malus spiritus essem, vel phantasmate vobis illuderem; Videte manus meas & pedes meos. Nam αὐτὸς ἐγώ Ego ipse sum (Ego sum qui loquitur, Esaj.LII.6.) Contrectate me & videte. Nam spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere. Luc.XXIV.37.38.39. Noluit enim Jesus videri spiritus, spectrum, vel habens corpus, quod per modum spiritus in loco fit, hoc est, corpus non corpus, sed spiritus. Apparuerunt etiam Angeli corpore vero induti; sed metuebant discipuli, ne spiritus malus esset. qualis corpora solida & vera non facit. Utque magis etiam animos dubitantium confirmaret, jussit afferri βρώσιμον ἐσκυλεντum; & allata parte assi piscis, & favi mellis, iis coram comedit. Sed plus etiam ad firmandam eorum fidem valuit, quod scripturis Moisis, Prophetarum & Psalmorum de se ante inculcatis, & denuo ad animum & memoriam eorum revocatis iis aperuit mentem, ut scripturas intelligerent, Luc.XXIV.41-48. Discipuli viso Domino magnopere laetati sunt. Unde denuo iis Pacem precatus Dominus, eadem adversus omnes terrores eos munivit, & ad suscipiendum munus animum iis addidit. Quemadmodum me misit Pater, inquiens, sic ego mitto vos; quin & afflatus signo iis Spiritum S. impertiens; quia Spiritus S. flatus instar operatus, Joh.III.8. & cum flatu magno in illos descensurus erat, Act.II.2. cum hac promissione: Quorum peccata remiseritis, (remissionem praedicando, consolando eos, quos Spiritu S. duce, & luce verbi Dei consolari conveniens erit) remittentur eis; quorum retinueritis, retinebuntur, Joh. XX.20-23. Octavo post die Sexta vice Apostolis omnibus, Thoma etiam, qui praeteris resurrectionem Christi in dubium revocaverat, nec prius se crediturum, quam vestigia clavorum in manibus ejus viderit, digitum vestigiis iis inseruerit, & manum lateri immiserit, asseruit; praesente iterum Hierosolymae apparuit, ibid.v.25. &c. Non enim negligere Thomam, nimia incredulitate, sive quod populum indignum, qui a Christo reviseretur, habuit; sive quod opinio de carnali Regno altas nimis radices egit, laborantem voluit. Eodem modo, ut ante octiduum, ad eas accedens, clausis foribus, in medio eorum sestitit, Pacem nuntiat, & ad Thomam dicit: Fer digitum tuum huc, & vide manus meas; & fer manum tuam, & infere in latus meum, & ne existe incredulus, sed fidelis, v.27. Licet enim prudentiae sit non quidvis ἀξιοπιστος recipere & probare; tamen verbo Dei, & veritati verbo Dei & pietati convenienti, & testimoniis eorum, qui facta Dei visa, quae suspecta esse non possunt, praedicant, ratiocinationes opponere, & nimiam ἀξιόπιστον evidentiam exigere non convenit; quia sic fides definiret esse fides, & non Deo obsequeretur, sed Deum potius sibi obsequentem reddere auderet. Ideo Thomas sine mora ratiocinationes & dubitationem suam Christo subjicit, & in haec verba erumpit: Ὁ Κύριός μου, καὶ ὁ Θεός μου, Dominus meus, & Deus meus, v.28. non primo sic de Christo sentiens, cum jam ante Filium Dei viventis cum aliis Apostolis confessus fuerit; sed eum ipsum, quem praesentem palpaverat, Dominum & Deum illum, quem ante hac agnoverat, esse confessus. Sed mox Thomae sic confitenti Christum a se visum & contrectatum, ceu beatiores eos, qui non viderint & crediderint, Christus ipse v.29. praefert; quia magis Deum glorificant, qui mentem Dei habent, & minus carnalia phantasmata patiuntur; atque mox Christo Coelum ingresso, & ad judicium ultimum usque in eo perseveranter mansuro, fideles res majores & gloriosiores, non sine demonstratione Dei & potentiae ejus, visuri & auditur erant, quam Apostoli viderunt & audiverunt. Unde statim Johannes subjicit, multa & alia signa Jesum coram discipulis suis fecisse, quae in hoc libro scripta non sint, quia scripta sufficiant ad hoc, ut credamus, quod Jesus sit Christus, Filius Dei, v.30.31. q.d. non obfuturum beatitudini majori non videntium, & non visa credentium, quod non omnia signa Christi viderunt, quia ne quidem omnia scribi Deus voluit.
units.tr: In Judaea: first, and therefore after the other four appearances mentioned above, fifthly, to the apostles, with Thomas absent, on the Lord's day after the doors were shut in the evening, later [ὑστερον], as Mark has it, that is, not "last" as the Vulgate has it, or "finally" as Beza and the Syriac render it, but "afterwards," as Erasmus rightly gives it, and the Arabic (compare Matth. 21:32; John 13:36; Heb. 12:11). He appeared at Jerusalem (Mark 16:14; Luke 24:36, etc.; John 20:19–25). He came to them when it was evening [ὀψὲ γενομένης], since it was already late, and with the doors shut [θυρῶν κεκλεισμένων] for fear of the Jews (John 20:19). Whether he entered by his own almighty power, or others opened the doors to him as he came and knocked, is not stated. Standing thus in the midst of them, he said to them, "Peace be to you" [Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν], or in the Punic tongue, "Avete" (Luke 24:36). The Vulgate adds, "It is I; do not be afraid." The Syriac and Arabic have the same, but the Greek manuscripts do not read it, and it does not fit well with what follows. To those who were astonished at his sudden coming and thought they saw a spirit [πνεῦμα] (a spectre, a devil), Christ speaks: "Why are you troubled?" [Τί τεταραγμένοι ἐστέ;] Why do doubts rise in your hearts? As if I were an evil spirit, or were mocking you with a phantom. "See my hands and my feet. For I am myself" [αὐτὸς ἐγώ]. I am he who speaks (Isaiah 52:6). Handle me and see; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me to have." (Luke 24:37–39). For Jesus did not wish to be seen as a spirit or a spectre, or as one having a body in the manner of a spirit that is in a place, that is, a body that is not a body but a spirit. Angels too have appeared clothed in a real body, yet the disciples feared that it was an evil spirit, such as does not make solid and true bodies. And to confirm still more the minds of the doubters, he ordered food [βρώσιμον] to be brought, and when a piece of a roasted fish and a honeycomb had been brought, he ate them before them. But what did more to establish their faith was that he opened their minds, so that they understood the Scriptures, by expounding to them, through the writings of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms, what had already been said about himself, and bringing it back to their mind and memory (Luke 24:41–48). The disciples rejoiced greatly on seeing the Lord. Therefore the Lord, greeting them with peace again, fortified them with the same words against all terrors, and gave them courage to take up their office. "As the Father has sent me, so I send you," he said; and breathing on them, he imparted to them the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit works like a breath (John 3:8), and was about to descend upon them with a mighty rushing wind (Acts 2:2), with this promise: "Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them", that is, by preaching remission and comforting those whom it will be fitting to comfort, under the leading of the Holy Spirit and the light of the Word of God; "whose sins you retain, they are retained" (John 20:20–23). Eight days later, on the sixth occasion, he appeared again at Jerusalem to all the apostles, including Thomas, who had called the resurrection of Christ into doubt beforehand and had asserted that he would not believe until he saw the marks of the nails in his hands, and put his finger into the marks and his hand into his side (ibid. v. 25, etc.). He did not neglect Thomas, whether because of excessive unbelief, or because the people were unworthy to be visited by Christ, or because the opinion of a carnal kingdom had struck too deep roots, but he wished to deal with him in his struggle. In the same way as eight days before, he came to them with the doors shut, stood in the midst of them, announced Peace, and said to Thomas: "Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put your hand and thrust it into my side, and do not be unbelieving, but believing" (v. 27). For although it is the part of prudence not to receive and approve just anything that is credible [ἀξιοπιστος], nevertheless it is not fitting to set one's reasonings against the Word of God and the truth agreeing with the Word of God and with godliness, and against the testimony of those who preach the deeds of God that they have seen, which cannot be suspected; nor to demand an excessive evidence of what is credible [ἀξιόπιστον], for then faith would cease to be faith, and would not obey God, but would dare to make God obey itself. Therefore Thomas without delay submitted his reasonings and doubts to Christ, and broke out in these words: "My Lord and my God" [Ὁ Κύριός μου, καὶ ὁ Θεός μου], Dominus meus, & Deus meus (v. 28). He was not thinking this of Christ for the first time, since he had already confessed the Son of the living God together with the other apostles; but he confessed that the very one whom he had touched while present was the Lord and God whom he had acknowledged before. But Christ himself immediately preferred to Thomas, who thus confessed him as one he had seen and handled, those more blessed ones who have not seen and yet have believed (v. 29). For those who have the mind of God and suffer less from carnal phantasms glorify God more; and soon, when Christ had entered heaven and was to remain there until the last judgment, the faithful were to see and hear greater and more glorious things, not without the demonstration of God and his power, than the apostles saw and heard. Hence John immediately adds that Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book, because what is written is sufficient for this, that we may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (v. 30, 31); as if to say that it would not stand in the way of the greater blessedness of those who do not see and believe what is not seen, that they did not see all the signs of Christ, since God did not even wish all of them to be written down.

units.la: Reliquae sunt pluribus, duae in Judaea. luit, justit, sed scripta pauciora ad ἀπιστοφοείαν eorum sufficiant.
units.tr: The rest were seen by many people, two of them in Judaea. He paid the penalty, he was justified, but fewer things were written down, sufficient for their unbelief [ἀπιστοφοείαν].

units.la: LIII. In Galilæa apparitiones duæ factæ sunt. Nam & ante resurrectionem se iis in Galilæam præiturum prædixerat; & resuscitatus per Mariam Magdalenam discipulis, ut in Galilæam, visuri ibi Dominum irent, mandaverat. Prior igitur in Galilæa, eáque numero Septima (nam τέλευ Tertiam Johannes cap. xxi. 14. vocat, inter eas nempe, quæ pluribus factæ sunt) ad mare Tiberiadis contigit. Hanc apparitionem solus Johannes cap. xxi. fere totó descripsit. Erant ibi unà Petrus, Thomas, Nathanael, Filii Zebedæi, & alii duo, piscantes, sed nihil ea nocte ceperant. Mane in litore stat Jesus, sed nondum piscantibus agnitus; obsonium petit, & cum se habere negassent, rete ad dexteram partem navigii projici jubet. Parent illi, & ingentem piscium multitudinemceperunt. Johannes dilectus ille Christi discipulus primus prodigium illud cum animo suo reputans, Jesum agnoscit, ejúsque indicium Petro facit, qui amiculo succinctus mari se committit, ut vel ocyús ad Dominum veniret, vel rete piscium facilius in terram traheret. Reliqui cum navigio veniunt, σύροντες τὸ δίκτυον trahentes rete, piscibus magnis centum quinquaginta tribus exuberans. In terram eluctati prunas positas, piscem iis impositum & panem inveniunt. Prandium instruitur, in quo discipuli non ausi sunt percunctari eum, quis esset, εἰδότες ὅτι ὁ Κύριός ἐστι scientes quòd Dominus sit, v. 12. In quibus emblema est, quo significare Christus voluit, quòd piscationis spiritualis instituendæ ipse Dominus & arbiter sit, & quòd benedicente ipso ii, quos ex Judæis & gentibus, etiam pisces magnos, potentes, obstinatos conversuri Apostoli erant, unum & commune in Regno Dei convivium, ex eodem igne paratum, eodem cibo instructum celebraturi essent. Ecce ego mittam piscatores multos, & piscabuntur illos, Jerem. XVI, 16. Finito prandio Petrum abnegatorem adoritur, & ex eo scisicitatur: Simon Jona (fili columbæ, non amplius Cepha, Petre) amas me magis quàm hi, cùm jactaveris, non scandalizaturum te in me, etiamsi omnes scandalizarentur, Matth. XXVI. 33. Marc. XIV. 29. Petrus humiliùs respondens, ad conscientiam Domini provocat: Ne Domine, inquiens, tu nosti, quòd amem te. Jubet igitur eum pascere agnos suos. Secunda vice interroganti similiter respondet. Tertia vice interrogante Domino, tristatur, & respondet: Domine, tu omnia nosti, nosti quòd diligam te. Cui denuo Dominus: Pasce oves meas, v. 15, 16, 17. Sed ne sibi amplius suffenus esset, clarè ipsi martyrium portendit, v. 18, 19. eique, ut se insequatur, præcipit, Johanne dilecto illo, sponte & injusso eum sequente. de cujus fatis percontanti Petro idem respondet: Si eum velim manere, donec veniam, quid ad te? v. 21, 22. q. d. non morietur, donec Regnum meum manifestabitur. Sed quid tamen tua refert? Non enim ad curam tuam, sed meam pertinet, qui, & quibus donis instruci, & quandiu Ecclesiæ & Regno Dei inservire debeant. Subit posterior in Galilæa apparitio, eáque numero Octava, à solo Matthæo cap. xxviii. 16 - f. consignata, & celeberri-
units.tr: LIII. Two appearances took place in Galilee. Before the resurrection he had said that he would go before them into Galilee, and after his resurrection he had told the disciples, through Mary Magdalene, to go into Galilee to see the Lord there. The first, therefore, was in Galilee, and it was the seventh in number (for John, at chapter 21:14, calls it the third [τρίτον] among those appearances which were made to several people). It happened by the Sea of Tiberias. John alone describes this appearance almost entirely, in chapter 21. Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee, and two others were there together, fishing, but they had caught nothing that night. In the morning Jesus stood on the shore, but he was not yet recognised by the fishermen. He asked for something to eat, and when they said they had nothing, he ordered them to cast the net on the right side of the boat. They obeyed and caught a huge number of fish. John, that disciple whom Christ loved, thought over the marvel in his mind, recognised Jesus, and told Peter so. Peter, girded with his outer garment, threw himself into the sea so that he might come to the Lord more quickly, or so that he might more easily drag the net of fish to land. The others came with the boat, dragging the net [σύροντες τὸ δίκτυον], full of one hundred and fifty-three large fish. Once on land they found a fire of coals laid out, with a fish and bread placed on it. A meal was prepared, and the disciples did not dare to ask him who he was, knowing that it was the Lord [εἰδότες ὅτι ὁ Κύριός ἐστι], v. 12. In these things there is an emblem by which Christ wished to signify that the Lord himself is the master and director of spiritual fishing, and that the apostles were going to gather, by his blessing, both Jews and Gentiles, even the large, powerful, stubborn fish, into one common feast in the kingdom of God, prepared over the same fire and furnished with the same food. Behold, I will send many fishers, and they will fish for them, Jer. 16:16. When the meal was finished, he turned to Peter, the one who had denied him, and asked him: Simon son of Jonah (son of the dove, no longer Cephas, Peter), do you love me more than these? When you boasted that you would not be made to stumble because of me, even if all were made to stumble, Matt. 26:33; Mark 14:29. Peter answered more humbly, appealing to the Lord's knowledge: No, Lord, you know that I love you. So Jesus told him to feed his lambs. To the second question he gave a similar answer. When the Lord asked a third time, he was saddened and answered: Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you. To him again the Lord said: Feed my sheep, vv. 15, 16, 17. But so that Peter should not be too self-assured, he clearly foretold his martyrdom, vv. 18, 19, and ordered him to follow him, while the beloved John followed of his own accord and without being told. When Peter asked about John's fate, the Lord gave this answer: If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? vv. 21, 22. That is, he will not die until my kingdom is made manifest. But what does that matter to you? For it is not your concern, but mine, to determine with what gifts, and for how long, each man should serve the Church and the kingdom of God. Then follows the later appearance in Galilee, the eighth in number, recorded by Matthew alone, chapter 28:16 ff., and celebrated

units.la: LIV. Novissima Christi apparitio, eáque Nona illa est, qua in monte Oliveti, & ea parte montis, quæ Bethania, appellatur; Hierosolymæ proxima, Undecim suis apparens, iisdem valedixit, & à nube susceptus, inspectantibus illis, in Cœlum sublatus est; Luc. XXIV. 50. Act. I. 4-10. Accidit illa die post resurrectionem quadragesimo, ibid. I. 3. Antea in Galilæa adhuc, uti videtur, cum undecim existens, vel in itinere ex Galilæa Bethaniam versus, vel Hierosolymæ, uti alii ex Act. I. 3 - 12. colligunt; testes suæ passionis & resurrectionis aciverat; ὑμεῖς δὲ ἐστε μάρτυρες τούτων Vos autem estis testes eorum, Luc. XXIV. 48. Eritis mihi testes & Hierosolymis & in tota Judæa & Samaria, & usque ad ultimas terras, Act. I. 8. Ut verò ad testimonium hoc promptiores aptiorésque evadant, iisdem Spiritum S. promittit. Ecce ego mittam in vobis ... λίαν ἐ Πατρὸς μὰ promissionem Patris mei in vos, Luc.XXIV.49. Recipietis Spiritus S. virtutem, postquam supervenerit in vos,& eritis mihi testes, &c. Act.I.8. Cumque promissio hæc Hierosolymis impleri debuerit, mandatum iisdem dat, ut Hierosolymis maneant. Vos autem sedete in civitate Hierusalem, usque dum virtute ex alto induamini, Luc.XXIV.49. Act.I.4. Percontantibus iis: Domine, num hoc tempore exhibes Regnum Israeli? (Regnum Dei, v.3. subjectionem omnium gentium, non Regnum temporale, cujus restitutionem sperare, vel expetere nonnisi per summum stuporem potuissent) respondet: Non est vestrum nôsse tempora, sive opportunitates, quas Pater in sua ipsius potestate statuit, ibid. v.6. 7. Non negat Christus, se exhibiturum hoc Regnum, sed tempus ejus repræsentandi revelare iis renuit, & ministerium hoc Regnum per testimonium suum promovendi iis injungit. Merito eorum curiositatem & coercet, quia amplius scire, quàm revelatum erat, cupiebant. Sed Deus quædam in potestate sua statuit, & de iis sic locutus est, ut interim promissionibus conditionatis, comminationibus & dilationibus, tanquam per occasionem, locus esset. Ita Regnum Ecclesiæ omnino promisit, sed cum conditione certaminum & afflictionum. Ideo Jobus Phiphazo opponit: Quare ab omnipotente non sunt recondita tempora? q. d. cur tu id in dubium revocas? Job. XXIV.1. Demum educit eos extra (Galilæam, vel potius Hierosolymam) in Bethaniam, ibi sublatis manibus suis benedixit iis, Luc.XXIV.50. Ubi uni benedicendum erat, id fieri impositione manuum, (Genes.XXVII.4.7.12.21. XLVIII.9.14.15.&c.) Ubi pluribus sublatis, seu protensis super eorum capita, pro quibus preces offerebantur, manibus id fieri suevit. Ita Aharon attollens manus suas super populum, benedixit illis, Levit.IX.12.
