Vix impleta benedictione Jesus in altum elevatus, & in Cœlum sublatus est, Luc.XXIV.51. Act.I.9. LV. Ascensio hæc Christi in Cœlum, Secundus Exaltationis gradus, imò proprie ipsa exaltatio fuit. Ἀναλήψεως sursum receptionis, Marc.XVI.19. Luc.IX.51. Act.I.11. nec non ἀναβάσεως, ascensionis, Joh.III.13. XX.17. Act.II.34. Ephef.IV.8.9.10. nominibus venit. Ille ipse, qui descendit in inferiores partes terræ (ex Cœlo in terram, neque in terram tantùm, sed in inferiores ejus partes, Psalm.CXXXIX.15. ubi & seu superioribus terræ viventium partibus) ipse est, qui etiam ascendit longè supra Cœlum, Ephef.IV.8.9. Ascendisti in altum, egisti prædam, dona accepisti in hominibus, Psalm.LXVIII.19. Qui descendit, idem est, qui ascendit super omnes Cœlos, &c. Ephef. IV.10. Si enim in terra Christus mansisset, Sacerdos noster non fuisset. Hebr.VIII.4. Sicut igitur Sacerdos summus semel quotannis, senescente æstate, post exordium novi anni vulgaris, revolvente anno (Exod. XXXIV.22.) ante festum non fine sanguine in Sanctum Sanctorum intrabat, Levit.XVI.14. ita Christus fuso sanguine suo & rupto velo carnis suæ initio temporis gratiæ & libertatis in Cœlum intravit, & viam ad Cœlum apertam nobis dedicavit, & Ecclesiam Cœlestem cum terrestri ad unum; unam summam redigens unam Dei domum fecit. planè ut Sacerdote velum amovente utrumque tabernaculum unum & indivisum fuit, Hebr.VI.19.20. IX.23.24. Ephef.I.10. LVI. Ascensionis proin hujus veritas omni dubitatione & exceptione major est. Nam & prædicta est, tum in V.T. Deut.XXX.11.12. Psal.XLV.5. XLVII.6. LXVIII.19. Prov. XXX.4. Esaj.LII.13. Amos.IX.6. tum in Novo Test. Joh.III.13. VII.33. XVI.7.8. & adumbrata est exemplis Enochi & Eliæ; nec non typo Sacerdotis in Sanctum Sanctorum intrantis: & in tempore revera successit. Nam discipulis aspectantibus sursum receptus est in Cœlum: Διέςη ἀπ' αὐτῶν disjunctus ab illis est, & quidem in nube, quæ id Christo præstitit, quod currus & equiinei Eliæ, Act.I.9. Neque suspicione ulla testes, ejus rei Apostoli laborare possunt, quando & numero plures, & nulla temporali mercede alia quàm odii implacabilis mundi, & dirissimorum suppliciorum, ita in toto mundo testati sunt: & Stephanus æquè ac Paulus eum in Cœlo viderunt: & Spiritus Christi juxta promissionem Apostolis destinato tempore ex Cœlo missus est: & Regnum, quod in Cœlo gerit, tot illustribus documentis patefactum est: & universa Religio Christiana eam postulat. Qui Dominus è Cœlo fuit, Cœlo excludi non potuit, sed in gloriam intrare debuit. Luc. XXIV.26. Qui justitiam omnem implevit Matth. III.15. etiam justitiæ coronam in Cœlo accipere debuit, 2.Tim.IV.8. Qui nisi in Cœlum intrasset, membra ejus consummari, cum cœlestibus recapitulari, suum, & spem viam Christi pro iis intercedentis in Cœlis habere recentem & vivum in Cœlum aditum habere, & in Cœlum denique assumi non possent. Sed Christus profestus est, ut pararet nobis locum, & rursum veniens nos ad se adsumeret, Joh.XIV.2.3. Cumque plures etiam filii in gloriam jam tum adducti fuerint, principem salutis per passiones consummari, & in gloriam etiam introduci oportuit, Hebr. II.10. LVII. Fidem Ascensionis Christi in Cœlum non minuit illud, quòd in hostium, Judæorum inprimis conspectu non ascendit. Sicut enim Regnum ejus non debuit venire cum observatione & pompa, Luc. XVII.20. Ita cum pompa in Cœlum ascendere noluit, tum ut fidei locus esset, cùm beatiores sint, qui non videntes credunt, Joh.XX.29. tum quia abundè signorum jam viderant Judæi, neque iis tamen moveri se passi sunt: tum quia revelatione justitiæ ex Cœlo, & donorum atque judiciorum efficaci dispensatione suam in Cœlo præsentiam patefacere maluit: tum quia suæ in Cœlo præsentiæ demonstrationem conspicabilem ex eodem reditu ad judicium novissimum differre constituit, Matth. XXIV.26.27. XXV.31.32. Illud quoque di-lutum lutum est, quod Christi hostes objectant, Apostolos non vidisse Dominum in Coelum ipsum ingredientem, quia nubes ab eorum oculis eum submoverit. Nam saltem duo Angeli cum coelesti gloria apparentes, eum in Coelum receptum esse, testati sunt. Viri Galilaei, inquiunt, quid statis intuentes in Coelum? Hic Jesus, qui sursum receptus est a vobis in Coelum, ita veniet, quemadmodum spectastis eum proficiscentem in Coelum, Act. I. 11. Etiam consecuta juxta promissionem effusio Spiritus S. in Apostolos Christi in Coelum, ex quo ab eodem effusus est, introitum confirmat. Eodem facit, quod & Stephanus & Paulus Jesum in Coelo viderunt, & Apostoli omnia, quae patrarunt, miracula, in nomine Christi in Coelis regnantis, se patrasse, professi sunt, συνεπιμαρτυροῦντος τοῦ Θεοῦ σημείοις κ. τέρασι &c. una testimonium Deo praebente signis & prodigiis, quibus annunciationem suam confirmarunt, Hebr. II. 4. Frustra etiam miraculosae ascensionis Christi in Coelum fidem obscurare annixus est Philostratus, scriptis octo de vita & rebus gestis Apollonii Thyanei libris, ex quibus Jesum inter & Thyaneum comparationem instituendi occasionem Hierocles libro, quem Φιλαλήθη inscripsit, captavit. Nam Thyaneum illum doctrinae, sanctitatis ac mirificae virtutis fictitium simulachrum in Coelum etiam, testibus Nymphis ab eodem Philostrato allegatis, ascendentem, invalescenti jam Christi in Coelum evecti fidei & doctrinae opponere ausi sunt. Sed fabulae scenam pridem Eusebius, & post eum alii aperuerunt. Nam ad Christi plane exemplar hanc Philostratus effigiem expressit, & pleraque ex Jesu Christi historia Thyaneo applicavit, ne quid Ethnici Christianis invidere possent. Qua re Christi gloriam incautus amplificavit, dum veram ejus virtutem, alteri falso adscriptam, meritis laudibus extulit, & aliis laudandam mirandamque propositi. Quod historiae illius cum historia Evangelii de Christo συγκεῖσθαι manifeste probat. Ne dicam Thyaneum hunc vaferrimum & sacerrimum magum fuisse. Hoc enim ei crimen, Euphrates Tyrius Philosophus celebris impegit. Eandem ob causam sacris Eleusiniis eum Hierophanta arcuit, & ab antro Trophonii Sacerdotes excluserunt, & pro mago a Domitiano captus & in carcerem detrusus est. Quin & Xiphilinus in Caracalla ex Dione tradidit, Caracallam magis & praestigiatoribus adeo delectatum esse, ut Thyaneum honoribus & monumentis etiam, qualia Heroibus consecrantur, coluerit. Similibus exemplis Coelum mirabiliter icandentium abundant monumenta fabularia, veluti Semeles, Ganymedis, Endymionis & Titheni, qui a Jove, Luna & Aurora rapti finguntur; item Britomartis, quae in Aegina oculis hominum erepta est; Bellerophontis, quem Pegasus tulit in Coelum, sed infelici successu; Ariadnes, quae & sideribus inserta est; Aesculapii, cui fulmen viam in Coelum aperuit; Herculis a Minerva aliisque diis illuc invecti; Bacchi, qui a Titanibus membratim dilaceratus redivivus & integer Coelum conscendit; Iphigeniae, immolatori a Diana ereptae, & in Coelum ipsum translatae, & similium, inprimis Romuli, quem uno telte Julio Proculo, a Daemone nascenti
units.tr: LIV. The last appearance of Christ is the ninth, when he appeared to the eleven on the Mount of Olives, in that part of the mount called Bethany, near Jerusalem. There he bade them farewell, and while they looked on he was taken up into heaven and received by a cloud; Luc. XXIV. 50. Act. I. 4-10. It happened on the fortieth day after the resurrection, ibid. I. 3. Earlier, while he was still in Galilee, as it seems, when he was with the eleven, either on the way from Galilee towards Bethany or at Jerusalem, as others gather from Act. I. 3-12, he had appointed them witnesses of his passion and resurrection: "But you are witnesses of these things [ὑμεῖς δὲ ἐστε μάρτυρες τούτων]," Luc. XXIV. 48. You shall be my witnesses both in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth, Act. I. 8. So that they might be readier and fitter for this testimony, he promises them the Holy Spirit: Behold, I send upon you ... [ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ Πατρός μου] the promise of my Father upon you, Luc. XXIV. 49. You shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit when he has come upon you, and you shall be my witnesses, etc. Act. I. 8. Since this promise was to be fulfilled at Jerusalem, he gives them the command to remain at Jerusalem: But you are to sit in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high, Luc. XXIV. 49; Act. I. 4. When they asked him, Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel? (the kingdom of God, v. 3, the subjection of all nations, not a temporal kingdom, whose restoration they could hope for or desire only through the greatest stupidity), he answers: It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father has set in his own power, ibid. vv. 6, 7. Christ does not deny that he will set up this kingdom, but he refuses to reveal to them the time of its establishment, and he enjoins on them the task of advancing this kingdom through their testimony. Rightly he restrains their curiosity, because they wished to know more than had been revealed. But God has fixed some things in his own power, and has spoken of them in such a way that, meanwhile, there is room for conditional promises, threats and delays, as it were by the way. Thus he has indeed promised the kingdom to the Church, but with the condition of conflicts and afflictions. Therefore Job answers Zophar: Why are times not hidden by the Almighty?, as if to say: why do you call this into doubt? Job XXIV. 1. Finally, he led them out (from Galilee, or rather from Jerusalem) as far as Bethany, and there, lifting up his hands, he blessed them, Luc. XXIV. 50. Where one person was to be blessed, this was done by the laying on of hands (Gen. XXVII. 4, 7, 12, 21; XLVIII. 9, 14, 15, etc.); where several were blessed, it was customary to do it by lifting or stretching out the hands over the heads of those for whom prayers were offered. So Aaron, lifting up his hands over the people, blessed them, Levit. IX. 12. Scarcely had the blessing been completed when Jesus was lifted up on high, and taken up into heaven, Luc. XXIV. 51; Act. I. 9. LV. This ascension of Christ into heaven was the second step of his exaltation; indeed it was properly the exaltation itself. It is named by the words [ἀναλήψεως] reception upward, Marc. XVI. 19; Luc. IX. 51; Act. I. 11, and also [ἀναβάσεως] ascent, Joh. III. 13; XX. 17; Act. II. 34; Ephes. IV. 8-10. He who descended into the lower parts of the earth (from heaven to earth, and not only to the earth but to its lower parts, Psalm CXXXIX. 15, where also the upper parts of the land of the living are meant) is the same who also ascended far above all heavens, Ephes. IV. 8, 9. You have ascended on high, you have led captivity captive, you have received gifts among men, Psalm LXVIII. 19. He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, etc., Ephes. IV. 10. For if Christ had remained on earth, he would not be our priest, Hebr. VIII. 4. Just as the high priest entered into the Holy of Holies once a year, at the end of summer, after the beginning of the civil new year, when the year had come round (Exod. XXXIV. 22), and entered not without blood (Levit. XVI. 14), so Christ, having poured out his blood and torn the veil of his flesh, at the beginning of the time of grace and liberty entered into heaven, and dedicated for us a way open to heaven, and, bringing the heavenly Church and the earthly together into one sum, made one house of God; just as, with the priest removing the veil, both tabernacles were one and undivided, Hebr. VI. 19, 20; IX. 23, 24; Ephes. I. 10. LVI. Therefore the truth of this ascension is greater than any doubt or objection. For it was foretold both in the Old Testament, Deut. XXX. 11, 12; Psalm XLV. 5; XLVII. 6; LXVIII. 19; Prov. XXX. 4; Isa. LII. 13; Amos IX. 6, and in the New Testament, Joh. III. 13; VII. 33; XVI. 7, 8; it was foreshadowed by the examples of Enoch and Elijah, and also by the type of the priest entering into the Holy of Holies; and it truly followed in time. For, while the disciples looked on, he was taken up into heaven: he was parted from them [διέστη ἀπ' αὐτῶν], and indeed in a cloud, which did for Christ what the chariot and horses of fire did for Elijah, Act. I. 9. Nor can the apostles, the witnesses of this matter, be suspected of any deceit, since they were many in number, and without any temporal reward other than the implacable hatred of the world and the most dreadful punishments, they bore witness in all the world. Stephen as well as Paul saw him in heaven. The Spirit of Christ was sent from heaven at the appointed time, as he had promised the apostles. The kingdom which he rules in heaven has been revealed by so many illustrious proofs. And the whole Christian religion demands it. The Lord who came from heaven could not be shut out of heaven, but ought to enter into glory, Luc. XXIV. 26. He who fulfilled all righteousness, Matth. III. 15, ought also to receive the crown of righteousness in heaven, 2 Tim. IV. 8. Unless he had entered into heaven, his members could not be perfected, be recapitulated with the heavenly, have a recent and living way of access to heaven, have Christ's intercession for them in the heavens as their hope, and finally be taken up into heaven. But Christ went away to prepare a place for us, and coming again would take us to himself, Joh. XIV. 2, 3. And since many sons had already been brought into glory, it was fitting that the author of salvation should be perfected through sufferings and also be brought into glory, Hebr. II. 10. LVII. The fact that Christ did not ascend into heaven in the sight of his enemies, above all the Jews, does not diminish the faith in his ascension. For just as his kingdom ought not to come with observation and display, Luc. XVII. 20, so he was unwilling to ascend into heaven with display: partly so that there might be a place for faith, since they are more blessed who do not see and yet believe, Joh. XX. 29; partly because the Jews had already seen signs in abundance, and yet they had not allowed themselves to be moved by them; partly because he preferred to make his presence in heaven known by the revelation of righteousness from heaven and by the effective dispensing of gifts and judgments; partly because he determined to defer a visible demonstration of his presence in heaven to his return at the last judgment, Matth. XXIV. 26, 27; XXV. 31, 32. That objection of Christ's enemies is also refuted, that the apostles did not see the Lord entering heaven itself, because a cloud removed him from their eyes. For at least two angels appeared with heavenly glory and testified that he had been received into heaven: Men of Galilee, they said, why do you stand looking into heaven? This same Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven, Act. I. 11. Also, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the apostles of Christ, which followed according to the promise, confirms his entry into heaven, since it was poured out by him. To the same effect is the fact that both Stephen and Paul saw Jesus in heaven, and the apostles all professed that the miracles they performed were done in the name of Christ who reigns in heaven, [συνεπιμαρτυροῦντος τοῦ Θεοῦ σημείοις καὶ τέρασι] God also bearing witness with signs and wonders, by which they confirmed their preaching, Hebr. II. 4. Philostratus also strove in vain to obscure the faith in the miraculous ascension of Christ into heaven, in his eight books on the life and deeds of Apollonius of Tyana, from which Hierocles, in the book he entitled Philalethes, seized the occasion to draw a comparison between Jesus and the Tyanean. For they dared to set against the growing faith and doctrine of Christ, who had been carried up to heaven, that fictitious image of the Tyanean, of doctrine, holiness and wonderful power, who was also said, according to the witnesses Philostratus cites (the Nymphs), to have ascended into heaven. But Eusebius, and after him others, long ago laid bare the fabric of this fable. For Philostratus formed this image on the plain model of Christ, and applied to the Tyanean most of the history of Jesus Christ, lest the heathens should have anything to envy the Christians. In doing so he carelessly magnified the glory of Christ, while he extolled with deserved praise the true virtue of Christ, falsely ascribed to another, and proposed the Tyanean to others as one to be praised and admired. That this story is manifestly [συγκεῖσθαι] put together with the Gospel history of Christ is clear. Not to mention that this Tyanean was a most crafty and most wicked magician. For Euphrates of Tyre, a famous philosopher, charged him with this crime. For the same reason the hierophant excluded him from the Eleusinian rites, and the priests shut him out from the cave of Trophonius; and as a magician he was seized by Domitian and thrown into prison. Indeed Xiphilinus, in the life of Caracalla, reports from Dio that Caracalla was so delighted with magicians and conjurers that he honoured the Tyanean with the kind of honours and monuments with which heroes are consecrated. There are abundant fabulous monuments of similar examples of men wonderfully carried up to heaven, such as Semele, Ganymede, Endymion and Tithonus, who are said to have been seized by Jupiter, the Moon and Aurora; likewise Britomartis, who was snatched from the eyes of men in Aegina; Bellerophon, whom Pegasus carried to heaven, but with an unhappy outcome; Ariadne, who was also placed among the stars; Aesculapius, for whom a thunderbolt opened the way to heaven; Hercules, carried thither by Minerva and other gods; Bacchus, who, torn limb from limb by the Titans, rose again alive and whole and ascended to heaven; Iphigenia, the sacrificial victim snatched away by Diana and translated into heaven itself; and others like them, above all Romulus, who, according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book II, tried to persuade people that he had been taken up into heaven, with the single witness Julius Proculus, a demon having been added to the birth. These things, and similar ones, were fabricated by the demon to obscure the ascension of Christ, and they should at least have produced among the Gentiles the effect that the ascension of Christ into heaven would be at least probable, and since not…

units.la: ipsi addito, in Coelum actum esse Dionysius Halicarnassaeus lib. I I, persuadere conatus est. Haec & similia a Daemone ad Ascensionem Christi offuscandam confecta id tamen apud Gentiles efficere debuerunt, ut Christi in Coelum ascensionem saltem probabilem, & cum non tantum testimoniis omni exceptione majoribus, sed etiam operationibus, quas Christo Regi Coelum inhabitanti tot praedictiones & argumenta vindicant, nitatur, certam credparent. Quem in finem a vetustis Patribus, Origene, Eusebio, aliisque exempla haec paganis objecta legere est.
units.tr: That he was carried up into heaven was also something Dionysius of Halicarnassus tried to persuade his readers of in book 2. The devil devised these and similar stories to obscure Christ's ascension, and they were meant to achieve at least this among the Gentiles: that Christ's ascension into heaven would seem probable, and would be held as certain, even though it rests not only on testimonies beyond all exception but also on the works that the many predictions and proofs vindicate for Christ, the King who dwells in heaven. To this end, the ancient Fathers, Origen, Eusebius and others, can be read objecting these examples to the pagans.

units.la: LVIII. Ascensio Christi in Coelum & ἀνάληψις sursum receptio, & ἀνάβασις ascensio fuit. Ἀνάληψις, quatenus a Patre in gloriam assumptus, seu sursum receptus est. Factum est ἐν τῷ συμπληροῦσθαι τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ἀναλήψεως cum implerentur dies sursum receptionis, Lu c.IX. 51. Ubi Budaeus ἀνάληψιν agnitionem Christi a Patre, antea velut abdicati, interpretatur; quia ἀναλαμβάνειν τὸν παῖδα opponitur τῷ ἀ-πεκρίνεσθαι; sicut apud Latinos agnitio liberorum opponitur abdicationi. Sed de hoc quicquid sit, saltem Marc. XVI. 19. ubi dicitur ἀνελήφθη εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν, & Act. I. 11. ubi Jesus ἀναλήφθεὶς εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν dicitur, sursum receptio, assumptio in Coelum significatur. S. Paulus; Ἀνελήφθη ἐν δόξῃ sursum receptus est in gloriam, 1. Tim. III. 16. Et disertius Esajas: Ex coarctatione & judicio לקח assumptus est, cap. LIII. 8. Quomodo etiam de Enocho dicitur; Non amplius erat כי לקח אתו אלהים quia assumpsit eum Deus, Genes. V. 24. Et David: Deus redimet animam meam ex potestate inferni, כי יקחני cum acceperit, assumpserit me, Psal. XLIX. 16. Lucas: ἀνεφέρετο εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν sursum ferebatur in Coelum, Luc. XXIV. 51. ἀνεφέρθη sublatus est, Act. I. 9. Significatur voluntas Patris, Jesum secundum carnem assumentis, sursum recipientis, evehentis, & in domum paternam introducentis, in qua voluntate Christi δικαίωσις justificatio, nec non δοξασμός glorificatio, qua Deus Pater ipsum obedientia defunctum, & secundum carnem noviter in Coelum admissum, gloria in Coelo coronavit, continetur. Sed fuit ascensio etiam Ἀνάβασις, hoc est, ascensio jure meriti quaesita; seu voluntas Filii, qua secundum potentiam & potestatem suam, non alienam, ad Patrem profectus est. ut cum quis sua potestate, jure, ope, in domum suam, cujus dominus est, intrat. Οὐδεὶς ἀναβέβηκεν εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν, Nemo ascendit in Coelum, nisi qui descendit, Joh. III. 13. coll. cum Psal. LXVIII. 19. Ephes. IV. 9. Ἀνάληψις Patri, ἀνάβασις Filio tribuitur; sed una utriusque voluntas est. Sed nemo tamen in Coelum ἀναβέβηκε ascendit, sicut filius ascendit. Licet enim ante Christum multi in Coelum introducti sint, secundum spiritum, nonnulli etiam secundum corpus, quia jam Christi tempore in domo Patris πολλοὶ μοναὶ multae mansiones fuerint, Joh. XIV. 2. hoc est, πολλοὶ μονὴν ποιήσαντες ἐκεῖ multi ibi mansionem facientes, uti ipse Christus ib. v. 23. explicat. & multi filii in gloriam introducti sint, Hebr. II. 10. tamen nemo ascendit in Coelum sicut Christus, tanquam Filius, suo non alieno jure, potestate, merito, & in domum suam, cujus
units.tr: LVIII. Christ's ascension into heaven was both ἀνάληψις [anālēpsis], a taking up or receiving up on high, and ἀνάβασις [anabasis], an ascent. It was an ἀνάληψις insofar as he was taken up, or received up on high, by the Father into glory. It came about, ἐν τῷ συμπληροῦσθαι τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ἀναλήψεως, when the days of his being received up were being fulfilled, Luke 9:51. Here Budaeus interprets ἀνάληψις as the Father's acknowledgement of Christ, who had previously been, as it were, disowned; because ἀναλαμβάνειν τὸν παῖδα [to acknowledge the child] is set against ἀπεκρίνεσθαι [to disown]; just as among the Latins acknowledgement of children is set against disinheritance. But whatever be the case here, at least in Mark 16:19, where it is said that he ἀνελήφθη εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν [was taken up into heaven], and in Acts 1:11, where Jesus is said to be ἀναλήφθεὶς εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν [taken up into heaven], a receiving up on high, an assumption into heaven, is signified. St Paul says: ἀνελήφθη ἐν δόξῃ [he was taken up in glory], he was received up into glory, 1 Tim. 3:16. And Isaiah more plainly: from restraint and judgement [Hebrew: lāqaḥ] he was taken, ch. 53:8. In the same way it is said of Enoch: He was no more, for [Hebrew: kī lāqaḥ ʾōtô ʾĕlōhîm] God took him, Gen. 5:24. And David: God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave, [Hebrew: kī yiqqaḥanī] when he has received, has taken me, Ps. 49:16. Luke: ἀνεφέρετο εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν [he was carried up into heaven], was borne up into heaven, Luke 24:51; ἀνεφέρθη [he was lifted up], was taken up, Acts 1:9. What is signified is the will of the Father, who takes up, receives up on high, raises and introduces the Son, according to the flesh, into his father's house; and in this will is contained Christ's δικαίωσις [dikaiōsis], justification, and also his δοξασμός [doxasmos], glorification, by which God the Father, having crowned him in heaven with glory after his death in obedience, and newly admitted him into heaven according to the flesh. But the ascension was also an Ἀνάβασις [anabasis], that is, an ascent sought by right of merit; or the will of the Son, by which he went up to the Father by his own power and authority, not another's, as when someone enters his own house, of which he is lord, by his own power, right and help. No one has ascended into heaven, except him who descended, John 3:13, compared with Ps. 68:19 and Eph. 4:9. Ἀνάληψις is attributed to the Father, ἀνάβασις to the Son; but the will of both is one. Yet no one else ascended into heaven as the Son ascended. For although before Christ many were introduced into heaven in spirit, and some even in body, since already in Christ's time there were many mansions in the Father's house, John 14:2, that is, many dwelling there and making a mansion, as Christ himself explains in the same passage at v. 23, and although many sons have been brought into glory, Heb. 2:10, nevertheless no one ascended into heaven as Christ did, as Son, by his own right, power and merit, and into his own house, of which

units.la: {i} jus ipse dominus erat, ibid. III. 6. & ut Mediator ac sequester glorificationis & salutis nostrae. Unde jam jam in Coelum ascensurus datam sibi πᾶσαν ἐξουσίαν omnem potestatem in Coelo & terra, praefatus est, Matth. XXVIII.18. Et jus illud indicat verbum προεύομαι proficiscor, quod Christus apud Johannem frequentat. cap. xiv. 2.3.12.28. & in historia ascensionis repetitur, Act. I.10.11. nec non illud, quod purificatione peccatorum per se ipsum facta, Hebr. I.3. in id, quod intra velamen est (hoc est, Coelum ipsum) προεδρομῶν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν εἰσῆλθε prodromus pro nobis ingressus est Jesus, ibid. VI.19.20.
units.tr: he himself was lord, Heb. 3:6, and as Mediator and surety of our glorification and salvation. Hence, about to ascend into heaven, he said that all power in heaven and earth had been given to him, Matt. 28:18. And that right is indicated by the word προεύομαι [proeuomai], I go forth, which Christ frequently uses in John, ch. 14:2, 3, 12, 28, and which is repeated in the account of the ascension, Acts 1:10, 11; and also by the statement that, having made purification of sins by himself, Heb. 1:3, he entered, as forerunner, for us (that is, into heaven itself) into that which is within the veil, Heb. 6:19, 20.

units.la: LIX.
units.tr: LIX.

units.la: Coelum igitur, in quod Christus ascendit, non inferius illud est, quod caput nostrum cingit; sed supremum, Coelum coelorum, quod S. Paulo tertium, 2. Cor. XII. 2. Prophetis שְׁמֵי Solium Domini, Esaj. LXVI. 1. dicitur; in quo est Pater noster, Matth. VI.9. Transiit enim Coelos, puta primum, in quo aer est, & secundum, in quo stellae, sol & sidera sunt, Hebr. IV.14. atque sic factus est ὑψηλότερος sublimior Coelis inferioribus, aspectabilibus, ibid. VII.26. Estque Coelum illud supremum locus & mansio Christi & beatorum. In domo Patris mei multae mansiones sunt. Si aliter esset, dicerem vobis. Proficiscor, ut parem vobis τόπον locum, Joh. XIV.2. Ubi μονή est mansio ejus, qui in Coelo, velut domo sua, manet, habitat: at τόπος locus ad manendum sive habitandum. Sensus igitur verborum Christi est; sunt jam, qui in Coelo habitent, mansionem suam habeant. Et si maxime nulli essent, & nemo hactenus Coelum intrasset, me tamen ad illud proficiscente, non deerit vobis locus in Coelo, in quo maneatis, quia hunc in finem eo proficiscor, ut locum vobis praeparem. Coelum porro, in quod Christus ascendit, locum esse, etiam alia evincunt. Nam ἄνω sursum est, Joh. XI.41. Act. II.19. Col. III.2. Unde ascensio ἀνάβασις, ἀναλήψις dicitur. Et Coelum hoc Christum δέχεται recipit, ut thronus Regem, usque ad tempus restitutionis omnium, Act. III.21. Alior enim Coelis visibilibus factus est, Hebr. IV.14. VII.26. & super omnes Coelos visibiles ascendit, Ephes. IV.10.
units.tr: Heaven, therefore, into which Christ ascended, is not that lower heaven which surrounds our head, but the highest, the heaven of heavens, which St Paul calls the third, 2 Cor. 12:2, and which the prophets call the throne of the Lord [Hebrew: shāmayim], Isa. 66:1; in which is our Father, Matt. 6:9. For he passed through the heavens, namely the first, in which is the air, and the second, in which are the stars, the sun and the constellations, Heb. 4:14; and so he became higher than the heavens, the lower, visible ones, Heb. 7:26. And that highest heaven is the place and dwelling of Christ and of the blessed. In my Father's house there are many mansions. If it were otherwise, I would tell you. I go to prepare a place [τόπον] for you, John 14:2. Here μονή [monē] is the mansion of one who remains and dwells in heaven as in his own house; but τόπος [topos], place, is for remaining or dwelling. The sense of Christ's words is therefore this: there are already those who dwell in heaven and have their own mansion. And even if there were none at all, and no one had yet entered heaven, still, while I go to it, there will be no lack of a place in heaven for you to remain, because I go there for this very purpose, to prepare a place for you. Moreover, that heaven into which Christ ascended is a place is shown by other things as well. For ἄνω [ano], upward, is used, John 11:41, Acts 2:19, Col. 3:2; hence the ascension is called ἀνάβασις and ἀναλήψις. And this heaven receives Christ, as a throne receives a king, until the time of the restoration of all things, Acts 3:21. For he has been made higher than the visible heavens, Heb. 4:14, 7:26, and ascended above all the visible heavens, Eph. 4:10.

units.la: LX.
units.tr: LX.

units.la: Qui omnipraesentiam carnis Christi tuentur, parum feliciter heic se extricant. Nam ascensionem Christi in Coelum alii quidem recentiores veram & localem, quae loci mutatione constat, profitentur, at reapse tollunt, non consecutam corporis Christi ascendentis in Coelum absentiam a terra, seu terrae relictionem, sed mutationem duntaxat modi praesentiae in terra, ex visibili videlicet in invisibilem, adeoque non loci saltem in terra, sed status duntaxat mutationem afferentes: alii vetustiores Coelum illocale, incorporeum, quod ubique fit, statuentes, ascensionem Christi locale penitus abnegarunt, & in nescio quam dispensationem, evanescentiam, ἀφανισμόν dispar ritionem solam converterunt. Quae plane vana sunt, & ascensionem Christi infidelium ludibrio exponunt. Scriptura vero consulto terminum utrumque localem, a quo Christus ascendens recessit, & ad quem accessit, nec non motum intermedium exprimit. Terminus a quo expressus est verbis, ἀπὸ τῶν ἄνω
units.tr: Those who defend the omnipresence of Christ's flesh do not extricate themselves very successfully here. Some of the more recent writers do profess that Christ's ascension into heaven was true and local, consisting in a change of place, but in fact they remove the consequence: the absence of Christ's ascending body from the earth, or its departure from the earth. They allow only a change in the mode of his presence on earth, namely from visible to invisible, so that the change affects only his state and not his place on earth. Some of the older writers held that heaven is non-local and incorporeal, existing everywhere, and so they wholly denied that Christ's ascension was local, and turned it entirely into some dispensation, evanescence, and disappearance [ἀφανισμόν], I know not what. These are plainly vain notions, and they expose Christ's ascension to the mockery of unbelievers. Scripture, however, deliberately expresses both the local terminus from which Christ departed when he ascended, and the one to which he came, as well as the intervening motion. The terminus from which is expressed by the words from the things above [ἀπὸ τῶν ἄνω]

units.la: disjunctus est, recessit ab iis, discipulis in terra ipsum sursum subvectum spectantibus, Luc. XXIV.51. Ergo in terris esse ἀπέστη, propinquitate substantiae corporis sui esse desiit. Hic Jesus ὁ ἀναλαμβανόμενος ἀφ' ὑμῶν à vobis (in terra existentibus) assumptus in Coelum, sic veniet (redibit, ante abiens) sicut vidistis eum euntem in Coelum, Act. I.11. Ideo Christus praemonuit: Si dixerint vobis: Ecce in eremo est; ne exeatis! Ecce in ciboriis est; ne credite. Nam sicut fulgur exit ab ortu, & lucet usque ad occasum, ita erit adventus Filii hominis q.d. Non erit amplius in terra, nisi ex Coelo descendens; nec descendet ex Coelo, nisi modo plane visibili, & illustri; Matth. XXIV.26.27. Nam si adhuc in terra esset, ne Sacerdos quidem esset, quia non fungeretur in Coelo intercessione pro nobis, per vivam corporis redivivi repraesentationem, Hebr. VIII.4. Quae non modum praesentiae corporis Christi in terra, sed rem ipsam, praesentiam corporalem omnem in terra tollunt. Terminus ad quem ponitur Coelum, supra nubes sursum. Elevatus est, & nubes suscepit ipsum, Act. I.9. & quidem εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν in Coelum, quod v. II. ter ponitur. Et rei totius gestae veritas ab Angelis ipsis ad sensus oculorum Apostolorum judicium apud oculos spectantes, ut oculis suis crederent, refertur: quando jubent ipsos credere, similiter & Coelo rediturum Christum. Οὕτως ἐλεύσεται ὃν τρόπον ἐθεάσασθε sic veniet, quemadmodum vidistis eum proficiscentem in Coelum, ibid. v. II. Laborabit non parum fides ascensionis Christi, si aliud hic creditur, quam quod oculis suis se spectasse Apostoli etiam alibi, Joh. I.14. Act. X.40. 41.42. I. Joh. I.1. testantur. Sed & motus intermedius exprimitur, ubi ascendisse, sublatus, profectus in Coelum, ab Apostolis disjunctus dicitur; quae corpori tributa motum, seu translationem ex uno loco in viciniam alterius significant. Cum igitur & terram, quae locus est, Christus reliquerit, & Coelum, novum locum acquisiverit, & ex illo in hunc locum motus, translatus fuerit, quid ascensio vera, localis est, si haec non est? Utut ergo statum Christus in Coelum ascendens mutaverit: at mutavit etiam locum; neque illum mutare sine hujus mutatione potuit. Nam qui statum visibilitatis mutans, in eodem tamen loco invisibiliter manet, quomodo ille ascendit, proficiscitur, migrat, sursum vehitur? Nimiae vero ὀλιγοπιστίας est, distantiam causantium, quam emetiri per motum localem corpus vix intra plures centenos annos valeat. Quid enim non potuit corpus Christi, rectore & vectore Deo Patre, qui Christum assumpsit: rectore Spiritu eo, a quo spiritual appellatur? Inprimis cum constet, viginti quatuor horarum spatio totam Coeli machinam circumvolvi, & Solem unico momento radios suos ad terram jaculari?
units.tr: he was parted, he departed from those disciples who on earth watched him being carried upward (Luke 24:51). Therefore he ceased to be on earth, that is, he ceased to be in the nearness of his bodily substance. This Jesus, who is taken up from you [ὁ ἀναλαμβανόμενος ἀφ' ὑμῶν] (you who are on earth) taken up into heaven, will come in this way (he will return, having gone away before) just as you saw him going into heaven (Acts 1:11). Therefore Christ forewarned: If they say to you, "Behold, he is in the wilderness," do not go out; "Behold, he is in the inner rooms," do not believe it. For as the lightning comes out of the east and shines even to the west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be (Matt. 24:26–27), as if to say: He will no longer be on earth, unless he comes down from heaven; and he will not come down from heaven except in a manner that is entirely visible and conspicuous. For if he were still on earth, he would not even be a priest, since he would not be exercising intercession for us in heaven, through the living representation of his risen body (Heb. 8:4). These people remove not merely the mode of Christ's bodily presence on earth, but the thing itself, all bodily presence on earth. The terminus to which is set as heaven, above the clouds. He was lifted up, and a cloud received him (Acts 1:9), and indeed into heaven [εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν], which is mentioned three times in verse 11. And the truth of the whole event is reported by the angels themselves, so that the Apostles' judgment rests on the matter seen before their eyes, that they might believe with their own eyes, when they are commanded to believe that Christ will likewise return from heaven. In this way he will come, just as you have seen him going into heaven [Οὕτως ἐλεύσεται ὃν τρόπον ἐθεάσασθε] (ibid., verse 11). The faith in Christ's ascension would labour not a little if here one believed something other than what the Apostles also testify they saw with their own eyes elsewhere (John 1:14; Acts 10:40–42; 1 John 1:1). But the intervening motion is also expressed, where he is said to have ascended, been lifted up, and gone into heaven, and to have been parted from the Apostles; these words, applied to a body, signify motion, or transfer, from one place to the neighbourhood of another. Since therefore Christ has left the earth, which is a place, and has acquired heaven as a new place, and has been moved and transferred from the one place to the other, what is true local ascension, if this is not? Although Christ, ascending into heaven, changed his state, he also changed his place; nor could he change the one without changing the other. For how does he ascend, depart, migrate, or be carried upward, if, changing his state of visibility, he nevertheless remains invisibly in the same place? It is, moreover, a sign of too little faith to make the distance an excuse, a distance which a body could scarcely traverse by local motion within several hundred years. For what could the body of Christ not do, with God the Father as its guide and conveyor, who took Christ up, and with that Spirit as its guide, from whom he is called spiritual? Especially since it is established that the whole machinery of heaven revolves in the space of twenty-four hours, and the sun hurls its rays at the earth in a single moment?

units.la: LXI. Christus in Coelum ascendens captivam duxit eaptivitatem, & accepit dona in hominibus, Psal. LXVIII.19. Ephes. IV.8. שבי captivitas captivitas ca-ptivos notat. qui nec sancti Patres, quos ex limbo liberatos, & cum Christo Coelum ingressos Pontificii fingunt; nec sancti, qui post resurrectionem Christi & ipsi resurgentes ex monumentis exiverunt, fuerunt. Neutri enim שבי captivi-
units.tr: LXI. Christ, ascending into heaven, led captivity captive, and received gifts among men (Ps. 68:19; Eph. 4:8). Shevi [שבי], captivity, denotes captives. Neither the holy Fathers, whom the Papists imagine were freed from Limbo and entered heaven with Christ, nor the holy men who, after Christ's resurrection, rose themselves and came out of the tombs, were such captives. For neither

units.la: Lenchus erroris, quod Christus in Coelum ascendens non praesentiam humanitatis, sed visibilem duntaxat modum praesentiae terrae subduxerit, adeoque ascensio in Coelum non loci, sed status mutatio fuerit. captivitas fuerunt; & illi in Limbo nunquam extiterunt. Captivi hostes in bello victi & capti sunt. Talis Diabolus, morte, peccato & inferno armatus fuit, quos hostes Christus ascendens revinctis quasi manibus ligavit, in triumpho suo duxit, ostentui habuit; & spolia iis sua, fideles, electos, a Patre sibi datos eripuit; secumque in Coelos ceu praedam opimam Patri sistendam, introduxit. Etiam שבי captivitas poterit tolletur, ומלקיח עריץ & praeda robusti evadet. Adversarium quoque tuum ego judicabo, & filios tuos servabo. Et comedere faciam spoliatores tuos carnem suam, & tanquam musto, sanguine suo inebriabunt se, &c. Esaj. XLIX.24. 25. Quomodo potest intrare quis in domum robusti, & vasa ejus diripere, nisi prius vinxerit robustum, & tum domum ejus diripiet? Matth. XII.29. Eadem opera accepit Christus בארם מתנות dona in hominibus, dona a Patre donata iis, quos Christo dedit, puta Spiritum filiationis, & alia omnia, quae ad Regnum & gloriam Christi pertinent, ipse Christus, perinde ut homines ipsos, haereditatem suam accepit, ut in iis glorificaretur; & ut sic accipiens dona simul acciperet פעלת opera; laboris sui praemium & mercedem, Esaj. XLIX.4 Dona enim illa per gratiam dantur hominibus propter Christum, quia ipse fidelium caput, & fideles ejus haereditas sunt, ipse causa, auctor, impetrator donorum, in fidelibus haec dona, ut impetrata a se accipit, S. Paulus inde colligit, Christum ascendisse supra omnes Coelos ἵνα πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα, ut impleret omnia, Ephes. IV. 10. Ascensio enim ejus in Coelum est signum meriti ejusdem, & potestatis implendi omnia donis; & simul causa impletionis alicujus, quia per eam declaratus est Christus & Dominus (Act. II.36.) ut crederemus in ipsum, & credentes omnem laetitiam animo conciperemus. Et dona illa ad completionem omnium comparata esse, v. 11. ostendit; ubi praecones etiam suae ex mortuis resurrectionis, & in Coelum ascensionis datos recenset.
units.tr: Refutation of the error that, in ascending into heaven, Christ withdrew not his human presence but only the visible mode of his presence from the earth, so that his ascension into heaven was a change not of place but of state. were shevi captives; and they never existed in Limbo. Captives are enemies conquered and taken in war. Such was the Devil, armed with death, sin and hell, whom Christ, ascending, bound as though with tied hands, led in his triumph, and exhibited as a spectacle; and he took from them their spoils, the faithful, the elect whom the Father had given him, and, bringing them with him into the heavens, presented them to the Father as rich booty. Even the captive of the mighty shall be taken away, and the prey of the tyrant [ומלקיח עריץ] shall be delivered. I will contend with him who contends with you, and I will save your children. And I will make your oppressors eat their own flesh, and they shall be drunk with their own blood as with sweet wine, etc. (Isa. 49:24–25). How can anyone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man, and then he will plunder his house? (Matt. 12:29). At the same time Christ received gifts among men [בארם מתנות], the gifts given by the Father to those whom he gave to Christ, namely the Spirit of adoption and all the other things that belong to the kingdom and glory of Christ. Christ himself, just as he received men themselves as his inheritance, so that he might be glorified in them, and so that in receiving gifts he might at the same time receive works [פעלת], the reward and wage of his labour (Isa. 49:4). For those gifts are given to men through grace, on account of Christ, because he is the head of the faithful and they are his inheritance; he himself is the cause, author and obtainer of the gifts, and he receives them in the faithful as gifts obtained by himself. St. Paul infers from this that Christ ascended above all the heavens so that he might fill all things (Eph. 4:10). For his ascension into heaven is the sign of his merit, and of his power to fill all things with gifts; and at the same time it is the cause of the fulfilment of something, because through it Christ was declared Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36), so that we might believe in him, and, believing, might conceive all joy in our minds. And verse 11 shows that those gifts were prepared for the completion of all things, where he also recounts the heralds of his resurrection from the dead and of his ascension into heaven who were given.

units.la: LXII. Superest Tertius idemque summus exaltationis Christi gradus, sessio ad dextram Dei.
units.tr: LXII. The third and highest step of Christ's exaltation remains: his sitting at the right hand of God.

units.la: Quae praedicta est, Psal. CX.1. נאם יהוה לאדני שב Dixit Jehova Domino meo לימיני Sede ad dextram meam, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Ubi voce לאדני Deum significari, inde liquet, quia Davidis Dominus vocari non potuit nisi is, cujus David servus erat. Solius autem Dei David servus erat. Hoc Pharisaeis Christus objicit, Matth. XXII.43.44. Luc. XIX.41-44. Chaldaeus habet: Dixit Dominus במימריה in verbo suo ad ponendum me Regem toti Israeli, Ubi מימרא Verbum Domini Paraphrasis pro יהוה ipso ponere solet. Messiam vero intelligi, inde liquet, quia is est אדון Dominus totius Ecclesiae, & ipsius etiam Davidis, cujus Deus & creator est, & cujus Filii Davidis effecti, David haereditas & peculium est; cui etiam in carne sua aeque atque aliis sanctis, justitiam & salutem acquisivit. Nam etiam ut Angelus faciei foederis, habitans in rubo, toti Israeli, ut Deus eorum, manifestatus est. Hunc igitur Christum & Dominum Ecclesiae Jehova, Pater jubet sedere ad dextram suam; & eadem voluntate ac potestate etiam propria ad dextram Dei sedit; sicut filius a Patre jussus mensae assidere, non nihil agit. Deus Pater Christum ex mortuis resuscitans ἐκα-θισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις collocavit ad dextram juam in supra coelestibus, Ephes. I.20. Filius purificatione peccatorum per se ipsum facta sedit in dextra magnificentia in excelsis, Hebr. I.3. Ipse unam pro peccatis victimam offerens εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ τῆς Θεοῦ in perpetuum sedit in dextra Dei, ibid. X.12. quibus locis sedendi ad dextram jus & potestas a purgatione peccatorum per se ipsum, & oblata pro peccatis hostia arcessitur.
units.tr: This was foretold at Psalm 110:1: "The LORD said to my Lord [נאם יהוה לאדני], Sit at my right hand [לימיני] until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." That "Lord" (לאדני) means God is clear from the fact that David's Lord could be none other than the one whose servant David was. David was the servant of God alone. Christ puts this to the Pharisees at Matt. 22:43-44 and Luke 20:41-44. The Chaldee paraphrast renders it: "The Lord said in his Word [bemimreh] to make me king over all Israel," where the word memra, the Word of the Lord, is commonly used by the paraphrast in place of Jehovah himself. That the Messiah is meant is clear because he is the Lord [adon] of the whole Church and of David himself, whose God and Creator he is, and whose Son David's descendants have become. David's inheritance and possession is the Son, and in his flesh he has acquired righteousness and salvation for David, as for the other saints. For he was also made manifest to all Israel as their God, as the Angel of the face of the covenant who dwelt in the bush. Jehovah the Father therefore bids this Christ, the Lord of the Church, sit at his right hand. By the same will and power, he himself also sat at the right hand of God, just as a son who is bidden by his father to sit at table does not act on his own initiative. God the Father, raising Christ from the dead, "set him at his right hand in the heavenly places" [ekathisen en dexia autou en tois epouraniois] (Eph. 1:20). The Son, having made purification for sins by himself, "sat at the right hand of the majesty on high" (Heb. 1:3). He himself, having offered one sacrifice for sins, "sat for ever at the right hand of God" [eis to dienekes ekathisen en dexia tēs Theou] (Heb. 10:12). In these passages the right, that is, the authority to sit there, is derived from the cleansing of sins by himself and from the sacrifice offered for sin.

units.la: LXIII. Deus cum spiritus sit, nec dextram nec sinistram habet. Sed ימין dextra ei tribuitur ad significandam vel potentiam, cujus dextra organon est; quomodo jurasse per dextram suam & per brachium roboris sui, Esaj. LXII.8. & dextra sua exaltasse Christum Deus Pater Act. II. 33. dicitur. vel honorem, cum dextram ei, quem honore afficimus, cedimus. Christus τῇ δεξιᾷ τῆς Θεοῦ dextra Dei, hoc est, potentia Patris (Act. II. 33. V.31.) & ad dextram Dei, ad eam sessurus, exaltatus est. Posterior sensus hujus loci est; ubi non dextra simpliciter, sed sessio ad dextram Christo tribuitur. Ad dextram vero, hoc est, potentiam sedere nemo dicitur. Ac ne vox quidem sedendi proprie Christo tribuitur; quia cum dextram Deus non habeat, ad eam sedere in Coelo proprie non potest. Sedere igitur heic signum honoris & potestatis est; & Sessio ad dextram honorem & potestatem, qua quis in ordine ad alium, vel in communione alterius gaudet, notat. Apud plerasque enim gentes dextra honoratior est, quam sinistra; nequicquam repugnante Goropio Becano in sua Hermathena, ubi exemplis & ratiunculis nonnullis probare satagit, plerisque gentibus sinistrum locum dextro honestiorem habitum esse. cujus tela Lipsius Elect. lib. II 2. valide retudit. Imbelle certe illud est, quod naturam, quae cor, vitae illum fontem, nobis ad sinistram collocavit, id ipsum voceferari asserit. Quomodo Xenophon de Cyro tradidit, solitum eum amicos locare ad laevam, ut cordi propiores essent. Sed id novum & Cyro proprium; nec trahendum ad morem totius gentis. denique non honori, sed affectui testando fuit. In Turcis solis aliter res habet, quos honestiorem habere laevam Busbequius docuit: causam allegantes, quia eam partem gladius honestet, & qui ad dextram, obnoxium eum & subjectum alterius manu; sinister contra eum expeditum habeat. Quae causae non causae sunt, militares, imo barbarae, gente barbara non indignae. Pro dextro certe loco etiam natura, quae usum induxisse videtur, pugnat, quia vires dextra parte majores, & hepar splene melius; & e renibus, testiculis, manibus, pedibus potiora omnia dextra fecit. Causam Aristoteles de Part. Anim. lib. III.9. reddit, quod τὰ μερῶν δεξιὰ θερμότερα membra dextra calidiora sint. Etiam movere & agere dextri est: moveri & pati sinistri. Cum tamen res haec rituum antiquorum sit, illa ab usu potius, quam a ratione spectari, & testimoniis magis, quam argutiis firmari debet. Cujusmodi usus vestigia etiam Scriptura exhibet. Nam mater Solomonis
units.tr: LXIII. God, since he is spirit, has neither right hand nor left. But the right hand [yamin] is ascribed to him, either to signify power, of which the right hand is the instrument, in the way that God is said to have sworn "by his right hand and by the arm of his strength" (Isa. 62:8), and that God the Father "exalted" Christ "by his right hand" (Acts 2:33); or to signify honour, since we yield the right hand to one whom we wish to honour. Christ was exalted to "the right hand of God," that is, to the power of the Father (Acts 2:33; 5:31), and to be seated "at the right hand of God," that is, to sit there. This second sense applies to this passage, where the sitting at the right hand, not the right hand simply, is ascribed to Christ. But no one is said to sit at the right hand, that is, in power. Nor is even the word "sitting" properly ascribed to Christ; since God has no right hand, he cannot properly sit at it in heaven. Sitting here is therefore a sign of honour and power, and "sitting at the right hand" denotes the honour and power which someone enjoys in relation to another, or in fellowship with another. For among most nations the right hand is more honourable than the left. Goropius Becanus, in his Hermathena, labours in vain to prove by examples and some petty arguments that among most nations the left place was considered more honourable than the right; Lipsius has forcefully repulsed his weapons (Elect. II.2). It is certainly a feeble claim that nature, which placed the heart, that fount of life, on our left, has itself named the left side as such. Xenophon reports of Cyrus that he was accustomed to place his friends on his left, so that they might be closer to his heart; but that was a novelty peculiar to Cyrus, and it should not be drawn into the custom of a whole nation. In the end it was a mark of affection, not of honour. Only among the Turks is the matter otherwise; Busbequius informed us that they regard the left as more honourable, giving as their reason that the sword honours that side, while one who is on the right is subject to and under the hand of another, whereas the one on the left has his sword free. These reasons are no reasons at all; they are military, or rather barbarous, and not unworthy of a barbarous people. Nature too, which seems to have established the custom, certainly fights for the right-hand place, since the right side has greater strength, and the liver is better than the spleen; and nature has made all the more excellent parts, from the kidneys, testicles, hands and feet, on the right. Aristotle gives the reason in De Partibus Animalium III.9: the right parts of the body are warmer [ta merōn dexia thermotera]. Moreover, to move and act belongs to the right, to be moved and to suffer to the left. Yet since this matter belongs to ancient rites, it ought to be judged by usage rather than by reason, and to be confirmed by testimonies rather than by subtleties. Scripture too shows traces of such usage. For the mother of Solomon,

units.la: Tertius & supremus exaltationis Christi gradus est sessio ejus ad dextram Dei, Psal. CX.1. praedicta. monis ad filii sui solio insidentis dextram honoris ergo proxima consedit. Sedit Rex super folium suum, & posuit folium matri suæ, ויושב לימינו & sedit ad dextram ejus, 1. Reg. II. 19. Etiam mater filiorum Zebedæi petiit, ut in Regno Christi sederent duo filii ejus, alter ad dextram, alter ad sinistram, Matth. XX. 21. Marc. X. 37. Proprie ergo in rebus humanis sedere ad dextram, præsertim Regis, quietam & honorificam corporis desidentis positionem, ut in illa matris Solomonis sessione ad dextram Filii: improprie, cum de Regis dextra agitur, per synecdochen, cum hujusmodi quieta & honorifica sessione conjuncta gubernandi potestas, ut in altera illa ambita filiorum Zebedæi sessione ad dextram Christi, significatur. Christo autem tributa sessio ad dextram Dei improprie ejusdem honorem & potestatem summam, in exaltatione post meritum obedientiæ eidem collatam, significat.
units.tr: The third and highest step of Christ's exaltation is his sitting at the right hand of God, foretold at Psalm 110:1. ...monis, sitting next to the right hand of her son who was seated on his throne, out of honour. "The king sat on his throne, and set a throne for his mother; and she sat at his right hand" [veyoshev limino] (1 Kings 2:19). Likewise the mother of the sons of Zebedee asked that in Christ's kingdom her two sons might "sit, one on the right hand and the other on the left" (Matt. 20:21; Mark 10:37). Therefore, in human affairs, "to sit at the right hand," especially of a king, properly denotes a quiet and honourable posture of the seated body, as in the sitting of Solomon's mother at the right hand of her son. Improperly, when the king's right hand is in question, by synecdoche, it signifies the power of governing joined with such a quiet and honourable sitting, as in that other request of the sons of Zebedee to sit at the right hand of Christ. The sitting at the right hand of God ascribed to Christ therefore signifies, improperly, his honour and supreme power, conferred upon him in exaltation after the merit of his obedience.

units.la: LXIV. Sed sessionem hanc Christi ad dextram Dei Patris ipsæ Scripturæ luculenter explicant. Nam cum honore summo, Nomine quod super omne nomen est, Phil. II. 9. omnem etiam potestatem in Cœlo & in terra accepisse eum, Matth. XXVIII. 18. testantur. Dextra Dei ὑψωθεὶς exaltatus est. Act. II. 33. Glorifica me, inquit, apud te ea gloria, quam habebam, antequam mundus esset apud te, Joh. XVII. 5. Oportebat Christum pati, & intrare in gloriam suam, Luc. XXIV. 26. Dominum & Christum eum fecit Deus, Act. II. 36. Superexaltavit eum, & donavit ei Nomen super omne nomen, &c. Phil. II. 9. Sedit ad dextram ejus in supercœlestibus, supra omnem principatum, & potestatem, & potentiam, & dominatum, & supra omne nomen, quod nominatum est in hoc seculo & in futuro; & subjecit omnia pedibus ejus; & dedit eum caput super omnia Ecclesiæ (quæ verba Christi sessionem ad dextram Patris clarissimè definiunt) Ephes. I. 20, 21, 22. Quomodo etiam S. Paulus verba Davidis, sedere ad dextram Domini per βασιλεύειν regnare interpretatur, dicens: Oportet eum regnare, usque dum ponant omnes hostes sub pedibus ejus, 1. Cor. XV. 25. Et S. Petrus eandem sessionem ad dextram Dei per ὑποταγὴν subjectionem Angelorum & potestatum, & potentiarum similiter explicat, 1. Pet. III. 22. Atque hic ille ἀρπαγμὸς raptus maris illius, qui omnes gentes baculo ferreo pascere debuit, ad Deum & thronum ejus est, Apoc. XII. 5. Duplex enim veluti dextrain Scriptura, uti diximus, distinguitur, altera δεξιὰ & θρόνῳ Dextra throni magnificentiæ in excelsis, Hebr. I. 3. VIII. 1. altera δεξιὰ τῆς δυνάμεως dextra potentiæ Dei, Matth. XXVI. 64. Luc. XXII. 69. Illa summum ejus honorem & gloriam: hæc cum honore eam conjunctam potestatem & potentiam significat.
units.tr: LXIV. The Scriptures themselves set out clearly this sitting of Christ at the right hand of God the Father. They testify that he received, with the highest honour, "the name which is above every name" (Phil. 2:9), and also "all power in heaven and on earth" (Matt. 28:18). "Exalted [hupsōtheis] to the right hand of God" (Acts 2:33). "Glorify me," he says, "with that glory which I had with you before the world was" (John 17:5). "Ought not Christ to have suffered and entered into his glory?" (Luke 24:26). "God has made him Lord and Christ" (Acts 2:36). "God has highly exalted him and given him the name which is above every name," etc. (Phil. 2:9). "He sat at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all principality and power and might and dominion, and above every name that is named in this age and in that which is to come; and he has put all things under his feet, and has given him to be head over all things to the Church" (these words of Christ clearly define the sitting at the Father's right hand) (Eph. 1:20-22). Likewise St Paul interprets the words of David, "to sit at the right hand of the Lord," by basileuein, "to reign": "He must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet" (1 Cor. 15:25). St Peter explains the same sitting at the right hand of God in a similar way, by hupotagē, the subjection of angels, powers and might (1 Pet. 3:22). And this is the harpagmos, the "catching up" of that Son of the woman who was to rule all nations with an iron rod, "to God and to his throne" (Rev. 12:5). For, as we have said, Scripture distinguishes a twofold right hand: one is the right hand of the throne of majesty on high (Heb. 1:3; 8:1), and the other is the right hand of the power of God (Matt. 26:64; Luke 22:69). The former signifies his supreme honour and glory; the latter signifies the power and might joined with that honour.

units.la: LXV. Ex his ad liquidum perducimus, quòd sessio Christi ad dextram Patris ejusdem suprema glorificatio, cum potestate id omne ad gloriam suam & salutem Ecclesiæ faciendi & exequendi, quod obedientia sua, ut Mediator, promeruit, conjuncta sit. Quòd enim non sedentem Filium Dei, sed ἐκ δεξιῶν & Θεοῦ ἑστῶτα ad dextras Dei stantem Stephanus Act. VII. 56.
units.tr: LXV. From these things we make it clear that the sitting of Christ at the right hand of the Father is his supreme glorification, joined with the power to do and carry out, for his own glory and the salvation of the Church, everything that his obedience as Mediator has merited. For Stephen saw the Son of God not sitting but standing at the right hand of God [ἐκ δεξιῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἑστῶτα], Act. VII. 56.

units.la: vidit, non honorem vel potestatem Filii hominis minuit, sed ejus in regenda, protegenda Ecclesia, & judicandis hostibus suis præsentiam & promptitudinem indigetat. Non enim sic ad ad dextram Dei sedet, ut honore & gloria sua fruens quiescat, & nullam vel Ecclesiæ suæ, vel hostium adversus ipsum & Ecclesiam insurgentium rationem habeat; quasi sic sedens ad dextram Dei otiosi beatitudinem, qualem Epicurus pro sola beatitudine venditavit, & Reges otiosi ac inglorii consectantur, affectasset; sed gloriam, potentiam & potestatem suam Ecclesiæ, & per eam amplificandæ suæ ipsius gloriæ impendit. Neque sic gloriosè regnat, ut Propheta & Sacerdos Ecclesiæ esse desinat, quia non tantum ut Rex ad dextram Dei sedet, sed etiam ut כהן לעולם Sacerdos in æculum, Psal. CX. 4. Portabit gloriam, sedebit ac dominabitur in solio suo. Erit quoque Sacerdos in solio suo, & consilium pacis erit inter utrumque, Zach. VI. 13. Sedens igitur ad dextram Dei, ut Propheta, Ecclesiam donis implet, ei Spiritum donat, dona distribuit, Ephes. IV. 11. ut Sacerdos victimam ante faciem Patris repræsentat, & pro nobis interpellat; & voluntate sua, qua hæreditatem suam & ejus glorificationem postulat, nos justitiæ & gloriæ participes facit. Psal. II. 8. Rom. VIII. 34. Hebr. VII. 25. IX. 24. X. 12, 13. ut Rex, Caput & Dominus Ecclesiæ eam Spiritu & verbo suo regit, tuetur, omnia pedibus suis subjicit, expectans, donec inimici ejus scabellum ipsius ponantur, Psal. CX. 1. Ephes. I. 20, 22. Hebr. X. 12, 13. & cuncta hæc sic gerit ad summi honoris & gloriæ suæ incrementum.
units.tr: This does not diminish the honour or power of the Son of man, but indicates his presence and readiness in ruling and protecting the Church and in judging his enemies. For he does not sit at God's right hand in such a way as to rest, enjoying his honour and glory, and taking no account either of his Church or of the enemies who rise against him and the Church, as if by sitting thus at God's right hand he aimed at the idle blessedness that Epicurus peddled as the only happiness, which idle and inglorious kings pursue. Rather, he devotes his glory, power and authority to the Church, and through it to the enlargement of his own glory. Nor does he reign in such glory that he ceases to be Prophet and Priest of the Church, for he sits at God's right hand not only as King but also as [כהן לעולם] Priest for ever, Psal. CX. 4. He shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne. And he shall be a priest upon his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both, Zach. VI. 13. Sitting therefore at God's right hand, as Prophet he fills the Church with gifts, gives it the Spirit and distributes gifts, Ephes. IV. 11; as Priest he presents the victim before the face of the Father and intercedes for us, and by his will, by which he asks for his inheritance and its glorification, he makes us partakers of righteousness and glory, Psal. II. 8, Rom. VIII. 34, Hebr. VII. 25, IX. 24, X. 12, 13; as King, Head and Lord of the Church he rules and guards it by his Spirit and word, subjects all things to his feet, waiting until his enemies are placed as a footstool for his feet, Psal. CX. 1, Ephes. I. 20, 22, Hebr. X. 12, 13. And he does all these things for the increase of his own highest honour and glory.

units.la: LXVI. Sessio ad dextram Patris Christo secundum utramque naturam competit, quia secundum utramque Mediator est, & munus Mediatoris in Cœlo gloriosè exequitur. Sed secundum divinam improprie quoad solam φανέρωσιν manifestationem gloriæ: quoad humanam proprie & reapse. Divinæ enim naturæ Majestas demum post ascensionem in Cœlos in pleno fulgore suo enituit, & illustrissimè patefacta est. Tum enim illa humilis & obscuræ conditionis nubes, quæ ante resurrectionem Divinæ Majestatis gloriam obnubilaverat, & quasi velo quodam contexerat, plenè planèque discussa est. Neque obstat, quòd Divina natura nihil accipere possit. Sicut enim Deus exinanitur, dum in carne mortali conspicitur, ex argumentis in Scriptura descriptis in humilitate fide cognoscendus: ita dum caro ex mortuis resuscitata in Cœlo locatur, ad oculum jam demonstratur, eum, cujus caro sic in Cœlum transvehitur, esse Filium Dei, Regem Ecclesiæ, & in gloriam suam, ad Regnum suum gerendum intrare. Et hoc omne non Deus accipit, ceu novum aliquid, quo ipse indigeat, sed ceu vetus, sibi vindicat, ad utilitatem non propriam, sed Ecclesiæ, ad cujus salutem & gloriam manifestatio illa refertur. Blasphemè proin Socini assectæ in collocatione Christi ad dextram Dei Patris primum dominationis & Regni Christi initium collocant. Cùm tamen David decem circiter ante sessionem illam seculis Christum Dominum suum vocaverit, Psal. CX. 1, Matth. XXII. 43, 44, 45. & Christus inde à prima conceptione
units.tr: LXVI. The sitting at the Father's right hand belongs to Christ according to both natures, since according to both he is Mediator and carries out the office of Mediator gloriously in heaven. But according to the divine nature it belongs improperly, only as to the manifestation of glory; according to the human nature it belongs properly and in reality. For the majesty of the divine nature shone forth in full brilliance only after the ascension into heaven, and was most illustriously revealed. Then that cloud of humble and obscure condition, which before the resurrection had obscured the glory of the divine majesty and, as it were, covered it with a veil, was fully and completely dispelled. Nor does it stand in the way that the divine nature can receive nothing. For just as God is emptied while seen in mortal flesh, and is to be known in humility by faith from the arguments described in Scripture, so when the flesh raised from the dead is placed in heaven, it is now demonstrated to the eye that he whose flesh is thus carried into heaven is the Son of God, the King of the Church, and enters into his glory to exercise his kingdom. And God does not receive all this as something new of which he has need, but claims it for himself as something old, for a use not his own but the Church's, to whose salvation and glory that manifestation is referred. Therefore the Socinians blasphemously place the first beginning of Christ's dominion and kingdom in his being set at God's right hand. Yet David, about ten centuries before that sitting, called Christ his Lord, Psal. CX. 1, Matth. XXII. 43, 44, 45; and Christ was called Lord from his very conception and birth,

units.la: {a} Ephes. I. 20, 21, 22 (marginal references, right margin, small type). ceptione & nativitate Dominus, Luc.I.43. II. II. salutatus fuerit; & Dominum gloriæ crucifixum esse, Apostolus I.Cor.II.8. affirmaverit; & Christus ipse in diebus carnis suæ excellens illud & Deo proprium Domini indigetamentum sibi asseruerit, dicens: Vos me vocatis ὁ Διδάσκαλος καὶ ὁ Κύριος Magister ac Domine, & recte facitis. Sum enim. Itaque si ego lavi pedes vestros ὁ Κύριος καὶ ὁ Διδάσκαλος Dominus & Magister, etiam vos invicem pedes lavare debetis; Joh.XIII.13.14. Accedit, quòd Christus idem ante exaltationem pedum osculum, ad quod mulier se demisit, acceptum gratúmque habuit; & Simoni hospiti indigné id ferenti præposteram de se existimationem exprobravit, Luc.VII.38.45. & Johannes Baptista, indignum se esse, qui vel maximè servilem operam solvendi corrigias calceamentorum, vel bajulandi calceamenta, Christo præstaret, quippe qui superne veniens ἐπάνω πάντων super omnes esset, Matth.III.11. Marc.I.7. Joh.III.28.31.
units.tr: {a} Ephes. I. 20, 21, 22. from his conception and birth, Luc. I. 43, II. 11; and the Apostle affirmed that the Lord of glory was crucified, I. Cor. II. 8; and Christ himself, in the days of his flesh, claimed for himself that outstanding title proper to God, Lord, saying: You call me [ὁ Διδάσκαλος καὶ ὁ Κύριος] Master and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet [ὁ Κύριος καὶ ὁ Διδάσκαλος] Lord and Master, you also ought to wash one another's feet, Joh. XIII. 13, 14. Moreover, Christ himself accepted with favour the kissing of his feet, to which a woman stooped, and rebuked Simon the host, who took it ill, for his preposterous opinion of him, Luc. VII. 38, 45. And John the Baptist said that he was unworthy to render to Christ even the most servile service, to loosen the thongs of his sandals or carry his sandals, since he who is coming from above [ἐπάνω πάντων] is above all, Matth. III. 11, Marc. I. 7, Joh. III. 28, 31.

units.la: LXVII. In gloriæ sessionis hujus ad dextram Dei partem etiam caro, seu humanitas Christi venit.
units.tr: LXVII. That the flesh, or humanity, of Christ also shares in this glorious session at the right hand of God.

units.la: Cujus ad dextram Dei sessio est summus apex glorificationis, seu μεγαλοπρεπείας δόξα magnifica gloria ejus, 2.Pet.I.16. in illa super omnes creaturas Deo proxima beatitudine, qua in summa excellentia perfectionis & gaudii animæ & corporis fruitur, consistit. Hanc S. Paulus εἰκόνα τῆς imaginem Filii, cui nos συμμόρφους conformes fieri oportet, ut ille sit primogenitus inter multos fratres, vocat, Rom.VIII.29. Huc pertinet illa unctio Christi, de qua Psal.XLV.8. Diligis justitiam, & odio habes improbitatem. Propterea unxit te Deus tuus oleo lætitiæ præ consortibus tuis. Ubi unctio per oleum lætitiæ cum justitia & odio improbitatis per particulam causalem vel rationalem Propterea connectitur, ut demonstretur, unctionem per oleum lætitiæ effectum vel consequens esse justitiæ præstitæ. Proin etiam oleum lætitiæ non tam ad gratiæ in terris, quàm ad gloriæ in cœlis unctionem spectat. Quod & series Psalmi flagitat, in quo Christi Regis & Reginæ Ecclesiæ gloriosæ epithalamion canitur. De quo pleno gaudio, in sessione ad dextram Dei comprehenso, ipse Christus alibi gloriatur, dicens: Scire me facies iter vitæ, satietatis lætitiarum apud faciem tuam, amœnitatum, quæ sunt in dextra tua perpetuò, Psal.XVI.11. Perperam verò Bellarminus de Christo lib.III.15. Sessionem hanc ad dextram Dei humanitati datam esse non in se, sed in suppositio statuit; quia sic proprie dicta exaltatio humanitatis Christi nulla foret, & sola improprie dicta exaltatio Personæ Divinæ in Natura Divina relinqueretur; atque simul etiam consolatio tum illa, qua fideles unà cum Christo sedere in supercœlestibus, hoc est, beatè in capite suo Christo quiescere, Ephes.II.6. Joh.XIV.3. tum illa, qua Ecclesia, gloriosa, Reginæ adinstar, ad dextram Christi Sponsi sui collocanda, Psal.XLV.10. Matth.XIX.28. XXV.33. describitur, planè enervaretur. Utraque enim perit, si non in humanitate sua Christus gloriosæ & beatæ quietis, quàm non cum Patre, sed cum Ecclesia communem habet, sequester est.
units.tr: His session at the right hand of God is the highest peak of glorification, or his magnificent glory (μεγαλοπρεπείας δόξα), 2 Pet. 1:16, and it consists in that blessedness, next to God above all creatures, in which he enjoys the highest excellence of perfection and joy in both soul and body. St Paul calls this the image [εἰκόνα] of the Son, to which we ought to be made conformed [συμμόρφους], so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers, Rom. 8:29. To this belongs the anointing of Christ spoken of in Psalm 45:8: You love righteousness and hate wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions. Here the anointing with the oil of gladness is linked, by the causal or reasoning particle Therefore, with the love of righteousness and the hatred of wickedness, to show that the anointing with the oil of gladness is the effect or consequence of the righteousness performed. Hence the oil of gladness refers not so much to the anointing of grace on earth as to the anointing of glory in heaven. The course of the psalm also demands this, since in it a glorious marriage song is sung for Christ the King and the Queen, the Church. Christ himself boasts elsewhere of this full joy, which is comprehended in the session at God's right hand, saying: You will make known to me the path of life; in your presence is fullness of joys, and at your right hand are pleasures for evermore, Ps. 16:11. But Bellarmine, De Christo book 3, chapter 15, wrongly lays down that this session at God's right hand is given to the humanity not in itself, but in the person. For in that case the properly so-called exaltation of Christ's humanity would be nothing, and only the improperly so-called exaltation of the Divine Person in the divine nature would remain; and at the same time the consolation would be utterly weakened by which the faithful are comforted that they sit in the heavenly places with Christ, that is, rest blessedly in Christ their head, Eph. 2:6; John 14:3, and that by which the glorious Church, like a queen, is described as to be placed at the right hand of her Bridegroom, Ps. 45:10; Matt. 19:28; 25:33. For both are lost unless Christ, in his humanity, is the mediator of that glorious and blessed rest which he shares not with the Father but with the Church.

units.la: LXVIII. Sessio Christi, quà hominis, ad dextram Dei, in perfectione animæ & corporis ejus gliscit.
units.tr: LXVIII. The session of Christ, as man, at the right hand of God, increases the perfection of his soul and body.

units.la: Et animæ quidem ejus summè excellens perfectio in scientiæ & potentiæ ad intellectus & voluntatis pristinæ & ab ipso ortu perfectæ rectitudinem accedente ad summum usque gradum amplificatione consistit. Unde plenam & perfectissimam, qualis in creaturam cadere potest, Dei summi boni cognitionem; amorem, & in eodem delectationem exoriri necesse fuit. Etiam Corporis Christi excellens perfectio ex sessione illa manans, summum ejus robur, pulchritudo, forma, splendor eximius est. Pulcher es præ filiis hominum. Effusa est gratia in labia tua. Propterea benedixit tibi Deus in secula, Psal.XLV.3. Ideo σῶμα τῆς δόξης Corpus gloriosum, cum quo configuranda nostra sunt, Phil.III.21. vocatur. Quam gloriam corporis Christi visibilem esse Scriptura docet, ajens θεωρεῖσθαι videri posse, Joh.XVII.26. ὀφθῆναι spectari oculis Filium hominis sedentem ad dextram potentiæ, Matth.XXVI.64. Stephanum vidisse Filium hominis stantem ad dextram Dei, Act.VII.56. & visuros nos eum καθὼς ἐστι sicut est, 1.Joh.III.2. Facit huc præludium & umbra gloriæ illius, quæ olim in statu humili intercesserit; quando Christus μετεμορφώθη transfiguratus est coram discipulis, & splenduit facies ejus sicut Sol, Matth.XVII.2. Unde S.Petrus se & alios tum præsentes fuisse ἐπόπται τῆς μεγαλειότητος spectatores magnitudinis ejus, gloriatur, 2.Pet.I.16.
units.tr: The supremely excellent perfection of his soul consists in an increase of knowledge and power, rising to the highest degree, of his intellect and will, which were perfect in rectitude from his very birth. Hence it was necessary that there should arise in him a full and most perfect knowledge of God, the highest good, such as can fall to a creature, together with love and delight in the same. The excellent perfection of the body of Christ, flowing from that session, is its highest strength, beauty, form and remarkable splendour: You are fairer than the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you for ever, Ps. 45:3. Therefore it is called the glorious body [σῶμα τῆς δόξης], to which our bodies are to be conformed, Phil. 3:21. Scripture teaches that this glory of Christ's body is visible, saying that he can be seen [θεωρεῖσθαι] (John 17:24), that he was seen [ὀφθῆναι] by eyes, the Son of man sitting at the right hand of power, Matt. 26:64, that Stephen saw the Son of man standing at the right hand of God, Acts 7:56, and that we shall see him as he is [καθὼς ἐστι], 1 John 3:2. To this there is a prelude and a shadow of that glory which formerly shone forth in his humble state, when Christ was transfigured before the disciples, and his face shone like the sun, Matt. 17:2. Hence St Peter glories that he and the others present at that time were eyewitnesses of his majesty [ἐπόπται τῆς μεγαλειότητος], 2 Pet. 1:16.

units.la: LXIX. Non ergo Christus post ascensionem ad dextram Dei considens novum corpus, exuto redivivo illo, in quo post resurrectionem ex mortuis se videndum & palpandum præbuit, induit, uti Sociniani fingunt, sed eidem quoad substantiam corpori novam gloriam superinduit.
units.tr: LXIX. Therefore Christ, sitting at the right hand of God after the ascension, did not put on a new body, having laid aside that risen body in which he showed himself to be seen and touched after the resurrection from the dead, as the Socinians pretend; but he added a new glory to the same body as to its substance.

units.la: Pestilens enim nimis error est, Christum sic mutantium, imò & transsubstantiationem, ut alium, quoad substantiam in Cœlis habeamus, quàm eum, qui ex Spiritu S. conceptus, ex B. Virgine natus, mortuus, ex morte resuscitatus in Cœlum ascendit. Ergone ascendendo corpus suum exuit, destructioni, annihilationi subjecit; ut cùm ante ex terra vindicatum fuerit, nunc demum in pulverem, ad incitas, imò ad nihilum redigi debuerit? Ubi exaltatio, coronatio corporis, quod exinanitum, passum, mortuum est? Quomodo sic αἷμα διὰ τοῦ per proprium sanguinem intravit in Sanctuarium, Hebr.IX.12? Quomodo sanguis idem Christi nobis παρρησίαν fiduciam ingrediendi in sanctuarium ea via, quam nobis recentem & novam dedicavit per velum, hoc est, carnem suam? ibid. cap.X.19.20. Cum alione corpore Sacerdos ille in Sanctum, cum alio in Sanctum Sanctorum ingressus est? Vel, an ingrediendo in Sanctuarium corpus suum prius destruxit, atque sic mortuus iterum est, vel potius in infernum non existentiæ descendit? Quomodo sic edentes carnem ejus, & bibentes sanguinem ejus communionem cum corpore ejus fracto, & sanguine fuso sortimur, 1.Cor.X.16? Quomodo sic redituras ad judicium est, ὃν τρόπον quemadmodum visus est proficisci in Cœlum, Act.I.11? vel videbunt eum oculi, qui eum confixerunt, Apoc.I.7? Næ piget pluribus ἀποπιμάζειν hostium Christi convellere, quorum πρῶτον ψεῦδος est, quòd Christus in resurrectione corpus mortu
units.tr: For it is an exceedingly pestilent error to change Christ in this way, or even to transubstantiate him, so that we have in heaven another Christ as to his substance than the one who was conceived of the Holy Spirit, born of the blessed Virgin, died, rose from the dead and ascended into heaven. Did he then, by ascending, cast off his body and subject it to destruction and annihilation, so that, having been claimed from the earth before, it must at last be reduced to dust, to ashes, indeed to nothing? Where is the exaltation and crowning of a body which was humbled, suffered and died? How did he enter in through his own blood [αἷμα διὰ τοῦ] into the sanctuary, Heb. 9:12? How does the same blood of Christ give us boldness [παρρησίαν] to enter into the sanctuary by that way, which he dedicated for us as new and living through the veil, that is, his flesh? Heb. 10:19–20. Did that priest enter into the holy place with one body and into the Holy of Holies with another? Or did he, by entering the sanctuary, first destroy his body, and so die again, or rather descend into hell in a state of non-existence? How do we, by eating his flesh and drinking his blood, partake of communion with his broken body and shed blood, 1 Cor. 10:16? How will he come again to judgement in the same manner [ὃν τρόπον] as he was seen to go into heaven, Acts 1:11? Or will the eyes which pierced him see him, Rev. 1:7? Indeed I am reluctant to root out at greater length the enemies' errors about Christ, of which the first falsehood is that Christ in the resurrection kept a mortal body (the substance of flesh and blood cannot be glorified—see above)...

units.la: Sessio carnis mortale retinuerit, & substantia carnis & sanguinis glorificari non possit, de quo supra.
units.tr: The session: that he kept a mortal body, and that the substance of flesh and blood cannot be glorified, as discussed above.

units.la: LXX. Neque etiam errores eorum, qui omnipræsentiam carnis Christi propugnant, & sessioni ejusdem ad dextram Dei, saltem quoad ejus ἐνέργειαν inædificant, dissimulandi sunt. Eorum certè confusam in explicanda & ad omnipræsentiam carnis detorquenda sessione hac labium non parum etiam errores ipsos confundit. Alii enim, Brentius, Andreæ & Suevi ferè Christum secundum carnem in primo conceptionis momento ad dextram Dei sedísse contendunt. Alii ascendere in Cœlum, & sedere ad dextram Dei proæquipollentibus accipiunt. Etiam sessionem ad dextram Dei & Deitatem Christi hominis idem esse, Jac. Andreæ affirmat. Quin & Cœlum & dextram Dei ἰσο-δυναμίαν nonnulli, velut Matthias Hoë, alii pronuntiant. Sed quid sic fiet ascensioni in Cœlum, si, quod iidem asserunt, Cœlum ubique est? Quid ipsi dextræ Dei, & sessioni ad eandem, si dextra Cœlum est?
