Cúmque sessio ad dextram Dei honorem, gloriam, potestatem totius Christi, & secundum naturam utramque, utrique convenienter significet, non priùs ex eo honore & potestate carni per sessionem accedente ejusdem omnipræsentia probari potest, quàm aliunde probatum fuerit, carnem omnipræsentem esse. Neque enim idem honor, dignitas personæ & naturarum Christi est, quod ubiquitas; cùm illa sit axioma personæ & naturarum, hæc proprietas essentialis Deitatis. Cúmque omnipræsentia carnem destruat, adeóque etiam honorem carnis, qui non in sessione ad dextram Dei vertitur, pessumdet, ad honorem & gloriam Christi pertinere non potest. Tum si dextra Deitas est, & caro, quia ad dextram illam sedet, omnipræsens efficitur. Præterea etiam Christum secundum humanitatem ad dextram Dei sedere jam confirmavimus. Non ergo dextra Dei simpliciter Deitas est, adeóque nec sedens ad dextram idcirco θεὸν π Divinum quid, quoad naturam & proprietates ejus, participat. Accedit, quòd Scriptura Christum non ubique, sed in Cœlo duntaxat ad dextram Dei sedere, & hujus rei gratia etiam in Cœlum ascendisse disertè testificatur. Sedit in dextra ἐν ὑψηλοῖς in Cœlestibus, Ephef.I.20. ἐν ἐπουρανίοις in Cœlis, Hebr. VIII.1. Ubi phrasis illa in Cœlis non gloriæ vel Majestatis Cœlestis, sed loci determinationem esse, inde liquet, quòd Cœlum τόπος Locus Joh. XIV.3. statuitur, & gloria sessionis ad dextram Dei periphrasi jam ante circumscripta est. Deniquè sessio Christi ad dextram Dei præsentiam corporalem carnis Christi in Cœna Domini non obscurè evertit, tum quia Christus secundum carnem ad dextram Dei sedere demum post ascensionem in Cœlum cœpit; at in Cœna jam ante præsens fuit; ut sessio hæc ad præsentiam Christi corporalem in Cœna Domini nihil attineat: tum quia ad dextram Dei secundum carnem collocatus est in Cœlis, Hebr. VIII. 1. non in terra, vel Pane Eucharistico: tum quia in Cœlo collocata ad dextram Dei est caro Christi visibilis, uti supra probavimus; cùm in Cœna invisibilis, adeóque à sedente ad dextram Dei diversa, statuatur.
units.tr: LXX. Nor must we pass over the errors of those who defend the omnipresence of Christ's flesh and try to bind it to his session at God's right hand, at least as to its energy [ἐνέργειαν]. Their confused labour in explaining this session and twisting it toward the omnipresence of the flesh confounds not a little even their own errors. For some, such as Brenz, Andreae and the Swabians, maintain that Christ according to the flesh sat at the right hand of God in the first moment of conception. Others take ascending into heaven and sitting at God's right hand to be equivalent. Jacob Andreae affirms that the session at God's right hand and the Deity of the man Christ are the same thing. Some, like Matthias Hoë, even declare heaven and the right hand of God to be of equal power [ἰσο-δυναμίαν]. But what then becomes of the ascension into heaven, if, as they themselves assert, heaven is everywhere? What becomes of the right hand of God itself, and of the session at it, if the right hand is heaven? And since the session at God's right hand signifies the honour, glory and power of the whole Christ, and according to each nature, appropriately to each, the omnipresence cannot be proved from the honour and power which come to the flesh through the session, unless it has first been proved from elsewhere that the flesh is omnipresent. For the honour, dignity of the person and the natures of Christ is not the same as ubiquity, since the former is an attribute of the person and natures, while the latter is an essential property of the Deity. And since omnipresence destroys the flesh, and thus also destroys the honour of the flesh, which does not consist in the session at God's right hand, it cannot belong to the honour and glory of Christ. Furthermore, if the right hand is the Deity, and the flesh, because it sits at that right hand, is made omnipresent... Moreover, we have already confirmed that Christ sits at God's right hand according to his humanity. Therefore the right hand of God is not simply the Deity, and so the one sitting at the right hand does not for that reason share in something divine [θεῖόν τι] as to the nature and properties of that Deity. Besides, Scripture plainly testifies that Christ sits at the right hand of God not everywhere but in heaven alone, and that for this reason he also ascended into heaven. He sits at the right hand in the heavenly places [ἐν ὑψηλοῖς], Eph. 1:20; in the heavens [ἐν ἐπουρανίοις], Heb. 8:1. That the phrase in the heavens here marks a determination of place, and not a glory or heavenly majesty, is clear from the fact that heaven is set down as a place [τόπος], John 14:3, and that the glory of the session at the right hand of God was already circumscribed by a periphrasis. Finally, the session of Christ at the right hand of God does not obscurely overthrow the corporeal presence of Christ's flesh in the Lord's Supper: first, because Christ according to the flesh began to sit at God's right hand only after the ascension into heaven, whereas in the Supper he was already present before; so this session has nothing to do with Christ's corporeal presence in the Lord's Supper; second, because Christ's flesh, according to the flesh, was placed at God's right hand in the heavens, Heb. 8:1, not on earth or in the Eucharistic bread; third, because the flesh of Christ placed in heaven at God's right hand is visible, as we proved above, whereas in the Supper it is held to be invisible, and therefore different from the one sitting at God's right hand.

units.la: LXXI. Unum addo, Christum ad dextram Dei Patris collocatum non ideo supra Patrem eveĉtum esse, uti Socinus, Deum Patrem post sessionem Christi ad ejus dextram usque ad finem mundi, Regno exuens, & illud Christo vicario & quodammodo honoratiori, sed cum voluntate Patri subjecta, adeóque non tam cum dominio, quàm cum consensu cum voluntate Patris, gerendum, sine suffragiis resignans, deliravit. Cui secundas fecisse famosus ille Maldonatus, in Psal.CX.1. videtur; asserens, dextram in sessione Christi non solùm significare Christum æqualem Patri, sed etiam majorem &c. administratione scilicet Regni, non autem re ipsa. Sed omnia Filio ad dextram Dei sedenti subjecta sunt, ὅταν δὲ εἴπωσιν πάντα πρᾶξαντ πάντα præter eum, qui ei omnia subjecit, 1.Cor.XV.27. Neque sessio ad dextram honoris eminentioris eo, ad cujus dextram sedetur; sed honoris symbolum est, qui inter æquales æqualis, inter inæquales inæqualis est. Quomodo Principes, qui ad dextram alios collocant, eos honorant, sed non præcisè supra se. Ita Nero Tiridatem Armeniæ Regem juxta se dextro latere collocans, uti Suetonius in Nerone cap. XIII. loquitur, Tiridate inferior non fuit. Solomon matrem suam honoravit; at non supra se, quia honorando nec Reginam, nec se poten-tiorem fecit. Et sponsa stans ad dextram sponsi, Psal.XLV.10. à Sponso honoratur, quantum honorari & glorificari potest; ita ut nemo alius supra eam honoretur, non ut sponsa ampliori honore, quàm Sponsus afficiatur: Et in ritu hoc humano non tam persona Regis alios ad dextram collocantis, quàm thronus, qui sedem non sinistram duntaxat habet, sed bilaterem, dextram & sinistram, in quarum medio thronus sublimior eminet, attendi debet. Quomodo aliter esse nequit, quin ille, qui sedet à dextero throni latere, ut aliis superior, sic inferior Rege, sit. Eò respexit mater filiorum Zebedæi, Johannis & Jacobi, quæ in Regno Christi unum eorum ad dextram, alterum ad lævam Christi collocari petiit. At dispar tamen sessionis Christi ad dextram Patris ratio est, quia nulla loci tertii, seu læviæ mentio est. Hoc solum ergo significatur, quòd Deus Filium glorificaverit, & quidem ea gloria, quam apud Patrem habuit, antequam mundus esset, Joh.XVII.5. Quod ex ascensione etiam patet, quia Deus assumendo eum declaravit, eum ex Cœlo venïsse, Filium unigenitum, & Deum Israelis esse. Non ergo sic Filius majore vel minore honore affectus est, quàm qui Patri competit. quia uterque unum sunt, & Regnum Patris est Regnum Filii, gloria Filii gloria Patris. Venturus est Filius hominis in gloria Patris, Matth.XVI.27. Cùm venerit Filius hominis, & omnes Angeli cum ipso, tum sedebit ἐπὶ θρόνου δόξης αὐτοῦ super throno gloriæ ipsius, ibid.XXV.31. ubi gloria, cum qua appa-rebit Filius, & thronus, in quo sedebit, gloria ejus & thronus ejus, Patris appellatur. Non tamen sessio ad dextram Patris præcisè æqualitatem cum Patre significat, quia Personæ omnes ab æterno æquales & unum fuerunt, neque tamen ad alterius dextram ab æterno sedit, sed respectu Naturæ Divinæ, novam gloriæ illius, qua Patri Filius æqualis est, vindicationem cum introductione ad gloriam à Patre & respectu Naturæ humanæ honorem & gloriam, sed humanitati à λόγῳ assumptæ convenientem, hoc est, gloriam supra omnes creaturas Deo proximam notat.
units.tr: LXXI. I add one point: the claim that Christ, placed at the right hand of God the Father, was therefore raised above the Father is the view of Socinus, who raved that God the Father, after Christ sat at his right hand until the end of the world, laid aside his reign and handed it over to Christ as his vicar and in some sense more honoured, though subject to the Father's will, so that it is to be exercised not so much with dominion as with consent to the Father's will, and he resigned it without votes. The famous Maldonatus seems to have come second to him in this, in in Psal.CX.1., asserting that the right hand in Christ's session signifies not only that Christ is equal to the Father but also greater, etc., that is, in the administration of the kingdom, but not in fact. But all things are subjected to the Son who sits at the right hand of God: ὅταν δὲ εἴπωσιν πάντα [when they say that all things are subjected], that is, all things except him who subjected all things to him (1 Cor. 15.27). Nor is sitting at the right hand a sign of a more eminent honour in the one at whose right hand one sits; it is a symbol of honour which is equal among equals and unequal among unequals. So princes who seat others at their right hand honour them, but not so as to place them above themselves. Thus Nero, seating Tiridates, King of Armenia, at his right side, as Suetonius says in Nerone cap. XIII., did not make Tiridates his superior. Solomon honoured his mother, but not above himself, since by honouring her he made her neither queen nor more powerful than himself. And the bride standing at the right hand of the bridegroom (Psal. 45.10) is honoured by the bridegroom as much as honour and glory can be given, so that no one else is honoured above her, yet not so that the bride is endowed with a greater honour than the bridegroom. In this human custom we must attend not so much to the person of the king who seats others at his right hand as to the throne, which has not only a left seat but a two-sided one, right and left, with the higher throne standing out in the middle. It cannot be otherwise: he who sits at the right side of the throne is superior to the others but inferior to the king. The mother of the sons of Zebedee, John and James, had this in mind when she asked that one of them be placed at Christ's right hand and the other at his left in his kingdom. But the session of Christ at the right hand of the Father is different, because there is no mention of a third place, or of the left. So this signifies only that God glorified the Son, and indeed with that glory which he had with the Father before the world was (John 17.5). This is also clear from the ascension, since by taking him up God declared that he had come from heaven, the only-begotten Son, and that he is the God of Israel. Therefore the Son is not honoured with a greater or lesser honour than belongs to the Father, because both are one, and the kingdom of the Father is the kingdom of the Son, and the glory of the Son is the glory of the Father. The Son of man is to come in the glory of the Father (Matt. 16.27). When the Son of man comes, and all the angels with him, then he will sit ἐπὶ θρόνου δόξης αὐτοῦ [on the throne of his glory] upon the throne of his glory (ibid. 25.31), where the glory with which the Son will appear and the throne on which he will sit are called his glory and his throne, that is, the Father's. Yet sitting at the right hand of the Father does not signify precisely equality with the Father, since all the Persons were equal and one from eternity, and yet the Son did not sit at the right hand of another from eternity; rather, with respect to the divine nature, it denotes a new vindication of that glory by which the Son is equal to the Father, together with his introduction into glory by the Father; and with respect to the human nature, it denotes honour and glory belonging to the humanity assumed by the λόγῳ [Word], that is, a glory next to God above all creatures.

units.la: LOCUS DECIMUS NONUS, De OFFICIO JESU CHRISTI. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: NINETEENTH HEAD, On the Office of Jesus Christ. A SUMMARY.

units.la: Missionis Jesu in carnem, humiliationis & glorificationis ejusdem causa fuit officium quod ut Mediator salutis nostrae procurandae gratia suscipere debuit. 1. Officium Christi Mediatorium definitur. 2. Ejus Naturam, nomina & res ipsae declarant. 3. Nomen praecipuum & proprium est ΙΗΣΟΥΣ JESUS ab Angelo impositum, ex Hebraeo יהושוע quod in ישוע Jesuah posteriores Hebraei mutarunt, & denique in ישו Jesu, ex more Syrorum, iidem contraxerunt. 4. Ita dictus est, quia populum suum salvat a peccatis. 5. Cujus sodales nequiter se Lojolae socii, qui daemoniorum potius spiritus a Spiritu S. insigniuntur, jactant. 6. Vim nominis illius Sociniani, ejusmodi Salvatorem fingentes, qui ne unius quidem hominis peccatum expiaverit, abnegant. 7. Cujus culpae rei etiam Pontificii sunt, Salvatores alios Jesu sociantes, atque ita Jesu imperfectum Salvatorem facientes. 8. Idem משיח Χριστὸς Unctii nomine venit, ab unctione, quae ad laetitiam, honorem & officium referri solet. 9. Christi seu Messiae nomen JESU, ceu ὄνομα διαφορώτερον tribuitur ad pridem promissum Salvatorem significandum. 10. Hoc nomine Jesus venit ob unctionem non externam, sed spiritualem, quae triplex est, aeterna ad officium destinatio, temporalis inhabitatio Deitatis in carne habitantis, nec non dignitatis Regiae eidem collatae. 11. Jesu prae veteribus unctis Prophetis, Sacerdotibus & Regibus praerogativa. 12. Idem Jesus Christus etiam μεσίτης Mediatoris aliisque nominibus synonymis, velut Sponsoris, Testatoris, Angeli foederis, Sacerdotis, Paracleti &c. venit. 13. Muneris Mediatorii causa communiter est tota S. Trinitas, sed in personis distincta ratio operandi est. 14. Christus Mediatoris munus secundum utramque naturam obiit. 15. Pontificiorum & Stancari uni Naturae humanae μεσιτείαν vindicantium, elenchus. 16. Eorundem argumenta ad incudem revocantur. 17. Mediatoris nomen non dicit mediam Divinam inter & humanam naturam excellentiam. 18. Ideo etiam Christus Mediator, & qua Mediator, adorari debet. 19. Mediator Jesus est Deum inter & homines, adeoque etiam se inter, qua filius est, & homines. 20. non Deum inter & Angelos. 21. Mediatio ipsa in reconciliatione consistit. 22. Quae non sola ad amorem Dei adductio est, uti Socinus fingit, sed hanc consequitur, & simul πλήρης est, cum & Deum homini, & hominem Deo conciliet. 23. In Mediatore Christo non sic meritum ejus ab efficacia divelli debet, ut pro aliis meruisse simpliciter, pro aliis etiam efficaciter, cum Remonstrantibus, dicatur. 24. Nam Mediator est merito & efficacia simul, adaequate, indivise & effective. 25. Officium Mediatoris Christi commune est omni statui Ecclesiae post peccatum, sed diversimode ante & post Christum administratum. 26. Triplex est, Propheticum, Sacerdotale & Regium. 27. Prophetico munere Christus etiam in V. T. defunctus est. 28. Sed tum maxime & proprie, cum in carne apparuit, juxta Vaticinium, Deut. XVIII.18.19. quod explicatur. 29. & quidem inde a primo conceptionis momento. 30. Neque adeo is voluntatem Dei raptus post Baptismum in Coelum demum didicit. quod profanum Socini ὑπνημα est. 31. Cujus argumenta discutiuntur. 32. Initium publicae muneris Prophetici functionis a Baptismo Johannis factum est. 33. Fuitque illa Legalis vel Evangelica. Illa in explicatione, non rogatione novae Legis operum perum constitit. 34. Secus quàm Sociniani aliùque pertendunt. 35. Quorum argu-mentis fit satis. 36. Christus Matth.V.17–f. non novam Legem Evangelicam tulit, sed hypocriticam scribarum justitiam, vindicata vera Legis justitia, redarguit. 37. Quod ex verborum Christi serie amplius probatur. 38. Præcipuum doctrinæ Christi genus Evangelicum fuit. 39. Ante omnia enim prædicavit Regnum Cœlorum, resipi-scentiam & fidem. 40. Summa præconii Christi. 41. Modus doctrinæ & Prophe-tiæ omnis à Christo prædicatæ, cum summa præconii efficacia conjunctus. 42. Non lo-cutus est ut scribæ, sed ut potestatem habens, & vera πει𝔇ω, seu suada. 43. Præco-nium illud suum etiam operibus seu miraculis omni exceptione majoribus confirma-vit. 44. Miracula Christi doctrinæ ejusdem mirificam lucem affuderunt. 45. Do-ctrina & miracula Christi ordine certo processerunt; quia & prius docuit, quàm fecit, & ordine etiam fecit. 46. Miracula insignia Jesum patrasse, ne Veteres quidem Ju-dæi, Josephus & Thalmudistæ; ac nec gentiles etiam inficiati sunt. 47. Sed per Beel-zebulem edita esse, Pharisæi veteres & recentiores Judæi blasphemant; adversus quos miraculorum Christi tum veritas. 48. tum Divinitas asseritur. 49. Eadem sic e-dita esse, ut Deus per ea non tentaverit populum, sed Veritati attestatus sit, proba-tur. 50. Objectiones miraculis Christi obductæ diluuntur. 51. Etiam exemplo vi-tæ. 52. nec non mortis suæ Christus doctrinam suam corroboravit. 53. Neque ta-men is ob muneris Prophetici fidele ministerium Salvator mundi, sensu Sociniano, salu-tari debet. 54. Sacerdotium Christi definitur & explicatur. 55. Sacerdos esse Chri-stus nisi ιεράπευτ non potuit 56. Sacerdotii Christi conditio externa ex Hebr. VII.13-26. explicatur. 57. Ejusdem Sacerdotii ex Hebr.VII.26. panditur. 58. Functionum Sacerdotii Christi & veteris Levitici differentia ex Hebr.VII.27 28. ex-ponitur. 59. Singula hæc Sacerdotio Missatico e diametro opposita sunt. 60. Vi-ctima Sacerdotii Christi ipse Christus fuit; & quidem potissimùm in genere piacula ri tum pro peccato, tum pro reatu. 61. Sacrificii Christi partes juxta typum præstantis-simum victimarum, quarum corpora extra castra cremabantur, & sanguis in adytum inferebatur, tres constituuntur, Voluntaria oblatio sui ipsius in victimam, mors, & re-præsentatio, seu oblatio hostiæ in Cœlo. 62. Ordo partium illarum in functione Sa-cerdotii Christi ostenditur. 63. Voluntariæ oblationis, qua Christus se, ut victimam, Deo Patri ad mortem obtulit, necessitas. 64. Mors Christi, ceu victimæ, vim expi-andi peccata habuit; utpote quæ sine morte Christi expiari non potuissent. 65. Mor-tem Christi rationem pœnæ & expiationis vicariæ habuisse, demonstratur. 66. Scri-pturæ morti Christi expiationem peccatorum & satisfactionem pro iisdem tribuunt. 67. Eadem Morti & Sanguini Christi ἀπολύτρωσιν, redemptionem, & quòd λύτρον, ἀντίλυτρον pro peccatis nostris sit, vindicant. 68. Socinianorum objectiones, quòd redemptio Christo tributa metaphorica, non propria sit, proponuntur; 69. & fusius discutiuntur. 70. Emphasis locutionum, quibus Christi mors ὑπὲρ pro nobis, & ἀντὶ vice nostra oppetita dicitur, urgetur & vindicatur. 71. Veritatem satisfactionis Christi illud quoque valide arguit, quòd Christus ex ligno suspensus pro nobis execratio factus dicitur. 72. Omnis typorum veterum & sacrificiorum inprimis schola satisfa-ctioni Christi attestatur. 73. Sublata satisfactione Christi immane syrma absurdita-tum sequitur. 74. Hæreticorum veterum & recentiorum satisfactionem Christi su-gillantium & negantium historia. 75. Fines illi, quos Socinus morti Christi aptavit, subducta satisfactionis basi, nihili sunt. 76. Argumenta satisfactioni Christi opposita proponuntur. 77. & dissolvuntur sigillatim, velut, quòd nomen satisfactionis nus-piam extet. 78. Quòd impossibilis sit, quia pœna ab uno in alium transferri, impius ju-stificari, unius morte omnium vita redimi non possit, & Christus æternam mortem non subierit. 79. Quòd supervacanea sit, quia Deus peccata sine satisfactione remittere potuerit, ceu absolutæ potestatis dominus & creditor, qui debitori debita sine satisfa-ctione remittere possit. 80. Quòd Deus æquè satisfactionem remittere, ac eandem eti-am, ut judex & legislator, à Lege sua recedendo, in alium transferre possit. 81. Quòd satisfactio Voluntati Dei repugnet, quia is in V.T. peccata sine satisfactione remiserit, & multò magis id faciat in N.T. quod tempus gratiæ est, & in quo se peccata gratis remissurum promisit; & placatus satisfactionem non ampliùs exigat. 82. Quòd sa-tisfactio cum remissione ex mera gratia pugnet, quia Deus peccatum χαρίζεται dicitur, & ἀνυσιῶν sit, satisfactionem exigere & peccatum remittere. 83. Obedientia Mor-tis Christi respectu nostri etiam meriti rationem habuit. quod proprië dictum, & ex con-digno fuit. 84. Ejus magnitudo & infinitas ex naturæ humanæ sanctitate & obedientia, eminentia ejusdem cum λόγῳ unitâ, & dignitate Personæ θεανθρώπῳ æstima- ri debet. 85. Socinianorum meritum Christi perinde ut satisfactionem ejus abnegan- tium elenchus. 86. Effectus mortis, satisfactionis & meriti Christi. 87. Christus i- is, pro quibus mortuus est, etiam Spiritum S. regenerationem & fidem promeruit. 88. Satisfactionis & meriti Christi abnegati rei etiam Pontificii & Remonstrantes pera- guntur. 89. Argumento Remonstrantium, quòd satisfactione posita concipi non pos- sit, quomodo Deus conditionem pœnitentiæ & fidei à peccatore Deo reconciliando exi- gere potuerit, occurritur. 90. Nec pro Angelis, nec pro hominibus quibusvis, sed pro solis electis Christus mortem sustinuit. 91. Veterum, Germadii & Massilianorum, nec non recentiorum mortem Christi pro omnibus & singulis hominibus obitam asserentium historia. 92. Eorundem argumenta ad partes vocantur. 93. Tertia sacrificii Chri- sti pars, victimæ in Cœlo repræsentatio & nova oblatio est. 94. Ad eam intercessio & interpellatio Christi pro nobis refertur. 95. Quæ in patrocinio eorum, qui Christo dati sunt, Sacerdotali & perpetuo apud Deum Patrem consistit. 96. Socinianorum intercessionis Sacerdotalis & efficacis vim ingressui Christi in Cœlum derogantium, elen- chus. 97. Regium Christi munus definitur, & Scripturæ testimoniis confirma- tur. 98. Causa Regiæ potestatis Christo collatæ est acquisitio populi, ceu peculiaris sibi & hæreditarii. 99. Regnum illud, quod merito mortis suæ Christus sibi acquisivit Mediatorium, à naturali & essentiali Regno ejusdem, ut Filii Dei, distinctum est. 100. Sed sola ratione, non re, quia etiam Mediatorium, nisi Deus exercere non potuis- set. 101. Regnum isthoc non præter, vel citra, sed secundum voluntatem Patris ad- ministrat; neque adeò Christo regnante Deus Majestatis suæ solio cessit. 102. Regio munere fungitur Christus θεάνθρωπος, Deus & homo; sed quà homo potestate, & exercitio potestatis dependente. 103. Regnum Christi non externum, vel temporale, sed spirituale & Cœleste totum est. 104. Nam & Regnum Cœlorum Regnum dici- tur: & Rex Cœlestis: & Lex spiritualis: & bona interna omnia spiritualia & cœ- lestia: & hostes ejus spirituales sunt. 105. Judæorum & Pontificiorum Regnum Christi in temporale convertentium elenchus. 106. Eorundem pro Regno Christi tem- porali argumenta diluuntur. 107. Spirituale Regnum Christi populi ejusdem guber- natione. 108. & defensione constat. 109. Regnum Christi æternum est. 110. Sed ejus œconomia & administratio differentiam recipit, quia Christus aliter illud in V. T. aliter in N. T. administravit, & administrat. 111. Ne in Cœlo quidem post finem mundi Christus Regnum illud abdicabit, sed aliter administrabit, cessatura ordinatione Regni communis essentialis ad Mediatorium, & Christo in Patre omnia complente re- gnaturo. 112. Loci 1.Cor.XV.24–27. perspicua paraphrasis. 113. Regium Christi munus mirè Pontificii & Sociniani corrumpunt. 114. Christus Rex idem Messias est, quæ vox non temporalem dominum & Principem significat, qualem Ju- dæi indurati frustra hactenus expectarunt. 115. Judaici illius Messiæ absurditas & vana expectatio. 116. Venisse Messiam verum demonstratur, tum ex iis, quæ Mes- siæ adventum præcedere debuerunt, & ante, non post Jesu adventum contigerunt. 117. Tum ex iis, quæ, Messia adventante, extare debuerunt, & pridem non amplius ex- tant. 118. Tum ex articulo temporis à Daniele signato. 119. Nebulæ à Judæis va- ticinio Danielis offusæ discutiuntur. 120. Exceptio Judæorum, quòd Messiæ adven- tus per peccata populi retardetur, eliditur. 121. Eorundem argumenta adventui Messiæ opposita, & à R.Isac Filio Abrahami in Chiffuk Emmunah collecta, ad examen revocantur. 122. Jesum Messiam esse, tum iisdem argumentis, quibus Messiæ adven- tus confirmatur; tum ex iis, quæ Jesu apparente visa & audita sunt: tum ex hæredi- tate gentium; seu fide illa, qua gentes Jesum, non obstantibus obstaculis pluribus, pro Messia receperunt: Tum ex Prophetia demonstratur. 123. Parallelia inter ea, quæ de Messia Prophetæ prædixerunt, & quæ de Jesu historia Evangelica prædicat, instituitur. 124. Objectiones Judæorum, quibus Jesum Messiam non esse argutantur, opposi- tæ Jesu tum Deitati: Tum nativitati ex Virgine: Tum genealogiæ: Tum miraculis & Regno spirituali: tum doctrinæ: 125. Tum vaticiniis; 126. Tum vitæ, refellun- tur. 127. Præjudicia Judæorum, quòd nemo Principum, sed sola turba, quæ legem non noverit, in Jesum crediderit; quòd Galilæus fuerit: quòd Majores sui, qui Jesum repudiarunt & damnarunt, viri probi fuerint, discussa. 128.
units.tr: The office that the Mediator had to undertake for the sake of procuring our salvation was the purpose of Jesus' mission into the flesh, of his humiliation and of his glorification. 1. The Mediatorial office of Christ is defined. 2. His nature, names and the things themselves declare it. 3. His chief and proper name is JESUS [ΙΗΣΟΥΣ], given by the angel, from the Hebrew יהושוע [Jehoshua], which later Hebrews changed into ישוע [Jeshua], and finally, after the manner of the Syrians, contracted into ישו [Jesu]. 4. He is so called because he saves his people from their sins. 5. The Companions of Loyola wickedly boast of being his fellows, though they are rather marked by the spirits of demons than by the Holy Spirit. 6. The Socinians deny the force of that name, feigning a Saviour who has not expiated even the sin of one man. 7. The Papists are also guilty of this fault, joining other saviours to Jesus and so making Jesus an imperfect Saviour. 8. The same Christ, the Messiah [משיח], Christos [Χριστός], comes under the name of Anointed, from the anointing that is usually referred to joy, honour and office. 9. The name Jesus is given to Christ or Messiah, as a more excellent name [ὄνομα διαφορώτερον], to signify the Saviour promised long before. 10. Jesus came under this name because of an anointing that is not external but spiritual, which is threefold: the eternal appointment to the office, the temporal indwelling of the Deity in the flesh that it inhabited, and also the royal dignity conferred upon him. 11. The prerogative of Jesus over the anointed prophets, priests and kings of old. 12. The same Jesus Christ also came as Mediator [μεσίτης] and under other synonymous names, such as Surety, Testator, Angel of the covenant, Priest, Paraclete, etc. 13. The whole Holy Trinity is in common the cause of the Mediatorial office, yet the manner of working is distinct in the persons. 14. Christ discharged the Mediatorial office according to both natures. 15. Refutation of the Papists and of Stancarus, who claim the mediation for the human nature alone [μεσιτεία]. 16. Their arguments are brought back to the anvil. 17. The name Mediator does not signify an excellence midway between the divine and the human nature. 18. Therefore Christ is also to be worshipped as Mediator, and as Mediator he must be adored. 19. Jesus the Mediator is between God and men, and thus also between himself, as he is the Son, and men. 20. He is not between God and the angels. 21. Mediation itself consists in reconciliation. 22. It is not merely a bringing of men to the love of God, as Socinus imagines, but follows upon that and is at the same time complete, since it reconciles both God to man and man to God. 23. In the Mediator Christ, his merit must not be so separated from its efficacy that he is said merely to have merited for some and effectively for others, as the Remonstrants say. 24. For the Mediator is at once meritorious and efficacious, adequately, indivisibly and effectively. 25. The office of the Mediator Christ is common to every state of the Church after the fall, but it has been administered in different ways before and after Christ. 26. It is threefold: prophetic, priestly and royal. 27. Christ also discharged the prophetic office in the Old Testament. 28. But it was then most fully and properly done when he appeared in the flesh, according to the prophecy of Deut. XVIII.18.19., which is explained. 29. And indeed from the first moment of conception. 30. Nor did he learn the will of God only after his baptism, when he was caught up into heaven, which is the profane dream of Socinus. 31. His arguments are examined. 32. The beginning of the public discharge of the prophetic office was made at the baptism of John. 33. And it was either legal or evangelical; the former consisted in the explanation, not the abrogation, of the works of the Law, and not in the perfection of works, as Socinians and others contend. 34. Socinians and others maintain otherwise. 35. Their arguments are sufficiently answered. 36. Christ, at Matth. V.17, did not bring in a new evangelical Law, but refuted the hypocritical righteousness of the scribes, vindicating the true righteousness of the Law. 37. This is further proved from the sequence of Christ's words. 38. The chief kind of Christ's teaching was evangelical. 39. For above all he proclaimed the Kingdom of heaven, repentance and faith. 40. The sum of Christ's preaching. 41. The manner of all the teaching and prophecy proclaimed by Christ, joined with the efficacy of the sum of his preaching. 42. He did not speak as the scribes, but as one having authority, and with true persuasion [πειθώ], or eloquence. 43. He also confirmed that preaching of his by works, that is, by miracles greater than any objection. 44. The miracles of Christ shed a wonderful light on his teaching. 45. The teaching and the miracles of Christ proceeded in a fixed order, since he both taught before he did, and also acted in order. 46. That Jesus performed notable miracles, neither the ancient Jews, Josephus and the Talmudists, nor even the Gentiles have denied. 47. But that they were done through Beelzebub, the ancient Pharisees and the more recent Jews blaspheme; against whom both the truth and the divinity of Christ's miracles are asserted. 48. Also. 49. It is proved that they were so done that God did not test the people through them, but bore witness to the truth. 50. Objections brought against the miracles of Christ are refuted. 51. Also by the example of his life. 52. And Christ confirmed his teaching also by his death. 53. Yet he is not, in the Socinian sense, the Saviour of the world because of the faithful discharge of the prophetic office. 54. The priesthood of Christ is defined and explained. 55. Christ could not be a priest unless he were also a [ιεράπευτ] (sacrificer). 56. The external condition of Christ's priesthood is explained from Heb. VII.13–26. 57. The same priesthood is set out from Heb. VII.26. 58. The difference between the functions of Christ's priesthood and of the old Levitical priesthood is set forth from Heb. VII.27–28. 59. All these things are diametrically opposed to the Socinian priesthood. 60. The victim of Christ's priesthood was Christ himself; and indeed chiefly in the kind of sacrifices offered both for sin and for guilt. 61. The parts of Christ's sacrifice, according to the most excellent type of victims, whose bodies were burned outside the camp and whose blood was carried into the inner sanctuary, are three: the voluntary offering of himself as victim, his death, and the representation, or offering of the sacrifice in heaven. 62. The order of those parts in the function of Christ's priesthood is shown. 63. The necessity of the voluntary offering by which Christ offered himself as victim to God the Father unto death. 64. The death of Christ, as of a victim, had the power of expiating sins, since sins could not have been expiated without the death of Christ. 65. It is demonstrated that the death of Christ had the character of punishment and of vicarious expiation. 66. The Scriptures ascribe to the death of Christ the expiation of sins and satisfaction for them. 67. The same Scriptures claim for the death and blood of Christ redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις], and that he is a ransom [λύτρον] and a substitute ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for our sins. 68. The Socinian objections, that the redemption ascribed to Christ is metaphorical and not proper, are set forth; 69. and are examined more fully. 70. The emphasis of the expressions by which Christ's death is said to have been undergone for us [ὑπὲρ] and in our place [ἀντί] is pressed and vindicated. 71. The truth of Christ's satisfaction is also strongly argued from this, that Christ, hanged on a tree, is said to have been made a curse for us. 72. The whole school of the old types and sacrifices, above all, bears witness to the satisfaction of Christ. 73. If Christ's satisfaction is removed, an immense train of absurdities follows. 74. History of the heretics, ancient and recent, who have disparaged and denied the satisfaction of Christ. 75. The ends that Socinus assigned to the death of Christ, once the foundation of satisfaction is removed, are nothing. 76. The arguments opposed to Christ's satisfaction are set out, 77. and are answered one by one; for example, that the name of satisfaction nowhere occurs. 78. That it is impossible, because punishment cannot be transferred from one to another, the impious cannot be justified, and the life of all cannot be redeemed by one man's death, and Christ did not undergo eternal death. 79. That it is superfluous, because God could have remitted sins without satisfaction, as the lord of absolute power and creditor, who can remit debts to a debtor without satisfaction. 80. That God can remit satisfaction as easily as, as judge and lawgiver, he can transfer the same, by departing from his own Law, to another. 81. That satisfaction repugns the will of God, since he remitted sins without satisfaction in the Old Testament, and does so much more in the New, which is the time of grace, in which he promised to remit sins freely; and being appeased, he no longer requires satisfaction. 82. That satisfaction contradicts remission from mere grace, because God is said to forgive [χαρίζεται] sin and is not one who both exacts satisfaction and remits sin. 83. The obedience of Christ's death also had the character of merit with respect to us, which is properly so called and is according to worth. 84. Its greatness and infinity must be estimated from the holiness and obedience of human nature, its eminence joined with the Word, and the dignity of the Person, God-man [θεάνθρωπος]. 85. Refutation of the Socinians, who deny the merit of Christ just as they deny his satisfaction. 86. The effects of the death, satisfaction and merit of Christ. 87. For those for whom Christ died, he also merited the Holy Spirit, regeneration and faith. 88. The Papists and the Remonstrants, who also deny the satisfaction and merit of Christ, are attacked. 89. The argument of the Remonstrants, that once satisfaction is granted it cannot be conceived how God could require of the sinner, to be reconciled to God, the condition of repentance and faith, is met. 90. Christ underwent death neither for the angels nor for any men whatever, but for the elect alone. 91. History of the ancient Germadians and Massilians, and of recent writers too, who assert that the death of Christ was undergone for all and each man. 92. Their arguments are called to account. 93. The third part of Christ's sacrifice is the representation of the victim in heaven and the new offering. 94. To this the intercession and interpellation of Christ for us is referred. 95. This consists in the priestly and perpetual advocacy before God the Father for those who have been given to Christ. 96. Refutation of the Socinians, who deny the priestly and effective intercession, and the force of Christ's entrance into heaven. 97. The royal office of Christ is defined and confirmed by testimonies of Scripture. 98. The cause of the royal power conferred on Christ is the acquisition of a people, as his own peculiar and hereditary people. 99. That Kingdom which Christ acquired for himself by the merit of his death is Mediatorial, and is distinct from his natural and essential Kingdom as Son of God. 100. But only in reason, not in fact, since even the Mediatorial Kingdom could not be exercised except by God. 101. This Kingdom he administers not apart from or without, but according to the will of the Father; nor, while Christ reigns, does God yield the throne of his majesty. 102. Christ, God-man, discharges the royal office as God and man; but as man, by a power that depends on the exercise of power. 103. The Kingdom of Christ is not external or temporal, but wholly spiritual and heavenly. 104. For it is called the Kingdom of heaven; and the Heavenly King; and the spiritual Law; and all good things inward, spiritual and heavenly; and its enemies are spiritual. 105. Refutation of the Jews and Papists who turn the Kingdom of Christ into a temporal one. 106. Their arguments for a temporal Kingdom of Christ are answered. 107. The spiritual Kingdom of Christ consists in the government of his people, 108. and in their defence. 109. The Kingdom of Christ is eternal. 110. But its economy and administration admit of difference, since Christ administered it otherwise in the Old Testament and otherwise in the New, and administers it so. 111. Not even in heaven after the end of the world will Christ abdicate that Kingdom, but he will administer it otherwise, the ordering of the common essential Kingdom relative to the Mediatorial one ceasing, and Christ, having completed all things in the Father, will reign. 112. A clear paraphrase of 1 Cor. XV.24–27. 113. The Papists and Socinians grievously corrupt the royal office of Christ. 114. Christ the King is the same Messiah, a word that signifies not a temporal lord and prince, such as the hardened Jews have hitherto vainly expected. 115. The absurdity and vain expectation of that Jewish Messiah. 116. That the true Messiah has come is shown, both from those things which ought to have preceded the coming of the Messiah, and which happened before, not after, the coming of Jesus. 117. And from those things which, at the Messiah's coming, ought to have been present and which have long since ceased to exist. 118. And from the time-point marked by Daniel. 119. The mists cast by the Jews over the prophecy of Daniel are dispelled. 120. The Jewish exception, that the coming of the Messiah is delayed by the sins of the people, is refuted. 121. Their arguments against the coming of the Messiah, collected by R. Isaac son of Abraham in the Chizzuk Emunah, are brought to examination. 122. That Jesus is the Messiah is demonstrated: both by the same arguments by which the coming of the Messiah is confirmed; and from those things which were seen and heard at the appearance of Jesus; and from the inheritance of the Gentiles, or that faith by which the Gentiles received Jesus as Messiah despite many obstacles; and from prophecy. 123. A parallel is drawn between what the prophets foretold about the Messiah and what the Gospel history proclaims about Jesus. 124. The objections of the Jews, by which they argue that Jesus is not the Messiah, are opposed: to his Deity; to his birth of a virgin; to his genealogy; to his miracles and spiritual Kingdom; to his teaching; 125. to the prophecies; 126. and to his life, are refuted. 127. The prejudices of the Jews, that none of the rulers but only the crowd, which does not know the Law, believed in Jesus; that he was a Galilean; that their ancestors, who rejected and condemned Jesus, were upright men, are discussed. 128.

units.la: I. Ausa maximè sontica, & gravissima omnium fuerit oportet, quæ hoc effecit, ut Sermo caro fieret, Deus in carne manifestaretur, Filius Dei in mortem traderetur, & ex mortem vindicatus in supremam sessionis ad dextram ipsius Dei gloriam eniteretur. Si nihil unquam Deus & Natura frustra fecerunt, frustra certè non fuit illud opus, de quo Deus ipse dixit: Faciam mirabilia, אשר לא נבראו quæ non creata sunt in tota terra, & in omnibus gentibus; Videbitque universus populus, in cujus medio es מעשה יהוה Opus Domini, quia נורא tremendum erit, quod ego facturus sum, Exod. XXXIV.10. Creavit Jehova חדשה novum (non visum, non auditum unquam) in terra: Fœmina circumdedit masculum, Jerem. XXXI.22. Neque alia tantæ rei causa fuit, quàm ἀδοxία beneplacitum illud Dei, quo nos in Christo, Sponsore, Mediatore, Salvatore nostro, & Uncto Dei ab æterno elegit, ut in eo haberemus ἀπολύτρωσιν redemptionem per sanguinem ejus, remissionem peccatorum, juxta divitias gratiæ ejus, Ephes. I.4.7. Ideo enim Semen Mulieris promissum est, ut contereret caput Serpentis, & in eo omnes familiæ terræ benedicerentur. Tunc dixi: Ecce veni; in volumine libri scriptum est de me, ut facerem voluntatem tuam, Deus mi, Psal. XL.8.9. In qua voluntate sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Jesu Christi, semel factam, Hebr. X.9.10. πιστὸς ὁ λόγος, καὶ πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος. Fidelis est sermo, & omni exceptione dignus, quòd Christus Jesus venerit in mundum ἁμαρτωλὸς σῶσαι ad salvandum peccatores, 1. Tim. I.15. Hæc enim doctrina, quòd Jesus in mundum venerit, peccatorum salvandorum gratiâ, sana illa & νεὶα unicè dominans doctrina est, per quam Deus honoratur, & homo ab odio Dei & proximi ad amorem Dei atque virtutum ejus; & ad amorem proximi traducitur. atque ad Dei imaginem renovatur; adeóque dubitationi nulli ansam præbet, vel relinquit, &, ut vera lux conscientiæ omni se patefacit, verè fidelis sermo & omni exceptione dignus.
units.tr: I. The deed that brought it about that the Word became flesh, that God was manifested in the flesh, that the Son of God was delivered to death, and that, vindicated from death, he was raised to the supreme glory of sitting at the right hand of God, must surely have been the most heinous and the gravest of all deeds. If God and Nature have never done anything in vain, then certainly that work was not in vain, of which God himself said: "I will do marvels which have not been created in all the earth or among all the nations; and all the people among whom you are shall see the work of the LORD, for it is tremendous [נורא] what I am about to do" (Exod. 34:10). "The LORD has created a new thing [חדשה] in the earth, never seen or heard of before: a woman shall encompass a man" (Jer. 31:22). Nor was there any other cause for so great a matter than that good pleasure of God [εὐδοκία], by which he chose us in Christ, our Surety, Mediator, Savior, and the Anointed of God, from eternity, so that in him we might have redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις] through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace (Eph. 1:4, 7). For this reason the Seed of the woman was promised, that he would crush the head of the serpent, and in him all the families of the earth would be blessed. "Then I said, Behold, I come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me that I should do your will, O my God" (Ps. 40:8–9). "By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ, made once for all" (Heb. 10:9–10). "Faithful is the saying, and worthy of all acceptance [πιστὸς ὁ λόγος, καὶ πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος]: that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners [ἁμαρτωλοὺς σῶσαι]" (1 Tim. 1:15). For this doctrine, that Jesus came into the world to save sinners, is that sound and divine doctrine which alone reigns, through which God is honored and man is turned from hatred of God and neighbor to the love of God and of his virtues, and to love of neighbor, and is renewed into the image of God. It therefore leaves no occasion or room for doubt, and, as the true light of conscience, it reveals itself to everyone. Truly, it is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance.

units.la: II. Ideo ergo Jesus Christus in mundum venit, mortuus, & ad dextram Dei exaltatus est, ut officio Salvatoris & Mediatoris Deum inter & homines suscepto gloriam Dei nimium peccato læsam restitueret, & peccatores salvaret. Estque officium illud μεσιτεία Mediatio Deum inter & homines; seu functio illa Mediatoris Jesu Christi, quam ipse secundum voluntatem Patris & unctionem Spiritus S. ad homines peccatores, sibi datos, Deo reconciliandos ac salvandos, sponte suscepit, & secundum utramque naturam, solus peregit & peragit. Nam, unus est Deus, unus & Mediator Dei & hominum, Christus Jesus, qui dedit se ipsum redemptionis pretium pro omnibus, 1. Tim. II.5.6. Filius hominis venit non ut sibi ministraretur, sed ut ipse ministraret, & animam suam pretium redemptionis pro multis ponere; Matth. XX.28. Neque in alio ullo est salus. Neque aliud nomen sub cœlo datum est in hominibus; per quod servari nos oportet, Act. IV.12. Quod convenit promissioni Divinæ: Et erit אדיר Dux, Heros ejus ex ipso, ומשלו & domi-
units.tr: II. Therefore Jesus Christ came into the world, died, and was exalted to the right hand of God, so that, by the office of Savior and Mediator undertaken between God and men, he might restore the glory of God, which had been too greatly injured by sin, and save sinners. That office is mediation between God and men [μεσιτεία]; that is, the function of the Mediator Jesus Christ, which he himself, according to the will of the Father and the anointing of the Holy Spirit, freely undertook for sinful men given to him, to reconcile and save them to God, and which he alone, according to both natures, performed and performs. For "there is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself a ransom for all" (1 Tim. 2:5–6). "The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many" (Matt. 20:28). Nor is there salvation in any other, nor is there another name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). This agrees with the divine promise: "And his leader [אדיר] shall be from himself, and his ruler shall come forth from his midst."

units.la: nator ejus ex ipsius medio exibit; והקרבתיו & faciam eum appropinquare ad me, & accedet ad me. Nam quis ille est ערב את לבו לגשת אלי qui in fidem suam recepit cor suum, ut ad me accedat? hoc est, qui peccator cùm sit, tamen cordi suo spondere possit, fore ut ad me, qui ignis consumens sum, accedat sine noxa sua, ut à me aliquid petat, vel aliquid tanquam gratum mihi offerat, sine sponsore alio? Jerem. XXX.21.
units.tr: nator ejus ex ipsius medio exibit; "and I will make him draw near to me, and he shall approach me." For who is he who has pledged his heart [ערב את לבו לגשת אלי] to come near to me? That is, who, though he is a sinner, could nevertheless stand surety for his own heart, that he might draw near to me, who am a consuming fire, without harm to himself, to ask something of me, or to offer me something as acceptable, without any other surety? (Jer. 30:21).

units.la: III. Officii hujus naturam intimam tum Nomina, quæ rerum notas Cicero dixit, tum res ipsa declarant. Nomina ejus, qui officium hoc gerit, multifaria sunt. Præcipua & διαφορώτερα nomina illa, ut innumera alia, inprimis Metaphorica, omittam, sunt Jesu, Christi, Mediatoris, Sponsoris, Testatoris, Vindicis, Principis salutis, &c. De posterioribus illis Loc. XI. §21. dicere occupavimus. De prioribus illis Jesu, Christi, & Mediatoris paucis etiam hoc dicendum.
units.tr: III. The inner nature of this office is declared both by the names, which Cicero called the marks of things, and by the thing itself. The names of the one who performs this office are many. I shall omit the chief and most distinctive names, as well as countless others, especially the metaphorical ones, such as Jesus, Christ, Mediator, Surety, Testator, Vindicator, Prince of salvation, and so on. About the latter names we have already undertaken to speak in Loc. XI, §21. About the former, namely Jesus, Christ, and Mediator, something must also be said briefly here.

units.la: IV. Nomen Personæ tantæ, quæ officium salvandi genus humanum in se suscepit ἰδιον & ἐξαίρετον est 'Ιησοῦς Jesus; ab ipso Angelo Gabriele nondum nato impositum. Pariet Maria Filium, & vocabis nomen ejus 'Ιησοῦν Jesum, Matth. I.21. Et vocatum est (in circumcisione) nomen ejus 'Ιησοῦς Jesus, quod vocatum est ab Angelo, priusquam in utero conciperetur, Luc. II.21. Hebraicum nomen est יהושוע Jehoschua, quod in libris Josuæ, Judicum, Samuelis & Regum extat; at postea scribi cœpit ישוע Jesua, literis ה & ו usu detritis. Ad manum ejus erant Eden, Minjamin וישוע & Jesua, 2. Paralip. XXXI. 15. Is ipse filius Nun, quem Moses יהושע Jehosuam vocat, Nehem. VIII. 17. ישוע Jesua appellatur. Et Jehosua Pontifex ille maximus, cum Judæis è Babylone Hierusalem redux, ab Haggæo cap. I.1. & Zach. III.1. &c. יהושע Jehoschua filius Josadak, apud Esdram verò cap. III.2.8. & Nehem. VIII.17. &c. ישוע Jesua filius Josadak insignitur. Tandem & ultima litera י paulatim & ipsa evanuit, & nomen ישוע & יהושע contractum est in nomen ישו Jesu, ex more Syrorum, qui literas ה & י elidunt, uti author Lexici Thalmudici, quod Baal Aruch inscribitur, notavit. Secuti hanc soni facilitatem Judæi Græca lingua usi, scripserunt 'Ιησᾶ, circumflexa ultima. Cùmque terminatio illa in sermone Græco inusitata esset, neque casuum variationem admitteret, facilioris constructionis gratia duo casus formati sunt, more Græcorum, rectus addito σ, & quartus addito ν. Sicut ergo dicitur ὁ Μανασσῆς, τὸν Μανασσῆν, ita quoque dictum est ὁ 'Ιησοῦς, τὸν 'Ιησοῦν. quomodo hoc nomen apud Græcos interpretes, Syracidem & Scriptores N.T. scribitur & declinatur. Nam Hebræum י ut & ה Græcis pronunciatu difficilima sunt; neque alii facilè id proferunt, nisi qui à pueritia didicerunt. Uti Abenezra apud Eliam Levitam notavit. Nomen isthoc 'Ιησῆς per compendium quidam scripserunt IHΣ cui scriptioni litera H majuscula, secunda in Græca scriptura IHΣOTΣ, & in characteribus majusculo eadem H Latinorum, occasionem dedit. Etiam Christiani veteres crebrò nomen Jesus per I & H Græcis literis I H scripserunt, & quidem subjecta litera T hoc modo I T H quæ tres literæ cùm numerum efficiant 318. (nam I decem H octo & T trecentos significat) mysterium venati sunt, quasi 318, vernæ Abrahami hostes suos debellantes crucis Christi typus extitisset. Hoc Prudentius Præfat. in Psychom. innuisse Drusio Quæst. Hebr. lib. II. q. 21. & Doctissimo Le Moine, amico, cùm in vivis esset, singulari, Var. Sacr. T.II. pag.77. &c. visus est.
units.tr: IV. The name of so great a Person, who took upon himself the office of saving the human race, is proper and unique: Jesus, imposed by the Angel Gabriel himself before he was born. "She shall bring forth a son, and you shall call his name Jesus" (Matt. 1:21). "And when eight days were completed for his circumcision, his name was called Jesus, which had been given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb" (Luke 2:21). The Hebrew name is Jehoshua [יהושוע], which occurs in the books of Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings; but later it began to be written Jeshua [ישוע], with the letters ה and ו worn away by use. Eden, Miniamin, and Jeshua were at his hand (2 Chron. 31:15). That same son of Nun, whom Moses calls Jehoshua [יהושע] (Neh. 8:17), is called Jeshua [ישוע]. And the high priest Jehoshua, when he returned from Babylon with the Jews to Jerusalem, is named in Haggai 1:1, Zechariah 3:1, and so on, Jehoshua the son of Jehozadak [יהושע בן יהוצדק]; but in Ezra 3:2, 8 and Nehemiah 8:17, and so on, he is designated Jeshua the son of Jozadak [ישוע בן יוצדק]. Finally, even the last letter י gradually disappeared, and the name ישוע and יהושע was contracted into the name ישו, Jesu, after the custom of the Syrians, who elide the letters ה and י, as the author of the Talmudic lexicon called Aruch has noted. The Jews, following this ease of sound and using the Greek language, wrote Ἰησᾶ, with the last syllable circumflexed. Since that ending was unusual in Greek speech and did not admit variation of cases, two cases were formed for the sake of easier construction, after the manner of the Greeks: the nominative with the addition of σ, and the accusative with the addition of ν. Just as one says ὁ Μανασσῆς, τὸν Μανασσῆν, so also one said ὁ Ἰησοῦς, τὸν Ἰησοῦν; in this way the name is written and declined among the Greek translators, Ben Sira, and the writers of the New Testament. For the Hebrew י and ה are most difficult for Greeks to pronounce, and others pronounce them easily only if they learned them from childhood, as Abenezra noted in Elias Levita. Some have written this name Ἰησῆς in abbreviation as IHΣ, and the capital H of the Latins gave occasion to this writing, IHΣOTΣ in Greek script. Also the early Christians often wrote the name Jesus with the Greek letters I H, and indeed with T added below, thus I T H; these three letters, since they make the number 318 (for I signifies ten, H eight, and T three hundred), they took as a mystery, as if the 318 servants of Abraham, defeating their enemies, had been a type of the cross of Christ. Prudentius seems to have hinted at this in Praefatio in Psychomachiam, as Drusius notes in Quaestiones Hebraicae lib. II, q. 21, and it seemed so to the most learned Le Moine, a friend of mine, while he was alive, in a notable way, in Variae Sacrae T. II, p. 77, and so on.

units.la: V. Qui ex veteribus nomen ′Ιησοῦς à Græco ἰάομαι sano deflexerunt, non notationem in animo habuisse, sed ingenii quodam lusu vocem Græcam quæsivisse, quæ Hebraicæ non sola significatione, sed sono etiam cohæreret, videntur; secuti morem Philonis, qui ita ad Græcas voces alludere amat, ut ab Hebræa notatione quàm minimùm recedat. Omnino enim vox Hebræa est, & יהושע (quod cum Græco ἰάομαι sanare, curare sono & significatu convenit) derivatur; quæ in Kal inusitata, in Hiphil הושיע σώζειν salvare, salvum præstare significat. הושיע salvavit Jehova unctum suum, Psal. XX.7. Ita Σωτῆρα Salvatorem notat, & quidem populi Dei & sui שׁ מ ἁμαρτιῶν à peccatis suis, uti ipse Angelus Matth. I. 21. perspicuè explicat. Olim quidem יהושע Jehosua, filius Nun σωτὴρ Salvator populi Israelis fuit. Ille cùm prius dictus esset הושע Hosea Salvator, nomen isthoc in יהושע Jehosuæ nomen mutavit Moses, quando servum hunc suum cum aliis undecim ad explorandam terram Canaan ablegavit, sive innuere voluit, Josuam hunc esse, de quo dici debeat: יהושע · Ille salvabit: sive, quæ Doctissimi Pearsoni Expos. in Symb. p.125. conjectura est, additum ′ indicium fuit nominis Divini י (nam litera ה in יהושע prima & in י ultima in una voce jungi non possunt, quin altera absorbeatur) perinde ac si dixisset Moses, Dei Salvator, seu à י Jah constitutus יהושע Salvator. Quod etiam Jesu Christo, qui σωτῆρα τοῦ Θεοῦ Salus Dei Luc.II.30. III.6. insignitur, aptari potest. Præter Josuam illum filium Nun, יהושע Jehosua ′Ιησοῦς nomen etiam alii, velut Beth-Semita 1. Sam. VI.14. præfectus urbis quidam, 2. Reg. XXIII.8. Sacerdos ille magnus Hagg.I. 1. filius Sirach & ejusdem avus; & in N.T. ille dictus justus, Col.IV.11. & Bar-Jesus, filius Jesu, magus famosus, Act. XIII.6. gesserunt. Sed rectè de talibus Bernhardus in Cant. Serm. 15. dixit: Habuit Judæa quosdam Jesus, quorum vacuis gloriatur vocabulis. Illa enim nec lucent, nec pascunt, nec medentur. Illi enim nomina vel vacua, vel saltem spirituali salute nulla prægnantia habuerunt. Nostèr verò Jesus est Servator populi sui à peccatis, qualis illorum nemo fuit, verus enim à peccatis Salvator idem Deus est, per quem gratia & veritas facta est. Nam Lex data est per Mosen: Gratia & Veritas (seu πλήρωμα plenitudo Gratiæ & Veritatis) per Jesum Christum facta est, Joh. I. 17. Esse ergo Jesum, Servatorem à peccatis, inter nomina Dei, & soli Deo reservata, est. Ego Jehova, & non est ultra Deus præter me. Deus justus יהוה & Salvator non est יהושע præter me, Esaj.XLV.21. hoc est, non tantum sine me nemo servat, sed præter me Servator nemo est. Ideo Deus dicit: Domus Jehuda miserebor ביהוה אלהיהם ורחשעתים & salvabo eos in Jehova Deo suo, Hos. I.7. Est enim veri nominis salvatio, qua sic homo salvatur, ut sublata maledictione ex peccato oriunda, & adducta justitia perfecta, nec corpore nec anima perire possit. quæ non est nisi à Deo, nonnisi in Deo, nonnisi per Deum; & uni soli que Jesu competit, qui consummatus obedientibus sibi omnibus, factus est causa æternæ salutis, Hebr. V.9. & ἀρχηγὸς σωτηρίας princeps, author salutis, ibid. II.10.
units.tr: V. Those among the ancients who derived the name Ἰησοῦς from the Greek ἰάομαι, to heal, seem not to have had etymology in mind, but to have sought, in a certain play of wit, a Greek word that agreed with the Hebrew not only in meaning but also in sound, following the custom of Philo, who loves to allude to Greek words in such a way that he departs as little as possible from the Hebrew derivation. For the word is altogether Hebrew, and is derived from יהושע (which agrees in sound and meaning with the Greek ἰάομαι, to heal or cure), a form that is not used in Qal, but in Hiphil means הושיע, σώζειν, to save, to make safe. "The LORD has saved [הושיע] his anointed" (Ps. 20:7). Thus it denotes the Savior [Σωτήρ], and indeed the Savior of his people [שׁ מ] from their sins [ἁμαρτιῶν], as the angel himself plainly explains in Matt. 1:21. Formerly indeed Jehoshua, son of Nun, was the savior [σωτήρ] of the people of Israel. When he was first called Hoshea, Salvation, Moses changed this name into the name Jehoshua, when he sent this servant of his with eleven others to explore the land of Canaan; or perhaps he wished to indicate that this was the one of whom it ought to be said: יהושע, "He will save." Or, as the most learned Pearson conjectures in Expositio in Symbolum, p. 125, the added ′ was an indication of the divine name י (for the letter ה cannot be joined to a final י in one word without one of them being absorbed), just as if Moses had said, a Savior of God, or Jehoshua, a Savior appointed by Jah. This may also be applied to Jesus Christ, who is called the Salvation of God [σωτήριον τοῦ Θεοῦ] (Luke 2:30; 3:6). Besides that Joshua, son of Nun, others also bore the name Jehoshua, Jesus: for example, a certain prefect of the city of Beth-Shemesh (1 Sam. 6:14), the high priest Jeshua, son of Jehozadak (Hag. 1:1), the son of Sirach and his grandfather of the same name, and in the New Testament the one called Justus (Col. 4:11), and Bar-Jesus, son of Jesus, a notorious magician (Acts 13:6). But Bernard rightly said of such men in In Cantica, Sermon 15: Judaea had certain Jesuses, in whose empty names it boasts. For these neither shine, nor feed, nor heal. For those men had names that were either empty, or at least pregnant with no spiritual salvation. But our Jesus is the Savior of his people from their sins, which none of those others was; for the true Savior from sins is the same God through whom grace and truth came. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth [that is, the fullness of grace and truth] came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). To be Jesus, the Savior from sins, therefore belongs among the names of God, and is reserved for God alone: I am the LORD, and there is no God besides me; a just God and a Savior, there is none besides me (Isa. 45:21). That is, not only does no one save without me, but there is no Savior apart from me. Therefore God says: I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them by the LORD their God (Hos. 1:7). For it is salvation in the true sense, by which a man is saved in such a way that, with the curse arising from sin removed and perfect righteousness brought in, he can perish neither in body nor in soul. This is not from anyone but God, not in anyone but God, not through anyone but God, and it belongs to Jesus alone, who, having been made perfect, became to all who obey him the cause of eternal salvation (Heb. 5:9), and the author [ἀρχηγός] of salvation (Heb. 2:10).

units.la: VI. Immanis proin & intolerandus eorum factus est, qui se Jesu sodales & Jesuitas jactant. Nam Christus quidem seu Unctus הבריח μέτοχοι consortes, sodales ejusdem unctionis participes, Psalm. XLV. 8. qui propterea & ipsi χρισταὶ Christiani, Act. XI.26. XXVI.28. 1.Pet.IV,16. dicuntur, habet. At Jesus typos licèt habuerit cognomines, socios tamen salvationis, à se solo præstitæ, nullos habet. Non est Salvator יולתי præter me, Esaj.XLV.21. Solus Judas Jesu ἑταῖρος socius, hoc est, אנוש כעריך homo ἑταῖρος, paris æstimationis, ab ipso Jesu appellatus est Matth. XXVI.50. (Psal.LV.14.) sed ironia, non proprietate vocis. Neque mirandus, detestandus licet, est ille ἁρπαγμὸς raptus nominis Jesu, cùm universa hominum illorum manifesta & secretiora instituta & fides non aliò tendant, quàm ad raptum & frustrationem gloriæ Jesu, & ad divisionem ejus, planè ut tales ἑταῖροι socii Jesu sint, qualis perditissimus Judas fuit; & quales illi sunt, qui Curios simulant & Bacchanalia vivunt. Adversus eos ipsa Sorbona decretum A.MDLIV. 1.Decemb. publicatum ejusmodi cudit: Hæc Societas videtur in negotio fidei periculosa, pacis Ecclesiastica perturbativa, Monastica religionis everstiva, & magis ad destructionem quàm ad ædificationem. Ipsa appellatio planè blasphema, schismatica, arrogans & irreligiosa est, quia vel solos sese Jesu discipulos, vel sibi solis collatam Jesu Domini gratiam & salutem, vel denique ejus in Divino munere ἑταῖροι socios se nequiter mentiuntur. Quantò rectius antesignani sui Lojolæ, quæ vox Hebraicè scripta (לילה) noct< urnum tenebrionem significat, sodalitium professi fuissent, cùm nihil cum Jesu commune habeant, non ad salvandum, sed ad destruendum orbem Christianum, adeóque non Jesu, sed Asmodæi sodales, novissimè venerint; quos pridem Spiritus S. hoc stigmate compunxit, quòd ex ore Draconis, Bestiæ, & Pseudoprophetæ, ceu spiritus immundi, similes ranis exiverint, & ceu πνεύματα δαιμονίων spiritus daemoniorum (ob astutiam, qua ceu δαίμονες, vel δαιμόνες scioli res suas mundanas artificiosè admodum & fallaciter componere norunt) proficiscantur ἐπὶ βασιλείας ad (vel potiùs in) Reges terræ & totius orbis habitabilis, ut eos congregent in prælium diei illius magnæ Dei omnipotentis, Apoc. XVI. 13. 14. Nam Spiritum S. verbis his sacerrimum hoc hominum genus, ejus nativitatem & molimina indigetasse, iis, qui vaticinium & institutà sectæ, missionis inprimis votum contenderint, ambiguum non erit.
units.tr: VI. Those who call themselves companions of Jesus and boast of being Jesuits have become monstrous and intolerable. Christ, that is the Anointed, has companions [הבריח] and partners [μέτοχοι], sharers in the same anointing (Psalm 45:8). For this reason they are also called Christians [χρισταὶ] (Acts 11:26, 26:28; 1 Pet. 4:16). But Jesus, although he had namesakes who were types of him, has no associates in the salvation wrought by himself alone: "There is no Saviour besides me" (Isa. 45:21). Judas alone was called a companion [ἑταῖρος] by Jesus himself, that is, a man [אנוש כעריך] of equal standing (Matt. 26:50; Ps. 55:14), but this was said with irony, not in the proper sense of the word. Nor is that robbery of the name of Jesus to be wondered at, detestable though it is, since all the open and secret arrangements and beliefs of those men aim at nothing else than the robbing and frustrating of Jesus' glory and its division. Their aim is that they may be such companions [ἑταῖροι] of Jesus as the most abandoned Judas was, and like those who feign the Curii and live Bacchanalian lives. Against them the Sorbonne itself issued a decree of this kind on 1 December 1554: "This Society appears dangerous in matters of faith, disturbing to ecclesiastical peace, destructive of monastic religion, and more for destruction than for building." The very name is plainly blasphemous, schismatic, arrogant and irreligious, because they falsely claim either that they alone are the disciples of Jesus, or that the grace and salvation of Jesus the Lord has been granted to them alone, or finally that they are his companions [ἑταῖροι] in his divine office. How much more rightly would they have professed the fellowship of their forerunner Loyola! The word, written in Hebrew (לילה), means a night-dweller, a gloomy one. For they have nothing in common with Jesus. They have come forth recently not to save but to destroy the Christian world, and so they are companions not of Jesus but of Asmodeus. The Holy Spirit long ago marked this people with a brand: they come forth from the mouth of the dragon, of the beast and of the false prophet, like unclean spirits like frogs, and as spirits of demons [πνεύματα δαιμονίων] (on account of the cunning by which, as demons or half-wise demons, they know how to arrange their worldly affairs very artfully and deceitfully). They set out to the kings of the earth and of the whole inhabited world (or rather, they go into them), to gather them into battle on the great day of God Almighty (Rev. 16:13–14). That the Holy Spirit in these words pointed out this most accursed race of men, its birth and its machinations, will not be doubtful to anyone who considers those who claim prophecy and the founding of the sect, and above all the vow of mission.

units.la: VII. Jesu, seu Salvatoris populi à peccatis ejus, vim omnem & potestatem Sociniani abnegant. negant. Ejusmodi enim Salvatorem fingunt, qui ne unius quidem hominis unicum pecca-tum proprie sustulerit & expiaverit. Neque id mirandum, cum semel iis placuerit, etiam Dei-tatem veram eidem abdicare. Nam qui verus Deus non est, nec verus Salvator populi a pecca-tis ejus esse potest. Coguntur ergo homines il-li eo descendere, ut Christum Jesum seu Salva-torem dici asserant, quia servat docendo, & viam justitiae per opera demonstrando: sic tamen ut operibus iis admixta sint peccata, & ea justitia ex operibus admixtam remissionem peccato-rum habeat. Sed nulla talis vel salvatio, vel a peccatis justificatio ex ore Dei unquam audita est, vel audiri potuit, quia justificatio & salvatio ex operibus cum remissione peccatorum plane ἀποτ est. Una enim ex operibus justifica-tio est, ex formula Legis: Qui fecerit haec homo, in iis vivet, Levit. XVIII. 5. Talis vero justifi-catio per se remissionem peccatorum excludit, quia eadem Lex, quae facienti, seu perfecte ob-servanti vitam addicit, etiam non facienti, transgredienti, & non in omnibus manenti maledi-ctionem comminatur & infligit, non remissio-nem promittit; utpote quae χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν sine miserationibus est, Hebr. X. 28. Tum si indi-care praecepta operum, ex quibus aliquis justifi-cetur, est σῴζειν salvare a peccatis, etiam Moses Jesus, seu Salvator fuit. Nam & ille facientem opera Legis justificari & salvari Levit. XVIII. 5. docuit. Sed tantum abest, ut is Salvator fue-rit, ut potius θάνατου minister mortis & condemnationis (. Cor. III. 7. 9.) fuerit; imo fassus fuerit, se indicando hanc justitiam Israeli maledictionem & mortem pro-posuisse. Testor adversus vos hodie Coelum & ter-ram, quod vitam & mortem, benedictionem & male-dictionem vobis proposui, Deut. XXX. 19. Nam quod Christum perfectiora Mosaicis praecepta docuisse regerunt, hilum non facimus; tum quia ea praecepta docuit, quae faciens per ea vi-vit: tum quia eam legem tulit, cui ipse Chri-stus subjectus obedivit, Matth. III. 15. V. 17. Gal. IV. 4. tum quia nullum praeceptum Chri-sti est, quod in Mose & Prophetis testimonium non habeat. Praeterea justitia, quae a Christo nobis donatur, efficit, ut τὸ δικαίωμα & νόμου jus legis, seu id, quod Lex ut justitiam, vitae cau-sam, exigit, in nobis impleretur, Rom. VIII. 4. Id vero non doctrina justitiae imperfectae cum remissione peccatorum conjuncta, sed legis per Christum impletio, & obedientia nobis donata efficit. At nec Jesus Salvator dici potest, quia primus vitae aeternae promissiones ediderit. Nam & veteres crediderunt, sperarunt, vitam aeternam adepti sunt. At licet Christus etiam docendo salvet, imo & Christi ministri docen-do se & alios salvent, 1. Tim. IV. 16. tamen ea salvatio per doctrinam, salutem per justitiam & obedientiam Christi partam supponit. Nam ex passionibus obedientiam didicit, & consumma-tus factus est omnibus ipsi obedientibus causa salu-tis aeternae, Hebr. V. 8. 9. Eam vero salutem & obedientiam Christus verbo & Spiritu suo do-cet, ejusque nos participes reddit.
units.tr: VII. The Socinians deny all power and authority to Jesus as the Saviour of his people from their sins. They invent a Saviour who has not truly removed and atoned for even the single sin of a single man. It is no wonder that, once they had taken this view, they also renounced his true divinity. For one who is not true God cannot be the true Saviour of his people from their sins. Those men are therefore forced to descend to the point of asserting that Christ is called Jesus or Saviour because he saves by teaching and by showing the way of righteousness through works, yet in such a way that sins are mixed in with those works, and that righteousness made up of works admixed with sins has the forgiveness of sins. But no such salvation, or justification from sins, has ever been heard from the mouth of God, or could be heard, because justification and salvation by works together with the forgiveness of sins are plainly contradictory. For justification by works is according to the formula of the Law: "The man who does these things shall live in them" (Lev. 18:5). Such justification by itself excludes the forgiveness of sins, because the same Law which promises life to the one who does, that is, who perfectly observes, threatens and inflicts a curse on the one who does not, who transgresses and does not remain in all things, and it does not promise forgiveness, since it is [a law] "without mercies" [χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν] (Heb. 10:28). Moreover, if to point out the precepts of works by which someone is justified is "to save from sins" [σῴζειν], then Moses also was a Jesus, or Saviour. For he too taught that the one who does the works of the Law is justified and saved (Lev. 18:5). But he was so far from being a Saviour that he was rather a "minister of death" [θάνατος] and of "condemnation" (2 Cor. 3:7, 9). Indeed he himself confessed that by pointing out this righteousness he had set before Israel curse and death: "I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse" (Deut. 30:19). As to their objection that Christ taught precepts more perfect than those of Moses, we make nothing of it. For first, he taught those precepts by which the one who does them lives; and second, he brought in that law to which Christ himself was subject and obeyed (Matt. 3:15; 5:17; Gal. 4:4); and third, there is no precept of Christ which does not have testimony in Moses and the Prophets. Moreover, the righteousness which is given to us by Christ brings it about that the "righteous requirement" [τὸ δικαίωμα] and "the right of the law" [νόμου], that is, what the Law demands as righteousness, the cause of life, "might be fulfilled in us" (Rom. 8:4). This is effected not by a doctrine of imperfect righteousness joined with the forgiveness of sins, but by the fulfilling of the Law through Christ and by the obedience given to us. Nor can Jesus be called Saviour because he was the first to publish the promises of eternal life. For the men of old also believed, hoped, and obtained eternal life. Yet although Christ saves even by teaching, and indeed Christ's ministers save themselves and others by teaching (1 Tim. 4:16), that salvation through teaching presupposes salvation obtained through the righteousness and obedience of Christ. For "he learned obedience from the things he suffered," and "being made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him" (Heb. 5:8–9). Christ teaches that salvation and that obedience by his word and Spirit, and makes us partakers of it.

units.la: VIII. Illi quoque Jesum Salvatorem ab-negant, qui salutem ab alio quam ab ipso expe-ctant. Cujus culpae manifeste rei sunt Ponti-
units.tr: VIII. Those too deny Jesus as Saviour who expect salvation from another than himself. The Papists are manifestly guilty of this fault,

units.la: ficii, qui γνώσις Salvatoris actus, redemptio-nem, intercessionem, satisfactionem, meritum, non sine raptu nominis Jesu horrendo creaturis vindicant, & in raptu eo proram & puppim re-ligionis suae collocant. Atqui Jesus vel verus Salvator a peccatis non est; vel perfectus & so-lus Salvator est, neminemque adeo in partes procurandae salutis ascisci, quia Deus esse, & indissolubilem vitae potentiam habere debet, & frater (ἀδελφός nudus) fratrem redimere, & Deo pretium redemptionis ejus solvere non potest, quia pretiosa nimis est redemptio animai-psorum, ut in seculum (a redemptione tali prae-itanda) desinere debeat, Psal. XLIX. 8. 9. & Sal-vator noster fieri debet dominus noster, cui nos confidere, gratias agere, in quo gloriari, quem glorificare, & ad quem, ceu finem nostrum nos esse convenit. Ideo Petra (Jesu) perfectum est opus, & omnes viae ejus judici-um sunt, Deut. XXXII. 4. Qui nominaverit no-men Jehovae (Jehovam Salvatorem suum esse crediderit, & professus fuerit, seque ei ut Sal-vatori suo tradiderit, atque ita in vera fide eum invocaverit) salvabitur. Joel. II. 32. In nullo e-nim alio est salus; & nullum aliud Nomen sub coe-lo in hominibus datum est, in quo oporteat salvari, (quem Salvatorem cum fide & gratiarum ac-tione agnoscere possimus) quam Jesu Christi, Act. IV. 12. Qui si salutem integram non prae-stitisset, ne quidem Salvator appellari posset. Impossibile quin etiam est, ut partem salutis Deus a creatura expectari velit, quia sic gloriam suam creaturae communicaret. quod fieri ne-quit. Ego Jehova; hoc nomen meum est, & glo-riam meam non dabo alteri, Esaj. XLII. 8. Cum-que in salute omnia, quae ad liberationem a pec-cato, & ad aeternam beatitudinem pertinent, contineantur, qui a peccatis liberat, & aeternum beat, verus perfectus, unicus Salvator sit opor-tet. Praeterea nec δικαίωμα Christi, aeterna sa-lutis causa, imperfectum esse potest, quia Chri-stus & omnem justitiam implevit, Matth. III. 15. & ab execratione Legis nos redemit, factus pro no-bis execratio, Gal. III. 13. Accedit, quod iis, qui in partes salutis hominibus procurandae vocan-tur, nefarie attribuitur tum ἀξία dignitas Deitatis, siquidem peccatorum remis-sionem & beatitudinem nobis meruisse statu-untur: tum Divina potentia, siquidem homi-num salvator eosdem ex morte spirituali vivi-ficare debet. Neque illud obstat, quod etiam fides, baptismus, praecones verbi, oratio fidelis σῴζειν salvare dicuntur, Marc. XVI. 16. 1. Tim. IV. 16. Jac. V. 15. 1. Pet. III. 21. & Evangelium est po-tentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I. 16. Non enim sic vel fides, vel opera hominis qua-liacunque, vel dignitas hominis causa salutis, sed illae res salutares propter causam salutis sta-tuuntur. Fides enim Christo, causae salutis, (Hebr. V. 9.) & Principi salutis (ibid. II. 10.) nos conjungit, ut in ipso sumus, vivamus; & ab ipso etiam merito Christi unice pendet. Labor prae-conum salutis, & ipsum Evangelium salvat, qua-tenus salutem omnem in Jesu solo ostendunt; & Spiritus S. per verbum auditum audientes convertit ad Christum, & in fide Christi confir-mat. Oratio fidelis salvat ut signum Spiritus, qui spiritus precum est, & fidei erga Christum. DeniDenique & Baptismus salvat, ut sigillum interrogationis conscientiæ bonæ in Deum. Hæc omnia sic salvant, hoc est, saluti per solum Jesum partæ sic ministrant, ut tamen salutem obediendo, Legis jus implendo, reconciliando, Deum placando, justitiam & vitam promovendo neutiquam procurent.
units.tr: who, not without a horrible seizure of the name of Jesus, ascribe to creatures the work of the Saviour: redemption, intercession, satisfaction and merit. In that seizure they place the prow and the stern of their religion. But either Jesus is not a true Saviour from sins, or he is the perfect and only Saviour, and so no one is to be admitted as a partner in procuring salvation. For God must be God and have an indissoluble power of life. A brother cannot redeem a brother, nor can he give God the price of redemption, "because the redemption of their souls is precious, and it must cease for ever" (if such redemption were to be provided), Ps. 49:8–9. Our Saviour must also become our Lord, in whom we trust, for whom we give thanks, in whom we glory, whom we glorify, and to whom it is fitting that we be directed as our end. Therefore "the Rock, his work is perfect, and all his ways are judgment" (Deut. 32:4). "Whoever calls on the name of Jehovah," that is, whoever believes and professes that Jehovah is his Saviour, and has given himself to him as his Saviour, and so has called upon him in true faith, "shall be saved" (Joel 2:32). "For there is salvation in no other, nor is there any other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (which name we can acknowledge as Saviour with faith and thanksgiving), "than the name of Jesus Christ" (Acts 4:12). If he had not provided full salvation, he could not even be called Saviour. Moreover, it is impossible that God should wish a part of salvation to be expected from a creature, since in that way he would communicate his glory to a creature, which cannot be done: "I am Jehovah; this is my name, and I will not give my glory to another" (Isa. 42:8). Since all things that pertain to deliverance from sin and to eternal blessedness are contained in salvation, the one who delivers from sins and blesses eternally must be the true, perfect and only Saviour. Furthermore, the righteousness of Christ, the cause of eternal salvation, cannot be imperfect, since Christ has fulfilled all righteousness (Matt. 3:15) and has redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us (Gal. 3:13). Add to this that to those who are called to take a part in procuring salvation for men there is wickedly attributed both the dignity of the Deity, since they are said to have merited for us the forgiveness of sins and blessedness, and divine power, since the saviour of men must quicken them from spiritual death. Nor does it stand in the way that faith, baptism, the heralds of the word, and the prayer of the faithful are also said to "save" [σῴζειν] (Mark 16:16; 1 Tim. 4:16; Jas. 5:15; 1 Pet. 3:21), and that "the gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes" (Rom. 1:16). For neither faith nor any works of man, nor the dignity of man, is set up as the cause of salvation in this way. Rather, those things are set up as saving because of the cause of salvation. For faith joins us to Christ, the "cause of salvation" (Heb. 5:9) and the "Prince of salvation" (Heb. 2:10), so that we are in him and live, and it depends solely on his merit. The labour of the heralds of salvation, and the gospel itself, saves insofar as they show all salvation in Jesus alone. The Holy Spirit, through the word heard, converts hearers to Christ and confirms them in faith in Christ. The prayer of the faithful saves as a sign of the Spirit, who is the Spirit of prayers, and of faith towards Christ. Finally, baptism saves as the seal of the appeal of a good conscience towards God.
