All these things save in this way, that is, they minister to the salvation obtained through Jesus alone, but they in no way bring about salvation by obeying, by fulfilling the right of the Law, by reconciling, by appeasing God, or by promoting righteousness and life.

units.la: IX. Jesum ad salvationem à peccatis à Deo προεχειροτονηθὲν ante designari, (Act. X.41.) ordinari Deus voluit. Quæ designatio, ordinatio unctionis rationem habuit. Sicut Græci, qui luctatores ungebant ad certamen ἀλείφειν ungere dicebant, pro imponere munus. Inde eiognomen משיח Messiæ, seu Χριστὸς Christi, Unctì impositum etiam est. In universum unctio vel lætitiam quandam & honorem, vel officium contulit. Lætitiæ collatæ exempla sunt Psalm. XXIII.5. Impinguasti oleo caput meum, & CXLI.5. Increpet me justus; erit instar olei capiti meo. Honoris symbolum erat unctio cadaverum, Joh. XI.2. XII.3. Muneris collati vestigia sunt in hominibus gradus celsioris. Ita enim olim Prophetæ, Sacerdotes & Reges ungebantur. De Sacerdotibus & Regibus res nota est. Ita enim הכהן המשיח Sacerdos unctus Levit. IV.3. dicitur. Et David de se: Ego hodie ך ומשיח מלך tener & unctus Rex, 2. Sam. III.39. Idem de Saule משיח יהוה הוא Messias, Unctus Domini hic, 1. Sam. XXIV.7. Etiam Elias Elisæum ungere לנביא in Prophetam jussus, non legitur quidem eum oleo perfudisse, (quanquam forte perfudit) sed pallium suum in eum injecisse; quod unctionis etiam, seu ordinationis ad munus Prophetæ speciem quandam habuit, 1. Reg. XIX.16. Ad Prophetas etiam nonnulli illud משיחי Unctorum Dei nomen, Psal. CV.15. reflexerunt, conferentes historiam Genes. XX.7. Ubi Deus Abrahamum, qui inter unctos illos Psal. CV.9. refertur, נביא Prophetam insignit.
units.tr: IX. God willed that Jesus be designated and ordained beforehand for salvation from sins, having been προεχειροτονηθὲν [procheirotonēthen] (Acts 10:41). This designation and ordination took the form of anointing. The Greeks, who anointed wrestlers for the contest, called this ἀλείφειν [aleiphein], "to anoint," though they meant the imposing of an office. Hence the title משיח [Messiah], or Χριστὸς [Christos], "Christ," was also given to the Anointed One. In general, anointing conferred either a certain joy and honour, or an office. Examples of joy conferred are Psalm 23:5, "You anointed my head with oil," and Psalm 141:5, "Let the righteous strike me; it shall be like oil upon my head." Anointing was a sign of honour in the anointing of corpses, John 11:2; 12:3. Traces of an office conferred are found in men of higher rank. For in this way prophets, priests and kings were anointed of old. The facts about priests and kings are well known. Thus the priest is called הכהן המשיח [the anointed priest], Lev. 4:3. David said of himself, "I am today a tender and anointed king" (ומשיח מלך), 2 Sam. 3:39. Of Saul the same is said: משיח יהוה הוא [he is the Messiah, the Lord's anointed], 1 Sam. 24:7. Elijah too was ordered to anoint Elisha לנביא [as prophet], and it is not read that he poured oil on him (though perhaps he did), but that he cast his mantle over him. This too had a certain appearance of anointing, or ordination to the office of prophet, 1 Kings 19:16. Some have also referred the name משיחי [my anointed ones], Ps. 105:15, to the prophets, comparing the history in Gen. 20:7, where God marks Abraham, who is counted among those anointed (Ps. 105:9), as a prophet, נביא [nabi].

units.la: X. Sed Christi, seu משיח Uncti hoc nomen ἴδιος & ἀντωνομαστικῶς Jesu convenit, ceu ὄνομα διαφορώτερον Nomen præstantius (Hebr. I.4.) & ea significatus cum emphasi, qua nemini aliii competit. Ideo jam in V.T. hoc nomine inclaruit. Prima Hanna, Samuelis mater, in Cantico suo exultabunda nomen hoc cievit; Jehova, inquiens, judicabit fines terræ, & dabit robur Regi suo, משיחו קרן וירם & exaltabit cornu Messiæ sui, 1. Sam. II.10. Quam Prophetiam Christo quadrare satis illud arguit, quòd eo tempore Rex in Israele non fuit; & Saul Rex factus miserè periit; David verò morti vicinus declaravit, quòd beneplacitum suum omne in eo sit, quòd domus sua germinatura non sit, 2. Sam. XXIII.5. & nec in Saule, nec in Davide salus fuit; & denique Deus ipse non Davidem cornu hoc facit, sed Davidi germinaturum cornu promittit. Ibi faciam germinare cornu Davidi; instruxi lucernam למשיחי Unctio, Christo meo, Psal. CXXXII.17. Etiam Uncti & Unctionis hujus alibi mentio est. Consilium ceperunt adversus Jehovam ומשיחו & Unctum ejus, ibid. II.2. משוח Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo justitiæ, ibid. XLV.8. Spiritus Domini fuit super me יען משה אותי quia unxit me Jehova ad annuntiandum mansuetis, Esaj. LXI.1. Sapientia de se: מעולם נסכתי à seculo uncta sum. Prov. VIII.
units.tr: X. But the name Christ, or משיח [Messiah], the Anointed, belongs peculiarly and by way of pre-eminence to Jesus, as a name more excellent (Heb. 1:4), and it carries this meaning with an emphasis that belongs to no one else. Therefore this name was already famous in the Old Testament. First Hannah, the mother of Samuel, exulting in her song, invoked this name: "Jehovah," she says, "will judge the ends of the earth, and will give strength to his king, and will exalt the horn of his Messiah" (משיחו), 1 Sam. 2:10. That this prophecy fits Christ well is shown by the fact that at that time there was no king in Israel; Saul, when made king, perished miserably; and David, near to death, declared that all his delight lay in this, that his house would not sprout (2 Sam. 23:5). Neither in Saul nor in David was there salvation. Finally, God himself does not make David this horn, but promises that a horn will sprout for David: "There I will make a horn to sprout for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed" (למשיחי), Ps. 132:17. The Anointed and this anointing are also mentioned elsewhere: "They took counsel against Jehovah and against his anointed" (ומשיחו), Ps. 2:2; "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of justice," Ps. 45:8; "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because Jehovah has anointed me" (משחני) "to announce good news to the meek," Isa. 61:1. Wisdom says of herself: "From of old I have been anointed" (מעולם נסכתי), Prov. 8:23.

units.la: 23. Et Daniel de eodem: Post septimanas sexaginta duas משיח יכרת excindetur Messias, Dan. IX.26. Ex hoc potissimum Danielis, uti videtur, loco Nomen Messiæ ei tributum, qui populi Salvator promissus, Hebræis & aliis etiam familiare fuit. Nam in Paraphrasibus Chaldaicis plusquam septuaginta locis legitur Nomen משיח quod Interpretes illi posuerunt, quoties promitti Servatorem & Liberatorem populi suspicarentur. Loca omnia magno studio & industria Buxtorfius Lex. Thalm. p. 1269. &c. collegit. Etiam in sacris Novi Fœderis tabulis vestigia occurrunt, ex quibus eo tempore vulgare & cunctis notum hoc vocabulum fuisse liquet. Sic enim Andreas Simoni dixit: εὑρήκαμεν τὸν Μεσσίαν invenimus Messiam, Joh. I.42. Nam Μεσσίας Græci dixerunt, quem Hebræi משיח expresso ּ per ער, & ultima litera ה pronunciatu difficili in ς mutata, quod in peregrinis vocibus aliàs etiam usitatum est. Et Græcorum more etiam Latinis משיח Messias appellatur. Ad Samaritanos etiam propagatum esse Messiæ Nomen, mulier Samaritana ostendit, dicens: Scio, quòd Μεσσίας venit, ibid. IV.25. Idem Hebræi Græcè loquentes non tam Messiam, quàm Χριστὸν Christum appellarunt. Licèt enim Græci olim Χριστὸν non Unctum, sed id, quo quis ungebatur, vocaverint; tamen Interpretes LXX. Χριστὸν ubique pro Unctio usurparunt; atque iis Χριστὸς idem est, quod χρισθεὶς vel χεχρισμένος, Unde Suidas: Χριστὸς, ὁ χεχρισμένος ἐν ἐλαίῳ Christus, qui unctus est oleo. Etiam Johannes haud aliter mulieris Samaritanæ verba exponit: Οἶδα ὅτι Μεσσίας ἔρχεται, ὁ λεγόμενος Χριστός. Novi, quòd Messias venit, qui dicitur Christus, ibid. Nam quòd Justinus Martyr Apol. I. Χριστὸν dictum ait, quia Deus per eum cuncta ἐκτισε καὶ ἐκόσμησε condidit & exornavit, dilutum nimis est; quia aliud est χρίειν ungere. Ergo Χριστὸς in Græcorum lingua tam tritum evasit, quàm משיח in Hebraica, ad diu promissum Servatorem significandum. Unde Angelus: Σωτὴρ, ὅς ἐστι Χριστὸς Κύριος. Servator, qui est Christus Dominus, Luc. II.11. Neque ii tantùm, qui Jesum summo amore & studio prosecuti sunt, sed inimici etiam ejus eo nomine ipsum insigniverunt. Velut Pilatus dicens: Quem vultis dimittam vobis, Barraban, an Jesum, τὸν λεγόμενον Χριστὸν, qui dicitur Christus, Matth. XXVII.17.22? Etiam Ethnicis hoc nomen innotuit, & sic quidem, ut vix cognito nomine Jesu, agnomen Christi in usum nominis transierit. Ita enim Tacitus A. XV.44. Auctor nominis ejus Christus, qui, Tiberio imperitante, per Procuratorem Pontium Pilatum supplicio affectus erat. Lampridius in Alexandro Severo cap. 29. Imperatorem eum in lararío suo Divos principes, optimos electos, & animas sanctiores, Apollonium, Christum, Abrahamum & Orpheum habuisse, scribit; & cap. 41. eundem Christo Templum facere, eúmque inter Deos recipere voluisse, narrat. Sed ii ipsi gentiles eximium hoc Jesu nomen, mutata litera in Chrestum transformarunt, quasi à Χρηστὸς quod benignum, suavem notat, originem nomen ilthoc duxisset, quod Pithoeus Adv. lib. II.3. Patrum testimoniis allegatis ostendit, & ex Suetonio in Claud. cap. 25. liquet; per inscitiam, an contumeliam, quia iidem dem Gentiles Χρηστολόγον Chrestologum appella-runt, qui bene loqueretur, & male faceret, uti Le-vinus Torrentius ad Sueton. l. c. docet, ita Je-sum appellaverint, in incerto est. Sed de no-mine eo satis.
units.tr: Daniel says the same of the same: "After sixty-two weeks the Messiah (משיח) shall be cut off," Dan. 9:26. It seems that the name Messiah, as Saviour promised to the people, was given to him chiefly from this passage of Daniel, and it became familiar to the Hebrews and to others too. For in the Chaldee paraphrases the name משיח [Messiah] is read in more than seventy places, which those interpreters put in wherever they suspected that a Saviour and Deliverer of the people was promised. Buxtorf, Lex. Talm. p. 1269 and following, collected all these places with great zeal and diligence. Traces also occur in the sacred books of the New Testament, from which it is clear that this word was then in common use and known to all. So Andrew said to Simon, "We have found the Messiah" (εὑρήκαμεν τὸν Μεσσίαν) [heurēkamen ton Messian], John 1:42. The Greeks called him Μεσσίας [Messias], which the Hebrews write as משיח [Messiah], the vowel being marked by a point and the final letter ה changed into ς, as the difficult pronunciation required, a practice otherwise common in foreign words. After the Greek manner, Messias is also called Messias by Latin writers. That the name Messiah had spread even to the Samaritans is shown by the Samaritan woman, who says, "I know that Messias comes" (John 4:25). Hebrews who spoke Greek called him not so much Messiah as Χριστὸν [Christon], Christ. For although the Greeks formerly used χριστὸν not of the anointed but of that with which someone was anointed, nevertheless the Seventy everywhere used Χριστὸν for the Anointed. To them Χριστὸς means the same as χρισθεὶς or χεχρισμένος [anointed]. Hence Suidas: "Christ, he who has been anointed with oil." John likewise explains the words of the Samaritan woman in the same way: "I know that Messias comes, who is called Christ" (Οἶδα ὅτι Μεσσίας ἔρχεται, ὁ λεγόμενος Χριστός), ibid. As for Justin Martyr, who says in Apol. I that Christ was so called because God through him created and adorned all things (ἐκτισε καὶ ἐκόσμησε), that is too feeble, since χρίειν means to anoint. So Χριστὸς became as common in the Greek language as משיח in Hebrew, to signify the Saviour long promised. Hence the angel: "a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord" (Σωτὴρ, ὅς ἐστι Χριστὸς Κύριος), Luke 2:11. Nor did only those who followed Jesus with the greatest love and zeal call him by this name; his enemies too marked him with it. So Pilate says, "Whom do you wish me to release for you, Barabbas or Jesus, the one called Christ (τὸν λεγόμενον Χριστὸν)?" Matt. 27:17, 22. The name was known even to Gentiles, and so much so that, the name Jesus being scarcely known, the surname Christ passed into use as his name. Thus Tacitus, Ann. XV.44: "the author of this name, Christus, who under the reign of Tiberius had been put to death by the procurator Pontius Pilate." Lampridius, in the life of Alexander Severus, ch. 29, writes that the emperor kept in his lararium the deified princes, the best and chosen, and holier souls: Apollonius, Christ, Abraham and Orpheus. In ch. 41 he relates that the emperor wished to build a temple to Christ and to receive him among the gods. But these same Gentiles changed the letter in this excellent name Jesus and made it Chrestus, as if the name derived its origin from χρηστὸς, which means kind and pleasant, as Pithoeus shows in Adv. II.3, citing the testimonies of the Fathers, and as is clear from Suetonius, Claud. ch. 25. Whether through ignorance or contumely is uncertain, since the same Gentiles called a Chrestologus one who speaks well, and does ill, as Levinus Torrentius teaches ad Suet. l.c., and so they called Jesus by this name. But enough on that name.

units.la: XI. Jesum oleo externo unctum & deli-butum esse, non constat. Sed unctus tamen est unctione spirituali, & excellentiore longè, quae in impositione officii omnium praestantissimi & vere Divini, cum summo honore, incitatio-ne ad defungendum officio eo alacriter, colla-tione charismatum, & demonstratione pote-statis ei datae, consistit. Triplex enim illa un-ctio est, aeterna destinatio ad officium: tempo-ralis inhabitatio Deitatis in carne, & collatio charismatum ad officium exequendum; deni-que temporalis demonstratio personae in carne habitantis; nec non Regiae potestatis eidem da-tae. De prima Unctione sic Sapientia loquitur, מָשִׁיחַ מִקֶּדֶם נִסַּכְתִּי מֵרֹאשׁ מֵעוֹלָם מֵאָז ... à seculo uncta sum à capite (initio) & primis terrae, Prov.VIII.23. Ubi Unctio per metonymiam est αἰωνιότητα, aeterna desi-gnatio Filii haeredis omnium facta velut in con-sistorio Trinitatis; quo Filius, aeterna Dei Sa-pientia, ante jacta mundi fundamenta destina-tus ad hoc est, ut officium salvandi homines in tempore susciperet. Cui Unctioni sponsio aeter-na & postulatio haereditatis respondet. Huic succedit secunda Unctio in tempore, & diebus carnis factae, per inhabitationem Deitatis in car-ne, & collationem charismatum, ad exequen-dum officium necessariorum, carni factam. Nam & haec unctionis adinstar est. Spiritus Do-mini Jehovae super me (plenitudo Deitatis tota in me corporaliter habitat) רוּחַ אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה עָלָי quia (vel ideo) unxit me Dominus ad annuntian-dum Evangelium mansuetis, Esaj.LXI.1. Super quo Spiritus Domini est, super eo unguenti in-star pretiosissimi effunditur; juxta illud spon-sae: juxta odorem unguentorum tuorum bonum o-lei instar effunderis nomine tuo, Cant.I.3. Christus enim in carne apparens talis & tantus apparuit, qualem & quantum eum fore Sancti Dei ho-mines per Spiritum ejus loquentes praedixerunt, atque ille nominibus suis omnibus ἀπεσταλμένος appellari & manifestari potuit. sicut o-leum ex alabastro fracto effusum sua εὐωδία bona fragrantia totam domum replet, & eidem virtutem suam testatur. Unctio haec Christi in carne manifestati tum intus, tum foris specta-tur. Intus in testificatione Spiritus S. interna ad conscientiam Christi hominis; qua accedente ad verbum Propheticum lectum, & vocem Dei Patris è Coelo auditam vocatio Hominis Chri-sti à Deo Patre ad officium, juxta Hebr.V.1. constat; connexam habens infusionem dono-rum Spiritus S. uberrimam, per quam κατ' ἐξοχὴν à Spiritu S. unctus dicitur; & sine qua vo-catio illa dicta in solidum non constat; Requi-escet super eum Spiritus Jehovae: Spiritus sapien-tiae & intelligentiae, spiritus consilii & roboris, scien-tiae & timoris Jehovae; & odorari faciet cum ti-more Jehovae, &c. Esaj.XI.2.3. Quae Spiritus S. unctio in Christi incarnatione in utero Virginis conceptione & animae ejus nova creatione, in perfecta justitia & sanctitate coepit: αὐξανω vero suam succeffivo incremento & profectu in sapientia, statura, gratia apud Deum & homi-nes habuit, donec ad functionem muneris publi-cam anno circiter XXX. aetatis Luc.II.52. ac-cessit; quando ipsi in Jordane baptizato visi-bili descensu Spiritus S. in specie columbae, & mansione supra ipsum (Matth.III.16.17.Joh. I.32.33.34.) juxta verbum Patris & Sacramen-tum Baptismi obsignata est. Unctio proin illa facta est per collatam à λόγῳ inhabitante pleni-tudinem gratiae & donorum, qualis ad mune-ris Prophetici veritatem infallibilem, victimae humanae sanctitatem ἀναμάρτητον, & Regiam spiritualium donorum distributionem necessa-ria fuit. Foris Unctio haec spectabatur in testi-monio Patris, quo is Christo, ut vocato à se, a-deóque unctio Salvatori applausit. Quod fuit vel mediatum per Angelos, Luc.I.28. II.13. vel immediatum ipsius Patris, ter editum, semel in Baptismo ad Jordanem, Matth.III.17. iterum in monte sancto, ubi transfiguratus est, Matth.XVII.f. 2.Pet.I.17. demum instante passione, Joh.XII.28. Tertia Unctio est illa in tempore etiam, sed non in diebus carnis, verum in Coelo facta, per demonstrationem Filii Dei in carne habitantis, ex collata eidem gloriosa dignitate & potestate Regia. Jesum ex Nazareth ἔχρισεν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεὸς unxit eum Deus in Spiritu (post ascensionem in Coelum operante per prae-dicationem, & illustri modo effusso, ut Spiritu Christi à quo impetratus est, in Apostolos & discipulos ejus, nec non ut Spiritu filiationis per fidem Evangelii dato, Gal.III.14.) & δυνάμει potentia Divinitatis, seu operibus Divinis, quae propria voluntate patravit; Act.X.38. Nam Deus Pater datione ea Spiritus S. & potentia Di-vina Jesum demonstravit Regem, Sacerdotem & Prophetam verba Dei loquentem, sive Κύριον πάντων Dominum omnium, ibid.v.36. non tan-tum quia omnia, quae Patris sunt, etiam Filii sunt, propter unitatem essentiae & operationis; sed etiam, quia Pater ipsi omnia in manum tra-didit, ut morte pro Ecclesia obita illam ut hae-reditatem jure redemtionis haberet, & omnibus dominaretur. Quod S.Petrus ibid.II.36.sic ex-pressit: Κύριον καὶ Χριστὸν Dominum & Christum (Unctum) eum Deus fecit, hoc est, demonstravit eum Dominum gloriae, cui Regnum debetur, & Christum Filium Dei in carne manifestatum, Prophetam, Sacerdotem & Regem; atque sic eum compotem sui dominii & officiorum suo-rum patratorem in plenissima operatione esse voluit. Et ante S. Petrum ipse Deus Pater: מָשַׁחְתִּי מַלְכִּי Unxi Regem meum super Sion mon-tem sanctitatis meae, Psal.II.6. Propterea unxit te Deus; Deus tuus, שֶׁמֶן שָׂשׂוֹן oleo laetitiae (qualis in Rege glorioso est) prae consortibus tuis, ibid. XLV.8. Unctionis hujus geminae posterioris alterius in terra, alterius in Coelo peractae, ty-pum David gessit, qui prius, vivente adhuc Sau-le, unctus, privatus aliquantisper vixit, & ad pa-scendas oves patris reversus est, 1.Sam.XVI. 13. Post mortem vero Saulis in Hebron Rex Judae unctus est, 2.Sam.II.4. ac demum Israe-lis universi Rex unctus, eadem unctione pera-cta arcem Sionis occupavit, ibid.V.3. Qua postrema unctione Davidis unctionis Chri-sti in coelesti coronatione colophonem figu-ratum esse, oracula Prophetica Davidis, & ma-xime dictum illud S. Petri: Sciat tota domus Israel, Israel, quòd hunc Dominum & Christum Deus fecit, Act.II.36. comparantibus liquet.
units.tr: XI. It is not established that Jesus was anointed with external oil and smeared with it. But he was anointed with a spiritual anointing, and a far more excellent one, which consists in the bestowal of the most excellent and truly divine office, with the highest honour, the incitement to discharge that office eagerly, the conferral of gifts, and the demonstration of the power given to him. For this threefold anointing consists of: the eternal designation to the office; the temporal indwelling of the Deity in the flesh, and the conferral of gifts for carrying out the office; and finally the temporal demonstration of the person dwelling in the flesh, together with the royal power given to him. Concerning the first anointing, Wisdom speaks thus: "The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his way, before his works of old. I was anointed from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was" [מָשִׁיחַ מִקֶּדֶם נִסַּכְתִּי מֵרֹאשׁ מֵעוֹלָם מֵאָז] Prov. 8.23. Here the anointing is, by metonymy, the eternal designation (αἰωνιότης) of the Son, the heir of all things, made as it were in the council of the Trinity; by which the Son, the eternal Wisdom of God, was destined before the foundations of the world were laid to undertake the office of saving men in time. To this anointing corresponds the eternal promise and the claim to the inheritance. Next follows the second anointing, in time and in the days of the flesh, made by the indwelling of the Deity in the flesh and by the conferral of gifts needed for carrying out the office, given to the flesh. For this too is in the manner of an anointing: "The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me" [רוּחַ אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה עָלָי] (the whole fullness of the Deity dwells bodily in me), "because (or therefore) the Lord has anointed me to preach good tidings to the meek", Isa. 61.1. Upon him on whom the Spirit of the Lord rests, the precious ointment is poured out like oil; according to the bride's words: "Because of the savour of your good ointments your name is as ointment poured forth", Song 1.3. For Christ, appearing in the flesh, appeared such and so great as the holy men of God, speaking through his Spirit, had foretold he would be, and he could be called and made manifest by all his names as the one sent (ἀπεσταλμένος). Like oil poured out of a broken alabaster box, his good fragrance (εὐωδία) fills the whole house and bears witness to his power. This anointing of Christ manifested in the flesh is seen both inwardly and outwardly. Inwardly, in the inward witness of the Holy Spirit to the conscience of the man Christ; when, to the prophetic word read and the voice of God the Father heard from heaven, is added the calling of the man Christ by God the Father to the office, according to Heb. 5.1. This is joined with the most abundant infusion of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which he is called, above all, the one anointed by the Holy Spirit; and without which that calling cannot be considered complete. "The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord; and he shall make him quick of understanding in the fear of the Lord", etc., Isa. 11.2.3. This anointing of the Holy Spirit began in the incarnation of Christ, in his conception in the Virgin's womb and the new creation of his soul, in perfect righteousness and holiness; but it grew by successive increase and progress in wisdom, stature, and grace with God and men, until he came to the public discharge of his office at about thirty years of age, Luke 2.52. Then, when he was baptized in the Jordan, the anointing was sealed by the visible descent of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, and by its remaining upon him (Matt. 3.16,17; John 1.32-34), according to the word of the Father and the sacrament of Baptism. That anointing therefore came about through the fullness of grace and gifts conferred by the Word dwelling in him, such as was necessary for the infallible truth of the prophetic office, for the sinless holiness (ἀναμάρτητον) of the human sacrifice, and for the royal distribution of spiritual gifts. Outwardly this anointing was seen in the testimony of the Father, by which he gave approval to Christ as one called by himself, and therefore anointed, the Saviour. This came either mediately through angels (Luke 1.28; 2.13), or immediately from the Father himself, uttered three times: once at the baptism in the Jordan (Matt. 3.17), again on the holy mount where he was transfigured (Matt. 17.5; 2 Pet. 1.17), and finally as the passion drew near (John 12.28). The third anointing is that which also takes place in time, but not in the days of the flesh; it was made in heaven, by the manifestation of the Son of God dwelling in the flesh, through the glorious dignity and royal power conferred on him. "God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Spirit" [ἔχρισεν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεὸς] (after his ascension into heaven, working through the preaching, and poured out in a remarkable manner, as the Spirit of Christ, by whom it was obtained, into the Apostles and his disciples, and also as the Spirit of sonship given through faith in the Gospel, Gal. 3.14) "and with power" [δυνάμει] of the Godhead, or by the divine works which he himself performed by his own will (Acts 10.38). For God the Father, by that gift of the Holy Spirit and the divine power, demonstrated Jesus as King, Priest, and Prophet, speaking the words of God, or as "Lord of all" [Κύριον πάντων], ibid. v. 36; not only because all that belongs to the Father also belongs to the Son, on account of the unity of essence and operation, but also because the Father delivered all things into his hand, so that, having died for the Church, he might have her as his inheritance by the right of redemption and rule over all. St. Peter expressed this thus (Acts 2.36): "God has made him Lord and Christ" [Κύριον καὶ Χριστὸν] (anointed), that is, he demonstrated him to be the Lord of glory, to whom the kingdom is due, and the Christ, the Son of God manifested in the flesh, Prophet, Priest, and King; and so he willed him to be the possessor of his dominion and of his offices, and the one who carries them out in the fullest operation. And before St. Peter, God the Father himself said: "I have set my King upon Zion, my holy hill" [מָשַׁחְתִּי מַלְכִּי], Ps. 2.6. "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness" [שֶׁמֶן שָׂשׂוֹן] (such as belongs to a glorious king) "above your fellows", ibid. 45.8. Of this twofold anointing, the latter part performed on earth and the other in heaven, David bore the type: he was anointed first while Saul was still alive, lived for a while in private, and returned to tend his father's sheep (1 Sam. 16.13). After Saul's death, however, he was anointed king of Judah at Hebron (2 Sam. 2.4), and at last, anointed king over all Israel, he occupied the citadel of Zion by the same anointing (ibid. 5.3). That David's last anointing foreshadowed the crown of Christ's heavenly coronation as its completion is made clear by comparing the prophetic oracles of David with the saying of St. Peter: "Let all the house of Israel know that God has made this same Jesus both Lord and Christ", Acts 2.36.

units.la: XII. Christi præ veteribus unctis Prophetis, Sacerdotibus & Regibus προφητικοί & excellentia eximia est; ferè ut ille proprie, hi tenuiter admodum uncti & Christi dicantur. Nam Mosè Prophetarum eminentissimo (Num.XII. 6.7.8.) præstantiorem longè esse, illud arguit, quòd post Mosen sublatum venturus & mansurus Propheta expectandus à Mose ipso prænuntiatur. Prophetam illis suscitabo de medio fratrum suorum,sicut tu, & ponam verba mea in ore ejus, & loquetur omnia quæ præcepero illi. Erit autem,quicunque non audiverit verba mea, quæ loquetur in nomine meo אדרש מעמו reposcam ab eo, Deut. XVIII.18.19. Moses fidelis erat in tota domo Dei ως θεράπων ut famulus, in martyrium eorum, quæ dicenda erant, Christus autem tanquam super domum suam, Hebr.III.5.6. Unde licèt post resurrectionem Apostolos fratres suos nominare haud erubuerit, Joh.XX.17. Hebr.II.11. tamen nullos unquam in Prophetico munere fratres vel collegas agnovit,contestatus apud Apostolos : Unus est καθηγητής Doctor, Christus; omnes autem vos fratres, Matth.XXIII.8. Et ipse, ceu φῶς Lux ipsa, Johanni Baptistæ de Luce illa testanti opponitur, Joh.I.8.9. Sacerdotii ejus eminentiam supra Aharonicos ex eo,quòd Sacerdos sit secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, Psal. CX.4. S.Paulus Hebr.VII.1. &c. demonstrat. Non tantùm enim Sacerdos ille ante initium dierum carnis suæ extitit, sed etiam Sacerdotes, quotquot ab initio mundi extiterunt, ceu typos & vicarios suos, ad tempus obnoxios habuit,functuros usque ad adventum ejus expiatione typica, & intercessione vicaria, Hebr. VIII.5. IX.5. X.1. Denique in Regio Christi munere eminens ejus axioma non Monarchia vel Regno terreno,in terris visibili, sed spirituali in Ecclesiam dominio, & spirituali atque cœlesti Ecclesiæ tutela constat. Nam ita Christus venturus erat filiæ Sionis, & filiæ Hierusalem Rex pauper, humilis, Zach.IX.9. ut tamen humilem adventum ejus consequi ingressus in gloriam ad dextram Dei debuerit. Dixit Jehova Domino meo: Sede ad dextram meam, ibi dominaturus donec hostes scabellum pedum suorum ponat, Psal.CX.1. Ego primogenitum ponam eum, עליון excelsum Regibus terræ, ibid. LXXXIX.28.
units.tr: XII. The excellence of Christ above the anointed prophets, priests and kings of old is outstanding: as those were anointed and called Christs only in a slight and limited sense, so he is so in the proper sense. For that he is far greater than Moses, the most eminent of the prophets (Num. 12.6-8), is shown by the fact that after Moses' death a prophet who was to come and remain was foretold by Moses himself: "I will raise them up a prophet from among their brethren, like unto you, and will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him. And it shall come to pass that whoever will not hear my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him" [אדרש מעמו], Deut. 18.18,19. "Moses was faithful in all his house as a servant" [ὡς θεράπων], for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken; "but Christ as a son over his own house", Heb. 3.5,6. Hence, although after the resurrection he was not ashamed to call the Apostles his brethren (John 20.17; Heb. 2.11), yet he never acknowledged any brethren or colleagues in the prophetic office, testifying to the Apostles: "One is your Teacher (καθηγητής), Christ; and all you are brethren", Matt. 23.8. And he himself, as the Light (φῶς) itself, is set over against John the Baptist, who bore witness to that Light (John 1.8,9). The eminence of his priesthood above the Aaronic priests, from the fact that he is a priest after the order of Melchizedek (Ps. 110.4), is demonstrated by St. Paul (Heb. 7.1, etc.). For that priest existed not only before the beginning of the days of his flesh, but he also had as his types and vicars, for a time subject to him, all the priests who have existed from the beginning of the world, who would serve until his coming through typical expiation and vicarious intercession (Heb. 8.5; 9.5; 10.1). Finally, in the royal office of Christ his outstanding axiom consists not in a monarchy or earthly kingdom visible on earth, but in a spiritual dominion over the Church and a spiritual and heavenly protection of the Church. For Christ was to come thus: "Behold, your King comes to you; he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon a donkey", to the daughter of Zion and the daughter of Jerusalem, Zech. 9.9; yet his lowly coming had to be followed by his entry into glory at the right hand of God. "The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool", there to reign, Ps. 110.1. "I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth" [עליון], ibid. 89.28.

units.la: XIII. Idem Jesus Christus etiam μεσίτης Mediator nuncupatur: Unus Deus, εἷς καὶ μεσίτης unus etiam Mediator Dei & hominum, Homo Jesus Christus, 1.Tim.II.5. Melioris Testamenti Mediator est, Hebr. VIII.6. Propterea Testamenti novi Mediator est, &c. ibid.IX.15. Accessistis ad Testamenti novi Mediatorem, ibid.XII.24. Μεσίτης, hoc est, Mediatoris nomen sacris scriptoribus proprium esse Erasmus censuit. Cæterum viri docti observarunt, etiam Philonem Judæum & Scholiasten Thucydidis vocem μεσίτης, & Apulejum vocem Mediatoris frequentasse. In universum verò μεσίτης Mediator is est, qui stat inter Deum & homines quosdam μέσω medius, seu nudè ut מתווך internuntius, renuntiator, seu fidejussione, sponsione, vadimonio pro alterius debito apud creditorem vel judicem obito. Priori sensu Moses Μεσίτης Media
units.tr: XIII. The same Jesus Christ is also called Mediator [μεσίτης]: There is one God, and also one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus [εἷς καὶ μεσίτης], 1 Tim. 2.5. He is the Mediator of a better covenant, Heb. 8.6. Therefore he is the Mediator of the new covenant, &c., ibid. 9.15. You have come to the Mediator of the new covenant, ibid. 12.24. Erasmus thought that the name Mediator [μεσίτης], that is, of the Mediator, belonged peculiarly to the sacred writers. Learned men have, however, observed that Philo the Jew and the scholiast on Thucydides also used the word μεσίτης, and that Apuleius used the word Mediator. In general, a mediator [μεσίτης] is one who stands between God and certain men, in the middle [μέσω], either simply as a go-between, a messenger, reporter [מתווך], or by surety, pledge or bail, undertaking another's debt before a creditor or judge. In the former sense Moses comes under the name of Mediator [Μεσίτης]

units.la: toris nomine venit, Gal.III.19.20. quia עמד stabat inter Jehovam & populum להגיד ut hunc renuntiaret verbum Jehovæ, Deut.V.5. Tametsi verò etiam Christus est מלאך הברית Angelus seu Nuntius, Internuntius Fœderis,Malach.III.1. tamen nomen Mediatoris ei tributum non nudè internuntii officium notat; sed κυρίως ἢ ἰδίως principaliter & proprie fidejussionem seu vadimonium pro nobis obitum, ad nos Deo per novum fœdus gratiæ adducendos. Per Christum habemus προσαγωγὴν adductionem in fide ad gratiam illam, Rom. V.2. Per Christum habemus accessionem ambo in uno spiritu ad Patrem, Ephes.II.18. III.12. Hominum enim per peccatum à Deo divulsorum in fœdere novo gratiæ καταλλαγὴς agglutinatio cum Deo non fit immediata conventione & pacto Dei cum hominibus, sicut Angeli sancti Deo agglutinati sunt, & manent, & nos Deo in futura vita, ubi ipsæ erit omnia in omnibus, agglutinabimur, (quæ immediata unio in Scripturis nomine Visionis Dei à facie ad faciem venit) sed reconciliatione hominum cum Deo, mediante illo Fœdere, quo Christus Patri sua fidejussione, quam homo factus implevit, fœderatus est. Synonyma vocabula sunt Ἐγγυητὴς Sponsoris, Διαθήκης Testatoris, כהן Sacerdotis, Παράκλητος Intercessoris, Ἐπηλ-πλοκ Vindicis, מלאך יהוה Angeli Domini. Nam qui κρείττονος Διαθήκης Mediator, Hebr.VIII.6. dicitur, quia ejus interventu Testamentum factum, & executioni mandatum est; idem κρείττονος Διαθήκης ἐγγυητὴς Testamenti præstantioris sponsor, ibid.VII.22. appellatur, quia æternam promptámque voluntatem habet ea προθύμως & liberter faciendi, quæ Salvatorem ad justitiam peccatoris & sanctificationem ejusdem facere necesse erat. Propter quam voluntatem, quia in ea propositum dandi hæreditatem & Regnum suum communicandi includitur, etiam Διαθήκης Testator ibid.IX.16. Luc.XXII.29. insignitur. Eodem כהן Sacerdotis cognomen, species Sacerdotis pro genere Mediatoris posita, facit. Nam כהן Sacerdos est, qui accedit, seu jus accedendi habet. sicut apud homines etiam כהנים dicuntur, qui proximæ admissionis amici sunt, juxta Regem & summum Principem, 2.Sam.VIII.18. 1.Chron.XVIII.17. Ideo Sacerdotibus tribuitur נגש אל יהוה accedere, approximare ad Dominum, Exod.XIX.22. & Sacerdos notatur per קרוב propinquum, Levit.X.3. An parum vobis est, quòd separaverit Deus Israelis להקריב אתכם ut faciat vos accedere ad ipsum, jure Sacerdotii vobis commissi, Num.XVI.9? Sacerdotis enim est pro populo accedere ad Deum, peccatum populi ferre, Levit.X.17. quæ μεσιτεία mediatio quædam est. Talis autem Christus est, qui æterno Spiritu se obtulit, Hebr.IX.14. Etiam παράκλητος Advocatus vel Intercessor Mediatoris rationem habet. Talem se Christus voluntate & sponsione sua ante passionem, & merito suo post passionem obitam gessit, satisfactione sua malum & iram ab iis, qui ipsi dati sunt, averruncans, atque ita peccatum illorum portans, & patrocinium pro peccatoribus suscipiens, tanquam is, qui onus pro iis in judicio respondendi in se suscepit. Quo sensu etiam מלאך Angelus inter-
units.tr: Gal. 3.19, 20, because he stood [עמד] between Jehovah and the people, to declare [להגיד] to them the word of Jehovah, Deut. 5.5. Although Christ is also the messenger of the covenant [מלאך הברית], angel or messenger, intermediary of the covenant, Mal. 3.1, yet the name of Mediator given to him does not signify merely the office of an intermediary, but principally and properly [κυρίως ἢ ἰδίως] the undertaking of surety or bail for us, to bring us to God through the new covenant of grace. Through Christ we have access [προσαγωγήν] in faith into this grace, Rom. 5.2. Through Christ we both have access [accessionem] in one Spirit to the Father, Eph. 2.18; 3.12. For men divided from God by sin are not brought into reconciliation [καταλλαγή] with God in the new covenant of grace by an immediate agreement and pact between God and men, as the holy angels are joined to God and remain joined, and as we shall be joined to God in the future life, where God will be all in all (this immediate union is called in Scripture the vision of God face to face). Rather, men are reconciled to God through that covenant by which Christ, made man, bound himself to the Father by his surety, which he fulfilled. Synonymous terms are surety [Ἐγγυητής], testator [Διαθήκης], priest [כהן], advocate [Παράκλητος], vindicator [Ἐπηλ-πλοκ] and Angel of the Lord [מלאך יהוה]. For he who is called the Mediator of a better covenant, Heb. 8.6, because by his intervention the covenant was made and put into execution, is also called surety of a better covenant [κρείττονος Διαθήκης ἐγγυητής], ibid. 7.22, because he has an eternal and ready will to do readily [προθύμως] and willingly what was necessary for the Saviour to do, to make the sinner righteous and to sanctify him. Because this will includes the purpose of giving the inheritance and communicating his kingdom, he is also marked as testator of the covenant [Διαθήκης Testator], ibid. 9.16; Luke 22.29. The title priest [כהן] likewise, the species of priest put for the genus of mediator, fits him. For a priest [כהן] is one who draws near, or who has the right of drawing near. Among men too, those are called כהנים who are friends of closest access, next to the King and the chief Prince, 2 Sam. 8.18; 1 Chron. 18.17. Hence priests are described as נגש אל יהוה, to draw near, to approach the Lord, Exod. 19.22, and the priest is designated by קרוב, near, Lev. 10.3. "Is it too little for you that the God of Israel has separated you" להקריב אתכם, so that he may make you draw near to him, by the right of the priesthood committed to you, Num. 16.9? For it is the office of a priest to draw near to God for the people, to bear the sin of the people, Lev. 10.17, which is a kind of mediation [μεσιτεία]. Such is Christ, who offered himself through the eternal Spirit, Heb. 9.14. Also Advocate or Intercessor [παράκλητος] has the character of Mediator. Christ acted in this role by his will and surety before his passion, and by his merit after the passion. By his satisfaction he averted evil and wrath from those given to him, and so bore their sin and took up the patronage of sinners, as one who had taken upon himself the burden of answering for them in judgment. In this sense also the Angel [מלאך] inter-

units.la: Iesu præ veteribus unctis Prophetis Sacerdotibus & Regibus prærogativa.
units.tr: The pre-eminence of Jesus above the anointed prophets, priests and kings of old.

units.la: Idem Iesus Christus etiam μεσίτης aliisque nominibus synonymis, velut Sponsoris, Testatoris, Angeli fœderis, Sacerdotis, Paracleti &c. venit. Interpres, vel Orator vocatur; cujus Oratoris munus ex verbis, quae ei tribuuntur, פדהו Redime eum, ne descendat in foveam; כפר מצאתי Inveni redemptionis pretium, cognoscitur, Job. XXXIII.23. coll. cum Hebr. IX.12. Ubi Christus αιωνίαν λύτρωσιν ευρέμενος aeternam redemptionem invenisse dicitur. Eandem μεσιτείαν vox ונא ἐπιλήπωρ Vindex, assertor, passim, velut Genes.XLVIII.16. Esaj.XLI.14. XLIII.1. LII.3. LXIII.4. Job.XIX.25. Hebr.II.16. Christo tributa significat; quia jure communis carnis & sanguinis, juxta praeceptum diligendi fratrem, bona & mala fratris sua reputat, injurias ejus vindicat, bona procurat, & quidem per פדות ἀπολύτρωσιν redemptionem. Nam vocabulum hoc significat liberum facere sola manu & potentia, si quis sola violentia alienatus fuerit: sin vero is, qui liberatur, reatu nexus & jure constrictus sit, per כפר λύτρον, obliterationem debiti, & vindicationem ex potestate aliena in suam haereditatem. Ne timeas, quia האלתיך vindicavi te, vocavi nomen tuum, לי אתה Meus es tu, Esaj.XLIII.1. Idem denique Mediator crebro יהוה מלאך Angelus Domini καὶ ἐξοχὴν vocatur, quia à Deo missus munere salvandi fungitur. cui disertè נאלה ἐπιλύτην seu vindicias Jacobus Genes.XLVIII.16. tribuit. Vocum & epithetorum horum Christi cum voce & epitheto Mediatoris ἱσδυναμία satis inde constat, quòd & Sponsor, & Testator, & Sacerdos, & Intercessor atque Orator, & Vindex, & Angelus Domini non aliter Christus dici potest, quàm quatenus is μέσος medius est Deum inter & peccatores, atque utrosque morte sua, velut pretio pro peccato, quod Lex requirit, reconciliat.
units.tr: The same Jesus Christ comes also under the name μεσίτης and other synonymous names, such as Surety, Testator, Angel of the covenant, Priest, Paraclete, and so on. He is called Interpreter or Orator, and the duty of this Orator is known from the words ascribed to him: "Deliver him from going down to the pit; I have found a ransom" [פדהו ... כפר מצאתי] (Job 33.23, compared with Heb. 9.12), where Christ is said to have "found eternal redemption" [αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν εὑρέμενος]. The same office of Mediator is signified by the word גאל [ונא ἐπιλήπωρ], Vindicator, defender, which occurs throughout, for example Gen. 48.16; Isa. 41.14; 43.1; 52.3; 63.4; Job 19.25; and is ascribed to Christ in Heb. 2.16. For by the law of common flesh and blood, in accordance with the precept to love one's brother, he counts his brother's good and evil as his own, avenges his wrongs, and procures his goods, and indeed by redemption [פדות, ἀπολύτρωσιν]. For this word means to set free by a hand and power alone, when someone has been alienated by mere violence. But if the one who is set free is bound by the chain of guilt and by right, then it is done by כפר, λύτρον, the cancelling of the debt, and the vindication from another's power into one's own inheritance. "Fear not, for I have redeemed [האלתיך] thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine" [לי אתה] (Isa. 43.1). Lastly, the same Mediator is often called, eminently, the Angel of the LORD [מלאך יהוה], because he, sent by God, performs the office of saving. To him Jacob plainly ascribes גאל, the redeemer or vindicator (Gen. 48.16). From these names and epithets of Christ it is sufficiently clear, together with the title and epithet Mediator, that he can be called Surety, Testator, Priest, Intercessor, Orator, Vindicator, and Angel of the LORD only insofar as he is in the middle [μέσος] between God and sinners, and reconciles both by his death, as a price for sin, which the law requires.

units.la: XIV. Fuerunt Nomina Jesu Christi & Mediatoris, quae naturam officii, quod in se suscepit, utcunque exprimunt; quae quoad rem ipsam amplius exponenda nobis est. Et Muneris quidem illius Mediatorii, ceu operis externi, causa communiter & indivisè tota S. Trinitas est; singulariter verò, & quoad operandi in eo opere modum, singulae Deitatis Personae, Pater missione, Spiritus S. unctione, Filius susceptione & executione. Pater enim, sicut Deitatis, ita operationis omnis principium, Filium misit in mundum, ut peccatores salvaret, Joh. III.17.34. VII.28. Gal.IV.4. eundem missum edita voce coelesti consecravit, Matth.III.17. XVII.5. & solenni juramento confirmavit. Juravit Jehova, & non poenitebit eum. Tu es Sacerdos in saeculum, secundum ordinem Melchisedeci. Psal.CX.4. Unde Christum Pontificem constitutum esse non χωρὶς ὁρκωμοσίας sine jureju-rando, sicut Levitae, Sacerdotes sine jurejurando constituti sunt, sed μετὰ ὁρκωμοσίας cum jurejurando, & quidem μετὰ τὸν νόμον post Legem, ut Sacerdotium legale & debilius quandoque a-movendum esse liqueret, Apostolus Hebr.VII.21.28. conclusit. Nam sermo ille jurisjurandi, & quidem ἀμεταμελήτῳ poenitudinis omnis expers τὸ ἀμεταθέτον τῆς βουλῆς consilii, seu propositi (nulli quippe conditioni adstricti) immutabilitatem, ibid.VI.17. significat. Etenim Deum poenitere non potest, quia Deus est; & si posset, tamen is juramentum mutare non potest, quia, verax & ἀψευδὴς est. Deus poenitere eorum, quae mutare decrevit, dicitur; sicut homines eorum, quae mutant, poenitere dicuntur. Sed propositum Christum mittendi, vocandi, & ordinandi Sacerdotem in Deo sine ejusmodi poenitentia metaphorica est. Ideo etiam jurejurando illud corroboravit. Atque haec causa est, quòd Christus missionem suam ubique ad Deum Patrem refert. Is enim Testamenti gratiae, Christo Mediatore sanciti, author, & bonorum suorum filiis gratiae dispensandorum arbiter est; ut sic in ἀληροφορίᾳ τῆς ἐλπίδος & gaudio perfecto Deum Patrem nostrum appellaremus, & diligeremus. quae vera pietas est, neque aliter in nobis effici potest, quàm si hoc modo Deus, ejusque in Christo erga nos amor innotescat. Spiritui S. tribuitur Unctio illa, qua dona Christo collata sunt; sed non sine Patre, qui & ipse Filium suum unxit, collato ei Spiritu, Esaj. XI.1.2. & gloria coelesti, ceu oleo laetitiae eum delibutum reddens, Psal.XLV.8. sed officium hoc obeundum missus à Deo Patre Filius Jesus Christus suscepit, & in sua persona executus est. Sacrificium & oblationem noluisti, corpus autem mihi adaptasti. Ecce adsum, ut faciam, Deus, voluntatem tuam, Hebr.X. s. 7. Ipse se exinanivit, accepta forma servi, Phil.II.7.8. Christus proin in ceteris causarum muneris hujus & proxima & solitaria est, quia unus Mediator est Jesus Christus, 1.Tim.II.5. & is torcular solus calcavit, Esaj. LXIII.3.
units.tr: XIV. The names Jesus Christ and Mediator express, in some measure, the nature of the office which he undertook; now the thing itself must be set out more fully. As to the cause of that mediatorial office, as an external work, the whole Holy Trinity is the common and undivided cause; but singly, and as to the mode of operating in that work, each Person of the Deity acts: the Father by sending, the Holy Spirit by anointing, the Son by undertaking and executing. For the Father, as the principle of the Deity and of all operation, sent the Son into the world to save sinners (John 3.17, 34; 7.28; Gal. 4.4). He consecrated the same Son, when sent, by a voice from heaven (Matt. 3.17; 17.5), and confirmed it by a solemn oath: "The LORD sware, and will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek" (Ps. 110.4). Hence the apostle concludes (Heb. 7.21, 28) that Christ was made high priest not without an oath [χωρὶς ὁρκωμοσίας], as the Levites were made priests without an oath, but with an oath [μετὰ ὁρκωμοσίας], and indeed after the law [μετὰ τὸν νόμον], so that it might be clear that the legal and weaker priesthood would at some point be removed. For that word of the oath signifies the immutability [τὸ ἀμεταθέτον] of the counsel or purpose, which is free of all unrepentance [ἀμεταμελήτῳ] (since it is bound by no condition) (Heb. 6.17). For God cannot repent, because he is God; and even if he could, he could not change the oath, since he is true and without falsehood [ἀψευδής]. God is said to repent of those things which he has decreed to change, as men are said to repent of the things they change. But the purpose in God to send Christ, to call him, and to ordain him priest is without any such repentance, which is only metaphorical. Therefore he confirmed it also by an oath. And this is the reason why Christ everywhere refers his mission to God the Father. For he is the author of the covenant of grace, sanctioned by Christ the Mediator, and the arbiter of his good things, to be dispensed to the children of grace, so that in the full assurance of hope [ἀληροφορίᾳ τῆς ἐλπίδος] and perfect joy we may call and love our Father God. This is true piety, and it cannot be produced in us in any other way than if God and his love towards us in Christ become known in this manner. To the Holy Spirit is ascribed that anointing by which gifts were conferred on Christ; yet not without the Father, who himself anointed his Son, by conferring the Spirit on him (Isa. 11.1, 2), and making him anointed with the oil of gladness, that is, with heavenly glory (Ps. 45.8). But the Son, Jesus Christ, sent by God the Father, undertook this office to be discharged, and executed it in his own person: "Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me ... Lo, I come to do thy will, O God" (Heb. 10.5, 7). "He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant" (Phil. 2.7, 8). Christ therefore is, in the other causes of this office, both the nearest and the only one, because "there is one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim. 2.5), and he alone has trodden the winepress (Isa. 63.3).

units.la: XV. Mediatoris munus Christus secundum utramque naturam suscepit & obiit.
units.tr: XV. Christ undertook and discharged the office of Mediator according to both natures.

units.la: Sicut enim post incarnationem duae in Filio Dei naturae, duo in uno supposito agendi principia sunt: ita utriusque naturae operationes ad μεσιτείαν concurrunt, & ab operationibus illis producta ἀποτελέσματα ad utramque naturam referuntur. Nam annuntiare Evangelium, orare, pati, mori Humana: at Voluntatem Dei ex sinu Patris proferre & immediatè revelare, Joh.I.18. potestatem habere animam ponendi & assumendi, ibid.X.18. sese offerre per spiritum aeternum, Hebr. IX.14. sanctificare victimam, Matth.XXIII.19. Virtute sua Coelos penetrare, Hebr.IV.14. Omnium preces, gemitus audire, Apoc.VIII.3. Ecclesiam potentia sua tueri, Joh.X.28. Matth. XVI.18. Divina operatio est. Sed & apotelesmata Mediatoris, qualia sunt, Ecclesiam proprio sanguine acquirere, Act. XX.28. Matth.XX.28. reconciliare, Rom.V.10.11. Col.I.21.22. mundare à peccatis, 1.Joh.I.7. salvare, Matth.I.21. &c. Θεανθρωπικά sunt, & ad utramque naturam pertinent, faciente unaquaque quod ἴδιον suum, sibi proprium est. Divina porro natura in opere Mediationis vel aliquid agit, vel nihil agit. Si nihil agit, necesse non habuit naturam humanam assumere. Neque etiam necessum fuit, ut Mediator inter Deum & homines ἀνθρωπῷ esset. Si aliquid agit, Christus secundum eam naturam, ceu principium formale actionis illius, Mediator est, quia omne operans per formam suam, ex qua operationes fluunt, operatur. Par Humanae naturae ratio est. quae si nihil in hac μεσιτείᾳ agit, potuit à λόγῳ non assumi; sin aliquid, ab opere & operatione μεσιτείας excludi non potest. Cùmque Mediator sit, qui inter partes dissidentes medius eas reconciliat, Christus certè secundum utramque naturam
units.tr: For just as after the incarnation there are two natures in the Son of God and two principles of action in one person, so the operations of each nature contribute to the mediation, and the effects produced by those operations are referred to each nature. For to preach the Gospel, to pray, to suffer and to die belong to the human nature; but to bring forth the will of God from the bosom of the Father and to reveal it immediately (John 1:18), to have power to lay down and to take up his soul (John 10:18), to offer himself through the eternal Spirit (Heb. 9:14), to sanctify the victim (Matt. 23:19), to penetrate the heavens by his own power (Heb. 4:14), to hear the prayers and groanings of all (Rev. 8:3), to defend the Church by his power (John 10:28; Matt. 16:18), these are a divine operation. But the effects of the Mediator, such as to acquire the Church with his own blood (Acts 20:28; Matt. 20:28), to reconcile (Rom. 5:10-11; Col. 1:21-22), to cleanse from sins (1 John 1:7), to save (Matt. 1:21), and so on, are theanthropic, and they pertain to both natures, each doing what is proper to it. Now the divine nature in the work of mediation either does something or does nothing. If it does nothing, it had no need to assume a human nature; nor would it have been necessary for the Mediator between God and men to be man. If it does something, Christ is Mediator according to that nature as the formal principle of that action, because everything that acts, acts through its form, from which its operations flow. The same reasoning holds for the human nature: if it does nothing in this mediation, it could not have been assumed by the Word; but if it does something, it cannot be excluded from the work and operation of the mediation. And since a Mediator is one who, standing between parties at variance, reconciles them, Christ certainly, according to both natures,

units.la: inter partes dissidentes medius est, eásque reconciliat. Nam naturam Divinam cum Deo, Humanam cum hominibus communem habens, à Deo per exinanitionem, ab Hominibus per gratiam unionis cum λόγῳ & immunitatem à peccato differt, & utrasque reconciliat, Rom.III. 24.25. Ephes.I.17. &c. Col.I.20. quibus locis reconciliatio facta per Christum dicitur; facta per mortem Filii Dei, per eum, in quo plenitudo Deitatis habitat, hoc est, per eum, qui Deus & homo est. Praeterea secundum utramque naturam Propheta, Sacerdos & Rex est; Propheta, quia Patrem nemo novit, nisi Filius, & cui revelare is voluerit, Matth. XI.27. & in novissimo diebus Deus per Filium locutus est, Hebr.I.1. Sacerdos, quia per Spiritum æternum se obtulit Deo inculpatum, ibid.IX.14. Rex, quia Deus omnia eidedit in manus, Joh.III.35. & Filius Altissimi regnabit in domo Jacobi in æternum, Luc.I.32.33. Secundum quam porro naturam Propheta, Sacerdos & Rex est, secundum eandem Mediator est; quia hi ejusdem muneris Mediatorii actus sunt. Denique secundum eandem naturam Christus Mediator est, secundum quam Sponsor est, quia idem Mediator & Sponsor est. At secundum utramque naturam Sponsorem esse, supra Loc.XI.22. probare occupavimus. Secundum utramque igitur etiam Mediator est.
units.tr: stands between the parties at variance and reconciles them. For, having the divine nature in common with God and the human nature in common with men, he differs from God by his emptying and from men by the grace of union with the Word and by immunity from sin, and he reconciles both (Rom. 3:24-25; Eph. 1:17; Col. 1:20, etc.). In these passages the reconciliation is said to be made through Christ, made by the death of the Son of God, by him in whom the fullness of the Godhead dwells, that is, by him who is God and man. Moreover, according to both natures he is Prophet, Priest and King: Prophet, because no one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (Matt. 11:27), and in these last days God has spoken by the Son (Heb. 1:1); Priest, because through the eternal Spirit he offered himself without blemish to God (ibid. 9:14); King, because the Father has given all things into his hands (John 3:35), and the Son of the Most High shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever (Luke 1:32-33). Moreover, the nature according to which he is Prophet, Priest and King is the nature according to which he is Mediator, since these are acts of the one mediatorial office. Finally, he is Mediator according to the same nature according to which he is Surety, since the Mediator and the Surety are the same. But we have already undertaken to prove (above, Loc. 11, §22) that he is Surety according to both natures. Therefore he is also Mediator according to both.

units.la: XVI. Christum ergo Mediatorem tollunt, qui solius naturae humanae in μεσιτεία operationem agnoscunt; Divinae autem operationem ab eadem removent. Quae Lombardi haeresis est, Sent.lib.III.D.19. decernentis, Christum Mediatorem esse & dici secundum humanitatem, non Divinitatem. Cui Thomas p.III.q.22.art.2. consentit. Quorum sententiam Bellarminus Controv.lib.cap.1. illustravit distinctione principii quod & quo, illud verbum Dei incarnatum, non Deum solum, sed etiam hominem; hoc est, personam θεάνθρωπος; hoc humanitatem, scilicet. Sic placuit Magistris illis ἀγιολατρείᾳ suae stabiliendae, ut nudos homines, Sanctulos suos, Mediatores esse posse, evincerent. Eadem errore pallebat Stancarus Regiomontanus Professor, sed gente Mantuanus; Collegae suo Osiandro asserenti, Christum ut verum Deum Jehovam, secundum naturam suam Divinam esse nostram justitiam, & non secundum naturam humanam, atque illam essentialem Dei justitiam in nobis habitare, & efficere, ut juste agamus (perimenti ita Gratiae illius necessitatem, qua Mediator homo ex muliere fieri & Legi subjici Gal.IV.4. debuit) merito, sed non recta ratione obloquens, stultorum more, in contrarium errorem currens, & è Charybdi in Scyllam incidens. Divinitatem ab opere & operatione Mediatoris seclusit, atque sic nodum secare, quam solvere maluit.
units.tr: XVI. Therefore those who acknowledge an operation in the mediation only of the human nature, and remove the operation of the divine nature from it, take away Christ as Mediator. This is the heresy of Lombard, who decreed in Sent. lib. III, dist. 19 that Christ is Mediator and is called Mediator according to his humanity, not his divinity. Aquinas agrees with him in P. III, q. 22, art. 2. Bellarmine, in his Controversies, book 1, ch. 1, illustrated their opinion by the distinction between that which and by which: the Word made flesh is that which, not only God but also man, that is, the theanthropic person; the humanity is that by which. So those teachers were pleased, in order to establish their own worship of saints, to argue that mere men, their little saints, could be mediators. The Regiomontane professor Stancarus, a Mantuan by birth, fell into the same error. He objected to his colleague Osiander, who asserted that Christ, as the true God Jehovah, is our righteousness according to his divine nature and not according to his human nature, and that this essential righteousness of God dwells in us and makes us act righteously. (In this way Osiander destroyed the necessity of that grace by which the Mediator had to be made man, born of a woman and made subject to the Law, Gal. 4:4.) Stancarus rightly objected, but not by sound reasoning: like fools, he ran into the opposite error and fell from Charybdis into Scylla. He excluded the divinity from the work and operation of the Mediator, and so preferred to cut the knot rather than untie it.

units.la: XVII. Vanissimae vero Pontificiorum & Stancari, pro haeresi sua ratiocinationes sunt. Licet enim S. Paulus Mediatorem illum unum Dei & hominum definiverit ἄνθρωπον Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν hominem Christum Jesum, non Deum, I.Tim. II.5. non tamen Deum exclusit. Hominem enim, hoc est, personam hominis, in qua etiam Deitas est, non humanitatem Mediatorem nominavit. Logica dispositio haec est: Homo Jesus Christus est Mediator Dei & hominum. Ubi prius Homo non potest esse restrictivum, quia est nomen speciei; sed posterius, Jesus Christus, quia individuale etiam restrictivum est. Non enim quivis homo Mediator est, verum ille, qui ab Angelo Jesus appellatus est. Hominis autem vocabulum addidit, sive amorem Mediatoris indicaturus, quia Hominis est secundum praeceptum dilectionis proximi, diligere omnes; sicut supra v.1. pro omnibus hominibus orare jussit; sive praescius idololatriae Papalis, cui homines inde colorem quaesituri erant; quod sine hominibus sanctis Mediatoribus nullus ad Deum aditus pateat. Sed Spiritus S. praemonuit, fideles non destitui Mediatore homine, qui Jesus Christus est, non Sancti. Eundem Mediatorem à Deo, hoc est, à persona Patris, non à Deitate S. Paulus distinxit. Addo Mediatorem etiam oeconomia officii à Deo φυσικῶς dicto distingui, licet ab oeconomia illa officii Deitas secludi non posset. Mera porro φλυαρία, non ratio est, quod Mediatorem, ceu medium, à Deo distare debere, adeoque secundum Deitatem Mediatorem esse non posse objectant. Eadem enim ratione nec secundum humanitatem Mediator esse posset, adeoque plane Mediator non esset. Nam ceu Medius, etiam ab hominibus distare debet. Sed satis est, quod ab utroque, Deo & homine, distat, ceu θεάνθρωπος, & oeconomiam Mediatoris gerens. Nam nec Deus quà talis, nec homo seorsim θεάνθρωπος est. Et Mediator à Deo non secundum φύσιν seu naturam Deitatis, sed secundum oeconomiam officii distinguitur: plane ut ab hominibus non secundum humanitatem, sed secundum oeconomiam & relationem muneris Mediatorii distat. Si Mediator secundum Deitatem Christus esse non potest, quia nemo apud se ipsum, vel sui ipsius Mediator esse potest; neque secundum humanitatem Mediator esse potest, quia nemo idem est cum eo, pro quo Mediatorem agit. Aliud igitur longe est, Deum Filium esse; aliud Mediatorem esse; aliud offensum esse, ut Deum: aliud Mediatorem agere ut θεάνθρωπον. Neque omnino absurdum est, variante respectu, Mediatorem esse sui ipsius, quia quod apud alios agit, ut persona ab ipsis diversa, id apud se agit, modo & relatione muneris à se diversus. Et Filius Deus à se ipso Deo distinguitur, quatenus non Deus duntaxat, sed etiam homo est. Idem Filius homo à se ipso homine distinguitur, quatenus non homo duntaxat, sed etiam Deus est. Distinctio porro illa Bellarmini, quod Christus, quà Deus, ab homine quidem differat, at non à se, ut Deus est, adeoque quà Deus, Mediator seu medius esse non possit: at quà homo differat tum à Deo, quia homo est, tum ab hominibus peccatoribus, quia ipse justus est; adeoque quà homo, Mediator & medius esse potuerit; nil nisi συνίνη ἰπποκεῖα est, tum quia sic mediationis ratio constituitur non ὁμολογίας, sed ex partibus longe distantibus, nimirum substantiali in humana natura, quatenus à Deo distinguitur; attributiva & merè ποιητική, quatenus ab hominibus, per solam scilicet justitiam distinguitur; quomodo nec apud homines Mediator esse potest, qui non ergo utramque partem benevolus, sed ita distractus est, ut alteram partem benevolentia, alteram consanguinitate, at non benevolentia attingat: tum quia pari ratione Filius Dei naturalis à se ipso per relationem status exinanitionis distingui poterit: tum quia Mediatoris hominis requisitum est, non tantùm justitia, sed etiam communio carnis & sanguinis: tum quia ratio dari non potest, cur Mediatio relata ad Patrem ἀρχηγικῶς, ad nos naturalis esse debeat; unde consequens erit, ut Christus apud Patrem Mediator sit non ἐκ τῆς ὁμοουσίου, sed ἐκ τῆς ὁμοιουσίου (quod Cyrillus Dial. 1. cum Herm. in Arianis damnavit) quia homo justus non potest Deo dici ὁμοούσιος; & ut Christus ne quidem medius sit, quia longè magis à Patre, quàm à nobis distaret: tum denique, quia distantia talis ad mediationem non sufficit, cùm in justitia unius hominis, quà talis est, sufficiens valor ad satisfaciendum justitiæ Dei pro peccatoribus non reperiatur. Sacerdos porro Christus est, & sacrificat ut Mediator, & secundum naturam non humanam duntaxat, sed Divinam etiam, quia æterno Spiritu se Deo obtulit, Hebr. IX, 14. & Deitas Christi, potestatem habentis ponendi animam, mortem operata est; & ad sacrificium etiam pertinet altare, quod Christi Deitas, quæ donum sanctificavit, fuit. Denique neque sic naturarum proprietates in Christo confusæ sunt, quia operationes totidem naturarum distinctæ ad idem numero opus propter unionem hypostaticam concurrunt. Agit enim, uti verissimè Leo ad Flav. dixit, utraque forma cum alterius communione, quod proprium; Verbo operante, quod verbi est, & carne exequente, quod carnis est.
units.tr: XVII. The arguments of the Papists and of Stancarus in support of their heresy are most empty. For although St. Paul defined that one Mediator between God and men as a man, Christ Jesus (ἄνθρωπον Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν), not God (1 Tim. 2:5), he did not thereby exclude God. For he named as Mediator the man, that is, the person of the man, in whom there is also the Godhead, not the humanity. The logical arrangement is this: the man Jesus Christ is the Mediator of God and men. Here the first term, man, cannot be restrictive, because it is the name of a species; but the second, Jesus Christ, is restrictive, because an individual name is also restrictive. For not any man is the Mediator, but he who was called Jesus by the angel. He added the word man, either to indicate the Mediator's love, since it is in keeping with the precept of love of neighbour that he should love all men, just as above, in v. 1, he commanded prayers for all men; or, foreseeing the Papal idolatry, by which men would seek a pretext from this, that without holy men as mediators no access to God lies open. But the Holy Spirit forewarned that the faithful are not left without a man Mediator, who is Jesus Christ, and not the saints. St. Paul distinguished the same Mediator from God, that is, from the person of the Father, not from the Godhead. I add that the Mediator is also distinguished, in the economy of office, from God as naturally so called, although the Godhead cannot be separated from that economy of office. Moreover, it is mere nonsense, and not reasoning, to object that the Mediator, as a middle, ought to be distant from God, and therefore cannot be Mediator according to the Godhead. For by the same reasoning he could not be Mediator according to the humanity either, and so would not be Mediator at all. For as a middle, he ought also to be distant from men. But it is enough that he is distant from both, God and man, as the theanthropos, and as one who discharges the economy of the Mediator. For neither God as such nor man alone is theanthropos. The Mediator is distinguished from God not according to the nature (physis) or nature of the Godhead, but according to the economy of office, just as he is distinguished from men not according to the humanity, but according to the economy and relation of the mediatorial office. If Christ cannot be Mediator according to the Godhead, because no one can be a mediator with himself or of himself, neither can he be Mediator according to the humanity, because no one is the same as the one for whom he acts as mediator. Therefore it is one thing to be God's Son, another to be Mediator, and another to be offended as God, and another to act as Mediator as the theanthropos. Nor is it at all absurd that, with a changing respect, one should be a mediator of oneself, since what one does toward others, as a person distinct from them, one does toward oneself, being distinct from oneself by mode and relation of office. The Son of God is distinguished from himself as God, insofar as he is not only God but also man. The same Son as man is distinguished from himself as man, insofar as he is not only man but also God. But Bellarmine's distinction, that Christ as God indeed differs from man but not from himself as God, so that as God he cannot be Mediator or middle, while as man he differs both from God, because he is man, and from sinful men, because he himself is just, so that as man he could be Mediator and middle, is nothing but a [συνίνη ἰπποκεῖα] fiction; both because the ground of mediation is thus constituted not from one agreement but from parts far apart: substantial in the human nature insofar as it is distinguished from God, and attributive and merely poetic insofar as it is distinguished from men by justice alone; and in such a way a mediator cannot even be among men, who is not benevolent toward both parties, but so divided that he touches one party by benevolence and the other by kinship, but not by benevolence; both because by the same reasoning the natural Son of God could be distinguished from himself by the relation of the state of emptying; and because a man as Mediator needs not only justice but also communion of flesh and blood; and because no reason can be given why the mediation, related to the Father as its origin, should be natural to us; whence it would follow that Christ is Mediator before the Father not from the same substance (ἐκ τῆς ὁμοουσίου) but from a like substance (ἐκ τῆς ὁμοιουσίου), which Cyril in his first Dialogue, together with Hermias, condemned among the Arians, since a just man cannot be called of the same substance (ὁμοούσιος) with God; and that Christ would not even be a middle, since he would be far more distant from the Father than from us. Lastly, because such a distance does not suffice for mediation, since in the justice of a single man, as such, no sufficient value is found to satisfy the justice of God for sinners. Christ is moreover Priest, and sacrifices as Mediator, and this according not to the human nature alone but also according to the divine, because he offered himself to God through the eternal Spirit (Heb. 9:14); and the Godhead of Christ, who had power to lay down his soul, effected the death; and the altar pertains also to the sacrifice, which was the Godhead of Christ, which sanctified the gift. Finally, the properties of the natures are not thus confused in Christ, because the operations of the distinct natures concur to one numerically identical work on account of the hypostatic union. For, as Leo said most truly in his letter to Flavian, each form acts in communion with the other, what is proper to it: the Word operating what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh.

units.la: XVIII. Inanis metus fuit Stancari, quo Orthodoxos percellere, & iisdem invidiam conflare laboravit, ne si Mediator Christus secundum naturam Divinam dicatur, Patre minor, cum Arianis, idem statuatur. Mediatoris enim nomen non est trahendum ad mediam Deum inter & homines naturam, neque ad dignitatem Personæ Mediatoris Divina inferiorem, & Divinam inter & humanam mediam, ad quam Mediator vel quà Deus deprimi, vel quà homo est, exaltari debuerit, vel potuerit. Qualem pre-cariam Mediatoris adorationem etiam Remonstrantes moderni, uti ex Philippo à Limborch Theol. Christ. lib. II. 18. liquet, tueri non verecundantur, patulas idololatriæ Pontificiæ januas munientes. Licèt enim Mediator, quà talis, propter communionem utriusque naturæ Divinæ & humanæ, medius sit, tamen non ideo vel ante, vel post exinanitionem factam Personæ Filii in natura Divina ullam ἐλαττωσιν minoritatem, vel Patris in eadem natura ἐξοχὴν majoritatem infert. Nam ante exinanitionem nullo schemate in natura Divina vel Filius minor Patre, vel Pater major Filio dici potuit. Cùmque in eam non cadat τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα mutationis obumbratio, Jac. I. 17. ipsa quoque exinanitio fieri ἀτρέπτως debuit. Nam in illa minor quidem factus est Patre, at non in forma Dei, verùm in assumpta forma servi. Proin etiam post exinanitionem 7ò Mediator non merè Servum Dei, sed magnum Deum & Servatorem Jesum Christum Tit. II. 13. necnon δόξαν ὡς μονογενοῦς παρὰ πατρὸς Gloriam ut unigeniti à Patre, Joh. I. 14. per naturam Patri cum Filio communem, adeò ut in illa Patrem intueri licuerit, ibid. XIV. 9. notat. Unde verus Deus Israelis se solum Salvatorem Israelis esse protestatur. Verè tu es Deus abscondens te אלהי ישראל מושיע Deus Israelis Salvator, Esai. XLV. 15. Israel נושע salvatus est in Jehova salute æterna, ibid. v. 17. אל זרך Deus justus & Salvator non est præter me, ibid. v. 21. Ego, Ego sum, qui deleo prævaricationes tuas propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordabor, ibid. cap. XLIII. 25. Delevi, ut nubem, prævaricationes tuas, & veluti nubem peccata tua. ibid. cap. XLIV. 22. Et de Filio ipse Pater sic loquitur: Ecce Deus vester! Ipse veniet & salvabit vos, ibid. XXXV. 4. Dic civitatibus Judæ: Ecce Deus vester: Ecce Dominus Jehova veniet, ibid. XL. 9, 10. Domus Jehudæ miserebor, & salvabo eos in Jehova Deo suo, Hos. I. 7. Ideo Filius ille donandus, & Puer nasciturus אל גבור Deus robustus, Pater æternitatis, Esai. IX. 6. & consignificandæ naturæ humanæ, quam assumpturus erat, עמנו אל Immanuel, ibid. VII. 14. VIII. 8. indigetatur. Etiam qui promittitur Davidi excitandus Germen justum, mox nominandus יהוה צדקנו Jehova justitia nostra Jerem. XXXIII. 15. dicitur. Licèt igitur Mediator non sit, qui non simul homo est, & homo, quà talis, Deus non sit; tamen ψιλὸς ἀνθρωπος nudus & merus homo לא יהוה Non-Jehova, Deut. XXXII. 27. Mediator esse non potuit: ac proin Filius Mediator Deus, nec Patre minor est. Non enim duplex Mediator, sed unus est; in quo quicquid Divinum est, Deus, quicquid humanum; homo sibi vindicat.
units.tr: XVIII. Stancarus's fear was groundless, and he took pains to alarm the orthodox and stir up hatred against them, lest, if Christ the Mediator were said to be less than the Father according to the divine nature, the same position as the Arians would be established. For the name of Mediator is not to be drawn to a nature midway between God and men, nor to a dignity of the Person of the Mediator lower than the divine and midway between the divine and the human, to which the Mediator would have had to be lowered as God, or raised as man, or could have been. The modern Remonstrants, as is clear from Philippus à Limborch, Theol. Christ. II.18, do not hesitate to defend such a precarious worship of the Mediator, thereby opening wide the doors of Papist idolatry. For although the Mediator, as such, is in the middle because of the communion of both natures, divine and human, nevertheless this does not imply any lowering [ἐλαττωσις] or minority of the Son in the divine nature, either before or after the emptying of the Person of the Son, nor any eminence [ἐξοχή] or majority of the Father in that same nature. For before the emptying, in no form in the divine nature could the Son be called less than the Father, or the Father greater than the Son. And since no shadow of change [τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα] falls upon that nature (Jas. 1.17), the emptying itself ought to have taken place without change [ἀτρέπτως]. For in it he was made indeed less than the Father, but not in the form of God; rather in the assumed form of a servant. Therefore also after the emptying, the Mediator is not merely the servant of God, but "our great God and Savior Jesus Christ" (Tit. 2.13), and the glory "as of the only-begotten from the Father" (John 1.14), through the nature common to the Father with the Son, so that in him it was lawful to behold the Father, as is noted in John 14.9. Hence the true God of Israel declares that he alone is the Savior of Israel: "Truly you are a God who hides yourself, the God of Israel, the Savior" [אלהי ישראל מושיע], Isa. 45.15. "Israel is saved [נושע] in the Lord with an everlasting salvation," ibid. v. 17. "A righteous God [אל צדיק] and Savior, there is none besides me," ibid. v. 21. "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins," ibid. 43.25. "I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like a mist," ibid. 44.22. And the Father himself speaks thus concerning the Son: "Behold your God! He himself will come and save you," ibid. 35.4. "Say to the cities of Judah: Behold your God! Behold the Lord Jehovah will come," ibid. 40.9, 10. "I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and will save them in the Lord their God," Hos. 1.7. Therefore that Son who is to be given, and the Child who is to be born, is called "mighty God [אל גבור], Father of eternity," Isa. 9.6, and, to signify the human nature which he was about to assume, "Immanuel [עמנו אל], God with us," ibid. 7.14, 8.8. The Branch who is promised to David to be raised up is also said soon to be named "The Lord our righteousness [יהוה צדקנו]," Jer. 33.15. Although, therefore, no one is a Mediator who is not at the same time man, and the man, as such, is not God, nevertheless a mere and bare man [ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος], "not-Jehovah" [לא יהוה] (Deut. 32.27), could not be Mediator. Accordingly the Son is the Mediator, God, and is not less than the Father. For there is not a double Mediator but one; in whom whatever is divine is claimed by God, and whatever is human by the man.

units.la: XIX. Iccirco etiam Christus Mediator, & quà Mediator, religiosè advocandus est. Cùm enim, quà Mediator Deus sit, etiam quà Mediator adorandus est. Et cùm Jehova adorari debeat, etiam debet, qui factus est, quod est, sive qui secundum promissionem Israeli factus est in Deum, puta Redemptorem, Mediatorem, qui ipse Jehova est. Ut omnes τιμῶσι honorent Filium, sicut honorant Patrem; Joh. V. 23. Adorent eum omnes Angeli Dei, Hebr. I. 6. Superexaltavit eum Deus, ut in nomine Jesu omne genu flectat, Phil. II. 10, 11. Religiosa verò adoratio uni soli-que Deo debetur, Deut. VI. 13. X. 20. Matth. IV. 10. Apoc. XIX. 10. XXII. 9. & sicut Deo debetur, ita etiam ipsi ut Creatori & Mediatori debetur, quod plurib° Loc. XIV. Th. 26. in Explication. II. Præc. astruximus. Neque illud obstat, quòd Mediator Deus & homo est, & quà homo ad Mediatoris personam concurrens licèt, adorari tamen nondebet. Humanitas enim ad Mediatoris personam concurrit, non ut persona à persona λόγῳ separata, sed ut σύσσημα assumptum, vel adjunctum personæ τῷ λόγῳ per voluntatem & gratiam Patris & suam unitum, velut Templum, in quo ὁ λόγος habitaret & adoraretur; non quòd ipsum, cùm creatura sit, adoraretur. Unicum enim in Christo, ante & post ejus incarnationem σάρκωσις est, religiosa adoratione colendum, nempe τὸ ὁμοούσιον Deitatis & personæ Divina, cum qua caro ἀδιαιρέτως unita est, at adorari non debet. Hoc enim esset carnem θεοποιεῖν Deum facere. Neque refert, quòd Damascenus & cæteri Patres carnem adorandam esse docuerunt, quia illi vocabulo σαρκὸς carnis non humanitatem, sed hominem, hoc est, totam personam Christi intellexerunt. In adoratione verò Christi Mediatoris naturarum ejusdem dem proprietates nec confundendæ, nec æquandæ sunt; Sed à Christo Mediatore Deo id expetendum est; ut faciat secundum utramque naturam, quod illi secundum utramque naturam facere & operari proprie convenit. Nam Deitas per humanitatem ceu organum suum operatur. Ut ergo etiam quod humanitatis est, operetur, rite ab eo, non adorata licet humanitate, expetimus. Una enim est adoratio & λατρεία religiosa, qua, absque confusione & transfusione proprietatum Divinarum adoratur Christus, tantum qua parte Deus est, non qua parte homo est; & sub ratione illa formali, qua Mediator est; quia qua Mediator & formale objectum fidei est, quæ fertur in eum ut Salvatorem, datorem gratiæ & Sacerdotem unicum: & nos ut Semen suum & filios spirituales sibi animam suam sacrificium ponenti, Esaj. LIII. 10. promissos & ceu pueros sibi datos, Hebr. II. 13. intuetur; & tum in Baptismi Sacramento, ut veniens per aquam & sanguinem, 1. Joh. V. 6. purificans & lavans nos per sanguinem ab omni peccato, ibid. I. 7, Apoc. I. 5. aspergens nos sanguine, ceu Mediator novi fœderis, Hebr. XII. 24. tum in S. Cœna ut panis, qui è Cœlo descendit, carnem manducandam & sanguinem bibendum habens, Joh. VI. 32. &c. 51. 54. adoretur: & ceu sacerdos magnus, qui Cœlos transivit, tentatus in omnibus similiter absque peccato, cum fiducia adiri, ad consequendam misericordiam, & inveniendam gratiam debet, Hebr. IV. 14. 15. 16. Nimis ergo jejunè, ne dicam impiè vocem Mediatoris explicant, qui eum non primam causam efficientem, nec primum ac supremum authorem omnis boni & salutis, sed causam inferiorem instrumentalem, & hac ratione bonorum collatorem, in cujus nomine, propter quem, & per quem in Deum tendimus, in eum credimus, eum adoramus, interpretantur. Nam in Christo Mediatore causæ inferiori instrumentali ὁ λόγος, causa prima & principalis, instrumentalem elevans, perficiens, & per illam agens, personaliter unitus est. Neque is collator bonorum spiritualium est per instrumentum illud, quod in sua persona gestat, & per quod in diebus carnis suæ purificationem peccatorum operatus est; sed per Spiritum S. per quem nos baptizat, & unionis suæ participes nos reddit, Matth. III. 11.
