Instrumentum verò illud à nobis absens in Cœlo, in nos absentes causalitate causæ instrumentalis, in nos ad unctionis nostræ apotelesma influentis, agere, vel Spiritum S. in cordibus nostris arrhabonem dare non potest; quamvis ad unctionem nostram, & collationem bonorum spiritualium humana voluntas cum Divina conspiret, atque sic vicem causæ συνεργουμένης & procatarcticæ fungatur.
units.tr: XIX. For this reason also Christ the Mediator, and as Mediator, is to be invoked religiously. For since, as Mediator, he is God, he is also to be adored as Mediator. And since Jehovah must be adored, so also must he who has been made what he is, that is, who according to the promise has been made to Israel God, namely Redeemer and Mediator, who is himself Jehovah. "That all may honor the Son, as they honor the Father" (John 5.23). "Let all the angels of God worship him" (Heb. 1.6). "God has highly exalted him, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow" (Phil. 2.10, 11). But religious worship is due to one God alone (Deut. 6.13, 10.20; Matt. 4.10; Rev. 19.10, 22.9); and just as it is due to God, so it is also due to him as Creator and Mediator, which we have shown at length in Locus XIV, Th. 26, in the Explication of the Second Commandment. Nor does it stand in the way that the Mediator is God and man, and that the human nature, as contributing to the person of the Mediator, may be worshipped but ought not to be. For the humanity contributes to the person of the Mediator not as a person separated from the person of the Word, but as an assumed subsistence, or as something joined to the person of the Word and united to it by the will and grace of the Father and of himself, like a temple in which the Word dwells and is worshipped; not that the humanity itself, since it is a creature, is to be worshipped. For there is one thing in Christ, before and after his incarnation, that is to be honored with religious worship, namely the consubstantial [τὸ ὁμοούσιον] Deity and the divine Person with whom the flesh is united inseparably [ἀδιαιρέτως], but it is not to be worshipped as flesh. For this would be to make the flesh a god [θεοποιεῖν]. Nor does it matter that Damascene and the other Fathers taught that the flesh is to be worshipped, because by the word "flesh" [σάρξ] they understood not the humanity but the man, that is, the whole person of Christ. In the worship, however, of Christ the Mediator, the properties of the same natures are neither to be confused nor equated; but from Christ the Mediator, who is God, that is to be sought which it properly belongs to him to do and to effect according to each nature. For the Deity works through the humanity as through its instrument. Therefore, when we ask him rightly to work also what belongs to the humanity, we ask this of him without worshipping the humanity. For there is one adoration and religious worship [λατρεία] by which Christ is worshipped without confusion or transfusion of the divine properties, only in so far as he is God, not in so far as he is man, and under that formal aspect by which he is Mediator; because it is as Mediator that he is the formal object of faith, which is directed toward him as Savior, giver of grace and sole Priest; and it looks upon him as the one who gives his soul as a sacrifice for sin, and who sees his seed and spiritual children promised (Isa. 53.10), and given to him as children (Heb. 2.13). And he is to be worshipped then in the Sacrament of Baptism, as coming by water and blood (1 John 5.6), cleansing and washing us from every sin by his blood (ibid. 1.7; Rev. 1.5), sprinkling us with blood, as the Mediator of the new covenant (Heb. 12.24); and then in the Lord's Supper, as the bread which comes down from heaven, having flesh to be eaten and blood to be drunk (John 6.32, etc., 51, 54). And as the great priest who has passed through the heavens, tempted in all things like us, yet without sin, he is to be approached with confidence, to obtain mercy and find grace (Heb. 4.14, 15, 16). Therefore they explain the title of Mediator too meagerly, not to say impiously, who interpret him not as the first efficient cause, nor as the first and supreme author of all good and of salvation, but as an inferior instrumental cause, and in this way a bestower of goods, in whose name, on account of whom, and through whom we tend toward God, believe in him, and worship him. For in Christ the Mediator, the Word, the primary and principal cause, is personally united to the inferior instrumental cause, raising it up, perfecting it, and acting through it. Nor is he the bestower of spiritual goods through that instrument which he bears in his own person, and through which he effected the purification of sins in the days of his flesh; but through the Holy Spirit, by whom he baptizes us and makes us partakers of his union (Matt. 3.11). But that instrument, absent from us in heaven, cannot act upon us who are absent, by the causality of an instrumental cause flowing into the effect of our anointing, nor can it give the Holy Spirit in our hearts as a pledge; although human will concurs with the divine will for our anointing and for the bestowal of spiritual goods, and thus takes the place of a cooperating and preparatory cause.

units.la: XX. Mediator porro Christus est non quorumvis, seu inter quosvis; sed Deum inter & homines. Est enim μεσίτης Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων Mediator Dei & hominum, seu Deum inter & homines. 1. Tim. II. 5. Deus pars offensa, homo offendens est; uterque inimicus; ille, quia offensus ob legem ejus violatam, imaginem à se datam conspurcatam, gloriam dominii & independentiæ delibatam, sanctitatem amissam, & cum injustitia, quam naturaliter Deus odit, commutatam: hic ob ipsius peccati labem & offensam, cui insitum est odisse, quem læserit, inprimis quia natura conscius δικαιώματος juris il-
units.tr: XX. Christ is the Mediator not of just anyone, nor between just any parties, but between God and men. For he is "Mediator of God and men" [μεσίτης Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων], that is, between God and men (1 Tim. 2:5). God is the offended party; man is the offending party; both are enemies. God is the offended party because his law has been violated, the image he gave has been defiled, the glory of his dominion and independence has been impaired, holiness has been lost and exchanged for injustice, which God naturally hates. Man is the offender, and sin's stain and offence is naturally inclined to hate the one it has wronged, chiefly because man, being conscious by nature of the righteous ordinance [δικαίωμα] of that God,

units.la: lius Dei, secundum quod peccatores sunt ἄξιοι θανάτου morte digni, Rom. I. 32. judicem vindicémque gloriæ suæ novit & horret. Ira Dei ex Cœlo revelatur super omnem impietatem & injustitiam, ibid. I. 18. Inimici reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filii ejus, ib. V. 10. Neque obstat Mediatori, quòd etiam Filius offensus est. Nam sicqua Deus absolute pars offensa est, ut tamen quà Mediator, Deus & homo, idémque exinanitus, partes dissidentes Deum & hominem reconciliare possit œconomicè. Qui duplex in una persona respectus absurdus equidem videri non debet; cùm talem ipse Christus in parabola illa Filii à Patre familias ad agricolas infideles missi, Matth. XXI. 37. se ostenderit; & talem etiam mediationis actum à suis observandum disertè prescripserit, jubens fratrem nos offendentem μεταξὺ ἡμῶν καὶ αὐτὸν μόνον inter nos & ipsum solum reprehendere, atque ita, si mens huic læva non sit, κερδαίνειν lucrari, ibid. XVIII. 15. Exempla etiam eorum, qui offensi offendentes conciliarunt, in Scripturis & praxi hominum obvia sunt. Ita enim Deus apud primos parentes, Genef. III. 14. 15. &c. & per ministros suos apud omnes vocatos, 2. Cor. V, 19. 20. Israelitæ apud Benjaminitas, Judic. XX. 11. 12, &c. David apud rebelles subditos, 2. Sam. XIX. 12. &c. offensi omnes apud offendentes se interposuerunt. Olim etiam Senatu Romano à plebe dissidente, Menius Agrippa & ipse Senator Mediatoris Senatum inter & plebem munere perfunctus est. Neque insolens est, Regis filium in parente à subditis offensum, reconciliandis apud Patrem perduellibus Mediatorem se interponere.
units.tr: by which sinners are "worthy of death" [ἄξιοι θανάτου] (Rom. 1:32), knows and dreads him as the judge and avenger of his glory. "The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness" (ibid. 1:18). "We were reconciled to God through the death of his Son while we were enemies" (ibid. 5:10). Nor is it an objection to the Mediator that the Son too was offended. For God is the offended party absolutely, yet as Mediator, both God and man and the same one emptied of his glory, he can reconcile the disagreeing parties, God and man, in an economic sense. This double respect in one person ought not to seem absurd, since Christ himself showed it in the parable of the son sent by the householder to the faithless husbandmen (Matt. 21:37). He also expressly prescribed such an act of mediation to his own people, bidding us to reprove a brother who offends us "between us and him alone" [μεταξὺ ἡμῶν καὶ αὐτὸν μόνον], and so, if the mind is not perverse, "to gain" [κερδαίνειν] him (ibid. 18:15). Examples of offended parties who reconciled offenders are common both in Scripture and in human practice. Thus God dealt with the first parents (Gen. 3:14, 15, etc.), and through his ministers with all who are called (2 Cor. 5:19, 20). The Israelites dealt with the Benjaminites (Judg. 20:11, 12, etc.), and David with his rebellious subjects (2 Sam. 19:12, etc.). In each case the offended parties interposed themselves between the offenders. Formerly, too, when the plebs had fallen out with the Roman Senate, Menenius Agrippa, himself a senator, performed the office of mediator between the Senate and the plebs. Nor is it unusual for a king's son, when his father has been offended by subjects, to interpose himself as mediator with the Father to reconcile the rebels.

units.la: XXI. Neque aliorum Mediator Christus est, quàm hominum. Nam qui Angelorum etiam Mediatorem faciunt, Scripturarum præsidio destituuntur. Nusquam enim (nullibi Scripturarum) Angelos, sed semen Abrahæ assumpsit, Hebr. II. 16. Quorum verò Mediator Christus est, eorundem naturæ consors esse debet, uti ibid. V. 11. 12. &c. Apostolus demonstrat. Ideo Mediator hominum, 1. Tim. II. 5. novi Fœderis, Hebr. IX. 15. XII. 24. præstantioris Testamenti, ibid. VIII. 6. quod non utique cum Angelis, sed cum domo Judæ & Israelis initum est, Jerem. XXXI. 31. &c. appellatur. Cúmque Angeli nec offensi peccato nostro sint, ut pars principalis, cùm non Deus, sed servi Dei, adversus quos non peccavimus, sint: nec ipsi Deum offenderint, quia ceu sancti Matth. XXV. 31. semper voluntatem Dei in Cœlis faciunt, ibid. VI. 10. Psal. CIII. 20. 21. Mediatore equidem nulli indigent. Actus certè formales Mediatoris sunt προσκαλεῖν advocare, ἐντυγχάνειν intercedere, ἱλάσκειν placare, 1. Tim. II. 5. 6. Rom. VIII. 34. 1. Joh. II. 1. 2. qui similésque circa peccata & peccatores solos occupari possunt. Accedit, quòd in altera vita salutem adepti, non demum per Mediatorem adepturi ἰσάγγελοι Angelis similes futuri sumus, Luc. XX. 36. Non ergo Angeli Mediatore ad salutem indigent. Nam quòd per Christum & sanguinem crucis ejus omnia, εἴτε τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, εἴτε τὰ ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις sive ea, quæ in terra, sive ea, quæ in Cœlis sunt, in ipsum ἀποκαταλλάξαι reconciliari Apostolus Col. I. 20. & omnia quæ in Cœlis, & quæ in terra sunt, in eodem ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι recapitulari, seu unum in κεφαλαίωμα caput, summam redigi, idem
units.tr: XXI. Christ is the Mediator not of angels as well as of men. Those who make him the Mediator of angels too are without the support of Scripture. For "nowhere" does he take hold of angels, "but the seed of Abraham" (Heb. 2:16). Whoever has Christ as their Mediator must share the same nature, as the Apostle shows in the same place (Heb. 2:11, 12, etc.). Therefore he is called "the Mediator of men" (1 Tim. 2:5), "of the new covenant" (Heb. 9:15; 12:24), and "of a better testament" (ibid. 8:6), which was indeed made not with angels but "with the house of Judah and Israel" (Jer. 31:31, etc.). Since the angels are not offended by our sin as the principal party (they are not God, but servants of God, against whom we have not sinned), and they have not offended God himself, because as "holy" ones (Matt. 25:31) they always "do the will of God in heaven" (ibid. 6:10; Ps. 103:20, 21), they certainly have no need of a Mediator. The formal acts of the Mediator are to "call to" [προσκαλεῖν], to "intercede" [ἐντυγχάνειν], and to "propitiate" [ἱλάσκειν] (1 Tim. 2:5, 6; Rom. 8:34; 1 John 2:1, 2), and these can be exercised only in regard to sin and sinners. Moreover, we who obtain salvation in the other life will be "equal to the angels" [ἰσάγγελοι] and like them (Luke 20:36), not obtaining it later through a Mediator. Therefore the angels have no need of a Mediator for salvation. As for the Apostle's statement that through Christ and "the blood of his cross" all things, "whether things on earth or things in heaven" [εἴτε τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, εἴτε τὰ ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις], are reconciled "to him" [ἀποκαταλλάξαι] (Col. 1:20), and that all things "in heaven and on earth" are to be "summed up in one" [ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι] in the same one, that is, brought under one head [κεφαλαίωμα] and sum,

units.la: Mediator Iesus est Deum inter & homines, adeóque etiam se inter, quà Filius est, & homines.
units.tr: Jesus the Mediator is between God and men, and thus also between himself, as he is the Son, and men.

units.la: Non Deum inter & Angelos. dem Ephef.I.10. dixit,proprie non ad Angelos, sed Sanctos in terra degentes & Coelites referendum est. Hi enim, non illi Deo reconciliari, pace facta per sanguinem crucis Christi, debuerunt. Licet enim Coelites jam prius efficacia meriti Christi Deo reconciliati fuerint, tamen non ante mortem Christi praefente & actuali merito intercedente reconciliati sunt. Christus enim novi Testamenti Mediator propterea fuit, ut morte ejus intercedente eis ἀπολύτρωσιν τ ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ ad redemptionem praevaricationum sub primo Testamento promissionem acciperent vocati aeterna haereditatis, Hebr.IX.15. Semel in consummatione seculorum, ad abolitionem peccati, per victimam suam manifestatus est, ibid.v.26. Quomodo etiam Coelestes & Terrestres Sancti ad unam summam, seu unitatem τ πεπληρωμένων consummatorum redig', quatenus post mortem Christi Sancti terrestres ab omni servitute & accusatione peccati liberi, neque amplius servi, sed amici, gnari mysteriorum Christi, Joh.XV.15. coll.cum Ephef.I.9.perinde ut, qui jam in Coelis degebant, consummati sunt, neque etiam Coelites ipsi fine nobis consummari debuerunt, Hebr.XI.40. & Sancti terrestres ad spiritus justorum consummatorum pervenerunt, ibid.XII.23. Est ergo ἀνακεφαλαίωσις recapitulatio, hoc est, conjunctio & ἑνώσεις Unitio Coelestium & Terrestrium Sanctorum in libertate propter justitiam seculorum a Christo adductam. Ac licet etiam Angeli in Coelo sint, tamen illi nec Deo reconciliari debuerunt, quia ejus hostes nunquam fuerunt, nec ut pars principalis, nobis reconciliati sunt, sed ut συνδοῦλοι conservi; nec ad illud κεφαλαίωμα proprie pertinent, quia non in plenitudine demum temporum, & ejusdem oeconomia, sed statim a confirmatione sua consummati sunt. Ac licet Deus jervis suis (Angelis) non fidat, (quia fine Dei gratia perseverantem in bono voluntatem non habent, & boni licet, tamen non essentialiter, nec necessario boni sunt) & vel in Angelis stultitiam poneret (fi cum Deo contendere sustinerent; praeterquam quod eorum sapientia cum Divina comparata mera stultitia foret) Job.IV.18. XV.15. adeoque illi & Dei gratia confirmati sunt, & ejusdem gratia in justitia sua confervantur, lapsuri aeque ac Angeli apostatae, fi sibi permitterentur; tamen gratia Dei, qua in bono & confirmati sunt, & confervantur jugiter, Mediatoris Christi beneficio illis conciliata nuspiam dicitur. Ut saltem ἀγεσφῶν fit Mediatoris redemptionis & confirmationis, vel conservationis a nonnullis frequentata distinctio. Scriptura enim duplicis tantum Mediatoris, puta typici, Mosis, & veri Christi, Mediatoris Dei & hominum fe ipsum dantis ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus, 1.Tim.II.5. 6.& quidem μεσίτης ἑνὸς Mediatoris unius, adeoque etiam μεσιτείας mediationis unius ejusdem que meminit; & conservationem Angelorum cum eorundem creatione sic conjungit, Col.I. 16.17. ut v.18.19. eandem a redemptione Ecclesiae, cujus solius respectu Christus Mediator appellatur, manifeste distinguat. Quicquid ergo gratiae & beneficii Christus Angelis contulit, illud omne qua Deus, non qua μεσίτης Mediator, ac forte ne quidem qua μέσω medius, quia nec medius est inter Deum & Angelos, nec qua medius inter Patrem & Spiritum S. peculiare unendi munus accepisse uspiam dicitur, contulit. Plura eandem in rem Loc.VIII.29. diximus.
units.tr: Not between God and angels. Properly, the words of Ephes. 1:10 are to be referred not to angels but to saints living on earth and the heavenly ones. For these, not those, had to be reconciled to God, peace having been made through the blood of Christ's cross. For although the heavenly ones were already reconciled to God through the efficacy of Christ's merit, yet they were not reconciled before the death of Christ, through his present and actual merit interceding. For Christ was the Mediator of the new testament for this reason: that through his death interceding, those who are called might receive "the redemption of the transgressions under the first testament" (ἀπολύτρωσιν τῶν ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεων), the promise of eternal inheritance (Heb. 9:15). He was manifested once, at the consummation of the ages, for the abolition of sin through his sacrifice (ibid. 9:26). In the same way, the heavenly and the earthly saints are brought back into one sum, or unity, of the perfected ones, inasmuch as after Christ's death the earthly saints, free from all bondage and accusation of sin, are no longer servants but friends, knowing the mysteries of Christ (John 15:15, compared with Eph. 1:9), just as those who already dwelt in heaven were perfected. Nor ought the heavenly ones themselves to be perfected without us (Heb. 11:40), and the earthly saints came to the spirits of the just made perfect (ibid. 12:23). Therefore recapitulation (ἀνακεφαλαίωσις) is the conjoining and unification (ἕνωσις) of the heavenly and earthly saints in the liberty brought by Christ for the righteousness of the ages. And although angels too are in heaven, yet they neither had to be reconciled to God, since they were never his enemies, nor were they reconciled to us as the principal party, but as fellow-servants (συνδοῦλοι); nor do they properly belong to that head (κεφαλαίωμα), since they were perfected not in the fullness of times and of the same economy, but immediately from their confirmation. And although God does not trust his servants, the angels (since they have no will to persevere in good without the grace of God, and they are good, though not essentially nor necessarily so), and although he would lay folly upon the angels (if they dared to contend with God, quite apart from the fact that their wisdom compared with the divine would be sheer folly) (Job 4:18; 15:15), and though they have indeed been confirmed by his grace and are preserved in their righteousness by the same grace, liable to fall just as the apostate angels would have fallen if they had been left to themselves, yet the grace of God by which they were confirmed and are continually preserved is nowhere said to have been obtained for them by the benefit of the Mediator Christ. So that the distinction, frequently drawn by some, between the redemption of the Mediator and his confirmation or conservation is not obscure. For Scripture speaks of only two Mediators: the typical one, Moses, and the true Christ, Mediator of God and men, who gave himself as a ransom (ἀντίλυτρον) for all (1 Tim. 2:5, 6), and indeed it speaks of the one Mediator and of one mediation (μεσιτείας). Also, it joins the preservation of the angels with their creation in such a way (Col. 1:16, 17) that, in vv. 18, 19, it clearly distinguishes it from the redemption of the Church, with respect to which alone Christ is called Mediator. Whatever grace and benefit Christ has conferred upon the angels, he has conferred it all as God, not as Mediator (μεσίτης), nor perhaps even as one in the middle (μέσος), since he is not in the middle between God and the angels, nor is he said anywhere to have received a peculiar office of uniting as the middle one between the Father and the Holy Spirit. We have said more on this same matter in Loc. VIII.29.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Mediatio ipsa in καταλλαγῇ reconciliatione partium diffidentium consistit. Omnia sunt ἐκ Θεοῦ ἐξ καταλλάξαντος ex Deo, qui nos reconciliavit sibi per Jesum Christum, & dedit nobis ministerium reconciliationis. Veluti Θεὸς ἦν ἐν Χριστῷ κόσμον καταλλάσσων ἑαυτῷ Deus erat in Christo (in Christo Deus apparuit, Spiritus Domini ipso fuit) mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputans ipsis offensas eorum, 2.Cor.V.18.19. καταλλάσσειν reconciliare idem est quod πεῖσαι χάριτι, in gratiam recipere; ut perinde fit, reconciliavit nos sibi per Christum. ac fi dixisset, ἵνα ἐχάρισεν ἡμᾶς ἐν ἠγαπημένῳ in gratiam recepit nos, gratos nos fecit in dilecto, Ephef.I.6. In quo enim Deus nos acceptat, velut sibi gratos, non amplius ob peccatum hostes nauseatos, fastiditos, in eodem nos καταλλάσσει reconciliat. Etiam sic explicari potest, ut intelligatur Deus nobis Filium suum dedifle in pacem & acceptationem, ut καταλλαγή opponatur τῇ ἐχθρᾳ καὶ ὀργῇ inimicitiae & irae. Nam justificati sanguine ejus, salvabimur per eum ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς ab ira. Si enim ἐχθροὶ ὄντες καταλλαγέντες cum hostes fuissemus, reconciliati fumus; quanto magis reconciliati salvabimur in vita ejus, Rom.V.9.10. Ipse modus reconciliationis in eo consistit, quod Christus per sanguinem suum inimicitiam, quae ex peccato utrosque Deum & hominem inter gliscebat, sustulit, amicitiam restituit, atque id effecit, ut Deus ex judice damnante judex absolvens, & vitam donans fieret, μὴ λογιζόμενος τὰ παραπτώματα non imputans peccata hominibus, sed justitiam Christi illis imputans. Unde reconciliatio & passa dicitur per sanguinem crucis Christi, Col.I.20. Reconciliationis illius diversi veluti gradus fuerunt, puta discretio & dijudicatio causae inter partes diffidentes, offensum justum, & offendentem injustum: pactorum & conditionum, sub quibus partes fine detrimento sanctitatis & justitiae Dei postliminio coalescerent, expositio, & per sponsionem implendi eas susceptio: intercessio pro offendentibus: satisfactio pro iisdem: satisfactionis illius applicatio: & reconciliatorum conservatio & gubernatio. Ex quibus Christus alia apud Deum, alia apud homines peregit, atque peragit, ut vere fit Mediator Dei & hominum, 1.Tim.II.5.
units.tr: Mediation itself consists in reconciliation (καταλλαγῇ) of parties at odds. "All things are of God, who has reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ and has given us the ministry of reconciliation" [τὰ δὲ πάντα ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ καταλλάξαντος ἡμᾶς ἑαυτῷ διὰ Χριστοῦ, καὶ δόντος ἡμῖν τὴν διακονίαν τῆς καταλλαγῆς]. So too: "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself" [Θεὸς ἦν ἐν Χριστῷ κόσμον καταλλάσσων ἑαυτῷ], that is, God appeared in Christ, and the Spirit of the Lord was in him, "reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their offences to them" (2 Cor. 5:18, 19). To reconcile (καταλλάσσειν) is the same as to win over by grace (πεῖσαι χάριτι), that is, to receive into favour. So it comes to the same thing whether it says "he has reconciled us to himself through Christ" or "he has made us accepted" [ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ], that is, "he received us into favour, made us acceptable in the Beloved" (Eph. 1:6). For in whom God accepts us, as pleasing to himself, no longer as enemies loathed and despised on account of sin, in the same person he reconciles us to himself. It can also be explained in this way, that God gave us his Son for peace and acceptance, so that reconciliation (καταλλαγή) is set over against enmity and wrath [τῇ ἔχθρᾳ καὶ ὀργῇ]. For having been justified by his blood, we shall be saved through him "from wrath" [ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς]. For if, while we were enemies [ἐχθροὶ ὄντες], we were reconciled [καταλλαγέντες] by the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life (Rom. 5:9, 10). The very manner of reconciliation consists in this: that Christ, by his blood, removed the enmity which had flared up between God and man on account of sin, restored friendship, and brought it about that God, from a condemning judge, became a judge who absolves and gives life, "not reckoning their trespasses" [μὴ λογιζόμενος τὰ παραπτώματα] against men, but imputing to them the righteousness of Christ. Hence reconciliation is also said to be effected through the blood of the cross of Christ (Col. 1:20). There were, as it were, different stages of this reconciliation: namely, the examination and judging of the case between parties at odds, the offended party being just and the offender unjust; the setting out of the terms and conditions under which the parties could be joined again without loss to the holiness and justice of God, and the taking on of the obligation to fulfil them by promise; intercession for the offenders; satisfaction for them; the application of that satisfaction; and the preservation and governance of those reconciled. In these matters Christ has done, and continues to do, some things before God and others before men, so that he truly becomes the Mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2:5).

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Non ergo Mediatoris reconciliatio in sola adductione ad amorem Dei consistit, uti Socinus, Mediatorem deprimens, & Scripturas exenterans, fingit. Licet enim Christi morte ad amorem Dei invitemur, ut ex oforibus Dei ejusdem amasii fiamus: tamen in hoc amore reconciliatio cum Deo non consistit, quia reconciliationem sequitur, non facit. Deus enim non reconciliatus prius tantum abest ut ab hominibus diligi possit, ut potius, tanquam judex male dicens, & mortem peccatori intentans, non possit non horreri & odio haberi. Non potest mundus vos odisse, ἐμὲ δὲ μισεῖ me autem odit, ibid. VII. 7. Ubi vero reconciliatus homo est per sanguinem Christi, tum demum reconciliatio illa fit argumentum, quo suadetur amor Dei, & ratio Deum amandi, ei gratias agendi, & eundem glorificandi. Quia enim Deus fuit in Christo, mundum dum reconcilians sibi, non imputans iis offensas eorum: ideo in hominibus posuit ministerium reconciliationis, tanquam Deo per eos rogante petentibus: Καταλλαγῆτε τῷ Θεῷ Reconciliamini Deo, (convertimini, credite Evangelio, desinite odisse Deum, aversari cognitionem ejus; incipite amare Deum, ut reconciliati, filii, Evangelio, quod reconciliationis sermo est, obedientes: sanctificate eum, justificate, glorificate Deum, laudes ejus narrate, canite, Esaj.XLIII.21.) qui (vel quia) eum, qui non norat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut nos fieremus justitia Dei in eo, 2. Cor.V.19.20.21. Maxima enim amandi Deum & pacem cum eo colendi ratio est, quòd nobis peccatoribus, & gratia Dei indignis, id praestitit Deus, per quod justitia Dei fieremus, & eam in rem impendit, quod maximum est, ut eum, qui peccatum non noverat, peccatum, seu maledictionem propter peccatum fecit, ut nos fieremus justitia Dei in Christo, hoc est, in Christo essemus, habentes justitiam non illam, quae ex lege est, sed illam, quae est per fidem Christi, justitiam ex Deo in fide, Phil.III.9. Nam quòd Socinus reconciliationem à Mediatore impetratam μονόπλευρον facit, ex parte hominis solius, non Dei, ut homo conciliari debuerit Deo, at non homini Deus, utpote placatus & amans homines, non iratus, non hostis homini; Mediatoris veri abnegatio verissima est. Nam verus Mediator se ipsum dat ἀντίλυτρον pro hominibus, hoc est, λύτρον pretium solvit Deo, id apud Deum praestando, quod Lex à peccatore requirit, ad placandum & conciliandum eum, 1.Tim.II.5.6. Qui ergo Deum soluto pretio non placat, non peccatori conciliat, verus Mediator non est. Ideo S. Paulus non tantùm homines jubet reconciliari Deo, 2.Cor.V.20. sed etiam Deum nos reconciliasse ἑαυτῷ sibi (velut prius inimico, irato) per Jesum Christum, ibid.v.18.19. dixit. Quò inprimis Sacerdotium Christi spectat. Nam Christus Sacerdotio functus est apud Deum, victimam ei offerendo, & patrocinium peccatoris apud ipsum suscipiendo. Omnis enim sacerdos pro hominibus, vel loco hominum constituitur τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν in iis, quae ad Deum pertinent, ut offerat dona & victimas, Hebr.V.1. Vicariam igitur poenam Deo per sacrificium solvens Christus eum offensum reconciliavit. Ideo etiam Jesum Christum παράκλητον πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα, Patronum, advocatum apud Patrem habere dicimur, 1.Joh. II.1. qui ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐντυγχάνει pro nobis intercedit, Rom.VIII.34. & ἐμφανίζεται τῷ προσώπῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν in conspectu Dei pro nobis apparet; Hebr.IX.24. Sacerdos cum hostia, Patronus, advocatus apud Deum Patrem non offensum, non irascentem homini necessarius non est. Et Deus quidem hominem odit & amat. Odit, quia hominis ante ἱλασμὸν placamentum, quo Deus justificans sanctificatur, is status est, ut si placamentum non detur, salvari non posset, ira & odio Dei manente. Deus enim est מקור Deus vindicatarum Psal.XCIV.1. πῦρ καταναλίσκον ignis consumens, Hebr.XII.29. Mundi sunt oculi Dei, ne videat malum & ad iniquitatem respiciat, Habac.I.13. Peccatum odit, Psal.V.6. non liberè & contingenter, sed naturalis puritatis & sanctitatis suae necessitate, ut lux, quae necessitate naturae suae tenebras arguit & fugat, Joh.III.19.20. Ephes.V.11.13. 2.Cor. VI.14. de quo pluribus supra. Idem verò etiam amat τὴν εὐδοκίαν, propositum faciendo ante secula in Christo Jesu, Ecclesiam per sanguinem ejus ab ira redimendi; Ephes.I.5.&c. III.11. & τὴν ἐυαρέστιαν, gratos habens in Christo, qui in nobis per fidem habitat, ibid.1.6. III.17.
units.tr: The reconciliation of the Mediator therefore does not consist solely in drawing men to the love of God, as Socinus pretends, belittling the Mediator and gutting the Scriptures. For although we are invited by the death of Christ to love God, so that we become friends of God, yet reconciliation with God does not consist in this love, because reconciliation comes before it and does not result from it. For a God who has not yet been reconciled is so far from being able to be loved by men that, rather, as a judge who speaks evil and threatens death to the sinner, he cannot but be dreaded and hated. "The world cannot hate you, but me it hates" [ἐμὲ δὲ μισεῖ] (John 7:7). But when a man has been reconciled through the blood of Christ, then that reconciliation becomes the ground on which the love of God is urged, and the reason for loving God, giving thanks to him and glorifying him. For because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing to them their offences, therefore he has placed in men the ministry of reconciliation, as though God were entreating through them: "Be reconciled to God" [Καταλλάγητε τῷ Θεῷ], (that is, turn back, believe the Gospel, cease to hate God and to turn away from the knowledge of him; begin to love God; as reconciled sons, be obedient to the Gospel, which is the word of reconciliation; sanctify him, justify him, glorify God, recount his praises, sing: Isa. 43:21). "Him who knew no sin he made to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him" (2 Cor. 5:19–21). For the greatest way of loving God and cultivating peace with him is that God has granted to us sinners, who are unworthy of his grace, that through which we might become the righteousness of God; and to this end he has done what is greatest: he made him who knew no sin to be sin, or a curse on account of sin, so that we might become the righteousness of God in Christ, that is, that we might be in Christ, "having a righteousness not which is of the law, but which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith" (Phil. 3:9). For as for Socinus, who makes reconciliation obtained by the Mediator "one-sided" [μονόπλευρον], on the part of man only and not of God, so that man ought to be reconciled to God, but God not to man, as though he were appeased and loving toward men, not angry, not hostile to man: this is the most complete denial of the true Mediator. For the true Mediator gives himself as a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for men, that is, he pays the price [λύτρον] to God, by doing before God what the law requires of the sinner, in order to appease and reconcile him (1 Tim. 2:5, 6). He, therefore, who does not appease God by payment of the price, does not reconcile the sinner, and is not a true Mediator. Hence St Paul not only bids men "be reconciled to God" (2 Cor. 5:20), but also says that God has reconciled us to himself [ἑαυτῷ] (as formerly an enemy, an angry one) "through Jesus Christ" (ibid. 5:18, 19). This pertains above all to the priesthood of Christ. For Christ acted as priest before God, by offering himself as a victim and by taking up the advocacy of the sinner before him. For "every priest is appointed for men, or in the place of men, in those things which pertain to God" [τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν], to offer gifts and sacrifices (Heb. 5:1). Christ, therefore, by paying to God a vicarious penalty through sacrifice, reconciled the offended God to us. Hence we are also said to have Jesus Christ as our "advocate with the Father" [παράκλητον πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα], a "patron" and "advocate before the Father" (1 John 2:1), who "intercedes for us" [ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐντυγχάνει] (Rom. 8:34), and "appears in the presence of God for us" [ἐμφανίζεται τῷ προσώπῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν] (Heb. 9:24). A priest with a victim, a patron, an advocate before God the Father, is not needed for one who is offended and angry with man. And God indeed both hates and loves man. He hates him, because before the propitiation [ἱλασμός], the placating by which God is justified and sanctified, man is in such a state that, if no propitiation were given, he could not be saved, the wrath and hatred of God remaining. For God is "the God of vengeance" [מקור] (Ps. 94:1), "a consuming fire" [πῦρ καταναλίσκον] (Heb. 12:29). "Your eyes are too pure to look on evil, and you cannot look on iniquity" (Hab. 1:13). He hates sin (Ps. 5:6), not freely and contingently, but by the necessity of his natural purity and holiness, as light, which by the necessity of its nature exposes and drives out darkness (John 3:19, 20; Eph. 5:11, 13; 2 Cor. 6:14), of which we have spoken at greater length above. Yet he also loves [ἀγαπᾷ] "the good pleasure" [τὴν εὐδοκίαν], purposing before the ages in Christ Jesus to redeem the Church from wrath through his blood (Eph. 1:5, etc.; 3:11), and "the grace" [τὴν χαριτόω] "making us acceptable in Christ, who dwells in us through faith" (ibid. 1:6; 3:17).

units.la: XXIV. Impiè etiam in Mediatore Christo meritum ejus ab efficacia sic Remonstrantes aliique divellunt, ut ad reconciliationem actualem, & salutem hominis parum vel nihil Christo Mediatori relinquant. Non tantùm enim duplicem illum mediationis & salvationis modum, Christo proprium, cum modis aliis confundunt, asserentes Christum non esse Salvatorem solo praeconio, exemplo & martyrio, sed etiam vero erga Deum merito & efficacia: sed etiam duos hosce modos posteriores à se invicem divellunt, dum partim essentialem & inseparabilem eorum nexum negant, partim aliud objectum meriti, puta omnes & singulos homines, aliud objectum efficacia, solos credentes & in fide perseverantes, statuunt. Ac demum utrumque illum modum evertunt & destruunt. Nam & meritum tollunt, quia Christum cuiquam remissionem peccatorum, Spiritum S. & vitam aeternam meruisse inficiantur, & tantùm jus ac potestatem miserendi hominum, iisque salutis quas velit, conditiones praescribendi Patri acquisivisse pertendunt; pronunciantes insuper assa & cruda voce, meritum Christi non respicere homines immediatè, & salvo eo omnes homines damnari posse, si nemo eorum praescriptas conditiones implere velit: & efficaciam abnegant, dum vocationem, fidem ac novam obedientiam ita ab hominis arbitrio suspendunt, ut sola voluntas hominis causa sit, cur alii resipiscant & credant, alii non; ea sola, non gratia Christi ad salutem efficax sit, & efficacia ea sit circa salutem, non circa fidem, utpote consequens fidem sine Christi merito & efficacia ingeneratam, non eam praecedens. Quae vaegrandem in religione Christiana νομὴν gangraenam habent, & Christum Mediatorem pauperem nimis faciunt, Salvatorem verò plane configunt & crucifigunt.
units.tr: XXIV. Impiously too, the Remonstrants and others so tear apart the merit of Christ the Mediator from its efficacy that they leave little or nothing to Christ the Mediator for the actual reconciliation and salvation of man. For they not only confuse that twofold mode of mediation and salvation, proper to Christ, with other modes, asserting that Christ is the Saviour not only by proclamation, example and martyrdom, but also by true merit and efficacy before God; they also separate these two latter modes from each other, partly by denying their essential and inseparable bond, partly by setting up one object for the merit, namely all and each of men, and another object for the efficacy, namely only believers and those who persevere in faith. And finally they overturn and destroy both modes. For they abolish merit, since they deny that Christ merited for anyone the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit and eternal life, and they contend that he acquired for himself only the right and power to show mercy to men and to prescribe to the Father whatever conditions of salvation he wishes; they moreover pronounce, in a harsh and crude voice, that the merit of Christ does not regard men immediately, and that all men may be damned, even with that merit intact, if none of them is willing to fulfil the prescribed conditions. And they deny efficacy, since they make calling, faith and new obedience depend so much on man's will that the will of man alone is the cause why some repent and believe and others do not; that is the only thing that makes it effective for salvation, not the grace of Christ, and that efficacy concerns salvation, not faith, since it is supposed to follow faith and to be produced without the merit and efficacy of Christ, not to precede it. These doctrines have a great gangrene in the Christian religion, and make Christ a Mediator who is too poor, while they utterly strike down and crucify the Saviour.

units.la: XXV. Sed Christiana religio firmiter constantérque, ceu νυξίαν δόξαν, & ubique βεβαίου fidei dogma, tenet, quòd Christus Mediator & Salvator sit Merito utique & Efficacia, non quocunque, certè non impio & heterodoxo, verùm & Scripturis diserte tradito sensu, hoc est, μόνως adaequate, αδιαιρέτως indivise, & ενεργητικῶς effective. Merito Salvator est, quia sanguine suo salutem nobis acquisivit, Act.XX.28. Efficacia, quia acquisitam salutem confert, & collatam semel conservat. Utroque modo Salvator est μόνως adaequate, quia nullus aliis modus mediationis vel salvationis concurrit, à quo Christus κατ' ἐξοχὴν Mediator vel Salvator dici possit. Nam quòd insuper docendo & miracula patrando eum reconciliare & salvare nos nonnulli asserunt, generaliùs illi reconciliandi, salvandi rationem & modum considerant, non in eo, quod Christo proprium est, & per quod non à servis duntaxat, suis, Prophetis & Apostolis, sed ab ipso etiam Patre & Spiritu S. distinguitur, spectant, Etiam ἀδιαιρέτως indivise Christum meri-to &
units.tr: XXV. But the Christian religion firmly and constantly holds, as a manifest and everywhere certain dogma of faith [νυξίαν δόξαν; βεβαίου], that Christ is Mediator and Savior both by merit and by efficacy, and not in just any sense, certainly not in an impious or heterodox one, but in the sense plainly delivered in Scripture. That is, He is Mediator and Savior solely and adequately [μόνως adaequate], indivisibly [ἀδιαιρέτως indivise], and effectively [ενεργητικῶς effective]. He is Savior by merit because He acquired salvation for us with His own blood, Acts 20:28. He is Savior by efficacy because He confers the salvation He has acquired and, once conferred, preserves it. He is Savior in both ways solely and adequately [μόνως adaequate], because no other mode of mediation or salvation concurs by which Christ could be called Mediator or Savior above all [κατ' ἐξοχὴν]. For as to what some assert, that He also reconciles and saves us by teaching and by working miracles, they consider the manner and method of reconciling and saving in a more general way, and do not look to what is proper to Christ and by which He is distinguished not only from His servants, the prophets and apostles, but also from the Father and the Holy Spirit. Also, Christ is Mediator and Savior indivisibly [ἀδιαιρέτως indivise] by merit and by

units.la: In Mediatore, Christo non sic meritum abesse ejus divelli debet ut pro aliis meruisse simpliciter, pro aliis etiam efficaciter cum Remonstrantibus dicatur. to & efficacia Mediatorem & Salvatorem Scriptura definit, quia nec meritum ab efficacia divellit, nec omnino subjectis disparat. Nam efficacia meriti ejus finis & fructus est. Filium hominis exaltari decet, ut omnis in eum credens non pereat, sed vitam æternam habeat. Ita enim dilexit Deus mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum dederit, ut omnis in eum credens non pereat, sed vitam æternam habeat, Joh. III. 14. 15. 16. Eum, qui peccatum non novit, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut fieremus justitia in ipso, 2. Cor. V. 21. Christus nos redemit ab execratione Legis, factus pro nobis execratio, ut in gentes benedictio Abrahami fieret in Christo Jesu, Gal. III. 13. 14. Sine efficacia enim meriti Christus frustra mortuus esset. qui frustra mori non potuit, ibid. II. 21. Ego, dixi, in vanum laboravi, in cassum & frustra vim meam consumpsi. Certè judicium meum est apud Dominum, & opera pretium meum cum Deo meo, Esaj. XLIX. 4. Et justitia, remissio peccatorum & salus nostra ex merito Christi, ceu proprius effectus ex propria causa emanat. Et quibus Christus remissionem peccatorum, Spiritum S. & vitam æternam meruit, iisdem haec beneficia donat & applicat. Ut nec meritum efficacia latius, nec efficacia merito strictior fit. Propter laborem animæ suæ videbit semen, saturabitur. Cognitione sui justificabit justus servus meus multos, & iniquitates eorum portabit, ibid. LIII. 11. Posset tamen nec semen videre, saturari, qui labore an imæ plus quàm Herculeo defunctus est, si meriti efficacia penes hominum lubricitatem staret, & quod meruit, non donaret pariter iis, quibus meruit. Sed exceptione omni major illa Christi promissio est: Oves meas cognovi, & sequuntur me, & vitam æternam iis do, & non peribunt in æternum, & nemo eas ex manu mea rapiet, Joh. X. 27. 28. Talis ergo Pastor Christus est; qui odoratur timorem Domini, quippe non secundum visum oculorum, vel auditum aurium judicans, Esaj. XI. 3. sed corda inspiciens, Joh. II. 25. & eos, qui ipsi dati sunt, illuminans & flectens, ut praeuntem sequantur, & nemo eos rapiat, vel brabæo suo, æternâ vitâ ab eodem ipsis danda, defraudet. Nam qui proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro omnibus nobis eum tradidit, quomodo non cum ipso omnia nobis gratificabitur? Quis accusabit electos Dei? Deus est, qui justificat. Quis condemnans? Christus mortuus est, magis etiam resuscitatus, qui est in dextra Dei, qui pro nobis intercedit: Rom. VIII. 32--35. Denique ἐνεργητικῶς effectivè & emanativè cohærent, quia merito Christi, ceu ab eodem proximè emanans, non tantum nobis salus, nec salus mediante libera voluntate hominis, sed etiam remissio peccatorum, & Spiritus S. author fidei & novæ obedientiæ, acquisita est, ibid. III. 25. V. 8. 9. 10. & ejusdem efficacia non tantum nobis donatur salus, postquam credidimus, sed etiam Spiritus S. antequam credamus, ut poenitentiam, fidem, novam obedientiam, & perseverantiam in omni bono, salutem denique in nobis operetur. Ego cùm exaltatus fuero, omnes ad me traham, Joh. XII. 32. hoc est, efficacia justitiæ meæ, & potentia brachii mei, Esaj. LII. 9. 10. efficiam, ut per fidem, salutis causam, ad me veniant, confugiant. Per dextram Dei exaltatus, promissione Spiritus S. à Patre accepta, effudit illud, quod nunc videtis, & auditis, Act. II. 33. Hunc Deus Principem & Salvatorem exaltavit dextra sua, ut daret poenitentiam
units.tr: In the Mediator, Christ's merit must not be so separated from His efficacy that it is said, with the Remonstrants, that He merited simply for some and efficaciously for others. Scripture defines Him as Mediator and Savior by merit and by efficacy, because it neither divides merit from efficacy nor sets them at odds with each other in their objects. For the efficacy of His merit is its end and fruit. "The Son of man must be lifted up, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life," John 3:14–16. "He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him," 2 Cor. 5:21. "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us, that the blessing of Abraham might come upon the Gentiles in Christ Jesus," Gal. 3:13–14. For without the efficacy of His merit Christ would have died in vain, and He who could not die in vain, Gal. 2:21. "I said, I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing and in vain. Surely my judgment is with the Lord, and my reward with my God," Isa. 49:4. And righteousness, remission of sins, and our salvation flow from the merit of Christ as a proper effect flows from its proper cause. And to those to whom Christ merited remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, and eternal life, to these same people He gives and applies these benefits. So merit is not wider in its reach than efficacy, nor is efficacy narrower than merit. "He shall see the fruit of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied. By his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many, and he shall bear their iniquities," Isa. 53:11. Yet he could not see his seed or be satisfied, he who has undergone labor of soul greater than that of Hercules, if the efficacy of merit depended on the fickleness of men, and did not also give what it merited to those for whom it merited. But that promise of Christ is greater than any exception: "I know my sheep, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand," John 10:27–28. Christ is such a Shepherd; He "smells the fear of the Lord, judging not by the sight of the eyes or the hearing of the ears," Isa. 11:3, but "knowing the hearts," John 2:25, and He illumines and bends those who have been given to Him, so that they follow Him as their leader, and no one snatches them away, or cheats them of their prize, eternal life to be given them by Him. For "he who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? Who will accuse God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus is the one who died, and more than that, was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us," Rom. 8:32–35. Finally, effectively and emanatively [ἐνεργητικῶς effectivè & emanativè] they cohere, because by the merit of Christ, as flowing directly from Him, not only salvation but also remission of sins and the Holy Spirit, the author of faith and of new obedience, have been acquired for us, not salvation through the free will of man, Rom. 3:25, 5:8–10. And by His efficacy not only is salvation given to us after we have believed, but also the Holy Spirit is given before we believe, so that He may work in us repentance, faith, new obedience, perseverance in all good, and finally salvation. "When I am lifted up, I will draw all to myself," John 12:32, that is, by the efficacy of my righteousness and the power of my arm, Isa. 52:9–10, I will bring it about that they come to me and take refuge in me through faith, the cause of salvation. "Exalted at the right hand of God, having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out what you now see and hear," Acts 2:33. "God has exalted this man at his right hand as Prince and Savior, to give repentance"

units.la: & remissionem peccatorum Israeli, ibid. V. 31.
units.tr: "and forgiveness of sins to Israel," Acts 5:31.

units.la: XXVI. Officium Mediatoris Christi commune est omni statui Ecclesiæ post peccatum. Nam Christus Jesus heri & hodie idem est, & in seculA, Hebr. XIII. 8. Sed aliter tamen Mediator fuit ante incarnationem, aliter post eam. Ante incarnationem Mediator fuit tum futuro merito, ceu Agnus mactatus à jacto mundi fundamento, Apoc. XIII. 8. tum efficacia meriti futuri semper præsente, utpote per & propter quam etiam Patres ante Christum redempti, salvati sunt, Act. XV. 11. Hebr. II. 10. Meritum enim est in genere causarum moralium, quarum ea indoles est, ut effectum producant, antequam eæ actu existant, quomodo sponsio efficit, ut liberatio fontis solutionem pretii antecedere possit. Huc ergo Christi sponsio, intercessio pro peccatoribus, testificatio Patris de Filio, ipsius Filii de se, & Spiritus S. de eodem; denique sanctificatio seminis electi referendæ sunt. Spopondit enim Christus ante jacta fundamenta mundi. Eadem sponsio effecit intercessionem pro peccatoribus, postquam peccatum in mundum intravit. Quando enim homo peccavit, voluntas Filii, qua decrevit peccatores per justitiam suam vivificare, intercessio pro iis & semine electo, iram Dei ab eo avertens, facta est. In omni angustia eorum vix quisquam eos angustiis affecit, quin Angelus faciei Jehovæ (qui erat apud Deum, in quo, ceu imagine, Deus videbatur) eos salvaret. Is per dilectionem suam & clementiam suam asseruit ipsos (velut dicens Deo; Mei sunt, Tu mihi eos dedisti, pro iis satisfaciam, Joh. XVII. 6. 9.) suscepit eos & bajulavit eos omnibus diebus seculi (verbo potente sponsionis suæ, Hebr. I. 3.) Esaj. LXIII. 9. Si fuerit apud eum מלאך Angelus Interpres, unus ex mille, Job. XXXIII. 23. Sponsio hæc & intercessio actus Sacerdotis fuit. Accessit Testificatio Patris de Filio: Ecce Ego mitto Angelum meum, Exod. XXIII. 20. Benedicentur in eo omnes gentes terræ, Genes. XVIII. 18. Jehova dixit ad me: Filius meus es Tu, Psal. II. 7. Tantum in Jehova (de me dixit) justitia & robur. Ad eum accedet quisque: & pudefient omnes excandescentes in ipsum. In Jehova justificabuntur, & gloriabuntur omne Semen Israelis, Esaj. XLV. 24. 25. Concinit testificatio Filii de se: Ponam inimicitiam, Genes. III. 15. Fiam tibi in Deum, ibid. XVII. 7. Ecce venio. In volumine libri de me scriptum est, &c. Psal. XL. 8. Hæc testificatio, ad quam totum Dei verbum referendum est, Christo, ut Prophetæ & Regi, competit, quia locutus est, non ut Minister, sed ut Dominus & Rex per legatos suos, Hebr. I. 1. Denique etiam Christus sibi sanctificavit semen electum; sine discrimine, ante & post diluvium, usque ad vocationem populi Israelitici, quem velut peculium suum ex populis omnibus, cui innotescere t, delegit, & cujus electos cum paucis proselytis sanctificavit. In quo species quædam Regni fuit. Dein Sacerdotes etiam constituit, qui pecuinam & ἀλογον victimam, veri sacrificii typum & umbram, pro populo offerrent, quos velut vestitum induit, & suo tempore iterum exuit. Sed efficacia tamen hæc meriti futuri pro conditione temporis, qua Princeps, salutis per passiones nondum consummatus fuit, parcior, & obscurior fuit; uti in loco vidimus. Post incarnationem in statu quidem Exina-
units.tr: XXVI. The office of the Mediator Christ is common to every state of the Church after sin. For "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever," Heb. 13:8. Yet the Mediator was one way before the incarnation and another way after it. Before the incarnation He was Mediator both by future merit, as "the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world," Rev. 13:8, and by the efficacy of future merit always present, through and on account of which the Fathers also before Christ were redeemed and saved, Acts 15:11, Heb. 2:10. For merit belongs to the class of moral causes, whose nature is to produce their effect before they actually exist, as a promise brings about that the release of a debt may precede the payment of the price. To this belong, therefore, Christ's promise, His intercession for sinners, the Father's testimony concerning the Son, the Son's own testimony concerning himself, the Holy Spirit's testimony concerning the same, and finally the sanctification of the elect seed. "For Christ promised before the foundations of the world were laid." The same promise brought about intercession for sinners after sin entered the world. For when man sinned, the will of the Son, by which He had decreed to make sinners live through His righteousness, became intercession for them and for the elect seed, turning away God's wrath from them. "In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them; in his love and in his pity he redeemed them; he lifted them up and carried them all the days of old," Isa. 63:9 (as if saying to God: they are mine, you have given them to me, for them I will make satisfaction, John 17:6, 9; by the powerful word of his promise, Heb. 1:3). "If there be with him an interpreter, an angel, one among a thousand," Job 33:23. This promise and intercession was the act of the Priest. To it was added the testimony of the Father concerning the Son: "Behold, I send my angel," Exod. 23:20; "In him shall all the nations of the earth be blessed," Gen. 18:18; "The Lord said to me, You are my Son," Ps. 2:7; "Surely in the Lord (he said of me) are righteousness and strength; to him shall come, and all who are incensed against him shall be put to shame. In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified and glory," Isa. 45:24–25. The Son's testimony concerning himself agrees with this: "I will put enmity," Gen. 3:15; "I will be a God to you," ibid. 17:7; "Behold, I come. In the roll of the book it is written of me," etc., Ps. 40:8. This testimony, to which the whole Word of God is to be referred, belongs to Christ as Prophet and King, because He spoke not as a minister but as Lord and King through His envoys, Heb. 1:1. Finally, Christ also sanctified the elect seed for himself, without distinction, before and after the flood, down to the calling of the Israelite people, whom He chose from all peoples as His own possession, to be made known, and whose elect, together with a few proselytes, He sanctified. In this there was a certain image of a kingdom. Then He also appointed priests, who would offer for the people the sacrificial animal, the type and shadow of the true sacrifice, whom He clothed as with a garment and in due time stripped off again. But this efficacy of future merit, according to the condition of the time, in which the Prince of salvation had not yet been consummated through sufferings, was more sparing and more obscure, as we have seen in its place. After the incarnation, indeed in the state of exinanition

units.la: Mediatoris Christi commune est omni statui Ecclesiæ post peccatum, sed diversimode ante & post ejus incarnationem administratum. Exinanitionis factus est Mediator & Salvator tum merito præsente, quia animam suam λυτρον pro multis posuit, Matth.XX.28. & Ecclesiam sanguine suo acquisivit, Act.XX.28. tum efficacia, quia Filius hominis potestatem habuit in terra remittendi peccata, Matth.IX.6. & actu ea remisit, Luc.VII.48. & Spiritu S.baptizavit, Matth.III.11. & vitam æternam donavit, Luc. XXIII.43. Joh.X.28. sed efficacia tamen quamvis illa V.T. major; tamen respectu status exaltationis minor fuit; adeo ut nondum glorificato eo Spiritus S.nondum fuerit, ibid.VII.39. & Christus, ad Patrem proficiscens eundem discipulis, licet aliquatenus eo jam donatis, Luc.IX.55. promiserit, Act.I.5.8. sed in statu exaltationis Mediator & Salvator idem est, tum merito præterito, quia semel ex morte resuscitatus, non amplius moritur, Rom.VI.9.10. tum efficacia ejusdem amplissima & evidentissima, quam effusione Spiritus S. in omnem carnem, Act.II.16. 17.33. missione doctorum omnis generis, Ephes.IV.11. & prædicatione Evangelii per totum orbem terrarum, ac multorum millium conversione, Matth.XXVIII.19. Act.II.41.47. &c. testificatus est.
units.tr: The office of Mediator Christ is common to every state of the Church after the fall, but it was administered in different ways before and after his incarnation. In his state of humiliation, the Mediator and Saviour acted both by his merit, which was then present, since he gave his soul as a ransom [λυτρον] for many, Matt. 20:28, and acquired the Church with his own blood, Acts 20:28; and by his efficacy, since the Son of Man had power on earth to forgive sins, Matt. 9:6, actually forgave them, Luke 7:48, baptized with the Holy Spirit, Matt. 3:11, and bestowed eternal life, Luke 23:43; John 10:28. Yet this efficacy, though greater than under the Old Testament, was less than in the state of exaltation. So much so that, before he was glorified, the Holy Spirit was not yet given, John 7:39, and Christ, departing to the Father, promised the Spirit to his disciples, although they had already received him in some measure, Luke 9:55, Acts 1:5, 8. But in the state of exaltation the Mediator and Saviour is the same, both by his past merit, since, once raised from death, he no longer dies, Rom. 6:9, 10, and by his most ample and evident efficacy, which he attested by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit on all flesh, Acts 2:16, 17, 33, by the sending of teachers of every kind, Eph. 4:11, and by the preaching of the Gospel throughout the whole world and the conversion of many thousands, Matt. 28:19; Acts 2:41, 47, etc.

units.la: XXVII. Triplex Mediatoris Christi Officium est, Propheticum, Sacerdotale & Regium.
units.tr: XXVII. The threefold office of Mediator Christ is prophetic, priestly and kingly.

units.la: Nam Jesus Christus nobis factus est Sapientia, Justitia, Sanctificatio & Redemptio, 1.Cor.1.30. Sapientia; ut Propheta Cœlestis Sapientiæ doctor, ea nobis revelans, quæ à Patre audivit: Justitia, ut Sacerdos veram justitiam afferendo se ipsum nobis impetrans; Sanctificatio, ut Rex veræ, interna & spiritualis illius sanctitatis & gloriæ Cœlestis author. Quibus partibus λυτρωσις Redemptio perficitur. Tum Christum Mediatorem verum unctio V.T. adumbravit. Christus enim corpus est umbrarum, quas inter Unctio non postrema fuit, adeo ut ab unctione Χριστος Unctus dicatur. Nam corporalis unctorum veterum spiritualem Jesu figuravit. Trium autem generum homines, Prophetas, Sacerdotes & Reges ungi olim consuêsse, supra ostendimus. Cum ergo antiquæ unctionis veritas in Christo quærenda sit, sicut Prophetæ, Sacerdotes & Reges externis unctionibus muneri suo consecrati sunt; ita Christus à Deo ipso unctus Propheta, Sacerdos & Rex existere debuit. Et Mosen Prophetam Christi Prophetæ, Aharonidas Sacerdotes Christi Sacerdotis, & Reges populi Israel, Davidem inprimis Christi Regis typum gessisse, abunde liquet. Accedit nativa hominis peccato corrupti conditio & indigentia, cui subleyandæ Christus Mediator factus est. Nam natura homo & ignorantia rerum spiritualium tenebris immersus; & à Deo alienatus, & ad eundem redeundi plane impos est. Christus igitur, qui venit σωσαι το ἀπολωλος salvaturus id, quod periit, Matth.XVIII.11. triplici huic miseriæ averruncandæ triplicem medelam opposuit, Nam ignorantiam, ut Propheta, pepulit, Matth. XXIII.10. alienationem à Deo & vita ejus, ut Sacerdos, sustulit, Ephes.II.13. & impotentiam redeundi ad Deum, ut Rex, supplevit, Psal.XXIII.3.4. CXXXIX.24. Apoc.VII.17. Insuper salutis nobis conferendæ ratio triplex isthoc munus Christo imposuit. Nam & de salute, in cujus fruitione felicitas nostra consistit, nos instruere, ut Propheta per doctrinam: & eandem Legis sancte faciendo acquirere, ut Sacerdos per sanguinem & acquisitam salutem conferre, ut Rex per spiritum suum debuit. Denique sic munus etiam suum executus est. Nam primo voluntatem Patris docuit, & doctrinam suam miraculis obsignavit, ut Propheta: tum Sacerdotem se gessit, offerendo in terra sanguinem proprium, & cum eodem cœleste sanctuarium ingrediendo, ibique coram facie Patris se sistendo: ac demum in Cœlo, ut Rex coronatus gloriâ, ad dextram Patris consedit. Sed variat tamen ordo intentionis & executionis. Nam in ordine intentionis præcedit Regnum, ceu Mediationis finis, quia Deus ante omnia Filio ut Regi multos fratres gloria æterna implendos dedit: excipit Sacerdotium, ut medium ad hunc finem, quia propter hanc causam ei datum est justitiam parare: ac demum Propheta subsequitur, quia ei ut Prophetæ datum est justitiam, salutem & gloriam ad obedientiam fidei annuntiare. Contrarius plane ordo executionis est, in quo Christus primo tanquam Propheta, justitiæ ac salutis præco extitit; inde, tanquam Sacerdos ad altare accedens, Deo Patri se ipsum victimam obtulit; & postremo tanquam Rex ad dextram Dei consedit. Hæc tamen, ceu connexa simul Christo data sunt; & sic implicantur, ut nec Sacerdos & Propheta esse desierit, nec Rex Sacerdotium plane exuerit. Nam Sacerdos manet in seculum, Hebr. VII.21. Ps.CX.4. & Regni ejus finis non est, Luc.I.33.
units.tr: For Jesus Christ has been made to us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, 1 Cor. 1:30. As wisdom, he is the heavenly prophet and teacher of heavenly wisdom, revealing to us what he heard from the Father. As righteousness, he is the priest who, by offering himself, obtains true righteousness for us. As sanctification, he is the king and author of that true, inward and spiritual holiness and heavenly glory. By these parts redemption [λυτρωσις] is accomplished. The anointing of the Old Testament also prefigured Christ as true Mediator. For Christ is the body of those shadows, among which anointing was not the least, so that from the anointing he is called Christ [Χριστος], that is, the Anointed. For the bodily anointing of the ancients prefigured the spiritual anointing of Jesus. We have shown above that men of three kinds, prophets, priests and kings, were anciently accustomed to be anointed. Since, then, the truth of the ancient anointing is to be sought in Christ, just as prophets, priests and kings were consecrated to their office by external anointings, so Christ ought to exist as prophet, priest and king, anointed by God himself. And it is abundantly clear that Moses bore the type of Christ the prophet, the sons of Aaron the type of Christ the priest, and the kings of the people of Israel, and David above all, the type of Christ the king. To this is added the natural condition and need of man, corrupted by sin, for relieving which Christ was made Mediator. For by nature man is immersed in the darkness of ignorance of spiritual things, is alienated from God, and is wholly unable to return to him. Christ, therefore, who came "to save that which was lost" [σωσαι το ἀπολωλος], Matt. 18:11, opposed a threefold remedy to this threefold misery: as prophet he drove out ignorance, Matt. 23:10; as priest he removed the alienation from God and from his life, Eph. 2:13; and as king he supplied the inability to return to God, Ps. 23:3, 4; 139:24; Rev. 7:17. Moreover, the threefold manner of conferring salvation on us imposed this threefold office on Christ. For, as prophet, he was to instruct us about the salvation in whose enjoyment our happiness consists, through his teaching; as priest, he was to procure it by making satisfaction for the law through his blood, and to bestow it, as the salvation acquired, by which we are made holy; and as king, he was to confer it through his Spirit. Finally, he also carried out his office in this way. First, as prophet, he taught the will of the Father and confirmed his doctrine by miracles. Then he acted as priest, offering his own blood on earth and entering with it into the heavenly sanctuary, there presenting himself before the face of the Father. And at last, in heaven, as king crowned with glory, he sat down at the right hand of the Father. Yet the order of intention and the order of execution differ. In the order of intention, the kingdom comes first, as the end of the mediation, because God, before all things, gave the Son, as king, the many brothers to be filled with eternal glory. Next comes the priesthood, as the means to this end, since for this cause it was given to him to procure righteousness. Lastly, the prophetic office follows, since as prophet it was given him to announce righteousness, salvation and glory to obedience of faith. The order of execution is plainly the reverse: in it Christ first appeared as prophet, the herald of righteousness and salvation; then, approaching the altar as priest, he offered himself as victim to God the Father; and finally, as king, he sat down at the right hand of God. Yet these were given to Christ as things joined together, and they are so intertwined that he neither ceased to be priest and prophet, nor did the king altogether put off the priesthood. For the priest remains for ever, Heb. 7:21; Ps. 110:4, and of his kingdom there is no end, Luke 1:33.

units.la: XXVIII. Prophetia Christi est, qua is voluntatem Dei de nostra salute sibi immediatè monstratam plenè planeque revelavit.
units.tr: XXVIII. Christ's prophetic office is that by which he fully and plainly revealed the will of God concerning our salvation, which was shown to him immediately.

units.la: Fecit id, ut Deus, & Dei Filius ante Incarnationem, ut Angelus Jehovæ, hoc est, is, qui mittendus erat à Jehova, assertor Seminis Abrahami, & Sponsor Testamenti. Is enim, qui Serpentem inter & mulierem inimicitiam posuit, Sanctificator fidelium jam in Paradiso locutus est, Gen.III.15. Fuit enim antequam Abrahamus esset, Joh.VIII.58. Jacobi Goel fuit, Genes.XLVIII.16. Hos.XII.4.5. Mosi in rubo apparuit, Exod.III.4.6. à cujus gratia idem Moses benedictionem precatus est, Deut.XXXIII.16. cum quo etiam locutus fuit die magni comitii, Act.VII.38. Ideo המדבר Loquentis ei nomen fuit. Propterea cognoscet populus meus nomen meum, quòd ego ille המדבר Loquens, seu, qui locutus sum, Ecce me. Esaj.LII.6. Ego, Ego locutus sum (non ut alius, sed אני ut Ego) adduxi illum (Cyrum) & prosperavit viam suam. Accedite ad me, audite hoc; לא מראש בסתר Non ab initio in occulto locutus sum, ante tempus, quo id extitit, Ego ibi eram. Et nunc Dominus misit me, & Spiritus ejus, ibid.XLVIII.15.16. Pertinent hæc ad tempus restitutionem Templi sequens, & eundem locutum esse ante Templi restitutionem, ab initio, & post Templi restitutionem missum esse: ejusdem esse vocare Cyrum, & mitti à Deo & Spiritu ejus, significant. Apud Danielem המדבר פלמוני nomine venit. Et audivi unum Sanctum loquentem, dixitque alter Sanctus המדבר לפלמוני Palmoni loquenti; usque quò visio jugis sacrificii? cap.VIII.13. Ubi פלמוני idem est quod פלוני אלמוני ὁ δεῖνα, ἀνώνυμος, non nemo, Ruth.IV.1. qui Christus intelligitur, habens occulta in numerato (unde vocem eam à מלא Mirabile, arcanum, & מנה numeravit nonnulli nulli derivant; haud inscita saltem πεῳδῖα) gnarus ἐπιλύειν dissolvere, interpretari parabolas, ænigmata, Marc. IV.34. quale illud fuit, quod ille Palmoni loquens statim vers.14. extricavit; & AngeloGabrieli, ut Danielem visionem istam suo velut Loquentis, nomine doceret, ceu Angelo major v.16. præcepit. Verus adeò nnyb nnbx Zophnath-Paaneach, ἑιδὼς τὰ κρυφία, ἐυρετὴς τῶν κρυφίων Arcanorum Magister & inventor Christus fuit, cujus typum sub tali nomine Josephus gessit, Genef. XLI.45. Verus itidem מבין חידות Doctor, Magister ænigmatum; Cujus ea in re vicarium Antichristus se venditat, Dan. VIII.23. sed verius longè de se Christus dicit: Aperiam in parabola os meum, אפתח במשל חידות scaturiginis more effundam ænigmata ab antiquo, Psalm. LXXVIII.2. Ille enim maxima cum certitudine eructavit, scaturivit ænigmata, hoc est, revelavit μυστήριον χρόνοις αιωνίοις σεσιγημένον Mysterium temporibus secularibus (מקדם ab antiquo, uti Psalmus loquitur) tacitum, Rom. XVI.25. Nunquam enim narratum est, uti factum est, licet futurum prædictum fuerit; at non ita clare tamen prædictum, uti factum est, neque ita prius recitatum, uti postea visum & auditum est. Utpote cujus quædam partes non dictæ sunt, & totus ordo atque καιροὶ tempora in Dei potestate reposita manserunt, Act. I.7. Ephes. III.5. 1.Petr. I.10.11.12. Sunt etiam alia Prophetæ synonyma. Nam & Pastor ille Magnus, quem Deus olim promittebat Ecclesiæ, Esaj. XL.11. Ezech. XXXIV.23: 24. tanquam עמיתי גבר Virum proximum suum, Zach. XIII.7. & in tempore eidem exhibuit, Matth. XXVI.31. Joh. X.2.14. &c. Hebr. XIII.20. tanquam Pastorem & Episcopum animarum, 1.Pet. II.25. Rabbi & καθηγητὴς Doctor atque Ductor unicus, Matth. XXIII.10. & Ἀπόστολος ὁμολογίας Apostolus confessionis nostræ, Hebr. III.1. appellatur.
units.tr: He did this as God and as the Son of God before the Incarnation, as the Angel of Jehovah, that is, the one who was to be sent by Jehovah, the champion of the seed of Abraham and the Surety of the covenant. For he who put enmity between the serpent and the woman, the Sanctifier of the faithful, already spoke in Paradise (Gen. 3.15). For he was before Abraham was (John 8.58). He was the Redeemer of Jacob (Gen. 48.16; Hos. 12.4, 5). He appeared to Moses in the bush (Exod. 3.4, 6), and from his grace Moses sought a blessing (Deut. 33.16). With him Moses also spoke on the day of the great assembly (Acts 7.38). Therefore his name was [המדבר] the Speaker. So "my people shall know my name, that I am he [המדבר] who speaks, or who has spoken: Behold, here I am" (Isa. 52.6). "I, I have spoken (not as another, but [אני] as I). I have brought him (Cyrus) and he has prospered his way. Come near to me and hear this: [לא מראש בסתר] I have not spoken in secret from the beginning; before the time when it came to be, I was there. And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit" (ibid. 48.15, 16). These words refer to the time following the restoration of the Temple, and they signify that the same one who had spoken from the beginning, before the restoration of the Temple, was sent after it; that to call Cyrus and to be sent by God and his Spirit belong to the same one. In Daniel he comes under the name [המדבר פלמוני]: "And I heard one Holy One speaking, and another Holy One said to [המדבר לפלמוני] Palmoni, who was speaking, 'How long will the vision of the continual sacrifice last?'" (ch. 8.13). Here פלמוני means the same as פלוני אלמוני, ὁ δεῖνα, ἀνώνυμος, "someone," "a certain one" (Ruth 4.1). He is understood to be Christ, who has hidden things stored up (some derive the word from מלא, wonderful, secret, and מנה, to number; this is certainly no uninformed guess) and who knows how to [ἐπιλύειν] unravel and interpret parables and riddles (Mark 4.34). Such was the riddle that this Palmoni, speaking, immediately unravelled at v. 14. And he commanded the angel Gabriel to teach Daniel this vision under the name of the Speaker, as one greater than an angel (v. 16). Indeed the true [nnyb nnbx] Zaphnath-Paaneah, [ἑιδὼς τὰ κρυφία, ἐυρετὴς τῶν κρυφίων] knower of hidden things and discoverer of hidden things, was Christ, the master and discoverer of secrets, whose type Joseph bore under such a name (Gen. 41.45). Likewise the true [מבין חידות] Teacher, master of riddles: in this matter Antichrist puts himself forward as Christ's vicar (Dan. 8.23). But far more truly Christ says of himself: "I will open my mouth in a parable, [אפתח במשל חידות] I will pour out riddles from of old, like a spring" (Ps. 78.2). For he most certainly sent forth riddles like a spring, that is, he revealed the [μυστήριον χρόνοις αιωνίοις σεσιγημένον] mystery kept silent through eternal ages, (from [מקדם] of old, as the Psalm says) kept hidden (Rom. 16.25). For it was never told in the way it was done, though it had been foretold that it would happen. Yet it was not foretold as clearly as it was done, nor was it recited beforehand in the way it was afterwards seen and heard. For some parts of it were not spoken of, and the whole order and [καιροὶ] times remained reserved in God's power (Acts 1.7; Eph. 3.5; 1 Pet. 1.10–12). There are also other synonyms for prophet. For that Great Shepherd whom God once promised to the Church (Isa. 40.11; Ezek. 34.23, 24), as [עמיתי גבר] the man who is my fellow (Zech. 13.7), and who presented himself at the proper time (Matt. 26.31; John 10.2, 14, etc.; Heb. 13.20), is called Shepherd and Bishop of souls (1 Pet. 2.25); Rabbi and [καθηγητὴς] Teacher and sole Guide (Matt. 23.10); and [Ἀπόστολος ὁμολογίας] Apostle of our confession (Heb. 3.1).

units.la: XXIX. Nunquam non Christus Propheta fuit, sicut nunquam non Salvator & Mediator, sed tum maximè, cùm in carne apparuit, ceu Apostolus confessionis, Heb. III.1. hoc est, missus in carnem secundum promissionem, ut verba Dei loqueretur, in quæ non tantum jurar&mus, & cui Amen responderemus, fœdus & pacem cum Deo facientes, Esaj. XXVII.5. sed quem etiam auctorem justitiæ & vitæ confitentes Deo gloriam daremus, ei astipularemur, & sic justi & amici Dei fieremus.
units.tr: XXIX. Christ was always a Prophet, just as he was always Saviour and Mediator, but he was so especially when he appeared in the flesh, as the Apostle of our confession (Heb. 3.1). That is, he was sent in the flesh according to the promise, to speak the words of God; to these words we not only swear allegiance, and to which we respond Amen, making covenant and peace with God (Isa. 27.5), but also, confessing him as the author of righteousness and life, we give glory to God, agree with him, and so become righteous and friends of God.

units.la: Multifariè enim & multis modis Deus olim Patribus locutus est per Prophetas, sed in novissimo diérum locutus est nobis in Filio, Hebr. I.1. Talis Propheta diserte promissus est. Prophetam è medio tui, è fratribus tuis (Israelitam, habentem carnem & sanguinem fratrum) כמני sicut ego (non minorem me, qui omnibus Prophetis aliis majorem sum, Num. XII.6.7.8. & me ipso etiam major, quia de ipso testatus sum, Joh. V.46.) suscitabit tibi Jehova. Illum audietis, Deut. XVIII.15. Et mox Deus ipse; Prophetam suscitabo illis de medio fratrum suorum, sicut tu; & ponam verba mea in ore ejus, & loquetur eis omnia, quæ præcepero illi. Erit autem, quicunque non audiverit verba mea, quæ loquetur in nomine meo, ego requiram ab eo, ibid. v.18.19. Manifestè Propheta ille futurus à Mose distinguitur. Nam Moses non potuit loqui verba Dei, sed à Deo præcepta & præscripta annuntiare, prædicare tantùm, ut alienâ, non propria, ut loquens ex terra, non ex Cœlo potuit; sed Propheta ille promissus Verba Dei locutus est, ut Deus, ut loquens ex Cœlo. Qui ex terra est, ex terra loquitur. Qui ex Cœlo venit, supra omnes est. Et quæ vidit ac audivit, testatur. Quem enim misit Deus, τὰ ῥήματα Θεοῦ λαλεῖ verba Dei loquitur, Joh. III.31.32.34. hoc est, loquetur, testabitur τὰ λαλήσ quæ loquenda supersunt, Hebr. III.5. absolvit sermonem Dei, quem is, ut Deus Israelis, adhuc ad Israelem & ad Gentes loqui volebat, quémque eum loqui, ut nomini huic satisfaceret, conveniebat, qualia sunt: Respicite ad me & salvamini omnes fines terræ, Esaj. XLV.22. hoc est; Credite in me, quòd ego sum justitia, salus, victoria. Qui enim post omnes expectandus fuit, is aut talia verba, nunquam hactenus audita loqui debuit, aut frustra expectandus fuit. Non enim potuisset loqui, nisi ex terra, ut Johannes, & quivis alius. Atque ita Deus non haberet eos sermones ad Israelem, quos ipsum fundere ad populum oportuit, cùm Deus illorum Deus, sanctificator, justitia, clypeus, salus, denique Pater ipsorum factus esset. Ex quibus liquidum est, verba Dei apud Mosen: Ponam verba mea in ore ejus, tantundem significare, ac si dixisset: Loquetur ea verba, quæ Israel expectare, desiderare debet, ut aliquando audiat ex Deo suo, ut in eo lætari, ei gratias agere, & consummatè glorificari posset. Loquetur verba mea, ut sua, quia Ego Pater & Propheta ille erimus unum; & ego Angelus Dei ille Propheta ero. Nam & Moses quidem ea verba, quæ Israel auditurus erat, locutus est, testis quippe eorum quæ loquenda erant, Hebr. III.5. Neque tamen de eo dictum est, vel dici potuit: Ego ponam verba mea in os ejus, sed de alio Propheta à Mose distincto Deus illa dixit. Ideo Jesu Christo soli oraculum illud vindicarunt & Johannes Baptista, ingenuè negans, se Prophetam illum esse, Joh. I.21. & Mulier Samaritana, dicens: Scio, quòd Messias ὁ λεγόμενος Χριστὸς qui Christus dicitur, veniet, ἀναγγελεῖ ἡμῖν πάντα annuntiabit nobis omnia, ibid. IV.25. & S.Petrus Act. III.22.23. illud Christo, & quidem cum Pronomine demonstrativo, tanquam τῷ ῥήτῃ ἐκείνῳ Prophetæ illi, ne verba illa per enallagen numeri ad omnes Prophetas sequentes, sed ut singulariter ad Prophetam principem, Christum referenda esse constet, diserte applicans: & S.Paulus Christum in Prophetici muneris functione generatim supra Prophetas V.T. Hebr. I.1. nominatim supra Mosen, ut servum inferiorem ipso Filio Dei, omnium Domino, Ibid. III.1-6. efferens. Et verò necesse plane fuit, ut veniret aliquando Propheta ille eximius, qui verba Dei loqueretur, quia justitia nisi per Filium Dei adduci non potuit, & Regnum illi dandum fuit, & non tantum expectari secundum promissionem, sed etiam videri, & Evangelium ex ore ejus ad lætitiæ consummationem, audiri, & de ipso dici: Ecce Deus vester, Esaj. XL.9. & ipse de se dicere: Ego sum, qui loquitur, hoc est, Ego loquor, non alius, ibid. LII.6. debuit.
units.tr: God, who in many portions and in many ways spoke of old to the fathers through the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son (Heb. 1.1). Such a Prophet was expressly promised: "A prophet from among you, from your brethren, like me [כמני]" (an Israelite, having the flesh and blood of his brethren; not less than me, who am greater than all the other prophets, Num. 12.6–8, and even greater than myself, since I bore witness to him, John 5.46), "Jehovah your God will raise up for you. Him you shall hear" (Deut. 18.15). And soon God himself says: "I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren, like you, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. And it shall be that whoever does not hear my words, which he speaks in my name, I will require it of him" (ibid. vv. 18, 19). Clearly that future Prophet is distinguished from Moses. For Moses could not speak the words of God; he could only announce and proclaim what was commanded and prescribed by God, speaking as one who utters another's words, not his own, as one speaking from the earth and not from heaven. But that promised Prophet spoke the words of God, as God does, as one speaking from heaven. He who is of the earth speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all. And what he has seen and heard, he testifies (John 3.31, 32, 34). For he whom God sent speaks the words of God. That is, he will speak and testify the things still to be spoken (Heb. 3.5), he completes the word of God, which he, as God of Israel, still wished to speak to Israel and to the Gentiles. And it was fitting that he speak such things as would satisfy this name, such as: "Look to me and be saved, all you ends of the earth" (Isa. 45.22); that is, believe in me, for I am righteousness, salvation and victory. For he who was to be awaited after all others ought either to speak words never heard until now, or else he was awaited in vain. For he could not have spoken except from the earth, like John and any other man.
