And thus God would not have those words to Israel which he ought to pour out to the people, since God had become their God, their sanctifier, righteousness, shield, salvation, and finally their Father. From these things it is clear that the words of God in Moses, "I will put my words in his mouth," mean just as much as if he had said: He will speak those words which Israel ought to expect and desire, so that at last it may hear from its God, rejoice in him, give thanks to him, and be able to glorify him fully. He will speak my words as his own, because I, the Father, and that Prophet will be one, and I, the Angel of God, will be that Prophet. For Moses indeed spoke those words which Israel was to hear, being a witness of the things that were to be spoken (Heb. 3.5). Yet it was not said of him, nor could it be said, "I will put my words in his mouth," but God spoke those words of another Prophet, distinct from Moses. Therefore that oracle was claimed for Jesus Christ alone: by John the Baptist, who frankly denied that he was that Prophet (John 1.21); and by the Samaritan woman, who said, "I know that the Messiah, who is called Christ, will come; he will announce all things to us" (ibid. 4.25); and by St Peter, who expressly applied it to Christ (Acts 3.22, 23), and indeed with a demonstrative pronoun, "to that Prophet," so that it is established that those words are to be referred, by a change of number, not to all the following prophets but singularly to the chief Prophet, Christ. And St Paul sets Christ above the prophets of the Old Testament in general in the exercise of the prophetic office (Heb. 1.1), and by name above Moses, as a servant inferior to the Son of God, the Lord of all (ibid. 3.1–6). And indeed it was entirely necessary that that eminent Prophet, who would speak the words of God, should one day come, because righteousness could not be brought in except through the Son of God, and the kingdom had to be given to him; and he had to be not only awaited according to the promise but also seen, and the Gospel had to be heard from his mouth for the completion of joy; and it had to be said of him, "Behold your God" (Isa. 40.9), and he himself had to say of himself, "I am he who speaks," that is, "I speak, not another" (ibid. 52.6).

units.la: XXX. Prophetæ isthoc munus in forma servi obiit idem ille, qui ante & post assumptam servi formam ἀτεκίνησις unus cum Patre & Spiritu S. summus Doctor fuit & est, & qui omnes Prophetæ
units.tr: XXX. The same one who undertook this office of prophet in the form of a servant, who before and after assuming the form of a servant is unmoved [ἀτεκίνησις], one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, was and is the supreme Teacher, and he is the one who is over all the prophets.

units.la: Sed tum maximè & proprie, cùm in carne apparuit, juxta vaticinium Deut. XVIII. 18.19. quod explicatur.
units.tr: But he did this most fully and properly when he appeared in the flesh, according to the prophecy of Deut. 18:18-19, which is explained there.

units.la: Et quidem à primo conceptionis momento. Prophetas, quotquot in mundo fuerunt, Spiritu suo afflavit. Nam à primo conceptionis momento officio Prophetæ defunctus est Filius Dei Θεάνθρωπος, secundum naturam Divinam Διδάσκαλος, & per illam in ipso habitantem Αυτο-διδάσκαλος, à se ipso edoctus & ad humanæ sapientiæ efformationem institutus, & factus διδακτικὸς ad oris humani apertionem. Statim enim à primo conceptionis momento Magisterio huic Θεανθρωπικῷ Angeli & homines, Evangelium de Christo exhibito prædicantes, inserviverunt; velut Angelus Gabriel conceptionem & nativitatem ejus, authore Christo annuncians, Luc. I. 26. Elizabetha Johannem in utero gestans, ad Mariam matrem Domini gratulabunda invisens, ibid. v. 41.42. &c. Maria cantico Dominum & Servatorem suum celebrans, ibid. v. 46. &c. Zacharias simili cantico cornu salutis erectum domui Davidis prædicans, ibid. v. 67.68. &c. Angeli & Pastores Bethlehemitici Jesu Christi nativitatem ebuccinantes, ibid. II. 10-20. Simeon & Anna Prophetissa festivo concentu eandem prosequentes, ibid. v. 25.36. &c. Et ne dubia sit Prophetici muneris Christi origo, ipsemet diserte affirmat, Deum neminem vidisse unquam, sed unigenitum Filium, qui in sinu Patris fuit, ἐκεῖνον Illum enarrasse, Joh. I. 18. neminem ascendisse in Cœlum, nisi qui è Cœlo descendit, Filium hominis, Ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, qui est in Cœlo, ibid. III. 13. VI. 62. exivisse à Patre, XVI. 28. Venisse supernè è Cœlo. III. 31. illic vidisse & audivisse, quæ loquutus est, v. 32. Quæ manifestum est pertinere ad incarnationem Christi, qua ipse è Cœlo in terram descendit, omnibus thesauris sapientiæ & cognitionis in eo reconditis, Col. II. 3. onustus.
units.tr: Indeed, he did it from the first moment of conception. He breathed his Spirit into all the prophets who have ever been in the world. For from the first moment of conception the Son of God, the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], performed the office of prophet: according to his divine nature he is Teacher [Διδάσκαλος], and through the divine nature dwelling in him he is self-taught [Αυτοδιδάσκαλος], instructed by himself and appointed to shape human wisdom, and made teachable [διδακτικός] in opening his human mouth. For from the first moment of conception, angels and men who preached the gospel of Christ made manifest served this God-human teaching office. Thus the angel Gabriel announced his conception and birth, with Christ as the author (Luke 1:26). Elizabeth, carrying John in her womb, visited Mary the mother of the Lord and greeted her with joy (ibid. vv. 41-42, etc.). Mary celebrated her Lord and Savior in a canticle (ibid. v. 46, etc.). Zacharias, in a similar canticle, proclaimed the horn of salvation raised up for the house of David (ibid. vv. 67-68, etc.). The angels and the shepherds of Bethlehem proclaimed the birth of Jesus Christ (ibid. 2:10-20). Simeon and the prophetess Anna joined in the same festive chorus (ibid. vv. 25, 36, etc.). And lest the origin of Christ's prophetic office be in doubt, he himself affirms it plainly: no one has ever seen God, but the only-begotten Son, who was in the bosom of the Father, has declared him [ἐκεῖνον] (John 1:18); no one has ascended into heaven except him who came down from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven [Ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ] (ibid. 3:13; cf. 6:62); he came out from the Father (16:28); he came from above, from heaven (3:31); there he saw and heard what he spoke (v. 32). It is clear that these words pertain to the incarnation of Christ, by which he came down from heaven into the earth, laden with all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in him (Col. 2:3). ## XXXI.

units.la: XXXI.

Immanis est Scripturarum hatrum detorsio per paradoxum illud socini, Schmalcii & aliorum, quòd Christus homo natus in Cœlum prius ascenderit, ut à Deo Evangelium disceret, quàm homines docere coepit, & quidem ascenderit eo modo, quo post resurrectionem in Cœlum assumptus est. Id factum post Baptismum tempore quadraginta dierum & noctium, quos jejunus in deserto consumpsit, pronunciant. Quam sententiam in se spectatam piam esse, & ad gloriam D. Jesu facere, parùm piè Limborchius, Socinianis caput demulcens, dixit; Nam & Scripturis adversatur, & gloriæ Doctoris & Prophetæ Christi detrahit. Scriptura enim Christum ἐφάπαξ semel eis τὰ ἅγια in Sanctuarium intrasse, Hebr. IX. 12. & descendisse πρῶτον prius, quàm ascendit, asserit. Illud verò (quod dicitur) ascendit, quid est, nisi quòd & descendit prius in inferiores partes terræ? Ephes. IV. 9. non quando post ascensum vel raptum illum descendit (sic enim prius ascendisset, non descendisset; nec valeret argumentatio Pauli, quia sic ascendere potuisset, qui prius non descendit) sed quando primitus in terram venit, & procedente tempore etiam in inferiores terræ partes, sepulchrum, descendit. Historia porro Evangelica docet, Christum eo tempore, quo ipse in deserto per quadraginta dies & noctes agitavit, fuisse tentatum à Sathana, & fuisse μετὰ θηρίων cum feris, Marc. I. 13, & eundem in finem in desertum subductum fuisse πειρασθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ Διαβόλου, ut à Diabolo tentaretur, Matth. IV. 1. Verius ergo tum ad inferos descendit, quàm in Cœlum
units.tr: The twisting of these Scriptures is monstrous, through that paradox of the Socini, Schmalcius and others, that Christ, born as a man, first ascended into heaven to learn the gospel from God, before he began to teach men; and indeed that he ascended in the same way that he was taken up into heaven after the resurrection. They declare that this happened after his baptism, during the forty days and nights he spent fasting in the wilderness. Limborch, stroking the head of the Socinians, said that this opinion, considered in itself, is pious and tends to the glory of Lord Jesus, but he said it not very piously. For it both conflicts with the Scriptures and detracts from the glory of Christ as Teacher and Prophet. Scripture asserts that Christ entered once for all into the holy places, the sanctuary (Heb. 9:12), and that he descended first [πρῶτον] before he ascended. But what does it mean that he ascended, unless he had first descended into the lower parts of the earth? (Eph. 4:9). This refers not to a descent after the ascension or rapture (for then he would have ascended first and not descended; and Paul's argument would not hold, since one who had not first descended could have ascended in that way), but to his first coming into the earth and, as time went on, his descent into the lower parts of the earth, the sepulchre. Moreover, the evangelical history teaches that Christ, at the time when he was driven about in the wilderness for forty days and nights, was tempted by Satan and was with the wild beasts [μετὰ θηρίων] (Mark 1:13), and to this end he was led into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil (Matt. 4:1). Therefore he then descended to the underworld rather than ascended into heaven.

units.la: ascendit. Nec profectò pium, vel Christo gloriosum, vel Scripturis & religioni non contumeliosum est dicere, Christum post Baptismum, quando jam ad munéris Prophetici functionem voce cœlesti Patris & descensu Spiritus S. super eum, ut Filius unicè audiendus sacratus fuit, ex terra in Cœlum raptum fuisse, ut ibi demum Evangelium disceret, quia sic Christus primo ortu suo non fuisset ἐκ τῶν ἀνω ex iis, quæ supra sunt, sed ἐκ τῶν κάτω ex iis, quæ infra sunt; non ἐκ τῆς ἀέρος ex Cœlo; contra quam Johannes Baptista testatus est, Joh. III. 31. & ipse Christus pronunciavit, ibid. VIII. 23. Præposterum planè fuisset, Christum primò consecrari in Prophetam & Doctorem audiendum, & postdemum in Cœlum abripi ad discendum, cùm ne apud homines quidem rite doctores creentur & pronuntientur, qui nondum, quod docearent, didicerunt, sed demum non docendo discere, vel porro discere, sed primò discere tenentur: & Scripturæ ipsæ imperfectionis & insufficientiæ insimulantur, quasi in iis non extaret πίστις exemplar doctrinæ, Rom. VI. 17. quàm doceret Christus, adeóque necesse fuisset adoptare impias illas voces: Quis nobis ascendet in Cœlum &c? Deut. XXX. 12. Rom. X. 6. & religionis ipsius vera antiquitas destruitur, quasi non ante raptum illum ex deserto in Cœlum cunabula sua habuisset. Cùm tamen Christus heri & hodie idem, & in sæcula fuerit, Hebr. XIII. 8. & Christus atque Apostoli cuncta sua ex Mose & Prophetis confirmaverint. Non ergo Christus demum circa annum ætatis trigesimum miraculosa illa in Cœlum ascensione Theologiam didicit, sed, quà Deus, λόγος, Sapientia Patris fuit ante montes fundatos, colles formatos, ab æterno unctus, à principio, ante terram; fuit apud Patrem אמון alumnus seu εἰς τὸν κόλπον ὢν Πατρὸς in sinu Patris, Joh. I. 18. Prov. VIII. 23.25.30. quâ homo verò, quoad charismatum collationem in terra, non in Cœlo unctus Luc. II. 40. III. 22. IV. 1.14.15. διὰ βρέφους, λόγῳ ipso ductore & doctore, Theologiam, quam doceret quod adeò verum est, ut etiam post resurrectionem ex mortuis Scripturas discipulis suis aperuerit & interpretatus fuerit, ibid. XXIV. 44.45 &. in nomine Christi Spiritus S. per Apostolos Evangelium docens nihil docuerit extra ea, quæ Prophetæ & Moses locuti sunt, Actor. XXVI. 22.
units.tr: Nor is it truly pious, or glorious to Christ, or insulting to the Scriptures and to religion, to say that Christ, after his baptism, when he had already been consecrated by the heavenly voice of the Father and the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him to the prophetic office, as the Son who alone is to be heard, was then caught up from the earth into heaven to learn there at last. For in that case Christ, at his first birth, would not have been from those things above, but from those things below; not from heaven. This is contrary to what John the Baptist testified (John 3:31) and Christ himself declared (ibid. 8:23). It would be absurd for Christ to be first consecrated as the Prophet and Teacher to be heard, and only afterwards carried up into heaven to learn. Even among men, teachers are not rightly appointed and presented as teachers if they have not yet learned what they are to teach; rather they are required first to learn, not to teach by not teaching, or to go on learning. The Scriptures themselves would also be accused of imperfection and insufficiency, as if the pattern of doctrine [πίστις ... exemplar doctrinæ] (Rom. 6:17), which Christ was to teach, were not in them; and it would be necessary to adopt those impious words, Who will ascend into heaven for us? (Deut. 30:12; Rom. 10:6). And the true antiquity of religion itself would be destroyed, as if it had had no cradle before that rapture from the desert into heaven. Yet Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever (Heb. 13:8), and Christ and the apostles confirmed all their teaching from Moses and the Prophets. Therefore Christ did not learn theology at about the thirtieth year of his age through that miraculous ascension into heaven. Rather, as God, the Word, he was the Wisdom of the Father, before the mountains were founded, before the hills were formed, anointed from eternity, from the beginning, before the earth; he was with the Father as the nursling [אמון], or, as John says, in the bosom of the Father [εἰς τὸν κόλπον ὢν Πατρὸς] (John 1:18; Prov. 8:23, 25, 30). As man, however, he was anointed with gifts on earth, not in heaven (Luke 2:40; 3:22; 4:1, 14-15), from infancy [διὰ βρέφους], with the Word himself as his guide and teacher. That he taught the theology which he taught is so true that even after his resurrection from the dead he opened and interpreted the Scriptures to his disciples (ibid. 24:44-45). And in the name of Christ, the Holy Spirit, teaching through the apostles the gospel, taught nothing beyond those things which the Prophets and Moses had spoken (Acts 26:22).

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Propudiosò adeò dogmati neutiquam Christus ipse favet, dicens: Nemo ascendit in Cœlum, nisi qui descendit ex Cœlo, Filius hominis, qui est in Cœlo, Joh. III. 13. Manifestè enim, uti diximus, descensum Christi ascensu priorem facit; & etiam cùm descendit, in Cœlo esse, adeóque Cœlum non deseruisse, asserit, συγκαταβαίνω tali Divinæ personæ in terris manifestationem innuens. Neque obstat, quòd Christus dixit: Οὐδεὶς ἀναβέβηκε Nemo ascendit in Cœlum, &c. Non enim ascensionem jam factam seu præteritam, sed futuram significat, imitans Prophetiam, quæ verbum præteriti temporis usurpavit: עלית למרום Ascendisti in altum, Psal. LXVIII. 19. Præsupponit enim Christus, Nicodemum, Israelis doctorem meminisse, scriptum esse à Davide de Christo, quòd ascenderit in altum, hoc est, ascensurus sit. Innuit ergo, id factum
units.tr: Christ himself by no means favours this dogma when he says: No one has ascended into heaven, except him who descended from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven, John 3:13. For he clearly makes the descent of Christ prior to the ascent, as we have said. And when he says that he descended, he asserts that he was in heaven and so had not left heaven, indicating the manifestation of this divine person on earth by συγκαταβαίνω [condescension]. Nor does it stand in the way that Christ said Οὐδεὶς ἀναβέβηκε [No one has ascended], etc. For he does not mean an ascent already made or past, but a future one, imitating prophecy, which used the past tense: עלית למרום [You have ascended on high], Ps. 68:19. For Christ presupposes that Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel, remembered that David had written of Christ that he would ascend on high, that is, that he was going to ascend. He therefore implies that this had not yet happened,

units.la: Ascensum scilicet ad Cœlum, qui est pleni Dei ascensus. {ctum} nondum esse, quia hactenus nemo Deum, vel quempiam ascendentem viderit, vel narraverit. Ergo de futuro hoc intelligendum, uti Prophetae solent loqui de futuris, ut praesentibus, quid in spiritu viderint, narrantes, & sic verba iis, qui rem, cum gereretur, visuri erant, praeeuntes. Ex ascensione hac, futura licet, colligit Christus, & post eum S. Paulus, ejusdem descensum priorem, seu manifestationem Dei in carne, praesupponens, quod descendens sit ἐκ τῶν ἄνω ex superioribus, hoc est, Deus. Idem sensus est verborum Christi: Hoc vos offendit? Si igitur conspexeritis filium hominis ascendentem, ubi erat πρότερον prius, Joh. VI. 62, supponens iterum descensum ascensu priorem. Cur enim alias non clare dixisset: denuo ascendentem, postquam noviter ascendens iterum descendit? Praeterea Christus est λόγος Sermo Dei, Joh. I. 1. Imago Dei & splendor gloriae ejus, Col. I. 15. Hebr. I. 3. reconditos in se habens thesauros sapientiae & cognitionis, Col. II. 3. Sed non ideo in Coelum rapi & ibi doceri Voluntatem Dei debuit, ut eam hominibus plenissime annunciare posset. Sunt enim nomina illa pleraque naturae, sive personae secundum naturam Divinam, non officii, & quae officium connotant, naturae humanae in Coelo institutionem minime comprobant. Nam a λόγω & Spiritu Dei quotidie in Scripturis proficiens, edoctus fuit. Alia denique Mosis & Pauli ratio fuit. Ille enim non in Coelum raptus fuit, sed cum Deo in monte fuit duas quadragesimas: hic in tertium Coelum raptus est; sed servus uterque, non Filius, Deus in carne manifestatus, qui, qua Deus, institutione nulla induit, qua homo, oraculum praesentissimum habuit.
units.tr: namely the ascent to heaven, which is the ascent of the fullness of God. For no one had yet seen or reported that God, or any man, had ascended. This must therefore be understood of the future, as the prophets were accustomed to speak of future things as present, relating what they had seen in the Spirit, and so going before with words those who were to see the thing when it was done. Christ, and after him St Paul, draws his conclusion from this ascent, although it is future, presupposing the prior descent or manifestation of God in the flesh, since he who descends is ἐκ τῶν ἄνω [from above], that is, God. The same sense is found in the words of Christ: Does this offend you? If then you see the Son of man ascending where he was before [πρότερον], John 6:62, again presupposing the descent prior to the ascent. For why would he not otherwise have said plainly: ascending again, after he had newly ascended and descended once more? Moreover, Christ is the λόγος [Word] of God, John 1:1; the image of God and brightness of his glory, Col. 1:15; Heb. 1:3; having in himself hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Col. 2:3. But he did not therefore need to be caught up into heaven and taught there the will of God, in order to be able to proclaim it most fully to men. For those names are mostly of his nature, or of his person according to the divine nature, not of his office, and they imply the office, and do not at all prove that the human nature was instructed in heaven. For he was taught daily by the λόγος and the Spirit of God, advancing in the Scriptures. Finally, the case of Moses and Paul was different. For Moses was not caught up into heaven, but was with God on the mountain for two forties; Paul was caught up into the third heaven; but each was a servant, not the Son, God manifested in the flesh, who, as God, put on no office, and, as man, had the most present oracle.

units.la: XXXIII. Publicam muneris Prophetici functionem Christus a Johanne baptizatus, & Coelesti Patris voce: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo acquiesco; Αὐτὸς ἀκούετε Hunc audite, Matth. III. 17. & XVII. 5. commendatus, obire coepit. Et varias Prophetia atque Sermo Christi partes habuit.
units.tr: XXXIII. Christ, baptized by John and commended by the heavenly Father's voice: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; Αὐτοῦ ἀκούετε [Hear him], Matt. 3:17 and 17:5, began to perform the public function of the prophetic office. And he bore various parts of prophecy and of the preaching of Christ.

units.la: Ante omnia enim falsam justitiam redarguit, ac tum demum, Evangelium praedicans, veram justitiam in se solo reperiri ostendit, & fidem sibi uni soliqueque habendam esse docuit. Universa proin ejus Prophetia circa demonstrationem verae justitiae Legis, & impletionem ejusdem a se uno soloque peractam, & sola in ipsum fide ab homine peccatore participandam, occupata, vel Legalis, vel Evangelica fuit.
units.tr: XXXIV. Christ's legal prophecy consisted in the explanation of the true righteousness that the Law requires. For without this, and without a firm knowledge of it, Christ could not be recognised as the true Saviour, since his whole salvation turned on the exhibition of that true righteousness which the Law had demanded in the covenant of works.

units.la: XXXIV. Legalis Christi Prophetia in explicatione verae justitiae, quam Lex requirit, continuit. Absque hac enim, & ejus solida cognitione Christus verus Salvator agnosci non poterat, quia tota ejus salvatio in exhibitione verae justitiae, quam Lex in foedere operum exegerat, vertebatur.
units.tr: XXXIV. Christ's legal prophecy consisted in the explanation of the true righteousness which the Law requires. For without this, and without a solid knowledge of it, Christ could not be recognised as the true Saviour, because his whole salvation consisted in the exhibition of the true righteousness which the Law had demanded in the covenant of works.

units.la: Non ergo Christus novum Legislatorem, sed Doctorem & Prophetam, Legis semel a Deo per Mosen latae τὸ πνευματικὸν rationem spiritualem, Rom. VII. 14. adeoque veram Legis justitiam, quam ipse impleturus in carnem venerat, demonstrantem, egerat. Licet enim etiam Legem fidei tulerit, & ejusdem obedientiam praeceperit, ibid. I. 5. III. 27. atque eatenus etiam ππο Legislatoris nomine veniat, atque insuper etiam Legalia praecepta & praxin character...
units.tr: Christ, therefore, acted not as a new Lawgiver, but as Teacher and Prophet, demonstrating the spiritual sense [τὸ πνευματικὸν] of the Law once given by God through Moses, Rom. 7:14, and so the true righteousness of the Law, which he had come into the flesh to fulfil. For although he also gave the law of faith and commanded obedience to it, Rom. 1:5; 3:27, and so in that respect he also comes under the name of Lawgiver, and moreover also has the character of teaching legal precepts and practice ...

units.la: XXXV. Diversi abeunt quotquot justitiam & salutem hominis a justitia non Christi credentibus imputata, sed hominis propria suspendunt.
units.tr: XXXV. Those who depart from the truth, all of whom make the righteousness and salvation of man depend on his own righteousness, and not on the righteousness of Christ imputed to believers.

units.la: Cum enim opera Legis ubique a justificatione hominis Scriptura excludat, opera non quaevis, sed Legis tantum Mosaicae excludunt, at Legem novam a Christo Legem Mosis vel perficiente, vel inducente, adeoque novo Legislatore, latam & promulgatam, ejusque justitiam ab homine, imperfecte licet, praestitam, justitiae & vitae causam esse pertendunt, manifesta cum Legis, Evangelii, & Christi ipsius clade. Apertum est Concilii Tridentini Sess. VI. Can.
units.tr: For while Scripture everywhere excludes works from the justification of man, they exclude not all works but only the works of the Mosaic Law. They contend that the new Law, given and promulgated by Christ, either perfecting or introducing the Law of Moses, and so by a new Lawgiver, and the righteousness of this law, performed by man, though imperfectly, is the cause of righteousness and life. This is a manifest overthrow of the Law, the Gospel, and Christ himself. It is clear from the Council of Trent, Session 6, Canon ...

units.la: Initium publicae muneris Prophetici functionis a Baptismo Johannis factum est.
units.tr: The beginning of the public function of the prophetic office was made at the baptism of John.

units.la: Fuitque illa vel Legalis, vel Evangelica. Illa in explicatione non rogationem novae Legis Operum constitiit.
units.tr: And that function was either legal or evangelical. The former, in its explanation, did not establish the requirement of works under a new Law.

units.la: Secus quam Socinianii id, eaque perpendunt. VI. Can. 21. anathema: Si quis dixerit, Christum Jesum à Deo hominibus datum esse ut Redemptorem, cui fidant, non etiam ut Legislatorem, cui obediant, anathema sit. Etiam Socinus Explicat. cap. V. Matth. & Catechesis Rackoviana de Offic. Christ. Propphet. cap.9. aliique asseclæ Christum novam Legem, abolita Mosaica, ceu imperfecta, tulisse, singula præcepta novis additamentis interpolasse, & post omnia abnegationem sui, crucis tolerantiam & sequelam Christi noviter præcepisse, statuit. Quos etiam Anabaptistæ, & Remonstrantes, Puppius, Episcopius, alii, justitiarii & ipsi, sectantur.
units.tr: The Socinians, by contrast, do not weigh these things in this way. Council of Trent, Canon 21: anathema. If anyone shall say that Christ Jesus was given by God to men as Redeemer, in whom they are to trust, and not also as Lawgiver, whom they are to obey, let him be anathema. Socinus himself, in his Explanation of Matthew, chapter 5, and the Racovian Catechism, On the Office of Christ as Prophet, chapter 9, and other followers, hold that Christ gave a new Law, as the Mosaic Law had been abolished as imperfect, that he interpolated the individual precepts with new additions, and that after all these things he newly commanded self-denial, endurance of the cross and following Christ. The Anabaptists, and the Remonstrants, Puppius, Episcopius and others, who are themselves justiciaries, also follow them.

units.la: XXXVI. Præcepit sanè Christus non pauca ad amorem Dei & proximi, in quo totius Legis cardo vertitur, pertinentia. Novum præceptum do vobis, ut diligatis alii alios. Sicut ego dilexi vos, ita & invicem vos diligatis, Joh.XIII.34. Hoc meum mandatum est, ut diligatis vos invicem, sicut ego dilexi vos, ibid.XV.12. Hoc mandatum ab ipso (Christo) habemus, ut qui diligit Deum, diligat etiam fratrem suum, 1.Joh.IV.21. Cæterum præcepta illa non simpliciter nova, vel noviter à Christo data sunt, ut impleta justificationis causa existant; sed vetera fuerunt, & à Christo, tum per explicationem & genuini sensus ejus per doctores populi in publica Catechesi perversi exegesin, tum per ejusdem impletionem ab ipso factam novam renovata sunt. Explicatio ad vitandam hypocrisin, abnegationem nostri, agnitionem Christi veri Mediatoris, inflammationem precum ad impetrandum Spiritum sanctificantem, & promptiorem intelligentiam Legis, per quam sanctificatio nostra verior & integrior fit. Impletio verò ad justitiæ acquisitionem, & conversationis Christianæ exemplar facit. Ita & vetera & nova Christi præcepta fuerunt. Fratres, non novum mandatum vobis scribo, sed vetus mandatum, quod habuistis à principio; (inde à Patriarchis & à Mose) Iterum mandatum novum scribo vobis, quod verax est in ipso (Christo quia veritas promissionis, quæ in Christo est, & ejus obedientia nos novo quodam jure ad amorem Dei & odium Diaboli obligat) & in nobis (fidelibus N.T. quia impletio promissionis in nobis per sanctificationem nostri ad fidem non jam promissionis veteris, sed veritatis ejus in Christo exhibitæ, nobis quodammodo fit lex Spiritus S. ad amandum Deum, & Sathanam odio habendum) quia tenebræ (servitutis umbrarum & indurationis per totum illud tempus, quo Deus gentes deseruit) transeunt, & lux vera (in exemplo Christi, prædicatione Evangelii, illuminatione etiam gentium, & regeneratione Spiritus) lucet. 1.Joh.II.7.8. Neque etiam novum & ab antiquo nunquam auditum est præceptum illud Christi: Si quis post me venire vult, abneget se ipsum, & tollat crucem suam, & sequatur me, Matth.XVI.24. Cùm enim obedientia Christi nobis imitanda sit, obedientia & impletio Veteris mandati à principio auditi, 1.Joh.II.7. utique sequela Christi, habens comitem abnegationem sui & patientiam crucis, præceptum peculiare & simpliciter novum Christi haberi non potest. Abnegatio enim nostri, qua Deum respicit, & tolerantia crucis propter Deum, ejusque ad crucem vocationem præcepti primi, quod erga Deum reverentiam, patientiam & obedientiam imperat; eadem verò abnegatio nostri, qua proximum spectat, & cupiditates nostras refrænat & extinguit, decimi præcepti virtus est. Imitatio verò Christi in totam Legem fertur, ceu exemplar vitæ & actionum ipsius. Ideo etiam in V.T. sanctissimi quique, juxta mandatum Dei Jer. IV.3.4. Ezech.XVIII.30.31. tum se ipsos abnegarunt, se ipsos totos in obsequium Dei redigentes, cupiditates hujus seculi coërcentes, carnem cum desideriis suis crucifigentes; velut Abrahamus, Genes.XI.XII.XXII. Levitæ, Deut. XXXIII.8.9. Jobus Deum in adversis celebrans, cap.I.II. Eli, David, Hiskias gravissimas castigationes Dei pio animo sustinentes, 1.Sam.II.III. 2.Sam.XVI. 2.Reg.XX. Moses, Daniel, Socii ejus, voluptates omnes fastidientes, Hebr.XI.25.26. Dan.I.8. &c. tum crucem religionis & Christi causa impositam patienter tulerunt, velut Moses, Heb.XI.25.26. Prophetæ subAchabo, 1.Reg. XVIII. Daniel & ejus Socii, Dan.III.VI. tota Ecclesia Judaica sub Antiocho: tum Deum Christum secuti, imitati sunt, quotquot juxta præceptum illud Legis: Sanctificate vos, & estote sancti, quia sanctus sum, Levit.XI.44.45. se ipsos per Spiritum Dei sanctificantes Deo, Christo, qui unum cum Patre est, Joh.X.30, conformarunt, & virtutes Christi, fiduciam, humilitatem, patientiam, amorem inimicorum, assiduitatem in officio, precibus &c. imitati sunt, quos inter facile primas Abraham & David tenuerunt. Conferturequidem Moses cum Christo, & hic illi longè præfertur, Hebr.II.1.2.3. III.6. at non in Legislatione, juxta quam sibi invicem opponuntur, Joh.I.17. sed partim in genere doctrinæ, quod illic legale, hic Evangelicum: partim in dignitate & gloria, qua Christus Mosen longissimè antecellit. Quod porrò magno cum pietatis schemate iidem crepant, in N.T. vitam Angelicam, adeóque perfectiorem simul Legem requiri, non sine fermento Pharisaico est; quia tum præsumunt, non esse nobis in hac vita degentibus impossibile vitam Angelicam traducere: tum Legem Divinam moralem, quam S.Paulus spiritualem Rom.VII.14. dixit, indignis modis deprimunt, quasi ad solam vitam animalem, non spiritualem informandam valuerit. Ubi & illud pessimi commatis est, quòd proportionem præcepta inter & promissa urgentes, in N.T. cœlestia promissa sanctitatem pariter cœlestem flagitare asserunt. Nam promissa utriusque Testamenti quoad rei summam eadem, certè non terrestria duntaxat, sed spiritualia & cœlestia fuerunt, & proportio sanctitatem inter hominis & cœlestem gloriam nulla est. Non enim condigna sunt passiones hujus temporis (& quantò minùs actiones) futura gloria, quæ in nobis revelabitur, ibid.VIII.18. Cùm feceritis omnia, quæ præcepta sunt vobis, dicite: Servi inutiles sumus. Nam quod facere debuimus, fecimus, Luc.XVII.10. Neque aliud sibi voluit illa S. Petri, Maxima & pretiosa promissa vobis donata sunt: ut per hæc participes fiatis Divinæ naturæ, elapsi ex corruptione, quæ in mundo est per cupiditatem, 2.Pet.I.4. Non enim is verborum illorum sensus est, quòd citra maxima & pretiosa illa promissa operæ pretium non sit ex corruptione, quæ in mundo per cupiditatem est, effugere, & cum Deo ambulare, sed is potius, quòd maxima & pretiosa illa promissa acrius stimulare nos debeant ad elabendum ex corruptione, quæ in mundo est, per cupiditatem, quæ mundum à Divinæ naturæ, id est, Dei consortio, seu à communione cum Deo, separat.
units.tr: XXXVI. Christ indeed commanded not a few things pertaining to the love of God and neighbour, on which the whole hinge of the Law turns. A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. As I have loved you, so also you should love one another, John 13:34. This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you, ibid. 15:12. We have this commandment from him (Christ), that whoever loves God should love his brother also, 1 John 4:21. But those precepts were not simply new, nor newly given by Christ so as to exist as a cause of justification fulfilled. They were old, and were renewed by Christ, both through the explanation of their genuine sense, against the perverse exegesis of the teachers of the people in public catechesis, and through his own fulfilment of them, which made them new. The explanation serves to avoid hypocrisy, to deny ourselves, to acknowledge Christ as the true Mediator, to kindle prayer for the sanctifying Spirit, and to give a readier understanding of the Law, through which our sanctification becomes truer and more complete. The fulfilment, however, makes for the acquisition of righteousness and provides a pattern of Christian conduct. So both the old and the new precepts of Christ were. Brothers, I write to you no new commandment, but an old commandment which you have had from the beginning (from the Patriarchs and from Moses onward); again I write to you a new commandment, which is true in him (Christ, because the truth of the promise which is in Christ, and his obedience, bind us by a certain new right to love God and hate the Devil) and in you (the faithful of the New Testament, because the fulfilment of the promise in us, through the sanctification of our faith, is no longer of the old promise but of its truth exhibited in Christ, and so becomes for us in a certain manner a law of the Holy Spirit, to love God and to hold Satan in hatred) because the darkness (of the bondage of shadows and of hardening throughout that whole time in which God left the nations) passes away, and the true light (in the example of Christ, the preaching of the Gospel, the illumination also of the nations, and the regeneration by the Spirit) shines. 1 John 2:7-8. Nor is that precept of Christ new, nor has it never been heard of from of old: If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me, Matt. 16:24. For since the obedience of Christ is to be imitated by us, the obedience to and fulfilment of the old commandment heard from the beginning, 1 John 2:7, namely the following of Christ, having as its companions self-denial and patience in the cross, cannot be regarded as a peculiar and simply new precept of Christ. For the self-denial by which we regard God, and the endurance of the cross for God's sake, and the calling to the cross, belong to the first precept, which commands reverence, patience and obedience towards God. But the same self-denial by which we regard our neighbour, and which restrains and extinguishes our desires, is the virtue of the tenth precept. The imitation of Christ, moreover, extends to the whole Law, as the pattern of his life and actions. Therefore also in the Old Testament the most holy men, according to the command of God (Jer. 4:3-4; Ezek. 18:30-31), both denied themselves, bringing their whole selves into obedience to God, restraining the desires of this age, and crucifying the flesh with its desires; as Abraham (Gen. 11, 12, 22); the Levites (Deut. 33:8-9); Job, praising God in adversity (ch. 1, 2); Eli, David and Hezekiah, bearing with a pious mind the most grievous chastisements of God (1 Sam. 2, 3; 2 Sam. 16; 2 Kings 20); Moses, Daniel and his companions, despising all pleasures (Heb. 11:25-26; Dan. 1:8, etc.). And they patiently bore the cross imposed for religion and for the sake of Christ, as Moses (Heb. 11:25-26); the prophets under Ahab (1 Kings 18); Daniel and his companions (Dan. 3, 6); the whole Jewish Church under Antiochus. And they followed and imitated God-Christ, as many as, according to that precept of the Law, Sanctify yourselves, and be holy, for I am holy (Lev. 11:44-45), sanctifying themselves to God through the Spirit of God, conformed themselves to Christ, who is one with the Father (John 10:30), and imitated the virtues of Christ: confidence, humility, patience, love of enemies, diligence in duty and in prayer, and so on. Among these Abraham and David easily hold the first places. Moses is indeed compared with Christ, and is greatly preferred to him (Heb. 2:1-3; 3:6), but not in respect of legislation, by which they are set against each other (John 1:17); rather partly in the kind of doctrine, in that the one is legal and the other evangelical, and partly in dignity and glory, in which Christ far surpasses Moses. As to what the same men boast, with a great show of piety, that in the New Testament an angelic life and therefore a more perfect Law is required, it is not without Pharisaic leaven. For they presume, first, that it is not impossible for us living in this life to lead an angelic life; and secondly, they debase the divine moral Law, which St Paul called spiritual (Rom. 7:14), in unworthy ways, as if it were capable of shaping only the animal life and not the spiritual. Here too is a most wicked saying: by insisting on the proportion between precepts and promises, they assert that in the New Testament heavenly promises demand a likewise heavenly holiness. For the promises of both Testaments, as to their main substance, are the same. They were certainly not merely earthly but spiritual and heavenly, and there is no proportion between human holiness and heavenly glory. For the sufferings of this present time (and much less our actions) are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us, ibid. 8:18. When you have done all the things that are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; for what we ought to have done, we have done, Luke 17:10. Nor did St Peter mean otherwise: Very great and precious promises are given to us, that by these you may be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust, 2 Pet. 1:4. For the sense of those words is not that without those very great and precious promises it is not worth the effort to escape the corruption that is in the world through lust and to walk with God. It is rather that those very great and precious promises ought more keenly to spur us to escape the corruption that is in the world through lust, which separates the world from the divine nature, that is, from the fellowship of God, or from communion with God.

units.la: XXXVII. Nulla etiam erroris σκιάφασις est in disceptatione illa seria Christi cum justitia Pharisæorum, quam Matth.V. 17-f. instituit. Nam cum justitia simulata Pharisæorum, per traditiones suas, & malam ἐγχείρησιν in docenda Lege τὸ ῥητὸν ejusdem, neglecta δανοία, & omissis βαρύτερος & νόμως gravioribus Legis Matth.XXIII.23. temerè & inciter vexantium; non cum justitia vera & genuina, quam Lex Mosis secundum γνήσιον & spiritualem sensum suum, Deo Legislatore, sanctitate ejus, & imagine Dei in homine dignum, dictat, contendit. Prædictum enim est futurum, ut filii Levi discedant à via, & multos faciant impingere in Lege & corrumpant fœdus Levi, Malach.II.8. Ideo in die adventus sui factus est ignis conflatoris & sicut smegma fullonum; & sedit conflans & purificans argentum, purificans filios Levi; & fundens eos, ut aurum & argentum, ibid. III.2.3. Christus ergo dicens: Audivistis quòd dictum sit veteribus, &c. Ego verò dico vobis, &c. Matth. V.21.22. nec Mosis Legem in sensu suo genuino refutandam suscepit, nec se auctorem tulit præcepti vel non dati Veteribus, vel non ita præcisè & exactè inculcati, quasi quod sub V.T. propositum fuerit per modum consilii, nunc demum sub N.T. exigatur per modum præcepti. Nam ipsa vox, ἡκούσατε audivistis, stylo Hebraico notat, traditione accepistis. Nam שמע Hebræis est non ex scripto, sed ex ore, &c. traditione orali audire vel percipere aliquid, quomodo frequentissima Thalmudis & Majmonidis locutio est משמועה למדו Auditione didicerunt, id est, traditione. Verba proin sequentia: ἐρρέθη τοῖς ἀρχαίοις quòd dictum fit Veteribus perinde sonant, ac si dictum esset: Vetus est traditio, quæ per multa secula obtinuit; vel: Traditio hæc est חכמים ראשונים Sapientum veterum (sic enim veteres Magistros Tradentes καταχητὰς Catechetas suos appellant) Christus verò subjiciens: Ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν. Ego verò dico vobis, v.22. non novam legem se ferre, sed Scribarum glossas refutare, quæstionem determinare & rectiora docere, innuit. Nam apud Hebræos eosdem confutantis, docentis, vel quæstionem determinantis formula est: ואני אומר Et ego dico. Huc merito referimus verba Esajæ: Et erit in novissimo dierum, & erit mons domus Jehovæ in vertice montium, &c. Et ibunt populi multi, & dicent: Venite & ascendamus ad montem Jehovæ, & ad domum Dei Jacob ויורנו & docebit nos, Esaj.II.2.3. Ubi sic David Kimchi: המורה הוא מלך המשיח Doctor hic est Rex Messias.
units.tr: XXXVII. There is also no shadow of error in that serious debate of Christ with the righteousness of the Pharisees which he undertook in Matt. 5:17ff. For he was contending with the feigned righteousness of the Pharisees: with their traditions, with their wretched handling [ἐγχείρησιν] of the teaching of the Law, with its letter [τὸ ῥητὸν] taken while its meaning [διάνοια] was neglected, and with the weightier matters of the Law left aside (Matt. 23:23), rashly and violently harassing others. He was not contending for the true and genuine righteousness which the Law of Moses, according to its genuine [γνήσιον] and spiritual sense, dictates as worthy of God the Lawgiver, of his holiness, and of the image of God in man. For it was foretold that the sons of Levi would depart from the way, make many stumble in the Law, and corrupt the covenant of Levi (Mal. 2:8). Therefore on the day of his coming he would be a refiner's fire and like the fuller's soap; he would sit refining and purifying the silver, purifying the sons of Levi, and pouring them out like gold and silver (ibid. 3:2-3). Christ therefore, saying "You have heard that it was said to the ancients," etc., and "But I say to you," etc. (Matt. 5:21-22), neither undertook to refute the Law of Moses in its genuine sense, nor presented himself as the author of a precept not given to the ancients, or not so precisely and exactly inculcated. It was not as if what had been proposed under the Old Testament by way of counsel were now at last under the New exacted by way of command. For the very word ἠκούσατε ["you have heard"], in Hebrew style, means "you have received by tradition." For שמע [shema] among the Hebrews means to hear or receive something not from writing but from the mouth, by oral tradition. This is why the most frequent phrase in the Talmud and in Maimonides is משמועה למדו [mishmu'ah lamdu], "they learned by hearing," that is, by tradition. Accordingly the words that follow, ἐρρέθη τοῖς ἀρχαίοις ["it was said to the ancients"], sound just as if it had been said: "It is an old tradition, which has held for many ages"; or: "This tradition is that of the first sages" [חכמים ראשונים, chakhamim rishonim] (for so they call their old teachers who handed down tradition, their catechists, καταχητάς). Christ, however, by adding Ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ["But I say to you"], v. 22, indicates that he is not bringing a new law, but refuting the glosses of the Scribes, settling the question and teaching what is more correct. For among the Hebrews the formula of one who refutes, teaches or determines a question is: ואני אומר ["And I say"]. To this we rightly refer the words of Isaiah: "And it shall come to pass in the last days, that the mountain of the house of Jehovah shall be established at the top of the mountains... And many peoples shall go and say: Come, and let us go up to the mountain of Jehovah, and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us" [ויורנו], Isa. 2:2-3. On which David Kimchi says: "This teacher is King Messiah" [המורה הוא מלך המשיח].

units.la: XXXVIII. Sed ipsa verborum Christi series docet, Christo rem esse cum justitia simulata Pharisæorum, non cum ea, quam Mosis Lex præcipit. Nam Christus diserte protestatur, non venisse se, ut solveret, sed ut impleret Legem. Mutatio autem legis ex imperfecta in perfectam quædam solutio est: & impletio Legis non est superadditio Legis novæ ad vetustam, sed stabilitio Legis, quæ extat, per obedientiam ejusdem. Tum Servator v.18. asserit, ne jota quidem, vel κεραία apiculum (minutias prominentes literarum, sicut cornua à cornigerorum capitibus prominent, quæ κεραία discrimen inter literas cognatæ formæ, velut ב & כ, nec non ר & ד &c. statuunt, vel lineolam, incisuram, quæ duabus utrinque extremitatibus, velut cornibus quibusdam constat, oppositè ad Jota) transiturum ex Lege, donec omnia fiant. Siquid ergo Legi superaddere Christus voluisset, dixisset utique: Jota vel apex non præteribit à Lege, & præceptis, quæ ego superaddo. Postea Christus commina-tur, eum, qui unum ex minimis præceptis istis (puta Legis, de qua loquitur) solverit, & ita homines docuerit, minimum in Regno Cœlorum (civem Ecclesiæ infimum, imò ne civem quidem, sed ἀνόμου, qualis Antichristus est) vocatum iri; sed qui fecerit & docuerit, eum magnum vocatum iri in Regno Cœlorum, v.19. Atque ut id confirmet, eorum, qui legem solvunt, exemplum ponit Scribas & Pharisæos; illos Legis tractatores in populo maximè celebres; hos à sanctitate & religione exacta nomen habentes; tanquam non habentes justitiam perfectam, quæ ad intrandum in Regnum Cœlorum sufficiat. Dico vobis, inquit, nisi justitia vestra abundaverit supra justitiam Scribarum & Pharisæorum, non poteritis intrare in Regnum Cœlorum; v. 20. Hanc ergo Scribarum & Pharisæorum justitiam, non justitiam Legis Mosaicæ carpere & configere Christus instituit. Non enim eandem justitiam Scribarum & Pharisæorum cum justitia Legis Mosis fuisse, satis inde constat, quòd Servator noster justitiam & obedientiam à Scribis & Pharisæis præceptam passim, ceu hypocriticam (qualis non fuit justitia Legis Mosaicæ) graviter increpat & damnat; contra à discipulis suis, si in Regnum Cœlorum ingredi, hoc est, ad Civitatem Dei in hac vita, ceu digni Cives & filii Dei v.47. 48. velint, postulat, ut doceant & agnoscant justitiam & obedientiam perfectiorem, quæ ipsius Legis Divinæ moralis à Mose promulgatæ est; & ut habeant justitiam, cujus fructus potiores sint quàm fructus justitiæ Pharisæorum. Justitia autem, quæ in Regno Cœlorum valet, est obedientia Christi Legi Mosis subjecti imputata, sive donata illis, qui per fidem unum cum Christo sunt, cujus fructus, propter meritum Christi longè exuberantiores sunt iis, qui à justitia Pharisæorum pullularunt. Adeò enim Scribæ & Pharisæi à vera justitia Christi aberrarunt, ut non tantùm non discipuli Regni Cœlorum, hoc est, non Israelitæ, & filii Abrahami, benedictionum Abrahami hæredes, censeri potuerint; sed ne quidem ad intelligentiam Legis, & veræ justitiæ pervenerint; nedum fructus vera pœnitentia dignos tulerint, Matth.III.7.9. Hoc procedente capite Christus demonstrat, & Pharisæorum justitiam verbis subinde Legis Mosaicæ fucatam, at genuino, salutari, spirituali ejusdem sensu penitus orbatam & destitutam; veram Legis justitiam non esse, nedum eam, per quam à se obitam homo peccator salvari possit, comprobat. Ubi ipsa verba inter Veterum, nudis subinde Legis corticibus constantia, & Christi iisdem opposita antithesis planè interiorem justitiæ Pharisæorum & Scribarum mentem denudat;
units.tr: XXXVIII. But the very sequence of Christ's words shows that Christ was dealing with the feigned righteousness of the Pharisees, not with the righteousness that the Law of Moses prescribes. For Christ plainly declares that he came not to dissolve but to fulfil the Law. Now a change of law from imperfect to perfect is a kind of dissolution, but the fulfilling of the Law is not the superadding of a new law to the old one. It is the establishing of the Law that already exists, through obedience to it. Then the Saviour, at v.18, asserts that not even a jot, or κεραία, a tittle (the small projecting strokes of letters, just as horns project from the heads of horned animals; these κεραῖαι mark the difference between letters of similar shape, such as ב and כ, and also ר and ד, and so on; or a little line or notch, which has two ends on either side like horns, set opposite to the jot), will pass from the Law until all things are done. If therefore Christ had wished to add something to the Law, he would surely have said: A jot or tittle will not pass from the Law and the precepts which I add. Afterwards Christ threatens that whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments (that is, of the Law, of which he is speaking) and so teaches men shall be called least in the Kingdom of Heaven (the lowest citizen of the Church, or rather not even a citizen but ἄνομος, a lawless one, such as Antichrist is), but whoever does and teaches them shall be called great in the Kingdom of Heaven, v.19. And to confirm this, he sets before them the example of those who break the Law: the Scribes and Pharisees, the interpreters of the Law most celebrated among the people, who had their name from exact holiness and religion, as if they did not have the perfect righteousness that suffices for entering the Kingdom of Heaven. I tell you, he says, unless your righteousness exceeds the righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the Kingdom of Heaven, v.20. Christ therefore set out to find fault with and confront this righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees, not the righteousness of the Mosaic Law. That the righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees was not the same as the righteousness of the Law of Moses is sufficiently clear from this: our Saviour everywhere sharply rebukes and condemns the righteousness and obedience prescribed by the Scribes and Pharisees as hypocritical (which the righteousness of the Mosaic Law was not). On the contrary, from his disciples he requires, if they wish to enter the Kingdom of Heaven, that is, the City of God in this life, as worthy citizens and sons of God (vv.47-48), that they teach and acknowledge a more perfect righteousness and obedience, that of the divine moral Law itself as promulgated by Moses, and that they have a righteousness whose fruits are better than the fruits of the righteousness of the Pharisees. The righteousness that holds good in the Kingdom of Heaven, however, is the obedience of Christ, who was subject to the Law of Moses, imputed or given to those who are one with Christ through faith. Its fruits, on account of the merit of Christ, are far more abundant than those which sprang from the righteousness of the Pharisees. For the Scribes and Pharisees had so strayed from the true righteousness of Christ that they could not only not be counted as disciples of the Kingdom of Heaven, that is, as Israelites and sons of Abraham, heirs of the blessings of Abraham, but did not even attain to an understanding of the Law and of true righteousness, much less bear fruits worthy of true repentance (Matt. 3.7-9). Proceeding in this chapter, Christ shows, and proves, that the righteousness of the Pharisees, disguised from time to time with the words of the Mosaic Law but utterly bereft and destitute of its genuine, saving, spiritual sense, is not the true righteousness of the Law, much less that by which a sinful man could be saved through what he has done. Here the very words, the ancients' teaching, consisting of bare husks of the Law, set in antithesis to the words of Christ, plainly lay bare the inner mind of the righteousness of the Pharisees and Scribes.

units.la: Christus Matth.V. 17-f. non novam Legem Evangelicam tulit, sed hypocriticam Scribarum justitiam, vindicata vera Legis justitia, redarguit.
units.tr: Christ, in Matt. 5.17f., did not bring a new Evangelical Law, but refuted the hypocritical righteousness of the Scribes, by vindicating the true righteousness of the Law.

units.la: Quod ex verborum Christi serie amplius probatur. dat; talem videlicet,quòd Lex Mosis externam coedem, at non iram, convitia, odia ἀπαροῦσα v. 21--27. adulterium, at non concupiscentiam mulieris, vel temeraria divortia,v.27--33.perjuria, at non profanationem nominis Dei in jurejurando, v.33--38. prohibuerit; & vicissim jus talionis permiserit, sed privata ultione exequendum v.38--43.amorem proximi & inimici odium praeceperit, v.43--f. vel sola disceptationis Christi ultima pericope,non cum Mose, nuspiam inimici odium praecipiente, sed cum scribis hypocritis eidem rem fuisse, clamat. Cui primae etiam pericopes verba illa: Audivistis dictum veteribus: Non occides. Qui autem occiderit, reus erit judicii, v.21. jungere licet. Nam verba illa: Qui occiderit, reus erit judicii, non Mosaica sunt, sed stylum Scribarum traditionalem sapiunt. Hanc ergo impiam Legis Divinae exenterationem sic graviter Christus refutavit & contudit,ut ipsi Legi Mosis nitorem,sanctitatem & interiorem vim suam in solidum restituerit. Nam iram,convitia,odium, profanationem nominis Divini in jurejurando, concupiscentiam mulieris, temeraria divortia, privatam vindictam,& odium inimicorum,ipsis Decalogi praeceptis, & eorundem sensu à Mose ipso, Prophetis, Christo & Apostolis explicatiora reddita vetari,non minus quàm externos graviores actus à Lege prohibitos, extra dubitationis aleam positum est,& ex Decalogi ipsius explicatione, supra à nobis fusiùs tradita,liquet. Mitto consilia perfectionis Evangelicae, quae à Christo Legi superaddita esse, nequicquam Pontificii pertendunt. De quibus infra pluribus.
units.tr: This is proved further from the sequence of Christ's words. The Law of Moses forbade external murder, but not anger, reproaches and hatred (vv.21-27); adultery, but not lustful desire for a woman, nor rash divorces (vv.27-33); perjury, but not the profaning of God's name in an oath (vv.33-38). Conversely, it permitted the law of retaliation, but to be carried out by private vengeance (vv.38-43), and it commanded love of the neighbour and hatred of the enemy (vv.43-f.). The last paragraph of Christ's discourse alone cries out that he was dealing, not with Moses, who nowhere commands hatred of the enemy, but with the hypocritical scribes. The first paragraph may also be joined with these words: "You have heard it said to the ancients: Thou shalt not kill; but whoever kills shall be liable to judgment" (v.21). For the words "whoever kills shall be liable to judgment" are not Mosaic but savour of the traditional style of the Scribes. Christ therefore so sharply refuted and crushed this impious disembowelling of the divine Law that he fully restored to the Law of Moses its brightness, holiness and inner force. For that anger, reproaches, hatred, profaning the name of God in an oath, lust for a woman, rash divorces, private vengeance and hatred of enemies are forbidden by the precepts of the Decalogue itself, and by their sense as more fully explained by Moses himself, the Prophets, Christ and the Apostles, no less than the more serious external acts forbidden by the Law, is beyond all chance of doubt, and is clear from the explanation of the Decalogue itself, which we have set out more fully above. I pass over the counsels of evangelical perfection, which the Papists vainly contend were superadded to the Law by Christ. Of these more below.

units.la: XXXIX. Sed potius & principale doctrinae Christi genus Evangelicum fuit. Missus enim & unctus est à Jehova ad annuntiandum Evangelium seu bonum nuntium mansuetis,pauperibus,humilibus,Esaj.LXI.1.Luc.IV.18. Ideo Evangelium κατ' ἐξοχὴν appellatur. Διδαχὴ & Κυρίου Doctrina Domini, Christi, Act. XIII.12. Μαρτύριον & Χριστοῦ testimonium Christi, 1.Cor.I.6. Apoc.I.2. Σωτηρία Salus, quae coepit λαλεῖσθαι dici per Dominum, Hebr.II.3. Nam Doctrinae Evangelicae objectum est, juxta illud S. Pauli: Non judicavi quidquam scire inter vos nisi Jesum Christum, eumque crucifixum, 1. Cor. II.2.praeterea in praedicando Evangelio praecipua quoq; ejusdem in terra industria desudavit. Venit enim Salvator à peccatis, Matth.I.21.adeoq; non minas Legis & condemnationem ingeniaturus, sed gratuitas Evangelii promissiones praedicaturus. Non tantùm enim Deus Israelis voluit esse tonans,fulgurans, Coelum & terram liquefaciens,vel Legem promulgans, aut in futurum aliquid promittens,sed etiam Deus veritatis, justitiae,pacis,salutis,vitae & consolationis. Qua cum re vehementer conspirat modus agendi Divinus cum Elia, 1.Reg.XIX.11.12.ubi non in vento,terraemotu, igne erat Deus, sed venit קול דממה דקה vox aurae lenis,& locutus est Deus. Merito igitur sic sponsa eum decantat: Pulcher es prae filiis hominum חןׁ בשפתיך Effusa est gratia in labia tua, Psal.XLV.3.Sermo tuus & sapiens est, omnia recta, justa, honesta loquens, & omne arcanum Divinae voluntatis explicans, & clamans gratiosus, oneratos & fessos invitans, & Evangelii praedicatione erigens contri-
units.tr: XXXIX. But the principal kind of Christ's teaching was rather evangelical. For he was sent and anointed by Jehovah to announce the Gospel, or good news, to the meek, the poor and the humble (Isa. 61.1; Luke 4.18). Therefore it is called the Gospel pre-eminently [κατ' ἐξοχήν]. It is the teaching [διδαχή] of the Lord, the doctrine of Christ (Acts 13.12); the testimony [μαρτύριον] of Christ (1 Cor. 1.6; Rev. 1.2); the salvation [σωτηρία] which began to be spoken of through the Lord (Heb. 2.3). For the object of evangelical doctrine is, according to St Paul's words: "I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified" (1 Cor. 2.2). Moreover, in preaching the Gospel he laboured with especial diligence on earth. For the Saviour came to save from sins (Matt. 1.21), and so he was not going to devise threats and condemnation of the Law, but to preach the free promises of the Gospel. For the God of Israel did not wish to be only the thundering, flashing God who shakes heaven and earth, or who promulgates the Law, or promises something in the future, but also the God of truth, righteousness, peace, salvation, life and consolation. The divine manner of acting with Elijah agrees strongly with this, where God was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but came as a voice of gentle breeze [קול דממה דקה], and God spoke (1 Kings 19.11-12). Rightly therefore the bride sings of him: "You are fairer than the sons of men; grace [חן] is poured into your lips" (Ps. 45.3). His speech is wise, speaking all things that are right, just and honourable, explaining every secret of the divine will, and crying out graciously, inviting the burdened and weary, and raising up the contrite by the preaching of the Gospel.

units.la: tos. Nam etiam de Lege concionatus est, quatenus illa Evangelio subservit.
units.tr: For he also preached about the Law, insofar as it serves the Gospel.

units.la: XL. Ante omnia praedicavit μετάνοιαν re-sipiscentiam, & approximationem Regni Coelorum, Tunc coepit Jesus praedicare & dicere: Resipiscite: Appropinquavit enim Regnum Coelorum, Matth.IV.17. Initium ergo publicae praedicationis suae hoc fuit, quòd resipiscendum sit, quia Regnum Coelorum sit prae foribus. Idem prius Johannes Baptista praedicaverat.Regnum intelligitur illud, quod promissum erat Patribus, & quod fideles expectaverant, & Coelorum Regni nomine venit, non tantum quia Deus Rex dicitur habere thronum in Coelo, sive Coelum & terram replet, atque adeo non est in terra sicut homo; quo sensu מלך שמים Rex Coelorum,Dan. IV.34. vocatur; sed inprimis, quia est Regnum Dei Coeleste, non terrestre, in quo Christus Ecclesiam sibi soli in communione bonorum coelestium, justitiae & libertatis subjicit. Approximavit illud initio praedicationis Christi, nondum aderat,quia Christus nec dum ex statu servitutis in Coelum translatus fuit, nec ad dextram Dei,ut Rex consedit, nec Spiritum ἐξέχεα effudit. Hujus Regni respectu semper sunt in Regno Coelorum,qui in Christo sunt:Rursus venit Regnum Coelorum, quando Templum & altare destructum est, & sacrificiorum usus cessavit; quia tum finis fuit dierum priscorum, & initium novi seculi, abolito Coelo priore & terra vetere; & creato novo Coelo,& nova terra,in quibus justitia habitat, 2.Pet.III.13. Appropinquans illud Regnum Coelorum μετάνοιαν resipiscentiam, hoc est, mutationem consilii & propositi,reversionem ad Deum, conversionem ab operibus malis,& falsa justitia, ad agnitionem verae justitiae,fundatae in Testamento Dei & sponsione Mediatoris jam praesentis, & fide recipiendi; qualis resipiscentia cor patrum, Malach.IV.6. Φρόνησις δικαίων sensus justorum Luc.I.17. appellatur; exigere Christus admonet, praecipiens: Resipiscite, quia appropinquavit Regnum Coelorum. Regnum enim Coelorum sine resipiscentia tali nec videri,nec haberi potuit,tum quia ἀσέβεια sunt, Regnum Dei, quod justitiae est, venire & non resipiscere à falsa justitia, sed manere in suo statu: tum quia dignum est, ut bona Regni Coelorum homines ad resipiscentiam commoveant, & inexcusabiles sint, qui ea negligunt. Alibi cum resipiscentia fidem conjungit. Praedicavit Jesus Evangelium Regni Dei, dicens: Impletum est tempus, & appropinquavit Regnum Dei: Resipiscite igitur,& credite Evangelio, Marc.I.15. Primum enim resipiscentiae opus erat credere non amplius promissioni, sed Evangelio, in quo revelatur justitia Dei ex fide in fidem, Rom.I.17. Ideo se missum dixit εὐαγγελίζεσθαι ad evangelizandum, Luc.IV.18. in quantum id ante exaltationem & glorificationem ejus fieri poterat. Licèt enim,quis & qualis esset, vulgò non pronunciavit, sed id ex dictis & factis suis colligendum omnibus reliquit; tamen aliquando se Filium Dei esse,non obscurè & hostibus & discipulis suis professus est. Hostibus, velut cùm Joh.V.17. Deum Patrem suum appellavit; unde rectè Judaei collegerunt, quòd πατέρα ἴδιον ἐλεγε τὸν Θεὸν, ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ Θεῷ, Patrem proprium Deum dixit, æqualem se ipsum faciens Deo, ibid. v. 18. & ipse statim v. 19.20. &c. se ὁ υἱὸν Filium Dei palam professus est. Discipulis quoque se Filium Dei viventis nuncupantibus id ipsum fassus est, Matth. XVI.16.17. Joh. VI.69. XI.27. & iisdem familiarius exposuit, quæ apud multos per parabolas loquebatur, Matth. XI. 25.26. XIII.11.37. &c. Marc. III.34. Fuitque ea in re mirum temperamentum Majestatis & humilitatis, ut & loqueretur ea, quæ nonnisi Deus, Filius Dei loqui poterat; & loqueretur in humili specie, iisque verbis, quæ Christum pronunciaturum esse, Scripturæ testabantur; licet eorum vis, propter loquentis humilitatem, multos lateret. Ita omnes ad fidem ad se invitans, & remissionem peccatorum atque vitam promittens apud alios, propter virtutem loquentis, dictorum veracitatem, & oculorum mentis operationem, fidem invenit, apud alios vero, humilitate ejus offensos, non invenit.
units.tr: XL. Above all he preached repentance [μετάνοια], that is, resipiscence, and the approach of the Kingdom of Heaven. "Then Jesus began to preach and to say: Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand" (Matt. 4.17). The beginning of his public preaching was therefore this: that one must repent, because the Kingdom of Heaven is at the door. John the Baptist had preached the same before him. The Kingdom meant is that which was promised to the Fathers and which the faithful had looked for. It comes under the name of the Kingdom of Heaven not only because God is called King, who has his throne in heaven, or who fills heaven and earth and so is not on earth as a man is (in which sense he is called מלך שמים, King of Heaven, Dan. 4.34), but above all because it is the heavenly Kingdom of God, not an earthly one, in which Christ subjects the Church to himself alone, in fellowship of heavenly goods, righteousness and liberty. It drew near at the beginning of Christ's preaching, but was not yet present, because Christ had not yet been translated from the state of servitude into heaven, nor had he sat down as King at the right hand of God, nor had he poured out the Spirit [ἐξέχεα]. In respect of this Kingdom, those who are in Christ are always in the Kingdom of Heaven. Again the Kingdom of Heaven came when the Temple and altar were destroyed and the use of sacrifices ceased; for then was the end of the former days and the beginning of a new age, the former heaven and old earth being abolished, and a new heaven and new earth created, in which righteousness dwells (2 Pet. 3.13). This approaching Kingdom of Heaven calls for repentance [μετάνοια], that is, a change of counsel and purpose, a return to God, a turning from evil works and false righteousness to the knowledge of true righteousness, founded in the covenant of God and in the promise of the Mediator now present, and in the faith of receiving him. Such repentance of the fathers (Mal. 4.6) is called the wisdom of the righteous [φρόνησις δικαίων], the sense of the just (Luke 1.17). Christ admonishes them to require this, commanding: "Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand." For the Kingdom of Heaven could be neither seen nor possessed without such repentance: both because it is impious for the Kingdom of God, which belongs to righteousness, to come while men do not repent of false righteousness but remain in their state; and because it is fitting that the good things of the Kingdom of Heaven should move men to repentance, and that those who neglect them are inexcusable. Elsewhere he joins faith with repentance: "Jesus preached the Gospel of the Kingdom of God, saying: The time is fulfilled, and the Kingdom of God is at hand. Repent therefore, and believe the Gospel" (Mark 1.15). For the first work of repentance was to believe no longer the promise but the Gospel, in which the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith (Rom. 1.17). Therefore he said he was sent to evangelize [εὐαγγελίζεσθαι] (Luke 4.18), so far as this could be done before his exaltation and glorification. For although he did not generally announce who and what he was, but left all to gather it from his words and deeds, yet at times he professed openly, and not obscurely, that he was the Son of God, both to enemies and to his disciples. To enemies, as when he called God his Father (John 5.17); whence the Jews rightly inferred that he "called God his own Father, making himself equal to God" [πατέρα ἴδιον ἔλεγε τὸν Θεόν, ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ Θεῷ] (ibid. v.18); and immediately afterwards (vv.19-20, etc.) he openly professed himself the Son of God. To his disciples also, when they named him the Son of the living God, he confessed the same (Matt. 16.16-17; John 6.69; 11.27); and he explained more familiarly to them what he spoke in parables to many (Matt. 11.25-26; 13.11, 37, etc.; Mark 3.34). In this matter there was a remarkable blending of majesty and humility: he both spoke those things which only God, the Son of God, could speak, and he spoke in a humble guise and in those words which the Scriptures testified that Christ would pronounce, although their force lay hidden from many because of the humility of the speaker. Thus, inviting all to faith in himself and promising forgiveness of sins and life, he found faith among some, on account of the power of the speaker, the truthfulness of his words and the working of the mind's eye; but among others, offended by his humility, he did not find it.

units.la: XLI.
units.tr: XLI.

units.la: Ad doctrinam hanc Christi Evangelicam referenda sunt ante omnia, quæcunque is de gratia salutari & misericordia Dei erga peccatores locutus est. Nam Lex per Mosen data est: Gratia & veritas per Jesum Christum facta est, Joh. I.17. tum eodem pertinent quæcunque de persona, statu, officio & beneficiis Christi, inprimis justitia ejus per fidem imputata, & redemptione ejusdem loquuntur. Ejusdem generis sunt, quæ de fide in Christum, ejusque natiua indole & proprietatibus, nec non de resipiscentia salutari agunt. Accedunt Sacramenta a Christo instituta, sigilla fœderis gratiæ & justitiæ ab eodem Christo adductæ. Neque etiam ab indole Evangelicæ doctrinæ abludunt, quæcunque Christus de Ecclesia, ejus capite & Petra, cui illa inædificanda sit, nec non de ejus in mundo gubernatione, perpetuitate, certaminibus, victoriis & triumphis passim docuit. Quo inprimis consignatissima ejusdem de Regno suo, ejusdemque in mundo vicissitudinibus vaticinia referri merentur. Cujusmodi sunt illa de Gentium conversione, Matth. XXII.2.&c. Joh. IV.23. X.16. &c. de commixtione Ecclesiæ cum hypocritis & utrorumque separatione, in parabola ζ σπέρματος Satoris mysterii plenissima, Matth. XIII.3. &c. de satis urbis & orbis, Ecclesiæ per Pseudo-prophetas corruptione, restitutione & decursu ad ultimum usque judicium, ibid. XXIV.4.-f. de periodis variis Ecclesiæ suæ militantis; Agni, Bestiæ duplicis, Babylonicæ meretricis fatis & plagis, nec non Ecclesiæ liberatione & Regno, toto libro Apocalypseos seu Revelationis, quam Deus Filio suo impertitus est, ut eandem servis suis communicaret, Apoc. I.1.&c.-f. Taceo prædictiones particulares non paucas, velut de passionibus suis instantibus, Matth. XVI.21. Petri abnegatione, & martyrio, Apostolorum scandalo, Judæ infidelitate, aliisque ejusmodi; quæ non parum Prophetiæ Christi excellentiam commendant, inprimis cum futurorum notitia in illo fuerit præstantior longè quam in Prophetis hominibus. In his enim fuit levis quædam corruscatio, & sicut lumen in aëre, modo accedens, modo recedens: in illo sicut lux in ipso sole perseveranter manens & manans: In ipso erat vita, & vita erat lux hominum. Erat φῶς ἀληθινὸν lux vera, illuminans omnem hominem, qui venit in mundum, Joh. I.4.-9.
units.tr: Before all else, to this Evangelical doctrine of Christ must be referred whatever he said about the saving grace and mercy of God towards sinners. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, John 1.17. Likewise pertaining to it is whatever speaks of the person, state, office and benefits of Christ, above all his righteousness imputed through faith, and his redemption. Of the same kind are those passages that treat of faith in Christ, its native character and properties, and also of saving repentance. To these are added the sacraments instituted by Christ, seals of the covenant of grace and righteousness brought in by the same Christ. Nor do they differ from the character of the Evangelical doctrine whatever Christ taught everywhere about the Church, its head and rock on which it is to be built, and about its governance in the world, its perpetuity, conflicts, victories and triumphs. Especially deserving to be referred here are his very certain prophecies about his Kingdom and its changing fortunes in the world. Such are those about the conversion of the Gentiles, Matt. 22.2 etc.; John 4.23, 10.16 etc.; about the mixing of the Church with hypocrites and the separation of both, in the parable of the seed of the sower [ζ σπέρματος Satoris], most full of mystery, Matt. 13.3 etc.; about the destruction of the city and the world, the corruption of the Church by false prophets, its restoration and course until the final judgment, ibid. 24.4 ff.; about the various periods of his militant Church; the fates and plagues of the Lamb, of the double beast and of the Babylonian harlot, and also the deliverance of the Church and its Kingdom, throughout the whole book of the Apocalypse or Revelation, which God gave to his Son to communicate to his servants, Rev. 1.1 etc. I say nothing of the not few particular predictions, such as of his impending sufferings, Matt. 16.21, of Peter's denial and martyrdom, of the scandal of the Apostles, of Judas's unbelief, and others of this kind; which greatly commend the excellence of Christ's prophecy, especially since his knowledge of future things was far more eminent in him than in the human prophets. For in them there was a slight flashing, like light in the air, now approaching, now receding; in him it was like the light of the sun itself, remaining and flowing constantly: In him was life, and the life was the light of men. He was the true light [φῶς ἀληθινὸν], which enlightens every man who comes into the world, John 1.4-9.

units.la: In his cognitio obscura, inevidens fuit; in illo clara, evidens, certa; in his finita, mutabilis; in illo infinita, immutabilis, æterna. Denique cùm contrariorum eadem notitia sit, ad Evangelii doctrinam aliena quadam vi referuntur, quæcunque Christus contra hypocrisin, infidelitatem, impœnitentiam profanationem & contemptum mysteriorum religionis Christianæ graviter declamavit.
units.tr: In them the knowledge was obscure and not evident; in him it was clear, evident and certain; in them finite and changeable, in him infinite, unchangeable and eternal. Finally, since the knowledge of opposites is the same, whatever Christ vehemently declaimed against hypocrisy, unbelief, impenitence, profanation and contempt of the mysteries of the Christian religion is referred to the doctrine of the Gospel by a certain foreign force.

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: Eximius inprimis Prophetiæ & doctrinæ omnis à Christo prædicatæ modus fuit, Divinam & incredibilem efficaciam comitem habens. Licet enim Dei verbum in ore etiam ministrorum Christi efficax organon sit, quo is utitur ad conversionem & salutem hominis; tamen Ministros inter & Dominum Christum discrimen maximum hactenus intercedit, quod illi ministerium obeuntes aures populi ferire, at cor ipsum præconio suo nudo vincere non possunt; hic & aures & cor hominis in potestate sua tenens, & Spiritus sui cor aperientis conferendi arbitrium habens Matth. III.11. Joh. XVI.7. utrumque ad obsequium verbi sui subigere potis est. Ita Johannes aqua baptizavit: Christus Spiritu S. & igne, Matth. III.11. Illi per Spiritum Christi manifestarunt passiones Christi & ejus glorias, I.Pet. I.11. Spiritu Christi eos ducente in omnem veritatem, eoque loquente non à se ipso, sed audita loquente, & ventura annuntiante, Joh. XVI.13. Hic cùm solus Patrem noverit, ut Filius, à se ipso & ex se ipso, non aliunde revelandi voluntatem ejus, cui lubet, potestatem & auctoritatem summam habet. Nemo novit Patrem, nisi Filius, & cui Filius eum revelare vult, Matth. XI.27. Illi præsentes ore vel calamo doctrinam semel sibi traditam docuerunt. Hic & præsens in diebus carnis suæ ore, potente verbo & Spiritu suo docuit: & absens, atque in Cœlo ad dextram Dei Patris considens, misso Spiritu & datis Apostolis, Evangelistis, Prophetis, Pastoribus, Doctoribus Ecclesiam docuit. Illi αὐτόπται non sunt, neque aliter, quam manifestatione veritatis ad conscientiam fidem sibi conciliant, 2.Cor. IV.2. neque se ipsos prædicant, sed Christum Jesum Dominum, se ipsos autem servos fidelium propter Jesum, ibid. v. 5. Hic αὐτόπτης est, & immediate cordibus hominum affulget. Etiamsi ego testor de me ipso, tamen verum est testimonium meum, Joh. VIII.14. Splendescit in fidelibus φωτισμὸς δ' Εὐαγγελίας τῆς δόξης lumen Evangelii gloriæ Christi, qui est imago Dei, 2.Cor. IV.4.
units.tr: Especially remarkable in his prophecy and in all the doctrine preached by Christ was its manner, which carried with it a divine and incredible efficacy. For although the Word of God, even in the mouth of Christ's ministers, is an effective instrument which he uses for the conversion and salvation of man, yet between the ministers and the Lord Christ there has hitherto been this very great difference: they, in discharging their ministry, can strike the ears of the people, but cannot conquer the heart itself by their bare proclamation; whereas he, holding both the ears and the heart of man in his power, and having the authority to confer the Spirit who opens the heart, Matt. 3.11; John 16.7, is able to bring both into obedience to his word. Thus John baptized with water; Christ baptized with the Holy Spirit and fire, Matt. 3.11. They, through the Spirit of Christ, made known the sufferings of Christ and his glories, 1 Pet. 1.11; the Spirit of Christ leading them into all truth, and speaking through them not of himself but what he heard, and announcing things to come, John 16.13. Since he alone knows the Father, as the Son, from himself and out of himself, not from elsewhere, he has the highest power and authority to reveal his will to whomever he pleases. No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him, Matt. 11.27. They, while present, taught by mouth or pen the doctrine once delivered to them. He, both while present in the days of his flesh, taught by his mouth, with a powerful word and his Spirit; and while absent, sitting in heaven at the right hand of God the Father, having sent the Spirit and given Apostles, Evangelists, Prophets, Pastors and Teachers, he has taught the Church. They are not eyewitnesses [αὐτόπται], nor do they win faith to themselves in conscience except by the manifestation of truth, 2 Cor. 4.2; nor do they preach themselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord, and themselves as servants of believers for Jesus' sake, ibid. v. 5. He is an eyewitness [αὐτόπτης], and immediately shines on the hearts of men. Even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, John 8.14. The illumination of the Gospel of glory [φωτισμὸς δ' Εὐαγγελίας τῆς δόξης], that is, the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, shines in believers, 2 Cor. 4.4.

units.la: XLIII.
units.tr: XLIII.

units.la: Hoc ergo inprimis non humano, sed θεοδιδάκτῳ fastigio muneris Prophetici Christi tribuendum est, quòd locutus dicitur longè aliter, quàm Scribæ. Erat enim διδάσκων docens ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων tanquam potestatem habens, & non ut Scriba, Matth. VII.29. adeò ut doctrina ejus auditores perculerit, Marc. I.22. Luc. IV.32. ἐξεπλήσσοντο percellebantur omnes, qui eum audiebant, super intelligentia & responsis ejus, ibid. II.47. Oratio enim ejus fuit vivida, ardens cum πνεῦμα ζωῆς conjuncta; Scribarum contrà elumbis, torpida, languens. Hebræorum doctores sueti erant accipere רשות ἐξουσίαν potestatem docendi, & legem interpretandi; neque quicquam nisi nomine & authoritate Magistrorum suorum, nisi מצות אנשים מלמדה præceptum hominum condocefactum Esaj. XXIX, 13. traditum à majoribus suis loquebantur, traditionum vanitatibus, Grammaticarum observationum tricis & Cabbalæ nugacis mendacisque mysteriis unicè inhærentes. Demonstratio verò ex S. literis, ad conscientiam apud eos rara vel nulla fuit. Nihilominus suam illam ρῆσιν ἐξουσίαν potestatem docendi jactantes, sic Christo insultarunt: Ἐν ποίᾳ ἐξουσίᾳ ταῦτα ποιεῖς Qua potestate fretus hæc facis? Quis tibi dedit potestatem istam? Matth. XXI.23. Sed potestatem licet non habuerit ab hominibus, at habuit tamen, locutus quippe, populo ipso judice, ut potestatem habens, & loquendo cunctos percellens, quia tanquam testis fidelis locutus est ea, quæ in Cœlo ipso vidit & audivit, attestante hominum conscientia, quòd doctrina ejus vera & sancta sit. Ecce populis testem dedi eum נגיד ומצוה ducem & præceptorem, Esaj. LV.4. Qui desuper venit, super omnes est. Et quod vidit & audivit, hoc testatur, & testimonium ejus nemo (ψυχικὸς animalis) accipit. (quia est supra omnem cogitationem hominum, & à consiliis eorum discrepat, & nisi compressa & coercita concupiscentia, quæ naturaliter obluctatur, recipi nequit, adeóque etiam scandalo est non gentibus duntaxat, sed etiam Judæis, ut testem eum ex Cœlo esse, vel inde constare possit.)
