Qui accepit ipsius testimonium, obsignavit, quòd Deus verax sit. Quem enim misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur, Joh. III.31-34. Multa habeo de vobis loqui & judicare. Sed qui misit me, verus est. Et ego, quæ audivi ex ipso, dico in mundum &c. Cùm exaltaveritis Filium hominis, tunc cognoscetis, quòd ego sim, & quemadmodum me docuit Pater meus (cujus Spiritus super me est, qui est Spiritus sapientiæ, prudentiæ, cognitionis, timoris Dei, Esaj. XI.2. & qui mihi dedit לשון למדים linguam eruditorum, ibid. L.4.) sic loquar, Joh. VIII.26. &c. Didicit enim à Patre ut homo; ut Deus in sinu Patris existens vidit & audivit. Unde multi ex populo, auditis sermonibus ejus, dixerunt: Οὗτος ἐστιν ἀληθῶς ὁ Προφήτης. Hic revera Ille (Deut. XVIII.15, promissus) Propheta est, Joh. VII.40. Nunquam sic locutus homo; sicut hic homo, hoc est, tam præclarè, tam efficaciter, & ad cor & conscientiam nostram locutus est, quomodo nemo alius, ibid. v.46. Ut in eo impletum sit illud Dei ad animam electam: על נפשי ודברתי אנכי Ego (ceu vera πειθω suada & suadela, suadens & persuadens) pelliciam; seu persuadebo ipsi, & loquar ei ad cor, quæ cordi sunt, & cor corroborant, afficiunt, Hos. II.14. Ideo discipuli Emmauntem profecti, penetrante illa suada Christi vehementer commoti & compuncti; Nonne, inquiunt, cor nostrum erat in nobis urens (quia juxta Solem illum justitiæ positum ejus ardentes radios persensit) cùm loqueretur nobis in via, & cùm nobis aperiret Scripturas? Luc. XXIV.32. Nam gladius Spiritus, anceps, romphæa ex ore Cœlestis hujus Prophetæ, inter septem candelabra aurea ambulantis prodit, Apoc. I.16. Sunt enim verba ejus sagittæ illæ acutæ, de quibus sponsa חציך שנונים Sagittæ tuæ acutæ sunt. Populi subter te cadunt, Psal. XLV.6. Cujusmodi verba illa, quibus Saulem ad se Christus convertit: Saul, Saul, quid me persequeris, &c. fuerunt, Act. IX.4. De quibus sic Augustinus, ad Psal. 45: præclarè: De Cœlo emissa est sagitta, corde percussus est Saulus;
units.tr: This, therefore, must above all be attributed not to human skill but to the divinely taught [θεοδιδάκτῳ] eminence of Christ's prophetic office: he is said to have spoken quite differently from the scribes. For he was [διδάσκων] teaching [ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων] as one having authority, and not as a scribe, Matt. 7:29, so that his teaching struck his hearers, Mark 1:22; Luke 4:32. [ἐξεπλήσσοντο] All who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers, ibid. 2:47. For his speech was lively and burning, joined to [πνεῦμα ζωῆς] the spirit of life; the scribes' speech, by contrast, was feeble, sluggish and languid. The teachers of the Hebrews were accustomed to claim [רשות ἐξουσίαν] authority to teach and to interpret the law, and they spoke nothing except in the name and authority of their own masters, and [מצות אנשים מלמדה] the commandment of men taught by rote, Isa. 29:13, handed down by their forefathers, clinging solely to the vanities of tradition, to the trifles of grammatical observations, and to the frivolous and false mysteries of the Cabbala. Demonstration from Holy Scripture that reached the conscience was rare or non-existent among them. Nevertheless, boasting of that authority [ῥῆσιν ἐξουσίαν] to teach, they insulted Christ thus: [Ἐν ποίᾳ ἐξουσίᾳ ταῦτα ποιεῖς] By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you that authority? Matt. 21:23. But although he had no authority from men, yet he had it, for he spoke as one having authority, the people themselves being the judges, and by his speaking he astonished everyone, because, as a faithful witness, he spoke those things which he had seen and heard in heaven itself, the conscience of men bearing witness that his teaching is true and holy. "Behold, I have given him to the peoples as a witness, [נגיד ומצוה] a leader and commander," Isa. 55:4. "He who comes from above is above all. And what he has seen and heard, that he testifies; and no one [ψυχικὸς] (natural man) receives his testimony." (Because it is above all human thought and differs from their counsels, it cannot be received unless concupiscence, which naturally struggles against it, is restrained and held in check; and so it is a stumbling-block not only to the Gentiles but also to the Jews, so that this alone can show that he is a witness from heaven.) "He who has received his testimony has set his seal that God is true. For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God." John 3:31-34. "I have many things to say and to judge concerning you. But he who sent me is true, and what I have heard from him, I say to the world," etc. "When you have lifted up the Son of man, then you will know that I am he, and that as my Father taught me, so I speak," John 8:26 etc. (whose Spirit is upon me, the Spirit of wisdom, prudence, knowledge and the fear of God, Isa. 11:2, and who has given me [לשון למדים] the tongue of the learned, ibid. 50:4). For he learned from the Father as man; as God, existing in the bosom of the Father, he saw and heard. Hence many of the people, when they heard his words, said: [Οὗτος ἐστιν ἀληθῶς ὁ Προφήτης] This is truly the Prophet. Here indeed is that Prophet promised in Deut. 18:15, John 7:40. "Never has a man spoken as this man does," that is, he spoke so eloquently, so effectively, and to our heart and conscience, as no one else did, ibid. v. 46. Thus in him was fulfilled that word of God concerning the chosen soul: [על נפשי ודברתי אנכי] "I will entice her" (as true persuasion and suasion, persuading and convincing); or I will persuade her, "and speak to her heart," that is, to the things that are of the heart, which strengthen and move the heart, Hos. 2:14. Therefore the disciples going to Emmaus, deeply moved and pierced by that penetrating persuasion of Christ, said: "Was not our heart burning within us," (for they felt the burning rays of that Sun of righteousness) "while he spoke to us on the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?" Luke 24:32. "For a sharp two-edged sword goes forth from the mouth of this heavenly Prophet, who walks among the seven golden candlesticks," Rev. 1:16. "For his words are those sharp arrows, of which the bride says: [חציך שנונים] Your arrows are sharp; the peoples fall beneath you," Ps. 45:6. Such were those words with which Christ turned Saul to himself: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" etc., Acts 9:4. Of these Augustine rightly says in his commentary on Ps. 45: "An arrow was sent from heaven; Saul was struck in the heart."

units.la: nondum Paulus, adhuc creatus, nondum prostratus, accepit sagittam ac cecidit, in corde. Non quòd prostratus est in faciem, ibi cecidit, in corde; sed ubi ait: Domine, quid vis me facere? Modò ibat ad Christianos castigandos & producendos ad pœnam, & modò dicit Christo: Quid jubes me facere? O sagittam acutam & potentissimam, qua accepta cecidit Saulus, ut esset Paulus. Denique ad ἐξαίρετον & Divinitatem sermonis Christi etiam præconii ejus gratia & suavitas pertinet. Longè enim rectius γλυκυλόγος Dulciloquus appellandus venit, quàm ille tantopere ab Homero celebratus Nestor, de quo Iliad. α. sic ille cecinit: Τῆς ἡ γλώσσης μέλιτος γλυκίων ῥέεν αὐδή. Illius ex ore melle dulcior fluxit oratio. De quo sic sponsa: Pulcher es præ filiis hominum: Effusa est gratia in labia tua, Psal. XLV.3. Et Deus ipse: Ecce Servus meus, &c. Non clamabit, nec exaltabit, nec audire faciet in platea vocem suam, (indignabundi scilicet, impatientis, ἀλαζὼν more strepet, tumultus ciebit; quia se ipsum κενὸν εξινανίρε, humiliare debuit, voluit.) Arundinem quassatam non franget, & linum fumigans non extinguet (infirmos eriget, consolabitur, salvabit, quia propter pauperes, non divites & plenos, propter peccatores, non justos veniet) Esaj. XLII.1.2.3. Ideo omnes mirati dicuntur ἐπὶ τοῖς λόγοις τῆς χάριτος super sermonibus gratiæ, qui procedebant ex ore ejus, Luc. IV.22. Est enim, uti iterum Sponsa laudat הכו מתקים וכלו מחמדים זה דודי Palatum ejus dulcedo mera (sermo ejus dulcissimus) & totus est desiderabilis. Hic est dilectus meus, Cant. V.16. Multorum instar hæc sunto: Venite ad me omnes fatigati & onerati. Ego reficiam vos, Matth. XI.28. Quicquid oraveritis Patrem meum in nomine meo, dabit vobis, Joh. XVI.23. Respicite ad me, & salvamini omnes fines terræ, Esaj. XLV.22. Heus omnis sitiens, venite ad aquam, ibid. LV.1. Tam suavia, dulcia nullus homo ex terra loqui potuit. Mittendus fuit Propheta, qui in sinu Patris fuit, & Patrem nobis ostendere potuit, & in cujus amore Dei amorem cerneremus, quíque verba Dei, quæ hactenus ille locutus non est, sed locuturum se ad consummationem lætitiæ promiserat, loqueretur, ut ita, qui Deitatem Christi tollunt, etiam officium ejus Propheticum tollere censeri debeant.
units.tr: Not yet Paul, still being made, not yet cast down, he received the arrow and fell in the heart. Not that he was thrown on his face there; he fell there in the heart, when he said: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" Just now he was going about to punish Christians and bring them to punishment, and now he says to Christ: "What do you bid me do?" O sharp and most powerful arrow, by which Saul, having received it, fell, so that he might be Paul. Finally, the excellence and divinity of Christ's speech also pertains to the grace and sweetness of his preaching. For he ought much more rightly to be called [γλυκυλόγος] sweet-speaking than that Nestor so greatly praised by Homer, of whom in the first book of the Iliad he sang thus: [Τῆς ἡ γλώσσης μέλιτος γλυκίων ῥέεν αὐδή] "Speech sweeter than honey flowed from his tongue." Of Christ the bride says: "You are fairer than the sons of men; grace is poured out on your lips," Ps. 45:3. And God himself: "Behold my Servant," etc. "He will not cry out, nor lift up his voice, nor make it heard in the street" (that is, he will not rage in indignation or impatience, nor stir up tumult with boastful bluster, because he willed to humble himself and empty himself). "A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoking flax he will not quench" (he will raise up the weak, console them, and save them, for he comes for the poor, not the rich and full, and for sinners, not the righteous), Isa. 42:1-3. Therefore all "marvelled at the words of grace" [ἐπὶ τοῖς λόγοις τῆς χάριτος] that proceeded from his mouth, Luke 4:22. For, as the bride again praises him: [הכו מתקים וכלו מחמדים זה דודי] "His mouth is sweetness itself; his speech is altogether sweet, and he is wholly desirable. This is my beloved," Cant. 5:16. Let these serve as examples of many: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you," Matt. 11:28. "Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you," John 16:23. "Look to me and be saved, all you ends of the earth," Isa. 45:22. "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters," ibid. 55:1. No man from the earth could speak so sweetly and pleasantly. A Prophet had to be sent who was in the bosom of the Father, who could show us the Father, in whose love we might discern the love of God, and who would speak the words of God, which he had not hitherto spoken but had promised to speak at the fulfilment of joy. Thus those who deny the deity of Christ ought also to be judged to remove his prophetic office.

units.la: XLIV. Salus nostra per Christum non tantum λαλεῖσθαι dici, prædicari, sed etiam dicta βεβαιοῦσθαι confirmari, stabiliri debuit, Hebr. II.3. Christus quidem ἀξιώσεως etiam absque operibus agnosci potuit & debuit, sed voluit tamen Deus eum ἐκ πεῖρας & per doctrinam, & per opera innotescere ad nostram fidem confirmandam, & obstinatos inexcusabiles reddendos βεβαιώσεως μαρτυρίας confirmatio testimonii, seu præconii Evangelici, 1.Cor. I.6. miraculis, exemplo vitæ & mortis, & martyrio facta est. Non tantum enim Deus Pater Filio suo verba, quæ loqueretur, sed etiam opera, quæ faceret, & quibus verbis pondus adderet, dedit. Et miracula quidem tum ad Propheticum, tum ad Sacerdotale, tum ad Regium Christi munus pertinent. Ad Propheticum, quatenus Prophetiæ ejus annexa, eidem robur addiderunt ad fidem populi, ut à Deo missus Salvator recipetetur. Quo respectu Patrem eorum authorem appellavit. Ad Sacerdotale, quatenus per ea morbos, mortem omnem
units.tr: XLIV. Our salvation through Christ had to be not only spoken of and preached, but the things spoken had also to be confirmed and established, Heb. 2:3. Christ indeed could and ought to have been recognised by his dignity even without works, but God nevertheless willed that he be made known [ἐκ πεῖρας] by experience, both by his teaching and by his works, to confirm our faith and to render the obstinate inexcusable. The [βεβαιώσεως μαρτυρίας] confirmation of the testimony, that is, of the Evangelical proclamation, 1 Cor. 1:6, was effected by miracles, by the example of his life and death, and by his martyrdom. For God the Father gave his Son not only the words he was to speak but also the works he was to do, and by which he would add weight to his words. And miracles indeed pertain to Christ's prophetic, to his priestly, and to his kingly office. To the prophetic office, insofar as they, being joined to his prophecies, added strength to them for the faith of the people, so that the Saviour sent from God might be received. In this respect he called the Father their author. To the priestly office, insofar as through them diseases, all death...

units.la: Præconium illud suum etiam operibus seu miraculis omni exceptione maioribus confirmavit.
units.tr: He also confirmed that proclamation of his by works, that is, by miracles, which are greater than any objection could be raised against.

units.la: Note: the right margin notes are: "Praeconium illud suum etiam operibus seu miraculis omni exceptione maioribus confirmavit." omnémque peccati vim à suis abstulit. Ad Regium, quatenus, ut potestatem habens destruendi opera Sathanæ, ea patravit. Ante omnia ergo miracula ut Propheta, doctrinæ suæ firmandæ patravit. Cúmque varia miraculorum genera sint, utpote quorum alia sunt, quæ admirationem habent à substantia operis, cui in rerum natura simile dari non potest, velut cùm Josuæ tempore Sol & Luna in medio cursu substiterunt, Josh. X. 12. 13. alia à modo productionis, quæ vel ordinariè per causas naturales & modo à natura præscripto, fieri sueta, extra ordinem illum vel in momento, vel brevissimo tempore producuntur, velut cùm Virga Aaronis floruit & germinavit, Num. XVII. 8. vel sine adhibitis mediis externis producuntur, ut nubes & columna ignis duces Israelitarum in deserto; vel adhibitis mediis externis, sed minimè ad effectum talem proferendum idoneis producuntur; velut cùm ex contactu ossium Elizæi mortuus ad vitam excitatus legitur, 2. Reg. XIII. 21. alia à Divinæ Benignitatis declaratione; velut cùm manna populo ex Cœlo depluit: alia à patefactione iræ & judicii, velut cùm terra seditionis Coreh, Dathan & Abiram dehiscere visa est: alia à patratione in Cœlo, ut Solis statio: alia à patratione in terra, velut aquarum ex petra baculo percussa fluxus: alia à patratione in aqua, velut æquoris Erythræi divisio; singulorum istorum specimina Christus immediatè vel per Apostolos edidit, stupendo & inaudito operum Divinorum ab uno editorum concursu. Nam & quoad substantiam operis cæco visum restituit, Joh. IX. 7. &c. quoad modum productionis extra ordinem aquam in vinum convertit, ibid. II. 7. 8. quod brevi adeò tempore & extra matricem propriam natura efficere non potest: & sine externis mediis adhibitis dæmonia ejecit, leprosos fanavit, mortuos resuscitavit: & adhibitis mediis, sed non idoneis, veluti luto & sputo cæco nato visum reddidit: & declarandæ benignitati & clementiæ suæ singula fere ἀληθῶν beneficiis afficiens omnes Act. X. 38. patravit, exceptis paucis, quibus iram & judicium suum prodidit, velut cùm Gadarenorum porcos potestati Diaboli subjecit, Matth. VIII. 31. 32. & ficui fructum foliis ostentatis mentienti maledixit; Marc. XI. 13. &c. & moribundus in Cœlo eclipsin, Matth. XXVII. 45. effecit; in terra motum ejusdem, & petrarum fissuram, ibid. v. 51. effecit: & in aëre silere ventos; in mari quiescere fluctus, ibid. VIII. 26. jussit. Merito igitur Nicodemus ad Christum dixit: Magister, novimus, quòd à Deo Doctor prodieris: Nemo enim hæc signa facere potest, quæ tu facis, nisi Deus sit cum eo, Joh. III. 2. Et cæcus ille: Nisi hic fuisset ex Deo, non potuisset facere quicquam, ibid. IX. 33.
units.tr: Note: the right margin notes read: "He also confirmed that proclamation of his by works or miracles, greater than any objection," and "he took from his own people all power of sin." To the king, insofar as, having power to destroy the works of Satan, he performed them. Above all, therefore, as a prophet, he performed miracles to confirm his teaching. Since there are various kinds of miracles, some of which draw our wonder from the substance of the work, for which nothing similar can be found in the nature of things, as when the sun and moon stood still in their course in the time of Joshua (Josh. 10:12, 13); others from the mode of production, when things that normally happen through natural causes and in the manner prescribed by nature are produced outside that order, in an instant or in a very short time, as when Aaron's rod budded and sprouted (Num. 17:8); or are produced without any external means, as the cloud and the pillar of fire that led the Israelites in the wilderness; or are produced with external means that are in no way fit to bring about such an effect, as when we read that a dead man was raised to life by contact with the bones of Elisha (2 Kings 13:21); others from the declaration of God's kindness, as when manna rained down on the people from heaven; others from the revelation of wrath and judgment, as when the earth seemed to open and swallow Korah, Dathan and Abiram in their rebellion; others from works in heaven, such as the standing still of the sun; others from works on earth, such as the flow of water from the rock struck by the staff; others from works in water, such as the division of the Red Sea. Christ himself, either immediately or through the apostles, displayed examples of each of these, in a wonderful and unheard-of concurrence of divine works performed by one person. For as to the substance of the work, he restored sight to the blind man (John 9:7, etc.); as to the mode of production, outside the ordinary order, he turned water into wine (ibid. 2:7, 8), which nature cannot do in so short a time and outside its proper womb; without external means he cast out demons, cleansed lepers, and raised the dead; with means applied but not fit for the purpose, as with clay and spittle he gave sight to the man born blind; and, showing his kindness and mercy by benefiting people in almost every way [ἀληθῶν], he performed all of them (Acts 10:38), except for a few in which he revealed his anger and judgment, as when he subjected the swine of the Gadarenes to the power of the devil (Matt. 8:31, 32), and cursed the fig tree that falsely displayed leaves without fruit (Mark 11:13, etc.); and when he was dying he caused an eclipse in heaven (Matt. 27:45), an earthquake on earth and the splitting of rocks (ibid. v. 51); and he commanded the winds to be still in the air and the waves to rest on the sea (ibid. 8:26). Rightly, therefore, Nicodemus said to Christ: "Rabbi, we know that you have come as a teacher from God; for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him" (John 3:2). And the blind man said: "If this man were not from God, he could do nothing" (ibid. 9:33).

units.la: XLV. Tot, & tantis miraculis exhibitis, Christus præconio suo gratiæ & Evangelii mirificam lucem affudit, incredibile pondus addidit.
units.tr: XLV. With so many and such great miracles displayed, Christ shed a wonderful light upon his proclamation of grace and the Gospel and gave it an incredible weight.

units.la: Nam aperiens cæcorum oculos eum se esse, qui ignorantiæ tenebris obscuratos hominum animos Divinæ sapientiæ & veritatis luce collustret. Mutorum linguas solvens, se linguas hominum ligatas, ne Deum & magnalia ejus prædicare vellent, vel vetarent, resolvere ad celebrandam gloriam Dei, gratiásque ei funden das: Surdorum aures patefaciens, se cordis aures peccato & obstinatione induratas aperire, vel potius in corde aures ad audiendum & intelligendum formare. Morbos quosvis mirabili ratione sanans, se sanatorem peccatorum, quæ morborum causæ & aculei sunt, esse: Dæmonia corporibus hominum exigens & exturbans, se vitia ex animis hominum expellere & expectorare, plantas ad gressum reformare, & animos, ut ab erroribus vitæ ad salutem progredi valeant, corroborare: Leprosos incurabiles sanans, se lepra peccatorum horribili laborantes sanguine suo purificare, & ad spiritualem salutem revocare: Mortuos resuscitans, se à morte peccati & inferno ad vitæ cœlestis fruitionem promovere & perducere potenter, docuit.
units.tr: For by opening the eyes of the blind he showed that he is the one who illumines the minds of men, darkened by the shadows of ignorance, with the light of divine wisdom and truth. By loosing the tongues of the dumb, he showed that he unbinds the tongues of men, which were tied so that they would not, or would not be allowed to, proclaim God and his great deeds, so that they may celebrate the glory of God and pour out thanks to him. By opening the ears of the deaf, he showed that he opens the ears of the heart, which have been hardened by sin and obstinacy, or rather that he forms in the heart ears for hearing and understanding. By healing diseases of every kind in a wonderful manner, he taught that he is the healer of sins, which are the causes and the sting of diseases. By driving out and casting out demons from the bodies of men, he taught that he expels and banishes vices from men's souls, restores the feet to walking, and strengthens minds so that they may advance from the errors of life to salvation. By healing incurable lepers, he taught that he purifies those suffering from the horrible leprosy of sin with his own blood and calls them back to spiritual health. By raising the dead, he taught that he powerfully moves and brings those from the death of sin and from hell to the enjoyment of heavenly life.

units.la: Etiam miracula cum Christi nativitate, baptismo, morte, resurrectione ex morte, ascensione conjuncta, eorundem veritatem, & Divinam potentiam συνεργίαν comprobarunt. Ita Miracula Christi visibile quoddam Evangelium: sicut orale præconium audibile fuerat. Unde discipulis Johannis Jesum interrogantibus, esset ne ipse Messias à Judæis expectatus, ipse Jesus respondit: Euntes renunciate Johanni, quæ audivistis & vidistis: Cæci vident, claudi ambulant, leprosi mundantur, surdi audiunt, mortui resurgunt, Matth. XI. 3. 4. 5. Luc. VII. 18. &c. quod perinde erat, ac si Messiam se verbis professus esset. Quamobrem etiam contumaciam eorum damnat, qui visis prodigiis in eum non crediderunt. Si, inquit, opera non fecissem in eis, quæ nemo alius fecit, peccatum non haberent, Johan. XV. 24.
units.tr: The miracles, joined with Christ's birth, baptism, death, resurrection from the dead and ascension, also confirmed the truth of these things and the divine power working together with them. Thus Christ's miracles were a kind of visible Gospel, just as his spoken proclamation was an audible one. Hence, when the disciples of John asked Jesus whether he was the Messiah expected by the Jews, Jesus himself answered: "Go and report to John what you have heard and seen: the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise," Matth. XI. 3, 4, 5; Luke VII. 18, etc., which was just the same as if he had professed himself the Messiah in words. For this reason he also condemns the obstinacy of those who, though they saw the prodigies, did not believe in him: "If," he says, "I had not done among them works which no one else has done, they would not have sin," John XV. 24.

units.la: XLVI. Cæterùm ordine certo doctrina & miracula processerunt.
units.tr: XLVI. Moreover, his teaching and his miracles came in a fixed order.

units.la: Nam & prius docuit quàm fecit, & ordine etiam fecit. Olim quidem Deus corporalia beneficia populo suo præstans, signa liberationi præmisit, Exod. IV. 2. 3. &c. Judic. VI. 17. 21. 37. Frustra enim confirmandis fidelium animis miracula post acceptum beneficium adjecta fuissent. Contra res in miraculis Christi habet. Christus enim prius per præconium, quàm per miracula inclarescere voluit. Primum enim ejus signum fuit aquæ in vinum conversio, Joh. II. 7. 8. &c. Atqui jam ante per doctrinæ promulgationem & Apostolorum vocationem innotuerat. Nam beneficia corporalia hominibus præstita & percepta nullam amplius dubitationem habere possunt. At Christi doctrina, ex Cœlo an ex terra sit, dubitationem apud homines animales & infirmos habuit, quæ Spiritu Dei, cooperantibus signis, discuti debuit. Tum & hic ordo in miraculis seu operibus ipsis Christi obtinuit, quòd per minora miracula majoribus prælusit, & velut auspicium fecit. Pater diligit Filium, & omnia ipsi ostendit, quæ ipse facit; (faciendo, operando, non rem ignotam docendo, adeóque non institutione, sed opere, quod in utroque, Patre & Filio, unum est;) & μείζονα τούτων majora his (quæ hactenus fecit) ostendet ei opera, ut vos admiremini, ibid. V. 20. Signum primum in Cana Galilææ editum erat, quòd fluvialem undam in vinum lætificans commutavit. Inde non semel eurienti turbæ cibos in deserto præbuit. Ab alimentis ad morborum sanationem progressus est; tandem & mortem expugnavit, resuscitatis iis, qui jam defleti & humati erant.
units.tr: For he taught before he worked miracles, and he also worked them in order. Of old, God first bestowed bodily benefits on his people and sent signs ahead of their deliverance (Exod. 4:2, 3, etc.; Judg. 6:17, 21, 37). For miracles added after a benefit had been received would have been pointless for strengthening the faith of believers. With Christ's miracles the case is different. Christ wished to become famous first through proclamation and only then through miracles. His first sign was the turning of water into wine (John 2:7, 8, etc.), but by then his teaching had already become known through its public proclamation and the calling of the apostles. Benefits to the body, once given and received, can leave no further doubt. But the question whether Christ's doctrine was from heaven or from earth was a doubt among natural and weak men, and it had to be resolved by the Spirit of God, with the signs co-operating. The same order also held in the miracles, or works, of Christ themselves: he prefaced greater miracles with lesser ones and, as it were, made a beginning with them. The Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself does (doing and working, not teaching a thing unknown; so the work is one in both Father and Son, not one of instruction). And he will show him greater works than these (that he has done so far), so that you may marvel (John 5:20). The first sign was done in Cana of Galilee, when he gladdened the river water by turning it into wine. After that, more than once, he gave food to a hungry crowd in the wilderness. From food he advanced to the healing of diseases, and at last he overcame death itself by raising those who had already been mourned and buried.

units.la: XLVII. Miracula Jesum edidisse, etiam inter Judaeos res confessa est.
units.tr: XLVII. That Jesus performed miracles has been admitted even among the Jews.

units.la: Ac ne iis quidem temporibus, quibus inter eos versatus est, & prodigia edidit, rem inficiabantur; sed vel magicis artibus facta esse causabantur, dicentes: Hic non ejicit daemones, nisi in Beelzebub, principe daemoniorum, Matth. XII.24. vel die Sabbathi, adeoque non ordine facta murmurabant, Joh. V.10.16. Etiam Josephus Jesum Thaumaturgum laudavit. Hv ǯ, inquit lib. XVIII.4. Erat enim mirabilium operum patrator. Licet enim haec & sequentia de Jesu, quem Virum sapientem, si modo virum eum nuncupare fas sit; appellat; verba in suspicionem vocatis Viri docti, Blondellus, Tanaquillus Faber, alii vocare conati sint; tamen eorum satis & Codicum veterum ac recentiorum manuscriptorum & editorum constans lectio, & Eusebii Demonstr. Evang. lib. IV. & Histor. lib. I. II. illa tanquam genuina & legitima repraesentantis; nec non Hieronymi lib. de Script. Eccl. in Josepho; Sozomeni Histor. lib. I. II. Isidori Pelusiotae lib. IV. Epist. 215. Cedreni, Nicephori Callisti, Suidae, aliorum eadem citantium & Josepho vindicantium authoritas: & ratio ipsa, quae Josephum, Scriptorem non indiligentem, historiam Christi, maximos in ea gente, & toto fere orbe motus excitantis, quin & sectam de nomine suo, Josephi jam tempore celebrem condentis, attingere voluisse & debuisse; inprimis cum fratris Christi Jacobi, Lib. XX. 8. & Hieronymo indice, etiam Johannis Baptistae, ceu veri Prophetae (verba tamen illa in codicibus recentioribus non occurrunt, a falsariis, uti videtur, erasa) meminerit; & orationis filum, atque dictionis color, talis, qualis Hellenistarum esse solet; tuentur. Sed haec παρέργα ὁδόν. At in libro etiam Thalmudico Avodah Zarah, & in Midras Cohelet, aliisque Veterum Hebraeorum libris vim veneni per nomen Jesu fuisse repressam, traditur. Quod & ipse Christus Marc. XVI. 18. promiserat. Sed & Nominis Jesu invocatione daemones expellere tentabant circumforanei quidam Judaei Exorcistae; Paulum salutari hac arte morbos sanantem imitari conantes. Quod filiis Sceuae, Sacerdotum principis, infeliciter ceciderit, cum male multaret eos daemon, atque his verbis incesseret: Jesum novi, & Paulum scio. Vos autem qui estis? Act. XIX.14.15. Accedit, quod Messiam maxima patrandorum prodigiorum facultate praeditum, & Mose ipso longe superiorem fore, iidem Thalmudistae, & Midras Coheleth tradiderunt; & revocaturum eum mortuos ad vitam R. Levi Ben-Gerson agnoscit. Talia igitur cum a Jesu praestita esse constet, illustrissimo hoc signo Messiam eum esse, vel palam fateri, vel suspicari certe debuerunt. Etiam Gentiles miranda facinora Jesu in publicos Pilati Commentarios retulisse, Justinus Apol. II. testatur, ad eos provocans passim; quod non fecisset, apud Imperatores Christianorum causam agens, nisi re nota publice & explorata. Quin & edita a Christo prodigia non pauca esse, nec Celsus, nec Julianus in Christianos scribentes negare ausi sunt. Denique & Muhammedani in Alcorano non solum prodigiis a Christo patratis fidem adjungunt, sed plura etiam, ab Evangelistis non memorata ex incertis Traditionibus, vel apocryphis libris hausta eidem affingunt.
units.tr: Even in the days when he lived among them, they did not deny that he performed wonders. Instead they claimed that they were done by magical arts, saying: He casts out demons only by Beelzebub, the prince of the demons (Matt. 12:24), or they grumbled that the works were done on the Sabbath and so not in good order (John 5:10, 16). Josephus also praised Jesus as a wonder-worker. For he was, as he says in book 18, chapter 4, a doer of wonderful works [Ἦν γὰρ παραδόξων ἔργων ποιητής]. For although this passage and what follows about Jesus, whom he calls a wise man, if indeed it is lawful to call him a man, have been suspected by learned men such as Blondel and Tanaquil Faber, who tried to reject them, the agreed reading of the old and more recent manuscripts and printed editions still stands for them, as does the authority of Eusebius, who cites it as genuine and authentic in his Demonstration of the Gospel, book 4, and in his History, books 1 and 2; and likewise of Jerome, in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, under Josephus; of Sozomen, History, books 1 and 2; of Isidore of Pelusium, Letters, book 4, letter 215; and of Cedrenus, Nicephorus Callistus, Suidas and others who quote the same passage and vindicate it for Josephus. The reasoning itself supports this: Josephus was no careless writer, the history of Christ stirred the greatest movements among that nation and almost throughout the whole world, and he was bound and obliged to touch on the sect that bore Christ's name, already famous in Josephus's own time. This is especially so since, according to Jerome, he also mentioned the brother of Christ, James (Book 20, ch. 8), and John the Baptist as a true prophet (although those words do not occur in the more recent manuscripts, having been erased, it seems, by forgers). The thread of the narrative and the colour of the diction are also such as Hellenistic writers usually have. But these are by-the-way remarks [παρέργα ὁδόν]. In the Talmudic book Avodah Zarah, and in the Midrash Kohelet and other ancient Hebrew books, it is related that the power of poison was checked through the name of Jesus, which Christ himself had promised in Mark 16:18. Also, some wandering Jewish exorcists tried to cast out demons by invoking the name of Jesus, imitating Paul, who healed diseases by this saving art. It went badly for the sons of Sceva, a chief priest, when the demon mistreated them and attacked them with these words: I know Jesus, and I know Paul, but who are you? (Acts 19:14, 15). In addition, the same Talmudists and the Midrash Koheleth handed down that the Messiah would be endowed with the greatest power to perform wonders and would far surpass Moses himself; and R. Levi Ben-Gerson acknowledges that he would restore the dead to life. Since it is established that such things were done by Jesus, they ought either to have openly confessed that he was the Messiah by this most illustrious sign, or at least to have suspected it. Justin, in his Apology II, testifies that the Gentiles also recorded Jesus's wonderful deeds in the public records of Pilate, appealing to them repeatedly. He would not have done so, pleading the Christian cause before the emperors, unless the matter had been publicly known and tested. Indeed, neither Celsus nor Julian, writing against the Christians, dared to deny that Christ performed not a few miracles. Finally, the Muslims in the Koran not only accept the miracles performed by Christ, but also attribute to him more, drawn from uncertain traditions or apocryphal books and not recorded by the Evangelists.

units.la: XLVIII. Nihilominus Pharisaeorum veterum miracula Christi Beelzebuli authori imputantium, impia progenies, recentiores Judaei alii quidem conficta, alii non Divina, sed Diabolica; omnes fere talia, qualia Pseudoprophetae edebant, & per quae Deus populum tentavit, fuisse blasphemant. Eorum igitur & Veritas, & Divinitas, & aptitudo ad procurandam salutem populi demonstranda est. Veritatem Miraculorum Christi eadem argumenta evincunt, quae Historiae & Scripturae S. N.T. Veritatem demonstrant. Neque fieri potuisset, ut undecim Apostoli, LXX. Discipuli, aliique Christum pro Messia, Deo, Salvatore suo reciperent, & ejus veritatis gratia, nulla temporali mercede, infanda adeo paterentur, imo homines plebeji, miseri, rerum omnium, quibus mundus seduci potest, velut astus, calliditatis, eloquentiae, &c. inopes veritatem eorum Judaeis, Graecis, Romanis, sacra sua, quibus innutriti erant abdicantibus, persuaderent, si vel ipsi talia confinxissent, vel fraus & mendacium iis suboluisset, vel ab impostoribus etiam falsa credere subacti essent. Nam quod primos authores eorum spem suam in mendaciis & fraudibus posuisse Judaei mentiuntur, nullam veri speciem habet, tum quia satis constat, eos, qui miracula illa primi prodiderunt, ab omni fraude & mendacio adeo abhorruisse, ut ne ad dissimulandam quidem ad breve tempus fidei suae professionem ullis fidiculis vel tormentis subigi potuerint: tum quia homines plebeji & idiotae non ita fraudes & mendacia architectari potuerunt, ut ab hominibus catis, sagacibus, & manus oculatas habentibus deprehendi non possent: tum quia tot homines, viri & mulieres, locis a se invicem distiti in fraudes adeo variantes, adeo calidas callidasque, constanter adeo & unanimiter conspirare non potuissent; nec etiam, nullo operae & perfidiae suae vel in hoc vel in altero saeculo pretio voluissent: tum quia impium ejusmodi facinus de illis credi, & dogmata eorum, pietatis plenissima, & vita nullius criminis comperta, vel ab inimicissimis etiam hostibus, solam imperitiam accusantibus insimulata, vetant: tum quia illa, quae miraculosam Ascensionem Christi in Coelum consecuta sunt, ejusmodi fuerunt, ut cum specie quadam fingi nullo modo potuerint: tum quia S. Paulus, qui ex hoste Christi, non sine miraculo, Apostolus factus, ad Corinthios scribens, varia Spiritus S. charismata fidelibus concessa commemorat, & signa Apostolatus sui operata esse apud eosdem in omni tolerantia ἐν σημείοις, ἐν τέρασι, & δυνάμεσι signis (nomine & potestate Christi patratis) prodigiis & virtutibus; 2. Cor. XII.12. gloriatur, mendacii convincendus nullo negotio a tota Ecclesia, ad quam scripsit, si dictis ejus certa fides non constitisset.
units.tr: XLVIII. Nevertheless, the impious progeny of the old Pharisees, who ascribed Christ's miracles to Beelzebub the author of evil, and the more recent Jews, some of whom say they were fabricated, and others that they were not divine but diabolical, all blaspheme that nearly all of them were of the kind that false prophets performed, and by which God tested his people. Therefore their truth, their divinity, and their fitness for procuring the salvation of the people must be demonstrated. The same arguments that establish the truth of history and of Holy Scripture of the New Testament also prove the truth of Christ's miracles. It could not have happened that eleven apostles, seventy disciples and others would have received Christ as the Messiah, God and their Saviour, and for the sake of this truth would have endured such unspeakable sufferings, without any temporal reward. Nor could poor and wretched common men, lacking all the things by which the world can be deceived, such as cunning, craft, eloquence and so on, have persuaded Jews, Greeks and Romans to renounce their own sacred rites in which they had been brought up, if they had invented such things themselves, or if fraud and lies had crept in among them, or if they had been compelled by impostors to believe falsehoods. For the Jews lie when they claim that the first authors of this faith put their hope in lies and frauds, and this has no appearance of truth. This is so for several reasons. First, it is sufficiently well established that those who first reported these miracles shrank so far from all fraud and falsehood that they could not be forced by any racks or torments even to pretend, for a short time, that they had not professed their faith. Second, common men and untrained people could not have devised frauds and lies so well that they could not be detected by shrewd, sagacious men who had sharp eyes. Third, so many people, men and women, scattered in different places, could not have agreed so constantly and unanimously in frauds so varied and so ingenious and cunning, nor would they have wished to, since they would gain no reward for their labour and treachery, either in this age or the next. Fourth, the faith of such people was full of piety, and their lives were found free of any crime, and even their most hostile enemies, who accused them only of ignorance, could not charge them with such an impious deed. Fifth, the things that followed Christ's miraculous ascension into heaven were of a kind that could in no way be feigned with any show of plausibility. Sixth, St Paul, who was made an apostle from an enemy of Christ, not without a miracle, writing to the Corinthians, recalls the various gifts of the Holy Spirit granted to believers, and boasts that the signs of his apostleship were done among them with all patience, in signs, in wonders and in powers [ἐν σημείοις, ἐν τέρασι, ἐν δυνάμεσι] performed by the name and power of Christ, with miracles and mighty deeds (2 Cor. 12:12). If his words had not rested on a sure faith, he could easily have been convicted of lying by the whole Church to which he wrote.

units.la: XLIX. Par ratio Divinitatis miraculorum Christi est. Nam naturali vi patrata non esse, satis apparet, quia per naturae vim fieri non potest, ut solo contactu morbi graves & quidem subito tollantur, & mortui jam sepulti & foetentes resuscitentur. Quod si ad naturalem efficaciam aliquo modo opera ista referri potuissent,
units.tr: XLIX. The same reasoning holds for the divinity of Christ's miracles. That they were not wrought by natural power is clear enough: by the force of nature it cannot happen that grave diseases are removed at once by mere contact, or that men long dead and buried and stinking are raised. But if these works could in any way have been referred to natural efficacy,

units.la: n tuissent, dictum & objectum id pridem fuisset ab iis, qui se aut Christi in terris agentis, aut Evangelii ipsius hostes profesi sunt. Simili argumento colligitur, nec praestigias fuisse, quia pleraque opera palam gesta sunt, inspectante populo, & in populo multis eruditis, Christo malevolentibus, & cuncta ipsius opera accurate observantibus. Adde, quod similia opera fuerunt, saepiusque repetita, & ipsi effectus non momentanei, sed permanens opus post se relinquentes: Processerunt ergo, quod & Judaei ipsi fatentur, a virtute plus quam humana, id est, a Spiritu, eoque vel malo, vel bono. A malo spiritu prophetata esse, Pharisaei olim blasphemarunt, dicentes, Jesum daemonia ejicere in Beelzebule, principe daemoniorum. Matth. XII. 24. Quibus Jesus respondit: Omne Regnum a se ipso divisum desolatur: & omnis civitas & domus a seipsa divisa non consistit: Et si Sathanas Sathanam ejicit, ipse divisus a se ipso est. Quomodo ergo Regnum ejus consistit? ibid. v. 25, 26. q.d. Si Sathanae ope daemonia ex corporibus obsessorum pello, ejusque ita Regnum destruo, se ipsum & Regnum suum libens volens Sathanas destruit. Similis omnium operum Christi ratio fuit, quae ad concutiendum & evertendum Sathanae Regnum, & ad solvenda ejus opera, 1. Joh. III. 8. unice comparata fuerunt. Nam & ipsa doctrina Jesu, quam miraculis his muniebat, malis spiritibus e diametro adversatur. Vetat enim malos spiritus coli, abstrahit omnes ab omni immunditia morum, qua tales spiritus delectantur. Et ubicunque doctrina ea bona fide recepta est, illico daemonum cultus collabitur, magicae artes frigent, unus Deus, cum odio inexpiabili & detestatione daemonum colitur. Ipse enim Porphyrius, Eusebio de praep. Evang. lib. V. 1. citante, fassus est, ex quo Jesus coli coeptus est, publicam Deorum opem neminem sentire. Et Oracula praedicato Jesu obmutuisse, quasi fracta tum penitus daemonum vi, & silentio iis impositio, constat; & Gentiles ipsi queruntur. Verisimile autem non est, tam imprudentes esse daemones, ut ea faciant, & quidem saepissime, ex quibus maximum dedecus & detrimentum iis accedat. At nec Sapientiae & bonitati Dei convenit, ut passus fuerit astu daemonum illudi hominibus ab omni malitia alienis, & sui metuentibus. quales primos Christi discipulos fuisse, vita eorum inculpata, & multae calamitates conscientiae causa toleratae manifestum faciunt. Neque hic moramur putidissima figmenta recentiorum verborum in Toldos Jeschu mentientium, quod Jesus in Templo שם המפורש Nomen Dei ineffabile lapidi a Davide fundamentum fodiente reperto, & in Sancto Sanctorum collocato, insculptum, & a duobus molossis aereis latratu suo adventantes prodentibus custoditum, clanculum & arte magica Templum intrans invenerit, didicerit, membranae inscripserit, & membranam hanc, scissa carne, &, ne dolorem sentiret, enuntiato nomine, intra carnem cruris sui abstruserit, ejusque pronunciatione mortuos suscitaverit, Leprosos sanaverit, similiaque patraverit. Placet equidem confessio haec, quod vera, non fictitia sint Christi miracula, & quod non daemonis, sed Nominis Tetragrammati ope opera tanta peregerit. De caetero ecquem lapidis hujus, & inscripti eidem Nominis Tetragrammati, a Davide inventi, in Sancto Sanctorum collocati, conservati idoneum testem dabunt? An Scriptores sacros, qui Davidis & Templi res praecipuas exquisite descripserunt? Altum apud eos de re hac silentium est. An Josephum, qui Templum, & quicquid in Templo memoratu dignum inerat, accurate etiam recensuit? At nec ϗ, nec μν ille hac de re. Si David & Solomon lapidem eum in potestate sua habuerunt, cur ipsi arte ea usi non sunt, nullisque miraculis claruerunt? Cur molossi Jesum non prodiderunt? Magica arte eos inhibitos fuisse nugantur; quasi Deus homini mago suppetias laturus & concessurus fuerit, ut tremendum Nomen suum furtim sublatum irreverenter adeo profanaret, & nominatione ejus tot & tanta miracula ederet. Sed & illud flagrantis mendacii futilitatem prodit, quod parum sibi Judaei circa tempus lapidis hujus mystici in Sacrarium illati constant. Alii enim, uti diximus, a Davide id factum delirant: alii Helenae Reginae Izatae Adiabenorum Regis uxoris temporibus, & munificentia monumentum isthoc conditum tradunt. Posterius hoc si recipitur, post tempora demum Jesu id factum fuerit, quia Helena illa Claudio demum imperante vixit. Sed pluribus etiam commenti vanitatem Celeb. Wagenseilius Confut. lib. Toldos Jeschu § IX. &c. confixit. Alio etiam mendacio impietatem suam Christianis nominis hostes cumularunt, suppositio sub Jesu nomine libro, magicas artes complexo, quibus eum miracula fecisse fingunt. Verum insciter fallaciam hanc ingressi sunt, cum Petro & Paulo inscriptum a Jesu opus tradiderunt, quasi Jesu familiaris Paulus fuisset, qui aliquanto post Jesu mortem in Christianorum castra transiit. Adversus figmenti hujus conditores vehementer incandescens Augustinus de Cons. Evang. lib. I. 9. merito quaerit, cur, qui librum hunc, in quo portentifica Jesu ars tradita est, legere possunt, eadem, quae ipse miracula patrare non possint, & an, qui tantum γοητειας prodigiisque vivus mortuusque valuit, iisdem, antequam natus esset, efficere potuerit, ut S. Prophetae Spiritu Dei afflati de se ea praedicerent, quae opere deinde completa sunt? Adde, Pauli, adeoque etiam Jesu discipulos θεσεγα sectatos contulisse libros, & coram omnibus combussisse, Act XIX. 19. Adeo Jesus & ejus discipuli a Magicis artibus abhorruerunt. Non ergo miracula Christi impuro spiritu authore processerunt. Si a bonis mentibus, at Deo inferioribus, profecta esse dixeris, eo ipso fatebere, illa Deo placuisse, & ad Dei honorem pertinuisse, cum bonae mentes nihil nisi Deo acceptum & gloriosum faciant. Talia tamen sunt Christi opera, ut a bonis etiam Angelis obstetricantibus patrari non potuerint, cum mortuorum suscitatio, totius naturae, Coeli, terrae, maris obsequium solius vocis nutus & voluntatis Christi testificationi praestitum, & prodigia patrandi facultatis communicatio Apostolis ab eodem, Matth. X. 8. Luc. X. 19. facta, & plura alia infinitae potentiae causam, adeoque Deum ipsum, qui עשה נפלאות לבדו solus mirabilia facit, Psal. LXXII. 18. authorem testantur.
units.tr: they would have been said and objected long ago by those who professed themselves enemies either of Christ while he was on earth or of the Gospel itself. By a similar argument it is inferred that they were not tricks, because most of the works were done openly, in full view of the people, and among the people were many learned men hostile to Christ, who observed all his works carefully. Add that the works were of a similar kind and often repeated, and that their effects were not momentary but left a lasting work behind them. They therefore proceeded, as the Jews themselves admit, from a power more than human, that is, from a spirit, and one either evil or good. The Pharisees once blasphemed that his prophesying came from an evil spirit, saying that Jesus casts out devils by Beelzebub, the prince of the devils. Matth. XII. 24. To which Jesus replied: Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand. And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then shall his kingdom stand? ibid. vv. 25, 26. That is, if by Satan's help I drive devils out of the bodies of the possessed, and so destroy his kingdom, then Satan of his own accord destroys himself and his own kingdom. The same account holds for all the works of Christ, which were designed solely to shake and overthrow Satan's kingdom and to undo his works, 1 Joh. III. 8. For the very doctrine of Jesus, which he confirmed by these miracles, is directly opposed to evil spirits. It forbids the worship of evil spirits and draws everyone away from the uncleanness of life in which such spirits delight. And wherever that doctrine has been received in good faith, at once the worship of demons collapses, magic arts grow cold, and the one God is worshipped with an inexpiable hatred and detestation of demons. Indeed Porphyry himself, as Eusebius cites him in Praep. Evang. book V, confessed that since Jesus began to be worshipped, no one has felt the public help of the gods. And it is established that the oracles fell silent once Jesus was preached, as if the power of the demons had then been wholly broken and silence imposed on them; and the Gentiles themselves complain of it. It is not likely, however, that the demons are so unwise as to do things which, and that very often, bring them the greatest shame and loss. Nor does it agree with the wisdom and goodness of God that he should have allowed men free from all malice and fearing him to be deceived by the cunning of demons, as the first disciples of Christ were: their blameless lives and the many hardships they bore for conscience' sake make this plain. Nor do we linger here over the most foul fictions of recent writers, who in the Toldos Jeschu lie that Jesus, having found in the Temple the ineffable Name [שם המפורש] of God, which was engraved on a stone that David had found while digging the foundations and placed in the Holy of Holies, and which was guarded by two bronze mastiffs that gave warning with their barking as he approached, entered the Temple secretly by magic art, learned the Name, wrote it on parchment, and, cutting his flesh so that he would feel no pain, hid the parchment within the flesh of his thigh; and by pronouncing the Name he raised the dead, healed lepers, and did similar things. Indeed I am content with this admission, that Christ's miracles were true and not fictitious, and that he performed such great works not by a demon but by the power of the Tetragrammaton. As for the rest, who will give a suitable witness to this stone and to the inscribed Name of the Tetragrammaton, found by David and placed and kept in the Holy of Holies? The sacred writers, who described carefully the chief matters concerning David and the Temple? On this they keep a deep silence. Josephus, who also listed accurately the Temple and whatever in it was worth mentioning? But he says nothing on this matter either. If David and Solomon had that stone in their power, why did they not use that art and become famous for miracles? Why did the mastiffs not betray Jesus? They babble that they were restrained by magic art, as if God would come to the aid of a magician and allow him to steal away his awesome Name and so profane it irreverently, and to work by naming it so many and such great miracles. But the futility of this blazing lie is also shown by the fact that the Jews agree poorly among themselves about the time when this mystical stone was brought into the sanctuary. For some, as we said, dream that David did it; others hand down that this monument was founded in the times of Helena, queen of Izates, king of the Adiabeni, through her generosity. If this latter is accepted, the thing was done only after the time of Jesus, since that Helena lived under the emperor Claudius. But the vanity of the fiction has been shown in many ways by the learned Wagenseil in his Confutatio of the Toldos Jeschu, §IX etc. The enemies of the Christian name have also heaped up their impiety with another lie: a book forged under the name of Jesus, containing magic arts, by which they pretend he worked his miracles. But they entered upon this deceit clumsily, since they handed the work down as written by Peter and Paul, as if Paul had been a familiar of Jesus, though he went over to the Christian camp some time after Jesus' death. Augustine, vehemently incensed against the authors of this fiction, rightly asks (De cons. Evang. I. 9) why those who can read this book, in which the marvel-working art of Jesus is handed down, cannot perform the same miracles themselves; and whether he who while alive and dead was so powerful in sorcery [γοητείας] and prodigies could, before he was born, have brought it about that the holy prophets, inspired by the Spirit of God, foretold of him the things that were afterwards fulfilled. Add that the disciples of Paul, and so also of Jesus, gathered their curious books [περίεργα] and burned them before everyone, Act. XIX. 19. So far did Jesus and his disciples shrink from magic arts. Therefore the miracles of Christ did not proceed from an impure spirit as their author. If you say they came from good minds, but inferior to God, you thereby confess that they pleased God and pertained to the honour of God, since good minds do nothing but what is acceptable and glorious to God. Yet Christ's works are of such a kind that they could not have been done even with good angels assisting: the raising of the dead, the obedience of all nature, of heaven, earth and sea, to the mere voice, nod and will of Christ as testimony to him, and his communication to the apostles of the power to work miracles, Matth. X. 8, Luc. X. 19, and many other things, testify to a cause of infinite power, and so to God himself, who alone does wonders, Psal. LXXII. 18, as their author.

units.la: L. Sed Deo cooperante licet, at tentante populum suum edita esse Christi miracula, clamitant. Atqui Deus ipse, inquiunt, Pseudoprophetæ etiam signo & portento edito & eventu ipso comprobato מרד apostasiam à Jehova Deo populi sui suadenti fidem omnem derogavit, eo argumento, quòd tali modo tentet populum suum, an diligat Jehovam toto corde, & tota anima, Deut. XIII. 1.2. &c. Fatendum equidem est, & signa quædam à Pseudo-prophetis, Diaboli instigatione edi posse cooperante Deo, nec sine Deo, uti Sathanas non sine Deo Serpentem loquelæ suæ organon fecit: & signa quædam, post veritatem publicatam, non veritatis doctrinæ, sed Divinæ tentationis & judicii signa esse posse. Neque enim omnia miracula fidem faciunt verbis ejus, qui miracula edit. Inprimis enim illa excitant homines, & attonitos reddunt, ne dormiant, & segnescant ad animadvertendum opera Dei, sive per ea docere, sive tentare intenderit. Tum verò per miracula Deus docet, cùm fiunt ab iis, qui in nomine Jehovæ, & verbum Jehovæ loquuntur: tum per eadem, à quocunque patrata tentat, cùm etiam post nomen Dei cognitum & manifestatum fiunt ab iis, qui nec in nomine Jehovæ, nec verbum Jehovæ loquuntur. Prioris, non posterioris generis miracula Christi fuerunt. Nam ille nec Pseudo-propheta fuit, nec miracula Pseudo-prophetarum miraculis similia patravit. Pseudopropheta non fuit, quia non docuit מרד apostasiam à Jehova, Deo Israelis, nec novum Numen, vel novam religionem, à Mose non præscriptam, uti Judæi, & sub specie pietatis Sociniani blasphemant, sed Deum Abrahami, Isaci & Jacobi, quem omnes justi ante ejus in carnem adventum coluerunt, suasit, imò promissionem ab eodem Deo factam, quòd velit populo suo fieri in Deum, Genes. XVII.8. implevit. Ideo in nomine Patris sui se venisse, loqui, operari; & operari ὁμοίως similiter ut Pater, Joh. V.19. & unum esse cum Patre, ibid. X.30. & Mosen de se scripsisse ibid.cap.V.46. protestatur. At nec miracula ejus similia illis, quæ Pseudoprophetæ, per quos Deus tentat, patrant, fuerunt. Quæcunque enim fecit, secundum præcedentes de ipso prophetias facta sunt, eo tempore, quo fieri debebant, juxta Prophetiam: Ecce ego, & pueri, quos dedit mihi Jehova לאתות ולמופתים in signa & portenta in Israel, Esaj. VIII.18. Nullibi verò prædictum est, Pseudo-Christum venturum ante Christum, & miraculis celebre nomen sibi facturum, uti etiam multis ante Christum seculis nulla miracula priùs, quàm Christus surgeret, edita sunt; & ex tribu Juda vix quisquam per miracula inclaruit; ac ætate Christi nemo ante illum, ac ne Johannes Baptista quidem, adventantis Christi præco, Joh. X.41. & nemo unus in Templo, præter solum Christum, Templi Dominum, Matth. XXI. 14. signa fecit: & nullius unquam nativitas & mors tantis miraculis insignita fuit, quantis nativitas & mors Christi insignita est. Hæc unius soliusque Christi decora, Pseudo Christus vel Pseudo-propheta nullus unquam sibi vindicavit. Accedit, quòd miraculis Christi verba, quæ Christum loqui oportuit, & justitia, & emendatio hominum potentissima & certissima miraculorum fulcra, sociata sunt. Præterea tot & tanta, & tam insignita, atque extra suspicionis & dubitationis aleam posita, & tam crebra, nulla unquam frustratione interrupta Christi miracula fuerunt; ut ante & post ipsum similia nunquam patrata sint. Imperium exercuit in Cœlum, aquas, ventos, arbores, pisces, morbos, dæmones, mortem ipsam. Tota enim illi serviit rerum Natura, eúmque Deum & Dominum suum agnovit. Et nunquam non ei vocata salus respondit. At Ægyptiorum Magis vermium & pediculorum exercitus se non stiterunt. Quin & miracula Christum non tantùm parem, sed etiam majorem Mose ostenderunt. Testatus enim est hominibus, quid in corde ipsorum esset; iisque tum bonis, velut Nathanaeli, Joh. I.48.49. aliisque vera fide ad ipsum confugientibus; tum malis, veluti Pharisæis & Judæ proditori. De Christo enim prædictum est: הריחו ביראת יהוה odorabitur (velut sacrificium sibi oblatum) timorem Domini, & non secundum visa oculorum suorum, & audita aurium suarum judicabit, Esaj. XI.3. Unde Veteres Hebræi inter characteres Messiæ numerant, odorari improbos. Et Simon ille Pharisæus; Hic, inquit, Jesus, si esset Propheta, nosset, quæ & qualis hæc fæmina sit, Luc. VII. 39. Merito ergo de se Christus dixit, Opera se facisse, quæ ... hemo alius fecit, Joh. XV. 24. Denique Christus propria, non aliena potestate, & ad suam etiam gloriam miracula fecit: An creditis, quòd possim hæc facere? Matth. IX. 28. Pater meus hucusque operatur; & ego operor; & quidem ὁμοίως similiter, Joh. V. 17.19. Hoc initium signorum fecit Jesus in Cana Galilæa, & manifestavit gloriam suam, ibid. II. 11. Hæc infirmitas non est ad mortem, sed propter gloriam Dei, ut glorificetur Filius Dei per eam, ibid. XI.4. Id verò nulli mero homini, nulli verò, nedum falsô Prophetæ datum est.
units.tr: L. But they cry out that Christ's miracles were indeed performed, yet with God cooperating in order to tempt his people. For, they say, God himself rejected all faith in a false prophet, even one who gave a sign and a wonder and whose sign was confirmed by the event, when that prophet urged apostasy [מרד] from Jehovah, the God of his people, and he did so on this ground: that God in this way tests his people, whether they love Jehovah with all their heart and all their soul, Deut. XIII. 1.2. etc. It must indeed be admitted that certain signs can be performed by false prophets at the instigation of the devil, with God cooperating, and not without God, just as Satan made the serpent the instrument of his speech, not without God. It must also be admitted that certain signs, after the truth has been published, can be signs not of the doctrine of truth but of divine temptation and judgment. For not all miracles make faith in the words of the one who performs them. They chiefly arouse men and make them astonished, lest they sleep and grow sluggish in noticing the works of God, whether he intends to teach or to tempt by them. Then God indeed teaches by miracles when they are done by those who speak in the name of Jehovah and the word of Jehovah. He tempts by the same miracles, whoever works them, when they are done, even after the name of God has been known and made manifest, by those who speak neither in the name of Jehovah nor the word of Jehovah. The miracles of Christ were of the former kind, not the latter. For he was neither a false prophet, nor did he perform miracles similar to those of false prophets. He was not a false prophet, because he did not teach apostasy [מרד] from Jehovah, the God of Israel, nor a new deity or new religion not prescribed by Moses, as the Jews blaspheme and the Socinians blaspheme under the guise of piety. Rather, he persuaded [them of] the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whom all the righteous worshipped before his coming in the flesh, and he fulfilled the promise made by that same God, that he would wish to be God to his people, Gen. XVII.8. Therefore he declared that he had come, spoken and worked in the name of his Father, and works similarly [ὁμοίως] as the Father, John V.19, and that he is one with the Father, ibid. X.30, and that Moses wrote of him, ibid. chap. V.46. Nor were his miracles similar to those which the false prophets, through whom God tests, perform. For whatever he did was done according to the prophecies about him that went before, at the time when they had to be done, according to the prophecy: Behold, I and the children whom Jehovah has given me are for signs and wonders in Israel [לאתות ולמופתים], Isa. VIII.18. Nowhere is it foretold that a false Christ would come before Christ and make for himself a name famous for miracles. Likewise, for many centuries before Christ no miracles were performed before Christ arose; and hardly anyone from the tribe of Judah became famous through miracles. In the age of Christ no one before him performed signs, not even John the Baptist, the herald of the coming Christ, John X.41, and no one in the Temple except Christ alone, the Lord of the Temple, Matt. XXI.14. And never was anyone's birth and death marked by such great miracles as the birth and death of Christ. A false Christ or false prophet never claimed these honours for himself; they belong to one and only Christ. Add to this that the words Christ had to speak, and righteousness and the reform of men, the most powerful and certain supports of miracles, were joined to his miracles. Besides, the miracles of Christ were so many, so great, so remarkable, placed beyond the chance of suspicion and doubt, and so frequent, never interrupted by any failure, that similar ones were never performed before or after him. He exercised dominion over heaven, waters, winds, trees, fishes, diseases, demons, and death itself. For all of nature served him and acknowledged him as its God and Lord, and his summoned salvation never failed to answer him. But the swarms of lice and gnats raised by the magicians of Egypt did not stop. Indeed his miracles showed Christ to be not only equal to Moses but greater. For he testified to men what was in their heart: to good men, such as Nathanael, John I.48.49, and others who with true faith fled to him, and to evil men, such as the Pharisees and Judas the betrayer. For it is foretold of Christ: he will smell [הריחו] (as a sacrifice offered to him) the fear of the Lord [ביראת יהוה], and he will not judge according to what his eyes see or what his ears hear, Isa. XI.3. Hence the ancient Hebrews number among the marks of the Messiah that he detects the wicked. And that Pharisee Simon said: This man, Jesus, if he were a prophet, would know who and what sort of woman this is, Luke VII.39. Rightly, therefore, Christ said of himself that he had done works which no other man has done, John XV.24. Finally, Christ performed miracles by his own power, not another's, and also for his own glory: Do you believe that I can do this? Matt. IX.28. My Father works until now, and I work; and indeed similarly [ὁμοίως], John V.17.19. Jesus made this beginning of signs in Cana of Galilee and manifested his glory, ibid. II.11. This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified through it, ibid. XI.4. This was given to no mere man, and certainly not to a false prophet.

units.la: LI. Nec Christi Thaumaturgi, nec operum ejus dignitatem & fidem minuit, quòd ipse nihil à semetipso se operari, & nonnisi ostendente Patre, se operari fassus est, Joh. V.19. & Lazarum resuscitaturus Dei Patris sui opem implora-vit, ibid. XI.41.42. & in patria sua ullam virtutem facere potuisse, Marc. VI.5. negatur; & miracula sua celari interdum jussit, Matth. VIII. 4. & Scribarum quoque filii dæmones pepulisse, ibid. XII.27. leguntur; & denique Christus ipse signa & prodigia jactantes, & dicentes: Ecce hic Christus, vel ibi; audiri vetuit, ibid. XXIV. 23.24. Nam à se ipso nihil operari potuit, quia nec à se ipso est, sed à Patre est. Et à quo est, ab eodem operari debuit. Una Patris & Filii essentia, una voluntas, una operatio est; quia ὁμοίως similiter eadem voluntate & potentia operantur, Joh. V.19. sed utriusque origo à Patre est; seu Principium utriusque à Patre est. Cùmque omnis creatura malum faciendo, & originem suam relinquendo, à se aliquid velle, operari; & velle, operari, quod Deus non vult, vel operatur, adeóque à Deo dissentire possit; Christus qui à semetipso nihil velle vel operari potuit; neque aliud velle vel operari potuit; quàm quod Pater vult & operatur, non ut creatura, sed ut creator & Deus opera sua fecerit oportet. Nam is Patris opus facit, & in eo Pater cognoscitur. Est enim Angelus faciei. Videt igitur, quod Pater facit, qui nihil facit sine Filio, quicquid facit, per Filium facit, ibid.I.3. Non ergo δᾶξις Ostensio illa externa institutio, vel prælusio operis per diversam voluntatem & potentiam inferiorem imitandi, sed communis operatio ejusdem numero operis est. Lazarum suscitaturus imploravit equidem Patris opem, sublatis sursum oculis, dicens: Pater gratias tibi ago, quod me audivisti. Ego vero sciebam, quod semper me audias, ibid.XI.41.42. ut homo scilicet, & servus fidelis simul atque Filius dilectus, qui nihil non in nomine Patris faciebat; non agens gratias ut alii homines, qui orantes voluntatem Dei & donum ejus non norunt prius, quàm id accipiant, & suam voluntatem quandoque improvidam Divinæ correctioni subjicere coguntur; sed ut is, qui noverat semper se exaudiri, quia novit quid Pater ipsi monstraverit, quod ipse faciat, ut id similiter faciat, ibid.V.19. & omne consilium Patris, & opera ab eo sibi data facienda, Testamentum Dei, hæreditatem suam, oves suas novit. Impleat Deus כל משאלותיך omnia postulata tua, Psal.XX.6. Quod de nullo homine mero dici potest. Quòd verò in patria sua μηδεμίαν δύναμιν ποιῆσαι ἠδύνατο nullam virtutem facere Christus potuit, Marc.VI.5. non id impotentiæ ejus, (nam quosdam saltem impositis manibus curasse dicitur) sed ἀπιστίας infidelitatis hominum culpa factum ilico v.6. docet. Non poterat, quia deficiebat occasio, nullis se offerentibus, qui ipsi ut Thaumaturgo considerent. Si quid potes, (inquiebat parens lunatici ad Jesum) juva nos, misertus nostri, Jesus autem dixit ipsi: Τὸ εἰ δύνασαι πιστεῦσαι. Πάντα δυνατὰ τῷ πιστεύοντι. Hoc (ut τὸ sit pro τοῦτο Poëticè vel Atticè, teste Budæo) si potes, nempe credere, quòd ego tibi opitulari possim; vel: Illud, si potes, credere (reponens homini verba sua, Εἰ τι δύνασαι q.d. tu mihi dicis: Si quid potes; ego regero tibi: Τὸ εἰ δύνασαι illud si & tu potes; si credere potes, ego juvare possum) Omnia fieri poterunt tibi credenti, ibid.IX.22.23. Ergo non credenti nihil fieri potest, ob defectum non virtutis in faciente, sed fidei in patiente. Non enim πᾶσαν decens est, non credentes juvare, adeóque nec δυνατὸν possibile, quia potentiæ Divinæ objectum est τὸ Θεοπρεπὲς, id, quod Deum & virtutes ejus decet. Potens hæc Christi impotentia: popularium verò ejus, qui poterant non credere, impotens potentia fuit. Quòd verò Christus leproso à se sanato dixit: Ὅρα μηδενὶ εἴπῃς· Vide nemini dixeris; sed vade, ostende te Sacerdoti, & offer donum tuum, quod Moses ordinavit, in testimonium illis, (Sacerdotibus) Matth.VIII.4. & cæcis sanatis; Videte, ne quis cognoscat, ib.IX.30. Neque vicum ingredere, neque id dic cuiquam in vico, Marc.VIII.26. non ideo factum, quòd miraculis à se factis dissideret, quia aliàs curatos à se non ad Sacerdotes, juxta Legem Lev.XIV.3.4.10. explorandos ableggasset, & quidem εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς in testimonium illis, seu convincendis illis, quòd ceu morborum, adeóque etiam peccatorum sanator verus Messias sit: sed quia id tum humilitati, tum sinceritati ejus, nihil facientis propter applausum hominum, neque, juxta prædictionem, clamantis, vel extollentis vocem suam in plateis, Esaj.XLII.2. tum charitati ejus, ne adversus cum Pharifæi irritarentur, sed ut quærendis
units.tr: LI. Nor does it diminish the dignity and credibility of Christ the wonder-worker or of his works that he confessed he could do nothing of himself, but only as the Father showed him, John V.19; or that when about to raise Lazarus he implored the help of his Father God, ibid. XI.41.42; or that it is written that he could do no mighty work in his own country, Mark VI.5; or that he at times ordered his miracles to be kept quiet, Matt. VIII.4; or that the sons of the scribes are read to have cast out demons too, ibid. XII.27; or finally that Christ forbade those who boast of signs and wonders, saying Behold, here is Christ, or there, to be heard, ibid. XXIV.23.24. For he could do nothing of himself, because he is not from himself but from the Father. And from whom he is, from the same he ought to work. The Father and the Son have one essence, one will, one operation, because they work similarly [ὁμοίως] by the same will and power, John V.19; but the origin of both is from the Father, or the principle of both is from the Father. Since every creature, by doing evil and abandoning its origin, can will and do something of itself, and so will and do what God does not will or do, and can thus dissent from God, Christ, who could will and do nothing of himself, and could will or do nothing other than what the Father wills and does, must have done his works not as a creature but as creator and God. For he does the Father's work, and in him the Father is known. For he is the Angel of the face. Therefore he sees what the Father does, and he, who does nothing without the Son, whatever he does, does through the Son, ibid. I.3. So that showing is not an external instruction, or a preliminary exercise of work to be imitated by a different and lower will and power; it is a common operation of one and the same numerical work. He indeed implored the Father's help, lifting up his eyes, saying: Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I indeed knew that you always hear me, ibid. XI.41.42. He did so as man, and as a faithful servant and beloved Son at once, who did nothing except in the name of the Father. He gave thanks not as other men do, who, praying, do not know the will of God and his gift until they receive it, and are sometimes forced to submit their own imprudent will to divine correction; but as one who knew he was always heard, because he knew what the Father had shown him, so that he likewise does what he himself does, ibid. V.19. He knew every counsel of the Father, and the works given him to do, the covenant of God, his inheritance, his sheep. May God fulfil all your requests [כל משאלותיך], Ps. XX.6. This can be said of no mere man. But that Christ could do no power [μηδεμίαν δύναμιν ... ἠδύνατο] in his own country, Mark VI.5 (for it is said that he cured some by laying on hands), was not due to any lack of power but, as he teaches immediately at v.6, to the fault of men's unbelief [ἀπιστίας]. He could not, because the occasion was lacking, since no one offered himself to regard him as a wonder-worker. The father of the lunatic said to Jesus: If you can do anything, help us, having pity on us; but Jesus said to him: If you can believe [Τὸ εἰ δύνασαι πιστεῦσαι]. All things are possible to one who believes [Πάντα δυνατὰ τῷ πιστεύοντι]. This (taking τὸ for τοῦτο, as is poetic or Attic usage, according to Budaeus) means if you can, namely believe that I can help you; or it means: That, if you can, believe. He returns the man's own words to him: Εἰ τι δύνασαι, that is, you say to me, "If you can do anything"; I answer you: Τὸ εἰ δύνασαι, "that, if you too can," i.e. if you can believe, I can help. All things will be possible for you who believe, ibid. IX.22.23. Therefore nothing can be done for one who does not believe, not because of any lack of power in the doer, but because of a lack of faith in the one who is acted upon. For it is not fitting [πᾶσαν] to help those who do not believe, and so it is not possible [δυνατὸν], because the object of divine power is what is becoming to God [τὸ Θεοπρεπὲς], that which befits God and his virtues. This impotence of Christ was powerful; the power of his fellow countrymen, who could refuse to believe, was impotent. As for Christ's words to the leper he had healed, See that you tell no one [Ὅρα μηδενὶ εἴπῃς]; but go, show yourself to the priests, and offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them [εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς], Matt. VIII.4; and to the blind men he healed: See that no one knows it, ibid. IX.30; and: Do not enter the village, nor tell anyone in the village, Mark VIII.26, these were not said because he disowned the miracles he had performed. Otherwise he would not have sent the healed men away to the priests for examination according to the Law, Lev. XIV.3.4.10, and indeed as a testimony to them, that is, to convince them that the true Messiah is a healer of diseases and thus also of sins. Rather, it was for his humility and sincerity, as one who did nothing for the applause of men, nor, according to the prophecy, cried out or raised his voice in the streets, Isa. XLII.2; then for his charity, lest the Pharisees be provoked against him; and so that he might more freely devote himself to seeking out his sheep

units.la: ovibus suis sine impedimento deinceps etiam liberius vacare posset: tum denique prudentiæ ejusdem, quia non properè nimis & saltu, sed gradu in ora famámque hominum venire, Judæis tempus examinandi dicta & facta sua largiri, & demum per resurrectionem, ceu maximum signum, & cæteris omnibus præcedentibus lucem fœneraturum; pondus iis ad publicam & duraturam omnium famam addere, & auctoritate conciliare voluit, congruebat. Quales ob causas etiam discipulis interdixit, ne cuiquam dicant, quòd ipse Jesus Christus esset, Matth.XVI.20.Luc.IX.21. Non pauca tamen ejus miracula jam ante mortem Christi innotuerant palam, adeò ut dicere potuerit: Si opera non fecissem, quæ nullus alius fecit, peccatum non haberent. Nunc verò & viderunt, & oderunt me & Patrem meum, Joh.XV.24. Porro etiam Scribarum filios dæmonia ejecisse, ipse Christus Matth.XII.27. fatetur; illorum tamen opus suis operibus neutiquam adæquat, sed hypocrisin tantùm Judæorum, suum, non filiorum Scribarum exorcismum damnantium, cùm tamen clarius esset, quòd ipsorum filii non in spiritu sanctitatis dæmonia nonnunquam iis cedentia, ejicerent, pulsat. Forte etiam filii illi Scribarum appellato Christi nomine in dæmonia potestatem exercuerunt, juxta illa Johannis: Magister, vidimus quendam, qui in nomine tuo dæmonia ejicit, Luc.IX.49. nec non verba Christi ipsius: Multi dicent: In nomine tuo dæmonia ejecimus, Matth.VII.22. Denique Christus dicens: Tum si vobis dixerint: Ecce hic est Christus, vel ibi, ne credite. Surgent enim Pseudo-Christi, & Pseudo-prophetæ, & edent signa & prodigia magna, adeò ut si fieri posset, electos seducturi sint, ibid.XXIV.23.24. non se præstigiatorem, quippe utentem iisdem artibus, quibus qui utuntur, jure præstigiatores, Pseudochristi, Pseudoprophetæ existimantur; fassus est; uti ex verbis iis Celsus apud Originem contra Cels.lib.II. deliravit; sed potiùs discipulos suos adversus eorum fraudes, qui incantationibus & præstigiis sibi Christi nomen arrogaturi erant, præmunivit. Tantum enim abest, ut prodigiorum editores damnaverit, ut potiùs & ipse tot signa fecerit, quæ si sigillatim scriberentur, ne ipse quidem mundus libros scribendos caperet, Joh.XXI.25.(è re enim fuit nimia librorum copia non obrui fideles, ne in legendo omnis religio sita esse videretur, & actio intermitteretur) & miraculorum perpetrandorum facultatem discipulis suis promiserit: Signa, inquiens, credentes hæc sequentur: In nomine meo dæmonia ejicient, Linguis novis loquentur, Serpentes tollent, &c.Marc.XVI.17.18.
units.tr: ...the sheep without hindrance, and so that he could devote himself more freely to them from then on. Finally, it was fitting that his prudence should allow the Jews time to examine his words and deeds, since he came into the view and reputation of men not too hastily or by leaps, but step by step. He also wanted his resurrection, the greatest sign, to give light to everything that had gone before and to lend weight and authority to his public and lasting reputation among all. For these same reasons he forbade the disciples to tell anyone that he was Jesus Christ (Matt. 16:20; Luke 9:21). Yet many of his miracles had already become publicly known before Christ's death, so that he could say: If I had not done among them the works that no other man has done, they would not have sin. But now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father (John 15:24). Moreover, Christ himself admits (Matt. 12:27) that the sons of the scribes also cast out demons, yet he does not place their work on a level with his own. He attacks only the hypocrisy of the Jews, who condemned his exorcisms while not condemning those of the scribes' sons, even though it was clearer still that their sons sometimes cast out demons who yielded to them, though not by a spirit of holiness. Perhaps those sons of the scribes also exercised power over demons by invoking the name of Christ, in line with John's words: Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name (Luke 9:49), and with Christ's own words: Many will say, "In your name we have cast out demons" (Matt. 7:22). Finally, when Christ says: Then if anyone says to you, "Look, here is Christ," or "There he is," do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise, and they will show great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect (ibid. 24:23-24), he did not admit that he was a mere wonder-worker. Such men, using the same arts that wonder-workers use, are rightly regarded as wonder-workers, false christs and false prophets. Rather, by those words Christ forewarned his disciples against the frauds of those who, through incantations and tricks, would claim the name of Christ for themselves; Celsus, as Origen reports against Celsus, book II, raved otherwise. Indeed, Christ was so far from condemning those who performed miracles that he himself did so many signs that, if they were written down one by one, the world itself could not contain the books that would be written (John 21:25). (For it was indeed useful that the faithful should not be overwhelmed by too great an abundance of books, lest all religion seem to lie in reading, and action be neglected.) He also promised his disciples the power to work miracles: These signs will follow those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons, they will speak with new tongues, they will take up serpents, etc. (Mark 16:17-18).

units.la: LII. Cum miraculis Christi Exemplum vitæ & mortis ejus conjunctum, & à nobis religiosè imitandum, ejusdem veritatem pariter confirmavit. Ad hoc vocati estis, quòd etiam Christus passus sit pro vobis, relinquens vobis ὑπογραμμὸν exemplar, ut sequamini vestigia ejus, 1.Pet.II.21. Christi enim obedientia nobis est ὑπογραμμὸς exemplar, ut, sicut ille per passiones ad gloriam suam enixus est, ita etiam nos per afflictiones ad Regnum Cœleste gratissemur, Rom.VIII.17. Ideo imitandum se nobis proposuit. Discite à me, quia mansuetus & humilis sum corde, Matth.XI.29. Μιμηταί imitatores estote mei, sicuti & ego Christi Christi, 1. Cor. XI. 1. Et vos imitatores facti estis nostri, & Domini, recipientes sermonem in afflictione multa, cum gaudio Spiritus S. 1. Thess. I. 6.
