Christus nempe archetypon & speculum est omnis justitiae & obedientiae, sanctitatis, misericordiae, veritatis, imago Dei invisibilis. Illius exemplum παραδειγμα incentivum, Hebr. X. 24. & ἰσχυρα valida incitatio, adhortatio, ibid. VI. 18. ad similes virtutes esse debet. Neque Sanctos aliter imitari convenit, quam quatenus & illi Christum imitantur; & ejus imaginem in se relucentem habent. Aliud tamen est μίμησις imitatio, aliud ἀκολούθησις sequela Christi. Illa conformatio obsequii ad exemplar sanctitatis, quo Christus praevit: haec obsequium mandatis ejus praestandum notat. Aliud etiam imitatio Dei, aliud imitatio Christi est. Illa Matth. V. 48. Ephes. V. 1. praecepta est expressio imaginis Dei, qua homo non ad aequalem sanctitatem cum Divina sanctitate, sed ad analogiam similitudinem cum Deo obligatur. Cum qua imitatio sanctitatis Christi Divinae convenit. Ad quam operum Divinae Omnipotentiae, vel miraculorum, quae solus Deus facit, Psalm. LXXII. 18. & jejunii Christi quadragesimalis miraculosi neutiquam pertinet: quia eorum efficientia principalis mere Divina est. Haec est exempli humanae sanctitatis & obedientiae Christi imitatio, non qua se Deum ipsum exhibuit, sed qua & ipse se Dei imitatorem exhibuit in forma servi factus sub Lege, & in omni virtutum choragio, amore & timore Dei, fide & fiducia in Deum, precibus ad Deum, sanctificatione nominis Dei, obedientia parentibus & Magistratui debita, humilitate & erga quosvis obsequio innoxio, modestia, lenitate, φιλανθρωπία erga pauperes & afflictos quosvis, mansuetudine, longanimitate, condonatione offensarum, &c. inde a puero, per omnes dies carnis suae lucidissimam nobis facem praetulit. In officiorum ipsorum functionibus licet Christum imitari, qua is Mediator, summus Propheta, Sacerdos & Rex est, nemini datum sit: tamen non tantum qua Christiani, unctionis ipsius mystico consortio, Prophetae, Sacerdotes, Reges & ipsi effecti, 1. Pet. II. 5. 9. Apoc. I. 6. quodammodo Christum Prophetam, Sacerdotem & Regem imitari, sed etiam humilitatis, fidelitatis & charitatis humanae affectus, quos ille in munere suo obeundo exeruit, piae aemulationis ardore exprimere tenemur. Scripturae enim Christum nobis imitandum proponunt in capessenda & obeunda vocatione muneris ejus, in qua nec sibi honorem non vocatus sumpsit, Hebr. V. 4. 5. nec lucrum suum, vel se ipsum quaesivit, Phil. II. 4. 5. nec opprobriis & contradictionibus impiorum succubuit, Hebr. XII. 2. 3. & in vita omni ac morte zelum dilectionis Dei & proximi invictum demonstravit, 1. Joh. III. 16.
units.tr: LII. Christ's life and death, which are joined with his miracles and which we must religiously imitate, likewise confirmed the truth of his teaching. You were called to this, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example [ὑπογραμμὸν], that you should follow in his steps (1 Pet. 2:21). For Christ's obedience is our example [ὑπογραμμὸς], so that, just as he entered into his glory through sufferings, so we too might enter the heavenly kingdom through afflictions (Rom. 8:17). Therefore he set himself before us as one to be imitated: Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart (Matt. 11:29). Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Cor. 11:1). And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, receiving the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit (1 Thess. 1:6). Christ is indeed the archetype and mirror of all righteousness and obedience, holiness, mercy and truth, the image of the invisible God. His example should be an incentive [παράδειγμα] (Heb. 10:24) and a strong stimulus and exhortation [ἰσχυρὰ] (ibid. 6:18) to similar virtues. Nor is it fitting to imitate the saints except insofar as they too imitate Christ and bear his image shining in themselves. Yet imitation [μίμησις] is one thing and following [ἀκολούθησις] Christ is another. The former is the conforming of obedience to the pattern of the holiness that Christ went before in; the latter denotes the obedience that must be rendered to his commands. Imitation of God is also one thing, and imitation of Christ another. The former is commanded (Matt. 5:48; Eph. 5:1) as the expression of God's image, by which man is bound not to an equal holiness with divine holiness, but to a likeness analogous to God. With this agrees the imitation of Christ's divine holiness. It does not extend to the works of divine omnipotence, or to the miracles that God alone performs (Ps. 72:18), nor to Christ's miraculous forty-day fast, because their principal efficacy is purely divine. This is the imitation of Christ's human holiness and obedience as an example: not in that he showed himself to be God, but in that he himself showed himself an imitator of God, made in the form of a servant and under the Law, and in every dance of the virtues: love and fear of God, faith and trust in God, prayer to God, sanctifying the name of God, obedience due to parents and to the magistrate, humility and innocent deference toward all, modesty, gentleness, philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία] toward the poor and all the afflicted, meekness, patience, forgiveness of offences, and so on. From boyhood onward, through all the days of his flesh, he held out to us the most radiant torch. Although we may not imitate Christ in the actual performance of his offices, as he is Mediator, supreme Prophet, Priest and King, yet we are not only, as Christians, by the mystical fellowship of his anointing, made prophets, priests and kings ourselves (1 Pet. 2:5, 9; Rev. 1:6), and so in some measure imitate Christ as Prophet, Priest and King; we are also bound to express, with the ardour of pious emulation, the affections of humility, faithfulness and human love which he displayed in discharging his office. For the Scriptures set Christ before us as one to be imitated in undertaking and discharging the calling of his office, in which he did not take the honour to himself without being called (Heb. 5:4-5); did not seek his own gain or himself (Phil. 2:4-5); did not yield to the reproaches and contradictions of the wicked (Heb. 12:2-3); and in his whole life and death showed an unconquered zeal for the love of God and neighbour (1 John 3:16).

units.la: LIII. Denique Christus supremo actu suo, morte & martyrio, non parum etiam coelestem doctrinam suam confirmavit, & velut obsignavit. Praecipio tibi coram Deo, qui omnia vivificat, & Jesu Christo, μαρτυρησαντος, qui testificatus est coram Pontio Pilato pulchram illam confessionem, ut serves praeceptum immaculatum &c. 1. Tim. VI. 13. Qua emphasi Jesus Christus ὁ μάρτυς ὁ
units.tr: LIII. Finally, by his supreme act, his death and martyrdom, Christ also confirmed, and as it were sealed, his heavenly doctrine no little. I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and before Christ Jesus, who witnessed [μαρτυρήσαντος] before Pontius Pilate the noble confession, that you keep the commandment without stain, etc. (1 Tim. 6:13). With this emphasis Jesus Christ is marked as the martyr [ὁ μάρτυς] ...

units.la: πιστὸς fidelis ille Testis Apoc. I. 5. insignitur. Quo in Martyrio Christi conspicua imprimis fuit exemplaris illa patientia ejus, qua injustum judicium innocens sine contradictione sustinuit, & injurias sibi factas juste judicanti commisit, 1. Pet. II. 23. 24. Cujus innocentiae attestati sunt insignite improbi, puta Judas clamans: Peccavi justum sanguinem prodens, Matth. XXVII. 4: & Pilatus Judex, fassus, se in eo nullam mortis causam invenire, Joh. XVIII. 38. Deo una testificante per somnium uxoris Pilati, quod ad Pilatum in Tribunali sedentem relatum effecit, ut testificationem suam, publica manuum ablutione, quasi protestatione quadam usus, iteraverit; Matth. XXVII. 19. 24. Ac licet is lata sententia Christum morti adjudicaverit, nullius tamen criminis reum peregit, vel peragere potuit. Nam occasione consuetudinis non sine fraude Legis receptae, optionem quidem innocentem inter & nocentem Judaeorum libidini cum permisisset, praeter & contra intentionem atque expectationem ejus cadente & sonante voce populi, sententiam mortis non tam consulto tulit, quam, Judaeorum & Caesaris metu, sibi extorqueri infelix passus est, ibid. XXVII. 15. Marc. XV. 6. Luc. XXIII. 17. Joh. XIX. 15. 16. 38. Qui etiam mortis Christi causam fictitiam crucii inscribens talem: Jesus Nazarenus Rex Judaeorum, qualem quidem se esse nunquam dixerat, sed significaverat tamen, cum revera talis fuerit, Dominum Jesum justum judicavit, & ea mente Jesum Regem Judaeorum appellavit; adeo ut Judaeis inique ferentibus, & postulantibus, ut titulum deleret, & scriberet, quod dixerit; Rex Judaeorum sum, morem gerere dedignatus sit, ipso Deo negotium ita dirigente, quia Jesus vere is fuit, in quem, quae de Rege Judaeorum & Filio Dei praedicta erant, competerent: quacunque mente haec Pilatus scripserit, & scripta, ringentibus etiam Judaeis, confirmaverit, ibid. XIX. 19--23: Palam igitur erat, Christum occisum esse innocentem, adeoque ceu Martyrem & Confessorem Coelesti veritati a se ipso in Evangelio patefactae sanguine suo innocenter profuso suffragatum esse.
units.tr: ...faithful [πιστὸς] witness (Rev. 1:5). In Christ's martyrdom, his exemplary patience stood out above all, by which, though innocent, he endured an unjust judgment without complaint, and committed his wrongs to the One who judges justly (1 Pet. 2:23-24). His innocence was attested by notable wicked men: Judas, crying out, I have sinned in betraying innocent blood (Matt. 27:4); and the judge Pilate, who confessed that he found no cause of death in him (John 18:38). God also bore witness through a dream of Pilate's wife, which was reported to Pilate as he sat on the judgment seat, so that he repeated his testimony by a public washing of his hands, as a kind of solemn protest (Matt. 27:19, 24). And although that sentence condemned Christ to death, it did not make him guilty of any crime, nor could it. For, on the occasion of a custom that was not without fraud against the received Law, he indeed allowed the choice between an innocent man and a guilty one to be left to the lust of the Jews. Yet, beyond and against his intention and expectation, when the voice of the people rose and echoed, he did not so much pass sentence of death deliberately as, unhappily, suffer it to be wrung from him by fear of the Jews and of Caesar (ibid. 27:15; Mark 15:6; Luke 23:17; John 19:15-16, 38). He too, when he inscribed the feigned cause of Christ's death on the cross, in these words: Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, which he had never said he was, but which he had indicated, since in truth he was such, judged the Lord Jesus to be just, and with that intention called Jesus King of the Jews. So when the Jews unjustly took it ill and demanded that he erase the title and write instead that he said, I am King of the Jews, he disdained to comply, God himself so directing the matter, because Jesus was truly the one in whom the things foretold of the King of the Jews and the Son of God applied. Whatever intention Pilate had in writing these things, and though the Jews were raging, he confirmed what he had written (ibid. 19:19-23). It was therefore plain that Christ was killed while innocent, and so, as a martyr and confessor, he bore witness with his innocently shed blood to the heavenly truth revealed by himself in the Gospel.

units.la: LIV. Neque tamen Christus ob muneris Prophetici fidele ministerium in diebus carnis obitum Servator mundi, ex sensu Socinianorum, salutari potest. Praeterquam enim quod haeretici illi ne verum quidem Prophetam Christum agnoscunt, functione muneris Prophetici, nec non Sacerdotalis & Regii solida προφητικῶν eum destituentes, neque majoris eum aestimantes, quam Prophetam merum quemvis, qualis Salvator hominum esse non potest; ipsum etiam in functione muneris hujus fastigium παντοκράτορα, quo ipsi, ut Prophetae Divino ad fidei obedientiam subjicimur; simpliciter spectatum, Servatorem eum non facit. Nam eo sensu ex eo ut Propheta etiam Angeli discunt, & ei aeque ac homines subjiciuntur. Nam principatibus & potestatibus, qui in supercaelestibus sunt; (Angelis & Sanctis in Coelo) per Ecclesiam sapientia Dei multifaria notificatur; quatenus cognoscunt, quid Deus in Ecclesia sua per Christum fecerit, & quomodo promissiones suas impleverit, Ephes. III. 9. 10. Angeli in ea, quae per evangelium vangelizantes annuntiata sunt, introspicere cupiunt, 1.Pet.I.12. Neque tamen, Angelorum Christus Salvator est. In salvifica ergo illa muneris Prophetici functione Servatorem Christus non simpliciter se gessit, sed quatenus gratiam illam praedicavit, qua ipse nobis, opus habentibus coelesti Medico, medicina fit, Matth.IX.12. neque quatenus medicinam illam & salutem nude praedicavit, sed ut a se, ceu Sacerdote, impetrandam, & ceu Rege nobis conferendam & extribuendam laetissimo praeconio suo annuntiavit; neque tantum foris per verbum auditum illam authentice docuit docetque, sed etiam non atramento, verum Spiritu Dei viventis, non tabulis lapideis, sed tabulis cordis carneis inscribit, 2.Cor.III.3. Nullius ergo ad salutem nostram Prophetia Christi, aeque atque Regii muneris functio, nisi animata utraque a Sacerdotalis muneris functione, pretii esse potest. De qua nunc dicendum.
units.tr: LIV. Yet Christ did not become the Saviour of the world by the faithful discharge of his prophetic office during the days of his flesh, as the Socinians hold. Those heretics do not even acknowledge Christ as a true Prophet. They deprive him of the solid prophetic [προφητικῶν] functions of his office, and of his priestly and kingly functions as well. They regard him as no more than any mere prophet, and no such person can be the Saviour of men. Nor does his prophetic office, viewed simply in itself, make him the Saviour, even at its summit, the almighty [παντοκράτορα] authority to which we submit, as to a divine Prophet, in obedience of faith. For in that sense angels also learn from him as a Prophet, and are subject to him just as men are. The principalities and powers in the heavenly places (angels and saints in heaven) learn through the Church the manifold wisdom of God, insofar as they come to know what God has done in his Church through Christ and how he has fulfilled his promises (Ephes. 3:9, 10). The angels desire to look into those things which have been announced by those who preached the gospel (1 Pet. 1:12). Yet Christ is not the Saviour of angels. In that saving function of his prophetic office, therefore, Christ did not act as Saviour simply by proclaiming that grace by which he becomes medicine for us, who need a heavenly physician (Matt. 9:12). Nor did he act merely by proclaiming that medicine and salvation in bare terms. He announced with his most joyful proclamation that this grace is to be obtained from him as Priest, and is to be bestowed and granted to us by him as King. Nor has he taught, nor does he teach, this only outwardly and authentically through the spoken word. He also writes not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of the fleshly heart (2 Cor. 3:3). Therefore the prophecy of Christ, like the function of his kingly office, is of no value for our salvation unless both are animated by the function of his priestly office. Of this we must now speak.

units.la: LV. SACERDOTIUM, seu Sacerdotale Christi munus est, quo is, ceu constitutus a Patre Sacerdos per obedientiam exinanitionis suae usque ad mortem crucis, Deo Patri pro peccatis eorum, qui ipsi dati sunt, se ipsum aeterno Spiritu offerendo perfecte satisfecit, & apud eundem pro nobis continenter intercedit. Sacerdotis nomen Christo venturo tributum est. Juravit Jehova, & non paenitebit eum: Tu es כהן Sacerdos in aeternum, juxta ordinem Melchisedeci, Psal.CX.4. ubi כהן non significat eminentiam talem, qualis eorum est, qui in terra post Regem vocantur כהנים לפלך proximi Regi, uti Kimchius delirat, quia inducitur כהן secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, qui ipse Rex, non Regi proximus fuit, & simul etiam כהן לאל עליון seu כהן non Regis terreni, sed Dei Altissimi, cui benedictio populi, & decimarum acceptio tribuitur: adeoque qua כהן non Regi proximus, vel ministrans, sed Sacerdos fuit. Intelligitur igitur Sacerdotium, non quale Aaronicum fuit, sed quod μετ' ὀρκωμοσίας cum jure jurando datur ei, qui ad dextram Dei consedit. De quo dictum est. Ille aedificabit Templum Jehova, & ipse accipiet Majestatem, & considebit, & potestate utetur in throno ejus, כהן והיה & erit, vel perseverabit esse Sacerdos in throno ejus, & consilium pacis erit inter ambos eos, Zach.VI.13. Eodem faciunt illa Danielis: Septimanae septuaginta decisae sunt ad consummandum peccata ולכפר & ad expiandam pravitatem, & ad adducendam justitiam sanctorum, Dan.IX.24. Inprimis in Sacerdotio utroque Melchisedeci & Aaronis Christi Sacerdotium figuratum & adumbratum fuisse, sed diverso modo, quia cum Sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, non Aaronis fuerit, nihilominus per Sacerdotium Aaronis multifarie Sacerdotium ejus repraesentatum fuit; pluribus Loc.XV.65. & c. 83.84. oltendimus. Ex professo S.Paulus Divinissima ad Hebraeos Epistola, Sacerdotium Christi explicans, decies eum ᾿Αρχιερέα Pontificem, & septies ἱερέα Sacerdotem appellat.
units.tr: LV. The priesthood, or priestly office of Christ, is that by which he, appointed priest by the Father, through obedience unto the death of the cross, in his self-emptying, fully satisfied God the Father for the sins of those given to him, by offering himself through the eternal Spirit, and continually intercedes for us before the same Father. The name of priest was ascribed to Christ who was to come: The LORD has sworn, and will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek (Ps. 110:4). Here the word kohen [כהן] does not signify that kind of eminence which belongs to those who are called, in the land, kohanim le-melech, that is, next to the king, as Kimchi raves, because Christ is introduced as a priest after the order of Melchizedek, who was himself a king, not one next to a king. At the same time he was kohen of God Most High, not of an earthly king, to whom the blessing of the people and the receiving of tithes are ascribed. Thus he was a priest, not one next to a king or serving him. Therefore the priesthood intended is not that of Aaron, but that which is given with an oath [μετ' ὀρκωμοσίας] to him who sat down at the right hand of God. Of him it is said: He shall build the temple of the LORD, and he shall bear the majesty, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both (Zech. 6:13). Daniel's words agree: Seventy weeks are determined to finish transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness (Dan. 9:24). Above all, in both priesthoods, that of Melchizedek and that of Aaron, the priesthood of Christ was foreshadowed and prefigured, but in different ways. Although he was a priest after the order of Melchizedek and not of Aaron, nevertheless his priesthood was represented in many ways by the priesthood of Aaron. We have shown this in more detail at Loc. 15, §§ 65 ff., and §§ 83, 84. The apostle Paul, in his most divine Epistle to the Hebrews, expounding the priesthood of Christ, calls him High Priest ten times and priest seven times.

units.la: LVI. Sacerdos verus apud Deum pro hominibus non merus homo, sed aeque ac Propheta, ἀνθρωπος Deus & homo esse debuit. Nam Spiritu aeterno se ipsum Deo obtulit, Hebr.IX.14. Et quia secundum ordinem Melchisedeci Sacerdos constitutus est, debuit esse ἀπάτωρ sine Patre secundum humanam, ἀμήτωρ sine matre secundum Divinam naturam, non habens initium dierum, nec finem vitae; manens Sacerdos εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς in perpetuum, ib.VII.3. non factus talis secundum legem praecepti carnalis, sed κατὰ δύναμιν ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτου secundum potentiam vitae indissolubilis, ib.v.16. qui posset σῴζειν εἰς τὸ παντελὲς salvare perfecte per ipsum accedentes ad Deum, πάντοτε ζῶν semper vivens ad intercedendum pro ipsis, v.25. Qui proin non tantum ipse extitit ante initium dierum carnis suae, utpote semper vivens, nec habens initium dierum suorum, sed etiam sibi, ut vicarios, obnoxios habuit, quotquot ab initio mundi ante ipsum extiterunt, Sacerdotes, typica expiatione & vicaria intercessione, usque dum ille in carnem venit, defungentes. Unde ὑποδείγματα καὶ σκιὰ τῶν ἐπουρανίων exemplari & umbrae coelestium eos inservisse Apostolus ib.VIII.5. coll.cum IX.9.10. X.1. dixit. Licet tamen προεχειροτονημένος ante designatus, seu ante carnem constitutus Sacerdos fuerit, tamen Sacerdotio eo defungi ante incarnationem non potuit, propter Sacerdotes vicarios, qui tum officio defungebantur, & testabantur, desiderari veram olim futuram functionem veri Sacerdotii; quosque, cum ipse Sacerdotio fungi coepisset, non aliter quam corpus umbram dispellere, & velut veterascens σκεύος παλαιὸν indumentum, quo se ad tempus velaverat, exuere debuit.
units.tr: LVI. A true priest before God for men must not be a mere man, but, like the Prophet, must be God and man. For he offered himself through the eternal Spirit to God (Heb. 9:14). And since he was constituted a priest after the order of Melchizedek, he had to be without father [ἀπάτωρ] according to his human nature, and without mother [ἀμήτωρ] according to his divine nature, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, remaining a priest for ever [εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς] (Heb. 7:3). He was not made such according to the law of a carnal commandment, but according to the power of an indissoluble life [κατὰ δύναμιν ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτου] (Heb. 7:16), and he was able to save completely [σῴζειν εἰς τὸ παντελὲς] those who come to God through him, always living [πάντοτε ζῶν] to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25). Therefore he did not only exist before the beginning of the days of his flesh, as one always living and having no beginning of days of his own, but he also had, as his substitutes, bound to himself all the priests who from the beginning of the world existed before him, and who served and died in typical expiation and vicarious intercession, until he came into the flesh. Hence the apostle says that they served as an example and shadow of heavenly things [ὑποδείγματα καὶ σκιὰ τῶν ἐπουρανίων] (Heb. 8:5; compare 9:9, 10; 10:1). Although he was designated beforehand, that is, appointed priest before the flesh [προεχειροτονημένος], yet he could not discharge that priesthood before the incarnation, because of the vicarious priests who then performed their office and bore witness that the true priesthood of the future was still awaited. And when he had begun to exercise the priesthood himself, he had to lay aside, as a body casts off its shadow, the old garment [σκεύος παλαιὸν], which is the covering he had put on for a time, and as it were growing old.

units.la: LVII. Sed qualis Sacerdos Christus esse, & quemadmodum Sacerdotio defungi debuerit S.Paulus, instituta Sacerdotii Aaronici, ceu nihil consummantis, cum Sacerdotio Christi; quod non Leviticum, sed secundum ordinem Melchisedeci est; comparatione, disertius etiam Hebr.VII.23--f. docuit. Ante omnia Sacerdotis Christi conditionem externam, quod ex tribu Juda oriri, non vocari secundum legem carnalis praecepti, & jurejurando aeternus Sacerdos constitui debeat, v. 13-26. Primum ergo Tribus non Levi, sed alterius, ex qua nemo altari inserviit, particeps esse debuit, v.13. Nam περὶ Ἰούδα... λόγον inquit, ὅτι ἐξ Ἰούδα ἀνατέτραλκεν ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν, manifestum est, quod ex Juda germinavit Dominus noster. In quam tribum nihil de Sacerdotio Moses locutus est, v.14. Unde translato ad tribum hanc Juda Sacerdotio (vero) necessario legis Sacerdotii Levi (figurati & nihil consummantis) μετάθεσιν translationem seu mutationem, abolitionem instituendam fuisse v.14. innuerat. Tum Levitas secundum legem praecepti carnalis, at Christum, Sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, secundum potentiam vitae indissolubilis extitisse v.16. asserit, idque eo argumento probat, quia ipsi dictum est: Tu es Sacerdos in saeculum, secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, v.17. Lex, quae Aaronem Sacerdotem instituit, fuit ἐντολῆς σαρκικῆς praecepti carnalis, dati iis, qui ipsi caro erant, & circa carnalia fere occupabantur, & ceu caro moriebantur; qualis Lex esse perpetua, & manere in Regno eo, quod totum spirituale est, & in quo adoratores Deum in Spiritu & veritate adorant, Joh.IV.23.24. non potuit. At Sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedeci Christus, γέγονε κατὰ δύναμιν ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτου secundum potentiam vitae indissolubilis factus est, utpote Sacerdos in saeculum, hoc est, non ab eo demum tempore. re, quo in Cœlum ascendens ad dextram Dei consedit, quasi vita indissolubilis Sacerdotis huius non aliud quàm immortalitas ejus post resurrectionem ex morte esset, uti Socinianî fingunt; tum quia jam ante v.3. Apostolus innuebat, Sacerdotem hunc non habere initium vitæ; tum quia Dominus Davidis, qualem Christum David, Psal.CX.1. dixit, simpliciter æternus vitam ἀπλῶς absolutè indissolubilem habet; tum quia juramentum Dei de permansione Sacerdotii hujus in æternum ad τὸ γεγονέναι ἱερέα Sacerdotem factum esse, adeóque ad omnem Sacerdotis illius statum, etiam illum, quo Sponsor & Mediator Testamenti fuit, pertinet: tum quia Filium Dei se dicit τὸν ζῶντα viventem illum (cujus est, non posse mori) & eum qui factus fuit mortuus, & est vivens in secula, Apoc.I.18. tum quia potentiam habere vitæ indissolubilis non alii, quàm Deo, cujus vita ex potentia propria dissolvi non potest, & qui ἔχει ζωὴν ἐν ἑαυτῷ vitam in se ipso independentem, & sine principio Joh.V.26. habet, competit. Cùm enim Christi Sponsio & μεσιτεία mediatio ejus adventu antiquior fuerit, etiam ante adventum ejus juramentum, quo ei æternum Sacerdotium juravit, extiterit, & ipse vitam, adeóque indissolubilem habuerit, oportet. Quomodo enim, qui non erat, vitæ indissolubilis potentiam non habuerat, hæc præstare potuit? Denique Sacerdotes Levitæ constituti, à Deo vocati sunt secundum legem præcepti carnalis: at Christus non tantùm secundum potentiam vitæ indissolubilis, sed etiam ἐ χωρὶς ὁρκωμοσίας non sine juramento, per illum, qui dixit ad eum: Juravit Dominus, & non pœnitebit eum: Tu es Sacerdos in seculum secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, v.20.21. Illi constituti sunt sine juramento, sic ut pœnitere Deum constitutorum, hoc est, eorum Sacerdotium, ceu nihil consummans, mutare, abolere potuerit, & immutabili consilio, voluerit, atque actu abolevit. Sed Sacerdotis secundum ordinem Melchisedeci constituti Deum pœnitere non potuit, quia etiam μετὰ τὸν νόμον post legem, qua Aharonidis Sacerdotium commissum est, v.28. Deus juravit, & quidem non aliis de ipso, ceu non extante, sed ipsi Domino Davidis, Christo, ut jam tum viventi, extanti, quòd Sacerdos in æternum sit. idque propter τὸ ἀμετάθετον τῆς βουλῆς immutabile consilium, ibid.V.I.17. Nulla enim suberat promissionis conditio. Deum enim proprie pœnitere non potest, quia Deus est: & si posset, at juramentum mutare non potest, quia verax & mentiri nescius est. Non caret mysterio, quòd in Psalmo CX.4. jurata illa promissio narratur, vel quasi repetitur hoc loco, postquam de Regno Christi, de ejus collocatione in throno, de missione sceptri ex Zione, de voluntario obsequio populi Sacerdotii Christi fructibus jam actum fuerat. Prævidit nempe Spiritus Dei, jam amplificatâ Ecclesiâ oriturōs homines, qui primò Sacerdotium Christi, ceu ejus vicarii & successores; ac mox etiam ejusdem Regnum invaduri, & meritum atque justitiam per ipsum adductam oppugnaturi, denique intercessoris honorem Sanctis asserturi essent. Ideo in parte Prophetiæ tempori illi respondente asseverationem hanc juratam posuit, tum ut Antichristo, falso Sacerdoti & Regi à fidelibus
units.tr: LVII. But the apostle Paul, comparing the institutions of the Aaronic priesthood, which accomplished nothing, with the priesthood of Christ, which is not Levitical but after the order of Melchizedek, taught more plainly what kind of priest Christ had to be and how he had to discharge the priesthood (Heb. 7:23 ff.). First of all, he taught the external condition of the priest Christ: that he must come from the tribe of Judah, that he is not called according to the law of a carnal commandment, and that he must be appointed an eternal priest by an oath (vv. 13–26). First, then, he had to belong to a tribe not of Levi, but of another, from which no one has served at the altar (v. 13). For he says concerning Judah: it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Judah [ὅτι ἐξ Ἰούδα ἀνατέτραλκεν ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν]. Moses said nothing about the priesthood in regard to this tribe (v. 14). From this he had hinted that, since the priesthood was transferred to the tribe of Judah, there must of necessity be a translation [μετάθεσιν], that is, a change and abolition, of the law of the Levitical priesthood, which was figurative and accomplished nothing, in order to establish the true priesthood (v. 14). Then he asserts that the Levites were according to the law of a carnal commandment, but that Christ, the priest after the order of Melchizedek, was according to the power of an indissoluble life (v. 16). And he proves this by the argument that it was said to him: Thou art a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek (v. 17). The law that appointed Aaron as priest was a law of carnal commandment [ἐντολῆς σαρκικῆς], given to those who were themselves flesh and were largely occupied with fleshly things, and who died as flesh. Such a law could not be perpetual, nor remain in that kingdom which is wholly spiritual, and in which the worshippers worship God in spirit and truth (John 4:23, 24). But Christ, the priest after the order of Melchizedek, has been made according to the power of an indissoluble life [κατὰ δύναμιν ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτου], as a priest for ever, that is, not only from that time on which he ascended into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. As if the indissoluble life of this priest were nothing other than his immortality after rising from the dead, as the Socinians imagine! Indeed, the apostle had already hinted before (v. 3) that this priest has no beginning of life. Again, the Lord of David, whom David called Christ (Ps. 110:1), simply has absolutely [ἀπλῶς] an indissoluble life, which is eternal. Again, God's oath concerning the perpetual continuance of this priesthood refers to his having become a priest, and therefore to every state of that priest, including that in which he was the surety and mediator of the covenant. Again, he calls himself the Son of God, the living one [τὸν ζῶντα] (whose it is not to be able to die), and he who was dead and is alive for ever (Rev. 1:18). Again, to have the power of an indissoluble life belongs to no one but God, whose life cannot be dissolved by its own power, and who has life in himself [ἔχει ζωὴν ἐν ἑαυτῷ], independent and without beginning (John 5:26). For since the suretyship and mediation of Christ were older than his coming, and the oath by which the eternal priesthood was sworn to him also existed before his coming, he must have had life, and therefore an indissoluble life. For how could he, who was not yet, have been able to bring about these things without having the power of indissoluble life? Finally, the Levitical priests were appointed by God according to the law of a carnal commandment. But Christ was made not only according to the power of an indissoluble life, but also not without an oath [ἐχωρὶς ὁρκωμοσίας], by him who said to him: The Lord has sworn, and will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek (vv. 20, 21). The others were appointed without an oath, so that God could repent of those whom he appointed, that is, could change and abolish their priesthood as accomplishing nothing, and he did so, in his unchangeable counsel, and in fact abolished it. But God could not repent of appointing a priest after the order of Melchizedek, because after the law by which the priesthood was committed to the sons of Aaron, God swore (v. 28), and indeed not concerning him as one not yet existing, but to the Lord of David himself, Christ, who was already then living and existing, that he is a priest for ever. And this is on account of the immutability of his counsel [τὸ ἀμετάθετον τῆς βουλῆς] (v. 17). For there was no condition attached to the promise. God, indeed, properly cannot repent, because he is God. And even if he could, he cannot change his oath, because he is true and does not know how to lie. It is not without mystery that this sworn promise is related in Psalm 110:4, or repeated here, after the things concerning the kingdom of Christ, his enthronement, the sending of the sceptre out of Zion, and the willing obedience of the people, the fruits of his priesthood, had already been treated. The Spirit of God foresaw that men would arise, when the Church had already grown large, who would first attack the priesthood of Christ as his vicars and successors, and soon afterwards would seize his kingdom too, and would assail the merit and righteousness brought by him, and finally would claim for the saints the honour of intercession. Therefore, in the part of the prophecy corresponding to that time, he placed this sworn assertion, so that the true, only, and sworn priest and king might be set against the Antichrist, the false priest and king, and so that the faithful might be strengthened. Just as the sworn priesthood of Christ cannot be overthrown, so the Church, to which his priesthood is profitable at all times, cannot perish.

units.la: opponi verus, unicus idémque juratus Sacerdos & Rex posset: tum ut fideles confirmarentur, sicut Sacerdotium Christi juratum expugnari non potest; ita nec Ecclesiam, cui Sacerdotium ejus omni tempori prosit, intercidere posse.
units.tr: to be opposed to Antichrist, the false priest and king, by the faithful. A true, unique and sworn priest and king could be set against him. Then, so that the faithful might be confirmed: just as the sworn priesthood of Christ cannot be overthrown, neither can the Church perish, for whose benefit his priesthood avails in every age. ## LVIII.

units.la: LVIII.

Hæc Sacerdotis Christi externa conditio fuit. Interiorem verò ejusdem conditionem & constitutionem idem S. Paulus statim v.26. pandit, scribens; Talis nos decuit Sacerdos ὅσιος, ἄκακος, ἀμίαντος, κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν, καὶ ὑψηλότερος τῶν οὐρανῶν γενόμενος, Sanctus, sine vitio, non coinquinatus, separatus à peccatoribus, & altior Cœlis factus. Plane ergo veri Sacerdotis Christi, & typicorum seu Leviticorum disparata ratio est. Hi sancti erant sanctitate legali, externa, quatenus lustralibus aquis, vestium imperatarum indutu, unguento quodam variis ex aromatibus confecto, ac pecorum sanguine sacrati, Exod.XXIX. Quibus similibúsque umbratilibus rebus virtutes illas, quæ in vero Sacerdote postulantur, adumbrare, at præstare nullo modo potuerunt. Nam & ipsi peccatores erant, vitiis manibúsque suis obnoxii, non una labe deformes, adeóque ex peccatorum censu; adeò ut pro iis etiam sacrificandum fuerit, licèt quodammodo duces atque πέρωτοι eorum, qui peccata sua ipsi confitebantur & accusabant, non sine ipse remissionis, fuerint. Hic verò Sacerdos verus & perfectus, virtutes omnes integras præstare debuit; absque quo fuisset, nec authoritate & gratia valere apud Deum, ut ei clientes suos efficaciter commendare posset; nec bonitate & misericordia erga homines pollere, ut patrocinio eorum apud Deum defungi vellet; nec vitam immortalem, qua fretus perpetuum patrocinium illud præstaret, habere (quæ tria inprimis consummatum Sacerdotium decent) potuisset. Debuit ergo esse tum ὅσιος ἁγιος Pius, Sanctus, Psal.XVI. 10. hoc est, אִישׁ חָסִיד vel חָסִיד בעל studio boni, recti, amoris erga Deum & proximum, ad gloriam illi, & gratiam ac misericordiam huic impertiendam, præditus. Tum ἄκακος sine vitio, malo, qui non habeat τὸ κακὸν τῷ ἐγκειμένον malum adjacens, Rom.VII.18.21. Tum ἀμίαντος non inquinatus, non natus impurus, Job.XIV. 4. vel in peccato, Psal.LI.7. vel peccans in Adamo, Rom.V.12. quippe non natus communi lege, vel judicio: Tum κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν, vivens licèt inter peccatores, cum iis agens, ambulans, utpote quorum gratia in mundum venit, Matth.IX.11.12. Luc.XIX.10. tamen à peccatoribus separatus, neque cum illis in ullo peccato communicans, quia non peccator, sed peccatorum medicus & Salvator venit. Hæ perfecti & consummati Sacerdotis aliorum peccata expiantis dotes sunt. Ipsa enim Sacerdotii Levitici lex sanctitatem saltem legalem & externam Sacerdotibus præcipiens, docuit; Deum à peccatoribus sacrificium peccata expians non accipere. Debuit ergo esse usquequaque justus, habens eam obedientiam, quam Lex ad jus petendi vitam exigit; seu δικαιώματα meritum justitiæ, opus jus petendi vitam operanti concilians; Rom.V.16. quod ibid.v.18.19. in ὑπακοὴ obedientiâ constituit. Denique etiam ὑψηλότερος τῶν οὐρανῶν altior Cœlis esse debuit, dignus, qui in Coelo ad dextram Patris residet, quod soli Filio Dei, qui de Coelo descendit, convenit. Nam ad Deum tanquam Patrem accedere nisi per Sacerdotem Filium ad Deum per non-Deum non licet.
units.tr: This was the external condition of Christ's priesthood. The same St. Paul, in verse 26, sets out its inner condition and constitution, writing: "Such a high priest became us: holy [ὅσιος], harmless [ἄκακος], undefiled [ἀμίαντος], separated from sinners [κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν], and made higher than the heavens [ὑψηλότερος τῶν οὐρανῶν]." Plainly, then, the true priest of Christ and the typical or Levitical priests differ in their whole character. Those were holy with a legal, external holiness, insofar as they were consecrated by lustral waters, by putting on prescribed garments, by a certain ointment compounded from various spices, and by the blood of beasts (Exod. 29). By such shadowy things they could foreshadow those virtues which are required in the true priest, but they could in no way actually possess them. For they themselves were sinners, subject to their own faults and failings, not stained by a single blemish but counted among sinners. Therefore sacrifice had to be made for them too, although they were in some sense leaders and first-fruits of those who confessed and accused their own sins, and who were not without a share in forgiveness. But this true and perfect priest ought to possess all the virtues in full. Without them he could not have availed with God, in authority and grace, to commend his clients effectively to him. Nor could he have been strong in goodness and mercy towards men, so as to be willing to discharge their advocacy before God. Nor could he have had the immortal life on which he could rest and provide that perpetual advocacy (and these three things above all befit a fully accomplished priesthood). He ought therefore to be holy [ὅσιος], pious, and "holy" (Ps. 16:10), that is, a man of piety [אִישׁ חָסִיד], or one possessed of zeal for what is good and right, of love for God and neighbour [חָסִיד בעל], endowed to render glory to God and to bestow grace and mercy on men. Then he must be harmless [ἄκακος], without fault or evil, one who has no evil lying close at hand [τὸ κακὸν τῷ ἐγκειμένον] (Rom. 7:18, 21). Then undefiled [ἀμίαντος], not polluted, not born impure (Job 14:4), not in sin (Ps. 51:7), nor sinning in Adam (Rom. 5:12), since he was not born under the common law or judgment. Then separated from sinners [κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν]: though living among sinners, dealing with them, and going about with them, since it was for their sake that he came into the world (Matt. 9:11-12; Luke 19:10), yet separated from sinners and not sharing with them in any sin, because he came not as a sinner but as the physician and Saviour of sinners. These are the qualities of the perfect and complete priest who makes atonement for the sins of others. For the law of the Levitical priesthood itself, which required only a legal and external holiness of its priests, taught that God does not accept from sinners a sacrifice that atones for sins. He therefore had to be altogether righteous, having that obedience which the Law requires for a right to seek life. This is the merit of righteousness, that is, the δικαιώματα, which brings about the work that gives a right to life (Rom. 5:16), and which Paul in verses 18-19 places in obedience [ὑπακοή]. Finally, he had to be higher than the heavens [ὑψηλότερος τῶν οὐρανῶν], worthy to sit in heaven at the right hand of the Father, which belongs only to the Son of God, who came down from heaven. For no one may approach God as Father except through the Son, the priest; it is not lawful to come to God through one who is not God.

units.la: LIX, Etiam functiones Sacerdotum Leviticorum,& veri ac perfecti Sacerdotis Christi, Hebr.VII.27.28. Apostolus distinguit, Illi necesse habuerunt prius pro suis peccatis offerre, deinde pro populi, v.27. Sed non par hujus ratio est, quia peccatum non habet, peccatum licet, seu sacrificium pro peccato nostro factus. Lex enim constituit Sacerdotes habentes ἀσθένειαν infirmitatem: sermo vero jurisjurandi, quod post legem est, Filium in aeternum consummatum, v.28. Filius in aeternum consummatus, & Sacerdos talis, qualem paulo ante Apostolus descripsit, nulla peccata, pro quibus offerret, habuit, nullam ἀσθένειαν infirmitatem sive moralem, vitiosam; sive ex peccato proprio contractam naturalem, qualis peccati poena & passio est. Quod igitur Socinians Christum pro suis peccatis obtulisse asserunt, ne pro nostris eum obtulisse, fateri necesse habeant; & peccata illa Christi, pro quibus obtulerit, ejusdem infirmitates, & dolores, qui peccatorum poenae sint, interpretantur, Apostolo utrumque de Sacerdote, Filio in aeternum consummato, neganti in os obloquuntur. Neque etiam quivis dolor peccati poena est. Peccatum enim fert, qui poenam peccati fert, non quisquis dolet. Etiam Deo dolor tribuitur, qui peccatum nuspiam vocatur. Christi dolor, pavor, vibex nostra sanatio est. Quid ergo pro dolore & infirmitate sua obtulit? An passiones, lachrymas suas? Atqui pro nobis, non pro suis peccatis, id est, doloribus & passionibus passus est, cum nemo pro suis doloribus & passionibus patiatur; & lachrymas effudit, non propter suos dolores, quod vaecordes & abjecti animi homines faciunt, sed indolescens nobis, ex charitate erga nos. Tum Sacerdotes Levitae πρῶτον prius pro suis, ἔπειτα deinde pro populi peccatis obtulerunt. At Christus ἐφάπαξ semel, ibid.v.27. non prius pro se, ac dein pro populo; neque iterans talia; sed semel. Vel pro suis igitur, vel pro populi peccatis obtulit. Nam pro utrisque non obtulit; quia alias prius & posterius obtulisset. Atqui pro suis peccatis non obtulit, quia, ceu Pontifex πεπείρων nos accedentes ad Deum decens, pius, sine vitio, non coinquinatus, a peccatoribus separatus, peccata, pro quibus offerret, non habuit. Ergo pro peccatis populi. Denique Sacerdotes Levitae aliquid extra se, idque vel inanimatum, in fertis, vel animatum in victimis, obtulerunt. At Sacerdos, Filius in aeternum consummatus, ἑαυτὸν se ipsum obtulit, ibid. v.27. non sanguinem juvencorum & hircorum. Per Spiritum aeternum se ipsum immaculatum obtulit Deo, ibid,IX.14. Hic demum ille rationalis cultus est, non in mutae & brutae pecudis mactatione vel crematione, sed in animae sanctae perfecta obedientia, ejusque obedientiae in morte crucis demonstratione consistens. Tali enim victima, obedientia & justitia ipsius Christi, Deus & honorari potuit, quia nulla alia re homo se secundum imaginem Dei esse ostendit, nec alia conditione jus vitae aeternae impetrat, nec aliter Deo honor independentiae per peccatum laesus vindicari potest; & placari debuit, quia tantae personae tanta humiliatio sola sufficit ad ostendendam sanctitate Dei, & quantum peccata, quae Ecclesiae remittuntur, merantur, ut Deus per fidem ab improbo, quem justificat, justificari, justus agnosci & celebrari possit.
units.tr: LIX. The apostle also distinguishes the functions of the Levitical priests from those of the true and perfect priest, Christ (Heb. 7:27-28). Those priests, he says, "had need first to offer for their own sins, and then for the people's" (v. 27). But the case is not the same for this one, who had no sin, though he was made sin, that is, a sacrifice for our sin. "For the law appoints men as high priests who have infirmity [ἀσθένειαν]; but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son, who has been perfected for evermore" (v. 28). The Son, perfected for evermore, and such a priest as the apostle described a little before, had no sins for which he needed to offer, and no infirmity, whether moral and faulty, or natural and contracted through sin of his own, such as the punishment and suffering of sin are. So the Socinians, who assert that Christ offered for his own sins, must either admit that he did not offer for ours, or else interpret those sins of his, for which he offered, as his infirmities and pains, which are the punishments of sins; in doing so they fling their taunts in the face of the apostle, who denies both of the priest, the Son perfected for evermore. Nor is every pain a punishment of sin. He bears sin who bears the punishment of sin, not whoever grieves. Pain is even ascribed to God, yet God is nowhere called sinful. The pain, fear and tears of Christ were our healing. What, then, did he offer for his pain and infirmity? His sufferings and his tears? But he suffered for us, not for his own sins, that is, his pains and sufferings, whereas no one suffers for his own pains and sufferings. And he shed tears not on account of his own sorrows, as foolish and base-spirited men do, but grieving for us, out of love for us. Then the Levitical priests offered "first for their own sins, then for the sins of the people" [πρῶτον … ἔπειτα]. But Christ offered "once for all" [ἐφάπαξ] (v. 27), not first for himself and then for the people, nor repeating such offerings, but once. So he offered either for his own sins or for the sins of the people. He did not offer for both, for otherwise he would have offered first and afterwards. But he did not offer for his own sins, because, as a high priest who fitted us, who approach God [πρέπων], "holy, harmless, undefiled, separated from sinners," he had no sins for which he would need to offer. Therefore he offered for the sins of the people. Finally, the Levitical priests offered something outside themselves, either lifeless, in fruits, or living, in victims. But the priest, the Son perfected for evermore, offered "himself" [ἑαυτόν] (v. 27), not the blood of bullocks and goats. "Through the eternal Spirit he offered himself without blemish to God" (Heb. 9:14). This is at last that reasonable worship, consisting not in the slaughter or burning of a dumb and brutish beast, but in the perfect obedience of a holy soul, and in its demonstration of that obedience in the death of the cross. For by such a victim, namely by the obedience and righteousness of Christ himself, God could be honoured, since man shows himself to be made in the image of God by no other means, and obtains the right to eternal life by no other condition, and the honour of his independence, injured by sin, cannot be vindicated in any other way. And he had to be reconciled, since the bearing of such humiliation by so great a person alone suffices to show both the holiness of God and how much the sins that are forgiven to the Church deserve, so that God, through faith, may justify the ungodly whom he justifies, be acknowledged as just, and be celebrated.

units.la: LX. Singula haec, quibus verum, perfectum, consummatum Christi Sacerdotium S. Paulus descripsit, & a Levitico per characteres conspicuos disparavit, Sacerdotium & Sacrificium Missale, ceu minime Christianum non unum numero cum sacrificio Christi, ut Missifices impudenter & audacissime mentiuntur, confundunt. Nam a conditione tum externa, tum interna, qualem in vero & consummato Sacerdote Apostolus requirit; & functionibus, quas idem Christo Sacerdoti, a Leviticis distinctas asserit, penitus destituitur. Conditione externa caret, quia Sacerdotes Missifices nec ex tribu Juda germinant, nec Sacerdotes secundum potentiam vitae indissolubilis sunt, quia meri homines caduci & mortales; nec ordinantur per sermonem jurisjurandi Divini, quia de sacerdotio & sacrificio eorum nulla unquam promissio Divina, nedum jurata facta est. Ac multo magis etiam conditio interna deficit, quia non sunt Pontifices πεπείρων decentes, per quos ad Deum accedere liceat: non ὅσιοι pii, sine vitio & maculatla, maculantes quippe & se ipsos & alios; nec a peccatoribus separati, sed cum iisdem in peccato praeceteris communicantes, non Dei, sed gloriae & lucri sui carnalis Sacerdotes: denique non sublimiores Coelis, sed coeno immersi, ex terra, non ex Coelo sunt. Denique & functiones toto Coelo distinctae sunt. Non enim pro peccatis tantum populi offerunt, sed pro suis etiam: neque semel, sed identidem, frequenter, quoties inprimis pretio oblationem conducere populo, & addicere sibi lubet: denique neque se ipsos, sed extra se rem vilissimam, nihili, quam accidens sine substantia, ens vagum & indeterminatum definiunt. Ab Aharonico etiam Sacerdotio Missale abluditi, quia Missifices nec ex tribu Levi germinant, nec secundum Legem Divinam praecepti carnalis constituuntur; nec sanctitate Legali & externa Divinitus praecepta ulla pollent, nec ullum quod offerant sacrificium Divinitus praeceptum habent. Non ergo sacerdotium illud vel Leviticum vel Christianum, sed Antichristianum est.
units.tr: LX. Each of these features by which St. Paul described the true, perfect and complete priesthood of Christ, and distinguished it from the Levitical by its conspicuous marks, the Mass priesthood and the Mass sacrifice, which are by no means Christian, confuse with the sacrifice of Christ, though not one in number with it, as the Missifices shamelessly and most audaciously lie. For they are utterly lacking in the external condition, as well as the internal, which the apostle requires in the true and perfect priest, and in the functions which he assigns to Christ the priest, distinct from the Levitical. They lack the external condition, because the Missifices do not spring from the tribe of Judah, nor are they priests according to the power of an indissoluble life, since they are mere men, frail and mortal. Nor are they ordained by the word of the divine oath, since no divine promise, much less a sworn one, has ever been made about their priesthood and sacrifice. And the internal condition is even more completely wanting, because they are not high priests who fit us, through whom it is lawful to approach God. They are not holy, pious, without fault or stain; rather they stain both themselves and others. They are not separated from sinners, but share with them in sin, and are priests not of God but of their own carnal glory and gain. Finally, they are not higher than the heavens, but sunk in mire, of the earth and not of heaven. And their functions too are wholly different. For they offer not only for the sins of the people, but also for their own; not once, but over and over, frequently, whenever it pleases them to hire out the offering for money to the people and to bind it to themselves. Finally, they offer not themselves, but something outside themselves, a most worthless thing of no account, which they define as an accident without substance, a vague and indeterminate being. The Mass priesthood is also far removed from the Aaronic priesthood, because the Missifices do not spring from the tribe of Levi, nor are they appointed according to the Divine Law of carnal descent; they possess no divinely commanded legal and external holiness, and they have no sacrifice commanded by God to offer. That priesthood, therefore, is neither Levitical nor Christian, but Antichristian.

units.la: LXI. Cum enim omnis Sacerdos pro hominibus constitutus in iis, quae ad Deum spectant, donum vel victimam pro peccatis offerendam habeat: Christus verus & perfectus Sacerdos victima carere non potuit. Sed peculiare ei est, quod ipse & Sacerdos & Victima est. Nam ἑαυτὸν se ipsum aeterno Spiritu obtulit, Hebr. VII.27.IX.14. Qua vero in re sacrificii seu victimae hujus ratio constiterit, analogia cum sacrificiis Leviticis docet. Et Levitica quidem vicaria fuerunt, alia solida sive holocausta; alia piacularia: alia salutaria seu Pacifica; quae singula qualia fuerint, & quemadmodum Christum ejusque sacrificium figuraverint, Loc. XV. 28--30. nec non 70.71.72. fuse exposuimus. Licet tamen singula illa sacrificium Christi quodammodo figuraverint, tamen sacrificium Christi verum non
units.tr: LXI. Since every priest appointed for men has, in the things that pertain to God, a gift or victim to offer for sins, Christ, the true and perfect Priest, could not lack a victim. But it is peculiar to him that he is both Priest and Victim. For he offered himself [ἑαυτὸν] through the eternal Spirit (Heb. 7:27; 9:14). In what respect this sacrifice or victim consists is taught by its analogy with the Levitical sacrifices. The Levitical sacrifices were vicarious: some were solid or whole burnt offerings (holocausts), some were sin offerings (piacular), and some were peace or fellowship offerings (salutary). We have set out at length, in Locus XV (28–30) and also at 70, 71 and 72, what each of these was like and how each foreshadowed Christ and his sacrifice. Yet although each of those sacrifices foreshadowed the sacrifice of Christ in some way, the true sacrifice of Christ was modelled not on every kind, but on one particular kind of sacrifice.

units.la: Funtiones Sacerdotii Christi & veteris Levitici differentia ex Hebr. VII. 27.28. exponuntur. non ex quovis; sed uno quodam sacrificiorum genere fuit. Cumque S.Literæ sacrificio huic ἀϕεσιν abolitionem seu obliterationem peccati, ibid.IX.26, ‏כפר‏ seu ἱλασμὸν propitiationem seu expiationem peccatorum, Dan.IX.24. 1.Joh.II.2. tribuant: & Christum Sacerdotem δι' ἑαυτοῦ per se ipsum purificationem peccatorum fecisse, Hebr.I.3. per proprium sanguinem populum suum sanctificasse, ibid.XIII.12. & μίαν θυσίαν ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν unam victimam pro peccatis obtulisse, ibid. X.12. asserant, dubitari non potest, quin piacu-lari in genere, & quidem tum ‏חטאת‏ pro peccato, tum ‏אשם‏ pro reatu contineatur. Non quòd non etiam vim holocausti & pacifici habeat (nam & totum se Deo obtulit, & pacem Dei nobis conciliavit) sed quòd præcipua & principalis ejus vis in peccati expiatione, & peccatoris propitiatione posita fuerit. Cumque victimas inter piaculares omnes illæ, quarum corpora extra castra cremabantur; & sanguis in die expiationis in adyto intimo spargebatur, sacrificium Christi evidentissimè & perfectissimè omnium adumbraverint, quæ ratio fuit typi illius omnium typorum piacularium præstantissimi, eandem esse sacrificii Christi, quod inveritate & unicum & perfectissimum est, consequitur.
units.tr: The functions of Christ's priesthood and the difference from the old Levitical priesthood are explained from Heb. 7:27–28. Since the Holy Scriptures ascribe to this sacrifice the abolition or obliteration of sin [ἄφεσιν] (Heb. 9:26), the propitiation or expiation of sins [כפר, or ἱλασμὸν] (Dan. 9:24; 1 John 2:2), and assert that Christ the Priest made purification of sins through himself [δι' ἑαυτοῦ] (Heb. 1:3), sanctified his people by his own blood (Heb. 13:12), and offered one sacrifice for sins [μίαν θυσίαν ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν] (Heb. 10:12), there can be no doubt that it belongs to the piacular kind, under both חטאת [chattat], for sin, and אשם [asham], for guilt. Not that it lacks the force of a holocaust and a peace offering (for he offered the whole of himself to God, and reconciled us to God's peace), but its principal and chief force lies in the expiation of sin and the propitiation of the sinner. And since, among the piacular victims, those whose bodies were burned outside the camp and whose blood was sprinkled in the innermost sanctuary on the day of atonement most clearly and most perfectly of all foreshadowed the sacrifice of Christ, and this was the reason for that type, the most excellent of all piacular types, it follows that the same is the sacrifice of Christ, which is in truth both unique and most perfect.

units.la: LXII. Istæ ergo victimæ, quibuscum sacrificium Christi, ceu typis præstantissimis, conferri debet, juvencus & hircus fuerunt, quorum alter pro Sacerdote summo & familia Aharonica, alter pro toto populi coetu die expiationis immolabatur.
units.tr: LXII. The victims, therefore, with which Christ's sacrifice, as the most excellent types, must be compared, were the young bull and the goat. Of these, the one was sacrificed for the high priest and the family of Aaron, the other for the whole assembly of the people on the day of atonement.

units.la: Has victimas primò Pontifex ad aram in atrio Sacerdotum positam adducebat, atque sic Deo primùm offerebat: dein adductas & sic oblatas mactabat: demum earundem sanguinem in adytum intimum mox illatum aspergebat, exta in ara adolebat, corpora autem extra populi castra, sive urbem Hierosolymitanam, penitus comburi curabat, uti fusiùs in Loco explicavimus. Et Pontifex quidem victimam ad aram adducens, seu Deo primùm offerens, nec non eandem jugulans populum repræsentabat. Cùm enim in hominum singulorum sacris suam quisque victimam pro ara sistere, manu sua consecrare, & sic consecratam vel ipse, vel ejus nomine Sacerdos mactare, Levit. I.3-7. debuerit; in totius coetus sacrificiis, quale fuit solenne illud die expiationis, victimæ adductio & mactatio, aliàs à Senatore, aliàs à Pontifice, sed coetus personam sustinente, facta, adeoque proprie Pontificalis non fuit. Sed proprie Pontificalis seu Sacerdotalis fuit posterior illa oblatio seu adolitio profectorum, & sanguinis aspersio in Sancto Sanctorum facta.
units.tr: The high priest first brought these victims to the altar set in the court of the priests, and so offered them to God first. Then, having brought them and so offered them, he slaughtered them. Finally he sprinkled their blood in the innermost sanctuary, which he had just entered, burned the fat on the altar, and saw to it that the bodies were burned up entirely outside the camp of the people, that is, outside the city of Jerusalem, as we have explained more fully in the Locus. The high priest, in bringing the victim to the altar, that is, in offering it first to God, and likewise in slaughtering it, represented the people. For in the sacrifices of individual men, each was to set his own victim before the altar, consecrate it with his own hand, and then, once consecrated, either himself or a priest in his name was to slaughter it (Lev. 1:3–7). But in the sacrifices of the whole assembly, such as that solemn sacrifice of the day of atonement, the bringing and slaughter of the victim were done sometimes by a senator and sometimes by the high priest, but while sustaining the person of the assembly. So this was not strictly pontifical. Strictly pontifical or priestly, however, was that later offering, the burning of the fat, and the sprinkling of the blood made in the Holy of Holies.

units.la: Ex his palam fit, sacrificium Christi, cujus piaculare illud in die expiationum peractum præ cæteris omnibus eximius typus fuit; tribus potissimùm actibus & ritibus, puta tum voluntaria ejus ad mortem cruentam oblatione: tum morte ipsa: tum ingressu in Cœlum victimæ jam mactatæ nomine, eóque erga homines animo, ut eos Deo commendaret; confectum esse. Has certè, non vel alias, vel plures Sacrificii Christi partes Scripturæ commemorant. Christus cùm advenit Sacerdos summus futurorum bonorum, per majus & perfectius tabernaculum non manufactum, hoc est, non hujus conditionis; neque per sanguinem hircorum vel vitulorum, sed per pri-
units.tr: From these things it is plain that the sacrifice of Christ, of which that piacular rite performed on the day of atonements was an outstanding type above all others, was accomplished chiefly by three acts and rites: namely, his voluntary offering of himself to a bloody death; the death itself; and his entry into heaven in the name of the victim now slain, with that disposition towards men by which he would commend them to God. The Scriptures certainly record these, and not other or more parts of Christ's sacrifice: "Christ, when he came as high priest of the good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, and not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own"

units.la: prium sanguinem intravit semel in sancta, æterna redemptione inventa. Si enim sanguis taurorum & hircorum, & cinis vaccæ irrorans contaminatos sanctificat ad carnis munditiem; quantò magis sanguis Christi, qui se ipsum per Spiritum æternum obtulit immaculatum Deo, purificabit conscientiam vestram à mortuis operibus ad serviendum Deo viventi? Hebr.IX.11-15. Singulas has sacrificii Christi partes & actus, nec non singularum illarum vim propriam curatius paulò explicabimus.
units.tr: blood, entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption. For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on the defiled, sanctify to the cleanness of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? (Heb. 9:11–15). We shall explain these individual parts and acts of Christ's sacrifice, and the proper force of each, somewhat more carefully.

units.la: LXIII. Prima sacrificii Christi pars, ejus voluntaria ad mortem cruentam oblatio, tum peracta est, cùm Filius Dei se ad mortem imminentem ultrò Deo obtulit.
units.tr: LXIII. The first part of Christ's sacrifice, his voluntary offering of himself to a bloody death, was accomplished when the Son of God freely offered himself to God as death drew near.

units.la: Quod ejus ad mortem se accingentis dicta & facta probant. Dicta, velut cùm mortem adituirus dixit: Pro illis ego memetipsum ἁγιάζω sanctifico, ut & ipsi in veritate sanctificati sint, Joh.XVII.19. Ubi ἁγιάζειν sanctificare idem est quod προσφέρειν offerre, quomodo etiam Hebræa vox ‏קדש‏, quæ proprie sanctificare significat, passim, velut, Exod.XIII.2. Levit.XXII.2.3. Deut.XV.19. &c. pro oblatione usurpatur. Apostolus, Hebr. IX.14. sic illud effert: ἑαυτὸν προσήνεγκε se ipsum obtulit.
units.tr: That he was preparing himself for death is proved by his words and deeds. His words, for example when about to face death: "For their sakes I sanctify [ἁγιάζω] myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth", John 17:19. Here to sanctify [ἁγιάζειν] is the same as to offer [προσφέρειν]. The Hebrew word ‏קדש‏ [qadash], which properly means to sanctify, is likewise used for offering throughout, as in Exod. 13:2, Lev. 22:2, 3, Deut. 15:19, etc. The Apostle, Heb. 9:14, expresses it thus: "he offered himself" [ἑαυτὸν προσήνεγκε].

units.la: Et preces illæ, quibus Christus; Joh.XVII. fusis ad mortem suam se consecrabat, conveniunt cum iis, quibus Pontifex Judæorum victimas die expiationis ante aram consecravit seu obtulit, quarum formulas Majmonides passim ex Misna & Siphra repetit.
units.tr: The prayers by which Christ consecrated himself to death in John 17 also agree with those by which the High Priest of the Jews consecrated, or offered, the victims before the altar on the Day of Atonement. Maimonides repeatedly quotes their formulas from the Mishnah and Sifra.

units.la: Sicut enim Pontifex ille victimas istas Deo offerens primò sibi & familiæ suæ, mox toti familiæ Aharonicæ, ac demum universo coetui salutem à Domino precabatur: ita Christus se ad mortem consecrans & Deo offerens primò se & glorificationem suam v.1-9. tum suos, inprimis Apostolos, v.9-20. ac demum omnes credentes in ipsum v.20-f. enixissimis precibus commendavit. Tum ergo, cùm preces hasce fudit, se Deo ut victimam obtulit. Facta ejus id ipsum comprobant. Illico enim post fusas illas preces ad locum eum se contulit, ex quo se ad judicium, atque inde ad supplicium ductum, & pro victima piaculari mactatum iri intellexit. His dictis Jesus cum discipulis suis trans torrentem Cedron, &c. Joh.XVIII.1.
units.tr: For as that High Priest, offering these victims to God, prayed for salvation from the Lord first for himself and his household, then for the whole family of Aaron, and finally for the whole assembly, so Christ, consecrating himself to death and offering himself to God, first commended himself and his glorification (vv. 1–9), then his own, especially the Apostles (vv. 9–20), and finally all who believe in him (vv. 20 to the end), with most earnest prayers. Therefore, when he poured out these prayers, he offered himself to God as a victim. His deeds confirm this. Immediately after these prayers he went to the place from which he understood he would be led to judgment, and then to execution, and be slain as the sin-offering. "When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron," etc., John 18:1.

units.la: Altera sacrificii ejus pars, mactatio successit tum, cùm mortem extra Hierosolymam (ubi exta victimæ, quibus maximè adumbrabatur, cremari solebant) subiit. Tertia, ingressus in Cœlum victimæ mactatæ nomine, cùm resuscitatus ex mortuis Cœlum, Sancto Sanctorum adumbratum, ingressus, coram Deo comparuit, ut Deum nobis maximè propitium redderet.
units.tr: The second part of his sacrifice, the slaughter, followed when he underwent death outside Jerusalem, where the entrails of the victims, which chiefly foreshadowed him, were burned. The third, "his entry into heaven in the name of the slain victim," took place when, raised from the dead, he entered heaven, foreshadowed by the Holy of Holies, and appeared before God, so as to make God most favourable to us.

units.la: Sicut enim Pontifex Judæorum victimarum sanguinem, ceu animas, intimo Templi adyto illatum in cædis ante confectæ signum propitiatorium versus spargebat: ita Christus Cœlum ingressus, non animam duntaxat, sed etiam corpus suum, ceu victimam pro peccatis nostris cæsam, Deo Patri stitit, qui actus ab aliis oblationis posterioris, ab aliis repræsentationis victimæ nomine venit. De eo sic S.Paulus. Non in manu facta Sancta Jesus intravit; exemplaria verorum, sed in Cœlum ipsum; νῦν ἐμφανισθῆναι τῷ προσώπῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ ut appareret nunc vultui Dei pro nobis, neque ut sæpe offerret se ipsum, sicut Pontifex intrat in Sancta per singulos annos in sanguine alieno, &c. Hebr.IX.24.25. Ubi Dei vultui pro nobis appareapparere, & semetipsum Deo offerre unam rem aliter atque aliter consideratam, illud ut continuatam, hoc ut inchoatam significat.
units.tr: For as the High Priest of the Jews sprinkled the blood of the victims, as though it were their life, carried into the innermost sanctuary of the Temple, towards the mercy seat, as a sign of the slaying already accomplished, so Christ, entering heaven, presented before God the Father not only his soul but also his body, as a victim slain for our sins. Some call this act the later offering, others the representation of the victim. Paul speaks of it thus: "Christ has not entered into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God for us [νῦν ἐμφανισθῆναι τῷ προσώπῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ], nor that he should offer himself often, as the High Priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own," etc., Heb. 9:24, 25. Here "to appear before the face of God for us" and "to offer himself to God" are one thing considered in two ways: the former signifies it as continuing, the latter as begun.

units.la: LXIV. Singulae hae sacrificii Christi partes peculiarem in procuranda nobis salute vim obtinuerunt. Nam voluntaria illa ad mortem cruentam oblatio id praestitit, quod mors ejus non ultra oppetita praestare non potuisset. Nam in ea fuit μαρτύριον testimonium doctrinae Christi & ὑπογραμμὸς exemplar obedientiae & charitatis; & ἁγιασμὸς sanctificatio, consecratio, qua se totum Deo sanctificando, adeoque sanctus & ipse ad gratiam apud Patrem sibi conciliandam devovit. Ante omnia igitur acerbae morti se sponte offerendo Evangelio suo fidem magnam conciliavit. Nam sanguis ejus μαρτυρεῖ testari, 1. Joh. V. 8. & ipse praeclaram confessionem coram Pontio Pilato edidisse, 1. Tim. VI. 13. dicitur. Si vero invitus & nolens mortem subiisset, & ultro se Deo Patri non obtulisset, morte sua dictorum a se veritatem non obsignasset. Tum voluntaria hac oblatione obedientiae suae erga Deum, & charitatis erga proximum exemplum discipulis suis tradidit. Mors enim, quam ultro adiit, gravissima fuit, & tantis cum cruciatibus conjuncta, ut se a Deo desertum esse queri necesse habuerit. Nihilominus patientissimè illam, utpote libenter prudenterque suscep-tam, sustinuit, spem propositae sibi in tantis malis gloriae inconcussam servavit, nulla ira, ne quidem in carnifices suos, efferbuit, convitia convitiando non retudit, & pro hostibus suis oravit. Quibus rebus maximum obsequii erga Deum, charitatis erga homines, spei promissae gloriae, humilitatis & patientiae exemplum dedit; quantum nullum aliud hactenus fuit, vel deinceps futurum est. Charitas proin Christi urget nos, aestimantes hoc, quod si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui sunt; & pro omnibus mortuus est, ut & qui vivunt, jam non sibi vivant, sed ei, qui pro eis mortuus est & resurrexit, 2. Cor. V. 14. 15. Denique voluntaria illa sui ad mortem oblatio summam ei apud homines potestatem, & apud Patrem gratiam conciliavit: qua fretus valido hominum apud Deum patrocinio defungi potuit. Unde pro Apostolis suis preces ad Deum fundens eo argumento usus est, quod pro iis se sanctificaverit, hoc est, ad mortem se obtulerit. Sanctifica eos in veritate: (in cognitione & amore veritatis magis magisque eos promove, ut velut φωστῆρες in mundo luceant) Sermo tuus (quem iis tradidi, in ore eorum posui solus) Veritas est. Quemadmodum me misisti in mundum, & ego eos misi in mundum. Et pro iis ego sanctifico me ipsum, (offero me Deo, cui quod offertur, sanctificatur, quia ipse sanctus est; & ad sanctificandum eum facit) ut & ipsi sanctificati sint in Veritate, (me offerente me ipsum ad mortem, & ipsi ad sanctitatem in veritate renoventur) Joh. XVII. 17, 18, 19.
units.tr: LXIV. Each of these parts of Christ's sacrifice had its own particular power in procuring our salvation. For that voluntary offering of himself to a bloody death achieved what his death, undertaken unwillingly, could not have achieved. In it there was his testimony [μαρτύριον] to the doctrine of Christ, his example [ὑπογραμμὸς] of obedience and love, and his sanctification [ἁγιασμὸς], or consecration, by which he devoted himself wholly to God, and so, being himself holy, devoted himself to win favour with the Father. Above all, then, by freely offering himself to a bitter death, he gained great credit for his Gospel. For his blood is said to "bear witness" [μαρτυρεῖ], 1 John 5:8, and he is said to have made a noble confession before Pontius Pilate, 1 Tim. 6:13. But if he had undergone death unwillingly and reluctantly, and had not offered himself to God the Father of his own accord, he would not have sealed the truth of what he had taught by his death. Moreover, by this voluntary offering he gave his disciples an example of obedience to God and of love towards neighbour. For the death he freely underwent was most grievous and joined with such torments that he was compelled to complain that he was forsaken by God. Nevertheless he bore it most patiently, as something undertaken willingly and wisely; he kept unshaken the hope of the glory set before him amid such evils; no anger, not even against his executioners, flared up in him; he did not repay insults with insults; and he prayed for his enemies. By these things he gave the greatest example of obedience to God, of love towards men, of hope in the promised glory, and of humility and patience, such as no other has been or will be. "For the love of Christ constrains us, because we judge this: that if one died for all, then all have died; and he died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them," 2 Cor. 5:14, 15. Finally, that voluntary offering of himself to death won him supreme power among men and favour with the Father, relying on which he could discharge the powerful intercession of men before God. Hence, pouring out prayers to God for his Apostles, he used this argument: that "he sanctified himself for them," that is, offered himself to death. "Sanctify them in the truth" (advance them more and more in the knowledge and love of truth, so that they may shine in the world as lights [φωστῆρες]). "Your word" (which I have delivered to them, and placed in their mouths alone) "is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world. And for their sakes I sanctify myself" (I offer myself to God, to whom what is offered is made holy, because he is holy and makes holy whom he makes holy) "that they also may be sanctified in truth" (as I offer myself to death, they too are renewed to holiness in truth), John 17:17, 18, 19.

units.la: LXV. Altera sacrificii Christi pars ipsa ejus Mors hanc proprie vim habuit, ut per eam peccata nostra expiarentur, & Deo pro iis in solidum satisfieret. Nam Deus, qua summa clementia & misericordia est, peccatores quosdam salvare: & qua pari justitia est, eosdem, nisi expiato peccato, sine συνδείξει δικαιοσύνης demonstratione justitiae peccatum punientis, salvare nolu-it: ac ne potuit quidem, quia justitia peccatum puniens ei naturalis est. Quod in loco amplissimè probavimus. Accedit, quod per Evangelium Lex, seu Legis δικαίωμα non retractatur, nec citra mutabilitatem Dei retractari potuit. An legem per fidem abolemus? Neutiquam: sed legem ἱστῶμεν stabilimus, Rom. III. 31. Nam Lex operum peccatori mortem comminata, & obedienti vitam promittens, non aliter rata esse, quam morte peccatori, vel ei, qui locum peccatoris subiit, inflicta, & vita nonnisi obedienti, aut obedientis locum subeunti, & δικαίωμα ἕ νόμω praestanti collata, potuit. Evangelium ergo, seu fides in Evangelio patefacta Christum mortis suae obedientia & sacrificio poenas peccatorum solventem, & δικαίωμα ἕ νόμω pro iisdem implentem revelans, legem operum stabilit, non abolet. Deus enim sententiam semel latam rescindere citra sui abnegationem non potuit. Ideo sine sanguinis effusione peccatorum remissionem non fieri, Hebr. IX. 22. iram Dei super illis, qui non credunt, manere, Joh. III. 36. & eosdem, antea quam credant, irae filios esse, Ephes. II. 3. & ab ira ventura liberari debere, ceu ὑπόδικος obnoxios Deo ad judicium, 1. Thess. I. 10. Scripturae asseverant.
units.tr: LXV. The second part of Christ's sacrifice, his death itself, had this particular power: through it our sins were expiated, and full satisfaction was made to God for them. For God, who is of highest clemency and mercy, willed to save certain sinners; and, being equally just, he was unwilling to save the same sinners without a demonstration of justice [συνδείξει δικαιοσύνης], that is, without punishing sin, unless the sin was expiated. Indeed he could not do so, because justice that punishes sin is natural to him. We have proved this most fully in its place. Besides, through the Gospel the Law, or the righteous requirement of the Law [δικαίωμα τοῦ νόμου], is not revoked, nor could it be revoked without a change in God. "Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid; yea, we establish the law," Rom. 3:31. For the Law of works, which threatens death to the sinner and promises life to the obedient, could be valid only if death was inflicted on the sinner, or on the one who took the sinner's place, and life was granted only to the obedient, or to one who takes the place of the obedient and fulfils the righteous requirement [δικαίωμα] of the Law. Therefore the Gospel, or the faith revealed in the Gospel, which reveals Christ paying the penalties of sinners by the obedience and sacrifice of his death, and fulfilling the righteous requirement [δικαίωμα] of the Law on their behalf, establishes the Law of works and does not abolish it. For God could not rescind a sentence once pronounced without denying himself. Hence the Scriptures affirm that "without shedding of blood there is no remission of sins," Heb. 9:22; that "the wrath of God abides on those who do not believe," John 3:36; that they are, before they believe, "children of wrath," Eph. 2:3; and that they must be delivered "from the wrath to come," as those who are "liable [ὑπόδικος] to God's judgment," 1 Thess. 1:10.

units.la: LXVI. Haec ergo peccati illorum, qui salvantur, expiatio, & pro iisdem satisfactio plena & solida morti Christi uni soliquae accepta refertur. Jam enim supra Loc. XV, 72. inprimis ex Esaj. LIII. 5. 6. 10. 11. 12. probare occupavimus, quod victimae piaculares vicariam ejus, pro quo offerebantur, poenam sustinentes typus fuerint mortis Christi, utpote quae & ipsa vicariae poenae & expiationis peccati rationem habuerit. Nam & vulneratum esse propter praevaricationes, contritum propter iniquitates nostras esse: & peccata nostra in Servum illum justum impositta esse, מוסר שלמינו paradigma, exemplar poenale, cujus poena alter coercetur, & σωφρονίζεται, ne & ipse puniatur Prov. VII. 22. XV. 10. & simul peccati ipsius noxa demonstratur; ad pacem nostram factum esse; & afflictum esse propter id, quod a nobis ישׁ exigebatur (exigebatur autem satisfactio pro poena) & animam ejus se positurum אשם & peccata multorum laturum, distertis verbis, Esaj. LIII. 3. &c. praedictum est. Vere ergo Christus satisfecit, quoad אשם reatum. Nam vox אשם in piaculari victima usitata, & reatum quidem, & reatus causam, hoc est, culpam, & satisfactionem pro reatu significat: Postremo hoc sensu Christus vitam ultro ponendo, seu mortem oppetendo, Deum & fratrem peccatorem diligens animam suam אשם posuit. (in mortem dedit) tanquam אשם satisfactionem pro culpa ad reatus solutionem. Sic ergo peccata nostra ei impacta sunt; sic propter ea vulneratus, contritus מוסר paradigma factus est; sic peccata nostra tulit, ut haec faciendo, seu patiendo potius, fieret אשם victima piacularis pro reatu, hoc est, satisfaciens pro culpis alienis ad solutionem reatus eorundem. Quod S. Paulus confirmat ajens, Deum Christum, qui peccatum non fecit, imo ἁμαρτίαν, ἁμαρτία ... Ipsa-justitia (uti Chrysostomus loquitur) fuit, pro nobis peccatum fecisse, 2. Cor. V. 21. hoc est, sacrificium περὶ ἁμαρτίας, Rom. VIII. 3. seu חטאת, Levit. IX. 15. pro peccato; & אשם nec non מוסר exemplar, peccatum ab ipso exigendo, Esaj.LIII. 5. sic eum tractando & latas ei poenas imponendo, quae peccato & remissione ejus dignae sunt, ut & foeditas atque cumulus peccati remissi, & sanctitas Dei peccatum remittentis in tanta & tam innocente persona sufficienter cognoscatur. Neque tantum satisfecit quoad reatum, sed etiam quoad jus filiorum, quia omnem justitiam implevit, Matth.III. 15. hoc est, omne mandatum, quod ipsi ut Sponsori & Sacerdoti datum est, obiit, adeo ut nobis a Deo justitia factus dicatur, 1.Cor.I.30. Accedit, quod Christus vel per se, vel sanguine, vel sacrificio suo peccata nostra expiasse, lustrasse, purificasse dicitur. Nam si ἑαυτὸν καθαρίσαμον ποιησάμενος per se ipsum (ut sacrificatum) purificatione facta peccatorum nostrorum consedit ad dextram Majestatis in sublimi, Hebr.I.3. Et sanguis Jesu Christi purificat nos ab omni peccato, 1.Joh.I.7. ubi καθαρίζειν notat purificare seu purgare a peccato per ejus expiationem. Ita enim Lex de ejus, qui mortuum contrectasset, expiatione: ישרה Et purus (plene purgatus, piatus) erit in vespera, Num.XIX.19. Clare autem Moses כפר pro alibi explicat.
