Hoc die expiationem faciet super vos ( כפר vobis dat ad peccatum obliterandum ) לטהר ad purificandum vos coram Jehova, טהרו puri eritis, Levit.XVI.30. Et LXX. Interpretes Exod.XXIX.36. כפר καθαρισμὸν purificationem reddunt. Sic ergo Christus per se ipsum & sanguine suo nos purificavit, ut peccatum, & peccati poenam abstulerit, eique contrariam puritatem & jus vitae coelestis nobis conciliaverit, quod victimae piacularis munus fuit. Cum quo convenit verbum ἁγιάζειν sanctificare, quod S. Paulus usurpat, dicens: Altare habemus, de quo edendi potestatem non habent, qui tabernaculo inserviunt. Quorum enim animalium sanguis pro peccato in Sancta per Pontificem infertur, horum corpora cremantur extra castra. Propter quod etiam Jesus, ut sanctificaret populum per sanguinem, extra portam passus est. Hebr.XIII.10.11.12. Ubi ἁγιάζειν idem est quod lustrare, expiare. Quo vero modo haec sanctificatio, lustratio per Christi sanguinem facta fit, Apostolus clare docuit. Cum enim de Christo ut victima piaculari, & de ejus sanguine, ut de sanguine victimae piacularis loquatur, talis populum sanctificandi & peccata ejus expiandi ratio morti ejus extra castra tribuenda est, qualem ipsa victimae piacularis ratio propria postulat. Atqui victimae piaculares omnes peccata, propter quae immolabantur, poena vicaria expiarunt. Ergo eadem ratione Christus populi sui peccata expiavit; atque sic eundem sanguine suo sanctificavit.
units.tr: LXVI. Therefore the atonement for the sins of those who are saved, and the full and solid satisfaction made for them, is traced to the death of Christ alone, and to it only is it accepted. For above, at Loc. XV, 72, we have already undertaken to prove, chiefly from Isaiah 53:5, 6, 10, 11, 12, that the sin offerings, bearing as substitute the punishment of the one for whom they were offered, were types of the death of Christ, since that death too had the character of a substitutionary punishment and an atonement for sin. For Scripture asserts that he was wounded for our transgressions and bruised for our iniquities, and that our sins were laid upon that righteous Servant; that the chastisement of our peace [מוסר שלמינו] was upon him, a paradigm, a penal exemplar, by whose punishment another is restrained and brought to his senses [σωφρονίζεται], lest he himself be punished (Prov. 7:22; 15:10), and at the same time the harm of the sin itself is shown; that he was made for our peace; that he was afflicted for that which was required of us [ישׁ] (and satisfaction was required in place of punishment); and that he would make his soul a guilt offering [אשם] and bear the sins of many, as is foretold in plain words (Isa. 53:3, etc.). Christ therefore truly satisfied as regards the guilt [אשם], that is, the reatus. For the word אשם, used of the sin offering, signifies both the guilt itself and the cause of guilt, that is, the fault, and also satisfaction for the guilt. Finally, in this sense Christ, by freely laying down his life, that is, by undergoing death, loving God and his sinful brothers, placed his soul as a guilt offering [אשם] (he gave it unto death) as a satisfaction for the fault, for the release from guilt. So therefore our sins were laid upon him; so, on account of them, he was wounded, bruised, and made a paradigm of chastisement [מוסר]; so he bore our sins, so that by doing these things, or rather by suffering them, he might become a sin offering [אשם], a victim of atonement for guilt, that is, one satisfying for the faults of others so as to release them from guilt. This St. Paul confirms, saying that God made Christ, who knew no sin, nay, who was righteousness itself (as Chrysostom puts it), [ἁμαρτίαν] sin for us (2 Cor. 5:21), that is, a sacrifice for sin [περὶ ἁμαρτίας] (Rom. 8:3), or [חטאת] a sin offering (Lev. 9:15), for sin; and [אשם] a guilt offering, and [מוסר] a paradigm, by requiring sin of him (Isa. 53:5). Thus, by treating him so and imposing on him punishments fitting for sin and for its remission, the foulness and the accumulated weight of the sin forgiven, and the holiness of God who forgives sin, are sufficiently made known in so great and so innocent a person. And he satisfied not only as regards the guilt, but also as regards the right of the sons, because he fulfilled all righteousness (Matt. 3:15), that is, he discharged every command given to him as Surety and Priest, so that he is said to have been made righteousness from God for us (1 Cor. 1:30). Add to this that Christ is said to have expiated, cleansed and purified our sins, either by himself, or by his blood, or by his sacrifice. For when he had by himself [ἑαυτὸν καθαρίσαμον] made purification of our sins (as one sacrificed), he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Heb. 1:3); and the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7), where [καθαρίζειν] to cleanse means to purify or purge from sin through his atonement. For so the Law speaks of the atonement for one who had touched a dead body: [וטהר] and he shall be clean (that is, fully purged and atoned) in the evening (Num. 19:19). Moses too clearly explains [כפר] elsewhere: on this day he shall make atonement for you ([כפר] he gives you for the obliteration of sin) [לטהר] to cleanse you before Jehovah, [טהרו] you shall be clean (Lev. 16:30). And the Septuagint, in Exod. 29:36, render [כפר] by purification [καθαρισμὸν]. So Christ, by himself and by his blood, cleansed us, so that he took away sin and the punishment of sin, and secured for us the purity opposite to it and the right to heavenly life, which was the office of the sin offering. With this agrees the word sanctify [ἁγιάζειν], which St. Paul uses, saying: We have an altar, of which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin are burned outside the camp. Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate (Heb. 13:10–12). Here [ἁγιάζειν] to sanctify is the same as to purify, to make atonement. Now in what manner this sanctification and purification is effected by the blood of Christ, the Apostle has clearly taught. For since he speaks of Christ as a sin offering, and of his blood as the blood of a sin offering, the manner of sanctifying the people and atoning for their sins must be ascribed to his death outside the camp in the same way as the proper manner of the sin offering itself requires. But all sin offerings atoned by vicarious punishment for the sins on account of which they were offered. Therefore by the same reasoning Christ atoned for the sins of his people, and so sanctified them by his blood.

units.la: LXVII. Sed clarissime Scriptura Christo ejusque morti כפרה expiationem peccatorum nostrorum, adeoque pro iisdem satisfactionem tribuit. Septuaginta hebdomadae decisae sunt, &c לכפר עון ad expiandam pravitatem, Dan.IX.24. Proprie, notante R.Sol.Jarchi כפרה notat קנוח ἀπολύτρωσιν, Hebr.IX.26. obliterationem veluti nominis in tabulis expensi scripti. Ita, Esaj. XXVIII.18. ויכפר בריתכם Et obliterabitur foedus vestrum, inducetur, delebitur. Sicut scriptura atramento inducto, & quod in tabula scriptum est, quovis colore deletur, R. D.Kimchi Scripturae Morti Christi expiationem peccatorum & satisfactionem pro iisdem tribuunt. per עונות הסיר auferre peccata explicat. No ergo עון כפרה ablationem, obliterationem peccati, ne Deus ejus amplius recordetur, Jerem. XXXI.34. Defectiones nostras אתה תכפרם tu eas deles, per כפר λύτρον ἀντὶ λύτρου, quod ipse tu das, Psal.LXV.4. כפר על החטאתינו Induc peccata nostra, imputans nobis justitiam Sponsoris, ut condones peccata, tanquam inducto illis tectorio, ibid. LXXIX.9. Non ergo Christus עון כפר expiavit pravitatem eam simpliciter condonando, sed morte sua expiando, ut condonari posset. Ideo in Lege de Sacerdote diceba-tur, כפר עליהם ונסלח להם faciet expiationem super illis (in fide offerentibus) & condonabitur illis, Levit.IV.20. ut ita כפר condonationis causam potius, quam condonationem significet. Sed convenit inprimis cum כפרה vox altera פדות ἀπολύτρωσις redemptio, quae vox scriptoribus N.T. familiaris est. Nam כפר proprie tectorium (quomodo Deus ad Noam: כפרת teges, induces eam intus & extus בכפר tectorio, Genes.VI.14.) impropriè λύτρον pretium redemptionis, quo peccatum & ejus poena inducitur, tegitur, obliteratur, nec non ἀντιλύτρον fontis vice datum, fonti succedaneum תמורה ἀντάλλαγμα permutationem (quae vox de victima piacolari Levit.XXVII.10. usurpatur) significat. אם כפר Si (λύτρα, uti Graeci) lytron ei imponetur; & dabit redemptionem animae suae, Exod.XXI.30. Fratrem nemo redimendo redimet, nec dabit Deo כפרו redemptionis pretium pro eo; Nam pretiosa est פדין נפשם redemptio animae eorum, Psal.XLIX.8.9. Ubi כפר & נפש & פדין alternant. Ita Exod. XXX.12.13. Dabunt quisque כפר נפשו λύτρον, pretium animae suae Jehovae, dimidium sicli. Non accipietis כפר לנפש רצח lytron animae homicidae, Num.XXXV.31. Et Christus ipse ad Patrem suum: Redime illum, ne descendat in foveam. Nam inveni כפר λύτρον pretium redemptionis ejus. Job.XXXIII.24. Cum igitur כפר λύτρον notet, etiam τῷ כפרה vox ἀπολυτρώσεως redemptionis respondeat oportet. Quo inprimis Hebraeorum usitata locutio pertinet, qua alterum alteri כפרה ἀπολυτρώσεων fieri dicunt. Ita in Misch. Sanhedr. cap.2. אנו כפרן Nos tibi ἀπολυτρώσεως fimus. Et Misch. Neg. cap.2, בני ישראל אני כפרן Filiis Israel sim ego ἀπολυτρώσεως. Et Jam. Fol.23. הרי הוא כפרתכם Hic fit vobis ἀπολυτρώσεως. Cujusmodi locutiones ita explicat Baal Aruch in voce כפר Omni in loco, quo quis dixerit הרינו כפרתו sim ipse illi ἀπολυτρώσεως, haec sententia declaratur: הרינו במקומו לסכל עונתיו Ultinam ipse ejus in locum supponar, ut iniquitates ejus feram. Quod perinde est, ac si quis dicat: Ego ipse, ille ut lustretur, in me peccata ejus suscipio. LXVIII. Scripturae autem N.T. morti & sanguini Christi ἀπολυτρώσεων, hoc est, πλείων λυτρώσεων redemptionem, quae vere liberos facit; & quod λύτρον atque ἀντιλύτρον sit pro peccatis nostris, passim tribuunt. Justificamur gratis ipsius gratia, διὰ τῆς ἀπολυτρώσεως τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ per redemptionem in Christo Jesu, quem praestituit Deus Propitiatorium per fidem in ipsius sanguine, Rom.III.24.25. Christus Jesus factus nobis a Deo est ἀπολύτρωσις redemptio, 1.Cor.I.30. In quo Eadem morti & sanguini Christi ἀπολυτρώσεων redemptionem, & quod λύτρον, ἀντιλύτρον pro peccatis nostris sit, ut indicant.
units.tr: LXVII. But Scripture most clearly attributes to Christ and his death the כפרה [kipparah, atonement], the expiation of our sins, and therefore satisfaction for them. "Seventy weeks are determined... to make an end of transgression, לכפר עון [lekhappēr ʿāwôn, to make atonement for iniquity]" (Dan. 9:24). Properly, as R. Solomon Jarchi notes, כפרה [kipparah] signifies קנוח [qinnûaḥ], wiping away, or, as the Greek puts it, ἀπολύτρωσιν [apolytrōsin, redemption] (Heb. 9:26), the obliteration, as it were, of a name written in an account book. So in Isaiah 28:18, ויכפר בריתכם [wĕyukhpar bĕrîtkem, and your covenant shall be annulled], that is, it shall be brought in, blotted out: just as writing is wiped out with ink, and what is written on a tablet is erased with any colour. Rabbi David Kimchi explains עונות הסיר [ʿăwōnôt hēsîr, to take away iniquities] as the taking away of sins. Therefore the Scriptures attribute to the death of Christ the expiation of sins and satisfaction for them. There is no כפרה [kipparah] of iniquity, that is, no removing and obliterating of sin, so that God may not remember it any more (Jer. 31:34). In Psalm 65:4, "Our transgressions, אתה תכפרם [attah tekhappərem], you shall purge them," כפר [kipper] is used in the sense of λύτρον ἀντὶ λύτρου [lytron anti lytrou, a ransom for a ransom], which you yourself give. In Psalm 79:9, כפר על החטאתינו [kappēr ʿal haḥaṭṭāʾōtênû, purge away our sins] means: impute to us the righteousness of the Surety, so that you may pardon sins, as if a plaster had been spread over them. So Christ did not expiate the iniquity of sin simply by forgiving it, but by expiating it with his death, so that it might be forgiven. Therefore in the Law concerning the priest it was said, כפר עליהם ונסלח להם [kipper ʿălêhem wĕnislaḥ lāhem, he shall make atonement for them, and it shall be forgiven them] (Lev. 4:20), faciet expiationem super illis, he shall make atonement for them (those offering in faith), and condonabitur illis, it shall be forgiven them. So that כפר [kipper] signifies rather the cause of forgiveness than forgiveness itself. But the word פדות [pĕdût, redemption], ἀπολύτρωσις [apolytrōsis, redemption], which is very familiar to the writers of the New Testament, agrees above all with כפרה [kipparah]. For כפר [kipper] properly means a plaster or coating (as God said to Noah: כפרת [kopher, coat] teges, induces, you shall coat it inside and out בכפר [bakkōpher, with pitch], Gen. 6:14), and figuratively λύτρον [lytron], the price of redemption, by which sin and its penalty are covered, hidden, and obliterated, and also ἀντιλύτρον [antilytron], given in place of a fountain, a substitute for the fountain. תמורה [tᵉmûrāh, exchange], ἀντάλλαγμα [antallagma, exchange], signifies a substitution (a word used of the sin offering in Lev. 27:10). אם כפר [ʾim kopher, if a ransom], Si (λύτρα, as the Greeks say) lytron ei imponetur, if a ransom is laid upon him, et dabit redemptionem animae suae, and he shall give the redemption of his life (Exod. 21:30). Fratrem nemo redimendo redimet, nec dabit Deo כפרו [kopherô, its ransom] redemptionis pretium pro eo: no man can redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him (Ps. 49:8, 9). For the redemption of their soul is costly, פדין נפשם [pidyōn napsham], which is the price of redemption of their soul. Here כפר [kopher], נפש [nepesh] and פדין [pidyon] alternate. So at Exod. 30:12-13, each shall give כפר נפשו [kopher napsho, the ransom of his soul] as λύτρον [lytron], the price of his soul, to the LORD, half a shekel. Non accipietis כפר לנפש רצח [kopher lĕnepesh rōtséaḥ, ransom for the life of a murderer], you shall take no ransom for the life of a murderer (Num. 35:31). And Christ himself speaks to his Father: Redime illum, ne descendat in foveam. Nam inveni כפר λύτρον pretium redemptionis ejus. Deliver him, that he may not go down into the pit: for I have found a ransom, כפר [kopher], the price of his redemption (Job 33:24). Since therefore כפר [kopher] signifies λύτρον [lytron], the word כפרה [kipparah] must also correspond to ἀπολυτρώσεως [apolytrōseōs, of redemption]. To this belongs especially the usual Hebrew expression by which they say that one person becomes כפרה [kipparah], ἀπολυτρώσεων [apolytrōseōn, a redemption], for another. Thus in Mishnah Sanhedrin ch. 2: אנו כפרן [ʾānû kapparān, we are your ransom], we are your redemption. And in Mishnah Nega ch. 2: בני ישראל אני כפרן [bĕnê Yisrāʾēl ʾănî kapparān, I am a ransom for the sons of Israel], I am a redemption for the sons of Israel. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, fol. 23: הרי הוא כפרתכם [hārî hû kapparātkem, he is your ransom], he is made your redemption. Baal Aruch explains such expressions in the word כפר [kopher] as follows: wherever someone says הרינו כפרתו [harînû kapparātô, I would be his ransom], this sense is declared: הרינו במקומו לסכל עונתיו [harînû bimqômô lĕsakkēl ʿawōnōtāyw, would that I were put in his place to bear his iniquities]. This is just as if someone said: "I myself take his sins upon me, so that he may be cleansed." LXVIII. But the Scriptures of the New Testament attribute to the death and blood of Christ the ἀπολυτρώσεων [apolytrōseōn], that is, the πλείων λυτρώσεων [pleiōn lytrōseōn, the fuller redemption], which truly sets free, and that λύτρον [lytron] and ἀντιλύτρον [antilytron] are for our sins, everywhere. "We are justified freely by his grace, διὰ τῆς ἀπολυτρώσεως τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ [dia tēs apolytrōseōs tēs en Christō Iēsou, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus], whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood" (Rom. 3:24, 25). "Christ Jesus was made by God to us ἀπολύτρωσις [apolytrōsis], redemption" (1 Cor. 1:30). In quo, in whom, they likewise indicate the same: the redemption of death and blood of Christ, and that λύτρον [lytron] and ἀντιλύτρον [antilytron] are for our sins.

units.la: quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ejus, remissionem peccatorum, Ephes.I.7. Col.I.14. Propterea (Christus) Testamenti Novi Mediator est, ut morte facta εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν ad redemptionem transgressionum primi Testamenti promissionem accipiant vocati æternæ hæreditatis, Hebr.IX.15. Quibus in locis ἀπολύτρωσις non quamvis redemptionem notat, sed eam, quæ in expiatione per victimam piacularem factam cernitur. Id quod & sanguinis, & remissionis peccatorum adjecta mentio demonstrat; illius nempe utrei expiatione partæ. Quas duas res simul commemorans & conjungens Apostolus expiationem victimarum piacularium sanguine apud Judæos factam, & peccatorum condonationem expiatione illa facta respexit. Faciet expiationem super illis, & condonabitur illis, Levit.IV.20. Quæ sic distincta Christo S.Paulus applicat, dicens: Omnia pœne in sanguine secundum Legem mundantur (expiantur,) & sine sanguinis effusione non fit peccatorum remissio, Hebr.IX.22. Quæ ergo victimæ veteris ratio, & vis fuit, eandem morti Christi tribuit. Atqui victimæ veteris ratio fuit, ut cæsæ ejus vicaria pœna peccati veniam reo impetraret. Par ergo mortis Christi, & factæ per eandem redemptionis vis & ratio fuit. Neque redemptionem metaphoricam, hoc est, liberationem à pœnis peccati per annuntiationem remissionis peccatorum gratuitæ non irritam, uti Socinus pertendit, satis illud evincit, quòd eædem Scripturæ morti & sanguini Christi etiam vim λύτρα & ἀντιλύτρα tribuunt. Filius hominis non venit, ut sibi ministraretur, sed ministraret, & daret animam suam λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν redemptionis pretium pro multis, Matth.XX.28. Quod igitur Esajas dixit, servum justum animam suam positurum אשם satisfactionem, seu victimam piacularem pro peccato, Esaj.LIII.10. id ipsum Christus verbis his expressit, ajens, Filium hominis animam suam λύτρον dare, ponere. Quod vel inde etiam liquet, quia victima quæque piacularis à Judæis כפר λύτρον, ἀντιλύτρον dici, & victimæ animæ, sive vita vice ipsius sontis dari solet. Cùm ergo Christus de morte sua, seu vita pro multis posita, ut de vita victimæ piacularis pro sontibus data, loquatur, eam morti suæ iisdem verbis vim tribuisse censeri debet, quæ ad victimam piacularem pertinet, quæ in peccatorum remissione per pœnam vicariam consistit. Consona sunt illa S.Pauli: Unus est Mediator, &c. qui dedit se ipsum ἀντιλύτρον redemptionis pretium pro omnibus, 1.Tim.II.5.6. hoc est, permutatione, volente & consentiente Deo Patre, facta dedit se loco eorum, quorum Mediator est, ut ipsis parceretur, & peccata iis condonarentur: sic tamen, ut ipse veniret in eorum locum, portans peccata ipsorum & obedientia ac sanguis ejus fieret τιμὴ pretium, quo eos sibi sanctificandos & glorificandos emeret, 1.Pet.I.18.19. Ejus porro λύτρα typus etiam est in argento capitationis, de quo sic Lex: Cùm ceperis numerum filiorum Israel per numeratos eorum, dabunt singuli כפר נפש lytron animæ suæ Jehovæ, &c. Dives non augebit, pauper non diminuet de dimidio siclo, &c. Exod.XXX.12-15. Typus sic ad veritatem reducitur: Gratis venditi estis ולא בכסף תגאלו & non argento redimemini, Esaj.LII.3. Explicatius verò sic: Οὐ φθαρτοῖς
units.tr: By whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins (Eph. 1.7; Col. 1.14). Therefore (Christ) is the Mediator of the New Testament, so that, by a death made εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν [for the redemption] of transgressions under the first Testament, those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance (Heb. 9.15). In these places ἀπολύτρωσις does not signify redemption in the general sense, but that which is seen in expiation made through a sin-offering. The added mention of both blood and forgiveness of sins shows this, since each is the fruit of that expiation. In recalling and joining these two things together, the Apostle had in view the expiation made among the Jews by the blood of sin-offerings, and the pardon of sins obtained through that expiation: "He shall make atonement for them, and it shall be forgiven them" (Lev. 4.20). S. Paul applies these distinct things to Christ, saying: "Almost all things are cleansed by blood according to the Law (expiated), and without shedding of blood there is no remission of sins" (Heb. 9.22). So what was the nature and force of the old sacrifice, he ascribes to the death of Christ. But the nature of the old sacrifice was that the substitute punishment of the slain victim obtained pardon of sin for the guilty. Therefore the force and nature of Christ's death, and of the redemption effected through it, is the same. Nor does this prove a metaphorical redemption, that is, liberation from the punishments of sin through the proclamation of free forgiveness of sins that is not void, as Socinus contends. This is sufficiently refuted by the fact that the same Scriptures ascribe to the death and blood of Christ the force of λύτρα and ἀντιλύτρα [ransom and substitute-ransom]. "The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom (λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν) for many" (Matt. 20.28). Therefore what Isaiah said, that the righteous servant would place his soul as an אשם, a satisfaction or sin-offering for sin (Isa. 53.10), Christ expressed in these words, saying that the Son of man gives and lays down his soul as a ransom. This is also clear from the fact that every sin-offering is called by the Jews כפר, λύτρον, ἀντιλύτρον, and a soul is customarily given in place of the guilty person's life. Since therefore Christ speaks of his death, his life laid down for many, as of the life of a sin-offering given for the guilty, he must be judged to have ascribed to his death, in the same words, the force that belongs to a sin-offering, which consists in the remission of sins through vicarious punishment. S. Paul's words agree: "There is one Mediator... who gave himself ἀντιλύτρον, a ransom price, for all" (1 Tim. 2.5, 6). That is, by an exchange, with God the Father willing and consenting, he gave himself in the place of those of whom he is Mediator, so that they might be spared and their sins forgiven; yet in such a way that he himself came into their place, bearing their sins, and his obedience and blood became τιμή, the price with which he bought them to be sanctified and glorified for himself (1 Pet. 1.18, 19). Moreover, his λύτρα is also prefigured in the silver of the poll-tax, of which the Law says: "When you take the number of the children of Israel by their counting, they shall each give a ransom (כפר נפש, lytron) for his soul to Jehovah... The rich shall not increase, nor the poor diminish, from the half shekel" (Exod. 30.12–15). The type is thus brought back to the truth: "You were sold for nothing, and ולא בכסף תגאלו you shall not be redeemed with money" (Isa. 52.3). More explicitly: "You were not redeemed with corruptible" [Οὐ φθαρτοῖς

units.la: ἀργυρίῳ καὶ χρυσίῳ ἐλυτρώθητε, ἀλλὰ τιμίῳ αἵματι. Non corruptibili argento & auro, sed pretioso sanguine Agni immaculati Christi redempti estis, 1.Pet.I.18.19. Faciunt huc etiam illa S.Pauli: Christus ἐξηγόρασεν redemit nos ab execratione Legis, factus pro nobis execratio, Gal.III.13. Ubi verbum ἐξηγόρασεν vim vocis ἀντιλύτρα explicans, significat, peccata omnia, à quibus Lex nos liberare non potuit, imò propter quæ nobis maledixit, per Christi vitam ἀντιλύτρα nomine pro nobis positam expiata & remissa esse. Eandem denique ob causam Christus ἱλασμὸς propitiatio pro peccatis nostris dicitur. In hoc est charitas, non quòd nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quòd ipse prior dilexit nos, & misit Filium suum ἱλασμὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν propitiationem pro peccatis nostris, 1.Joh.IV.10. Quorum verborum hic sensus est, quòd Deus nos malè licèt erga ipsum affectos tantopere dilexerit, ut Filium suum morte sua peccata nostra expiaturum in mundum miserit. Nam morti Christi ἱλασμὸν seu כפרה expiationem hanc (quomodo etiam LXX. Interpretes vocem כפר passim ἱλασμὸν, ἐξιλασμὸν, ἐξιλασμα reddunt: velut, Exod.XXX.10. Levit.XXIII.27.28. Num.V.8. & alibi) tribui, satis inde liquet, quia amor Dei Filium suum ἱλασμὸν futurum mittentis, ex eo maximè emicuit, quòd Filium huncce suum morti exposuit: quodque ἱλασμὸς περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν non aliter esse potuit, quàm quatenus ceu victima piacularis pro nobis substitutus peccata nostra expianda in se suscepit. Quæ peccatorum expiatio, quoties victima piaculari facta est, pœnæ vicariæ rationem habuit.
units.tr: ἀργυρίῳ καὶ χρυσίῳ ἐλυτρώθητε, ἀλλὰ τιμίῳ αἵματι] silver and gold, but with precious blood. You were redeemed, not with corruptible silver and gold, but with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb, Christ (1 Pet. 1.18, 19). Those words of S. Paul also bear on this: "Christ ἐξηγόρασεν redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us" (Gal. 3.13). Here the verb ἐξηγόρασεν, explaining the force of the word ἀντιλύτρα, signifies that all sins, from which the Law could not free us, and on account of which indeed it pronounced its curse upon us, have been expiated and remitted through the life of Christ, set in our place as an ἀντιλύτρα. Finally, for the same reason Christ is called ἱλασμός, propitiation, for our sins. "In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he first loved us, and sent his Son ἱλασμὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, a propitiation for our sins" (1 John 4.10). The sense of these words is that God so greatly loved us, though we were ill disposed towards him, that he sent his Son into the world to expiate our sins by his death. That expiation (כפרה, or ἱλασμός, as the Seventy generally render the word כפר by ἱλασμός, ἐξιλασμός, ἐξιλασμα, as in Exod. 30.10, Lev. 23.27–28, Num. 5.8, and elsewhere) is clearly ascribed to the death of Christ. For the love of God, sending his Son to be a propitiation, shone out chiefly in this, that he exposed this Son of his to death; and a propitiation for sins could be nothing other than the Son's taking upon himself, as a sin-offering substituted for us, our sins to be expiated. Such an expiation of sins, whenever it is made by a sin-offering, has the character of vicarious punishment.

units.la: LXIX. Demonstrationis hujus vim non infringunt, quæ Socinus obducit, velut quòd כפר פדה ἀπολύτρωσιν & λύτρων sæpe liberationem absque pretio significent; velut cùm Moses λυτρωτὴς appellatur, Act.VII.35. & de Jonathane dicitur; פדה Redemerunt populus Jonathanem, hoc est, liberarunt sine pretio, 1.Sam. XIV.45. & Christus quoque redemptus sine pretio certè dicitur, Psal.XXXI.6. & Deus ipse שוב כפר bonus ignoscere dicitur, 2.Chron.XXX.18. & פדה Deo liberatori tribuitur à Davide, 2.Sam. IV.9. Vivit Dominus, qui פדה redemit, vel liberavit animam meam ex angustiis: & Solomon divitias כפר λύτρον animæ, qualecunque impendium dixit, Prov.XIII.8. & idem iniquitatem veritate & misericordia כפר redimi dixit, ibid. XVI.6. & liberatis jam per Christum ἀπολύτρωσις redemptio, hoc est, liberatio, sed sine novo pretio tribuitur, Rom.VIII.23. Ephes.IV.30. quòd nullus sit acceptor λύτρα seu pretii, cùm redempti dicamur ab execratione Legis, Gal.III.13. & ab iniquitatibus nostris, Tit.II.14. quibus tamen pretium nullum persolutum fuerit; quòdque adeò ipsa redemptio & λύτρον metaphoricè, non proprie dicantur eo sensu, quòd sicut proprie dicta λύτρωσις causa est liberationis è captivitate vel servitute, sic Christus in mortem traditus ab omni reatu peccatorum nos absolverit: quòd ad λύτρον & τιμὴν pretium, quo Christus nos redemit, non pertinuerit, ut pœnam vicariam pro emptis subeat: quòd, cùm Deus Christum pro nobis in mortem tradiderit, non motus ad id morte Christi, (quia morte sua mereri non potuit, ut ipse pro nobis moreretur) tantam
units.tr: LXIX. The objections that Socinus raises do not undermine this demonstration: for instance, that כפר, פדה, ἀπολύτρωσις and λύτρα often signify liberation without a price. For example, Moses is called λυτρωτής (Acts 7.35), and of Jonathan it is said: "They redeemed (פדה) Jonathan," that is, freed him without price (1 Sam. 14.45); Christ too is certainly said to be redeemed without price (Ps. 31.6); God himself is called שוב כפר, good to forgive (2 Chron. 30.18); and David ascribes פדה to God as deliverer: "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed (פדה) my soul out of distress" (2 Sam. 4.9). Solomon said that riches are the כפר λύτρον of a man's soul, whatever the cost (Prov. 13.8), and the same writer said that iniquity is כפר, redeemed, by truth and mercy (Prov. 16.6). Redemption, ἀπολύτρωσις, that is liberation but without a new price, is ascribed to those already freed through Christ (Rom. 8.23; Eph. 4.30). Since no ransom or price is received, we are said to be redeemed from the curse of the Law (Gal. 3.13) and from our iniquities (Titus 2.14), though no price was paid for them. And so redemption and λύτρον are called metaphorical and not proper, in the sense that, just as proper redemption is the cause of liberation from captivity or servitude, so Christ, delivered up to death, absolved us from all guilt of sins; that it did not pertain to the λύτρον and τιμή, the price with which Christ redeemed us, that he should undergo vicarious punishment in place of those bought. And that, since God delivered Christ up to death for us, he was not moved to this by Christ's death (because by his death he could not merit that he himself should die for us), so great is his benevolence toward us that he showed he was willing to forgive us with no account taken of Christ's death. Finally, that, since God gave Christ his life and blood, a proper redemption and satisfaction, held to be obtained by the life and blood of Christ rendered to God, would be nothing other than a certain ludicrous transaction, by which God gave to himself from his own, and made satisfaction to himself from his own.

units.la: Socinianorum objectiones, quòd redemptio Christo tributa metaphorica, non propria sit, propensuntur. tam ejus erga nos benevolentiam esse constet, ut nulla habita ratione mortis Christi nobis ignoscere se velle ostenderit: quòd denique, cùm Deus Christo vitam & sanguinem dedit, redemptio & satisfactio proprie dicta, quæ ejusdem vita & sanguine Deo reddito parta statuitur, non aliud quàm commercium quoddam ludicrum fuisset, quo sibi Deus de suo dedit, sibique satis de suo fecit.
units.tr: The objections of the Socinians, that the redemption ascribed to Christ is metaphorical and not proper, are weighed. So clear is his benevolence toward us that he showed he was willing to forgive us with no account taken of Christ's death. Finally, since God gave Christ his life and blood, a proper redemption and satisfaction, held to have been procured by that life and blood rendered back to God, would be nothing other than a certain ludicrous transaction, by which God gave himself something from his own and made satisfaction to himself from his own.

units.la: LXX. Sed nihil profecto efficit φρικτὴ illa περιτρέπεια, qua homines illi inimici crucis Christi maximum Dei beneficium, & capitalissimam veritatem illam, quòd Christi obedientia & passio vera redemptio & verum pretium sit, & veri pretii effectum, nempe jus postulandi possessionem & hæreditatem suam habuerit, oppugnant. Nam Moses quidem λυτρωτὴς Redemptor etiam, Act. VII. 35. appellatur. Sed λυτρὸν respondet Hebræo פדה quod vel liberationem captivi, interveniente pretio, si nexus sit juris: vel interveniente non pretio, sed potentia majore, si captivitas sola vi & injuria constet, significat. Sive igitur priore sensu Moses à S. Stephano λυτρωτὴς dictus est, quatenus ob potentem illam manum Dei, qua ad dictum ejus Pharao percussus est, ut Israelitæ injustè à Pharaone detenti liberarentur ex captivitate Ægyptiaca, nihil hoc facit ad ἀπολύτρωσιν illam, quæ Christo tribuitur, quia Moses λυτρώσεις illa non pretio, sed potentia sola interveniente, & captivos non jure, sed sola vi nexos liberante facta est, cùm ἀπολύτρωσις per Christum pretio interveniente, & jure nexos liberante facta sit. Sive posteriore sensu λυτρωτὴς dictus est, quatenus Israelitas liberavit per sanguinem, qui illis per eum datus est, ut eo fuso & poltibus illito Angelus interfector domum ipsorum præteriret, & ipsi tanquam filii Dei ex Ægypto exirent; talis utique fuit interveniente pretio, sed typico: adeoque ipse etiam λυτρωτὴς typicus exitit; Christus verus est; utrumque pretium habens, & per illud jure captos liberans; sed ille typicum, sanguinem Agni, hic verum, sanguinem sui ipsius. Eodem sensu verba כפר & פדה Deo, 2.Sam.IV.9. 2.Chron.XXX.18. tributa, liberationem Divinam vel per solam potentiam ex captivitate injusta sine interveniente pretio, vel interveniens pretium ex captivitate justa Sathanæ, significant. Priore sensu de Deo usurpata Christi redemptionem per interveniens pretium non tollit, quia diversi generis illa liberatio est: posteriore sensu eam confirmat. Ita David dicens: אלהים פדה Deus redimet animam meam, Psal.XLIX.16. & הוא פדה Ipse redimet Jerusalem ex pravitatibus suis, ibid. CXXX.8. & defectiones nostras אתה תכפרם tu eas deles, ibid. LXV.4. redemptionem & deletionem eam per כפר λυτρον, sacrificium Christi à Patre dati factam intelligit. Populus verò Jonathanem פדה redimens sine pretio, periculo iniquè objectum liberavit, 1.Sam.XIV.45. Sed dispar Christi ratio est, cui pretium, & per illud liberatio ex captivitate justa per peccatum promerita tribuitur. Neque verba illa, Psal.XXXI.6. In manum tuam depono Spiritum meum, פדית אותי redemisti me Deus verax; Christi sunt, sed Ecclesiæ fiduciam suam in redemptione Christi testantus. Sed & Solomon dicens; divitias homini esse כפר נפשו lytron animæ ejus, Prov. XIII 8. non aliud quàm liberationem vitæ divitis per pretium pecuniæ suæ, adeoque proprie dictam, non qualecunque impendium, intelligere potuit, quali diviti pauperem, qui non audit increpationem, hoc est, à nemine vexatur, vel increpatur, ut in vitæ periculum veniat, & λυτρῶ redimi debeat, præfert. Convenit cum eo dictum: Quicquid habet aliquis; id pro vita sua daturus est, Job.II.4. Etsi maximè כפר λυτρον eo loco, qualecunque impendium significaret: at vox ἀντίλυτρα, quæ Christi sanguini tribuitur, significantior est, quàm ut solum impendium notet. Idem Solomon dicens, in gratia & veritate כפר expiari pravitatem, Prov.XVI.6. redemptionem Christi propriam non tollit, sed confirmat, quia solam veram peccati expiationem esse, quæ in amore, quo Deus electos in Christo diligit, & in redemptione per sanguinem ipsius consistit, & gratia & veritas per Jesum Christum, Joh.I.17. dicitur, docet. Neque illud obstat, quòd etiam liberati jam per Christum ἀπολυτρῶσθαι redimi dicuntur, Rom.VIII.23. Ubi filii Dei ἀπολύτρωσιν & σωματος redemptionem corporis expectare, & Ephes.I V.30. ubi Spiritu S. obsignati εἰς ἡμέραν ἀπολυτρώσεως in diem redemptionis dicuntur. Cùm enim non spiritus duntaxat, sed corpus etiam nostrum πωλῆς pretio emptum sit, 1.Cor.VI.20. redemptionis Spiritus fructus indicatur υἱοθεσία adoptio, cujus Spiritum nos accepisse Apostolus, Rom.VIII. 15. dixit. Redemptionis verò corporis fructus expectandus dicitur redemptio corporis à morte, utraque pendens à pretio illo, quo Christus & animam & corpus nostrum emit. Adeoque liberationem Apostolus intellexit, at non sine λυτρῷ, sed talem, qualis solutionem & λυτρὸν sequitur, & quæ in judicio fit, qualis intelligitur, Job.XXXIII.24. פדעהו Redime eum, ne descendat in foveam. Nam כפר λυτρον pretium redemptionis inveni. Ubi porro verum pretium, ejusque vera solutio, vera captivitas nocentis, & vera liberatio est, ibi deesse non potest acceptor, hoc est, is, qui pretium accipiat. Qui non est Diabolus, cui, ceu Lorario, non Domino captivorum nihil debetur; sed Deus judex. Is enim accipit, qui judex est, qui propter sanctitatem & legem suam hominem captivum tradidit; qui ut Deus Sionis sanctus & justificans reum ac damnatum, exaltatur per judicium, & sanctificatur per justitiam, Esaj.V.16. Ille acceptor pretii est, cui honos suus per peccatum violatus & contaminatus restituitur: cujus longanimitas & gratia planè indecens esset, nisi justitia ea, tanquam verè gratum & minimè aspernabile sacrificium, extaret. Qui maledictioni subjicere, peccatum condonare, justificare, & per sacrificium justificari atque sanctificari potest. Et judices quidem humani non possunt pretium accipere, sed secundum leges judicare tenentur; & cùm pretium accipiunt, corrumpi se patiuntur, ut à lege recedant. At Deus pretium accipiens non recedit à lege, sed secundum legem peccatum condonat, peccatorem in Sponsore, Mediatore Testamenti & Sacerdote justificat. Ac licèt vox accipiendi, si rigidè sumatur, non factis, sed solis rebus aptari soleat, factis tamen satisfieri, & liberationem impetrari posse, dubitari nequit, & præcipuè apparet in ea liberatione, quæ per poenæ translationem fit. Poena tamen proprie non accipitur, quia in ea nemo proprie & naturaliter creditor est; neque etiam utilitas propria punientis, sed bonum commune & ordo rerum spectatur. Proin ἀντιλύτρωσις loquendo acceptor hic nullus requiritur, nisi, libeat admodum improprie acceptorem dicere judicem, tanquam juris & æqui ac communis boni curatorem. Quo non obstante etiam in poena λύτρον proprie locum habet. Quomodo Zaleuci oculus fuit λύτρον oculi filii; & in decimatione qui puniuntur, λύτρον totius legionis sunt. Latini etiam veteres, quorum lingua tota Græcæ depravatio fuit, litera una interposita, λύτρον lustrum & λυτρέιν lustrare dixerunt. Lustrare ergo urbem est a poena liberare per lustrum, hoc est, per poenam succedaneam, quod & piaculum dicitur. In poenis ergo ἱλασμός, λύτρον, λύτρωσις, καθαρσμός placamen, lustrum idem sunt. Non redempti sumus equidem a Deo per alienationem, ut pretio dato non amplius ejus simus: at redempti tamen sumus Deo, Apoc. V.9. per reconciliationem, Rom. V.9, ab execratione Legis, Gal.III.13. tanquam a poena, & ab iniquitatibus nostris, Tit.II.14. tanquam a laqueis, quibus constricti eramus a Deo judice, ut principaliter detinente. Non ergo illis, sed huic pretium solvendum fuit. Quid nunc ad redemptionem proprie dictam amplius desideramus? Si metaphorica, seu quasi redemptio est, est etiam quasi lex peccatori mortem comminans, quasi justus Deus, quasi transgressio Legis; quasi reatus mortis, quasi maledictio Legis, quasi captivitas, quasi justificatio a peccato, &, uno verbo, quasi Deus. Et plane redemptio metaphorica, qualem Socinus commentus est, redemptionem sine emptione, emptionem sine pretio, pretium sine valore, valorem sine solutione, solutionem sine absolutione ponit. Quomodo sic Sion per judicium redimitur, & reduces ejus (resipiscentes) per justitiam? Esa. I.27. Quomodo Jehova per judicium exaltatur, & Deus ille Sanctus per justitiam sanctificatur, ibid. V.16. Cumque Socinus, Crellius & alii omnia, quæ ad veram & proprie dictam redemptionem requiruntur, adesse, solo acceptore, seu eo, qui pretium accipiat, excepto, sæpe fateantur, αὐτοκατακέκριτοι sunt. Nam acceptorem rigide sumptum in factis, velut solutione poenæ, non requiri; & latius sumptum adesse, jam demonstravimus. Inane porro est, quod ad λύτρον & τιμὴν seu pretium, quo aliquis emitur, poenam vicariam pro empto subeundam non pertinere garriunt. Quando enim pretii nomen in victima piacularI ponitur, ita nomen illud intelligi debet, uti victimæ talis ratio postulat. Commutatio ergo illa, quæ inter nos & Christum, qui se ipsum propter peccata nostra pro victima piaculari exposuit, intercessit, ejusmodi intelligitur, qualis inter fontem quemvis & victimam ejus piacularem intercedit, & cum poena vicaria semper conjuncta est. Et Deus quidem Christum pro nobis in mortem tradidit solo amore εὐδοκίας beneplaciti seu benevolentiæ suæ erga genus humanum, non morte vel sacrificio Christi motus, quia ut in mortem traderetur, vel moreretur pro nobis, morte sua impetrare nec potuit, nec debuit. Potuit tamen Deus, qua erga genus humanum ἐπιθυμία & charitate est, salva justitia sua, cum Filio suo, ut animam suam sacrificium pro eo poneret, & satis justitiæ suæ faceret, transfigere. Non enim Filium suum mittendo, ut morte sua pro nobis satisfaceret, vel peccata expiavit, vel sine ejus expiatione peccatori se ignoscere velle declaravit; sed causam & medium expiationis peccatorum procuravit. Neque denique, quia Deus Christo vitam & sanguinem dedit, iccirco de suo sibi satisfecisse, & ludicrum quoddam commercium instituisse censeri debet. Non enim Christi vita & sanguis simpliciter Deo pro peccatis nostris satisfecit, sed vita & sanguis ejus summis ipsius cum doloribus, summo erga Deum obsequio fusus. Hoc vero obsequium; hos dolores Christus sibi proprios habuit. Ita damnati in inferno poenas in animabus & corporibus a Deo ipso datis luentes, nihilominus eidem pro peccato poenas persolvunt, neque in supplicio tali ludicri quicquam vel Deus, vel damnati committere putantur.
units.tr: LXX. But that dreadful distortion [περιτρέπεια], by which those enemies of the cross of Christ attack the greatest benefit of God and that chief truth, that the obedience and passion of Christ are a true redemption and a true price, and that the effect of a true price, namely the right to claim possession and inheritance, is secured, accomplishes nothing at all. For Moses is indeed called "redeemer" [λυτρωτὴς] at Acts 7:35. But λύτρον corresponds to the Hebrew פדה, which signifies the liberation of a captive, either by means of a price, if the bond is one of law, or by means of a greater power and no price, if the captivity rests on force and injustice alone. So if Stephen called Moses "redeemer" in the first sense, because by that mighty hand of God, which struck Pharaoh at his word, the Israelites unjustly held by Pharaoh were freed from Egyptian captivity, this has nothing to do with that redemption [ἀπολύτρωσιν] which is ascribed to Christ. For Moses' redemption was made without a price, by power alone, and it freed captives held not by right but by force alone, whereas the redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις] effected through Christ was made by a price and freed those held by right. If Stephen meant the second sense, that Moses was a redeemer because he freed the Israelites through the blood given to them by God, so that when it had been poured out and smeared on the doorposts the destroying angel would pass over their houses, and they themselves as sons of God would go out of Egypt, then this was indeed a redemption by an intervening price, but a typical one. Thus Moses too was a typical redeemer, while Christ is the true redeemer, having both a price and freeing the captives by right: Moses with the typical blood of the lamb, Christ with the true blood of himself. In the same sense the verbs כפר and פדה, when ascribed to God (2 Sam. 4:9; 2 Chron. 30:18), signify divine liberation either by power alone from unjust captivity without any intervening price, or by a price intervening from the just captivity to Satan. When these verbs are used of God in the first sense, they do not remove Christ's redemption by an intervening price, because that liberation is of a different kind; in the second sense they confirm it. So David says: "God will redeem my soul" (Ps. 49:16); "He himself will redeem Israel from all its iniquities" (Ps. 130:8); and "You will cover our transgressions" (אתה תכפרם, Ps. 65:4). By this redemption and covering he understands the redemption and atonement effected through the sacrifice given by the Father in Christ, which is the כפר λυτρον. The people, indeed, redeemed Jonathan (פדה) without a price, when they freed him from an unjust danger (1 Sam. 14:45). But Christ's case is different: to him is ascribed a price, and through it liberation from the just captivity merited by sin. Nor do those words in Psalm 31:6, "Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O faithful God" (פדית אותי), belong to Christ; they express the Church's trust in the redemption of Christ. Solomon too, saying that riches are to a man the כפר נפשו, the λύτρον of his soul (Prov. 13:8), could mean nothing other than the liberation of the rich man's life by the price of his money, and so a redemption properly so called, not any sort of outlay. He sets the rich against the poor, who does not hear rebuke, that is, who is harassed or rebuked by no one so as to be brought into danger of life and so have to be redeemed by a λύτρῳ. The saying agrees with this: "Whatever a man has he will give for his life" (Job 2:4). Even if in that place כפר λυτρον signified any sort of outlay, the word ἀντίλυτρα, which is ascribed to Christ's blood, is too strong to mean mere outlay. Solomon's words that iniquity is כפר expiated "by mercy and truth" (Prov. 16:6) do not remove Christ's proper redemption but confirm it, since they teach that the only true expiation of sin consists in the love with which God loves the elect in Christ and in the redemption by his blood, and that "grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" (John 1:17). Nor is there any objection in the fact that those already freed through Christ are said to be redeemed [ἀπολυτρῶσθαι] (Rom. 8:23), where the sons of God await ἀπολύτρωσιν, the redemption of the body; or in Ephesians 4:30, where those sealed by the Holy Spirit are said to be sealed εἰς ἡμέραν ἀπολυτρώσεως, unto the day of redemption. For not only our spirit but our body too has been bought with a price [πωλῆς] (1 Cor. 6:20). The fruit of the Spirit's redemption is indicated by υἱοθεσία, adoption, which the Apostle says we have received in the Spirit (Rom. 8:15). The fruit of the redemption of the body is said to be awaited as the redemption of the body from death, both depending on that price by which Christ has bought both our soul and our body. Thus the Apostle understood a liberation not without a λύτρον, but one that follows the payment and the λύτρον, and that takes place at judgment. Such is the sense of Job 33:24, פדעהו, "Redeem him, that he may not go down into the pit", for I have found a כפר λύτρον, a price of redemption. Where there is a true price, and its true payment, a true captivity of the guilty, and a true liberation, there the recipient cannot be absent, that is, the one who receives the price. This is not the devil, to whom, as to a jailer and not as to the Lord of captives, nothing is owed; it is God as judge. For he receives who is judge, who on account of his holiness and his law has handed over the captive man; who, as the holy God of Zion, justifies the guilty and condemned, and is exalted in judgment and sanctified in righteousness (Isa. 5:16). That recipient of the price is the one whose honour, violated and defiled by sin, is restored; whose long-suffering and grace would be wholly unbecoming unless that righteousness stood as a truly acceptable and in no way despicable sacrifice. He can subject to curse, forgive sin, justify, and be justified and sanctified through a sacrifice. Human judges, indeed, cannot receive a price, but are bound to judge according to the laws; and when they do receive a price they allow themselves to be corrupted, so as to depart from the law. But God, when he receives the price, does not depart from the law; according to the law he forgives sin and justifies the sinner in the Surety, the Mediator of the covenant and the Priest. And although the word "to receive", if taken strictly, is usually applied not to deeds but to things alone, it is beyond doubt that satisfaction can be made by deeds, and liberation obtained, and this appears especially in that liberation which takes place by the transfer of punishment. Yet properly speaking the punishment is not "received", because no one is properly and naturally the creditor in it; nor is the proper advantage of the one punishing looked to, but the common good and the order of things. Therefore, in speaking of an antiredemption [ἀντιλύτρωσις], no recipient is required here, unless one is pleased to call the judge, in a very improper sense, the recipient, as guardian of law and of equity and of the common good. Notwithstanding this, a λύτρον does properly have a place in punishment too. So the eye of Zaleucus was a λύτρον for the eye of his son; and those who are punished by decimation are a λύτρον for the whole legion. The ancient Latins also, whose whole language was a corruption of Greek with one letter inserted, said lustrum for λύτρον and lustrare for λυτρέιν. To lustrate a city is therefore to free it from punishment by a lustrum, that is, by a substitute punishment, which is also called a piaculum. So in punishments ἱλασμός, λύτρον, λύτρωσις and καθαρσμός, placation, lustrum, are the same thing. We have indeed not been redeemed by God through alienation, so that once a price was paid we would no longer be his; but we have been redeemed to God (Rev. 5:9) through reconciliation (Rom. 5:9), from the curse of the law (Gal. 3:13) as from a punishment, and from our iniquities (Titus 2:14) as from snares by which we were bound by God as judge, who holds us principally. So the price was to be paid not to them but to him. What more do we now want for redemption properly so called? If it is a metaphorical or quasi-redemption, then there is also a quasi-law threatening the sinner with death, a quasi-just God, a quasi-transgression of the law, a quasi-guilt of death, a quasi-curse of the law, a quasi-captivity, a quasi-justification from sin, and, in one word, a quasi-God. Indeed the metaphorical redemption that Socinus invented posits a redemption without a purchase, a purchase without a price, a price without value, value without payment, and payment without absolution. How then is Zion redeemed through judgment, and her returning ones (the penitent) through righteousness (Isa. 1:27)? How is Jehovah exalted through judgment, and that holy God sanctified through righteousness (ibid. 5:16)? And since Socinus, Crellius and others often admit that everything required for true and properly so called redemption is present, except only the recipient, that is, the one who receives the price, they condemn themselves. For that the recipient, taken strictly, is not required in the deeds, as in the payment of a penalty, and that taken more widely he is present, we have already shown. Equally empty is their prattle that the vicarious punishment to be undergone for the one bought does not belong to λύτρον and τιμή, or price, by which someone is bought. For when the name of price is put on a sacrificial victim, the name must be understood as the nature of such a victim demands. So that exchange which took place between us and Christ, who offered himself for our sins as a sacrificial victim, is to be understood as the kind that takes place between any source and its sacrificial victim, and it is always joined with vicarious punishment. God indeed delivered Christ to death for us solely by the love of his good pleasure [εὐδοκίας], that is, of his benevolence towards mankind, not moved by the death or sacrifice of Christ; for neither could nor ought he to obtain by his death that he should be delivered to death or die for us. Yet God, through that desire [ἐπιθυμία] and charity which he has towards mankind, could, with his Son and his justice preserved, bring it about that the Son should lay down his soul as a sacrifice for them and satisfy his justice. For by sending his Son not so that he might satisfy for us by his death, he did not expiate sins, nor declare that he was willing to forgive the sinner without their expiation; rather he provided the cause and means of the expiation of sins. Nor, finally, because God gave life and blood to Christ, should it be judged that he thereby satisfied himself out of his own resources and set up a sort of game of exchange. For the life and blood of Christ did not simply satisfy God for our sins; rather his life and blood, poured out with the greatest sufferings and in the greatest obedience to God, did so. This obedience and these sufferings Christ had as his own. Just so the damned in hell, paying the penalties that God himself has imposed on their souls and bodies, nonetheless pay penalties to him for their sin, and in such punishment neither God nor the damned are thought to commit anything of a game.

units.la: LXX. Emphasin non exiguam ad probandam Christi satisfactionem per poenam vicariam exantlatam habent Scripturæ locutiones, quibus Christi mors ὑπὲρ pro nobis, imò etiam ἀντὶ vice, loco nostro oppetita dicitur.
units.tr: LXX. The phrases of Scripture in which Christ's death is said to be undergone "for us" [ὑπὲρ] and even "instead of" [ἀντὶ], "in our place" [loco nostro], give no small emphasis to proving Christ's satisfaction through a vicarious penalty.

units.la: Hoc est sanguis meus Novi Testamenti, qui περὶ πολλῶν pro multis effusus est, Matth.XXVI.28. Christus, cum adhuc peccatores essemus, ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν pro nobis mortuus est, Rom.V.8. Si unus ὑπὲρ πάντων pro omnibus mortuus est, nempe isti omnes mortui sunt, &c. 2.Cor.V.15. Fecit eum, qui non novit peccatum, ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν pro nobis peccatum, ib. v.21. Christus ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν pro nobis factus est execratio, Gal.III,13. Jesus Christus dedit se ipsum redemptionis pretium pro omnibus, 1.Tim.II.6. Gloria & honore coronatus est, ut gratia Dei ὑπὲρ πάντος pro omnibus mortem gustaret, Heb.II.9. Justus ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων pro injustis passus est, 1.Pet. III.18. Similia loca, Joh.X.11.15. XI.50.51, Rom.XIV.15. 1.Cor.XV.3. Ephes.V.2. 1.Pet. IV.1. extant. Cunctæ hæ locutiones eam vim habent, ut pro quo Christus mortuus dicitur, pro eo se ἀντίλυτρον redemptionis pretium dedisse, juxta analogiam loci, 1.Tim.II.6. & pro eo sanguinem suum effudisse ad remissionem peccatorum, ipso Christo indice, Matth.XXVI.28. intelligatur. Ea enim a Christo & S. Paulo in verbis illis morti Christi vis tribuitur, quam ea cum victima piaculari, vicariam poenam sustinente communem habuit; ut dubitari non possit, quin ὑπὲρ locum, vicem seu substitutionem mortis Christi in locum debitæ mortis nostræ significet. De locis similibus simile judicium est. Inprimis id evidens est ex verbis S. Pauli, si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, omnes ergo mortui sunt, 2.Cor.V.15. Quid enim his verbis aliud, quàm mors Christi, ut victimæ vicariam pro hominibus poenam subeuntis, significari potest? Eadem vis est phrasium, quibus Christus ὑπὲρ aut περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν pro peccatis nostris, aut propter peccata nostra mortuus dicitur. Christus mortuus est ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν pro peccatis nostris, 1.Cor. XV.3. Christus dedit semetipsum pro peccatis nostris, ut eriperet nos de præsenti seculo nequam, Gal. I.4. Christus semel περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ὑπὲρ pro peccatis passus est, justus pro injustis, 1.Pet.III.18. Quibus locis ὑπὲρ pro idem esse quod διὰ propter, ex Rom.IV.25.ubi Christus Greek propter peccata nostra traditus dicitur, liquet; adeóque peccata mortis Christi causa impulsiva: at expiatio eorundem causa ejus finalis innuitur. Id duntaxat ὑπὲρ inter & ἀντὶ in locis citatis interest, quòd ὑπὲρ apertius finem, tacitè causam impellentem: ἀντὶ verò apertius causam impellentem, tacitè finem significat. Sed utramque peccata causam impellentem, & peccatorum expiationem causam finalem designare, inde colligitur, quòd tum Christus ἱλασμὸς ἀντὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, 1.Joh.IV.10. dicitur, tum ipse peccata nostra, ut Sponsor & Legi satisfaciens in corpore suo tulit super lignum, ut pro iis fieret κατάρα: tum eædem illæ locutiones, in sacrificiis etiam piacularibus poni solent; utpote quæ & ὑπὲρ & ἀντὶ ἁμαρτιῶν propter & pro peccatis oblata, Heb.V.1. VII.27, X.18.26. XIII.11. dicuntur; & quotiescunque in iis ponuntur, peccatorum expiationem significant. Ita lex præscripsit: Anima quæ peccaverit, &c. ... (ita LXX: Interpp.reddunt) offeret pro peccato, quod peccavit, juvencum vitulum, &c. Levit.IV.2.3. Ubi idem est quod ὑπὲρ propter, vel ἀντὶ pro. Neque aliam ob causam sacrificium piaculare appellatur sacrificium peccati, seu pro & propter peccatum expiandum oblatum. Quo verò modo Christus, ut victima piacularis peccata nostra expiaverit, ipsa victimæ talis ratio ostendit. Nam victimam quamque piacularem peccatum, pro quo, vel propter quod immolabatur, pœna vicaria subita expiasse, in loco fusius demonstravimus. Licèt ergo ὑπὲρ, ubi de peccatis, pro quibus, vel propter quæ Christus mortuus est, usurpatur, non notet substitutionem in locum, vel vicem alterius, (Christi enim mors in locum peccatoris, non peccati surrogata est; neque peccata mori; vel pœnas pati possunt, sed peccatores) sed causam impulsivam & finalem mortis Christi; tamen inde Christi vicaria mors & satisfactio æquè solidè demonstratur. Qui enim moritur alieni peccatoris alienis peccatis impulsus, atque eum in finem, ut peccata illa expiet eo modo, quo in sacrificiis pro peccato expiari solent, is loco & vice peccatoris alterius, cujus peccata vicaria victima sua expiat, moritur. Neque porrò illud obstat, quòd sicut Christus ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν pro nobis animam suam posuit, nos etiam similiter ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀδελφῶν pro fratribus animam ponere jubemur, 1.Joh.III.16. & Paulus ὑπὲρ pro Colossensibus passus dicitur, Col.I.24. neque tamen vel nos loco fratrum justitiæ Dei satisfacere possumus; vel pro Colossensibus S. Paulus satisfecit. Non enim simpliciter pro fratribus mori jubemur, sicut Christus pro nobis mortuus est; sed ita, ut non dubitemus vitam nostram bono, vel, si gloria Dei id postulaverit, etiam loco eorum profundere, quemadmodum Christus non dubitavit animam suam; dare redemptionis pretium pro multis, Matth.XX.28. quod ipsi, ceu uni Mediatori proprium fuisse S. Paulus, 1.Tim.II.6. testatur. Ad exemplum sufficit generalem quandam esse similitudinem, etsi differentia sit in modo speciali, cujus tamen mentio fit subinde rei certius denotandæ gratia. Ita S.Petrus 1.Epist.II.19, &c. exemplo Christi
units.tr: This is my blood of the New Testament, which is shed for many [περὶ πολλῶν], Matt. 26:28. While we were still sinners, Christ died for us [ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν], Rom. 5:8. If one died for all [ὑπὲρ πάντων], then all have died, etc., 2 Cor. 5:15. He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us [ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν], ibid. v. 21. Christ became a curse for us [ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν], Gal. 3:13. Jesus Christ gave himself as a ransom for all, 1 Tim. 2:6. That by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone [ὑπὲρ παντὸς], Heb. 2:9. The righteous suffered for the unrighteous [ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων], 1 Pet. 3:18. Similar passages are found at John 10:11, 15; 11:50–51; Rom. 14:15; 1 Cor. 15:3; Eph. 5:2; 1 Pet. 4:1. All these expressions carry this force: that for whom Christ is said to have died, for him he is understood to have given his life as a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] in accordance with the analogy of 1 Tim. 2:6, and for him to have shed his blood for the forgiveness of sins, as Christ himself declares in Matt. 26:28. For Christ and St. Paul ascribe to the death of Christ, in these words, the same power which a sacrificial victim bearing a vicarious penalty has in common with it. So there can be no doubt that [ὑπὲρ] signifies the place, stead or substitution of Christ's death in the place of our deserved death. Similar passages are to be judged in the same way. This is especially plain from the words of St. Paul: "If one died for all, then all have died," 2 Cor. 5:15. For what else can these words signify than the death of Christ as that of a victim undergoing a vicarious punishment for men? The same force attaches to the phrases in which Christ is said to have died [ὑπὲρ] or [περὶ] "for our sins" [ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν], or "because of our sins." Christ died [ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν] "for our sins," 1 Cor. 15:3. Christ gave himself [ὑπὲρ] "for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present evil age," Gal. 1:4. Christ once suffered [περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ὑπὲρ] "for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous," 1 Pet. 3:18. From these passages it is clear that [ὑπὲρ] means the same as [διὰ], "because of", as is evident from Rom. 4:25, where Christ is said to have been delivered [διὰ] "because of our sins." Thus the sins are the impelling cause of Christ's death, while their expiation is indicated as its final cause. The only difference between [ὑπὲρ] and [ἀντὶ] in the passages cited is that [ὑπὲρ] more openly expresses the final end and tacitly the impelling cause, whereas [ἀντὶ] more openly expresses the impelling cause and tacitly the end. That both sins are the impelling cause and the expiation of sins the final cause is gathered from the fact that Christ is called [ἱλασμὸς ἀντὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν] "a propitiation for our sins," 1 John 4:10, and from the fact that he himself, as Surety and satisfier of the Law, bore our sins in his own body upon the tree, so that he became a curse [κατάρα] for them. Moreover, these same expressions are usually applied to propitiatory sacrifices as well, since they are said to be offered [ὑπὲρ] and [ἀντὶ] "for sins" [ἁμαρτιῶν], that is, "because of and for sins," Heb. 5:1; 7:27; 10:18, 26; 13:11. And wherever they occur in such contexts they signify the expiation of sins. So the law prescribed: If a soul shall sin, etc. (so the Septuagint translators render it) he shall offer for the sin which he has sinned a young bullock, etc., Lev. 4:2–3, where [ὑπὲρ] is the same as [propter] "because of", or [ἀντὶ] "instead of". For no other reason is a sacrifice for sin called a sacrifice of sin, that is, offered to expiate sin for and because of sin. How Christ, as a propitiatory victim, expiated our sins is shown by the very nature of such a victim. For we have demonstrated at length elsewhere that every propitiatory victim expiated, by a vicarious punishment undergone, the sin for which or because of which it was slain. Therefore, although [ὑπὲρ], where it is used of the sins for which or because of which Christ died, does not denote substitution in the place or stead of another (for Christ's death was substituted in the place of the sinner, not of the sin, since sins cannot die or suffer penalties, but sinners can), but rather the impelling and final cause of Christ's death, nevertheless Christ's vicarious death and satisfaction are demonstrated just as solidly from this. For he who dies, moved by the sins of another and to this end, that he may expiate those sins in the manner in which sins are customarily expiated by sacrifices for sin, dies in the place and stead of the other sinner, whose sins his vicarious victim expiates. Nor does it stand in the way that, just as Christ laid down his life [ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν] "for us," we too are similarly commanded to lay down our lives [ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀδελφῶν] "for the brethren," 1 John 3:16, and that St. Paul is said to have suffered [ὑπὲρ] "for the Colossians," Col. 1:24. Neither can we satisfy the justice of God in the place of the brethren, nor did St. Paul satisfy for the Colossians. For we are not commanded simply to die for the brethren as Christ died for us; rather, we are to be so ready that we do not hesitate to pour out our life for their good, or, if the glory of God requires it, even in their place, just as Christ did not hesitate to give his soul and to give a ransom for many, Matt. 20:28. St. Paul testifies that this was proper to him alone, as the one Mediator, 1 Tim. 2:6. For the example it is enough that there is a general similarity, even though there is a difference in the specific mode, which is sometimes mentioned in order to denote the matter more certainly. Thus St. Peter, 1 Pet. 2:19ff., urges patience in afflictions, which we suffer though innocent, by the example of Christ.

units.la: patientiam in afflictionibus, quas insontes patimur, urget. Satis hoc erat ad comparationem; sed additur, v.21. Christum passum esse ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν pro nobis, quod non ad comparationem, sed ad rem ipsam, hoc est, passionem Christi, cujus modus ipsi proprius erat, pertinet. Alias frustra Paulus quæreret: An Paulus ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν pro vobis crucifixus est? 1.Cor.I.13. Poterat enim & ipse pro Ecclesia crucifigi, sicut se pati pro Colossensibus, puta ædificandis, dixit, Col.I.24. & postea magno Ecclesiæ bono ipse gladio percussus, Petrus crucifixus est. Sed eo modo, quo Christus crucifigi, pœnas vice nostra ferendo, nec Paulus, nec alius quisquam potuit. Vox ergo illa ὑπὲρ pro de Christi morte usurpata peculiare quid denotat, quod nemini mortalium communicari potest. Posset autem, si mortis Christi utilitas gradu tantum, non etiam fine proprio à morte Apostolorum segregaretur.
units.tr: patience in afflictions, which we suffer though innocent. That was enough for the comparison; but he adds, v. 21, that Christ suffered [ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν] "for us," and this pertains not to the comparison but to the thing itself, that is, to Christ's passion, whose mode was proper to him. Otherwise Paul would ask in vain: Was Paul crucified for you [ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν]? 1 Cor. 1:13. For Paul too could have been crucified for the Church, just as he said he suffered for the Colossians, that is, for their edification, Col. 1:24; and later Peter was crucified, after being struck with the sword for the great good of the Church. But no one, neither Paul nor any other, could be crucified in the way Christ was crucified, by bearing penalties in our place. So that word [ὑπὲρ], used of Christ's death, denotes something peculiar which cannot be communicated to any mortal. It could, however, be separated from the death of the Apostles only if the benefit of Christ's death differed merely in degree, and not also in its own proper end.

units.la: LXXI.
units.tr: LXXI.

units.la: Sed omni exceptione majus est, quòd S.Paulus τὸ ὑπὲρ & ἀντὶ tanquam ἱσοδυναμοῦντα ponit, dicens, Christum se ipsum dedisse ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων, pretium ἀντὶ & ὑπὲρ vice omnium, & pro omnibus, 1.Tim.II.6. Et alibi: Christus venit, ut daret animam suam λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν pretium vice multorum, Matth.XX.28. Marc.X.45. Quoties autem ea particula personis accommodatur; unius in locum alterius succession notat. Sic Archelaus in Judæa regnasse dicitur ἀντὶ Ἡρώδου τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ vice Herodis patris sui, hoc est, successisse in Regnum patris sui, Matth.II.22. Et Petrus jubetur staterem dare ἀντὶ pro se & Christo, ibid.XVII.27. quia ipse unus in ea actione duorum vicem sustinebat. Neque aliter apud profanos Scriptores εἰς ἀντὶ πολλῶν, & similia. Etiam in rebus particula ea commutationem significat. Velut cùm dicitur reddi κακὸν ἀντὶ κακοῦ malum pro malo, 1.Pet.III.9. Rom.XII.7. ὀφθαλμὸς ἀντὶ ὀφθαλμοῦ, ὀδοὺς ἀντὶ ὀδόντος oculus pro oculo, dens pro dente, Matth.V.38. ὄφις ἀντὶ ἰχθύος serpens pro pisce, Luc.XI.11. τὰ πρωτοτόκια ἀντὶ βρώσεως μιᾶς primogenituræ jus pro uno cibo, Hebr.XII.16. Miserum Sotini heic plane constricti κρησφύγετον est, fatentis equidem ἀντὶ commutationem significare; at regerentis, ubi de redemptione agitur, locum esse isti præpositioni ἀντὶ, licèt captivus, puta à prædonibus, nihil pro redemptione debeat. Non enim ex voce ἀντὶ directè solutionem inferimus: sed inde colligimus, vice nostra Christum mortuum, hoc est, nisi Christus mortuus esset, nos fuisse moriturōs, & mortuo eo nos mortuos censeri, neque æterna morte morituros ipsos esse. Nam vox ἀντὶ juncta personæ, & verbo δῶναι requirit, ut persona in Genitivo indicata idem in genere aut specie datura fuerit; quod nunc aliuṡ dedit. Neque refert, jurénè id detur, ut in nexo ob debitum, an injuria; ut in capto à prædonibus. Sed hoc posito, futurum scilicet, ut nos morte afficeremur, nisi Christus mortuus esset; solutio deinde ex rei ipsius natura facilè colligitur. Nam vel injuria morte afficiendi fuimus; vel jure. At non injuria, quia mortem commeriti sumus. Ergo jure; Si jure, eramus igitur mortis debitores. Ab hoc mortis debito Christus nos liberavit aliquid dando. Dare autem aliquid, ut per id ipsum alter à debito liberetur, est solvere, vel satisfacere. Ergo locutio illa, δοῦναι ψυχὴν ἀντὶ πολλῶν dare animam pro multis, vel vice multorum, commutationem veram, non metaphoricam sonat.
units.tr: But more than any objection, St Paul treats τὸ ὑπὲρ and ἀντὶ as equivalent when he says that Christ gave himself as an ἀντίλυτρον [ransom in exchange] ὑπὲρ πάντων, a price in the place of and on behalf of all, 1 Tim. 2:6. And elsewhere: Christ came to give his soul λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν [a ransom in place of many], that is, a price in the stead of many, Matt. 20:28; Mark 10:45. Whenever that particle is applied to persons, it denotes one person succeeding into the place of another. So Archelaus is said to have reigned in Judea ἀντὶ Ἡρώδου τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ [in place of Herod his father], that is, to have succeeded to his father's kingdom, Matt. 2:22. And Peter is ordered to pay the tax ἀντὶ [for] himself and Christ, ibid. 17:27, because he alone, in that transaction, stood in the place of both. Nor do the profane writers use it otherwise: εἰς ἀντὶ πολλῶν and similar phrases. In things, too, the particle signifies exchange. Thus when it is said that evil is to be returned κακὸν ἀντὶ κακοῦ [evil for evil], "not evil for evil," 1 Pet. 3:9; Rom. XII.7; ὀφθαλμὸς ἀντὶ ὀφθαλμοῦ, ὀδοὺς ἀντὶ ὀδόντος [eye for eye, tooth for tooth], Matt. 5:38; ὄφις ἀντὶ ἰχθύος [a serpent for a fish], Luke 11:11; τὰ πρωτοτόκια ἀντὶ βρώσεως μιᾶς [birthright for one meal], Heb. 12:16. The wretched refuge of Socinus, who is here plainly cornered, is a miserable one. He admits that ἀντὶ signifies exchange, but replies that where redemption is concerned this preposition has its place even when a captive, say one taken by pirates, owes nothing for his ransom. We do not, however, infer the payment directly from the word ἀντὶ. We gather from it that Christ died in our place, that is, that unless Christ had died we would have been going to die, and that, with him dead, we are reckoned as dead and are not to die the eternal death. For the word ἀντὶ, joined to a person and to the verb δῶναι [to give], requires that the person named in the genitive would have given the same thing in kind or species; but this one gave something else. It makes no difference whether this is given by right, as in a debt, or by wrong, as with one captured by pirates. But granting this, namely that we would have been put to death unless Christ had died, the answer is then easily drawn from the nature of the thing itself. For either we were to be put to death by wrong, or by right. But not by wrong, since we had deserved death. Therefore by right. If by right, then we were debtors of death. From this debt of death Christ freed us by giving something. But to give something so that by that very act another is freed from debt is to pay or to satisfy. Therefore that expression, δοῦναι ψυχὴν ἀντὶ πολλῶν [to give his soul in place of many], or "to give his life for many," or "in the stead of many," means a true exchange, not a metaphorical one.

units.la: LXXII. Insuper & hoc veritatem satisfactionis Christi valide probat, quod Christus ex ligno suspensus pro nobis κατάρᾶ execratio factus est. Nam Dei ipsius vox est: קללת אלהים תלוי Maledictio Dei suspensus est, Deut. XXI.23. Unde Christum, quippe ex ligno suspensum, maledictionem factum esse, & quidem pro nobis, atque sic nos emisse, ut liberi essemus ab execratione, S. Paulus colligit, dicens: Christus nos emit, ut liberi essemus ab execratione Legis, dum pro nobis execratio factus est. Scriptum enim est: Maledictus omnis, qui pendet in ligno, Gal.III.13. Cum ergo, ex sententia Legis Dei, omnis homo, ex ligno suspensus, ne justis quidem exceptis (nam etiam sanctissimi poterant σκολοπίζεσθαι, πυραμιζεσθαι, σαυρίζεσθαι) ceu reus quodammodo peccati, ferens reatum vel typicum (uti suspen-li in V.T. quem typum alibi expositum) vel verum, eumque vel proprium, vel alienum (qualem & verum & alienum Christus ferebat) execratio, & propter execrationem peccato incumbentem de ligno suspensus fuerit; etiam Christum de ligno suspensum κατάρᾳ execrationem factum, & quidem pro nobis, quia ipse fuit χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας sine peccato, Hebr. IV.15. adeoque pro se nulli maledictioni obnoxius; Apostolus conclusit, non argute, uti Socinus blasphemat, sed solide, & non sine ἀποδείξει πνεύματος demonstratione spiritus. Qui autem pro nobis factus est maledictio, is nostra peccata tulit; & propter peccata nostra maledictionem, hoc est, poenam mortis, quam Lex peccatori maledicens comminata est, subiit, adeoque loco nostro mortuus Divinae justitiae satisfecit, atque sic satisfaciendo a maledictione Legis liberatos & redemptos nos sibi ut Domino novo, emit. Κατάρα enim passim poenam ex Legis sanctione provenientem significat, velut; Gal.III.13. Matth.XXV.41. Et hic addita Legis mentio ἐπικατάρατον maledictum aliter accipi vetat, imprimis cum ἐπικατάρατον τῷ Θεῷ maledictum Deo, hoc est, poenae a Deo irrogatae, & quidem ignominiosissimae obnoxium. Hoc est quod S. Petrus dixit: Qui (Christus) peccata nostra ipse pertulit in corpore suo super lignum, ut peccatis mortui justitiae vivamus, cujus livore sanati sumus, 1.Pet.II.24. Dilutum est illud Socini, quod Christus nostri causa in quandam Legis execrationem incidens, nos interea a vera Legis execratione liberaverit. Nam quaedam illa execratio quid aliud est, quam peccati quaedam poena; & peccati quaedam poena pro nobis tolerata quid aliud est, quam liberatio a vera execratione & morte aeterna. Neque minus dilutum est illud Crellii, quod Christus morte sua, ceu magno impendio, doctrinam ac foedus novum, quod nobiscum Dei nomine pepigit, & in quo remissio peccatorum gratuita promittitur, sanciens pro nobis maledictio factus sit. Christus enim maledictio pro nobis factus non simpliciter morte sua novam Legislationem & novum foedus, in quo remissio peccatorum sine satisfactione promitteretur, sanxit, sed ad maledictionem auferendam hoc quod passus est, ut Sponsor passus est. Ideo mortem aditurus dixit; Principem hujus mundi (Diabolum) venire, mortem sibi irrogaturum, Joh.XIV.30. innuens, se iponsione sua in manum & ditionem Diaboli habentis potestatem mortis, & jam jam sibi calcaneum contriturī, venisse. Mors ergo Christi a κατάρᾳ maledictione, potestate Diaboli & peccato provenit. Si per Legislationem novam maledictio aboleri potuisset, frustra Christus mortuus esset. Si enim ad fidem novae Legislationi faciendam miraculo opus fuit, potuit alio quovis signo, & melius etiam per resuscitationem alicujus de peccatoribus Legislatio confirmari, & promissioni fides fieri. Denique nec Christus venit ad novam promissionem proferendam, sed ad veterem, multis modis confirmatam, praestandam venit.
units.tr: LXXII. Moreover, this also strongly proves the truth of Christ's satisfaction, that Christ, hanged on a tree, was made a curse for us. For it is the very word of God: קללת אלהים תלוי [qillelat elohim talui; "the curse of God is the one hanged"], "he who is hanged is accursed of God," Deut. 21:23. Hence St Paul draws the conclusion that Christ, being hanged on a tree, was made a curse, and indeed for us, and so redeemed us that we might be free from the curse; he says: "Christ redeemed us, that we might be free from the curse of the Law, being made a curse for us. For it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree," Gal. 3:13. Since, then, by the sentence of God's Law, every man hanged on a tree, even the just not excepted (for even the most holy could be impaled, crucified, or hanged on a stake), is in a certain way as a guilty party of sin, bearing guilt, whether typical (as the hanging in the Old Testament, which we have explained elsewhere as a type) or real, and that either his own or another's (and Christ bore both real and another's), and is hanged on the tree because of the curse that rests upon sin, so too Christ, hanged on a tree, was made a curse, and indeed for us, because he himself was χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας [without sin], Heb. 4:15, and so in himself liable to no curse. The Apostle concluded this, not cleverly, as Socinus blasphemously says, but soundly, and not without the ἀπόδειξις πνεύματος [demonstration of the Spirit]. He who was made a curse for us bore our sins; and because of our sins he underwent the curse, that is, the penalty of death, which the Law threatens against the sinner who is accursed; and so, dying in our place, he satisfied divine justice, and thus, by satisfying, he redeemed us, freed from the curse of the Law, and acquired us for himself as a new Lord. For κατάρα [curse] everywhere signifies the penalty arising from the sanction of the Law, as in Gal. 3:13; Matt. 25:41. And here the mention of the Law added to ἐπικατάρατον [accursed] forbids it to be taken otherwise, especially since it is ἐπικατάρατον τῷ Θεῷ [accursed of God], that is, subject to a penalty inflicted by God, and indeed the most disgraceful kind. This is what St Peter said: "He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that we, dead to sins, might live to righteousness; by whose stripes you were healed," 1 Pet. 2:24. The objection of Socinus is refuted, namely that Christ, falling for our sake under a certain curse of the Law, meanwhile freed us from the true curse of the Law. For what is that certain curse but a certain penalty for sin? And what is a certain penalty for sin borne for us but deliverance from the true curse and from eternal death? No less refuted is the saying of Crellius, that Christ, made a curse for us, by his death, as at great cost, ratified the doctrine and the new covenant which he made with us in God's name, and in which the free remission of sins is promised. For Christ, made a curse for us, did not simply by his death ratify a new legislation and a new covenant in which remission of sins would be promised without satisfaction; rather, he suffered what he suffered in order to remove the curse, as a Surety suffers. Therefore, about to die, he said that the Prince of this world (the Devil) was coming, who would bring about his death, John 14:30, indicating that he had come, having put himself under surety into the hand and power of the Devil, who held the power of death, and who was just about to bruise his heel. The death of Christ therefore arose from the curse, the power of the Devil and sin. If the curse could have been abolished through a new legislation, Christ would have died in vain. For if a miracle was needed to make the new legislation credible, another sign could have served, and better still, the legislation might have been confirmed, and faith in the promise produced, through the raising of one of the sinners. Finally, Christ did not come to proclaim a new promise, but to fulfil the old one, which had been confirmed in many ways.

units.la: LXXIII. Dein & omnis typorum veterum & sacrificiorum inprimis schola satisfactioni Christi attestatur. Inter typos Agnus (peccatoris hieroglyphicon, Esaj.LIII.6. 1.Pet.II, 25.) ferens peccatum, Joh.I.29. Serpens exaltatus, in quo nihil nisi mendacium & dolus, vel saltem imputatio peccati & maledictionis spectari potest, ibid.III.14. eminent. Ipse Sacerdos, Christi typus, adolens partem cibi ipsius, qui pro corpore substituebatur, ferre peccatum populi dicebatur, Levit.X.17. & victimas piaculares inprimis vicariam poenam eorum, pro quibus substituebantur, sustinentes, Christi corpus adumbrasse Apostolus, Heb.X.1-5. ex Psal.XL.7.8.9. docet: atque nos supra, Loc.XV.65.66. coll. cum §27. fusius comprobavimus. Cumque & Agnus & Serpens, & victimae vices aliorum gerentes, peccata eorum, quorum vicem gerebant, gestaverint & expiaverint, vel in rei veritate, vel in typo Christum verum Agnum, Serpentem, victimam figurante gestaverint & expiaverint oportet. At non in rei veritate, quia peccatum ad Christum usque in mundo manst, neque actu expiatum est. Ab Adamo enim ad Legem peccatum fuit in mundo, Rom. V.13 Si enim in mundo non fuisset, & ante Mosen expiatum fuisset, Lex peccatum nondum expiatum commemorans, accusans & damnans, post promissionem subintrare non potuisset, ibid.IV.15.V.20. Gal.III.10.19.22.
