At neque a Mose ad Christum usque peccatum abolitum fuisse, satis constat, tum quia Lex, sive ministerium condemnationis omni tempore auditum est: tum quia Lex subintravit propter transgressiones accusandas potius quam piandas, cum nihil consummaverit, Hebr.VII.19. tum quia sacrificia & oblationes, per quas commemoratio peccati facta est, usque & usque frequentatae sunt: tum quia eadem sacrificia ad expiationem peccati idonea non fuerunt, uti Loc.XV.63. latius demonstravimus. Ergo in Christo, vero illo Agno, Serpente & victima figurante, demum peccata gestarint & expiarint oportet. In sola enim morte Christi, ceu vera & perfecta victima est ἄφεσις perfecta, solida & consummata peccati remissio & ἀθέτησις aboli-tio, Hebr.IX.29. ut peccati fidelium commemoratio amplius fieri, & chirographum exigi non posset. Usus enim sacrificiorum & figurarum omnium fuit χειρόγραφον adversus eos, qui iis utebantur, Col.II.14. tandiu videlicet, quandiu Veritatem satisfactionis Christi illud quoque valide probat, quod Christus ex ligno suspensus pro nobis execratio factus dicitur. Omnis typorum veterum, & sacrificiorum inprimis schola satisfactionis Christi asseruit. diu fuit ἀσθένεια transgressio nondum per idoneum sacrificium deleta.
units.tr: LXXIII. Next, the whole school of the old types and sacrifices, above all, bears witness to Christ's satisfaction. Among the types stand out the Lamb (the hieroglyph of the sinner, Isa. 53:6; 1 Pet. 2:25), bearing the sin, John 1:29; the serpent lifted up, in which nothing but deceit and guile, or at least the imputation of sin and curse, can be seen, John 3:14. The priest himself, a type of Christ, burning a part of the food which was substituted for the body, was said to bear the sin of the people, Lev. 10:17; and the sin-offerings, above all those bearing the vicarious punishment of those for whom they were substituted, the Apostle teaches prefigured the body of Christ, Heb. 10:1-5, from Ps. 40:7-9; and we have demonstrated this more fully above, Loc. XV.65, 66, compared with §27. And since both the Lamb and the Serpent, and the victims which bore the places of others, bore and expiated the sins of those whose place they bore, they must have borne and expiated them either in the reality or in the type, the true Lamb, Serpent and victim being foreshadowed in Christ. But not in the reality, because sin remained in the world until Christ and was not actually expiated. For from Adam to the Law sin was in the world, Rom. 5:13. For if it had not been in the world, and had been expiated before Moses, the Law, recalling, accusing and condemning sin not yet expiated, could not have entered in after the promise, ibid. 4:15; 5:20; Gal. 3:10, 19, 22. But that sin was not abolished from Moses to Christ is quite clear: both because the Law, or the ministry of condemnation, was heard at all times; and because the Law entered in because of transgressions to be accused rather than atoned for, since it made nothing perfect, Heb. 7:19; and because the sacrifices and offerings, through which the remembrance of sin was made, were repeated again and again; and because those same sacrifices were not fit for the expiation of sin, as we have shown more fully at Loc. XV.63. Therefore the sins must finally have been borne and expiated in Christ, the true Lamb, Serpent and victim foreshadowed. For in the death of Christ alone, as the true and perfect victim, there is ἄφεσις [remission], perfect, solid and complete remission of sin, and ἀθέτησις [abolition], Heb. 9:26, so that the remembrance of the sins of believers could no longer be made, and the handwriting could not be demanded. For the use of sacrifices and all types was a χειρόγραφον [handwriting] against those who used them, Col. 2:14, namely for as long as the transgression had not yet been wiped out through a fitting sacrifice. This also strongly proves the truth of Christ's satisfaction, that Christ, hanged on a tree, is said to have been made a curse for us. The whole school of the old types and sacrifices, above all, asserted the satisfaction of Christ. It was a weakness for as long as the transgression had not yet been wiped out through a fitting sacrifice.

units.la: LXXIV. Denique sublata satisfactione Christi vicaria horrendarum absurditatum syrma ex parte Dei, rei, Servatoris & nostri consequitur. Ex parte Dei, tum quia frustra is legem promulgasset, eique comminationem adjunxisset, cum nec qui observaret, nec qui transgressorem ejus puniret, existeret: tum quia Dei sanctitas & puritas per communionem cum peccatore non expiato mirum in modum collutulata fuisset: tum quia ejus mortem peccatori comminantis sapientia & veracitas non parum nutasset. Verbo, Deus plane sic se abnegasset. Ex parte Rei, quia satisfactione sublata in illo decantato adeo Redemptionis opere non plus Christus praestitisset, quam quod justus aliquis Aristides, vel temperatus Socrates, vel rigidus Baptista, vel Thaumaturgus Apostolus, vel callinicus Martyr aliquis praestare potuit. Nam eodem modo etiam hi aliena Dei potentia ex morte resuscitari, & immortalitati hominibus conferendae eo modo fidem facere potuerunt, atque Christus potuit; cum resuscitatio talis nullam in resuscitando virtutem, omnem in resuscitante Deo ponat, & nemo non ab eodem resuscitari potuerit. Cur enim resuscitatio Petri aut Pauli, aut Martyris, aut alterius justi cuiuspiam non eandem vim persuadendi immortalitatem, siquidem vestigia eorum calcemus, habeat, quam ipsius Christi? Cum quicquid per merum & solitarium hominem agitur, non magis hujus, quam alterius ope & ministerio peragi necesse sit. Homo enim hominem a consortio operis non excludit. Ex parte Servatoris, qui si pro peccatis nostris Deo in solidum non satisfecit, multum certe sudavit, at parum promovit, chirographum delevit, at debitum non expunxit, morte, ceu stipendio peccati, multatus est, at apocham nullam consecutus est. Ex parte Nostri, cum sub peccato venundati, nondum interveniente satisfactionis pretio, a corpore mortis hujus liberati non simus, nec ulla fiducia coram throno gratiae comparere valeamus cum justitia Dei, & Deus ipse judex non-dum placatus torvis oculis peccatorem aspiciat.
units.tr: LXXIV. Finally, if Christ's vicarious satisfaction is removed, a train of horrible absurdities follows, on the part of God, of the work, of our Saviour, and of ourselves. On the part of God: because he would have promulgated the law in vain and attached a threat to it, when there would be neither anyone who kept it nor anyone who punished its transgressor; because the holiness and purity of God would have been wonderfully sullied by fellowship with an unexpiated sinner; and because his wisdom and truthfulness, in threatening the sinner with death, would have wavered not a little. In a word, God would thus have denied himself. On the part of the work: because, with satisfaction removed, Christ in that much-vaunted work of redemption would have achieved no more than a just man such as Aristides, or a temperate Socrates, or a stern Baptist, or a wonder-working apostle, or some glorious martyr could achieve. For these men too could have been raised from the dead by the power of another, and could have given men assurance of immortality in the same way as Christ; since such a resurrection ascribes no power to the one raised but all power to the God who raises him, and anyone at all could have been raised by him. For why should the resurrection of Peter, or Paul, or a martyr, or any other just man not have the same force to persuade us of immortality, provided we tread in their footsteps, as the resurrection of Christ himself? For whatever is done by a mere solitary man must be done no more by his help and ministry than by another's; a man does not exclude another man from partnership in the work. On the part of the Saviour: who, if he did not fully satisfy God for our sins, certainly sweated much but accomplished little; he blotted out the handwriting but did not cancel the debt; he was punished with death, as the wages of sin, but obtained no receipt. On the part of ourselves: since, sold under sin, and no price of satisfaction having yet intervened, we are not freed from this body of death, nor can we have any confidence to stand before the throne of grace with the justice of God, while God himself, the judge not yet appeased, looks on the sinner with stern eyes.

units.la: LXXV. Satisfactionem Christi, ceu salutis nostrae ἀσφάλειαν, uti Athanasius vocat, & uti veteres alii appellant, fidei anchoram, spei asylum, charitatis normam, religiose semper Ecclesia orthodoxa amplexa est; Gnosticos, Valentinianos Sabellianos, Samosathenianos, Arianos Christi merito & satisfactioni iniquiores refutavit, & infami haereseos stigmate notavit. Sed quod liberato ab impuro spiritu accidit, ut rediret hostis septem nequioribus spiritibus stipatus, Matth. XII. 43. fierentque adeo novissima pejora prioribus, id hic quoque accidit, Diabolo, dormientibus vigilibus, zizania sua seminante. Nam seculo XII. ingruentibus Sophistarum tenebris apud Gallos homo versutus & multifaria eruditione praeditus Petrus Abaillardus satisfactionem Christi una cum prisci haereticis impie & sacrilege convellere visus est, quo nomine a Bernhardo & synchronis, Samsone Archiepiscopo Rhemensi, Gaufrido Catalaunensi, Aloiso Atrebatensi apud Innocentium II. ceu
units.tr: LXXV. The satisfaction of Christ, as the security of our salvation [ἀσφάλεια], as Athanasius calls it, and as other ancient writers call it, the anchor of faith, the refuge of hope, the rule of love, has always been devoutly embraced by the orthodox Church; and she has refuted the Gnostics, the Valentinians, the Sabellians, the Samosatenes, and the Arians, who were rightly more hostile to the person and satisfaction of Christ, and has branded them with the infamous stigma of heresy. But what happened to the man freed from an unclean spirit, that the enemy returned, accompanied by seven worse spirits (Matt. 12:43), and so the last state became worse than the first, has happened here too, while the devil, when the watchmen slept, sowed his tares. For in the twelfth century, when the darkness of the Sophists was closing in, among the Gauls Peter Abelard, a crafty man endowed with varied learning, seemed to assail the satisfaction of Christ impiously and sacrilegiously, together with the ancient heretics; for this he was denounced to Innocent II as the author of a new heresy by Bernard and his contemporaries, Samson, archbishop of Reims, Geoffrey of Châlons, and Aloisius of Arras.

units.la: novae haereseos author, delatus est. Nihilominus scripta apologia palam professus est, quod solus Filius Dei incarnatus sit, ut nos a servitute peccati, & jugo Diaboli liberaret, & supremae aditum vitae morte sua nobis reseraret. Vel igitur resipuit, vel, pro temporum illorum caligine, qua paulo ingenio & doctrina caeteris praestantes, ceu alienis a fide traduci solebant, falsa ei sententia a malevolis impacta est. Superiore demum seculo qui haeretici Deitatem Christi, iidem satisfactionem ejusdem oppugnarunt, prae caeteris autem consultius & animosius Faustus Socinus, qui libris tribus de Christo Servatore contra Gallum Covetum scriptis satisfactionem Christi γυμνὴ κεφαλὴ oppugnavit, & morti Christi alios longe fines, quam satisfactionem pro peccatis nostris, seu persolutionem poenarum peccatis nostris debitarum, tribuit. Nam remissionem peccatorum plane gratuitam cum asseruisset, ne nihil Christo & morti ejus in remissionis peccatorum & salutis nostrae negotio tribuere, videretur, cum Scriptura nihil non, imo σωτηρίαν εἰς τὸ παντελὲς salvationem perfectam & aeternam, Hebr. VII. 25. ei tribuat; quatuor ob causas Christum mortuum esse confinxit, puta ut morte sua tum praeconio remissionis peccatorum testimonium perhiberet: tum jus donandae remissionis peccatorum consequeretur: tum exemplum patientiae & obedientiae nobis praeberet: tum nobis id ipsum persuadendam requiritur, fidem scilicet; sive, ut Socinus explicat, spem consequendae aeternae vitae. Principalem vero mortis Christi finem, satisfactionem, qua summota fines illi in nihilum recidunt, ceu impossibilem sic exibilavit, ut clarissima Scripturae eam in rem testimonia per inusitatos tropos explicare sas sibi esse putaverit. Sic enim de Christo Servat. lib. III. 6. loquitur: Neque satis admirari possum, quid iis in mentem venerit, qui primi nobis istam satisfactionem fabricarunt; cum ea, quae fieri non posse aperte constat, Divinis etiam oraculis ea facta fuisse in specie diserte attestantibus, nequaquam admittantur; & iccirco sacra verba in alium sensum, quam ipsa sonant, per inusitatos etiam tropos, quandoque etiam explicantur. Ego quidem etiamsi non semel, sed saepe id in sacris monimentis scriptum extaret, non idcirco tamen ita rem prorsus se habere crederem, ut vos opinamini. Cum enim id omnino fieri non possit, non secus atque in multis aliis Scripturae testimoniis, und cum caeteris omnibus facio, aliqua, quae minus incommoda videretur, interpretatione adhibita eum sensum ex ejusmodi verbis elicerem, qui & sibi ipsi constaret, & perpetuo ejusdem Scripturae tenori non adversaretur. Quibus verbis ulcus & gangraena Theologiae Socinianae plane nudatur, rationis humanae cristas sic erigentis, ut quicquid illi fieri non posse videtur, abnegari, & clarissima Scripturae testimonia diserte id confirmantia per inusitatos tropos, & adhibitas minus incommodas explicationes in alium sensum detorqueri possint, monstrum horrendum infandae haereseos & stultae praesumptionis!
units.tr: Nevertheless, in a written apology he openly professed that the Son of God alone was incarnate, so that he might free us from the slavery of sin and the yoke of the devil, and by his death open to us the way to supreme life. Either, therefore, he repented, or, because of the darkness of those times, when men who excelled others a little in talent and learning were wont to be branded as alien to the faith, the false opinion was fastened upon him by malicious men. In the last century, those heretics who attacked the deity of Christ also assailed his satisfaction; and among them Faustus Socinus, more shrewdly and boldly than the rest, attacked the satisfaction of Christ, "bare-headed," in three books written against Gallus Coveus on Christ the Saviour, and assigned to the death of Christ far different ends than the satisfaction for our sins, or the payment of the penalties owed for our sins. For, having asserted that the forgiveness of sins is wholly gratuitous, lest he seem to assign nothing to Christ and his death in the business of the remission of sins and our salvation, when Scripture ascribes to him not only salvation but "perfect and eternal salvation" [σωτηρία εἰς τὸ παντελές] (Heb. 7:25), he contrived that Christ died for four reasons: namely, that by his death he might bear witness to the proclamation of the remission of sins; that he might acquire the right to grant the remission of sins; that he might set before us an example of patience and obedience; and that he might persuade us of the very thing that is required, namely faith, or, as Socinus explains, the hope of obtaining eternal life. But the principal end of Christ's death, satisfaction, by the removal of which these other ends fall to nothing, he so hissed off as impossible, that he thought the clearest testimonies of Scripture on this matter had to be explained by unusual tropes. For he speaks thus about Christ the Saviour, book III, chapter 6: "Nor can I sufficiently wonder what came into the minds of those who first fabricated for us that satisfaction, since it is clearly impossible, and such things are by no means admitted even though the divine oracles expressly attest that they were done in fact; and therefore the sacred words are explained in a sense other than they sound, sometimes even by unusual tropes." I, indeed, even if this were written in the sacred records not once but often, would not therefore believe that the matter stands altogether as you suppose. For since it cannot possibly be so, I, as in many other testimonies of Scripture, and with all the others, by applying some interpretation which seems less inconvenient, elicit from such words that sense which both agrees with itself and does not oppose the constant tenor of the same Scripture. By these words the ulcer and gangrene of Socinian theology is plainly laid bare, which raises the crests of human reason in such a way that whatever seems to it impossible is denied, and the clearest testimonies of Scripture expressly confirming it can be twisted into another sense by unusual tropes and explanations applied as less inconvenient: a horrible monster of unspeakable heresy and foolish presumption!

units.la: LXXVI. Sed fines illi, quos morti Christi Socinus aptavit, satisfactionis ejusdem basi subducta ad remissionem peccatorum & salutem peccatoris nihil omnino profliunt. Primus
units.tr: LXXVI. But those ends which Socinus assigned to the death of Christ, once the foundation of its satisfaction is withdrawn, contribute absolutely nothing to the forgiveness of sins and the salvation of the sinner. The first

units.la: p
units.tr: p

units.la: enim ille finis, quo mors Christi praeconio remissionis peccatorum testimonium perhibere statuitur, eandem remissionis peccatorum effectum faciens (omnis enim testis re, de qua testatur, posterior est) aperte refragatur Scripturae, quae mortem & sanguinem Christi remissionis peccatorum non effectum, sed causam statuit. In Christo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ejus, remissionem peccatorum, Ephes.I.7. Col.I.14. Sanguis Jesu Christi, Filii ejus, purificat nos ab omni peccato, 1.Joh.I.7. Sine sanguinis effusione nulla peccatorum remissio est, Hebr.IX.22. Tum Martyres eadem ratione sanguinem fudisse in remissionem peccatorum, & nos per ipsorum sanguinem remissionem peccatorum consequi posse dici posset. Sed reclamat Scriptura, & privilegium hoc Christo eximium facit. Neque etiam testatio de doctrina & remissione peccatorum mortem Christi flagitavit, cum miracula sufficere potuerint. Nusquam tamen miraculis, sed uni soliqueque morti Christi effectus hic tribuitur; quod per illam habeamus remissionem peccatorum. Par ratio est finis Secundi, quod Christus sua morte jus donandae remissionis peccatorum consecutus sit. Nam ipse Socinus asserens, quod Christus in terris vivens hoc jus habuerit & exercuerit, finem hunc evertit. Quod enim meum est, id amplius meum fieri non potest. Neq; haec Christi potestas ad poenas duntaxat temporales averruncandas valuisset. Nam Christus dicens: Ut sciatis, quod potestatem habeat Filius hominis in terra remittendi peccata, dicit Paralytico: Surgens tolle lectum tuum & vade in domum tuam, Matth.IX.6. morborum sanationem signum juris remittendi peccata facit, quia qui effectum peccatorum tollit, idem causam tollere censetur; & verba illa, ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς in terra non effectum restringunt, quasi poenas tantum hujus vitae Christus sustulerit, sed actionis locum ἐμφανικῶς, uti etiam alibi, ibid. XVIII.18. denotant. Hoc ergo Christus voluit, sibi quantumvis in terris agenti, jus tamen illud adeo eximium ac coeleste competere: neque aliud v.8. mirabatur populus, quam quod jus tantum hominibus (hoc est κατ' ἐναλλαγὴν uni ex hominibus) datum esset. Ipse etiam Christus paralytico prius peccata remisit, quam ejus paralysin curavit, & temporalem poenam sustulit. Praeterea Scripturae modum connexionis inter mortem & remissionem vocibus ἱλασμὸς placaminis, expiationis, ἀπολυτρώσεως redemptionis per pretium explicant, quae ad jus donandae veniae sine satisfactione aptari nequeunt. Tertius finis, quod in Christi morte exemplum patientiae & obedientiae nobis propositum sit, non ad remissionem peccatorum, sed ad sanctificationem & gloriae aeternae consecutionem pertinet; & sic finem mortis Christi secundarium explicat, ut principalem non tollat. Mors enim Christi non tantum ὑπόδειγμα exemplar patientiae, sed etiam λύτρον pretium redemptionis, & causa remissionis peccatorum est. Quartus denique finis, ut mors Christi nobis fidem, seu spem vitae aeternae consequendae, quae ad obtinendam remissionem peccatorum requiritur, persuadeat, plane alienus est. Quomodo enim mors adeo cruenta hominis innocentissimi per se ad hoc valeret, ut nobis persuadeat, sanctè viventibus summa gaudia a Deo parata esse ? Commenti hujus absurditatem videns Socinus ait, mortem Christi hoc quidem non efficere, sed resurrectionem ejus ex mortuis, & quae resurrectionem eam consecuta sunt; mortem autem praecedere debuisse. Sed hoc si vellet Scriptura, resurrectioni ex mortuis, seu potius evectioni in Coelos, & sessioni ad dextram Dei, non morti & sanguini remissionem peccatorum tam saepe, & verbis tam significantibus tribuisset.
units.tr: end, namely that the death of Christ bears witness to the proclamation of the remission of sins, makes the effect of remission of sins the same (for every witness is subsequent to the thing to which he testifies), and so clearly contradicts Scripture, which sets the death and blood of Christ down not as the effect of the remission of sins but as its cause. "In Christ we have redemption through his blood, the remission of sins" (Eph. 1:7; Col. 1:14). "The blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7). "Without shedding of blood there is no remission of sins" (Heb. 9:22). By the same reasoning it could be said that the martyrs shed their blood for the remission of sins, and that we obtain the remission of sins through their blood. But Scripture protests, and makes this privilege peculiar to Christ. Nor did the testimony concerning doctrine and the remission of sins require the death of Christ, since miracles could have sufficed. Yet this effect is nowhere attributed to miracles, but to the death of Christ alone, that through it we have the remission of sins. The reasoning is the same for the second end, that Christ "by his death acquired the right to grant the remission of sins." For Socinus himself, while asserting that Christ had and exercised this right while living on earth, overturns this end. For what is mine can no longer be made more mine. Nor could this power of Christ have availed merely to avert temporal punishments. For when Christ says, "That you may know that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins, he says to the paralytic, 'Rise, take up your bed, and go home'" (Matt. 9:6), the healing of diseases is made a sign of the right to forgive sins, because he who removes the effect of sins is deemed to remove their cause; and the words "on earth" [ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] do not restrict the effect, as if Christ had removed only the punishments of this life, but indicate the place of the action "in a manner of speaking" [ἐμφανικῶς], as also elsewhere (ibid. 18:18). Christ therefore wished that this so exalted and heavenly right belonged to him, though he was acting on earth; nor did the people marvel at anything else in verse 8 than that such a right had been given "to men" (that is, by exchange [κατ' ἐναλλαγήν], to one of men). Christ himself also forgave the paralytic's sins before he cured his paralysis and removed the temporal punishment. Moreover, the words "propitiation" [ἱλασμός], "expiation," and "redemption by a price" [ἀπολύτρωσις] by which Scripture explains the manner of connection between death and remission cannot be adapted to a right to grant pardon without satisfaction. The third end, that in the death of Christ an example of patience and obedience has been set before us, pertains not to the remission of sins but to sanctification and the attainment of eternal glory; and thus it explains the secondary end of Christ's death in such a way that it does not remove the principal one. For the death of Christ is not only the pattern [ὑπόδειγμα] of patience, but also the ransom [λύτρον], the price of redemption, and the cause of the remission of sins. The fourth end, finally, that the death of Christ persuades us of faith, or the hope of obtaining eternal life, which is required for obtaining the remission of sins, is wholly foreign. For how could a death so bloody, of a most innocent man, by itself avail to persuade us that the greatest joys are prepared by God for those who live holily? Seeing the absurdity of this invention, Socinus says that the death of Christ does not indeed accomplish this, but his resurrection from the dead and the things that followed the resurrection do; yet the death ought to have preceded. But if Scripture had wished this, it would not so often, and in words so significant, have ascribed the remission of sins to the resurrection from the dead, or rather to his exaltation into heaven and his sitting at the right hand of God, rather than to the death and blood.

units.la: Illa enim adeo frequens & usitata conjunctio remissionis peccatorum cum morte Christi effectum aliquem non communē, sed proprium, non longe remotum, sed propinquum indicat. Quid enim ambages istae? Remissio peccatorum non contingit nisi sanctè viventibus: Sanctimoniam vitae efficit fides & spes praemii: fidem ingenerat exemplum Christi ob vitae sanctimoniam a mortuis excitati & glorificati: excitationem illam mors antecessit: Ergo remissio peccatorum per mortem Christi obtinetur. Ita pro causa non propinquum aliquid, aut saltem modico intervallo remotum, sed longissimè ab effecto dissitum affertur. Id vero si uno in Scripturae loco fieret, forte minus mirum esset; sed toties tam obscurē, imò tam frigidè Scripturam loqui, quis sanus crediderit? Neque illud ad rem Socini facit, quod Christus resuscitatus ad nostram justificationem, Rom.IV.25. dicitur, tum quia resurrectio Christi, cum sit effectus justitiae per mortem ejus paratae, simul est testimonium justificationis credentium, & medium fidei ac regenerationis nostrae per Spiritum filiationis: tum quia jam prius Christus traditus dicitur propter peccata nostra expianda scilicet; & quod sic morti Christi separatim adscribitur, imò hoc loco non obscurē adimitur. Neque Christum ex mortuis resuscitatum esse propter justificationem nostri credere possunt, qui nos per obedientiam novorum praeceptorum justificari asserunt. Cùm ergo fines illi morti Christi à Socino assignati fallant, vel satisfactio ejusdem agnosci, vel Christus & ejusdem mors pro nobis obita abnegari debet, quod posterius hostes Deitatis & satisfactionis Christi, quae pari passu ambulant, strenuè faciunt.
units.tr: Indeed, this conjunction of the forgiveness of sins with the death of Christ, so frequent and so common, points to an effect that is not general but proper to it, and not remote but close at hand. For what are these circumlocutions? Forgiveness of sins comes only to those who live holily. Faith and the hope of reward produce holiness of life. The example of Christ, raised from the dead and glorified because of his holy life, produces faith. That raising was preceded by his death. Therefore the forgiveness of sins is obtained through the death of Christ. In this way a cause is alleged that is not close at hand, or at least not separated by a small interval, but lies far removed from the effect. If this occurred in a single passage of Scripture, it would perhaps be less surprising. But who of sound mind would believe that Scripture speaks so often, and in such an obscure, indeed such a lifeless, manner? Nor does it help Socinus that Christ is said in Romans 4:25 to have been raised again for our justification. This is so because the resurrection of Christ, being the effect of the righteousness procured by his death, is at the same time a testimony to the justification of believers and a means of faith and of our regeneration through the Spirit of adoption. It is also because Christ is said earlier to have been delivered up for our sins, that is, to make expiation for them; and so the death of Christ is ascribed to them separately, and in that very place it is not obscurely granted. Nor can those believe that Christ was raised from the dead for our justification who assert that we are justified by obedience to the new precepts. Since, then, the ends that Socinus assigns to the death of Christ are false, either his satisfaction must be acknowledged, or Christ and his death undergone for us must be denied. The latter is what the enemies of the deity and of Christ's satisfaction, which walk side by side, vigorously do.

units.la: LXXVII.
units.tr: LXXVII.

units.la: Sed satisfactionem Christi, a-junt illi, nec memorari uspiam in Scripturis; & impossibilem esse, quia poena capitalis ab uno in alterum transferri nequeat, protestante Deo, Ezech.XVIII.19.20. se innocentem pronocente nolle punire, & abominationi sibi esse, qui impium justificat, & justum condemnat, Prov.XVII.15. atque insuper unius morte vita omnium redimi non posset, nec Christus aeternam mortem, fremitum & desperationem damnatorum subiverit; & supervacaneam esse, quia Deus peccata sine satisfactione remittere potuerit, ceu absolutae potestatis dominus, & creditor, qui debitori debita, seu peccata, quae debitorum nomine veniunt, remittere potest, nulla satisfactione praevia; inprimis cùm justitia puniens ei essentialis non sit; & voluntati inprimis Dei contrariari, quia tum in V.T. peccata sine ulla satisfactione remiserit; & multò magis in N.T. quod tempus gratiae est, illa sic remittat, uti in foedere gratiae seu N.T. peccata se remissurum, Jerem. XXXI.34. &c, promisit: tum Deus nobis placatus catus.
units.tr: But they say that the satisfaction of Christ is nowhere mentioned in the Scriptures, and that it is impossible, because a capital punishment cannot be transferred from one person to another. God declares that he will not punish the innocent in place of the guilty, and that he abhors him who justifies the wicked and condemns the righteous (Ezek. 18:19–20; Prov. 17:15). Moreover, the life of all could not be redeemed by the death of one alone, nor could Christ have undergone eternal death, the gnashing and despair of the damned. They also say it is superfluous, because God could have remitted sins without satisfaction, as the lord of absolute power and as a creditor, who can remit to a debtor his debts, or sins, which go by the name of debts, with no prior satisfaction. Above all, since the justice that punishes is not essential to him. And it is contrary to the will of God above all, because in the Old Testament he forgave sins without any satisfaction, and much more in the New Testament, which is the time of grace, he remits them in this way, as he promised in the covenant of grace, or New Testament, that he would forgive sins (Jer. 31:34, etc.). Then God would be placated toward us.

units.la: {a} Argumenta satisfactionis Christi opposita proponuntur. catus nulla satisfactione & reconciliatione indiguerit: & cum remissione peccatorum ex mera gratia Dei pugnare; cùm Deus exemplo Regis illius, Matth. XVIII. 27. 35. & eo modo, quo & nos peccata proximo nostro sine satisfactione ulla remittere jubemur, Ephes. IV. 32. Matth. VI. 12. χαρίζεσθαι gratificari, hoc est, sibi aliquid adimere & suo commodo se ipsum privare tetstetur: & remissio gratuita duas has partes habeat, ut & debitor per eam omni obligatione solvatur, & creditor sibi satisfieri nolit. Hæc Achillea illa scilicet argumenta sunt, quibus à Catholicæ & verè Christianæ fidei tramite se transversum abripi Socinus, cæcæ rationis suæ potius, quàm Spiritus Dei ductum secutus, passus est. Quæ paucis nunc diluenda sunt.
units.tr: {a} The arguments opposed to Christ's satisfaction are set forth. God, already placated, would have needed no satisfaction or reconciliation. And the satisfaction conflicts with the forgiveness of sins from the mere grace of God, since God, following the example of that king (Matt. 18:27, 35), and the manner in which we too are commanded to forgive our neighbour's sins without any satisfaction (Eph. 4:32; Matt. 6:12), shows that to gratify [χαρίζεσθαι] means taking something from oneself and depriving oneself of one's own advantage. And a free remission has these two parts: the debtor is released from every obligation by it, and the creditor does not wish to be satisfied. These are indeed the Achilles' heel arguments by which Socinus, following the blind reasoning of his own mind rather than the leading of the Spirit of God, allowed himself to be dragged aside from the path of the Catholic and truly Christian faith. These arguments must now be refuted briefly.

units.la: LXXVIII. Satisfactionis equidem vocabulo illo forensi in hoc negotio Scriptura nusquam utitur. At Ecclesiam adversariorum importunitas & fallacia ea uti ad significandam voluntariam poenarum nobis debitarum persolutionem à fidejussore Christo pro nobis praestitam, coegit. Neque tamen simpliciter ἀγεχ-φῶ vox est, cùm phrasis illa ικανὸν ποιῆσαι, Marc. XV. 15. idem quod satisfacere, hoc est, tantum facere, quantum postulanti vel desideranti satis est, sonet; plane uti Act. XVII. 9. ικανὸν λαμβάνειν satis accipere ab eo, qui satis facit, notat. Et Philem. v. 19. ἐγὼ ἀποτίσω idem est, quod Ego satisfaciam, uti etiam Novella 115. habet. Sed de eo quicquid sit, in causa mortis Christi, qua Deo fieri satis debuit, abundè parium & æquivalentium vocum est: velut כפר λυτρωσις, ἀντιλυτρωσις, ἱλασμὸς, &c. Res verò ipsa longè testatissima est: uti ex iis, quæ diximus, colliguequescit.
units.tr: LXXVIII. Scripture nowhere uses that forensic word satisfaction in this matter. But the importunity and trickery of the adversaries have forced the Church to use it to signify the voluntary payment, made for us by Christ as our surety, of the penalties we owed. Nor is it simply a word of its own; the phrase ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι [to make enough] in Mark 15:15 means the same as to satisfy, that is, to do as much as is enough for one who asks or desires it. In the same way, Acts 17:9, ἱκανὸν λαμβάνειν [to take enough], means to receive sufficient security from the one who makes satisfaction. And in Philemon 19, ἐγὼ ἀποτίσω [I will repay] is the same as I will make satisfaction, as Novella 115 also has it. But whatever be the case with that, in the cause of Christ's death, by which satisfaction had to be made to God, there is an abundance of equivalent and parallel words, such as כפר [kipper], λυτρωσις [redemption], ἀντιλυτρωσις [ransom], ἱλασμὸς [propitiation], and so on. The thing itself, however, is very amply attested, as may be gathered from what we have said.

units.la: LXXIX. Impossibilitatem satisfactionis Christi ab adversariis jactatam, Dei satisfactionem decernentis, postulantis, admittentis, & Christi præstantis voluntas infringit.
units.tr: LXXIX. The will of God, which decrees, demands and accepts satisfaction, and the will of Christ, who renders it, overturns the claim of our opponents that Christ's satisfaction was impossible.

units.la: Nam quod Legi impossibile erat, id Deus fecit, mittens Filium suum in similitudine carnis peccati, & pro peccato condemnavit peccatum in carne, Rom. VIII. 3. Cùm enim Deus se obstrinxerit, quòd nolit peccatum impunitum dimittere, non impossibilis satisfactio, sed impossibilis sine satisfactione peccati condonatio fuit. Licet ergo fieri non posset, ut Deus innocentem invitum pro nocente puniat; at innocentem volentem & fidejubentem, qualis Christus fuit, veniens ultrò ad faciendam voluntatem Dei, Psal. XL. 8. 9. pro nocente puniri, nihil vetat. Sic Ruben pro Benjamine spopondit, Genes. XLII. 37. Et iponsionem quamvis ratam esse Deus voluit. Fili mi, si spoponderis pro amico tuo, complosisti alieno manu tua. Illaqueatus es verbis oris tui, captus es eloquiis oris tui, Prov. VI. 1. 2. quod non in pecuniariis duntaxat, sed etiam criminalibus causis obtinet: Licet enim vita & corpus unius non possit fieri vita & corpus alterius; tamen casus & periculum unius fieri potest alterius, intercedente vadimonii & sponsionis pacto, & consensu judicis. Quomodo vix pro justo quis moriatur; nam pro bono quis forsitan mori sustineat. Commendat autem suam charitatem erga nos Deus, quòd cùm adhuc peccatores essemus, Christus pro nobis mortuus est, Rom. V. 7. 8. In Christum enim poena peccatis nostris debita mandato speciali Patris, & voluntaria sponsione Filii Patri obsequentis translata est, Joh. X. 18. XIV. 31 Phil. II. 7. 8. Hebr. X. 6. 7. Quod ipsum non natura, non Lex, non communis consuetudo, sed Evangelium nobis revelat. Sine Lege justitia Dei (quæ est per fidem Jesu Christi pro nobis mortui) patefacta (in re & causa sua exhibita) est; cui testimonium Lex & Prophetæ perhibent, Rom. III. 21. Non ergo Deus, Ezech. XVIII. 19. 20. ajens, animam, quæ peccavit, mori, & Filium iniquitatem Patris portare non debere, sponsionem ejusmodi & vicariam mortem fieri etiam jure posse negat; neque quid in negotio redemptionis secundum Evangelium facere constituerit, edisserit, sed quid Deus secundum Legem, sive ordinariè faciat, quid item nos facere velit, docet. Idem sensus est verborum Solomonis, quòd abominatio sit Domino, qui justificat impium, & qui justum condemnat, Prov. XVII. 15. Nam hoc non obstante certè Deus justificat impium, Rom. IV. 5. & eum, qui non novit peccatum, adeóque justum, fecit peccatum, impositis ei peccatis condemnavit, 2. Cor. V. 21. & utrumque juste fine dubio, quia omnes viæ Dei rectæ sunt. Sed impium justificat non in se, sed in Filio suo justo, qui impietatem morte sua expiavit: & justum condemnavit, quia sponte libens volensque peccata nostra expianda in se suscepit, & supra lignum tulit. Pugnat cum justitia Divina peccatorem vocare justum in se, ut consideratur tanquam creatura Dei Legi irrevocabili subjecta. Sed cum eodem secundum Legem agente non pugnat, ut homo etiam peccator Filii Dei, Creatoris sui, se ipsum pro eo, ad justitiam ei impetrandam offerentis membrum & peculium fiat, ejusque hæreditatem cernat. Quin ab hac ipsa Lege & justitia proficiscitur, ut Deus talem Sacerdotem & deprecatorem exaudiat, & ei implantatum peccatorem non condemnet, sed potius justificet. Quòd porro unius morte multorum vel omnium vitam redimi non posse clamitant, communi etiam usui, quo haud raro pro uno captivo Duce vel Rege omnes captivi dimittuntur, repugnat. Sed unum pro omnibus mortuum esse, diserte S. Paulus, 2. Cor. V. 15. testatus est; & præstare, ut unus homo moriatur pro populo, & non tota gens pereat, Cajaphas, non à se ipso, se prophetans, quòd Jesus pro gente moriturus esset, dixit, Joh. XI. 50. 51. Nempe mors non hominis, sed Dei, Act. XX. 28. sed Domini gloriae, 1. Cor. II. 8. sufficiens pro vita omnium λύτρον fuit. Præterea necfieri potuit, ut Christi Sponsor justus & innocens, qui ex amore Dei & nostri mortem pro nobis oppetiit, & Deo Patri obediens fuit, æternam mortem sustineret; vel in condemnationem æternæ mortis veniret. Lex enim omnem obedientem justificat, omnem justum glorificat. Neque Deus & gloria ejus frustra quæritur, vel similis est aquæ, quam Tantalus petit, vel spectro Ixionis, sed ספיה ישראל exspectatio Israelis, Jerem. XIV. 8. audit. Non patiebatur igitur vel justitia, vel, supposito beneplacito de servando aliquo semine, Lex Dei, ut obediens sic exercitationi subjiceretur, ut non etiam obedientiæ præmium, justitiam & vitam eorum, pro quibus obedivit, consequeretur. Non ergo ad redemptionem nostram æterna mors Sponsori æquè ac damnatis in inferno exantlan
units.tr: For what was impossible for the Law, God did, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and condemning sin in the flesh for sin (Rom. 8:3). For since God has bound himself not to let sin go unpunished, the impossibility lay not in satisfaction but in forgiving sin without satisfaction. Therefore, although it could not happen that God should punish an innocent person against his will in place of a guilty one, nothing prevents an innocent person who is willing and who offers surety, as Christ was, coming of his own accord to do the will of God (Ps. 40:8, 9), from being punished in place of the guilty. So Reuben gave surety for Benjamin (Gen. 42:37), and God willed that the surety should stand: My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have struck hands with a stranger. You are snared by the words of your mouth, you are taken by the sayings of your mouth (Prov. 6:1, 2). This holds not only in monetary matters but also in criminal cases. For although the life and body of one person cannot become the life and body of another, nevertheless the risk and the peril of one can become the risk and peril of another, by the agreement of bail and suretyship and with the consent of the judge. So scarcely will anyone die for a righteous man; for perhaps someone would dare to die for a good man. But God commends his love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:7, 8). For the punishment due to our sins was transferred to Christ by a special command of the Father and by the voluntary suretyship of the Son, who obeyed the Father (John 10:18; 14:31; Phil. 2:7, 8; Heb. 10:6, 7). Not nature, not the Law, nor common custom, but the Gospel reveals this to us. Without the Law the righteousness of God has been made manifest, which is through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe, and which the Law and the Prophets bear witness to (Rom. 3:21). Therefore God, when he says in Ezekiel that the soul that sins shall die and that the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father (Ezek. 18:19, 20), does not deny that such a surety and vicarious death can also be lawful. Nor does he set out what he has decided to do in the matter of redemption according to the Gospel. He teaches only what God ordinarily does according to the Law, and likewise what he wishes us to do. The sense of Solomon's words is the same: that it is an abomination to the Lord to justify the wicked and to condemn the righteous (Prov. 17:15). For notwithstanding this, God certainly justifies the wicked (Rom. 4:5), and he made him who knew no sin to be sin, laying our sins on him, who was righteous, and condemning him (2 Cor. 5:21); and both acts are undoubtedly just, because all the ways of God are right. But he justifies the wicked not in himself but in his righteous Son, who expiated impiety by his death; and he condemned the righteous because he willingly and gladly took upon himself to expiate our sins and bore them on the cross. It is contrary to divine justice to call a sinner righteous in himself, considered as a creature of God subject to an unalterable Law. But it is not contrary to the same justice, acting according to the Law, that a sinful man should become a member and a possession of the Son of God, his Creator, who offers himself for him to obtain righteousness for him, and that he should inherit his inheritance. Indeed, it is from this very Law and justice that God hears such a priest and intercessor, and does not condemn a sinner implanted in him, but rather justifies him. Furthermore, the claim that the life of many or of all cannot be redeemed by the death of one is contrary also to common practice, by which all captives are often released for the sake of one captive leader or king. But St. Paul plainly testified that one died for all (2 Cor. 5:15); and Caiaphas, not speaking of himself, prophesied that it was expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish, and that Jesus was going to die for the nation (John 11:50, 51). Indeed, it was not the death of a man but of God (Acts 20:28), the death of the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8), that was a sufficient ransom [λύτρον] for the life of all. Moreover, it could not happen that Christ, the just and innocent Surety, who out of love for God and for us died for us, and who was obedient to God the Father, should undergo eternal death, or come into the condemnation of eternal death. For the Law justifies every obedient person and glorifies every righteous person. Nor is God and his glory sought in vain, or is he like the water that Tantalus seeks, or the phantom of Ixion; but he hears the hope [ספיה] of Israel (Jer. 14:8). Therefore neither justice nor the Law of God, given the good pleasure of preserving some seed, would allow that the one who obeyed should be subjected to the trial in such a way that he would not also obtain the reward of obedience, namely righteousness and life for those for whom he obeyed. Therefore eternal death was not to be endured by the Surety for our redemption in the same way as by the condemned in hell, since he could overcome death as God, and as the just and obedient one he ought to obtain the reward. The eternity of punishment, the gnashing of teeth and despair, belong together with the punishment of death not by reason of the judgment of God, who inflicts punishment and for whom infinite punishment suffices, whether in duration or in price, but by reason of the subject, who was merely finite and so could not pay an infinite price, and who was also corrupted, labouring under hatred of God and impatience, raging against God and despairing because he could not see an end.

units.la: Et dissolvuntur sigillatim, revelut quòd nomen satisfactionis nusquam in Scriptura exstet.
units.tr: And these objections are answered one by one, as well as the fact that the word "satisfaction" nowhere appears in Scripture.

units.la: Quòd impossibilis sit, quia pœna ab uno in alium transferri, impius justificari, unius morte omnium vita redimi non possit, & Christus æternam mortem non subierit. exantlanda fuit, quia ut Deus mortem vincere potuit, ut justus & obediens praemium consequi debuit. Æternitas vero poenae, fremitus & desperatio cum poena mortis non ratione judicis Dei, poenam irrogantis, cui poena infinita sive in duratione, sive in pretio sufficit, sed ratione subjecti tum mere finiti, quod infinitum pretium penstare non potest; tum corrupti etiam, quod odio Dei & impatientia laborans adversus Deum fremit, & exitum non cernens desperat, cohaerent.
units.tr: That it is impossible because punishment cannot be transferred from one person to another, the wicked cannot be justified, the life of all cannot be redeemed by the death of one, and Christ did not undergo eternal death, is answered as follows: Christ had to undergo eternal death in our place, so that, as God, he could overcome death, and as the just and obedient one, he ought to obtain the reward. The eternity of punishment, the gnashing of teeth and despair, belong together with the punishment of death, not by reason of the judgment of God, who inflicts punishment and for whom infinite punishment suffices, whether in duration or in price, but by reason of the subject, who was merely finite and so could not pay an infinite price, and who was also corrupted, labouring under hatred of God and impatience, raging against God and despairing because he could not see an end.

units.la: LXXX. Neque etiam supervacanea esse satisfactio Christi potuit, quam & justitia & voluntas Dei unicè postulavit. Merus enim fucus est, potestatis Divinae praetextu ejusdem justitiam in discrimen vocantium, & voluntatem abolentium. Deus noster in Coelis est, quicquid vult facit, Psal. CXV.3. Et absolutae quidem potestatis dominus Deus est, cui facere licet quicquid vult, sed non quicquid ceu se indignum, & quo ipsum abnegaret, & velut ὑποπεζύτεσθαι sub-sannari, Gal. VI.7. pateretur; non vult. At indignum Deo est, peccatum non punitum remittere, quia sic justitia ejus, & abnegata justitia Deus ipse abnegaretur. De quo in loco multa satis diximus. Potest equidem creditor pecuniae debitori remittere debitum, nulla satisfactione praestita, & ubi id fit, non id in vitio, sed in laude ponitur. Et sunt etiam peccata ὀφειλήματα debita, Matth. VI.12. ex consuetudine illa loquendi, qua peccata Hebraeis appellantur. Sumus enim debitores gratitudinis Deo praestandae non tantum propterea, quia nos fecit, sed etiam quia nos in Filios suos suscepit. Ubi vero gratitudo illa multis nominibus obstricta deficit, & ingratitudo per offensam Dei subit, etiam poenae debitores fimus, nisi Deus in Christo eam nobis condonaverit. Alia igitur debiti pecuniarii, alia poenalis ratio est. Illud remittere creditori liberum est. Hoc non aeque, saltem ei, qui non ut creditor, sed ut rector universi consideratur. Deus autem, ubi de poenis & earum inflictione agitur, proprie non, uti Socinus contendit, vel creditoris vel partis offensae, cui, qua tali, jus puniendi non est; sed rectoris κρίσιν habet. Nam & poenas infligere, aut a poenis liberare, quem punire possis, non est nisi rectoris, qua talis, primo & per se; velut in familia patris, in Republica Regis, in Universo Dei: & poena ultimum est in coactione, quae nonnisi superiori, seu supereminenti potestati convenit: & Jacobus unum esse legislatorem, qui servare & perdere possit, cap. IV.12. docet. Ad Rectorem porro etiam jus puniendi pertinet; quod tamen non est jus absoluti dominii, vel crediti, quod liberè remitti, vel non remitti possit. Nam jus absoluti dominii, & jus crediti ejus gratia, qui id jus habet, comparatum est. At jus puniendi non punientis, sed communitatis alicujus causa existit. Tum cum justitia non pugnat, de jure dominii vel crediti cedere, quia ea proprietatis natura est, ut ea uti, vel non uti liceat. At peccata quaedam, velut non resipiscentium, remittere, in rectore, etiam Deo, injustum esse, Socinus fatetur. Et in universum Abraham: An judex universae terrae non faciat judicium? Genes. XVIII.25. Accedit, quod nemo ob id justus vel injustus dicitur, quod domino suo utitur,
units.tr: LXXX. Nor could the satisfaction of Christ be superfluous, which both the justice and the will of God alone demanded. For it is a mere pretence, under the cloak of divine power, to put in jeopardy the justice of God and to abolish his will. Our God is in the heavens; whatever he wills, he does (Ps. 115:3). God is indeed the Lord of absolute power, who may do whatever he wills; but he does not will to do whatever would show himself unworthy, whatever would deny himself, and whatever would allow him to be mocked [ὑποπεζύτεσθαι] (Gal. 6:7). But it is unworthy of God to remit an unpunished sin, because thus his justice would be denied, and God himself would be denied with his justice. We have said enough about this in its place. A creditor may indeed remit a debt to a debtor for money without any satisfaction being made, and when this happens it is not put down to fault but to praise. And sins are also debts [ὀφειλήματα] (Matt. 6:12), by that manner of speaking by which sins are called debts in Hebrew. For we are debtors to God for gratitude, not only because he made us, but also because he has taken us up as his sons. But where that gratitude, bound by many ties, fails, and ingratitude arises through offence against God, we are also debtors of punishment, unless God has forgiven us this in Christ. Therefore the reason for a monetary debt is one thing and that for a penal debt another. The former a creditor is free to remit; the latter is not equally so, at least for one who is regarded not as creditor but as ruler of the universe. But God, when punishments and their infliction are at issue, does not properly have the judgment [κρίσιν] of a creditor or of the injured party, as Socinus contends, to whom, as such, there is no right to punish; he has the judgment of a ruler. For to inflict punishments, or to free someone from punishment whom you could punish, belongs only to a ruler as such, primarily and in himself: as in the household of a father, in the commonwealth of a king, in the universe of God. And punishment is the last resort in compulsion, which belongs only to a superior or supereminent power; and James teaches that there is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy (James 4:12). Moreover, the right to punish also belongs to a ruler; yet this is not a right of absolute dominion or of a credit, which can be freely remitted or not remitted. For the right of absolute dominion and the right of a creditor are established for the benefit of the one who holds that right. But the right to punish exists not for the sake of the one who punishes but for the sake of some community. Hence there is no conflict with justice in yielding a right of ownership or of a credit, because such is the nature of property that one may use it or not use it. But Socinus admits that it is unjust in a ruler, even in God, to remit certain sins, such as those of the unrepentant. And in general Abraham says: Shall not the judge of all the earth do right? (Gen. 18:25). Besides, no one is called just or unjust for using or not using what belongs to his lord: he demands a debt or does not demand it. But a ruler who does not remit punishments, but severely exacts them, is usually praised for justice, as in Rev. 16:5.

units.la: vel non utitur: creditum exigit, vel non exigit. At rector poenas non remittens, sed severe exigens, justitiae nomine laudari solet, velut Apoc. XVI.5. Neque creditorem requiri, vox debiti peccato tributa evincit, quia vox debendi non semper relationem duas inter personas, creditorem & debitorem, postulat, sed hoc unum etiam arguere potest, quod peccator reus sit debendi & solvendi poenam rectori, non ut creditori, sed ut judici. Ita bene meritis praemium debetur, nullo creditore.
units.tr: Or he does not demand it. But a ruler who does not remit punishments and exacts them strictly is usually praised for justice, as in Rev. 16.5. Nor does the word debiti, applied to sin, prove that a creditor must be involved, since the word debendi does not always require a relation between two persons, creditor and debtor. It can also prove this one thing: the sinner is guilty of owing, and of paying the penalty, to the ruler, not as to a creditor but as to a judge. So too a reward is owed to deserving deeds, with no creditor at all. ## LXXXI.

units.la: LXXXI.

Sed cùm licuerit Deo Rectori etiam Judici & Legislatori sic à Lege sua recedere, ut poenam non sonti, quod Lex requirebat, sed ex hypothesi quidem nostra fontis loco insonti, Christo videlicet infligeret; & satisfactionem propriam reo remitteret: eidem licuisse etiam satisfactionem alienam non exigere, & legem suam, quae peccatori poenam comminatur, non exercere, colligunt. Praeposterum est, quod vim objectionis hujus declinaturi nonnulli in substitutione vadis in locum rei relaxationem quandam legis, seu dispensationem, qua legis manentis obligatio circa personas, quibus poenam Lex comminata est, utpote arbitraria & positiva, sublata fit, confinxerunt. Quae causae quaedam non obscura desertio est. Si enim relaxata Lex poenalis, quia in alium poena translata est, nihil obstat, quo minus relaxari, imo & aboleri, ne poena peccatum sequatur, potuerit. Non enim magis quoad peccatorem, quam quoad peccatum, quoad unam, quam quoad alteram partem relaxari, atque ita in universum aboleri potuit. Quis enim relaxationis hujus modum finemque statuet? Et annon sic Christus Legem solvisset potius quam implevisset? Neque parum etiam Legis relaxatio de ejusdem authoritate delibat. Non ergo in translatione poenae in Christum Sponsorem Legis relaxatio statui, sed ejusdem executio agnosci debet; quia cùm Christus in poena ferenda vicem nostram subiverit, non à nobis separatus & divulsus, sed nobiscum, ceu frater fratri vindex, nos ceu Abrahae femen assumens, pueris sibi datis, caro & sanguis, carnem & sanguinem nostrum proximè participans, nobis ceu carni & sanguini suo, & sanctificans iis, qui sanctificantur, qui utrique ἐξ ἑνὸς ex uno sunt, Hebr. II.11-16. ceu caput corpori, membra ejus, ex carne & ossibus ejus, v. 30. Vitis palmiti, Joh. XV.1.2. Sponsus sponsae, & conjux conjugi, qui una caro sunt, Ephes. V.29. &c. arctissimè conjunctus, quicquid ille fecit & passus est salutis nostrae causa, nos ceu ἓν unum cum ipso fecisse & passi esse censemur. Judicamus hoc, quòd si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, igitur omnes mortui sunt, 2. Cor. V.15. Et συμφυτοι γεγοναμεν complantati facti sumus similitudine mortis ejus, Rom. VI.5. Neque de nihilo est, quòd Christus se offerens Deo victimam dixit: Ἐγὼ ἐν αὐτοῖς. Ego in iis sum, Joh. XVII.23. & S. Paulus dixit: Χριστῷ συνεσταυρωμαι una cum Christo crucifixus sum. Vivo autem non amplius ego, sed vivit in me Christus, Gal. II.20. Si ergo solvisse censetur, qui per alium solvit, & quod quis per alium facit ipse facere dicitur; multò magis solvisse, legi satisfecisse, mortui ipsi κεῖνοντται judicantur, pro quibus solvit, satisfecit, mortuus est Christus, arctè adeò cum iis conconjunctus & velut σωσωματωθεὶς concorporatus, conglutinatus, ut inde etiam Ecclesia Χριστοῦ Christi nomine veniat, 1.Cor.XII.12. Christi ergo obedientia & mors, nostra obedientia & mors est. Ille in nobis est, & nos in ipso. Ille nostra dedecora & mala in se suscepit; nos ejus ornamenta & bona nostra facimus. In ipso poenam peccati sustinuimus; in ipso Legis justitiam implevimus, à peccatis absolvimur, justi & haeredes vitae pronuntiamur. A quo vero? A Deo, ut justo, Legislatore, judice, non contra, sed juxta Legem, quae aeterna, immutabilis & irrevocabilis est. Neque forte Moses rigidior est Deo ipso, vel Lex rigidior justitia Dei, quae licet debitum exigat a debitore ipso, tamen cum is solvendo non fit, sponsorem, qui ejus loco solvat, non abnuit, & sponsionem solutionémque admittit, atque in ea acquiescit. Neque enim Deus sic Legem suam adstrinxit, ut citra ejus abolitionem gratiae locum nullum reliquerit. Et Legi in solidum satisfieri, ceu justus & verax: & gratiae locum cedere, ceu bonus & misericors voluit.
units.tr: But they argue that since God, as Ruler, Judge and Lawgiver, was free to depart from his law in such a way that he inflicted on the innocent, namely Christ, the punishment that the law demanded from the guilty (on our hypothesis, as a substitute for the source of sin), and so remitted the guilty party's own satisfaction, he was also free not to require another's satisfaction, and not to enforce his law, which threatens the sinner with punishment. It is a perverse move that some, seeking to escape the force of this objection, have invented, in place of substituting a surety for the debtor, a certain relaxation or dispensation of the law, by which the obligation of the abiding law, with respect to the persons threatened with punishment, is removed as arbitrary and positive. This is a plain abandonment of the cause. For if the penal law could be relaxed because the punishment was transferred to another, nothing prevents it from being relaxed, indeed abolished, so that punishment does not follow sin. For the law could no more be relaxed as regards the sinner than as regards the sin, or as regards one party rather than the other, and so could be abolished altogether. Who would set the manner and limit of such a relaxation? And would not Christ in this way have dissolved the law rather than fulfilled it? Nor would a relaxation of the law take little away from its authority. Therefore the transfer of punishment to Christ, the surety of the law, should not be regarded as a relaxation of the law, but as its execution. For when Christ undertook our place in bearing the punishment, he did not stand apart from us and cut off, but with us, as a brother avenging a brother, assuming the seed of Abraham, "the children given to him, flesh and blood, sharing closely in our flesh and blood" (Heb. 2.11–16), as to his own flesh and blood, sanctifying those who are sanctified, who are both [ἐξ ἑνὸς] of one. He is "the head to the body, his members, of his flesh and of his bones" (v. 30); "the vine to the branch" (John 15.1, 2); "the bridegroom to the bride, and the husband to the wife, who are one flesh" (Eph. 5.29), and so on. Being most closely joined to us, whatever he did and suffered for our salvation, we are reckoned to have done and suffered as [ἓν] one with him. "We judge this, that if one died for all, then all died" (2 Cor. 5.15). And we "have been [συμφυτοι] grown together in the likeness of his death" (Rom. 6.5). It is not without reason that Christ, offering himself to God as a victim, said: "I am [in them]" (John 17.23); and Paul said: "I am [crucified] together with Christ. I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me" (Gal. 2.20). If, then, he is reckoned to have paid who pays through another, and what someone does through another is said to be done by himself, much more are those for whom Christ paid, satisfied the law and died, themselves judged to have paid, to have satisfied and to have died, since Christ is so closely joined with them and, as it were, [συσσωματωθείς] made one body with them, cemented together, so that the Church is even called by the name of Christ (1 Cor. 12.12). Therefore the obedience and death of Christ are our obedience and death. He is in us, and we in him. He took our disgraces and evils upon himself; we make his adornments and goods our own. In him we have borne the punishment of sin; in him we have fulfilled the justice of the law; we are absolved from sins, and pronounced just and heirs of life. But by whom? By God, as just Lawgiver and Judge, not against but according to the law, which is eternal, unchangeable and irrevocable. Nor is Moses perhaps harsher than God himself, or the law harsher than the justice of God, which, although it demands the debt from the debtor himself, yet when he is not able to pay, does not refuse a surety who pays in his place, and admits the promise and payment, and rests in it. For God did not so bind his law that he left no place for grace without abolishing the law. He willed that the law be fully satisfied, as just and true, and that place be given to grace, as good and merciful.

units.la: LXXXII. At nec Voluntati Dei satisfactio repugnat.
units.tr: LXXXII. Nor does satisfaction stand against the will of God.

units.la: Placuit enim Patri, pace per sanguinem crucis Christi facta, per eum sibi omnia reconciliare, Col.I.20.21. Sacrificia & holocausta pro peccato noluisti. Corpus autem adaptasti mihi, &c. Hebr. X.5.&c. Et causas voluntatis hujus Scriptura tum in justitia Dei, qua peccatores morte digni sunt, Rom.I.32. tum in Veritate, qua iisdem mortis poenam comminatus est, Genes.II.17. ostendit. Patres porro ante Christum non sine Christo & satisfactionis ejus futurae efficacia remissionem peccatorum & salutem adeptos esse, Scriptura, Act.XV.11. Hebr.IX.15. testatur, & fusius alibi demonstravimus. Eandem vero salutis & remissionis peccatorum in utroque Testamento rationem esse, eadem Scriptura, Act.XV.11. Hebr.XIII.8. confirmat. Et Novum quidem Testamentum Gratiae merae, non permixtae cum legali ira & servitute fuit; sed nonnisi in Christo & ejus merito fundatae.
units.tr: For it pleased the Father, having made peace through the blood of Christ's cross, to reconcile all things to himself through him (Col. 1:20, 21). "Sacrifice and burnt offering for sin you did not desire; but a body you have prepared for me," etc. (Heb. 10:5, etc.). Scripture shows the causes of this will both in the justice of God, by which sinners are worthy of death (Rom. 1:32), and in his truth, by which he threatened the same penalty of death (Gen. 2:17). Moreover, Scripture testifies (Acts 15:11; Heb. 9:15) that the Fathers before Christ obtained forgiveness of sins and salvation not apart from Christ and the efficacy of his future satisfaction, and we have demonstrated this more fully elsewhere. The same Scripture confirms (Acts 15:11; Heb. 13:8) that the manner of salvation and forgiveness of sins is the same in both Testaments. The New Testament was indeed a covenant of pure grace, not mingled with legal wrath and servitude, but founded only in Christ and his merit.

units.la: Gratos nos fecit in dilecto, in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ejus, remissionem peccatorum, Ephes.I.6,7. Gratia Dei erga peccatores, justitia ejus erga Christum Deo morte sua satisfacientem se exeruit. Promissionem quin etiam foederalem de remissione peccatorum sub Novo Foedere, quae Jerem.XXXI.31. &c. extat, in Christi sanguine fundatam fuisse, Apostolus locuples testis est, asserens, Christum N.T. Mediatorem esse, ut intercedente morte, ad redemptionem transgressionum sub priori Testamento, vocati aeternae haereditatis promissionem accipiant, Hebr.IX.15. Fuisse porro Deum sic peccatori placatum, ut nulla per satisfactionem pro peccato reconciliatio cum ipso necessaria fuerit, plane à Scripturis dissonum esse, supra §XXIII. ostendimus.
units.tr: "He has made us accepted in the Beloved, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins" (Eph. 1:6, 7). The grace of God toward sinners revealed itself through the justice of God toward Christ, who by his death satisfied God. That the covenant promise of forgiveness of sins under the New Covenant, which stands at Jer. 31:31, etc., was also founded on the blood of Christ, the Apostle bears full witness, asserting that Christ is the Mediator of the New Testament, so that by means of his death, for the redemption of the transgressions under the former testament, those who are called might receive the promise of the eternal inheritance (Heb. 9:15). Moreover, that God was so appeased toward the sinner that no reconciliation with him through satisfaction for sin was necessary, is plainly at odds with Scripture, as we showed above in §XXIII.

units.la: Mediator certe noster cum fuerit Christus, & Deum iratum, offensum, inimicum nobis, & nos inimicos Deo reconciliavit. Si placatus nobis fuit Deus sine Christo & sanguine ejus, quare ἱλασμὸν & ἱλασμὸν placamentum Christum fecit? Rom.III.25. 1.Joh.II.2. Quòd vero Deo καταλλάσσειν reconciliari nos, non Deum nobis, S.Paulus, 2.Cor.V,19.20. dixit, inde est, quod Deus pars offensa, homo offen-
units.tr: Since our Mediator is certainly Christ, and God was angry with us, offended, and hostile to us, he reconciled us, who were enemies, to God. If God was placated toward us without Christ and his blood, why did he make Christ a placation [ἱλαστήριον] and propitiation [ἱλασμόν] (Rom. 3:25; 1 John 2:2)? That we are reconciled to God [καταλλάσσειν], and not God to us, St Paul said (2 Cor. 5:19, 20). The reason is that God is the offended party and man the offender.

units.la: dens est. Qui vero alterum offendit, dicitur ei, quem offendit, reconciliari. Vade, prius διαλλάγηθι reconciliare fratri tuo à te offenso, Matth.V.24. Si separatur mulier καταλλαγήτω reconcilietur marito à se offenso, 1.Cor.VII.11. Sed duplex reconciliatio, 2.Cor.V.19.20. indigetatur; prior qua Deus mundum sibi reconciliavit per Christum, v.19. posterior, quam Apostoli, ut Legati Dei & Christi, urgebant apud homines, dicentes: Reconciliamini Deo, hoc est, convertimini ad Deum, v.20. Prior est reconciliatio Dei cum homine, seu conversio Dei antehac aversi ad homines, ad id instituta, ut homines peccatorum remissionem per Christum accipiant; Constitit enim in non-imputatione peccatorum, uti verba sequentia, μὴ λογιζόμενος non imputans iis peccata, & quidem propter Christum, quem hunc in finem pro nobis peccatum fecit. ibid.v.21.
units.tr: He who offends is said to be reconciled to the one he has offended. "Go first, be reconciled [διαλλάγηθι] to your brother whom you have offended" (Matt. 5:24). "If a wife is separated, let her be reconciled [καταλλαγήτω] to her husband whom she has offended" (1 Cor. 7:11). But in 2 Cor. 5:19, 20 a double reconciliation is spoken of. The first is that by which God reconciled the world to himself through Christ (v. 19). The second is that which the Apostles, as ambassadors of God and Christ, urged upon men, saying, "Be reconciled to God," that is, turn to God (v. 20). The first is the reconciliation of God with man, or the turning of God, previously averted, toward men. It was instituted so that men might receive forgiveness of sins through Christ. For it consists in the non-imputation of sins, as the following words show: "not imputing their sins to them" [μὴ λογιζόμενος], and indeed on account of Christ, "whom he made sin for us for this purpose" (ibid. v. 21).

units.la: Si igitur per reconciliationem hanc, qua Christus pro nobis peccatum factus Deo mundum reconciliavit, peccata nobis non imputantur, quae absque Christo & reconciliatione ejus nobis imputanda fuissent, ante reconciliationem eam Deum homini iratum, offensum, non placatum fuisse, manifeste sequitur.
units.tr: If therefore, through this reconciliation by which Christ, made sin for us, reconciled the world to God, sins are not imputed to us, which would have had to be imputed to us without Christ and his reconciliation, it manifestly follows that before that reconciliation God was angry with man, offended, and not placated.

units.la: LXXXIII. Denique nec Remissio peccatorum gratuita cum satisfactionis Christi veritate ἀνυπεύθυνος est.
units.tr: LXXXIII. Finally, the free forgiveness of sins is not without accountability [ἀνυπεύθυνος] if the truth of Christ's satisfaction is maintained.

units.la: Non enim simpliciter gratuita est, sed cum conditione satisfactionis, non quidem propriae, quae sola cum gratia remissionis pugnat, sed alienae, Christi Sponsoris. Nam S.Paulus cum alibi, tum Rom.III.24.25. gratiae Dei justificantis & peccata remittentis, diserte Christum ἱλαστήριον placamentum per sanguinem, & quidem ad demonstrationem justitiae, idque propter πάρεσιν dissimulationem & tolerantiam peccatorum antegressorum subordinat. Quomodo vero gratiae subordinatur, si ab eadem excluditur, evertitur? Et quae in justificatione ἔνδειξις demonstratio justitiae est, si etiam quoad Christum gratuita est? Gratuita ergo est respectu nostri, impetrata satisfactionis merito respectu Christi. Nam Deus sic est misericors, gratiosus, longanimis, multus gratia & veritate, condonans pravitatem, defectionem & peccatum, ut tamen (נקה לא ינקה) absolvendo (peccatorem) non absolvat (Christum Sponsorem) vel dissimulatione non utatur, hoc est, non simpliciter impunitatem det, vel se ipsum & justitiam suam abneget, sed remittendo peccatum revera justificet, & secundum Legem suam, quae lex immutabilis veritatis est, judicet, Exod.XXXIV.6,7. Neque obstat parabola, qua Regis, servo simpliciter debitum remittentis exemplo debita remittere jubemur, Matth.XVIII.27-35. tum quia non is scopus parabolae, ex quo solo argumentari licet, est, ut sine satisfactione peccatum a Deo remitti posse doceat, vel nos remittere debeamus, sed modo ut fratribus remittamus: tum quia non agit de judiciali processu judicem inter & reum, sed de mutuis inter conservos officiis: Judicis est punire, conservi ignoscere. Apostol vero jubens condonare invicem, sicut & Deus in Christo condonavit, Ephes.IV.32. Christi satisfactionem allegat, ut innuret, Dei in peccati condonatione non à nobis satisfactionem postulantis, sed sine merito & satisfactione propria condonantis exemplo, & propter Christum, gratis offensas fratri
units.tr: For it is not simply free, but is given with the condition of satisfaction. This is not satisfaction of one's own, which alone conflicts with the grace of remission, but of another's, Christ, the Surety. For St Paul, both elsewhere and in Rom. 3:24, 25, expressly subordinates to the grace of God, who justifies and remits sins, Christ as the placation [ἱλαστήριον] through blood. He does so for the demonstration of justice, and because of the passing over [πάρεσιν], that is, the forbearance and tolerance of earlier sins. But how is Christ subordinated to grace if he is excluded from it, and is not rather overthrown? And what is the demonstration [ἔνδειξις] of justice in justification, if it is free also with respect to Christ? It is therefore free with respect to us, but obtained by the merit of satisfaction with respect to Christ. For God is so "merciful, gracious, long-suffering, abundant in grace and truth, forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin," yet so that (נקה לא ינקה) while absolving the sinner he does not absolve (the Surety Christ), nor does he use "dissimulation," that is, he does not simply grant impunity or deny himself and his own justice. Rather, by remitting sin he truly justifies, and he judges according to his Law, which is the law of immutable truth (Exod. 34:6, 7). Nor does the parable stand in the way, in which we are commanded to forgive debts by the example of the king who simply remits the debt of his servant (Matt. 18:27–35). This is so both because that is not the scope of the parable, from which alone an argument may properly be drawn; its scope is not to teach that sin can be remitted by God without satisfaction, or that we ought to remit debts only in that way, but only that we should forgive our brothers. And it is so because it does not deal with a judicial process between judge and defendant, but with mutual duties between fellow-servants. It belongs to the judge to punish, and to the fellow-servant to forgive. But the Apostle, commanding, "forgive one another, as God in Christ also forgave you" (Eph. 4:32), appeals to Christ's satisfaction, to intimate that God, in forgiving sin, does not demand satisfaction from us. He forgives without merit and without proper satisfaction, and this is the example, and on account of Christ we freely forgive offences to our brother.

units.la: Quòd satisfactio voluntati Dei repugnet, quia is in V.T. peccata fine satisfactione remiserit, & multò magis id faciat in N.T. quod tempus gratiae est, & in quo se peccata gratis remissurum promisit; & placatus satisfactionem non amplius exigat. tribus condonandas esse. Deus offensas offendentibus χαρίζεσθαι condonat. Ergo etiam homo offensus condonare offendenti tenetur, qui multo minus jus erga fratrem, quàm Deus erga hominem habet. Sed non si homo homini offensam sine satisfactione condonare potest & debet, etiam Deus homini sine satisfactione peccata remittere potest vel debet. Diversus omnino condonationis modus est. Homo sine satisfactione condonare tenetur, quia nihil habet, propter quod ei satisfactio debeatur. At Deus nonnisi in Christo condonare potest, quia habet propter quod sine satisfactione peccata condonare non potest, nempe ut quando peccata condonat, etiam se ipsum sanctificet & justificet. Ut sit justus, & justificans ex fide Jesu, Rom.III.26. idque propterea, ut nos ei condonationem peccati attribuentes, eum glorificemus, & credentes in Christum, atque misericordiam Patris, & amorem Filii diligentes, virtutes Dei reverea-mur & prædicemus. Par ratio est Orationis Dominicæ: Remitte nobis debita nostro, ὡς sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris, Matth.VI.12. Tenendum enim est, exempla sumi non tantùm à rebus, quæ proximo genere eædem sunt, sed & ab iis, quæ aliquid similitudinis habent, præsertim cùm iis idem aliquod nomen ob similitudinem imponitur. Ita Christus vetat judicare ne ipsi judicemur, Matth.VII.1.2, ubi judicare illud prius ab altero toto genere distat, quia illud libertatis, hoc potestatis est. Eodem modo peccata remittere longè aliud est in privatis laesis, aliud in Deo & rectoribus. Huic opponitur punire: illi poenam postulare, optare, conqueri. Distant ergo intrinsecus; at extrinsecus quodammodo conveniunt. Causa impellens ad utrumque est benignitas, seu φιλανθρωπία; effectus, quòd is, qui peccavit, ab incommodo liberatur aut re ipsa, aut quantum in remittente est. Quæ convenientia sufficit, ut exemplo sua vis constet. Falsum porro est, quod Socinus ceu certissimum ponit, ad vocis χαρίζεσθαι gratificari (Eph.IV.32. Col.II.13.) significationem requiri, ut qui χαρίζεται gratificatur sibi aliquid adimat, & suo se jure vel commodo privet. Ita nobis ἐχαρίσθη in Christum credere & pro Christo pati, Phil.I.29. Christus cæco ἐχαρίζετο τὸ βλέπειν gratificabatur ut videret, Luc.VII.21. nulla proprii commodi vel juris neglecti ratione habita. Sufficit, ut ad patientem aliquid commodi, præsertim indebiti, perveniat, etiamsi agenti nihil decedat. Πρῶτον ψεῦδος est, quòd Socinus Deum condonantem vel punientem non ut rectorem vel judicem, cui in condonando vel puniendo nihil decedit vel accedit, sed ut pœnæ creditorem considerat. Denique duæ illæ partes remissionis, ut & debitor per eam ab omni obligatione liberetur, & creditor sibi satisfieri nolit; non cuivis; sed absolutæ tantùm remissioni insunt. Remissio verò peccatorum gratuita, utpote in Christo & morte ejus fundata non absoluta, sed conditionata est, utpote in qua Deus misericordiam simul & justitiam exercere volens, debitorem obligatione solvit ex misericordia, satisfieri verò sibi vult à Sponsore ejus exjustitia: quem tamen Sponsorem Deus ipse nobis ex gratia dedit.
units.tr: The objection is that satisfaction goes against the will of God, because he forgave sins without satisfaction under the Old Testament, and much more so under the New, which is the time of grace, and in which he promised that he would forgive sins freely, and, being appeased, no longer demands satisfaction. God forgives offences to offenders [χαρίζεσθαι]. Therefore the offended man is also bound to forgive the offender, who has far less right over his brother than God has over man. But, the answer runs, if a man can and ought to forgive an offence to another man without satisfaction, God too can or ought to remit sins to man without satisfaction. The manner of forgiveness is entirely different. A man is bound to forgive without satisfaction because he has nothing on account of which satisfaction is owed to him. But God can forgive only in Christ, because he has something on account of which he cannot forgive sins without satisfaction, namely that, when he forgives sins, he also sanctifies and justifies himself, "that he may be just and the justifier of him who has faith in Jesus" (Rom. 3:26). And this is so that, by attributing the forgiveness of sin to him, we may glorify him, and believing in Christ, loving the mercy of the Father and the love of the Son, we may truly revere and proclaim the virtues of God. The Lord's Prayer provides the same reasoning: "Forgive us our debts, as [ὡς] we also forgive our debtors" (Matt. 6:12). It must be held that examples are taken not only from things that are the same in the nearest genus, but also from those that have some likeness, especially when the same name is given to them on account of that likeness. Thus Christ forbids us to judge, lest we ourselves be judged (Matt. 7:1, 2), where judging in the first sense differs from the other in an entirely different genus, because the one belongs to liberty and the other to power. In the same way, to remit sins is quite different when wrongs are done to private persons and when they are done to God and to rulers. To the latter the opposite is to punish; to the former it is to demand, desire, or complain of the penalty. They differ therefore intrinsically, but extrinsically they agree in some way. The impelling cause of both is kindness, or philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία]; the effect is that the one who has sinned is freed from harm, either in fact or as far as the one forgiving is concerned. This agreement is enough for the example to hold its force. Moreover, it is false, as Socinus assumes as most certain, that the meaning of the word to show favour [χαρίζεσθαι] (Eph. 4:32; Col. 2:13) requires that the one who shows favour takes something from himself and deprives himself of his own right or advantage. Thus it was granted to us [ἐχαρίσθη] to believe in Christ and to suffer for Christ (Phil. 1:29). Christ granted [ἐχαρίζετο] to the blind man the gift of sight (Luke 7:21) with no regard to any loss of his own advantage or right. It is enough that something of advantage, especially something undue, comes to the one who suffers, even if nothing is lost to the one who acts. Socinus's first falsehood is that he considers God, in forgiving or punishing, not as ruler or judge, to whom nothing is lost or gained by forgiving or punishing, but as a creditor of the penalty. Finally, those two parts of remission, namely that the debtor is freed from every obligation through it, and that the creditor does not wish to be satisfied, belong not to every remission but only to an absolute remission.
