But the free forgiveness of sins, being founded in Christ and his death, is not absolute but conditional. In it God, wishing to exercise mercy and justice at the same time, releases the debtor from obligation out of mercy, but wishes to be satisfied by his Surety out of justice, and this Surety God himself has given to us out of grace.

units.la: LXXXIV. Quæ porro obedientia Christi
units.tr: LXXXIV. What further obedience of Christ

units.la: respectu Dei Satisfactio, eadem respectu nostri Meritum fuit. Nam Christus pro nobis Patri satisfecit, at nobis vitam meruit. In universum meritum est opus, quod mercedem consequi idoneum est. Nam mereri à μισθῷ quod λαμβάνειν, λαγχάνειν accipere, adipisci, consequi Hesychius interpretatur; proprie est opere quodam idoneo aliquid, quod μισθὸς mercedis rationem habere potest, accipere, adipisci, consequi. Potest autem opus aliquod bonum consequi, vel ex sola gratia & promissione: vel ex justitia propter ἀξίωσιν dignitatem & ἰσότητα æqualitatem operis & bonum illud, quod opus consequitur. Non illud, sed hoc meritum proprie dictum constituit. Nam nec opus illud, cui bonum promittitur, si cum bono eo commensum non habuerit (quale opus fuisset primi hominis, si legem perfectè implevisset) meritum proprie dictum est; licet meritum expacto, adeòque proprie dictum appellari soleat. Sed proprie dictum meritum unius soliusque Christi operibus, iisque non quibusvis, non naturalibus, quæ in eo natura vel sola, vel interventu voluntatis operabatur, sed liberè voluntariis & moralibus, amore Dei & proximi, usque ad mortem pro Dei gloria & salute proximi, consummatissimo, convenit. Nam omnes meriti proprie dicti conditiones iis examussim quadrant. Opera enim obedientiæ Christi & ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων ex propriis sunt, quia ἀναγκαῖα opera: & indebita, quia nonnisi à vade & Sponsore, cujus sine fidejussione nullum ὀφείλημα debitum fuit, edita: & cum bono, quod iis consecutus est, propter infinitam personæ dignitatem, commensum plenum habentia fuerunt, adeòque meriti proprie dicti & ex condigno omnes numeros impleverunt. Ideo obedientia & justitia Christi δικαίωμα hoc est, αἰτίας δικαιώσεως causæ justificationis sive justitiæ, per quam quis justus constituitur, & jus vitæ exigendæ habet; nomine venit. Sicut per unius lapsum in omnes homines in condemnationem, ὥτω ἠμὴ δι ἑνὸς δικαιώματος εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους εἰς δικαίωσιν ζωῆς; sic etiam per unius justitiæ meritum, vel causam in omnes homines in justificationem vitæ, hoc est, unius Christi meritum & obedientia unica ad justificationem vitæ omnium, qui justificantur, redundat, Rom.V.18. Christus ἀρχηγὸς τῆς σωτηρίας princeps salutis, Hebr.II.10. τελειωθεὶς ἐγένετο πᾶσιν αἴτιος σωτηρίας αἰωνίας consummatus omnibus causa salutis æternæ factus, ibid. V.9. eandem ob causam dicitur.
units.tr: With respect to God, the same obedience that is Christ's satisfaction was with respect to us his merit. For Christ satisfied the Father on our behalf, and he merited life for us. In general, a merit is a work that is fitting for obtaining a reward. The Greek word for reward [μισθῷ] comes from the verb meaning to receive [λαμβάνειν], and Hesychius explains it as to receive, to obtain, to attain [λαγχάνειν]. Properly, by some fitting work a person receives, obtains or attains something that can have the character of a reward. A good work may obtain a good either from grace and promise alone, or from justice, on account of the worth [ἀξίωσιν] and the equality [ἰσότητα] between the work and the good that the work obtains. The second kind, not the first, constitutes merit in the proper sense. A work to which a good is promised, if it has no commensurate relation to that good (such as the work of the first man would have been had he fully kept the law), is not merit in the proper sense, although it is commonly called merit by pact and so is said to be merit in the proper sense. But proper merit belongs to the works of one person only, Christ, and not to just any works: not to natural works, which in him nature performed either alone or through the will's agency, but to works that are freely voluntary and moral, most perfect in love of God and neighbour, carried through even to death for God's glory and the salvation of his neighbour. For all the conditions of proper merit fit these works exactly. The works of Christ's obedience were from his own resources [ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων], because they were necessary works [ἀναγκαῖα]; and they were not owed, because they were performed by a surety and sponsor, for whom no debt [ὀφείλημα] existed without his undertaking; and, since they had a full commensurate relation to the good which he obtained through them, on account of the infinite dignity of his person, they fulfilled every requirement of proper merit, merit ex condigno. Therefore the obedience and righteousness of Christ are called a righteous claim [δικαίωμα], that is, the cause [αἰτίας] of justification, or the righteousness by which a person is constituted just and has the right to demand life. As through one man's fall condemnation came upon all men, so the Greek is: "so also through one righteous act [δικαιώματος] came justification of life to all men" [εἰς δικαίωσιν ζωῆς]. So too, through the merit of one righteousness, the cause of justification of life flows out to all men; that is, the merit and single obedience of the one Christ flows out to the justification of life of all who are justified, Rom. 5:18. For the same reason Christ is called the author of salvation [ἀρχηγὸς τῆς σωτηρίας], Heb. 2:10, and, made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all [τελειωθεὶς ἐγένετο πᾶσιν αἴτιος σωτηρίας αἰωνίας], Heb. 5:9.

units.la: LXXXV. Licèt tamen meritum hoc non fit infinitum extensivè, quatenus non omnia bona meriti illius ambitu concludantur, cùm saltem unionem hypostaticam & visionem verbi in instanti conceptionis sibi non meruerit: infinitum tamen est intensivè, quia tantum est, ut nullo finito præmio exhauriri, vel æqualiter compensari valeat. Explenitudine ejus omnes accepimus gratiam pro gratia, Joh.I.16. Æstimari autem meriti Christi illa magnitudo & infinitas debet tum ex naturæ humanæ innocentia, sanctitate & obedientia omnimoda, quæ verum illud δικαίωμα est, cui vitam ipsa Lex addixit, Levit.XVIII.5. tum ex eminentia naturæ Christi humanæ, non per se consideratæ, sed quatenus illa cum λόγῳ unita, & consortio cum λόγῳ intimio- Obedientia Mortis Christi timiore sanctificatione plane eximia ita effulsit, ut in ipso & operationibus ejus Deus, cui placentia semper fecit, Joh. VIII.29. singulare beneplacitum habuerit, Matth. III.27. tum praeprimis ex dignitate personae ϑεανθρώπου, cujus, ceu veri Dei, sanctitas infinita est. Unde sanguis ille, quo purgamur, vocatur αἷμα τοῦ Θεοῦ sanguis Filii Dei, 1. Joh. I.7. & redempta Ecclesia sanguine Dei, Act. XX.28. & Christus Dominus gloriae crucifixus, 1. Cor. II.8. dicitur. Non potest non personae hujus dignitas multum ad obedientiae πιστὴν pretium & acceptationem ejusdem apud Deum conferre, ut sic longe plus ad meritum & acceptationem ejus fuerit unum pati, quam si totum simul genus humanum aeternam poenam subiret. Sed meriti tamen valor nec a sola obedientia, nec a sola personae obedientis dignitate, sed ab utraque, & a jure Filii, quem Deus diligit, in quo solo beneplacitum habet, & cujus gloriam quaerit, & a jure servi justi pendet, non exclusa etiam morte, in qua obedientiae coronis & consummatio fuit. Decuit enim eum, propter quem, & per quem omnia sunt, postquam multos filios in gloriam introduxit, Principem salutis, per passiones consummare, Hebr. II. 10. Amen, Amen dico vobis, nisi granum tritici cadat in terram, & moriatur, ipsum manet solum. Si vero moriatur, multum fert fructum, Joh. XII.24. Nam Filius Dei ex iis, quae passus est, didicit obedientiam. Hebr. V. 8.
units.tr: LXXXV. Although this merit is not infinite extensively, in that not all the goods are included within its compass, since at least he did not merit for himself the hypostatic union or the vision of the Word at the instant of conception, it is nevertheless infinite intensively, because it is so great that no finite reward can exhaust it or equally compensate it. From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace, John 1:16. The greatness and infinity of Christ's merit must be estimated from several things: from the innocence, holiness and complete obedience of his human nature, which is that true righteous claim to which the Law itself adjudged life, Lev. 18:5; from the eminence of Christ's human nature, considered not in itself but as united with the Word and in the closest fellowship with the Word, which shone forth with a holiness quite outstanding, so that in him and in his works God, to whom he always did what pleases him, John 8:29, had a singular good pleasure, Matt. 3:27; and above all from the dignity of the God-man [θεανθρώπου], whose holiness, as that of true God, is infinite. Hence that blood by which we are cleansed is called the blood of God, the blood of the Son of God, 1 John 1:7, and the Church redeemed with the blood of God, Acts 20:28, and Christ the Lord of glory is said to have been crucified, 1 Cor. 2:8. The dignity of this person cannot but contribute greatly to the price of his faithful obedience [πιστὴν] and to its acceptance with God, so that to suffer for him was far more to his merit and acceptance than if the whole human race together had undergone eternal punishment. But the value of the merit depends neither on the obedience alone nor on the dignity of the obedient person alone, but on both together, and on the right of the Son whom God loves, in whom alone he has good pleasure and whose glory he seeks, and on the right of the righteous servant. Death is not excluded either, for in death was the crown and completion of his obedience. For it became him, for whom and through whom all things exist, after bringing many sons into glory, to make the Prince of their salvation perfect through sufferings, Heb. 2:10. Amen, amen I say to you, unless a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it remains alone; but if it die, it bears much fruit, John 12:24. For the Son of God learned obedience from the things he suffered, Heb. 5:8.

units.la: LXXXVI. Qui satisfactionem Christi vicariam tollunt, eosdem & meritum ejusdem vicarium tollere necesse est.
units.tr: LXXXVI. Those who deny Christ's vicarious satisfaction must also deny his vicarious merit.

units.la: Nam dicis tantum gratia Ostorodus & Veidovius in Enchirid. Socin. cap. 7:3. se meritum Christi agnoscere profitentur, quatenus sua obedientia sibi gloriam & potestatem coelestem, ac consequenter nobis credentibus aeternam salutem obtinuit, ac veluti mercedem laborando comparavit, Phil. II.9. Esaj. LIII.12. sic tamen ut meritum hoc gratiae Dei non opponatur, sed subordinetur. Ubi adverbio illo consequenter, pro necessaria connexione illa, quam Scriptura docet, qua non potuit Christus sibi gloriam coelestem sua obedientia mereri, quin una Ecclesiae, quae corpus ipsius est, vitam & salutem aeternam mereretur, consequentiam futuri contingentis obtrudunt, cujus, moriente Christo, nullam determinatam veritatem, sed dubiam expectationem an facta per ipsum redivivum ex mortuis promulgatione Evangelii, mundus in ipsum crediturus esset, nec ne, fuisse contendunt. Absque illa connexione certa, qua Christus una sibi, ut capiti, & nobis, ut corpori gloriam & vitam aeternam meritus sit, opus ei non fuisset, ut obedientia sibi gloriam & potestatem coelestem obtineret, ac veluti mercedem laborando compararet, quia dives erat, 2. Cor. VIII.9. & gloriam, qua glorificatus est, apud Patrem habuit, antequam mundus esset, Joh. XVII.5. Sed meruit Christus sibi vitam & gloriam illam, qua, in communione corporis mystici, ipse aeternum beatus est, ut in se & a se membra sua aeternum justa & beata reddat. Ex quo merito proinde & vitae gloriaeque communionem cum corpore, & jus quoque reliquum corpus secum vivificandi habet; ita tamen, ut simul Christi supra ejusdem gloriae consortes praerogativa sit, qua ipse est πρωτότοκος primatum tenens in omnibus, Col. I.18. Quam in
units.tr: For Ostorodus and Veidovius, in their Enchiridion of the Socinians, chapter 7, admit that they acknowledge the merit of Christ only in so far as by his obedience he obtained for himself glory and heavenly power, and consequently eternal salvation for us who believe, and acquired it by his labour as a reward, Phil. 2.9; Isa. 53.12, yet in such a way that this merit is not set against the grace of God but made subordinate to it. In this, by the word "consequently" they (in place of the necessary connection which Scripture teaches, that Christ could not merit heavenly glory for himself by his obedience without at the same time meriting eternal life and salvation for the Church, which is his body) foist on us a consequence that depends on a future contingent event. They contend that, at Christ's death, there was no determinate truth of this kind, only an uncertain expectation of whether the world would believe in him, or not, once the gospel was published by him after he had risen from the dead. Without that certain connection, by which Christ merited glory and eternal life both for himself as head and for us as his body, there would have been no need for his obedience to obtain for himself glory and heavenly power, and to acquire them as a reward for labour, since he was rich, 2 Cor. 8.9, and had the glory which he had with the Father before the world was, John 17.5. But Christ merited for himself that life and glory by which, in communion with his mystical body, he is eternally blessed, so that he might make his members eternally righteous and blessed in himself and from himself. Hence, by this merit, he also has a share with the body in life and glory, and the right to quicken the rest of the body with himself. Yet at the same time this is a pre-eminence of Christ above his fellow-sharers in that glory, by which he is the firstborn (πρωτότοκος), holding the primacy in all things, Col. 1.18. We have said more on this matter in Locus 11.29.

units.la: rem plura Loc. XI.29. diximus. Illud quoque ὑπαλον est, quod Christi meritum gratiae Dei iidem subordinant. Cujus assertionis haec crypsis est, quod freti verbis Apostoli, asserentis Sacerdotem sicut pro populo, ita etiam pro se ipso offerre debere pro peccatis, Hebr. V.3. & Christum in diebus carnis suae precationes & intercessiones ad eum, qui ipsum ex morte salvare poterat, cum clamore valido & lachrymis obtulisse, ibid. V.7. & eidem non fuisse necesse, sicut Sacerdotibus, primo pro propriis peccatis victimas offerre, ac demum pro populi, cum hoc semel fecerit, se ipsum offerens, ibid. VII.27. Christum eximunt quidem Divinarum legum transgressionibus, at non infirmitatibus carnis, quas illic Apostolus peccata appellet, ob quae Christus sacerdotis veteris adinstar suas cum clamore valido & lachrymis supplicationes debuerit; uti ita meritum ejus gratiae non opponi, sed subordinari posset. Licet vero gratiae vocabulo laxius accepto recte etiam Calvinus Institit. II. 17.1. pronunciaverit, si quis simpliciter & per se Christum judicio Dei opponere velit, non fore locum merito, quia sine gratia quadam Christus dari & ejus meritum pro salute hominis a Deo acceptari non potuisset: tamen meritum ipsum Christi, tanta videlicet, & tantae personae obedientia, nulli gratiae seu condonationi infirmitatum subordinari, sed potius opponi debet. Unde ex Legis impletione per obedientiam Christus a Patre justificationem sibi vindicat. Prope est justificans me. Quis contendet mecum? Consistamus una. Quis adversarius meus? Accedat ad me, Esaj. L.8. Justificatus est in Spiritu, hoc est, in potentia Divinitatis suae, qua vivificatus est, 1. Tim. III.16. Si ex gratia, non ex operibus. Alias gratia non esset gratia. Si vero ex operibus, non amplius est gratia. Alias opus non esset opus, Rom. XI.6. Denique neque illud meritum Christi tollit, quod Deo satisfecisse eum statuimus, & in solutione debiti merito locus non est, quia non proprio creditori, debitum a se contractum solvendo, sed alieno, debitum pro aliis solvendo satisfecit, quali in casu satisfactio & meritum probe consistunt.
units.tr: It is also plain that those same men subordinate Christ's merit to the grace of God. The hidden point behind this assertion is this: relying on the words of the Apostle, who says that the priest must offer for his own sins as well as for the people's, Heb. 5.3, and that Christ, in the days of his flesh, offered prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears to him who could save him from death, ibid. 5.7, and that it was not necessary for him, as for the priests, first to offer sacrifices for his own sins and then for the people's, since he did this once for all when he offered himself, ibid. 7.27, they indeed exempt Christ from transgressions of the divine laws, but not from infirmities of the flesh, which the Apostle there calls sins, and for which Christ, like the priests of old, had to make supplications with strong crying and tears. In this way his merit could be made subordinate to grace, and not set against it. Yet although Calvin, taking the word "grace" more loosely, rightly declared in Institutes II.17.1: if anyone wishes to set Christ simply and by himself against the judgment of God, there is no room for merit, because without a certain grace Christ could not have been given, and his merit could not have been accepted by God for the salvation of man; nevertheless the merit of Christ itself, namely the obedience of so great a person, ought not to be made subordinate to any grace or pardon of infirmities, but rather set over against them. Hence by his obedience in fulfilling the Law, Christ claims justification for himself from the Father: He is near who justifies me. Who will contend with me? Let us stand together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me, Isa. 50.8. He was justified in the Spirit, that is, in the power of his divinity, by which he was quickened, 1 Tim. 3.16. If it is by grace, it is no longer by works; otherwise grace would not be grace. But if it is by works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work would not be work, Rom. 11.6. Finally, the satisfaction we affirm Christ made to God does not abolish that merit either, and there is no room for merit in the paying of a debt. For he did not satisfy his own creditor by paying a debt he had himself contracted, but paid a debt owed by others, on their behalf. In such a case satisfaction and merit rightly go together.

units.la: LXXXVII. Operae pretium est, sedulo ruminare, quid Christus morte sua Deo Patri satisfaciens, & pro nobis merens profecerit.
units.tr: LXXXVII. It is worth our while to ponder carefully what Christ accomplished by his death, in satisfying God the Father and in meriting for us.

units.la: Ante omnia enim Deum sanctificavit, ceu justificantem impium sine injustitia & macula. Deus Christum praestituit propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ejus, &c. ut esset ipse justus & justificans ex fide Jesu, Rom. III.25.26. Tum satisfactione praestita praeceptum fidei in Christum, & promissionem justitiae per fidem fundavit. Quia enim Pater Filium tradidit, & Filius Patri se obtulit, consequens est, tum, ut omnibus imperari possit, ut Christum unicum Salvatorem agnoscant, persuasissimumque habeant, beatos esse, quotquot ei confidunt, eum diligunt, justitiam in ipso sitiunt, & per eum pacem cum Deo faciunt, quia omnes tenentur testimonium Dei recipere, fiduciam in Christo collocare, eum quaerere & glorificare; tum ut omnes mandato huic parentes, & in Christum credentes, non pereant, sed habeant vitam aeternam, Joh. III.16. Ingens enim hoc magni amoris Dei, quo is Ecclesiam omnium gentium dilexit, pignus est, quod, sicut is Filium dedit, cujus sanguis revera erat ἡμιν πολύτιμος, quíque dignus erat, ut omnium hæres ac dominus fieret, ita effecit, ut omnium in ipsum credentium justitia & vita firmo certóque talo staret. Qui enim per fidem ipsi insiti & in eum baptizati sunt, reputantur pro mortuis, qui à peccato justificati sunt. Quotquot in Jesum Christum baptizati sumus, in mortem ejus baptizati sumus. Unà consepulti sumus cum ipso per baptismum in mortem, &c. Si complantati facti sumus similitudini mortis ejus, etiam resurrectionis erimus, &c. Qui mortuus est, justificatus est à peccato. Si mortui sumus cum Christo, cum eodem vivemus, Rom. VI. 3-9. Mortificati estis legi per corpus Christi, ibid. VII.4. Per Legem Legi mortuus sum, ut Deo vivam, Gal. II.19. Unde omnes electi viam munitam accedendi ad Deum, ostium expectationis apertum, manum porrectam ad adducendum ipsos, firmum fundamentum, in quo spem suam exaedificent, & ansam apprehendendi spem, ut expositam, Hebr. VI.18. habent. Praeterea Christus morte sua Deo satisfaciens impetravit & promeruit καταλλαγὴν reconciliationem eorum, qui ei dati sunt, & ante fuerunt ἐχθροί, ἀπεχθεῖς hostes, impii, peccatores, impotentes, filii irae, & nunc mortis Christi merito participes fiunt omnium benedictionum spiritualium in Christo, ut sint sancti & inculpati coram eo in charitate, Ephes. I.3.4. Nam propter Christi satisfactionem redemptis non imputantur peccata, 2.Cor. V.19. utpote per mortem Christi obliterata & deleta, & in carne ejus judicata. Cumque peccata iis non imputentur, eo ipso efficaciter vocantur, regenerantur, Christo per fidem inseruntur, in eo & per eum justificantur, & tandem in judicio Dei sancti & immaculati in charitate Divina comparent. Pro nemine ergo mortuus est, quin eum actu reconciliarit; nec quemquam reconciliavit, cui peccata alterius imputari possint; nec cuiquam peccata non imputat, qui non regeneretur, vocetur efficaciter, fide donetur, justificetur. Accedit, quòd satisfactio Christi praestita & credentibus libertatem ab accusatione peccati, à chirographo ipsis subcontrario, & servitute elementorum affert: & pacem gentibus conciliat: & Christum ipsum non tantùm ut Filium, sed etiam ut justum servum justificat & beat: & Filium Dei πιστὸν κτίστην fidelem creatorem, 1.Pet. IV.19. demonstrat, eique omnem gloriam virtutum Divinarum vindicat, ut eum sicut Patrem, & in ipso Patrem honoremus.
units.tr: First of all, he sanctified God, as the one who justifies the ungodly without injustice or stain: God set forth Christ as a propitiation through faith in his blood, etc., that he might himself be just and the justifier of him who has faith in Jesus, Rom. 3.25, 26. Then, by the satisfaction he rendered, he established the command of faith in Christ and the promise of righteousness through faith. For since the Father gave up the Son and the Son offered himself to the Father, it follows both that all may be commanded to acknowledge Christ as the only Saviour and to hold it as most certain that all who trust in him are blessed, who love him, who thirst for righteousness in him, and who make peace with God through him; for all are bound to receive God's testimony, to place their trust in Christ, to seek him and to glorify him. And so that all who obey this command, and believe in Christ, may not perish, but have eternal life, John 3.16. For this is a great pledge of the great love of God, by which he loved the Church of all nations: just as he gave the Son, whose blood was truly precious to us (τιμιος? [πολύτιμος] precious), and who was worthy to become heir and lord of all, so he has ensured that the righteousness and life of all who believe in him stand on a firm and sure foundation. For those who have been ingrafted into him through faith and baptized into him are reckoned as dead, who have been justified from sin. As many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death. We were buried with him by baptism into death, etc. If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection, etc. He who has died has been justified from sin. If we have died with Christ, we shall also live with him, Rom. 6.3-9. You were made dead to the Law through the body of Christ, ibid. 7.4. Through the Law I died to the Law, that I might live to God, Gal. 2.19. Hence all the elect have a fortified way of access to God, an open door of expectation, an outstretched hand to lead them, a firm foundation on which to build their hope, and a handle for laying hold of the hope set before us, Heb. 6.18. Moreover, Christ, by satisfying God through his death, obtained and merited the reconciliation (καταλλαγή) of those who were given to him, and who were formerly enemies (ἐχθροί), hated (ἀπεχθεῖς), enemies, ungodly, sinners, helpless, children of wrath; and now, by the merit of Christ's death, they become partakers of all spiritual blessings in Christ, that they may be holy and blameless before him in love, Eph. 1.3, 4. For on account of Christ's satisfaction, sins are not imputed to the redeemed, 2 Cor. 5.19, since they have been blotted out and destroyed by the death of Christ and condemned in his flesh. And since sins are not imputed to them, they are by that very fact effectually called, regenerated, ingrafted into Christ through faith, justified in him and through him, and at last appear in the judgment of God holy and spotless in divine love. Therefore he did not die for anyone without actually reconciling that person; nor did he reconcile anyone to whom the sins of another could be imputed; nor does he not impute sins to anyone who is not regenerated, effectually called, endowed with faith, and justified. Besides, the satisfaction of Christ, once rendered, brings to believers freedom from the accusation of sin, from the handwriting that stood against them, and from the bondage of the elements; it reconciles the Gentiles to peace; it justifies and blesses Christ himself not only as the Son but also as the righteous servant; and it shows the Son of God to be a faithful Creator (πιστὸν κτίστην), 1 Pet. 4.19, and vindicates to him all the glory of the divine perfections, so that we may honour him as we honour the Father, and in him the Father.

units.la: LXXXVIII.
units.tr: LXXXVIII.

units.la: Inprimis illud praemunien-dum & tenendum firmiter est, quòd Christus iis, pro quibus morte sua Deo Patri suo satisfecit, Spiritum S. & ejusdem eximium, & ad salutem unicè necessarium donum, regenerationem ad fidem meruerit & impetraverit. Hoc enim solum perfectum Salvatorem, Principem salutis αἴτιον σωτηρίας αἰωνίου causam salutis aeternae, Heb. II.10. V.9. eorum, pro quibus mortuus est, facit. absque quo fuisset, parum vel nihil morte sua profecisset, neque adeò ἡμιν pretiosus ejus sanguis fuisset. Ante omnia igitur, pro quibus morte sua Deo satisfecit, iisdem Spiritum S. adoptionis & regenerationis ad fidem causam meruit & impetravit. Nam qui proprium Filium suum pro nobis in mortem tradidit, annon cum eo omnia nobis gratificabitur? Rom. VIII.32. Ideo enim se legi subjecit, ut eos, qui sub Lege erant, redimeret, ut adoptionem filiorum acciperemus. Quia verò estis filii, emisit Deus Spiritum Filii sui in corda vestra, qui clamat, Abba Pater.
units.tr: First of all, this must be borne in mind and firmly held: Christ merited and obtained for those for whom he satisfied God the Father by his death the Holy Spirit, and his singular gift, which alone is necessary for salvation, namely regeneration unto faith. For this alone makes him the perfect Saviour, the Prince of salvation [αἴτιον σωτηρίας αἰωνίου], the cause of eternal salvation (Heb. 2.10; 5.9) for those for whom he died. Without this, his death would have profited little or nothing, and his precious blood would not have been precious to us [ἡμῖν]. Therefore, above all, for those for whom he satisfied God by his death, he merited and obtained for them the Spirit of adoption and the cause of regeneration unto faith. For he who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? (Rom. 8.32). For this reason he submitted himself to the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive the adoption of sons. And because you are sons, God sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father.

units.la: Christus iis, pro quibus mortuus est, etiam Spiritum S. regenerationem & fidem promeruit. dixit Jehova: Dabo legem meam in medio eorum, & cordi eorum inscribam eam, Jer.XXXI.31-34. Inscriptio illa legis in cor ipsa fidei & resipiscentiæ donatio est. Tum enim Lex Dei, seu Lex justitiæ, fidei cordi fidelium promissionis inscribitur, cùm fides cordi donatur, ut Christum & justitiam ejus intimè recipiant & diligant. Eodem facit promissio: Spargam super vos aquas puras & purificabimini. Ab omnibus fœditatibus vestris, & ab omnibus stercoribus vestris purificabo vos. Et dabo vobis cor novum, & spiritum novum dabo in medio vestri, & auferam cor illud lapideum ex carne vestra, & dabo vobis cor carneum. Et Spiritum meum dabo in medio vestri, ut in statutis meis ambuletis, & judicia mea observetis & faciatis-Ezech. XXXVI.25-28. Quibus verbis gemina renovationis seu regenerationis causa מים טהורים aquæ puræ, hoc est, obedientia Christi, Sponsoris & Sacerdotis nostri, sacrificium pro peccato offerentis, quam omnes ῥαντισμοὶ καὶ βαπτισμοὶ aspersiones & lotiones V. T. significarunt, aspergenda, hoc est, imputanda per fidem: & רוח Spiritus Dei, in medio populi ponendus, cui potentia & efficientia tribuitur; ut Israel in statutis & judiciis Dei ambulet. Quod paucis Christus explicavit, dicens Nicodemo: Amen, Amen dico tibi: Nisi quis genitus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest intrare in Regnum Dei, Joh.III.5. Eandem ob causam & cum Christo convivificati, conresuscitati, conlocati in supercœlestibus in Christo Jesu, Ephes. II.5.6. dicimur; quia videlicet Deus Pater Christum vivificans & in Cœlum extollens, ei ut Principi salutis per passiones consummato vivificationem ex morte peccati, adeòque regenerationem, resuscitationem & glorificationem nostri obsignavit; & vetus homo noster cum Christo crucifixus est, Rom. VI.6: quia vi crucifixionis & mortis Christi impetrata nobis est veteris hominis destructio, ne serviamus peccatis: & in circumcisione Christi nos circumcisi circumcisione, quæ non fit manibus, Col.II.11: dicimur, quia Christo sponsori circumciso, repurgatio cordis nostri per fidem obsignata est. Et vos mortuos in peccatis & præputio carnis vestræ convivificavit cum ipso, ibid. v.13. Idem Christus de se μάλα ἐμφανικῶς. Ego ἐὰν ὑψωθῶ cum elatus fuero ex terra, (crucifixus fuero, nam & crucifixio הרמה elevatio Judæis dici suevit) omnes (sine discrimine, Judæos & gentes) ἐλκύσω πρὸς ἐμαυτόν trahamad me ipsum, (efficacia justitiæ meæ, & potentia brachii mei impetrabo, promerebor, efficiam, ut veniant ad me, salutis causâ ad me confugiant, mihi confidant, in me חמדה voluptatem & delicias habeant, Hagg.II.8. Malach.III.1.) Joh. XII.32-33. Eandem denique mortis Christi ad regenerationem & fidem nostram efficaciam comprobat, quòd tum Filius præordinatus est, ut sit primogenitus inter multos fratres, Rom. VIII.29. & sibi populum peculiarem redemit, Tit. II.14. & nos liberos fecit, non tantùm à jugo Legis, sed etiam à servitute peccati & Sathanæ, Rom. VIII.34-39: tum Deus Christo ponenti animam suam משם satisfactionem promisit, quòd visurus sit Semen, Esaj. LIII.10. ubi & Seminis multiplicatio infallibile satisfactionis Christi consequens statuitur; & præsertim נפש animæ voluntati Christi λύτρον Deo proponenti, & sibi datis tradenti, Seminis novi proventus acceptus refertur: tum Christus se tradidisse, ut Ecclesiam sanctificaret, purgans illam lavacro aquæ in verbo, Ephes. V.25.26. & ut redimeret & purificaret sibi populum peculiarem, æmulum bonorum operum, Tit. II.14. dicitur: tum nos electi in Christo sumus sancti & inculpati coram ipso, adeóque filii per ipsum sola fide & regeneratione id sortiti, ut sancti & filii simus; Ephes. I.4.5. nec non servati & vocati vocatione sancta, secundum Dei propositum proprium, & gratiam, quæ data est nobis in Christo Jesu ante tempora secularia, 2.Tim. I.9. dicimur. Illa enim salvatio & vocatio sancta, quid aliud est quàm adductio ad Deum per regenerationem & fidem in Christum? Et illud ἐν Χριστῷ in Christo, in quo electi sumus; & in quo data nobis est gratia ante tempora secularia, gratiosam illam conjunctionem capitis & membrorum, Sponsoris & reorum, æterno Dei consilio factam notat, secundum illa: Quodcunque mihi dedit Pater, ad me veniet, Joh. VI.37. Hæc est voluntas Patris, ut quicquid mihi dedit, ne perdam ex eo; ibid. v. 39: Ecce ego & pueri, quos dedit mihi Deus, Hebr. II.13.
units.tr: Christ also merited for those for whom he died the Holy Spirit, regeneration and faith. The LORD said: I will put my law in the midst of them, and I will write it on their heart (Jer. 31.31-34). That writing of the law on the heart is the bestowing of faith and repentance itself. For the law of God, or the law of righteousness, is then written on the heart of believers, when faith is given to the heart, so that they inwardly receive and love Christ and his righteousness. The promise does the same: I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be clean. From all your filthiness and from all your idols will I cleanse you. A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them (Ezek. 36.25-28). In these words the twofold cause of renewal or regeneration is set forth: the clean water [מים טהורים], that is, the obedience of Christ, our Surety and Priest, offering a sacrifice for sin, which all the sprinklings and washings [ῥαντισμοὶ καὶ βαπτισμοὶ] of the Old Testament signified, is to be sprinkled, that is, imputed through faith; and the Spirit of God [רוח], to be placed in the midst of the people, to whom power and efficacy are ascribed, so that Israel may walk in the statutes and judgments of God. Christ explained this briefly when he said to Nicodemus: Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God (John 3.5). For the same reason we are said to be quickened together with Christ, raised up together, and made to sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus (Eph. 2.5-6). That is, because God the Father, quickening Christ and exalting him into heaven, sealed to him, as the Prince of salvation perfected through his sufferings, the quickening of our life from the death of sin, and so our regeneration, resurrection and glorification. And our old man has been crucified with Christ (Rom. 6.6), because by the power of the crucifixion and death of Christ the destruction of the old man has been obtained for us, so that we should no longer serve sin. And we are said to be circumcised in the circumcision of Christ, a circumcision made without hands (Col. 2.11), because the cleansing of our heart through faith has been sealed to us, Christ being our circumcised Surety. And you, being dead in your sins and the uncircumcision of your flesh, has he quickened together with him (ibid. v. 13). Christ himself spoke about himself very plainly: I, if I be lifted up from the earth [ἐὰν ὑψωθῶ] (that is, if I be crucified; for crucifixion was also commonly called lifting up [הרמה] by the Jews), will draw all men [ἐλκύσω πρὸς ἐμαυτόν], that is, Jews and Gentiles without distinction, unto myself. (By the efficacy of my righteousness and the power of my arm I will obtain, I will merit, I will bring it about that they come to me, flee to me for salvation, trust in me, and have in me their desire [חמדה] and delight; cf. Hag. 2.8; Mal. 3.1) (John 12.32-33). Finally, he confirms this efficacy of the death of Christ for our regeneration and faith by the fact that the Son was foreordained to be the firstborn among many brethren (Rom. 8.29), and redeemed to himself a peculiar people (Titus 2.14), and made us free, not only from the yoke of the law, but also from the bondage of sin and Satan (Rom. 8.34-39). Then God promised Christ, who made his soul an offering for sin [משם, satisfactio], that he shall see his seed (Isa. 53.10). Here the multiplication of the seed is established as the infallible consequence of Christ's satisfaction; and especially the new seed's yield is ascribed as acceptable to the will of Christ, who offered his soul [נפש] as a ransom [λύτρον] to God and delivered himself up for them. Then it is said that Christ gave himself up that he might sanctify the Church, cleansing it with the washing of water by the word (Eph. 5.25-26), and that he might redeem and purify for himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works (Titus 2.14). Then we are said to be chosen in Christ, holy and blameless before him, and therefore sons through him, obtaining this by faith alone and by regeneration, so that we may be holy and sons (Eph. 1.4-5); and also to be saved and called with a holy calling, according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began (2 Tim. 1.9). For what else is that salvation and holy calling than the bringing to God through regeneration and faith in Christ? And that phrase in Christ [ἐν Χριστῷ], in whom we were chosen, and in whom grace was given us before the world began, denotes the gracious union of Head and members, Surety and guilty ones, made by the eternal counsel of God, according to those words: All that the Father gives me shall come to me (John 6.37); This is the will of the Father, that of all that he has given me I should lose nothing (ibid. v. 39); Behold, I and the children whom God has given me (Heb. 2.13).

units.la: LXXXIX. Et satisfactionis & meriti Christi abnegatores Socinianos supra tetigimus. Neque multò saniores Pontificii utrumque nefariè infringunt; Nam & satisfactionem Christi temerè ita concidunt, ut factam esse pro solo peccato originali & actualibus ante Baptismum commissis, nec non post baptismalibus gravioribus, seu, uti loquuntur, mortalibus, non venialibus, & quoad reatum culpæ & pœnæ æternæ; non temporalis asserant, & pro reliquis hominES de suo satisfacere debere pronuntient: & Christum denuo in Missa quotidie creberriméque adeò occidi, crucifigi, & ad propitiationem peccatorum viventium & mortuorum offerri constituunt: & creaturis, Sanctis, ipsísque passionis atque mortis Christi instrumentis, inprimis signo crucis id tribuunt, quod solius mortis Christi est: & Christum in anima sua pœnas infernales luisse, adeóque, quod consequens inde est, ab infernalibus cruciatibus nos liberasse; inficiantur: & in templis, Missa inprimis, & ludis scenicis Christum ἀνασταυροῦν καὶ ἀναδεικνύειν denuo crucifigere & ostentui habere, Heb: VI.6. summo cum piorum scandalo & horrore; religioni nulli ducunt. Ad Meritum Christi ubi pervenitur, explosa & exsibilata imputatione justitiæ Christi, adeóque ῥαντισμῷ aspersione sanguinis Christi, hanc unam merito Christi vim relinquunt, quòd promerueris, ut homines propria justitia in Baptismo infusa, & deinceps incrementis suis augescente vitam mereantur; quasi sanguis Christi non peccata nostra expiaverit; & à mortuis operibus nos purificaverit lustraveritque; sed justitiam & merita nostra tinxerit, ut immediata vitæ causa esse possint: Quo pacto Christus nec princeps & causa salutis æternæ, nec princeps & consummator fidei esse poterit. Quæ errorum Antichristianorum monstra alibi debellamus. Deniq; Remonstrantes etiam tantùm non Christi satisfactionem & meritum nefariè abolent, asserentes, Christum mortuum esse eo fine, ut Deus Pater nobiscum de novo, sub qua vellet conditione; de remissione peccatorum & justificatione contrahendi jus haberet. Atqui stante Christi obedientia & morte
units.tr: LXXXIX. We have already touched upon the Socinians, the deniers of the satisfaction and merit of Christ. Not much more sound are the Papists, who wickedly violate both. For they rashly cut down the satisfaction of Christ, asserting that it was made only for original sin and for actual sins committed before baptism, and also for the graver sins committed after baptism, or, as they say, mortal sins, not venial ones, and only as to the guilt and the eternal punishment, not the temporal; and they pronounce that men must make satisfaction for the rest from their own resources. They also hold that Christ is daily and very frequently slain, crucified and offered again in the Mass for the propitiation of living and dead sinners; and they attribute to creatures, to the saints, and even to the instruments of Christ's passion and death, above all to the sign of the cross, what belongs to the death of Christ alone; and they deny that Christ suffered the pains of hell in his soul, and consequently (which follows from this) that he delivered us from infernal torments. And in their temples, above all in the Mass, and in stage plays, they make Christ crucified again and put to open shame [ἀνασταυροῦν καὶ ἀναδεικνύειν] (Heb. 6.6), to the great scandal and horror of the godly, and they do not regard it as irreligious. As for the merit of Christ, where they arrive at it, having exploded and hissed down the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, and thus the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, they leave this one power to the merit of Christ: that it merited for men that, with the righteousness infused in baptism and growing by their own increments, they should merit life; as if the blood of Christ had not expiated our sins, nor purified and cleansed us from dead works, but had only tinged our righteousness and merits so that they might be the immediate cause of life. By this means Christ could be neither the author and cause of eternal salvation, nor the author and finisher of faith. We elsewhere combat these monsters of Antichristian errors. Finally, the Remonstrants, too, almost wickedly abolish the satisfaction and merit of Christ, asserting that Christ died for this end only: that God the Father should have a right to enter into a new covenant with us, on whatever condition he wished, concerning the remission of sins and justification. But while the obedience and death of Christ stand...

units.la: Satisfactionis & meriti Christi abnegati reiciam Pontificii & Remonstrantes peraguntur morte unica tantùm ad justitiam perveniendi via est: neque ulla alia possibilis est: Qui verò illa via justificantur, non ex legali pacto, sed ex Testamento per modum fœderis applicato, & ex δικαιώματι ἢ νόμῳ, seu obedientia, quam Lex ut justitiam sponsoris approbare potest, eáque gratis donata & imputata. Aliter enim vel remittentur peccata actu absque fide, ut homo ad novi pacti conditionem admittatur, vel Christus remissibilitatem peccati meritus non fuerit, quippe ad quam præstatio novæ conditionis non necessaria est.
units.tr: The Papists and the Remonstrants, who deny the satisfaction and merit of Christ, reject it. Christ's death alone is the only way to righteousness, and no other way is possible. Those who are justified by that way are justified not by a legal pact but by the Testament applied by way of covenant, and by the righteous requirement [δικαίωμα] or law, that is, by the obedience which the Law can accept as the righteousness of the surety, and which is given freely and imputed. Otherwise either sins would be forgiven in fact without faith, so that a man is admitted to the condition of the new covenant, or Christ would not have merited the forgivableness of sin, since the performance of a new condition is not necessary for that.

units.la: XC. Nam dilutum oppidò est, quod iidem Remonstrantes ceu φερόνιμον quidpiam urgent, impossibile esse, ut intelligatur, quomodo Deus, satisfactione Christi posita, conditionem pœnitentiæ & fidei à peccatoribus exigere potuerit, ut per eam in gratiam cum ipso redirent, & remissionem peccatorum consequerentur. Licèt enim impossibile sit, ut post satisfactionem Christi per pœnitentiam & fidem, tanquam per opus & conditionem novi pacti legalis justificemur; tamen nec satisfactio Christi sine communione cum ipso ad justitiam prodesse nobis potuit. Communio autem cum Christo sola fide; sicut fides per regenerationem & purificationem cordis obtinetur. Cur igitur mors & satisfactio Christi nonnisi fide recepta à morte æterna liberare posset, in promptu causa est. Cùm enim lex à peccatore mortem & satisfactionem exigat, & mors & satisfactio, non à nobis, sed à Christo præstita sit, Deo mortem alienam admittenti & nobis donanti, nemini nisi illam donatam apprehendenti & per eandem veniam peccatorum & vitam æternam recipienti impertiri placuit. Hoc nempe pœnam inter vicariam & propriam fontis cujusque interest, quòd sua fontis pœna, si modò culpæ par sit, legis ad pœnam obligationem per se deleat & dissolvat. At pœna vicaria hoc non præstat, nisi gratiam ejus, qui puniendi jus habet, & vicariam pœnam admittit, impetrando. Neque impetrari Dei gratia, nisi communionem cum pœna vicaria principalis debitor habeat, potest. Sed ipsa tamen mors Christi hoc effecit & promeruit, ut fides, communionis illius vinculum, omnibus illis, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, donaretur, absque quo fuisset, mors Christi planè inutilis fuisset; quia fides non est naturæ, sed gratiæ, non quorumvis, sed electorum opus, Ephes.II.8. 2.Thess.III.2. Actor. XIII.48. nec nisi in Christo, in quo electi sumus, & in quo data nobis est gratia ante tempora secularia, Ephes.I.4. 2.Tim.I.9. donari potuit. Ex quo & illud intelligere est, mortem Christi, pœnæ vicariæ rationem habentem, cum gratia Dei ἀσύνγνων haud fuisse; quia gratia Dei factum est, ut Christus pro nobis moreretur, & ut illius mors ad peccatorum remissionem & æternam vitam nobis valeret.
units.tr: XC. For it is quite worthless what the same Remonstrants press, as if it were some piece of prudence, that it is impossible to understand how God, once Christ's satisfaction has been set forth, could require from sinners the condition of repentance and faith, so that through them they might return into grace with him and obtain the forgiveness of sins. For although it is impossible that after Christ's satisfaction we should be justified through repentance and faith, as through a work and condition of a new legal covenant, yet neither could Christ's satisfaction have profited us for righteousness without communion with him. Communion with Christ, however, is by faith alone, just as faith is obtained through regeneration and the purification of the heart. Why, then, the death and satisfaction of Christ could free from eternal death only when received by faith, the cause is ready at hand. For since the law demands death and satisfaction from the sinner, and since the death and satisfaction were performed not by us but by Christ, it pleased God, who admits another's death and grants it to us, to impart it to no one except him who lays hold of it as given and by it receives the pardon of sins and eternal life. Indeed, the difference between a vicarious penalty and one's own penalty is this: one's own penalty, if it is equal to the guilt, by itself cancels and dissolves the obligation of the law to punishment. A vicarious penalty does not do this unless, by entreaty, it wins the favour of him who has the right to punish and who admits the vicarious penalty. Nor can God's favour be obtained unless the principal debtor has communion with the vicarious penalty. But the death of Christ itself brought this about and merited that faith, the bond of that communion, should be given to all those for whom Christ died; without faith the death of Christ would have been altogether useless, because faith is not of nature but of grace, and is the work not of everyone but of the elect (Eph. 2:8; 2 Thess. 3:2; Acts 13:48), and it could be given only in Christ, "in whom we were chosen and in whom grace was given us before the ages" (Eph. 1:4; 2 Tim. 1:9). From this too it is to be understood that the death of Christ, which has the character of a vicarious penalty, was not [ἀσύνγνων] at odds with the grace of God; for it was by the grace of God that Christ died for us, and that his death might avail us for the forgiveness of sins and eternal life.

units.la: XCI. Pro quibus Christus satisfecit, pro iisdem se obtulit & mortuus est, eorum peccata tulit, & eosdem pretiosò sanguine suo sibi emit & redemit. Hæ enim Scripturæ parallelæ phrases sunt. Hi autem non sunt vel Angeli, quorum ἐπιλήπτωρ assertor & redemptor non est, Hebr. II.16. nec homines quivis, sed σπέρμα Ἀβραὰμ Semen Abrahæ, non carnale illud, sed spirituale & promissionis, quod est ex fide, Gal.III.7.8, atque illud ex circumcisione & præputio, Rom.IV.11-18. Omnésque adeò fideles & electi. Licèt enim ad nonnullos etiam pereuntes, externè vocatos, ex morte Christi & consequente eandem prædicatione Evangelii beneficia quædam redundent, sed ἀναπλήρωσιν & incrementum damnationis potiùs, quàm salutem eorum tendentia, Hebr. VI.4.5.2.Pet.II.20. tamen non pro iis, sed pro solis electis Christus animam suam ⸗ satisfactionis pretium & sacrificium posuit. pro solis iis se obtulit, solos eos sanguinis sui pretio redemit. Nam Christi mortem pœnæ vicariæ rationem habuisse, supra ostendimus. Pro quibus ergo mortuus est, eorum vice & loco mortuus est; & quorum vice mortuus est, illi ipsi mortui censentur. Judicamus, quòd si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, omnes mortui sint, 2.Cor.V.15. Quod ex iis etiam locis, quibus mors Christi ἀντίλυτρον, ἀντίλυτρον, ἰλασμός, καταλλαγὴ pro iis, pro quibus mortuus est; appellatur, liquet. Nam voces eæ substitutionem in locum alterius notant. Pro quibus Christus se victimam, satisfactionem, pretium redemptionis, placamentum Deo dedit, obtulit, illorum loco & vice talem se dedit, obtulit. Perinde igitur est, ac si ipsi pro peccatis suis mortui Deo se victimam, placamentum, redemptionis suæ pretium obtulisset. Tales autem, qui in judicio Dei habentur, illi ceu in Christo pro se moriente mortui, expiati à peccatis absolvuntur, justitiam & vitam consequuntur. Qui enim mortuus est (in se, vel in Christo) is à peccato justificatus est, Rom. VI.7. Et qui à peccato justificatus est, is salvatur. Quos enim Deus justificavit, eos glorificavit, ibid. VIII.30. Accedit, quòd pro quibus Christus mortuus est, pro iisdem morte eadem sua Spiritum S. regenerationem & fidem, per quam cum Christo uniuntur & communionem habent, meruit & impetravit. Qui enim Filium suum pro nobis omnibus in mortem tradidit, quomodo non cum eo omnia nobis gratificaretur? ibid. v.32. Non gratificatur πάντα omnia, qui hoc unum gratificatur, ut liberè volenti meritum Christi applicari possit: sed qui præcipua & unicè salutaria, per quæ homo actu salvatur, donat, quæ inter Spiritus S. gratia regenerans & fides, quæ Christum apprehendit & sibi applicat, locum quam maximè habet. Et Christi satisfactionem & meritum præcipuè ad donationem Spiritus S. regenerationis & fidei valere, supra §LXXXVIII. luculenter demonstravimus. Cùm ergo Christus nec pro omnibus victimam se Deo obtulerit, nec eo moriente omnes & singuli mortui & à peccato justificati censeantur: nec omnes & singuli Spiritus S. regenerationis & fidei, quam Christus iis, pro quibus mortuus est, promeruit, participes sint, evidens est, non pro omnibus & singulis, sed pro solis iis, qui justificantur, regenerantur, salvantur, mortuum esse. Ideo Scripturæ non pro omnibus & singulis, certè non pro reprobis, sed pro solis electis & fidelibus mortuum esse, haud obscurè docent. Reprobi enim ad Semen serpentis, non Mulieris, Christum pertinent, Genes.III.15. Sicut verò Christus, Semen illud Mulieris, se ipsum pro Serpente non impendit, ita nec pro ejus semine. Parens enim & partus ejusdem generis sunt. Et justus ille servus in cognitione sui non omnes, sed דבר multos justificat, Esaj.LIII.11. Salvator est non omnium, sed populi & corporis sui, Matth. 1.21. Ephes. V.23.25. animam suam λυτρον pretium redemptionis dedit ἀντὶ πολλῶν pro multis, Matth. XX.28. sanguinem suum ad remissionem peccatorum effudit ἐπὶ πολλῶν pro multis, ibid.XXVI.28. Ecclesiam, hoc est, vocatos, electos, fideles proprio sanguine suo acquisivit, Act.XX.28. redemptionem fecit τῷ λαῷ αὐτῆς populo suo, Luc.I.68. animam suam posuit pro ovibus suis, Joh.X.11. ut similia innumera, quibus id ipsum vel expresse, vel dianoetice asseritur, omittam. Quae sufficientiae & efficaciae meriti & mortis Christi, ut pro omnibus sufficienter, pro paucis efficaciter, mortuus dicatur, distinctio minime diluit. Licet enim meritum mortis Christi propter ἀπειρίας pretii dignitatem & infinitatem, sufficiens in se sit pro omnibus, & impendi possit omnibus, quibus Deus impendi vult, non tamen ex consilio Dei, & intentione Christi morientis pro aliis sic sufficit, ut pro iis impensa dicatur, at nihil efficiat; pro aliis & sufficit & efficit, tum quia potentialis ejusmodi sufficientia non id praestat, ut mors Christi actu pro hoc vel illo impendatur, sicut λύτρα cujusvis valor, qualis & quantuscunque ille est, non tamen actu ad hoc sufficit, ut impendatur pro quovis, sed tantum ut impendatur pro eo, cui impendi dominus λύτρα vult: tum quia aliàs Christi mors etiam pro daemonibus oppetita dici eadem ratione posset, cum propter pretii infinitatem per se aequè pro illorum, atque pro reproborum salute suffecerit: tum quia aliàs Deus consilio & intentione sua eorum respectu, apud quos nihil efficit, excideret. Deus enim Filium in mortem tradens, & Filius mortem oppetens non aliud quàm redemptionem, liberationem, salutem eorum, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, propositum sibi habere potuit. Sufficientia verò meriti salutem non producens & applicatio secundum potentiam, quae in actum exit, qualis quaeso sufficientia, qualis applicatio est? Possibilis, inquies. Sed quid hoc ad rem? Quale beneficium, qualis sufficientia & applicatio est meriti Christi, promereri alicui id, quod ad salutem sufficit, at eam non efficit, & cujus actualis applicatio hominis levissimi desultoria voluntate impediri potest? Cum tamen applicatio & efficacia meriti Christi à fide pendeat, eandem fidem merito Christi acceptam referendam esse, jam liquidò probavimus. Vel igitur nihil Christus morte sua pro quoquam effecit: vel simul fidem, & cum fide applicationem & efficaciam meruit. Quis medicum ferat medicamentum promittentem, quod applicari possit, at ipso etiam praescio & volente applicetur nunquam? Quantò levius est, tale quid affirmare de amore Dei Filium dantis, & de morte Christi, beneficio tali, quo nullum aliud in mundo pretiosius extat? Si mors Christi ut victima pro omnibus oppetita est, (nam victimae & poenae vicariae rationem habuit, neque aliter pro quoquam, quàm ut victima oppeti potuit) tum omnes actu expiat. Victima enim acceptata expiat, remissionem peccatorum & dationem seminis per regenerationem ejusque justificationem & glorificationem impetrat, sive certò dandam obtinet, juxta illud, Psal.LXVIII.19. Ascendisti, cepisti dona accepisti in hominibus.
units.tr: XCI. For whom Christ made satisfaction, for those same he offered himself and died; he bore their sins, and he bought and redeemed those same with his precious blood for himself. For these are phrases in Scripture that are parallel. These, however, are not angels, whose help-giver [ἐπιλήπτωρ] or redeemer Christ is not (Heb. 2:16), nor are they any men at all, but the seed of Abraham [σπέρμα Ἀβραάμ], not the fleshly seed but the spiritual seed of promise, which is of faith (Gal. 3:7, 8), and that which is of circumcision and of uncircumcision (Rom. 4:11–18). Thus they are all the faithful and elect. For although some benefits of Christ's death, and of the preaching of the Gospel that follows it, also fall upon some who perish, who are called outwardly, yet these benefits tend rather to the filling up and increase of their damnation than to their salvation (Heb. 6:4, 5; 2 Pet. 2:20); nevertheless Christ laid down his soul as the price of satisfaction and as a sacrifice not for those but for the elect alone. He offered himself for these alone; he redeemed these alone with the price of his blood. For we have shown above that the death of Christ had the character of a vicarious penalty. Therefore, for whom he died, in their stead and place he died; and those in whose stead he died are themselves regarded as having died. We judge that if one died for all, then all have died (2 Cor. 5:15). This is clear also from those passages in which the death of Christ is called [ἀντίλυτρον], [ἀντίλυτρον], [ἰλασμός], [καταλλαγή] for those for whom he died. For those words denote substitution in the place of another. For those for whom Christ gave and offered himself as victim, satisfaction, the price of redemption, and propitiation to God, in their place and stead he gave and offered himself. It is therefore just as if they themselves had offered themselves to God as victim, propitiation, and the price of their redemption for their own sins. Those, moreover, who are reckoned in the judgment of God, as dead in Christ dying for them, are absolved from sins expiated, and obtain righteousness and life. For "he who has died is justified from sin" (Rom. 6:7), and he who is justified from sin is saved; "for whom God justified, them he also glorified" (ibid. 8:30). Besides, for whom Christ died, by that same death he merited and obtained for them the Holy Spirit, regeneration and faith, through which they are united with Christ and have communion with him. "For he who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how will he not with him also freely give us all things?" (ibid. 8:32). He does not give "all things" who grants only this one thing, that the merit of Christ may be applied to whoever freely wishes it; rather he gives the principal and uniquely saving things through which a man is actually saved, among which the regenerating grace of the Holy Spirit and faith, which lays hold of Christ and applies him to oneself, hold by far the first place. And we have clearly demonstrated above, at §88, that the satisfaction and merit of Christ avail chiefly for the bestowal of the Holy Spirit, of regeneration and of faith. Since therefore Christ did not offer himself as victim to God for all, and since not all and each are reckoned dead and justified from sin by his dying, and since not all and each partake of the Holy Spirit, of regeneration and of faith, which Christ merited for those for whom he died, it is evident that he died not for all and each, but for those alone who are justified, regenerated and saved. Therefore the Scriptures teach plainly that he died not for all and each, certainly not for the reprobate, but for the elect and faithful alone. For the reprobate belong to Christ as the "seed of the serpent," not of the "woman" (Gen. 3:15). Just as Christ, that seed of the woman, did not offer himself for the serpent, so neither did he for its seed; for parent and offspring are of the same kind. And that "righteous servant," "by the knowledge of himself," does not justify all but "many" [רַבִּים] (Isa. 53:11). He is Saviour not of all but of his "people" and his "body" (Matt. 1:21; Eph. 5:23, 25); he gave "his soul a ransom" [λύτρον] "for many" [ἀντὶ πολλῶν] (Matt. 20:28); he poured out "his blood for the forgiveness of sins" [ἐπὶ πολλῶν] "for many" (ibid. 26:28); he "acquired the Church," that is, those called, elect and faithful, "with his own blood" (Acts 20:28); he "made redemption for" [τῷ λαῷ αὐτῆς] "his people" (Luke 1:68); he "laid down his soul for his sheep" (John 10:11). I omit innumerable similar passages in which the same thing is asserted either expressly or by implication. Nor does the distinction dissolve these passages, by which it is said that Christ died "sufficiently" for all and "efficaciously" for a few. For although the merit of Christ's death, on account of the dignity and infinity of its [ἀπειρίας] price, is in itself sufficient for all and can be applied to all to whom God wills to apply it, yet it is not sufficient for others in such a way that it is said to have been applied for them but effects nothing, according to the counsel of God and the intention of Christ dying; for some it both suffices and effects. This is so because such a potential sufficiency does not bring about that the death of Christ is actually applied to this or that person, just as the value of any ransom, whatever and however great it is, does not actually suffice to be paid for anyone, but only to be paid for him for whom the master wishes the ransom to be paid. And because otherwise the death of Christ could be said by the same reasoning to have been undergone also for the demons, since by the infinity of its price it would equally suffice for their salvation as for that of the reprobate. And because otherwise God, by his counsel and intention, would fall short with respect to those among whom he effects nothing. For God, in delivering up his Son to death, and the Son, in undergoing death, could have purposed nothing other than the redemption, deliverance and salvation of those for whom Christ died. But a sufficiency of merit that does not produce salvation, and an application that is merely "according to power" and does not come into act, what sort of sufficiency and what sort of application is that, I ask? "A possible one," you will say. But what does that matter to the case? What sort of benefit, what sort of sufficiency and application is it of Christ's merit to merit for someone what suffices for salvation but does not effect it, and whose actual application can be hindered by the most fickle will of a man? Yet since the application and efficacy of Christ's merit depend upon faith, and we have now clearly proved that the same faith is to be referred to the merit of Christ as its source, either Christ by his death effected nothing for anyone, or at the same time he merited faith, and with faith the application and efficacy. Who could bear a physician who promises a medicine that can be applied, yet which is never applied even though he himself foreknows and wills it? How much more trifling is it to affirm such a thing concerning the love of God who gave his Son, and concerning the death of Christ, a benefit than which no other more precious exists in the world? If the death of Christ was undergone as a victim for all (for it had the character of a victim and a vicarious penalty, and could not be undergone for anyone otherwise than as a victim), then all are in fact expiated. For an accepted victim expiates, and obtains the forgiveness of sins and the bestowal of seed through regeneration, and its justification, and glorification, or obtains as certain to be given, according to that saying, "You ascended, you took captives, you received gifts among men" (Ps. 68:18).

units.la: Christus enim in iis, pro quibus mortuus est, & qui sui sunt, compensationem & mercedem obedientiae suae accipit. Pro quibuscunque igitur mortuus est, iisdem mors ejus ad expiationem & remissionem peccati, vitam & salutem ita sufficit, ut simul eandem efficiat. Neq; profectò ex sua vel Patris intentione mortuus esse dici potest pro iis, quos jam infernò damnatos, quos ad mortem peccare, quos filios perditionis esse noverat. Hoc enim fecisset nec pie, quia contra voluntatem Dei, utpote tales nō salvantis, vel salvare volentis, sed jam actu damnantis & punientis, vel damnare & punire volentis, Matth.XXIII.33. Luc.XVI.25.26. Joh. VIII.24.44.XVII.12. 1.Pet.III.19. 2.Pet.II.5.6. nec sapienter, quia frustra. Scite Remigius Archiepiscopus Lugdunensis Lib. de tenenda Scriptura verit. in Auctario Bibliothecae Patr. Tom. II. Esset, inquit, haec mera & inaudita praesumptio, ut nullus hominum etiam impiorum, & apud inferos irrevocabiliter damnatorum fuerit, pro quo Christus passus non fuerit. Cum pro solis illis defunctis passionem sustinuerit, qui eum, dum in corpore viveret, fideliter venturum, & mundum sua passione redempturum crediderunt. Hoc est Catholicum, hoc Ecclesiae fidei ab initio commendatum. Cum porro Christus, pro quibus animam suam in mortem effudit, & quorum peccata tulit, pro iisdem intercesserit, Esaj.LIII.12. adeóque oblatio sacrificii in mortem, & oratio seu intercessio pro peccatoribus apud Patrem in mortis Christi negotio indissolubili nexu cohaereat, sed satis constat, non pro omnibus, sed pro solis electis & sibi datis Christũ intercessisse. Ego pro iis oro. Non pro mundo oro, sed pro iis, quos mihi dedisti, quia tui sunt, Joh. XVII.9. Pro iis (quos mihi dedisti) sanctifico memet ipsum, ibid.v.19. Neque certè pro aliis, quàm pro salvandis orare potuit; quia oratio ejus, victimae oblatae pretio nixa semper efficax est. Ego noveram, quòd me semper exaudias, ibid.XI.42. Cum ergo pro quibus Christus orat, salvantur, necesse est eos etiam salvari, pro quibus se ipsum obtulit. Qui non singuli homines, sed soli electi & fideles sunt. Nec repugnat, quòd Patrem oravit pro iis, qui crucifixionis ejus authores fuerunt. Pater mi, remitte iis, nesciunt enim quod faciunt, Luc.XXIII.34. quia oratio illa indefinita est, nec ad mundum impiorum pertinet; pro quibus ex hypothesi Christus à Patre non esset exauditus, quod affirmationi ejus, Joh.XI.42. repugnat. Accedit, quòd Deus eos, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, maxima & amplissima dilectione complexus est. Majorem hac dilectione nemo habet, ut quis animam ponat pro amicis suis, Joh.XV.13. Commendat Deus charitatem suam erga nos, quòd cum essemus peccatores, Christus pro nobis mortuus est: Rom.V.8. Sic (tantopere) dilexit Deus mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum dederit, &c. Joh.III.16. At reprobos summo amore Deus adeò complexus non est, ut potiùs eos maximè oderit, Rom.IX.13. Circa eandem verò personam ejusdem amor maximus & odium intensissimum, adeóque contrarii in summo gradu affectus conciliari non possunt. Praeterea non omnes & singuli populorum, tribuum & gentium, sed selectae tantùm ex iis, & obsignatae myriades stolas suas lavisse & dealbasse in sanguine Agni, Apoc.VII.4.14. dicuntur tur. Quin & salvati hoc suum privilegium profitentur. Mactatus es, & redemisti nos Deo per sanguinem tuum ex omni tribu, lingua & populo, non singulos tribuum, linguarum, populorum, ibid.V.9. Denique Deus iis, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, beneficium mortis Christi, utpote pro iis impensae, promulgat & patefacit. Talis enim notificatio ad sufficientiam beneficii & meriti talis minimum haud dubie requiritur. At Christus pluribus populis, nedum individuis sub utroque Testamento ne fando quidem auditus est. Inane vero κενησφυμεν est, quod Deus in Adamo & Noacho, vel per opera communis providentiae omnes vocaverit. Quomodo enim in Adamo vel Noacho vocavit eos, ad quos verbum suum non fecit, & qui Deum loquentem, vel revelantem nunquam audiverunt? Auditus enim est ex verbo Dei, Rom.X.17. Neque notificationi & vocationi huic magis, quam ipsi beneficio mortis Christi impensae hominum culpa & ingratitudo obstare potuit. An hominum infidelitas, Dei fidelitatem antiquabit? ibid. III.3.
units.tr: For Christ receives the recompense and reward of his obedience in those for whom he died and who are his own. Therefore his death is sufficient, for whomever he died, to make expiation and remission of sin, and life and salvation, and at the same time it actually brings these about. Nor can it be said that he died, by his own intention or that of the Father, for those whom they knew to be already condemned to hell, who were destined to death in sin, and who were sons of perdition. For that would have been neither piously done, since it would be against the will of God, as he does not save such people, or wish to save them, but already actually condemns and punishes them, or wishes to condemn and punish them (Matt. 23:33; Luke 16:25–26; John 8:24, 44; 17:12; 1 Pet. 3:19; 2 Pet. 2:5–6); nor wisely, since it would be in vain. Remigius, Archbishop of Lyons, writes well in his book On Holding to the Truth of Scripture, in the Appendix to the Library of the Fathers, vol. II: It would be, he says, a mere and unheard-of presumption, if there were any man, even an impious one, and one irrevocably condemned in hell, for whom Christ had not suffered. For he endured the passion only for those dead who believed that he would come faithfully while he lived in the body, and would redeem the world by his passion. This is the Catholic teaching, this is what the Church has committed to faith from the beginning. Again, Christ interceded for those for whom he poured out his soul unto death and whose sins he bore (Isa. 53:12). Since the offering of the sacrifice unto death and the prayer or intercession for sinners before the Father are bound together by an indissoluble tie in the business of Christ's death, and since it is quite clear that he did not intercede for all, but only for the elect and those given to him: I pray for them. I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours (John 17:9); For their sake (whom you have given me) I sanctify myself (ibid. v. 19). Nor could he have prayed for any others than those to be saved, because his prayer, resting on the price of the sacrifice offered, is always effective: I knew that you always hear me (ibid. 11:42). Therefore, since those for whom Christ prays are saved, it is necessary that those also be saved for whom he offered himself. These are not individual men, but only the elect and the faithful. Nor does it count against this that he prayed to the Father for those who were the authors of his crucifixion: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34), because that prayer is indefinite and does not pertain to the world of the impious, for whom, on that hypothesis, Christ would not have been heard by the Father, which contradicts his affirmation (John 11:42). Add to this that God embraced those for whom Christ died with the greatest and fullest love: Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends (John 15:13); God commends his love toward us, that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:8); God so (so greatly) loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, etc. (John 3:16). But God has not so embraced the reprobate with the highest love that he rather hates them most (Rom. 9:13). Moreover, the greatest love and the most intense hatred cannot be reconciled concerning the same person, and so contrary affections in the highest degree cannot be harmonized. Besides, it is not all and each of the peoples, tribes and nations, but only a select number from them, the sealed myriads, who are said to have washed and whitened their robes in the blood of the Lamb (Rev. 7:4, 14). Indeed, the saved themselves profess this privilege: You were slain, and by your blood you redeemed us to God out of every tribe, tongue and people, not each individual of the tribes, tongues and peoples (ibid. 5:9). Finally, God proclaims and makes known to those for whom Christ died the benefit of Christ's death, as having been bestowed on them. For such a notification is undoubtedly required, at the very least, for the sufficiency of such a benefit and merit. But Christ has not been heard of by many peoples, much less by individuals, under either Testament, not even by hearsay. And it is empty talk [κενησφυμεν] that God called all in Adam and Noah, or through the works of common providence. For how did he call in Adam or Noah those to whom he did not speak his word, and who never heard God speaking or revealing? For faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Rom. 10:17). Nor could the guilt and ingratitude of men have hindered this notification and calling any more than they could hinder the benefit of Christ's death, which was bestowed for them: Will the unfaithfulness of men make void the faithfulness of God? (ibid. 3:3).

units.la: XCII. Non semel in Ecclesia quaestio de amplitudine mortis Christi disceptata est.
units.tr: XCII. The extent of Christ's death has been disputed in the Church more than once.

units.la: Jam olim Pelagiani, inprimis Gennadius cum Semipelagianis seu Massilienfibus suis Divinae benevolentiae & gratiae erga quosdam propositum eversuri, eo quod Gentilium fatum, libertatis excidium, necessitatis asylum, desperationis barathrum, praecepti, exhortationis, correptionis, orationis interitum, & duas naturas, duas massas, insania plus quam Manichaea, inducat; tanquam balin quandam errori suo Voluntatem Dei, quae & salvare omnes, & pro omnibus & singulis Christum in mortem dare statuerit, substraverunt. Cui errori mature se Augustin oppositum passim, uti collectis ejus testimoniis Jansenii August. de Grat. Christi lib. III.20. ostendit, asserens, non pro omnibus & singulis Christum mortuum esse, sed pro iis duntaxat, quibus mors ejus ad salutem profuit. Omnes, sic ille alicubi loquitur; fecit suas oves, pro quibus est omnibus passus: quia ut ipse pro omnibus pateretur, factus est ovis. Et in Joh.tract.47. Fecit ipse etiam suorum sanguinem pretiosum, pro quibus dedit sanguinis pretium. Et Epist.48. Christus est propitiator peccatorum nostrorum, non tantum nostrorum, sed totius mundi, propter triticum, quod est per totum mundum. Sed Magistri sui doctrinam sanam nonnihil inflexit & corrupit Prosper Aquitanicus, qui diversis in locis, inprimis lib. de articulis falso Augustino impositis (qui inter Augustini opera Tomo VII. relatus licet, non tamen Augustini sed Prosperi est) artic.I. Objectionem Vincentianam, quod Prosper statuat; Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum pro omnium hominum redemptione passum esse, sic diluit. Quod ad magnitudinem & potentiam pretii, & quod ad unam pertinet causam generis humani, sanguis Christi redemptio est totius mundi. Sed qui hoc seculum sine fide Christi, & sine regenerationis sacramento pertransfeunt, redemptionis alieni sunt. Cum itaque propter unam omnium causam a Domino nostro in veritate suscepram rectè omnes dicantur redempti, & tamen non omnes a captivitate sint eruti, redemptionis proprietas haud dubie penes illos est, de quibus Princeps mundi foras missus est, & jam non membra Diaboli, sed vasa Christi sunt. units.tr: Long ago the Pelagians, above all Gennadius, together with the Semipelagians or Massilians who followed them, set out to overthrow the divine benevolence and grace towards certain people. Their argument was that this doctrine brings in fate for the Gentiles, the ruin of liberty, a refuge for necessity, an abyss of despair, and the loss of precept, exhortation, correction and prayer, and that it posits two natures and two masses, a madness worse than the Manichaeans'. They undermined the will of God, which had determined both to save all and to give Christ to death for all and each, as though it were a kind of snare for their own error. Augustine was early opposed to this error and resisted it everywhere, as Jansenius shows from his collected testimonies (August. de Grat. Christi lib. III.20.). Augustine asserted that Christ did not die for all and each, but only for those to whom his death brought salvation. All, he says somewhere, are his sheep, for whom he suffered: for that he himself might suffer for all, he became a sheep. And in In Joh. tract. 47: He made his own blood precious for those whom he gave as the price of blood. And in Epist. 48: Christ is the propitiation for our sins, not only for ours, but for the whole world, on account of the wheat which is throughout the whole world. But Prosper of Aquitaine somewhat bent and corrupted the sound doctrine of his master. In various places, above all in the book on articles falsely imposed on Augustine (which, though it is listed among Augustine's works in Tome VII., is really Prosper's), article I., he answers the Vincentian objection, which says that Prosper lays down that our Lord Jesus Christ suffered for the redemption of all men, in this way: As regards the greatness and power of the price, and as regards the one cause of the human race, the blood of Christ is the redemption of the whole world. But those who pass through this age without faith in Christ and without the sacrament of regeneration are strangers to the redemption. Since, therefore, all are rightly said to be redeemed on account of the one cause undertaken by our Lord in truth, and yet not all are rescued from captivity, the property of redemption undoubtedly belongs to those of whom the Prince of the world has been cast out, and who are no longer members of the Devil but vessels of Christ. units.la: mortalitatis, quod confectum est de carne nostra, & virtute Divina, habet quidem in se, ut omnibus prosit: sed si non bibitur, non medetur. Redemptionis igitur proprietatem solis illis, qui salvantur: at magnitudinem & potentiam pretii omnibus & singulis asserit. Haec cunabula sunt distinctionis Sufficientiae & Efficaciae mortis & redemptionis Christi, quae procedente tempore a quibusdam recepta, & ad consilium morientis & redimentis Christi relata sensum incommodum, & parum Scripturis convenientem habet. Augustini saniore hac de re doctrina paulatim sic corrupta demum a Godescbalco (quae vox Francica seu Germanica veteri lingua θεοδουλον Dei servum notat) Orbacensi in Gallia Monacho Benedictino Augustinianae doctrinae studiosissimo orthodoxa de morte Christi doctrina vindicata est, oppugnatore acerrimo Hincmaro Rhemensi Archiepiscopo, qui in Epistola ad Nicolaum I. inter propositiones Gottescbalci hanc tertio loco ponit, quod non pro totius mundi redemptione, id est, non pro omnium hominum salute & redemtione Dominus & Salvator noster Jesus Christus crucifixus & mortuus sit, sed tantum pro his, qui salvantur. Sed ipse ab Hincmaro in carcerem compactus propugnatorem cordatum Remigium Lugdunensem Archiepiscopum, quo ἐργοδιωκτη in Concilio Valentino A.D CCC LV. celebrato canones, Capitulis conventus Carisinei & Johannis Scoti Erigenae, oppositi & cusi sunt, quorum quarto definitum est, pro solis credentibus pretium mortis Christi datum esse. Atque canones iidem Anno D CCC LIX. in Concilio Lingonensi repetiti & confirmati sunt. Gottescbalcus captivus in sententia sua adeò obfirmatus mansit, ut aquae & olei ferventis examini, quod pro illorum temporum consuetudine Judicium Dei habebatur & nominabatur, promptissime se obtulerit. Historiam Gottescbalci una cum ejusdem confessionibus Celeber. Ussherius Armachanus fusius prodidit. Sed vicit tamen error; & in Ecclesia Papali alii quidem, inprimis Lombardus Lib.III.Dist.80. & Thomas Summa de Verit.Mat. 26.q.6. Prosperum secuti Christum pro omnibus sufficienter, pro salvandis efficaciter mortuum esse statuerunt, asserentes, redimi omnes, quatenus solvitur omnibus captivitatis necessitas: at non redimi omnes, quatenus non omnibus solvitur captivitas. In Concilio Tridentino Sess.VI.cap.3. pronunciatum est, Christum pro omnibus mortuum esse, sed non omnes mortis ejus beneficium accipere. Cum tamen definitio haec sic satis ambigua sit, deinceps circa sensum definitionis in partes itum est. Nam plerique, Jesuitae inprimis, in Semipelagianorum castra euntes simpliciter pro omnibus & singulis mortuum esse, sed servata omnibus libertate mortem Christi sibi applicandi, pertenderunt. Quibus se opponens Cornelius Jansenius de Grat.Christi Salv.lib.III.20. Augustini sententiae arctius inhaesit, ne quidem Prosperi de Redemptionis magnitudine seu potentia, & proprietate, hoc est, sufficientia & efficacia distinctione, quia, inquit, ipsa phrasis, qua quis dicitur pro aliquo redemptionem dare, prae se ferre videtur redemptionem, ex redimentis animo, in usum & liberationem captivorum offerri & dirigi, quae oblatio ac directio Christi Christi inanis esse non potest: & quia aliàs etiam pro dæmonibus se dedisse redemptionem dici posset: ac denique, quia Prospero antiquior ac doctior Augustinus nunquam in scriptis suis fatetur, Christum pro omnibus, nullo excepto, redemptionem se dedisse, vel crucifixum esse, vel mortuum, sed tantùm pro illis, quibus mors ejus profuit.
