Nihilominus Jansenii aselectæ, Calvinismi invidiam declinaturi, in Catechesi q.65. docent: Christum mortuum esse pro omnibus, ut daret gloriam electis, & gratias transitorias quibusdam e reprobis. Quæ Prosperi sententia à Jansenio ipso improbata fuit. Perperam certè pro iis Christus mortuus dicitur, qui propter mortem Christi gratias quasdam transitorias accipiunt, neque salvantur tamen, cùm Scripturæ usu non aliter Christus pro aliquo mortuus dicatur, quàm sensu substitutionis in locum reorum ad eorundem peccata expianda, & justificationem actualem promerendam.
units.tr: mortality, which was made from our flesh and by divine power, has indeed in itself that it may benefit all; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal. Prosper therefore ascribes the property of redemption only to those who are saved, but the greatness and power of the price to all and each. These were the cradle of the distinction between the sufficiency and the efficacy of the death and redemption of Christ. In the course of time this distinction was received by some, and it was related to the purpose of the dying and redeeming Christ in a sense that is inconvenient and scarcely agrees with Scripture. Augustine's sounder doctrine on this matter was gradually corrupted in this way, until at last Gottschalk (a name which in the old Frankish or German tongue means servant of God [θεοδουλον]), a Benedictine monk of Orbais in Gaul, most devoted to Augustine's doctrine, vindicated the orthodox doctrine of Christ's death. His most fierce opponent was Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, who in his letter to Nicholas I puts among Gottschalk's propositions, in third place, that our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ was not crucified and dead for the redemption of the whole world, that is, not for the salvation and redemption of all men, but only for those who are saved. Hincmar, however, cast Gottschalk into prison, and Remigius, Archbishop of Lyons, a sound defender of the truth, was then pressed into the fight. At the Council of Valence, held in A.D. 855, the canons were drawn up by this taskmaster [ἐργοδιώκτης] Remigius, opposed to the Chapters of the Council of Quierzy and to John Scotus Erigena. In the fourth of these it was decided that the price of Christ's death was given for believers only. The same canons were repeated and confirmed at the Council of Langres in A.D. 859. Gottschalk remained so hardened in his opinion while in captivity that he most readily offered himself to the test of boiling water and oil, which in those times was regarded and called the judgement of God. The distinguished Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, related the history of Gottschalk at length, together with his confessions. But error nevertheless prevailed. In the Papal Church, some, above all Lombard (Book III, Dist. 80) and Thomas (Summa, de Verit. Mat.; 26, q. 6), followed Prosper and maintained that Christ died for all sufficiently, but for the saved efficaciously, asserting that all are redeemed inasmuch as the necessity of captivity is loosed for all, yet not all are redeemed inasmuch as captivity is not loosed for all. At the Council of Trent (Sess. VI, cap. 3) it was declared that Christ died for all, but not all receive the benefit of his death. Since this definition is quite ambiguous, the parties then disputed over its meaning. Most, and above all the Jesuits, going over to the camp of the Semipelagians, insisted that Christ died simply for all and each, but that the freedom of all to apply the death of Christ to themselves was preserved. Opposing them, Cornelius Jansenius (de Grat. Christi Salv., lib. III.20.) adhered more closely to the view of Augustine. He rejected even Prosper's distinction between the greatness or power and the property of redemption, that is, between sufficiency and efficacy. For, he says, the very phrase by which someone is said to give redemption for another seems to imply that the redemption is offered and directed, from the mind of the redeemer, for the use and liberation of captives; and this offering and direction cannot be empty in Christ. Otherwise it could be said that he also gave redemption for demons; and finally, because Augustine, older and more learned than Prosper, never admits in his writings that Christ gave himself as a redemption for all without exception, or was crucified or died, but only for those to whom his death was profitable. Nevertheless, the Jansenists, wishing to avoid the odium of Calvinism, teach in their Catechism, question 65, that Christ died for all, that he might give glory to the elect and transitory graces to some of the reprobate. This opinion of Prosper was disapproved by Jansenius himself. Certainly Christ is wrongly said to have died for those who receive certain transitory graces on account of Christ's death yet are not saved, since in the usage of Scripture Christ is not said to have died for anyone except in the sense of substitution, in the place of the guilty, to expiate their sins and to merit actual justification.

units.la: In Ecclesia Evangelica Reformatores ambiguè locuti sunt. Pro solis salvandis mortuum esse Christum, non obscurè Lutherus & Calvinus docuerunt. Demum Anno circiter sexagesimo Marbachius & Zanchius contentionis serram reciprocarunt; ille pro universali: hic pro particulari redemptione pugnans. Illi ferè Augustani: huic Helvetii, aliique Reformati Zanchii sententiam suffragio suo firmantes, accesserunt; donec sub seculi hujus initium Remonstrantes Semipelagianis secundas facere denuo coeperunt, mortem Christi sic pro omnibus obitam asserentes, ut liberum cuivis sit, eam applicando suam facere vel non: Omnibus sufficientem à Christo impetratam asserentibus, negantibus aliis.
units.tr: In the Evangelical Church the Reformers spoke ambiguously. Luther and Calvin taught, not obscurely, that Christ died only for those who are to be saved. At last, about the year 1560, Marbach and Zanchius renewed the saw of contention, the one fighting for universal redemption, the other for particular redemption. The Augsburg theologians mostly went over to the former; the Swiss and other Reformed theologians came to the side of Zanchius and confirmed his opinion with their vote. Then at the beginning of this century the Remonstrants began again to give the second place to the Semipelagians, asserting that the death of Christ was undergone for all in such a way that it is free for anyone to make it his own by applying it, or not to do so. They asserted that Christ obtained a sufficiency for all, and denied that he did so for others.

units.la: ad partes vocantur.
units.tr: are called to take sides.

units.la: Eorundem argumenta de omnibus dicitur. In Christo omnes vivificabuntur, 1.Cor.XV.22.quod Apostolus statim, v. 23.de iis, qui Christi sunt, explicat. Summa huc redit, quod Omnes illi, pro quibus Christus mortuus dicitur, illi sint, qui per illum, ceu secundum Adamum, & in ipso ad novam paternitatem pertinent; quemadmodum in primo Adamo omnes mortui sunt, quorum pater factus erat Adam primitivæ benedictionis lege, cùm diceret Deus: Crescite & multiplicamini; jam tum significans, in libro suo Psal.CXXXIX.16. descriptos esse, qui ordine naturæ ab Adamo nasci deberent. Jam & ὁ κόσμος mundus ille, cujus peccatum Agnus ille Dei αἴρειν ferre debuit, Joh.I.29. quem Deus adeò dilexit, ut Filium suum unigenitum dederit, ibid.III.16. Cujus σωτὴρ Salvator, ibid.IV.42.dicitur; cui vitam dare, & pro cujus vita carnem dare, ibid.VI.33. 51. quem Deus in Christo sibi reconciliasse, 2.Cor.V.19. pro cujus denique peccatis Christus se ipsum ἱλασμὸν placamentum dedisse, 1.Joh.II.2. dicitur, qui non alii quàm fideles & electi sunt; & κόσμω mundi nomine veniunt, non tantùm quia ex mundo electi, & in mundo sunt, sed inprimis quia in N.T. non ex uno populo Israele, sed ex mundo etiam gentium, hactenus à Deo & fœdere Dei extorrium & abalienatarum sunt. In quibus impleta est promissio Dei Abrahamo facta: Benedicentur in te omnes familiæ terræ, Gen.XII.3. Benedicentur in Semine tuo omnes gentes terræ, ibid.XXII.18. Porro omnes familiæ & omnes gentes terræ æquipollent mundo, teste S.Paulo, Rom.IV.13. Ubi Abrahamum per promissionem eam factum esse κληρονόμον κόσμου haeredem mundi, hoc est, familiarum, gentium, quarum pater factus dicitur, docet. Promissio autem illa, quòd in Abrahamo benedictionem accepturæ sint omnes familiæ & gentes terræ, hoc est, mundus, significat, quòd Deus per fidem in Christum, tanquam Sponsorem, gentes justificaturus sit, teste eodem Apostolo, Gal.III.8.16. Atque id non de universitate hominum, qui in mundo sunt, sed de universitate Seminis promissionis, ablata distinctione, accipiendum esse patet, quia non omnes & singuli per fidem justificantur: tum quia S. Paulus, Rom.IV.16. Omne Semen, omnésque adeò familias terræ in Abrahamo benedicendas explicat id, quod est ex fide Abrahami, qui est pater omnium nostrum, non secundum carnem, sed secundum promissionem. Quoties ergo benedictio gentium, mundi hæreditas, mors Christi pro omnibus, Deus gentium prædicatur; ratione Seminis promissionis, ad excludendam distinctionem respectu populorum, non exceptionem respectu singulorum, intelligi debet. Quòd porro δεσπότης Dominus eos ipsos falsos Prophetas & Doctores, qui ipsum abnegarunt, emisse, vel mercatus esse, 2.Pet.II.1. dicitur, non eum sensum habet, quòd Christus Dominus eos morte sua, ut victima & λύτρων pretio redemptionis pro iis Deo oblato redemerit, sed quòd eos mortis suæ impendio sui quadantenus beneficii fecerit, quatenus morte sua id etiam effecit, ut quibusdam etiam reprobis Evangelium prædicaretur, atque ii per vocationem externam à pollutionibus mundi gravioribus, erroribus & idololatria liberarentur, & unà cum fidelibus
units.tr: Their arguments are drawn from passages which speak of "all". In Christ all shall be made alive, 1 Cor. 15:22, which the Apostle immediately explains in verse 23 as referring to those who are Christ's. The sum of this comes to this: all those for whom Christ is said to have died are those who, through him, as the second Adam, and in him, belong to a new fatherhood, just as in the first Adam all have died, of whom Adam became the father by the law of the original blessing, when God said, Increase and multiply. This already signified that they were written in his book (Ps. 139:16) who by the order of nature were to be born from Adam. Again, that world [ὁ κόσμος], whose sin that Lamb of God had to take away [αἴρειν], John 1:29, which God so loved that he gave his only Son, ibid. 3:16, whose Saviour [σωτὴρ] he is called (ibid. 4:42), to which he is to give life, and for whose life he is to give his flesh (ibid. 6:33, 51), which God reconciled to himself in Christ (2 Cor. 5:19), and for whose sins Christ is said to have given himself as a propitiation [ἱλασμὸν] (1 John 2:2), are none other than believers and the elect. They come under the name of world [κόσμος] not only because the elect are out of the world and in the world, but chiefly because in the New Testament they are drawn not from the one people of Israel alone but from the world of the Gentiles, who until then were estranged from God and the covenant of God. In them the promise made by God to Abraham is fulfilled: In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Gen. 12:3), In your Seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed (ibid. 22:18). Moreover, all the families and all the nations of the earth are equivalent to the world, as St Paul witnesses (Rom. 4:13). There he teaches that Abraham, by that promise, was made heir of the world [κληρονόμον], that is, of the families and nations of which he is said to have become the father. That promise, that in Abraham all the families and nations of the earth, that is, the world, shall receive the blessing, signifies that God would justify the Gentiles through faith in Christ as Surety, as the same Apostle witnesses (Gal. 3:8, 16). And that this must be understood not of the whole number of men who are in the world but of the whole body of the seed of promise, the distinction being removed, is plain, because not all and each are justified through faith. Moreover, St Paul, Rom. 4:16, explains that every seed, and so all the families of the earth to be blessed in Abraham, is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all, not according to the flesh but according to the promise. Therefore, whenever the blessing of the Gentiles, the inheritance of the world, the death of Christ for all, or God as the God of the Gentiles is proclaimed, this must be understood with respect to the seed of promise, in order to exclude a distinction between peoples, not an exception with respect to individuals. Again, that Lord [δεσπότης] is said (2 Pet. 2:1) to have bought or purchased those very false prophets and teachers who denied him does not mean that Christ the Lord redeemed them by his death as a victim, and by the price of a ransom [λύτρων] of redemption offered to God for them; rather, by the outlay of his death he made them in some measure partakers of his benefit, inasmuch as by his death he also brought it about that the Gospel was preached even to some of the reprobate, and that these, through external calling, were freed from the grosser pollutions of the world, from errors and idolatry, and, together with the faithful,

units.la: agnoscerent Christum verum Ecclesiæ Regem & Dominum esse. Quorum erat, non iterum abnegare Regem & Dominum illum, sed fide constante adhærere ei, qui sui eos beneficii morte sua fecerat. Si enim cùm effugissent πυσματα ἐκ κόσμου pollutiones seculi in cognitione Domini & Salvatoris Jesu Christi, iisdem iterum impliciti deficiant, facta sunt postrema pejora prioribus, 2.Pet.II.20. Beneficiorum ejusmodi, quibus Christi morte sua tales sibi devinxit, & velut ἀγοράσας emit, reprobi participes sunt nō ex consilio & proposito eos sanandi secundū Testamentū, sed ex voluntate longanimitatem, potentiam & divitias misericordiæ in vasa misericordiæ, & denique impotentiam & duritiem humani cordis demonstrandi, Rom.IX.22.23. Præterea S.Paulus dicens, gravi pœna dignum esse, qui Filium Dei conculcat, & sanguinem Testamenti profanum ducit, ἐν ᾧ ἡγιάσθη in quo sanctificatus est, Heb.X.29. non infidelem illum, Filium Dei conculcantem, sed Filium Dei sanguine Testamenti sanctificatum, hoc est, ut principem salutis per passiones suas consummatum esse, ibid.II.10. innuit. Idem Rom.XIV.15. vetans, cibo perdere eum, pro quo Christus mortuus est, non perdi actu posse eum, pro quo Christus mortuus est, sed interitum ejus à maleferiatis tentari, & quantum in iis est, promoveri posse, docet. Sed non quicquid tales tentant & conantur, evenit, quia salus hominum non tam lubrico talo stat. Quomodo non ideo Christus ἀνασταυροῦσθαι denuo crucifigi poteat, quia non desunt, qui denuo eum crucifigunt, hoc est, crucifigere conantur, Hebr. VI.6. Frivola porro ratiocinatio est, argutantium, Christum pro omnibus mortuum esse, quia omnes tenentur in Christum credere. Quod sophisma à Daniele Hofmanno Helmstadiensi primitus cusum avidè Remonstrantes arripuerunt. Præterquam enim quòd non omnes & singuli, sed soli ii, quibus Christus revelatus est, in eum credere tenentur: Omnes quidem & singuli tenentur credere illam ἱκανότητα & sufficientiam Dei, qua is possit fieri Deus peccatoris, per Christum justificandi, si Deus in verbo suo medium illud proponat. Quæ obligatio à Lege est. Omnes etiam illi, quibus Evangelium prædicatum est, tenentur credere, Christum propositum esse placamentum ad Divinæ justitiæ demonstrationem, & apparuisse gratiam Dei salutiferam, quæ jubet credere & resipiscere, hoc est, abnegare se ipsum, omnémque impietatem, confugere ad Christum, ceu unicam salutis arcem, in ipso solo justitiam quærere, & in præsente hoc seculo vivere sobriè, justè & piè, Tit.II.12. Quæ obligatio ab Evangelio est. Sed hoc non est credere in Christum, sed credere aliquid de Christo, quod credere etiam ii tenentur, qui in Christum, tanquam Salvatorem suum pro se mortuum, credere nullatenus tenentur. Neque enim Christum suum Salvatorem esse, & pro se mortuum esse, credere tenetur is, qui vitiosis affectibus mancipatus est, & indulget, sed is demum, qui sibi & operibus suis renuntiat, coram Dei misericordia prosternitur, & non aliunde quàm ex Christi merito salutem expectat. Hi proprii credentis in Christum actus sunt, non communes omnibus vocatis, sed electis eximii. Per gradus enim fides ad Christum accedit. Praecedit enim abnegatio sui, fuga & receptus ad Christum; Sequitur demum consolatio illa ceu fructus justitiae Christi non pertinens nisi ad conscientias contritas, esurientes & sitientes justitiam, qua sic fugiens ad Christum simul ἀληθοφορέηως, firmiter credit, Christum pro se mortuum, & certò sibi omnia peccata remissa esse, quae non tam fides electorum in Christum, quàm fides eorundem de Christo est: ille fidei actus formalis, hic consolatorius; ille quoad actum directum & reflexum, quo credens se credere sentit & credit, praecedens; hic consequens. de quo plura in loco.
units.tr: they should acknowledge Christ as the true King and Lord of the Church. It was their duty not to deny that King and Lord again, but to cling to him with steadfast faith, the one who by his death had made them partakers of his benefit. For if, having escaped the pollutions of the world [μιάσματα ἐκ κόσμου] through the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse than the first, 2 Pet. 2:20. Reprobate persons do share in such benefits, by which Christ bound them to himself through his death and, as it were, bought [ἀγοράσας] them. They do not share in them through God's purpose and intention to heal them according to the covenant, but in order to display God's long-suffering, his power and the riches of his mercy towards the vessels of mercy, and finally to display the helplessness and hardness of the human heart, Rom. 9:22-23. Moreover, when St Paul says that a person deserves a heavier punishment who tramples the Son of God and counts as unclean the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified [ἐν ᾧ ἡγιάσθη], Heb. 10:29, he does not mean an unbeliever trampling the Son of God, but the Son of God sanctified by the blood of the covenant. That is, he implies that the author of salvation was made perfect through his sufferings, ibid. 2:10. Likewise, in Rom. 14:15, when he forbids destroying with food the one for whom Christ died, he teaches that the one for whom Christ died cannot actually be destroyed, but that his ruin may be attempted by evil men and, so far as lies in them, promoted. Yet not everything that such men attempt and try to do comes about, because the salvation of men does not stand on so slippery a die. Nor, for that reason, can Christ be crucified again [ἀνασταυροῦντας], because there are not lacking those who crucify him again, that is, who try to crucify him, Heb. 6:6. Moreover, it is a futile argument of the hair-splitters that Christ died for all because all are bound to believe in Christ. The Remonstrants eagerly seized upon this sophism, first devised by Daniel Hofmann of Helmstedt. For apart from the fact that it is not all and each, but only those to whom Christ has been revealed, who are bound to believe in him, all and each are bound to believe in that ability and sufficiency of God by which he is able to become the sinner's God by justifying him through Christ, if God sets forth that means in his word. This obligation comes from the Law. Likewise, all to whom the Gospel has been preached are bound to believe that Christ has been set forth as a propitiation to show the justice of God, and that the saving grace of God has appeared, which commands us to believe and repent, that is, to deny ourselves, and all ungodliness, to flee to Christ as the only refuge of salvation, to seek righteousness in him alone, and to live soberly, righteously and godly in this present age, Titus 2:12. This obligation comes from the Gospel. But this is not to believe in Christ; it is to believe something about Christ, which is required even of those who are in no way bound to believe in Christ as their Saviour who died for them. For a person who is enslaved to sinful passions and indulges them is not bound to believe that Christ is his Saviour and died for him. Rather, it is the person who renounces himself and his own works, prostrates himself before the mercy of God, and looks for salvation from no source other than the merit of Christ. These are the proper acts of one who believes in Christ, not common to all who are called but peculiar to the chosen. For faith comes to Christ by degrees. First comes the denial of self, flight and refuge to Christ. Then at last follows that consolation, which, as the fruit of the righteousness of Christ, belongs only to consciences that are contrite and hunger and thirst for righteousness. Thus fleeing to Christ, with full assurance [ἀληθοφορίᾳ], one firmly believes that Christ died for him and that all his sins are certainly forgiven. This faith of the elect is not so much faith in Christ as faith concerning Christ: the former is the formal act of faith, the latter the consolatory act; the former is prior with respect to the direct and reflexive act by which the believer feels that he believes and does believe, the latter is consequent. More on this in its place.

units.la: Sicut Evangelium non omnibus hominibus, sed solis illis praedicatur, quos Deus saltem externa vocatione dignatur, neque etiam omnes illi, quibus Evangelium praedicatur, statim & prima vice jubentur & obligantur credere in Christum, sed illi soli, qui peccata sua, & defectum gloriae sentientes, justitiam esuriunt & sitiunt: (sic enim verba Evangelii habent: Resipiscite & credite, Marc. I. 15.) sic non omnes etiam, qui jubentur & obligantur credere in Christum, statim primâ vice & instantiâ jubentur & obligantur credere; Christum pro se mortuum esse, sed illi demum, qui priores gradus scalae hujus, qua per fidem in Coelum itur, jam conscenderunt. Nequicquam verò Christum pro omnibus mortuum esse iidem inde colligunt, quia omnium & singulorum naturam assumpsit. Ad hoc enim, ut Christi mors pro quopiam obita dicatur, non sufficit naturae utrorumque communio & μέθεξις, sed voluntas & consilium Dei Patris & Filii, nec non communio Spiritus requiritur. Qui enim Spiritum Christi non habet, non est ejus, Rom. VIII. 9. ipsi datus, in eo electus ad υἱοθεσίαν non est, Joh. XVII. 9. Ephes. I. 4.5. adeóque nec inter eos, pro quibus Christus se obtulit, censeri potest. Aliter longè S. Paulus, Heb. II. 14. 15. argumentatur, nimirum, quia pueri carnem & sanguinem participant, ideò etiam Christum similiter eorundem participem esse debuisse, ut per mortem aboleret eum, qui imperium habebat mortis, & liberaret eos, qui metu mortis per totam vitam servituti obnoxii erant. Et Christus homo factus, & legi amandi proximum subjectus, non omnibus & singulis hominibus summum illum amoris gradum debuit, ut pro omnibus & singulis moreretur.
units.tr: Just as the Gospel is preached not to all men but only to those whom God at least deigns to call outwardly, and not all to whom the Gospel is preached are immediately and at the first time commanded and obliged to believe in Christ, but only those who, feeling their sins and their lack of glory, hunger and thirst for righteousness (for this is how the words of the Gospel run: Repent and believe, Mark 1:15), so too not all who are commanded and obliged to believe in Christ are at once, at the first time and on the first urging, commanded and obliged to believe that Christ died for them. That obligation falls only on those who have already climbed the earlier rungs of this ladder by which one goes to heaven through faith. Yet the claim that Christ died for all, which these men infer from the fact that he assumed the nature of all and each, is utterly vain. For, in order that Christ's death may be said to have been undergone for someone, a sharing of nature and communion is not enough. The will and purpose of God the Father and the Son is required, and also the communion of the Spirit. For whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ is not his, Rom. 8:9. He is not given to him, and is not chosen in him for adoption [υἱοθεσίαν], John 17:9, Eph. 1:4-5, and so cannot be counted among those for whom Christ offered himself. St Paul argues quite differently in Heb. 2:14-15: because children share in flesh and blood, Christ too was bound to share in the same, so that by death he might destroy him who had the power of death, and free those who through fear of death were all their lives subject to bondage. And Christ, made man and subject to the law of loving one's neighbour, did not owe that highest degree of love to all and each men, so as to die for all and each.

units.la: Sicut enim homines proximum diligendi lege constricti, non pro omnibus & singulis aliis, saltem non pro iis, quos à Deo odio haberi, imò etiam reprobari noverunt, tenentur, neaffectus Dei Creatoris & creaturae diffidean: ita nec Christus homo pro omnibus & singulis, certè non pro iis, quos sibi à Patre non datos, à Deo non diligi ad salutem, sed odio haberi noverat, mori tenebatur. Nihilominus morte sua non redemptorum & pereuntium exitio indoluit, Matth. XXVI. 24. Christi φιλανθρωπία est quidem illa eximia & incredibilis erga universum genus humanum, sed tamen voluntate Patris circumscribitur. Ut enim quà homo, pro suo erga omnes homines amore omnes salvos cupiat, tamen aliter Patri videri intelligens, affectum suum contrahit, eumque ad Patris voluntatem adigit, & quod optimo justissimóque consilio Dei fit, ei congratulatur. Denique nec solidior suaviórque ex universali, quàm ex particulari morte Christi consolatio fluit, tum quia illud, quod omnibus hominibus, electis & reprobis commune est, consolationem solidam fundare nequit; tum quia ὁ ἐξ ἐναντίας mortis Christi efficaciam & applicationem ad individua, quae consolationis basis est, particularem, non universalem faciunt; tum quia à morte Christi particulari, certis indiciis, quòd pro me vel te obita sit, investiganda, rectà ad fiduciam in Deo & Christo itur; ab universali verò per ambages longas, intricatas, perplexas & inutiles; tum denique, quia optima & efficacissima illa afflictorum consolatio est, quam ipse S. Paulus nobis praevivit, dicens: Quis condemnabit? Christus est, qui mortuus est, Rom. VIII. 34. Unde prompta illa consolatio est: Pro quo Christus mortuus est, is non condemnabitur. Pro me (quod certis τεκμηρίοις mihi constat) Christus mortuus est. Ergo non condemnabor. Summa consolatio est, quòd novimus, nos non condemnatum, sed salvatum iri. Fundamentum consolationis est, quòd novimus, Christum pro nobis mortuum esse. Universalis vero redemptio Christi tum majoris illius propositionis vim labefactat non parum, quia ex hypothesi ejus multi, imò plerique, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, damnantur: tum minori propositioni illi infirmum fulcrum substernit; quale est, quòd pro me, quia homo sum, Christus mortuus sit: adeóque fiducia mortis Christi, & manantium ex eadem beneficiorum, non aliud sit, quàm communis omnibus humanitas. Cum tamen non per humanitatis, sed per fidei in Christum sensum communionem cum morte Christi adipiscamur. Fides enim in justitiam Christi efficit, ut potentiam resurrectionis Christi, & κοινωνίαν παθημάτων communionem passionum ejus, conformati cum morte ejus, obtinearnus, Phil. III. 10. Ad fidem verò illam in nobis confirmandam satis est, quòd promissiones Evangelii respectu non omnium & singulorum hominum, sed credentium communes & quodammodo universales sunt. Nam etiam populum Dei habere suam universitatem & plenitudinem, rectè Ambrosius de Voc. Gent. lib. I. dixit; & consolationis nervus est, non quòd de genere hominum, sed quòd de genere populi Dei sumus.
units.tr: For just as men, bound by the law of loving their neighbour, are not obliged to do so for all and each other person, at least not for those whom they know to be hated by God, indeed even reprobated, since the feelings of God the Creator and of the creature are not the same, so Christ as man was not bound to die for all and each, certainly not for those whom he knew were not given to him by the Father, and were not loved by God unto salvation but were hated. Nevertheless, by his death he did not grieve over the destruction of those who were redeemed and perish, Matt. 26:24. The love of Christ for mankind is indeed that remarkable and incredible love towards the whole human race, but it is nonetheless bounded by the will of the Father. For although, as a man, he would desire all to be saved out of his love for all men, yet understanding that it is otherwise seen by the Father, he restrains his affection, submits it to the Father's will, and rejoices that what is done is done by the best and most just counsel of God. Finally, comfort does not flow more solidly or sweetly from the universal death of Christ than from his particular death. First, because what is common to all men, elect and reprobate, cannot found solid comfort. Second, because the converse, the efficacy and application of Christ's death to individuals, which is the basis of comfort, makes it particular, not universal. Third, because from a particular death of Christ, to be sought by certain signs that he died for me or for you, one goes directly to trust in God and Christ, whereas from a universal death one goes by long, tangled, perplexing and useless detours. Last, because the best and most effective comfort of the afflicted is the one St Paul himself set before us, saying: Who shall condemn? It is Christ who died, Rom. 8:34. Hence the ready consolation: He for whom Christ died will not be condemned. Christ died for me (which is certainly known to me by sure tokens [τεκμηρίοις]). Therefore I shall not be condemned. The highest consolation is that we know we shall not be condemned but saved. The foundation of the consolation is that we know Christ died for us. Moreover, the universal redemption by Christ not a little weakens the force of that major premise, because on its hypothesis many, indeed most, for whom Christ died are damned; and it lays a feeble prop under that minor premise, namely that Christ died for me because I am a man, so that trust in the death of Christ and in the benefits flowing from it would be nothing other than the common humanity of all. Yet we obtain communion with the death of Christ not through a sense of common humanity but through faith in Christ. For faith in the righteousness of Christ brings it about that we obtain the power of Christ's resurrection, and the [κοινωνίαν παθημάτων] communion of his sufferings, being conformed to his death, Phil. 3:10. To strengthen that faith in us, it is enough that the promises of the Gospel are, not with respect to all and each man but to believers, common and in a certain way universal. For Ambrose rightly said, in On the Calling of the Gentiles, book 1, that the people of God also have their universality and fullness; and the strength of consolation lies not in our being of the human race but in our being of the people of God.

units.la: XCIV. Tertia sacrificii Christi pars, victima puta jam ante in terra oblatae & mactatae, in Coelo facta nova seu oblatio seu repraesentatio coram facie Dei, eam vim habuit, ut Christus coram facie Dei cum victima, sanguine suo apparens, pro nobis patrocinando, interpellando, Deo nos propitiare, commendare efficaciter non desineret.
units.tr: XCIV. The third part of Christ's sacrifice, namely the victim already offered and slain on earth, became in heaven a new offering, or presentation, before the face of God. Its effect was that Christ, appearing before the face of God with the victim and with his own blood, never ceases to plead for us, to intercede, to propitiate God toward us, and to commend us effectively.

units.la: Non in manufacta Sancta intravit Christus, exemplaria verorum, (vel verorum instar habentia) sed in Coelum ipsum, ut appareat nunc faciei Dei pro nobis, neque ut saepe offerat, sicut Pontifex intrat in Sancta quotannis cum sanguine alieno, Hebr. IX. 24. 2. Semper vivit εἰς τὸ ἐντυγχάνειν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ad interpellandum pro iis, ibid. VII. 25. Quis condemnabit? Christus is, qui mortuus est, magis etiam qui resurrexit; qui etiam est apud Dei dextram, & pro nobis ἐντυγχάνει intercedit, Rom. VIII. 34. Si quis peccaverit, παράκλητον advocatum habemus apud Patrem, Jesum Christum Dominum, I. Joh. II. 1. Si enim inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filii ejus, quanto magis gis reconciliati servabimur ἐν τῇ ζωῇ αὐτοῦ in vita eius? Rom.V.10.
units.tr: Christ did not enter into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true ones (or which have the likeness of the true ones), but into heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God for us; nor does he enter to offer himself often, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own, Heb. 9:24. 2. He always lives to make intercession [εἰς τὸ ἐντυγχάνειν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν] for them, ibid. 7:25. Who shall condemn? It is Christ who died, yes, rather who has risen again, who is also at the right hand of God, and makes intercession [ἐντυγχάνει] for us, Rom. 8:34. If anyone sins, we have an advocate [παράκλητον] with the Father, Jesus Christ the Lord, 1 John 2:1. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved in his life [ἐν τῇ ζωῇ αὐτοῦ]? Rom. 5:10.

units.la: XCV. Facit ergo huc Christi Pontificis Coelum ingressi, & coram facie Patris cum sanguine suo proprio, pro nobis effuso comparentis Intercessio & Interpellatio pro iis, pro quibus se ipsum Deo Patri ad mortem obtulit, & mortuus est. Etenim in terra etiam oratione tum generali & communi, ex humano affectu profecta, pro iis etiam, qui ipsum crucifixerunt, Luc.XXIII.34. tum speciali mediatoria & sacerdotali pro iis, qui ipsi a Deo Patre dati erant, Joh.XVII.6.&c. intercessione defunctus est; & pro se etiam in diebus carnis suae precationes & intercessiones ad eum, qui ex morte servare eum poterat, cum clamore & lacrymis obtulit, Hebr.V.7. sed alterius plane generis illa est, qua Coelum cum sanguine proprio ingressus defungitur. Non enim ibi amplius in genua procumbit, nec supplicatione deprecatoria apud Patrem iratum, cum clamore valido & lachrymis utitur; sed se & victimam suam sistendo & praesentando, ejusdem vi hereditatem sibi dandam & conservandam postulat: Postula a me, & dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam, & proprietatem tuam extrema terrae, Psal.II.8. Ubi Deus Pater voluntatem suam velut accommodat voluntati Filii. Unde Ecclesiae illa sive precatio, sive gratulatio: Det tibi secundum cor tuum, & omne consilium tuum impleat. Impleat Jehova omnes petitiones tuas, ibid.XX.5.6. In terra vero Filius voluntatem suam voluntati Patris accommodavit. Quanquam non ut ego volo, sed ut tu, Matth. XXVI.39. Aliud ergo est petitio quaevis, aliud postulatio. Illa conditionata esse potest: haec nonnisi absoluta est, licet secundum decretum Patris sapientissimum fiat. Nam Deus Pater Filio dedit potestatem omnis carnis, ut quoscumque dedit ipsi, iis daret vitam aeternam, Joh.XVII.2. Eo innuitur unitas voluntatis Patris & Christi. Est igitur intercessio Christi in Coelo ejusdem παρακλήσεως advocatio pro nobis per gloriosum patrocinium, quo causam nostram apud Deum agit; sanguinem suum, exantlatos pro Ecclesia labores, denique crucem ipsam testans & ostentans: Postulatio haereditatis Christi vi hostiae oblatae & jugiter faciei Dei repraesentatae; deprecatio irae, & sanctificationis populo suo impertiendae jugis petitio. Etiam ἐρωτήσεως rogationis, orationis nomine venit. Ἐρωτήσω τὸν Πατέρα Rogabo Patrem (ceu Sacerdos consummatus & Rex) & dabit vobis alium Paracletum, ibid. XIV.16. Estque intercessio, postulatio, rogatio illa non tam expressa, vel proprie dicta, quae verbis fit (quanquam nec illa Christum homini nem dedecet) quam interpretativa & improprie dicta, quae re aliqua, puta repraesentatione hostiae, & sanctificatione haereditatis promeritae per donationem Spiritus S. fidei & vitae aeternae peragitur.
units.tr: XCV. Therefore the intercession and pleading of Christ the High Priest, who has entered heaven and appears before the face of the Father with his own blood, poured out for us, belongs here, for those for whom he offered himself to God the Father and died. For on earth he also died, interceding, first by a general and common prayer, arising from human feeling, even for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34), and then by a special mediatorial and priestly intercession for those whom the Father had given to him (John 17:6, etc.); and for himself too, in the days of his flesh he offered prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him who was able to save him from death, Heb. 5:7. But the intercession by which he, having entered heaven with his own blood, now carries on his work is clearly of a different kind. For there he no longer bends his knee, nor uses a suppliant plea with loud cries and tears before an angry Father; rather, by presenting and displaying himself and his victim, he demands by the power of that victim that the inheritance be given to him and kept for him: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession, Ps. 2:8. Here God the Father seems to accommodate his will to the will of the Son. Hence the Church's words, whether prayer or congratulation: May he grant you according to your heart, and fulfil all your counsel. May Jehovah fulfil all your petitions, ibid. 20:5, 6. On earth, however, the Son accommodated his will to the will of the Father: Nevertheless not as I will, but as you will, Matt. 26:39. Thus one thing is a petition, another a demand. The former may be conditional; the latter is only absolute, although it is done according to the Father's most wise decree. For God the Father gave the Son power over all flesh, so that he might give eternal life to all whom he has given him, John 17:2. By this the unity of will of the Father and the Son is indicated. Christ's intercession in heaven is therefore the same advocacy of consolation for us, through the glorious patronage by which he pleads our cause before God, bearing witness to and displaying his blood, the labours he undertook for the Church, and finally the cross itself: it is a demand for the inheritance of Christ by the power of the offering made and continually presented before the face of God; a plea against wrath, and a constant request for the sanctification to be bestowed on his people. It is also called ἐρώτησις, request or prayer [ἐρωτήσω]. I will ask the Father (as the consummate Priest and King), and he will give you another Paraclete, ibid. 14:16. And this intercession, this demand, this asking, is not so much express or properly so called, as made in words (although such asking is not unbecoming to Christ as a man), but is interpretative and improperly so called, carried out by a certain thing, namely the presentation of the victim and the sanctification of the inheritance earned, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, of faith and of eternal life.

units.la: XCVI. Sicut morte sua Christus tanquam Sacerdos Deo pro peccatis nostris satisfecit in solidum: ita suo in Coelum ingressu cum sanguine proprio ceu Patronus & Advocatus noster apud Deum, nos eidem propitiavit, & preces nostras Deo commendavit, jugiterque commendat. Neque enim illa, quam in Coelo suscepit, salutis nostrae procuratio circa homines duntaxat, sed quam maxime circa Deum nobis propitiandum & placandum distringitur. Quia enim cum sanguine proprio Coelum ingressus est, & eum Deo Patri obtulit ac repraesentavit, apparens coram facie Dei, Hebr.IX.24. manifestum est, eum aliquid apud Deum praestitisse. Id autem apud Deum praestitit, quod victima piacularis praestare potest. At potest illa peccatorem Deo placare & propitium reddere. Tum Christus sic pro nobis apud Patrem intercedit & interpellat, ut apud eum patroni & advocati munere hac in re fungatur. Filioli mei, haec scribo vobis, ne peccetis. Et si quis peccaverit, habemus παράκλητον Paracletum apud Deum, Jesum Christum justum, 1.Joh.II.1. Graecis autem παράκλητος is dicitur, qui ut Advocatus seu Patronus alterius apud alterum causam agit. mani ad Demetrium: Ἐὰν ἐπὶ ἐντύγχωσι κατὰ σὲ Si te deinceps accusaverint Judæi: adversus te faciemus judicium, 1.Macchab.VIII.31. Cùm igitur ἐντυγχάνειν contra ac ἐντυγχάνειν semper valeat, sicut illud accusatoris, ita hoc Patroni seu Advocati sit oportet. Aliter verò Spiritus S. ὑπερεντυγχάνειν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν interpellare pro nobis, Rom.VIII.26. & ὑπὲρ ἁγίων pro Sanctis, ib.v.27. dicitur, non quia ut Cœlestis Patronus, apparens coram facie Dei,ad dextram solii ejus assidens, preces nostras Deo commendat & efficaces reddit, quod solius Christi,qui manens in æternum, sempiternum sacerdotium habet, & salvare in perpetuum potest, accedentes per semetipsum ad Deum,Hebr.VII.24.25. est, sed quia preces & gemitus nostros format, & clamor atque gemitus nostri ὃ φρονήματος voluntatis & studii Spiritus S. pro nobis signum sunt. Quæ voluntas intercessionis instar habet, quia est voluntas Paracleti,hoc est,ejus, qui nobis datus est,& cujus Templum fumus. Neque intercessioni & patrocinio huic Christi in Cœlo obstant ejusdem verba, dicentis: In illo die in nomine meo petetis,& non dico vobis, quòd ego rogabo Patrem super vobis. Ipse enim Pater amat vos,quia vos me amastis, Joh.XVI.26.27. quia non se rogaturum seu intercessurum pro suis negat, sed non dicere, quòd rogaturus pro iis Patrem sit, eò quòd Pater eos diligat,affirmat; quasi diceret,se inpræsentiarum illud præterire,quòdCœlum ingressus pro iis rogaturus sit, & majus quid commemorare,quòd Pater sua sponte eos diligat,quia & ipsi Filium diligunt. Solet enim Christus de duabus rebus agens, unam præterire, vel in speciem, non revera removere, ut eò magis alterum illustret. uti loca similia, velut Joh.V.45.46.47.&c.contendenti liquet.
units.tr: XCVI. Just as by his death Christ as Priest fully satisfied God for our sins, so by his entry into heaven with his own blood, as our Patron and Advocate before God, he has propitiated God toward us, commended our prayers to him, and continually commends them. For the care of our salvation that he has taken up in heaven is not concerned only with human beings, but above all with God, who must be propitiated and appeased for us. For since he entered heaven with his own blood, offered and presented it to God the Father, appearing before the face of God, Heb. 9:24, it is evident that he has accomplished something before God. And what he accomplished before God is what an atoning victim can accomplish; and such a victim can make a sinner pleasing to God and render him gracious. Thus Christ intercedes and pleads for us before the Father in such a way that in this matter he performs the office of patron and advocate. My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. And if anyone sins, we have a Paraclete [παράκλητον] with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, 1 John 2:1. Now among the Greeks, one is called paraklētos who pleads the cause of another before someone else, as an advocate or patron. Compare the letter to Demetrius: If the Jews accuse you hereafter, we will pass judgment against you [Ἐὰν ἐπ' ἐντύγχωσι κατὰ σὲ], 1 Macc. 8:31. Since entynchanein always means the opposite of the accuser's act, as it does here, it must mean the act of a patron or advocate. In a different sense the Holy Spirit is said to intercede [ὑπερεντυγχάνειν] for us, Rom. 8:26, and for the saints, ibid. 8:27. This is not because he appears as our heavenly Patron before the face of God, sitting at the right hand of his throne, and commends and makes effective our prayers before God; that belongs to Christ alone, who, remaining for ever, has an everlasting priesthood, and is able to save completely those who come to God through him, Heb. 7:24, 25. Rather, the Spirit forms our prayers and groanings, and our cry and groaning are a sign of the will and zeal of the Holy Spirit [τὸ φρόνημα] for us. This will has the force of intercession, because it is the will of the Paraclete, that is, of him who has been given to us and whose temple we are. Nor does his word, saying, In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father for you. For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me, John 16:26, 27, stand in the way of this intercession and patronage of Christ in heaven. For he does not deny that he will ask or intercede for his own; he states that he does not say that the Father will be asked for them, because the Father loves them. It is as if he said that for the present he passes over the fact that, having entered heaven, he will plead for them, and that he is mentioning something greater: that the Father loves them of his own accord, because they also love the Son. For Christ, when speaking of two things, is accustomed to pass over one, or to set it aside in appearance but not in reality, so that he may the more clearly illustrate the other. As passages like John 5:45–47 make clear to anyone who considers them closely.

units.la: XCVII.
units.tr: XCVII.

units.la: Sicut Morti Christi victimæ piaculatis & satisfactionis: ita ejusdem in Cœlum ingressui intercessionis Sacerdotalis & efficacis vim Socciniani eripiunt. Nam & falsò,& dicis causa Christum in Cœlo demum Sacerdotem factum esse asserunt. Falsò,quia perinde ut in V. T. Pontifex typicus in sanctuarium interius ut talis introiit, non in eo factus demum est: ita in N. T. verus Pontifex Christus in Cœlum ceu Sancta non manibus facta ut talis introiit,non in Cœlo demum factus est. Nam ceu Pontifex per proprium sanguinem semel in Sacrarium ingressus est, æternam redemptionem nactus, Hebr.IX.12. Purificatione peccatorum nostrorum per se ipsum facta sedit ad dextram Majestatis illius in locis excelsissimis, ibid.1.3. In terra nempe vocatus ad Sacerdotium, eodem, quantum debuit, in terra defunctus est, ad mortem se, ceu victimam piacularem sanctificando & offerendo,Joh.XVII.1.&c.& eandem sustinendo. Tradidit se ipsum pro nobis oblationem & victimam Deo in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ, Ephes.V.2. Quòd vero Christum, si in terris mansisset,Sacerdotem esse potuisse. S.Paulus Hebr.VIII.4. negat,non in Cœlo demum Sacerdotem eum factum esse; sed Sacerdotem in terris factum in Cœlum ingredi, & non terrestri, sed cœlesti tabernaculo inservire, quia non Leviticus Sacerdos, qualis in terra est & manet,sed verus,Cœlesti tabernaculo in terra primùm, ac dein in Cœlo etiam invigilans, fuit, debuisse arguit. Ideo idem S. Paulus Christum cùm advenisset Sacerdos summus, futurorum bonorum,per majus & perfectius tabernaculum intrasse in Sancta, ibid.IX.11.docet. Qui ergo cùm advenisset Sacerdos fuit, & munere Sacerdotis fungi coepit,is ut Sacerdos in Cœlum introiit, & reliquam Sacerdotii functionem in Cœlo obiit. Etiam dicis causa Christum in Cœlo Sacerdotem factum esse asserunt,tum quia ejus Sacerdotium figuratum duntaxat,non proprium fuisse pertendunt; quem errorem alibi perstrinximus: tum quia Sacerdotium tale nonnisi administrationem Regni ejus, adeòque ab hoc non re,sed ratione duntaxat distinctum faciunt,cùm tamen Scriptura utrumque, distincto etiam throno disparet: Dominabitur in throno suo: erit quoque Sacerdos in throno suo, Zach.VI.13. actibus formalibus, oblatione victimæ, & intercessione Sacerdotali pro peccatoribus, Rom.VIII.34. 1.Joh.II.1.2. & defensione ac liberatione Ecclesiæ Regia,Psal.CX.1. &c. differant; & differentia typi,Sacerdotium Aharonis, & Regnum Davidicum, realiter distincta præcesserint. Ejusmodi ergo Sacerdotem, Sacerdotii cassi adeò & infirmi auspicia in Cœlo capientem Christum cùm fecerint, mirè etiam Intercessionem ejusdem infringere debuerunt. Non enim proprie Sacerdotalem, hostiæ oblatæ merito innixam, sed precariam quasi usurpationem potestatis ejus,& curam salutis nostræ, non qua, ut patronus, nos & nostra generatim vel speciatim preces nostras Deo commendet, sed qua precario quodam in Ecclesiam imperio eandem regat, definiunt. Unde infirmam in Christum hominem fidem nasci oportet,cùm is juxta ipsos nec quicquam nobis meruerit, nec patrocinio pro nobis apud Deum utatur,& potestatem nullam nisi precariam & alteri obnoxiam habeat, ac multò satius sit rectà Deum adire, quàm tali sponsore & interprete niti, qui non solùm fidem nostram roborare non possit, sed & in Dei ipsius contumeliam cedat, quasi ipsi soli, sine homine fidejussore, qui pro ipso spondeat,confidere non possimus. Frivolum verò etiam est, quòd preces proprie dictas cum perfecta & independente potestate non consistere argutantur: quia Intercessio Christi non per preces & supplicationes, quales in diebus carnis obtulit, Hebr.V.7.8. sed per patrocinium apud Deum efficax, voluntatem communem cum Patre, & postulationem justam hæreditatis morte, ceu victima,ipsi acquisitæ, peragitur.
units.tr: The Socinians rob Christ's intercession of its priestly and effective power just as they rob his death of its force as a sacrifice for sin and as satisfaction. They claim, both falsely and only for the sake of argument, that Christ became a priest in heaven at last. It is false because, just as the typical high priest in the Old Testament did not become a priest only when he entered the inner sanctuary but was already a priest, so the true High Priest Christ, when he entered heaven, a place not made with hands, did not become a priest only there. For as a priest "he entered once into the holy place by his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption" (Heb. 9:12), and "when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high" (Heb. 1:3). He was called to the priesthood on earth, and there, as far as he had to, he died, sanctifying and offering himself to death as a sacrificial victim (John 17:1, etc.) and enduring it. "He gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour" (Eph. 5:2). As for the claim that Christ could have been a priest had he remained on earth, the apostle Paul denies it (Heb. 8:4). He argues that Christ did not become a priest only in heaven, but that having become a priest on earth he entered heaven, and that he had to minister in a heavenly, not an earthly, tabernacle, because he was not a Levitical priest such as those on earth are and remain, but a true priest who was to watch over the heavenly tabernacle first on earth and then also in heaven. Therefore the same apostle teaches that Christ, when he came as high priest of the good things to come, entered the holy places through a greater and more perfect tabernacle (Heb. 9:11). So he who, having come, was a priest and began to discharge the office of priest, entered heaven as priest and completed the rest of his priestly work there. The Socinians also claim, only for the sake of argument, that Christ became a priest in heaven, partly because they contend that his priesthood was merely figurative and not real, an error we have already criticised elsewhere; and partly because they make this priesthood nothing more than the administration of his kingdom, and so distinct from it in reason only and not in fact, although Scripture separates the two, with a distinct throne as well: "He shall reign on his throne, and he shall be a priest on his throne" (Zech. 6:13). The two differ in their formal acts: the offering of the victim, and priestly intercession for sinners (Rom. 8:34; 1 John 2:1-2), and the royal defence and deliverance of the Church (Ps. 110:1, etc.); and the type, the Aaronic priesthood and the Davidic kingdom, had these as really distinct offices. Having made Christ a priest of this kind, one who takes up in heaven the office of a priesthood that is so empty and weak, they were bound also to undermine wonderfully his intercession. For they define it not as a properly priestly intercession resting on the merit of the sacrifice offered, but as a kind of precarious usurpation of his power and care for our salvation. It is not that he, as advocate, commends us and our prayers to God, in general or in particular; rather, by a certain precarious rule over the Church, he governs it. Hence faith in Christ as man must necessarily be weak, since by their own account he has merited nothing for us, uses no advocacy for us before God, and has no power except a precarious one dependent on another. It is far better to approach God directly than to lean on such a sponsor and interpreter, who not only cannot strengthen our faith but also turns to the dishonour of God himself, as though we could not trust God alone without a human surety to vouch for us. Equally trifling is their quibble that proper prayers cannot coexist with a perfect and independent power. Christ's intercession is carried out not through "prayers and supplications, such as he offered in the days of his flesh" (Heb. 5:7-8), but through an effective advocacy before God, a common will with the Father, and a just claim to the inheritance he acquired for us by his death, as a victim.

units.la: XCVIII. Regium Christi munus est, quo Ecclesiam suam verbo & Spiritu suo gubernat, & contra omnes hostes tuetur atque conservat.
units.tr: XCVIII. The kingly office of Christ is that by which he governs his Church by his Word and Spirit, and defends and preserves it against all enemies.

units.la: Regem fore Jesum, consignatissima oracula testantur. Primus Bileamus id vaticinatus est, dicens: Incedit stella ex Jacob,& surgit sceptrum ex Israele,& defligit angulos Moab,& demolitur omnes filios Seth. Et Israel strenuè aget,& dominabitur aliquis ex Jacobo,& perdet superstitem de urbe, Num.XXIV.17.18.19. Inde Deus ipse in benedictione Mosis: Et factus est Rex in Jeschurum, quando congregata sunt capita populi, una tribus Israelis, Deut.XXXIII.5. Deinceps Hannah in Cantico: Jehova judicabit fines terræ, & dabit robur invictum Regi suo,& efferet cornu מְשִׁיחוֹ מִשִׁיחִ Unctii fui, 1.Sam.II.10. ubi propter Regiam illam dignitatem primùm מָשִׁיחַ Messiæ, Unctiî nomine venit. Inde passim in Psalmis Davidis Regnum hoc decantatur. Deus Pater; Ego, inquit, unxi Regem meum in Sionem montem sanctum meum, Psal.II.6. Primogenitum faciam illum, שליין למלכי ארץ summum Regibus terræ, ib. LXXXIX. 28. Dixit Dominus Domino meo. Sede ad dextram, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum, &c. ibid. CX.1. &c. Et Davidi ipsi Regiam hanc prolem Deus promisit: Statuam semen tuum post te, quod egredietur è ventre tuo, & firmabo Regnum ejus. Ipse ædificabit domum Nomini meo, & firmabo solium Nomini ejus in Regnum. Firma erit domus tua, & Regnum tuum usque in seculum coram te thronus tuus erit firmus usque in seculum, 2.Sam. VII.12.13.16. David ipse in novissimis suis: Dixit Deus Israelis mihi, locuta est Rupes Israelis. Dominator erit in timore Dei. Et lucente matutino exorietur Sol, &c. Nam non sic est domus mea apud Deum; sed fœdus perpetuum posuit mihi expositum inter omnes & servatum, quòd omnis salus mea, & omne beneplacitum, cùm non germinabit domus mea, (ut habeat splendorem mundanum, quia Sol ille justitiæ exorietur, cùm domus mea quasi in cineribus jacebit, ad inchoandum Cœleste Regnum) ibid. XXIII.3.4.5. Inde Esajas: Puer natus est nobis: Filius datus est nobis, & venit Principatus in humerum ipsius, & nuncupatum est Nomen ejus Mirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Pater æternitatis, Princeps pacis, Esaj.IX.6. Idem tanquam Rex stirpis Davidicæ expectandus proponitur: Serviant Jehovæ Deo suo, & Davidi Regi suo (Davidis semini, Regi Cœlesti) Jer.XXX.9. Constituam super ipsas Pastorem unum, & pascet eas, Servum meum Davidem. Et ego Jehova ero ipsis in Deum, & servus meus David Princeps in medio earum, Ezech.XXXIV.23.24. Postea convertentur filii Israel, & quærent Jehovam Deum suum, & Davidem Regem suum, Hos.III.5. Conspicuè inprimis Daniel Regnum Jesu Cœleste, spirituale, æternum describit: In diebus Regum illorum eriget Deus Cœli Regnum, quod in seculum non corrumpetur, Dan.II.44. Quin & eo nomine ad gaudium, & jubila vocavit Zacharias: Exulta valde Filia Sion: jubila Filia Jerusalem: Ecce Rex tuus veniet tibi justus & נושע Salvatus ipse est, (ex passionibus suis, morte ereptus) inops & vectus asino, imò pullo filio armenti asinarum, Zach.IX.9. Sedebit & dominabitur in solio suo; erit quoque Sacerdos in solio suo, ib.VI.13. Angelus de Jesu ex Maria nasciturò: Hic erit magnus, & Filius Altissimi vocabitur. & dabit ei Dominus Deus thronum Davidis (thronum servi Domino throni, Davidi, ceu semini suo promisso) & regnabit super domum Jacob, & Regni ejus non erit finis, Luc.I.32.33. Denique Christus Pilato interroganti: Ergone Rex es tu? respondit: Tu dicis, quia Rex sum ego. Ego ad hoc natus sum, & ad hoc veni in mundum, ut testimonium dem veritati, Joh.XVIII.37. Quæ illa καλὴ ὁμολογία pulchra confessio est, quam Christus coram Pontio Pilato edidit, 1.Tim.VI.13. & morte sua confirmavit.
units.tr: That Jesus would be king is attested by the most certain oracles. First Balaam prophesied it, saying: "There shall come a star out of Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth. And Israel shall do valiantly, and out of Jacob shall one have dominion, and shall destroy him that remaineth of the city" (Num. 24:17-19). Then God himself, in the blessing of Moses: "And he was king in Jeshurun, when the heads of the people were gathered together, the tribes of Israel together" (Deut. 33:5). Next Hannah, in her song: "The LORD shall judge the ends of the earth, and he shall give strength unto his king, and exalt the horn of his anointed [מְשִׁיחוֹ]" (1 Sam. 2:10), where, on account of that royal dignity, the word "Messiah" [מָשִׁיחַ], that is, "Anointed," is first used. Thereafter this kingdom is sung throughout the Psalms of David. God the Father says: "Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion" (Ps. 2:6); "I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth" [עליון למלכי ארץ] (Ps. 89:27); "The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool" (Ps. 110:1, etc.). And God promised this royal offspring to David himself: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build an house for my name, and I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever. And thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever" (2 Sam. 7:12-13, 16). David himself, in his last words: "The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spake to me: He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God. And he shall be as the light of the morning, when the sun riseth... For although my house be not so with God, yet he hath made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and sure: for this is all my salvation, and all my desire, although he make it not to grow" (2 Sam. 23:3-5). The meaning is that the sun of righteousness will rise, while his house will lie as if in ashes, so that the heavenly kingdom may be begun, not with worldly splendour. Then Isaiah: "Unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace" (Isa. 9:6). The same figure is set forth as a king of David's line to be expected: "They shall serve the LORD their God, and David their king" (that is, David's seed, the heavenly King) (Jer. 30:9). "I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David. And I the LORD will be their God, and my servant David a prince among them" (Ezek. 34:23-24). "Afterward shall the children of Israel return, and seek the LORD their God, and David their king" (Hos. 3:5). Daniel above all describes the heavenly, spiritual, eternal kingdom of Jesus with clarity: "In the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed" (Dan. 2:44). Zechariah too called men to joy and exultation on this very ground: "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy king cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation [נושע] (saved from his sufferings, rescued from death), lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass" (Zech. 9:9). "And he shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne" (Zech. 6:13). The angel, speaking of Jesus to be born of Mary: "He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David (the throne of the servant, promised to David and his seed, as the throne of the Lord), and he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end" (Luke 1:32-33). Finally, when Pilate asked Christ, "Art thou a king then?", he answered: "Thou sayest that I am a king. To this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth" (John 18:37). This is the "good confession" [καλὴ ὁμολογία] which Christ made before Pontius Pilate (1 Tim. 6:13), and he confirmed it by his death.

units.la: XCIX. Regia potestas Christo conferri debuit, quia morte sua consecutus est, & sibi, velut peculium, substantiam acquisivit populum סגלה עם λαὸν περιούσιον Populum peculii, Tit. II.14. hoc est, velut thesaurum, qui seponitur, servatur, custoditur, ut dives inde, qui possidet, censeatur, & magnificentiam suam ostendere possit; λαὸν εἰς περιποίησιν (ita סגלה Malach. III.17. redditur) populum acquisitionis, vel in conservationem, permanentem, uti res acquisitæ, ceu caræ, pretiosæ acquirenti conservantur, seponuntur, ut inde acquirens splendidus, magnificus fiat, 1.Pet.II.9. Ideo etiam Seminis, Esaj.LIII.10. נחלה ואחזה hæreditatis & possessionis, Psal.II.8.Hebr.1.2. נדבה עם Populi spontaneitatum, Psal. CX.3. nomine venit. Semen, hæreditas, possessio, populus isthic ab eodem, ceu Rege & Domino, ex mundo, qui totus in malo jacet, segregari, in unum corpus Ecclesiæ redigi, donis illis, per quæ ad vitam æternam, verbo & Spiritu Dei duce, perveniat, locupletari; legibus & statutis, conscientias ad obedientiam constringentibus, devinciri; per ministros & præfectos ab eodem constitutos in politia conveniente & recti tramite contineri; adversus hostium corporalium & spiritualium insultus & violentiam protegi, bonis & privilegiis eximiis ditari atque dotari; judiciis hostibus ejus repræsentatis commendari; denique æterna gloria impleri debuit. Ideo Deus ab æterno Christum Regem elegit, & in tempore Dominum & Christum fecit, Act.II.36. cœlesti Unctione in Regem sacravit, Psal.II.6. eum superexaltavit, & ceu Regem, ad dextram suam collocavit, dato ei nomine supra omne nomen, ut in ejus nomine omne genu se flectat, Phil.II.9.10. Oportuit eum, ut Rex talis fieret, intrare in gloriam suam, Luc.XXIV.26. Est Servator corporis sui, Ecclesiæ, Ephes.V.23. non tantùm ut Propheta & Sacerdos, sed etiam ut Rex, salutem partam ei potenter conferens. Jehova Rex est; Ipse salvabit nos, Esaj.XXXIII.22. Proprium enim Regis munus est, ut salutem subditorum suorum procuret, uti etiam Aristoteles Polit. lib. III.7. agnoscit, tum demum Principem veri Regis nomen mereri & obtinere, cùm saluti communi subditorum consulit. Denique inter tot salutis impedimenta, tantam facilitatem pereundi, hostium conglobatorum, cum quibus nobis πάλη lucta est, Ephes.VI.12. sub Regis Christi solius umbra fideles delitescunt, quia mundo & inferno potentior est; utpote Rex Regum & Dominus dominantium, Apoc.XVII.14. cujus conspectum non ferunt Diaboli, Matth.VIII.29. Cujus verba sunt: Ero pestis tua, ô mors, & perditio tua, ô inferne, Hos.XIII.14. & qui fidelibus suis animum addens, Confidite, inquit, ego vici mundum, Joh. XVI.33. C. Regnum hoc Christo ut Mediatori, & Salvatori sui corporis convenit. Aliud enim Christi etiam Regnum, commune ei cum Patre & Spiritu S. essentiale, aliud ei, ut Mediatori, eximium, Personale, Mediatorium & Oeconomicum est. Illud Christus, ut Deus, unà cum Patre & Spiritu S. exercet in creaturas omnes, quas, sicut verbo solo fecit, ita eodem verbo fert, conservat & gubernat, Deus scilicet magnus Jehova, & Rex magnus super omnes Deos, Psal.XCV.3. Rex æternus, à cujus ira contremiscit terra, & cujus indignationem metuunt gentes, Jer.X.10. Deus Cœli & terræ, Matth.XI.27. Hoc ut Θεάνθρωπος Deus & homo, Mediator & Salvator fidelium, exercet erga Ecclesiam, ceu electos solos, in quorum cordibus verbi sui efficacia & Spiritu operatur. Causa Regiæ potestatis Christo collatæ est acquisitio populi ceu peculii. operatur. Par licèt in utroque Regis Majestas & honor glúcat, dispar tamen utriusque administratio est. Illud Christus, quâ Deus tantùm, operans ὁμοίως similiter ut Pater, Joh. V. 17.19. hoc quâ Deus & homo, factus à Patre Dominus & Christus, Act. II.36. administrat. Unde Esajas posterius hoc Regnum describens praestruit: Puer natus est nobis, Filius datus est nobis, Esaj. IX. 6. Illud in decreto providentiæ, quo Deus res omnes à se creatas conservare & gubernare decrevit: hoc in decreto electionis, quo Deus nos in ipso elegit & praedestinavit ad adoptionem filiorum, Ephes. I.4.5. fundatur. Illud creaturas omnes suo ambitu complectitur: hoc in Ecclesia terminatur, nisi quatenus hujus etiam hostes potentia sua coërcet; & scabellum pedum suorum facit. Cætera omnia, quæ in mundo sunt, parent, sed non voluntate & consilio parent. Solus homo in Regno Christi voluntate, consilio, amore paret. Illud, quatenus exercetur in creaturas omnes ratione carentes, quæ Deum nec cognoscunt, nec amant, sed ei tamen famulantur, quia ab eo ad gratiam vel judicium, ceu organa adhibentur; proprie Regnum non est: hoc, quia sedem in mente hominis amantis habet, proprie Regnum est. Regnum enim est, ubi obedientia amoris est. Illius effecta communia in omnes creaturas, diversis licet gradibus redundant: hujus beneficia ad solos fideles spectant. Illud causas secundas, Coelum, Solem Lunam, elementa, Deos vicaria potestate pollentes, ceu instrumenta quædam dominationis ascisit. Hoc solus Christus Dominus, sine Regibus & Dominis exercet. Licet enim nihil in mundo sit, quin fidelium utilitati volente Domino, inserviat, Rom. VIII.28. ita ut omnia ipsorum sint, 1.Cor. III.22. tamen mundus, Coelum, Sol, Luna, Elementa & res aliæ visibiles ratione ordinis à Deo primitus instituti media & instrumenta, quorum ministerio Regnum gratiæ promoveatur, aut Ecclesiæ salus adjuvetur, non sunt. Prædicant illa Divinæ sapientiæ, bonitatis, patientiæ, longanimitatis gloriam: at gratiam salutarem non testantur. Ac ne ipsi quidem Prophetæ, Pastores, Doctores; quos Christus ad corporis sui ædificationem instituit, & quibus etiam salvandi munus tribuitur, ibid. IX. 22. 1.Tim. IV.16. insita & naturali virtute quidquam hic moliuntur, sed ascititia solius Christi & Spiritus ejus; Verbum suum in ore eorum ponentis, & in solidum omnia operantis. Tantùm in te, Deus, & nullus ultra. Verè tu es Deus, abscondens te, Deus Israelis Salvator, Esaj. XLV. 14. 15. Paulus plantat, Apollo rigat, sed Deus dat incrementum, 1.Cor. III.6.
units.tr: XCIX. Kingly power had to be conferred on Christ because by his death he obtained it, and he acquired for himself, as a kind of special property, a substance: a people [סגלה עם; λαὸν περιούσιον] a people of peculiar possession, Tit. II.14. That is, like a treasure that is set apart, kept and guarded, so that the one who possesses it is reckoned rich and can display his magnificence. He is a people [λαὸν εἰς περιποίησιν] for acquisition, or for preservation, as the word סגלה is rendered at Malachi 3.17, a people kept for permanence, just as acquired things, being dear and precious, are preserved and set aside by the one who acquired them, so that the acquirer becomes splendid and magnificent, 1 Pet. 2.9. Therefore he is also named by the terms seed (Isa. 53.10), [נחלה ואחזה] inheritance and possession (Ps. 2.8; Heb. 1.2), and [נדבה עם] a people of freewill offerings (Ps. 110.3). The seed, the inheritance, the possession and the people are there, from the same One as King and Lord, to be separated from the world, which lies wholly in evil, and gathered into one body of the Church. They are enriched with those gifts through which they attain eternal life, by the Word and Spirit of God as their guide. They are bound by laws and statutes that bind consciences to obedience. Through ministers and rulers appointed by him they are kept in a fitting polity and in the straight path. They are protected against the assaults and violence of bodily and spiritual enemies, and enriched and endowed with excellent goods and privileges. They are committed to judgments that represent his enemies, and finally they were to be filled with eternal glory. Therefore God from eternity chose Christ as King, and in time made him Lord and Christ (Acts 2.36). He anointed him as King with heavenly anointing (Ps. 2.6), exalted him above all, and set him at his right hand as King, giving him the name above every name, so that at that name every knee should bow (Phil. 2.9, 10). It was necessary for him, if he was to become such a King, to enter into his glory (Luke 24.26). He is the Saviour of his body, the Church (Eph. 5.23), not only as Prophet and Priest but also as King, powerfully conferring the salvation he has obtained. "Jehovah is King; he himself will save us" (Isa. 33.22). For it is the proper office of a king to care for the salvation of his subjects, as even Aristotle acknowledges (Polit. III.7): a prince then deserves and obtains the name of true king when he looks to the common salvation of his subjects. Finally, amid so many obstacles to salvation, such an ease of perishing, and such a gathering of enemies, with whom our wrestling is (Eph. 6.12), the faithful hide under the shadow of Christ the King alone, because he is more powerful than the world and hell, being King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 17.14). The devils cannot endure his presence (Matt. 8.29). His words are: "I will be your plague, O death, and your destruction, O hell" (Hos. 13.14). Encouraging his faithful, he says: "Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world" (John 16.33). C. This kingdom belongs to Christ as Mediator and Saviour of his body. For there is another kingdom of Christ, common to him with the Father and the Holy Spirit, which is essential, and another, peculiar to him as Mediator, which is personal, mediatorial and economical. The former Christ, as God, exercises together with the Father and the Holy Spirit over all creatures, which, as he made them by his word alone, so by the same word he bears, preserves and governs. This is God, the great Jehovah, and the great King above all gods (Ps. 95.3); the eternal King, at whose wrath the earth trembles and whose indignation the nations fear (Jer. 10.10); the God of heaven and earth (Matt. 11.27). He exercises the latter as Theanthropos, God and man, Mediator and Saviour of the faithful, towards the Church, as towards the elect alone, in whose hearts he works the efficacy of his word and Spirit. The cause of the kingly power conferred on Christ is the acquisition of a people as a special possession. Although in both there is equal majesty and honour of the King, the administration of each is unequal. The former Christ administers as God alone, working in like manner with the Father (John 5.17, 19); the latter he administers as God and man, made by the Father Lord and Christ (Acts 2.36). Hence Isaiah, describing this later kingdom, foreshadows it: A child is born to us, a son is given to us (Isa. 9.6). The former is founded in the decree of providence, by which God decreed to preserve and govern all things created by himself; the latter in the decree of election, by which God chose us in him and predestined us to adoption as sons (Eph. 1.4, 5). The former embraces all creatures within its compass; the latter is confined to the Church, except insofar as he also restrains its enemies by his power and makes them his footstool. All other things in the world obey, but they do not obey by will and counsel. Only man in the kingdom of Christ obeys by will, counsel and love. The former, insofar as it is exercised over all creatures lacking reason, which neither know nor love God but nevertheless serve him, because they are used by him as instruments for grace or judgment, is not properly a kingdom. The latter, because it has its seat in the mind of a loving man, is properly a kingdom, for a kingdom is where there is the obedience of love. The effects of the former extend in common to all creatures, though in different degrees; the benefits of the latter pertain to the faithful alone. The former takes to itself, as instruments of its dominion, secondary causes: heaven, sun, moon, the elements, and gods wielding power by vicarious authority. The latter the Lord Christ alone exercises, without kings and lords. For although nothing in the world exists which does not serve the good of the faithful, the Lord willing (Rom. 8.28), so that all things are theirs (1 Cor. 3.22), yet the world, heaven, sun, moon, elements and other visible things are not, by the order first instituted by God, means and instruments through whose ministry the kingdom of grace is advanced or the salvation of the Church is aided. They proclaim the glory of divine wisdom, goodness, patience and long-suffering, but they do not bear witness to saving grace. Nor do even the prophets, ministers and teachers whom Christ instituted for the building up of his body, and to whom the office of saving is also assigned (ibid. IX.22; 1 Tim. IV.16), undertake anything here by innate and natural power, but by the borrowed power of Christ alone and his Spirit, who puts his Word in their mouths and works all things wholly. Only in you, God, and none beside; truly you are God, hiding yourself, the God of Israel, the Saviour (Isa. 45.14, 15). Paul plants, Apollos waters, but God gives the increase (1 Cor. 3.6).

units.la: CI. Nihilominus Regnum Personale & Mediatorium Christi, si plenitudo potestatis, quam ipse in Coelo & terra habet, Matth. XXVIII. 18. quæque Nomen Jesu super omne nomen, in quo omne genu flectendum est, vocatur, Phil. II.9.10. spectatur, à Regno ejusdem communi & essentiali non re, sed sola ratione differt. Nam etiam per illud Deo Patri ὁμοούσιον esse, vel inde colligitur, quòd is, coram quo omne genu flectendum, non alius quàm Jehova esse potest. Dixit Jehova, Creator Coelorum &c. Per me juravi, egressum est ex ore meo in justitia verbum; & non revertetur, quòd in nomine meo flectetur omne genu, per me jurabit omnis lingua, Esaj. XLV. 18.23. Quod
units.tr: CI. Nevertheless, the personal and mediatorial kingdom of Christ, which is viewed as the power he has in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28.18), and which is called the name Jesus above every name, in which every knee must bow (Phil. 2.9, 10), differs from his common and essential kingdom not in substance but only in the mode of consideration. For that he is of one essence with God the Father can be gathered even from this, that he before whom every knee must bow can be none other than Jehovah. Jehovah, the Creator of the heavens, etc. By myself I have sworn; a word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness and will not return: that to my name every knee shall bow, by me every tongue shall swear (Isa. 45.18, 23). Which

units.la: Sed sola ratione, non re, quia etiam Mediatorium nisi Deus exercere non potuisset.
units.tr: But only in the mode of reasoning, not in reality, because even the mediatorial kingdom could not have been exercised except by God.

units.la: velut de Christo dictum S. Paulus Rom. XIV.11. citat. Cúmque totus etiam mundus, vita & mors, præsentia & futura fidelium sint, 1.Cor. III.22. & eorum usibus inserviant; non potest Christus Regnum suum Personale in Ecclesiam sine essentiali & communi in totum mundum exercere. Quamobrem nec novus Rex & Legislator in Religione Christiana credi vel salutari debet Christus ad dextram Patris exaltatus, qui nunc demum in N.T. Mosi successerit; sed is Mosis fidelis servi jam olim Dominus & Deus; in Legislatione & fundatione Reipublicæ Israelis. Rex Israelis, Jehova ipse, unicus ille Legislator, Esaj. XLIV.1. Joh. I.50. Jacob. IV.12. extitit. Neque plane Regnum Christi Mediatorium Personæ Filii, quà Mediatori; œconomicè appropriatum Majestatem Regni inferiorem Regno Dei Altissimi, sed personale jus Filio Dei quæsitum notat, quo ipse Ecclesiam sibi ut capiti mysticè unitam, in se & à se vivificatam glorificat, & communem etiam mundi universi gubernationem ad ejus salutem ordinat. Unde Regnum Dei κατ' ἐξοχὴν Regni Christi nomine venit. Judicabit vivos & mortuos κρίνειν ζῶντας καὶ νεκροὺς ἐπιφάνειαν αὐτοῦ, καὶ τὴν βασιλείαν αὐτοῦ; hoc est, cùm apparebit, & Regnum occupabit, 2.Tim. IV.1. Dominus me salvum faciet in Regnum suum coeleste, ib. v. 18. Locupletem in modum vobis suppeditabitur introitus in æternum Regnum Domini nostri & Salvatoris Jesu Christi, 2.Pet. I.11. Si patimur, etiam unà regnabimus, 2.Tim. II.12.
units.tr: as Saint Paul says, quoting it of Christ, Rom. 14:11. And since the whole world also, life and death, present and future, belongs to the faithful, 1 Cor. 3:22, and serves their uses, Christ cannot exercise his personal kingdom over the Church without exercising his essential and common kingdom over the whole world. Therefore Christ, exalted at the right hand of the Father, who is said to have succeeded Moses in the New Testament, ought not to be believed or confessed as a new King and Lawgiver in the Christian religion. He was already long ago the Lord and God of Moses, his faithful servant, in the legislation and foundation of the commonwealth of Israel. The King of Israel, Jehovah himself, the one and only Lawgiver, has been.

units.la: CII. Regnum isthoc Personale Christus etiam quà Deus, non præter vel citra, sed secundum voluntatem Patris gerit. Potest enim, ut Deus & Mediator, quæ vult, omnia. Sed nihil vult, quin idem Deo Patri gratum & acceptum fit. Quæ talia sunt, omnia vult. Deo autem gratum acceptúmque est; ut Jesus Christus, quem ipse tam μεσίτην hominum apud se, quàm suum apud homines constituit, non tantùm populum vera doceat; legibus contineat, Spiritu sanctificet, ad vitam æternam resuscitet, sed etiam eum sibi, ut Patronus commendet. Hoc enim omne ad honorem Dei pertinet, eíque gloriosum est. Non ergo, Christo regnante, Deus Majestatis suæ solio cessit, neque Jesu Christo, ut Mediatori, ita Regnum tradidit, ut illud sibi abrogaverit, aut semetipsum Christo subjecerit. Aliàs nullas nisi ad Christum ut μεσίτην preces fundere liceret. Cùm contra ab Apostolis & Ecclesia Catholica semper factum sit. Christus quidem factus omnium judex omnia nunc in Ecclesia sua administrat; sed secundum voluntatem Patris, quia fieri non potest, ut in quo vivimus, movemur & sumus, Act. XVII.28. qui omnia in omnibus implet, 1.Cor. XV.28. Ephes. I.23. & cuncta intuetur, eorum, quæ ad Ecclesiam pertinent, nihil cogitet, nihil velit, nihil ad se pertinere putet; atque ita Christo administranda derivit, ut nihil ipse de rebus nostris apud se statuat, sed cuncta susque deque habeat. Est igitur omnino aliqua Dei erga nos voluntas; & Christus ut Pontifex noster id agit, id inprimis vult, ut benevola & propitia semper Dei erga nos voluntas sit; & eam ob causam nos Deo commendat. Ex quo illud maximè liquet, Regno & Sacerdotio Christi aprimè convenire, neque unum alterum, quæ Socinianorum cavillatio est; labefactare.
units.tr: CII. Christ also administers this kingdom as God, not apart from or without the Father, but according to the Father's will.
