For as God and Mediator he can do whatever he wills, and he wills nothing that is not also pleasing and acceptable to God the Father. He wills all such things. Now it is pleasing and acceptable to God that Jesus Christ, whom the Father has appointed as mediator [μεσίτην] of men with himself and as the Father's own with men, should not only teach the people the truth, restrain them by laws, sanctify them by the Spirit and raise them to eternal life, but also commend them to God as their Patron. For all this pertains to the honour of God and is glorious to him. Therefore, Christ reigning does not mean that God has yielded the throne of his majesty, nor has God so handed the kingdom over to Jesus Christ as Mediator that he has taken it from himself or subjected himself to Christ. Otherwise it would be lawful to pour out prayers only to Christ as Mediator, whereas the Apostles and the Catholic Church have always done the opposite. Christ, indeed, having been made judge of all, now administers all things in his Church, but according to the will of the Father. It cannot be otherwise, because "in him we live, move and have our being," Acts 17:28, and he who "fills all in all," 1 Cor. 15:28; Eph. 1:23, and beholds all things, could not fail to think of, will and consider as his own whatever pertains to the Church. Nor has he so transferred the administration to Christ that he himself decides nothing about our affairs and regards everything with indifference. There is therefore certainly some will of God toward us, and Christ, as our High Priest, carries this out. Above all he wills that God's will toward us should always be benevolent and gracious, and for this reason he commends us to God. From this it is most clear that the kingdom and the priesthood of Christ agree very well, and that neither overthrows the other, which is the sophistry of the Socinians.

units.la: Regnum hoc non præter, vel citra; sed secundum voluntatem Patris administrat, neque adeò Christo regnante Deus Majestatis suæ solio cessit.
units.tr: This kingdom is administered not apart from or without the Father, but according to his will; nor, with Christ reigning, has God yielded the throne of his majesty.

units.la: CIII. Officio hoc Regio fungitur Christus Θεάνθρωπος, Deus & Homo; Deus ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem, tutelam & glorificationem regnans αὐτοκρατορικῶς: Homo non ut Dominus universi, sed ut Patris mandatarius, potestate finita & dependente utens. Sicut enim ad intercessionem Sacerdotalem etiam naturæ humanæ viscera & commiseratio: ita ad Regni hujus administrationem ejusdem etiam cura & opera requiritur. Nam & in præsens Angelis bonis & malis ad Ecclesiæ salutem dominatur: & in judicio visibili universali Angelorum & hominum viventium & mortuorum etiam humana natura, quod suum est, faciet. Potestatem dedit etiam judicium faciendi, quia Filius hominis est, Joh. V.27. Constituit diem, in quo judicabit orbem habitabilem in justitia ἐν ἀνδρὶ ᾧ ὥρισεν per virum, quem ad id destinavit, Act. XVII. 31. Sed quà homo regnat potestate dependente & finita: quà Deus independente & infinita. Neque enim sibi Sociniani constant, asserentes, Christum habere potestatem dependentem, sed ea per voluntatem & potentiam independentem uti. Nam voluntas & potentia independens soliusDei est, non creaturæ ullius, qualem Christum faciunt. Si enim creatura per potentiam independentem ageret, Deus hoc, quod sic creatura agit, nec vellet, nec faceret, nec prima rerum omnium causa foret, & à creaturæ consilio & voluntate Dei us dependeret. In Regno suo nihil Christus agit, nisi quod Pater velit fieri: nihil sibi subjicit, nisi quod Pater ei subjicit. Vel igitur voluntas & potentia Christi erit dependens, quod illi negant: vel voluntas Patris & Filii una est; sicut Christus ipse dicit: Nihil potest facere Filius à se ipso, nisi quod viderit Patrem facientem, ut id similiter faciat, Joh. V. 19.
units.tr: CIII. Christ, the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], discharges this royal office, as God reigning for the building up, protection and glorifying of the Church, by his own authority [αὐτοκρατορικῶς]; and as man, not as Lord of the universe but as the Father's agent, exercising a finite and dependent power. For just as the compassion and tender feeling of human nature is required for his priestly intercession, so the care and work of that same nature is required for the administration of this kingdom. For even now he rules over good and bad angels for the salvation of the Church, and at the visible universal judgment of angels and of living and dead men, he will also act through his human nature, which is his own. "He has given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man," John 5:27. "He has appointed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has ordained" [ἐν ἀνδρὶ ᾧ ὥρισεν], Acts 17:31. But as man he reigns with a dependent and finite power; as God, with an independent and infinite power. The Socinians are not consistent with themselves, for they assert that Christ has a dependent power, but that he uses it through an independent will and power. For an independent will and power belong to God alone, not to any creature, which is what they make Christ. If a creature acted through independent power, God would neither will nor do what the creature so does, and he would not be the first cause of all things, but would depend on the counsel and will of the creature. In his kingdom Christ does nothing except what the Father wills to be done, and subjects nothing to himself except what the Father subjects to him. Therefore either the will and power of Christ is dependent, which they deny, or the will of the Father and of the Son is one; as Christ himself says: "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing; for whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise," John 5:19.

units.la: CIV. Regnum, quod Christus gerit, non est de hoc mundo, neque adeò per modum Regni mundani & humani geritur; sed planè Divinum, & gloria ejus summa. Regnum meum non est ex hoc mundo. Si Regnum meum esset ex mundo; ministri mei certassent, ne traderer Judæis. Nunc verò Regnum meum non est ἐντεῦθεν hinc. Joh. XVIII.36. Quasi diceret: Non sum Rex ut Herodes, ut Cæsar, ut Rex Parthorum. Non illo modo regno. Non talibus legibus, armis populum subjicio. Non illo modo populus meus cognoscitur. Non tale bonum est, quod populo meo imperior, quale illud, quod Romani suo imperiuntur. Non tale judicium in Regno meo agito, quale in humano die agitari solet. Non est Regnum meum ex mundo, ex hominibus, qui in terra sunt, eorum consilio, præcepto, potestate, authoritate & nomine; neque ex rebus, quæ in terra sunt. Talis si esset, ministri mei, Angeli & homines fideles, ex quibus collecto exercitu facile me à violentia vestra expediissem. Sed ea res opus non est, cùm etiam potestati vestræ subjectus, & vinculis vestris constrictus regnare non desinam. Mox v. 37. coram Pilato se Regem professus, ad hoc se natum esse, ad hoc in mundum venisse docet, ut testimonium daret veritati, quòd vi- delicet sit Deus, quæ prima veritas est: quòd omnia ad gloriam suam fecerit, docendo justitiam Dei, & eam per obedientiam & passionem suam demonstrando, ut in justitia Deus Abrahami, Isaci & Jacobi cognosceretur: quòd vera sit
units.tr: CIV. The kingdom that Christ administers is not of this world, nor is it carried on in the manner of a worldly and human kingdom, but is wholly divine and of the highest glory. "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have fought, that I should not be delivered to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here [ἐντεῦθεν]," John 18:36. As if he were saying: I am not a king like Herod, like Caesar, like the King of the Parthians. I do not reign in that way. I do not subject the people by such laws or arms. My people are not recognised in that way. The good I impose on my people is not like that which the Romans impose on theirs. I do not carry out in my kingdom such judgment as is usually carried out in human courts. My kingdom is not "of this world," that is, of men who are on earth, by their counsel, precept, power, authority and name, nor of things which are on earth. If it were such, my servants, the angels and faithful men, would have gathered an army from whom I could easily have freed myself from your violence. But that is not necessary, since I shall not cease to reign even though I am subject to your power and bound with your chains. Soon after, at verse 37, confessing before Pilate that he is king, he teaches that "for this I was born, and for this I came into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth," namely that he is God, who is the first truth; that he has made all things for his own glory, teaching the justice of God and demonstrating it by his obedience and passion, so that God might be known in the justice of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; that

units.la: Lex, obedienti, & nonnisi obedienti vitam promittens, verææ promissiones; verus cultus ille, qui non in ritibus & litera, sed in spiritu peragitur; verum fœdus, quod cum hominibus super sacrificio initum est, Psal. L. 5. cujus Lex & promissio verè in Christo impleta est. Hæc ἀληθινὴ veritas secundum pietatem est, cujus Christus ὁ πιστὸς μάρτυς fidelis testis, Apoc. I. 5. factus est. Sceptrum igitur Regni Christi est verbum veritatis, quod ex Sione progredi fecit, Psal. CX.2. Esaj. II. 3. quod in ore puerorum & lactentium, Psal. VIII.3. Evangelizantium, Esaj. LII.7. posuit. Modum regnandi Christus his statim verbis exprimit: Omnis, qui est ex veritate, audit vocem meam, Joh. XVIII.37. quasi diceret: In hoc Regni mei vis consistit, quòd habeo tales, qui ex veritate sunt, qui veritati illi obediunt, & vocem meam audiunt, testimonium meum recipiunt, illi attendunt, & veritatem amant. Hæc enim illa ὑπακοὴ τῆς πίστεως obedientia fidei, Rom. I.5. ὁμολογίας εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον Χριστοῦ, subjectio confessionis in Evangelium Christi, 2. Cor. IX. 13. est. Quam fidei subjectionem & veritatis amorem qui tollunt, & cum mendacio commutant, illi Regnum Christi corrumpunt & tollunt. Ideo Christus idem Pharisæis interrogantibus, quando venturum sit Regnum Dei, respondit: Non venit Regnum Dei μετὰ παρατηρήσεως cum observatione, (pompa, splendore mundano, qui à quovis homine observari potest, nemine ignorante, quis in quoque territorio summa potestate utatur) neque dicent; Ecce hic est, vel ecce ibi est; Ecce enim, Regnum Dei ἐντὸς ὑμῶν intra vos (in mente, conscientia, voluntate hominum, testimonium Jesu & justitiam ejus recipientium) est, Luc. XVII.20.21. Quando enim Regnum Cœlorum venit, adest Scriptura cum iis argumentis, quibus Divinitas ejus cognosci potest; adsunt voces, facta, passiones, quæ cuncta conspicabilia sunt. Sed nemini nisi fideli liquidò constat, hanc Scripturam esse verbum Dei, testimonium Jesu Christi esse Spiritum Prophetiæ, Jesum esse Dominum, Christum, justitiam credentis, & fideles esse populum ejus, in quibus regnat & vivit. Non ergo Regnum Christi παρατηρητὸν aspectabile, nec nisi intra hominis credentis & Deum amantis penetrale est. Quod difertius etiam S. Paulus definit, dicens: Non est Regnum Dei esca & potus, sed justitia & pax, & lætitia in Spiritu S. Nam qui in his servit Christo, placet Deo, & hominibus probatus est, Rom. XIV.17. 18. Qui ergo habent justitiam Dei, Christi per fidem; pacem cum Deo; & lætitiam in Spiritu S. dignam authore Spiritu Dei, qui Deus noster nos consummat, & in cordibus nostris, ut arrhabo, positus est, is Christo, ut Regi, ut Domino, & ut ei, ad quem omnis gloria pertinet, servit. Regnat Christus, quando sic dominatur subditis, sic à subditis glorificatur; &, ut sic dominetur & glorificetur, verbo & Spiritu suo efficit. Concinit illud Johannis: Vidi Cœlum apertum. Et ecce equus candidus, & sedens in eo fidelis & verus, & in justitia judicat & belligerat, Apoc. XIX. 11. Justitia enim, quam adduxit, quam prædicavit, cui homines subjici voluit, quam donat suis; adeóque jus salvandi oves suas, non patitur, ut non judicet; ut non consoletur credentes in se, & iram adversus fideles non exerceat. Id ipsum etiam Prophetæ prædicarunt. Judicabit in justitia tenues, & demonstrationem faciet in æquitate mansuetis terræ, & percutiet terram virga oris sui, & spiritu labiorum suorum interficiet improbum, Esaj. XI.4. Quis excitavit ab Oriente, cui justitia occurrit ad omnem gressum ejus? ibid. XLI.2. Propinqua est salus mea, ut veniat, & justitia mea ut reveletur, ib. LVI.1. Justitia ejus eum fulcivit, & induit justitiam velut loricam, ibid. LIX.16.
units.tr: the law is true, promising life to the obedient and to none but the obedient; that the promises are true; that the true worship is that which is carried on not in ritual and letter but in spirit; that the true covenant, made with men concerning sacrifice, Ps. 50:5, whose law and promise have truly been fulfilled in Christ. This is the true [ἀληθινὴ] truth according to godliness, of which Christ was made the faithful [ὁ πιστὸς μάρτυς] witness, Rev. 1:5. "The sceptre therefore of Christ's kingdom is the word of truth, which he has caused to go forth from Zion," Ps. 110:2; Isa. 2:3, which he has placed "in the mouth of children and infants," Ps. 8:3, and of those who "proclaim the good news," Isa. 52:7. Christ expresses the manner of his reigning at once in these words: "Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice," John 18:37. As if he were saying: The strength of my kingdom consists in this, that I have such people as are of the truth, who obey that truth and hear my voice, who receive my testimony, attend to it and love the truth. For this is that "obedience of faith" [ὑπακοὴ τῆς πίστεως], Rom. 1:5, "the subjection of your confession [ὁμολογίας] to the gospel of Christ" [εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον Χριστοῦ], 2 Cor. 9:13. Those who take away this subjection of faith and love of the truth, and exchange it for a lie, corrupt and destroy the kingdom of Christ. Therefore Christ, when the Pharisees asked him when the kingdom of God would come, answered: "The kingdom of God does not come with observation" [μετὰ παρατηρήσεως], that is, with worldly pomp and splendour, which any man can observe, and which everyone knows who holds supreme power in any territory. "Nor will they say, Behold, here it is, or behold, there it is; for behold, the kingdom of God is within you" [ἐντὸς ὑμῶν], that is, in the mind, conscience and will of men who receive the testimony and righteousness of Jesus, Luke 17:20-21. For when the kingdom of heaven comes, Scripture is present with those arguments by which its divinity can be known; voices, deeds and sufferings are present, all of which are visible. But it is clear to no one except the faithful that this Scripture is the word of God, that the testimony of Jesus Christ is the spirit of prophecy, that Jesus is Lord and Christ, the righteousness of the believer, and that the faithful are his people, in whom he reigns and lives. The kingdom of Christ, therefore, is not observable to the eye, and is found only within the inner sanctuary of the man who believes and loves God. St Paul defines this more plainly, saying: "The kingdom of God is not meat and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. For he who in these things serves Christ is pleasing to God and approved by men," Rom. 14:17-18. Those, therefore, who have "the righteousness of God, of Christ, through faith," "peace with God," and "joy in the Holy Spirit," worthy of the Spirit of God as author, who completes us and has been placed in our hearts as a pledge, serve Christ as King, as Lord, and as him to whom all glory belongs. Christ reigns when he so rules his subjects and is so glorified by them; and he brings it about by his word and Spirit that he should so rule and be glorified. John's words agree: "I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse, and he who sat on it was called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war," Rev. 19:11. For the righteousness which he has brought, which he has preached, to which he wishes men to be subject, and which he gives to his own, does not allow him, since he has the right to save his sheep, not to judge; nor does he fail to comfort those who believe in him and to exercise wrath against the unfaithful. The prophets too proclaimed this same thing: "He shall judge the poor in righteousness, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth, and he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked," Isa. 11:4. "Who has raised up one from the east, whom righteousness meets at every step?" ibid. 41:2. "My salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed," ib. 56:1. "His righteousness upheld him, and he put on righteousness like a breastplate," ibid. 59:16.

units.la: CV. Expressis his testimoniis alia quoque accedunt, quæ intimam Regni hujus indolem spiritualem & cœlestem testantur; velut, quòd Regni Cœlorum & Regni Dei nomine venit, quia Cœleste est & quoad Regem, qui verus Deus, immediatè regnans desuper venit, & super omnes est. Joh. III.31. Dominus ex Cœlo, 1.Cor.XV.47. Rex gloriæ, Psal. XXIV.7. Dominus gloriæ, 1.Cor. II.8. & quoad ortum, quia non humanis consiliis, sed cœlesti prudentia & ratione constituitur; & quoad statum, quia in rebus Cœlestibus, Divinis, mysticis occupatur totum, & quoad actum, quia in dispensandis cœlestibus beneficiis cœlesti ratione totum exercetur: quòd Lex, qua regnum istud gubernatur, spiritualis est, utpote quam Spiritus S. ipse author ejus, cordi inscribit, & quæ cultum Dei verum & spiritualem præcipit, nec ab aliis, quàm à spiritualibus impletur, & æternam, cœlestem vitam promittit: quòd cultus Regi Christo debitus totus internus & spiritualis, Joh. IV.24. 1.Pet. II.5. quòd Subditi sunt spirituales, 1.Cor. II.15. Gal. VI.1. Homo interior & abscónditus, in spiritu, non litera, Rom. II.29. Spiritu Deo servientes, Phil. III.3. occultus cordis homo, 1.Pet. III.4. ex Dei Spiritu regeniti, Joh. III.5. Spiritu adversus carnem belligerantes, Gal. V.17. quorum corpora etiam spiritualia erunt, 1.Cor. XV.43.44. quòd bona omnia in Regno hoc collata, honos, divitiæ, sapientia, justitia, deliciæ, gaudium, esca, potus, caro & sanguis Christi, illa edenda, hic bibendus, &c. interna & spiritualia, cœlestia, non externa, conspicabilia, & terrestria sunt, uti vidimus: quòd media, per quæ ad Christum Regem venimus, & cum eodem unimur, Verbum Dei, Spiritus ejus, fides, spiritualia omnia sunt: quòd denique etiam hostes hujus Regni, quos Christus debellare, & sub pedibus suorum conterere habet, sunt Spiritualia nequitiæ in supercœlestibus, Ephes. VI.12. Regnum scilicet Sathanæ, Regno Christi è diametro oppositum, cujus Rex est tenebrarum Princeps, Col. I.13. qui latente spirituali nequitia, tyrannide, fraudibus & impostúris imperium suum plantavit, profert, & in æterna morte finiet. Sicut enim Diabolus, Princeps hujus mundi, in conscientiis hominum per ignorantiam & contumaciam adversus Deum invisibiliter regnat: ita Christus Rex Ecclesiæ, triumphato per mortem crucis Diabolo, in cordibus fidelium per fidem, charitatem & perseverantiam in bono regnat.
units.tr: CV. Besides these testimonies, others also show the inner spiritual and heavenly character of this kingdom. It is called the kingdom of heaven and kingdom of God because it is heavenly with respect to its King, who is the true God, reigning immediately, who comes from above and is over all (John 3:31). He is the Lord from heaven (1 Cor. 15:47), the King of glory (Ps. 24:7), the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8). It is heavenly with respect to its origin, since it is established not by human counsels but by heavenly wisdom and reason; with respect to its state, since it is wholly occupied with heavenly, divine and mystical things; and with respect to its action, since everything is carried out in the heavenly dispensing of heavenly benefits. The law by which this kingdom is governed is spiritual, since the Holy Spirit himself, its author, writes it on the heart. It prescribes the true and spiritual worship of God, is fulfilled by none but spiritual people, and promises eternal, heavenly life. The worship owed to Christ the King is wholly inward and spiritual (John 4:24; 1 Pet. 2:5). Its subjects are spiritual (1 Cor. 2:15; Gal. 6:1). The inward and hidden man is in the spirit, not the letter (Rom. 2:29). They serve God in the Spirit (Phil. 3:3); the hidden man of the heart (1 Pet. 3:4); those born again of God's Spirit (John 3:5). They fight against the flesh with the Spirit (Gal. 5:17), and their bodies will also be spiritual (1 Cor. 15:43-44). All the good things conferred in this kingdom (honour, riches, wisdom, righteousness, delights, joy, food, drink, the flesh and blood of Christ, to be eaten there and drunk here, etc.) are inward, spiritual and heavenly, not outward, visible and earthly, as we have seen. The means by which we come to Christ the King and are united with him, the Word of God, his Spirit, and faith, are all spiritual. Finally, the enemies of this kingdom, whom Christ must overcome and crush under his feet, are the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. 6:12). That is, the kingdom of Satan, diametrically opposed to the kingdom of Christ, whose king is the prince of darkness (Col. 1:13). Hidden in spiritual wickedness, he has established his rule by tyranny, fraud and deceit, extends it, and will end it in eternal death. For just as the Devil, the prince of this world, reigns invisibly in men's consciences through ignorance and obstinacy against God, so Christ, the King of the Church, having triumphed over the Devil through the death of the cross, reigns in the hearts of believers through faith, love and perseverance in good.

units.la: CVI. Hanc propriam Regni Christi indolem Judæi solidè ignorant. Nam externum, carnale, temporale, pomposum & conspicabile semel amissum, armis carnalibus à Messia recuperandum, latè proferendum, brevi tamen finiendum fingunt; neque altiores omnino spes animo suo volutant. Judæos imitati Pontificii de Regno temporali Christi variis inter se sententiis digladiantur: uti Vasquesii & Valentiæ in Thomæ 3.q.22. disputationes produnt. Quærunt enim: Utrum Christus secundum humanam naturam in omnes & singulas universos dominium habeat? Utrum jus Regis temporalis in omnes Mundi Monarchias ei competerit? Utrum jus Regium temporale saltem in Judæos ratione generationis carnalis obtinuerit? & similia. Reapse verò Regnum Christi in mundanum & temporale, cui in mundo Papa, supremus temporalium omnium dominus & arbiter pro Vicario Christi rectore, præsit, spiritualibus omnibus profligatis, pridem converterunt. Sed tantum abest, ut Christus externum in mundo Regnum erexerit, ut potiùs sacrorum illud Regnum, neque humanum, quod in Ecclesia adhuc extabat, abrogaverit, Sacerdotum thronos, & veterum Regulorum solium everterit, & ne ejus posthliminio erigendi occasio vel necessitas esset, carnalem illum cultum, meliori superinducto, deleverit, denique Regni ejus sedem ac palatium, Templum Hierosolymitanum, ejusque domicilium, Hierosolymam, everterit. Et ne in externo nomine & carne quisquam gloriaretur, carnalem illum populum repudiatum Cœlo solóque extorrem errare toto orbe jussit, & eidem gentium populum, velut suum, & spiritualiter à se regendum succenturiavit. Ideo Messiam Regem, sed mitem, vel pauperem pullo asinæ vectum Zacharias cap. IX.9. inducit. Et Deus ipse: Domus Jehudæ miserebor, & salvabo eos in Jehova Deo suo. At non salvabo eos arcu & gladio, & bello, & equis, & equitibus, Hos. I.7. Neque alium hunc Regem quàm externa specie contemptibilem, Esaj. LIII.2.3. &c. Occidendum ibid. & Psal. XXII.17. confodiendum, Zach. XII.10. sed percussurum tamen terram virga oris sui, & spiritu labiorum suorum interfecturum impios, Esaj. XI.4. non clamaturum, neque exaltaturum in platea vocem suam, ibid. XLII.2. Serpentis Diaboli caput contriturum, Genes. III.15. Familiis terræ benedicturum, ibid. XXII.18. justitiam, pacem, redemptionem spiritualè allaturum, Ps. LXXII.2.4.7.14. Dan. IX.24. peccata hominum affusis aquis puris expiaturum, Ezech. XXXVI.25. ut innumera ejusmodi præterearn. Neque etiam, quod Papæ gnathones somniant, spirituali imperio temporale Christus superinduxit, tum quia Christi, omnem licet in Coelo & terra potestatem, quatenus ad salutem Ecclesiæ illa refertur, nacti, officium Regium totum in regenda, salvanda & tutanda Ecclesia occupatum, temporali dominio, quod ad salutem Ecclesiæ non proficit, nil indiget: tum quia tantum abest, ut dominio ejusmodi polluerit, ut pauperrimus non habuerit, ubi caput reclinaret, Luc. IX.58. 2.Cor. VIII.9. & servus dominantium esset, Esaj. XLIX.7. Veniens in mundum, non ut sibi serviretur, sed ut ipse aliis ministraret, Matth. XX.28. Et fugiens eos, qui Regem ipsum creare paraverant, Joh. VI.15. tum quia nemini de Principatu temporali controversiam unquam movit, quin potius Reges gentium in jure suo confirmavit, Matth. XXV.21. & Cæsari dari, quæ Cæsaris sunt, jussit, ibid. XXII.21. tum quia Christus Rex temporalis nec electione, nec successione, nec belli jure, nec hæreditate, nec superioris donatione factus est. Nam quòd in mundum veniens, venisse eis τα ἴδια in propria, Ioh.I.11.dicitur, & creaturis omnibus ad Ecclesiæ salutem & protectionem liberè utitur, non eum Regem temporalem, sed Regem Coelestem & Omnipotentem Dominum arguit.
units.tr: CVI. The Jews utterly fail to grasp this proper character of Christ's kingdom. For they imagine that the outward, carnal, temporal, showy and visible kingdom, once lost, is to be recovered by the Messiah with carnal arms, extended widely, but to be brought to an end soon; nor do they entertain any higher hopes in their minds. Imitating the Jews, the Papists wrangle among themselves with various opinions about Christ's temporal kingdom, as the disputations of Vasquez and Valentia on Thomas, 3. q. 22, reveal. For they ask: Does Christ, according to his human nature, have dominion over each and every person? Does the right of a temporal king belong to him over all the monarchies of the world? Did the temporal kingly right over the Jews, at least, belong to him by reason of carnal descent? and similar questions. Indeed, they have long since turned the kingdom of Christ into a worldly and temporal one, over which the Pope, the supreme lord and arbiter of all temporal things, presides as ruler in place of Christ's Vicar, having destroyed all spiritual things. But so far was Christ from setting up an outward kingdom in the world that he rather abolished that sacred kingdom, which was not of this world but still existed in the Church. He overthrew the thrones of the priests and the seat of the old kings, and, so that there should be no occasion or need for its restoration, he destroyed that carnal worship by introducing a better one. Finally, he destroyed the seat and palace of his kingdom, the Temple of Jerusalem, and its dwelling place, Jerusalem. And lest anyone should glory in an outward name and in the flesh, he ordered that carnal people, rejected by heaven and exiled from their land, should wander over the whole world, and he put in their place the people of the Gentiles, as his own, to be ruled by him spiritually. Therefore Zechariah (9:9) introduces the Messiah as a King, but a meek one, poor and riding on a colt, the foal of an ass. And God himself says: I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and will save them by the Lord their God. But I will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by battle, nor by horses, nor by horsemen (Hos. 1:7). Nor is this King other than one despised in outward appearance (Isa. 53:2-3, etc.), to be slain (ibid.; Ps. 22:17), to be pierced (Zech. 12:10), but who will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and slay the wicked with the breath of his lips (Isa. 11:4); who will not cry out, nor lift up his voice in the street (ibid. 42:2); who will crush the head of the serpent, the Devil (Gen. 3:15); who will bless the families of the earth (ibid. 22:18); who will bring righteousness, peace and spiritual redemption (Ps. 72:2, 4, 7, 14; Dan. 9:24); who will cleanse the sins of men by sprinkling clean water (Ezek. 36:25), and countless others of this kind I pass over. Nor did Christ, as the Pope's flatterers dream, add a temporal dominion to a spiritual rule. This is so, first, because Christ, having obtained all power in heaven and on earth, insofar as it relates to the salvation of the Church, occupies his whole kingly office in ruling, saving and protecting the Church, and has no need of temporal dominion, which does not benefit the salvation of the Church. Second, because he was so far from being polluted by such dominion that, being most poor, he had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58; 2 Cor. 8:9), and was the servant of those who rule (Isa. 49:7). He came into the world not to be served, but to serve others (Matt. 20:28), and he fled from those who were about to make him king (John 6:15). Third, because he never stirred up a dispute about temporal principality with anyone, but rather confirmed kings of the nations in their right, and ordered that the things that are Caesar's be given to Caesar (Matt. 22:21; cf. 25:21). Fourth, because Christ was never made a temporal king by election, succession, the right of war, inheritance, or the gift of a superior. For when he came into the world, it is said that he came to his own [τὰ ἴδια] (John 1:11), and he freely uses all creatures for the salvation and protection of the Church. This shows that he is not a temporal king but the heavenly King and Almighty Lord.

units.la: CVII. Neque etiam Judæorum, pro temporali Messiæ Regno argumenta pondus habent. Nam quæ illi crudè nimis & κατὰ σάρκα accipiunt; velut cum passim Regnum Christi regibus corporalibus adumbratur; mysticè & spiritualiter, modo loquendi ex forma humana desumpto, quem ipsi דרך של בני אדם & בלשון בני אדם appellant, interpretanda esse, facilè liquet, tum quia in Scriptura, Prophetarum inprimis, multa mysticè intelligenda esse adeò non inficiantur ipsi, ut nihil apud eos interpretatione tali frequentius sit: tum quia de Messiæ Regno temporali sensum exilem, vel nullum; de spirituali amplissimum & salutarem maximè fundunt: tum quia temporale & transitorium, & mundano cuivis simile Messiæ Regnum tanti non fuit, ut à principio mundi, omnibus Patribus tam πλυμερῶς & πολυτρόπως prædici debuerit; at spirituale omnes & singulos fideles concernit, & universum pœne mundum implicat: tum quia ad literam expohita ἀτοπα, ἀσυμφωνα, naturæ, verbo, voluntati & legi Dei atque rationi adversantia multa involvunt. Cujusmodi incommodis vitandis ipsi Judæi ad sensus mysticos convolare solent. Talia sunt, quæ de lupo & agno unà commorantibus, &c. Esaj.XI.6.7.8.de altari in media terra Ægypti, ibid. cap.xix.19. de quinque civitatibus in Ægypto, lingua Chananæa loquentibus, ibid.v.18. de suffimento in omni loco offerendo, Malach.I.11. aliàque ejusmodi plurima prædicuntur. Promissio porro Davidi de Semine ejus thronum ejus in perpetuum occupaturo, 2.Sam.VII.12. nec non Solomoni de throno Regni ejus in æternum stabiliendo, 1.Reg.IX.4.5. facta partim Davidi absolutè, spiritualiter intelligi debet, juxta Davidis ipsius sententiam, omne in eo beneplacitum testantis, quòd domus sua germinatura non sit, 2.Sam.XXIII.4.5. partim, quatenus Solomoni facta est, conditionem annexam habuit, si in præceptis Dei ambulaverit. Et vocatur etiam Regnum Messiæ passim Regnum Davidis, Israelis, sed spirituale illud, non temporale, sicut & ipse Messias, ceu à Davidis Regno figuratus, & ex ejus semine natus Davidis, sed spiritualis illius nomine, Ezech.XXXIV.23.24. Hos.III.5. venit. Hic dicet: Jehovæ ego sum, & ille invocabit in nomine Jacob. Et alius scribet manu sua: Jehovæ sum, בשם ישראל יכנה de nomine Israelis se nominabit, ascisçendus scilicet in Ecclesiam Israelis spiritualem; & Jacobi atque Israelis fidem professurus, Esaj.XLIV.5. Leve est præ ut sis mihi servus, erigere tribus Jacobi: & retentos Israelis reducere. Et dabo te in lucem gentium, ut fiat (perveniat) salus mea ad finem terræ, ib.XLIX.6. Regnum enim temporale Israelis in spirituale converti debuit, in quo non armis virisque, sed verbo & spiritu Christus regnare, spiritualia bona omnibus credentibus impertiri, spirituales hostes profligare debuit. Illo die erigam tugurium Davidis jacens (post ruinam Regni posterorum Davidis, dabo Davidi Semen promissum, Christum, in quo salutem & εὐδοκίαν suam David omnem fixit, 2.Sam.XXIII.5. & sepiam ruptúras illorum, & destructa ipsius (Davidis) resuscitabo (Christi Filii Davidis, corpus destructum resuscitabo) & ædificabo illud ut diebus sæculi, (in majestate & gloria non minore, imò majore, quam fuit tempore Davidis, Zach.XII.8.) ut hæreditent reliquias Edomi & omnium gentium super quibus nuncupatum fuerit nomen meum (ut omnes familiæ terræ fiant Semen Abrahami, & Abrahamus hæres mundi; peculium Christi) ait Jehova faciens hoc, Amos IX.11.12. Parabola porro illa duorum baculorum nominibus Josephi & Judæ inscribendorum, ut fiant in manu ipsius unus baculus, seu unum lignum continuum; hoc est, duorum Regnorum seu sceptrorum in unum commutandorum, & ex omnibus gentibus colligendorum, atque in terram suam adducendorum, ut fiant gens una in terra in montibus Israel, & Rex unus ipsis sit, & servus Dei David Rex super ipsis sit, & Pastor unus omnibus, Ezech.XXXVII.19-25. non temporale Regnum sub Rege temporali Messia, sed post unionem tribuum in terram Canaan Babylone & ex aliis captivitatis locis reducum mox secuturum Regnum spirituale, sub uno Rege & Pastore, Christo, Davidis Filio, portendit. Loquitur enim de Regno novo, quod erit Regnum justitiæ: de Pastore uno, v.24. cujus est mori pro grege suo, & de salvandis Israelitis ex omnibus habitationibus ipsorum, in quibus peccarunt & iisdem purificandis, ut sint Deo populus, & Deus illis Deus sit, v.23. nec non iisdem in judiciis Dei ambulaturis & statuta Dei observaturis, v.24. denique promittit, fore, ut cum iis pangat fœdus pacis, fœdus sæculi, & det Sanctuarium suum in medio eorum in sæculum (de quo fusius cap.xL. &c. sermo est) & habitet super ipsis (ut singuli ejus templum sint) & sit ipsis Deus, & illi sibi populus, v.26.27. & ut sic cognoscant gentes, quòd Jehova sanctificet Israelem, cum sanctuarium ejus in medio eorum erit in sæculum, v.28. Quæ omnia Regnum Messiæ à temporali, quale Davidis erat, vehementer distinctum sonant. Nec majoris momenti illud est, quòd Judæi omnes Gogi & Magogi bellum, Ezech. XXXVIII. XXXIX. à Messia gerendum esse, neque abeo, nisi temporali Rege, geri posse objectant. Falluntur enim vehementer, cum Prophetiam illam de Rege & Pastore uno cum bello adversus Gogum & Magogum connectentes, à Messia bellum illud gerendum esse asserunt. Gogi & Magogi nominibus hostes Ecclesiæ, quales-cunque illi, sive Turcæ, sive Antichristiani insinuantur, quibuscum bello decernere non Messias, ut Rex & Imperator temporalis, sed Ecclesiæ Reges, Nutritii & Patroni, sub auspiciis tamen Messiæ, ut Regis Coelestis, non terrestris, ut Jehovæ, non ut meri hominis, ut אל Vindicis & Assertoris Seminis sui (unde Judæi Gogi expeditionem בימי נאלה in diebus ἀνταλλήψεως seu vindicationis ex manu hostium per Messiam ponunt) non ut qualiscunque Bellatoris hominis, debuerunt. Et sic dixit Dominus Deus: Ecce ego ad te Gog, princeps primarie Mesech & Tubal. Et reducam te, & dabo hamos in maxillas tuas, &c. cap.XXXVIII.3.4. Vocabo contra ipsum in omnes montes meos gladium, dictum Domini Dei. Gladius viri in fratrem suum erit; Et disceptabo cum ipso peste, &c. Et cognoscent, quòd ego sim Jehova. v. 21.22.23. Messiam verò veluti a Jehova eo distinctum, vel sub Jehova carnalibus armis adversus Gogum conflicturum nusquam Prophetia innuit.
units.tr: Nor do the arguments of the Jews for a temporal kingdom of the Messiah carry any weight. They take many things crudely and "according to the flesh" (κατὰ σάρκα) that, wherever the kingdom of Christ is foreshadowed by earthly kings, must be interpreted mystically and spiritually, in the manner of speech taken from human custom, which they themselves call "the way of the sons of men" [דרך של בני אדם] and "the language of the sons of men" [בלשון בני אדם]. This is easily shown. First, the Jews themselves do not deny that many things in Scripture, especially in the Prophets, are to be understood mystically; indeed nothing is more common among them than such interpretation. Second, they draw from the Messiah's temporal kingdom only a meagre sense, or none at all, while from his spiritual kingdom they draw a very rich and saving meaning. Third, a temporal and transitory kingdom of the Messiah, like any worldly kingdom, was not so important that it should have been foretold from the beginning of the world by all the Fathers so many times and in so many ways (πολυμερῶς and πολυτρόπως). But a spiritual kingdom concerns all and each of the faithful and embraces almost the whole world. Fourth, if the words are expounded literally, they involve many absurdities (ἄτοπα) and inconsistencies (ἄσυμφωνα), things at odds with the nature of things, with the word of God, with his will and law, and with reason. To avoid these difficulties the Jews themselves are accustomed to take refuge in mystical senses. Of this kind are the things said of the wolf and the lamb dwelling together (Isa. XI.6-8), of an altar in the middle of the land of Egypt (Isa. XIX.19), of five cities in Egypt speaking the language of Canaan (Isa. XIX.18), of incense to be offered in every place (Mal. I.11), and many other similar things that are foretold. Moreover, the promise made to David that one of his seed would occupy his throne forever (2 Sam. VII.12), and the promise to Solomon that his royal throne would be established forever (1 Kings IX.4-5), were partly made to David absolutely and must be understood spiritually, according to David's own judgement, when he testifies that in him there is every delight, since his house would not sprout forth (2 Sam. XXIII.4-5). Partly, insofar as it was made to Solomon, it had a condition attached: if he walked in the precepts of God. The kingdom of the Messiah is also called everywhere the kingdom of David and of Israel, but it is that spiritual kingdom, not a temporal one, just as the Messiah himself came not as one shaped after the kingdom of David and born of his seed in the mere sense of a David, but in the name of the spiritual David (Ezek. XXXIV.23-24; Hos. III.5). "Here one will say: I am of the LORD, and he will call upon the name of Jacob. And another will write with his own hand, I am the LORD's, and he will call himself by the name of Israel" [בשם ישראל יכנה], that is, he will be taken into the spiritual Church of Israel, and will profess the faith of Jacob and of Israel (Isa. XLIV.5). "It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and restore the preserved of Israel. I will also give you for a light to the Gentiles, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth" (Isa. XLIX.6). For the temporal kingdom of Israel had to be turned into a spiritual one, in which Christ would reign not with arms and men but with the word and the Spirit, would impart spiritual goods to all who believe, and would overthrow spiritual enemies. "In that day I will raise up the fallen tabernacle of David" (after the ruin of the kingdom of David's descendants I will give to David the promised seed, Christ, in whom David placed all his salvation and all his delight, 2 Sam. XXIII.5). "And I will repair their breaches, and I will raise up its ruins (that is, the ruined body of Christ, the Son of David, I will raise up), and I will build it as in the days of old" (in a majesty and glory not less, but greater, than in the time of David, Zech. XII.8), "that they may possess the remnant of Edom and of all the nations over whom my name is called" (so that all the families of the earth become the seed of Abraham, and Abraham the heir of the world, the peculiar people of Christ), says the LORD who does this (Amos IX.11-12). Further, that parable of the two sticks to be inscribed with the names of Joseph and Judah, so that they become one stick in his hand, or one continuous piece of wood (that is, two kingdoms or sceptres to be changed into one, and gathered from all nations and brought into their own land, so that they become one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel, and have one king, and David, the servant of God, be king over them, and one shepherd for all: Ezek. XXXVII.19-25), does not foretell a temporal kingdom under a temporal king Messiah, but a spiritual kingdom that will follow soon after the union of the tribes in the land of Canaan, with those returned from Babylon and other places of captivity, under one king and shepherd, Christ, the Son of David. For it speaks of a new kingdom which will be a kingdom of righteousness; of one shepherd (v. 24), whose office is to die for his flock; and of the saving of the Israelites from all their dwelling places in which they sinned, and the cleansing of the same, so that they may be God's people and God may be their God (v. 23); and likewise of their walking in the judgements of God and keeping his statutes (v. 24). Finally, it promises that he will make with them a covenant of peace, an everlasting covenant, and will set his sanctuary in their midst forever (a matter discussed more fully in chapters XL and following), and will dwell among them (so that each of them is his temple), and will be their God and they his people (vv. 26-27); and so the nations will know that the LORD sanctifies Israel, when his sanctuary is in their midst forever (v. 28). All these things sound strongly as if the kingdom of the Messiah were distinct from a temporal kingdom such as that of David. Nor is it of greater weight that the Jews object that the war against Gog and Magog (Ezek. XXXVIII-XXXIX) must be waged by the Messiah, and that this cannot be done except by a temporal king. They are greatly mistaken, for in connecting that prophecy of one king and shepherd with the war against Gog and Magog, they assert that the Messiah must wage that war. The names Gog and Magog indicate the enemies of the Church, whoever they are, whether Turks or Antichristians; in waging war against them, the Messiah ought not to act as a temporal king and emperor, but the kings, nurses and patrons of the Church should do so, under the auspices of the Messiah as a heavenly king, not an earthly one, as Jehovah and not as a mere man, as El [אל], the avenger and defender of his seed (whence the Jews place the expedition against Gog in the days of deliverance [בימי נאלה], that is, of rescue (ἀνταλλήψεως) from the hand of enemies through the Messiah), and not as any warrior of a human kind. And so the Lord God said: "Behold, I am against you, Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. And I will turn you about and put hooks into your jaws," etc. (Ezek. XXXVIII.3-4). "I will call a sword against him on all my mountains, says the Lord God. Every man's sword will be against his brother; and I will plead against him with pestilence," etc. "And they shall know that I am the LORD" (vv. 21-23). But nowhere does the prophecy indicate the Messiah as distinct from Jehovah in this way, or as fighting against Gog with carnal arms under Jehovah.

units.la: CVIII. Spirituale Regnum Christi gubernatione populi sui, & ejusdem defensione contra omnes hostes constat.
units.tr: CVIII. The spiritual kingdom of Christ consists in the governing of his people and in its defence against all enemies.

units.la: Has enim duas partes sessio Christi ad dextram Patris complectitur. Dixit Jehova Domino meo: Sede ad dextram meam, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Virgam roboris tui mittet Jehova e Sione, &c. Dominus ad dextram tuam in die irae suae deflixit Reges. Judicat in gentibus; plenum est cadaveribus, &c. Psal.CX.1.2.5.6. Oportet ipsum regnare usque dum ponat inimicos scabellum pedum ejus; Ultimus hostis abolebitur mors, 1.Cor.XV.25.26. Est autem Gubernatio populi Christi externa vel interna: Externa Verbo Legis & Evangelii inprimis perficitur. Virgam roboris tui mittet Jehova e Sione, Psal.CX.2. Habet enim Christus ‎מטה עז Virgam, sceptrum roboris: quod est Lex Christi, Evangelium, potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom.I.16. E Sione exibit Lex, & verbum Jehovae de Jerusalem, Esaj.II.3. Mich.IV.2. Hoc sceptrum robustum est, quia agitatur brachio Domini, Esaj.LII.10. LVIII.1. cujus proinvis & a Spiritu S. comite; quo duce & comite missum in totum terrarum orbem, praedicatur tanta cum efficacia, ut Christo servandos subjiciat. Nam ipse Jehova sceptrum hoc emittit, atque illud per potentiam Spiritus S. efficax reddit. Et stabit, & pascet in robore Domini, & in elatione nominis Dei sui, Mich.V.4. Verbo, quo nomen & virtutes Dei indicantur; Hoc verbo Christus voluntatem suam, refipiscentiam, fidem & novam obedientiam imperat. Approximavit Regnum Dei. Resipiscite & credite Evangelio, Marc.I.15. Interna per Spiritus S. efficaciam peragitur. Nam Christus Spiritu suo verbum potens & efficax reddit, mentes illuminat, Joh.VI.45. ad cognitionem veritatis ducit, ibid.XVI.13. resipiscentiam, fidem, novam obedientiam operatur, Act.V.31. Legem cordibus suorum inscribit, Jer.XXXI.33. Utroque se gubernari petit David. Priore sic orans: Rege me, Domine, secundum verbum tuum, Psal.CXIX.116.169. Posteriore, dicens: Spiritus tuus bonus dirigat me via plana, ib.CXLIII.10.
units.tr: For the session of Christ at the right hand of the Father embraces these two parts: "The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool. The LORD shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion, etc. The Lord at thy right hand shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath. He shall judge among the nations; he shall fill the places with the dead bodies, etc." Ps. 110:1, 2, 5, 6. "He must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet. The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death," 1 Cor. 15:25, 26. The governing of Christ's people is external or internal. The external is carried out chiefly by the Word of the Law and of the Gospel. "The LORD shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion," Ps. 110:2. For Christ has the rod of strength [מטה עז], the sceptre of power, which is the Law of Christ, the Gospel, "the power of God unto salvation to everyone that believeth," Rom. 1:16. "Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem," Isa. 2:3; Mic. 4:2. This sceptre is strong, because it is wielded by the arm of the Lord, Isa. 52:10; 53:1, whose companion and comrade is the Holy Spirit. Sent through the whole world under the leading and companionship of the Spirit, it is preached with such efficacy that it brings those who are to be saved into subjection to Christ. For Jehovah himself sends forth this sceptre and renders it effective through the power of the Holy Spirit. "And he shall stand and feed in the strength of the LORD, in the majesty of the name of the LORD his God," Mic. 5:4. By the Word, in which the name and powers of God are declared, Christ commands his will, repentance, faith and new obedience: "The kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel," Mark 1:15. The internal governing is carried out through the efficacy of the Holy Spirit. For Christ, by his Spirit, makes the Word powerful and effective, enlightens minds, John 6:45, leads them to the knowledge of the truth, ibid. 16:13, and works repentance, faith and new obedience, Acts 5:31. "I will put my law in their inward parts," Jer. 31:33. David asks to be governed in both ways: in the former, praying thus: "Order my steps in thy word," Ps. 119:116, 169; in the latter, saying: "Thy good Spirit shall lead me into the land of uprightness," ibid. 143:10.

units.la: CIX. Defensio populi Christi est, qua is eundem contra omnes hostes potenter tuetur & conservat.
units.tr: CIX. The defence of Christ's people is that by which he powerfully protects and preserves them against all enemies.

units.la: Non simplex enim hostium genus Ecclesia infestum habet; Sathanam & inferorum portas, seu robur omne, mundum, carnem, seu intestina vitia, hominemque sibi parum concordem, & mortem. Hi enim partim tentationibus suis & interno tumultu fideles solicitant, partim externa vi & terrore continuè infestant. Adversus tentationes Sathanae, mundi & carnis eos partim verbo, partim Spiritu suo tuetur. Illo promittit & minatur, acclamans identidem: Quisquis me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, & ego eum confitebor coram Patre meo, qui est in Coelis. Quisquis vero me negaverit coram hominibus, eum etiam negabo coram Patre meo, qui est in Coelis, Matth.X.32.33. Hoc tum confervat fidem, ne plane deficiat, Luc.XXII.32. tum timorem Domini in cordibus eorum confirmat, ne ab ipso recedant, Jer.XXXII.40. tum veterem illum hominem, qui contra spiritum concupiscit, mortificat, Rom.VIII.13. Gal.V.17. Contra violentiam Sathanae, qui ceu lupus infernalis, assiduè Dominicum ovile circumgemit, nec non mundi & mortis sic eos tuetur, ut partim irritum faciat consilium gentium, irritas reddat cogitationes populorum, Psal.XXXIII.10. partim frangat eorum potentiam, ne quantum cupiunt, noceant, vulnerans in die furoris sui Reges, defligens caput super terram amplam, ibid.CX.5.6: comminuens & consumens (velut dissipando, infar paleae ventilando, atque glumas a frumento separando) omnia Regna reliqua, Dan.II.44. & Ecclesiam ponens ‎אבן lapidem onerosum omnibus populis, quo quicunque se onerant, (conantur eum sustollere) lacerando lacerantur, seu incidendo inciduntur, Zach.XII.3. partim eosdem prorsus aboleat in consummatione seculorum. Ubi & Sathanam suis & fidelium pedibus subjiciet, Rom.XVI.20. & mundum, seu inimicos scabellum pedum suorum ponet, Psal.CX.1. mortem denique, hostem ultimum, in victoriam absorbebit, 1.Cor.XV.26.54.
units.tr: For the Church does not have a single kind of enemy hostile to it: Satan and the gates of hell, or all strength, the world, the flesh, or the inward vices, and man, who is not wholly at one with himself, and death. For these partly harass the faithful by their temptations and inward tumult, partly constantly assail them with external force and terror. Against the temptations of Satan, the world and the flesh, he protects them partly by his Word, partly by his Spirit. By the Word he promises and threatens, crying out repeatedly: "Whosoever shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven. But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven," Matt. 10:32, 33. This both preserves faith, so that it does not utterly fail, Luke 22:32, and confirms "the fear of the Lord in their hearts, that they may not depart from him," Jer. 32:40, and mortifies that old man who "lusts against the Spirit," Rom. 8:13; Gal. 5:17. Against the violence of Satan, who like a infernal wolf ever prowls around the Lord's fold, and likewise against the world and death, he so protects them that he partly "makes void the counsel of the nations and brings to nought the devices of the peoples," Ps. 33:10, and partly breaks their power, so that they cannot harm as much as they desire, "wounding the kings in the day of his wrath, and striking through the head over a wide land," ibid. 110:5, 6; grinding and consuming (as by scattering, or winnowing like chaff, and separating the husks from the grain) all the remaining kingdoms, Dan. 2:44; and setting the Church as a stone, a burden to all peoples, by which whoever burdens himself (who tries to lift it) is torn in pieces by it, or cut by its cutting, Zech. 12:3. Partly he will utterly abolish these same enemies at the consummation of the ages. There he will also put Satan under the feet of his own and of the faithful, Rom. 16:20, and will set the world, or his enemies, as a footstool for his feet, Ps. 110:1; finally he will swallow up death, the last enemy, in victory, 1 Cor. 15:26, 54.

units.la: CX. Sicut Jesus Christus heri, hodie & in secula idem est: ita etiam Rex perpetuus est, & erit, & Regnum ejus aeternum est. Est enim ‎אבי עד Pater aeternitatis, Esaj.IX.6. Firmabo solium Regni ejus usque in seculum, 2.Sam.VII.13. Solium tuum, Deus, in seculum & seculum, Psal.XLV.7. Temporibus Regum illorum suscitabit Deus Coeli Regnum, quod in secula non destruitur, & Regnum ipsum populo alieno non relinquetur; comminuet & consumet omnia illa Regna, ipsum autem perstabit in secula, Dan.II.44.&c. Regni ejus non erit finis, Luc.I.33. Nam & Rex aeternus est, ‎πάντοτε ζῶν semper vivens, Hebr.VII.25. nec mori amplius potest, Rom.VI.9.10. & Populus aeternus est, quem nemo vel ex manibus ejus rapiet, Joh.X.28. vel a charitate Dei separabit, Rom.VIII.35. & Regimen ipsum populi hujus aeternum est, per immediatam & immutabilem Dei operationem, 1.Cor.XV.28. Licèt enim in Coelesti gloria hostes Ecclesiae nulli futuri sunt, adversus quos illa a Christo Rege defendi debeat; manebit tamen Ecclesia ut corpus, Christo ut capiti & Regi sic unita, ut ceu populus maximè spontaneus per obedientiam liberrimam Christo subsit, Spiritu ejus tota impleatur, & Regi suo atque Agno perpetua gratiarum actione & glorificatione ejus cohaereat.
units.tr: CX. As Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever, so also he is and will be a perpetual King, and his kingdom is eternal. For he is "the Father of eternity" [אבי עד], Isa. 9:6. "I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever," 2 Sam. 7:13. "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever," Ps. 45:6. "In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed; and the kingdom shall not be left to other people; it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever," Dan. 2:44, etc. "Of his kingdom there shall be no end," Luke 1:33. For he is an eternal King, ever living [πάντοτε ζῶν], Heb. 7:25, and can no more die, Rom. 6:9, 10; and the people is eternal, which no one shall snatch out of his hands, John 10:28, or separate from the love of God, Rom. 8:35; and the governing of this people is itself eternal, through the immediate and unchangeable operation of God, 1 Cor. 15:28. For although in heavenly glory there will be no enemies of the Church against whom it must be defended by Christ the King, nevertheless the Church will remain as a body, united to Christ as its head and King in such a way that, as a most willing people, it is subject to Christ through most free obedience, is wholly filled with his Spirit, and cleaves to its King and Lamb in perpetual thanksgiving and glorification of him.

units.la: CXI. Sed oeconomia tamen & administratio Regni aeterni licet differentiam recipit.
units.tr: CXI. But the economy and administration of the eternal kingdom admit of difference.

units.la: Nam in V. T. populum quidem Israelis, quasi proprium peculium, delegit ex omnibus populis, cui innotesceret, quem sub carnali disciplina haberet, & cujus electos cum paucis proselytis sanctificaret. Vos eritis mihi Regnum Sacerdotale & gens sancta, Exod.XIX.6. Sed singulari plane modo Christus Regnum istud administravit. Praeterquam quod, qua Deus, etiam civili imperio populo illi praefuit, atque ea in re spiritualis Regni sui sub V. T. typum gessit, uti supra Loc.XVI.7. ostendimus. Etiam in Ecclesiae V. T. Regno singulare & privum quid obtinuit, quatenus in eo sibi associavit Principes & potestatem habentes, qui subjicerent eundem populum, in quo seriem Dei continebatur. batur, elementis mundi, curámque gererent, ut Lex præcepti carnalis in vigore permaneret; quique eodem fine judicia exercerent. Dein constituit Sacerdotes, qui pecuinam & ἀλογον victimam pro populo offerrent, typum & umbram melioris sacrificii. Hos ad tempus induit, velut vestitum. Sed non erat hoc merè & verè Regnum Dei: neque dum hac facie Christus se obtulit, hominibus unius populi, & iis dominatus est, ea Dei בעילה δεσποτεία dominatio erat, quia Christus non solus Rex & princeps erat, neque ei soli, sine principibus, servis & rebus terrestribus, servire vera libertas erat. Neque etiam ibi tanta, quanta in Regno Dei eximiè dicto esse poterat, lætitia, dilectio & gratiarum actio fuit, cùm deessent, quæ ad severitatem potius, quàm ad gratiam referri deberent. Hæc igitur externa Regni Christi facies aboleri, &Principes ac Potestates sociæ ejus ἀπεκδυσάμενοι exui Col II.15. Christo in carnem adventante, debuerunt. Cujus rei præco fuit Johannes Baptista, dicens: Resipiscite. Appropinquavit enim Regnum Cœlorum, Matth. III.2. Ubi Regnum Christi vocatur Regnum Cœlorum, non tantùm ut, Dan. IV.34. quia Deus habere thronum in Cœlo, atque adeò non est in terra, ut homo, sed multò magis, quia est Regnum Dei Cœleste & non terrestre. Intelligitur modus gubernandi proprius Novo Testamento, quo Deus Ecclesiam sibi soli, & quidem in communione cœlestium quoad justitiam & libertatem subjicit. De quo Regno Christus dicit: A diebus Johannis Baptistæ usque nunc Regnum Cœlorum βιάζεται vim patitur, (vel agit) & βιασταὶ vim facientes, rapiunt illud, Matth. XI.12. Venit enim cum impetu quodam ad destructionem & abolitionem veteris illius formæ Regni sub V.T. quia Filius Dei ea facturus, quæ Prophetæ prædixerant, & Lex præmonstraverat, aderat: & ii etiam, qui ad Regnum illud pertinebant, magno animo, studio, cura, aviditate & fiducia, velut in certamine, subigentes carnem atque concupiscentiam, & omnia, quæ in mundo sunt, abnegantes, illud rapturiebant, ad se trahere coeperunt. Regnum isthoc habet suos profectus, ut paulatim latius & absolutius fiat. Auspicatus enim illud Christus est, quando ad dextram Dei sedens Spiritum S. in Apostolos effudit, qua effusione quodammodo à Patre unctus & Christus atque Dominus factus est, Act. II.36. quia is actus Christi & pleno jure Domini fuit. Effusionem illam ministeriorum ad concinnationem corporis ejus constitutio, Ephes. IV.10-13. secuta est; quorum interpolatio, ex ministerio in principatum mutatio à Bestia & Antichristo facta, ejusdem Regni Christi φθορὰ corruptio Apoc. XI.8. fuit. Accedit assumptio populi ex gentibus, & Regni à Judæis ablatio. Aliter etiam Christus regnavit hactenus inter hostes, aliter, ubi hostes ejus scabellum pedum ejus positi fuerint. Id verò Christus hactenus in medio hostium, inter quos est Sathanas, vetus homo, Antichristus, & ultimus, mors; verbo & Spiritu suo regnans effecit, ut de medio tolleretur Politia Judæorum, Draco seu Diabolus, populum Romanum adversus Ecclesiam incitans, de throno suo concedere cogeretur, & vinculis constringeretur, ne amplius gentes seduceret; ut Ecclesia post longum bellum cum Bestia, in quo Sancti victi, seu, illibata eorum fide & sanctitate, oppressi sunt, resurgeret; Evangelium æternum prædicaretur; ipsa ex Babylone educeretur: Babylon cadere inciperet, & porta plurimis, si Babylone exire velint, pateret. Hucusque Regnum illud Cœlorum promotum est, expectantibus & enixis votis ac desideriis nostris acceleranti-bus nobis tempus illud, quo omne Regnum adversarium profligabitur, ut Christus ubique regnet, & tandem subactis hostibus Christi omnibus adveniat Regnum Gloriæ, ac nos quidem liberemur à corpore mortis, ut simus cum Christo, & appetat ultimus dies, quo etiam corpora nostra ad se assumpturus est.
units.tr: For under the Old Testament God chose from all peoples the people of Israel, as his own peculiar treasure, that he might make himself known to them, rule them under a carnal discipline, and sanctify their elect together with a few proselytes: You shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, Exod. 19.6. Yet Christ administered this kingdom in a singular and quite distinctive way. Besides, as God he also presided over that people with civil authority, and in this respect bore the type of his spiritual kingdom under the Old Testament, as we showed above, Loc. 16.7. In the Old Testament kingdom of the Church, too, he obtained something singular and private, inasmuch as he associated with himself princes and rulers who were to subject that same people, in whom the line of God was contained, and who were to take care, under the elements of the world, that the law of carnal precept remain in force; and who by the same purpose were to exercise judgments. Then he appointed priests, who were to offer for the people a victim of sheep and cattle, a type and shadow of the better sacrifice. These he put on for a time, as a garment. But this was not the true and proper kingdom of God; nor, while Christ presented himself in this form and ruled over the men of one people, was it the lordship of God [δεσποτεία], because Christ was not the sole King and Prince, and true freedom was not to serve him alone, without princes, servants and earthly things. Nor was there then as much joy, love and thanksgiving as could properly be expected in the kingdom of God, since those things were lacking which ought to be attributed rather to severity than to grace. Therefore this external appearance of Christ's kingdom had to be abolished, and his princes and powers, having put off (ἀπεκδυσάμενοι) their rule, had to be stripped of it, Col. 2.15, when Christ came in the flesh. John the Baptist was the herald of this matter, saying: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand, Matt. 3.2. Here the kingdom of Christ is called the kingdom of heaven, not only in the sense of Dan. 4.34, because God has his throne in heaven and so is not on earth as man is, but much more because it is the heavenly and not the earthly kingdom of God. The mode of governing proper to the New Testament is understood, by which God subjects the Church to himself alone, and indeed in fellowship with the heavenly ones as regards righteousness and freedom. Of this kingdom Christ says: From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence (or acts), and violent men (βιασταί) seize it, Matt. 11.12. For it came with a certain impetus for the destruction and abolition of that old form of the kingdom under the Old Testament, because the Son of God, about to do the things the prophets had foretold and the law had prefigured, was present; and those too who belonged to that kingdom, with great courage, zeal, care, eagerness and confidence, as in a contest, subduing the flesh and concupiscence and renouncing all that is in the world, began to draw it to themselves and seize it [βιάζεται, βιασταὶ, ἁρπάζουσιν]. This kingdom has its advances, so that it gradually becomes wider and more complete. For Christ inaugurated it when, sitting at the right hand of God, he poured out the Holy Spirit on the Apostles, by which outpouring he was in a certain way anointed by the Father and made Christ and Lord, Acts 2.36, because that act was the act of the Christ and Lord with full right. The outpouring was followed by the appointment of ministries for the building up of his body, Eph. 4.10-13; and the corruption of these, the change from ministry into principality made by the Beast and Antichrist, was a destruction [φθορά] of this very kingdom of Christ, Rev. 11.8. Added to this is the taking up of the people from the Gentiles and the removal of the kingdom from the Jews. Hitherto Christ has also reigned in one way amid his enemies, and in another way when his enemies shall have been placed as a footstool for his feet. Now hitherto Christ, reigning by his word and Spirit in the midst of his enemies, among whom are Satan, the old man, Antichrist, and last of all death, has brought it about that the polity of the Jews was taken out of the way, that the dragon or devil, who stirred up the Roman people against the Church, was forced to give up his throne and was bound in chains, so that he could no longer lead the nations astray; that the Church should rise again after the long war with the Beast, in which the saints were conquered, or, though their faith and holiness remained unimpaired, were oppressed; that the eternal Gospel should be preached; that the Church herself should be led out of Babylon; that Babylon should begin to fall, and a door should stand open to many, if they wish to go out of Babylon. Thus far that kingdom of heaven has been advanced, while we, with expectant and eager prayers and longings, hasten that time in which every adverse kingdom will be overthrown, so that Christ may reign everywhere, and at last, when Christ's enemies have all been subdued, the kingdom of glory may come, and we indeed may be freed from the body of death, so that we may be with Christ; and the last day may draw near, on which he will also take our bodies up to himself.

units.la: CXII.
units.tr: CXII.

units.la: Ac ne in Cœlo quidem post finem mundi Christus Regnum suum Mediatorium abdicabit; vel ipse à Deo Patre Regno eo exue-tur. Nam Regnum ejus æternum esse supra probavimus. Sedebit nempe Christus ad dextram Dei εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς in perpetuum, Hebr. X.12. adeóque etiam regnabit in perpetuum; quia sessio Mediatoris ad dextram Dei ejusdem Regni Mediatorii gloriosa functio est. Et eodem in æternum etiam fungitur. Licet enim actio Mediatoris meritoria cessaret, & cessare debuerit, quia alias imperfecta, adeóque meritoria non esset; tamen voluntas illius, qua postulat hæreditatem, & bonum hæreditatis suæ, non cessabit. Profligatis universis hostibus Regni illius, consummata, neque ulla potestate adversaria unquam turbanda ejus tranquillitas & gloria erit. Idem Regnum erit, sed facies ejus & gubernatio non turbida iterum, & vicissitudinibus distincta, sed pacata, gloriosa, æquabilis & immutabilis erit. Christus dicit: Ego vitam æternam do ipsis, Joh. X.28. Ego sum vita, ibid. XI.25. XIV.6. Scriptura de eodem testatur, in ipso est vita, ibid. I.4. Filius habet vitam in se, & vivificat, quem vult, ibid. V.26.21. Quæ clarissimè indicant, Christum vivificare in æternum & merito, & potentiæ suæ efficacia, adeóque habere Regnum æternum. Aliud proin etiam in Cœlesti gloria Regnum Christi Mediatorium, aliud ejusdem cum Patre & Spiritu S. commune Regnum naturale, seu essentiale erit. Illi sola Ecclesia suberit: huic etiam Diabolus, Angeli ejus, & damnati omnes suberunt. Sed cessabunt, ut diximus, hostes, qui Ecclesiam denuo perturbent, vel corrumpant. Cessabit in Ecclesia illud, quod est ἐκ μέρους ex parte; cessabit id, quod hactenus impediit, quò minùs omnia implerentur cœlesti gloria, & Deus omnia esset in omnibus, vitiositas, caro, corruptio, lucta, mors: cessabit denique illa Regni S.S. Trinitatis communis seu naturalis ordinatio ad Regnum Christi Mediatorium, utpote non ultra necessaria, quàm quoad Ecclesiæ salus novissimo die per glorificationem consummata, & ad metam perducta fuerit. Hac cessante Regni Christi œconomia cum imperfectione ejusmodi conjuncta, non cessabit, sed initium capiet & æternùm durabit œconomia ejusdem gloriosa, cum πληρώσει impletione Ecclesiæ, quæ Deo, qui omnia in omnibus erit, plena, Christo Regi & capiti suo conjunctissima, eidem per amorem & voluntariam obedientiam, gratiarum actionem & glorificationem ejus in æternum serviet.
units.tr: Nor will Christ lay down his mediatorial kingdom even in heaven after the end of the world, nor will it be taken from him by God the Father. For we have shown above that his kingdom is eternal. He will sit at the right hand of God forever [εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς], Heb. 10:12, and so he will also reign forever, since the Mediator's sitting at the right hand of God is a glorious function of that same mediatorial kingdom, and he performs it eternally. For although the meritorious action of the Mediator will cease, and ought to cease (otherwise it would be imperfect and so not meritorious), his will, by which he claims his inheritance and the good of his inheritance, will not cease. When all the enemies of that kingdom have been overthrown, its tranquillity and glory will be complete and never again disturbed by any hostile power. It will be the same kingdom, but its aspect and government will no longer be turbulent and divided by changes; it will be peaceful, glorious, even and unchanging. Christ says: I give them eternal life, John 10:28; I am the life, ibid. 11:25, 14:6. Scripture bears witness to the same: in him is life, ibid. 1:4; the Son has life in himself and gives life to whom he will, ibid. 5:26, 21. These passages most clearly indicate that Christ gives life eternally, both by his merit and by the efficacy of his power, and so possesses an eternal kingdom. Therefore in the heavenly glory there will be one kingdom of Christ as Mediator, and another, the common natural or essential kingdom which he shares with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The former will be subject to the Church alone; the latter will be subject also to the Devil, his angels, and all the damned. But, as we have said, the enemies who would again disturb or corrupt the Church will cease. There will cease in the Church what is ex parte [ἐκ μέρους], in part; there will cease whatever has hitherto hindered all things from being filled with heavenly glory and God being all in all: vice, flesh, corruption, strife, death. Finally, that arrangement of the kingdom of the Holy Trinity which is common or natural, and which is ordered toward the mediatorial kingdom of Christ, will cease, since it is no longer necessary than until the salvation of the Church is completed by glorification on the last day and brought to its goal. When this has ceased, the economy of Christ's kingdom, which was joined with such imperfection, will not cease but will begin, and its glorious economy will last forever, with the fulfilment [πλήρωσις] of the Church, which will be full to God, who will be all in all, most closely joined to Christ its King and head, and will serve him forever through love and willing obedience, giving thanks and glorifying him.

units.la: CXIII. Hoc, non aliud S.Paulus finem Regni Christi, 1.Cor.XV.24. &c. ad demonstrandam resurrectionem ex mortuis describens, sibi voluit. Verbis ejus, quae inter δυσνόητα intellectu difficilia ipse S.Petrus 2.Epist.III.16. agens de adventu Domini, & novo Coelo & nova terra posuisse videtur, lucem perspicua paraphrasi foenerari juvabit.Postea, inquit ille, v.24. erit finis (mundi & imperfectionis rerum omnium, quia abolebitur id, quod ex parte est, cum perfectum venerit, 1.Cor.XIII.10.) cum tradiderit Regnum Deo & Patri (cum & Regnum naturale ad muneris Mediatorii in mundo functionem ordinatum, utpote non amplius necessarium, ut Mediator, deponet, & cum Patre, ut Filius, non ut Mediator amplius, exercebit: & actum Regni sui sic consummabit, ut tradat Ecclesiam, Regnum suum, Deo Patri, omni perfectione & gloria consummata implendum, ut nihil in eo nisi Deus, hoc est, Divina operatio, gratia & amoris illius aeterni atque ineffabilis efficacia locum habeat. Sicut enim voluntate Patris & Filii regeniti, justificati, sanctificati, & manu Patris atque Filii confirmati sumus, Joh.X.28.29. ita voluntate & manu Patris sanctitate perfecta, & laetitia gloriosa implebimur. Et sicut Pater nunc cognoscitur in Filio & in eodem inter hostes dominante regnat: ita abolita imperfectione omni, cum Deus Pater omnia erit in omnibus, & omnia ei subjecta fuerint, Filius in Patre omnia implente regnabit. Hoc enim illud Regnum est, ad quod erigendum Deus Pater Filium suum misit, quodque ad Patrem redire debuit, sic tamen, ut & Filius ipse in Ecclesia sibi & Patri subjecta glorificetur & admirabilis fiat, 2.Thess.I.10. faciens, ut Deus omnia in omnibus sit) cum aboleverit omnem principatum (dominium, per quod fit, ut unus alteri subjiciatur, unius voluntas ab alterius nutu pendeat) & potestatem (jus illud, quo quis in alterum aliquid potest) & potentiam (vim, qua utitur is, qui jus habet, vel non habet. Nam cum alii aliis dominantur, jure vel injuria, eos sibi subjiciunt, nondum Deus omnia in omnibus est, sibi soli omnia subjicit, omnia implet. Qui a Deo impletur, alio nullo, a quo regatur, & cujus mandatis cum voluntate & libertate ejus haud raro pugnantibus constringatur, indiget) v.25. Nam oportet eum regnare (ideo mortuus est, ideo resurrexit, in Coelum ascendit, ut ceu Rex haberet populum, haereditatem sibi soli obnoxiam, cui ut Rex praeesset & dominaretur) donec ponat omnes hostes suos sub pedes suos, (David Psal.CX.1.id Patri; Paulus hic Filio tribuit. Sed idem David etiam Filio robur & exercitum tribuit. Utrumque ergo potestatem & robur subjugandi habet. Particula αχρις & donec aliquando rei terminum, aliquando gradum majorem vel profectum significat. Sive hic terminum notat, finis Regni Christi non absolute, sed κατα τον secundum quid, administratio ejus inter hostes, cui succedet alia facies Regni, qua Filius in Patre omnia, abolito Principatu, potestate & potentia aliena, immediate implente regnabit, significatur: sive gradum majorem vel profectum, sensus erit, Regnum illud, quod nunc inter hostes Christus administrat, nondum perfecte & consummate esse Regnum Dei; adeoque si-
units.tr: CXIII. This, and nothing else, is what St Paul meant by the end of Christ's kingdom, 1 Cor. 15:24 etc., when he described the resurrection from the dead. It will help to bring light to his words, which St Peter, speaking of the coming of the Lord and of a new heaven and new earth, seems to have found hard to understand [δυσνόητα] (2 Pet. 3:16), by means of a clear paraphrase. Afterwards, he says, v. 24, there will be the end (of the world and of the imperfection of all things, since what is in part will be abolished when the perfect comes, 1 Cor. 13:10), when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father (when he will lay down the kingdom which was ordered to the function of his mediatorial office in the world, as no longer necessary to him as Mediator, and will exercise it with the Father as Son, no longer as Mediator; and he will so complete the act of his kingdom that he hands over the Church, his kingdom, to God the Father, to be filled by him with all perfection and glory, so that nothing remains in it but God, that is, the divine working, grace, and the efficacy of that eternal and ineffable love). For just as we have been begotten again, justified, and sanctified by the will of the Father and the Son, and confirmed by the hand of the Father and the Son (John 10:28, 29), so we shall be filled by the will and hand of the Father with perfect holiness and glorious joy. And just as the Father is now known in the Son and reigns through him, ruling among enemies, so, when all imperfection has been abolished and God the Father is all in all, and all things have been made subject to him, the Son will reign in the Father, filling all things. For this is that kingdom which God the Father sent his Son to establish, and which ought to be returned to the Father; yet in such a way that the Son himself is glorified in the Church, which is subject to him and to the Father, and is made wonderful (2 Thess. 1:10), so that God may be all in all. When he has abolished every principality (dominion, by which one is made subject to another, the will of one depending on the nod of another), and power (that right by which someone has power over another), and might (the force which he uses who has the right, or does not have it. For while some rule over others, rightly or wrongly, and subject them to themselves, God is not yet all in all; he subjects all things to himself alone and fills all things. He who is filled by God needs no other by whom he is ruled, and who constrains him by commands which often conflict with his will and freedom), v. 25. For he must reign (therefore he died, therefore he rose, and ascended into heaven, so that as King he might have a people, an inheritance bound to him alone, over which he might preside and rule as King), until he has put all his enemies under his feet (David ascribes this to the Father, Ps. 110:1; Paul here ascribes it to the Son. But the same David also ascribes strength and army to the Son. So he has both the power and the strength to subdue. The particle ἄχρις [until], and donec, sometimes signifies the end of a thing, sometimes a greater degree or progress. If here it denotes an end, the end of Christ's kingdom is not absolute but relative [κατὰ τὸν]: his administration among enemies is meant, to be succeeded by another aspect of the kingdom, in which the Son will reign immediately in the Father, filling all things, with principality, power, and might abolished and put aside; if it denotes a greater degree or progress, the sense will be that the kingdom which Christ now administers among his enemies is not yet perfect and complete as the kingdom of God,

units.la: niendum & cum perfectione, quod κατ' εξοχην Regnum Patris erit, commutandum esse,) v.26. Ultimus hostis aboletur Mors. (nam mors corporis impedit απληρωσιν impletionem Patris, quae non ad spiritum duntaxat, sed etiam ad corpus extenditur: adeoque ceu hostis, cum non sit sequela naturae, sed a peccato, & destructio naturae, vitae, quam Deus homini dedit, contraria, aboleri prius debet quam perfecte Christus, vel Pater in Christo regnet,) v.27. Omnia enim posuit sub pedibus ejus, (Psal.CVIII.7. Si omnia, etiam principatum, potestatem, potentiam, carnem, mortem, quibus si semper subjicirentur, qui Christi membra sunt, Christus ipse in iisdem membris suis iis subjiceretur.) Quando autem dicit, quod omnia sint subjecta, manifestum est, quod excepto subjiciente (Patre, qui Christo tum ob dignitatem personae, tum ob meritum omnia subjecit) ipsi omnia, v.28. Cum autem subjecta ipsi fuerint omnia, tum & ipse Filius subjicietur subjicienti ipsi omnia, (tum secundum eam naturam, qua Filius naturaliter divinitati subjectus est; tum secundum omnia membra sua, & filios, seu genituram & populum suum, Psal.CX.3. Non quod antea non fuerit subjectus, sed quia tum ut frater noster primogenitus nos gloriae suae participes reddet, qui hucusque in servili vilitate in mundo egimus. Quandiu aliquid in membris Filii est nondum subjectum Patri, velut peccatum, caro, mors, nondum Filius totus Patri subjectus intelligitur. Cessabit autem illa differentia status, & incipiet communio status fraterna, ut in throno ejus sedeamus. Erit autem & Filius homo velut unus fratrum, subjectus Deo, & praemium suae subjectionis reportans) ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus (ut nihil sit etiam in membris Filii, quod non sit a Deo, non amplius peccatum, miseria, afflictio, mors, sed mera justitia, beatitudo, laetitia, gloria & immortalitas; atque ita, qui Dei sunt, plane consummentur, ut Deus in ipsis non sit aliquid duntaxat, sed παντα omnia, & perfecte illis fiat in Deum: Id vero ut fieret, Christum Regnum, populum suum tradere debuit Deo Patri gloria ejus implendum, & modis omnibus consummandum. Hoc non obstante in perpetuum Rex noster Caput nostrum corpus suum spiritu & gloria implens, Mediator noster manebit, quia virtute subjectionis ejus, qua factus est sub Legem, & nos sibi subjiciendos impetravit, nos ipsi in uno corpore subjecti cum ipso beabimur, & aeterna illius gratia in aeternum conservabimur, & quidem ab ipso. Potest enim εἰς τὸ παντελές in perpetuum, seu omne tempus eos, qui per ipsum accedunt ad Deum, salvare, semper vivens ad interce-dendum pro ipsis: & unica oblatione in perpetuum sanctificatos consummavit, Hebr.VII.25. X.14. Coram Deo & Domino Jesu Christo, qui judicaturus est vivos & mortuos, καὶ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν βασιλείαν αὐτοῦ cum apparitione sua, & Regno suo,2.Tim.IV.1.)
units.tr: and must be brought to an end and changed into perfection, which will be the kingdom of the Father par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν]). V. 26.
