The last enemy, death, is abolished (for bodily death prevents the fulfilment [ἀπλήρωσις] of the Father, which extends not only to the spirit but also to the body; and so, as an enemy, since it is not a consequence of nature but comes from sin, and is contrary to nature and to the life which God gave to man, it must be abolished before Christ, or the Father in Christ, can reign perfectly). V. 27. For he has put all things under his feet (Ps. 8:7. If all things, including principality, power, might, flesh, and death, are subjected to him, then those who are members of Christ, if they were always subject to these, would be subject to them in his own members). But when it says that all things are subjected, it is plain that he who subjected all things to him is excepted (the Father, who subjected all things to Christ, both because of the dignity of his person and because of his merit). V. 28. But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him (both according to that nature by which the Son is naturally subject to the Godhead, and according to all his members, and his sons, or offspring and people, Ps. 110:3. Not that he was not subject before, but because then, as our firstborn brother, he will make us partakers of his glory, we who hitherto have lived in servile lowliness in the world. As long as anything in the members of the Son is not yet subject to the Father, such as sin, flesh, or death, the Son is not understood to be wholly subject to the Father. But that difference of state will cease, and the fraternal communion of state will begin, so that we may sit on his throne. The Son too will be a man, as one of the brethren, subject to God and receiving the reward of his subjection), so that God may be all in all (so that there is nothing even in the members of the Son which is not from God, no longer sin, misery, affliction, or death, but pure righteousness, blessedness, joy, glory, and immortality; and thus those who belong to God will be wholly perfected, so that God is not merely something in them but all things [πάντα], and they are made perfectly into God. For this to happen, Christ had to hand over the kingdom and his people to God the Father, to be filled with his glory and completed in every way). Nevertheless, our King and Head, filling his body with spirit and glory, will remain our Mediator forever, because by the virtue of his subjection, by which he was made subject to the law and obtained for us that we should be subjected to him, we, subject in one body with him, shall be blessed with him, and kept forever by his eternal grace, and indeed by him. For he is able to save to the uttermost [εἰς τὸ παντελές], forever, that is, at all times, those who come to God through him, always living to make intercession for them; and by one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified (Heb. 7:25, 10:14). Before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead, and his appearing and his kingdom [καὶ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν βασιλείαν αὐτοῦ], with his appearing and his kingdom (2 Tim. 4:1).

units.la: CXIV. Sicut Sacerdotale, ita Regium Christi munus Pontificii & Socinliani mire corrumpunt. Illi enim Christo Regi & Capiti in Coelo συμβασιλεις Conreges multos, & in terris Regem & caput visibile atque Vicarium Papam sociantes, non parum de gloria Regis & Capitis Christi delibant; saltem Regnum ejus Coelo Coeleste & merum simile faciunt illi, quo sub V. T. Principatus & Potestates induit, quos sub N. T. ἀπεκδυσάμενος exuens traduxit publicè, triumphans de iis in se ipso, Col.II.15. Quam in rem plura in loco. Hi verò tum Regem Christum recentem ac modernum tantùm faciunt, ex quo videlicet victa morte in Coelum ascendit, & triumphalia adeptus est; diversa Regni ejus tempora modò clariora, modò illustria minùs, variantémque oeconomiam discernere non valentes: tum naturam Regni talem tradunt, ut illud Patri subordinatum, ab eo donatum, & quoad potestatem quidem dependens, sed quoad exercitium potentiae & voluntatis independens (quae ἀσυγχυτως supra confiximus) sit, utpote qui in V.T. solus regnans, in Novo Christum socium & collegam asciverit, divisum cum eo imperium possederit, & servato sibi reliquo mundo, Ecclesiam potissimùm regendam ipsi tradiderit: tum Regnum Christi naturale in Coelum & terram, ejúsque ordinationem ad Mediatorium penitus tollunt, & Mediatorium arctissimis limitibus constringunt: tum denique, ut Christum Regem χριστὸν vel ἀνεγχθῆς factum asserunt, eundem ἀπογαιον & ἐφημερον faciunt, utpote qui die novissimo Regnum abdicaturus, & de Rege subditus & privatus iterum futurus sit. Quae recitasse refutasse est. Falsissimis enim hypothesibus hactenus profligatis nituntur.
units.tr: CXIV. Just as they corrupt Christ's priestly office, so the Papists and the Socinians wonderfully corrupt his kingly office. The Papists associate with Christ, the King and Head in heaven, many co-kings [συμβασιλεῖς], and on earth they set up a visible King and Head, the Pope as Vicar. In doing so they take no small part of the glory of Christ the King and Head. At the very least they make his kingdom in heaven wholly like that heavenly kingdom which, under the Old Testament, the Principalities and Powers possessed, and which under the New Testament he "put off" [ἀπεκδυσάμενος], leading them captive openly and triumphing over them in himself (Col. 2:15). I have treated this matter at greater length elsewhere. The Socinians, for their part, make Christ a King only recent and modern, from the time when, having conquered death, he ascended into heaven and obtained his triumphal dignity. Unable to distinguish the different periods of his kingdom, which are now more evident and now less clear, and to discern the varying economy, they teach the nature of his kingdom in such a way that it is subordinate to the Father and granted by him, and dependent indeed as to its power but independent as to the exercise of its power and will (which we have established above, "without confusion" [ἀσυγχύτως]). For, they say, the Father, who alone reigned in the Old Testament, took Christ as partner and colleague in the New, shared the empire with him, and, keeping the rest of the world for himself, handed over the governing of the Church chiefly to him. Further, they entirely remove Christ's natural kingdom over heaven and earth, and its ordering toward the Mediatorship, and they confine the Mediatorship within the narrowest limits. Finally, they assert that Christ became King as one "anointed" [χριστὸν] or "begotten" [ἀνεγχθῆς], and they make him "earthly" [ἐπίγειον] and "ephemeral" [ἐφήμερον], as one who would lay down his kingdom on the last day and would again become a subject and a private person. To recite these views is to refute them, for they rest on most false hypotheses, already overthrown.

units.la: CXV. Cùm Jesus noster Rex & quidem
units.tr: CXV. Since our Jesus is King, and indeed

units.la: משיח Unctus & merus Rex in N.T. factus sit, & talis in aeternum perseveraturus sit, advenisse Messiam tum, cùm Jesus Christus venit, ad liquidum perducitur. De eo tamen cum Judaeis justo Dei judicio induratis acris nobis contentio est. Illi enim cùm Messiae promissionem, tot vaticiniis testatam in dubium vocare non sustineant, imò etiam fundamentales inter fidei suae articulos referant, negantes salutem ei contingere, qui Messiam venturum negat, ejus praestationem in Jesu factam praefracte inficiantur. Utque faciliùs id sibi aliisque persuadeant, pro Messia spectrum aliquod obtrudunt, nimirum Messiam geminum, unum ex tribu Josephi oriundum, sed miserum illum, nullisque triumphis inclytum, quippe in praelio contra exercitum Gogi moriturum inglorium: alterum & veriorem illum, hominem tamen merum, ex tribu Juda & semine Davidis oriundum, hominem strenuum, & in rebus gerendis felicem, qui armis virisque succinctus servientem populum libertati restitueret; cum quo principes & duces populi essent; qui talia patraret, qualia patravit Moses, qui Aegyptium caecidit: Israelitas per mare traduxit, eúmque in deserto terram Canaan versus duxit. Has cogitationes eorum, quibus Christus scandalum futurum erat, repraesentavit Jesajas, cap.LXIII.10-14. Ipsi, inquit, inobedientes exiterunt, & dolore afflecerunt Spiritum Sanctum ipsius, & versus est ipsis in inimicum, ipse pugnavit in ipsos. Recordatus est (populus ille) dies seculi, Moisis, populi ejus. Ubi qui fecerat illos ascendere ex mari? cum Pastoribus ovium suarum (septuaginta Senioribus.) Ubi qui posuit in medium ipsius Spiritum Sanctum suum? Qui fecit ambulare ad dextram Moisis brachium deorisuum? qui fidit aquas coram ipsis, ut faceret si-
units.tr: Since Jesus was made the anointed one, the Messiah [מָשִׁיחַ], and a King in the New Testament, and will continue such for ever, it is brought clearly to light that the Messiah came when Jesus Christ came. Yet on this point we have a sharp dispute with the Jews, who have been hardened by the just judgment of God. For though they do not dare to call into doubt the promise of the Messiah, attested by so many prophecies, and indeed even count it among the fundamental articles of their faith, saying that one who denies that the Messiah is to come has no salvation, they stubbornly deny that this promise was fulfilled in Jesus. To persuade themselves and others the more easily, they thrust forward a certain phantom in place of the Messiah, namely a twofold Messiah: one descended from the tribe of Joseph, but a wretched man, distinguished by no triumphs, who would die inglorious in battle against the army of Gog; and the other, the truer one, yet a mere man, descended from the tribe of Judah and the seed of David, a vigorous man, fortunate in his undertakings, who, armed and girded with men and weapons, would restore the enslaved people to liberty, with princes and leaders of the people about him. He would do such things as Moses did when he struck down the Egyptian, led the Israelites through the sea, and brought them through the desert toward the land of Canaan. Isaiah set forth these thoughts of those to whom Christ would be a stumbling block (Isa. 63:10–14): They, he says, became disobedient, and grieved his Holy Spirit, and he turned to be their enemy, and he himself fought against them. That people remembered the days of old, of Moses, his people. Where is he who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock (the seventy elders). Where is he who put his Holy Spirit in the midst of them? Who caused his glorious arm to go at the right hand of Moses? Who divided the waters before them, to make himself an everlasting name?

units.la: bi nomen seculi? Qui fecit ambulare illos in abyssis, ut equus in deserto, non offendebant. Ut jumentum, quod in vallem descendit, Spiritus Jehova faciebat ipsum acquiescere. Sic duxisti populum tuum ad faciendum tibi nomen decorum. Talia ergo cùm nec Jesus, nec alii hactenus patraverint; cùmque non viderint illi ita populum in duodecim tribubus per aspectabilia judicia à potestate Romanorum liberari, & sic per totum mundum ad occupandam terram Canaan duci, sicut olim à potestate Pharaonis per Mosen liberatus & in terram Canaan introductus est, haec, non alia potior, ipsis Regni Christi abnegandi ratio fuit.
units.tr: Who led them through the depths, as a horse in the wilderness, so that they did not stumble. As a beast that goes down into the valley, the Spirit of Jehovah caused it to rest. So you led your people, to make for yourself a glorious name. Since neither Jesus nor others have hitherto done such things, and since they did not see the people of the twelve tribes delivered from the power of the Romans by visible judgments, and thus led through the whole world to take possession of the land of Canaan, as once they had been delivered from the power of Pharaoh through Moses and brought into the land of Canaan, this, and no weightier reason, was the ground on which they denied the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: CXVI. Sed hoc ipsissimarum tenebrarum, quibus Judaeos Deus justus judex implicavit, argumentum est. Nam Messiam, qualis promissus est, Deus videlicet & homo, non occisurus alios, sed occidendus ipse, & morte sua aeternam salutem & vitam non corporis duntaxat, sed inprimis spiritus credentium restauratus; quin & Rex non temporalis, sed spiritualis & Coelestis, non unius gentis, vel carnalis populi, sed totius mundi, (uti hactenus fuse demonstravimus) nulli agnoscunt; atque sic carnalium praejudiciorum suorum scotomate percusi turpissimè & infelicissimè errant; quasi tot vaticinia de Messia & Salvatore inde à principio revelationis ad finem usque non alium, quàm sospitatorem unius populi, non salutis animae in Coelis cum Deo uniendae, & aeternùm beandae; sed corporis solius in terris, porcorum instar saginandi proviserom, tot seculorum tractu populum suum in horribili exilio, summisque angustiis, citra spem solidam liberationis relinquentem; & si fata quandoque voluerint, ut in mundum eum in finem, tot seculorum flagrantibus desideriis appetitus & praeconiatus tandem lento pede veniat, brevissimi temporis spatio liberationis temporalis & corporalis unius populi pertinacis, abdicato in perpetuum mundo reliquo, cura defungentem, portenderint. Tantae videlicet molis erat unam gentem, quam culpa propria Deo hominibúsque invisam reddidit, à servitute corporali liberare, & geniali quidem. sed peritura statim, fluxàque adeò felicitate in mundo mactare. Si non aliud fundamentalis ille fidei de Messia articulus mysterium continet, quid Abrahamo, quid Mosi, quid tot Regibus, Prophetis, universo populo contulit? Cur tam solicitè à Prophetis nuntiatur, toties, non minùs prospero quàm adverso populi statu, non minùs sub bonis Regibus, quàm sub tyrannis inculcatur? sed quod majus est, cur iis ipsis, qui Messiam, Regem terrestrem conspecturi non erant, praedicatur, & sonore vehementérque magis, quàm iis, qui tempore ejus vitam degent? Scripturae Mosis & Prophetarum, quas à Deo esse, & ad salutem conducere, nobiscum Judaei agnoscunt, in luxum, delicias, vanitates vehementer detonant: haec omnia cum aerumnis, funeribus, sordibus commutaturum minantur. Quam ergo illae laetitiam & felicitatem sub Messia augurantur, temporalis illa, à qua toties homines revocantur, esse non potest; spiritualis mera est. Exulta valde filia Sion, jubila filia Jerusalem, Ecce Rex tuus veniet tibi, &c. inquit Jehova, Zach.IX.9. Cur ita Christus Rex idem Messias est, quae vox non temporalem Dominum & Principem significat; qualem Judaei indurati frustra hactenus expectant. ita? Post tot seculorum fluxus exurget Rex magnus in Israele. Quid absurdius? Hic, ajunt, optimam pacem faciet. Quid mea refert, si bello vexor? Carceres aperiet. Quid juvat, si interim situ & squalore computresco? De caeteris orbis gentibus triumphabit. Haec quid ad me, quem gentes certatim conculcant, & in triumphum manibus post terga revinctis circumducunt? Pater si quid filium post obitum feliciter gesturum sperat, filii causa laetatur, sed brevis laetitia est. At quis nepotum post plurima secula gloria exultat, inprimis si praecedentes longo tempore in umbra mortis sessuros auguratur? Ergo laetitia ista latius pateat oportet: & qui eam praedicunt, utique praesentiunt, praesentesque afficiuntur & incalescunt: qui audiunt, jam degustant: in mentibus suis Regni illius privilegiis gaudent, priusquam Rex ipse tantopere expetitus in terra nascatur. Spiritualis, inquam, illa laetitia est, quae futuri Regis fructum animo adeo gestiente, exultante praecipit. Demus vero, sectatores & spectatores Judaici istius Messiae omnibus hujus vitae voluptatibus & commodis perfrui: quis tandem finis ejus erit? Morietur, inquiunt, & generatio ejus cum eo. Hic vero quot annos Messias ille victurus sit, inter se digladiantur; dum alii quadraginta, alii septuaginta, alii etiam quadringentis annis vitam ejus definiunt: illi, quod quadraginta annos Israel in deserto erraverit: illi, quod septuaginta annos Babylone agitaverit; hi quod quadringentorum annorum Aegyptiaca captivitas fuerit. Singuli hoc argumento pugnant, quod dies Messiae adaequaturi sint tempus aliquod afflictionis populi, juxta illud: Laetifica nos juxta dies, quibus nos afflixisti: annos, quibus vidimus malum, Psal. XC. 15. Sed eodem argumento alii dies Messiae diebus exilii Romani aequabunt. Sed de hoc quicquid sit, quam procul haec absunt ab ea laetitia, quam Prophetae aeternam pollicentur? Transegerint illi centum annos in deliciis & luxu; quid nisi prolixae epulae, quas primus somnus paucis horis deleverit? Et si omnino morien-dum, quid dein superest? Sin altera nobis post hanc vita restat, quid praeter triste desiderium? Quorsum ob brevem & momentaneam voluptatis coruscationem tanta laetitia afficiantur patres? Multo minus certe, quam ob epulas nuptiales, quas saltem proles aliqua consequatur. In his volutabris miseri Judaei haerent, quasi aut extra hanc vitam homo non vivat, aut puerilem prorsus vitam perpetuo vivere debeat. Absurdum hoc alio absurdo tegunt, fingentes, eos omnes, qui Messiam expectarunt, in vitam redituros, quin & impios ipsos, ut invidia disrumpantur; quasi in gloria viventes rediturisint, ut hominis istius magnificentiam spectent, a peccati vinculo liberi denuo se vinciendos daturi sint, ut licentiam hanc intueantur, qui aeterna beatitudine in Coelo fruuntur, inde descensuri sint, ut boum & vervecum adipe satientur. Haec vero tandem quid? nisi ac si quis ex somno ad potandum surgat, potus mox rursus obdormiscat. Quod si haec in Palaestina geruntur, & in vitam omnes redeunt, quae Palaestina capiendis; quis Leviathan satiandis sufficiet? Et si gentes etiam admittuntur, quale tandem Templum erit? Et si omnes eo sacrificia sua conferunt, quid Hierusalem nisi carnificina & laniena perpetua erit. Judaea ipsa quid nisi sanguinis diluvium? Sed non gentes in Hierosolymam colligendas, verum Hierosolymam inter gentes spargendam; non gentes in Templum confluxuras, sed gentes, earum corda, Templum Dei, in quo is adoretur, futuras, Prophetae praenuntiarunt. Cumque Deus sanguinis effusiones nostras, arietum adipes, altarium suffumigationes adeo aspernetur, quis nisi de Epicuri metallo ficto cor habens, ad ejusmodi convivium nos invitari, eas nobis epulas a Deo praeparari credat? Justum Dei judicium est, quod qui Filium Davidis verba Dei loquentem, & opera Dei facientem rejecerunt, identidem deinceps nescio quos, genus Davidis mentientes, & latronum facinora patrantes, homines temerarios & scelestos pro Messia amplexi sunt; pudendo & exitiali cum successu. Ego, sic Jesus ipse dixit, & praedixit, veni in nomine Patris mei (quem solum testem nomino, cujus solius potestatem & auctoritatem praedico, gloriam quaero,) & non accipitis me. Si alius veniat in nomine proprio (sine testimonio Dei, propria authoritate,) illum accipietis, Joh. V.43. Nam oves quidem Christi, relictis Scribis & Pharisaeis per deserta currentes ad eum venerunt, ejus vocem audiverunt, & Messiam ac Salvatorem suum agnoverunt; sed multi etiam falsis Christis & falsis Prophetis adhaeserunt, discipuli Scribarum & Pharisaeorum, aut alioqui rerum novarum cupidi, homines scelesti & temerarii. Ita cum Barocheba fecerunt celeberrimi Judaeorum Patriarchae, qui in Thalmude utramque paginam faciunt; ac inter eos etiam R. Akiba. Et Moses Majmonides auctor est eum, qui filius Davidis, fortis ac strenuus est, praesumi esse Messiam, donec contrarium appareat. Secundum quam regulam sequendi sunt impostores in perniciem sequentium, uti non semel Judaei malesani praesentissimo malo suo impostores, velut sub Adriano Barcochebam, qui post כּוֹכְבָא בַּר filius mendacii dictus est; sub Theodosio juniore Mosen Cretensem, Majmonidis tempore in Persia Davidem al David, Praestigiatorem & Magum: superiore seculo in Germania R. Lemlem: & non ita pridem famosum Sabathai Sebhi a prodromo Nathane Levi commendatum; & denique prae desperatione ad Turcas deficientem secuti sunt. Sed verae oves Christum, Pastorem illum bonum, non impostores secutae sunt. Omnes, qui ante me venerunt, fures sunt, & praedones, sed non audiverunt eos oves. Ego sum ostium. Per me si quis intrabit, salvabitur, & intrabit & exibit, & νομὴν pastum inveniet. Oves meae vocem meam audiunt, & ego cognosco eas, & sequuntur me, & ego vitam aeternam do eis, & non peribunt in seculum, & non rapiet eas quisquam ex manu mea. Joh. X. 8. 9. 27. 28.
units.tr: CXVI. But this is the very argument of the thick darkness in which God, the just judge, has enveloped the Jews. They do not acknowledge the Messiah as he was promised: God and man, who was not to kill others but himself to be killed, and who by his death was to restore eternal salvation and life, not of the body only but above all of the spirit of believers. Nor do they acknowledge him as a King who is not temporal but spiritual and heavenly, King not of one nation or carnal people but of the whole world, as we have hitherto demonstrated at length. Struck by the blindness of their carnal prejudices, they err most shamefully and most unhappily, as if so many prophecies about the Messiah and Saviour, from the beginning of revelation to its end, pointed to no other than a saviour of one people, not of the soul to be united with God in heaven and blessed for ever, but of the body alone on earth, to be fattened like swine. On this view God had provided for his people only to leave them for so many ages in horrible exile and extreme distress, without any solid hope of deliverance. And if at last the fates should will that he come into the world, at the end of so many ages, longed for with burning desire and proclaimed, and come slowly at last, he would in the briefest span of time, the world left behind and abandoned for ever, concern himself with the temporal and bodily liberation of one stubborn people alone. Surely it would be a matter of great weight to free from bodily servitude one nation which by its own fault had made itself hateful to God and men, and to bless it with an earthly happiness that is fleeting and soon to perish. If that fundamental article of faith about the Messiah contains no other mystery, what did it contribute to Abraham, to Moses, to so many kings and prophets, and to the whole people? Why is it announced so earnestly by the prophets, so often, in a prosperous state of the people no less than in an adverse one, and impressed no less under good kings than under tyrants? But what is greater: why is it preached to those very men who were not going to see the Messiah as an earthly king, and preached with more sound and vehemence than to those who lived in his time? The Scriptures of Moses and the Prophets, which the Jews acknowledge with us to be from God and to lead to salvation, they vehemently denounce as luxury, delights and vanities, and threaten that the Messiah will change all these into miseries, funerals and filth. Therefore the temporal joy and happiness which they promise under the Messiah, the joy to which men are so often called back, cannot be what they imagine; it is purely spiritual. "Exult greatly, daughter of Zion, shout, daughter of Jerusalem; behold, your King shall come to you, etc., says Jehovah," Zach.IX.9. Why is Christ the King the same Messiah, when that word does not signify a temporal Lord and Prince, such as the hardened Jews have vainly awaited until now? So? "After so many ages a great king shall arise in Israel." What could be more absurd? "Here," they say, "he will make the best peace." What does it matter to me if I am harassed by war? "He will open the prisons." What good is it if meanwhile I rot in filth and squalor? "He will triumph over the other nations of the world." What is that to me, whom the nations trample eagerly and lead about in triumph with their hands bound behind their backs? If a father hopes that his son will achieve something prosperously after his death, he rejoices for the son's sake, but the joy is brief. But who exults in the glory of grandsons after very many ages, especially if he foresees that the generations before them will sit for a long time in the shadow of death? That joy, therefore, must extend more widely. Those who proclaim it surely anticipate it, and are affected and kindled by what is present; those who hear it already taste it; in their minds they rejoice in the privileges of that kingdom before the King himself, so eagerly desired, is born on earth. It is a spiritual joy, I say, which urges and exults in the fruit of the future King with a soul so eager. Grant, however, that the followers and spectators of that Jewish Messiah enjoy all the pleasures and comforts of this life: what will be the end of it? "He will die," they say, "and his generation with him." Here, however, they dispute among themselves how many years that Messiah is to live. Some define his life as forty years, others seventy, others even four hundred: the first because Israel wandered forty years in the desert, the second because it was troubled seventy years at Babylon, the third because the Egyptian captivity lasted four hundred years. Each fights with this argument, that the days of the Messiah are to equal some period of affliction of the people, according to that: "Make us glad according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us, and the years wherein we have seen evil," Psal. XC. 15. But by the same argument others will make the days of the Messiah equal to the days of the Roman exile. Whatever be the case, how far removed are these from that joy which the prophets promise as eternal? Suppose they spend a hundred years in delights and luxury: what is that but long feasts, which the first sleep will erase in a few hours? And if we must altogether die, what then remains? But if another life awaits us after this one, what is there but sad longing? Why should the fathers be filled with such joy for a brief and momentary flash of pleasure? Far less surely than for wedding feasts, which at least some offspring follows. In these mire-pits the wretched Jews stick, as if either man does not live outside this life, or must live a wholly childish life for ever. They cover this absurdity with another, feigning that all who expected the Messiah will return to life, and even the impious themselves, so that they may burst with envy. As if those living in glory would return, to behold the magnificence of that man; as if those freed from the bond of sin would again give themselves to be bound, to look upon this licence; as if those who enjoy eternal blessedness in heaven would descend thence, to be sated with the fat of oxen and rams. But what are these things in the end? They are like someone who rises from sleep to drink and, once he has drunk, falls asleep again at once. And if these things happen in Palestine, and all return to life, what Palestine would suffice to feed the Leviathan? And if the Gentiles too are admitted, what sort of Temple will it be? And if all bring their sacrifices there, what will Jerusalem be but a perpetual slaughterhouse and butchery? And Judea itself, what but a flood of blood? But the prophets foretold not that the Gentiles would be gathered into Jerusalem, but that Jerusalem would be scattered among the Gentiles; not that the Gentiles would flow into the Temple, but that the Gentiles, their hearts, would be the Temple of God in which he is worshipped. And since God so spurns the outpourings of our blood, the fat of rams and the smoke of altars, who, unless he has a heart of Epicurus' counterfeit metal, would believe that we are invited to such a feast, and that God prepares such banquets for us? It is the just judgement of God that those who rejected the Son of David, who spoke the words of God and did the works of God, have since embraced, to their shame and ruin, with disastrous success, I know not whom: men pretending to be of the line of David, rash and wicked men who commit the deeds of robbers, as their Messiah. "I," thus Jesus himself said and foretold, "have come in the name of my Father" (whom alone I name as witness, whose sole power and authority I proclaim, whose glory I seek) "and you do not receive me. If another come in his own name" (without the testimony of God, by his own authority) "him you will receive," John V.43. For indeed the sheep of Christ, leaving the Scribes and Pharisees, came running to him through the deserts, heard his voice and acknowledged him as their Messiah and Saviour; but many also clung to false Christs and false prophets, being disciples of the Scribes and Pharisees, or otherwise men greedy for novelties, wicked and rash. So did the most celebrated patriarchs of the Jews with Bar Cochba, whose names fill both pages in the Talmud, and among them also R. Akiba. And Moses Maimonides is the authority for the rule that whoever is a son of David, brave and vigorous, is to be presumed the Messiah until the contrary appears. By this rule impostors are to be followed, to the destruction of their followers, as more than once mad Jews have followed impostors to their own most present ruin: under Hadrian Bar Cochba, who after [כּוֹכְבָא בַּר, Kokhba] was called "son of a lie"; under Theodosius the Younger Moses of Crete; in Persia, in Maimonides' time, David al David, a trickster and magician; in Germany in the last century R. Lemlem; and not long ago the notorious Sabbatai Sevi, commended by the forerunner Nathan Levi; and finally, out of despair, they followed those who defected to the Turks. But the true sheep followed Christ, that good Shepherd, not impostors. "All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not hear them. I am the door. If anyone enters through me he will be saved, and will go in and out, and find pasture [νομὴν]. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they shall not perish for ever, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand." John X. 8. 9. 27. 28.

units.la: CXVII. Sed missis his, rei ipsius arcem invadamus.
units.tr: CXVII. But setting these aside, let us attack the citadel of the matter itself.

units.la: Venisse ergo Messiam, σημεῖα καιρῶν signa temporum, quibus is venturus praedictus est, examussim impleta confirmant. Nam & quae Messiae apparitionem praecedere debuerunt, ante Jesu apparitionem contigerunt: & quae de Messia apparente extare adhuc debuerunt, illa pridem non amplius extant: & tempus mortis Messiae a Daniele signatum ante plurima
units.tr: That the Messiah has come, the signs of the times [σημεῖα καιρῶν], by which he was foretold to come, confirm by exact fulfilment. For both the things that ought to have preceded the Messiah's appearance happened before Jesus appeared, and the things that ought still to have remained after the Messiah appeared have long since ceased to exist. The time of the Messiah's death, marked out by Daniel, passed away many centuries ago.

units.la: § 2 rima secula effluxit. Quæ Messiæ apparitionem præcedere debuerunt, præcipua sequentia sunt. Israel deduci in captivitatem Assyriacam, Juda in Babylonicam: Babylonicum Imperium destrui: Populo Israelis captivo libertas redeundi in patriam à Cyro concedi: Templum secundum, & urbs Hierosolyma ædificari: Græci Persas subjugare: Duodecim tribus in terra & extra eam habitantes sub Seniorum regimine uniri; & mox etiam αυτονομίαν recuperare, in immensum, ut sabulum maris, multiplicari, subactis populis antehac non subjectis, Idumæis; Sacerdotes diadema sumere: Romani Judæos, domitis circumquaque vicinis, indagine cingere, terram ingredi; Judæos provinciam Imperii sui facere; & toti Orbi habitabili, ipsíque etiam Israeli Σωτηρίαν indicere debuerunt. Et tum Messias à Prophetis promissus venturus erat. Quæ Prophetias legentibus obscura esse non possunt. Omnium instar sunt illa Mosis, qui Prophetiæ Canonem fixit: Fiet, innuit ille, cum supervenient tibi omnia hæc, benedictio (sub judicibus, Regibus, Davide & Solomone) & maledictio (in divisione Regni, deportatione in captivitatem decem tribuum & tribus Judæ) & revocabis ad animum in omnibus gentibus, quò te Jehova Deus tuus propulerit; & converteris, (in captivitate Babylonica) & restituet Jehova jaturas tuas, & miserabitur tui, & rursus colliget te ex omnibus gentibus, & deducet te ad terram (modo tum extraordinario per Cyrum, Darium, Artasastam secundum, sive Mnemonem, tum ordinario, data libertate terram Patrum adeundi) & hæreditabis eam (denuo solus eam obtinebis) & faciet tibi bene, & multiplicabit te magis quàm Patres tuos (accessione facta populorum antehac non subjectorum, velut Idumæorum) & circumcidet Jehova cor tuum, & cor seminis tui, ut diligas Jehovam Deum tuum toto corde & tota anima propter vitam tuam, (dato Messia, qui te à timore mortis, servitute, terrore, jugo, accusatione peccati, &c. velut præputio quodam liberet,) Deut.XXX.1-6. Similia difertiora & specialiora vaticinia, Num.XXIV.18.19. Esaj.XL. 1-5. Jer.III.14-18. Ezech.XX.35. XXI.31.32. Hos.I.10.11. legere est. Hæc autem omnia ante plus sedecim secula contigisse locupletissimus & notissimus testis historia est.
units.tr: Many centuries ago. The chief things that ought to have preceded the Messiah's appearance are these: Israel was led into captivity by the Assyrians, Judah into the Babylonian captivity; the Babylonian empire was to be destroyed; freedom to return to their homeland was to be granted by Cyrus to the captive people of Israel; the second Temple and the city of Jerusalem were to be built; the Greeks were to subdue the Persians; the twelve tribes, living in the land and outside it, were to be united under the rule of elders, and soon also to recover autonomy [αὐτονομίαν], and to be multiplied beyond measure, like the sand of the sea; the Idumaeans, peoples previously not subject, were to be subdued; the priests were to take up the diadem; the Romans, having subdued the neighbouring peoples on every side, were to surround the Jews with a net and enter the land; the Jews were to be made a province of their empire; and they were to proclaim salvation [Σωτηρίαν] to the whole inhabited world, and to Israel itself. And then the Messiah promised by the Prophets was to come. These things cannot be obscure to those who read the Prophets. Those of Moses, who fixed the canon of prophecy, are the pattern of all the rest. He indicates: It shall come to pass, when all these things shall come upon you, the blessing (under the judges, kings, David and Solomon) and the curse (at the division of the kingdom, the deportation into captivity of the ten tribes and of the tribe of Judah), and you shall call them to mind among all the nations to which Jehovah your God has driven you; and you shall return (in the Babylonian captivity), and Jehovah will restore your fortunes, and will have mercy on you, and will gather you again from all the nations, and will bring you back to the land (now by an extraordinary means through Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes the Second, or Mnemon, and then by an ordinary means, freedom being given to go up to the land of the fathers), and you shall inherit it (you alone shall again possess it), and he will do you good, and multiply you more than your fathers (by the addition of peoples previously not subject, such as the Idumaeans), and Jehovah will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, that you may love Jehovah your God with all your heart and all your soul for your life (the Messiah being given, who would free you, as it were from a foreskin, from the fear of death, from slavery, from terror, from the yoke, from the accusation of sin, etc.), Deut. 30.1–6. Similar and clearer and more specific prophecies can be read: Num. 24.18, 19; Isa. 40.1–5; Jer. 3.14–18; Ezek. 20.35; 21.31, 32; Hos. 1.10, 11. Now, that all these things happened more than sixteen centuries ago is attested by the most abundant and well-known history.

units.la: CXVIII. Tum quæ Messia apparente extare debuerunt, pridem non ampliùs extant.
units.tr: CXVIII. Next, the things that ought still to have existed when the Messiah appeared have long since ceased to exist.

units.la: Nam Sceptrum & Legislator, qui esset ex medio pedum Judæ, non fuerat recessurus antequam veniret Schilo, Genes.XLIX.10. hoc est, ut suprà exposuimus, Judaica tribus habitura erat sceptrum, aut saltem Legislatorem, Legis Interpretem & executorem, & principes potestate coercendi & castigandi præditos. Venturus erat ad Templum suum, Malach.III.1. stante Templo, seu domo posteriore, quam implere gloria sua Messias, desiderium illud gentium, debuit, Hagg.II.7.8.9. Utrobique enim de Messia agi multa fidem faciunt, velut quòd Mal.III.1. sermo est de Angelo mittendo, hoc est, de præcone, cujus vox in deserto audiri debuit, Esaj.XL.3. qui infra IV.5. vocatur Elias Propheta, cujus munus fuit, velut imminente Regno Messiæ, præparare viam Domino, & convertere cor patrum ad filios & cor filiorum ad patres, ib.6, hoc est, sua doctrina vocare Israelitas ad pœnitentiam & fidem Messiæ, ne Abrahamum promissioni credentem & cæteros filiorum suorum puderet, Esaj.XXIX.22.23. quod præconium non Messiæ filii Josephi, uti Abenezra nugatur, neq; Angeli mortis uti Raschi fingit; sed Johannis Baptistæ fuit, Matth.III.2. Marc.I.5. utpote qui postultimum Prophetarum Malachiam proximus pœnitentiæ doctor venit, Israelem ad fidem patrum revocavit, & Messiæ atque Regni ejus adventum prænuntiavit: quod Mal.III.1. ad Templum suum venturus vocatur Dominus, qui ibid.II.17. vocatur Deus judicii, Filius Regis, cui dandum judicium, Psal.LXXII.1. Esaj. XL.3.4. quem Israelitæ quærebant, & Angelus fœderis, de quo, in quo & per quem est fœdus, novum scilicet illud, quod Jer.XXXI.31. promissum est; quo Angelo fœderis iidem delectabantur, vel delectari debebant; quem Messiam intelligi R. David Kimchi, Abenezra, Maimonides ipsi fatentur: quòd denique, Hagg.II.7. desiderium gentium non alius quàm Schilo, cui erit obedientia gentium, Genes.XLIX.10. ad cujus Legem Insulæ durabunt, Esaj.XLII.4. & in quo gentes conversæ delicias sibi facturæ erant, intelligitur. Frustra gloriam domus posterioris Judæi vel de rebus quibusdam externis; vel de duratione longiore, cùm decem annis longiùs steterit; vel de muneribus Regum Darii, Artaxerxis &c. vel de additamentis Herodis explicant. Talia enim tantæ promissionis mensuram neutiquam implent: inprimis cùm Deus ipse, Hagg.II.8.dicens: Meum est argentum, & meum est aurum, protestatus sit, in rebus caducis gloriam Templi non consistere, neque omnino iis se indigere; sed majorem longè Templi gloriam fore. Et qualiacunque secundi Templi ornamenta, neutiquam illud supra Solomonici Templi gloriam extollunt, cùm vel sola Arca fœderis cuncta Templi secundi multis parasangis superet. Structura verò Herodis fuit tentatio Sathanæ & stratagema, quo homines inescare voluit, ut de vera gloria Templi non cogitantes Templo illi considerent, & Dominum gloriæ crucifigerent. Denique sic Templum secundum illustrari gloria supra primum debuit, ut pax fieret, & gentes accederent. Atqui nulla pax nisi spiritualis, consistens in expiatione peccati, & quidem sub Jesu Messia. Ideo Abarbanel defertis veteribus, majorem illam gloriam ad Templum tertium sub Messia refert. cùm tamen diserte Prophetia dixerit: Implebo domum hanc: & Major erit gloria domus hujus posterioris, vel secundâ. Nam, quòd non secundum seu sed ultimum inter plura significare objicit, vel solum dictum Dei, Esaj.XLIV.6. Ego primus & ego ultimus, diluit. Proinde quivis primum sive immediate, sive mediate consequens, seu post veniens intelligitur. Accedunt alia etiam, quæ veniente Messia extare debuerunt; velut quòd Damascus nascente Immanuele debuit esse caput Syriæ, ibid.VII.8.14. quòd Messias debuit esse Servus potestatem habentium, Sacerdotum, Principum populi, ib.XLIX.7. minor fieri Diis, Psalm.VIII.6. quòd in pace, terra omnibus bonis abundante nasci debuit, Esaj.VII.15.16. quòd Bethlehem nondum destructa, parva licet, & vix inter civitates Judæ numeranda, extare, adeóque simul stirps Davidica deprimi, simul familiæ Judæ integræ perstare debuerunt: quòd urbs Sancta, visio, sacrificia, oblationes durare usque ad excidium Messiæ debuerunt, Dan.IX.24–f. Cùm ergo nec Scriptrum, nec Legislator, nec domus seu Templum posterius; nec Damascus, ceu caput Judææ, nec inter Judæos Dii, potestatem habentes; nec terra Canaan, ceu Judæorum terra pacata, & bonis temporalibus abundans; nec Bethlehem illa, quæ tempore Michææ fuit; nec familiæ Judæ integræ & distinctæ; nec urbs Sancta; nec visio, nec sacrificiorum & oblationum cultus amplius extent; Messiam advenisse invicta demonstratio est.
units.tr: For the sceptre and the lawgiver, who would come from between the feet of Judah, would not depart until Shiloh came, Gen. 49.10. That is, as we have explained above, the tribe of Judah was to hold the sceptre, or at least a lawgiver, an interpreter and executor of the Law, and rulers endowed with power to restrain and punish. He was to come to his Temple, Mal. 3.1, while the Temple was standing, or the latter house, which the Messiah, the desire of all nations, was to fill with his glory, Hag. 2.7–9. For in both places many things establish that the Messiah is meant: for example, Mal. 3.1 speaks of the messenger to be sent, that is, of a herald whose voice was to be heard in the wilderness, Isa. 40.3, who is called below (4.5) Elijah the Prophet, whose office was, as the kingdom of the Messiah was at hand, to prepare the way for the Lord, and to turn the heart of the fathers to the children and the heart of the children to the fathers, ibid. 6; that is, by his teaching to call the Israelites to repentance and faith in the Messiah, lest Abraham, who believed the promise, and the rest of his sons, should be put to shame, Isa. 29.22, 23. This proclamation was not that of the son of Joseph the Messiah, as Aben Ezra trifles, nor of the angel of death, as Rashi feigns; but it was that of John the Baptist, Matt. 3.2; Mark 1.5, who, as the teacher of repentance coming next after Malachi, the last of the Prophets, called Israel back to the faith of the fathers and foretold the coming of the Messiah and of his kingdom. That is why in Mal. 3.1 the Lord who is to come to his Temple is called (ibid. 2.17) the God of judgment, the Son of the King, to whom judgment is to be given, Ps. 72.1; Isa. 40.3, 4; whom the Israelites were seeking; and the angel of the covenant, concerning whom, in whom and through whom is the covenant, namely that new covenant which was promised, Jer. 31.31; the angel of the covenant in whom they delighted, or ought to have delighted. That this is the Messiah, R. David Kimchi, Aben Ezra and Maimonides themselves confess. Finally, in Hag. 2.7 the desire of the nations is none other than Shiloh, to whom the obedience of the nations shall be, Gen. 49.10, for whose law the islands shall wait, Isa. 42.4, and in whom the converted nations were to find their delight. In vain do the Jews explain the glory of the latter house either by certain external things, or by its longer duration, since it stood for ten years longer, or by the gifts of the kings Darius, Artaxerxes, etc., or by the additions of Herod. For such things by no means fill the measure of so great a promise, especially since God himself, saying in Hag. 2.8 The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, testified that the glory of the Temple does not consist in perishable things, nor does it need them at all; but that its glory would be far greater. And whatever the ornaments of the second Temple were, they by no means exalt it above the glory of Solomon's Temple, since the Ark of the covenant alone surpasses all of the second Temple by many parasangs. Herod's building, however, was a temptation of Satan and a stratagem by which he wished to lure men, so that, not thinking about the true glory of the Temple, they would admire that Temple and crucify the Lord of glory. Finally, the second Temple had to be made more illustrious in glory than the first, so that peace would come, and the nations would draw near. But there is no peace except a spiritual one, consisting in the expiation of sin, and indeed under Jesus the Messiah. Therefore Abarbanel, abandoning the older interpreters, refers that greater glory to a third Temple under the Messiah, although the Prophecy plainly said: I will fill this house: and the glory of this latter house (or second) will be greater. For his objection that the word means not second or after but last among several is answered by the saying of God alone, Isa. 44.6: I am the first and I am the last. Accordingly, whatever immediately or mediately follows the first, or comes after, is understood by it. There are also other things which ought to have existed when the Messiah came: for example, that Damascus was to be the head of Syria while Immanuel was being born, ibid. 7.8, 14; that the Messiah was to be the servant of those who have power, that is, of the priests, the princes of the people, ibid. 49.7; to be made a little lower than the gods, Ps. 8.6; that he was to be born in peace, in a land abounding in every good thing, Isa. 7.15, 16; that Bethlehem, not yet destroyed, though small and hardly to be counted among the cities of Judah, was to remain, and at the same time the stock of David was to be humbled while the whole family of Judah was to remain; that the holy city, the vision, the sacrifices and the oblations were to last until the destruction of the Messiah, Dan. 9.24ff. Since, then, neither sceptre nor lawgiver, nor the latter house or Temple; neither Damascus as the head of Judea, nor gods among the Jews holding power; neither the land of Canaan as a Jewish land at peace and abounding in temporal goods; neither that Bethlehem which existed in the time of Micah; neither the whole and distinct families of Judah; neither the holy city; neither the vision, nor the cult of sacrifices and oblations, any longer exist, it is an unanswerable demonstration that the Messiah has come.

units.la: CXIX. Jam & tempus mortis Messiæ ab Angelo Danieli loquente signatum pridem effluxit.
units.tr: CXIX. Now too the time of the Messiah's death, which the Angel marked out long ago when speaking to Daniel, has already run out.

units.la: Juvabit & hic consignatissimum vaticinium Danielis brevi paraphrasi explicatius reddere. Sic autem illud, Dan.IX.24–f. sonat. v.24. Consldera sermonem, & adverte visionem; septimanas septuaginta (Prophetice, uti Ezech.IV.6. dies pro anno & Levit.XXV.8. שבע שבתות שנים septem Sabbatha, seu septimanæ annorum dicuntur. ut ita LXX. septimanæ annos 490. conficiant) decisæ sunt super populo tuo, (intra tempus illud colligendo & amplificando) & super urbe sancta tua, (habitura intra illud tempus Deum inhabitatorem cum populo & Regno suo) ad coërcendam defectionem (ne deinceps amplius in populo sint & censeantur defectores, apostatæ à foedere Dei) & ad consummandum peccata, (non ut non sint peccata, sed ut illi, qui hactenus ἁμαρτωλοὶ peccatores, nil nisi peccantes erant & nominabantur, gentiles, peccare desinerent) & ad expiandam pravitatem, (ne Deus ejus amplius recordetur, sicut hactenus impositis sacrificiis & oblationibus recordatus est; quæ proin expiatio non per sacrificia fieri debuit; inprimis cùm expiatione hac data nec sacrificiis, nec sanctuario amplius futurus locus sit) & ad adducendam justitiam æternam (causam justitiæ in consummatione sua, δικαίωμα Christi, peccata expiantis, & Legem nostro loco implentis) & ad obsignandam visionem & Prophetiam (implendum quicquid de salute per figuras adumbratum & per Prophetas prædictum fuit, & simul finem visioni & Prophetiis imponendum) & ad ungendum Sanctum Sanctorum (non terrestre illud, quippe quod destruendum, v.26. innuitur; sed terrestri respondens, ut figuræ veritas respondet, quod Domus non manufacta, in qua Deus perpetuò habitat, Ecclesia N.T. Domus Dei viventis est; in qua est Arca foederis, Christus, Cherubim, σκίνωσις, Unctio Spiritus S. effusi in omnem carnem, non ex mensura dati,) v.25. Et agnosce & anima advertite, ab exitu sermonis de reducendo, & de ædificandis Hierosolymis usque ad משיח נגיד Unctum Principem septimanas septem & septimanas sexaginta duas, quibus denuo ædificabuntur. quoad forum & fossam, (inde à verbo, seu edicto vel Cyri, quo populo potestas data fuit redeundi in terram, & ædificandi urbem; de quo 2.Chron.XXXVI.22.23; Esr.I.1–4. legere est; vel, uti exactius alii Artaxerxis Longimani, cujus anno VII. Ezra diplomate ejus munitus in Judæam ascendit.
units.tr: It will also help here to set out Daniel's very clearly sealed prophecy in a somewhat fuller paraphrase. It reads thus, Dan. IX.24 ff. Verse 24: "Consider the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks" (spoken of prophetically, as in Ezek. IV.6, where a day stands for a year; and in Lev. XXV.8 שבע שבתות שנים [shiv'a shabbatot shanim], "seven sabbaths" or seven weeks of years, so that the seventy weeks make 490 years) "are determined upon your people" (to be gathered and increased within that time), "and upon your holy city" (in which, within that time, God is to dwell as the inhabitant of His people and kingdom), "to restrain transgression" (so that from then on they are no longer to be counted as transgressors and apostates from God's covenant), "and to make an end of sins" (not that there would be no sins, but that those who until then were ἁμαρτωλοί [hamartōloi], sinners, nothing but sinners and so called, the Gentiles, should cease to sin), "and to make atonement for iniquity" (so that God no longer remembers their iniquity as He had until then, when sacrifices and offerings were laid upon them; this atonement, therefore, was not to be made by sacrifices, especially since, with this atonement given, there will be no further place either for sacrifices or for a sanctuary), "and to bring in everlasting righteousness" (the cause of righteousness, in its completion, δικαίωμα [dikaiōma] of Christ, expiating sins and fulfilling the Law in our place), "and to seal up the vision and prophecy" (whatever concerning salvation was foreshadowed by figures and foretold by the prophets must be fulfilled, and at the same time an end is to be put to vision and prophecy), "and to anoint the Most Holy" (not that earthly place, which is indicated to be destroyed in v. 26, but one answering to the earthly, as the truth answers to the figure: the house not made with hands, in which God dwells perpetually, the Church of the New Testament, the house of the living God; in which are the ark of the covenant, Christ, the cherubim, σκίνωσις [skēnōsis], the anointing of the Holy Spirit poured out on all flesh, given not by measure). Verse 25: "Know therefore and understand, from the going forth of the word to restore and build Jerusalem until the Anointed Prince, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks" (משיח נגיד [māshiaḥ nāgîd]), "in which it shall be built again, as to the market-place and the moat" (counting from the word or edict of Cyrus, by which the people was given power to return to the land and rebuild the city; on which see 2 Chron. XXXVI.22–23 and Ezra I.1–4; or, as others more exactly reckon, of Artaxerxes Longimanus, in whose seventh year Ezra went up into Judea, armed with his decree).

units.la: Esr.VII. & VIII. expectandus est principatus Messiæ prodromi in sanctum sanctorum, & primogeniti ex mortuis, Regnum Cœleste auspicaturi; sed distinctis temporibus, ita ut septimanæ septem, seu anni 49. sint vel tempus à primo anno Cyri Judæis copiam struendi Templi facientis usque ad tempus illud; quo sub Artaxerxe Mnemone Templum sine atrio tamen externo structum fuit; vel, juxta alios, illud; quod inde ab Ezra ascendente in Judæam fluxit sexaginta duæ hebdomadæ, seu anni 434. sint tempus illud; vel quo Nehemias impetrata ab Artaxerxe Mnemone potestate, cœpit rursus ædificare urbem quoad forum, ut portas habeat; quia fora apud portas erant; & fossam, seu muros superpositos profundis illis vallibus; quæ Hierosolymæ pro fossa erant; & valli τυγωπιῶ ad urbem superiorem muniendam; denique fossis manufactis, ubi profunditas vallium naturale munimentum non præstabat. A tempore Nehemiæ illo urbis ædificatio sæpius facta est; sive cùm pomoeria prolata; sive cùm veteres muri instaurati sunt; sive cùm Herodes circa adventum Christi in ædificanda urbe, muris, turribus & Templo reficiendo operam ingentem navavit. Hoc igitur opus Deus populo illi per omne illud tempus attribuit, ut plerunque in pace domos & muros ædificarent. Alii vero tempus illud ab anno XLIX. inde ab Artaxerxis A.VII. fluente, inchoant;) & in angusta erunt tempora (sive quædam, velut cùm sub Dario Hystaspis impedientur ædificare Templum, & ab Artaxerxe Longimano idem vetabantur, Esdr.IV.5.6.7. & sub Assuero Estheræ marito populus ingens periculum adiit, sive omnia usque ad Messiam, cùm identidem magnis cum angustiis populo conflictandum fuerit,) v.26. Et post septimanas illas sexaginta duas excidetur Unctus, (ex eo tempore Unctus, cujus unctione verum sanctuarium ungendum erit; ejúsque oblatio & Regnum singulos in dies expectandum est. Ad hoc enim unctus est, ut נגיד princeps esset. Ut verò Princeps fieret, prius excindi, inde exaltari, & Coelum, sessurus ad dextram Patris, ingredi debet) & non erit ipsi, (ad incitas redigetur, nec quisquam cum eo erit, nisi soli malefici cum ipso crucifixi) & urbem & sanctum corrumpet populus Principis advenæ (Romani per Vespasianum, suo tempore, non confestim post Messiæ excidium) & finis ejus erit cum inundatione, & usque ad finem belli, decisæ sunt desolationes (vastitates rigidæ, sine ulla commiseratione, exceptione vel conservatione reliquiarum,) v.27. Et faciet prævalere fœdus propter multos septimana una, (Messias excisus, at mox resuscitatus, & jam Rex efficiet, ut fœdus pacis sit in orbe non minùs saltem quàm sepimana una; ad bellum usque Judaicum; idque propter multos, qui evasuri, & ad Principem unctum confugituri sunt) & dimidio septimanæ faciet cessare sacrificium & donum, (admissis ad Ecclesiam etiam præputiatis; qualis erat Cornelius centurio, nec dum finita illa heptaeteride, circa ejus medium) & super ala abominationum erit desolans (alæ abominabili, quam Zelotas, Idumæos, Johannem, Eleazarum, impurissimos homines, qui Templum occuparunt & defenderunt, intelligere licet; imminebit desolator, populus Princeps. Principis advenæ) & quidem usque ad consummationem & decisionem, quæ deßillabit in stupentem, (sic plaga illa in stupentem, Judæos amentes, incredulos, induratos, ne veritati & Regi unćto credant, effundetur, ut internecione deleatur, nec ulla spes supersit, ut talis Respublica & urbs cum tali sanćtuario, & tales Sacerdotes atque Legislatores aliquando reviviscant.) Hactenus vaticinium. Cùm igitur omnia illa facta sint, quæ fieri priùs, quàm Messias justitiæ adducendæ causa pateretur, & in Regnum suum intraret, non poterant; & sacrificia non tantùm cessarint in populo Dei, admissis ad communionem Ecclesiæ etiam præputiatis, sed etiam Sanćtuarium ipsum deletum sit, & ea deletio sit כלה consummatio; contra Christus passus, resuscitatus, in Cœlum susceptus prædicetur; & sanćtum sanćtorum effuso Cœlitus Spiritu, & omnino dato Spiritu filiationis unćtum sit; & Prophetiæ verificentur, imò obsignatæ sint, ut non amplius loquantur de futuris, sed rerum extantium testes fiant; & prædicato anno gratiæ peccatum finitum, defećtio coërcita, justitia seculorum adducta sit; Et præterea illæ annorum hebdomadæ ante multa secula diffluxerint, & urbs sanćta non minus septuaginta hebdomadis gavisa sit, nulla superesse dubitatio potest, quin Prophetia illa impleta sit, & venerit Messias, & ille ipse sit, qui excisus & in Cœlum, ut thronum gratiæ sublatus prædicatur.
units.tr: Ezra VII and VIII: the principate of the Messiah, the forerunner who is to introduce the entrance into the holy of holies and the firstborn from the dead, the beginning of the Heavenly Kingdom, is to be looked for, but at distinct times. So the seven weeks, or 49 years, are the time from the first year of Cyrus, when the Jews were given the opportunity of building the Temple, until the time when under Artaxerxes Mnemon the Temple was built, though without an outer court; or, according to others, the sixty-two weeks, or 434 years, which flowed on from the time Ezra went up into Judea, are the period until Nehemiah, having obtained power from Artaxerxes Mnemon, began again to build the city "as to the market-place," so that it might have gates, since the markets were by the gates; and "as to the moat," that is, the walls set upon those deep valleys, which served Jerusalem as a moat, and the rampart τυγωπιῶ [tygōpiō] for fortifying the upper city; and finally by moats dug by hand where the depth of the valleys did not supply a natural defence. From Nehemiah's time the building of the city was often carried out, whether when the boundaries were extended, or when the old walls were restored, or when Herod, around the coming of Christ, expended great effort on building the city and repairing its walls, towers and Temple. This work, then, God gave to that people throughout all that time, so that for the most part they might build houses and walls in peace. Others, however, begin that period from the forty-ninth year, flowing from the seventh year of Artaxerxes. "And the times shall be straitened" (whether some, as when under Darius Hystaspis they were hindered from building the Temple and were likewise forbidden by Artaxerxes Longimanus, Ezra IV.5–7; and when under Ahasuerus, husband of Esther, the people faced great danger; or all the way until the Messiah, since the people had to struggle with great distress again and again). Verse 26: "And after those sixty-two weeks the Anointed shall be cut off" (from that time the Anointed, by whose anointing the true sanctuary is to be anointed, and whose offering and kingdom are to be awaited day by day. For He was anointed to be נגיד [nāgîd], prince; but to become Prince He must first be "cut off," and then exalted, and enter heaven to sit at the right hand of the Father), "and shall have nothing" (He will be reduced to nothing, and no one will be with Him except the wicked who were crucified with Him), "and the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary" (the Romans under Vespasian, in their own time, not immediately after the cutting off of the Messiah), "and its end shall be with a flood, and until the end of the war desolations are decreed" (harsh devastations, without any pity, exception or preservation of remnants). Verse 27: "And he shall make a covenant prevail for many for one week" (the Messiah, cut off, yet soon raised up and now King, will bring it about that a covenant of peace exists in the world for at least one week, that is, until the Jewish war; and this "for many," who would escape and take refuge with the anointed Prince), "and in the middle of the week he shall cause sacrifice and offering to cease" (uncircumcised men being admitted to the Church also, as Cornelius the centurion was, even before that heptad was finished, around its midpoint), "and on the wing of abominations shall be one who desolates" (by the wing of abominations one may understand the Zealots, the Idumeans, John, Eleazar, most impure men, who occupied and defended the Temple; the desolator, the people of the prince, the prince who is to come, shall hang over it), "and indeed, until the consummation and decision, which shall be poured out upon the desolate one" (so that the blow will be poured out upon the astonished, the Jews, foolish, unbelieving, hardened, so that they do not believe the truth and the anointed King; they will be destroyed by slaughter, and no hope will remain that such a commonwealth and city, with such a sanctuary, and such priests and lawgivers, will ever revive). Thus far the prophecy. Since, therefore, all those things have been done which could not be done before the Messiah suffered for the sake of bringing in everlasting righteousness and entered into His kingdom; and since sacrifices have not only ceased among the people of God, with the uncircumcised also admitted to communion in the Church, but the sanctuary itself has been destroyed, and that destruction is the כלה [kālāh], the consummation; whereas Christ is proclaimed as having suffered, risen again, and been taken up into heaven; and the holy of holies has been anointed by the Spirit poured out from heaven, the Spirit of adoption given in full; and the prophecies have been fulfilled, indeed sealed, so that they no longer speak of things to come but become witnesses of things now existing; and since, with the year of grace proclaimed, sin has been ended, rebellion restrained, and everlasting righteousness brought in; and moreover, since those weeks of years ran out many centuries ago, and the holy city has enjoyed not less than seventy weeks, no doubt can remain that that prophecy has been fulfilled, that the Messiah has come, and that He is the very one who is proclaimed as cut off and taken up into heaven, as the throne of grace.

units.la: CXX. Nil nisi stuporem & cordis ἀσυνεσίαν audaciam sapiunt illa, quæ disertissimo huic vaticinio Danielis, ejúsque explicationi, quæ ex analogia promissionum, phraseon Scripturæ & ipsa re facta fidem habet, opponunt. Leve quidem illud est, quòd dissensum Christianorum in explicando eo vaticinio urgent, cùm & ipsi in explicandis vaticiniis creberrimè dislideant, & quascunque explicationes, dummodo impletionem veram, & impletionem in vero Messia, Jesu, illæ removeant, tolerent. Christianorum verò explicationes, si ab una Johannis Marshami Angli, qui totam Prophetiam hanc finitam esse tempore Antiochi Epiphanis contendit, (cui accuratè Celeb. Wagenseilius in Mantissa de LXX. Hebdomadis Danielis respondit) discesseris, in rei summa conveniunt, in sola temporis incipientis & intermedii notatione dislident: dum alii hebdomadas illas ab anno quarto Zedekiæ Regis, quo Jeremias, cap. xviii.1. &c. de captivorum reditu ex Babylone vaticinari coepit: alii ab hoc Angeli ad Danielem sermone & nuntio: alii ab Edićto Cyri Regis liberum populo reditum in patriam indulgentis, 2.Chron.XVI.22.&c.alii ab anno secundo Darii Nothi, ex Esr. cap.vi. alii ab anno septimo Artaxerxis Longimani, occasione, Esr. VII.1. numerare incipiunt: alii earundem sinem in Christi Baptismo, alii in passione Domini, alii in excidio urbis & Templi collocant. Enimverò cum Judæis non de annis aliquot, vel de seculo, sed de intervallo quindecim seculorum contentio nobis est; &, quod probè attendendum, nunc post impletum vaticinium longius tempus, & longius mille annis, præteriit, ea intercapedine, quæ inter prolationem hujus Oraculi, & complementum illius intercedere debuit. In supputatione temporum Dionysius Halicarnasæus Histor. lib.VII. loquitur, si quis paucis annis fallatur, in vetusto & multorum annorum historia ferendum fit: sed totis duabus aut tribus (imò quindecim) ætatibus à vero aberrare non permittitur. Verisimile est, Deum non voluisse exammussim indicare annum emortualem Christi, sed paululum relinquere scrutationi fidelium; nonnihil etiam occasionis oblocutionibus infidelium. Nam gloria Dei est occultare sermonem, ut indoles sermonis studium & fidem exerceat, Prov.XXV.2. Neque ad fidem hujus Oraculi exaćtissima certitudo Chronologiæ, nullam difficultatem relinquens, necessaria est; sed sufficit ἐν ταλάντει cum latitudine quadam hæc accipere. Non enim in temporis puncto nos hærere, sed ipsarum rerum gestarum momenta ponderare nos Deus voluit. Neque minùs Judæis in computo LXX hebdomadum, quàm ipsis Christianis convenit. Illud verò majus est, & rei cardo, quòd alii quidem, Itali cumprimis, hebdomadas non annorum, sed Jubilæorum, contra omnem S. Scripturæ loquendi usum, quæ non alias quàm dierum & septimanarum hebdomadas agnoscit, intelligi asserunt: alii per נגיד משיח Unćtum principem vel Cyrum, uti Lipmannus, Saadias, Jarchi, Jacchiades, Menasse; vel Nehemiam, uti Abenezra; vel Jehosuam Sacerdotem, ut R. Levi Ben Gerson: vel Zorobabelem, uti Abarbanel, intelligunt. Cùm verò Danielis ille Messias seu Unćtus Princeps is ipse fit, quem post septem & sexaginta duas hebdomadas excidendum idem mox asserit, an illorum quisquam post tot demum hebdomadas excisus est? Nam quòd per משיח illum, qui excidendus dicitur, sanćtuarium unćtum, vel opus sanćtuarii Cyri Unćti intelligendum esse clamitant, frivolum nimis est. Nam in eadem pericopa varius vocis משיח sensus obtinere non potest; & Sanćtuarium quomodo opus Cyri unćti appelletur, ipsi viderint. De eo Messia Principe & excidendo agitur, cujus munus est coërcere defećtionem, consummare peccata, expiare pravitatem, adducere justitiam seculorum, quod frustra illi vel Cyro, vel Nehemiæ, vel Jehosuæ Sacerdoti, vel Zorobabeli authori tribuerint. Falsum inprimis est, quod Menasse Ben Israel, Abarbanel, Jacchiades, & plerique alii vaticinio hoc denuntiari pertendunt, non Messiæ post hebdomadas sexaginta novem mortem, sed propter peccata populi, quæ post liberationem ex captivitate Babylonica, stante secundo Templo patraturus fit, exilium novum populi post LXX hebdomadas & destrućtam Hierosolymam, in quo purgandus fit populus ab Idololatria, homicidio, adulterio; & qua finita purgatione, seu coërcitione defećtionis, consummatione peccati & expiatione pravitatis demum justitia seculorum adducenda, Prophetiæ vis aućtior futura, & denuo sacrificia sub tertio Templo restituenda sint. Unde Abarbanel verba illa שבעים שבעים נחתך על העם sic explicat, ut sensus fit, post septuaginta hebdomadas seu 490. annos prosperitatem & gloriam Hierosolymæ cessaturam, & novam longinquam in exilio calamitatem subituram, ut ita החתיך excifio illa nihil aliud fit, quàm decretum denuo subeundi longum & triste exilium; vel Separatio in eo exilio populi ab urbe, & urbis à populo, per quam Israelitæ in terra Domini non amplius habituri, sed hæc ab illis relinquenda sit. Qua explicatione nihil infrunitum magis est. Nam verbi חתך in Hebræo ἀπαξ λεγόμενον sensus ex Chaldæis petendus est. Illis autem חתך scindere, decidere notat. Cúmque verbum נחתך cum voce שבעים hebdomadæ in casu recto construatur, vim textui Abarbanel facit, cùm modò prosperitatem populi cum ejus exilio commutandam, modò populum ab urbe separandum significari nugatur. quasi scriptum sit, אחר post septuaginta hebdomadas tale quid futurum. Etiam glossam Judaicam particula על quam Judæi plane omittunt, convincit. Non enim simpliciter septimanæ definitæ, sed definitæ על העם super populo & urbe dicuntur, ut videlicet coërceatur defectio, & expietur pravitas, non per pœnitentiam in exilio post elapsas illas hebdomadas denuo indicendo, sed nondum elapsis hebdomadis, seu ipsa illa hebdomadarum periodo. Præterea excidium Urbis-Templi vel populi in exilium missi non est כפר חטאת expiatio peccati, sed potiús vindicta, juxta Deut. XXXII.20.21. & quidem non peccati duntaxat in captivitate Babylonica non expiati, sed infidelitatis parentum, & omnis sanguinis effusi inde à condito mundo, à sanguine Habelis usque ad sanguinem Zachariæ filii Barachiæ, Matth. XXIII.35. idque propter פשע apostasiam à Rege suo, & stuporem, per quem videntes non viderunt, & audientes non audiverunt, Esaj.VI.9. & non crediderunt Messiæ, sed eum & filios ac filias ejus occiderunt, Deut.XXXII.19. Expiatio verò est gratiæ & clementiæ, & condonationem efficit, ibid. XXXII.43. Esaj.XXI.8. Psalm.LXV.4. &c. Significat enim peccati abolitionem per ἀντίλυτρον, quod non est nisi justitia, qua Deus sanctificatur, & ut justè impium justificans justificatur. Ideo etiam Israelitarum peccata non habuerunt כפרה expiationem, nisi per sanguinem victimarum, & quasi λύτρον pretium. Sed in illis non erat ἐξιλασμός, sed tantùm externa, carnalis, typica quædam purificatio; vera autem fuit Messiæ, qui sanguine proprio peccata nostra, non post, sed intra hebdomadas LXX. delevit. Post excidium verò urbis & novum atque diuturnum exilium restitutio Templi & populi in pristinum statum expectanda non fuit, quia excidium hoc v.27. dicitur כלה ונחרצה ἀντέλλια & ὑπετομία consummatio & decisio novissima (confer Esaj.X.22.23. Rom.IX.27.28.) vocatur. Promissio verò pacem, justitiam & conversionem gentium Templo secundo deputat, Hag.II.8.9. Zach.VIII.3. Si tertium Templum ædificandum esset, nunquam visio & Prophetia obsignaretur. Nunquam Herosolyma est עיר האמת urbs veritatis (uti Zach.VIII.3. appellatur.) si semper visio & Prophetia manet. Vana enim est Prophetia quæ nunquam impletur. Neque etiam in sacrificiorum restitutione adductio æternæ justitiæ est, quia illa justitia non foret major, quàm priscorum, qui sacrificia habuerunt & amiserunt. Quod amitti potest, non est causa æternæ justitiæ. Jam & Sanctum Sanctorum, quod spatio temporis decisi ungendum promittitur, aliud est à penetrali Templi manufacti. Ita templum ædifi-
units.tr: These objections show nothing but stupidity and a lack of understanding [ἀσυνεσίαν], and an audacity that matches it, when they are set against that most eloquent prophecy of Daniel and its explanation, which gains credit from the analogy of the promises, from the phrases of Scripture, and from the event itself. Their complaint that Christians disagree in explaining that prophecy is trivial, since they themselves quarrel constantly over the explanation of prophecies, and they tolerate any explanation at all, provided it removes the true fulfilment, that is, fulfilment in the true Messiah, Jesus. If you set aside the single view of the Englishman John Marsham, who contends that the whole prophecy was finished in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes (and the learned Wagenseil has carefully answered him in his Mantissa on the seventy weeks of Daniel), the Christian explanations agree in substance and differ only in marking the beginning and the intervening period. Some begin the weeks from the fourth year of King Zedekiah, when Jeremiah (ch. 18:1 ff.) began to prophesy about the return of the captives from Babylon; others from the message and announcement of the angel to Daniel; others from the edict of King Cyrus granting the people free return to their country (2 Chron. 36:22 ff.); others from the second year of Darius Nothus (Ezra 6); others from the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, on the occasion described in Ezra 7:1. Others place their end at the baptism of Christ, others at the passion of the Lord, others at the destruction of the city and the Temple. Indeed, our dispute with the Jews concerns not a few years or a single century, but an interval of fifteen centuries. And, what must be carefully noted, a longer time than a thousand years has now passed since the prophecy was fulfilled, in addition to the interval that ought to have lain between the utterance of this oracle and its completion. In reckoning times, Dionysius of Halicarnassus says in his History, book 7, that if someone is wrong by a few years in an ancient history covering many years, it must be tolerated; but to be out by two or three whole ages (indeed by fifteen) is not allowed. It is likely that God did not wish to indicate the exact year of Christ's death, but to leave a little room for the investigation of the faithful, and also some occasion for the objections of unbelievers. For it is the glory of God to conceal a matter, so that the nature of the matter may exercise the zeal and faith of people (Prov. 25:2). Nor is an exact chronology, leaving no difficulty at all, necessary for faith in this oracle; it is enough to take these dates with some latitude [ἐν ταλάντει]. For God wished us not to cling to a point of time, but to weigh the significance of the events themselves. Nor does this suit the Jews in their computation of the seventy weeks any less than it suits Christians. More serious, and the very hinge of the matter, is that some, the Italians especially, assert that the weeks are to be understood not as weeks of years but as weeks of Jubilees, contrary to all the usage of Holy Scripture, which recognizes no weeks other than weeks of days and of seven days. Others understand by the "anointed prince" [נגיד משיח] Cyrus, as Lipmann, Saadiah, Jarchi, Jacchiades and Menasseh do; or Nehemiah, as Abenezra does; or the priest Jeshua, as R. Levi ben Gershom does; or Zerubbabel, as Abarbanel does. But since this Messiah or Anointed Prince of Daniel is the very one whom the same passage asserts will be cut off after sixty-two weeks, was any of these men cut off after so many weeks? For the claim that by the "Messiah" who is said to be cut off we must understand the anointed sanctuary, or the work of the anointed Cyrus, is too frivolous. For the same word "Messiah" cannot have a varying sense within one and the same passage; and how the sanctuary could be called the work of anointed Cyrus, they themselves must see. The passage concerns that Messiah the Prince who is to be cut off, whose office is to restrain transgression, to bring sin to its end, to atone for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness; these tasks they vainly attribute to Cyrus, or Nehemiah, or the priest Jeshua, or Zerubbabel the author. Above all, it is false what Menasseh ben Israel, Abarbanel, Jacchiades and most others contend, that this prophecy foretells not the death of the Messiah after sixty-nine weeks, but a new exile of the people after seventy weeks and the destruction of Jerusalem, which the Messiah is to bring about while the second Temple stands, on account of the sins of the people committed after their deliverance from Babylonian captivity, sins of idolatry, murder and adultery; and that once this purging, that is, the restraint of transgression, the bringing of sin to its end, and the atonement for iniquity, is completed, everlasting righteousness is at last to be brought in, the force of the prophecy is to be greater, and sacrifices are to be restored again under a third Temple. Hence Abarbanel explains the words "seventy weeks are decreed upon the people" [שבעים שבעים נחתך על העם] so that the sense is: after seventy weeks, that is 490 years, the prosperity and glory of Jerusalem will cease, and a new and long calamity will be undergone in exile; thus the word "cut off" [החתיך] is nothing other than a decree to undergo again a long and sad exile; or a separation of the people in that exile from the city, and of the city from the people, so that the Israelites will no longer dwell in the land of the Lord, but this land is to be abandoned by them. Nothing is more unsound than this explanation. For the sense of the Hebrew word חתך, which occurs only once [ἅπαξ λεγόμενον], must be sought from the Chaldeans. Among them חתך means "to cut, to cut off." And since the verb נחתך is construed with the noun "weeks" in the nominative case, Abarbanel does violence to the text when he trifles that it signifies now that the prosperity of the people is to be exchanged for their exile, now that the people is to be separated from the city, as if the text had read "after" [אחר] seventy weeks something of that sort would happen. The Jewish gloss is also refuted by the particle על, which the Jews plainly omit. For the weeks are not simply called "determined weeks," but "determined upon the people and the city" [על העם], namely so that transgression may be restrained, and iniquity atoned for; this is not to be done by repentance in exile, to be proclaimed again after those weeks have run their course, but while the weeks have not yet run out, within that very period of weeks. Moreover, the destruction of the City-Temple, or the sending of the people into exile, is not an atonement for sin [כפר חטאת], but rather vengeance, in accordance with Deut. 32:20, 21; and not merely the sin left unatoned in the Babylonian captivity, but the unbelief of the fathers and all the blood shed since the foundation of the world, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah (Matt. 23:35), and this on account of the apostasy [פשע] from their King, and the dullness by which seeing they did not see, and hearing they did not hear (Isa. 6:9); and they did not believe the Messiah, but killed him and his sons and daughters (Deut. 32:19). But atonement belongs to grace and mercy, and brings about forgiveness (ibid. 32:43; Isa. 21:8; Ps. 65:4 etc.). For it signifies the abolition of sin by means of a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον], which is nothing but the righteousness by which God is sanctified, and by which he, justly justifying the ungodly, is himself justified. Therefore the sins of the Israelites also had no atonement [כפרה] except through the blood of victims, and as it were a price of ransom [λύτρον]. But in those sacrifices there was no propitiation [ἐξιλασμός], only an external, fleshly, somewhat typical purification; but the true one was that of the Messiah, who blotted out our sins with his own blood, not after, but within the seventy weeks. After the destruction of the city, however, and the new and lasting exile, the restoration of the Temple and the people to their former state was not to be expected, because this destruction is called in v. 27 "consummation and decision" [כלה ונחרצה], the last end [ἀντέλλια] and cutting off [ὑπετομία] (compare Isa. 10:22, 23; Rom. 9:27, 28). But the promise assigns peace, righteousness and the conversion of the nations to the second Temple (Hag. 2:8, 9; Zech. 8:3). If a third Temple were to be built, the vision and prophecy would never be sealed. Jerusalem would never be the city of truth [עיר האמת] (as it is called in Zech. 8:3), if the vision and prophecy remained always. For a prophecy that is never fulfilled is empty. Nor is the restoration of sacrifices the bringing in of everlasting righteousness, because that righteousness would be no greater than that of the ancients, who had sacrifices and lost them. What can be lost is not the cause of everlasting righteousness. Moreover, the Most Holy Place, which is promised to be anointed after the cutting off of time, is something other than the inner sanctuary of a Temple made by hands. Thus the Temple to be built by the Branch [צמח] is distinguished from the Temple of Zerubbabel (Zech. 6:13). But that is not a third Temple made by hands proper to Israel; what is promised there and in Ezekiel is not in Zion and the tribe of Judah (Ezek. 45:1, 4, 5, 6, 7; 48:8, 9, 10). Nor, therefore, is that third Temple the one...

units.la: candum à צמח Germine à Templo Zorobabelis, Zach.VI.13. distinguitur. Sed illud non est Templum tertium manufactum Israeli proprium; quod ibi & apud Ezechielem promittitur, non est in Sione & tribu Judæ, Ezech.XLV.1. 4.5.6.7. XLVIII.8.9.10. Neque proin tertium illud Templum id est, ad quod venire Messias debuit, quia is venire debuit ad Sionem, Psal.II. 6. LXXVIII.68. CXXXII.13.17. Denique inprimis attendi scopus Dei oraculum hoc dantis debet, qui est consolari Danielem, & cum eo omnes fideles, & illorum expectationem alere, atque ὑπομονή excitare. Cum eo scopo non conveniebat, jubere pios, ut, exceptis paucis diebus angustiæ, attenderent & numerarent annos, quibus ad finem labentibus non magnum & inæstimabile bonum, sed ineffabile malum & exitium, dissipatio populi duratura tanto tempore, ut nullus finis præstitutus inveniri posset, sequatur. Ergone Deus annos parvæ εὐημερίας numerari voluit, at tantæ calamitatis in exilio obventuræ non voluit? Quid verò multis? Judæorum væcordia & ἀπιστία Solis radiis scripta est, quia tempora in talibus Prophetiis definita putare sub anathemate vetuerunt. Nam in Massechet Sanhedrin, cap.11. hæc legere est: תפח רוחן של מחשבי קצין Rumpatur spiritus eorum, qui computant terminos. Et R. Lipman in Nizzachon n.334. תפח נשמתם בגהנם של מחשבי הקיצים Pereat spiritus eorum in gehenna, qui terminos computant. Quin & Prophetæ Danielis paraphrasin ne adornaret Chaldæus Interpres Divinitus vetitum eum esse Magistri perhibent Massechet Megill. c.1. דאית ביה קיף המשיח quia in eo finis Messiæ continetur.
