XXII.8), Amaziah against Amos (Amos VII.10), and the priest Pashhur against Jeremiah (Jer. XX.7.8). Who does not know that some have charged others, even the most innocent, with crimes? For if accusation is enough, who will be innocent? Christ was not a Samaritan, because he worshipped and taught the true God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, not a foreign god. He was not a blasphemer, although he called himself the Son of God. For he was the Son of God, and he showed it by his works. Nor did he seduce people to worship other gods, but by turning the hearts of the children to the hearts of the fathers he persuaded them of the same God whom the fathers worshipped. Moreover, that he cast out demons not by Beelzebul but by the Spirit of God (Matt. XII.25, etc.), he proved powerfully, so that the Jews were reduced to silence [ἐχεμυθίαν]. And what sort of accusers did Christ have? His enemies, goaded by the gadfly of envy, burning with a deadly hatred of him, not on account of any crime of Christ but on account of his zeal, by which he brought their hypocrisy and wickedness into the open; in short, they were judges and witnesses in their own cause. Nor does it stand in the way that not even his brothers believed in him, John VII.5. For the counsel they gave Christ, that he should go into Judea and manifest himself to the world, and so come out in public [ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ], revealed that they too laboured under carnal prejudice about raising an earthly kingdom. They cherished the same thoughts as the other Jews, namely that

units.la: Jesus, ceu alter Moses, populum à servitute temporali liberaret, quod de iis, Esaj. LXIII. 10-15. prædictum est. Neque etiam prædictionem illam Esajæ; Non faciet, ut audiatur in publico vox sua, cap. XLII.2. similésque alias meditati sunt. Non ergo contemptus, sed iniqua contemptus causa respici debet. Alias enim etiam Cain Habelem, Ismael Isacum, Esavus Jacobum, filii Jacobi fratrem Josephum, fratres Davidis eundem, amici Jobum contempserunt sine ullo sanctitatis horum præjudicio. Quo verò animo proximi Christi erga eundem futuri fuerint, etiam prædictiones, Psal. XLI.9.10. LV. 12.13.14. Mich. VII.5.6. testantur, Et fuerunt illi fratres non germani vel uterini, sed consanguinei, vel ὁμιλοῦντες. Sed quos genuinos fratres suos censuerit, ipse sapientissimè declaravit, dicens: Qui fecerit voluntatem Patris mei in Cœlis, is meus frater, mea soror, & mea mater est, Matth. XII.50. Sed Judæos impulsore Christo assiduè tumultuatos esse, adeóque Christum seditiosum hominem fuisse, teste Svetonio in vita Claudii, cap.25. Lusitanus Judæus probat. Id ipsum etiam hostes Christi passim ei objecerant, quasi regiam dignitatem affectasset, Luc. XXIII. 2.5. Sed à crimine in solenni judicio, eum Pilatus judex, & Herodes ipse absolverunt, ibid. v. 14, 15. Quin & Christus in diebus carnis suæ tum doctrina, tum facto suo calumniam diluit, Matth. XVII.24.25.26. Joh. XIX.11. Et tam vera de Christo Svetonius, quàm de Mose Galenus prodidit. Nam ne nomen quidem genuinum ei innotuit, cùm Chrestum, non Christum insignivit. Seditiosos fuisse non Christum, vel Christianos, sed horum hostes Judæos, satis ipse Josephus diligentissimus Judaici belli, seditione populi provocati, scriptor prodidit. Ausi porro Judæi etiam sunt Christum furti crimine arcessere, eò quòd in ligno suspensus, non lapidibus obrutus fuerit; quasi vel fures ex ligno suspendi Lex Divina, vel Romanorum etiam jusserit, vel fures fuerint filii Saulis suspensi, 2.Sam. XXI.9. vel non fuerit Achan lapidibus obrutus, Jos. VII.20.26. Veriorem longè mortis Christi causam S. Petrus prodidit, dicens: Christus semel pro peccatoribus mortuus est, justus pro injustis, 1.Pet. IV.18. Sed maniacum etiam fuisse, & propter maniam vinculis constrictum blasphemant, prætextu verborum, Marc. III.21. Cùm hæc audivissent ejus propinqui, venerunt, ut prehenderent eum. Dixerunt enim, ὅτι ἐξέστη quòd apud se ipsum non sit; Propinqui illi haud dubiè fratres illi, qui in eum non crediderunt, Joh. VII.5. fuerunt. Illi venerunt prehensuri Jesum, vel quia ob turbæ, cui etiam hostes Jesu immisceri potuerunt, confluxum, eum periclitari crediderunt; vel quia urbi Nazaretho ab Herodianis & Romanis Jesu causa metuerunt: vel quia alias ob causas omnino turbæ subducendum putarunt. Illi dixerunt, fingentes prætextum, vel metuentes, vel piam fraudem, vel bonum dolum struentes, quòd apud seipsum non sit. Sed quod illi sic dixerunt, non iccirco verum fuisse consequitur. Ita mox, v.22. Scribæ dixerunt: Habet Beelzebulem, & per principem daemoniorum daemonia ejicit. Quòd procul à vero aberrat. Etiam servi illi de Elisa ad Jehu dixerunt: Cur venit ὁ ἐπίλητος insanus, arreptitius ille ad te, 2.Reg. IX.11? Sed dicto fides non constitit.
units.tr: Jesus, like another Moses, would free the people from temporal servitude, which is foretold of them in Isaiah LXIII.10-15. Nor did they consider that prophecy of Isaiah, He shall not make his voice heard in public, ch. XLII.2, or other similar ones. The cause to be considered, then, is not contempt but unjust contempt. For Cain despised Abel, Ishmael Isaac, Esau Jacob, the brothers of Joseph, son of Jacob, the brothers of David, and Job's friends despised Job, without any prejudice to the holiness of these men. What the attitude of Christ's neighbours towards him would be is attested by the prophecies too (Ps. XLI.9.10; LV.12.13.14; Mic. VII.5.6). And those brothers were not full brothers or uterine brothers, but cousins, or companions [ὁμιλοῦντες]. But whom he judged to be his true brothers he himself most wisely declared, saying: Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven, he is my brother, sister and mother (Matt. XII.50). But that the Jews were constantly stirred up to tumult at Christ's instigation, and so that Christ was a seditious man, as Suetonius attests in the Life of Claudius, ch. 25, the Lusitanian Jew proves. Christ's enemies also charged him with this everywhere, as if he had aimed at royal dignity (Luke XXIII.2.5). But Pilate the judge and Herod himself acquitted him of the charge in a solemn trial (ibid. v.14,15). Indeed Christ in the days of his flesh refuted the slander both by his teaching and by his deed (Matt. XVII.24-26; John XIX.11). And Suetonius reported things about Christ as true as Galen reported about Moses. For the name Christ was not even known to him, since he called him Chrestus, not Christ. That it was not Christ or the Christians but their enemies, the Jews, who were seditious, the very careful writer of the Jewish war, Josephus himself, shows well enough, for the people were provoked to rebellion. Moreover the Jews dared to charge Christ with the crime of theft, because he was hanged on a tree and not stoned, as if the Divine Law, or the Romans too, had ordered thieves to be hanged on a tree, or as if the sons of Saul who were hanged were thieves (2 Sam. XXI.9), or as if Achan had not been stoned (Josh. VII.20.26). Peter told a far truer cause of Christ's death, saying: Christ died once for sinners, the just for the unjust (1 Pet. IV.18). But they also blaspheme that he was mad and bound with chains on account of madness, on the pretext of his words (Mark III.21): When his relatives heard this, they came to seize him. For they said that he is out of his mind [ὅτι ἐξέστη]. Those relatives were undoubtedly the brothers who did not believe in him (John VII.5). They came to seize Jesus either because they believed he was in danger from the crowd, into which enemies of Jesus could also mix, or because they feared for the town of Nazareth from the Herodians and Romans on account of Jesus, or because for other reasons they thought he had to be withdrawn from the crowd altogether. They said, inventing a pretext, out of fear, or devising a pious deceit or a good trick, that he is not in his right mind. But it does not follow that what they said was true. So soon after, v.22: The scribes said: He has Beelzebul, and by the prince of demons he casts out demons, which is far from the truth. Likewise those servants said of Elisha to Jehu: Why did this madman [ὁ ἐπίλητος] come to you? (2 Kings IX.11). But a saying does not establish faith.

units.la: Denique neque legem de honorandis parentibus violavit, dicens: Quæ mater mea, & qui fratres mei? Matth. XII.48. Quid tibi & mihi mulier? Joh. II.4. Nam quà homo, fuit parentibus ὑποτασσόμενος subjectus, Luc. II.51. At quà Deus, fuit ἀμήτωρ sine matre, Hebr. VII.3. & quà Mediatoris officium sustinens, imperata matris agnoscere non debuit. Quare me quæsivistis? An nesciebatis, quòd oportuerit me vacare iis, quæ Patris sunt, Luc. II.49?
units.tr: Finally, he did not violate the law on honouring parents when he said: Who is my mother, and who are my brothers? (Matt. XII.48), or What have you to do with me, woman? (John II.4). For as a man he was subject [ὑποτασσόμενος] to his parents (Luke II.51), but as God he was without mother [ἀμήτωρ] (Heb. VII.3), and in carrying out the office of Mediator he ought not to acknowledge the commands of his mother. Why did you seek me? Did you not know that I must be occupied with the things of my Father? (Luke II.49)

units.la: CXXVIII. Non argumenta, sed mera præjudicia sunt, quæ præterea Judæi Jesu Domino & Messiæ verillimo objiciunt.
units.tr: CXXVIII. The objections which the Jews also raise against the Lord Jesus, the true Messiah, are not arguments but mere prejudices.

units.la: Si Jesus verus Messias fuit, inquiunt, quis magis illum agnoviisset, vel recepisset, quàm magna illius ætatis Judæorum Synagoga, quam penes Ecclesiæ authoritas stetit? Num quis, ita Pharisæi loquuntur, ex Principibus credidit in eum, aut ex Pharisæis? Sed turba hæc, quæ non novit Legem, execrabilis est, Joh. VII.48. Quasi non prædictum sit, fore, ut Messias ab architectis rejiciatur, Psal. CXVIII.22. & sit deficiens viris & principibus, Esaj. LIII. 3. Sed hoc Dei adversus principes Judæorum judicium fuit. De quo sic Esajas. Vade, & dic populo huic: Audite audiendo, & ne intelligite: & videte videndo, & ne cognoscatis. Impinguando impinguavit cor populi hujus, & aures ejus aggravando aggravavit, & oculos ejus oblinendo oblevit: ne videat oculis suis, & auribus suis audiat, & cor ipsius intelligat, & convertatur, & sanet eum. Et dixit: Quousque, Domine? Et dixit: Donec vastatæ fuerint urbes absque habitatore: & domus, absque homine; & terra vastitate effecta fuerit solitudo; & elongaverit Jehova homines: & multum erit desertum in medio terræ, Esaj. VI. 9-12. Idem Esajas descripturus, qua humilitate & simplicitate venturus esset Messias, ut pro nobis pateretur, quem Sacerdotes & primores illi, ut ambitioni & cupiditati suæ abblandirentur, triumphabundum expectabant. Quis, ita præconum Evangelii nomine loquitur, auditui nostro credidit, & brachium Jehovæ super quo revelatum est? cap. LIII. 1. Sed Pharisæi magno præjudicio populum fidelem, qui Christum recepit, onerant; Turba, inquiunt, hæc, qui non norunt Legem, maledicti sunt, Joh. VII.49. quasi non æquè Legem intellexissent atque primores, adeóque non judicio, sed affectu abrepti Christum amplexi essent. Hic rursus evenit, quod ante prædictum est. Sapientia Sapientum populi peribit, & prudentia prudentum occultabit se, Esaj. XXIX. 14. Cor tuum meditabitur terrorem: Ubi Scriba, ubi trutinans? ibid. XXXIII.18. Quæ testimonia conjungens Apostolus, ad tempus appatitionis Christi accommodat, 1.Cor. I.19. 20. addens epilogum: Nonne infatuavit Deus sapientiam hujus mundi? Nempe Sapientes Judæorum eo tempore multi erant in quæstionibus Legalibus, sed ad signa temporum non attendebant, & opus, quod Deus moliebatur, ignorabant. Quærebant justitiæ Legem, & Zelum habebant, sed non secundum scientiam, à justitia Legis aberrabant, Rom. IX.31. X.2. Nimium enim traditioni & authoritati Patrum suorum sidebant. Plebs contrà non attendens nisi ad promissionem, & in conscientia sua convicta, quòd Christi
units.tr: If Jesus was the true Messiah, they say, who would have recognised or received him more readily than the great Synagogue of the Jews of that age, in whose hands the authority of the Church rested? Has any of the rulers believed in him, or any of the Pharisees? But this crowd, which does not know the Law, is accursed, as the Pharisees put it, John 7:48. As if it had not been foretold that the Messiah would be rejected by the builders, Psalm 118:22, and would be despised and rejected by men and princes, Isaiah 53:3. But this was God's judgment upon the chief men of the Jews, and Isaiah speaks of it thus: Go, and say to this people: Hear and hear, but do not understand; see and see, but do not perceive. Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and be healed. Then I said, Lord, how long? And he answered, Until the cities be wasted without inhabitant, and the houses without man, and the land be utterly desolate; and the LORD have removed men far away, and there be a great forsaking in the midst of the land, Isaiah 6:9-12. The same Isaiah, describing the humility and simplicity with which the Messiah would come to suffer for us, whom those priests and chief men awaited in triumph, so as to flatter their ambition and greed, says: Who has believed our report, speaking in the name of the heralds of the gospel? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? chap. 53:1. But the Pharisees burden the faithful people who received Christ with a great prejudice: This crowd, they say, which does not know the Law, is cursed, John 7:49, as if they had not understood the Law just as well as the chief men, and so had embraced Christ not by judgment but carried away by feeling. Here again what was foretold before comes to pass: The wisdom of the wise shall perish, and the understanding of the prudent shall be hidden, Isaiah 29:14. Your heart shall meditate terror: where is the scribe? where is he that weighs? ibid. 33:18. The Apostle, joining these testimonies, applies them to the time of Christ's appearing, 1 Cor. 1:19-20, adding this conclusion: Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? Indeed, the wise men of the Jews at that time were many in questions of the Law, but they did not attend to the signs of the times and were ignorant of the work God was undertaking. They sought the Law of righteousness and had zeal, but not according to knowledge; they went astray from the righteousness of the Law, Rom. 9:31; 10:2. For they trusted too much in the tradition and authority of their fathers. The common people, on the other hand, attended only to the promise, and, convicted in their own conscience, that Christ...

units.la: Præjudicia Judæorum, quòd nemo Principum, sed sola turba, quæ non novit Legem, execrabilis est, quæ genuinè nos gemunt, non noveris; in lesum credideris: quid Galilæus fueris: quòd Majores sui, qui leguntur repudiarunt & damnarunt, viri probi iuerint, diffusa.
units.tr: The prejudices of the Jews, that no one of the rulers, but only the crowd which does not know the Law, is accursed, which you would truly lament, you have not known; you have believed in Jesus; what you were as a Galilean; that their ancestors, whom they read of, rejected and condemned, were upright men, spread abroad.

units.la: Christi doctrina amorem Dei efficiat, ad audiendum & recipiendum Christum expeditior fuit, cum nec praejudiciis devinciretur, nec per χενοδοξίαν turpe ipsi videretur, doceri & discere, nec ambitionis & dominationis stimulis concitaretur. Fieri nempe potest, ut varia & delicata eruditio ad cognitionem veritatis impedimentum afferat. Veritas enim salutaris in uno consistit, & omnes ejus partes per illud unum inter se conjunguntur. Qui igitur illud unum ignorat, vel ad illud non identidem respicit, & memoriam multis oneravit, quae qualia sint, dijudicare non potest, quia ea in uno non potest connectere, nullum eruditionis suae usum habere potest. At cui Deus eum fontem, in quo omnis thesaurus sapientiae & prudentiae continetur, revelare voluerit, ei non est difficile in viis Dei incedere, in quibus alii impingunt. Non tamen ex turba Nicodemus, sed Pharisaeus & ἀρχῶν τῶν Ἰουδαίων princeps Judaeorum, Joh. III.1. qui Christo adhaesit, & praejudicantes, atque turbam ob Legis ignorantiam traducentes Judaeos his verbis reprehendit: Num lex nostra judicat hominem, si non audiat ab ipso prius, & cognoverit, quid faciat? ibid. VII.51. q. d. vos turbam ignorare Legem, & execrabilem ideo esse clamitatis, & contra Legem ipsi agitis. Sed reliqui Pharisaei scommate dictum hoc excipientes; An & tu, inquiunt, Galilaeus es? Scrutare & vide, quod Propheta ex Galilaea non sit excitatus, ibid. v.52. Atque hoc novum praejudicium fuit. Quasi Deus Prophetas mittens homines ingeniosos, exercitatos, & inter homines elegantes in terris optimis educatos legere cogeretur, vel satis esset ad damnandum Christum, quod, cum ex Galilaea veniret, docere tanquam Propheta a Deo missus auderet. Potuit tamen Propheta Bethlehemi nasci, & in Galilaea habitare, atque inde in Judaeam ad docendum progredi. Neque prolin etiam Judaeos a suscipienda Jesu disciplina retinere debuit praeconcepta opinio, de virtute ac probitate Majorum suorum, ac maxime Sacerdotum, qui Jesum praejudicio damnarunt, & dogma ejus repudiarunt. Nam quales saepe Majores eorum fuerint, Lex & Prophetae testantur, a quibus saepe appellantur, incircumcisi auribus & corde, Jerem. IV.4. VI.10. Populus labiis Deum honorans, corde autem ab eo remotissimus, Esaj. XXIX.13. Majores eorum fuerunt, qui Josephum fratrem suum, parum abfuit, quin interficerent, re autem ipsa in servitutem vendiderunt; qui Mosen perpetuis vexationibus ad vitae taedium egerunt, ducem suum ac liberatorem, cui terra, mare, aer obediebant; qui panem coelitus missum fastidiverunt; qui velut de summa injuria conquesti sunt, cum aves comestas adhuc ructarent: qui Davide, tanto ac tam bono Rege deserto, rebellem filium secuti sunt; qui Zachariam, Jojadae filium trucidarunt in loco sanctissimo, victimam crudelitatis suae ipsum Sacerdotem facientes. Pontifices & Sacerdotes fuerunt, qui Jeremiae falso crimine mortem machinati sunt, & effecerunt, ut usque ad diem captae Urbis captivus detineretur. De quibus Jeremias dixit: Sicut bruta animalia facti sunt Pastores, & Jehovam non requisiverunt. Propterea non intellexerunt, & pascua eorum dispersa sunt, Jerem. X.21. quorum, tempore ipsius Jesu, atrocissima facinora Josephus describit. Neque de Synedrio melius existimandum, praesertim cum eo tempore Senatores non veteri more cooptati, sed ex potentium nutu legi solerent; ut & Pontifices, non jam perpetua, sed annali & saepe empta dignitate. Non mirari ergo debemus, si homines arroganti tumidi; ambitione & avaritia insatiabiles in furorem acti sunt, conspecto homine, qui sanctissima praecepta afferens, vitam ipsis suam ipsa vivendi divinitate exprobravit. Neq; aliud illi crimini datum, quam quod optimo cuique; velut Michae a falsis Prophetis, quod veritatem adversus illos asseruisset, I.Reg. XXII.22.23.24. Eliae ab Achabo, quod pacem Israelis turbasset, I.Reg. XVIII.17. Luc. XXIII.2. Jeremiae a Sacerdotibus, quod adversus Templum vaticinatus esset, Jerem. XXVI.6.11. Matth. XXVII.40. Joh. II.19.20.21. Neque tantum Esajas praedixit, fore ut tempore Messiae Servus Dei, Sacerdotes, scribae, cum consummatus esse deberet, sit caecus & surdus, Esaj. XLII.19. coll. cum VI.9–12. Sed etiam Hebraeorum Magistri Veteres in Sanhedrin, Ketubhoth & Sota scriptum reliquerunt, temporibus Messiae homines fore canina impudentia, asinina contumacia, & ferina crudelitate. Traditio R. Jehudae in Masora ad titulum de Sanhedr. C. Helech: Quo tempore, inquit, adveniet filius David, rari erunt Sapientes in Israel, & Sapientia Scribarum putrescet, & domus institutionis Divinae lupanar erit.
units.tr: The teaching of Christ, which kindles the love of God, was better placed to hear and receive Christ, since it was bound by no prejudices, nor did it seem shameful to it, through vainglory [κενοδοξία], to be taught and to learn, nor was it stirred by the goads of ambition and domination. It can indeed happen that a varied and refined learning becomes a hindrance to the knowledge of the truth. For saving truth consists in one thing, and all its parts are joined together through that one thing. Whoever therefore is ignorant of that one thing, or does not keep returning to it, and has burdened his memory with many things, cannot judge what sort they are, because he cannot connect them in the one thing, and so he cannot make any use of his learning. But to one to whom God has been pleased to reveal that fountain, in which the whole treasure of wisdom and prudence is contained, it is not difficult to walk in the ways of God, in which others stumble. Yet it was not from the crowd that Nicodemus came, but a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews [ἀρχῶν τῶν Ἰουδαίων], a prince of the Jews, John 3:1, who clung to Christ, and who rebuked the Jews, who were prejudging and dismissing the crowd for its ignorance of the Law, with these words: Does our law judge a man before it hears him, and knows what he does? ibid. 7:51, as if to say: you complain that the crowd does not know the Law, and therefore is accursed, yet you yourselves act against the Law. But the rest of the Pharisees, taking up this saying with a sneer, said: Are you also a Galilean? Search and see that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee, ibid. v. 52. And this was a new prejudice. As if God, when sending prophets, were bound to choose men of talent, trained, and brought up among men of refinement in the best lands; or as if it were enough to condemn Christ that he came from Galilee and dared to teach as a prophet sent by God. The prophet could indeed have been born in Bethlehem and yet dwell in Galilee, and from there go on to teach in Judea. Nor should the preconceived opinion about the virtue and probity of their ancestors, and especially of the priests, who condemned Jesus by prejudice and rejected his doctrine, have kept the Jews from accepting the discipline of Jesus. For the Law and the Prophets bear witness what their ancestors often were, and they are often called by them uncircumcised in ears and heart, Jer. 4:4; 6:10. A people that honours God with their lips, but whose heart is far from him, Isaiah 29:13. Their ancestors were the men who nearly killed their brother Joseph, and in fact sold him into slavery; who wore Moses down with constant vexations until he was weary of life, their leader and deliverer, whom land, sea and air obeyed; who despised the bread sent from heaven; who complained, as if of a great wrong, while they were still belching the birds they had eaten; who, deserting David, so great and so good a king, followed a rebellious son; who slew Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada, in the most holy place, making the priest himself the victim of their cruelty. There were high priests and priests who plotted the death of Jeremiah on a false charge, and brought it about that he was kept a prisoner until the day the city was taken. Of them Jeremiah said: The shepherds have become brutish, and have not sought the LORD. Therefore they have not prospered, and all their flocks are scattered, Jer. 10:21. Josephus describes their most atrocious crimes in the time of Jesus himself. Nor should we think better of the Sanhedrin, especially since at that time the senators were not chosen by the old custom, but were usually appointed at the nod of the powerful; and likewise the high priests held their office not for life, but for a year and often purchased. We ought not to wonder, then, if men proud and puffed up with arrogance, insatiable in ambition and greed, were driven to fury when they saw a man who, bringing the most holy precepts, reproached them for their own lives, which were so unlike his teaching. Nor was any other charge laid against him than that he was against the best men, as Micaiah was by the false prophets because he had maintained the truth against them, 1 Kings 22:22-24; as Elijah was by Ahab because he had troubled the peace of Israel, 1 Kings 18:17; Luke 23:2; as Jeremiah was by the priests because he had prophesied against the Temple, Jer. 26:6, 11; Matt. 27:40; John 2:19-21. Nor did Isaiah only foretell that in the time of the Messiah the Servant of God, when he ought to have been made perfect, would be blind and deaf, the priests and scribes, Isaiah 42:19, compared with 6:9-12. But also the old teachers of the Hebrews, in the tractates Sanhedrin, Ketubhoth & Sota, have left it written that in the times of the Messiah men would be of dog-like shamelessness, of ass-like obstinacy, and of beast-like cruelty. The tradition of R. Jehuda in the Masora, under the title de Sanhedr., chapter Helech: At the time, he says, when the son of David comes, the wise men in Israel will be few, the wisdom of the scribes will rot, and the house of divine instruction will become a brothel.

units.la: LOCUS VICESIMUS De OECONOMIA FOEDERIS GRATIÆ Sub EVANGELIO. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: LOCUS VICESIMUS: On the Economy of the Covenant of Grace under the Gospel. A Summary.

units.la: Jesus Christus è Cœlo missus Propheta, Sacerdos & Rex evangelizari debuit. 1. Vocis Evangelii origo indagatur, & homonymia explicatur. 2. Judæorum probrosa vocis detorsio. 3. Evangelium definitur, & Scripturæ testimoniis generalibus explicatur. 4. Ante promissum est per Prophetas in Scripturis, velut per Prophetam novum, Christum, à Mose distinctum, prædicandum. 5. Summa Evangelii ex Rom. I 2. 3. 4. exponitur. 6. Christus ut Mediator melioris & Novi Testamenti utramque ejus paginam facit. 7. Testamenti Novi, quod in Evangelio prædicatur, definitio & explicatio. 8. Prædictiones & prafigurationes ejusdem variæ. 9. Jeremiæ inprimis & Ezechielis. 10. Ejus introducendi necessitas ex Veteris Testamenti antiquatione colligitur. 11. Judæorum vaticinium Jeremiæ detorquentium, & Novum Testamentum oppugnantium elenchus. 12. Novi Fœderis seu Testamenti promissiones ipsum fœdus seu Testamentum novum, non renovatum arguunt. 13. Judæorum argumenta contraria refelluntur. 14. Novum Testamentum propriam & peculiarem œconomiam habet. 15. Oeconomia illa Fœderis gratiæ sub Evangelio, & Testamenti præceptis & promissionibus propriis absolvitur. Lex Evangelii explicata. 16. Est Lex obedientiæ astipulationis in Evangelium Christi, hoc est, fidei in Christum per passiones consummatum. 17. Quæ ex testimonio, 1. Joh. V. 10. 11. 12. illustratur. 18. Lex fidei demonstrationem Evangelii ejusque manifestationem ad conscientiam comitem habet. Cujus firmamenta sunt sapientia, convenientia cum Scripturis Propheticis, & Pietatis fructus. 19. Pelagianorum, Pontificiorum, Socinianorum, &c. Legem Evangelii in legem novam operum convertentium elenchus. 20. Eorundem argumenta ad partes vocantur. 21. Libertinorum aliorumque Respiscentiæ & Pietatis legem & studium ab Evangelio removentium impietas. 22. Fides & respiscentia non est conditio propriè dicta Evangelii. 23. Evangelium nulla consilia à præceptis distincta, & perfectionem Evangelii constituentia commendat. 24. Quod pluribus astruitur. 25. Vota Monastica, consiliorum horum apex, Evangelio contrariantur. 26. Argumenta pro consiliis Evangelicis refelluntur. 27. Neque Christus sub Evangelio nova præcepta, Lege Mosis non comprehensa rogavit. 28. Quod probatur, inductione tum eorum præceptorum, quæ Priori Decalogi Tabulæ adjecta statuunt. 29. Tum eorum, quæ Posteriori Tabulæ adjecta statuunt. 30. Evangelium propriis & præstantioribus promissis gaudet. 31. Quæ non Fœdere æterno Gratiæ, nec Testamento Vetere & Typico, sed Novo nituntur, & non sine gravi culpa negliguntur. 32. Regula generalis, qua Promissionum Novi Testamenti præstantiorum intelligentia informari debet, figitur. 33. Scripturæ consummationem Christi & fidelium Novo Testamento attribuunt. 34. Consummatio Ecclesiæ sub N. T. definitur & explicatur. 35. In omnia N. T. bona, quæ Evangelio, quàtali, propria sunt, illa se diffundit. 36. Maxima illa Novi Testamenti prærogativa est quòd in ea prædicatur Jesus Christus, qui in mundum venit, ut peccatores salvaret. 37. In Jesu Christo consummato etiam membra ejus consummata intelliguntur. 38. Bona. fidelium Novi Testamenti eximia summatim comprehensa. 39. Primum est exhibitio justitiæ perfectæ per mortem Christi. 40. Cum qua consummata redemptio, justificatio & cum Deo reconciliatio cohæret. 41. Discrimen justificationis sub Vetere & Novo Testamento. 42. Proximum N.T. Bonum est donatio Spiritus Promissionis. 43. Differentia œconomiæ N.& V.Test. quoad donationem Spiritus. 44. Spiritus promissionis præcipuum opus est Filiatio seu Adoptio eorum, qui in Evangelio credunt. 45. Hunc qui acceperunt, Deum Patrem, merè paternum affectum in Christo erga fideles exerentem, appellant. 46. Ejusdem Spiritus promissionis operatio est Revelatio plenior, & eximia sapientia fidelium sub N.T. quæ jam olim prædicta & promissa. 47. Et per Christum mysteria Regni Cœlorum reludentem præstita est. 48. Comparatio quoad Bonum isthoc Veteris & Novi Testamenti. 49. Sapientiam & notitiam majorem fiducia, amor & timor Dei intensior sequitur. 50. Etiam libertate singulari fideles N.T. gaudent. 51. Quæ in immunitate ab execratione Legis, exorto inde timore, & servitute Legis præceptorum in placitis consistit. 52. Potissimum vero in eo, quod à Vetere domino liberati solum Christum cognoscimus, eique soli servimus, & in eo ad Deum, ceu patrem nostrum cum omni fiducia accedimus. 53. Libertatis illius comes Pax est, in V.T. luculenter prædicta; 54. & in Novo per Christum exhibita. 55. Una cum Pace illa datur hæreditas gentium, seu communio cum hominibus in terra, nullo discrimine; 56. nec non communio fidelium in terra cum spiritibus consummatis in Cœlo. 57. Salvo Ecclesiæ militantis & triumphantis discrimine arctior fidelium Ecclesiæ N.T. cum Cœlestibus communio est, quàm fuit fidelium Ecclesiæ V.T. 58. Bonorum N.T. hactenus explicatorum comes singularis Lætitia. 59. Eáque plane [Greek], cùm etiam lugentium sit. 60. Præstantia N.T. in externum etiam cultum se diffundit, qui non amplius servilis, carnalis, sed ingenuus & spiritualis est. 61. Non obstante Sacramentorum, quæ terrestribus elementis constant, usu. 62. Qualis N.T. cultus, tale etiam Ministerium est. 63. Licèt Evangelium pereuntibus etiam sit occultatum, & odor mortis ad mortem; non tamen amplius velamen habet, nec ministerium ejus literæ occidentis. 64. sed Spiritus, justitiæ; 65. & sermo merè reconciliationis est. 66. Fidelibus N.T. etiam hæreditas, & dominium eorum, quæ extra ipsos sunt, competit. 67. Denique, & obsignatio Bonorum N.T. quæ per Sacramenta N.T. fit, perfectior & consummatior est. 68. Tanta ergo salus, quam Evangelium præstat, omni maximo studio affectanda est, & amorem Dei in Christo, ita nos diligentis impensiorem postulat. 69. Ignorantia vel neglectus consummationis, gratiæ sub Evangelio, & bonorum N.T. omnes ferè hæreses, & magnas in Theologia difficultates peperit. 70. quod inductione errorum, quos Judæi inprimis, Socinianí & Pontificii ob perversam de Præceptis & Promissis N.T. doctrinam errant, probatur. 71. Oeconomia Fœderis Gratiæ sub Evangelio distincta tempora habuit; præparationis, ratificationis, & peremptoriæ executionis. 72. Omnibus illis temporibus Testificatio de Christo obtinere debuit. 73. Præconum Evangelii & Testium Christi missio in V.T. prædicta est. 74. Et plerosque illos fore viles, abjectos, quosdam etiam infames, omnes rudes, pariter prædictum est; & talibus uti Deo placuit, varias ob causas, quæ ex 1.Cor.II.17–f. III. IV.1–8. breviter indigetantur. 75. Primus Evangelii, post conticescentes Prophetas, præco Johannes Baptista extitit; qui etiam ante nativitatem à Prophetis promissus, & per Gabrielem & Zachariam, non sine miraculo, testem, præcursor Domini designatus est; & in ipso matris utero Salvatorem salutavit, & per os matris prophetavit. 76. Ministerium ejus præconio Resipiscentiæ, Testimonio de Christo & Baptismo absolvitur. Resipiscentiæ enim præco à Prophetis promissus est, & talem se gessit. 77. Testimonium Christo, ceu servus Domino, post se venturo quidem, sed ante se facto, ratione officii, & se priore atque præstantiore, ratione personæ, illustre inprimis perhibuit. 78. Et concionem de Pœnitentia, & Testimonium de Christo Baptismo obsignavit. 79. Ex quibus, merè Evangelicum fuisse Johannis Ministerium, conficitur. nequicquam differentibus Pontificiis, & Amyraldo, qui ex Legali & Evangelico mixtum facit. 80. Quorum argumentis occurritur. 81. Johannes Prophetarum omnium maximus, imò major Propheta fuit; sed minimus tamen in Regno Cœlorum eo major est. 82. Post Johannem Christus Evangelium, ut Dominus & causa ejus tum adventu suo, tum per Johannem, tum oretenus, in cruce inprimis, prædicavit. 83. Idem Testes & Præcones Evangelii sui, nec non ministros sibi elegit Apostolos, eósque plures, & numero duodecim, quibus tertius & decimus Paulus accessit. 84. Ordo vocationis, & nomina Apostolorum. 85. Apostoli [Greek] Testes fuerunt Resurrectionis Christi; perinde missi, uti Christus ipse à Patre missus est. 86. Ministerii sui tyrocinium ante mortem Christi fecerunt, missi à Christo in Judæam
units.tr: Jesus Christ, sent from heaven, ought to be proclaimed as Prophet, Priest and King. 1. The origin of the word "Gospel" is investigated, and its homonymy explained. 2. The Jews' shameful distortion of the word. 3. The Gospel is defined and explained by general testimonies of Scripture. 4. Before the Gospel came, Christ was proclaimed in the Scriptures through the Prophets, as a new Prophet, distinct from Moses. 5. The sum of the Gospel is set out from Romans 1:2–4. 6. Christ, as Mediator of the better and New Testament, makes up both pages of it. 7. Definition and explanation of the New Testament, which is proclaimed in the Gospel. 8. Its various predictions and foreshadowings. 9. Especially those of Jeremiah and Ezekiel. 10. The necessity of its introduction is inferred from the abrogation of the Old Testament. 11. Refutation of the Jews who twist the prophecy of Jeremiah and attack the New Testament. 12. The promises of the New Covenant or Testament show that the covenant itself, the New Testament, is not a renewed one. 13. The contrary arguments of the Jews are refuted. 14. The New Testament has its own proper and distinct economy. 15. That economy of the covenant of grace under the Gospel is completed by the precepts and proper promises of the Testament. The law of the Gospel is explained. 16. It is the law of obedience, consenting to the Gospel of Christ, that is, of faith in Christ, consummated through his sufferings. 17. This is illustrated from 1 John 5:10–12. 18. The law of faith has as its companions the demonstration of the Gospel and its manifestation to the conscience. Its supports are wisdom, agreement with the prophetic Scriptures, and the fruit of piety. 19. Refutation of the Pelagians, Papists, Socinians, etc., who turn the law of the Gospel into a new law of works that earn salvation. 20. Their arguments are brought forward and answered. 21. The impiety of the Libertines and others who remove from the Gospel the law and the pursuit of repentance and piety. 22. Faith and repentance are not properly speaking a condition of the Gospel. 23. The Gospel commends no counsels distinct from its precepts, and constituting a perfection of the Gospel. 24. This is confirmed by many arguments. 25. Monastic vows, the summit of these counsels, are contrary to the Gospel. 26. The arguments for the evangelical counsels are refuted. 27. Nor did Christ under the Gospel ask for new precepts not comprehended in the Law of Moses. 28. This is proved by an enumeration of the precepts that they add to the first table of the Decalogue. 29. And of those that they add to the second table. 30. The Gospel rejoices in its own and more excellent promises. 31. These promises rest not on the eternal covenant of grace, nor on the Old and typical Testament, but on the New, and are not neglected without grave fault. 32. A general rule is laid down by which the understanding of the more excellent promises of the New Testament ought to be shaped. 33. Scripture attributes the consummation of Christ and of believers to the New Testament. 34. The consummation of the Church under the New Testament is defined and explained. 35. It extends itself to all the goods of the New Testament that are proper to the Gospel as such. 36. The greatest prerogative of the New Testament is that in it is proclaimed Jesus Christ, who came into the world to save sinners. 37. In Jesus Christ as consummated, his members too are understood as consummated. 38. The outstanding goods of believers under the New Testament, summarily comprehended. 39. The first is the display of perfect righteousness through the death of Christ. 40. With this is joined the consummated redemption, justification, and reconciliation with God. 41. The difference of justification under the Old and New Testaments. 42. The next good of the New Testament is the gift of the Spirit of promise. 43. The difference between the economy of the New and Old Testaments as regards the gift of the Spirit. 44. The chief work of the Spirit of promise is the sonship, or adoption, of those who believe in the Gospel. 45. Those who have received this Spirit call God their Father, who in Christ shows a purely paternal affection towards believers. 46. Another operation of the same Spirit of promise is the fuller revelation and the remarkable wisdom of believers under the New Testament, which was foretold and promised long ago. 47. And this was bestowed through Christ, who unfolds the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. 48. A comparison of this good of the Old and New Testaments. 49. Greater wisdom and knowledge are followed by greater confidence, and a more intense love and fear of God. 50. Believers of the New Testament also enjoy a singular liberty. 51. This consists in freedom from the curse of the Law, and from the fear that arises from it, and from servitude to the precepts of the Law in matters of ceremony. 52. Above all it consists in this, that, freed from the old master, we know Christ alone, serve him alone, and in him approach God, as our Father, with all confidence. 53. Peace is the companion of that liberty, clearly foretold in the Old Testament; 54. and it was exhibited in the New through Christ. 55. Together with that peace is given the inheritance of the Gentiles, or fellowship with men on earth without any distinction; 56. and also the fellowship of believers on earth with the spirits made perfect in heaven. 57. With the distinction between the Church militant and the Church triumphant preserved, the fellowship of believers of the New Testament Church with the heavenly ones is closer than that of believers of the Old Testament Church. 58. A singular joy accompanies the goods of the New Testament explained so far. 59. And this joy is plainly [Greek], since it belongs also to those who mourn. 60. The excellence of the New Testament extends even to external worship, which is no longer servile and carnal, but free and spiritual. 61. This holds notwithstanding the use of the sacraments, which consist of earthly elements. 62. Such as the worship of the New Testament is, such also is the ministry. 63. Although the Gospel is hidden even from those who are perishing, and is a fragrance of death to death, yet it no longer has a veil, nor is its ministry a ministry of the letter that kills. 64. but of the Spirit, of righteousness; 65. and it is a word of pure reconciliation. 66. To believers of the New Testament belong also the inheritance and the lordship over those things which are outside themselves. 67. Finally, the sealing of the goods of the New Testament, which takes place through the sacraments of the New Testament, is more perfect and more complete. 68. Such great salvation, which the Gospel brings, is to be sought with the utmost zeal, and the love of God in Christ, who thus loves us, demands it the more earnestly. 69. Ignorance or neglect of the consummation of grace under the Gospel, and of the goods of the New Testament, has given rise to almost all heresies and great difficulties in theology. 70. This is proved by an enumeration of the errors which the Jews above all, the Socinians and the Papists fall into through their perverse doctrine of the precepts and promises of the New Testament. 71. The economy of the covenant of grace under the Gospel has distinct periods: of preparation, of ratification, and of the final execution. 72. In all those periods the testimony concerning Christ ought to hold. 73. The sending of the heralds of the Gospel and the witnesses of Christ was foretold in the Old Testament. 74. It was likewise foretold that most of them would be cheap, despised, and some even infamous, all of them unlearned; and it pleased God to use such men for various reasons, which are briefly indicated from 1 Corinthians 2:17 to 3:4–8 and 4:1–8. 75. The first herald of the Gospel after the Prophets fell silent was John the Baptist, who, though promised by the Prophets even before his birth, and designated through Gabriel and Zechariah, not without a miracle, as the witness and forerunner of the Lord, also greeted the Saviour in his mother's womb, and prophesied through his mother's mouth. 76. His ministry is completed by the proclamation of repentance, by the testimony concerning Christ, and by baptism. For the herald of repentance was promised by the Prophets, and he so conducted himself. 77. He bore a most illustrious testimony to Christ, as a servant to his Lord, coming after him in time but before him in office, and prior and more excellent in person. 78. And he sealed the sermon concerning repentance and the testimony concerning Christ with baptism. 79. From these things it follows that John's ministry was purely evangelical, against the Papists who think otherwise, and against Amyraldus, who makes it a mixture of the legal and the evangelical. 80. Their arguments are answered. 81. John was the greatest of all the Prophets, indeed more than a Prophet; yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. 82. After John, Christ proclaimed the Gospel, as the Lord and its cause, both by his coming, by John, and by word of mouth, above all on the cross. 83. The same Christ chose for himself the witnesses and heralds of his Gospel, and also the Apostles as ministers, many of them, twelve in number, to whom Paul, the thirteenth, was added. 84. The order of calling and the names of the Apostles. 85. The Apostles were witnesses of Christ's resurrection, sent in the same way as Christ himself was sent by the Father. 86. They made the apprenticeship of their ministry before the death of Christ, sent by Christ into Judea

units.la: ad praedicandam approximationem Regni Coelorum. 87. Hoc tyrocinio posito post mortem Christi ab eodem etiam ad gentes mittuntur; idque quia Israel tum, cum gentes vocandae erant, juxta Prophetias rebellis, & ad praeconium tale ineptus futurus erat. 88. Ordo missionis Apostolis mandatae, & ab iisdem susceptae. 89. Prius quam mitterentur, virtute ex alto induti, inunEgi & Spiritu baptizari debuerunt. 90. Id Pentecostes festo successit, quando symbolo insidentium illis flammantium linguarum donum linguarum, & sapientiae ad magnalia Dei eloquenda, atque illud non momentaneum, sed permanens acceperunt. 91. Apostolorum principale Privilegium fuit, quod Testes & Praecones Resurrectionis Christi, atque universales, & infallibiles Evangelii Praecones & Doctores extiterunt. 92. Eorundem privilegia & Praerogativae accessoriae aliae. 93. Habuerunt etiam Apostoli signa Apostolorum, Patientiam, Prodigia & virtutes. 94. Christus per eos opera majora fecit illis, quae vivus patravit; eaque veri nominis miracula ad attestandum veritati, non ad tentandum comparata. 95. Ad Praerogativas Apostolorum perperam Hierarchici dominationem in fide, & quidem in Petro principalem, & ad posteros traducendam, in reliquis delegatam referunt. 96. Hypothesis mystea Saraviae, quod Apostolatus semper in Ecclesia vigeat, & legitimis Episcopis omnibus competat, ad incudem revocatur. 97. Post institutos Apostolos Christus in terra adhuc degens septuaginta discipulos misit. inter quorum praeconium Sathanam e Coelo cadentem Spiritu vidit. 98. Inter Testes Christi & Praecones Evangelii etiam Prophetae, ab Apostolis distincti, extiterunt. quorum donum, quatenus extraordinarium & temporale, vel ordinarium & perpetuum fuerit, ostenditur. 99. Nec non Evangelistae. 100. Et Evangelio jam publicato, & Ecclesia constituta, Pastores & Doctores. 101.
units.tr: To preach the approach of the kingdom of heaven. 87. After this period of apprenticeship, the Apostles were sent by the same Christ, after his death, also to the Gentiles. This was because Israel, at the time when the Gentiles were to be called, was rebellious according to the prophecies and would be unfit for such a proclamation. 88. The order of the mission entrusted to the Apostles and taken up by them. 89. Before they were sent, they had to be clothed with power from on high, anointed and baptized with the Spirit. 90. This followed the feast of Pentecost, when, under the symbol of tongues of flame settling on them, they received the gift of tongues and of wisdom to proclaim the great works of God, and this gift was not momentary but permanent. 91. The principal privilege of the Apostles was that they were witnesses and heralds of the resurrection of Christ, and that they were universal and infallible preachers and teachers of the Gospel. 92. Other privileges and secondary prerogatives of the same men. 93. The Apostles also had the signs of apostles: patience, prodigies and powers. 94. Through them Christ did greater works than those he performed while alive, and these were real miracles, provided to attest the truth, not to test it. 95. The Hierarchists wrongly refer the prerogatives of the Apostles to a principal dominion over the faith, chiefly in Peter, to be handed down to his successors, and in the rest to be delegated. 96. The mystical hypothesis of Saravia, that the apostolate always flourishes in the Church and belongs to all lawful bishops, is put back on the anvil. 97. After the Apostles were appointed, Christ, while still living on earth, sent out seventy disciples; in their preaching he saw Satan falling from heaven by the Spirit. 98. Among the witnesses of Christ and the heralds of the Gospel there were also prophets, distinct from the Apostles. It is shown whether their gift, insofar as it was extraordinary and temporary, or ordinary and perpetual, was. 99. Likewise the evangelists. 100. And once the Gospel had been published and the Church established, pastors and teachers. 101.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: ESUS CHRISTUS e Coelo missus, ex muliere natus, Legi subjectus, humiliatus ad mortem usque, ex morte resuscitatus, ad dextram Dei collocatus, Salvator, Propheta, Sacerdos & Rex populi sui, una cum beneficiis & promissis praestantioribus non ingrato apud mundum silentio iterum sepeliri, sed praedicari, denuntiari, & alte proclamari debuit. Ideo S. Paulus postquam dixit, unum esse Mediatorem Dei & hominum, hominem Christum Jesum, qui dedit se ipsum redemptionis pretium pro omnibus; ilico addidit, το μαρτυριον τοις καιροις ιδιοις testimonium temporibus propriis, 1. Tim. II. 6. quasi diceret, quod Christus se ipsum redemptionis pretium dedit pro omnibus, id esse argumentum martyrii illius, quo Deus homines contestatur, ut sibi de veritate promissionum suarum interroganti respondeant ναι Etiam, & de justitia glorificationis sui, gratiarum actionis & fiduciae in se, 'Αμην, Amen, 2. Cor. I. 20.
units.tr: JESUS CHRIST, sent from heaven, born of a woman, made subject to the Law, humbled even to death, raised from the dead, set at the right hand of God, the Saviour, Prophet, Priest and King of his people, ought not to be buried again in silence by an ungrateful world, together with his benefits and his more excellent promises, but ought to be preached, announced and loudly proclaimed. Therefore, after St Paul said that there is one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself a ransom for all, he immediately added [το μαρτυριον τοις καιροις ιδιοις] "the testimony in its own times", 1 Tim. 2:6, as if to say that the fact that Christ gave himself a ransom for all is the proof of that testimony by which God calls men to witness, so that, when they are asked about the truth of his promises, they answer [ναι] "Yea", and about the justice of his glorification, the thanksgiving and trust placed in him, [Αμην] "Amen", 2 Cor. 1:20.

units.la: Quod testimonium nomine Dei omnibus hominibus annuntiari debet, quia tum Christo gratitudinem & studium gloriae ejus; tum proximo votum communionis tanti boni, nempe foederis cum Deo debemus. Et testimonium hoc fieri Deus voluit καιροις ιδιοις propriis temporibus, hoc est certis, distinctis & opportunis temporibus: ut primo illud Judaeis, inde gentibus, suo ordine, atque, cum inter eas absolvisset, vocatis ex Babylone, demum toti mundo praedicaretur: per σοφιαν πολυποικιλον sapientiam multifariam, Eph. III. 10. Non igitur statim post mortem Christi Deus saeculo finem imponere, sed partim ab electis supereminentem suam gratiam celebrari, ib. II. 7. 2. Petr. III. 9. partim per gloriationem suam hostes suos vel irritare & exasperare, vel ad mentiendum sibi adigere, & de ingratis supplicium sumere voluit. Ideo Christus: Populus, in-
units.tr: This testimony ought to be announced to all men in the name of God, because we owe it both to Christ, as gratitude and zeal for his glory, and to our neighbour, as a wish for communion in so great a good, namely in the covenant with God. And God wished this testimony to be given [καιροις ιδιοις] "in its own times", that is, at certain, distinct and opportune seasons: so that first it should be proclaimed to the Jews, then to the Gentiles in their order, and, when he had finished among them and called those from Babylon, at last to the whole world, [σοφιαν πολυποικιλον] "by the manifold wisdom", Eph. 3:10. Therefore God did not wish to put an end to the age immediately after the death of Christ, but partly that his surpassing grace should be celebrated by the elect, Eph. 2:7; 2 Pet. 3:9, and partly that by his own glorying he might either provoke and exasperate his enemies or compel them to lie to him, and exact punishment from the ungrateful. Therefore Christ says: "The people

units.la: quit, quem formavero mihi, laudem meam narrabunt, visuri scilicet, quae ad gloriam, nomen & virtutes meas ostendendas, fecero, Esaj. XLIII. 21.
units.tr: which I have formed for myself shall declare my praise", namely, they will see what I have done to display my glory, name and virtues, Isa. 43:21.

units.la: II. Haec origo est Evangelii. Quae vox a Scriptoribus N.T. sumta est ex LXX. Interpretibus, qui verbum בשר laeta, carnea, mollia annuntiare, ευαγγελιζεσθαι, & בשורה Ευαγγελιον, & quandoque (velut, 2. Sam. XVIII. 27. 2. Reg. VII. 9.) etiam Ευαγγελιαν reddunt. Augustinus contr. Faust. lib. II. 6. Omnes, inquit, qui Graece vel tenuiter nōrunt, Evangelium bonum nuntium, aut bonam annuntiationem interpretantur. Idem ergo est quod דבר טוב, λογον αγαθος, καλον ρημα verbum bonum, רחש לבי דבר טוב Eructat, vel vivificit cor meum verbo bono, sermone suavi, jucundo, grato, Psal. XLV. 2. Gustarunt καλον Θεου ρημα bonum Dei verbum, Hebr. VI. 5. Semel, velut I. Sam. IV. 17. בשור per antiphrasin in malam partem accipi videtur, de eo, qui Eli mortem filiorum suorum nuntiabat: Ubi tamen Graeci non ευαγγελιζομενον, sed ηυδακοτα habent. Sed utraque vox Hebraea בשר & בשורה & Graeca Ευαγγελιζεσθαι & Ευαγγελιον improprie vel proprie accipitur.
units.tr: II. This is the origin of the Gospel. This word was taken by the New Testament writers from the Septuagint, who render the Hebrew word בשר (good news, joyful, tender things) as [ευαγγελιζεσθαι] "to announce good news", and בשורה as [Ευαγγελιον] "Gospel", and sometimes also (as in 2 Sam. 18:27; 2 Kings 7:9) as [Ευαγγελιαν]. Augustine, Against Faustus, book 2, ch. 6: "All who know even a little Greek," he says, "interpret Gospel as good news or good announcement." So it is the same as the Hebrew דבר טוב, [λογον αγαθος, καλον ρημα] "a good word", רחש לבי דבר טוב [my heart is stirred with a good word, my tongue is the pen of a ready writer], that is, "my heart pours forth a good word, a sweet, pleasant, agreeable speech", Ps. 45:2. They have tasted [καλον Θεου ρημα] "the good word of God", Heb. 6:5. Once, as in 1 Sam. 4:17, the Hebrew word בשור seems to be taken in a bad sense, of the man who announced to Eli the death of his sons; there, however, the Greek does not have [ευαγγελιζομενον] but [ηυδακοτα]. But both the Hebrew words בשר and בשורה and the Greek [Ευαγγελιζεσθαι] and [Ευαγγελιον] are taken improperly or properly.

units.la: Improprie per metonymiam signi praemium pro bono nuntio significat. Semel, 2. Sam. I V. 10. ubi David de eo, qui Saulis mortui nuntium ferebat, a se occiso dicit, quod frustra speraverit fore, ut daret ei בשורה Ευαγγελιον praemium pro laeto nuntio. Quo sensu etiam Homerus Odyss. ξ. Ευαγγελιον δε μοι εσω Evangelium, praemium pro laeto nuntio, mihi posco. Eodem tropo etiam sacrificium pro laeto nuntio oblatum significat apud Xenophontem & Ciceronem, qui ad Atticum lib. II. 27. O suaves, inquit, Epistolas tuas uno tempore mihi datas duas, quibus ευαγγελια quae reddam, nescio, deberi quidem plane fateor. Per Synecdochen seu Metonymiam continentis tum rem laetam, quae nuntiatur, Rom. I. 1. 1. Cor. IV. 15. IX. 14. 2. Cor. VIII. 18. tum librum, quo res laeta, historia Christi, describiscribitur, Marc. I. 1. 2.Cor.VIII. 18. significat. Proprie autem rei laetae annuntiationem, praedicationem notat, sensu vel latiore, vel strictiore & pressiore. Latiore annuntiationem, promissionis exhibendi Christi, quae aliàs simpliciter εὐαγγελία promissio appellatur; strictiore annuntiationem exhibiti Christi, qui prius ut exhibendus & promissus nuntiatus est, quae κατ' ἐξοχὴν Εὐαγγέλιον appellatur. Uterque sensus conjungitur, Hebr.IV.2. ἐσμὲν εὐηγγελισμένοι, καθάπερ κἀκεῖνοι, Sumus evangelizati sicut & illi. Priorem sensum seorsim duo loca habent. Velut ibid. v.6. Οἱ πρότερον εὐαγγελισθέντες quibus prius evangelium praedicatum est, ii non intrarunt. 1.Pet.IV.6. Ad hoc mortuis εὐηγγελίσθη Evangelium praedicatum est. Posterior, qui hujus loci est, in vocibus Εὐαγγέλιον & εὐαγγελιζόμενοι passim obvius est. Respipiscite & credite Evangelio, Marc.I.15. Ne timete, εὐαγγελίζομαι ὑμῖν annuntio vobis magnum gaudium, quod natus hodie fit vobis Salvator, qui est Christus Dominus, Luc.II. 10.11. Non pudet me Evangelii Christi, Rom.I.16. Quàm speciosi sunt pedes εὐαγγελιζομένων evangelizantium! ibid.X.15. Eundem sensum caetera loca omnia, exceptis iis, quae pro latiore sensu attulimus, continent. Opponitur ei voci σιγή silentium priscorum temporum, quibus illa res bona, ut extans, annuntiata nondum fuit. Et qui potest vos confirmare juxta Evangelium meum, & praeconium Jesu Christi, juxta revelationem mysterii temporibus saecularibus σεσιγημένου taciti, ibid. XVI.25. Nam oculus non vidit, & auris non audivit, & in cor hominis non ascenderunt, quae praeparavit Deus diligentibus ipsum, Esaj.LXIV.4. 1.Cor. II.9. Inprimis olim gentes הדות aenigmata non audiverunt, Psalm.LXXVIII.2. CXLVII. 19.20.
units.tr: Improperly, by metonymy of the sign, the word means the reward given for good news. Once, in 2 Sam. 4:10, where David says of the man who brought him news of Saul's death, whom he had killed, that he had vainly hoped he would give him a reward for his joyful news, the Hebrew word is בשורה [Ευαγγελιον], a reward for good news. In this sense Homer also, Odyssey 10: "I demand a reward for good news [Ευαγγελιον] from me." In the same trope, Xenophon and Cicero use the word for a sacrifice offered for good news; Cicero, to Atticus, book 2, letter 27: "O sweet letters of yours, two given to me at one time, to which I do not know what good news [ευαγγελια] I should return; I plainly admit that they are owed." By synecdoche, or metonymy of what contains, the word signifies both the joyful thing that is announced, Rom. 1:1; 1 Cor. 4:15; 9:14; 2 Cor. 8:18, and the book in which the joyful thing, the history of Christ, is described, Mark 1:1. Properly, however, it denotes the announcement or preaching of a joyful thing, in a wider or a narrower and closer sense. In the wider sense it is the announcement of the promise of the Christ to be given, which elsewhere is simply called [εὐαγγελία] "promise". In the narrower sense it is the announcement of the Christ already given, who was first announced as to be given and promised, and this is called [κατ' ἐξοχὴν] "Gospel" in the pre-eminent sense. Both senses are joined in Heb. 4:2: [ἐσμὲν εὐηγγελισμένοι, καθάπερ κἀκεῖνοι,] "we have been evangelized, as they also were." Two passages contain the former sense separately: for example, in the same place, v. 6, [Οἱ πρότερον εὐαγγελισθέντες] "those who were first evangelized", to whom the Gospel was preached, did not enter in. 1 Pet. 4:6: for this reason [εὐηγγελίσθη] the Gospel was preached to the dead. The latter sense, which belongs to our passage, is found throughout in the words "Gospel" and [εὐαγγελιζόμενοι] "those who evangelize". "Repent and believe the Gospel", Mark 1:15. "Fear not, for [εὐαγγελίζομαι ὑμῖν] I announce to you great joy, that today there is born to you a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord", Luke 2:10–11. "I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Christ", Rom. 1:16. "How beautiful are the feet of [εὐαγγελιζομένων] those who evangelize!", ibid. 10:15. All the other passages, except those which we have cited for the wider sense, contain the same sense. It is opposed to the word [σιγή] "silence" of earlier times, when that good thing had not yet been announced as present. "And who can establish you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery [σεσιγημένου] kept secret for long ages", Rom. 16:25. "For eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him", Isa. 64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9. Above all, the Gentiles of old did not hear the הדות [riddles], Ps. 78:2; 147:19–20.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Sicut Evangelii rem ipsam, ita nomen etiam Judaei oderunt. Nam vocem etiam Evangelii nefarie pervertunt, & modo cum אוון גליון vanitate revelationis, modo cum עוון גליון iniquitate revelationis commutant. Quam blasphemiam metu Christianorum prodere in libris excusis verentur, hiatu relicto, manu demum sua exemplaribus suis adscribere solent. uti in Thalmud. Massech & Schabbat cap.9. & En Israel sol.72. semel iterumque videre est. Sed nullus dissimulat R. Elias Germanus in Lexico, quod Thisbi vocat, p.17. Evangelium lingua Graeca sonare בשורה טובה bonum nuntium, & cùm doctores nomen ejus inverterunt, vocantes און גליון eos facere id, quod לא נבון גליון non retum est.
units.tr: The Jews hate the name as much as the thing itself. They wickedly distort even the word Evangelium, changing it at one time to vanity of revelation [אוון גליון] and at another to iniquity of revelation [עוון גליון]. Out of fear of the Christians they are reluctant to set down this blasphemy in printed books. They leave a gap, and then, with their own hand, they usually write it into their own manuscript copies. This can be seen once and again in the Talmud, tractates Massech. and Schabbat, chap. 9, and in Ein Israel, sol. 72. Yet R. Elias Germanus does not conceal it in his Lexicon, which he calls Thisbi, p. 17. He says that the Greek word Evangelium means good news [בשורה טובה], and that when their teachers distorted the name, calling it evil revelation [און גליון], they made it into what is not a wise revelation [לא נבון גליון].

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Est autem Evangelium, ut rem ipsam finiamus, laeta annuntiatio foederis & Testamenti gratiae novi, quo per & propter Christum in carne manifestatum, per passiones consummatum, ex morte resuscitatum & glorificatum, sub conditione resipiscentiae & fidei ejusdem merito donanda plena & consummata reconciliatio cum Deo, justitia, remissio peccatorum, adoptio, libertas, pax, regeneratio Spiritus, & vita aeterna promittitur & donatur; facta a prodromo Jesu, Johanne Baptista, Jesu Christo ipso, & Apostolis Resurrectionis Christi testibus. S. Paulus paucis verbis vocat, λόγον τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν sermonem veritatis, annuntiationem laetam salutis nostrae, Ephes.I. 13. In Evangelio enim praedicatur veritas, tum quia in eo ostenditur, quòd Deus sit ἀληθὴς verus & πιστὸς fidelis, utpote cujus promissiones in Christo sunt nae & Amen, 2.Cor.I.20. tum quia ex Evangelii testimonio cognoscitur, quid Deus sit, ejus videlicet voluntas, amor, bonitas, nomen, virtutes, justitia inprimis & misericordia & gloria, tum quia Evangelium haec omnia demonstrat non in umbris, parabolis & aenigmatibus, sed clare, ut in ipso corpore, substantia & imagine rerum, Col.II.17. Hebr.X.1. tum quia testimonium hoc & Divina veritas est typus & ostensio veritatis, cujus cognitione homo illuminatus & amore imbutus sapiens, sanctus, Deóque similis est; tum quia in Christo Lex Dei, quae Lex charitatis est, vera est, quippe habens jam exemplum, ut non amplius in solis tabulis lapideis & in litera, sed in vivo exemplari extet, eóque adeò amabili, ut in ejus amore etiam amor Dei nos & fratres nostros amantis, & amor Sanctitatis Dei, & sic amor boni & amor fratrum, velut in radice & fonte conti-neatur. Ideo Evangelium ἀληθεῖαν veritatem etiam alibi, Gal.III.1.V.7. & Christum, qui in eo praedicatur πλήρη ἀληθείας plenum veritate, Joh. I.14. Scriptura dixit. In eodem Evangelio est Εὐαγγέλιον τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν laeta annuntiatio salutis nostrae, quia in eo annuntiatur, quòd Christus Salvator pacem, justitiam, salutem ab omni reatu, captivitate, jugo, accusatione attulerit, & se ipsum obtulerit non tantùm pro Judaeis, sed etiam pro gentibus, Joh. XI.52. Matth. XXVI.28. idque secundum promissionem, qua dicitur: In Semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes, Gen.XII.3. XXII.18. Nam leve est, dixit Jehova, ut sis mihi servus ad suscitandas tribus Jacob, & ad reducendam desolationem Israelis. Etiam dedi te in lucem gentium, ut sis ישועתי salus mea usque ad extremum terrae, Esaj.XLIX.6. Etiam ἀποκάλυψις revelatio mysterii, Rom.XVI.25. appellatur, quia in eo γνωρίζεται μυστήριον notificatur mysterium Evangelii, Ephes.VI.19. hoc est, res per se ab hominum expectatione, cogitatione & consilio remota. Nam & a nemine sciri potest, nisi ab eo, cui à Deo revelatum est, & qui ψῆφον λευκὴν calculum illum album, Apoc.II.17. accepit; & etiamsi ejus annuntiatio promissa fuerit, tamen ea non fuit facta nisi ultimis temporibus, ut ita, quae annuntiantur, supra expectationem sint, Esaj. LXIV.3. 1.Cor.II. 9. Ac licet etiam revelatum sit Testamentum Dei per promissionem, & annuntiatio rei gestae facta, & imago rerum publicata sit; tamen homo animalis non recipit quae Spiritus Dei sunt, ibid.14. Sed & χάρις Gratia κατ' ἐξοχὴν nomine venit. Lex data est per Mosen: Gratia & veritas per Jesum Christum facta est, Joh.I.17. Gratia, plena videlicet, per quam accedentes liberantur à jugo, & quae data est per ἀπολύτρωσιν redemptionem, Rom.III.24. Ephes.I.7. quae χάρις & Θεοῦ σωτηρίας gratia Dei salutaris, Tit.II.11. appellatur, quia ejus effectus omnimoda salus est. Plures aliae Evangelii appellationes sunt, puta tum generales, cùm Lex, verbum, testimonium, praeceptum, doctrina, via veritatis insignitur: tum speciales, velut cùm per periphrasin & vocabuli explicationem bonum Dei Verbum, sanus sermo, sana doctrina, κήρυγμα: ex causa Evangelii efficiente, Verbum Dei, testimonium Dei, Christi, Spiritus, Sapientia Dei, beneplacitum voluntatis Dei: ex objecto, promissio, Evangelium Christi, Verbum
units.tr: To finish with the thing itself: the Gospel is the joyful proclamation of the covenant and the new Testament of grace. Through Christ, who was manifested in the flesh, perfected by his sufferings, raised from the dead and glorified, and on the condition of repentance and faith, there is promised and given, by the merit of Christ, full and complete reconciliation with God, righteousness, forgiveness of sins, adoption, liberty, peace, regeneration by the Spirit, and eternal life. This was announced by the forerunner of Jesus, John the Baptist, by Jesus Christ himself, and by the apostles, witnesses of his resurrection. Saint Paul calls it in a few words the word of truth, the gospel of our salvation [λόγον τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν], Ephes. 1.13. The Gospel is called truth, first, because in it God is shown to be true [ἀληθής] and faithful [πιστός], since his promises are in Christ yea and amen, 2 Cor. 1.20; second, because from the testimony of the Gospel we learn what God is, namely his will, love, goodness, name, virtues, above all his justice, mercy and glory; third, because the Gospel sets all these things forth not in shadows, parables and riddles, but clearly, as in the body itself, the substance and the image of the things, Col. 2.17, Heb. 10.1; fourth, because this testimony is the divine truth, and the type and manifestation of truth, by whose knowledge a man, enlightened and imbued with love, is wise, holy and like God; fifth, because in Christ the law of God, which is the law of love, is true, since it now has its example, so that it no longer stands only on tablets of stone and in the letter, but in a living pattern, and one so lovable that in love for him there is contained, as in a root and fountain, the love of God who loves us and our brothers, the love of God's holiness, and so the love of the good and the love of the brethren. For this reason the Gospel is called truth [ἀληθεῖαν] elsewhere in Scripture, Gal. 3.1, 5.7, and Christ, who is preached in it, is called full of truth [πλήρη ἀληθείας], John 1.14. The same Gospel is called the gospel of our salvation [Εὐαγγέλιον τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν], that is, the joyful announcement of our salvation, because it proclaims that Christ the Saviour has brought peace, righteousness and deliverance from all guilt, captivity, yoke and accusation, and offered himself not only for the Jews but also for the Gentiles, John 11.52, Matt. 26.28. This was according to the promise in which it is said: In your Seed all the nations shall be blessed, Gen. 12.3, 22.18. For Jehovah said: It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to restore the desolation of Israel. I have also given you as a light to the Gentiles, that you may be my salvation [ישועתי] to the end of the earth, Isa. 49.6. The Gospel is also called the revelation [ἀποκάλυψις] of the mystery, Rom. 16.25, because in it the mystery of the Gospel is made known [γνωρίζεται μυστήριον], Ephes. 6.19; that is, a thing which in itself lies beyond human expectation, thought and counsel. Nor can anyone know it except the one to whom it has been revealed by God, and who has received the white stone [ψῆφον λευκήν], Rev. 2.17. And even though its announcement was promised, it was not made until the last times, so that what is announced lies beyond expectation, Isa. 64.3, 1 Cor. 2.9. And although the testament of God was revealed through promise, and the announcement of the event was made, and the image of the things was made public, still the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, ibid. 14. Moreover, grace comes in the name grace [χάρις] par excellence. The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, John 1.17. This is full grace, through which those who come are set free from the yoke, and which is given through redemption [ἀπολύτρωσιν], Rom. 3.24, Ephes. 1.7. It is called the grace of God that brings salvation [χάρις Θεοῦ σωτηρίας], Tit. 2.11, because its effect is salvation in every respect. There are many other names for the Gospel. Some are general, when it is designated as law, word, testimony, precept, doctrine, the way of truth. Others are special, as when by periphrasis and explanation of the term it is called the good Word of God, sound speech, sound doctrine, preaching [κήρυγμα]. From its efficient cause it is called the Word of God, the testimony of God, of Christ, of the Spirit, the wisdom of God, the good pleasure of the will of God. From its object it is called the promise, the Gospel of Christ, the Word

units.la: Evangelium definitur; & Scriptura testimoniis generalibus explicatur. Verbum Christi, Evangelium Regni, Testamentum Novum, Verbum, Lex, auditus fidei: ex effectibus, Sermo vitae, verbum gratiae Evangelium pacis, Lex libertatis, Evangelium gloriae beati Dei: ex adjunctis, annuus acceptationis Jehovae, Seculum futurum, Evangelium aeternum, arcanum voluntatis Divinae, beneplacitum, &c. ex similibus, bonus odor, bonum semen, vinum novum, sibilus, fons aquae salientis in vitam aeternam, lux, cibus, pascua, mensa, calix exuberans; ex eventu & accidente, scandalum crucis, stultitia praedicationis, stultitia Dei, odor mortis ad mortem; appellatur.
units.tr: of the Gospel; and Scripture explains it by general testimonies. It is called the Word of Christ, the Gospel of the Kingdom, the New Testament, the Word, the Law, the hearing of faith. From its effects it is called the word of life, the word of grace, the Gospel of peace, the law of liberty, the Gospel of the blessed glory of God. From its attendant circumstances it is called the year of the Lord's acceptance, the age to come, the eternal Gospel, the hidden will of the Divine, good pleasure, and so on. From its likenesses it is called a good fragrance, good seed, new wine, a signal, a fountain of water springing up to eternal life, light, food, pasture, a table, an overflowing cup. From its outcome and accident it is called the offence of the cross, the foolishness of preaching, the foolishness of God, the odour of death to death.

units.la: V. Evangelium isthoc Deus προεπηγγείλατο ante promisit per Prophetas suos in Scripturis Sanctis, Rom.I.2. Nihil enim in N. T. praedicari debuit, quin ante promissum fuerit in posterioribus temporibus praedicandum. Nam & Moses fidelis servus Dei in tota domo ejus fuit, εἰς μαρτύριον τῶν λαλησομένων in testimonium eorum, quae dicenda erant; adeoque eorum etiam, quae ἐπ' ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν in novissimis diebus dicenda & a toto populo Dei ex Judaeis & gentilibus colligendo audienda erant, Hebr.III.5.coll.cum I.1. Deus enim aliquid in posterum dicendum sibi reservavit, quod nec Patres ante Mosen, nec populus Israel ad montem Dei constitutus audivit. Prophetam ex medio tui, ex fratribus tuis parem mihi excitabit tibi Jehova Deus tuus. Ei auscultabitis, Deut.XVIII.15. Dabo verba mea in os ejus, & loquetur ad eos, quicquid ei praecipiam, ibid. v. 18. Si Moses jam tum eodem modo & omne verbum Dei loqui potuisset, novo Propheta, qui Mose non minor esset, opus haud fuisset. Et hactenus Moses & novus ille Propheta promissus differunt, quod Deus verba sua in hujus, non illius ore positurus erat. Licet enim Moses etiam verba Dei locutus sit, tamen ejus verba fuerunt verba non Dei & Domini, sed servi. Ideo sermonibus suis praeponere suevit: Et locutus est Dominus ad Mosen. Ipse ergo ex terra locutus est, ut servus, qui ex terra erat. Sed verba Dei, velut in os suum posita loquitur is, qui Dominus ex Coelo est, qui & quod se, ut domino dignum est, & quo gloria Dei in solidum & reapse manifestatur, loquitur: quod non Moses, sed novus ille Propheta fecit. Ille enim Promissionem locutus est; hic Evangelium. Sed ut Deus fiat in Deum, & omnem Dei, ut benigni Patris, mensuram & affectum impleat, non sola Promissio, sed Evangelium, cum lege fidei, quae Lex Christi est, omni alia Lege sequeltrata, conjunctum efficit. Habuit enim & locutus est Christus, verbum, quod Moses nec habuit, nec locutus est: Venite ad me omnes, quotquot fatigati & onerati estis; & ego ἀναπαύσω faciam vos requiescere, Matth.XI.28. Neque enim Moses venientibus ad se quietem, per adductam videlicet justitiam, & consummatum principem salutis, nuntiare potuit. Contentus enim nuntiare, quod apud Deum sit Angelus vindex, & ventus sit Propheta, qui verba sanctificantis & justificantis Israelem loqueretur, de caetero onus grave patribus impositum, quod portare non potuerunt, Act.XV.10. De Evangelio etiam alii Prophetae locuti sunt. Inprimis David & Esajas. Ille, Psal.LXVIII.12. Jehova dat אמר dictum המבשרות צבא רב evangelizantium turbam, exercitum magnum. Hic cap.XL.9. In montem altum ascende tibi מבשרת ציון Evangelizatrix Tzionis,
units.tr: V. God promised this Gospel beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, Rom. 1.2. For nothing ought to be preached in the New Testament which had not been promised beforehand to be preached in later times. For Moses also was a faithful servant of God in all his house, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken [εἰς μαρτύριον τῶν λαλησομένων], that is, of the things that were to be said, and so of those things which were to be said in the last days [ἐπ' ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν] and which were to be heard by the whole people of God gathered from Jews and Gentiles, Heb. 3.5, compared with 1.1. For God reserved for the future something to be said which neither the fathers before Moses nor the people of Israel, gathered at the mount of God, had heard. The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among you, from your brethren, like me; you shall hear him, Deut. 18.15. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him, ibid. v. 18. If Moses had already been able in the same way to speak every word of God, there would have been no need for a new prophet, who would be no less than Moses. And in this respect Moses and that new prophet promised differ: God was going to put his words in the mouth of the latter, not of the former. For although Moses also spoke the words of God, his words were the words not of God and Lord but of a servant. Therefore he was accustomed to prefix his discourses with: And the Lord spoke to Moses. He himself therefore spoke from the earth, as a servant who was of the earth. But the one who is Lord from heaven speaks the words of God as if they were placed in his own mouth; he speaks in such a way as befits a Lord, and so that the glory of God is manifested fully and in reality. Moses did not do this, but that new prophet did. For Moses spoke the promise; this one spoke the Gospel. But so that God may become God in him, and fill the whole measure and affection of God as a kind Father, he does not make the promise alone but the Gospel, joined with the law of faith, which is the law of Christ, and with every other law set aside. For Christ had and spoke a word that Moses neither had nor spoke: Come to me, all you who are weary and heavy laden, and I will give you rest, Matt. 11.28. For Moses could not announce rest to those who come to him, namely through the righteousness that is brought in and the perfected Prince of salvation. He was content to announce that there is an avenging angel with God and that there is a wind, a prophet, who would speak words sanctifying and justifying Israel; and in other respects the heavy yoke laid on the fathers, which they could not bear, Acts 15.10. Other prophets also spoke of the Gospel, above all David and Isaiah. David, Psalm 68.12: Jehovah gives the word; the evangelizing host is great [המבשרות צבא רב]. Isaiah, chap. 40.9: Get you up into the high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion [מבשרת ציון], evangelist of Zion

units.la: extolle cum viribus vocem tuam. Evangelizatrix Hierosolymae; extolle, ne metuas. Dic oppidis Judae: Ecce Deus vester. Et LII.7. Quam pulchri sunt in montibus pedes מבשר evangelizantis, qui promulgat pacem, qui annuntiat bonum, qui promulgat salutem; qui dicit Sioni: Rex factus est Deus tuus. Et cap.LXI.1.2. Jehova unxit me לבשר ad evangelizandum mansuetis, ad praedicandum captivis libertatem, &c.
units.tr: Lift up your voice with strength, O herald of Jerusalem; lift it up, and do not be afraid. Say to the cities of Judah: "Behold your God!" And at 52:7: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the one who brings good tidings [מבשר], who publishes peace, who announces good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion: Your God reigns." And at ch. 61:1-2: "The Lord has anointed me [לבשר] to preach good tidings to the meek, to proclaim liberty to the captives," etc.

units.la: VI. Evangelii summam paucis verbis idem S. Paulus complexus est dicens: Evangelium Deus ante promiserat per Prophetas, &c. περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ de Filio suo, qui extitit ex semine Davidis secundum carnem, qui definite notatus est Filius Dei in potentia secundum Spiritum sanctitatis ex resurrectione mortuorum, Jesu Christo Domino nostro; Rom.I.2.3.4. Fundamentum igitur & objectum Evangelii est Jesus Christus, Dominus noster, secundum carnem ex Semine Davidis, homo: secundum Spiritum sanctitatis, seu Deitatem, Filius Dei in potentia, hoc est, naturalis & proprius, utpote talis ex resurrectione ex mortuis definite notatus. Cum promissione id commune Evangelium habet, quod salus peccatoris in Christo solo consistit, & is Filius Dei est: At proprium Evangelio est, quod ille Jesus est, sive is homo, qui eo nomine insignitus est; & quod in eo, ceu Jesu Christo Domino nostro, qui talis est, & dignitate atque potentia, Apoc.V.12. & donatione omnium in manum ejus, & potestate, Joh.III.35. Hebr.I.2. & merito, cum omnia fecerit & passus sit, per quae Salutis Princeps consummari potuit & debuit; habemus redemptionem a reatu & effectu reatus, servitute, ne alii, quam ipsi, nos ceu suos asserenti, & sanguine suo ementi, subsimus. Nam Filium Dei, Evangelii objectum, esse Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, velut interjecta parenthesi probat; quia is secundum carnem ex Semine Davidis natus, & secundum Spiritum sanctitatis ex resurrectione ex mortuis Filius Dei in potentia Dei demonstratus est. Ideo in titulo Jesu Christi Domini nostri Evangelicae praedicationis summa etiam alibi ponitur. Nemo potest dicere Dominum Jesum, nisi in Spiritu S. 1.Cor.XII.3. Si quis non diligit Dominum Jesum Christum, sit anathema, Maranatha, Dominus noster venit. ibid.XVI.22. Omnis lingua confiteatur, quod Dominus sit Christus Jesus ad gloriam Patris, Phil.II.11. Omnis spiritus, qui confitetur, quod Jesus sit Christus, qui in carne venit (non tam sono & strepitu syllabarum, quam vi nominum) ex Deo est, 1.Joh.IV.2.
units.tr: In a few words the same St Paul sums up the substance of the gospel, saying: "God had promised beforehand by his prophets the gospel concerning his Son [περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ], who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, and who was declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord" (Rom. 1:2-4). The foundation and object of the gospel, therefore, is Jesus Christ our Lord, a man according to the flesh from the seed of David, and according to the Spirit of holiness, that is, according to his deity, the Son of God in power, that is, the natural and proper Son, who as such was declared so by his resurrection from the dead. The common ground of the gospel and the promise is that the salvation of the sinner rests in Christ alone, and that he is the Son of God.
