What is peculiar to the gospel is that he is that Jesus, that man who was marked with that name; and that in him, as Jesus Christ our Lord, who is such both in dignity and power (Rev. 5:12), and in the gift of all things into his hand and his authority (John 3:35; Heb. 1:2), and by his merit, since he has done and suffered all things through which the Prince of Salvation could and had to be made perfect, we have redemption from guilt and from the effect of guilt, that is, from slavery, so that we are not subject to anyone other than himself, who claims us as his own and bought us with his blood. For the apostle shows, as if in a parenthesis, that the Son of God, the object of the gospel, is Jesus Christ our Lord, since he, born according to the flesh from the seed of David, and according to the Spirit of holiness, was demonstrated to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead. Therefore the sum of evangelical preaching is also placed elsewhere in the title "Jesus Christ our Lord": "No one can say 'Lord Jesus' except in the Holy Spirit" (1 Cor. 12:3); "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed; Maranatha, our Lord comes" (1 Cor. 16:22); "every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of the Father" (Phil. 2:11); "every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God" (1 John 4:2). The confession is judged not so much by the sound and noise of the syllables as by the force of the names.

units.la: VII. Cum tamen Jesus Christus Dominus noster in Evangelio praedicetur ut Mediator melioris & Novi Testamenti, Hebr.VIII.6. praedicatio Novi Testamenti illius, & praestantiorum ejusdem promissionum & benedictionum, Evangelii, & novae ac distinctae sub eodem Foederis gratiae oeconomiae utramque paginam facit. Licet enim foedus & Testamentum gratiae quoad praecipua unum sint, aeternum etiam & immutabile, tamen illud, quoad ascititia & rerum πλεῖωσιν consummationem, & melius & novum efficitur, non ut innovetur duntaxat, sed etiam ut novetur, cum ab eo separatur id, quod subintroductum est, & prioris temporis fuit, & nihil consummavit, imo etiam μεμψιν reprehensionem quandam, ἀπλῆς imperfectum habuit, & nova
units.tr: VII. Yet since Jesus Christ our Lord is preached in the gospel as the Mediator of the better and new covenant (Heb. 8:6), the preaching of that New Testament, and of its more excellent promises and blessings, which is the gospel, makes both pages of the new and distinct economy under the same covenant of grace. For although the covenant and testament of grace is one as to its principal matters, and eternal and unchangeable, nevertheless, as to its added elements and the fulfilment [πλήρωσιν] of things, it has been made both better and new. It has been renewed not merely in the sense of being restored, but also in the sense of being made new, since that which was introduced in addition, and belonged to an earlier time, has been separated from it, and had accomplished nothing; indeed it even had a certain blame [μέμψιν] and was imperfect [ἀτελῆ], and new

units.la: {a} ante promissum est per Prophetas in Scripturis, velut per Prophetam novum, Christum & Mosen distinctum, praedicandum. nova quædam hactenus promissa, sed nunc demum præstita exhibentur.
units.tr: {a} was promised before through the prophets in the Scriptures, as something to be proclaimed through a new prophet, distinct from Christ and Moses. Certain new things, promised until now, are now at last set forth as actually performed.

units.la: VIII. Est autem Testamentum Novum ea pars Consilii Divini, quam is, abolitis iis, quæ promissioni superaddita sunt ad tempus usque διορθώσεως correctionis, & nova dedicatione & confirmatione æterni Testamenti gratiæ per sanguinem Christi; denique & meliorum promissionum donatione, ultimo tempore mundi in Israele exequi, & in mundo per Evangelii præconium innotescere voluit. Testamentum vocamus non typicum illud, quod aboleri debuit, sed verum, ipsum æternum Testamentum gratiæ, quo Deus bona spiritualia & cœlestia hæredibus suis in Christo legavit. Novum vero, tum quia Veteri abrogato successit: tum quia ceu Testamentum merum noviter a typis & Lege promissioni superaddita separatum, & veluti purgatum novum quodammodo apparuit: tum quia hæredib° meliora, nova bona Hebr. VIII.6. attulit; Cœlumq; novum, immutato Ecclesiæ statu, & Terram novam Evangelio ad Christum conversam, 2. Pet. III.13. fecit: tum quia in eo Fœderi Gratiæ novus ἐγκαινισμός, nova dedicatio & confirmatio per sanguinem Christi accessit. In eo quod dixit, novum, antiquavit primum, Hebr. VIII.13. Hoc (poculum) est sanguis Novi Testamenti, sigillum, quo Testamentum sanguinis Christi dedicatione novatum obsignatur; Matth. XXVI.28. Non ergo Testamentum Novum est Veteris accessio, quemadmodum Vetus Testamentum typicum Israeli datum fuit accessio Testamenti de Patribus atque omnibus hæredibus iustitiæ facti, & Promissionis illius, quæ Patribus data est. Nam Testamentum illud typicum & Lex æternum Testamentum gratiæ & promissionem non abolevit. Fieri enim potuit, ut præter promissionem subintraret Lex. Quamvis Lex & promissio contrariarentur, non ut Lex promissionem tolleret, sed ut bonum promissum, nempe redemptio, per accusationem & abundantiam peccati, & manifestationem condemnationis, quam Lex servitutem imponens aliquatenus operabatur, necessarium ostenderetur. At Testamentum Novum Vetus παλαιώσεν antiquavit. Illud fuit Testamenti veri Gratiæ & Promissionis ἐπουράνιος superadditio, Gal. III.19. hoc Testamenti typici veteris & Legis, quæ παρεισῆλθε subintraverat, Rom. V.20. διόρθωσις correctio, Hebr. IX.10. quæ consummationem, seu purificationem conscientiæ, ib. v.14. affert.
units.tr: VIII. The New Testament is that part of the divine counsel which God willed to carry out in Israel at the last time of the world, and to make known in the world through the proclamation of the gospel: the old things that were added to the promise, until the time of correction [διορθώσεως], having been abolished, and the eternal covenant of grace having been newly dedicated and confirmed by the blood of Christ, and finally the better promises having been given. We call that the Testament not the typical one, which had to be abolished, but the true one, the eternal testament of grace itself, by which God bequeathed spiritual and heavenly goods to his heirs in Christ. It is called New, both because it succeeded the Old, which was abrogated; and because, as a pure testament newly separated from the types and from the Law added to the promise, it appeared in some way new and as if purified; and because it brought to its heirs better, new goods (Heb. 8:6); and because it made a new heaven, with the state of the Church changed, and a new earth, with the world converted to Christ by the gospel (2 Pet. 3:13); and because in it there came to the covenant of grace a new renewal [ἐγκαινισμός], a new dedication and confirmation by the blood of Christ. In saying "new," he has made the first old (Heb. 8:13). "This is the cup, the blood of the New Testament, the seal by which the testament is sealed, renewed by the dedication of Christ's blood" (Matt. 26:28). The New Testament, therefore, is not an addition to the Old, in the way the typical Old Testament given to Israel was an addition to the covenant made with the Fathers and with all the heirs of righteousness, and to that promise which was given to the Fathers. For that typical testament, and the Law, did not abolish the eternal testament of grace and the promise. For it could happen that the Law entered in besides the promise. Although the Law and the promise were in opposition, the Law did not take away the promise, but it showed that the good promised, namely redemption, was necessary, through the accusation and abundance of sin, and through the manifestation of condemnation, which the Law, imposing slavery, in some measure brought about. But the New Testament made the Old obsolete [παλαιώσεν]. The former was the heavenly addition [ἐπουράνιος] of the true testament of grace and promise (Gal. 3:19); the latter, that of the old typical testament and of the Law, which had come in beside (παρεισῆλθε) (Rom. 5:20), the correction [διόρθωσις] (Heb. 9:10), which brings about the completion or purification of the conscience (ibid. v. 14).

units.la: IX. Læta annuntiatio Testamenti illius novi apud Patres Christo antiquiores magna in expectatione fuit. Salutem tuam, Jehova, expecto, Genes. XLIX.18. Præstolor Jehovam, qui abscondit faciem suam à domo Jacobi, & expectavi eum. ut videam eum, quem nemo hactenus vidit: qui nondum manifestatus est, Esaj. VIII.17. A seculo non audiverunt, non auscultarunt. Oculus non vidit præter te Deum, qui facit ei, qui præstolatur ipsum, ibid. LXIV.4. Si tergiversetur, præstolare eum, quia veniendo veniet; Habac. II.3. Ideo futura quasi præsentia fecerunt, & de iis, tanquam de præsentibus, in spiritu cum gaudio locuti sunt. Quod fidei veterum opus חזון visio, hoc est, mentis à præsentibus avocatæ, & in considerationem rerum futurarum transmissæ propter sperata & non visa, tanquam visa, exultatio vocatur, עוד חזון Adhuc visio erit ad tempus præstitutum usque, & veniet sub finem præceo & non fallet expectationem, Habac. II.2. Fides enim est ἔλεγχος μὴ βλεπομένων demonstratio eorum, quæ non videntur, sive ea extent; sive expectentur in futurum, Hebr. XI.1. Ut ergo in futuris exultare & deliciari quodammodo Patres possent; Deo etiam promissionem & Prophetiam de Christo & bonis ejus per Novum Testamentum præstandis multiplicare placuit. Prophetæ quæ siverunt & scrutati sunt, in quod & quale tempus Spiritus Christi, qui in ipsis erat, significaret Christi passiones & glorias sequentes, 1. Pet. I.10, 11. Præcipuas promissiones repetere non pigebit. Prima promissio spem & expectationem in futurum fecit. Semen Mulieris conteret caput Serpentis, Gen. III.15. Inde Abrahamo promissio repetita est his verbis: Fiam Semini tuo in Deum, Genes. XVII.8. In Semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes, ibid. XXII.18. Etiam Moses circumcisionem cordis in posterum promisit. Converteris ad Jehovam Deum tuum, & auscultabis vocei ejus, & circumcidet Jehova cor tuum, ad diligendum Jehovam Deum tuum, ex toto corde tuo, Deut. XXX.2, 6. Canta sterilis, quæ non peperit, fragorem fac cantu, & hinni, quæ non doluit, Nam multi sunt filii desolatæ præ filiis maritatæ, dixit Jehova, Esaj. LIV.1. Quas duas matres Sarai & Hagarem, duo Testamenta figurasse, Apostolus, Gal. IV.24. significat. Nam si duæ matres sunt, & duarum matrum filii diversa conditione sunt, utique duo etiam Testamenta sunt, quibus utrumque Semen, & utrique Semini sua conditio datur. Idem Esajas de vocatione Gentium & contumacia Israelitarum sic loquitur: Respondi non interrogantibus: obtuli me non quærentibus me. Dixi: Ecce me, ecce me, ad gentem non nominatam de nomine meo. Expandi manus meas toto die ad populum refractarium, Esaj. LXV.1, 2. Dein v.3-8. queritur de apostatis, & v.8. ostendit, se memorem fore misericordiæ suæ, addens v.10-16. se insigne iudicium acturum, quo populum suum & defectores distinguat. Tum vero, v.16, 17. Qui benedicat sibi, inquit, in terra, benedicet sibi in Deo Amen (gloriando & consolationem Divinam atque benedictiones spirituales in Christo vendicando) & jurans in terra, jurabit in Deo Amen, cum oblivioni tradita fuerint angustiæ priores, & cum abscondita fuerint ab oculis meis. Nam ecce ego creo Cœlos novos, & terram novam, & non erit memoria priorum, neque venient in mentem. Quæ novitas Novum Testamentum indicat, quia consummatio illa novitatis locum habere nequit, nisi sub Novo Testamento, sub quo omnia nova creatura sunt. Si quis in Christo est, nova creatura est. Vetera præterierunt. Ecce nova facta sunt omnia, 2. Cor. V.17.
units.tr: IX. The joyful announcement of that new testament was held among the Fathers, who were earlier than Christ, in great expectation. "I wait for your salvation, O Lord" (Gen. 49:18). "I will wait for the Lord, who hides his face from the house of Jacob, and I will look for him, that I may see him whom no one has yet seen, who has not yet been manifested" (Isa. 8:17). "From of old they have not heard, nor perceived; no eye has seen a God besides you, who works for the one who waits for him" (Isa. 64:4). "If he delays, wait for him, for he will surely come" (Hab. 2:3). Therefore the Fathers made future things as if present, and spoke of them in the spirit with joy as though they were present. This exultation of the faith of the ancients is called חזון, vision, that is, the mind withdrawn from present things and carried into consideration of future things, on account of things hoped for and not seen, as though they were seen. "The vision is yet for an appointed time, and at the end it will speak and not lie; though it tarry, wait for it" (Hab. 2:2-3, Hebrew "עוד חזון"). For faith is "the proof of things not seen," the demonstration of those things which are not seen, whether they exist or are expected in the future (Heb. 11:1). So, that the Fathers might in some way exult and take delight in future things, it also pleased God to multiply the promise and prophecy concerning Christ and his blessings, to be fulfilled through the New Testament. The prophets who prophesied and searched diligently into what time and what kind of time the Spirit of Christ within them signified, when he foretold the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow (1 Pet. 1:10-11). I will not hesitate to repeat the principal promises. The first promise made hope and expectation for the future: "The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent" (Gen. 3:15). Then the promise was repeated to Abraham in these words: "I will be God to your seed" (Gen. 17:8); "In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed" (ibid. 22:18). Moses also promised circumcision of the heart for the future: "You shall return to the Lord your God and obey his voice, and the Lord your God will circumcise your heart, to love the Lord your God with all your heart" (Deut. 30:2, 6). "Sing, O barren woman, who did not bear; break forth into singing and shout, you who did not travail; for the children of the desolate are more than the children of the married wife, says the Lord" (Isa. 54:1). The Apostle indicates that these two mothers, Sarah and Hagar, signified two testaments (Gal. 4:24). For if there are two mothers, and the sons of the two mothers are in different conditions, then there are certainly two testaments too, by which each seed and each seed's condition is given. The same Isaiah speaks thus about the calling of the Gentiles and the obstinacy of the Israelites: "I was found by those who did not ask for me; I was made manifest to those who did not seek me. I said, 'Here I am, here I am,' to a nation that was not called by my name. I stretched out my hands all day to a rebellious people" (Isa. 65:1-2). Then, in vv. 3-8, he complains of the apostates, and in v. 8 he shows that he will remember his mercy, adding in vv. 10-16 that he will execute a remarkable judgment by which he distinguishes his people from the defectors. Then indeed, in vv. 16-17: "He who blesses himself in the land," he says, "shall bless himself in the God of truth, Amen" (boasting and claiming divine consolation and spiritual blessings in Christ), "and he who swears in the land shall swear by the God of truth, Amen, since the former troubles have been forgotten and have been hidden from my eyes. For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind." This newness indicates the New Testament, because that fulfilment of newness cannot take place except under the New Testament, under which all things are a new creation. "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new" (2 Cor. 5:17).

units.la: X. Sed de Fœdere & Testamento Novo expressius Jeremias & Ezechiel loquuntur. Ille cap. XXXI.31-35. Ecce dies veniunt, ait Jehova, & pangam cum domo Israel, & cum domo Juda ברית חדשה fœdus novum. Non ut fœdus, quod pepigi cum Patribus ipsorum die, quo apprehendi manum eorum, ut educerem eos ex Ægypto; qui irritum fecerunt fœdus meum: & ego dominatum in eos exercui, ait Jehova. Sed hoc erit fœdus, quod pangam domui Israel post dies illos, ait Jehova: Do legem meam in medium ipsorum, & super corde eorum scribam eam; & fiam ipsis Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi
units.tr: X. But Jeremiah and Ezekiel speak more explicitly about the covenant and the New Testament. Jeremiah, chapter 31, verses 31-35: "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant [בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה, berith chadashah] with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the LORD. But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, saith the LORD: I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people."

units.la: Ieremiæ in primis & Ezechieli. mihi populus. Et non docebunt amplius quisquam proximum suum, & quisquam fratrem suum dicendo: cognoscite Jehovam. Nam omnes ipsi cognoscent me, non minus parvus ipsorum, quam magnus ipsorum, dicit Jehova. Nam condonabo pravitatem eorum, & ipsum peccatum eorum non recordabor amplius. Quod vaticinium & veteris Foederis seu Testamenti abolitionem & Novi Testamenti introductionem, & Novi Testamenti bona magna cum emphasi pandit. Occasio vaticinii fuit vetus & jactatum apud Judaeos adagium: Patres comederunt amphacem, uvam acerbam, & dentes filiorum stupent, v.29. Quod adagium Judaeis tritum fuisse, etiam Ezech. XVIII. 1.2. dicitur. Omnes homines ab Adamo peccatum traxerunt: & Judaei, etiam fideles & sancti, propter transgressionem Patrum Legis onus grave portarunt. Haec querelae, adagialiloquutione apud Judaeos vulgatae, causa fuit. Sed cessaturam quandoque cum ipso onere hoc propter Patrum transgressiones impositio querelam, Propheta asserit, praedicens venturos dies, quibus foedere illo, quo onus ejusmodi populo impositum est, abolito successurum sit foedus novum, finem oneri & jugo illi, atque simul etiam querelae populi facturum; utpote in quo nil nisi fides, resipiscentia, remissio peccatorum, sine ejus recordatione &c. obtinere debeat. Hic vero Ezechiel cap. XVI. 60. 61.62. Erigam, inquit, tibi foedus seculi. Et recordaberis viarum tuarum, & subterfugies prae pudore, cum accipies sorores tuas majores te ad minores te, & dabo illas tibi in filias, & non ex foedere tuo. Et erigam ego foedus meum tecum, & cognosces, quod ego Jim Jehova. Cum Samaria, Sodoma & caeteris gentibus loquitur. Ex illis filias Hierosolymae promittit, sed ex alio Testamento quam eo, quod Hierosolyma terrestris primo accepit. Terrestris enim Hierosolyma initio Testamentum ejusmodi accepit, ut esse metropolis populi, cujus haereditas erat terra Canaan, & ut Templum in ea esset, in quo Sacerdotium Aharonicum exerceretur, a Deo ipso electa, ut memoriam nominis sui in ea poneret. Sed non ex tali Testamento, terrestri Hierosolymae eximio, gentes Hierosolymae promittuntur filiae, sed ex alio, adeoque novo illo, quod Jeremias promiserat; quia Abrahamus sine lege habuit promissionem, fore eum haeredem mundi, seu patrem multarum gentium.
units.tr: Especially Jeremiah and Ezekiel. "And they shall not teach every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the LORD: for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them, saith the LORD: for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more." This prophecy discloses both the abolition of the old covenant or testament and the introduction of the New Testament and its blessings, with great emphasis. The occasion of the prophecy was an old proverb common among the Jews: "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge," v. 29. That this proverb was well known among the Jews is also indicated at Ezekiel 18:1-2. All men have derived sin from Adam, and the Jews, even the faithful and holy, have borne the heavy yoke of the Law because of the transgressions of their fathers. This complaint, spread among the Jews in the form of a proverb, was the cause. But the Prophet asserts that this complaint will one day cease together with the burden itself, which was laid on the people because of their fathers' transgressions. He foretells days to come when, the covenant by which such a burden was imposed upon the people having been abolished, a new covenant will follow, which will bring an end to that yoke and burden and at the same time to the people's complaint; for in it nothing ought to prevail but faith, repentance and the forgiveness of sins, without remembrance of them, and so on. But Ezekiel, chapter 16, verses 60-62, speaks here: "I will establish unto thee an everlasting covenant. Then thou shalt remember thy ways, and be ashamed, when thou shalt receive thy sisters, thine elder and thy younger: and I will give them unto thee for daughters, but not by thy covenant. And I will establish my covenant with thee; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD." He speaks with Samaria, Sodom and the other nations. From among them he promises daughters to Jerusalem, but by a different covenant from the one which earthly Jerusalem first received. For earthly Jerusalem at the beginning received a covenant of this kind, that it should be the metropolis of the people whose inheritance was the land of Canaan, and that the Temple should be in it, in which the Aaronic priesthood would minister, chosen by God himself to set there the memory of his name. But it is not by such a covenant, the covenant that was peculiar to earthly Jerusalem, that the nations are promised as daughters to Jerusalem, but by another, and indeed that new one which Jeremiah had promised; because Abraham had the promise, without the law, that he would be the heir of the world, or the father of many nations.

units.la: XI. Novi Testamenti necessitatem ipsa Veteris Testamenti, seu eorum omnium, quae Promissioni ante Mosen, & sub eo acceperunt, antiquatio evincit. Quam Loc.XV. f.98.99. argumento tam generali, quod mere umbraticum illud fuerit, & corpus in Messia praestari debuerit: tum specialibus a natura Legum illius Testamenti, utpote quae nec necessariae per se, sed ex placito Divino uni populo ad certum usque tempus impositae fuerunt; nec ceu justitia, vel pars justitiae per se quenquam Deo commendare potuerunt; a praedictionibus, Sacerdotii & dignitatis Messiae conditione, & peremptoria ejus per excidium Templi destructione petitis, probare occupavimus. Cum ergo cultus Dei sub Messia non cessaturus, sed ita perficiendus fuerit, ut corporalibus mere spiritualia & caelestia succedant, res ipsa confirmat,
units.tr: XI. The antiquation of the Old Testament itself, or of all those things which were received under the promise before Moses and under him, proves the necessity of the New Testament. We have set out to prove this from the Lecture XV, pp. 98-99, with the general argument that the old covenant was merely shadowy and that the body was to be supplied in the Messiah; and then from special arguments drawn from the nature of the laws of that covenant, which were imposed on one people for a certain time, not necessary in themselves but by divine decree, and which could not commend anyone to God as righteousness, or as part of righteousness; and from the predictions concerning the priesthood, the condition of the dignity of the Messiah, and the decisive destruction of the Temple by its overthrow. Since, therefore, the worship of God under the Messiah was not going to cease but was to be perfected in such a way that spiritual and heavenly things would succeed bodily ones, the matter itself confirms that

units.la: alii & meliori, praestantioribus promissis sancito Testamento locum esse debuisse. Neque enim haereditas bonorum spiritualium & caelestium nisi ex Testamento datur.
units.tr: another and better covenant, sanctioned by more excellent promises, had to have its place. For the inheritance of spiritual and heavenly goods is not given except by a testament.

units.la: XII. In contrarium pertinaci studio Judaei nituntur, Novum Testamentum, & cum eodem Evangelium impie abnegantes. Nam nono fidei suae articulo sic illi profitentur: Ego credo fide perfecta, quod Lex Mosaica nulli mutationi sit obnoxia, neque alia Lex a Creatore, cujus nomen benedictum sit, unquam expectanda veniat. Nihilominus aiusest Abarbanel in Jerem. XXXI.31.q.5. ex verbis Jeremiae Testamentum Novum promittentis concludere, Deum tempore futurae redemptionis populo suo daturum esse Legem novam & aliam, loco illius, quam, inquit, habemus. Sed hoc, inquit idem, repugnat fundamento, quo credere tenemur, Legem perpetuam & subinde immutabilem fore. Aliud ergo Deus per Jeremiam promisit: aliud Judaei in fundamentis suis credere tenentur, quod Theomachin est. Sed R. David Kimchi in catrata quidem illa, sed ope MS. a Cl. Pocockio restituta glossa sic verba Jeremiae de Testamento vel Foedere Novo detorquet, ut dicat, promitti a Jeremia non novitatem Foederis, sed stabilimentum ejus; eo quod futurum sit firmum atque stabile, non iterum irritum reddendum, sicut prius illud foedus in monte Sinai cum Israelitis initum; juxta verba Prophetae. Non ut foedus, quod pepigi cum Patribus ipsorum, &c. qui irritum fecerunt foedus meum. Mosaicum igitur foedus communiter illi interpretantur, utpote juxta Majmonidis illa, cap.9. Jesud. Hathor. subsistens in secula seculorum, adeoque nunquam abrogandum, sed sic tamen sub Messia stabiliendum, ut non amplius violetur, & hoc sensu foedus novum, hoc est, observantia fideli renovatum & stabilitum dicitur. Quae Hesperides sunt. Nam & illud ipsum quod Vetus & Novum foedus hactenus etiam differant, quod illud statim violatum & irritum factum est juxta illud Mosis: Recesserunt cito de via, quam praecepi: Exod. XXXII.8. hoc sic violari, ut irritum reddatur, nequit, quia in eo Lex non cortici dun-taxat, vel tabulae lapideae, sed cordibus foederatorum ab ipso Deo inscribitur, Jerem. XXXI.33. & sempiternum illud est, promissionem habens, fore, ut Deus non recedat a foederatis, quo minus iis benefaciat, sed timorem suum det in corda eorum, ut a se non deficiant, &c. ibid. XXXII.39. 40. longe majorem differentiam, quam Foederis ejusdem ut veteris & renovati duntaxat arguit. Nam promissionum differentia est efficiens, ut illud irritum reddi potuerit, hoc non potuerit. Frustra vero stabiliri sub Messia Foedus Mosaicum per observantiam Legis Mosis pertendunt, quia Messias peccata, a quibus Lex Mosis liberare non potuit, expiaturus, non justitiam propriam stabiliturus venire debuit. Negat insuper Propheta, Foedus Novum pangendum esse sicut foedus cum Patribus initum. Cum vero servilis litera, uti Kimchi in libro Michlol sol.25. docet, ut plurimum serviat ad comparationem instituendam, qua diversa inter se comparari solent, apparet, non de uno eodémque fœdere, sed diversis, sibique ἀντιδιῃρημένως oppositis sermonem esse, adeóque fœdus cum Patribus initum, ראשונה prius & novum, illud שנית posterius esse. Ideo vocis חדשה emphasin merito S. Paulus sic urget: ἐν τῷ λέγειν καινὴν, πεπαλαίωκε τὴν πρώτην, in eo, quòd dixit, Novum, antiquavit prius, Hebr. VIII.13. Licet enim verbum חדש renovari significet, tamen adjectivum חדש semper novum, veteri oppositum, diversum, aliud significat. Surrexit מלך חדש novus Rex, Exod.I.8. Elegebant אלהים חדשים Deos novos, alios, Jud.V.8. ישן מפני חדש Vetus propter novum educetis, Levit.XXVI.10. Et Jeremias XXXI.22. Creabit Jehova חדשה novum in terra: Fœmina circumdabit virum. Unde LXX. per ἕτερον aliud subinde reddunt. Præterea Deus apud Jeremiam præfatus הני ימים באים Ecce dies veniunt, v.31. & subjungens: Fœdus feriam אחרי הימים ההם post dies illos, v.33. non obscurè dies alios à diebus Veteris Testamenti distinctos, & ejusmodi quidem, quibus adagium illud, quòd Patres omphacem comederint, & filiis dentes stupeant, hoc est, quòd onus Legis propter Patrum transgressiones sustineant, unà cum onere illo Legis V. T. cessaturum sit, innuit.
units.tr: XII. The Jews strive with stubborn zeal against this, impiously denying both the New Testament and the Gospel with it. For in the ninth article of their faith they profess thus: "I believe with perfect faith that the Mosaic Law is subject to no change, and that no other Law will ever come from the Creator, blessed be his name." Nevertheless, Abarbanel on Jeremiah 31:31, question 5, concludes from the words of Jeremiah promising a New Testament that God, at the time of the future redemption, will give his people a new Law, different in place of the one, he says, that we have. But this, he says, contradicts the foundation which we are bound to believe, namely that the Law is perpetual and therefore unchangeable. So God promised one thing through Jeremiah; the Jews are bound to believe something else in their foundations, which is a theomachy. But Rabbi David Kimchi, in his gloss, which is indeed in that clouded edition but was restored with the help of a manuscript by the distinguished Pococke, twists the words of Jeremiah about the New Testament or covenant in such a way as to say that Jeremiah promises not a novelty of the covenant but its establishment, because it will be firm and stable and not again to be rendered void, as that former covenant made at Mount Sinai with the Israelites was; according to the words of the prophet: "Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers, etc., which my covenant they brake." Therefore they commonly interpret the Mosaic covenant in this way, following Maimonides' words in chapter 9 of Yesodei ha-Torah, that it endures for ever and ever, and so is never to be abrogated; but nevertheless it is to be established under the Messiah in such a way that it is no longer violated, and in this sense it is called "new covenant," that is, renewed and established by faithful observance. These are Hesperidean fancies. For also the fact that the Old and New covenants still differ in this, that the former was immediately violated and made void according to Moses' words, "They have turned aside quickly out of the way which I commanded them" (Exod. 32:8), while the latter cannot be violated so as to be made void, because in it the Law is written not merely on bark or stone tablets but on the hearts of those in covenant by God himself, Jer. 31:33, and it is everlasting, having the promise that God will not turn away from those in covenant, so as to refrain from doing them good, but will put his fear in their hearts so that they do not fall away from him, etc., ibid. 32:39-40, argues a much greater difference than merely that of an old and renewed covenant of the same kind. For the difference in the promises is what made the one capable of being rendered void and the other not. And they strive in vain to establish the Mosaic covenant under the Messiah through observance of the Law of Moses, because the Messiah was to come to make atonement for sins, from which the Law of Moses could not free, and not to establish his own righteousness. The Prophet moreover denies that the New Covenant is to be made like the covenant that was made with the fathers. And since the literal language, as Kimchi teaches in the book Michlol, fol. 25, usually serves to set up a comparison in which different things are normally compared with one another, it is evident that the discourse concerns not one and the same covenant but different ones, opposed to each other antidiairemenōs [ἀντιδιῃρημένως]; so the covenant made with the fathers is the first [ראשונה], and the new is the second [שנית]. For this reason St. Paul rightly presses the emphasis of the word "new" in this way: "In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old" [ἐν τῷ λέγειν καινὴν, πεπαλαίωκε τὴν πρώτην], Heb. 8:13. For although the verb חדש signifies to be renewed, the adjective חדש always means new, different, other, opposed to old. "There arose a new king" [מלך חדש], Exod. 1:8. "They chose new gods" [אלהים חדשים], that is, other gods, Judg. 5:8. "Ye shall bring out the old because of the new" [ישן מפני חדש], Lev. 26:10. And Jeremiah 31:22: "The LORD hath created a new thing in the earth [חדשה]: A woman shall compass a man." Whence the Seventy often render it by heteron [ἕτερον], "another." Moreover God, in Jeremiah, introduces it with "Behold, the days come" [הנה ימים באים], v. 31, and adds: "I will make a covenant after those days" [אחרי הימים ההם], v. 33, clearly distinguishing those days from the days of the Old Testament; and indeed days of such a kind that he hints that the proverb that the fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge, that is, that they bear the burden of the Law because of their fathers' transgressions, will cease together with that burden of the Old Testament Law.

units.la: XIII. Quid verò multis? Ipsæ Fœderis, seu Testamenti Novi promissiones à Jeremia descriptæ non vetus Fœdus Mosaicum renovatum, sed diversum à vetere fœdere, Fœdus Evangelicum sonant, quia promissiones illæ sub Veteri Testamento non fuerunt, neque omnino cum statu Patrum congruunt. Ipsum enim fundamentum promissionum Novi Testamenti, nempe פדות גאלה ἀπολύτρωσις redemptio per non argentum, Esaj.LII.3. per veri nominis justitiam, ibid.I.27. V.16. non extitit nisi in fine dierum priorum. Necessariò autem diversus status redemptorum, & non redemptorum est, quia his, si Christus non venisset, ob peccata nec dum expiata pereundum necessariò fuisset: Illorum peccata jam expiata intelliguntur. Redemptionem sequitur prædicatio boni, salutis, justitiæ, Psal.XL.10.11. Esaj.LII.7. Qua prædicatione, sicut nomen Dei rebus ipsis manifestatum celebratur, ita Lex Dei ponitur in medio Israelis, ut qui narrationem de Salvatore & salute procurata audiverunt, ignorare non possint, quid faciendo homo peccator faciat voluntatem Dei, & se ad eum convertat, ut cum ipso amicitiam habeat. Hoc illud apud Jeremiam est: Dabo Legem meam in medio eorum, v.33. oppositè ad umbras & ænigmata V. T. quibus vigentibus, ceu cortice quodam Lex fidei & Christus ipse velatus est, at remotis omnia nunc Legis fidei arcana panduntur, & gloria Domini revelata facie spectatur, 2.Cor.III.18. Accedit, quòd Deus in Novo Testamento Legem illam cordibus inscribit, ibid. Jerem. hoc est, eam intelligi, amari, credi, retineri, & jugi meditatione ad perfectiorem sapientiam augescere facit. Ut jam non ampliùs circumcisi in litera Legis ambulantes, sed ii soli, qui se Legem Dei in corde scriptam habere testantur, pro populo Dei, cui ipse in Deum fieri velit, censeantur. Addit, Non docebunt ampliùs quisquam proximum suum, & quisquam fratrem suum, dicendo: cognosce Jehovam. Nam omnes ipsi cognoscent me, &c. v.34. Quod dici de Vetere Testamento non poterat, utpote in quo expectabatur Propheta, qui Verba Dei loqueretur: & Moses atque Prophetæ testes erant eorum, quæ in posterum dicenda erant; & clavis cognitionis doctoribus commissa fuit, & abscondi potuit, & leges παιδαγωγικὰ patrum locum habuerunt; & Lex carnalis præcepti ab hominibus urgeri & præcipi debuit. Denique condonabo, inquit Jehova, pravitatem eorum, & peccati eorum non recordabor amplius, ibid. At in V.T. in sacrificiis fuit ἀνάμνησις τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν recordatio peccati, Col.II.14. Heb. X.3. utpote nondum expiati, sed expiandi, & uno die auferendi, Dan.IX.24. Zach.III.9. Psal.XL.7, 8.9.10. Ac licèt condonatio peccati, seu non imputatio ad æternam damnationem ibi fuerit, non tamen condonatio peccati velut expiati, & ad servitutem ferendam non imputati, fuit. Hæc plus quàm renovationem & novam stabilitionem ejusdem fœderis sonant.
units.tr: XIII. But why say more? The very promises of the covenant, or New Testament, described by Jeremiah do not sound like the Mosaic covenant renewed, but like a covenant different from the old one, an Evangelical covenant. Those promises were not made under the Old Testament, and they do not agree at all with the state of the Fathers. For the very foundation of the promises of the New Testament, namely redemption [פדות גאלה] [ἀπολύτρωσις] through what is not silver, Isa. 52.3, and through justice in the true sense of the name, ibid. I.27, V.16, did not exist until the end of the former days. The condition of the redeemed and of the unredeemed is necessarily different, because for the latter, had Christ not come, perishing would necessarily have followed on account of sins not yet expiated; the sins of the former are understood to be already expiated. Redemption is followed by the proclamation of good, of salvation, of justice, Ps. 40.10, 11; Isa. 52.7. Just as the name of God is celebrated in the very things made manifest, so by this proclamation the Law of God is set in the midst of Israel, so that those who have heard the account of the Saviour and of the salvation obtained cannot be ignorant of what a sinful man must do in order to do the will of God, and to turn to him, so as to have friendship with him. This is what is meant in Jeremiah: "I will put my Law in the midst of them," v. 33, in contrast to the shadows and enigmas of the Old Testament, under which the Law of faith and Christ himself were veiled as under a kind of bark; but now, with those removed, all the hidden things of the Law of faith are laid open, and the glory of the Lord is beheld with unveiled face, 2 Cor. 3.18. Moreover, God in the New Testament writes that Law on hearts, ibid., Jer. That is, he causes it to be understood, loved, believed and retained, and by continual meditation to grow into fuller wisdom. So that now not the circumcised who walk in the letter of the Law, but those alone who testify that they have the Law of God written in their heart, are to be counted as the people of God, to whom he himself wishes to be God. He adds: "They shall no longer teach each his neighbour, and each his brother, saying, Know the Lord; for they shall all know me, etc.," v. 34. This could not be said of the Old Testament, in which a prophet was expected who would speak the words of God; Moses and the prophets were witnesses of those things which were to be said in the future; the key of knowledge was committed to teachers and could be hidden; the laws served as a tutor [παιδαγωγικὰ] for the fathers; and the carnal law of precept had to be pressed and enjoined on men. Finally, "I will forgive," says the Lord, "their wickedness, and I will remember their sin no more," ibid. But in the Old Testament, in the sacrifices, there was a remembrance of sins [ἀνάμνησις τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν], Col. 2.14; Heb. 10.3, since they were not yet expiated but to be expiated, and to be taken away in one day, Dan. 9.24; Zech. 3.9; Ps. 40.7, 8, 9, 10. And although there was in that case a forgiveness of sin, or a non-imputation to eternal damnation, there was not a forgiveness of sin as already expiated, and not imputed for the bearing of servitude. These things mean more than a renewal and a new establishment of the same covenant.

units.la: XIV. Frivola sunt Judæorum argumenta, quibus probare contendunt, Fœdus novum, ejusque Legem esse ipsum Fœdus Mosaicum renovatum & observantia stabilitum. Nam quæ pro immutabilitate Legis Mosaicæ etiam Ritualis objectant, Loc.XV. §.100. diluimus. Habebit sanè Messias Legem suam. Ad Legem ejus insulæ sperabunt, Esaj.XLII.4. Sed Legem eam esse id omne & solum, quod Moses præcepit, falsum est. Multa enim à Mose præcepta fuisse temporaria & mutabilia, δόγματα puta seu placita, supra etiam demonstravimus. Neque Lex Messiæ est: Qui fecerit illa, vivet in illis: sed: Respicite ad me, & salvamini omnes fines terræ, ibid. XLV.22. Justus in fide ejus (Præconis) vivet, Habac.II.4. תורה enim non tantùm id est, quod Moses præcepit, sed notat etiam demonstrationem viæ justitiæ, quam Moses etiam tradidit, at nec solam illam per se, nec eo modo, quo Messias. Non enim ad se, sed ad Rupem salutis, Angelum Fœderis, Prophetam magnum respicientibus, confugientibus salutem promisit. Neque illud obstat, quòd etiam post datam circumcisionem cordis dicitur: Revertemini, & audietis vocem Domini Dei vestri, facietisque omnia præcepta, quæ hodie præcipio vobis, &c. quando audietis vocem Domini Dei vestri, & שמרתם præcepta & statuta ejus custodietis, &c. Deut. XXX.6.8.10. Nam ipsa circumcisio cordis secundum excellentiam dicta talis est, ut prisci s temporibus dari, & cum ritibus conjungi non potuerit. Est enim circumcisio à conscientia reatus. At quandiu Christus sacrificium non obtulit, tandiu etiam reatus non desiit, adeóque etiam conscientia reatus cordi incubuit. Ideo Israelitæ, offerendo sacrificia pro reatu & peccato, quotidie confessionem reatus ipsis æquè ac toti mundo incumbentis, ediderunt; & figuræ omnes oblationis Christi spem Israelis testatæ sunt. Ubi verò spes liberationis tantùm est, ibi nec dum conscientia plenè consummata & liberata est. Neque alia probatione opus est, quàm quòd ipsa conscientia & ratio dictat, constitutiones ejusmodi non inservire, nisi ad concludendum eos, quibus imponuntur, sub peccatum, & ad testandum illis, quòd opus habeant salute Dei, justitia, pace & sacrificio justitiæ ab idoneo Sacerdote oblatæ. Præcepta igitur illa & statuta, quorum observantia etiam post circumcisionem cordis datam urget, sunt Decalogus, qua regula charitatis Dei & proximi, æqua judicia Rerum publicarum. Quantum vero ad figuras, ritus, & disciplinam subjicientem servituti earum Mosis præceptum non est, ut in iis semper ambuletur, quia idem supra cap.XXIX.19. Satiatam à Sitiente distinxit, & circumcisionem cordis, cum observantia rituum ἀναγκαίου, promisit. Neque tamen plane sub Messia præcepta etiam illa ritualia & judicialia singularia cessant, sed magis in spiritu & veritate exercentur. Neque aliter Moses illa populo commendaverat, ostendens passim, citra spiritum ceremonias esse otiosas, inanes, & Deo abominabiles. Veniet hora & nunc est, cum veri adoratores adorabunt Patrem in Spiritu & veritate. Nam Pater tales adoratores quærit. Spiritus est Deus, & adorantes eum in Spiritu & veritate adorare decet, Joh.IV.23.24. Falluntur vero non parum Judæi, quod חקות ubique ritus explicant, cum præcepta cujuscunque generis, quæ sunt οεσμοὶ definitiones, & modum ac limitationem certam habent, חקים dicantur. Nam חק modum cujusque rei significat. Neque proin etiam Verba Mosis: Et diliges Dominum Deum tuum, & observabis observationem ejus, & חקות statuta & judicia, & præcepta ejus omnibus diebus, Deut.XI.1. Judæos juvant, quia rituum vel præceptionum ritualium nulla diserta mentio est. Quid insuper impedit semper diligi Deum, & observari præcepta ejus omnia, quæ ipse Deus in certa tempora præscripsit; nempe præcepta, quæ tempori libertatis conveniebant. Etiam כל הימים omnes illi dies, certos dies, nempe dies expectationis, in quibus tunc populus constitutus erat, significare possunt. Frequens etiam in eorundem Judæorum ore est locus Mosis: תורה צוה לנו משה מורשה קהלת יעקב quæ sic illi reddunt, ut Legem Mosis jungant cum hæreditate, hoc sensu: Legem dedit Moses nobis, hæreditatem, toti cœtui Jacob, Deut.XXXIII.4. Sed perperam sic illi construunt, quia non extat signum Dativi, nec est forma regiminis מורשת. Rectius Lex & hæreditas distinguuntur hoc sensu: Moses præcepit Legem nobis ex sermonibus Domini: hæreditatem accepit cœtus Jacob. Si tamen Lex, quam præcepit Moses, est hæreditas cœtus Jacobi, non est ea Lex, quam nec Abraham acceperat, cum fide justificatus est, nec Patres acceperunt. Quomodo enim id hæreditas esse potest, ex quo non datur hæreditas? Nam Sodoma & Samaria, & reliquæ gentes non dantur Judæ in filias ex Testamento Judæ, Ezech. XVI.61. Præterea nec Lex illa Messiæ, quam insulæ sperant vel expectant, Esaj.XLII.4. vel gentibus, vel Israeli ceremonias injungit. Non gentibus, tum quia promissio dicit, quod gentes sint benedicendæ in Abrahamo & Semine ejus, eo certè Semine, cujus Legem gentes expectabunt: quæ benedictio non minor futura erat, quàm ipsius Abrahami, cui fides sua in justitiam reputata est: tum quia Messias esse debuit in Lucem gentium, ibid.XLIX.6. & ad easdem missurus erat, qui annuntiarent Evangelium de justitia, bono & salute, non jugum illis imponerent, ibid. LII. 7. Psal.XL. 11. tum quia pacem ad gentes loqui debuit, Zach.IX.10. tum quia gentes Israeli dandæ erant filiæ non ex Testamento Judæ, sed novo, Ezech.XVI.3. Non Israeli, tum quia Gentes expectare debuerunt Legem Messiæ, quæ non alia gentibus, alia Israeli præscribi debuit: tum quia prædicaturus erat Israeli
units.tr: XIV. The arguments of the Jews, by which they strive to prove that the New Covenant and its Law is the Mosaic covenant renewed and established by observance, are worthless. For what they object concerning the immutability of the Mosaic Law, even the ritual part, we have refuted at Loc. XV. §.100. Certainly the Messiah will have his Law: the islands will hope for his Law, Isa. 42.4. But that this Law is everything and only what Moses commanded is false. For we have also shown above that many things commanded by Moses were temporary and changeable, decrees or ordinances [δόγματα]. Nor is the Law of the Messiah: "He who does those things shall live in them," but: "Look to me, and be saved, all ends of the earth," ibid. 45.22; "The just shall live by his faith" (of the herald), Hab. 2.4. For תורה [torah] does not mean only what Moses commanded, but also denotes the demonstration of the way of justice, which Moses also handed down; yet not that alone by itself, nor in the manner in which the Messiah does. For he promised salvation not to those looking to themselves, but to those fleeing to the Rock of salvation, the Angel of the covenant, the great Prophet. Nor is it an objection that even after the circumcision of the heart was given it is said: "Return, and you will hear the voice of the Lord your God, and you will do all the commandments which I command you today," etc., when you shall hear the voice of the Lord your God, and you shall keep [שמרתם] his precepts and statutes, etc., Deut. 30.6, 8, 10. For the circumcision of the heart, so called pre-eminently, is of such a kind that it could not be given in earlier times, nor joined with rites. For circumcision is from the conscience of guilt. But as long as Christ had not offered the sacrifice, so long the guilt did not cease, and so the conscience of guilt lay upon the heart. Therefore the Israelites, by offering sacrifices for guilt and sin, daily gave out a confession of the guilt that lay on them, as on the whole world; and all the figures of the oblation of Christ bore witness to the hope of Israel. But where there is only the hope of deliverance, there the conscience is not yet fully consummated and freed. No other proof is needed than that conscience and reason itself dictate that such ordinances serve only to shut up those on whom they are imposed under sin, and to testify to them that they need the salvation of God, justice, peace, and the sacrifice of justice offered by a fitting priest. Those precepts and statutes, therefore, whose observance continues to press even after the circumcision of the heart has been given, are the Decalogue, the rule of love of God and neighbour, and the fair judgments of civil governments. As for figures, rites, and a discipline subjecting people to their servitude, there is no precept of Moses that one should always walk in them; for the same Moses, above at chap. 29.19, distinguished the satisfied from the thirsty, and promised circumcision of the heart together with the observance of the necessary rites. Nor, however, do those ritual and judicial precepts, taken individually, altogether cease under the Messiah; rather they are exercised more in spirit and in truth. Nor did Moses commend them to the people otherwise, showing everywhere that ceremonies without the spirit are idle, empty, and abominable to God. The hour comes, and now is, when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father seeks such worshippers. God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth, John 4.23, 24. But the Jews are not a little mistaken in explaining חקות [chukkot] everywhere as rites, since precepts of any kind, which are bonds [οεσμοὶ] of definition, and have a fixed measure and limitation, are called חקים [chukim]. For חק [chok] signifies the measure of each thing. Nor do the words of Moses help the Jews: "And you shall love the Lord your God, and keep his charge, and his חקות statutes, and his judgments, and his precepts, all the days," Deut. 11.1, because there is no express mention of rites or ritual precepts. Moreover, what prevents God from always being loved, and all his precepts being kept, which God himself prescribed for certain times, namely precepts that suited the time of liberty? Also כל הימים [kol hayyamim], "all the days," may signify certain days, namely the days of expectation in which the people was then placed. Also frequent on the lips of the same Jews is the passage of Moses: תורה צוה לנו משה מורשה קהלת יעקב [torah tsiwah lanu Mosheh morashah qehillat Yaaqov], which they render so as to join the Law of Moses with an inheritance, in this sense: "Moses gave us the Law, an inheritance to the whole assembly of Jacob," Deut. 33.4. But they construe it wrongly, because there is no sign of the dative, nor is it the construct form of מורשת [morashat]. More rightly the Law and the inheritance are distinguished in this sense: Moses commanded the Law to us from the words of the Lord; the assembly of Jacob received the inheritance. But if the Law which Moses commanded is the inheritance of the assembly of Jacob, it is not that Law which Abraham did not receive when he was justified by faith, nor which the Fathers received. For how can that be an inheritance, when no inheritance is given from it? For Sodom and Samaria and the other nations are not given to Judah as daughters from the covenant of Judah, Ezek. 16.61. Moreover, neither does that Law of the Messiah, which the islands hope for or expect, Isa. 42.4, impose ceremonies either on the Gentiles or on Israel. Not on the Gentiles: both because the promise says that the Gentiles are to be blessed in Abraham and in his Seed, certainly that Seed whose Law the Gentiles will expect, which blessing was to be no less than that of Abraham himself, whose faith was reckoned to him for righteousness; and because the Messiah was to be a light of the Gentiles, ibid. 49.6, and was to send to them those who would announce the Gospel of justice, good, and salvation, not impose a yoke upon them, ibid. 52.7; Ps. 40.11; and because he was to speak peace to the nations, Zech. 9.10; and because daughters were to be given to Israel from the Gentiles not from the covenant of Judah but from the new, Ezek. 16.3. Not on Israel: both because the Gentiles ought to expect the Law of the Messiah, which was not to be prescribed to one people in one way and to another in another; and because he was going to proclaim to Israel

units.la: libertatem & dimissionem ex carcere, Esaj.LXI.1. Zach.IX.11. tum quia Dominus ad gentes versurus erat labium clarum, ut serviant illi uno humero, eodem modo, quo Israel, Zeph.III.9. tum quia abdicaturus erat Pastores & Principes, ne amplius sint Pastores, Ezech.XXXIV.10. Psalm. LXXXII.6. nominatim etiam Sacerdotes, Malach.II.12. Ipse autem futurus erat omnium unus Pastor, Ezech.XXXIV.23.24. tum quia Prophetia salutem promittit omni credenti in Præconem, & nomen Jehovæ nuncupanti, Habac.II.4. Esaj.XXVIII.16. Joel.II.32. tum quia ritus & ceremoniæ abrogandæ fuerunt. quod operosè supra probavimus. Denique nec Deus apud Malachiam dicens: Recordamini Legis Mosis, servi mei, quam præcepi illi in monte Horeb ad totum Israelem, משפטים וחקים definitiones & judicia, Malach.IV.4.5. jussit, cum Christus venerit, observare omnia, quæ Moses imperaverat, sed simpliciter memoriæ mandare jubet Legem Mosis, usque dum mittatur Elias, magnus ille præcursor Messiæ, ad quem usque Lex & Prophetæ prophetare debuerunt. Præterquam quòd ibi nec distinctè ritus commemorantur, sed cum Lege definitiones & judicia per appositionem junguntur.
units.tr: liberty and release from prison, Isa. 61:1; Zech. 9:11. Because the Lord was about to turn to the nations a pure lip, that they should serve him with one shoulder, in the same way as Israel, Zeph. 3:9. Because he was about to depose the shepherds and princes, so that there should no longer be shepherds, Ezek. 34:10; Ps. 82:6, and in particular the priests, Mal. 2:12. He himself was to be the one shepherd of all, Ezek. 34:23-24. Because the prophecy promises salvation to every believer in the Herald, who calls upon the name of Jehovah, Hab. 2:4; Isa. 28:16; Joel 2:32. Because the rites and ceremonies were to be abrogated, which we have demonstrated at length above. Finally, in Malachi God does not command, when Christ has come, that all the things Moses prescribed be observed, when he says: "Remember the law of Moses, my servant, which I commanded him in Horeb for all Israel, [מִשְׁפָּטִים וְחֻקִּים] definitions and judgments," Mal. 4:4-5. Rather, he simply bids them commit the law of Moses to memory until Elijah is sent, that great forerunner of the Messiah, up to whom the Law and the Prophets were to prophesy. Moreover, in that passage the rites are not distinctly mentioned; rather, definitions and judgments are joined to the Law by apposition.

units.la: XV. Sicut Vetus Testamentum peculiarem œconomiam habuit; ita & Novum suum & propriam habet.
units.tr: XV. Just as the Old Testament had its own peculiar economy, so the New also has its own and proper economy.

units.la: Deus notificavit nobis mysterium voluntatis suæ, secundum beneplacitum suum, quod propositum fuerat in se, εἰς οἰκονομίαν & πληρώματος τῶν καιρῶν ad dispensationem plenitudinis temporum, Ephes.I.9.10. Ubi Oeconomia seu Dispensatio plenitudinis temporum dignam & convenientem plenitudini temporum seu iis temporibus, quibus omnia impleta & consummata sunt, & quæ sunt ἄκρον summum temporum mundi; πλήρωμα αἰώνων fines seculorum, I.Cor.X.11. ultima hora, I.Joh.II.18. rerum, puta Fœderis Gratiæ & Testamenti Novi administrationem notat. Oportebat enim inprimis in plenitudine temporum talia fieri, quæ ostenderent & probarent, Deum, sapientissimum rectorem, sicut omnia, ita etiam illa suo tempore pulchrè, Eccles.III.11. fecisse. ut ita ad laudem gloriæ Gratiæ etiam ἐντιπεπονα decentia dispositionis temporum, & decentia glorificationis Christi exhibiti faciat. Cùm enim Deus diversa mundi ante judicium ultimum tempora ita distinxerit, ut alia ad dies priores, alia ad plenitudinem temporum, diebus prioribus succedanea referret; & priora illa suam œconomiam, aptámque tempori expectationis Christi faciem impleverint, non potuerunt posteriora tempora œconomia illis conveniente destitui. Habuit enim omnino Israel duo tempora; unum, quo puer fuit; alterum, quo pueritia omnia tolli, & virilis sapientia ac prudentia omnis effundi debuit. Planè enim etiam consentaneum Sapientiæ Dei fuit hoc modo agere cum mundo, antequam ultimum judicium appelleret, ut partim Filium suum glorificaret, Joh. XVII. 1-7. & servos suos ad perfectionem, per quam in ultimo hoc tempore propiùs ad Deum, & cœlestia gaudia, non stantes ampliùs in loco, in quo chirographum contra se consignent, accederent, & in bona conscientia maxima promissa adipiscerentur; adduceret: partim etiam mundum, seu ingratos ex Judæis & gentibus vocaret, juxta parabolam: Postremò ad ad ipsos misit Filium suum, dicens: Reverebuntur Filium meum, Matth. XXI. 37.
units.tr: God has made known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he had purposed in himself, unto the dispensation of the fullness of times [εἰς οἰκονομίαν πληρώματος τῶν καιρῶν], Eph. 1:9-10. Here "economy" or "dispensation of the fullness of times" denotes the dispensation and administration of the covenant of grace and the New Testament, suited and fitting to the fullness of times, that is, to those times in which all things have been fulfilled and completed, and which are the very end [ἄκρον] of the times of the world; the fullness of the ages [πλήρωμα αἰώνων], the ends of the ages, 1 Cor. 10:11; the last hour, 1 John 2:18. For it was necessary above all that in the fullness of times such things should be done as would show and prove that God, the wisest ruler, had done all things, including these, beautifully in their season, Eccl. 3:11, and so would make the fitting arrangement of the times also serve the praise of the glory of grace and the glorification of the Christ who had been revealed. For since God had so distinguished the various periods of the world before the last judgment, referring some to the former days and others to the fullness of times as successors to the former days, and since those earlier periods had fulfilled their own economy and the face suited to the time of expectation of Christ, the later times could not be left without an economy fitting to them. Israel indeed had two periods: one in which it was a child, and another in which all childishness was to be removed and the full wisdom and prudence of manhood poured forth. It was also altogether consistent with the wisdom of God to deal with the world in this way before he summoned the last judgment: partly so that he might glorify his Son, John 17:1-7, and bring his servants to that perfection by which, in this last time, they might draw nearer to God and the heavenly joys, no longer standing in the place in which they sign a bond against themselves, and might attain the greatest promises in a good conscience; partly also so that he might call the world, that is, the ungrateful among Jews and Gentiles, according to the parable: Last of all he sent to them his Son, saying: They will reverence my Son, Matt. 21:37.

units.la: XVI. Dispensatio illa Foederis Gratiae & Testamenti Novi sub Evangelio obtinet, & praeceptis potissimum & promissis propriis abrogatur. Habet enim etiam sub Novo Testamento Christus תורת Legem suam לתורתו אתיים יחלו Legem ejus insulae sperant, expectant, Esaj. XLII. 4. Istud est foedus, &c. Dabo תורתי legem meam in medio eorum, & cordi eorum inscribam eam, Jerem. XXXI. 33. q.d. Sic vobiscum agam, ut videri possim semper ad vos dicere: Ecce haec Lex mea, haec clara & minime velata expositio viae justitiae est; efficiamque, ut eam libentes recipiatis, diligatis, ea delectemini, & ejus non obliviscamini. Licet enim Evangelium proprie non sit Lex, sed annuntiatio rei laetae & amabilis ad gloriam Dei, tamen annuntiatio illa absque naturali obligatione, contestatione & adjuratione hominis, eam veritatem amabilem & Deo gloriosam audientis, confitentis & ad gloriam Dei celebrantis, & bonum hoc, & ejusque authorem Deum in Christo amantis, fieri non potuit. Ideoque Evangelium, seu testificatio & annuntiatio isthaec Dei per se vim habet praecepti, quatenus animae rectae tantum non vim facit ad se recipiendum, affirmandum, laudandum & amandum. Quae quidem vis suavissima quaedam πειθωνάγκη est similis luci, quae se amare cogit; rebus pulchris & pretiosis, quae concupiscentiam sui extorquent; & sponso, qui sponsam enixe amans, eam ad se redamandum compellit. Atque laeta annuntiatio talis revera rationem habet תורת Legis, hoc est, demonstrationis viae ejus, qua peccator amando Deum amantem, & virtutes ejus, & amorem ejus, ad Deum & vitam pervenire potest.
units.tr: XVI. That dispensation of the covenant of grace and the New Testament holds under the Gospel, and is especially marked by its own precepts and promises. For Christ has also under the New Testament his law [תורה, לתורתו אִיִּים יְחַלּוּ], "the isles shall wait for his law," that is, they hope for and expect it, Isa. 42:4. This is the covenant, etc. I will put my law [תורתי] in their midst, and will write it on their heart, Jer. 31:33. That is to say: I will so deal with you that I may seem always to speak to you thus: "Behold, this is my Law; this is the clear and by no means veiled exposition of the way of righteousness; and I will bring it about that you receive it gladly, love it, take delight in it, and do not forget it." For although the Gospel is not properly a law, but the announcement of a joyful and lovable thing to the glory of God, nevertheless that announcement could not be made without a natural obligation, an attestation and an adjuration of the man who hears, confesses and celebrates to God's glory that lovable truth, and loves this good and God as its author in Christ. Therefore the Gospel, that is, this testimony and announcement of God, has of itself the force of a precept, inasmuch as it does scarcely any violence to a righteous soul to receive, affirm, praise and love it. This force is a most sweet kind of persuasion-necessity [πειθωνάγκη], like light that compels one to love it, like beautiful and precious things that extort desire for themselves, and like a bridegroom who, loving the bride ardently, compels her to love him in return. And such a joyful announcement truly has the character of the Law [תורה], that is, it shows the way by which the sinner, loving God who loves him, and loving his virtues and his love, can come to God and to life.

units.la: XVII. Non igitur aliud haec Lex esse potest, quam Lex ὑποταγῆς τῆς ὁμολογίας εἰς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον & Χριστῷ subjectionis, seu obedientia a stipulationis in Evangelium Christi, 2. Cor. IX. 13. Quae subjectio ab eodem S. Paulo ὑπακοὴ τῆς πίστεως obedientia fidei appellatur, Rom. I. 5. Per fidem enim subjicimur, obedimus Evangelio, recipientes alacri cum ὁμολογίᾳ, assensu laetum ejus de salute nostra testimonium. In fide est subjectio, obedientia, quae τῇ εὐαγγελίᾳ mandato praestatur. Praecipitur quippe & mandatur fides, non nova Lege, sed novo testimonio & nova re. Lex enim Naturae, & Lex amoris Dei omnem hominem ad id obligat, ut Deum glorificet, omni ejus verbo & testimonio credat, ad ipsum accedat, & convertatur, salutem ejus non negligat, Deum ut longanimem, de gratia sua testantem diligat, eique gratias agat. Porro subjectio illa fidei consistit in ὁμολογίᾳ stipulatione seu assensu cordis, quo homo testimonio, mandato, obtestationi Dei in verbo suo astipulatur, ad illa Ne & Amen respondet, atque ita cum Deo foedus init, & quidem in ὁμολογίᾳ stipulatione tali εἰς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον in Evangelium Christi. Licet enim fides, assensus noster feratur in omne verbum & testimonium Dei, nonnamen quivis assensus ad foedus cum Deo habendum & amicitiam cum ipso contrahendam conducit. Natura enim homo veritati Divinae reluctatur, 1. Cor. II. 14. Jud. v. 10. Ita assensus in verbum illud Dei: Qui fecerit ea homo, in iis vivet, amorem Dei operari non potest, quia solum illud, si nullum aliud verbum audiatur, vel cognoscatur apud hominem peccatorem manet litera, neque cordi inscribitur. Sed in Evangelio ἡ φιλανθρωπία καὶ χρηστότης & Θεοῦ amor erga homines & bonitas Dei, Tit. II. 11. III. 4. ostenditur. Ibi dicitur: Gustate & videte, quod bonus sit Dominus, Psal. XXXIV. 9. Nam id in corde sentire; & velut oculis videre licet. Atque hoc est Evangelium Christi, seu de Christo, Rom. I. 2. 3. Non enim aliud nomen sub coelo nominatum est, in quo oporteat nos salvari, Act. IV. 12. In solo illo ad Deum accedere licet, Hebr. VII. 25. 26. Cum Deo foedus per sacrificium fieri oportet, Psal. L. 5. 14. 23. adeoque per Sacerdotem, qui non alius quam Christus est, Extra quem cum nulla salus sit, etiam subjectio, & quidem subjectio astipulationis nisi in admissione Evangelii Christi esse non potest.
units.tr: XVII. Therefore this Law can be nothing other than the law of subjection to the confession of the Gospel and to Christ [ὑποταγῆς τῆς ὁμολογίας εἰς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον καὶ Χριστῷ], that is, the obedience of a covenant-pledge to the Gospel of Christ, 2 Cor. 9:13. This subjection the same St. Paul calls obedience of faith [ὑπακοὴ τῆς πίστεως], Rom. 1:5. For by faith we are subjected to, and obey, the Gospel, receiving with a glad confession [ὁμολογία], that is, with assent, its joyful testimony concerning our salvation. In faith there is subjection, obedience, which is rendered to the gospel [τῇ εὐαγγελίᾳ] as a command. For faith is indeed commanded and enjoined, not by a new law but by a new testimony and a new thing. For the law of nature and the law of the love of God obliges every man to this: to glorify God, to believe every word and testimony of his, to draw near to him and be converted, not to neglect his salvation, and to love God as patient and testifying to his own grace, and to give thanks to him. Moreover, that subjection of faith consists in confession [ὁμολογία], a covenant-pledge or assent of the heart, by which a man stands surety with God's testimony, command and solemn charge in his word, and answers to those words Yes and Amen, and so enters into covenant with God; and indeed in such a pledge of confession unto the Gospel of Christ. For although our faith and assent is directed to every word and testimony of God, yet not every assent is conducive to having covenant with God and contracting friendship with him. For by nature man struggles against divine truth, 1 Cor. 2:14; Jude 10. Thus assent to that word of God, the man who does these things shall live in them, cannot work the love of God, because that word, if no other word is heard or known, remains merely a letter to a sinful man and is not written on the heart. But in the Gospel the love of God toward men and the goodness of God [ἡ φιλανθρωπία καὶ ἡ χρηστότης τοῦ Θεοῦ] is shown, Titus 2:11; 3:4. There it is said: Taste and see that the Lord is good, Ps. 34:9; for it is possible to perceive this in the heart and, as it were, to see it with the eyes. And this is the Gospel of Christ, or concerning Christ, Rom. 1:2-3. For there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved, Acts 4:12. Only in him is it permitted to draw near to God, Heb. 7:25-26. A covenant with God must be made through sacrifice, Ps. 50:5, 14, 23, and so through the priest, who is none other than Christ. Since there is no salvation outside him, subjection, and indeed subjection of pledge, cannot exist except in the admission of the Gospel of Christ.

units.la: XVIII. Luculenter id ipsum S. Johannes explicat, dicens: Si testimonium hominum accipimus, testimonium Dei majus est de Filio suo. Qui credit in Filium Dei, habet testimonium hoc in se. Qui non credit Deo, ipsum mendacem facit, quia non credidit testimonio, quod testatus est Deus de Filio suo. Et hoc est id testimonium, quod vitam aeternam nobis dederit Deus, & haec vita in Filio ipsius sit. Qui habet Filium, habet vitam; qui non habet Filium Dei, non habet vitam, 1. Joh. V. 9-12. Quibus verbis tum praedicatio Evangelii, tum Lex eidem annexa exponitur. Praedicatio Evangelii illa statuitur, quod Deus miserit Filium suum, & quod in eo, ut causa, exhibita sit vita aeterna. Lex eidem annexa est communio cum Filio, seu ἔχειν τὸν υἱὸν habere Filium, v. 12. idque per fidem. Nam communio illa cum Filio obtinetur per Spiritum S. Ubi ille operari in nobis incipit, jam habemus Spiritum Filii. Is autem ante omnia in nobis operatur fidem, qua recipimus testimonium de Filio: Nam qui credit in Filium Dei, is habet testimonium in se ipso, v. 10. Ergo qui in Filium credit, ad eum confugit, animamque suam ei committit, is testimonium Dei in se habet. Nullo autem modo id in se habet, qui in eum non credit; imo Deum mendacem facit, quia non credit testimonio, quod Deus de Filio suo testatur. Testatur enim, beatum esse, quicunque ad eum confugit, Psal. II. 12. Qui igitur ad eum non confugit, is non credit Deo, beatum dicenti, qui ad eum confugit.
units.tr: XVIII. St John explains this very clearly, saying: "If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, because it concerns his Son. He who believes in the Son of God has this testimony in himself. He who does not believe God makes him a liar, because he has not believed the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son. And this is the testimony: that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He who has the Son has life; he who does not have the Son of God does not have life." 1 John 5:9-12. These words set forth both the preaching of the Gospel and the law attached to it. The preaching of the Gospel is that God has sent his Son, and that eternal life has been offered in him as its cause. The law attached to it is communion with the Son, or "having the Son" [ἔχειν τὸν υἱὸν], v. 12, and this comes through faith. For that communion with the Son is obtained through the Holy Spirit. When the Spirit begins to work in us, we already have the Spirit of the Son. He, above all, works faith in us, by which we receive the testimony concerning the Son. For "he who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself," v. 10. Therefore he who believes in the Son, who flees to him and commits his soul to him, has the testimony of God in himself. But "he who does not believe in him" has it in no way; indeed he "makes God a liar, because he does not believe the testimony that God bears concerning his Son." For God testifies "that all who flee to him are blessed," Psal. II. 12. Therefore he who does not flee to him does not believe God, who calls blessed the one who flees to him.

units.la: XIX. Haec porro praedicatio, quod in Filio Dei sit vita aeterna, & quod credens in eum, habeat in se Filium & vitam aeternam, demonstrationem & φανέρωσιν manifestationem ad omnem conscientiam hominum coram Deo comitem habere debet, Rom. XVI. 26. 2. Cor. IV. 2. Nam in praedicatione Evangelii debet gratia Dei ἐφανερωθεῖσα εἰς ἡμᾶς ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει exuberare in nos in omni sapientia & prudentia, Ephes. I. 8. De sapientia autem judicat conscientia, an doctrina Christi habeat fundamentum certum, in quo omnes partes veritatis concentrentur, ita ut illae inter se conveniant, omnie mendacium respuant, ut quod de Deo, de nobis, de operibus Dei & ejus tolerantia novimus, cum fundamento illo εὐαρμόστως conveniat & conspiret. Nempe, si Deus velit peccata condonare, quod ejus longanimitas sperare finit, quod eum non deceat ea nisi punita & expiata in Filio lio sperare, cum qua veritate omnia, quæ ad pietatem & honorem Dei conjuncta sunt, pertinent. Hoc internum & maximè γνήσιον Evangelii firmamentum est. Accedit convenientia Evangelii cum Scripturis Propheticis; quod alterum paulo magis obvium fidei firmamentum est. Sed maxima veritatis Evangelii demonstratio Pietas est, Nam scopus Dei gratiam exercentis est, ut per bona opera celebretur. In iis enim charitas Dei efficax per sanctificationem noscitur, & justitiæ Christi per fidem acceptæ obsignatio est. Oportuit enim hominibus indicare, quibus operibus Deus delectetur & rité colatur; quod studium bonorum operum ex gratia consequatur: quódque ii, qui bonis operibus carent, spem salutis nullam habeant; ii contra, qui iis in fide vera operam dant, de sua salute certi sint. Ideo Christus & Apostoli veram resipiscentiæ indolem & bonorum operum species enucleatè tradiderunt, eáque ex fide & charitate, genuinis & limpidis fontibus suis, derivarunt, & consolationem iis, qui operam illis darent, certam promiserunt; contra eorum ofores iræ reliquerunt, & eos, qui non ex vera fide, sed in speciem, ut honori coram hominibus vel quæstui suo litarent, quæ bona sunt, faciunt, ceu hypocritas ἀπέχειν τὸν μισθὸν mercedem nullam habere, imò damnationi subesse demonstrarunt. Præclarè eam in rem S. Paulus: Affulsit gratia Dei salutaris omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos, ut abnegata impietate & mundanis cupiditatibus, temperanter & juste & pie vivamus in hoc seculo, expectantes beatam illam spem & affulgentiam gloriæ magni illius Dei, & Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi; qui dedit semetipsum pro nobis, ut nos redimeret ab omni adversus legem delicto, & purificaret sibi populum peculiarem, æmulatorem bonorum operum. (non populum pigrum, inertem, languidum, somnolentum, facientem ex duplici corde, sed cum zelo, studio, serio proposito, lætitia) Hæc loquere, & mone, & redargue cum omni imperio, Tit. II. 11–15. Non convenit enim populum Christi non differre ab aliis populis, qui non sunt Christi, inprimis cùm Christi nomen ἐπικαλεῖσθαι nominare & invocare, adeóque ab omni injustitia recedere debeat. Recedat ab omni injustitia, qui nominat nomen Christi, 2. Tim. II. 19. Qui enim Christum Regem & Dominum suum nominat, eum quoque facere, quæ ipsi grata sunt, & non placere hosti ejus, oportet. Qui bona facit, Christo; qui mala, hosti ejus placet. Estque tanta doctrinæ hujus suavitas, ut nemo in Christum credens non prius sentiat propemodum, se ita esse cupere, quam doceatur, se talem esse debere. Unde S. Johannes dicit: Novum præceptum scribo vobis, quod verum est in ipso, (Christo) & in vobis (credentibus,) 1. Joh. II. 8. Nam id ipsum, quod scribi potest de voluntate Dei, fides in Christum credentibus etiam sine Scriptura dictat, corde ipsorum vice Dei dicente: Quærite faciem meam, Psal. XXVII. 8. Legem enim Dei scriptam in cordibus suis habent, Jerem. XXXI. 33. Merito igitur Christus jugum suum ζυγὸν suave, onus suum ἐλαφρὸν leve, Matth. XI. 20. & S. Johannes ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ ... βαρεῖαι præcepta ejus non gravia esse dixerunt, quia per amorem Dei, qui est à Dei regenerantus Semine, verbo & Spiritu Dei, in ipsis manente, observantur. Hæc est dilectio
units.tr: XIX. Moreover, this preaching, that eternal life is in the Son of God, and that the one who believes in him has the Son and eternal life in himself, ought to have as its accompanying demonstration and manifestation [φανέρωσιν] to every human conscience before God, Rom. XVI. 26; 2 Cor. IV. 2. For in the preaching of the Gospel the grace of God, "made manifest to us [ἐφανερωθεῖσα εἰς ἡμᾶς] in all wisdom and prudence," ought to abound toward us, Ephes. I. 8. Now conscience judges the wisdom of a doctrine by asking whether the teaching of Christ has a certain foundation, in which all parts of truth converge, so that they agree with one another and reject every lie; and whether what we know of God, of ourselves, of the works of God and of his forbearance, agrees and harmonizes [εὐαρμόστως] with that foundation. Namely: if God is willing to pardon sins, which his long-suffering allows us to hope for, it would not befit him to do so except with sins punished and expiated in the Son. With this truth are bound up all the things that pertain to the piety and honour of God. This is the internal and most genuine [γνήσιον] firmament of the Gospel. To it is added the agreement of the Gospel with the prophetic Scriptures, which is a second support of faith, somewhat more obvious. But the greatest demonstration of the truth of the Gospel is piety. For the aim of God, who exercises grace, is that he be glorified through good works. In these the efficacious love of God is recognised through sanctification, and they are the seal of the righteousness of Christ received through faith. For it was necessary to show men with what works God is delighted and duly worshipped; that the zeal for good works follows from grace; and that those who lack good works have no hope of salvation, while those who devote themselves to them in true faith may be certain of their salvation. Therefore Christ and the apostles set forth clearly the true character of repentance and the form of good works, and derived them from faith and love, their genuine and clear sources. They promised a sure consolation to those who devoted themselves to these things. On the other hand, they left the wrath of God upon those who do not act from true faith but only in outward show, doing what is good to win honour before men or to serve their own gain; these they showed to be like hypocrites, who "have their reward" [ἀπέχειν τὸν μισθὸν], having no reward at all, and indeed subject to condemnation. St Paul puts this excellently: "The saving grace of God has appeared to all men, teaching us that, renouncing impiety and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously and godly in this present age, looking for that blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from every iniquity and purify for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works" (not a lazy, sluggish, languid, sleepy people, double-hearted, but one with zeal, eagerness, earnest purpose and joy). "Speak these things, and exhort and rebuke with all authority," Tit. II. 11–15. For it is not fitting that the people of Christ should not differ from other peoples who are not Christ's, especially since they name and invoke the name of Christ [ἐπικαλεῖσθαι], and so ought to withdraw from all injustice. "Let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from injustice," 2 Tim. II. 19. For he who names Christ his King and Lord ought also to do what is pleasing to him, and not to please his enemy. He who does good pleases Christ; he who does evil pleases his enemy. And so great is the sweetness of this doctrine that no one who believes in Christ fails to feel, almost before he is taught it, that he desires to be such as he ought to be. Hence St John says: "I write to you a new commandment, which is true in him (Christ) and in you (believers)," 1 John II. 8. For what could be written about the will of God, faith itself dictates to those who believe in Christ even without Scripture, their own heart speaking in God's place: "Seek my face," Psal. XXVII. 8. "For they have the law of God written in their hearts," Jer. XXXI. 33. Rightly, therefore, Christ calls his yoke [ζυγὸν] easy and his burden [ἐλαφρὸν] light, Matth. XI. 20; and St John says that his commandments [ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ] are not grievous [βαρεῖαι], because they are kept through the love of God, which abides in those born of God's seed, word and Spirit. This is the love

units.la: Dei, ut præcepta ipsius observemus. Et præcepta ipsius gravia non sunt. Quia omne quod ex Deo genitum est, vincit mundum. Et hæc est victoria, quæ vicit mundum, fides vestra, 1. Joh. V. 3, 4. Præterquam quòd etiam timorem mortis, terrorem & accusationem peccati, & molesta illa rituum atque judiciorum singularium opera Evangelium tollit, & pro timore charitatem consummatissimam per lætitiam Spiritus S. introducit.
units.tr: of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not grievous. For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that overcomes the world: your faith. 1 John V. 3, 4. Moreover, the Gospel also removes the fear of death, the terror and accusation of sin, and those troublesome works of rites and particular judgments, and in place of fear it introduces most perfect love through the joy of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: XX. Hæc cùm ita sint, manifestum est, Pelagianorum, Pontificiorum, Socinianorum, etc. Legem Evangelii in novam Legem operum convertunt: tum eos, qui ab Evangelio resipiscentiam, amorem Dei, bona opera secludunt, Evangelio ipsi, & Novo sub eo Testamento, ejusque Legi cladem machinari. Illi Pelagiani veteres & novi, Pontificii inprimis & Socinians Evangelium proprio & speciali significatu doctrinam operum, gradu perfectionis à Lege distinctam definiunt. Nempe illi Evangelium à Lege non genere doctrinæ, sed gradu distinguunt, asserentes, Legem esse doctrinam operum imperfectam, Evangelium perfectam: illam semen & radicem, hoc arborem ipsam complecti. Qui capitalis Evangelii devoratorius error est, quia Evangelium non obnuntiatio est rei scævæ, strictioris, quàm quod in Lege requiritur, debiti, sed annuntiatio rei lætæ, & ... bonum verbum, Psal.
