XLV. 2. de gratia Dei salutifera, per quam peccata & debita omnia adversus Legem commissa, & sanguine Christi expiata delentur, & gratiosè condonantur. Ne timete. Ecce ego annuntio vobis gaudium magnum, quod continget omni populo, quod natus vobis hodie est Salvator, qui est Christus Dominus, in civitate Davidis, Luc. II. 10, 11. Paulus separatus in Evangelium Dei, de Filio ejus, &c. Rom. I. 1, 3. Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti: Justitia enim in eo revelatur ex fide in fidem, ibid. v. 16, 17. Sine Lege justitia Dei manifestata est, testimonium habens ex Lege & Prophetis. Justitia verò Dei per fidem in Jesum Christum, &c. ibid. III. 21, 22. Ideo hanc gratiam inter & Legem operum perpetua antithesis est. Per Christum nobis remissio peccatorum annuntiatur; & ab omnibus, quibus non potuistis per Legem Mosis justificari, in hoc omnis credens justificatur, Act. XIII. 38, 39. Justificamur gratis (sine merito operum) gratia ejus, per redemptionem Jesu Christi, quem Deus præstituit Propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ejus propter remissionem peccatorum præcedentium, &c. Ubi igitur gloriatio est? Exclusa est. Per quam Legem? Operum? Non, sed per Legem fidei, Rom. III. 24. &c. Si ex gratia, non amplius ex operibus. Alias gratia non amplius est gratia. Si ex operibus, non ex gratia. Alias opus non amplius est opus, ibid. XI. 6. Salvavit nos vocantis vocatione sancta, non secundum opera, sed secundum propriam propositum, & gratiam, quæ nobis datur in Christo Jesu ante tempora sæcularia, quæ manifestata est per apparitionem Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi, qui mortem quidem abolevit, vitam autem & incorruptibilitatem illustravit per Evangelium, 2. Tim. I. 9, 10. Cùmque justitiarii plerique nulli diffiteri possint, quin justitia, quam fideles in hac vita præstant, imperfecta, & numeris suis neutiquam absoluta sit, quid absurdius fingi potest, quàm quod illi tenentur, dari justitiam ex imperfecta observatione ne perfectiorum præceptorum? Ac ne quidem justitia operum, quæ remissione peccatorum indiget, qualem illi tuentur, vel justos facit, vel vera justitia est. Justitia enim operum in observatione perfecta mandatorum, at remissio peccatorum in condonatione defectus observationis illius consistit. Accedit, quòd ea propria Evangelii conditio est, quòd vitam sub conditione solius fidei, non operum, pollicetur, Joh. III.16. Marc. XVI.16. ne quis nisi in Deo glorietur, 1.Cor.I.31. Pugnat autem cum ingenio fidei, accipere præcepta ad justitiam, & non credere, Deum in Christo esse justitiam nostram. Neque per ea præcepta amor Dei, qualis in fide, saltem non sine fide est, efficitur, aut odium Dei, quo peccator naturaliter laborat, extirpatur. Si enim caro concupiscit contra legem imperfectiorem, ex qua nunquam de salute sua certus esse poterit, concupiscet. Neque vel voluntas aliquid externum dicendi, faciendi vel patiendi ad hoc, ut Deo id imputes, aut in eo apud Deum glorieris, amor Dei, qui in solo Deo deliciatur, sed cordis duplicis voluntas est: vel per doctrinam operum Deus peccatori amabilis reddi potest. Quamobrem doctrina illa hypocritas, superbos, utpote in justitia propria gloriantes, Legis Dei corruptores & extenuatores, denique peccati sui palliatores efficit; & toti Evangelio, quod Christum salutis causam, & credentes in ipsum, in eodem ad bona opera creatos, ut in iis ambulent, & ad vitam æternam per sanctificationem Spiritus perveniant; & justitiam per fidem in merito ejus fundatam docet, contrariatur. Cúmque Evangelium fit potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom.I.16. nec non ministerium vitæ & Spiritus, 2.Cor.III.6.8. manifestum est, illud sensu proprio non esse doctrinam operum, quia tum potentia Dei sese non in operante, sed in credente de fide in fidem exerit, & ad justitiam, quam Deus propter Christum donat, non quam operibus suis acquirit, Rom.I.16. efficax est: tum ministerium Spiritus, & vitæ ministerio literæ & mortis, ad quam doctrina operum, à Spiritus S. gratia seporata, refertur, opponitur, 2.Cor.III.6.7. Neque illud de nihilo est, quòd doctrina operum pro operibus mercedem debitam, saltem ex pacto, tribuit; Evangelium contra nec mercedem pro operibus, sed absque operibus tribuit, Rom.IV.4.5.6. eámque prorsus indebitam & gratuitam, ibid. & V I.23. Denique de perfectiore justitia operum sub Evangelio quàm sub Lege prædicata supra profligavimus. Cùm in Decalogo præcepta sint, quæ qui facit, in iis vivit, Levit. XVIII.5. Ezech.XX.11. perfectiora à Christo annuntiari non potuerunt, quia non dantur præcepta alia atque alia, in quibus homo vivat. Hæc enim, utpote in quibus homo vivat. Hæc enim, utpote in quibus imago Dei consistit, eadem semper sunt, neque omnino variari possunt. Ideo Scripturæ illa à placitis, quæ mutari possunt, & in quibus non est justitia, distinguit.
units.tr: XX. Since these things stand as they do, it is clear that the Pelagians, Papists, Socinians and others who turn the Law of the Gospel into a new law of works, and who exclude from the Gospel repentance, the love of God and good works, are plotting the ruin of the Gospel itself and of the New Covenant under it, and of its Law. The old and new Pelagians, and above all the Papists and Socinians, define the Gospel, in its proper and special sense, as the doctrine of works, distinguished from the Law by a degree of perfection. They do not distinguish the Gospel from the Law by the kind of doctrine but by degree, asserting that the Law is an imperfect doctrine of works and the Gospel a perfect one, the Law embracing the seed and root and the Gospel the tree itself. This is the devouring error at the heart of the Gospel, because the Gospel is not an announcement of a harsh and stricter debt than what is required in the Law, but an announcement of good news, and a good word, Ps. 45:2, concerning the saving grace of God, by which all sins and debts committed against the Law are blotted out through the blood of Christ and freely forgiven. Fear not, for behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people: for unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord, Luke 2:10, 11. Paul, separated unto the gospel of God, concerning his Son, etc., Rom. 1:1, 3. The gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; for therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith, ibid. vv. 16, 17. But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ, etc., ibid. 3:21, 22. Hence there is a perpetual antithesis between this grace and the Law of works. Through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins; and by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses, Acts 13:38, 39. Being justified freely (without the merit of works) by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, for the remission of sins that are past, etc. Where is boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith, Rom. 3:24, etc. If by grace, then it is no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if of works, then it is no more grace: otherwise work is no more work, ibid. 11:6. Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began, but is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel, 2 Tim. 1:9, 10. Since most of the justiciaries cannot deny that the righteousness which the faithful render in this life is imperfect and by no means complete in its parts, what more absurd fiction can be devised than their claim that righteousness is given from an imperfect observance of the more perfect precepts? Nor does the righteousness of works, which needs the remission of sins, as they maintain it, either make men righteous or is true righteousness. For the righteousness of works consists in the perfect observance of the commandments, but the remission of sins consists in the pardon of the defect of that observance. Moreover, it is the peculiar condition of the Gospel that it promises life under the condition of faith alone, not of works, John 3:16, Mark 16:16, so that no one may glory except in God, 1 Cor. 1:31. But it is contrary to the nature of faith to receive precepts for righteousness and not to believe that God is our righteousness in Christ. Nor through those precepts is the love of God, such as is found in faith, or at least not without faith, brought about, nor is the hatred of God, under which the sinner naturally labours, rooted out. For if the flesh lusts against the more imperfect law, from which it can never be certain of its salvation, it will lust. Nor does the will to say, do or suffer anything outward, in order that you may impute it to God or glory in it before God, constitute the love of God, which delights in God alone; rather it is the will of a double heart. Either through the doctrine of works God can be made lovable to the sinner, or not. Therefore that doctrine makes hypocrites, proud men who glory in their own righteousness, corrupters and belittlers of the Law of God, and finally covers over their sin; and it is opposed to the whole Gospel, which teaches that Christ is the cause of salvation, and that believers in him are created in him unto good works, that they should walk in them, and attain eternal life through the sanctification of the Spirit, and that righteousness is founded through faith in his merit. Since the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, Rom. 1:16, and also the ministry of life and of the Spirit, 2 Cor. 3:6, 8, it is clear that in its proper sense it is not the doctrine of works: for the power of God then does not manifest itself in the one who works but in the believer, from faith to faith, and it is effective for the righteousness which God gives on account of Christ, not for that which a man acquires by his own works, Rom. 1:16. Then too the ministry of the Spirit is set against the ministry of the letter and of death, to which the doctrine of works, separated from the grace of the Holy Spirit, is referred, 2 Cor. 3:6, 7. Nor is it without reason that the doctrine of works assigns a due reward for works, at least by covenant, whereas the Gospel gives no reward for works but gives apart from works, Rom. 4:4, 5, 6, and that reward wholly undue and gratuitous, ibid., and 6:23. Finally, we have above refuted the claim that a more perfect righteousness of works is preached under the Gospel than under the Law. Since the precepts in the Decalogue are such that whoever does them shall live in them, Lev. 18:5, Ezek. 20:11, more perfect ones could not have been announced by Christ, because no different precepts are given in which man may live. For these, since in them the image of God consists, are always the same and cannot be varied at all. Therefore Scripture distinguishes those precepts from the decrees which can be changed and in which there is no righteousness.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Est sanè Evangelium Lex, Jerem. XXXI.33. Rom.III.27. VIII.2. Gal.VI.2. Jac.I.25. sed non Lex operum, verùm πίστεως fidei, legi operum opposita, Rom.III.27. Lex Spiritus vitæ in Christo Jesu, ibid. VIII.2. quia sicut ipsritus vitæ palmitis in vite vivit: ita Lex Spiritus vitæ Christi, seu Christi justitia nobis donata, & per fidem apprehensa, ceu Lex quædam in nobis efficit vitam Christi, ut in eo, ceu membra in capite vivamus: Lex perfecta libertatis, Jac.I.25. quia Lex fidei & charitatis τελειότης perfecta voluntas Dei, Rom.XII.2. omnem hominem perficiens, Deóque similem reddens, nos à servitute non peccati duntaxat, sed etiam legali liberat, ut jam nobis ceu liberis & liberatis agere liceat.
units.tr: The Gospel is indeed a law (Jer. 31:33; Rom. 3:27; 8:2; Gal. 6:2; Jas. 1:25), but not the law of works. It is the law of faith [πίστεως], set over against the law of works (Rom. 3:27). It is "the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus" (Rom. 8:2), because just as the life of the Spirit lives in the vine's branch, so the law of the Spirit of Christ's life, that is, the righteousness of Christ given to us and apprehended by faith, works in us as a kind of law, so that we live the life of Christ in him, as members living in the head. It is "the perfect law of liberty" (Jas. 1:25), because the law of faith and love is [τελειότης] the perfect will of God (Rom. 12:2). It makes every man perfect and renders him like God, and it frees us not only from the servitude of sin but also from the legal kind, so that we may now act as free and liberated persons.

units.la: Eorundem argumenta ad partes revocantur.
units.tr: The arguments of the same authors are traced back to their proper sides.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Oppositus huic error Libertinorum aliorumque est, refispiscentiam & bona opera ab Evangelio secludentium, quem supra §. 16. confiximus. gi opponitur, solius fidei in Christum stipulationem contineat, neque omnino refipiscentiam, prout hæc fidei opponitur, vel bona opera postulet, tamen quatenus cum Lege componitur, atque hæc ei subordinatur, refipiscentiam & bona opera minimè dedignatur, sed in sinum contuberniumque suum ultro recipit. Cum enim Evangelium κυρίως sit concio fidei, & ad fidem sine contritione & dolore perveniri non potest, atque insuper fides charitatem ἀδιάκριτον comitem habeat, neque omnino sine charitate & bonis operibus operosa, vera & sincera sit, hinc in praxi & usu Legem, uti illa opera non ut causam vitæ, sed ut normam sanctimoniæ; gratitudinis & conformitatis cum Christo præscribit, asciscit, ejusque hunc in finem non dominio, sed ministerio utitur. Unde denominatione à potiori facta totum necessariæ ad salutem peccatoris doctrinæ genus Evangelium appellatur: Licet fides ab eo dominante, resipiscentia verò fidei opposita & nova obedientia à Lege, quam sic Evangelium associat, ministrante præscribatur. Neque arduum est, significatus illos vocis Evangelii ex propriis ejus objectis & effectis discernere. Nam proprie dicti Evangelii objecta sunt gratia Dei, meritum Christi, fides: effecta verò justificatio, tranquillitas conscientiæ peccatoris, gaudium in Spiritu S. Joh. I. 17. Rom. I. 16. 17. II. 21. 22. V. 1. Gal. III. 25. Hæc ergo propriam Evangelii naturam & significationem declarant: reliqua, puta agnitio peccati, desperatio de se & viribus suis, proftratio, timor pœnæ seorsim consideratus, adeòque contritio, quatenus illa merè legalis est, & delineatio veræ sanctitatis & amoris Dei & proximi, quibus Evangelium carere nequit, à Lege Evangelio ministrante proficiscuntur. Atque hæc sic distincta & cum grano salis intellecta controversiam Augustanos inter ipsos, & ab his nobis motam de concione Evangelii, an illa fidei duntaxat, an simul fidei & pœnitentiæ sit, minuere apta nata sunt. Nam nec pœnitentia, qualis in Evangelio exigitur, cum amore Dei & fiducia conjuncta, legalis esse potest: & quæ in pœnitentia fidei non sunt, vel legalia sunt, quatenus cum fide non junguntur; vel Evangelica sunt, quatenus cum fide conjuncta à Lege quidem, sed non dominante, verum Evangelio inserviente proveniunt, & usus ipse Legis salutaris non à Lege, sed ab Evangelio proficiscitur.
units.tr: Opposed to this is the error of the Libertines and others, who exclude repentance and good works from the Gospel, which we refuted above in §16. Although the Gospel, as opposed to the law, contains only the promise of faith in Christ, and does not by any means demand repentance as opposed to faith, or good works, nevertheless, insofar as it is set alongside the Law and the Law is made subordinate to it, it does not disdain repentance and good works, but willingly receives them into its bosom and fellowship. For since the Gospel properly [κυρίως] is the preaching of faith, and faith cannot be reached without contrition and sorrow, and moreover faith has love [ἀδιάκριτον] as its inseparable companion, and cannot be true and sincere without being active through love and good works, therefore in practice and use the Law prescribes those works, not as the cause of life, but as the rule of holiness, of gratitude and of conformity to Christ. The Gospel takes the Law to this end, using it not as lord but as servant. Hence, by naming the whole teaching necessary for the sinner's salvation from its principal element, the whole is called the Gospel, although faith is prescribed by the Gospel as ruling, and repentance (which is opposed to faith) and the new obedience are prescribed by the Law as serving, which the Gospel thus joins to itself. Nor is it difficult to distinguish those senses of the word "Gospel" from its proper objects and effects. For the proper objects of the Gospel are the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and faith; its effects are justification, the tranquillity of the sinner's conscience, and joy in the Holy Spirit (John 1:17; Rom. 1:16, 17; 2:21, 22; 5:1; Gal. 3:25). These therefore declare the proper nature and meaning of the Gospel. The rest, namely the recognition of sin, despair of oneself and one's own strength, prostration, fear of punishment considered apart, and so contrition, insofar as it is merely legal, and the outlining of true holiness and of the love of God and neighbour, which the Gospel cannot do without, come from the Law serving the Gospel. These distinctions, when rightly drawn and understood with a grain of salt, are fitted to diminish the controversy among the Augustana men themselves, and raised by them against us, over the preaching of the Gospel, whether it is of faith alone or of faith and repentance together. For repentance, as it is required in the Gospel, joined with love of God and trust, cannot be legal. And those things in repentance which are not of faith are either legal, insofar as they are not joined with faith, or evangelical, insofar as they arise, joined with faith, from the Law indeed, but not as ruling; rather as serving the Gospel. The salutary use of the Law itself comes not from the Law but from the Gospel.

units.la: XXIII. Hallucinatio etiam gravis est Socinianorum & Remonstrantium, qui Fidem & Refipiscentiam conditionem proprie dictam Evangelii, viribus nostris præstandam faciunt; eò quòd hæc fœderis ratio sit, ut fœderatorum unus stipuletur officium, promittátque bonum; alter officium ad promissionem obtinendam restipuletur.
units.tr: XXIII. The Socinians and Remonstrants also fall into a serious error, who make faith and repentance, properly speaking, the condition of the Gospel, to be performed by our own powers. They argue that this is the nature of a covenant: one of the covenanting parties stipulates a duty and promises a good; the other stipulates a duty to obtain the promise.

units.la: Sed fidem & refipiscentiam partem esse hæreditatis morte Christi nobis acquisitæ, satis constat, & pluribus etiam Loc. XIX. 26. & 88. confirmavimus. Non potest igitur esse conditio proprie dicta, de bono & peculio nostro præstanda. Neque ideo stipulatio & mandatum fidei deest, vel mandatum credendi & resipiscendi fidem & refipiscentiam in conditionem proprie dictam, viribus nostris implendam, commutat, sed potius medium illud est, quo Deus fidem ac pœnitentiam in hæredibus efficit. Et hactenus Evangelium à Lege differt, quòd hæc vitam sub conditione obedientiæ viribus propriis præstandæ pollicetur: illud salutem, & quicquid viribus suis acquirere peccator, ad salutem necessarium nequit, nobis addicit in Christo, Sponsore nostro.
units.tr: But it is sufficiently clear that faith and repentance are part of the inheritance acquired for us by the death of Christ, which we have also confirmed at greater length in Loc. XIX §§26 and 88. Therefore they cannot be a condition properly so called, to be performed from our own goods and resources. Nor, for that reason, is the stipulation and command of faith lacking, nor does the command to believe and repent turn faith and repentance into a condition properly so called, to be fulfilled by our powers. Rather, faith and repentance are the means by which God produces them in the heirs. And in this respect the Gospel differs from the Law: the Law promises life under the condition of obedience to be performed by one's own powers, while the Gospel assigns us, in Christ our Surety, salvation and whatever the sinner cannot acquire by his own powers and yet needs for salvation.

units.la: XXIV. Sicut Lex Evangelii à Lege operum toto Coelo dissidet: ita nec consilia à præceptis fidei vel operum disparata commendat. Impiè enim Pontificii Consiliorum nomine bona quædam opera à Christo nobis non imperata, sed demonstrata, non mandata, sed commendata obtrudunt. Quæ etiam καθ' ἐξοχὴν Evangelica & perfectionis Evangelicæ consilia appellare non erubescunt, eò quod in Evangelio, tanquam Lege perfectiore proponantur, suadeantur, & ad majorem sanctitatis perfectionem omnes eos, qui speciali voto ad eorum observantiam se obstringunt, provehant.
units.tr: XXIV. Just as the Law of the Gospel is utterly at odds with the law of works, so it does not commend counsels as separate from the precepts of faith or works. For the Papists impiously foist upon us, under the name of Counsels, certain good works not commanded by Christ but shown, not enjoined but commended. They are not ashamed to call these, by preeminence [καθ' ἐξοχὴν], the evangelical counsels and counsels of evangelical perfection, because they are set forth in the Gospel as a more perfect law, are recommended, and urge all those who bind themselves by a special vow to observe them toward a greater perfection of holiness.

units.la: Et hactenus etiam illa à præceptis seu operibus ad salutem necessariis differre pertendunt, quòd difficiliora his & perfectiora sint, non promiscuè in quosvis, sed in certi duntaxat ordinis homines cadant, observantiam non necessariam, sed arbitrariam habeant, & observata præmium amplius, aureolam videlicet: neglecta verò pœnam nullam promereantur. De numero consiliorum ejusmodi ipsimet consultores discrepant. Alii enim ex concione Christi in monte habita duodecim: alii plura vel pauciora, omnes ferè præcipua tria. Continentiam, obedientiam & paupertatem, iisque superstructa totidem vota continentiæ perpetuæ, obedientiæ regularis, & paupertatis spontaneæ, Monachis eximia faciunt.
units.tr: And so they also contend that these counsels differ from the precepts or works necessary for salvation in that they are more difficult and more perfect; that they do not fall upon all indiscriminately but only upon men of a certain order; that their observance is not necessary but optional; and that if they are observed a greater reward is earned, namely a crown (aureola), while if they are neglected no punishment is merited. The counsellors themselves disagree about how many such counsels there are. Some take twelve from Christ's sermon on the mount; others more or fewer; nearly all count three principal ones: continence, obedience and poverty. Built upon these, they make for the Monks three distinguished vows of perpetual continence, of regular obedience, and of voluntary poverty.

units.la: Fatemur equidem ultro, dari opera quædam indifferentia, quæ cujusque arbitrio subjiciuntur, 1 Cor. VII. 25. 26. Act. V. 4. quin & in verbo Dei extare consilia de rebus ejusmodi indifferentibus, quæ à præceptis non immerito distinguuntur, 1 Cor. VII. 26. 1 Tim. V. 14. Sed eadem consilia naturam suam generalem <bl>ἀδιάφορον</bl> illam exuunt, & ex specialibus quibusdam causis atque circumstantiis, quæ rem per se liberam aliquando necessariam huic vel illi personæ, in hac vel illa circumstantia efficiunt, in præcepta non quidem communia & absoluta, nisi quantum ad <bl>ἐτοιμασίαν</bl> seu præparationem animi, sed personalia & conditionata, ratione ætus commutant.
units.tr: We readily grant that there are certain indifferent actions, which are left to each person's judgement (1 Cor. 7:25, 26; Acts 5:4). Indeed, counsels about such indifferent matters are found in God's Word, and they are not unjustly distinguished from precepts (1 Cor. 7:26; 1 Tim. 5:14). But these counsels lay aside their general indifferent nature, and, through certain special causes and circumstances which make a thing free in itself at some time necessary for this or that person in this or that circumstance, they change in their action from counsels into precepts that are not common and absolute (except as regards the preparation [ἐτοιμασίαν] or readiness of mind), but personal and conditional.

units.la: Quomodo cùm liberum, & nulli communi præcepto illigatum sit, uxorem ducere, stipendium accipere pro labore, ob certam causam & in certa circumstantia huic vel illi non nubendi, & ministerium <bl>διδασκάλου</bl> obeundi necessitas injungitur. Cæterùm, qui rei hujus cardo est, observationem consiliorum, quatenus in genere sine specialibus circumstantiis consideratur, per se Deo gratam esse, vel majus etiam præmium mereri; vel consilia Pontificiorum, quæ & quatenus ex Verbo Dei proponuntur, non esse ullo modo præcepta; vel esse perfectionis, sive status perfectionis, in Christianismo, vel esse meritoria & supererogatoria, hoc est, majoris meriti & mercedis, quàm sit obedientia Divinorum mandatorum, vel denique
units.tr: Thus, although it is free, and not bound by any common precept, to marry, or to take wages for labour, yet for a certain reason and in a certain circumstance it is laid upon this or that person not to marry, or the necessity of undertaking the ministry of a teacher [διδασκάλου] is imposed. But the crux of the matter is this: whether the observance of counsels, considered in general without special circumstances, is pleasing to God in itself or merits a greater reward; or whether the counsels of the Papists, which and insofar as they are proposed from the Word of God, are in no way precepts; or whether they belong to perfection, or to a state of perfection, in Christianity; or whether they are meritorious and supererogatory, that is, of greater merit and reward than the obedience of God's commandments; or finally

units.la: {y} Evangelium nulla consilia à præceptis distinguat. que vota illa Monastica, maximè perpetua, & irrevocabilia, quæ Ecclesiæ sentina & Plutonius sunt, inde deduci & stabiliri pernegamus.
units.tr: whether the Gospel distinguishes no counsels from precepts. We flatly deny that those monastic vows, especially the perpetual and irrevocable ones, which are the sink of the Church and its Pluto, are deduced and established from there.

units.la: XXV. Etenim quæ illi consilia Evangelica ex verbo Dei recensent, proprie non consilia, sed præcepta sunt, alia quidem in genere, alia in specie, alia directè & per se, alia obliquè & per accidens, sive propter aliud. Nam dilectio inimici, patientia injuriæ, datio mutui, fuga abnegationis peccandi, abnegatio sui, castitas, voluntaria paupertas, aliáque, quæ consiliorum Evangelicorum nomine venditant, verbo Dei tanquam necessaria officia præcipiuntur. Dico vobis, diligite inimicos vestros, Matth. V. 44. Si esuriverit inimicus tuus, ciba ipsum, &c. Rom. XII. 20. Dico vobis: Ne resistite improbo, &c. Matth. V. 39. Nemini malum pro malo reddite, Rom. XII. 17. Petenti da, & ab eo, qui à te mutuum petierit, ne te averte, Matth. V. 42. Si quis potest me venire voluerit, abneget se ipsum, &c. ibid. XVI. 24. Habemus libertatem circumducendi uxorem sororem; sed non usus sum quoquam eorum. Præstat enim mihi mori, quam ut gloriatio mea irrita fit, 1. Cor. IX. 5. 15. Quisquis se non abdicaverit facultatibus suis, (cùm id gloria Dei & salus ejus postulat) non potest discipulus meus fieri, Luc. XIV. 33. In his omnibus non libera hominis optio conceditur, sed in casu, in quo talia exerceri Verbum Dei jubet, necessitas exercendi diserto mandato imponitur. Tum consilia, quæ vocant, Evangelica, non sunt Evangelii sive proprie & stricte, sive latius ita dicti. Non proprie & stricte dicti, quia sic Evangelium non est nisi doctrina fidei; hæc autem sive universa, sive singula non circa fidem, sed circa mores versantur. Non late dicti, quia illud tum fidei, tum morum præcepta & officia præscribit, non consilia commendat. Accedit, quòd omne bonum opus ad moralem perfectionem hominis pertinet, & pars quædam imaginis Divinæ est. Nullum ergo opus bonum demonstratum, non imperatum, commendatum, non mandatum, quale consilium illi faciunt, datur. Moralis enim perfectio & imago Dei non nudè demonstratur & commendatur, sed imperatur. Estote perfecti, ut Pater vester, qui est in Cœlis, perfectus est, Matth. V. 48. Sancti estote, quia sanctus sum ego, Jehova vester, Levit. XIX. 2. Quod reliquum est, fratres, quæcunque sunt vera, veneranda, justa, pura, amabilia, boni nominis, si quæ virtus, si quæ laus, hæc reputate, Phil. IV. 8. Quin & bonorum operum summa verbis Legis Mosaicæ comprehenditur, sic sancientis: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, ex tota anima tua, & ex omni cogitatione tua, Matth. XXII. 37. 38. Quibus verbis non inferioralis gradus amoris sic præcipitur, ut superior sit consilii, quæ Bellarmini glossa est, sed amor Dei in omni sua latitudine & mensura, ipso Thoma fatente, nullum gradum dilectionis esse in consilio, sed omnes in præcepto, quatenus hoc præceptum continet & medium & finem, & nihil potest addi ad dilectionem, quæ ut finis sine mensura appetatur. De quo alibi plura. Vel igitur Consilia ad perfectionem, sanctitatem, imaginem Dei in homine & amorem Dei pertinent, vel non. Si pertinent, præcepta, non demonstrata duntaxat & commendata sunt; quia perfectio, sanctitas, imago Dei & amor Dei, præcepta utique singula, non demonstrata duntaxat & commendata sunt.
units.tr: XXV. Indeed, the so-called evangelical counsels that they list from the Word of God are not properly counsels but precepts, some in kind and some in particular, some directly and in themselves, others indirectly and by accident, or on account of something else. For love of enemies, patience under injury, lending, refusal to sin, self-denial, chastity, voluntary poverty, and the others that they peddle under the name of evangelical counsels, are enjoined by the Word of God as necessary duties. "I say to you, love your enemies" (Matt. 5:44). "If your enemy is hungry, feed him," etc. (Rom. 12:20). "I say to you, do not resist the evil one," etc. (Matt. 5:39). "Repay no one evil for evil" (Rom. 12:17). "Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you" (Matt. 5:42). "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself," etc. (ibid. 16:24). "Have we not the right to take along a sister as wife? But I have used none of these rights, for it is better for me to die than to have my boasting made void" (1 Cor. 9:5, 15). "Whoever does not renounce all his possessions (since the glory of God and his salvation require it) cannot be my disciple" (Luke 14:33). In all these matters, no free choice is granted to a man; rather, where the Word of God commands such things to be practised, the necessity of practising them is imposed by an express command. Then, the so-called evangelical counsels are not of the Gospel, either properly and strictly so called, or in the wider sense of the term. Not in the proper and strict sense, because in that sense the Gospel is nothing but the doctrine of faith; and this doctrine, whether taken as a whole or in its parts, is concerned not with faith but with morals. Nor in the wider sense, because the Gospel then prescribes precepts and duties both of faith and of morals; it does not commend counsels. Moreover, every good work pertains to the moral perfection of man and is a part of the image of God. Therefore no good work is set forth that is not commanded, commended but not enjoined, of the kind that those counsels present. For moral perfection and the image of God are not merely displayed and commended, but commanded. "Be perfect, as your Father who is in heaven is perfect" (Matt. 5:48). "Be holy, for I am holy, Jehovah your God" (Lev. 19:2). "Finally, brethren, whatever is true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, of good report, if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think on these things" (Phil. 4:8). Indeed, the sum of good works is comprehended in the words of the Mosaic Law, which thus ordains: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind" (Matt. 22:37–38). By these words a lower degree of love is not so enjoined that a higher degree is left to counsel (this is Bellarmine's gloss); rather, the love of God in its whole extent and measure, as Thomas himself admits, contains no degree of love in counsel, but all degrees in precept, inasmuch as this precept contains both the means and the end, and nothing can be added to love, which is sought as an end without measure. More on this elsewhere. Either, then, the counsels pertain to the perfection, holiness, image of God in man, and love of God, or they do not. If they pertain to these, they are not merely displayed and commended but are precepts; for perfection, holiness, the image of God, and the love of God are surely each commanded, not merely displayed and commended.

units.la: Si non pertinent, nec bona opera, nec omnino laudabilia, sed ἀνπλήξ rejicienda sunt. Et in Deo quidem consilium proprie dictum non magis quàm Deitatis pluralitas locum habet. Quelecunque vero locum in eo habet, à præcepto distingui non potest, quia non aliter consulit, quàm ut ἐχων ἐξουσίαν habens potestatem, authoritatem jubendi. Quomodo consilium quodvis cum authoritate conjunctum præcepti rationem habet. Christus enim Angelo Laodicensium dicens: Consilium do tibi, ut emas à me aurum igne examinatum, ut dives fias; vestimenta alba, ne manifesta fiat nuditas tua, & collyrio inunges oculos, ut videas, Apoc. III. 18. sic consulit, ut justisse censendus sit, quia non parens consilio pauper, pudendus, cæcus fit. Consilium nempe Dei voluntas Dei est. At voluntate Dei, tanquam Lege, omnes tenemur. Hæc est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra, ut abstineatis à scortatione, &c. 1. Thess. IV. 3. 4. &c. Differentiæ porro, quas consilia inter & præcepta illi constituunt, fictiæ sunt. Ratione materiæ præcepti materiam faciliorem, bonam, naturæ principiis innixam: at consilii difficiliorem, meliorem, & naturæ principiis sublimiorem faciunt. Quæ mali commatis sunt, cùm nec difficilius sit cœlibatum colere, si continentiæ donum habueris, quàm in conjugio vivere; nec melior sit, si de bonitate morali sermo sit, cœlibatus quàm conjugii status; nec naturæ principiis minùs ille quàm hic congruat. Par ratio est subjecti, quod in præceptis promiscuè omnes, in consiliis solos eos, qui ad statum perfectionis aspirant, faciunt. Omnes enim ad id, quod melius est, tenentur, quia ad perfectionem & summum gradum amoris omnes tenentur, & imperfectio ejus, qui in secundis consistit, in vitio est. At consilium melius aliquid præscribere pertendunt; Sed & pleraque illa, quæ consilia illi appellant, velut abnegatio sui, patientia injuriæ &c. omnes singulosque homines devinciunt. Sunt etiam præcepta, quæ non omnibus præscribuntur. Alia enim viris, alia mulieribus, alia senioribus, alia adolescentioribus imperantur, Ephes. V. 22. &c. Col. III. 18. &c. Tit. II. 2. 3. 4. &c. Excepta tamen speciali vocatione, quæ præcepti; non consilii rationem habet, nihil in Evangelio traditur, quod ad unum Christianorum ordinem pertineat. Sicut non varium & multiplex Christianorum genus est. Omnes estis filii Dei per fidem in Christum Jesum. Non est Judæus vel Græcus, servus vel liber, Gal. III. 26. &c. Neque certius est discrimen ratione formæ, quòd præceptum vi sua obliget, consilium liberæ observantiæ sit. Si enim ea consilii excellentia est, ut melius, justius, sanctius aliquid præscribat, quàm præceptum, tum vi insitæ illius pulchritudinis, bonitatis, sanctitatis omnes ad observantiam obligabit. Nam etiam δοκιμάζειν τὰ διαφέροντα præstantiora explorare, adeóque etiam sectari jubemur, Rom. II. 18. Phil. I. 10. Neque etiam liberum cuiquam vel solutum est, se ipsum non abnegare, inimicum non diligere, injurias patienter non ferre, Christum non sequi, Deo ad cœlibatum vel paupertatem vocanti non parére. Denique & illud, quod ratione finis seu effectus obtrudunt, discrimen, juxta quod præceptum observatum præmium, violatum pœnam; consilium verò observatum ma-jus jus præmium, seu aureolam, neglectum poenam nullam, sed solius aureolæ jacturam post se trahat; fictitium totum est; quia consilia Dei ipsius, cum authoritate quippe Divina conjuncta, impune non negligi, jam supra ostendimus. Saltem poena damni, eos, qui recta, imo Divina consilia aspernantur, manet. A poena autem damni poena sensus ἀιδιάστως & est. Taceo hypocrisin eorum, qui cum Legem, cujus quàm consiliorum opera impletu faciliora esse scisc-unt, perfectè nec impleant, nec implere possint, ad difficiliora tamen factu se offerunt; & plura se facere posse, quàm quibus faciendis obstricti sunt, atque ultra gradum amoris Dei ab eodem præscripti se eniti posse, jactant; & officia, velut Deo indebita, cum toti nexu & mancupio Dei sint, crepant, Deóque velut aureolarum debitori imputant. Non ergo consilia hæc Evangelicæ perfectionis sunt, sed יצר רשעים consilia improborum, Psal.I.1. & præcepta hominum condocefacta, Esaj.XXIX.13. hoc est, cogitationes hominum irregenitorum, & Divinæ justitiæ expertium de ratione obliterandi peccatum, & placendi Deo. Nam pro præcepto fidei & poenitentiæ placuit inimicis Dei blandiloquis ea ratio, ut Deo imponerent & mentirentur. Cui hypocrisi doctrina de Consiliis Evangelicis sic succollare debuit, ut per eam sub specie religionis augendæ homines à Lege Dei, Christo & vera resipiscentia ad falsa merita, ad aliud χάραγμα, signaturam aliam, Divinæ Legis χαράγματα adulterium, ad falsas satisfactiones, ipsámque ὑπόστασιν abduci possent. Et esse dogma illud de Consiliis occultiorem quandam ὑπόφυσιν dogmatis Encratitarum sive Apostolicorum & Pelagianorum, ex iis, quæ Bellarminus de Mon. cap.8. habet, colligere est.
units.tr: If they do not pertain to these, then they are neither good works nor laudable at all, but are to be rejected. In God, indeed, a counsel properly so called has no more place than plurality of Godhead does. Whatever counsel does have a place in him cannot be distinguished from a precept, because he counsels in no other way than as one who has authority [ἔχων ἐξουσίαν], the power to command. Thus any counsel joined with authority has the character of a precept. For Christ, speaking to the angel of the Laodiceans, says: "I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, that you may become rich; and white garments, that your nakedness may not be exposed; and anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see" (Rev. 3:18). He so counsels that he must be judged to have commanded, because the one who does not obey the counsel of a parent becomes poor, shameful, and blind. Indeed, the counsel of God is the will of God. And we are all bound by the will of God as by a Law: "This is the will of God, your sanctification, that you abstain from fornication," etc. (1 Thess. 4:3–4). Moreover, the distinctions that they draw between counsels and precepts are fictitious. With respect to the matter, they make the matter of the precept easier, good, and based on the principles of nature, but the matter of the counsel more difficult, better, and more sublime than the principles of nature. These are the words of a bad sort, since it is no more difficult to cultivate celibacy, if you have the gift of continence, than to live in marriage; nor is celibacy a better state, if the discussion concerns moral goodness, than the state of marriage; nor does it accord less with the principles of nature than marriage does. The same reasoning holds for the subject: they make the precepts binding on all men without distinction, but the counsels only on those who aspire to the state of perfection. For all are bound to that which is better, since all are bound to perfection and the highest degree of love, and the imperfection of one who remains in the second rank is a fault. But the counsel aims to prescribe something better; yet most of those things that they call counsels, such as self-denial, patience under injury, and so on, bind all and each individual man. There are also precepts that are not prescribed to all. For some are commanded to men, others to women, some to the elderly, others to the younger (Eph. 5:22ff.; Col. 3:18ff.; Titus 2:2–4, etc.). Yet, apart from a special calling, which has the character of a precept and not of a counsel, nothing is handed down in the Gospel that pertains to only one order of Christians. Just as there is no varied and manifold kind of Christians: "You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. There is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free" (Gal. 3:26ff.). Nor is the distinction more certain in respect of form, namely that a precept binds by its own force while a counsel is a matter of free observance. For if the excellence of a counsel is such that it prescribes something better, more just, or more holy than a precept, then by the force of that inherent beauty, goodness, and holiness it will bind all to observance. For we are also commanded to "test the things that differ" [δοκιμάζειν τὰ διαφέροντα], that is, to examine what is more excellent, and so also to pursue it (Rom. 2:18; Phil. 1:10). Nor is it free or permitted for anyone not to deny himself, not to love his enemy, not to bear injuries patiently, not to follow Christ, or not to obey God calling him to celibacy or poverty. Finally, the distinction they draw by reason of the end or effect, namely that the observed precept has a reward and the violated one a penalty, while the observed counsel has a greater reward, or aureole, and the neglected counsel has no penalty but drags after it only the loss of the aureole, is wholly fictitious; for we have already shown above that the counsels of God himself, being joined with divine authority, are not neglected with impunity. At least the penalty of loss remains for those who scorn right, indeed divine, counsels. But from the penalty of loss the penalty of sense is inseparably [ἀδιαστάτως] present. I say nothing of the hypocrisy of those who, while they neither fully fulfil nor are able to fulfil the Law, whose works of counsel they know to be easier to perform, offer themselves for the more difficult tasks; who boast that they can do more than they are bound to do, and can strive beyond the degree of love of God prescribed by him; who crow about duties as though they were not owed to God, since they belong to the whole bond and bondage of God, and impute them to God as a debtor of aureoles. Therefore these counsels are not counsels of evangelical perfection, but "the counsel of the wicked" [עצת רשעים], the counsels of the ungodly (Ps. 1:1), and "precepts of men taught by rote" (Isa. 29:13), that is, thoughts of unregenerate men, ignorant of divine righteousness, about the way of wiping out sin and pleasing God. For, instead of the precept of faith and repentance, those flattering enemies of God devised this method, so that they might impose upon God and lie to him. To this hypocrisy the doctrine of evangelical counsels was bound to lend support, so that under the appearance of increasing religion men might be drawn away from the Law of God, from Christ and true repentance, to false merits, to another mark [χάραγμα], another stamp, an adulteration of the marks [χαράγματα] of the divine Law, to false satisfactions, and to apostasy [ἀπόστασιν] itself. And that this doctrine of counsels is a rather hidden origin [ὑπόφυσιν] of the dogma of the Encratites or Apostolics and of the Pelagians, one may gather from what Bellarmine says in De monachis, chapter 8.

units.la: XXVI. Inprimis vota Monastica Consiliorum horum supremus apex, multum ab Evangelio, nedum ab Evangelii perfectione dissident. Nam vovere quidem, hoc est, dedito animo, & firmo cordis proposito Deo promittere aliquid, sive præceptum, sive indifferens in potestate voventis positum, ad Dei honorem, salutem propriam & proximi bonum pertinens, sive sit rei alicujús largitio, sive abstinentia, sive factum, sive aliud, ad pietatem facere potest. Unde Scripturæ ejusmodi vota ad ὅρκως juramenta referunt. Juravit David Jehovæ נדר vovit Potenti ipsius Jacob, Psal.CXXXII.2. Et sicut votum facere est sinceritatis in proposito, ita exequi illud est amoris majoris quidem, quàm qui in socordi reperitur, non tamen supra præceptum. Cæterum nec ad Evangelium proprie id pertinet, nec in eo supererogationis vel consilii actus, sed adminiculum quoddam Legis est, & eatenus etiam sub Evangelio locum habet, quatenus ipsa Lex sub eodem obtinet. Neque ullum votum legitimum & ad honorem Dei faciens agnoscimus, nisi vel in mandato officio, vel in generatim approbato cultu determinando, vel in orationis, meditationis & pietatis adminiculo. Sed votum nuncupare de rebus, de quibus nihil Deus dixit, quæque ad cultum cordis nihil faciunt, ad ἐθελοθρησκείαν cultum voluntarium, imo ad irrisionem ipsius Dei pertinet. Huc referimus vota Monastica, seu δόγματα placita, decreta illa, de quibus Apostolus: Cur placitis hominum, velut viventes in mundo, vos ob-
units.tr: XXVI. First of all, monastic vows, the supreme peak of these counsels, differ greatly from the Gospel, let alone from the perfection of the Gospel. To vow, that is, to promise something to God with a devoted mind and firm purpose of heart, whether it is a command or something indifferent that lies within the power of the one vowing and pertains to God's honour, one's own salvation and the good of a neighbour, whether it is a giving of some thing, an abstinence, an action or something else, can serve piety. Hence the Scriptures refer such vows to oaths [ὅρκους]. David swore to Jehovah and vowed [נדר] to the Mighty One of Jacob (Ps. 132:2). Just as to make a vow belongs to sincerity of purpose, so to perform it belongs to a love greater than that found in the careless, yet not above what is commanded. Otherwise it does not properly belong to the Gospel, nor is there in it any act of supererogation or of counsel, but it is a certain aid of the Law, and to that extent it also has a place under the Gospel, insofar as the Law itself holds under the same. Nor do we acknowledge any vow as lawful and making for God's honour, unless it is in a commanded duty, or in determining a worship generally approved, or as an aid to prayer, meditation and piety. But to vow concerning things about which God has said nothing, and which contribute nothing to the worship of the heart, belongs to self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκείαν], indeed to the mockery of God himself. To this we refer monastic vows, or the decrees [δόγματα] and inventions of men, of which the Apostle says: Why do you let yourselves be bound by the decrees of men, as though living in the world? (Col. 2:20)

units.la: stringi finitis? Ne tangas, (mulierem) ne gustes, (certos cibos, sive omnino, sive certis diebus) ne contrectes, (bona vel propria & dominio tuo subjecta) quæ rationem quidem sapientiæ in cultu voluntario, &c. habent. Col.II.21-23. Quibus si votum obedientiæ in ἐντολὰς ἀνθρώπων præcepta hominum κατακεχρ subjicientium & præmio defraudantium, ibid.v.18. seu τῆς πετασμονῆς τῆς ἐκ ἐν ἡ καλύπτ obsequii, quod non est ex vocante, Gal.V.8. & θρησκείαν Ayselan cultum Angelorum & beatarum mentium, Col.II.18. & horum omnium finem ταπεινοφροσύνη τῆς σαρκὸς repletionem carnis, ibid.v.23. addideris, perfecta fictitiae religionis Monasticæ idea exsurget. Apertissime enim S. Paulus, futurorum adeò præscius, ut velut præsentia describat, digitum in famosissima illa cœlibatus, paupertatis & obedientiæ vota intendit; ut directius oculum Monachatus impetere non potuerit. In specie votum absolutum Cœlibatus perpetui temerarium, & cum Verbo Dei pugnat. Christus enim Matth.XIX.12. dicens: Qui potest capere, capiat; diserte sibi vel aliis Legem cœlibatus perpetui dicere vetat. Non enim qui nunc χωρεῖ capit, certus est, fore ut semper capiat. Liberum igitur permitti vult τῷ δυναμένῳ χωρεῖν ei qui capere potest, &, qui ἀνάγκην necessitatem non habet, 1. Cor.VII.37. Vovere continentiam fragili aetate, Dei tentatio est; & qui pueros virginesque Monasteriis includunt, perinde faciunt, atque si Molocho eos immolarent. Par ratio est voti Paupertatis spontaneæ, quæ mendicitas, hoc est, ἀταξία inordinatio, 2.Thess.III.11. cum verbo Dei tum jubentis vescipane in sudore vultus, Genes.III.19. 2.Thess.III.10. tum vetantis, ne mendicus in populo Dei reperiatur, Deut.XV.4. nec non cum voto Sapientis, qui paupertatem deprecatus est, Prov.XXX.8. & cum Pauli sententia, quòd beatius sit dare, quàm accipere, Act.XX.35. pugnat. Impedit etiam votum paupertatis majus bonum, quia officia charitatis erga fratres indigos sufflaminat. Denique & votum Obedientiæ regularis cum subjectione judicii proprii & voluntatis in judicium & voluntatem alterius, non tantum cum præcepto Apostoli jubentis, ut servi secundum carnem libertatis suæ in Christo sint memores, 1.Cor.VII.22. & libertatem, si possint, quærant, ibid.v.21. & omnino cum libertate Christiana, in qua stare jubemur. Gal.V.1. nec non cum statu N.T. in quo non est δοῦλος & ἐλεύθερος, servus & liber, ibid.III.28. sed etiam cum obedientia religiosa, quæ soli Deo, Matth.IV.10. non ulli homini, 1.Cor.VI.20. VII.23. 2.Cor.I.24. debetur; nec non cum bona conscientia, quæ postulat δοκιμάζειν τὶ διαφέρoντα explorare, quæ meliora sunt, Rom.II.18. è diametro pugnat. Palam igitur est, à votis Monasticis & Legem Dei, cui illa contrariantur, & Evangelium, quod Legem non abolet, sed stabilit, ibid.III.31. abhorrere plurimum.
units.tr: Do not touch (a woman), do not taste (certain foods, whether altogether or on certain days), do not handle (goods or things subject to your ownership). These indeed have the appearance of wisdom in self-chosen worship, etc. (Col. 2:21–23). If to these you add the vow of obedience to the precepts of men [ἐντολὰς ἀνθρώπων], subjecting men to the precepts of men and defrauding them of the reward (ibid. v. 18), or the persuasion [πεισμονῆς] that is not from him who calls (Gal. 5:8), and the worship of angels and of blessed minds (Col. 2:18), and the end of all these, the satisfying of the flesh [πλησμονὴν τῆς σαρκός] (ibid. v. 23), the complete idea of a fictitious monastic religion will arise. For most clearly St Paul, so well foreseeing the future that he describes it as if present, pointed his finger at those most notorious vows of celibacy, poverty and obedience, so that the monastic life could not have been assailed more directly. Specifically, the absolute vow of perpetual celibacy is rash and fights against the Word of God. For Christ, saying in Matt. 19:12, "He who is able to receive it, let him receive it," expressly forbids himself or others to make a law of perpetual celibacy. For he who now receives [χωρεῖ] does not know that he will always be able to receive. He wills therefore that freedom be permitted to the one who is able to receive [τῷ δυναμένῳ χωρεῖν], and to him who has no necessity [ἀνάγκην] (1 Cor. 7:37). To vow continence in a fragile age is to tempt God; and those who shut up boys and virgins in monasteries do just as if they were sacrificing them to Moloch. The same reasoning applies to the vow of voluntary poverty, which is begging, that is, disorder [ἀταξία] (2 Thess. 3:11); it fights both against the word of God, which commands that we eat bread in the sweat of our face (Gen. 3:19; 2 Thess. 3:10), and forbids that a beggar be found among the people of God (Deut. 15:4); and also against the vow of the wise man, who prayed against poverty (Prov. 30:8), and against Paul's saying that it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35). The vow of poverty also hinders a greater good, because it hampers the duties of charity towards needy brethren. Finally, the vow of regular obedience, with the subjection of one's own judgement and will to the judgement and will of another, fights not only against the precept of the Apostle, who bids that slaves according to the flesh remember their freedom in Christ (1 Cor. 7:22), and seek freedom if they can (ibid. v. 21), and altogether against Christian liberty, in which we are commanded to stand (Gal. 5:1); and also against the state of the New Testament in which there is neither slave nor free (ibid. 3:28); but also against religious obedience, which is owed to God alone (Matt. 4:10) and not to any man (1 Cor. 6:20; 7:23; 2 Cor. 1:24); and likewise against a good conscience, which requires us to prove [δοκιμάζειν] what things are better, what is more excellent (Rom. 2:18). It is therefore plain that we utterly abhor monastic vows, both from God's law, to which they are opposed, and from the Gospel, which does not abolish the Law but establishes it (ibid. 3:31).

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Frivola sunt, quæ pro Consiliis suis argumenta Adversarii cudunt. Non enim S. Paulus, 1.Cor.IX. fusè demonstrans, se liberè abstinuisse accipiundis stipendiis, quibus frui æquè atque alii potuerit, se vel consilio à præcepto distincto obsecutum esse, vel supererogasse, & majus præmium meruisse declarat. Licèt enim liberum ei fuerit stipendia à Corinthiis accipere, si res in se abstracte consideretur, ratio-
units.tr: Frivolous are the arguments which the adversaries devise in support of their counsels. For St Paul, in 1 Cor. 9, showing at length that he freely abstained from accepting wages, which he could have enjoyed just as others did, does not declare that he obeyed a counsel distinct from a precept, or that he went beyond duty and merited a greater reward. For although it was lawful for him to accept support from the Corinthians, if the matter is considered in itself and abstractly, by reason-

units.la: Vota Monastica, consiliorum horum apex, Evangelio contrariantur.
units.tr: Monastic vows, the peak of these counsels, are opposed to the Gospel.

units.la: Argumenta pro consiliis Evangelicis refelluntur. ratione tamen vitandi scandali & Evangelii propagandi neutiquam hoc illi liberum fuit. Imò certis in locis, & certarum personarum ratione habita accipiundis iis abstinere debuit, ne gloriæ Dei,& propagationi Evangelii officerer, multósque adeò offenderet. Nam abstinebant etiam Pseudapostoli, & abstinentia hac S. Pauli authoritatem & gratiam, qua apud Corinthios pollebat, deprestum ibant, se verò iisdem insinuabant, ut zizania falsæ doctrinæ suæ facilius spargerent possent. Inde Evangelii propagationi non levis remora objecta est, quam Paulus simili abstinentia tollere debuit, ut qua in re Pseudapostoli gloriabantur, similes illi essent, nec haberent, quo inde supra eum gloriari possent, 2. Cor.XI.12. Etiam remoram Evangelii Christi nullam objicere, & libertate suâ non abuti, 1. Cor. IX.12, sic voluit. Sic faciendo non fecit opus indebitum supererogationis, quod liberè omittere, & quo aureolam in vita futura sibi promereri potuerit, sed Apostolico munere, quod ei à Christo impositum erat, bene legitimèque defunctus est, atque sic, non aliter, rebus ita stantibus, defungi debuit. Aliter si fecisset, peccasset graviter, nec omnino gloriam Domini sui procurasset. In universum enim res omnes, quæ in se nec bonæ, nec malæ, sed adiaphoræ sunt, cùm per circumstantias loci, temporis & personarum circumscribuntur & determinantur, bene vel malè fiunt, atque ita ἀδιαφορίαν suam exuunt. Et quæ certo loco & tempore & à certis personis laudabiliter & bene fiunt, alio loco & tempore, & ab aliis vel iisdem personis facta in vitio cubant. Nihil ergo circumstantiarum ratione habita non debitum vel indebitum, bonum vel malum, præmio vel poena dignum est. Neque magis ad rem faciunt ejusdem Apostoli verba: De Virginibus non habeo mandatum Domini, γνώμην δὲ δίδωμι, ibid. VII. 25. Non enim ibi γνώμη Consilium, uti Vulgatus & Erasmus reddunt, sed sententiam notat. Aliud enim est γνώμη, aliud βουλή. Ita S. Paulus idem: Γνώμην ἐν τούτῳ δίδωμι Sententiam in hoc do. 2. Cor. VIII.10. Ea autem erat de re non arbitraria, sed necessaria sententia Pauli, de eleemosynis scilicet Hierosolymam mittendis. Est ergo illa γνώμη sententia Apostoli non quidem ἐπιταγὴ præceptum Domini commune ad omnes & singulos pertinens; sed præceptum tamen, quia quod Apostolus Spiritum Dei habens 1. Cor. VII.40. sensit, perinde ut dictatus quivis Spiritus S. obligabat; præceptum puta personale & conditionatum, pertinens non ad omnes, sed ad eos demum, quibus ὁ Θεὸς ἐμέρισε Deus admensus est donum continentiæ, & quos κέκλη-κεν ὁ Κύριος vocavit Dominus, v.17. Non ergo sententia ea indefinita est, respectu omnium & singulorum, ita ut in arbitrio omnium sit eam amplecti vel repudiare; & amplectentes aureolam mereantur, repudiantes poena nulla maneat. Sic nec indefinita simpliciter est sententia Christi, Matth.XIX.13. Qui potest capere, capiat. Non enim omnibus ut capiant, consulitur, cùm Christus diserte dixerit: Οὐ πάντες χωροῦσι Non omnes capiunt. v.11.12. sed id solis δυναμένοις ii qui capere possunt, & οἷς δέδοται quibus datum est, præcipitur. Par ratio est verborum Christi, non consulentis utique, sed præcipientis juveni, in notitiam sui ipsius perdu-
units.tr: Arguments for the evangelical counsels are refuted. Yet by reason of avoiding offence and of spreading the Gospel, it was by no means lawful for him to take them. Indeed, in certain places, and with regard to certain persons, he ought to have abstained from receiving them, lest he hinder the glory of God and the spread of the Gospel, and so offend many. For the false apostles also abstained, and by this abstinence they tried to lower the authority and favour which Paul had among the Corinthians, while they insinuated themselves with them, so that they could more easily sow the tares of their false doctrine. Hence a no small hindrance to the spread of the Gospel was placed in the way, which Paul had to remove by a similar abstinence, so that in this matter the false apostles boasted, he might be like them and not have anything by which they could boast above him (2 Cor. 11:12). He also wished to put no hindrance in the way of the Gospel of Christ, and not to abuse his liberty (1 Cor. 9:12). In so doing he did not do an undue work of supererogation, which he could freely have omitted, and by which he could have earned a crown in the life to come for himself; but he discharged well and lawfully the apostolic office which Christ had laid upon him, and in such circumstances he ought to have discharged it in no other way. Had he acted otherwise, he would have sinned grievously and would not have promoted the glory of his Lord at all. For in general, all things which are in themselves neither good nor evil, but indifferent [adiaphora], when they are circumscribed and determined by the circumstances of place, time and persons, are done well or badly, and so they lose their indifference. And things which are done praiseworthily and well in a certain place, at a certain time, and by certain persons, when done in another place, at another time, and by others or the same persons, lie in fault. Nothing therefore, with circumstances taken into account, is not due or undue, good or evil, worthy of reward or punishment. Nor do the words of the same Apostle help more to the point: "Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give judgement" (1 Cor. 7:25). For there γνώμη does not mean counsel, as the Vulgate and Erasmus render it, but signifies opinion. For γνώμη is one thing, βουλή another. So St Paul likewise says: "I give judgement in this" (2 Cor. 8:10). But that was a judgement of Paul not on an arbitrary matter but on a necessary one, namely concerning the sending of alms to Jerusalem. That γνώμη therefore is the Apostle's judgement, not indeed a command [ἐπιταγὴ] of the Lord common to all and each, but nevertheless a precept, because what the Apostle, having the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 7:40), judged, bound just as any dictate of the Holy Spirit did; a personal and conditional precept, namely, pertaining not to all but only to those to whom God has apportioned the gift of continence [ὁ Θεὸς ἐμέρισε], and whom the Lord has called [κέκλη-κεν ὁ Κύριος] (v. 17). This judgement, therefore, is not indefinite with respect to all and each, so that it is in everyone's power to embrace or reject it, and those who embrace it merit a crown, while those who reject it remain without punishment. Nor is the saying of Christ simply indefinite, Matt. 19:13: "He who is able to receive it, let him receive it." For he is not counselled that all may receive it, since Christ expressly said: "Not all receive it" (v. 11–12), but it is commanded to those alone who are able to receive it [δυναμένοις], and to whom it is given [οἷς δέδοται]. The same reasoning applies to the words of Christ, who is not counselling but commanding the young man, leading him to knowledge of himself: "If you wish to be perfect" (not with the Evangelical, but with the legal perfection, which alone he boasted of), "go, sell your goods, and give to the poor, and come, follow me" (ibid. v. 21).

units.la: cendo: Si perfectus esse (non Evangelica, sed Legali, quam solam is jactabat, perfectione) vis, vade, vende bona tua, & da pauperibus, & veni, & sequere me. ibid. v.21. Nam quod sic Christus jussit, occupare vel non occupare juveni liberum minimè fuit. Christus enim occasione juvenis hujus, imperata non facientis, sed tristi animo facessentis, dixit: Amen, dico vobis; quòd difficulter dives ingredietur Regnum Cœlorum, v.23. Atqui consilia negligere, cum periculo salutis conjunctum esse, ipsimet οἱ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων negant. Quomodo præterea Deum ex toto corde diligere dici is potest, qui auditis ejus sive consiliis, sive præceptis λυπούμενος tristis (uti de juvene illo, v.22. dicitur) abit, & quid Deus consulat, vel præcipiat, pensi non habet? Certè eum, qui Christum sequi renuit, ex discipulorum suorum numero idem excludit, ibid. XVI.24. At qui discipulus Christi non est, nec Christianus est. Nam quòd eundem juvenem Christus intuitus dilexisse Marc. X.21. dicitur; non eum sensum habet, quòd eum, ceu sibi gratum vel obsequentem dilexerit; sed quòd eum amanter, utpote de sua salute utcunque anxium & percontantem exceperit. Quomodo Varino etiam ἀγαπᾶν idem est, quod ὑποδέχεσθαι excipere; & eodem sensu passim LXX. Interpretes τὸ ἀγαπᾶν explicant, velut Psalm. LXXVIII. 37. CXVI.1. &c. Juvenem enim serio quærentem, serio respondentem dignum Christus pro sua φιλανθρωπία judicavit, quem amanter compellaret, et benignè instrueret, exoscularetur, eo modo, quo Hebræorum magistri caput ejus, qui non indocte respondisset, exosculari solebant. Præterea nec Eunuchi, se ipsos propter Regnum Cœlorum castrantes. Matth. XIX. 12. ex consilio id facere censentur, sed ex vocatione singulari, quæ præcepti vim habet, juxta limitationem ipsius Christi, v.11.12. Non omnes sermonem hunc capiunt, sed quibus datum est; Qui potest capere, capiat: quibus verbis Christus testatur, non omnes cœlibatus, seu propositi constantis cœlibatum colendi, capaces esse; sed nonnullis omnino necessarium conjugium esse. Denique Philosophi quidem in omni opere bono duplicem perfectionem, alteram necessariam simpliciter ad rei essentiam pertinentem; alteram arbitrariam, ad majorem rei sive operis dignitatem facientem, & accommodatum utrique præmium, ordinarium, pro cujusque laboribus etiam jure debitis, & extraordinarium pro singularibus quibusdam meritis; distinguunt. Qui forte fons est erroris de Consiliis. Cùm enim in S. literis N. T. nonnulla horridiùs dici viderentur, quàm ut sapientibus Ethnicorum placere possent, inventum est moderamen ex distinctione præceptorum & consiliorum accommodatione quadam ad placita Philosophorum, præcipuè Stoicorum de officio communi & vero perfecto. Sed Christiana religio perfectionis differentiam similem neutiquam agnoscit. Quin potiùs evidens perfectionis Philosophicæ & Christianæ disparitas est. Illa enim externa, & naturalis, hæc interna & supernaturalis est, Matth. V.21. &c. Illa inhærens est; hæc etiam imputata per fidem Christi. Illa mercedem debitam apud homines, hæc præmium gratuitum à Deo consequitur. Illa perfectionem utramque in operum præstatione; hæc unam eandem andémque in fide, perfectissimam Christi justitiam prensante, collocat.
units.tr: ...cendo: If you wish to be perfect (not in the Gospel sense, but in the legal perfection, which alone he boasted of), go, sell your goods, give to the poor, and come, follow me. Ibid. v.21. For Christ did not leave it to the young man's choice whether or not to take up what he commanded. Christ, speaking on the occasion of this young man, who did not do what was commanded but went away sorrowful, said: Verily I say unto you, that a rich man shall hardly enter the kingdom of heaven, v.23. Yet even those of men [οἱ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων] deny that neglecting counsels is joined with danger to salvation. Moreover, how can someone be said to love God with his whole heart if, on hearing God's counsels or precepts, he goes away grieved (as is said of that young man, v.22) [λυπούμενος], and has no concern for what God advises or commands? Certainly the same Christ excludes from the number of his disciples the one who refuses to follow him, ibid. XVI.24. But whoever is not a disciple of Christ is not a Christian either. As for the statement that Christ, looking upon that same young man, loved him (Mark X.21), this does not mean that he loved him as pleasing or obedient to himself, but that he received him lovingly, as one anxious in some way about his own salvation and asking questions. Thus with Varinus too, to love [ἀγαπᾶν] means the same as to receive [ὑποδέχεσθαι], and in the same sense the Septuagint everywhere renders the word to love, as at Psalm 78:37, 116:1, etc. For Christ, in his love of mankind [φιλανθρωπία], judged the young man, who was seriously seeking and seriously answering, worthy to be addressed lovingly and kindly instructed, and to be kissed, in the way the rabbis were accustomed to kiss the head of a pupil who had answered not unlearnedly. Furthermore, nor are eunuchs, who make themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, Matt. 19:12, thought to do this from counsel, but from a singular calling, which has the force of a precept, according to Christ's own limitation, vv. 11–12: Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it is given. He that is able to receive it, let him receive it. By these words Christ testifies that not all are capable of celibacy, or of keeping celibacy by a settled purpose, but that for some marriage is altogether necessary. Finally, the philosophers indeed distinguish in every good work a twofold perfection: one necessary, belonging simply to the essence of the thing; the other optional, adding to the greater dignity of the thing or work, and a reward suited to each: an ordinary reward, due by right for each one's labours, and an extraordinary reward for certain singular merits. This is perhaps the source of the error about counsels. For since some things in the New Testament Scriptures seemed to be said too harshly to please the wise men of the Gentiles, a remedy was found in distinguishing precepts from counsels, with some accommodation to the opinions of the philosophers, chiefly the Stoics, concerning common duty and true perfection. But the Christian religion by no means acknowledges a similar difference of perfection. Rather, there is a plain disparity between philosophical and Christian perfection. For the former is external and natural, the latter internal and supernatural, Matt. 5:21 etc. The former is inherent; the latter is also imputed through faith in Christ. The former obtains a reward owed among men; the latter a free reward from God. The former places perfection in both the performance of works; the latter places one and the same perfection in faith, laying hold of the most perfect righteousness of Christ.

units.la: XXVIII. Mittimus hic eorundem Pontificiorum, nec non Socinianorum, & iisdem secundas facientium Anabaptistarum & Novatorum capitalem haeresin, quod Christus sub Evangelio non tantum singulis Decalogi praeceptis nonnulla ad perfectiorem & Angelicum Dei in N. T. cultum pertinentia adjecerit, sed etiam toti Decalogo nova quaedam praecepta, sub eo minime comprehensa, velut abnegationem sui, tolerantiam crucis, & Christi in virtutibus moralibus, praecipue autem in fiducia erga Deum, charitate Dei & proximi, humilitate & precum assiduitate, imitationem adjunxerit. Hoc videlicet conspirantes illi agunt, ut Evangelium in novam Legem transforment, & justitia fidei conculcata justitiam operum stabiliant, adeoque simul legem & Evangelium solvant. Nam nec Lex manca adeo & mutila vera Dei lex est: nec Evangelium est, quod salutis arcem in novae Legis obedientia constituit; & Christi ipse Pseudopropheta secundum Legem Divinam immutabilem Deut. XIII. 1. &c. occidendus nefarie statuitur, si novam Legem protulit, veteremque interpolavit, & veri Redemptoris atque Salvatoris axioma idem perdidit, si non aliam ob rationem in carnem venit, quam ut meliora & perfectiora & servatu difficiliora praecepta rogaret, ac de caetero justitiam ipse non afferret. Sed erroris hujus fibras jam supra Loc. XIX. §. 24. 35. &c. incidimus. Unum restat, ut quae a Christo singulis praeceptis addita nugantur, dissertius paulo ad incudem revocemus.
units.tr: XXVIII. We pass over here the capital heresy of the same Papists, as well as of the Socinians, and of the Anabaptists and Novatians who follow them: that Christ under the Gospel not only added to individual precepts of the Decalogue some things pertaining to a more perfect and angelic worship of God in the New Testament, but also joined to the whole Decalogue certain new precepts, not included in it at all, such as self-denial, endurance of the cross, and of Christ in moral virtues, especially, however, in trust toward God, love of God and neighbour, humility and constancy in prayer, and imitation. Clearly by this they conspire to turn the Gospel into a new Law, and, trampling underfoot the righteousness of faith, establish the righteousness of works, and so at the same time dissolve both Law and Gospel. For the Law, so maimed and mutilated, is not the true law of God, nor is it the Gospel that places the citadel of salvation in obedience to a new Law. And Christ himself is impiously set down as a false prophet, to be put to death according to the immutable law of God, Deut. 13:1 etc., if he brought a new law and corrupted the old, and lost the axiom of the true Redeemer and Saviour, if he came in the flesh for no other reason than to request better, more perfect and harder-to-keep precepts, and did not himself bring righteousness henceforth. But we have already touched the roots of this error above, Loc. XIX §§ 24, 35 etc. One thing remains: that we bring back to the anvil, a little more clearly, what they foolishly claim Christ added to individual precepts.

units.la: XXIX. Quoad priorem Decalogi Tabulam. Primo igitur Praecepto novum orandi modum, in Oratione Dominica praescriptum, & novum Dei cultum in Christo & per eum superadditum illi afferunt. Sed modus quidem orandi a Christo praescriptus, si ex forma ac dispositione sua aestimetur, novus est; perinde ut modus orandi a Davide in Psalmis introductus novus fuit; sin ex materia, hoc est, ex ipsis rebus petendis, nec non eorum petitionibus judicetur, nihil prorsus continet, quod precibus Sanctorum in V. T. non sit expressum, uti loca Psal. CXV. 1. LXVII. 2. XXV. 4. §. Prov. XXX. 8. Psal. XXV. 11. XIX. 14. cum singulis petitionibus comparanti liquet. Dilutum vero illud est, quod imitationem Angelorum, & remissionem peccatorum N. T. promissa faciunt. Nam etiam David exemplis Angelorum se ad Dei laudes excitavit, Psal. CIII. 20. Petimus, ut imitetur Angelos humana fragilitas, inquit Hieronymus; sed suo modo, hoc est, sincere & ex animo. Perfectio vero in Coelis proposita est, ubi demum ἰσάγγελοι erimus, Luc. XX. 36. Idem David alios remissionem peccatorum orare docuit, Psal. XIX. 13. XXXII. 6. Neque illud obstat, quod Lex Mosis capitis poenam quibusdam transgressoribus dictavit, Num. XV. 30. 31. Aliud enim forum soli, aliud forum poli est. Remissionem peccatorum apud illud, non apud hoc expetimus. Altera de novo Dei cultu in Christo & per eum additio, nil nisi horrendam in Filium Dei blasphemiam, qua is & Deitate sua cum Patre communi, & honore Divino spoliatur, spirat. Neque praeceptum Primum ullam additionem vel exceptionem admittit, sed simpliciter praecipit, Non erit tibi Deus alius in conspectu meo. Neque praeceptum illud dogmate, sed veritate & natura nititur. Non potest etiam esse Deus Israelis nisi Jehova. Atis, qui dixit: Fiam qui sum: Fiam Deus tuus, etiam factus est Deus Israelis, & non alius. Ideo status N. T. dicitur Regnum Dei ... quia Deus in eo non habet socium, vel socios. Neque vel Deus Divina adoratione mediate coli, vel quisquam in cultu Divino Deo sic subordinari potest, ut honor Divinus per eum, ceu inferiorem, ad Deum transeat. Honor enim, qui transit, non est Divinus, quia Divinus honor in eo subsistit, qui eo, ut summo afficitur. Etiam in V. T. fuerunt Θεοὶ λεγόμενοι, Dii dicti, seu nominati, licet solus Jehova, non illi Divino honore afficerentur. Si igitur sub N. T. Christus factus est Θεὸς λεγόμενος, non ideo vel factus est Jehova, Deus Israelis, vel Divino cultu affici debet: non plus inde, quam a Diis nominatis V. T. accedere potuerit. Praeterea nec Jehova aliter ab Israele cognosci potuit, quam ut habens Filium & Spiritum, & volens Filium dare Redemptorem & Spiritum Paracletum, atque sic Deus ipsorum fieri. Ideo Scriptura Sermonem, qui est in Decalogo, adeoque etiam haec verba: Ego sum Jehova Deus tuus, &c. attribuit Angelo, qui habitaverat in rubo, quem & Jehovam appellat, Act. VII. 38. coll. cum Exod. III. 2. 4. 6. 7. 12. 13. Sententia proin primi Praecepti est, Nomen illud, Jehova Deus Israelis, & ejusdem Nominis gloriam non esse tribuendam ulli extra Angelum, qui in rubo apparuit. Accedunt mandata sub V. T. de adorando Christo Filio, Psal. II. 12. XLV. 12. XCVII. 7. nec non exempla Angelorum, Esaj. VI. 2. 3. Abrahami, Gen. XVIII. 23. Jacobi, XLVIII. 16. Danielis, cap. IX. 17. totiusque; Ecclesiae Esaj. LXIII. 16. LXIV. 8. &c. de quo in Loco plura diximus. Secundi Praecepti ἀναφιλήτως faciunt fugam idolorum, juxta illa: Si quis te conscientiam habentem viderit in idoleo accumbentem, &c. 1. Cor. VIII. 10. Dilecti mei, fugite idololatriam, ibid. X. 14. Custodite vos ab idolis, 1. Joh. V. 21. Cum ergo in V. T. imaginum adoratio prohibita fuerit, in Novo etiam imaginum fugam praeceptam, & participationem omnem eorum, quae idolis consecrata sunt, quin & locorum ipsorum, quibus eae coluntur, frequentationem interdictam ajunt. Quasi licuerit in V. T. interesse cultui idololatrico, & videri similem idololatris. Hoc enim dum superadditum scisciunt, revera ut minus idololatriam caveamus efficiunt; quia plane constat, veteres idololatriam fugisse. Nam etiam idola gentium comburere, altaria destruere, lucos succidere jussi sunt, Exod. XXIII. 24. Deut. IV. 5. XII. 2. 3. Imo interdictum iis est, ne vel nomina idolorum in os assumerent, Exod. XXIII. 13. Hos II. 16. 17. consortium cum idololatris religioni noxium ullum colerent, Deut. VII. 2. 3. Ideo etiam Naaman Syrus frequentati idolei veniam anxie adeo expetiit, 2. Reg. V. 18. Si igitur veteribus licuit adesse idololatrico cultui, cum tamen idololatriam omnem, loca, nomina idolorum, societatem cum idololatris omnem fugere jussi sint, videtur id aeque nobis licere. Similes sunt Praecepti Tertii appendices; velut quod in N. T. non solum Deum, sed etiam Christum testem invocare liceat; quod non tantum non pejerare, sed ne jurare rare quidem nunc, nisi in rebus gravissimis & & magno cum Dei metu fas sit. Cùm verò in V. T. Christum ut unum illum Jehovam unâ cum Patre adoratum fuisse, alibi comprobaverimus, etiam testem eundem invocare licuisse, sequitur. Imo invocatum talem esse, ex Esaj. XLV.23.Rom.XIV.11.constat. Neque etiam leviter jurare in V.T. licuit. Quin justus ab injusto hac nota discretus fuit, quòd hic נשבע juraret; ille שבועה ירא juramentum timeret, Eccles.IX.2. De quo in loco plura. Quartum Præceptum non ullo additamento auctum, sed penitus sublatum asserunt. Quod disertis Christi verbis, Matth.V.17.contrariatur. Neque certè vel sanctificatio quietis nostræ, quam Deus sub N.T. dedit, vel deputatio certi temporis ad congregationes sacras sublata est. De quo etiam alibi plura.
units.tr: XXIX. As for the first table of the Decalogue. First, they claim that the First Commandment is given a new mode of prayer in the Lord's Prayer and a new worship of God in Christ, added through him. But the mode of prayer prescribed by Christ is new if it is judged by its form and arrangement, just as the mode of prayer introduced by David in the Psalms was new. If it is judged by its matter, that is, by the things asked for and the petitions themselves, it contains nothing that was not already expressed in the prayers of the saints in the Old Testament. Comparing each petition with the passages shows this: Psalm 115:1; 67:2; 25:4; Prov. 30:8; Psalm 25:11; 19:14. The claim that the New Testament promises the imitation of angels and the remission of sins is refuted. David too roused himself to praise God by the example of the angels, Psalm 103:20. "Human frailty is asked to imitate the angels," says Jerome, "but in its own way, that is, sincerely and from the heart." Perfection, however, is set before us in heaven, where at last we shall be isangeloi [ἰσάγγελοι, equal to the angels], Luke 20:36. The same David taught others to pray for the remission of sins, Psalm 19:13; 32:6. Nor does it stand in the way that the Law of Moses prescribed the death penalty for some transgressors, Num. 15:30, 31. For there is one court for the earth and another for heaven. We seek the remission of sins in the latter, not the former. The other addition, a new worship of God in Christ and through him, breathes nothing but horrible blasphemy against the Son of God, by which he is stripped of his Deity, which he shares with the Father, and of divine honour. Nor does the First Commandment admit any addition or exception. It simply commands, "You shall have no other God before me." Nor does that commandment rest on doctrine but on truth and nature. Nor can there be a God of Israel except Jehovah. He who said, "I will be who I am: I will be your God," was made the God of Israel, and no other. Therefore the state of the New Testament is called the "Kingdom of God" ... because God has no partner or partners in it. Nor can God be worshipped with divine adoration mediately, nor can anyone be so subordinated to God in divine worship that the divine honour passes through him, as through an inferior, to God. For honour that passes through is not divine, since divine honour rests in the one who is honoured as supreme. In the Old Testament too there were "gods so called," dii dicti, or "named," although Jehovah alone was not honoured with divine worship by them. So if under the New Testament Christ has been made a "god so called," he has not for that reason become Jehovah, the God of Israel, nor ought he to be worshipped with divine honour. No more can accrue to him from this than could accrue from the named gods of the Old Testament. Moreover, Jehovah could not be known by Israel otherwise than as having a Son and a Spirit, willing to give the Son as Redeemer and the Spirit as Paraclete, and so becoming their God.
