Therefore Scripture attributes the speech in the Decalogue, and so also these words, "I am Jehovah your God," etc., to the Angel who "dwelt in the bush," whom it also calls Jehovah, Acts 7:38, compared with Exod. 3:2, 4, 6, 7, 12, 13. The sense of the First Commandment, therefore, is that the name "Jehovah, God of Israel," and the glory of that same name, are not to be ascribed to anyone other than the Angel who appeared in the bush. To these are added the commands under the Old Testament to worship Christ the Son, Psalm 2:12; 45:12; 97:7, as well as the examples of angels, Isa. 6:2, 3; of Abraham, Gen. 18:23; of Jacob, 48:16; of Daniel, ch. 9:17; and of the whole Church, Isa. 63:16; 64:8, etc., of which we have said more in the Locus. For the Second Commandment they without hesitation enjoin flight from idols, according to: "If anyone sees you, who have knowledge, reclining in an idol's temple," etc., 1 Cor. 8:10; "My beloved, flee from idolatry," ibid. 10:14; "Keep yourselves from idols," 1 John 5:21. Since the adoration of images was forbidden under the Old Testament, they say that under the New Testament flight from images is commanded, and all participation in things consecrated to idols, and even attendance at the very places where they are worshipped, is forbidden. As if it were permitted under the Old Testament to take part in idolatrous worship and to appear similar to idolaters! For while they insist on this as an addition, they in fact bring it about that we guard less against idolatry, since it is plain that the ancients fled idolatry. For they were ordered to burn the idols of the nations, overthrow altars and cut down groves, Exod. 23:24; Deut. 4:5; 12:2, 3. Indeed they were forbidden even to take the names of idols on their lips, Exod. 23:13; Hos. 2:16, 17, and to cultivate any alliance with idolaters that was harmful to religion, Deut. 7:2, 3. Hence Naaman the Syrian also anxiously sought pardon for attending the idol temple, 2 Kings 5:18. If therefore the ancients were allowed to be present at idolatrous worship, although they were ordered to shun all idolatry, the names of idols and all fellowship with idolaters, it seems that this is equally permitted to us. Similar are the appendages of the Third Commandment. For instance, they say that under the New Testament it is lawful to invoke not only God but also Christ as witness; and that not only is perjury forbidden but even swearing is now rarely lawful, except in the most serious matters and with great fear of God. Since we have proved elsewhere that Christ was worshipped under the Old Testament together with the Father as that one Jehovah, it follows that it was also lawful to invoke him as witness. Indeed, from Isa. 45:23 and Rom. 14:11 it is plain that he is so invoked. Nor was it lawful under the Old Testament to swear lightly. Indeed the righteous was distinguished from the unjust by this mark: the one swears [נשבע, nishba], the other fears an oath [שבועה ירא, yare shevuah], Eccl. 9:2, on which more in its place. They say the Fourth Commandment was not enlarged by any addition but wholly abolished. This contradicts the explicit words of Christ, Matt. 5:17. Certainly neither the sanctification of our rest, which God gave under the New Testament, nor the setting apart of a fixed time for sacred assemblies has been abolished. On this too we say more elsewhere.

units.la: XXX. Neque etiam posterioris Tabulæ Præceptis quicquam Christus adjecit. Nam quod illi Quintò Præcepto additum statuunt, quòd nunc Magistratus, Domini, mariti, non ut Dominos tantum, sed ut Patres inferioribus se præbere debeant, juxta, Coloss.IV.1. Ephes V.21.&c. Col.III.19.&c. exemplo Dei ipsius, qui ante Dominus, nunc Pater in Christo factus sit; quòdque nunc etiam inimici diligendi sint, frivolum est. Nam dilectionem inimici communem fuisse utrique Testamento, alibi comprobavimus. Magistratus verò, Domini & Mariti æquè in Veteri atque in N.T. אבות Patrum nomine veniunt, velut, Genes.XLI.43. XLV.8. Exod.XII.3. Job.XXIX.16. 2.Reg.V.13. Idem ut potestate sua clementer, leniter, paternè utantur, passim admonentur, Deut. XVII.15. &c. XXIV.1. Mal.II.14.15.16. Sed & Deus in V.T. non Domini duntaxat, verùm etiam Patris nomine cultus & invocatus est; Esaj. LXIII.16. LXIV.8. Malach. I.6.II.10. Sexto Præcepto accessisse, ne fratri irascamur, vel verbis asperis & facie austera, quæ vindictæ fomites igniculíque sunt, alios offendamus, juxta Matth. V.21.22. Ephes.IV.31. neve injurias ullo modo ulciscamur, juxta Matth. V.39.40. &c. nequicquam iidem nugantur. Nam iram & μηνιᾶν omnem adversus fratres etiam Lex Divina prohibuit, Levit.XIX.18. Prov.XXVII.3.Eccles.VII.9.Neque aliud Deus sibi voluit, cùm Caini adversus fratrem ἀσφ- θόνιαν, invidentiam & austeritatem graviter increpuit, Genes.IV.6. 1.Joh.III.12.15. Ac licet irascenti ignis gehennæ supplicium disertis verbis dictatum non sit, tamen sub generali maledictione Legis continetur, Deut.XXVII.26.Sed & ira habens comitem vindictæ cupiditatem, diserte prohibita est. ܥܡܢ ܠܐ Non ulciscēris te, neque recondes odium adversus filios populi tui, Levit.XIX.18. Lex ipsa jubens amare, non odisse proximum, omnem commotionem animi, quæ non est ex charitate, & cum ea, & quæ perseverantior in odium exit, prohibet. Quòd verò vindictam etiam publicam per Magistratum olim concessam sub N.T. prohibitam esse ex Matth. V.39.40.41.colligunt, merâ Evangelii corruptela est, quam & scopus Christi solam privatam vindictam cohibentis: & factum ejusdem, Magistratui jus vindictæ asserentis, Joh.XVIII.23. & S.Pauli Act.XXIII.2.3. exemplum & generalis de officio Magistratus doctrina, Rom.XIII.
units.tr: XXX. Nor did Christ add anything to the precepts of the second table either. For what they claim was added to the Fifth Commandment, that magistrates, masters and husbands must now show themselves to their inferiors as fathers and not merely as lords, according to Col. 4:1; Eph. 5:21, etc.; Col. 3:19, etc., following the example of God himself, who, once Lord, has now become Father in Christ, and that enemies must now be loved as well, is trivial. For we have shown elsewhere that love of enemies was common to both Testaments. But magistrates, masters and husbands alike, in the Old and the New Testament, come under the name of fathers [אבות, abot], as in Gen. 41:43; 45:8; Exod. 12:3; Job 29:16; 2 Kings 5:13. That they are repeatedly admonished to use their power mercifully, gently and paternally is shown by Deut. 17:15, etc.; 24:1; Mal. 2:14, 15, 16. Moreover, in the Old Testament God too was worshipped and invoked not only under the name of Lord but also under the name of Father: Isa. 63:16; 64:8; Mal. 1:6; 2:10. To the Sixth Commandment, they say, has been added that we must not be angry with a brother, nor offend others by harsh words and stern faces, which are the fuel and sparks of revenge, according to Matt. 5:21, 22; Eph. 4:31; nor avenge injuries in any way, according to Matt. 5:39, 40, etc. These things they talk about to no purpose. For even the divine Law forbade all anger and resentment against brothers, Lev. 19:18; Prov. 27:4; Eccl. 7:9. Nor did God desire anything else when he sharply rebuked Cain for his envy and bitterness against his brother, Gen. 4:6; 1 John 3:12, 15. And although the punishment of the fire of Gehenna is not stated in explicit words for the one who is angry, yet he is included under the general curse of the Law, Deut. 27:26. But anger that has the desire for vengeance as its companion is also expressly forbidden: "You shall not avenge yourself, nor bear a grudge against the children of your people," Lev. 19:18 (in the Chaldee paraphrase, "lo tinqom"). The Law itself, which commands us to love and not hate our neighbour, forbids every movement of the mind that does not come from charity, and that which goes on into more lasting hatred. But that vengeance, even the public vengeance once exercised by the magistrate, is forbidden under the New Testament, they gather from Matt. 5:39–41. This is a mere corruption of the Gospel, which is clearly refuted by the purpose of Christ, who restrains only private vengeance; by his own act, asserting the magistrate's right of vengeance, John 18:23; by the example of Paul, Acts 23:2, 3; and by the general doctrine of the office of the magistrate set forth in Rom. 13:1, etc.

units.la: 1.&c.prodita luculenter refellunt. Ejusdem ferè commatis sunt, quæ Septimo Præcepto adjecta somniant, velut quòd impudicus aspectus mulieris sit adulterium coram Deo, Matth.V.28. quòd divortium mulieris, extra adulterii causam, adulterium & ipsum sit; ibid. v.32. quodque omnis scortatio, turpiloquentia & εὐτραπελία, quam Gentiles Philosophi inter virtutes laudarunt, flagitiosa sit, 1.Thess.IV.3. 4.Ephes.V.3.4. s.Nam & oculi adulteri æquè atque mala voluntas æquè in V.T. prohibiti sunt, Exod.XX.17. ubi concupiscentia in genere, adeóque & impura voluntas, & oculi impudici, ejusdem membra & arma, quatenus illa ἀφνιαζειν; & spiritum rectorem excutere solent, damnantur, quod etiam exempla, Gen.XXXIX. 7-10.Job.XXXI.9.Ezech.XXIII.16. comprobant: & divortiorum licentia in prima conjugii institutione coercita est, Genes.II.24.Matth. XIX.8. & quidem ceu בגד perfidia, Mal.II.14. tolerata licet σκληροκαρδίαν ob populi duritiem; & obscœnitas quævis rerum & verborum generali de sanctimonia Lege Levit.XI.44.45. specialiúmque etiam præceptorum analogia, Deut.XXII.20. XXIII.2.13. Ezech.XVI.15. XVIII.6. cohibita est. Præcepto Octavo interdictum avaritiæ, qua stimulante possessiones ad vitæ sustentationem non necessariæ appetuntur; nisi forte quod abundat, in pauperes erogetur; nec non exactæ & quasi Divinæ temperantiæ in omni vita servandæ, ne nobis impendamus, quod aliis jure charitatis debetur; mandatum additum esse, pertendunt. Verùm avaritiam & luxuriam omnem in victu & amictu æquè in V.T. atque in Novo prohibitam esse diserte Scripturæ, Exod.XX.17. XXII.25. XXV.8. Deut.XXI.20. Psal.CXIX.36. Prov. XXIII.20.Esaj.III.17.20. probant. Nam quòd promissiones temporales bonorum terrenorum fibulam avaritiæ luxasse illi clamitant, frustra sunt, quia temporalia quædam bona fidelibus V.T. promissa sunt, non ut iis confidant, vel ea ultra modum appetant, sed ut spiritualium bonorum quibusdam velut delinimentis suavíque promulsíde uterentur. Dilutum verò & illud est, quòd Præcepto Nono mendacii cujusvis interdictum additum, omnésque detractiones, calumnias, censuras iniquas domum sub N.T. Rom.I.30. Ephes.IV.25. 1.Pet. II.1, serió prohibitas affirmant. Plenas enim interdictis earum rerum esse tabulas V.T. in explicatione Præcepti hujus ostendimus. Denique ad Præcepti Decimi enervationem pertinet, quòd ei additum iidem perhibent, ne inclinemus cor ad res cupitas, etiamsi non cogitemus cupita facere. Id enim semper sanctitati repugnat, & unà cum concupiscentia, quæ talis esse non desinit, sive ei homo repugnet, sive indulgeat, vetatur. Ideo S. Paulus Rom.VII.7.8. totum genus illicitæ concupiscentiæ Dei Lege damnari docet. Proin etiam omnes species ejus, omnésque specierum gradus damnari pariter, consequens est.
units.tr: 1. etc. These clearly refute the doctrines handed down. Of much the same kind are the additions they dream up to the Seventh Commandment: for example, that an impure look at a woman is adultery before God (Matt. 5:28); that a wife's divorce, apart from the cause of adultery, is itself adultery (ibid. v. 32); and that all fornication, obscene talk and wit [εὐτραπελία], which the Gentile philosophers praised among the virtues, are shameful (1 Thess. 4:3–4; Eph. 5:3–4). For in the Old Testament the adulterous eye, and an evil will alike, are forbidden (Exod. 20:17), where concupiscence in general, and so an impure will and wanton eyes, the members and weapons of lust, which are wont to dull [ἀφνιάζειν] and shake loose the ruling spirit, are condemned. The examples also confirm this (Gen. 39:7–10; Job 31:9; Ezek. 23:16). The licence of divorce was restrained at the very institution of marriage (Gen. 2:24; Matt. 19:8), and though it was tolerated because of the people's hardness of heart [σκληροκαρδίαν], it was still treated as perfidy [בגד] (Mal. 2:14). Every kind of obscenity in words and deeds is restrained by the general law of holiness (Lev. 11:44–45) and by analogy with the special precepts (Deut. 22:20; 23:2, 13; Ezek. 16:15; 18:6). Under the Eighth Commandment, they argue, what was added was a prohibition of greed, by which possessions not necessary for sustaining life are sought after, unless perhaps the surplus is given to the poor; and also a command to keep, in every part of life, a strict and almost divine temperance, so that we do not spend on ourselves what is owed to others by the right of charity. But that greed and all luxury in food and clothing are forbidden alike in the Old Testament and in the New, the Scriptures expressly prove (Exod. 20:17; 22:25; 25:8; Deut. 21:20; Ps. 119:36; Prov. 23:20; Isa. 3:17, 20). As for their cry that the temporal promises of earthly goods have loosened the clasp of greed, it is in vain, because certain temporal goods were promised to the believers of the Old Testament not so that they should trust in them or desire them beyond measure, but so that they might use them as a kind of sweetener and pleasant relish for the spiritual goods. Equally weak is their claim that, under the Ninth Commandment, a prohibition of every kind of lie was added, and that all detractions, calumnies and unjust censures are seriously forbidden in the New Testament (Rom. 1:30; Eph. 4:25; 1 Pet. 2:1). For we have shown, in explaining this Commandment, that the tables of the Old Testament are full of prohibitions of those things. Finally, it belongs to the weakening of the Tenth Commandment that they also maintain that there was added to it: do not incline the heart to desired things, even if we do not intend to do what is desired. For this always runs counter to holiness, and together with concupiscence, which never ceases to be such, whether a man resists it or indulges it, is forbidden. Therefore St Paul teaches that the whole kind of unlawful concupiscence is condemned by God's Law (Rom. 7:7–8). It follows, in the same way, that all its species, and all the degrees of its species, are equally condemned.

units.la: XXXI. Fuit Lex Evangelii. Ad Promissa, Evangelium ejusdem utramque fere paginam facientia, tractatio flectit.
units.tr: XXXI. The Gospel was a law of promise. The treatment turns to the promises, which make up nearly both pages of the Gospel.

units.la: Nam Lex ipsa fidei in promissa illa fertur, ut ea læto præconio annuntiata credenti applicet. Divina potentia in cognitione vocantis nos per gloriam & virtutem τῷ ἰδίῳ κλήσει. τιμια ἐπαγγέλματα maxima & pretiosa promissa nobis largita est, ut per hoc fieretis Divinae naturae participes, effugientes à corruptione, quae in mundo est, in concupiscentia, 2. Pet. I.4. Ἐπαγγέλματα promissa vocat, quia Deus per Mosen & Prophetas bona promissa aliquando praestanda promisit. Quae & μέγιστα maxima sunt, quia gloriosa & potiora omnibus; & τίμια pretiosa, quia & cum virtute sunt, & ad bonum nostrum aeternum conferunt: & Divinae naturae participes faciunt, quia per ea communionem cum Deo in Christo habemus, ut nobis sit in Deum, & nos ipsi simus populus, Jer. XXXI.33.34. Summa enim promissorum est: Fiam tibi & Semini tuo in Deum, Genes. XVII.7.8. Ego Jehova Sanctificator vester, Exod. XXXI.13. Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, qui benedixit nobis omni benedictione spirituali in supercoelestibus in Christo, Ephes. I.3. Non est Regnum Dei esus & potus, sed justitia, pax & gaudium in Spiritu Sancto, Rom. XIV.17. Fusius vero etiam explicantur, Jer. XXXI.33.34. Hebr. VIII.10 11.12. Hoc est Foedus, quod pangam cum domo Israel post dies illos, inquit Jehova: Do Legem meam in medio ipsorum, & super corde eorum scribam eam, & fiam ipsis Deus, & illi mihi fient populus. Et non docebunt amplius quisquam proximum suum, & quisquam fratrem suum, dicendo: Cognoscite Jehovam. Nam omnes ipsi cognoscent me, non minus parvus ipsorum, quam magnus ipsorum, ait Jehova. Nam condonabo pravitatem eorum, & peccati eorum non recordabor amplius.
units.tr: For the law of faith itself is carried in those promises, so that, announced with a joyful proclamation, it may apply them to the believer. "His divine power has given us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and virtue [τῷ ἰδίῳ κλήσει]. By these he has given us great and precious promises [τίμια ἐπαγγέλματα, μέγιστα], that through them you might become partakers of the divine nature, escaping the corruption that is in the world through lust" (2 Pet. 1:3–4). He calls them promises [ἐπαγγέλματα] because God, through Moses and the Prophets, promised good things to be bestowed at some time. They are also the greatest [μέγιστα], because they are glorious and more excellent than all others; and precious [τίμια], because they carry power and contribute to our eternal good; and they make us partakers of the divine nature, because through them we have communion with God in Christ, so that he may be our God and we may be his people (Jer. 31:33–34). For the sum of the promises is this: "I will be God to you and to your seed" (Gen. 17:7–8); "I am the Lord who sanctifies you" (Exod. 31:13); "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ" (Eph. 1:3); "The kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom. 14:17). They are explained more fully in Jer. 31:33–34 and Heb. 8:10–12: "This is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my law in their midst, and write it on their heart, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall no longer teach each one his neighbour and each his brother, saying, 'Know the Lord.' For all of them shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord. For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more."

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Sunt ergo Promissa haec Bona illa ἐξαίρετα, quae Deus olim per Christum sub Novo Testamento credentibus praestanda promisit, & in Christo demum praestitit. Quam jucundi pedes sunt מבשרי שוב evangelizantium Bona, verè & consummatè Bona, Esaj. L II.7. Hinc Evangelium דבר שוב בשורה verbum bonum Psal. XLV.2. Hebr. VI.5. Mich. VI.8. appellatur. Nituntur enim Testamento, non quovis illo, non Aeterno gratiae, cujus promissiones communes sunt omnibus credentibus omnium temporum: non Veteri & Typico, quod ad populum Israel ab omnibus aliis separatum spectans, antiquari, & cum ejusdem populi Ecclesia & Politia expirante ipsum quoque expirare debuit, Sed Novo; quo de Jos. 8.9. &c. fusius egimus. Ideo Διαθήκη κρείττων Testamentum melius, cujus Mediator Christus est, κρείττονος ἐπαγγελίαις melioribus promissionibus sancitum vel in Legis formulam redactum Apostolus, Hebr. VIII.6. dixit; comparans Testamentum melius cum Testamento Veteri & antiquando, quia non fuit ἀμεμπτος querimoniae expers, ibid. v.7. Meliores ergo illae promissiones sunt, quia Testamentum novum ipsum quoque melius est; & quatenus opponuntur promissionibus Testamenti gratiae Aeterni, quod apud Patres etiam obtinuit, & promissis communibus atque essentialibus, absque quibus salus non constat, absolvitur, sola τελειωσει consummatione nostri in hac vita per Redemptionem Christi ab his distinguuntur: quatenus vero promissionibus Testamenti Typici & Veteris opponuntur, abolito typo remipsam, typo figuratam repraesentant. Has igitur promissiones sic distinctas, & Oeconomiae Foederis Gratiae Evangelicae, Oeconomiae inprimis Foederis Gratiae Legali opositae, eximias propriasque cognoscere utile cumprimis & salutare est, ut eadem opera cognoscamus πολυποίκιλον σοφίαν & Θεοῦ multifariam sapientiam Dei; & quibus in rebus fors fidelium sub Evangelio, quam tenet Dominus, Ps. XVI.5. excedat fortem Sanctorum ante Christum, qui cupiverunt videre, quae nos videmus, & non viderunt; & audire, quae nos audimus, & non audiverunt, Matth. XIII.17. & ne cessemus indesinenter exclamare: Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, qui benedixit nobis in omni benedictione spirituali in supercoelestibus in Christo, Ephes. I.3.
units.tr: These promises, then, are those excellent good things which God once promised to bestow on believers under the New Testament through Christ, and which he finally bestowed in Christ. "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring the good tidings [מבשר טוב] of good things," truly and perfectly good, Isa. 52:7. Hence the Gospel is called "a good word" [דבר טוב בשורה], Ps. 45:2; Heb. 6:5; Mic. 6:8. For it rests on a Testament, not on any Testament whatever: not on the eternal covenant of grace, whose promises are common to all believers of every age; nor on the Old and typical Testament, which looked to the people of Israel as separate from all other peoples, and which had to be abolished and, together with the Church and polity of that people, had to expire as well. It rests on the New Testament, concerning which we have treated more fully at Josh. 8:9 and following. Therefore the Apostle, in Heb. 8:6, calls it a "better covenant" [διαθήκη κρείττων], whose Mediator is Christ, established on "better promises" [κρείττοσιν ἐπαγγελίαις], or reduced to the form of a law, comparing this better Testament with the Old one, which was to be done away with, because it was not "faultless" [ἄμεμπτος], free from complaint, ibid. v. 7. Those promises are therefore "better" because the New Testament itself is better. Insofar as they are set against the promises of the eternal covenant of grace, which held good also among the Fathers, and against the common and essential promises without which salvation does not stand, they are distinguished from these only by the consummation [τελείωσις] of our state in this life through the redemption of Christ. Insofar as they are set against the promises of the typical and Old Testament, they represent the thing itself, once the type has been abolished, which the type prefigured. It is therefore most useful and salutary to know these promises, distinguished in this way, and set against the economy of the covenant of evangelical grace, and especially against the economy of the covenant of legal grace, in their excellence and their own character; so that by the same work we may come to know "the manifold wisdom of God" [πολυποίκιλον σοφίαν Θεοῦ], and in what respects perhaps the lot of the faithful under the Gospel, which the Lord holds, Ps. 16:5, surpasses the lot of the saints before Christ, who desired to see what we see and did not see it, and to hear what we hear and did not hear, Matt. 13:17; and so that we may not cease to cry out without pause: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ," Eph. 1:3.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Ne erremus in re, in qua non omnes τὸ ἐν forte φρονίμως, τὸ ἐν etiam λέγειν, Ariadneo filio opus est. Cujus instar erit regula quam pridem sapienter cordati & consummati Theologi fixerunt, quod Scriptura diversa beneficia Foederis gratiae, velut remissionem peccatorum, effusionem Spiritus S. justificationem, inscriptionem Legis in corda, cognitionem Dei, aliaque ejusmodi saepe ita adscribat Oeconomiae N.T. perinde ac si illa filiis Dei in V.T. plane non contigisset, quamvis illis obtigerint, eo quod non eo gradu, mensura & perfectione iis obtigerunt. Ita cum Spiritus S. donatio nunquam credentibus defuerit, tamen ante glorificationem Christi eum fuisse diserte Johannes negat. Οὔπω γὰρ ἦν, inquit, Πνεῦμα ἅγιον, ὅτι ὁ Ἰησοῦς οὐδέπω ἐδοξάσθη. Nondum enim erat Spiritus S. quia Jesus nondum glorificatus erat, Joh. VII.39. Nondum erat, quia nondam tanta mensura, tanto perfectionis gradu erat, quanta post glorificationem Jesu donatus est. Par ratio est omnium illorum beneficiorum, quae sub N.T. demum danda promittuntur, Jer. XXXI.31. &c. perinde ac si ante N.T. non obtinuerint; cum tamen omnino obtinuerint, sed non cum τελειώσει consummatione sua, quae demum sub N.T. quando Foederi & Testamento Gratiae per ejusdem dedicationem per sanguinem Christi colophon accessit, & supremum velut, quale in terra obtinere potuit, fastigium impositum est. Non ergo beneficia ejusmodi de foederatis veteribus negantur absolute, sed comparate; non simpliciter, sed oeconomice; non quoad τὸ ὄν rem, sed quoad τὸ ποιον rei qualitatem, puta mensuram & consummationem, nec non dictionem Oeconomicam, secundum quam beneficium aliquod in emphasi & excellentia de foederatis veteribus negatur, quod simpliciter negatum existimari non debet. Ita veteribus non obtigisse justitiam, justificationem, remissionem peccatorum, Spiritum S. &c. oeconomica dictione, qua oeconomia imperfectior cum oeconomia perfectiore comparatur, & verbis Spiritui S. consuetis contenditur, verum est; quod ἁπλῶς simpliciter dictum non constat. Quae observatio logomachiis plurimus jugulum incidit, & de re ipsa concordes, at verbis, vel verborum non accurate satis Spiritus S. stylo conformatorum aucupiis discordantes facile conciliat.
units.tr: We must not err in a matter where not all have the wit to see clearly and to speak clearly; for it needs Ariadne's thread [τὸ ἐν φρονίμως, τὸ ἐν λέγειν]. The rule that wise and seasoned theologians laid down long ago will serve as that thread: Scripture often ascribes the various benefits of the covenant of grace, such as the remission of sins, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, justification, the writing of the law on the heart, the knowledge of God, and other such things, to the economy of the New Testament, just as if they had not at all fallen to the sons of God under the Old Testament, although they did fall to them, though not in that degree, measure and perfection. Thus, although the gift of the Holy Spirit was never lacking to believers, John plainly denies that he was yet present before the glorification of Christ: "For the Holy Spirit was not yet [Οὔπω γὰρ ἦν Πνεῦμα ἅγιον], because Jesus was not yet glorified [ὅτι ὁ Ἰησοῦς οὐδέπω ἐδοξάσθη]," John 7:39. He was not yet present, because he was not yet in such measure and at such a degree of perfection as he was given after the glorification of Jesus. The same reasoning holds for all those benefits which are promised to be given only under the New Testament, Jer. 31:31 and following, as if they had not been obtained before the New Testament; yet they were indeed obtained, but not in their consummation, which at last, under the New Testament, when the covenant and Testament of grace received its seal through the dedication by the blood of Christ, was added, and the highest summit, such as could be attained on earth, was set upon it. Such benefits are therefore not denied absolutely to the covenanted of old, but comparatively; not simply, but economically; not as to the substance of the thing [τὸ ὄν, rem], but as to its quality [τὸ ποιόν, rei qualitatem], namely its measure and consummation, and also the economic manner of speaking, according to which some benefit is denied to the covenanted of old in an emphatic and excellent sense, which ought not to be thought simply denied. Thus it is true that justice, justification, the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, and so on, were not obtained by the Old Testament saints, in the economic manner of speaking, in which the more imperfect economy is compared with the more perfect and the usual language of the Holy Spirit is used; but it is not established as true when said absolutely [ἁπλῶς]. This observation easily cuts the throat of very many verbal contests, and reconciles those who agree in the matter itself but disagree over words, or over the search for expressions not sufficiently exact in the style of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: XXXIV.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: In universum ergo Scriptura fideles N.T. τελειῶσθαι consummari asserit. Ut omnes unum sint, quemadmodum tu Pater in me, & ego in te, ut & ipsi in nobis unum sint, &c. Ego in ipsis, & tu in me, ut sint πεπληρωμένοι εἰς ἓν consummati in unum, Joh. XVII.21.23. quia quod summum & perfectissimum in hac vita haberi potest.
units.tr: In general, then, Scripture asserts that the faithful of the New Testament are made perfect [τελειῶσθαι], that is, consummated. "That they may all be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us," etc. "I in them, and you in me, that they may be made perfect [πεπληρωμένοι] into one," John 17:21, 23. This is because it is the highest and most perfect state that can be had in this life.

units.la: Scripturae consummationem Christi & fidelium Novo Testamento attribuunt. potest, adepti, commune id habent omnes, & quidem in Deo uno, qui ut unus est, ita iis uno modo fit in Deum, ut eodem modo in eo glorientur. Lex nihil τελείωσις consummavit. sed subintroductio melioris spei, per quam approximamus Deo, Hebr.VII.19. Cum enim τελείωσις consummatio, ut subsequens quid differre & a Lege procul ostendi debuerit, manifestum est, non in Lege, vel a Lege, sed in Evangelio & ab eo praestari eam debuisse; & praestitam esse per ἐλπίδα spem, non qualemcunque, sed eam, per quam remoto velo, in Christo proximè, & solo eo mediante, ad Deum accedimus. Quo statu nihil perfectius in hac vita existit. Nam etiam τελείωσις συνειδήσεως consummatio conscientiae, per quam ad Deum tranquillo corde, testante nobis conscientia, quòd id, quod unum Deo gratum & acceptum est, in solidum teneamus, accedimus, & quam non umbrae, non Lex, non munera & sacrificia, sed καιρὸς διορθώσεως tempus correctionis praestare potuit, in eodem statu obtinet, Hebr.IX.9.10. Umbram habens Lex futurorum bonorum, nunquam potest accedentes τελειῶσαι consummare, ibid.X.1. quia non Lex, sed Evangelium solidum plenúmque gaudium, & eum gradum amoris, in quo in hac etiam vita Deus amari & glorificari potest, parit. Non enim expectatio, sed adeptio & visio rei expectatae expectantem perficit. Si τελείωσις consummatio per Leviticum Sacerdotium facta est, quid opus erat secundum ordinem Melchisedeci Sacerdotem alium constitui? ibid.VII.11. Et Patres quidem licet testimonium adepti per fidem, non tamen promissione, (κατ' ἐξοχὴν tali, Christi puta & bonorum N.T. quae illis facta est tum explicitè in verbo de benedictione & sanctificatione in Semine; tum ἀντιγμάτως δεύτερον in figuris & umbris) potiti sunt, Deo de nobis κρεῖττον τι melius quid providente, ne sine nobis consummarentur, hoc est, ut & illi in Coelo per aspectum gloriae, & nos in terra etiam per fidem & collationem bonorum praestantiorum, adeóque nos non sine illis consummaremur; ibid.XI.39.40. Neque illud de nihilo est, quòd S. Paulus verba Dei apud Jeremiam cap.XXXI.31. אכרת Feriam cum domo Israel, & cum domo Jehudah foedus novum, sic exponit: συντελέσω consummabo super domum Israel, & super domum Juda foedus novum, Hebr.VIII.8. quasi dicat, Perficiam foedus meum, ut jam foederis Gratiae, per introductionem praestantiorum promissorum, mensuram omnem impleat.
units.tr: Scripture attributes the consummation of Christ and of the faithful to the New Testament. They all hold this in common, and indeed in the one God, who is one and so becomes one to them in one way, so that they glory in him in the same way. The Law consummated nothing [τελείωσις], but there was a bringing in of a better hope, through which we draw near to God, Heb. 7:19. For since consummation [τελείωσις] must be something that goes beyond and is shown to differ from the Law, it is clear that it was to be provided not by the Law or from the Law, but in and by the Gospel. And it has been provided through a hope [ἐλπίς], not just any hope, but that through which, the veil being removed, we draw near to God, directly in Christ and through him alone. Nothing more perfect than this state exists in this life. For there is also the consummation of conscience [τελείωσις συνειδήσεως], by which we approach God with a quiet heart, conscience bearing witness to us that we hold firmly to what alone is pleasing and acceptable to God. This consummation, which neither shadows, nor the Law, nor gifts and sacrifices, but only the time of correction [καιρὸς διορθώσεως] could provide, is possessed in the same state, Heb. 9:9–10. The Law, having a shadow of good things to come, can never make those who draw near perfect [τελειῶσαι], Heb. 10:1. For it is not the Law but the Gospel that brings solid and full joy, and that degree of love in which God can be loved and glorified even in this life. For it is not expectation but the attaining and seeing of what was expected that perfects the one who expects. If consummation [τελείωσις] was accomplished through the Levitical priesthood, why was there any need for another priest to be raised up according to the order of Melchisedec? Heb. 7:11. And indeed the Fathers, though they obtained the testimony of faith, yet not the promise (in the highest sense, namely the good things of Christ and of the New Testament, which were made to them both explicitly in the word about blessing and sanctification in the Seed, and a second time in figures and shadows [ἀντιγμάτως δεύτερον]), had it, God providing something better for us, so that they should not be consummated without us, that is, that they in heaven through the sight of glory, and we on earth through faith and the bestowal of better goods, might not be consummated without them; Heb. 11:39–40. Nor is it without meaning that St Paul expounds the words of God in Jeremiah 31:31, "I will make a new covenant [אכרת] with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah," thus: "I will consummate [συντελέσω] a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah," Heb. 8:8, as if to say: I will bring my covenant to perfection, so that the covenant of grace, through the introduction of better promises, might fill up its whole measure.

units.la: XXXV. Est igitur consummatio Ecclesiae sub N.T. is status fidelium, quo in Christo, Principe salutis, per passiones consummato, & ipsi in terra adhuc existentes sic consummantur, ut sublato tum reatu, nec non accusatione & effectibus reatus, qui in Sanctos ad ipsorum humiliationem cadebant: tum interstitio illo, quo a gentibus dispescebantur, cum laetitia Deum ament, in spe ad eum, tanquam Sacerdotes, accedant, in omnibus haereditatem, velut Reges, adeant, & plenam, qualis in hac vita obtinere potest, justitiam, libertatem & pacem possideant. Proin non absoluta illa, & omnibus numeris exacta, sed comparata cum statu fidelium prioris temporis est; neque etiam talis, qualis est δικαίων τετελειωμένων justorum consummatorum in Coelo, Hebr. XII.23. Licet enim ad spiritus justorum consummatorum in Coelo accessisse nos ibidem Apostolus dicat, quatenus cum illis secundum spiritum in Coelo consummatis (licet corpora eorum in terra adhuc quiescant) justitiae, pacis & laetitiae in Christo communionem in hac etiam vita habemus: tamen non aequè ac illi in Coelo, nos in terra etiam consummamur. Alia enim Coelestis, alia terrestris fidelium consummatio est. Sicut haec in Coelo locum habere non potest; ita nec illa in terra obtingit. Non quod jam acceperim, ἢ ἤδη τετελειωμαι aut jam consummatus sim, sed persequor, si & apprehendam, propter quod & apprehensus sum a Christo Jesu, Phil.III.12. Non enim in hac vita consummamur in veritate illa, ad quam vivificati cum Christo resurreximus, quia dicere non possumus, nos non habere peccatum, carnem, defectum, nos esse divites, neque quicquam nobis deesse, Rom.VII.4. Gal.V.17.1.Joh.1.8.9.10. Apoc.III.17. Quandiu in homine peccatum, caro, mortalitas, luctà est, tandiu Deus non est πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν omnia in omnibus, 1.Cor.XV.28. neque adeò perinde uti Coelites in Coelo, nos etiam in terra consummamur. Neque etiam S. Paulus dicens: Bonum certamen certavi, cursum consummavi, fidem servavi, 2.Tim.IV.7. in hac etiam vita se simpliciter consummatum profitetur; sed de absoluto curriculo suo, non perveniendo ad perfectionem, sed Evangelium Christi sufficienter, juxta mensuram sui canonis, fideliter & irreprehensibiliter praedicando impensè sibi gratulatur. Loquitur enim de καλῷ ἀγῶνι bono certamine. Atqui etiam in luctâ spiritus adversus carnem καλῶς ἀγωνίζεται bene certatur. Retinuisse se fidem in Christum, eique in obeundo ministerio fidem illibatam servasse dicit; at sic ita se τετελεωμένον consummatum, ut nihil amplius sibi desit, non dicit. Quin potius se coronam justitiae, quae in perfecta sanctificatione & laetitia est, propediem in Coelo sibi imponendam, nondum impositam, expectare testatur.
units.tr: XXXV. The consummation of the Church under the New Testament is therefore that state of the faithful in which, Christ, the Author of salvation, having been consummated through his sufferings, they themselves, still existing on earth, are so consummated that guilt is removed, and also the accusation and the effects of guilt, which used to fall upon the saints to their humiliation; and that separation by which they were set apart from the nations is removed; so that they love God with joy, approach him in hope as priests, enter into the inheritance in all things as kings, and possess a full righteousness, liberty and peace, such as can be had in this life. Hence it is not that absolute state, exact in every respect, but one compared with the state of the faithful of earlier times; nor is it such as the consummation of the just made perfect in heaven [δικαίων τετελειωμένων], Heb. 12:23. For although the Apostle there says that we have come to the spirits of the just made perfect in heaven, inasmuch as we, in spirit, have communion with them in heaven (though their bodies still rest on earth) in righteousness, peace and joy in Christ, even in this life, yet we are not consummated on earth in the same way as they are in heaven. For the heavenly consummation is one thing, and the earthly consummation of the faithful another. As the former cannot take place here, so the latter does not occur on earth. Not that I have already received, or am already made perfect [ἢ ἤδη τετελειωμαι], or am already consummated, but I press on, if I may also lay hold of that for which I was laid hold of by Christ Jesus, Phil. 3:12. For we are not consummated in this life in that truth into which we rose, quickened with Christ, because we cannot say that we have no sin, no flesh, no defect, that we are rich and lack nothing, Rom. 7:4; Gal. 5:17; 1 John 1:8–10; Rev. 3:17. As long as sin, flesh and mortality struggle in a man, God is not all in all [πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν], 1 Cor. 15:28, and we are not consummated on earth in the same way as the heavenly ones in heaven. Nor does St Paul, when he says, I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith, 2 Tim. 4:7, profess himself simply consummated even in this life. He rejoices exceedingly, not in having reached perfection, but in having completed his course, preaching the Gospel of Christ faithfully and blamelessly, sufficiently according to the measure of his canon. For he speaks of the good fight [καλῷ ἀγῶνι]. Yet even in the struggle of the spirit against the flesh the good fight is fought well [καλῶς ἀγωνίζεται]. He says that he kept hold of faith in Christ, and that in discharging his ministry he kept the faith unblemished; but he does not say that he is so consummated [τετελεωμένον] that nothing more is lacking to him. Rather, he testifies that he awaits the crown of righteousness, which consists in perfect sanctification and joy, to be placed upon him shortly in heaven, not yet placed.

units.la: XXXVI. Consummatio haec oeconomica in omnia Novi Testamenti bona, in Evangelio praeconiata, se diffudit. Ante omnia enim Jesus Christus, Novi & Melioris Testamenti Mediator, & bonorum omnium N.T. author & ipse in Evangelio consummatus praedicatur. Nam moribundus exclamavit τετέλεσται consummatum est, Joh.XIX.30. q.d. jam certamen meum peregi; implevi, quae mihi ut Sponsori & Sacerdoti, ad damnandum peccatum, & adducendam justitiam seculorum incumbunt. Ipsi enim passio erat sua τελείωσις consummatio. Ideo Herodi renuntiari jussit: Ecce ego daemonia ejicio, & hodie atque cras sanationes perficio, καὶ τῇ τρίτῃ τελεῦμαι & tertio die consummor, Luc. XIII.32. Nam decebat Deum, propter quem omnia sunt, & per quem omnia sunt, multis filiis in gloriam jam introductis, Principem salutis per passiones τελειῶσαι consummare, Hebr.II.19. Quia enim per passiones aeternam redemptionem invenit, justitiae effectum acquisivit, & in iisdem sic tentatus est, ut de vera & perfecta ejus obedientia liqueret, ideo in iisdem τελείωσιν consummationem Christi Scripturae statuunt. Erat ille hactenus Sponsor, & sponsionis ejus vi filii in gloriam introducti sunt. Sed nec dum ille vadimonium obivit, donec moreretur, & moriendo justitiae Dei in solidum satisfaceret. Demum ex iis, quae passus est, didicit obedientiam, & τελειωθεὶς consum consummatus factus est omnibus illi obedientibus αἴτιος σωτηρίας αἰωνίου causa salutis æternæ, ibid. V. 8.9. Sine consummatione illa Salus nostra τῆς ... confici non potuit, quia Deum ἐπρέπε decebat, ibid.II.10. hoc est, virtutibus ejus, quas semper occultare, & occultando negare nec voluit, nec potuit, consentaneum erat, ut per passiones, ceu salutis æternæ causa, consumma- retur. Ideo etiam Sacerdos εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετελειωμένον in æternum consummatus, ibid.VII.28. appellatur, quia in eo, & quidem in seculum consummato nulla alia consummatione indigemus, sed τελείαν παρρησίαν plenariam fiduciam & libertatem filiorum adipiscimur.
units.tr: XXXVI. This economical consummation spread itself to all the goods of the New Testament proclaimed in the Gospel. First of all, Jesus Christ, Mediator of the New and Better Covenant, and the author of all the goods of the New Testament, is proclaimed as himself consummated in the Gospel. For when dying he cried out, It is finished [τετέλεσται], John 19:30, as if to say: now I have finished my contest; I have fulfilled what was laid upon me as Surety and Priest, to condemn sin and bring in everlasting righteousness. For his passion was his own consummation. Hence he told them to report to Herod: "Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am consummated [καὶ τῇ τρίτῃ τελεῦμαι]," Luke 13:32. For it befitted God, for whom and through whom are all things, having brought many sons into glory, to make the Author of their salvation perfect through sufferings [τελειῶσαι], Heb. 2:10. For because through sufferings he found eternal redemption and obtained the effect of righteousness, and was so tested in them that his true and perfect obedience was made clear, therefore Scripture places the consummation of Christ in them. Until then he had been Surety, and by the power of his suretyship the sons were brought into glory. But he had not yet discharged his bond until he died and, by dying, fully satisfied the justice of God. Finally, from what he suffered he learned obedience, and having been made consummate [τελειωθεὶς] became the cause [αἴτιος σωτηρίας αἰωνίου] of eternal salvation to all who obey him, Heb. 5:8–9. Without that consummation our salvation could not be accomplished [τῆς ... confici non potuit], because it befitted God [ἐπρέπε], Heb. 2:10. That is, it was fitting, for his virtues, which he never wished or was able to hide and deny by concealing them, that he should be consummated through sufferings as the cause of eternal salvation. Therefore he is also called a Priest consummated for ever [εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετελειωμένον], Heb. 7:28, because in him, consummated for the age, we need no other consummation, but obtain full confidence and the freedom of sons [τελείαν παρρησίαν].

units.la: XXXVII. Maximum illud Evangelii
units.tr: XXXVII. That greatest result of the Gospel

units.la: ἀποτέλεσμα est, quod in eo prædicatur Christus Jesus, qui in mundum venit, ut peccatores salvaret, 1.Tim.I.15. qui ceu Germen ex alto nos in visceribus misericordiæ Dei nostri visitavit, Luc.I.78. nec visitavit tantum, sed etiam justitiam omnem implevit, Matth.III.15. Deum ἐξηγήσατο enarravit, Joh.I.18. locutus est verba Dei, ibid.III.34. sanguinem pro nobis effudit, Matth.XXVI.28. animam λύτρον pretium redemptionis nostræ dedit, ibid. XX.28. mundum Deo conciliavit, 2.Cor.V.19. victa morte super omnes Cœlos ascendit, Ephes. IV.10. Ad dextram Dei pro nobis intercedit, Rom. VIII.34. gloriosa nimirum intercessione, in sanguine Testamenti æterni fundata, Hebr.XIII.20. Atque sic consummatus Salutis princeps, & perfecta salutis nostræ causa extitit. Extra controversiam (fatentibus id tum iis, qui credunt: tum iis, qui non credunt, quia illud ceu nimis mirabile respuunt) magnum (רחוב latum, Deo gloriosum, & magnitudini ejus maxime consentaneum) est pietatis mysterium: Deus est manifestatus in carne, justificatus in Spiritu, visus Angelis, prædicatus gentibus, creditus in mundo, susceptus in gloria, 1.Tim.III.16. Radix illa Jesse stat לנס in vexillum populorum, Esaj.XI.10. Sicut enim signum vexillum, pharus, φρυκτωρία, malus in monte positus conspicuus est omnibus: ita nunc Christus stat in signum, ut in se per verbum suum conspicuus sit. Ipse vero, non alius, stat in signum, ut quamvis non videatur, tamen cunctis ad fidem per se sufficienter innotescat. Ipsum enim Evangelium nobis est pro αὐτοψία oculari visione Christi; & vel ideo maxime πιστὸν credibile est, quia Christus, quem admodum promissus est, venit, & à Deo demonstratus est Christus & Dominus, cum tali efficacia & evidentia dictorum & factorum, & effusione Spiritus S. ut Evangelium non prius libros quam aures hominum & animos impleverit: Libri autem ab Apostolis scripti & traditi sint indubitati testes eorum, quæ alii viderunt & audiverunt. Licet ergo Christus à terris absens in Cœlo ad dextram Dei sedeat, Evangelium tamen præsentem & conspicabilem eum nobis facit & καὶ ὀφθαλμῶς προγεγραμμένον ante oculos depingit, velut crucifixum in nobis, Gal. III.1. quia non tantum coram oculis totius mundi crucifixus est, verum etiam in nobis, coram animis nostris, ut videamus eum filium Dei, qui dilexit nos, & se ipsum pro nobis tradidit.
units.tr: The greatest result of the Gospel is this: in it Christ Jesus is proclaimed, who came into the world to save sinners, 1 Tim. 1.15; who as the Branch from on high has visited us in the bowels of mercy of our God, Luke 1.78; and who not only visited us but also fulfilled all righteousness, Matt. 3.15; declared God [ἐξηγήσατο], John 1.18; spoke the words of God, ibid. 3.34; poured out his blood for us, Matt. 26.28; gave his soul as a ransom [λύτρον], the price of our redemption, ibid. 20.28; reconciled the world to God, 2 Cor. 5.19; having conquered death, ascended above all the heavens, Eph. 4.10; intercedes for us at the right hand of God, Rom. 8.34, with glorious intercession, founded in the blood of the eternal testament, Heb. 13.20. And so the consummated Prince of Salvation has stood forth as the perfect cause of our salvation. Beyond controversy (as both those who believe and those who do not believe admit it, the latter rejecting it as too wonderful) great [רחוב: broad, glorious to God, and most fitting to his greatness] is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached to the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory, 1 Tim. 3.16. That root of Jesse stands [לנס] for an ensign of the peoples, Isa. 11.10. For just as a standard, a beacon, a signal fire, or a mast set on a mountain is visible to all, so now Christ stands as a sign, that he may be made conspicuous in himself through his word. He himself, and no other, stands as a sign, so that although he is not seen, he is nonetheless made sufficiently known to all for faith through himself. For the Gospel itself is for us an eyewitness [αὐτοψία], the ocular vision of Christ; and it is most of all for this reason credible [πιστὸν], because Christ has come just as he was promised, and has been shown by God to be Christ and Lord, with such efficacy and evidence in his words and deeds, and with such an outpouring of the Holy Spirit, that the Gospel filled the ears and minds of men before it filled books. The books written and handed down by the Apostles are unquestionable witnesses of those things which others saw and heard. Although Christ, absent from earth, therefore sits in heaven at the right hand of God, the Gospel nevertheless makes him present and visible to us, and paints him before our eyes [ὀφθαλμῶς προγεγραμμένον], as crucified among us, Gal. 3.1, because he was crucified not only before the eyes of the whole world but also in us, before our minds, so that we may see him as the Son of God, who loved us and gave himself up for us.

units.la: XXXVIII. In Christo Capite consummato etiam fideles, membra ejus, consummati intelliguntur. Estis in ipso (Christo) πεπληρωμένοι completi, qui est caput omnis principatus & potestatis, Col.II.10. Ecclesia est corpus Christi, τὸ πλήρωμα πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν πληρουμένου complementum, vel completum ejus, qui omnia in omnibus complet, Ephes.I.23. III.19. Est enim Tzion (spiritualis maximè, ex qua Lex exivit, Esaj.II.2. perfectio pulchritudinis, Psal. L.2. quia gratiam Dei plenam & consummatam in Christo consummato possidet. Nam explenitudine ejus nos omnes accepimus χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος gratiam pro gratia, Joh.I.16. Quid enim desiderare possumus, quod ex ejus plenitudine & divitiis non acceperimus, qui factus est nobis sapientia à Deo & justitia, & sanctificatio & redemptio, 1.Cor.I.30. Nam Lex per Mosen data est; gratia (plena, quæ per Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν præstatur) & veritas (res, complementum typorum, imago rerum) per Jesum Christum, Joh.I.17. Ideo Christus in Evangelio, ceu τελειωτὴς & πίστεως consummator fidei, Hebr.XII.2. proponitur. Nam & promissa & sperata dat: & fidelibus πεῖσμα firmitudinem fidei, ne ulla seductione vel terrore labefactetur: & fidelium imprimis expectantium salvationem à peccatis & à jugo ad tempus impositio servitutem, in lætitiam, gratiarum actionem & usum libertatis in accedendo ad Deum commutat. Quod effecit ut Sacerdos, initians viam illam πρόσφατον recentem ad Deum, Hebr.X.20. & annuntians remissionem plenam peccatorum, & Spiritum virtutis, charitatis, filiationis secundum mensuram eorum, quæ ab ipso implentur, effundens, Ephes.I.13-23. Qui descendit, ipse etiam est, qui ascendit super omnes Cœlos, ut omnia impleret, ibid.IV.10. Omnia & in omnibus Christus est, Col.III.11. ut caput, per Spiritum omnia sibi uniens, ut causa omnium, ut implens omnia se ipso & donis suis. Ut jure merito Jesum præstitum Messiam sic Ecclesia alloquatur: Tu coronas annum (שנת annum) beneplaciti Domino, Esaj.LXI.2.) שובך bono tuo, & semita tua stillant pinguedinem, Psalm. LXV.12. XXXIX. Pertinent ergo huc proprie eximia illa uberrima & διαφορώτερα Novi Testamenti Bona, quibus fideles à Christo per passiones consummato, & ipsi consummati in hac vita supra Patres fideles V.T. eminent. Quæ diversimodè Scripturæ enumerant, quia & individuo nexu cohærent: & modo explicitè in speciebus, modo implicitè in genere spectantur. Unde modò pauciora, modò plura statuuntur, Solius Benedictionis nomine, Gen.XXII.18. Gal. III.14. Ephes.I.3. veniunt, quia in omnibus Divina benedictio conspicua est, Jeremias cap. XXXI.31-34. quatuor, Inscriptionem Legis Dei in corda, adoptionem, notitiam Dei, nulli authenticæ institutioni humanæ subjectam, & peccatorum remissionem in emphasi. Daniel cap.IX.24. Sex, coercitionem defectionis, peccati obsignationem, pravitatis expiationem, justitiæ seculorum adductionem, visionis & Prophetiæ obsignationem, & Sanctuarii unctionem: Angeli Luc.II.14. tria, Glorificationem Dei in excelsis, pacem in terris, & benevolentiam in hominibus: S.Paulus Rom. XIV.17. itidem tria, justitiam, pacem & lætitiam in Spiritu S. faciunt. Explicatiora in τελείωσι consummatione Justitiæ, Adoptionis per Spiritum promissionis, Sapientiæ, Sanctitatis, Libertatis, Pacis, Communionis cum Cœlitibus, Lætitiæ & Consolationis {a} membra eius consummata intelliguntur solationis, Cultus, Prædicationis, Hæreditatis rerum extra nos, & Obsignationis conspiciuntur. Cuncta enim Evangelii ἀτελεσματα in Scripturis sparsim tradita ad hæc, nisi fallor, capita redigunter. Et sunt hæc Bona in universum Fœderis gratiæ. Sed quicquid de illis œconomia Promissionis, & inprimis Legis itadelibavit, ut illa ἀτελεστεραimperfectiora quodammodo sub œconomiis illis evaserint, illud omne Evangelium sub Novo Testamento perficit & consummat.
units.tr: XXXVIII. In Christ the Head, the faithful, his members, are also understood to be made complete. "You are complete in him (Christ), who is the head of every principality and power," Col. 2.10. The Church is the body of Christ, the fullness [τὸ πλήρωμα] of him who fills all things in all, Eph. 1.23; 3.19. For Zion (chiefly the spiritual Zion, from which the Law went forth, Isa. 2.2) is the perfection of beauty, Ps. 50.2, because she possesses the full and perfected grace of God in the consummated Christ. For from his fullness we have all received, "grace for grace" [χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος], John 1.16. For what can we desire that we have not received from his fullness and riches, he who has been made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption, 1 Cor. 1.30? For the Law was given through Moses; grace (full grace, which is bestowed through Jesus Christ) and truth (the reality, the fulfilment of the types, the image of the things) came through Jesus Christ, John 1.17. Therefore Christ is set forth in the Gospel as the perfecter [τελειωτής] and "consummator of faith," Heb. 12.2. For he both gives the things promised and hoped for, and gives the faithful a firm anchor [πεῖσμα] of faith, so that it is not overthrown by any seduction or terror; and above all for the faithful who look for salvation from sins, he changes the yoke of servitude imposed for a time into joy, thanksgiving, and the use of liberty in drawing near to God. This has brought it about that the Priest, "initiating the way" [πρόσφατον] new to God, Heb. 10.20, and announcing the full remission of sins, and pouring out the Spirit of power, love and sonship according to the measure of those things which are filled up by him, Eph. 1.13-23. "He who descended is himself also he who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things," ibid. 4.10. "Christ is all and in all," Col. 3.11, as head, uniting all things to himself through the Spirit, as cause of all, filling all things by himself and by his gifts. Thus the Church rightly addresses the Messiah now exhibited: "You crown the year [שנה] of the Lord's good pleasure," Isa. 61.2; "your goodness [שובך]" and "your paths drip with fatness," Ps. 65.12.

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Primum igitur & palmarium Novi Testamenti Bonum Justitia, seu perfectæ justitiæ per mortem Christi exhibitio est. Nam illa inprimis olim promissa, & in tempore per obedientiam à Christo Legi agendo & patiendo præstitam exhibita est. In Justitia firmaberis, Esaj.LIV.14. In Jehova justificabuntur & gloriabuntur omne Semen Israel, ibid.cap.XLV.25. Prope est justitia mea ut reveletur, ibid.cap.LVI.1. Ecce dies venient, ait Jehova, & excitabo David Germen justum, quod regnabit Rex & prosperabitur, & faciet judicium & justitiam in terra. In diebus ejus salvabitur Juda, & Israel habitabit securè, & hoc nomen ejus, quo quis vocabit eum, יהוה צדקנו Jehova Justitia nostra, Jer.XXIII.5.6. Septuaginta hebdomadæ sunt, &c. לחביא צדק עולמים ad adducendam justitiam seculorum, Dan.IX.24. Quod adducendum esse Angelus dicit, illud prius adductum non fuit. In Evangelio revelatur δικαιοσύνη δεοῦ justitia Dei, Rom.III.21. vel justitia ἐκ Θεοῦ ex Deo, Phil.III.9. ἐκ πίστεως ex fide, Rom.I.17. III.22. X.6. Phil.III.9. quia fides est, qua credimus, Jesum traditum propter lapsus nostros, & resuscitatum propter justificationem nostram, Rom.IV.25. quæ nos Christi & justitiæ ejus compotes facit. Per fidem induimus Christum, Gal.III.26.27. Pallio justitiæ cooperuit me, Jesaj.LXI.10. Unde fides in justitiam imputari dicitur, Rom.IV.5. Regnum Dei non est esca & potus, sed justitia, &c. ibid.XIV.17. Plena est Scriptura testimoniis, quibus justitia seu obedientia legi à Christo moriente præstita decantatur. Nam vel ipse in plenitudine temporum eam præstitit: vel nunquam ea præstita est, vel præstabitur, atque ita generis humani salus conclamata est.
units.tr: The first and chief good of the New Testament is righteousness, that is, the bestowal of perfect righteousness through the death of Christ. For this was promised long ago and was actually bestowed in time, when Christ rendered it by obeying and suffering under the Law. "In righteousness you shall be established," Isa. 54:14. "In the LORD shall all the seed of Israel be justified and shall glory," ibid. ch. 45:25. "My righteousness is near to be revealed," ibid. ch. 56:1. "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and righteousness in the earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely; and this is the name whereby he shall be called, יהוה צדקנו [Jehovah our Righteousness]," Jer. 23:5–6. "Seventy weeks are determined... to bring in everlasting righteousness [לחביא צדק עולמים]," Dan. 9:24. The angel says that this righteousness was to be brought in, and that it had not been brought in before. In the Gospel "the righteousness of God [δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ] is revealed," Rom. 3:21, or "the righteousness which is of God [ἐκ Θεοῦ]," Phil. 3:9; "[the righteousness] which is by faith [ἐκ πίστεως]," Rom. 1:17; 3:22; 10:6; Phil. 3:9. This is because faith is that by which we believe that Jesus "was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification," Rom. 4:25; and faith makes us partakers of Christ and of his righteousness. "As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ," Gal. 3:26–27. "He hath covered me with the robe of righteousness," Isa. 61:10. Hence faith is said to be imputed for righteousness, Rom. 4:5. "The kingdom of God is not meat and drink, but righteousness," etc., ibid. 14:17. Scripture is full of testimonies in which the righteousness, or obedience to the Law, rendered by Christ dying is proclaimed. For either he himself rendered it in the fulness of time, or it was never rendered, or will never be rendered, and so the salvation of the human race would be lost.

units.la: XLI.
units.tr: XLI.

units.la: Cum justitiæ Christi exhibitione ipsa consummata ἀπολύτρωσις redemptio, δικαίωσις justificatio, qua peccator credens propter Christi justitiam remissionis peccatorum & justitiæ universæ à Lege ad vitam requisitæ compos fit, & καταλλαγή reconciliatio cohærent. Quia enim Christus legi satisfecit, ejusque justitiam omnem implevit, iccirco ii, qui sub N.T. sunt, plenæ & consummatæ redemptionis, justificationis, peccatorum remissionis & reconciliationis participes fiunt. Clarum enim est, beneficia isthæc in τελειώσει & emphasi sua olim ceu futura promissa & in tempore demum exhibita esse. Gratis venditi estis & absque pretio תנאלו redimemini, Esaj.LII.3. In cognitione sui justus servus meus multos justificabit, & iniquitates eorum portabit, ibid.LIII.11. Condonabo pravitatem eorum, & peccati eorum non recordabor amplius, Jerem. XXXI.34. Septuaginta hebdomadæ decisæ sunt, &c. לכפר עון ad expiandum peccatum, Dan.IX.24. Delebo pravitatem terræ illius uno die, unico sacrificio ἐφάπαξ semel, Zach.III.9. Quibus testimoniis, ut plura gemella omittam, diserte futura quædam אתלו ἀπολύτρωσις redemptio, peccati condonatio, justificatio promittitur. Et talis quidem promittitur, qualis durantibus sacrificiis obtinere non potuit. Nam ubi est remissio peccatorum (soluto pretio & facta eorum expiatione, adeoque plena & consummata) ibi non amplius est oblatio pro peccato, Hebr.X.18. Ubi ergo oblatio pro peccato est, ibi remissio non est. Ideo hæc cuncta in tempore à Christo per passiones consummato allata dicuntur. In ipso habemus ἀπολύτρωσιν redemptionem per sanguinem ejus, Col.I.14. Is factus est nobis ἀπολύτρωσις redemptio, 1.Cor.I.30. Justificamur gratis gratia ejus, per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Jesu, quem proposuit nobis Propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ejus, ad demonstrationem justitiæ ejus διὰ τὴν πάρεσιν τῶν προγεγονότων ἁμαρτημάτων propter remissionem, vel dissimulationem (nam & sanguis Christi eum in finem effusus est, ut per eum præteritæ peccata expiarentur, & quia nondum expiata præterita peccata, sed dissimulatione quadam velut olim expianda, transmissa sunt, sanguis Christi effundi debuit,) peccatorum præteritorum, Rom.III.24.25. Nam peccata præterita nondum fuso sanguine Christi, in eodem punita nondum hactenus fuerunt, adeoque dissimulata antehac, hoc est, actuali poena nondum soluta, expiata, & sic in emphasi nondum condonata, demum morte Christi intercedente condonari, remitti potuerunt. Propter hoc enim Christus Novi Testamenti Mediator est, ut morte intercedente ad redemptionem transgressionum sub primo Testamento, promissionem acciperent vocati æternæ hereditatis, Hebr.IX.15. Semel is in consummatione seculorum per ablationem sui ipsius manifestatus est εἰς ἀθέτησιν τῆς ἁμαρτίας ad abolitionem peccati, ibid.v.24. quam peccati abolitionem plenariam etiam plenaria & consummata cum Deo καταλλαγή reconciliatio conjecuta est. Nam si, cùm essemus inimici, reconciliati summus Deo per mortem Filii ejus, quanto magis reconciliati salvabimur in vita ejus? Rom.V.10.
units.tr: With the bestowal of Christ's righteousness are joined the redemption accomplished in it [ἀπολύτρωσις], justification [δικαίωσις], by which the believing sinner, on account of Christ's righteousness, becomes a partaker of forgiveness of sins and of all the righteousness which the Law required for life, and reconciliation [καταλλαγή]. For because Christ satisfied the Law and fulfilled all its righteousness, therefore those who are under the New Testament become partakers of full and complete redemption, justification, forgiveness of sins and reconciliation. For it is clear that these benefits, in their perfection and emphasis, were promised in former times as things to come, and were bestowed only in time. "You have been sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money [תנאלו]," Isa. 52:3. "By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many, for he shall bear their iniquities," ibid. 53:11. "I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more," Jer. 31:34. "Seventy weeks are determined... to make reconciliation for iniquity [לכפר עון]," Dan. 9:24. "I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day [ἐφάπαξ, once for all]," Zech. 3:9. In these testimonies, to omit many similar ones, certain things are plainly promised for the future: redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις], forgiveness of sin, justification. And they are promised in such a form as could not be obtained while the sacrifices continued. For where there is remission of sins (the price having been paid and their expiation made, and so full and complete), there is no longer any offering for sin, Heb. 10:18. Where there is an offering for sin, therefore, there is no remission. Hence all these things are said to have been brought in time by Christ, who consummated them through his sufferings. "In him we have redemption [ἀπολύτρωσιν] through his blood," Col. 1:14. "He was made unto us redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις]," 1 Cor. 1:30. "We are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness, for the remission [διὰ τὴν πάρεσιν] of the sins that are past," Rom. 3:24–25. Or, rendered as "the passing over of the sins that were committed beforehand," the sense is that the sins were passed over, or overlooked, and not yet expiated, and so the blood of Christ had to be shed. For sins past, not yet punished in the shedding of Christ's blood, had until then been overlooked, that is, not yet cleared by actual punishment nor expiated, and so not yet forgiven in their full weight; they could be forgiven and remitted only by the intercession of Christ's death. For this reason Christ is the Mediator of the New Testament, so that, by his death intervening for the redemption of the transgressions under the first Testament, those who are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance, Heb. 9:15. Once, in the consummation of the ages, he was manifested "for the putting away [εἰς ἀθέτησιν] of sin by the sacrifice of himself," ibid. v. 26 (24 in some editions). By this full abolition of sin there also follows full and complete reconciliation [καταλλαγή] with God. For "if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved by his life," Rom. 5:10.

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: Fuit iane etiam Abrahamo fides sua reputata in justitiam, Genes.XV.6. Rom.IV.3. Idem ἐδικαιώθη justificatus est, ibid. & reconciliatus Deo, quippe nuncupatus אהב φίλος, amicus Dei, 2.Paralip.XX.7. Jac.II.23. Et quæ Abrahami, patris credentium, ratio, eadem filiorum credentium omnium fuit. Nihilominus justitia, justificatio & reconciliatio consummata bonum Novi Testamenti, seu uti S. Paulus, Rom.XIV.17. appellat, Regni Cœlorum est. Veteres enim, qui sub jugo fuerunt, non quatenus sub jugo fuerunt, etiam justificati fuerunt, sed quatenus in Deum cum Abrahamo crediderunt. Tum justificatio Activa, seu amor ille Dei, quo eos, quos Christo dedit, diligit, & eorum Deus esse vult, adeoque in Christo justos & habentes jus vitæ cenlet, & εὕρηκε invenit, Phil.III.9. Bonum Veteris & Novi Testamenti ex æquo est. At justificatio Passiva, hoc est, sententia illa Dei, qua is justitiam ad animam credentis pronuntiat, dicendo ei velut ad cor & intimando: Ego sum Deus tuus; quoad sensum gratiæ, qua peccator justificatur, & peccata ei remittuntur, gradus recipit, & modo imperfectior, chirographi deletionem, peccati abolitionem & expiationem excludens; modo perfectior, illa includens, & commemorationem reatus adhuc extantis excludens, est. Neque enim justificatio Vete-
units.tr: Thus Abraham too had his faith reckoned to him as righteousness, Gen. 15:6; Rom. 4:3. The same man was justified [ἐδικαιώθη], ibid., and reconciled to God, being called [ʾōhēb], that is, friend of God [φίλος], 2 Chron. 20:7; James 2:23. The reason for Abraham, father of believers, was the same as for all the children of believers. Nevertheless, righteousness, justification and consummate reconciliation are the good of the New Testament, or, as St Paul calls it, Rom. 14:17, the Kingdom of Heaven. For the ancients who lived under the yoke were justified, not insofar as they lived under the yoke, but insofar as they believed in God with Abraham. Then there is active justification, that is, that love of God by which he loves those whom he has given to Christ and wills to be their God, and so regards them as righteous and as having a right to life in Christ, and finds them [εὕρηκε], Phil. 3:9. The good of the Old and New Testament is the same. But passive justification, that is, that sentence of God by which he pronounces righteousness to the soul of the believer, speaking to him as it were to the heart and making it known: "I am your God." As regards the sense of grace by which the sinner is justified and his sins are remitted, it admits of degrees: it is at one time more imperfect, excluding the cancelling of the bond, the abolition of sin and expiation; at another time more perfect, including these and excluding the remembrance of the guilt still standing. For the justification of the Old

units.la: Discrimen justificationis sub Veteribus & Novo Testamento.
units.tr: The difference of justification under the Old and the New Testament.

units.la: Veterum ad eum gradum processit, qui in Novo Testamento obtinet. Nam per Evangelium revelatur justitia Dei ut in sua causa,Rom.I.17. & prædicatur sine lege, ibid.III.21. sine peccatorum ἀναμνήσει commemoratione legali, Hebr.X.3. & προσφορᾶς περὶ ἁμαρτίας oblatione pro peccato, ib. v.18. adeóque τελείως perfectè, non deficiente amplius justitiæ causa,qua nondum extante, & per passiones nondum consummata,ipsa justitia numeris omnibus non consummata, non eundem justificationis & peccatorum remissionis sensum parere potuit. Adhuc enim fuit chirographum, non ante crucem Christi, cui affigi, & cum Christo velut expirare debuit,abolitum. Condonavit vobis omnes lapsus, ἐξαλείψας τὸ καθ' ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον τοῖς δόγμασιν ὃ ἦν ὑπεναντίον ἡμῖν postquam delevit chirographum in placitis nobis subcontrarium, & illud ex medio sustulit, clavis illud cruci affigens, Col.II.13.14. Chirographi formula erant δόγματα placita, seu præcepta in placitis posita, per quæ Deus ab Israelitis in suis προσφοραῖς περὶ ἁμαρτίας oblationibus pro peccato, Hebr.X.18. confessionem peccati adhuc extantis & nondum deleti exegit. In iis erat τὸ ἀσθενὲς καὶ ἀνωφελὲς infirmitas & inutilitas quædam, ibid.VII.18. hoc est, imperfectio illa, per quam peccata commemorat & exprobrat quotidie in sacrificiis anxietatem, perturbationem, tristitiam, metum pepererunt. Erat adhuc ṿꞌꞋ exactio debiti, sed nondum erat ṇṇṇ qui propter debitum affigeretur, & illud expungeret,Esaj.LIII.7. Expuncto & cruci affixo propter solutionem debiti chirographo, peccato sanguine Messiæ deleto simul peccati per legem commemoratio, exprobratio & suborti inde molestiores animi affectus cessarunt, serenitásque cordis circa peccati remissionem & justificationem consummatam longè major, quàm hactenus affulsit. Filius Dei missus est in similitudine carnis peccati, & Deus condemnavit peccatum in carne ἵνα πληρωθῇ τὸ δικαίωμα ἐν ἡμῖν, ut compleretur in nobis, quod lex justo attribuit, Rom.VIII.3.4.
units.tr: reached that degree which it holds in the New Testament. For through the Gospel the righteousness of God is revealed as in its own cause, Rom. 1:17, and is preached without law, ibid. 3:21, without legal remembrance of sins, Heb. 10:3, and offering for sin, ibid. v. 18, and so perfectly, the cause of righteousness no longer lacking. The righteousness itself, not yet existing and not yet consummated in all respects through sufferings, could not produce the same sense of justification and remission of sins. For the handwriting was still not abolished before the cross of Christ, to which it had to be nailed and with Christ, as it were, expire. "He has forgiven us all our trespasses, blotting out the handwriting against us in its decrees, which was contrary to us" [ἐξαλείψας τὸ καθ' ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον τοῖς δόγμασιν ὃ ἦν ὑπεναντίον ἡμῖν], and he took it out of the way, nailing it to the cross, Col. 2:13-14. The forms of the handwriting were δόγματα, decrees, or precepts laid down in ordinances, by which God demanded from the Israelites, in their sin-offerings [προσφοραῖς περὶ ἁμαρτίας], Heb. 10:18, confession of sin still standing and not yet blotted out. In them there was weakness and unprofitableness [τὸ ἀσθενὲς καὶ ἀνωφελὲς], ibid. 7:18, that is, that imperfection by which the sacrifices brought sins daily to mind and reproached them, and produced anxiety, disturbance, sadness and fear. There was still the exaction of the debt, but there was not yet the one who would be fastened to the cross for the debt and would erase it, Isa. 53:7. When the handwriting was erased and nailed to the cross in payment of the debt, sin being blotted out by the blood of the Messiah, at the same time the remembrance of sin through the law, the reproach, and the more troublesome emotions of the mind arising from it ceased, and a serenity of heart concerning the remission of sin and consummate justification far greater than hitherto shone forth. God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and condemned sin in the flesh, [ἵνα πληρωθῇ τὸ δικαίωμα ἐν ἡμῖν] that the requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, which the law attributes to the righteous, Rom. 8:3-4.

units.la: XLIII. Christus mortuus, & in Cœlo ad dextram Dei collocatus non reliquit suos ὀρφανούς orphanos, Joh.XIV.18.
units.tr: XLIII. Christ, dead and placed in heaven at the right hand of God, did not leave his own as orphans, John 14:18.

units.la: Rogavit enim Patrem,ut daret illis alium Paracletum, Spiritum veritatis, v.16.17. Quem & Pater in nomine ejus misit,ibid. v.26.Quisque manet cum Sanctis in seculum, ibid. v.16. De quo etiam Christus; Qui credit in me, fluvii è ventre ejus manabunt aquæ viva. Hoc verò dixit de Spiritu, quem credentes in illum accepturi erant. Nec dum enim erat Spiritus S. (tanta copia effusus) quia Jesus nondum glorificatus erat, ibid. VII.38.39. Non accepistis Spiritum rursum ad metum, sed πνεῦμα υἱοθεσίας Spiritum filiationis,in quo clamamus,Abba (quod oris tenerioris, infirmioris est) Pater (quod perfectiorum est,) Rom. VIII.15.Quia estis filii,emisit Deus Spiritum Filii sui in corda vestra,clamantem,Abba, Pater, Gal.IV.6. Obsignati estis Spiritu promissionis,qui est pignus hæreditatis nostræ, Ephe.I.13.14. Sicut in tempore Spiritus S. credentibus ita datus est: ita jam olim, velut in N.T. dandus promissus est. Effundam in domum Davidis Spiritum gratiæ & supplicationis,Zach.XII.10.Intelligitur effusio Spiritus S.in ea mensura, quæ gratiæ in Christo Jesu consummatæ convenit, qui precationes, seu δεήσεις clamores à credentibus ceu jam filiis ad Deum ceu Patrem directas operatur. Cujus donationis Spiritus S. ordinariæ signum luculentum extraordinaria & miraculosa ejusdem effusio in omnem carnem,Joel.II.28.prædicta, & in Pentecoste prima, & post eam varië impleta fuit. Nam hæc & certi temporis fuit, & argumentum dati Christi & Spiritus filiationis, & revelationis Regni Dei,nec non medium perficiendi Prophetiam, ut illa apud Ecclesiam ordinaria deinceps esset,extitit.
units.tr: For he asked the Father to give them another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, vv. 16-17, whom the Father also sent in his name, ibid. v. 26, who remains with the saints forever, ibid. v. 16. Of him Christ also said: "He who believes in me, from his belly shall flow rivers of living water." He said this of the Spirit whom believers were to receive. For the Holy Spirit (poured out in such abundance) was not yet because Jesus was not yet glorified, ibid. 7:38-39. "You have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but the spirit of adoption [πνεῦμα υἱοθεσίας], in which we cry, Abba (which is the language of a tender and weaker mouth), Father (which belongs to the more mature), Rom. 8:15. "Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father", Gal. 4:6. "You were sealed with the Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance", Eph. 1:13-14. As the Holy Spirit was given to believers in time, so he was promised long before, as it were, to be given in the New Testament. "I will pour out on the house of David the spirit of grace and supplication", Zech. 12:10. The effusion of the Holy Spirit is to be understood in that measure which befits the grace consummated in Christ Jesus, who works the prayers, or δεήσεις, the cries, which believers, now as sons, direct to God as Father. The clear sign of this ordinary gift of the Spirit was his extraordinary and miraculous effusion upon all flesh, foretold in Joel 2:28, and fulfilled at the first Pentecost and afterwards in various ways. For this was both for a certain time, and a proof of the given Christ and of the Spirit of adoption, and of the revelation of the Kingdom of God, and a means of fulfilling prophecy, and so it came to be ordinary thereafter in the Church.

units.la: XLIV. Nulla certè Fœderis gratiæ œconomia Spiritu gratiæ vacare potuit.
units.tr: XLIV. Certainly no economy of the covenant of grace could be without the Spirit of grace.

units.la: Nam & ii ipsi, qui crediderunt promissioni Scripturæ, discentis, fore, ut credentes in Christum abundarent tanquam fluminibus aquæ vitæ, Prov.V.15.16.XI.25. Joh.VII.38. sine Spiritu Dei promissioni non crediderunt. Testatur enim S. Petrus, Prophetas in Spiritu Christi de ipsius passionibus & sequentibus gloriis locutos esse,I.Pet.I.11.& S.Paulus; nos habere ἀντὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς πίστεως eundem Spiritum fidei, juxta id quod scriptum est: Credidi,ideo locutus sum. Etiam nos,inquit,credimus,ideo loquimur,2.Cor.IV.13. Sed & Esajas, in quorum ore ponit verbum Dei, in iisdem etiam Spiritum Dei collocat. Hoc est fœdus meum cum ipsis: Spiritus meus, qui est super te, & verba mea,quæ posui in ore tuo,non recedent ab ore tuo, & ab ore Seminis tui, & ab ore Seminis Seminis tui, dicit Jehova,à nunc & in seculum, Esaj.LIX.21. Etiam David orat: Spiritum tuum sanctum ne aufferas à me,Psal.LI.13. Tu Deus meus es, Spiritus tuus bonus ducat me in terram planam! ibid.CXLIII.10. Cúmque sine Spiritu Dei nemo Jesum Dominum vocare possit, 1.Cor.XII.3. satis constat tamen, Davidem Christum Dominum suum appellasse,Psal.CX.1.Sicut autem per Spiritum S.crediderunt promissioni, quæ pollicebatur, effusum iri Spiritum S. ita per eundem Spiritum S. adventum Christi,& Spiritus S. effusionem sitiverunt. Idem proin Spiritus sitim incendit,qui eandem extinxit. Sed quem fœdus gratiæ quoad remæquat, eundem varians Fœderis gratiæ œconomia, quoad rei gradum & τελείωσιν disparat, adeò ut variantis illius œconomiæ ratione ante Christum glorificatum ἐυπω nondum fuisse Spiritum S.disertè dicatur, Joh.VII.39. quia nondum ut Spiritus promissionis atque adoptionis meræ, & eo gradu & τελειωσει operationis ante datus fuit. Is enim Spiritus, qui in Patribus V. T. fidem testimonii Dei cum spe venturi Christi operabatur, Christo jam glorificato fidem in Christum jam consummatum, & quidem cum lætitia consummata & amore perfecto filiorum Dei operaturus erat. Sicut in filiis Dei Legi subjectis fuit Spiritus adoptionis seu filiationis non meræ,sed cum servitute mixtæ, qui simpliciter πνεῦμα δουλείας Spiritus servitutis,Rom.VIII.15.appellatur,quia filiis quidem hæredibus & dominis omnium sed, νηπίοις pueris & œconomis,atque exactoribus subjectis,& eatenus nil distantibus à servis, Gal.IV.1.2.3.datus est: ita cùm Christus glorificatus esset, futurus erat Spiritus ἐν gratiæ merè & in solidum,& ṙṙṙ precum ,seu implorationis gratiæ, Zach.XII.10. sive πνεῦμα υἱοθεσίας Spiritus filiationis, seu adoptionis, Rom.VIII.15. qui κατ' ἐξοχὴν πνεῦμα Θεοῦ Spiritus Dei, & πνεῦμα υἱὸς Θεοῦ Spiritus Filii Dei,ibid.v.9. 1.Cor.II.12. III.16. Gal.IV.6.&c, vocatur.
units.tr: For those who believed the promise of Scripture, which said that believers in Christ would abound like rivers of living water (Prov. 5:15–16; 11:25; John 7:38), did not believe the promise without the Spirit of God. For St Peter testifies that the prophets spoke in the Spirit of Christ concerning his sufferings and the glories that would follow (1 Pet. 1:11). St Paul also says that we have the same spirit of faith [τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς πίστεως], according to what is written: "I believed, therefore I spoke." We also believe, therefore we speak (2 Cor. 4:13). Moreover, Isaiah, into whose mouth God puts his word, also places the Spirit of God in the same men: "This is my covenant with them: my Spirit that is upon you, and my words that I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed, nor from the mouth of your seed's seed, says the LORD, from now and for ever" (Isa. 59:21). David also prays: "Take not your holy Spirit from me" (Ps. 51:13), and "You are my God; let your good Spirit lead me into the land of uprightness" (Ps. 143:10).
