Ex quibus liquidò cognoscitur, ad reconciliationem gentium requisitam fuisse mortem Christi, seu αἷμα ἡ σταυρὸς sanguinem crucis Christi; quia inimicitia gentium erat in carne Christi, Ephes. II. 15. & nonnisi rupto hoc velo, vel Judæi prope ad Deum accedere, vel gentes adduci poterant: Dedicavit Christus nobis ὁδὸν πρόσφατον ἡ ζῶσαν viam recentem (qualis est via N. T. in quo demum Deo, ut plenissime justificanti, & libertatem à jugo servitutis danti gratias agere; in nomine Christi omnia petere, in fiducia sacrificii Christi oblati ad Deum proximè accedere licet; & quæ, tabernaculo priori stationem Pontificis habente, manifestata nondum fuit, Hebr. IX. 8.) & vivam (utpote vivorum, cùm ad Templum, altare etiam mortui in peccatis accedere potuerint) per velum, hoc est, carnem ejus (fractam, in cœlum sublatam, & jam se habentem ut velum reductum, quod oculos, quò minùs in intima Sanctuarii penetrent, & ibi animi oculis Christum non ut velum, sed ut arcam & Propitiatorium, super quo Deus habitat, contueantur, morari nequit) Hebr. X. 20. Ideo etiam Christus ante mortem suam vetuit discipulos proficisci in via gentium, Matth. X. 5. 6. X. 5.6. & negavit se missum esse, nisi ad oves perditas domus Israel, ibid. XV. 24. & gentes vocavit canes, ibid. v.26. & minister circumcisionis diserte appellatur, Rom. XV. 8. Sed mortuus tamen est non pro solis Judæis, sed pro omnibus; 2. Corinth. V. 15. 1. Timoth. II. 6. &c. pro mundi vita, Joh. VI. 51. hoc est, non tantum pro Judæis, sed etiam pro gentibus. Ex quo tempore gentes non amplius seclusæ, sed pace cum Deo & Ecclesia inita, in fœderis sanctitatem cooptatæ sunt. Ne dicat filius alienigenæ, qui adhæret Jehovæ dicendo: Separando separavit me à populo suo. Ne dicat Eunuchus: Ecce arbor arida sum. Esaj. LVI. 3. Consequens est, non imputatio peccati mundi, 2. Cor. V. 19. Vocatio gentium, & Ecclesiæ inter gentes plantatio.
units.tr: LV. The outcome corresponded to the predictions. For Christ was made our peace (both between all men and God, and between the different kinds of men, hitherto divided by deadly enmities), who has made both (Jews and Gentiles) one (body, as in himself as its head), and has broken down the middle wall of partition (the Law of commandments contained in ordinances, which sharply divided the Jews from the nations, with the enmity blazing between them and their religions set in direct opposition, he took away, and so opened the wide door to peace; at the same time abolishing) the enmity which was in his flesh (not yet broken, the veil not yet torn, the Law, like that middle wall, endured until the satisfaction had been made, and so the breaking and tearing had not yet taken place, and the Gentiles had no access to the Church), while he reduced the Law of commandments contained in ordinances to nothing; so that he might create the two in himself into one new man (the Gentiles, to be raised as if newly from the death of sins and the uncircumcision of the flesh, and the Jews themselves, though sanctified and believing, to be created anew by the Spirit of adoption given to the promise), making peace; and might reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, having slain the enmity in himself (Eph. 2:14-16). It pleased God through him (Christ) to reconcile all things to himself [εἰς αὐτὸν], making peace through the blood of his cross, through him (both by his obedience, sufferings, reproaches and death, and by the worth and dignity of his person), both things in heaven and things on earth (angels, blessed spirits, and those who come to God on earth, Jews and Gentiles). And you, who were once alienated, and enemies in mind through evil works, has now reconciled (freed from wrath and enmity) in the body of his flesh through death (through his obedience even to death, and death of the cross), to present you holy and without blemish, and blameless before him (Col. 1:20-23). From these words it is plainly known that the death of Christ, or the blood of the cross of Christ [αἷμα ἡ σταυρὸς], was required for the reconciliation of the Gentiles, because the enmity of the Gentiles was in the flesh of Christ (Eph. 2:15), and only when this veil was torn could either the Jews draw near to God or the Gentiles be brought in. Christ has dedicated for us a new and living way [ὁδὸν πρόσφατον καὶ ζῶσαν] (such is the way of the New Testament, in which at last it is permitted to give thanks to God, as fully justifying and granting liberty from the yoke of servitude; to ask all things in the name of Christ, and to draw near to God in confidence in the sacrifice of Christ offered; a way which was not yet made manifest while the earlier tabernacle still held its station for the high priest, Heb. 9:8), and living (as belonging to the living, since even the dead in sins could approach the Temple and the altar), through the veil, that is, his flesh (broken, taken up into heaven, and now standing as a veil drawn back, which cannot keep the eyes from penetrating the innermost parts of the sanctuary, and from there beholding Christ with the eyes of the mind, not as a veil, but as the ark and the mercy seat upon which God dwells) (Heb. 10:20). Therefore Christ also, before his death, forbade the disciples to go into the way of the Gentiles (Matt. 10:5-6), and he said that he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 15:24), and he called the Gentiles dogs (Matt. 15:26), and he is plainly called a minister of the circumcision (Rom. 15:8). Yet he died not for the Jews only, but for all (2 Cor. 5:15; 1 Tim. 2:6), for the life of the world (John 6:51), that is, not only for the Jews but also for the Gentiles. From that time the Gentiles were no longer shut out, but, peace having been made with God and the Church, they were admitted into the holiness of the covenant. Let not the son of the foreigner, who has joined himself to the LORD, say: The LORD has utterly separated me from his people. Let not the eunuch say: Behold, I am a dry tree (Isa. 56:3). It follows that there is no imputing of the sins of the world (2 Cor. 5:19), the calling of the Gentiles, and the planting of the Church among the Gentiles.

units.la: LVI. Unà cum Pace hac data est hæreditas decoris, exercitus gentium; Jerem. III. 19. De qua hæreditate gentium etiam Esajas: Accedet Proselytus ad ipsos & agglutinabuntur ad domum Jacobi. Et accipient illos populi, & deducent eos in locum ipsorum, & pro hæreditate illos sibi vendicabunt domus Israelis in terra Jehovæ, &c. Jesaj. XIV. 1. 2. Christo autem, tanquam Filio & hæredi omnium, obedientia populorum, Gen. XLIX. 10. & hæreditas gentium diserte promissa est. Postula à me, & dabo gentes hæreditatem tuam, & proprietatem tuam fines terræ, Psal. II. 8. Funes mihi ceciderunt in amœnis; etiam hæreditas decora mihi, ibid. XVI. 6. Dominabitur à mari ad mare, & à fluvio Euphrate ad fines terræ, ib. LXXII. 8. Quæ autem Christo promittuntur, omnibus etiam fidelibus promittuntur, quia quæcunque Christi sunt, fidelium sunt; propter unitatem & communionem capitis & membrorum. Ideo etiam Abrahamo promittitur: Benedicentur in te omnes familiæ terræ, Gen. XII. 3. Patrem multitudinis gentium posui te, ib. XVII. 5. Benedicentur in Semine tuo omnes gentes terræ, ib. XXII. 18. Unde S. Paulus colligit, Abrahamum & semen ejus esse κληρονόμον κόσμου hæredem mundi, Rom. IV. 13. illius videlicet, pro quo Christus mortuus est, Zach. III. 9. Joh. VI. 33. 1. Joh. II. 2. & quem Christus hæreditatem accipit, & nos in ipso accipimus; qui fit peculium Christi, cum quo communionem habemus. Quæ hæreditas mundi cum celebratione Nominis Dei in gentibus conjungitur. Ab ortu Solis usque ad occasum magnum est Nomen meum in gentibus, & in omni loco incensum offeretur Nomini meo, & oblatio munda. Magnum erit nomen meum inter gentes, dicit Jehova; Mal. I. 11. Sed hæreditas illa gentium per vices & gradus proficiens, neque parum etiam per Draconem, Bestiam & ejus imaginem (Apoc. XII. XIII.) ad tempus interturbata τελείωσιν consummationem & complementum suum præstolatur, ut plenitudo gentium intret, & totus Israel salvetur; Rom. XI. 25.26.
units.tr: LVI. Together with this peace there is given also an inheritance of glory, the forces of the nations (Jer. 3:19). Of this inheritance of the nations Isaiah also speaks: The proselyte shall join himself to them, and they shall cleave to the house of Jacob. And the peoples shall take them and bring them to their place, and the house of Israel shall possess them as servants in the land of Jehovah, etc. (Isa. 14:1, 2). Obedience of the peoples is promised to Christ as Son and heir of all (Gen. 49:10), and the inheritance of the nations is expressly promised to him: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession (Ps. 2:8). The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places; yes, I have a goodly heritage (ibid. 16:6). He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth (ibid. 72:8). What is promised to Christ is also promised to all believers, because all that belongs to Christ belongs to the faithful, on account of the unity and communion of the Head and the members. For this reason it is also promised to Abraham: In you shall all the families of the earth be blessed (Gen. 12:3); I have made you a father of many nations (ibid. 17:5); In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed (ibid. 22:18). Hence St Paul concludes that Abraham and his seed are heir of the world [κληρονόμον κόσμου] (Rom. 4:13), that is, of that world for which Christ died (Zech. 3:9; John 6:33; 1 John 2:2). Christ receives this inheritance, and we receive it in him; we become his peculiar people, with whom we have communion. This inheritance of the world is joined with the celebration of the name of God among the nations: From the rising of the sun even to its going down my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense shall be offered to my name, and a pure offering; for my name shall be great among the nations, says Jehovah (Mal. 1:11). But that inheritance of the nations, advancing by turns and degrees, and not a little disturbed for a time by the Dragon, the Beast and its image (Rev. 12, 13), waits for its consummation [τελείωσιν] and completion, so that the fullness of the nations may come in and all Israel may be saved (Rom. 11:25, 26).

units.la: LVII. Ejusdem Pacis œconomicæ pars quædam non ignobilis degentis in terra Ecclesiæ cum Spiritibus consummatis in cœlo, & merè cœlestibus eorundem bonis communio est. Quæ ἀνακεφαλαίωσις adunationis, vel confusionis utrumque in unam summam nomine venit. De qua S. Paulus: Notum nobis fecit arcanum voluntatis suæ, secundum beneplacitum suum, quod propo-
units.tr: LVII. There is also a certain not inconsiderable part of this economic peace: the communion of the Church living on earth with the spirits made perfect in heaven, and with their purely heavenly goods. This recapitulation [ἀνακεφαλαίωσις], that is, the uniting or confusing of both into one sum, is so called. St Paul speaks of it: He made known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he had purposed in himself

units.la: fuerat in se ad dispensationem plenitudinis temporum, ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι adunandi, vel in unam summâ confundendi omnia in Christo, tum quæ in cœlo, tum quæ in terra, in ipso. Eph. I. 9.10.11. Ubi ἀνακεφαλαιοῦσθαι idem est quod ἑνοῦσθαι uniri, seu recapitulari, in unam summam, uti æra solent; colligi; & confundi, summatim comprehendi, (velut Rom. XIII. 9.) κεφαλαίωμα enim summam numerorum notat. In eo autem unio hæc & collectio eorum, qui in Cœlo & in terra sunt, nempe in Christo, consistit, quòd sicut ii, qui in Cœlis sunt, cognoscunt mysterium voluntatis Dei, & nomen atque amorem Dei; & liberi sunt ab omni servitute & accusatione peccati, & pro justis, amicis consummatis habentur: ita etiam, qui in terris sunt in Christo. Quæ τελείωσις consummatio eorum, qui in terris sunt; dicitur; quia sicut Sancti in Cœlo consummati sunt, ita hi per Christum & in Christo in terra consummati pariter sunt. Deus enim de nobis (N. T. fidelibus) melius quid providit, ne (Patres V. T. qui promissionem in terra non adepti, adeóque in terra non consummati demum in Cœlo libertate accepta consummati sunt) fine nobis (at non sine illis, qui in terra existentes promissione potiti non sunt) consummarentur; (non utique hi quidem in Cœlo, sed in terra; in qua, promissione; quam veteres non reportarunt, exhibita Deus melius quid de iis providit) Hebr. IX. 40. Accessimus enim ad montem Sion (non Sinai, sed Sion, quem montem Deus elegit, ut ibi N. Testamentum patefaceret; Ps. LXVIII. 16. LXXVIII. 68. CXXXII. 13-18; Esaj. II. 3. Jerem. XXXI. 12. 13. 14.) ad urbem Dei vivi, Hierosolymam cœlestem (cujus, non æque ac terrestris Hierosolymæ, Deus, Christus ex morte vivificatus constructor, sanctificator, rector, habitator, throni ejusdem Cœlestis infessor est, & cujus incolæ sunt quotquot in Cœlo & in terra consummationis participes, recapitulati; & in unam summam redacti sunt) ad myriades Angelorum (ceu conservorum; & ejusdem civitatis civium; ministrorum Dei ad salutem hæredum missorum) Panegyrin & concionem primogenitorum, qui in Cœlis conscripti sunt (universitatem omnium electorum, qui sunt ἀπαρχαὶ primitiæ Deo & Agno; Apoc. XIV. 4. Ecclesia Dei viventis, 1. Tim. III. 15. qua cum nullo negotio coalescere omnibus datur; cùm in V.T. ad Panegyrin seu קהל ישראל coetum Israelis non omnibus; obstante διαστολὴ distinctione, coalescere datum fit; & qui cum illo coaluerunt, non continuò ad panegyrin primogenitorum in Cœlis conscriptorum venerint; quia in eo cœtu non pauci in Cœlis non conscripti, fuerunt) & judicem Deum omnium (Deum; qui nos in Christo judicat; imò Christum, cui Deus pater judicium omne dedit; Joh. V. 22.27. ut velut ab eo justificati & absoluti videamus faciem ejus cum lætitia) & spiritus justorum consummatorum (ad eos, qui in V. T. defuncti rectà in Cœlum migrarunt, & donum justitiæ cum lætitia adepti sunt. Sicut enim illi in Cœlis sic consummati sunt, ut non amplius elementis mundi, pædagogis & œconomis ac puerilibus crepundiis distinerentur: ita fideles N. T. præstita λυτρώσει liberatione per solutionem pretii, non tantùm à reatu peccati; sed etiam à commemoratione ejusdem & servitute durissima & scrupulosissima, in terra consummantur, & cum illis secundum spiritum consummatis in hac etiam vita communionem libertatis, justitiæ & lætitiæ habent) & Testamenti Novi Mediatorem (non Mediatorem Typicum Mosen, sed verum, Christum viventem, glorificatum & in Cœlesti throno collocatum, Mediatorem N. T. seu justitiæ in libertate habendæ, & Sponsorem Testamenti; quo hæreditas gloriæ, & animæ post mortem consummatio datur) & sanguinem aspersionis præstantiora præ Habele loquentem (quippe jam fusum & aspersum, donatum, imputatum conscientiis credentium ad purificationem omnem à peccatis; antehac nondum expiatis; quin & loquentem meliora præ sanguine Habelis; quia non vindictam, sed salutem eorum; qui aspersi sunt; postulat) Hebr. XII. 22-25.
units.tr: for the dispensation of the fullness of times, to gather together [ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι], that is, to unite or sum up into one total, all things in Christ, both those in heaven and those on earth, in him (Eph. 1:9, 10, 11). Here ἀνακεφαλαιοῦσθαι means the same as ἑνοῦσθαι, to be united, or to be recapitulated into one sum, as accountants do; to be gathered together, or to be summarily comprehended (as in Rom. 13:9), for κεφαλαίωμα denotes the sum of numbers. This union and gathering together of those who are in heaven and on earth, namely in Christ, consists in this: just as those who are in heaven know the mystery of God's will and the name and love of God, and are free from all servitude and accusation of sin, and are regarded as just and as perfected friends, so too are those who are on earth in Christ. This perfecting [τελείωσις] of those who are on earth is so called because, just as the saints are perfected in heaven, so these, through Christ and in Christ, are likewise perfected on earth. For God has provided something better for us (the New Testament faithful), that they (the Fathers of the Old Testament, who, not having obtained the promise on earth, and so not perfected on earth, were at last perfected in heaven when they received freedom) should not be made perfect without us (but not without those who, existing on earth, did not obtain the promise); (certainly not these in heaven, but on earth; in which, when the promise was made manifest, God provided something better concerning them, which the ancients did not attain) (Heb. 11:40). For you have come to Mount Sion (not Sinai, but Sion, which mountain God chose so that there he would reveal the New Testament; Ps. 68:16; 78:68; 132:13–18; Isa. 2:3; Jer. 31:12–14) and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (of which, unlike earthly Jerusalem, God is the builder, and Christ, quickened from death, is the sanctifier, ruler, inhabitant, and the one who sits upon its heavenly throne; and whose inhabitants are all who, recapitulated and gathered into one sum, share in the perfection, both in heaven and on earth), and to myriads of angels (as fellow-servants and fellow-citizens of the same city, sent as ministers of God for the salvation of the heirs), to the general assembly and church of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven (the whole body of the elect, who are the firstfruits [ἀπαρχαὶ] to God and to the Lamb; Rev. 14:4), the Church of the living God (1 Tim. 3:15), with which all are given to unite without difficulty; whereas in the Old Testament it was not given to all to unite with the assembly of Israel [קהל ישראל], since the distinction stood in the way; and those who united with it did not at once come to the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, since in that assembly there were not a few who were not enrolled in heaven); and to God the judge of all (God, who judges us in Christ; nay, Christ, to whom the Father has given all judgment, John 5:22, 27, so that, as if justified and acquitted by him, we may see his face with joy); and to the spirits of just men made perfect (those who died under the Old Testament and went straight to heaven, and obtained the gift of righteousness with joy). For just as they are perfected in heaven, so that they are no longer held by the elements of the world, pedagogues, stewards, and childish trifles, so the New Testament faithful, having obtained redemption [λυτρώσει], that is, liberation by the payment of a price, not only from the guilt of sin but also from the remembrance of it and from its most harsh and scrupulous servitude, are perfected on earth, and with those who are perfected according to the spirit have in this life also communion of freedom, righteousness and joy; and to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant (not Moses, the typical mediator, but the true Christ, living, glorified and placed upon the heavenly throne, the Mediator of the New Testament, or of righteousness to be held in freedom, and the Surety of the covenant, by whom the inheritance of glory and the consummation of the soul after death are given); and to the blood of sprinkling, which speaks better things than Abel (since it has already been shed and sprinkled, given and imputed to the consciences of believers for purification from all sins, which had not yet been expiated before; nay, it speaks better things than the blood of Abel, since it asks not for vengeance but for the salvation of those who have been sprinkled) (Heb. 12:22–25).

units.la: LVIII. Salvo proin Ecclesiæ Militantis & Triumphantis discrimine, arctior longè in N. T. Ecclesiam inter utramque communio, tum ratione bonorum & privilegiorum, tum ratione occupationis & cultus Dei obtinet.
units.tr: LVIII. Therefore, without prejudice to the distinction between the Church Militant and the Church Triumphant, there is far closer communion between the two in the New Testament Church, both in respect of goods and privileges and in respect of the office and worship of God.

units.la: Nam bona hæreditatis, quæ fidelibus N. T. tribuuntur; merè spiritualia & cœlestia sunt. Benedixit nobis Deus in omni benedictione spirituali in cœlestibus in Christo, Ephes. I. 3. Benedictiones merè πνευματικαὶ spirituales, non amplius cum carnalibus & litera mixtæ sunt, quæ à Spiritu S. effunduntur, & ejus gratiæ & effusioni conveniunt; sive eæ in spiritum nostrum solum competunt, sive etiam in corp', cujus resuscitatio etiam spiritui tribuitur. Rom. VIII. 11. 1. Cor. XV. 44. quæ etiam ponuntur ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις in supercœlestibus, quia non includuntur spatio terrestri, vel sphæra illarum rerum, quæ supra nos sunt, & in cognitionem nostram veniunt, velut sidera: & quæ excedunt omnia illa cœlestia, quæ propter nos facta sunt. Quæ proin Cœli tertii, seu Cœli cœlorum sunt. Unde secundus homo, qui dicitur Dominus ex Cœlo, etiam ἐπουράνιος supercœlestis 1. Cor. XV. 47. 48. 49. appellatur, quia cum esset supra omnes, & in iis, quæ visibilia sunt, antea non essët visus, sed supra illa, quæ videntur, locum parasset, in quo se per gloriam suam Angelis & consummatis spiritibus manifestaret, inde descendit, & in carne se manifestavit. Et spirituales ejusmodi Benedictiones in supracœlestibus etiam in terra dari; Christus testis est, dicens: Si terrestria locutus sum vobis, & non creditis, quomodo si dicam vobis Cœlestia, credetis? Joh. III. 12. Sunt enim quædam bona ἐπίγεια terrestria quæ in terra donantur, sunt & ἐπουράνια Cœlestia, quæ in Cœlis repòsita sunt. Nihilominus & priora illa Cœlestia dici possunt, quia pertinent ad Regnum Dei, quod est Regnum Cœlorum, Matth. III. 2. non tantum quia Deus thronum habet in Cœlo, vel potius Cœlum & terram implet; atque adeò non est in terra ut homo; sed multò magis; quia est Regnum Dei cœleste, & non terrestre; utpote quo Deus sic Ecclesiam gubernat, ut eam sibi subjiciat soli, & quidem in communione bonorum cœlestium quoad justitiam & libertatem. Opponitur enim illi Regno, in quo præter Deum dispensatores & tutores dominabantur, Gal. IV. 2. 3. & Ecclesia elementis mundi subjecta non habuit communionem cum cœlestibus in plena justitia & libertate. Ideo πλήρωμα
units.tr: For the goods of the inheritance that are bestowed on New Testament believers are purely spiritual and heavenly. God has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in heavenly places in Christ (Eph. 1:3). The blessings are purely spiritual [πνευματικαὶ]; they are no longer mixed with carnal things and the letter; they are poured out by the Holy Spirit and agree with his grace and outpouring, whether they pertain to our spirit alone or also to the body, whose resurrection is likewise ascribed to the Spirit (Rom. 8:11; 1 Cor. 15:44). They are also placed in the heavenly places [ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις], that is, above the heavens, because they are not contained within earthly space, or within the sphere of those things which are above us and come within our knowledge, such as the stars, and which surpass all those heavenly things that were made on our account. Therefore they belong to the third heaven, or the heaven of heavens. Hence the second man, who is called the Lord from heaven, is also called heavenly [ἐπουράνιος] (1 Cor. 15:47–49), because, though he was above all and had not previously been seen among visible things, but had prepared a place above those things which are seen, in which he might manifest himself through his glory to the angels and to the perfected spirits, he came down from there and manifested himself in the flesh. And that such spiritual blessings in the heavenly places are also given on earth, Christ is witness, saying: If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? (John 3:12). For there are certain earthly [ἐπίγεια] goods that are given on earth, and there are heavenly [ἐπουράνια] goods that are laid up in heaven. Nevertheless, those former things may also be called heavenly, because they pertain to the kingdom of God, which is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 3:2); not only because God has his throne in heaven, or rather fills heaven and earth, and so is not on earth in the way a man is; but much more because it is a heavenly and not an earthly kingdom, inasmuch as God so governs the Church that he subjects it to himself alone, and indeed in communion of heavenly goods as regards righteousness and freedom. For that kingdom is set over against the one in which, besides God, stewards and guardians ruled (Gal. 4:2, 3), and in which the Church, subject to the elements of the world, did not have communion with heavenly things in full righteousness and freedom. Therefore the fullness [πλήρωμα]

units.la: LIX. Omnium præcedentium illorum Bonorum comes ἀγαλλίασις Lætitia singularis est.
units.tr: LIX. Singular joy [ἀγαλλίασις] accompanies all the aforementioned goods.

units.la: Nam Regnum Dei etiam χαρὰ ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ Lætitia in Spiritu S. (Spiritu non amplius servitutis, sed Filiationis, fidem reconciliationis, libertatis filiorum; παρρησίαν, amorem Dei & omnium virtutum ejus cum lætitia, authore Spiritu Dei non cum mensura dato digna operante) est, Rom. XIV. 17. Ad quam sic Paulus hortatur: χαίρετε ἐν τῷ κυρίῳ; Gaudete in Domino, Phil. III. 1: χαίρετε ἐν κυρίῳ πάντοτε, Gaudete in Domino semper; iterum dico, Gaudete; ibid. IV. 4. Christi certè nativitas & prædicatio magnum gaudium affert, Angelo teste: Ecce, evangelizo vobis χαρὰν μεγάλην gaudium magnum, quod erit omni populo. Quoniam natus est vobis hodie Salvator, qui est Christus Dominus in urbe Davidis, Luc. II. 10. 11. Hæc locutus sum vobis, ut lætitia mea (hilaritas Sponsi super Sponsa, Esaj. LXII. 5.) in vobis maneat; & lætitia vestra πεπληρωθῇ impleatur, Joh. XV. 11. Hucusque non petiistis quicquam in Nomine meo. Petite & accipietis, ut lætitia vestra sit πεπληρωμένη completa, ibid. XVI. 24. Quidni enim exuberaret & impleretur lætitia eorum, qui tantis bonis τηλικαύτῃ σωτηρίᾳ tanta Salute (Hebr. II. 3.) præ veteribus illis nunc maktantur? Qui omnia ad vitam & pietatem spectantia (2. Pet. I. 3.) tali tantáque mensura, non modo, nec trimodio, sed toto horreo, quale quidem Ecclesiæ in terra adhuc militanti competere potest, possident? Qui causas metuendi, quas veteres habuerunt, jacturam terrestris hæreditatis & pignoris per exilium, afflictiones, intempestivam mortem; necnon serviendi elementis mundi, & torvos pædagogos tutoresque aspectandi necessitatem, & peccati ipsius velut nec dum expiati quotidianam in sacrificiis commemorationem, & similia φθαρτὰ, per Christi sanguinem in terra etiam consummati; & cum Cœlestibus solis communionem habentes, procul habent, & contra in præsentem salutem & Evangelium unicè intenti remissionem peccatorum & justitiam in Christo donatam amplectuntur, & in Deo atque virtutibus ejus deliciantur? Quibus denique ipsa in afflictionibus & morte consternatio, perdito per Christum peccati & maledictionis omnis aculeo, magna lætitiæ & gloriationis seges & materia est? Nam gloriamur in spe gloriæ Dei, (per professionem spei vitæ æternæ, & quia Deus illuminando, sanctificando, lætificándo & glorificando nos gloriosus & admirabilis in nobis fieri vult.) Non hoc solum autem, sed & gloriamur in afflictionibus, scientes, quòd afflictio patientiam operatur. &c. Rom. V. 2. 3. &c. Postquam enim sublata est accusatio legis, Christo pro nobis in mortem tradito, nihil in afflictione superesset, nisi communio passionum Christi, & efficacia earum, in mortificatione veteris hominis, ut participes fiamus sanctitatis Dei; nec non glorificatio Christi & martyrium, Phil. I. 29. Act. V. 41. Joh. XXI. 19. 1. Pet. II. 19. 20. 21. & quòd sunt γυμνασίαι exercitationes, δοκιμασίαι probationes, πειρασμοὶ tentationes, quibus fides & charitas manifestatur, Heb. XII. 11. 1. Pet. I. 6. 7. Jac. I. 12. Quæ cuncta fœcunda non lugendi, sed impensè gaudendi materies sunt. Πᾶσαν χαρὰν ἡγήσασθε omnem lætitiam ducite, fratres, cùm in tentationes varias incideritis, scientes, quòd probatio fidei vestræ operetur patientiam, patientia autem opus perfectum habeat, Jac. 1. 2. 3. 4. Si enim lætandum nobis est, quando, quæ videntur, bona accipimus; certè omni lætitia exultandum est, quando Deus ad angustias vocat, quia hoc longè nobis salutarius, Deo gloriosius, & ad spem vivam utilius est. Aliqua lætitia est, rebus suavibus oblectari: omnis lætitia, tentari, affligi.
units.tr: For the kingdom of God is also joy [χαρὰ] in the Holy Spirit, the Spirit no longer of bondage but of adoption, faith of reconciliation, freedom of the sons, boldness [παρρησίαν], and love of God and of all his virtues with joy, given by the Spirit of God, who works worthily and not by measure (Rom. XIV. 17). To this joy Paul exhorts us thus: rejoice in the Lord [χαίρετε ἐν τῷ κυρίῳ] (Phil. III. 1); rejoice in the Lord always [χαίρετε ἐν κυρίῳ πάντοτε]; again I say, rejoice (ibid. IV. 4). Certainly the birth and proclamation of Christ bring great joy, as the angel testifies: "Behold, I bring you good news of great joy [χαρὰν μεγάλην], which will be for all the people. For today there is born to you a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David" (Luke II. 10, 11). "I have spoken these things to you, that my joy (the bridegroom's gladness over the bride, Isa. LXII. 5) may remain in you, and that your joy [πεπληρωθῇ] may be fulfilled" (John XV. 11). "Hitherto you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy [πεπληρωμένη] may be complete" (ibid. XVI. 24). For why should the joy of those overflow and be filled, who now, compared with the men of old, are blessed with such great salvation [τηλικαύτῃ σωτηρίᾳ] (Heb. II. 3), who possess all things pertaining to life and godliness (2 Pet. I. 3) in such a measure, not merely by the peck, nor by the bushel, but by the whole granary, such as may indeed befit the Church still militant on earth? Those who have the causes for fear that the men of old had, the loss of earthly inheritance and pledge through exile, afflictions, untimely death, the necessity of serving the elements of the world and of looking toward stern tutors and guardians, and the daily remembrance of sin in sacrifices, as if it were not yet expiated, and similar perishable things, (though these were also brought to an end on earth through the blood of Christ), and who have communion with the heavenly things alone, keep such fears far away. On the contrary, intent only on the present salvation and the Gospel, they embrace the remission of sins and the righteousness given in Christ, and delight in God and his virtues. Finally, for them even consternation in afflictions and death, once the sting of sin and of every curse has been destroyed through Christ, is a great harvest and matter of joy and boasting. For we glory in the hope of the glory of God (through the profession of the hope of eternal life, and because God, by enlightening, sanctifying, gladdening and glorifying us, wishes to be made glorious and wonderful in us). And not only this, but we also glory in afflictions, knowing that affliction produces patience, etc. (Rom. V. 2, 3, etc.). For once the accusation of the law has been removed, Christ having been delivered to death for us, nothing remains in affliction except the communion of Christ's sufferings and their efficacy in the mortifying of the old man, so that we may become partakers of the holiness of God; likewise the glorifying of Christ and martyrdom (Phil. I. 29; Acts V. 41; John XXI. 19; 1 Pet. II. 19, 20, 21). And these are exercises [γυμνασίαι], proofs [δοκιμασίαι], and temptations [πειρασμοὶ], by which faith and love are made manifest (Heb. XII. 11; 1 Pet. I. 6, 7; Jas. I. 12). All these are fruitful matter not for mourning but for unrestrained rejoicing. Count it all joy [Πᾶσαν χαρὰν ἡγήσασθε], my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience, and patience must have its perfect work (Jas. I. 2, 3, 4). For if we ought to rejoice when we receive what seems good, certainly we ought to exult with all joy when God calls us into distress, because this is far more salutary for us, more glorious to God, and more useful for living hope. There is a joy in being delighted by pleasant things; there is a joy, in being tempted and afflicted, that is entire.

units.la: LX. Christianorum igitur lætitia ἀγαλλίασις est, multò magis quàm illa Stoicorum, suaviter somniantium, Sapientem suum vel in tormentis Beatum esse. Nam Christiani ὡς λυπούμενοι ἀεὶ χαίροντες tanquam contristati semper gaudent, 2. Cor. VI. 10. Hæc enim Dei in illorum animis potentia operatur, ut ubi nulla causa externa lætitiæ elicit, imò omnes causæ externæ, tum quæ ipsos infestant, tum quæ ad συμπάθειαν eos commovent, tristitiam suadent, nihilominus ἀεὶ semper gaudeant, nimirum propter consolationem Evangelii, Spiritus S. præsentiam, bonam conscientiam, & spem vivam, quæ in iis est. Et qui Deum propter salutem datam diligit, in Divina veritate delicia-tur, conscientiam consummatam sentit, adversa eleganter fert, offensas æquo animo condonat, & in omnibus ἀγαθωσύνῃ est, næ is tranquillum animum gerit semper Deo gratias agit, neque unquam μεμψίμοιρος est; Et qui tales sunt, videntur λυπούμενοι contristati, quia non diligunt mundum, & ea, quæ in mundo sunt, non ἀγαθοὶ ... τῆς ἐν κακὰ πράγματα gratos habent eos, qui mala faciunt, sed potiùs cùm mala vident, πενθοῦσι lugent; cum timore & tremore salutem suam operantur, & id omne, quod amori Dei & proximi contrariatur, fugiunt, neque delectantur eo, quo caro titillatur & saginatur. Qua tamen iidem Deum diligunt, & ardentiùs a Christo ad mortem usque dilecti eum diligunt, iccirco lætantur semper. Ideo S. Paulus inter fructus Spiritus S. primore
units.tr: LX. The joy of Christians, therefore, is exultation [ἀγαλλίασις], far more than that of the Stoics, who pleasantly dream that their Wise Man is blessed even under torments. For Christians, as sorrowful yet always rejoicing [ὡς λυπούμενοι ἀεὶ χαίροντες], as if grieved yet always rejoicing (2 Cor. VI. 10). For this is the power of God working in their souls, so that where no external cause draws forth joy, but indeed all external causes, both those that trouble them and those that move them to sympathy [συμπάθειαν], urge sadness, they nevertheless always [ἀεὶ] rejoice, namely on account of the consolation of the Gospel, the presence of the Holy Spirit, a good conscience, and the living hope that is in them. He who loves God for the salvation given, delights in divine truth, feels a conscience made complete, bears adversity gracefully, forgives offences with an even mind, and is in all things of goodness [ἀγαθωσύνῃ]; indeed he keeps a tranquil mind, always giving thanks to God [semper Deo gratias agit], and is never discontented with his lot [μεμψίμοιρος]. And those such as these seem grieved [λυπούμενοι], because they do not love the world, and do not regard as good those things that are in the world. They do not take pleasure in those who do evil things [ἀγαθοὶ ... τῆς ἐν κακὰ πράγματα], but rather, when they see evils, they mourn [πενθοῦσι]; they work out their salvation with fear and trembling, and flee from everything that opposes the love of God and of neighbour, and they do not delight in that by which the flesh is tickled and fattened. Yet the same people love God, and, loved by Christ even unto death, they love him more ardently, and therefore they rejoice always. Hence St. Paul joins love and joy first among the fruits of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: loco charitatem & lætitiam copulat. Fructus Spiritus est charitas, lætitia, &c. Gal. V. 22. Lætitia enim charitati cùm semper adest, tùm potissimùm sub N. T. ubi omnis metus, dolor, mœror expulsus est. Charitas saturalætatur. Qui enim Deum habet, eúmque Patrem appellare potest, ejus benignam faciem videt, familiare colloquium, quo & ad sapientiam formatur; & in omni conditione, rebus secundis & adversis, refocillatur, audit; & arrhabonem ab eo possidet, & nomen ejus novit, & scit, intercessorem fratrem apud eum esse, & semper proximè ad eum accedere, nullo repulsæ metu potest, & hæreditatem mundi cernit, & gloriæ hæres dictus est, & ut hæreditas Dei obsignatus est, næ is non potest non lætari. Estq; lætitiæ illius fulcrum & nutricula bona conscientia quòd novimus nos Deum amare. Nemo qui Deum amat, verè tristari potest, quia scit, cuncta sibi ad salutem proficere, & eum, quem amat, revera bonum, & amabilem esse, & amorem sui remunerari: imò qui vivit in eo, qui ipsum amat, & ipsum jam sui participem facit. Unum ergo insatiabiliter agendum, ut sentiamus nos amare; & λυπούμενοι licet, semper tamen lætabimur. Non enim, uti præclare Ambrosius lib. I. de Jacob. cap. 7. loquitur, frangitur sapiens doloribus corporis, nec vexatur incommodis, sed etiam in ærumnis beatus est, quia non in delectatione corporis vitæ beatitudo est, sed in conscientia pura ab omni labe peccati, per Christum plane pleneque remissi. Nostram Christiano sensu facimus memorabilem illam Senecæ de Benef. lib. IV. 22. vocem: Licèt corpus ipsum plenum bona conscientia stillet, placebit illi ignis, per quem bona fides collucebit.
units.tr: The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, etc. (Gal. V. 22). For joy is always present with love, and especially under the New Testament, where all fear, pain and sorrow have been driven out. Love is fully glad. For he who has God, and can call him Father, sees his kindly face, has familiar converse with him, by which he is also formed in wisdom, and in every condition, prosperous and adverse, is refreshed and hears; and he possesses a pledge from him, and knows his name, and knows that a brother is an intercessor with him, and can always approach him very near, with no fear of rejection; and he discerns the inheritance of the world, and is called an heir of glory, and is sealed as God's inheritance. Such a man cannot but rejoice. And the support and nurse of that joy is a good conscience, because we know that we love God. No one who loves God can truly be sad, because he knows that all things work together for his salvation, and that the one whom he loves is truly good and lovable, and that love for himself is rewarded; indeed, he who lives in him who loves him, and makes him already a partaker of himself. Therefore there is one thing to be done without ceasing: that we feel that we love. And although we are grieved, yet we shall always rejoice. For, as Ambrose says well in Book I on Jacob, chapter 7, the wise man is not broken by bodily pains, nor troubled by discomforts, but even in distress he is blessed, because blessedness does not lie in bodily delight, but in a conscience pure from every stain of sin, fully and completely remitted through Christ. In a Christian sense we make memorable that saying of Seneca, On Benefits, Book IV, 22: Although the body itself drips with a good conscience, the fire by which good faith shines will please it.

units.la: LXI. Præstantia Novi Testamenti in Æternum etiam Ecclesiæ cultum se diffundit.
units.tr: LXI. The excellence of the New Testament extends also into eternity to the worship of the Church.

units.la: Qui non amplius servilis, carnalis & elementis mundi addictus, sed ingenuus, masculus, spiritualis est. Nam Spiritus est Deus, (Divinus, æternus, perfectissimus & beatissimus, & jam Pater in Christo nobis factus) & qui adorant eum, in Spiritu & veritate adorent oportet, Joh. IV. 24. In Spiritu, hoc est, cultu tali, quem Spiritus non servitutis, sed filiationis, qui κατ' ἐξοχὴν Spiritus Jehovæ audit, sanctificando operatur, & quem mens & voluntas hominis, quæ spiritus etiam est; absque quo nullus membrorum motus placere Deo potest, dictat. Cultus enim Dei principaliter in animo consistit; & quæ membris fiunt, secundum id, quod Spiritus hominis, & dictatus charitatis, & rectum judicium hominis ad gloriam Dei faciendum esse judicat. Absque hoc est, non cultus Dei, sed μυκτηρισμὸς ludificatio mera, & temeraria Nominis Divini usurpatio est. In veritate, hoc est, cum confessione veritatis promissionum, prophetiarum & figurarum. Adoratio illa in Spiritu in oppositione literæ & carnalis præcepti (qualis adoratio etiam Hierosolymis fuit) intelligitur merè, quia quodammodo illi etiam in spiritu adorabant; sed non sine literæ & carnalis præcepti observantia, adeóque non merè: in oppositione verò montis Samaritarum Garizim, in quo superstitio & hypocrisis exercebatur, intelligitur verè. Tempus enim instabat, ut & literalis adoratio, quæ in multis erat sine Spiritu, in fidelibus verò non in solo Spiritu; & superstitiosa adoratio, quæ qua planè non erat in Spiritu, à populo Israelitico auferretur; & soli illi adoratores censerentur, qui in Spiritu & veritate adorarent,&, interprete S. Paulo, Deo vivo (in quo est perpetua vita, & nihil quod mori posset, adeóque nil nisi spiritus, sanctam, bonam & immutabilem voluntatem habens; & charitas, ut sola charitate ei similes evadere possimus) & vero (qui nec mentiri, nec promissiones suas non implere, & rebus ipsis repræsentare potest; imò implevit & repræsentavit in Christo) servirent, 1. Thess. I. 9. In V. T. non deerat Spiritus; sed is erat servitutis, qui etiam Sanctos literæ & carni inservire subegit. Neque iidem poterant in confessione veritatis, sive rei exhibitæ, sed promissæ & speratæ duntaxat adorare. Et hactenus illi quoq; in Spiritu & Veritate adorarunt,quia Spiritus servitutis etiam fuit Spiritus sanctificationis, sed subjiciens servituti præcepti carnalis; & quia spes erat fides veritatis promissionum, & expectatio rei ipsius. Qua adoratione carentes, licet omnia in litera & carne facerent, Deo nulli placuerunt, quia in litera & carne non est similitudo Dei; qui Spiritus, sapientia, vita, amor, lux est; & in Dei similitudine cultus Deo placens consistit. Circumcisio enim vel præputium, mactatio animalium, sanguinis aspersio, lotiones, ciborum & dierum differentiæ non ea sunt, in quibus Dei similitudo & imago consistit. Umbræ hæ fuerunt, donec veritas non tantum promissionis, sed etiam rei promissæ, sive ejus ὑπαρξις & præsentia illas dispelleret. Dispulsis illis, locus non est adorationi nisi in Spiritu, qui sanctificando efficit veritatis cognitionem,& amorem,&gratiarum actionem pro eo, quod Spiritus servitutis compellebat ad servitutem elementorum mundi, propter veritatis promissionem, & rei ipsius expectationem.
units.tr: The New Testament's worship is no longer servile, carnal and bound to the elements of the world, but free, manly and spiritual. For God is Spirit (divine, eternal, most perfect and most blessed, and now made our Father in Christ), and those who worship him must worship in Spirit and truth, John 4:24. In Spirit means with the kind of worship which the Spirit of sonship, who is called the Spirit of Jehovah par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], works by sanctifying, and which the mind and will of man, which is also a spirit, dictates. Without this, no movement of the limbs can please God. For the worship of God consists chiefly in the soul, and what is done by the members follows from what the spirit of man, the dictate of charity and the right judgment of man, judges ought to be done for the glory of God. Without this there is no worship of God, but mere mockery [μυκτηρισμὸς], a trifling and reckless use of the Divine Name. In truth means with the confession of the truth of the promises, prophecies and figures. That worship in Spirit, understood in contrast to the letter and the carnal precept (which was also the worship at Jerusalem), is taken merely in a qualified sense, since in a certain way they also worshipped in spirit there, but not without observing the letter and the carnal precept, and so not merely. But in contrast to Mount Gerizim of the Samaritans, where superstition and hypocrisy were practised, it is taken truly. For the time was coming when both literal worship, which in many was without the Spirit, and in the faithful was not in the Spirit alone, and superstitious worship, which was not at all in the Spirit, would be removed from the Israelite people, and only those would be counted as worshippers who would worship in Spirit and truth, and, as St Paul explains, serve the living God (in whom is perpetual life and nothing that could die, and who therefore is nothing but spirit, having a holy, good and unchangeable will, and charity, so that only by charity can we become like him) and the true God (who can neither lie nor fail to fulfil his promises, and can present them in the things themselves; indeed he has fulfilled and presented them in Christ), 1 Thess. 1:9. In the Old Testament the Spirit was not lacking, but it was the Spirit of servitude, which compelled even the saints to serve the letter and the flesh. Nor could they worship in the confession of the truth of a thing exhibited, but only of a thing promised and hoped for. And so far they too worshipped in Spirit and truth, since the Spirit of servitude was also the Spirit of sanctification, but subjecting them to the servitude of the carnal precept; and because hope was the faith in the truth of the promises, and the expectation of the thing itself. Lacking this worship, though they did everything in letter and flesh, they pleased God in no way, because in letter and flesh there is no likeness of God, who is Spirit, wisdom, life, love and light; and the worship that pleases God consists in the likeness of God. For circumcision or uncircumcision, the slaughter of animals, the sprinkling of blood, washings, and the distinctions of foods and days are not the things in which the likeness and image of God consist. These were shadows, until the truth, not only of the promise but also of the promised thing, or its existence and presence, dispelled them. With them dispelled, there is room for worship only in Spirit, which, by sanctifying, produces the knowledge of the truth and love, and thanksgiving for what the Spirit of servitude had compelled men to render in servitude to the elements of the world, on account of the promise of truth and the expectation of the thing itself.

units.la: LXII. Neque ideo cultus Novi Testamenti non merè spiritualis est, quia in eo etiam Sacramentorum & signorum religio obtinet. Non enim quævis signa & pignora cultum literalem vel carnalem efficiunt, sed signa, elementa& pignora rerum nondum exhibitarum, quibus, qui colit, cum anxietate quadam inservire tenetur. At veritate exhibita Sacramentis N. T. non sunt ejusmodi signa vel elementa mundi, sed ἐπαγγελιῶν... firmamenta stipulationis bonæ (& consummatæ) conscientiæ, hoc est, fidei & charitatis experimento, tanquam arrhabone Spiritus obsignatæ per resurrectionem Christi, qui resuscitatus est ad nostri justificationem, 1. Pet. III. 21. & quasi verba visibilia, quibus Christus nobis præbet semetipsum, Regnum suum, & remissionem peccatorum, nos autem vicissim ei pro donis illis gratias agimus. Pontificii contra Sacramentis tanquam ex opere operato justificantibus utentes, non tantum elementis mundi iterum se subjiciunt, sed etiam revera elementis mundi id tribuunt, quod Dei in Christo est. Neque etiam proprie Deus in Sacramentis colitur. Nunquam enim potest Deus non major esse creatura, atque adeò nunquam in similitudine creaturæ colitur. Licet ergo Deus Sacramenta & symbola gratiæ, per quæ nos doceret, & quibus gratiam exhibitam obsignaret, instituerit;
units.tr: LXII. The worship of the New Testament is not therefore not wholly spiritual because in it the religion of the sacraments and signs also holds sway. For not every sign and pledge produces literal or carnal worship; rather it is signs, elements and pledges of things not yet exhibited, to which the one who worships is bound to serve with a certain anxiety. But with the truth now exhibited, the sacraments of the New Testament are not such signs or elements of the world, but the firm pledge of a good (and sealed) conscience (1 Pet. 3:21), that is, sealed by the experience of faith and charity, as a pledge of the Spirit, through the resurrection of Christ, who was raised for our justification (Rom. 4:25). They are also, as it were, visible words by which Christ offers himself to us, his kingdom and the forgiveness of sins, and we in turn give thanks to him for those gifts. The Papists, on the other hand, using the sacraments as if they justified ex opere operato, not only subject themselves again to the elements of the world, but actually attribute to the elements of the world what belongs to God in Christ. Nor is God properly worshipped in the sacraments. For God can never be less than a creature, and so he is never worshipped in the likeness of a creature. Therefore, although God instituted sacraments and symbols of grace, by which he might teach us and by which he might seal the grace given,

units.la: {a} Non obstante Sacramentorum, quæ terrestribus elementis constant, usu.
units.tr: {a} Notwithstanding the use of the sacraments, which consist of earthly elements.

units.la: tamen existimandum non est, velle Deum in Sacramentis coli, vel mentem nostram ejusmodi rebus, vel tanquam similitudini, vel tanquam Deo coli: Deus Altissimus non habitat in Templis manufactis, Act. VII. 48. Neq; colitur manibus hominum, nullius indigus, ipse vero dans omnibus vitam, & halitum & omnia, ib. XVII. 25. Per Sacramenta vero Deum colimus, quando eum non colimus in Sacramento & elemento; sed per ea excitamur ad cogitandum ea, quæ Deus per ea docet, & in fiducia ab eo petendum, quæ illis sigillis & pignoribus nobis ad se in fide accedentibus spondet.
units.tr: yet we should not think that God wishes to be worshipped in the sacraments, or that our mind is to worship such things either as images or as God: The Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands, Acts 7:48. Nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath and all things, ibid. 17:25. But we worship God through the sacraments when we do not worship him in the sacrament and the element; rather we are stirred by them to think on what God teaches through them, and to ask from him in trust what he promises to us, who come to him in faith by these seals and pledges.

units.la: LXIII. Cum cultus N. T. spiritualis sit, Minisferium ejusdem spirituale etiam sit oportet. Deus nos idoneos fecit Ministros Novi Testamenti, non litera, sed Spiritus, 2.Cor. III. 6. Unde Ministerium V. T. non tantum litera, sed etiam mortis, v. 7. & condemnationis, v. 9. at Ministerium N. T. & Spiritus v. 8. & justitia v. 9. appellat. Veteris ergo Testamenti Ministri erant tum litera, hoc est, verbi, quod per se, primò & solum, non adducto alio verbo, hominem convertere & vivificare, hoc est, regenerare & sanctificare, vel propter se & primo in cordibus scribi non poterat; cujusmodi verbum erat illud: Qui fecerit illa, vivet in iis: Maledictus sit: &c. Gal. III. 10.12. item verbum de purificationibus legalibus, Hebr. VII. 18.19. IX. 9.13.14. X. 1.2. nec non promissiones temporalium bonorum: Tum mortis, quia verbum ejusmodi non vivificabat, justificabat, sed occidebat, declarando, mortem esse stipendia peccati; & peccatorem esse sub maledictione; quin & peccatum irritando, efficiendo, ut id abundet & illud peccaminosum secundum excessum demonstrando, Rom. V. 20. VII. 8-13. Tum denique condemnationis, quia Lex omnes homines, etiam Israelitas convincebat peccati, eos impuros declarabat, ciborum ac rerum distinctione ab altari arcebat; peccatum commemorabat, & exprobrabat, proximum ad Deum aditum intercludebat. Licet enim sub V. T. non defuerint Sancti, qui per verbum V. T. illuminati fuerint, ut Deum amarent, qui etiam per fidem testimonium acceperunt, quòd sint hæredes justitiæ & vitæ, Heb. XI. 39. & eodem tempore præter legem subingressam nunquam non promissio in Paradiso audita, & predicata sonuerit: tamen ipse Apostolus 2.Cor. III. 14-18. docet, Verbum illud, quo Deus homini peccatori, ut amabilis commendatur, perinde fuisse velatum, atque facies Mosis è monte descendentis circumpositio velamine abscondita fuit: utrevelata facie gloriam Domini speculari non licuerit. Nempe in aditu verbi collocata fuerunt verba illa: Qui fecerit illa, vivet in iis: Maledictus, &c. Quin & præceptis multifariis de cultu externo & sacrificiis adjectum fuit verbum de remissione. Unde stupidis & induratis cogitatio incessit peccata sua non obsistere justitiæ. Quia igitur sermo ille solus induration emollire non potuit, litera & quidem occidentis, condemnantis nomine venit. Nucleus vero illius sermonis & medulla, virtus atque bonum, quod in eo ostendebatur, nec palam, nec solum, sed sub cortice & involucris propo-
units.tr: LXIII. Since the worship of the New Testament is spiritual, its ministry too must be spiritual. God has made us fit ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit, 2 Cor. 3:6. Hence Paul calls the ministry of the Old Testament not only the letter, but also of death (v. 7) and of condemnation (v. 9), while he calls the ministry of the New Testament of the Spirit (v. 8) and of righteousness (v. 9). The ministers of the Old Testament were therefore, on the one hand, of the letter, that is, of the word which, of itself, first and alone, without another word being added, could not convert and quicken man, that is, regenerate and sanctify him, or be written first and for its own sake in hearts. Such a word was this: He who does those things shall live in them; cursed be he, etc. (Gal. 3:10, 12); likewise the word about legal purifications (Heb. 7:18-19; 9:9, 13-14; 10:1-2), and also the promises of temporal goods. On the other hand, they were of death, because a word of this kind did not quicken or justify, but killed, by declaring that death is the wages of sin and that the sinner is under a curse; indeed by stirring up sin, bringing it about that sin might abound and become exceedingly sinful, as it shows (Rom. 5:20; 7:8-13). Finally, they were of condemnation, because the Law convicted all men, even the Israelites, of sin, declared them unclean, and by the distinction of foods and things kept them from the altar; it recalled sin and reproached them, and it shut off the approach of the neighbour to God. For although under the Old Testament there were not lacking saints who, enlightened by the word of the Old Testament, loved God, and who by faith received the testimony that they were heirs of righteousness and life (Heb. 11:39), and although at the same time, besides the law which had been introduced, the promise heard in Paradise never failed to be made known and to sound forth, yet the Apostle himself teaches (2 Cor. 3:14-18) that that word by which God commends himself as lovable to sinful man was in the same way veiled, just as the face of Moses, when he came down from the mountain, was hidden by a veil placed around it, so that it was not permitted to look upon the glory of the Lord with an unveiled face. Indeed, at the entrance of the word were placed those words: He who does those things shall live in them; cursed, etc. Moreover, along with the many precepts about external worship and sacrifices, a word about forgiveness was also added. So a thought crept into the dull and hardened that their sins did not stand in the way of justice. Since, therefore, that word alone could not soften the hardness, it came under the name of letter, and indeed of the letter that kills and condemns. But the kernel and marrow of that word, the power and the good which was shown in it, was set forth not openly nor alone, but under the bark and wrappings

units.la: {b} Qualis N. T. cultus, tale etiam Ministerium est. proponebatur. Proin is sermo, ceu litera, aures verberavit, sed ad cor ipsum penetrare non potuit.
units.tr: {b} As the worship of the New Testament is, so also is its ministry set forth. Therefore that discourse, like a letter, struck the ears, but could not penetrate to the heart itself.

units.la: LXIV. Tametsi vero etiamnum Evangelium pereuntibus occultatum, 2. Cor. IV. 3. Judæis scandalum & Græcis stultitia, 1. Cor. I. 23. & multis odor mortis ad mortem, 2. Cor. II. 16. sit, tamen non amplius simpliciter est κεκαλυμμένον velatum, sed φῶς Lux, ibid. IV. 3. 6. neque adeo litera eo sensu; quo Lex ante Christum fuit. Nam id, quod Judæi ante oculos videbant, quod primo audiebant, quod promissionibus verbis brevissimis, si cum verbo legis illa comparetur, comprehensæ, circumpositum fuit ejusmodi fuit, ut per illud nemo vivificari potuerit; adeoque nonnisi Litera occidens fuit. Alia ratio est Evangelii, quod nunc per se, primo & immediate auditur, inculcatur, insatiabiliter ita exponitur, ut non amplius audiatur Lex, velut nobis in servitutem iterum redigendis dicta; imo audiatur verbum, quod non amplius simus sub Lege, sed sub Gratia. Neque amplius videntur, vel, ceu facienda, prædicantur illa omnia, quæ Israelitas per omnem vitam exercitos habebant: imo videntur, quæ illi non viderunt: audiuntur, quæ non audiverunt. Cessante Lege & ministerio præcepti carnalis, maledictione silente, accusatione lapsus peccati & reatus expirante, non aliud nunc ministerium exercetur, quam verbi illius, quod primo & per se cordi à Spiritu S. inscriptum animas convertit, oculos illuminat, & fatuos sapientes reddit. Quod autem eo audito quidam scandalizantur, non occasione obscuritatis cujuspiam verbi, vel speciei extrinsecus objectæ, & intelligentiam sufflaminantis, sed per insitum homini naturali lucis odium evenit. Hoc est judicium, quod Lux venit in mundum, & homines dilexerunt magis tenebras, quàm Lumen. Mala enim opera eorum fuerunt. Omnis enim qui mala facit, odit lucem, & non venit ad lucem ne opera ejus reprehendantur; Joh. III. 19. 20. Qui ergo hypocrita non credit Evangelio, per ipsa illa verba, quæ in ore habet, damnatur: & qui aliud docet, se apostatam ostendit; neque quicquam, quo se Christianum demonstret, habet.
units.tr: LXIV. Although the Gospel is still hidden from those who are perishing, 2 Cor. 4:3; a scandal to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks, 1 Cor. 1:23; and to many a fragrance of death unto death, 2 Cor. 2:16; nevertheless it is no longer simply veiled [κεκαλυμμένον] but is Light [φῶς], ibid. 4:3, 6, and so it is not a letter in the sense in which the Law was before Christ. For what the Jews saw before their eyes, what they first heard, and what was contained in the very brief promissory words, when compared with the word of the Law, was of such a kind, with its surrounding matter, that no one could be made alive through it; so it was only the letter that kills. The Gospel is of another character. What is now heard first, directly and of itself, is pressed home and set forth without ceasing, so that the Law is no longer heard as spoken to us as those to be brought back into bondage. Rather what is heard is the word that we are no longer under the Law but under grace. Nor are all those things preached any more as seen or as to be done, which the Israelites had exercised throughout their whole lives. Rather, things are seen which they did not see, and heard which they did not hear. With the Law ceasing, the ministry of the carnal precept gone, the curse silent, and the accusation of the fall of sin and its guilt expired, no other ministry is now carried on than that of the word which, first and of itself, inscribed on the heart by the Holy Spirit, converts souls, illumines the eyes, and makes the foolish wise. That some are scandalized on hearing it does not happen because of any obscurity in a word, or some external object that hinders understanding, but through the hatred of light implanted in natural man. This is the judgment, that light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, for their works were evil. For everyone who does evil hates the light, and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved; John 3:19, 20. Therefore the hypocrite who does not believe the Gospel is condemned by the very words he has in his mouth; and whoever teaches otherwise shows himself an apostate, and has nothing by which to demonstrate that he is a Christian.

units.la: LXV. Est igitur Ministerium N. T. διακονία Πνεύματος & διακαιοσύνης, Ministerium Spiritus & justitiæ, 2. Cor. III. 6. 8. Spiritus, quia non aliud loquitur, quàm quod Spiritus S. in N. T. datus cordibus ad amorem Dei recta inscribit; atque id palam & sine involucro loquitur, jubens id, quod loquitur, plenissimè & gloriosissimè intelligi; neque adeo fideles vel propositione formulæ fœderis operum, & maledictionis, vel figuris & tegumentis variis distringit, sed remoto velo omni; fractóque cortice rem ipsam & fundamentum, Jesum Christum Dominum; per passiones consummatum; ostendit; denique id loquitur; quod credimus, dicimus Abba, Pater, atque ita accipimus Spiritum filiationis; & filii Dei vivi evadimus. Qui merus Spiritus est; non Lex carnalis præcepti; omnes filios Israelis tum carnales; tum secundum promissionem commiscens: & Spiritus promissionis est; quia eum amorem in nobis operatur, qui nobis amantibus ut filiis, & Deo amato; ut Patri convenit. Justitiæ etiam ministerium est; non quod meliora justitiæ præceptæ præscribat & proponat, cùm ἀκαιοσύνης justitia κατακρίσει condemnationi opponatur, adeoque jus vitæ illis, qui in Christum credunt, acquisitum notet; sed tum, quia prædicat justitiam & condonationem peccatorum, Jerem. XXXI. 34. Hebr. VIII. 12. Psal. XXII. 32. Is. LI. 10. 11. tum Deo cooperatur ad Regnum Christi erigendum, quod justitiæ ipsius debitum est, Esaj. LIII. 11. tum quia servos justitiæ ad vitam facit.
units.tr: LXV. The ministry of the New Testament is therefore the ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness [διακονία Πνεύματος καὶ δικαιοσύνης], 2 Cor. 3:6, 8. It is of the Spirit, because it speaks nothing other than what the Holy Spirit, given in the New Testament to hearts, rightly writes to the love of God. It speaks this openly and without a veil, bidding what it says to be understood most fully and most gloriously. It does not therefore distract the faithful with the proposition of the formula of the covenant of works and of the curse, nor with various figures and coverings. Rather, with every veil removed and the shell broken, it shows the thing itself and the foundation, Jesus Christ the Lord, consummated through his sufferings. Finally, it speaks what we believe, and we say "Abba, Father", and so we receive the Spirit of adoption and become sons of the living God. It is pure Spirit, not the carnal law of precept, which mingles all the sons of Israel, carnal as well as according to promise; and it is the Spirit of promise, because it works in us that love which suits us as sons loving, and God as loved Father. It is also a ministry of righteousness: not because it prescribes and sets forth better precepts of righteousness, since righteousness [δικαιοσύνη] is opposed to condemnation [κατάκρισις], and so denotes the right to life acquired for those who believe in Christ; but both because it preaches righteousness and the forgiveness of sins, Jer. 31:34; Heb. 8:12; Ps. 22:32; Isa. 51:10, 11; and because it cooperates with God in raising up the kingdom of Christ, which is owed to his righteousness, Isa. 53:11; and because it makes servants of righteousness unto life.

units.la: LXVI. Est etiam Ministerium N. T. λόγος καταλλαγῆς sermo reconciliationis, 2. Cor. V. 19.
units.tr: LXVI. The ministry of the New Testament is also the word of reconciliation [λόγος καταλλαγῆς], 2 Cor. 5:19.

units.la: quia Ministri N. T. palam prædicant; Deum in carne apparuisse; & mundum sibi, non imputando eis offensas, reconciliasse; & pro Christo (propter causam & gloriam Christi) legatione funguntur tanquam Deo per eos hortante (non imperando, fidei dominando; velut apud servos, sed adhortando, suaviter monendo; orationis παρακλήσεως; velut apud liberos, utendo, & quidem non suis; sed Dei verbis) rogantes vel petentes Christi causa (cujus interest; ut hac via, blandaque ratione hæreditate sanguine suo parta, quam & ipse sic per nos מרבה postulat, Psal. II. 8. & non cum terrore, sed cum omni suavitate adire vult, potiatur) Reconciliamini Deo (reconciliato per Christum; qui pro vobis peccatum factus est; Deo, ipsi quoque eidem reconciliamini; inimicitiam, odia ponendo, arcem salutis apprehendendo, pacem cum Deo pangendo, Regnum & justitiam ejus quærendo; Evangelio credendo, respicendo, Deum diligendo; præceptis ejus obediendo) 2. Cor. V. 20. Ex quibus verbis Evangelici Ministerii à Legali differentia amplius cognoscitur. Nam in V. T. Pædagogi & œconomi cum imperio & duriter sic loquebantur: Ut Deum placetis, sacrificia λατρεία offerte, date compensationem pro peccato vestro, lavate, purificate vos; sin, velut immundi, castra Dei purgate; &c. Evangelici contrà ministerii sermo in mera παρακλήσει adhortatione & δεήσει petitione, rogatione consistit; non imperio tanquam apud servos, sed suavis & συναγωγὴ velut apud ingenuos est. Non enim frangere; sed ædificare: non terrorem incutere; sed amorem infigere contendit. Christus quippe, pro quo legatione funguntur; חמדת כל הגוים delicia omnium gentium venire; Hagg. II. 8. & non clamare, non extollere in platea vocem, calamum quassatum non contundere, linum fumigans non extinguere Esaj. XLII. 2. 3. voluit. Non aliud ergo jam Evangelica tuba sonat, quàm Reconciliamini Deo; sermonem reconciliationis recipite, os aperite, ut à Deo illud impleatur; Deo gratias agite, laudem sacrificate, &c. Non enim accessimus ad montem tractabilem; & accensum ignem, & turbinem, & caliginem, & procellam, & tubæ sonum, & vocem verborum, quam qui audiverunt, deprecati sunt, ne sibi adderetur sermo, &c. Sed accessimus ad montem Sion, & civitatem Dei viventis; Hierosolymam cælestem, myriadas Angelorum, Panegyrin & concionem primogenitorum, qui in Cœlis conscripti sunt; & judicem Deum omnium, & spiritus justorum consummatorum, & Testamenti Novi Mediatorem Jesum, & sanguinem aspersionis, præstantiora loquentem præ Abel, Hebr. XII. 18-24.
units.tr: because the ministers of the New Testament openly preach that God has appeared in the flesh and has reconciled the world to himself, not imputing their offences to them; and they act as ambassadors for Christ (for the cause and glory of Christ), as though God were exhorting through them. They do not command as to slaves, lording it over faith, but exhort and gently admonish, by the word of comfort [παράκλησις]; as among free men, using, and indeed not their own words but the words of God. They beseech or ask in Christ's cause, for it is his interest that, in this way and by this gentle method, he may obtain the inheritance won by his own blood, which he also asks of us in this way (Ps. 2:8), and which he wishes to approach not with terror but with all sweetness. Be reconciled to God (who is reconciled through Christ, who was made sin for you): be reconciled to him yourselves too, by laying down enmity and hatred, by laying hold on the citadel of salvation, by making peace with God, by seeking his kingdom and righteousness, by believing the Gospel, by turning back, by loving God, and by obeying his precepts; 2 Cor. 5:20. From these words the difference between the Evangelical ministry and the Legal may be understood more clearly. For in the Old Testament the tutors and stewards spoke thus with authority and harshly: "That you may please God, offer sacrifices of service [λατρεία], give compensation for your sin, wash, purify yourselves; otherwise, as unclean, purge the camp of God," and so on. The language of the Evangelical ministry, by contrast, consists in pure exhortation [παράκλησις] and petition [δέησις], asking and requesting; it is not command as to servants, but gentle and as it were a gathering [συναγωγή] among free men. For it does not seek to break, but to build up; not to strike terror, but to implant love. Christ indeed, for whom they act as ambassadors, willed to come as the desire of all nations (Hag. 2:8), and not to cry out or raise his voice in the street, not to break a bruised reed or quench a smoking flax (Isa. 42:2, 3). Therefore the Evangelical trumpet now sounds nothing other than "Be reconciled to God; receive the word of reconciliation; open your mouth that it may be filled by God; give thanks to God, offer praise," and so on. For you have not come to a mountain that can be touched, and burning fire, and darkness, and storm, and the sound of a trumpet, and a voice of words, which those who heard it begged should not be spoken to them any further. But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels, the festal assembly and church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect, and to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood, which speaks better things than Abel; Heb. 12:18-24.

units.la: LXVII. Est & eximia fidelibus N. T. Hæreditas omnium, quæ extra ipsos sunt. Deus æqui-dem dem hominem à se creatum מושל Dominum rerum omnium fecit, Gen. I. 26. Sed dominium illud ἐξ τὸ δοκεῖν restrinxit. In V.T. Ecclesiæ hæreditatem terræ Canaan, ceu pignoris meliorum donavit. Dixit enim ad Abrahamum: Dabo tibi & Semini Tuo post te terram peregrinationum tuarum in possessionem perpetuam, ibid.XVII. 8. Ista est terra, quæ cadet vobis בנחלה in hæreditatem, terra Canaan. Num.XXXIV. 2. In eadem vero terra in hæreditatem data non pauca etiam credentium usibus Divinitus subtracta sunt. Quædam enim, ceu immunda, gustare, vel attrectare nefas fuit. Nunc vero omnia pura sunt puris, Tit. I. 15. Nihil enim amplius ceu impurum prohiberi iis, qui puri, hoc est, per sanguinem Christi purificati & expiati planè sunt, potest. Si cum Christo mortui estis elementis mundi, quid ut viventes in mundo, dogmata suscipitis? Ne tangas, neque gustes, neque contrectes; quæ omnia sunt εἰς φθορὰν τῆς ἀποχρήσεως ad corruptionem usu secundum mandata hominum, Col.II.21. 22. Omnia, quæ in macello venduntur, edite, nihil examinantes propter conscientiam, quia Domini est terra, & plenitudo ejus, &c. 1.Cor. X.25.26. Fuit etiam in V.T. terra Dei, & non idolorum. Neque tamen Deus Regnum in tota terra habuit. Soli Israeli in terra sua collocato se revelavit, & Leges suas dedit. Omnis reliqua terra immunda fuit. Non habitant in terra Domini; & in terra Assur immundum comedunt, Hos. IX. 3. Nihil enim aliud Deus gentibus dedit, nisi Cœlum, terram & sidera, Deut. IV. 19.20. Sed voluit esse portio Israelis. Quamobrem Israelitæ, ne reliquarum gentium instar essent providere & diligenter inquirere debuerunt, an ea, quæ comederent, idololatria contaminata essent, nec ne. Postquam vero Deus coepit habere Regnum in gentibus in toto mundo, quoad victum seu cibum discrimen inter populos cessare debuit: Ideo Psal. VIII. cùm dixisset David v. 2. Dei Nomen valde magnum esse in universa terra: & v.6. glorificationem Christi commemorasset, statim v. 7. subjicit: Omnia (sublata distinctione, quæ erat commemoratio peccati) posuisti sub pedibus ejus; Pecudes & boves, universa illa, bestias agri, volucres Cœli, pisces maris, &c. claudens v. 10. Jehova Domine noster, quàm grande est Nomen tuum in tota terra! Et S. Paulus cibos interdici vetat, tum quia omnis creatura bona, & nulla rejectanea est, si cum gratiarum actione accipiatur: tum quia, etiamsi nos peccatores simus, sanctificatur, seu sancta nobis fit per sermonem Dei, & intercessionem Mediatoris, 1.Tim. IV. 3.4.5. Sed parum id est; Nam, inquit S. Paulus, nemo glorietur in hominibus. Omnia enim vestra sunt, (omnes homines à Deo missi, unà cum donis ipsorum & verbis, quæ loquuntur, vestri; usibus vestris consecrati sunt; non vos illorum estis, ut in servitutem ab iis redigi positis) sive Paulus, sive Apollos, sive Cephas, (& quanto magis, qui successor Cephæ audire vult) sive mundus, (cujus hæreditatem cum Abrahamo aditis) sive vita, sive mors, (quia vobis datum est, ut per utramque Deum glorificare possitis) sive præsentia, sive futura (quæ & in V.T. fuerunt, & in Novo sunt) omnia vestra sunt, (examini & ἀναχωρήσει vestræ subjecta, ut in fide nova à veteribus, dicta Dei à dictis hominum distinguatis) Vos vero Christi, (ut illi soli immediatè omnes & singuli adhærescatis) Christus autem Dei, (non hominum, non multitudinis hominum, sed Dei Patris, qui illum misit, & ad cujus cognitionem & fidem immediatè illenos adducit) 1.Cor.III.21.22.23.
units.tr: LXVII. The faithful of the New Testament also have an excellent inheritance of all things which are outside themselves. God indeed made man, created by him, ruler [מושל] of all things (Gen. 1:26); but he restricted that dominion in appearance only [ἐξ τὸ δοκεῖν]. In the Old Testament he gave the Church the inheritance of the land of Canaan, as a pledge of better things. For he said to Abraham: I will give to you and to your seed after you the land of your sojournings as a perpetual possession, ibid. 17:8. This is the land which shall fall to you by lot [בנחלה] as an inheritance, the land of Canaan; Num. 34:2. Yet in that same land given as an inheritance, not a few things were withdrawn by God from the use of believers. For some things, as unclean, it was unlawful to taste or even touch. But now all things are pure to the pure, Titus 1:15. For nothing further can be forbidden as unclean to those who are truly pure, that is, purified and cleansed by the blood of Christ. If you died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though living in the world, do you submit to decrees? "Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch"; all of which are for corruption in the using, according to the commandments of men; Col. 2:20-22. Eat whatever is sold in the meat market, asking no question for conscience' sake; for the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof, etc.; 1 Cor. 10:25, 26. In the Old Testament too the land was God's, and not of idols. Yet God did not have his kingdom over the whole earth. He revealed himself only to Israel, settled in its own land, and gave his laws to it; all the rest of the earth was unclean. They do not dwell in the land of the Lord; and in the land of Assyria they eat unclean food; Hos. 9:3. For God gave nothing else to the nations than heaven, earth, and stars; Deut. 4:19, 20. But he willed to be the portion of Israel. Therefore the Israelites, so as not to be like the other nations, had to take care and diligently inquire whether the things they ate were contaminated by idolatry or not. But after God began to have his kingdom among the nations throughout the whole world, the distinction between peoples as to food and drink ought to have ceased. So in Psalm 8, after David had said in verse 2 that the name of God is very great in all the earth, and in verse 6 had recalled the glorification of Christ, he immediately added in verse 7: You have put all things under his feet (the distinction, which was a reminder of sin, being removed): sheep and oxen, all of them, and the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven, the fish of the sea, etc., closing in verse 10: O Lord our Lord, how excellent is your name in all the earth! And St. Paul forbids the forbidding of foods, both because every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected, if it is received with thanksgiving, and because, even though we are sinners, it is sanctified, or made holy for us, by the word of God and the intercession of the Mediator; 1 Tim. 4:3-5. But this is a small matter. For, says St. Paul, let no one glory in men. For all things are yours (all men sent by God, together with their gifts and the words they speak, are yours; they are consecrated to your uses; you are not theirs, so as to be reduced by them into servitude), whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas (and how much more he who wishes to hear the successor of Cephas), or the world (whose inheritance you have entered with Abraham), or life, or death (because it has been given to you that through both you may be able to glorify God), or things present, or things to come (which were both in the Old Testament and are in the New), all are yours (subject to your examination and withdrawal, so that in the new faith you may distinguish the words of God from the words of men, as the ancients did not); and you are Christ's (so that you cleave to him alone, immediately, all and each of you), and Christ is God's (not of men, not of a multitude of men, but of God the Father, who sent him, and to the knowledge and faith of whom he leads us immediately); 1 Cor. 3:21-23.

units.la: LXVIII.
units.tr: LXVIII.

units.la: Quæ Bonorum N.T. ratio est, eadem est obsignationis Bonorum illorum, quæ in Sacramentis N.T. obtinet. Quia enim status ipse N.T. melior & consummatior est, etiam signis aliis, τελείωσιν consummationem illam significantius & efficacius repræsentantibus, neque amplius Ecclesiam in servitutem redigentibus, sed de communione cum Christo & morte ejus, inque eo adoptione & justitia ad spem vitæ coufirmantibus, opus fuit. Sunt ergo & illa τελειώσεως consummationis, quia spem meliorem, per quam Deo approximamus, Hebr.VII.19: obsignant, & quidem, uti S. Augustinus, de Doctr. Christi. lib. III.9. loquitur, pauca pro multis, facta facilima, intellectu augustissima, observatione castissima, sicuti est Baptismi Sacramentum, & celebratio corporis & sanguinis Domini. In Sacramentis veteribus fuit reatus detectio & commemoratio, in his est ejus deletio & consolatio: in illis gentium disgregatio; in his congregatio: in illis futuri obscurior præmonstratio; in his rei gestæ commemoratio; illa fuerunt σκιαὶ umbræ futurorum, & eatenus signa nuda, quatenus corpus, rem, imaginem rerum ipsarum velut exhibitam non significarunt, sed exhibendam præfigurarunt; hæc corpus & rem exhibitam significant & obsignant; proin in iis propter additam Evangelii lucem omni luce clariorem, nil nisi meralux, veritas, res, charitas, fiducia, libertas, gaudium & satietas obtinet.
units.tr: The New Testament good things are sealed in the same way as the sacraments of the New Testament seal them. Because the New Testament state is itself better and more complete, other signs were also needed, which represent that completion [teleiōsin] more significantly and effectively. These signs no longer bring the Church into servitude, but confirm, from communion with Christ and his death, and in him adoption and righteousness, unto the hope of life. So these too belong to completion [teleiōseōs], since they seal the better hope through which we draw near to God, Heb. 7:19. Indeed, as Augustine says in De doctrina Christiana III.9, they are few for many, very easy to perform, most august in understanding, most chaste in observance, such as the sacrament of Baptism and the celebration of the body and blood of the Lord. In the old sacraments there was the detection and remembrance of guilt; in these there is its removal and consolation. In those there was the scattering of the Gentiles; in these the gathering together. In those there was a rather obscure foreshadowing of what was to come; in these there is the remembrance of what has been done. Those were shadows [skiai] of the things to come, and were bare signs only so far as they did not signify the body and the thing, the image of the things as if already exhibited, but foreshadowed what was still to be exhibited. These signify and seal the body and the thing exhibited. Therefore in them, because of the added light of the Gospel, brighter than all light, nothing holds sway but pure light, truth, reality, love, confidence, liberty, joy and satisfaction.

units.la: LXIX.
units.tr: LXIX.

units.la: Atque hæ promissiones, hæc Bona illa ἀλλοφωτες sunt, quibus in œconomia plenitudinis temporum (Ephes. I.10.) Evangelium proprie dictum non tantùm Legem, sed ipsam etiam promissionem ad Christum usque audi-tam superat; & Fœdus ipsum atq; Testamentū Gratiæ consummat. Quæ salus indefesso studio affectanda, & pensi maximi habenda est.
