S.Paulus ostendit inquiens: τῶς ἐκφόβοῦμεν τηλικαύτης ἀμελήσαντες Quomodo effugiemus, tanta salute (jam in causa sua, Principe salutis per passiones consummato, extante) neglecta? Hebr. II.3. Tanta enim salus non utique ἀμέλεταν neglectum, sed σπουδὴν studium, curam longè intensiorem, amorem Dei tanta bona in Christo donantis, flagrantiorem, & novo velut præcepto Joh. XIII. 34. 1. Joh. II. 8. ob veteris in exemplo novo diligentis nos Christi βεβαίωσιν confirmationem, mandatam altissimèque infixam, postulat. Nam ἐπεφάνη ἡ χάρις ... Θεοῦ (illuxit, Solis justitiæ radiosa proles, cedentibus umbris & nocte Legis) gratia Dei salutifera (unà cum Christo Sole justitiæ, ישועה Σωτηρίας Θεοῦ Salutari Dei, quod est Christus in carnem missus; Gratia omnis, quæ per ejus obedientiam, morte oppetita præstitam, & Spiritum Filiationis manifestatur & credentibus donatur; Testamentum illud Dei, & εὐδοκία, quia bonum ei visum est, & σκεῦος, qua statuit & decrevit Judæos simul & gentes, in uno corpore creare novam creaturam, ad credendum in Deum, eum amandum, ei gratias agendum, & eundem glorificandum) αὐτὸν δίκαιον.
units.tr: These promises and these good things are ἀλλοφωτες [of another light], in which, in the economy of the fullness of times (Eph. 1:10), the Gospel properly so called surpasses not only the Law but even the promise heard until Christ, and it completes the covenant itself and the Testament of grace. This salvation is to be sought with unwearied zeal and held in the greatest esteem. St. Paul shows this, saying: τῶς ἐκφόβοῦμεν τηλικαύτης ἀμελήσαντες [How shall we escape, if we neglect so great a salvation?], already accomplished in its own cause, the Prince of salvation having been perfected through sufferings and standing, Heb. 2:3. For so great a salvation does not demand ἀμέλεταν [neglect], but σπουδὴν [zeal], a far more intense care and a more fervent love of God, who gives such great goods in Christ. It demands this as if by a new command, John 13:34; 1 John 2:8, that we should love with the new example of Christ, which confirms the old command, and is deeply fixed. For ἐπεφάνη ἡ χάρις ... Θεοῦ [the grace of God has appeared], (it shone forth, the radiant offspring of the Sun of righteousness, the shadows and the night of the Law giving way) the saving grace of God, together with Christ the Sun of righteousness, ישועה [yeshuah] Σωτηρίας Θεοῦ [the salvation of God], the Salvation of God, which is Christ sent into the flesh. It is all the grace that is manifested through his obedience, performed by his death, and the Spirit of sonship, and is given to believers; that testament of God, and εὐδοκία [good pleasure], because it seemed good to him, and σκεῦος [purpose], by which he determined and decreed to create the Jews and the Gentes alike in one body as a new creature, to believe in God, to love him, to give thanks to him, and to glorify him in turn; αὐτὸν [him] δίκαιον [righteous].

units.la: Denique & Obsignatio Bonorum N.T. quæ per Sacramenta N.T. fit, perfectior & consummatior est. {*}δεύτατε erudiens nos, ( non legis instar operum omne opus, & quidem præsens & perpetuum; stipulans; sed, quod gratiæ proprium est, puerorum & charissimorum filiorum instar regens, & ad virilem perfectionem & plenitudinem Christi perducere satagens, in παιδεία institutione hac tua omni cum longanimitate & φιλανθρωπίᾳ, tum pueris in Christo se accommodans, & fumigans lignum non extinguens; nec calamum quassatum frangens: tum viros exercens, & per homines proficientes infatuos; simplices, pueros, ut omnes serventur; exuberans, quin & ipsos docentes & regentes erudiens, ut & ipsi erudiant alios in justitia cum omni longanimitate & mansuetudine; 2. Tim. II.24.25.26. III.16. ut abnegata impietate & mundanis cupiditatibus (tum ignorantia, odio, blasphemia Dei; tum amore non veri boni, velut veri boni, & amore mali, ceu boni,) temperanter & juste & pie vivamus in hoc seculo, (dum in carne, in corpore peccati & mortis fumus) expectantes beatam illam spem & ἐπιφάνειαν affulgentiam gloriæ magni illius Dei & Salvatoris Jesu Christi; qui dedit seipsum pro nobis, ut nos redimeret ab omni peccato, & purificaret sibi populum peculii, æmulatorem bonorum operum; Tit. II. 11-15. Totus igitur hic Evangelii cursus duplicem inter ἐπιφάνειαν affulgentiam, nempe Gratiæ salutiferæ, v. 12: & Gloriæ, v 13: sic impense laborare & desudare debet, ut per Gratiæ illius παιδείαν Evangelio & Salutari nostro dignam ad cœlestem Gloriam grassemur. Neque grassabimur ordine & feliciter, si Evangelii institutionem, postulata & promissa semper & indefesso studio ad animum non revocaverimus.
units.tr: Finally, the sealing of the New Testament goods, which is effected through the sacraments of the New Testament, is more perfect and more complete. δεύτατε erudiens nos [teaching us] (not as a law, making every work a work of obligation, and that a present and perpetual one, stipulating; but, as is proper to grace, ruling as children and dearly beloved sons, and striving to bring them to the manly perfection and fullness of Christ). In this παιδεία [instruction] of yours, you show all long-suffering and φιλανθρωπίᾳ [kindness], accommodating yourself to children in Christ, not quenching the smoking flax nor breaking the bruised reed; and also exercising men, and advancing those who are foolish, simple and childish through men, so that all may be saved. You abound, teaching and instructing even those who teach and rule, so that they in turn may instruct others in righteousness with all long-suffering and meekness, 2 Tim. 2:24-26; 3:16, so that, denying impiety and worldly lusts (both ignorance, hatred and blasphemy of God, and love of what is not truly good as if it were truly good, and love of evil as if it were good), we may live soberly, righteously and godly in this present world (while we are in the flesh, in the body of sin and death), looking for that blessed hope and the appearing [epiphaneian] of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ; who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify to himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works, Titus 2:11-15. Therefore this whole course of the Gospel, lying between the ἐπιφάνειαν [appearing] of the saving grace, v. 12, and of the glory, v. 13, ought to labour and toil so earnestly that, through the παιδείαν [instruction] of that grace, we may advance worthily of the Gospel and of our salvation towards the heavenly glory. We shall not advance in order and happily unless we always recall to mind the instruction, the demands and the promises of the Gospel with unwearied zeal.

units.la: LXX. Magni momenti hæc de œconomia Fœderis Gratiæ, & differentia utriusque Testamenti doctrina, ex Scripturis hausta est.
units.tr: LXX. This doctrine of the economy of the covenant of grace, and of the difference between the two Testaments, is of great importance and has been drawn from Scripture.

units.la: Ab ejus enim ignoratione & neglectu omnes fere hæreses & difficultates in Theologia plurimæ proveniunt. Nihil de Judæis dicam, qui perpetuitatem œconomiæ priscæ & legis placitorum omnibus, quod ajunt, interdictis defensitantes, facile eò prolapsi sunt, ut veram justitiam, & præstantiam Regni Messiæ abnegarent, & in hugis quibusdam constituerent; denique Novum Testamentum ex terra in Cœlum ablegarent; aliaque longe facie ibidem induerent.
units.tr: For almost all the heresies and many of the difficulties in theology arise from ignorance or neglect of it. I say nothing of the Jews, who, defending the perpetual validity of the old economy and the statutes of the law against everything, as they say, that is forbidden, easily slid so far that they denied the true righteousness and the excellence of the kingdom of the Messiah, reduced it to certain shadows, and in the end banished the New Testament from earth to heaven, clothing it there in quite another form.

units.la: Quorum impia eam in rem placita supra confiximus. Et circa ejusdem œconomiæ Evangelicæ Legem, quæ fidei & respicentiæ solius est, errores Pontificiorum & Socinianorum, Evangelium in novam Legem operum transformantium jam etiam jugulare occupavimus.
units.tr: We have already set down their impious opinions on this point. And concerning the law of the same Gospel economy, which belongs to faith and repentance alone, we have already begun to strangle the errors of the Papists and the Socinians, who transform the Gospel into a new law of works.

units.la: LXXI. Sed circa Evangelii Promissa & Novi Testamenti Bona αἱ περιτομαί haud excusatius iidem peccant. Nam Socinianos universa illa vel tollere, sublata satisfactione & proprie dicta λυτρώσει Christi; vel falso fundamento inædificare, non est cur longo sermone confirmemus.
units.tr: LXXI. But the same men sin no less inexcusably concerning the promises of the Gospel and the good things of the New Testament, [the promises]. For that the Socinians either take all of these away, with satisfaction and the strictly so-called redemption of Christ removed, or build them upon a false foundation, there is no reason to confirm at length.

units.la: Pontificii vero palam in illa incurrunt, & dum illa vel aperte abnegant, vel per cuniculos subruunt, manifestum faciunt, se illos esse, qui μὴ ὁμολογοῦσι τὸν Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα qui non confitentur, Christum Jesum in carne venisse, adeoque se non esse ex Deo, sed Antichristi spiritu turgere, 1. Joh. IV.3. Nam & Jesum Christum per passiones consummatum principem & causam salutis factum esse, introducto Sacerdotio, sacrificio, Mediatoribus, satisfactionibus, meritis novis inficiantur: & justitiæ seculorum adductionem, sublata ejusdem per idem imputatione, per solam fidem justificatione & plenaria reconciliatione abnegant: & Spiritum Filiationis cum Spiritu servitutis ad metum, potestate humana, elementis mundi, prædagogia Legis & ceremoniarum, impuritate, anxietate & perplexitate conscientiæ reductis, commutant: & sapientiam communem totius Ecclesiæ, novo Propheta infallibili, populum ad cæcam credulitatem & obedientiam obligante, & novo verbo, novis revelationibus atque definitionibus eundem ludificante, denique novum velamen oculis populi imponente, obtrusō tollunt: & Fiduciam, Amorem Dei & Sanctitatem perpetua mandata dubitatione, immediato ad Deum aditu negato, affectu omni erga creaturas potius quam Creatorem directo, & amore Dei omni humanis præceptionibus illigato, non tam minuunt, quam destruunt: & libertatem filiorum Dei, propositā denuo ad justificationem peccatoris Lege, & ejusdem diris; timore mortis ob incertitudinem gratiæ & metum Purgatorii incusso; jugo legis adstricto, & sarcinis gravioribus, quam veteres illæ erant, per Verbi Divini prohibitionem, cæremonias infinitas in partem cultus conversas, cæcam obedientiam, jugum cœlibatus, confessionem auricularem &c. illigatis; denique novis, & longe dirioribus prædagogis; curatoribus, œconomis, legislatoribus, judicibus introductis, profligant: Pacem & conscientiæ consummatæ & populorum, per tyrannidem conscientiæ horribilem, & cum Cœlitibus consummatis, consummatione in terris, quin & ipsa morte, omnia sublata, penitus contur-bant: & Hæreditatem Gentium, per eandem tyrannidem, anathemata adversus innocentes vibrata, & dominationem Papæ in temporalibus & spiritualibus raptam, infringunt: & Lætitiam fidelium, quæ Evangelii utramque fere pagi-nam facit, perpetua conscientiarum fluctuatione, servitute, prædagogia, pœnarum, ignis Purgatoriani metu dominante crudeliter dis-turbant: & Cultum externum carnalem, servilem, elementis mundi addictum spirituali & vero omni exturbato, exercent: & Ministerium cultus cum dominio & Hierarchia commutatum, non tam Spiritus, quam Literæ, mortis & condemnationis obeunt: & Hæreditatem omnium, quæ extra fideles sunt, per interdicta nefaria ciborum, dierum, conjugii: nec non vota temeraria paupertatis, cœlibatus & obedientiæ; quin & subjectionem illorum, qui laicorum nomine veniunt, sub Clericorum & Hierarchiæ fidei dominantis, nec non veterum & recentiorum hominum, jugum, diris modis affligunt: & denique beneficiorum Evangelii Obsignationem in Sacramentis veris obscuratis, & falsis Hierarchiæ fere ambitioni & avaritiæ velificantibus, gravem, onerosam, veris mysteriis vacuam, falsis plenam, intellectu non augustam; observatione non castam, sed incestam efficiunt. Plane ut nullo jure Evangelici, sed Evangelii omnis & Evangelici Nominis decoctores jure meritóque audiant, & ne quidem ad eam gloriam assurgant, ad quam fideles ante Christum, bonorum Fœderis Gratiæ per promissionum missionum & Legis ipsius promissioni ministrantis adminiculum, participes, per communnem Ecclesiæ V. & N. T. fidem & salutem enitebantur. Nam hi per promissiones Fœderis Gratiæ, licet non consummatas, salvati sunt: illi FœderisGratiæ promissionibus &Bonis etiam non consummatis, adeóque in universum destituuntur.
units.tr: The Papists openly fall into these errors, and while they either flatly deny those promises or undermine them by secret tunnels, they make it plain that they are the ones who do not confess Jesus Christ to have come in the flesh [μὴ ὁμολογοῦσι τὸν Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα], and so that they are not of God but swell with the spirit of Antichrist, 1 John 4:3. For they deny that Jesus Christ, made perfect through sufferings, became the author and cause of salvation, by introducing a priesthood, sacrifice, mediators, satisfactions and new merits. They deny that the bringing in of the righteousness of the ages is accomplished, by taking away its imputation through the same act, and that justification by faith alone and full reconciliation are possible. They exchange the Spirit of adoption for the spirit of bondage to fear, by bringing back human power, the elements of the world, the tutelage of the Law and of ceremonies, and the impurity, anxiety and perplexity of conscience. They set aside the common wisdom of the whole Church by thrusting in a new infallible prophet who binds the people to blind credulity and obedience, who mocks them with a new word, new revelations and definitions, and who finally lays a new veil over the eyes of the people. They do not so much diminish as destroy trust, love of God and holiness, by denying the perpetual command of doubt-free trust, immediate access to God, directing all affection toward creatures rather than the Creator, and binding the love of God to all human precepts. They overthrow the liberty of the children of God, by restoring the Law, with its curses, for the justification of the sinner, by inspiring fear of death from the uncertainty of grace and dread of Purgatory, by binding the yoke of the law and burdens heavier than those of old, through the prohibition of the Word of God, through countless ceremonies turned into parts of worship, blind obedience, the yoke of celibacy, auricular confession and so on, and finally by introducing new and far harsher tutors, curators, stewards, lawgivers and judges. They utterly disturb peace of conscience and of the people, through the dreadful tyranny over conscience, and they take away fellowship with the perfected saints in the consummation on earth, and even in death itself. They break the inheritance of the Gentiles, through the same tyranny, by hurling anathemas against the innocent and seizing the dominion of the Pope in temporal and spiritual affairs. They cruelly disturb the joy of the faithful, which fills almost every page of the Gospel, by a constant wavering of consciences, by servitude, tutelage, and fear of punishments and of the fire of Purgatory ruling over them. They practise external worship that is carnal, servile, and bound to the elements of the world, with all that is spiritual and true cast out. Their ministry of worship, exchanged for lordship and hierarchy, dies to the letter rather than the Spirit, to death and condemnation. They afflict with harsh burdens the inheritance of all who are outside the faithful, through the wicked prohibitions of foods, days and marriage, together with the rash vows of poverty, celibacy and obedience; and also through the subjection of those who are called laymen to the dominating faith of clerics and the hierarchy, and through the yoke of men both old and recent. And finally, they make the sealing of the benefits of the Gospel in the true sacraments obscured, and the false sacraments, which favour the ambition and avarice of the hierarchy almost above all, heavy, burdensome, empty of true mysteries, full of falsehoods, not august to understand, and not chaste to observe, but impure. Plainly, therefore, they have no right to be called Evangelical; rather, they are rightly and deservedly regarded as the destroyers of the Gospel and of every Evangelical name. Nor do they rise even to that glory to which the faithful before Christ strove, sharing in the good things of the covenant of grace through the promises and missions and the help of the Law that ministered to the promise, through the common faith and salvation of the Church of the Old and New Testament. For those men were saved through the promises of the covenant of grace, though not yet fulfilled; these men, with the promises and good things of the covenant of grace not fulfilled, are altogether destitute.

units.la: LXXII. Oeconomia Fœderis Gratiæ sub Evangelio ἰδίως καιρὸς propria tempora (1.Tim. H.6.) habuit.
units.tr: LXXII. The economy of the covenant of grace under the Gospel had its own times (1 Tim. 6:6) [ἰδίοις καιροῖς].

units.la: Non enim innovationi isti unum aliquod temporis momentum, sed peripheria & latitudo quædam tribui debet. Primo ejus auspicio à Salvatoris adventu capto, Novum Testamentum per præparationem & prædicationem ejusdem in carne jam manifestati promulgatum: at morte ejusdem, quæ Veteri Testamento finem imposuit, ratificatum, ac demum cum excidio Reipublicæ Judaicæ peremptoriæ executioni mandatum fuit. Planè ut alia ratio Præparationis N. T. inde à nato Christo incipientis: alia ratificationis in morte Christi factæ: alia peremptoriæ executionis cum casu Reipublicæ Judaicæ conjunctæ ratio fuerit. Proin etiam Regnum Cœlorum modò à Johanne Baptista, ratione Præparationis: modò à Resurrectione Christi ob ratificationem morte Christi factam: modò à Judæorum excidio ob N.T. peremptoriam executionem Scripturæ auspicantur. A Johanne, juxta illa Christi: A diebus Johannis Baptistæ usque huc Regnum Cœlorum vim facit; & vim facientes illud rapiunt, Matth. XI. 12.13. Quo tempore V. T. œconomia planè adhuc obtinuit, Christo ipso se & discipulos suos illi submittente. Nihilominus jam tum commeatus ad N. T. factus est, & Evangelium promulgari cœpit. A resurrectione Christi juxta ejus verba: Dico vobis, quòd à nunc non bibam amplius ex hoc genimine vitis ad diem illum usque, quo bibam vobiscum novum in Regno Patris mei, ibid. XXVI.29. Quo tempore V. T. & servitute omni jure abrogata, legalia tamen statuta ob infirmitatem quorundam liberè exerceri, at non rigidè à quoquam præscribi poterant. Ab Excidio Reipublicæ Judaicæ quod idem Christus his verbis innuit: Dico vobis, verè sunt nonnulli eorum, qui adstant, qui mortem non gustabunt, usque dum viderint Regnum Dei, Luc. IX. 27. & quidem venientis ἐν δυνάμει in potentia, Marc. IX. 1. Hoc demum tempore legalis cultus tum illicitus in universum, tum impossibilis fieri cœpit. Liquet etiam inde, circa confinia utriusque œconomiæ quandam illarum mixturam obtinuisse. Nam & nova œconomia cum Johanne Baptista, qui, si epocham temporis spectamus, ministerio suo Evangelico sub V. T. functus est, cœpit: & vetus œconomia finem cum casu demum Reipublicæ Judaicæ, ante quem pridem nova œconomia obtinuit, accepit. Cujus mixturæ ratio à singulari sapientia, bonitate & Οικονομία Dei, qui paulatim œconomiam veterem abolere, & novam introducere voluit, ut ex tenebris oppositis lux amabilior splendesceret, & infirmiores paulatim ex caligine ea, in qua nonnullæ stellæ micabant, ad eam lucem, quam Sol de se fundit, cùm ex alto Cœlo imminet, traducerentur, & sensim sine sensu corroborati felicius emergerent, arcessi debet.
units.tr: This innovation should not be assigned to a single moment of time, but to a certain periphery and breadth. At its beginning, taken from the Saviour's coming, the New Testament was promulgated through the preparation and proclamation of him now manifested in the flesh. It was ratified by his death, which put an end to the Old Testament, and at last it was committed to peremptory execution with the destruction of the Jewish commonwealth. Clearly the manner of the New Testament's preparation, beginning from the birth of Christ, was one thing; the manner of its ratification, made in the death of Christ, another; and the manner of its peremptory execution, joined to the fall of the Jewish commonwealth, a third. Accordingly the kingdom of heaven is said to begin sometimes from John the Baptist, with respect to the preparation; sometimes from the resurrection of Christ, on account of the ratification made by his death; and sometimes from the destruction of the Jews, on account of the peremptory execution of the New Testament Scripture. It begins from John, according to those words of Christ: From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force, Matt. 11:12-13. At that time the economy of the Old Testament still clearly held sway, Christ himself submitting both himself and his disciples to it. Nevertheless, a passage to the New Testament had already been made, and the Gospel had begun to be proclaimed. It begins from the resurrection of Christ, according to his words: I tell you, from now on I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father, ibid. 26:29. At that time the Old Testament had been abrogated, with all its servitude, yet its legal statutes could be freely observed on account of the weakness of some, though no one could prescribe them rigidly. It begins from the destruction of the Jewish commonwealth, which Christ himself indicated in these words: I tell you, truly there are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God, Luke 9:27; and indeed of its coming ἐν δυνάμει [in power] in power, Mark 9:1. Only at this time did the legal worship begin to become altogether unlawful and impossible. It is also clear from this that around the boundaries of the two economies a certain mixture of them prevailed. For the new economy began with John the Baptist, who, if we look at the epoch of time, exercised his evangelical ministry under the Old Testament; and the old economy received its end only with the fall of the Jewish commonwealth, before which the new economy had long been in force. The reason for this mixture must be sought in the singular wisdom, goodness and economy of God, who wished gradually to abolish the old economy and introduce the new, so that light might shine more lovingly out of opposing darkness, and the weaker might be drawn little by little out of that gloom, in which some stars glimmered, into the light which the sun pours forth from itself when it hangs in the high heavens, and be strengthened gradually, without their noticing, so that they might emerge more happily.

units.la: LXXIII. Temporibus illius propriis N. T. μαρτύριον Testificatio de Christo, ejus morte & resurrectione obtinere debuit. Nam Christus dedit seipsum redemptionis pretium pro omnibus εἰς μαρτύριον καιροῖς ἰδίοις ad testimonium temporibus propriis, 1.Tim. II.6. de quo §. 1. diximus. Quia enim Christus non debuit manere in terra, sed in thronum gloriæ assumi, in quo sedens Sacerdotio suo per jugem intercessionem, fungeretur, iccirco oportuit esse Μάρτυρες Testes dictorum & factorum, inprimis passionum, mortis & ascensionis ejus in Cœlum, qui ea renuntiarunt; & ut fideliter, corde & constanter renuntiare possent, eosdem indui virtute ex alto, mitti ad μαρτύριον illud perhibendum; & missionis suæ argumentis & indiciis magnis atque evidentibus instrui, ut eorum præconium, ceu Divinum & omni exceptione majus ab omnibus reciperetur oportuit. Frustra enim Christus mortuus esset, si per Evangelii præconium mors ejus mundo annuntiata non fuisset. Hi Evangelistæ, præcones Christi præsentis & morituri, vel mortui & absentis sunt; de quibus adhuc dicendum.
units.tr: LXXIII. In its own proper times the New Testament ought to have the testimony [μαρτύριον] concerning Christ, his death and his resurrection. For Christ gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in its own times (1 Tim. 2:6) [εἰς μαρτύριον καιροῖς ἰδίοις], of which we spoke in §1. For since Christ was not to remain on earth but to be taken up into the throne of glory, where, sitting, he would perform his priesthood by unceasing intercession, it was necessary that there be witnesses [μάρτυρες] of the things said and done, above all of his sufferings, death and ascension into heaven, who would report them. And so that they might report them faithfully, from the heart and constantly, they had to be clothed with power from on high and sent to bear that testimony; and they had to be furnished with great and evident proofs and signs of their mission, so that their proclamation would be received by all as divine and beyond every objection. For Christ would have died in vain if his death had not been announced to the world through the proclamation of the Gospel. These evangelists, heralds of Christ present and about to die, or of Christ dead and absent, are yet to be discussed.

units.la: LXXIV. Præcones Evangelii & Testes ejusmodi mittendos fuisse, S. Paulus Rom. X.13–17. gemino Scripturæ V. T. testimonio confirmat.
units.tr: LXXIV. That heralds of the Gospel and witnesses of this kind were to be sent, St Paul confirms from a twofold testimony of the Old Testament (Rom. 10:13-17).

units.la: Prius ex Joel. II. 32. petitum est, ubi sic Deus: Et erit, quicunque Nomen Jehovæ invocabit salvabitur vel præservabitur. Unde missionem præconum Christi sic colligit: Quomodo vero invocabunt, in quem non crediderint? Quomodo credent, quod non audiverint? Quomodo vero audient sine prædicante? Quomodo autem prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? v. 14.15. Posterius ex Esaj. LII. 7. depromptum sic habet: Quam decori (εὐαγγελίζεσθαι) digni Deo ipsos mittente, & de Filio suo per ipsos præconium faciente) sunt in montibus (in quibus ab uno ad alterum per totam terram discurrendo ambulant) pedes evangelizantium Pacem, evangelizantium (ut Paulus reddit) Bona (puta illa ἕξοχα N.T.) qui faciunt audiri salutem; qui dicunt Tzioni: Rex factus est Deus tuus! Jam ante David de ejusmodi Evangelistis: Dominus, inquit, dat dictum (Christus, hæres omnium, cui data est omnis potestas in Cœlo & in terra, mysterium moriendo aperit, promissum præstat, Evangelium primus facto suo nuntiat) boni præcones, vel præconiatrices sunt exercitus multus, (exercitus & acies erunt Evangelistarum) Psal. LXVIII. 12.
units.tr: The first is taken from Joel 2:32, where God says: "And it shall be that whoever calls on the name of Jehovah shall be saved or preserved." From this he infers the sending of Christ's heralds thus: "But how shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent?" vv. 14-15. The second, taken from Isaiah 52:7, runs thus: how beautiful are the feet of those who bring the good news (εὐαγγελίζεσθαι) [euangelizesthai], worthy of God who sends them and makes a proclamation concerning his Son through them, as they run from one to another across the whole earth on the mountains. The feet of those who preach peace, who preach good news (as Paul renders it) of good things (namely those excellent things of the New Testament) [ἕξοχα], who cause salvation to be heard, who say to Zion: Your God has become king! Earlier still, David spoke of such evangelists: "The Lord", he says, "gives the word" (Christ, heir of all, to whom all power in heaven and on earth is given, opens the mystery by dying, fulfils the promise, and first announces the Gospel by his deed); "the good heralds, or women heralds, are a great host" (the host and army will be the evangelists), Ps. 68:12.

units.la: LXXV. Hos plerosque viles, contemptibiles, & quosdam etiam infames fore pariter prædictum est. Filii ipsius, labes eorum, generationis perversæ & tortuosæ, Deut. XXXII. 5. Ejusmodi erant Galilæi, & publicani etiam, velut Matthæus, qui telonio relicto Christum secutus est. Unde de Christo Esaias: destitutus viris, non habens secum viros, Esaj. LIII. 3. Non enim, qui eum comitati sunt viri fuerunt, sed parvuli & lactentes, ex quorum ore fundavit Deus robur Ecclesiæ ipsis inferorum portis insuperabile; Psal. VIII. 3. & pueri, Esaj. VIII. 18. nihil habentes, nisi quod ex hominibus nati essent. Ad laudem enim Dei pertinebat per infirmos, γεγεννημένοι rudes, nec magni ingenii, nec magni animi compertos, quod validum & robustum sit, exequi, tum ut in solo Domino gloriaremur: tum ne vel vi ad fidem homines adigere, adeóque fidei dominari, vel σταφισμένοις μύθοις & venustè fictis hominum fabulis simplicium credulitati illudere, & Evangelium cauponari viderentur. Misit me Christus ad evangelizandum, non in sapientia sermonis, tum ne crux Christi evacuaretur, hoc est, ne intentio Dei, quam in praeconio crucis Christi, respectu tum pereuntium, tum salvandorum, Deus sibi proposuit, obscuraretur, & irrita fieret, 1. Cor. I. 17-f. tum ne vel ὑπεροχὴ λόγοις ἢ Σοφίας excellentia sermonis & sapientiae testimonium Dei de Jesu Christo, eóque crucifixo everteret; vel fides nostra sit in sapientia potius hominum, quam in potentia Dei, ibid. II. 1 --5. tum quia sapientia Divini sermonis, quam loquebantur, captum omnem hominis superat, & à solo homine spirituali, non animali, vel carnali ullo cognosci potest, ibid. v. 5 --16. III. 1.--8. tum quia qui sapiens videri vult in hoc seculo, stultus fieri debet, ut sapiens fiat, cum sapientia hujus mundi stultitia sit apud Deum, ibid. v. 18--21. tum quia indignum est gloriari in hominibus, cum omnia nostra sint, ib. v.21 - f. tum quia praecones Evangelii sunt ministri Christi & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei, neque habent judicium, sed examini Domini sui unicè subsunt, ibid. IV. 1 - 5. tum quia non sapiendum est supra id quod scriptum est, ib. v.6. tum denique quia nos ipsos non discernimus, nec quicquam habemus, quod non acceperimus, adeóque gloriari non licet, cùm nemo unus alio praestantior sit, ibid. v. 7. &c.
units.tr: LXXV. It was likewise foretold that most of these would be base and contemptible, and some even infamous. Not his sons, but their blemish: a perverse and crooked generation (Deut. 32:5). Such were the Galileans, and tax collectors too, such as Matthew, who left the toll booth and followed Christ. Hence Isaiah says of Christ: "Forsaken by men, having no men with him" (Isa. 53:3). For those who accompanied him were not men but little children and infants, out of whose mouth God founded a strength of the Church that even the gates of hell could not overcome (Ps. 8:3), and boys (Isa. 8:18), having nothing except that they were born of men. For it belonged to the praise of God that through the weak, rude-born [γεγεννημένοι], found neither of great talent nor of great spirit, he should accomplish what is strong and robust, both so that we might glory in the Lord alone, and so that men should not seem to compel faith by force and thus lord it over faith, or to mock simple credulity with cunningly fashioned human fables [σταφισμένοις μύθοις], and to peddle the Gospel like a huckster. "Christ sent me to preach the gospel, not in the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied" (1 Cor. 1:17): that is, lest the purpose of God, which he set before himself in the proclamation of the cross of Christ with respect both to those who perish and to those who are saved, be obscured and made void (ibid.); lest the excellence of speech or wisdom [ὑπεροχὴ λόγοις ἢ Σοφίας] overturn the testimony of God concerning Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2:1-5); or lest our faith rest on the wisdom of men rather than the power of God (ibid.); (2:5-16; 3:1-8) since the wisdom of the divine word which they preached surpasses all human comprehension and can be known only by the spiritual man, not by the natural or carnal man. (3:18-21) Since whoever wishes to seem wise in this age must become a fool, that he may become wise, for the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. (3:21) Since it is unworthy to glory in men, for all things are ours. (4:1-5) Since the heralds of the Gospel are ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, and have no judgment of their own, but are subject to the scrutiny of their Lord alone. (4:6) Since one must not think beyond what is written. (4:7 etc.) Finally, since we do not distinguish ourselves, and have nothing that we have not received, and therefore it is not lawful to glory, since no one is more excellent than another.

units.la: LXXVI. Prophetiis jam conticescentibus, sub finem visionis primus Evangelii praeco Johannes Baptista extitit; praesentis, sed nondum mortui, verùm morituri Christi Testis & Nuntius. Extitit homo, missus à Deo, nomen ei Johannes. (יוחנן Dominus gratiam exercuit) Hic venit εἰς μαρτυρίαν in testificationem, ut testaretur de Luce, ut omnes per ipsum crederent, Joh. I. 6. 7. Jam ante nativitatem, quae in missione hac includitur, tum per verba Prophetarum promissus & auctoratus: tum per Gabrielem & Zachariam, non sine miraculo, testem, designatus praecursor Domini est: tum in utero matris Salvatorem suum saltu salutavit, & per os matris suae de ipso testatus est: Mittendi ejus promissio à Propheta Malachia facta est his verbis: Ecce ego mitto vobis Eliam Prophetam, antequam veniat dies Jehovae magnus ille & terribilis, ut convertat cor patrum ad filios, & cor filiorum ad Patres ipsorum, ne veniam & percutiam terram anathemate, Malach. IV. 5. 6. supra cap. III. 1. dixerat: Ecce ego mittam angelum meum, ut vacuam faciat viam ante me: & derepente veniet ad templum suum Dominus ille, &c. Et Eliae igitur, & Angeli nomine venit. Eliae, non proprie Thesbitae illius, uti Judaei, & qui hic pollicem iisdem premunt, Pontificii pertendunt, tum quia is non venit ante Christi Domini ad Templum suum venientis manifestationem in carne, ut cor Patrum ad filios, & cor filiorum ad Patres converteret: tum quia immediatus adventus Domini cum Praecursore suo post Malachiam promittitur; sed improprie & analogicè talis, hoc est, Eliae mystici Thesbitae similis, venientis scilicet ἐν πνεύματι καὶ δυνάμει Ἠλίου in spiritu & virtute Eliae, Luc. I. 17. adeóque Eliae fervente adversus superstitionem & impietatem zelo animóque praediti. Angeli verò, quia à Deo ante Christum manifestatum mittendus praeco fuit. De eodem sic vaticinatus est Esajas: Vox clamantis in deserto (in quo & ipsa vox clamantis audita est; & extiterunt Judaei, cùm vox illa sonaret, quia plurimi extra terram palantes, velut in deserto gentium errarunt, & ipsi terram Canaan incolentes, Herodi, Romanorum servo, adeóque Imperio Romano, gentium deserto subjecti fuerunt, ut ita Deserti mentione etiam character temporis designetur) Parate viam Domini, rectificate in solitudine aggerem Deo nostro. Omnis vallis extolletur, & omnis mons ac clivus humiliabuntur, & fiet lamosum in planitiem, & protuberantia in planam vallem. Et revelabitur gloria Domini, & videbunt omnis caro simul, quod os Domini locutum sit, Esaj. XL. 1--6. Prophetis hisce Gabriel & Zacharias, Johannis pater, nondum eo nato, suffragati sunt. Gabriel enim Zachariam visione perculsum sic erigit: Ne time, &c. Erit magnus coram Domino. Vinum & siceram non bibet. Et Spiritu S. implebitur adhuc in utero matris suae. Et multos filiorum Israel convertet ad Dominum Deum suum. Et praebit ipsi in Spiritu & virtute Eliae, ad convertenda corda Patrum erga filios, & inobedientes (filios) ἐν φρονήσει δικαίων in studio, vel ad studium seu sensum justorum (patrum, à quibus quoad fidem in Christum & veram justitiam inobedientes illi filii dissidebant) ad praeparandum Domino populum aptum, Luc. I. 12-18. Etiam Zacharias non sine miraculo adempti ei & restituti sermonis, Spiritu S. impletus, sic filio applausit: Et tu, puer, Propheta Altissimi cluebis. Antecedes enim ante faciem Domini, ad praeparandas ei vias, ut des populo suo cognitionem salvationis, quae est in remissione peccatorum eorum, &c. ibid. v. 76. 77. Denique & ipse Johannes in utero matris, Spiritu S. repletus, (ibid. v. 15.) Servatorem suum ἀγαλλιάσει saltu, seu exultatione salutavit, & per os matris suae de eodem testatus est, ibid. 44. 45.
units.tr: LXXVI. With prophecy now falling silent, at the close of the vision John the Baptist arose as the first herald of the Gospel: a witness and messenger of Christ, who was present but not yet dead, and who was about to die. "There came a man sent from God, whose name was John" (Yochanan, "the Lord has shown grace"). "He came for a witness [eis martyrian], to bear witness of the Light, that all might believe through him" (John 1:6-7). Even before his birth, which is included in this mission, he was designated as the forerunner of the Lord: promised and authorised by the words of the Prophets, and, through Gabriel and Zechariah, appointed as a witness not without a miracle. While still in his mother's womb he greeted his Saviour with a leap and bore witness to him through his mother's mouth. The promise of his sending was made by the Prophet Malachi in these words: "Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes, to turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse" (Mal. 4:5-6). Earlier, in chapter 3:1, he had said: "Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me; and suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple," and so on. He came, then, in the name both of Elijah and of the Angel. "Elijah" is not to be taken strictly as that Tishbite, as the Jews, and those who here press their thumbs on the same point, the Papists, contend. This is because he did not come before the manifestation of the Lord coming in the flesh to his temple, to turn the heart of the fathers to the children and the heart of the children to the fathers; and because the immediate coming of the Lord with his forerunner is promised after Malachi. Rather, he came improperly and by analogy, that is, as one like the mystical Tishbite Elijah, namely coming in the spirit and power of Elijah [en pneumati kai dynamei Ēliou] (Luke 1:17), and so endowed with the fervent zeal and spirit of Elijah against superstition and impiety. But he is called Angel, because he was the herald to be sent by God before Christ was manifested. Isaiah prophesied concerning him in the same way: "A voice of one crying in the wilderness" (in which wilderness the voice of the crier was indeed heard; and the Jews, when that voice sounded, were there, since very many of them were wandering abroad, as though in the wilderness of the nations, and they who lived in the land of Canaan were subject to Herod, the servant of the Romans, and thus to the Roman Empire, the wilderness of the nations; so that by the mention of the wilderness the character of the time is also indicated): "Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places a plain. And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see together that the mouth of the Lord has spoken" (Isa. 40:1-6). Gabriel and Zechariah, the father of John, supported these Prophets before he was born. For Gabriel, raising Zechariah who was struck with the vision, speaks thus: "Fear not... He will be great before the Lord. He shall drink no wine or strong drink. And he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb. And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. And he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah [en phronēsei dikaiōn], to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just (the fathers, from whom those disobedient children differed as to faith in Christ and true righteousness), to prepare for the Lord a people fit" (Luke 1:12-18). Zechariah too, who had his speech taken away and restored not without a miracle, filled with the Holy Spirit, thus addressed his son: "And you, child, will be called the Prophet of the Most High. For you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give his people knowledge of salvation in the remission of their sins," etc. (ibid. vv. 76-77). Finally, John himself, filled with the Holy Spirit in his mother's womb (ibid. v. 15), greeted his Saviour with a leap of joy [agalliasei], and through his mother's mouth bore witness to him (ibid. vv. 44-45).

units.la: LXXVII. Officium Johannis tribus partibus absolvebatur: Praeconio Resipiscentiae, Testimonio de Christo praesente, & Baptismo. Resipiscentia enim praeco fuit, qui cor Patrum ad filios, & filiorum cor ad Patres converteret, Mal. IV. 6. hoc est, efficeret, ne Abrahamum & caeteros puderet filiorum suorum, Esaj. XXIX. 22. & ut filii ἀπειθεῖς immorigeri ad φρόνησιν δικαίων sensum & studium justorum patrum, hoc est, sententiam rectam de Deo, de Christo, vera justitia converterentur: qui complanare & vacuam facere viam coram Jehova, Malach. III. 1. hoc est, praeconio poenitentiae ad recipiendum Christum homines praeparare: qui in deserto clamare; Parate viam Domini, rectificate in solitudine aggerem Deo nostro, Esaj. XL. 3. hoc est, magna cum παῤῥησία & contentione jubere debuit, ut obstacula, errores, praejudicia, sententiae falsae in animo radicatae, quae Christo recipiendo & Evangelicae doctrinae obstare poterunt, ex via removeantur, & ex Mose atque Prophetis, quis sit ille agger, via recta, quis Christus, quae ejus dicta & facta, passiones, justitia vera, statu regni Dei, discatur, & simul via illa ametur; quod est attollere portas, patefacere fores Regi, Psal. XXIV. 7. 9. Hoc praeconium reapse Johannes nes obiit, prædicans in deserto Judæa, & dicens: Resipiscite. Appropinquavit enim Regnum Cœlorum, Matth. III. 2. hoc est, convertimini à viis & operibus malis ad conversationem bonam, inprimis à falsa justitia, quæ in abstinentia à malis operibus externis, in affectatione gratiæ Dei per cultum externum & afflictionem corporis; ad agnitionem veræ justitiæ, in Sponsione Mediatoris præsentis, & Testamento Dei propediem per sanguinem Mediatoris obsignando & ratificando, fundatæ; in fide vera præsentem Christum recipite, & fructus fidei pœnitentia dignos, veræ pœnitentiæ & sanctificationis testes, ferte, v. 8. In propinquo enim est Regnum Cœlorum, quod expectatis, & quod sine resipiscentia prensari nequit, tum quia dignum est, ut bona Regni Cœlorum, homines ad resipiscentiam [illegible, ~1 word] commoveant, & qui ea negligunt, inexcusabiles sunt: tum quia, Regnum Dei venire, & eos, qui à falsa justitia non resipiscunt, in suo statu persistere, [illegible, ~1 word] sunt. Ad præconium illud seria [illegible, ~1 word] Pharisæorum & Sadducæorum; ad Baptismum suum simulata cum pietate accedentium, facit. Hos enim statim atque vidit, ceu [illegible, ~1 word] terrificis minis, & suavioribus minis increpat, dicens: Progenies Viperarum, quis demonstravit vobis, quòd (sine vera pœnitentia, cum falsæ justitiæ fide, fucatis factis, & tristi sanctimonia vestra) venturam iram effugituri sitis? Facite igitur fructus dignos pœnitentia. Et ne videamini vos dicere, vel apud vos cogitare posse: Patrem habemus Abraham, atq; ita in vado salus nostra est, ut nullus filius Israel in futuro seculo non habiturus sit portionem, quod etiam in Sanhedrim cap. II. Judæi omnes sibi temere promittunt) Dico enim vobis, quòd Deus ex lapidibus istis Abrahamo liberos excitare (gentium, lapidum duritiem nunc habentium, multitudinem Abrahamo promissam advocare, petram in stagnum aquarum, & silicem in rivum aquarum convertere, Psal. CXIV. 8.) potis est. Et jam securis (judicia Dei per Romanorum potentiam exequenda) radici arborum (illorum qui inter vos arbores videntur, principum & potestatum populi) imminet. Omnis igitur arbor non proferens bonum fructum, excinditur, & in ignem conjicitur, Matth. III. 7.–11. Luc. III. 7. 8.
units.tr: LXXVII. The office of John was carried out in three parts: the proclamation of repentance, the testimony concerning Christ present, and baptism. For he was the herald of repentance, who was to turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to the fathers (Mal. 4:6); that is, to bring it about that Abraham and the others would not be ashamed of their children (Isa. 29:22), and that the disobedient, stubborn children would be turned to the wisdom of the just [phronēsin dikaiōn], that is, to the right judgment and zeal of the righteous fathers concerning God, concerning Christ, and true righteousness. He was to make level and empty the way before Jehovah (Mal. 3:1), that is, by the proclamation of repentance to prepare men to receive Christ. He was to cry in the wilderness: "Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight in the desert a highway for our God" (Isa. 40:3), that is, he had to command with great boldness [parrhēsia] and earnestness that the obstacles, errors, prejudices, and false opinions rooted in the mind, which could hinder the reception of Christ and the Gospel doctrine, be removed from the way; and that from Moses and the Prophets men should learn what that highway, the straight way is, who Christ is, his sayings and deeds, his sufferings, true righteousness, and the state of the kingdom of God; and at the same time that they should love that way. This is to lift up the gates and open the doors for the King (Ps. 24:7, 9). John indeed carried out this proclamation, preaching in the wilderness of Judea and saying: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" (Matt. 3:2); that is, turn from evil ways and works to a good manner of life; above all from the false righteousness, which is founded on abstinence from outward evil works, on seeking the grace of God through outward worship and bodily affliction; to the knowledge of true righteousness, founded on the surety of the Mediator now present and on the covenant of God soon to be sealed and ratified through the blood of the Mediator; receive by true faith the Christ who is present, and bring forth fruits of faith worthy of repentance, witnesses of true repentance and sanctification (v. 8). For the kingdom of heaven, which you await, is at hand, and it cannot be seized without repentance; both because it is fitting that the good things of the kingdom of heaven should move men to repentance, and whoever neglects them is inexcusable; and because, when the kingdom of God comes, those who do not repent of false righteousness and persist in their state will be [illegible]. The address fits the serious [illegible] of the Pharisees and Sadducees who came to his baptism with feigned piety. For as soon as he saw them, as if [illegible], he rebuked them with terrifying threats and gentler words, saying: "You brood of vipers, who has shown you that (without true repentance, with the faith of false righteousness, with deceitful deeds and your gloomy sanctimony) you will escape the coming wrath? Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance. And do not think or say among yourselves: 'We have Abraham as our father,' as though our salvation were so secure that no son of Israel would fail to have a share in the age to come (which all Jews rashly promise themselves, also in Sanhedrin chapter 2). For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham (that is, to call together from the Gentiles, who now have the hardness of stones, the multitude promised to Abraham, to turn the rock into a pool of water, and the flint into a spring of water, Ps. 114:8). And now the axe (the judgments of God to be executed through the power of the Romans) is laid to the root of the trees (of those who seem among you to be trees, the princes and powers of the people). Every tree therefore that does not bring forth good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire" (Matt. 3:7-11; Luke 3:7-8).

units.la: LXXVIII. Sed utramque fere paginam Officii Johannis ejusdem [illegible, ~1 word] Testimonium de Christo, ejus scilicet manifestatione, honore, officio & Persona fecit.
units.tr: LXXVIII. Indeed, nearly both pages of John's same office bore witness to Christ, namely to his manifestation, honour, office and person.

units.la: Tametsi enim Christus protestatus fuerit, se ab homine, ipso etiam Johanne, testimonium non accipere, quasi ipse eo indigeret, neque alia validiori ratione sibi, utpote qui ceu Lux & Sol justitiæ ad probandam lucem sibi sufficiat; authoritatem conciliare posset, tamen illud admisit, ut ipsi Judæi [illegible, ~1 word] salventur, saluti eorum sic consulens, ut saltem cogitarent, tantum virum nonnisi ex certa scientia testimonium hoc sibi perhibere velle, Joh. V. 33. 34. Hic ergo venit [illegible, ~1 word] in testimonium, ut testificaretur de luce, ut omnes crederent per ipsum. Non erat ille lux, sed ut testaretur de luce, ibid. I. 7. 8. Huc enim omne fere ejus ministerium spectavit, ut testaretur [illegible, ~1 word] de luce vera, Christo, ut eum tanquam authorem justitiæ, datorem Spiritus S. & statorem salutis omnes agnoscerent, justitiam ejus, & consolationem per eandem sitirent, ipsíque, ut Principi vitæ & Redemptori animas suas in bonis factis committerent. Licet igitur Judæi [illegible, ~1 word] ad horam in luce ejus Johannis exultare & hilarescere voluerint, gavisi vehementer, tam sanctum, veracem, abstinentem virum, in cujus sapientia & sanctitate supra omnium gentium sapientes gloriari in proclivi esset, inter se caput extulisse: non tamen ille vera lux fuit, sed tantum [illegible, ~1 word] lucerna ardens & lucens, à luce lumen suum omne mutuata, ceu Phosphorus; & [illegible, ~1 word] luminare, lucem gestans, præ cæteris, qui ante ipsum fuerunt, tum zelo singulari ardens, tum testimonio de Luce præsente lucens, ibid. V. 35. Ideo de Johanne Baptista idem Johannes Evangelista: Johannes testatur de ipso & clamat: (non sine ingenti [illegible, ~1 word] testificatione gratiæ Domini, qui tum electis ovibus suis ipsum [illegible, ~1 word] tanquam exerto capite præsolantibus hoc præconio absque mora & cunctatione clamore eo innotescere: tū omnibus, passis quasi ulnis, ut sub alis suis congregarentur, occurrere: tum sui cognoscendi argumentum evidentissimum edere voluit) Hic est, de quo dicebam: Qui post me venit, ante me factus (collocatus) est, quia prior me erat, ibid. I. 15. 30. Testimonii hujus sensus est, Christum serius licet Johanne Baptista manifestatum, officio tamen, honoris & personæ dignitate longè eum antecellere. Scilicet Christus post Johannem venit, qui post eum, ceu prodromum ejus, manifestatus est; & statim, [illegible, ~1 word] derepente atque citius illum; cui viam parabat, secutus est; Idem [illegible, ~1 word] ante eum factus est, ratione muneris & officii, utpote qui [illegible, ~1 word] majori, quàm qua ipse Johannes gloria dignus habitus est, & majorem gloriam habet, Hebr. III. 3. cùm Christum [illegible, ~1 word] crescere, at Johannem [illegible, ~1 word] minorem fieri (Joh. III. 30.) oportuerit, & ille hoc [illegible, ~1 word] robustior fuerit, Marc. I. 7. Luc. III. 16. Licet cætera non surrexerit in natis mulierum major Johanne, Matth. XI. 11. Denique [illegible, ~1 word] prior Johanne fuit ratione dignitatis personæ, quia; uti verba hæc ipse Evangelista expositi, Johannes cum Christo collatus dignus non erat, ut huic corrigias calcei solveret, hoc est, minister, servus ejus existeret, quia apud Hebræos servi empti calceum ementi solvere, in signum emptionis solebant; Joh. I. 27. Homo enim peccator cinis & pulvis dignus non est, ut Deo ministret; & Divina dignatio mera est, quòd homo Dei minister creatur. Christus autem, personæ ratione [illegible, ~1 word] prior Johanne & longè ante Johannem & [illegible, ~1 word] multò prior & anterior fuit, quippe cujus exitus sunt ab ante, à diebus sæculi, Mich. V. 1. Prov. VIII. 22–30. Qui [illegible, ~1 word] in principio (ante Johannis [illegible, ~1 word]) fuit, Joh. I. 1. Neque aliàs ratio constaret, quare Christus Baptistæ præponeretur. Nisi enim ante Johannem fuisset, nec fuisset Dominus & Jehova, cui præcursoris officium Johannes præstaret, nec Dominus Davidis vel Johannis, neque baptizans in Spiritu S. [illegible, ~1 word] simpliciter, nempe ut sine ipso nemo, ac ne Johannes quidem Spiritu S. baptizatus sit, Luc. III. 16. Accedit & aliud Johannis
units.tr: For although Christ declared that he did not receive testimony from man, not even from John himself, as if he needed it, and although he could win authority for himself by a stronger means, since as the Light and Sun of righteousness he is sufficient to prove his own light, he nonetheless allowed it, so that the Jews themselves might be saved, consulting their salvation in such a way that at least they would consider that so great a man bore this witness to him only from certain knowledge, John 5:33, 34. He came as a witness, to bear witness of the light, that all might believe through him. He was not that light, but was sent to bear witness of the light, ibid. 1:7, 8. For nearly all his ministry looked to this, that he should bear witness to the true light, Christ, so that all would acknowledge him as the author of righteousness, the giver of the Holy Spirit and the establisher of salvation, and would thirst for his righteousness and consolation through it, and would commit their souls, in good works, to him as the Prince of life and Redeemer. Therefore, although the Jews for a time wished to rejoice and be glad in the light of this John, and gladly exulted that such a holy, truthful, abstemious man, in whose wisdom and holiness it was easy to boast above the wise of all nations, had raised his head among them, yet he was not the true light, but only a burning and shining lamp, borrowing all his light from the light, like Phosphorus; a luminary bearing light beyond all who had gone before him, burning with a singular zeal and shining with testimony to the Light who was present, ibid. 5:35. Hence the Evangelist John also said of John the Baptist: John bears witness of him and cries out (not without a great testimony to the grace of the Lord, who, while his chosen sheep were waiting for him with heads raised high, wished to make him known by this proclamation, cried out without delay or hesitation, and then ran to all, as if with outstretched arms, that they might be gathered under his wings, and gave a most evident sign of his own recognition): This is he of whom I spoke: He who comes after me has been placed (set) before me, because he was before me, ibid. 1:15, 30. The sense of this testimony is that Christ, though made known later than John the Baptist, far surpasses him in office, in honour and in dignity of person. Christ, that is, came after John, who was made known after him as his forerunner; and immediately, suddenly and more swiftly, he followed the one who was preparing his way. The same one was placed before him by reason of his office and function, since he was deemed worthy of greater glory than John himself, and has greater glory, Heb. 3:3, when Christ had to increase and John had to become less (John 3:30), and the former was mightier, Mark 1:7; Luke 3:16. Although in other respects there has not arisen among those born of women one greater than John, Matt. 11:11. Finally, he was before John by reason of the dignity of his person, because, as the Evangelist himself explained these words, John, compared with Christ, was not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal, that is, to be his minister and servant, since among the Hebrews a bought servant used to loosen the sandal of the buyer as a sign of purchase; John 1:27. For a sinful man, dust and ashes, is not worthy to minister to God, and it is a mere act of divine condescension that a man is created as a minister of God. But Christ, by reason of his person, was before John and far before John, and much earlier and prior, since his goings forth are from of old, from the days of eternity, Mic. 5:1; Prov. 8:22–30. He who was in the beginning (before John) was, John 1:1. Otherwise there would be no reason why Christ should be placed before the Baptist. For if he had not been before John, he would not have been the Lord and Jehovah, to whom John as forerunner rendered his office, nor the Lord of David or of John, nor would he be the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit without qualification, namely so that without him no one, not even John, was baptized with the Holy Spirit, Luke 3:16. There is also another testimony of John's.

units.la: Testimonium Christo, ceu servus Dominos post se venturo, quidem, sed ante se factus ratione officii, & se priore & præstantiore, ratione personæ, illustre inprimis perhibuit. hannis testimonium, quod Christo ad Baptismum ejus venienti perhibuit. Visò enim Jesu ad se veniente, dixit: Ecce (quasi δαχτυλοδεικνυ- μένῳ digito eum monstrans, in quo justitiam & vitam quærere solo licet, & qui posthac publicè ὁ ᾿Αμνὸς in signum, vexillum prostare debet, Esaj. XL. 10. Matth. XXIV. 30. Ut omnes ad eum accedant, Esaj. XLV. 24. ad eum respiciant, Zach. XII. 10. super eo fœdus cum Deo faciant, Psal. L. ꝓ. 14. 23.) ὁ ᾿Αμνὸς Agnus ille Dei (tot agnorum balatu & cruore in Templo pridem vocatus & postulatus, præcognitus à Deo ante jacta mundi fundamenta, ut esset victima pro peccatis 1. Pet. I. 20.) qui (solus) tollit peccata mundi, seu peccata Judæorum & gentium ad quos secundum promissionem benedictio venire debuit, per obedientiam præcepti dilectionis fratrum in se suscipit, expiat, delet, tollit, ut credentibus nullo amplius modo imputari valeant, Joh. I. 29.
units.tr: Another testimony, which he bore to Christ when Christ came to his baptism, is especially outstanding. The one who comes after him as Lord, yet was made before him by reason of office, and is prior and more excellent by reason of person, is set forth by John. For seeing Jesus coming to him, he said: Behold (pointing him out with the finger [δαχτυλοδεικνυμένῳ], the one in whom alone righteousness and life may be sought, and who afterwards must be publicly displayed as a sign, a standard, Isa. 40:10; Matt. 24:30), so that all may come to him, Isa. 45:24, look upon him, Zech. 12:10, and make a covenant with God concerning him, Ps. 50:14, 23; the Lamb [ὁ Ἀμνὸς] of God (that Lamb who had long been called and demanded in the Temple by the bleating and blood of so many lambs, foreknown by God before the foundation of the world, to be the sacrifice for sins, 1 Pet. 1:20), who (alone) takes away the sin of the world, that is, the sins of the Jews and the Gentiles to whom the blessing was to come according to the promise, by the obedience of the precept of love of the brethren he takes upon himself, makes atonement for, blots out and removes, so that they can no longer be imputed to believers in any way, John 1:29.

units.la: LXXIX. Et Concionem de Pœnitentia, & Testimonium de Christo Sacramento Baptismi obsignavit. Nam, more apud Proselytos consueto, omnes concioni pœnitentiæ audientes, & Testimonio de Christo, abjectis vanis ac inanibus illis, quibus hactenus insveverant, fidem substringentes sacra unda lustravit. Exitit Johannes baptizans in deserto, & prædicans Baptismum ad remissionem peccatorum. Et exivit ad eum tota Judææ regio, & Hierosolymitæ, & baptizati sunt omnes in Jordanis fluvio ab ipso, confitentes peccata sua, Marc. I. 4. ꝓ. Ego quidem baptizo vos aqua ad resipiscentiam, (resipiscentibus Divino jussu signaculum justitiæ in Christo promptæ & expositæ confero, non iterum ad servitutem elementorum mundi, sed ad continuationem resipiscentiæ.) Sed qui post me venit, robustior me est, Ipse vos baptizabit in Spiritu S & igne. (baptismo sum obsignaturus Spiritum sanctificationis, filiationis, charismatum) Matth. III. 11. Erat autem & Johannes baptizans in Ænon juxta Salim, quia aquæ multæ erant ibi, & accedebant, & baptizabantur, Joh. III 23. Johannes baptizavit Baptismum resipiscentiæ, populo dicens, ut credant in eum, qui post ipsum veniret, id est, in Christum Jesum, Act. XIX. 4. Fuit ergo Baptismus Johannis obsignatio tum stipulationis resipiscentiæ, tum testimonii ejus de Christo, quòd resipiscentes & credentes in Christum post Johannem venturum habeant spem justitiæ, remissionis peccatorum & vitæ tum charismatum singularium, qui linguarum ignearum symbolo credentibus die Pentecostes, & deinceps, conferenda erant: Baptisma enim illud tum invitavit ad resipiscentiam, & eandem stipulatus est; tum resipiscentibus remissionem peccatorum præsentem, & charismatum singularium donationem futuram obsignavit: ne Pontificii aquas ejus, uti Tertullianus olim locutus est, viduas & infœcundas, nec Spiritus S. fœtas amplius mentiantur. Eodem vero Baptismo etiam Christus ipse tingi voluit, quia eum omnem justitiam implere, Matth. III. 15. hoc est, non circumcidi duntaxat, atque sic ad obedientiam Legis, & servitutem ejus se obligare; sed etiam baptizari, atque sic signaculum justitiæ & remissionis peccatorum nostrorum, quæ spondendo sua fecerat, ut caput sui corporis, recipere oportuit. Aliás enim Christus ille est, qui peccata remittit, quòd & Johannes professus est, dicens: Ego opus habeo à te baptizari, tua sanctificatione & justificatione indigeo, ibid. v. 14. Sed de hoc Baptismo plura in loco.
units.tr: LXXIX. John also sealed his sermon on repentance and his testimony concerning Christ with the sacrament of baptism. For, in the manner customary among proselytes, he cleansed with the holy water all who heard his sermon of repentance and his testimony about Christ, who, having cast off the vain and empty things to which they had hitherto been accustomed, bound their faith to him. John came baptizing in the desert and preaching a baptism for the remission of sins. And the whole region of Judea went out to him, and the people of Jerusalem, and all were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins, Mark 1:4, 5. I indeed baptize you with water for repentance (to those who repent I confer, by divine command, the seal of righteousness made ready and set forth in Christ, not to a return to the bondage of the elements of the world, but to the continuation of repentance). But he who comes after me is mightier than I; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire (I am to seal by baptism the Spirit of sanctification, of sonship and of gifts), Matt. 3:11. John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there, and people came and were baptized, John 3:23. John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people that they should believe in him who would come after him, that is, in Christ Jesus, Acts 19:4. Therefore the baptism of John was a sealing both of the covenant of repentance and of his testimony concerning Christ, that those who repent and believe in Christ, who was to come after John, should have hope of righteousness, remission of sins and life, and also of singular gifts, which were to be conferred on believers on the day of Pentecost and afterwards, under the symbol of fiery tongues. For that baptism both invited to repentance and bound it by covenant; and it both sealed to those who repent the present remission of sins and the future bestowing of singular gifts. Thus the Papists may no longer falsely say that its waters are, as Tertullian once put it, widowed and barren, nor pregnant with the Holy Spirit. Christ himself also wished to be washed with this same baptism, because he wished to fulfil all righteousness, Matt. 3:15, that is, not merely to be circumcised, and so bind himself to the obedience of the Law and its servitude, but also to be baptized, and so to receive, as the head of his body, the seal of righteousness and of remission of our sins, which he had made his own by undertaking them. For otherwise he is the one who forgives sins, as John also professed, saying: I have need to be baptized by you; I need your sanctification and justification, ibid. v. 14. But more on this baptism in its place.

units.la: LXXX. Ex his merè Evangelicum fuisse Johannis Baptistæ Ministerium, ad liquidum perducimus. Quicquid enim fiat de Epocha temporis, in quod ministerium illud incidit, nondum utique vel de jure, vel de facto antiquato Veteri Testamento; sed & Novi Testamenti præparatione jam tum vigente (de quo supra diximus) ipse tamen typus doctrinæ, cui ministerium suum Johannes confirmavit, non utique lex, sed Evangelium fuit. quicquid Pontificii & Anabaptistæ, latibulum suæ hæresis deLegis & Evangelii differentia quærentes, obstrepant; concedente nonnihil iisdem Cl. Amyraldo, qui Ministerium Johannis ita temperatum fuisse, ut neque propriè Lex esset, neque Evangelium, sed aliquid ex utroque conflatum; comitante illud Spiritu velut ex utriusque mixtura compositò, ut neque merè Spiritus adoptionis, neque merè servitutis esset, sed medius inter eos affectus, qui ex Legis & Evangelii prædicatione producuntur; docuit; ut ita, qua similitudine idem rem illustrat, Lex noctis similis sit, multis de Christo vaticiniis, tanquam sideribus quibusdam interlucentibus distinctæ: Evangelium diei, cùm Sol jam exortus cuncta purissimo & splendidissimo lumine complet: Johannis ministerium diluculo, cùm nondum exorto sole, attamen annitente ad horizontem luce quadam, Cœlum albescit, quæ neque nox, neque dies, sed aliquid intermedium est. Verùm Sol justitiæ, in cujus alis est sanitas, cum ipso etiam Christo nato ortus, seu manifestatus est, Mal. IV.2. Nam & Sermo ille, qui caro factus est, φῶς Lux fuit, Joh. I. 1. ꝓ. 14. Eo nascente visitavit nos ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους oriens (Sol) ex alto, Luc. I. 78. Quid verò multis? Lex & Prophetæ usque ad Johannem. Ex eo Regnum Dei evangelizatur; & quisque illi vim infert; ibid. XVI. 16. A diebus Johannis Baptistæ hucusque Regnum Cœlorum vim facit, cum impetu quodam ad destructionem & abolitionem formæ priscæ populi Dei tendens, &c. Matth. XI. 12. Nihil igitur de Lege, quatenus illa subintravit, Johannes docuit, quin potiùs illud ipsum Evangelium docuit, quod circa nativitatem Christi per Angelos & homines, qui Spiritu Prophetico de ejus in carnem adventu locuti erant, & quod ipse Christus per se & discipulos suos prædicavit, videlicet, adesse natum ex muliere, promissum Messiam, ut verum agnum Dei, corporis sui sacrificio peccata tollentem. Eandem doctrinam Evangelicam Baptismi Sacramento in nomine Domini Jesu Christi Act. XIX. 4. 5. administrato obsignavit. Et cum eodem Johannis Baptismo Evangelica promissio Spiritus S. & remissionis peccatorum conjuncta fuit similiter ut cum Baptismo Apostolorum in diePentecostes, ibid. II. 38. coll. cum Matth. III. 11. Marc. I. 4. 8. Luc. III. 16. Neque Christus ipse Johannis Baptismum impensè adeò desiderasset, si cum Baptismo per Apostolos administrato, & ab eodem in Cœlos ascendente in usum Ecclesiæ Catholicæ dedicato ἱσπμ non fuisset. Uterque pro visibili signo & sigillo justitiæ Christo inhærentis, & credentibus in ipsum ipsum imputatæ, in mystica unione credentium, & membrorum cum Christo capite, habere debuit. Denique cum Evangelii summa præcepto credendi in Christum & resipiscendi, nec non promissione justitiæ & remissionis peccatorum absolvatur; non aliud Johannes præcepit, non aliud docuit.
units.tr: LXXX. From these points we make it clear that the ministry of John the Baptist was purely evangelical. Whatever may be said about the period of time in which that ministry fell, the Old Testament was not yet abrogated either in law or in fact, and the preparation for the New Testament was already in force (as we said above). Still, the type of doctrine which John confirmed by his ministry was certainly not law but Gospel. The Papists and Anabaptists may clamour whatever they like, seeking a hiding place for their heresy in the difference between Law and Gospel. The distinguished Amyraldus, who conceded something to them, taught that John's ministry was so tempered that it was properly neither Law nor Gospel but something compounded of both, accompanied by the Spirit as if by a mixture of the two, so that it was neither purely the Spirit of adoption nor purely that of bondage, but an intermediate disposition produced by the preaching of Law and Gospel together. He illustrates the point with a comparison: the Law is like the night, distinguished by many prophecies about Christ, like stars shining through; the Gospel is like the day, when the sun, now risen, fills all things with its purest and brightest light; John's ministry is like the dawn, when the sun has not yet risen but a certain light striving toward the horizon makes the sky grow white. This light is neither night nor day but something in between. But the Sun of righteousness, with healing in its wings, rose or was made manifest together with Christ himself at his birth (Mal. 4:2). For that Word which was made flesh was light [φῶς] (John 1:1, 14). At his birth he visited us as the dayspring from on high [ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους] (Luke 1:78). But why say more? The Law and the Prophets were until John. From then on the Kingdom of God is preached, and everyone presses into it (ibid. 16:16). From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, tending with a certain impetus to the destruction and abolition of the old form of the people of God (Matt. 11:12). Therefore John taught nothing of the Law, insofar as it had come in between; rather he taught that very Gospel which was announced around the birth of Christ by angels and men who spoke by the prophetic Spirit concerning his coming in the flesh, and which Christ himself preached through himself and his disciples: namely, that the promised Messiah, born of a woman, was at hand, as the true Lamb of God who would take away sins by the sacrifice of his body. He sealed this same evangelical doctrine by the sacrament of Baptism administered in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 19:4–5). And the evangelical promise of the Holy Spirit and of the forgiveness of sins was joined to the same baptism of John, just as it was to the baptism of the Apostles on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:38; compare Matt. 3:11; Mark 1:4, 8; Luke 3:16). Nor would Christ himself have so earnestly desired John's baptism unless it were in agreement with the baptism administered through the Apostles, and afterwards dedicated, when he had ascended into heaven, to the use of the Catholic Church. Each was to have, as a visible sign and seal of the righteousness which is in Christ and imputed to believers, a place in the mystical union of believers and members with Christ their head. Finally, since the sum of the Gospel is comprised in the command to believe in Christ and to repent, and in the promise of righteousness and forgiveness of sins, John commanded nothing else and taught nothing else.

units.la: LXXXI. Imbellis est dissentientium ratio, quòd ministerium Johannis æquè ac Baptismus ejusdem, à ministerio & Baptismo Apostolorum essentialiter disparatum fuerit. Nam quoad Baptismum Johannis, τὸ ἐν ὕδατι petitur. Nos enim in loco identitatis essentialis ejusdem fidem facimus. Qualis verò Baptismus fuit, tale etiam ministerium, Baptismo ut signaculo suo respondens, fuerit oportet. Sacramenta enim visibile verbum sunt. Neque etiam, quod Amyraldus urget, præconium resipiscentiæ, & responsa, quæ Johannes baptizandis secundum Legem Mosis dedit, obstant, quo minus Evangelicus fuerit typus doctrinæ, quam Johannes prædicavit. Nam fuit semper Prophetarum, Johannis, Christi, Apostolorum prædicantium, atque etiam num est Ministrorum Evangelii doctrina bipertita, partim Legalis, partim Evangelica. Legale est, quicquid & vitæ & morum informationem, ut mandatis Dei conformiter vivamus, spectat: Evangelicum verò, quicquid gratiam Dei & Christi, à nobis fide amplectendam exhibet. Proin & Legem & Evangelium docuerunt Prophetæ usque ad Johannem, & Johannes, & Christus & ejusdem Apostoli; sed hac methodo, ut Lex usque ad Johannem esset pædagogus ad Christum adducens atque impellens: deinceps verò canon & norma gratitudinis pro dono Dei. Qui hæc confundunt, illi per efficaciam erroris sicut Johanni, ita etiam Christo ante mortem & ascensionem ejus typum doctrinæ ad obtinendam justitiam Evangelicam sufficientem abrogare coguntur. Quantum verò ad minas & Johannis, quibus Pharisæos perculit, non minùs certe terribiliter Christi Pharisæos percellentis minæ & adversus eosdem invectivæ fuerunt. Nam eosdem γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν progeniem viperarum, Matth. XII. 35. appellavit; & gravissimum iis væ & judicium passim, inprimis ibid. XXIII. 13. &c. obnuntiavit. Denique nec temporis illius, in quod ministerium Johannis incidit, articulus magis legale ejusdem Ministerium facit; quam tempus Christi ad mortem ejus usque, quadenum Novum Testamentum vim suam accepit, Christi Ministerium legale efficit; vel Evangelium evertit.
units.tr: LXXXI. The objection of the dissenters is weak, namely that the ministry of John, like his baptism, was essentially different from the ministry and baptism of the Apostles. For as regards John's baptism, what is sought is "the in water" [τὸ ἐν ὕδατι]. But we make the same point in the place of essential identity. Whatever sort of baptism it was, the ministry too must have been of a kind that corresponds to its baptism as its seal, since sacraments are visible words. Nor does what Amyraldus presses stand in the way: the proclamation of repentance and the answers John gave to those to be baptized according to the Law of Moses do not prevent his teaching from being an evangelical type of the doctrine he preached. For the teaching of the ministers of the Gospel has always been twofold, partly legal and partly evangelical, as it was for the Prophets, John, Christ and the Apostles when preaching, and so it still is. Legal is whatever concerns the formation of life and morals, so that we live in conformity with the commandments of God; evangelical is whatever sets forth the grace of God and Christ, to be embraced by us in faith. Accordingly the Prophets up to John taught both Law and Gospel, and so did John, and Christ and his Apostles; but by this method, that the Law up to John was a schoolmaster leading and driving us to Christ, and thereafter it is the rule and norm of gratitude for the gift of God. Those who confuse these things are compelled, by the efficacy of error, to abolish the type of doctrine sufficient for obtaining Gospel righteousness, not only in the case of John but also in the case of Christ before his death and ascension. As for the threats of John, with which he struck the Pharisees, the threats and invectives of Christ against the same Pharisees were certainly no less terrible. For he called them "offspring of vipers" [γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν] progeniem viperarum, Matt. 12:35, and everywhere he pronounced a most grievous woe and judgment upon them, especially in ibid. 23:13 etc. Finally, the period of time in which John's ministry fell does not make that ministry more legal, any more than the time of Christ up to his death, by which the New Testament received its force, makes Christ's ministry legal or overthrows the Gospel.

units.la: LXXXII. Hoc ergo fuit ministerium Johannis; Prophetarum omnium maximi & Evangelizantium primi; teste ipso Christo: Quid ad videndum exiistis? Prophetam? Certè, dico vobis etiam majorem Prophetam.. Matth. XI. 9. Nam omnes Prophetæ & Lex usque ad Johannem prophetarunt, ibid. v. 13. Non ergo ex illorum Prophetarum numero fuit: sed Propheta tamen fuit. Et tu, puerule, προφήτης ὑψίστου Propheta Altissimi vocaberis. Præibis enim ante faciem Domini ad præparandum vias ejus, Luc. I. 76. Propheta igitur, non eadem ratione, qua illi, sed illis major Propheta fuit, quia præsentem & ortam Israelitis lucem testatus est, & præco Regni Dei jam appellentis, & vi se ingerentis, fuit,
units.tr: LXXXII. Such, then, was the ministry of John: the greatest of all the Prophets and the first of those who preached the Gospel, as Christ himself testifies: What did you go out to see? A prophet? Certainly, I tell you, even more than a prophet. Matt. 11:9. For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John, ibid. v. 13. He therefore was not of the number of those Prophets, yet he was a Prophet. And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High [προφήτης ὑψίστου]; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, Luke 1:76. He was a Prophet, then, not in the same way as they, but a greater Prophet than they, because he bore witness to the light already present and risen among the Israelites, and he was the herald of the Kingdom of God now drawing near and pressing in with force.

units.la: & Christo post se manifestando viam paravit, & ut talis ante faciem Domini προσέμπευσε præivit. Talis enim Propheta, Angelus, Elias à Deo missus est. Licet enim miracula non æquè ut Elias patraverit, testibus Judæis, σημεῖον ἐν ἀλλ signum nullum ab eo editum esse, Joh. X. 41. ne Messias, cujus prodromus tantum, & resipiscentiæ, secundum Prophetias, præco fuit, existimaretur; tamen necipsi defuit auctoratio per miraculum in Zacharia, & præ nuntiationem Angeli. Neque poterat eo tempore venire seductor sub similitudine ejus, quem Prophetia descripserat. Et qui reduxit filios ad cor Patrum, hoc est, pœnitentiam docuit, & fidem Patrum filiis demonstravit, is seductor non fuit; imò prodromus Christi fuit. Et sanè veritas illorum, quæ de Domino Jesu dixit, fidelitati ejus attestatur. Nam omnia, quæ Johannes de Jesu dixit, ἀληθῆ vera erant, ibid. X. 41. Imò hoc ipsum, quod post ipsum veniens omnes numeros Messiæ implevit, eum Prophetam & prodromum ejusmodi Messiæ fuisse, evincit. Dixit Jesus illis: Profecti nuntiate Johanni, quæ vidistis & audivistis; quòd cœci videant, claudi ambulent, leprosi mundentur, surdi audiant, mortui resuscitentur, pauperibus evangelizetur, Luc. VII. 22. Accedit, quòd Johannes venit cum Spiritu & virtute Eliæ, ibid. I. 17. hoc est, cum singulari zelo, exemplari sanctitate, quæ in habitu etiam & victu ejus se exeruit; & evidenti Spiritus in ipso loquentis manifestatione, qualis etiam in Elia extitit. Nam eventus ipse, qui instar verbi Divini, aut certè clavis ad verbum Dei se habet, docuit, Johannem illum fuisse, qui præconio resipiscentiæ, & munere prodromi Christi, à Prophetis prædicti, functus fuerit, atque ita cum spiritu & virtute Eliæ venerit. Denique quæ de Christo locutus fuit, antequam ab illo, & in illo fierent, illa sic omnia postea facta sunt, Joh. X. 41. Fieri autem non potuit, ut quis de alio post se veniente res tantas; eventu liquidò comprobatas, absque Spiritu Dei prædicere potuerit. Merito igitur Christus vice versa ejusmodi testimonium ipsi perhibuit: Amen dico vobis, non surrexit inter natos ex mulieribus major Johanne Baptista, cui scilicet majus & gloriosius munus sit concreditum; Matth. XI. 11. Sed hoc non obstante, minimus, ibidem inquit; in Regno Cœlorum ipso major est; quia in Regno Cœlorum illo, cujus auspicia in Christi exaltatione jacientur; minimus fidelium Johannem, ante Christi mortem & Regni Cœlorum initium necatum, neque adeò Bonorum N. T. participem, consummatione post facta, & minimis etiam præstita, antecellet. Ideo munere suo expleto; Christo decessit, & Veteris Testamenti Cœlum clausit.
