units.tr: and he prepared the way for Christ to be manifested after him, and as such went before the face of the Lord [προπορεύσῃ]. For such a Prophet, an Angel, Elijah was sent by God. Although he did not perform miracles as Elijah did, the Jews bearing witness that he did no sign at all, John 10:41, so that the Messiah, of whom he was only the forerunner and herald of repentance according to the Prophecies, would not be thought to be him, nevertheless he was not without authentication by a miracle in the case of Zechariah, and by the announcement of an angel. Nor could a deceiver come at that time under the likeness of him whom Prophecy had described. And he who turned the hearts of the fathers to the children, that is, taught repentance and showed the faith of the fathers to the children, was not a deceiver; rather he was the forerunner of Christ. And indeed the truth of what he said about the Lord Jesus bears witness to his faithfulness. For all the things John said about Jesus were true, ibid. 10:41. Indeed the very fact that, coming after him, he fulfilled all the marks of the Messiah proves that John was a Prophet and forerunner of such a Messiah. Jesus said to them: Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: that the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have the Gospel preached to them, Luke 7:22. In addition, John came in the spirit and power of Elijah, ibid. 1:17, that is, with singular zeal and exemplary holiness, which also showed in his dress and diet, and with the clear manifestation of the Spirit speaking in him, such as was also in Elijah. For the outcome itself, which stands like the Divine word, or certainly like the key to the word of God, has shown that John was the one who performed the office of herald of repentance and forerunner of Christ foretold by the Prophets, and so came in the spirit and power of Elijah. Finally, what he said about Christ before those things happened from him and in him, in this way all those things were afterwards fulfilled, John 10:41. But it could not happen that anyone should foretell such great matters about another coming after him, matters clearly confirmed by the event, without the Spirit of God. Rightly, then, Christ in turn bore this testimony to him: Amen, I say to you, there has not arisen among those born of women a greater than John the Baptist, to whom indeed a greater and more glorious office had been entrusted; Matt. 11:11. But notwithstanding this, the least, he says in the same place, in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he; because in that kingdom of heaven, whose beginnings would be laid at Christ's exaltation, the least of the faithful surpasses John, who was put to death before Christ's death and the beginning of the kingdom of heaven, and so was not a sharer in the good things of the New Testament, which were bestowed even on the least after the consummation had taken place. Therefore, having completed his office, he gave way to Christ and closed the heaven of the Old Testament.

units.la: LXXXIII. Post Johannem Christus Evangelium prædicavit, sed ut Dominus, & causa ejus, non ut famulus. In novissimo diérum (priorum; quomodo 1. Pet. I. 20. Christus manifestatus dicitur ἐπ' ἐσχάτων τῶν χρόνων novissimis temporibus) Deus locutus nobis est in Filio; Hebr. I. 1. Salus coepit dici per Dominum, ibid. II. 3. Nam & ipse adventus Salvatoris est veluti sermo ejus de salute jam extante; in causa sua, nempe consummatione Principis salutis mox absolvenda: Sed magis etiam locutus est per Baptistam præcursorem suum. Maximè vero, quando ipse ad discipulos suos, & totum populum locutus est: imò quando de cruce, tanquam triumphali curru, τὸ τπλεσϑη consummatum est, prædicavit; tandemque ex mortuis redux cum discipulis suis de Regno Dei sermonem fecit. Neque aliud locutus est; quàm salutem, quia non venit, ut judicaret mundum, sed ut mundus per eum salvaretur, Joh. III. 17. Ideóque non locutus est, nec loqui potuit sermonem accusantem peccatum, & illud commemorantem. Alias fuisset Minister peccati, Gal. II. 17. Quippe potentiæ peccati, quæ est reum facere, declarare & accusare, succenturiatus fuisset. Sed Spiritus Dei super eo fuit, quia unxit eum Jehova לבשר ad evangelizandum mansuetis, ad obligandum confractos corde, ad prædicandam captivis libertatem, & vinctis acutum visum, ad prædicandum שנת רצון annum acceptationis Jehovæ, &c. Esaj. LXI. 1. 2. Luc. IV. 18. Qui mansuetis primus evangelizat, is est, qui facit pacem, & adducit justitiam, ut mansueti gaudere, & omnibus relictis ad eum accedere, possint. Sed de Christo per gratiam in labiis ejus diffusam Psalm. XLV. 3. sic Evangelizante pluribus Loc. XIX. §. 39. 40. &c. egimus.
units.tr: LXXXIII. After John, Christ preached the Gospel, but as Lord and for his own cause, not as a servant. In the last of these days (of the former days; as in 1 Pet. 1:20, where Christ is said to have been manifested in the last times [ἐπ' ἐσχάτων τῶν χρόνων]), God has spoken to us in the Son (Heb. 1:1). Salvation began to be spoken of through the Lord (ibid. 2:3). For the very coming of the Saviour is, as it were, his speech about salvation already at hand, in its cause, namely the completion of the Prince of salvation, which was soon to be accomplished. Yet he also spoke more through his forerunner, the Baptist. He spoke most of all when he addressed his disciples and the whole people; indeed, when he proclaimed from the cross, as from a triumphal chariot, that it is finished [τὸ τετέλεσται] (John 19:30), and finally, returned from the dead, he discoursed with his disciples about the kingdom of God. He spoke of nothing other than salvation, because he did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17). Therefore he did not speak, nor could he speak, a word accusing sin and recalling it. Otherwise he would have been a minister of sin (Gal. 2:17), since he would have served as a helper to the power of sin, which is to make guilty, to expose and to accuse. But the Spirit of God was upon him, because Jehovah anointed him לבשר to preach good tidings to the meek, to bind up the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives and opening of the eyes to the bound, to proclaim שנת רצון the acceptable year of Jehovah, etc. (Isa. 61:1, 2; Luke 4:18). He who first preaches good tidings to the meek is the one who makes peace and brings righteousness, so that the meek may rejoice and, leaving everything, may come to him. But we have treated of Christ, whose lips were anointed with grace (Ps. 45:3), as the one who evangelised to many, at Loc. XIX §§ 39, 40, etc.

units.la: LXXXIV.
units.tr: LXXXIV.

units.la: Salus sic à Christo dici coepta ab iis, qui audiverunt usque ad nos ἐκκλησίων στα-bilita est, Hebr. II. 2. Ante omnia enim Christus è tota discipulorum suorum turba elegit duodecim, qui cum ipso essent Marc. III. 14. Joh. VI. 70. ejus dicta exciperent, & aliis narrarent, ὃς καὶ Ἀπόστολος ὠνόμασε, quos etiam Apostolos, missos à se nominavit Luc. VI. 13. voce familiari Hebræis, apud quos שליחי & שלוחי Apostoli etiam Moses & Aharon dicti sunt, uti ex Chaldæo Paraphraste Jerem. II. 1. liquet. Ea vox apud eosdem non nuntium duntaxat, sed nuntium vices mittentis gerentem significat. Ita in Bab. Berach. sol. 34. שליחי של אדם כמותו Apostolus cujusque est sicut ipse, à quo deputatur. Apostoli autem vox modo latius quemvis etiam ab Apostolis missum notat; quomodo etiam Barnabas Act. XIV. 14. Andronicus & Junias, Rom. XVI. 7. Epaphroditus Phil. II. 25. Apostoli vocantur: modò κατ' ἐξοχὴν duodecim à Christo electos notat. Tales Christus delegit, tum ut socios, comites & ministros, quorum ope & ministerio in terris agens, sive ad comparanda hujus vitæ ὑπηρεσίας, sive ad alia uteretur, haberet: tum ut iisdem præ aliis mysteria Regni Cœlorum reseraret, Matth. XIII. 11. & in eorum sinum doctrinam suam, & verba quæ ipsi Pater dedit, deponeret, Joh. XVII. 8. tum ut testes αὐτόπται καὶ αὐτήκοοι dictorum & factorum suorum, resurrectionis inprimis haberet, Luc. XXIV. 48. Act. I. 22. X. 41. XXII. 15. 1. Joh. I. 1. tum ut haberet ἀπαρχὴν ἕνα τῶν αὐτῶ κτισμάτων primitias quasdam creaturarum suarum, Jac. I. 18. quas virtute ex alto induceret, & ad partem sortis sanctorum aptaret, Luc. XXIV. 49. Act. I. 8. Col. I. 12. tum ut Ecclesia ex Judæis & Gentibus colligenda præcones & doctores in messe Domini operarios, Matth. IX. 37. hominum piscatores, ibid. IV. 19. Luc. V. 10. haberet: tum denique, ut haberet qui defectus passionum Christi in carne sua vicissim implerent, Col. I. 24. & morte sua Dominum glorificarent. Joh. XXI. 19. Eosdem at plures elegit, ut in ore plurium sit veritas, & plures inter se operas mundi totius Evangelio subjiciendi partirentur; & fundamentum Ecclesiæ, ceu periti architecti, jacerent: Et duodecim elegit, quia ad duodecim tribus Israelis, iisque innectendas gentes mitti debuerunt. Sicut verò duodecim Patriarchæ & tribus uno Patriarcha, & una tribu aucti sunt: ita Apostolorum numerus, cooptato in chorum eorum Paulo, qui ex Benjaminis tribu oriundus, Prophetiæ illius: Benjamin lupus lanians, mane comedit prædam, & vesperi spolia divisit, Genes. XLIX. 27. partem implevit; quia sicut Saulus primus in exortu Reipublicæ Judaicæ prædas comedit: ita Saulus hic alter, Apostolus, in ultimo tempore spolia distribuit. Hac enim Phrasi Christo amplificatio Regni promissa est: Cum robustis, vel numerosis dividet spolia, Esaj. LIII. 12. Effecit enim inprimis Paulus, Gentium Apostolus; ut πληρώματα τῶν ἐθνῶν plenitudo Gentium jam tum intrare inciperet.
units.tr: Salvation, thus begun to be spoken by Christ, was confirmed to us by those who heard him [ἐβεβαιώθη] (Heb. 2:3). For first of all, out of the whole crowd of his disciples, Christ chose twelve, who were to be with him (Mark 3:14; John 6:70), to receive his sayings and to relate them to others; these he also named Apostles [ὃς καὶ Ἀπόστολος ὠνόμασε], that is, sent by himself (Luke 6:13). It is a word familiar to the Hebrews, among whom שליחי and שלוחי (apostles) were also used of Moses and Aaron, as is clear from the Chaldee paraphrast on Jer. 2:1. Among the same people the word signifies not merely a messenger, but one who acts in the place of the one who sends him. So in Babylonian Berachot, fol. 34: שליחי של אדם כמותו, the apostle of any man is as himself, by whom he is appointed. Moreover, the word apostle is used more broadly of anyone sent even by the apostles; thus Barnabas is called an apostle (Acts 14:14), and Andronicus and Junias (Rom. 16:7), and Epaphroditus (Phil. 2:25). But in the strict sense [κατ' ἐξοχήν] it denotes the twelve chosen by Christ. Christ chose such men: first, as companions, comrades and ministers, whose help and service he would have while living on earth, whether to provide the necessities of this life or for other purposes; second, that he might unlock to them, above others, the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 13:11), and deposit in their bosom his teaching and the words which the Father had given him (John 17:8); third, that he might have witnesses of his sayings and deeds [αὐτόπται καὶ αὐτήκοοι], above all of his resurrection (Luke 24:48; Acts 1:22; 10:41; 22:15; 1 John 1:1); fourth, that he might have some first-fruits of his creatures [ἀπαρχὴν τινα τῶν αὐτοῦ κτισμάτων] (James 1:18), whom he would bring in by power from on high and fit for a share in the inheritance of the saints (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:8; Col. 1:12); fifth, that he might have, for gathering the Church from Jews and Gentiles, heralds and teachers, labourers in the Lord's harvest (Matt. 9:37), and fishers of men (ibid. 4:19; Luke 5:10); and finally, that he might have men who would in turn fill up what was lacking in the sufferings of Christ in their flesh (Col. 1:24), and glorify the Lord by their death (John 21:19). He chose these and more, so that in the mouth of many there might be truth, and so that many might share among themselves the labour of subjecting the whole world to the Gospel, and lay the foundation of the Church, like skilled architects. And he chose twelve because they were to be sent to the twelve tribes of Israel and to the Gentiles to be joined with them. Just as the twelve patriarchs and tribes were increased by one patriarch and one tribe, so the number of the Apostles, with Paul admitted into their company, who sprang from the tribe of Benjamin, fulfilled that prophecy: Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he devours the prey, and at evening he divides the spoil (Gen. 49:27). For as Saul at the beginning of the Jewish commonwealth ate the prey, so this other Saul, the Apostle, at the last time distributed the spoils. For by this phrase an enlargement of the kingdom was promised to Christ: He shall divide the spoil with the strong, or with the many (Isa. 53:12). For Paul, the Apostle of the Gentiles, above all brought about that the fullness of the Gentiles [πλήρωμα τῶν ἐθνῶν] might already begin to enter.

units.la: LXXXV.
units.tr: LXXXV.

units.la: Quis primus Apostolus vocatus fuerit, non plane constat. Alii Andreæ eum honorem vindicant, quem propterea πρωτόκλη-τον appellant. Alii Simonem pariter & Andream πρωτόκλητος, utpote ante alios omnes vocatos, nominant. Neque defuerunt, qui Philippo hunc honorem haberent. Illud verisimile est, Christum vocationem suorum Apostolorum à binis fratribus Simone & Andrea, Bethsaida Galilææ oriundis, sic tamen ut Andreæ, quippe Simonem prima vice ad Jesum adducentis Joh. I. vers. 41. 42. sive vocatio, sive cum Christo familiaritas præcesserit; inchoasse; quemadmodum olim ad ministerium Legis Moses & Aharon simul vocati fuerunt. Simonem & Andream Jacobus & Johannes, filii Zebedæi, quibus nomen Boanerges; filiorum tonitru, Christus imposuit, exceperunt, Matth. IV. 18. 21. Marc. III. 17: Hi quoque piscatores, & in opere eo κοινωνοὶ socii Simonis & Andreæ fuerunt, Matth. IV. 18. Luc. V. 10. Quintus Philippus fuit, quem Christus in Galilæam exire volens invenit & vocavit, Joh. I. 44. Sextus Bartholomæus, cujus rara in sacris mentio. Septimus Thomas Δίδυμος Geminus dictus; ibid. XI. 16. XIV. 5. XX. 24. &c. Octavus Matthæus ὁ τελώνης Publicanus, quem Jesus à telonio se sequi jussit, dictus etiam Λευις ἡ Αλφαίου Levi Alphæi, Matth. IX. 9. Marc. II. 14. Nonus Jacobus Alphæi: frater, seu consanguineus Domini, Matth. XIII. 55. dictus ὁ μικρὸς minor, Marc. XV. 40. Decimus Lebbæus, cognominatus Thaddæus, alias Judas, Jacobi frater, Matth. X. 3. Luc. VI. 16. Act. I. 13. Undecimus Simon ὁ Καναναῖος Zelotes, frater Thaddæi & Jacobi minoris, Mat. XIII. 55. Duodecimus Judas Iscariotes, quasi איש קריות vir ex Kerioth, oppido Judæ Jos. XV. 25. oriundus; nisi sic dictus est, quia fuit איש שקר vir mendacii, proditor Christi. Talis enim in sacro choro juxta Scripturas etiam comparere debuit. Nam & Achitophelis exemplum præcesserat, & David in persona Christi amicum aliquem suum proditionis accusat, Ps. XLI. 10. cujus extincti fœda morte ἐπισκοπὴ Episcopatus & ἀποστολὴ Apostolatus per sortem Matthiæ cessit, Psal. CIX. 8. Act. I. 20. 25. 26. Quibus omnibus serius paulò Saulus, Pauli deinceps nomine insignis, accessit, quo de supra.
units.tr: It is not altogether certain who was the first of the Apostles to be called. Some claim that honour for Andrew, whom they therefore call protoklētos [πρωτόκλητον], the first-called. Others name Simon and Andrew alike as the first-called [πρωτόκλητος], since they were called before all the rest. Some have also given this honour to Philip. It is likely that Christ began the calling of his Apostles with the two brothers Simon and Andrew, natives of Bethsaida in Galilee. It is likely, however, that Andrew, who brought Simon to Jesus for the first time (John 1:41-42), came first, whether by calling or by earlier acquaintance with Christ. So of old Moses and Aaron were called together to the ministry of the Law. James and John, the sons of Zebedee, whom Christ named Boanerges, that is, sons of thunder, joined Simon and Andrew (Matt. 4:18-21; Mark 3:17). These too were fishermen, and in that work they were partners [κοινωνοί] of Simon and Andrew (Matt. 4:18; Luke 5:10). The fifth was Philip, whom Christ found when he wished to go out into Galilee, and called (John 1:44). The sixth was Bartholomew, whose mention in Scripture is rare. The seventh was Thomas, called Didymus [Δίδυμος], that is, Twin (ibid. 11:16, 14:5, 20:24, etc.). The eighth was Matthew, the publican [ὁ τελώνης], whom Jesus bade follow him from the toll-booth; he is also called Levi, son of Alphaeus [Λευις ἡ Αλφαίου] (Matt. 9:9; Mark 2:14). The ninth was James, son of Alphaeus, brother or kinsman of the Lord (Matt. 13:55), called "the less" [ὁ μικρός] (Mark 15:40). The tenth was Lebbaeus, surnamed Thaddaeus, otherwise Judas, brother of James (Matt. 10:3; Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13). The eleventh was Simon the Canaanite [ὁ Καναναῖος], the Zealot, brother of Thaddaeus and of James the less (Matt. 13:55). The twelfth was Judas Iscariot, as if a man of Kerioth [איש קריות], that is, of the town of Kerioth in Judah (Josh. 15:25); unless he was so called because he was a man of lies [איש שקר], the betrayer of Christ. For such a man had to appear in the sacred band, according to the Scriptures. The example of Ahithophel had gone before, and David, speaking in the person of Christ, accuses a friend of his of betrayal (Ps. 41:10). After Judas was cut off by a foul death, his office of bishop [ἐπισκοπή] and his apostleship [ἀποστολή] passed by lot to Matthias (Ps. 109:8; Acts 1:20, 25-26). A little later Saul, afterwards known by the name Paul, joined all these, as was said above.

units.la: LXXXVI. De Apostolis in universum sic loqui-
units.tr: LXXXVI. Concerning the Apostles in general, speaking thus:

units.la: Idem Testes & Præcones Evangelii sui, nec non ministros sibi elegit Apostolos & quosque plures, & numero duodecim quibus tertius & decimus Paulus accessit.
units.tr: The same Jesus chose for himself Apostles, witnesses and heralds of his Gospel, and also ministers, and more besides; the number was twelve, to which the thirteenth, Paul, was added.

units.la: loquitur Petrus: Hunc (Jesum) Deus suscitavit tertio die, & dedit eum conspicuum fieri non omni populo, sed μάρτυσι τῆς προχειροτονημένοις testibus ante Divino suffragio electis a Deo, nobis qui unà cum eo edimus & bibimus, postquam ex mortuis resurrexit, & mandavit nobis, ut praedicaremus populo, quòd ipse sit definitus a Deo judex vivorum & mortuorum, Act. X. 40.41.42. Fuerunt ergo Divino suffragio electi testes resurrectionis Christi, utpote qui post resurrectionem iis ἐμφανὴς conspicuus factus est, cum quo comederunt & biberunt: accepto mandato, ut eum populo Judicem vivorum & mortuorum, cui omnes Prophetæ testimonium perhibent, fore ut remissionem peccatorum per nomen ejus accipiat omnis, qui in ipsum credit, ibid. v. 43. praedicarent. Unde S. Petrus Apostolum simpliciter μάρτυρα τῆς ἀναστάσεως testem resurrectionis Christi ibid. I.22. finit.
units.tr: Peter speaks thus: "God raised this Jesus on the third day and granted that he be made manifest, not to all the people, but to witnesses [μάρτυσι τῆς προχειροτονημένοις] chosen beforehand by God, to us who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead; and he commanded us to preach to the people that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead" (Acts 10:40-42). The witnesses of Christ's resurrection, therefore, were chosen by Divine suffrage, since he was made manifest [ἐμφανής] to them after the resurrection, and they ate and drank with him. They had received the command to preach to the people that he is the judge of the living and the dead, to whom all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins through his name (ibid. v. 43). Hence St Peter simply calls an Apostle a witness [μάρτυρα] of the resurrection of Christ (Acts 1:22).

units.la: Accipietis potentiam venturi supra vos Spiritus S. Et eritis mihi testes in Hierusalem, & in omni Judæa, & Samaria, & usque ad ultimum terræ, ibid. I.8. Ac ne S. Paulus quidem Apostolus esse, nisi Christum ex mortuis resuscitatum in Coelo vidisset, poterat. Deus Patrum nostrorum te designavit, ut cognoscceres voluntatem ejus, & videres illum justum, & vocem ejus ex ore ejus audires, quòd sis ipsi futurus μάρτυς testis apud omnes homines eorum, quæ vidiveras & audiveras, ibid. XXII.14.15. Nonne sum Apostolus? Nonne Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum vidi? 1. Cor. IX. 1. Hoc Evangelium de Jesu Christo ex mortuis resuscitato, & a se viso, ut praedicarent in toto terrarum orbe, missi sunt. Profecti discipulos facite omnes gentes, &c. Matth. XXVIII. 19. Profecti in mundum universum, praedicate Evangelium omni creaturæ. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur, Marc. XVI. 15.16. Non vos elegistis me, sed ego elegi vos, & posui vos, ut vadatis, & fructum multum feratis, & fructus vester maneat, Joh. XV. 16. Sicut me misit Pater, ita ego mitto vos: Comparata non authoritate & potestate, quæ in Christo a Patre misso, & Apostolis a Christo missis minimè æqualis fuit; sed missione & missionis instructione, ib. XX.21. Finis enim missi a Patre Christi, unde & ipse Ἀπόστολος Apostoli nomine venit, Heb. III, 1. erat, ut & Filius mitteret Apostolos, atque per eos auditorum & visorum testes, atque praecones justitiæ, Ecclesiam sibi ex toto mundo colligeret, ut sic benedictio ad gentes perveniret. Non ergo alia cum ἀποστολικὴ instructione missi sunt, quàm cum qua & Filius missus est, ut quod ex Filio de justitia audiverant, id ipsum praedicarent, neque quicquam addendo vel detrahendo mutarent; sicut nec ipse Filius, qui ab ipsis praedicari debuit, mutatur. Regnum enim ipsius, non proprium erigi debuit. Nihil ergo ultra id, quod Filius locutus erat, loqui debuerunt. Omnia, sic ipse, quæ audivi a Patre, indicavi vobis, Joh. XV. 15. Audivit autem, quæ ad cognitionem Nominis Dei & plenitudinem lætitiæ faciebant. Hæc Apostolis indicavit, hæc, non alia hi praedicare potuerunt, debuerunt. Tum Filius hominis venit, non ut dominaretur, vel ei servirent alii, sed ut ipse serviret aliis, Matth. XX. 28. Marc. X. 45. Pari ratione nec Apostoli missi sunt ad dominandum, sed ad serviendum. Principes gentium dominantur eis, &c. Vos autem non sic. Sed qui inter vos magnus esse voluerit. esto sicut minister. Et qui inter vos voluerit esse primus, esto vester servus, Matth. XX. 25. 26. 27.
units.tr: "You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth" (ibid. 1:8). Nor could even St Paul be an Apostle unless he had seen Christ raised from the dead in heaven. "The God of our fathers has appointed you to know his will, and to see the Just One, and to hear the voice from his mouth, because you are to be his witness [μάρτυς] to all men of what you have seen and heard" (ibid. 22:14-15). "Am I not an Apostle? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?" (1 Cor. 9:1). "They were sent to proclaim this Gospel of Jesus Christ, raised from the dead and seen by themselves, throughout the whole world. Go, make disciples of all nations," etc. (Matt. 28:19). "Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved" (Mark 16:15-16). "You did not choose me, but I chose you, and appointed you that you should go and bear much fruit, and that your fruit should remain" (John 15:16). "As the Father sent me, so I send you" (ib. 20:21). Here the comparison is not of authority and power: Christ, sent by the Father, and the Apostles, sent by Christ, were by no means equal. The comparison is of the mission and of the instruction given for it. For the Son of God, whom the Father sent, and who is therefore called Apostle (Heb. 3:1), had this purpose: that he should also send Apostles, and through them witnesses of what they had heard and seen, and heralds of righteousness, to gather for himself a Church from the whole world, so that the blessing might reach the nations. The Apostles were therefore sent with no other apostolic instruction than that with which the Son himself was sent: that they should preach what they had heard from the Son about righteousness, and change nothing by adding or taking away, just as the Son himself, who was to be preached by them, is not changed. For his kingdom, not their own, was to be set up. They ought therefore to speak nothing beyond what the Son had said. "All things, as he himself said, which I heard from the Father, I have made known to you" (John 15:15). He heard, however, what served the knowledge of God's Name and the fullness of joy. These things he made known to the Apostles; these, and no others, they could and ought to preach. Then: "The Son of man came not that he might be ruled, or that others should serve him, but that he himself might serve others" (Matt. 20:28; Mark 10:45). By the same reasoning the Apostles also were sent not to rule but to serve. "The princes of the nations lord it over them," etc. "But it shall not be so among you. Whoever wishes to be great among you, let him be as a minister; and whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be your servant" (Matt. 20:25-27).

units.la: LXXXVII. Apostoli ministerii & praeconii tyrocinium jam ante mortem Christi Judæis fratribus suis resipiscentiam & approximationem Regni Coelorum praedicando fecerunt, obsequentes mandato Christi: Profecti, praedicate, dicentes: Approximavit Regnum Coelorum, Matth. X.7. sic, procursu velut in Ecclesiæ campum facto, cui deinde perarando se totos impensuri erant, Evangelii semen per Judæam & Galilæam diffuderunt, reliquum tempus, hauriendæ Christi disciplinæ lateri ejus assiduè haerentes traduxerunt. Cum simili mandato Christus etiamseptuaginta discipulos misit, injungens iis: Dicite iis: Appropinquavit vobis Regnum Dei, Luc. X.9. Ne videlicet quemquam lateret, expectationem Israelis esse praeforibus, & jam Christum, cui Regnum datum erat, in mundo versari, & in eo esse, ut propediem fasces principatus sui capessat; ut audita & visa cum Prophetiis contenderent, & credentes in Christum Regni Dei participes fierent. LXXXVIII. Hoc demum posito tyrocinio, post mortem & exaltationem Christi Ἀπολλῶ suam obire coeperunt; postquam iis sibi & pavoris sui consilio relictis, dispersis, & ex fuga ab ipso Christo collectis Christus profectionem non ad Judæos duntaxat, sed etiam ad gentes, notitia mortis & resurrectionis ejusdem imbuendas mandavit, Matth. XXVIII. 9. Joh. XX. qui Apostolatus praecipuus character erat. Non enim ad populi tantum Israelitici tribus, sed ad gentes etiam eos mitti oportuit, quia & hæ per fidem salvandæ erant. Credere autem nisi audientes, audire nisi ex missis ad praeconium non potuerunt. Atque ideò magis necessarium erat, quia Israel, dum gentes compellarentur, rebellis futurus erat. Respondinon interrogantibus, praesto fui non quaerentibus. Expandiveram manus meas omni tempore ad populum refractarium, Esaj. LXV. 1.2. Quo argumento S. Paulus suam ad gentes legationem Rom. X. 14-21. defendit. Cui consentaneum est, quòd Deus de caecitate servi sui, quem missurus esset, ita queritur: Surdi (gentes, quae verbum Dei non audiviistis) audite, & caeci (qui opera Dei magnifica apud Israelem facta non vidistis, ad solum spectaculum Coeli, terræ & operum Dei in mundo stupentes) intuemini ad videndum. Quam surdorum & caecorum compellationem & fanationem caecitate & surditate populi sui statim tuetur, exclamans: Quis caecus nisi servus meus, quis surdus nisi legatus meus, quem mittaterem? Quis caecus ut qui consummatus est, (apud quem salutis consummatio jam facta est) & caecus ut servus Jehovæ? Esaj. XLII. 18.19. clarissimum illud est, quod Prophetia dicit, fore ut Lex Domini & verbum ejus ex Hierosolyma proficiscatur ad gentes, & sic gentes ad Deum accedant, & unionem cum Sione, seu Christo revelato, & membris ejus, verae Sionis, quae posthac in toto mundo futura erat, civibus, quaerant; Esaj. II. 2. 3. LXXXIX. Sed ordinem tamen missio Divina, Apostolis ejusmodi injunxit, ut primò Hierosolymæ & in Judæa, Esaj. II. 2. 3. Act. II. 14. &c. apud filios Regni, Matth. VIII. 12. ad quos
units.tr: LXXXVII. Before Christ's death, the apostles served their apprenticeship in the ministry and the proclamation of the gospel. Obeying Christ's command, they preached repentance and the nearness of the kingdom of heaven to their Jewish brethren: Go, preach, saying: The kingdom of heaven is at hand, Matt. 10.7. In this way, as though making a running start onto the field of the Church, which they were afterwards to cultivate wholeheartedly, they scattered the seed of the gospel through Judea and Galilee, and spent the rest of the time clinging constantly to Christ's side and drinking in his teaching. Christ sent out the seventy disciples with a similar command, charging them: Say to them: The kingdom of God has drawn near to you, Luke 10.9. The purpose was that no one should fail to understand that the expectation of Israel was at the door, and that Christ, to whom the kingdom had been given, was already present in the world and about to take up the rods of his rule; so that they might set what they had heard and seen alongside the prophecies, and that, believing in Christ, they might become partakers of the kingdom of God. LXXXVIII. Only after this apprenticeship was complete did they begin to carry out their apostolate, after the death and exaltation of Christ. Left to their own counsel of fear, scattered, and gathered from their flight by ChristHimself, they were commanded by Christ to go forth and to be instructed in the knowledge of his death and resurrection, not only for the Jews but also for the nations, Matt. 28.9; John 20. This was the chief character of the apostolate. For they had to be sent not only to the tribes of the Israelite people but also to the nations, since these too were to be saved through faith. But they could not believe unless they heard, nor hear unless they were sent to preach. And so it was all the more necessary, because Israel, while the nations were being summoned, was going to be rebellious. I was found by those who did not ask; I was at hand for those who did not seek me. I stretched out my hands all day long to a rebellious people, Isa. 65.1,2. With this argument St Paul defends his mission to the nations, Rom. 10.14–21. Consistent with this is the way God complains of the blindness of the servant whom he was going to send: Deaf (you nations, who have not heard the word of God), hear; and blind (you who have not seen the wonderful works of God among Israel, and who stand amazed only at the spectacle of heaven, earth and the works of God in the world), look and see. He immediately upholds this address to the deaf and blind, and their healing, against the blindness and deafness of his own people, exclaiming: Who is blind but my servant? Who is deaf but my messenger whom I send? Who is blind as one who is made perfect (among whom the perfecting of salvation has already been accomplished), and blind as the servant of Jehovah? Isa. 42.18,19. Very clear is what the prophecy says, that the law of the Lord and his word shall go forth from Jerusalem to the nations, and so the nations shall come to God and seek union with Zion, that is, with the revealed Christ and his members, the citizens of the true Zion, who were to be throughout the whole world from then on; Isa. 2.2,3. LXXXIX. Nevertheless, the divine mission laid this order upon the apostles: that they should first preach at Jerusalem and in Judea, Isa. 2.2,3; Acts 2.14 etc., among the sons of the kingdom, Matt. 8.12, to whom

units.la: quos promissiones pertinebant Rom. IX. 4. Act. II. 39. & quorum exemplo in Semine quippe Abrahami gentes benedicenda erant, Genes. XXII. 18. inde in Samaria, Act. VIII. 5. & auspicio jacto (erant enim Samaritani hybridæ, ex Judæorum & gentium disciplina religionem miscellam constantes) demum apud gentes præconiarent. Quem ordinem non sortes jactæ, ut apocrypha traditio habet, sed ipse Spiritus Dei, gressus Apostolorum singulariter, uti ex Act. VIII. 29. XIII. 2. colligere est, dirigens constituit.
units.tr: the promises pertained, Rom. 9.4; Acts 2.39; and by whose example the nations were to be blessed in the Seed of Abraham, Gen. 22.18. Then they were to preach in Samaria, Acts 8.5, and, once a beginning had been made there (for the Samaritans were a hybrid people, whose religion was a mixture of Jewish and pagan practice), finally among the nations. This order was set not by casting lots, as the apocryphal tradition has it, but by the Spirit of God himself, who directed the steps of the apostles individually, as can be gathered from Acts 8.29; 13.2.

units.la: XC. Priusquam mitterentur Apostoli, virtute ex alto indui debuerunt. Ego mitto promissionem Patris mei super vos. Vos autem sedebitis in urbe Hierosolyma, donec induamini virtute ex alto, Luc. XXIV. 49. Mandavit iis, ne ab Hierosolyma discederent, sed ibi manentes expectarent promissionem Patris, quam ex eo audiverunt, Act. I. 4. Sicut nempe Christus publicè inungi, & à Deo Christus ac Dominus coram omnibus fieri ibid. II. 36. debuit, ut ita compellaretur, seu rebus ipsis ostenderetur Sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, Hebr. V. 10. ita Apostoli, oleo sacro, à capite Aaronis Cœlestis in ejusdem Barbam & fimbrias togæ ejus talaris descendente, Psal. CXXXIII. 2. & ipsi χρίσμα unctionem à sancto illo habentes, 1. Joh. II. 20. inungi S. Spiritu capitis sui Christi debuerunt, ut muneri arduo obeundo pares redderentur. Eadem Apostolorum inunctio etiam Baptismi Spiritus S. nomine venit. Johannes quidem baptizavit aqua, vos autem baptizabimini Spiritu S. iste non multis post diebus, Act. I. 5. Baptismus ille non Fluminis, sed Flaminis fuit, æque atque inunctio in consecuta mox Pentecoste, contigit; quando Apostoli oleo Spiritus S. liberalissimè perfusi sunt; & domus, in qua isthæc peracta sunt, Spiritu S. ita repleta fuit, ut in eam velut καλυμμένην quandam Apostoli demersi videantur. Sicut nempe Paschate & Dominica Paschatis festum sequta typus præcedens per resurrectionem Christi manè diei solis factam impletus fuit, ita etiam harum primitiarum Ecclesiæ Christianæ, quas אדירי duces eorum in quibus est voluptas Dei, Christus ipse, Ps. XVI. 3. appellat, in Pentecoste consecratio, & per ignem cœlestem inflammatio procedere debuit. Non enim sine gravi ratione Judæi septimanas & dies ad oblationem usque primitiarum anxiè adeò computare jussi sunt.
units.tr: XC. Before they were sent out, the apostles had to be clothed with power from on high. I send the promise of my Father upon you. But you shall sit in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high, Luke 24.49. He commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait there for the promise of the Father, which they heard from him, Acts 1.4. Just as Christ had to be anointed publicly, and be made Christ and Lord before all by God, Acts 2.36, so that he might be compelled, that is, shown by the facts themselves, to be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, Heb. 5.10; so the apostles, with sacred oil coming down from the head of Aaron in heaven onto his beard and the fringes of his long robe, Ps. 133.2, and themselves having the anointing [χρῖσμα] from that Holy One, 1 John 2.20, had to be anointed with the Holy Spirit by their head, Christ, so that they might be made equal to the arduous office they had to discharge. This same anointing of the apostles also comes under the name of baptism with the Holy Spirit: John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now, Acts 1.5. That baptism was not of water but of wind, just as the anointing that came soon afterwards at Pentecost took place, when the apostles were most abundantly drenched with the oil of the Holy Spirit; and the house in which these things were done was so filled with the Holy Spirit that the apostles seem to have been plunged into it as into a kind of covering. Just as the type that went before was fulfilled, after the Passover and the festival that followed it, by the resurrection of Christ early on the day of the sun, so also the consecration of these first-fruits of the Christian Church, whom Christ himself calls the excellent ones [אדירי], the princes in whom is the delight of God, Ps. 16.3, had to proceed at Pentecost, with the inflaming by heavenly fire. For not without weighty reason were the Jews commanded to count the weeks and days so anxiously up to the offering of the first-fruits.

units.la: XCI. Hoc ergo Pentecostes festo cum unâ concordes adessent, ἅπαντες omnes sive Apostoli, uti Codices quidam diserte legunt, ἅπαντες Ἀπόστολοι omnes Apostoli; sive, quod Camerario aliisque videtur, cæteri quoque discipuli cum illis collecti, quod tum ex Act. I. 15. ubi discipuli Petro concinante collecti turba capitum quasi centum viginti dicuntur: tum ex eo, quòd ἅπαντες illi, non solos Apostolos, sed inaugurationi eorum præsentes discipulos alios, qui unctionem & Baptismum hunc expectabant, notare videntur: tum quia demum v. 14. Petri & undecim diserta mentio fit, cùm ante ἅπαντες omnes generaliter dicti fuerint: tum quia etiam super alios, velut Centurionem, æquè ac super Apostolos & fratres ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ in principio Spiritus S. lapsus, Act. XI. 15. coll. cum v. 1. dicitur; colligi posse videtur, facto repente sonitu ex cœlo, tanquam ruentis flatus violenti, domum totam, in qua considebant, concutiente, visæ sunt linguæ dispertitæ, instar ignis, super unoquoque eorum consistentes; atque ita omnes ἐπλήσθησαν Πνεύματος ἁγίου, repleti sunt Spiritu S. καὶ coeperunt ἑτέραις γλώσσαις aliis linguis ad Judæos proselytosque, qui ex omni terrarum orbe isthuc festum agituri confluxerunt, loqui, prout Spiritus iis dabat; τὰ μεγαλεῖα Θεοῦ magnalia, magnifica Dei opera effari, Act. II. 1-12. Nam quòd Erasmus miraculum illustre adeò non in Apostolis, quippe sua lingua locutis, sed in auditoribus Apostolorum dicta, perinde ac si suam quisque linguam audivisset, intelligentibus contigisse asserit, ratione, nisi fallor, omni destituitur; quia sic non Apostoli, sed eorum auditores Spiritu S. baptizati fuissent. Neque etiam satis dignitati miraculi consulunt, qui cum III. Salmasio ejus fructum, πολυγλωττίαν, plurium linguarum notitiam & usum in Apostolis, sic Spiritu S. afflatis, non ultra diem illum, quo Judæis & Proselytis coram in linguas varias ora sua resolverunt; duravisse statuunt. Nam linguarum variarum notitia iis in orbem terrarum profecturis aprime necessaria fuit. Cumque credentes plures χαρίσματα γλωσσῶν linguarum donum habuisse ex Marc. XVI. 17. 1. Cor. XII. 10. XIV. 2. &c; constet; quin & S. Paulus discipulis Ephesiis per impositionem manuum Spiritum S. sic contulerit, ut statim illi linguis loquerentur, Act. XIX. 6. ne quid vel Dodonæis oraculis, quæ unicuique secundum nativam linguæ suæ proprietatem responsa dedisse, Mythici ferunt; vel Apollonio alicui Thyaneo, quem linguarum omnium callentem fuisse, licet nullam didicerit, Philostratus, Christo & Apostolis eundem, uti alibi diximus, opponens, Apoll. vita I. I. 13. finxit; tribueretur dubitare non licet, quin & ipsis collatum in Pentecoste linguarum donum usque perseveraverit. Hæc ergo Spiritus S. effusio tam evidentibus signis & effectibus illustris initiatio illa effusionis Spiritus S. in Ecclesiam N. T. fuit, quæ Joel. II. 28. promissa est. Non enim quod promissum ibi est, secundum omnem mensuram impletum est in Apostolis aliisque, qui die Pentecostes unâ erant. Nam in N. T. omni tempore, omnibusque credentibus promissio Spiritus datur, Gal. III. 14. Sed ut hoc donum ad Ecclesiam perveniret, initiò Spiritum S. in Apostolos & Evangelistas copiosissimè effundi oportuit, ut per eos verbum Dei in mundo uberrimo modo extaret, tandemque tota terra cognitione Dei impleretur, sicut mare plenum est aquis, Esaj. XI. 9. Atque licet etiam mirabile illud fuerit, quòd ignea linguæ flammæ, & quasi faces in Apostolis sic visæ sunt, tamen illud longè mirabilius fuit, quòd de mysterio & μεγαλείως Dei rectè & cordatè loqui, & quæ prudenter cogitarunt: tot linguis eloqui potuerunt, docente illos Spiritu Dei non tantùm quid loqui deberent; sed etiam signa per internum magisterium suppeditante, quibus apud diversarum terrarum incolas diversis juxta cujusque captum uterentur. Aderant enim ab Oriente Parthi, Medi, Elamitæ, seu Persæ, Mesopotami, Judæi: à Septentrione Cappadoces, Ponti, Asiæ; Phrygiæ, Pamphyliæ: à Meridie, Ægyptii, Cyrenæi: ab Occidente Romani Cretenses: inter Orientem & Meridiem Meridiem siti Arabes. Quod igitur tot gentium & plagarum mundi incolis coram geitum est, fama celebrari, & in totius mundi notitiam pervenire facile potuit. Quin & ipsa Apostolorum & Evangelistarum scripta fidem faciunt, eos revera Spiritu Dei imbutos fuisse, & efficacia Spiritus S. in iis & per eos operantis inde manifesta est, quod per praeconium eorum Christus in mundo creditus est. Neque in apparatu eorum alia defuerunt charismata, quae ipsos & in se ipsis ornarent, & apud omnes admirabile ipsorum ministerium redderent.
units.tr: XCI. So when they were all together in one place on this feast of Pentecost, all [ἅπαντες]: either the apostles, as certain codices plainly read, all apostles [ἅπαντες Ἀπόστολοι]; or, as Camerarius and others think, the other disciples gathered with them too. This is suggested by Acts 1.15, where the disciples gathered together at Peter's speech are said to be a crowd of about one hundred and twenty persons; by the fact that the word all seems to refer not to the apostles alone but to the other disciples present at their inauguration, who were waiting for this anointing and baptism; and by the fact that the explicit mention of Peter and the eleven comes only at verse 14, whereas all was said in general before. It also seems that it can be gathered from Acts 11.15, compared with verse 1, that the Holy Spirit fell upon others too, such as the centurion, just as upon the apostles and brethren, in the same way [ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ] at the beginning. Accordingly, a sudden sound came from heaven, as of a rushing violent wind, filling the whole house in which they were sitting; and there appeared to them tongues divided, like fire, resting upon each one of them; and so they were all filled with the Holy Spirit [ἐπλήσθησαν Πνεύματος ἁγίου] and began to speak with other tongues [ἑτέραις γλώσσαις] to the Jews and proselytes who had come together from every part of the world to keep that feast, speaking as the Spirit gave them utterance, and to proclaim the mighty works of God [τὰ μεγαλεῖα Θεοῦ], Acts 2.1–12. For the view of Erasmus, that this illustrious miracle happened not in the apostles, who spoke in their own tongue, but in their hearers, who each heard what was said as though in his own language, is, unless I am mistaken, wholly without reason; for then it would have been not the apostles but their hearers who were baptized with the Spirit. Nor do those who, with Salmasius, claim that the fruit of this, the gift of many tongues, a knowledge and use of several languages in the apostles so inspired by the Spirit, did not last beyond that day, when they opened their mouths in various languages before the Jews and proselytes, do justice to the dignity of the miracle. For knowledge of various languages was most necessary for those who were to go out into the world. And since it is established that believers had the gift of tongues [χαρίσματα γλωσσῶν], Mark 16.17; 1 Cor. 12.10; 14.2, and indeed St Paul conferred the Holy Spirit on the Ephesian disciples by the laying on of hands so that at once they spoke with tongues, Acts 19.6, we cannot doubt that the gift of tongues conferred on Christ and the apostles at Pentecost continued to persevere. Nothing should be attributed to the Dodonaean oracles, which the mythical tales say gave answers to each person according to the native character of his own language, nor to that Apollonius of Tyana, who, although he learned no language, is said by Philostratus to have been skilled in all languages, Philostratus setting him up, as I have said elsewhere, against Christ and the apostles, Apoll. vita I.1.13. This outpouring of the Holy Spirit, illustrious for such evident signs and effects, was therefore that initiation into the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Church of the New Testament which was promised in Joel 2.28. For what was promised there was not fulfilled in full measure in the apostles and the others who were together on the day of Pentecost. For in the New Testament, at all times and to all believers, the promise of the Spirit is given, Gal. 3.14. But for this gift to reach the Church, the Holy Spirit had first to be poured out most abundantly upon the apostles and evangelists, so that through them the word of God might stand forth in the world in the most abundant manner, and at last the whole earth be filled with the knowledge of God, as the sea is full of waters, Isa. 11.9. And although that marvel was great, that tongues of fire and what seemed like torches appeared over the apostles, it was far more wonderful that they could speak rightly and wisely of the mystery and magnalia of God, and could utter in so many tongues what they had prudently considered, the Spirit of God teaching them not only what they ought to say but also supplying them, through inner instruction, with the signs by which they might use various forms of speech according to each hearer's capacity among the inhabitants of various lands. For there were present, from the East, Parthians, Medes, Elamites, that is Persians, Mesopotamians, Jews; from the North, Cappadocians, people of Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia; from the South, Egyptians, Cyrenians; from the West, Romans and Cretans; and between East and South, the Arabs, who lie to the south. What was done thus before inhabitants of so many nations and regions of the world could easily be made known by report and come to the knowledge of the whole world. Indeed, the very writings of the apostles and evangelists bear witness that they were truly imbued with the Spirit of God, and the efficacy of the Holy Spirit working in them and through them is manifest from the fact that, through their preaching, Christ came to be believed in the world. Nor were there lacking among them other gifts, which both adorned them personally and made their ministry admirable to all.

units.la: XCII. Non paucae igitur, nec contemnendae sic unctorum & baptizatorum Spiritu S. Apostolorum praerogativae, & privilegia fuerunt. Ante omnia enim a Christo immediate vocati & missi Testes αὐτόπται ἢ αὐτήκοοι dictorum & factorum, inprimis mortis & Resurrectionis Christi, & Praecones Doctoresque Evangelii ex Scripturis Propheticis, earumque impletione per Christum demonstrandi universales in toto terrarum Orbe evaserunt, quo de supra diximus. Utque munere suo cum successu defungi possent, ex immediata Christi & Spiritus S. revelatione cognitionem Evangelii & mysteriorum saltitis hauserunt. Cum haec dixisset Christus, afflavit eos, & dixit iis: Accipite Spiritum S. qui videlicet vobiscum sit, vos vivificet, illuminet, roboret, regat, tueatur, & conservet, Joh. XX. 22. Cum venerit Spiritus ille veritatis; ducet vos in omnem veritatem, & futura vobis renuntiabit, ibid. XVI. 13, Quae promissio sic πτωτως & ἐξόχως ad Apostolos, in totum mundum ad praedicandum Evangelium omni creaturae, ut ad omnes id pervenirent, & in omne tempus manet, mittendos, pertinet; ut tamen suo illuminationis gradu ad omnes etiam fideles pertineat, cum illorum nemo non cognoscat fundamentum fidei, & teneat sermonem Dei, ex quo discere & proficere indies paratus sit. Ideo S. Paulus: Non ab homine, inquit, accepi Evangelium, sed per revelationem Jesu Christi, Gal. I. 12, ut ita constet, revelationem Jesu Christi non esse revelationem hominis & qua hominis, cui Jesus Christus opponitur, sed Dei. Secundum revelationem notificavit mihi mysterium, Ephes. III. 3. Haec illa δύναμις Virtus est, qua ex alto induti sunt, Luc. XXIV. 49. quod a Spiritu Dei sic docti ductique Evangelium recte & cum ἀπόδειξιν Πνεύματος demonstratione Spiritus, virtutibus & prodigiis, & eloquio claro apud gentes praedicare potuerunt, revelationem atque Divinam inspirationem eorundem ἀναμαρτησία & in praeconio obeundo infallibilitas doctrinae consequebatur. Quae ipsis non minus quam Prophetis Θεοπνεύστοις Veteris Ecclesiae adfuit. Ille Spiritus vos docebit omnia, & faciet vos meminisse omnium, quae dixi vobis, Joh. XIV. 26. ducet vos in omnem veritatem, XVI. 13. Licet enim ante effusionem in eos Spiritus S. parcior eorum, ceu tyronum adhuc in Schola Christi, notitia fuerit, nec simplex subinde haesitatio & πτοησις praecipitantia, trepidatio, fuga, Psal. XXXI. 23. CXVI. 11. eos corripuerit, ut ex Matth. XVI. 22, XX. 24. Luc. XVIII. 34. colligere est; imo & Petrus Christum abnegaverit, & eundem Judas prodiderit: tamen nec in prima eorum ad Israelem ζύμη fermentum opinionum errorum praedicationi suae admiscuerunt, Christo iis promittente: Dabitur vobis in hora illa, quid loquamini. Non enim vos estis loquentes, sed Spiritus Patris vestri, loquens in vobis, Matth. X. 19. 20. Luc. XII. 12. & post mortem Christi & effusum in eos Spiritum S. publice docentes, & Evangelium praedicantes, vel scribentes nullo amplius errore pallere, vel a veri tramite seduci potuerunt. Eorum enim verbum lucerna fuit, quae in veritatem, non in errorem duxit. Alia nihilominus praeconii eorum publici & scriptionis: alia privae conversationis fuit. In illo errare, ob Spiritus S. φοβεῖν & dictamen non potuerunt: in hoc potuerunt. Uti S. Petri, qui columna cum esset, aliquando arundo factus est, non recto pede incedens juxta veritatem Evangelii, eoque etiam a S. Paulo κατηγορημένος damnandus, Gal. II. 11. 14. cum & ipse Petrus se a gentilibus subducens, ne cum iis vesci videretur, factum suum antea damnaverit, dicens: Quid tentatis Deum, cervici discipulorum jugum imponentes? Act. XV. 10. & factum hoc tum proprium Petri peccatum, tum alieni peccati illecebra fuerit. Opinionem enim necessitatis abstinendi a certis cibis si non imperio, saltem exemplo, uti S. Augustinus loquitur, docuit. Et illa ipsa Paulum inter & Petrum contentio praeconii Petri publici, vel scriptionis etiam infallibilitatem non concussit, tum quia contentionis illius finis conservatio illibatae veritatis, cui Petrus monitus ultro cessit, fuit: adeoque omnis illa tempestas sine Ecclesiae noxa detonuit: tum quia idem Petrus nec in fidei doctrina, nec in dogmate ullo erravit, nec erravit Evangelium vel praedicando, vel literis consignando, sed in sola conversatione aliquid humanitus passus est. Praedicatio porro & conscriptio Evangelii ex Divina inspiratione: Conversatio, actiones & mores eorundem ex modo & mensura regenerationis pendebant. Inspiratio perfecta, regeneratio imperfecta fuit. Inspirati ergo & illuminati Divinitus perfecte errare non potuerunt: at regeniti in hac vita imperfecte peccare potuerunt. Habemus thesaurum in vasis testaceis, ut excellentia potentiae sit Dei, & non ex nobis, 2. Cor. IV. 7. At de caetero nec absoluta, nec ἀνυπεύθυνος Apostolorum infallibilitas fuit. Nam & ipsorum doctrina non praetoria authoritate, sed Spiritus demonstratione nixa, examini subjecta fuit. Nam & S. Paulus habuit ἀναχεῖρονος examinantes: nec ἀνάκρισιν examen recusavit, sed ἀπολογία usus est. Apologia haec mea examinantibus me est, 1. Cor. IX. 3. Idem: Tanquam prudentibus loquor: Judicate, quod dico ibid. X. 15. Ne scilicet putemus, cuiquam Mortalium authoritatem & ἀνυπεύθυνον ad dicendum aliquid ἀξιοπιστίας competere, quod Papae Apostolicam authoritatem & successionem mentitus prae se fert. Accedit, quod Spiritus S. ductus Apostolis per gradus & partes accessit, prout Ecclesiae tempora id suadebant. Unde etiam post Pentecosten nonnisi idoneo exacto spatio de Gentium vocatione & rituum abolitione Act. X. XV. moniti sunt.
units.tr: XCII. The prerogatives and privileges of the Apostles, anointed and baptized with the Holy Spirit, were therefore not few, nor to be despised. First of all, they were called and sent immediately by Christ as witnesses [αὐτόπται or αὐτήκοοι] of the things said and done, above all of the death and resurrection of Christ, and as preachers and teachers of the Gospel, able to demonstrate from the prophetic Scriptures and their fulfilment in Christ, universally throughout the whole world, as we said above. So that they could discharge their office successfully, they drew their knowledge of the Gospel and of the mysteries of salvation from the immediate revelation of Christ and the Holy Spirit. When he had said these things, Christus breathed on them and said to them: Receive the Holy Spirit, who is with you indeed, to quicken, enlighten, strengthen, rule, protect and preserve you, John 20:22. When that Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth and will declare to you things to come, ibid. 16:13. This promise pertains in the fullest and most eminent way to the Apostles, who were sent to preach the Gospel to every creature, so that it might reach everyone, and it remains for all time. Yet it pertains also to all the faithful, according to each one's degree of illumination, since none of them is ignorant of the foundation of faith, and holds the word of God, from which he is ready to learn and to make progress daily. Therefore St Paul says: I received the Gospel not from man, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ, Gal. 1:12, so that it is established that the revelation of Jesus Christ is not a revelation of man, or from man, to which Jesus Christ is opposed, but of God. By revelation he made known to me the mystery, Eph. 3:3. This is that power [δύναμις] by which they were endued from on high, Luke 24:49, so that, taught and led by the Spirit of God, they could rightly preach the Gospel with the demonstration of the Spirit [ἀπόδειξις Πνεύματος], with virtues, prodigies and clear speech among the nations. From their revelation and divine inspiration followed their freedom from error [ἀναμαρτησία], and in discharging their preaching the infallibility of their teaching. This was present to them no less than to the Prophets [Θεοπνεύστοι] of the Old Church, who were inspired by God. That Spirit will teach you all things, and will make you remember all that I have said to you, John 14:26; he will lead you into all truth, 16:13. For although before the outpouring of the Holy Spirit their knowledge was rather meagre, as befits novices still in the school of Christ, and not only simple hesitation but panic, rashness, trembling and flight troubled them, Ps. 31:23; 116:11, as may be gathered from Matt. 16:22; 20:24; Luke 18:34; indeed Peter denied Christ and Judas betrayed him. Nevertheless, in their first preaching to Israel they did not mix the leaven [ζύμη] of erroneous opinions into their proclamation, Christ promising them: It will be given you in that hour what you shall say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you, Matt. 10:19–20; Luke 12:12. And after Christ's death, and once the Holy Spirit had been poured out upon them, they could no longer fall into any error, nor be seduced from the path of truth, when teaching publicly, preaching the Gospel, or writing. For their word was a lamp that led into truth, not into error. Nevertheless, their public preaching and writing was one thing, their private conversation another. In the former they could not err, because of the fear [φόβος] of the Holy Spirit and his dictation; in the latter they could. Thus Peter, who was a pillar, at one time became a reed, not walking straightly according to the truth of the Gospel, and so was to be condemned by St Paul as one accused, Gal. 2:11, 14, since Peter himself, withdrawing from the Gentiles lest he seem to eat with them, had previously condemned his own act, saying: Why do you tempt God by placing a yoke on the necks of the disciples? Acts 15:10. That deed was both Peter's own sin and an enticement to another's sin, for he taught, if not by command at least by example, as St Augustine puts it, the opinion that it was necessary to abstain from certain foods. Nor did that very contention between Paul and Peter shake the infallibility of Peter's public preaching or writing. This was so, first, because the purpose of that contention was the preservation of the unimpaired truth, to which Peter, when warned, willingly yielded; and so that whole storm thundered without harm to the Church. And second, because Peter erred neither in the doctrine of faith nor in any dogma, and the Gospel erred neither in his preaching nor in his writing; he suffered something merely human only in his conduct. Moreover, the preaching and writing of the Gospel came from divine inspiration, while their conduct, actions and morals depended on the measure and degree of their regeneration. Inspiration was perfect; regeneration was imperfect. Those inspired and illuminated by God could therefore not err completely, but the regenerate in this life can sin imperfectly. We have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us, 2 Cor. 4:7. Otherwise, however, the infallibility of the Apostles was neither absolute nor free from accountability. For their teaching too rested not on imperious authority but on the demonstration of the Spirit, and was subject to examination. St Paul himself had examiners [ἀνακρίνοντες], and he did not refuse examination [ἀνάκρισις] but made use of a defence [ἀπολογία]. This is my defence to those who examine me, 1 Cor. 9:3. Likewise: I speak as to wise men; judge what I say, ibid. 10:15. We should certainly not suppose that any mortal has an authority, and an unaccountable [ἀνυπεύθυνον] claim to be believed when speaking, such as the Pope falsely claims for himself, pretending apostolic authority and succession. Moreover, the Spirit led the Apostles gradually and in parts, as the times of the Church suggested. Hence even after Pentecost they were admonished about the calling of the Gentiles and the abolition of the rites only after a suitable interval, Acts 10, 15.

units.la: XCIII. Fuerunt & alia Apostolorum ἀπλεονεξίαι κτήματα & Privilegia accessoria, velut, quod illis claves Regni Coelorum, & potestas remittendi & retinendi peccata, nec non solvendi & ligandi singulari modo, & proprio ac genuino, reliquis Ecclesiae Ministris inclinato sensu concessae sunt, Matth. XVI.
units.tr: XCIII. The Apostles also had other additional gifts and privileges, such as that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to them, together with the power of remitting and retaining sins, and of loosing and binding in a singular way, in their own and genuine sense, which is denied to the other ministers of the Church, Matt. 16.

units.la: Apostolorum principale privilegium fuit, quod Testes & Praecones Resurrectionis Christi, atque universales & infallibiles Evangelii Praecones & Doctores exstiterunt.
units.tr: The chief privilege of the Apostles was that they were the witnesses and heralds of Christ's resurrection, and the universal and infallible preachers and teachers of the Gospel.

units.la: Eorundem Privilegia & praerogativae accessoria alia. Matth. XVI. 19. XVIII. 18. Joh. XX. 23. Act. II. 41. X. 44. XV. 7. quòd per impositionem manuum Spiritum S. aliis etiam largissimè contulerunt; ibid. VIII. 6--19. XIX. 6. quod nec Mosi, nec Veterum cuiquam datum est: quòd signa etiam in poenam infidelium, vel fidelium, ut spiritus eorum per corporum afflictationem salvaretur, patrarunt, cum virga sua Apostolica venientes, 1. Cor. IV. 21. severitate secundum potestatem à Domino datam utentes, 2. Cor. XIII. 10. Sathanæ quosdam tradentes, ad perniciem carnis, ut Spiritus servetur in die Domini Jesu, 1. Cor. V. 3. 5. qua potestate non pro lubitu, nec ad destructionem, sed ex sapientissimo Dei consilio, & ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ usi sunt: quod prædicatio illorum, utpote præsentem semper Spiritum oltendens, miram efficaciam exeruit, uti vel solâ Petri concio; ex qua Ecclesia uno die incrementum ter mille animarum cepit; Act. II. 41: quod nulli affixi loco, certò licet affixi Canoni, seu lineæ prædicationis, à Deo ipsis assignatæ (2. Cor. X. 13-16.) ut sicut testificatio habuit propria sua tempora, ita etiam locis propriis, non angustum illum & concisum, sed augustiorem & latiorem districtum habentibus distinguerentur; communes Ecclesiæ doctores constituti sunt: quòd denique circumacto præconii sui orbe, sic statione sua decesserunt, ut ἀπόστολοι plane fuerint, neque cuiquam in munere proprie Apostolico lampada tradere potuerint. Ex quibus Apostolici muneris supra omnia alia excellentia abundè cognoscitur. Ut merito de illis explicentur illa Solomonis: Egredimini, & spectate, Filiæ Sionis, Regem Solomonem (Christum) בעטרה cum corona; qua coronavit eum mater ejus in die sponsalium, & in die lætitiæ cordis ejus, Cant. III. 11. Verè enim & ante alios omnes Christi corona fuerunt Apostoli, qui verbum ejus locuti, & pro ipso passi sunt, & Christo, ceu sponso fuerunt להתנאר ad ornandum, Esaj. LX. 21. impositia ei à matre Sponsi, Patribus & populo electo V. T. ex quibus est secundum carnem, & qui ipsum spe & exspectatione pepererunt. Quibus etiam specialis illa promissio facta est, fore, ut in παλιγγενεσία sedeant super duodecim thronis, judicantes duodecim tribus Israelis, Matth. XIX. 28. Luc. XXII. 29. 30. quia tum in ea regeneratione, qua Cælum novum & terra nova, in qua justitia habitet, fieri debuit, 2. Pet. III. 13. in thronis sedebunt, doctrina sua & præconio omni Ecclesiam judicaturi, singulari illo jure; licet & fidelibus omnibus judicium hoc competat, quatenus idem cum Apostolis loquuntur: tum in altera vita doctrinæ; quam hic prædicarunt, suffragio Christi judicis sententiam confirmabunt. Quæ maxima eorum dignitas est.
units.tr: Their other privileges and accessory prerogatives were these. (1) They conferred the Holy Spirit very abundantly on others also by the laying on of hands, Matt. 16:19; 18:18; John 20:23; Acts 2:41; 10:44; 15:7; 8:6–19; 19:6, which was not given to Moses or to any of the ancients. (2) They also worked signs for the punishment of unbelievers or even of believers, so that their spirit might be saved through affliction of the body. They came with their apostolic rod, 1 Cor. 4:21, using severity according to the power given them by the Lord, 2 Cor. 13:10, delivering certain persons to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus, 1 Cor. 5:3, 5. They used this power not at their pleasure, nor for destruction, but according to the most wise counsel of God and for the edification of the Church. (3) Their preaching, showing the Spirit always present, exerted a wonderful efficacy, as Peter's sermon alone shows, by which the Church gained three thousand souls in one day, Acts 2:41. (4) Though fixed to no place, they were certainly fixed to the canon or line of preaching assigned to them by God (2 Cor. 10:13–16); so that just as their witness had its own times, so too they were distinguished by their own places, not a narrow and cramped district but a wider and broader one. (5) They were appointed as common teachers of the Church. (6) Finally, having completed the circuit of their preaching, they died at their post, so that they were truly apostles, and could hand on the torch to no one in the proper apostolic office. From these facts the excellence of the apostolic office above all others is abundantly clear. Hence rightly are those words of Solomon explained of them: Go forth and behold, daughters of Zion, King Solomon (Christ) with the crown [בעטרה], with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousals, and on the day of the joy of his heart, Song 3:11. For truly, before all others, the Apostles were Christ's crown: they spoke his word and suffered for him, and were to Christ, as to the bridegroom, for adornment [להתנאר], Isa. 60:21, placed on him by the mother of the Bridegroom, namely the Fathers and the chosen people of the Old Testament, from whom he came according to the flesh, and who bore him by hope and expectation. To them also that special promise was made, that in the regeneration [παλιγγενεσία] they would sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel, Matt. 19:28; Luke 22:29–30. For in that regeneration, in which a new heaven and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells, must come about, 2 Pet. 3:13, they will sit on thrones, judging the whole Church by their doctrine and preaching, by a singular right; although this judgment also belongs to all the faithful, insofar as they speak the same things as the Apostles. And in the other life, by the vote of Christ the Judge, they will confirm the sentence of the doctrine that they preached here. This is their greatest dignity.

units.la: XCIV. Habuerunt Apostoli præter doctrinam etiam Σημεῖα τ' Ἀποστόλων Signa Apostolorum, hoc est, argumenta, ex quibus ceu inso-lentioribus, Divina eorum ad prædicandum Evangelium missio comprobari potuit. Signa Apostoli in nobis patrata sunt, ἐν πάσῃ ὑπομονῇ, ἐν σημείοις καὶ τέρασι καὶ δυνάμεσιν in omni patientia, in signis & prodigiis & virtutibus, 2. Cor. XII. 12. Nam salus Domini cœpta dici ab iis, qui audiverunt, in nos confirmata est; unà testificante Deo signis & prodigiis & multiformis virtutibus &
units.tr: XCIV. Besides their doctrine, the Apostles also had the signs of the Apostles [Σημεῖα τ' Ἀποστόλων], that is, arguments by which their divine mission to preach the Gospel could be proved, as it were by means of unusual occurrences. The signs of an Apostle have been wrought among us [ἐν πάσῃ ὑπομονῇ, ἐν σημείοις καὶ τέρασι καὶ δυνάμεσιν], in all patience, in signs and wonders and mighty deeds, 2 Cor. 12.12. For the salvation of the Lord, which was first spoken by those who heard it, was confirmed to us, God also bearing witness with signs and wonders and various mighty deeds and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will, Heb. 2.3, 4.

units.la: distributionibus Spiritus S. secundum voluntatem ejus; Hebr. II. 3. 4. Potissimum equidem Apostolatus signum est doctrina: ut sine quo-noni Si quis voluerit facere voluntatem ejus, qui me misit, cognoscet de doctrina, utrum ea ex Deo sit, an ego ex me ipso loquar, Joh. VII. 17. Potest tamen doctrinam veritatis habere, qui non est Apostolus. Signa ergo Apostoli necessaria fuerunt, ex quibus de eorum ad prædicandum Evangelium missione liqueret; ut eorum verbum acciperetur tanquam verbum Dei, non minus quàm Verbum Mosis. Si enim Christus ipse ita venit; ut haberet testimonium à Deo, & per verbum ipsius, & per opera, quæ fecit, ibid. X. 25. 38. XIV. 10. 11: etiam Apostoli; per quos Christus loqui voluit ad populum & ad gentes; non tantùm demonstratione ex verbo; sed etiam aliis signis cognosci debuerunt; ita ut etiam pueri dubitare non possent, se ab illis veritatem discere posse. Quod Christus ipse per Esajam prædixit, dicens: Ecce ego & pueri, quos dedit mihi Jehova, in signa & prodigia, in Israele à Jehova Deo exercituum, qui habitat in monte Sion, Esaj. VIII. 18. Signa illa Apostolus, Patientiam, Prodigia & Virtutes ponit. Patientiam, quia tot persecutiones, plagæ, carceres, ærumnæ, labores, supplicia, quæ animo intrepido, volentes gestientesque adiverunt, certissima signa & ἐνέργειαι fuerunt, non sine missione, institutione & impulsu illos ad Evangelii præconium profectos esse, utpote qui timere haberent illud Οὐαί Ψε, nisi prædicarent, 1. Cor. IX. 16. Prodigia, in quibus evidens majoris potestatis demonstratio fuit. Denique Virtutes seu גבורות Potentiæ, Divinæ quippe potentiæ effecta. In quibus etiam μεγίσματα & Πνεύματος distributiones Spiritus, qui Spiritus est fidei, timoris & charismatum ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem facientium, per quæ salus per Christum parta stabilitur & solidatur; ut per ea efficax sit, inter quæ donum linguarum cum παρρησία & eloquentia ad magnos & parvos erudiendos accommodatissima, miraculum omni exceptione majus est. Tum vertam ad populum linguam claram, ut omnes nominent nomen Domini, & serviant ipsi humero uno, Zophon. III. 9. Ne quid dicam de sapientia illa, quam piscatores locuti sunt; de manifestatione veritatis ad conscientiam, Prophetia, Scripturarum & mysteriorum notitia, per quæ sicut salutem docuerunt, & legem Christi in conspectu omnium ita posuerunt, ut per eos Christus lux gentium fieret, & oculos cæcorum aperiret: ita illa salutis factæ maxima operatio fuerunt.
units.tr: Chiefly, indeed, the doctrine itself is the sign of the apostleship, as in the words: If anyone is willing to do the will of him who sent me, he will know concerning the doctrine whether it is from God or whether I speak from myself, John 7.17. Yet one who is not an Apostle may hold the doctrine of truth. Therefore the signs of the Apostles were necessary, by which it might be made clear that they had been sent to preach the Gospel, so that their word would be received as the word of God, no less than the word of Moses. For if Christ himself came in such a way that he had testimony from God both through his word and through the works he did (ibid. 10.25, 38; 14.10, 11), then the Apostles also, through whom Christ willed to speak to the people and the nations, had to be recognised not only by the demonstration from the word but also by other signs, so that even children could not doubt that they could learn the truth from them. Christ himself foretold this through Isaiah, saying: Behold, I and the children whom Jehovah has given me are for signs and wonders in Israel from Jehovah, God of hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion, Isa. 8.18. The Apostle names these signs as patience, wonders and powers. Patience, because the many persecutions, blows, prisons, hardships, labours and tortures which they endured with fearless spirit and eager willingness were most certain signs and workings that they had set out to proclaim the Gospel not without being sent, instructed and impelled, since they had reason to fear that woe [Οὐαί μοι], if they did not preach, 1 Cor. 9.16. Wonders, in which there was clear demonstration of greater power. Finally, powers, or gebhuroth [גבורות], that is, mighty deeds, which are effects of divine power indeed. Among these are also the miracles and the distributions of the Spirit, which is the Spirit of faith, of fear, and of gifts serving the building up of the Church, through which the salvation obtained through Christ is established and strengthened; and through these is effective the gift of tongues, together with boldness and eloquence most suited to instructing great and small, a miracle surpassing every objection. Then I will turn to the peoples a clear language, that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him with one shoulder, Zeph. 3.9. Not to mention that wisdom which the fishermen spoke, the manifestation of truth to conscience, the knowledge of prophecy, of the Scriptures and of mysteries, by which, as they taught salvation and set the law of Christ before the eyes of all, so that through them Christ became the light of the nations and opened the eyes of the blind; these were the greatest workings of the salvation accomplished.

units.la: XCV. Non necesse est commemorare Signa & Prodigia & opera, quæ Christus per Apostolos fecit. Quæ magna certè, imò perinde ut aliorum credentium majora etiam fuerunt illis, quæ Christus sine iis fecit. Amen amen dico vobis; Qui credit in me, opera quæ ego facio, & ille faciet, & his μείζονα majora faciet, quia ego ad Patrem proficiscor; & quod petiveritis in nomine meo, hoc faciam, ut glorificetur Pater in Filio. Joh. XIV. 12. Pater dedit Filio, quæ in Regno suo faceret, opera. Eadem facienda daturus erat Filius credentibus in ipsum, hoc est, sic ipse facturus erat, ut fierent ad verbum credentium, & nomen Christi, qui ea facturus erat, nominanum. Quæ sic per credentes, adeòque etiam
units.tr: XCV. It is not necessary to recount the signs, wonders and works which Christ did through the Apostles. These were certainly great, indeed just as the greater works of other believers were greater than those which Christ did without them. Truly, truly I say to you, he who believes in me, the works which I do he also will do, and he will do greater works [μείζονα], because I go to the Father; and whatever you ask in my name, that I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son, John 14.12, 13. The Father gave the Son works to perform in his kingdom. The Son was going to give the same works to those who believe in him; that is, he himself was going to act so that they came about at the word of believers, and the name of Christ, who was going to do them, would be invoked. Works done in this way through believers, and so also...

units.la: {a} Christus per eos opera majora fecit illis, quæ virtus patravit, cadem veri non minus mirabilia, ad attestandum veritatis, non ad tantum comparata. etiam Apostolos in Regno suo facturus erat, μείζονα majora præsentibus appellat, non quòd vel major potentia Apostolorum futura sit, vel non eadem, qua miracula ante mortem edidit, potentia per Apostolos illa facturus fuerit, sed quia & plura illa futura, & majorem effectum habitura erant. Tale est, dicere monti alicui: Μετάβηθι ἐντεῦθεν ἐκεῖ. Tollere hinc & tolletur; Nihil vobis impossibile erit, &c. Matth. XVII. 20. Nam hoc per allegoriam tantundem est, ac si diceretur, fore, ut juxta fidem Ecclesiæ, & fidelium prædictionem, maxima imperia, quæ montium instar sunt, Christo cedant, atque sic in planitiem abeant. Sicut Babylon, mons magnus, coram Zorobabele redactus est in planitiem, Zach. IV. 7. Taceo ἀνάστασιν, resuscitationem mortuorum. Ipsæ Apostolorum prædictiones de Judæorum induratione & exitio, Ecclesiæ persecutione, mutatione imperii, adventu Antichristi ejusque violentia, liberatione Ecclesiæ, & his omnibus similibusque exacte respondens eventus, inter μείζονα majora ejusmodi opera referenda sunt. Cumque Apostoli miracula & signa ejusmodi virtute & authoritate ipsius Christi patraverint, & prædicatio illorum fuerit non tantum ἐν ἀποδείξει δυνάμεως demonstratione potentiæ, seu evidentiæ miraculorum, sed etiam Πνεύματος Spiritus, seu evidente demonstratione Spiritus in ipsis loquentis, facta cum manifestatione veritatis ad conscientiam, 2. Cor. IV. 2. & cum charitate, mansuetudine, patientia, omnique virtute Apostolis digna, 1. Cor. II. 4. 2. Cor. VI. 4–11. & prædictum non sit, exituros seductores in mundum, qui faciant miracula coram gentibus, & illis persuadeant, ut relictis idolis profiteantur se credere in Deum Israelis, & verba Mosis ac Prophetarum, & eum ament, propter donum justitiæ glorificent, & animas suas non vivificent, neque diligant usque ad mortem, Psal. XXII. 30. Apoc. XII. 8. Miracula illa & Divina & veritatis, non mendacii, & ad attestandum doctrinæ; non ad tentandum comparata fuisse, consequitur.
units.tr: {a} Christ, through them, performed works greater than those his power had wrought, works no less wonderful, prepared not merely for ... to attest the truth. Since he was going to do in his kingdom even through the Apostles, he calls them greater [μείζονα] than those which were present, not because the power of the Apostles would be greater, or because the power by which he worked the miracles before his death would not be the same power through which he would do them through the Apostles, but because those works were going to be more numerous and to have a greater effect. Such is the saying to a mountain: Move from here to there [Μετάβηθι ἐντεῦθεν ἐκεῖ]. Remove from here and it will be removed; nothing will be impossible for you, etc., Matt. 17.20. For allegorically this amounts to the same as saying that, according to the faith of the Church and the prediction of the faithful, the greatest empires, which are like mountains, will yield to Christ and so pass away into a plain, just as Babylon, a great mountain, was reduced to a plain before Zerubbabel, Zech. 4.7. I say nothing of the resurrection, the raising of the dead. The Apostles' predictions of the hardening and destruction of the Jews, the persecution of the Church, the change of empire, the coming of Antichrist and his violence, the deliverance of the Church, and the event corresponding exactly to all these and similar things, are to be reckoned among such greater works. And since the Apostles wrought miracles and signs of this kind by the power and authority of Christ himself, and their preaching was not only in demonstration of power [ἐν ἀποδείξει δυνάμεως], that is, in the evident proof of the miracles, but also of the Spirit [Πνεύματος], that is, in the evident demonstration of the Spirit speaking in them, made by the manifestation of truth to conscience, 2 Cor. 4.2, and with love, gentleness, patience, and every virtue worthy of Apostles, 1 Cor. 2.4; 2 Cor. 6.4–11, and since it was not foretold that seducers would go out into the world who would do miracles before the nations and persuade them to abandon idols and profess that they believe in the God of Israel and in the words of Moses and the Prophets, and to love him and glorify him for the gift of righteousness, and they would not give life to their souls, nor love their lives unto death, Ps. 22.30; Rev. 12.8, it follows that those miracles were prepared as divine and true, not lying, and to attest the doctrine, not to test it.

units.la: XCVI. Ad prærogativas Apostolorum hactenus à nobis contextas perperam Hierarchici referunt, quòd à Christo Ecclesiæ Principes ac Domini & S. Petrus quidem, ceu potestate principali ad posteros per successionem propaganda; reliqui verò cum potestate delegata, & in iisdem terminata dati fuerint. Quia in re summam rei Christianæ verti, Bellarminus audacter asserit. Cæterum figmentum illud Papæ: non spirituali certè, sed carnali Regno statumi nando cusum est. Imperium certè & dominium omne Apostolis Christus disertis verbis abdicavit. Nôstis, quòd Principes gentium dominantur illis, & Magnates potestatem in eos exercent, Vos autem non sic. Sed qui inter vos magnus esse voluerit, esto sicut Minister, Matth. XX. 25–26. Quibus verbis Christus dominatione quavis, nullo temporalium & spiritualium discrimine, Apostolis interdixit. Inprimis cum dominatio in spiritualibus longè Divinior sit, quàm quæ in corporalibus exercetur. Nam hæc in corpora, quæ hominibus subesse possunt, illa in conscientias & spiritus, qui soli Patri spirituum subsunt, exerceri potest. Ideo S. Paulus Hoc, inquit, dicô, quòd unusquisque vestrûm dicit: Ego quidem sum Pauli; Ego verò Apollo, ego verò Cephæ, ego verò Christi. Divisus est Christus? An Paulus crucifixus est pro vobis, aut in nomen Pauli baptizati estis? 1. Cor. I. 12, 13. Non dominamur fidei, sed cooperarii sumus lætitiæ vestræ, 2. Cor. I. 24. Missi enim sunt Apostoli, ut testes eorum, quæ viderunt & audiverunt. Et iisdem sic testantibus credendum fuit, quòd talia viderint & audiverint, quia testimonium hoc fingi non potuit, & Deo ac ejus nomine dignum fuit, & juxta prædictionem Divinam succeßit, & in testibus signa missionis Christi, variæque virtutes apparuerunt, & testimonium eorum eventus conveniens & prædictus olim respondit.
units.tr: XCVI. The Hierarchs wrongly refer to the prerogatives of the Apostles, hitherto set out by us, that from Christ the princes and lords of the Church were given, and that Saint Peter indeed was given the principal power to be propagated to posterity by succession, while the others were given a delegated power, terminating in themselves. Bellarmine boldly asserts that the sum of the Christian religion turns on this point. Moreover, that fiction of the Pope was devised for establishing not a spiritual but a carnal kingdom.
