Christ certainly renounced in plain words all rule and dominion for the Apostles: You know that the princes of the nations lord it over them, and the great exercise power over them; but it shall not be so among you. Whoever among you wishes to be great, let him be as a minister, Matt. 20.25, 26. By these words Christ forbade the Apostles every kind of domination, without any distinction between temporal and spiritual matters. Especially since domination in spiritual things is far more divine than that which is exercised over bodily things. For the latter can be exercised over bodies, which can be subject to men, whereas the former can be exercised over consciences and spirits, which alone are subject to the Father of spirits. Therefore Saint Paul says: I say this, that each of you says, "I indeed am of Paul," "I am of Apollos," "I am of Cephas," "I am of Christ." Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptised in the name of Paul? 1 Cor. 1.12, 13. We do not lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers for your joy, 2 Cor. 1.24. For the Apostles were sent as witnesses of what they saw and heard. And they were to be believed as they testified that they had seen and heard such things, because this testimony could not have been invented, was worthy of God and of his name, came to pass according to the divine prediction, and the signs of Christ's mission and various powers appeared in the witnesses, and their testimony was answered by a fitting outcome that had been foretold long before.

units.la: {a} Ad prærogativas Apostolorum perperam Hierarchici dominationem in fide, & quidem in Petro principatem, & ad posteros tradendum, in reliquis delegatam, referunt. Petrus denominatus est; ita ut eadem Petra, Rupes, Christus & Petrum & Ecclesiam sustineat, & nec Petrus sine Ecclesia; nec Ecclesia sine Petro in hac rupe sit. Neque igitur Petrus Rupes est, in qua Ecclesia Dei viventis aedificata est; sed Lapis vivus, cui Ecclesia in Rupe coædificatur, quod magnum satis est; & Petro sufficit: ut sicut Abraham; pater & exemplar credentium priscis temporibus fuit; ita sub Novo Testamento Petrus velut τῶν ἡγεμόνων dux eorum, in quibus est voluptas Dei Psal. XVI. 3: habeatur. Sed eandem in rem plura in loco.
units.tr: Those who call themselves hierarchs wrongly refer to the prerogatives of the Apostles their dominion over faith, and indeed the primacy in Peter, and the handing down of what was entrusted to the rest to their successors. Peter is so named that the same rock, which is Christ, sustains both Peter and the Church, and neither is Peter without the Church, nor the Church without Peter on this rock. Peter, then, is not the Rock on which the Church of the living God was built, but a living stone, with whom the Church is co-built upon the Rock. That is great enough, and it is sufficient for Peter. Just as Abraham was the father and pattern of believers in ancient times, so under the New Testament Peter should be regarded as the leader [τῶν ἡγεμόνων] of them, in whom all my delight is (Ps. 16:3). But more on the same point elsewhere.

units.la: XCVII. Haud adeo probi commatis & illorum hypothesis est; qui Hierarchiae succollaturi cum Hadriano Saravia pertendunt, hodieque Apostolatum in Ecclesia vigere debere; & Apostolis in Apostolatu non equidem Papam solum; sed omnes legitimos Episcopos succedere. Licet enim ministerium praedicandi Evangelium & Sacramenta administrandi, nec non ἐπισκοπὴ inspectio non solius gregis Dominici; sed ipsorum etiam Presbyterorum ab Apostolis ad Episcopos veros & Pastores Ecclesiae omnino transiverit; atque eodem sensu Ecclesia vetus omnes Episcopos Apostolorum successores dixerit, uti ex Irenaeo adv. haer. lib. III. 3. Cypriano Epist. lib. IV. 9. Hieronymo Epist. ad Evagr. liquet; tamen illa Ἀποστολή proprie dicta cum praerogativis & signis Apostolorum, quae tradidimus, conjuncta una cum Apostolis penitus expiravit, ut jam Apostolum resurrectionis Christi à se visi testem, immediatè à Christo vocatum & virtute ex alto indutum, dicere, cui nunquam Christus visus est, & cujus fallibile, nec universale praeconium est, sit dicere Apostolum non Apostolum. Quotusquisque dicere potest: Signa Apostoli in me patrata sunt in omni patientia, in signis, prodigiis & virtutibus? 2. Cor. XII. 12. Officium equidem docendi & baptizandi, Divina vocatio & generalis promissio ad omnes ministros Dei non minus quam ad Apostolos pertinet; sed specialis determinatio de praedicatione Evangelii inter omnes gentes, modus vocationis immediatus & extraordinarius, nec non specialis promissio infallibilitatis & doni miraculorum Apostolis sic eximia fuere, ut nulli alii post eorum tempora congruant. Ita Mosi & Aharoni in ordinariis officii Sacerdotalis & regiminis Politici partibus nonnulli successerunt, at in extraordinariis & temporariis, eductione populi ex Aegypto, promulgatione Legis, fundatione Sacerdotii nemo. Promissio vero illa: Ecce vobiscum omnibus sum usque ad consummationem seculi, Matth. XXVIII. 20. non ad solos equidem Apostolos, sed ad fideles omnium temporum pertinet. Sed dispar ratio est mandati, quo Apostolis profectio in totum mundum imperata est; quam non aeque late patere, atque promissio patet, vel inde constat, quod promissio omnibus fidelibus, mandatum vero illud non omnibus fidelibus datum est, Neque Apostoli dignitatem propriè Apostolicam iis, quos comites & συνεργοὶ asciverunt, communicarunt. Nam etiam Priscilla à Paulo ut συνεργὸς in Christo assumpta est, Rom. XVI. 3; quae tamen Apostolica dignitate nunquam fuisset: & omnes Ecclesiae Ministri Θεοῦ συνεργοὶ Dei cooperarii 1. Cor. III. 9, cluent, cùm tamen solos Episcopos Apostolis successisse Hierarchi-
units.tr: XCVII. The hypothesis of those is not very sound, who, in support of the hierarchy, with Adrian Saravia maintain that the apostolate should still flourish in the Church today, and that not only the Pope but all lawful bishops succeed the Apostles in the apostolate. For although the ministry of preaching the Gospel and administering the sacraments, and also the oversight (episkopē) not only of the Lord's flock but also of the presbyters themselves, has entirely passed from the Apostles to the true bishops and pastors of the Church, and although in the same sense the ancient Church called all bishops successors of the Apostles, as is clear from Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3; Cyprian, Epistles 4.9; and Jerome, Letter to Evagrius; yet that apostleship properly so called, together with the prerogatives and signs of the Apostles which we have set out, has wholly expired along with the Apostles. So to call someone an apostle who was a witness of Christ's resurrection seen by himself, immediately called by Christ and clothed with power from on high, one to whom Christ was never seen, and whose proclamation is fallible and not universal, is to call a non-apostle an apostle. How many can say: "The signs of an apostle were wrought among you in all patience, by signs, wonders and mighty works" (2 Cor. 12:12)? The office of teaching and baptizing, the divine calling and the general promise, pertain no less to all ministers of God than to the Apostles. But the specific charge to preach the Gospel among all nations, the immediate and extraordinary mode of calling, and the special promise of infallibility and the gift of miracles were so singular to the Apostles that they suit no one after their time. Thus some succeeded Moses and Aaron in the ordinary parts of the priestly office and civil government, but in the extraordinary and temporary tasks, leading the people out of Egypt, promulgating the Law, and founding the priesthood, no one did. That promise, "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world" (Matt. 28:20), pertains not to the Apostles alone but to the faithful of all times. But the command by which the Apostles were sent into the whole world is of a different kind. It does not extend as widely as the promise does, and this is clear from the fact that the promise was given to all believers, while that command was not given to all believers. Nor did the Apostles communicate the strictly apostolic dignity to those whom they took as companions and fellow-workers [συνεργοί]. For Priscilla too was taken by Paul as a fellow-worker in Christ (Rom. 16:3), yet she never held apostolic dignity; and all ministers of the Church are called God's fellow-workers [Θεοῦ συνεργοί] (1 Cor. 3:9), while the hierarchs contend that only bishops succeeded the Apostles.

units.la: ci contendant. Evangelistae certè, qui Apostolorum lateri haeserunt, & συνεργοὶ eorum facti sunt; longè infra horum dignitatem subsederunt, cùm etiam Ephes. IV. 11. ab Apostolis proprie dictis distinguantur. Si quando igitur & hi Apostolorum nomine insigniuntur, non Apostoli κατ' ἐξοχὴν, sed minorum gentium intelligi debent. Fuerunt enim Apostolorum Apostoli. Et quantò minùs sequentium temporum Episcopi propter solam ἐπισκοπὴν, quam in gregem Christi, & Presbyteros alios habent; ad culmen Apostolicae dignitatis consurgere putandi sunt? Denique nec illud caute satis Hierarchici asserunt, quòd Apostoli opus praedicandi Evangelii & plantandae Ecclesiae affectum successoribus perficiendum, reliquerint; neque Apostolica Legatio simul cum Apostolis in Coelum migraverit: Nam Apostoli τὸν δρόμον cursum suum perfecerunt, 2. Tim. IV. 7. In omnem terram exivit sonus eorum, & in fines habitabilis verba eorum, Rom. X. 18. Evangelium est apud vos & in toto mundo, & fructificat, quemadmodum in vobis, Col. I. 6. Non subduxi me, quò minus vobis annuntiarem omnem voluntatem Dei, Act. XX. 20. 27. Praedicato in mundo Christo, notificato mysterio, nuntiatis in gentibus imperviis illuminatis edoctisque omnibus, quae communio sit mysterii absconditi à saeculis in Deo, Ephes. III. 5. 8. 9. obsignandum erat verbum Dei, ut fides fieret promissioni, fore; ut nemo amplius doceat proximum suum dicendo: Cognoscite Dominum, Jerem. XXXI. 34. Ideo Judas, qui ultimos inter scripsit, omni diligentia scribens, de communi salute, non invenit, quod adderet, τῇ ἅπαξ παραδοθείσῃ τῆς ἁγίοις πίστει fidei semel sanctis traditae, Jud. v. 3. Satis verò est, quòd illi, ceu periti architecti fundamentum, quo omnia continentur & nituntur, posuerunt; cui superaedificare ad culmen usque domus, aliis etiam non Apostolis in proclivi fuit, 1. Cor. III. 10.
units.tr: Evangelists certainly, who clung to the side of the Apostles and became their fellow-workers, stood far below their dignity, since in Eph. 4:11 they are distinguished from the Apostles properly so called. If therefore these too are sometimes given the name of apostles, they must be understood not as apostles par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχήν] but as apostles of the lesser sort, for they were apostles of the Apostles. And how much less should the bishops of later times be thought to rise to the summit of apostolic dignity on account of the oversight (episkopē) alone which they hold over Christ's flock and the other presbyters? Finally, the hierarchs do not assert this cautiously enough, that the Apostles left the work of preaching the Gospel and planting the Church to be completed by their successors, and that the apostolic embassy did not depart to heaven together with the Apostles. For the Apostles finished their course (2 Tim. 4:7 [τὸν δρόμον]). "Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world" (Rom. 10:18). "The Gospel is among you and in all the world, and it bears fruit, as it does among you" (Col. 1:6). "I have not shrunk from declaring to you the whole counsel of God" (Acts 20:20, 27). With Christ preached in the world, the mystery made known, the message announced among the nations that had been untrodden, and all enlightened and taught what is the fellowship of the mystery hidden from ages past in God (Eph. 3:5, 8, 9), the word of God had to be sealed, so that faith might be given to the promise, and so that no one would any longer teach his neighbour by saying, "Know the Lord" (Jer. 31:34). Therefore Jude, who wrote last of them, writing with all diligence about our common salvation, found nothing to add to "the faith once delivered to the saints" (Jude 3 [τῇ ἅπαξ παραδοθείσῃ τοῖς ἁγίοις πίστει]). But it is enough that they, like skilled architects, laid the foundation on which everything is held and rests; to build upon it, up to the roof of the house, was easy even for others who were not apostles (1 Cor. 3:10).

units.la: XCVIII. Post institutos Apostolos Christus in terra adhuc degens, paulò ante excessum suum alios etiam ex comitatu suo, Septuaginta puta discipulos misit.
units.tr: XCVIII. While Christ was still living on earth, shortly before his departure, he sent out others from his company as well, namely seventy disciples.

units.la: Post hæc (post Apostolos duodecim vocatos & missos) designavit Dominus etiam alios septuaginta, misitque eos binos ante faciem suam in omnem urbem & locum, quò futurum erat, ut ipse veniret. Dicebat igitur iis; Messis quidem multa, sed operarii pauci. Rogate ergo Dominum messis, ut emittat operarios in messem suam. Luc. X. 1. 2. Iisque ac Apostolis dictum est: Qui vos audit, me audit; & qui vos aspernatur, me aspernatur, ibid. v. 16: Qui reversi Christo laetabundi retulerunt, etiam daemonia per nomen ejus sibi subjici, v. 17. Quibus Christus applaudens, respondit, vidisse se Sathanam ut fulgur è Coelo cadentem, v. 18; hoc est, inter praeconium illud Spiritu se vidisse casum Sathanae ex Coelo, atque jam tum cum throno suo, in quo hactenus dominans gentibus & filiis tenebrarum, & peccatum continuè accusans, sederat, deturbari coepisse, & magis magisque deturbatum iri, ne in potestate habere posset eos, quos Deus Pater Filio suo dedit. Addit verò, non ea re potissimum exultandum ipsis esse, quòd daemonia sibi subjicerentur; sed potiùs quòd nomina in Coelis descripta intelligerent, v. 20. Parum enim est Sathanae dominari, si in Coelo cum Christo regnaturos nos esse, confidere non possumus.
units.tr: After this (after the twelve Apostles had been called and sent), the Lord also appointed seventy others and sent them out two by two before his face into every city and place to which he himself was about to come. He therefore said to them: "The harvest is indeed great, but the workers are few. Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest." Luke 10:1–2. And to them, as to the Apostles, it was said: "He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me" (ibid. v. 16). When they returned joyfully to Christ and reported that even the demons were made subject to them through his name (v. 17), Christ responded to them with approval, saying that he had seen Satan falling from heaven like lightning (v. 18). That is, in the midst of that proclamation by the Spirit, he had seen the fall of Satan from heaven, and that Satan had already begun to be cast down from his throne, from which until then he had ruled over the nations and the children of darkness and had continually accused sinners, and that he would be cast down more and more, so that he could no longer hold power over those whom God the Father has given to his Son. But he adds that they ought not to rejoice chiefly because the demons were subjected to them, but rather because their names were written in heaven (v. 20). For it is a small thing for Satan to be overthrown, if we cannot be confident that we shall reign with Christ in heaven.

units.la: XCIX. Apostolis Scripturae etiam Prophetas & Evangelistas conjungunt. Dedit Christus alios Apostolos, alios Prophetas, alios Evangelistas, Ephes. IV. 11. Omnes Apostoli Prophetae & Evangelistae fuerunt, sed non vicissim. Postulavit Evangelii praeconium etiam Prophetas ejusmodi, qui licet Apostoli non essent, tamen cum Apostolis commune ejusmodi charisma haberent, ut & fatorum Regni Christi sub Evangelio conscii illa praedictionibus suis panderent, & res occultas reserarent, exemplo Prophetarum qui Hierosolymis Antiochiam venerunt, nominatim Agabi, qui per spiritum famem imminentem magnam, Act. XI. 27. 28. nec non vincula Pauli, ibid. XXI. 10. significavit. Et Δυνατοὶ ἐν γραφαῖς potentes in Scripturis, quae, Christo exhibito & exinanito atque exaltato jam contigerunt, ex Prophetiis eventura, & Prophetiis conformiter facta, demonstrarent, Divinasque res ex Verbo Dei praedicarent, & ad conscientiam ex Scripturis προφητεύσεις manifestarent. Habentes secundum gratiam vobis datam charismata diversa εἰς προφητείαν, sive Prophetiam, quae fieri debet secundum analogiam fidei, &c. Rom. XII. 6. Cum zelo quaerite spiritualia, magis vero ut prophetetis, 1. Cor. XIV. 1. Talis Propheta Apollos fuit, qui fervens spiritu demonstravit per Scripturas, Jesum esse Christum, Act. XVIII. 24. 25. 28. Super ejusmodi Prophetarum & Apostolorum fundamento aedificati dicimur, Ephes. II. 20. Et mysterium nunc revelatur sanctis Apostolis & Prophetis, ibid. III. 5. Si habeam Prophetiam, & noverim omnia mysteria & omnem cognitionem: 1. Cor. XIII. 2. Prophetias ne exinanite. 1. Thess. V. 20. Hoc dono pollentes dicuntur προφητεύειν prophetare, 1. Cor. XI. 4. 5. Quibus hanc prophetandi legem dixit Apostolus, tum ut duo vel tres loquantur (ne nimis multi uno tempore loquantur & audientes confundant, adeoque sermo sit ἀκαταστασία infructuosus; quod in publica inprimis ζυζητοῦσι locum habet) tum ut illis loquentibus οἱ ἄλλοι alii (omnes audientes, quisque pro suo captu, praecipue illi, qui donum διακρίσεως πνευμάτων discretionis spirituum habent, 1. Cor. XII. 10.) dijudicent (an quod Prophetae dicunt, suscipi ut verbum Dei, & an illi, qui loquuntur, ut servi Dei & fratres recognosci debeant, & quidem secundum testimonium & sermonem Jesu, sive fundamentum & analogiam fidei, Rom. XII. 6.) 1. Cor. XIV. 29. Proclive autem judicatu est, quatenus donum illud Prophetia in Ecclesia extraordinarium temporale & interruptum, vel ordinarium, perpetuum & permanens sit, vel esse debeat. Nam ratione praedictionum de rebus futuris, revelationis arcanorum, & demonstrationis Regni Dei ex Scripturis Propheticis, & in universum explicationis Scripturarum majore cum zelo & singulari cum dono & successu, sic extraordinarium, temporale & interruptum est, ut Apostolica potissimum aetate ob Spiritus S. ampliorem effusionem, subinde etiam sine studio sola impositione manuum, vel alio extraordinario modo viguerit, & procedente tempore quieverit, & eclipsin passum fuerit, modo ἀναζωπυρεῖν ignis instar sub cinere latentis revivis cere & inflammari, sed non sine studio & industria, quoad Scripturae explicationem, visum fuerit, quod inprimis in nobili illa Reformationis Ecclesiasticae Pentecoste apparuit. Ratione vero explicationis Scripturae cum Spiritus S. mensura communi, ad Ecclesiae conservationem & propagationem necessaria & sufficiente ordinarium, perpetuum & permanens est. Nunquam enim Ecclesiae Prophetae, Doctores & Testes, vel in ipsis flammis & multiplice patientia loquentes, desunt. Sicut porro testimonium Apostolorum fideles quasi αὐτόπται & αὐτήκοοι eorum, quae Christus dixit, fecit & passus est, quin & resurrectionis ipsius facit: ita per Prophetas ejusmodi fit, ut verba Dei intelligant, & in iis Spiritus S. ad ipsos loquatur.
units.tr: XCIX. The Scriptures also join the Prophets and Evangelists to the Apostles. Christ "gave some to be Apostles, some Prophets, some Evangelists" (Eph. 4:11). All the Apostles were Prophets and Evangelists, but not conversely. The proclamation of the Gospel also required Prophets of this kind, who, although they were not Apostles, nevertheless shared with the Apostles a similar gift, so that, being aware of the destinies of Christ's kingdom under the Gospel, they might set them forth in their predictions and unlock hidden things, after the example of the Prophets who came from Jerusalem to Antioch, especially Agabus, who through the Spirit signified a great famine that was coming (Acts 11:27–28), and also the chains of Paul (ibid. 21:10). And there were those who were powerful in the Scriptures [Δυνατοὶ ἐν γραφαῖς], who, once Christ had been shown forth, emptied, and exalted, could demonstrate from the prophecies what was to come, and what has come to pass in accordance with the prophecies, and could proclaim divine matters from the Word of God, and make known from the Scriptures the prophecies to the conscience. "Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us" [εἰς προφητείαν], "whether prophecy, which must be exercised according to the analogy of faith," etc. (Rom. 12:6). "Earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy" (1 Cor. 14:1). Apollos was such a Prophet, who, fervent in spirit, demonstrated from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ (Acts 18:24–25, 28). We are said to be "built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles" of this kind (Eph. 2:20). And "the mystery is now revealed to the holy Apostles and Prophets" (ibid. 3:5). "If I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge" (1 Cor. 13:2). "Do not despise prophecies" (1 Thess. 5:20). Those endowed with this gift are said to prophesy [προφητεύειν] (1 Cor. 11:4–5). To these the Apostle gave this law of prophesying: first, that "two or three speak" (so that not too many speak at one time and confuse the hearers, and so the discourse become unfruitful [ἀκαταστασία], which especially takes place in public disputations [ζητοῦσι]); and second, that while they speak, "the others" (all the hearers, each according to his capacity, and especially those who have the gift of discerning of spirits [διακρίσεως πνευμάτων], 1 Cor. 12:10) "judge" (whether what the Prophets say is to be received as the Word of God, and whether those who speak are to be acknowledged as servants of God and brothers, and indeed according to the testimony and word of Jesus, that is, the foundation and analogy of faith, Rom. 12:6) (1 Cor. 14:29). Now it is not difficult to judge whether that gift of prophecy in the Church is extraordinary, temporary and interrupted, or ordinary, perpetual and permanent, or ought to be so. For with respect to predictions of future things, the revelation of hidden things, the demonstration of God's Kingdom from the prophetic Scriptures, and, in general, the explanation of the Scriptures with greater zeal, singular gift and success, it is extraordinary, temporary and interrupted: it flourished especially in the Apostolic age, because of the fuller outpouring of the Holy Spirit, sometimes even without study, by the mere imposition of hands or some other extraordinary means; and as time went on it grew quiet and suffered an eclipse, and, like fire lying hidden under ashes, it was revived and inflamed again, though not without study and diligence in the explanation of Scripture, as appeared especially in that noble Pentecost of the ecclesiastical Reformation. But with respect to the explanation of Scripture, with the ordinary measure of the Holy Spirit that is necessary and sufficient for the preservation and propagation of the Church, it is ordinary, perpetual and permanent. For the Church never lacks Prophets, Teachers and Witnesses, even speaking amid the flames and in manifold suffering. Just as the faithful, as eyewitnesses and earwitnesses [αὐτόπται, αὐτήκοοι] of what Christ said, did, and suffered, bear testimony to the Apostles, and indeed to his resurrection, so through such Prophets it comes about that they understand the words of God, and in them the Holy Spirit speaks to them.

units.la: C. Evangelistae, ab Apostolis, Prophetis, Pastoribus & Doctoribus distincti, non quivis Evangelii praecones, sed ii demum, qui praeter Apostolos Historiam Christi per singularem gratiam & assistentiam Spiritus S. voce vel scripto, vel utroque explicarunt, non tantum ut αὐτόπται, sed etiam ut qui fideliter exceperunt, & παρηκολουθηκότες ἄνωθεν πάσιν ἀκριβῶς desuper seu coelitus omnia accurate assecuti sunt ab iis, qui ἀπ' ἀρχῆς αὐτόπται a principio ipsi viderunt & audiverunt, ut sic Ecclesia ἀσφάλειαν certitudinem sermonum, de quibus edocta est, haberet; (Luc. I. 1-4.) intelliguntur. Tales non tantum Matthaeus & Johannes αὐτόπται, & qui ἀπ' ἀρχῆς a principio omnia viderunt & audiverunt, sed non ut Apostoli, sed ut Evangelistae scripserunt (neque enim omnes Apostoli scripserunt) sed alii etiam, Apostolorum συνεργοί & συνεργοί cooperarii fuerunt. Ab Apostolis enim in partem muneris Apostolici ascititi, & ad diversa etiam loca missi sunt, ut vel prima Evangelicae praedicationis fundamenta ibi ponerent, vel rigando, super fundamentum ab aliis positum superstruendo, coepta absolverent, & vices eorum fungerentur, Pastores oppidatim constituerent, ἐυξίαν ordinarent, defectus corrigerent, & subinde etiam per singularem afflatum Spiritus S. scriptione Ecclesiam aedificarent. In eorum numero fuerunt Timotheus, Pauli γνήσιος, 1. Tim. I. 2. qui & Εὐαγγελιστὴς Evangelista 2. Tim. IV. 5. insignitur; Titus, ejusdem συνεργός 2. Cor. VIII. 23. Barnabas, individuus ejusdem comes usque; ad πάρεξυσμόν, qui inter eos ob Johannem Marcum, quem comite Barnabas ascisicere voluit, at renuit Paulus, subortae est, Act. XV 37. 38. 39. Silas, ejusdem Pauli comes, ib. v. 40. Marcus inprimis Petri, & Lucas Pauli perpetui comites; qui Εὐαγγελια sua scripserunt: aliique etiam ex LXX. illorum, quorum opera Christus etiam usus est, uti videtur, numero. Hoc nempe ad donum gratiae Christi etiam pertinebat, ut ea, quae dixit & fecit, quibusvis modis inclarescerent, & a nemine ignorari, vel in dubitationem vocari possent: neque posthac a quoquam alio ea repetere necesse esset. Ea de causa inprimis Ecclesiae quatuor Evangelistae dati sunt, qui ut testes & notarii omni exceptione majores historiam dictorum & factorum Christi contexerent. In quorum scriptis etsi alii ab aliis omissa sarcire voluerint, tamen quoad ea, quae Christus dixit, fecit & passus est, summa convenientia, & plenissima omnia Majestatis, sapientiae & justitiae θεοπνευστος. apparent. Nihil iis utilius, quia vitam Christi, cujus unius vestigiis nobis inhærendum, qui solus justitia, lux, vita nobis est, recitant; nihil suavius, quia Evangelium, Benedictiones, glorias Christi levato velo aperiunt: nihil certius & ἀσφαλέστερον, quia diversis temporibus à diversis scripta in rei summa pulchrè convenient, cum Mose & Prophetis concordant, non favoris & gratiæ hominum aucupium, sed merum pietatis & veritatis, patientia tot malorum & sanguine obsignatæ, zelum, studium, ardorem spirant: nihil perfectius, quia multa licet Christus dixerit & fecerit, quæ scripta non sunt, Joh. XXI. 25. tamen quæ ad pietatem & vitam necessaria sunt, plenissimè omnia scripserunt: nihil sublimius, quia iis magnum illud sine controversia mysterium (1.Tim.III.16.) panditur: nihil refertius mirabilibus exemplis, quia ibi sermonem, seu Deum carnem factum, passum, resuscitatum, miracula in omnibus mundi partibus patrata, Diaboli tentationes elisas, Angelorum bonorum ministeria prompta aliaque ἀνιγματωδῶς legere est.
units.tr: C. The Evangelists, distinguished from Apostles, Prophets, Pastors and Teachers, are not just anyone who proclaims the Gospel, but those who, besides the Apostles, through singular grace and the assistance of the Holy Spirit, set forth the history of Christ by voice or in writing, or both; and they are understood to be those who not only were eyewitnesses but also faithfully received, and "had followed all things accurately from the beginning" [παρηκολουθηκότες ἄνωθεν πάσιν ἀκριβῶς], that is, had learned them from those who from the beginning themselves saw and heard (Luke 1:1–4), so that the Church might have the certainty [ἀσφάλειαν] of the words in which it has been taught. Not only Matthew and John, who were eyewitnesses and had seen and heard everything from the beginning, but also others wrote as Evangelists rather than as Apostles (for not all the Apostles wrote), were cooperators [συνεργοί] of the Apostles. For they were taken by the Apostles into a share of the Apostolic office and were also sent to various places, to lay the first foundations of the Evangelical preaching there, or, by watering what had been laid by others, to complete what was begun, and to take their place, to set up Pastors in each town, to order the polity, to correct defects, and at times also to build up the Church by writing, through a singular inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Among their number were Timothy, Paul's true son (1 Tim. 1:2), who is also labeled an Evangelist [Εὐαγγελιστὴς] (2 Tim. 4:5); Titus, the same man's fellow worker (2 Cor. 8:23); Barnabas, the inseparable companion of the same man, up to the sharp disagreement [πάρεξυσμόν] that arose between them over John Mark, whom Barnabas wished to take as his companion but Paul refused (Acts 15:37–39); Silas, the same Paul's companion (ibid. v. 40); Mark especially Peter's, and Luke Paul's constant companions, who wrote their Gospels; and, it seems, others also from the number of the Seventy, through whose labors Christ also made use. For this also pertained to the gift of Christ's grace, that the things he said and did should be made known in every way, and that no one could be ignorant of them or call them into doubt, and that it should not be necessary for anyone afterwards to repeat them. For this reason especially four Evangelists were given to the Church, who, as witnesses and recorders above all exception, were to weave together the history of Christ's words and deeds. In their writings, although some have wished to supply what others omitted, nevertheless, with respect to what Christ said, did, and suffered, there is the greatest agreement, and all things appear most fully as the majesty, wisdom and justice of God-breathed [θεόπνευστος] Scripture. Nothing is more useful to us, because they recount the life of Christ, in whose footsteps alone we must cling, since he alone is our righteousness, light and life; nothing is sweeter, because the Gospel, the blessings and glories of Christ, they open with the veil lifted; nothing is more certain and more secure [ἀσφαλέστερον], because writings composed at different times by different men agree beautifully in the sum of the matter, accord with Moses and the Prophets, and breathe not a seeking after the favor and grace of men, but pure piety and truth, zeal, earnestness and ardor, sealed by patience under so many evils and by blood; nothing is more perfect, because although Christ said and did many things that were not written (John 21:25), they have written most fully everything that is necessary for piety and life; nothing is more sublime, because in them that great mystery, beyond dispute (1 Tim. 3:16), is laid open; nothing is more full of wonderful examples, because in them one reads of the Word, that is God, made flesh, suffering, raised from the dead, of miracles wrought in every part of the world, of the devil's temptations overcome, of the ready ministries of good angels, and of other things set forth in riddles [ἀνιγματωδῶς].

units.la: CI. Horum munerum beneficio Evangelio semel publicato, & Ecclesia constituta cum ad institutionem, tum ad conversationis & necessitatum variarum moderamen, alii etiam Ministri, Pastores & Doctores dati sunt, de quibus in loco fusius.
units.tr: CI. By the benefit of these offices, once the Gospel had been published and the Church established, both for instruction and for the regulation of conduct and various needs, other ministers, pastors and teachers were also given, concerning whom more will be said at greater length in the proper place.

units.la: LOCUS VICESIMUS PRIMUS. De GRATIA VOCATIONIS
units.tr: LOCUS VICESIMUS PRIMUS. On the GRACE OF VOCATION

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: DEUS sicut ab æterno in Christo nobis benedixit: ita in tempore in eodem, ceu Dilecto suo, nos ad eum pertinentes omni gratia cumulat. 1. Ideo nobis non tantùm justitiam & vitam per Christum procuravit, sed eandem per & propter ejus meritum donat & applicat; æquè late patente acquisitione & applicatione ejusdem. 2. Χαρίτωσις seu gratiæ in Christo donatio ad vitæ initium & progressum in hac, & consummationem ejusdem in altera vita pertinet. 3. In hac vita gratia vocationis prima est; cujus origo ostenditur. 4. Gratia vocationis definitur quoad rem & nomen. 5. Et Scripturæ testimoniis illustratur. 6. Necessitas ejus ab æterna vocatione & testamento Dei, ejusdem gloria, & hominis salvandi impotentia arcessitur. 7. Solorum electorum & per Christum redemptorum est. 8. Alterius enim planè generis non electorum vocatio est. 9. Quos non Deus sic vocat, ut iis fidem & resipiscentiam dare decreverit, vel velit, dummodo vocanti non resistat. 10. Quæ nihilominus & ipsa sincera & seria est. 11. Electi sic ad fidem & salutem vocantur, ut ad eandem etiam adducantur, juxta æternum Dei propositum, sed non sine mediis. 12. Quæ inter etiam opera naturæ, ejusque longanimitas & beneficentia est. 13. Sed vocatio per naturam spem veram vivam & non pudefacientem haud efficit. 14. Potentius longè vocationis illius medium Dei verbum est. 15. Cui tria insunt, testimonium, mandatum & promissio. 16. Vocatio per verbum externa, quia per homines præcones procedit, ad reprobos etiam quosdam pervenit, sed sine eorum ad Testamentum Dei, & salutaria Christi beneficia jure ullo. 17. Nullum inde periculum est, ne vel nondum conversi promissionem sibi non applicare, vel conversi, sed tentati, ex tentationibus eluctari non valeant. 18. Externa vocatio non est universalis, omnium & singulorum hominum. 19. Argumenta illam asserentium ad partes vocata. 20. Vocatio externa electorum cum interna Spiritus S. compellatione conjunctissima est. 21. Idem verbum homo prædicat, & Spiritus S. cordi inscribit. 22. Aliter longè Deus vocans cum electis filiis suis, quàm cum omnibus aliis agit. 23. Status eorum, qui vocantur, & dum vocantur, geminus est, internus & externus. Ille internis qualitatibus cognoscitur, velut quòd natura peccatis catis corrupti sunt; hic externis, velut quòd sunt infantes, stulti, infirmi. 24. Et ab æterno electi, in tempore per Christum sic redempti sunt, ut mors Christi vocationis etiam causa sit. 25. Operatio Spiritus S. per verbum foris prædicatum, & intus cordi inscriptum vocantis supernaturalis, omnipotens & efficacissima est. 26. Actus Spiritus S. vocantis & trahentis circa voluntatem & intellectum hominis. 27. Vocatio electorum libera est; neque illi ante vocationem suam ullum semen electionis cordi suo insitum habent. 28. Historia hæresEon, quibus doctrina sana de gratia vocationis corrupta est. 29. Veluti Manichæorum, Enthusiastarum, Pelagianorum. 30. Quibus strenuè Augustinus se opposuit, cujus argumenta pro gratia convertente strictim recensentur. 31. Pelagianorum impiam de gratia Dei doctrinam Socinus revocavit, asserens illam natura, arbitrio, remissione peccatorum, & promissione vitæ æternæ absolvi. 32. Eorum argumentis occurritur. 33. Semipelagianorum seu Massilienßium de gratia convertente hæresis. 34. Quorum castra Scholastici & Scotistæ inprimis & Jesuitæ Præscientistæ; 35. Et Remonstrantes concesserunt. 36. Augustanorum de gratia vocationis universali & sufficiente opinio, & saniorum inter eosdem interpretatio benignior exponitur. 37. In opinionum de gratia vocationis & libero arbitrio labyrintho Ariadneo filo opus est; ut & Manichæismi & Pelagianismi scopuli vitentur; 38. Inprimis status naturæ corruptæ & gratiæ, & hujus initium & progressus distinguendus venit. 39. Cardo rei in quæstione de gratia vocationis in eo vertitur: An datis omnibus gratiæ adminiculis, duobus eodem[que] loco dispositis, vocatus alter actu convertatur, alter liberè dissentiendo eandem gratiæ virtutem irritam reddat? Affirmant Semipelagiani & affectæ omnes: negant Orthodoxi. 40. Primò, quia Scriptura post lapsum voluntati omnia detrahit, & quicquid boni est, gratiæ discernenti acceptum refert. 41. Exceptio, quòd gratiæ motio in se sit indifferens, & differentia omnis à congruitate, vel applicatione, vel intentione Divina oriatur: vel æqualitas gratiæ in motionis, non beneficii æqualitate consistat; vel gratia principaliter, voluntas sub gratia agat, elisa. 42. Gratiæ congruæ figmentum evertitur. 43. Et argumentis eam astruentibus occurritur. 44. Secundò, quia vocatio & conversio peccatoris nomine creationis, regenerationis, vivificationis; insitionis in oleam, sumptionis in hæredem vel notationem per sortem venit. 45. Exceptioni, quòd naturaliter inter & spiritualiter mortuos discrimen intercedat, & non quivis reprobi in peccatis mortui dicantur. 46. Quin & in ipsa vita naturali principium aliquod vitæ supernaturalis hæreat, occurritur. 47. Tertiò, quia vocatio & conversio hominis ab infinita potentia Dei omnipotenter agente, procedit, quod inprimis ex Ephes. I. 19. probatur. 48. Qui locus illustris adversus παραξεμνιας asseritur. 49. Quartò, quia omnes à Deo vocati etiam trahuntur, nec nisi trahente Deo Patre ad Filium veniunt. 50. Limborchii tractum illum Dei extenuantis & admoralem Dei operationem detorquentis elenchus. 51. Quintò, quia, juxta catenam salutis, quos Deus vocavit, eos justificavit & glorificavit; adeóque omnes juxta propositum Dei vocati certò glorificantur; quod de vocatis secundum gratiam sufficientem communem dici non potest. 52. Exceptio, quòd in loco eo de vocatione non ad salutem, sed ad crucem & passiones agatur, diluitur. 53. Sextò, quia semipelagianizantium sententia pluribus absurdis laborat. 54. Objectiones eorundem discussæ, velut, Primò, quòd Scripturæ passim, Deum non tantum voluisse, ut convertantur homines, sed etiam conversionis remedia adhibuisse, quibus converti potuissent, & tamen eosdem vocationi non paruisse, sed rebellasse testentur; 55. Secundò quòd Deus conversionem novi cordis & Spiritus comparationem, fidem & resipiscentiam mandet, adeóque in arbitrio hominis relinquat. 56. Tertiò, quòd omnes actus & operationes, quibus verbum Dei circa homines operatur, testentur, homines in quovis instanti gratiam recipere, vel respuere posse. 57. Quartò, quòd vocatio externa absque gratia sufficiente, & propositò servandi eos, qui vocantur, Dei sapientiæ, bonitati & æquitati repugnet. 58. Quintò, quòd sic gratiam inter & liberum arbitrium discordia æstuaret, quæ tamen concordare debeant. 59. Concordia gratiam Dei, & voluntatem humanam inter qualis vigere debeat? 60. Sextò, quia à Deo sapientissimo doctore & monitore alienum sit, ut, quæ suadet & mandat, eadem in nobis operetur. 61. Vocationis Divinæ opus Regeneratio est. 62. In qua & vetus atque exterior homo deponitur, & novus atque interior homo cordis induitur: sine ullo medio inter utrumque statu. 63. Et vetustus homo exuendus, & novus induendus in utraque hominis parte, anima & corpore locum habet. 64. Regenerationis causas & Principia Christus Joh. III. 5. duo statuit tuit, aquàm, seu obedientiàn Christi; 65. Et Spiritum Dei; cujus arcanam operationem ibidem explicat. 66. Non ex sanguine & voluntate carnis, sed ex semine Verbi Dei & exemplo fidei succedit. 67. Non quodvis verbum Dei, sed verbum promissionis & Evangelii semen illud est, & quidem incorruptibile. 68. Ei incrementum dat Spiritus S. 69. Sicut vocatio, ita etiam regeneratio à virtute Dei omnipotente, & omnipotenter agente, nulla praevia dispositione, vel praeparatione ad regenerationem idonea, procedit. 70. Libertinorum & Fanaticorum, Spiritum regenerantem in turbulentum phantasma commutantium deliria perstringuntur. 71. Regenerationis in hac vita imperfectio tum ex lucta residua carnis & Spiritus, quam inprimis suo exemplo S. Paulus Rom. VII. 14. &c. asseruit. 72. Tum ex testimoniis aliis Scripturae. 73. Tum ex regenerationis profectu probatur. 74. Causae permanentis in regenitis carnis & luctae cum eadem edisseruntur. 75. Novatianorum, Catharorum, Pelagii, Tridentinorum & Fanaticorum, regenitorum perfectionem & impeccantiam propugnantium historia. 76. Argumentis eorundem occurritur. Velut quòd, Deus, gratia Dei, Christus unà cum peccato consistere non possint. 77. Quòd peccans sit ex Diabolo, & regeniti ob semen Dei in iis permanens non peccent, passim in Scriptura regenitis perfectio tribuatur; iidem in omnibus mandatis Dei ambulare dicantur, in Christo omnia valeant; Deum toto corde diligant &c. 78. Vocanti Deo homo vocatus respondet per fidem in Christum, quam ipsa vocatio operatur. 79. Fidei diversa in Scripturis notio evolvitur. 80. Aliae est fides, quae creditur, alia, qua creditur, alia, argumentum, quo rei credendae fides conciliatur. 81. Fidei generalis definitio; & ejusdem ab iis, quae videntur, vel per causas cognoscuntur; distinctio. 82. Respicit illa testem, ejusque veracitatem & testimonium, & in solum Deum fertur. 83. Estque legalis vel Evangelica. 84. Evangelica vel communis vel propria est. Illa historica, eaque vel mortua, vel ad tempus viventis speciem habens: & miraculosa est. 85. Propria definitur. 86. Communis & propriae fidei differentia essentialis est. 87. Propria & justificans habitus Divinitus infusus est. 88. Quod pluribus asseritur. 89. Solutis Remonstrantium argumentis contrariis. 90. Deus fidem infundit & donat, tum propter Filii meritum. 91. Tum per operationem Spiritus S. 92. In Christum Redemptorem, & salutaria ejus beneficia proprie fertur. 93. Neque nude, sed Christum & gratiam ejus apprehendendo, sibique applicando. 94. Pontificiorum & Remonstrantium argumenta objecto huic fidei opposita ad incudem revocantur. 95. Perperam Augustani objectum fidei salvificae gratiam universalem objectivam & subjectivam constituunt, cùm sine utroque fides generari & exerceri possit. 96. Actus, quibus fides circa objectum suum occupatur, antecedentes, comitantes, formalis & consequentes sunt. 97. Antecedentes sunt tum Notitia Christi & gratiae in Christo; 98. per quam, velut speculum quoddam, fides Christum & gratiae ejus praestantiam, plenitudinem, sufficientiam, & ad opitulandum προθυμίαν intuetur. 99. Nequicquam Pontificiis ejus in locum fidem implicitam, in Ecclesiae, non verbi Dei, oraculis stupentem substituentibus. 100. Quorum argumenta ad examen revocantur. 101. Tum assensus theoricus. 102. Humiliatio, sui ipsius abnegatio, & pia contentio. 103. Comitantes fidei salvificae actus sunt tum assensus practicus, seu fiducialis. 104. Quo credens Christum ut caput suum, in quavis fortuna, perpetuò & cum sui in voluntarium obsequium ejus deditione recipere gestit; 105. Tum sanctum ejus & justitiae ejus desiderium, seu refugium ad eundem. 106. Formalis fidei justificantis actus ejusdem fiduciālis apprehensio est. 107. Qui phrasibus Scripturae fidem justificantem proprie circumscribentibus illustratur. 108. Apprehensio Christi fiducialis est; sed diversa tamen fiducia assensus practici, apprehensionis ipsius Christi, & consequentis eandem acquiescentiae in Christo, & tranquillitatis animi est. 109. Quod similitudinibus tum hominis in torrentem aquae prolapsi, & in hoc periculo arboris supra torrentem expansae frondem apprehendentis, 110. Tum homicidae involuntarii ad asylum se recipientis; necnon cervi ad aquarum alveos anhelantis, & ex iisdem bibentis, amplius illustratur. 111. Consequentes fidei actus sunt gratia ejusdem vivificans, purificans, tranquillans, corroborans & fructificans. 112. Pontificiorum fidei justificantis formam non in fiducia meriti Christi, sed charitatis propriae collocantium Antichristianismus. 113. Fidei tum assensui practico, tum apprehensioni Christi, tum confidentiae eandem consequenti, fiduciam inesse probatur. 114. Et argumenta fiduciae opposita disputantur. 115. Fides totam animam, etiam voluntatem ejus occupat. 116. Nec fides charitate destituta vera fides est nec charitas
units.tr: God, as from eternity He has blessed us in Christ, so in time, in the same Christ, as His Beloved, He heaps every grace upon us who belong to Him. 1. Therefore He has not only procured for us righteousness and life through Christ, but He also bestows and applies the same through and on account of His merit; the acquisition and the application of it extend equally far. 2. Charitosis [χαρίτωσις], or the bestowal of grace in Christ, pertains to the beginning and progress of life in this world, and to its consummation in the other life. 3. In this life the grace of calling comes first; its origin is shown. 4. The grace of calling is defined as to its thing and its name. 5. It is also illustrated by the testimonies of Scripture. 6. Its necessity is derived from the eternal calling and covenant of God, from His glory, and from man's inability to save himself. 7. It belongs only to the elect and to those redeemed through Christ. 8. For the calling of the non-elect is of an entirely different kind. 9. God does not so call those whom He has not decreed, or is not willing, to give faith and repentance, provided they do not resist the one calling. 10. Yet this calling too is sincere and earnest. 11. The elect are so called to faith and salvation that they are also brought to it, according to the eternal purpose of God, but not without means. 12. Among these means are also the works of nature, and its long-suffering and beneficence. 13. But calling through nature does not produce a true, living hope that does not disappoint. 14. The far more powerful means of that calling is the Word of God. 15. In it three things are present: testimony, command and promise. 16. The external calling through the word, since it proceeds through human heralds, reaches even some reprobate, but without any right to God's covenant and to the saving benefits of Christ. 17. From this there is no danger that either the not-yet-converted might fail to apply the promise to themselves, or the converted, when tempted, might be unable to struggle free of their temptations. 18. The external calling is not universal, to all and each of men. 19. The arguments asserting that it is universal are addressed to the parties concerned. 20. The external calling of the elect is most closely joined with the internal compulsion of the Holy Spirit. 21. Man preaches the same word, and the Holy Spirit inscribes it on the heart. 22. God, calling, deals far differently with His elect sons than with all others. 23. The state of those who are called, and while they are being called, is twofold, internal and external. The former is known by internal qualities, for example that by nature they are corrupted by sins; the latter by external ones, for example that they are infants, foolish and weak. 24. The elect were redeemed from eternity, and in time through Christ, in such a way that the death of Christ is also the cause of their calling. 25. The operation of the Holy Spirit, supernatural, omnipotent and most efficacious, works through the word preached outwardly and through the word inscribed inwardly on the heart by the one calling. 26. It is the act of the Holy Spirit calling and drawing, acting upon the will and the intellect of man. 27. The calling of the elect is free; nor do they, before their calling, have any seed of election implanted in their heart. 28. The history of the heresies by which the sound doctrine of the grace of calling has been corrupted. 29. Such as those of the Manichaeans, the Enthusiasts and the Pelagians. 30. Against them Augustine strenuously opposed himself, and his arguments for converting grace are briefly reviewed. 31. Socinus revived the impious doctrine of the Pelagians concerning the grace of God, asserting that it is settled by nature, by the will, by the remission of sins and by the promise of eternal life. 32. Their arguments are met. 33. The heresy of the Semipelagians, or Massilians, concerning converting grace. 34. The Scholastics and especially the Scotists, and the Jesuit Praescientists, have taken up their camp. 35. And the Remonstrants have conceded to them. 36. The opinion of the Augustana writers concerning a universal and sufficient grace of calling is set forth, and the more benign interpretation of the saner among them. 37. In the labyrinth of opinions about the grace of calling and free will, we need Ariadne's thread, so that the rocks of both Manichaeism and Pelagianism may be avoided. 38. Above all, the state of corrupt nature and the state of grace, and the beginning and progress of the latter, must be distinguished. 39. The hinge of the question about the grace of calling turns on this: when all the aids of grace are given, arranged in the same place for two persons, does one who is called actually convert, while the other, by freely dissenting, renders the same power of grace void? The Semipelagians and all the partisans affirm it; the Orthodox deny it. 40. First, because Scripture takes away from the will everything after the fall, and ascribes whatever good there is to discerning grace. 41. Objection: the motion of grace is in itself indifferent, and every difference arises from congruity, or from application, or from divine intention; or the equality of grace consists in the equality of the motion, not of the benefit; or grace acts chiefly, while the will, struck down, acts under grace. 42. The fiction of congruous grace is overthrown. 43. And the arguments asserting it are met. 44. Second, because the calling and conversion of the sinner are described by the names of creation, regeneration and vivification, of engrafting into the olive tree, of adoption as heir, or of designation by lot. 45. Objection: there is a difference between the naturally and the spiritually dead, and not every reprobate is said to be dead in sins; this is met. 46. Indeed, a certain beginning of supernatural life clings even to natural life itself; this is met. 47. Third, because the calling and conversion of man proceed from the infinite power of God acting omnipotently; this is proved chiefly from Ephesians 1:19. 48. This illustrious passage is maintained against the ...

units.la: verae fidei forma est. 117. Nihilominus in fide justificante amor Dei includitur, sed distinctus ab ea charitate, quam Scriptura fidei contra distinguit. 118. Quam fidei justificantis formam non esse, pluribus asseritur. 119. Socinianorum fidei essentiam in obedientia legali collocantium sententia, & sententiae cryptis. 120. Argumenta eorundem pro obedientia legali fidei diluitur. 121. Fidei salvificae ordo, iter & tota ratio concluditur: 122.
units.tr: the form of true faith. 117. Nevertheless, the love of God is included in justifying faith, but it is distinct from that charity which Scripture sets over against faith. 118. That this is not the form of justifying faith is argued at length. 119. The opinion of the Socinians, who place the essence of faith in legal obedience, and the hidden arguments of that opinion. 120. Their arguments for legal obedience as the form of faith are refuted. 121. The order, path and whole reasoning of saving faith are concluded: 122.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: DEUS ita in Christo nobis omni benedictione spirituali in supercoelestibus benedixit, ut non tantum ante fundationem mundi nos in eo elegerit, ut essemus sancti & immaculati in conspectu ejus in charitate, & nos praedestinaverit ad adoptionem per eundem in se ipsum, secundum voluntatis suae beneplacitum: ad laudem gloriae & gratiae ejus: sed etiam in tempore in eadem gratia nos cumulaverit. Nam ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ gratia nos cumulavit in Dilecto, Christo, Eph. I. 3-6. hoc est, non tantum nos ab aeterno in Christo elegit, & ad adoptionem per eum praedestinavit, sed etiam secundum aeternam gratiam in tempore in Dilecto gratia cumulavit, nos ceu amatos, & in oculis ejus gratiam invenientes re ipsa pro gratiosis & dilectis in Filio dilecto: non demum ut Sponsore & Angelo Jehovae intercessore, sed jam dato Sacerdote, Rege & Propheta; tractavit; & maximae, qualis in hac vita dari potest, gloriosaeque gratiae compotes reddidit. Quae χαρίτωσις donatio gratiae & benedictionum spiritualium δείγμα specimen, & electionis atque praedestinationis ἔνδειγμα indicium est. Ideo etiam Christus, seu sermo caro factus dicitur πλήρης χάρις plenus gratia, Joh. I. 14. & in solo illo Deus חנון gratiosus est, Exod. XXXIV. 6.
units.tr: GOD has so blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places that he not only chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blemish before him in love, and predestined us to adoption through the same Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of his glorious grace; but also in time he has heaped us with that same grace. For he has heaped grace upon us [ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ] in the Beloved, Christ (Eph. 1:3-6). That is, he not only chose us from eternity in Christ and predestined us to adoption through him, but also, according to his eternal grace, in time he has heaped grace upon us in the Beloved. He has treated us as those who are loved, and who find grace in his eyes, and has in fact regarded us as gracious and beloved in the beloved Son. He has treated us not merely as a surety, nor only as the Angel of Jehovah, the intercessor, but as the Priest, King and Prophet now given. He has made us partakers of that greatest and most glorious grace which can be given in this life. This heaping of grace is a specimen [δείγμα] of the gift of grace and of spiritual blessings, and an indication [ἔνδειγμα] of election and predestination. For this reason Christ, or the Word made flesh, is also called full of grace [πλήρης χάρις] (John 1:14), and in him alone is God gracious [חנון] (Exod. 34:6).

units.la: II. Ad Gratiam hanc, qua nos filios suos per gratiam dilectos, in Filo Dei per naturam dilecto Deus nos in tempore cumulavit, pertinet, quod pro favore plane immerito non tantum justitiam & vitam seu salutem per Christum nobis impetrari curavit; sed eandem etiam in eodem Christo, per & propter ejus meritum nobis confert, donat & applicat. Nam qui Filio suo proprio non pepercit, sed eum pro nobis omnibus tradidit, quomodo non cum ipso τὰ πάντα omnia nobis χαρίσεται gratificabitur? Rom. VIII. 32. Distincta igitur justitiae & salutis impetratio & ejusdem applicatio & donatio est: at separata non est, sed conjunctissima, & aeque late patens. Quibus enim Christus morte sua justitiam & salutem acquisivit, iisdem, non aliis, illa donatur & applicatur, & vicissim. Nam iisdem, pro quibus mortuus est, etiam Spiritum S. & Spiritus S. ad salutem unice necessarium, donum, regenerationem & fidem meruit, quod supra Loc. XIX. §. 88. invictis argumentis asseruimus. Plane igitur necesse est, ut omnibus, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, mors ejusdem applicetur, & Spiritus S. una cum operationibus ejus, regeneratione, fide, justitia, sanctificatione, quibus applicatio illa constat, donetur. Hoc enim solum perfectum Salvatorem, Principem salutis, & αἴτιον σωτηρίας αἰωνίας causam salutis aeternae (Hebr. II. 10.) eorum, pro quibus mortuus est, facit.
units.tr: II. To this grace, by which God in time has heaped his favour upon us, who are his sons beloved through grace, in the Son of God beloved by nature, belongs the fact that, for a favour entirely undeserved, he has not only taken care that justice and life, or salvation, be obtained for us through Christ, but also that he confers, gives and applies the same in the same Christ, through and on account of his merit. For he who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things [τὰ πάντα ... χαρίσεται] (Rom. 8:32)? There is therefore a distinction between the obtaining of justice and salvation and their application and gift; but they are not separated, rather they are most closely joined and extend equally far. For those for whom Christ by his death has acquired justice and salvation, to them, and to no others, these are given and applied, and conversely. For for those for whom he died he also merited the Holy Spirit, who alone is necessary for salvation, the gift of regeneration and faith; as we have asserted with unanswerable arguments above, Loc. XIX §88. It is therefore plainly necessary that the death of Christ be applied to all for whom he died, and that the Holy Spirit be given, together with his operations, regeneration, faith, justice and sanctification, of which that application consists. For this alone makes him a perfect Saviour, the Prince of salvation, and the cause [αἴτιον] of eternal salvation (Heb. 2:10) to those for whom he died.

units.la: III. Sicut porro salus nostra in hac vita inchoatur & proficit, in altera vero consummatur: ita χαρίτωσις seu gratiae illa donatio in Christo dilecto ad vitae spiritualis initium & progressum in hac vita, & consummationem in altera pertinet. Illa Gratia vocationis, justificationis & sanctificationis: haec glorificatione aeterna absolvitur. Nam quos Deus praecognovit, praedestinavit, &c. hos vocavit, quos vocavit, illos justificavit, quos justificavit, illos glorificavit. Rom. VIII. 29. 30. Beneficia isthaec licet universo foederi gratiae, & singulis ejus oeconomiis communia sint; hoc tamen loco praecipue tractari merentur, quia sub N. T. eminent, & juxta Philosophi illud, perfectum quodque rei mensura est.
units.tr: III. Moreover, just as our salvation begins and advances in this life but is consummated in the next, so that gracious gift of God, which is heaped upon us in the beloved Christ, pertains to the beginning and progress of the spiritual life in this life, and to its consummation in the next. The grace of calling, of justification and of sanctification belongs to the former; the latter is completed by eternal glorification. For whom he foreknew, he also predestined... and whom he called, them he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified (Rom. 8:29-30). Although these benefits are common to the whole covenant of grace and to each of its economies, yet they deserve to be treated especially in this place, because they stand out under the New Testament, and according to the saying of the Philosopher, each thing's perfection is its measure.

units.la: IV. Peccatum hominem a communione & amicitia Dei avertit, & ad amicitiam ac communionem cum Sathana convertit. Aversi a Deo, qui ignis consumens est, & cum peccatore communionem habere nequit, sponte sua redire ad eum nec possunt, nec volunt. Nam & aversio illa separatio quaedam a Deo, ejusque communione, & mors in peccatis est, conjunctumque Dei odium & fugam habet; & accedentes ad Deum (peccatores ad amicitiam & communionem ejus redire gestientes) credere oportet, quod fit, (peccatori propitius) & remunerator sit iis, qui quaerunt ipsum, Hebr. XI. 6. Atqui nec mortuus in peccato sponte ad Deum venire potest, nec qui Deum odit & fugit, venire vult: nec credere peccator, quod Deus sibi propitius esse velit, nisi Deo ad gratiam vocante, & fiduciam in gratia sua praecipiente, poteste. Primus ergo post Christum redemptorem datum gratiae Dei in Christo actus est, hominem peccatorem ad se vocantis, convertentis, ducentis atque trahentis, quae Vocationis gratia est.
units.tr: IV. Sin turns man away from communion and friendship with God, and turns him toward friendship and communion with Satan. Turned away from God, who is a consuming fire and cannot have communion with a sinner, they can neither return to him of their own accord nor will to do so. For that aversion is a certain separation from God and from his communion, and a death in sins; it carries with it hatred of God and flight from him. And those who approach God (sinners who long to return to his friendship and communion) must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him (Heb. 11:6). But neither can a man dead in sin come to God of his own accord, nor can one who hates and flees God wish to come. Nor can a sinner believe that God is willing to be propitious to him, unless God calls him to grace and commands him to trust in his grace. The first act of the grace of God given in Christ the Redeemer is therefore that by which he calls the sinful man to himself, converts him, leads and draws him; this is the grace of calling.

units.la: V. Est autem, ut accuratius finiam, Gratia Vocationis voluntarius & immeritus ille Dei favor, quo is ab aeterno in Christo electos, & velut haeredes in Testamento Dei scriptos, vocatosque, in tempore vero per Christum redemptos in eodem tempore natura peccatores, in peccatis mortuos, & plerosque simplices, ignobiles supernaturali, ineffabili & omnipotente sua vi per praeconium verbi sui externum & Spiritum S. ad communionem gratiae & gloriae suae ita invitat, trahit, ducit, imo novos creat, ex morte peccati vivificat & regenerat, ac simul etiam fide in Christum donat, & per eam cen communionis cum Deo in Christo vinculum, sibi unit, ut Deo sic vocante, trahente, infallibiliter adducantur, & ad communionem ejus postliminio perveniant. Unde liquet, sermonem hic non esse de vocatione aliqua ad munus in Ecclesia vel Politia obeundum, sed longe sublimiore & sanctiore ad communionem cum Deo, ejusque gratia & gloria; quae fit per segregationem a foece mundi, & reductionem ad Deum: eaque non aeterna, quae aeterno consilio, destinatione & testamento, quo certi quidam haeredes ex mundo quandoque segregandi ab aeterno definiti sunt, facta, & proin etiam ἀμεταμέλητος absque poenitentia est, Rom. XI. 29. sed de temporali, in qua vocationis aeternae executio est, & quae fit ἐνέργεια operatione Dei in tempore homines quosdam non nude invitantis, & aures
units.tr: V. To finish more precisely: the Grace of Calling is that voluntary and undeserved favour of God by which he invites, draws and leads to the communion of his grace and glory those whom he has chosen from eternity in Christ, and written as heirs in the testament of God, and called; and in time, redeemed by Christ, who by nature are sinners at that same time, dead in sins, and mostly simple and ignoble. By his supernatural, ineffable and omnipotent power, through the external proclamation of his Word and the Holy Spirit, he even creates them anew, quickens and regenerates them from the death of sin, and at the same time bestows faith in Christ, and through it, as the bond of communion with God in Christ, unites them to himself, so that, being thus called and drawn by God, they are infallibly brought in and return by right of restoration to his communion. From this it is clear that the discussion here is not about some calling to an office to be discharged in the Church or the commonwealth, but about a far higher and holier calling to communion with God and his grace and glory. This is effected through separation from the dregs of the world and restoration to God. It is not the eternal calling, which is made by the eternal counsel, decree and testament, by which certain heirs, to be separated at some point from the world, have been defined from eternity; and therefore it is also without repentance [ἀμεταμέλητος] (Rom. 11:29). It concerns rather the temporal calling, in which the eternal calling is executed, and which is effected by the operation [ἐνέργεια] of God in time, who not merely invites certain men

units.la: Gratia vocationis definitur quod ad rem & nomen. & aures compellantis, vel per verbum suum officium iis notificantis, & fructum obsequenti promittentis (quo sensu etiam quidam non electi dicuntur κλητοὶ vocati; Matth. XX. 16. sed per verbum simul & Spiritum cor ipsum hominis alloquentis, & ad se, & participationem bonorum suorum invitantis pariter atque potenter trahentis. Quæ ipsa illa electio temporalis æternæ respondens, de qua Johan. XV.16. 1.Cor. I. 20. &c. nec non Divinæ voluntatis efficacia illa est, qua quæcunque præcipit, & vocat, stant. Ipse dixit, & factum est. Ipse jussit, & stetit, Psal. XXXIII. 9. Propter voluntatem tuam omnia sunt, & creata sunt; Apoc. IV. 11. denique similis illi vocationi, qua קרא הדורות מראש vocat generationes ab initio, hoc est, jubet illas adesse, & suo tempore nasci, Esaj. XLI. 4. qua homines קרא מבטן vocat ex utero, ibid. XLIX. 1. qua Christum servum suum קרא בצדק vocavit in justitia, ibid. XLII. 6. קרא והביא vocavit & adduxit, ibid. XLVIII. 15. & quae ea, quae non erant, vocavit, ac si essent. Rom. IV. 17. Vocatio igitur hic per metonymiam causæ pro effectu, ipsam adductionem notat. Quo sensu etiam Genes. XXI. 12. dicitur: vocabitur tibi semen, hoc est, dabitur, sistetur, adducetur propter vocationem meam. Et Prov. IX. 18. In profundis inferni sunt קראיו vocati ejus adulteri, hoc est, qui pellecti ad eam accesserunt. Passim in Scripturis conversionis, regenerationis, illuminationis, tractus, inscriptionis legis Dei in cor, vivificationis & renovationis nominibus venit.
units.tr: The grace of calling is defined with respect to the thing and the name. ...and calls to their ears, or by his Word notifies them of their duty and promises fruit to the obedient (in which sense some who are not elect are also called κλητοὶ, "called": Matt. 20:16); but who, by his Word and at the same time by the Spirit, addresses the very heart of man, and invites him to himself and to participation in his goods, drawing him both powerfully and effectively. This is that temporal election corresponding to the eternal election, of which John 15:16 and 1 Cor. 1:20, etc., speak; and it is also that efficacy of the divine will by which whatever he commands and calls, stands. He spoke, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood (Ps. 33:9). Because of your will all things are and were created (Rev. 4:11). Finally, it is similar to that calling by which he calls the generations from the beginning [קרא הדורות מראש], that is, commands them to be present and to be born in their time (Isa. 41:4); by which he calls men from the womb [קרא מבטן] (Isa. 49:1); by which he called his servant Christ in righteousness [קרא בצדק] (Isa. 42:6); [קרא והביא] called and brought (Isa. 48:15); and by which he calls those things which are not as though they were (Rom. 4:17). Calling here therefore, by metonymy of cause for effect, denotes the very bringing near. In this sense also it is said in Genesis 21:12: "in Isaac shall your seed be called," that is, it shall be given, set up, brought forth on account of my calling. And in Proverbs 9:18: "In the depths of hell are [קראיו] his called ones, the adulterers," that is, those who, enticed, came to her. Throughout the Scriptures it comes under the names of conversion, regeneration, illumination, drawing, the writing of God's law upon the heart, quickening and renewal.

units.la: VI. Vocationis hujus passim Scripturæ meminerunt. In monte Sion & Jerusalem erit פליטה evasio, sicut dixit Jehova, & inter superstitibus אשר יהוה קרא quos Dominus vocat, non tantum per verbum, sed etiam per Spiritum, ea efficacia, qua vocat ea, quæ non sunt, ut quæ sunt, Joel. II. 32. vel III. 5. Vocabo eum, qui non est populus meus, populum meum, non dilectam, ut sit dilecta, Hos. I. 10. II. 23. Non veni, ita Christus, καλέσαι ad vocandum justos, sed peccatores ad pœnitentiam, Matth. IX. 13. S. Paulus ad Romanos: Quos inter etiam vos estis, κλητοὶ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ vocati Jesu Christi. Omnibus iis, qui sunt Romæ, dilectis Dei κλητοῖς ἁγίοις vocatis sanctis, hoc est, iis, quorum vocatio corda purificavit, Rom. I. 6. 7. Idem diligentes Deum κλητοὺς κατὰ πρόθεσιν vocatos secundum propositum, ibid. VIII. 28. appellat, quia in tempore ea vocatione, per quam Deus æternum suum propositum & testamentum exequitur, vocati sunt. Quos secundum propositum illud Dei vocatos esse Apostolus eo argumento probat, quod Deus, quos præcognovit (quorum in æterna πρόθεσις seu proposito salvandi quosdam curam paternam habuit) etiam prædefinivit, conformes imagini Filii sui, &c. quos prædefinivit, hos & κἀλεσεν vocavit, hoc est, ab æterno ad se adducere decrevit, & in tempore adduxit, v. 29. 30. Non enim vocationem qualemcunque, vel nudam invitationem, sed adductionem etiam ibi intelligi, res ipsa loquitur, quia vocati etiam justificati & glorificandi dicuntur. Nemo autem nisi per vocationem ad Deum adductus justificari & glorificari potest. Vocatio enim Dei, ἀμεταμέλητος expers pœnitudinis est, Rom. XI. 29. ideoque non emanent, quos Deus ita vocavit, & qui veniunt, non excluduntur foras, Joh. VI. 37. Ne-
units.tr: VI. The Scriptures often speak of this vocation. "On Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be an escape [פליטה], as the LORD has said, and among the survivors whom the Lord calls [אשר יהוה קרא]": he calls them not only by the Word but also by the Spirit, with that efficacy by which he calls things that are not as though they were (Joel 2:32 or 3:5). "I will call that which was not my people, my people; and her who was not beloved, beloved" (Hos. 1:10; 2:23). Christ says, "I came not to call [καλέσαι] the righteous, but sinners to repentance" (Matt. 9:13). Paul to the Romans: "among whom you also are the called [κλητοὶ] of Jesus Christ"; "to all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called [κλητοῖς] saints", that is, those whose calling has purified their hearts (Rom. 1:6, 7). He calls those who love God "called according to purpose [κλητοὺς κατὰ πρόθεσιν]" (ibid. 8:28), because in time they were called by that calling through which God carries out his eternal purpose and covenant. Paul proves that they were called according to God's purpose by this argument: those whom God foreknew (for in his eternal purpose [πρόθεσις], that is, his purpose of saving some, he had a fatherly care for them), these he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, and so on; and those whom he predestined, these he also called [ἐκάλεσεν], that is, he decided from eternity to bring to himself, and in time he brought them (vv. 29, 30). For the thing itself shows that the calling meant here is not any sort of calling, or a bare invitation, but also a bringing near, since those who are called are also said to be justified and glorified. Now no one can be justified and glorified unless he is brought to God by calling. For the calling of God is without regret [ἀμεταμέλητος] (Rom. 11:29), and therefore those whom God has so called do not perish, and those who come are not cast out (John 6:37).

units.la: que vocatio illa ad crucem, vel passiones intelligitur, ut Episcopius & affectæ ejus pertendunt; quia nec id agit Apostolus, ut offendat, eos, qui crucem patienter tolerant, justificari, sed id potius, quod amantibus Deum nihil ad salutem desit, ac ne ipsa quidem crux obsit; & planè à veritate abhorrum est, quòd patientia crucis causa vel conditio justificationis sit, cùm sicut fidei; ita etiam justitiæ consequens sit. Justificati fide &c. gloriamur in afflictionibus, scientes, quòd afflictio patientiam operetur, &c. Rom. V. 1. 3. De eadem vocatione loquitur S. Petrus. Vestra est promissio, & filiorum vestrorum, & omnium qui sunt longè, quoscunque advocaverit Dominus Deus noster; scil. ad eandem sortem Sanctorum, Act. II. 39. Et iterum Paulus: Fidelis est Deus, per quem vocati estis in communionem Filii ipsius; 1. Cor. I. 9. Quibus affinia sunt loca Gal. I. 15. 2. Thessal. II. 14. Hebr. IX. 15. Quoties etiam Apostolus κλητὸς vocatos appellat, credentes intelligit, hoc est, per vocationem ad fidem adductos. Vocatis Judæis & Græcis Christus est potentia & Dei sapientia, 1.Cor. I. 24. statim enim v. 30. explicantur vocati illi, quòd sint ii, qui ex Deo sunt in Christo. Quorum etiam cœtus κλήσεως vocationis nomine venit. Videte fratres τὴν κλῆσιν vocationem vestram, hoc est, κλητοὺς vocatos vestros, &c. ib. v. 26. Idem S. Paulus vocationem κλήρωσις dationis, vel sumptionis in hæreditatem nomine insignit. In Christo ἐκληρώθημεν forte notati, vel forte in hæreditatem sumpti; vel Christo hæreditas dati sumus, prædefiniti secundum propositum ejus, Ephes. I. 11. Non enim ibi sortis projectio, sed datio & quasi manutentio notatur, juxta illud Christi: Tu tenes sortem meam. Funiculi mei ceciderunt in amœnis, Psal. XVI. 5. 6. Cumque vocatio hæc similis primæ creationi, qua Deus vocavit quæ non sunt, velut ea quæ sunt, Rom. IV. 17. & generationi naturali, qua idem vocat generationes, Esaj. XLI. 4. quædam velut nova creatio & generatio, seu παλιγγενεσία, iteratus quasi exortus sit; huc referenda sunt, quæcunque Scriptura de nova creatione, regeneratione, seu spirituali vivificatione habet, quam in rem infra plura dicemus.
units.tr: Nor is that calling to the cross or to sufferings meant, as Episcopius and his followers contend. For the Apostle does not set out to show that those who bear the cross patiently are justified; rather he is showing that nothing is lacking to salvation for those who love God, and that not even the cross itself does them harm. It is altogether foreign to the truth that patience under the cross is the cause or condition of justification, since, just as faith, so also righteousness is a consequence of justification: "Being justified by faith ... we glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience," etc. (Rom. 5:1, 3). St Peter speaks of the same calling: "The promise is to you and to your children, and to all who are afar off, as many as the Lord our God shall call" (Acts 2:39); namely, to the same lot of the saints. And again Paul: "God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son" (1 Cor. 1:9). Similar are Gal. 1:15, 2 Thess. 2:14, and Heb. 9:15. Whenever the Apostle calls people "called" [κλητὸς], he means believers, that is, those brought by the calling to faith. "To the called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power and wisdom of God" (1 Cor. 1:24); for immediately at v. 30 those called are explained as those who are of God in Christ. Even the company of the called [κλήσεως] is named by the term "calling." "Consider, brethren, your calling [τὴν κλῆσιν], that is, your called ones [κλητοὺς]" (ibid. v. 26). The same Apostle marks the calling by the term "lot" [κλήρωσις], that is, the giving or taking up into an inheritance: "In Christ we have obtained an inheritance [ἐκληρώθημεν]," perhaps marked as taken up into an inheritance, or perhaps we are given to Christ as an inheritance, predestined according to his purpose (Eph. 1:11). Here it is not the casting of lots that is meant, but a giving, and as it were a holding in hand, in accordance with Christ's saying: "You hold my lot; the lines have fallen to me in pleasant places" (Ps. 16:5, 6). And since this calling is like the first creation, by which God called things that are not as though they were (Rom. 4:17), and like natural generation, by which the same God calls generations (Isa. 41:4), it is in some sense a new creation and generation, or a palingenesia [παλιγγενεσία], as if a renewed rising. To this belong whatever Scripture says about new creation, regeneration, or spiritual quickening, on which we shall say more below.

units.la: VII. Necessitatem vocationis hujus temporalis tum æterna vocatio & testamentum Dei: tum ejusdem gloria: tum hominis salvandi impotentia evincunt. Æterna Vocatio & Testamentum Dei, quia utrumque illud executionem in tempore postulat. Non potuit enim Deus ab æterno decernere & jubere, ut, qui præcogniti prædestinatique sunt, etiam ad Christum venire, si in tempore eosdem vocare & ad Christum adducere noluit. Atqui vocatio æterna, seu verbum Jehovæ, quod stat in seculum, Esaj. XL. 8. quo Pater dixit, Filio daturum se hæreditatem, & Filius hæreditatem eam poposcit; antecessit creationem cœli & terræ, comprehensa in vocatione, qua omnia ab initio, quemadmodum extiterunt, aut adhuc existent, vocata, & esse jussa sunt. Non enim Adam & filii ejus simpliciter, ut quædam ζῷα animalia, sed ut hæredes salutis vocati sunt. Absque qua vocatione Deus omnia & hominem ipsum frustra creasset, quia sic gloriæ Dei ex operibus ejusdem præco defuisset. Æternæ huic vocationi Apostolus adscribit, quòd hæredes salutis in tempore
units.tr: VII. The necessity of this temporal calling is proved by God's eternal calling and covenant, by his glory, and by man's inability to save himself. God's eternal calling and covenant prove it, because both demand their execution in time. For God could not have decreed and ordained from eternity that those who were foreknown and predestined should also come to Christ, if he had been unwilling to call them in time and bring them to Christ. But the eternal calling, or the word of Jehovah, which stands for ever (Isa. 40:8), by which the Father said that he would give an inheritance to the Son, and the Son asked for that inheritance, came before the creation of heaven and earth. In that calling all things were called and ordered to be, just as they came into being from the beginning, or still exist. For Adam and his sons were called not simply like some living creatures [ζῷα], but as heirs of salvation. Without this calling God would have created all things and man himself in vain, because then the herald of God's glory from his works would have been wanting. The Apostle ascribes to this eternal calling the fact that heirs of salvation come to Christ in time and are saved in him.

units.la: Et Scripturæ testimoniis illustrantur. pore ad Christum accedunt, & in eo salvantur. In Isaco vocabitur tibi semen, Rom. IX. 7. ex Genes. XXI. 12. hoc est, Isaco dedi semen, quod voco vel vocabo; quos vocabo, ut sint tuum semen, eos vocabo, ut sint semen & filii Isaci, ut ita, quod est secundum electionem, propositum maneret, non ex operibus, sed ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος, ib. v. 11. ut ita קרא & καλέω in locis illis non meram nominationem, sed adductionem per imperium & voluntatis propositum significet. Cumque aeterna vocatio facta sit per Testamentum, similis illi, quo paterfamilias opum suarum haeredes delegit, necesse est, ut haeredes ejusmodi in aeterno Testamento vocati & designati in tempore ad Christum veniant, seu ab eodem redempti, ad eum adducantur, fideique participes reddantur. Propterea enim Christus Novi Testamenti Mediator est, ut, morte obita ad redemptionem transgressionum, quae sub priori erant, promissionem acciperent κεκλημένοι τὴν αἰώνιον κληρονομίαν vocati aeternae haereditatis. Hebr. IX. 15. Firmissima enim vocatio illa testamentaria est, & non tantum promissione Patribus de semine dando facta, nec non fide illorum, qua promissionem Dei immutabilem & irrevocabilem fecerunt, quia ipsis fidem sibi habentibus mentiri non potest, sed inprimis pacto Patris cum Filio haereditatem dedit: imo jure Filii ex justitia haereditatem postulantis nituntur, ac proin in tempore etiam expleri necessario debuit. Tum & gloriae Dei intererat, ut in tempore quidem evocarentur, ne deesset, qui virtutes ejus, qui ex tenebris nos vocat ad lucem admirabilem, narrarent, 1. Pet. II. 9. Denique & ἀδυναμία impotentia illa hominis peccatoris salvandi, qui in peccato mortuus, imo natura a Deo abalienatus, ab eo, ceu judice severo abhorrens, ad Deum accedere non potest, nec vult, imo Deo insultat, dicens: Recede a nobis, Job. XXII. 17. vocationem & adductionem omnipotentem Dei postulat. Ideo Protoplasti lapsi non ipsi ad Deum redierunt, sed potius a facie Dei se occultarunt, donec Deus eos, ceu pastor oves, gratiose requireret, imo vocaret verbo suo, dicendo; ubi es? & prior inimicitiam ipsos inter & Serpentem poneret, quae inimicitiae positio ipsa Dei vocatio fuit, Genes. III. 9. 15.
units.tr: And these are illustrated by testimonies of Scripture. In time they come to Christ and are saved in him. "In Isaac shall your seed be called" (Rom. 9:7), from Gen. 21:12; that is, I have given Isaac a seed, which I call or shall call; those whom I shall call to be your seed, I shall call to be the seed and sons of Isaac, ut so that quod est secundum electionem, propositum maneret, non ex operibus, sed ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος, "the purpose according to election might remain, not of works, but of him who calls" (ibid. v. 11). So in those passages קרא and καλέω do not mean a mere naming, but a bringing near through command and the purpose of the will.
