And since the eternal calling is made through a testament, like that by which a householder chooses heirs for his goods, it is necessary that heirs of this kind, called and designated in the eternal testament, should in time come to Christ, that is, be redeemed by him, be brought to him, and be made partakers of faith. For this reason Christ is the Mediator of the New Testament, ut so that, morte obita ad redemptionem transgressionum, quae sub priori erant, promissionem acciperent κεκλημένοι τὴν αἰώνιον κληρονομίαν vocati aeternae haereditatis, his death having taken place for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the former covenant, those who are called might receive the promise of the eternal inheritance (Heb. 9:15). For that testamentary calling is most firm, and is not only made by the promise of giving a seed made to the Fathers, nor only by their faith, by which they made the promise of God unchangeable and irrevocable, since God cannot lie to those who trust him; but above all God gave the inheritance by the covenant of the Father with the Son. Indeed they rest on the right of the Son, who asks for the inheritance by justice, and therefore it had to be fulfilled in time also, of necessity. Moreover, it was also for the glory of God that they should be called in time, so that there would not be lacking those who might tell of virtutes ejus, qui ex tenebris nos vocat ad lucem admirabilem, the virtues of him who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light (1 Pet. 2:9). Finally, the inability of sinful man to save himself, who is dead in sin, and indeed by nature alienated from God, shrinking from him as a stern judge, cannot come to God and does not want to, and even insults God, saying, Recede a nobis, "Depart from us" (Job 22:17), requires the omnipotent calling and bringing near of God. Therefore the fallen first parents did not return to God themselves, but rather hid themselves from the face of God, until God, like a shepherd seeking his sheep, graciously sought them and even vocaret called them by his word, saying: ubi es? "Where are you?" And first he set inimicitiam enmity between them and the Serpent, and this setting of enmity was itself God's calling (Gen. 3:9, 15).

units.la: VIII. Vocatio electorum & per Christum redemptorum est.
units.tr: VIII. The calling belongs to the elect and to those redeemed through Christ.

units.la: Soli enim hi ita vocantur, ut etiam adducantur, & novi creentur atque generentur. Soli sunt, quorum Deus non tantum aures verbo suo per homines praedicato ferit, sed etiam corda aggreditur, ea aperit, legem suam eis inscribit, illa mutat, & ad amorem sui inflammat. Soli secundum testamentum Dei, & κατὰ πρόθεσιν secundum propositum, hoc est, praecogniti & praedestinati prius vocantur, & ceu vocati & ita fide donati justificantur & glorificantur, Rom. VIII. 28.29.30.
units.tr: For only these are called in such a way that they are also brought in, and are created and begotten anew. They alone are those whom God does not merely strike on the ears by the word preached through men, but whose hearts he also reaches, opening them, writing his law upon them, changing them, and inflaming them to love of himself. Only these are called first according to the covenant of God, and according to purpose [κατὰ πρόθεσιν], that is, foreknown and predestined, and, as those called, and thus endowed with faith, they are justified and glorified, Rom. 8:28-30.

units.la: IX. Alius enim plane generis est vocatio eorum, qui non electi relinquuntur & rejiciuntur. Quomodo plures vocati quam electi dicuntur, Matth. XX. 16. Neque omnes ad nuptias vocati venerunt ibid. XXII. 3. Nam vocati non electi non vocantur secundum propositum & testamentum Dei ut in eo scripti haeredes, sed secundum judicium & dispensationem Dei, qua eos in externa electorum communione tolerat per verbum de sua bonitate, ipsorum
units.tr: IX. The calling of those who are not chosen but are left and rejected is plainly of another kind. Hence many are called, but few are chosen is said, Matt. 20:16. Nor did all who were invited come to the wedding, ibid. 22:3. For those called who are not chosen are not called according to the purpose and covenant of God, as heirs written into it, but according to the judgment and dispensation of God, by which he bears with them in the external fellowship of the elect, testifying through the word to his goodness, and convicting them of their own

units.la: vero malitia convincit, atque non venientibus ad nuptias Filii Regis, excusationem praecidit. Vocantur etiam non tam immediate a Deo, cor afficiente, mutante & regenerante, quam mediate per homines qui aures ferire possunt, ad cor ipsum vero penetrare non possunt; Atque sic vocantur verbo ab hominibus praedicato, ut tamen non adducantur per Spiritum Dei ad communionem Dei, neque fide, & resipiscentia donentur, sed in miseria sua relinquantur; imo damnationis suae incrementis ex ipsorum illorum beneficiorum, quae ad eosdem ex Evangelii praeconio nec pauca nec exigua redundant, abusu provenientibus mactentur, utpote semper resistentes Spiritui S. per verbum ab hominibus scriptum vel praedicatum loquenti, & secundum duritiem suam & cor poenitere nescium sibi ipsis iram in diem irae thesaurizantes, Rom. II. 5. Ac licet vocatio talis, seu notificatio foederis in nonnullis etiam conjunctum habeat ἐλεγχον Spiritus, a quo illuminati perducuntur ad gustum doni coelestis, boni Dei verbi & virtutum futuri seculi, Heb. VI. 4. tamen illa cum mutatione cordis ad amorem Dei, fide radicata & resipiscentia conjuncta nunquam est, neque omnino illa ad κρείττονα καὶ ἐχόμενα σωτηρίας meliora illa & cum salute connexa ibid. v. 9. proficit. Denique vocantur non tam propter se, quam propter electos, in quorum medio habitant, & ad quos alias solos verbum Evangelii pertinet. Accidit enim, ut verbum Dei, ceu semen illud bonum in agro, in quo electi, propter quos solos Evangelium praedicatur, cum reprobis commixti sunt, sparsum incidat non tantum in electos, terram bonam, sed etiam in reprobos, velut propter viam, vel in terram petrosam, vel in vepres, Matth. XIII. 19-23. Homo enim est, qui semen illud serit. Cumque is terrae illius partes foetas & steriles, electos & reprobos discernere non valeat, evenit, ut ad utrosque illud pertingat. Sed in parte terrae sterili semen illud deficit, & deinde aufertur, vel cum eo seductio & potentia mortis secundae ingreditur, ut qui vocati sunt, & amore veritatis, ut salventur, non ardent, mendacio credant, indurentur, pejusque pereant. Ideo praecones verbi Dei ibi, ubi electi nulli sunt, praedicare prohibentur, non obscuro indicio, quod reprobi vocationem suam electis acceptam referre debeant. Transeuntes Paulus & Timotheus Phrygiam & Galaticam regionem, prohibiti sunt a Spiritu S. loqui sermonem in Asia. Venientes autem juxta Mysiam, tentarunt in Bithyniam proficisci. Et sivit eos Spiritus Act. XVI. 6.7. Unde etiam vocatio per verbum non contingit omnibus ubivis hominibus, Deo justum judicium & liberam gratiam per vices dispensante. Vide benignitatem & severitatem Dei; erga lapsos severitatem; erga te benignitatem; si quidem permanseris in benignitate. Alioquin & tu excideris, Rom. XI. 22.
units.tr: wickedness, and cutting off the excuse of those who do not come to the wedding of the King's Son. They are also called not so much immediately by God, who touches, changes and regenerates the heart, as mediately through men, who can strike the ears but cannot penetrate to the heart itself. Thus they are called by the word preached by men, yet they are not brought by the Spirit of God into communion with God, nor are they endowed with faith and repentance, but are left in their misery. Indeed, they are destroyed by the abuse of those very benefits, which flow to them from the proclamation of the gospel in no small or slight measure, growing into the increase of their own damnation, since they always resist the Holy Spirit speaking through the word written or preached by men, and, according to their hardness, and a heart unable to repent, they store up for themselves wrath on the day of wrath, Rom. 2:5. And although such a calling, or notification of the covenant, in some cases also has joined with it a conviction [ἔλεγχον] of the Spirit, by which they are enlightened, and led to taste the heavenly gift, the good word of God, and the powers of the age to come, Heb. 6:4, yet it is never joined with a change of heart to the love of God, rooted in faith and connected with repentance, and it never profits them toward better things and things accompanying salvation [κρείττονα καὶ ἐχόμενα σωτηρίας], ibid. v. 9. Finally, they are called not so much for their own sake as for the sake of the elect, in whose midst they dwell, and to whom alone the word of the gospel otherwise belongs. For it happens that the word of God, like that good seed in the field, in which the elect, for whose sake alone the gospel is preached, are mixed with the reprobate, falls scattered not only on the elect, good ground, but also on the reprobate, as by the way, or on stony ground, or among thorns, Matt. 13:19-23. For it is man who sows that seed. Since he cannot distinguish the fruitful and barren parts of that ground, the elect and the reprobate, it comes about that the seed reaches both. But on the barren part of the ground the seed fails, and is then taken away, or with it deception and the power of the second death enter in, so that those who are called do not burn with love of the truth in order to be saved, believe a lie, are hardened, and perish all the more. Therefore the heralds of the word of God are forbidden to preach where there are no elect, by no obscure sign that the reprobate ought to attribute their calling to the elect. Paul and Timothy, passing through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they came to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit did not permit them, Acts 16:6-7. Hence calling through the word does not come to all men everywhere, since God dispenses his just judgment and free grace in turn. Behold the goodness and severity of God: toward those who fell, severity; toward you, goodness, if you continue in his goodness; otherwise you also will be cut off, Rom. 11:22.

units.la: X. Neque omnino Deus reprobos quosdam sic vocat, ut decreverit, vel velit iis aeque atque electis dare fidem & resipiscentiam, dummodo Spiritui S. vocanti non resistant, quae nonnullorum λεπτολογία est. Nulla enim datur decreta Dei, quae homines vel creatura ulla frustrari possint; sed efficacia omnino sunt, certissimumque eventum habent. Quibus ergo decrevit dare fidem & refipiscentiam, iis eandem in tempore per verbum&Spiritum S.confert. Tum omnes homines per se & natura sua Spiritui S. repugnant, quia semper φρόνημα σαρκὸς dium carnis est inimicitia adversus Deum, Rom. VIII. 7. & quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, animali homini stultitia sunt, 1.Cor. II. 14. Qui non repugnant Spiritui S. illud aut ex se, aut ex Spiritu S. habent. Si ex se, ipsi igitur se discernunt, quod Apostolo ibid. IV. 7. repugnat, & fidem ex se habent, quæ tamen Dei donum est Ephes. II. 8. 9. Sin ex Spiritu S. non igitur is vult vel intendit efficaciter operari conversionem saltem in iis, à quibus repugnantiam non tollit; alias eam operaretur, quia in Cælo est, & facit quicquid vult, Psal. CXV. 3. Repugnantiam igitur tollere est speciaiis ejus ut operatio; sic etiam intentio, respectu eorum, qui credunt & convertuntur, & de quibus dicitur: Verbum meum, quod egredietur de ore meo, non revertetur ad me vacuum, sed faciet quod volo, Esaj. LV. 11. Electio assequitur, reliqui indurantur: Rom. XI. 7. Præterea quòd quidam vocati non veniunt vel adducuntur, ejus rei causa penes ipsos quidem residet, quia & habitu pravi natura sunt, & actu obstinatos se gerunt; quæ causa omnem prætextum & excusationem homini adimit, & justitiam Dei mirificè illustrat. Neque tamen ideirco nulla causa est etiam ex parte Dei vocantis. Is enim dum foris vocat per verbum, intus nec illuminat, nec cor flectit, nec fidem donat: imò ab æterno sicut à salute, ita à mediis etiam salutis, illuminatione, renovatione, fide eosdem decretorie exclusit.
units.tr: X. Nor does God call certain reprobate men in such a way that he has decreed, or wills, to give them faith and repentance just as to the elect, provided they do not resist the Holy Spirit calling them. This is the hair-splitting [λεπτολογία] of some. For no decrees of God are given which men or any creature can frustrate; rather they are wholly effective, and have a most certain outcome. To those therefore to whom he has decreed to give faith and repentance, he confers the same in due time through the word and the Holy Spirit. Yet all men, by themselves and by their nature, resist the Holy Spirit, because the mind of the flesh is enmity against God [φρόνημα σαρκὸς ἔχθρα εἰς θεόν], Rom. 8:7, and the things of the Spirit of God are foolishness to the natural man, 1 Cor. 2:14. Those who do not resist the Holy Spirit have this either from themselves, or from the Holy Spirit. If from themselves, then they distinguish themselves, which contradicts the Apostle, ibid. 4:7, and they have faith from themselves, which is nevertheless the gift of God, Eph. 2:8-9. But if from the Holy Spirit, then he does not will or intend to work conversion effectively, at least in those whose resistance he does not remove; otherwise he would work it, since he is in heaven and does whatever he wills, Ps. 115:3. To remove resistance, therefore, is a special operation of his; so too is intention, with respect to those who believe and are converted, and of whom it is said: My word, which goes out of my mouth, shall not return to me empty, but shall accomplish what I desire, Isa. 55:11. The elect obtain it, and the rest are hardened, Rom. 11:7. Moreover, that certain called men do not come or are not brought in, the cause of this resides indeed in themselves, because they are evil by nature in their disposition, and in their acts they behave obstinately; this cause takes away from man every pretext and excuse, and wonderfully illustrates the justice of God. Yet for all that there is no cause also on the side of God who calls. For while he calls outwardly through the word, inwardly he neither enlightens, nor bends the heart, nor gives faith. Indeed, from eternity, as from salvation, so also from the means of salvation, illumination, renewal and faith, he has decretively excluded these same men.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Inanis planè vocationem electorum & reproborum Dei ipsius etiam respectu æquiparantium metus est, ne vocatio reproborum cum decreto & intentione non dandi fidem, refipiscentiam & salutem non conjuncta, sincera, vel seria satis sit. Parùm enim Dei τῇ ἐλλιπεῖ convenire ajunt, ut eos etiam, quibus salutem & media salutis dare non decrevit, ad salutis participationem vocare, & ut omnes veniant, velle, dicatur. Sive enim ferium opponatur jocoso, Deus in negotio vocationis neutiquam ludit; sive simulato, æquè non simulat, quia non aliud foris verbo profitetur, intus aliud animo tegit; sed planam, apertam & constantem voluntatem suam vocatione hominibus declarat. Cùmque vocationis partes sint mandata & promissiones, quotquot vocat, iis seriò refipiscentiam & fidem mandat & imperat. Vult enim, ut resipiscant & credant, voluntate præcipiente & approbante; licèt non velit voluntate decernente, & ad donandam fidem & refipiscentiam efficaci. Jure suo utramque imperat, & quia imperat, eam se approbare testatur. Sed operari eam non vult, neque hactenus, ut in reprobis existeret, decrevit; quia alias vel decretum irritum esset, quod Deo indignissimum est, vel eandem in iis sic operaretur, ut in iis exi-stat, quod Scripturæ & experientiæ repugnat. Sed & vocatio promittit salutem, at non promiscuè cuivis, vel sine conditione, sed credenti & resipiscenti. Vocatio ipsa externa, utpote per homines Evangelii sagenam in mare conjicientes & cuncti generis piscibus implentes, sed ita, ut ad litus illi tandem explorandi veniant; facta indeterminata est, &
units.tr: Those who fear that the calling of the elect and of the reprobate, even when set beside God's own purpose, is empty are groundless. They fear that the calling of the reprobate, which is not joined to a decree and intention to withhold faith, repentance and salvation, is not sincere or earnest enough. They say that it hardly suits God [τῇ ἐλλιπεῖ] to call to a share in salvation those to whom he has decided not to give salvation or the means of salvation, and that it is said he wills that all should come. For if earnest is opposed to jesting, God is in no way playing in the business of calling; and if it is opposed to feigned, neither does he feign, since he does not profess one thing outwardly in the word while hiding another in his mind. Rather, by the calling he declares to people his plain, open and constant will. Since the parts of the calling are commands and promises, he earnestly commands and enjoins repentance and faith on all whom he calls. For he wills that they repent and believe, by a will that commands and approves; although he does not will with a will that decrees and is effective in bestowing faith and repentance. By his right he commands both, and because he commands them he testifies that he approves them. But he does not will to work them, nor has he hitherto decreed to bring them about in the reprobate; for otherwise either the decree would be void, which is most unworthy of God, or he would work them in such a way that they exist in the reprobate, which contradicts Scripture and experience. But the calling also promises salvation, yet not indiscriminately to anyone or without condition, but to the believing and repentant. The external calling itself, since it is carried out by men casting the net of the Gospel into the sea and filling it with fish of every kind, yet in such a way that they come at last to the shore to be sorted, is made indeterminate, and

units.la: nominatim nec electos, nec reprobos indigetat. Omnis credens non peribit, sed habebit vitam æternam, Joh. III. 16. Hæc est voluntas ejus, qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt Filium & in eum credit, habeat vitam æternam. Et ego eum resuscitabo in ultimo die, ib. VI. 40. Quod cùm verissimum sit, & Deo par jus sit à reprobis postulandi fidem & refipiscentiam, atque legis obedientiam, cùm mandatum illud fidei & refipiscentiæ, præsuppositio testimonio de salute quibusdam in Christo danda, pars sit legis, quæ etiam abnegationem justitiæ propriæ peccatoris, omnisque alius remedii & solatii miseriæ non revelati, nec non amorem Dei impium in Christo justificantis, & fiduciam illam, qua animam nostram Deo committimus in bonis factis, præcipit; manifestum est à mandato tali omnem fallitatem & hypocrisin abesse: At nec promissio conditionata, & sine subjecti determinatione notificata hypocrisin arguit, quia indicat veritatem certissimam, complexam, quæ ex Testamento & decreto Dei fluit, quàmque Deus æquè ac decretum suum de salute redemptorum, unde ista veritas fluit, vult & approbat. Est enim veritas illa ipsissima legis sententia, quæ non potest condemnare, vel non absolvere, vel vitam non promittere iis, qui in Christo sunt, & in eo Legi satisfecisse censentur. Quin potiùs vocatio ejusmodi indeterminata Dei sapientiam, veracitatem & constantiam arguit, quia per eam in reprobis tantò clariùs carnis impotentia, & Dei immorigeros punientis justitia patefecit; electi verò tantò majorem solicitudinem, & sui scrutationem ad firmandam electionem & vocationem suam, adhibere discunt.
units.tr: does not name either the elect or the reprobate. Whoever believes will not perish, but will have eternal life, John 3:16. This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life. And I will raise him up on the last day, ib. 6:40. Since this is most true, and God has an equal right to require faith, repentance and obedience to the law from the reprobate, and since that command of faith and repentance, which presupposes the testimony about salvation to be given to certain people in Christ, is part of the law, which also enjoins the renunciation of one's own righteousness, the abandonment of every other remedy and comfort for a wretchedness not revealed, the impious love of God who justifies in Christ, and that trust by which we commit our souls to God and not to good works, it is clear that every falsehood and hypocrisy is absent from such a command. Nor does a conditional promise, announced without determination of the subject, argue hypocrisy, since it indicates a most certain and comprehensive truth, which flows from the Testament and decree of God, and which God, just as much as his decree concerning the salvation of the redeemed from which this truth flows, wills and approves. For that truth is the very sentence of the law, which cannot condemn, or fail to absolve, or fail to promise life to those who are in Christ and are regarded as having satisfied the Law in him. Indeed, such an indeterminate calling rather argues the wisdom, truthfulness and constancy of God, since through it the impotence of the flesh and the justice of God punishing the disobedient are made clearer in the reprobate; while the elect learn to apply all the more care and self-examination to confirm their election and calling.

units.la: XII. Sed missa heterogenea illa reproborum vocatione, ad augustiorem illam, quæ electorum est, redimus. Non enim hic cortex vocum, sed pondus librandum est. Juxta quod longè alia electorum, quàm reproborum vocatio est. Nam electi secus longè quàm reprobi sic ad salutem vocantur, ut vocati etiam afficiantur, trahantur, & adducantur, idque juxta æternum propositum & Testamentum, & absolutè licèt non sine mediis, quæ tamen eorum respectu non sunt conditiones in eorum arbitrio positæ, sed beneficia Dei libera, juxta æternum propositum & Testamentum ejus vocandis omnibus cum infallibili efficacia & operatione adhibenda & conferenda.
units.tr: XII. But setting aside that calling of the reprobate, which is of a different kind, let us return to the more exalted calling, that of the elect. For here it is not the husk of words but the weight that must be weighed. In accordance with this, the calling of the elect is quite different from that of the reprobate. For the elect are called to salvation in a way very different from the reprobate: being called, they are also moved, drawn and brought in, and this according to the eternal purpose and Testament, and absolutely, although not without means; yet these means, with respect to them, are not conditions placed in their own power, but free benefits of God, to be applied and conferred with infallible efficacy and operation upon all who are called, according to his eternal purpose and Testament.

units.la: XIII. Sicut omnes promiscuè homines, ita etiam electi per opera Dei, ejúsque longanimitatem & χρηστότης beneficentiam quodammodo ad Deum ejúsque communionem quærendam vocantur. Neque enim natura ipsa mutaeft, sed multis modis inclamat homini, ut in rebus terrenis non acquiescat, sed per hanc quasi scalam ad meliora, cœlestia & æterna ascendat. Quid enim opera Dei in natura se proferentia aliud quàm figuræ quædam & symbola rerum cœlestium sunt? Quod & Seneca Præfat. Quæst. Nat. pluribus exposuit, exclamans inter alia: O quàm contempta res est homo, nisi supra humana se erexit! Nam naturæ voce invitantur homines, ut quærant Deum, si forte palpando ipsum invenire queant, Act. XVII. 27. Et invisibilia Dei à conditu mundi operibus animadversa providentur, æterna ejus potentia & Deitas, Dettas, Rom. I. 20. Quod pluribus etiam Hie-ropsaltes Psal. XIX. 1–6. persequitur. Neque tantùm ad quærendum sese per naturam Deus hominem invitat, sed etiam potiundi sui spem nonnullam sua longanimitate, beneficentia & subjectione naturæ, ut præter ingenium suum, & velut invita vanitate inserviens libe-rationem expectet, facit. An divitias beneficen-tiæ ejus, & tolerantiam & longanimitatem contemnis, ignarus, quòd beneficentia Dei te ad resipi-scentiam ducat? Rom. II. 4. Vanitati subjecta est creatura, non volens, sed propter subjicientem, in spe, quòd & ipsa creatura liberanda sit a servitute corruptionis in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei, ibid. VIII, 20. 21.
units.tr: XIII. Just as all people without distinction, so also the elect are called, through the works of God and his long-suffering and [χρηστότης] kindness, in some measure to seek God and communion with him. For nature itself has not changed, but in many ways it cries out to man that he should not rest content in earthly things, but by this, as it were a ladder, should ascend to better, heavenly and eternal things. For what are the works of God displayed in nature but certain figures and symbols of heavenly things? Seneca too set this out at length in the preface to his Natural Questions, exclaiming among other things: O how contemptible a thing is man, unless he raises himself above human things! For people are invited by the voice of nature to seek God, if perhaps they might feel after him and find him, Acts 17:27. And the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are seen through the things that are made, his eternal power and Godhead, Rom. 1:20. The psalmist of Psalm 19:1–6 pursues this at greater length. Nor does God invite man only to seek him through nature, but by his long-suffering, his kindness and the subjection of nature he also gives some hope of attaining him, so that, beyond its own nature, and as if serving against its will in vanity, it awaits liberation. Or do you despise the riches of his kindness, and forbearance and long-suffering, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? Rom. 2:4. The creature was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that the creature itself also will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God, ib. 8:20, 21.

units.la: XIV. Cæterùm hæc per naturam vocatio conscientiam licet ad cogitandum, Deum posse justificare hominem impium, & ad quærendum eum & cognitionem voluntatis ejus excitat; tamen spem veram, vivam & nunquam pudefacientem non suppeditat, quia nec ejus indicio justitia Dei & justificatio impii innotescit; neque ob cæcitatem & stultitiam suam homo à Deo desertus non potest tolerantia Dei abuti. Unde gentes per naturam ad Dei longanimitatem & beneficentiam invitatæ licet, multis tamen seculis vocationem, quæ ad fidem, amorem Dei, & conversionem peccatoris necessaria est, non habuerunt, Deo illos deserente, & sub inobedientiam includente, Rom. XI. 32. hoc est, ita judicio suo indurante, ut ostenderet iram suam, & quòd eas æterno proposito ad salutem æternam vocare non decreverit.
units.tr: XIV. However, although this calling through nature stirs the conscience to think that God can justify the ungodly man, and to seek him and the knowledge of his will, it does not supply a true, living and never-disappointing hope; for by its testimony the righteousness of God and the justification of the ungodly do not become known; nor can a man forsaken by God, because of his blindness and folly, abuse the forbearance of God. Hence the nations, though invited by nature to the long-suffering and kindness of God, nevertheless for many ages did not have the calling which is necessary for faith, the love of God, and the conversion of the sinner, God leaving them and shutting them up under disobedience, Rom. 11:32; that is, hardening them by his judgment, so that he might show his wrath, and because he has not decreed by his eternal purpose to call them to eternal salvation.

units.la: XV. Alio ergo potentiore medio electi vocantur, verbo scilicet Dei, non quovis illo, sed eo, per quod Deus homini peccatori amabilis fit. Hoc verbum est notificatio Testamenti, sive propositi æterni Dei, quòd is in Christo peccatorem redimere, per gratiam & potentiam suam propter meritum Salvatoris, efficere, ut is opera Diaboli oderit, & Deum creatorem & redemptorem, novæ vitæ, justitiæ & gloriæ auctorem diligat; atque eo modo hominem sanctificare decreverit. Unde S. Petrus dixit: Verbum Dei, quod in æternum perstat, esse ῥῆμα τὸ εὐαγγελισθὲν εἰς ὑμᾶς verbum quod evangelizatur, sive prædicatur ad nos, 1. Pet. I. 25. hoc est, βουλὴ & θελημα& consilium voluntatis Dei, seu ἀγάπησιν τῶν αἰώνων, ὃν ἐποίησεν ἐν Χρι-στῷ propositum seculorum, quod fecit in Christo, Ephes. I. 11. III. 11. prædicari iis, qui vocantur, ut habeant argumentum & motivum amandi eum, & sine timore serviendi ei, quem propter peccata sua & justitiam ipsius suopte ingenio non potest non odisse.
units.tr: XV. Therefore the elect are called by another and more powerful means, namely the word of God, not just any word, but that by which God makes himself lovable to the sinful man. This word is the announcement of the Testament, or eternal purpose of God, that he has decreed to redeem the sinner in Christ, by his grace and power, on account of the Saviour's merit, and to bring it about that he hates the works of the devil and loves God as Creator and Redeemer, the author of new life, righteousness and glory; and so to sanctify the man. Hence St. Peter said: The word of the Lord abides for ever, and this is the word that was preached to you [ῥῆμα τὸ εὐαγγελισθὲν εἰς ὑμᾶς], the word which is evangelized, or preached, to us, 1 Pet. 1:25. That is, the counsel and will [βουλὴ, θελημα], the counsel of the will of God, or the purpose [πρόθεσιν] of the ages, which he made in Christ, Eph. 1:11; 3:11. This is preached to those who are called, so that they may have a reason and motive for loving him, and may serve him without fear, whom, on account of their sins and his righteousness, they cannot by their own nature avoid hating.

units.la: XVI. Tria in verbo hoc, quo electi vocantur, insunt, Testimonium, Mandatum & Promissio. Testimonium est de salute in Christo data. Hoc est testimonium, quòd vitam æternam nobis dedit Deus. Et hæc vita in Filio ejus est, 1. Joh. V. 11. Hoc Testimonium vocatur Evangelium, quod antecedit promissio salutis per Christum parandæ. Evangelium hoc primò peccatoribus sensu peccatorum & iræ Dei contritis gratiam Dei in Christo offert; tum revelans eam, quæ à temporibus seculorum tacita fuit, Rom. XVI. 25. tum declarans, quod natura sit incomprehensibilis, & vel stultitia vel offendiculum ratione, 1. Cor. I. 2. tum ostendens ejus participandæ modum per fidem. Si credideris in corde tuo, quòd Deus eum suscitaverit ex mortuis, salvaberis. Corde enim creditur ad justitiam; ore fit confessio ad salutem, Rom. X. 9. 10. Tum etiam Evangelium fidem operatur, ceu efficax & potens organon. Est enim potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, ibid. I. 16. Fides est ex auditu. Auditus autem per verbum Dei, ibid. X. 17. Atque hoc verbum de gratia proprie est λόγος ἐμφυτος, sermo, qui implantatur, cordi inscribitur, animas convertit, recreat. Jac. I. 21. Jer. XXXI. 33. Psal. XIX. 8. cujus solius auditu, cognitione & inscriptione peccator Deum amare, glorificare potest. Mandatum est resipiscendi & credendi Evangelio, hoc est, abnegata justitia propria, cujus stabiliendæ conatus non est nisi hypocrisis & abnegatio justitiæ Dei, nec non neglecto omni alio remedio salutis Deum ut justificatorem impii in Christo amandi, & ei animam suam in bonis factis commendandi. Quod mandatum, præsuppositio Testimonio Dei de salute electis in Christo data, pars legis est, jubentis credere omni Dei testimonio, & omnem voluntatem ejus revelatam implere. Quæ etiam lex ei, qui vocatur, prædicata non tantùm in agnitionem peccati ducit, Rom. III. 20. VII. 7. & defectus pravitatémque naturæ, multiplicémque in actionibus ἀνομίαν ostendit; sed etiam maledictionem comminatur; & utroque illo actu ad gratiam Evangelii, peccatoribus, laborantibus & oneratis, pauperibus spiritu, & trepidantibus ad Dei verbum destinatam præparat. Denique Promissio de salute omni credenti donanda, seu declaratio universalis de salute omni credenti certò conferenda eodem verbo prædicatur. Quam non tam voluntatis generalis, & nullum certum subjectum respicientis, vel suspensi desiderii aut voti in Deo; quàm certæ veritatis complexæ ex decreto & testamento Dei fluentis, & à Deo sic approbatæ, ut tamen fidem illam cui salus promittitur, in solis electis operari decreverit, declarationem esse, non semel monuimus.
units.tr: XVI. Three things are contained in this word by which the elect are called: testimony, command and promise. The testimony is the good news of salvation given in Christ. This is the testimony that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son, 1 John 5:11. This testimony is called the gospel, and it goes before the promise of salvation to be obtained through Christ. The gospel first offers God's grace in Christ to sinners who are crushed by a sense of their sins and of God's wrath. Then it reveals what was kept secret since the world began, Rom. 16:25. Then it declares that the nature of this grace is beyond comprehension and, to reason, either foolishness or a stumbling block, 1 Cor. 1:23. Finally, it shows the way of partaking of it through faith: If you believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation, Rom. 10:9-10. The gospel also works faith, as an effective and powerful instrument, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, ibid. 1:16. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing comes through the word of God, ibid. 10:17. This word of grace is properly an implanted word [λόγος ἔμφυτος], a word that is planted in the heart, written upon it, converts souls and renews them, James 1:21; Jer. 31:33; Ps. 19:8. By hearing, knowing and having this word written on the heart alone, a sinner is able to love and glorify God. The command is to repent and to believe the gospel, that is, to renounce one's own righteousness, the attempt to establish which is nothing but hypocrisy and a rejection of the righteousness of God, and, neglecting every other remedy for salvation, to love God as the justifier of the ungodly in Christ, and to commend one's soul to him in good works. This command, presupposing the testimony of God concerning the salvation given to the elect in Christ, is a part of the law, which commands us to believe every testimony of God and to fulfil all his revealed will. This law, when it is proclaimed to the one who is called, not only leads to the knowledge of sin, Rom. 3:20; 7:7, and shows the defect and corruption of nature and the manifold lawlessness [ἀνομία] in actions, but also threatens a curse; and by both of these acts it prepares sinners, who are labouring and burdened, poor in spirit and trembling at the word of God, for the grace of the gospel that is destined for them. Finally, the promise that salvation is to be bestowed on everyone who believes, or the universal declaration that salvation is to be surely conferred on everyone who believes, is proclaimed by the same word. This is a declaration not so much of a general will of God that regards no definite subject, or of a suspended desire or wish in God, but of a certain truth that is complex, flowing from the decree and testament of God, and so approved by God that, nevertheless, he has decreed that the faith to which salvation is promised should be wrought only in the elect; as we have pointed out more than once.

units.la: XVII. Vocatio per Verbum, quatenus illa per homines, sive peculiari docendi officio, sive communi charitatis lege, qua incitante eùnt populi multi; & dicent, venite & ascendemus ad montem Jehovæ &c. Jes. II. 3. obstrictos peragitur, externa est. Ac licèt proprie ad solos electos pertineat, & Συμβεβηκὸς tamen, licet non sine dispensatione Divina ad reprobos etiam illam pervenire, supra, indicata etiam rei ejus causa, ostendimus. Sed non iccirco iis æquè atque electis jus & fas est Testamentum Dei sibi vendicare, velut ἰχυρὸν παράκλησιν & καθᾶπερ γέννων consolationem, vel incitationem fortem confugientium ad Christum, ad arripiendam spem expositam Hebr. VI. 18. sibi applicare; quia ad Christum cum abnegatione sui, & glorificatione Dei, cum vera fame & siti justitiæ, non confugiunt, quæ lex iis, qui vocati ad salutem contendunt, dicta est. Licèt enim vocati ab homine jubeantur credere in Christum, tamen nihil iis absolutè sic promittitur; neque sic ad consolationem, vel salutare aliquod beneficium capessendum citantur; sed tantùm ad officium illud, ad quod auditum fidei præconium nium eos obligare potest; ac nonnisi eo præsti-to ad salutem, adeóque non decretoria voce Dei ad aliquid, quod Evangelio proprium & eximium est; sed hominis ministerio, promissionem conditionatam ; ex Dei Testamento fluentem & Divinitus approbatam pronuntiantis, ad officium in mandato fidei suppositò de salute per Christum conferenda testimonio vi ipsius Legis debitum absolutè, ad beneficium salutare cum conditione vocantur.
units.tr: XVII. The external call through the Word, insofar as it is carried out by men, either by the special office of teaching or by the common law of charity, by which, when urged on, many peoples go and say, "Come, let us go up to the mountain of Jehovah," etc., Isa. 2:3, is external. And although it properly pertains to the elect alone, it is nevertheless an accident [συμβεβηκός] that this call, though not without divine dispensation, also reaches the reprobate, as we have shown above, including the reason for this. But for that reason the reprobate do not have the same right and warrant as the elect to claim God's testament for themselves, as a strong consolation [ἰσχυρὰν παράκλησιν] and as an anchor [καθάπερ ἄγκυραν] of the soul, and to apply it to themselves as a strong encouragement to those who flee to Christ, to lay hold of the hope set before them, Heb. 6:18. For they do not flee to Christ with self-denial and the glorifying of God, with a true hunger and thirst for righteousness, which is the law that is given to those who strive, being called, toward salvation. For although those called by man are commanded to believe in Christ, nothing is absolutely promised to them in this way, nor are they summoned in this way to take hold of consolation or any saving benefit. They are only summoned to that duty to which the proclaimed message of faith can bind them. And only when this duty has been performed do they come to salvation. So they are not called, by a decisive voice of God, to something that is proper to and distinctive of the gospel; rather, through the ministry of man, announcing a conditional promise that flows from God's testament and is divinely approved, they are called, by the very force of the law, as a debt absolutely owed to the duty that the testimony concerning salvation through Christ supposes in the command of faith, and called to the saving benefit under the condition.

units.la: XVIII. Neque sic periculum est, ne vel nondum conversi promissionem Evangelicam sibi non applicare, vel conversi, sed tentati idem ex tentationum gurgite non satis eluctari valeant, quem metum nobis vocationem per verbum Evangelii ad solos electos restringentibus nonnulli incutere conantur. Nam nondum conversi vel electi vel reprobi sunt. Illi per gratiam vocationis certò sibi promissionem Evangelii, quando hora vocationis illorum adest, applicant. De his non laboramus, quia iis à Deo relictis, nihil unquam promissum est; neque adeò, quod sibi applicent, habent. Quoad conversos tentatos, illi ex tentationum fluctibus non vocationis Evangelicæ ad reprobos etiam directæ remis velisque (quàm parum enim ad consolationem facit, quod cum reprobis commune est?) sed electionis illorum ex certissimis criteriis, in Dei verbo & conscientiæ sensu patefactis confirmatæ præsidio liberari debent.
units.tr: XVIII. Nor is there therefore any danger that those not yet converted will be unable to apply the evangelical promise to themselves, or that those who are converted, but tempted, will not be able to struggle sufficiently out of the whirlpool of temptations. This is the fear that some try to instil in us, who restrict the call through the word of the gospel to the elect alone. For those not yet converted are either elect or reprobate. The former apply to themselves with certainty the promise of the gospel through the grace of the call, when the hour of their calling arrives. We are not concerned about the latter, because, since they have been abandoned by God, nothing has ever been promised to them, and so they have nothing that they could apply to themselves. As for the converted who are tempted, they ought to be freed from the waves of temptations not by the oars and sails of the evangelical call, which is also directed to the reprobate (for how little does it help consolation that it is shared with the reprobate?), but by the protection of their election, which is confirmed by the most certain criteria made manifest in the word of God and in the sense of conscience.

units.la: XIX. Tametsi verò externa vocatio aliena quadam vi ad reprobos etiam dirigitur, tamen ad omnes & singulos homines promiscuè nunquam directa est; nunquam dirigitur. Cùm enim verbum Dei propter solorum electorum vocationem prædicetur, satis constat, non quovis tempore, omnibus in locis mundi electos extitisse, vel existere. Ideo vocatio per auditum habet ἰδίως καιρὸς propria tempora, 1. Tim. II. 6. & certum μέτρον κανὸν certam mensuram regulæ, vel lineæ 2. Cor. X. 13. 15: missionis suæ, adeò ut nec uno tempore ad omnes & singulos pervenerit, nec diversis temporibus hucusque ad omnes pervenerit, certo indicio, quod & vocatio, & salus nonnisi ex testamento, cujus notificatio ipsa vocatio est; detur. Ideò & olim gentiles; & post Judæos à vocatione hac Deus definito judicio suo excludit; includens omnes sub inobedientiam, ut omnium misereretur, Rom. XI. 32. Quin & gentium in V. T. decretoriam rejectionem novitas vocationis earundem ad salutem sub N. T. evincit. Mysterium Christi in præcedentibus ætatibus non est cognitum filiis hominum, sicut nunc revelatum est sanctis Apostolis ejus & Prophetis in Spiritu; quod etiam gentes sint cohæredes, & concorpores, & participes promissionis ejus in Christo per Evangelium, Ephes. III. 4. 5. 6. Quibus verbis μαλα ἐμφαλνίσις mysterium Christi non in hoc ponitur, quod gentes factæ sint cives Ecclesiæ in uno corpore, ibid. II. 16. hoc est; unâ cum Judæis, quia non hoc est principale καταλλαγὴς reconciliationis negotium, ut gentes cum Judæis in uno corpore Ecclesiæ externæ socientur, sed potiùs ut nova adoptione per Christum Deo reconcilientur. Unde etiam Gentium sub N. T. vocatio ad salutem proponitur; ut illustre προσδοκημα gratuitæ reconciliationis Dei nobiscum, cùm adhuc essemus peccatores & inimici;
units.tr: XIX. Although the external call is directed, by a certain external force, even to the reprobate, nevertheless it is never directed, and never is directed, to all and each of men without distinction. For since the word of God is preached for the sake of calling the elect alone, it is quite clear that the elect have not existed, or do not exist, at all times and in all places of the world. Therefore the call through hearing has its own proper times [ἰδίοις καιροῖς], 1 Tim. 2:6, and a certain measure of the rule [μέτρον τοῦ κανόνος], or line, 2 Cor. 10:13, 15, of its mission. So it has neither reached all and each at one time, nor, at different times up to now, has it reached all. This is a sure sign that both the call and salvation are given only from the testament, of which the notification is the call itself. Therefore God, by his definite judgment, has excluded from this call both the Gentiles of old and, afterwards, the Jews, shutting up all under disobedience, that he might have mercy on all, Rom. 11:32. Indeed, the newness of the call of the Gentiles to salvation under the New Testament proves the decisive rejection of the Gentiles in the Old Testament. The mystery of Christ was not made known to the sons of men in former ages, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ through the gospel, Eph. 3:4-6. In these words the mystery of Christ is not placed, in a very clear disclosure [μάλα ἐμφανίσεως], in this, that the Gentiles have been made citizens of the Church in one body, Eph. 2:16, that is, together with the Jews. For this is not the principal business of reconciliation, that the Gentiles should be joined with the Jews in one external body of the Church, but rather that they should be reconciled to God through Christ by a new adoption. Hence also the call of the Gentiles under the New Testament to salvation is set forth as a remarkable pledge of God's free reconciliation with us, when we were still sinners and enemies,

units.la: Rom. V. 8. 10. quando Gentes antonomasticè vocat ἁμαρτωλὸς peccatores, eásque alibi hoc titulo à Judæis secernit, dicens: Nos natura Judæi, non ex gentibus peccatores, Gal. II. 15. non quòd quoad naturalem corruptionem utrique pares non fuerint; cùm Paulus idem dixerit: Eramus & nos natura filii iræ, sicut & reliqui, Ephes. II. 3. Sed quia extrinseca nascendi in Gentilismo & in populo Judaico conditio propter fœdus gratiæ & vocationem externam Judæis & liberis ipsorum dispensatum, & à gentibus ablatum impar fuit: ut ita φύσις natura, ibid. omnium Adami posterorum naturalium propagationem naturalem; at Gal. II. 15. Judaici populi cognationem, secundum quam Judæi κλάδοι & φύσιν rami secundum naturam, Rom. XI. 21. appellantur, significet.
units.tr: Romans 5:8, 10. When he calls the Gentiles sinners in the special sense (ἁμαρτωλοί), and elsewhere separates them from the Jews under this title, saying, We are Jews by nature, not sinners from the Gentiles, Gal. 2:15. This is not because the two were not equal in their natural corruption, since Paul also said, We too were by nature children of wrath, just as the rest, Eph. 2:3. Rather, the external condition of birth among the Gentiles was unequal to that of the Jewish people, who had the covenant of grace and the external calling entrusted to them and to their children, and from which the Gentiles were excluded. So "nature" (φύσις), as in Eph. 2:3, means the natural propagation of all Adam's natural posterity, whereas in Gal. 2:15 it means the kinship of the Jewish people, by which the Jews are called the branches according to nature (Rom. 11:21).

units.la: XX. Dilutum est, quòd in Adamo ante diluvianos, in Noacho postdiluvianos usque ad Christum; post Christum per Apostolos omnes vocatos esse asserunt. Nam vocatio per signa ad vocationem directa, & ab iisdem intellecta esse, minimè constat. Illud quoque nimis ἀναγματοῦ est; quòd vocationem externam, ut universalem facere possint, quavis χειραγωγία, qua homo ad Deum duci potest, sive ea per verbum Dei lectum; vel prædicatum, sive per naturam, sive per Ecclesiæ famam fiat, definiunt. Nam per naturæ vocem neminem salutariter vocari, jam supra constituimus. Hac enim via ad Deum ire velle, Evangelii abnegatio est. Graviter S. Augustinus contra Jul. Introducis, inquit, hominum genus, quod placere Deo possit sine fide Christi, lege naturæ. Hoc est, unde vos maximè detestatur Ecclesia Christiana. Neque hic de notitia Dei; quæ ex contemplatione naturæ, vel insitis principiis practicis, vel fama & rumore rauco, sed de vocatione publica ad communionem & amicitiam cum Deo, quæ sine revelatione & notitia Christi iniri nequit, & ex qua fides oriri potest, quæstio instituitur. Quomodo enim invocabunt, in quem non crediderint? Quomodo credent ei, de quo non audiverint? Quomodo audient absque prædicante? Quomodo prædicabunt, cùm missi non fuerint? Rom. X. 14. 15. Talis ergo vocatio & fidei causa esse debet, & missionem postulat. Frustra autem intentionem saltem Dei, juxta quam omnes & singulos sic vocari velit, imò etiam præcipiendo, promittendo, & tribus distinctis vicibus manifestando exequatur, ingeminant; quia nec intentio talis probari potest, & diversæ dispensationi fœderis gratia ab ipso Deo profectæ; quæ ἰδίως καιρὸς propria tempora habuit, repugnat: & executio nimium vacillat; cùm nec præceptum, nec promissio universalis uspiam occurrat; & patefactio primò duobus hominibus, Adamo & Evæ; mox octo, Noæ & sociis ejus in arca; denique per Apostolos, qui omnes & singulos homines, imò etiam populos vocare non potuerunt, universalis dici non posset. Neque etiam communis Christo cum omnibus hominibus natura gratiam quoque & notificationem ejus communem ac promiscuam facit; quia præter naturæ illius communionem propius cum ipso vinculum necessarium est, fidei & Spiritus S. Denique nec incredulitas mundi, quæ toties in Scriptura accusatur; & causa damnationis, juxta verba Christi
units.tr: XX. It is refuted that they assert that before the Flood all were called in Adam, after the Flood until Christ in Noah, and after Christ through the Apostles. For it is by no means clear that a calling through signs directed to calling was also understood by those same people. It is also far too absurd that, in order to make the external calling universal, they define it as any guidance (χειραγωγία) by which a man can be led to God, whether this happens through the reading or preaching of the Word of God, through nature, or through the report of the Church. For we have already established above that no one is savingly called by the voice of nature. To wish to go to God by this way is the denial of the Gospel. Augustine rightly says, sharply, against Julian: You introduce a kind of men who can please God without faith in Christ, by the law of nature. This is precisely what the Christian Church most of all detests in you. Nor is the question here about the knowledge of God that comes from contemplating nature, from innate practical principles, or from hearsay and vague rumour. It concerns the public calling to communion and friendship with God, which cannot be entered without revelation and knowledge of Christ, and from which faith can arise. How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent? Rom. 10:14, 15. Such a calling must therefore be the cause of faith and requires a mission. Those who insist that God's intention at least, by which he wills that all and each be so called, is carried out by commanding, promising, and making it known on three distinct occasions, do so in vain. For such an intention cannot be proved, and it conflicts with the diverse dispensation of the covenant of grace, which comes from God himself and has its own proper times. And the execution is far too unsteady, since no universal command or promise appears anywhere, and the revelation was first made to two people, Adam and Eve, then to eight, Noah and his companions in the ark, and finally through the Apostles, who could not call all and each person, or even all peoples, and so cannot be called universal. Nor does Christ's common nature with all men make grace and its proclamation common and promiscuous to all, since beyond the communion of that nature a closer bond is necessary, that of faith and the Holy Spirit. Finally, the unbelief of the world, which is so often charged against it in Scripture, and which, according to the words of Christ,

units.la: tt Christi : Qui non credit, jam condemnatus est, Joh. III. 18. ponitur, universalem vocationem arguit. Nam incredulitas illorum intelligitur, qui de Christo audiverunt, & tamen non credunt, & salutem tantam negligunt, digni qui judicentur, quia se ipsos condemnant dum non dignos se vita aeterna judicant, Act. XIII. 46. Sed & illi, qui non audiverunt, adeóque negativè increduli sunt, eo ipso quòd Christus iis datus non est, nec de eo aliquid audiverunt, manent in peccato & sub ira Dei, adeóque jure meritòque judicantur.
units.tr: Christ's words: He who does not believe is already condemned, John 3:18, is given as the cause of damnation, does not argue for a universal calling. For the unbelief meant is that of those who have heard of Christ and yet do not believe, and neglect so great a salvation; they are worthy of judgment because they condemn themselves, while they judge themselves unworthy of eternal life, Acts 13:46. But those too who have not heard, and so are negatively unbelieving, because Christ has not been given to them and they have heard nothing of him, remain in sin and under the wrath of God, and are therefore justly and rightly judged.

units.la: XXI. Vocatio externa electorum per verbum ab hominibus praedicatum cum interna Spiritus S. compellatione conjunctissima est. Absque hac enim esset, illa nihil prodesset. Nam verbum ab hominibus praedicatum ferit aures hominis naturalis & in peccato mortui, qui nec aures castigatas ad audiendum, nec oculos illuminatos ad videndum, nec cor subactum ad amandum & obsequendum habet, Esaj. VI. 9. Omne verbum quantumvis Divinum, verissimum, sapientissimum, per se suavissimum & maximè amabile ad peccatorem, in peccato adhuc mortuum factum, & a Spiritu S. cordi non inscriptum, manet litera, peccatorem occidit, eúmque ad peccandum irritat, 2. Corinth. III. 6. Rom. V. 20. VII. 8. Peccatum pestilentissimum, quod per legem in homine peccatore efficitur, est odium Dei, & sanctitatis ejus, & judicii ipsius. Verbi Dei praeco illud proponit, commendat, robur & potentiam ejus demonstrat, occasionem cogitandi de rationibus, propter quas ad Deum redeundum est, suppeditat. Sed quid hoc ad mortuum, imò Dei & verbi ejus hostem infensissimum? Quantavis vehementia, eloquentia, authoritate, diligentia in id incumbat, efficere nequit, ut naturalis homo eas causas, ceu veras gravesque admittat, & approbet & diligat. Plantat ille, rigat, sed nihil est plantans, vel rigans, sed Deus, qui incrementum dat, 1. Cor. III. 6. 7. Non igitur sine Deo de veritate verbi quemquam is convincere, nedum homini peccatori verbum Dei amabile reddere, vel ei amorem ejus instillare potest, hoc enim munus Dei & Spiritus S. est. Fidelis Deus est, per quem vocati estis ad communionem Filii ejus Jesu Christi, ibid. I. 9. Homo enim animalis non capit ea, quae Spiritus Dei sunt. Stultitia ei sunt, non potest cognoscere, quia spiritualiter dijudicantur, ibid. II. 14. Deus illud Spiritus S. digito inscribit cordi, Jerem. XXXI. 33. atque sic implantatum efficit, Jac. I. 21. & simul ut, cui sic lex inscripta & implantata a Spiritu Dei est, condelectetur legi Dei, operatur, Rom. VII. 22. Ideò fides, amor & timor Dei & verbi ejus Spiritus S. authori passim accepta feruntur, adeò ut ab iis donis Spiritus fidei, 1. Cor. XII. 9. 2. Cor. IV. 13. amoris, 2. Timoth. I. 7. & timoris, Esaj. XI. 2. nuncupetur. Spiritus Sancti enim operationes appropriatae sunt, illuminare mentes, Ephes. I. 17. 18. 1. Cor. II. 10. corda regenerare, Joh. III. 3. fidem operari, 2. Cor. IV. 13. Christo nos unire & in nobis per dona sua, arrhabonis instar, ibid. I. 22. Denique Deus, qui dixit, ut ex tenebris lux splendeat, fulsit in cordibus vestris, ad illuminationem cognitionis gloriae Dei in conspectu Jesu Christi, ibid. IV. 6.
units.tr: XXI. The external calling of the elect through the Word preached by men is most closely joined with the internal compulsion of the Holy Spirit. For without this the former would profit nothing. The word preached by men strikes the ears of natural man, who is dead in sin, and who has neither ears taught to hear, nor eyes enlightened to see, nor a heart subdued to love and obey (Isa. 6:9). Every word, however Divine, most true, most wise, in itself most sweet and most lovable, remains a letter to a sinner who is still dead in sin and whose heart has not been written upon by the Holy Spirit; it kills the sinner and stirs him up to sin (2 Cor. 3:6; Rom. 5:20; 7:8). The most pestilential sin, which is produced in the sinner by the law, is hatred of God, of his holiness and of his judgment. The preacher of the Word sets this out, commends it, demonstrates its strength and power, and supplies occasion to think about the reasons why one must return to God. But what is this to a dead man, or rather an utterly hostile enemy of God and his Word? However much he applies himself to this with vehemence, eloquence, authority and diligence, he cannot bring it about that the natural man accepts, approves and loves these reasons as true and weighty. One plants, another waters, but it is not the planter or the waterer who matters, but God who gives the increase, 1 Cor. 3:6, 7. Therefore no one can convince anyone of the truth of the Word without God, much less make the Word of God lovable to a sinful man or instil its love in him; for this is the work of God and of the Holy Spirit. God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 1:9. The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned, 1 Cor. 2:14. God writes that Spirit upon the heart with his finger, Jer. 31:33, and so makes it implanted, James 1:21, and at the same time works it so that the one in whom the law has thus been written and implanted by the Spirit of God delights in the law of God, Rom. 7:22. Therefore faith, love and fear of God and of his Word are everywhere ascribed to the Holy Spirit as author, so much so that he is named from these gifts the Spirit of faith, 1 Cor. 12:9; 2 Cor. 4:13, of love, 2 Tim. 1:7, and of fear, Isa. 11:2. For the operations of the Holy Spirit are appropriated to him: to enlighten the minds, Eph. 1:17, 18; 1 Cor. 2:10, to regenerate the hearts, John 3:3, to work faith, 2 Cor. 4:13, to unite us to Christ and to dwell in us through his gifts, as a pledge, 2 Cor. 1:22. Finally, God, who said, Let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, 2 Cor. 4:6.

units.la: XXII. Idem verbum est, quod & homo praedicat, & Spiritus S. cordi inscribit: una prophetie vocatio, sed cujus causa & medium duplex, organicum homo verbum extus praedicans, principale, Spiritus S. intus illud cordi inscribens. Ejus exemplum conspicuum est in Lydia purpuraria, cui Paulus Evangelium praedicavit, Deus cor aperuit, ut a Paulo praedicata non tantùm auribus externis hauriret, sed in primis corde aperto reciperet, intelligeret, crederet & amaret, Act. XVI. 14. Ut verbum Dei per hominem praedicatum, & per Spiritum S. inscriptum audiamus, recipiamus & diligamus; auribus apertis opus est. Et auribus quidem corporis praeconium Evangelii humanum percipimus. Sed nihil juvat aures corporis arrigere homini verbum loquenti, si aures cordis clausae obseratèque maneant. Ne obduretis cor vestrum sicut in Meriba, sicut in die Massa in deserto, Psal. XCV. 8. Sic homo redditur verbi Dei auditor, sed factor non redditur, Jac. I. 22. Aures cordis apertae ipsa voluntas hominis, verbo Dei attendentis illud, ceu verbum bonum, Divinum & usquequaque excellens, cum gaudio & gratiarum actione, intromittentis, diligentis, & cum omni obsequio exprimentis, sunt. Et aures quidem cordis natura graves clausae & obthuratae, Psalm. LVIII. 5. Esaj. VI. 10. Zach. VII. 11. averse, Prov. XXVIII. 9. segnes, Hebr. V. 11. & praeputio obductae, Jerem. VI. 10. Act. VII. 51. sunt Eas aperire, emollire, arrigere, applicare, circumcidere, quis nisi cordis formator Deus potest?
units.tr: XXII. It is the same word that man preaches and the Holy Spirit writes upon the heart. There is one calling, but its cause and means are twofold: the man who preaches the word outwardly is the instrumental means, and the Holy Spirit who writes it inwardly on the heart is the principal cause. A clear example of this is Lydia the seller of purple, to whom Paul preached the Gospel, and God opened her heart, so that she took in what Paul preached not only with her outward ears, but above all received it with an opened heart, understood it, believed it and loved it, Acts 16:14. For us to hear, receive and love the Word of God, preached by man and written by the Spirit, our ears must be opened. Indeed, through the ears of the body we perceive the human proclamation of the Gospel. But it does nothing to help to prick up the ears of the body toward a man who speaks, if the ears of the heart remain shut and barred. Do not harden your hearts as at Meribah, as on the day of Massah in the wilderness, Ps. 95:8. In this way a man is made a hearer of the Word of God, but he is not made a doer, James 1:22. The ears of the heart are the will of man itself, opened, attending to the Word of God, receiving it with joy and thanksgiving as a good word, Divine and in every way excellent, loving it, and expressing it in all obedience. But the ears of the heart are by nature heavy, shut and stopped up, Ps. 58:5; Isa. 6:10; Zech. 7:11; turned away, Prov. 28:9; sluggish, Heb. 5:11; and covered over with foreskin, Jer. 6:10; Acts 7:51. Who but God, the former of the heart, can open them, soften them, make them attentive, apply them, and circumcise them?

units.la: XXIII. Aliter ergo longè Deus vocans agit cum filiis suis, quàm cum aliis omnibus, quos hominum ministerio etiam vocari finit. De electis enim intelligenda sunt illa Pauli: πιστός ὁ καλών, ὅς ἴ πιστός fidelis est ille vocans, qui etiam faciet, adducet, 1. Thess. V. 24. His igitur aperit cor, dat cor novum, largitur Spiritum regenerationis, infundit animis eorum semen seu verbum suum, quatenus illud est potentia Dei ad salutem, eósque non jubet tantùm quaerere salutem in Christo, & eam sperare sub conditione, uti caeteros, sed cùm circumciderit cor ipsorum, Deut. XXX. 6. & dederit ipsis oculos ad videndum, aures ad audiendum, cor ad intelligendum, ibid. XXIX, 4. ut non modò venire possint, sed etiam ut veniant, & penitus Christo credant, eósque, uti Augustinus loquitur, voluntatibus illorum, quas in iis operatus est, traxerit: demum consolatur, & velut certa jam eorum salute, confidere jubet; loquens velut ad cor: Ne metuas parve grex, quia placuit Patri vobis dare Regnum. Luc. XII. 32. Gaudete, quod nomina vestra scripta sunt in Coelis. ibid. X. 20. Confide fili, remissa tibi sunt peccata, Matth. IX. 2. Vobis datum est nosse mysteria Regni Coelorum, ibid. XIII. 11. Invocabit nomen meum, & ego respondebo ipsi. Dicam; hic est populus meus; & ipse dicet: Hic Deus meus. Zach. XIII. 9. Dic animae meae. Ego sum salus tua, Ps. XXXV. 3. Hos & novit de nomine. Exod. XXXIII. 17. & vocat nomine, Joh. X. 3. Haec igitur consummata vocatio est, mensuram omnem & emphasin nominis illius implens, qua Spiritu intus renovante, illuminante, flectente, trahente, fundante, solidante, confirmante, obsignante, homo in Regno gratiæ nova creatura fit, sicut per vocationem, & imperium ejusdem in Regno naturæ creatura factus est. Unde etiam κλῆσις ἢ Θεῦ vocatio Dei, Rom. XI. 29. ἡ ἄνω supera vocatio, Phil. III. 14. & ἐπουράνιοι cœlestis, Heb. III. 1. appellatur, ut cum ἐκλογῇ electione, ut causa sua 2. Pet. I. 10. copulatur. Quemadmodum etiam S. Paulo perinde est dicere κατ' ἐκλογὴν secundum electionem, & ἐκ ἢ καλοῦντος ex vocante, Rom. IX. 11.
units.tr: XXIII. God's way of calling his sons is therefore very different from his way with all the others whom he allows to be called through the ministry of men. Those words of Paul must be understood of the elect: πιστὸς ὁ καλῶν, ὃς καὶ ποιήσει [faithful is he who calls you, who also will do it], he will bring it about, 1 Thess. 5:24. To these he opens the heart, gives a new heart, bestows the Spirit of regeneration, and pours into their souls his seed or word, insofar as it is the power of God unto salvation. He does not merely command them to seek salvation in Christ and to hope for it on condition, as he does with the rest. Rather, when he has circumcised their heart, Deut. 30:6, and has given them eyes to see, ears to hear, and a heart to understand, ibid. 29:4, they are enabled not only to come but actually to come, and to believe fully in Christ. He draws them, as Augustine puts it, by those wills of theirs which he himself has worked in them. At last he comforts them, and, as if their salvation were now certain, bids them trust, speaking as if to the heart: Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom, Luke 12:32. Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven, ibid. 10:20. Take heart, son, your sins are forgiven, Matt. 9:2. To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, ibid. 13:11. He will call upon my name, and I will answer him. I will say, "This is my people," and he will say, "This is my God", Zech. 13:9. Say to my soul, "I am your salvation", Ps. 35:3. These he knows by name, Exod. 33:17, and calls by name, John 10:3. This, then, is the complete calling, filling up every measure and the full meaning of that name. By it, through the Spirit renewing, enlightening, bending, drawing, establishing, strengthening, confirming and sealing within, a man becomes a new creature in the kingdom of grace, just as through the calling and command of God he was made a creature in the kingdom of nature. Hence it is also called the calling of God, Rom. 11:29 [κλῆσις τοῦ Θεοῦ]; the upward calling, Phil. 3:14 [ἡ ἄνω κλῆσις]; and heavenly, Heb. 3:1 [ἐπουράνιοι]; and it is joined with election as its cause, 2 Pet. 1:10. In the same way it is all one to Paul to say according to election [κατ' ἐκλογήν] and of him who calls [ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος], Rom. 9:11.

units.la: XXIV. Status eorum, qui vocantur, & dum vocantur, geminus, internus & externus est. Ille internis, hic externis illorum qualitatibus dignoscitur. Secundum qualitates internas peccatis corrupti, & in iisdem mortui sunt. Eramus natura filii irę, sicut & reliqui, Ephes. II. 3. Vos in lapsibus mortuos unà cum Christo vivificavit. Gratia enim salvati estis, ibid. v. 5. Col. II. 13. Sunt ἐσκοτισμένοι τῇ διανοίᾳ obtenebrati mente, abalienati à vita Dei, propter ignorantiam, quæ in iis est, & propter indurationem cordis eorum, Ephes. IV. 18. Non capaces eorum, quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, 1. Cor. II. 14. duri & lapidei corde, Ezech. XI. 19. proni tantùm ad malum omni tempore, inde à pueritia, Genes. VI. 5. VIII. 21. inimici Dei, & Legi ejus subjici nescii, Rom. VIII. 7. amentes, rebelles, errantes, servientes voluptatibus & cupiditatibus variis, Tit. III. 3. Secundum qualitates externas sunt infantes & maximam partem stulti, infirmi, ignobiles, sed coram mundo; quoad gratiam verò DEI æternam electi, & in tempore à Christo redempti. Non vocat enim Deus hominem sapientem & fortem, sed fatuum & debilem, הוי Quis fatuus est? Divertat huc. Quis expers cordis? Dicit ipsi: Venite, vescimini de pane meo, Prov. IX. 4. 5. Videte vocationem vestram, (vocatos vestros) fratres, quòd non multos sapientes secundum carnem, (sapientia carnali, Politica, inprimis Ecclesiam, ceu Regnum quoddam terrenum, humanis consiliis gubernantes) non multos potentes, (potentia & brachio carnali Ecclesiam regere conantes) non multos nobiles, sed stulta mundi (non Philosophos, Pharisæos, Scribas, sed rudes & in mundi oculis cum cruce sua stultos) elegit Deus, ut confundat sapientes, & impotentia mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat potentes. Et ignobilia mundi, & pro nihilo habita elegit Deus, & quæ nihil sunt, ut eos, qui aliquid sunt, aboleat, ut non glorietur illa caro coram ipso, 1. Cor. I. 26-30. Nemo se decipiat. Si quis inter vos videtur sapiens esse in hoc sæculo, fiat stultus, ut sapiens fiat, deponat id, quod apud homines sapientia videtur, & id discat, quod hominibus stultitia esse videtur, ibid. III. 18. Ideò Christus: Gratias tibi ago, Pater, quòd hæc occultasti sapientibus & intelligentibus & revelasti infantibus, Matth. XI. 25.
units.tr: XXIV. The state of those who are called, both before and while they are being called, is twofold, internal and external. The former is known by their internal qualities, the latter by their external ones. As to their internal qualities, they are corrupt through sins and dead in them. We were by nature children of wrath, as the rest were, Eph. 2:3. He made us alive together with Christ when we were dead in our trespasses; for by grace you have been saved, ibid. v. 5; Col. 2:13. They are darkened in their understanding [ἐσκοτισμένοι τῇ διανοίᾳ], alienated from the life of God, through the ignorance that is in them and the hardening of their heart, Eph. 4:18. They cannot receive the things of the Spirit of God, 1 Cor. 2:14. They are hard and stony of heart, Ezek. 11:19; inclined only to evil at all times from their youth, Gen. 6:5, 8:21; enemies of God, not subject to his law, Rom. 8:7; foolish, disobedient, going astray, slaves to various lusts and pleasures, Titus 3:3. As to their external qualities, they are infants and for the most part foolish, weak and of low birth, but in the eyes of the world. As to the eternal grace of God, however, they are elect, and in time they are redeemed by Christ. For God does not call a man who is wise and strong, but one who is foolish and weak. Ho! [הוי] Who is foolish? Let him turn in here. To the one who lacks understanding he says, "Come, eat of my bread", Prov. 9:4-5. Consider your calling, brethren, that not many of you are wise according to the flesh (with worldly wisdom, governing the Church above all by human counsels, as if it were some earthly kingdom), not many are powerful (trying to rule the Church by power and carnal arm), not many are noble; but God has chosen the foolish things of the world (not philosophers, Pharisees or scribes, but the simple, who in the world's eyes are fools with their cross), that he might shame the wise; and God has chosen the weak things of the world, that he might shame the strong. God has chosen the low and despised things of the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in his presence, 1 Cor. 1:26-30. Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become foolish, that he may become wise. Let him set aside what seems wisdom among men, and learn what seems foolishness to men, 1 Cor. 3:18. Therefore Christ says: I thank you, Father, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to infants, Matt. 11:25.

units.la: XXV. Ad statum illum externum etiam retulimus gratiam Dei, secundum quam ab æterno electi, & in tempore per mortem Christi redempti sunt. Fons nempe vocationis gratia electionis æternæ, & redemptionis Christi temporalis est. Fit enim illa κατ' ἐκλογὴν secundum propositum æternum, Rom. VIII. 28. quod propositum est κατ' ἐκλογὴν ἢ Θεῦ secundum electionem Dei, ibid. IX. 11. Ideò ἀμεταμελήτως pœnitudinis expers est; ibid. XI. 29. æque ac πίστεως
units.tr: XXV. To that external state we also refer the grace of God, by which the elect were chosen from eternity and in time redeemed through the death of Christ. The source of calling is indeed the grace of eternal election and of Christ's redemption in time. For the calling takes place according to an eternal purpose [κατ' ἐκλογὴν secundum propositum æternum], Rom. 8:28, and that purpose is according to the election of God, ibid. 9:11. Therefore it is free from repentance [ἀμεταμελήτως], lacking any regret, Rom. 11:29, just as the purpose of faith itself is.

units.la: propositum ipsum. Firmum enim stat fundamentum, & habet sigillum hoc: Novit Dominus eos, qui sui sunt, 2. Tim. II. 19. Quin & ex electione æterna, ceu causa sua, arcessitur, Rom. VIII. 28. 29. 30. Salvavit nos & vocavit vocatione sancta, ut essemus scilicet filii ipsius, non secundum opera nostra (quæcunque lex præcipit, quia nihil nos præstamus ad hoc, ut vocemur, regeneremur, & in Regnum lucis transferamur) sed secundum proprium propositum, & gratiam datam nobis in Christo Jesu ante tempora seculáría, 2. Tim. I. 9. Neque aliud vocatio est, quàm temporalis electio, seu separatio à mundo, quæ manu & operatione Dei fit, in tempore verò Christus se ipsum dedit pro nobis, ut redimeret nos ab omni defectione, & purificaret sibi populum peculiarem, æmulum bonorum operum, Tit. II. 14. Non tantùm ergo Christus mortuus est, ut nos redimeret ab omni iniquitate, solvendo legem peccati & mortis, ut Lex, quæ non poterat condemnare peccatum potens coram tribunali Dei dominium in peccatorem ad mortem, non posset non condemnare peccatum, & auctorem peccati Diabolum, petentem in Dei judicio dominium in electos Dei à Christo redemptos ad mortem, atque sic peccatum nobis ad condemnationem non imputaretur amplius neque etiam vocationem & sanctificationem nostram impedire posset; sed etiam, ut nos purificaret sibi populum peculiarem, æmulum bonorum operum, hoc est, ut nos, ceu peculium Dei, rem non perdendam, vel alienandam, sed in æternum retinendam, sibi purificaret, separaret, sanctificaret populum, cujus ipse Rex, Dominus & caput esset, à quo cognosceretur; & amaretur; qui omnem in ipso fiduciam collocaret; à quo glorificaretur; in quo ipse viveret. Non possumus enim esse Christi, si non sumus ad ipsum. Non ejus populus, nisi in nobis sit & regnet Spiritus ejus, corda nostra per fidem purificans. Non enim Spiritus Dei habitat in corde impuro, in quo impietas & mundanæ cupiditates regnant. Ejus proin purificationis initium, vocatio nostra, morti & redemptioni Christi accepta referri debet. Ex ejus enim merito Deus gratiam abundanter effundit in nos in omni sapientia & prudentia, Ephes. I. 8. Pluribus verò id ipsum Loc. XIX. 88. confirmavimus.
units.tr: itself. For the foundation stands firm, and has this seal: The Lord knows those who are his, 2 Tim. 2:19. Indeed, it is drawn from eternal election as its cause, Rom. 8:28-30. He saved us and called us with a holy calling, that we should be his sons, not according to our works (whatever the law commands, since we contribute nothing toward being called, regenerated, and transferred into the kingdom of light), but according to his own purpose and the grace given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages began, 2 Tim. 1:9. Calling is nothing other than temporal election, or separation from the world, which is effected by the hand and operation of God. In time, Christ gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works, Titus 2:14. Christ therefore did not die merely to redeem us from all iniquity by dissolving the law of sin and death, so that the law, which could not condemn sin, would not be able to condemn sin, and the devil, the author of sin, who claimed in God's judgment dominion over the elect of God redeemed by Christ, leading to death, would no longer have sin imputed to us for condemnation, nor be able to hinder our calling and sanctification. He died also that he might purify for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works, that is, that he might cleanse, separate and sanctify for himself us, as God's peculiar possession, a thing not to be lost or alienated but kept for ever, a people of which he himself would be King, Lord and Head, by whom they would be known and loved, who would place all their trust in him, by whom he would be glorified and in whom he himself would live. For we cannot be Christ's if we are not his, and we are not his people unless his Spirit is in us and reigns, purifying our hearts through faith. For the Spirit of God does not dwell in an impure heart in which ungodliness and worldly desires reign. Therefore the beginning of this purification, our calling, must be referred to the merit and redemption of Christ. For by his merit God pours out grace abundantly upon us in all wisdom and prudence, Eph. 1:8. We have confirmed this same point at greater length in Loc. XIX. 88.

units.la: XXVI. Operatio Spiritus S. per verbum foris prædicatum, & intus cordi inscriptum nec naturalis, nec moralis, vel mediata; per verbum & alia externa media, tantùm, uti novissimè Pajonus Aurelianensis Ecclesiastes persuadere laboravit, sed supernaturalis immediata ineffabilis, omnipotens & efficacissima est. Nam Spiritus S. sic vocans novos creat homines electos, in peccatis mortuos vivificat; cæcos illuminat, duros emollit, pravos & perversos convertit; ad Christum trahit, atque ita recipientibus, patientibus tantùm, non etiam agentibus vel cooperantibus novas qualitates indit, illos novas creaturas facit, sicut prima creatione creaturas fecit. Est enim vocatio re ipsa efficacia Spiritus S. mentem illuminantis & cor aperientis, & verbi illius Dei, quod in sæcula manet, 1. Pet. I. 25. & quo ante secula filios & hæredes salutis vocavit. Quæ Spiritus S. & verbi vis & efficacia talis & tanta est, ut hominem & voluntatem ejus Deo per amorem subjiciat;
units.tr: XXVI. The operation of the Holy Spirit, which works through the word preached outwardly and written inwardly on the heart, is not natural, not moral, and not mediate, through the word and other external means alone, as the Aurelian minister Pajonus has lately laboured to persuade. It is supernatural, immediate, ineffable, almighty and most efficacious. For the Holy Spirit, in calling, creates new elect men, makes alive those who are dead in sins, gives sight to the blind, softens the hard, and converts the crooked and perverse. He draws them to Christ, and so gives new qualities to those who only receive and suffer, not to those who act or cooperate, and makes them new creatures, as he made creatures in the first creation. For the calling is in fact the efficacy of the Holy Spirit illuminating the mind and opening the heart, and of that word of God which abides for ever, 1 Pet. 1.25, by which he called the sons and heirs of salvation before the ages. Such is the force and efficacy of the Holy Spirit and of the word, and so great is it, that it subjects man and his will to God through love.

units.la: Status eorum, qui vocantur, & dum vocantur, geminus, internus & externus. Illæ internis qualitatibus cognoscitur, velut quòd natura peccatis corrupti sunt; hic externis, velut quòd sunt infantes, stulti, infirmi. jiciat, & nolentem volentem, ex fugiente accedentem, ex renitente voluntarium sacrificium (Psal. CX. 3.) faciat. Propterea S. Paulus Ephesiis precatus est, ut Deus Domini nostri Jesu Christi, Pater ille gloriæ, det illis Spiritum sapientiæ & revelationis in cognitione ipsius, revelatos oculos mentis eorum, ut sciant, quæ sit spes vocationis illorum, & quæ divitiæ gloriæ & hæreditatis ejus in Sanctis, & quæ sit supereminens magnitudo potentiæ ejus in credentibus κατα τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ juxta operationem roboris virium ipsius, quam exeruit in Christo, dum eum ex mortuis suscitavit, Eph. I. 17-20. Et eandem ἐνέργειαν & δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ τὴν ὑποταξαι ἑαυτῷ τὰ πάντα operationem sive efficaciam, qua sibi subjicere omnia potest, Phil. III. 21. Cujus operatio est circumcidere cor, & facere, ut amemus Deum, Deut. XXX. 6. Dare cor unum & Spiritum in visceribus, amovere cor lapideum, & dare cor carneum, Ezech. XI. 19. 20. XXXVI. 26. 27. Convertere, Jerem. XXXI. 18. trahere, Cant. I. 4. Joh. VI. 44. &c. regenerare ex aqua & Spiritu, ibid. III. 5. condere in Christo Jesu ad bona opera, Ephes. II. 10. novum condere & facere, 2. Cor. V. 17. Gal. VI. 15. Operari & velle & operari, Phil. II. 13. potentiam suam in infirmitate hominis consummare, 2. Cor. XII. 9. Θεὸς δυνάμεις Divina sua potentia largiri omnia, quæ ad vitam & pietatem sunt, 2. Pet. I. 3. Adeò quidem, ut nostra ὑποταγὴ τῆς ὁμολογίας εἰς Εὐαγγέλιον Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ subjectio astipulationis nostræ in Evangelium Jesu Christi 2. Cor.
