IX. 13. sit revera ex eo, qui omnia ὑπέταξε subjecit Filio hominis, Psal. VIII. 7. & fides sit donum Dei, Ephes. II. 8. & ejus donatio sit donatio Christi, quia accipientibus Christum datur potestas, ut fiant filii Dei, Joh. I. 12. & super illis, qui credunt, brachium Domini, eos afferens reveletur, Esaj. LIII. 1. secundum illud: Omnis qui nominatur de nomine meo, quem ad gloriam meam בראתיו יצרתיו אף עשיתיו creavi, formavi, feci, ibid. XLIII. 7. Populus quem formavi mihi, gloriationem meam narrabunt, ibid. v. 21. Cum viderit ילידי natos suos, opus manuum mearum in medio sui, sanctificabunt nomen meum, &c. ibid. XXIX. 23. Populus tuus, נצר מטע virgultum plantationis meæ, & opus manuum mearum ut glorificer, ibid. LX. 21. Neque alia causa est, quòd diverso adeò cum fructu prædicetur verbum Dei etiam de gratia, seu Evangelium, dum aliorum mentes excæcat Deus hujus seculi, ne radiet ipsis lux Evangelii gloriæ Christi, qui est imago Dei, 2. Cor. IV. 4. sed potius iis sit stultitia, 1. Cor. I. 23. & odor mortis ad mortem, 2. Cor. II. 16. in aliis autem Deus, qui dixit, ut ex tenebris lux splendescat, fulgeat in cordibus illorum ad illuminationem cognitionis gloriæ Dei in facie Jesu Christi, ibid. IV. 6. & Evangelium sit potentia Dei ad salutem, Rom. I. 16. Hæc omnia vocationem arguunt & supernaturalem, quia excedunt vires totius naturæ creatæ, & profunditates Dei revelant, 1. Cor. II. 10. & admirabilem, quia talia nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in mentem hominis venerunt, ibid. v. 9. & omnipotentem & efficacissimam, infallibilémque eventum habentem, quia procedit ab ea virtute & potentia, qua Deus omnia creat, generat, vivificat, & qua Christum ex mortuis suscitavit, & nos denique suscitaturus est.
units.tr: The state of those who are called, both before and while they are called, is twofold, internal and external. The former is known by internal qualities, for instance that by nature they are corrupted by sins; the latter by external ones, for instance that they are infants, foolish and weak. It subjects, and from the unwilling it makes the willing, from the one who flees it makes the one who comes, from the one who resists it makes a willing sacrifice (Ps. 110.3). Therefore St Paul prayed that the Ephesians might have God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, give them the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of their mind being enlightened, that they may know what is the hope of their calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, and what the exceeding greatness of his power in those who believe (κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ) according to the working of the strength of his might, which he exerted in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, Eph. 1.17-20. And the same energy and power (ἐνέργειαν) by which he is able to subject all things to himself (τὴν ὑποταξαι ἑαυτῷ τὰ πάντα), the operation or efficacy by which he can subject all things, Phil. 3.21. Of this operation the effect is to circumcise the heart and make us love God, Deut. 30.6; to give one heart and a spirit within, to take away the stony heart and to give a heart of flesh, Ezek. 11.19, 20; 36.26, 27; to convert, Jer. 31.18; to draw, Song 1.4; John 6.44, etc.; to regenerate of water and the Spirit, ibid. 3.5; to create in Christ Jesus unto good works, Eph. 2.10; to make and create anew, 2 Cor. 5.17; Gal. 6.15; to work both to will and to work, Phil. 2.13; to perfect his power in the weakness of man, 2 Cor. 12.9; his divine power grants all things that pertain to life and godliness (θεῖα δυνάμει), 2 Pet. 1.3. So much so that our subjection of confession to the Gospel of Jesus Christ (ὑποταγὴ τῆς ὁμολογίας εἰς Εὐαγγέλιον Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ), 2 Cor. 9.13, is truly from him who subjected all things to the Son of man, Ps. 8.7; and faith is the gift of God, Eph. 2.8; and its giving is the gift of Christ, because to those who receive Christ power is given to become the sons of God, John 1.12; and the arm of the Lord is revealed over those who believe, bringing them to him, Isa. 53.1, according to that saying: everyone who is named by my name, whom I have created for my glory (בראתיו יצרתיו אף עשיתיו) I have created, formed, made, ibid. 43.7; the people whom I have formed for myself shall declare my praise, ibid. v. 21; when he sees his (ילידי) children, the work of my hands in the midst of him, they will sanctify my name, etc., ibid. 29.23; your people (נצר מטע) the branch of my planting, the work of my hands that I may be glorified, ibid. 60.21. Nor is there any other cause why the word of God, and the Gospel too, concerning grace, is preached with such diverse fruit: the god of this world has blinded the minds of others, lest the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine on them, 2 Cor. 4.4; but rather it is foolishness to them, 1 Cor. 1.23, and the smell of death unto death, 2 Cor. 2.16; while to others God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, shines in their hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, ibid. 4.6; and the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation, Rom. 1.16. All these things show that the calling is supernatural, because they exceed the powers of all created nature and reveal the depths of God, 1 Cor. 2.10; and wonderful, because such things neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, ibid. v. 9; and almighty and most efficacious, having an infallible outcome, because it proceeds from that virtue and power by which God creates, generates and makes alive all things, by which he raised Christ from the dead, and by which he will at last raise us also.

units.la: XXVII. Præterea Deus Verbo & Spiritu
units.tr: XXVII. Moreover, God by his Word and Spirit

units.la: suo vocans, trahens, ducens & convertens tum voluntatem movet, ut ad verbi annuntiati argumentum, veritatem & bonitatem attendat, tum intellectum collustrat, ut veritatis ac salubritatis Evangelii, ad quam sic attendit, convincatur, eiq; assentiatur: tum deniq; voluntatem eandem flectit & determinat, ut sermonem verum bonumque, cui attendimus & consentimus, diligamus, & veluti vivum in nobis efficiamus. Quæ tria aprime necessaria sunt, quia & mens hominis male sibi conscia Dei verbum timet, neque, ceu rebus terrenis immersa & alligata, Divinas contemplari amat, imo eas odit horrétque: & mens hominis cæca sapientiam Dei stultitiam reputat: & voluntas contumax bonum cognitum licet, utpote concupiscentiis suis adversans nec capere nec diligere potest. Sed accedente omnipotente virtute Dei, & exerto ac revelato brachio ejusdem cor hominis refractarium domatur, mollitur, renovatur, & novum creatur; mens cœlesti lumine perfunditur; atque ita mutatus & renovatus, ac velut novus genitus homo facilè verbo salutis attendit, illud animo attento considerat, assensu dignatur & diligit. Et singuli Dei convertentis actus eventum succesumque certissimum habent. Deo enim volente jubente perinde hæc fiunt, atque volente jubente Cœli & terra, & exercitus eorum creati sunt. Ipse dixit & fuit. Ipse præcepit, & factum est. Ps. XXXIII. 6. 9. Voluntati ejus quis resistit? Rom. IX. 19. Ac licet primus ille & secundus actus per generalem Dei gratiam quodam modo etiam in non electis locum habere possit: & tertius tamen in solis electis obtinet: & primus quoque & secundus ut salutaris sit, speciali gratia indiget, atque speciali hac gratia Dei productus in solis etiam electis invenitur.
units.tr: calls, draws, leads and converts his own. He moves the will so that it attends to the argument, truth and goodness of the announced word. He enlightens the understanding so that it is convinced of the truth and saving power of the Gospel, to which it thus attends, and assents to it. Finally, he bends and determines the same will so that it loves the true and good word to which we attend and with which we agree, and makes it, as it were, a living thing within us. These three acts are plainly necessary, because the human mind, conscious of its guilt, fears God's word, and, being immersed and bound in earthly things, does not love to contemplate divine things but actually hates and shudders at them. The blinded human mind counts God's wisdom foolishness, and the stubborn will, although it knows the good, cannot receive or love it, since it opposes its own lusts. But when the almighty power of God comes in, and his arm is stretched out and revealed, the human heart, which resists, is subdued, softened and renewed, and is created anew. The mind is flooded with heavenly light, and so the man, changed and renewed, and as if newly born, readily attends to the word of salvation, considers it with an attentive mind, and deigns to assent to and love it. Each act of God's converting work has a certain outcome and success. For when God wills and commands, these things happen just as, at his will and command, the heavens and the earth, and all their host, were made. He spoke and it was. He commanded and it stood fast. Ps. 33.6, 9. Who has resisted his will? Rom. 9.19. And although that first and second act may in a certain way have a place even among the non-elect through God's general grace, the third act is found only in the elect; and the first and second, if they are to be saving, also need a special grace, which is found, produced by God's special grace, only in the elect.

units.la: XXVIII. Qui sic à Deo vocantur electi, nec statim ab utero, nec eodem omnes tempore, sed prout Deo illis gratiam suam dispensare visum est, in ovile Christi per vocationem aggregantur. Ante verò quàm ad summum Pastorem illum colligantur, in communi deserto dissipati aberrant; nec ab aliis ulla re differunt, nisi quòd singulari Dei misericordia protegantur, ne ante vocationem suam in ultimum mortis præcipitium ruant. In ipsis ergo nil nisi Adami progeniem, communem massæ corruptionem redolens, conspicere est. Quòd non in extremam usque & desperatam impietatem feruntur, non ingenita aliqua illorum bonitate evenit, sed quia in eorum salutem oculus Dei excubat, & manus veluti extenta est. Non enim, quod non nullorum ἐνέργημα est, cordibus eorum semen aliquod electionis insitum est, cujus virtute semper ad pietatem & timorem Dei inclinentur. Nam qui à S. Paulo Ephes. II. 1. &c. internus vocationem præcedens status describitur, granum hujus seminis nullum ostendit. Eratis, inquit, mortui in lapsibus & peccatis, in quibus ambulastis secundum seculum mundi hujus, juxta principem potestatum aëris, qui nunc agit in filiis contumacibus. Inter quos & nos versabamur aliquando in concupiscentia carnis nostræ, facientes, quæ carni & menti libebant. Et eramus natura filii iræ, sicut & cæteri, v. 1. 2. 3. Idem cùm denuntiasset, nec scortatores, nec idololatræ, nec adulteros, nec molles, nec concubitores cum
units.tr: XXVIII. Those who are thus called by God, the elect, are gathered into Christ's fold through vocation, neither all at once from the womb nor all at the same time, but as God has seen fit to dispense his grace to them. Before they are gathered to that chief Shepherd, they wander scattered in the common wilderness, and they differ in nothing from others, except that they are protected by the singular mercy of God, lest before their calling they fall into the final precipice of death. In them, therefore, nothing is to be seen but the offspring of Adam, smelling of the common corruption of the mass. That they are not carried off into extreme and hopeless impiety does not happen through any innate goodness of theirs, but because the eye of God watches over their salvation and his hand is, as it were, stretched out. For a seed of election is not implanted in their hearts, as some hold, by which they are always inclined to piety and the fear of God. For the state preceding internal vocation, described by St. Paul in Ephesians 2.1 and following, shows no grain of such a seed. You were, he says, dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, who now works in the sons of disobedience. Among them we too once lived in the lusts of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest, vv. 1-3. When he had said the same, that neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor effeminate, nor abusers of themselves with

units.la: Actus Spicum masculis, nec fures, nec avaros regni Dei hæredes futuros; statim subjungit: Καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε. Et tales nonnulli eratis; sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, &c. 1. Cor. VI. 10. 11. Et alibi: Sicut præbuistis membra vestra serva impuritati, & iniquitati ad iniquitatem; Ita nunc sistite membra vestra serva justitiæ. Quem igitur fructum ex illis habuistis, in quibus nunc merito erubescitis? Rom. VI. 19. 21. Quale justitiæ germen fuit in Rahab ante fidem? Jos. II. 1. In Manasse, cum Hierosolyma Prophetarum sanguine rataret? 2. Reg. XXI. 16. In latrone, qui inter ultimos tandem spiritus de resipiscentia cogitavit? Frustra Paulum, qui in Pharisaismo suo irreprehensibilis vixit, Phil. III. 6. objectant, quia talis fuit secundum justitiam externam & legalem, qualis Luc. XVIII. 11. 12. describitur; & quæ ad hoc requirebatur, ut quis sacros locos adire posset, nec censuram metuere, & testimonium hominis probi mereri posset. Qui sic apud homines ἀμέμπτοι sunt, fiducniam habent apud homines, sed non apud Deum, neque ea in rea reprobis differunt. Quos ergo Deus è communi perditionis gurgite eruere statuit, eos in suam opportunitatem differt, & tantùm conservat, ne in peccatum in Spiritum S. incidant, vel in peccato suo moriantur.
units.tr: men, nor thieves, nor covetous persons shall inherit the kingdom of God, he immediately adds: Καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε [And such were some of you]; but you were washed, you were sanctified, etc. 1 Cor. 6.10, 11. And elsewhere: As you once yielded your members to uncleanness and iniquity, leading to more iniquity, so now yield your members to righteousness, leading to sanctification. What fruit did you then have from the things of which you are now ashamed? Rom. 6.19, 21. What germ of righteousness was there in Rahab before faith? Josh. 2.1. In Manasseh, when he filled Jerusalem with the blood of the prophets? 2 Kings 21.16. In the thief, who at the last gasp at length thought of repentance? They object to Paul, who lived blameless in his Pharisaism, Phil. 3.6, in vain, because he was such in external and legal righteousness as is described in Luke 18.11, 12, and such as was required for one to be able to approach the sacred places, not to fear censure, and to earn the testimony of an upright man. Those who are thus blameless before men have confidence before men, but not before God, and in this respect they do not differ from the reprobate. Those whom God has decided to snatch from the common whirlpool of perdition, he defers to his own appointed time, and meanwhile only preserves, lest they fall into the sin against the Holy Spirit or die in their sin.

units.la: XXIX. Hæc de vocatione Dei ejusque per omnipotentem Dei vim operatione & infallibili successu capitalis doctrina & Scripturis allatis testatissima est: & plane cum statu hominis per peccatum corrupto miserrimo congruit: &Dei gloriosæ gratiæ maximè consentanea est. Ne ergo miremur, Sathanam, cujus regnum in Deo ejusque gloria deprimenda, & homine, dominationis suæ instrumento, supra Deum ejusque gratiam & gloriam evehendo, & denique in infernum præcipitando maximè occupatur, veritati huic semper infensum se gessisse. Deum enim & gloriam ejus pertinacissimè odit, & hominem honoris specie nequiter supplantat. Hæc causa est tot errorum & hæresOn, gratiam & potentiam Dei minuentium & humanæ voluntatis & arbitrii potentiam exaltantium, quorum Historiam paucis texere è re fuerit.
units.tr: XXIX. This is the chief doctrine concerning God's calling, and its operation through the omnipotent power of God and its infallible success, and it is most fully attested by the Scriptures cited. It plainly agrees with the most wretched condition of man corrupted by sin, and is most consonant with the glorious grace of God. Let us not wonder, therefore, that Satan, whose kingdom is chiefly occupied with diminishing God and his glory, and with exalting man, the instrument of his own dominion, above God and his grace and glory, and finally with casting him down into hell, has always been hostile to this truth. For he most stubbornly hates God and his glory, and wickedly supplants man under the appearance of honour. This is the cause of so many errors and heresies diminishing the grace and power of God and exalting the power of the human will and free choice. It will be fitting to weave a brief history of them.

units.la: XXX. In Ecclesia Christiana latè graßabantur tum Manichæi, fingentes, omnia fato fieri, & pro eodem, & externis motibus mentis & voluntatis bonos vel malos esse: tum Enthusiastæ, qui absque exercitiis resipiscentiæ & fidei conversionem hominis per immediatum & sensibilem Spiritus S. operationem & velut afflatum fieri asserebant. Etiam Patres non pauci τὸ αὐτεξούσιον seu liberum arbitrium, pravo Philosophorum exemplo ita extollebant, ut gratiam Dei ab ejus usu suspenderent. Et palam Origenes ἀπαθείαν & ἀναμαρτησίαν docuit, statuens, posse hominem in hac vita tantam ad perfectionem pervenire, ut affectibus vacuus omni periculo careat. Manichæis & Enthusiastis renitens, Patribus errantibus consentiens Pelagius Brito, ex Monacho Presbyter factus, ingenii, doctrinæ & vitæ innocentis laude celebris, omnè gratiæ Divinæ succesum à libero arbitrio suspendit; nactus adjutores Cœlestium, à quo Cœlestiani, & Julianum, Episcopum Capuanum, acri ingenio & pari eloquentia juvenem; & asseclas non paucos, Rufinum, Evagrium, Sulpi-
units.tr: XXX. In the Christian Church the Manichaeans spread widely, feigning that all things happen by fate, and that by the same fate men are good or bad through their outward movements of mind and will. The Enthusiasts also spread, who asserted that the conversion of man takes place without the exercises of repentance and faith, through an immediate and perceptible operation of the Holy Spirit, as if by a breath. Not a few of the Fathers also, following the bad example of the philosophers, so extolled autexousion, that is, free choice, that they made the grace of God depend on its use. And Origen openly taught apatheia and anamartesia, holding that a man in this life can attain to such perfection that, free from passions, he is without any danger. Opposing the Manichaeans and Enthusiasts, and agreeing with the erring Fathers, Pelagius the Briton, a monk who became a presbyter, famous for his talent, learning and reputation for an innocent life, made the whole success of divine grace depend on free choice. He found helpers in Caelestius, from whom came the Caelestians, and in Julian, bishop of Capua, a young man of keen wit and equal eloquence, and not a few followers: Rufinus, Evagrius, Sulpicius, Jovian and others. In the East there were also the Novatians, or Meletians. These men removed altogether the necessity of grace converting and regenerating, once man's corruption through sin was taken away; and they attributed everything to the freedom of the will, which they held to be innate in man, and which they also placed in a state of indifference towards good and evil.

units.la: tium, Jovianum, alios; In Oriente etiam Novatianos, sive Meletianos. Illi corruptione hominis per peccatum sublata gratiæ converten-tis & regenerantis necessitatem pariter sustulerunt; & ad libertatem arbitrii, quippe homini congeniti, cuncta retulerunt; quam etiam in indifferentia ad bonum & malum constituerunt; in eadem indifferentia imaginem Dei, ad quam homo conditus sit & perseveraverit, & humanæ conditionis decus supra animalia reliqua constitutum, collocantes. Cùm tamen in S. Literis nihil frequentius occurrat, quàm nomen χάρις gratia, Pelagius primò ipsam naturam nomine gratiæ venire asseruit; utpote quæ à Deo donata una cum libero arbitrio fuerit. Sic dicere impiè soliti sunt: A Deo habemus, quòd homines sumus: à nobis, quòd justi sumus. Sed gratiæ talis confessionem nimis fraudulentam Augustinus & Catholici cùm explosissent merito, ille novum fucum faciens, gratiam in Lege constituit. Sicut oculos, aures, naturali licet videndi & audiendi facultate præditos, ab objectis tamen excitari oportet, ut videant & audiant: ita Lege & doctrina adjuvari liberum arbitrium debere statuebat; sic tamen, ut iis tantùm attentio excitetur, & cognitio promoveatur; imò etiam sine iis non pauca sciri vel agi possint. Qua ratione plus ille libero arbitrio arrogavit, quàm sensibus, quia licèt oculi, aures, lucem, colorem, sonos naturaliter recipere possunt, tamen producere eosdem non possunt. Qui gratiæ significatus merus Judaismus fuit. Judæis enim proprium est sublata Christi gratia, in lege gloriari, Rom. II. 23. Addidit tandem, argumentis Catholicorum motus, gratiam Christi liberaliter velut concedens; salvari hominem per liberum arbitrium sub statu naturæ, Legis Mosis & Gratiæ Christi. Hoc vos, sic Augustinus ad Bonifac. lib. I.21. exprobrat, non vultis, inimici gratiæ Christi, ut eadem gratia Jesu Christi salvi facti credantur antiqui; sed distribuitis tempora secundum Pelagium, in cujus libro hoc legitur, & ante legem dicitis salvos factos per naturam, deinde per Legem, postremò per Christum, quasi hominibus duorum superiorum temporum, ante Legem scilicet & in Lege sanguis Christi non fuerit necessarius. Sed & Christi gratiam subdolè & dicis gratia confessus est, cùm non aliud quàm naturam, id est, naturales vires arbitrii, utcunque doctrina Christi adjutas intellexerit. Tria enim adjutoria Christum peccatoribus attulisse, remissionem peccatorum, iis qui peccarunt (nam quosdam peccati planè exsortes statuit) collatam, planè gratuitam & satisfactionis omnis expertem, & ideò iis, qui sub Evangelio vivunt, necessariam, quia sub eo peccandi consuetudo magis quàm sub Lege Naturæ & Mosis, utpote quæ facilè expleri potuerit, inoleverit: Doctrinam Evangelicam, quam respicere ad cavendas & superandas futurorum peccatorum tentationes plurimùm referat; & Exemplum virtutis Christi, quo ipsa doctrina Evangelica expressa fuerit. Quam gratiâ licèt plenis buccis ceu Evangelio propriam crepare sveverit, nil tamen à lege illa distat, quia forinsecus haud secus ac lex auribus insonat, at cor ipsum non mutat. Addidit his etiam ad extremum internam gratiam, seu internum auxilium possibilitatis, Unum in intellectu, quo efficiatur; ut Per revelationem Dei facienda noverimus,non cognita faciamus: alterum in voluntate, quam adjuvari ajebat, tum per concursum generalem, tum per corroborationem ejus, ut faciliùs operetur: tum per infusa quædam Spiritus S. dona, infusámque justitiam quandam, nempe internam animi renovationem, quæ fiat per habitualem gratiam in remissione peccatorum, quam tamen nonnisi pro peccatis præteritis, non futuris cavendis vitandisque, auxilium ferre docuit; cùm id non fiat per adjutorium remissionis habitualis, sed per actuale Divinæ inspirationis, qua juvemur, ne concupiscentia post remissum peccatum superstite & tumultuante superemur: tum denique per effecta quædam Baptismi, cujusmodi sint, purgare animam, renovare, regenerare, justificare, sanctificare, &c. Quæ omnia magnificis licèt verbis confessa libero tamen hominis arbitrio subjecit; utpote à cujus determinatione tota Dei gratia, & qualiscunque illa pendeat. Ac revera hæc nihil aliud quàm recoctus Ethnicismus, aut ad summum Judaismus, seu potiùs Sadducæismus cuncta liberæ hominis proæresi subjiciens & turpe naturæ gratiáque adulterium fuerunt, per quæ servitus & mors in peccato tolli, & voluntas ad volendum & operandum bonum præparari nullo modo potuit.
units.tr: For by the corruption of man through sin, they equally removed the necessity of grace that converts and regenerates. They attributed everything to freedom of the will, which they said is born in man, and they placed it in an indifference toward good and evil. In that same indifference they located the image of God, in which man was created and has persisted, and the dignity of the human condition, set above the other animals. Yet nothing occurs more often in the Holy Scriptures than the word χάρις [grace]. Pelagius first asserted that nature itself comes under the name of grace, since it was given by God together with free will. They were accustomed to speak impiously in this way: We have from God that we are men; from ourselves that we are righteous. But Augustine and the Catholics, having rightly rejected this confession of grace, which was too deceptive, Pelagius, putting on a new disguise, established grace in the Law. He taught that, just as the eyes and ears, although endowed with the natural faculty of seeing and hearing, must still be stirred by objects in order to see and hear, so free will ought to be aided by the Law and by doctrine. He held that this aid only arouses attention and promotes knowledge, and that indeed many things can be known or done even without these. By this reasoning he ascribed more to free will than to the senses, since the eyes and ears can receive light, colour and sounds naturally, yet cannot produce them. This sense of grace was pure Judaism, for it is peculiar to the Jews, with the grace of Christ set aside, to glory in the law, Rom. 2.23. Finally, moved by the arguments of the Catholics, he added the grace of Christ, conceding it as if generously, and maintained that man is saved through free will under the state of nature, the Law of Moses and the grace of Christ. Augustine reproaches him in this way in Against Boniface: This you, he says, (Pelagius) do not wish, enemies of the grace of Christ, that the men of old be believed saved by the same grace of Jesus Christ (to Boniface, book 1, chapter 21). Instead you divide the times according to Pelagius, in whose book this is read, and you say that before the Law men were saved by nature, then by the Law, and finally by Christ, as if the blood of Christ were not necessary for men of the two earlier periods, namely before the Law and under the Law. But he also confessed the grace of Christ deceitfully, and called it grace only in name, since he understood nothing other than nature, that is, the natural powers of the will, however they might be helped by the teaching of Christ. For he said that Christ brought three aids to sinners: the forgiveness of sins, granted to those who have sinned (for he claimed that some are entirely free of sin), entirely gratuitous and free of any satisfaction, and therefore necessary for those who live under the Gospel, because under the Gospel the custom of sinning has taken firmer root than under the law of nature and of Moses, since it could be easily satisfied; the Evangelical doctrine, which contributes greatly to avoiding and overcoming the temptations of future sins; and the example of the virtue of Christ, by which the Evangelical doctrine itself was expressed. Although he was accustomed to trumpet this grace with full cheeks, as proper to the Gospel, it nonetheless differs in no way from that Law, because it sounds outwardly to the ears just as the Law does, yet does not change the heart itself. At the end he added to these the internal grace, or internal help of possibility, one aspect in the intellect, by which it is brought about, so that we may know through the revelation of God what is to be done, not that we may do what we know; and another in the will, which he said is aided both by general concurrence and by its strengthening, so that it may work more easily, and also by certain gifts of the Holy Spirit infused, and by a certain infused righteousness, namely the internal renewal of the mind, which takes place through habitual grace in the forgiveness of sins. Yet he taught that this help is given only for past sins, not for avoiding and shunning future ones; for this does not happen through the aid of habitual forgiveness, but through the actual inspiration of God, by which we are helped, lest, after sin has been forgiven, concupiscence remaining and stirring up, we be overcome by it; and finally through certain effects of Baptism, such as cleansing the soul, renewing, regenerating, justifying, sanctifying, and so on. Although he confessed all these things in magnificent words, he nevertheless subjected them to the free choice of man, since the whole grace of God, and whatever sort it is, depends upon its determination. And in truth these things are nothing other than a rehashed Heathenism, or at most Judaism, or rather Sadducism, subjecting everything to the free choice of man; and they were a shameful adulteration of nature and grace, by which bondage and death in sin could not in any way be removed, nor the will be prepared to will and to do good.

units.la: XXXI. Iccirco Catholici, Augustinus inprimis ille Pelagianæ impietatis malleus, Prosper Aquitanicus, Fulgentius, aliíque Veteres, Conciliorum etiam definitionibus adjuti in id maximè incubuerunt, ut venenum illud maturè ex Ecclesia tolleretur, & malum in herba suffocaretur. Stabat enim illis sententia, ejusmodi gratiæ auxilio naturam voluntatis à servitute sua liberari & expediri, ut bonum velit & operetur, neutiquam posse. Atq; eam in rem adversus Pelagianos liberi arbitrii non defensores, sed deceptores, uti Fulgentius eos appellat, argumentis ponderosis militarunt; cujusmodi sunt; quòd necessaria insuper sit creatio novi hominis, regeneratio, mutatio & apertio cordis; quòd externa media parum vel nihil heic proficiant, & non uvas, sed labruscas tantùm proferant: quòd in revelatione sapientiæ non sit sufficiens ad salutem gratia, cùm S. Paulus etiam tertium in Cœlum raptus & periculum incurrens, ne excellentia revelationum efferretur, ter ad preces conversus, tandem audiverit: Sufficit tibi gratia mea, 2. Cor. XII. 9. quæ gratia amplior & sola sufficiens adjici non debuisset, si in revelatione sapientiæ vera & sufficiens gratia esset: quòd ejusmodi gratia concupiscentiam vegetam relinquat, imò robustiorem etiam, quia ne agnitum quidem bonum velle possit: quòd Lex bonum præcipiat, malum vetet, & de cætero arbitrio voluntatis vires ad illud operandum, hoc vitandum non conferat; imò majorem etiam difficultatem afferat, & quasi muro quodam interposito observantiam impossibilem reddat, quia non data sit ad peccatum minuendum, vel tollendum, sed augendum potiùs, quin & passim, inprimis Joh. I. 17. gratiæ opponatur: quòd modus ille, quo accessu legis peccatum auctius & validius fiat, Deum extra culpam collocet, quia id ex parte Dei & Legis merè per accidens, ex innato verò & consuetudine roborato hominis vitio per se oriatur; cùm Lex per se non fomes, sed limes ardoris sit, quamvis propter vitium hominis ex limite magis magisque exardescat; multùmque interest, non quid accipiat, sed quis accipiat, nec quale sit, quod datur, sed qualis sit ille, cui datur: quòd Lex data sit, ut hominis superbia peccatorum agnitorum magnitudine frangatur: quòd Lex non Judæorum duntaxat, sed etiam Christianorum respectu, ante acceptam gratiam sit potentia peccati: quòd ad liberandam voluntatem vis cujuscunque doctrinæ & revelationis eadem sit, quæ legis est, quia per eam non aliud intellectui conferatur, quàm scientia, qua ostenditur, quàm magnum, utile, necessarium & gloriosum sit bonum facere, & malum declinare; & lex præmiorum pollicitatione, & poenarum comminatione armata longè efficacius, quàm hortatio, suasio vel consilium ullum ad operandum incitet; cùm Lex jubeat, hortatio, suasio consilium tantùm petat: quòd denique tota illa gratia Legis & doctrinæ Christianæ non aliud sit, quàm præconium justitiæ & salutis per naturam.
units.tr: XXXI. Therefore the Catholics, above all that hammer of Pelagian impiety, Augustine, along with Prosper of Aquitaine, Fulgentius and other ancient writers, aided also by the definitions of the Councils, laboured especially to ensure that this poison was removed from the Church in good time and the evil stifled while still in the grass. For they held the view that by such a grace the nature of the will could by no means be freed and set loose from its bondage, so that it wills and does good. To this end they fought against the Pelagians with weighty arguments, not as defenders of free will, but, as Fulgentius calls them, as its deceivers. Such arguments are these: that the creation of a new man, regeneration, change and the opening of the heart are also necessary; that external means avail little or nothing here, and bring forth not grapes but only wild grapes; that the grace of revelation of wisdom is not sufficient for salvation, since Saint Paul, caught up into the third heaven and in danger, lest he be puffed up by the excellence of the revelations, turned to prayer three times and at last heard: My grace is sufficient for thee, 2 Cor. 12.9. This greater grace, the one that alone suffices, would not have needed to be added, if the grace in the revelation of wisdom were true and sufficient; that such grace leaves concupiscence vigorous, indeed even stronger, since it cannot even will the good that is recognised; that the Law commands good, forbids evil, and then does not confer on the power of the will the strength to do the one or to avoid the other, but rather brings greater difficulty and, as if a wall had been placed between, renders obedience impossible, since it was not given to lessen or remove sin, but rather to increase it; and everywhere, especially John 1.17, it is set against grace; that the mode by which sin is made greater and stronger by the approach of the Law places God outside of blame, since this arises on the part of God and the Law merely by accident, but from the innate vice of man, strengthened by habit, arises of itself; whereas the Law is not in itself tinder but the boundary of the fire, although on account of the vice of man it blazes more and more from the boundary; and it matters greatly not what is received but who receives it, nor what is given but what sort of person it is to whom it is given; that the Law was given so that the pride of man might be broken by the greatness of the sins recognised; that the Law, not only in respect of the Jews but also of Christians, before grace is received, is the power of sin; that the force of any doctrine and revelation for freeing the will is the same as that of the Law, because through it nothing more is conferred on the intellect than knowledge, by which is shown how great, useful, necessary and glorious it is to do good and to turn from evil; and that the Law, armed with the promise of rewards and the threat of punishments, incites to action far more effectively than exhortation, persuasion or any counsel whatever, since the Law commands, while exhortation, persuasion and counsel only ask; and finally that the whole grace of the Law and of Christian doctrine is nothing other than a proclamation of righteousness and salvation through nature.

units.la: XXXII. Recoctor Pelagianismi & Sadducæismi Socinus totam salutis & cognitionis Dei causam in libero delectu arbitrii, utrum velit, sibi bonum, an rectum prosequi, collocans, gratiam non aliud quàm naturam, facultatem liberi arbitrii, remissionem peccatorum gratuitam, & promissionem vitæ æternæ fecit. Pernegat verò ipse, & pernegant ejus assecla, Deum ad se vocantem omnipotente vi sua in intellectum & voluntatem hominis agere, sed id tantùm satagere, ut vocando Evangelium prædicetur, cui tum extus per promissa & minas, tum intus per promissorum obsignationem in corde obedientis adjuto sine ulteriore Spiritus S. gratia sola animi volentis probitate obedire: & nolentis malitia non obedire possit. Evangelium enim æquè ac universam Scripturam à quovis attento lectore fine illuminatione Spiritus Sancti intelligi posse, neque Spiritus Sanci donum aliud quid esse, quàm donum miraculorum ad tempus concessum, vel ipsum Evangelium, & certam vitæ æternæ spem perpetuò manentem, asserunt. Denique vocatos secundum propositum appellari sciscunt, quotquot auditam Christi discipli- nam factis ipsis sequuntur, quia hoc DEI propositum sit, ut homines salutarem veritatem sibi annuntiatam amplectantur, & juxta eam vitam omnem instituant. Quæ crassè nimis Pelagiana & impia sunt, iisdémq; argumentis, quibus veteres Pelagii hærefin refutarunt confodi possunt. Neq; sanè omnes, quibus Evangelium prædicatur, eidem obedire sine singulari gratia Spiritus S. possunt, tum quia obstat naturæ lethalis, & sine speciali Dei gratia insanabilis corruptio: tum quia Judæi quidam, quibus Evangelium nuntiatum est, οὐκ ἠδύναντο πιστεύειν non potuerunt credere, Deo oculos illorum excæcante, & corda indurante, Joh. XII. 39. 40. & animalis homo ὁ ψυχικὸς οὐ δέχεται, non potest cognoscere ea, quæ Spiritus sunt, 1. Cor. II. 14. tum quia multis vocatis non est datum obedire Evangelio, Matth. XI. 25. XIII. 11. tum quia facultas obediendi, & fides ipsa non est omnium, 2. Thess. III. 2. sed electorum duntaxat, qui pauci sunt, Matth. XX. 16. Act. XIII. 48. Tit. I. 1. tum quia non idem in omnibus Evangelii praedicati effectus est, cùm aliis sit odor vitæ ad vitam, aliis odor mortis ad mortem, 2. Cor. II. 16. Cujus differentiæ ratio pessimè ex animi volentis probitate, & nolentis malitia arcessitur. Non enim est volentis, nec currentis, sed Dei miserantis, Rom. IX. 16. & dantis vel non dantis, Matth. XIII. 11. Phil. I. 29. Fides etiam non est ex nobis, sed Dei donum, Ephes. II. 8. probitas verò animi fidei effectum est, Actor. XV. 9. 1. Tim. I. 5. Infidelitatis verò causa tum Divina reprobatio & excæcatio, Joh. XII. 39.40. Rom. XI. 7. 8. tum animi malitia omnibus insita & naturalis, Ephes. II. 3. est. Denique nec vocati secundum propositum, Rom. VIII. 28. dicuntur, qui præceptis & disciplinæ Christi obediunt; Apostolus enim loquitur de proposito Dei, quod est secundum electionem, ibid. IX. 11. & mox ib. VIII. 29. per prænotionem, & prædestinationem conformium imagini Filii declaratur. Quæ non est voluntas vocandi per Evangelium quosvis (est enim quorundam prænotio & electio) vel dandi gratiam sufficientem quibusvis, sine operatione fidei. Nam gratia sufficiens operosa est, 2. Cor. XII. 9. & quæ fidem non operatur, non sufficit.
units.tr: XXXII. Socinus, a reviver of Pelagianism and Sadduceism, places the whole cause of salvation and of the knowledge of God in the free choice of the will, whether it chooses to pursue what is good for itself or what is right. He makes grace nothing other than nature, the faculty of free will, the gratuitous remission of sins, and the promise of eternal life. He flatly denies, and his followers deny, that God, calling man to himself, works in the intellect and will of man by his almighty power. He holds that God only takes care that the Gospel be preached in the call. The one who obeys is helped outwardly by promises and threats, and inwardly by the sealing of the promises in the heart. Without any further grace of the Holy Spirit, he can obey by the sheer uprightness of a willing mind, and by the malice of an unwilling mind he can refuse to obey. They assert that the Gospel, like all Scripture, can be understood by any attentive reader without the illumination of the Holy Spirit, and that the gift of the Holy Spirit is nothing other than the gift of miracles granted for a time, or the Gospel itself and the certain hope of eternal life that remains forever. Finally, they maintain that those are called "according to purpose" who, having heard the discipline of Christ, follow it in their deeds, because it is God's purpose that men embrace the saving truth announced to them and order their whole life accordingly. These views are grossly Pelagian and impious, and can be overthrown by the same arguments with which the ancients refuted the heresy of Pelagius. Indeed, not all to whom the Gospel is preached can obey it without the singular grace of the Holy Spirit. This is so, first, because the deadly corruption of nature, incurable without the special grace of God, stands in the way. Second, because certain Jews to whom the Gospel was announced "could not believe" [οὐκ ἠδύναντο πιστεύειν], God blinding their eyes and hardening their hearts (John 12:39, 40). Third, because "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God... and he cannot know them" [ὁ ψυχικὸς οὐ δέχεται] (1 Cor. 2:14). Fourth, because to many who are called it is not given to obey the Gospel (Matt. 11:25; 13:11). Fifth, because the ability to obey, and faith itself, is not the possession of all (2 Thess. 3:2), but only of the elect, who are few (Matt. 20:16; Acts 13:48; Titus 1:1). Sixth, because the Gospel, when preached, does not have the same effect in all: "to some it is a fragrance of life unto life, to others a fragrance of death unto death" (2 Cor. 2:16). The reason for this difference is wretchedly sought in the uprightness of the willing mind and the malice of the unwilling. For "it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy" (Rom. 9:16), and it is a matter of God "giving" or "not giving" (Matt. 13:11; Phil. 1:29). Faith too "is not of yourselves; it is the gift of God" (Eph. 2:8), and uprightness of mind is the effect of faith (Acts 15:9; 1 Tim. 1:5). The cause of unbelief is both divine reprobation and blinding (John 12:39, 40; Rom. 11:7, 8), and the malice of mind, which is innate and natural in all (Eph. 2:3). Finally, those who obey the precepts and discipline of Christ are not said to be "called according to purpose" (Rom. 8:28). For the Apostle speaks of the purpose of God, which is "according to election" (Rom. 9:11), and immediately afterwards (Rom. 8:29) this is declared through "foreknowledge" and "predestination to be conformed to the image of the Son." This is not a will to call all men through the Gospel (for there is a foreknowledge and election of some), nor a will to give sufficient grace to all without the working of faith. For "sufficient grace" is effectual (2 Cor. 12:9), and grace that does not work faith is not sufficient.

units.la: XXXIII. Qui Christo non credunt, gravius equidem in die judicii, quàm incolæ Sodomæ punientur, Matth. XI. 22. Non tamen consequens est, ut cum Socino dicamus, etiam infideles ejusmodi facultatem credendi à Deo accepisse, eò quòd nemo justè puniri possit, non præstans id, cujus præstandi facultatem non habuit. Nam etiam in humano foro ad carcerem, metalla, triremes damnatur debitor, licèt facultatem solvendi non habeat, ac ne habuerit quidem unquam. De foro autem Divino Christus docet, quòd in eo etiam damnandi illi sint, qui non potuerunt credere, Joh. XII. 39. Satis verò illud est ad asserendam justitiam Dei, quòd impotentes propria culpa impotentiam sibi accersiverunt. Neque etiam vel omne donum Dei, quale est salvificæ fidei, sic liberæ vocatorum acceptioni relinquitur, ut acceptio ejus non ab ulla gratia Dei efficaciter movente, sed à sola voluntate hominis pendeat. Nam tractum cœlestis Patris & efficaciam roboris potentiæ ejus requiri Scriptura Joh. VI. 44. & Ephes. I. 19. testatur: vel sola credendi facultas, non etiam actus, donum Dei, & quidem commune vocatis omnibus & sola prædicatione, non etiam Spiritus S. interna operatione in credentibus productum est. Nam & actus credendi gratiæ subjicitur, Phil. I. 29. & facultas credendi non sola externa prædicatione, sed etiam Spiritus S. cor aperientis, Act. XVI. 14. operatione in credentibus producitur: nec facultas credendi omnibus vocatis communis est, cùm quidam non possint credere Joh. XII. 39. Media externa communia esse possunt: interna solis electis destinata sunt. Neque ideò frustra Christus mortuus est, quia Ecclesiam sanguine suo redemptam ad fidem nominis sui, tum externâ prædicatione, tum interna conversione Ezech. XXXVI. 26. 27. certò adducit. Non etiam, quia per Spiritum homo renascitur, nondum renatus jam Spiritum habet, quia, sicut Deus in eo, quod creat; ita Spiritus S. in eo, quem regenerat simul agit & est. Uti etiam qui Spiritui resistit, & eundem expellit; non ideò Spiritum regenerantem habere censetur; sicut, qui fores pulsanti non aperit, non ideò hospitem domi habet. Licèt enim Spiritus S. agat per præconium verbi ad aures & intellectum, & cum ἐλέγχῳ suo sæpe convincat, attamen non sic habetur, ut donum, ut noster, ut habitans in nobis tanquam in templo, nisi per fidem cordis. Nam Spiritum S. habere, non est simpliciter eum habere, ut patratorem miraculi, vel ut per prædicatum Evangelium certam æternæ vitæ spem facientem, uti Sociniani nugantur, sed in ipso esse, templum ejus esse, ab eo duci: Spiritum veritatis mundus non potest accipere, quia eum non videt, neque cognoscit eum. Vos verò cognoscitis eum, quia apud vos est, & in vobis est, Joh. XIV. 17. Ubi Servator mundum opponit iis, pro quibus orat Patrem, ut iis det Paracletum, qui apud eos maneat, ad quos ipse venturus est; quibus sese manifestaturus est; quos describit ceu amantes ipsum, & sermonem ejus servantes; quos diligit Pater, & ad quos Pater & ipse venturi sunt: verbo, de renascentibus, non de non renatis. Soli igitur renascentes accipiunt Spiritum S. qui quidem ad tempus sunt in mundo, quia ceu donati Christo à Patre, cum mundo non pereunt. Mundum verò reliquos omnes, seu Judæos, seu gentes appellat. Unde in continuatione sermonis, ibid. XV. 19. quos opponit mundo, negat esse ex mundo, quia Christus eos elegerit ex mundo. Perspicuum igitur est, eorum esse Spiritum S. quos Christus è mundo elegit, & quos à mundo per Spiritum separat. Unde porro sequitur, esse apud ipsos Spiritum, & apud ipsos manere, & ab iis cognosci, & dari iis, ut doctorem & ductorem in omni veritate, ut consolatorem & arrhabonem, & pignus acquisitionis, sigillum, intercessorem apud Deum, Christum ἐμφανίζοντα & ostendentem. De cæterorum ille idem Spiritus, qui in regenitis est, mundum de peccato, justitia & judicio arguit. ibid. XVI. 9. 10. 11. Sed nemo tantùm ἐλέγχομενος & redargutus ideò Spiritum habere, & spiritualis esse dicitur. Præterea qui ex Deo est, hoc est, qui ex Deo natus est, (Joh. I. 13. 1. Joh. III. 9.) & ejus Spiritu agitur, Rom. VIII. 14. non qui qualicunque vitæ probitate, præditus est; verba Dei audit, Joh. VIII. 47. Denique Christus dicens: Si quis voluerit voluntatem Patris facere, cognoscet de doctrina, an sit ex Deo, Joh. VII. 17. non docet, fidem ex nativa quapiam animi probitate nasci (non enim ex fructu arbor, sed ex arbore fructus nascitur & cognoscitur, Matth. VII. 17.) sed, si quis facere velit voluntatem Dei, eum cogniturum de doctrina, an ex Deo sit, admonet. Quæ tamen voluntas non ex naturæ viribus, sed ex gratia Dei procedit. Deus enim est, qui in vobis operatur & velle & operari Phil. II. 13.
units.tr: XXXIII. Those who do not believe in Christ will indeed be punished more severely on the day of judgment than the inhabitants of Sodom (Matt. 11:22). Yet it does not follow, as Socinus says, that even unbelievers have received from God such a faculty of believing. No one can justly be punished for not doing what he had no faculty to do. Even in a human court a debtor is condemned to prison, to the mines, or to the galleys, although he has no ability to pay, and never had. But concerning the divine court, Christ teaches that those are condemned in it who "could not believe" (John 12:39). It is enough to assert the justice of God that the unable have brought their inability upon themselves by their own fault. Nor is every gift of God, such as saving faith, left to the free acceptance of those who are called, in such a way that its acceptance depends not on any effectually moving grace of God but on the will of man alone. For Scripture testifies that "the drawing of the heavenly Father" (John 6:44) and "the working of the strength of his power" (Eph. 1:19) are required. Or else only the faculty of believing, and not the act, is the gift of God, and this is common to all who are called and is produced by preaching alone, not by the inner operation of the Holy Spirit in believers. For the act of believing is also subject to grace (Phil. 1:29), and the faculty of believing is produced in believers not by external preaching alone, but also by the operation of the Holy Spirit, who "opens the heart" (Acts 16:14). Nor is the faculty of believing common to all who are called, since some "cannot believe" (John 12:39). External means can be common; inner means are destined for the elect alone. Nor is Christ therefore dead in vain, because he surely brings the Church, redeemed by his blood, to faith in his name, both by external preaching and by inner conversion (Ezek. 36:26, 27). Nor is it the case that, because a man is born again through the Spirit, one who is not yet reborn already has the Spirit. Just as God is in what he creates, so the Holy Spirit both acts in and is present in the one he regenerates. Likewise, one who resists the Spirit and drives him out is not thought to have the regenerating Spirit; just as one who does not open the door to a knocker does not therefore have a guest at home. For although the Holy Spirit works through the proclamation of the Word to the ears and the understanding, and often convicts with his conviction [ἐλέγχῳ], yet he is not regarded as a gift, as ours, as dwelling in us as in a temple, except through the faith of the heart. For to have the Holy Spirit is not simply to have him as the worker of miracles, or as the one who makes a certain hope of eternal life through the preached Gospel, as the Socinians babble. It is to be in him, to be his temple, to be led by him: "The world cannot receive the Spirit of truth, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you know him, for he dwells with you and is in you" (John 14:17). Here the Savior sets "the world" against those for whom he asks the Father, that the Father may give them the Paraclete, who may remain with them, to whom he himself will come, and to whom he will manifest himself. He describes them as loving him and keeping his word, as those whom the Father loves, and to whom the Father and he will come. In a word, he speaks of those who are being born again, not of those who are not reborn. Therefore only the reborn receive the Holy Spirit. These indeed are in the world for a time, yet, as given to Christ by the Father, they do not perish with the world. But he calls all the rest, whether Jews or Gentiles, "the world." Hence, in the continuation of the discourse (John 15:19), he says that those whom he sets against the world are not of the world, because Christ has chosen them out of the world. It is therefore clear that the Holy Spirit belongs to those whom Christ has chosen out of the world, and whom through the Spirit he separates from the world. It further follows that the Spirit is with them and remains in them, is known by them, and is given to them "as teacher and guide into all truth, as comforter and earnest," and as the pledge of acquisition, the seal, and "intercessor" before God, Christ [ἐμφανίζοντα] showing and manifesting. But the same Spirit who is in the reborn "convicts the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment" (John 16:9-11). Yet no one who is merely convicted and refuted is therefore said to have the Spirit or to be spiritual. Moreover, "he who is of God," that is, "who is born of God" (John 1:13; 1 John 3:9), and who is led by his Spirit (Rom. 8:14), is not one who is endowed with some uprightness of life; he "hears the words of God" (John 8:47). Finally, when Christ says, "If anyone wills to do the will of the Father, he will know concerning the doctrine whether it is of God" (John 7:17), he does not teach that faith is born from some natural uprightness of mind. For a tree does not bear fruit from fruit; rather, fruit is born from the tree and known by it (Matt. 7:17). He is rather admonishing that whoever wishes to do the will of God will come to know whether the doctrine is from God. Yet this will does not proceed from the powers of nature but from the grace of God. For "it is God who works in you both to will and to work" (Phil. 2:13).

units.la: XXXIV. Pelagio Semipelagiani, seu Massilienses, Johannes Cassianus, Presbyter Massiliensis, Faustus, aliique successerunt, à Pelagio hactenus divortium facientes, quòd naturalem corruptionem fassi sunt; at cum eodem paria facientes, cùm gratiam cooperantem asseruerunt, at operantem sustulerunt. Catholici enim gratiam Dei, qua homo ex impio pius fit, & bona opera facit, in operantem & cooperantem tem distinxerant. Quoniam, sic Augustinus de Grat. & lib. Arb. loquitur, ipse ut velimus, operatur incipiens, qui volentibus cooperatur, perficiens. Propter quod ait Apostolus, Phil. I. 6. certus sum, quoniam, qui operatur in vobis opus bonum, perficiet usque in diem Jesu Christi. Ut ergo velimus, sine nobis operatur. Cum autem volumus, & sic volumus, ut faciamus, nobiscum cooperatur: Tamen sine illo vel operante, ut velimus, vel cooperante cum volumus, ad pietatem nihil valemus. Gratiam illam operantem praeoperantis Prosper, & praevenientis etiam Augustinus; & cooperantem comitantis & subsequentis nominibus iidem insigniverunt. Hic vero Semipelagiani, Pelagio suo cooperantes, naturam, legem, & posteriorem etiam gratiam illam cooperantem, licet non plene, agnoverunt: sed operantem, praeoperantem, praevenientem oppugnarunt. Recte autem Prosper Epist. ad August. de reliq. haeref. Pelag. In iis, inquit, Pelagianae pravitatis reliquiis non mediocris virulentiae fibra nutritur, si principium salutis male in hominibus collocatur: si Divinae voluntati impie voluntas humana praefertur, ut ideo quis adjuvetur, quia voluit, non ideo quia adjuvatur, velit: si originaliter malus receptionem boni non a summo bono, sed a semet ipso inchoare male creditur; si aliunde Deo placetur, nisi ex eo, quod ipse donaverit. Sicut Pelagius sublata funditus Christi gratia & fide puram putam Philosophiam & Ethnicismum in Ecclesiam introducere statuit: ita Semipelagiani Christum, ceu naturae perditae Salvatorem, ejusque gratiam omnibus modis retinendam asseruerunt. Sed displicuit iis aeternae electionis illud propositum, quo quidam ex solo Dei beneplacito, nulla voluntatis humanae ratione habita, prae aliis ad gratiam & gloriam praedestinantur, Proin propositum Dei geminum, unum generale & conditionatum, omnes creatae voluntatis motus praecedens, & voluntatem Dei omnibus & singulis salutem dandi complexum, efficax, si ei homines consentiant, inefficax, si dissentiant: alterum speciale & absolutum, voluntatis motus consequens finxerunt. Ex generali proposito communia beneficia omnibus promiscue hominibus praeparata derivarunt; eaque vel remota, gratia quadam actuali & propinquiore, ut ad salutem prodesse possint, indigentia; cujusmodi sint incarnatio, redemptio, baptismus, &c. vel proxima, cujusmodi sint gratiae internae vel externae actuales, velut gratia institutionis Legis & Evangelii, quando & ubi illud creditum iri praeviderit; imaginis Divinae reliquiae, gratia interna sufficiens ad credendum, qualem primus homo habuerit, sine qua non agit homo, sed non qua agit, & cujus usus in libera voluntate hominis relinquatur; bonus usus liberi arbitrii, cui id tribuebant, ut non quidem merito, sed occasione ejus major gratia, id est, vera operans deinceps & velle & operari, consequatur. Summa est, eandem esse vocationem secundum propositum, qua & obedientes & non obedientes vocantur. Sed discerni illam voluntate sola hominis, omnibus etiam, qui vocantur; conferri gratiam & facultatem obediendi ex aequo sufficientem, qua excitati & adjuti, si voluerint, credant & obediant, si noluerint, non credant; nec obediant. Fusius haec Viri
units.tr: XXXIV. After Pelagius came the Semipelagians, or Massilians: John Cassian, presbyter of Marseilles, Faustus, and others. They separated from Pelagius only in that they admitted natural corruption. In other respects they agreed with him, for while they affirmed a cooperating grace, they denied an operating grace. The Catholics had distinguished the grace of God, by which a man is made godly from ungodly and does good works, into operating and cooperating. For, thus Augustine speaks in On Grace and Free Will, He himself works in us, beginning that we may will; he cooperates with those who will, bringing it to completion. For this reason the Apostle says, Phil. 1:6, I am confident that he who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Jesus Christ. So then, he works in us without us that we may will; but when we will, and so will that we may act, he cooperates with us. Yet without him, either working so that we will or cooperating when we will, we can do nothing toward godliness. Prosper called that operating grace preceding-operating, and Augustine called it preventing; the same writers named the cooperating grace accompanying and subsequent. The Semipelagians, however, while cooperating with their Pelagius, acknowledged nature, the law, and that later cooperating grace, though not fully; but they attacked the operating, preceding, and preventing grace. Prosper rightly says in his letter to Augustine, On the Remnants of the Pelagian Heresy: In these remnants of Pelagian perversity there is nourished a fibre of no small virulence, if the beginning of salvation is wrongly placed in men; if the human will is impiously preferred to the divine will, so that someone is helped because he willed, not that he might will because he is helped; if it is wrongly believed that a bad man begins to receive good from himself rather than from the supreme Good; if God is pleased in any way other than by what he himself has given. Just as Pelagius, having utterly removed the grace and faith of Christ, resolved to bring pure philosophy and paganism into the Church, so the Semipelagians asserted that Christ, as Saviour of lost nature, and his grace must be retained by every means. But they disliked that purpose of eternal election by which some are predestined to grace and glory before others, solely by God's good pleasure, without regard to any human will. Therefore they devised a twofold purpose of God: one general and conditional, preceding all motions of the created will, embracing God's will to give salvation to all and each, effective if men consent to it, ineffective if they dissent; the other special and absolute, following the motions of the will. From the general purpose they derived benefits common to all men without distinction, prepared for them; and these are either remote, needing some actual and nearer grace so that they may avail for salvation (such as the incarnation, redemption, baptism, etc.), or proximate, such as the internal or external actual graces: for example, the grace of the institution of the Law and the Gospel, when and where God foresaw that it would be believed; the remnants of the divine image, the internal grace sufficient for believing, such as the first man had, without which man does not act, though it is not that by which he acts, and whose use is left to the free will of man; and the good use of free choice, to which they attributed this, that a greater grace follows, not indeed as merit but on the occasion of it, namely the true grace that thereafter works both to will and to act. In short, they held that the calling according to purpose is the same for those who obey and for those who do not. But they held that the difference lies in the sole will of man, and that all who are called are given an equal and sufficient grace and ability to obey: when stirred and helped, if they will, they believe and obey; if they will not, they do not believe nor obey. The most learned men Forbes, Vossius, Ussher and Jansenius pursue these matters more fully.

units.la: doctissimi, Forbesius, Vossius, Usserius, Jansenius prosequuntur.
units.tr: The most learned men Forbes, Vossius, Ussher and Jansenius pursue these matters more fully.

units.la: XXXV. Sicut nihil est sub sole novi & id quod fuit, idem futurum est, & quod fit, idem fiet, Eccles. I. 9.10. ita Semipelagianorum illam orbitam sequentes triverunt. Eadem fabula diversis seculis a diversis agitur; & historia eadem, sed non idem apparatus, non theatrum idem. Nil dicam de controversia Godeschalkum, Remigium &c. inter & Hincmarum Rhemensem Archiepiscopum, & Johannem Erigenam Scotum, quorum illi Augustini & Prosperi vestigiis inhaerentes, gratiam Dei defenderunt; hi libertri arbitrii fimbrias mire dilatarunt. Inter Scholasticos aperte Semipelagianismus nidulatus est, apud quos necessaria argumentatio est: Ipse facit, quicquid in se est: Ergo Deus ei dat gratiam; licet saepe det gratiam iis, qui non faciunt quantum in se est. Illud vero facere quod in se est, definiunt, ex notione naturali & libero arbitrio recurrere ad illum, quem homo scit suum principium, & quem scit esse orandum sibi, & petendum ab illo lumen cognitionis fidei & boni. Albertus Magnus: In nobis, inquit, est aliquid facere, quo facto, habemus potestatem ex gratia. Quam in sententiam Lessius veteres & recentiores multos citat; uno excepto Gregorio Ariminensi, qui statuit, viribus naturae non posse fieri ullum opus moraliter bonum secundum omnes circumstantias, quod Pii V. & Gregorii XIII. anathema meruit. Concilii porro Tridentini Canon IV. Sess. VI. sic tonat: Si quis dixerit, liberum arbitrium hominis a Deo motum & excitatum nihil cooperari, assentiendo Deo excitanti atque vocanti, quo ad obtinendam justificationis gratiam se disponat ac praeparet; nec posse dissentire, si velit, sed velut inanime quoddam, nihil omnino agere, mereque passive se habere, anathema sit. In ipso tamen Concilio Dominicani, Thomam Aquinatem secuti, intrepide negarunt, opera vocationem antecedentia vere praeparatoria esse. Et nullas omnino partes esse in conversione liberi arbitrii, teste Suave Aloisius Catanaeus, & teste Pallavicino, Gregorius Senensis statuerunt. Et post Concilium etiam de modo gratiae convertentis, quaestione videlicet illa. An in negotio vocationis & conversionis nostrae, omnibusque adeo actibus fidelium supernaturalibus praecedat gratia Divina operatio adeo efficax, ut ea posita infallibiliter sequatur effectus a Deo praedefinitus, & praedeterminatus? mire digladiantur. Affirmant Thomam suum secuti Praedicatores, aliique, Praedeterminantium nomine insignes, qui gratiae convertentis efficaciam in praedeterminatione physica, uti appellant, hoc est, non nuda suasione morali, ancipitem eventum habente, sed physica, hoc est vera & reali efficientia, certum post se eventum habente, ponunt. Negant Franciscani, Scoto suo duce, eosque secuti Jesuitae inprimis, Molina suo chorago, Praescientistarum nomine famosi, docentes concursum gratiae Dei consistere non in motione aliqua voluntatem praedeterminante, sed in quadam illuminatione intellectus & motibus voluntatis, quibus Deus alliciat voluntatem, ut velit, vires volendi tribuat, simulque cum voluntate, si voluerit, concurrat. Quid vero libera voluntas cum quavis gratia, si daretur, vellet vel faceret, statuerunt, Deum explorare per scientiam conditionatam seu mediam.
units.tr: XXXV. As there is nothing new under the sun, and what has been is what will be, and what is done is what will be done, Eccl. 1:9–10, so the Semipelagians, following their track, wore out the same course. The same play is performed by different people in different ages; the story is the same, but the staging is not the same, nor the theatre. I say nothing of the controversy between Gottschalk, Remigius, etc., and Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, and John Erigena the Scot. The former, clinging to the footsteps of Augustine and Prosper, defended the grace of God; the latter wonderfully extended the fringes of free will. Among the Scholastics Semipelagianism openly nested, and among them the following argument is standard: He does what is in him; therefore God gives him grace; though God often gives grace to those who do not do what is in them. But they define doing what is in oneself as having recourse, by natural notion and free will, to him whom man knows as his beginning, whom he knows must be prayed to, and from whom he must seek the light of knowledge of faith and of good. Albert the Great: It is in us, he says, to do something, by doing which we have the power from grace. Lessius cites many ancient and recent writers to this effect, except Gregory of Rimini, who held that by the powers of nature no morally good work can be done according to all circumstances, a view that earned the anathema of Pius V and Gregory XIII. Moreover, Canon 4 of Session 6 of the Council of Trent thunders thus: If anyone says that the free will of man, moved and stirred by God, cooperates in nothing by assenting to God who stirs and calls, so that he disposes and prepares himself to obtain the grace of justification, and that he cannot dissent if he wills, but, like something inanimate, does nothing at all and is merely passive, let him be anathema. Yet within the Council itself the Dominicans, following Thomas Aquinas, boldly denied that works preceding the calling are truly preparatory. And, as Suárez, Luigi Cattaneo, and Pallavicino testify, Gregory of Siena held that there is no part at all for free will in conversion. And after the Council they fiercely contended over the mode of converting grace, namely the question: In the business of our calling and conversion, and indeed in all supernatural acts of the faithful, does a divine operation of grace so efficacious precede that, once it is posited, the effect predefined and predetermined by God infallibly follows? The Thomist Preachers and others, famous under the name of Predeterminists, affirm that the efficacy of converting grace lies in what they call physical predetermination, that is, not in mere moral persuasion, which has a doubtful outcome, but in physical efficacy, that is, true and real efficient causation, which has a certain outcome after it. The Franciscans, with Scotus as their leader, and especially the Jesuits who followed them, with Molina as their chorister, famous under the name of Scientists of Foreknowledge, deny this, teaching that the concurrence of God's grace consists not in any motion predetermining the will, but in a certain illumination of the intellect and motions of the will, by which God draws the will so that it wills, gives it the power of willing, and at the same time concurs with the will, if it wills. And they held that God explores, through conditional or middle knowledge, what free will would will or do with any grace, if it were given.

units.la: Quorum in castra Scholastici, Scotistae inprimis & Ieremis fuit Praesciemistae. mediam. Explorata per præscientiam ejusmodi (unde iis Præscientiarum nomen hæsit.) voluntate libera, dari gratiam, cum qua voluntas operatura prævidetur ex decreto Dei prævidensis, ut talis effectus fiat. De acerrimo partium illarum conflictu multa paucis Mariana de mort. & immort. lib. III. 8. dixit. En, inquit, scopulus, ad quem multæ confractæ sunt naves! En Euripus rapidus, in diversas & contrarias partes versó mari, velut monte præcipiti devolutus torrens, fervens rixis & contentionibus! Nusquam majori animo, neque odio partium magis implacabili hisce annis certatum est, usque eò, ut ad severa tribunalia ventum sit, dum utrique adversariis hæresis crimen affingunt, quo nihil est gravius. Ipse Romanus Pontifex appellatus jam aliquot annos ea controversia districtus nondum in pace litigantes posuit, novo decreto promulgato. Sed veterem litem nec dum Papa sopivit, licet insignis ille gratiæ præco Bradwvardinus in conclusione operis, quod adversus Pelagium & asseclas scripsit de causa Dei, his verbis Romanam Ecclesiam ad finiendam controversiam appellaverit. Simon dormis? Exsurge quæso. Sed adhuc ille dormit, nec ambigua litium fata dirimit. Imo tertius supervenit, Jansenius cum sectatoribus suis, qui & Prædeterminantium & Præscientiarum sententia improbata, Augustini illud auxilium Christi, & adjutorium Dei medicinale revocans, illud non in motione tantum virtuosa, sed in verissimo motu voluntatis, ineffabili delectatione objecti, quod proponitur; totum animum cum ingenti jucunditate sursum rapiente collevavit. Cúmque Prædeterminantes suam prædeterminationem actum vitalem esse inficiarentur; ille Christi adjutorium actum verum vitalem, & victricem, uti cum Augustino vocat, delectationem, qua anima haud secus afficitur, & in Deum movetur, ac quando simili delectatione rebus terrenis inhæret, fecit. Denique cum prædeterminatio physica omnibus agentibus necessaria statueretur ex vi causæ secundæ, quæ causæ primæ essentialiter subordinata est; ille adjutorium Christi læsæ voluntati necessarium esse asseruit, propter solum vulnus, quod peccantis voluntatis audacia ei inflixit.
units.tr: To their camp went the Scholastics, the Scotists above all, and the Jesuits, who were the Foreknowledgists. By foreknowledge of the free will so explored (whence they got the name Foreknowledgists), grace is given with which the will is foreseen to act, according to the decree of God foreseeing it, so that such an effect comes about. Mariana, in On the Death and Immortality, Book 3, chapter 8, has said much in few words about the bitter conflict of those parties: Behold, he says, a reef on which many ships have been broken! Behold a rapid whirlpool, the sea turned into different and opposite directions, a torrent rolling down as from a steep mountain, seething with quarrels and contentions! Never in these years has there been fought with greater spirit, or with a hatred of parties more implacable, to the point that they came to severe tribunals, while each side charges the other with the crime of heresy, than which nothing is more serious. The Roman Pontiff himself, appealed to, though for some years now occupied with that controversy, has not yet settled the litigants in peace, though he promulgated a new decree. But the Pope has not yet quieted the old dispute, even though that famous herald of grace, Bradwardine, in the conclusion of his work written against Pelagius and his followers, On the Cause of God, appealed to the Roman Church to end the controversy in these words: Are you asleep, Simon? Arise, I beg you. But that one still sleeps, nor does he settle the doubtful fates of the disputes. Indeed a third came on, Jansen with his followers, who, rejecting the opinion of both the Predeterminists and the Foreknowledgists, and recalling that saying of Augustine, the help of Christ, and the medicinal help of God, located it not merely in a virtuous motion, but in a most true motion of the will, by the ineffable delight of the object proposed, which carries the whole soul upward with great joy. And since the Predeterminists denied that their predetermination is a vital act, he made the help of Christ a true vital and victorious act, as he calls it with Augustine, delight, by which the soul is affected no less, and is moved toward God, than when it clings to earthly things with a similar delight. Finally, since physical predetermination was asserted to be necessary for all agents by the force of a secondary cause, which is essentially subordinate to the primary cause, he asserted that the help of Christ is necessary for the wounded will, on account of the wound alone that the audacity of the sinning will has inflicted upon it.

units.la: XXXVI. Sed vix ovum ovo simílius est, quàm Semipelagianorum & Remonstrantium de gratia vocationis & conversionis sensus est; Ut hi ex illorum putredine nati videri possint. Utrisque errandi occasionem decreti prædestinationis absoluti aversatio præbuit. Utrique gratiam in voluntate ipsum τὸ velle operantem rejiciunt, & eam, uti barbarè hi loquuntur, resistibilem faciunt; ita ut homo, sic Episcopius ex animi omnium sententia loquitur; sufficiens principium & dominus suarum actionum sit, qui licet sub Deo, liber tamen maneat; & potestate volendi & nolendi uti potest contra voluntatem & operationem Dei. Utrique gratiam efficacem & inefficacem à solo eventu statuunt: universalem & promiscuam urgent arbitrii libertatem per gratiam efficientem destrui; præcepta, exhortationes, promissiones, minas frustra fore clamitant: solam orationem necessariam esse asseruunt, absurdum reputantes, ut Deus ab homine fieri petat, quod per talem gratiam facere debet: Voluntatem Dei generalem conditionatam, quantum est ex parte Dei, & si homines ipsi velint, faciunt: mortem Christi pro omnibus oppetitam tuentur: Gratiam sufficientem, etiam internam, communem faciunt; ita ut intellectus irresistibiliter illuminetur; at voluntas respectu gratiæ indifferens maneat, & se ipsam sola determinet. In eo tamen sententiæ discrepant, quòd illi initium fidei & perseverantiam sibi adscripserunt, hi totam potestati suæ vendicant: illi post initium fidei veram Christi gratiam actualem agnoverunt, hi illam duntaxat, quæ initio debetur. Sed longius etiam progressi Remonstrantes, uti vera vibiam sequi solet, Pelagii ipsius castra ingressi peccatum originis negant, & ceu Augustini figmentum, ex Manichæismo haustum, sugillant: hominem peccato infirmatum, non mortuum asserunt: vitam spiritualem ab homine animali penitus separatam inficiantur: sine interna Spiritus S. gratia, solo rationis & judicii usu, Scripturas intelligi posse pronuntiant: nonnullos testimonio luminis naturæ, reliquos voce Evangelii ad Deum vocari asserunt: indifferentiam arbitrii plane Pelagianam defendunt: gratiam merè moralem, doctrina Legis & Evangelii, exhortationibus, correptionibus constantem faciunt: Denique nec majore Deum in homine convertendo vi, quàm Diabolus in pervertendo adhibet, uti blasphemant. Eo nunc loco Remonstrantium res sunt. Mali homines proficiunt in pejus, in errorem agentes, & errantes, 2. Tim. III. 13.
units.tr: XXXVI. But an egg is hardly more like an egg than the Semipelagians' and the Remonstrants' view of the grace of calling and conversion is like itself, so that the latter might seem to have been born from the rot of the former. For both, the occasion of error was their aversion to the doctrine of absolute predestination. Both reject grace that works in the will itself [τὸ θέλειν], and, to use their own barbarous term, make it resistible. So that man, as Episcopius speaks, by the judgment of all, is a sufficient principle and lord of his own actions, who, though under God, nevertheless remains free, and can use the power of willing and not willing against the will and operation of God. Both determine efficacious and inefficacious grace solely by the outcome. They insist that universal and indiscriminate freedom of choice would be destroyed by efficacious grace; they cry out that precepts, exhortations, promises and threats would be in vain. They assert that only prayer is necessary, thinking it absurd that God should ask of man what he ought to effect by such grace himself. They hold that God's general will is conditional, so far as it depends on God, and that if men themselves are willing, they are saved. They defend the death of Christ as suffered for all. They make sufficient grace, even inward grace, common to all, so that the understanding is illuminated irresistibly, but the will remains indifferent with respect to grace and determines itself alone. They differ in this, however: the Semipelagians ascribed to themselves the beginning of faith and perseverance, whereas the Remonstrants claim everything for their own power. The former acknowledged the true actual grace of Christ after the beginning of faith; the latter acknowledge only that grace which is owed at the beginning. But the Remonstrants have advanced even further: as truth usually follows vanity, they have entered the very camp of Pelagius himself, denying original sin and sneering at it as a fiction of Augustine drawn from Manichaeism. They assert that man is weakened by sin, not dead; they deny that the spiritual life is wholly separated from the natural man; they declare that the Scriptures can be understood without the inward grace of the Holy Spirit, by the use of reason and judgment alone; they maintain that some are called to God by the testimony of the light of nature, the rest by the voice of the Gospel; they defend a purely Pelagian indifference of the will; they make grace merely moral, consisting in the doctrine of Law and Gospel, in exhortations and rebukes; and finally, they blaspheme that God uses no greater force in converting man than the Devil uses in perverting him. Such is now the state of the Remonstrants. Evil men will proceed from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived, 2 Tim. 3:13.

units.la: XXXVII. Erasmus liberum arbitrium calamo, non animo decantaverat. Nam Epist. lib. XIX. 22. ad Lud. Vivem sic scripsit: Ut ingenue dicam, perdidimus liberum arbitrium. Illic aliud mihi, animus: aliud scribebat calamus. Sed calamo ejus Lutherus animo æquè atque calamo (nam ad conscientiam se cuncta retulisse, non semel protestatur) respondit, edito de servo arbitrio libro aureolo, quo inter alia verissimè profitetur, hominem in conversionis suæ principio plane nihil agere, sed tantum pati id, quod Deus in eo agit. Sed Magistri sui egregium factum quidam ejus discipuli, non eo, quo par erat, pretio æstimantes, sicut Christum omnibus meruisse salutem docent, it Deum omnes & singulos ad salutis communionem vocare, pariter pronuntiant. Quòd verò populi multi Evangelio destituuntur, ipsorum culpa, non ulla Dei voluntate evenire, sciscunt. Omnibus interim vocatis concedi gratiam sufficientem, & in omnibus verbi Divini auditoribus simul operari Spi. S. neq; aliud discrimen intercedere quàm quòd alii Spir. S. operanti cedant; alii resistendo obicem ponant; cùm non sic gratia Dei omnipotens agat omnipotenter, ut homo resistere non possit; denique pertendunt: Fatendum nihilominus est, saniores inter illos nec Pelagianorum, nec Semipelagianorum castra hactenus subivisse; Deo avertente ab iis venenum, quod lethale Ecclesiam aliàs perimeret. Nam & Pelagianum de liberi arbitrii usu idolum abominantur, & simul confitentur, quòd nunquam eventu sic homo gratiæ convertenti resistat; quin illa victrix evadat. Nam ad sententiam Augustini de Correp. & Grat. cap, 14. quòd Deo volenti salvum facere nullum resistat liberum arbitrium, quia sic velle aut nolle in volentis aut nolentis potestate est, ut Divinam voluntatem non impediat, nec potestatem superet, ita ipse Hulsemannus de Auxil. Grat. pag. 329. respondet: Hoc dicto patet, negari non resistibilitatem, sed eventualem resistentiam, quam & nos utique negamus, asserendo, nullum electum vocationi Divinæ finaliter resistere, quia ejusmodi propositio implicat. Idem pag. 317. diserte declarat, non esse impium dicere, electis esse peculiarem quandam gratiam à Deo præparatam, qua infallibiliter convertuntur. Quin & juxta Formulam Concordiæ pag. 673. Deus trahit hominem, quem convertere decrevit; sic autem eum trahit, ut ex intellectu cæcato illuminatus, & (NB.) ex rebelli voluntate fiat prona & obediens voluntas. Hoc nobis abunde sufficit. Nam resistibilitatem ipsam, si ea ad hominis corrupti & in peccato mortui, adeoque sibi relicti, naturam referatur, in dubium nulli revocamus. Denique & Lutherus, uti vidimus, & ejus assecla γνῶσιν hactenus nobiscum consenserunt, quòd homo in principio conversionis se merè passivè habeat. Solius decreti absoluti, non ex animi nostri sententia accepti, immeritus horror ad quædam minùs verbo Dei consentientia, gratiam inprimis sufficientem omnibus vocatis communem, compulisse videtur.
units.tr: XXXVII. Erasmus had sung of free choice with his pen, not with his heart. For in his letter (Epist. book 19, no. 22) to Ludovicus Vives he wrote thus: To be frank, we have lost free choice. There my mind is one thing, and my pen writes another.
