But Luther answered his pen with his heart as well as with his pen (for he protested more than once that he had referred everything to conscience), in the golden little book de servo arbitrio, in which, among other things, he most truly professes that man at the beginning of his conversion does absolutely nothing, but only suffers what God works in him. But some of his disciples, not valuing their master's splendid achievement at its proper price, declare alike that just as Christ merited salvation for all, so God calls all and each to the fellowship of salvation. They decide that when many peoples are deprived of the Gospel, this happens through their own fault and not by any will of God. Meanwhile they hold that sufficient grace is granted to all who are called, and that the Holy Spirit works simultaneously in all hearers of the Divine Word, and that there is no difference between them except that some yield to the working Spirit while others, by resisting, put up an obstacle; since the omnipotent grace of God does not act so omnipotently that man cannot resist it. Finally, they maintain these things. Nevertheless it must be admitted that the saner among them have hitherto not entered the camps of the Pelagians or the Semipelagians, God turning away from them the poison which would otherwise have destroyed the Church by death. For they both abhor the Pelagian idol of the use of free choice, and at the same time confess that in outcome man never so resists converting grace that it does not prevail. For, as Augustine says in de Correptione et Gratia, chapter 14, that no free choice resists God when he wills to save, because to will or not to will is in the power of the one willing or unwilling, so that it does not hinder the Divine will nor overcome its power, so Hulsemann himself responds (de Auxiliis Gratiae, p. 329): From this saying it is clear that what is denied is not resistibility but actual resistance, which we indeed also deny, asserting that no elect person finally resists the Divine calling, because such a proposition is self-contradictory. The same author, p. 317, plainly declares that it is not impious to say that the elect have a peculiar grace prepared by God, by which they are infallibly converted. Indeed, according to the Formula of Concord, p. 673: God draws the man whom he has decided to convert; and he draws him in such a way that, enlightened from a blinded understanding, and (note well) from a rebellious will, he becomes a willing and obedient will. This is quite enough for us. For we do not call into doubt resistibility itself, if it is referred to the nature of corrupt man, dead in sin and thus left to himself. Finally, Luther, as we have seen, and his followers' opinion [γνῶσιν] have hitherto agreed with us that man at the beginning of conversion is wholly passive. It seems that an undeserved horror of the absolute decree alone, not received from our own judgment, has driven some, who agree less with the Word of God, to hold a sufficient grace common to all who are called.

units.la: XXXVIII. In conflictantium opinionum & errorum de gratia Vocationis & libero arbitrio hominis labyrintho Ariadnes filo quodam opus est.
units.tr: XXXVIII. In the labyrinth of conflicting opinions and errors about the grace of calling and the free will of man, we need a certain thread, like Ariadne's.

units.la: Ante omnia suus gratiæ, & suus arbitrio locus relinquendus est. Si enim, uti scitè Augustinus Epist. 48. ad Valent. loquitur, non est Dei gratia, quomodo Deus salvat mundum? Si non est liberum arbitrium, quomodo judicat mundum? Quod sic Bernhardus de Grat. & Lib. Arb. reponit: Tolle liberum arbitrium, non erit, quod salvetur: tolle gratiam, non erit unde salvetur. Aureum inprimis est illud Bradvvardini de causa Dei c. 31. corollarium: Scriptura & Patres ex hac parte præcipuè non tantùm pium, sed etiam prudentem lectorem requirunt, qui dubia perpendat, opposita conferat, Doctores ipsos vel inter se, vel sibi ipsis non obscurè contradicentes ex Scripturis, vel testimoniis expressioribus exponat & corrigat; ne dum Pelagianismi refugit scyllam; incidat in Manichæismi & Euthusiasmi charybdin. Seopulis his evitatis naturæ corruptæ miseria & clades, gratiæ Divinæ necessitas & efficacia, denique liberi arbitrii conditio ejusmodi ex verbo solidè edoceri debet, ut gloriam & honorem Dei tum ex indignitate nostra, tum ex amplitudine gratiæ ejus efficacissimè illustret.
units.tr: First of all, the place of grace and the place of free will must each be preserved. For if, as Augustine rightly says in Epist. 48 ad Valent., there is no grace of God, how does God save the world? If there is no free will, how does he judge the world? Bernard answers this in de Grat. & Lib. Arb.: Take away free will, and there is nothing to be saved; take away grace, and there is nothing from which to be saved. Especially golden is that corollary of Bradwardine in de causa Dei c. 31: Scripture and the Fathers, on this point above all, require a reader who is not only pious but also prudent, one who weighs doubtful matters, compares opposing statements, and explains and corrects the teachers themselves, who contradict one another or themselves not obscurely, from the Scriptures or from more express testimonies; so that, while avoiding the Scylla of Pelagianism, he does not fall into the Charybdis of Manichaeism and enthusiasm. With these rocks avoided, the misery and ruin of corrupt nature, the necessity and efficacy of divine grace, and finally the condition of free will must be taught solidly from the Word, so that the glory and honour of God may be most effectively displayed both from our unworthiness and from the greatness of his grace.

units.la: XXXIX. Hic ante omnia statu natura corrupta & peccati, in quo nec dum regeniti & converti degunt, à statu gratiæ & conversionis, in quo homines peccatores vel convertuntur, vel conversi sunt, distinguendus venit.
units.tr: XXXIX. Here we must first distinguish the state of corrupt nature and sin, in which men not yet regenerated and converted live, from the state of grace and conversion, in which sinners are either being converted or have been converted.

units.la: In priore statu homo in cæteris omnibus liber, & intelligendi ac volendi facultate præditus; in spiritualibus verò & cœlestibus servus peccati, mortuus in peccatis, filius iræ, ingurgitans se peccato, uti piscis aquæ, super omnia perversus, Deo & legi ejus ita repugnans, ut se ei submittere nullo modo possit, omni prorsus libertate destituitur, quod Loc. X. 84. &c. fusiùs probavimus. In posteriore statu Conversionis & Gratiæ ejusdem initia à progressu & perseverantia, fundamentum ab ædificio, radix à ramo distinguenda pariter sunt. Initium, Fundamentum & Radix conversionis est novæ naturæ sanctæ qualitatis ac propensionis in corde humano, voluntate & affectibus generatio & productio, qua cor priùs in peccato mortuum vivificari, hoc est, vita spirituali donari incipit.
units.tr: In the former state, man is free in all other respects and endowed with the faculty of understanding and willing; but in spiritual and heavenly things he is a slave of sin, dead in sins, a child of wrath, plunging himself into sin like a fish into water, perverse above all things, and so opposed to God and his law that he can in no way submit himself to them; he is wholly deprived of freedom, as we proved at greater length in Locus X, §84 and following. In the latter state of conversion and grace, the beginnings of conversion must likewise be distinguished from its progress and perseverance, the foundation from the building, and the root from the branch. The beginning, foundation and root of conversion is the generation and production, in the human heart, of a new nature and a holy quality and inclination in the will and affections, by which the heart, previously dead in sin, begins to be made alive, that is, to be given spiritual life.

units.la: Quæ vivificatio spiritualis naturali corporis organici vivificationi & animationi per animæ rationalis cum eodem unione quodammodo respondet. Hoc initium, fundamentum & hæc radix in solidum à gratia Dei vivificante regenerante, creante, & omne liberum arbitrium ita præveniente, ut illud non supponat sive ut existens, sive ut operans, sed demum, ut causa effectum suum, efficiat & producat, dependet. Habemus igitur nos in ea operatione merè passive, ut materia patiens, & subjectum δεχτικόν, gratiosam illam Spiritus S. operationem recipiens, non ulla tamen vi vel coactione interveниente.
units.tr: This spiritual quickening corresponds in some way to the natural vivification and animation of an organic body through the union of the rational soul with that body. This beginning, foundation and root depends entirely on the quickening, regenerating and creating grace of God, which so anticipates all free will that it does not presuppose free will, either as existing or as acting; rather, as a cause brings about its effect, so grace brings about and produces the will. In this operation, therefore, we are purely passive, like matter that suffers, a receptive subject [δεκτικόν], receiving that gracious operation of the Holy Spirit, without any force or compulsion intervening.

units.la: Nam vis illa σφεργικόν seu vorticordia sic intellectum & voluntatem regenerat, habenas affectuum tractat & moderatur, ut voluntas velut ex mortuis resurgens cum quodam jubilo & spirituali lætitia creatorem & ἀναγεννώντα suum sponte sequatur, juxta illud sponsæ: Trahe me post te, & curremus, Cant. I. 4. & Jerem. XXXI. 18. 19. Converte me, & convertar, quia tu es Jehova, Deus meus. Et postquam ostensum fuerit mihi, applaudam femori.
units.tr: For that spherical power [σφαιρικόν], or whirling of the heart, so regenerates the intellect and the will, and so governs and moderates the reins of the affections, that the will, rising as if from the dead, follows its Creator and Regenerator [ἀναγεννῶντα] of its own accord, with a certain joy and spiritual gladness, according to the bride's words: Draw me after you, and we will run, Song 1:4; and Jeremiah 31:18-19: Turn me, and I shall be turned, for you are the LORD my God. And after I was shown, I struck my thigh.

units.la: Qua in re Tridentinis, & ipsis etiam Prædeterminantibus & Jansenitis liberi arbitrii in principio etiam conversionis à gratia, uti loquuntur, præventi, moti & excitati, cooperationem cum eadem, ad se ad gratiam justificationis obtinendam disponendum ac præparandum, asserentibus ingentis erroris dicam jam supra Loc. X. 86. conscripsimus. Progressus porrò, ædificium & ramus conversionis nostræ sunt effecta illa omnia, quæ gratiam Spiritus S. regenerantem, adeoque primam illam in regeneratione nobis inditam qualitatem, quæ veluti anima novi hominis est, proximè & immediatè sequuntur, quæque illam nobis primò, deinde aliis manifestant.
units.tr: On this point we have already written above, in Locus X, §86, against the Tridentines, and even against the Predeterminists and Jansenists, who assert that the free will, anticipated, moved and stirred up by grace (as they put it) even at the beginning of conversion, cooperates with grace, disposing and preparing itself to obtain the grace of justification; this is a great error. But the progress, the building and the branch of our conversion are all those effects that immediately and directly follow the regenerating grace of the Holy Spirit, and thus that first quality infused into us in regeneration, which is as it were the soul of the new man, and which first makes these effects known to us and then to others.

units.la: Pertinent huc sancti illi motus; cogitationes, desideria, opera, quibus, quod verè bonum est, cogitamus, eligimus, cupimus, volumus, & denique facimus. Atque hæc Spiritus S. non tantùm in nobis, sed etiam per nos operatur. Proin in iis voluntas humana non est tantùm subjectum recipiens & patiens, sed etiam instrumentum agens, quia Spiritus S. nostro intellectu, voluntate & affectibus in actibus hisce producendis uti dignatur. Facit enim, ut nos ipsi cogitemus, velimus, cupiamus, quæramus & faciamus ea, quæ sancta & Deo ἀνάγκῃ sunt.
units.tr: To this belong those holy motions: the thoughts, desires and works by which we think, choose, desire, will and finally do what is truly good. The Holy Spirit works these not only in us but also through us. Therefore in these the human will is not merely a receiving and suffering subject, but also an acting instrument, since the Holy Spirit deigns to use our understanding, will and affections in producing these acts. For he makes us ourselves think, will, desire, seek and do those things which are holy and pleasing to God [εὐάρεστα].

units.la: Atque sic in progressu illo & perseverantia voluntas humana non passivè tantùm se habet, sed à Spiritu Dei mota & acta ipsa quoque efficaciter agit, & nos ad bonum persequendum, malum fugiendum movet. Quo sensu illa jam vivens & valens non tam Deo cooperari, quàm suboperari dicitur, de quo in Loco plura. Et paucis eam in rem multa & ἐμφαλλικῶς S. Augustinus de Grat. & lib. Arbit. cap. 17. dixit; Deus inquit, ut velimus, operatur incipiens, qui volentibus cooperatur perficiens. Propter quod ait Apostolus: Certus sum, quoniam qui operatur in vobis bonum opus, perficiet usque in diem Jesu Christi. Ut ergo velimus, sine nobis operatur: cum autem tem volumus, & sic volumus, ut faciamus, nobiscum cooperatur; tamen sine illo vel operante, ut velimus, vel cooperante cum volumus, ad bona pietatis opera nihil valemus.
units.tr: And so, in that progress and perseverance, the human will not only is passive, but, moved and acted upon by the Spirit of God, also acts effectively itself, and moves us to pursue the good and flee evil. In this sense, the will, now living and strong, is said not so much to cooperate with God as to be subordinate to him in operation; more on this in the Locus. And St. Augustine said much briefly and forcefully on this point in de Grat. & lib. Arbit. c. 17: God, he says, works in us that we may will, beginning, and cooperates with those who will, completing. That is why the Apostle says: I am sure that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ, Philippians 1:6. So, that we may will, he works without us; but when we will, and will in such a way that we act, he cooperates with us; nevertheless, without him working that we may will, or cooperating when we will, we can do nothing to achieve good works of piety.

units.la: XL. Semipelagianorum & eorum, quos recentiores vestigia eorum premere diximus, Helena est gratia sufficiens, omnibus scilicet data, sed non omnipotente vi & omnipotenter sic agens, ut eventus necessario & immediatè sequatur, verùm morali operatione & suasione liberum hominis arbitrium, velut non plane in spiritualibus etiam per peccatum extinctum, sed vivens adhuc, sauciatum licèt, sic inclinans, ut conversionis tamen eventus in libera ejus potestate sit, & gratiæ sic inclinanti homo resistere, vel non resistere posset. Tota verò res & quæstio isthæc Deum inter & hominem, illius & hujus gloriam & potentiam disceptatur, atque ad hunc fere cardinem revocari potest: An datis omnibus gratiæ interne, prævenientis, excitantis & operantis adminiculis, duobus eodem modo dispositis, alter actu convertatur, alter liberè dissentiendo eandem gratiæ virtutem irritam seu inefficacem reddat? Affirmantem ubi demonstraverint Semipelagiani & semipelagianizantes, jam vicerit homo, vicerit arbitrium, & potestas hominis, & gratiæ sufficientis liber usus vel abusus de Deo ipso victo, & honore ejus honori arbitrii subjecto triumphum & Pæana canet. Negantem ubi nos demonstraverimus, Deus supra hominis stultitiam victor triumphatorque exisret, & simul funditus corruet, quicquid Philosophi de concursu Dei cum causis secundis, de viribus & facultate voluntatis humanæ; quicquid Pelagiani & Semipelagiani veteres & novi de hominis convertendi viribus, de gratia præveniente & subsequente, operante & cooperante, excitante & adjuvante; de gratia sufficiente efficaci & inefficaci; de voluntate Dei antecedente & consequente; de motionibus, auxiliis, prædeterminationibus, præscientia conditionata, de gratiæ communicandæ modo, infallibilitate, resistibilitate, necessitate, contingentia, &c. disputarunt, & adhuc disputant. Si enim datis gratiæ Dei convertentis omnibus adminiculis, duo subjectivè eodem modo dispositi infallibiliter convertuntur, non aliunde id evenire potest, quàm quia gratia Dei non communis & sufficiens aliqua ab arbitrio hominis alterutram in partem conversionis, vel in statu peccati perseverationis determinanda; sed singularis & eximia solis convertendis omnipotente sua vi omnipotenter agens, & repugnantiam ac resistentiam omnem vincens tolensque, neque tantum affectum conversionis infallibiliter imprimens, quod etiam οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας largiuntur, sed effectum ipsum certissimo cum eventu eliciens, primitus hominem non spiritualiter quidquam agentem vel molientem, sed spiritualem gratiam tantum recipientem, & quoad illam merè passivè se habentem convertit, & velut ex morte peccati vivificat & regenerat. Hoc ergo agamus.
units.tr: XL. The Semipelagians, and those whom we said the more recent men follow in their footsteps, hold to a sufficient grace, given to all, but not with an omnipotent power acting omnipotently so that the result follows necessarily and immediately; rather, by moral operation and persuasion, the free will of man, which is not wholly extinguished in spiritual matters by sin but still lives, though wounded, so inclines it that the outcome of conversion is nonetheless in its free power, and man can either resist or not resist grace inclining in this way. The whole matter and question is debated between God and man, concerning the glory and power of each, and it can be brought back almost to this hinge: given all the aids of inward, prevenient, stirring and operating grace, and two persons disposed in the same way, does one actually convert while the other, by freely dissenting, renders the same power of grace void or ineffective? If the Semipelagians and those who favour them demonstrate the affirmative, then man has already won, free will and the power of man have won, and the free use or abuse of sufficient grace has conquered God himself, and sings a triumph and paean with the honour of God made subject to the honour of free will. But if we demonstrate the negative, God will come forth as victor and triumphant over human folly, and at the same time all that the philosophers have said about the concurrence of God with secondary causes, about the powers and faculty of the human will, and all that the old and new Pelagians and Semipelagians have argued about the powers of man in conversion, about prevenient and subsequent grace, operating and cooperating, stirring and aiding, about efficacious and inefficacious sufficient grace, about the antecedent and consequent will of God, about motions, aids, predeterminations, conditional foreknowledge, the mode of communicating grace, its infallibility, resistibility, necessity, contingency, and so on, will utterly collapse. For if, given all the converting aids of God's grace, two subjectively equally disposed persons are infallibly converted, this can only happen because the grace of God is not a common and sufficient grace that is determined to one side or the other of conversion, or to perseverance in the state of sin, by the will of man; rather it is a singular and exceptional grace granted only to those who are to be converted, acting omnipotently by its own omnipotent power, overcoming and removing all repugnance and resistance. It not only imprints an affection for conversion infallibly, which even the opposing side [οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας] grants, but it also brings about the effect itself with most certain result: it converts man, who at first does nothing spiritual or attempts nothing spiritual, but only receives spiritual grace and is purely passive with respect to it, and it quickens and regenerates him as if out of the death of sin. Let us therefore proceed to this.

units.la: XLI. Planum igitur Primò omnium illud est, Scripturam voluntati nostræ post lapsum omnia detrahere, & gratiæ quicquid boni obvenit, in solidum acceptum referre. Nam figmentum omne cogitationum cordis humani יֵצֶר tantùm malum est omni die, Genes. VI. 5. Ut
units.tr: XLI. It is therefore plain, first of all, that Scripture takes away from our will everything it had after the Fall, and credits grace with the whole of whatever good comes to us. For every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart is only evil every day, Gen. VI. 5 [יֵצֶר]. So that

units.la: animalis homo non capit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Sunt enim ei stultitia, & non potest intelligere, quia spiritualiter dijudicantur, 1.Cor. II.14. Non sumus idonei ex nobis cogitare aliquid tanquam ex nobis, sed ἱκανότης idoneitas nostra ex Deo est, 2. Cor. III. 5. Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi (vocavi) vos. Joh. XV. 16. Deus est, qui in nobis operatur velle & perficere ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας pro beneplacito (non nostro, sed suo illo, seu θελήματος voluntatis illius, & quod est ἐνεργεῖν juxta propositum ejus, Ephes. I. 5. 11.) Phil. II. 13. Si homo quivis sufficientem gratiam habet, per quam posset si velit, non jam Deus operabitur τὸ θέλειν velle (nam sic velle non est nostrum, sed Deus facit velle, dando cor novum ad intelligendum, cor carneum, spiritum novum) sed τὸ δύνασθαι posse. Quamvis & nostra δύναμις potentia est ἐνδυναμοῦσθαι corroborari, Phil. IV. 13. agi à Spiritu Dei, à Deo creari, à Deo & ejus ἐνεργείᾳ operatione efficaci velle & operari, seu voluntatem & operationem accipere. Merum porro in verbis Apostoli ludibrium foret, si Deus diceretur operari velle, quia voluntati cooperatur, & cooperando facit velle, uti id Novatores explicant. Qui enim cum voluntate cooperatur, is non facit velle, sed tantum opus externum producere. Et Deo cum voluntate cooperante non sequitur conversio, sed jam in voluntate operante sive volente est conversio, sed quid multis? Deus operatur velle ut κλῆσις vocatio est. Quemadmodum cùm Deus creat, vocat, quæ non sunt, & non potest fieri, ut non sit, vel vocatum adsit; nec sibi existendi causa esse potest. Sic ergo operatur velle, ut voluntas nova se sistat, quæ ante non erat; & infallibiliter se sistat, & prius quàm se sistat, non velit, puta πνευματικὸν spirituale aliquid; quale est credere; resipiscere, Deum amare; adeóque nec volendo ancipitem gratiam determinet. Ideo ἐχαρίσθη πιστεύειν donatum nobis est in Christum credere, Phil. I. 29. & opus bonum in nobis inchoat, ib. v. 6. Deo omne bonum operis nostrum præveniente, non cum hominis voluntate cooperante. Nam qui sic inchoat bonum opus, ut inchoando ipsum velle det, cum illo sic inchoante voluntas cooperari non potest. Clarissimè verò idem S. Paulus: Quis te discrevit? Quid habes autem quod non acceperis? Si autem accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non acceperis? 1. Cor. IV. 7. Atqui qui cum eadem gratiæ mensura convertitur, cum qua alius non convertitur, næ is se ipsum discernit. Habet enim, quod non accepit, & unde glorietur. Sed solus Deus gratiam dando vel non dando homines discernit, distinguit Jehova pium sibi; Psal. IV. 4. Unde Bellarminus ipse de Grat. & Lib. Arb. lib. I. 12. sic Molinam; & qui ipsum sequuntur, suppresso nomine perstringit: Nonne dicere poterit is, qui credit, se discerni ab infidelì per liberum arbitrium, quia ipse inspirationem recepit, quam alter rejicit, nonne gloriari poterit contra infidelem, quòd ipse Dei gratiæ cooperatus sit, quam ille contempsit?
units.tr: the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned, 1 Cor. II. 14. Our sufficiency is not from ourselves, as though we could think anything of ourselves, but our sufficiency [ἱκανότης] is from God, 2 Cor. III. 5. You did not choose me, but I chose you (I called you), John XV. 16. It is God who works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure [ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας] (not our pleasure, but his own, or his will [θελήματος], and what is to work [ἐνεργεῖν] according to his purpose, Eph. I. 5, 11), Phil. II. 13. If any man has sufficient grace, by which he could act if he wished, then God does not yet work the willing [τὸ θέλειν] (for to will in this way is not ours, but God makes us will, by giving a new heart to understand, a heart of flesh, a new spirit), but only the being able [τὸ δύνασθαι]. Although our power [δύναμις] is also to be strengthened [ἐνδυναμοῦσθαι], Phil. IV. 13, to be moved by the Spirit of God, to be created by God, and by his efficacious operation [ἐνεργείᾳ] to will and to work, that is, to receive the will and the working. Moreover, it would be a mere mockery of the Apostle's words if God were said to work the willing because he cooperates with the will, and by cooperating makes us will, as the innovators explain it. For he who cooperates with the will does not make us will, but only brings about an external act. Nor does conversion follow from God cooperating with the will; rather, conversion is already in the will that works or wills. But why say more? God works the willing as calling [κλῆσις] is. Just as when God creates, he calls into being things that are not, and it cannot happen that a thing is not and yet the called thing is present, nor can it be the cause of its own existence; so he works the willing in such a way that a new will comes into being which did not exist before, and it comes into being infallibly; and before it comes into being it does not will anything spiritual [πνευματικὸν], such as believing, repenting, or loving God; and so it does not determine grace as something doubtful by its own willing. Hence "it has been given [ἐχαρίσθη] to us to believe in Christ," Phil. I. 29, and he "begins a good work in us," ibid. v. 6, God going before every good of our work, not with the human will cooperating. For he who so begins a good work that in beginning it he gives the very willing, cannot have the will cooperating with him in that beginning. Most clearly the same Paul says: "Who makes you to differ? And what have you that you did not receive? Now if you received it, why do you glory as if you had not received it?" 1 Cor. IV. 7. But he who is converted with the same measure of grace with which another is not converted, certainly distinguishes himself. For he has something that he did not receive, and something to glory in. But God alone, by giving or not giving grace, distinguishes men; Jehovah sets apart the godly for himself, Ps. IV. 4. Hence Bellarmine himself, in De Gratia et Libero Arbitrio, book I, chapter 12, so describes Molina, and, without naming him, strikes at those who follow him: Can not he who believes say that he is distinguished from the unbeliever by free will, because he himself received the inspiration which the other rejected? Can he not glory against the unbeliever that he himself cooperated with the grace of God which the other despised?

units.la: XLII. Apertè S. Paulo Molina, Lessius, alii discretionem omnem libero arbitrio vendicantes, & gratiæ efficaciam à solo eventu arcessentes; reclamant, & Pelagio strenuè litant. Tertius & cautius; si non castius alii Gratiæ Divinæ modo næ motionem in se indifferentem esse: at relative, respectu vel annexæ congruitatis: uti Bellarminus loquitur; vel debitæ applicationis, ut Fonseca, vel intentionis Divinæ, uti Suarez discrimen seu Διακρισιν discretionem illam facere asserunt; similitudine petita ab eleemosyna & gladio, quorum illa non eodem modo saturum & famelicum: hic non eodem modo securum & periclitantem afficit. Ita ex circumstantiarum talium varietate id evenire contendunt, ut levior gratiæ impulsus plus, gravior verò minùs promoveat. Sed Σοφὸν φάρμακον, non rationem id sapit. Nam congrua ista gratiæ explicatio ex intentione Divina vel ad gratiam solùm, vel ad liberum arbitrium solùm, vel ad utrumque ex æquo, vel inæqualiter refertur. Si ad liberum arbitrium in solidum, vel ex parte refertur, erit hæc Pelagii & Molinæ bis cocta crambe, & cum eadem mors gratiæ Dei. Si ad solam gratiam, non ergò illa amplius æqualis erit, quia alteri congrua applicatio defuit, quam alterius gratia inclusit. Atque ita non fuerint subjectivè æqualiter dispositi. Sed illi æqualitatem gratiæ in genere motionis, at non beneficii collocant, atque inde provenire ajunt, ut æqualis gratiæ motio utrisque ex parte Dei adhibita, ob diversam objectorum dispositionem, & occupatam à proponente opportunitatem diversos effectus producat. Sed præterquam quòd miserum nimis est, seclusò gratiæ beneficio ad nudam motionem confugere, eamque sine beneficio gratiæ nomine obtrudere; etiam motio hæc plane chimærica est: quia, si ob diversam convertendorum dispositionem diversus ejusdem motionis effectus prodit, quale cunque discrimen illud est, non à gratia, sed à recipientis, quæ superadditur, promptitudine illud fluet, atque sic homo habebit, quo se ipsum discernat, & unde glorietur. Dilutum verò & illud Remonstrantium est, quo Jesuitis suppetias ferunt, quòd gratia agat principaliter, voluntas verò cum & iub gratia, ut effectus jam gratiæ, non voluntatis sit. Nam ille gratiæ & voluntatis concursus vel coordinatus vel subordinatus est. Si subordinatus, prius gratia convertit, quàm voluntas operatur. Si coordinatus, parum refert, cujuscunque inæqualitatis sit, modo agens debilius, pueri instar ad gigantis robur in tractione navis nonnihil conferentis, momentum aliquod, utut debile conferat, absque quo agentis fortioris conatus non succederet. Quicquid verò illud gratiæ accessorium est, discrimen ponit, unde qui illud adjecit, seipsum discernit.
units.tr: XLII. Molina, Lessius, and others who claim all distinction for free will and derive the efficacy of grace solely from its result, clearly contradict St. Paul and struggle stoutly for Pelagius. A third party, more cautiously (if not more chastely), holds that the motion of Divine grace is in itself indifferent, but relatively so, with respect to an attached congruity, as Bellarmine speaks; or to a due application, as Fonseca; or to the divine intention, as Suarez: they maintain that this makes the distinction, or discrimination [Διάκρισιν], borrowing a similitude from alms and the sword, of which the former does not affect the full and the hungry in the same way, nor the latter the secure and the endangered in the same way. Thus they contend that from the variety of such circumstances it happens that a lighter impulse of grace advances a person more, and a heavier one less. But this is a clever remedy, not a reasoned one. For this congruous explanation of grace refers the divine intention either to grace alone, or to free will alone, or to both equally, or to both unequally. If it refers to free will wholly or in part, this will be the twice-cooked cabbage of Pelagius and Molina, and the same death of the grace of God. If it refers to grace alone, then it will not be equal in the two, because the congruous application was lacking to one, which the grace of the other included. And so they would not have been equally disposed in their subjects. But they place an equality of grace in the kind of motion, not in the benefit, and they say that from this it follows that an equal motion of grace applied by God to both, because of the different disposition of the objects and the opportunity seized by the proposer, produces different effects. But apart from the fact that it is too wretched to flee to a bare motion, leaving out the benefit of grace, and to press it on us without the name of grace, this motion is also quite chimerical. For if a different effect of the same motion arises from the different disposition of those to be converted, whatever difference that is will flow not from grace but from the readiness of the recipient, which is added on top of grace; and so man will have something by which he distinguishes himself, and something to glory in. Nor is that answer of the Remonstrants, with which they come to the aid of the Jesuits, any better: that grace acts principally, but the will acts with and under grace, so that the act is now the effect of grace, not of the will. For that concurrence of grace and will is either coordinate or subordinate. If subordinate, grace converts first, before the will acts. If coordinate, it matters little how unequal it is, provided that the weaker agent, like a boy helping a giant a little in hauling a ship, contributes some momentum, however feeble, without which the stronger agent's effort would not succeed. But whatever that accessory of grace is, it sets up a difference, by which he who added it distinguishes himself.

units.la: XLIII. Qui gratiam congruam, per quam homo discernatur, finxerunt, prope illi à Pelagii castris absunt. Ejusmodi enim gratia illa est, non quæ in voluntatem influat, sed in quam voluntas hoc vel illo modo disposita influat, & quæ eam volendo efficacem reddat. Non igitur propriè gratiam, sed ipsum potiùs hominem certis temporibus ad salutarem conversionem congruum ponunt, & gratiæ efficaciam ab ejus unius assensu suspendunt.
units.tr: XLIII. Those who invented a congruous grace, by which a man is distinguished, have come very near to the camp of Pelagius. For such a grace is not one that flows into the will, but one into which the will, disposed in this or that way, flows, and which by its willing makes grace effective. They therefore do not properly posit grace, but rather posit man himself as congruous for saving conversion at certain times, and make the efficacy of grace depend on the assent of that one man alone.

units.la: Atque ita homo se ipsum, non gratia Dei hominem discernit. Qui purus putus Pelagianismus est. Tum verò incongruum est, captatis momentis temporum, aliarumque circumstantiarum hominem in peccatis mortuum, tempestivo & congruo sua-
units.tr: And so man distinguishes himself, not the grace of God distinguishes man. This is pure Pelagianism. Moreover, it is absurd to want to lead a man dead in sins to the heavenly life by a timely and congruous persuasion, seizing on the moments of time and other circumstances, just as one might want to call back to life the ashes and bones of a dead man by some art of music and a suitable song.

units.la: su ad vitam cœlestem adducere velle, quàm mortui hominis cineres & offa Musicæ ope quadam & accommodato cantu ad vitam ciere vele. Ut nullo fundamento præscientia illa Dei, qua gratiam illam perité & congruè dispenset, innitatur. Dei porro gratia hominem saluti congruum facit, non invenit: quæ ut liberrima est, ita indignissimis sæpe adest, multósque foris etiam speciosos, & à seculi labe, uti videtur, remotos præterit. Cùmque congruitas illa gratiæ fundetur in certa dispositione hominis, in qua eo tempore, quo ad credendum vocatur, invenitur, atque ejusmodi dispositio hominis oriri possit, & sæpe oriatur à causis naturalibus, tota sic efficacia gratiæ ad naturam reducetur.
units.tr: Thus that foreknowledge of God, by which he skilfully and congruously dispenses that grace, rests on no foundation. But the grace of God does not find a man congruous for salvation; it makes him so. And since it is most free, it is often present to the most unworthy, and passes by many who seem outwardly excellent and, as it appears, remote from the stain of the world. And since that congruity of grace is founded on a certain disposition of the man, which is found in him at the time when he is called to believe, and since such a disposition can arise, and often does arise, from natural causes, the whole efficacy of grace is thus reduced to nature.

units.la: XLIV. Cùm Deus homines quosdam in peccatum lapsos quadam gratia sua coërcet & frænat, ad bonum multis modis excitat, & varie illuminat, non sic congruum eum speciali vocationi & conversioni facit, sed pro ineffabili sua sapientia quadam ampliore illuminatione sanctè ad convictionem impotentiæ carnis, quæ Deo subjici non potest, abutitur, ut eo magis justitia condemnationis humanæ naturæ & necessitas gratiæ appareat. Sed & cum electis suis aliquando &ferè ordinariè Deus ita agit, ut maturè ad agnitionem veritatis adducantur, & ab inquinamentis mundi perditi & in malo jacentis segregentur, & sæpe non longè à regno Cœlorum absint. Neque tamen ea vel congruentia, vel causa quædam est, ob quam illos conversionis gratia dignetur. Nam & tales abjicere posset, neque in tali statu partem aut potestatem regenerationis, per quam in regno Cœlorum collocentur, habent. Præterea nec dubium est, quin Deus vocationis circumstantias moderetur, nonnunquam graves tentationes, quarum natura est assensum difficiliorem reddere; amovendo; aliquando in magnum peccatum labi sinendo, ut contusa superbia humilitas resurgat; sæpe constringendo vinculis angustiarum, ut illecebris carnis summotis, & conscientia apud se in judicium vocata, aurem in angustia aperiat. Unde infantes, infirma elegisse, vocasse dicitur, Matth. XI. 25. 1.Cor. I. 19. &c. Jac. II. 5. quia ipsi gloriosum est homines in talibus circumstantiis vocare & beare, & contra in aliis circumstantiis justæ severitatis exemplum præbere, ne quis in se ipso glorietur. Nihilominus circumstantiæ ejusmodi homines non regenerant vel convertunt; & in nullo statu vel circumstantia homo carnalis vocationi congruus reddi potest. Ejus enim studium manet inimicitia contra Deum. Legi enim Dei non subjicitur, ὑπότασσεται ac ne potest quidem, Rom. VIII. 7.
units.tr: XLIV. When God restrains and bridles some men who have fallen into sin by a certain grace of his, and stirs them up to good in many ways and variously enlightens them, he does not thereby make them fit for special calling and conversion. Rather, in his ineffable wisdom, he sometimes uses a fuller illumination to convince the flesh of its impotence, which cannot be subject to God, so that the justice of the condemnation of human nature and the necessity of grace may appear all the more. But God also acts thus with his elect, sometimes and almost ordinarily, so that they are brought early to the knowledge of the truth and set apart from the defilements of the lost world, which lies in evil, and often they are not far from the kingdom of heaven. Yet this is neither a fitness nor a cause for which the grace of conversion deigns to choose them. For he could also cast such men off, and in such a state they have neither part nor power of regeneration, through which they are placed in the kingdom of heaven. Moreover, there is no doubt that God regulates the circumstances of calling: sometimes by removing grievous temptations, whose nature is to make assent more difficult; sometimes by allowing a man to fall into great sin, so that humility may rise again after pride has been bruised; often by binding him with the chains of distress, so that, the allurements of the flesh being removed and conscience called to judgment within itself, he may open his ear in his distress. Hence infants are said to be chosen and the weak things to be called (Matt. 11:25; 1 Cor. 1:19, etc.; James 2:5), because it is glorious for him to call and bless men in such circumstances, and on the other hand to give, in other circumstances, an example of just severity, so that no one may glory in himself. Nevertheless, such circumstances do not regenerate or convert men, and in no state or circumstance can the carnal man be made fit for calling. For his disposition remains enmity against God; for he is not subject to the law of God, and indeed cannot be (Rom. 8:7) [ὑποτάσσεται].

units.la: XLV. Sed argumenta sequentia prosequantur. Secundum igitur ea Scripturæ loca suppeditant, quibus conversio seu vocatio peccatoris creatio, regeneratio, vivificatio à mortuis, insitio in oleam, & sumptio in hæredem vel notatio per fortem, appellatur. Crea in me cor purum, Psal. LI. 12. Licèt enim jam tum, cùm sic praecaretur David habuerit cor purum, quia odium peccati, quod testabatur, & seria deprecatio atque fides nonnisi ex corde puro proficisci potuit; tamen creationem cordis puri à Deo petens innuit, tum cor purum se non habere à se ipso, sed à creante Deo: tum partem nondum in se venit. in se regenitam, sed indies regenerandam creatoris Dei omnipotentiam requirere: tum puritatem per prævalentem cupiditatem carnis imminutam non posse fine creatione quadam restitui: tum sicut initium puritatis in corde, ita ejusdem etiam amplificationem, per quam fit, ut novæ virtutes, novæ cogitationes bonæ, nova lux, cognitio, lætitia in homine existat, à Divina creatione existere. Sed & Christus vocationem & conversionem γέννησιν generationem, quæ ἄνωθεν desuper fit, & ex Spiritu & aqua, appellat, ejusque necessitatem argumentis maximis confirmat. Joh. III. 3. s. &c. Nam Deus secundum multam misericordiam suam nos ἀναγεννήσας regeneravit ad spem vivam per resurrectionem Jesu Christi, 1. Pet. I. 3. Sicut vero naturalis generatio est quædam vocatio generandi ex utero, Esaj. XLI. 4. XLIX. 1. ita spiritualis generatio, seu regeneratio quædam vocatio regenerandi ex eo statu, in quo non erat, vel in quo erat παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος vetustus homo abolendus, Rom. VI. 6. est. Ideo Deus Pater hominum, velut Israelis, & homines filii Dei vivi, Hos. I. 10. dicuntur. Nam צוּר יָלַד Rupes te genuit, Deut. XXXII. 18. Βυλήθησ ἀπεκύησεν ἡμᾶς volens genuit nos, Jac. I. 18. Quando homo in hunc mundum nascitur, non à Deo nascitur, sed à parentibus; à Deo autem creatur. Quando vero à Deo generatur, secundò generatur & τέκνον γίνεῖ filius fit, Joh. I. 12. Quam regenerationem etiam Bildad innuit, dicens: Onager homo nascitur, seu qui onager fuit, jam homo, imago Dei fit, Job. XI. 12. Denique à Deo vocatus, & per vocationem conversus velut ex mortuis vivificatur & resuscitatur. Vos mortuos in peccatis vivificavit unâ cum Christo, & unâ suscitavit. &c. Ephef. II. 1. s. 6. Ideò etiam τὸ ὑπερεξαίρετον μέγεθος supereminentem magnitudinem potentiæ, & ἐνέργειαν κράτος efficaciam roboris potentiæ suæ, quam exeruit in Christo, cùm eum ex mortuis resuscitavit, etiam erga πιστεύοντας credentes, quando fide donatos ex morte spirituali revocavit, adhibuisse ibid. I. 19. dicitur. Accedit, quòd vocatus & convertendus ab ipso Deo παρὰ φύσιν præter naturam oleæ inseritur. Potens enim Deus est, ut eos inferat oleæ. Nam si tu ex naturali excisus es oleastro, & præter naturam infertus es in oleam bonam, quanto magis ii, qui secundum naturam sunt (nati ex Patribus & in fœdere) inserentur oleæ suæ? Rom. XI. 23. 24. Denique vocatio & conversio venit nomine κλῆσις. In Christo ἐκλεγόμενοι in clerum seu hæreditatem Dei recepti, vel forte notati sumus, qui prædestinati sumus secundum propositum ejus, Ephef. I. 11. Atqui ad creationem, generationem novam, vivificationem ex mortuis, insitionem in oleam, acceptionem in hæreditatem, vel notationem, quæ per sortem fit, non plus unus confert, quàm alius. Nam ita etiam pro justificatione prima gratuita Bellarminus de justific. lib. IV. 18. argumentatur: Quemadmodum nemo potest opere suo se ipsum procreare, aut ex morte revocare: sic etiam homo per peccatum mortuus non potest se ipsum merito operum suorum justificare. Ergo pari etiam ratione homo in peccato mortuus, creandus, regenerandus, vivificandus &c. unus præ alio se convertere, vocanti, creanti, regenerati, vivificanti parere vel repugnare nequit.
units.tr: XLV. Let the following arguments follow on. Accordingly, the passages of Scripture which call the conversion or calling of the sinner a creation, regeneration, making alive from the dead, engrafting into the olive tree, adoption as heir, or designation by lot, support this. Create in me a clean heart (Ps. 51:12). For although David already had a clean heart when he prayed thus, since the hatred of sin which he professed, and his earnest entreaty and faith, could have come only from a pure heart, nevertheless in asking God for the creation of a clean heart he signals that he does not have a clean heart of himself but from God the Creator; that he has not yet come to a regenerate part of himself, but daily requires the omnipotence of God the Creator to be regenerated; that purity, diminished by the prevailing lust of the flesh, cannot be restored without a certain creation; and that just as the beginning of purity in the heart, so also its increase, by which new virtues, new good thoughts, new light, knowledge and joy come to exist in a man, exists from divine creation. Christ also calls conversion and calling a birth (γέννησις) which comes from above (ἄνωθεν), and of the Spirit and of water, and confirms its necessity with the greatest arguments (John 3:3ff., etc.). For God, according to his great mercy, has regenerated us (ἀναγεννήσας) to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ (1 Pet. 1:3). Just as natural generation is a certain calling to be born from the womb (Isa. 41:4; 49:1), so spiritual generation, or regeneration, is a certain calling to be reborn out of that state in which one was not, or in which one was the old man (παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος), who is to be put off (Rom. 6:6). Therefore God is called the Father of men, as of Israel, and men are called sons of the living God (Hos. 1:10). For Rock that begat you (צוּר יָלַד) (Deut. 32:18), and willing, he begat us (βουληθεὶς ἀπεκύησεν ἡμᾶς) (James 1:18). When a man is born into this world, he is born not of God but of his parents; but when he is begotten by God, he is begotten a second time and becomes a child (τέκνον γίνεται, John 1:12). Bildad also hints at this regeneration, saying: the wild ass is born a man, or he who was a wild ass is now a man, made the image of God (Job 11:12). Finally, called by God and converted through the calling, he is made alive and raised as from the dead. He made you alive, who were dead in sins, together with Christ, and raised you up together (Eph. 2:1ff., 6). Therefore he is said to have shown the surpassing greatness (τὸ ὑπερεξαίρετον μέγεθος) of his power and the working (ἐνέργειαν) of the might of his strength, which he exerted in Christ when he raised him from the dead, also toward those who believe, when he recalled them, given faith, from spiritual death (ibid. 1:19). Add to this that the one called and to be converted by God himself is grafted into the olive contrary to nature (παρὰ φύσιν). For God is able to graft them into their olive. For if you were cut out of the wild olive which is by nature, and grafted contrary to nature into a good olive, how much more will those who are according to nature (born of the fathers and in the covenant) be grafted into their own olive? (Rom. 11:23, 24). Finally, calling and conversion are named by the word κλῆσις. In Christ we are chosen (ἐκλεγόμενοι), received into the clergy, that is, the inheritance of God, or perhaps designated by lot, we who were predestined according to his purpose (Eph. 1:11). Yet one man contributes no more than another to creation, new generation, making alive from the dead, engrafting into the olive, reception into the inheritance, or designation which is made by lot. For Bellarmine argues in this way even for the first, gratuitous justification (De justificatione, Book IV, ch. 18): Just as no one can create himself by his own work, or recall himself from death, so too a man who is dead through sin cannot justify himself by the merit of his own works. Therefore, by the same reasoning, a man who is dead in sin, to be created, regenerated, made alive, etc., cannot prefer to convert himself, or resist the one calling, creating, regenerating, and making alive.

units.la: XLVI. Nequicquam verò hostes gratiæ regerunt, nihil similitudines has probare, quia mortuum inter naturaliter & spiritualiter discrimen multiplex intercedat; & mortuos in peccatis non quosvis reprobos, sed quosdam duntaxat omnis vocationis expertes intelligi: & vocatos solos innatam nolendi & volendi facultatem, solicitante primùm gratia, in actum producere, non vocatos non item. Sed tenuissimorum flatuum hæ bullæ sunt. Non enim similitudinum illarum in omnibus convenientia, sed scopus spectari debet. Retinet spiritualiter mortuus intellectum, voluntatem, libertatem, quam naturaliter mortuus non retinet. Sed nihilominus spiritualiter mortui intellectus, voluntas & libertas in bono naturali, civili, morali externo activa & vivax, nulla in spirituali vita, actu nullo pollet. Atque eatenus demum creari, regenerari, vivificari debet. Sicut horologium casu aliquo turbatum indicat nihilo minus tempus, sed falsò: pixis nautica fulmine vel aliàs à cynosura aversa constanter fidus obliquum vel oppositum indigetat: Vinum acescens colorem & quantitatem, sed cum qualitate edaci & noxia retinet: ita voluntas libera per mortem in peccato libera esse non definit, & liberè bonum illud, ad quod naturaliter fertur, appetit; sed ad bonum supernaturale & spirituale non assurgit, perinde ac si eatenus mortua esset. Non corrumpitur enim vel moritur quoad agendi radicem, sed quoad terminum salutarem, ut ad eum amplius aspirare, vel ad conversionem sui plus conferre quàm creatura, genitus, planè mortuus, horologium, acus nautica, acetum ad integritatem non habitam acquirendam, vel ad amissam perfectionem recuperandam potest, non valeat. Sicut verò vita est, nosse vitam & veritatem Deo gloriosam, eámque amare, & ejus amore moveri, regi, incitari; ita mors est, non quaerere bonum suum, ab eo separari, esse ἀδύνατον ineptum ad omne bonum opus, non condecorare Deum creatorem suum, & ejus oblivisci, atque ei rebellare, aliud pro eo bonum quaerere, se ipsum in libertatem afferere, & sibi finem, atque vim suam, Deum suum constituere. Quæ opera, sicut mortua sunt, ita mortem, hoc est, ἀδύνατον & ἀδυναμίαν imbecillitatem & impotentiam faciendi voluntatem Dei, adeóque vivendi, & actiones vitæ exercendi arguunt. Et mors hæc omnium haud dubiè irregenitorum, sive illi vocati, sive non vocati sint, quanquam ii, quibuscum nobis res est, universalem vocationem tuentur: Nam etiam vocati, si nondum regeniti sunt, vita illa spirituali carent, adeóque in peccato mortui, & , siquidem salvandi sunt, creandi, regenerandi, resuscitandi, & vineæ suæ inserendi sunt. Licèt enim gradatim crescat conversionis fructus, in instanti tamen, ut cum Philosophis loquar, per primum sui non esse forma ipsius imprimitur. Neque enim de eo quæstio est, an voluntas primo gratiæ impulsui assentiatur, sed de eo quæstio est, unde fit ille assensus liber, num à voluntate, an ab operante gratia, quæ in solidum illud restituit, ut voluntas primæ conversioni liberè assentiatur. Non enim assensum negamus, sed illum à gratia effectum esse contendimus.
units.tr: XLVI. Yet the enemies of grace vainly object that these similitudes prove nothing, because there is a manifold difference between natural and spiritual death; and that those dead in sins are to be understood not as any reprobates, but only certain men who lack all calling; and that only those who are called, when grace first stirs them, bring their innate power of willing and not-willing into act, while those not called do not. But these bubbles are of the thinnest breath. For the agreement of those similitudes is to be considered not in all respects, but in the point at issue. The spiritually dead man retains understanding, will and liberty, which the naturally dead man does not retain. Yet nonetheless the understanding, will and liberty of the spiritually dead man, active and lively in natural, civil, moral and external good, have no power at all in spiritual life. And so far, at last, he must be created, regenerated and made alive. Just as a clock disturbed by some accident still shows the time, but falsely; or a magnetic compass, averted from the pole star by lightning or otherwise, constantly points to the opposite, or away from its faithful guide; or sour wine keeps its colour and quantity, but with a corrosive and harmful quality: so the free will does not cease to be free through death in sin, and freely desires that good to which it is naturally inclined; but it does not rise to supernatural and spiritual good, just as if it were dead in that respect. For it is not corrupted or dead as to the root of acting, but as to the saving end, so that it cannot aspire further toward that end or contribute more to its own conversion than a creature, a begotten man, a clock, a compass needle, or vinegar can to acquiring an integrity it did not have or recovering a lost perfection. Just as life is to know God's life and truth as glorious, and to love it and be moved, ruled and urged by its love, so death is not to seek one's own good, to be separated from him, to be unfit (ἀδύνατον) for every good work, not to honour God the Creator and forget him, to rebel against him, to seek another good in his place, to assert oneself into liberty, and to make oneself one's end and strength, one's own god. These works, as they are dead, so they show death, that is, the inability (ἀδύνατον) and powerlessness (ἀδυναμία), the weakness and impotence to do the will of God, and therefore to live and to perform the actions of life. And this death without doubt belongs to all the unregenerate, whether they are called or not called; although those with whom we have to do defend a universal calling. For even the called, if they are not yet regenerate, lack that spiritual life, and so are dead in sins; and, if indeed they are to be saved, they must be created, regenerated, raised up, and engrafted into his vineyard. For although the fruit of conversion grows gradually, yet, to speak with the philosophers, the form is impressed on the thing in an instant, by its first non-being. For the question is not whether the will assents to the first impulse of grace, but whence that assent comes to be free: whether from the will, or from the operating grace, which restores the will entirely so that it may assent freely to the first conversion. For we do not deny assent, but we contend that it is effected by grace.

units.la: XLVII. Sed in ipsa vita naturali principium
units.tr: XLVII. But even in natural life itself, some principle

units.la: Exceptioni, quòd naturaliter inter & spirituaaliter mortuos discrimen intercedat, & non quivis reprobi in peccatis mortui dicantur. pium aliquod supernaturális vitæ patroni liberi arbitrii ponunt. Sic meus quondam retiarius, Abbas Augustinus Redingius; addens & illud, principium illud vitæ supernaturalis ad supernaturales operationes fidei, charitatis, pœnitentiæ, justificationi prævias elevari. Quod crudum & ἀσύνετον nimium est. Quomodo enim homo naturalis, animalis, in peccato mortuus actívum vitæ supernaturalis principium habere, & ad supernaturales operationes exercendas elevari, & simul animalis, naturalis, in peccato mortuus, quippe irregenitus, manere potest? Et principium tale irregenitus vel ex se ipso, vel ex vi per gratiam accepta habet. Si prius, vicit Pelagius. Si posterius, vel vis illa per gratiam accepta vitalis, vel non vitalis est: Si vitalis, vivit igitur irregenitus prius, quàm vivificetur. Per quod enim ante vivificationem sui cooperatur, id ante sui vivificationem habet. Si non vitalis, quomodo ea ad sui vivificationem cooperatur? Et vim illam cooperandi non vitalem per suam cooperationem, an sine ea accepit? Si prius, ergo antequam vim illam acciperet, aliam vim cooperandi habuit. Unde verò illam habuit? à se, an ex gratia? Si à se, ubi gratia? Si à gratia, an se cooperante, vel non cooperante? Si à se cooperante, vim igitur operandi habet prius quàm vivat. At vita prior est, quia operandi principium est. Si à se non cooperante, ergo primæ vivificationi suæ non cooperatur.
units.tr: To the objection that there is a difference between those who are naturally dead and those who are spiritually dead, and that not every reprobate is called dead in sins, the patrons of free will posit some principle of supernatural life. So did my former adversary, Abbot Augustinus Redingius, adding that this principle of supernatural life is raised up to the supernatural acts of faith, charity, repentance and justification that precede it. This is crude and unintelligible [ἀσύνετον] in the extreme. For how can a natural, animal man who is dead in sin have an active principle of supernatural life and be raised to perform supernatural acts, and yet at the same time remain an animal, natural man who is dead in sin, since he is unregenerate? An unregenerate man has such a principle either from himself or from a power received through grace. If from himself, Pelagius has won. If the latter, that power received through grace is either vital or not vital. If vital, then the unregenerate man is alive before he is quickened; for whatever he co-operates with before his quickening, he has before his quickening. If not vital, how does it co-operate in his quickening? And did he receive that non-vital power of co-operating without its co-operation, or with it? If first, then before he received that power he had another power of co-operating. But where did he get that power? From himself, or from grace? If from himself, where is grace? If from grace, did grace co-operate, or not? If grace co-operated, then he has a power of acting before he lives; but life comes first, since it is the principle of acting. If from himself without grace's co-operation, then he does not co-operate in his first quickening.

units.la: XLVIII. Argumento huic robur Tertium ab infinita Dei potentia omnipotenter convertentis & vocantis petitum, addit.
units.tr: XLVIII. He adds a third argument, drawn from the infinite power of God who converts and calls omnipotently, to strengthen this argument.

units.la: Hoc enim ad liquidum perductum facilè creationis, regenerationis, vivificationis metaphoricæ figmentum elidet. Si enim Deus vocans, convertens ejusmodi gratia utitur, quæ omnipotente vi & omnipotenter agit, manifestum erit, & creationem, regenerationem, vivificationem hominis, qui vocatur & convertitur, proprie, non metaphoricè totum esse: & duobus vocatis æqualiter dispositis nunquam fore, ut unus convertatur, alter conversioni reluctetur. Cui enim bono omnipotens virtus omnipotenter agens, si voluntas ita dispositæ est, ut gratiæ cooperari, & cooperando aliquatenus se ipsam convertere possit? Et omnipotenti virtuti omnipotenter agenti qua libertate freta voluntas resistere potest? Atqui in vocatione & conversione hominis gratiam Dei omnipotente virtute seu omnipotenter agere, supra §. XXVI. pluribus confirmavimus. Vel unus S. Paulus omni exceptione major est, prædicans illud ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ superéminentem magnitudinem potentiæ Dei erga nos, qui credimus, secundum ἐνέργειαν & κράτος ἰσχύος efficaciam roboris potentiæ, vel virium ejus, quam operatus est in Christo, dum eum excitavit ex mortuis, & collocavit ad dextram suam in supercœlestibus, Ephes. I. 19. 20. Nam & potentiam Dei & superéminentem magnitudinem potentiæ Dei, per quam factum est, ut crederemus, vehementer prædicat: & potentiam illam tum in genere, tum in specie explicat. In genere, quòd sit potentia par & consentanea efficaciæ roboris virium, quam operatus est in Christo. Ubi κράτος גבורה robur excessum supra potentiam omnis creaturæ, & supra id, quod Deus ordinarie in mundo facit: ἰσχύς חיל vires penetrationem voluntatis in effectum, ejusque certam assecutionem; & ἐνέργεια efficacia operationem roboris & virium in Christo jam extantem, & velut obsidem reliqui effectus significat.
units.tr: For if this is brought fully into the light, it will easily dispel the fiction of a metaphorical creation, regeneration and quickening. For if God, in calling and converting, uses a grace that acts with almighty power and omnipotently, it will be clear that the creation, regeneration and quickening of the man who is called and converted are wholly real, not metaphorical; and that when two men are called and equally disposed, one will never be converted while the other resists conversion. For to what purpose would an omnipotent power acting omnipotently be, if the will is so disposed that it can co-operate with grace and by co-operating convert itself in some measure? And what freedom could the will rely on to resist an omnipotent power acting omnipotently? Yet we have shown at length, above in §. XXVI., that in the calling and conversion of man the grace of God works by omnipotent power, or omnipotently. Paul alone is greater than every objection, when he proclaims that surpassing greatness [ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ] of the power of God towards us who believe, according to the working [ἐνέργειαν] and the might [κράτος] of the strength [ἰσχύος], the efficacy of the power of his strength, which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and set him at his right hand in the heavenly places, Eph. I. 19, 20. For he strongly proclaims both the power of God and the surpassing greatness of the power of God, by which it came about that we believed, and he explains that power both in general and in particular. In general, because it is a power equal and fitting to the efficacy of the strength of might which he worked in Christ. Here κράτος [Heb. גבורה] strength signifies a force that exceeds the power of every creature and what God ordinarily does in the world; ἰσχύς [Heb. חיל] might signifies the penetration of the will into its effect and its certain attainment of it; and ἐνέργεια efficacy signifies the operation of the strength and might already existing in Christ, and as it were a pledge of the remaining effect.

units.la: Nam hoc Dei illa potentia in Christo operata est, ut caput Ecclesiæ fieret, & ceu tale Ecclesiam impleret Deo, qui omnia in omnibus implet, v. 23. In specie, quòd sit potentia par ei, qua Deus Christum ex mortuis suscitavit, & in dextra Dei in supercœlestibus collocavit. Quæ potentia sicut infinita, & omnipotentia est, ita omnipotenter etiam & modo infinito egit: agitque adeò similiter in omnibus, qui ex spirituali morte vivificantur, & unà cum Christo ad dextram Dei collocantur.
units.tr: For by that power God worked in Christ, that he might become the head of the Church and, as such, fill the Church to God, who fills all in all, v. 23. In particular, because it is a power equal to that by which God raised Christ from the dead and set him at his right hand in the heavenly places. This power, being infinite and omnipotent, also works omnipotently and in an infinite manner; and so it works in the same way in all who are quickened from spiritual death and are set together with Christ at the right hand of God.

units.la: XLIX. Emphaticam adeò S. Pauli sententiam Lombardus, Thomas aliíque detorquent ad solos Apostolos, & gloriæ gradum illum, quo cæteris in cœlo eminebunt. Sed S. Paulus supereminentem magnitudinem illam potentiæ diserte refert ad ἡμᾶς τοὺς πιστεύοντας, nos credentes, sine ullo discrimine, & cum articulo τοὺς illos, credentes, quà tales insigniente. Fides enim omnium salvandorum donum commune est, & easdem in omnibus causas habet. Alii de ea potentia Dei, qua usurus est circa fideles, quando eos ex morte corporis suscitaturus est, sermonem esse falsò pertendunt. Clarum enim est, τῆς πίστεως cohærere sine interpunctione cum verbis ἐξ & ἐνέργειαν &c. ut credere dicantur secundum efficaciam roboris virium, & Apostolum loqui de ea potentia, per quam factum est simpliciter, ut crederemus, & quam exercuit in κλήσει vocatione quæ fundamentum spei hæreditatis, v. 18.
units.tr: XLIX. Lombard, Thomas and others twist this emphatic saying of Paul to refer only to the apostles and to that degree of glory by which they will stand out above others in heaven. But Paul expressly refers that surpassing greatness of power to us who believe [ἡμᾶς τοὺς πιστεύοντας], without any distinction, and with the article τοὺς marking them as believers. For faith is a common gift of all who are to be saved, and has the same causes in all. Others falsely contend that this is about the power of God which he will use towards the faithful when he is about to raise them from bodily death. For it is clear that of faith [τῆς πίστεως] is joined without a break to the words from [ἐξ] and efficacy [ἐνέργειαν], etc., so that they are said to believe according to the efficacy of the strength of might, and that the Apostle is speaking of that power by which it simply came about that we believed, and which he exercised in the calling [κλήσει], which is the foundation of the hope of the inheritance, v. 18.

units.la: Neque omnino scopus Apostoli fuit ad fidem resurrectionis carnis inducere, sed potiùs illuminatos oculos Ephesiis apprecatus est, ut vocationis suæ spem, divitias hæreditatis in sanctis, hoc est, abundantiam & excellentiam juris illius, quod adepti sunt per Christum in communione Sanctorum, & supereminentem magnitudinem potentiæ Dei, per quam effectum est, ut adeò alieni à Deo & Christo nihilominus ad eum adducti crederent. Neque sine causa S. Paulus supereminentem illam magnitudinem potentiæ, efficientis, ut credamus, prædicat; quia in vocatione, conversione, & ad fidem adductione hominis peccatoris illa quàm maximè se exerit. Sicut enim longè difficilius est figulo opus suum in frusta comminutum & corruptum in pristinam integritatem restituere, quàm novum fingere; & difficilius vita cadaveri restituitur, quàm corpus idoneum & præparatum spiritu vitæ animatur, quia hoc non sine miraculo, & extraordinaria virtute, illud ordinaria Dei potentia quotidie fit: ita DEUS potentiæ suæ magnitudinem excellentiore modo & gradu eminentiore in homine instaurando, redimendo, vivificando, & ad Christi imaginem reformando, quàm in illo noviter creando, & per generationem carnalem propagando patefecit. Licèt enim Deo omnipotenti ex æquo facilia omnia sint, in quibusdam tamen operibus excellens & eminens potentiæ Divinæ magnitudo magis quàm in aliis se patefacit & exerit. Tale inprimis est redemptionis humanæ longè gloriosissimum opus, utpote quod
units.tr: Nor was the Apostle's aim at all to induce belief in the resurrection of the flesh; rather he prayed that the Ephesians might have the eyes illuminated, so that they might know the hope of their calling, the riches of the glory of the inheritance in the saints, that is, the abundance and excellence of that right which they obtained through Christ in the communion of the saints, and the surpassing greatness of the power of God, by which it is brought about that those so alienated from God and Christ nonetheless are led to him and believe. Nor without reason does Paul proclaim that surpassing greatness of power which causes us to believe; for it displays itself most fully in the calling, conversion and bringing of a sinful man to faith. For just as it is far more difficult for a potter to restore a work broken into pieces and spoiled to its former wholeness than to fashion a new one, and just as it is more difficult to restore life to a corpse than to animate with the breath of life a body that is fit and prepared (because the one cannot be done without a miracle and an extraordinary power, while the other is done daily by the ordinary power of God), so God has revealed the greatness of his power in a more excellent manner and in a higher degree in restoring, redeeming, quickening and reforming man into the image of Christ, than in creating him anew and propagating him by carnal generation. For although all things are equally easy for almighty God, yet in some works the excellent and eminent greatness of the divine power shows itself and acts more than in others. Chief among these is the work of human redemption, by far the most glorious, since it is advanced in a manner and by a means far more august than any other.

units.la: Tertiùm, quia vocatio & conversio hominis ab infinita potentia Dei omnipotenter agente, procedit, quod inprimis Ephes. I. 19. probatur. quod modo medióque longè augustiore, quàm quodcunque aliud promotum est.
units.tr: Thirdly, because the calling and conversion of man proceeds from the infinite power of God acting omnipotently, which is chiefly proved by Eph. I. 19.

units.la: L. Neque illud Quarto leve est, quòd omnes, qui vocante Deo convertuntur, simul etiam à Deo trahuntur, nec nisi trahente Deo Patre ad Filium veniunt & convertuntur. Dixit Jesus. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater, qui misit me, ἑλκύσῃ traxerit eum, & ego resuscitabo eum ultimo die; Joh. VI. 44. Quisquis igitur ad Filium venit, à Patre is trahitur, & quidem tractu gemino. Priore enim Deus Pater ostendit, rectum, sanctum, justum & salutare esse ad Filium, quærendæ in ipso justitiæ & vitæ gratia, accedere. Fit id sermone & testimonio Dei, quod à se venisse is demonstrat; quódque in publico ponitur, ut ab omni conscientia hominum probari & explorari possit. Cùm verò homo excæcatus, in peccato mortuus & sapientia sua plenus sit, neque adeò lucem quærat, opus est tractu posteriore, quo oculi mentis illuminantur, cor durum & lapideum ex medio hominis aufertur, & cor carneum datur, ut Deum timere & glorificare velit. Disertè enim Christus testatur, sibi à Patre datos esse, quos velit venire, & quorum ipsam jacturam facere nolit. Quæ voluntas Dei efficax est, & Christo per Testamentum datos potenter trahit. Nam Filio postulandi eos jus dedit, ut eos ipsi postulanti det, Psal. II. 8. atque sic in communionem Filii vocet, & adducat, ut in ipso sint, 1. Cor. I. 9. 30. Neque tantùm sic Pater trahit, sed etiam Filius ad se trahit. Ego cùm ex terra elatus fuero, omnes traham ad me, Joh. XII. 32. Nam efficacia justitiæ suæ, & potentia brachii sui, (Esaj. LII. 9. 10.) impetrat & efficit, ut quos ille ex Judæis & gentibus redemit, ad se illi veniant, & salutis suæ causa confugiant, & in se תמדה delicias, voluptatem habeant. Hagg. II. 7. Mal. III. 1. Christus enim frustra, in cassum & sine fructu mori non potuit; & postulandi sibi hæreditatem jus habet. Positis ergo jam duobus æqualiter dispositis & à Deo Patre atque Filio sic tractis, an fieri potest, ut libera voluntate; & communi gratia omnibus ad veniendum sufficiente, unus ad Christum veniat, alter non veniat, sed trahenti Patri & Filio repugnet. Scilicet si Patris & Filii tractus voluntate humana impotentior est, ut huic, si homo velit, succumbere necesse habeat: Si brachium Jehovæ revelatum infirmum est, & non potiùs זרוע dominatur, potestate utitur. Esaj. XL. 10. L. 2. Nudavit Jehova brachium sanctum suum ad oculos gentium, & viderunt omnes fines terræ salutem Dei nostri; ibid. LII. 10.
units.tr: L. Nor is this fourth point of small weight: all who are converted by the calling of God are at the same time drawn by God, and they come to the Son and are converted only when God the Father draws them. Jesus said: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws [ἑλκύσῃ] him, and I will raise him up on the last day, John VI. 44. Whoever therefore comes to the Son is drawn by the Father, and indeed by a twofold drawing. For by the first drawing God the Father shows that it is right, holy, just and salutary to come to the Son in order to seek righteousness and life in him. This is done by the word and testimony of God, which shows that it comes from himself, and which is set forth publicly so that it may be approved and examined by every human conscience. But since man is blinded, dead in sin and full of his own wisdom, and does not seek the light, there is need of a second drawing, by which the eyes of the mind are enlightened, the hard and stony heart is taken away from within the man, and a heart of flesh is given, so that he is willing to fear and glorify God. For Christ plainly testifies that those whom he wills to come, and whose loss he is unwilling to suffer, have been given to him by the Father. This will of God is efficacious, and it powerfully draws those given to Christ by the Testament. For he gave the Son the right to ask for them, so that he might give them to the one asking, Ps. II. 8, and thus call and bring them into the communion of the Son, so that they are in him, 1 Cor. I. 9, 30. Nor does the Father alone draw in this way; the Son also draws to himself. And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all to me, John XII. 32. For by the efficacy of his righteousness and the power of his arm (Isa. LII. 9, 10) he obtains and brings it about that those whom he has redeemed from Jews and Gentiles come to him and flee to him for the cause of their salvation, and have in him delight [תמדה] and desire [voluntatem], Hag. II. 7; Mal. III. 1. For Christ could not die in vain, to no purpose and without fruit; and he has the right to ask for the inheritance. Therefore, if we now posit two men equally disposed and drawn in this way by God the Father and the Son, can it happen that by free will, and with a common grace sufficient for all to come, one comes to Christ and the other does not come, but resists the Father and the Son who are drawing him? Certainly, if the drawing of the Father and the Son is less powerful than the human will, so that, if a man wills, he must necessarily yield to it; or if the revealed arm of Jehovah is weak, and does not rather rule [זרוע] and use power. Isa. XL. 10; L. 2. Jehovah has bared his holy arm before the eyes of the nations, and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God; ibid. LII. 10.

units.la: LI. Gratiam hanc Trahentem ut communem, promiscuam, vel saltem congruam faciant veræ gratiæ adversarii, nullum non lapidem movent. Negat inprimis Limborchius à Christo per tractum Patris actionem Dei insuperabilem intelligi, quia aliàs Judæi à Christo reprehendi non potuissent, quòd ad ipsum non pervenerint, cùm non tracti à Patre venire nullo modo potuissent. Sed impotentia faciendi officium, quod suppositia revelatione Christi ipsa lex postulat, jumento proprio accersita justam μίμψιν habet. Neque perinde justam excusationem habet, qui deficiente Patris tractu venire ad Christum non potest, suo enim ore se condemnat, quasi excusationem haberet, sal-
units.tr: LI. In order to make this drawing (Trahentem) a common, indiscriminate, or at least congruous grace, the adversaries of true grace leave no stone unturned. First, Limborch denies that the Father's drawing is to be understood as an action of God that cannot be resisted through Christ. Otherwise, he argues, the Jews could not have been rebuked by Christ for not coming to him, since they could not have come unless drawn by the Father. But inability to perform a duty that the law itself demands, once Christ has been revealed, brings blame upon the person who has summoned that inability by his own fault. Nor does one who cannot come to Christ for want of the Father's drawing have a just excuse. He condemns himself by his own mouth, as if he had an excuse, at least if he believed that no one can come unless the Father draws him, and yet he does not murmur against it.

units.la: tem crederet, neminem venire posse, nisi quem Pater traxerit, & non obloqueretur. Nunc autem Deo μεμφομένῳ de ipso querente obloquitur & respondet, Rom. IX. 20. & sic agit tanquam si absque tractu Dei ad Christum venire posset, & omnia agit fiducia sui plenus: Denique neutiquam obsequitur Apostolo hortanti: Cum metu & trepidatione salutem vestram operamini. Deus enim est, qui operatur in vobis & velle & operari propter beneplacitum suum. Omnia facite sine oblocutionibus & ratiocinationibus, Phil. II. 12. 13. 14. Addit ille, tractionem amicam, & maxima sui parte moralem, cui facilè resisti possit, intelligi, ut si quis homini persuadere cupiens, ut aliquò egrediatur, manu apprehensa eum leniter trahat; cui tractioni ille, manum retrahendo, resistere possit. Imò potest, inquit, tractio esse moralis & suavis actio, quando quis eloquentia vel beneficiis homines post se trahit. Sic Deus vinculis charitatis Israelem traxit, Hos. XI. 4. Sed aliud protectò est trahentis manus & brachii Divini; aliud humani robur. Illud dominatur, Esaj. XL. 10. hoc infirmari & destitui à potentiore potest. Quas oves semel Deus manu sua apprehendit, ut Christo eas det, & quas Christus velut sibi datas prensat: illæ ex manu Dei elabi & dantis Christo Patris, & Christi accipientis manum destituere non possunt. Non rapiet quisquam oves ex manu mea. Pater meus, qui dedit eas mihi, omnibus major est. Et nemo potest illas ex manu Patris mei rapere. Ego & Pater unum sumus, Joh. X. 28. 29. 30. Non est ille tractus violentus, fateor, quia trahente Deo homo currit, Cant. I. 4. & simul homo trahitur & docetur, Joh. VI. 44. 45. constringitur, sed charitatis funibus, Hos. XI. 4. 2. Cor. V. 14. & Spiritus S. trahens Spiritus roboris & gratiæ; potentiæ & amoris est, 2. Tim. I. 9. At nec merè moralis idem est, quia suadendo, docendo, demonstrando nec nativæ tenebræ mentis dispelluntur, nec cordis duritties frangitur. Nec Deus Orator: sed author gratiæ est, & per stultam prædicationem crucis salvat, 1. Cor. I. 21. 22. 23. Præterea tractio illa, inquit, est datio, juxta Joh. VI. 37. Quicquid dat mihi Pater, ad me veniet. Certum ergo tractus ille eventum habet, & plus gratiæ habet, quàm sufficiens & promiscua illa, quia qui hoc pollet, non certò ad Christum venit, sed non venire, & resistere potest. Imo datio illa juxta Psal. II. 8. fit ad postulationem Christi, qua is postulat hæreditatem sibi in Testamento Patris promissam; adeòque solorum electorum est, singularemque gratiam iis datam, non communem & sufficientem, vel congruam etiam, propria dispositione & voluntate determinatam, atque sic demum efficacem redditam ostendit. Denique tractus ille, inquiunt; explicatur per ἕνα διδαχτὸν & Θεοῦ esse edoctum à Deo, v. 45. At doctio moralis actio est, & clara voluntatis Divinæ revelatione fit. Verùm ille trahitur, & trahendo docetur à Patre, ad quem verba Patris perveniunt, & cui Pater non aurem duntaxat corporis, sed etiam cor aperit, ut attendat, consideret, intelligat, discat & amet. Hoc enim non ab homine, sed ab ipso Jehova, verbum suum cordi inscribente, doceri est. Tractus enim Patris hoc efficit, ut ipso loquente, vocante, & ut homo, depositis præjudiciis, abnegatis concupiscentiis carnis suae attendat, & gloriam ipsi det, efficiente discat, hoc est, sapiens & prudens conscientiae & verbi luce conspirante, & sibi mutuo attestante evadat; atque sic jubente Patre ad Filium accedere ad eundem accedat. Doceri igitur à Jehova, est verè doceri & illuminari ab eo, & quidem solo, & eo modo, quo nemo homo docere potest, quod plus profecto est, quàm cùm homo πειθοῖς λόγοις persuasoriis sapientiae suae sermonibus aures ferit, sed ad cor loqui, & sermonibus suis illud subigere neutiquam potest.
units.tr: But now he murmurs against God, who is complaining about him, and answers back (Rom. 9:20), and so he acts as if he could come to Christ without God's drawing, and he acts wholly confident in himself. Finally, he by no means obeys the Apostle exhorting him: Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure. Do all things without murmurings and disputings (Phil. 2:12–14). He adds that the drawing is a friendly one, and for the most part moral, which can easily be resisted. It is as when someone who wants to persuade a man to go somewhere takes him gently by the hand and draws him along, and the man, by pulling his hand back, can resist that drawing. Indeed, he says, the drawing can be a moral and sweet action, when someone draws men after him by eloquence or by benefits. So God drew Israel with the cords of love (Hos. 11:4). But surely it is one thing for the hand and arm of the divine drawer, and another for human strength. The former rules (Isa. 40:10); the latter can be weakened and overcome by a stronger force. The sheep that God once seized by his hand, so that he might give them to Christ, and that Christ takes hold of as given to himself, cannot slip from the hand of God who gives them, nor from the hand of Christ who receives them.
