No one shall snatch the sheep out of my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand. I and the Father are one (John 10:28–30). I admit that this drawing is not violent, since when God draws, man runs (Song 1:4), and at the same time man is drawn and taught (John 6:44–45), is bound, but with the cords of love (Hos. 11:4; 2 Cor. 5:14). And the Holy Spirit who draws is the Spirit of strength and grace; it is of power and love (2 Tim. 1:9). But this is not merely moral, because by persuading, teaching and demonstrating, neither the native darkness of the mind is dispelled nor the hardness of the heart broken. Nor is God a mere orator; he is the author of grace, and by the foolishness of the preaching of the cross he saves (1 Cor. 1:21–23). Moreover, he says, that drawing is a giving, according to John 6:37: Whatever the Father gives me will come to me. That drawing therefore has a certain outcome and contains more grace than that sufficient and indiscriminate grace, because one who has this power does not come to Christ with certainty, but can fail to come and can resist. Indeed, according to Psalm 2:8, that giving takes place at the request of Christ, by which he asks for the inheritance promised to him in the Father's testament. It therefore belongs only to the elect, and it shows that a singular grace is given to them, not a common and sufficient one, or even a congruous one determined by their own disposition and will, and that it is thus at last made effective. Finally, they say that the drawing is explained by the phrase taught by God (John 6:45). But moral teaching is an action, and it happens through the clear revelation of the divine will. But the one who is drawn is also taught by drawing from the Father, to whom the Father's words come, and to whom the Father opens not merely the ear of the body but also the heart, so that he may attend, consider, understand, learn and love. For this is to be taught not by a man but by Jehovah himself, who writes his word upon the heart: to be taught is this. For the drawing of the Father brings it about that, with him speaking and calling, the man, laying aside prejudices and denying the lusts of his flesh, attends, gives glory to him, and learns, that is, becomes wise and prudent, the light of conscience and of the word agreeing and bearing witness to one another. And so, when the Father commands, he comes to the Son and comes to him. To be taught by Jehovah is therefore truly to be taught and enlightened by him, and that alone, and in the way that no man can teach, which is surely more than when a man strikes the ears with persuasive words [πειθοῖς λόγοις] of his own wisdom, but he cannot by any means speak to the heart and subdue it by his words.

units.la: LII. Quintum argumentum adamantina salutis catena, quae Rom. VIII. 29. 30. contexitur, suppeditat. Quos, inquit Apostolus, praecognovit, eos praedestinavit; quos praedestinavit, eos vocavit; quos vocavit, eos justificavit; quos justificavit, eos glorificavit. Plane rumpitur catena illa, si per vocationem Divinam gratia aequalis sic duobus interne offertur, ut uni liberum sit assentiri, alteri liberum sit assensum cohibere. Sic enim non quoscunque praedestinavit, eos vocavit, & quos vocavit, eos justificavit, & quos justificavit, eos glorificavit; quia poterunt esse vocati, adeoque etiam esse praedestinati, qui tamen nec justificentur, nec glorificentur. Quin & plane irritum cadet praedestinationis decretum, quia gratia illa aliquid ponit in Jacobo, praeter propositum Divinum, vel ei accessorium, quod illum ab Esavo discernit. Neque catenam illam aureanm integram servant adversarii, statuentes, propositum illud Dei, secundum quod praecogniti & praedestinati in tempore vocantur, justificantur & glorificantur, conditionatum esse ex praevisione per scientiam mediam moralis cujusdam persuasionis, cui praesciat Deus hunc vel illum non repugnaturum, licet ex arbitrii libertate repugnare possit. Quomodo, inquiunt, pastor ovi ramum viridem ostendit, parens filium nucibus illicit, quem certò secuturum novit, licet fieri posset, ut ista non moveant. Quam similitudinem ex Augustino urgent, sed praeter ejus mentem, quia de externis tantùm mediis, quae rejici possent, non de interna gratiae efficacia, quae praedestinationis decretum exequitur, similitudines illas adhibuit. Verùm moralis tantùm suasio ex objecto congruè propositò, solùm alliciens, at nihil efficiens, manente semper in convertendo arbitrio ad oppositum, conversionem infallibiliter operari non potest. Nam suasio apud eum, quem Scriptura convertenti ut caecum, surdum & mutum objicit, nullam obsequendi potentiam inveniens, nihil proficit. Quae enim Suadae medulla efficere & persuadere caeco, ut videat, surdo, ut audiat, muto ut loquatur, mortuo ut vivat, non adhibitis aliis mediis potis est? Et si efficacia gratiae ultra suasionem moralem non extenditur, non plus Deus ad peccatoris conversionem, quàm Diabolus ad ejus perversionem conferet. Nullum ergo propositum Dei conditionatum praescientiae effectus certi suasionis ejusmodi moralis innixum datur: adeoque vel propositum Dei aeternum nutat, vel catena salutis tota luxatur; vel gratia vocationis omnis efficax est, & infallibilem eventum habet; & nulla promiscua, communis, sufficiens omnibus, sed ancipitis eventus datur. Qui praedestinantur, ii praedestinantur, ut sint conformes cum imagine Filii Dei, Rom. VIII. 30. Et qui praedestinati sunt, ut tales essent, ii ab aeterno vocati, hoc est, jussi sunt, ut suo tempore renascantur in Christum: extra quem nulla cum ipso conformitas datur. Cùm igitur in tempore assumuntur, & Christo inseruntur, ut actu conformes sint cum imagine ejus, non utique per gratiam, sive qualitatem ambiguam in utrumque, non per sanctificationem hominis & non sanctificationem, sed per Spiritum vivificantem & sanctificantem, & operationem roboris potentiae ipsius: haec vocatio temporalis & unicè efficax est, utpote quae efficit, ut certò in Christo simus, & cum imagine ejus in justitia & gloria conformemur.
units.tr: LII. The fifth argument is supplied by the adamantine chain of salvation that is woven in Rom. 8:29–30. Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; those whom he justified, he also glorified. That chain is plainly broken if, through the divine calling, grace is offered internally in the same way to two persons, so that it is free for one to assent and free for the other to withhold assent. For then not all whom he predestined did he call, and not all whom he called did he justify, and not all whom he justified did he glorify, since those who are called, and so also predestined, may nonetheless be neither justified nor glorified. Indeed the decree of predestination would fall entirely void, because that grace adds something to Jacob, beyond or in addition to the divine purpose, which distinguishes him from Esau. Nor do the adversaries keep that golden chain intact, when they hold that the purpose of God, according to which those foreknown and predestined are called in time, justified and glorified, is conditioned by foresight through middle knowledge of a certain moral persuasion, to which God foreknows that this or that person will not object, although he could resist by the freedom of his will. As, they say, a shepherd shows a green branch to a sheep, and a parent entices a son with nuts, whom he knows will certainly follow, although it could happen that these things do not move him. They press this comparison from Augustine, but beyond his intention, because he used those comparisons only of external means, which could be rejected, not of the inner efficacy of grace, which carries out the decree of predestination. But a merely moral persuasion, proposed from a suitably presented object, which only attracts and effects nothing, while the will remains always free to turn to the opposite in its conversion, cannot infallibly bring about conversion. For persuasion does nothing for one whom Scripture presents to be converted as blind, deaf and dumb, finding in him no power of obedience. For what can the marrow of persuasion effect, and what can it persuade, without other means, into seeing the blind, hearing the deaf, speaking the dumb, or living the dead? And if the efficacy of grace is not extended beyond moral persuasion, God will contribute no more to the conversion of a sinner than the devil contributes to his perversion. There is therefore no purpose of God conditioned by foreknowledge, resting on the certain effect of such moral persuasion. Either, then, the eternal purpose of God wavers, or the whole chain of salvation is dislocated; or else all grace of calling is effective and has an infallible outcome, and no indiscriminate, common grace, sufficient for all but of doubtful outcome, is given. Those who are predestined are predestined so that they may be conformed to the image of the Son of God (Rom. 8:30). And those who were predestined so that they would be such were called from eternity, that is, they were ordered that in their time they should be born again in Christ, outside whom there is no conformity with him. Since, therefore, they are taken up in time and grafted into Christ, so that they may actually be conformed to his image, this is not done by a grace or quality that is ambiguous for either outcome, nor by the sanctification and non-sanctification of man, but through the Spirit who quickens and sanctifies and by the working of his strong power. This temporal calling is therefore uniquely effective, since it brings it about that we are certainly in Christ and are conformed to his image in righteousness and glory.

units.la: LIII. Aliam verò quercum Episcopius alii- que excutiunt, qui sicut praedestinationem de propósito vocandi ad crucem & passiones interpretantur; ita etiam vocationem non de prima hominum vocatione ad fidem, sed de vocatione fidelium ad crucem, qua Deus fidelles suo quosque tempore ad crucem vocat, intelligendam pertendunt, juxta illa S. Petri: In hoc vocati estis, quia & Christus passus est pro nobis, vobis relinquens exemplum, ut sequamini ejus vestigia, 1. Pet. II. 21. Sed non idem sermonis Pauli & Petri argumentum. Ille non solas passiones, sed etiam infirmitates, v. 26. imò omnia ad bonum cooperari diligentibus Deum, & vocatis secundum propositum v. 28. declarat; innuens non ab amore nostro, sed ἐκ τῆς καλέσεως ex vocante (Rom. IX. 11.) esse, quòd omnia nobis ad bonum cooperantur. Intelliguntur autem vocati ad amandum, & bonum, hoc est, ad gloriam. Vocatos verò secundum propositum statim definit, quòd videlicet ii sint, quos Deus praecognovit, praedestinavit conformes imagini Filii sui, atque tales vocavit, justificavit & glorificavit. Quae verba sic gratiae Divinae hostes προέγνωσις: Quos praecognovit (ante approbavit ut amantes, sed amore mutabili) eos praedestinavit (constituit sibi obedientes per passiones ad gloriam ducere) quos praedestinavit eos vocavit (quos sic constituit per passiones ad gloriam ducere, eos vocavit ad crucem) quos vocavit, eos justificavit (quos sic ad crucem vocavit, si eam lubenter tulerint, iis peccata remisit, & vires ad perseverandum dedit) quos justificavit, eos glorificavit (quibus sic peccata remisit, & vires ad perseverandum dedit, si rectè iis viribus usi fuerint, & perseveraverint, eos certò glorificabit) Quae non verborum Apostoli interpretatio, sed interpolatio; non πρόγνωσις, sed προορισμός est, quia ad hoc omnia illa comparata sunt, ut Paulus potiùs videatur falsum dicere, & sibi contradicere; vel nihil dicere & negare, quàm dicere id quod dicit; nempe vocatos ad haereditatem Testamento ea certò potiri, tum propter propositum Dei, qui frustra amari non potest, cùm diligatur ut charitas; tum propter Testamentum, quo Filius Dei constitutus est primogenitus: tum propter meritum ejus: tum propter communionem cum eo: tum propter voluntatis gratiosae naturam, quae cùm sit πρόγνωσις praenotio miserorum, etiam est destinatio conformium cum imagine Filii, & vocatio in communionem cum Filio; & sic justificatio & glorificatio fit. Voluntas
units.tr: LIII. Another knot is untied by Episcopius and others, who interpret predestination as a purpose of calling to the cross and to sufferings, and likewise contend that the calling is to be understood not as the first calling of men to faith but as the calling of believers to the cross, by which God calls the faithful to the cross each in his own time, according to the words of St Peter: For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps, 1 Pet. 2:21. But the argument of Paul and of Peter is not the same. Paul declares that not only sufferings but also infirmities, v. 26, and indeed all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose, v. 28, implying that all things work together for our good not from our love but ἐκ τῆς καλέσεως [ek tēs kleseōs], from the one who calls (Rom. 9:11). Those called are understood to be called to love and to good, that is, to glory. Paul then at once defines those called according to purpose: they are those whom he foreknew, and did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, and whom he thus called, justified and glorified. The enemies of divine grace explain these words in this way: προέγνωσις [proegnōsis]: whom he foreknew (that is, first approved as loving, but with a changeable love); them he predestinated (he determined to lead them to glory by sufferings, as those who would obey him); whom he predestinated, them he called (whom he thus determined to lead to glory through sufferings, them he called to the cross); whom he called, them he justified (whom he thus called to the cross, if they bear it gladly, to them he remits sins and gives strength to persevere); whom he justified, them he glorified (to whom he thus remits sins and gives strength to persevere, if they use that strength rightly and persevere, them he will surely glorify). This is not an interpretation of the Apostle's words but an interpolation. It is not πρόγνωσις [prognōsis] but προορισμός [proorismos], since all those things are arranged for this purpose. Paul would then seem to say what is false and to contradict himself, or to say nothing and deny what he actually says, namely that those called to the inheritance of the Testament surely obtain it: partly on account of God's purpose, for he who is loved as charity cannot be loved in vain; partly on account of the Testament, by which the Son of God was constituted firstborn; partly on account of his merit; partly on account of communion with him; and partly on account of the nature of his gracious will, which, since it is πρόγνωσις [prognōsis], the foreknowledge of the wretched, is also the destining of men to be conformed to the image of the Son, and the calling into communion with the Son; and thus justification and glorification take place. Will

units.la: Quia juxta catenam salutis, quos Deus vocavit, eos justificavit & glorificavit, adeòque omnes juxta propositum Dei vocati certò glorificantur: quod de vocatis secundum gratiam sufficientem communem dici non potest.
units.tr: Because according to the chain of salvation, those whom God called he also justified and glorified; and so all who are called according to God's purpose are certainly glorified. This cannot be said of those called according to common sufficient grace.

units.la: Voluntas enim Dei ad hominem miserum relata primò est προγνωσις praecognitio, sive ipsius aspectus & procuratio aeterna; inde destinatio ad conformitatem cum imagine Filii, quia nisi tali bono aeterno destinato frustra ejus miseretur: Post vocatio, seu jussio tum aeterna, ut suo tempore in Christum renascatur, tum temporalis, qua is assumitur, & Christo inseritur; demum justificatio, sive voluntas auferendi omnem accusationem peccati, & vitam dandi, ut justo, denique glorificatio, qua tum jus, tum actus coelestis gloriae confertur. Contra Novatorum illa προελωσις catenae salutis; & amorem ac praedefinitionem aeternam certorum haeredum προεοφενων ante definitorum, designatorum, & nominatim in catalogo Dei scriptorum, & Testamentum, quo Christo haereditas data est, & propositum Dei, propter quod Apostolus diligentibus Deum & vocatis secundum propositum omnia cooperari in bonum dixit; & vocationem efficacem, quae hic astruitur; & justificationem ex fide Christum apprehendente: & gloriationem in spe & in afflictionibus, adeoque universam fere gratiam Dei salutiferam, & Christianam religionem funditus evertit; & ex adverso cuncta ad voluntatem, vires & factum hominis refert, ut is vim suam habeat pro Deo suo, Habac. I. 11. Quibus gratia sufficiens dicis tantum causa, ne omnis gratia Dei abnegari videatur, conjungitur, plane praeter Scripturae sensum, in qua χαρις χαρις gratia sufficiens illa est, quae salutifera est, & potentiam Dei, quae in infirmitate nostra perficitur, comitem habet, 2. Cor. XII. 9. Gratiam vero, quam illi sufficientem dicunt, omnes homines habent. Asseruit equidem Apostolus τὸ πάσχειν pati amantibus Deum non obstare, quia est συμπάσχειν τῷ Χριστῷ una pati cum Christo, v. 17. hoc est, κοινωνεῖν τοῖς δὲ Χριστοῦ παθήμασι communicare Christi passionibus, 1.Pet. IV. 13. Sed nulla in his apparet conditio patientiae vel propositi Dei, vel justificationi hominis addita; neque voluit Apostolus argumento secuturae gloriae ad patientiam hortari; de qua, non ut conditione antecedente, sed ut effectu satis jam cap. V. 3. egerat. Neque omnino patientia conditio justificationis, sed donum cum ea donatum est; spei autem nutricula & roboratio est per δοκιμήν. Neque enim in verbis v. 17. ὑπὲρ συμπάσχομεν, ἵνα καὶ συνδοξασθῶμεν conditio est, quia τὸ ὑπέρ non significat Si, sed siquidem, & verba illa cum praecedentibus conjunguntur, ut paris veritatis, q. d. Si non essemus cohaeredes Christi, in vanum cum eo pateremur, ut cum ipso glorificemur. Si igitur communio passionum infert communionem gloriae, certissimum est, nos esse cohaeredes Christi, quia passiones nostrae sunt Christi passiones in nobis. Non igitur hic conditio haereditatis, consecutioni addita intelligitur, quia Paulus non hortatur ad patientiam, nec tali argumento utitur, quod nisi patienter mala feramus, jus filiorum amisisuri simus, sed simpliciter de communione ut in gloria, ita in passionibus loquitur. Ac licet alibi cum patientia consolationem hypothetico sermone conjungat, dicens: 'Ει συμπάσχομεν και συμβασιλευσομεν' si toleramus, etiam conregnabimus, 2. Tim. II. 12. tamen illam velut in vocatione propositam conditionem justifica-
units.tr: For the will of God, regarded in relation to wretched man, is first προγνωσις [prognōsis], foreknowledge, that is, his eternal regard and care for him; next the destining of him to be conformed to the image of the Son, for unless such an eternal good were destined for him, God would have mercy on him in vain; then vocation, or command, both eternal, that in due time he should be born again in Christ, and temporal, by which he is taken up and grafted into Christ; finally justification, that is, the will to remove every accusation of sin and to grant life to him as just; and lastly glorification, by which both the right and the act of heavenly glory are conferred. Against this, the Novatians hold that the foreknowledge of the chain of salvation is προεγνωσις [proegnōsis] only; and that the love and eternal predefinition of certain heirs, who were previously προορισθέντων [prooristhenton], defined, designated, and written by name in God's catalogue, and the Testament by which the inheritance was given to Christ, and the purpose of God, on account of which the Apostle said that all things work together for good to those who love God and are called according to purpose, and the efficacious calling which is here asserted, and justification by faith apprehending Christ, and boasting in hope and in afflictions, are all overturned, and indeed almost the whole saving grace of God and the Christian religion is utterly subverted. On the other hand, they refer everything to the will, the powers and the deed of man, so that he has his strength for his god, Hab. 1:11. To these they join sufficient grace, merely as a pretext, lest all grace of God seem to be denied; but this is plainly against the sense of Scripture, in which that sufficient grace is saving and has with it the power of God, which is made perfect in our weakness, 2 Cor. 12:9. Yet all men have the grace which they call sufficient. The Apostle indeed asserts that to suffer, τὸ πάσχειν [to paschein], does not hinder those who love God, because it is συμπάσχειν τῷ Χριστῷ [sympaschein tō Christō], to suffer together with Christ, v. 17, that is, κοινωνεῖν τοῖς τοῦ Χριστοῦ παθήμασι [koinōnein tois tou Christou pathēmasi], to share in the sufferings of Christ, 1 Pet. 4:13. But no condition of patience or of God's purpose appears in these words, nor is any condition added to the justification of man. Nor did the Apostle wish to exhort to patience by the argument of the glory to follow; of this patience he had already spoken, not as an antecedent condition but as an effect, at Rom. 5:3. Nor is patience at all a condition of justification; a gift is given along with it, and it is the nurse and strengthening of hope through δοκιμήν [dokimēn], proving. For in the words of v. 17, ὑπὲρ συμπάσχομεν, ἵνα καὶ συνδοξασθῶμεν [hyper sympaschomen, hina kai synedoxasthōmen], there is no condition, because ὑπέρ does not mean if, but siquidem, seeing that; and those words are joined with what precedes as a parallel truth, as if he said: If we were not co-heirs with Christ, we would suffer with him in vain, so that we might be glorified with him. If therefore the communion of sufferings brings communion of glory, it is most certain that we are co-heirs with Christ, because our sufferings are the sufferings of Christ in us. Therefore no condition of inheritance is here to be understood as added to the obtaining of it; Paul is not exhorting to patience, nor is he using the argument that unless we bear evils patiently we shall lose the right of sons. He speaks simply of communion, in glory as in sufferings. And although elsewhere he joins consolation with patience in a hypothetical sentence, saying: If we suffer, we shall also reign with him, Εἰ συμπάσχομεν καὶ συμβασιλεύσομεν, 2 Tim. 2:12, nevertheless he does not make that condition, as though set forth in the calling, into a condition of our justification,

units.la: tionis nostrae non facit, quia conditio justificationis apud Deum non potest esse nisi causa juris petendi vitam; quae in sola Christi obedientia est; in qua etiam sola spem nostram fundare licet; quia etiam Deus nos praedestinavit conformes imagini ipsius, ut ipse sit primogenitus in multis fratribus. Quae ad vindicandam adversus violentos violatores, humanae voluntatis adversus gratiam Dei patronos aureum illam salutis catenam sicuti dici necessario debuerunt; ita dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: because a condition of justification with God can only be the ground for claiming life, and this lies in the obedience of Christ alone, and in him alone is it lawful for us to ground our hope; since God also predestinated us to be conformed to the image of himself, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. These things, which had to be said to vindicate the golden chain of salvation against violent violators and against the defenders of human will against the grace of God, may be said to be sufficient.

units.la: LIV. Sextò ἀποπμάτων seu absurditatum plaustra sequuntur, si posita eadem gratia duorum cætera aequalium unus libera voluntate sua assentiri & converti, alter simili libertate dissentire, repugnare & perire potest. Sic enim plus libero hominis arbitrio, quàm Deo ipsi tribuendum fuerit; quia Deus tantum movet moraliter, & monet, at homo paret. Nemo autem eo quòd movetur & monetur, bonus est, sed eo quòd moventi & monenti paret. Atque ita bonus erit homo, quia vult, non quia Deus talem fecit, ut velit, & ex nolente volens fiat. Tum discrimen filiorum Dei & seculi sic non à gratia, sed à natura erit. Nam gratia rectè uti, hoc est, ei consentire, est liberi arbitrii, quod à natura est. Et cui, quaeso, ex adversaria' sententia salutem acceptam referam? An Deo, ut authori gratiae? At illa, nisi bene utar, resilit, excutitur. An Deo, ut arbitrii & naturae conditori? At natura communis est; quod discernitur, speciale est. Neque sic Deus eliget arbitrium, sed arbitrium eligit Deum, quia assensus meus efficiet, ut gratia mihi potius quàm alteri salutaris sit. Quis sic de se demisse, de Deo magnificè sentiet, cùm à se aliquid inveniat, quod à gratia non accepit? Quis in solo Deo fiduciam omnem collocabit, quam maximam partem ab assensu proprio pendere putat? Quid verò etiam de precibus & gratiarum actione fiet? Quid enim à Deo precabor? Gratiam sufficientem? At illam polliideo, & cum hypocritis communem habeo. An bonum usum istius gratiae? At hic à proprio nixu, & innata arbitrii differentia pendet. Quis autem serio petit, quod possidet? Et quis de eo Deo gratias aget, quod non accepit, sed ipse sibi contulit? Denique Jesuitarum & Remonstrantium moralis illa suasio non minus quàm gratia specialis & praedeterminans libertati arbitrii officit. Nam posita Divinae praescientiae de Jacobo convertendo & Esavo repugnante infallibilitate, quam junctim omnes defendunt, vel Jacobus necessario convertitur, vel non. Si necessario, quid ergo gratia specialis & praedeterminans plus quam praescientia infallibilis libertatis arbitrii proficit?
units.tr: LIV. Sixthly, the wagonloads of absurdities follow, if, with the same grace given to two equal persons, one can by his free will assent and be converted, while the other, with like freedom, can dissent, resist, and perish. For then more would have to be attributed to man's free choice than to God himself, since God only moves morally and admonishes, but man obeys. Yet no one is good because he is moved and admonished, but because he obeys the one who moves and admonishes. Thus man will be good because he wills, not because God made him such that he should will, and from unwilling should become willing. Then the difference between the sons of God and of the world will be from nature, not from grace. For to use grace rightly, that is, to consent to it, belongs to free choice, which is from nature. And to whom, I ask, on the opposing view, should I refer the salvation received? To God as author of grace? But that grace, unless I use it well, leaps back and is shaken off. To God as creator of the will and of nature? But nature is common; what distinguishes is special. Nor in this way does God choose the will, but the will chooses God, because my assent will make grace saving for me rather than for another. Who will think so humbly of himself and so magnificently of God, when he finds in himself something which he did not receive from grace? Who will place all his trust in God alone, when he thinks that the greater part of it depends on his own assent? What, moreover, will become of prayers and thanksgiving? For what shall I pray to God? Sufficient grace? But I already possess that, and I have it in common with hypocrites. The good use of that grace? But this depends on one's own effort and the innate difference of the will. Who seriously asks for what he already possesses? And who will give thanks to God for what he did not receive, but conferred on himself? Finally, that moral persuasion of the Jesuits and the Remonstrants hinders the freedom of the will no less than special and predetermining grace. For, granting the infallibility of divine foreknowledge concerning the conversion of Jacob and the resistance of Esau, which all defend together, either Jacob is necessarily converted or he is not. If necessarily, what then does special and predetermining grace accomplish beyond infallible foreknowledge, which leaves the freedom of the will intact?

units.la: LV. Sed nunc adversantium gratiae specialí & infallibili, & gratiae communis ac sufficientis cum ambiguo apud duos aequaliter dispositos eventu, placitum adeò dogma mordicus propugnantium argumenta ad incudem revocanda sunt. Ante omnia illi Scripturae illa testimonia cumulant, quibus & Deus non tantum voluisse, ut convertantur homines, sed ea etiam adhibuisse remedia, per quae converti potuissent, & homines rebellasse & non paruisse vocationi & voluntati huic Divinae dicuntur. Talia sunt: Quid est quod ultra facere debui vineae meae,
units.tr: LV. But now, since those who oppose the special and infallible grace, and the common and sufficient grace whose outcome is uncertain and equally open to both, are holding stubbornly to their favourite dogma, their arguments must be put back on the anvil. Above all, they pile up those passages of Scripture in which God is said not only to have willed that men be converted, but also to have applied remedies by which they could have been converted, and in which men are said to have rebelled, to have failed to obey the calling, and to have resisted this divine will. Such are: What more ought I to have done for my vineyard,

units.la: ce
units.tr: ...ce

units.la: nea meâ, & non feci? Quare expectavi ut faceret uvas, & fecit labruscas? Esaj. V. 4. Expandi manus meas toto die ad populum perversum, qui graduntur per viam non bonam post cogitationes suas: ad populum, qui irasci faciunt me in faciem meam semper, ibid. LXV. 2. 3. Fili hominis, in medio domus exasperantis habitas; qui oculos habent ad videndum, & non vident, & aures ad audiendum, & non audiunt, quia domus exasperans est, Ezech. XII. 2. Væ tibi Chorazin, væ tibi Bethsaida, quia, si Tyri & Sidone factæ essent virtutes, quæ factæ sunt vobis, in sacco & cinere poenitentiam egissent, &c. Matth. XI. 21. 22. Jerusalem, Jerusalem, quæ occidis Prophetas &c. quoties volui congregare filios tuos, sicut gallina congregat pullos suos, sub alas? Et noluistis, ibid. XXIII. 37. Pharisæi & Legisperiti consilium Dei spreverunt erga semet ipsos, non baptizati ab eo, Luc. VII. 30. Hæc dico, ut salvi fiatis. Et non vultis venire ad me, ut vitam habeatis, Joh. V. 34. 40. Vos semper resistitis Spiritui S. illi, sicut Patres vestri, ita & vos, Act. VII. 51. Sed plane hæc sunt. Alia enim ne quidem de repugnantia vocatorum loquuntur, velut illa Christi. Quoties volui congregare filios tuos &c. & noluistis. Matth. XXIII. 37. Nam nolentibus licet illis, qui Prophetas occiderunt, imo multum repugnantibus congregavit Christus, quos voluit Hierosolymae trucidatricis filios, discipulos & credentes non paucos. Noluerunt Patres, Principes Hierosolymae plerique saltem in conciliis ejus congregati, ut Christus ibi filios Dei jus habentes ad urbem sanctam, & communionem Sanctorum in ea, colligeret. Sed Christus ἠθέλησε συναγαγεῖν voluit congregare, hoc est, & propositum habuit eos congregandi, & illud executus est. Frustra explicationem hanc Limborchius eo argumento eludere conatur, quod Hierosolyma semper in Scriptura omnes incolas urbis notet. Non enim Christus simpliciter Hierosolymam, sed Hierosolymam occidentem compellavit, ad quam non omnes Hierosolymae filii pertinebant, certe non pertinebant discipuli Christi & credentes illi, quos ille congregavit. Reliqua testimonia de vocatione mere externa per homines externo praeconio facta; non de interna Spiritus Dei cor ipsum alloquente & tractante, mutare & convertere volente loquuntur. Sic plane Deus protestatus fecisse se vineae suae, quod ei faciendum erat, Esaj. V. 4. non hoc asserit, quod omne auxilium, & omnem gratiam populo suo dederit, tum quia diserte negatur, Deum ei dedisse oculos ad videndum, & cor ad intelligendum, Deut. XXIX. 4. tum quia ei καρδίαν ἐπιλογὴν promittitur circumcisio cordium in futurum, ibid. XXX. 6. tum quia Deus ipse in hac parabola distinguit gratiam sanctificationis a beneficiis communibus, quando dicit: Plantavi te optima vite, v. 2. Vitis Judæ est plantatio deliciarum ejus, v. 7. significans, Deum Patres, quorum semen & propago hi erant, cum quibus disceptatio instituitur, sanctificasse, & eos posuisse in exemplum posteris, quorum fructum frustra expectaverat; adeoque radicem illam, cum qua Deus foedus pepigit, sanctam fuisse, at ramos propter infidelitatem defractos esse, Rom. XI. 16. 17. &c. tum quia Deus in explicatione judicii inter alias poenas etiam negationem gratiae conversionis & sanctificationis praecipiendo nubibus ne pluant super illos pluviam, v. 6. ponit; ne scilicet inter ipsos amplius Ecclesia & populus Dei reperiatur; quod gratiam indifferentem & potestatem hominis ad sui conversionem sine auxilio efficaci & circumcisione cordis adversus quasi cornibus destruit: tum quia media, quae Deus circa vineam adhibuisse dicitur, mere externa sunt, sine ulla mentione. quod pluvia eam rigaverit, Solem super ea oriri fecerit, qui proprie fructus ex vinea eliciunt, & gratiae internae analoga sunt: tum denique quia alias non haberet locum gratia alii congrue, alii incongrue secundum beneplacitum Dei data. Sic enim ad quaestionem: Quid amplius facerem? responderi potuisset, hoc deesse ad Dei beneficia, quod gratiam, quam dedit, non congrue dedit. Non ergo in parabola hac quaesitum est, quo amplioris auxilio indiguerit vinea, ut uvas ferret (nam plus utique auxilii erat in iis, quos optimam vineam plantavit) sed, quae media salutis Israelitis tum de sua potestate praesumentibus, quasi non indigerent Divina regeneratione: tum adversus Dei judicium, quo is omnem carnem condemnat, contendentibus, defuerunt. Nullum certe tale salutis medium iis defuit. Omnia enim, quae Israelitae Deo obsequium promittentes petierunt & expectarunt, Deus fecit: & insuper in multis etiam cooperatus est, quae per Spiritus S. auxilium ad uvas proferendas fructuosa fuerunt. Quod porro expectasse se uvas, at labruscas invenisse, Deus v. 4. testatur, non proprie intelligi potest, quia nemo proprie expectat, quod futurum non est; at futuram non esse fructificationem illam Deus noverat; quia id ut futurum praedixit, & quale judicium Israeli irrogaturus esset, indicavit: sed ἀνθεωπινωσ propter tolerantiam & dilationem judicii malis irrogandi, sine desiderio, verisimilitudine rei, vel indifferentia hominis ad utrumque, qualia, ceu imperfectiones, in expectatione Dei cogitari non possunt. Neque enim similitudo extra scopum suum extendi debet. Scopus autem parabolae non est, explicare indifferentiam hominis, sed convincere eum, quod sit inexcusabilis. Hujus autem convincitur, non tantum si sit indifferens, sed etiam si sit malus, & impotens se subjiciendi Deo. Fructum vero expectare Deus dicitur, non propter similitudinem ignorantiae ingenii soli aut plantae; vel irriti desiderii; vel propter verisimilitudinem proditurae fructus, aut potestatem hominis ad fructificandum indifferentis; sed propter similitudinem tum in tolerantia fruticis & soli maligni; tum in exploratione & manifestatione malignitatis & ineptitudinis per cultum illum vineae & tolerantiam: tum in praeparatione judicii & exterminii: tum denique in apparentia externa ad spem fructus apud homines scilicet, non apud Deum. Qui expectationis, idem expansionis manus, Dei ad populum refractarium, Esaj. LXV. 2. 3. est. Notatur enim impropria phrasi tolerantia & longanimitas Dei in invitandis, & beneficiis non paucis mactandis Judaeis rebellibus, cogitationes suas sequentibus, & vae semper Deo facientibus; ad convincendos eos malitiae, duritiei & justi judicii, quod erga illos pronuntiaturus erat. Sed vel gratiam Dei iis per praeconium verbi, & electionem ac vocationem externam in populum fuisse ad conversionem sufficientem, neque distinctam ab ea, qua erga Sanctos in populo τὸ λείμμα reliquias utebatur; vel refractarios illos indifferentes fuisse ad gratiam sufficientem amplectendam, minimè consequitur. Qui porro Ezech. XII. 2. dicuntur oculos habere ad videndum, & non videre; aures ad audiendum, & non audire, illi quidem hactenus illuminati innuuntur, non ut hoc, quod oportet, viderent & intelligerent, quod in irregenitos non cadit, utpote quibus Deus non dat cor ad cognoscendum, nec oculos ad videndum, nec aures ad audiendum, Deut. XXIX. 4. quique sunt ἀπεσυτητοι τῆς ὠσίν incircumcisi auribus, Act. VII. 51. adeoque non possunt cognoscere ea, quae Spiritus, quia spiritualiter dijudicantur, 1. Cor. II. 14. sed tantum ut quaedam viderent, per quae duci possent ad videndum quae oportet videre; atque inprimis illud verbum, in quo vera sapientia continetur, pro verbo Dei agnoscerent.
units.tr: ...nea meâ, and did not do it? Why did I look for it to bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes? Isaiah 5:4. I have stretched out my hands all day long to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts; a people who provoke me to my face continually, ibid. 65:2, 3. Son of man, you dwell in the midst of a rebellious house; they have eyes to see and do not see, and ears to hear and do not hear, because they are a rebellious house, Ezek. 12:2. Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes, etc., Matt. 11:21, 22. Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets, how often would I have gathered your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings? And you would not, ibid. 23:37. The Pharisees and lawyers rejected the counsel of God for themselves, not being baptized by him, Luke 7:30. I say these things so that you may be saved. And you are not willing to come to me, that you may have life, John 5:34, 40. You always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you, Acts 7:51. But these passages are clearly of a different kind. For the others do not even speak of the resistance of those who are called, such as that saying of Christ: How often would I have gathered your children together, etc., and you would not, Matt. 23:37. For although those who killed the prophets were unwilling, indeed were strongly opposed, Christ nevertheless gathered together, from among the children of the city that murders, those whom he wished to gather: disciples and not a few believers. The fathers and the leaders of Jerusalem, most of them at least gathered in its councils, were unwilling that Christ should gather there the children of God, who had a right to the holy city and to fellowship with the saints in it. But Christ ēthelēse synagagein [ἠθέλησε συναγαγεῖν], he willed to gather them, that is, he had the purpose of gathering them and carried it out. Limborch tries in vain to evade this explanation by the argument that in Scripture "Jerusalem" always denotes all the inhabitants of the city. For Christ did not address Jerusalem simply, but Jerusalem that kills, and not all the children of Jerusalem belonged to her; certainly the disciples and those believers whom he gathered did not belong to her. The remaining testimonies speak of a calling that is purely external, made by men through an outward proclamation, and not of God's inward Spirit speaking to and dealing with the heart itself, willing to change and convert it. So clearly, when God declares that he did for his vineyard what was to be done, Isaiah 5:4, he does not assert that he gave to his people every help and every grace. This is so, first, because it is expressly denied that God gave them eyes to see and a heart to understand, Deut. 29:4; second, because circumcision of heart is promised to them for the future, ibid. 30:6, and the Hebrew word is used for a chosen [καρδίαν ἐπιλογὴν] heart; third, because in this parable God himself distinguishes the grace of sanctification from common benefits, when he says: I planted you a choice vine, v. 2, and: The vine of Judah is his pleasant plantation, v. 7, signifying that God had sanctified the fathers, whose seed and offspring these were, with whom the dispute is conducted, and had set them as an example to posterity, whose fruit he had vainly looked for; and so that root with which God made his covenant was holy, but the branches were broken off because of unbelief, Rom. 11:16, 17, etc.; fourth, because in declaring judgment, among other punishments, God commands the clouds not to rain upon them, v. 6, which means that the Church and people of God should no longer be found among them, and this destroys indifferent grace and man's power to convert himself without efficacious help and circumcision of heart, as if by its horns; fifth, because the means which God is said to have applied to the vineyard are purely external, with no mention that he watered it with rain or made the sun rise upon it, which properly bring forth fruit from a vineyard and are analogous to inward grace; and finally, because otherwise there would be no room for grace given to one congruently and to another incongruently, according to God's good pleasure. For thus to the question, "What more should I have done?" the answer could have been given: that what was lacking in God's benefits was that he did not give the grace he gave in a fitting way. Therefore the question of this parable is not how much more help the vineyard needed in order to bear grapes (for it certainly had more help in those whom he planted as the best vine), but what means of salvation were lacking to the Israelites, who at that time presumed upon their own power, as if they had no need of divine regeneration, and who contended against God's judgment, by which he condemns all flesh. Certainly no such means of salvation was lacking to them. For God did everything that the Israelites, promising obedience to God, asked for and expected; and besides, he also cooperated in many things which, through the help of the Holy Spirit, were fruitful for bearing grapes. Further, that God testifies, v. 4, that he expected grapes and found wild grapes cannot properly be understood, because no one properly expects what is not going to happen; but God knew that this fruitfulness would not come, since he foretold it as something that would not happen, and indicated what kind of judgment he was going to inflict on Israel. Rather, it is spoken anthrōpinōs [ἀνθρωπινῶς], in human fashion, because of his forbearance and the delay of the judgment to be inflicted on evil, and without any desire, probability of the thing, or indifference of man towards either outcome, which, as imperfections, cannot be thought of in God's expectation. For a likeness should not be extended beyond its purpose. The purpose of the parable, however, is not to explain man's indifference, but to convince him that he is inexcusable. And he is convicted of this not only if he is indifferent, but also if he is evil and unable to submit himself to God. God is said to expect fruit, not because of a likeness to the ignorance of the mind of the soil or the plant, or to a vain desire, or because of the probability that fruit would be produced, or because of man's power to bear fruit being indifferent; but because of a likeness in the forbearance of the bush and the wicked soil, and in the testing and manifestation of its malignity and unfitness through that cultivation of the vineyard and that forbearance, and in the preparation of judgment and destruction, and finally in the outward appearance that raises hope of fruit among men, but not before God. Of the same kind is the expectation, and the stretching out of God's hands to a refractory people, Isaiah 65:2, 3. For in an improper phrase it is pointed out that God was patient and long-suffering in inviting and in bestowing many benefits upon the rebellious Jews, who followed their own thoughts and always did evil to God; this was to convince them of their malice, hardness, and of the just judgment which he was about to pronounce against them. But it does not at all follow that God's grace was given to them through the proclamation of the word and through external election and calling, sufficient for conversion, and not distinct from that grace by which he dealt with the saints among the people, the to leimma [τὸ λείμμα], the remnant; nor that those refractory people were indifferent towards embracing sufficient grace. As for those who in Ezekiel 12:2 are said to have eyes to see and not see, ears to hear and not hear, these are indeed indicated as enlightened so far, not so that they might see and understand what they ought, which does not fall to the unregenerate, to whom God does not give a heart to know, nor eyes to see, nor ears to hear, Deut. 29:4; and who are aperitmētoi tōn ōtōn [ἀπεσυτητοι τῆς ὠσίν], uncircumcised in their ears, Acts 7:51, and so cannot know those things which are of the Spirit, because they are spiritually discerned, 1 Cor. 2:14. Rather, they were only to see certain things, by which they might be led to see what they ought to see; and above all, they were to acknowledge that word, in which true wisdom is contained, as the word of God.

units.la: Sed qui eo usque illuminantur, & oculos ad videndum, aures ad audiendum habent, possunt tamen non audire, non videre, quod audire & videre oportet; quia de eo quod vident & audiunt per oppositionem sapientiae carnalis, quae verba Dei etiam detorquere docet, possunt non recte cogitare, judicare. Quod cum faciunt, non jam vulgari more errant sed ita indurantur, ut putent id, in quo errant, verbum Dei esse. Qui fere ἀπερίπτωτοι incurabiles sunt. Causa non intelligentium ita verbum Dei eorum inobedientia est. Sapientia enim carnalis & ejus amor revera inobedientia est. Tales vocantur populus stultus & sine corde; qui habent oculos & non vires, aures & non audiunt, Jerem. V. 21. Illis verbum Dei existit opprobrium; eo non delectantur, ibid. VI. 10. Non ergo, qui ejusmodi oculos & aures habent, sufficientem gratiam habent, quia non eam habent, qua recte audire & videre possunt; sed potius tali prorsus destituuntur. Jam & Christus Tyrios & Sidonios in sacco & cinere resipiscentiam actuaros, si virtutes, quas idem apud Chorazinitas & Bethsaiditas patravit, apud eosdem patrata essent, asseverans, Matth. XI. 21. neutiquam id sibi voluit, quod cum aequali auxilio stet unum converti, & alterum non converti. An enim putamus, conversionem per externa miracula procedere posse? Quid Pelagianum magis? Sed aliud videlicet est in sacco & cinere conceptum dolorem testari, & eatenus poenitentiam externam agere: aliud & sublimius quiddam, per gratiam efficacem regenerari, & penitus converti. Sicut aliud est, quomodo apud medicos aliud est, humores noxios excutere & dissipare; aliud salubriori pharmaco exhaurire & aegrotum sanare. Ita comminatio Eliae terrorem incussit Achabo, terror humiliavit, humilitas vindictam Dei pro tempore avertit. Cilicium & saccus cum jejunio fuit, vera conversio non fuit. Hoc solum verba Christi evincunt, inter irregenitos & reprobos alios aliis nequiores esse, sic ut audito verbo Dei & visis signis alii aliter afficiantur: alii indurescant, alii trepidantes signa poenitentiae & doloris edant. Planum quin etiam est, Christo non de interna gratia, sed de externo tantum per
units.tr: But those who are enlightened to this extent, and have eyes to see and ears to hear, may still fail to hear and fail to see what they ought to hear and see. Because of the opposition of carnal wisdom, which even teaches them to twist the words of God, they may fail to think and judge rightly about what they see and hear. When they do this, they no longer err in the ordinary way, but are so hardened that they think the very thing in which they go wrong is the word of God. Such people are almost incurable [ἀπερίπτωτοι]. So the reason why they do not understand the word of God is their disobedience. For carnal wisdom and love of it are in fact disobedience. Such people are called a foolish and senseless people, who have eyes but do not see, and ears but do not hear, Jer. 5:21. The word of God is a reproach to them; they take no pleasure in it, ibid. 6:10. Therefore those who have such eyes and ears do not have sufficient grace, because they do not have the grace by which they could rightly hear and see; rather, they are wholly deprived of it. Christ also, asserting that the Tyrians and Sidonians would have repented in sackcloth and ashes, if the miracles which he performed among the Chorazinites and Bethsaidans had been performed among them, Matt. 11:21, certainly did not mean that one person is converted and another is not converted with equal help. For do we think that conversion can come about through external miracles? What could be more Pelagian? Clearly it is one thing to show grief conceived in sackcloth and ashes and so far to perform an external repentance; it is another, and something loftier, to be regenerated through efficacious grace and wholly converted. It is as in medicine: one thing is to expel and disperse harmful humours, another to drain them with a more wholesome remedy and heal the sick person. So Elijah's threat struck terror into Ahab, the terror humbled him, and the humility turned aside God's vengeance for the time being. There was sackcloth and fasting, but there was no true conversion. The words of Christ prove only this: among the unregenerate and the reprobate some are worse than others, so that when they hear the word of God and see the signs, some are affected in one way and some in another. Some harden, while others, trembling, show the signs of repentance and sorrow. It is also plain that Christ was speaking not of inward grace but only of outward help, through preaching and miracles.

units.la: praedicationem & miracula auxilio sermonem esse. Praeterea utcunque Tyriorum & Sidoniorum aeque ac Chorazinitarum & Bethsaidarum deplorata salus fuit, tamen hos illis comparatos obstinatiores esse Christus queritur, eo modo, quo quis Christianum corripiens diceret: Turca si esses, humanius mecum egisses. Denique etiam Christus hic respicit ad Prophetias, in quibus Tyri, ceu μητροπόλεως & speciminis gentium convertendarum, mentio fit, Psalm. XLV. 13. LXXXVII. 4. Hos. IX. 13. ut sic connexiva illa enuntiatio consectarium sit decreti Divini de gentibus potius quam indurati Judaeis (de quibus comminatio gravis Deut. XXXII. 19. &c. extat.) per fidem justificandis, in specie vero Tyriis & Sodomaeorum similibus, de quibus est Ezech. XVI. 57. Sed & Pharisaei & Legisperiti τὸ βουλὴ & θεὸς ἠθέτησαν εἰς ἑαυτούς consilium Dei irritum fecerunt vel potius rejecerunt, ad se, ne baptizarentur, Luc. VII. 30. non respuendo internam & sufficientem ad salutem gratiam, sed voluntatem Dei praecipientem, hoc est, προστάγμα mandatum Dei, & id quod Deo gratum est. Nam βουλὴ consilium etiam mandatum Dei datum significat, quod cum rejicitur, atque ita efficitur, ut εἰς τὸ κενὸν frustra & sine fructu datum sit, ἀθέτησις dicitur. Ita Christus alibi: 'O ἀθετῶν ἐμὲ καὶ μὴ λαμβάνων τὰ ῥήματά μου. Qui me rejicit, & non accipit verba mea, Joh. XII. 48. Ubi pro ἀθετῶν Syrus habet ܢܬܩ quod significat ὑποτ-ξεῖν frustrari, & non semel pro ἀθετῶν ponitur, velut Luc. X. 16. Qui vos audit, me audit και ὁ ἀθετῶν ὑμᾶς, ἐμὲ ἀθετεῖ. Ubi ἀθετῶν non significat irritum facere, sed rejicere, non audire. Conveniunt verba Lucae cum illis Solomonis exuistis, rejecistis omne consilium meum, & redargutioni meae assensi non estis, Prov. I. 25. Denique Stephanus Protomartyr exprobrans Judaeis; Durae cervicis & incircumcisis corde & auribus; Vos semper Spiritui S. resistitis, sicut & Patres vestri. Act. VII. 51. non loquitur de gratia Spiritus S. interna sufficiente, vel de causis conversionis, quae ab intentione Dei dependent, sed de modo convertendi externo qui hominum ministerio promovetur. Restiterunt illi Sp. S. externe per ministros suadenti & fistula verbi congreganti, non interne per gratiam efficacem operanti. Quod statim Stephanus, optimus verborum suorum interpres declaravit; dicens: Quem Prophetarum (qui locuti sunt ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίου φερόμενοι) lati a Spiritu S. 2. Pet. I. 21.) non persecuti sunt Patres vestri? & occiderunt eos, qui ante praedicarunt de adventu justi &c. v. 52. Et Deus ipse: Posuerunt cor suum silicem, ne audirent legem & verba, quae mandavit Jehova Deus exercituum in Spiritu suo per Prophetas priores, (cum manifestatione Spiritus S. per Prophetas loquentis) Zach. VII. 12. Alibi Sapientia: Convertimini ad redargutionem meam. Ecce scatebrae instar effundam vobis רוח Spiritum meum: (animum meum; quomodo vox רוח saepe in Spiritu Sancto accipitur, & ab ipso Corn. a Lapide & Mariana, sed multo magis statim a Deo ipso explicatur, dicente:) Faciam vos scire sermones meos. Quia vocavi, & renuistis, & rejecistis omne consilium meum, &c. Proverb. I. 23. 24.
units.tr: Moreover, although the salvation of the Tyrians and Sidonians, like that of the Chorazinites and Bethsaidans, was lamented, Christ nevertheless complains that these were more obstinate than those compared with them. He speaks as someone rebuking a Christian might: "If you were a Turk, you would have dealt more humanely with me." Finally, Christ here also looks back to the prophecies in which Tyre is mentioned as the mother city and specimen of the nations to be converted (Ps. 45:13; 87:4; Hos. 9:13). So that connecting statement is a consequence of the divine decree concerning the Gentiles, to be justified through faith, rather than concerning the hardened Jews (against whom a grave threat stands, Deut. 32:19 etc.), and especially concerning the Tyrians and those like the Sodomites (Ezek. 16:57). But also the Pharisees and lawyers "set aside the counsel of God against themselves" [τὴν βουλὴν τοῦ θεοῦ ἠθέτησαν εἰς ἑαυτούς], that is, they made the counsel of God void, or rather rejected it, so that they would not be baptized (Luke 7:30). They did not reject an internal grace sufficient for salvation, but the will of God commanding, that is, prostagma, the command of God, and that which is pleasing to God. For boulē also signifies the counsel, that is, the command of God given, and when this is rejected, so that it has been given in vain and without fruit (eis to kenon), it is called athetēsis [ἀθέτησις]. So Christ elsewhere: "He who rejects me and does not receive my words" [ὁ ἀθετῶν ἐμὲ καὶ μὴ λαμβάνων τὰ ῥήματά μου] (John 12:48). There the Syriac, for athetōn, has "netaq", which signifies to frustrate, and it is not used only once for athetōn, as in Luke 10:16: "He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects [ὁ ἀθετῶν ὑμᾶς] you rejects me [ἐμὲ ἀθετεῖ]." There athetōn does not mean to make void, but to reject, not to hear. The words of Luke agree with those of Solomon: "You have cast off [exuistis], you have rejected all my counsel, and have not assented to my reproof" (Prov. 1:25). Finally, Stephen the first martyr, reproaching the Jews: "Stiff-necked, and uncircumcised in heart and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did" (Acts 7:51). He does not speak of the internal and sufficient grace of the Holy Spirit, or of the causes of conversion, which depend on the intention of God, but of the external manner of converting, which is promoted by the ministry of men. They resisted the Holy Spirit externally, persuading through ministers and gathering by the trumpet of the Word, not operating internally through efficacious grace. Stephen himself, the best interpreter of his own words, made this plain at once, saying: "Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One" (v. 52), the prophets who spoke "being carried along by the Holy Spirit" [ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίου φερόμενοι] (2 Pet. 1:21). And God himself says: "They made their heart like flint, so that they would not hear the law and the words which the LORD of hosts sent by his Spirit through the former prophets" (with the manifestation of the Holy Spirit speaking through the prophets) (Zech. 7:12). Elsewhere Wisdom says: "Turn at my reproof. Behold, I will pour out my spirit [רוח] upon you like a spring" (here ruach means my mind, as the word ruach is often taken for the Holy Spirit by Cornelius a Lapide and Mariana, but it is explained much more clearly by God himself, who says): "I will make you know my words. Because I have called, and you refused, and you have rejected all my counsel" etc. (Prov. 1:23–24).

units.la: LVI. Tum adversarii loca illa, quibus
units.tr: LVI. Then the adversaries are accustomed to press those passages by which

units.la: Deus conversionem, resipiscentiam & fidem hominibus mandat, urgere solent. Ita enim Deus ipse: Circumcidite præputium cordis vestri, & cervicem vestram ne indurate ultra, Deut. X. 16. Projicite à vobis omnes prævaricationes vestras, quibus prævaricati estis, & facite vobis cor novum, & spiritum novum, & quare moriemini domus Israel? Ezech. XVIII. 31. Convertimini ad me, & ego convertar ad vos, Zach. I. 3. Resipiscite & convertimini, ut deleantur peccata vestra, Act. III. 19. Resipiscite & credite Evangelio, Marc. I. 15. Hoc est mandatum ejus, ut credamus in nomine Filii ejus Jesu Christi, & diligamus alii alios, 1. Joh. III. 23. Atqui, inquiunt illi, si Deus ipse gratia insuperabili hominem converteret, eique resipiscentiam & fidem donaret, conversionem, fidem &c. sub promissione præmii & comminatione pœnæ præscribere non posset. Quasi scilicet Dei mandatum mensura virium nostrarum, non officii nostri norma esset. Quæ ergo vires resurgendi ex morte corporis fuerunt, cùm Christus Lazaro mortuo mandavit: Lazare exi foras, Joh. XI. 43. & quæ erunt, cùm omnibus mandabit: Revertimini filii hominum; Psal. XC. 3. Cùm denique omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem Christi jubentem reverti, & prodibunt ad resurrectionem vitæ? &c. Joh. V. 28.29. Neque obstat, quòd ibi mandatum cum promissione & comminatione conjunctum est; hic non item, quia promissio & comminatio non ad mandatum ipsum, sed ad sanctionem mandati pertinet. Et sicut justi reverti, prodire, ita etiam credere, resipiscere, ex morte utraque resuscitari, reverti, prodire, resipiscere, sub præmio & pœna juberi potuerunt, quia ipsorum est prodire, reverti; credere, resipiscere, postquam ex utraque morte suscitati sunt. Initio patimur, sed passi ipsi quoque agimus. Quæ actio præcipi sub præmio & pœna potest. Etiam Christus quà homo, & Angeli cœlites Deo obediunt, sine ulla facultate peccandi & resistendi Deo: & mali angeli non obediunt Deo, & supplicio digni sunt sine ulla facultate Deo obediendi. Omnibus tamen his obedientiæ Lex dicta est. Nam creaturæ cujusvis Lex est, Deo creatori subesse. Neque ideo Deus impossibilia mandat; quia mandat id, quod possibile fuit homini integro, qui sua culpa, & impulsore Diabolo, ἀδυναμίαν, quæ nihil aliud est, quàm ζωλη-σεγχηλίαν, seu malæ voluntatis durities, contraxit, & Deus jus suum repetendi & exigendi id, cujus homo debendi reus est, quatenus Dei creatura est, & primitus unâ cum imagine obediendi vires à Deo accepit, hominis imaginem Dei conturbantis culpa non decoxit. Ac licet homo integer Christo ut Salvatori credere non potuerit, quia ut Salvator homini integro revelari non potuit; tamen potentiam credendi cuivis revelationi in Adamo accepit. Cùm ergo Christus post peccatum ut Salvator revelatus fuerit, tenetur homo credere ea ipsa potentia credendi, quam in Adamo habuit, & per peccatum amisit. Non enim potentia illa, quam actu non exeruit, nec exerere potuit, frustranea Adamo magis fuit, quàm potentia miserendi, & φιλοσοφία, quam Adamus habuit, licet eam ante peccatum non exeruerit, nec exerere potuerit. Quòd verò jubemur, nos ipsos circum-cidere, cor novum & spiritum novum nobis facere, credere, resipiscere, &c. id nihil detrahit gratiæ Dei, quò minùs circumcisio cordis, cor novum & spiritum novus &c. Divina creatio fit. Hoc solum significatur, quando Deus nos regenerat & sanctificat, id in nobis effici, ut ipsi cordis nostri malitiam, stultitiam, torporem & inertiam cognoscamus, eámque magis magisque deponere, mortificare & nos ipsos ad amandum & timendum solum Deum componere, nec non malas radices ex corde nostro eruncare discamus, & in cogitationibus cordis nostri nobis ne benedicamus. In id, qui non omni studio & labore incumbit; næ is à corde novo, & spiritu novo, quem solus Deus creat, longè abest. Ita David sibi faciebat cor novum orans: Cor purum crea mihi, Deus, & spiritum promptum ac firmum nova in medio mei, PSLI. 12. Si quid enim boni cogitamus, nisi non Deo, sed nobis confidimus, oramus utique & suspiramus, ut id Deus in nobis efficiat. Deus enim cor circumcidit & novum facit mandato dilectionis. Dum igitur mandat, hoc facit, quod eum facere necesse erat, qui corda circumcidit. Hoc autem facit verbo & Spiritu suo. Sic voluntas nostra cum Divina conspirat: sic Deus facit nos velle, circumcidens corda nostra facit, ut circumcidamus corda; faciens in nobis cor novum facit, ut nobis faciamus cor novum. Hæc prima in corde novitas est, ut sibi displicens se velit esse novum, & trahente Deo currat, Cant. I. 4. Tum claudus salit instar cervi, Esaj. XXXV. 6. Denique Dei mandata rectissimè intelligimus, ubi in preces illa commutamus, clamando ad Deum: Converte nos Jehova ad te, & convertemur, Thren. V. 21.
units.tr: They usually press the command of God for conversion, repentance and faith on people. God himself speaks thus: "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart, and stiffen your neck no more" (Deut. 10:16). "Cast away from you all your transgressions, by which you have transgressed, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit; for why will you die, house of Israel?" (Ezek. 18:31). "Turn to me, and I will turn to you" (Zech. 1:3). "Repent and turn, that your sins may be blotted out" (Acts 3:19). "Repent and believe the gospel" (Mark 1:15). "This is his command, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another" (1 John 3:23). But, they say, if God himself converted a man by an irresistible grace, and gave him repentance and faith, he could not prescribe conversion, faith and so on under the promise of a reward and the threat of punishment. As if, forsooth, the command of God were measured by our strength, and not the rule of our duty. What strength, then, did the dead Lazarus have to rise from the death of the body, when Christ commanded him, "Lazarus, come out" (John 11:43)? And what strength will the dead have when he commands all, "Return, sons of men" (Ps. 90:3)? Finally, when "all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of Christ bidding them return, and shall come forth to the resurrection of life" (John 5:28–29)? Nor does it stand in the way that in the former case the command is joined with a promise and a threat, but in this one it is not, because the promise and the threat pertain not to the command itself but to its sanction. And just as the righteous could be bidden to return and come forth, so also to believe and repent, and to be raised up from death in either sense, to return, come forth and repent, under a reward and a penalty; for it is their own act to come forth and return, to believe and repent, once they have been raised from death in either sense. At the beginning we are acted upon, but having been acted upon, we also act in turn; and this action can be commanded under a reward and a penalty. Christ also, as man, and the heavenly angels obey God, without any ability to sin or to resist God; and the evil angels do not obey God and deserve punishment, without any ability to obey God. Yet the name of law has been given to all this obedience, for it is the law of every creature to be subject to God its Creator. Nor does God therefore command impossibilities, because he commands what was possible for man in his integrity; man, by his own fault and at the instigation of the devil, contracted an inability, which is nothing other than obstinacy of the evil will [ζωλη-σεγχηλίαν], or the hardness of a bad will; and God retains his right to demand and exact what man is bound to owe, insofar as he is God's creature, and at the outset received from God, together with the image of obedience, the power to obey; the fault which disturbed the image of God in man did not destroy that power. And although man in his integrity could not believe in Christ as Saviour, because Christ as Saviour could not be revealed to man in his integrity, nevertheless he received in Adam the power to believe any revelation whatever. Therefore, since Christ has been revealed as Saviour after the sin, man is bound to believe by that same power of believing which he had in Adam and lost through sin. For that power, which he did not and could not exercise in act, was no more futile to Adam than the power of mercy and the wisdom [φιλοσοφία] which Adam had, although before the sin he did not and could not exercise them. But when we are commanded to circumcise ourselves, to make for ourselves a new heart and a new spirit, to believe, to repent, and so on, this takes nothing away from the grace of God, so that the circumcision of the heart, the new heart and the new spirit are not a divine creation. This only is signified: when God regenerates and sanctifies us, this is effected in us, that we come to know the malice, folly, torpor and sloth of our own heart, and learn to lay these aside more and more, to mortify them, to bring ourselves to love and fear God alone, and to root out the evil roots from our heart, and not to bless ourselves in the thoughts of our heart. He who does not apply himself to this with all zeal and labour is far from the new heart and the new spirit which God alone creates. So David, praying, made for himself a new heart: "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right and steadfast spirit within me" (Ps. 51:10). For if we think anything good, and trust not in God but in ourselves, we surely pray and sigh that God would effect this in us. For God circumcises the heart and makes it new by the command of love. Therefore, when he commands, he does what he must do who circumcises hearts. He does this, however, by his word and his Spirit. Thus our will agrees with the divine will: God makes us will, by circumcising our hearts he makes us circumcise our hearts; by making a new heart in us he makes us make for ourselves a new heart. This is the first newness in the heart, that displeasing to itself it wishes to be new, and "draws near, being drawn by God" (Song 1:4). Then "the lame man leaps like a deer" (Isa. 35:6). Finally, we understand the commands of God most rightly when we turn them into prayer, crying out to God: "Turn us, O Jehovah, to yourself, and we shall be turned" (Lam. 5:21).

units.la: LVII.
units.tr: LVII.

units.la: Addunt & exaggerant hostes gratiæ, quòd omnes actus & operationes, quibus verbum Dei circa homines operatur, testentur, hominem in quovis instanti libertate illud vel rejiciendi, vel recipiendi præditum esse. Cùm enim verbum Dei homini offertur, ad illud audiendum, inquiunt, non constringitur, sed sponte illud audit vel non audit. Ubi verbum audivit, non potest, quin illius clarè quippe propositi sensum intelligat. Actiones enim intellectus necessariæ sunt. At in potestate hominis est, verbum auditum & intellectum meditari; & cùm illud meditatus est, potest illud per liberam voluntatem recipere vel rejicere. Nam Deus dat potestatem eligendi vitam vel mortem, Deut. XXX. 19. suadet, ut homines illud recipiant & se emendent, Apoc. III. 18. Cùm suasio necessitatem non inferat: monet, ne illud rejiciant, Heb. III. 7. quæ monitio frustranea foret, si liberè recipere vel rejicere illud non posset: orat, optat, vovet, ut homo verbum recipiat, eíque obediat, Deut. V. 29. Psal. LXXXI. 14. Luc. XIX. 42. 2. Cor. V. 20. quod Deus seriò non faceret, si homo obedire nò posset, sicut nemo catenis constrictum orare seriò potest, ut ad se veniat, si vincula ei demere nolit: rejicientem verbum reprehendit, Joh. V. 40. Act. VII. 51. & damnat, Prov. I. 24.25.26. Joh. III. 19. recipientem laudat, Act. II. 41. XIII. 48. & beat, Joh. XIV. 21. Hactenus illi, sed ἀλόγως nimis & præter Scripturarum, quas vendi-tant, mentem. Quicquid enim verbum Dei auditum, intellectum, ruminatum propositá, vita & morte, ingeminatis admonitionibus, suasionibus, precibus, votis, promissionibus, comminationibus, beatitudinis spe facta, & damnationis terrore incusso operatur; illud omne brachio & sceptro Spiritus S. non erga quosvis, per sufficientis gratiae donationem, sed erga solos electos revelato & extenso operatur. Nam ut verbum Dei salutariter audiatur, intelligatur, ruminetur, ejusque consilia, svasiones, admonitiones, correptiones, promissiones & comminationes, quibus Deus apud hominem, quem non αλόγως, sed ceu creaturam rationalem λογικώς regit & moderatur, utitur, ad salutem proficiant, opus est, tum ut cordis nebulae, falsa sapientia & concupiscentia auferantur, Psal. CXIX. 18. tum ut conscientia excitetur ad id agnoscendum in verbo, quod de gloria Dei naturaliter notum est: tum ut aperiatur cor per dationem timoris Dei, ut verbum Dei auditum in cor intromittatur, consideretur, & cum eo, quod naturaliter notum est, comparetur, ut videamus, an id, quod de Deo revelatum est, ipso dignum sit, & in operibus ejus testimonium habeat: tum ut Deus infundat amorem sui, ut homo animadversa Dei erga Ecclesiam φιλανθρώπία & χενσότης maxima, propter violatum nomen Domini doleat, se ipsum abneget, & ad justitiam Dei anhelet: tum ut excitetur homo ad animadvertendum in verbo Dei, quae signa sint redemptionis, regenerationis & communionis Christi, & quae sit ἐξουσία potestas tantum bonum sibi vindicandi, nec non ad semetipsum explorandum, & dilectionem Dei velut Patris in se requirendum, & ad animam suam Deo in bonis factis committendam. Haec & similia omnia non communis aliqua gratia per Dei verbum operans, sed speciali & convertentis plane eximia, coruscatio Dei in cordibus ad radiationem cognitionis gloriae Dei in facie Christi, 2.Cor. IV. 6. ut qui in verbo lucet amabilis, etiam in corde ut amans & salvans luceat, efficit. Suasiones porro, adhortationes, obtestationes, comminationes, promissiones &c. etiam impotentes nos officii admonent, & in electis quidem ad conversionem, in reprobis ad convictionem & ἀναπολογησίαν validae & efficaces sunt. Neque ideo vel nullam laudem merentur, qui resipiscere, credere, diligere volunt, etiam si voluntatem illam non ex libero arbitrio, sed ex gratia Dei operantis in nobis velle & operari, habeant quia gloria, honor & pax est παντὸ τῷ ἔργαζομένω τὸ ἀγαθὸν omni operanti bonum opus, undecunque operetur, Rom. II. 10. vel nullam poenam merentur illi, qui sua culpa obedire non possunt, quia afflictio & angustiae sunt super omnem hominem κατεργαζόμενον τὸ κακὸν operantem malum, ibid. v. 9. & justum Dei judicium est adversus eum etiam, qui potentiam obediendi suopte vitio perdidit & ad peccandum induruit.
units.tr: The enemies of grace add to this and exaggerate it, arguing that all the acts and operations by which the Word of God works upon human beings testify that a person, at every moment, is endowed with the freedom either to reject or to accept it. For when the Word of God is offered to a man, they say, he is not compelled to hear it; he hears it or does not hear it of his own accord. Once he has heard the Word, he cannot fail to understand the sense of what has been clearly proposed, since the acts of the intellect are necessary. But it lies within a man's power to meditate on the Word he has heard and understood, and once he has meditated on it, he can accept or reject it by his free will. For God gives the power of choosing life or death, Deut. XXX. 19. He urges people to receive it and mend their ways, Rev. III. 18. But since urging does not impose necessity, He warns them not to reject it, Heb. III. 7. That warning would be pointless if they could not freely receive or reject it. He prays, desires and vows that a man should receive the Word and obey it, Deut. V. 29. Ps. LXXXI. 14. Luke XIX. 42. 2 Cor. V. 20. God would not do this in earnest if a man could not obey, just as no one can seriously ask a man bound in chains to come to him if he refuses to loosen his chains. He rebukes the one who rejects the Word, John V. 40. Acts VII. 51, and condemns him, Prov. I. 24, 25, 26. John III. 19. He praises the one who receives it, Acts II. 41. XIII. 48, and pronounces him blessed, John XIV. 21. So far they argue, but irrationally [alogōs] and beyond the sense of the Scriptures they flaunt. For whatever the Word of God works, once heard, understood and pondered, through the setting out of life and death, the repeated admonitions, persuasions, prayers, vows, promises, threats, the hope of blessedness and the terror of damnation, all of this He works by the arm and sceptre of the Holy Spirit, not toward everyone through the bestowal of sufficient grace, but toward the elect alone, in a revealed and extended manner. For if the Word of God is to be heard, understood and pondered unto salvation, and if God's counsels, persuasions, admonitions, corrections, promises and threats, by which He deals with a human being whom He does not govern irrationally [alogōs] but, as a rational creature, rationally [logikōs], are to profit that person for salvation, then several things are necessary. First, the clouds of the heart, false wisdom and concupiscence must be removed, Ps. CXIX. 18. Second, the conscience must be stirred to recognise in the Word what is naturally known of the glory of God. Third, the heart must be opened by the bestowal of the fear of God, so that the Word of God, once heard, may be admitted into the heart, considered and compared with what is known by nature, that we may see whether what has been revealed of God is worthy of Him and has its witness in His works. Fourth, God must pour in the love of Himself, so that a man, having perceived the very great philanthropy and kindness of God toward the Church, may grieve over the violated name of the Lord, deny himself, and long for the righteousness of God. Fifth, a man must be roused to notice in the Word of God what the signs of Christ's redemption, regeneration and communion are, and what the authority [exousia] is to claim so great a good for himself; and likewise to examine himself, to seek in himself the love of God as Father, and to commit his soul to God in good works. All these things and similar ones are not some common grace working through the Word of God, but a special grace, clearly of an eminent converting kind, the shining forth of God in hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ, 2 Cor. IV. 6. It causes the one who is lovable in the Word to shine also in the heart as loving and saving. Moreover, persuasions, exhortations, entreaties, threats, promises, and so on, though powerless, remind us of our duty, and in the elect they are effective and efficacious for conversion, while in the reprobate they are effective for conviction and without excuse [anapologēsia]. Nor, for that reason, do those who wish to repent, believe and love deserve no praise at all, even though they have that will not from free choice but from the grace of God working in us "to will and to work". For glory, honour and peace belong to every one who works good [panti tō ergazomenō to agathon], to everyone working good, wherever he works it, Rom. II. 10. Nor do those who, through their own fault, cannot obey deserve no punishment at all; for affliction and anguish are upon every man who works evil [katergazomenou to kakon], ibid. v. 9, and God's judgment is just against the one who, by his own fault, has lost the power of obeying and has hardened himself to sin.

units.la: LVIII.
units.tr: LVIII.

units.la: Porro vocationem externam absque gratia sufficiente & proposito servandi eos, qui vocantur, Dei sapientiae, bonitati & aequitati, seu rectitudini adversari iidem pertendunt. Si enim Deus Christum in mortem tradat, & eum proponat Propitiatorium, & iis, quibus sic eum proponit, non det gratiam vivificantem, cum omnes in peccatis & lapsibus mortui sint, quomodo, inquiunt, id sapientiae Dei convenit? Sed esse tamen vivificationem, per quam, qui vivificantur, nec mali, impotentes & mortui; nec recti, neque adeo vivi sint, planè ασύνατον etiam est. Caeterum non repugnat sapientiae Dei, homini permittere ut labatur: non justitiae, ut lapsum una cum prole damnet: non bonitati, ut ostendat gratiam suam, & ejus necessitatem homini ingrato & sibi confidenti; vel ut eum prope ad Regnum Dei adducat: non aequitati, ut ostendat hominis impotentiam & ἀναπολογησίαν, qui, cum sine Deo se nihil posse audit, id irridere, quam se ipsum abnegare mavult. Ac licet Deus omni tempore & loco per longanimitatem & beneficia sua invitet ad resipiscentiam, tamen verbum suum eo mittit, tanquam certo canone & certa linea, ubi Ecclesiam habet, & eam salvare, ingratos vero majoribus poenis afficere vult. In qua omni Divinae administrationis μικιλία Dei sapientia manifeste conspicitur.
units.tr: Moreover, the same men contend that an external calling without sufficient grace and without God's purpose of preserving those who are called is contrary to the wisdom, goodness and equity, or rectitude, of God. For they ask: if God delivers Christ to death and sets him forth as the propitiation, yet does not give life-giving grace to those to whom he thus sets him forth, since all are dead in sins and transgressions, how does this agree with the wisdom of God? But that there should be a vivification by which those who are made alive are neither evil, powerless and dead, nor righteous and therefore living, is altogether impossible [ἀσύνατον]. Moreover, it is not contrary to the wisdom of God to permit man to fall; nor to his justice to condemn the fallen man together with his offspring; nor to his goodness to show his grace and its necessity to an ungrateful man who trusts in himself, or to bring him near to the kingdom of God; nor to his equity to show man's powerlessness and lack of excuse [ἀναπολογησίαν], since the man who hears that he can do nothing without God prefers to mock this rather than deny himself. And although God, at all times and in all places, through his long-suffering and his benefits invites to repentance, yet he sends his word there as to a sure rule and a sure line, where he has a Church, and wills to save it, but to punish the ungrateful with greater penalties. In all this management of divine affairs, the wisdom of God is clearly seen in its manifold variety [μικιλία].

units.la: LIX. Denique discordiae litant, qui gratiam inter & liberum arbitrium concordiam hic desiderant, Nulla enim gratiam inter & libertatem voluntatis in spiritualibus se moventis concordia locum habere prius potest, quam voluntas, hactenus serva peccati, & in peccato mortua a peccato liberatur, & quoad bonum spirituale vivificatur. Quae enim potentis vocis Dei, qua mortui vivificantur, cum mortuis ipsis, prius quam vivificati sunt, concordia in operando esse potest? Neque tamen gratia liberum arbitrium tollit, sed a servitute peccati liberat. Si Filius vos liberaverit, ὁντως ἐλεύθεροι vere liberi eritis, Joh. VIII. 36. Non ergo, sic praeclare Augustinus ad Bonifac. lib. I. 19. loquitur, tollitur liberum arbitrium per gratiam, sed liberatur, id est, vere fit liberum. Non enim libertate consequitur gratiam, sed gratia libertatem. Ideo agimur & agimus, quia acti agimus. Non enim sic Templum suum de nobis aedificat, quasi de lapidibus, qui non habent motum suum: Levantur, a structore ponuntur. Non sic sunt lapides vivi. Ducimini, sed currite vos. Ducimini, sed sequimini, quia cum secuti fueritis, verum erit illud, quia sine illo nihil facere poteritis. Totum ex Deo, non tamen quasi dormientes, non quasi ut non conemur, non quasi ut non velimus. Sine voluntate tua non erit in te justitia Dei.
