Voluntas quidem non est nisi tua, justitia non est nisi Dei. Qui fecit te sine te, non te justificat, id est justum facit, sine te, Fecit nescientem, justificat volentem.
units.tr: LIX. Finally, those who here seek a concord between grace and free will are quarrelling in vain. For no concord between grace and the freedom of a will that moves itself in spiritual things can take place until the will, hitherto a slave of sin and dead in sin, is freed from sin and made alive as regards spiritual good. For what concord in working can there be between the powerful voice of God, by which the dead are made alive, and the dead themselves, before they are made alive? Yet grace does not abolish free will, but frees it from the slavery of sin. If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed [ὄντως ἐλεύθεροι], John 8:36. Thus Augustine speaks well in his letter to Boniface, book I, chapter 19: Therefore free will is not abolished by grace, but is set free, that is, it truly becomes free. For grace does not follow upon liberty, but liberty upon grace. Therefore we are moved and we act, because we are moved to act. For God does not build his temple out of us as out of stones that have no motion of their own: they are lifted up and set in place by the builder. Stones are not living in this way. You are led, but you must run yourselves. You are led, but you must follow, for when you have followed, that saying will be true, that without him you can do nothing. All is from God, yet not as though we were asleep, not as though we did not strive, not as though we did not will. Without your will there will be no righteousness of God in you. Indeed the will is yours alone, but righteousness is God's alone. He who made you without you does not justify you, that is, make you righteous, without you. He made you when you did not know him; he justifies you when you will.

units.la: LX. Hactenus igitur concors Dei gratia & hominis voluntas est, quod nec illa violenter agit, nec haec, trunci instar, violenter agitur; sed illa agit & omnipotenter & suaviter, nec sine delectatione voluntatis; haec agentem sic gratiam volendo, non nolendo, reluctando, & libenter, non aegre volendo sequitur. Tanto enim voluntas liberior est, quanto sanior & Divinae misericordiae & gratiae subjectior. Gratia vero ipsa & potenter & suaviter, & invicte & gratiose convertit. Nam Deus & Spiritu creat, regenerat, cor carneum dat, habitus supernaturales fidei & charitatis infundit: & verbo docet, inclinat, suadet, & rationibus variis, ceu vinculis amoris, & veris παρκλήσεις ad se trahit. Unde gratia Augustino nomine Victricis delectationis venit, quia cum jucunditate & suavitate summa efficaciam & potentiam summam, qua omnis
units.tr: LX. Thus the grace of God and the will of man are in agreement in this respect: grace does not act by violence, nor is the will driven violently, like a log. Rather, grace acts both omnipotently and sweetly, and not without the delight of the will, and the will, in this way, follows the acting grace by willing, not by unwilling, by not resisting, and by willing gladly, not reluctantly. For the will is the freer the healthier it is and the more subject to divine mercy and grace. Grace itself converts both powerfully and sweetly, both invincibly and graciously. For God by his Spirit creates, regenerates, gives a heart of flesh, and infuses supernatural habits of faith and charity; and by his word he teaches, inclines, persuades, and draws to himself by various reasons, as with the bonds of love, and by true exhortations [παρκλήσεις]. Hence grace is called by Augustine the victorious delight, because together with the greatest sweetness and gentleness it has the greatest efficacy and power, by which every hardness of heart is overcome.

units.la: Quarto, quod vocatio externa absque gratia sufficiente & proposito servandi eos, qui vocantur, Dei sapientiae, bonitati & aequitati, seu rectitudini adversari iidem pertendunt. omnis cordis durities vincitur conjunctam habet. Utraque simul juncta & infirmitatem hominis roborat, & odium peccati superat. Potens est, ne sit eis kenon inanis & frustranea: suavis, ne coacta, & a natura intelligente & rationali aliena videri possit. Sicut nempe peccati inelúctabilis servitus, quae peccatorem velut aheneo jugo alligatum tenet, cum deliciis carnis conjungitur; & bene agendi impotentia, malaque agendi necessitas maxima simul & voluntaria est: ita gratia regenerationis eidem opposita invicta & incredibili suavitate imbuta est. Cum enim vitam spiritualem, amorem Dei, fidem in Christum, & cum eodem communionem libertatem voluntatis a servitute solutae; operetur, quid his omnibus suavius esse possit? Sic foedissima delectatio peccati suavissima delectatione gratiae vincitur. Et sic gratia Dei trahit, non torquet, ut etiam doceat, Joh. VI. 44. 45. sic jugo innodat, ut sua chrestotes demulceat, Matth. XI. 30. Sic Spiritus S. potentia persuadet, ut etiam demonstret, 1. Cor. II. 4. Sic immensa virtute Dei convertit, ut etiam illuminatione plena gaudii perfundat, Ephes. I. 18. 19. constringit & ligat, sed charitatis & philanthropias funibus, Hos. XI. 4. 2. Cor. V. 14. Eandem ob causam Evangelium, quo convertimur, & potentia & sapientia, 1.Cor. I.24. & brachium Dei, quo nihil potentius, Esaj. LIII. 1. & dulcius melle ac stillatione favorum, Psal. XIX. 11. Lac, quo nihil suavius, 1. Pet. II. 2. tum Spiritus S. regenerans passim Spiritus & roboris & gratiae, potentiae & charitatis 2. Tim. I. 7. & sceptrum roboris, Psal. CX. 3. & oleum laetitiae, ibid. XLV. 7. appellatur. Quae cuncta gratiae libertatem voluntatis operantis vim, sed suavissimam & amicissimam illam insinuant: Hactenus ergo gratiae convertentis motio nec Physica nec Ethica proprie, sed supernaturalis & Divina, tum omnipotens, tum suavissima est, & utramque, Physicae & Ethicae seu moralis analogia quadam refert.
units.tr: Fourthly, the same men contend that external calling without sufficient grace and without God's purpose of preserving those who are called is contrary to the wisdom, goodness and equity, or rectitude, of God. Every hardness of heart is overcome, and it has these two things joined together. Both joined together strengthen the weakness of man and overcome the hatred of sin. Grace is powerful, lest it be empty and vain [eis kenon]; it is gentle, lest it seem forced and alien to an intelligent and rational nature. For just as the inescapable slavery of sin, which holds the sinner bound as with a bronze yoke, is joined with the delights of the flesh, and the impotence to do good and the greatest necessity of doing evil are at once both great and voluntary, so the grace of regeneration, which is opposed to this, is imbued with an invincible and incredible sweetness. For since it works spiritual life, the love of God, faith in Christ, and communion with him, and the freedom of a will loosed from slavery, what can be sweeter than all these? Thus the most foul delight of sin is overcome by the most sweet delight of grace. And so the grace of God draws, and does not torture, so that it also teaches, John 6:44-45; so it binds with a yoke, yet soothes with its kindness, Matthew 11:30. So the power of the Holy Spirit persuades, so that it also shows, 1 Corinthians 2:4. So by the immense power of God he converts, so that he also fills with illumination full of joy, Ephesians 1:18-19; he binds and ties, but with the cords of charity and love for mankind [philanthropias], Hosea 11:4; 2 Corinthians 5:14. For the same reason the Gospel, by which we are converted, is called both power and wisdom, 1 Corinthians 1:24; and the arm of God, than which nothing is more powerful, Isaiah 53:1; and sweeter than honey and the dripping of the honeycomb, Psalm 19:11; the milk, than which nothing is sweeter, 1 Peter 2:2. Then the regenerating Holy Spirit is everywhere called the Spirit of strength and of grace, of power and of love [potentiae & charitatis], 2 Timothy 1:7; and the sceptre of strength [roboris], Psalm 110:3; and the oil of gladness, ibid. 45:7. All these things imply that the freedom of the will is the working power of grace, but a most sweet and friendly power. Thus the movement of converting grace is properly neither physical [Physica] nor ethical [Ethica], but supernatural and divine [supernaturalis & Divina]; it is both omnipotent and most sweet, and in a certain analogy [analogia] it bears a likeness to both physical and ethical [Physicae & Ethicae], that is, moral, action.

units.la: LXI. Neque proin a Deo sapientissimo doctore & monitore alienum est, ut quae suadet & mandat, eadem in nobis operetur. Imo haec Foederis gratiae & Novi Testamenti supra foedus operum praerogativa est, quod Deus, secus atque in illo, quas exigit conditiones, ipse met praestat, & ultro hominibus largitur. Hoc est Foedus, quod pacisc ar cum domo Israelis, post dies illos, dicit Dominus: Indam legem meam menti eorum, & cordi eorum inscribam, & ero ipsis Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus, Jerem. XXXI. 33. Heb. VIII. 10. 11. Dabo illis cor unum, & Spiritum novum in medio illorum, & auferam cor lapideum, & dabo illis cor carneum, ut in statutis meis ambulent, & judicia mea observent & ea faciant. Ezech. XI. 19. 20. Inprimis id ex Pauli vocatione liquet, quam non sine externo hortatu & verbo Deus explicuit, licet is in solidum gratiae Dei, ejusque potenti virtuti accepta omnia referat. Gratia Dei sum, quod sum. 1.Cor.XV.10. Dominus Jehova aperuit mihi aurem, & ego non extiti inobediens, non retrocessi, Esaj. L. 5. Verba enim, quae Deus, Christus loquitur, sunt Spiritus & vita, Joh. VI. 6. 3. Et vivus est sermo Dei, efficax & penetrantior quovis gladio ancipite, Hebr. IV. 12.
units.tr: LXI. Therefore it is not foreign to God, the most wise teacher and admonisher, that he should work in us the very things that he persuades and commands. Indeed, this is the prerogative of the covenant of grace and of the New Testament above the covenant of works: that God himself provides the conditions which he requires, unlike in that covenant, and freely bestows them on men. This is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my law in their minds, and write it on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people, Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10-11. I will give them one heart, and a new spirit in the midst of them, and I will take away the stony heart, and give them a heart of flesh, that they may walk in my statutes, and observe my judgments, and do them, Ezekiel 11:19-20. This is clear above all from the calling of Paul, which God accomplished not without external exhortation and the word, although Paul refers all things wholly to the grace of God and its powerful virtue. By the grace of God I am what I am, 1 Corinthians 15:10. The Lord God has opened my ear, and I was not disobedient, I did not turn back, Isaiah 50:5. For the words that God, that is Christ, speaks are spirit and life, John 6:63. And the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, Hebrews 4:12.

units.la: LXII. Vocationis Divinae opus est 'Ava-
units.tr: LXII. The work of divine calling is 'Ava-

units.la: regeneratio seu deuteros genesis secunda quaedam generatio, & palingenesia iteratus velut exortus, nova nativitas. De eadem S. Petrus: Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, qui secundum multam misericordiam suam anagennesas hemas regeneravit nos ad spem vivam per resurrectionem Jesu Christi ex mortuis, 1. Pet. I. 3. Anagegennēmenoi, regeniti non ex semine corruptibili, sed incorruptibili, per sermonem vivum Dei & manentem in saeculum, ibid. v. 23. Et S. Paulus: Non ex operibus in justitia, quae feceramus nos, sed secundum misericordiam suam salvavit nos per lavacrum palingenesias regenerationis & anakainoseos renovationem Spiritus, Tit. III. 5. nisi forte in loco eo palingenesia iterata generatio, quippe distincta ab anakainosei renovatione Spiritus, qua ex morte peccatorum vivificamur, regeneramur, & novi homines velut ex Patre Coelesti, filii Dei vivi generamur, resurrectionem ex mortuis, quae nova quaedam nativitas in beatitudinem & gloriam coelestem, significat. Idem vero regenerationem hanc depositionem vetusti hominis, qui secundum concupiscentias deceptionis corrumpitur; renovationem, quae fit spiritu mentis, & induitionem novi hominis, qui secundum Deum in justitia & sanctitate veritatis creatus est, Ephes. IV. 22. 23. definit.
units.tr: regeneration, or deuteros genesis, a certain second generation, and palingenesia, as it were a repeated rising, a new birth. On this, St Peter says: Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has regenerated us [anagennēsas hēmas] to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, 1 Pet. 1:3. Having been born again [anagegennēmenoi], not of corruptible seed but of incorruptible, through the living word of God which abides for ever, ibid. v. 23. And St Paul: Not by works of righteousness which we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration [palingenesias] and the renewal of the Spirit [anakainoseōs], Titus 3:5. Unless perhaps in that place palingenesia means a repeated generation, distinct indeed from the renewal of the Spirit [anakainōsis], by which we are made alive from the death of sins; we are regenerated, and as new men are born, as it were, from the heavenly Father, sons of the living God, and this denotes a resurrection from the dead, a certain new birth into heavenly blessedness and glory. The same apostle defines this regeneration as the putting off of the old man, who is corrupted according to the lusts of deceit; the renewal which takes place in the spirit of the mind; and the putting on of the new man, who according to God is created in righteousness and holiness of truth, Eph. 4:22, 23.

units.la: LXIII. In regeneratione igitur hac tum palaios anthropos vetus homo, qualis ex Adamo, seu ex muliere nascitur, & ortu primo est, secundum concupiscentias deceptionis corruptus, qui & o exo anthropos exterior homo, 2. Cor. IV. 16. quia metropolin & arcem suam in carne seu membris corporis habet, Rom. VII. 5. 23. deponitur, & cum Christo ad abolitionem corporis peccati crucifigitur, quia ad abolitionem usque corporis ad concupiscendum tentantis proficit & Christi crucifixione procurata est, ibid. VI. 6. 12. tum kainos novus homo, & o esō interior, seu occultus homo cordis arcem & fontem novitatis in corde seu voluntate mente habens, ibid. VII. 22. 23. 2. Cor. IV. 16. induitur. Non quod depositio vetustatis assumptionem novitatis praecedat. Nam vetus homo nonnisi per calorem, odium nonnisi per amorem pellitur. Neque enim medius status datur. Nam quod quidam tepidi, nec frigidi, nec calidi, Apoc. III. 16. dicuntur, non medii regenitos inter & irregenitos, sed in sua vetustate diversi ab aliis intelliguntur, ut nempe nec aperte contrarii sint, nec integre & sincere cum Christo faciant, sed aliquid vetustatis deponant, aut potius similitudinem adversantium ex dictatu vetusti hominis deponant. Vetus enim homo varius & chamaeleonti similis est, cujus etiam non omnis mutatio in melius est, sed quandoque etiam in pejus. Nam & quandoque in novum hominem mutatus videtur, & tum eo magis in sua vetustate obfirmatur, & eo difficilius ad veram novitatem traducitur, velut quando oculos habet ad videndum, & non videt, Ezech. XII. 2. Ac multo minus Apostolus Rom. VII. 14. &c. de se, ceu irregenitum & regenitum inter, medio loquitur, cum se carnalem, sub peccato venditum quiritatur. Nam carnalem se appellat secundum naturam & reliquias pravitatis: venditum sub peccato, quia secundum residuam vetusti hominis carnem peccato ad finem vitae usque serviebat. Nam etiam a veteri servitute homini regenito pugna relicta est. Ideo emphatice S. Paulus dicit: Αὐτὸς ἐγὼ τῷ νοΐ μὲν δουλεύω νόμῳ Θεοῦ, τῇ δὲ σαρκὶ νόμῳ ἁμαρτίας. Ipse ego mente quidem servio legi Dei, carne vero legi peccati, ib. v.25. quasi diceret: Idem ego utrumque facio; & mente servio legi Dei, secundum novum hominem reliquum Christum agnosco Dominum, in eum credo, gestio esse servus justitiae ad gloriam Dei; carne vero peccato, litigo cum carne & lege, quae in membris stabulatur; secundum vetustum hominem, carnem adjacentem & captivum facere nitentem, servitutem peccati gemens dolensque patior. Tametsi vero status ejusmodi medius nullus datur, tamen prius deponere vetustum hominem jubemur, tum quia prius conspicitur depositio veteris hominis, quam novitatis assumptio, in perfectione quadam & operibus externis; tum quia studium hominis prius occupatur in extirpandis cogitationibus, desideriis, affectionibus & motibus vetustis, quam in exornatione & perfectione novi: tum denique quia ille terminus a quo, hic ad quem est.
units.tr: LXIII. In this regeneration, therefore, the old man [παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος], the man as he is born of Adam, or of a woman, and as he is in his first birth, corrupted according to the lusts of deceit, who is also the outward man [ὁ ἔξω ἄνθρωπος], 2 Cor. 4.16, because he has his capital and citadel in the flesh or the members of the body, Rom. 7.5, 23, is put off, and is crucified with Christ for the destruction of the body of sin, because the old man tends towards the destruction of the body, which tempts to lust, and this has been procured by the crucifixion of Christ, ibid. 6.6, 12. Then the new man [καινὸς ἄνθρωπος] and the inward [ὁ ἔσω] or hidden man, who has in the heart, that is, in the will and mind, the citadel and source of newness, ibid. 7.22, 23; 2 Cor. 4.16, is put on. Not that the putting off of the old state precedes the taking up of the new. For the old man is driven out only by warmth, and hatred only by love. Nor is there any middle state. For those who are called lukewarm, neither cold nor hot, Rev. 3.16, are not understood to be midway between the regenerate and the unregenerate, but they are understood to differ from others in their old state, namely that they are neither openly opposed to Christ nor serve him wholly and sincerely, but put off something of the old nature, or rather put off the likeness of the adversaries under the dictation of the old man. For the old man is changeable and like a chameleon, and not every change of his is for the better, but sometimes for the worse. Sometimes he seems to have been changed into the new man, and then he is all the more fixed in his old state, and is all the harder brought over to true newness, as when he has eyes to see and does not see, Ezek. 12.2. Much less does the Apostle, Rom. 7.14 and following, speak of himself as midway between the unregenerate and the regenerate, when he complains that he is carnal, sold under sin. For he calls himself carnal according to nature and the remnants of depravity; sold under sin, because according to the remaining flesh of the old man he was still serving sin until the end of his life. For even to the regenerate man the struggle with the old servitude is left. Therefore St Paul says emphatically: I myself with the mind serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin [Αὐτὸς ἐγὼ τῷ νοΐ μὲν δουλεύω νόμῳ Θεοῦ, τῇ δὲ σαρκὶ νόμῳ ἁμαρτίας], ibid. v. 25, as if he said: I myself do both things; with the mind I serve the law of God, and as the new man I acknowledge Christ as Lord, believe in him, and rejoice to be a servant of righteousness to the glory of God; but with the flesh I serve sin, I struggle with the flesh and the law which dwells in my members; according to the old man, I groan and grieve, suffering the servitude of sin, which the flesh clinging to me strives to make me captive. Although, indeed, no such middle state is given, yet we are commanded first to put off the old man, both because the putting off of the old man is seen before the putting on of newness, in a certain perfection and external works; and because the zeal of a man is first occupied in rooting out old thoughts, desires, affections and motions, before it is occupied in adorning and perfecting the new; and finally because the former is the starting point, and the latter the goal.

units.la: LXIV. Vetustus homo in regeneratione exuendus in utraque parte; anima & corpore locum habet. Nam vetustas illa in vana cogitatione & delectatione, nec non in actione secundum eandem, sive ea prohibita, sive jussa quidem, at non ex recto corde facta sit; constitit. Ejus typus est in πρότερον ἀναστροφὴν priore conversatione, Ephes. IV.22. In eo enim, quod prius fuimus, cernere est, quid sit veteris hominis; nempe, non cognoscere, quaerere verum Deum, ut summum bonum, falsas de Deo sententias habere, ab eo aversum esse; corrumpi secundum concupiscentias deceptionis, hoc est, per concupiscentiam ad falsa bona stimulantem, a rectitudine & sanctitate, in qua a Deo creati sumus, deficere. Sic vero vetustus ille homo totus deponendus nobis est, ut renovemur spiritu mentis, hoc est, in mentem nostram alium spiritum recipiamus, vel recipiamus Spiritum S. qui facit aliam mentem, sensum, studium, nempe τὸν Κυρίου, Χριστοῦ mentem Domini, Christi, 1. Cor. II.16. seu cogitationes & voluntatem similem cogitationibus & voluntati Christi; & ut induamus novum hominem, qui secundum Deum in justitia & sanctitate veritatis creatus est, Ephes. IV.23.24. Sicut autem vetustus ille homo omnes partes hominis irregeniti; ita novus omnes partes hominis regeniti complectitur. Licet enim novitas illa sit ἔσω interior & νοὸς mentis, tamen & etiam proficit, ut homo etiam vera loquatur ore, & confiteatur sua peccata, atque ea abneget, & ab iis faciendis desistat, & recta Deoque placentia faciat. Veteri enim homini tributa φθορὰ corruptio, quia in toto homine, & utraque ejus parte obtinet: Novo emendatio illius corruptionis & novitas, quae in utraque etiam ejus parte residet. Nam sanctificatio est hominis ὁλοπλὴς totius, puta ὁλοκληρῳ πνεύματι, ψυχῇ καὶ σώματι integri spiritus, animae & corporis, 1. Thess. V.23. Ejus novitatis ibidem Apostolus ponit tum ἁγιασμὸν, quod sit τῷ Θεῷ secundum Deum, hoc est, secundum imaginem Dei, restitutam puta; & quidem in justitia, quae jus filiorum Dei in Christo per fidem justificatorum, & in spe gloriae Dei gloriantium est; & sanctitate veritatis, seu rectitudine cogitationum, verborum & factorum veritati congruente: tum causam & originem, quae non humana, sed Dei κτίσις creatoris virtus & potentia est, quia homo novus secundum Deum κτίσθη creatus est. Nam partim in Christo nobis parta est & parata renovatio nostra; partim illa e Spiritus S. potentia & ἐνέργεια procedit: partim ante secula & jacta mundi fundamenta vocati sumus, ut illa, quae non sunt, a Deo vocantur, & mortui excitantur, Rom. IV.17.
units.tr: LXIV. The old man must be put off in regeneration in both parts, in soul and in body. For that old state consists in vain thought and delight, and also in action according to these, whether the action is forbidden, or indeed commanded but not done from a right heart. Its type is the former conversation [πρότερον ἀναστροφήν], Eph. 4.22. For in what we were before, we can see what the old man is: namely, not to know, nor to seek the true God as the highest good, to hold false opinions about God, to be turned away from him, to be corrupted according to the lusts of deceit, that is, through a desire that stirs us to false goods, to fall away from the uprightness and holiness in which we were created by God. Thus that old man must be put off entirely by us, that we may be renewed in the spirit of the mind, that is, that we may receive another spirit into our mind, or receive the Holy Spirit, who makes another mind, sense and zeal, namely the mind of the Lord, of Christ [τὸν Κυρίου, Χριστοῦ], 1 Cor. 2.16; or thoughts and a will similar to the thoughts and will of Christ; and that we may put on the new man, who after God is created in righteousness and holiness of truth, Eph. 4.23, 24. And just as the old man embraces all parts of the unregenerate man, so the new man embraces all parts of the regenerate man. For although that newness is inward [ἔσω] and of the mind [νοὸς], nevertheless it also works so that the man speaks true things with his mouth, confesses his sins, renounces them, desists from doing them, and does what is right and pleasing to God. For to the old man is ascribed corruption [φθορά], because it holds in the whole man and in both parts of him; to the new is ascribed the amendment and newness of that corruption, which also remains in both parts of him. For sanctification is of the whole man, that is, of the entire spirit, soul and body [ὁλοκληρῳ πνεύματι, ψυχῇ καὶ σώματι], 1 Thess. 5.23. In the same place the Apostle sets forth the holiness [ἁγιασμόν] of this newness, which is to God [τῷ Θεῷ], that is, according to the image of God, namely restored; and indeed in righteousness, which is the right of the sons of God, of those justified in Christ through faith, and who glory in the hope of the glory of God; and in holiness of truth, that is, in uprightness of thoughts, words and deeds agreeing with truth. Then there is the cause and origin, which is not human but the power and efficacy of God the Creator [κτίσις], because the new man was created [κτίσθη] according to God. For our renewal is partly acquired and prepared for us in Christ, partly it proceeds from the power and working [ἐνέργεια] of the Holy Spirit; and partly we were called before the ages and before the foundations of the world were laid, as God calls those things which are not as though they were, and raises the dead, Rom. 4.17.

units.la: LXV. Sed regenerationis causas illas & principia distinctius Christus ipse Nicodemo exposuit.
units.tr: LXV. But Christ himself set out the causes and principles of regeneration more distinctly to Nicodemus.

units.la: Postquam enim regenerationis necessitatem his verbis exposuit: Amen, Amen dico tibi ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν. Nisi quis nascatur desuper, non potest videre Regnum Dei, Joh. III. 3. Quaerenti Nicodemo: Quomodo homo potest nasci, qui senex est? Numquid potest in uterum matris suae iterum intrare & nasci? v.4. Christus respondit: Amen, Amen dico tibi; Nisi quis nascatur ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest intrare in Regnum Dei. v.5. Ubi regenerationis causas, Aquam & Spiritum ponit. Aquae vero nomine non intelligit vel Baptismum, tum quia ille non est causa regenerationis ex opere operato, sed signaculum regenerationis & communionis Regni Dei, & quatenus praedicatur, una cum verbo Dei medium morale regenerationis intellectum docendo, & voluntatem svadendo mutantis; quae ipsa mutatio regenerationis effectus est: tum quia impossibile non est, ut sine Baptismo aliquis regeneretur, & Regnum Coelorum intret: tum quia eo tempore, quo Christus loquebatur, doctor aliquis Israelis, qualis Nicodemus fuit, facile eum ignorare potuit sine culpa, qualem Christus Nicodemo v.10. exprobrat: vel ipsum Spiritum S. qui aquae purificantis rationem habet, usitata quadam hendyade, ut ita copulativa καὶ ponatur pro τουτέστιν hoc est, quomodo etiam Matth. III.11, ponitur, quia non solus utique Spiritus S. causa regenerationis est, sed aliud etiam, quod aquae nomine venit, meritum nempe obedientia, δικαίωμα & sanguis Christi, qui propter puritatem & purificandi vim aquae nomine, Hebr. X.22.23. 1. Joh. V.8. venit, & tum per aquam foeditatis, ad purificandam foeditatem ejus, qui morticinum vel cadaver attrectavit, Num.XIX.2. &c. aliasque lotiones adumbrata: tum disertè promissa & praedicta ab ipso Deo est, dicente: Et fundam super vos aquas mundas, & purificabimini ab omnibus impuritatibus vestris, & ab omnibus stercoribus vestris purificabo vos. Ezech. XXXVI.25. quae verba sic Jonathan Paraphrastes explicat Peccata vestra vobis remittam, sicut quis aqua aspersionis, & cinere vaccae rufae, quae pro peccato offertur, purificatur; & ab omnibus sordibus vestris purificabimini. Hanc ex aqua spirituali obedientiae & sanguinis Christi regenerationem mox v.13.14.&c. ipse Christus explicat, necessitatem sui descensus ex Coelo, & exaltationis suae in cruce, traditionisque in mortem pro mundo, ut omnis, qui in eum credit, habeat vitam aeternam, fusius demonstrans. Quod vero Christi mors & obedientia regenerationis hominis in filium Dei causa sit, patet, quia Christo data est haereditas & Regnum, & Deus salvandos in ipso elegit; neque
units.tr: For after he had stated the necessity of regeneration in these words, Truly, truly I say to you, unless someone is born anew [ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν]. Unless someone is born from above, he cannot see the Kingdom of God, John 3:3, and when Nicodemus asked, How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter his mother's womb again and be born? v. 4, Christ answered, Truly, truly I say to you, unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the Kingdom of God, v. 5. Here he names the causes of regeneration: water and Spirit. By the word water he understands neither Baptism (first, because Baptism is not a cause of regeneration by the work done, but a seal of regeneration and of communion in the Kingdom of God, and, insofar as it is preached together with the Word of God, a moral means of regeneration, teaching the understanding and persuading the will to change, and that change itself is the effect of regeneration; second, because it is not impossible that someone should be regenerated and enter the Kingdom of heaven without Baptism; third, because at the time when Christ was speaking, a teacher of Israel such as Nicodemus was could easily be ignorant of this without fault, which is what Christ reproaches Nicodemus for in v. 10). Nor does he mean the Spirit S. alone, which has the force of purifying water, by a common hendiadys, so that the copulative καὶ is put for τουτέστιν, that is, "and" means "that is," as is also the case in Matt. 3:11. For the Spirit is certainly not the sole cause of regeneration; there is also something else that comes under the name of water, namely the merit of obedience, δικαίωμα, and the blood of Christ, which, on account of its purity and its power to cleanse, comes under the name of water (Heb. 10:22, 23; 1 John 5:8), and which was foreshadowed by the water of impurity, used to cleanse the defilement of one who had touched a corpse (Num. 19:2, etc.) and by other washings. It is also expressly promised and foretold by God himself, who says, And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your impurities, and from all your filthy idols I will cleanse you (Ezek. 36:25). Jonathan the Paraphrast explains these words thus: I will forgive your sins, just as one is purified by the water of sprinkling and by the ashes of the red heifer, which is offered for sin; and you shall be cleansed from all your filth. Christ himself then explains this regeneration from the spiritual water of obedience and the blood of Christ in what follows, v. 13, 14, etc., setting out at length the necessity of his descent from heaven, of his exaltation on the cross, and of his being handed over to death for the world, so that everyone who believes in him may have eternal life. That the death and obedience of Christ are the cause of the regeneration of a man into a son of God is plain, because the inheritance and the Kingdom were given to Christ, and God chose those to be saved in him; nor could he die in vain, and he had the right to ask for the inheritance which God had decreed for him (Ps. 2:8), and by his merit he received gifts among men (ibid. 68:19). Hence in v. 17 he is said to have been handed over to death so that he might be saved through him; and to him, who sets his soul as the price of satisfaction, it is promised that he shall see the Seed (Isa. 53:10), that is, that for his death the Seed of God is to be begotten or regenerated, to whom the soul of the righteous servant of God will give the ransom acquired for sins. Thus the regeneration of Christ follows his pledge, his satisfaction, and his intercession or request; nor could regeneration in any way take place without such purifying water. For if the setting down of his soul as a ransom is the condition on which God sees the Seed, that is, has sons, then surely the ransom and righteousness, that is, obedience, which has the force of merit, is the cause of regeneration, since through it the sons of God are redeemed. For this reason Christ died, that he might gather together into one the scattered children of God (that is, those to whom adoption was destined), John 11:52, and that he might purify for himself a people, Titus 2:14. Indeed we were chosen in him so that we might be holy, such as we become through regeneration, Eph. 1:4. Of this we have also said more above, in §25.

units.la: {a} Regeneratio causas & principia Christus. ille frustra mori potuit; & jus ille habuit postu-landi hæreditatem, quam Deus ipsi decrevit, Psal. II. 8. & merito suo dona in hominibus acce-pit, ibid. LXVIII. 19. Unde v. 17. in mortem traditus dicitur, ut per ipsum servetur; & eidem animam pretium satisfactionis ponenti promittitur, quòd visurus sit Semen, Esaj. LIII. 10. hoc est, quòd propter mortem ejus generandum vel regenerandum sit Semen Dei, cui anima justi servi Dei. λύτρον pro peccatis acquisitum donatura & appositura sit. Sic regeneratio Christi sponsionem, satisfactionem & postulationem seu intercessionem sequitur: nec sine ejusmodi aqua purificante omnino regeneratio fieri potuit. Si enim à positione animæ ceu λύτρον pendet, ut Deus videat Semen, sive habeat filios, utique λύτρον & δικαίωμα seu obedientia, quæ vim meriti habet, causa est regenerationis, utpote per quam redempti filii Dei sunt. Ideò Christus mortuus est, ut filios Dei dispersos (seu eos, quibus υἱοθεσία adoptio destinata erat) in unum colligeret, Joh. XI. 52. & sibi purificaret populum, Tit. II. 14. quin & in eodem electi sumus, ut essemus sancti, quales per regenerationem fimus, Ephes. I. 4. de quo etiam plura supra §. XXV. diximus.
units.tr: {a} Regeneration: the causes and principles of Christ. He could not die in vain, and he had the right to ask for the inheritance which God had decreed for him, Ps. 2:8, and by his merit he received gifts among men, ibid. 68:19. Hence in v. 17 he is said to have been handed over to death so that he might be saved through him; and to him, who sets his soul as the price of satisfaction, it is promised that he shall see Semen, Isa. 53:10, that is, that on account of his death the Seed of God is to be begotten or regenerated, to whom the soul of the righteous servant of God will give the ransom acquired for sins. Thus the regeneration of Christ follows his pledge, his satisfaction, and his postulation or intercession; nor could regeneration in any way take place without such purifying water. For if the setting down of the soul as a ransom is the condition on which God sees the Seed, that is, has sons, then the ransom and the righteousness, that is, obedience, which has the force of merit, is surely the cause of regeneration, since through it the sons of God are redeemed. Christ died for this reason, that he might gather into one the scattered children of God (that is, those for whom adoption was destined), John 11:52, and that he might purify for himself a people, Titus 2:14. Indeed we were chosen in him so that we might be holy, such as we become through regeneration, Eph. 1:4. Of this we have also spoken more fully above, §25.

units.la: LXVI. Alterum regenerationis principium Christus facit Spiritum Dei. Non quòd regeneratio sit propria actio & efficientia Spiritus S. sed quia illa œconomicè ei appropriatur, & illis, qui regenerantur, Spiritus S. datur; ut in illis sit, & maneat, sicut pars substantiæ parentum manet in filiis. De eo etiam eadem promissio qua aquæ puræ promittuntur, statim sic loquitur: Et dabo vobis cor novum, & auferam cor lapideum, & dabo vobis cor carneum &c. Et Spiritum meum ponam in medio vestri, & faciam ut in definitionibus meis ambuletis, & judicia mea observetis, Ezech. XXXVI. 25. 26. 27. Nam cor lapideum auferre, & novum & carnale dare, quod in regeneratione fit, nisi Spiritus Dei omnipotens non potest. Animalis enim homo non recipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, 1. Cor. II. 14. Et necessitatem Spiritus S. ad regenerationem Christus ipse Nicodemo explicat & probat Joh. III. 6-13. ante omnia quidem ex anthithesi & comparatione generationis ex carne & Spiritu, dicens: Quod natum est ex carne, caro est: & quod natum est ex Spiritu, spiritus est, v. 6. q. d. qui ex homine carnali genitus est, ipse quoque carnalis, non spiritualis est, quia ψυχικοὶ animales, carnales non habent spiritum, Judæ v. 19. Cúmque ad Regnum Dei videndum, & in illud intrandum necesse sit, ut homo non caro, sed spiritus sit, quia Regnum Dei non perinde ut humanum aliquod, in quo populus Regem videt, sicut ovis pastorem, oculis videri carnalibus & πνευματικῶς observari potest, cùm in eo Deus ut Rex, & nominis ejus excellentia, & bona spiritualia, & cives ejusdem nonnisi mente & spiritu rectè cognoscantur; Spiritus porro, seu, ut homo spiritualis sit, nonnisi ex Spiritu generetur sicut caro ex carne nascitur; consequens planè est, ut regeneratio, seu hominis spiritualis generatio ex Spiritu fiat. Generationem verò ejusmodi non carnali, sed spirituali modo, adeóque per Spiritum S. succedere, statim docet, cùm generationem hanc, facili & obvio emblemate motus & operationis venti adumbrat. Ne mireris, ait, quòd dixi tibi: oportet vos nasci rursus. Spiritus quò vult spirat, & vocem ejus audis, sed nescis unde veniat, & quò vadat. Ita est omnis, qui natus est ex spiritu. v. 7. 8. Sicut igitur ventus flat, quò vult, & qui sonum ejus audit, nescit, unde veniat, & quò vadat; seu in qua regione priùs flaverit, & ad quam proficiscatur, neque adeò potestatem eum adducendi, retinendi & dimittendi habet: ita operatio illa Spiritus S. qua is novum hominem facit, intellectum illuminat, cor sanctificat, sic eum afficit, ut nesciat, quando Spiritus S. venturus sit, neque ipse eum prior excitet, advocet, adducat, neque sciat, quousque operationem suam extensurus sit, neque omnino eum in sua potestate habeat. Quo emblemate genitura illa spiritualis pulcherrimè explicatur. Sicut enim naturalis generatio à voluntate ejus, qui generat, non ejus, qui generatur, & se generari nescit, pendet: ita, qui à Deo per Spiritum S. regeneratur & renovatur, id soli gratiæ Dei acceptum referre in solidum debet. Nam vivere incipit, antequam de vita cogitaverit, vel ad vitam se præparaverit, & nescit, quos porro Deus generet, & quid Spiritus Dei in reliquo mundo, & se ipso etiam operaturus sit. Stupenti ad hæc Nicodemo, & à Christo reprehenso, quòd doctor Israelis talia ignorare non dubitaverit, novo argumento necessitatem regenerationis ex aqua & Spiritu Christus comprobat, dicens: Amen, Amen dico tibi; quod novimus, loquimur, & quod vidimus, testamur: & testimonium nostrum non accipitis. Si terrestria dixi vobis, & non creditis; quomodo, si dixero vobis cœlestia, credetis? v. 10. 11. 12. quasi diceret: Deus non tantùm per Spiritum suum olim locutus est per Prophetas, sed etiam nunc loquitur per me: qui homines per Spiritum meum regenerabo & vivificabo, ut Regnum Dei videant, & in illud intrent. Uterque propria, certa & comperta loquimur, quæ tam certò novimus, quàm Spiritus hominis novit, quid sit in corde suo; & quæ sic Dei sunt, ut etiam nostra sint, quia illa vidimus. Cùm ergo duos hos testes indicésque habeatis, vestrum erat nôsse, quòd Regnum Dei, in quo Deus suum & Filii sui Spiritum effusurus erat, præforibus sit. Sed vos carnales, inepti ad videndum Regnum Cœlorum, cùm ne terrestria quidem, ex quibus tamen cœlestia pendent, puta ea, quæ in terra geruntur, utpote in qua ex aqua & Spiritu homines generantur, Regnum Dei videtur & recipitur, intelligatis: multò minùs, si vobis cœlestia, seu consummationem salutis in Cœlo, expósuero, intelligetis.
units.tr: LXVI. Christ makes the Spirit of God the second principle of regeneration. Not that regeneration is the proper action and efficacy of the Holy Spirit, but because it is attributed to him in the economy, and the Holy Spirit is given to those who are regenerated, so that he may be in them and remain, just as a part of the substance of the parents remains in the children. Concerning him, the same promise by which clean water is promised speaks in the same way at once: And I will give you a new heart, and will take away the stony heart, and will give you a heart of flesh, etc. And I will put my Spirit in the midst of you, and will make you walk in my statutes, and keep my judgments (Ezek. 36:25–27). For to take away the stony heart and to give a new and fleshly heart, which takes place in regeneration, cannot be done except by the almighty Spirit of God. For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14). And Christ himself explains and proves to Nicodemus the necessity of the Holy Spirit for regeneration (John 3:6–13), chiefly first from the contrast and comparison between generation from flesh and from Spirit, saying: That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit (v. 6); that is to say, whoever is begotten of a carnal man is himself also carnal, not spiritual, since the natural (ψυχικοί) men, the carnal, do not have the Spirit (Jude 19). And since in order to see the Kingdom of God, and to enter it, a man must be not flesh but spirit, because the Kingdom of God cannot be seen with carnal eyes, nor observed spiritually (πνευματικῶς) in the way that some human kingdom can be observed, where the people see the king as sheep see the shepherd, since in it God is known as King, with the excellence of his name, the spiritual goods, and his citizens, only rightly by mind and spirit; and since the Spirit, or, that a man may be spiritual, is only begotten of the Spirit as flesh is born of flesh, it follows plainly that regeneration, or the spiritual generation of man, takes place from the Spirit. That this generation takes place not in a carnal but in a spiritual manner, and so through the Holy Spirit, he teaches immediately, when he shadows forth this generation by an easy and obvious image of the motion and operation of the wind: Do not wonder, he says, that I said to you, you must be born again. The Spirit blows where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit (v. 7, 8). Just as the wind blows where it wills, and he who hears its sound does not know where it comes from or where it goes, or in what region it first blew and whither it is going, and has no power to bring it, hold it, or let it go, so that operation of the Holy Spirit by which he makes a new man, illuminates the understanding, sanctifies the heart, and affects him in such a way, does not know when the Holy Spirit will come, and neither does he himself rouse, summon, or lead him first, nor does he know how far his operation will extend, and he does not in any way have him in his power. By this image that spiritual begetting is most beautifully explained. For just as natural generation depends on the will of the one who begets, not of the one who is begotten, who does not know that he is being begotten, so he who is regenerated and renewed by God through the Holy Spirit must fully ascribe this to the grace of God alone. For he begins to live before he has thought about life or prepared himself for life, and he does not know what further God will beget, or what the Spirit of God will still work in the rest of the world and in himself. Nicodemus was astonished at these things, and was rebuked by Christ for not hesitating to be ignorant of such things as a teacher of Israel. Christ confirms the necessity of regeneration from water and Spirit with a new argument, saying: Truly, truly I say to you, we speak what we know, and testify to what we have seen; and you do not receive our testimony. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? (v. 10–12). As if he were saying: God not only spoke of old through his Spirit by the prophets, but even now speaks through me, who will regenerate and vivify men by my Spirit, so that they may see the Kingdom of God and enter into it. We speak of things that are our own, certain and known, which we know as surely as the spirit of a man knows what is in his own heart; and which are so of God that they are also ours, because we have seen them. Since then you have these two witnesses and indicators, it was your duty to know that the Kingdom of God, in which God was to pour out his Spirit and the Spirit of his Son, is at hand. But you, carnal, unfit to see the Kingdom of heaven, since you cannot even understand earthly things, from which the heavenly depend, namely those things that happen on earth, as in it men are begotten from water and Spirit, and the Kingdom of God is seen and received: much less will you understand if I set out to you heavenly things, that is, the consummation of salvation in heaven.

units.la: LXVII. Generatio naturalis fit ex sanguinibus, voluntate carnis, & voluntate viri, Joh. I. 13. Quæ proin non potest esse ad rectitudinem, sapientiam & lucem, sed ad tenebras, caliginem cor cupiditatibus corruptum, audax ad ea, quæ non novit, blaiphemandum, & quæ Spiritus S. sunt, irridendum. Non talis regeneratio est. Licèt enim filii Dei etiam Semen mulieris & filii Abrahami dicantur, tamen eorum regeneratio non à mulieris vel Abrahami fœcunditate, vel eorum carne, voluntate & sanguine, sed à promissione Dei, & exemplo fidei, ceu semine quodam, originem habet. De promissione sic Apostolus: Nos verò, fratres, secundum
units.tr: LXVII. Natural generation comes about "from bloods, from the will of the flesh, and from the will of man" (John 1:13). Therefore it cannot lead to uprightness, wisdom and light, but only to darkness and dimness. It produces a heart corrupted by desires, bold to blaspheme what it does not know and to mock what belongs to the Holy Spirit. Such is not regeneration. For although the sons of God are also called "the seed of the woman" and "the sons of Abraham," their regeneration does not arise from the fertility of woman or Abraham, nor from their flesh, will and blood, but from the promise of God and the example of faith, as from a certain seed. Concerning the promise, the Apostle speaks thus: But we, brethren, according to

units.la: Non ex sanguine & voluntate carnis, sed ex Semine verbi Dei, & exemplo fidei succedit. dum Ifacum, ἐπαγγελίας τέκνα promissionis filii sumus, Gal. IV.28. Ut firma sit promissio omni Semini, non ex Lege tantùm, sed etiam ex fide Abrahami, qui est Pater omnium nostrûm, sicut scriptum est: Quoniam Patrem multarum gentium dedite, Rom.IV.16.17. De fidei exemplo idem: Abraham accepit sigillum justitiæ fidei in præputio, ut esset pater omnium credentium in præputio, ut iis imputaretur justitia; & pater circumcisionis non tantùm iis, qui ex circumcisione essent, sed iis etiam, qui incederent vestigiis fidei, quæ fuit in præputio Patris nostri Abrahami, ib. v. 11. 12. Hunc locum in paternitate filiorum Dei unà cum Abrahamo habent omnes fideles, tum quia spem habent proventus & generationis filiorum Dei: tum quia fide sua & bonis operibus prælucent. Habent enim etiam fideles singuli aliquid, quod in regeneratione aliorum filiorum Seminis instar est, velut confessionem verbi, & spei suæ in omni honestate, charitate & patientia. Unde S. Paulus dicit, se ὠδίνειν parturire Galatas, Gal. IV. 19. Et qui alios ad Christum adducunt, Patres in Christo Jesu per Evangelium generantes 1. Cor. IV. 15. dicuntur. Etiam præcedens Ecclesia sequentis quodammodo mater est; quia verbum illud, per quod homines carnales regenerantur, & filii Dei fiunt, in ore piorum est; & iidem in nomine Dei hominibus, ut cum Deo reconcilientur, suadent, 2. Cor. V. 20.
units.tr: Not from blood and the will of the flesh, but from the seed of the word of God and by the example of faith, it comes about that, as Isaac was, we are "children of promise" [ἐπαγγελίας τέκνα], the sons of promise (Gal. 4:28). The promise is made firm for all the seed, not only from the Law but also from the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all, as it is written: "For I have made you the father of many nations" (Rom. 4:16–17). On the example of faith, the same Apostle says: Abraham received the sign of the righteousness of faith while still uncircumcised, so that he might be the father of all who believe though uncircumcised, that righteousness might be imputed to them; and the father of circumcision, not only to those who are of the circumcision, but also to those who follow in the steps of the faith which our father Abraham had while uncircumcised (ibid. vv. 11, 12). All the faithful have a share in this fatherhood of the sons of God, together with Abraham, both because they hope for the offspring and generation of the sons of God, and because they shine forth by their faith and good works. Indeed, each of the faithful also has something which is like a seed in the regeneration of other sons, namely the confession of the word, and of their hope, in all honesty, love and patience. Hence St Paul says that he is in travail [ὠδίνειν] for the Galatians (Gal. 4:19). And those who bring others to Christ are called fathers begetting in Christ Jesus through the Gospel (1 Cor. 4:15). Also the earlier Church is in some sense the mother of the later one, because that word through which carnal men are regenerated and made sons of God is in the mouth of the godly, and they, in the name of God, urge men to be reconciled to God (2 Cor. 5:20).

units.la: LXVIII. Proprie igitur semen regenerationis est verbum promissionis seu Evangelii, per quod, ceu organon regenerationis solum Deus, & exemplo fidei suæ etiam homines alios regenerant. De quo sic S. Petrus: Regeniti sumus non ex semine corruptibili, sed incorruptibili, per sermonem vivum Dei & manentem in seculum; quia omnis caro est velut gramen &c. Verbum autem Domini manet in seculum. Hoc vero est verbum, quod evangelizatum est ad vos, 1. Petr. I. 23. &c. Semen proprie est, unde fœtus est; velut novus homo, filius Dei. Semen φθαρτὸν corruptibile est, ex quo qui nascitur, non perpetuò vivit; ἄφθαρτον incorruptibile, ex quo qui nascitur, perpetuò vivit, quôdque immortalitatis causa est. Tale regenerationis semen S. Petrus facit λόγον ζῶντος Θεοῦ καὶ μένοντος εἰς αἰῶνα, sermonem viventem Dei, & manentem in æternum, hoc est, sermonem talem, qui auditus & admissus efficax est ad generandam ἐλπίδα ζῶσαν spem vivam, non languidam & infirmam, sed cum παῤῥησίᾳ certa fiducia conjunctam, & non pudefacientem, sed semper exhilarantem, quæ non intermoritur, sed semper renovatur & refocillatur, & in eo, qui eam habet, manet, quia est semen Dei vivi & in æternum manentis. Semen Dei manet in ipso, 1. Joh. III. 9. De quo etiam S. Jacobus: Βουληθεὶς ἀπεκύησέν ἡμᾶς λόγῳ ἀληθείας volens (secundum εὐδοκίαν beneplacitum, quod propositum in se ipso, Ephes. I. 9. 11.) genuit nos sermone veritatis, Jac. I. 18. Sermo ille vivus Dei, & manens in æternum; sermo veritatis, ab eodem Petro v. 25. explicatur τὸ ῥῆμα τὸ εὐαγγελισθὲν verbum, quod evangelizatum est, hoc est, quo annuntiatum est, quòd Jesus sit Christus, cui Deus populum dedit, quem à peccatis salvaret, & sibi purificaret, cum præcepto fidei ad spem vivam, & amoris, ad amandum Christum, sicut ab eodem dilecti sumus. In hoc enim solo verbo proponitur,
units.tr: LXVIII. Properly, therefore, the seed of regeneration is the word of promise or the Gospel, through which God alone, as the instrument of regeneration, and also men by the example of their own faith, regenerate others. On this St Peter says: We have been born again not of corruptible seed but of incorruptible, through the living word of God which abides for ever; for all flesh is like grass, etc. But the word of the Lord abides for ever. "And this is the word which has been preached to you" (1 Pet. 1:23, etc.). A seed is properly that from which an offspring comes, like a new man, a son of God. A corruptible seed [φθαρτὸν] is one from which what is born does not live for ever; an incorruptible seed [ἄφθαρτον] is one from which what is born lives for ever, and which is the cause of immortality. St Peter calls such a seed of regeneration "the living word of God and abiding for ever" [λόγον ζῶντος Θεοῦ καὶ μένοντος εἰς αἰῶνα]: that is, a word which, when heard and received, is effective in generating a living hope [ἐλπίδα ζῶσαν], not weak and feeble, but joined with a sure confidence [παῤῥησίᾳ], not shaming but always cheering, which does not die out but is always renewed and revived, and remains in the one who has it, because it is the seed of the living God, who abides for ever. "His seed abides in him" (1 John 3:9). Of this the Apostle James also says: Willing [Βουληθεὶς], he brought us forth by the word of truth (James 1:18). He wills according to his good pleasure [εὐδοκίαν], which he purposed in himself (Eph. 1:9, 11). That living word of God, abiding for ever, which is the word of truth, is explained by the same Peter in v. 25 as the word which has been preached as good news [τὸ ῥῆμα τὸ εὐαγγελισθὲν], that is, the word by which it is announced that Jesus is the Christ, whom God gave to the people, to save them from their sins and to purify them for himself, with the command of faith to a living hope and of love, so that they might love Christ, as they are loved by him. For in this word alone is set forth

units.la: quid de Deo credendum sit, quo credito is glorificetur, & per quid homo ad amandum Deum, eique obediendum moveatur, ut sic, mutato corde & affectu, nova creatura & filius Dei fiat.
units.tr: what is to be believed about God, by believing which he is glorified, and through which man is moved to love God and to obey him, so that, with his heart and affections changed, he becomes a new creature and a son of God.

units.la: LXIX. Cùm tamen amabilis licèt ille & suavissimus Evangelii sermo ab homine animali, & Spiritu Dei carente non recipiatur, imò ei sit odor mortis ad mortem, 2. Cor. II. 16. manifestum est, verbum illud bonum auribus oblatum & inculcatum, imò quandoque cum gaudio etiam auditum, Hebr. VI. 5. ad regenerationem non sufficere, sed ultra ad eam requiri gratiam Spiritus S. qui semini incrementum det; imò creationem novi cordis & novi Spiritus, novæ & sanctæ cogitationis & voluntatis, Ezech. XXXVI. 26. Psal. LI. 12. Deus enim respiscentiam dat ad vitam, Act. XI. 18. creat in Christo Jesu, Ephes. II. 10. IV. 24. Col. III. 10. Vivificat ex præputio carnis, ibid. II. 13. fidem, timorem, amorem Dei donat; à quibus donis etiam Spiritus fidei, amoris & timoris Dei, Esaj. XI. 2. Zach. XII. 10. 1. Cor. XII. 9. 2. Cor. IV. 13. 2. Tim. I. 7. appellatur. Sicut nempe generatio hominis non est sine creatione, atque idem homo, qui parentum generatione productus est, Dei etiam vocantis generationes ab initio, Esaj. XLI. 4. creatione formatur: ita cum generatione supernaturali seu regeneratione Divina creatio concurrit. Denique sicut בעל maritus Ecclesiæ Deus, Christus, ὁ ἔχων νύμφιον qui sponsam habet, sponsus, Joh. III. 29. qui eam imprægnat, hoc est, semen filiorum Dei ipsi committit, ejusdem etiam ποιητὴς factor est, Esaj. LIV. 5. ita quorum Pater Deus est, eorundem creator est. An ego venire faciam ad partum, & non gignam, dixit Jehova? An ego, qui is sum, qui gignit, continebo me, quò minus pariam, dixit Dominus, ibid. LXVI. 9. Non tantùm ergo adjuvat partum parturientis, sed ipse etiam parit, semen suum in illis, qui de Deo non cogitaverant, ponit, ex quo in novos homines renascantur.
units.tr: LXIX. Although this lovely and most sweet word of the Gospel is not received by the natural man who lacks the Spirit of God, but is rather to him a smell of death unto death (2 Cor. 2:16), it is nevertheless plain that that good word offered to the ears and inculcated, and sometimes even heard with joy (Heb. 6:5), does not suffice for regeneration. Beyond it, the grace of the Holy Spirit is required, who gives increase to the seed, indeed the creation of a new heart and a new spirit, of new and holy thought and will (Ezek. 36:26; Ps. 51:12). For God gives repentance unto life (Acts 11:18), creates [us] in Christ Jesus (Eph. 2:10; 4:24; Col. 3:10), quickens [us] from the uncircumcision of the flesh (Col. 2:13), and bestows faith, fear and love of God. From these gifts the Spirit is also called the Spirit of faith, of love and of the fear of God (Isa. 11:2; Zech. 12:10; 1 Cor. 12:9; 2 Cor. 4:13; 2 Tim. 1:7). Just as the generation of a man is not without creation, and the same man who is produced by the generation of parents is formed by creation, as God is "calling the generations from the beginning" (Isa. 41:4), so a divine creation goes along with supernatural generation, that is, with regeneration. Finally, just as God, Christ, is the husband [בעל] of the Church, he who has the bride, the bridegroom (John 3:29), who makes her pregnant, that is, who entrusts to her the seed of the sons of God, and is also her maker [ποιητής] (Isa. 54:5), so the one whose Father is God is also his creature. "Shall I bring to the birth and not cause to bear? says the LORD. Shall I who cause to bring forth shut the womb? says your God" (Isa. 66:9). Therefore he not only helps the travail of the one in labour, but he himself also gives birth, placing his seed in those who had not thought of God, from which they are born again as new men.

units.la: LXX. Quæ vocationis Divinæ per verbum & Spiritum, eadem regenerationis ratio est. Nam Deus per verbum & Spiritum vocando regenerat. Sicut igitur vocatio, ita etiam regeneratio virtute Dei omnipotente, & omnipotenter agente, certissimumque succesfsum habente procedit. An enim, qui parere facit, non gignet? Esaj. LXVI. 9. Neque homo naturalis eam voluntate sua vel promovere, vel sufflaminare potis est. Spiritus S. enim regenerans vento similis est, ac proin, qui ex eo nascitur, natus quidem jam ejus operationem sentit, at dum nascitur, unde veniat, & quò vadat, ignorat, Joh. III. 8. tantum abest, ut ad regenerationem suam quicquam ipse conferat. Non enim homo, sed Deus βουληθεὶς volens solo beneplacito suo, secundum æternum propositum ἀπεκύησε gignit per semen verbi veritatis, Jac. I. 18. Homo dum generatur, intelligit & vult, sed naturalia, non spiritualia; quæ genitus demum, voluntate à peccati servitute liberata, velle incipit. Proin nec plus etiam in homine est, quo regenerationem suam adjuvet, quàm in eodem est, quo generationem suam promoveat. Licèt enim in iis, quos Deus regenerare vult, in antecessum Deus quædam, quæ actus præcedanei vocari solent, operetur multis modis, velut quòd verbum Dei audiunt, voluntatem Dei cognoscunt, miseriam suam cum dolore quodam agnoscunt, judicis Dei terrore perculsi pollutiones seculi & peccata conscientiam vastantia vitant, &c. quæ dein, cùm hora salutis eorum adest, in eo, qui regeneratur, non εἰς κενὸν δέχονται in vanum recipiuntur, 2 .Cor. VI. 1. sed utilia planè & fructuosa fiunt: tamen nulla vel dispositio, vel præparatio, vel congruentia, vel gratia sufficiens, non efficax in eo, qui nec dum regenitus est, agnosci potest. Quicquid enim in regenerando est, illud in irregenito est, qui ceu mortuus in peccato nullam planè ad regenerationem, ne λογισμῷ cogitando quidem, nec dum agendo vel perficiendo, ἱκανότητα aptitudinem habet, ibid. III. 5. Quæ igitur in regenerando dispositiones, præparationes ad gratiam videri possunt, per se hominis mortui opera mortua, nullam efficaciam ad regenerationem habentia sunt. In generatione quidem naturali dispositionibus quibusdam locus est: in resuscitatione corporis ex materia rudi corpus restituitur. At regeneratio non tantùm generatio nova, vel resuscitatio quædam rei in principiis suis latentis, sed creatio etiam, seu rei spiritualis ex nihilo spirituali productio est, Ephes. II. 10. Psal. LI. 12. In nihilo autem quæ dispositio, præparatio, aptitudo, congruentia est? Peccatum solum in irregenito regnat & vivit; quod tantum abest, ut regenerantem adjuvet, vel disponat regenerandum, ut, quantum in se est, præparationem, dispositionem omnem impediat, quin & Dei ipsius regenerantis gratiam, si fieri posset, omnem averruncet. Fortis ille & armatus (Diabolus) probè atrium suum custodit, ut in pace omnis possessio sit; donec ἰσχυρότερος fortior eo Christus ingrediatur, & eum vincat, armaturam, cui ille considebat, ei eripiat, & vasa spoliet, Luc. XI. 21.22. Ideò Tzophar ad Jobum: אִישׁ גָּבוֹר יִלָּבֵב Vir ἀξύνετος inanis (in cujus medio nihil est, cavo, cloacæ similis) cor accipit, & pullus onager homo (similis onagro, quia cupiditatibus suis obsequens se à Deo regi non patitur) nascitur, Job. XI. 12. Hic regenerandi status est. Sed de eo, quid gratia, & qualis gratia ad vocationem simul atque conversionem & regenerationem hominis conferat, & an voluntas hominis, vel liberum arbitrium quidquam conferre possit, abundè supra diximus.
units.tr: LXX. The reason of regeneration is the same as that of divine vocation through the word and the Spirit. For God regenerates by calling through the word and the Spirit. Just as the calling, so also regeneration proceeds by the omnipotent power of God, acting omnipotently and having a most certain success. "For shall he who causes to bring forth not beget?" (Isa. 66:9). Nor can a natural man either advance or hinder it by his own will. For the Holy Spirit, regenerating, is like the wind, and so the one born of him, though he is already aware of his operation after he is born, while he is being born does not know whence it comes or whither it goes (John 3:8). Far from contributing anything himself to his regeneration, the man does not do so. For it is not man but God who, willing [βουληθεὶς] by his good pleasure alone, according to his eternal purpose, begets [ἀπεκύησε] through the seed of the word of truth (James 1:18). While a man is being generated, he understands and wills, but things natural, not spiritual; once he is born, and his will is freed from the servitude of sin, he begins to will what is spiritual. Therefore there is no more in man by which he may help his regeneration than there is by which he may promote his generation. For although in those whom God wills to regenerate, God in advance works certain things, which are usually called preceding acts, in many ways, such as that they hear the word of God, know the will of God, recognise their misery with a certain grief, and, struck with the terror of the judgment of God, shun the pollutions of the age and the sins which lay waste the conscience, and so on; yet when the hour of their salvation arrives, these things are not received in vain [εἰς κενὸν δέχονται] in the one who is regenerated (2 Cor. 6:1), but become entirely useful and fruitful. Nevertheless, no disposition, preparation, congruity, or sufficient grace that is not effective can be recognised in one who is not yet regenerate. For whatever there is in regenerating, that is not in the unregenerate, who, being dead in sin, has no fitness [ἱκανότητα] for regeneration, not even in thinking by reasoning [λογισμῷ], much less in acting or accomplishing it (2 Cor. 3:5). Therefore whatever dispositions and preparations for grace may seem to exist in the work of regenerating are, in the dead man, dead works in themselves, having no efficacy for regeneration. In natural generation, indeed, certain dispositions have a place; in the resurrection of the body, a body is restored from crude matter. But regeneration is not merely a new generation or a certain resuscitation of a thing lying hidden in its principles, but a creation, that is, the production of a spiritual thing out of nothing spiritual (Eph. 2:10; Ps. 51:12). But what disposition, preparation, aptitude or congruity is there in nothing? In the unregenerate, sin alone reigns and lives. So far from helping the regenerating or disposing the one to be regenerated, it hinders every preparation and disposition, as far as it can, and would, if it were possible, avert the very grace of God who regenerates. The strong and armed one (the Devil) carefully guards his court, so that all his possessions are in peace, until Christ, stronger [ἰσχυρότερος] than he, enters, overcomes him, takes from him the armour in which he trusted, and divides his spoils (Luke 11:21–22). Hence Zophar says to Job: An empty man gets a heart [אִישׁ גָּבוֹר יִלָּבֵב], and a wild ass's colt is born a man (Job 11:12), that is, a man like a wild ass, who, obeying his desires, does not allow himself to be ruled by God. This is the state of one to be regenerated. But concerning what grace is, and what kind of grace contributes to vocation, conversion and regeneration of man at once, and whether the will of man or free choice can contribute anything, we have said enough above.

units.la: LXXI. Impiè de regeneratione sentiunt, qui cum Libertinis & Fanaticis eam in nescio quem Enthusiasmum & phreneticam intemperiem commutant, & regenitos, ceu in statum innocentiæ restitutos Dei filios, de libidine carnis non amplius solicitos esse, sed Spiritum solum ducem, sub cujus actione nunquam aberraturi sint, sequi oportere, blasphemant. Illi enim Spiritum Dei, qui sermone Dei vivo ad spem vivam regenerat, cum spiritu mundi & Sathanæ confundentes, gratia Dei ad lasciviam abutuntur, & delectum omnem turpis & honesti, justi & injusti, boni & mali, virtutis & vitii, discrimen eorum ex maledictione Adami veteris, per Christi gratiam sublata, arcessentes, tollunt. Tolle, inquiunt, vanam formidinem; Spiritus nil mali tibi imperabit, modò actioni ejus te secure subjicias. Quæ popularis eorum philosophia est, qui libidinum amentia excæcati, communem sensum exuerunt. Sed quem illi Christum, quem Spiritum, quod Evangelium fabricantur? Nos enim Christum unum, ejus Spiritum unum, quem Prophetæ commendarunt, Evangelium exhibitum prædicat, recognoscimus. Spiritus ille non homicidii, impuritatis, injustitiæ, fraudis patronus; sed author dilectionis, pudicitiæ, justitiæ, moderationis, veritatis: non vertiginosus, præceps, per fas & nefas inconsiderate ruens, sed plenus sapientiæ & intelligentiæ, qua justum inter & injustum rite discernitur: non dux ad dissolutam & effrœnam licentiam, sed modi moderationisque servandæ author est. Neque Christianis Spiritus Domini, regeneratione collatus, turbulentum phantasma, quod vel ipsi per somnium peperierint, vel ab aliis confictum acceperint, est; utpote cujus notitiam & ἀλήθειαν ex Scripturis religiose petunt. Ibi verò duo de eo traduntur. Prius, quòd nobis in sanctificationem datus sit, ut nos ab immunditiis & inquinamentis purgatos Divinæ voluntatis & justitiæ obedientiam perducat, quæ obedientia nonnisi domitis & subactis concupiscentiis constat. Posterius est, quòd sic Spiritus S. sanctificatione purgemur, ut multis vitiis, multáque infirmitate obsideamur, quamdiu mole corporis premimur. Quo fit, ut longo intervallo à perfectione dissitis nobis semper proficiendum, & cum vetusti hominis atque carnis reliquiis, domestico velut & periculosissimo omnium hoste luctandum nobis sit. Unde consequitur, excussa desidia & securitate semper intentis animis vigilandum nobis esse, ne carnis insidiis circumveniamur.
units.tr: LXXI. Those who change regeneration into I know not what enthusiasm and frenzied intemperance, along with the Libertines and Fanatics, think impiously. They blaspheme by claiming that the regenerate, as sons of God restored to a state of innocence, are no longer anxious about the lusts of the flesh, and that they ought to follow the Spirit alone as their guide, since they will never go astray under his direction. Confusing the Spirit of God, who regenerates us to a living hope by the living Word of God, with the spirit of the world and of Satan, they abuse the grace of God for licentiousness. They also remove every distinction between what is shameful and honourable, just and unjust, good and evil, virtue and vice, which they derive from the curse of the old Adam, supposedly taken away by the grace of Christ. "Cast away," they say, "vain fear. The Spirit will command you nothing evil, provided you submit securely to his action." This is the popular philosophy of men who, blinded by the madness of their lusts, have cast off common sense. But what Christ, what Spirit, and what Gospel do they fashion for themselves? We acknowledge one Christ and one Spirit, whom the prophets commended, and we preach the Gospel as it has been revealed. That Spirit is not the patron of murder, impurity, injustice, or fraud, but the author of love, chastity, justice, moderation, and truth. He is not giddy, headlong, rushing thoughtlessly through right and wrong, but full of wisdom and understanding, by which the just is rightly distinguished from the unjust. He is not a leader into dissolute and unbridled licence, but the author of measure and moderation. Nor is the Spirit of the Lord, bestowed on Christians in regeneration, a turbulent phantasm, which they have either dreamed up themselves or received fabricated by others. Rather, they seek the knowledge and truth [ἀλήθεια] of him devoutly from the Scriptures. There two things are handed down about him. The first is that he has been given to us for sanctification, so that he may lead us, purged from uncleanness and defilement, to obedience to the will and righteousness of God, an obedience which consists only in tamed and subdued lusts. The second is that we are purged by the sanctification of the Holy Spirit in such a way that we are still beset by many vices and much weakness, as long as we are weighed down by the burden of the body. Hence it follows that, since we are far removed from perfection by a long interval, we must always make progress, and must struggle with the remnants of the old man and of the flesh, the most dangerous enemy of all, as it were a domestic one. From this it follows that, shaking off sloth and complacency, we must keep watch with minds always alert, lest we be overcome by the snares of the flesh.

units.la: LXXII. Neque enim vel regeneratio in hac vita perfecta, vel regeniti perfecti sunt. Quandiu enim in mortali hac carne peregrinatur, cum veteris Adami reliquiis nec prima, nec progrediente hujus vitæ regeneratione penitus extinctis, luctantur, & ipsa regeneratio frequentissimas vicissitudines experitur, sicut nunc major, nunc minor ejus progredientis operatio sit. Non enim spiritum duntaxat, sed etiam carnem regeniti habent; & hos inter quàdam μάχη ἀντιστρατεύεσθαι est, ut modò caro, modò spiritus vincat vel vincatur. Caro (reliqua naturæ veteris peccato corruptæ infirmitas, ad peccandum continuè irritans & per se impotens) concupiscit adversus spiritum (regenerationis & Christi, qui nos Christo unit, implantat, ad novam vitam vivificat, regenerat, dona distribuit, & in omnem veritatem sanctitatémque ducit) & spiritus adversus carnem. Ταῦτα ἡ ἀντικεῖται ἀλλήλοις Hæc autem inter se opposita sunt, ut non quæ velitis, hæc faciatis, Gal. V. 17. Spiritus perfectionem concupiscit, ad eam adipiscendam movet, voluntatem Dei in terris fieri, sicut illa in Cœlo fit, gestit, zelum pro gloria Dei & regno Christi acuit. Caro omnia alia spirat, Deo & legi ejus, Christo, justitiæ & regno ejus contrariatur, Sathanæ Regno amplificando intenta tota est, & perfectionem modis omnibus impedire conatur. Hos inter luctam Deus ipse Agonothetes summus instituit, ut sibi contrarientur, & adversa velut acie confligant, in qua nec caro semper vincit, & Spiritus carnis infestationem experitur. Efficit enim
units.tr: LXXII. For neither is regeneration perfect in this life, nor are the regenerate perfect. For as long as they are wandering in this mortal flesh, they struggle with the remnants of the old Adam, which are not wholly extinguished either at the first regeneration or in the regeneration that progresses through this life. Regeneration itself experiences very frequent vicissitudes, so that its progressive operation is now greater, now less. The regenerate do not have only the spirit but also the flesh, and between these there is a certain [μάχη] conflict, [ἀντιστρατεύεσθαι] a mutual warfare, so that now the flesh and now the spirit conquers or is conquered. The flesh (the weakness of the rest of the nature corrupted by sin, which constantly incites to sin and is powerless of itself) lusts against the Spirit (of regeneration and of Christ, who unites us to Christ, implants us, quickens us to a new life, regenerates us, distributes gifts, and leads us into all truth and holiness), and the Spirit against the flesh. [Ταῦτα γὰρ ἀλλήλοις ἀντίκειται] "For these are contrary the one to the other, so that you cannot do the things that you would," Gal. 5:17. The Spirit longs for perfection, moves us to attain it, desires that the will of God be done on earth as it is in heaven, and sharpens zeal for the glory of God and the kingdom of Christ. The flesh breathes everything else; it is opposed to God and his law, to Christ, to righteousness and his kingdom; it is wholly intent on enlarging the kingdom of Satan and tries in every way to hinder perfection. God himself, the supreme Master of the contest, has set up this struggle between them, so that they are opposed to each other and clash as in a battle line. In this conflict the flesh does not always conquer, and the Spirit experiences the assaults of the flesh. For it brings about that you do not do what you would.

units.la: {y} Regeneratio in hac vita imperfecta ex lucta r... fidua carnis & spiritus, quam iuprimis suo exemplo, &c. Paulus Rom. VII. 14. &c. &c. fernii. enim caro, ne faciamus quod volumus. Quod de se ipso pluribus S. Paulus carni suae non parum succensens, exaggerat, dicens: Novimus, quod Lex spiritualis sit. Ego vero sum carnalis (secundum reliquias carnis, & quia non id omne, quod in me est, a Spiritu S. est) venundatus sub peccatum, (non plene a peccati servitute liberatus.) Quod enim operor (secundum carnem) non cognosco (tentatione carnis haud raro praeoccupante & me implicante, ut vix intelligam, quoties impingam, & occultos errores nesciam Psal. XIX. 13. Gal. VI. 1. & in optimis displicere mihi cogar) Non enim quod volo, hoc ago, sed quod odi, hoc facio (vellem bonum facere, & plus, quam facio; sed prohdolor! carne impediente non semper id exequor; imo peccatum mihi secundum spiritum invisum quam maxime patro) Si autem, quod non volo, hoc facio, consentio Legi, quod bona fit (quia hoc volo secundum Spiritum, quod Lex vult) Nunc autem non jam ego operor illud, sed quod habitat in me peccatum (ego non qua regenitus, a peccati dominio liber & solutus, & justitiae mancipatus, sed qua peccati, veteris Adami, non plane expurgati, sed sub Spiritus dominio in me adhuc habitantis particeps) Novi enim, quod non habitet in me, hoc est, in carne mea bonum, quia carnis concupiscentia ad malum fertur, & membra mea malo assueta difficulter a Spiritu reguntur.) Nam velle adjacet mihi, sed operari bonum non invenio, (sentio spiritum sponta-neum, gestientem ad bonum, sed non par operationis ratio, cui caro, Sathanas, mundus multum intercedit, ut vel non bonam, vel non perfecte bonam, & in qua placere mihi possim, inveniam.) Non enim quod volo, facio bonum, sed quod nolo, malum, hoc ago, (non quale volo, perfectum, usquequaque purum, rectum, sed quale nolo, peccati sordibus contaminatum, facio.) Condeletor Legi secundum interiorem hominem (sicut Deus, ita & ego secundum animi mei delector) video autem aliam legem in membris meis belligerantem adversus Legem mentis meae, (nihilominus tanta carnis meae, peccatum mihi imperantis, & in membris illud exequentis, impotentia est, ut experiri identidem cogar illam me a servitute & lege justitiae, qua Christo mancipatus sum, abstrahere, captivum abducere nitentem; & abstrahit illa, capit non raro, sed non abducit ad interitum, quia mihi vindex est.) Miser ego homo, quis me eripiet e corpore hujus mortis? (an miser ego in hac lucta durare, vel eluctari etiam ex corpore hoc mortali, sine spe Salvatoris a lucta hac liberaturi, possim?) Gratias ago Deo per Jesum Christum, Dominum nostrum (hic ille vindex, Sospitator meus, custodit, servat me, ne captivus a Sathana abducar, ne peccatum saluti meae obsit, imo ut plus quam victor in ipso existam) Rom. VII. 14-24. Vix hominis regeniti, cui Deus ipse regenerans hanc legem dixit, ut quandiu in corpore vivit, cum residua carne, hoste domestico luctetur, conditionem pensitant, qui S. Paulum se ipsum ut adhuc irregenitum, objurgare, non ut regenitum repraesentare statuunt. Nihil enim eorum homini irregenito, at regenito omnia quadrant. Nam & inde a v. 14. constante de se in praesenti loquitur, cum ante, ubi de se irregenito locutus est,
units.tr: {y} Regeneration in this imperfect life arises from the struggle between the flesh and the spirit, which Paul above all illustrates by his own example, etc. Paul, Rom. 7:14, etc. For the flesh is at work so that we do not do what we want. St Paul, greatly provoked against his own flesh, expounds this at length about himself, saying: We know that the law is spiritual. But I am carnal (according to the remnants of the flesh, and because not all that is in me is from the Holy Spirit) sold under sin (not fully freed from slavery to sin). For what I do (according to the flesh) I do not know (the flesh, pre-occupying me and entangling me, often makes it hard for me to understand how often I stumble and to be aware of hidden errors, Ps. 19:13; Gal. 6:1; and I am compelled to be displeased with myself even in my best deeds). For what I would, that I do not; but what I hate, that I do (I would wish to do good, and more than I do; but alas! the flesh hinders me, and I do not always carry it out. Indeed, I hate sin most intensely, as far as the Spirit is concerned). If then I do that which I would not, I consent to the law that it is good (because I wish, according to the Spirit, what the law wills). Now then it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me (I am not free and released from the dominion of sin as regenerate, and enslaved to righteousness, but I am a partaker, as sin of the old Adam, not wholly cleansed, but still dwelling in me under the dominion of the Spirit). For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh) dwelleth no good thing, because the lust of the flesh tends toward evil, and my members, accustomed to evil, are with difficulty ruled by the Spirit. For to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not (I feel the Spirit willing and eager for good, but there is not an equal ability to act, since the flesh, Satan, and the world intervene greatly, so that I find either not good, or not perfectly good, and in which I can be pleased with myself). For the good that I would I do not; but the evil which I would not, that I do (I do not do what I would, perfect, wholly pure and upright, but what I would not, I do, defiled by the filth of sin). I delight in the law of God after the inward man (as God does, so do I delight according to my mind). But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind (nevertheless, such is the powerlessness of my flesh, which commands me to sin and carries it out in my members, that I am constantly compelled to experience the attempt to drag me away from the slavery and law of righteousness, to which I am bound to Christ, and to lead me away captive; and it sometimes succeeds in seizing me, but does not lead me away to destruction, because he is my defender). O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? (Can I, wretched as I am, endure in this struggle, or struggle out of this mortal body, without hope of a Saviour who will free me from this conflict?)
