I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord (here is that defender and my Saviour, who guards and keeps me so that I am not led away captive by Satan, and so that sin does not harm my salvation, but so that I am more than a conqueror in him), Rom. 7:14-24. Those who decide to rebuke Paul as though he were still unregenerate, rather than presenting him as regenerate, scarcely weigh the condition of a regenerate man, to whom God himself, regenerating him, gave this law: that as long as he lives in the body, he should struggle with the remaining flesh, a domestic enemy. For none of these things fit an unregenerate man, but all of them fit the regenerate. For from verse 14 onward he speaks of himself in the present tense, whereas before, when he spoke of himself as unregenerate, he used past tense verbs; and of the unregenerate man it is said that he does not will what he does, but hates it; and that it is not he himself but the sin dwelling within him (so that in Paul there was some principle distinct from sin, which was nothing other than the Holy Spirit against the flesh...

units.la: verbis praeteritum significantibus usus fuerit; & de irregenito, quod id quod facit, non velit, sed oderit; quod non ipse, sed peccatum inhabitans (ut ita in Paulo principium aliquod a peccato distinctum fuerit, quod non erat nisi Spiritus S. adversus carnem concupiscens, Gal. V. 17.) peccatum faciat; quod τὸ θέλειν velle boni (quod Deus regenerans demum operatur Phil. II. 13.) nec non interiorem hominem & legem mentis habeat, & Lege una cum Deo delectetur, eique mente serviat; quod miseriae suae ingemiscat, & Deo per Jesum Christum gratias agat, dici, nemo ad statum irregeniti, in peccato mortui, & medii status impossibilitatem paulo attentior asseveraverit: Et denique S. Paulus ipse exclamans: Miser ego homo, quis me eripiet e corpore hujus mortis? v. 24. aperte innuit, statum illum suum, de quo loquitur, non utique regeneratione, sed demum morte corporis finiri.
units.tr: in the past tense, and of the unregenerate man, that what he does he does not want to do but hates; that it is not he himself but sin dwelling in him that does the sinning (so that in Paul there was some principle distinct from sin, which was nothing other than the Spirit lusting against the flesh, Gal. 5:17); that he has the willing [τὸ θέλειν] of good, which God works in the regenerate at last (Phil. 2:13), as well as the inner man and the law of the mind, and that he delights in the law of God and serves it with his mind; that he groans over his misery and gives thanks to God through Jesus Christ. No one who looked more carefully would maintain that these things are said of the state of the unregenerate, dead in sin, or that a middle state is impossible. And finally St Paul himself, crying out, "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?" (v. 24), clearly hints that the state of which he speaks is ended not by regeneration but, at last, by the death of the body.

units.la: LXXIII. Desino ex Scriptura pluribus illa commemorare, quibus regenerationis in hac vita imperfectio confirmatur, & regenitorum jactata a malesanis & carnali typho inflatis illa ἀναμαρτησία evertitur.
units.tr: LXXIII. I shall leave aside the many passages of Scripture that confirm the imperfection of regeneration in this life, and that overthrow the claim to sinlessness [ἀναμαρτησία] which the mad and those puffed up with carnal pride boast of among the regenerate.

units.la: Dicere enim S. Johannes: Si, inquit, dixerimus nos peccatum (inhabitans & se proferens in membris) non habere, nos ipsos seducimus, & veritas in nobis non est. Si dixerimus, quod non peccaverimus, (actu) mendacem eum facimus, (qui carnis omnem impotentiam tam manifeste accusat & convincit passim) & sermo Dei non est in nobis, I. Joh. I. 8. 10. Quae verba priora de praesenti eorum statu, quibus ipse Johannes se includit: non de praeterito irregenitorum, loquuntur. Dicit enim: Si dixerimus, nos peccatum non habere; & si dixerimus, quod non peccaverimus, non ante regenerationem, quis enim hoc dixerit? Ideo de τεκνίοις filiolis statim subjicit: Ne peccate, (ne putetis, ideo liberum vobis esse peccare, quia peccatum habetis) Et si quis peccaverit, Paracletum habemus apud Deum, I. Joh. II. 1. Filioli igitur, & qui Paracletum apud Deum habent, adeoque regeniti sunt, peccare etiam possunt. Christus quoque discipulos suos orare jussit: Remitte nobis debita nostra: Ne nos inducas in tentationem sed libera nos a malo, Matth. VI. 12. 13. Propter hoc (remissionum pravitatem) orabit te omnis pius, tempore opportuno; & cum exundaverint aquae multae, ipsum non attingent, Psal. XXXII. 6. Non quod non simul semelque omnibus regenitorum omnium peccatis per sanguinem Christi litura inducta sit, sed quia remissionis semel factae interior sensus & consolatio quotidie renovari debet. Grandem vero injuriam Deo facimus, fingentes animo nostro, quod Deus non sit major corde nostro, I. Joh. III. 20. adeoque cordis nostri latebras ignoret, nec in iis inveniat, propter quod judicium ejus deprecandum nobis est. Ne quid de sanctissimorum hominum, Patriarcharum, Mosis, Aharonis, Davidis, Solomonis, Petri gravissimis lapsibus dicam, quos Scriptura nobis & communis fragilitatis, & non cadendi, sed, cum ceciderimus, resurgendi exempla, & velut praecones verborum Apostoli: Μὴ ὑψηλοφρονῶ, ἀλλὰ φοβοῦ. Ne elato sis animo, sed time, Rom. XI. 20. propositi. Ideo etiam S. Paulus Corinthios, quos prius sanctificatos in Christo Jesu
units.tr: For St John says: "If we say that we have no sin" (dwelling in us and showing itself in our members), "we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we say that we have not sinned" (in act), "we make him a liar" (who so clearly and so constantly accuses and convicts all the impotence of the flesh), "and the word of God is not in us" (1 John 1:8, 10). These earlier words speak of the present state of those to whom John includes himself, not of the past state of the unregenerate. For he says, "If we say that we have no sin, and if we say that we have not sinned": this is not said before regeneration, for who would say such a thing then? So he goes on at once to his little children [τεκνία]: "My little children, sin not" (do not suppose that you are free to sin because you have sin), "and if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father" (1 John 2:1). So the little children, and those who have an advocate with God, and therefore are regenerate, can still sin. Christ also commanded his disciples to pray: "Forgive us our debts; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil" (Matt. 6:12–13). "For this shall every godly man pray unto you in a time when you may be found; and when the great waters overflow, they shall not reach him" (Ps. 32:6). This is not because the blot of all the sins of all the regenerate is not at once and together wiped out by the blood of Christ, but because the inner sense and comfort of a forgiveness once granted must be renewed every day. We do great wrong to God when we imagine in our minds that God is not "greater than our heart" (1 John 3:20), and so does not know the hidden places of our heart and does not find in them what we must pray that his judgment will not consider. I say nothing of the very grave falls of the holiest men, of the Patriarchs, of Moses, Aaron, David, Solomon, and Peter, which Scripture sets before us as examples both of common frailty, and not of falling, but of rising again when we have fallen, and as heralds, as it were, of the Apostle's words: "Be not highminded, but fear" [Μὴ ὑψηλοφρονῶ, ἀλλὰ φοβοῦ] (Rom. 11:20). Therefore St Paul also calls the Corinthians, whom earlier he had called "sanctified in Christ Jesus"

units.la: Tum ex simonilis aliis Scripturae Jesu vocatos sanctos, 1.Cor.I.2. appellaverat, mox pueros quidem in Christo, sed tamen non spirituales, verùm carnales, non in universum, sed quatenus carnalibus affectibus ad schismata se abripi passi sunt, appellat, cap.III.1. & alibi gravissimè hortatur: Pondere omni depositó, & peccato, quod nos facilè circumstat, per patientiam decurramus propositum nobis certamen, Heb. XII.1. Ad ἀγῶνα ergo προκείμενον certamen propositum, & quidem cum peccato ἐυπερίστατον nos ipsos circumstante, cingente, supplantante, adeóque proprio, citamur omnes μέχρις αἱ- μάτ ad sanguinem usque, ibid. v.4.
units.tr: and "called to be saints" (1 Cor. 1:2), as other similar passages of Scripture do, and soon after calls them "babes in Christ," yet "not spiritual but carnal" (1 Cor. 3:1). He means not that they were carnal in every respect, but that they allowed themselves to be swept into schisms by carnal affections. And elsewhere he exhorts very earnestly: "Laying aside every weight, and the sin which so easily surrounds us, let us run with patience the race that is set before us" (Heb. 12:1). So all of us are summoned to the race set before us [ἀγῶνα προκείμενον], with sin, which surrounds, encircles, and trips us up [ἐυπερίστατον], always standing around us, and so to the struggle "unto blood" [μέχρις αἵματος] (ibid. v. 4).

units.la: LXXIV. Accedit quòd regeneratio & renovatio nostra ceu proficiens, & in stadio usque progrediens, qualis cum perfectione ἀσύμ- φῶν est, describitur. Non segnescimus; sed etiamsi exterior homo noster corrumpitur, interior tamen renovatur ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ de die in diem, 2.Cor. IV.16. Licèt nempe in regenitis praeter corruptionem & destructionem nihil mundus videat, cùm exterior ille homo, corpus & anima, quorum illud pulvis est, hoc ἐπιθυμίαν concupiscentiam residuam habet, corrumpatur; tamen homo interior, seu occultus ille cordis homo, 1.Pet. III.4. seu ἁγιότης sanctitudo illa, quae in corde, mente & Spiritu domicilium suum metata, merè interna est, de die in diem, magis magisque ad perfectionem verae sapientiae, extirpationem errorum & vitiorum, & ad victoriam atque brabeon coelestis vocationis proficit. Fideles enim primò sunt νήπιοι ἐν Χριστῷ pueri in Christo, 1.Cor.III.1. ac demum ἄνδρες τέλειοι viri perfecti evadunt. Ita S. Johannes παιδία infantes, νεανίσκος juvenes, & πατέρες patres, 1.Joh.II.13, 14. distinguit. Semper enim ἐςχάτα πλείονα πρώτων ultima prioribus locupletiora evadunt, Apoc. II.19. Veri nempe Christiani non usque in secundis consistunt, sed progrediuntur versus Coelum, & inter primos etiam inveniri contendunt. Non progredi, regredi est. Denique Christus in cordibus fidelium primùm exoritur instar φωσφόρος Luciferi, 2.Pet.I.19. Sicut enim Lucifer exoriens paulatim lucem fundit, at tenebras noctis non simul semelque plene dispellit: sic Christus in cordibus fidelium exoriens, potens licèt, ceu Sol justitiae, cunctas cordis humani tenebras dissipare, nihilominus sic lucem suam dispensat, ut quantum ad salutem satis est, homo in luce ambulare possit; neque tamen quaedam, velut ignorantiae, cupiditatum carnis, amoris sui, &c. tenebrae protinus evanescant. Ac licèt paulatim Christus etiam ut Sol justitiae in cordibus eorundem exoriatur, tamen ut plenum jubar & meridianus Sol demum in altera vita illucescit, tenebrásque omnes plenissimè discutit. Iter justorum est ut lux jubaris, quod procedit & lucet usque ad diem confirmatum, Prov. IV.18. Eunt מחיל אל חיל de virtute in virtutem, vel de turma in turmam, donec compareant apud Deum in Sione, Psal.LXXXIV.8.
units.tr: LXXIV. Moreover, our regeneration and renewal is described as something that makes progress and advances through the course, as it is with perfection [ἀσύμφωνον]. "We faint not; but though our outward man is decaying, yet the inward man is renewed day by day [ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ]" (2 Cor. 4:16). Although in the regenerate the world sees nothing but corruption and destruction, since that outward man, body and soul, of which the body is dust and the soul has residual concupiscence [ἐπιθυμίαν], is decaying, nevertheless the inner man, the "hidden man of the heart" (1 Pet. 3:4), or that holiness [ἁγιότης] which has its dwelling in heart, mind, and spirit, and is purely internal, advances from day to day, more and more toward the perfection of true wisdom, the uprooting of errors and vices, and the victory and prize [βραβεῖον] of the heavenly calling. For the faithful are first "babes in Christ" [νήπιοι ἐν Χριστῷ] (1 Cor. 3:1), and at last become "perfect men" [ἄνδρες τέλειοι]. So St John distinguishes little children [παιδία], young men [νεανίσκοι], and fathers [πατέρες] (1 John 2:13–14). The last works always turn out greater than the first (Rev. 2:19). True Christians do not stop at the second stage, but press on toward heaven and strive to be found among the first. Not to advance is to go back. Finally, Christ rises in the hearts of the faithful at first like the morning star [φωσφόρος] (2 Pet. 1:19). For as the morning star, rising, sheds its light little by little and does not at once fully dispel the darkness of night, so Christ, rising in the hearts of the faithful, though powerful enough as the Sun of righteousness to scatter all the darkness of the human heart, nevertheless dispenses his light so that, as far as salvation requires, a man can walk in the light; yet certain darknesses, of ignorance, of carnal lusts, of self-love, and so on, do not vanish at once. And although Christ rises in their hearts only gradually as the Sun of righteousness, nevertheless he shines out fully, like the midday sun, only in the other life, and dispels all darkness completely. "The path of the just is as the shining light, which shines more and more unto the perfect day" (Prov. 4:18). "They go from strength to strength" [מחיל אל חיל], that is, from virtue to virtue, or from troop to troop, until they appear before God in Zion (Ps. 84:8).

units.la: LXXV. Neque sine gravi causa regeneratio in hac vita imperfecta relinquitur, & homini lucta cum peccato & Adamo vetere reliquo severè indicitur. Interest enim gloriae Dei, non tantùm ut ejus ceu ἀντικεῖμ- dominium, & libertas in lucta homini pro arbitrio ejus decernenda manifestatur, sed etiam ut po-
units.tr: LXXV. Nor without a serious cause is regeneration left imperfect in this life, and the struggle with sin and the old Adam is strictly laid upon man. For it is in the interest of God's glory not only that his dominion [ἀντικείμενον?] is made manifest, and that man's freedom to decide in the struggle by his own will is shown, but also that the po-

units.la: tentia gratiae ejus in infirmitate nostra consummetur. Ideò Deus S. Paulo, luctam hanc cum palo carni suae infixo, & Sathana ipso deprecanti respondit: Sufficit tibi gratia mea. Nam potentia mea in infirmitate consummatur, 2.Cor. XII.9. Sic enim Deus homini succumbenti ipse succollans זרעה עולם brachia aeterna Deut. XXXIII.27. supponens, & ἐκ ἀσθενείας ἡμῶν ζωαπλαμβάνομ infirmitatibus nostris opitulans, Rom. VIII.26. potentiam suam quàm maximè demonstrat. Ad honorem enim Dei pertinet, ut ipse exaltetur, & homo humilietur. Omnia haec manus mea fecit, & extiterunt omnia haec, ait Jehova. Et hunc intuebor, qui inops, & pauper Spiritu est, & trepidat ad verbum meum, Esaj. LXVI.2. Cùm enim plurima in mundo, apud electos inprimis, velut aeternus amor Dei, quo illos complectitur, regeneratio, vocatio in communionem Filii, adoptio, spiritualis prudentia, aliàque ejusmodi πλεονεκτήματα sint, quibus inflari, & ad gloriandum cum Laodicea Angelo, quòd divites sint, & nullius rei indigeant, Apoc. III.17. seduci possent; visum Deo est, crisitas has deprimere, & ferocientem carnem relicto in eadem hoste, & indicto hoc certamine contundere. Quamobrem etiam sanctissimos ἐν προσπώματα πλαμβάνεσθαι lapsibus praeoccupari Galat. VI.1. finit, tum ne efferantur, sed ut se coram oculis Dei humilient: tum ne nimio in pretio, cum honoris Dei detrimento, ab aliis habeantur: tum ut alii exemplo eorum territi timeant, & Deo cum timore serviant, & cum tremore exultent. In ipsa natura, quod & Philosophi, Plutarchus inprimis, observant, quicquid vacuum est, sursum, & quicquid praegnans plenúmque est, deorsum ferri videmus. Nam plenae bonae frugis aristae, vites, arbores humum versus inclinatae velut coram Deo se humiliant, eíque bonorum omnium acceptorum laudem gratiámque tribuunt. Quantò magis hominem coram Deo sic humiliari convenit, ut & Dei χειρ, & indignitate atque infirmitate sua deprehensa opulentiam & robur DEI unicè suspiciat. Sicut etiam Christus, in quo passus est ipse tentatus potest iis, qui tentantur, opitulari, Heb. II.18. & μετριοπαθῶν aequanimis esse ignorantibus & errantibus potest, quia & ipse infirmitate circumdatus fuit, ibid. V.2. ita Sancti infirmitatibus ejusmodi pressi ad juvandos convertendósque alios promptiores se gerunt. Denique progrediens illa exterioris hominis corruptio, & interioris renovatio, post se tum contemptum mundi, & eorum, quae videntur; tum desiderium domicilii illius coelestis & Divini, atque non ἐνδύσεως indutionis duntaxat justitiae Christi, sed etiam ὑπερενδύσεως superindutionis coelestis gloriae; tum fiduciam in Deo Patre, gaudium spirituale ex renovationis profectu, & ardorem placendi Deo trahit, quae S. Paulus 2.Corinth. IV.16-f. V.1.2. &c. amplissimè confirmat.
units.tr: wer of his grace is made perfect in our weakness. So God answered St Paul, who was struggling with the thorn fixed in his flesh and who prayed to be rid of Satan himself: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor. 12:9). For in this way God shows his power most fully: he supports the man who is giving way, sustaining him with "the everlasting arms" [זרעה עולם] (Deut. 33:27), and "helps our infirmities" [ἐκ ἀσθενείας ἡμῶν συναντιλαμβάνεται] (Rom. 8:26). For it belongs to the honour of God that he should be exalted and man humbled. "All these things has my hand made, and all these things have been, says the LORD. But to this man will I look, to him who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at my word" (Isa. 66:2). For since in the world, and especially among the elect, there are many advantages, such as God's eternal love by which he embraces them, regeneration, calling into communion with the Son, adoption, spiritual wisdom, and other such privileges, by which they might be puffed up and seduced into boasting, like the Laodicean angel, that they are rich and need nothing (Rev. 3:17), God has seen fit to humble these pride and to crush the fierce flesh, leaving the enemy within it and declaring this contest. For this reason he also allows the holiest men to be overtaken by falls, "Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault" [ἐν προσπώματι προλημφθῆ] (Gal. 6:1); both so that they will not be puffed up but humble themselves before the eyes of God, and so that they will not be held in too high esteem by others, to the detriment of God's honour, and so that others, frightened by their example, may fear, serve God with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Even in nature, as the philosophers, Plutarch above all, observe, we see that whatever is empty is borne upward, and whatever is full and heavy is borne downward. For full ears of good grain and vines and trees bend toward the ground, as if humbling themselves before God, and they ascribe to him the praise and thanks for all the good things they have received. How much more fitting is it for man to humble himself thus before God, so that, recognising God's hand and his own unworthiness and weakness, he looks up to God alone for wealth and strength. So also Christ, "in that he himself has suffered being tempted, is able to succour them that are tempted" (Heb. 2:18), and "can have compassion on the ignorant and on those who are out of the way, since he himself also is compassed with infirmity" (ibid. 5:2). So too the saints, pressed down by such infirmities, are more ready to help and convert others. Finally, that progressive corruption of the outward man and renewal of the inner man brings with it, first, contempt for the world and for what is seen; second, desire for that heavenly and divine dwelling place, and not only for the putting on [ἐνδύσεως] of the righteousness of Christ but also for the putting on over [ὑπερενδύσεως] of heavenly glory; third, trust in God the Father; fourth, spiritual joy from the progress of renewal; and fifth, an ardent desire to please God. St Paul confirms these at great length in 2 Cor. 4:16–5:2 and following.

units.la: LXXVI. Non defuerunt tamen in Ecclesia, neque hodieque desunt perfectionis regenitorum superbi buccinatores, qui non tantum cum Ephraimo cogitant, sed etiam dicunt. Profecto dives sum, inveni divitias mihi. In omnibus laboribus meis non invenient iniquitatem & peccatum, Hos. XII.9. & cum Corinthiis se fatu-ros: ros, divites esse & regnare sibi fingunt, 1. Cor. IV. 8. Est enim generatio quædam pura in oculis suis, quæ tamen à stercore non est lota, Prov. XXX. 12. Jam olim Novatus, ex Africa oriundus perfectionem ejusmodi professus est; Cui Cyprianus masculè se opposuit, Sed Novatus, cujus audacem & improbum animum Eusebius Hist. Eccles. lib. VI. 43. detegit, asseclas adeptus est Catharos, quos Fridericus II. Imp. in Constitutione Gazaros (Ʞᾶτζερ; quod nomen deinceps omnibus in fundamento fidei Christianæ errantibus hæsit) appellat. Mox Pelagius & Cœlestius perfectionem similem propugnarunt, quibus Augustinus Tractatum de perfectione justitiæ, & Hieronymus, qui Pelagium prædicatorem impeccantiæ insignit, tres libros dialogisticè scriptos opposuerunt. Repressa in Concilio non uno, Carthaginensi inprimis II. & III. hæresis nidum inter Scholasticos invenit, quibus Concilium Tridentinum Sess. VI. Can. 8. anathema dicens iis, qui dixerint; Dei præcepta homini etiam justificato, & sub gratia constituto ad observandum impossibilia esse, suffragatum est. Demum Weigelius explosa justitia Christi imputata, quam Antichristi justitiam imputativam blasphemavit, eúmque secuti fanatici non pauci, inprimis novi Pharisæi, prætextu liberationis à peccato per mortem Christi, communionis cum Christo & regenerationis, ἀναμαχετησαν regenitorum ex orco revocarunt; applaudente Sathana, quòd ut res ejusmodi inflatos reperes, quibus opinione regenerationis perfectæ & peccandi impotentiæ dementatis facilè persuasit, ut crederent, & se regenitos esse, & quicquid ultra, ceu regeniti seu ἐνομοι, seu ἀνομοι patrant, id omne peccato vacare, imo & Deo placere; ambulantes ita ἐν πνευματι in astutia, & ἐν ... secreta pudoris non abdicantes, sed retinentes tortius, 2. Cor. IV. 2. Hoc enim illud βαθη ... Satanæ illa profunditas Sathanæ est, quam dogma verbis speciosum, at re ipsa pestiferum maximè occultat.
units.tr: LXXVI. Yet the Church has never lacked, and even today does not lack, proud trumpeters of the perfection of the regenerate. They not only think with Ephraim but also say: Surely I am rich, I have found riches for myself. In all my labours they will not find iniquity or sin, Hos. 12:9. Like the Corinthians, they imagine that they are already full, that they are rich and reign as kings, 1 Cor. 4:8. "There is a generation that is pure in its own eyes, yet is not washed from its filth," Prov. 30:12. Long ago Novatus, a native of Africa, professed perfection of this kind, and Cyprian opposed him manfully. But Novatus, whose bold and wicked spirit Eusebius exposes in Hist. Eccles. lib. VI. 43., gained followers, the Cathari, whom the Emperor Frederick II in his constitution calls Gazari (a name that afterwards stuck to all who err in the foundation of the Christian faith). Soon Pelagius and Caelestius defended a similar perfection. Augustine wrote a treatise de perfectione justitiæ against them, and Jerome, who branded Pelagius as a preacher of impeccability, opposed them with three books written in dialogue form. Repressed in more than one council, especially the Second and Third Councils of Carthage, the heresy found a nest among the Schoolmen, and the Council of Trent (Sess. VI, can. 8) lent its support to it by pronouncing anathema on those who say: The commandments of God are impossible for man to observe, even when he is justified and placed under grace. Finally Weigel, having rejected the imputed justice of Christ, which he blasphemed as Antichristi justitiam imputativam, and not a few fanatics following him, especially the new Pharisees, under the pretext of liberation from sin through the death of Christ, of communion with Christ and of regeneration, have recalled the regenerate from the grave. Satan applauded, for he easily persuaded inflated men of this sort, whose minds were infatuated with the notion of perfect regeneration and of an inability to sin, that they were regenerate, and that whatever they did beyond this, whether as those under the law [ἔνομοι] or as lawless [ἄνομοι], was all free from sin and even pleasing to God. They walk thus ambulantes ita "in the Spirit," in craftiness [πανουργία], and do not renounce the hidden things of shame, but hold to them all the more tightly, 2 Cor. 4:2. This is that "depths of Satan" [τὰ βαθέα τοῦ Σατανᾶ] which the speciously worded but in fact pestilential dogma conceals so well: profunditas Sathanæ.

units.la: LXXVII. Negant illi ante omnia, Deum, gratiam Dei, Christum, regenerationem unà cum peccato consistere posse. Quod verum est de peccato quoad manentem ejus reatum & dominium: falsum, quoad ejus ἐνοικησιν inhabitationem qualemcunque, non ut imputetur ad damnationem, vel ut regnet in mortali corpore nostro, & in eodem pleno voluntatis consensu committatur; sed ut per Spiritum Dei cum carne conflictante mancipii refractarii adinstar, magis magisque mortificetur, & demum in morte penitus aboleatur. Licèt enim in renatis sic peccatum habitet, non tamen remis vehisque ad serviendum illi feruntur, sed parte regenita plus minusvè illi renituntur, prout fortior vel debilior tentatio premit & incumbit, aut virium plus minusvè ad ei reluctandum à Spiritu S. suppeditatur. Caro quidem illa veternosa & spiritus semper sibi adversantur, neque unquam redigi ad concordiam possunt. Sed duo tamen hæc adeò diversa principia per totam hominis regeniti animam sic diffunduntur, & eandem sedem occupant, ut non alia sui parte, potentia & facultate sit caro, alia verò spiritus, sed ubique ac totus, licèt non ὀλι- κως totaliter, sit caro; ubique item ac totus, at non in totum, sit spiritus, sicut in crepusculis non alia parte vel regione tenebræ solæ sunt, alia solum lumen; sed ubique per singulas ejus partes lux cum tenebris, & tenebræ cum luce commiscentur. Non possunt autemcontraria in summo gradu in eodem subjecto consistere; quia secundum Philosophorum illud, sunt pellentis naturæ; at possunt in remissiore; sicut aqua tepida tota remissè calere vel frigere dicitur. Sic igitur Spiritus S. gratia, Christus & regeneratio hominis cum peccato non jam ad damnationem imputato, vel regnante, sed remisso, & quoad culpam reliquam fracto subactóque, imò frangendo subigendóque indies consistere potest. Nam idem etiam campus, hosticum idem diversas hostium acies patitur, donec alter victor, victus alter & hosticum deserens, existat. Et ut verbo dicam, quod de Romanis, cùm adhuc eorum res floruissent, historia narrat, eos prælio sæpe vinci potuisse, bello nunquam, quia belli exitum prosperum semper habuerunt; ita in bello hoc intestino cum Diabolo & carne fieri potest, ut singulari conflictu aliquo, occulto Dei judicio, à peccato Christi miles infirmus vincatur; sed ut ab eodem enecetur, & vita spirituali omni privetur, fieri non potest.
units.tr: LXXVII. Above all, these men deny that God, the grace of God, Christ and regeneration can coexist with sin. This is true of sin as to its remaining guilt and dominion, but false as to its indwelling of whatever kind. Sin is not imputed to damnation, nor does it reign in our mortal body so as to be committed with full consent of the will. Rather, through the Spirit of God, which fights against the flesh like a stubborn slave, it is more and more mortified, and at last utterly abolished in death. For although sin dwells in the reborn in this way, they are not carried headlong into serving it. Instead the regenerate part resists it more or less, according as a stronger or weaker temptation presses and assails, or as more or less strength is supplied by the Holy Spirit to resist it. That old fleshly nature and the spirit are always opposed to each other, and can never be brought into concord. Yet these two so diverse principles are so spread through the whole soul of the regenerate man, and occupy the same seat, that the flesh is not one thing in one part, power and faculty, and the spirit another in another part. Rather the flesh is everywhere and wholly, though not totally in the sense of being entirely corrupt; likewise the spirit is everywhere and wholly, though not in its whole extent. In twilight, darkness is not alone in one part or region and light alone in another; rather, through each part, light is mingled with darkness and darkness with light. Contraries cannot exist in the highest degree in the same subject, since by the saying of the Philosophers they are of repelling nature; but they can exist in a lesser degree, just as lukewarm water is said to be wholly warm or cool in a mild degree. So the grace of the Holy Spirit, Christ and the regeneration of man can coexist with sin which is no longer imputed to damnation or reigning, but relaxed, and as to its remaining guilt broken and subdued, indeed being broken and subdued daily. For the same field suffers the same hostile battle-lines of the enemies, until one side emerges victor, the other vanquished and deserting the field. And, to say it in a word, what history relates of the Romans, when their affairs were flourishing, that they could often be beaten in battle, but never in war, because they always had a prosperous outcome of the war, can also be said of this internal war with the Devil and the flesh. It can happen that a weak soldier of Christ is overcome by sin in some single conflict, by a hidden judgement of God; but that he should be put to death by it and deprived of all spiritual life cannot happen.

units.la: LXXVIII. Neque quicquam in Scripturæ testimoniis adversantes præsidii habent. Dixit S. Johannes: Nostis quòd Ille (Christus) revelatus sit, ut peccata nostra auferret. Et peccatum in ipso non est. Quisquis in ipso manet, non peccat. Qui peccat, non vidit ipsum, neque novit ipsum. Qui justitiam facit, justus est, sicut & ipse justus est. Qui facit peccatum, ex Diabolo est, quia à principio Diabolus peccat. Ad hoc manifestatus est Filius Dei, ut opera Diaboli solvat. Quisquis natus est ex Deo, peccatum non facit, quia semen ejus in ipso manet; Et non potest peccare, quia ex Deo genitus est, 1. Joh. III. 5-10. Sed ille c. I. 8-10. se & sui similes adeóque regenitos peccatum habere & peccare pariter professus est. Cùm ergo Christum peccata nostra abstulisse dicit, de peccati reatu & dominio in hac vita loquitur; & peccantem ex Diabolo esse asserens, de eo, qui nil nisi peccat, & eo modo peccat, quo Diabolus, ab initio & continuè, & plena cum voluntate & delectatione peccans; loquitur. Neque enim sic peccant fideles, quia Filius Dei revelatus est, ut ejusmodi Diaboli opera solveret, ne in iis, qui in ipso sunt, locum habere amplius possint. Eodem sensu regenitos, qui in Christo sunt, peccare posse, vel peccare negat. Non enim sicut Diabolus, irregeniti, & nondum per Christum justificati, peccant; imò quà regeniti, & secundum Spiritum planè non peccant, quia peccatum à carne reliqua, nondum regenita, non à Spiritu regenerante & regenito est. Ideo de se peccante S. Paulus loquitur: Nunc ergo non amplius ἐγω ego (regenitus, vel interior homo) operor illud, sed peccatum in me habitans, Rom. VII. 17. Neque adeò quivis peccatores Regno Sathanæ, quod novi Pharisæi blaterant, includuntur; sed ii demum, qui Spiritus Dei carni resistente destituti, prudentes, libentes volentésque peccant, & eo modo peccant, quo regni illius tenebrarum Rex Sathanas peccat. Peccatum ipsum quodvis à Diabolo est; sed non quivis peccans; non certè ille, cui peccatum non imputatur, nec
units.tr: LXXVIII. Nor do those who oppose us have any support in the testimonies of Scripture. St John said: You know that He (Christ) was revealed to take away our sins. And in Him there is no sin. Whoever abides in Him does not sin. Whoever sins has not seen Him, nor known Him. Whoever does righteousness is righteous, as He is righteous. Whoever commits sin is of the Devil, because the Devil has sinned from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that He might destroy the works of the Devil. Whoever is born of God does not commit sin, because His seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he has been born of God, 1 John 3:5-10. Yet in 1:8-10 he likewise professed that he himself, and those like him and therefore regenerate, have sin and sin. Since he says that Christ has abstulisse [taken away] our sins, he speaks of the guilt and dominion of sin in this life. And when he asserts that one who sins is ex Diabolo esse [of the Devil], he speaks of one who does nothing but sin, and sins in the way the Devil does, ab initio [from the beginning] and continually, sinning with full will and delight. For the faithful do not sin in this way, because the Son of God was revealed to destroy such works of the Devil, so that they can no longer have a place in those who are in Him. In the same sense he denies that the regenerate, who are in Christ, can peccare posse [be able to sin], or peccare [sin]. For the unregenerate, and those not yet justified through Christ, sin as the Devil does; but as regenerate, and according to the Spirit, they plainly do not sin, because the sin that comes from the remaining flesh, not yet regenerate, is not from the regenerating and regenerated Spirit. Therefore St Paul speaks of himself as sinning: Now then it is no more I (the regenerate, or inner man) who do it, but sin dwelling in me, Rom. 7:17. Nor are all sinners therefore included in the kingdom of Satan, as the new Pharisees babble; rather, only those who, being destitute of the Spirit of God that resists the flesh, sin prudently, willingly and deliberately, and sin in the way in which Satan, the king of that kingdom of darkness, sins. Sin itself is from the Devil in every case, but not everyone who sins is; certainly not one to whom sin is not imputed, nor

units.la: { } Quòd peccans sit ex Diabolo, & regeniti ob semen Dei in iis permanens non peccent. dominatur; & qui infirmitates suas agnoscit, deplorat, & cum iisdem per Spiritum Dei assiduè luctatur. Ac proin nec doctrina de regenerationis imperfectione licentiam peccandi fovet. Nam S. Johannes peccatum in regenitis 1. Joh. I. 8. 10. agnoscens, illico tamen cap. II.1. addidit, hoc se filiolis suis scripsisse ne peccent. Confessio ergo ingenua peccati inhabitantis tantum abest, ut causa peccandi sit, ut potius repagulum sit; sicut cautior est, qui hostem apertum novit, quàm qui occultum ignorat. An igitur peccato patrocinari putabimus doctrinam, quæ ad certamen cum peccato vocat, & carni resistere, hominem veterem crucifigere, mortificare jubet? Quin potiùs infirmitas carnis, malum nobis adjacens, ignorantia & tentationes nostræ fortis instigatio & exsuscitatio & irritatio quædam ad non peccandum sunt. Debet enim homo regenitus, & charitas, quæ in eo est, habere velocitatem promptitudinem & zelum. An putatis, quòd inaniter Scriptura dicat: Adversus invidiam concupiscit Spiritus, qui in nobis habitare voluit? Jac. IV. 5. Neque enim vanum est, quòd Scriptura charitati zelum, quo nomine etiam invidia; venit; nec non robur, quale orci est, ignem & flammam Cant. VIII. 6. tribuit; & Spiritum adversus carnem concupiscere, atque ita adversus carnales affectus insurgere, neque minùs fortes motus animæ imprimere, quàm qui in carne fortissimi sunt; velut invidia testatur; Sicut igitur anima invidiâ laborans: ita anima, quæ gloriam Dei & salutem proximi desiderat, quandam colliquationem, macerationem, tabefactionem habet. Humanum dico, propter infirmitatem carnis vestræ; Sicut exhibuistis membra vestra serva immunditiæ & iniquitati ad iniquitatem, (ad repugnandum Legi) ita nunc exhibete membra vestra justitiæ ad sanctificationem, Rom. VI. 19. Ego corpus meum contundo, sugillo, in servitutem redigo, 1. Cor. IX. 27. Porro Scriptura & perfectionem præcipit, Matth. V. 48. VI. 10. Genes. XVII. 1. Hebr. VI. 1. & Ecclesiam, sponsam Christi, perfectam ejus Cant. VI. 8. appellat; & fideles in Christo factos divites esse in omni sermone, & in omni cognitione &c. 1. Cor. I. 5. &c. asserit, & quosdam perfectos esse, ibid. II. 6. Phil. III. 15. Hebr. V. 14. profitetur. Sed duplex scilicet perfectio est, una peccati omnis expers; altera, expers fuci & duplicis cordis; & peccati etiam, quatenus illud vel imputatur ad damnationem, vel dominatur homini: sed non peccati illius, quod post regenerationem in homine habitans Spiritu Dei magis magisque mortificatur, donec unà cum corpore peccati deponatur. Illa patriæ & metæ; hæc viæ & stadii est. Ad illam aspiramus, donec ad brabeum coelestis vocationis pertingamus; hanc in vita hac, quisque pro modulo regenerationis assequimur; sed ejusmodi, ut pro tentationum carnis ratione incrementi & decrementi capax sit. Illa omnibus modis numerisque consummata charitas Dei, cum homine carnem resíduam habente est; hæc sinceritas, spiritualis castitas, & integritas est ejus, qui solum Deum diligit, nec duobus dominis servit, nec adulterino amore pallet; nec perversus & eligens, quod respuit; & respuens, quod eligit, est; de quo dicitur Qui ambulat integrè, salvus erit & qui perversus duabus viis incedit, cadet in una, Prov. XXVIII. 18. Illa coronatur & brabeon habet; hæc luctatur & currit ut apprehendat, 1. Cor. IX. 24. 25. Illa Cœli est, in quo abolita carne, infirmitate, peccato, luctâ, defectu omni Deus erit omnia in omnibus, ibid. XV. 28. Quam licet in hac vita non consequimur, Deus tamen, ceu scopum proponit, & sectari, & ad eam, ceu brabeon viribus omnibus contendere, (Phil. III. 14.) jubet, quia ad eam consequendam ab æterno in Christo electi sumus, Ephes. I. 4. & in hac vita præparamur, ut ceu casta sponsa uni viro Christo sistamur, 2. Cor. XI. 2. & Deus periti pictoris adinstar, lineamenta ducentis, ac demum imaginem perfectam iis inducentis, gratiæ suæ lineamenta animæ regenitorum in hac vita imprimit, at Spiritus S. penicillo in altera vita planè plenéque exprimit, & ad summum splendorem atque pulchritudinem perducit. Quædam etiam Scripturæ loca perfectionem posteriorem comparatam, virorum puta & adultorum cum pueris comparatorum, insinuant. Ex quibus, quæcunque de perfectione & perfectis Scripturæ habent, nullo negotio intelliguntur. Scripturas enim non collidere, sed piè dextréque conciliare convenit. Jam & præcepta Dei non sunt gravia, Matth. XI. 30. 1. Joh. V. 3. & extant exempla eorum, qui Deum toto corde dilexerunt, & in omnibus præceptis Dei ambularunt. Sed hæc ad amussim & legis exacta Scripturis reliquis prorsus repugnarent, at secundum Evangelii amicissimè conspirant. Nam credenti, & per fidem in Christo existenti, omnia possibilia sunt, Marc. IX. 23. Omnia valeo in Christo me corroborante, Phil. IV. 13. Evangelium enim & gratiam regenerantem promittit, & remissionem peccatorum, quæ propter Christum non imputantur, prædicat, & Dei Patris in qualicunque, sincera modò & obedientia nostra, nec non beneplacitum in nobis propter Christum testatur. Ita igitur dilectio Dei ex toto corde &ambulatio in omnibus præceptis Dei sinceritati, integritati, contentioni & studio fidelium attestans, eorundem perfectionem, sed posteriorem illam, non priorem arguit; & præsuppositia natura corrupta atque gratia sanctificante; resipiscentiam sinceram firmo & minimè ambiguo animi judicio & propósito, siti & fame justitiæ eximio zelo, studio ac labore actam, qualem qui habet, studiosus appellatur, significat. Cujus etiam virtus est, toto corde contra connatam vitiositatem pugnare, toto corde se humiliare, sua peccata sine dolo confiteri, & remissionem eorum humiliter expetere. Ad vias enim Dei, in quibus sancti ambulant, etiam orationem & humilem peccati confessionem pertinere, licet ad eas peccata non pertineant, scitè Augustinus dixit. Jam & encomia illa magnifica regenitorum, cujusmodi sunt, quòd ex Deo nati sint, 1. Joh. III, 9. arbores justitiæ & plantatio Domini ad decus ejus, Esaj. LXI. 3. in quibus gloriatur, ibid. XLIX. 3. populus Dei peculiaris, Exod. XIX. 6. Deut. VII. 6. Spontaneus, Psal. CX. 3. electum genus, Regale Sacerdotium, populus sanctus, &c. 1. Pet. II.
units.tr: That the one who sins is of the devil, and that the regenerate, because the seed of God remains in them, do not sin, ne peccent. The regenerate man rules over sin, and he who recognises his weaknesses laments them and wrestles with them constantly through the Spirit of God. Nor does the doctrine of the imperfection of regeneration therefore encourage licence to sin. For St John, while acknowledging sin in the regenerate (1 John 1:8, 10), immediately added in chapter 2:1 that he had written this to his little children, ne peccent. A frank confession of the sin that dwells within is therefore so far from being a cause of sinning that it is rather a barrier against it, just as the one who knows his open enemy is more cautious than the one who ignores a hidden one. Shall we then suppose that the doctrine which calls us to a contest with sin, and bids us resist the flesh and crucify and mortify the old man, is an advocate of sin? Rather, the weakness of the flesh, the evil that clings to us, and our temptations are a strong incitement, an arousal and a certain provocation not to sin. For the regenerate man, and the love that is in him, ought to have speed, readiness and zeal. Do you think that Scripture speaks in vain when it says: "The Spirit who has willed to dwell in us lusts toward envy"? (James 4:5). For it is not in vain that Scripture ascribes to love zeal, a word which also means envy, and likewise strength such as that of the grave, fire and flame (Song 8:6); and that the Spirit lusts against the flesh, and so rises up against carnal affections and impresses motions of the soul no less strong than those which are most powerful in the flesh, as envy bears witness. Just as a soul labouring under envy is in a certain melting, wasting and consuming, so the soul that longs for the glory of God and the salvation of its neighbour suffers a similar wasting. I speak in human terms, because of the weakness of your flesh: as you once presented your members as slaves to uncleanness and iniquity, leading to iniquity (in opposition to the Law), so now present your members as slaves to righteousness, leading to sanctification (Rom. 6:19). I beat my body and bring it into subjection (1 Cor. 9:27). Further, Scripture also commands perfection (Matt. 5:48; 6:10; Gen. 17:1; Heb. 6:1), calls the Church, the bride of Christ, his perfect one (Song 6:8), and affirms that believers in Christ were made rich in all utterance and in all knowledge etc. (1 Cor. 1:5), and professes that some are perfect (ibid. 2:6; Phil. 3:15; Heb. 5:14). But there is clearly a twofold perfection: one free of all sin, the other free of guile and double-heartedness, and free of sin in so far as it is either imputed for condemnation or rules over a man; but not free of that sin which, dwelling in a man after regeneration, is more and more mortified by the Spirit of God until it is laid aside together with the body of sin. The former is the goal of the homeland; the latter belongs to the way and the race. We strive toward the former until we attain the prize of the heavenly calling; the latter we attain in this life, each according to the measure of his regeneration, yet of such a kind that it is capable of increase and decrease according to the manner of the flesh's temptations. The former is the perfect love of God, which is complete in every way and by every measure, when a man still has residual flesh; the latter is the sincerity, spiritual chastity and integrity of the one who loves God alone, serves not two masters, and does not grow pale with adulterous love; who is not perverse, choosing what he rejects and rejecting what he chooses. Of him it is said: "He who walks in integrity shall be saved," and "he who walks in two ways, perverse, shall fall in one" (Prov. 28:18). The former is crowned and has the prize; the latter wrestles and runs that he may lay hold (1 Cor. 9:24–25). The former belongs to heaven, where the flesh, weakness, sin, struggle and every defect having been abolished, God will be all in all (ibid. 15:28). Although we do not attain this in this life, God nevertheless sets it before us as a goal, and commands us to pursue it, and to strive for it with all our strength as for the prize (Phil. 3:14), because we were chosen in Christ from eternity to attain it (Eph. 1:4), and in this life we are prepared to be presented to Christ, one husband, as a chaste virgin (2 Cor. 11:2). God, like a skilled painter who first draws the outlines and at last brings the finished image, impresses the outlines of his grace on the souls of the regenerate in this life; the Holy Spirit, with his brush, paints them fully and perfectly in the other life, and brings them to the highest splendour and beauty. Certain passages of Scripture also hint at a later perfection, compared with the perfection of men, that is, of adults, as opposed to children. From these, whatever Scripture says about perfection and the perfect is understood without difficulty. For it is fitting to make Scripture not clash with itself, but to reconcile it piously and rightly. Now, the commandments of God are not grievous (Matt. 11:30; 1 John 5:3), and there are examples of those who loved God with all their heart and walked in all the commandments of God. But these things, if taken as exact to the measure and exact demands of the law, would be wholly at odds with the rest of Scripture; yet according to the Gospel they agree most harmoniously. For all things are possible to him who believes (Mark 9:23), and through faith in Christ: I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me (Phil. 4:13). The Gospel promises regenerating grace and proclaims the remission of sins, which for Christ's sake are not imputed, and testifies that God the Father accepts our obedience, however imperfect it may be if only it is sincere, and his good pleasure toward us for Christ's sake. Thus the love of God with the whole heart and the walking in all the commandments of God, attesting the sincerity, integrity, endeavour and zeal of believers, indicate their perfection, but the later perfection, not the earlier, presupposing a corrupt nature and sanctifying grace. It signifies a sincere repentance, carried out with a firm and unambiguous judgment and purpose of mind, with a thirst and hunger for righteousness, and with exceptional zeal, study and labour; one who has this is called studious. It is also the virtue of one who fights against his inborn vice with his whole heart, humbles himself with his whole heart, confesses his sins without deceit, and humbly seeks their forgiveness. For, as Augustine rightly said, prayer and humble confession of sin belong to the ways of God in which the saints walk, although sins do not belong to those ways. Again, those magnificent commendations of the regenerate, such as that they are born of God (1 John 3:9), trees of righteousness and the planting of the Lord for his glory (Isa. 61:3), in which he glories (ibid. 49:3), a peculiar people of God (Exod. 19:6; Deut. 7:6), willing (Ps. 110:3), a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy people, etc. (1 Pet. 2:9),

units.la: 1. Petr. II. 9. imago & gloria Dei, 1. Cor. XI. 7. Sanctum semen, Esaj. VI. 13. Templum Dei, 1. Cor. III. 16. Ecclesia Dei vivi, 1. Timoth. III. 15. &c, ejusmodi sunt, ut illa non à se, vel in se primò, sed in Christo capite, cui per fidem in hac vita conformantur, & cujus justitiæ & acquisitorum bonorum cœlestium participes sunt, habeant. Sicut enim per rubrum vitrum aspicientibus rubra omnia videntur: ita anima fidelium per sanguinem Christi aspecta pulcherrima apparet. Tum pulchritudinem illam à Spiritu S. regenerante, & ad imaginem Dei renovante, sed affectam tantum & adumbratam in hac vita, expressam & perfectam in altera, quando Christus veniet, ut in Sanctis suis glorificetur, & in fidelibus suis admirabilis fiat, 2. Thess. I. 10. & Deus omnia in omnibus erit, 1. Cor. XV. 28. habent. Hic Spiritus S. primitiæ sunt, Rom. VIII. 23. ibi plena messis erit. Sic verò gloriosi sunt in Christo, ut in se ipsis etiam pudendi sint. O Domine, tua est justitia, & nobis convenit pudor faciei, Dan. IX. 7. Præterea etiam Christi redemptio, propter & per quam regeneramur, perfecta equidem est; sed ejusdem applicatio & efficacia hac in vita ad perfectionis suæ statigium non assurgit. Aliàs ne mortis quidem necessitas regenitis incumberet: & regeneratio cœlestem eorundem gloriam sine ulla mora post se traheret. Satis est ad gloriam meriti Christi, quòd sanguis ejus peccati aculeum simul semelque sustulit, & mortis maledictæ periculum omne avertit; licet integrum decus & pristinæ amplitudinis ornamenta in altera demum vita restituat. Nec laudem alexipharmaci minuit, quòd vim veneni simul extinguit, & periculum mortis avertit; at plenam sanitatem paulatim restituit: nec de victoriæ patratæ gloria quicquam delibat, quòd & vulnera adhuc hiant, & fructus ejus pleni serò se proferunt: nec similiter de gloria meriti Christi pretiosissimi quidquam decerpit, quòd eo, quo diximus, modo asseratur, inprimis cùm operatio ipsa sapientissima, Deo gloriosa, & nobis proficua sit, quod abunde supra confirmavimus. Denique S. Paulus nos peccato mortuos, in eodem vivere porro debere negat, Rom. VI. 2. non hoc innuens, quòd sine peccato hanc vitam mortalium quisquam transigere possit; sed quòd fideles, peccato quippe mortui, hoc est, ab ejus damnatione & dominio liberati, ut eam non magis, quàm mortuus digressi à se Spiritus vitalem operationem ullam, sentiant, non amplius in peccato vivere, hoc est, uti ipse S. Paulus explicat, ejus dominio se subjicere v. 12. se ipsos servos peccato ad ejus obedientiam sistere, v. 16. peccato servire, v. 17. passiones peccati efficaces ad fructificandum morti fovere, ibid. VII. 5. debeant. Aliud enim longè est, non sine peccato esse, aliud in peccato vivere. Illud est peccati reliquias pati, & cum iis per Spiritum S. belligerari: hoc peccato cum omni cogitationum, cupiditatum, voluntatis, propositi, ardoris, animæ & corporis virium contentione & studio addictissimè servire, quæ non tam vera vita, quàm mors in peccatis est.
units.tr: the image and glory of God (1 Cor. 11:7), a holy seed (Isa. 6:13), the temple of God (1 Cor. 3:16), the Church of the living God (1 Tim. 3:15), etc., are such that they have them not from themselves or in themselves first, but in Christ the head, into whose image they are conformed in this life through faith, and of whose righteousness and acquired heavenly goods they are partakers. For just as to those who look through red glass everything appears red, so the souls of believers, seen through the blood of Christ, appear most beautiful. They have that beauty from the Holy Spirit who regenerates and renews them to the image of God, but it is only begun and shadowed in this life, and expressed and perfected in the next, when Christ comes to be glorified in his saints and to be admired in all who believe (2 Thess. 1:10), and God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28). Here the Holy Spirit is the firstfruits (Rom. 8:23); there the harvest will be full. Thus believers are so glorious in Christ that in themselves they are even to be ashamed. O Lord, righteousness is yours, and to us belongs open shame (Dan. 9:7). Moreover, the redemption of Christ, by and through which we are regenerated, is indeed perfect; but its application and efficacy in this life do not rise to the summit of its perfection. Otherwise, the necessity of death would not even press upon the regenerate, and regeneration would draw their heavenly glory after it without any delay. It is enough for the glory of the merit of Christ that his blood at once and together removed the sting of sin and averted every danger of accursed death, even though in the other life he restores the whole honour and the adornments of his former greatness. Nor does the praise of an antidote diminish because it at once extinguishes the force of the poison and averts the danger of death, but gradually restores full health; nor does it take anything from the glory of the victory won, because the wounds still gape and its fruits appear full only later. Likewise, it takes nothing from the glory of the merit of the most precious Christ that it is asserted in the way we have said, especially since the operation itself is most wise, glorious to God and profitable to us, as we have amply confirmed above. Finally, St Paul denies that we who are dead to sin ought to live any longer in it (Rom. 6:2), not implying that anyone can pass this mortal life without sin, but that believers, being dead to sin, that is, freed from its condemnation and dominion, should no longer live in sin, so that, just as a dead man has no vital operation from a spirit departed from him, they should feel nothing of it. St Paul himself explains what this means: they should not submit themselves to its dominion (v. 12), should not present themselves as slaves to sin for obedience (v. 16), should not serve sin (v. 17), and should not nurture the sinful passions that are effective to bear fruit for death (ibid. 7:5). For it is one thing not to be without sin, and quite another to live in sin. The former is to suffer the remnants of sin and to wage war against them through the Holy Spirit; the latter is to serve sin most devotedly, with all the striving and zeal of thoughts, desires, will, purpose, ardour, and the powers of soul and body. That is not so much true life as death in sins.

units.la: LXXIX. Vocationem esse hominis ad Deum & communionem ejus adductionem, sæpe jam diximus. Nulla porro communio cum Deo esse, nisi in Christo potest neque in Christo esse nisi per fidem, per quam cum eo ad justitiam & adoptionem filiorum complantamur, possumus: Unde qui credunt, per fidem sibi donatam Christum dono accepisse recte intelliguntur, Joh. I. 12. Vocatio igitur fidei largitio & donatio est, qua donata homo Deo vocanti veluti respondet. Pro te (tuo nomine tuisque verbis) dixit cor meum: Quærite faciem meam. Faciem tuam, Jehova quæro, Psal. XXVII. 8. Revertimini, filii adversantes, curabo aversationes vestras: Ecce nos accedimus ad te, quia tu es Jehova, Deus noster, Jerem. III. 22. Dicam, populus meus ipse est: & ipse dicet, Jehova Deus meus est. Hos. II. 23. Zach. XIII. 9. Unde καλεῖν vocare, & κλησις vocatio sæpe in Scripturis pro fide donatione accipitur, & κλητοι pro fide donatis. Abrahamus credidit Deo, qui vivificat mortuos, & vocat, quæ non sunt, velut quæ sunt, Rom. IV. 17. Fidelis est Deus, per quem vocati estis, in communionem Filii ejus Jesu Christi, 1. Cor. I. 9. Vocatis Judæis & Græcis Christus est potentia & sapientia Dei, ib. v. 24. quod mox v. 30. per τὸ ἐν ἡ Θεῷ εἶναι ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ex Deo esse in Christo Jesu exprimitur. Alibi: Hæc πεισμονὴ obedientia non est ex vocante vos, Gal. V. 8. Ut sciatis, quæ sit spes vocationis vestræ, Ephes. I. 18.19. Fidelis est, qui vocavit vos, qui etiam faciet, 1. Thessal. V. 24. Nempe Deus vocans promissionem gratiæ proponit. Homo respondens promissionem fide accipit, & promissam sibi gratiam applicat; ut ita Dei vocantis, & hominis per fidem respondentis partes ejusmodi Syllogismo aptè connectantur: Quicunque crediderit, justificabitur & salvabitur. Ego credo. Ergo justificabor & salvabor. Major Dei vocantis: Minor hominis respondentis est. De fide ergo, vocatione respondente, & per eandem homini donata dicendi hic locus est.
units.tr: LXXIX. We have often said already that the calling of a man is his summons to God and to communion with Him. There can be no communion with God except in Christ, and we cannot be in Christ except through faith, by which we are grafted into him for righteousness and the adoption of sons. Hence those who believe are rightly understood to have received Christ, given to them through the faith bestowed on them, John 1:12. Vocation, then, is the bestowal and gift of faith, by which the man who has been given faith answers God's call. My heart said on your behalf (in your name and in your words): Seek my face. Your face, Jehovah, I seek, Ps. 27:8. Return, rebellious sons, and I will heal your backslidings. Behold, we come to you, for you are Jehovah our God, Jer. 3:22. I will say, "He is my people," and he will say, "Jehovah is my God", Hos. 2:23; Zech. 13:9. Hence καλεῖν [to call] and κλῆσις [calling] are often taken in Scripture for the gift of faith, and κλητοί [the called] for those who have been given faith. Abraham believed God, who gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they were, Rom. 4:17. God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 1:9. To those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power and wisdom of God, ibid. v. 24; this is expressed a little later, at v. 30, through τὸ ἐν Θεῷ εἶναι ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ [to be of God in Christ Jesus]. Elsewhere: this persuasion [πεισμονή] does not come from him who calls you, Gal. 5:8. That you may know what is the hope of your calling, Eph. 1:18–19. Faithful is he who calls you, who also will do it, 1 Thess. 5:24. Clearly God, calling, sets forth the promise of grace; man, answering, receives the promise by faith and applies the grace promised to himself. So the parts of God calling and of man answering through faith are aptly joined in this syllogism: Whoever believes will be justified and saved. I believe. Therefore I shall be justified and saved. The major premise is God's calling; the minor is man's answer. So it is here that we should speak of faith, the answering calling, and of the faith given to man through that calling.

units.la: LXXX. Fidem proprie dictorum & conventorum constantiam & veritatem Cicero definit.
units.tr: LXXX. Cicero defines fidelity as the constancy and truth of things said and agreed upon.

units.la: Quæ cum fieri debeant, inde fidei nomen esse putant. Hinc dare, servare, frangere fidem: Græca, Punica fides. Neque alienus ille à Scriptura significatus est. Periit האמונה fides, & excisa est ab ore ipsorum, Jerem. VII. 28. באמונה in fide, seu veracitate faciebant, 2. Reg. XII. 15. Quid enim, si non crediderunt quidam? An incredulitas illorum Dei πίστιν fidem irritam reddet? Rom. III. 3. Ipsa doctrina Evangelii propter promissorum veracitatem & constantiam πίστις fides, Actor. VI. 7. Gal. I. 23. 1. Tim. IV. 1. &c. appellatur, & πιστὸς fidelis sermo, ibid. I. 15. sermonem veracem; quin & cùm de persona usurpatur, non tantum credentem, sed etiam in fide manentem, constantem, perinde ut Hebræum אמן significat. Sed plerunque & in hoc argumento fere semper Scriptura voce ea improprio & sensu passivo utitur, persuasionem firmam de dicti vel facti alicujus veritate significans: licet ei etiam activus sensus constantiæ involvi possit. In Prophetarum sermonibus אמונה, אמן & האמין hoc sensu frequentantur, velut: האמין Credidit Abraham Jehovæ, Genes. XV. 6. צדיק באמונתו יחיה Justus fide sua vivet, Habac. II. 4. Conf. Psal. II. 12. Esaj. VII. 9. XXVIII. 16. LIII. 11. 2. Reg. XII. 15. Descendit ab אמן gestare, gerere sinu, quod אמנה τροφὸς, θῆτες nutricis (Ruth. IV. 16.) curatoris, nutritii & אמנה nutricis(Ruth.IV.16.) est,
units.tr: Since these things ought to be done, they think the name fides [faith] comes from this. Hence the phrases to give, keep, and break faith, and Punic faith, Greek faith. Nor is this meaning foreign to Scripture. Faith [האמונה] has perished and has been cut off from their mouth, Jer. 7:28. They acted in faithfulness [באמונה], 2 Kings 12:15. For what if some did not believe? Will their unbelief make the faith [πίστις] of God void? Rom. 3:3. The very doctrine of the Gospel is called faith [πίστις] because of the truthfulness and constancy of its promises, Acts 6:7; Gal. 1:23; 1 Tim. 4:1, and so on; and a faithful saying [πιστὸς λόγος], ibid. 1:15, means a true saying. Indeed, when the word is used of a person, it means not only one who believes but one who remains in the faith, steadfast, just as the Hebrew אמן signifies. But in most cases, and almost always in this matter, Scripture uses this word in an improper and passive sense, signifying a firm persuasion of the truth of some saying or deed, though an active sense of constancy may also be included. In the sayings of the Prophets, אמונה, אמן and האמין are frequent in this sense, for example: Abraham believed [האמין] in Jehovah, Gen. 15:6; The just shall live by his faith [צדיק באמונתו יחיה], Hab. 2:4. Compare Ps. 2:12; Isa. 7:9; 28:16; 53:11; 2 Kings 12:15. It is derived from אמן [to bear, carry in the bosom], which means a nurse, a guardian, a foster-father, and אמנה [a nurse] (Ruth 4:16).

units.la: Vocanti Deo homo vocatus respondet per fidem. est, cui respondet יְמֵא ἐγκάλπι puer in sinu gestatus, lactens, Prov.VIII. 30. Est ergo יְמֵא se rejicere gestandum velut in veritatem & potentiam alterius, niti alio, committere se alteri; non sine πίστει fiducia in eo, ut vox ea non tantum testimonium alterius recipere, sed etiam ei, ut firmo certóque confidere significet. Frequentes, inprimis Græcæ voces conjugatæ sunt, πίστις, πιστὸς, πιστεύειν fides, fidelis seu credens, & credere, ἀ πεῖθομαι persuadeo, & hoc ab Hebraeo הָמִן quod in Pihel suadeo, persuadeo significat. Prima habitum, altera eum, qui habitum πίστεως fidei habet: tertia πεῖξιν operatio-nem, imò etiam ἔργον opus Joh.VI.29. significat.
units.tr: To God calling, man called responds through faith. To this corresponds יְמֵא [a child carried in the bosom, nursing], Prov. 8:30. So יְמֵא means to give oneself over to be carried, as it were, into the truth and power of another, to lean on another, to commit oneself to another; not without πίστει [trust] in him, so that the word signifies not only receiving another's testimony but also trusting in him as firm and certain. The Greek words of the same root are frequent, especially πίστις, πιστός, πιστεύειν [faith, faithful, to believe], that is, faithful or believing, and to believe; and πείθομαι [to be persuaded, to persuade], which comes from the Hebrew הָמִן, which in the Piel means to persuade. The first denotes a habit, the second the person who has the habit of πίστις [faith]; the third denotes πεῖξιν [an action], and even ἔργον [a work], John 6:29.

units.la: LXXXI. Ex his de homonymia vocis Fidei liquet. Non male enim Augustinus fidem, quæ creditur, & qua creditur, distinxit. Illa proprie & sensu activo τὸ πιστευόμενον id quod creditur, significat. Ita Evangelii doctrinam utpote, πίστν λόγον fide dignum sermonem 1. Tim. I. 15. nomine πίστεως fidei venire, supra citatis locis ostendimus. Et clarè S. Paulus: Mia πίστις Una fides, Ephes.IV. 5. ἀπὸ ἐλθεῖν τὴν πίστιν antequam veniret fides sub lege custoditi sumus, Gal. III.23. ubi fides tum Christum ceu πίστιν & fidei objectum, tum Legem Christi, Evangelium, quod ob repraesentationem promissionum & consummationem omnis doctrinæ fidei, seu rei maximè credendæ nomine venit; significat. Haec improprie & sensu passivo, tum πεκμήριον seu argumentum rei credendæ fidem faciens: tum habitum, vel actum mentis, quo de veritate testimonii persuasi eidem credunt & confidunt, significat. Argumentum rei credendæ fidei nomine venit. Act. XVII.31. Judicabit mundum in justitia per virum, quem definivit, πίστιν ... πᾶσι de quo fidem omnibus fecit, ex mortuis eum resuscitans. Ubi resuscitatio ex mortuis, argumentum infallibile Christi judicis constituti, πίστεως nomine venit. Habitum vel actum mentis, quo persuasi de veritate testimonii eidem credunt, passim significat, qui etiam significatus, hujus loci est.
units.tr: LXXXI. From this the ambiguity of the word faith is clear. Augustine rightly distinguished the faith which is believed [quae creditur] from the faith by which one believes [qua creditur]. The former properly denotes, in the active sense, τὸ πιστευόμενον [that which is believed]. Thus, as we have shown in the passages cited above, the doctrine of the Gospel, as πιστὸς λόγος [a faithful word], a saying worthy of trust, 1 Tim. 1:15, is called by the name of faith. And St. Paul says plainly: One faith [Μία πίστις], Eph. 4:5; Before faith came, we were kept under the law [πρὸ τοῦ ἐλθεῖν τὴν πίστιν], Gal. 3:23, where faith signifies both Christ, as πίστις and the object of faith, and the law of Christ, the Gospel, which is called by the name of faith, because it presents the promises and is the sum of all the doctrine to be believed most of all. These things, in an improper and passive sense, signify either the proof or argument that makes a thing believable, or the habit or act of the mind by which, persuaded of the truth of the testimony, people believe and trust in it. Argument of a thing to be believed comes under the name of faith: Acts 17:31, He will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has appointed, having given assurance [πίστιν] to all men, by raising him from the dead. Here the resurrection from the dead, an infallible argument that Christ has been appointed judge, comes under the name of faith [πίστεως]. The habit or act of mind, by which those persuaded of the truth of the testimony believe in it, is signified everywhere, and this meaning is the one relevant to this place.

units.la: LXXXII. In universum ergo fides est πίστις (Gal. V.8.) seu persuasio de veritate à sensibus remota per testimonium Dei revelantis. Quædam enim non remota à sensibus nostris interioribus & exterioribus, nobis ipsis testibus; alia à sensibus nostris remota testimonia aliena cognoscimus. Illa πίστις & sciri, haec πίστευε & credi vulgò dicuntur. Sed haec vocum differentia non tam à Scriptura, in qua πίστις & πιστὸς promiscuè accipitur; quàm à Philosophis est. Res ipsa dubitationem non habet. Nam etiam S. Paulus fidem ἔλεγχον τōν μὴ βλεπομένων demonstrationem eorum, quæ non videntur, Hebr.XI.1. & Bernhardus Consid. l. 5. eandem voluntariam & certam veritatis nec dum propalatæ prælibationem dixerunt. Possunt tamen & illa, quæ sciuntur, fidei Divinæ objici, nempe si vel rem scibilem seu sine testimonio demonstrabilem Deus suo testimonio confirmet, & demonstrationis viam & certitudinē in verbo suo aperiat; quod haud raro facit; vel Divino testimonio, quod Deus de rebus, quæ sola revelatione cognoscuntur, excitati, & ad id recipiendum amore veritatis inclinati mentem haesitantem, & opinionibus obrutam rerum, quæ cum rerum revelatarum conjunctæ sunt, investigatio-ni intendimus. Ita fide νοῦμεν animadvertimus, secula verbo Dei concinnata esse, Hebr.XI.3. Ubi fides revelationi Dei de creatione omnium ex nihilo innixa causa directrix & velut ἀνάλογισμὸν animadversionis & consideratio nis rerum invisibilium per ea, quæ facta sunt, (Rom.I.20.) statuitur: quia ea Deo revelanti inhærens etiam νόησιν & ζωὴν circa id, quod de Deo naturaliter cognosci potest, ad Dei sapientiam perfectius cognoscendam, & mentem ab errore liberandam, operatur. Neque adeò fides rationem perimit, sed excitat; non excæcat, sed illuminat; non premit, sed ab ignorantia erroribus & conscientiis liberat. De quo adversus Scholasticos, aliósque sic fidem à scientia separantes, quasi nulla utriusque connexio esset, & fides sapientiam Dei in testimonio ejus contemplandam procul à se amandaret, plura diximus. Sed maximè tamen fides circa ea occupatur, quæ rationem superant, & vel lacessere, atque cum ea altercari videntur: in quibus fidei nobilissima victoria est. Abrahamus contra spem sub spe credidit, & minimè infirmus fide, non consideravit corpus suum ipsius jam emortuum, Roman. IV.18.19.
units.tr: LXXXII. In general, then, faith [πίστις] (Gal. 5:8) is persuasion of the truth of something remote from the senses, through the testimony of God revealing it. For some things are not remote from our inner and outer senses, which are witnesses to us ourselves; other things we know through testimonies of others, remote from our senses. The former are commonly said to be known [scire], the latter believed [credere]. But this difference of words comes less from Scripture, in which πίστις and πιστός are used interchangeably, than from the Philosophers. The thing itself is not in doubt. For St. Paul calls faith ἔλεγχος τῶν μὴ βλεπομένων [the proof of things not seen], Heb. 11:1, and Bernard, in Consid. book 5, calls it a voluntary and certain foretaste of a truth not yet revealed. Yet those things which are known can also be set before divine faith: namely, if God confirms by his testimony a thing that is knowable, that is, demonstrable without testimony, and opens in his Word the way and certainty of the demonstration, which he often does; or when, by the divine testimony that God gives about things known only by revelation, we are roused and, inclined by love of the truth to receive it, we apply our hesitant mind, overwhelmed by opinions, to the investigation of things connected with the things revealed. Thus by faith we understand [νοοῦμεν] that the ages were framed by the word of God, Heb. 11:3. Here faith, resting on God's revelation of the creation of all things out of nothing, is set down as the guiding cause and, as it were, the ἀναλογισμός [reasoning] of consideration and reflection on invisible things through the things that have been made (Rom. 1:20), because faith, adhering to God revealing, also works νόησις [understanding] and ζωή [life] concerning what can be known naturally about God, to know the wisdom of God more perfectly and to free the mind from error. Nor does faith therefore destroy reason; it stirs it up. It does not blind, but illuminates; it does not oppress, but frees from ignorance, errors, and troubled consciences. On this we have said much against the Scholastics, and others who so separate faith from knowledge, as if there were no connection between them, and as if faith drove away from itself the contemplation of the wisdom of God in his testimony. But faith is especially occupied with those things that surpass reason, and that seem to assail it and to contend with it; in these is faith's most noble victory. Abraham, against hope, believed in hope, and, not weak in faith, did not consider his own body, already dead, Rom. 4:18–19.

units.la: LXXXIII. Fides respicit testem ejusque veracitatem, scientiam infallibilem & testimonium, qui non alius esse quàm Deus potest, utpote solus ἀληθὴς verus, Rom. III.4. Σοφὸς sapiens, 1.Tim. I. 17. ἀψευδὴς mentiri nescius Tit.I.2. est, & testimonio alio non indiget, Joh. V.34. & omnia, vitam & mortem in manu sua habet, & plenus gratia & veritate est, Joh. I.14. Unicus enim is fidei dominus est, juxta illud: Unus Dominus, una fides, Ephes.IV.5. Ideo, remoto omnia alio, profitemur nos credere in Deum, Joh. XIV.1. Rom. X.14. Licet enim ex usu Hebraeo credere in etiam Prophetis Exod.XIV.31.2.Paral.XX.20. sano sensu tribuatur, & ex Hebraismo illo Symbolum Nicaenum εἰς in Ecclesiam Sanctam &c: credere jubeat; tamen phrasis illa non temere affectanda est, ne Divinam Ecclesiae vel cuiquam homini authoritatem cum Pontificiis tribuere videamur. Neque enim ulli homini, vel Angelo per se certa fides haberi potest. Non homini, quia de suo loquens mendax est: & etiamsi vera ac Divina loquitur, tamen ex terra, ut minister & discipulus loquitur, Joh. III.31. Non Angelus, quia; si malus & tenebrarum is est, mendax est; si bonus & lucis, strictura lucis per ipsos, ut servos & ministros, nobis administratur. Ecce servis suis non confidit, & in Angelis suis ponit תחלה lucem, Job. IV.18. In Deum verò fides fertur ut ἀληθὴς veracem & ἀξιόπιστον fide per se dignum: adeóque ut ἡ ἀληθεια veracitas Dei, eáque prima & independens, immutabilis sola causa sit, ob quam ei creditur, & credi debet. Qui testimonium ejus recipit, obsignavit, quòd verax sit, Joh.III.33. Unde fidei falsum nullo modo subesse potest. Neque enim vel Abrahamus jussus mactare filium, vel Ezechias, indicta sibi morte, falsum credere jussi sunt; quia uterque ex mandato Dei, quid officii sui sit, colligere, & hoc solum firmiter credere, non eventum animo praecipere debuit.
units.tr: LXXXIII. Faith looks to the witness, to his truthfulness, and to his infallible knowledge and testimony. The witness can be none other than God, who is alone true [ἀληθὴς], as in Rom. 3.4; wise [Σοφὸς], as in 1 Tim. 1.17; and unable to lie [ἀψευδὴς], as in Titus 1.2. He needs no other testimony (John 5.34), he holds life and death in his hand, and he is full of grace and truth (John 1.14). For he is the sole Lord of faith, according to that saying: One Lord, one faith (Eph. 4.5). Therefore, setting aside everything else, we profess that we believe in God (John 14.1; Rom. 10.14). For although, by Hebrew usage, to believe in is also rightly applied in a sound sense to the prophets (Exod. 14.31; 2 Chron. 20.20), and although the Nicene Creed, by that same Hebraism, bids us believe in the holy Church [εἰς in Ecclesiam Sanctam], that phrase is still not to be rashly adopted, lest we seem, with the Papists, to ascribe divine authority to the Church or to any man. For no certain faith can be placed in any man or angel in himself. Not in man, because a man speaking of his own is a liar; and even when he speaks true and divine things, he speaks from the earth [ex terra], as a minister and disciple (John 3.31). Not in an angel, because if he is evil and of darkness he is a liar, and if he is good and of light, the rays of that light are administered to us through them as servants and ministers. Behold, he puts no trust in his servants, and charges his angels with folly (Job 4.18). Faith, however, is directed to God as true [ἀληθὴς], as truthful and worthy of faith in himself. Thus the truth [ἡ ἀληθεια] of God, which is first and independent, is the sole unchangeable cause on account of which he is believed and ought to be believed. He who receives his testimony has set his seal that God is true (John 3.33). Hence falsehood can in no way underlie faith. For neither Abraham, bidden to slay his son, nor Hezekiah, told that he was to die, was bidden to believe a falsehood. Each, from God's command, ought to gather what his duty was and to believe this alone firmly, not to anticipate the outcome in his mind.

units.la: LXXXIV. Fides Legalis vel Evangelica est. Illa persuasio de veritate cujusvis testimonii Divinitus revelati: hæc de veritate testimonii nii particularis de Christo Salvatore credentis, non in Lege, sed in solo Evangelio patefacti, est. Quæ non sic distinguuntur, ut nihil commune habeant. Nam Evangelica supposita jam revelatione Christi Salvatoris credentium, vi ipsius Legis, quamlibet revelationem testimonii Divini credere jubentis, obligat. Unde intellectu proclive est, quòd positivè increduli non tam vi Evangelii, quàm ipsius Legis, justæ damnationi subsint. Differentia verò in eo sita est, quòd lex Christum non revelat, adeóque simpliciter & absolutè fidem in eum non præcipit: at Evangelium Christum revelat, & fidem in ipsum, vi ipsius legis, fidem hominum testimonio cuivis Divino idoneè patefacto subjicientis, præcipit. Si per Angelos dictus sermo (Legis) firmus extitit, & omnis transgressio & inobedientia justam retributionem accepit; quomodo effugiemus nos tantam salutem negligentes, quæ à Domino dici cœpta, ab iis, qui audiverunt, in nos confirmata est? Hebr. II. 2. 3. Illa opus Legis est, & ad ea opera pertinet, de quibus dictum est: Qui fecerit illa, vivet in iis, adeóque ad fœdus operum pertinet; sed non justificat, nisi legaliter perfecta, & cum operibus, quæ Lex præcipit, reliquis omnibus conjuncta, qualis in peccatore nulla est. Hæc ad fœdus gratiæ pertinet, & justificat, at non ut opus, quia non operanti, sed se reum fatenti, credenti in Deum, qui justificat impium, fides ad justitiam imputatur, Roman. IV. 5.
units.tr: LXXXIV. Faith is either legal or evangelical. The former is the persuasion of the truth of any testimony divinely revealed; the latter is the persuasion of the truth of the testimony concerning Christ the Saviour, a testimony revealed not in the Law but in the Gospel alone, which is believed by the particular believer. These are not so distinguished that they have nothing in common. For the Gospel, with the revelation of Christ the Saviour now presupposed, binds by the force of the Law itself, which commands us to believe any revelation of divine testimony. Hence it is readily understood that those who positively disbelieve are liable to just condemnation less by the force of the Gospel than by the force of the Law itself. The difference lies in this: the Law does not reveal Christ, and so does not simply and absolutely command faith in him; but the Gospel reveals Christ and, by the force of the Law itself, commands faith in him, subjecting human faith to any divine testimony suitably laid open. If the word spoken through angels proved firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just retribution, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation, which, having begun to be spoken by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard? (Heb. 2.2, 3). That faith is the work of the Law and belongs to those works of which it is said, He who does those things shall live in them; and so it belongs to the covenant of works. But it does not justify, unless it is legally perfected and joined with all the other works which the Law commands, which is never the case in a sinner. Evangelical faith belongs to the covenant of grace and justifies, but not as a work, because to him who does not work, but believes in God who justifies the ungodly, and confesses himself guilty, faith is imputed for righteousness (Rom. 4.5).

units.la: LXXXV. Fides Evangelica communis vel propria est.
units.tr: LXXXV. Evangelical faith is either common or proper.

units.la: Communis etiam in reprobos & nondum regenitos: propria in solos electos cadit: Illa historica vel miraculosa est. Historica notitia & assensu eorum, quæ Deus in verbo suo revelavit, constat. Credis, Rex Agrippa Prophetis? Novi quòd credas. Agrippas Paulo dixit: Pœne mihi persuades, ut Christianus fiam, Actor. XXVI. 27. 28. Credis quòd Deus sit. Rectè facis. Nam & dæmonia id credunt, & contremiscunt, Jac. II. 19. Duobus gradibus constat, notitia verbi totius, sed præcipuè tamen historiæ de Jesu Christo, quam S. Paulus γνῶσιν, & ἀποφη-τὰν I. Cor. XIII. 2. appellat; & assensu, non fiduciali & practico, sed dogmatico & theoretico, nec speciali illo, qui salvificus est, sed generali. Qua proin præditi verbo Dei credunt & assentiuntur sicut historico probata vel probabilia narranti aliquis credit. Unde Historica nomen est. Sic verò credens & cognoscit veritatem verbi, & ei assentitur, partim lumine naturæ, partim operatione Spiritus S. sed generali illa. Estque fides hæc vel mortua prorsus, vel utcunque viva. Mortua est notitia verbi Dei, & assensus, sed absque omni salutari cordis motu, bonisque operis expers. Nam sic credens contremiscit, Jacob. II. 19. Et fidem sine operibus νεκρὰν mortuam ibid. v. 26. Apostolus dixit: sicut corpus sine spiritu, seu spiraculo vitæ, indicio vitæ, mortuum est. Viva utcunque est, qua cor movetur quidem, & gustu quodam Spiritus S. gaudens ad bona opera saltem exteriùs edenda impellitur, sed, quia radice caret, ad tempus duntaxat; utpote quæ afflictionis tempore prorsus evanescit. Aliàs ... temporalis nomine venit. Semen quod in petrosa spargitur, is est, qui sermonem audit, & mox cum lætitia eum recipit. Non enim in se ipso radicem habet; sed temporarius est. Afflictione enim vel persecutione obveniente mox scandalizatur, Matth. XIII. 20. 21.
