Impossibile est; ut qui semel illuminati sunt, & gustarunt donum Dei cœleste, & participes facti sunt Spiritus S. & gustarunt bonum Dei verbum, & virtutes futuri seculi, & prolapsi fuerint, ut denuò ad pœnitentiam renoventur, Hebr. VI. 4. 5. 6. Non tremorem hæc gignit, uti simpliciter mortua, neque omni sensu destituitur, sed credentem ante verum dolorem secundum Deum, præcox lætitia aliqua afficit, non spirituali, sed carnali illa, quæ non ex causis solidis, sed evanidis, puta commodis externis, & promissionibus Evangelii, citra resipiscentiam malè applicatis, atque ex eadem μοιφωσις aliqua pietatis, cum fuga profusæ impuritatis mundanæ 2. Pet. II. 20. oritur. Vos voluistis exultare ad horam in luce ejus, Joh. V. 35. Neque adeò illa (ζωτικὴ) salutaris est, quia quantavis illa notitia gustus boni Dei verbi, & lætitia ejus comes non ex fiduciali Christi apprehensione, sed ex doctrinæ vel novitate vel suavitate, ob prædicatam in Evangelio justificationem ex fide sine operibus & libertatem Christianam, vel utilitate ad opes & honores proficiscitur, denique vel deficit, vel afflictione & persecutione ingruente, deficeret, ad desperationem usque & abnegationem veritatis. Non enim habet radicem, seu στερεωμα soliditatem, qualis fidei, Col. II. 5. tribuitur. Sed ignorare tamen fidei suæ fluxam vanitatem eadem præditi possunt, donec eventu ipso de ejus instabilitate convincantur. Hierosolymis multi crediderunt in nomen Christi, videntes signa quæ fecerat: sed Jesus se iis non credidit, quia cognoverat omnes, Joh. II. 23. 24. Tanta & tam profunda cordis humani hypocrisis est. Provenit fides illa à Spiritu S. cujus participes ita credentes sunt, sed operatione ejus generali, electis & reprobis communi; & non destituitur operibus quibusdam; cujusmodi externa professio, Matth. X. 4. Act. VIII. 13. auditus verbi Dei, & dictante eodem, externa opera non pauca. Herodes audito Johanne πολλὰ ἐποίει multa fecit, & ἡδέως libenter eum audivit, Marc. VI. 20. Si insumam alendis egenis omnia, quæ mihi suppetunt, & si tradam corpus meum, ut comburar, charitatem autem (quæ ex vera fide est) non habeam, nihil mihi prodest, I. Cor. XIII. 3. Ievi proin & non duraturo gaudio luxurians quendam veluti stipularum ignem excitat, qui corda repurgare nequit, & tempestate oborta illico extinguitur, neque unquam maturos fidei fructus producere potis est. Vivam igitur utcunque dixi, hoc est, opinione ejus, qui eam habet, & aliorum, nec non simulatione actuum externorum; cum revera mortua sit. Novi opera tua, quia nomen habes, quòd vivas, & mortuus es, Apocal. III. 1. Denique Fides Miraculosa est persuasio cordis de edendo miraculo, ex singulari & occulta revelatione Divina procedens. Si πᾶσαν πίστιν omnem fidem haberem, adeò ut etiam montes transferre valeam, charitatem verò non habeam, nihil sum, I. Cor. XIII. 2. Ad illam non sufficit verbum Dei generale, sed specialis revelatio & promissio requiritur, qualem Gedeoni Deus fecit, dicens: Vade בכחך in virtute tua, & servabis Israelem e manu Midianitarum, Jud. VI. 14. nec non Apostolis ante & post resurrectionem, Matth. X. 1. Marc. XVI. 17. &c. Fidem eam Spiritus S. operatur dono speciali & extraordinario, sed reprobis & electis communi. Alii data sunt charismata fanationum in eodem Spiritu, 1. Cor. XII. 9. Multi dicent: In nomine tuo daemonia expulimus, & in nomine tuo virtutes multas fecimus, Matth. VII. 22. Nihilominus fides illa quatenus non nudè fertur ad obtinendam miraculi edendi potestatem, sed praecipuè in verbum, quod miraculo confirmatur, adeóque in fide miraculi veram, solidam & vivam fidem exercet, solorum electorum est, & eo nomine à Christo ibid. VIII. 10. IX. 22. commendatur. Opera fidei hujus sunt signa & miracula, quae cum ordinaria non sint, nec ipsa fides haec ordinaria esse potest. Et parva illa dicitur, atque grani sinapis adinstar, quia per se ad salutem nihil valet. Si habueritis fidem grani sinapis instar, dicetis monti huic: Transfertor illinc, & transferetur, ibid. XVII. 20.
units.tr: Common faith falls also on the reprobate and those not yet regenerate; proper faith falls only on the elect. The former is historical or miraculous. Historical faith consists in knowledge and assent to those things which God has revealed in his word. Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you believe. Agrippa said to Paul: You almost persuade me to become a Christian (Acts 26.27, 28). You believe that God is. You do well. For even the demons believe this and tremble (James 2.19). It consists of two degrees: knowledge of the whole word, but chiefly of the history of Jesus Christ, which St Paul calls knowledge [γνῶσιν] and prophecy [ἀποφη-τὰν] (1 Cor. 13.2); and assent, which is not fiducial and practical but dogmatic and theoretical, and not that special assent which is saving, but a general one. Those endowed with it believe the word of God and assent to it just as one believes a narrator of things proved or probable by history. Hence the name historical. Such a believer knows the truth of the word and assents to it, partly by the light of nature and partly by the operation of the Holy Spirit, but by that general operation. This faith is either utterly dead or somehow living. The knowledge and assent to the word of God are dead, without any saving motion of the heart, and lacking good works. For such a believer trembles (James 2.19). And faith without works is dead [νεκρὰν] (ibid. v. 26), as the Apostle said: as the body without spirit, that is, without the breath of life which is the sign of life, is dead. It is somehow living when the heart is indeed moved, and, rejoicing in some taste of the Holy Spirit, is impelled at least outwardly to perform good works; but because it lacks a root, it lasts only for a time, for it wholly vanishes in the time of affliction. Otherwise it is called temporal. The seed sown on rocky ground is he who hears the word and straightway receives it with joy. But he has no root in himself, and is temporary. For when affliction or persecution comes, he is at once offended (Matt. 13.20, 21). It is impossible that those who have once been enlightened, and have tasted the heavenly gift of God, and have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, should be renewed again to repentance (Heb. 6.4–6). This faith does not produce trembling, as purely dead faith does, nor is it entirely without feeling; it affects the believer, before true sorrow according to God, with a certain premature joy, which is not spiritual but carnal. It arises not from solid causes but from fleeting ones, namely external advantages and the promises of the Gospel, wrongly applied without repentance, and from the same sort of semblance of piety, along with flight from the gross pollutions of the world (2 Pet. 2.20). You were willing to rejoice for an hour in his light (John 5.35). Nor is this faith in fact saving. However great that knowledge of the taste of the good word of God, and the joy that accompanies it, it springs not from a fiducial apprehension of Christ but from the novelty or sweetness of the doctrine, namely the justification by faith without works proclaimed in the Gospel and Christian liberty, or from its usefulness for wealth and honours. Finally it either fails, or would fail when affliction and persecution press in, even to despair and denial of the truth. For it does not have a root, or firmness [στερεωμα], such as is ascribed to faith (Col. 2.5). Yet those endowed with it may be ignorant of the fluid vanity of their faith until, by the event itself, they are convinced of its instability. At Jerusalem many believed in the name of Christ, seeing the signs which he did; but Jesus did not trust himself to them, because he knew all (John 2.23, 24). So great and so profound is the hypocrisy of the human heart. This faith arises from the Holy Spirit, and those who so believe are partakers of him, but by his general operation, which is common to the elect and the reprobate. Nor is it without certain works, such as outward profession (Matt. 10.4; Acts 8.13), hearing the word of God, and, at its prompting, not a few outward works. Herod, having heard John, did many things [πολλὰ ἐποίει] and gladly [ἡδέως] heard him (Mark 6.20). If I bestow all that I have to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but do not have charity (which comes from true faith), it profits me nothing (1 Cor. 13.3). Hence this light and short-lived joy kindles a sort of straw-fire, which cannot cleanse the heart, and is at once extinguished when a storm arises; it is never able to produce the mature fruits of faith. I have said, therefore, that it is living in some way, that is, in the opinion of him who has it and of others, and by the pretence of outward acts, when in reality it is dead. I know your works, that you have the name of living, and yet you are dead (Rev. 3.1). Finally, miraculous faith is the persuasion of the heart that a miracle will be performed, proceeding from a singular and secret divine revelation. If I have all faith, so that I could even move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing (1 Cor. 13.2). For this the general word of God is not enough; a special revelation and promise is required, such as God gave to Gideon, saying: Go in your strength [בכחך] and you shall save Israel from the hand of the Midianites (Judg. 6.14), and likewise to the Apostles before and after the resurrection (Matt. 10.1; Mark 16.17, etc.). The Holy Spirit works this faith by a special and extraordinary gift, but one common to the reprobate and the elect. To another are given gifts of healing by the same Spirit (1 Cor. 12.9). Many will say: In your name we cast out demons, and in your name we did many mighty works (Matt. 7.22). Nevertheless, that faith, so far as it is not simply directed to obtaining the power to perform a miracle, but chiefly to the word which the miracle confirms, and so in the faith of the miracle exercises a true, solid and living faith, belongs to the elect alone, and on that account is commended by Christ (ibid. 8.10; 9.22). The works of this faith are signs and miracles, and since these are not ordinary, this faith itself cannot be ordinary. It is called small, and is like a grain of mustard seed, because in itself it is worth nothing for salvation: If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, Move from here, and it will be moved (ibid. 17.20).

units.la: LXXXVI. Fides propria est virtus supernaturalis à Deo homini infusa, qua is Christum Redemptorem & salutaria ejus beneficia, prout illa verbo Evangelii offeruntur, & Sacramentis obsignantur, non tantum certò cognoscit, iisque assentitur, sed etiam cum fiducia apprehendit, & sibi sigillatim adjudicat atque applicat.
units.tr: LXXXVI. Proper faith is a supernatural virtue infused into a person by God, by which he not only knows with certainty Christ the Redeemer and his saving benefits, as they are offered in the word of the Gospel and sealed by the sacraments, and assents to them, but also apprehends them with trust, and adjudges and applies them to himself individually.

units.la: Vocatur illa propria, quia est ἐκλεκτῶν & Θεῦ electorum Dei, Tit. I. 1. & ἁγίων Sanctorum, Apoc. XIII. 10. Licet etiam propter communem salutem κοινὴ communis, Tit. I. 4. & propter utilem fructum ἰσότιμον aeque pretiosa, 2. Pet. I. 1. dicitur. Unde etiam salvificae & justificantis in Scholis, absolutè πίστεως fidei nomine venit: Justus fide sua vivet, Rom. I. 17. Fide justificati &c. ibid. c. V. 1. Fides operans per charitatem, Gal. V. 6. fides ἀνυπόκριτος non simulata, 1. Tim. I. 5. ἁγιωτάτη sanctissima, Jud. 20. & de qua dicitur: ἡ πίστις πάντων Non enim omnium fides est, 2. Thess. III. 2. Sunt & alia fidei hujus nomina. Vocatur enim ὁμολογία aflipulatio, Heb. III. 1. ὁμολογίας εἰς τὴν ἐναγγελίαν subjectio aflipulationis in Evangelium Christi, 2. Cor. IX. 13. ὁμολογία τῆς ἐλπίδος aflipulatio spei indeclinabilis, Hebr. X. 23. Juramentum, juxta illa: Per me jurabit omnis lingua, Esaj. XLV. 23. datio manus, juxta illa Ezechiae תנו יד ליהוה date manum Jehovae, 2. Chron. XXX. 8. Et passim etiam sic credentes Deum & Christum nôsse, ad eum respicere, se recipere, venire, confugere; eum sitire, cupere, in eo inveniri, ei confidere, commendare spiritum & animam, eum quaerere, expectare, ei aglutinari, eum pro Rupe sua habere, &c. dicuntur.
units.tr: It is called proper because it belongs to the elect and of God [ἐκλεκτῶν καὶ Θεοῦ], Tit. 1.1, and to the saints [ἁγίων], Rev. 13.10. It is also called common, on account of the common salvation [κοινὴ], Tit. 1.4, and it is described as equally precious [ἰσότιμον], 2 Pet. 1.1, on account of its useful fruit. Hence also in the Schools the saving and justifying faith is called, without qualification, by the name of faith [πίστεως]: The just shall live by his faith, Rom. 1.17; justified by faith, etc., ibid. 5.1; faith working through love, Gal. 5.6; faith unfeigned [ἀνυπόκριτος], 1 Tim. 1.5; most holy [ἁγιωτάτη], Jude 20; and of which it is said: for all men have not faith [ἡ πίστις πάντων οὐ πάντων], 2 Thess. 3.2. There are also other names of this faith. It is called agreement [ὁμολογία], Heb. 3.1; subjection of agreement to the Gospel of Christ [ὁμολογίας εἰς τὴν εὐαγγελίαν], 2 Cor. 9.13; the unwavering agreement of hope [ὁμολογία τῆς ἐλπίδος], Heb. 10.23. It is called oath, according to that: Every tongue shall swear by me, Isa. 45.23; giving of the hand, according to that of Hezekiah, give the hand to the LORD [תנו יד ליהוה], 2 Chron. 30.8, date manum Jehovae. And everywhere, too, believers are described as knowing God and Christ, looking to him, betaking themselves, coming, fleeing for refuge to him; thirsting for him, desiring, being found in him, trusting in him, committing spirit and soul to him, seeking him, waiting for him, cleaving to him [aglutinari], holding him as their Rock, and so on.

units.la: LXXXVII. Communem & propriam fidem diligenter & solicitè sic distinguentibus Pontificii, aliúque succensent; qui & omnem fidem temporariam & amissibilem faciunt, & historicam, miraculosam & promissionis gratiae, sive justificantem eandem specie esse pertendunt.
units.tr: LXXXVII. The Papists and others are angry with those who distinguish common and proper faith so carefully and diligently. They maintain that all faith is temporary and capable of being lost, and they contend that historical faith, miraculous faith and the faith of promised grace, or justifying faith, are the same in kind.

units.la: Catechismus enim Tridentinus pag. 13. diserte fidem sine operibus mortuam, & fidem, quae per charitatem operatur, magnitudine tantum & dignitate dissere, idem autem genere esse statuit: & ad diversos fidei gradus, quibus eadem definitionis vis & ratio competat, refert. Cùm tamen iidem charitatem fidei formam & animam faciant, & fidem, quae ea destituitur, mortuam esse dicant, quis unquam fando audivit, corpus vivum & mortuum, animatum & inanimatum nonnisi gradu differre, nec diversa rerum genera constituere? Neque certè fides operibus destituta, quam cum daemoniis communem esse Jacobus cap. II. 19. docuit; solo gradu à fide electorum differre potest. Non enim, quae Bellarmini de Justif. lib. I. 15. impia glossa est, malorum hominum & daemonum fides differunt, quòd illa libera fit captivante nimirum pia voluntate intellectum in obsequium Christi; haec coacta, & ab ipsa rerum evidentia extorta fit. Scilicet malorum hominum pia voluntas, & quidem in obsequium Christi captivata est. Sunt equidem homines mali, quibus non sic fides extorquetur: sunt, qui carbonaria fide ducuntur. Sed non ideo eorum fides ingenua vel libera, vel fide, quam rerum evidentia extorquet, melior est. Subtilior Bellarmino Costerus malorum hominum & daemonum fidem quoad operationes, non quoad habitus & virtutes convenire nugatur. Praeterquam enim quòd discrimen ejusmodi in S. Jacobi verbis non apparet, vel sic etiam firmum ex Jacobi verbis petitum argumentum manet, quòd fides sine operibus, adeóque mortua, non eadem sit cum fide, qua quis salvatur, quia actus ejus cum actibus fidei, quam daemones habent, communes sunt. Quid verò communes dico? Nam daemones credentes, quòd Deus unus sit, φρίσσουσι contremiscunt; & merito, quia id dignum est ea veritate, quam quis verbis profitetur, & opere abnegat. At impiorum fides ne eò quidem proficit, quia nec timent Deum, quod necesse est volenti judicium ejus effugere; nec eum quaerunt, amant, vel ei secundum verbum ejus confidunt. Praeterea nec sola duratione fides impiorum & salvandorum differt, cùm discrimen insuper ingens satis & plane σπάνιος sit inter eos, qui radicem habent, & non habent; qui terra petrosa vel bona sunt, seu cor lapideum vel carneum habent; & fructus ἐν ὑπομονῇ in patientia gerunt, Luc. VIII. 15. & qui patientia omni destituti fructus nullos ferunt. Et si vel maximè sola duratione differrent, satis tamen ad differentiam non gradus, sed speciei est, quod de reproborum, adeóque communi dici non potest, quod de omni credente Christus citra ullam conditionem dixit: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur, Marc. XVI. 16. Jam & S. Paulus, 1. Cor. XII. 9. dicens, alii datam esse fidem eodem Spiritu: alii data esse charismata fanationum eodem Spiritu: fidem illam, qua homo omni veritati Divinae, quae vel per revelationem, vel per naturam, sed non sine fide revelationis cognoscitur, assentitur, à fide miraculorum seu charismatum sic distinguit, ut alii illam, alii hanc datam esse dicat. An dici potuit: Huic data est fides, non illi fideli, si fides miraculorum, gradu tantùm à fide salvifica differt? Nam ejusdem rei gradus inferior vel superior in re includi, non ab ea excludi debet. Plane enim fides Historica, miraculosa & justificans subjectis distinguuntur, quia in aliis historica est sine miraculosa & justificante, velut in Simone Magó, Act. VIII. 13. & hypocritis illis, quibus Christus se non commisit, Joh. II. 23. 24. in aliis miraculosa sine justificante, Matth. VII. 22. 1. Cor. XIII. 2. in aliis, & plerisque fidelibus justificans sine miraculosa. Causis quin etiam, objecto
units.tr: For the Tridentine Catechism, p. 13, expressly holds that faith without works is dead, and that faith which works through love differs only in magnitude and dignity, but is the same in kind; and it refers to different degrees of faith to which the same force and nature of definition belongs. Yet since these same men make love the form and soul of faith, and say that faith which lacks it is dead, who has ever heard it said that a living and a dead body, or an animated and an inanimate one, differ only in degree and do not constitute different kinds of things? Certainly faith destitute of works, which James, ch. 2.19, taught is common even to demons, cannot differ from the faith of the elect only in degree. For the faith of evil men and of demons does not differ, as Bellarmine's impious gloss in de Justif. I.15 has it, in that the one is free, the intellect being captivated by a pious will into obedience to Christ, while the other is forced and wrested from it by the very evidence of things. Clearly the pious will of evil men is captivated, and indeed into obedience to Christ. There are indeed evil men who are not brought to faith in this way; there are those who are led by a faith of charcoal-burners. But their faith is not on that account more noble or free, or better than the faith which the evidence of things wrests from them. Costerus, more subtle than Bellarmine, trifles that the faith of evil men and of demons agrees as to operations, not as to habits and virtues. For, apart from the fact that such a distinction does not appear in the words of St. James, even so the argument drawn firmly from James's words remains: that faith without works, and therefore dead, is not the same as the faith by which one is saved, because its acts are common to the acts of the faith which demons have. Why do I say common? For demons, believing that God is one, shudder [φρίσσουσι]; and rightly so, since this is worthy of the truth which one professes in words and denies in deed. But the faith of the impious does not even profit so far, since they neither fear God, which is necessary for one who wishes to escape his judgment, nor seek him, love him, or trust in him according to his word. Moreover, the faith of the impious and that of those who are to be saved does not differ merely in duration, since there is quite enough and a plainly rare [σπάνιος] difference between those who have a root and those who do not; who are on rocky or good ground, or have a stony or a fleshly heart; and who bear fruit in patience [ἐν ὑπομονῇ], Luke 8.15, and those who, destitute of patience, bear no fruit. And even if they differed only in duration, the difference would be enough to be one not of degree but of kind, and this cannot be said of the reprobate, and so of the common faith, which Christ said without any condition of every believer: He who believes and is baptized shall be saved, Mark 16.16. Again, St. Paul, 1 Cor. 12.9, saying that to one is given faith by the same Spirit, and to another gifts of healing by the same Spirit, distinguishes that faith by which a man assents to every divine truth known either through revelation or through nature, but not without the faith of revelation, from the faith of miracles or gifts, so that he says that the one is given to some and the other to others. Could it have been said: to this one is given faith, not to that faithful one, if the faith of miracles differed from saving faith only in degree? For the lower or higher degree of the same thing ought to be included in the thing, not excluded from it. Clearly historical, miraculous and justifying faith are distinguished by their subjects, since in some it is historical without miraculous and justifying faith, as in Simon Magus, Acts 8.13, and those hypocrites to whom Christ did not commit himself, John 2.23, 24; in others it is miraculous without justifying faith, Matt. 7.22, 1 Cor. 13.2; and in others, and most believers, it is justifying without miraculous faith. Moreover, in causes as well as in object, . . .

units.la: Fides propria definitur.
units.tr: Proper faith is defined.

units.la: Communis & propria fidei differentia essentialis est. objecto & effectibus discrepare, ex iis, quæ de fide justificante dicturi sumus, patebit.
units.tr: The essential difference between common and proper faith lies in object and effects, as will become clear from what we are going to say about justifying faith.

units.la: LXXXVIII. Fidem hanc justificantem non tam actum, quàm habitum, eúmque supernaturalem & à Deo infusum definimus. Non enim solo opere, vel actu transitorio, sed habitu seu qualitate durabili, quæ ad actu credendum habilem reddit; constat, secus quàm Remonstrantes pertendunt, cùm negant, ab initio, cùm fideles primò credere dicuntur, existere in illis habitum fidei, & hanc ceu ethicam virtutem, operis fidei longa & crebra exercitatione à quibusdam acquiri, statuunt, ne gratiæ hominum voluntatem ad fidem infallibiliter flectentis efficaciam eámque perseverantem, qualem infusio habitus necessario ponit, agnoscere cogantur. Sed ἀνλόγητον dogma multa convincunt. Sic enim illi, quibus ex hypothesi, nondum habitus acquisitus est, justi temporis exercitatione, noctu dormientes, unà cum veste fidem exuerent, quin & ad momenta singula fides periret, per intervalla aliud cogitantibus. Neque illi credentes denominari πιστοὶ fideles possunt, sicut Act. X.45. XVI. 1. alibíque passim vocantur. Denominatio enim illa non transeuntem actionem, sed habitus immanentis durabilem soliditatem, seu στερέωμα & confirmationem ac perseverantiam notat. Siquidem manetis τῇ πίστει τεθεμελιωμένοι ἐν ἐδραῖοι fide fundati & stabiles, Col. I. 23. Gaudeo videns τὸ στερέωμα τῆς εἰς Χριστὸν πίστεως ὑμῶν soliditatem fidei vestræ in Christum, ibid. II. 5. Radicati & superædificati in ipso, & confirmati in fide, ibid. v. 7. Ideò credentes in Christum dicuntur ἔχειν πίστιν habere fidem, Marc. XI. 22. 1. Tim. I. 19. & fides in credentibus esse & ἐνοικεῖν inhabitare 2. Tim. I. 5. dicitur. Neque illud obstat, quòd fides mandatur, cùm habitus & qualitates infusæ sub præceptum cadere non putentur. Licet enim actus Dei fidem, vel quemvis alium habitum donantis & infundentis, adeóque existentia habitus infusi sub præceptum non cadat ratione suæ originis, at cadere potest semel originaliter infusus, quatenus conservari, foveri, actionibus exprimi & demonstrari debet.
units.tr: LXXXVIII. We define this justifying faith not so much as an act as a habit, and one that is supernatural and infused by God. For it is established, not by a single work or transitory act but by a habit or lasting quality which makes a man able to believe in act, and this is contrary to what the Remonstrants contend when they deny that at the beginning, when the faithful are first said to believe, there exists in them a habit of faith, and assert that this habit, as an ethical virtue, is acquired by some through long and frequent exercise of the act of faith, so that they need not acknowledge the efficacy of grace, which infallibly and perseveringly bends the human will to faith, and which the infusion of a habit necessarily implies. But many arguments refute this absurd dogma. For on their hypothesis, those who have not yet acquired the habit would, by the just exercise of time, lose their faith along with their clothes while sleeping at night; indeed faith would perish at each moment through intervals in which they think of other things. Nor can those believers be called faithful [πιστοί], as they are called in Acts 10.45, 16.1, and elsewhere throughout. For that designation signifies not a passing action but the lasting firmness of a habit that remains, that is, steadfastness [στερέωμα] and confirmation and perseverance. Thus: if indeed you continue in the faith, grounded and steadfast [τῇ πίστει τεθεμελιωμένοι καὶ ἑδραῖοι], Col. 1.23; I rejoice to see the steadfastness [στερέωμα] of your faith in Christ, ibid. 2.5; rooted and built up in him, and established in the faith, ibid. v. 7. Therefore believers in Christ are said to have faith [ἔχειν πίστιν], Mark 11.22, 1 Tim. 1.19, and faith is said to be and to dwell [ἐνοικεῖν] in believers, 2 Tim. 1.5. Nor does it stand in the way that faith is commanded, since habits and infused qualities are not thought to fall under precept. For although the act of God giving and infusing faith, or any other habit, and therefore the existence of an infused habit, does not fall under precept by reason of its origin, yet a habit once originally infused can fall under precept, insofar as it must be preserved, cherished, expressed in actions and shown forth.

units.la: LXXXIX. Esse autem fidem habitum non acquisitum, qualis etiam, difficulter licet, amitti, sicut acquiri potest; sed infusum, qualis perpetim manet, Scriptura testatur. Nam in universum de omnibus gratiæ salutaris donis docet, quòd in nos effusa sint, & quòd per illa in nos effusa, ceu principia actionum operamur. Quid enim Spiritus S. omnibus fidelibus communis, quem qui non habet, Christi non est, Rom. VIII. 9. aliud est, quàm dona gratiæ Spiritus S.? Atqui Deus illum ἐξέχεεν ἐφ' ἡμᾶς πλουσίως effudit super nos copiosè per Jesum Christum Salvatorem nostrum, Tit. III. 6. Etiam gratia Dei ἐκκέχυται effusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum S. qui nobis datus est, Rom. V. 5. Habitat ille in nobis & id efficit, ut actiones corporis nostri mortificemus, & vivamus, ibid. VIII. 11. 13. Omnes porro credentes habere dicuntur πνεῦμα πίστεως Spiritum fidei: 2. Cor. IV. 13. hoc est, habere habitum fidei àSpiritu S. infusum, per quem credimus. Nam ipsa vox ἔχειν habere notat habitum, quia actiones transeuntes non habemus. Eodem modo Spiritus sapientiæ, Esaj. XI. 2. infusum sapientiæ habitum notat. Quid porro illa ῥίζα radix, Matth. XIII. 21. quæ verbum prædicatum recipit & retinet, & quam qui non habent, credentes licet, veri fideles non sunt, nec in fide perseverant, aliud est, quàm habitus fidei, qui in regeneratione hominis donatur & infunditur. Non esse acquisitum, inde liquet, quia quamprimum credimus, jam radicem illam gerimus. Neque actus fidei, sed habitus est, quia ab actu verbum recipiente distinguitur, & eodem deficiente fidei actus continuari non potest. Accedit, quòd conversio non in actu hominis, sed in ablatione cordis lapidei & donatione carnei, ut in præceptis Dei ambulemus, Ezech. XXXVI. 26. 27. consistit. Primum autem in corde carneo fides est, per quam cor purificatur, Act. XV. 9. Distinctius verò S. Paulus: Gratia servati estis per fidem; & hoc non ex vobis. Θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον Dei donum est, non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur. Ejus enim sumus ποίημα opus, κτισθέντες creati in Christo Jesu in bonis operibus, quæ præparavit Deus, ut in iis ambulemus, Eph. II. 8. 9. 10. Et fides igitur, & salus est à Dei gratia seu benignitate; & non est à nobis: & Dei δῶρον donum, datum, infusum nobis est, absolutè tale, ut & facultas credendi omnis, & quæ extra hominem est, revelatio, & quæ in hominis intellectu est illuminatio, quæ in voluntate est, habituum malorum repressio; voluntas credendi ut velis, & ipsum credere, donum Dei merum intelligatur. Cuncta enim hæc πίστεως fidei nomine intelliguntur. Nam Deus χαρίζεται gratificatur etiam τὸ εἰς Χριστὸν πιστεύειν credere in Christum, Phil. I. 29. Neque enim donum Dei in eo consistit, quòd fides ab argumentis non humanis, sed Divinis, quæ Deus non rogatus nobis in Christi miraculis, morte & resurrectione exhibuit, procedit, quasi solum hoc Dei donum sit, quòd Christus in mundum venit, mortuus, in Cœlum receptus, prædicatus est, sed inprimis illud, quòd cum Christo vivificati, suscitati, collocati in supercœlestibus sumus; ut demonstret Deus, excellentes divitias in bonitate erga nos in Christo Jesu, Ephes. II. 6. 7. Gratia & donatio illa excludit omnem gloriationem non in Deo, Roman. V. 11. sed apud Deum, ib. IV. 2. qua scilicet nos ipsi jactemus, tanquam habentes quicquam ex nobis. Atque eam ob rem debuimus κτισθῆναι creari in Christo, Eph. II. 10. & Deus excellentem magnitudinem potentiæ suæ erga credentes, ut credere velint, & possint, & quidem πιστεύοντες credentes κατὰ secundum operationem roboris virium ejus, ut fidem ex operatione roboris virium Dei procedere constet, exerit, ibid. I. 19. Non enim ibi agitur de magnitudine potentiæ, qua Deus usurus est circa credentes, cùm eos ex mortuis resuscitaturus; & gloriosos in Cœlo collocaturus est; sed de ea, qua in nobis operatur, ut credamus. Nam Præpositio illa κατὰ secundum à Participio πιστεύοντας credentes, cum quo citra interpunctionem in codicibus cohæret, avelli non debet: adeóque sensus est, fidem in nobis esse secundum efficaciam roboris virium Dei. Et ne putemus, credentes designari, in quos priùs credentes potentia illa se exerit, obstat, quòd non simpliciter dixit, potentiam illam se exerere εἰς ἡμᾶς πιστεύοντας in nos credentes, sed cum articulo εἰς ἡμᾶς τὰς πιστεύοντας, in nos, qui credimus. Articulus enim ille credentium, quà ta-
units.tr: LXXXIX. That faith is an acquired habit, of the kind that can be lost (though with difficulty) as it can be acquired, is not what Scripture teaches. Scripture teaches that faith is an infused habit, which remains constantly. In general it teaches about all the gifts of saving grace that they are poured out upon us, and that through these gifts poured out in us, as the principles of our actions, we work. For what is the Holy Spirit, common to all the faithful, whoever does not have him is not Christ's (Rom. 8:9), other than the gifts of the grace of the Holy Spirit? Yet God poured out upon us richly [ἐξέχεεν ἐφ' ἡμᾶς πλουσίως] through Jesus Christ our Saviour (Tit. 3:6). Also the grace of God has been poured out [ἐκκέχυται] in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). He dwells in us and brings it about that we put to death the deeds of the body, and live (ibid. 8:11, 13). Moreover, all believers are said to have the Spirit of faith [πνεῦμα πίστεως] (2 Cor. 4:13); that is, to have the habit of faith infused by the Holy Spirit, through which we believe. For the word to have [ἔχειν] itself denotes a habit, since we do not have transitory acts. In the same way the Spirit of wisdom (Isa. 11:2) denotes the infused habit of wisdom. What is more, that root [ῥίζα] (Matt. 13:21), which receives and keeps the preached word, and which those who lack it, though they believe, are not true believers and do not persevere in faith, is nothing other than the habit of faith, which is given and infused in the regeneration of a man. That it is not acquired is clear from this, that as soon as we believe we already bear that root. Nor is it an act of faith but a habit, since it is distinguished from the act of receiving the word, and when that act ceases the act of faith cannot continue. Besides, conversion consists not in an act of man but in the taking away of the stony heart and the giving of a heart of flesh, so that we walk in the commandments of God (Ezek. 36:26, 27). Now faith is first in the heart of flesh, through which the heart is purified (Acts 15:9). More distinctly, St Paul says: By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves. It is the gift of God [Θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον], not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship [ποίημα], created [κτισθέντες] in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared that we should walk in them (Eph. 2:8–10). Therefore both faith and salvation are from the grace or kindness of God, and are not from us; and the gift of God, given and infused into us, is of such a kind absolutely that the whole ability to believe, and the revelation which is outside man, and the illumination which is in the man's understanding, and the repression of evil habits which is in the will, and the willingness to believe, as well as believing itself, are understood to be the pure gift of God. For all these are understood under the name of faith. For God also bestows as a favour [χαρίζεται] to believe in Christ (Phil. 1:29). Nor does the gift of God consist in this, that faith comes from arguments not human but divine, which God, unasked, has displayed to us in the miracles, death and resurrection of Christ, as if this alone were the gift of God, that Christ came into the world, died, was taken up into heaven, and was preached; but above all in this, that with Christ we are made alive, raised up, and seated in the heavenly places; so that God may show the surpassing riches of his kindness toward us in Christ Jesus (Eph. 2:6, 7). That grace and gift excludes all boasting not before God (Rom. 5:11) but with God (ibid. 4:2), namely, that we should boast ourselves as though we had anything of our own. And for this reason we ought to be created [κτισθῆναι] in Christ (Eph. 2:10); and God shows the exceeding greatness of his power toward those who believe, that they may will and be able to believe, and indeed believing [πιστεύοντες] according to [κατὰ] the working of the strength of his might (Eph. 1:19), so that it is clear that faith proceeds from the operation of the strength of God's might. For there is not in that place a question of the greatness of power which God is going to use toward believers, when he will raise them from the dead and place them gloriously in heaven, but of that which works in us so that we may believe. For that preposition according to [κατὰ] should not be separated from the participle believing [πιστεύοντας], with which it coheres in the manuscripts without punctuation. The sense, therefore, is that faith is in us according to the efficacy of the strength of God's might. And lest we think that believers are meant, to whom that power is first displayed as believers, the fact that he did not simply say that the power is displayed toward us believers [εἰς ἡμᾶς πιστεύοντας], but with the article, toward us [εἰς ἡμᾶς τὰς πιστεύοντας], who believe, stands in the way. For that article of believers, insofar as [quà] it indicates a consideration of such persons, and their further description in the following words…

units.la: Propria & justificans habitus divinitus infusus est.
units.tr: A proper and justifying habit is infused by God.

units.la: Quod pluribus asseritur. lium, consideration em, & ulteriorem eorum in sequentibus verbis descriptionem indicat. Principium quoque illud Capitis secundi v. 1. Kai ὑμᾶς ὄντας νεκρούς ἐν τοῖς παραπτώμασιν & vos cum essetis mortui in lapsibus, ostendit, participium ἐγείραντας resuscitans cap. I. v. 20. ἀπὸ κοινῆς repetendum esse, ut ita manifeste Deus dicatur potentiam illam suam non tantum in Christo suscitando & in Coelum extollendo, sed etiam in nobis ex morte peccatorum suscitandis & fide donandis exeruisse.
units.tr: This is asserted in many passages. …lium: for the article of believers indicates the consideration of such persons, and their further description in the words that follow. The principle of the first chapter, verse 1 as well, And you, being dead in your trespasses [Καὶ ὑμᾶς ὄντας νεκρούς ἐν τοῖς παραπτώμασιν] (Eph. 2:1), shows that the participle raising up [ἐγείραντας] in chapter 1, verse 20, is to be repeated from the common [ἀπὸ κοινῆς] clause, so that God is plainly said to have displayed that power of his not only in raising Christ and exalting him into heaven, but also in raising us from the death of sin and bestowing faith upon us.

units.la: XC. Ratiunculis, quibusdam humani arbitrii Patroni fidem Divinitus non infundi, sed adjuvante utcunque Deo liberè acquiri evincere nequicquam conantur. Etenim sensu quodam etiam habitus sub mandatum cadere posse, jam vidimus. Inanis proin etiam illa ratiocinatio est: Si Deus gratia & invita potentia sua fidem in nobis producit, eam mandare non potest. Sicut nempe, licet Deus mortuos omnipotente virtute sua resuscitat, neque quisquam se suscitat ipse, vel resuscitare potest, tamen Deus jubebit nos, perinde ut Lazarum jussit, ex sepulchris prodire: ita licet principium fidei non actioni ulli, sed merae passioni nostrae subest, neque quisquam sibi fidem, vel credendi principium & actum dat; tamen Deus sancte jubet ut credamus, quia nos sumus, qui ex morte spirituali resuscitati credimus, & credere tenemur. Qui actionem totam in aliquo efficit, is eam non praecipit, fateor: sed qui efficit in aliquo, etiamsi sine ipso, efficiente puta, actionem, non suam, sed ejus, in quo efficit, is praecipere sane potest. Jam vero Deus non credit in nobis, sed credere nostrum efficit. Nostra ergo si est actio, pure putè quidem à Deo initio patimur, sed passi seu acti ipsi quoque liberè agimus. Actio ergo illa praecipi potest. Nec vel praecipitur eo minus, si effectum validius consequitur: vel omni laude caret apud homines, qui etiam ob dona Dei alia praedicant alios: vel praemio gratuito apud Deum destituitur; quamvis, quia Deus nostram actionem efficit, omne meritum & gloriatio nostra excluditur. Si in Deo vivimus, movemur & sumus, quomodo eundem gratia sua ad intellectus & voluntatis nostrae actionem hanc concurrere, & כל מעשינו פעל לנו omnia opera nostra operari Esaj. XXVI. 12. inficiabimur? Hoc Dei opus est, ut credatis in eum, quem ille misit, Joh. VI. 29. Si porrò Deus Legis impletionem in quovis statu praecipere sub poena potest, quidni etiam fidem? Non obstat enim, quod Evangelium verbum gratiae est, quia non in eo gratia consistit, quod homo vires credendi ex se, sine regeneratione habet; sed in eo potius, quod id ipsum, quod praecipit, ipse gratia sua in nobis operatur; secus atque in Lege factum. Et sic verbum fidei prope est ori nostro & cordi nostro, Rom. X. 5-10. ut tamen citra gratiam ἐκλογῆς electionis Judaeis infidelibus impossibile fuisse, ut credant, ibidem & cap. seq. Apostolus convicerit. Sicut rebelli subdito propter insitam maliti am aequè impossibile est pro rebellione satisfacere, atque gratiam remittentis Principis admittere, neque tamen gratiae non est, si neglecto priore posterius Princeps offerat: ita licet aequè impossibile fit Legem implere, & credere, deputandum nihilominus gratiae est, si Deus
units.tr: XC. Some advocates of human free will, by petty arguments, try in vain to prove that faith is not infused by God but is acquired freely, with God's help in whatever way. For we have already seen that in a certain sense even habits can fall under a command. Therefore that reasoning is also empty: If God produces faith in us by his grace and invincible power, he cannot command it. Just as, although God raises the dead by his almighty power, and no one raises himself or can raise himself, yet God commands us, just as he commanded Lazarus, to come forth from the tombs; so, although the principle of faith underlies not any action but our mere passivity, and no one gives himself faith or the principle and act of believing, nevertheless God rightly commands us to believe, because it is we who, raised from spiritual death, believe, and are bound to believe. I grant that one who brings about the whole action in someone does not command it; but one who brings about in someone, even without that someone's own agency, an action that is not his own but that of the one in whom he brings it about, can certainly command it. Now God does not believe in us, but makes our believing to be ours. If, therefore, the action is ours, then truly we are passive at the start from God, but as those who are passive or acted upon we also act freely. That action, therefore, can be commanded. Nor is it commanded any less because it attains its effect more powerfully; nor does it lack all praise among men, who also praise others for the gifts of God; nor is it deprived of a free reward with God; although, because God brings about our action, all merit and our boasting are excluded. If in God we live, move and have our being, how shall we deny that he concurs with his grace in this action of our intellect and will, and that all our works [כל מעשינו] he has worked for us (Isa. 26:12)? This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent (John 6:29). Moreover, if God can command the fulfilment of the Law under penalty in any state, why not faith as well? For it is no objection that the Gospel is a word of grace, because grace does not consist in this, that man has the power to believe of himself without regeneration; but rather in this, that the very thing he commands, he himself works in us by his grace; unlike what is done in the Law. And so the word of faith is near to our mouth and to our heart (Rom. 10:5–10); yet the Apostle proved, in the same place and in the following chapter, that without the grace of election it would have been impossible for unbelieving Jews to believe. Just as it is equally impossible for a rebellious subject, because of his innate malice, to make satisfaction for the rebellion and to accept the grace of the pardoning prince; yet it is not less a matter of grace if the prince, having disregarded the former, offers the latter; so although it is equally impossible to fulfil the Law and to believe, nevertheless it must be reckoned to grace if God has commanded not the fulfilling of the Law but belief in Christ…

units.la: non Legem implere, sed in Christum credere jusserit.
units.tr: not to fulfil the Law, but to believe in Christ, if God has commanded that.

units.la: XCI. Deus Pater fidem infundit & donat propter Filium per Spiritum S. Nam & Filium fidem morte sua promeruisse non semel ostendimus; & eidem authori fidem Sancti acceptam referunt. Ita Apostoli: Domine, πρόσθες ἡμῖν πίστιν adde nobis fidem, Luc. XVII. 5. Pater lunatici: Credo Domine, juva incredulitatem meam, Marc. IX. 24. Christus ipse: Nemo novit Patrem nisi Filius, & cui ille revelare voluerit, Matth. XI. 27. Et ad S. Petrum: oravi pro te, ne deficiat fides tua, Luc. XXII. 32. Oro pro credentibus propter sermonem ipsorum, Joh. XVII. 20. Notificavi nomen tuum hominibus, quos mihi dedisti ex mundo. Verba, quae mihi dedisti, iis dedi, ibid. v. 6. 8. Unde S. Paulus praedicans divitias gratiae Dei in benignitate, quae Ephesiis obtigit in Christo Jesu, ejusdem mox specimen in salute per fidem, ceu donum Dei, ponit, Ephes. II. 7. 8. Propter ipsum nobis datum est in ipsum credere, Phil. I. 29. Quod nunc vivo in carne, vivo ἐν πίστει τῆ τοῦ υἱοῦ Θεοῦ in fide, quae est Filii Dei, Gal. II. 20. Imò Jesus Christus laudatur fidei & ἀρχηγὸς dux, hoc est, causa fidei per meritum & potentiam ejus, sicut etiam est Princeps salutis filiorum Dei, eorum etiam, qui ante consummationem ejus in gloriam introducti sunt, (Hebr. II. 10.) & τελειωτὴς consummator ejusdem, quia & sperata dat, & fidelibus πεγυνὸν firmitudinem, soliditatem fidei dat, ne seductione vel terrore ullo labefactetur; & fidem fidelium expectantium salvationem à peccatis & jugo, in laetitiam, gratiarum actionem & usum libertatis in accedendo ad Deum mutat, ibid. XII. 2.
units.tr: XCI. God the Father infuses and bestows faith on account of the Son through the Holy Spirit. For we have shown more than once that the Son merited faith by his death, and Scripture likewise refers the faith of the saints to the same author. So the Apostles: Lord, add faith to us [πρόσθες ἡμῖν πίστιν], Luke 17:5. The father of the lunatic boy: Lord, I believe; help my unbelief, Mark 9:24. Christ himself: No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him, Matt. 11:27. And to St Peter: I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail, Luke 22:32. I pray for those who believe through their word, John 17:20. I have made your name known to the men whom you gave me out of the world. The words that you gave me I have given to them, ibid. vv. 6, 8. Hence St Paul, speaking of the riches of God's grace in kindness shown to the Ephesians in Christ Jesus, immediately sets forth salvation through faith as the gift of God, Eph. 2:7, 8. It has been granted to you for Christ's sake to believe in him, Phil. 1:29. The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God [ἐν πίστει τῆ τοῦ υἱοῦ Θεοῦ], Gal. 2:20. Indeed Jesus Christ is called the author [ἀρχηγὸς] and leader of faith, that is, its cause through his merit and power; he is also the Prince of the salvation of the sons of God, including those who were brought into glory before his consummation, Heb. 2:10; and the perfecter [τελειωτὴς] of faith, because he both grants what is hoped for and gives the believers steadfastness [πεγυνὸν], the firmness of faith, so that it is not shaken by any seduction or terror; and he turns the faith of believers, who await salvation from sins and the yoke, into joy, thanksgiving and the use of liberty in approaching God, ibid. 12:2.

units.la: XCII. Sed inprimis Spiritus S. opus fides est. Nam is κατ' ἐξοχὴν Πνεῦμα πίστεως Spiritus fidei vocatur. Habentes Spiritum fidei eundem, sicut scriptum est. Credidi, propterea locutus sum; & nos credimus, propterea loquimur, 2. Cor. IV. 13. Nulla enim non fides à Spiritu S. est. Abraham credidit, Genes. XV. 6. David credidit, Ps. CXVI. 10. Sed ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ Πνεύματι in eodem Spiritu, 1. Cor. XII. 9. Inprimis in N. T. est Spiritus fidei, quando expectationi fides Evangelii successit, 2. Cor. IV. 13. Gal. III. 23. &c. Inspirat ille fidem intus, & fidei professionem intrepidam expirat extus. Nam qui loquuntur, & profitentur Christum, persecutiones in mundo pati necesse habent: Quod ergo sic credunt, loquuntur & profitentur, non potest venire à carne, quia illa non jubet credere, loqui & profiteri, quod totus mundus odit. A Spiritu S. igitur est, quod credunt & loquuntur. Ideo etiam Deus illa, quae oculus non vidit, auris non audivit &c. revelavit ἀλλὰ διὰ Πνεύματος αὐτοῦ per Spiritum suum, 1. Cor. II. 10. Sicut enim Spiritus S. est à Patre & Filio, ita etiam propter voluntatem Patris & Filii vult, & propter meritum Filii mittitur, & ad gloriam ejus operatur. Idque convenit cum promissione de effusione Spiritus S. in omnem carnem, & inscriptione Legis Dei in corda hominum per donationem fidei, Esaj. XLIV. 3. Jerem. XXXI. 33. Ezech. XXXVI. 26. 27. Joel. II. 28. Neque etiam coelestem illam sapientiam nisi per Spiritum S. fidei authorem cognosci posse, S. Paulus ibid. probavit, pluribus argumentis, cujusmodi sunt, quòd nemo cognoscat, quid in Deo fit, nisi Spiritus Dei,
units.tr: XCII. But above all the work of faith belongs to the Holy Spirit. For he is called, par excellence, the Spirit of faith [Πνεῦμα πίστεως]. Having the same Spirit of faith, as it is written: I believed, therefore I spoke; and we too believe, therefore we speak, 2 Cor. 4:13. For there is no faith that is not from the Holy Spirit. Abraham believed, Gen. 15:6; David believed, Ps. 116:10; but in the same Spirit [ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ Πνεύματι], 1 Cor. 12:9. Above all in the New Testament he is the Spirit of faith, when the faith of the Gospel has succeeded to expectation, 2 Cor. 4:13; Gal. 3:23, etc. He inspires faith within, and breathes out a fearless profession of faith without. For those who speak and profess Christ must suffer persecution in the world. What they therefore believe, speak and profess, when the whole world hates it, cannot come from the flesh, since the flesh does not bid one believe, speak and profess what the whole world hates. It is therefore from the Holy Spirit that they believe and speak. For this reason too God has revealed those things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, etc., revealed [ἀλλὰ διὰ Πνεύματος αὐτοῦ] through his Spirit, 1 Cor. 2:10. For just as the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, so also he wills according to the will of the Father and the Son, is sent on account of the merit of the Son, and works to his glory. This agrees with the promise of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit on all flesh, and the writing of God's law on the hearts of men through the bestowal of faith: Isa. 44:3; Jer. 31:33; Ezek. 36:26, 27; Joel 2:28. Nor, as St Paul proved in the same place by several arguments, can that heavenly wisdom be known except through the Holy Spirit, the author of faith: for no one knows what is in God except the Spirit of God,

units.la: {y} Deus fidem infundit & donat propter meritum. Dei; qui profunditates Dei scrutatur, v. 10. 11. quòd quæ nobis donata sunt, cognosci nisi per Spiritum Dei, & comparationem spiritualium non possint, v. 12.13. quòd omnis homo animalis, Spiritum Dei non habens, à spiritualibus abhorreat, v. 14. quòd nonnisi à Spiritu S. effici possit, ut homo verè liber sit, omnia judicet, & à nemine judicetur, v. 15. At nec Spiritus ille fidei enthusiasticus est, quia fidem non sine verbi Dei praeconio inspirat, & verbum illud cordi potenter inscribit, & in eo obsignat. Quod ibidem S. Paulus, v. 13. 14. docet, ubi sic διδαktòs Πνεύματος ἁγίου λόγοις διδάσκοις Spiritus S. sermones ab eodem dictari asserit, ut tamen declaret statim, non ab homine animali, sed solo spirituali, seu ab operatione Spiritus S. quæ hominem spiritualem reddit, recipi & dijudicari.
units.tr: God infuses and bestows faith on account of the merit of God, who searches the depths of God, vv. 10, 11; that the things freely given to us cannot be known, nor compared with spiritual things, except through the Spirit of God, vv. 12, 13; that every natural man, not having the Spirit of God, shrinks from spiritual things, v. 14; that only the Holy Spirit can make a man truly free, judge all things, and be judged by no one, v. 15. But that Spirit of faith is not enthusiastic, for he does not inspire faith apart from the proclamation of the Word of God, and he powerfully writes that word on the heart and seals it there. St Paul teaches this in the same place, vv. 13, 14, where he says that the things are taught by the Holy Spirit, in words taught by the Holy Spirit [λόγοις διδάσκοις], affirming that the words are dictated by him; yet he immediately makes clear that they are received and judged not by the natural man, but only by the spiritual man, that is, by the working of the Holy Spirit, which makes a man spiritual.

units.la: XCIII. Fides salvifica in Christum Redemptorem & salutaria ejus beneficia fertur.
units.tr: XCIII. Saving faith is directed to Christ the Redeemer and to his saving benefits.

units.la: Aliud nempe fidei objectum genericum, aliud specificum est. Illud fidei communis commune & ipsum, Deus & omne ejus testimonium seu revelatio est: hoc, fidei salvificae proprium solus Christus Redemptor & ejus beneficia sunt. Sicut nempe Israelitae iisdem, quibus serpentem aeneum aspexerunt, oculis, multa alia aspexerunt, neque tamen salutem nisi aspectu serpentis consecuti sunt: ita iisdem fidei oculis quodvis Dei verbum, & in specie Christum, & gratiam Dei in Christo sic aspicimus, ut tamen non cujusvis verbi, sed solius verbi de Christo & gratia Dei in ipso aspectus nobis salutaris existat. Et de priori quidem, seu generico fidei objecto supra egimus. Specificum vero triplex, personale, verbale & reale est. Personale, Christus, non simpliciter ut Filius Dei, sed ut Redemptor & Propheta, quem Deus audire jussit. Hic est Filius meus ille dilectus, in quo acquiesco. Hunc audite; Matth. HI. 17. XVII. 5. Nemo cognoscit Filium nisi Pater, neque Patrem quis cognoscit nisi Filius, & cui Filius revelare voluerit, ibid. XI. 27. Qui ejus testimonium accipit, obsignavit, quòd Deus verax sit. Nam quem Deus misit, is verba Dei loquitur, &c. Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam æternam. Et qui Filio non obedit, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super ipsum, Joh. III. 33-f. Hoc nempe Christo datum est, ut revelet Patrem & se ipsum, & loquatur verba Dei, quibus credenti salus promittitur; ut qui Christo, & in Christum credit, vitam æternam habeat; qui verò ei non credit, is condemnetur. Ideò S. Paulus: Si, inquit, confessus fueris ore tuo Dominum Jesum, & credideris in corde, quòd Deus eum ex mortuis suscitaverit, salvaberis, Rom. X. 9. Nam quum Christus dixit: Qui credit in me, non credit in me, sed in eum, qui misit me, Joh. XII. 44. non se ipsum à fidei subjecto summovit, sed objectum ejus non distinctum à Patre, sed cum Patre unum dominum, juxta ejusdem verba: Ego & Pater unum sumus, ibid. X. 30. fecit. Verbale est Evangelium; in quo Christus & ejus beneficia promulgantur; de quo supra pluribus egimus. Reale denique est, quod Christus in Evangelio & promisso & exhibito velut credendum ad salutem revelat. Estque illud Christus cum omnibus salutaribus beneficiis suis, quibus nobis factus sapientia à Deo, justitia; sanctificatio & redemptio, 1 Cor. I. 30.
units.tr: There is one object of faith that is generic and another that is specific. The generic object, which is common to all faith, is God himself and all his testimony or revelation. The specific object, which belongs to saving faith alone, is Christ the Redeemer and his benefits. Just as the Israelites, with the same eyes with which they looked at the bronze serpent, also saw many other things, yet obtained salvation only by looking at the serpent, so with the same eyes of faith we look upon any word of God, and upon Christ and the grace of God in Christ. Yet the sight that saves us is not of just any word, but only of the word concerning Christ and the grace of God in him. We have already discussed the first, the generic object of faith. The specific object is threefold: personal, verbal and real. The personal object is Christ, not simply as the Son of God, but as Redeemer and Prophet, whom God commanded us to hear: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him" (Matt. 3:17; 17:5). "No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him" (ibid. 11:27). "He who receives his testimony has certified that God is true. For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God," etc. "He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him" (John 3:33–36). For Christ was given so that he might reveal the Father and himself, and speak the words of God, by which salvation is promised to the believer; so that whoever believes in Christ and on Christ has eternal life, but whoever does not believe him is condemned. Therefore Saint Paul says: "If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God has raised him from the dead, you will be saved" (Rom. 10:9). For when Christ said, "He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me" (John 12:44), he did not remove himself from being the subject of faith, but made its object not distinct from the Father, but one Lord with the Father, according to his own words: "I and the Father are one" (ibid. 10:30). The verbal object is the Gospel, in which Christ and his benefits are proclaimed, of which we have spoken at length above. Finally, the real object is what Christ, in the Gospel, reveals both as promised and as offered, to be believed for salvation. This is Christ himself with all his saving benefits, by which he has been made to us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification and redemption (1 Cor. 1:30).

units.la: mo crucis, ibid. v. 18. Christus crucifixus, ibid. v. 23. captivorum dimissio, caecorum restitutio, confractorum liberatio, annus Domini acceptus, Luc. IV. 18.19. Justitia Dei, quæ in Evangelio revelatur ex fide in fidem Rom. I. 17. remissio peccatorum, Luc. XXIV. 47. Salus, Heb. II. 3. denique omnia illa Novi Testamenti bona, de quibus supra fusius. Idem enim fidei & Evangelii objectum est. Unde promissionem specialis misericordiae in Christo omnium Sanctorum fides semper respexit. Pro hac (remissione peccatorum) omnis sanctus orabit tempore opportuno, Psal. XXXII. 5. 6. Tecum est remissio, ut timearis, ibid. CXXX. 4. Credimus nos per gratiam Jesu Christi servari, quemadmodum & illi, Actor. XV. 11. Huic (Christo) omnes Prophetæ testimonium dant, remissionem peccatorum accepturos per nomen ejus, qui crediderint in eum, ibid. X. 43. Accedit, quòd & gratia Dei in Christo, ejusque satisfactio illud ipsum est, quo apprehenso coram Deo justificamur: & remissio peccatorum est justitia fidei, Roman. IV. 11.13. seu justitia, quæ est ex fide, ibid. X. 6. & Lex peccata arguit & damnat, ac proin salvificae fidei objectum esse non potest, & fides salvifica æquè in Christum, atque oculi Israelitarum in serpentem æneum respexerunt, Joh. III. 14. 15. Num. XXI. 8.9. & aliud longè fides salvifica, quàm communis reproborum, quæ & daemoniorum est, respicere debet. Denique si gratia & misericordia Dei in Christo proprium fidei salvificae objectum non est, sequitur fidem, quatenus gratiam Dei in Christo apprehendit, non magis salvare, quàm quatenus doctrinæ de Diabolis & gehenna assentitur: Haec enim non minus quàm illa revelata est: & assensus non minus huic, quàm illi praeberi debet.
units.tr: the word of the cross (ibid. v. 18); Christ crucified (ibid. v. 23); the release of captives, the recovery of sight to the blind, the liberation of the oppressed, the acceptable year of the Lord (Luke 4:18–19); the righteousness of God, which is revealed in the Gospel from faith to faith (Rom. 1:17); the remission of sins (Luke 24:47); salvation (Heb. 2:3); and finally all those blessings of the New Testament of which we have spoken more fully above. For faith and the Gospel have the same object. Hence faith has always looked to the promise of special mercy in Christ among all the saints. "For this (the remission of sins) every saint shall pray at an opportune time" (Ps. 32:5–6). "With you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared" (ibid. 130:4). "We believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, just as they are" (Acts 15:11). "To him (Christ) all the prophets bear witness, that through his name all who believe in him shall receive the remission of sins" (ibid. 10:43). In addition, the grace of God in Christ, and his satisfaction, is that very thing by which, when it is laid hold of, we are justified before God; and the remission of sins is the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4:11, 13), or the righteousness which is of faith (ibid. 10:6). The Law convicts sins and condemns them, and therefore cannot be the object of saving faith; and saving faith must look to Christ just as the eyes of the Israelites looked to the bronze serpent (John 3:14–15; Num. 21:8–9), and it must look to something quite different from that general faith of the reprobate, which belongs also to the demons. Finally, if the grace and mercy of God in Christ is not the proper object of saving faith, it follows that faith, insofar as it lays hold of the grace of God in Christ, does not save any more than insofar as it assents to the doctrine concerning devils and hell. For the latter is no less revealed than the former, and assent must be given to it no less than to the former.

units.la: XCIV. Non nudè fides haec in objectum suum fertur, sed illud apprehendit, & ceu ad se pertinens, sibi applicat. Nam promissio gratiae in Christo non ut indefinita, sed ut determinata in Scriptura proponitur. Sic Deus ad Abrahamum. Ero Deus tuus & Seminis tui post te, Genes. XVII. 7. Quod S. Paulus respiciens dicit, non per legem promissionem factam esse Abrahae & Semini ejus, sed per fidem, ut esset secundum gratiam, & firma promissio esset toti Semini, Rom. IV. 13. 16. Quam determinationem, si supervacanea non fuit, Abrahamus sibi applicare debuit, & semen ejus debet. Nam qui ex fide sunt, sunt filii Abrahami, & benedicuntur cum fideli Abrahamo, Gal. III. 7.9. Apostoli iis, quos in fide erudiendos & confirmandos suscepepunt, promissionem gratiae in Christo peculiariter applicarunt. Gratias ago Deo meo semper de vobis, ob gratiam Dei, quæ vobis in Christo Jesu data est, I. Cor. I. 4. Fidelis Deus est, per quem vocati estis in communionem Filii ipsius Jesu Christi, ibid. v. 9. An nescitis, vos esse Templum Dei, & Spiritum Dei habitare in vobis? ibid. III. 16. Vos estis corpus Christi, & membra ejus ex parte, ib. XII. 27. Gratia servati estis per fidem, Eph. II. 8. Estis in eo completi, qui caput est omnis imperii & potestatis, in quo etiam circumcisi estis circumcisione quae fit sine manibus, &c. Col. II. 10. 11. 12. Vos estis genus electum, Sacerdotale, Regium Sacerdotium, &c. I. Pet. II. 9. Scribo vobis, filioli, quoniam remissa vobis sunt peccata, I. Joh. II. 12. Vos ex Deo estis, ibid. IV. 4. Huic applicationi
units.tr: XCIV. This faith is not directed to its object bare, but apprehends it and, as belonging to itself, applies it to itself. For the promise of grace in Christ is not set forth in Scripture as indefinite, but as determinate. So God said to Abraham: "I will be your God and the God of your seed after you" (Gen. 17:7). Saint Paul, considering this, says that the promise was made to Abraham and his seed not through the law, but through faith, so that it might be according to grace, and the promise might be firm to all the seed (Rom. 4:13, 16). If this determination was not superfluous, Abraham ought to have applied it to himself, and his seed ought to apply it. For those who are of faith are the sons of Abraham, and are blessed with faithful Abraham (Gal. 3:7, 9). The Apostles specially applied the promise of grace in Christ to those whom they had taken on to instruct and confirm in the faith. "I thank my God always for you, for the grace of God which has been given to you in Christ Jesus" (1 Cor. 1:4). "God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ" (ibid. v. 9). "Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?" (ibid. 3:16). "You are the body of Christ, and members of it in part" (ibid. 12:27). "By grace you have been saved through faith" (Eph. 2:8). "You are complete in him, who is the head of all rule and authority, in whom you were also circumcised with a circumcision made without hands," etc. (Col. 2:10–12). "You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood," etc. (1 Pet. 2:9). "I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven" (1 John 2:12). "You are of God" (ibid. 4:4). To this application [...]

units.la: In Christum Redemptorem & salutaria ejus beneficia propriè fertur.
units.tr: Faith is properly directed to Christ the Redeemer and to his saving benefits.

units.la: Neque nudè sed Christum & gratiam ejus apprehendendo & sibi applicando. cationi Apostolicæ fidem profesi vel astipulati sunt, vel non. Si astipulati sunt, utique eandem gratiam sibi applicarunt, vos mutando in nos, & singuli in ego & me si non sunt astipulati, fideles non fuerunt; Sed applicasse fideles sibi gratiam, Scripturæ diserte testantur. Quis ἡμᾶς nos separabit à charitate Christi ? Rom. VIII. 35. In his omnibus plus quàm victores sumus per eum, qui nos dilexit. ib. v. 37. Vitam, quam nunc vivo in carne, vivo per fidem Filii Dei, qui dilexit Me, & semetipsum pro Me tradidit, Gal. II.20. Elegit Nos in ipso, Ephes. I.4. Unà vivificavit Nos per Christum, ibid. II.5. Videte, qualem charitatem Nobis dedit Pater, ut Filii Dei vocemur. Charissimi, nunc filii Dei sumus, sed nondum patefactum est, quod erimus, 1. Joh. III.1.2. Sic Apostoli, à Spiritu Dei acti, & suam fidem professi sunt, & formarunt aliorum fidem. Si eodem modo applicare fideles omnes non audent, cur talem formam præscripserunt? Et promissiones sanè generales sunt, sed singulari assumptione applicantur. Quæ singularis assumptio cùm non sit fidei, quæ creditur, sed qua creditur, in verbo Dei scribi nec potuit, quia singularium hominum innumerorum est; nec debuit, quia non testimonio externo, sed interno conscientiæ & Spiritus S. in corde habitantis indiget. Qualis fides, qua credimus, esse debeat, in verbo Dei scriptum est. Sed quòd in nobis talis sit, qualem esse Deus in verbo jubet, in tabulis cordis legimus. Sic Paulus: Novi, cui crediderim, 2. Tim. I.12. Neque tamen is legerat in Scriptura, quòd ipse crederet, sed fidem suam in corde suo oculis fidei viderat. Par omnium fidelium ratio est. Suam quisque fidem, sic Augustinus de Trinit. lib. XIII.2. loquitur, apud semetipsum videt, in altero eam credit esse, non videt. Scitè etiam Bonaventura sent. lib. III. d. 23. Fides, inquit, essentialiter existens in anima cognoscitur per suam essentiam, idque non tantùm scientia notitiæ & discretionis, sed etiam experientiâ. Per hoc enim cognoscit aliquis se habere fidem, dum & se ipsum introrsus ingrediens experitur, utrum sit promptus ad credendum. Accedunt & aliæ rationes, quibus apprehensio & applicatio specialis gratiæ in Christo nititur, velut, quòd fides & spes indivulso nexu cohærent, quia fides est ὑπόστασις ἐλπιζομένων subsistentia eorum quæ sperantur, Hebr. XI.1. & qui vitam æternam sperat, is non tantùm vitam æternam futuram, sed etiam se vitæ ejus compotem fore, sibi recipit: quòd promissio citra specialem applicationem, seu acceptionem ejus inutilis est; imò propterea ex fide est hæreditas, ut firma sit promissio toti Semini, Roman. IV.16. quòd in humanis etiam contractibus promissio vel donatio per acceptationem demum rata fit: quòd Ministri verbi Dei beneficio clavium credentibus remissionem peccatorum annuntiant. Johan. XX.23, qua absolutione audita fideles credunt, peccata sibi remissa esse, quòd inprimis Deus fideles obsignat, & arrhabonem Spiritus in cordibus nostris dat, 2. Cor. I.22. Ephes. I.13.14. IV.30. & qui credit in Filium Dei, habet testimonium in se ipso, 1. Joh. V.10. & quidem testimonium hoc, quòd Deus nobis vitam æternam dedit, & hæc vita in Filio ejus est, ib. v.11. Cùm tamen testimonium tale credenti ipsi, non aliis factum sit; & arrhabo ei detur, qui rem sibi applicat & habet, non alii: quòd denique Sacramenta credentibus eam gratiam obsignant, non quæ aliis, sed quæ ipsis offertur. Abrahamus enim accepit sigillum justitiæ suæ, Rom. IV.11. Et Deus servat nos per lavacrum regenerationis, Tit. III.5. Quin & Ananias Paulo dixit: Exsurge, baptizare & ablue peccata tua, Act. XXII.16. Denique nec cœna theatricum spectaculum est, sed fidelibus quibusvis communionem corporis & sanguinis Christi obsignat, 1. Cor. X.16.
units.tr: Not bare, but by apprehending Christ and his grace and applying them to oneself. To the Apostolic application, either those who professed faith agreed [astipulati], or they did not. If they agreed, they surely applied the same grace to themselves, changing vos into nos, and each one into ego and me. If they did not agree, they were not faithful; but Scripture plainly testifies that the faithful did apply grace to themselves. Who shall separate us [ἡμᾶς] from the love of Christ? (Rom. 8:35). In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us (ibid. v. 37). The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Gal. 2:20). He chose us in him (Eph. 1:4). He made us alive together with Christ (ibid. 2:5). See what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God. Beloved, now we are children of God, but it has not yet been revealed what we shall be (1 John 3:1–2). Thus the Apostles, moved by the Spirit of God, professed their own faith and shaped the faith of others. If all the faithful do not dare to apply it in the same way, why did they prescribe such a form? The promises are indeed general, but they are applied by a singular assumption. Since this singular assumption belongs not to the faith which is believed [quae creditur], but to the faith by which it is believed [qua creditur], it could not be written in the Word of God, because it belongs to innumerable individual men; nor ought it to have been written, because it needs not external testimony, but the internal testimony of conscience and of the Holy Spirit dwelling in the heart. What kind of faith, by which we believe, ought to be, is written in the Word of God. But that in us it is such as God commands in his Word, we read on the tablets of the heart. So Paul: I know whom I have believed (2 Tim. 1:12). Yet he had not read in Scripture that he himself believed, but had seen his own faith in his heart with the eyes of faith. The reason is the same for all the faithful. Each one sees his own faith, so Augustine speaks in De Trinitate book 13, chapter 2, within himself; he does not see it, but believes that it is in another. Bonaventure also wisely says in the Sentences, book 3, distinction 23: Faith, he says, existing essentially in the soul, is known through its essence, and this not only by the knowledge of recognition and discernment, but also by experience. For by this one knows that he has faith, when, entering into himself, he experiences whether he is ready to believe. There are also other reasons on which the special apprehension and application of grace in Christ rests: for instance, that faith and hope cohere in an inseparable bond, because faith is the substance of things hoped for (Heb. 11:1), and he who hopes for eternal life takes to himself not only that eternal life will be his in the future, but also that he will be a partaker of it. The promise without special application, or acceptance of it, is useless; indeed, for this reason the inheritance is by faith, so that the promise may be firm to all the seed (Rom. 4:16). In human contracts too, a promise or gift is only ratified by acceptance. The ministers of the Word of God, by the power of the keys, announce the remission of sins to believers (John 20:23); on hearing this absolution the faithful believe that their sins are forgiven to them. Above all, God seals the faithful and gives the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts (2 Cor. 1:22; Eph. 1:13–14; 4:30). And he who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself (1 John 5:10), and indeed this testimony is that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son (ibid. v. 11). Since such testimony has been made to the believer himself, and not to others; and the pledge is given to him who applies the thing to himself and possesses it, not to another. Finally, the sacraments seal to believers that grace which is offered not to others, but to themselves. For Abraham received the seal of his righteousness (Rom. 4:11). And God saves us through the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5). Indeed Ananias said to Paul: Arise, be baptized and wash away your sins (Acts 22:16). Finally, the Supper is not a theatrical spectacle, but seals to all the faithful communion in the body and blood of Christ (1 Cor. 10:16).

units.la: XCV. Nimium fidei salvificæ objectum laessunt
units.tr: XCV. They harm the object of saving faith

units.la: XCV. Nimiùm fidei salvificæ objectum lacessunt, qui illud non specialem gratiam Dei in Christo, sed omnia, quæ Deus in verbo suo revelavit, faciunt, & credentibus jus promissam gratiam sibi applicandi, & Christum Redemptorem apprehendendi negant. Ita Pontificii, quibus applicatio misericordiæ Dei in Christo, non quæ antecedit, sed quæ per ipsam fidem specialis evadit, temerariæ præsumptionis crimen incurrit. Socmiani quoque, & conspirantes cum iisdem Remonstrantes in objectum speciale fidei impetum faciunt, negantes necessario eam in Christum ferri. Curcellæus ne quidem cognitionem Christi ad salutem simpliciter necessariam esse, asserit. Eò usque hominum illorum error prolabitur. Diluta hominum omnium argumenta sunt. Perperam enim alicubi, veluti Matth. IX. 28. Luc. VII.9. Mar. XVI.16. Joh. VI.68.69. fidem solius potentiæ & Divinitatis Christi exigi pertendunt, cùm ex locorum eorum circumstantiis facile colligatur, sic Deum fidem potentiæ & Divinitatis Christi exegisse, ut etiam fides misericordiæ sub ea intelligi debeat; & alia etiam fidei miraculosæ, alia salvificæ ratio sit. Neque si quidam crediturí fide justificante miracula edent, uti in Ecclesia Apostolica factum est, Marc. XVI.16.17. idem fidei justificantis & miraculorum objectum esse, consequitur. Ejusmodi enim objectum fidei salvificæ figendum est, quod salvandis omnibus comperat. Quomodo nec leprosi illius Christo dicentis. Si volueris, potes me purificare, Marc. I.40.41. fides justificans fuit, quia beneficium mere corporale spectavit. Crudum vero illud est, quòd Pharisæum illum cum fide specialis benevolentiæ rejectum, & publicanum sine ea justificatum, ex Luc. XVIII. 11.12. pronuntiant. Nullum enim in Pharisæo sua duntaxat opera decantante, & persuadente sibi se justum esse, reliquósque despiciente ibid. v.9. fidei specialis benevolentiæ vestigium apparet, licèt enim Deo gratias egerit, egit tamen superbè & arroganter, publicanum juxta se despiciens, & jactavit se, & cum Deo de justitia propria disceptavit magis, quàm oravit; Pelagianorum præsultor, non Christianorum incentor. In Publicano verò quàm expressa est gratiæ speciali confidentis oratio, & tundente præ humilitate pectus suum, & exclamante: Deus propitius esto mihi peccatori? v. 13. Neque nullam in speciali gratia Dei fiduciam collocarunt, qui auditis Petri & Pauli concionibus conversi sunt, Act. II. IV. X. XIII. XVII. vel fidem specialis gratiæ illi concionantes nullam exegerunt. Quid enim sibi volunt illa Petri: Resipiscite, & baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomine Jesu Christi in remissionem peccatorum. Vobis enim facta est promissio, &c. ibid. II. 38.39. ? Quid illa ejusdem: Huic omnes omnes Prophetæ testimonium dant, remissionem peccatorum accepturum, per nomen ejus, qui crediderit in eum? ibid. X. 43. Quid illa Pauli: Notum sit vobis, fratres, annuntiari vobis remissionem peccatorum per ipsum, & ab omnibus, à quibus per Legem Mosis absolvi non potuistis, ibid. XIII. 38. 39. Aureæ hæ gnomæ sunt, quibus genuina fidei esca exprimitur. Atque eodem eorundem Apostolorum de Christo, ejus morte & resurrectione conciones collineant, utpote quæ gratiam remissionis peccatorum in morte & resurrectione Christi fundant. Abrahamicæ porro fidei objectum non fuisse tantum promissionem numerosæ prolis, sed inprimis gratiæ Seminis, Christi, & benedictionis ejus ad omnes familias terræ perventuræ, abunde in loco probavimus. Non enim tenuem adeo sensum & medullam habet promissio: Ego scutum tuum, merces tua magna valde, Gen. XV. 1. Ero Deus tuus & Seminis tui, ibid. XVII. 7. Neque minus divitem sensum habent illa, quòd Jesus sit Christus, quæ quisquis credit ex Deo genitus dicitur, 1. Joh. V. 1. quia nec Jesus, nec Christus est, nisi ut Salvator à peccatis, & ad ipsum unctus, ut captivis liberationem nuntiaret; & Salvator meus, unctus mihi. Cùm verò in Symbolo Apostolico contineri fiduciam in misericordia Dei speciali negant, næ oculos illi clausos nimium tenent, ne videant id, quod Symboli anima est. Quid enim fides remissionis peccatorum & vitæ æternæ, quam in eo pro se credens quisque profitetur, est, si fides specialis gratiæ in Christo non est? Quid ter repetita phrasis: Credo in Deum Patrem: Credo in Jesum Christum: Credo in Spiritum S. nisi fiduciam gratiæ clamat? Quid enim est credere in eum? Credendo, inquit Augustinus, Tract. 29. in Joh. amare, credendo diligere, credendo in eum ire, & ejus membris incorporari. Ita sine fiducia gratiæ DEI non salvaberis, sed ab ipso, ceu igne consumente consumeris. Quòd mihi, tibi peccata remissa esse nuspiam in verbo Dei expressum est, nil fiduciæ huic, & applicationi speciali gratiæ derogat. Generales enim in eo promissiones extant, quas quisque καταφοσθεὶς certus in mente, seu corde suo fidei sibi applicat. Atque ita in propositione generali etiam speciale implicatur. Nam si omnis credens in Christum servatur, utique & ego credens, & fidei meæ sensum haud fallacem habens salvabor, vi promissionis scriptæ. Et quis non fidelium legit has sententias: Qui remittit Tibi omnes iniquitates Tuas: qui sanat iniquitates Tuas; qui redimit ex fovea vitam Tuam, qui coronat Te in misericordia, &c. Psal. CIII. 3. 4. Hæc enim unicuique laudes Dei celebranti dicuntur. Si promissionem Evangelii generalem credens sibi applicare non potest, tum nec peccator comminationem legis universalem sibi applicare potest, vel tenetur. Nam nec hujus nomen scriptum est. Frustra clamitant, propositionem absolutam: Ego credo in Filium Dei, non in verbo Dei, sed in fallaci opinatione hominis consistere. Sit opinatio illorum fallax. Quid hoc ad fideles? In illis enim est notitia omni humanæ rationis & sensuum judicio firmior, ex operatione Spiritus S. per lucem verbi Dei accensa & immoto verbo Dei innixa. Unde Philippus Eunucho dicens: Si credis toto corde, licet baptizeris, eidem respondenti: Credo Filium Dei esse Jesum Christum, non fallacem opinionem objecit, sed eum baptizavit, atque sic conditionem implevit; Act. VIII. 37. 38. Fideles certè se credere noverunt. David: Credidi, Psal. CXVI. 10. Apostoli: Nos credimus & cognovimus, te esse Christum illum, Filium Dei viventis, Joh. VI. 69. Lunatici pater, Credo Domine, Marc. IX. 24. Paulus suo & credentium nomine: Nos in Christum credidimus, ut justificemur ex fide Christi, Gal. II. 16. Scio, cui crediderim, 2. Tim. I. 12. Et tum sibi, tum aliis, qui cum ipso erant, eundem Spiritum fidei, quem David habuit, afferens dixit: Habemus eundem Spiritum fidei secundum illud, quod scriptum est; Credidi & ideo locutus sum, nos quoque credimus, &c. 2. Cor. IV. 13. Illum Spiritum Deus dat pignus in corda credentium, quos per illum obsignat ibid. I. 22. & arrham hæreditatis, Ephes. I. 14. de quo etiam supra diximus. Accedunt operationes Spiritus S. & fidei, quæ utrumque infallibiliter arguunt. Quomodo denique nos ipsos probare, an simus in fide, possumus, 2. Cor. XIII. 5. quod, an in nobis sit, nunquam certò cognoscimus? Jam & fides & peccatorum remissio cùm relata sint, simul sint oportet, quia ὁ relata simul natura sunt, ut fides misericordiæ & gratiæ justificantis nec prior hac, nec posterior natura sit.
