Nihilo minus manet ordo naturæ, juxta quem promissio de remissione peccatorum in Evangelio oblata prior est fides: at fides prior est applicatione, seu receptione promissionis, quomodo prius dives mendico eleemosynam offert, quàm mendicus manum, qua oblatam eleemosynam accipit & possidet. Deniq; fiducia, quatenus est persuasio de Dei gratia, prior est remissione peccatorum, & est ipsa fides justificans, non ea posterius aliquid. Confidentia verò illa, quam ex sensu remissionis peccatorum concipimus, ceu fidei justificantis effectus, eandem sequitur. Non enim mihi peccata remittuntur, quia sentio mihi remissa esse; sed sentio mihi remissa esse, quia remissa sunt. XCVI. Perperam verò etiam Augustani Fidei salvificæ objectum proprium gratiam universalem objectivam & subjectivam constituunt. Nam absolutè universalis, uti non sed mel ostendimus; nulla est. Et meminerimus, non nostrum esse, ut nobis formemus credendi rationes, quales esse nostro judicio debeant, vel possint: quò ex illarum dein præscripto fidei dogma constituamus. Cujus etiam usus nullius ad fidem usus vel momenti est; & quia nullius, perniciosum dogma fidei est; quæ si radicem nullam solidam habet, facilè deficit vel vacillat. Quid si enim ex universali isto principio deductam conclusionem obtineas, nimirum spectare ad te quoque gratiam Dei & meritum Christi, prout illud ad omnes spectare iis videtur, quid hinc solatii, vel fiduciæ salutaris? Et si vera & καταφοσθεὶς, seu de salute certos nos reddens fides illa est, quæ solo & unico fundamento promissionum universalium nititur, quivis profanus etiam, & in profanitate sua perfistens verè, & ad salutis certitudinem credere poterit, quia fundamentum quod dicitur, fidei universale unicum est. Atqui si dixerimus, quòd communionem habeamus cum Deo, & in tenebris ambulamus, mentimur, & non facimus veritatem. Si verò in luce ambulamus, sicut ipse est in luce, communionem invicem habemus, & sanguis JesuChristi Filii ejus purgat nos ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. I. 6. 7. quod totum deducitur ex ἐπαγγελίᾳ promissione illa, quam Apostoli audiverunt ab ipso, Filio Dei, quòd Deus sit lux, & tenebrae in ipso nulla sint, ibid. v. 5. ¦Hoc ergo axioma, si in toto Evangelio continetur, absit, ut fidei, quae utramque in Evangelio paginam facit, fundamentum ejusmodi faciamus, per quod credere & verè profiteri communionem cum Deo, & sanguine Christi iis quoque, in quibus merae tenebrae sunt, liceat. Si quis autem usus ad fidem erit dogmatis de universali gratia, in eo consistat, ut inde inferatur, nos servari posse. Quod apud eos, qui cum tentationibus colluctantur, exigui vel nullius est. Ut verò certam spem tentati concipiant, doctrina de gratia speciali in Christo credentibus promissa sola momentum habet. Et sanè constare nobis fides nostra sine fundamento absolutè universalis gratiae potest. Sufficit illa innitatur universali alicui propositioni, quae in verbo Dei extans maximam certitudinem habeat, qualis illa est, quae credentibus & resipiscentibus omnibus gratiam in Christo promittit. Quae propositio arx & acropolis Evangelii est. Illa ad fidem concipiendam sufficit, quia licet non omnibus hominibus, imò nemini nisi credenti & resipiscenti Dei gratiam & communionem mortis Christi polliceatur, tamen certissimam credenti & resipiscenti fidem facit, quòd salus in promissione hac facta ad se pertineat. Sic occurritur tentationi, quae à fide concipienda arcet hominem, in quo haetenus nihil fidei est. In tentationibus verò aliorum resipiscentiae & fidei observandi sunt gradus, qui serii quidem & sinceri vel primi ubique sunt, ulterioris fidei fundamentum praebent, juxta voces Evangelii, quae pauperes Spiritu, esurientes & sitientes justitiam, laborantes & onusios, Matth. V. 3. 6. XI. 28. omnes denique (quod efficax inprimis ad consolandum argumentum est) qui βέλεσι volunt Apocal. XXII. 17. sigillatim vocant, iisque liberum ad gratiam aditum faciunt, sub quibus universalibus ad concipiendam fidem rectè assumi, tum rei ipsius evidentia, tum praxis multorum infirmitate laborantium docet. Et sinceri illi, primi licet, regenerationis gradus salutis quoque certitudinem sigillatim efficiunt, quia Scriptura non tantum tales vocat, sed etiam eos beatos praedicat, & satietatem ad justitiam & Regni Coelorum spem pollicetur. Haec autem homini quàm certissima facere, efficacissimus confirmandae fidei modus est. Ac licet etiam certum sit, Deum non in omnibus velle operari fidem, abundè tamen argumenti homo ad fidem alacriter concipiendam habet, quia novit, nec se nominatim ab ea operatione excludi, & in omnium hominum verbum Dei audientium genere esse aliquos, quibus Deus hanc gratiam facit; & se quoque eorum in ordine esse, quos Deus exteriore vocatione dignatur, quod aliquam saltem spei faculam accendere potest. Per ejusmodi argumenta homo non quidem per se, qui nihil potest, sed efficiente & cuncta operante Dei gratia, inducì facilè potest, ut bono animo sit. Accidit, quòd is, qui cum tentatione tali luctatur, ut dubitet, an sibi quoque fidem largiri Deus velit, & eam in rem serio inquirit, haud dubiè etiam desiderat enixè, ut ex eorum, quibus facultas illa à Deo conceditur, numero sit; At desiderium tale amorem, amor cognitionem boni, & fidei qualiscunque fructum qualemcunque arguit.
units.tr: XCV. They wrong the object of saving faith when they make it not God's special grace in Christ but all the things God has revealed in his word, and when they deny that believers have the right to apply the promised grace to themselves and to lay hold of Christ the Redeemer. This is the error of the Papists, for whom the application of God's mercy in Christ is not what comes before faith but what emerges specially through faith itself, and so they incur the guilt of rash presumption. The Socinians likewise, and the Remonstrants who conspire with them, attack the special object of faith, denying that faith necessarily bears on Christ. Curcellaeus asserts that even the knowledge of Christ is not simply necessary for salvation. So far does the error of these men go. Their arguments have all been refuted. They wrongly contend, from passages such as Matt. 9:28, Luke 7:9, Mark 16:16 and John 6:68-69, that faith in the power and divinity of Christ alone is required, since from the circumstances of those passages it is easily gathered that God required faith in the power and divinity of Christ in such a way that faith in his mercy must be understood under it as well; and there is one kind of miraculous faith and another kind of saving faith. Nor does it follow, because some who believe with justifying faith work miracles, as happened in the apostolic Church (Mark 16:16-17), that the object of justifying faith and of miracles is the same. For the object of saving faith must be one that is evident to all who are to be saved. Thus the leper who said to Christ, If you will, you can make me clean (Mark 1:40-41), did not have justifying faith, because he looked only to a purely bodily benefit. It is crude, however, to pronounce from Luke 18:11-12 that the Pharisee was rejected for lacking faith in special benevolence, and the publican justified without it. For no trace of faith in special benevolence appears in the Pharisee, who extolled his own works, persuaded himself that he was righteous, and despised the others (v. 9). Although he gave thanks to God, he did so proudly and arrogantly, looking down on the publican beside him; he boasted, and argued with God about his own righteousness more than he prayed. He was the forerunner of the Pelagians, not the teacher of Christians. In the publican, on the other hand, how plain is the prayer of one trusting in special grace, beating his breast in humility and crying out, God, be merciful to me, a sinner (v. 13). Nor did those who were converted after hearing the sermons of Peter and Paul (Acts 2, 4, 10, 13, 17) place no confidence in God's special grace, nor did those preachers demand no faith in special grace. For what do those words of Peter mean: Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins. For the promise is made to you, and so on (Acts 2:38-39)? What of his words: To him all the prophets bear witness, that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive forgiveness of sins (Acts 10:43)? What of Paul's: Let it be known to you, brothers, that through him forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone is set free from all things from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses (Acts 13:38-39)? These are golden maxims, in which the genuine food of faith is expressed. And the sermons of these same apostles about Christ, his death and his resurrection aim at the same thing, since they ground the grace of forgiveness of sins in the death and resurrection of Christ. Moreover, we have shown at length in its place that the object of Abraham's faith was not only the promise of numerous offspring, but above all the grace of the Seed, Christ, and of his blessing that was to reach all the families of the earth. For the promise has no meagre sense or marrow: I am your shield, your reward will be very great (Gen. 15:1); I will be your God and the God of your seed (Gen. 17:7). Nor do those words, that Jesus is the Christ, which whoever believes is said to be born of God (1 John 5:1), have a less rich sense, because Jesus is not Christ except as the Savior from sins and anointed to him, to proclaim liberty to captives; and my Savior, anointed for me. But when they deny that trust in God's special mercy is contained in the Apostles' Creed, they keep their eyes shut too tightly to see what is the soul of the Creed. For what is the faith in the forgiveness of sins and eternal life, which each person professes when he believes for himself in it, if there is no faith in special grace in Christ? What is the threefold repeated formula, I believe in God the Father; I believe in Jesus Christ; I believe in the Holy Spirit, if not a cry of trust in grace? For what is to believe in him? By believing, says Augustine (Tract. 29 on John), to love, by believing to cherish, by believing to go into him and to be incorporated into his members. So without trust in the grace of God you will not be saved, but consumed by him as by a consuming fire. That it is nowhere expressed in God's word that my sins, or your sins, are forgiven takes nothing away from this trust and special application of grace. For there are general promises in it, which each person, fully assured in his mind or heart, applies to himself by faith. And so a special application is implied in a general proposition. For if every believer in Christ is saved, then certainly I too, believing and holding a sense of my faith that is not deceptive, shall be saved by the force of the written promise. And which of the faithful does not read these sentences: Who forgives all your iniquities; who heals all your diseases; who redeems your life from the pit; who crowns you with mercy, and so on (Ps. 103:3-4)? For these are said to each person who celebrates the praises of God. If the believer cannot apply to himself the general promise of the gospel, then neither can the sinner apply to himself, or is he bound to apply, the general threat of the law. For not even this is written with his name. In vain they cry out that the absolute proposition, I believe in the Son of God, rests not on the word of God but on a deceptive opinion of man. Let their opinion be deceptive. What does that matter to the faithful? For in them there is a knowledge firmer than all human reason and the judgment of the senses, kindled by the operation of the Holy Spirit through the light of God's word and resting on the unmoved word of God. Hence Philip, saying to the eunuch, If you believe with all your heart, you may be baptized, when he answered, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, did not raise an objection of deceptive opinion, but baptized him, and so fulfilled the condition (Acts 8:37-38). The faithful surely know that they believe. David: I believed (Ps. 116:10). The apostles: We believe and know that you are that Christ, the Son of the living God (John 6:69). The father of the lunatic boy: Lord, I believe (Mark 9:24). Paul, in his own name and that of believers: We have believed in Christ, that we may be justified by the faith of Christ (Gal. 2:16). I know whom I have believed (2 Tim. 1:12). And bringing forward the same spirit of faith that David had, both for himself and for those who were with him, he said: We have the same spirit of faith, according to what is written: I believed, and therefore I spoke; we also believe, and so on (2 Cor. 4:13). God gives this Spirit as a pledge in the hearts of believers, whom through him he seals (2 Cor. 1:22), and as the earnest of the inheritance (Eph. 1:14), of which we have also spoken above. There are added the operations of the Holy Spirit and of faith, which prove both infallibly. And how can we test ourselves, whether we are in the faith (2 Cor. 13:5), if we never know for certain whether it is in us? Now, since faith and the forgiveness of sins are relative to each other, they must exist together, because relatives are by nature simultaneous, so that faith in mercy and justifying grace is neither prior nor posterior to the other by nature. Nevertheless the order of nature remains, according to which the promise of forgiveness of sins offered in the gospel comes first, and faith comes after; for faith comes before the application or reception of the promise, just as a rich man offers alms to a beggar before the beggar stretches out the hand with which he receives and possesses the alms offered. Finally, trust, insofar as it is the persuasion concerning God's grace, comes before the forgiveness of sins, and is itself justifying faith; it is not something that follows. But that confidence which we conceive from the sense of the forgiveness of sins, as an effect of justifying faith, follows it. For my sins are not forgiven because I feel that they have been forgiven; rather I feel that they have been forgiven because they have been forgiven. XCVI. Moreover, the followers of the Augsburg Confession are wrong to make the proper object of saving faith the universal grace, objective and subjective. For absolute universality, as we have shown more than once, does not exist. And let us remember that it is not for us to frame for ourselves the grounds of believing, of what kind they ought or may be in our judgment, and then from their prescription to set up a dogma of faith. Such a dogma has no use or importance for faith; and because it has no use, it is a harmful dogma of faith, since a faith that has no solid root easily fails or wavers. For if from this universal principle you derive the conclusion that God's grace and the merit of Christ also belong to you, as they seem to belong to all, what comfort or saving trust does this bring? And if that faith is true and fully assured, that is, the faith that makes us certain of salvation, and it rests on the sole and single foundation of universal promises, then any profane person, persisting in his profanity, could truly believe and be certain of salvation, since the foundation said to be universal is one and the same for all. But if we say that we have fellowship with God and walk in darkness, we lie and do not practise the truth; but if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:6-7). All of this is derived from the message [ἐπαγγελίᾳ] which the apostles heard from the Son of God himself, that God is light and in him there is no darkness at all (v. 5). If, then, this axiom is contained in the whole gospel, far be it from us to make the foundation of faith, which makes up both pages of the gospel, such that it would be permitted to believe and truly to profess fellowship with God and the blood of Christ even to those in whom there is nothing but darkness. If there is any use of the dogma of universal grace for faith, it lies in this: that from it one may infer that we can be saved. But among those who struggle with temptations this is of little or no use. To conceive a sure hope, the tempted need the doctrine of special grace promised in Christ to believers. And indeed our faith can stand without the foundation of absolutely universal grace. It is enough that it rests on some universal proposition which, being in God's word, has the greatest certainty, such as that which promises grace in Christ to all who believe and repent. This proposition is the citadel and acropolis of the gospel. It suffices for conceiving faith, because although it does not promise God's grace and the fellowship of Christ's death to all men, indeed to no one except the believer and the penitent, it nonetheless makes the believer and penitent most certain of faith, that salvation pertains to him in this promise made. Thus one meets the temptation that keeps a man from conceiving faith, in a man who so far has no faith at all. But in the temptations of others, the stages of repentance and faith must be observed; those which are serious and sincere, even if they are the first, are everywhere the foundation for further faith, according to the words of the gospel which call individually the poor in spirit, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, those who labour and are burdened (Matt. 5:3, 6; 11:28), and finally everyone (which is a particularly effective argument for comfort) who wish [θέλουσι] (Rev. 22:17), and make a free way of access to grace for them. That these universal terms may rightly be taken up to conceive faith is shown both by the evidence of the matter itself and by the practice of many who labour under weakness. And those sincere men, even if the first stage of regeneration, also produce individually the certainty of salvation, because Scripture not only calls such people but also pronounces them blessed, and promises that they shall be satisfied with righteousness and have hope of the kingdom of heaven. To make these things most certain to a man is the most effective way of strengthening faith. And although it is also certain that God does not wish to work faith in all, yet a man has ample reason to conceive faith eagerly, because he knows that he is not by name excluded from that work, and that among the whole range of men who hear the word of God there are some to whom God gives this grace, and that he himself is among those whom God honours with outward calling, which can at least kindle some spark of hope. By arguments of this kind a man may easily be led to good courage, not indeed by himself, who can do nothing, but by the effective grace of God, who works all things. It happens that the one who struggles with such a temptation, so that he doubts whether God wishes to grant faith to him too, and seriously inquires into this, most certainly also earnestly desires to be among those to whom that ability is granted by God. But such a desire shows love, love shows knowledge of the good, and some fruit of faith, of whatever kind, shows that faith.

units.la: XCVII.

Sed operae pretium imprimis est cognoscere & distinguere fidei proficientis fibras, hoc est, actus illos, quibus circa objectum fidei proprium homo occupatur. Qui non unius generis sunt. Alii enim fidem justificantem sic praecedunt, ut sine iis non consistat; alii comitantur, alii eandem formant, alii consequuntur. Qui actus fidei sic distincti doctrinae de fide justificante, & ordine, quo eadem in Christum & beneficia ejus fertur, non exiguam lucem foenerantur. Actus fidem salvificam, praecedentes, sine quibus illa non consistit, notitia, assensus theoricus, humiliatio abnegatio sui ipsius, & animae pia quaedam contentio. Comitantes, assensus practicus, desiderium sanctum Christi & justitiae ejus, seu refugium ad Christum, & Spiritus contritio: Formalis fiducialis Christi apprehensio: Consequentes gratia fidei justificantis vivificans, purificans, tranquillans, corroborans & fructificans sunt. Quos actus sic distinguimus, ut tamen eos nec divellamus, nec temporis differentiam recipere, sed simul sic existere, ut posterior quisque priorem includat, prior verò posteriorem trahat, dicamus, de iis distinctè nobis agendum est.
units.tr: But it is worth our while, above all, to know and distinguish the fibres of growing faith, that is, those acts by which a person is occupied with the proper object of faith. These are not all of one kind. Some go before justifying faith so that it cannot exist without them; others accompany it, others form it, and others follow it. These acts of faith, distinguished in this way, shed no small light on the doctrine of justifying faith and on the order in which it is directed to Christ and his benefits. The acts that precede saving faith, without which it cannot exist, are knowledge, theoretical assent, humiliation, self-denial, and a certain pious striving of the soul. Those that accompany it are practical assent, holy desire for Christ and his righteousness (or flight to Christ), and the contrition of the Spirit. The formal act is the fiducial apprehension of Christ. The following acts are the grace of justifying faith, which quickens, purifies, calms, strengthens and makes fruitful. We distinguish these acts in this way, yet we neither separate them nor admit a difference of time between them. Rather, they exist together, so that each later act includes the earlier and the earlier draws in the later. Having said this, we must now treat them separately.

units.la: XCVIII.

Inter actus praecedentes fidei Notitia Christi & beneficiorum ejus agmen ducit, imò embryonis instar est, ex quo fides nascitur. Fides enim notitiam rei creditae necessario supponit. Estque illa non implicita duntaxat, sed, ratione fundamenti, explicita; neque ἢ ὅτι, quae causam revelati de Christo testimonii deceptet, sed ἢ ὅτι, quae revelationem testimonii apprehendit; denique non qualiscunque, sed efficax, comitem amorem & affectum rei cognitae habens. De qua passim Scripturae. Confident in te cognoscentes nomen tuum, Psal. IX. 11. Cognitione sui justus servus meus multos justificabit, Esaj. LIII. 11. Qui sapiens est, intelligit ista, intelligens agnoscat ista, Hos. XIV. 9. Unicum enim salutis obtinendae medium cognitio Dei Patris & Christi. Haec est vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te illum solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Jesum Christum, Joh. XVII. 3. Est enim fides γνῶσις τῆς ἀληθείας cognitio veritatis, Tit. I. 1. Ideo Scripturas scrutari, Joh. V. 39. praedicantem audire, Rom. X. 14. explorare omnia, & bonum retinere, 1. Thess. V. 21. judicare, quae dicuntur, 1. Cor. X. 15. non credere cuivis spiritui, sed probare spiritus, an sint ex Deo, 1. Joh. IV. 1. Solius Christi vocem audire, Joh. X. 4. 5. jubemur. Christus enim nobis factus est sapientia, 1. Cor. I. 30. Et credentes in Christum eum didicisse, Ephes. IV. 20. utpote διδαχτοὶ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ doctii Dei, vel à Deo, Joh. VI. 45. licet ex parte cognoscamus, & ἐν αἰνίγματι in speculo, per aenigma, 1. Cor. XIII. 9. 12. Facem ergo cognitio fidei praefert, juxta illa S. Pauli: οἶδα ᾧ πεπίστευκα Novi, cui crediderim, 2. Tim. I. 12. Sicut in conversione versione conversione ejusdem Pauli subitò αὐτὸν φῶς circumfulsit eum lux ex Cœlo, Act. IX. 3. ita Deus ante omnia intellectum eorum, in quibus fidem operatur, illuminat. Absque eo enim est, nox profunda cordi hominis incumbere non definit: & bona conscientia constare non potest, quam qui repellunt, circa fidem naufragium patiuntur, 1. Tim. I. 19. Quomodo fides ὑπόστασις subsistentia sperandorum Hebr. XI. 1. sine notitia rei apprehensæ & speratæ est? Nam objecta sua cordi credentis sic repræsentat, ut ea, velut in se subsistentia intimè intueatur. Denique non aliam ob causam credentes nomine lucis, Ephef. V. 8. intelligentium & sapientum, Matth. XI. 25. eorum, qui illuminatos oculos habent, Ephef. I. 18. veniunt; & incredulitas per cæcitatem, Rom. XI. 25. Ephef. IV. 18. ignorantiam, Act. XVII. 23. 30. tenebras, Joh. I. 5. Luc. I. 79. stultitiam, Rom. X. 19. Luc. XXIV. 25. describitur. Imò ignorantia erroris omnis mater est. Erratis nescientes Scripturas, Matth. XXII. 29. Recte proin Hieronymus contr. Lucif. Quæ ista, inquit, est simplicitas nescire quæ credas? Imò oculata est, & lynceos oculos habet, quia cognoscit Filium Dei lactentem, cognoscit in ligno pendentem, cognoscit morientem, siquidem latro in patibulo, magi in stabulo cognoscunt, iste clavis infixum, hi pannis involutum, uti scite Bernhardus Serm. 2. de Magis tribus loquitur.
units.tr: Among the preceding acts of faith, the knowledge of Christ and his benefits leads the way; it is indeed like an embryo from which faith is born. For faith necessarily presupposes knowledge of the thing believed. This knowledge is not merely implicit but, as to its foundation, explicit; it is not the that [ἢ ὅτι] which merely takes note that the testimony concerning Christ has been revealed, but the that which grasps the revealed testimony; finally, it is not knowledge of any sort, but effective knowledge, with love and affection for the thing known as its companions. Scripture speaks of this throughout. Those who know your name will trust in you, Ps. 9:11. By his knowledge my righteous servant will justify many, Isa. 53:11. Whoever is wise, let him understand these things, and whoever is intelligent, let him acknowledge them, Hos. 14:9. For the only means of obtaining salvation is the knowledge of God the Father and of Christ. This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, John 17:3. Faith is indeed knowledge of the truth [γνῶσις τῆς ἀληθείας], Titus 1:1. Therefore we are commanded to search the Scriptures, John 5:39; to hear the preacher, Rom. 10:14; to test all things and hold fast what is good, 1 Thess. 5:21; to judge what is said, 1 Cor. 10:15; not to believe every spirit, but to test the spirits, whether they are from God, 1 John 4:1. We are bidden to hear the voice of Christ alone, John 10:4–5. For Christ has become for us wisdom, 1 Cor. 1:30. And believers are said to have learned Christ, Eph. 4:20, as those taught by God [διδακτοὶ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ], or taught by God, John 6:45, although we know in part, and in a mirror, in an enigma [ἐν αἰνίγματι], 1 Cor. 13:9, 12. Knowledge therefore goes before faith, according to those words of St Paul: I know whom I have believed [οἶδα ᾧ πεπίστευκα], 2 Tim. 1:12. As in Paul's conversion a light from heaven suddenly shone around him, Acts 9:3, so God first illuminates the understanding of those in whom he works faith. Without this, the deep night does not cease to lie upon the human heart, and a good conscience cannot stand; those who reject it suffer shipwreck concerning the faith, 1 Tim. 1:19. How could faith be the substance of things hoped for [ὑπόστασις], Heb. 11:1, without knowledge of the thing apprehended and hoped for? For it presents its objects to the heart of the believer in such a way that he gazes upon them inwardly, as subsisting in themselves. Finally, believers are called by the name of light, Eph. 5:8, of the intelligent and wise, Matt. 11:25, of those who have enlightened eyes, Eph. 1:18, for no other reason; and unbelief is described by blindness, Rom. 11:25; Eph. 4:18, by ignorance, Acts 17:23, 30, by darkness, John 1:5; Luke 1:79, and by folly, Rom. 10:19; Luke 24:25. Indeed, ignorance is the mother of all error. You are wrong, not knowing the Scriptures, Matt. 22:29. Rightly therefore Jerome, against Lucifer, says: What kind of simplicity is it, he asks, not to know what you believe? Indeed faith has sharp eyes and lynx's eyes, because it knows the Son of God as an infant, knows him hanging on the cross, knows him dying: for the thief knew him on the gibbet, the magi knew him in the stable; the one knew him with nails driven through him, the others knew him wrapped in rags, as Bernard speaks wisely in Sermon 2 on the Three Magi.

units.la: XCIX. Per notitiam hanc, velut speculum quoddam, fides inprimis Christi præstantiam, plenitudinem, sufficientiam & propensionem ad succurrendum miseris intuetur. Præstantiam, quia eum, ceu insignitum præ millibus, Cant. V. 10. pretiosum unionem, Matth. XIII. 46. lapidem angularem pretiosum, Esaj. XXVIII. 16. qui nos ceu lapides vivos supra se extruit, 1. Pet. II. 5. intuetur. Omnia in ipso ἁρμοζόμενα præstantiora sunt, nomen, natura, virtus, πλεονεκτήματα plurima. Plenitudinem, quia eum cognoscit talem, in quo plenitudo Deitatis, Col. II. 9. tota plenitudo, ibid. I. 19. plenitudo meriti seu sanguinis & Spiritus: quarum illa liberamur à peccato, hac parta justitia exornamur. Sufficientiam, quia ad omnia nobis sufficit, ceu panis vitæ, Joh. VI. 35. Cujus sanguis verissimum illud balsamum Gileadis est; quique similis est arboribus sanctuarii, quarum fructus cibo, & folia sanationi inserviunt, Ezech. XLVII. 12. Denique propensionem ad succurrendum miseris. Nam & dives ipse est, & ex plenitudine ejus omnes χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος gratiam pro gratia accipimus, Joh. I. 16. Omnes sitientes venite, emite absque argento, & absque pretio vinum & lac, Esaj. LV. 1. Ad gratiam invitat, ampleƒti eam præcipit, non amplexis minatur, præstolatur gratiam facere, propterea effertur, ut misereatur nostri. Beati omnes, qui præstolantur ipsum, ibid. XXX. 18. Christi promissiones aureum illud sceptrum sunt, quod porrigit: Spiritus S. commotiones Jesum Christum ad nos venientem, & domicilium in cordibus nostris metantem portendunt. Talis Christi Salvatoris notitia, cùm præcedit, fides incenditur, & in amplexus Christi ruere gestit.
units.tr: 99. Through this knowledge, as through a kind of mirror, faith above all beholds the excellence, fullness, sufficiency, and readiness of Christ to help the wretched. It beholds his excellence, because it sees him as distinguished above thousands, Song 5:10; as a precious pearl, Matt. 13:46; as a precious cornerstone, Isa. 28:16, who builds us up on himself as living stones, 1 Pet. 2:5. Everything that belongs to him is more excellent: his name, his nature, his power, and very many privileges. It beholds his fullness, because it knows him as the one in whom is the fullness of the Godhead, Col. 2:9, all the fullness, ibid. 1:19: the fullness of merit, of blood and of Spirit. By the first we are freed from sin; by the second, through the righteousness obtained, we are adorned. It beholds his sufficiency, because he is sufficient for us in all things, as the bread of life, John 6:35. His blood is that most true balm of Gilead; and he is like the trees of the sanctuary, whose fruit serves for food and whose leaves serve for healing, Ezek. 47:12. Finally, it beholds his readiness to help the wretched. For he himself is rich, and from his fullness we all receive grace upon grace [χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος], John 1:16. All you who are thirsty, come, buy without money and without price, wine and milk, Isa. 55:1. He invites us to grace; he commands us to embrace it; he does not threaten those who refuse to embrace it. The Lord waits to be gracious to you, therefore he exalts himself to have mercy on you. Blessed are all who wait for him, ibid. 30:18. Christ's promises are the golden sceptre which he extends. The motions of the Holy Spirit signify Jesus Christ coming to us and making his dwelling in our hearts. When such knowledge of Christ the Saviour goes before, faith is kindled and eagerly rushes into the embrace of Christ.

units.la: C. Qui notitiam à fide separant, oculum illi fidei utrumque effodiunt, & cum Atheniensibus ϑεῷ Ἀγνώστῳ Deo incognito aram erigunt, Act. XVII. 23. Hic Pontificiorum stupor est, quibus, Bellarmino ipso caliginoso finitore, fides melius per ignorantiam, quam per notitiam definitur. Assensum enim esse fidem, non notitiam, & fidem ipsam implicitam, hoc est, crassissimam ignorantiam, modò universaliori positioni, in qua res credita potentia continetur, qualis Ecclesiæ proponentis infallibilitas est, assensus præbeatur, totámque adeò esse, ut per eam homo animum unicè inducat credere id, quod Ecclesia credit: pertendunt. Carbonarii fidem Hosius lib. III. de auêt. Script. sol. 261. ejusmodi laudavit, qua is credebat, quicquid Ecclesia credit; quid verò illa crederet interrogatus, respondit, quod ipse crederet; ignarus tum quid ipse, tum quid Ecclesia crederet. Et alia quidem explicitè, alia implicitè credenda esse, supra Loc. I. 48. ostendimus. Fides verò implicita quidem fidei præparatio est. Sunt enim in pueris & rudibus, conscientiam suam audientibus, fidei igniculi quidàm, quibus, cùm Evangelium audiunt, ad desiderium doctrinam illam cognoscendi exardescunt, eam ceu lac rationale appetunt, & tanquam verbum Dei, auctoritate Scripturæ roboratum, hauriunt. In quibus illa fidei τριμαθία præparatio efficit, tum ut quærant & credant omne verbum Dei, & sic ad φρόνησιν δικαίων sensum seu prudentiam justorum Luc. I. 17. perveniant: tum de Divinitate S. Literarum persuasi Scripturæ, tanquam verbo Dei, in omnibus per eam revelatis credant, & eam scrutari non desinant. Sed fides tamen in nullo homine, hac quidem in vita explicitè & distinctè omne id, quod in verbo DEI revelatum est, attingit. Omnes enim μαθηταὶ discipuli sumus, & ad perfectionem, non sine difficultate & suspiriis contendimus, paulatim ædificamur, & ad agnitionem Dei crescimus, Col. I. 10. donec ad unitatem fidei & cognitionis Filii Dei perveniamus, & in virum perfectum, ad mensuram staturæ complementi Christi, evadamus, Ephef. IV. 13. Col. II. 19. III. 10. Nemo tamen sine explicita notitia & fide fundamenti fidelis cluere potest. De cæteris plura ad sapientiam illam, quæ in perfectis est, 1. Cor. II. 6. requiruntur. Inprimis homo Dei ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructus esse, & uberiorem longè notitiam, quàm pueri in Christo, habere debet. Sed alia longè fidei implicitæ Pontificiorum ratio est, quæ non immediatè in verbum Dei, & in eodem revelata fertur, sed voluntaria quædam deditio in obsequium Papæ est, sine ulla dictorum & oraculorum ejus notitia solida ex Dei verbo, vel examine eorum ad Lydium Scripturæ lapidem. Eligit enim implicita hæc fides, implicata in fide non verbi Dei, sed labyrintho propositionis Ecclesiæ, & humanarum inventionum ἀλλοτρίως loqui & facere, quæ Papa cum obediente sibi multitudine loquitur & facit; adeòque non fides, sed apostasia à fide, & spiritualis fornicatio est.
units.tr: 100. Those who separate knowledge from faith gouge out both eyes of faith, and with the Athenians they erect an altar to the unknown God [ϑεῷ Ἀγνώστῳ], Acts 17:23. Here lies the stupidity of the Papists, who, with Bellarmine himself, a murky definer, hold that faith is better defined through ignorance than through knowledge. They contend that faith is assent, not knowledge; and that faith itself is implicit, that is, the crassest ignorance, provided assent is given to the more general proposition in which the thing believed is contained potentially, such as the infallibility of the proposing Church; and that faith is thus wholly of this kind, so that through it a person determines to believe whatever the Church believes. Hosius, in his third book On the Authority of Scripture, page 261, praised a faith of charcoal-burners of this sort, by which a man believed whatever the Church believes; but when asked what the Church believed, he answered that he believed what he himself believed, ignorant both of what he believed and of what the Church believed. We have shown above, at Locus 1, section 48, that some things must be believed explicitly and others implicitly. Yet implicit faith is indeed a preparation for faith. For in children and the unlearned, who listen to their conscience, there are certain sparks of faith, by which, when they hear the gospel, they burn with desire to know that doctrine, they seek it as rational milk, and they drink it in as the word of God, confirmed by the authority of Scripture. In them this preparation effects a threefold learning of faith: first, that they seek and believe every word of God, and so come to the wisdom of the just [φρόνησιν δικαίων], that is, the sense or prudence of the righteous, Luke 1:17; second, that, persuaded of the divinity of the Holy Writings, they believe in all things revealed by them as the word of God, and never cease to search them; third, [the preparation is complete when they are taught these things]. Yet no person, at least in this life, attains explicitly and distinctly everything that is revealed in the word of God. For we are all disciples [μαθηταί], and we strive toward perfection not without difficulty and sighing; we are gradually built up and grow into the knowledge of God, Col. 1:10, until we attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, and become a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, Eph. 4:13; Col. 2:19; 3:10. Yet no one can be a faithful builder without explicit knowledge and faith of the foundation. Other things are required for that wisdom which is among the perfect, 1 Cor. 2:6. Above all, the man of God must be thoroughly equipped for every good work, and must have a far fuller knowledge than children in Christ. But the implicit faith of the Papists is a quite different matter. It is not directed immediately to the word of God and to what is revealed in it; it is rather a voluntary surrender to the obedience of the Pope, with no solid knowledge of his sayings and decrees drawn from the word of God, or examined by the Lydian touchstone of Scripture. For this implicit faith chooses to be entangled not in faith in the word of God but in the labyrinth of the Church's proposition, and in human inventions, to speak and act otherwise [ἀλλοτρίως] than the Pope speaks and acts with the multitude obedient to him. Thus it is not faith but apostasy from faith, and spiritual fornication.

units.la: CI. Argumenta, quibus contra notitiam fidei pro fide implicita nitantur, nec speciosa, nec solida illa sunt. Frivolum inprimis illud Thomæ Aquinatis est, petitum ex verbis Jobi, Boves arabant, & asinæ juxta eos pascebantur, Job. I. 14. Nam minores, qui signentur per asinas, in credendo cohærere cum majoribus, per
units.tr: CI. The arguments by which they support implicit faith against knowledge of the faith are neither plausible nor sound. Above all, Thomas Aquinas's point is trifling. It is drawn from the words of Job, The oxen were ploughing, and the asses were feeding beside them (Job I. 14). He says the lesser people, signified by the asses, cohere with the greater in believing, the greater being signified by the oxen. This is trifling. (The rest continues below.)

units.la: bb per boves signatis, nugatur. Quæ allegoria nimis contorta, imò præter & contra intentionem Spiritus S. graditur. Minores equidem majoribus cohærere debent, sed non citra examen eorum, quæ majores dicunt. Possunt enim majores esse λεγόμενοι dicti, qui revera non sunt, imò Pseudoprophetæ & Spiritus non ex Deo sunt. Dixit etiam Jehova Esaj. VII. 9. non, Si non credideritis, non intelligetis, uti Græci & vetus Itala reddiderunt, sed rectius. Et si non creditis, quia non permanebitis, sed cadetis, uti ex Symmacho Hieronymus reddidit. Sensus est. Judæos non credere, neque acquiescere Divinæ gratiæ & potentiæ, sed eventurum nihilo minus, quod Deus prædixit, & fore, ut ipsi non permaneant, sed cadant. Ipse certè Vulgatus Interpres illa לא תאמנו non reddit, non intelligetis, sed non permanebitis. S. Paulus verò dicens: Si novero πάντων τὴν γνῶσιν omnem cognitionem & habuero omnem fidem &c. 1. Cor. XIII. 2. non fidem à cognitione separat, sed γνῶσιν cognitionem rerum abstrusarum, sive eruditionem theoreticam vel practicam illam, sed charitatis tamen expertem, qualis illa Bileami de populo Dei vaticinia insignia proloquentis; à fide omni, hoc est, non salvifica illa, sed persuasione de Divinis promissionibus & Divina potentia: qualis Israelitarum mare rubrum transeuntium, & illorum, qui in nomine Christi dæmonia ejecerunt, fuit, separari posse innuit, quod verissimum est; Potest nempe quis amore Dei destitutus naturaliter sciens omnipotentiam Dei, & veritatem ejus, & videns omnia miracula, quæ in Scripturis narrantur, & quorum fama mundum implevit, eò adduci, ut pronuntiet miraculum aliquod in nomine Dei; & tamen non assurgere ad fidem in Christum, quæ salvat, & charitate nunquam destituitur. Non enim omnis persuasio circa opera Divinæ potentiæ fides salvifica est. Idem verò S. Paulus se per prædicationem Evangelii captivare omnem mentem in obsequium Christi ajens, 2. Cor. X. 5. non notitiam à fide secludit, cùm ipse prius se ratiocinationes & omnem altitudinem oppositam τῇ γνώσει θεοῦ cognitioni Dei (ut ita in fide cognitio Dei sit) evacuare dixerit. In ipso igitur obsequio Christi notitia ejusdem continetur. Quis enim Christo non rite ex verbo Dei cognito obsequi potest? Licet enim multa in Scripturis sint, quæ captum hominis superant, neque plenè & perfectè, quemadmodum in se sunt, & à Deo cognoscuntur, cognosci possunt, tamen ad captivandam mentem in obsequium Christi cognitio eorum, quæ de Deo & Divinis proprietatibus ad salutem nostram cognosci debent, sufficit. Tum ergo mens hominis in obedientiam Christi captivatur, cùm credit id verum esse, quod Deum revelasse & testificatum esse novit; Licet id, quomodo in se sit, & ὃ τὸ διότι non comprehendat. Ita quòd Deus ubique sit, & omnia sciat, & quòd virgo peperit, novimus: sed quomodo id factum sit, nescimus: & hactenus mens captivanda ducitur; non ut τὸ ὅτι ignoret, sed ut τὸ διότι ne scrutetur. Plane enim fides & obsequium Christi mentem non excæcat, sed illuminat & perficit; at dum ex parte cognoscimus, non revelata scrutari vetat. Obedientia fidei passim laudata non brutum doctrinæ simpliciter ignotæ assensum, sed spontaneum agnitæ veritatis assensum significat. Idem enim S. Paulus, qui se gratiam & Apostolatum accepisse ᾔς ὑπακοήν τῆς πίστεως ad obedientiam fidei Rom. I. 5. dixit, id quoque affirmavit, quòd Deus splenderit in cordibus Apostolorum ad præbendum lumen cognitionis in facie Jesu Christi, 2. Cor. IV. 6. Præterea inscitè etiam ex verbis S. Pauli totum corpus mysticum esse oculum, & membra omnia corporis eundem actum habere negantis, Rom. XII. 4. 1. Cor. XII. 14. &c. colligunt, non omnes fideles oculatos esse, & omnia per fidem explicitè cognoscere debere. Nam nec omnium explicitam cognitionem, nec æqualem omnium ab omnibus exigimus, sed fidem rei simpliciter incognitæ assensum esse, negamus. Neque quia in eodem corpore mystico non omnia membra eundem actum habent, vel oculus sunt, alios fidem explicitam, alios implicitam habere, vel universam fidem, eo, quo illi asserunt, sensu implicitam esse sequitur. Sed quidam, velut Doctores in Ecclesia comparantur oculis, ob cognitionem ampliorem & munus dirigendi alios, non sic tamen, ut reliqui omnes oculis carere putentur. Nam & illi, qui cum auribus comparantur, non sic audire soli intelliguntur, ut reliqui omnes & auribus & auditu destituti putentur. Sed comparatio illa corporis naturalis & mystici in distinctione charismatum, munerum specialium, non communis fidei absolvitur. Ab hoc similitudinis scopo abstracta ratiocinatio nihil arguit. Non igitur vi allegoriæ magis implicita fides ad plebem rejicitur, quàm donum sanationum, vel genus linguarum ad solos doctores adstringitur. Denique ex eo, quòd etiam fideles mysteria fidei apprehendere & cognoscere possunt, rectè concluditur, non omnem apprehensionem & notitiam mysteriorum esse fidem. Sed fidem notitiam non supponere, vel includere, perperam inde concluditur. Latius enim apprehensio quàm fides patet; sed hæc tamen illa, ceu oculo suo, carere non potest.
units.tr: The allegory is far too strained, and it goes beyond and against the intention of the Holy Spirit. Lesser people indeed ought to cohere with greater ones, but not without examining what the greater ones say. For those called greater may be called so without really being so; indeed they may be false prophets, and spirits that are not from God. Jehovah also said (Isa. VII. 9), not If you do not believe, you will not understand, as the Greeks and the old Italic version rendered it, but more correctly And if you do not believe, you will not remain, but will fall, as Jerome rendered it from Symmachus. [לא תאמנו] The sense is that the Jews do not believe or rest in the grace and power of God, yet what God foretold will nonetheless come to pass, and they will not remain standing but will fall. The Vulgate translator himself does not render לא תאמנו as you will not understand, but as you will not remain. St Paul, saying If I know [πάντων τὴν γνῶσιν] all knowledge and have all faith, etc. (1 Cor. XIII. 2), does not separate faith from knowledge. By γνῶσις he means knowledge of abstruse things, or that theoretical or practical learning which lacks charity, such as Balaam had when he uttered his notable prophecies about the people of God. By all faith he means not that saving faith but the persuasion about the Divine promises and the Divine power, such as the Israelites had when they passed through the Red Sea, and those who cast out demons in the name of Christ. He hints that these can be separated, and this is quite true. Someone destitute of the love of God may naturally know the omnipotence and truth of God, may see all the miracles narrated in the Scriptures, whose fame has filled the world, and may be led so far as to pronounce some miracle in the name of God; yet he may not rise to faith in Christ, which saves, and which is never without charity. For not every persuasion about the works of Divine power is saving faith. Again, when St Paul says that through the preaching of the Gospel he takes every thought captive to the obedience of Christ (2 Cor. X. 5), he does not exclude knowledge from faith, since he had earlier said that he would destroy reasonings and every height raised against [τῇ γνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ] the knowledge of God, so that the knowledge of God is contained in faith. Knowledge of Christ is therefore contained in the very obedience to Christ. For who can rightly obey Christ without knowing from the Word of God? Although there are many things in the Scriptures that exceed the grasp of man, and cannot be known fully and perfectly as they are in themselves and as God knows them, nevertheless for taking the mind captive to the obedience of Christ, knowledge of those things which must be known about God and the Divine attributes for our salvation is sufficient. Then the mind of man is taken captive to the obedience of Christ when it believes that what God has revealed and attested to be true is true, even though it does not grasp how it is in itself, nor the why [τὸ διότι]. Thus we know that God is everywhere and knows all things, and that a virgin bore a child; but we do not know how this came about. So far the mind must be led captive, not so that it is ignorant of the that [τὸ ὅτι], but so that it does not pry into the why [τὸ διότι]. Plainly faith and obedience to Christ do not blind the mind but enlighten and perfect it; whereas, since we know only in part, it forbids us to pry into what has not been revealed. The obedience of faith, so often praised, signifies not a dull assent to a doctrine simply unknown, but a willing assent to a truth recognised. For St Paul, who said that he had received grace and apostleship unto obedience of faith [εἰς ὑπακοὴν τῆς πίστεως] (Rom. I. 5), also affirmed that God has shone in the hearts of the Apostles to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor. IV. 6). Moreover, they also foolishly infer from the words of St Paul, who denies that the whole mystical body is an eye and that all the members of the body have the same function (Rom. XII. 4; 1 Cor. XII. 14, etc.), that not all the faithful are seeing, and that they must not all know everything explicitly through faith. For we demand neither an explicit knowledge from all, nor an equal knowledge from all by all; but we deny that faith is a simple assent to a thing wholly unknown. Nor does it follow, in the sense they assert, that because in the same mystical body not all the members have the same function, or are eyes, some have explicit faith and others implicit faith, or that the whole faith is implicit. Rather, some are compared to eyes in the Church, on account of their wider knowledge and their duty of directing others; yet not so that all the rest are thought to lack eyes. For those who are compared to ears are not understood to hear alone, so that all the rest are thought to lack ears and hearing. That comparison, however, is drawn from the natural and mystical body in respect of the distinction of gifts and special offices, not of the common faith. Abstract reasoning drawn from the purpose of this comparison proves nothing. Therefore, by the force of an allegory, implicit faith is not thrown back upon the common people any more than the gift of healing or the gift of tongues is confined to teachers alone. Lastly, from the fact that even the faithful can apprehend and know the mysteries of faith, it is rightly concluded that not every apprehension and knowledge of the mysteries is faith. But it is wrongly concluded from this that faith does not presuppose or include knowledge. For apprehension extends more widely than faith; yet faith cannot be without it, as without its own eye.

units.la: CII. Post notitiam fidem assensus theoricus præcedit. Per hunc enim cognitæ veritati de Christo sic homo astipulatur, ut de ea per Spiritum S. convictus libens ceu vera & Divina recipiat, quæcunque Deus in verbo suo testatur de se ipso, de sanctitate; jure & justitia judicii sui, itémque de homine, quòd is sit reus; malus, damnatus, impotens, Deo indignus, de operibus Dei, quòd illa & extent, & recta atque Deum decentia sint; nominatim, quòd longanimitas Dei resipiscentia digna sit, & quòd Deus in plenitudine temporum id præstiterit, quod ad justitiam & salutem peccatoris fieri oportuit, quòd verus Messias sit, in cujus solius nomine nos salvari oporteat; quódque ita ἀληθὴς verus compertus sit. Qui accepit testimonium ejus, obsignavit, quòd Deus sit verus, Joh. III. 33: hoc est, quòd memor sit juramenti, quo se Patribus obligavit, & verbum suum impleverit. Hoc est ubera promissionis Divinæ sugere, quod non minus Deo acceptum est, quàm matri suave est, cùm infans ubera ejus sugit. Et philosophi quidem tres perfectionis in assensu gradus distinguunt, firmitatem, ut sit sine hæsitatione, certitudinem ut certo & solido fundamento mento innitatur; & evidentiam, ut non testimonio alieno nitatur, sed ex sensu vel ratione probetur. Fidei vero assensus firmitatem & certitudinem habet, quia verbo Divino infallibili nititur; at evidentia Philosophica destituitur; quia testimonio Dei, non sensu, vel ratione nititur. Ideo S. Paulus fidem definivit ὑπόστασιν & ἔλεγχον subsistentiam & demonstrationem ad firmitatem & certitudinem ejus designandam; sed τ' ἀ βλεπομένων eorum, quæ non videntur; quæ proin non a sensu, vel a ratione, sed a revelatione pendent. Quanquam nec illa, quæ a Deo revelata sunt, recte inevidentia dicantur. Nam & illud evidens est, quod per fortissima argumenta docilēs Dei, & attendentes verbo ejus ita confirmat, ut veritati sine omni dubitatione inhæreant. Tale vero testimonium & revelatio Dei est. Cujus summa sicut certitudo, ita evidentia est. Licet enim quæ creduntur, non videantur, & eo sensu inevidentia vulgo dicantur, tamen verba illa, quibus credenda revelantur, habent evidentem sententiam, ut mente nostra intueri possimus, quid in mente & animo loquentis sit, sive quid is velit a nobis intelligi, credi, sperari. Quamobrem S. Paulus etiam fidei ἔλεγχον demonstrationem tribuit, Hebr. XI. 1. Facit ergo rem evidentem, quemadmodum qui ex mathematicis principiis demonstratur, & facit velut ἀντότπος.
units.tr: CII. Before faith, knowledge is followed by theoretical assent. For through this assent a man so agrees with the truth known about Christ that, convinced of it by the Holy Spirit, he willingly receives as true and Divine whatever God testifies in his Word about himself, about his holiness, and about the justice and righteousness of his judgement; and likewise about man, that he is guilty, evil, condemned, powerless, unworthy of God; about the works of God, that they both exist and are right and becoming to God; and in particular, that the long-suffering of God is worthy of repentance, and that God in the fulness of time has accomplished what had to be done for the righteousness and salvation of the sinner; that he is the true Messiah, in whose name alone we must be saved; and that he has thus been found to be true [ἀληθής]. He who has received his testimony has certified that God is true (John III. 33); that is, he remembers the oath by which God bound himself to the fathers, and sees that he has fulfilled his word. This is to suck the breasts of the Divine promise, which is no less acceptable to God than it is sweet to a mother when the infant sucks her breasts. The philosophers indeed distinguish three degrees of perfection in assent: firmness, so that it is without hesitation; certainty, so that it rests on a sure and solid foundation; and evidence, so that it rests not on another's testimony but is proved by the senses or by reason. The assent of faith has firmness and certainty, because it rests on the infallible Word of God; but it lacks philosophical evidence, because it rests on the testimony of God, not on sense or reason. Therefore St Paul defined faith as substance [ὑπόστασις] and demonstration [ἔλεγχος], substance and demonstration, to designate its firmness and certainty; and as the evidence [ἔλεγχος] of things not seen [τῶν οὐ βλεπομένων], that is, things that are not seen, and which therefore depend not on sense or reason but on revelation. Yet even those things revealed by God are not rightly called non-evident. For that is evident which, by the strongest arguments, teaches the docile and those attending to his Word, and confirms them so that they cleave to the truth without any doubt. Such is the testimony and revelation of God. Its sum is as much evident as it is certain. For although the things believed are not seen, and in that sense are commonly called non-evident, nevertheless the words by which the things to be believed are revealed have a clear meaning, so that we can see with our minds what is in the mind and purpose of the speaker, that is, what he wishes us to understand, believe and hope. Hence St Paul also ascribes demonstration [ἔλεγχος] to faith (Heb. XI. 1). Faith therefore makes a thing evident, as one who is proved from mathematical principles is demonstrated, and it makes the believer as it were an eyewitness [αὐτόπτης].

units.la: CIII. Cum notitia & assensu tali humiliatio sui ipsius, abnegatio sui ipsius & pia contentio conjungitur. Humiliatio sui ipsius, qua de peccato & impotentia sua convictus coram Deo se ipsum, ceu natura miserum, irae Dei & aeternae damnationi obnoxium, & Divinae opis atque gratiae quam maxime indigum humiliat. Sicut semen frugi profundam terram: ita fides cor & spiritum profunde contritum praesumque poscit. Neque Christus prius dulcescit, quam peccatum amarescit; vel πνεῦμα quietis largitor est, quam homo κοπιῶν καὶ πεφορτισμένος laborans & oneratus est, Matth. XI. 28. Quomodo enim onus suum in Christum devolvet, qui illud non sentit? Ideo credentes κατανυσσόμενοι compunguntur, Act. II. 37. ut inflatus spiritus, compuncto velut folle, exeat, & vera humilitas atque depressio subeat. Ego quondam vivebam sine lege; veniente autem praecepto, peccatum revixit. Et ego mortuus sum, Rom. VII. 9. 10. Ex Lege enim peccati cognitio est: & peccatum cognitum vivis & sanguineis velut coloribus depictum, mortis sensum sine lege extinctum, operatur. Mortis ergo peccato commeritae sensum prius habeat oportet, qui per fidem vivere vult. Perculit Israelitas mare rubrum visui objectum, & Pharao cum exercitu a tergo imminens: Quanto magis peccatorem mare suorum peccatorum menti & conscientiae observans, & justitiae Dei a tergo vindicis horror percellere debet; ut in eo salutaris illa κατάνυξις compunctio oriatur. Abnegatio dein sui ipsius sequitur. Ante omnia enim credens in se ipsum descendat, quam ad Christum veniat; sibi ipsi propter impotentiam suam diffidat, quam Christo confidat oportet. Non enim, uti praeclare Bernhardus, fides, sed perfidia est, in se ipso habere fidem. Ideo S. Paulus: Propter Christum omnia reputo stercora, ut Christum lucrer, & inveniar in ipso, non habens justitiam, quae est ex lege, sed illam, quae est ex fide Christi, Phil. III. 8. 9. Neque enim prius homo Christo, oleae verae inseri & implantari potest, quam veterem illum fundum suum, in quo computrescendum ipsi fuerat, deserat. Denique his omnibus pia etiam credentis contentio accedit. Quam primum enim verbo & Spiritu Dei ad fidem vocatur, non ille iners sterlit, vel brachia concutiat, sed venire ad Christum, eumque, ceu arcem salutis, apprehendere contendit, & gratiam Dei in Christo amplecti gestit; non sine interlocutione quadam animae, qua in Dei verbo oblatam gratiam cum indignitate & miseria sua comparans, sanguinem Jesu Christi, velut purificantem ab omnibus peccatis, 1. Joh. I. 7. peccato, indignitati & miseriae suae opponit, ejusque, ceu medicinae unice salutaris pretium ex aequo aestimat.
units.tr: CIII. Joined with this knowledge and assent go humiliation of oneself, self-denial, and devout striving. Humiliation of oneself is the act by which a person, convicted before God of sin and of his own powerlessness, humbles himself as a wretched creature, liable to the wrath of God and eternal damnation, and in great need of divine help and grace. As good soil must be deeply ploughed before it bears grain, so faith demands a heart and spirit deeply broken and contrite. Christ is not sweet until sin has become bitter; the Spirit of rest is given only when a man is labouring and burdened, Matt. 11:28. For how will a man roll his burden upon Christ if he does not feel it? So believers are pricked in their hearts [κατανυσσόμενοι], Acts 2:37, so that their inflated spirit may escape, as if a bellows had been punctured, and true humility and lowliness may take its place. I was alive without the law once; but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died, Rom. 7:9-10. For the knowledge of sin comes through the law, and sin known, painted in living and bloody colours, works a sense of death, which without the law lies dormant. He who wishes to live by faith must therefore first have a sense of the death that his sin has deserved. The Israelites were dismayed by the Red Sea set before their eyes, and by Pharaoh with his army bearing down behind them. How much more ought the sea of his sins, watched by his mind and conscience, and the terror of God's justice pursuing him as an avenger from behind, to strike the sinner, so that that saving compunction [κατάνυξις] may arise in him. Self-denial follows next. For before the believer comes to Christ, he must first go down into himself; he must distrust himself because of his own powerlessness before he trusts in Christ. For, as the great Bernard says admirably, it is not faith but faithlessness to have faith in oneself. So the apostle Paul says: For Christ's sake I count all things to be loss, that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, Phil. 3:8-9. Indeed, a man cannot first be grafted and planted into Christ, the true olive, unless he leaves that old soil of his, in which he was destined to rot. Finally, to all these there is added the devout striving of the believer. For as soon as he is called to faith by the Word and Spirit of God, he does not lie idle or fold his arms, but strives to come to Christ and to lay hold of him as the stronghold of salvation, and eagerly embraces the grace of God in Christ. This is not without a certain inner dialogue of the soul, in which, comparing the grace offered in God's Word with his own unworthiness and wretchedness, he sets against his sin, unworthiness and misery the blood of Jesus Christ, which cleanses us from all sin, 1 John 1:7, and weighs its worth, as the only saving remedy, against them.

units.la: CIV. Excipiunt fidei actus Comitantes; puta assensus practicus, desiderium sanctum Christi & justitiae ejus, seu καταφυγὴ refugium ad Christum, & salutaris contritio spiritus. Assensus practicus illa ὁμολογία astipulatio seu πεισμονὴ persuasio intellectus practici est, qua Evangelium de Christo non tantum verum, sed etiam bonum, & sibi bonum amore & studio omni dignissimum, & promissiones gratiae de remissione peccatorum & salute omnibus credentibus & resipiscentibus, adeoque etiam sibi credenti & resipiscenti conferenda certissimas judicat. Quae illa πληροφορία seu plena persuasio de Dei gratia ad se etiam pertinente, Rom. IV. 21. Col. II. 2; Hebr. X. 22. est sive ab arbore bona ad ripam plantata, & fructibus bonis, quas φέρει fert, exuberante; sive a navi, quae plenis velis fertur, dicta. Est enim πληροφορία illa fidei ἀληθείας fides, seu assensus fiducialis, quae omnem dubitationem, ratiocinationem & ψιθυρισμὸν obmurmurationem excludit; idque per amorem veritatis, & sanctam resolutionem & propositum, quo nos Deo permittimus, & propter ipsius verbum nihil timemus. Cupimus unumquemque vestrum idem praestare studium πρὸς τὴν πληροφορίαν τῆς ἐλπίδος ad plenitudinem spei usque in finem, Hebr. VI. 11. Per hanc ὁμολογίαν homo ad Deum dicit: Tu es Dominus, Deus meus, Rex meus, justitia mea; Psal. IV. 2. V. 3. Esaj. XXXIII. 22. Jerem. XXXIII. 6. XXXIII. 16. Zach. XIII. 9. atque ita non tantum Ne, Etiam dicit omnes promissiones, & eas, ceu veras, affirmat, sed etiam ad easdem dicit, Amen, hoc est, easdem approbat, & applausu suo excipit. Haec quaedam veluti יְרוּשָׁה מֶלֶךְ jubilatio Regis, Jer. XLIX. 2. Num. XXIII. 21. qua Rex noster velut cum jubilo excipitur: nec non αἵρεσις electio viae justitiae & Salvatoris ac Domini, imo Patris; denique ὁμολογίαν, qua Deo foedus proponenti astipulamur & assentimur, Hebr. X. 23. est. Quae omnia, uti patet, non tantum in judicio animi, sed multo magis in affectu consistit, corde hominis vice Dei dicente: Quaerite faciem meam; & pro se respondente, atque ita astipulante: Faciem tuam, Jehova, quaero, Psal. XXVII. 8.
units.tr: CIV. The acts of faith are followed by its accompanying acts, namely, practical assent, holy desire for Christ and his righteousness, or refuge [καταφυγή] to Christ, and saving contrition of spirit. Practical assent is that agreement [ὁμολογία], or persuasion [πεισμονή], of the practical intellect, by which it judges the Gospel concerning Christ not only true but also good, and most worthy of all love and zeal for oneself, and judges most certain the promises of grace, concerning forgiveness of sins and salvation, which are to be conferred on all believers and penitent persons, and therefore also on oneself, if one believes and repents. This is the full assurance [πληροφορία] of God's grace reaching also to oneself, Rom. 4:21; Col. 2:2; Heb. 10:22, and it is described as coming from a good tree planted by the riverbank and abounding in the good fruit it bears, or from a ship carried along with full sails. For this full assurance is the faith of the truth, that is, fiducial assent, which excludes all doubt, reasoning and murmuring [ψιθυρισμός]; and it does so through love of the truth, and through a holy resolve and purpose, by which we commit ourselves to God and fear nothing on account of his word. We desire each one of you to show the same diligence [πρὸς τὴν πληροφορίαν τῆς ἐλπίδος], for the full assurance of hope until the end, Heb. 6:11. Through this agreement a man says to God: You are the Lord, my God, my King, my righteousness, Ps. 4:2; 5:3; Isa. 33:22; Jer. 33:6, 33:16; Zech. 13:9. And so he not only says No and Yes to all the promises, and affirms them as true, but also says Amen to them, that is, approves them and receives them with his applause. This is, as it were, the jubilation of the King [יְרוּשָׁה מֶלֶךְ], Jer. 49:2; Num. 23:21, by which our King is received as if with jubilation. It is also the choice [αἵρεσις] of the way of righteousness and of the Saviour and Lord, indeed of the Father; and finally it is the agreement [ὁμολογία], by which we concur with and assent to God when he proposes a covenant, Heb. 10:23. All these things, as is plain, consist not only in a judgement of the mind but much more in the affections, the heart of man speaking in God's place, Seek my face, and answering for himself, and so concurring: Your face, Jehovah, I seek, Ps. 27:8.

units.la: CV. Fiducialis ille assensus Christum ut caput suum, in gloria aeque ac ignominia, ex amore puro, sine fine & modo, & cum sui in voluntatem & obsequium ejus voluntaria & plena deditione, recipere gestit. Ut caput suum
units.tr: CV. This fiducial assent eagerly receives Christ as its head, in glory as well as in shame, out of pure love, without end or measure, and with a voluntary and full surrender of oneself to his will and obedience. As its head

units.la: quia sicut caput & dominatur & spiritu corpori suppeditat: ita Christum & ut Dominum, & ut Spiritus sui largitorem amabit. Nam & sceptro ille regit, & alis suis protegit: & officium stipulatur, & beneficium promittit. Utroque modo agenti, & se offerenti cedit & ὁμολογίᾳ ὑποθέσεως astipulatione sua subjicitur, 2. Cor. IX. 13. In gloria æquè ac ignominia, ibid. VI. 8. quia & cum ipso pati & mori paratus est, & vivere atque glorificari gestit, Rom. VIII. 17. 2. Tim. II. 12. Beati estis, si in nomine Christi opprobria patimini. Nam sic gloria & Spiritus Dei super vos quiescit, 1. Pet. IV. 14. Ne ignes quidem, siquidem Christus in iis est, vera fides horret; cui etiam crux scala ad Cœlum est. Ex amore puro, quia Christo propter Christum, non propter aliud quicquam se subjicit. Non est castus conjugis amor, qui propter dotem ardet: at nec vera fides, quæ Christum propter aliud appetit. Ne Cœlum quidem sine Christo idonea fidei dos est. Sine fine & modo, quia dissolutionem à Christo capite suo non patitur, imò cum corpus ἀνακλᾶν dissolvitur; credens cum Christo esse plenius incipit. Tanti enim boni, quo solo satiari possumus, æterna duratio esse debet. Denique cum sui in voluntatem & obsequium Christi voluntaria & plena deditione, quia & sponta-nea hæc ὑπακοὴ ... subjectio astipulationis in Evangelium Christi, 2. Cor. IX. 13. esse debet; & consensus invitus dissensus potiùs est: &, qui in Christi partes transit, non sui amplius juris est, sed Christi est nexu mancupioque. Vivo, non amplius ego, sed vivit in me Christus, Gal. II. 20. Non estis vestri, 1. Cor. VI. 19.
units.tr: because, just as the head both rules the body and supplies it with spirit, so the believer will love Christ both as Lord and as the giver of his Spirit. For he rules with his sceptre and protects with his wings, and he both demands service and promises benefit. The believer yields to Christ acting in either way, and submits himself to Christ's agreement of the undertaking [ὁμολογίᾳ ὑποθέσεως], 2 Cor. 9:13. In glory as well as in shame, 2 Cor. 6:8, because he is ready to suffer and die with him, and eagerly desires to live and be glorified, Rom. 8:17; 2 Tim. 2:12. Blessed are you if you suffer reproach for the name of Christ, for the glory and Spirit of God rests upon you, 1 Pet. 4:14. True faith does not shrink even from fires, since Christ is in them; for faith, the cross is a ladder to heaven. Out of pure love, because he submits himself to Christ for Christ's sake and for nothing else. The chaste love of a spouse is not that which burns for a dowry; nor is true faith that which seeks Christ for something else. Not even heaven without Christ is a fitting dowry for faith. Without end or measure, because he does not suffer separation from Christ his head; indeed, when the body is broken up, the believer begins more fully to be with Christ. For the eternal duration of so great a good, by which alone we can be satisfied, must be without end. Finally, with a voluntary and full surrender of oneself to the will and obedience of Christ, because this obedience must be spontaneous, and the submission of agreement to the Gospel of Christ, 2 Cor. 9:13; a consent given unwillingly is rather a dissent. And one who passes over to Christ's side is no longer his own master, but belongs to Christ by bond and by purchase. I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me, Gal. 2:20. You are not your own, 1 Cor. 6:19.

units.la: CVI.
units.tr: CVI.

units.la: Tali cum assensu sanctum desiderium Christi & justitiæ ejus, seu refugium ad Christum conjunctissimum est. Sicut cervus (cum à serpentibus vulneratus est, vel obesior à venatoribus urgetur) anhelat ad alveos aquarum, ita anima mea anhelat ad te ô Deus. Sitit anima mea Deum viventem, Psal. XLII. 2. 3. Beati, qui esuriunt & sitiunt justitiam, Matth. V. 6. validam incitationem habemus ... confugientes (qui persuasi de amore Dei erga hæreditatem Christi, sititi justitiæ exarserimus, ut ad Christum confugeremus, & in ipso inveniri cuperemus) arripiendi illam spem expositam, Hebr. VI. 18. Fieri enim non potest, quin qui se miserrimum novit, & persuasissimus est, nusquam alibi, quàm in solo Christo salutis remedium, & tabulam in naufragio, reperiri, ad Christum apprehendendum se accingat, & omnibus votis desideriúsque in eum feratur, eum ardentissimè cupiat, ex se ipso exiens ad eum confugiat, ad nomen Jehovæ tanquam turrim munitam currat, Proverb. XVIII. 10. ad Filium confugiat, se recipiat Psalm. II. 12. & omnibus modis eum, ceu arcem Dei apprehendere Esaj. XXVII. 5. & possidere studeat. Denique & assensus & desiderii ac fugæ illius ad Christum comes spiritus contritio non ex timore pœnæ, sed ex amore Christi Salvatoris profecta, & sic lachrymis cor hominis rigans, ut Spiritu gratiæ, velut rore quodam perfusum totum mollescat, & ad recipiendum Christum habile & idoneum reddat.
units.tr: With this assent goes most closely a holy longing for Christ and his righteousness, or a refuge in Christ. As the deer (when it is wounded by serpents, or when a heavier animal is pressed by hunters) pants after the water brooks, so my soul pants after you, O God. My soul thirsts for the living God, Ps. 42:2, 3. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, Matt. 5:6. We have a strong incentive: those who, persuaded of God's love toward the heirs of Christ, have been set on fire by a thirst for righteousness, so that they flee to Christ and desire to be found in him, to seize the hope set before us, Heb. 6:18. For it cannot but be that one who knows himself to be most wretched, and is fully persuaded that the remedy for salvation, and the plank in shipwreck, is to be found nowhere else than in Christ alone, will gird himself to lay hold of Christ, will be carried toward him with all his prayers and longings, will desire him most ardently, and, going out of himself, will flee to him. He runs to the name of Jehovah as to a strong tower, Prov. 18:10. He flees to the Son, takes refuge in him, Ps. 2:12, and strives in every way to lay hold of God's stronghold, Isa. 27:5, and to possess him. Finally, both the assent and that flight and longing toward Christ are accompanied by a contrition of spirit, not arising from fear of punishment but proceeding from love of Christ the Saviour. Thus it waters the human heart with tears, and as if bathed in a certain dew of the Spirit of grace, the whole heart is softened and made fit and suitable to receive Christ.

units.la: CVII.
units.tr: CVII.

units.la: Sequitur demum Formalis fidei justificantis actus, qui Christi ex Evangelio agnitti, assensu theorico & practico, non sine humiliatione, abnegatione sui, pia contentione, enixissimo desiderio & fuga ad ipsum & contritione salutari Spiritus approbati, ut Salvatoris unici, fiducialis apprehensio, receptio & cum eodem unio est. Sicut enim Deus animæ laboranti, & sensu peccatorum dejectæ, contritæ & oneratæ Filium suum, & ipse Filius Jesus Christus se ipsum cum omniplenitudine gratiæ & salutis in Evangelio offert: ita anima fidelis de plenitudine gratiæ & salutis in Christo ex ejusdem verbo fideliter edocta, firmiter persuasa, ad ipsum serió confugiens, communionem ejus impense desiderans, oblatum inæstimabile illud bonum summa cum lubentia accipit, ambabus ulnis amplectitur, Christo, rupi & arci salutis suæ innititur, se illi tradit, cum ipso tota unitur, & tam firmiter eum retinet, ut ab eo se divelli nunquam patiatur. Hic proprius & formalis fidei justificantis actus est. Justificat enim per Christum & in Christo, non quatenus ille ut Salvator unicus ex verbo DEI agnoscitur, assensu pio approbatur, enixè cum fame & siti spirituali, ceu lac sincerum vitæ spiritualis appetitur, & anima à se ipsa fugiendo ad ipsum tendit, eique cor & spiritum contritum pandit: sed quatenus Christum & justitiam ejus, fundum & fructum fidenter, vocatus quippe ad hoc & jussus, omnibusque Evangelii promissionibus ad id invitatus, & à Spiritu S. tractus, accipit, apprehendit, cum eo unitur, & communionem justitiæ & salutis habere incipit.
units.tr: Then at last comes the formal act of justifying faith. Christ, recognised from the Gospel, approved by the Spirit with a theoretical and practical assent, not without humility, self-denial, devout striving, most earnest desire and flight to him, and saving contrition, is the fiducial apprehension, reception and union with him. For just as God offers his Son to the labouring soul, which is cast down, contrite and burdened by a sense of its sins, and the Son Jesus Christ himself offers himself in the Gospel with the fullness of grace and salvation, so the faithful soul, faithfully taught from his word about the fullness of grace and salvation in Christ, firmly persuaded, fleeing earnestly to him and eagerly desiring communion with him, receives that offered inestimable good with the greatest delight, embraces it with both arms, leans upon Christ, the rock and stronghold of its salvation, gives itself to him, is united wholly with him, and holds him so firmly that it never allows itself to be torn from him. This is the proper and formal act of justifying faith. For a person is justified through Christ and in Christ, not insofar as he is acknowledged as the only Saviour from the word of God, approved by pious assent, earnestly sought with hunger and spiritual thirst, desired as the pure milk of spiritual life, and the soul, fleeing from itself, strives toward him and opens to him its heart and contrite spirit; but insofar as it confidently receives Christ and his righteousness, the foundation and the fruit. For being called to this and commanded, invited to it by all the promises of the Gospel, and drawn by the Holy Spirit, it receives and apprehends him, is united with him, and begins to have communion in righteousness and salvation.

units.la: CVIII. Hoc enim illud האמין ... credere in Christum est, nempe, quæ vis verbi האמין est, se periclitantem, & sine Christo pereuntem, Christo ad salutem gestandum dare, committere; in ejus ut Salvatoris sinum & brachia se fidenter conjicere; eo modo, quo alumni nutricibus se committunt, ab eorum uberibus pendentes, & ab iisdem sustentantur. Unde credentes etiam Christum λαμβάνειν, accipere, & eo נשען niti, אחז passis velut brachiis in eum se injicere, & apprehendere eum, induere, in eo reclinari, cum eo uniri, & adhærere passim dicuntur. E re fuerit, Scripturas eam in rem exscribere. Quotquot eum ἔλαβον, acceperunt, inquit Christus, iis dedit potestatem, ut filii Dei fierent, Joh. I. 12. nisi forte ibi Christum accipere dono dicuntur, quibus dono datur, quo sensu vox Act. I. 8. Rom. V. 11. 1. Cor. II. 12. IV. 7. Gal. IV. 5. accipitur. Sed distertior est vox προσλαμβάνειν recipere, quæ & assumere etiam notat. Sicut, inquit S. Paulus, παρελάβετε τὸν Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν recepistis Christum Jesum Dominum, in ipso ambulate, Col. II. 6. Ubi προσλαμβάνειν recipere Christum est unum cum Christo fieri, illum ut thesaurum & vitam suam, & ut caput corporis, ut habitantem, & viventem in se, ut Dominum & Salvatorem suum recipere & habere. Asa Rex: שלוך Tibi innitimur, 2. Paralip. XIV. 11. Deus ipse. Non perget Israel ulterius להשען inniti percutienti se, sed על innitetur Domino Sancto Israelis, Esaj. X. 20. Qui ambulavit in tenebris, nec fuit ei splendor, spuseret in nomine Jehovæ ... innitatur Deo suo, ibid. L, 10. Christus ipse Sponsus de Sponsa
units.tr: CVIII. For this is what the Hebrew he'emin [האמין] means, to believe in Christ: namely, that the force of the verb he'emin is to entrust, commit to Christ for carrying to salvation oneself who is in danger and perishing without Christ, to throw oneself confidently into the bosom and arms of him as Saviour, in the way that nurslings commit themselves to their nurses, hanging from their breasts and being sustained by them. Hence believers are also said everywhere to take [λαμβάνειν] Christ, to accept him, and to lean on him [נשען], to throw themselves into him with outstretched arms [אחז], and to lay hold of him, to put him on, to rest in him, to be united with him, and to cling to him. It will be useful to copy out the Scriptures on this matter. As many as received him [ἔλαβον], says Christ, to them he gave power to become the sons of God, John 1:12; unless perhaps there it is said that those receive Christ as a gift to whom he is given as a gift, in the sense in which the word is used at Acts 1:8, Rom. 5:11, 1 Cor. 2:12, 4:7, Gal. 4:5. But the word proslambanein [προσλαμβάνειν], to receive, which also signifies to take up, is more expressive. As you have received [παρελάβετε] Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, says St Paul, Col. 2:6. Here to receive Christ by prosl­ambanein is to become one with Christ, to receive and have him as one's treasure and life, and as the head of the body, as the one dwelling in and living in oneself, as one's Lord and Saviour. King Asa: We rest on you [שלוך], 2 Chron. 14:11, and God himself. Israel shall no longer lean on [להשען] the one who strikes him, but shall lean on [על] the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, Isa. 10:20. He who walked in darkness and had no light, let him trust in the name of Jehovah ... let him rely on his God, ibid. 50:10. Christ himself, the Bridegroom, concerning his Bride

units.la: quidem fiducialis apprehensio est. Sponsa sua: Quæ est hæc ascendens ex deserto מִתְרַפֵּק עַל דּוֹדֵיהָ quæ se injicit supra dilectum suum? Cant. VIII. 5. Ubi LXX. pro מִתְרַפֵּק habent ἀνακλιθεῖσα [?] super eo se firmans, stabiliens, fulciens; velut passis brachiis in eum se injiciens. Eadem Sponsa: אחזתיו ואל ארפנו Apprehendi eum, & non faciam eum missum, ibid. III. 4. David נִסְמְכְתִּי עָלֶיךָ super te reclinatus sum, tibi innixus suum, Psal. LXXI. 6. מִסְמַךְ יְהוָה Fultor est Jehova omnibus lapsantibus, ibid. CXLV. 14. Esajas, Deo Israelis נִסְמְכוּ innituntur, in eo, reclinantur, Esaj. XLVIII. 2. Clarè inprimis Deus יִחְזַק בְּמָעוֹז Apprehendet arcem meam; faciet pacem mihi, pacem faciet mihi, ib. XXVII. 5. Ubi arcem salutis vocat rupem salutis, ad quam מָנוֹס qui confugit, se recipit, beatus est, Psal. II. 12. Qui autem ad illam confugit, eam apprehendit, is pacem Deo facit, cessat cum Deo πολεμεῖν belligerari, & καταλλάσσεσθαι τῷ Θεῷ reconciliatur cum Deo, 2. Cor. V. 20. Ita Jobus: בִּצִדְקָתִי הֶחֱזַקְתִּי Justitiam meam apprehendi: non dimittam illam, Job. XXVII. 6. S. Paulus: Quotquot in Christum baptizati estis, Christum induistis, Gal. III. 27. ἐνδυσάμενοι induti, non reperiemur nudi: 2. Cor. V. 3. David: יחד uni, aduna cor meum, Ps. LXXXVI. 11. יִלְוּ Adjungentur, vel adhærebunt ei gentes multæ, Zach. II. 15.
