Ubi LXX. habent: καταφευξονται πρὸς τὸν Κύριον confugient ad Dominum. Quæ phrasis etiam apud Esaiam exstat תִּלְוּיִם עַל יְהוָה qui adjunguntur, adhærent Jehovæ, Esaj. LVI. 6. sicut nempe Vir יִלְוֶה adhæret uxori, Genes. XXIX. 34. Taceo Scripturas reliquas, quæ Christi inhabitationem, communionem cum fidelibus, qualis est cibi & potus cum corpore, vitis cum palmite, capitis cum corpore, arboris cum ramis, sponsi cum sponsa, lapidis angularis cum ædificio. Quibus aliisque Scripturæ phrasibus & similitudinibus πίστωσις ἐκ χυ-ρίως primò & principaliter fidei salvificæ unum solumque Christum apprehendentis, recipientis & cum eo ad salutem se unientis actus proprius & ἀπολαμβάνειν emphaticè exprimitur. Nihil enim est, per quod sic Christus apprehendatur, recipiatur, & per quod ipse peccatorem sibi innixum gestet, fulciat, sustentet, & cum eodem communionem illam habeat, si à τῇ πίστει εἰς Χριστὸν fide in Christum discesseris. Unde & phraseos illius, πιστεύειν εἰς Χριστὸν credere in Christum in pleno & proprio sensu aliud significare non potest, quàm Christo fidere, ei inniti, in eo recumbere, quiescere ad salutem, & se salutémque suam ei ut Salvatori unico committere.
units.tr: is indeed a fiducial apprehension. His Bride says: Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved [מִתְרַפֵּק עַל דּוֹדֵיהָ], Song 8:5? Here the LXX, for מִתְרַפֵּק, have anaklitheisa [ἀνακλιθεῖσα]? supporting, establishing, propping herself upon him, as if throwing herself upon him with outstretched arms. The same Bride: I have laid hold of him, and will not let him go [אחזתיו ואל ארפנו], ibid. 3:4. David: I lean upon you [נִסְמְכְתִּי עָלֶיךָ], I have leaned on you, Ps. 71:6. Jehovah is the support [מִסְמַךְ יְהוָה] of all who fall, ibid. 145:14. Isaiah: they lean [נִסְמְכוּ] on the God of Israel, they rest on him, Isa. 48:2. Above all, God clearly says: He shall lay hold of my stronghold [יִחְזַק בְּמָעוֹז], he shall make peace with me, he shall make peace with me, ibid. 27:5. Here he calls the stronghold of salvation the rock of salvation, to which whoever flees for refuge [מָנוֹס] is blessed, Ps. 2:12. But whoever flees to it and lays hold of it makes peace with God, ceases to wage war [πολεμεῖν] with God, and is reconciled to God [καταλλάσσεσθαι τῷ Θεῷ], 2 Cor. 5:20. So Job: I have held fast my righteousness [הֶחֱזַקְתִּי], I will not let it go, Job 27:6. St Paul: As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ, Gal. 3:27; clothed [ἐνδυσάμενοι], so that we shall not be found naked, 2 Cor. 5:3. David: unite my heart [יחד], Ps. 86:11. Many nations shall join themselves [יִלְוּ] to him, or shall cling to him, Zech. 2:15. Here the LXX have: they shall flee for refuge [καταφευξονται] to the Lord. The same phrase also occurs in Isaiah: those who join themselves [תִּלְוּיִם] to Jehovah, who cling to Jehovah, Isa. 56:6, just as a man cleaves [יִלְוֶה] to his wife, Gen. 29:34. I pass over the remaining Scriptures, which speak of Christ's indwelling and the communion of the faithful, such as the communion of food and drink with the body, of the vine with the branch, of the head with the body, of the tree with its branches, of the bridegroom with the bride, of the corner stone with the building. By these and other phrases and similitudes of Scripture, the proper and principal act of saving faith, which apprehends, receives and unites itself with Christ alone unto salvation, is expressed emphatically, pistōsis [πίστωσις] ... and apolambanein [ἀπολαμβάνειν]. For there is nothing through which Christ may thus be apprehended and received, and through which he himself may carry, prop up and sustain the sinner leaning on him, and have that communion with him, if you have departed from faith in Christ [τῇ πίστει εἰς Χριστὸν]. Hence also the phrase to believe in Christ [πιστεύειν εἰς Χριστὸν], in its full and proper sense, cannot mean anything other than to trust in Christ, to lean on him, to recline in him, to rest in him unto salvation, and to commit oneself and one's salvation to him as the only Saviour.

units.la: CIX. Colligimus hinc, apprehensionem illam Christi, quæ per fidem fit, fiduciales esse. Quomodo enim non confidens Christo ut Salvatori, eidem se & salutem suam fidere, ei ad salutem inniti, in eo reclinari, eum ut arcem salutis suæ apprehendere potest? Tenendum tamen est, fiduciam πίστωσιν λέγεσθαι. Nam modò assensum practicum seu fiducialem persuasionem de veritate & bonitate promissionum, quas ad se quoque pertinere credens confidit: modò actum receptionis & apprehensionis Christi, ceu Salvatoris, quo fidelis cognita & approbata veritate & bonitate promissionum velut ad se pertinentium, ad Christum confugit illum recipit, ampleētitur, & in illo unicè requiescit.
units.tr: CIX. From this we gather that the apprehension of Christ which takes place through faith is fiducial. For how can one who takes Christ as his Saviour, and who trusts himself and his salvation to him, leans on him for salvation, rests in him, and grasps him as the stronghold of his salvation, not be confident? It must be held, however, that trust is called [πίστωσις]. For sometimes it means the practical assent, or fiducial persuasion, of the truth and goodness of the promises, which the believer trusts apply to himself too. Sometimes it means the act of receiving and apprehending Christ as Saviour, by which the believer, having known and approved the truth and goodness of the promises as belonging to himself, flees to Christ, receives him, embraces him, and rests in him alone.

units.la: CX. Sicut nempe homo in profundum aquæ gurgitem prolapsus, mersus, & torrente aquæ abreptus, visa arboris supra torrentem se expandentis fronde conclamata jam salute fa-cile sibi persuadet, se apprehensa fronde salvum fore, & hoc auxilium sibi Divinitus provisum esse, ideóque omnibus viribus hoc satagit & enitur, ut frondem eam apprehendat, eíque innitatur; quin & eandem apprehendit & ei se frondem innititur, firmissimeque inhæret, atque ita innixus ei inhærensque sic ab interitu vindicatur, at nondum tamen metus omnis perturbationis & anxietatis expers fit; donec ad se ipsum redux, & cuncta reputans se in tuto & extra periculi aleam collocatum videt, atque sic demum salutis suæ certus & securus esse incipit, cùm prius quidem extra periculi aleam, sed nondum extra anxietatem & metum constitutus fuerit: sic planè fidei salvificæ & justificantis res habet. Nam peccato homo ad portas usque inferorum pervenit. Sed Deus ex alto prospectans, & peccatoris misertus verbo Evangelii, ad gratiam in Christo eundem vocat, & Spiritu S. sic trahit, ut de benigna voluntate Dei in Christo plenissimè edoctus & jam πληροφορηθεὶς persuasissimus ad Christum manus auxiliares erga se pandentem properet, ad eum veniat, eum, ut arcem salutis apprehendat, ei totus innitatur, & totum se ad justitiam & vitam committat. Atque ita fide sua justificatur, & extra mortis periculum collocatur, sed nondum omnis metus, perturbatio, anxietas evanescunt. Hic ergo fides non amplius in κινήσει motu suo, quo ad Christum, minùs actu directo contenderat, sed ἐν σταθῇ in tuta veluti statione & portu
units.tr: CX. Just as a man who has slipped into the depths of a whirlpool, is submerged, and is carried off by the torrent, when he sees a tree's branches spreading over the current and cries out for help, easily persuades himself that he will be safe if he grasps the branch, and that this help has been provided for him by God. Therefore he strives and struggles with all his strength to grasp that branch and lean upon it. Indeed, he does grasp it, clings to the branch, and holds on most firmly. Thus supported and clinging, he is rescued from destruction, yet he is not yet free of all fear, disturbance, and anxiety. Only when he comes back to himself, and, weighing everything, sees that he is placed in safety and outside the hazard of danger, does he at last begin to be certain and secure of his salvation; before this he was indeed outside the hazard of danger, but not yet outside anxiety and fear. It is plainly the same with saving and justifying faith. For by sin a man has come right to the gates of hell. But God, looking down from on high and taking pity on the sinner, calls him to grace in Christ by the word of the Gospel, and draws him by the Holy Spirit so that, having been most fully taught of God's kindly will in Christ, and now fully assured [πληροφορηθεὶς], he hastens to Christ, who stretches out helping hands towards him, comes to him, grasps him as the stronghold of salvation, leans wholly upon him, and entrusts himself entirely to righteousness and life. And so he is justified by his faith and placed outside the danger of death, yet all fear, disturbance, and anxiety do not yet vanish. Here faith is no longer in its movement [κίνησις], by which it strove toward Christ with direct action, but is in a firm standing [ἐν σταθῇ], as if placed in a safe station and harbour.

units.la: Apprehensio Christi fiducialis est; sed diversa tamen fiducia adsensus practicus apprehensionis ipsius Christi, & consequentis eandem acquiescentiam in Christo, & tranquillitatis animi est. & portu collocata, & in sinu Christi recumbens, eique firmissimè innixa, actu suo reflexo Christum Salvatorem suum, in cujus sinu jam quiescit, considerat, liberationem suam à peccato per mortis ejus meritum, quod suo demum pretio pensiculatius æstimat, meditatur, metum paulatim omnem discutit, & sibi in Christum credenti, propter ejusdem meritum & obedientiam peccata omnia remissa esse confidit, & ad serenitatem, tranquillitatem, consolationem indies majorem, licèt non sine lucta cum tentationibus subinde fidem oppugnantibus, sed nunquam expugnantibus, proficit. Tum anima Deum suum sic alloquitur: Dic animæ meæ: Salus tua sum, Psalm. XXXV. 3. & Spiritus S. ipse in nobis, & nos per eum clamamus Abba Pater, & idem Spiritus S. arrhabo nobis datus, Ϛυμμαρτυρεῖ unà testatur quòd sumus filii Dei; si verò filii etiam hæredes, Rom. VIII. 15. 16. 17. Sic fiduciam persuasionis actum fidei justificantem præcedere: fiduciam apprehensionis eundem constituerè; & fiduciam acquiescentiæ in eo, ceu fructum Christi & justitiæ ejus receptæ quo spiritualis securitas, confidentia perseverans, & consolatio omnis in nobis efficitur, & magis magisque exuberat, eum consequi, intelligere est.
units.tr: and placed in the harbour, and resting in the bosom of Christ and most firmly leaning on him, by its reflexive act considers Christ its Saviour, in whose bosom it now rests. It meditates on its deliverance from sin through the merit of his death, which it now values more carefully at its true price, and gradually drives away all fear. It trusts that all its sins are forgiven for the sake of Christ's merit and obedience, to the one who believes in him. And it advances toward serenity, tranquillity, and consolation that grow greater day by day, not without struggle against temptations that from time to time assail faith, yet never overcome it. Then the soul speaks to its God in this way: Say to my soul, I am your salvation (Ps. 35:3). And the Holy Spirit himself within us, and we through him, cry Abba, Father; and the same Holy Spirit, given to us as a pledge, bears witness together with our spirit that we are children of God; and if children, then also heirs (Rom. 8:15–17). Thus to understand is to see that the trust of persuasion goes before the act of justifying faith, the trust of apprehension constitutes it, and the trust of acquiescence in him, as the fruit of Christ and of the righteousness received, follows it, by which spiritual security, persevering confidence, and all consolation are produced in us and grow more and more abundant.

units.la: CXI. Homo enim fidelis, ut aliis similitudinibus rem maximi momenti & usus, depingamus, homicidæ instar involuntarii à vindice sanguinis ad necem petiti, magnitudinem peccati sui reputans, & vindictam Divinam metuens, Christum asylum & cornu salutis à Deo erectum Luc. I. 69. in verbo Dei invenit, eum quoque ad se pertinere ex sensu peccati & desiderio liberationis, ipso cumprimis Spiritu S. persuadetur, obtinendæ proin salutis suæ gratia ad eum confugit, cornu illud salutis apprehendit, & apprehenso demum eo statuit se in urbe ea degere, quam Deus asylum esse voluerit: hoc est, se cum Christo & morte ejus communionem habere, denique securitatem ex urbis illius inhabitatione, hoc est, remissionem peccatorum & salutem ex communione cum morte Christi sibi pollicetur, sic verba Christi sua faciens sibi gratulatus: Jehova portionis & calicis mei pars. Tu tenes, sustentas sortem meam. Funes mihi ceciderunt in amœnis, etiam hereditas mihi decora. Benedicam Jehovæ, qui consuluit mihi, &c. Psalm. XVI. 5. 6. 7. Denique fidelis cervi vel hominis sitientis adinstar ad extinguendam sitim aquas circumspicit & quærit, ad eásque sanguineChristi sibi monstratas properat, eas labiis suis bibendo recipit, ac demum obbibendo recepit, judicat, & sentit, eas secum jungi, & se illarum potu suaviter refocillari. Sicut cervi anhelant ad alveos aquarum, ita anima mea anhelat ad Te, ô Deus. Sitit anima mea Deum, Deum viventem, &c. Quid dejicis te anima mea, & fremis apud me? Expecta Deum. Nam adhuc confitebor illum, salutes faciei meæ, & Deum meum, ibid. XLII. 2. 3. 12. Heus omnis sitiens, venite ad aquas. Venite, emite sine argento, & sine pretio vinum & lac. Esaj. LV. 1. Qui ad me venit, non esuriet, & qui in me credit, non sitiet unquam, Joh. VI. 35.
units.tr: CXI. For, to depict the matter with other similes of the greatest weight and use: a believer, like an involuntary manslayer sought for death by the avenger of blood, reckoning the greatness of his sin and fearing the divine vengeance, finds in the word of God Christ as the refuge and horn of salvation raised up by God (Luke 1:69). The Holy Spirit above all persuades him, from a sense of sin and a desire for deliverance, that this refuge belongs to him too. So, to obtain his salvation, he flees to him, grasps that horn of salvation, and, having grasped it, resolves to dwell in that city which God wished to be a refuge; that is, he resolves to have fellowship with Christ and his death. Finally, he promises himself security from dwelling in that city, that is, forgiveness of sins and salvation from communion with the death of Christ. So, making the words of Christ his own, he rejoices: The LORD is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; you maintain my lot. The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places; yes, I have a goodly heritage. I will bless the LORD, who has given me counsel, etc. (Ps. 16:5–7). Finally, like a deer or a thirsty man looking about for water to quench his thirst, the believer seeks and hastens to the waters shown to him by the blood of Christ. He takes them in with his lips by drinking, and at last, by drinking deeply, judges and feels that they are joined with him, and that he is pleasantly refreshed by their draught. As the deer pants for the water brooks, so pants my soul after you, O God. My soul thirsts for God, for the living God, etc. Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, the help of my countenance and my God (Ps. 42:1–2, 11). Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters. Come, buy without money and without price wine and milk (Isa. 55:1). Whoever comes to me shall never hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst (John 6:35).

units.la: CXII. Sed ampliùs id ex actibus fidem consequentibus liquebit: quos gratia fidei justificantis vivificante, purificante, tranquillante, corroborante & fructificante absolvi diximus. Vivificans est, quia justus ex fide sua vivit, Habac. II. 4. Christus enim, quem illa apprehendit, vita est, Joh. XIV. 6. Et in ipso vita est, ibid. I. 4. Sicut palmes cum vite unitus succum, ita homo per fidem Christo unitus succum spiritualem percipit. Ego sum vitis, vos palmites. Qui manet in me, fructum fert multum, quia sine me non potestis quicquam, ibid. XV. 5. Sic enim ex aqua, seu sanguine Christi & Spiritu novi generamur ad Regnum Cœlorum, ibid. III. 5. Per eandem fidem charismata & officia nostra omnia ἀναζωπυρεῖ & reviviscunt. Sicut nempe Spiritus Dei semen & principium charismatum animæ hominis infundit: ita fides fons & origo operationis eorundem est; similis ponderibus horologii, sine quibus ejusdem rotæ nullatenus moventur. Omnia enim Spiritus S. charismata fides efficax reddit; velut charitatem, quia amoris Christi erga nos cogitatio amorem nostrum erga Deum accendit, & ad illum trahit, & charitas ex fide non simulata pullulat, 1. Tim. I. 5. humilitatem, quia & miseriæ peccatoris, & gratiæ aspectus per fidem humiliat & deprimit: patientiam, quia exploratio fidei operatur patientiam, Jac. I. 3. & fides Deum tum ut sapientem, qui afflictionibus fidelium exitum bonum conciliare novit, tum ut gratiosum & potentem, qui ab omni malo liberare vult & potest, intuendo patientiam efficit. Par ratio officiorum hominis Christiani, quæ per fidem vivificunt. Nihil enim sine fide oratio, quæ fidelis esse debet, Jac. V. 15. Nihil Evangelii auditus, quia Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I. 16. & sermo auditus temperari cum fide audientium debet, Hebr. IV. 2. Et viva igitur & vivifica fides est. Eadem purificans quoque est, quia corda per fidem purificantur, Act. XV. 9. Sicut lux aëra, ignis metalla, medicina corpus: ita fides purificat. Accedamus cum vero corde in fiducia fidei, aspersi corda à conscientia mala, & abluti corpus aqua pura. Hebr. X. 22. 23. Habemus mysterium fidei ἐν καθαρᾷ συνειδήσει in pura conscientia, 1. Tim. III. 9. Cœlestis enim planta cum sit fides, terræ impuræ mandari non potest. Sicut illa justificat, ita sanctificat etiam. In Cœlo enim ad justitiam, & in corde hominis ad sanctimoniam fructificat. Christus enim semel fide vera apprehensus virtutem exerit, qua peccatum & homo vetustus mortificatur, & novus indies proficit. Denique fides amoris Dei initium multò minus cum amore peccati, quàm lux cum tenebris consistit. Ἀσυγκλωστα hæc sunt. Tum & gratia fidei tranquillans est. Nam justificati per fidem pacem habemus apud Deum per Dominum Jesum Christum, per quem etiam accessum fidei nacti sumus ad gratiam illam, ἐν ᾗ ἑστήκαμεν, in qua stamus & gloriamur, &c. Rom. V. 1. 2. Non tantùm enim, uti supra ostendimus, in fide κίνησις motio est, per quam in Christum movens eum apprehendit; sed etiam in eodem apprehenso est στάσις statio, & illabefactabilis ille status, in quo bona per Christum apprehensum parta magis magisque ad animum revocantes verissimam animi tranquillitatem, serenitatem, confidentiam adipiscimur. Ostendit enim reconciliationem cum Deo per Christum, quæ pacis & tranquillitatis pia mater est. Ἐν ἐμοὶ in me habebitis pacem. In mundo
units.tr: CXII. But this will become clearer from the acts that follow faith, which we said are accomplished by the grace of justifying faith in making alive, purifying, calming, strengthening, and fruit-bearing. It is life-giving, because the just shall live by his faith (Hab. 2:4). For Christ, whom faith apprehends, is life (John 14:6); and in him is life (John 1:4). As a branch united to the vine receives its sap, so a man united to Christ by faith receives spiritual sap. I am the vine, you are the branches. He who abides in me bears much fruit, for without me you can do nothing (John 15:5). For thus we are born of water, that is, of the blood of Christ, and of the Spirit, into the kingdom of heaven (John 3:5). Through the same faith all our gifts and duties are rekindled [ἀναζωπυρεῖ] and revive. Just as the Spirit of God pours into the soul of man the seed and principle of spiritual gifts, so faith is the source and origin of their operation; it is like the weights of a clock, without which its wheels do not move at all. For effective faith makes all the gifts of the Holy Spirit work: love, because the thought of Christ's love for us kindles our love for God and draws it to him, and love arises from faith unfeigned (1 Tim. 1:5); humility, because the sight of the sinner's misery and of grace, seen through faith, humbles and lowers him; patience, because the testing of faith produces patience (James 1:3), and faith, by looking on God both as wise, who knows how to bring a good outcome from the afflictions of believers, and as gracious and powerful, who wills and is able to deliver from every evil, produces patience. The same is true of the duties of the Christian man that bring life through faith. For nothing is effective without faith: prayer, which ought to be faithful (James 5:15); nothing is effective in hearing the Gospel, since the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes (Rom. 1:16), and the word preached must be mixed with the faith of the hearers (Heb. 4:2). So faith is living and life-giving. The same faith is also purifying, because hearts are purified by faith (Acts 15:9). As light purifies the air, fire the metals, and medicine the body, so faith purifies. Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water (Heb. 10:22–23). They hold the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience (1 Tim. 3:9). For since faith is a heavenly plant, it cannot be committed to an impure earth. As it justifies, so it also sanctifies. For it bears fruit unto righteousness in heaven and unto holiness in the heart of man. For Christ, once apprehended by true faith, exerts a power by which sin and the old man are mortified, and the new man advances day by day. Finally, faith in the love of God cannot exist with the love of sin any more than light can exist with darkness. These things are inseparable [Ἀσυγκλωστα hæc sunt]. Then too the grace of faith is calming. For being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom also we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand [ἐν ᾗ ἑστήκαμεν], and rejoice, etc. (Rom. 5:1–2). For, as we have shown above, in faith there is not only motion [κίνησις], by which it moves toward Christ and apprehends him, but also in the one apprehended there is standing [στάσις], an unshakable state in which, as we keep recalling to mind the goods obtained through the apprehended Christ, we attain the truest tranquillity, serenity, and confidence of soul. For it shows the reconciliation with God through Christ, which is the devoted mother of peace and tranquillity. In me you shall have peace; in the world [Ἐν ἐμοὶ in me habebitis pacem. In mundo].

units.la: Tum homicidæ involuntarii ad asylum se recipientis; nec non cervi ad aquarum alveos anhelantis, & ex iisdem bibentis, amplius illustratur.
units.tr: The same point is further illustrated by the man-slayer who flees to the city of refuge, and by the hart that pants for the water-brooks and drinks from them.

units.la: Consequentes fidei effluunt. mundo afflictionem habebitis. Sed confidite. Ego vici mundum, Joh. XVI. 33. Fides ceu lapides vivos Christo petrae inaedificati, quae omnipotens omnipotenter sustinet, Esaj. XXVIII. 16. Matth. XVI. 18. 1. Pet. II. 5. Hic in celsis habitabit, arces petrarum sublimatio ipsius, panis ipsius datur, aquae ipsius permanent, Esaj. XXXIII. 16. Pax illa, quam fides efficit, exuberans omnem mentem, (ut nihil de ea dignum Deo cogitare possimus, quin verum sit) custodiet (praesidii instar) corda vestra & cogitationes vestras in Christo Jesu, Phil. IV. 7. Imo laetitiam ex tristitia, Joh. XVI. 20. gloriam ex ignominia, 1. Pet. IV. 14. velut uvas quasdam ex spinis & ficus ex tribulis Matth. VII. 16. colligit. Jam & corroborans fidei gratia est. Nam omnia valeo in corroborante me Christo, quem fides apprehendit, Phil. IV. 13. Haec est victoria nostra, quae mundum (carnem, concupiscentiam, tentationes) vincit, fides nostra. Quis est, qui vincat mundum, nisi qui credit, quod Jesus sit Filius Dei, 1. Joh. V. 4. 5. Fides enim in certamine adversus carnem, mundum & Sathanam, in afflictionibus & adversis omnibus cor hominis sustentat, & coelesti robore donat, animam propositis certissimae victoriae & consequentis gloriae promissionibus excitat, & in Christo invictam reddit. Ideo cum clypeo, & tali quidem, qui sanguine Christi tinctus & imbutus ignita mali tela extinguit, Eph. VI. 16. Comparatur Christus enim fide receptus etiam Leo ex tribu Juda est, Apoc. V. 5. Ut turris Davidis collum ejus, aedificata in molem pinnarum. Mille scuta suspensa sunt ab illa, omnes clypei fortium, quia fides omnibus clypeis Dei fortiter & prudenter utitur, Cant. IV. 4. Etiam per fidem nonnulli ignis vim extinxerunt, quorum patientia ne ignibus quidem succensis superari potuit, Hebr. XI. 34. Ignis quidem corpus consumere potuit; sed fides flammantes ignes vicit. Denique gratia fidei fructificans est, quia ceu foecunda mater bonis operibus impraegnatur, & fructus fert. Mortificati estis legi per corpus Christi, ut fiatis servi alteri ex mortuis resuscitato, ut fructificemus Deo, hoc est, ut gratia Dei in nobis redundet ad laudem ejus per fructum justitiae, Rom. VII. 4. Id enim Deo Filium, fide apprehendendum dante, dignissimum est. Ideo enim Christus pro nobis mortuus est, ut viventes non amplius nobis vivamus, sed ei, qui pro nobis mortuus est, & resuscitatus est, 2. Cor. V. 15. Deo vivere & fructificare Christo perinde est. Fides per charitatem efficax, operosa est, Gal. V. 6. Nam per fidem Christum recipimus: per charitatem idem receptus in nobis vivit, & sic vivimus per charitatem in fide Filii Dei, qui nos dilexit, & semetipsum pro nobis tradidit, Gal. II. 20. Atque eo modo fidem cooperari operibus S. Jacobus c. II. 22. dixit, quatenus in iis se vivam, fortem & operosam ostendit; sine quibus est, perinde ut corpus sine Spiritu, mortua, non fides, sed fidei umbra est, similis membris cadaveris, &c. quae non amplius organa sunt, sed dicuntur, ibid. v. 26.
units.tr: The consequences of faith flow forth. "In the world you will have affliction. But be of good cheer: I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). Faith, like living stones built upon Christ the rock, which the Almighty sustains almightily (Isaiah 28:16; Matthew 16:18; 1 Peter 2:5). "He shall dwell on high; the munitions of rocks shall be his place; bread shall be given him, his waters shall be sure" (Isaiah 33:16). That peace which faith produces, surpassing every mind (so that we cannot think anything worthy of God that is not true of it), "shall keep your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus" as a garrison (Philippians 4:7). Indeed, faith gathers joy out of sorrow (John 16:20), glory out of disgrace (1 Peter 4:14), and, as it were, grapes from thorns and figs from thistles (Matthew 7:16). Now too faith is a grace that strengthens: "I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me," whom faith apprehends (Philippians 4:13). This is our victory, our faith, which overcomes the world (the flesh, concupiscence, temptations). "Who is he that overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?" (1 John 5:4, 5). For faith, in the struggle against the flesh, the world and Satan, in afflictions and all adversities, sustains the heart of man and bestows heavenly strength; it rouses the soul with the promises of certain victory and of the glory that follows, and makes it invincible in Christ. Therefore it is armed with a shield, and indeed one that, dipped and steeped in the blood of Christ, quenches the fiery darts of the evil one (Ephesians 6:16). For Christ, received by faith, is also "the Lion of the tribe of Judah" (Revelation 5:5). "His neck is like the tower of David, builded for an armoury, whereon there hang a thousand bucklers, all shields of mighty men" (Song of Solomon 4:4), because faith uses all the shields of God bravely and wisely. Also "through faith some quenched the violence of fire, whose patience could not be overcome even when the fires were kindled" (Hebrews 11:34). Fire could indeed consume the body, but faith conquered the flaming fires. Finally, the grace of faith is fruitful, because, like a fruitful mother, it is made pregnant with good works and bears fruit. "You are made dead to the law through the body of Christ, that you should be married to another, to him who is raised from the dead, that we should bring forth fruit to God," that is, that the grace of God should overflow in us to his praise through the fruit of righteousness (Romans 7:4). For since God gives the Son to be apprehended by faith, this is most fitting. "For this reason Christ died for us, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who died for us and was raised again" (2 Corinthians 5:15). To live to God and to bear fruit to Christ amount to the same thing. "Faith working through love" is operative (Galatians 5:6). For through faith we receive Christ; through love he, thus received, lives in us; and so we live by love in the faith of the Son of God, "who loved me and gave himself for me" (Galatians 2:20). In this way St James (ch. 2:22) said that faith cooperates with works, insofar as it shows itself living, strong and operative in them; without them it is dead, just as the body without the spirit is dead. What is dead is not faith but the shadow of faith, like the limbs of a corpse, which are no longer organs but are called so (ibid. v. 26).

units.la: CXIII. Sic omnia quae fides salvifica sinu suo fert, nativam cumprimis indolem ejus justificantis explicatam dedimus. Eam vero mire Pontificii corrumpunt, pro vera fide spectrum quoddam inanis credulitatis substituentes. Non tantum fidei escam suam propriam, panem illum vitae, qui ex coelo descendit, & mundo vitam dat, Christum & gratiam omnem in Christo perversa de fidei objecto doctrina, surripiunt, & negata eidem notitia oculos ei effodiunt; sed etiam fiduciale Christi apprehensionem procul ab ea removent. Fiduciam enim gratiae in Christo ei inesse pernegant, & ejus in locum charitatem propriam, ceu formam fidei, dantem ei to einai esse illud omne, quod luculenter adeo Scripturae ubique fere fidei salvificae & justificanti vendicant, sufficere audent; quin & dissentientibus Concil. Trid. Sess. VI. can. 12. 28. anathema dicunt: Sic instituentes illi, nihil fidei, qua fides est, relinquunt, quod non in daemoniorum fide locum habere possit; & Christianum esse posse, qui sine charitate credit, ibidem can. 22. sub anathemate definiunt, quo sic securius Christum & justitiam ejus a negotio justificationis & salutis nostrae arceant, & hominem per charitatem suam salutis iuae architectum constituant, quae Antichristi certi ma nota est. Quis est mendax nisi is, qui negat quod Jesus sit Christus (qui eum a fide salvifica removent, & fiduciam non in eo, sed in charitate propria collocant) Hic est ille Antichristus, qui negat Patrem & Filium, 1. Joh. II. 22.
units.tr: CXIII. Thus we have explained the native character of saving faith, especially its justifying character, which faith bears in its bosom. The Papists, however, wonderfully corrupt this character, substituting for true faith a certain phantom of empty credulity. They not only steal from faith its proper food, that bread of life which came down from heaven and gives life to the world, namely Christ and all grace in Christ, by a perverse doctrine concerning the object of faith, and, by denying it knowledge of him, they put out its eyes; they also remove far from it the trusting apprehension of Christ. For they deny that trust in the grace of Christ belongs to it, and in its place they dare to put proper love, as the form of faith, giving it to einai [τὸ εἶναι], that is, its whole being, which the Scriptures everywhere, almost, plainly ascribe to saving and justifying faith. Indeed, they pronounce an anathema on those who dissent (Council of Trent, Sess. VI, can. 12, 28). Those who so teach leave nothing of faith, as faith, that could not have a place in the faith of demons. And the Council defines under anathema that a man can be a Christian who believes without love (ibid., can. 22). By this means they keep Christ and his righteousness more securely away from the business of our justification and salvation, and they make man, through his own love, the architect of his salvation, which is the certain mark of Antichrist. "Who is a liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ?" (those who remove him from saving faith and place trust not in him but in their own love) "This is that Antichrist who denies the Father and the Son" (1 John 2:22).

units.la: CXIV. Sed in fidei tum persuasione, tum objecti ejus, Christi, apprehensione, tum apprehensionem eam consequente statu & consolatione, quae separari, saltem in perpetuum nullo modo possunt, fiduciam inesse, non semel jam asseruimus merito. Quid enim aliud sibi nomina pistis eis Christon fidei in Christum cui Esaj. XII. 2. pavor opponitur, pepoithesis, athaeophoeia, parrhesia, quae passim de fide enuntiantur, & omnes illae fidei periphrases, quae credentem in Christum eundem apprehendere, eo niti, in eum recumbere, se conjicere, ei se unire, &c. testantur, uti ex testimoniis supra allatis liquet, volunt? Non nudi assensus haec pistis sunt. S. Paulus vero fidem definiens hypostasin ... elegchon ... eorum, quae sperantur, repraesentationem, vel pollicitationem & demonstrationem eorum, quae non videntur, Hebr. XI. 1. ostendit, sic fidem circa ea, quae sperantur, & non videntur, versari, tum ut sperata in anima credentis ceu praesentia subsistere, & anima credens illa sibi praesentia sistere, tanquam si jam illa haberet: seu pollicitari, tanquam periculum omne et aleam ambiguitatis subiens, dicatur; tum ut illa, quae non videntur; demonstret & arguat, ceu visa; adeoque firma & certa faciat, quae vis & vocis ... elegchon. Ejusmodi vero hypostasin & elegchon non utique nudus assensus, qui rei ad credentem non pertinenti habetur, sed fiducia inprimis, qua quis rem promissam suam facit, sibi praesentem, ad se pertinentem sibi recipit & pollicetur, generat. Neque obscure S. Paulus hypostasin per fiduciam declarat, Hebr. III. 6. 14. Et exempla fidei ib. XI. 2. &c. subiecta, fidem justificantem specifice declarantia ostendunt. Alibi 2. Cor. IX. 4. XI. 17. S. Paulus vocat hypostasin kauchaeseos fiduciam gloriationis, velut si quis dicat; hypostasis mou kauchasis fiduciam habeo gloriandi; vel, fidenter glorior, audeo gloriari. Ita hypostasis.
units.tr: CXIV. But we have already rightly asserted, and not once only, that trust belongs to faith, both in the persuasion of faith, and in its apprehension of its object, Christ, and in the state and consolation that follow that apprehension; these things cannot in any way be separated, at least not permanently. For what else do the words pistis eis Christon [πίστις εἰς Χριστόν] (faith in Christ, to which fear is opposed, Isaiah 12:2), pepoithesis [πεποίθησις], athaeophoeia [ἀθαρσοφορία], parrhesia [παρρησία], which are predicated of faith everywhere, and all those circumlocutions of faith which attest that the believer apprehends Christ, leans upon him, reclines on him, casts himself upon him, unites himself to him, and so on, wish to say, as is clear from the testimonies cited above? This is not a bare assent. St Paul, defining faith, shows that it is "hypostasis [ὑπόστασιν] ... elegchos [ἔλεγχον] of things hoped for, the representation or promise and demonstration of things not seen" (Hebrews 11:1). Thus faith is concerned with things hoped for and not seen, both so that what is hoped for subsists in the soul of the believer as present, and the believing soul sets those things before itself as present, as if it already had them; and it is said to promise, as one undergoing every danger and risk of uncertainty; and also so that it demonstrates and convicts those things which are not seen, as if seen, and so makes firm and certain the things that are the force of the words hypostasis and elegchos. Such hypostasis and elegchos are not produced by a bare assent, which is held to be of a thing not pertaining to the believer, but above all by trust, by which a man makes the promised thing his own, receives it as present to himself and as pertaining to himself, and pledges it. Nor does St Paul obscurely declare hypostasis to mean trust (Hebrews 3:6, 14). And the examples of faith subjoined in Hebrews 11:2 etc. show that they declare justifying faith specifically. Elsewhere (2 Corinthians 9:4; 11:17) St Paul calls hypostasis the kauchaeseos [καυχήσεως], the trust of boasting, as if one were to say: hypostasis mou kauchasis [ὑπόστασίς μου καύχησις], "I have confidence of boasting"; or "I boast confidently, I dare to boast." So hypostasis.

units.la: Pontificium fidei justificantis formam non in fiducia εὐφ[?] ἐλπίζ[?] est sibi res sperata promittere, subire periculum sperantium: & ὑπό-στασις simpliciter est fiducia, seu sponsio, qua nobis aliquid promittimus, vel gloriatio. Unde נחם Psal. XXXIX. 8. & מקוה Ruth. I. 12. LXX. habent ὑπόστασις. Syrus מבטחם perfuasionem vel certitudinem rei, velut ad se pertinentis, reddit, quæ fiducia carere non potest. Accedit, quòd fides & fiducia eadem oppositta habent, veluti τὸ διστάζειν, ἀμφιβάλλειν dubitare Matth. XIV. 31. Jac. I. 6. τὸ μετεωρίζεσθαι sublimia sapere, Luc. XII. 28. 29. ὀλιγοπιστίαν exigua fide praeditum esse, Matth. VI. 30. VIII. 26. XIV. 31. מורא timor & metus, Esaj. XII. 2. Luc. VIII. 25. Marc. V. 36. diffidentia, Rom. IV. 20. Quae omnia & fidei, & fiduciæ oppositia sunt. Unde Abrahamus, cùm ei præceptum esset: Noli timere, addita tum declaratione Divini propositi: Ego clypeus tuus ero: tum promissione seminis cum ipso in Semine Mulieris benedicendi dicitur credidisse, Genes. XV. 1. 2. 6. Ubi fides Abrahami timori ejusdem oppositia fiduciam necessariò includit. Imò per fidem astipulamur Deo stipulanti reclinationem in ipsum ut Salvatorem. Huic autem stipulationi non mero assensu in veritatem stipulationis, sed per fiduciam astipulamur. Nam ὁμολογία astipulatio illa non solam confessionem, vel veritatis testimonii, propter veracitatem testis: vel veritatis eorum, quæ Deus de se, & de nobis in verbo suo dicit; sed inprimis confessionem juris Dei ad exigendam à nobis glorificationem sui, & amorem atq; gratitudinem; nec non dominii Dei in redemptos, ut peculium suum significat. Quæ confessio in eo, uti supra etiam diximus, consistit, ut quis ad Deum dicat: Tu es Dominus meus, Rex meus, justitia mea, Ps. IV. 2. V. 3. Esaj. XXXIII. 22. Jerem. XXIII. 6. adeóque ad promissiones Dei Nai Etiam & Amen dicat. Præterea fidei justificantis effecta sunt remissio peccatorum, Actor. X. 43. justificatio, Rom. III. 28. Gal. II. 16. pax cum Deo, Rom. V. 1. Accessus ad Deum, ibid. v. 2. benedictio, Gal. III. 9. purificatio cordis, Act. XV. 9. Victoria Sathanæ, Eph. VI. 16. vita & salus æterna, Joh. III. 16. Marc. XVI. 16. Hæc autem singula non nudus assensus bonis malisque, quin & ipsi Diabolo communis, sed inprimis fiducia specialis gratiæ, & Christi apprehensi præstat: Non enim fide in Christum solam veritatem, ut simus eruditiores, sed sapientiam illam, qua vitam, tranquillitatem & beatitudinem assequimur; neque Deum tantùm ut veracem, sed inprimis ut bonum & benevolum nobis atque remuneratorem quærentium se aspicimus & recolimus. Comparatur enim cum aspectu ænei serpentis, Joh. III. 14. 15. cum sigillo, ibid. v. 33. cum cibo, ibid. VI. 35. 51. Atqui aspectus Serpentis ænei fiduciam comitem habuit: Sigillum quo Deus ut verax obsignatur, fiduciam exigit: cibus, qui nisi applicatus & in succum sanguinémque conversus, nihil prodest, fiduciam insinuat. Sed & fidei objectum proprium esse promissionem gratiæ in Christo, supra probavimus. Perpetua enim inter verbum promissionis, & fidem, quæ verbo illi innititur, relatio est. Atqui promissio gratiæ in Christo neutiquam nudo assensu, sed inprimis certa fiducia recipitur & applicatur. Neque fides justificans, qua Christus apprehenditur fiduciæ radix tantùm & basis est, sed fiducia ipsa, quia Christus à non confidente ipsi & merito ejus apprehendi non potest. Radix verò est fiduciæ illius, quæ confidentiæ nomine καυχήσεως venit, & fidem consequitur. Quòmodo denique, juxta Augustini decantatum illud, & ab ipso Lombardo Dist. 33. Lit. D. laudatum, credere in Deum est credendo amare, credendo in eum ire, credendo ei adhærere & membris ejus incorporari; si à fide in Deum & Christum salvifica fiducia removetur?
units.tr: The Papists do not place the form of justifying faith in confidence, which is to promise oneself the thing hoped for and to undertake the risk of those who hope. Hypostasis [ὑπόστασις] is simply confidence, or a pledge by which we promise something, or boasting. Hence the Seventy render the Hebrew words for comfort [נחם] (Ps. 39:8) and hope [מקוה] (Ruth 1:12) by hypostasis. The Syriac (mabṭaḥam) renders it as persuasion or certainty about a thing as belonging to oneself, which cannot lack confidence. Moreover, faith and confidence have the same opposites: doubting [διστάζειν] and wavering [ἀμφιβάλλειν] (Matt. 14:31; James 1:6); being anxious and unsettled [μετεωρίζεσθαι] (Luke 12:28–29); little faith [ὀλιγοπιστία], that is, being endowed with little faith (Matt. 6:30; 8:26; 14:31); fear and dread [מורא] (Isa. 12:2; Luke 8:25; Mark 5:36); and diffidence (Rom. 4:20). All these are opposed to both faith and confidence. Hence Abraham, when he was told Fear not, with the declaration of God's purpose added, I am your shield, and with the promise of blessing for his seed in the Seed of the Woman, is said to have believed (Gen. 15:1, 2, 6). Here Abraham's faith, set against his fear, necessarily includes confidence. Indeed, through faith we answer God's stipulation by resting on him as Saviour. We accept this stipulation not by mere assent to its truth, but through confidence. For that answering [ὁμολογία] signifies not only a confession, or testimony to the truth on account of the truthfulness of the witness, or an acknowledgment of the truth of what God says of himself and of us in his word; but above all a confession of God's right to demand from us the glorifying of himself, love and gratitude, and also of God's lordship over the redeemed, as his own possession. This confession consists, as we have also said above, in saying to God, You are my Lord, my King, my righteousness (Ps. 4:2; 5:3; Isa. 33:22; Jer. 23:6), and so saying to God's promises, Yea and Amen [ναί]. Moreover, the effects of justifying faith are: forgiveness of sins (Acts 10:43); justification (Rom. 3:28; Gal. 2:16); peace with God (Rom. 5:1); access to God (ibid. v. 2); blessing (Gal. 3:9); cleansing of the heart (Acts 15:9); victory over Satan (Eph. 6:16); eternal life and salvation (John 3:16; Mark 16:16). Now each of these is produced not by bare assent, which is shared by good and bad alike, even by the devil himself, but above all by the confidence of special grace and of Christ apprehended. For by faith in Christ we do not look to the truth alone, so that we may become more learned, but to that wisdom by which we attain life, peace and blessedness; nor do we regard and recall God merely as truthful, but above all as good, kind to us, and the rewarder of those who seek him. For faith is compared with looking at the bronze serpent (John 3:14–15), with a seal (John 3:33), and with food (John 6:35, 51). Yet the looking at the bronze serpent was accompanied by confidence; the seal by which God is attested as true requires confidence; and food, which profits nothing unless it is applied and turned into juice and blood, implies confidence. But we have also shown above that the proper object of faith is the promise of grace in Christ. For there is a constant relation between the word of promise and the faith that rests on that word. But the promise of grace in Christ is by no means received and applied by bare assent, but above all by sure confidence. Nor is justifying faith, by which Christ is apprehended, only the root and basis of confidence; it is confidence itself, since Christ and his merit cannot be apprehended by one who is not confident. The root, however, of that confidence which is called boasting [καυχήσεως] follows faith. Finally, how is it possible, according to that often-repeated saying of Augustine, praised by Lombard himself (Dist. 33, letter D), that to believe in God is by believing to love, by believing to go to him, by believing to cleave to him and be incorporated into his members, if saving confidence is removed from faith in God and Christ?

units.la: CXV. Quo sensu S. Paulus fidem ὑπόστασιν ἐλπιζομένων Hebr. XI. 1, definiverit, jam ostendimus. Nimis enim jejuni sunt, qui verba illa ad solum assensum theoricum & intellectus operationem detorquent. Credita enim subsistunt, non tam per assensum in intellectu, quàm per fiduciam in corde. Quod sic subsistit, & demonstratum videtur à voluntate fidente & amante abesse nequit. Unde etiam Polybius ὑπόστασιν per τόλμαν audaciam in bonam & malam partem, & τὸ ὑποστελλόμενον per τολμηρόν explicat. Apud Suidam: Gessit se in periculis ὑποστελλικῶς fortiter, imperterritè. Et Thomas Aquinas 2. quæst. 4. a. 1. scribit; per ὑπόστασιν illam habitudinem actus fidei ad finem, qui objectum voluntatis est, significari. Idem S. Paulus porro fidem etiam ἔλεγχον demonstrationem eorum, quæ non videntur, finiens, nec soli intellectui, nec nudo assensui illam tribuit. Nam fidem ejusmodi demonstrationem, ejusmodi argumentum eorum, quæ non videntur, quæ voluntatem intimè afficit, & certissima spe eorum, quæ non videntur, sustentet, adeóque fiducia impleat, facit. Talis enim demonstratio est, qua id, quod non videtur, tanquam præsens, subsistens & jam possessum, demonstratur & applicatur. Non igitur fides proprie est demonstratio, vel argumentum rei, sed improprie, & per metonymiam effecti. Nam, uti scitè Alexander Alensis p. 3. q. 68. m. 5. a. 2. observat, in Logicis argumentum facit fidem, sed in Theologicis fides facit argumentum. Porrò idem S. Paulus fidei actum facit credere, quòd Deus sit, & remunerator sit eorum, qui ipsum quærunt, Hebr. XI. 6. Id verò si ad solum assensum omnino, uti οἱ ἐξ εὐαγγελίας pertendunt, referri deberet, fiduciam non ideò excluderet, quia unius positio non est alterius comitantis remotio. Sed plus etiam est credere, quòd Deus sit, quàm nudus assensus existentiæ Dei habitus, quia Dei τὸ ὄντως, seu יהוה à quo יהוה Jehova dicitur; non in sola ejus existentia, sed etiam essentia & virtutibus, quas inter ejus justitia, impium sine abnegatione sui justificantis, nec non gratia & bonitas in Christo eminent, consistit. Et qui Deum remuneratorem quærentium se esse credit, is non sine fiducia in promissionem ejus, qui potestatem dat restipulandi à Deo in bona conscientia id, quod præmium Deus nominavit, ita credit. Perperam porro fiduciam solì spei, quam fiduciam corroboratam appellant, adversarii tribuunt. Distincta enim fidei & spei fiducia est. Quatenus enim promittenti astipulamur & subscribimus per fidem confidentes credimus: quatenus futura bona promissa expectamus cum patientia, promptitudine & desiderio obtinendi, confidentes speramus. Fides est fiducia boni præsentis, vel quasi præsentis & præteriti: Spes
units.tr: CXV. We have already shown in what sense St Paul defined faith as the substance [ὑπόστασιν] of things hoped for (Heb. 11:1). They are too shallow who twist those words into a merely theoretical assent and an operation of the intellect. For things believed subsist, not so much by assent in the intellect as by confidence in the heart. What thus subsists, and is shown forth, cannot be absent from a will that trusts and loves. Hence Polybius too explains hypostasis as boldness [τόλμαν], in a good and a bad sense, and explains what is drawing back [τὸ ὑποστελλόμενον] as bold [τολμηρόν]. In Suidas: he conducted himself in dangers [ὑποστελλικῶς], bravely, undaunted. And Thomas Aquinas (2.2, q. 4, a. 1) writes that by that hypostasis is signified the relation of the act of faith to its end, which is the object of the will. Again, St Paul, defining faith as proof [ἔλεγχον] of the demonstration of things that are not seen, assigns it neither to the intellect alone nor to bare assent. For he makes faith such a demonstration, such an argument of things that are not seen, as deeply affects the will, sustains it with the most certain hope of things not seen, and so fills it with confidence. For such a demonstration is one by which that which is not seen is shown and applied as present, subsisting and already possessed. Faith, therefore, is not properly a demonstration or argument of the thing, but improperly, by metonymy of the effect. For, as Alexander of Hales wisely observes (p. 3, q. 68, m. 5, a. 2), in logic the argument produces belief, but in theology belief produces the argument. Moreover, the same St Paul makes the act of faith to believe that God is, and is the rewarder of those who seek him (Heb. 11:6). But if this were to be referred wholly to bare assent, as those of the Gospel [οἱ ἐξ εὐαγγελίας] contend, it would not therefore exclude confidence, since the positing of one is not the removal of another that accompanies it. But to believe that God is is more than bare assent to the existence of God, because God's true being [τὸ ὄντως], or Yahweh [יהוה], from which he is called Jehovah, consists not only in his existence but also in his essence and attributes, among which his justice, justifying the ungodly without denial of himself, and also his grace and goodness, shine forth in Christ. And he who believes God to be the rewarder of those who seek him believes so not without confidence in the promise of him who gives the power to restipulate with God in a good conscience what God has named as reward. Moreover, the adversaries wrongly attribute confidence to hope alone, which they call strengthened confidence. For the confidence of faith and that of hope are distinct. Insofar as we answer the promiser and subscribe to him by faith, trusting, we believe; insofar as we await the promised future goods with patience, readiness and desire to obtain them, trusting, we hope. Faith is confidence in a present good, or one as if present and past. Hope

units.la: Et argumenta fiduciæ oppositæ discutiantur. Spes futuri. Fidei objectum est verbum rei, seu promissio: Spei res verbi, seu promissa. Neutra sine fiducia officio fungi potest. Conjunctissima nihilominus fidei & spei fiducia est, quia & fidei quodammodo spes inest, & spei fides. Qui enim credit promittenti sperat: & qui sperat, bona promissa se consecuturum credit. Sed & S. Paulus dicens, nos Ἀρχ πίστως per fidem habere παρρησίαν ἐν ἀπεργαγωγῶν ἐν πεποιθήσει fiduciam & accessum in confidentia, Ephes. III. 12. tantum abest, ut fiduciam a fide separet, ut a fide ejus Christi, hoc est, a formali actu fidei, qui apprehensio Christi ut Salvatoris, est, fiduciam illam & confidentiam, ceu consequentem fidei actum, quo is, qui Christum semel apprehendit, in eodem acquievit, & pulsa δειλία, φόβῳ ἡ δειλίας (qualis Patrum V. T. fuit) magis magisque corroboratur, derivet. In eo enim non sine fiducia apprehenso habemus & παρρησίαν fiduciam, seu libertatem gloriandi de remissione peccatorum per sanguinem ejus consummata, & accessum (ad Deum) in confidentia ad petendum id, quod filiorum Dei est. Nam in eo justitiam, & causam vitae aeternae, omniumque benedictionum habemus.
units.tr: The arguments opposed to confidence are examined. Hope concerns the future. The object of faith is the word of the thing, that is, the promise; the object of hope is the thing of the word, that is, the thing promised. Neither can perform its office without confidence. Nevertheless, confidence is most closely joined with both faith and hope, because in some sense hope is in faith, and faith in hope. For he who believes the promiser hopes, and he who hopes believes that he will obtain the promised goods. But St Paul too, saying that through faith we have boldness [παρρησίαν] and access [προσαγωγὴν] in confidence [ἐν πεποιθήσει] (Eph. 3:12), is so far from separating confidence from faith that he derives that confidence, from faith in Christ, that is, from the formal act of faith, which is the apprehension of Christ as Saviour, as an act following faith. By this act, one who has once apprehended Christ rests in him, and with fear [δειλία, φόβῳ ἡ δειλίας] (such as the Old Testament Fathers had) driven out, is more and more strengthened. For in him, apprehended not without confidence, we have boldness [παρρησίαν], that is, confidence or freedom of boasting concerning the remission of sins accomplished through his blood, and access (to God) in confidence to ask for what belongs to the sons of God. For in him we have righteousness, and the cause of eternal life, and of all blessings.

units.la: CXVI. Denique fidem in diversis subjectis, intellectu per assensum, in voluntate per fiduciam habitare posse Pontificii iidem alii-que, ἀλόγως inficiantur; eò quòd impossibile sit, ut una eademque facultas diversis subjectis insit. Nam fides animam totam occupat, nec unus simplex habitus, sed quasi aggregatum quid, mutationem totius animae importans, est, qualis habitus complexus etiam justitia originalis fuit. Scriptura certè eam τῇ καρδίᾳ cordi assignat, dicens, nos τῇ καρδίᾳ πιστεύομεν corde credere ad justitiam, sicut ore confitemur ad salutem, Rom. X. 10. Qui soli intellectui fidem assignant, non negant tamen, id, quod intellectus facit, a voluntate imperari. Scholastici enim in voluntate requirunt virtutem, quae intellectum ad tale judicium moveat, quo veritatem Dei obsignet, quam studiositatem & piam affectionem insigniunt. Sed ipsa studiositas & pia affectio non potest quodam Dei amore & fiducia, qualis in fide Christum apprehendente est, vacare, & post se fiduciam seu confidentiam trahit. Neque profecto solus intellectus vel Christo nos conjungit, vel principaliter conjungit. Et plane sicut ore confitemur, ita corde credimus. Atqui ore confitemur actum ex nobis, tanquam subjecto, eliciendo. Ergo corde, seu voluntate etiam credimus, non intellectum movendo: sed actum proprium circa objectum fidei eliciendo. Quomodo insuper credentes Deo dare gloriam, Rom. IV. 20. diligere gloriam ipsius, Joh. XII. 43. amare nomen Dei, Psal. V. 12. obedire, Rom. I. 5. subjici Deo, 2. Cor. IX. 13. citra voluntatem dici possunt? Sed supervacanea forte illa de subjecto fidei omnis disceptatio est, cum non desint Scholastici, Durandum secuti, qui intellectum & voluntatem distinctas animae potentias esse insufficientur; & assensum perinde ut omne judicium animi, accuratiores hodie Philosophi non tam intellectui, quam voluntati deputent.
units.tr: CXVI. Finally, the Papists and others like them irrationally deny that faith can reside in different subjects, in the intellect through assent and in the will through trust, on the ground that one and the same faculty cannot inhere in different subjects. For faith occupies the whole soul. It is not a single simple habit but a kind of aggregate, bringing about a change in the whole soul, just as original righteousness was a complex habit. Scripture certainly assigns faith to the heart: τῇ καρδίᾳ we believe τῇ καρδίᾳ πιστεύομεν, corde credere ad justitiam, just as we confess with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:10). Those who assign faith to the intellect alone do not deny that what the intellect does is commanded by the will. For the Scholastics require in the will a virtue that moves the intellect to that judgment by which it sets its seal to the truth of God, and they mark this as studiositatem & piam affectionem, zeal and pious affection. But studiositas & pia affectio cannot be without a certain love and trust in God, such as is in the faith that apprehends Christ, and it draws trust or confidence after it. Nor does the intellect alone join us to Christ, or join us principally. And just as we confess with the mouth, so with the heart we believe. But we confess with the mouth by eliciting an act from ourselves as the subject. Therefore we believe with the heart, that is, with the will also, not by moving the intellect but by eliciting its own act concerning the object of faith. Moreover, how can believers be said, without the will, to give glory to God (Rom. 4:20), to love his glory (John 12:43), to love the name of God (Ps. 5:12), to obey (Rom. 1:5), to be subject to God (2 Cor. 9:13)? But perhaps all that dispute about the subject of faith is superfluous, since there are Scholastics, following Durandus, who hold that intellect and will are not sufficiently distinct powers of the soul. And more careful philosophers today assign assent, like every judgment of the mind, not so much to the intellect as to the will.

units.la: CXVII. Profligata sic impie fidei salvificae fiducia, aliam ei formam, charitatem hominis, induerunt, sic tamen, ut sine ea vera fides, licet non viva, sed mortua, imò etiam Christianum efficiens, sit. Quod sub anathemate sic Tridentini Sess. VI. can. 28. definiverunt: Si quis dixerit, fidem quae amissa gratia remanet, non esse veram fidem, licet non sit viva, aut eum, qui fidem sine charitate habet, non esse Christianum, anathema sit. Supra vero cap. 15. novas suas creaturas, & fideles novos Tridentinos, nimirum fideles fornicarios, adulteros, molles, masculorum concubitores, fures, avaros, ebriosos, maledicos, rapaces &c. in scenam iidem produxerunt, exempli eorum, qui veram fidem habentes, & Christiani etiam sint, charitatis licet exortes, gratia. Inde monstrosa illa fidei informis & formatae distinctio nata est. Informem enim charitate destitui, ac nihilo minus aliquid dispositive ad justificationem sive adeptionem charitatis conferre: Formatam vero per charitatem, justificare pertendunt. Illam mortuam at veram nihilominus fidem: hanc vivam appellant. Quae sophistica plane & distorta sunt: quia nec mortua fides vera fides est, sed potius cadaver informe: & vera fides informis nulla est, quia sicut essentiam propriam: ita formam etiam propriam habet: & fides illa, cui Scriptura justificationem tribuit, pro forma non distinctae ab eadem virtutis habitum, sed propriam pariter, puta fiducialem apprehensionem Christi, uti supra ostendimus, habet.
units.tr: CXVII. Having thus impiously stripped saving faith of its trust, they have given it another form, the love of man, yet in such a way that true faith, though not living but dead, and even making a man a Christian, exists without it. The Council of Trent defined this under anathema, Sess. VI, can. 28: If anyone says that faith which remains after grace is lost is not true faith, though it is not living, or that the one who has faith without charity is not a Christian, let him be anathema. Earlier, in chapter 15, the same men brought onto the stage their new creatures and new faithful of Trent, namely fornicating, adulterous, effeminate, men-lovers, thieves, covetous, drunkards, slanderers, extortioners, and so on, as examples of those who have true faith and are even Christians, though they lack charity and grace. From this came that monstrous distinction between unformed and formed faith. They maintain that unformed faith is destitute of charity, yet contributes something dispositively to justification or to the obtaining of charity; but formed faith, that is, faith through charity, justifies. The former they call dead yet nonetheless true faith; the latter they call living. These are plainly sophistical and distorted notions. A dead faith is not true faith but rather a misshapen corpse; and an unformed true faith does not exist, because just as it has its own essence, so it has its own form. The faith to which Scripture ascribes justification has as its form not a habit of virtue distinct from it, but its own form, namely the trusting apprehension of Christ, as we have shown above.

units.la: CXVIII. Est tamen etiam in fide justificante amor Dei. Continetur enim etiam sub illo praecepto: Amabis Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde; in quo illud etiam involvitur: Credes Domino Deo tuo ex toto corde. Amare enim Dominum, ut Deum suum, est ei, ut authori foederis, per fidem adhaerescere. Unde credentes ἠγαπηκέναι dilexisse apparitionem Christi, 2. Tim. IV. 8. & hypocritae non excepisse amorem veritatis, 2. Thess. II. 10. dicuntur. Neque non potest non fides esse amor gloriae Dei, non tantum ut veracis in verbo, sed etiam ut virtutes suas per testimonium patefacientis. Nam qui credit, is Deo dat gloriam, Rom. IV. 20. & ἀγαπᾷ diligit gloriam ipsius, Joh. XII. 43. Cumque fides sit obedientia, Rom. I. 5. & ὑποταγὴ subjectio, 2. Cor. IX. 13. nemo Christo credendo obedit, eique subjicitur, nisi qui eum ut Dominum, & dominium atque imperium ejus diligit. Praeterea in foedere gratiae Christus Salvator ut Dominus noster, & justitia & salus, quae in illo est, fidei proponitur. Fides autem illa, quae receptio Christi ut Salvatoris, Domini, justitiam & salutem donantis est, & fiduciam in eodem omnem collocat, nisi amor esse non potest. Una charitate suaviter & veraciter obeditur, inquit Augustinus de bono perseverantia cap. 16. Sed non obstante hoc fides à charitate distinguitur. Aliud enim est amor Dei per testimonium ad foedus se offerentis: aliud amor omnium Dei attributorum, operum ejus & proximi: nec non ardor ille, in quem excrescimus, & tranquilla suavitas, qua in Deo deliciamur. Ille in fide est, hic à fide est, neque tamen omnino ab ea separari potest.
units.tr: CXVIII. Yet there is also love of God in justifying faith. For it is contained in that precept: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart (Deut. 6:5); and in it this too is included: You shall believe the Lord your God with all your heart. For to love the Lord as one's God is to cleave to him by faith, as to the author of the covenant. Hence believers are said to have loved Christ's appearing (2 Tim. 4:8), and hypocrites are said not to have received the love of the truth (2 Thess. 2:10). Nor can faith fail to be the love of God's glory, not only as he is true in his word but also as he makes his virtues known through testimony. For he who believes gives glory to God (Rom. 4:20) and loves his glory (John 12:43). And since faith is obedience (Rom. 1:5) and subjection (2 Cor. 9:13), no one believes Christ, obeys him, and submits to him unless he loves him as Lord, and loves his dominion and rule. Moreover, in the covenant of grace Christ is set before faith as our Saviour and Lord, and the righteousness and salvation that are in him. Faith, however, which is the reception of Christ as Saviour and Lord, who bestows righteousness and salvation, and which places all its trust in him, cannot be without love. By charity alone is obedience rendered sweetly and truly, says Augustine, De bono perseverantiae, ch. 16. Yet notwithstanding this, faith is distinguished from charity. For one thing is the love of God through testimony, as he offers himself to the covenant; another is the love of all God's attributes, his works, and his neighbour; and another is that ardour into which we grow, and the tranquil sweetness in which we delight in God. The former is in faith, the latter is from faith, yet it cannot altogether be separated from it.

units.la: CXIX. Etenim Scriptura veram fidem, quae ad salutem & justificationem aliquid confert, causam charitatis emanativae similem, non vel illam ab hac separabilem, vel hanc illius formam facit. Charitas est ex fide.
units.tr: CXIX. For Scripture makes true faith, which contributes something to salvation and justification, the cause, like an emanative cause, of charity. It does not make faith separable from charity, nor does it make charity the form of faith. Love springs from faith.

units.la: ii ex fide non simulata, 1. Tim. I. 5. Omnis credens, quòd Jesus sit Christus, ex Deo genitus est: & omnis qui diligit genitorem, diligit etiam genitum ex eo, 1. Joh. V. 1. Fides per charitatem ἐνεργουμένη operosa est, charitate non opus justificationis, sed sanctificationis promovens, & eo fructu se justificantem demonstrans, Gal. V. 6, ut quæ hoc opus non præstat, non illa augusta fides sit, quam Scriptura exigit & prædicat, sed ejus turpe simulachrum, informe cadaver, & inanis larva, Jac. II. 26. 26. Ubi fides sine operibus non vera fides, sed νεκρὰ mortua, & quidem v. 17. καθ' ἑαυτὴν in semetipsa, v. 14. λεγομένη quæ dicitur, & non est; & quæ non tantùm non esse hominis Christiani integrè perfecti, ut Sophistæ loquuntur, sed ne quidem esse hominis Christiani, sed esse hominis hypocritæ, & filii Sathanæ constituit. Si enim dixerimus, nos communionem cum eo habere (qualem fides sola præstat) & in tenebris ambulamus, mentimur, & non facimus veritatem, 1. Joh. I. 6. Sicut igitur nec sol, qui non illuminat, sol est; nec aqua, quæ non humectat, aqua: itâ nec vera fides est, quæ charitatem non operatur. Accedit, quòd vera Dei notitia, quæ fidei inest, nunquam charitatis & bonorum operum expers est. Qui dicit, cognovi eum, & mandata ejus non servat, mendax est, & in ipso veritas non est, (quomodo ergo vera fides?) ibid. II. 4. Quid verò multa? Qui propriis, & maximè domesticis non providet, adeóq; charitatem non exercet, is fidem abnegavit, & infideli pejor est, 1. Tim. V. 8. Quomodo ergo veram fidem habet? Denique vera fides Christo nos inserit, Joh. I. 12. Gal. II. 20. III. 26. corda purificat, Act. XV. 9. & Spiritum obsignantem habet, Eph. I. 13. At Christo inseri quemquam, vel cujusquam cor purificari, vel quemquam Spiritu Dei obsignari sine charitate, næ ἀσύμφωνον id planè est. Neque illud obstat, quòd πᾶσαν πίστιν omnem fidem charitate destitui posse S. Paulus, 1. Cor. XIII. 2. innuit, quia de fide omni miraculorum, vel persuasione de veritate prædictionum & promissionum ibi sermo est; quod ex scopo ejus colligitur. Nam de variis donis particularibus, eorúmque abusu agit; & fidem illam, quam charitate destitui posse innuit, supra cap. XII. 9. inter dona spiritualia non omnibus fidelibus communia numeraverat; & fidei illius opus statim definit, montes transferre. Neque etiam principes illi Judæorum credentes in Christum, neque tamen eum confitentes, & plus gloriam hominum, quàm Dei diligentes, Joh. XII. 42. 43. verè crediderunt, vel vera fide præditi fuerunt, quia verè credentes gloriam à se ipsis non accipiunt, & solius Dei gloriam quærunt, ibid. V. 44. Parabolæ quin etiam Christi Matth. XIII. 18. XXII. XXIV. multos quidem oretenus fidem profiteri sine charitate insinuant: at vera fide eos donatos esse, minimè testantur. Multi enim confitentur, Deum se scire, sed operibus abnegant, Tit. I. 16. Et quis tandem paleam, pisces putridos, hospites sine veste nuptiali, hœdos veros fideles & Christianos designare, asserere ausit?
units.tr: From unfeigned faith (1 Tim. 1:5). Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God, and everyone who loves the one who begot loves also the one begotten by him (1 John 5:1). Faith working through love [ἐνεργουμένη] is operative: by charity it promotes not the work of justification but of sanctification, and by that fruit it shows that it justifies (Gal. 5:6). So a faith that does not perform this work is not that noble faith which Scripture requires and proclaims, but its base image, a misshapen corpse and an empty mask (Jas. 2:26). Here faith without works is not true faith but dead [νεκρὰ], and indeed (v. 17) in itself [καθ' ἑαυτὴν], (v. 14) said to be [λεγομένη], which is said and is not; and such a faith makes a man not only not a fully perfected Christian, as the Sophists speak, but not even a Christian at all, but a hypocrite and a son of Satan. For if we say that we have fellowship with him (such as faith alone provides) and yet walk in darkness, we lie and do not do the truth (1 John 1:6). Just as neither a sun that does not shine is a sun, nor water that does not wet is water, so neither is a faith that does not produce love a true faith. Add that the true knowledge of God which is in faith is never without charity and good works. He who says, I know him, and does not keep his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him (how then is his faith true?) (1 John 2:4). Why say more? He who does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, and so does not exercise charity, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever (1 Tim. 5:8). How then does he have true faith? Finally, true faith engrafts us into Christ (John 1:12; Gal. 2:20; 3:26), purifies hearts (Acts 15:9), and has the Spirit sealing it (Eph. 1:13). But that anyone should be engrafted into Christ, or that anyone's heart should be purified, or that anyone should be sealed by the Spirit of God without charity, is plainly inconsistent. Nor does it stand in the way that St Paul hints that every faith [πᾶσαν πίστιν] can be destitute of charity (1 Cor. 13:2), because there he is speaking of the faith of miracles, or of the persuasion about the truth of predictions and promises, as is gathered from his purpose. For he treats of various particular gifts and their abuse; and the faith which he hints can lack charity he had already numbered, at 12:9, among the spiritual gifts not common to all believers; and he immediately defines its work as moving mountains. Nor did those rulers of the Jews, believing in Christ but not confessing him, and loving the glory of men more than the glory of God (John 12:42-43), truly believe or possess true faith, because those who truly believe do not receive glory from themselves but seek only the glory of God (ibid. 5:44). Indeed the parables of Christ (Matt. 13:18; 22; 24) also suggest that many profess faith with their lips without charity, but they by no means testify that such people have been given true faith. Many profess that they know God, but deny him by their works (Titus 1:16). And who would dare to assert that the chaff, the rotten fish, the guests without a wedding garment, and the goats designate true believers and Christians?

units.la: CXX. Fidei justificantis naturam etiam Socinianí plane pervertunt. Definiunt enim fiduciam in Deo per Christum collocatam, qua ei sub spe promissæ salutis obedimus. Et vulgò obe-
units.tr: CXX. The Socinians also completely pervert the nature of justifying faith. They define it as "a trust placed in God through Christ, by which we obey him in hope of the promised salvation," and commonly call it obe-

units.la: dientiam mandatorum Dei appellant; & bona opera non fructum, sed formam fidei esse statuunt. Quæ non aliò tendunt, quàm ut pro obedientia Christi nobis imputata subrogetur obedientia nostra à Christo præscripta, qua per nos ipsos Legi à Christo correctæ satisfiat; ita ut fides justificans re ipsa non differat à conversione & pœnitentia; nisi quòd causam ipsius conversionis ipsam speciatim à Christo præscriptam obedientiam denotet. Quod igitur in fidei definitione sano sensu, ἐγὼν esse debuit, ipsis παρέρχον est, sensu heterodoxo ab ipsis intellectum, nempe fiducia in Deo per Christum collocata. Cùm enim secundum Scripturam illa sit fiducia in sanguine Christi, Rom. III. 25. qua confidimus, Christum Θεάνθρωπον sua obedientia Deo Patri debitum nostrum solvisse, atque sic justificationem nostram coram Deo obtinuisse; illi eam intelligunt, qua Deum promittentem nobis, cum amnestia, seu impunitate peccatorum antecedentium, mercedem vitæ æternæ, si per obedientiam nostram legi ejus satisfecerimus, habemus pro veraci & fideli, & in promissione illa acquiescentes, nos ad illam amnestiam & mercedem, laboriosò opere pœnitentiæ comparandam accingimus. Verbo, in Christo, sed in opere proprio, & promissione mercedis illi reddendæ, fiduciam illi defigunt: & simul fiduciam illam in Deo per Christum collocantes profitentur, se majorem fiduciam habere in homine olim mortali, mortuo & nunc redivivo, quem negant, naturam Deum esse, quàm in Deo vivente & jurante: Vivo ego. Quasi talis pro Dei veracitate spondere potuerit; similis Josepho pro fratribus apud Pharaonem spondenti, qua similitudine Smalcius de Div. Christi cap. 11. & 19. utitur. Sed præterea fides justificans & obedientia Legis ἀλλ' ἀλλά πι-στῶν differunt. Illa infusus Divinitus habitus: hæc opus vel actio est: illa πίστις & ἀληθο-φορία; hæc ἐνέργεια: illa hujus causa, hæc illius effectus: illa justificat, Christo unit, filios Dei efficit; hæc tales à posteriore demonstrat: illa circa Evangelium; hæc circa legem occupatur: illa cum hac vita finitur; hæc permanet. Denique tantum abest, ut obedientia Legis fidei forma sit, ut in negotio justificationis eidem opponatur. Colligimus fide justificari hominem sine operibus Legis, Rom. III. 28. Scientes non justificari hominem ex operibus Legis, sed per fidem Jesu Christi, Gal. II. 16. Nam quòd sic fidem operibus perfectis Legis opponi, cùm fides nec opus perfectum, licèt à Deo pro tali habeatur; nec opus Legis sed Evangelii sit, illi pertendunt, nullam veri similitudinem habet. Ubique enim fides & opera Legis absolutè & simpliciter opponuntur. Neque illud πᾶν ξενούμενον fuit, an opera Legis perfecta justificent, sed an opera, quæ secundum Legem Judæi præstabant, justificent, quæ opera Legis, à Mose imperata, rectè dicuntur, quia facta sunt secundum Legem; licèt ei ad amussim non respondeant. Fides verò nec quà opus perfectum, pro quali à Deo, cujus judicium secundum veritatem est, Rom. II. 2. nec quà imperfectum justificat, quia operibus in justificatione simpliciter & perpetuò opponitur. Denique quatenus ut confidentia in Deo absolutè accipitur, uti adversarii accipiunt, non minùs opus Legis,
units.tr: dience to the commandments of God. They also hold that good works are not the fruit of faith but its form. These views aim at nothing other than this: that our obedience, prescribed by Christ, should be substituted for the obedience of Christ imputed to us, so that by our own efforts the Law, as corrected by Christ, is satisfied. In that case justifying faith would in fact differ in no way from conversion and repentance, except that it names as the cause of conversion the obedience itself prescribed by Christ. So what in a sound sense ought to have stood in the definition of faith, namely [ἐγὼν], is replaced by what they put in its place [παρέρχον], understood in a heterodox sense: "a trust placed in God through Christ." For according to Scripture faith is the trust in the blood of Christ (Rom. 3:25), by which we rely on the fact that Christ, the God-man [Θεάνθρωπον], paid to God the Father the debt we owed by his own obedience, and so obtained our justification before God. They understand it as the trust by which we hold God, who promises us, with the forgiveness or impunity of past sins, the reward of eternal life if we satisfy his law through our obedience, to be true and faithful; resting in that promise, we set ourselves to obtain that forgiveness and reward by the laborious work of repentance. In short, they fix their trust on Christ in name, but on their own work and on the promise of a reward to be paid for it. At the same time, while claiming to place their trust in God through Christ, they profess that they have more trust in a man once mortal, dead and now restored to life (whom they deny to be God by nature), than in the living God who swears, "I live". As if such a man could give surety for God's truthfulness, like Joseph standing surety for his brothers before Pharaoh, an analogy Smalcius uses in De divinitate Christi, chapters 11 and 19. Moreover, justifying faith and the obedience of the Law differ in [ἀλλὰ πίστεως]: the one is a habit infused by God, the other a work or action; the one is faith and full assurance [πίστις καὶ ἀληθοφορία], the other activity [ἐνέργεια]; the one is the cause of the other, the other its effect; the one justifies, unites us to Christ and makes us sons of God, while the other demonstrates such men by its fruits; the one is concerned with the Gospel, the other with the Law; the one ends with this life, the other endures. Finally, far from obedience to the Law being the form of faith, in the matter of justification it is set directly against faith: "We conclude that a man is justified by faith without the works of the Law" (Rom. 3:28); "Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the Law, but by faith in Jesus Christ" (Gal. 2:16). That faith is opposed to the perfect works of the Law, on the ground that faith is neither a perfect work, though God counts it as such, nor a work of the Law but of the Gospel, has no plausibility at all. Everywhere faith and the works of the Law are set against each other absolutely and simply. Nor was the whole question [πᾶν ζητούμενον] whether perfect works of the Law justify, but whether the works which the Jews performed according to the Law justify; these are rightly called works of the Law, commanded by Moses, because they were done according to the Law, although they do not correspond to it exactly. Faith, however, justifies neither as a perfect work, for which God, whose judgment is according to truth (Rom. 2:2), would take it, nor as an imperfect one, since in justification it is simply and constantly set against works. Finally, insofar as the adversaries take it absolutely as confidence in God, it is no less a work of the Law, and commanded by the first precept of the Decalogue, than other works.

units.la: Socinianorum fidei, sententia, & sententiae crypsu gis , prima Decalogi præcepto imperatum, quàm alia opera, est.
units.tr: Thus, even by the Socinians' own opinion and their hidden sense, faith is no less a work of the Law, commanded by the first precept of the Decalogue, than other works are.

units.la: CXXI. Est equidem fides opus, quippe animæ actio Divinitus mandata, per quam præcepto Christum cognoscendi, ei confidendi, & in eum recumbendi, obeditur. Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum, quem ille misit, Joh.VI.29. Operis igitur hujus actus est, non obedire Legi faciendorum, sed credere in eum, quem Deus misit, ut Legi satisfaceret. Et sic opus Dei est, quia Deus prima ejus causa est, & per eum ut justus, & justificans improbum, justificatur & glorificatur, ut etiam sit opus & actus credentis, cui à Deo fides datur, ut credat. Sicut rota à superiore mota ipsa quoque se movet & currit, ut unus & moventis rotam, & rotæ se moventis motus sit. Ideo etiam fidei ὑπακοὴ obedientia tribuitur. Per Christum accepimus gratiam & Apostolatum εἰς ὑπακοὴν πίστεως ad obedientiam fidei & aspersionem sanguinis Christi, 1.Pet. I.2. Ideo ἀπιστία infidelitas vocatur ἀπει-θεία inobedientia, & fidei opponitur, Joh.III.36. 1.Pet.II.8. Rom.II.8. Cùm enim fides habeat præceptum: Credite Evangelio, Marc.I.15. Hoc est præceptum ejus, ut credamus in nomine Filii ejus Jesu Christi, 1.Joh.III.23. qui præceptum illud implent, ei obediunt. Ita credere est obedire mandato credendi, sed non omne obedire est credere. Nam obedimus vel fidem verbo promissionis habendo, & Christum apprehendendo; vel opera præcepta faciendo, interdicta omittendo. Illa fidei, hæc Legis obedientia est. Neq; etiam Abrahamus justificatus est per obedientiam mandatorum Legis; sed per fidem, quæ ei in justitiam reputata est, quia per eam Christum ceu justitiam credentis recepit, Gen. XV.6. Mandatum verò ambulandi coram Deo, & ut integer sit, ibid.XVII.1. sic fidem in Christum involvit, ut tamen, sola fides in Christum mandatum illud non exhauserit. Mandatum enim & fidei & resipiscentiæ in eo continetur. Acli-cèt testata ab eodem promptitudine obedien-di mandato Dei, quo filium mactare jussus est, Deus ad eum dixerit: כי יען אשר עשית quia hoc fecisti &c. benedicendo benedicam tibi, ibid.XXII. 16.17. tamen fides ejus non fuit obedientia mandati illius, tum quia ante annos plus triginta fide justificatus dicitur, Genes.XV.§.6. tum quia particula כי יען quoniam vel quandoquidem non consequentis, vel causæ, sed consequentiæ & signi nota est. Quo verò sensu, Jac.II.ex operibus justificatus idem dicitur, infra dispiciemus.
