units.tr: CXXI. Faith is indeed a work, being an action of the soul commanded by God, by which obedience is rendered to the precept of knowing Christ, trusting in him and resting upon him. This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent (John 6:29). The act of this work, therefore, is not to obey the Law's commands to do, but to believe in him whom God sent to satisfy the Law. Thus it is the work of God, because God is its first cause, and through him as just, and justifying the wicked, the believer is justified and glorified; yet it is also the work and act of the believer, to whom faith is given by God that he may believe. As a wheel set in motion from above also moves itself and runs, so that the motion is both that of the one moving the wheel and of the wheel moving itself. Hence obedience [ὑπακοὴ] is also ascribed to faith. Through Christ we have received grace and apostleship, to bring about the obedience of faith [εἰς ὑπακοὴν πίστεως] and the sprinkling of the blood of Christ (1 Pet. 1:2). Hence unbelief [ἀπιστία] is called disobedience [ἀπείθεια], and is opposed to faith (John 3:36; 1 Pet. 2:8; Rom. 2:8). For since faith has a command, Believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15), this is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ (1 John 3:23), those who fulfil that command obey it. Thus to believe is to obey the command to believe, but not every obedience is faith. For we obey either by holding faith in the word of promise and laying hold of Christ, or by doing commanded works and omitting forbidden ones. The first is the obedience of faith, the second the obedience of the Law. Nor was Abraham justified by obedience to the commands of the Law, but by faith, which was reckoned to him as righteousness, because through it he received Christ as the righteousness of the believer (Gen. 15:6). The command to walk before God and be blameless (Gen. 17:1) involves faith in Christ in such a way that faith alone in Christ does not exhaust that command, for the command of faith and of repentance is contained in it. Although Abraham showed his readiness to obey God's command to sacrifice his son, and God said to him, because you have done this [כי יען אשר עשית] etc., in blessing I will bless you (Gen. 22:16–17), nevertheless his faith was not the obedience of that command. This is because he is said to have been justified by faith more than thirty years earlier (Gen. 15:6), and because the particle [כי יען] because or since marks not a consequent or cause but a consequence and a sign. In what sense James says, a man is justified by works (James 2), we shall examine later.

units.la: CXXII. Tenendus est denique ex iis, quæ dicta sunt, ordo, & iter velut fidei, quo illa ad consolationem credentis proficit, & sine deceptionis periculo ad praxin deducitur, ne quis non amans vel timens Deum, & purificationis veterum peccatorum suorum incuriosus, seu generatio pura in oculis suis, sed à stercore suo non lota, Prov.XXX.12. nimis citò & intempestivè eam sibi vendicet. Licèt enim non peccet ille, quì statim Christum, ut redemptorem ac Dominum suum, & Deum ut Patrem amat & clamat; Pater: tamen qui vitiosis affectibus adhuc mancipatus est, & indulget, temerè Christo ut pro se mortuo confidit, & consolationem remissionis peccatorum suorum vi, non pretio aufert. Omnes equidem verbo vocati in Christum credere jubentur, sed מאד רחבה latum valde est, Psalm.CXIX.96. & scalæ simile, quæ per gradus, non saltu superatur. Omnes ergo vocati ante omnia verbum Dei vocantis audire & cognoscere, atque ex eo νοεῖας δόξας principalia & velut dominantia capita eruere & amplexari tenentur. Sunt autem illa Legis, vel Evangelii. Legis præcipua hæc sunt, quòd universum genus humanum peccato pollutum sit originali, omnes actuali insuper adulti: quòd stipendium peccati maledictio & æterna mors sit. Evangelii verò hæc, quòd per solam Dei gratiam & misericordiam liberatio à peccato & morte contingat: quòd sine obedientia & satisfactione Legi præstita illa non contingat: quòd Christus ex consilio Dei eum in finem incarnatus, mortuus, resuscitatus sit, ut ἱλασμὸς propitiatio pro peccato, & perfectus Salvator, princeps salutis existeret: quòd sine communione cum Christo, ejus justitia & vita nemini salus contingat: quòd communio illa nemini nisi resipiscenti & in Christum credenti contingat: His rectè fundatis Evangelium procedit: fœdus gratiæ peccatori offert, omnes vocatos resipiscere, Christum Salvatorem unicum recipere & amplexari jubens, & recipienti atque amplectenti justitiam & vitam æternam promittens. Hic fidei primum opus est, quòd credens convictus in conscientia libenter & mox, non sine pudore se ipsum & propriam justitiam abnegat: Dei justitiam agnoscit, ei se subjicit, non sine firmo animi judicio, & πεισμονὴ illa, quòd sicut certò omnes, qui Christum habent, justitiam & vitam pariter habent, ita etiam quisque verbo Dei ad Christum amplectendum invitatus, si eum ut rupem salutis apprehendat, certò vitam per ipsum adepturus sit. Sed hæc persuasio firmiter redditur, quòd à Spiritu S. trahi ad Christum incipit. Inde fames & sitis justitiæ, desiderium flagrans, compunctio & contritio spiritus, conjuncta cum proposito animam Christo, ceu fido creatori & redemptori committendi, fuga à se ipso, & motus ad Christum. Demum succedit receptio & apprehensio fiduciali Christi, qua credens per fidem in ipsum recumbit, ei unitur & velut agglutinatur. Jam ergo periculum mortis & iræ Dei cessat, quia nulla in iis, qui in Christo Jesu sunt, condemnatio est, Rom.VIII.1. Sed se jam Christum, velut pro se mortuum, & cum eodem beneficia ejus, remissionem peccatorum, justitiam & vitam tenere, non audet sub prima sæpe initia, in tentationibus cumprimis gravioribus, gloriari. Imò sensus & gloriatio illa nonnisi anxia solicitudine, defatigatione, & gemitibus assiduis obtinetur. In hoc enim ingemiscimus, εἴγε καὶ ἐνδυσάμενοι αὐ-induti simus, annon nudi inveniamur, 2.Cor.V.2.3. Sed non potest non tamen hæc animæ immutatio statim, & quotiescunque credens promissionem, quam vix unquam fides ex oculis deponit, & à qua sacer ille ignis accenditur, respicit, persentisci, ut non quasi eminus cor Dei & Cœlum sibi apertum videat, quia ipse spiritus fidei, qui ex effectu suo noscitur, obsignatio in Christum est, Ephes.I.13.14. De cætero quantum δοκιμὴ exploratio per patientiam, & fructus Spiritus, & amorem proximi, minimùm offensas ei condonantis, crescit, tantum etiam plenitudo spei ad gloriationem in Deo ad πεποίθησιν fiduciam & lætitiam consummatam prosi-cit, cit. Quæ fidei consolatio, & in Christo velut pro se mortuo ad propitiationem pro peccatis confidentia, ad solos electos pertinens, minimè negligi, vel contemni, quasi vel non daretur, vel anti non esset, sed studiosè & cupidè quæri debet, ne metuamus Genef. XV. I. sed persuasissimum habeamus, quòd quærentes Deum, & sic amantes requiem animarum inventuri simus.
units.tr: CXXII. Finally, from what has been said, we must keep in view the order and path, as it were, of faith, by which it advances to the consolation of the believer and is brought without danger of deception into practice, lest anyone who does not love or fear God, and is careless about the purification of his former sins, or a generation pure in its own eyes, yet not washed from its filth (Prov. 30:12), claim it for himself too quickly and unseasonably. For he does not sin who at once loves and cries out, Christ as his Redeemer and Lord, and God as his Father, Abba; yet he who is still enslaved to vicious affections and indulges them rashly trusts in Christ as dead for himself, and seizes the comfort of forgiveness of sins by force rather than by price. All who are called by the Word are indeed commanded to believe in Christ, but the way is [מאד רחבה] exceedingly broad (Ps. 119:96), and it is like a ladder, which is climbed by steps, not by a leap. Therefore all who are called must first hear and know the Word of the calling God, and from it draw out and embrace the principal and, as it were, dominant heads of the saving [νοεῖας δόξας] opinions. These are either of the Law or of the Gospel. The chief points of the Law are these: that the whole human race is polluted by original sin, and adults additionally by actual sin; and that the wages of sin are curse and eternal death. The chief points of the Gospel are these: that deliverance from sin and death comes through God's grace and mercy alone; that it does not come without obedience and satisfaction rendered to the Law; that Christ was incarnate, died and rose again by the counsel of God for this end, that he might be a [ἱλασμὸς] propitiation for sin and a perfect Saviour and author of salvation; that salvation comes to no one without communion with Christ, his righteousness and life; and that this communion comes only to one who repents and believes in Christ. Once these things are rightly established, the Gospel proceeds: it offers the covenant of grace to the sinner, commanding all who are called to repent, to receive and embrace Christ as the only Saviour, and promising righteousness and eternal life to the one who receives and embraces him. This is the first work of faith: the believer, convicted in conscience, willingly and promptly, not without shame, renounces himself and his own righteousness, acknowledges God's righteousness and submits himself to it, not without a firm judgment of the mind; and there is that persuasion that, just as all who have Christ certainly have righteousness and life together, so also whoever is invited by the Word of God to embrace Christ, if he lays hold of him as the rock of salvation, will certainly obtain life through him. This persuasion is firmly produced when the Holy Spirit begins to draw him to Christ. Hence come hunger and thirst for righteousness, a burning desire, compunction and contrition of spirit, joined with a resolve to commit the soul to Christ as a faithful creator and redeemer, flight from oneself, and movement towards Christ. At last comes the reception and fiducial apprehension of Christ, by which the believer rests in him through faith, is united to him and, as it were, cemented to him. Now the danger of death and the wrath of God ceases, because there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:1). Yet at the early stages, and especially in heavier temptations, he does not dare to glory in holding Christ as dead for him, and with him his benefits: remission of sins, righteousness and life. Indeed that sense and glorying are obtained only with anxious care, weariness and constant groaning. For in this we groan, if indeed being clothed we are not found naked (2 Cor. 5:2–3). Yet this change of soul cannot but be perceived at once, and whenever the believer looks at the promise, which faith scarcely ever takes from its eyes, and from which that sacred fire is kindled, so that he does not see the heart of God and heaven opened to him as if from afar; for the very Spirit of faith, known by its effect, is the seal in Christ (Eph. 1:13–14). Moreover, as the [δοκιμὴ] proving through patience, the fruit of the Spirit and love of neighbour, which at least forgives offences, grows, so also the fullness of hope advances to glorying in God, to [πεποίθησιν] confidence and perfected joy. This consolation of faith, and confidence in Christ as dead for us as the propitiation for sins, belongs only to the elect and must by no means be neglected or despised, as though it were not given or did not exist; it must be sought eagerly and with desire, so that we need not fear (Gen. 15:1), but may be firmly persuaded that by seeking God, and thus loving him, we shall find rest for our souls.

units.la: LOCUS VICESIMUS SECUNDUS: De GRATIA JUSTIFICATIONIS. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: TWENTY-SECOND TOPIC: On the Grace of Justification. A SUMMARY.

units.la: Cum Gratia Vocationis Gratia Justificationis cohæret. 1. Cujus doctrina maximi momenti est. 2. Nequicquam illud extenuantibus quibusdam, qui in religione nec calidi, nec frigidi sunt. 3 Vocis justificandi Latinæ notio evolvitur. 4. Vocum originalium צדק & δικαιόω notio forensis est, non justitiæ infusionem, sed ceu justi in judicio Dei declarationem & absolutionem significans. 5. Justificatio vel Peccatoris, vel justi est. Summa de justificatione peccatoris. 6. Justificationis ejusdem definitio, & ex Rom. III. 24. 25. illustratio. 7. Deus solus justificat, isque Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. 8. Status hominis justificandi internus est, quòd peccati convictus, & æternæ mortis reus est. 9. Debitum, quod ab homine justificando Deus exigit, duplex est, & solvendi poenam peccato commeritam, & obedientiam, sive justitiam universalem præstandi; utrumque vel in se, vel in sponsore. 10. Status justificandi hominis externus est, quòd ab æterno ad id electus, in tempore vocatur & separatur, Christo sequestro, ut ante justificationem perire non possit. 11. Causa Deum intus ad justificandum movens Dei gratia, seu gratiosus favor est. 12. Tridentinorum & Bellarmini, gratiam illam non benignum favorem Dei, sed rectitudinem habitus charitatis infusi interpretantium, impietas. 13. Eorundem argutiæ ad incudem revocantur. 14. Causa extra Deum eundem ad justificandum peccatorem movens est δικαίωμα, opus seu justitia perfecta quod Lex Dei ab eo, qui justus declarari debet, exigit. 15. Quæ ἀπολύτρωσις redemptio & justitia Christi est. 16. Cujus necessitas astruitur. 17. In judicio Dei ad justificandum peccatorem inprimis illa efficax est. 18. Judæorum de hac justificationis causa cum Christo & Apostolis contentio; propriam eidem justitiam surrogantium. 19. Post Christum & Apostolos Judæi in errore propriæ justitiæ induruerunt. 20. Eorundem vestigiis Socitiani insistentes, causam eandem justitiam Christi, à justificatione removentes, planè hanc evertunt. 21. Impurum eorum dogma, quòd homo peccator ex pura misericordia justificetur. 22. Tridentinorum de justificationis causa definitio; quòd meritoria sit passio Christi, at formalis justitia inhærens. 23. Quæ veritatis & mendacii fœda commixtio est. 24. In judicio enim Dei, in quo peccator absolvendus est, justitiæ & charitatis inhærentis donatio momentum nullum habet. 25. Figmentum causæ justificationis formalis duplicis, intrinsecæ & extrinsecæ, seu exemplaris, ut illa sit justitia hominis inhærens, hæc justitia Christi; à Walenburgiis inprimis cusum, discutitur. 26. Bellarmini fucus, quòd merita Christi nobis imputentur, quia ea nobis à Deo donata, ut Deo Patri pro peccatis nostris offerre possemus, abstergitur, & ejusdem fraudulentia detegitur. 27. Error eorundem, quòd homo per justitiam propriam, ut formalem justificationis causam, justificetur, Verbi Divini testimoniis configitur. 28. Et justitiariorum rationibus contrariis occurritur. 29. Sola Christi justitia causa illa est, quæ ad absolvendum peccatorem in Dei judicio valet 30. Sed illa tamen quodammodo nostra esse debet. 31. Nostram justitiam vel donatam, vel propriam, non præcisè propriam Lex requirit. 32 At justitia Christi peccatori in judicio Dei donatur & imputatur. 33. Imputationis vox in hoc argumento attributionem rei alienæ notat. 34. Duplex tamen imputatio est, rei vel alienæ, vel propriæ; & neutra licet infusionem justitiæ significat; prior tamen hujus loci est, & à mercatoribus ad forum Divinum translata est. 35. Imputatio alienæ justitiæ Christi probatur tum ex testimonio Davidis & Pauli, Rom. IV 6.7 8. cujus πα̃ρεξεμπνεία refelluntur. 36. Tum ex Rom. V.12 &c. ubi antithesi primum inter & secundum Adamum instituta, peccati Adami & justitiæ Christi imputatio clarissimè docetur. 37. Tum aliis argumentis. 38. Tridentinorum imputationem justitiæ Christi anathemate ferientium insania perstringitur. 39. Justitiam Christi imputatam, ceu putatitiam, fictitiam, imaginariam & phantasticam nequiter adversarii proscindunt. 40. Argumenta justitiæ Christi imputationi opposita refelluntur. 41. Remonstrantium infida assertio, quod peccatori justitia propria fidei imputetur à Judæorum & Socinianorum impietate parum abest. 42. Argumentis prægnantibus illa refellitur. 43. Limborchii pro eadem objectiones elisæ. 44. Justitia Christi homini peccatori imputata non essentialis Dei, sed Legalis Christi Mediatoris justitia est. 45. Quæ non in passionibus solis, sed in tota Christi obedientia ad mortem usque crucis continuata consistit. 46. Quod pluribus asseritur. 47. Cargii & Piscatoris contrariis argumentis fit satis. 48. Justificationis partes remissio peccatorum & adjudicatio vitæ sunt, quæ beneficia ita distinguenda sunt, ut separari non debeant. 49. Remissio peccatorum eorundem condonatio, & non imputatio est. 50. Non peccatorum expulsio & abolitio, uti perperam Pontificii eam explicant. 51. Qui etiam errore contrario post peccati abolitionem reatum poenæ saltem temporalis ejusdem remanere pertendunt, quod pluribus refellitur. 52. Contraria eorundem argumenta ad limam revocantur. 53. Error hic humanas satisfactiones propriας & alienas non parum satisfactioni Christi iniquas peperit. 54. Quarum vanitas pluribus argumentis convincitur. 55. Et argumentis contrariis nequicquam suffulcitur. 56. Satisfactionum remissionem per indulgentias non religio, sed nundinatio in Ecclesiam invexit. 57. Quæ & Scripturæ & rationi, & propriis adversariorum hypothesibus adversantur. 58. Argumenta pro iisdem mota expenduntur. 59. Pseudo-Politicorum, Herberti, aliorum, remissionem peccatorum sugillantium, eò quòd religionem molliat, deliria perstringuntur. 60. Communes etiam notiones gratuitæ peccatorum remissioni, & Numinis placationi vel ificantur. 61. Pars altera justificationis adjudicatio vitæ, seu hæreditatis est, 62. Justitiam Christi Deus peccatori non sine conditione imputare voluit, quæ nec Legis obedientia perfecta, vel imperfecta; nec satisfactio propria, nec sacrificii alicujus oblatio, nec charitas, nec bona opera, sed sola in Christum fides esse potuit. 63. Fide hominem justificari, omnes consentiunt, sed circa modum, quo illa justificat, gravis dissensus est. Pontificiis enim, ut prima dispositio; Socinianis ut gratuita Dei acceptilatio justificat. 64. Non justificat ut opus, vel ut justitia sive sola, sive cum aliis conjuncta: vel propriè. 65. Sed impropriè & metonymicè, quatenus causæ principalis opus fidei, ut organo tribuitur: 66. Hoc sensu & solam fidem justificare probatur, tum quia in Scriptura ubique fidei justificatio, vita & communio cum Christo tribuitur. 67. Tum quia opera, ceu causæ, à justificatione, vita & communione cum Christo excluduntur, & fides ad justitiam imputari, Rom. IV 4.5. dicitur. 68. Tum quia justificatio & salus ex gratia, non ex operibus datur. 69. Justificationis primæ, ceu gratuitæ, & secundæ, ceu operosæ, figmentum Socinianum rejicitur. 70. Aliis etiam argumentis justificatio ex sola fide, non ut opere, sed ut organo, confirmatur. 71. Particulam exclusivam Sola Scripturæ sensus requirit, & versiones nonnullæ, Patrum inprimis consensus stabiliunt. 72. Argumenta Fidei soli, non ut operi, sed ut organo, justificanti à Pontificiis & Socinianis opposita diluuntur. 73. Remonstrantium objectio, quòd satisfactio Christi efficiat, ut fides nobis ad justitiam imputetur, adeòque illa non relative, sed ut opus justificet, neque habitui animi πιστῷ sui objecti tribui possit, dissolvitur. 74. Finis justificationis Dei gloria & salus atque consolatio electorum est. 75. Justificatio una specie in omnibus; & una numero in singulis est. 76. Indivisum eum actum justificationis primæ & secundæ, & revivisecentiæ peccatorum commentum Scholasticum; nec non opinio eorum, qui peccatorum remissionem revocabilem statuunt, incidunt. 77. Indivisus & perfectus in se justificationis actus ratione sensus divisus & imperfectus est. Alia enim justificationis activa, alia passiva ratio est. 78. Activa indivisa, perfecta, æqualis omni tempore fuit: Passiva divisa, imperfecta & inæqualis est. 79. Justificatio justi definitur, & a justificatione peccatoris distinguitur. 80. Distinctam peccatoris & justi justificationem nexus utriusque, duplex Dei, cui homo subjicitur, judicium, duplex à qua justificandus absolvitur, condemnatio; duplex denique hominis tribunal comprobant. 81. Ex distinctione eadem consensus S. Paulum inter & S. Jaco-
units.tr: The grace of justification is joined to the grace of calling. (1) The teaching on this is of the greatest importance. (2) Some who are neither hot nor cold in religion nevertheless try to belittle it, to no purpose. (3) The meaning of the Latin word justificare is unfolded. (4) The meaning of the original words צדק and δικαιόω is forensic, signifying not the infusion of righteousness but the declaration and absolution of a person as righteous in the judgment of God. (5) Justification is either of the sinner or of the righteous person. Summary of the justification of the sinner. (6) A definition of justification is given and illustrated from Romans 3:24–25. (7) God alone justifies, and he is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. (8) The inner state of the person to be justified is that he is convicted of sin and liable to eternal death. (9) The debt that God requires of the person to be justified is twofold: to pay the penalty deserved by sin, and to render obedience, or universal righteousness; each of these either in himself or in a surety. (10) The outer state of the person to be justified is that, having been chosen for this from eternity, he is called and set apart in time, with Christ as mediator, so that he cannot perish before justification. (11) The cause that moves God within to justify is the grace of God, that is, his gracious favour. (12) The impiety of the Tridentines and Bellarmine, who interpret that grace not as God's kindly favour but as the rectitude of an infused habit of charity. (13) Their subtleties are brought back to the anvil. (14) The cause outside God that moves him to justify the sinner is the dikaiōma, the perfect work or righteousness which the law of God requires from the one who is to be declared righteous. (15) This is the redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις] and the righteousness of Christ. (16) Its necessity is established. (17) In the judgment of God this is above all the effective cause for justifying the sinner. (18) The contention of the Jews with Christ and the Apostles over this cause of justification, when they substituted their own righteousness. (19) After Christ and the Apostles the Jews hardened in the error of their own righteousness. (20) The Socinians, following in their footsteps, remove the same cause, the righteousness of Christ, from justification, and so utterly overthrow it. (21) Their impure dogma, that a sinful man is justified by pure mercy alone. (22) The definition of the Tridentines concerning the cause of justification: that the passion of Christ is meritorious, but that formal righteousness is inherent. (23) This is a foul mixture of truth and falsehood. (24) For in the judgment of God, in which the sinner must be absolved, the bestowing of inherent righteousness and charity has no weight at all. (25) The fiction of a twofold formal cause of justification, intrinsic and extrinsic or exemplary, so that the one is inherent human righteousness and the other the righteousness of Christ, coined chiefly by the Walenburgs, is examined. (26) Bellarmine's pretence that the merits of Christ are imputed to us, because they were given to us by God so that we might offer them to God the Father for our sins, is wiped away, and his deceit is exposed. (27) The error of the same men, that man is justified by his own righteousness as the formal cause of justification, is refuted by the testimonies of the Divine Word. (28) And the arguments of the advocates of works-righteousness are met with contrary arguments. (29) The righteousness of Christ alone is that cause which is effective for absolving the sinner in the judgment of God. (30) Yet nevertheless it must in some way be ours. (31) The law requires our righteousness either as given to us or as our own, not merely as our own. (32) But the righteousness of Christ is given to the sinner and imputed to him in the judgment of God. (33) In this argument the word imputation denotes the ascribing of a thing belonging to another. (34) There is, however, a twofold imputation, of a thing either foreign or one's own; and neither means the infusion of righteousness. The former, however, is the one relevant here, and it has been transferred from merchants to the divine forum. (35) The imputation of the foreign righteousness of Christ is proved both from the testimony of David and Paul, Romans 4:6–8, whose evasions [παρεξεμπνεία] are refuted. (36) And from Romans 5:12 etc., where, with the antithesis first set up between the first and second Adam, the imputation of the sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ is most clearly taught. (37) And by other arguments. (38) The madness of the Tridentines, who anathematise the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, is exposed. (39) The adversaries wickedly tear apart the imputed righteousness of Christ as though it were reckoned, fictitious, imaginary and phantasmal. (40) The arguments opposed to the imputation of Christ's righteousness are refuted. (41) The faithless assertion of the Remonstrants, that the righteousness of faith is imputed to the sinner as his own, differs little from the impiety of the Jews and Socinians. (42) That assertion is refuted by weighty arguments. (43) The objections of Limborch in favour of the same view are overthrown. (44) The righteousness of Christ imputed to the sinful man is not the essential righteousness of God but the legal righteousness of Christ the Mediator. (45) This consists not in his sufferings alone but in the whole obedience of Christ continued unto the death of the cross. (46) This is asserted by many. (47) The arguments of Cargius and Piscator to the contrary are answered. (48) The parts of justification are the remission of sins and the adjudication of life; these benefits are to be distinguished in such a way that they must not be separated. (49) The remission of sins is the pardoning of them, not their imputation. (50) It is not the expulsion and abolition of sins, as the Papists wrongly explain it. (51) Some, too, by the opposite error, maintain that after the abolition of sin the guilt of at least temporal punishment remains; this is refuted by many arguments. (52) Their contrary arguments are brought back to the file. (53) This error has brought forth human satisfactions, both one's own and those of others, which are not a little unfair to the satisfaction of Christ. (54) Their vanity is proved by many arguments. (55) And it is propped up in vain by contrary arguments. (56) The remission of satisfactions through indulgences was introduced into the Church not by religion but by commerce. (57) These things are opposed both to Scripture and to reason, and to the adversaries' own hypotheses. (58) The arguments put forward for them are weighed. (59) The delusions of the pseudo-politicians, of Herbert and others, who disparage the remission of sins on the ground that it softens religion, are exposed. (60) Common notions too, which are favourable to free remission of sins and to appeasing the Deity, are disparaged. (61) The second part of justification is the adjudication of life, or of the inheritance. (62) God was willing to impute the righteousness of Christ to the sinner, but not without a condition; this condition could be neither the perfect or imperfect obedience of the law, nor one's own satisfaction, nor the offering of any sacrifice, nor charity, nor good works, but only faith in Christ. (63) All agree that man is justified by faith, but there is a serious dispute about the manner in which faith justifies. For the Papists hold that it justifies as a first disposition, the Socinians that it justifies as God's free acceptilation. (64) It does not justify as a work, or as righteousness, whether alone or joined with others, properly speaking. (65) But improperly and metonymically, inasmuch as the work of faith, as the instrument, is ascribed to the principal cause. (66) In this sense it is proved that faith alone justifies, both because throughout Scripture justification, life and communion with Christ are ascribed to faith. (67) And because works, as causes, are excluded from justification, life and communion with Christ, and faith is said to be imputed for righteousness, Romans 4:4–5. (68) And because justification and salvation are given by grace, not from works. (69) The Socinian fiction of a first justification, as free, and a second, as laborious, is rejected. (70) By other arguments too, justification by faith alone is confirmed, not as a work but as an instrument. (71) The exclusive particle sola demands the sense of Scripture, and some versions, above all the consensus of the Fathers, establish it. (72) The arguments of the Papists and Socinians against faith alone justifying, not as a work but as an instrument, are dissolved. (73) The objection of the Remonstrants, that the satisfaction of Christ brings it about that faith is imputed to us for righteousness, and so faith justifies not relatively but as a work, and cannot be ascribed to the habit of a mind [πιστῷ] trusting in its object, is dissolved. (74) The end of justification is the glory of God, and the salvation and comfort of the elect. (75) Justification is one in species in all, and one in number in each. (76) The Scholastic fiction of an undivided act of first and second justification and of a revival of sins, and also the opinion of those who hold that the remission of sins is revocable, fall into error. (77) The undivided and perfect act of justification in itself is divided and imperfect in respect of our sense, for the active aspect of justification is one thing and the passive aspect another. (78) The active aspect was undivided, perfect and equal at all times; the passive aspect is divided, imperfect and unequal. (79) The justification of the righteous person is defined and distinguished from the justification of the sinner. (80) The connection between the two, the twofold judgment of God to which man is subject, the twofold condemnation from which the one to be justified is absolved, and finally the twofold tribunal of man, confirm the distinct justification of the sinner and of the righteous person. (81) From this same distinction the agreement between St Paul and St James is most fully set out, and it is shown that the former speaks of the justification of the sinner and the latter of the justification of the righteous person, the former asserting that a man is justified by faith alone, the latter by works. (82) The arguments of those who strive to make faith and works joint causes of justification, as in the case of St James, are met.

units.la: Jacobum; quorum ille ex sola fide, hic ex operibus hominem justificari asserit; plenissimus exponitur; & illum de justificatione peccatoris, hunc de justificatione justi agere ostenditur. 82. Argumentis eorum, qui S. Jacobum fidem & opera causas socias justificationis facere pertendunt, occurritur. 83. Justificatio justi per gradus in hac vita, morte corporis & resurrectione ejusdem proficit. 84. Effecta justificationis per fidem varia sunt, inprimis Adoptio & Libertas spiritualis. Adoptio vel humana vel Divina; eaque vel generalis & integri populi; 85. Vel specialis & singulorum est. 86. Ejus causa Deus Triunus est, variante œconomia personarum. 87. Completitur regeneratio nem ex Deo, cognitionem nominis Dei, & eorum quæ facit; fiduciam ad Deum & jus hæreditatis, etiam gentium. 88. Latè dicta adoptio omnium temporum est; strictè dicta Ecclesiæ N.T. strictissime dicta cœlestis gloriæ. 89. Infidelium & Muhammedanorum adversus adoptionem hanc sanna. 90. Ejusdem fructus. 91. Libertas spiritualis duplex est, vel essentialis, omnium temporum; 92. Vel accidentalis, propria N. T. 93. Regulæ, quibus Libertas Christiana dirigitur, tres sunt. Prima, ne Libertas in libidinem vel licentiam degeneret. 94. Secunda, ut eandem in usu rerum indifferentium fides & charitas dirigat. 95. Tertia, ne prætextus dominationis fiat. 96. Reliqua justificationis effecta conscientiæ tranquillitas, liber ad Deum accessus, filialis timor, nova obedientia, & certitudo gratiæ præsentis & futuræ sunt. 97.
units.tr: Jacob. Of these two, the one asserts that a man is justified by faith alone, the other that he is justified by works. The point is set out most fully, and it is shown that the former speaks of the justification of a sinner and the latter of the justification of a man already just. 82. The arguments of those who contend that St. James makes faith and works joint causes of justification are answered. 83. The justification of the just advances by degrees in this life, through the death of the body and its resurrection. 84. The effects of justification through faith are various, chiefly adoption and spiritual liberty. Adoption is either human or divine, and the divine is either general, of a whole people, 85. or special, of individuals. 86. Its cause is the triune God, the economy of the persons varying. 87. It brings regeneration from God, knowledge of the name of God and of what he does, confidence towards God, and a right of inheritance, even for the Gentiles. 88. Adoption taken broadly belongs to all ages; taken strictly, to the Church of the New Testament; taken most strictly, to heavenly glory. 89. Unbelievers and Muhammadans rail against this adoption. 90. Its fruits. 91. Spiritual liberty is twofold: either essential, belonging to all ages, 92. or accidental, proper to the New Testament. 93. There are three rules by which Christian liberty is directed. The first: that liberty not degenerate into lust or licence. 94. The second: that faith and charity direct its use of indifferent things. 95. The third: that it not become a pretext for domination. 96. The remaining effects of justification are tranquillity of conscience, free access to God, filial fear, new obedience, and assurance of present and future grace. 97.

units.la: I. UM Gratia Vocationis Gratia Justificationis proximè cohæret. Nam quos Deus vocat, eos Christo donat, eóque vult venire ad Christum, imò ad eum trahit & ducit. Quicquid mihi dat Pater, ad me veniet: & venientem ad me non ejiciam foras, Joh. VI.37. Qui sic vocati, tracti & ducti ad Christum veniunt cum eodem junguntur & uniuntur, eum in finem, ut cum eo communionem habeant. Vocat enim Deus εἰς κοινωνίαν τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ in communionem Filii ejus Jesu Christi Domini nostri, 1.Cor.I.9. Quæ communio justitiæ illius seculorum, quam sanguine suo Christus acquisivit, ut quotquot ipsius sunt, non obstante peccato & impotentia sua jus habeant ad vitam æternam, participes reddit. Atque hæc ipsa per fidem in Christum, communionem cum eodem & justitia ejus ad jus vitæ præstantem, justificatio est. Connexionem eandem aurea illa salutis catena confirmat. Nam οὓς ἐκάλεσε, τούτους καὶ ἐδικαίωσε Quos vocavit, eos etiam justificavit, Rom.VIII.30.
units.tr: I. The grace of vocation is closely joined to the grace of justification. For those whom God calls, he gives to Christ, and he wills that they come to Christ, indeed he draws and leads them to him. "All that the Father gives me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out" (John 6:37). Those who are thus called, drawn and led come to Christ, and are joined and united with him, to the end that they may have fellowship with him. For God calls us "into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord" (1 Cor. 1:9) [εἰς κοινωνίαν τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ]. This fellowship makes all who belong to Christ partakers of that righteousness of the ages which Christ acquired by his blood, so that, notwithstanding their sin and their weakness, they have a right to eternal life. And this very thing, namely faith in Christ, fellowship with him and his righteousness as the ground of a right to life, is justification. The golden chain of salvation confirms this connection: "Whom he called, them he also justified" (Rom. 8:30) [οὓς ἐκάλεσε, τούτους καὶ ἐδικαίωσε].

units.la: II. Maximi momenti doctrina sana de justificatione peccatoris coram tribunali Dei est. Nam quod de remissione peccatorum, quæ justificationis pars est, Augustinus in aureolo suo ad Laurentium Enchiridio cap. 64. dixit: Per hanc stat Ecclesia, quæ in terris est. Per hanc non perit, quod perierat, & inventum est: de universa justificatione merito dixeris. Hæc regia cœlestis veritatis arx, hæc acropolis, hoc propugnaculum est, quo cadente, vel ruinam minitante cuncta cadunt, vel subsidunt: stante & florente religio universa stat & floret, atque in tuto consistit. Ideóque Deus ipse Ecclesiæ promisit simul & edixit: בצדקה תכונני In justitia stabilieris & longè aberis ab oppressione, & non timebis, & à contritione, quia non appropinquabit tibi, Esaj. LIV.14. Quisquis igitur de hac salute edoctus salutariter est, eámque tenet, is nec Christum, nec verba fundamenti abnegare, nec gloriam Dei in discrimen adducere, nec conscientiam lethaliter vulnerare, nec errorem ullum ad exitium præcipitantem committere potest. Scopus enim totius Evangelii est, ut justus agnoscatur Deus, καὶ δικαιῶν & justificans, Rom.III.26. & ut homo, qui non potest justitiam suam constituere, Dei justitiam obtineat, ib.X.3. Ad quam inter τὰ πρῶτα prima & principalia quærenda hortatur Christus: Quærite, inquiens, πρῶτον primò Regnum Dei & justitiam ejus, Matth. VI. 33. Quippe Regnum Dei est justitia, pax & gaudium in Spiritu S. Rom. XIV. 17.
units.tr: II. The sound doctrine of the justification of a sinner before the tribunal of God is of the utmost importance. What Augustine said in his little golden book to Laurentius, the Enchiridion, chapter 64, of the forgiveness of sins, which is a part of justification, may rightly be said of the whole of justification: "Through this the Church which is on earth stands; through this what was lost does not perish but is found." This is the royal citadel of heavenly truth, this the acropolis, this the bulwark: when it falls, or threatens to fall, everything falls or sinks; while it stands and flourishes, all religion stands and flourishes and is secure. Therefore God himself promised and declared to the Church: "In righteousness shalt thou be established; thou shalt be far from oppression, for thou shalt not fear; and from terror, for it shall not come near thee" (Isa. 54:14) [בצדקה תכונני]. Whoever, then, has been taught this salvation in a saving way and holds it, can neither deny Christ nor the words of the foundation, nor bring the glory of God into peril, nor wound the conscience mortally, nor commit any error that plunges into ruin. For the aim of the whole Gospel is that God may be recognised as "just, and the justifier" (Rom. 3:26) [καὶ δικαιῶν], and that man, who cannot establish his own righteousness, may obtain the righteousness of God (Rom. 10:3). Christ urges us to seek this first among the first and chief things: "Seek first" (Matt. 6:33) [πρῶτον] "the kingdom of God and his righteousness." For the kingdom of God is righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom. 14:17).

units.la: III. Horribile certè judicium illud, quod Judæos justitiam suam quærentes & Dei justitiæ se non subjicientes, Rom. X. 3. pressit & oppressit, incitare debet, ut justitiam Dei diligenter quæramus, & à Judæis atque Antichristo licet allatas tratam & oppugnatam, illibatam & inconcussam semper retineamus. Neque nos moveat cantus Sirenum, quo nonnulli Pontificios æquè ac Protestantes inter, nec calidi nec frigidi, sed ἀμφότεροι cum blanda lingua & corde duplici loquentes, simplicioribus persuadere laborant, vocum non sententiarum utrosque inter divortium esse. Quibus Antonius de Dominis Archiepiscopus Spalatinus de Repr. lib. VII. 11. prælusit, ajens; dissidia illa, an justificatio in sola remissione peccatorum & imputatione justitiæ, an vero etiam in interna renovatione ponenda sit, metaphysica videri posse, haud absimilia Disputationi Logicæ vel Metaphysicæ potius, in quonam ponenda sit essentialis vel formalis ratio quantitatis, an in mensura, an in divisibilitate, an vero in extensione partium, &c. Cui suffragantes Guilhelmus Forbesius Consid. Pacif. lib. II. 4. Walenburgii de Unit. & Schism. lib. II. 9. & novissime Benignus Bossuetus, Meldensis Præsul, dissensum in hoc argumento verbalem potiùs quàm realem, saltem non fundamentalem esse, sustinuerunt. Quæ microscopii instar sunt, quod oculis illorum admovetur, quibus transitus ex castris Christi ad castra Antichristi sic suadetur, ut hiatum ingentem utrosque inter non observantes, saltum audacter tentent, & sine horrore abyssi, sua ad Ecclesiam Romanam apostasia, ipsimet se præcipitent. Optaremus sanè, vera vel vero affinia esse, quæ illi persuadere nobis connituntur. Sic enim spe firma nos lactarent, futurum, ut ad nos Pontificii accedant, & nobiscum sequantur & communibus labiis Christum adorent; non ut nos illi revocent ad se, ut sequamur nomen huma-
units.tr: III. That dreadful judgment which pressed upon and overwhelmed the Jews, who sought to establish their own righteousness and did not submit themselves to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10:3), ought to stir us to seek the righteousness of God diligently, and, though it has been assailed and attacked by the Jews and by Antichrist, to keep it always unimpaired and unshaken. Nor let us be moved by the siren song of those who, standing between Papists and Protestants, neither hot nor cold but speaking both ways with a smooth tongue and a double heart, labour to persuade the simpler sort that the division between the two sides is only one of words, not of matters. Antonius de Dominis, Archbishop of Spalato, gave them a prelude in his De republica ecclesiastica, book VII, chapter 11, saying that those quarrels, whether justification is to be placed in the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness alone, or also in inward renewal, may seem metaphysical, not unlike the logical or rather metaphysical dispute as to where the essential or formal nature of quantity lies: in measure, in divisibility, or in the extension of parts, and so on. Guilielmus Forbesius, Considerationes modestae et pacificae book II, chapter 4, Walenburch, De unitate et schismate book II, chapter 9, and most recently Benignus Bossuet, Bishop of Meaux, have supported this, holding that the disagreement on this subject is verbal rather than real, or at least not fundamental. These arguments are like a microscope held up to the eyes of those to whom the passage from the camp of Christ to the camp of Antichrist is so recommended that, not noticing the vast gulf between the two, they boldly attempt the leap and, without any horror of the abyss, cast themselves headlong by their own apostasy into the Church of Rome. We would indeed wish that the things they try to persuade us of were true or akin to the truth. For then we would be cheered with a firm hope that the Papists would come over to us, follow with us, and adore Christ with common lips, rather than that they should call us back to themselves, so that we follow a human name and take into our bosom a sink of errors.

units.la: Nepu... nec calidi, nec frigidi sunt. humanum, & colluviem errorum in sinum no-strum recipiamus. Ecclesiæ Evangelicæ dictum putemus: Sic ait Jehova: si convertaris & reducam te, coram me stabis. Et si educas pretiosum à vili, ut os meum. Redeant illi ad te, & tu non revertéris ad illos, Jerem. XV. 19. Simul etiam Pontificii tandem ipsi damnarunt dogmata sua cum doctrina de justificatione gratuita per solam fidem in Christum è diametro pugnantia. Cujusmodi sunt merita operum, fiducia in propria dignitate & congruitate, satisfactionibus humanis, indulgentiis, Purgatorio, sacrificio Missatico, invocatione Sanctorum, idoli sui Maozim, imaginum, Papæ ipsius, suffragiis pro defunctis, aliisque ejusmodi, quibus resectis Papatus inane cadaver est. Sed in rem ipsam descendere, & quantum distent æra lupinis, non in nium verborum tricis, sed rerum notionibus demonstrare animus est.
units.tr: Let us take as spoken to the Evangelical Church these words: "Thus saith the LORD: If thou return, then will I bring thee again, and thou shalt stand before me; and if thou take forth the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth. Let them return unto thee, but return not thou unto them" (Jer. 15:19). At the same time, the Papists themselves have at last condemned their own dogmas, which are diametrically opposed to the doctrine of justification freely through faith alone in Christ. Such are the merits of works, confidence in one's own dignity and congruity, human satisfactions, indulgences, Purgatory, the Mass as sacrifice, the invocation of the saints, their idol Maozim, images, the Pope himself, suffrages for the dead, and other things of this kind; with these cut away, the Papacy is an empty corpse. But my intention is to go down to the matter itself, and to show how far apart the wheat and the tares are, not by the tricks of empty words but by the meanings of things.

units.la: IV. Vox justificandi barbara, non Latio, sed Ecclesiæ, voce ea emphasin vocum originalium exprimere studenti, originem debet. Licet enim analogia sua in voce simplices duas justum & facere resolvatur: sicut sanctificare pariter in duas sanctum & facere resolvatur, tamen ex usu, analogiæ proferendæ non eum significatum habet, ut justificare sit infusa justitia justum facere. Nam quod in verbo sanctificare quidem τὸ facere notat efficientiam, quæ naturam alterat novæ qualitatis introductione, id non τῷ facere, sed subjectæ materiæ imputandum. Sed non raro extra compositionem ipsum simplex facere Latinum, sicut ποιεῖν Græcum apud authores sacros & profanos nullam ejusmodi efficientiam significat. Velut in verbis Christi: Aut poiêsate arborem bonam & fructus bonos &c. Matth. XII. 33. Si dicamus, nos non peccasse, mendacem facimus ipsum, 1. Joh. I. 10. Et par ratio est verborum sanctificare, glorificare, magnificare, in quibus de Deo enuntiatis τῷ facere nullam efficientiam significat. Accedit, quòd peccatorem in judicio justificare, seu justum declarare & absolvere etiam significet justum facere; non justitiam propriam infundendo, sed Christi justitiam imputando. Cui enim Deus illam imputat, eum justum facit. Et de eo quicquid fit, cùm vox justificandi emphasin originalium exprimat, harum significatus, non alius illi aptari debet.
units.tr: IV. The word justificandi is barbarous; it originates not in Latin but in the Church, from one who wished by this word to express the emphasis of the original words. For although by its analogy the word resolves into the two simple parts justum and facere, just as sanctificare resolves into sanctum and facere, yet by usage, the analogy to be carried over does not have that meaning, that justificare is to make just by infused righteousness. For what in the word sanctificare indeed indicates the facere as an efficacy which alters the nature by introducing a new quality, is to be imputed not to the facere but to the matter subjected to it. But often outside composition the simple Latin facere, just as the Greek ποιεῖν in sacred and profane authors, signifies no efficacy of that kind. So in the words of Christ: "Either make [ποιήσατε] the tree good, and its fruit good" (Matt. 12:33), and "If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar" (1 John 1:10). The reasoning is the same for the words sanctificare, glorificare, magnificare, in which, when said of God, facere signifies no efficacy. Moreover, to justify a sinner in judgment, that is, to declare him just and absolve him, also means to make him just; not by infusing one's own righteousness, but by imputing the righteousness of Christ. For he whom God imputes it to, he makes just. And whatever is done about this, since the word justificandi expresses the emphasis of the originals, no other meaning than theirs ought to be fitted to it.

units.la: V. Missa igitur justificandi voce, originales pensitandæ sunt, atque dispiciendum illud, in hoc argumento sensum forensem, quo quis in judicio justus declaratur, & absolvitur: an physicum, seu ex morali & physico compositum, uti loquuntur, quo prius peccator in se motu & mutatione quadam interna in se & inhærenter justus fit, quod posterius primus Thomas Aquinas finxit; habeant. Notissima autem est Hebræa vox צדק in Pihel, הצדיק in Hiphil, quæ nunquam interné justum facere; & in hoc argumento semper justum, & habentem jus petendi vitam in judicio declarare significat. Quod inprimis manifestum ex iis locis est, quibus τῷ הרשיע condemnare, & τῷ הצדיק perversum pronunciare sensu intransitivo opponitur. Ita Moses: הצדיקו את הצדיק יהרשיעו את הרשע Justificant justum & condemnabunt improbum, Deut. XXV. 1. Abominatio sunt צדיק רשע ומרשיע צדיק justificans improbum & condemnans justum, Prov.
units.tr: V. Therefore, setting aside for the moment the word justificandi, the original terms must be weighed, and it must be examined whether in this matter they carry the forensic sense, by which someone is declared just and absolved in judgment, or the physical sense, or a sense compounded of the moral and the physical, as they say, by which the sinner first becomes just in himself through some inner motion and change within himself and inherently, which latter notion Thomas Aquinas devised. The Hebrew word צדק [tsdq] in Piel, and הצדיק [hitsdiq] in Hiphil, are very well known, and they never mean inwardly to make just; in this matter they always mean to declare someone just, and to declare in judgment one who has a right to ask for life. This is clearest from those passages in which הרשיע [harshia], to condemn, is set against הצדיק [hitsdiq], to pronounce perverse, in the intransitive sense. Thus Moses: הצדיקו את הצדיק יהרשיעו את הרשע [hitsdiqu et hatsaddiq yarshiu et harasha] They justify the just and condemn the wicked, Deut. 25:1. It is an abomination: justifying the wicked and condemning the just, Prov.

units.la: XVII. 15. Si justus fuero, os meum ירשיעני condemnabit me; Si integer fuero ויפקשני perversum me pronuntiabunt, Job. IX. 20. Cùm verò certum sit nec הרשיע esse improbum, nec הצדיק perversum facere, quia in judicio nemo improbus vel perversus fit, sed pronuntiatur, & ut talis condemnatur: manifestum etiam est, הצדיק non esse justum facere, sed pronuntiare, definire. Semel Dan. XII. 3. מצדיקי הרבים justificantes multos significat justificationi multorum operam dantes, seu ad justificationem perducentes. Cum ל Dativi signo construct um, justificationem alicui conciliare; notat. Cognitione sui צדיק עבדי לרבים justificabit, seu justificationem conciliabit justus servus meus multis, Esaj. LIII. 11, sensu prægnante; quasi diceretur: יעשה להם הצדקה fiet, procurabitur iis justitia, seu δικαίωμα opus, quod jus petendi vitam conciliat. Hebrææ voci Græca δικαιοσύνη respondet. Cujus cùm multiplex sit notio, nulla tamen est justum inhærenter facientis, & cùm Hebrææ voci respondet, perpetua est justum pronuntiantis. Si qui tamen Theologi sunt, qui in voce hac δικαιοσύνη donationem justitiæ inhærentis agnoscunt; illorum sententia nec orthodoxæ sententiæ obest, nec adversanti patrocinatur, quia illi ipsi fatentur, sensum eum à præsenti negotio alienum esse, & commodiora loca occurrere, in quibus forensis significatus manifestior fit. Et qui in explicatione locorum, Rom. VIII. 30; Tit. III. 7, seorsim sentit Beza, non tamen ibi verbum δικαιοῦν de sola donatione justitiæ inhærentis, sed longè de eo omni, quod per Christum, sive per imputationem, sive per Spiritus S. efficaciam, ut simus ἄρτιοι perfecti in ipso, accipimus, intelligit. De loco Apoc. XXI. 11. infra. Etiam sapientia à filiis justificata, hoc est, agnita & celebrata, Matth. XI. 19. Luc. VII. 35. Christus in spiritu justificatus, hoc est, perfectus Servator virtute Divinitatis per obedientiam Legis, quam pro nobis spopondit, omnem impletam, declaratus, 1. Tim. III. 16. mortuus δικαιωθεὶς ἀπὸ ἁμαρτίας justificatus à peccato, seu liberatus est, quia per mortem corporis lucta cum peccato cessat, introitus in gloriam sequitur, & justificatio per fidem plenissimè demonstratur, Rom. VI. 7. Denique Abrahamus ex operibus δικαιωθη justificatus est, & nos ex operibus justificamur, quia opera declarant & demonstrant justificationem per fidem, Jac. II. 21. 24. Hæc testimonia licet de peccatoris coram tribunali Dei justificatione proprie non loquantur, neque adeò in iis vox δικαιοσύνη argumentum præsens spectet, tamen nec significationem justitiæ inhærentis acceptæ habent, & celebrationem vel declarationem & demonstrationem justitiæ notat. Atque ita vox δικαιοσύνη vel non alium, vel non crebriorem & genuinum magis sensum, quam forensem & judiciale sustinet, & constanter fere servat analogiam judicii, sive formandi à priori ex causis rei, sive indicandi & demonstrandi à posteriori ex effectibus & signis consequentibus, quod in hoc inprimis argumento etiam voces cognatæ justificationis, cujusmodi sunt judex, ira Dei, judicium, accusator, reus, reatus, testis, debitor, advocatus, δικαίωμα, absolutio, & phrases æquipollentes, vocari in judicium, non judicari, fidem imputari ad justitiam, tegere, remittere peccata, &c. manifestè forenses omnes liquidò tenuntur. VI. Enu-
units.tr: XVII. 15. If I am just, my mouth will condemn me; if I am whole, they will pronounce me perverse, Job 9:20. But since it is certain that neither הרשיע [harshia] means to make wicked, nor הצדיק [hitsdiq] to make perverse, because in judgment no one is made wicked or perverse, but is pronounced such and condemned as such, it is also clear that הצדיק does not mean to make just, but to pronounce, to define. Once, in Dan. 12:3, מצדיקי הרבים [matsdiqe harabbim] means justifying many, that is, those who labour for the justification of many, or who bring them to justification. With the dative sign ל, it means to bring about justification for someone. By his knowledge my righteous servant will justify, that is, my just servant will bring about justification for many, Isa. 53:11, in a pregnant sense, as if one said: יעשה להם הצדקה [yaaseh lahem hatsdaqah] it will be done, justice will be procured for them; that is, δικαίωμα, the deed which secures the right to ask for life. The Greek δικαιοσύνη corresponds to the Hebrew word. Although its meaning is manifold, none of its senses is making someone inherently just, and where it corresponds to the Hebrew word it is always declaring someone just. If there are some theologians who in this word δικαιοσύνη recognise the bestowal of inherent righteousness, their view neither harms the orthodox position nor supports the opposing one, for they themselves admit that this sense is foreign to the present business, and that more suitable passages occur in which the forensic meaning is clearer. Beza, who thinks otherwise in explaining Rom. 8:30 and Tit. 3:7, does not take the verb δικαιοῦν there to mean merely the donation of inherent righteousness, but understands it of everything we receive through Christ, whether by imputation or by the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, so that we may be ἄρτιοι, perfect, in him. On the passage Rev. 21:11, see below. Likewise wisdom is justified by her children, that is, acknowledged and celebrated, Matt. 11:19; Luke 7:35. Christ was justified in the Spirit, that is, declared the perfect Saviour by the power of the Godhead, through his obedience to the Law, which he undertook for us and fulfilled in full, 1 Tim. 3:16. He was dead, justified from sin, δικαιωθεὶς ἀπὸ ἁμαρτίας, that is, freed, because by the death of the body the struggle with sin ceases, entrance into glory follows, and justification by faith is most fully displayed, Rom. 6:7. Finally, Abraham was justified by works, ex operibus δικαιωθη, and we are justified by works, because works declare and demonstrate justification by faith, James 2:21, 24. Although these testimonies do not speak properly of the justification of a sinner before the tribunal of God, and the word δικαιοσύνη in them does not concern the present subject, nevertheless they do not carry the sense of inherent righteousness received, but denote celebration, or declaration and demonstration, of righteousness. And so the word δικαιοσύνη bears either no other sense, or no more frequent and genuine sense, than the forensic and judicial one, and it nearly always keeps the analogy of judgment, whether forming a judgment à priori from the causes of the thing, or indicating and demonstrating à posteriori from consequent effects and signs. In this matter especially, the cognate words of justification, such as judge, wrath of God, judgment, accuser, defendant, guilt, witness, debtor, advocate, δικαίωμα, absolution, and equivalent phrases, to be called into judgment, not to be judged, faith to be imputed for righteousness, to cover, to remit sins, etc., are all clearly held to be forensic. VI. Enu-

units.la: {y} Vox justificandi Latinæ notio erolvitur.
units.tr: {y} The meaning of the Latin word justificandi is unfolded.

units.la: VI. Enucleatæ sic voces in ipsam rei perceptionem nos provehunt. Nam duplex quidem justificatio Evangelica, de qua in præsentiarum agimus, est, una Peccatoris, altera Justi. Prioris illius summa est; Hominem in Adamo peccatorem & spiritualiter mortuum, coram tribunali Dei convictum esse impietatis, & propter eandem reum esse mortem æternam debendi. In judicio autem hoc Deum solum nos justificare non propter nos, vel justitiam nostram, vel rectitudinem ullam, quam in nobis intueatur; quia in peccatore, impio, & in peccatis mortuo talem nullam intueri potest, sed propter solum Christum, qui pro peccatore in æterno Dei consilio spopondit, & in tempore vadimonium obiit, pro peccatore mortuus est, omnem Legis justitiam implevit, atque sic & ipse in Dei judicio ab omni debito absolutus plenissime justificatus est. Cum vero Lex ab homine peccatore justitiam exigat, atque homo justitiam Legis non habens in Dei judicio consistere non posset, sed condemnetur, justitiam Christi eum habere, atque sic eum cum Christo & ejus justitia uniri oportere docemus.
units.tr: VI. Once the words have been unfolded in this way, they lead us to the very perception of the matter. For the Evangelical justification, which we are now discussing, is indeed twofold: one of the sinner, the other of the just. The sum of the former is this: man, a sinner in Adam and spiritually dead, is convicted before the tribunal of God of impiety, and on account of it is liable to eternal death. In this judgment God alone justifies us, not on account of us, or our righteousness, or any uprightness which he might see in us, since in a sinner, an impious man dead in sins, he can see no such thing, but on account of Christ alone, who in the eternal counsel of God stood surety for the sinner, and in time underwent the surety-bond, died for the sinner, and fulfilled all the righteousness of the Law; and so he himself, having been absolved in the judgment of God from every debt, was most fully justified. But since the Law demands righteousness from the sinful man, and a man without the righteousness of the Law could not stand in God's judgment but would be condemned, we teach that he must have the righteousness of Christ, and so must be united with Christ and his righteousness.

units.la: Tum autem eam homo habet, & cum Christo atque justitia ejus unitur, non cum justitia hæc ei implantata inhæret, quod impossibile est; sed cum Deus in judicio eam homini donat, applicat & imputat judiciali actu, ut ejus & effectuum ejus, qui peccatorum remissio, & jus petendi vitam cœlestem sunt, perinde particeps sit, atque si eam ipse præstitisset; quæ omnis imputationis judicialis ratio est. Sed justitiam sic donatam & imputatam homo accepit, apprehendat & sibi applicet oportet.
units.tr: But man has this righteousness, and is united with Christ and his righteousness, not by its being implanted in him and inhering in him, which is impossible, but when God in judgment gives it to man, applies it and imputes it by a judicial act, so that he may share in it and in its effects, which are the remission of sins and the right to ask for heavenly life, just as if he had performed it himself. This is the whole account of judicial imputation. But man must accept the righteousness so given and imputed, and apprehend it and apply it to himself.

units.la: Hic ergo docemus, Deum nobis communicare Spiritum suum, qui filiorum Dei corda, cum vocantur, & hora salutis eorum adest.
units.tr: Here, therefore, we teach that God communicates to us his Spirit, who is present in the hearts of the sons of God when they are called, and at the hour of their salvation.

units.la: VII. Paucis igitur ut rem definiamus: Justificatio peccatoris est actus judicialis, quo Deus judex hominem peccati convictum & æternæ mortis reum, sed ab æterno tamen electum, & in tempore vocatum propter Christi Sponsoris vadimonium in tempore obeuntis, & à debito, quod in se libens volensque suscepit, in Dei etiam judicio perfectè absoluti & justificati obedientiam & justitiam gratis homini donatam & imputatam, atque sola fide in eundem apprehensam & applicatam, justum declarat, à peccato ejusque condemnatione absolvit, & æternæ vitæ compotem reddit, ad gloriam justitiæ & misericordiæ ejus, & salutem æternam hominis.
units.tr: VII. To define the matter briefly: Justification of a sinner is a judicial act by which God, as judge, declares just a man convicted of sin and liable to eternal death, yet elected from eternity and called in time, on account of the surety-bond of Christ the Sponsor, who underwent it in time, and on account of the debt which he freely and willingly took upon himself; the obedience and righteousness of Christ, given freely to man and imputed to him, and apprehended and applied to him by faith alone, perfectly absolving and justifying him also in the judgment of God, absolves him from sin and its condemnation, and makes him a partaker of eternal life, to the glory of God's justice and mercy and the eternal salvation of man.

units.la: Nihil hæc definitio habet, quod non contineatur in verbis S. Pauli, dicentis: Justificamur gratis gratia ejus, per redemptionem quæ est in Christo Jesu, quem Deus proposuit propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ejus, ad demonstrationem justitiæ ejus, propter remissionem peccatorum ante factorum, in tolerantia Dei ad ostensionem justitiæ suæ in præsenti tempore, ut sit ipse justus & justificans eum, qui est ex fide Jesu Christi, Rom. III. 24–27. nis illius scopus unicus, ἔνδειξις δικαιοσύνης demonstratio justitiæ, ut Deus demonstretur justus & justificans eum, qui est ex fide Jesu, v.2 r.26. Hæc omnia paucis idem etiam Apostolus alibi constrinxit, dicens: Η χάρις βασιλεύει διὰ δικαιοσύνης εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν. Gratia regnat per Justitiam in vitam æternam per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, ibid. V.21. Sed hæc paucis sic definita & asserta deinceps uberius demonstranda, & adversus errores quosvis fortiter asserenda sunt.
units.tr: Nothing in this definition is not contained in the words of St Paul, who says: We are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness, because of the remission of previously committed sins, in the forbearance of God, to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he may be just and justifier of him who is of the faith of Jesus, Rom. III. 24–27. The sole scope of that passage is the demonstration of righteousness, ἔνδειξις δικαιοσύνης, so that God may be shown just and justifier of him who is of the faith of Jesus, v. 26. The same Apostle summed up all these things briefly elsewhere, saying: Η χάρις βασιλεύει διὰ δικαιοσύνης εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν. Grace reigns through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord, ibid. V. 21. But these matters, thus briefly defined and asserted, are to be demonstrated more fully afterwards, and strongly maintained against whatever errors arise.

units.la: VIII. Ante omnia Θεὸς ὁ δικαιῶν Deus est, qui justificat, Rom.VIII.33. Ille enim Judex totius terræ est, Genes.XVIII.25. κρίνων πάντων Judex universorum, Hebr.XII.23. Ei ταῖς Soli peccatur, Psal.LI.6. Quis potest remittere peccata, εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ Θεὸς nisi solus Deus? Marc.II.7. Sic enim ille de se: Ego, ego deleo defectiones vestras, & peccatorum vestrorum non recordor amplius, Isaj.XLIII.25. Ille λογίζεται δικαιοσύνην imputat justitiam absque operibus, Rom.IV.6. Eius vero solius est vitæ & mortis judicium administrare, qui natura supremus & ἀνυπεύθυνος mundi judex est: ejus de Lege impleta vel violata judicare, qui legis author est: ejus peccatum remittere, adversus quem peccatum est: ejus reum absolvere, cujus ille justa constitutione reatum incurrit. Sed sic tamen justificationis opus commune personæ omnibus Deitatis est, quia justificamur non tantum à Patre, sed etiam in nomine Jesu Christi, & in Spiritu Dei nostri, 1.Cor. VI.11. ut tamen in œconomia salutis singulæ privum aliquid & singulare conferant. Nam Deus Pater κατ' ἐξοχὴν justificat, ut Judex velut pro tribunali sedens. Nam Deus (Pater velut Judex) erat in Christo mundum sibi reconcilians, non imputans ei peccata, judex factus ex condemnante in Christo absolvens, 2.Cor.V.19. Filius justificat ut sponsor & advocatus. Quis est qui condemnaret? Christus pro nobis mortuus, magis etiam suscitatus est, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, & pro nobis intercedit, Rom.VIII.34. Absque Christo pro nobis mortuo, suscitato, ad dextram Dei sedente, & pro nobis intercedente fuisset, nec accusatio, nec condemnatio cessare, nec Deus justificare potuisset. Sed condemnatio tolli debuit tum morte Christi, quia peccata nostra in eum conjecta sunt, Esaj.LIII.6.8.12. & ipsum pro nobis peccatum Deus fecit, ut essemus justitia Dei in ipso, 2.Cor.V.21. tum ejus resurrectione, quæ quasi vox Dei est justificantis eos, pro quibus mortuus est, & qui in ipso reperiuntur: tum ejus sessione ad dextram Dei, quia sedens ad dextram Dei demonstratus est Rex & judex, sub sceptra sua populum colligens, & expectans, donec omnia ponantur sub pedibus ejus; neque adeo condemnari possunt, in quibus ille regnat, & pro quibus mortuus est, cum aliâs sit judex, & ipse potestatem in omnia habeat: tum intercessione ejusdem pro nobis, quia in cœlum intravit, ut se ostenderet Deo, & pro nobis intercederet, Hebr.IX.24. X.12.13. Denique Spiritus S. justificat, quia Cancellarii instar absolutionis diplomata & sententiam Dei in conscientia & cordibus electorum pronuntiat & intimat, eandem σφραγίδα objignat, Ephes.I.13. & de ea, ceu arrhabo datus, cerimillimos reddit.
units.tr: VIII. Above all, God is he who justifies, who justifies, Rom. VIII.33. For he is the Judge of all the earth, Gen. XVIII.25, judging all things [κρίνων πάντων], the Judge of all, Heb. XII.23. Sin is committed against him alone, Ps. LI.6. Who can forgive sins but God alone? Mark II.7. For thus he speaks of himself: I, I am he who blots out your transgressions, and I will remember your sins no more, Isa. XLIII.25. He imputes righteousness without works [λογίζεται δικαιοσύνην], Rom. IV.6. It is his alone to administer the judgment of life and death, since he is by nature the supreme and unaccountable judge of the world; his alone to judge whether the Law has been fulfilled or violated, since he is its author; his alone to forgive the sin, since it is committed against him; his alone to absolve the guilty, whose guilt he has incurred by a just constitution. Yet the work of justification is common to all the persons of the Deity, since we are justified not only by the Father but also in the name of Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God, 1 Cor. VI.11; still, in the economy of salvation each person contributes something peculiar and singular. For God the Father justifies preeminently [κατ' ἐξοχήν], as Judge sitting as it were on the tribunal. For God (the Father as Judge) was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their sins to them, having become judge, from condemning to absolving, in Christ, 2 Cor. V.19. The Son justifies as surety and advocate. Who is he that condemns? It is Christ who died for us, yes rather who was raised, who is also at the right hand of God and makes intercession for us, Rom. VIII.34. Without Christ having died for us, been raised, sat at the right hand of God, and interceded for us, neither accusation nor condemnation could have ceased, nor could God have justified. But condemnation had to be removed: by the death of Christ, since our sins were laid upon him, Isa. LIII.6.8.12, and God made him sin for us, so that we might be the righteousness of God in him, 2 Cor. V.21; by his resurrection, which is as it were the voice of God justifying those for whom he died and who are found in him; by his sitting at the right hand of God, because by sitting at the right hand of God he is shown to be King and Judge, gathering the people under his scepter and waiting until all things are put under his feet; nor can those be condemned over whom he reigns and for whom he died, since he is otherwise the judge and has power over all things; by his intercession for us, since he entered heaven to appear before God and intercede for us, Heb. IX.24, X.12.13. Finally, the Holy Spirit justifies, because, like a chancellor, he pronounces and intimates the decree of God's absolution in the consciences and hearts of the elect, sets his seal [σφραγίδα] to the same, Eph. I.13, and, given as an earnest of it, makes them certain of it.

units.la: IX. Justificandus homo peccati convictus, & æterna mortis reus, sed ab æterno tamen electus, & in tempore vocatus est. Duplex igitur hominis justificandi status, internus & externus est. Internus, secundum qualitatem internam & priam est, quod peccati convictus & æternæ mortis reus est; Deus enim justificans δικαιοῦ τὸν ἀσεβῆ justificat impium, Rom.IV.5. Omnes peccarunt & destituuntur gloria Dei; δικαιούμενοι δωρεάν proin justificantur gratis, &c. ibid.III.23.24. Non enim sani opus habent medico, ἀλλὰ κακῶς ἔχοντες sed male habentes: Non veni vocare justos, sed peccatores, &c. Matth.IX.12.13. Nam justificatio peccati remissio, & vitæ per justitiam Christi adjudicatio est. Justificandus igitur in se ipso, & peccator & mortis æternæ reus est. In Judicio enim hoc omne os clauditur, & totus mundus, velut ὑπόδικος obnoxius Deo objicitur, Rom.III.19. Et infantes quidem non peccant ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς παραβάσεως 'Αδὰμ ad similitudinem, seu imitatione transgressionis Adami, ibid.V.14. Nihilominus natura filii iræ sunt, sicut omnes homines, Ephes.II.3. Adulti alii ante regenerationem ἀπλαβεῖς virtuosi sunt, quales in Judæismo fuerunt S.Paulo similes, καὶ δικαιοσύνην τῶν ἐν νόμῳ ἀμεμπτοι juxta justitiam externam quæ in Lege est, inculpati, Phil.III.6. & in Christianismo sunt non regeniti quidem, sed tamen sanctioris disciplinæ jugo, & Divinæ providentiæ fræno cohibiti à scandalis & crassioribus mundi inquinamentis abstinent: alii facinorosi & scandalosi, quales Corinthios nonnullos Apostolus describit, 1.Cor.VI.9.10.11. Neque tamen vel illos, licet non æquè gravem damnationem meritos, sua illa externa probitas ad justificationem provehit, juxta illa Apostoli: Οὐδὲν σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ nullius rei (criminis gravioris, scandali) mihi ipsi conscius sum, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐν τούτῳ δεδικαίωμαι, sed non in hoc justificatus sum, ib. IV.4. vel hi peccatorum suorum numero & pondere justificationi obicem ponunt; exceptis solis, qui in Spiritum S. peccant. Quin paradoxa carnis judicio assertione, magis justificantur à Deo peccatis onusti publicani, quàm exquisitissimi Pharisæi; ante regenerationem Paulo similes, Luc.XVIII.10–14. & præveniuntur tales in Regno Dei ab ipsis publicanis & meretricibus, Matth.XXI.31. ut ita veritas Dei in hominum mendacio cumulatiori fit abundantior, ad gloriam ejus, Rom.III.7.
units.tr: IX. The man to be justified is convicted of sin, guilty of eternal death, yet elected from eternity, and called in time. The status of the man to be justified is therefore twofold, internal and external. The internal status, according to his internal and proper quality, is that he is convicted of sin and guilty of eternal death; for God, justifying, justifies the ungodly [δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἀσεβῆ], Rom. IV.5. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God; being justified freely [δικαιούμενοι δωρεάν], they are justified freely, etc., ibid. III.23.24. For those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are badly off [ἀλλὰ κακῶς ἔχοντες]: I came not to call the righteous but sinners, etc., Matt. IX.12.13. For justification is the remission of sin and the adjudication of life through the righteousness of Christ. The one to be justified is therefore, in himself, both a sinner and guilty of eternal death. For in this judgment every mouth is stopped, and the whole world is set before God as liable [ὑπόδικος], Rom. III.19. Infants indeed do not sin after the likeness [ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι] of the transgression of Adam, ibid. V.14, that is, by imitation; nevertheless they are by nature children of wrath, as all men are, Eph. II.3. Other adults before regeneration are virtuous, such as in Judaism were like St. Paul, and as to the righteousness which is in the Law [καὶ δικαιοσύνην τῶν ἐν νόμῳ] blameless, Phil. III.6; and in Christianity there are those not yet regenerate but restrained by the yoke of stricter discipline and the bridle of divine providence, who abstain from scandals and the grosser pollutions of the world. Others are wicked and scandalous, such as the Apostle describes in some Corinthians, 1 Cor. VI.9.10.11. Yet neither those, though they have not merited so grave a condemnation, does that outward uprightness advance to justification, according to the Apostle's words: I am conscious of nothing against myself [Οὐδὲν σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ] (of no grave crime or scandal), but I am not justified by this [ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐν τούτῳ δεδικαίωμαι], 1 Cor. IV.4. Nor do these put an obstacle to justification by the number and weight of their sins, except only those who sin against the Holy Spirit. Indeed, though it seems a paradox to the judgment of the flesh, sinful tax collectors are more justified by God than the most exquisite Pharisees, who before regeneration were like Paul, Luke XVIII.10–14; and such people are anticipated in the Kingdom of God by the tax collectors and harlots themselves, Matt. XXI.31, so that thus the truth of God, amid the greater lie of men, becomes more abundant, to his glory, Rom. III.7.

units.la: X. Facit huc debitum, quod juxta Legis δικαιώμα, Deus, ut creditor, ab homine peccatore justificando exigit. Quod in justificatione Evangelica, secus atque in Legali, geminum est, obligatio puta tum ad pœnam, quæ in hac non obtinuit, & partim in justitia Dei naturali, qua Deus ut Zelotes peccatum odit: partim in nexu fœderis operum violati fundatur: tum ad obedientiam, seu justitiam universalem personæ, quæ in utraque justificatione obtinet, & tum in creationis beneficio absolutè; tum in promissione vitæ æternæ melioris consequendæ, ex hypothesi fundatur: Obligatio prior ad pœnam tantum abest, ut posteriorem ad obedientiam extinguat, ut magis cumulet, quia impossibile est, ut obedientia Legis à creatura auferatur, atque Deus illam debendi ream non habeat, vel exlegem patiatur. Nam etiam qui partem non habet in gratia Christi, & legis nexu ad pœnam ligatus est, tamen ὀφειλέτης ἐστὶν ὅλον τὸν νόμον τηρῆσαι debitor est servandi totam Legem, Gal.
units.tr: X. Here belongs the debt, which God, as creditor, demands of the sinful man to be justified according to the righteous ordinance [δικαίωμα] of the Law. In evangelical justification, unlike legal justification, this debt is twofold: an obligation indeed to punishment, which in this justification does not hold, and which rests partly on God's natural justice, by which God as a zealot hates sin, and partly on the bond of the violated covenant of works; and an obligation to obedience, or the universal righteousness of the person, which holds in both justifications, and rests absolutely on the benefit of creation, and hypothetically on the promise of the eternal life to be obtained later. The former obligation to punishment is so far from extinguishing the latter obligation to obedience that it rather adds to it, because it is impossible that obedience to the Law be taken away from the creature, and that God should not have it as a debt or allow it to be lawless. For even one who has no part in the grace of Christ, and is bound to punishment by the bond of the Law, is nonetheless a debtor to keep the whole Law [ὀφειλέτης ἐστὶν ὅλον τὸν νόμον τηρῆσαι], Gal.

units.la: kk
units.tr: kk

units.la: Gal.V. 3. Neque tamen solutio poenae exigitur ut justitia, vel, ab obedientia & justitia illa universali separata, in se justitiam, vel partem justitiae, quae simpliciter justum facere posset, sed tantum absolutionem a reatu, & restitutionem in integrum ad inhoandam postliminio justitiam dicit. Nam poenam pati non est opus bonum a Lege praeceptum facere, sed est opus bonum non factum fuere. Neque ulla in passionibus proprie justitia est, licet illae ceu cos justitiam & patientiam in demonstratione activa charitatis erga Deum & proximum acuere possit, uti in Christo acuerunt. Rectius ergo justitia passiva dicitur activa, passionibus explorata & ex illis eluctans. Quibus animadversis ruit πεῶτον illud ψεύδῳ, quod justitia perfecta peccatori ad justificationem necessaria in sola peccatorum remissione consistat; & non activa, sed passiva duntaxat justitia Christi peccatori imputetur, quod justificationi Evangelicae evertendae est.
units.tr: Gal. V.3. Nor, however, is the payment of punishment demanded as righteousness, or, separated from that obedience and universal righteousness, as righteousness in itself or a part of righteousness which could simply make a man just; it signifies only absolution from guilt and restoration to integrity, so that righteousness may be resumed by postliminy. For to suffer punishment is not the performance of a good work commanded by the Law, but is a good work that has not been done. Nor is there any proper righteousness in sufferings, although they can sharpen righteousness and patience in the active demonstration of love towards God and neighbour, as they did in Christ. Thus passive righteousness is more rightly called active, being tested by sufferings and struggling out of them. With these points observed, that first falsehood [πρῶτον ψεῦδος] falls, namely that the perfect righteousness necessary for the sinner's justification consists in the remission of sins alone, and that not active but only passive righteousness of Christ is imputed to the sinner; this is destructive of evangelical justification.

units.la: XI. Status externus peccatoris justificandi est, quod ab aeterno ad id electus est, & in tempore vocatur.
units.tr: XI. The external state of the person to be justified is that he was chosen for this from eternity and is called in time.

units.la: Nam quos Deus praecognovit, illos praedestinavit, quos praedestinavit, illos vocavit, quos vocavit, illos justificavit, Rom.VIII. 29.30. Fit autem vocatio justificationem illam praecedens separatio illa arcana, qua Deus quos praecognovit, in tempore ἀφορίζει separat, hoc est, oculo providentiae suae discernit, ut ita firmum stet fundamentum Dei habens sigillum hoc: Novit Dominus, qui sui sunt. 2.Tim.II.19. Quo sigillo quicunque in mundum veniunt, in tempore justificandi, ita obsignati sunt, ut non pollint cum mundo perire, vel in peccatis suis mori, quamvis non ab initio sic κεχωρισμένοι separati characterem impressum in anima habeant, quo ante justificationem a reliquo mundo differant, vel ab hominibus discerni possint.
