Ita S. Paulus licet demum adultus in Christo esse incepit, Rom.XVI.7. tamen se ab utero matris suae separatum esse dixit, Gal.I.15.16. Et ovium nomine Christo veniunt, qui nondum ad ovile adducti, sed demum adducendi sunt, Joh.X.16. Quin & de credituris, non credentibus Corinthiis Dominus ad S.Paulum dixit: Quoniam est mihi populus multus in hac urbe, Act.XVIII.10. Denique omnes a Christo convertendi & justificandi πρόβατα ἀπολωλότα oves perditae, Matth. XV.24. dicuntur, relicto reliquis perituris nomine filiorum perditionis, Joh.XVII.12. Christus enim inde ab utero matris est sequester salutis justificandorum, quamvis nondum ipsis reve-latae, sed demum opportuno tempore cum regeneratione revelandae; in quo justificationis ipsorum thesaurus ἀποκεκρυμμένος recónditus, ipsisque, ut depositum singulis erogandum, servatus est: ex quo ipse consummata obedientia sua, justificatus, & sponsor ipsis donatus est; excitatus videlicet propter δικαίωσιν justificationem nostri, obedientia sua consummata quaesitam, Rom.IV.25.
units.tr: For those whom God foreknew, he also predestined; those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified (Rom. 8:29-30). The call is preceded by that hidden separation, by which God, in time, separates [ἀφορίζει] those whom he foreknew, that is, he distinguishes them by the eye of his providence. So the foundation of God stands firm, bearing this seal: "The Lord knows those who are his" (2 Tim. 2:19). Everyone who comes into the world with this seal is sealed so that they cannot perish with the world or die in their sins, even though they are not from the beginning set apart [κεχωρισμένοι] in this way and do not bear in the soul an impressed mark by which they differ from the rest of the world, or can be distinguished by men before their justification. Thus Paul, although he began to be in Christ only as an adult (Rom. 16:7), nevertheless said that he had been set apart from his mother's womb (Gal. 1:15-16). And those who have not yet been brought to the fold, but are yet to be brought in, come to Christ under the name of sheep (John 10:16). Indeed, the Lord said to Paul concerning the Corinthians, who were not yet believing: "I have many people in this city" (Acts 18:10). Finally, all who are to be converted and justified by Christ are called lost sheep [πρόβατα ἀπολωλότα] (Matt. 15:24), leaving the rest, who are to perish, under the name of sons of perdition (John 17:12). For Christ, from his mother's womb, is the mediator of salvation for those who are to be justified, although it is not yet revealed to them, but is to be revealed at the proper time with regeneration. In him the treasure of their justification [δικαίωσιν] lies hidden [ἀποκεκρυμμένος] and is kept, to be dispensed to each as a deposit. From it he himself, having completed his obedience, was justified and was given to them as surety. He was raised, that is, for our justification, which was obtained by his completed obedience (Rom. 4:25).

units.la: XII. Causa Deum intus ad justificandum percatorem movens ejusdem gratia, non ulla justificandi dignitas est.
units.tr: XII. The cause that moves God within to justify the sinner is his grace; there is no worthiness in the one being justified.

units.la: Nam justificamur δωρεάν τῇ αὐτοῦ χάριτι gratis ipsius gratia, Rom.III. 24. ubi δωρεάν, seu חנם Esaj.LV.1.2. nil nisi causam promerentem, opus vel dignitatem & meritum hominis, quod sit causa juris petendi
units.tr: For we are justified freely by his grace [δωρεάν τῇ αὐτοῦ χάριτι], Rom. 3.24, where freely [δωρεάν], or in Hebrew [חנם] (Isa. 55.1, 2), excludes any cause that would earn the justification: any work, dignity or merit of man, which would be the ground for claiming a right to life.

units.la: vitam, negat, & δικαιοῦσθαι μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ justificari non operantem, Rom.IV.5. insinuat. Neque enim Deus in homine justificando invenit id, quod lex postulat faciendum, ut quis in eo, quod fecerit, vivat: imo nec quicquam in eo invenit boni, quia justificat τὸν ἀσεβῆ impium, ibid. Neque ullo officio compensatur donum justitiae, ut sit instar illius contractus: Do ut des. Nunquid pro merito retribuitis mihi? Joel.III.4. Licet enim justificemur fide, nihilominus gratis justificamur, quia fides non est proprie dicta conditio, vel causa juris petendi mercedem; imo ipsa quoque Dei donum est; ut qui gratis justificari dicuntur, donum fidei, ut justi sint, accipere intelligantur. Neque tamen vox δωρεάν meritum & satisfactionem Christi excludit, quia non excludit ἀντλύτρωσιν, sed tantum causam, quae in nobis sit, promerentem. At χάρις gratia illa, qua justificari dicimur, veram justificationis in Deo causam ponit, quae ejus benevolentia, amor & misericordia est. Ita cum justitia Dei ejusdem gratia conjungitur. Propter justitiam tuam educes animam meam ex angustia; & propter gratiam tuam disperdes inimicos meos, Psalm. CXLIII.11.12. Et passim salus peccatoris gratiae & misericordiae Dei accepta refertur, utpote quae fons & irrigua illa icaturigo est, ex qua omnes salutarium beneficiorum rivi ad nos manant. In specie autem Justificatio a χάρις gratia & dilectione Dei provenit, quia justitia, propter quam justi in Dei judicio pronuntiamur, ex solo Dei erga homines amore aeterno admissa, decreta & definita, in tempore credentibus donatur & sic donata in judicio Dei, ceu δικαίωμα & νόμος ab hominibus acceptatur. Deus enim non fuit debitor nisi ex pacto gratuito admittendi Sponsorem, nos ei inserendi & in eodem nos justificandi. Totum hoc χάρις gratia & σωτηρίας donationis in gratia, Rom.V.15. est, & φιλανθρωπίαν amorem erga genus humanum spirat.
units.tr: It denies that, and implies that one is justified without working [δικαιοῦσθαι μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ], Rom. 4.5. For God, in justifying a man, does not find what the law requires to be done, so that the man might live by what he has done. Indeed, he finds nothing good in him at all, since he justifies the ungodly [τὸν ἀσεβῆ], ibid. Nor is the gift of righteousness repaid by any service, as in that contract: I give so that you may give. "Do you repay me for my merit?" Joel 3.4. For although we are justified by faith, we are nonetheless justified freely, because faith is not properly a condition or a cause that claims a reward; indeed faith itself is God's gift, so that those who are said to be justified freely are understood to receive the gift of faith in order to be righteous. Yet the word freely does not exclude Christ's merit and satisfaction, since it excludes not the ransom [ἀντλύτρωσιν] but only a cause that would earn it from within us. But that grace [χάρις] by which we are said to be justified posits the true cause of justification in God, namely his benevolence, love and mercy. Thus the righteousness of God is joined with his grace: "For thy righteousness' sake bring my soul out of trouble, and of thy mercy cut off mine enemies," Ps. 143.11, 12. Everywhere the salvation of the sinner is ascribed to the grace and mercy of God, as to the fountain and ever-flowing spring from which all the streams of saving benefits flow to us. More specifically, justification arises from God's grace and love, because the righteousness on account of which we are pronounced righteous in God's judgment was admitted, decreed and defined from God's eternal love toward men alone, and is given in time to believers; and so given, it is accepted by men in God's judgment as a statute [δικαίωμα] and law [νόμος]. For God was under no obligation except that which arose from the free covenant to admit the Surety, to join us to him, and in him to justify us. All of this is grace [χάρις] and the gift of salvation [σωτηρίας] in grace, Rom. 5.15, and it breathes love for mankind [φιλανθρωπίαν].

units.la: XIII. Horrendum profecto illud est, quod Tridentini Sess. VI.can.2. propositionem illam: Gratia, qua justificamur, est tantum favor Dei, anathemate notare non horruerunt.
units.tr: XIII. It is truly horrible that the Tridentines, Session VI, canon 2, did not shrink from condemning with an anathema the proposition: "The grace by which we are justified is only the favour of God."

units.la: Et inepte, imo impudenter Bellarminus contendit, Apostolum, Rom.III.24. per χάριν gratiam intelligere rectitudinem habitus charitatis infusi. Adeo nullum in verbis Apostoli locum habitui illi infuso, qui sit forma justitiae Dei, invenit, ut coactus fuerit, eo absurditatis procedere, ut potius fontem justificationis, amorem Dei, ex pericopa verborum ejus tolleret, imo justificationem per solum amorem negaret, & vocem, quae eum notat, pro religionis suae ingenio in qualitatem hominis transubstantiaret. Quam etiam plane imperite, imo blaspheme cum Thoma Aquinate faciunt gratiam gratum facientem, oppositae ad gratiam gratis datam, seu charismata, quae hominibus non tam propter suam, quam propter aliorum salutem dantur. Quasi haec esset illa χάρισμα gratiae donatio, de qua Apostolus: In qua gratia Christi ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς gratia nos cumulavit in Dilecto illo, in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ejus, &c. Ephes.I.6.7. Quae tantum abest, ut charitatis habitum infusum, ceu causam justitiae, stabiliant, ut potius evertant, quia omnem gratiam
units.tr: And Bellarmine argues foolishly, indeed shamelessly, that the Apostle, Rom. 3.24, understands by grace [χάριν] the rectitude of a habit of infused charity. So completely does he find no place in the Apostle's words for that infused habit, which is the form of God's righteousness, that he was driven to such absurdity as to remove from the passage the fountain of justification, the love of God, and to deny that justification comes through love alone. He also changes the word that signifies this into a quality of man, according to the temper of his own religion. Equally inept, indeed blasphemous, is what Thomas Aquinas does when he sets gratia gratum faciens (grace that makes one pleasing) against gratia gratis data (grace freely given), that is, the charismata, which are given to men not so much for their own salvation as for that of others. As if this were that gift of grace [χάρισμα] of which the Apostle speaks, in which grace of Christ he has made us graced [ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς] in that Beloved, in whom we have redemption through his blood, etc., Eph. 1.6, 7. This is so far from establishing an infused habit of charity as the cause of righteousness that it rather overturns it, because they take away every grace

units.la: Tridentinorum & Bellarmini, gratiam illam non benignum favorem Dei, sed rectitudinem habitus charitatis infusi interpretantium impietas. tiam extra nos in Christo, Dilecto illo solo, collocant. Sed Apostolus dicens, Rom. III. 24. nos gratia αὐτοῦ ejus Dei justificari, &c. satis ostendit, nihil in nobis esse, quod sit causa juris filiorum; & gratiam, non justitiae habitum, sed justitiae donandae causam esse, denique justitiam nostram, sive jus nostrum a redemptione pendere & provenire: atque id nostrum fieri per fidem v. 28. quia per fidem in sanguine ejus, & fiduciam in eo accedimus ad ἱλαστήριον propitiatorium, & in eo solo Deum placatum & nostrum invenimus. Si porro δωρεὰν gratis justificamur, non igitur ex habitu, vel ulla re, quae in nobis sit, justificamur: neque χάρις ejusmodi habitum in homine notare potest. Dilutum enim plane est, quod voce δωρεὰν tantum opus meritorium excludi ajunt, quia si habitus est justitia, multo magis opus justitia erit. Habitus enim non donatur, quin Deus & τὸ θέλειν velle, & τὸ ἐνεργεῖν operari in nobis, operetur, quia Deus nos regenerat operando, ut velimus & faciamus. Illa vero voluntas, quam Deus operatus est, ut actum, manet in nobis ut habitus, ut ex ea frequenter & constanter operemur. Denique vera gratia gratum faciens est proprietas Dei non habitus noster: χάρις gratia, non δωρεὰ in χάριτι donum ex gratia, cujus homo non subjectum, sed terminus est. Non ex operibus, quae sunt in justitia, & quae fecerimus nos (& quanto minus ex habitu charitatis, cum opus, non habitus justificet, juxta illud: Fac hoc & vives) ὡς ἀλλὰ ἐξ τὸν αὐτοῦ ἔλεον sed secundum misericordiam suam salvavit nos, Tit. III. 5. Nam omnes peccarunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei, & ut tales δικαιοῦνται justificantur, Rom. III. 24. 25.
units.tr: ...the impiety of the Tridentines and Bellarmine, who interpret that grace as the rectitude of infused charity rather than God's benign favour. They place grace outside us, in Christ that Beloved alone. But the Apostle, saying that we are justified by his grace, that is of God, etc., Rom. 3.24, sufficiently shows that there is nothing in us which is the cause of the right of God's children; that grace is the cause of righteousness to be bestowed, not a habit of righteousness; and finally that our righteousness, or our right, comes from and depends on redemption, and becomes ours through faith, v. 28, because through faith in his blood, and by trust in him, we approach the propitiatory [ἱλαστήριον], and in him alone we find God appeased and our own. If then we are justified freely [δωρεὰν], we are not justified by a habit or by anything that is in us; nor can grace of that kind denote a habit in man. It is quite false to say that by the word freely only meritorious work is excluded, since if a habit were righteousness, much more would a work be righteousness. A habit is not given unless God also works in us both to will [τὸ θέλειν] and to work [τὸ ἐνεργεῖν], because God regenerates us by working, so that we will and do. That will which God worked in us as an act remains in us as a habit, so that we act from it frequently and constantly. Finally, true grace that makes one pleasing is a property of God, not our habit: grace [χάρις], not a gift in grace [δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι], of which man is not the subject but the terminus. Not from works that are in righteousness, which we have done (and still less from the habit of charity, since work, not habit, justifies, according to that saying: "Do this and you shall live"), but according to his mercy he saved us [ὡς ἀλλὰ ἐξ τὸν αὐτοῦ ἔλεον], Titus 3.5. For all have sinned and come short of the glory of God, and are justified as such, Rom. 3.23–25 [δικαιοῦνται].

units.la: XIV. Frivola sunt, quae gratiae huic & favori Dei Bellarminus obducit, argumenta. Pertendit ille, voce δωρεὰν gratis liberalitatem Dei, sine merito justificantis, ceu causam efficientem, at voce χάρις gratiae justitiam infusam, ceu causam formalem justificationis intelligi. Atqui S. Paulus etiam ubi δωρεὰν donationem, quae liberalitatis est, expresse dicit, non refugit adjungere χάριν gratiam. Ἡ χάρις ἔστι Θεοῦ, καὶ ἡ δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι τῇ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου Gratia Dei, & donatio in gratia unius hominis, Rom. V. 15. Οἱ τὴν περισσείαν τῆς χάριτος καὶ τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς δικαιοσύνης λαμβάνοντες qui abundantiam gratiae & donum justitiae accipiunt, vers 17. Et si maxime χάρις gratia rem donatam significaret, nulla necessitas foret intelligendi magis donum inhaerens, quam jus Dei donatum, quod & ipsum per metonymiam χάριτος gratiae nomine venire potest. Neque etiam Apostolus nos justificari dixit διὰ χάριτος per gratiam, quod non favori, sed causae formali, vel meritoriae instrumentali soli quadrare Bellarminus nugatur, sed τῇ χάριτι αὐτοῦ gratia ejus, hoc est, amore & favore Dei. Et amor certe Dei non est inanis. Sed non ideo immediate & tantum sanctos facit, sed id efficit, ut peccata nobis non imputentur, redemptio nobis praestetur, vocemur, regeneremur ad fidem, in Christo simus, in Christo justi simus, & denique sanctificemur.
units.tr: XIV. The arguments Bellarmine draws against this grace and favour of God are worthless. He contends that the word δωρεὰν [freely] means God's free liberality, without the merit of the one justifying, as the efficient cause, but that the word χάρις [grace] means the infused righteousness, as the formal cause of justification. Yet St Paul, even where he expressly says δωρεὰν, a gift which belongs to liberality, does not hesitate to add χάριν [grace]: "The grace of God, and the gift in the grace of one man" [Ἡ χάρις ἔστι Θεοῦ, καὶ ἡ δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι τῇ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου], Rom. 5:15. "Those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness" [Οἱ τὴν περισσείαν τῆς χάριτος καὶ τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς δικαιοσύνης λαμβάνοντες], v. 17. Even if χάρις meant the gift bestowed, there would be no need to understand the gift as an inherent quality rather than the right of God bestowed, which itself can also be called by the name of grace through metonymy. Nor did the Apostle say that we are justified "through grace" [διὰ χάριτος], which Bellarmine trifles suits only a formal cause or an instrumental meritorious cause and not God's favour; he said "by his grace" [τῇ χάριτι αὐτοῦ], that is, by the love and favour of God. And the love of God is certainly not empty. Yet it does not therefore make saints immediately and merely; it brings it about that sins are not imputed to us, that redemption is provided for us, that we are called, regenerated to faith, are in Christ, are righteous in Christ, and finally are sanctified.

units.la: XV. Extra Deum in judicio hoc requiritur רִיב causa per & propter quam Deus peccatorem absolvat, & jure coelestis vitae donet. Quae
units.tr: XV. Outside God, in this judgment, there is required a cause [רִיב] through and on account of which God absolves the sinner and grants him a right to heavenly life.

units.la: δικαίωμα aliquod, seu opus perfectum, quod Lex Dei ab eo, qui justus declarari debet, exigit, esse debet, & sine quo nec homo integer, nec peccator justificari potest. Quia enim juris petendi vitam non aliam causam ipse praescripsit, quam τὸ ποιεῖν Facere id, quod Lex praecipit; & non facienti mortem & condemnationem commi-natus est, non ita, ceu justus, sanctus & verax, causam illam, seu postulatum δικαιώματος in judicio ad justificandum peccatorem, amittere potest, ut quemquam sine ea justificet. Secus enim non ferret judicium rectum, imo ipse, quod cogitare blasphemum est, tenebras pro luce, amarum pro dulci prensaret, & delicta praemio compensaret. Sed novimus quod judicium Dei sit secundum veritatem, adversus eos, qui talia faciunt, peccant, Rom. II. 2. Et Deus absolvendo non absolvit peccatorem, citra δικαιώματα Exod. XXXIV. 7. Et hactenus justificatio legalis esse non definit; utpote quae ab Evangelica non quoad essentiam, quae in respectu causae, seu δικαιωματος, consistit; sed quoad solas circumstantias, subfitituto in peccatoris locum Christo, Legis δικαίωμα implente, quia impossibile erat Legi per carnem debilitate peccatori per δικαιωμα proprium, quod nullum habuit, peccatum remittere, & jus ad vitam conferre, Rom. VIII. 3. Neque quoad causam illam judicii immutabilem & perpetuam thronus justitiae Dei a throno misericordiae separari, & abillo separato ad hunc tuto provocari potest, licet rhetoricatione quadam, cum grano salis accipienda, vulgo id fieri soleat. Misericordia enim non in remissione causae, vel in relaxatione justitiae, cujus respectu non ita tribunal Dei aboleri, vel mitigari potest, ut ab eo provocatio dari possit, sed in datione & acceptatione Mediatoris, δικαιωμα & νόμος justitiam Legis omnem implentis, & causam in judicio requisitam repraesentantis, consistit.
units.tr: There must be some righteous requirement [δικαίωμα], or perfect work, which the law of God demands from the one who is to be declared righteous, and without which neither an innocent man nor a sinner can be justified. For since he himself prescribed no other cause of the right to seek life than doing [τὸ ποιεῖν] what the law commands, and threatened death and condemnation to the one not doing it, God, as just, holy and true, cannot in this way lose that cause or claim of righteous requirement [δικαίωμα] in judgment so as to justify a sinner without it. Otherwise he would not render a right judgment; indeed he would (which it is blasphemous even to think) take darkness for light and bitter for sweet, and reward sins with a prize. But we know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things, Rom. 2:2. And God, in absolving, does not absolve the sinner without requirement [δικαιώματα], Exod. 34:7. And so far legal justification does not cease to be justification; for it differs from the evangelical not in its essence, which consists in relation to the cause or requirement [δικαιώματος], but only in its circumstances, Christ being substituted in the sinner's place and fulfilling the requirement [δικαίωμα] of the Law, because it was impossible for the Law, weakened through the flesh, to remit sin for the sinner through his own requirement [δικαίωμα], which he did not have, and to confer a right to life, Rom. 8:3. Nor, with respect to that unchangeable and perpetual cause of judgment, can the throne of God's justice be separated from the throne of mercy and appeal be safely made from the one to the other, although this is commonly done by a kind of rhetorical figure, to be taken with a grain of salt. For mercy does not consist in the remission of the cause or the relaxation of justice, by respect to which the tribunal of God cannot be abolished or softened so that an appeal can be made from it; it consists in the giving and acceptance of the Mediator, who fulfils every requirement [δικαίωμα] and law of justice and represents the cause required in judgment.

units.la: XVI. Causam hanc in justificatione peccatoris Apostolus ἀπολύτρωσιν redemptionem Christi appellat. Justificamur gratis ipsius gratia διὰ τῆς ἀπολυτρώσεως per redemptionem, quae est in Christo Jesu, Rom. III. 24. Absque redemptione enim Christi justificatio peccatoris nulla est, quia δικαίωσις non potest esse citra δικαίωμα neque omnino fieri potest, ut Deus in veritate judicet, peccatorem esse justum & habere jus non modo non metuendi mortem, sed etiam expectandi & petendi vitam, si causa juris illius, quae δικαίωμα est, absit. Quam causam modo ἀπολύτρωσιν redemptionem Christi, modo δικαίωμα opus justificans, quod causa justitiae seu justificationis esse possit. & δικαίωμα, & νόμος id, quod Lex justificat, quia ejus μορφωσις delineatio in lege extat; Scriptura appellat. Nam Christus tale opus praestando & repraesentando redemit, factus pro nobis peccatum, ut nos fieremus justitia Dei in ipso, 2. Cor. V. 21. Hanc justificationis causam extra Deum alii justificationis causam meritoriam, alii materialem appellant, sensu eodem. Meritoriam, quia est illud ipsum, quo nobis, proprie loquendo, justificationem promeruit: Materialem, quia illa res est, quae in judicio Dei nobis ad justitiam imputatur. Quam etiam causam Scriptura modo in toto Christo, qui יְהוָה justitia nostra appellatur, Jer. XXIII. 6. & nobis factus δικαιοσύνη justitia dicitur, 1. Cor. 1, 30. I.30. & passus est δικαιῳ- σύνῃ ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων justus pro injustis, 1. Pet. III.18. modò in ejus Redemptione, Rom.III.24. Obedientia, ibid.V.19. Paupertate, 2.Cor.VIII.9. Vibicibus & livore, Esaj.LIII.5. Sanguine, 1.Pet.I.19. 1.Joh.I.7. Crucifixione, Gal. III.13. Coloss.I.20. Morte, Rom.V.8.10. Hebr. II.14. collocat. Quæ phraseologia verbis seu modo explicandi diverso, in rei explicatæ veritate pulchrè consentit.
units.tr: XVI. The Apostle calls this cause in the justification of the sinner the redemption [ἀπολύτρωσιν] of Christ. "We are justified freely by his grace through the redemption [διὰ τῆς ἀπολυτρώσεως] that is in Christ Jesus," Rom. 3:24. For without the redemption of Christ the justification of the sinner is nothing, because justification cannot exist without a requirement [δικαίωμα], nor can it at all come about that God judges in truth that the sinner is righteous and has a right not only not to fear death but also to expect and seek life, if the cause of that right, which is the requirement [δικαίωμα], is absent. This cause Scripture calls now the redemption of Christ, now the requirement [δικαίωμα], the justifying work, which can be the cause of righteousness or of justification, and the requirement [δικαίωμα] and law, namely that which the Law justifies, because its pattern [μορφωσις] stands delineated in the law. For Christ, by performing and representing such a work, redeemed us, being made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him, 2 Cor. 5:21. This cause of justification outside God, some call the meritorious cause of justification, others the material cause, in the same sense. Meritorious, because it is that very thing by which, properly speaking, he merited justification for us; material, because it is that thing which in God's judgment is imputed to us for righteousness. Scripture also places this cause sometimes in the whole Christ, who is called Jehovah our righteousness [יְהוָה], Jer. 23:6, and who was made for us righteousness [δικαιοσύνη], 1 Cor. 1:30, and who "the righteous suffered for the unrighteous" [δικαίῳ σύνῃ ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων], 1 Pet. 3:18; sometimes in his redemption, Rom. 3:24; in his obedience, ibid. 5:19; in his poverty, 2 Cor. 8:9; in his stripes and bruises, Isa. 53:5; in his blood, 1 Pet. 1:19, 1 John 1:7; in his crucifixion, Gal. 3:13, Col. 1:20; in his death, Rom. 5:8, 10, Heb. 2:14. These different expressions, in their different wording or manner of explanation, agree beautifully in the truth of the thing explained.

units.la: XVII. Neque omnino aliter res habere potest. Nam Deus Adamum jure creationis & legalis fœderis ad perfectam justitiam & rectitudinem, seu ad facienda omnia, quæ recta conscientia dictat, & in lege morum continentur, obligavit; neque alia conditione ei vitam promisit. Sicut verò imago Dei alia esse non potest, quàm ὁσιότης τῆς ἀληθείας sanctitas veritatis, Ephes.IV.24. hoc est, sanctitas æternæ veritatis ac sapientiæ Lege nixa: ita nec Legis δικαιώματα mutari potest, ut vel illud amplius non postulet Deus, vel ut aliud postulet. Postverò quàm homo peccavit, Lex non magis mutata, quàm Deus ipse aliud δικαίωμα præscribens, & insuper peccatori maledicens, nullum hominem peccatorem absolvere, vel ei, justitiæ experti jus vitæ addicere potuit. Ex operibus Legis non justificabitur omnis caro in conspectu ejus, Rom.III.20. neque quisquam per totam Legem à reatu & statu peccati liberari & justificari potest. Act. XIII.39. obstante non sola voluntate Dei, sed etiam tum naturali ejus decoro, qui seipse, & quod imagini suæ convenit, abnegare, vel diffidens à se & imagine sua præmio afficere non potest, imò non abominari non potest: tum carnis impotentia, quæ se legi subjicere non potest: tum denique Legis peccatori maledictionem comminantis immutabilitate, sed Deus dives potuit peccatorem justificare, seu justum in judicio pronuntiare aliena justitia, si quis esset, qui sacerdos fieri, & idoneum atque Deo gloriosum sacrificium pro peccatore offerre, eúmque Deo reconciliare posset. Idoneum imprimis sacrificium, quo Deus se oblectat est sacrificium justitiæ, Psal.LI.21. seu obedientia, quæ secundum Legem jus vitæ petendæ parit: qua præstita Deo dignum est & peccata remittere, & vitam æternam donare. At hoc sacrificium offerri nisi ab eo, cujus peculium salvandi existunt, non potest. Si igitur Sacerdos exstet, qui oblata pro peccato victima salvandorum dominus esse, & gloriam sanctitatis Dei passionibus & justitia sua afferere possit, eum exaudiri posse Lex & conscientia dictat, quia sic simul Deus glorificatur, simul homo salvatur. Cùm igitur talis Sacerdos Vindex & assertor per sacrificium, obedientiam & justitiam Legi debitam, ab æterno extiterit, & post peccatum talis nominatus, ac in plenitudine temporis consummatus sit, manifestum est, in eo, seu obedientia & justitia ejus esse causam, seu δικαίωμα illud, quod quicunque habent, per Legem legi moriuntur, non amplius debitores ipsi moriendi vel implendi legem ad justitiam & vitam, sicut mortui alicui rei, ejus actum vitalem nullum edunt. Gal.II.19. & in iis δικαίωμα & νόμος justitia legis impletur, Rom.VIII.4. ceu in iis, quod lex justitiæ causa & ad vitam addicendam exigit, per καινωνίαν cum Christo
units.tr: XVII. Nor can the matter be otherwise at all. For God bound Adam, by the right of creation and of the legal covenant, to perfect righteousness and uprightness, that is, to doing all that a right conscience dictates and that is contained in the law of morals; nor did he promise him life on any other condition. And just as the image of God can be nothing other than holiness of truth [ὁσιότης τῆς ἀληθείας], Eph. 4:24, that is, holiness resting on the law of eternal truth and wisdom, so the requirement [δικαιώματα] of the Law cannot be changed, so that God either no longer demands it or demands something else. But after man sinned, the Law was not changed any more than God himself was, prescribing another requirement [δικαίωμα] and, moreover, cursing the sinner; so he could not absolve any sinner or assign a right to life to one experienced in unrighteousness. "By the works of the Law no flesh will be justified in his sight," Rom. 3:20, nor can anyone at all be freed from guilt and the state of sin and be justified through the whole Law, Acts 13:39. There stands in the way not only God's will, but also his natural dignity, which cannot deny himself and what befits his image, or, distrustful of himself and his image, reward with a prize, indeed cannot fail to abhor; and the impotence of the flesh, which cannot subject itself to the law; and finally the unchangeableness of the Law threatening the sinner with a curse. But God, being rich, could justify the sinner, that is, pronounce him righteous in judgment, by an alien righteousness, if there were someone who could become a priest, offer an acceptable and to God glorious sacrifice for the sinner, and reconcile him to God. Above all, the acceptable sacrifice in which God delights is "the sacrifice of righteousness," Ps. 51:21, that is, obedience, which according to the Law brings forth the right to seek life; once this is rendered, it is worthy of God both to remit sins and to grant eternal life. But this sacrifice cannot be offered except by him whose people are those to be saved. If then there exists a priest who, having offered the victim for sin, can be lord of those to be saved and can assert the glory of God's holiness by his sufferings and his righteousness, the Law and conscience dictate that he can be heard, because thus God is glorified and man is saved at the same time. Since then such a priest, as Vindicator [Vindex] and advocate through sacrifice, obedience and righteousness due to the Law, existed from eternity, and after sin was so named and was consummated in the fullness of time, it is plain that in him, that is, in his obedience and righteousness, lies the cause, or that requirement [δικαίωμα], which all who have it "die to the Law through the law" [per Legem legi moriuntur], no longer debtors to die or to fulfil the law for righteousness and life, just as the dead perform no vital act toward anything. Gal. 2:19. And in them "the righteous requirement [δικαίωμα] and the law" [νόμος], "the righteousness of the law is fulfilled," Rom. 8:4, as in them, which the law demands as the cause for awarding life, through fellowship [καινωνίαν] with Christ our Priest and Saviour, is complete; and this is itself the cause of justification.

units.la: Sacerdote & Salvatore nostro, plenum extat; quæ ipsa justificationis causa est.
units.tr: ...in our Priest and Saviour, is complete; and this is itself the cause of justification.

units.la: XVIII. Hæc causa in judicio Dei ad peccatorem justificandum inprimis efficax est. Nam per Christi obedientiam, justitiam, redemptionem & mortem peccatum condemnatur, ut condemnare amplius non possit, quia in Christo, qui peccatum pro nobis factus est, punitum est, execratio tollitur, quia Christus pro nobis execratio factus est, Gal.III.13. & justitia, vita & salus adducitur, quia is nobis à Deo justitia factus est, 1.Cor.I.30. & in ipso vita est, Joh.I.4. & qui habet Filium, vitam habet, 1.Joh.V.12. Neque lex vel condemnare eum, qui per fidem in Christo est, & ejus δικαίωμα habet: vel eum non pro filio Dei agnoscere, & illi obedientiæ, quam in redemptore obtinet, vitæ mercedem non imputare potest. Nulla condemnatio in iis est, qui sunt in Christo Jesu, Rom.VIII.1. Is enim peccatum damnavit in carne, ut jus Legis in nobis impleretur, ib.v.3.4. Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Qui proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit ipsum. Quomodo non cum ipso nobis largietur omnia? Quis accusabit electos Dei? Christus est, qui justificat. Quis condemnabit? Christus qui mortuus est: imò excitatus, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, & pro nobis intercedit, v. 31-35. Sevocanda huc sunt, quæ de satisfactione & merito mortis Christi supra amplissimè diximus.
units.tr: XVIII. This cause is, in God's judgment, especially effective for justifying the sinner. For through Christ's obedience, righteousness, redemption and death, sin is condemned so that it can no longer condemn, because it was punished in Christ, who was made sin for us. The curse is removed, because Christ was made a curse for us, Gal. 3:13. And righteousness, life and salvation are brought in, because he was made by God our righteousness, 1 Cor. 1:30, and in him is life, John 1:4, and he who has the Son has life, 1 John 5:12. Nor can the law either condemn the one who is in Christ through faith and has his δικαίωμα [righteous requirement], or refuse to acknowledge him as a son of God, or withhold the reward of life from that obedience which he obtains in the Redeemer. There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, Rom. 8:1. For he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the just requirement of the Law might be fulfilled in us, ibid. vv. 3, 4. If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him freely give us all things? Who will bring a charge against God's elect? It is Christ who justifies. Who will condemn? It is Christ who died, or rather who was raised, who is also at the right hand of God, and who intercedes for us, vv. 31-35. What we have said most fully above about satisfaction and the merit of Christ's death should be brought in here.

units.la: XIX. De causa hac Justificationis peccatoris coram Deo, Christo & Apostolis cum Judæis acerrima contentio fuit. Hi enim ἀγνοοῦντες τὴν δικαιοσύνην τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ τὴν ἰδίαν δικαιοσύνην ζητοῦντες στῆσαι, τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐχ ὑπετάγησαν: ignorantes justitiam Dei, & propriam justitiam statuere quærentes, justitiæ Dei se non subjecerunt, Rom.X.3. Ἰδίαν δικαιοσύνην propriam justitiam illam Apostolus v.5. appellat δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ νόμου justitiam, quæ est ex lege, de qua Moses scribit: Qui fecerit ea homo, vivet in iis. Lev. XVIII.5. Sed non ita Judæi hæc intellexerunt, uti intelligere debuerunt. Quomodo enim justitiam suam statuere quæsivissent, si, quemadmodum oportebat, cognovissent, peccatum, pro quo quotidie sacrificarunt, propriam justitiam prorsus excludere? Sed confuderunt illi justitiam Dei & propriam, justitiam Dei vocantes factum aliquod, quod Deus à peccatore exigeret, ut propter illud eos justificaret. Quale factum erat omissio peccatorum graviorum & infamium, quam vocarunt μετάνοιαν conversionem, vexationem corporis per jejunia, nec non sacrificia & oblationes. Sic enim Pharisæus ille, propriæ justitiæ suæ decantator: O Deus, gratias tibi ago, quòd non sum, sicut reliqui homines, rapaces, injusti, adulteri, & sicut ille publicanus. Jejuno bis die Sabbathi, decimo omnia, quæ possideo. Luc.XVIII.11. 12. Per & propter talia, saltem ut conditionem & causam sine qua non, Deum Israelem justificare velle crediderunt. Reipsa igitur propriam justitiam constituere voluerunt, quia ex factis, quam constituere volentes justitiæ Dei se subjici putarunt. Non ergo, quod justitiarii hodierni suam causam à Judæorum causa discreturi, pertendunt, Apostolus Judæorum hunc errorem perstringit, quòd pro causa salutis justitiam Legis externam, quæ per frequentes actio-
units.tr: XIX. Over this cause of the justification of the sinner before God, there was a most bitter dispute between Christ and the Apostles on the one side and the Jews on the other. For these, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, did not submit themselves to the righteousness of God, Rom. 10:3. The Apostle, in v. 5, calls this their own righteousness the righteousness which is of the law (δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ νόμου), of which Moses writes: The man who does these things shall live by them, Lev. 18:5. But the Jews did not understand these words as they ought to have. For how could they have sought to establish their own righteousness if, as they should have, they had recognised that sin, for which they sacrificed every day, wholly excludes one's own righteousness? But they confused the righteousness of God with their own, calling by the name righteousness of God some deed which God required of the sinner, so that for its sake he would justify them. Such a deed was the omission of the graver and more shameful sins, which they called μετάνοια, conversion; the mortification of the body by fasts; and also sacrifices and offerings. For thus that Pharisee, the eulogist of his own righteousness: O God, I thank you that I am not like other men, robbers, unjust, adulterers, or like that tax collector. I fast twice a week, and I give a tenth of all that I possess, Luke 18:11, 12. By and because of such things they believed that God of Israel wished to justify them, at least as the condition and cause without which it could not be. In fact, therefore, they wished to establish their own righteousness, because they thought that by establishing it from works they were submitting to the righteousness of God. Therefore it is not the case, as present-day justiciaries, wishing to distinguish their cause from that of the Jews, maintain, that the Apostle is here attacking the error of the Jews in that they sought, as the cause of salvation, an external righteousness of the Law, which is prepared by frequent actions...

units.la: Judaeorum de hac justificationis causa cum Christo & Apostolis contentio: propriam justitiam ... ctiones paratur, & in civili vita aliquid valet; constituere voluerunt; sed hunc potius cum justitiariis omnibus communem, quòd justitiam Dei collocantes in factis, definiverunt; jus illud, quod Deus concedit ex facto tali, quod pro conditione vitæ dixerunt esse justitiam Dei. Neque enim Apostolus hoc loco cum Judæis de perfectione legis, sed de justitia, per quam homo justificatur, sine illa justitia Legis seu factorum, an justitia fidei, quæ in Christo est, disceptat. Judæi igitur talem justitiam perfectam statuere quærentes veram Dei justitiam repudiarunt & blasphemarunt, non in thesi, ut dicerent se Dei justitiam rejicere, sed in hypothesi & reapse; quia negarunt justitiam fidei in Christum sine factis. Nam hanc fidei justitiam esse illam justitiam Dei, Apostolus v. 6. 7. &c. asserit, & telte ipso Mose probat, dicens: Ἡ ἐκ πίστεως δικαιοσύνη quæ ex fide justitia est, sic dicit: Deut.XXX.11.12. Ne dicas in corde tuo. Quis ascendet in cœlum? Id est, Christum deducere. Aut quis descendet in abyssum? Hoc est, Christum ex mortuis reducere. Sed quid dicit? Prope te est verbum in ore tuo, & in corde tuo. Hoc est verbum fidei, quod prædicamus.
units.tr: The dispute of the Jews with Christ and the Apostles over this cause of justification: they wished to establish their own righteousness... which is prepared by frequent actions and has some value in civil life. But he rather rebukes this error, which is common to all justiciaries, that by placing the righteousness of God in works they defined it as that right which God grants on the basis of such a deed, which they called the righteousness of God in terms of the condition of life. For the Apostle does not here dispute with the Jews about the perfection of the Law, but about the righteousness by which a man is justified: whether it is the righteousness of the Law or of works without faith, or the righteousness of faith which is in Christ. Therefore the Jews, in seeking to establish such a perfect righteousness, rejected and blasphemed the true righteousness of God. They did this not in theory, by saying they rejected the righteousness of God, but in practice and in fact, because they denied the righteousness of faith in Christ without works. For the Apostle, in vv. 6, 7 and following, asserts that this righteousness of faith is that righteousness of God, and proves it by the testimony of Moses himself, saying: The righteousness which is of faith speaks thus (Ἡ ἐκ πίστεως δικαιοσύνη), Deut. 30:11, 12: Do not say in your heart, Who will ascend into heaven? That is, to bring Christ down. Or who will descend into the abyss? That is, to bring Christ back up from the dead. But what does it say? The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart. This is the word of faith which we preach.

units.la: XX. Post Christi & Apostolorum tempora errori huic capitali Judæi præfractè inhærunt. Licet enim in Tractatu Berachot definiverint, neminem justum censeri nisi בורקתי שׁל הקבה in justitia Sancti Benedicti, tamen justitiam illam (Dei) Sancti Benedicti eodem illi sensu intellexerunt, quo vetustiores Judæi δικαιο- σύνῳ Θεῷ justitiam Dei; quæ videlicet in pœnitentia, jejuniis, Festo expiationis eum in finem instituto, ut totius anni peccata expientur, præviâ eidem mactatione galli gallinacei, qui in locum peccatoris illum offerentis succedat; afflictionibus, morte ipsa & misericordia Dei, quibus Deus remissionem peccatorum & vitam addixerit, confitlat. Quæ ipsa quoque ostendunt, illos propriam justitiam in factis conspicuam, constituere, & justitiæ Dei veræ non subjici. Nam sic nec peccati gravitatem & reatum, nec justitiam Dei, δικαίωμα verum, à lege requisitum, ad absolutionem peccatoris exigentis, agnoscunt; & obedientiam legis statutorum pro vera justitia, in judicio Dei valida, venditant; & sacrificiis justitiam tribuunt, quæ verius peccatorum & maledictionis Divinæ ἀνάμνησιν commemorationem continebant; & חתם הטור chirographi, non apochæ rationem habebant; & corpus umbræ respondens, Christum, finem Legis; verumque adeò pro peccatis sacrificium & Mediatorem atque Redemptorem unicum abnegant; & pœnitentiam à fide in Christum separantes, fucatam Deo obtrudunt; & mortem temporalem solam peccati stipendium faciunt; & misericordiæ Dei obtentu ejusdem justitiam evertunt. Quæ πεπω- σε ψευδῆ non semel jugulavimus. Neque eorundem pro infidelitate sua argumenta, superius Loc.XIII.61. ad incudem revocata, repetere libet.
units.tr: XX. After the time of Christ and the Apostles, the Jews stubbornly clung to this chief error. For although in the tractate Berachot they defined that no one is counted righteous unless he is [צדקתו של הקב"ה] in the righteousness of the Holy One, blessed be he, yet they understood that righteousness of the Holy One, blessed be he, in the same sense in which the earlier Jews understood the righteousness of God (δικαιοσύνη Θεοῦ). That is, they held it to consist in repentance, fasting, and the Day of Atonement instituted to this end, so that the sins of the whole year might be expiated, with the prior slaughter of a rooster which was to take the place of the sinner who offered it; in afflictions, in death itself, and in the mercy of God, by which God was said to have granted forgiveness of sins and life. These things also show that they set up a righteousness of their own, visible in works, and did not submit to the true righteousness of God. For thus they acknowledged neither the gravity and guilt of sin, nor the true righteousness of God, the δικαίωμα required by the law, which demands the absolution of the sinner. They put forward the observance of the statutes as true righteousness, valid in God's judgment. They attributed to sacrifices a righteousness which in truth contained a remembrance (ἀνάμνησις) of sins and of the divine curse. They had the account of the bond [חתם הטור], not the receipt. They had the body which corresponds to the shadow, but not Christ, the end of the Law. So they deny the one true sacrifice for sins and the one Mediator and Redeemer. Separating repentance from faith in Christ, they thrust a counterfeit upon God. And they make temporal death alone the wages of sin, and they overthrow righteousness by appealing to the mercy of God. We have already refuted these false fabrications (πεπωσμένα ψευδῆ) more than once. Nor is it pleasing to repeat their arguments for their unbelief, which were already brought to the anvil above, in Loc. XIII.61.

units.la: XXI. Judæorum vestigiis insistentes Socinus & gregales ejus causam eandem justificationis, & cum eadem justificationem funditus evertunt. Asserunt enim, Deum nos justificare ex pura misericordia absque compensatione vel satisfactione ulla, vel nostra, vel Christi, qui γνῶσι Judæorum error est. Ne tamen cum Judæis Christum penitus à justificatione excludere videantur; per eundem, seu obedientiam & mortem ejus nobis peccata condonari ajunt, quatenus Christus per ea, quæ jussu Dei propter salutem nostram fecit & passus est, tum cognitionem, tum effectum justificationis in nobis producit. Ipsam verò justificationem seu plenariam à reatu peccatorum absolutionem tum demum in plerisque re ipsa peragi statuunt, cùm à morte liberati ad æternam vitam perducuntur, ut ita beneficium hoc spe tantùm in hac vita obtineant. Sicut nempe iis electio & vocatio, ita & justificatio alia non plena, nec firma: alia plena & firma est. Illam hujus vitæ & illorum esse, qui fidem Deo habentes, parati sunt omnia promissionum obtinendarum gratia facere; hanc tum demum & illis contingere, qui se perseveranter obedientes præstiterint. Multa enim, inquit Socinus, inter calicem supremáque labra cadere possunt. Cujus rei exemplum Abrahamum faciunt, non omnino justum à Deo pronuntiatum nisi postquam, præter alia suæ in Deum fiduciæ, ejusque præceptorum obedientiæ specimina, tandem ipso ita jubente unigenitum filium ei immolare non recusavit. Quæ cuncta ad Christum & justificationem Evangelicam per Christum ex religione Christiana exturbandam spectant. Abrahamum certè in præputio, adeóque sexaginta ante immolationem Isaci annis justificatum esse Apostolus, Rom.IV.9.10.11. docet. Ergò ille in præputio justificatus & sacramento circumcisionis auctoratus, annos sexaginta cum Deo ambulavit, ut salutis funambulus: de cujus corde & animo ne ipse quidem Deus firmiter aliquid statuere ante tentationem ejus potuerit? Adeò ille לב הלב supplantans cor habuit? De priore etiam illa & minùs plena justificatione intelligendum est; quod asserunt, Deum nos ex pura misericordia, sine satisfactione & compensatione ulla nostra vel Christi justificare. Nam ea conditione Deum sic justificare docent, si in posterum ad iram non provocetur; sin, in ipsa fide & resipiscentia, quæ oblatæ à Deo justificationi ex parte hominis respondeat, sitam esse satisfactionem, qua homo ipse Legi satisfaciat.
units.tr: XXI. Following in the footsteps of the Jews, Socinus and his followers utterly overthrow this same cause of justification, and with it justification itself. For they assert that God justifies us from pure mercy, without any compensation or satisfaction, either ours or Christ's, which is (γνῶσι) the error of the Jews. Yet, lest they seem with the Jews to exclude Christ entirely from justification, they say that our sins are forgiven us through his obedience and death, insofar as Christ, by what he did and suffered by God's command for our salvation, produces in us both the knowledge and the effect of justification. But they hold that justification itself, that is, the full absolution from the guilt of sins, is for the most part really carried out only when, freed from death, they are brought to eternal life; so that they obtain this benefit only in hope during this life. Accordingly, for them there is election and calling, and also a justification that is not full nor firm, and another that is full and firm. The former belongs to this life and to those who, having faith in God, are ready to do all things for the sake of obtaining the promises; the latter falls to them only when they have shown themselves perseveringly obedient. For many things, says Socinus, can fall between the cup and the lips. They take Abraham as an example of this: he was not pronounced wholly righteous by God until, besides other proofs of his trust in God and his obedience to his commands, he at last, at God's command, did not refuse to sacrifice to him his only son. All these things aim at overturning Christ, and the justification which is by Christ, the Evangelical justification, in the Christian religion. The Apostle, however, teaches that Abraham was justified in uncircumcision, and thus sixty years before the sacrifice of Isaac, Rom. 4:9, 10, 11. Therefore, if he was justified in uncircumcision, and sealed by the sacrament of circumcision, did he walk with God for sixty years like a tightrope walker on salvation? Could God himself not firmly decide anything about his heart and mind before his trial? Did he have a heart that supplants [לב הלב]? What they assert, that God justifies us from pure mercy, without any satisfaction or compensation of ours or of Christ, must also be understood of that earlier and less full justification. For they teach that God justifies on this condition, that in the future he is not provoked to anger. And if this is not so, they say that the satisfaction by which man himself satisfies the Law lies in faith itself and in repentance, which, offered by God, corresponds to justification on the part of man.

units.la: XXII. Sed & justificatio illa prior, quam ex pura misericordia contingere pronuntiant, impurum sanè dogma est. Contrariatur enim puritati naturæ Divinæ; per quam fieri non potest, ut Deus ad peccatum conniveat, & impunitate illud donet. Puri sunt oculi tui, ne videas malum, & respicere ad iniquitatem non poteris, Habac.I.13. Odisti omnes operantes iniquitatem, Psal.V.6. Non liberè utique & contingenter, sed naturalis puritatis & sanctitatis suæ necessitate. Lux enim est, quæ necessitate naturæ suæ tenebras arguit & fugat, Joh.III.19.20. Ephes.V.13. Non tantùm igitur pœnam & vindictam sanctè exercere potest, sed etiam nisi exerceret, se ipsum abnegaret, quod ἀ δύναται non potest, 2.Tim.II.13. Cùmque justitiæ Dei omnino satisfaciendum sit, vel ipsi, vel nostro loco alius satisfacere debet. Nos autem solvendo non sumus, & impotentiam nostram prædicari parabola Regni Cœlorum & Regis creditoris toris rigidíque exactoris Evangelium justit, dicens: Simile est Regnum Coelorum Regi, qui voluit rationem conferre cum suis. Et cùm coepisset conferre, oblatus ei est quidam debitor decies mille talentorum. Cùm autem non posset hæc reddere, jussit eum Dominus ejus venundari & uxorem ejus, & liberos ejus, &c. Matth. XVIII. 23. 24. 25. Summa verò Evangelii de Christo facto nobis sponsore est: נפש ... Exigitur solutio. & ipse afflictus est, Esaj. L III. 7. Ipse dedit se ἀντίλυτρον redemptionis pretium pro omnibus, 1. Tim. II. 6. Non per ea, quæ jussu propter salutem nostram fecit & passus est, cognitionem & effectum justificationis in nobis producendo, uti illi fingunt, sed morte sua λύτρωσιν redemptionis nostræ λύτρον persolvendo. Ideo Deus justificat in Christo. Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputans eis offensas eorum. Fecit eum, qui non novit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum, ut nos justitia Dei in ipso fieremus, 2. Cor. V. 19. 21. Denique remissio peccatorum, quæ in Evangelio offertur talis est, ut per eam demonstretur justitia Dei, Rom. I II. 25. 26. Non igitur ex pura misericordia Dei citra ullam satisfactionem, procedit. Sed satisfactionis hujus necessitatem in loco pluribus demonstravimus & vindicavimus.
units.tr: XXII. But that earlier justification, which they claim comes about from pure mercy, is indeed an impure doctrine. It is opposed to the purity of the divine nature, by which it cannot happen that God should overlook sin and pardon it without punishment. Thine eyes are too pure to behold evil, and thou canst not look on iniquity, Hab. 1:13. Thou hatest all workers of iniquity, Ps. 5:6. Not freely and contingently, but by the necessity of his natural purity and holiness. For he is light, which by the necessity of its nature reproves and drives out darkness, John 3:19-20; Eph. 5:13. Therefore he can not only exercise punishment and vengeance justly, but if he did not exercise them he would deny himself, which ἀδύνατον [is impossible], 2 Tim. 2:13. And since the justice of God must be fully satisfied, either he himself or another in our place must satisfy it. But we are not able to pay, and the Gospel bids us to consider our inability in the parable of the Kingdom of Heaven, of the king who was a creditor, stern and rigid exactor: "The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants. And when he began to settle, one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents. But since he could not repay, his lord ordered him to be sold, with his wife and children, etc." Matt. 18:23-25. The sum of the Gospel concerning Christ is that he has been made our surety: [nephesh] ... Solution is required. and he himself was afflicted, Isa. 53:7. He gave himself ἀντίλυτρον [a ransom] for all, a price of redemption, 1 Tim. 2:6. Not by what he did and suffered at God's command for our salvation, producing in us the knowledge and effect of justification, as they imagine, but by paying with his death λύτρωσιν [redemption] for our redemption, the λύτρον [ransom]. Therefore God justifies in Christ. God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their offences to them. He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God, 2 Cor. 5:19, 21. Finally, the forgiveness of sins which is offered in the Gospel is such that through it the justice of God is shown, Rom. 3:25-26. Therefore it does not proceed from the pure mercy of God without any satisfaction. But we have demonstrated and vindicated the necessity of this satisfaction at greater length in its place.

units.la: XXIII. Justificationis causam etiam Pontifici lancinant.
units.tr: XXIII. The Papists also tear apart the cause of justification.

units.la: Concedunt equidem illi, & plenis buccis δικαιώματα seu meritum Christi jactant. Sed hominem peccatorem nihilominus partim per Sacramenta & sacrificium Missæ, partim per habitum infusum charitatis, partim per satisfactiones temporales, partim per merita propria & aliena justificari, hoc est, à reatu peccati absolvi, & jus vitæ consequi pertendunt. Tridentini enim Sess. VI. cap. 7. Jesum Christum quidem esse causam justificationis meritoriam, quia sua sanctissima passione in ligno crucis nobis justificationem meruit, & pro nobis Deo Patri satisfecit, fatentur; sed demum, ajunt, unica formalis causa justificationis est justitia Dei, non qua ipse justus est, sed qua nos justos facit, qua videlicet ab eo donati, renovamur spiritu mentis nostræ, & non modò reputamur, sed vere justi nominamur & sumus, justitiam in nobis recipientes &c. Addunt: Quanquam nemo possit esse justus, nisi cui merita passionis Domini nostri Jesu Christi communicantur, id tamen in hac impii justificatione fit dum ejusdem sanctissimæ passionis merito per Spiritum S. charitas Dei effunditur in cordibus eorum, qui justificantur, atque ipsis inhæret. Unde in ipsa justificatione cum remissione peccatorum hæc omnia simul infusa accipit homo per Jesum Christum, cui inseritur per fidem, spem & charitatem.
units.tr: They indeed concede, and with full mouths boast of the δικαιώματα [righteous acts] or merit of Christ. Yet they maintain that the sinful man is nevertheless justified partly through the sacraments and the sacrifice of the Mass, partly through the infused habit of charity, partly through temporal satisfactions, partly through his own and others' merits; that is, that he is absolved from the guilt of sin and attains the right to life. For the Council of Trent, Session VI, chapter 7, acknowledges that Jesus Christ is indeed the meritorious cause of justification, because by his most holy passion on the wood of the cross he merited justification for us and satisfied God the Father on our behalf; but then, they say, the only formal cause of justification is the justice of God, not that by which he himself is just, but that by which he makes us just, namely, that by which we, being endowed by him, are renewed in the spirit of our minds, and are not only reckoned but truly named and made just, receiving justice within us, etc. They add: although no one can be just unless the merits of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ are communicated to him, yet this takes place in the justification of the impious when, by the merit of that most holy passion, the charity of God is poured out through the Holy Spirit into the hearts of those who are justified and dwells in them. Hence in justification itself, together with the remission of sins, the man receives all these things infused at once through Jesus Christ, into whom he is grafted through faith, hope and charity.

units.la: XXIV. Mirum hoc veritatis & mendacii μίγμα est, dignum ea Bestia, quæ habet cornua Agni, & loquitur ut Draco, Apoc. XIII. 11. Nam Agninum quidem illud est, quòd δικαιώματ meritum, redemptionem & satisfactionem Christi à justificatione non excludunt. Sed Draconis loquelam sapit, quòd terminorum logicorum præstigiis horrendum illud iniquitatis mysterium occultant, quo Jesu Christi meritum, redemptionem & justitiam ab unica formali causa justificationis separantes non obscurè negant, Jesum Christum & ejus justitiam esse causam illam unicam proximam & immediatam, per & propter quam peccator in Dei judicio justus declaratur, seu à peccato & pœna ejus absolvitur, & jure petendi vitam æternam donatur; atque in ejus locum justitiam, seu charitatem, quæ, inquiunt, homini justificato inhæret & infunditur, substituunt. Non ergo Christo, & merito atque obedientiæ ejus id tribuunt, quod in judicio Dei ad sustinendam causam peccatoris justificandi, ut à peccato absolvi, & jure petendi vitam obedienti promissam potiri possit; absque qua justificatio cassa & nulla est, requiritur; sed id, quòd omni merito, obedientia & justitia sua id unicè meruerit, ut per Spiritum S. charitas Dei diffundatur in cordibus eorum, qui justificantur, atque in ipsis inhæret; hoc est, ut Deus homini donet charitatem infusam, & ei inhærentem, per & propter quam, ceu unicam formalem justificationis causam, in judicio Dei à peccato absolvatur, & ceu jam justus, jus petendi vitam æternam, quo propter peccati m, & non impletam perfecto opere justitiam legis excidit, possideat. Hoccine aliud est, quàm Christum & meritum mortis ejus à Dei judicio, in quo justificatio peragitur, removere, nisi quatenus ille donationem justitiæ humanæ propriæ, quæ tamen vim ἰλαστήριον & δικαιώματα habere nunquam potest, promeruit; & loco ejus hominem atque justitiam ejus infusam, Deo irato judici, ceu causam unicam formalem justificationis, qua ille commotus peccatorem à peccato & æterna damnatione absolvat, & jure potiundæ vitæ æternæ beet, obtrudere: hoc est, vim suam facere Deum suum, Habac. I. 11. negare, quòd Jesus Christus venerit in carnem, ut ipse justitia nostra fieret, 1. Joh. IV. 3. denique ex homine ipso Christum facere?
units.tr: XXIV. This is a strange mixture of truth and falsehood, worthy of that beast which has the horns of a lamb and speaks like a dragon, Rev. 13:11. For it is lamb-like in that they do not exclude the δικαιώματα [righteous acts], merit, redemption and satisfaction of Christ from justification. But it savours of the dragon's speech in that by the sleight of logical terms they conceal that dreadful mystery of iniquity, by which, separating the merit, redemption and righteousness of Jesus Christ from the sole formal cause of justification, they not obscurely deny that Jesus Christ and his righteousness are that sole proximate and immediate cause, through and on account of which the sinner is declared just in the judgment of God, or is absolved from sin and its punishment, and is granted the right to ask for eternal life; and in its place they substitute the justice, or charity, which, they say, inheres in and is infused into the justified man. Therefore they do not attribute to Christ and his merit and obedience that which is required in the judgment of God to sustain the cause of the sinner to be justified, so that he may be absolved from sin and obtain the right to ask for the life promised to the obedient (without which justification is void and null); but they attribute to his merit, obedience and righteousness alone that the charity of God should be poured out through the Holy Spirit into the hearts of those who are justified and dwell in them; that is, that God should give man infused charity, dwelling in him, through and on account of which, as the sole formal cause of justification, he may be absolved from sin in the judgment of God, and, as one already just, possess the right to ask for eternal life, which he has lost through sin and through failing to fulfil the law by perfect work. Is this anything other than to remove Christ and the merit of his death from the judgment of God, in which justification is accomplished, except insofar as the latter has merited for us the bestowal of a human justice of our own, which can never have the power of ἱλαστήριον [propitiation] and δικαιώματα [righteous acts]; and in its place to thrust upon the angry judge, God, the man and his infused justice as the sole formal cause of justification, by which the judge, moved, absolves the sinner from sin and eternal damnation and makes him worthy to obtain the right to eternal life? This is to make their own strength their god, Hab. 1:11; to deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh so that he himself might become our righteousness, 1 John 4:3; and finally, to make Christ out of the man himself?

units.la: XXV. Etenim in Dei severo judicio, cui homo peccator, æternæ damnationis reus, vel absolvendus, si causa absolutionis adsit; vel condemnandus, si illa desit, objicitur, non id agitur, ut homini donetur justitia & charitas inhærens, per quam Deum & proximum diligat, sed ut sine justitiæ Divinæ pœnam à peccatore exigentis, & justitiam Legis universalem, quàm debendi homo ut creatura, imago Dei & fœderatus reus fuit, neque post peccatum reus esse desiit, detrimento à peccato, & æterna condemnatione absolvi, & jure obedientiæ perfectæ à se vel Sponsore præstitæ petendi vitam æternam beari postliminio possit. Hoc ergo si non meruit Christus omni obedientia & justitia sua, nihil meruit. Manet enim homo peccator sub ira, & ἀνάθεμα Deo, quia in judicio Dei, deficiente causa, seu δικαιώματα, à peccato & damnatione absolvi non potuit, nedum jure petendi vitam beari potuit. Impossibile autem fuisset, homini nondum à peccato absoluto, promereri donationem justitiæ inhærentis; & si possibile id maximè fuisset, nihil tamen ad salutem hominis profuisset. Sicut enim homicidæ in judicio ad vitam temporalem retinendam Angelica vita in carcere transacta nihil prodest, quia per eam reatus peccati commissi non tollitur, & non ideo non puniendus ille est, quia aliquot annos vel dies ante aut post admissum homicidium manus animúmque ab hoc scelere abstinuit: ita peccatorem in Dei judicio non tuetur adversus mortem commeritam quantacunque justitia & charitas sive Divinitus Tridentinorum de justificationis causa definitio, quòd meritoria sit passio Christi, at formalis justitia inhærens. Quæ veritatis & mendacii fœda commixtio est. vinitus propter meritum aliquod infusa & donata, sive acquisita, quia reatus peccati manet, neque ulla obedientia expungi, sed sola morte, quam lex peccatori decrevit, solvi potest. Ita ex Tridentinorum sententia reapse nec meritum Christi, nec infusus ille charitatis habitus quicquam ad justificationem confert. Manet enim homo peccator in Dei judicio, & cum omni causa hac meritoria & formali unica, qualem Tridentini exposuerunt, causa cadit, aeternumque damnatur. Unde consequens est Pontificiam religionem omni justificatione coram tribunali Dei destitui. Quae non aliam ob causam ab ea non admittitur, imo despuitur, & diris anathematis configitur, quam ut justificatio gratuita, remissio peccatorum & vera justitia per solam crucem Christi per res pretio addictas, seu venales, cujus modi imprimis Missae, satisfactiones alienae & satisfactionum propriarum in hac vita relaxatio, per indulgentias, aliaque ejusmodi ad stabilimentum Regni Hierarchici carnalis excogitata, quae per nostrum de justificatione dogma ruere, ipse Soto in Concilio Tridentino arguit; suppleatur. Hic enim rhodus, hic saltus est.
units.tr: XXV. For in the severe judgment of God, to which the sinful man, liable to eternal damnation, is brought either to be absolved, if a cause of absolution is present, or to be condemned, if it is lacking, the question is not whether justice and inherent charity are given to man, by which he may love God and his neighbour; but whether, without the satisfaction of the divine justice which exacts punishment from the sinner, and without the universal justice of the law, which man as a creature, the image of God and a bound party to the covenant, owed and did not cease to owe after sin, he can be absolved from the injury of sin and eternal condemnation, and by right of perfect obedience performed by himself or by his Surety, be restored to the right to ask for eternal life. Therefore, if Christ did not merit this by all his obedience and righteousness, he merited nothing. For man the sinner remains under wrath and accursed before God, because in the judgment of God, the cause or δικαιώματα [righteous acts] being lacking, he could not be absolved from sin and damnation, much less be made blessed with the right to ask. Moreover, it would have been impossible for man, not yet absolved from sin, to merit the bestowal of inherent justice; and even if this had been possible in the highest degree, it would nevertheless have profited nothing for man's salvation. For just as a murderer, in order to keep his temporal life before the judge, gains nothing by having spent his life in prison like an angel, because by this the guilt of the crime committed is not removed, and he is not therefore to be exempt from punishment because for some years or days before or after the homicide he kept his hand and mind from this crime: so too no amount of justice and charity, whether infused and bestowed by God on account of some merit or acquired, protects the sinner in the judgment of God against the death he has deserved, since the guilt of sin remains, and it cannot be wiped out by any obedience, but only by the death which the law has decreed for the sinner. The Tridentine definition of the cause of justification, that the passion of Christ is meritorious but inherent justice is formal, is a foul mixture of truth and falsehood. Thus, according to the sentiment of the Tridentines, in fact neither the merit of Christ nor that infused habit of charity contributes anything to justification. For the sinful man remains in the judgment of God, and with every such cause, meritorious and formal alone, as the Tridentines have set it out, he falls and is eternally condemned. Whence it follows that the Papist religion is destitute of all justification before the tribunal of God. It is not admitted by it for any other reason, nay it is spat upon and pierced with dreadful anathemas, than that gratuitous justification, remission of sins and true righteousness through the cross of Christ alone are overthrown by things bought and sold for a price, such as, above all, the Mass, the satisfactions of others, and the relaxation of one's own satisfactions in this life through indulgences, and other such things devised for the establishment of the carnal Hierarchical Kingdom, which, as Soto himself argues at the Council of Trent, fall down if our doctrine of justification stands. Here is the Rhodes, here the leap.

units.la: XXVI. Neque ie expediunt, vel consensum Pontificios inter & Evangelicos muniunt, qui cum Walenburgii aliisque causam justificationis formalem duplicem intrinsecam, justitiam hominis inhaerentem, & extrinsecam, quam etiam exemplarem, & conditionem causae formalis appellant, meritum & justitiam Christi faciunt. Sed justitia inhaerens, posterior quippe justificatione, ejus nec causa, nec causa formalis, nec formalis intrinseca est. Meritum etiam & justitia Christi nec extrinseca nobis est, quia Christus nobis factus est justitia, 1. Cor. I. 30. nos finius justitia in ipso, 2. Cor. V. 21. habemus justitiam per fidem Christi, ex Deo justitiam in fide, Phil. III. 9. donum justitiae accipimus, Rom. V. 27. fides seu justitia Christi fide apprehensa nobis imputatur ad justitiam, ibid. IV. 5. nec etiam exemplaris duntaxat justificationis causa est, quasi Christi justitia nihil aliud esset quam exemplar justitiae inhaerentis, non causa vitae, propter quam solam in foro Dei justificamur, seu justi pronuntiamur: nec conditio tantum causae formalis, seu justitiae inhaerentis, quia sic non esset vera causa justificationis nostrae, sed tantum regenerationis, seu, uti loquuntur ipsi, facultatis bene operandi, quae justificationem impii sequitur, & sine ea nullo modo obtinere potest: sed ipsa & unica causa, sive meritoria illa, sive formalis appelletur. (Humani enim termini verbo Dei praescribere non debent) justificationis, propter quam solam in foro Dei justi pronuntiamur & absolvimur. Sola enim justitia Christi, nec extrinseca illa, nec inhaerens nobis, sed una cum Christo, & in ejus communione nobis donata, in judicio Dei, ut nos salvat, & efficit, ut per legem (a Christo impletam) legi mortui (ab ea liberati) Gal. II. 19. vivificemur. Communionem autem cum Christo & justitia ejus in fide habemus, quae propriam justitiam abnegat, & Dei justitiam sitit, ut ei & misericordiae ejus animas nostras in bonis factis ad laudem ejus committamus.
units.tr: XXVI. Nor do they help, or do they strengthen the agreement between the Papists and the Evangelicals, who, with Walenburg and others, make the merit and righteousness of Christ into the twofold formal cause of justification: an intrinsic one, the righteousness of man inhering in him, and an extrinsic one, which they also call exemplary, and the condition of the formal cause. But inherent righteousness, being subsequent to justification, is neither its cause, nor its formal cause, nor its intrinsic formal cause. Nor is the merit and righteousness of Christ extrinsic to us, since Christ has been made righteousness for us, 1 Cor. 1.30; we are made the righteousness of God in him, 2 Cor. 5.21; we have righteousness through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is from God through faith, Phil. 3.9; we receive the gift of righteousness, Rom. 5.17; faith, or the righteousness of Christ apprehended by faith, is imputed to us for righteousness, ibid. 4.5. Nor is it merely an exemplary cause of justification, as if the righteousness of Christ were nothing other than an example of inherent righteousness, and not the cause of life, on account of which alone we are justified, or pronounced righteous, in the court of God. Nor is it merely the condition of the formal cause, that is, of inherent righteousness; for thus it would not be the true cause of our justification, but only of regeneration, or, as they themselves put it, of the "faculty of doing good works", which follows the justification of the ungodly and without which it cannot be obtained in any way. Rather, it is the one and only cause, whether it be called meritorious or formal (for human terms ought not to be prescribed to the Word of God), of the justification on account of which alone we are pronounced and absolved as righteous in the court of God. For the righteousness of Christ alone, neither that extrinsic one nor one inhering in us, but given to us together with Christ and in communion with him, in the judgment of God saves us and brings it about that, "through the law" (fulfilled by Christ), "we are made alive to the law" (freed from it by Christ), Gal. 2.19. We have communion with Christ and his righteousness in faith, which denies its own righteousness and thirsts for the righteousness of God, so that we may commit our souls, in good works, to him and to his mercy, to his praise.

units.la: XXVII. In eo etiam fucum Bellarminus, & cum eodem Walenburgii ejus verbis consensum cum Christo & Beliale machinari, ad irretiendos simplices, conati, faciunt, quod se nobiscum profiteri ajunt, nobis imputari merita Christi, quia nobis donata sunt, & possumus ea offerre Deo Patri pro peccatis nostris, quia Christus onus satisfaciendi in se suscepit, nosque Deo Patri reconciliavit. Si orthodoxo Scripturae sensu sic loquuntur, & credunt, quod ore profitentur, cur pro justitia inhaerente, ceu causa justificationis formalis, tanquam pro aris & focis suis, sed magis tamen pro his, quam pro illis, tanto studio & zelo belligerantur? Nam revera is, cui merita & satisfactiones Christi, onus satisfactionis in se suscipientis, sic imputantur, ut ea Deo Patri pro peccatis suis offerre possit, ille per & propter merita Christi, ceu justificationis extra Deum causam unicam a peccatis absolvitur, adeoque justificatur. Nam hoc ipsum Scripturae sensu, justificare est: Si ita illi sentiunt, & illis placet Christus ille doctor ad justitiam, unum superent, ut Tridentini Concilii anathemata deleant, & dextras nobiscum jungant. Sed latet anguis in herba. Nam merita quidem Christi nobis imputari fatentur, at justitiam ejus imputari praefracte negant; quasi non Christus justitiam Legis omnem implendo meruerit, & merita Christi aliud esse, quam justitia vitae & passionum vitam nobis promerens, & a peccatis absolvens, possint. Sed in re maximi momenti Sophistae ludunt, ut incautis imponant. Non enim merita Christi nobis in judicio Dei immediate ad justitiam & vitam sic imputari sentiunt, ut Christi merita & justitia, per fidem nobis donata & imputata, sola & unica justificationis causa, exclusa ab hac causalitate inhaerente justitia omni, sint: sed ut sint causa meritoria, uti loquuntur, extrinseca, exemplaris, & conditio causae formalis justificationis, hoc est, ut propter illa Deus justitiam homini infundat, cujus, ceu unicae causae formalis justificationis vi homo justificetur. Quae nec vera imputatio meritorum Christi est: nec illa imputatio est, quam Scriptura docet. Non vera, quia qui suo opere alteri beneficium meretur, ejus opus alteri non necessario imputatur. Imputatio enim est judicium uni tribuentis, quod alter fecit, vel passus est. Non etiam haec imputatio illa meritorum Christi est, quam in justificatione Scriptura urget, quia Christi merita peccatori imputari docet, non quatenus propter ea Deus movetur ad justitiam propriam homini infundendam, sed quatenus illa per fidem reputantur pro justitia, seu judicantur esse justitia illa, quam Lex Dei ab homine ad vitam & salutem requirit, Rom. IV. 4. Sicut enim cum Christo in judicio Dei peccata nostra imputata sunt, Esai. LIII. 6. & ipse pro nobis peccatum factus est, 2. Cor. V. 21. non ipse inhaerentem peccati habitum nactus est: ita cum ejus opera & merita homini imputantur, non eo inhaerentem justitiae habitum accipere intelliguntur, sed opera & merita Christi ejus esse, cui imputata sunt, judicantur; ut ipsi pro peccato suo mortui esse, & Legi Dei in solidum satisfecisse censeantur. Dulcissima enim illa αντιλαγη, optatissima permutatio est, ut quemadmodum Christo imputata peccata nostra fuerunt, ita nobis justitia ejus nobis imputetur, semper ob oculos nobis versetur oportet. Hic aliquid aliud qui supponunt, quo justificemur, hi fundamentum nostrae cum Deo reconciliationis evertunt.
units.tr: XXVII. In this too Bellarmine, and with him Walenburg, by his words, seek to weave a deception and to contrive an agreement between Christ and Belial, to ensnare the simple, when they profess to agree with us that "the merits of Christ are imputed to us, because they have been given to us, and we can offer them to God the Father for our sins, because Christ took upon himself the burden of satisfaction and reconciled us to God the Father." If they speak and believe in the orthodox sense of Scripture what they profess with their mouths, why do they wage war with such eagerness and zeal for inherent righteousness, as the formal cause of justification, as if for their altars and hearths, yet more for that than for these? For truly, he to whom the merits and satisfactions of Christ, and the burden of satisfaction taken upon himself by Christ, are imputed so that he can offer them to God the Father for his sins, is absolved from sins, and so justified, through and on account of the merits of Christ, as the sole cause of justification outside God. For this very thing, in the sense of Scripture, is "to justify". If they think thus, and if that Christ, the "teacher of righteousness", pleases them, let them overcome the one point, that they may remove the anathemas of the Council of Trent, and join right hands with us. But there is a snake in the grass. For they indeed confess that the merits of Christ are imputed to us, but they stubbornly deny that his righteousness is imputed; as if Christ had not merited the righteousness of the whole Law by fulfilling it, and as if the merits of Christ could be anything other than the righteousness of his life and sufferings, which obtains life for us and absolves us from sins. But these Sophists play tricks on a matter of the greatest moment, so that they may deceive the unwary. For they do not hold that the merits of Christ are imputed to us immediately, in the judgment of God, unto righteousness and life, in such a way that the merits and righteousness of Christ, given and imputed to us through faith, are the sole and only cause of justification, with all inherent righteousness excluded from this causality. Rather, they hold that they are the meritorious cause, as they put it, the extrinsic cause, the exemplary cause, and the condition of the formal cause of justification; that is, that God, on account of them, infuses righteousness into man, by the power of which, as the sole formal cause of justification, man is justified. This is neither a true imputation of the merits of Christ, nor the imputation which Scripture teaches. Not a true one, because one who merits a benefit for another by his work does not necessarily impute his work to the other; for imputation is the judgment by which one attributes to another what that other has done or suffered. Nor is it that imputation of the merits of Christ which Scripture urges in justification, because it teaches that the merits of Christ are imputed to the sinner, not in the sense that God is moved by them to infuse righteousness of his own into man, but in the sense that through faith they are reckoned as righteousness, or judged to be that righteousness which the Law of God requires of man for life and salvation, Rom. 4.4. For just as our sins were imputed to Christ in the judgment of God, Isa. 53.6, and he himself was made sin for us, 2 Cor. 5.21, without his having acquired a habit of sin inhering in him, so when his works and merits are imputed to a man, they are understood not to make him receive a habit of righteousness inhering in him, but his works and merits are judged to be his to whom they are imputed, so that he is deemed to have died for his sin and to have fully satisfied the Law of God. For that most sweet exchange, the most desired substitution (ἀντάλλαγη), is that just as our sins were imputed to Christ, so his righteousness should be imputed to us, and it must always be kept before our eyes. Those who suppose anything else by which we are justified undermine the foundation of our reconciliation with God.

units.la: XXVIII.
