Sed justificari hominem per justitiam propriam, seu infusum charitatis habitum, ut formalem justificationis causam, sive illud, unde homo peccator titulum & jus expectandi & petendi vitam habet, & quod Deus sine abnegatione sui pro tali titulo & fundamento ad vitam adjudicandam habet, & sapientissime ordinavit atque dedit, in quo solo justificationis vera ratio consistit, Scripturae universae repugnat. Etenim illa docet, hominem justificari gratis, gratia Dei, Rom. III. 24. Ubi gratiam, favorem, benevolentiam & χαρις Dei, qua ille non imputat nobis peccata, sed propter solam Christi redemptionem ea nobis remittit, & justos nos pronunciat, notari, supra ostendimus. Neque profecto in hoc negotio unquam gratiae nomine infusa qualitas intelligitur. Neque tantum gratiae Dei justificationem acceptam Scriptura refert, sed etiam illam ex justitia propria, & operibus, quae nos fecerimus, contingere, diserte negat. Colligimus, fide justificari hominem; χωρις εργων νομος sine operibus legis, ibid. III. 28. Scientes, ὁτι ἐξ ἐργων νομου, quod non justificetur homo ex operibus legis, Gal. II. 16. At justitia propria & inhaerens secundum legem exercetur, & legis opera protrudit. Clare Apostolus: Ut inveniar in ipso (Christo) non habens meam justitiam, quae ex lege est, sed illam, quae est per fidem Christi, justitiam ex Deo in fide, Phil. III. 9. Omnia autem legis opera, non viribus duntaxat naturae facta, neque legis tantum ceremonialis opera: omnemque justitiam propriam, sive per alienum meritum conciliatam & donatam, sive propriis viribus acquisitam, sic Scripturae removent. Non enim vel opera, vel justitiam propriam distinguunt; & καυχησιν gloriationem omnem, Rom. III. 27. excludunt, quae nisi remotis universis operibus, excludi nequit; & ipsius Abrahami, Patris credentium opera, ibid. IV. 2. &c. imo etiam Pauli regeniti, 1. Cor. IV. 4. Gal. II. 16. quin & ea, ad quae in Christo Jesu conditi sumus, Ephes. II. 10. excludit, & operibus & justitiae propria nusquam opera ex gratia facta, vel justitiam gratis donatam, sed fidem in Christum, & justitiam Dei, quae in fide est, opponunt. Nam non eum, qui ἐργάζεται operatur, sed qui credit in eum, qui impium justificat, justificari, Apostolus, Rom. IV. 5. pronuntiat; fidem omni operi, qualecunque illud sit, & quibuscunque viribus patratum sit, e diametro opponens. Et ne solam justitiam ex operibus legis ceremonialis excludi putemus, credere id vetat ipse Apostolus illam etiam justitiam, quae est ex factis vivificantibus, seu operibus, quae qui fecerit, in iis vivet, ibid. X. 5. ex qua est agnitio peccati, ibid. III. 20. quae iram operatur, ibid. IV. 15. quae universum mundum damnat, & Deo ὑπόδικον obnoxium reddit, ibid. III. 19. cordibus hominum inscripta est, ibid. II. 15. denique cujus violatae reos & gentibus & Judaeos, ibid. I. II. III. 1-24. peregit, excludens. Accedit, quod justificatio peccatoris illa est, qua ejus peccata expiantur, & debita, quorum in Adamo reus factus est, expunguntur. Atqui expiationem peccati admissi nulla antecedente vel consequente integerrima etiam obedientia, sed sola poena, quam lex dictat, exantlata expiari, supra probavimus. Neque enim lex poenitentiae conditionem admittit, quia legem iritam faciens χωρις διχαιωματων sine miseratione moritur, Heb. X. 28. & Christi adventu opus non fuisset, si lex poenitentiae tacitam conditionem includeret. At nec justitia, quam homo propriam habere potest, omnibus numeris consummata est, qualem solam vitae causam lex admittit. Imperfecta enim justitia, quae peccati admixtas scorias habet, ipsa apud Deum rea est; neque proin justificare, seu jus vitae cuiquam afferre potest. Et qui in uno impingit, reus est omnium, Jacob. II. 10. Atqui πολλοι ἁμαρτωλοι in multis impingimus omnes, ibid. III. 2. Quomodo justus est mortalis coram Deo? Si velit litigare coram eo, non poterit ei respondere ad unum ex mille, Job. IX. 2. 3. 20. Neque satisfaciunt, qui justitiam hominis habitualem perfectam, at actualem imperfectam esse regerunt. Nam opus, non habitus justificat. Fac hoc, & vives; Rom. X. 5. Habitum justitiae perfectum Adamus integer habuit; neque tamen cum eo justificatus est. Imo actualis ejus obedientia explorari debuit. Et acceptat quidem Deus in Christo qualemcunque rectitudinem eorum, qui justificati sunt: at pro perfecta, quae justitiae & vitae causa esse potuit, non acceptat, nisi illam, quae ad Legis Divinae rigidam amussim facta est. Obstat enim justitia & veracitas Dei, nec non peccatoris conditio. Ac licet Christi gratia justitiae nostrae defectum tegat, illa ipsa tamen operibus nostris in ordine ad effectum justificationis & salutis opponitur, Rom. XI. 6. Neque leve illud est, quod Scriptura justificationem per remissionem peccatorum definit. Per Christum annuntiatur vobis remissio peccatorum, & ab omnibus, quibus non potuistis in lege Mosis justificari, Act. XIII. 38. 39. David dicit beatitudinem illius hominis, cui Deus imputat justitiam sine operibus; Beati, quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, quorum tecta peccata sunt. Beatus vir, cui Dominus non imputat peccatum, Rom. IV. 6. 7. 8. Ubi imputatio justitiae, seu justificatio & remissio, seu non imputatio peccati aequipollent. Hinc Pharisaeus opera sua jactans justificatione excidit: Publicanus pro τω ιλασμω humiliter supplex domum suam δεδικαιωμενος justificatus rediit, Luc. XVIII. 11. 13. 14. Frivolum plane est, quod remissionem peccatorum non sola condonatione reatus peccati, sed etiam abluptione culpae per peccati expulsionem constare, & ad justificationem insuper renovationem hominis requiri pertendunt. Licet enim homini peccati reatus condonetur, quin idem a culpa peccati dominantis abluatur; tamen distincta haec beneficia sunt, quia reatus peccati per remissionem in justificatione, macula vero peccati dominantis, remissione peccati jam facta, in sanctificatione tollitur. Parum vero Tridentini sibi constant, cum justificationis duas partes, remissionem peccatorum, & renovationem mentis constituunt. Paulus enim Rom. IV. 6. 7. &c. ubi modum, quo homo coram Deo justificatur, plene declarat, justificationem tionem perfectam in peccatorum remissione & æquipollente eidem imputatione justitiæ sine operibus, adeóque sine renovatione mentis, collocat. Justitia certè inhærens, vel maculæ peccati deletio nec peccatorum remissio, nec justitiæ imputatio est; quia illa peccatorum condonatio ubique declaratur, hæc cum infusione habitus ἀσνφαλῶ est, quia, quod infunditur, non imputatur, & justitia infusa in operando, imputata in credendo consistit. Et posse remissionem peccati absque infusione justitiæ sua natura separari, satis docet experientia communis hominum, qui remittunt debita & injurias etiam illis, quibus neque divitias, neque justitiam conferunt vel infundunt. Sanè reconciliatio nostri cum Deo per mortem Filii, redemptio per sanguinem ipsius, & justificatio æquipollent, Rom. III. 24. V. 9. 10. Atqui reconciliatio nostri cum Deo per mortem Filii sola remissione peccatorum, 2. Cor. V. 18. 19. Redemptio quoque per sanguinem Christi eadem sola, Ephes. I. 7. Col. I. 14. definitur. Ergo par justificationis ratio est. Denique remissio peccatorum, & renovatio mentis realiter distinguuntur, quia diversissimis formis essentialibus constituuntur. Ergo eandem justificationem ingredi non possunt. Unde Andradius χερισφυγέτω quodam elapsurus statuit, Tridentinos, justificationem remissione peccatorum & renovatione mentis definientes, per remissionem peccatorum non intellexisse non imputationem peccati jam admissi, seu ablationem reatus peccati, sed ipsissimam charitatem infusam, quæ sua potentia peccatum mortificet & expungat. Ut jam remissio peccatorum & quotidiana renovatio & sanctificatio peccatoris in Schola Pontificiorum unum idémque sit. Quæ licentia immanis est quidvis pro lubitu asserentium. Denique si justitia inhærens forma est justi, seu jus habendis ad petendam vitam, atque sic causa vitæ, ea niti, in ea gloriari, ei confidere licet. Nam aliud docere, aliud credere non convenit. Quod credimus esse formam justitiæ, & causam juris nostri, ei in bona conscientia inniti debemus. Sed adversarii tamen modestiores fatentur, tutius esse, ut piæ conscientiæ merito Christi, quàm justitiæ propriæ confidant. Ergo intuta & falsa est doctrina, quæ docet, id quod in nobis est, esse δικαιω-μα & νόμως, atque ita fiduciæ nostræ fundum. Et si Christi justitia sola tutò nitimur, non peccamus, censentes, nos sic Deo gratias agere, & in eum credere debere, ut fateamur, nos non habere justitiam propriam, propter quam vitam adipisci valeamus, sed eam à Deo per justitiam Christi donatam nos expectare debere.
units.tr: XXVIII. But that a man is justified by his own righteousness, or by the infused habit of charity, as the formal cause of justification, meaning that which gives the sinner a title and right to expect and claim life, which God, without denying himself, holds as such a title and ground for awarding life, which he has most wisely ordained and given, and in which alone the true nature of justification consists, is opposed by all of Scripture. For Scripture teaches that man is justified freely, by the grace of God (Rom. 3:24). There we have already shown that grace means favour, goodwill and the χάρις of God, by which he does not impute our sins to us but forgives them for the sake of Christ's redemption alone, and pronounces us righteous. Certainly in this matter the grace of God is never understood as an infused quality. Scripture does not merely say that we are justified by the grace of God; it also plainly denies that we are justified by our own righteousness and by the works we have done. We conclude that a man is justified by faith, without the works of the law (Rom. 3:28). Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law [ἐξ ἔργων νόμου] (Gal. 2:16). But one's own inherent righteousness is exercised according to the law, and it puts forward the works of the law. The Apostle says clearly: that I may be found in him (Christ), not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness from God by faith (Phil. 3:9). Scripture removes all works of the law, not only those done by the powers of nature alone, nor only the works of the ceremonial law, and likewise every righteousness of one's own, whether procured by another's merit and bestowed, or acquired by one's own powers. Scripture does not distinguish between works and one's own righteousness; it excludes all boasting (Rom. 3:27), which cannot be excluded unless all works are set aside; it excludes even the works of Abraham, the father of believers (Rom. 4:2, etc.), indeed the works of Paul himself after his regeneration (1 Cor. 4:4; Gal. 2:16), and even those works for which we were created in Christ Jesus (Eph. 2:10). Nowhere do they set works done from grace, or a freely given righteousness, against works and one's own righteousness; they set faith in Christ, and the righteousness of God which is in faith, against them. For the Apostle declares that it is not the one who works who is justified, but the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5), setting faith directly against every work, of whatever kind it is and by whatever powers it is performed. And lest we think that only righteousness from the works of the ceremonial law is excluded, the Apostle himself forbids us to believe this, since he also excludes that righteousness which is from living-making deeds, or works, which whoever does, shall live by them (Rom. 10:5); through which comes the knowledge of sin (Rom. 3:20); which works wrath (Rom. 4:15); which condemns the whole world and makes it liable [ὑπόδικον] to God (Rom. 3:19); is written in the hearts of men (Rom. 2:15); and finally, by which Jews and Gentiles alike have been made guilty of its violation (Rom. 1–3:1–24). Moreover, the justification of a sinner is that by which his sins are atoned for and the debts, in which he became guilty in Adam, are blotted out. But we have already shown above that the atonement for a sin committed is made not by any most perfect obedience, before or after, but only by the punishment which the law prescribes being endured. For the law does not admit of a condition of repentance, since he who sets aside the law dies without mercy, apart from the righteous requirements [χωρὶς διακαιωμάτων] (Heb. 10:28); and there would have been no need for the coming of Christ if the law of repentance included a tacit condition. Yet the righteousness which a man can have as his own is not complete in every respect, such as the law alone admits as the cause of life. For imperfect righteousness, which has the dross of sin mixed into it, is itself guilty before God, and therefore cannot justify, or bring a right to life, to anyone. And whoever stumbles in one point is guilty of all (Jas. 2:10). But we all stumble in many things [πολλοὶ ἁμαρτωλοί] (Jas. 3:2). How can a mortal be just before God? If he wishes to contend with him, he cannot answer him one in a thousand (Job 9:2, 3, 20). Nor do those satisfy who reply that a man's habitual righteousness is perfect, but his actual righteousness is imperfect. For it is the deed, not the habit, that justifies. Do this, and you will live (Rom. 10:5). Adam, while still whole, had a perfect habit of righteousness; yet he was not justified by it. Indeed his actual obedience had to be tested. God does indeed accept, in Christ, whatever uprightness there is in those who are justified; but he does not accept it as the perfect righteousness which could be the cause of justice and life, but only that which is made according to the rigid rule of the divine law. For the justice and truthfulness of God stand in the way, as does the condition of the sinner. And although the grace of Christ covers the lack of our righteousness, yet that very grace is set against our works in relation to the effect of justification and salvation (Rom. 11:6). Nor is it a small point that Scripture defines justification as the remission of sins. Through Christ the forgiveness of sins is announced to you, and by him everyone is justified from all things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses (Acts 13:38, 39). David speaks of the blessedness of the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin (Rom. 4:6, 7, 8). Here the imputation of righteousness, or justification and remission, or the non-imputation of sin, are equivalent. Hence the Pharisee, boasting of his works, fell from justification; while the publican, humbly pleading for propitiation, went home justified [δεδικαιωμένος] (Luke 18:11, 13, 14). It is quite frivolous to contend that the remission of sins consists not only in the pardon of the guilt of sin, but also in the washing away of the fault through the expulsion of sin, and that renewal of man is required in addition to justification. For although the guilt of sin is pardoned to a man, it does not follow that he is at once washed from the fault of the sin that rules him. These are distinct benefits, because the guilt of sin is removed by remission in justification, while the stain of the dominant sin is removed in sanctification, once the remission of sin has already taken place. The Tridentines are indeed hardly consistent with themselves when they make the two parts of justification the remission of sins and the renewal of the mind. For Paul, Rom. 4:6, 7, etc., where he fully sets out the manner in which a man is justified before God, places perfect justification in the remission of sins and in the imputation of righteousness, equivalent to it, without works, and so without renewal of the mind. Certainly inherent righteousness, or the wiping away of the stain of sin, is neither the remission of sins nor the imputation of righteousness; because the forgiveness of sins is declared everywhere, while the infusion of a habit is [ἀσφαλῶς] securely something else, since what is infused is not imputed, and infused righteousness consists in working, while imputed righteousness consists in believing. And the common experience of men shows well enough that remission of sin can be separated by its nature from the infusion of righteousness, since men forgive debts and injuries even to those to whom they neither give nor infuse riches or righteousness. Surely the reconciliation of us with God through the death of the Son, redemption through his blood, and justification are equivalent (Rom. 3:24; 5:9, 10). But the reconciliation of us with God through the death of the Son is defined by the remission of sins alone (2 Cor. 5:18, 19). Redemption also through the blood of Christ is defined by the same alone (Eph. 1:7; Col. 1:14). Therefore the manner of justification is the same. Finally, the remission of sins and the renewal of the mind are really distinct, because they are constituted by entirely different essential forms; therefore they cannot enter into the same justification. Hence Andradius, about to slip away as if through his hands, held that the Tridentines, in defining justification by the remission of sins and the renewal of the mind, did not understand by remission of sins the non-imputation of a sin already committed, or the removal of the guilt of sin, but the very charity infused, which by its power mortifies and blots out sin. So that now the remission of sins, daily renewal and sanctification of the sinner are one and the same thing in the school of the Papists. This licence is monstrous, for anyone to assert whatever he pleases. Finally, if inherent righteousness is the form of the righteous man, or the right to claim life, and thus the cause of life, it is lawful to rest on it, to glory in it and to trust in it. For it is not fitting to teach one thing and believe another. What we believe to be the form of righteousness and the ground of our right, we ought to rest on with a good conscience. But even the more moderate adversaries confess that it is safer for a pious conscience to trust in the merit of Christ rather than in its own righteousness. Therefore the doctrine which teaches that what is in us is [δικαίωμα καὶ νόμος] a righteous requirement and a law, and so the ground of our trust, is unsafe and false. And if we rest securely on the righteousness of Christ alone, we do not sin, since we judge that we should thank God and believe in him in such a way as to confess that we do not have a righteousness of our own by which we may obtain life, but must look to God to bestow it on us through the righteousness of Christ.

units.la: XXIX. Habent Justitiarii ex Scripturis detortis ratiunculas, quas paucis diluemus.
units.tr: XXIX. The Justitiarii have little arguments drawn from twisted Scriptures, which we will briefly refute.

units.la: Ante omnia χάριν seu gratiam illam, qua nos justificari Apostolus Rom. III. 24. dixit, ad inhærentem justitiam violenter illi detorquent, quod supra jam diluimus. Similis παρεμμένει est illius charitatis, quæ in corda nostra per Spiritum S. diffusa, Rom. V. 5. dicitur, quæ neque in justificatione homini donari dicitur, & non tam hominis, quàm Dei, seu activa est, utpote quæ sola spei non pudefacientis fundamentum est, & in cordibus credentis ratione sensus & effectuum diffunditur. In justificatione porro,
units.tr: First of all, they violently twist that grace [χάριν], or grace, by which Paul says in Rom. 3:24 that we are justified, into inherent righteousness, which we have already refuted above. Similar [παρεμμένει] is that charity which, according to Rom. 5:5, is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. It is not said to be given to man in justification; it is active rather than a matter of man, that is, of God. It is the sole ground of a hope that does not put us to shame, and it is spread abroad in the hearts of believers by way of feeling and effects. Moreover, in justification,

units.la: Et Justitia-riorum ra-tionibus contrariis occurritur.
units.tr: And the arguments of the Justitiarii are met with contrary arguments.

units.la: hominem peccatorem καθισταθῆναι constitui, non declarari, vel haberi tantùm justum, & quidem quatenus τὴν περισσείαν τῆς χάριτος τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς δικαιοσύνης λαμβάνοντες abundantiam gratiæ & doni justitiæ accipit, ibid. v. 17. 19. nequicquam iidem objectant. Quasi non æquè per obedientiam unius, seu Adami primi, adeóque imputatam peccator constitui justus posset, atque per inobedientiam unius hominis, Adami secundi, imputatam etiam (supra v. 12.) multi ἁμαρτωλοὶ κατεστάθησαν peccatores constituti sunt, ibid. v. 19. ut ita constitutio illa veritatem ac certitudinem non tam qualitatis inhærentis, quàm relationis significet. Accedit, quòd Apostolus in futuro dicit: καταστήσονται constituentur justi, respectu tum promissionis, tum eidem respondentis consummationis, quæ fiet novissimo die, quo vi & valore obedientiæ seu δικαιώμα-τῶν Christi, quotquot ejus populus, hæreditas, Sponsa & membra sunt, & cum eo communionem habent, inculpati sine macula & ruga coram Deo sistentur, ut dicatur iis: Venite benedicti, hæreditate &c. Matth. XXV. 34. Illa verò abundantia gratiæ & doni justitiæ, quam accipientes in vita regnare v. 17. dicuntur, meram Dei liberalitatem & propositum perducendi ad finem vocationis & summum bonum, & justitiæ Christi donationem, qua præditi per eum regnabunt in vita, significat. Per quid enim perveniemus ad regnum vitæ, si non per gratiam & justitiæ Christi donum, & Christum ipsum? Hæc est voluntas Patris, qui me misit, ut quod mihi dedit, de eo non perdam, sed illud resuscitem ultimo die, Joh. VI. 39. Gratiæ Dei χάρις abundantia est, quòd Pater nos dedit Christo, & nos non perire, sed resuscitari ultimo die voluit; donum justitiæ, quod sicut nos Christo, ita ipse nobis datus & donatus est. Idem S. Paulus, justos conformari cum imagine Christi, Rom. VIII. 29. asserit: sed non in justitia inhærente perfecta & consummata, quæ δικαίωμα & causa justitiæ ac vitæ peccatoris esse posset; sed tum in justitia ejus, cum qua imputata per fidem communionem habemus: tum in inhærente propria, sed pro mensura gratiæ Spiritus S. & illa quidem in justificatione, hac in sanctificatione donata: tum denique in gloria. Etenim si conformitas illa nostra cum imagine Christi omni modo esset, neque exceptionem ullam pateretur, consequens foret, fideles etiam originaliter justos, & sine peccato esse, & justitiam suam pro δικαιώματα tali, quo aliis peccatoribus justitia & vita conciliari posset, constituere posse, quod cogitatu dictúque blasphemum foret. Alibi S. Paulus dixit, salvos nos factos esse per lavacrum regenerationis & renovationis Spiritus S. quem effudit in nos abunde per Jesum Christum Salvatorem nostrum, ut δικαιωθέντες justificati ejus gratia hæredes fiamus secundum spem vitæ æternæ, Tit. III. 5. 6. 7. non id docens, quòd renovatio sit ipsa justificatio, vel regeneratio; sed quòd Baptismus sit lavacrum regenerationis, institutum eum in finem, ut justificati hæreditatem obtineant. Jam & Regnum Dei, quod justitia etiam est, ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν intra nos est, Luc. XVII. 21. Rom. XIV. 17. Sed non ideo justitia, quæ vitæ peccatoris causa est, ei inhærens & propria est. Nam & justitia Regni Cœlorum, non nostra, sed Dei in Evangelio revelata ta ex fide in fidem,Rom.I.17. quæ primis capitibus Epistolæ hujus describitur, est: & Regnum Dei intus est, non quòd omnia ad Regnum Dei pertinentia homini inhæreant, sed quia eo tempore,quo Christus ita locutus est, Regnum Cœlorum,licèt sine observatione & pompa,appropinquavit, imò & vim passum est: & fideles Regni hujus cives, cum Christo cœlesti Rege, & bonis ejus communionem habent,eámque fidei suæ fructibus testantur. Præterea justitiam per Adamum oblatam, quæ inhærens fuit, restituit Christus, quoad ejus primitias in hac vita,& quoad consummationem in altera, quando Deus erit omnia in omnibus,1.Cor.XV.28. Neque tamen in hac vita restituitur, qualis in Adamo fuit, quia illa & originalis & peccati omnis expers, & mutabilis & merito Christi acquisita fuit; hæc non item. Sicut autem Adamus per justitiam,quam habuit,originalem justificatus non fuit,sed opere demum,quod à Deo exploratus edere debuit, præstito justificari potuisset: ita multò minùs homo peccator per infusum justitiæ habitum, ceu causam vitæ justificari potest.
units.tr: that a sinner is constituted [καθισταθῆναι], not merely declared or held to be just, and indeed in so far as he receives the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness [τὴν περισσείαν τῆς χάριτος τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς δικαιοσύνης λαμβάνοντες], as Rom. 5:17, 19 says, they object in vain. As if a sinner could not be constituted just, by imputation, through the obedience of one, that is, of the first Adam, just as, by imputation, through the disobedience of one man, the second Adam, many were constituted sinners [ἁμαρτωλοὶ κατεστάθησαν] (Rom. 5:19, see also v. 12). So that constitution signifies the truth and certainty not so much of an inherent quality as of a relation. Besides, the Apostle says in the future, they shall be constituted [καταστήσονται] just, with respect both to the promise and to the consummation which corresponds to it, which will take place on the last day. On that day, by the force and value of the obedience, or righteous acts [δικαιώμα-τῶν], of Christ, all who are his people, his inheritance, his bride and members, and who have communion with him, will be presented blameless and without spot or wrinkle before God, so that to them is said: "Come, blessed, inherit," etc. (Matt. 25:34). But that abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness, which those who receive it are said to reign in life (Rom. 5:17), signifies the pure liberality of God, his purpose of bringing us to the end of our calling and the highest good, and the gift of Christ's righteousness, by which those endowed with it through him will reign in life. For by what means shall we attain to the kingdom of life, if not through grace and the gift of Christ's righteousness, and Christ himself? "This is the will of the Father who sent me, that of all he has given me I should lose nothing, but raise it up at the last day" (John 6:39). The abundance of God's grace [χάρις] is that the Father has given us to Christ, and willed that we should not perish but be raised up on the last day. The gift of righteousness is that, just as we were given to Christ, so he himself has been given and bestowed upon us. Paul likewise asserts that the just are conformed to the image of Christ (Rom. 8:29), but not in perfect and consummated inherent righteousness, which could be the righteous act [δικαίωμα] and cause of the justice and life of a sinner. It is rather in his righteousness, with which we have communion through faith by imputation; in our own inherent righteousness, given in measure by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the latter in justification, the former in sanctification; and finally in glory. For if this conformity of ours with the image of Christ were complete in every way and admitted no exception, it would follow that believers are also originally just and without sin, and that they could constitute their own righteousness as a righteous act [δικαιώματα] of such a kind that it could procure righteousness and life for other sinners. That would be blasphemous to think or to say. Elsewhere Paul says: "We have been saved through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour, so that, justified [δικαιωθέντες] by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life" (Titus 3:5-7). He does not teach there that renewal is itself justification or regeneration, but that Baptism is the washing of regeneration, instituted to this end, that the justified may obtain the inheritance. Again, the Kingdom of God, which is also righteousness, is within you [ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν] (Luke 17:21; Rom. 14:17). Yet it does not follow that the righteousness which is the cause of a sinner's life is inherent in him and his own. For the righteousness of the Kingdom of Heaven is not ours but God's revealed in the Gospel, from faith to faith (Rom. 1:17), as is described in the first chapters of this Epistle. And the Kingdom of God is within you not because everything pertaining to the Kingdom of God adheres to man, but because at the time when Christ spoke thus, the Kingdom of Heaven, though without observation and pomp, drew near, and indeed suffered violence. Believers, citizens of this Kingdom, have communion with Christ the heavenly King and his goods, and attest this by the fruits of their faith. Moreover, Christ restores the righteousness offered through Adam, which was inherent, in its first fruits in this life, and in its consummation in the other, when God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28). Yet it is not restored in this life in the form it had in Adam, because that righteousness was both original, free from all sin, and unchangeable, and was not acquired by Christ's merit; this one is not so. Just as Adam was not justified by the original righteousness he possessed, but could have been justified only by the work he was bound to perform, once tested by God, so much less can a sinner be justified by an infused habit of righteousness as the cause of life.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Cùm ergo justitia inhærens homini δικαίωμα seu causa vitæ & juris ad vitam, qualis in judicio Dei ad justificationem requiritur, nullo modo esse posset, sequitur, solam Christi justitiam & meritum causæ hujus in Dei judicio vices sustinere. Neque ab hac si discesseris, alia ostendi potest. Et hanc solam ejusmodi δικαιώματα esse, supra comprobavimus. Ideo hæc justitia, cui adducendæ Filius servi conditionem subiit,Dei justitia tum à Prophetis passim,inprimis, Psal.CXLIII.1.11. Esaj. LVI.1. tum ab Apostolo Rom.I.17. III.22. X.3. & justitia à Deo,Esaj.LIV.17. ex Deo,Phil. III.9. & Deus justitia nostra, Psal.IV.2. justitia nostra, Jer.XXIII.6. XXXIII.15.16. appellatur. Est enim jus à Deo donatum; & Deus ipse ὑπακοήν obedientiam Filii, quæ meritum vitæ esse potest,præstat,& nonnisi in communione cum Christo illa obtinetur; & ea sola cum gloria Dei ad excludendam gloriationem hominis conjuncta est, & Deus per propositionem Filii sui,ceu ἱλαστήριον ejus, in quo Deus placatus invenitur, justitiam & decentiam suam in eo confitentem, quòd justificat impium,qui in Christo Jesu est,demonstrat.
units.tr: Since, then, inherent righteousness cannot in any way be the δικαίωμα [righteous claim], that is, the ground of life and of a right to life, which is required for justification in the judgment of God, it follows that the righteousness of Christ alone, and the merit of this ground, stands in for us before the judgment of God. If one departs from this, no other ground can be shown. We have already proved above that this alone is such a δικαίωμα. For this reason this righteousness, to which the Son of God submitted to the condition of a servant in order to bring it forward, is called the righteousness of God by the Prophets everywhere, especially at Ps. 143.1, 11 and Isa. 56.1, and by the Apostle at Rom. 1.17, 3.22, 10.3; also righteousness from God (Isa. 54.17), from God (Phil. 3.9), God our righteousness (Ps. 4.2), and our righteousness (Jer. 23.6, 33.15–16). For it is a right given by God, and God himself provides the obedience of the Son, which can be the merit of life [ὑπακοή]. It is obtained only in communion with Christ, and it alone is joined with the glory of God so as to exclude human boasting. And God, by setting forth his Son as his ἱλαστήριον [propitiation], in whom God is found reconciled, shows that he is just in this, that he justifies the ungodly who are in Christ Jesus.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Sed justitia tamen illa Dei Christi merito acquisita,quodammodo nostra esse debet; neque non nostra in Dei judicio ad justificationem nostram quicquam valet. Lex enim ab homine justificando obedientiam & justitiam perfectissimam exigit. Eam nisi quodammodo possideat homo, & Deo in judicio ejus integerrimo præstare valeat,justificari,hoc est, justus pronuntiari, &, peccator quidem,à peccato absolvi, & vita potiri non potest. Sicut autem debitor æs quidem alienum expungere tenetur,sed non ita,ut nonnisi ex peculio suo illud expungere teneatur,& non per Sponsorem seu vadem à judice probatum, solutionem promittentem, & æs pro debitore appendentem,expungere illud possit,atque dum pro ipso Sponsor sic solvit. Solutio ei debitori imputatur,& per eam creditori in solidum satisfactum censetur; ita peccator omnino solutio-
units.tr: But that righteousness of God, acquired by the merit of Christ, must in some sense be ours, and it is of no avail for our justification in God's judgment unless it is in some sense ours. For the law demands from the man to be justified the most perfect obedience and righteousness. Unless a man in some sense possesses this, and is able to render it to God in his most upright judgment, he cannot be justified, that is, pronounced righteous, and, though a sinner, be absolved from sin and obtain life. Just as a debtor is indeed bound to discharge his debt, but not in such a way that he must discharge it only from his own means, and so a surety or bondsman approved by the judge, who promises payment and weighs out the money on the debtor's behalf, cannot discharge it; and while the surety pays for him in this way, the payment is imputed to the debtor, and by it the creditor is deemed fully satisfied; so the sinner altogether owes payment to God

units.la: nem Deo debet,& justitiam præstare tenetur; sed non ita ex peculio suo, adeóque propriam, qua omni destituitur,præstare tenetur, ut aliena Sponsoris,à Deo ipso dati & acceptati satisfactio & justitia peccatori in judicio Dei imputata non sufficiat. Quæ Sponsoris justitia licèt aliena sit qualitate,quia Christo inhæret,& ab eodem acquisita solo est: tamen nostra est lege propter justitiam à vade præstitam absolvente,& judicio Dei, quo non imputatur nobis peccatum,sed imputatur nobis,atque sic donatur justitia Christi, ceu causa vitæ; ut sic qui qualitate injusti sumus,lege & judicio Dei formaliter justi,nec culpæ,nec accusationi,nec pœnæ obnoxii censeamur & simus. Lex enim eum,qui in Christo est, & justitiam ejus habet, nec accusare,nec damnare potest,sed absolvere tenetur; quæ sic potentia peccati,pro quo satisfactum non est, 1.Cor. XV.56. dicitur,& ἀδύναμον impotentiam peccatum nondum expiatum & remissum condemnandi, Rom. VIII.3. habet, ut etiam peccatorem,pro cujus peccato à Christo plenissimè satisfactum est, absolvere à peccato,& justum pronuntiare possit,imò debeat. Quæ non Legis & Evangelii confusio,sed distinctio & genuina explicatio est, quia in Evangelio & fœdere gratiæ non aliter salvamur, quàm per impletionem conditionis,sub qua vita æterna in lege & fœdere operum promissa est; sed non à nobis, verùm à Christo Sponsore præstitam, in qua ita lex, seu potiùs secundum Legem suam legislator, & judex Deus acquiescit, ut eum, pro quo Christus à Deo judice acceptatus ejus postulatum & justitiam omnem implevit,non tantùm non condemnare possit, sed etiam penitus absolvat. Nam Lex Spiritus vitæ Christi (justitia Christi, quæ per Spiritum ejus lex Christi facta est,& nos Spiritui Christi sic addicit, ut nos,tanquam suos,occupet,in nobis habitet & vivat) in Christo Jesu liberum me fecit à lege peccati & mortis (à servitute peccati,cui Lex peccatorum, mancipavit,& sententia mortis me liberavit,ut lex non amplius servituti peccati me subjicere,vel condemnare possit) Rom.VIII.2. Justificatio certè legalis & Evangelica non in eo differunt,quòd qui Evangelicè justificantur, aliter quàm per & propter impletionem conditionis in lege ad vitam requisitam, hoc est,obedientiam perfectam & perseverantem justificentur, sed in eo, quòd cùm ipsi conditionem hanc non impleverint nec omnino implere potuerint,impletio à Sponsore facta iis imputetur.
units.tr: and is bound to render righteousness. But he is not bound to render it from his own means, and so from his own righteousness, of which he is wholly destitute, in such a way that the satisfaction and righteousness of the surety, given and accepted by God himself and imputed to the sinner in God's judgment, would be insufficient. Although this righteousness of the surety is alien in quality, because it inheres in Christ and is acquired by him alone, nevertheless it is ours by the law, on account of the righteousness supplied by the bondsman, which absolves us, and by the judgment of God, by which sin is not imputed to us but righteousness is imputed to us, and so the righteousness of Christ is given to us as the cause of life; so that we who are unrighteous in quality may be counted and be formally righteous by the law and judgment of God, liable neither to guilt, nor accusation, nor punishment. For the law can neither accuse nor condemn the one who is in Christ and has his righteousness, but is bound to absolve him. This law, which thus has the power of sin, for which satisfaction has not been made, is called "the power of sin" [1 Cor. 15:56], and has the impotence [ἀδύναμον, adynamon] to condemn sin not yet atoned for and remitted [Rom. 8:3], so that it is able, and indeed ought, to absolve from sin and pronounce righteous even the sinner for whose sin Christ has fully made satisfaction. This is not a confusion of Law and Gospel, but their distinction and genuine explanation, because in the Gospel and the covenant of grace we are saved in no other way than through the fulfilment of the condition under which eternal life was promised in the law and the covenant of works; yet this fulfilment is not performed by us but by Christ our Surety. In it the law, or rather God as lawgiver and judge according to his own law, is so satisfied that he who has been accepted by God the judge, for whom Christ has fulfilled his demand and all righteousness, can not only not be condemned, but is altogether absolved. For "the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death" [Rom. 8:2] (the righteousness of Christ, which by his Spirit has become the law of Christ, and so assigns us to the Spirit of Christ that it takes possession of us as its own, dwells and lives in us), freeing me from the servitude of sin, to which the law of sin enslaved me, and from the sentence of death, so that the law can no longer subject me to the servitude of sin or condemn me. Legal and evangelical justification certainly do not differ in this: that those justified in the Gospel are not justified otherwise than through and on account of the fulfilment of the condition required for life in the law, that is, perfect and persevering obedience; rather they differ in this: that although they themselves have not fulfilled this condition, and could not fulfil it at all, the fulfilment done by the Surety is imputed to them.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Nam qui legem obedientiam simul perfectam & perseverantem, simul propriam essentialiter requirere pertendunt, næ illi malè saluti peccatoris consulunt,& Socinianis aperte velificantur. Cùm enim Deus legem propter ejus immutabilitatem, & suam veracitatem nunquam relaxaverit, si propriam illa obedientiam & justitiam ita postulat,ut postulatum justitiæ propriæ de essentia legis sit,nondum illi à quoquam satisfactum est, & peccator legi adhuc subjectus, Christo ut Domino suo addici & mancipari non potest. Vivit ita lex, & dominatur homini, quandiu vivit; sicut mulier obnoxia est legi viri, quandiu is cum lege sua mulierem re integra vinciente, vivit; & adultera est,si legem eam,marito & lege matrimonii trimonii vivente, violet, Rom. VII. 1--5. Lex igitur obedientiam perfectam & perseverantem postulat. At cum propriam postulat, id non est de essentia justitiae, quam lex requirit. Licet ergo lex obedientiam propriam exigat, tamen per impletionem conditionis in lege requisitae, & à Sponsore nostro praestitae justificamur, & vitam consequimur. Perinde ut non obstante eo, quòd lex peccatori poenam comminatur: comminationi eo satisfit, cùm Christus poenam in se suscipit & exantlat. Non enim id poenae mortis peccanti denuntiatae essentiale est, ut infligatur peccanti, sed ut infligatur ob peccatum. Quod similitudine praemii, gratiae & ultionis manifestum est. Nam praemium saepe in bene meriti liberos, vel cognatos; & gratia in propinquos ejus, qui beneficium contulit; & ultio, si in potestate puniendis id sit, in ejus, qui offendit, amicos conferri solet, neque eo desinunt esse, quod sunt, praemium, gratia, ultio. Pari ratione conditioni obedientiae ad vitam requisitae illud essentiale est, ut impleatur: sed non ut impleatur ab eo, qui eam debendi reus est. Quod in debitis pecuniariis inprimis clarissimum est. Solvere debitor tenetur centum florenorum debitum. De essentia debiti est, ut omnino creditori bona fide solvatur. Nam ei per restitutionem pecuniae creditae ab alio etiam velut Sponsore factam satisfit, quia tantum recepit, quantum debit. Denique licet homo peccator justificandus justitiam propriam, quam nullam habet, ejerare teneatur; tamen nec simpliciter alienam, sed quodammodo suam, propter Sponsoris cum eo communionem, & justitiae Sponsoris in judicio Dei imputationem, praestat. Ideo Jehova dicitur justitia nostra, Jerem. XXIII. 5. 6. XXXIII. 15. 16. & nobis factus justitia, 1. Cor. I. 30. & nos fieri justitiam Dei in Christo, 2. Cor. V. 21. Judicamus enim, si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, quòd omnes mortui sint, ibid. v. 15.
units.tr: Those who insist that the law requires obedience that is at once perfect, persevering, and essentially one's own are doing a poor service to the salvation of sinners, and they openly run before the wind with the Socinians. For since God has never relaxed the law, on account of its immutability and his own truthfulness, if it demands obedience and righteousness as one's own, so that the demand for one's own righteousness belongs to the essence of the law, then the law has not yet been satisfied by anyone, and the sinner, still subject to the law, cannot be assigned and handed over to Christ as his Lord. The law lives and rules over a man for as long as it lives, just as a woman is bound to her husband's law for as long as he lives, the law holding her while the marriage is intact; and she is an adulteress if she violates that law while her husband and the law of marriage are alive (Rom. 7:1–5). The law therefore demands perfect and persevering obedience. But when it demands this as one's own, that is not of the essence of the righteousness which the law requires. Therefore, although the law exacts obedience as one's own, we are nevertheless justified, and obtain life, through the fulfilment of the condition required by the law and rendered by our Surety. It is just as, notwithstanding the fact that the law threatens punishment to the sinner, the threat is satisfied when Christ takes that punishment upon himself and endures it. For it is not essential to the punishment of death threatened against the sinner that it be inflicted on the sinner, but that it be inflicted on account of sin. This is clear from the analogy of reward, grace and vengeance. For a reward is often conferred on the children or kinsfolk of one who has deserved well; grace is conferred on the relatives of the one who conferred the benefit; and vengeance, where the avenger has the power to punish, is commonly directed at the friends of the offender; and they do not cease to be what they are: reward, grace, vengeance. By the same reasoning, what is essential to the condition of obedience required for life is that it be fulfilled, but not that it be fulfilled by the one who is bound to owe it. This is most clearly seen in money debts. A debtor is bound to pay a debt of a hundred florins. It is of the essence of a debt that it be fully paid to the creditor in good faith. For the creditor is satisfied by the restitution of the money lent, even when it is made by another as surety, because he has received exactly what is owed him. Finally, although a sinner who is to be justified is bound to render a righteousness of his own, which he does not have, nevertheless he offers not simply an alien righteousness but, in a certain sense, his own, on account of the communion of the Surety with him and the imputation of the Surety's righteousness in the judgment of God. Therefore Jehovah is called our righteousness (Jer. 23:5–6; 33:15–16), and Christ was made righteousness for us (1 Cor. 1:30), and we are made the righteousness of God in him (2 Cor. 5:21). For we judge that, if one died for all, then all have died (ibid. v. 15).

units.la: XXXIII. Enimvero Christi justitiam, satisfactionem & meritum in Dei judicio nobis donari, & imputari, atque sic donata & imputata ea nos justificari, negari non potest.
units.tr: XXXIII. Indeed, that Christ's righteousness, satisfaction and merit are given to us and imputed to us in the judgment of God, and that we are justified by them so given and imputed, cannot be denied.

units.la: Sicut enim soluta à fidejussore pecunia debitori, pro quo soluta est, imputatur, & exhibita à vade satisfactio ei, cujus nomine exhibita est, imputatur pariter: ita Christi Sponsoris nostri satisfactio ex gratia Dei Patris nobis, quorum vice illa praestita est, donatur & imputatur: atque sic imputata & donata justitia Christi illa ipsa est, qua in judicio Dei justificamur. Ea enim justitia sola justificamur, qua liberatus à reatu nostro est vas & Sponsor noster. Atqui is à reatu nostro plenissimè liberatus est vi satisfactionis à se pro nobis praestitae. Ergo sola ea plenissimè justificamur. Ecquis vero negaverit, qua debitorum nostrorum solutione deletum est chirographum nobis subcontrarium, Col. II. 14. eadem nos Deo creditori nostro desiisse ipsi esse obnoxios? Qua justitia redempti sumus à condemnatione & maledictione Legis, Gal. III. 13. eadem nos esse justificatos? Qua satisfactione pro nobis satisfactum est justitiae Divinae perfectissimè, nósque adeò Deo reconciliati fuimus, ut nos in filios & haeredes adoptarit, ea nobis Deum omnino placatum esse? Qua denique propitiatione peccata nostra expiata & perfectè purgata sunt, ea nos obtinere jus ingrediendi in Templum Dei?
units.tr: For just as money paid by a surety is imputed to the debtor for whom it was paid, and satisfaction offered by a bondsman is likewise imputed to the one in whose name it was offered, so the satisfaction of Christ our Surety is, by the grace of God the Father, given and imputed to us, in whose place it was rendered; and the righteousness of Christ, so imputed and given, is that very righteousness by which we are justified in the judgment of God. For we are justified by that righteousness alone by which our Surety and bondsman was freed from our guilt. But he has been most fully freed from our guilt by the power of the satisfaction he rendered for us. Therefore by that alone we are most fully justified. Who would deny that by the same payment of our debts by which the handwriting that was against us was blotted out (Col. 2:14), we have ceased to be bound to God our creditor? Who would deny that by the same righteousness by which we were redeemed from the condemnation and curse of the law (Gal. 3:13), we have been justified? Who would deny that by the satisfaction made for us, the justice of God has been most perfectly satisfied, and that we have been so reconciled to God that he has adopted us as sons and heirs, and that God is wholly appeased toward us? And who would deny that by the propitiation by which our sins have been expiated and perfectly cleansed, we obtain the right to enter the temple of God?

units.la: XXXIV. Justitiam illam Christi nobis imputari, donari, atque sic nostram fieri, Scripturae testantur. Ante omnia enim ipsam vocem imputationis, sensu adscribendi, adjudicandi, attribuendi, numerandi, censendi inter sua, quae proprie sua non sunt; frequentant. Ei qui operatur, merces ... non imputatur secundum gratiam, sed ... secundum debitum. Ei vero qui non operatur, sed credit in eum, qui justificat impium, imputatur fides ejus (seu id quod credit, quod Christus & ejus justitia est) ad justitiam, Rom. IV. 4. 5. Sic enim se ipsum explicat Apostolus, dicens, quòd Abraham us Deo crediderit, & id ei ad justitiam imputatum fit, vers. 3. 22. Non scriptum est, addit, propter ipsum solum, quòd ei imputatum fit, sed etiam propter nos, quibus vult imputare credentibus in eum, qui suscitavit Dominum nostrum Jesum ex mortuis, qui traditus est propter peccata nostra, & excitatus est propter justificationem nostram, vers. 23--25. Ubi manifeste objectum fidei, quod justificationis & salutis unicam & solam in se causam meritoriam continet, pro fide, quae nobis ad justitiam imputatur, asseritur. Unde concludit: Justificati igitur fide (ad justitiam imputata) pacem habemus erga Deum, cap. V. 1.
units.tr: XXXIV. The Scriptures testify that this righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, given to us, and so made ours. For above all they frequently use the very word "imputation" in the sense of ascribing, adjudging, attributing, reckoning, or counting among one's own things those that are not properly one's own. "To him who works, the wages are not imputed according to grace, but according to debt. But to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is imputed (that is, what he believes, that Christ and his righteousness are) for righteousness" (Rom. 4:4–5). For the Apostle explains himself in this way, saying that Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness (vv. 3, 22). It is not written, he adds, for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him, but also for ours, to whom it will be imputed, who believe in him who raised our Lord Jesus from the dead, who was delivered up for our sins and raised for our justification (vv. 23–25). Here the object of faith, which contains within itself the sole and only meritorious cause of justification and salvation, is asserted in place of the faith that is imputed to us for righteousness. Hence he concludes: Therefore, having been justified by faith (imputed for righteousness), we have peace with God (ch. 5:1).

units.la: Neque enim fides ut opus aut qualitas ad justitiam imputari potest, quia imputatur non operanti, sed id quod fides apprehendit, seu res credita, Christus & justitia ejus imputatur. Eodem etiam sensu Paulus voce alibi utitur. Si praeputium jura legis servaverit, nonne praeputium illius ... pro circumcisione reputabitur? ibid. II. 26. Ubi liquet, circumcisionem, quae gentilitati deerat, ei imputatum iri, id est, adjudicatum iri, si jura legis servet. Alibi: In prima defensione nemo mihi adfuit, sed omnes me deseruerunt. ... Ne iis imputetur, 2. Tim. IV. 16. Ubi desertionis ... petit Apostolus iis, à quibus tempore maximè necessario deserebatur, non imputari, hoc est, à Deo perinde, ac si non esset, haberi, eíque non adjudicari. Non obstat igitur, quòd Apostolus in hoc argumento non verbo composito, sed simplici usus est, quia non absolute dictum, sed cum addito dandi casu, semper vim compositi habet. Neque aliter Vulgatus reddit, quàm imputare. Unde Varinus: Puerorum peccata Deus patribus imputat. Quomodo etiam vox Hebraea licet primò significet putare, cogitare, tamen etiam pro & accipitur, Levit. XVII. 4. Num. XVIII. 27. 30. Quidni ergo etiam Genes. XV. 6. & reputatum & imputatum dicamus? Inprimis cùm Apostolus significanter vertat non reputata est justitia, sed in justitiam, Rom. IV. 22.
units.tr: For faith cannot be imputed for righteousness as a work or a quality, because what is imputed is not the act of believing but what faith apprehends, namely the thing believed: Christ and his righteousness are imputed. Paul uses the word in the same sense elsewhere: If the uncircumcised keep the requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision? (Rom. 2:26). Here it is clear that circumcision, which the Gentile lacked, will be imputed to him, that is, adjudged to him, if he keeps the requirements of the law. Elsewhere: At my first defence no one stood by me, but all deserted me. ... May it not be imputed to them (2 Tim. 4:16). Here the Apostle asks that the desertion by which he was abandoned in his most pressing hour should not be imputed to those who deserted him, that is, that they should not be regarded by God as if they had not deserted him, nor be adjudged guilty of it. It is therefore no objection that the Apostle in this argument used the simple verb and not a compound; for when it is not used absolutely but with a dative added, it always has the force of the compound. Nor does the Vulgate render it otherwise than imputare. Hence Varinus: God imputes the sins of children to their fathers. Likewise the Hebrew word, although it primarily means to think, to reckon, is also taken for to impute (Lev. 17:4; Num. 18:27, 30). Why then should we not also say, from Gen. 15:6, that it was reckoned and imputed? Especially since the Apostle significantly translates not it was reckoned as righteousness but into righteousness (Rom. 4:22).

units.la: XXXV. Verbum porro & imputare modò refertur ad propria, modò ad aliena, quae imputantur. Ad propria relatum significat id, quod in aliquo verè est, ejusdem
units.tr: XXXV. Moreover, the verb to impute is sometimes referred to one's own things, and sometimes to the things of others that are imputed. When referred to one's own, it signifies what truly is in someone, to acknowledge as belonging to the same person,

units.la: At justitia Christi peccatori in judicio Dei donatur & imputatur.
units.tr: But the righteousness of Christ is given and imputed to the sinner in the judgment of God.

units.la: Impuratio vox in hoc argumento attributionem rei alienae notat.
units.tr: The word imputation, in this argument, denotes the attribution of a thing that belongs to another.

units.la: Duplex tamen imputatio est, rei vel alienae, vel propriae. dem esse agnoscere, judicare, & vel ad poenam vel ad praemium referre; quomodo Rom. IV. 8. λογίζεσθαι imputari, vel non imputari peccatum, & Pinchaso zelus suus ad justitiam imputatus, Psal. CVI. 31. dicitur. Ad aliena relatum significat tribuere alicui, vel adjudicare, quod tamen ejus non est, nec ei inhaeret, sed alii inhaeret, vel adest; velut cum Paulus ad Philemonem dixit: si quid laeserit, ἐλλόγει μοι, mihi imputa, ego rependam, Philem. vers. 18.19. Neuter tamen ille significatus infusionem notat. Non prior, quia quae pro talibus agnoscuntur, judicantur, jam insunt, non infunduntur. Non posterior, qui maxime hujus loci est, quia nec Paulo Onesimi, nec Christo nostra peccata inhaerebant cum utrisque imputata fuerint. Utraque nempe imputatio judicialis actus est extrinsecus illi, cui aliquid sive proprium sive alienum imputatur. Et in nostro argumento fides imputari ad justitiam dicitur sine operibus μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ non operanti, Rom. IV. 5. Sed cui fides, seu justitia aliena Christi apprehensa ad justitiam imputatur, ei etiam opus aliquod proprium, cui fides cooperatur, imputari ad justitiam, alio modo, hoc est, declarari a Deo argumentum justitiae & benedictionis paratae & praemii potest. Quomodo & Christus communionem, quam cum ejus afflictis habuerimus, ad justitiam reputabit, seu argumentum benedictionis, justitiae & haereditatis declarabit, Matth. XXV. 34.35. & Pinchaso zelum suum Deus reputavit justitiam, Psal. CVI. 31. quia declaravit, eum ex zelo pro se id fecisse, & ei foedus suum addixit, & in gratiae suae argumentum ei Sacerdotium perpetuum dedit, Num. XXV. 11. 12. 13. Talis est justificatio ex operibus, de qua Jacobus, & ex eodem nos infra. Sed haec, uti diximus, imputatio operis proprii non est hujus loci, ubi imputatio operis alieni intelligitur, & ubi phrasis illa λογίζεσθαι reputari vel imputari fidem ad justitiam, metaphorica est, & a mercatoribus ad forum Divinum translata videtur. Solent nempe tabulas accepti & expensi conficere, & in his erogata, adeoque debita, in illis pro debitis accepta & soluta scribere. Deus non incuriosus & negligens sui honoris & beneficii est. Rigidus computator est. In libro ejus scriptum est, quid expenderit & dederit nobis, & quid nos ei debeamus. Cumque in altera pagina accepti nostra obedientia & solutio scribi non posset, cum copiam bonam ejerare debeamus, nec omnino solvendo pares simus; quid ibi scribitur, ut justificemur? Christi utique δικαιώματα sive meritum, quod ad multorum justificationem valet; ejus participes simus, & quae donum est sanctificantis Dei, per cujus Spiritum, qui eam operatur, in unum corpus baptizamur.
units.tr: Imputation is twofold, of what belongs to another and of what belongs to oneself. To impute is to acknowledge, to judge, and to refer something either to punishment or to reward. So in Rom. 4:8 sin is said to be reckoned [λογίζεσθαι] as imputed or not imputed, and in Ps. 106:31 Phinehas's zeal is said to have been imputed to him for righteousness. When referred to what is another's, it means to ascribe or adjudge to someone what is not his and does not inhere in him, but inheres in or is present in another. So when Paul said to Philemon, if he has wronged you, [ἐλλόγει μοι] put it to my account, I will repay it, Philem. 18-19. Yet neither of these senses denotes infusion. Not the first, because what is acknowledged as belonging to someone is judged already to inhere, not infused. Not the second, which is the one most relevant to this place, because Onesimus's wrongs did not inhere in Paul, nor our sins in Christ, when they were imputed to them. Both kinds of imputation are judicial acts, external to the one to whom something, whether his own or another's, is imputed. In our subject, faith is said to be imputed for righteousness without works, to the one not working [μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ], Rom. 4:5. But to the one to whom faith, or the alien righteousness of Christ laid hold of, is imputed for righteousness, some work of his own, to which faith contributes, can also be imputed for righteousness, in another way. That is, God can declare it to be a sign of righteousness, of the blessing prepared, and of the reward. Thus Christ too will reckon for righteousness the fellowship we have had with his afflicted, or will declare it a sign of blessing, righteousness and inheritance, Matt. 25:34-35. And God reckoned Phinehas's zeal to him as righteousness, Ps. 106:31, because he declared that he had done it out of zeal for him, assigned him his covenant, and gave him a perpetual priesthood as a token of his grace, Num. 25:11-13. Such is justification by works, of which James speaks, and of which we shall speak below. But this imputation of one's own work, as we have said, does not belong to this place, where the imputation of another's work is meant, and where the phrase λογίζεσθαι, faith being reckoned or imputed for righteousness, is metaphorical and seems to have been transferred from merchants to the divine court. Merchants, after all, keep ledgers of receipts and expenditures, and in them write what has been paid out and so is owed, and in the other column what has been received or paid as owed. God is not careless or negligent of his own honour and benefits. He is a strict reckoner. In his book it is written what he has laid out and given us, and what we owe him. Since our obedience and payment cannot be written on the other page, because we ought to bring a good account and are in no way able to pay, what is written there so that we may be justified? Surely the δικαιώματα, that is, the merit of Christ, which avails for the justification of many. Let us be partakers of it, and of the gift of God who sanctifies, through whose Spirit, who works it, we are baptized into one body.

units.la: XXXVI. Idem S. Paulus imputationem justitiae Christi ex Davidis testimonio evincit.
units.tr: XXXVI. The same St. Paul proves the imputation of Christ's righteousness from the testimony of David.

units.la: Sicut, inquit, David dicit beatitudinem hominis ᾧ ὁ Θεὸς λογίζεται δικαιοσύνην χωρὶς ἔργων, cui Deus imputat, vel reputat justitiam sine operibus. Beati (Psal. XXXII. 1.2.) quorum remissa sunt peccata, quorum tecta sunt peccata. Beatus vir, ᾧ οὐ λογίσηται Κύριος ἁμαρτίαν cui non imputaverit Dominus peccatum, Rom. IV. 6.7.8. Quibus verbis justificatio definitur remissione peccatorum, & quidem per & propter justitiam illam, quae imputatur sine operibus, & eo ipso, quod imputatur, peccata remittit & tegit. Omnis autem remissio peccatorum imputativa est, quia remittere peccatum Paulo & Davidi idem est, quod non imputare peccatum; & hoc idem, quod justitiam imputare absque operibus. Sicut creditor acceptam refert pecuniam debitori, cum eam pro soluta se habere fatetur.
units.tr: As Paul says, David speaks of the blessedness of the man to whom God imputes righteousness [ᾧ ὁ Θεὸς λογίζεται δικαιοσύνην] without works, that is, reckons righteousness without works. Blessed (Ps. 32:1-2) are those whose sins are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin [ᾧ οὐ λογίσηται Κύριος ἁμαρτίαν], Rom. 4:6-8. In these words justification is defined as the remission of sins, and indeed through and on account of that righteousness which is imputed without works; and by the very fact that it is imputed, it remits and covers sins. Now every remission of sins is imputative, because for Paul and David to remit sin is the same as not to impute sin, and this is the same as to impute righteousness apart from works. Just as a creditor who admits that he holds the money as paid credits it back to the debtor.

units.la: {y} Imputatio aliena justitiae Christi probatur tum ex testimonio Davidis & Pauli Rom. IV. 6.7.8. nec implicitè ad justificationem pertinet, quia Apostolus justitiam imputari sine operibus, seu μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ non operanti dixit. Atqui in justitiæ ratione idem est non operans, quod in civili politia non solvens. Quare imputari justitiam non operanti, idem est, quòd acceptari non solutum pro se. Puta. Sed de ea supra pluribus egimus. Accedit & illud, quòd ei, cui fides ad justitiam imputatur, cui justitia imputatur sine operibus, cui peccatum remittitur & non imputatur, is justificatur ut ἀσεβὴς impius. Nam ei, qui non operatur, sed credit ἐπὶ τὸν δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἀσεβῆ in eum, qui justificat impium, fides imputatur ad justitiam, Rom.IV.5. Atqui omnis justificatio impii imputativa est. Nam qui per inhærentem justitiam justificatur, is non ut ἀσεβὴς impius, sed ut jam justus per propriam & insitam justitiam justificatur. Vel ergo impius planè non justificatur, vel aliena & imputata justitia justificatur. Atqui Deum justificare impium. Apostolus dixit. Ergo aliena & imputata justitia justificat.
units.tr: {y} The imputation of Christ's alien righteousness is proved both from the testimony of David and Paul, Rom. 4:6-8, and it pertains to justification not only implicitly, because the Apostle said that righteousness is imputed without works, or to the one not working [μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ]. But in the reckoning of righteousness, not working is the same as not paying in civil affairs. Therefore to have righteousness imputed to one who does not work is the same as to have one who has not paid accepted as paid for himself. This is clear. But we have treated this at length above. Add also that he to whom faith is imputed for righteousness, to whom righteousness is imputed without works, to whom sin is remitted and not imputed, is justified as ἀσεβὴς, the impious. For to the one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the impious [ἐπὶ τὸν δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἀσεβῆ], faith is imputed for righteousness, Rom. 4:5. But all justification of the impious is imputative. For one who is justified by inherent righteousness is not justified as impious, but as already righteous, through his own and implanted righteousness. Either, then, the impious man is not justified at all, or he is justified by an alien and imputed righteousness. But the Apostle says that God justifies the impious. Therefore it is by an alien and imputed righteousness that he justifies.

units.la: XXXVII. Eandem justitiæ Christi imputationem luculenter Apostolus, Rom.V.12. &c. instituta primum & secundum Adamum inter antithesin, confirmat: Licet enim ibi verbo λογίζεσθαι imputandi non utatur, æquipollente tamen utitur, cùm δικαίωμα seu opus illud justificans Christi, quod justitiæ causa est, propter quod homo justificatur, χάρισμα gratiosam donationem, oppositè ad παράπτωμα lapsum v.15. & δωρεὰν ἐν χάριτι donationem in gratia, ibid. & δώρημα donum, v.16. appellat. Nam ejusmodi δικαίωμα, χάρισμα & δώρημα Adami secundi, oppositum lapsui Adami primi, non utique inhærens homini, sed Christo, Adamo primo, justitia intelligitur, sicut παράπτωμα lapsus Adami primi non hominibus ex eo progenitis inhæsit, sed Adamo primo soli. Utrumq; verò & δικαίωμα justitia, seu justitiæ meritum, causa, & παράπτωμα lapsus in posteris seu personis ad utrumque Adamum pertinentibus, & ab utroque repræsentatis nonnisi per imputationem esse potuit. Quod igitur Apostolus præcedente capite per λογίζεσθαι imputare, id ipsum hoc capite per χαρίζεσθαι gratificari & δωρεῖν donare expressit. Nam quæ bona aliena homini immerenti imputantur, illa ei, ad jus aliquod consequendum donantur. Apostolus autem demonstraturus, nos aliter non potuisse justificari, quàm in Christo, ut secundo Adamo, & in eo verè & plenè justificari, cum justificatione nostra per & propter δικαίωμα Christi, ceu secundi Adami condemnationem generis humani per & propter παράπτωμα Adami primi confert. Comparatio integra & contracta ejusmodi est: Sicut ex uno Adamo κρίμα judicium, vel crimen, quod judicatur, venit εἰς κατάκριμα ad condemnationem, seu terminatur in condemnatione, vers. 16. per unum παράπτωμα lapsum Adami illius, v. 17. 18. ira ex uno Christo, Adamo secundo, seu venturo χάρισμα & δώρημα donum justitiæ gratuitum redundavit ad justificationem vitæ per unum δικαίωμα justitiæ meritum, seu ὑπακοὴ obedientiam Adami secundi, Christi, v. 14.15.&c. Quod paucioribus Apostolus sic constringit: Igitur (concludens rem) sicut per unum lapsum in omnes homines ad condemnationem: ita & per unum justitiæ meritum in omnes homines in justificatio-nem vitæ, vers. 18. Licet verò, quæ Bellarmini ὑγίασις est, etiam Adamus primus posteros suos peccatores, & secundus suos justos etiam inhærenter, ille propagata in suos inhærente injustitia, hic suis communicata per regenerationem inhærente justitia, constituerit; tamen Apostoli scopus hoc loco non fuit id docere. Manifestum id est ex Adami primi peccato, in quo comparationis τύπος est. Dicit enim Apostolus: omnes in uno peccasse, v. 12. unius lapsu multos mortuos esse, v. 15. judicium esse ex uno lapsu ad condemnationem, v. 16. per unius lapsum in omnes homines venisse judicium ad condemnationem, v. 18. per unius inobedientiam nos peccatores constitui, v. 19. Quæ phrases manifestè denotant id, quod Adamus fecit per lapsum suum ad condemnationem hominis, non labem, qua se & posteros suos per lapsum suum infecit. Id certè Christi obedientia & δικαίωμα nobis donatum ad justificationem vitæ proximè & immediatè valet, quod Adami inobedientia ad κατάκριμα condemnationem hominis proximè & immediatè valuit. Atqui Adami inobedientia ad condemnationem hominis proximè & immediatè id valuit, ut homo propter eam Adamo inhærentem, at judicio Dei posteritati ejus imputatum non inhærenter justus esset, sed condemnaretur. Ergo Christi etiam obedientia & δικαίωμα nobis ad justificationem vitæ donatum proximè & immediatè id valet, ut, qui Christi sunt, propter illam obedientiam ejus, Christo inhærentem, at judicio Dei nobis imputatam non inhærenter justi essent, sed justi, & habentes jus vitæ, condemnationi oppositum, pronuntiarentur. Sicut etiam κατάκριμα condemnatio est reatus ad mortem imputatio: ita eidem opposita justificatio justitiæ ad vitam imputatio esse debet. Atque fortiùs hæc comparatio Pontificios stringit, quod Bellarminus ipse de amiss. Grat. lib. V.17. fatetur, inobedientiam Adami communicari nobis eo modo, quo communicari potuit, quod transiit, nempe per imputationem. Omnibus enim imputari, qui ex Adamo nascuntur, quoniam omnes in lumbis Adami extiterint, in eo & per eum peccaverint, cùm ipse peccavit.
units.tr: XXXVII. The Apostle, in Rom. 5:12ff., clearly confirms the same imputation of Christ's righteousness by setting up an antithesis between the first and second Adam. For although he does not there use the verb λογίζεσθαι, to impute, he uses an equivalent: he calls Christ's δικαίωμα, that justifying act which is the cause of righteousness, on account of which man is justified, a χάρισμα, a gracious gift, opposed to the παράπτωμα, the fall, in v. 15; and a δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι, a gift in grace, ibid.; and a δώρημα, a gift, in v. 16. For these δικαίωμα, χάρισμα and δώρημα of the second Adam, opposed to the fall of the first Adam, are understood to be righteousness not inhering in man but in Christ, the second Adam. Just as the παράπτωμα, the fall of the first Adam, did not inhere in the men born from him, but only in the first Adam. Yet both the δικαίωμα, the righteousness or merit that is the cause of righteousness, and the παράπτωμα, the fall, could only be in the posterity, or the persons related to each Adam and represented by each, through imputation. Therefore what the Apostle expressed in the previous chapter through λογίζεσθαι, to impute, he expresses in this chapter through χαρίζεσθαι, to bestow favour, and δωρεῖν, to give. For the good things of another that are imputed to a man who has not earned them are given to him so that he may obtain some right to them. The Apostle, wishing to show that we could not be justified otherwise than in Christ as the second Adam, and that in him we are truly and fully justified, compares our justification through and on account of Christ's δικαίωμα with the condemnation of the human race through and on account of the fall of the first Adam, as the condemnation brought by the second Adam. The comparison, full and abbreviated, is this: as through one Adam judgment, or the crime which is judged, came εἰς κατάκριμα to condemnation, that is, ended in condemnation, v. 16; through the one fall of that Adam, v. 17-18; so through the one Christ, the second Adam, or the one who is to come, the gift χάρισμα and the gift δώρημα, the free gift of righteousness, abounded to justification of life through the one δικαίωμα, the merit of righteousness, or ὑπακοή, the obedience of the second Adam, Christ, v. 14-15, etc. The Apostle compresses this in fewer words: Therefore (concluding the matter), as through one fall to condemnation for all men, so also through one righteous act to justification of life for all men, v. 18. But although, as Bellarmine's ὑγίασις, the first Adam made his posterity sinners and the second his posterity righteous, even inherently, the first through the injustice propagated and inhering in his own, and the second through the inherent righteousness communicated to his own by regeneration, the Apostle's aim in this passage was not to teach that. This is clear from the sin of the first Adam, which is the type of the comparison. For the Apostle says: all sinned in one, v. 12; many died through the fall of one, v. 15; judgment came from the fall of one to condemnation, v. 16; judgment came to all men through the fall of one to condemnation, v. 18; through the disobedience of one we were made sinners, v. 19. These phrases clearly denote what Adam did through his fall for the condemnation of man, not the stain by which he infected himself and his posterity through his fall. Certainly Christ's obedience and the δικαίωμα given to us avail for justification of life as directly and immediately as Adam's disobedience availed for the κατάκριμα, the condemnation of man, directly and immediately. But Adam's disobedience availed for the condemnation of man directly and immediately in this way: that man, because of it, was judged by God not to be inherently just through what inhered in Adam, but to be imputed to his posterity, and so would be condemned. Therefore Christ's obedience too, and the δικαίωμα given to us for justification of life, avails directly and immediately in this way: that those who are Christ's, on account of his obedience, which inheres in Christ but is imputed to us by God's judgment, would be declared not inherently just, but just, and holding a right to life, opposed to condemnation. Just as κατάκριμα, condemnation, is the imputation of guilt to death, so justification, its opposite, ought to be the imputation of righteousness to life. And this comparison presses the Papists more strongly, because Bellarmine himself admits, de amissione gratiae, book V, ch. 17, that Adam's disobedience is communicated to us in the way in which it could be communicated, which passed over, namely by imputation. For all who are born of Adam are imputed with it, since they all existed in the loins of Adam, and sinned in him and through him when he himself sinned.

units.la: XXXVIII. Cætera pro imputatione justitiæ Christi argumenta ad compendium ponamus. Christus sanè nobis factus justitia dicitur, 1.Cor. I.30. Jehova justitia nostra, Jer.XXIII.6. Ergo non ipsi nobis justitia sumus, sed justi per imputationem sumus. Neque nobis justitia factus est tantùm efficienter, quia meritum ejus causa efficiens inhærentis justitiæ est. Non enim justitia Christi proximè id efficit, ut inhærens justitia nobis donetur, sed ut à peccato absolutè jus vitam petendi adipiscamur. Quod citra imputationem non fit. Sicut verò Christus justitia, ita etiam sapientia, sanctificatio & redemptio nobis factus est; sed variante modo. Non enim quia factus nobis est justitia per imputationem, etiam sapientia per similem imputationem nobis factus est. Nam sapientia nuda qualitas est, quæ de nemine prædicari potest, cui non inhæret. At justitia in hoc argumento non est nuda qualitas, sed conjunctum respectum ad præmium vel pœnam habet; quem respectum alii, quibus qualitas illa proprie non inhæret, habere, dummodo iis imputetur, possunt. Sicut tamen nemo alterius sapientia sic sapere potest,ut sapientia alterius ei inhæreat: ita alterius justitia vel injustitia justus vel injustus esse inhæsive nemo potest. At potest quis intuitu alienæ justitiæ vel injustitiæ pœna vel præmio affici haud secus, ac si justitia vel injustitia in eo hæreret, vel ab eo præstita esset. Faciunt huc etiam illa S. Pauli: Fecit,ut qui non novit peccatum,pro nobis peccatum esset,ἵνα ἡμεῖς γενώμεθα δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ ut essemus justitia Dei in ipso,2. Cor.V.21. Sicut ergo Christus pro nobis peccatum factus est: ita nos facti sumus justitia Dei in Christo. Atqui ille pro nobis peccatum factus est, quia peccata nostra ipsi imputata,impacta sunt,ut ea in corpore suo supra lignum ferret. Ergo nos quoque justitia Dei in Christo facti sumus, quia Christi justitia nobis imputatur. Hanc enim dulcissimam & plenam consolationis ἀντάλλαγὴν & permutationem in negotio salutis nostræ obtinere Deus voluit. Scitè Augustinus Enchir. ad Laur. cap.41. Ipse, inquit, peccatum, ut nos justitia, nec nostra, sed Dei simus; nec in nobis, sed in ipso; sicut ipse peccatum non suum,sed nostrum; nec in se,sed in nobis constitutum similitudine carnis peccati,in qua crucifixus est, demonstravit. Ipse Bellarminus non diffitetur,peccata nostra Christo imputari quoad debitum satisfaciendi, quòd illa sponte suscepit. Addit etiam; justitiam Christi nobis imputari,quoad satisfactionem, quam pro nobis præstitit. Hæc qui fatentur, quomodo negare possunt, Christi justitiam ita nobis imputari,ut propter eam justi censeamur & pronuntiemur. Sicut enim ille,cui à creditore solutio sponsoris imputatur, tam plenè à debito absolvitur, ac si ipse proprio ære luisset: sic cui λύτρον Christi imputatur,is tam plenè à peccatis absolvitur, ac si ipse Deo de suo satisfecisset. Quj autem in judicio Dei à debito absolvitur, is justus censetur, quia nonnisi per justitiam Christi absolutio illa fit. Præterea nullus peccator manens peccator aliter justificari quàm per imputationem potest, quia peccatum & inhærens justitia directè opponuntur. Sicut enim idem simul bonum & malum dici non potest: ita nemo simul justus & peccator. Atqui fideles omnes,quandiu hic vivunt,manent peccatores, nec quisquam, præter Christum ἀναμάρτητος est. Nam quòd sanguine Christi lavamur, & à peccatis sanamur,ipsam hanc imputationem evincit, quia sanguis Christi significat pœnas, quas Christus pro nobis pertulit. Quod sine imputatione ne cogitari quidem potest. Sanatio verò à peccatis ad sanctificationem relata in hac vita inchoatur,in altera demum perficitur. Sicut enim quæ sanantur corpora,non usque quaque morbo carent: ita quæ animæ sanantur,hoc est,sanari incipiunt, aliquid in se peccati habent, quod magis magisque,rubiginis instar in olla, tergitur & atteritur, sed in morte demum penitus abstergitur, & tollitur. Denique ipsum verbum צדק δικαιῶν, justificare forensem significatum habere,non justum inhærenter faciendi, sed eum, qui inhærenter injustus est,justum pronuntiandi & absolvendi, initio disputationis hujus probatum dedimus. Unde & illud consequens est, justificationem imputativam esse. Οπε ἐδί δἑξαι.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Let us set out briefly the remaining arguments for the imputation of Christ's righteousness. Christ is indeed said to have been made righteousness for us, 1 Cor. 1:30, and Jehovah our righteousness, Jer. 23:6. Therefore we are not ourselves righteousness, but we are righteous by imputation. Nor has he been made righteousness for us merely in an efficient way, since his merit is the efficient cause of inherent righteousness. For Christ's righteousness does not directly bring it about that inherent righteousness is bestowed on us, but that we obtain from sin, absolutely, the right to seek life, and this does not happen without imputation. Just as Christ has been made righteousness for us, so he has also been made wisdom, sanctification and redemption, but in a different way. It does not follow that because he has been made righteousness for us by imputation, he has also been made wisdom for us by a similar imputation. For wisdom is a bare quality, which cannot be predicated of anyone in whom it does not inhere. Righteousness, however, in this argument is not a bare quality, but carries with it a relation to reward or punishment; and others, in whom that quality does not properly inhere, can have this relation if it is imputed to them. Yet just as no one can be wise by another's wisdom so that that wisdom inheres in him, so no one can be righteous or unrighteous by inherence through another's righteousness or unrighteousness. But someone can be affected with punishment or reward on account of another's righteousness or unrighteousness, just as if that righteousness or unrighteousness were in him or had been performed by him. Those words of St. Paul also bear on this: He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him, 2 Cor. 5:21 [ἵνα ἡμεῖς γενώμεθα δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ]. Therefore, as Christ was made sin for us, so we have been made the righteousness of God in Christ. But he was made sin for us because our sins were imputed to him and laid upon him, so that he might bear them in his body on the tree. Therefore we too have been made the righteousness of God in Christ, because Christ's righteousness is imputed to us. God willed that this exchange and substitution, most sweet and full of comfort, should hold in the matter of our salvation.
