Augustine wisely says (Enchiridion to Laurentius, ch. 41): He himself became sin, so that we might be righteousness; not our own, but God's; not in ourselves, but in him; just as he showed that the sin was not his own, but ours, and was placed not in himself but in us, in the likeness of sinful flesh, in which he was crucified. Bellarmine himself does not deny that our sins are imputed to Christ as regards the debt of satisfying, since he took them up of his own accord. He adds too that Christ's righteousness is imputed to us as regards the satisfaction which he has rendered for us. How can those who admit this deny that Christ's righteousness is imputed to us in such a way that we are counted and pronounced righteous on account of it? For as one to whom a surety's payment is imputed by the creditor is absolved from the debt as fully as if he had paid it with his own money, so one to whom Christ's ransom is imputed is absolved from sins as fully as if he had himself satisfied God from his own resources. And one who is absolved from debt in God's judgment is counted righteous, because that absolution takes place only through the righteousness of Christ. Moreover, no sinner who remains a sinner can be justified in any way other than by imputation, because sin and inherent righteousness are directly opposed. For as the same thing cannot be called both good and bad at once, so no one is at once righteous and a sinner. But all believers, as long as they live here, remain sinners, and no one is sinless [ἀναμάρτητος] except Christ. That we are washed by the blood of Christ and healed from sins itself proves this very imputation, since the blood of Christ signifies the punishments which Christ bore for us, and this cannot even be conceived without imputation. But the healing from sins, as it relates to sanctification, begins in this life and is only completed in the next. For just as bodies that are healed are not entirely free from disease, so souls that are healed (that is, begin to be healed) still have something of sin in them, which is rubbed off and worn away little by little, like rust in a pot, and is only wholly wiped away and removed in death. Finally, we have already shown at the beginning of this disputation that the word צדק [tsedeq] and δικαιῶν [dikaiōn] have the forensic meaning of justifying, that is, of pronouncing and absolving one who is inherently unrighteous as righteous, not of making someone inherently righteous. From this it also follows that justification is by imputation. Here is what must be shown.

units.la: XXXIX. Sed hanc tamen justitiæ Christi imputationem, ceu justificationis causam unicam,diro anathemate Tridentini configere non erubuerunt. Si quis dixerit,inquiunt, Sess. VI. Can.11. hominem justificari vel sola imputatione justitiæ Christi, vel sola peccatorum remissione,exclusa charitate & gratia,quæ in cordibus eorum per Spiritum S. diffundatur, atque illis inhæreat, anathema sit. Idem tamen cap.7. à formali justificationis causa justitiam,qua justi reputamur, penitus removerunt, ne putemus,ex eorum mente, hominem imputata Christi justitia,sed non sola justificari. Hi scilicet, qui Sanctorum, Monachorum inprimis suorum satisfactiones & merita atque indulgentiarum fumos aliis imputari pertendunt,& in tali imputatione atque mercimonio religionis suæ si non aras, saltem focos omnes collocant,committi in Divinam justitiam clamant, si Christi satisfactio & justitia homini imputari dicatur. Scilicet non potest homini peccatori & omnium rerum indigo imputari justitia Christi: at potest justitia hominis,quæ simulata tota & hypocritica est.
units.tr: XXXIX. Yet the Tridentine fathers were not ashamed to hurl this imputation of Christ's righteousness, as the sole cause of justification, with a dreadful anathema. If anyone says, they declare, Session 6, Canon 11, that a man is justified by the imputation of Christ's righteousness alone, or by the remission of sins alone, excluding charity and grace which is poured out in their hearts by the Holy Spirit and inheres in them, let him be anathema. Yet in the same session, chapter 7, they have entirely removed from the formal cause of justification the righteousness by which we are counted righteous, lest we should think, in their view, that a man is justified by the imputed righteousness of Christ but not by that alone. Those, of course, who contend that the satisfactions and merits of the saints, above all of their own monks, and the smoke of indulgences, are imputed to others, and who set up altars, if not everywhere, at least hearths, in this imputation and merchandise of their religion, cry out that the Divine righteousness is being violated if it is said that the satisfaction and righteousness of Christ is imputed to a man. Clearly it is not possible for the righteousness of Christ to be imputed to a sinful man who lacks everything; yet the righteousness of a man, which is wholly feigned and hypocritical, can be imputed.

units.la: XL. Addunt clamores tragicos,quòd justitiam putatitiam, fictitiam, imaginariam, phantasticam,quæ non aliud sit,quàm fictio cogitationis humanæ, velut cùm quis corvum album,qui sit niger, & monetam aureàm, quæ cuprea sit,fingit; justitiæ veræ inhærenti anteferamus: illam hac repudiata,formalem justificationis causam statuamus; hominem utcunque introrsum turpem & maculosum, externa ista justitiæ veste obtectum, velut sepulchrum dealbatum, quod intus ossibus mortuorum & omni spurcitia plenum est; virginem fatuam, quæ non habet oleum justitiæ in lampade sua, & alienum oleum ei sufficiat; lupum in vestimento ovis venientem, quæ Decani impudens & impotens paratragœdiatio est; Deo obtrudamus. Dignissima profectò autoribus suis hæc μυ- μολυχέα sunt,qui veram justitiam Dei,quæstus sui gratia, abnegare & blasphemare,quàm justitiam suam verè putatitiam, fictitiam, imaginariam, phantasticam cum Apostolo ad lucrandum Christum γνάθου συνέκαλα εἶναι pro stercoribus ducere,Phil.III. 8. hoc est, & oleum tum alienum tum proprium, atque operam omnem Christi etiam pro nobis navatam perdere & Deo loco justitiæ Christi stercora sua obtrudere malunt. Cùm enim Deus in judicio peccata nostra Christo,& Christi justitiam nobis imputat, nihil hic νομιζόμενον putatitium vel fictitium est,perinde ac si fingeretur esse,quod non est; quia nec peccata nostra Christo, nec justitiam Christi nobis inhærere, quod falsum omnino esset.& rectiùs in adversarios, qui justitiam omnem homini inhærere fingunt,competit,putamus. Vox enim imputandi nihil aliud hic significat,quàm simplex & justum Dei judicium,quòd sicut Deus Christo Sponsori nostra peccata impegit, atque illa in se suscepit, & morte sua expiavit, ut peccator ad vitam æternam perduci posset: ita illi,qui credunt in Christum,& in eo sunt, propter justitiam Christi capitis & Filii,in judicium non veniant,& ut filii adoptivi atque hæredes vitam æternam, quæ à lege merces obedientiæ proponitur,consequi dono debeant,perinde atque si ipsi obedientiam dientiam hanc patrassent, & nullum peccatum commisissent. Quod judicium Dei κατ' ἀλήθειαν secundum veritatem, Rom. II.2. & justum est, quia verissimum est, quod Deus judicat, eos, qui credunt, esse in Filio, & omnis juris ipsius, ut fratris primogeniti esse compotes; & justum est, quia justum utique est, ut Deus Filium Sponsorem, Sacerdotem, Mediatorem justificet, & ei פעלה opera sua pretium tribuat, omnesque cordis ejus petitiones impleat; & Deus δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἐκ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ justificans eum, qui est ex fide Jesu, justus est, Rom. III. 26. quia peccatorem justificans per Christum demonstratur justus, ad gloriam sapientiæ, justitiæ, potentiæ veritatis & gratiæ ejus. Imputatio igitur hæc si fictio dici debeat, non est fictio poëtica vel logica, qualis eorum est, qui aureos montes, canes tricipites, cygnos nigros &c. fingunt, sed fictio juris, cujus, ut Juris consulti ajunt, effectus realissimus est, quia tantum operatur, quantum veritas; velut cum quis propter adoptionem fingitur esse filius alicujus, ut maxime ab ipso non sit genitus, attamen omnibus filiorum juribus gaudet. Quod revera nobis imputatur & donatur, quod imputatur à Deo, qui verax & justus est, potensque ad dandum ea, quæ dare & donare vult, id nostrum esse non vane & stultorum instar putamus, fingimus, imaginamur, sed revera & jure divinitus concessum nobis vindicamus. Multum certe duo inter hæc interest, cum, qui justus nullo modo est, nullamque nec perfectam nec imperfectam justitiam habet, justus putatur; & cum Deus electis suis justitiam Christi imputat, & propter eam eos justificat, à peccatis absolvit & justos pronuntiat. Hoc si putare est, Deo igitur, non homini putare, non sine blasphemia tribuitur: & qui sic cavillatur, dignus est, qui tandem coram tremendo tribunali Dei non alia quàm sua ἱστερ-corea justitia vestitus, & de cætero ἐυρεθεὶς γυμνὸς nudus inventus, 2. Cor. V. 3. æternum pereat. Denique eum, qui sic per imputatam Christi justitiam justificatur, etiam in se ipso, vi & merito ejusdem Christi, atque operatione Spiritus S. sanctificari, & ad imaginem Dei, per peccatum originale fœdatam mirè & dissipatam sic renovari, ut mens ejus magis magisque cœlesti lumine collustretur, cor durum emolliatur, amore boni & odio mali inflammetur, affectus refractarii coërceantur, & peccatum ipsum, quoad maculam non simul semelque equidem in eo tollatur, sed dominio omni spolieтur, atque subjugum mittatur, ὁμολογουμένως afferimus. Quæ detegendæ & convincendæ eorum, qui orthodoxam de imputatione justitiæ Christi sententiam maledictis suis proscindunt, perversitati & stultitiæ sufficiunt.
units.tr: XL. They add tragic outcries, that we set up over true inherent righteousness a righteousness which is reckoned, fictitious, imaginary, fantastical, which is nothing but a fiction of human thought, as when someone imagines a white raven that is black, or a golden coin that is made of copper; that we impose on God a man who is within foully stained and spotted, covered by this outward garment of righteousness, like a whitewashed tomb which is inside full of dead men's bones and every filth; a foolish virgin who has no oil of righteousness in her lamp and whose borrowed oil suffices for her; a wolf coming in sheep's clothing. These are the impudent and impotent tragic performances of the Dean. Truly these ravings [μυμολυχέα] are most fitting for their authors, who prefer, for the sake of gain, to deny and blaspheme the true righteousness of God, and to count their own righteousness, which is truly reckoned, fictitious, imaginary, fantastical, as dung, in the Apostle's words, for the sake of gaining Christ [Phil. 3:8, σκύβαλα], that is, to waste both borrowed and their own oil, and all the labour Christ undertook even for us, and to impose their own dung on God in place of the righteousness of Christ. For when God in judgment imputes our sins to Christ and Christ's righteousness to us, nothing here is merely reckoned or fictitious, as if it were pretended to be what it is not; for neither our sins are inherent in Christ, nor Christ's righteousness in us, which would be entirely false. We rather think that this applies more correctly to our opponents, who pretend that all righteousness inheres in man. For the word imputing here means nothing other than the simple and just judgment of God, by which, just as God laid our sins upon Christ our Surety and took them upon himself and expiated them by his death, so that the sinner might be brought to eternal life, so those who believe in Christ and are in him, on account of the righteousness of Christ, the Head and Son, do not come into judgment, and as adopted sons and heirs they ought to obtain, by gift, eternal life, which the law proposes as the reward of obedience, just as if they themselves had performed this obedience and had committed no sin. This judgment of God is according to truth [κατ' ἀλήθειαν], secundum veritatem, Rom. 2:2, and it is just, because it is most true that God judges those who believe to be in the Son, and to be partakers of all his right, as brothers and firstborn; and it is just, because it is altogether just that God should justify the Son as Surety, Priest and Mediator, and give him the reward of his works [פעלה, pe'ullah], and fulfil all the petitions of his heart; and God is justifying him who is of the faith of Jesus, just [δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἐκ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ], Rom. 3:26, because in justifying a sinner through Christ he is shown to be just, to the glory of his wisdom, righteousness, power, truth and grace. If this imputation ought to be called a fiction, it is not a poetic or logical fiction, such as that of those who imagine golden mountains, three-headed dogs, black swans and so on; it is a legal fiction, whose, as the jurists say, effect is most real, because it works as much as the truth does; as when someone, by adoption, is pretended to be the son of another, though he is in no way begotten by him, yet enjoys all the rights of sons. What is truly imputed to us and granted to us, what is imputed by God, who is true and just and able to give what he wills to give and grant, we do not vainly and foolishly reckon, fancy or imagine to be ours, but we claim it as truly and by divine right conceded to us. Certainly there is a great difference between these two things: when one who is in no way righteous, and has no righteousness, either perfect or imperfect, is reckoned righteous, and when God imputes the righteousness of Christ to his elect and on account of it justifies them, absolves them from sins and pronounces them righteous. If this is reckoning, then to put it this way is ascribed to God, not to man, and not without blasphemy; and whoever so carps deserves to perish eternally, since at last before the dreadful tribunal of God he will be clothed in no righteousness but his own [ἱστερ-corea], and will be found naked [ἐυρεθεὶς γυμνὸς] for the future, 2 Cor. 5:3. Finally, we affirm, plainly and openly, that the one who is thus justified by the imputed righteousness of Christ is also sanctified in himself, by the power and merit of the same Christ and by the operation of the Holy Spirit, and is so renewed to the image of God, which was wonderfully marred and scattered by original sin, that his mind is more and more illumined by heavenly light, his hard heart is softened, he is inflamed with love of good and hatred of evil, his unruly affections are restrained, and sin itself, as to its stain, is indeed not removed in him all at once, but is stripped of all its dominion and sent into subjection. These things are sufficient to expose and refute the perversity and folly of those who slander the orthodox view of the imputation of Christ's righteousness with their abuse.

units.la: XLI. Sed aliis etiam telis justitiam imputatam iidem impetunt.
units.tr: XLI. But they also attack imputed righteousness with other weapons.

units.la: Negant, uspiam legi, quòd Christi justitia nobis imputetur. Sed legi id Rom. IV. 5.6. ubi fides ad justitiam imputari, & justitia imputari sine operibus dicitur, jam ostendimus. Faciunt huc etiam illa Christi: יהוה יחשב לי Dominus imputabit mihi. (Ergo & corpori Christi, sed Christo, ut suum proprium, corpori, ut id, quod est à Christo) passiones & obedientiam meam, Psal. XL. 18. Sed legitur etiam, quod plus est, quàm imputari, nempe eam nobis donari, Rom. V. 15. 16. 17. ut nos fiamus justitia Dei in Christo, 2. Cor. V. 21. qui nobis factus est justitia, 1. Cor. I. 30. nos ῥαντίζεσθαι aspergi sanguine Christi, 1. Pet. I. 2. in eo lavari, 1. Cor. VI. 11. purificari, Heb. I. 3. 1. Joh. I. 7. Apoc. VII. 14. in eo χαρίζεσθαι gratia donari, Ephes. I. 6. Sed necessariam esse imputationem, iidem negant, quia remissio peccati ejusdem plenaria abolitio sit, & fides, ipes & charitas hominis perfecta sit.
units.tr: They deny that anywhere in Scripture it is written that Christ's righteousness is imputed to us. But it is written in Rom. 4:5-6, where it is said that faith is imputed for righteousness and that righteousness is imputed without works; we have already shown this. To the same point are the words of Christ, יהוה יחשב לי [The LORD will reckon to me], The Lord will impute to me. (Therefore the passions and obedience are imputed to the body of Christ, but to Christ as his own, and to the body as that which is from Christ), Ps. 40:18. Moreover it is read that something more is given than imputation, namely that this righteousness is donated to us, Rom. 5:15-17; that we become the righteousness of God in Christ, 2 Cor. 5:21; that he was made righteousness for us, 1 Cor. 1:30; that we are sprinkled [ῥαντίζεσθαι] with the blood of Christ, 1 Pet. 1:2; that we are washed in him, 1 Cor. 6:11; purified, Heb. 1:3, 1 John 1:7, Rev. 7:14; and that we are graciously given [χαρίζεσθαι] by grace in him, Eph. 1:6. But those same men deny that imputation is necessary, because the remission of sin is a full abolition of it, and the faith, hope and love of man are perfect.

units.la: Quæ non obscura Christi abnegatio est. Si enim absque imputatione meriti & δικαιώματος Christi peccata remittuntur, ut penitus aboleantur & hominis justitia, fides, spes, charitas perfecta est, qualis ad justificationem requiritur, cui bono Christus? Sed hypotheses illas non semel jam profligavimus. Insuper justitiæ Christi imputationem cum rectâ ratione pugnare nugantur, quia ab ea justi denominari non possumus. Cùm enim sic argumentantur: cùm in aliquo duæ contrariæ formæ sunt, una inhærens, altera extrinseca, fine dubio denominatio absolutè sumitur à forma inhærente, potiùs quàm extrinseca. Quomodo æthiops candida licèt vestè indutus, non candidus ab extrinseca illa forma; sed niger ab interna forma denominatur. Sic, inquiunt illi, homo inhærenter injustus, at justus per imputationem, non justus, sed injustus denominari debet, quia injustitia inhæret, justitia imputata extrinseca est. Et sicut sponsa, quo simili Walenburgii utuntur, quæ habet teruncium apud se, à sponso donatum, dives magis dicitur à teruncio, quem in manu habet, quàm à divitiis, quas habet in communione cum Sponso; ita homo, qui inhærentem justitiam qualemcunque habet, ab hac potiùs, quàm ab imputata justus formaliter denominatur. Quæ tricæ meræ sunt. Nam etiam Christus à forma extrinseca peccatum pro nobis factus, 2. Cor. V. 21. dicitur, qui ab intrinseca justus fuit. Neque semper denominatio est ab inhærente, sed potiùs à potiori. At imputata justitia potior inhærente justitia est. Neque regula illa, quòd à forma intrinseca potiùs, quàm extrinseca denominatio fieri debeat, universaliter vera est. Esto enim debitor reus debendi centum florenos, pro quo alius solverit. Juxta Bellarminum liber non denominabitur propter alienam solutionem sponsoris, sed in se debitor. Quæ hæc insania? Tum ergo canon ille valet, cùm duæ formæ contrariæ sunt. At contrariæ formæ non sunt in diversis generibus. Itaque Æthiops ille dicetur utrumque, & niger & albus, niger cute, albus vestibus, quæ nulla contrarietas, sed respectus tantum diversitas est. Similiter justus imputativè, & peccator (non impius, qui imputata Christi justitia talis esse definit) inhærenter non pugnant; neque quicquam obstat, quò minus utrumque de uno eodémque prædicari queat. Walemburgiorum verò similitudo propiùs ad impietatem accedit, quia post peccatum ne teruncius quidem justitiæ propriæ superet, qui in Dei judicio ad justificationem valeat; & blasphemum sit, pluris æstimari divitias nostras, quàm divitias Christi imputatas, absque quibus est, nobis marcescendum est. Addunt illi; Christum nobis eam justitiam restituisse, quam in Adamo perdidimus. Quæ non imputata, inquiunt, sed inhærens fuit. Cæterùm quod in Adamo amissimus, vel finis ultimus indivulsa cum Deo communio, vel medium ad finem fuit. Illum nobis Christus restituit. Sed & hoc restituit, at nobiliore & eminentiore modo pro justitia nostra mutabili, defectibili, justitiam Dei immutabilem, indefectibilem, & inhærentem etiam, sed non talem, quæ in judicio Dei momentum haberet, quia impossibile fuit, ut homini peccatori justitia talis infunderetur, per quam & peccatum expiaretur. Christus igitur non id tantum, quod in Adamo habuimus, reddere, sed etiam mala, quæ in eo contraximus, depellere necesse habuit. Præterea non si justitia Christi nobis imputatur, æquè justi, redemptores, salvatores censemur, atque ille est, quia fieri non potest, ut qui imputative justus est, æquè justus sit, atque qui inhærenter est. Justitiæ enim denominatio non tantùm in ipsa justitia, sed etiam in modo habendi justitiam est. At qui justitiam ipse suam habet, longè nobiliore modo justus est, quàm qui alienam duntaxat habet. Quamobrem nec redemptor, salvator haberi potest, quia qui aliena justitia redemptus est, aliena justitia redemptor dici nequit, & qui alium à peccato redimit, justitiam inhærentem perfectam habere debet, qualem redemptus non habet. Neque enim Petro justitia Christi imputatur secundum omnem latitudinem efficaciæ, & prout est λύτρον & meritum pro fidelibus in genere, sed in quantum ipse ea opus habet. Vicissim etiam non ideo Christus peccator & mancipium Diaboli fuit, quia nostra ei peccata imputata sunt. Nam peccati fœditas, unde peccator & Diaboli mancipium dicitur, non sic in eum transfundi potuit, ut ei inhæreret. Ideo peccatum pro nobis factum, non peccator, 2. Cor. V. 21. Est & hæc illorum ἀντιλυτρωτ πεδσεια, quòd imputata Christi justitia & obedientia simul necesse sit imputari tum redemptionem totius mundi, quia obedientia & mors Christi illa ipsa Christi justitia est, quæ fuit propitiatio totius mundi: tum Divinitatem Christi, quia illa à carne separari non potest. Nam redemptio mundi non ipsa obedientia, sed effectum obedientiæ Christi est. Non est autem necesse omnia effecta applicari ei, cui quædam applicantur: sicut non quia calor Solis pyro applicatur ad maturitatem pyrorum, necesse est eidem applicari maturitatem omnium pomorum & segetum, quæ ab eodem calore Solis fluit. Scitè Bernhardus, ille justitiæ imputatæ incomparabilis præco, super Cont. Serm. 61. Domine, inquit, memorabor justitiæ tuæ solius. Ipsa est enim & mea. Nempe factus es mihi tu justitia à Deo. Numquid mihi verendum, ne ut una ambobus sufficiat? Non est pallium breve, quod secundum Prophetam non possit operire duos. Justitia tua, justitia in æternum. Quid longius æternitate? Et te & me operiet largiter. Neque etiam Deitatem Christi applicari nobis necesse est, quia obedientia Christi non est Deitatis effectum per se, sed καὶ ἄλλο. Quanquam etiam totus Christus noster est, Filius datus nobis est. Puer natus nobis est; Esaj. IX. 6. Verbum pro nobis caro factum est, Joh. I. 14. Sed non ideo reputamur filii Dei naturales, sicut Christus Filius Dei naturalis est, uti iidem υἱοποιήσαι, quia nemo reputari filius naturalis potest. Nam illud ipsum reputari filios est non esse filios naturales. Denique imputatio justitiæ Christi non superbiæ, sed humilitatis mater est. Quis enim supercilium attollat, qui novit & credit, nihil sibi in peculio proprio esse, quod Dei judicio opponat? Qui salutem suam ab uno solóque Christo & ejus gratia expectat. Neque enim quivis impurus sic æqualis Christo, cujus infinita justitia est, reputatur. Nam qui hanc spem habet, sanctificat se, sicut ipse sanctus est, 1. Joh. III. 3. Et sic ille justitiæ Christi, quæ infinitum pretium habet, & habere debet, particeps est, ut tamen in se ipso infinitam justitiam nullo modo habeat, sed finitam imperfectam, nulliúsque ad justificationem pretii. Illa potius doctrina, quæ justitiam hominis propriam justificationis causam facit, fœta superbiæ mater est, tum adversus Deum, cui se homo, ceu immaculatum ostentat, qui plenus est spurcitie, & cum Pharisæo Luc. XVIII. 11. 12. in quadam abstinentia à criminibus & voluptatibus justitiam suam collocat, tum adversus proximum, dum acerbus est in illos, qui lapsi sunt; qui sæpe magis Deum timent, & sanctitatem amant, quàm ille ab externis maculis propter gloriam, quam apud homines captat, se continens.
units.tr: This is no obscure denial of Christ. For if sins are forgiven without the imputation of Christ's merit and righteousness [δικαιώματος], so that they are wholly abolished, and man's righteousness, faith, hope and love are perfect, as justification requires, then what need is there of Christ? But we have already overthrown these hypotheses more than once. Further, they trifle that the imputation of Christ's righteousness conflicts with sound reason, because we cannot be called righteous from it. For they argue thus: when two contrary forms are in one thing, one inherent and the other extrinsic, the denomination is undoubtedly taken absolutely from the inherent form rather than the extrinsic. Thus an Ethiopian, though clothed in white, is not called white from that extrinsic form, but is named black from his inner form. So, they say, a man who is inherently unrighteous, but righteous by imputation, ought to be named not righteous but unrighteous, because unrighteousness inheres while imputed righteousness is extrinsic. And just as the bride, which is the similitude the Walenburgians use, who has a farthing with her, given by the bridegroom, is called rich from the farthing she holds in her hand rather than from the riches she has in communion with the Bridegroom, so a man who has whatever inherent righteousness is named righteous formally from that rather than from the imputed. These are mere trifles. For Christ too is said to have been made sin for us from an extrinsic form, 2 Cor. 5:21, though he was intrinsically righteous. Nor is the denomination always from the inherent, but rather from the stronger. And imputed righteousness is stronger than inherent righteousness. Nor is that rule, that the denomination ought to be made from the intrinsic rather than the extrinsic form, universally true. For suppose a debtor owes a hundred florins and another has paid them for him. According to Bellarmine the debtor will not be named free by the surety's payment, but remains a debtor in himself. What madness is this? That rule then holds when the two forms are contrary. But contrary forms are not in different genera. Therefore that Ethiopian will be called both black and white: black in his skin, white in his clothing; and this is no contrariety, only a difference of relation. Similarly, one who is righteous by imputation and a sinner inherently (not an impious man, who by the imputed righteousness of Christ ceases to be such) do not conflict; nothing prevents both from being predicated of one and the same person. But the likeness of the Walenburgians comes closer to impiety, because after sin not even a farthing of one's own righteousness remains that could avail for justification before the judgment of God; and it is blasphemous to value our riches above the imputed riches of Christ, without which we must wither. They add that Christ restored to us that righteousness which we lost in Adam, which, they say, was not imputed but inherent. But what we lost in Adam was either the ultimate end, unbroken communion with God, or a means to that end. Christ restored that to us. But he restored it also in a nobler and more eminent way: in place of our changeable and defectible righteousness he gave the immutable and indefectible righteousness of God, which also inheres, but not in such a way as to have weight in the judgment of God, since it was impossible for such a righteousness to be infused into a sinful man that would also expiate sin. Christ therefore had to do more than render what we had in Adam; he also had to drive away the evils we had contracted in him. Moreover, if the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, we are not thereby counted equally righteous, redeemers and saviours as he is, because one who is righteous by imputation cannot be as righteous as one who is righteous inherently. For the denomination of righteousness lies not only in the righteousness itself but also in the manner of having it. But he who has his own righteousness is righteous in a far nobler manner than one who has only another's. Wherefore neither can he be called a redeemer or saviour, because one redeemed by another's righteousness cannot be named a redeemer by another's righteousness, and he who redeems another from sin must have perfect inherent righteousness, which the redeemed does not have. For the righteousness of Christ is not imputed to Peter with every breadth of its efficacy, nor as it is a ransom and merit for the faithful in general, but only so far as he needs it. Conversely, Christ was not a sinner and a slave of the Devil because our sins were imputed to him. For the foulness of sin, from which one is called a sinner and a slave of the Devil, could not be so transfused into him as to inhere in him. Therefore he was made sin for us, not a sinner, 2 Cor. 5:21. Also part of their anti-redemption [ἀντιλυτρωτ πεδσεια] chain of argument is this: if Christ's righteousness and obedience are imputed, then the redemption of the whole world must be imputed too, because the obedience and death of Christ are that very righteousness of Christ which was the propitiation for the whole world; and also the divinity of Christ, because it cannot be separated from the flesh. But the redemption of the world is not the obedience itself but the effect of Christ's obedience. Nor is it necessary that all effects be applied to one to whom some are applied: just as, because the heat of the sun is applied to a pear to ripen it, it is not necessary that the ripening of all the fruits and crops which flow from that same heat of the sun be applied to the same pear. Bernard, that incomparable herald of imputed righteousness, rightly says on Sermon 61 on the Song of Songs: Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone. For it is also mine. Indeed you have been made to me righteousness from God. Am I to fear lest it suffice for only one of us? The cloak is not too short, which, according to the Prophet, cannot cover two. Your righteousness is righteousness for ever. What is longer than eternity? It will cover both you and me abundantly. Nor is it necessary that the deity of Christ be applied to us, because the obedience of Christ is not an effect of the deity in itself, but [καὶ ἄλλο] has something else. Although all of Christ is ours: a son is given to us, a child is born to us, Isa. 9:6; the Word was made flesh for us, John 1:14. Yet we are not thereby considered natural sons of God, as Christ is the natural Son of God, which is why they make us adopted sons; because no one can be reckoned a natural son. For that very phrase to be reckoned sons means not to be natural sons. Finally, the imputation of Christ's righteousness is the mother not of pride but of humility. For who would lift up his brow, if he knows and believes that he has nothing of his own to set against the judgment of God, and who expects his salvation from Christ alone and his grace? For no impure man is thus reckoned equal to Christ, whose righteousness is infinite. For he who has this hope purifies himself, as he is pure, 1 John 3:3. And so he shares in the righteousness of Christ, which has and must have an infinite worth, yet in himself he by no means has an infinite righteousness, but a finite and imperfect one, of no worth for justification. Rather that doctrine which makes man's own righteousness the cause of justification is the mother of pride: against God, before whom man displays himself as spotless though he is full of filth, and, like the Pharisee in Luke 18:11-12, places his righteousness in a certain abstinence from crimes and pleasures; and against his neighbour, while he is harsh towards those who have fallen, who often fear God more and love holiness more than that man who keeps himself from outward stains for the glory he seeks among men.

units.la: XLII. Infelix Remonstrantium secta
units.tr: XLII. The unhappy sect of the Remonstrants

units.la: in deterius proficiens semper in hoc argumento simul Judæorum & Socinianorum vestigia legit, & Pontificiis lenocinatur. Limborchius Lib. VI. 4. tres justificationis significatus distinguens secundum quos modò ipsam legem Dei, quæ justitiam docet, Psal. CXIX. 5. 8. 16. 20. &c. modò justitiæ acquisitionem, per quam is, qui ante injustus fuit, revera justus fit: modò justitiæ declarationem, seu absolutionem à reatu, & tractationem tanquam justi, sensu forensi significat; secundum, qui Pontificiorum est, sic refellit, ut asserat equidem adversus eos pluribus argumentis, quòd justificatio fit actus judicialis, & imputatione rei cujuspiam constet: at simul iisdem caput demulceat, dicens, statuendum omnino cum ipsis videri, justitiam inhærentem requiri, ut remissionem peccatorum, seu justificationem à Deo consequamur. Ipse justificationis partes duas, remissionem peccatorum & justitiæ imputationem statuit. Illam voluntatem non infligendi poenam, quam peccata promeruerunt, hanc gratiosam æstimationem, seu potius acceptationem non justitiæ Christi, sed justitiæ nostræ imperfectæ, quam fidem & resipiscentiam appellat, & quæ, si Deus rigidè nobiscum agere vellet, in judicio Dei consistere non posset, pro perfecta, propter Jesum Christum, definit. Verbo, imputationem justitiæ nostræ imperfectæ, fidei & resipiscentiæ pro justitia perfecta, idque propter meritum Christi, justificationis causam coram judicio & tribunali Dei tremendo unicam asserit. Ante ipsum Arminius ipse & Episcopius fidem imputari ad justitiam non metonymicè, sed proprie, quatenus opus aliquod est, docuerunt. Et Episcopio quidem fides illa, quæ in justitiam reputatur, ipsa religio Christiana est, complexa præceptum credendi in Christum, seu fidem per charitatem efficacem, quam promissio clara æternæ justitiæ & remissionis peccatorum comitetur. Opera verò fidei huic oppositæ ei omnis alia religio & cultus, qui sine illa religione Christiana, vel contra illam, vel etiam simul cum illa exercetur, neque adeo tam gratiosam promissionem, vel tale praeceptum fidei comprehendit. Ut ita Apostolicae de justificatione per fidem, & non per opera disputationis scopus sit, quod justitia & remissio peccatorum sola fide, seu exercitio religionis Christianae, non per opera, id est, alterius cujusvis religionis, quae opera alia, quam quae sine promissione veniae per Christum praecipiuntur, agnoscit, exercitium obtineri posse. Quae parum a Judaeorum & Socinianorum impietate abesse, res ipsa clamat. Nam cum Judaeis justitiam propriam exclusa justitia Dei constituunt: Cum Socinianis acceptilationem, seu justitiae imperfectae fidei imputationem & reputationem pro justitia perfecta statuminant. Adeo similes labra lactucas habent, & justitiariorum omnium vota atque sententiae conspirant.
units.tr: The unhappy sect of the Remonstrants, always going from bad to worse on this subject, follows at once the footsteps of the Jews and the Socinians and flatters the Papists. Limborch, in Book VI, chapter 4, distinguishes three senses of justification. In one sense it means the law of God itself, which teaches righteousness (Ps. 119:5, 8, 16, 20, etc.). In another it means the acquisition of righteousness, by which one who was previously unrighteous really becomes righteous. In a third, in the forensic sense, it means the declaration of righteousness, or absolution from guilt and being treated as righteous. The second sense, which belongs to the Papists, he refutes in such a way that he does indeed argue against them with many arguments that justification is a judicial act and consists in the imputation of something. At the same time, however, he soothes their head by saying that it must altogether be held with them "that inherent righteousness is required in order that we obtain remission of sins, or justification, from God." He himself posits two parts of justification: remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness. The first is the will not to inflict the punishment that sins have deserved. The second is the gracious estimation, or rather acceptance, not of the righteousness of Christ but of our imperfect righteousness, which he calls faith and repentance, and which, if God wished to deal rigorously with us, could not stand in the judgment of God. He defines this imperfect righteousness as perfect on account of Jesus Christ. In short, he asserts that the imputation of our imperfect righteousness, that is, of faith and repentance, as perfect righteousness, and that on account of the merit of Christ, is the sole cause of justification before the dreadful judgment and tribunal of God. Before him, Arminius himself and Episcopius taught that faith is imputed to righteousness not metonymically but properly, insofar as it is some work. For Episcopius, indeed, that "faith" which is reckoned to righteousness is the Christian religion itself, comprising the command to believe in Christ, or faith working through effective love, accompanied by the clear promise of eternal righteousness and remission of sins. The "works" opposed to this faith are every other religion and worship which is practised without that Christian religion, or against it, or even alongside it, and which does not include such a gracious promise or such a command of faith. Thus the aim of the apostolic discussion of justification by faith and not by works is that righteousness and remission of sins can be obtained by faith alone, that is, by the exercise of the Christian religion, and not by works, that is, by any other religion which acknowledges works other than those commanded without the promise of forgiveness through Christ. The thing itself cries out how little this differs from the impiety of the Jews and the Socinians. For with the Jews they set up their own righteousness, with the righteousness of God excluded; with the Socinians they set up acceptilation, that is, the imputation and reckoning of the imperfect righteousness of faith as perfect righteousness. So alike are they, having, as it were, the same lips, and the wishes and opinions of all these justifiers conspire together.

units.la: XLIII. Sed alia longe facies est justificationis illius, quam consentiens Scriptura, S. Paulus inprimis dedita opera tradit. Haec enim est justificatio impii, qua peccator, ut talis absolvitur in judicio Dei, idque ideo, quia omnes peccarunt, & gloria Dei destituuntur, Rom. III. 23. quaeque consistit in imputatione justitiae sine operibus, & remissione peccatorum, cap. IV. 6. 7. gratis gratia Dei per redemptionem Christi, cap. III. 24. At haec justificatio, quae fit ex operibus fidei, quae nihil aliud sunt, quam ipsa religio Christiana, & ejus exercitium, non justificatio impii, sed pii & justi est, utpote qua Deus pro justo eum habet, qui justitiam cum spe veniae peccatorum intercurrentium exercet; & fit sine imputatione justitiae sine operibus, & non est imputatio fidei in justitiam sine operibus; neque fit δωρεὰν gratis, vel χάριν gratia, sed ex operibus; denique nec in remissione peccatorum consistit, nec ipsa remissio est. Cumque fides, & justificatio per fidem legem non irritam reddat, sed stabiliat, ibid. v. 31. haec justificatio legem abolet & cassat, quia aliud δικαίωμα, aliam justitiam admittit, quam eam, quam lex omnibus numeris perfectam & consummatam praecipit. Non possumus autem aliter legi mori, quam per legem, ut Deo vivamus, Gal. II. 19. hoc est, a lege liberari nisi per legem impletam, & per legem Spiritus vitae in Christo Jesu, hoc est, per justitiam Christi, cujus virtute Spiritus S. nos a Lege liberos facit, Rom. VIII. 2. Alias frustra Christus mortuus esset, & Deus Te & Filium suum abnegaret, neque omnino fides operi opponi posset, & gloriatio hominis foret non in Deo, saltem non mere in Deo, sed in nobis quoque; imo in nobis tantum, quia non tantum in Deo. Deus enim gloriam nominis sui omnem, non partem gloriae postulat. Cumque partem gloriae non admittat, tota sic gloria infra Deum in homine subsidat oportet. Neque sic Apostolus recte inter ἐργαζόμενον καὶ μὴ ἐργαζόμενον operantem & non operantem, ibid. IV. 4. 5. distinxisset, atque inde conclusisset, Abrahamum non ex operibus justificatum esse. Omnino enim sic justificatus esset ἐργαζόμενῳ operans, & illi merces ex debito, non ex gratia imputata esset. Nam si ex operibus, non amplius ex gratia. Alias opus non est opus. ibid. XI. 6. Atqui Abrahamo merces imputata est non operanti, sed credenti, non ex debito, sed ex gratia. Nam
units.tr: XLIII. But the justification which Scripture, and especially St Paul, deliberately sets forth is of quite a different appearance. For this is the justification of the ungodly, by which a sinner, as such, is absolved in the judgment of God, and this because all have sinned and come short of the glory of God (Rom. 3:23). It consists in the imputation of righteousness without works, and the remission of sins (ch. 4:6, 7), being justified freely by his grace through the redemption of Christ (ch. 3:24). But this justification, which comes from the works of faith (which are nothing other than the Christian religion itself and its exercise), is not the justification of the ungodly but of the pious and just. For God regards as just the one who exercises righteousness with the hope of forgiveness for the sins that intervene. It comes about not through the imputation of righteousness without works, and faith is not imputed to righteousness without works. Nor does it come about freely [δωρεὰν] or by grace [χάριν], but from works. Finally, it does not consist in the remission of sins, nor is it that remission. And since faith, and justification through faith, does not make the law void, but establishes it (ibid. v. 31), this justification abolishes and annuls the law, because it admits another righteousness [δικαίωμα], another justice, than that which the law commands as perfect and complete in every respect. Yet we cannot die to the law except through the law, that we may live to God (Gal. 2:19), that is, be freed from the law only by the law being fulfilled, and through the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus, that is, through the righteousness of Christ, by whose power the Holy Spirit makes us free from the Law (Rom. 8:2). Otherwise Christ would have died in vain, and God would deny both himself and his Son, and faith could not be set against works at all, and the glorying of man would be not in God, or at least not purely in God, but in us also; indeed in us alone, since not in God alone. For God demands all the glory of his name, not a part of it. And since he does not admit a part of the glory, the whole glory must necessarily rest beneath God in man. Nor would the Apostle rightly have distinguished between him who works [ἐργαζόμενον] and him who does not work (ibid. 4:4, 5), and then concluded from this that Abraham was not justified by works. For in that case he would have been justified as one who works, and the reward would have been imputed to him as a debt, not as a gift of grace. For if by works, then no longer by grace. Otherwise work is not work (ibid. 11:6). But the reward was imputed to Abraham not as one working, but as one believing, and not as a debt but as a gift of grace. For

units.la: & sine illo opere, quod jam credens, & verae religioni addictus patravit, justificatus est. Non enim τὸ κενώμενον fuit, an justitia sit ex falsa religione, superstitione, idololatria: sed omnino, an sine opere & justitia propria ex sola fide in Christum? Ideo idem S. Paulus negat, Deum salvos nos fecisse ἐξ ἔργων τῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν ex operibus in justitia, quae, inquit, feceramus nos: sed ex misericordia sua, Tit. III. 5. Misericordia autem Dei omne id, quod in nobis & ex nobis est, ceu salutis causam, excludit: & opera in justitia facta verae religionis opera sunt. Quin & haereditas vi solius promissionis nobis datur. Non enim per legem Abrahae aut Semini ejus cessit promissio, ut esset haeres mundi, sed per justitiam fidei. Si enim qui ex lege sunt, haeredes sunt, exinanita est fides, & abolita promissio. Ideo ex fide, ut secundum gratiam, ut firma sit promissio omni semini, Rom. IV. 13. 14. 16. Quicquid Deus promittit, id ipse praestat, & ideo, quia promisit. Aliud enim promittere, aliud jubere est. Atque in hoc ipso foederis gratiae a foedere operum differentia consistit, quod in eo Christus praestitit, quae lex jubet, quia peccatori id impossibile est: in hoc homo, quae lex jubebat, & integris adhuc viribus ab homine praestari poterant, praestare tenebatur. Et num quid putamus, Deum pro justitia perfecta reputare posse eam justitiam hominis, quam Lex, adeoque ejusdem authorem, idem Deus secundum Legem suam arguit & repuit? Etenim lex, seu Deus secundum legem suam perfectam justitiam, omnis labis & deficientis in amore gradus expertem exigit; non ὑπερεδών connivens ad defectum. Deum enim non perfecte amare, nec ex toto corde, &c. nec proximum sicut se ipsum, quid aliud quam peccatum & transgressio Legis est? Si imperfecta obedientia sufficit, quae mensura, quis modus servabitur? Ubi conscientia sic acquiesceat, ut certa fit, eam obedientiam se praestitisse, quae sufficere posset? vel majorem dispensationem dari in hoc, quam in alio praecepto; & hunc, quam alium defectum excusationem esse; hoc peccatum magis quam aliud remitti? Atqui Christus ipse. Nolite, inquit, putare, me venisse, ut Legem vel Prophetas solvam. Non veni ut solvam, sed ut impleam, Matth. V. 17. Praeterea ubinam invenire est illa opera meritoria, quae perfectam & perpetuam observantiam includunt, & quibus merces datur ex debito, & quibus fides opponitur? Vel illa sunt, quae ex fide fiunt, vel illa, quae fidem antecedunt, sine ea, vel contra eam fiunt. Non illa, quia credenti merces ex gratia, & fides ipsa in justitiam imputatur, neque adeo in iis perfecta obedientia, cui merces ex debito imputari possit, consistit. Non haec, quia cum sine fide impossibile sit Deo placere, obedientia sine fide praestita neque quidem vera, nedum perfecta obedientia esse potest. Meras ergo chimaeras justificationis ejusmodi assertores spirant. Accedit, quod veram gratiae & misericordiae notionem iidem corrumpunt, & pro ea ἐπιείκειαν quandam & ἀνοχὴν tolerantiam, consistentem in παρόψει dissimulatione perpetua substituunt: cum tamen propter tolerantiam & dissimulationem praeteritorum peccatorum Christus in tempore mori debuerit, ad demonstrationem justitiae Dei, & convictionem, quod Deus in justificatione & salute lute peccatoris ἐμπεπτωκότα tali uti nolit, & citra abnegationem justitiae suae non posset, Rom.III. 25. Gratia certe illa, qua justificamur, non ἐμπ- τωκότα, sed mera gratia est, quia, uti recte Augustinus, Gratia non est gratia ullo modo, si non est gratuita omni modo. Nam si ex gratia, non ex operibus, ibid.XI.6. Sic gratia justificamur, ut etiam δωρεὰν gratis justificemur, adeoque ex mera ἀδοχία erga nos Dei justificantis. Versatur enim gratia illa circa hominem peccatorem, cui si quid praeter justitiam Christi imputare Deus vellet, non aliud quam peccatum suum ad damnationem imputaret. Rex ille, qui servo decem mille talenta debenti reo gratiam impertitus est, totum debitum remisit, non ἐμπεπτωκότα usus est; quali utitur judex, qui jus moderatur, & cum totum obtinere non posset, partem ejus retinet. Ejusmodi ἐμπεπτωκότα licet in judice humano, ob legis generalitatem, obtinere posset; tamen in Deo locum non habet, ut de lege sua, quae ipsa justitiae regula, ex aeterna lege justitiae expressa, adeoque essentialiter immutabili ita dispensset. Denique judicium Dei secundum veritatem est, ibid.II.2. Non ergo justitiam imperfectam pro perfecta reputare potest. Licet enim sic imperfectam non reputaret perfectam, tamen imperfectae id jus tribueret, quod secundum legem suam soli perfectae tribuit, quod non est κρίνειν δικαίαν κρίσιν judicare justum judicium, vel secundum veritatem judicare.
units.tr: and he was justified without that work which, already believing and devoted to the true religion, he had performed. For the question is not whether righteousness comes from a false religion, superstition, or idolatry; the question is altogether whether one is justified without works and without one's own righteousness, by faith alone in Christ. Therefore the same St Paul denies that God saved us from works in righteousness which we had done [ἐξ ἔργων τῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν], but according to his mercy (Tit. 3:5). The mercy of God excludes everything that is in us and from us, as the cause of salvation. And works done in righteousness are the works of the true religion. Indeed, the inheritance too is given to us by the power of the promise alone. For the promise did not come to Abraham or his seed through the law, that he should be heir of the world, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void and the promise is abolished. Therefore it is of faith, that it might be according to grace, so that the promise might be sure to all the seed (Rom. 4:13, 14, 16). Whatever God promises, he himself performs, and that because he has promised. For to promise is one thing, to command another. And in this very thing lies the difference between the covenant of grace and the covenant of works: in the one Christ performed what the law commands, because it is impossible for a sinner; in the other man was bound to perform what the law commanded, and which could be performed by man while his powers were still whole. And do we think that God can reckon as perfect righteousness that righteousness of man which the Law, and therefore its author, the same God according to his Law, condemns and rejects? For the law, or God according to his law, demands perfect righteousness, free from every stain and every degree of deficiency in love; it does not connive at deficiency. For not to love God perfectly, nor with the whole heart, etc., nor one's neighbour as oneself, what else is this than sin and transgression of the Law? If imperfect obedience suffices, what measure or what limit will be kept? When could conscience rest so as to be certain that it has rendered that obedience which could suffice? Or that a greater dispensation is given in this than in another precept, and that this defect, rather than another, is an excuse, and that this sin is forgiven rather than another? Yet Christ himself said: Do not think that I came to destroy the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to destroy, but to fulfil (Matt. 5:17). Moreover, where can one find those meritorious works which include perfect and perpetual observance, and for which the reward is given as a debt, and which are set against faith? They are either those which are done from faith, or those which precede faith, or are done without it or against it. Not the first, because the reward to the believer is given by grace, and faith itself is imputed to righteousness, and so perfect obedience, to which the reward could be imputed as a debt, does not consist in them. Not the second, because since without faith it is impossible to please God, obedience rendered without faith cannot even be true obedience, much less perfect obedience. The advocates of such a justification therefore breathe out mere chimeras. Besides, these same men corrupt the true notion of grace and mercy, and substitute for it a certain clemency [ἐπιείκειαν] and forbearance [ἀνοχὴν], consisting in perpetual overlooking [παρόψει] and dissimulation. Yet on account of forbearance and the dissimulation of past sins, Christ had to die in time, to demonstrate the righteousness of God, and to show that God, in the justification and salvation of a sinner, does not wish to use connivance [ἐμπεπτωκότα] with such a person, and could not do so without denying his own righteousness (Rom. 3:25). Certainly that grace by which we are justified is not connivance [ἐμπεπτωκότα] but pure grace, because, as Augustine rightly says, grace is not grace in any way, if it is not gratuitous in every way. For if by grace, not by works (ibid. 11:6). Thus we are justified by grace so that we are justified also freely [δωρεὰν], and so from the pure goodwill [ἀδοχία] of God toward us as justifier. For that grace is concerned with a sinful man, to whom, if God wished to impute anything besides the righteousness of Christ, he would impute nothing but his own sin, unto condemnation. That king who granted pardon to the servant who owed him ten thousand talents, remitted the whole debt, and did not use connivance [ἐμπεπτωκότα], as a judge does who moderates the law, and, when he cannot obtain the whole, keeps back part of it. Such connivance may be possible in a human judge, on account of the generality of the law; yet in God it has no place, since he would not dispense in this way with his own law, which is the very rule of righteousness, expressed from the eternal law of righteousness and therefore essentially unchangeable. Finally, the judgment of God is according to truth (ibid. 2:2). Therefore he cannot reckon imperfect righteousness as perfect. For even if he did not reckon imperfect righteousness as perfect, he would still be granting to the imperfect what, according to his law, he grants only to the perfect. This is not to judge a righteous judgment [κρίνειν δικαίαν κρίσιν], that is, to judge according to truth.

units.la: XLIV. Tam praegnantibus argumentis convictam spuriam justificationem suam paucis & frivolis ratiunculis idem Limborchius sustentare conatur.
units.tr: XLIV. Limborch, with a few paltry and frivolous little arguments, tries to sustain his spurious justification, which has already been refuted by such weighty arguments.

units.la: Nam remissionem peccatorum non tantum fidei, sed etiam operibus adscribi pertendit ab ipso Christo, dicente: Si remiseritis hominibus peccata eorum, remittet vobis etiam Pater vester Caelestis, Matth.VI.14. Jusserat idem Christus paulo ante sic precari. Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris, v.12. Utrobique non causa remissionis peccatorum, quam toties gratuitam Scriptura praedicat, sed indubitata nota fidei justificantis exponitur, nempe minimus ille motus charitatis inchoatae, ut debitoribus nostris, & iis, qui nos offenderunt, debita & offensas condonemus, ut sensus sit, si remiseritis hominibus peccata, certissimum argumentum habebitis, quod & vestra peccata remissa vobis sint. Neque obstat futurum ἀφήσει remittet, quia & solennis quaedam remissio futura est in futuro seculo, ib.XII.32. & quotidiana remissione, seu intimatione remissionis, & consolatione de peccatis remissis nobis opus est. Simplex igitur verborum sensus est, veniam dare oportere eos, qui venia ipsi opus habent, & veniam dedisse, datae veniae γνώσεως indubium esse. qui multum diligunt, certissimum argumentum habent, multa peccata sibi remissa esse, quia dilectio illa testificatio spei bonae, adeoque dilectio gratitudinis est, Luc.VII.47. Nemo diligere, nemo peccata alteri remittere potest, nisi spiritu Dei praeditus, & Dei amans. At Spiritum Dei & amorem ejusdem nemo nisi jam Deo reconciliatus & justificatus habet. Nam cum inimici essemus, Deo reconciliati sumus per mortem Filii ejus, Rom. V.10. In hoc est charitas, non quod nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quod ipse dilexerit nos, & misFerit Fi-
units.tr: For he insists that the remission of sins is ascribed not only to faith but also to works, citing Christ himself, who says: If you forgive men their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, Matth.VI.14. Shortly before, the same Christ had taught us to pray: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors, v.12. In both places the cause of the forgiveness of sins, which Scripture so often proclaims to be free, is not being stated. Instead, the undoubted mark of justifying faith is being pointed out, namely that small beginning of charity by which we pardon our debtors and those who have offended us, forgiving their debts and offences. The sense, then, is: if you forgive men their sins, you will have a most certain sign that your own sins are forgiven you as well. Nor does the future tense ἀφήσει [will forgive] stand in the way, since there is also a solemn remission still to come in the future age, ib.XII.32, and we need daily remission, or the intimation of remission, and comfort about sins already forgiven us. The plain sense of the words, therefore, is that those who themselves need pardon ought to grant it, and that the knowledge [γνώσεως] of having granted pardon is beyond doubt. Those who love much have a most certain argument that their many sins have been forgiven them, because that love is a token of good hope, and so it is a love of gratitude, Luke VII.47. No one can love, and no one can forgive sins to another, unless he is endowed with the Spirit of God and loves God. But no one has the Spirit of God and his love unless he is already reconciled to God and justified. For while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, Rom. V.10. In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent

units.la: lium suum, ut esset propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, 1.Joh.IV.10. Sed & S.Petrus dicens: Resipiscite & convertimini, ut deleantur peccata vestra, Act. III.19. resipiscentibus & conversis deleri peccata innuit, at per opera justificari hominem neutiquam docet. Nam resipiscentiae latius sumptae & conversionis initium fides est, quae Christo nos inserit, & vi justitiae & obedientiae ejusdem donatae, & apprehensae peccata delet. Et incredulitas quidem, condemnationis causa, cum operibus malis conjuncta est, imo & ipsa opus malum est, quia est violatio legis illius, quae jubet omne testimonium Dei in verbo ejus patefactum recipere, & salutem a Deo oblatam non negligere. Si omnis transgressio & inobedientia justam retributionem accepit, quomodo effugiemus tantam salutem negligentes? Heb.II.2.3. Incredulitati opposita fides conjuncta similiter opera habet, & quodammodo opus est, quia est actus hominis Deo revelanti Christum, ut causam justitiae & salutis, obedientis; sed non justificat ut opus, vel pars justitiae, sed ut instrumentum, seu manus Christum λαμβάνοντα accipiens, apprehendens, Joh.I.12. Quomodo nec manus mendici eleemosynam oblatam amplectens vel pars est eleemosynae, quae offertur, vel ut pars eleemosynae illius mendicum locupletat, sed ipsa vacua & inops demum ab eleemosyna apprehensa impletur. Praeterea etiam ultimum judicium, in quo sententiae justificationis & condemnationis executio publica & solennis locum habebit, secundum opera maxime pronuntiabitur, Matth. VII.21. XVI.27. XXV.35. &c. & executio sententiae ipsi sententiae repugnare non debet. Sed non ideo justificationis aeque ac condemnationis sententia fertur secundum opera, ceu justitiae causam, quia justificatur impius, & credens non ἐργαζόμενος operans; sed secundum opera, ceu fidem & justificationem per fidem a posteriori demonstrantia. Δεῖξον μοι demonstra mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis, Jac.II.18. Fides enim, & justificatio per eandem cum in oculos hominum non incurrat, & in hac vita, & in ultimo judicio coram hominibus aliis argumentis, quae ab homine etiam cognosci possunt, & cum fide atque justitia Christi per fidem apprehensa nexum Divinitus ordinatum habent, demonstrari debet. Nequicquam vero Limborchius sequi inde urget, quod homo impius, imo quatenus impius adhuc consideratus justificetur. Nam διαρρήδην Apostolus dixit, Deum justificare τὸν ἀσεβῆ impium, Rom.IV.5. Et impium etiam justificari, qua impius est, & impius consideratur, licet non impius manens, sed per justificationem justus & sanctus inhaerenter factus, res ipsa loquitur. Nam in justificatione homini peccata remittuntur, & justitia aliena imputatur. At nisi impio & injusto peccata remitti, & aliena justitia imputari non potest. Ideo etiam electi, quando Christo per fidem uniuntur, & reconciliationem accipiunt, justificantur ut ἀμαρτωλοὶ peccatores, ib.V.8. & ut ἐχθροὶ hostes, v.10. Et qui non credunt, ut justificentur gratia Dei, ἀσεβεῖς, ἀμαρτωλοὶ improbi, damnati in omnibus Scripturis nuncupantur. Quod eo etiam evidentius fit, quia solo sanguine Christi abluimur a peccatis, idque tum in nobis peragitur, quando credimus. Inde credentes lavare stolas
units.tr: his Son to be the propitiation for our sins, 1.Joh.IV.10. But when St Peter says, Repent and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out, Act. III.19, he indicates that sins are blotted out for those who repent and turn, but he by no means teaches that a man is justified by works. For faith is the beginning of repentance, taken in the wider sense, and of conversion; it engrafts us into Christ, and by the power of his justice and obedience, which is given and apprehended, it blots out sins. Unbelief, indeed, the cause of condemnation, is joined with evil works; indeed it is itself an evil work, because it violates that law which commands us to receive every testimony of God revealed in his Word, and not to neglect the salvation offered by God. If every transgression and disobedience has received a just retribution, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? Heb.II.2.3. Faith, which is opposed to unbelief, likewise has works joined to it, and in a way it is a work, because it is the act of a man obeying God who reveals Christ as the cause of righteousness and salvation. But it does not justify as a work, or as a part of righteousness, but as an instrument or hand [ὄργανον] that takes and apprehends Christ [λαμβάνοντα], Joh.I.12. Just as the beggar's hand that receives an offered alms is not part of the alms that is offered, nor does it enrich the beggar as part of that alms, but rather the beggar, empty and needy, is at last filled by the alms that he has taken hold of, so too faith justifies as an instrument. Moreover, the last judgment, in which the sentence of justification and of condemnation will be publicly and solemnly carried out, will be pronounced chiefly according to works, Matth. VII.21, XVI.27, XXV.35, etc., and the execution of a sentence ought not to contradict the sentence itself. But the sentence of justification, like that of condemnation, is not pronounced according to works as the cause of righteousness, as if the ungodly is justified and the believer is not working [ἐργαζόμενος]; rather it is pronounced according to works as demonstrating faith, and justification through faith, after the fact. Show me [Δεῖξον μοι] your faith from your works, Jac.II.18. For faith and justification through it do not fall under human eyes, and in this life, and in the last judgment before other men, they must be demonstrated by other evidences which can also be recognised by man, and which have a divinely ordained bond with the faith and the righteousness of Christ apprehended through faith. Limborch, however, is wrong to press from this that a man who is ungodly, indeed a man considered as still ungodly, is justified. For the Apostle has said expressly that God justifies the ungodly [τὸν ἀσεβῆ], Rom.IV.5. And the fact itself speaks: an ungodly man is justified in so far as he is ungodly and is considered ungodly, although he does not remain ungodly, but through justification becomes just and holy inherently. For in justification sins are remitted to the man, and an alien righteousness is imputed to him. But sins cannot be remitted to, nor an alien righteousness imputed to, one who is not ungodly and unrighteous. Therefore also the elect, when they are united to Christ through faith and receive reconciliation, are justified as sinners [ἁμαρτωλοί], ib.V.8, and as enemies [ἐχθροί], v.10. And those who do not believe, that they might be justified by the grace of God, are called in all the Scriptures ungodly [ἀσεβεῖς], sinners [ἁμαρτωλοί], wicked and condemned. This is made all the more evident because we are cleansed from sins by the blood of Christ alone, and this is done in us when we believe. Hence believers are said to wash their robes

units.la: Limborchii pro eadem objectiones vindicae. stolas in sanguine Agni, Apoc. VII. 14. & Christus purgare Ecclesiam à peccatis per lavacrum aquæ in verbo, Eph. V. 26. dicuntur. Si ambulamus in luce, sicut ipse est in luce, communionem invicem habemus. Et sanguis Jesu Christi, Filii ejus, purificat nos ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. I. 7. Neque tamen, si impius justificatur, etiam fidem à justificatione excludi consequitur; sicut non si pauper & omnium rerum indigus aliena liberalitate ditatur, etiam manum liberale donum prensantem excludi necesse est. Satis est, quòd fides non ut opus, vel ut justitia, sed ut organon, alienam justitiam donatam carpens justificat, quódque simul justificatur impius, simul ex statu damnationis in statum securitatis & justitiæ per fidem transponitur. Simul enim atque credimus, apud Deum esse redemptionem & remissionem, & ad eum, in quo est justitia nostra, confugimus, non tam amore impunitatis, quàm studio gloriæ Dei, & nos ei committimus, quærentes habere bonam conscientiam coram ipso, & signaculum Spiritus S. jam justi sumus. Nam obedimus præcepto Dei, qui nos jussit nil metuere, & ei, ut clypeo confidere, & amplissimam à se mercedem expectare. Neque ullum doctrinæ huic periculum subesse, vel contradictio gliscere potest; quia fieri nequit, ut vel Deus peccatorem aliter ad donum justitiæ accipiendum vocet, vel homo id aliter accipiat, vel frustra sit, qui Deum, præsertim secundum verbum ipsius, ut tanti boni datorem, amaverit. Denique & infirmus ille Arminii adversus justitiæ Christi imputationem Achilles est, arguentis illud, quod nobis à Deo imputatur ad justiam, non debere ipsum esse justitiam perfectam, sed aliquid, quod pro justitia perfecta habeatur, & à Deo acceptetur. Alioquin, inquit, si illud ipsum, quod nobis imputari dicitur, perfecta justitia fuerit, quomodo imputari justitiæ loco dicetur? Verum perfectam quidem justitiam, si nobis insit & inhæreat, non necesse est nobis imputari, quia jam nostra est. Potiùs imputari justitia, factum, meritum alienum, quod in alio, & ab alio est, dicitur, cùm pro nobis à Deo acceptatur, & pro nostro habetur. Atqui si justitia illa, etiam perfectissima, aliena fuerit, seu alii, velut Christo, inhæserit, & ab eodem præstita & profecta, non in nobis, nec à nobis fuerit, cur non nobis imputabitur, cùm eam fide apprehensam nobis applicaverimus.
units.tr: Limborch's objections in defence of the same point are answered. their robes in the blood of the Lamb, Apoc. VII.14, and Christ is said to cleanse the Church from sins by the washing of water in the word, Eph. V.26. If we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another; and the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin, 1.Joh.I.7. Yet it does not follow that, if the ungodly is justified, faith is excluded from justification, any more than, if a poor man who lacks everything is enriched by another's generosity, his hand that grasps the generous gift must necessarily be excluded. It is enough that faith justifies not as a work, nor as righteousness, but as an instrument [ὄργανον], laying hold of the alien righteousness that is given; and that at the same moment the ungodly is justified, he is transferred from a state of condemnation into a state of security and righteousness through faith. For as soon as we believe that there is redemption and remission with God, and we flee to him in whom is our righteousness, not so much from love of impunity as from zeal for the glory of God, we commit ourselves to him, seeking to have a good conscience before him, and we are already just, with the seal of the Holy Spirit. For we obey the command of God, who bids us fear nothing, and to trust in him as in a shield, and to expect from him a most ample reward. Nor can any danger or growing contradiction threaten this doctrine, because it cannot happen that God should call a sinner to receive the gift of righteousness in another way, or that a man should receive it in another way, or that one who has loved God, especially according to his Word, as the giver of so great a good, should love in vain. Finally, that weak Achilles of Arminius against the imputation of Christ's righteousness is also refuted, when he argues that what is imputed to us by God as righteousness ought not itself to be perfect righteousness, but something that is held to be perfect righteousness and accepted by God. Otherwise, he says, if that very thing which is said to be imputed to us were perfect righteousness, how could it be said to be imputed in place of righteousness? But perfect righteousness, if it is in us and inheres in us, need not be imputed to us, because it is already ours. Rather, an act or merit is said to be imputed when it is something alien, which is in another and from another, and is accepted by God on our behalf and regarded as ours. Yet if that righteousness, even most perfect, is alien, or has inhered in another, such as Christ, and has been performed and proceeded from him, and is not in us nor from us, why should it not be imputed to us, since we have applied it to ourselves by apprehending it through faith?

units.la: XLV.
units.tr: XLV.

units.la: Justitia Christi, quæ justificandis imputatur, non essentialis, seu æterna & infinita Deitatis Christi justitia est, quod perperam in controversia de Christo Mediatore adversus Stancarum Osiander asseruit. Hæc enim, cùm per essentiæ Divinæ simplicitatem sit Deitas ipsa, venire in rationes justitiæ illius, quæ homini imputatur, citra monstrosam ejus Deificationem, non potest. Legalis igitur est, seu exacta ad amussim Legis illius, sub cujus conditione Deus fœdus operum cum homine integro pepigit. Quæ lex obedientiam perfectam quoad partes, gradus & perseverantiam ab homine exegit, & transgressori mortem comminata est. Cùmque eam homo transgressus fuerit, & transgressione sua ita mortem commeruerit, ut tamen, ceu creatura Dei manens, à debito obediendi & implendi legem absolutus minimè fuerit, uti Loc. IX. 26. fusiùs comprobavimus, manifestum fit, Christum, qui in fœdere gratiæ locum peccatoris subiit, & μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν formam servi assumens, Phil. II. 7. ejus loco ὑπὸ νόμον γενόμενον sub lege factus, seu legi subjectus est, Gal. IV. 4. non tantùm pro nobis mortem subire, & execrationem fieri; sed etiam justitiam omnem implere debuisse. Absque hoc enim fuisset, legi factum satis non esset, neque benedictio, & vitæ hæreditas, utpote jure plenæ obedientiæ & δικαιώματος Christi non quæsita; donari nobis posset.
units.tr: The righteousness of Christ that is imputed to those who are justified is not the essential righteousness of Christ's deity, that is, the eternal and infinite righteousness of the Godhead, which he wrongly asserted against Stancarus in the dispute about Christ the Mediator. For since, by the simplicity of the divine essence, that righteousness is the Godhead itself, it cannot come into the account of the righteousness that is imputed to man without a monstrous deification of him. It is therefore legal: that is, exact to the very line of that law, under whose condition God made the covenant of works with man in his integrity. That law demanded from man perfect obedience in its parts, degrees and perseverance, and threatened death to the transgressor. Since man transgressed it and by his transgression deserved death, yet remained as God's creature and was by no means released from the duty of obeying and fulfilling the law (as we have shown more fully in Loc. IX, 26), it is plain that Christ, who in the covenant of grace took the place of the sinner, "taking the form of a servant" [μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν] (Phil. 2:7), and in his place "made under the law" [ὑπὸ νόμον γενόμενον], that is, made subject to the law (Gal. 4:4), was bound not only to undergo death for us and become a curse, but also to fulfil all righteousness. Without this, the law would not have been satisfied, and the blessing and the inheritance of life could not be given to us, since they were not obtained by the right of Christ's full obedience and righteousness [δικαίωμα].

units.la: Justitia Christi homini peccatori imputata non essentialis Dei, sed legalis Christi Mediatoris justitia est. docti sic justitiam Christi partiuntur, vel sepa-rant etiam, ut omnino alia activa, quam imputari fatentur, alia passiva (totidem videlicet ejusdem justitiae partes reapse distinctae) dicatur, & illi meritum vitae, huic meritum liberationis a morte distincte tribuatur. Una enim justitia, unum δικαίωμα, una obedientia Christi est, quam & vitam universam ad normam legis Divinae componendo, & patienter atque ex amore Dei & hominis patiendo demonstravit, quaeque proin in ipsa etiam morte, ex charitate Dei & hominis obita, activa fuit. Majorem charitatem nemo habet hac, qua quis animam suam ponit pro amicis suis, Joh. XV. 13. Nam in rigore & per se nulla in passionibus justitia est, nisi quatenus in iis charitatis erga Deum & proximum activa demonstratio, & quaedam veluti cos, justitiam & patientiam acuens, est, ut pro justitia passiva rectius justitiam activam passionibus exploratam, & ex illis elucantem, seu ὑπακοὴν obedientiam, quam ex passionibus didicit, Hebr. V. 8. dicas. Sicut vita Christi perpetua quaedam crux, & actiones ejus passiones, quippe a persona exinanita & humiliata profectae, fuerunt: ita etiam in Christi morte & passione actio omnium nobilissima, exercitium dilectionis inimici, humilitatis, patientiae, obedientiae, fiduciae, omniumque virtutum plenissimum emicuit. Ideo Scriptura δικαίωμα, seu causam justitiae, simpliciter nomine ὑπακοῆς obedientiae, Rom. V. 18. 19. & δικαιοσύνης justitiae, 2. Cor. V. 21. insignit. In passionibus autem ejus est τελείωσις consummatio justitiae, Hebr. II. 10. & ejusdem πειρασμὸς tentatio, ibid. 18. cap. IV. 15. Obedientia illa respectu personae agentis vel patientis ταπείνωσις humiliatio, & ἐξινάνωσις exinanitio voluntaria: respectu legis & pacti cum Patre, ὑπακοὴ obedientia, & δικαιοσύνη justitia: respectu extremi actus & coronidis mors, crux, passio, oblatio, sanguis appellatur. Quae observata disputationi de imputatione justitiae Christi activae & passivae finem imponere possunt.
units.tr: The righteousness of Christ imputed to the sinner man is not the righteousness of God in its essence, but the legal righteousness of Christ the Mediator. Some scholars divide or even separate the righteousness of Christ in such a way that they call one part active, which they admit is imputed, and another part passive (these being, in fact, distinct parts of the same righteousness), and they assign to the one the merit of life and to the other the merit of deliverance from death, as though these were different things. For there is one righteousness, one act of righteousness [δικαίωμα], one obedience of Christ, which he displayed both in ordering his whole life according to the norm of the divine law, and in suffering patiently and out of love for God and man. Therefore this obedience was active even in his death, which he underwent out of charity toward God and man. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lays down his life for his friends (John 15:13). For strictly speaking, there is in sufferings no righteousness in themselves, except insofar as in them there is an active demonstration of love toward God and neighbour, and a kind of whetstone, as it were, sharpening righteousness and patience. Hence it is more correct to call the active righteousness, tested by sufferings and shining forth from them, passive, or obedience [ὑπακοὴ], which he learned from what he suffered (Heb. 5:8). Just as the whole life of Christ was a kind of perpetual cross, and his actions were sufferings, since they proceeded from a person emptied and humbled, so also in the death and passion of Christ the most noble action shone forth, the exercise of love toward an enemy, of humility, patience, obedience, trust, and of all virtues in fullest measure. Therefore Scripture names the righteousness, or the ground of righteousness [δικαίωμα], simply obedience [ὑπακοῆς] (Rom. 5:18, 19), and righteousness [δικαιοσύνης] (2 Cor. 5:21). In his sufferings, however, there is the consummation [τελείωσις] of righteousness (Heb. 2:10), and its trial [πειρασμὸς] (ibid. 2:18; 4:15). That same obedience, with respect to the person acting or suffering, is called humiliation [ταπείνωσις] and voluntary emptying [ἐξινάνωσις]; with respect to the law and the compact with the Father, it is obedience [ὑπακοή] and righteousness [δικαιοσύνη]; with respect to its final act and crown, it is called death, cross, passion, offering, blood. These observations can put an end to the dispute about the imputation of Christ's active and passive righteousness.

units.la: XLVII. Sed presslus tamen ut agamus in re, quae ad justificationis sanitatem doctrinam magni momenti est, Scripturae certe obedientiam Christi nusquam ad solam mortem vel passionem ejus restringunt.
units.tr: XLVII. But, to speak more precisely about a matter of great importance for the soundness of the doctrine of justification, the Scriptures certainly nowhere restrict the obedience of Christ to his death or passion alone.

units.la: XLVII. Sed pressius tamen ut agamus in re, quae ad justificationis saniorem doctrinam magni momenti est, Scripturae certe obedientiam Christi nuspiam ad solam mortem vel passionem ejus restringunt. Quin potius justitiam nostram vel indefinite obedientiae Christi tribuunt, celebri illo loco, Rom. V. 19. Sicut per unius hominis inobedientiam peccatores constituti multi sunt: ita per unius obedientiam justi constituentur multi; ubi non solam mortis Christi obedientiam intelligi liquet, quia Christus ex passionibus obedientiam didicisse, Heb. V. 8. dicitur: vel ad Christi mortem, crucem, sanguinem, passionem, sacrificium vere ἱλαστήριον in cruce peractum, ceu redemptionis, remissionis peccatorum, reconciliationis nostrae causam, sic ἀπολυτρώσεως illimitate referunt, ut illa demum in morte Christi & cruce, tanquam ejus gradu & actu extremo desinat & terminetur. Ipse se exinanivit, forma servi accepta &c. factus obediens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, Phil. II. 8. Quibus verbis Apostolus non justitiam distinguit, & in partes concidit, sed unicam obedientiam Christi perfectissimam, ab incarnatione Christi inchoatam, per totum vitae ejus curriculum extensam & continuatam, atque in morte demum terminatam & consummatam proponit, eamque sine discrimine κένωσιν, ταπείνωσιν, ὑπακοήν exinanitionem, humiliationem, obedientiam appellat; nec aliter universam Christi vitam, quam ut perpetuam submissionem, humiliationem, gradatim ad extremum usque terminum, crucem videlicet, sub qua & sepultura triduana intelligitur, procedentem, definit. Non demum in morte obediens fuit, sed μέχρι θανάτου usque ad mortem. Accedit, quod quam voluntatem Christi David de obedientia legi per universam vitam sanctissimam praestita, Psal. XL. 7. &c. explicat, eandem Paulus Heb. X. 7. &c. de oblatione corporis Christi interpretatur. Paulus sic loquitur: Quapropter ingrediens in mundum dixit: Sacrificia & oblationem noluisti; Corpus autem adaptasti mihi: Tunc dixi: Ecce adsum, in capite libri de me scriptum est, ut faciam, O Deus, voluntatem tuam. Qua voluntate sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Jesu Christi semel factam. At voluntatem hanc David Psal. XL. 7. &c. ad alia etiam, quam ad oblationem in cruce factam restringit. Facere, inquit, voluntatem tuam, o Deus mi, delector, & lex tua in medio viscerum meorum est. Praedico justitiam tuam in congregatione multa. Ecce labia mea non cohibeo, o Jehova, tu nosti; &c. Jam & pretium illud, quo empti sumus, non in passionibus duntaxat, sed in passionibus etiam legi Divinae conformatis Scripturae collocant. Non corruptibilibus rebus, auro vel argento redempti estis, sed pretioso sanguine Agni immaculati & incontaminati, 1. Pet. I. 18. 19. Talis nos decebat Pontifex, sanctus, &c. Hebr. VII. 26. 27. Qualis autem erat sanguis agni, qualis victima Sacerdotis, talis nobis imputatur.
