Negari porro nequit, quin Christus apud Deum Patrem ἔγγυος Sponsor fuerit ejus implendae legis, quam homo implere debuit, juxta mandatum: Fac hoc & vives; At legem illam, quae facere jubet, non patiendo duntaxat in cruce, sed toto vitae suae sanctissimae decursu, & ex charitate ipsa moriendo, implevit. Neque pro in ad vitam & salutem nostram sufficiebat, ut reatus nobis incumbens sacrificio mortis Christi auferretur; sed obedientia a primo momento ad extremum usque actum vitae producta & continuata requisita est. Tali enim, non alii lex, innocentem facere, & peccatorem tum facere, tum pati jubens, vitam promisit. Pro iis, inquit, sanctifico me ipsum, ut & ipsi sanctificati sint in veritate, Joh. XVII. 19. Et poenae reatum ab obedientiae debito non emancipare, fusius in loco ostendimus. Dignum inprimis notatu, quod per Christum δικαίωμα & νόμος ἐν ἡμῖν πληρωθῇ justitiam legis in nobis impleri, Rom. VIII. 4. dixit; ubi justitia legis nec poenas, nec solas poenas notat, tum quia illa in nobis impleri dicitur, cum tamen justitia, & jus legis sit non tantum maledicere peccatori, sed etiam postulare facta, ut per ea homo vivat: tum quia Christus justitiam legis in nobis implevit, quam lex per carnem infirmata implere non potuit. At lex ad poenam exigendam & peccatori infligendam potentissima fuit. Denique doctrina haec tum ad Christi ipsius gloriam, tum ad conscientiae nostrae plenam pacem, consolationem & securitatem plurimum facit. Ad Christi gloriam, quia ei gloriosum magis
units.tr: XLVII. But, to speak more precisely about a matter of great importance for the sounder doctrine of justification, the Scriptures nowhere restrict the obedience of Christ to his death or passion alone. Rather, they ascribe our righteousness to the obedience of Christ in general, in that famous passage, Rom. 5:19: As by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one many will be made righteous. Here it is clear that the obedience meant is not only the obedience of Christ's death, since Christ is said to have learned obedience from what he suffered (Heb. 5:8). Nor do they refer redemption, without limit, to Christ's death, cross, blood, passion, or sacrifice truly accomplished on the cross as the propitiation [ἱλαστήριον] and cause of our redemption, remission of sins and reconciliation, in such a way that it ends and terminates in Christ's death and cross as the last step and final act of his obedience. He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, etc., becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil. 2:8). In these words the Apostle does not distinguish righteousness or divide it into parts, but sets forth one most perfect obedience of Christ, begun from his incarnation, extended and continued through the whole course of his life, and at last ended and completed in death. He calls it without distinction emptying [κένωσιν], humiliation [ταπείνωσιν], obedience [ὑπακοήν]. Nor does he describe the whole life of Christ otherwise than as a perpetual submission and humiliation, advancing step by step to its last limit, namely the cross, under which is understood also the three days of burial. He was not obedient only at the end in death, but unto death [μέχρι θανάτου]. Moreover, the will of Christ, which David explains as the obedience to the law rendered through his whole most holy life (Ps. 40:7 ff.), Paul interprets in Heb. 10:7 ff. as the offering of Christ's body. Paul speaks thus: Wherefore, when he came into the world he said: Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; but a body you prepared for me. Then I said: Behold, I come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will, O God. By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. But David (Ps. 40:7 ff.) restricts this will not only to the offering made on the cross, but applies it also to other things: I delight to do your will, O my God, and your law is within my heart. I proclaim your righteousness in the great congregation. Behold, I do not restrain my lips, O LORD, you know it; etc. Again, Scripture places the price by which we were bought not only in the sufferings, but in the sufferings conformed to the divine law also. You were redeemed not with corruptible things, with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of a lamb unblemished and undefiled (1 Pet. 1:18, 19). Such a high priest was fitting for us, holy, etc. (Heb. 7:26, 27). But as the blood of the lamb was, and as the victim of the priest was, so it is imputed to us. Nor can it be denied that Christ was before God the Father the surety [ἔγγυος] of the fulfilment of that law, which man was bound to fulfil according to the command: Do this and you shall live. But he fulfilled that law, which commands doing, not merely by suffering on the cross, but through the whole course of his most holy life, and by dying out of love itself. Nor was it sufficient for our life and salvation that the guilt lying upon us should be removed by the sacrifice of Christ's death; but obedience carried out and continued from the first moment to the last act of life was required. For the law, which commands the innocent to be made innocent and the sinner both to do and to suffer, promised life only on such terms, and not otherwise. For their sake I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth (John 17:19). We have shown more fully in the proper place that the guilt of punishment is not freed from the debt of obedience. It is especially worthy of note that through Christ the righteousness of the law [δικαίωμα] was said to be fulfilled in us (Rom. 8:4), where the righteousness of the law denotes neither punishments nor punishments alone: first, because it is said to be fulfilled in us, whereas the righteousness and right of the law consists not only in cursing the sinner, but also in requiring deeds by which man may live; and second, because Christ fulfilled in us the righteousness of the law, which the law, weakened through the flesh, could not fulfil. Yet the law was most powerful in exacting punishment and inflicting it on the sinner. Finally, this doctrine contributes greatly both to the glory of Christ himself and to the full peace, consolation and security of our conscience. It contributes to the glory of Christ, because it is more glorious to him, and especially effective in extolling the riches of his grace, if it is established that he is our whole Christ, and that he did not only undergo an ignominious death for us, but also passed for us a holy, laborious life of practice; nor did he, in living, act for his own sake, and in dying...

units.la: Quod plu-ribus asseritur. gis est, & ad extollendas gratiæ ejus divitias inprimis efficax, si constet, illum ὀλόκληρον nostrum esse, neque tantum ignominiosam mortem pro nobis subiisse, sed vitam etiam sanctam, exercitam, laboriosam pro nobis transegisse; nec vivendo quidem suum, moriendo autem nostrum, sed tum vivendo, tum moriendo nostrum tantum tum legem universam implendi, tum moriendi debitum expunxisse. Ad conscientiæ quoque plenam pacem, consolationem & securitatem facit, si certi fuerimus, in Christo reperiri id omne, quo nos indigere sentimus, ut coram Dei judicio intrepidè comparearnus. At conscientia nostra nos constrictos convictosque tenet, quòd nobis peccatoribus, ut coram Deo justificari possimus, & admissi peccati expiatio, & naturæ totius sanctitas, & perfecta Divinæ legis impletio necessaria sit. Hæc vero cunctasi in Christo ita reperiuntur, ut simul nobis liberaliter donentur, & imputentur, nihil ad conscientiæ pacem, consolationem & servitutem ultra desiderari poterit. Sive igitur Sathanas reatum poenæ æternæ peccato contractum objicit, & inferorum horrores excitat, Christus pro nobis execratio factus, plagis à Deo percussus, mortuus est; sive ortus nostri impuritatem, & originalis labis fœditatem objicit, Christi originalis sanctitas & innocentia eam resarcit; sive legem à nobis violatam variis modis, nec omnino præstitum à nobis officium causatur, Christi obedientia, qua legi in solidum satisfecit, defectum compensat. Scitè Bernhardus in Sententiis: Triplici morbo laborat genus humanum, principio, medio & fine. Nativitas immunda, vita perversa, mors periculosa. Venit Christus, & contra triplicem hunc morbum triplex remedium opposuit. Natus enim est, vixit, mortuus est. Atque ejus nativitas purgavit nostram, mors illius destruxit nostram, & vita illius instruxit nostram. Non quòd singulis hisce partibus, tanquam causis reciprocis effectus hos adaptandos putemus, sed quòd nullum periculum, vel metus excessus sit, ne nimium Christo confidamus, suspicantes, vel plura nobis ad salutem deesse, quàm desunt: vel plura quàm opus est, in Christo ad justitiam & vitam nobis imputari.
units.tr: ...which is asserted by many, is more glorious for him, and is especially effective in extolling the riches of his grace, if it is established that he is our wholeness [ὀλόκληρον], and that he not only underwent a shameful death for us but also lived a holy, disciplined and laborious life on our behalf. He did not live for himself and die for us. Rather, both by living and by dying he was ours: by living he fulfilled the whole law for us, and by dying he cancelled the debt of death. This doctrine also brings peace, consolation and security to the conscience, if we are certain that everything we feel we lack is found in Christ, so that we can appear fearlessly before the judgment of God. Our conscience holds us bound and convicted, because for us sinners to be justified before God we need the atonement for sin admitted, the holiness of our whole nature, and the perfect fulfilment of the divine law. But when all these things are found in Christ in such a way that they are given to us and imputed to us freely, nothing more can be desired for the peace, consolation and security of the conscience. So whether Satan lays before us the guilt of eternal punishment incurred by sin and stirs up the horrors of hell, Christ, made a curse for us and struck by God with blows, has died; whether he lays before us the impurity of our birth and the foulness of original stain, the original holiness and innocence of Christ make amends for it; whether he accuses us of having violated the law in various ways and of not having rendered the duty required of us at all, the obedience of Christ, by which he fully satisfied the law, makes up for the deficiency. Bernard rightly says in the Sentences: "The human race suffers from a threefold disease, at its beginning, its middle and its end: an unclean birth, a perverse life, a dangerous death. Christ came, and against this threefold disease he set a threefold remedy. For he was born, he lived, he died. His birth cleansed ours, his death destroyed ours, and his life built up ours." We do not mean that these effects must be matched to each of these parts as if they were reciprocal causes, but that there is no danger or fear of excess that we might trust in Christ too much, by supposing either that we lack more for salvation than we do lack, or that more is imputed to us in Christ for righteousness and life than is needed.

units.la: XLVIII. Neque verò metuendum est, ne nimis legalis sic fiat justificatio nostra.
units.tr: XLVIII. Nor indeed is it to be feared that our justification should thereby become too legal.

units.la: Licet enim illa non sit ex lege, sed ex fide, sit tamen in Christo secundum legem. Lex neminem justificat. Sed id tamen, quod justificationis materia & fundamentum est, legis præscripto respondere debet, cùm Apostolus doceat, per justificationem Evangelicam, in nobis τὸ δικαίωμα & νόμος justitiam legis impleri, Rom. VIII. 4. Ratio verò, cur satisfactio Christi & redemptio nostra frequenter adeò morti & sanguini Christi tribuatur, in promptu est, quia summum suum fastigium & colophonem in morte Christi consecuta est. Nam Christus ἐτελειώθη διὰ τῶν παθημάτων consummatus est per passiones, Hebr. II. 10. Sed à charitate & justitia illa, quam in morte Deo præstitit, vita ante acta, ceu perpetua quædam exinanitio & humiliatio secludi non debet. Unica obedientia, unica humiliatio fuit, quæ morte Christi complementum sortita est. Ita ejusdem virtutis, constantiæ vel fortitudinis est, tum hostem strenuè pugnando repellere, tum dolores, cruciatus, tormenta, mortem repellere. Nihil ergo vetat, mortis generosæ mentione facta congeneres vitæ actiones subintelligi. Quomodo pii & regeniti non tantum charitatis opera exercentes, & in tota vita pietati studentes, sed etiam, necessitate ita postulante, gloriosò martyrio veritatem & pietatem ante actam obsignantes, eadem pietate, sanctitate, charitate inchoata, continuata & provecta ad finem usque id faciunt. Sed negant illi, remissionem peccatorum, quàm Scriptura morti Christi acceptam fert, ab imputatione justitiæ ad vitam reapse differre, quia is, qui à poena capitali absolvitur, eo ipso jus vitæ habeat. Cæterùm non observant, non agi hic de justificatione ejusmodi, qua judex vel prætor crimine capitali arcessitum insontem pronuntiat, atque à morte absolutum ulteriori vitæ relinquit, sed de ea, qua judex sive brabeuta & præmiorum secundum legem diribitor, quempiam ob rem præclarè gestam, & conditionem, quam lex requirit, exactè impletam, præmio dignum judicat. Scriptura enim de vita æterna, quæ in justificatione homini adjudicatur, tanquam שכר פעולה operæ pretio, seu præmio, legem facientibus promisso & proposito loquitur: Homo, qui facit hæc, vivet in iis, Levit. XVIII. 5. Si vis ingredi ad vitam, serva mandata, Matth. XIX. 17. Reposita mihi est corona justitiæ, quam reddet mihi Dominus in illa die, ille justus judex, 2. Timoth. IV. 8. Justificatio enim est sententia Dei judicis omnium (Hebr. XII. 23.) talis, qua peccatoris propter Christum partim poena mortis & maledictionis remittitur, partim benedictio & vita, non ea duntaxat, quam in Adamo habuimus & amisimus, quæ terrena adhuc & Paradisiaca fuit, sed cœlestis, spiritualis & æterna, quam Adamus nondum habuit, per eundem Christum adjudicatur. Hac ergo spe vitæ æternæ, cùm in Adamo homo exciderit, & peccato reatum mortis contraxerit, non tantùm à morte liberari, & in integrum restitui, sed etiam, quia hac in integrum restitutione non plus ei reddi potuit, quàm in Adamo habuit, jus vitæ æternæ, & justitiam perfectam legis ad jus hoc acquirendum necessarium consequi debuit. Neutrum verò cùm præstare ipse potuerit, necessarius ei sponsor fuit, qui & poenas pro peccatore ad ejus liberationem & restitutionem necessarias subiret, & justitiam legis perfectam, causam juris vitam consequendi repræsentaret. Dilutum verò & illud est, quòd justitiam activam conditionem in Mediatore requisitam, sine qua Mediator esse, vel morte sua aliquid nobis promereri non potuerit, non materiam nostrae justificationis fuisse pertendunt. Nam & conditio in Mediatore fuit, & materia justificationis, peccatori imputata. Constat enim etiam illa debitori imputari, quæ nummis pro ipso solutis, ceu conditiones quædam valorem conciliant, veluti quòd aurei, argentei sunt. Et si obedientia Christi activa materiam justificationis non ingreditur, neque peccatori ad justitiam imputatur, quæ igitur illa justitia est, ob quam peccator in justificatione sic justus censetur, ut jus petendi vitam æternam habeat? Mera enim passio hoc nomine venire non potest, quia alias etiam damnati in inferno, cùm poenam luunt, simul hanc justitiam praestarent, vel in statu essent jus vitae aeternae promerendi. An sine impletione legis propria vel imputata quisquam salvari potest? Annon potius secum justitiam perfectam legis ferre tenetur, qui viam in Coelum adfectat? An qui ob crimen virgis caesus est, poenam illam sustinendo omnes numeros boni civis implesse, imo dignus, qui propter ea ad summos in Republica honores evehatur, censeri potest? Sed opus omnino nobis est veste, qua coram facie Dei compareamus. In hoc suspiramus, &c. an futurum sit, ut etiam induti, non nudi inveniamur. Non enim exuere, sed superindnere cupimus, 2. Corinth. V.2.3.4. Quae haec vestis est? Instauratio, inquiunt, imaginis Divinae amissae, quam passione sua Christus nobis meruit. Sed haec justificationis & sanctificationis confusio, & hujus supra illam evectio quaedam est. Atqui Deus justificat impium, Rom. IV. 5. Ergo imago Dei, vel justitia inhaerens non ea justitia est, per & propter quam justificamur, vel ob quam Deus in hoc negotio judicem agens, & secundum legem suam judicans, jus petendi vitam aeternam nobis impertiatur. Licet enim merito mortis Christi etiam imago Dei in justificatis restituatur, tamen in justificando nullas illa omnino partes habet. Utraque quidem justitia imputata & inhaerens cum veste comparatur, illa Rom. XIII. 14. 2. Cor. V. 3. Gal. III. 27. haec Ephes. IV. 24. Apoc. XIX. 8. sed lato cum discrimine. Illam comparituri coram tribunali Dei induimus, ut a peccatis, quae vestis ista tegit, absolvamur, & jus vitae aeternae, quod vestis ista requirit, obtineamus. Hac ornamur intus, tum ut gratos nos pro jure eo concesso geramus; tum ut justificationem apud nos ipsos firmam reddamus; tum ut ad actualem ejus fruitionem nos praeparemus.
units.tr: For although justification is not from the law but from faith, it is nevertheless in Christ according to the law. The law justifies no one. Yet what is the matter and foundation of justification must still correspond to the prescription of the law, since the Apostle teaches that through the gospel justification, "the righteous requirement of the law [τὸ δικαίωμα] and the law [νόμος]" is fulfilled in us, Rom. 8.4. The reason why the satisfaction of Christ and our redemption are so often ascribed to the death and blood of Christ is plain: his highest summit and crown was reached in the death of Christ. For Christ was made perfect through sufferings [ἐτελειώθη διὰ τῶν παθημάτων], Heb. 2.10. Yet the love and righteousness which he showed to God in his death should not be cut off from the life lived before it, as if it were a kind of continual emptying and humbling. There was one obedience and one humbling, which received its completion in the death of Christ. Thus it belongs to the same virtue, steadfastness or courage, to repel an enemy by fighting bravely and to repel pains, torments, tortures and death. Nothing therefore prevents the mention of a noble death from implying the actions of his life that belong with it. So too the pious and regenerate, who not only perform works of love and devote themselves to piety throughout their life, but who also, when necessity demands it, seal the truth and piety by a glorious martyrdom, carry this same piety, holiness and love, begun, continued and advanced, to the end. But these people deny that the remission of sins, which Scripture attributes to the death of Christ, really differs from the imputation of righteousness to life, because one who is acquitted of a capital penalty thereby has a right to life. But they do not observe that we are not here speaking of that kind of justification by which a judge or praetor pronounces an innocent man, accused of a capital crime, free and leaves him to the rest of his life after releasing him from death. Rather we are speaking of that justification by which a judge, or arbiter, or distributor of rewards according to the law, judges someone worthy of a reward because of a deed well done and a condition which the law requires has been exactly fulfilled. For Scripture speaks of eternal life, which is adjudged to man in justification, as the wage of work [שכר פעולה], or reward, promised and set before those who keep the law: "The man who does these things shall live by them," Lev. 18.5; "If you would enter into life, keep the commandments," Matt. 19.17; "There is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day," 2 Tim. 4.8. For justification is the sentence of God, the judge of all (Heb. 12.23), by which the penalty of death and the curse are partly remitted to the sinner for Christ's sake, and partly blessing and life are adjudged through the same Christ, not only the life we had and lost in Adam, which was still earthly and paradisiacal, but a heavenly, spiritual and eternal life, which Adam did not yet have. Therefore, since man fell in Adam and incurred the guilt of death through sin, in hope of this eternal life he must be freed not only from death and restored to his former state, but also, since in such a restoration nothing more could be given back to him than he had in Adam, he must obtain the right to eternal life and the perfect righteousness of the law necessary for acquiring this right. Since he could not perform either of these himself, he needed a surety who would both undergo the punishments necessary for the sinner's deliverance and restoration, and would represent the perfect righteousness of the law, the ground of the right to obtain life. Again, the claim that the active righteousness required in the Mediator, without which he could not be Mediator or merit anything for us by his death, was not the matter of our justification, is weak. For it was both a condition in the Mediator and the matter of justification imputed to the sinner. It is established that even that which secures value as a kind of condition is imputed to the debtor, when coins paid on his behalf have the qualities of gold or silver. And if the active obedience of Christ does not enter into the matter of justification and is not imputed to the sinner for righteousness, then what is that righteousness by which the sinner is counted righteous in justification, so as to have a right to ask for eternal life? Mere suffering cannot be called by this name, for then the damned in hell, while they pay their penalty, would at the same time render this righteousness, or would be in a state of meriting a right to eternal life. Can anyone be saved without the fulfilment of the law, either one's own or imputed? Is not rather the one who aims at the way to heaven bound to carry with him the perfect righteousness of the law? Or can someone who has been beaten with rods for a crime, by enduring that punishment, be considered to have fulfilled every requirement of a good citizen, or even to be worthy of being raised to the highest honours in the commonwealth for that reason? But we absolutely need a garment in which we may appear before the face of God. In this we groan, etc., whether it will be that we are found clothed, not naked. For we desire not to be unclothed, but to be further clothed upon, 2 Cor. 5.2-4. What is this garment? They say it is the restoration of the divine image lost, which Christ merited for us by his suffering. But this is a confusion of justification and sanctification and a kind of elevation of the latter above the former. Yet God justifies the ungodly, Rom. 4.5. Therefore the image of God, or inherent righteousness, is not that righteousness through and for which we are justified, or by reason of which God, acting as judge in this business and judging according to his law, bestows on us the right to ask for eternal life. For although by the merit of Christ's death the image of God is also restored in those who are justified, nevertheless it has no part at all in justifying. Both imputed and inherent righteousness are compared to a garment: the former in Rom. 13.14, 2 Cor. 5.3, Gal. 3.27; the latter in Eph. 4.24, Rev. 19.8, but with a wide difference. We put on the former when we are about to appear before the judgment seat of God, so that we may be absolved from the sins which that garment covers, and obtain the right to eternal life, which that garment requires. With the latter we are adorned inwardly, so that we may conduct ourselves as thankful for the right granted to us, so that we may make our justification firm in ourselves, and so that we may prepare ourselves for its actual enjoyment.

units.la: Parum etiam solidum illud est, quod praecipue moveri solet, Christum, tanquam Dei creaturam pro se obedientiam legi Dei morali praestandam reum debendi fuisse, neque proinde illam peccatori imputari posse. An enim putabimus, Adamum uno eodemque peccato & sibi & posteris peccare potuisse: at Christum eadem justitia sibi & nobis prodesse, non potuisse? Praesertim cum Adamus non sua sponte se obedientiae pro posteris debitorem fecerit, at Christus sponte se legi, cui persona ejus ante incarnationem parere non tenebatur, obnoxium fecerit, & tanquam sponsor pro nobis manum complosserit. Accedit, quod obedientia Christi opus fuerit. At Christus, qua Deus, obedientiam debendi reus non fuit.
units.tr: This is also a weak argument, though it is often pressed: that Christ, as a creature of God, owed the obedience of the moral law for himself, and so that obedience cannot be imputed to a sinner. Would we say that Adam by one and the same sin could sin both for himself and for his posterity, but that Christ could not by the same righteousness benefit both himself and us? Especially since Adam did not of his own accord make himself a debtor of obedience on behalf of his posterity, whereas Christ of his own accord bound himself to the law, which his person was not bound to obey before the incarnation, and clasped hands as a surety for us. Besides, Christ's obedience was a work. But Christ, as God, was not a debtor of obedience.

units.la: Sed missis his, negamus certe, Christum, qua is homo & creatura Dei fuit, reum fuisse debendi obedientiam meritoriam, hoc est, talem, qua sibi jus vitae demum mereretur. Cum enim venerit in forma servi, Phil. II. 7. & legi subjectus, Galat. IV. 4. & Sponsor, fidejussor melioris testamenti, Hebr. VII. 22. quis eum obedientiam servi, legi ad promerendam vitam subjecti, fidejussionis pro se debuisse affirmaverit? Potuisset enim creatura Dei esse, & non sic obligari ad justitiam meritoriam & fidejussoriam; uti omnes consummati in Coelo, & fruentes jam gloria, ceu creaturae Dei, obedientiam Deo debent, neque tamen vel meritoriam, vel fidejussoriam debent. Ideo
units.tr: But setting these aside, we certainly deny that Christ, as he was a man and a creature of God, was a debtor of meritorious obedience, that is, of such obedience as would earn life for himself. For since he came in the form of a servant, Phil. 2:7, and was made under the law, Gal. 4:4, and became a surety of a better testament, Heb. 7:22, who would assert that he owed for himself the obedience of a servant and of one subject to the law to earn life, and the obedience of a surety? For he could have been a creature of God without being bound in this way to meritorious and surety righteousness, just as all who are perfected in heaven and already enjoy glory owe obedience to God as creatures of God, yet owe neither meritorious nor surety obedience. Therefore

units.la: Christus non sibi, sed nobis natus est, Esai. IX. 6. nec alio fine in mundum venit, & homo factus est, quam ut esset Mediator Dei & hominum, nec alio fine vixit & mortuus est, quam ut munus illud exerceret & exequeretur: ita inter homines agens nihil fecit vel passus est, quin ad munus illud Mediatoris suscep tum pertineret. Sicut qui pro alio fidejussit, ante fidejussionem liber, post eam debitor factus est, debitum autem non pro se, sed pro alio solvit, ita ut solutio alteri imputetur: ita Christus pro nobis fidejubendo, & juxta fidejussionem in carnem veniendo, se quoque debitorem servandae legis fecit, adeoque non pro se, sed pro nobis debitum illud legis exsolvit: ut ita quicquid, ut Sponsor pro nobis gessit; non ipsi sed nobis imputari debeat. Ita qui prius liber & sui juris, amici liberandi causa, alieno imperio se subjecit, sive sedem in ejus ditione figendo, sive se servituti ejus mancipando, sive quavis ratione alia jure suo cedendo, simul atque in alienam ditionem migraverit, illius jam subditus & servus est, cujus Regnum subiit.
units.tr: Christ was born not for himself but for us, Isa. 9:6, and he came into the world and was made man for no other end than to be the Mediator between God and men; nor did he live and die for any other end than to perform and carry out that office. So in acting and suffering among men he did nothing, and underwent nothing, that did not pertain to the office of Mediator he had undertaken. As one who has stood surety for another, free before the suretyship but a debtor after it, pays the debt not for himself but for the other, so that the payment is credited to that other, so Christ, by standing surety for us and by coming in the flesh in accordance with the suretyship, also made himself a debtor to keep the law, and therefore paid that debt of the law not for himself but for us. Thus whatever he did as our Surety should be imputed not to himself but to us. In the same way, one who was formerly free and his own master, and who for the sake of a friend to be freed submits himself to a foreign rule, whether by fixing his home under that rule, or by pledging himself into its servitude, or by surrendering his right in some other way, as soon as he has migrated into that foreign dominion becomes a subject and servant of the one whose kingdom he has entered.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem illuc se non sui, sed amici liberandi causa contulit: ita non pro se, sed pro amico se totum nexu & mancupio obnoxium fecit, & quodcunque in ea civitate ministerium obit, illud omne non ipsi, sed amico imputatur. Par ratio est Christi Mediatoris, servi formam assumentis, ut in ea legi Divinae se subjicere, & nos redimere posset. Porro S. Paulus Rom. IV. 6.7. beatum praedicat, cui Deus imputat justitiam sine operibus; & justitiam sine operibus ex testimonio Davidis ei imputari asserit, cui Deus peccata remittit; non quod remissio peccatorum totam justificationem absolvat, sed quia peccati remissio & vitae adjudicatio, quae per imputatam universam Christi justitiam obtingunt, beneficia adeo conjuncta sunt, ut, utram nominemus, utramque intelligere necesse habeamus.
units.tr: Just as he went there not for his own sake but for the sake of the friend he was to free, so he made himself wholly liable to the bond and pledge not for himself but for his friend, and whatever service he performs in that state is credited not to himself but to his friend. The same reasoning holds for Christ the Mediator, who took the form of a servant so that in that form he could submit himself to the divine law and redeem us. Moreover, St. Paul, Rom. 4:6, 7, pronounces blessed the one to whom God imputes righteousness without works, and he asserts from the testimony of David that righteousness without works is imputed to the one whose sins God forgives. He does not mean that the remission of sins accomplishes the whole of justification, but that the remission of sins and the adjudication of life, which come about through the imputation of the whole righteousness of Christ, are so closely joined as benefits that whichever one we name, we must understand both.

units.la: Nemo enim remisso peccato a morte liberatur, quin in vitam idem inducatur; nemo odio Dei subtrahitur, quin amore succedente ejusdem foveatur; nemo a poenis absolvitur, quin glorificetur. Amen, Amen dico vobis, qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei, qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam; & in condemnationem non venit, sed transfivit a morte ad vitam, Joh. V. 24. Cum vero non detur aditus ad Deum nisi reconciliatis in sanguine Christi per remissionem peccatorum, cum qua adjudicatio vitae & beatitudo cohaeret, & remissionem peccatorum non fieri ex operibus clarissime constet, atque vel inde maxime constet, justificationem seu beatitudinem non contingere ex operibus, quod solum probare Apostolus intendit, ideo remissionem peccatorum, ceu conspectiorem beatitudinis & justificationis partem, in qua maxime gratia Dei elucesceit, adversus meritum operum nominare satis habuit; sed non exclusa adjudicatione ad vitam, per eandem imputationem justitiae. Nam sine hac beatitudo illa constare non potuisset, & Apostolus imputationem justitiae totius Christi ad totum peccatorum remissione, & vitae adjudicatione constantem, abunde in praecedentibus & sequentibus stabilivit. An, ita paulo ante, legem inanem reddimus per fidem? Minime. Sed legem stabilimus, in Christo, qui
units.tr: For no one is freed from death by the remission of sin without being led at the same time into life; no one is withdrawn from the wrath of God without being cherished by his love in turn; no one is absolved from punishments without being glorified. Truly, truly I say to you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life; and he does not come into condemnation, but has passed from death to life, John 5:24. Since there is no access to God except for those reconciled in the blood of Christ through the remission of sins, to which the adjudication of life and blessedness cohere, and since it is most clearly established that the remission of sins does not come from works, and especially since it is established from this that justification or blessedness does not come from works (which alone the Apostle intends to prove), he was content to name the remission of sins, as the more conspicuous part of blessedness and justification, in which the grace of God shines most brightly, against the merit of works. He did not thereby exclude the adjudication to life through the same imputation of righteousness. For without this that blessedness could not stand, and the Apostle had amply established in what precedes and follows that the imputation of the righteousness of the whole of Christ, consisting in the remission of all sins and the adjudication of life, is so. Do we then make void the law through faith? By no means. Rather we establish the law, in Christ, who

units.la: cam eam loco nostro implevit, Rom. III. 31. Sicut per inobedientiam unius hominis peccatores constituti multi sunt, ita per obedientiam unius justi multi constituentur, ibid. v. 19. Cùmque justificatio hominis sit apotelesma totius justitiæ Christi à nativitate ejus inchoatæ, & in morte consummatæ, perperam dissentientes argutantur, si justitia activa Christi nobis imputetur, fore, ut per eam jam justi simus, neque adeò passionum & mortis Christi imputatione indigeamus. Sic enim justitiæ Christi non plenæ & consummatæ, sed imperfectæ justificatio tribuitur, quæ vi legis ipsius violatæ perfectum ἀποτέλεσμα esse debet, & ad expiationem peccati passionibus carere non potest. Nam Deus cum Christo omnia nobis gratificatur, ib. VIII. 32. Denique neque illud consequens est, ut, si Christi justitia illa, qua legem implevit, nobis imputatur, nos ab omni obedientia legis absolvamur. Alia enim obedientia filialis, in hac vita inchoata, in altera perfici nda, qua debitores sumus spiritui, non carni: alia servilis & meritoria, qua legis debitum ad promerendum vitam rigide exigitur, & totum perfecto actu sic implendum est, ut absque impletione tali nemo vitam ingredi possit. Utrius sque norma lex est, sed diversimodè; illic gratitudinis, hic rigidæ exactionis. Ad illam tenemur: ab hac liberati sumus. Si Filius vos liberavit, verè liberi eritis, Joh. VIII. 36. Justo lex non est posita, 1.Tim. I. 9.
units.tr: fulfilled it in our place, Rom. 3:31. As by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one many will be made righteous, ibid. v. 19. And since the justification of a man is the apotelesma [ἀποτέλεσμα, the completed result] of the whole righteousness of Christ, begun at his birth and completed in his death, those who dissent argue wrongly that if the active righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, we would thereby already be righteous, and would not need the imputation of Christ's sufferings and death. For in this way justification would be ascribed to the righteousness of Christ not as full and complete but as imperfect, whereas by the force of the law which has been violated it must be a perfect apotelesma, and cannot lack the sufferings for the expiation of sin. For God with Christ freely gives us all things, ibid. 8:32. Finally, it does not follow that if that righteousness of Christ by which he fulfilled the law is imputed to us, we are released from all obedience to the law. For there is one obedience that is filial, begun in this life and to be perfected in the next, by which we are debtors to the Spirit, not to the flesh; and there is another that is servile and meritorious, by which the debt of the law is rigidly demanded in order to earn life, and the whole must be fulfilled by perfect act, so that without such fulfilment no one can enter life. The norm of both is the law, but in different ways: the one of gratitude, the other of rigid exaction. We are bound to the former; from the latter we have been freed. If the Son makes you free, you will be truly free, John 8:36. The law is not laid down for the righteous, 1 Tim. 1:9.

units.la: XLIX. Justificatio remissionem peccatorum & vitæ, seu hæreditatis adjudicationem completitur. Nam cui justitia Christi per passiones consummata imputatur, illi & peccata condonantur, & jus vitæ addicitur; quia legi vitam promittenti, & quidem per peccatum violatæ in solidum satisfit, atque ita per Christum omne δικαίωμα in nobis impletur, Rom. VIII. 4. Id ipsum quoque Paulus, ibid. IV. 6. 8. inde probat, quòd is, cui Deus non imputat peccatum, μακαρίζεται beatus prædicatur. Si beatitudo cum remissione peccatorum connexa est, cum eadem etiam hæreditas vitæ connexa est, quia sine ea nemo beatus esse potest. Apostolo perinde erat dicere, δεδικαιωμένον justificatum & μακάριον beatum. Et ex fide, non ex operibus esse, eodem μακαρισμῷ beatitudinis elogio probat. Statim enim cum remissione peccati beatitudo connectitur. Sed remissionem peccati non esse ex opere, Apostolus, velut ex terminis clarum, supponit. Cùmque idem Apostolus ib. vers. 5. dixerit, fidem imputari ad justitiam, ea fides non est tantùm, qua creditur remissio peccatorum præteritorum, sed etiam qua creditur Deum justificare impium, justificare autem est habere pro eo, qui præmium vitæ æternæ jure petere & expectare potest. Et rem ita se habere necesse est, tum quia ad satisfactionem etiam δικαίωμα requiritur, & δικαίωμα importat δικαιοσύνλω: tum quia remissio peccatorum fit per redemptionem, redemptio autem emptionem in hæreditatem & peculium includit: tum quia ut extra Christum non potest esse remissio; ita in Christo non potest non justitia reperiri. Faciunt huc argumenta omnia, quibus supra fidem fecimus, justitiam Christi omnem nobis imputari eum in finem, ut tum peccata nobis condonentur, tum jus ad vitam æternam con-
units.tr: XLIX. Justification is completed by the remission of sins and the adjudication of life, or of the inheritance. For to the one to whom the righteousness of Christ, perfected through his sufferings, is imputed, both sins are forgiven and a right to life is granted; for the law which promises life, and which has been violated through sin, is fully satisfied, and so through Christ every dikaiōma [δικαίωμα, requirement of righteousness] of the law is fulfilled in us, Rom. 8:4. Paul himself also proves this from the same passage, Rom. 4:6, 8, where the one to whom God does not impute sin is pronounced blessed [μακαρίζεται]. If blessedness is connected with the remission of sins, then the inheritance of life is also connected with it, since no one can be blessed without it. For the Apostle it was the same to say justified [δεδικαιωμένον] and blessed [μακάριον]. And by the same blessing [μακαρισμῷ] of blessedness he proves that it is from faith, not from works. For blessedness is joined at once with the remission of sin. But the Apostle presupposes, as is clear from the terms themselves, that the remission of sin is not from works. And since the same Apostle said in verse 5, faith is imputed for righteousness, that faith is not only the faith by which the remission of past sins is believed, but also the faith by which it is believed that God justifies the ungodly. To justify, however, is to hold as righteous the one who can rightly seek and expect the reward of eternal life. And it must be so, both because satisfaction also requires a dikaiōma, and a dikaiōma implies dikaiosynē [δικαιοσύνη, righteousness]; and because the remission of sins comes through redemption, and redemption includes purchase into an inheritance and a possession; and because just as there can be no remission outside Christ, so righteousness cannot fail to be found in Christ. All the arguments by which we have above established that the whole righteousness of Christ is imputed to us serve this purpose: that both sins are forgiven to us and a right to eternal life is obtained.

units.la: sequendam habeamus. Sed sic tamen beneficia hæc distinguuntur, ut nihilominus etiam connexa, imò & innexa intelligi debeant. Quomodo Apostolum Rom. IV. 6. 7. nominata remissione peccatorum etiam addictionem vitæ & hæreditatis intellexisse, non semel jam ostendimus. Nam qua justitia peccatorum condonationem Christus nobis promeruit, eadem jus ad vitam promeruit, tum quia actiones Christi omnes, ceu actus personæ exinanitæ & humiliatæ, etiam passiones, & vicissim, fuerunt: tum quia & remissio peccatorum viam ad jus vitæ stravit, & qui jus vitæ habet, eidem peccata condonata intelliguntur: tum quia eadem utriusque causa est, imputatio justitiæ Christi totius in principio vitæ ejus inchoatæ, & in morte consummatæ. Neque obstat, quod Calvinus Antid. Concil. Trid. Sess. VI. cap. 7. justificationem in sola peccatorum remissione posuit; quia exclusivam sola non adjudicationi vitæ, sed renovationi naturæ, quam Tridentini in sua definitione una cum remissione peccatorum ad justificationem requirunt, opposuit.
units.tr: ...which we ought to follow. Yet these benefits are so distinguished that they must nonetheless be understood as connected, indeed as bound together. That the Apostle, in Rom. 4:6-7, by the name of forgiveness of sins also meant the adjudication of life and inheritance, we have already shown more than once. For the righteousness by which Christ merited for us the forgiveness of sins is the same by which he merited the right to life. This is so because all the actions of Christ, as acts of a person emptied and humbled, were also sufferings, and conversely. It is so also because the forgiveness of sins paves the way to the right to life, and those to whom life is due are understood to have their sins forgiven. And it is so because the cause of both is one: the imputation of the whole righteousness of Christ, begun at the start of his life and completed in his death. Nor does it stand in the way that Calvin, in his Antidote to the Council of Trent, Sess. VI, cap. 7, placed justification in the forgiveness of sins alone. For he set the exclusive alone not against the adjudication of life, but against the renewal of nature, which the Tridentines, in their definition, require along with the forgiveness of sins for justification.

units.la: L. Remissio peccatorum est actus Dei judicis, quo is peccatori credenti peccati reatum & pœnam propter Christum condonat. Beatus est, cujus defectio sublata, cujus peccatum tectum est. Beatus homo, cui Jehova non imputat pravitatem, Psal. XXXII. 1. 2. Rom. IV. 7. 8. Ubi auferre, tegere, non imputare sic conveniunt, ut unum alterum explicet. Nam peccata ablata sunt ferendo, quia Christus illa tulit in corpore suo supra lignum, 1. Petr. II. 24. ceu Agnus Dei illa sustulit, Joh. I. 29. Eadem tegu ntur induto Christo & ejus justitia: non imputantur, cùm pœna eorum à peccatore non exigitur, neque ille propter ea ampliùs accusatur. Benedic, anima mea, Jehova, &c. qui condonat omnem pravitatem tuam, medetur omnibus morbis tuis, Psal. CIII. 2. 3. Deus erat in Christo mundum sibi reconcilians, μὴ λογιζόμενος αὐτοῖς τὰ παραπτώματα non imputans iis peccata, 2. Corinth. V. 19. Phrasis ipsa, remittere peccata metaphorica est à creditoribus & debitoribus petita. Nam illi misericordia moti debitum ab his, solvendo impariubus, non exigentes, sed condonantes remittere dicuntur. Ideo remissionem peccatorum Christus parabola Regis creditoris & servorum debitorum, Matth. XVIII. 23. &c. alterius cujusdam creditoris & duorum debitorum, Luc. VII. 41. & ex adverso similitudine debitoris in carcerem conjecti, & usque ad solutionem ultimi quadrantis in eo detenti, Matth. V. 25. 26. declarat, & eo quoque confirmat, quòd nos peccatorum, tanquam ὀφειλημάτων debitorum remissionem quotidie à Deo petere jubet, ibid. VI. 12. Verè enim debita peccata sunt, quia peccator eorum pœnam Deo debet. Tum ergo Deus peccata remittit, cùm eorum pœnam non exigit, sed condonat. Quo sensu etiam non tantùm auferri, tegi, non imputari, sed etiam non observari, ut propter ea damnemur, Psal. CXXX. 3. deleri, non videri, projici post tergum, demergi in profundum maris, facies ab iis averti &c. dicuntur, quia qui peccatorum pœnam non exigit, illa veluti expungit, non videt, ut puniat; in profundum maris projicit, ne ad pœnam imputari possint. Cùm enim Christus pœnam nostram solverit, atque ea
units.tr: L. The forgiveness of sins is an act of God as judge, by which he, for Christ's sake, releases the sinner who believes from the guilt and punishment of sin. "Blessed is he whose transgression is taken away, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man to whom the LORD does not impute iniquity," Ps. 32:1-2; Rom. 4:7-8. Here "taking away," "covering," and "not imputing" agree in such a way that each explains the other. For sins are taken away by bearing them, because Christ "bore our sins in his own body on the tree," 1 Pet. 2:24, and as the Lamb of God he "took them away," John 1:29. The same sins are "covered" when Christ and his righteousness are put on. They are "not imputed" when their punishment is not demanded of the sinner, and he is no longer accused on account of them. "Bless the LORD, O my soul... who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases," Ps. 103:2-3. "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning their trespasses against them" [μὴ λογιζόμενος αὐτοῖς τὰ παραπτώματα], 2 Cor. 5:19. The very phrase "to forgive sins" is a metaphor taken from creditors and debtors. For when creditors, moved by mercy, do not demand a debt from debtors who cannot pay, but cancel it, they are said to "forgive" it. Therefore Christ, by the parable of the king and his servants who owed debts, Matt. 18:23ff., and of another creditor and two debtors, Luke 7:41, and by the opposite likeness of a debtor thrown into prison and kept there until he paid the last penny, Matt. 5:25-26, declares the forgiveness of sins. He also confirms this by bidding us daily ask God for the forgiveness of our debts [ὀφειλημάτων], Matt. 6:12. For sins truly are debts, since the sinner owes their punishment to God. God therefore forgives sins when he does not exact their punishment but cancels it. In this sense sins are said not only to be "taken away," "covered," and "not imputed," but also "not observed, so that we are condemned on account of them," Ps. 130:3; "blotted out," "not seen," "cast behind the back," "sunk into the depths of the sea," and "hidden from God's face," and so on. For he who does not exact the punishment of sins wipes them out as it were, does not look at them so as to punish, and casts them into the depths of the sea so that they cannot be imputed for punishment. For since Christ has paid our punishment, and that...

units.la: Justificatio partes remissio peccatorum & adjudicatio vitæ sunt; quæ beneficia sic distinguenda sunt, ut separari tamen non debeant.
units.tr: Justification has two parts: the forgiveness of sins and the adjudication of life. These benefits must be distinguished in such a way that they nevertheless should not be separated.

units.la: Remissio peccatorum eorundem condonatio, & non imputatio est. ea solutio Divinitus imputata nobis sit, non potest illa denuo à nobis exigi, cùm bona fides non patiatur idem debitum bis exigi. Nulla condemnatio in iis est, qui in Christo Jesu sunt, Rom. VIII. 1.
units.tr: The forgiveness of sins is the cancelling of debts, that is, non-imputation. Once that payment has been imputed to us by God, it cannot be demanded of us again, since good faith does not allow the same debt to be exacted twice. "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus," Rom. 8:1.

units.la: LI. Gravissimè circa remissionem peccatorum Pontificii hallucinantur. Nam remissionem peccati de expulsione potiùs ejus & abolitione vitiositatis, quàm de reatus ablatione, seu liberatione à condemnatione interpretantur. Quod phraseologiæ remittendi, condonandi, non imputandi peccata, è diametro repugnat. Alioqui si remissio peccatorum etiam vitiositatis inhærentis abolitio esset, ut illa perfecta est, sic hæc quoque perfecta foret, quod Scripturæ testimoniis, & justificatorum omnium, in quibus, quoad vixerunt, perpetua carnem inter & spiritum lucta fuit, exemplis repugnat. Sed aliter videlicet peccata sublata sunt, & tolluntur in cruce, aliter tolluntur in justificatione, aliter in sanctificatione. In cruce ea Christus sustulit satisfaciendo: in justificatione tolluntur non imputando: in sanctificatione paulatim enervando, abolendo. Verba igitur tollendi, delendi, longissime projiciendi &c. ad justificationem relata non propria, sed metonymica sunt, quibus peccata ipsa tolli, deleri &c. dicuntur, quia ipsorum consequens, reatus, seu obligatio ad poenam, seu poena ipsa tollitur. Sunt peccata etiam μολυσμοὶ & μιάσματα inquinamenta, ratione labis seu maculæ, quam insitam habent. Et à labe illa & pollutione etiam mundantur fideles, imperfectè in vita, perfectè in morte; at sanctificationis non justificationis beneficio. Porro medicus corporalis peritus sic morbos & vulnera corporis sanat, ut pro viribus suis illa etiam aboleat & destruat. Non impotentior vel infelicior medicus spiritualis Christus spirituales morbos penitus abolet & destruit. Cùm tamen omnipotens licet medicus, cui nihil insanabile est, causa voluntaria fit, quæ liberè agit, & actus suos dispensat non momento, nec uno beneficio & gradu, sed successivè & gradatim abolendo. Præterea cùm corpori mortuo vera vita restituitur, mortem omnino penitus extingui necesse est, quia idem corpus simul vivum & mortuum esse non potest. Sed dispar vivificationis spiritualis hactenus ratio est, quòd simul quidem ac homo justificatur, peccatum, quod imputatum mors animæ est, non imputatum sic moritur, & homo justitiæ & vitæ Christi per justificationem particeps vivit, atque per sanctificationem quoad justitiæ etiam inhærentis dominium vivificatur, ut tamen non simul semélque vetustus homo per concupiscentias totus corruptus moriatur, sed spiritu actus corporis mortificante (Rom. VIII. 13.) paulatim planè moriatur, atque ita homo interior renovetur ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ de die in diem, 2. Cor. IV. 16. Ibi ergo mors carnis, hominis exterioris & vetusti unà cum vita spiritus, hominis novi & interioris, Deo sic dispensante, consistit. Alias, si cui vita restituta est, in eo simpliciter abolitum peccatum est, nemini profectò Mortalium vita restituta fuerit, quia nemo ante mortem peccati prorsus expers est. Desino retundere calumnias Becani, quòd sic injuriam merito Christi inferamus, & Pharisæis similes Christum medicum obtrudamus, qui ægrotum non sanet, sed pallio tectum & involutum dimittat, nec plagas & vulnera tollat, sed tegat & occultet. Quæ similesque aniles nugæ & deliria ex iis, quæ diximus, planè evanescunt; & in adversarios ipsos, acri thyrso inhærentis justitiæ suæ percussos, & veram Christi justitiam fastidientes fortiùs longè retorqueri possunt.
units.tr: LI. The Papists go most seriously astray concerning the forgiveness of sins. For they interpret the forgiveness of sins as their expulsion and abolition of sinfulness, rather than as the removal of guilt, or deliverance from condemnation. This is directly contrary to the phrasing "to forgive, to cancel, not to impute sins." Otherwise, if the forgiveness of sins were also the abolition of inherent sinfulness, then, since forgiveness is complete, this abolition too would be complete. That contradicts the testimonies of Scripture and the examples of all the justified, in whom there was a continual struggle between flesh and spirit as long as they lived. But clearly sins are removed in one way on the cross, in another way in justification, and in another way in sanctification. On the cross Christ took them away by satisfaction. In justification they are taken away by non-imputation. In sanctification they are gradually weakened and abolished. Therefore the words "to take away," "to blot out," "to cast far away," and so on, when applied to justification, are not proper but metonymical. By them sins themselves are said to be taken away or blotted out, because what follows from them, the guilt or obligation to punishment, or the punishment itself, is taken away. Sins are also called defilements and stains [μολυσμοὶ & μιάσματα], pollutions, because of the stain or spot they have implanted in us. And believers are cleansed from that stain and pollution, imperfectly in this life and perfectly in death, but this is a benefit of sanctification, not of justification. Moreover, a skilled bodily physician heals the diseases and wounds of the body in such a way that, as far as his powers allow, he also abolishes and destroys them. Christ, the spiritual physician, is no less powerful or less fortunate, and he completely abolishes and destroys spiritual diseases. Yet although he is the almighty physician, to whom nothing is incurable, he is a voluntary cause who acts freely and dispenses his acts not in a moment, nor by one benefit and one step, but successively and gradually abolishing. Furthermore, when true life is restored to a dead body, death must be wholly extinguished, because the same body cannot be both living and dead at once. But the manner of spiritual quickening is so far different: as soon as a man is justified, sin, which imputed is the death of the soul, is not imputed, and so it dies; and the man, through justification, lives as a partaker of the righteousness and life of Christ. Through sanctification he is quickened as to the dominion of inherent righteousness as well. Yet the old man is not corrupted entirely by concupiscences and killed all at once. Instead, "by the Spirit he puts to death the deeds of the body" (Rom. 8:13), and so is gradually and truly put to death, and thus "the inner man is renewed day by day" [ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ], 2 Cor. 4:16. There, then, the death of the flesh, of the outer and old man, exists together with the life of the Spirit, of the new and inner man, God so dispensing. Otherwise, if life were restored to someone and sin were simply abolished in him, no mortal would ever have been restored to life, since no one is entirely free of sin before death. I cease to refute the calumnies of Becanus, that by this we do injury to the merit of Christ and, like the Pharisees, put forward Christ as a physician who does not heal the sick but sends him away covered and wrapped in a cloak, and who does not remove the wounds and sores but hides and conceals them. These and similar old wives' tales and delusions are entirely undone by what we have said, and they can be hurled back far more forcefully against the adversaries themselves, who are struck by the sharp thyrsus of their own inherent righteousness and despise the true righteousness of Christ.

units.la: LII. Iidem verò, qui per remissionem peccatorum illa expelli & penitus aboleri mortem pertendunt, errore contrario, post peccati abolitionem in homine reatum pœnæ peccati saltem temporalis manere, & humana, adeóque propria satisfactione in hac vita, & post hanc vitam in Purgatorio expiari debere asserunt. Malè profecto mendacia hæc cohærent. Etenim si remissio peccatorum penitus peccata ipsa expellit, obliterat & abolet, quis reatus, quæ pœna luenda ab homine superesse potest? Reatus enim vinculum quoddam culpam inter & pœnam est. Vinculo hoc per culpæ abolitionem disrupto, quis reatus, quæ obligatio ad pœnam manet? Et parum solicitus erit de remissione culpæ, qui pœnam sibi remissam novit. Non enim satisfit pro pœna, sed pœna satisfacit pro culpa. Neque aliud est remittere culpam, quàm non punire. Nec Christus aliter pro culpa nostra, quàm pœnam culpæ debitam ferendo satisfecit. Si enim causa sublata effectus, qui nondum extra causam suam exivit, tollitur, etiam sublata culpa, quæ pœnæ peccati causa est, ipsa poena, quæ nondum ulla erat, cùm peccatum remitteretur, tollatur necesse est. In justificatis certè, seu iis, qui in Christo Jesu per fidem sunt, οὐδὲν κατάκριμα nulla condemnatio est, Rom. VIII. 1. non nulla duntaxat æterna, sed planè nulla condemnatio. Universalium enim negantium necessaria est veritas, non indefinita, ut plerunque affirmantium. Et aliena planè, & in meritum Christi perfectissimum contumeliosa temporalis illa pœna & satisfactio est. Cùm enim Christus pro tota pœna abundè satisfecerit, alienum est à justitia Dei, pro uno eodémque debito geminam solutionem exigere, & ad cumulum aut supplementum aliquid addere, quo tamen non fiat plenior, nec perfectior solutio. Frivolum verò est, asserere, quòd Christus plenariam omnium peccatorum remissionem nobis promeruerit, sed meriti ejus efficacia quoad actum secundum non in hac vita, ubi Deus misericordiam & judicium temperat, sed in æterna demum vita plenè se exerat. Nam remissio peccatorum ejusque efficacia, quoad non imputationem peccatorum in hac etiam vita perfecta est, quia una oblatione consummavit in sempiternum omnes sanctificatos, Heb. X. 14. Si εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς in sempiternum, ergo semper. Neque τελείωσις consummatio sine efficacia meriti quoad actum secundum locum habere potest, quia consummatio omnis actualis, non potentialis est. Cùmque perfectæ sint causæ, Deus remittens, & justitia Mediatoris, etiam opus seu effectum perfectum fit oportet. Cum remissione verò peccati judicium proprie dictum consistere non potest. Qui enim remittit, & plenissimè condonat, is non judicat. Judicare quippe peccatum imputare, & non condonare est. Si vel semel pœnæ exiguntur, nunquam remissio peccati perficitur, nunquam Christi merita perfectè applicantur, quæ summa contumelia perfectissimi meriti Christi est. Accedit, quòd Deus se peccatorum à justificatis admissorum non recordaturum se amplius Esaj. XLIII. 24. Jerem. XXXI. 31–34. promisit. Deus autem iis in rebus, quarum non recordatur, nihil agit, proinde nec punit. Infamis ille servus est, qui ex Deo σκληρὸν durum & austerum Dominum facit, ibi metentem, ubi nihil seminavit. Sed etiam dirissimi Domini, quorum prorsus non recordantur, in iis nihil agunt; ac proin nec puniunt. Quomodo in reconciliationibus si quis pólliceatur, se non fore memorem offensæ, eò ipso certum facit, se nullam vindictam sumpturum. Unde celebre ἀμνηστία hominen, quæ non ἀμνηστία, sed subdola reconciliatio censetur, cùm minimus vindictæ locus est. Sic durissimo homine Deum duriorem dominum faciunt, qui eum non recordantem peccati, & simul vindicantem inducunt. Et quomodo Christus Chirographum nobis subcontrarium delevit, Col. II. 14. si partem debiti non dissolvit, à nobis demum dissolvendum? Quomodo fideles filii, amici, dilecti Dei, reconciliati cum eodem Joh. I. 12. 13. XV. 14. 15. Rom. V. 8. 9. dicuntur, si poenis & suppliciis propriè dictis ab eodem infligendis in hac & altera vita subjacent? Enim verò cùm Deus jubeat nos remittere proximo culpam simul & poenam, an consentaneum est, Deum velle nos esse clementiores, quàm ipse est? Estote misericordes, condonantes vobis mutuò offensas, sicut & Deus in Christo vobis condonavit, Ephes. IV. 32. Et potest homo sic condonare offensas, ut vindictam ipse non exerceat, sed in gravioribus injuriis quandoque vindictam potestati publicæ commendet. Deus verò condonans præter se alium, cui vindictam alia authoritate exercendam committat, neminem habet. Quòd si poenis nostris Deo satisfaciendum pro peccatis nostris esset, quis poenam culpæ ἀντίψυχον ferre posset? Nam Christo judice, is qui proximum fatuum appellavit, reus gehennæ ignis est, Matth. V. 22. & Paulus maledicentem proximo ex Regno Cœlorum excludit, 1. Corinth. VI. 10. Quotusquisque verò ejusmodi peccatorum expers est? Pro quibus tamen de suo nemo aliter satisfacere, quàm per æternum cruciatum, poterit. Denique per hoc dogma fidelibus omnis inter ærumnas consolatio adimitur, & rebus per se amaris; insuper fel & absinthium affunditur, siquidem calamitates suas ut vindictam & poenam propriè dictam à Deo inflictam, non ut remedia & paternas castigationes intueri debeant. Fideles enim de Dei erga se amore persuasi in cruce gloriantur, & ærumnas pro Christo honestas censent, ac veluti adversa vulnera, & cicatrices in pectore, virtutis argumenta: At uri & torqueri ad satisfactionem, & poenas pro peccatis pendere, non modò gloria non est; sed causa anxietatis & gradus ad desperationem.
units.tr: LII. Those who maintain that death is driven out and utterly abolished by the remission of sins fall into the opposite error. They assert that after the abolition of sin, the guilt of the penalty of sin, at least temporal, remains in a person, and that it must be expiated by human and therefore one's own satisfaction in this life, and after this life in Purgatory. These falsehoods certainly do not hang together. For if the remission of sins utterly drives out, obliterates and abolishes the sins themselves, what guilt or what penalty to be paid by the person can remain? Guilt is a kind of bond between sin and punishment. When this bond is broken by the abolition of the sin, what guilt or what obligation to punishment remains? And a person who knows that the punishment has been remitted to him will hardly be anxious about the remission of the sin. For satisfaction is not made for the punishment; rather the punishment satisfies for the sin. To remit the sin is nothing other than not to punish. Nor did Christ satisfy for our sin in any other way than by bearing the punishment due to sin. For if, when the cause is removed, the effect that has not yet gone beyond its cause is also removed, then once the sin, which is the cause of the punishment of sin, is taken away, the punishment itself, which did not yet exist when the sin was remitted, must necessarily be taken away too. Certainly "for those who are justified, that is, who are in Christ Jesus through faith, there is no condemnation [οὐδὲν κατάκριμα]", Rom. 8.1: not some eternal condemnation only, but plainly no condemnation at all. For universal negatives require a universal truth, not an indefinite one, as those who usually affirm supposed. That temporal punishment and satisfaction is altogether alien, and an insult to the most perfect merit of Christ. For since Christ has abundantly satisfied for the whole punishment, it is foreign to the justice of God to demand a double payment for one and the same debt, and to add something by way of surplus or supplement, by which the payment would not be made fuller or more perfect. It is also frivolous to assert that Christ merited for us the full remission of all sins, but that the efficacy of his merit in its second act does not fully display itself in this life, where God tempers mercy and judgment, but only in eternal life. For the remission of sins and its efficacy, as far as the non-imputation of sins, is complete even in this life, because "by one offering he has perfected for ever all who are sanctified", Heb. 10.14. If "for ever" [εἰς τὸ διηνεκές], then "always". Nor can perfection [τελείωσις] take place without the efficacy of the merit in its second act, because all perfection is actual, not merely potential. And since the causes are perfect, namely God remitting and the righteousness of the Mediator, the effect too must necessarily be perfect. Moreover, judgment properly so called cannot consist together with remission of sin. For one who remits and fully pardons does not judge. To judge is indeed to impute sin, and not to pardon it. If punishments were exacted even once, the remission of sin would never be completed, and the merits of Christ would never be fully applied, which would be the greatest insult to the most perfect merit of Christ. Add that God promised that he would no longer remember the sins committed by those who are justified, Isa. 43.24; Jer. 31.31–34. But God does nothing in those matters which he does not remember, and therefore does not punish them. That man is infamous who makes God a hard [σκληρόν] and austere lord, reaping where he has not sown. But even the most cruel lords, when they utterly do not remember certain things, do nothing in those matters, and therefore do not punish them. Just as, in reconciliations, if someone promises that he will not be mindful of an offence, he thereby makes it certain that he will take no vengeance. Hence the well-known amnesty [ἀμνηστία] is not regarded as a true amnesty but as a sly reconciliation, since there is no room at all for vengeance. Thus by making God a harder lord than the hardest man, they introduce him as one who does not remember the sin and at the same time takes vengeance. And how has Christ blotted out the handwriting against us, Col. 2.14, if he did not dissolve a part of the debt, which must in the end be dissolved by us? How are the faithful called sons, friends, beloved of God, reconciled to him, John 1.12–13; 15.14–15; Rom. 5.8–9, if they are subject in this life and the next to punishments and torments properly so called, to be inflicted by him? Indeed, since God commands us to remit to our neighbour both fault and punishment, is it consistent that God wishes us to be more merciful than he himself is? "Be kind to one another, forgiving one another, as God in Christ also forgave you", Eph. 4.32. A man can forgive offences in such a way that he does not himself exercise vengeance, but in more serious injuries sometimes commits vengeance to the public power. But God, forgiving, has no one other than himself to whom he might commit vengeance to be exercised by another authority. But if we had to satisfy God for our sins by our own punishments, who could bear a punishment [ἀντίψυχον] as a ransom for the fault? For before the Judge Christ, whoever calls his neighbour a fool is liable to the fire of hell, Matt. 5.22; and Paul excludes the reviler of his neighbour from the kingdom of heaven, 1 Cor. 6.10. Yet how few are free of such sins? For which no one could satisfy from his own resources otherwise than by eternal torment. Finally, through this dogma all consolation is taken from the faithful amid their troubles, and bitter things are made more bitter still; indeed gall and wormwood are poured in, since they ought to regard their calamities as vengeance and punishment properly so called inflicted by God, not as remedies and paternal chastisements. For the faithful, persuaded of God's love towards them, glory in the cross and count their afflictions honourable for Christ's sake, and regard them as wounds received in battle and scars on the breast, proofs of virtue. But to be burned and tormented in satisfaction, and to pay penalties for sins, is not only not glorious, but a cause of anxiety and a step towards despair.

units.la: LIII. Fatemur equidem, Deum post remissam culpam infligere mala quædam solere, quæ poenarum nomine veniunt, & veræ poenæ apud damnatos sunt. Sed poenæ tamen, vel secundum rem, seu materialiter, vel secundum rei definitionem, seu formaliter intelliguntur. Ita omnia incommoda hujus vitæ aliquo modo poenæ peccatorum sunt: sed etiam possunt esse non poenæ. Quomodo comedere panem in sudore vultus sui poena Adamo assignata fuit, quæ tamen annexam Dei benedictionem habet, nec poena est, nisi cùm frustra est. Ejusmodi igitur incommoda post remissam culpam poenæ sunt, quoad rem & materialiter, non quoad rei definitionem & formaliter. Quia enim poena est correlativum peccati, quod per eam, ceu destructionem quandam peccatoris expiari debet, iccirco id, quod tum poena est, si novam relationem sumat, non amplius poena dici potest. Sumit autem novam relationem, quoties bonum finem sortitur. Ita sectio membri in corpore vulnus est, si ab hoste; curatio, si à medico proficiscatur. Nam ab hoste ad perniciem, à medico ad salutem suscipitur, quæ mera relatio est. Et sumere ejusmodi incommoda novam relationem necesse est, quia diligentibus Deum omnia cooperantur in bonum, Rom. VIII. 28. Hoc demum sensu nunquam remisso peccato poena retinetur; sub ratione poenæ propriè dictæ. Neque enim incommoda illa satisfactiones; sed commonefactiones sunt: non ultiones judicis, sed castigationes Patris: non poenæ, sed medicinæ, quibus cavere poena longè gravior esset. Maxima poena est à Deo sic non puniri, nec salutariter corripi, quia conscientiis callus obducitur, & peccatores alto veterno indormiunt, donec subitò obruantur. Quem diligit Dominus, castigat; & flagellat omnem filium, quem ad se recipit, Heb. XII. 6. Afflictio patientiam operatur, patientia experimentum, experimentum spem; spes autem non pudefacit, Rom. V. 3. 4. Populo Israelitico in moscholatriam collapso & poenitenti Deus non culpam duntaxat, sed etiam poenam remisit. Supplicanti enim Mosi, ut Deus populo peccatum condonet, responsum est: Abi nunc, deduc populum, &c. Exod. XXXII. 31. 32. 33. Quod autem alio tempore, nempe פקד בעונם in die visitationis suæ, se visitaturum in iis peccatum comminatus est, ibid. v. 34. & revera visitavit, ejus judicii causa fuit continuata culpa ἀμεταμελήτων in populo, quibus idololatriæ culpa nunquam remissa, sed tantùm Divina Nemesis procrastinata est. Neque obstat, quòd judicio huic non soli ἀμεταμέλητοι, sed etiam poenitentes impliciti sunt; quia, uti scite Augustinus de Civit. Dei Lib. I. 8. loquitur, sub uno igne aurum rutilat, palea fumat; & sub eadem tribula stipulæ comminuuntur, frumenta purgantur: nec ideo cum oleo amurca confunditur, quia eodem preli pondere exprimitur, & una eademque vis irruens bonos probat; malos vastat, damnat, exterminat. Mors ipsa temporalis, quæ à prima sui origine poena propriè dicta fuit, in fidelibus poena esse desinit, & peccati depositio, Rom. VII. 24. ἀφιξις discessus in patriam, Act. XX. 29. ad Christum, Phil. I. 23. & transitus ad meliorem vitam Joh. V. 24. est. Quam etiam Paulus optavit, ἐπιθυμίαν ἔχων εἰς τὸ ἀναλῦσαι cupiens dissolvi, Phil. I. 23. Et fideles etiam à Domino κείνου judicantur, 1. Cor. XI. 32. sed ne unà cum mundo condemnentur. Proin judicium illud παιδεία castigatio, non κατάκριμα condemnatio, seu poena propriè dicta est. Sed & per afflictiones resarcitur injuria ex peccato facta, quoad abolitionem
units.tr: LIII. We certainly admit that God is accustomed, after a sin has been remitted, to inflict certain evils which go under the name of punishments, and which are true punishments among the damned. But punishments are understood either according to the thing itself, that is materially, or according to the definition of the thing, that is formally. Thus all the inconveniences of this life are in some way punishments of sins, but they may also not be punishments. Just as eating bread in the sweat of one's face was assigned to Adam as a punishment, yet it has God's blessing attached and is not a punishment unless it is in vain. Such inconveniences, therefore, after the remission of the sin, are punishments as regards the thing and materially, not as regards the definition of the thing and formally. For since punishment is the correlative of sin, which must be expiated through it, as a kind of destruction of the sinner, what is then a punishment, if it takes on a new relation, can no longer be called a punishment. It takes on a new relation, however, whenever it obtains a good end. Thus the cutting off of a limb in the body is a wound if it comes from an enemy, but a cure if it proceeds from a physician. For what is undertaken by an enemy is for destruction, but by a physician for salvation, which is a pure relation. And such inconveniences must necessarily take on a new relation, because "to those who love God all things work together for good", Rom. 8.28. In this sense alone, with sin remitted, punishment is never retained under the aspect of punishment properly so called. For those inconveniences are not satisfactions but admonitions: not the avenging of a judge but the chastisements of a Father: not punishments but medicines, by which to be spared would be a far graver punishment. The greatest punishment is not to be punished by God in this way, nor to be salutarily corrected, because a callus is drawn over the conscience and sinners sleep in deep lethargy until they are suddenly overwhelmed. "Whom the Lord loves he chastens, and he scourges every son whom he receives", Heb. 12.6. "Affliction works patience, patience experience, experience hope; and hope does not put to shame", Rom. 5.3–4. To the people of Israel, fallen into calf-worship and repentant, God remitted not only the fault but also the punishment. For when Moses petitioned that God would pardon the people's sin, the answer was: "Go now, lead the people, etc.", Exod. 32.31–33. But that at another time, namely when he would visit them in "the day of his visitation" [פקד בעונם, paqad baʿawonam], he threatened to visit their sin upon them, ibid. v. 34, and indeed he did visit it: the cause of that judgment was the continued guilt of the unrepentant [ἀμεταμελήτων] among the people, for whom the guilt of idolatry was never remitted, but only divine retribution was postponed. Nor is it an objection that not only the unrepentant but also the penitent were involved in this judgment; for, as Augustine says wisely in the City of God, book 1 chapter 8, under one fire gold shines and chaff smokes, and under the same threshing-sledge the straw is crushed and the grain is cleansed; nor is oil mixed with lees because both are pressed by the same weight of the press, and one and the same rushing force tests the good and lays waste, condemns and destroys the bad. Temporal death itself, which from its very origin was a punishment properly so called, ceases to be a punishment in the faithful, and is a laying aside of sin, Rom. 7.24; a departure [ἄφιξις] into the homeland, Acts 20.29; a going to Christ, Phil. 1.23; and a passage to a better life, John 5.24. This Paul also desired, having "the desire to depart" [ἐπιθυμίαν ἔχων εἰς τὸ ἀναλῦσαι], Phil. 1.23. And the faithful are also judged by the Lord, 1 Cor. 11.32, but so that they are not condemned along with the world. Therefore that judgment is chastisement [παιδεία], not condemnation [κατάκριμα], that is, not punishment properly so called. But also through afflictions the injury done by sin is made good, as far as the removal of the scandal in the Church is concerned,

units.la: Contraria eorundem argumenta ad limam revocantur. nem scandali in Ecclesia, non quoad compensationem justam offensæ apud Deum, utpote quæ solius Christi merito & satisfactione fit. Nam ἀντίκαγμα compensatio injuriæ Deo illatæ infinita esse debet, uti injuria ipsa infinita est; neque nisi vel obedientia, quæ infiniti pretii est, vel æterna morte peragitur. Denique nec confundenda hic sunt, maximè distincta, peccatum adversus Deum, & adversus Deum simul ac homines admissum: nec non pœna utrique cum discrimine debita. Etenim Divinum forum humano non præjudicat; & peccatum à Deo remissum retineri simul ac puniri ab hominibus æquissimo judicio potest. Unius enim ejusdemque peccati adversus legem politicam diversa est noxa, quæ in societatem humanam redundat, & iniquitas atque injuria, quæ in Deum legislatorem summum committitur. Illa sine hac, & hæc sine illa compensari potest, & non raro compensatur; quia nec facinorosis omnibus, pœnas judici humano dantibus, Deus in suo foro peccatum remittit; nec quibus Deus propter Christum peccatum perfectissimè remittit, illi à debito luendæ pœnæ politicæ, non tam Deo, quàm humano judici, ex Dei tamen præscripto reddendæ, liberantur.
units.tr: Their opposing arguments are brought to the file. The punishment for scandal in the Church is not in question as to a just compensation for the offence before God, since that is made solely by the merit and satisfaction of Christ alone. For the ἀντίκαγμα [antikama], the compensation for injury done to God, must be infinite, just as the injury itself is infinite; and it is accomplished only by obedience, which is of infinite worth, or by eternal death. Finally, the sin committed against God and the sin committed against God and men at once must not be confused here, and they must be carefully distinguished, as must the punishment owed to each with its own difference. For the divine court does not prejudge the human one, and a sin remitted by God can, with the most righteous judgment, be retained and punished by men. For the harm of one and the same sin against the civil law is different from the iniquity and wrong committed against God, the supreme lawgiver; the former harm spreads into human society. The one can be made good without the other, and often is; for God does not remit sin in his own court for all the criminals who pay penalties to the human judge, nor are those whom God perfectly forgives for Christ's sake freed from the debt of paying the civil penalty, which is owed not so much to God as to the human judge, though it is to be paid according to God's prescription.

units.la: LIV. Error hic de retenta post remissionem culpæ pœna temporali, venenatus fons est erroris alterius de satisfactionibus humanis propriis & alienis, vel sponte susceptis, vel à Deo aut sacerdote injunctis, & in hoc vel futuro seculo Deo præstandis, quibus demum præstitis perfecta peccatorum remissio & redemptio agnosci debeat.
units.tr: LIV. This error about the temporal punishment retained after the remission of guilt is a poisonous spring of another error, concerning human satisfactions, both one's own and those of others, whether undertaken voluntarily or imposed by God or by a priest, and to be rendered to God in this or the future age; and once these have been rendered, the complete forgiveness and redemption of sins is supposed to be acknowledged.

units.la: Sic enim qui Christi justitiam propriæ justitiæ mangonio prius suppresserunt, satisfactionem ejusdem humanarum satisfactionum velut coronide corrumpere religioni non duxerunt. Et satisfactionibus ejusmodi alii pœnas æternas, alii temporales duntaxat persolvi asserunt. Neque enim concordes eorum calculi sunt. In eo tamen consentire videntur, quòd satisfactio sit reddita voluntaria æquivalentis aliâs indebiti. Catechismus Romanus Lib. II. c. 5. q. 52. eandem rei debitæ integram solutionem & compensationem, qua homo pro peccatis commissis aliquid Deo persolvit, definit. Ejusmodi satisfactiones iis sunt sublesta quædam opera, gerræque siculæ, flagellationes, Laconicæ διαμαςηγώσεως incitamentum, jejunia piscaria, eleemosynæ Monachis divitibus erogatæ, peregrinationes nudipedales ad reliquias sanctorum, recitatio precularum superstitiosè toties, & quidem in lingua incognita, repetitæ, battologia & πολυλογία à Christo damnata, χαμαιζῆλον, nodosus funis sub interula, qui lumbos exulceret, cranium pro cervicali suppositum, aliâque ejusmodi, quæ laboriosorum operum nomine venditant, & non ita pridem Antonius Arnoldus Sorbonæ Doctor spisso volumine velut universali seculi hujus impœnitentiæ faventia, applaudentibus Theologis & Episcopis pluribus, exagitavit. Quarum rerum adeò disparium cum merito Christi copulatio non minùs Christo contumeliosa est, quàm si quis gemmas carbonibus sociaret, aut contra legem Mosis bovem cum asino aratro alligaret. Talia enim ad lydium verbi Dei lapidem explorata tantum abest, ut Deo satisfaciant, ut etiam pœnam mereantur, & ad lancem judicii Divini ponderata immensum quantum peccata novo pondere premant.
