units.tr: For those who first buried the righteousness of Christ under the huckstering of their own righteousness did not think it wrong to corrupt its satisfaction, as with a crowning touch, by adding human satisfactions. Some assert that by such satisfactions eternal punishments are paid, others only temporal ones. Their reckonings do not agree. Yet they seem to agree in this, that satisfaction is a voluntary rendering of an equivalent otherwise not owed. The Roman Catechism (Book II, ch. 5, q. 52) defines it as the full payment and compensation of a debt, by which a man pays something to God for sins committed. Satisfactions of this kind are such things as paltry works and Sicilian tricks: flagellations, the Laconian incitement [διαμαστιγώσεως] to scourging, fish fasts, alms given by rich monks, barefoot pilgrimages to the relics of saints, the recitation of prayers repeated so superstitiously, and that in an unknown tongue, battology and much speaking [πολυλογία], which Christ condemned, grovelling on the ground [χαμαιζῆλον], a knotted cord under the shirt that chafes the loins, a skull put under the head as a pillow, and other things of this sort, which are sold under the name of laborious works. Not long ago Antoine Arnauld, Doctor of the Sorbonne, in a thick volume, favouring as it were the universal impenitence of this age, attacked them, with many theologians and bishops applauding. To join the merit of Christ to things so unlike is no less an insult to Christ than if someone set gems among coals, or yoked an ox with an ass to the plough, contrary to the law of Moses. For such things, when tested on the Lydian touchstone of the Word of God, do not satisfy God; they even deserve punishment, and when weighed in the scales of divine judgment they press sins down with immense new weight.

units.la: LV. Cùm verò Deum peccata hominibus gratis, gratia sua, per redemtionem, quæ est in Christo Jesu, quem idem solum ἱλαστήριον propitiatorium in sanguine ejus statuit, ita perfecte remisisse, ut nec æterna, nec temporalis pœna ab homine ipso in Christum credente exantlanda sit, abundè jam comprobaverimus, nullum satisfactionibus humanis locum esse posse, ultrò consequitur.
units.tr: LV. Since we have now amply shown that God has so perfectly remitted sins to men, freely, by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God alone set forth as the propitiatory [ἱλαστήριον] in his blood, that neither eternal nor temporal punishment is to be endured by the man himself who believes in Christ, it follows of its own accord that there can be no place for human satisfactions.

units.la: Habet enim satisfactio Christi infinitam perfectionem & valorem, adeòque per eam à Deo judice peccatum commissum, & debita peccato pœna ad justam ἰσότιμος seu æqualitatem reduci possunt. Quo posito si aliam satisfactionem Deus ab homine exigeret, justitiam excederet, & quod blasphemum dictu est, ad immanitatem præcipitaret. Nam quòd satisfactionem Christi infinitam humana satisfactione non supplerì, sed applicari regerunt, nullum veri colorem habent. Fide enim, non humana satisfactione, vel opere ullo satisfactionem Christi applicari, Scripturæ docent; & illa hanc destruit, non applicat. Neque enim Deus contrarium per contrarium, remissionem per pœnam, hoc est, lucem per tenebras, medicinam per venenum applicat. Modi quoque per quos Christi beneficia nobis applicantur, ex Scriptura discendi, non ex humano cerebro, cui summa mentiendi libido inest, hauriendi sunt.
units.tr: For the satisfaction of Christ has infinite perfection and worth, and so through it the sin committed and the punishment owed to sin can be brought by God the judge to a just equal honour [ἰσότιμος], that is, to equality. Given this, if God were to demand another satisfaction from a man, he would exceed justice and, what is blasphemous to say, drive it into savagery. For their claim that the infinite satisfaction of Christ is not supplemented by human satisfaction but applied to it has no semblance of truth. For the Scriptures teach that the satisfaction of Christ is applied by faith, not by human satisfaction or any work; and human satisfaction destroys it rather than applies it. For God does not apply the contrary by the contrary, remission by punishment, that is, light by darkness, medicine by poison. The ways by which the benefits of Christ are applied to us are to be learned from Scripture, not drawn from the human brain, which has a great lust for lying.

units.la: Et in Veteri quidem Testamento fuerunt satisfactiones improprie tales, victimæ legales, quæ satisfactionis satisfactionis nomine venientes reatum non sustulerunt, sed indicarunt, & Christum præfigurarunt. Quod autem typicum fuit, in Novo Testamento, præstita vera satisfactione per Christum, Esaj. LIII. 10. 2.Cor. V. 21. expirare debuit; sicut præsente corpore umbra expirat. Accedit, quòd satisfactione humana Christi satisfactioni addita, potentior foret reatus Adami ad nos servituti pœnæ tum æternæ tum temporali subigendos, quàm obedientia Christi fuit ad nos ab omni maledictione liberandos, quod Apostolus Rom. V. 15. negat.
units.tr: And in the Old Testament there were indeed improper satisfactions of this kind, the legal victims, which, coming under the name of satisfaction, did not remove guilt but indicated it and foreshadowed Christ. But what was typical in the Old Testament ought to have ceased in the New Testament, once the true satisfaction had been made through Christ (Isa. 53:10; 2 Cor. 5:21), just as the shadow ceases when the body is present. Moreover, if human satisfaction were added to the satisfaction of Christ, the guilt of Adam would be more powerful to subject us to the bondage of punishment, both eternal and temporal, than the obedience of Christ was to free us from every curse, which the Apostle denies (Rom. 5:15).

units.la: Cùmque nostram inter satisfactionem finitam, & Dei offensam infinitam distantia pariter infinita sit, illa hanc nullo modo attingere, ac pro in placare minimè potest. Nam vel sola attingit, vel cum satisfactione Christi conjuncta. Non sola, quia finita est. Non conjuncta cum satisfactione Christi, quia, ut mollissimè loquamur, perinde facit, qui illam huic conjungit, ac qui candela Solis meridiani lucem, gutta mare, teruncio Croesi divitias, mendici veteramento assuto regiam togam augere, vel exornare sustinet. Ac frustra hic satisfactionum Christi & humanarum subordinationem, qualis in generatione causarum secundarum est, oggerunt.
units.tr: And since the distance between our finite satisfaction and the infinite offence against God is equally infinite, the former cannot in any way reach the latter, and can by no means placate it. For either it reaches it alone, or it is joined with the satisfaction of Christ. Not alone, because it is finite. Not joined with the satisfaction of Christ, because, to speak most gently, he who joins the one to the other does the same as he who would think that a candle adds light to the noonday sun, a drop adds to the sea, a penny adds to the riches of Croesus, or a beggar's patched rag adds to or adorns a royal robe. And here they vainly bring forward the subordination of Christ's satisfaction and human satisfactions, such as exists in the generation of secondary causes.

units.la: Satisfacere enim pro peccato nemo Mortalium potest, quia redemptionis pretium, quod infinitum esse debet, nemo habet. Cedit ergo in summam contumeliam Christi tam disparatarum satisfactionum conjunctio, neque aliter humanæ satisfactiones Christi satisfactioni, quàm cera igni, & tenebræ luci subordinari possunt. Quicquid porro homo facit, id omne Deo & Christo debendi reus est, & acceptum gratiæ.
units.tr: For no mortal can make satisfaction for sin, because no one possesses the price of redemption, which must be infinite. Therefore the conjunction of satisfactions so unlike is the greatest insult to Christ, and human satisfactions cannot be subordinated to the satisfaction of Christ in any other way than wax to fire or darkness to light. Moreover, whatever a man does, he is bound to owe it all to God and Christ and to count it as received from grace.

units.la: Error hic humanas satisfactiones propias & alienas, non parum Christi satisfactioni injuriosas, perpetuit. gratiæ Dei referri debet, quod procul à satis-factione veri nominis abest. Præterea neque homo infallibilem certitudinem de redemptione peccatorum per satisfactiones habere potest. Cùm enim satisfactio, vi nominis, delicto æqualis esse debeat, ejus tamen æqualitatis certa ac definita mensura nec ex Dei verbo, nec ex ratione definiri potest. Nam quòd satisfactionum mensuram in actu signato definitam esse in verbo Dei; at in actu exercito definiri, ob incertam semper & dubiam applicationem, non posse fingunt, nullius commatis est, quia nec actus ille signatus ostendi potest, & exerciti incertitudo satisfactionum vim omnem resolvit, imò desperationis mater est. Præterea satisfactiones etiam cum meritis operum pugnant, quia quod mercedem aliquam in gratia & gloria meretur, nullam amplius dignitatem, qua pro pœna satisfacere possit, habet. Omnis enim illa dignitas in merendo exhausta & consumpta est. Et bona opera pœnalia vocare, gravis adversus virtutes injuria est. Denique ipsi adversarii satisfactiones non parum suspectas reddunt. Nam à vera pœnitentia separabiles eas esse, indulgentiarum suppetiis comprobant. Cajetanus quoque ingenuè fatetur, Divino præcepto pœnitentem non teneri eas suscipere; & posse easdem à pœnitente renui Scotus, Biel, Navarrus, Medina, alii asserunt. Circa effectum earundem maximè discordes, alii culpam & pœnam, alii pœnam æternam, alii temporalem tantùm iis redimi statuunt. Quin & de ordine satisfactionum disputant, ante, an post absolutionem imponendæ sint.
units.tr: This error perpetuates human satisfactions, one's own and those of others, which are not a little injurious to the satisfaction of Christ. What is far from true satisfaction should be ascribed to the grace of God. Moreover, a man cannot have infallible certainty about the redemption of sins through satisfactions. For since satisfaction, by the force of its name, ought to be equal to the offence, yet a certain and defined measure of that equality can be determined neither from the Word of God nor from reason. For their claim that the measure of satisfactions is defined in the Word of God in the signate act, but cannot be defined in the exercised act, because the application is always uncertain and doubtful, has no force, since that signate act cannot be shown, and the uncertainty of the exercised act dissolves all the force of satisfactions; indeed it is the mother of despair. Moreover, satisfactions also clash with the merits of works, because whatever merits some reward in grace and glory has no further dignity by which it could satisfy for punishment. For all that dignity has been exhausted and used up in merit. And to call good works penal is a grave injury to the virtues. Finally, the adversaries themselves make satisfactions not a little suspect. For they prove by the aid of indulgences that these can be separated from true repentance. Cajetan also frankly admits that a penitent is not bound by divine precept to undertake them, and others, Scotus, Biel, Navarrus, Medina, assert that they may be refused by the penitent. Concerning their effect they are most divided: some hold that both guilt and punishment are redeemed by them, others that eternal punishment, others that temporal punishment only. Indeed they also dispute about the order of satisfactions, whether they should be imposed before or after absolution.

units.la: LVI. Nequicquam verò Adversarii pœnitentiam, toties mandatam nobis in satisfactionem commutant. Dixit equidem Augustinus, seu potius Gennadius Massiliensis de dogm. Ecclesiæ cap. 54. pœnitentiæ satisfactionem esse, quòd peccatorum causas excidat, & earum suggestionibus aditum non indulgeat. Sed nihil ad rem hoc facit, quia peccata removere, vitare non est proprie satisfacere; vel pœnam pro peccato subire. Alia longè est satisfactio pœnarum. Nam hæc est genus pœnæ. At pœnitentia non est genus pœnæ, quia est mutatio mentis in melius, seu acquisitio novi habitus inhærentis, quæ pœna non est. Ita Deus ipse: Impius omni peccato suo, &c. Ezech. XVIII. 21. Ubi averti à peccato, seu pœnitentiam agere, mutationem, per quam peccata quis deserit, manifestè designat. Neque etiam semper qui pœnitentiam agit, ipse damnum resarcire, & injuriam compensare tenetur. Nam ubi plena & solida remittentis liberalitas est, & injuria à lædente aliter quàm disciplina præteriti & cautione futuri sarciri non potest; & ab alio jam farta est, ibi nulla compensationis necessitas est. Tum Johannes jubens facere fructus dignos pœnitentia, Matth. III. 8. non opera pœnalia mandat, tum quia fructus pœnitentia dignos baptizandis mandat, quibus satisfactiones nullas ii injungunt: tum quia illi, qui fructus hos non ferunt excidendi & in æternum ignem abjiciendi dicuntur; quod de iis, quibus æternam pœnam remissam esse illi statuunt, dici nequit, tum quia fructus tales ii etiam facere possunt & debent, quibus tota
units.tr: Nor, however, do our opponents rightly turn repentance, which is commanded to us so often, into satisfaction. Augustine did say, or rather Gennadius of Marseilles did in On the Dogmas of the Church, chapter 54, that the satisfaction of repentance is cutting off the causes of sins and not giving entry to their suggestions. But this has nothing to do with the matter, because to remove sins and avoid them is not properly to satisfy, or to undergo a penalty for sin. The satisfaction of penalties is a quite different thing, for it is a kind of punishment. Repentance, however, is not a kind of punishment, since it is a change of mind for the better, or the acquiring of a new inherent habit, and that is not a punishment. God himself speaks thus: "The wicked man, from all his sin," etc., Ezek. 18:21. There, "turning away from sin," that is, repenting, clearly designates the change by which someone forsakes his sins. Nor is the one who repents always himself bound to make good the damage and compensate the injury. For where the one who forgives is full and generous, and the injury cannot be repaired by the offender in any way other than by the amendment of the past and the caution for the future, and where it has already been made good by another, there is no necessity of compensation. Again, John, bidding them "bear fruits worthy of repentance" (Matt. 3:8), does not command penal works; and he commands fruits worthy of repentance of those to be baptized, to whom the advocates of satisfaction impose no satisfactions. Again, those who do not bear such fruits are said to be cut down and cast into eternal fire; this cannot be said of those whom they themselves declare to have been released from eternal punishment. And again, such fruits can and must be produced even by those from whom the whole

units.la: Et argumentis contrariis nequicquam juffulciuntur.
units.tr: And they are vainly propped up by contrary arguments.

units.la: pœna remissa est. Nam Bellarminus ait, aliquando tam vehementem esse posse dolorem contritionis, ut tota pœna remittatur. Fructus ergo illi pœnitentia digni sunt omne genus bona opera, cùm non verbis duntaxat testamur, nos iram venturam fugere, sed re etiam testamur, acrem nobis esse peccati sensum, & vivam pœnitentiam, quæ in opera exeat. Judicium porrò illud, cujus I. Cor. XI. 32. mentio est, non pœnam proprie dictam, sed παιδεία castigationem paternam esse ipse Apostolus declarat, dicens: judicati à Domino castigamur, ne cum mundo condemnemur. Seipsum igitur judicat, qui culpam agnoscit & dolet; quod qui facere negligit, is à Deo immisso judicio, non sponte occupata satisfactione castigatur. Neque etiam illa vindicta, quam in Corinthiis Apostolus, 2. Cor. VII. 11. laudat, satisfactio propria, sed excommunicationis sententia à Corinthiis ex Apostoli præscripto adversus incestuosum lata fuit, quod etiam Cajetanus, Clarius, Godellus, aliique plures agnoscunt. Qui porro de alio pœnam expetit, is pœnam non sustinet. Satisfactionem verò Christi per propriam satisfactionem applicari debere, falsum esse; jam supra convicimus. Insaniæ proximum est, nugari, quòd solutio per solutionem, satisfactio per satisfactionem, pœna per pœnam applicari debeat. Et in rebus quidem naturalibus causæ nonnullæ ad finitum effectum producendum primæ causæ subordinari possunt. Sed negotii redemptionis & remissionis peccatorum dispar ratio est, quia sicut nulla virtus finita creare, ita nec redimere, satisfacere, pœnam infinitam pro peccato, quod infinitum reatum habet, exsolvere ulla ratione potest. Nam pretiosa nimis est redemptio animæ eorum, Psal. XLIX. 9 Quod verò Divinam justitiam exigere, ut aliter in gratiam recipiantur, qui ante baptismum per ignorantiam, aliter qui post baptismum per scientiam peccant, tricantur, satisfactionum necessitatem ibi, ubi peccata remittuntur, non evincit. Utrique enim remittuntur, credenti in Christum, qui pro nobis plenissimè satisfacit, neutri satisfacienti. Nam nec satisfactionem talem Nebucadnezari, non circumcisio certè; vel in gremium Ecclesiæ recepto (qualibus solis satisfaciendi munus adversarii injungunt) Daniel suasit, dicens: O Rex, consilium tuum placeat tibi, & peccata tua per justitiam (rectè cogitata, dicta, facta) avelle, Dan. IV. 24. Peccata enim per assumptionem contrarii deponuntur. Perperam enim verbum Græcus reddit, λυτρόω, & juxta eundem Vulgatus, redime. Nunquam enim hoc verbum λυτρώσασθαι pretio redimere significat. Quòd autem Syrus etiam vertit facit id ob generalem notionem liberandi, quam verbum alicubi Psal. CXXXVI. 24. Thren. V. 8. habet. Neque satisfactioni favet Solomon, dicens: In gratia & veritate expiatur peccatum, Prov. XVI. 6. Qua enim ratione gratia & veritas satisfactionem notare potest? Sensus est, peccatum gratia & veritate Dei oblite-rari, & velut ἐξιλάσκεσθαι expiari, quia id veritas sanctitatis & justitiæ requirit. Nam gratia & veritas per Jesum Christum facta est, Johan. I. 17.
units.tr: penalty has been remitted. For Bellarmine says that "sometimes the grief of contrition can be so vehement that the whole penalty is remitted." Therefore every kind of good work is worthy of that repentance, since we testify not merely in words that we flee the coming wrath, but also in deed that we have a keen sense of sin and a living repentance that comes out in works. Moreover, that "judgment" which is mentioned in 1 Cor. 11:32 is not a penalty properly so called, but a "chastisement" (paideia) of a father; the Apostle himself declares this when he says: "When we are judged by the Lord, we are chastened, that we should not be condemned with the world." Therefore he who acknowledges and grieves over his guilt judges himself; he who neglects to do this is chastened by the judgment sent from God, not by a satisfaction voluntarily undertaken. Nor is that "avenging" which the Apostle praises in the Corinthians (2 Cor. 7:11) a proper satisfaction; it was the sentence of excommunication pronounced by the Corinthians against the incestuous man according to the Apostle's directive, as Cajetan, Clarius, Godellus and many others also acknowledge. Moreover, he who demands a penalty from another does not himself undergo the penalty. That the satisfaction of Christ must be applied through our own satisfaction is false; we have already refuted this above. It is close to madness to talk nonsense that payment must be applied by payment, satisfaction by satisfaction, penalty by penalty. In natural things, indeed, some causes can be subordinated to the first cause in producing a finite effect. But the matter of redemption and the remission of sins is of a different kind, for just as no finite power can create, so no finite power can by any means redeem, satisfy, or pay an infinite penalty for a sin that has infinite guilt. For "the redemption of their soul is too precious" (Ps. 49:8–9). As for the claim that divine justice demands that those who sin before baptism through ignorance be received back into grace in one way, and those who sin after baptism through knowledge in another, this does not prove the necessity of satisfactions in the place where sins are remitted. For both are remitted to the one who believes in Christ, who fully satisfied for us, and to neither of them as satisfying. For Daniel did not advise Nebuchadnezzar to such a satisfaction, nor circumcision certainly, nor reception into the bosom of the Church (which are the only things for which the adversaries impose the duty of satisfaction), but said: "O King, let my counsel please you, and redeem your sins by righteousness (thinking, speaking and doing what is right)" (Dan. 4:24). For sins are laid aside by the taking up of the contrary. The Greek word is wrongly rendered as lytroō [λυτρόω], and following it the Vulgate likewise has "redeem." For the verb lytrōsasthai [λυτρώσασθαι] never means to redeem with a price. As for the Syriac also translating it in the sense of "making," this is due to the general sense of "freeing," which the word has in some places (Ps. 136:24; Lam. 5:8). Nor does Solomon favour satisfaction when he says: "By grace and truth iniquity is purged" (Prov. 16:6). For how can "grace and truth" signify satisfaction? The sense is that sin is blotted out by the grace and truth of God, and is expiated as it were by exilaskesthai [ἐξιλάσκεσθαι], because the truth of holiness and justice requires this. For "grace and truth came by Jesus Christ" (John 1:17).

units.la: Non alia enim expiatio peccati est, quàm in amore, quo Deus electos in Christo diligit, & in redemptione per sanguinem ipsius. Quæ Dei gratia & veritas plena purificationis & remissionis peccati causa est. Sed satisfactiones inprimis utiles esse, clamant, eò quòd ad habitus vitiorum eradicandos, virtutum inserendos plurimùm conducant, Christo nos conformment, & homines, peccata leviora putantes suffiaminent, ne in peccata graviora præcipites ruant, & iram in diem iræ sibi thesaurizent. Quasi quicquid hominibus utile videtur, statim in religione constituendum sit. Quidni ergo cum Novatianis veniam lapsis omnem negant, quia utilissimum illud ad coërcendos peccatores videri potest? Sed tali συλλεγωγία vitiorum habitus non eradicari sed foveri, adolescere, confirmari, & virtutes oppositas extinguì palam est, quia homines levissimi quique peccata levibus adeò pœnis dispungi stolidè sibi fingunt, & tantùm de Christi meritis, quæ sola apud Deum iratum judicem valent, delent, quantum satisfactionibus illi suis tribuunt. Neque satisfactionum Pontificiarum ludibria & oculiferia, sed crux Divinitus immissa, satisfactionis propriæ typho destituta, & persecutio Christi causa infracto animo tolerata Christo Fratri nostro primogenito nos conformant. Alia etiam peccati pro eo atque meretur æstimandi subsidia præsto sunt; lex iram denuntians, ira ex Cœlo revelata adversus omnem impietatem, peccati meritum, æternæ pœnæ gravitas, denique ipsius Filii Dei ad tollendum illud exinanitio. Necesse autem est homines satisfactionibus nugatoriis defunctos peccata rem jocularem arbitrari, quæ tam levibus piaculis dilui credunt. Denique si qui vetusti Patres satisfactiones commendant, verbis subinde iisdem, sed diversum sensum habentibus loquuntur. Nemo enim unus pro pœnis temporalibus ipsi Deo satisfieri; satisfieri pro peccatis per opposita bona opera, peccati habitum tolli, contrarium habitum induci, satisfactiones & pœnas eas veniam & remissionem præcedere, iis peccata redimi asseruit. Ac licèt veterum δημηγεσίας omnes ad amussim simplicitatis Christianæ, & Apostolicæ sinceritatis vix exigi possint, fidenter tamen pronuntiamus, nostram sententiam, quæ pœnitentiam in mutatione vitæ, per quam resipiscens & præterita peccata deplorat, & oppositas iis virtutes comparat, propiùs, imò planè ad mentem Patrum accedere. Quanquam & illud, quòd satisfieri Deo dicunt, commodè explanari potest, ne pœnitentiæ aut internum sensum, aut externa opera ad amussim potiùs nostri judicii, quàm voluntatis Divinæ in verbo ejus expressæ exigenda esse putemus. Et satisfactionis nomine ut plurimùm canonicam, in foro Ecclesiæ, non humanam, in foro Dei, intelligunt. Neque hîc verba sola ἱππολαίως attendenda, sed rerum definitiones ponderandæ sunt. Pridem enim est, quòd sicut pueri nolis sonantibus affingunt, quod ipsi cantillant, sic degenerans Papistarum natio veteribus accepta referunt, quæ ipsi ad quæstum suum excogitarunt. Sed eam in rem plurima & omni exceptione majora Cl. Dalleus libris septem de Pœnis & Satisfactionibus editis, dixit.
units.tr: For there is no other expiation of sin than in the love with which God loves his elect in Christ, and in redemption through his blood. This grace and truth of God is the full cause of the purification and remission of sin. But they cry out that satisfactions are especially useful, because they greatly contribute to uprooting the habits of vices and implanting virtues, conform us to Christ, and check men who, thinking their lesser sins trivial, might otherwise rush headlong into greater sins and store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath. As if whatever seems useful to men must at once be established in religion! Why then not also deny with the Novatians all pardon to the fallen, since that seems a most useful means of restraining sinners? But it is plain that by such syllegōgia [συλλεγωγία] the habits of vice are not uprooted but fostered, grow, become confirmed, and the opposite virtues are extinguished; for the lightest men foolishly imagine that their sins are wiped out by such light penalties, and they attribute to satisfactions of their own as much as they ascribe to the merits of Christ, which alone avail before God as an angry judge. Nor do the Papist satisfactions, which are mere mockeries and eyewash, conform us to Christ our firstborn brother; but the cross sent by God, which is free from the pride of one's own satisfaction, and persecution for Christ's sake endured with an unbroken spirit do. There are also other means of estimating sin as it deserves: the law threatening wrath, the wrath of God revealed from heaven against all ungodliness, the desert of sin, the gravity of eternal punishment, and finally the emptying of the Son of God himself to take that away. Moreover, men who have discharged themselves by trifling satisfactions must necessarily regard sin as a jesting matter, since they believe it is washed away by such light expiations. Finally, if certain ancient Fathers commend satisfactions, they speak at times in the same words, but with a different meaning. For no one of them has asserted that satisfaction is made to God himself for temporal penalties, but that satisfaction is made for sins through opposing good works, that the habit of sin is taken away and the contrary habit induced, and that satisfactions and penalties of this kind precede pardon and remission, and that sins are redeemed by them. And although the public speeches (dēmēgesiai [δημηγεσίας]) of the ancients can scarcely all be required to meet the standard of Christian simplicity and apostolic sincerity, we confidently affirm that our view, which places repentance in a change of life, by which the one who repents deplores past sins and acquires the virtues opposed to them, comes closer, indeed quite plainly, to the mind of the Fathers. Yet also what they say, that one "satisfies God," can be fittingly explained, so that we do not think that the inward sense or outward works of repentance should be measured by the standard of our own judgment rather than by the will of God expressed in his Word. And by the name of "satisfaction" they mostly understand the canonical satisfaction in the forum of the Church, not the human satisfaction in the forum of God. Nor are only the words to be considered here hippolaiōs [ἱππολαίως], but the definitions of the things must be weighed. For it has long been the case that, just as children attach to hollow reeds the sounds they themselves chant, so the degenerate Papist race refers to the ancients whatever it has devised for its own gain. On this matter the renowned Dallaeus has said much, in seven books On Penalties and Satisfactions, which are more than sufficient and beyond every exception.

units.la: LVII. Sicut unda undam, ita error errorem trudit & protrudit.
units.tr: LVII. As one wave drives on another, so error pushes forward and drives out error.

units.la: Non satis enim vi-sum superstitioni est, humanis satisfactionibus Christi satisfactionem obumbrare; nisi humanis etiam indulgentiis, pretio addictis, Divinam remissionem miris modis offuscaret. Nam satisfactiones in proprias & alienas distinguere placuit. Proprias, quas sibi quisque operationibus suis in remedium peccatorum suorum procuret: Alienas, quæ sunt aliorum pro aliis. Et has rursum in privatas & publicas. Privatas à privatis affectibus, velut liberorum erga parentes, amicorum erga amicos, qui affligunt se ipsos, sperantes inde solatium ventum iis, qui post discessum ex corpore non amplius pœnas debitas dare, neque eas omnino exsolvere possunt. Publicas ab Ecclesiæ authoritate. Qua in parte longæ sunt Indulgentiarum ambages, inventi novissimi & intricatissimi, infinitis contentionibus obscurati, altercantibus in oppositas partes sententiis. Summa est, nihil perire apud Deum sive meritorum, sive satisfactionum, sed merita nonnisi sua cuique prodesse: Satisfactiones verò etiam pro aliis. Evenire autem, ut multi Sancti plura passi sunt, quàm sibi opus fuerit. Id ergo quod abundat, necesse est aut perire, aut aliis inservire, qui pauciora patiantur. Ut verò inservire aliis possint, colligi in Thesaurum, quem vocant, Ecclesiæ, ex meritis Christi & passionibus Sanctorum constantem. Hunc Thesaurum commendatum esse clavibus Ecclesiæ, dispensandum indies pro necessitate aliorum. Idque fieri tum ab Episcopis, sed circumcisa authoritate: tum inprimis à Papa pro plenitudine potestatis. Dispensandi porrò mensuras esse à peccatis, & à tempore. A peccatis, in dimidium, trientem & quadrantem. A tempore, in dies variè multiplicatos. Et Episcopis quidem licere indulgentias dare in dies quadraginta, & in annos singulos, si festum sit Ecclesiæ consecratæ, neque ultra, & cuique in suæ diœcesis finibus. At Papa, cujus diœcesin unam totum terrarum orbem faciunt, quocunque libuerit, locorum & temporum pervadere posse, scisçunt. Unde annorum infinitorum impotentissimi lusus. Nam annorum ultra multoties centena millia audiuntur. Denique Jubilæi nomen celebratum ab annis aliquot, instituti primùm in annos centesimos, paulò post in quinquagesimos, demum in vicenos quintos. Neque tamen liberalitatem hanc infinitam esse, sed iis solis prodesse placuit, qui vel sibi suo nomine, vel aliis redemerint. Redimendi modus opere pœnali constat, puta visitatione Ecclesiæ alicujus certis diebus descripta, vel manibus adjutricibus, sine quibus nihil fieri, audacter disputant, atque ita plus juris in thesaurum iltum divitibus, quàm pauperibus largiuntur. Hæc summa longissimæ disputationis est, quæ Scholasticos miris antinomiis exercuit: sed papalis nervus, & Evangelii Christi clades est.
units.tr: For superstition has not thought it enough to overshadow Christ's satisfaction with human satisfactions. Unless it also clouded the divine remission in marvellous ways by means of human indulgences, sold for money, it would not be content. For they have chosen to divide satisfactions into proper and alien. Proper satisfactions are those each person procures for himself by his own works as a remedy for his sins. Alien satisfactions are those of some for others. These in turn are divided into private and public. Private satisfactions come from private affections, such as children's toward their parents, or friends' toward friends, who afflict themselves, hoping thereby to bring comfort to those who, after departing from the body, can no longer pay the penalties they owe, nor pay them off at all. Public satisfactions come from the authority of the Church. In this part there is a long tangle of indulgences, a most recent and most intricate invention, obscured by endless disputes, with opinions contending on opposite sides. The sum is this: nothing is lost before God, whether of merits or of satisfactions. But merits benefit only the one who has them, whereas satisfactions benefit even others. Now it happens that many saints have suffered more than was necessary for themselves. What is in excess must therefore either perish or serve others who have suffered less. So that it may serve others, it is gathered into what they call the Treasury of the Church, made up of the merits of Christ and the sufferings of the saints. This treasury is said to be committed to the keys of the Church, to be dispensed daily as others' needs require. This is done by bishops, though with restricted authority, and above all by the Pope, by the fullness of his power. Moreover, the measures of dispensing are reckoned by sins and by time. By sins: by a half, a third, or a quarter. By time: in various multiples of days. Bishops, they say, may grant indulgences for forty days and for each year, if it is the feast of a consecrated church, and no further, and only within the bounds of their own diocese. But the Pope, whose diocese they make the whole round of the earth, may (they know) range over any places and times he pleases. Hence come the most unbridled games with endless years, for mention is regularly made of more than a hundred thousand years. Finally, the name of Jubilee, celebrated for some years, was first instituted for every hundredth year, soon after for every fiftieth, and at last for every twenty-fifth. Yet they have not been willing to make this bounty unlimited, but only to benefit those who have bought it either for themselves in their own name, or for others. The mode of purchase consists in a penal work, such as a visit to some church on prescribed days, or helping hands, without which, they boldly argue, nothing can be done. And so they bestow more right in that treasure on the rich than on the poor. This is the sum of a very long dispute, which has troubled the Scholastics with strange contradictions. But it is the sinew of the papacy and the ruin of the Gospel of Christ.

units.la: LVIII. Cùm enim peccata, eorumque pœnas tum æternas, tum temporales gratis, gratia Dei, per redemptionem Jesu Christi, & sanguinem ejus, velut placamentum & λυτρον unicum, sine ullo opere & satisfactione humana remitti, abundè jam comprobaverimus; Indulgentias Papales ἐν ᾧδενὶ ἀφεσμῷ non Megarense. rense aliquod, sed Divinum oraculum ponit. Jugiter in auribus nostris meliflua illa Dei vox personat: Omnes sitientes venite ad aquas. Vos, quibus non est argentum, venite, emite & comedite: Venite, inquam, & emite absque argento & absque pretio vinum & lac, Esaj. LV. 1. Frustra enim per illos Divinam remissionem & indulgentiam applicari garriunt. Gratia enim Dei omnis, & peccatorum ac poenarum remissio uno modo apprehenditur; eo videlicet, quo Christi justitia & beneficia universa apprehenduntur, quam fidem salvificam & justificantem esse, mox demonstrabimus. In re certe seria magnique momenti aerariscatores Pontificii immaniter ludunt, qui remissionem Divinam peccatorum & meritum atque satisfactionem Christi modo per satisfactiones proprias, modo per alienas, modo per indulgentias humanas, poenarum temporalium gratiam facientes, imo ipsum jus Dei pro arbitrio humano relaxantes, applicari dictitant. Quem tandem portum tranquillitatis in fluctuante judicio hominum afflicta conscientia sortiri poterit? Vel justitia Dei exigit, ut satisfaciamus ipsi, & satisfactione nostra gratuitam remissionem peccatorum a Christo impetratam applicemus, vel non exigit. Si exigit, quomodo eandem applicari per indulgentias, satisfactionis propriae necessitatem destruentes, dicunt? Si non exigit, cur non contenti satisfactione Christi actum agunt, & cui jam satisfactum est, ultra satisfacere, nimium scilicet pii & justi, contendunt? Sed totum hoc indulgentiarum negotium falsis hypothesibus nititur, cujusmodi sunt, quod peccatis remissis poena aliqua retineatur: quod homo satisfacere pro ea teneatur: quod Ecclesia judiciali authoritate peccata remittere possit: quod detur thesaurus Ecclesiae a Papa ex plenitudine potestatis, quam nullam habet, dispensabilis; cum tamen nec Sancti vel pro aliis satisfacere, vel plus quam debent, praestare possint; vel Christi satisfactiones nondum in consilio, pacto & acceptatione Dei Patris applicatae, adeoque superfluae dentur. Sanctorum passiones ipse Durandus a thesauro hoc in 4. Sent. D. 20. q. 3. f. 7. excludit, his argumentis fretus, quod haec eorum intentio non fuerit, & quicquid S. Martyres sustinuerunt, ultra quam peccata ipsorum meruerunt, iis vel plane remuneratum, vel in assumpto corpore remunerandum sit. Cumque reatus peccati infinitus satisfactionem infinitam postulaverit, nihil in passione Christi non erogatum vel pro unico peccato redundavit. Scriptura vero per thesaurum illum Ecclesiae clavim putei abyssi, Apocal. IX. 2. appellat. Accedit, quod indu gentiae, fatentibus ita Durando, Roffensi, Cajetano, aliis nullum in Scripturis fundamentum habent: quod Evangelium & in eodem Claves Regni Coelorum foede corrumpunt, declarationem remissionis peccatorum, quae earum beneficio fit, irritam facientes, & de integro remissionem venum exponentes; quod studium respiscentiae verae, & solidae pietatis enervant, & hominibus securitatis pulvillos sub axillis consuunt, dum per eas satisfactiones, quarum innumera opera laboriosa, preces, eleemosynas, jejunia collocant, relaxari docent: quod peccatores vanis promissis laetant, poenarum temporalium re-
units.tr: For we have now sufficiently shown that sins, and their punishments both eternal and temporal, are remitted freely, by the grace of God, through the redemption of Jesus Christ and his blood, as the sole propitiation and ransom [λύτρον], without any work or human satisfaction. The Papal indulgences set up not some Megarian decree but a divine oracle, ἐν ᾧδενὶ ἀφεσμῷ [in no remission]. In our ears that sweet voice of God sounds continually: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters; and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price (Isa. 55.1). For they vainly babble that the divine remission and indulgence are applied by these means. The whole grace of God, and the remission of sins and punishments, is apprehended in one way only: namely, the way in which the righteousness and all the benefits of Christ are apprehended. We will shortly demonstrate that this is saving and justifying faith. In a matter truly serious and of great moment, the Papist money-changers play a monstrous game, who insist that the divine remission of sins and the merit and satisfaction of Christ are applied now through their own satisfactions, now through those of others, now through human indulgences, which make a grant of the grace of temporal punishments, and indeed loosen the very right of God at human pleasure. Into what harbour of tranquillity can a troubled conscience ever come amid the fluctuating judgement of men? Either the justice of God requires that we should satisfy it ourselves, and by our own satisfaction apply the gratuitous remission of sins obtained by Christ, or it does not require this. If it requires it, how do they say that it is applied through indulgences, which destroy the necessity of one's own satisfaction? If it does not require it, why, not content with the satisfaction of Christ, do they act, and contend that one must satisfy beyond what has already been satisfied, being, of course, too devout and too just? But this whole business of indulgences rests on false hypotheses, of which kinds are these: that some punishment remains after sins are forgiven; that man is bound to satisfy for it; that the Church can remit sins by judicial authority; that there is a treasury of the Church, given by the Pope from the fullness of a power, which he does not have, and which is dispensable; whereas neither the saints can satisfy for others, nor render more than they owe; and the satisfactions of Christ, not yet applied by the counsel, covenant and acceptance of God the Father, are thought to be superfluous. Durandus himself excludes the sufferings of the saints from this treasury, in 4 Sent. d. 20 q. 3 f. 7, relying on these arguments: this was not their intention, and whatever the holy martyrs endured beyond what their sins merited has either been fully rewarded to them, or is to be rewarded in the body they have assumed. And since the guilt of sin, being infinite, demanded an infinite satisfaction, nothing in the passion of Christ was left unused, or overflowed for a single sin. Scripture indeed calls that treasury of the Church the key of the bottomless pit (Rev. 9.2). Moreover, indulgences, as Durandus, Rofensis, Cajetan and others concede, have no foundation in the Scriptures. They foully corrupt the Gospel and in it the Keys of the Kingdom of Heaven, rendering void the declaration of remission of sins which is made by their means, and selling remission anew for money. They weaken the zeal for true repentance and solid piety, and they sew cushions of security under men's armpits, while they teach that by those satisfactions, whose countless laborious works, prayers, alms and fastings they lay down, sins are relaxed. They delight sinners with empty promises, promising the re-

units.la: missionem pollicentes, quarum, quatenus Divinae castigationes sunt, nemo filiorum Dei in hac vita exors fuit, vel esse potest, si vel maximè omnes facultates suas in comparandas indulgentias erogaret; & quarum post hanc vitam nemini in Christum credenti metus esse potest; quod Ecclesiae primitivae, quales nunc in usu sunt, plane incognitae fuerunt, neque ante Seculum XII. quo inprimis religio in barbariem & nundinationem converti coepit, in notitiam pervenerunt; & pro indulgentiis factae emulgentiae & venales tesserae sunt, quando omni perfracto pudore, praetextu eleemosynarum ad dedicationes templorum & hospitalium, peregrinationum; in universum vero non sine tinnitu munerum, trapezitarum mensae in templo Dei erectae & impune exercitae sunt, donec a Viris Dei, Christi Spiritu & zelo inflammatis, restituta Evangelii de gratuita remissione peccatorum doctrina, destructae, & foeneratores sacri res suas sibi habere justi sunt. Nequid de viperina illa astutia dicam, qua Pontifices indulgentias strenuis Regni sui promachis erogantes, eosdem ad infideles & haereticos, quos appellabant, sub jugum Papae mittendos accenderunt, quod belli sacri, Waldensium aliorumque historia prodit. Sed sua etiam vineta indulgentiarii strenue coedunt. Si enim, uti Papa in Bulla Jubilaei A. MDC. edita promisit, super indulgentias plenissima omnium peccatorum indulgentia & remissio poenae contingit, cur qui eas consecuti sunt de remissione peccatorum & salute sua dubitare adhuc jubentur? Si Papa absolutam potestatem habet per indulgentias è Purgatorio, quas velit, animas liberandi, cur tam durus est, ut non confestim omnes liberet & Purgatorium sic evacuet? Nam quod Papam animas è Purgatorio non liberare per modum absolutionis, sed suffragii, & talem indulgentiarum concessionem effectum infallibilem non sortiri, regerunt, non placet Medinae, aliisque, qui Bellarmino teste, contendunt, animas defunctorum, quae in Purgatorio sunt, pertinere ad jurisdictionem Papae & posse ab eo indulgentias percipere per modum absolutionis.
units.tr: promising the remission of temporal punishments. Insofar as these are divine chastisements, none of the sons of God has been, or can be, exempt from them in this life, even if he were to spend all his resources on buying indulgences; and after this life, no one who believes in Christ can have any fear of them. These things were wholly unknown to the primitive Church, as it now practises them, and did not come to be known until the twelfth century, when religion first began to degenerate into barbarism and into a marketplace. In place of indulgences, there were made hawked and sold tokens, when, every shame cast aside, money was collected under the pretext of alms for the dedication of churches and hospitals and for pilgrimages. In general, not without the clink of gifts, the money-changers' tables were set up in the temple of God and carried on with impunity, until the doctrine of the free remission of sins in the Gospel was restored by men of God inflamed with the Spirit and zeal of Christ, the tables were destroyed, and the sacred usurers were justly left to keep their own goods. Not to mention that viperish cunning by which the Popes, who granted indulgences to the valiant champions of their kingdom, inflamed them to be sent under the yoke of the Pope against the infidels and heretics, as they called them, as the history of the holy wars and of the Waldenses and others shows. But the indulgence-sellers also vigorously cut their own vines. For if, as the Pope promised in the bull of the Jubilee published in the year 1600, "upon indulgences the most complete remission of all sins and of the punishment falls", why are those who have obtained them still bidden to doubt the remission of their sins and their salvation? If the Pope has absolute power to free souls from Purgatory through indulgences, whichever he wishes, why is he so hard-hearted that he does not free them all at once and so empty Purgatory? For as to the claim that the Pope does not free souls from Purgatory "by way of absolution" but "by way of intercession", and that such a grant of indulgences does not have an infallible effect, Medina and others do not approve of this reply. According to Bellarmine, they contend that "the souls of the dead who are in Purgatory belong to the jurisdiction of the Pope and can receive indulgences from him by way of absolution".

units.la: LIX. Fuisissima sunt, quae indulgentiarum institores ex detortis Scripturis pro nundinatione sua asserunt. Dixit equidem David, se socium esse omnium eorum, qui Deum timent, Psal. CXIX. 63. Sed non de satisfactionibus propriis, nec de alienis, nec de satisfactionum, vel potius carbonum thesauro illo quicquam in mentem ei venit. Nam se timentium Deum socium appellans, pietatis, non illius, quae quaestui habetur, sed purae & solidae societatem professus est. Et Christus Petro & Apostolis claves Regni Coelorum, & cum iisdem potestatem solvendi & ligandi, peccata remittendi & retinendi impertiens, Matth. XVI. 19. X VIII. 18. Joh. XX. 23. modum eum remittendi peccata, quo eorum poenae temporales retentae propter satisfactiones alienas in thesauro reservatas remittuntur, minime probavit, tum quia textus eos ad forum poenitentiae, non ad indulgentias pertinere. Durandus fatetur; & Pontificii potestatem remittendi & retinendi peccata, Joh. XX. 23. collatam ad potestatem ordinis: at potestatem indulgentias dispensandi ad potestatem jurisdictionis pertinere
units.tr: LIX. The most shameless claims that the sellers of indulgences make for their trade rest on twisted Scripture. David did say that he was a companion of all who fear God (Ps. 119:63). But nothing about his own satisfactions, or those of others, or that treasury of satisfactions (or rather of coals), ever entered his mind. In calling himself a companion of those who fear God, he professed a fellowship of piety, not the kind that is pursued for gain, but a pure and solid fellowship. Christ gave Peter and the Apostles the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and with them the power of loosing and binding, of remitting and retaining sins (Matt. 16:19; 18:18; John 20:23). Yet he did not thereby approve that way of remitting sins by which their temporal punishments, which are retained, are remitted on account of the satisfactions of others that are reserved in the treasury. This is so, first, because those texts pertain to the forum of repentance, not to indulgences. Durandus admits as much. The Papists refer the power of remitting and retaining sins (John 20:23) to the power of order, but they contend that the power of dispensing indulgences belongs to the power of jurisdiction.

units.la: Argumenta pro iisdem mota expenduntur. nere pertendunt : tum quia Christus suo & Scripturæ more de remissione peccati plenaria quoad culpam & pœnam omnem, eaque merè gratuita, non pretio addicta, loquitur, & potestatem uno actu ab æterna & temporali pœna absolvendi, non uni Apostolo, sed omnibus æquo jure, & in eorum persona omnibus Ecclesiæ Pastoribus contulit. Paulus verò indulgentiam pœnitenti incestuoso dispensans, & dicens: Ω᾽ δὲ ὴ χαρίζεσθε, καὶ ἐγὼ cui aliquid gratificamini, etiam ego, 2. Cor. II. 10. ne jota quidem emulgentias Papales confirmat. Condonat enim non solus Apostolus, sed cum eodem Corinthii, imò hi priùs quàm ille: condonat excommunicato, cùm tamen excommunicati non sint in statu gratiæ, vel in Ecclesia, adeóque nec indulgentiarum capaces: condonat scandalum & tristitiam, quam peccato suo incestuosus produxerat, nec non excommunicationem meritam, quam indulgentiarum materiam esse pernegant, eò quòd liberatio ab excommunicatione ad jurisdictionem pœnitentialem exteriorem pertineat. Cùmque S. Paulus nullam incestuoso post remissum peccatum in Sacramento confessionis pœnam injunxerit, gratificatio ejus Papalis indulgentia esse non potuit. Idem verò Paulus Col. I. 24. testatur, se ἀντἀναπληρῶν vicissim adimplere reliquias afflictionum Christi in carne sua pro corpore, quod Ecclesia est. Sed de communione & communicatione satisfactionum ex thesauro Ecclesiæ per indulgentias, quæ satisfactiones relaxent, nec χεὶ nec μὴ. Nemo enim homo merus vel pro se ipso, vel pro aliis satisfacere justitiæ Dei, & solutione sufficientis pretii vel se, vel alios debitis pœnis eximere potest. Hoc sibi vult, se, tanquam unum aliquod corporis mystici sub uno capite Christo membrum ἀντιπαναπληρῶν vicissim, hoc est, gratitudinis lege, implere reliquias afflictionum Christi, hoc est, mystici corporis Christi, cui, ut & singulis ejus membris, ipsique inprimis etiam Paulo, ut ex Act. IX. 16. liquet, suum crucis demensum Deus partitus est; idque in carne sua, & ὑπὲρ τῆς σώματός pro corpore Christi, quod Ecclesia est; non vice ejus, ἱλασμὸν satisfactionem præstando, quæ ei à Papa imputari potest, quia ad plenam satisfactionem nihil passionibus Christi defuit, Joh. XIX. 30. & infinito illarum valori nihil omnino addi potuit, sed bono & commodo ejus sic patiendo, ut inde fructus & ædificatio uberrima ad Ecclesiam redundet, uti ipse Paulus 2. Cor. I. 6. Phil. I. 12. 14. explicat. Neque enim patiendo pro aliis satisfecit, vel meruit quicquam, quia, uti scitè Cyprianus loquitur, Christus in nobis luctatur & coronatur. Porrò satisfactio Christi sic infinitum pretium habuit, ut tota tamen applicetur, non quicquam non applicatum in Papæ venalem thesaurum colligendum redundet. Impium inprimis est dicere, satisfactiones Christi ab hominibus iis applicari, quibus ipse Deus & Christus eas applicare non dignatur, quasi plus gratiæ homo, & ipse peccator, atque morte dignus, habeat, quàm Deus. Sed unicuique totus Christi sanguis, qui infiniti pretii est, applicatur, quia non guttatim nos redemit, sed totius sanguinis profluvio, ut rectè unusquisque dicat: Sanguis Jesu Christi me purgat ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. I. 7. Quod con-
units.tr: The arguments brought forward for these claims are weighed. They contend, first, that Christ, in his own manner and in the manner of Scripture, speaks of a remission of sin that is full as to both guilt and all punishment, and that is purely gratuitous, not bound to a price; and that he conferred the power of absolving from eternal and temporal punishment in a single act, not on one Apostle only, but on all with equal right, and in their persons on all the ministers of the Church. But when Paul dispensed indulgence to the incestuous penitent and said, "To whom you forgive anything, I also" (ᾧ δέ τι χαρίζεσθε, κἀγώ; 2 Cor. 2:10), he does not confirm the Papal indulgences even a jot. For it was not the Apostle alone who forgave, but the Corinthians with him, and indeed they before he did. They forgave one who was excommunicated, although the excommunicated are not in a state of grace or in the Church, and so are not capable of indulgences. They forgave the scandal and sorrow that his sin had caused, and also the excommunication he had deserved; and the opponents deny that this is a matter of indulgence, because release from excommunication belongs to the external penitential jurisdiction. And since St Paul imposed no penance on the incestuous man after his sin was remitted in the sacrament of confession, his forgiveness cannot have been a Papal indulgence. Paul himself testifies (Col. 1:24) that he fills up in turn (ἀνταναπληρῶ) what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ, in his flesh, for the body, which is the Church. But this says nothing about the sharing and communication of satisfactions from the treasury of the Church through indulgences that relax them, neither in the sense of instead of nor of for. For no mere man can satisfy the justice of God, either for himself or for others, nor by paying a sufficient price free himself or others from the debts of punishment. What Paul means is that he, as one member of the mystical body under the one head, Christ, fills up in turn, that is, by the law of gratitude, what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ, that is, of the mystical body of Christ. To this body, and to each of its members, and especially to Paul himself, as Acts 9:16 makes plain, God has allotted his share of the cross. He does so in his flesh, and for the sake of the body of Christ, which is the Church (ὑπὲρ τοῦ σώματος). He does not do so as a substitute, offering a propitiatory satisfaction (ἱλασμόν), which could be imputed to him by the Pope. Nothing was lacking to the full satisfaction of Christ's passion (John 19:30), and nothing at all could be added to its infinite value. Rather, Paul suffers for the good and benefit of the Church, so that abundant fruit and edification flow from it to the Church, as Paul himself explains (2 Cor. 1:6; Phil. 1:12, 14). For by suffering he did not satisfy for others, nor did he merit anything. As Cyprian rightly says, Christ wrestles and is crowned in us. Moreover, Christ's satisfaction has such infinite worth that it is nevertheless applied in full, and nothing unapplied remains to be gathered into the Pope's saleable treasury. It is especially impious to say that the satisfactions of Christ are applied by those men to whom God and Christ himself do not deign to apply them, as though a man, a sinner worthy of death, had more grace than God. But the whole blood of Christ, which is of infinite worth, is applied to each person, because he redeemed us not by drops but by a full outpouring of blood, so that each can rightly say, "The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses me from all sin" (1 John 1:7).

units.la: sideratio tum mortis Christi, quæ singulis tota applicatur, Rom. V. 10. tum Baptismi, in quo singulis non gutta, sed totus sanguis Christi obsignatur: tum Cœnæ, in qua singuli totum sanguinem Christi bibunt, amplius confirmat. Ita uno eodémque solido Solis lumine tum universus mundus, tum singuli homines illustrantur. Audax proin facinus est redemptionis nostræ pretium dissecantium, quod solidum & indivisum Deus esse voluit, & tale pro singulis lex Dei postulavit. Neque peregrinam illam λεπλολογίαν, quam Scholasticorum & Bullarum Papæ, cui Deus venter est, vanitas peperit, quod verbi Divini hypostasis infinitam dignitatem cuilibet sanguinis Christi guttulæ, cuilibet actioni ejus meritoriæ, & reliqua omnia superflua idonea sint, quæ thesauro Ecclesiæ vindicentur, moramur. Nusquam enim ita Scriptura loquitur, imò contrarium testatur, quæ ubique δικαίωμα justitiæ perfectæ opus, quo uno solóque redemptio nostra secundum legem, à peccatore non profusionem guttulæ sanguinis, vel unam actionem meritoriam, sed justitiam perfectam & mortem peccatoris exigentem, procurari potuit. Reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filii ejus, Rom. V. 10. Reconciliavit nos in corpore carnis suæ per mortem, Col. I. 21. 22. An sic guttas, guttulas etiam comminisci licet? An particula hac mortis unus, alia alius redemptus est? Annon potiùs tota morte simul universus mundus, simul homines singuli redempti sunt? Si hypostasis verbi singulis sanguinis Christi guttis infinitum valorem perhibuit, an amori erga Filium Dei unigenitum convenlens fuit, ut maledictæ adeò neci eum exponeret, quem vel guttula profusa totius mundi redemptorem facere potuisset? Ita pensi non habent Deum tyrannum facere, dum thesauris terrestribus inde locupletentur. Est quoque Sanctos inter, uti aliarum rerum, ita quoque afflictionum & passionum communis sensus, & arctissima communio, sed satisfactionum nulla. Neque ubi communio est, etiam communicatio est, quia communio rem communem supponit, cujus omnes æqualiter participes fiunt, Ephes. IV. 4. communicatio non item, quia fit erga indigentem. Pro in communio Sanctorum hujus vel illius particularem satisfactionem evertit, nósque ad unicam satisfactionem Christi, ceu rem communem, manuducit. Communicatio quoque bonorum, quæ fideles inter vigere debet, communicabilium, non incommunicabilium bonorum est. Cùm verò pro se nemo satisfacere posset, ac multò minùs pro aliis, satisfactiones communicabile bonum esse non possunt, ac nulla proin à satisfactionibus per indulgentias relaxatio locum habere potest. Et quæcunque opera vel passiones fidelium sunt, illas pro se quisque ex vocatione Dei, non pro aliis, facere & tolerare debent. Quisque suum onus gestabit, Galat. VI. 5. Ideo virgines prudentes stultis oleum suum denegarunt, Matth. XXV. 9. Noe, Daniel, Job ne proprios quidem infantes rediment, Ezech. XIV. 14. 20. Denique nec Ecclesia prisca indulgentiarum usum habuit. Causam Roffensis hanc perhibet; quòd ipsum quoque Purgatorium, sine quo nullæ indulgentiæ, serò in Ecclesia cognitum receptúmque fuerit. GregoGregorium quidem M. stationibus indulgentias addidisse Thomas & Altisiodorensis, Gregorio plusquam sexcentis annis recentiores tradiderunt, sed sine Gregorio teste. Concilia vero Viennense, Lugdunense, Claromontanum & sera, & particularia, & Papalium in summo corruptionis apice mancipiorum conventicula potius, quam Concilia fuerunt. Certè duodecim priorum seculorum Concilia de indulgentiis ejusmodi ne gry quidem habent. Nec nomen, nec omen Papalium indulgentiarum veteris Ecclesiae consensu firmari potest. Musteum earum inventum est ad hoc, ut superstitione captae animae quaestui habeantur.
units.tr: This is confirmed further by the consideration of Christ's death, which is applied in its entirety to each person (Rom. 5:10); of Baptism, in which the whole blood of Christ, not a mere drop, is sealed to each person; and of the Supper, in which each person drinks the whole blood of Christ. Thus one and the same solid light of the sun illumines both the whole world and each individual man. It is therefore a rash deed to divide the price of our redemption, which God willed to be solid and undivided, and which the law of God required to be such for each person. Nor shall we linger over that foreign babble of the Scholastics and of the Papal bulls, which the vanity of one whose god is his belly has produced, namely that the infinite dignity of the hypostasis of the divine Word is suited to each drop of Christ's blood and each of his meritorious actions, and that all the remaining superfluities are to be claimed for the treasury of the Church. Scripture nowhere speaks in this way; on the contrary, it testifies otherwise. Everywhere it presents the righteous act (δικαίωμα) of perfect justice as the work by which alone our redemption could be procured according to the law, not by the outpouring of a drop of blood or a single meritorious act, but by perfect justice, which demands the death of the sinner. "We are reconciled to God through the death of his Son" (Rom. 5:10); "He reconciled us in the body of his flesh through death" (Col. 1:21-22). Is it permissible, then, to invent drops and droplets as well? Is one person redeemed by one particle of this death and another by a different particle? Rather, is not the whole world redeemed at once by the whole death, and each individual person redeemed at once? If the hypostasis of the Word gave infinite value to each drop of Christ's blood, was it consistent with love for his only-begotten Son that God should expose him to such a cursed death, when a single drop shed could have made him the redeemer of the whole world? They have no scruple in making God a tyrant, while they enrich themselves from earthly treasuries by doing so. Among the saints there is indeed a common feeling, and a very close communion, in other things and in afflictions and sufferings; but in satisfactions there is none. Where there is communion, there is not necessarily communication, because communion presupposes a common good in which all share equally (Eph. 4:4), whereas communication is directed toward one who is in need. Thus the communion of saints overturns the particular satisfaction of this or that person, and leads us to the single satisfaction of Christ as a common good. The communication of goods, which ought to flourish among the faithful, concerns goods that can be communicated, not goods that cannot. Since no one can satisfy for himself, much less for others, satisfactions cannot be a communicable good, and so no relaxation of satisfactions through indulgences can have any place. Moreover, whatever works or sufferings the faithful have, each ought to perform and endure for himself, by the calling of God, and not for others: "Each shall bear his own burden" (Gal. 6:5). For this reason the wise virgins refused their oil to the foolish (Matt. 25:9). "Noah, Daniel and Job would not deliver even their own sons" (Ezek. 14:14, 20). Finally, the ancient Church did not use indulgences at all. Bishop Fisher of Rochester maintains this as the reason: indulgences were not known or received in the Church until late, and neither was Purgatory itself, without which there are no indulgences. Thomas and the Altisiodorensis, who were more than six hundred years later than Gregory, handed down that Gregory the Great added indulgences to the stational churches, but they cite no witness from Gregory himself. The councils of Vienne and Lyons, and the late councils of Clermont and others, as well as the particular assemblies of the Papalists, which were in the high summit of corruption, were rather gatherings of slaves than councils. Certainly the councils of the first twelve centuries contain nothing of this kind of indulgence at all. Neither the name nor the omen of Papal indulgences can be confirmed by the consent of the ancient Church. Their must was invented for this purpose only: that souls captured by superstition might be made a source of gain.

units.la: LX. Vix operae pretium est memorare Pseudopoliticos, qui peccatorum remissionem albo dente ridThis. Nam Eduardus Herbertus molliri religionem & minus severam reddi doctrina de peccatorum condonatione & justificatione per Christum delirat; eò quòd homines ex facili delictorum condonatione citius ad volutabrum revertantur, & in foediora crimina delabantur. Dum enim ex subsidiaria opera (sic Christi gratiam appellat) salutem suam impetrari posse credunt, quae ad ipsorum partes spectant, ut plurimum eos destituere vel negligere cavillatur. Nempe naturalibus & communibus notionibus suis dementatus, Christianam religionem, utpote discrimen inter homines statuentem, & gratia Christi nixam, sic confossam reddere voluit. Quasi quae religio gratiam Dei, & remissionem peccatorum confitetur, eandem ad lasciviae illecebram trahi permittat. Sed stans firmum Dei fundamentum hoc sigillum habet: Novit Dominus, qui sui sunt. Et: Desistat ab iniquitate omnis, qui nomen Christi nominat, 2. Tim. II. 19. Et quae gratia Dei salutaris omnibus hominibus affulsit, eadem erudit nos, ut abnegantes impietatem & mundanas concupiscentias sobrie, juste & pie vivamus in hoc seculo, Tit. II. 11. 12. Sed communem tamen experientiam testem ille appellat, quod ex externis auxiliis potius, quam ex virtute & interna poenitentia salutem aeternam homines expetant. Quidni vero sic expeterent, quorum optimi etiam miseriam & impotentiam suam extra Dei gratiam compertam habent? Sine gratiae Dei sensu non ullus amor Dei hominem occupare potest, sed metus potius & horror Numinis odium & aversationem Dei suadet. Ideo David: Si pravitates observes, Jah, quis stabit? כי עמך הסליחה למען תורא Nam apud te est condonatio, ut timearis, Psal. CXXX. 3. 4. Sine venia igitur fieri non potest, ut timeatur Deus. Nam Deus justificandis sanctificationem destinavit & paravit. Ejus initium est timor Dei, quo aestimatur Dei sanctitas, & hominis impuritas & indignitas, atque necessitas justificationis Divinae, & sigilli ejus, donatae, & quàm dignum sit Deo & justis gloriam Dei illustrare, ut humiliter cum Deo nostro ambulemus, & verbum ejus cum reverentia, submissione, cura atque solicitudine audiamus, retineamus & observemus. Qui ergo audiunt, dari gratiam, justificationem, peccatorum remissionem, illi Deum amant, timent, & in Deum credunt. Nullis enim justitia & remissio annuntiatur, nisi credentibus. Et in ipsa fide amor & timor Dei est. Quid porro communes de Deo notiones extra gratiam Dei & Christum in animis infidelium effecerint, S. Paulus Rom. capp. I. II. III. potenter demonstravit, quae ruminare potius, quam Christianam religionem sic pipulo differre, Pseudo-Politicorum, illorum inprimis, qui Christianum adhuc nomen profitentur, fuerat.
units.tr: LX. It is scarcely worth the trouble to mention the Pseudo-Politicians, who laugh at the remission of sins with a white tooth. Edward Herbert raves that religion is softened and made less strict by the doctrine of the forgiveness of sins and justification through Christ, because men, once their sins are easily pardoned, return more quickly to the mire and slide into more shameful crimes. For while they believe their salvation can be obtained through subsidiary works (so he calls the grace of Christ), he sneers that these works, which belong to their own part, mostly fail or neglect them. Indeed, driven mad by his own natural and common notions, he wished to pierce the Christian religion in this way, since it sets a distinction between men and rests on the grace of Christ. As if a religion that confesses the grace of God and the forgiveness of sins would allow itself to be dragged into the allurements of lust! But the firm foundation of God stands and has this seal: The Lord knows those who are his. And: Let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity, 2 Tim. 2:19. And the grace of God that brings salvation has appeared to all men, and that same grace teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly desires, and to live soberly, righteously and godly in this present age, Titus 2:11, 12. Yet he calls on common experience as his witness, that men seek eternal salvation from external helps rather than from virtue and inward repentance. But why would they not seek it so, when even the best of them have discovered their own misery and powerlessness outside the grace of God? Without a sense of God's grace no love of God can take hold of a man; rather, fear and dread, and the hatred and aversion toward the Deity, persuade him. So David: If you should mark iniquities, O Jah, who could stand? [כי עמך הסליחה למען תורא] For with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared, Ps. 130:3, 4. Therefore God cannot be feared without pardon. For God has designed and prepared sanctification for those he justifies. Its beginning is the fear of God, by which we weigh the holiness of God, the impurity and unworthiness of man, the necessity of divine justification and of its seal (the gift), and how fitting it is for God and for the righteous to make the glory of God shine forth, so that we may walk humbly with our God, and hear, hold and keep his word with reverence, submission, care and concern. Those, therefore, who hear that grace, justification and the forgiveness of sins are given, love and fear God and believe in God. For justification and remission are announced to none except believers. And in faith itself there is the love and fear of God. Furthermore, what common notions about God have produced in the minds of unbelievers apart from the grace of God and Christ, St Paul has powerfully shown in Romans chapters 1, 2 and 3. It was the habit of the Pseudo-Politicians, especially of those who still profess the Christian name, to chew over these notions rather than to deal with the Christian religion in such a trifling way.

units.la: LXI. Etenim si vel communes notiones integras & defaecatas attendimus, licet illae Christum, & remissionem peccatorum per ejusdem ἱλασμὸν non revelent, tamen remissionis peccatorum & ἱλασμὰς propitiationis Numinis si salvi esse cupimus, necessitatis & possibilitatis non obscuram suspicionem hominis insgenerabunt. Conscientia enim hominis peccati & miseriae humanae ignarum esse non patitur. Deum vero peccatis ita offendi, ut peccatorem poenae subjicere, nisi idoneè placatus, velit & debeat, eadem conscientia & cogitationes hominis invicem defendentes & accusantes, dictant. Sicut vero natura, vel Deus potius, naturae author nares ad odoratum, linguam ad loquelam, aures ad auditum comparavit, ita conscientiam ejusque dictamina & notiones anticipatas de Deo, felicitate bonorum, & poenis improborum eadem homini ingeneravit, ut virtuti studeat, & sicubi Deum offendit, placari eundem conetur. Placabilem autem Deum esse, ejusdem longanimitas, tolerantia, misericordia, clementia dubitare non sinunt. Nam juxta Ovidii illud:
units.tr: LXI. Indeed, if we attend to the common notions in their whole and purified form, although they do not reveal Christ, nor the forgiveness of sins through his propitiation, nevertheless, if we wish to be saved, they will beget in man an unclear but real suspicion of the necessity and possibility of remission of sins and of propitiation [ἱλασμὸς] of the Deity. For conscience does not allow man to be ignorant of sin and of human misery. That same conscience, and the thoughts that defend and accuse one another, dictate that God is so offended by sins that he both wills and ought to subject the sinner to punishment unless he is properly appeased. Just as nature, or rather God the author of nature, fitted the nose for smelling, the tongue for speech and the ears for hearing, so the same God implanted in man conscience, its dictates, and the anticipated notions of God, of the happiness of the good and the punishments of the wicked, so that he may strive after virtue, and, wherever he has offended God, try to placate him. That God is placable, his long-suffering, forbearance, mercy and clemency do not allow us to doubt. For according to the saying of Ovid:

units.la: Quò quisque est major, magis est placabilis ira. Et si nihil magno & praeclaro viro dignius esse placabilitate & clementia, rectè Cicero dixit, Deum, sicut offendi potest, ita placari posse ἀνεξαγώνιον erit. Sed placari tamen non sine remedio aliquo Deum posse natura etiam gentiles docuit; qui (exceptis solis Epicuraeis, qui Deum, tranquillitati & quieti suae indormientem nec promeritis capi, nec ultionem prosequi pertenderunt) placandi Numinis ritus varios excogitarunt, eosque vel humaniores, velut, si juxta Horatianum illud, Coelo supinas quis tulerit manus Nascente luna, &c. Si thure placarit, & horna Fruge lares, avidaque porca; si juxta Apollinis à Porphyrio memoriae proditum de sacrificiis oraculum, victimae quadrupedes, eaque nigri coloris omnibus diis ex aequo immolentur. Si Lustralia constituantur, quibus suae, ove & tauro caesis Diis litetur, &c. vel crudeliores, vel ut si homines immolarentur, vel sui immolationem homines voverent, vel infantes Molocho sacrarent &c. Philosophi vero aliique emunctiorum narium placandi Numinis, sine consilio Oraculorum, eam rationem ineundam esse dictarunt, ut quisque se ad sapientiam & puritatem convertat, & exiguarum impensarum libamine Deos propitiet, crudelitati vero, pompae & sumptibus sacrificiorum parcat. Maxima tamen Gentilium pars placationis instituendae ritus sibi praescribere formidans, illos Divinitus per Oracula, Vates, Augures, aliósque quibus cum Diis commercium esse putabatur, religiosè consultos, discere non sine ratione maluit. Cùm enim natura dictet, credibile esse, quòd Deus peccato offensus ratione aliqua placari possit, & referre non parum, ut placetur; neque tamen naturae lumine modum placandi Numinis dignosci posse animadanimadverterent, aliunde notitiam illam petendam esse merito statuerunt. Sed oraculis tamen omni exceptione majoribus illi destituebantur. Qua in re Christianæ religionis excellentia inprimis conspicua est, quòd à revelatione, seu oraculo, modum placandi Numinis & condonandarum offensarum per Christum certissimum patefaciente, eóque iis testibus, qui mentiendi causas procul habuerunt omnes, & testimonio suo capitibus suis damna innumera sævissimaque supplicia inconciliarunt, confirmato dependet. Naturales igitur notiones placandi Numinis & remissionis peccatorum necessitatem & possibilitatem non obscure docent, sed modum ἱλασμὸς seu propitiationis & remissionis peccatorum per Christum, ejusque obedientiam ad mortem usque crucis sola revelatio Divina omni exceptione major patefacit.
units.tr: The greater the man, the more placable his anger. And if it was rightly said by Cicero that nothing is more worthy of a great and distinguished man than placability and clemency, then that God, who can be offended, can also be appeased, is not without reason. But even the Gentiles, by nature, taught that God can be placated, not without some remedy. Except for the Epicureans alone, who thought that God, sleeping in his tranquillity and rest, is neither moved by merits nor pursues vengeance, they devised various rites for appeasing the Deity. Some of these were milder, as in the Horatian line: If anyone should lift up his hands palm upward to heaven when the moon is rising, etc. If he has appeased the household gods with incense and meal, and with a greedy sow; or as in the oracle concerning sacrifices recorded by Porphyry from Apollo: four-footed victims, and those of black colour, are to be sacrificed alike to all the gods. Or if lustral rites are instituted, by which the gods are propitiated with the slaughter of sheep and bulls, etc. Others were crueller, as when men were sacrificed, or when men vowed their own immolation, or dedicated infants to Moloch, etc. The philosophers and others of keener scent, however, laid down that, without the counsel of oracles, the way to appease the Deity is for each to turn himself to wisdom and purity, to propitiate the gods with the offering of small expenses, and to spare cruelty, display and the costs of sacrifices. Yet the greatest part of the Gentiles, fearing to prescribe for themselves the rites of appeasement, preferred to learn them, not without reason, by seeking counsel from the gods divinely through oracles, seers, augurs, and others who were thought to have intercourse with the gods. For while nature dictates that it is credible that God, offended by sin, can be placated by some means, and that it matters not a little that he be placated, yet, since they perceived that the manner of appeasing the Deity cannot be discerned by the light of nature, they rightly determined that the knowledge of it must be sought from elsewhere. But those who lacked such things were left without oracles of all exceptions. In this matter, above all, the excellence of the Christian religion is conspicuous: that it depends, for its confirmation, on a revelation or oracle that most certainly sets forth the manner of appeasing the Deity and of pardoning offences through Christ, and on witnesses who were far from every cause of lying and who, by their testimony, drew upon their own heads countless losses and most savage punishments. Natural notions therefore teach obscurely the necessity and possibility of appeasing the Deity and of the forgiveness of sins; but the manner of propitiation [ἱλασμὸς], that is, of the remission of sins through Christ and his obedience unto death on the cross, is revealed by divine revelation alone, which is greater than every exception.

units.la: LXII. Altera justificationis pars Vitæ seu hæreditatis adjudicatio est.
units.tr: LXII. The second part of justification is the adjudication of life, or of inheritance.

units.la: Nam propter Christi justitiam & obedientiam non tantum peccata homini condonantur, sed etiam jus petendi vitam cœlestem & æternam eidem addicitur. Non aliter enim salus homini constare potuit; qui absolutus licet à peccatis, jus tamen vitæ gloriosæ rapiendæ vel occupandæ non habet, nisi tribuente illud eadem Christi justitia, per quam legi vitam cœlestem & gloriosam sub conditione obedientiæ promittenti satisfactum in solidum est. Ideo etiam vox צדק justitiæ sæpissimè jus in rem bonam complectitur. Hæc hæreditas servorum Domini, & justitia illorum à me, Esaj. LIV. 17. Non est pars & justitia, & memoria, Nehem. II. 20. Justitia illa hominis est, quòd Filius Dei & hæres omnium bonorum ejus est. Supplicat Deo & gratum ipsum habet (peccata condonat) & videt faciem ejus cum jubilo, & reddit homini justitiam suam, (sensum justitiæ suæ) Job. XXXIII. 26. Quæ juris vitæ concessio realiter cum adoptione convenit, neque aliter ab hac distinguitur, quàm quòd vita æterna in justificatione ut debitum, in adoptione verò ut hæreditas spectatur; & Deus ibi judicis, hic Patris personam sustinet. Sed de adoptione hac pluribus infra.
units.tr: For on account of Christ's righteousness and obedience, not only are sins forgiven to a man, but the right to seek heavenly and eternal life is also granted to him. Otherwise salvation could not have been secured for man. A man who is absolved from sins still has no right to seize or lay hold of glorious life, unless the same righteousness of Christ bestows it, by which full satisfaction has been made to the law that promised heavenly and glorious life under the condition of obedience. Hence the word צדק (righteousness) very often includes a right to a good thing. "This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord, and their righteousness from me," Isa. 54:17. "There is no portion, righteousness, or memorial," Neh. 2:20. That righteousness of man is that the Son of God is also heir of all his goods. "He prays to God, and God is gracious to him (he forgives sins), and he sees his face with joy, and restores to man his righteousness" (the sense of his righteousness), Job 33:26. This grant of a right to life agrees in reality with adoption, and is distinguished from it only in that eternal life is viewed in justification as a debt, but in adoption as an inheritance; and in the one God plays the part of judge, in the other of Father. But more on this adoption below.

units.la: LXIII. Justitiam Christi Deus peccatori non sine conditione aliqua imputare voluit.
units.tr: LXIII. God was not willing to impute Christ's righteousness to the sinner without some condition.

units.la: Neque tamen decebat eandem, quam lege tulerat, perfectæ obedientiæ conditionem exigere, tum quia illa præstitu impossibilis fuisset: tum quia ab æquitate planè alienum id fuisset. Non potuisset etiam exigere, ut pro peccatis nostris ipsi vel in solidum, vel ex parte, vel in hac vita, vel post hanc vitam satisfaceremus, atque ea conditione justitiæ Christi participes reddere-mur; tum quia impossibile id fuit: tum quia sic liberari non potuissemus; tum quia in justitiæ Dei & Christi contumeliam id redundasset.
