Neque etiam, ut oblato pro peccatis nostris sacrificio justitiam Christi apprehendere-mus, fieri potuit. Nam etiam in sacrificio vel tota satisfactio, vel saltem præcipua ejus pars posita est. Neque alius sacerdos esse, quàm Christus: aliud sacrificium quàm Christi sacrificium in cruce oblatum, potuit. At nec caritas, vel bona opera conditionis illius vicem fungi potuit, quia sic sanctificatio medium ad glorificationem fuisset, cùm res contra habeat.
units.tr: Yet it was not fitting to demand the same condition of perfect obedience that he had laid down by law. This was partly because that obedience would have been impossible to render, and partly because such a demand would have been wholly foreign to equity. Nor could he have required that we make satisfaction for our sins to him, either wholly or in part, in this life or after it, and that on this condition we be made partakers of Christ's righteousness. This was partly because it is impossible, partly because in that way we could not have been freed, and partly because it would have redounded to the dishonour of the righteousness of God and of Christ. Nor could it come about that we lay hold of Christ's righteousness by offering a sacrifice for our sins. For even in sacrifice the whole satisfaction, or at least its chief part, is located. Nor could there be any priest other than Christ, or any sacrifice other than Christ's sacrifice offered on the cross. But neither love nor good works could take the place of that condition, because then sanctification would be the means to glorification, whereas the matter stands the other way round.

units.la: Atque id non Scriptura tantùm ubique docet, sed etiam ratio evincit, quia conveniens non est, ut cui Deus peccata nondum condonavit, ei donum charitatis, quo nullum sanctius vel præstabilius est, impertiatur. Apud te condonatio est, ut timeatris, Psal. CXXX. 4. Ejusmodi ergo conditio bonitati & sapientiæ Dei convenient fuit, quæ & omnium maxime necessaria, & æqua, & facilis esset. Talis fides in Christum est. Nullum enim opus ab homine exigi poterat, quin fidem ut causam includeret. Neque æquum fuit Christi justitiam & pretiosam satisfactionem cuiquam imputari vel donari, quin tantum beneficium non libens volensque agnosceret & apprehenderet, quam agnitionem & apprehensionem justitiæ Christi ipsam fidem esse, pluribus supra Loc. XXI. 88. &c. altruximus. Ubi totius fidei justificantis naturam explicuimus.
units.tr: Scripture does not only teach this everywhere, but reason also proves it, because it is not fitting that God should bestow the gift of love, than which none is holier or more excellent, on one to whom he has not yet forgiven sins. "With you is forgiveness, that you may be feared," Ps. 130:4. Therefore such a condition was suited to the goodness and wisdom of God, being at once most necessary of all, fair, and easy. Such is faith in Christ. For no work could be required of man that did not include faith as its cause. Nor was it just that Christ's righteousness and precious satisfaction should be imputed or given to anyone, unless he willingly and gladly acknowledged and laid hold of so great a benefit. That acknowledgement and apprehension of Christ's righteousness is faith itself, as we have argued at length above, Loc. XXI. 88, etc., where we explained the whole nature of justifying faith.

units.la: LXIV. Fide hominem justificari, tam claris & disertis Scripturarum testimoniis constat, ut id inficias ire nemo hactenus ausus fuerit. Sed modus, quo illa justificat, in controversiam venit.
units.tr: LXIV. That man is justified by faith is so clearly and plainly established by the testimonies of Scripture that no one has yet dared to deny it. But the manner in which faith justifies is in controversy.

units.la: Nam Pontificii in Concilio Tridentino Sess. VI. cap. 6. & can. 9. Fidem justificare definiverunt per modum dispositionis seu præparationis ad justificationem, qua peccator fidem ex auditu concipiens liberè & primò in Deum, moveatur, credens vera esse, quæ Divinitus revelata & præmissa sunt, atque illud inprimis, in Deo justificari impium per gratiam ejus, si à Divinæ justitiæ timore ad considerandam ejus misericordiam se convertat, in spem erigatur, atque sic Deum diligat, adversus peccata moveatur, per odium & detestationem, hoc est, per eam pœnitentiam, quæ ante Baptismum præstari debet: si denique proponat suscipere Baptismum, inchoare novam vitam, & mandata Dei servare. Ita Fides prima illis ad justificationem motio & præparatio est, & qua talis prima motio sola justificare, quia ad primam illam motionem sola concurrat, à Walenburgiis imposturibus; ambigua & fallaci maximè dictione statuitur, sed habens tamen comites & pedisequas præparationis & dispositiones plures, timorem, spem, dilectionem, pœnitentiam antebaptismalem, propositum Baptismi & observantiæ mandatorum Dei; quibus demum præviis dispositionibus universis viam sterni infusioni habitus charitatis, seu formalis causæ justificationis dogmatizant. Sociniani Fidem gratuitam Dei acceptilationem interpretantur, quà scilicet visum Deo sit fidem, qua quis paratus est omnia consequendæ promissionis Divinæ gratia facere, & pro viribus facit; reputare pro justitia, sive perfecta impletione Legis; sicut olim sub Fœdere legali obedientia fuit universalis justitia, ex qua vita Dei pendebat, quoratum fere vestigiis Remonstrantes insistunt, qui & ipsi fidem imperfectam mandatorum Dei obedientiam statuunt. Omnibus his commune est, quòd fidem opus & justitiam, qua homo proprie, per se, & sine respectu ad objectum suum justificetur, faciunt, hoc fere cum discrimine, quòd Pontificii præcipuè oppugnant fidei naturam, eam in generalem assensum verbi Dei, & præviam justificationis dispositionem convertentes. Sociniani ejus objectum, justitiam & satisfactionem Christi impetunt. Remonstrantes strantes denique ejus usum, apprehensionem justitiæ imputatæ Christi evertunt.
units.tr: For the Papists, at the Council of Trent, Session VI, chapter 6 and canon 9, have defined that faith justifies by way of a disposition or preparation for justification. By this, the sinner, receiving faith from hearing, is moved freely and first towards God, believing those things to be true which are divinely revealed and promised, and especially that he is justified before God by his grace, if from fear of divine justice he turns to consider God's mercy, is raised up to hope, and thus begins to love God, and is moved against sins by hatred and detestation, that is, by that repentance which ought to be performed before baptism. Finally, he resolves to receive baptism, to begin a new life, and to keep God's commandments. Thus for them the first faith is the motion and preparation for justification. That this first motion alone justifies, since only it concurs with that first motion, is laid down by the Walenburgian impostors in an ambiguous and very deceptive phrase. Yet it has many companions and attendants of preparation and disposition: fear, hope, love, repentance before baptism, the purpose of baptism, and observance of God's commandments. When all these preceding dispositions are in place, they teach that the way is prepared for the infusion of the habit of love, which is the formal cause of justification. The Socinians interpret faith as God's gracious acceptilation: that is, it has seemed good to God to reckon as righteousness, or as the perfect fulfilment of the Law, the faith by which someone is ready to do everything to obtain the divine promise, and does what he can. Just as formerly under the legal covenant universal obedience was righteousness, on which the life of God depended, so the Remonstrants follow nearly the same footsteps, who also hold that faith is an imperfect obedience to God's commandments. Common to all these is that they make faith a work and a righteousness by which a man is properly and in himself justified, without regard to its object. This is roughly the difference: the Papists chiefly attack the nature of faith, turning it into a general assent to the Word of God and a preceding disposition for justification. The Socinians assail its object, the righteousness and satisfaction of Christ. Finally, the Remonstrants overturn its use, namely the apprehension of the imputed righteousness of Christ.

units.la: LXV. Orthodoxi fidem ut opus & justi-tiam, sive solam, sive cum aliis conjunctam proprie justificare pernegant. Neque enim ut principalem vel formalem, sed merè ut organicam causam justificationis causam faciunt, quatenus videlicet ceu organon & manus Christum salutarem unicè in naufragio tabulam & arcem salutis, & ex ejusdem plenitudine <bl>χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος</bl> gratiam pro gratia Joh. I. 16. capessit, apprehendit & applicat. Hoc solo sensu <bl>πίστις</bl> æquè pretiosa fides, 2. Pet. I. 1. appellatur, non quòd quocunque alio opere per se pretiosior sit, sed quia manum suam implet Christo, qui solus <bl>τιμίῳ αἵματι</bl> pretioso sanguine tanquam Agni immaculati nos redemit, 1. Pet. I. 19. Nam itatim Petrus æquè pretiosam illam fidem, quam <bl>λαχὼν</bl> sortitos, hoc est, Divina sorte vel destinatione, ceu donum Dei, accepisse dicit, <bl>ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ</bl> in justitia Dei nostri & Servatoris nostri Jesu Christi esse docet: nominans proin fidem æquè pretiosam in justitia Christi, quia pretium habet à justitia Christi, quam manu spirituali sua ad hoc Divinitus creata prensat, & sibi applicat. Fides enim per se non majus pretium, quàm reliqua dona Dei habet: imò extra functionem suam essentialem apprehendi Christum & divitias ejus, nullum habet, sicut mendici manus non apprehendens <bl>δωρημα</bl> donum oblatum æquè paupertina & vilis atque mendicus ipse est. Ita cerae & auri ejusdem magnitudinis per se pretium diversissimum, & illius cum hoc comparati fere nullum est: at cera eadem Testamento vel Diplomati, quo maxima bona hæredi legantur & addicuntur appensa, & bona legata obsignans, longè maximi, & auri exiguæ atque æquæ magnitudinis valorem plurimùm superantis pretii est. Quid enim fides sine objecto apprehensio, sine Christo, nisi oculus sine luce, auris sine sono, phantasma merum est? Quæ si sine Christo, adeóque proprie & per se justificare putatur, Christi locum & manus ipsa impiè invadit, & quod Christi est, sacrilegio maximo sibi vindicat. Est equidem fides donum Dei, Ephes. II. 8. Sed Christus & justitia ejus, quæ sola à peccatis absolvit, & jus vitæ donat, non est. At nec ut opus justificat, quia <bl>χωρὶς ἔργων</bl> sine operibus, Rom. III. 28. & justificari <bl>διὰ πίστεως</bl> per fidem, ceu medium & organon, ibid. v. 25. nuspiam <bl>διὰ τὴν πίστιν</bl> propter fidem dicimur. Denique nec fides justificare dicitur, quatenus ipsa gratiam, charitatem operatur, & corda purificat. Licèt enim fidei actus consequens quidem <bl>καρπποφῶν</bl> fructificans detur, juxta quem, postquam Christum apprehendit & eo apprehenso peccatorem justificavit, etiam fœta mater novæ obedientiæ, reliquarum virtutum & bonorum operum evadit, tamen non ut sic fructificans, sed seorsim & sola, non tamen solitaria, sola justificationem efficiens; at non sola exititit, justificat. Sicut enim in sole calor & splendor inseparabiles licèt sint, tamen Sol nec ut splendens calefacit, nec ut calefaciens splendet: sic fides & charitas, per quam illa operosa est, inseparabiles licèt sint, tamen sola fides, non charitas justificat. Scitè enim Lutherus in justificatione Christum & fidem solam tanquam sponsum & sponsam in thalamo esse, dixit.
units.tr: LXV. The orthodox flatly deny that faith, whether alone or joined with other things, properly justifies as a work and a righteousness. For they make faith the cause of justification not as principal or formal cause, but merely as an organic cause, inasmuch as, like an instrument and hand, it grasps, apprehends and applies Christ the Saviour, the only plank in shipwreck and the citadel of salvation, and receives "grace for grace" [χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος] from his fullness, John 1:16. Only in this sense is faith called "equally precious" [πίστις], 2 Pet. 1:1: not because it is in itself more precious than any other work, but because it fills its hand with Christ, who alone redeemed us with "precious blood" [τιμίῳ αἵματι], as of a spotless Lamb, 1 Pet. 1:19. For Peter at once says that he has received that equally precious faith which he has obtained by lot [λαχὼν], that is, by divine lot or appointment, as a gift of God. He teaches that it is "in the righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ" [ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ]. So he calls faith equally precious in the righteousness of Christ, because it has its worth from the righteousness of Christ, which it grasps with the spiritual hand that God created for this very purpose, and applies to itself. For faith in itself has no greater worth than the other gifts of God. Indeed, apart from its essential function of apprehending Christ and his riches, it has none, just as a beggar's hand that does not take the gift offered is as poor and worthless as the beggar himself. So wax and gold of the same size have very different values in themselves, and the comparison of the one with the other is almost nothing. Yet the same wax, attached to a will or charter by which the greatest goods are bequeathed and assigned to an heir, and sealing the goods bequeathed, is of far greater worth, far surpassing the value of gold of small and equal size. For what is faith without its object, an apprehension without Christ, but an eye without light, an ear without sound, a mere phantom? If it is thought to justify by itself and properly, without Christ, it impiously invades the place and hand of Christ, and with the greatest sacrilege claims for itself what belongs to Christ. Faith is indeed a gift of God, Eph. 2:8. But it is not Christ and his righteousness, which alone absolves from sins and bestows the right to life. Nor does it justify as a work, since we are justified "without works" [χωρὶς ἔργων], Rom. 3:28, and are justified "through faith" [διὰ πίστεως], as a means and instrument, ibid. v. 25; nowhere are we said to be justified "on account of faith" [διὰ τὴν πίστιν]. Finally, faith is not said to justify insofar as it works grace and love and purifies hearts. For although the act of faith has a consequence that bears fruit, by which, after it has apprehended Christ and, Christ being apprehended, has justified the sinner, it also becomes the fruitful mother of new obedience, of the other virtues and of good works, nevertheless it does not justify as fruit-bearing, but separately and alone; yet not solitary, it justifies alone, though not as a lone agent. For just as in the sun heat and light, though inseparable, yet the sun does not warm as it shines, nor shine as it warms, so faith and love, through which faith is active, though inseparable, yet faith alone, not love, justifies. Luther aptly said that in justification Christ and faith alone are like a bridegroom and bride in the bridal chamber.

units.la: LXVI. Cùm ergo Fides non dignitate quadam propria, nec ut opus, vel δικαίωμα, nec proprie & per se, sed improprie ac metonymicè, quatenus objectum fidei, quod causa principalis justificationis est, proprie justificet, hujus verò effectum fidei, ut instrumento tribuatur; atque eo sensu sola justificet; obscurus esse modus, quo ei justificationem Scriptura tribuit; non potest. Justificat enim sola tum quatenus est organon & medium communionis nostræ cum Christo, per quam primo cum Christo certa fiducia apprehenso unimur, & uno spiritu in idem corpus baptizamur, 1. Cor. XII. 13. tum per eandem, ceu ὁμολογίαν Deo in fœdere gratiæ eandem stipulanti ὁμολογοῦμεν astipulamur, & Deo velut desponsamur, atque ita fœdus & amicitia cum Deo per peccatum interrupta in Christo apprehenso restauratur: tum quatenus in fide est acceptatio promissionis, quæ eam irrevocabilem facit. Cùm enim justitia in verbo Dei esurienda & sitienda, & ceu arx Dei apprehendenda, offeratur & porrigatur, per fidem, qua eam sitimus, esurimus, ut arcem Dei apprehendimus, & cum eadem sic unimur, Christus unà cum justitia sua noster fit, atque sic nos justificat. Qua fide sic corda filiorum Dei erga Christum afficiuntur, uti infantes recens nati erga lac maternum affici solent, 1. Pet. II. 2. ut sic bonis Christi se expleri sincerè expectant, & in Deum & Christum cum omni fiducia se conjiciant, de quo plurima superiùs diximus.
units.tr: LXVI. Since faith justifies, not by any dignity of its own, nor as a work or dikaioma [δικαίωμα], nor properly and in itself, but improperly and metonymically (in that the object of faith, which is the principal cause of justification, justifies properly, and its effect is ascribed to faith as an instrument), and since it justifies alone in this sense, the manner in which Scripture ascribes justification to faith is not hard to see. Faith justifies alone, first, in so far as it is the organ and means of our communion with Christ, by which, having first laid hold of Christ with certain trust, we are united to him and are baptized into one body by one Spirit, 1 Cor. 12:13. Second, through faith we respond with homologia [ὁμολογίαν] to God, who in the covenant of grace demands this agreement, and we say homologoumen [ὁμολογοῦμεν] in return, and are betrothed to God. In this way the covenant and friendship with God, broken by sin, is restored in Christ, who is laid hold of. Third, faith justifies alone in so far as acceptance of the promise is found in faith, which makes that justification irrevocable. For since righteousness is offered and held out in the word of God, to be hungered and thirsted for, and to be laid hold of as the fortress of God, we thirst and hunger for it through faith, and we lay hold of it as the fortress of God, and by this we are united to it. Christ, together with his righteousness, becomes ours, and so he justifies us. By this faith the hearts of the children of God are disposed towards Christ as newborn infants are normally disposed towards their mother's milk, 1 Pet. 2:2, so that they sincerely look to be filled with the good things of Christ, and cast themselves upon God and Christ with all confidence. We have said a great deal about this above.

units.la: LXVII. Per solam fidem eo modo nos justificari, Scriptura testatur, ubicunque fidei justificationem vitam & communionem cum Christo tribuit, quod creberrimè facit. Multorum locorum instar sunto: Justitia Dei revelatur ex fide in fidem, Rom. I. 17. Deus justificat ex fide Jesu, cap. III. 26. Concludimus, fide justificari hominem, ibid. v. 28. Ut justificemur ex fide Christi, Gal. II. 16. Justus ex fide vivet, Habac. II. 4. Rom. I. 17. In fide Filii Dei vivo, Gal. II. 20. Manifestum est, quòd justus ex fide vivat, ibid. III. 11. Per fidem Christus habitat in cordibus nostris, Ephes. III. 17. Radicati & superædificati in Christo, & confirmati in fide, Col. II. 7. Si aliquid fidem vel antecedens (nihil tamen aliud quàm servitus peccati antecedit) vel consequens, quale charitas est, justificaret, cur sic constanter Scriptura fidei justitiam & vitam vendicaret? Imò sic fidei justificatio & vita ne quidem assignari posset. Nam justificatio & vita vel jam præcessisset, vel demum consequeretur. Cùm enim justificatio sit sententia Dei judicis, à peccato absolventis, & jus vitæ addicentis, necesse est ἐν ἀπιστῳ, & simul semélque non succedlivè illa fiat. Ideo justitia revelari diserté ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν ex fide in fidem Rom. I. 17. dicitur, quia fidei nil nisi fides, non opera succenturiantur; ut ita fides ejus non tantùm ἀρχὴ principium, radix, prima motio sit, uti Tridentini pertendunt, sed etiam τέλος finis, sicque archetelos statuatur. Licèt enim actus quosdam præcedaneos & fidei justificanti prævios dari, quales ex lege agnitio peccati, ex Evangelio agnitio Christi & promissionum gratiæ, aliíque supra; ubi actus fidei antecedentes explicavimus.
units.tr: LXVII. Scripture bears witness that we are justified in this way, by faith alone, wherever it ascribes justification, life and communion with Christ to faith, which it does very often. Let these many passages stand as examples: The righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, Rom. 1:17. God justifies by the faith of Jesus, ch. 3:26. We conclude that a man is justified by faith, ibid. v. 28. That we might be justified by the faith of Christ, Gal. 2:16. The just shall live by faith, Hab. 2:4; Rom. 1:17. I live in the faith of the Son of God, Gal. 2:20. It is evident that the just lives by faith, ibid. 3:11. Christ dwells in our hearts through faith, Eph. 3:17. Rooted and built up in Christ, and established in the faith, Col. 2:7. If something either preceding faith (though nothing precedes it except the servitude of sin) or following it, such as love, justified, why would Scripture so consistently claim justification and life for faith? Indeed, justification and life could not even be assigned to faith in this way. For justification and life would either already have come before, or would follow afterwards. Since justification is the sentence of God as judge, absolving from sin and adjudging the right to life, it must happen en apistō [ἐν ἀπιστῳ] and at once and all together, not successively. Therefore it is said expressly that righteousness is revealed ek pisteōs eis pistin [ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν], from faith into faith, Rom. 1:17, because nothing but faith is set in faith's place, not works; so that faith is not only the archē [ἀρχὴ], the beginning, root and first motion, as the Tridentines contend, but also the telos [τέλος], the end, and so is set as archetelos, beginning and end. For although we allow that certain acts precede faith and prepare for justifying faith, such as the knowledge of sin from the law, the knowledge of Christ and of the promises of grace from the Gospel, and others besides, which we explained above where we dealt with the acts of faith that precede justification, we do not deny this.

units.la: 0 ● mus; à nobis expositi sunt nulli diffiteamur, & eosdem dispositionum, sine quibus non, nomine improprie à Theologis quibusdam appellari sano sensu haud ægre patiamur; tamen dari dispositiones & præparationes justificationis formales, quibus introductio formæ in subjectum adjuvetur, sive fide priores (quod ipsi Tridentini negant) sive fidem consequentes, cujusmodi sex numero, timorem, spem, dilectionem, pœnitentiam, propositum Baptismi & novæ obedientiæ iidem numerant, non sine gravi ratione inficiamur. Nam dispositiones formales, quibus introductio formæ in subjectum adjuvatur, qualitatibus, quæ introducuntur homogeneæ esse debent; utpote à quibus gradu solo, non natura differunt; & insuper introductionem formæ ipsius in subjectum antecedere, & formam inchoare debent. Atqui in justificatione nec qualitas ulla in subjectum introducitur, quia illa actus judicialis, quo Deus Christi justitiam credenti in judicio suo imputat, est; non qualitatis inhærentis infusione & exercitio peragitur: nec dispositiones à Tridentinis enumeratæ justitiæ illi, per & propter quam solam justificamur, homogeneæ seu congeneres sunt, quia justificatio fit absque operibus, cum dispositiones illæ opera non sint, & pleræque legis opera sint; & justificatio relativa, dispositiones verò qualitates inchoatæ sint, & pleraque illa, una fide excepta, justificationem sequantur, non præcedant; & denique fides justificationem acceptatam non inchoet, sed simul semelque, ceu actum indivisibilem perficiat. Nam per fidem accedimus ad Deum, & accedentes simul justificamur. Quomodo enim non justificati, non reconciliati ad Deum, qui ignis consumens est, accedere audint? Sola igitur fides, vel ipso Apostolo, cujus testimonium ad fidem, ceu dispositionem inchoantem, illi detorquent, judice, accessui ad Deum, in quo justificatio est, præordinari debet. Reliquæ omnes spuriæ sunt, non dispositiones ad justificationem, sed jam justificatorum qualitates vel actus sunt.
units.tr: 0 ● We have set out these things; no one should deny them, and in a sound sense we would not be troubled if some theologians improperly call the same things dispositions without which not. Yet we cannot without serious reason deny that there are dispositions and preparations for justification that are formal, by which the introduction of the form into the subject is helped, whether they come before faith (which the Tridentines themselves deny) or follow faith. Those whom the same men count as six, namely fear, hope, love, repentance, the purpose of baptism and of new obedience, are of this kind. For formal dispositions, by which the introduction of the form into the subject is helped, must be homogeneous with the qualities that are introduced, since they differ from them in degree only and not in nature. Moreover, they must precede the introduction of the form itself into the subject and begin the form. But in justification no quality is introduced into the subject, because that act of judgment by which God, in his judgment, imputes the righteousness of Christ to the believer, is not accomplished by the infusion and exercise of an inherent quality. Nor are the dispositions listed by the Tridentines homogeneous or congeneric with that righteousness through which, and on account of which alone, we are justified. This is because justification happens without works, whereas those dispositions are works, and most of them are works of the law. Justification is relational, whereas those dispositions are inchoate qualities, and most of them, apart from faith, follow justification rather than precede it. Finally, faith does not merely begin the justification that is accepted; it completes it at once and all together, as one indivisible act. For through faith we draw near to God, and in drawing near we are at once justified. For how could those who are not justified, not reconciled to God, who is a consuming fire, dare to draw near? Therefore faith alone, in the judgment of the Apostle himself, whose testimony they twist to make faith a disposition that merely begins, must be ordained as the approach to God, in whom justification lies. All the others are spurious. They are not dispositions towards justification, but qualities or acts of those already justified.

units.la: LXVIII. Atque id magis etiam ex iis Scripturæ testimoniis, quibus non solum fidei justificatio, vita & communio cum Christo tribuitur, sed etiam opera, ceu causæ, à justificatione, vita & communione cum Christo excluduntur, & fides atque opera opponuntur, colligere est.
units.tr: LXVIII. This may be gathered even more from those testimonies of Scripture in which justification, life and communion with Christ are ascribed not only to faith, but also works are excluded, as causes, from justification, life and communion with Christ, and faith and works are set against each other.

units.la: Concludimus igitur, fide justificari hominem sine operibus legis, Rom. III. 28. Ei, qui operatur, merces non imputatur secundum gratiam, ib. IV. 4. 5. Quibus verbis S. Paulus non solum fidem & opera opponit, uti alibi gratiam & opera, ibid. XI. 6. ut authoritate ejus tutò affirmare nobis liceat, sola fide nos justificari, quia justificamur non operantes, cum tamen, judice Apostolo, ipsa opera inter & fidem immediata oppositio sit; sed etiam oppositionis illius, & justificationis ex sola fide veritatem demonstrat. Argumentatur enim cap. IV. 3. ex eo, quòd Scriptura Gen. XV. 6. dicat: Credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatum est ei ad justitiam. Ex quo dicto duo efficit, quòd ea fides, quæ ad justitiam imputatur, sit fides in eum, qui impium justificat: & quòd is non operans, sine operibus & merito suo ullo justificetur. Satis enim liquet, eam fidem, quæ ad justitiam imputatur, non illud animæ & conscientiæ judicium esse, quo quis credit, se operantem, hoc est, facientem ea, quæ legis sunt; victurum, quia hoc judicium, non accedente testimonio alio, non tam fides, quàm naturalis cognitio est, neque de eo quicquam Abraham ex fide justificato Deus locutus est.
units.tr: We conclude therefore that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law, Rom. 3:28. To him who works, the reward is not imputed according to grace, ibid. 4:4, 5. In these words St Paul does not merely set faith against works, as he elsewhere sets grace against works, ibid. 11:6, so that on his authority we may safely affirm that we are justified by faith alone, because we are justified not by working. Rather, in the judgment of the Apostle, works and faith are an immediate opposition, and he demonstrates the truth of that opposition and of justification by faith alone. For he argues in ch. 4:3 from what Scripture says in Gen. 15:6: Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness. From this statement he draws two conclusions: first, that the faith which is imputed for righteousness is faith in him who justifies the ungodly; and second, that he who does not work is justified without works and without any merit of his own. It is quite clear that the faith which is imputed for righteousness is not that judgment of the soul and conscience by which someone believes that he is working, that is, doing the things of the law, and will live by them. This is because such a judgment, without other testimony added, is less faith than natural knowledge, and God did not speak of Abraham as justified by faith in any such thing.

units.la: Tum quia opera, ceu causæ, à justificatione, vita & communione cum Christo excluduntur, & fides ad justitiam imputari, Rom. IV. 4. 5. dicitur. re unico glorietur, Rom. V. 11. 1. Cor. I. 31. Phil. III. 3. Gratia verò sola omnem gloriationem hominis apud Deum excludit, Rom. III. 27. IV. 1. In eo, quod nostrum est, gloriari licet. Et per fidem salvari maxima gratia est. Convertit Deus ad nos labium selectum & clarum, atque nobiscum loquitur, non de peccato, & praeceptis gravibus, sed de pace, libertate, vita, justitia, Salvatore, foedere, Regno & gloria, quae in Filio parata sunt omnibus in eum credentibus. Cumque justificatio non aliud sit, quam donatio & imputatio justitiae & meriti Christi, gratuita omnino esse debet. Si enim in nobis aliquid esset, cujus dignitate vel valore justificari possemus, cui bono imputatio justitiae & meriti alieni? Ita Adamus integer aliena justitia vel merito opus non habuit, quia proprio vitam merreri potuit. Qui ergo per alienam justitiam & meritum vivit, is propria justitia vivere non potest. Si igitur justificatio ex gratia est, non est ex opere. Si gratia, non amplius ex operibus. Alias gratia non amplius gratia esset. Si vero ex operibus, non amplius est ex gratia. Alias opus non amplius esset opus, Rom. XI. 6. Gratiae vero cum tribuitur justificatio & quidem per fidem, Ephes. II. 8. manifestum est, quaevis opera fidem & antecedentia & consequentia excludi. Antecedentia, sive illa perfecta sunt, qualia nemo peccator habet, sive imperfecta, bona tamen, quia sic opera tamen iunt, & ante fidem nil nisi peccatum habemus, & fides, per quam salvamur, initium novum & vitae & salutis aeternae est. Per eam enim corda purificantur, Act. XV. 9. & per eam ex morte peccatorum vivificamur. Consequentia, quia gratia Dei per fidem salvamur, Ephes. II. 8. Nam per fidem Christum accipimus, & ei implantamur, qui princeps, auctor & causa salutis est, Heb. II. 10. XII. 2. Quae igitur fidem sequuntur, non possunt causa salutis statui. Alias justificatio & salvatio per fidem rescinderetur.
units.tr: Again, because works, as causes, are excluded from justification, life and communion with Christ, and faith is said to be imputed for righteousness, Rom. 4:4, 5, therefore let him who glories glory in the Lord, Rom. 5:11; 1 Cor. 1:31; Phil. 3:3. But grace alone excludes all boasting of man before God, Rom. 3:27; 4:1. One may glory in what is one's own. And it is the greatest grace to be saved through faith. God turns to us a pure and chosen lip, and speaks with us not of sin and grievous precepts, but of peace, liberty, life, righteousness, the Saviour, the covenant, the kingdom and glory, which are prepared in the Son for all who believe in him. And since justification is nothing other than the gift and imputation of the righteousness and merit of Christ, it must be wholly gratuitous. For if there were something in us by whose worth or value we could be justified, to what purpose would the imputation of another's righteousness and merit be? Thus Adam, in his integrity, had no need of an alien righteousness or merit, because he could earn life by his own. Therefore whoever lives through another's righteousness and merit cannot live by his own righteousness. If justification is from grace, then it is not from works. If by grace, then it is no more of works; otherwise grace is no more grace. But if of works, then it is no more of grace; otherwise work is no more work, Rom. 11:6. Since justification is ascribed to grace, and indeed through faith, Eph. 2:8, it is clear that every work is excluded, both those that precede faith and those that follow it. Works that precede faith are excluded, whether they are perfect, which no sinner has, or imperfect yet good, for we have nothing before faith but sin, and the faith through which we are saved is the new beginning of life and of eternal salvation. For through faith hearts are purified, Acts 15:9, and through faith we are made alive from the death of sin. Works that follow faith are excluded, because by the grace of God we are saved through faith, Eph. 2:8. For through faith we receive Christ and are implanted into him, who is the prince, author and cause of salvation, Heb. 2:10; 12:2. Therefore those things which follow faith cannot be set up as the cause of salvation. Otherwise justification and salvation through faith would be annulled.

units.la: LXX. Non consulunt Divinae gratiae Pontificii asserentes justificationem primam, qua per justitiam homini infusam is ex injusto & impio justus efficitur, gratuitam esse; at secundam qua justitia infusa per opera exercetur & crescit, adeoque is ex justo justior evadit, ex operibus, eorumque merito obtingere. Justificationem enim non infusione justitiae, sed imputatione obedientiae & meriti Christi peragi, supra probavimus. Tum ex mente Papistarum prima justificatio pertinet ad eum, qui ex injusto justus, ex servo peccati non servus fit, quod cum factus est, tum demum secunda incipit. At justificari coram Deo ad universum salutis humanae cursum, donec ad coronam perventum sit, pertinet. Qui ergo gratis, non ex opere coram Deo justificatur, is in solidum sic justificatur, ut alia justificatione opus minime sit. Insuper nec plane gratuita est justificatio, ad quam homines praeviis dispositionibus fide & operibus propriis se praeparant, qualem primam illam esse, contendunt. Ac licet gratis justitiam homini infundi concedant, tamen justitia infusa, quam formalem justificationis causam faciunt, habitus justitiae proprius, donatus licet, est. Qui igitur habitu eo justificatur, is justitia propria justificatur. Nam quod quis habet, quocunque titulo habeat, proprium est. Et qui
units.tr: LXX. The Papists do not respect divine grace when they assert that the first justification, by which a man is made righteous from unrighteous and ungodly through the righteousness infused into him, is gratuitous, but that the second, in which the infused righteousness is exercised and grows through works, so that a man becomes more righteous from being righteous, comes from works and their merit. For we have proved above that justification is effected not by the infusion of righteousness but by the imputation of the obedience and merit of Christ. Moreover, according to the mind of the Papists, the first justification belongs to the one who becomes righteous from unrighteous, and from a slave of sin becomes not a slave; only when this has happened does the second begin. But being justified before God belongs to the whole course of human salvation until the crown is reached. Therefore, he who is justified before God freely and not by works is justified entirely in such a way that there is by no means need of another justification. Furthermore, the justification which they contend is the first one, and which they say is not gratuitous and not meritorious, is not truly gratuitous at all, since men prepare themselves for it by prior dispositions of faith and their own works. And although they concede that righteousness is poured into man freely, nevertheless the infused righteousness, which they make the formal cause of justification, is a habit of righteousness belonging to the man himself, even if it is given as a gift. Therefore, he who is justified by that habit is justified by his own righteousness. For whatever a man has, by whatever title he has it, is his own. And

units.la: ex re propria, sive habitus, sive actus illa sit, justificatur δωρεάν gratis, & quidem χάριν gratia, hoc est, nullo habitu vel opere proprio, sed ex re, quae propria est. Quomodo qui nummo gratis donato aes alienum exsolvit, ei aes alienum non ex gratia remittitur, quia re sua debitum expunxit. Praeterea homo in prima illa justificatione, quam gratuitam esse, non meritoriam asserunt, vel perfecte Deo reconciliatur, vel non. Si prius, quid opus est justificatione secunda, quae ulterius justificet? Si posterius, qua ratione secunda merebitur, cum per primam non absolvamur? Accedit & hoc, quod dum primae justificationis causam meritoriam Christi justitiam statuunt, secundae habitum infusum; si ex secunda justificatione, quam ex prima perfectior quis prodeat, consequens erit, ut opera nostra Christi meritum vel superent, quod blasphemum est, vel perficiant, quod eidem contumeliosum est. Denique sic initium justificationis erit Dei & gratiae ejus; at progressus & perfectio operum nostrorum. Quae diabolica blasphemia est. Quid enim hoc aliud est, quam adorare opera manuum nostrarum, gloriam Creatoris & Redemptoris creaturae, & Deo justificationis initium, homini ejusdem perfectionem tribuere? Hoc Sathanas velit, cujus studium est honori Dei detrahere. Divinus honor est credere, quod solius Dei opus sit impium justificare. Qui igitur operibus suis justificationis absolutionem tribuunt, annon ii Sathanica impietate Creatorem & Redemptorem suum blasphemant?
units.tr: he who is justified by a thing that is his own, whether that thing is a habit or an act, is justified freely [δωρεάν], and indeed by grace [χάριν], that is, not by any habit or work of his own but by something that is truly his own. It is like someone who pays off a debt with a coin given to him freely: his debt is not remitted to him by grace, because he has cancelled the debt with his own property. Besides, in that first justification, which they say is gratuitous and not meritorious, a man is either perfectly reconciled to God or he is not. If the former, what need is there for a second justification to justify him further? If the latter, how will the second merit anything, since we are not absolved through the first? This also follows: while they establish the meritorious cause of the first justification as the righteousness of Christ, they establish the infused habit as the cause of the second. If someone should come forth more perfect from the second justification than from the first, it will follow that our works either surpass the merit of Christ, which is blasphemous, or complete it, which is insulting to him. Finally, in this way the beginning of justification would belong to God and his grace, but the progress and perfection to our works. This is a diabolical blasphemy. For what else is this than to worship the works of our hands, to give the glory of the Creator and Redeemer to a creature, and to attribute the beginning of justification to God but its perfection to man? Satan would wish this, whose aim is to take away the honour of God. It is the divine honour to believe that it is the work of God alone to justify the ungodly. Those, therefore, who ascribe the absolution of justification to their works, do they not, with Satanic impiety, blaspheme their Creator and Redeemer?

units.la: LXXI.
units.tr: LXXI.

units.la: Non desunt alia etiam argumenta, quibus fidem non ut opus, vel proprie, sed ut organon, & improprie & relative, & solam justificare certam fidem facimus. Negari enim non potest, justificationem in remissione peccatorum, quam Evangelium promittit, consistere. Nam & ipsi Tridentini remissionem peccatorum partem justificationis constituerunt. Atqui nulla in homine facultas est, quae remissionem hanc in Evangelio oblatam acceptare possit, quam fides. Sola enim illa Deo promittenti & remissionem offerenti credit, & credendo eam accipit; non vel spes, vel charitas. Illa enim non rem promissam apprehendit, sed quatenus futura adhuc est, expectat: haec eandem apprehensam & jam possessam amat; utraque applicatae jam & apprehensae remissionis peccatorum fructus est. Tum per solam fidem justitia Christi & satisfactio nobis imputatur, Rom. III. 22. IV. 5. Sola igitur justificat. Praeterea eo jure justificamur, quo sumus filii Dei, & membra Christi. At filii Dei & membra Christi per fidem non per opera sumus. Opera enim filii Dei & membra Christi jam facti edimus. Spirituales enim aeque ac naturales & animales operationes existentiam subjecti operantis praesupponunt. Cumque fides nostra in hac vita imperfecta sit, quia ex parte cognoscimus, I. Cor. XIII. 9. & multiplicis fidei defectus optimi quisque conscientiam habent, utique proprie, per se, vel per gratuitam acceptilationem justificare non potest. Nam quod proprie & per se justificat, universalem justitiam habere debet, qualem non habet justitia imperfecta sive ex natura sua, quia ei omnimoda cum lege Dei con-
units.tr: There are not lacking other arguments by which we show that faith justifies alone, not as a work, or properly, but as an instrument, improperly and relatively, and that it is a certain faith. For it cannot be denied that justification consists in the remission of sins, which the Gospel promises. Indeed the Tridentine fathers themselves made the remission of sins a part of justification. But there is no faculty in man capable of accepting this remission offered in the Gospel except faith. For faith alone believes God promising and offering the remission, and by believing receives it; not hope or charity. For hope does not lay hold of the promised thing but, insofar as it is still future, waits for it; charity loves it already laid hold of and possessed. Both are fruits of the remission of sins already applied and apprehended. Moreover, it is through faith alone that the righteousness and satisfaction of Christ are imputed to us, Rom. 3:22, 4:5. Therefore faith alone justifies. Furthermore, we are justified by the right by which we are sons of God and members of Christ. But we are sons of God and members of Christ through faith, not through works. For we produce the works of sons of God and members of Christ only after we have become such. For spiritual operations, just like natural and animal ones, presuppose the existence of the acting subject. And since our faith in this life is imperfect, because we know in part, 1 Cor. 13:9, and the best of men have a consciousness of the many defects of their faith, it cannot, properly and of itself, or through gratuitous acceptance, justify. For that which justifies properly and of itself must have a universal righteousness, which imperfect righteousness, by its own nature, does not have, since it lacks complete conformity with the law of God; or else it justifies through gratuitous acceptance, since

units.la: Aliis etiam argumentis justificatio ex sola fide, non ut opus, sed ut organo, confirmatur. conformitas deest; vel per gratuitam acceptationem, tum quia judicium Dei secundum veritatem est, Rom. II. 2. tum quia in gratuita justificatione Deus justitiam suam demonstrat, ibid. III. 25. 26. adeoque imperfectam justitiam pro perfecta non acceptat: tum quia nusquam in verbo suo testatur, quod fidem, ceu opus hominis, pro justitia a nobis Deo debita accipere, sed potius, quod ipse Jehova justitia nostra esse Jerem. XXIII. 6. velit, & quod nos justitia Dei in ipso simus, 2. Cor. V. 21. Denique fidem non ut opus & proprie, sed ut organon, adeoque metonymice, quatenus Christum & ejus justitiam, quae sola proprie justificat, apprehendit, justificare, multa evincunt. Velut quod fides accipit Christum, Joh. I. 12. donum justitiae, Rom. V. 17. remissionem peccatorum, Act. XXVI. 18. accipere autem instrumenti est: quod dicimur justificari ex fide, Rom. I. 17. III. 30. IX. 30. per fidem, ibid. III. 24. 25. 30. Ephes. II. 8. in fide, Gal. II. 20. fide, Rom. III. 28. quae omnia instrumenti notionem habent: quod Rom. III. 24. 25. in subordinatione causarum justificationis ad eundem effectum fides nonnisi instrumenti vice fungi possit, a qua causae principales Deus, gratia Dei, redemptio Christi, qui factus est placamentum in sanguine ejus: justitia & imputatio, quae in verbo justificandi continetur, & demonstratio justitiae Dei ad gloriam ejus distinguuntur.
units.tr: Justification by faith alone is also confirmed by other arguments, not as a work but as an instrument. ...conformity is lacking; or through gratuitous acceptance, both because the judgment of God is according to truth, Rom. 2:2, and because in gratuitous justification God demonstrates his righteousness, ibid. 3:25, 26, and so he does not accept imperfect righteousness in place of perfect; and because nowhere in his word does he testify that he accepts faith, as a human work, in place of the righteousness that we owe to God, but rather that Jehovah himself wishes to be our righteousness, Jer. 23:6, and that we are the righteousness of God in him, 2 Cor. 5:21. Finally, many things prove that faith justifies not as a work and properly, but as an instrument, and so metonymically, insofar as it lays hold of Christ and his righteousness, which alone justifies properly. For example, faith receives Christ, John 1:12; the gift of righteousness, Rom. 5:17; the remission of sins, Acts 26:18; but to receive belongs to an instrument. We are said to be justified by faith, Rom. 1:17, 3:30, 9:30; through faith, ibid. 3:24, 25, 30, Eph. 2:8; in faith, Gal. 2:20; by faith, Rom. 3:28; all of which carry the notion of an instrument. Also, Rom. 3:24, 25, in the subordination of the causes of justification to the same effect, shows that faith can only act in the place of an instrument. The principal causes are distinguished from it: God, the grace of God, the redemption of Christ, who was set forth as a propitiation in his blood; the righteousness and imputation, which are contained in the word justifying; and the demonstration of the righteousness of God to his glory.

units.la: LXXII. Particulam exclusivam Sola Scriptura non usurpat; sed ejus sensum clarissime definit.
units.tr: LXXII. The exclusive particle sola is not used by Scripture, but Scripture defines its sense most clearly.

units.la: Nam nos ει μη δια πιστεως 'Ιησου Χριστου nonnisi fide Jesu Christi, & sine operibus legis justificari diserte affirmat: Cumque inter fidem & opera immediata oppositio sit, operibus a justificationis negotio remotis sola fides relinquitur. Neque aliud medium est, quod Christo nos uniat, & ejus justitiam apprehendat, quam fides. Sola igitur justificat. Proin sensum Scripturae non literam respexit Lutherus, ubi in loco celebri, Rom. III. 28. exclusivam particulam (allein) addidit, non verbi, sed rei interpretem agens; neque id exemplo novo. Nam & Christus ipse verba Dei: Dominum Deum tuum timebis, & illi servies, Deut. VI. 13. X. 20. allegans, & sensum potius quam verba respiciens, particulam μονον addidit sic citans: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, και αυτω μονω λατρευσεις & ei soli servies, Matth. IV. 10. Cui tamen eo nomine Sathanas Sophista omnium maximus, dicam scribere ausus non est.
units.tr: For Paul plainly affirms that we are justified only through faith in Jesus Christ [ει μη δια πιστεως 'Ιησου Χριστου], and not by the works of the law. Since there is a direct opposition between faith and works, once works are removed from the business of justification, faith alone remains. Nor is there any other means that unites us to Christ and lays hold of his righteousness except faith. Faith alone therefore justifies. Luther therefore looked to the sense of Scripture and not to the letter when, in the famous passage Rom. 3:28, he added the exclusive particle "alone" (allein), acting as an interpreter of the thing and not of the word. Nor was this a new precedent. For Christ himself, quoting the words of God, You shall fear the Lord your God, and serve him, Deut. 6:13, 10:20, looked to the sense rather than the words and added the particle μονον [only], citing it thus: You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him only [και αυτω μονω λατρευσεις], Matt. 4:10. Yet Satan, the greatest of all sophists, did not dare on that account to find fault with him in writing.

units.la: Simili exemplo Veneta editio A. 1546. excusa locum Apostoli Gal. II. 16. reddidit, ma solo per la fede, hoc est, sed solummodo per fidem in Jesum Christum. Et editio Italica Francisci Virginii Bresciani A. 1551. Venetiis edita sic locum Rom. III. 28. reddidit: Non per observationem legis (ma sola per fiducia) sed per solam fiduciam in merito Christi justificari poteris. Germanica quoque Versio Scripturae Norinbergae 52. annis ante Lutheri versionem excusa particulam exclusivam (Nur) in loco Gal. II. 16. habet. Et Patres nec pauci, nec obscuri exclusiva usi sunt. Origenes Lib. IV. ad Rom. ad Cap. III. 27. sic commentatur: Dicit Apostolus, sufficere solius fidei justificationem, ita ut credens quis tantummodo justificetur, etiamsi nihil ab eo operis expletum fuerit. Hilarius Can. 8. in Matth.
units.tr: In a similar way the Venetian edition of 1546 rendered Gal. 2:16 as "but only through faith", that is, "but only through faith in Jesus Christ." The Italian edition of Francesco Virginio of Brescia, published at Venice in 1551, rendered Rom. 3:28 thus: "You can be justified not by observance of the law (but by trust alone) but by trust alone in the merit of Christ." The German version of Scripture printed at Nuremberg 52 years before Luther's version also has the exclusive particle (only) in Gal. 2:16. Nor have the Fathers, and not obscure ones either, failed to use the exclusive form. Origen, in Book IV on Romans, on Rom. 3:27, comments thus: The Apostle says that justification by faith alone is sufficient, so that a believer is justified merely by believing, even if no work has been performed by him. Hilary, on Matthew, Canon 8.

units.la: LXXIII. Ficulnea argumenta sunt, quae capitali huic de fide & impropre ceu organo & sola justificante doctrina conspirantes Pontificii, Sociniani & Remonstrantes obducunt.
units.tr: LXXIII. These are flimsy arguments, which the Papists, Socinians and Remonstrants pile up against this principal doctrine, that faith justifies improperly, as an organ and alone.

units.la: Nam quod Scriptura fidei primam motionem ad justificationem tribuat, ex Heb. XI. 6. Rom. X. 13. 14. Joh. I. 12. neutiquam Pontificii probant. Prima & ultima movet, neque remissio peccatorum tarda ejusmodi molimina & temporum discrimina admittit. Credere oportet accedentem ad Deum, Hebr. XI. 6. sed in ipso illo accessu ad Deum in Christo justificatio consistit. Fide, enim stamus, Rom. XI. 20. & per eam φρουρουμεθα custodimur ad salutem, 1. Pet. I. 5. Et fides ad invocationem nominis Dei Rom. X. 13. 14. requiritur, non ut prima motio ad justificationem, sed ut causa ad suum effectum. Quin & accipientibus Christum potestas, dignatio, jus, ut filii Dei fiant, tribuitur, Joh. I. 12. quam potestatem habentes justificati jam sunt. Aliud enim est ἐξουσία potestas, quam qui habent, jàm ex Deo nati sunt, ibid. v. 13. adeóque actu filii Dei sunt: aliud δύναμις potentia ab actu separata. Timor Domini ἀποστρέφει τὰ ἁμαρτήματα peccata depellit, Eccles. I. 27. quoad reatum in justificatione, quoad abolitionem in sanctificatione. Spe quoque salvati sumus, Rom. VIII. 24. sed non justificati. Et à dilectione Dei remissio peccatorum, Luc. VII. 47. ut à signo & πίστει indubitato eandem declarante, non ut à dispositione vel causa suspenditur.
units.tr: The Papists by no means prove from Heb. XI. 6, Rom. X. 13, 14 and John I. 12 that Scripture ascribes the first movement toward justification to faith. Faith moves both first and last, and the forgiveness of sins does not admit such delays or intervals of time. You must believe that he who comes to God, Heb. XI. 6, but justification in Christ consists in that very coming to God. By faith you stand, Rom. XI. 20, and through faith we are guarded unto salvation [φρουρούμεθα], 1 Pet. I. 5. Faith is required for calling on the name of God, Rom. X. 13, 14, not as the first movement toward justification but as the cause of its effect. Moreover, those who receive Christ are given the power, the dignity and the right to become children of God, John I. 12, and those who have this power are already justified. For the power [ἐξουσία] which they have is one thing; they are already born of God, ibid. v. 13, and so are actually children of God. Power [δύναμις] as potency, separated from act, is another thing. The fear of the Lord drives away sins [ἀποστρέφει τὰ ἁμαρτήματα], Eccles. I. 27, as to guilt in justification, and as to their removal in sanctification. We have also been saved by hope, Rom. VIII. 24, but not justified by it. And the forgiveness of sins follows from the love of God, Luke VII. 47, as from a sign and an indubitable proof of the same, not as if it hung upon love as its disposition or cause.

units.la: Quomodo etiam S. Johannes dicens: Qui non diligit fratrem, manet in morte, 1. Joh. III. 14. non charitatem vivificationis & exclusæ mortis atque damnationis causam facit, sed carentiam ejus mortui in peccatis signum declarat. Sed & resipiscere & baptizari in remissionem peccatorum Apostolus Act. II. 38. jubet, non quòd vel resipiscentia, quatenus vitæ mutationem in melius conjunctam habet, vel Baptismus ad justificationem præparet. Quomodo enim præparabit Baptismus, sigillum justitiæ fidei? Quomodo resipiscentia respectu mutationis vitæ, quæ & ipsa inhærens justitia est, & justificationem sequitur? Non igitur hæc ut causa, verùm ceu testimonium & confirmatio ac obsignatio remissionis peccatorum per Christum jam acceptæ inducuntur. Etiam ex operibus justificatum esse Abrahamum, & justificari nos Jacobus cap. II. 21. 24. dixit, quia justificatio per fidem ex operibus à posteriori declaratur & demonstratur; atque sic impletur Scriptura, dicens, fidem ad justitiam imputari, ibid. v. 23. & fides ex operibus consummatur, ibid. v. 22. quomodo gratia Dei in infirmitate hominis consummatur, id est, ut causa ab effectu demonstratur, 2. Cor. XII. 9. Quæ illa justificatio justi est, de qua mox dictum sumus. Tribus enim modis justificamur, effectivè à Deo, apprehensivè à fide, & declarativè, seu demonstrativè ab operibus. Fides verò in actu justificationis est instrumentum apprehendens & applicans Christum & bona ejus, in persona initium virtutum: in affectu janua & vita ad novam obedientiam & gloriam. Parum etiam constat, quòd fidem non apprehendendo, sed impetrando & promerendo justitiam justificare pronuntiant; ut ita fidei in justificatione tribuatur, quod negatur operibus, quæ non justificant, id est, justitiam non promerentur. Cùm enim fides nec tempore, nec natura, ceu opus justitiam præcedat, eam impetrare & promereri non potest. Sola Christi justitia absolutionem à peccatis & jus vitæ promeruit. Neque S. Paulus fidei tribuit, quod operibus negat. Negat nos operibus quovis modo justificari. At fidem quovis modo, adeóque etiam promerendo justificare non docet. Præterea non si sola fides justificat, etiam sola salvat; quia ex ordinatione Dei plus ad salutem, quàm ad justificationem requiritur. Et sola licet justificet, non tamen solitaria, & à sanctificante virtute separata justificat. Exclusiva enim illa sola ad prædicatum potiùs quàm ad subjectum referenda est. Non enim quæritur quæ virtutes quibus cohabitent, sed quid cuique proprium sit. Aliud causa justificationis, aliud qualitas justificati est. Est quoque fides justificans viva, formata, efficax. Sed vita,
units.tr: So too when St John says, He who does not love his brother abides in death, 1 John III. 14, he does not make love the cause of life and the exclusion of death and condemnation; he declares that the lack of it is a sign of one dead in sins. Likewise the Apostle in Acts II. 38 bids us repent and be baptized for the remission of sins, not because repentance, insofar as it carries with it a change of life for the better, or baptism prepares us for justification. For how would baptism, the seal of the righteousness of faith, prepare for it? How would repentance, with respect to the change of life, which is itself inherent righteousness, follow justification? These things are therefore introduced not as causes but as the testimony, confirmation and sealing of the forgiveness of sins already received through Christ. Likewise James, ch. II. 21, 24, said that Abraham was justified by works and that we are justified by works, because justification by faith is declared and demonstrated from works a posteriori; and so the Scripture is fulfilled which says that faith was imputed to him for righteousness, ibid. v. 23, and faith is made perfect by works, ibid. v. 22, just as the grace of God is made perfect in the weakness of man, 2 Cor. XII. 9, that is, the cause is shown from its effect. That justification of the righteous is the one of which we spoke a little while ago. For we are justified in three ways: effectively by God, apprehensively by faith, and declaratively, or demonstratively, by works. Faith, however, in the act of justification is the instrument that apprehends and applies Christ and his benefits; in the person it is the beginning of the virtues; in its affection it is the gate and the life of new obedience and glory. It is also little established when they declare that faith justifies not by apprehending but by obtaining and meriting righteousness. In this way faith would be credited with what is denied to works, which do not justify, that is, do not merit righteousness. For since faith precedes righteousness neither in time nor in nature, as a work does, it cannot obtain or merit it. Christ's righteatousness alone has merited absolution from sins and the right to life. Nor does St Paul ascribe to faith what he denies to works. He denies that we are justified by works in any way, but he does not teach that faith justifies in any way, even by merit. Moreover, if faith alone justifies, it does not follow that it alone saves, since by God's ordinance more is required for salvation than for justification. And although faith alone justifies, it does not justify alone, separated from the sanctifying virtue. For that exclusive alone is to be referred to the predicate rather than to the subject. For the question is not which virtues dwell together, but what is proper to each. The cause of justification is one thing; the quality of the justified person is another. Justifying faith is also living, formed and effective. But its life,

units.la: forma & efficacia ejus, qua justificat, non justitia, charitas, vel ullum opus hominis est, quia hæc omnia fidei in justificationis negotio opponuntur, & extra illud fides, spes & charitas ut distinctæ virtutes in Scripturis proponuntur, sed fiducialis apprehensio est, quod pluribus supra demonstravimus. Nam & ipsi Sophistæ fidem in solo intellectu collocantes rationem reddere non possunt, quomodo quod in intellectu, non in voluntate est, pro forma & vita sua charitatem habere possit. Efficax tamen per charitatem est, quatenus per eam, ceu effectum, non justificando, sed renovando & sanctificando operatur.
units.tr: form and efficacy, by which it justifies, is not righteousness, love or any work of man, because all these are set over against faith in the business of justification; and apart from that business, faith, hope and love are set forth in Scripture as distinct virtues. Rather, it is a fiducial apprehension, as we have shown at greater length above. For even the Sophists, who place faith in the intellect alone, cannot give a reason how what is in the intellect and not in the will could have love as its form and life. Yet faith is effective through love, insofar as it works through love, as through an effect, not by justifying but by renewing and sanctifying.

units.la: LXXIV. Illud quoque Remonstrantium telum, quòd satisfactio Christi efficiat, ut fides nostra nobis in justitiam imputetur, adeóque non relativè, ut organon, sed inhærenter; quia actus credendi per meritum Christi gratiosa apud Deum acceptilatio fit, justificet; non semel hebetavimus. Satisfactio certè Christi justitiam partis offensæ, non fidem rei spectavit. Non enim fidei nostræ; sed Deo Christus satisfecit. Nam quòd iidem ulterius ratiocinantur; quòd habitui animi non tribuatur πιστὸν seu affectus sui objecti; sicut quia scientia mea apprehendit triangulum habere tres angulos æquales duobus rectis, non recte infertur. Ergo scientia mea habet tres angulos æquales duobus rectis; & pariter fidei, quæ habitus est, objecti sui, satisfactionis Christi, πιστὸν affectus, seu effectus, qui justificatio est, non recte sic attribuatur, ut dici possit, nos sola fide justificari, perperam plane instituunt. Justificatio enim fidei attribuitur non proprie, sed metaleptice, quatenus objecti actus propter arctam connexionem inter illum & habitum, usitata Scripturæ phrasi in habitum transfertur. Ita spe salvati sumus, Rom. VIII. 24. Ubi salus, quæ objecti est, habitui tribuitur. Et ὁ ἴδιος ἰησοῦς, Amor meus crucifixus est, inquiebat Ignatius, hoc est, ille, quem amo, & semper amaturus sum. Porro Scriptura fidem nobis imputari ad justitiam passim, velut Gen. XV. 6. Rom. IV. 3. 5. 9. 23. 24. dicitur. At imputari eam ut opus, & proprie, nusquam dicit. Imò contrarium innuit, asserens, fidem imputari sine operibus, & fidem nobis ad justitiam imputari, dum justitia nobis imputatur per fidem, prout Apostolus ibid. IV. 5. 6. & III. 22. rem istam æquipollenter declarat. Neque enim effectum causæ principalis adscribi instrumentali primò, proprie, aut per se, terminis citra ambiguitatem intellectis, hoc est, ita ut virtuti ejus, dignitati vel merito, sive proprie, sive per acceptulationem tribuatur, adscribi potest. Denique quæ de subordinatione imputationis fidei ad justitiam, quæ proprie sic dicitur, & imputationis justitiæ, quæ Christi dicitur, secundum quam fides obedientiam Christi apprehendens immediatè & formaliter, at justitia & meritum Christi mediante & efficiente imputatione fidei imputetur iidem Remonstrantes fingunt, aliena & ἄτοπα plane sunt. Nam & fidem proprie ad justitiam imputari, supponunt, non probant: & modos subordinatæ imputationis commi-niscuntur tum novos, tum contrarios, quia fidem cùm opus faciant, nullum opus satisfactioni & merito Christi subordinari potest, tum plane ἀνυπότακτος. Etenim si fides ad justitiam imputatur, quatenus Christi justitiam apprehendit, utique improprie & instrumentaliter tantum imputatur: proprie autem Christi justitia & meritum imputatur.
units.tr: LXXIV. That weapon of the Remonstrants too, namely that the satisfaction of Christ brings it about that our faith is imputed to us for righteousness, and so is not relative, as an instrument, but inherent, because the act of believing becomes a gracious acceptance before God through the merit of Christ and so justifies, we have blunted more than once. The satisfaction of Christ looked to the righteousness of the offended party, not to the faith of the offender. For Christ satisfied God, not our faith. As for their further reasoning, that the habit of the mind is not credited with the πιστὸν [object of faith] or affection of its object, the inference is not sound: just as it does not follow that because my knowledge apprehends that a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, my knowledge has three angles equal to two right angles. In the same way they are utterly mistaken when they argue that faith, which is a habit, does not rightly have attributed to it the πιστὸν [faith's object] or affection of its object, that is, the satisfaction of Christ, or its effect, which is justification, so that it could be said that we are justified by faith alone. For justification is attributed to faith not properly but metaleptically: because of the close connection between the act of the object and the habit, Scripture's customary phrasing transfers the act to the habit. Thus we have been saved by hope, Rom. 8:24, where salvation, which belongs to the object, is attributed to the habit. And My love is crucified, said Ignatius [ὁ ἴδιος ἰησοῦς], that is, he whom I love, and whom I shall always love. Further, Scripture everywhere says that faith is imputed to us for righteousness, as in Gen. 15:6, Rom. 4:3, 5, 9, 23, 24. But nowhere does it say that faith is imputed as a work, and properly so. On the contrary, it implies the opposite, asserting that faith is imputed without works and that faith is imputed to us for righteousness, while righteousness is imputed to us through faith, as the Apostle declares the same thing equivalently in Rom. 4:5, 6 and 3:22. For, with the terms understood without ambiguity, the effect of the principal cause cannot be ascribed to the instrument primarily, properly, or in itself, in such a way that it is attributed to its power, dignity or merit, whether properly or through acceptation. Finally, what these same Remonstrants invent about the subordination of the imputation of faith to righteousness, which is properly so called, and the imputation of righteousness, which is called Christ's, according to which faith, apprehending the obedience of Christ immediately and formally, but the righteousness and merit of Christ are imputed mediately and effectively through the imputation of faith, is wholly alien and absurd. For they assume that faith is imputed properly to righteousness; they do not prove it. And they devise modes of subordinate imputation that are both new and contrary: since they make faith a work, no work can be subordinated to the satisfaction and merit of Christ, and faith is wholly unsubordinated [ἀνυπότακτος]. For if faith is imputed to righteousness insofar as it apprehends the righteousness of Christ, then it is imputed only improperly and instrumentally; but properly it is the righteousness and merit of Christ that is imputed.

units.la: LXXV. Finis justificationis supremus est πάντων δόξης laus gloriae gratia, Ephes. I. 6. seu gloria & agnitio Dei & virtutum ejus, cujusmodi inprimis misericordia & justitia sunt. Nam qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, 1. Cor. I. 31. & quidem partim in demonstratione justitiae, quatenus Christum propositum, ut esset placamentum pro nobis, ad demonstrationem justitiae, Rom. III. 25. Omnes enim peccarunt, & ὑστεροῦνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ indigent gloria Dei, seu praevertuntur a gloria Dei, dum nempe is impium gratis justificat, ibid. v. 23. Omnis qui vocatur in nomine meo (qui nominat nomen meum, Joel. II. 32.) ad gloriam meam creavi eum, & formavi eum, & feci eum, Esaj. XLIII. 7. Haec Jehovae gloriatio, qua se supra omnem sapientiam & cogitationem humanam, & gloriationem Deorum omnium extollit, est, quod ipse impium justificat, Rom. IV. 5. Quam gloriam & gloriationem suam non potest dare alteri, Esaj. XLII. 8. & in Vocatione justi servi sui cum justitia ponit, & eodem omne opus gratiae suum revocat, ibid. XLVIII. 11. Qui sacrificat confessionem (confitetur Sacerdotem Christum, & sacrificium ejus, quo mediante Deus foedus nobiscum facit) is me glorificat, & munit viam, qua ipsum faciam videre salutem Dei, Psal. L. 23. Post summum hunc finem subordinatus salus electorum, & eorundem firmissima in vita & morte consolatio est. Quos justificavit, eos glorificavit, Rom. VIII. 30. Gratia salvati estis, Ephes. II. 8. Justificati per fidem habemus pacem apud Deum, per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, &c. Rom. V. 1. Quis accusabit electos Dei? Deus est, qui justificat. Quis condemnans? Christus ille, qui mortuus est, magis etiam, qui resuscitatus est, ibid. VIII. 33. 34.
units.tr: LXXV. The supreme end of justification is the praise of the glory of grace [ἔπαινον δόξης τῆς χάριτος], Ephes. I. 6, or the glory and acknowledgment of God and of his virtues, chief among which are mercy and justice. For he who glories, let him glory in the Lord, 1. Cor. I. 31. This is so partly in the demonstration of justice, in that God set forth Christ to be a propitiation for us, for the demonstration of his justice, Rom. III. 25. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God [ὑστεροῦνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ], that is, they lack the glory of God, or are cut off from it, since God freely justifies the ungodly, ibid. v. 23. Everyone who is called by my name (who names my name, Joel. II. 32) I created for my glory, I formed him and I made him, Esaj. XLIII. 7. This boast of Jehovah, by which he exalts himself above all human wisdom and thought, and above the glorying of all gods, is that he justifies the ungodly, Rom. IV. 5. He cannot give this glory and boasting of his to another, Esaj. XLII. 8. In calling his righteous servant he places it together with righteousness, and by the same act he recalls every work of grace to himself, ibid. XLVIII. 11. He who offers the sacrifice of confession (who confesses the priest Christ and his sacrifice, through whose mediation God makes covenant with us) glorifies me, and prepares the way by which I may show him the salvation of God, Psal. L. 23. Subordinate to this highest end is the salvation of the elect, and their most firm consolation in life and death. Whom he justified, them he also glorified, Rom. VIII. 30. By grace you are saved, Ephes. II. 8. Being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc., Rom. V. 1. Who will accuse God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is the one who condemns? Christ, who died, or rather who was raised, ibid. VIII. 33, 34.

units.la: LXXVI. Justificatio una specie in omnibus, & una numero in singulis est. Una specie in omnibus, quia justificationis τὰ κύρια seu principales causae apud omnes electos omni tempore eaedem sunt. Deus enim omnes credentes gratis, gratia, per redemptionem Christi, ejusdemque justitiae imputationem per solam fidem justificat. Per gratiam Domini Jesu Christi credimus salvari (nos) sicut & illi, Act. XV. 11. Quandoquidem unus Deus, qui justificabit circumcisionem ex fide, & praeputium per fidem, Rom. III. 30. Per fidem justificati inducuntur Abrahamus, Pater credentium, Genes. XV. 6. Rom. IV. 2. 3. David, ibid. v. 6. 7. Sancti illi, qui commemorantur, Hebr. XI. qui per fidem Deo placuerunt, vers. 6. testimonium justitiae obtinuerunt, v. 4. ejus, quae ex fide est, justitiae haeredes facti sunt, v. 7. Nec dissimile aliter justificati in V. vel N. T. exemplum occurrit. Una numero in singulis, quia justificatio est actus indivisus, perfectam omnium peccatorum remissionem credenti simul semelque eo tempore, quo primum homo vocatur, adferens, & nullo unquam tempore revocatur. Nam sanguis Christi applicatus a Deo, & fide apprehensus, purgat nos ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. I. 7. nihil in nobis condemnationis relinquit, Rom. VIII. 1. Deo nos plene reconciliat, ibid. V. 9. 10. eoque pacem & tranquillitatem conscientiae nobis adfert, ibid. v. 1. quae affulgere nequit vel unico retento peccato, utpote cujus stipendium maledictio, Deut. XXVII. 26. & mors est, Rom. VI. 23. Sicut etiam David beatos praedicat, quorum iniquitates remissae sunt, Psal. XXXII. 1. Ita Christus fide servatos pronuntiat, quibus peccata remiserat, Matth. IX. 2. Luc. VII. 48. 50. Praeterea Deus remissionem peccatorum semel donatam nunquam revocat, propter justitiae & promissionis suae juramento confirmatae immutabilitatem, Heb. VI. 17. 18. Remissio enim peccatorum est donum justitiae, Rom. V. 17. idque electis proprium, ibid. VIII. 32. 33. Atqui dona Dei, quae electis singulariter conferuntur, & vocatio secundum propositum, sunt sine poenitentia, ibid. XI. 29. Atque Prophetica haec de re phraseologia confirmat. Deleo, ut densam nubem, defectiones tuas, & velut nubem, peccata tua, Esaj. XLIV. 22. Abjecisti post tergum tuum omnia peccata mea, ibid. XXXVIII. 17. Propitiabor iniquitati eorum, & peccati eorum non recordabor amplius, Jerem. XXXI. 34. Abjecturus es in profundissimum maris omnia peccata istorum, Mich. VII. 19.
units.tr: LXXVI. Justification is one in kind in all, and one in number in each individual. It is one in kind in all because its chief causes [τὰ κύρια], or principal causes, are the same for all the elect at all times. For God justifies all believers freely, by grace, through the redemption of Christ and the imputation of his righteousness, by faith alone. We believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, just as they are, Act. XV. 11. Since there is one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith, Rom. III. 30. Abraham, the father of believers, is brought forward as one justified by faith, Gen. XV. 6; Rom. IV. 2, 3. So too is David, ibid. v. 6, 7. Those saints who are commemorated in Heb. XI., who pleased God through faith, vers. 6, obtained testimony of righteousness, v. 4, and became heirs of the righteousness which is by faith, v. 7. Nor does any example of justified persons in the Old or New Testament differ from this. It is one in number in each individual because justification is an undivided act, bringing to the believer the complete remission of all sins at once, at the same moment in which the man is first called, and it is never revoked at any time. For the blood of Christ, applied by God and apprehended by faith, cleanses us from all sin, 1. Joh. I. 7; it leaves no condemnation in us, Rom. VIII. 1; it fully reconciles us to God, ibid. V. 9, 10; and so it brings peace and tranquillity of conscience to us, ibid. v. 1. This peace cannot shine forth even if a single sin is retained, since the wages of sin is a curse, Deut. XXVII. 26, and death, Rom. VI. 23. So David also pronounces blessed those whose iniquities are forgiven, Psal. XXXII. 1. Likewise Christ pronounces saved by faith those to whom he had remitted their sins, Matth. IX. 2; Luc. VII. 48, 50. Moreover, God never revokes a remission of sins once granted, on account of the immutability of his justice and promise, confirmed by an oath, Heb. VI. 17, 18. For the remission of sins is the gift of righteousness, Rom. V. 17, and this belongs to the elect, ibid. VIII. 32, 33. But the gifts of God, which are bestowed singularly on the elect, and the calling according to his purpose, are without repentance, ibid. XI. 29. The prophetic phraseology on this matter confirms it: I blot out your transgressions like a thick cloud, and your sins like a cloud, Esaj. XLIV. 22; you have cast all my sins behind your back, ibid. XXXVIII. 17; I will be merciful to their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more, Jerem. XXXI. 34; you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea, Mich. VII. 19.

units.la: LXXVII. Nugantur ergo Pontificii, qui justificationis primae & secundae, superius discussae commento unum illum & indivisum justificationis actum incidunt. Quibus neutiquam verba illa Angeli: Qui justus est, justificetur έτι amplius Apoc. XXII. 11. patrocinantur, quia iis verbis non justificatio peccatoris, de qua in praesentiarum nobis sermo est, sed justificatio peccatoris & justi, de qua mox dictum fumus, dilinguitur. Qui semel simulque per fidem justificatus, & a peccato absolutus est, is amplius justificari, id est, justificationem suam per fidem semel peractam operibus declarare, demonstrare & manifestare debet. Eadem opera & illa ruunt, quae iidem de revivescentia peccatorum semel remissorum fabulantur: discorde tamen de revivescentiae illius modo sententia, uti apud Becanum de Sacram. cap. 33. q. 1. legere est. Fermentum quoddam illa etiam Orthodoxorum quorundam sententia habet, qui remissionem peccatorum semel factam irritam fieri posse docent. Aliud longe argumenta supra allata evincunt; inprimis promissio foederalis, quod Deus peccatorum nostrorum non velit recordari amplius, Jerem. XXXI. 34. Quae non habet conditionem illam tacitam, si non iterum peccemus. Plane enim irrita alias promissio erit, quia nemo certus est, se non peccaturum iterum; & de omnibus peccatis, adeoque etiam futuris, promissio loquitur. Filioli mei, haec scribo vobis, ne peccetis. Et si quis peccaverit, Paracletum habemus apud Patrem, Jesum Christum justum, 1. Joh. II. 1. Cum remissione peccatorum glorificatio individuo nexu cohaeret. Quos justificavit, eos glorificavit, Rom. VIII. 30. In quibus vero remissionem peccatorum irritam fieri statuunt? In electis, an in reprobis? Atqui electi asseququntur, ibid. XI. 7. Semen Dei in illis manet, 1. Joh. III. 9. Obsignati sunt Spiritu redemptionis, Ephes. IV. 30. Custodiuntur virtute Dei per fidem ad salutem, 1. Pet. I. 5. Reprobis vero peccata nunquam remittuntur, quia fidem, quae electorum est, Tit. I. 1. & qua sola homo justificatur, nunquam habent. Frustra illi parabolam Christi, in qua creditor ille, qui cum Deo peccata remittente comparatur, servum crudelem & ingratum, cui prius debita condonaverat, revocata sententia tortoribus tradidit, Matth. XVIII. 27. &c. objiciunt. Non enim omnes ejus parabolae particulae, & circumstantiae, sed solus scopus applicari Deo creditori debet. Scopus autem est suadere, condonandas esse fraternas offensas iis, qui sua peccata a Deo remitti cupiunt. Ita, inquit Christus in ἐπιμνήσω, Pater meus caelestis faciet vobis, nisi remiseritis suo quisque fratri ex cordibus vestris offensas eorum, v. 35. Unde male infertur, Deum peccata semel remissa iterum imputare velle, cum id solum intenderit, eos, qui fratribus offensas non remiserint, crudelis servi exemplo gravissimas poenas daturos. Id vero fieri poterit, licet peccata semel dimissa non imputentur.
units.tr: LXXVII. The Papists therefore trifle when, by the invention of a first and a second justification, which we discussed above, they break up that one and undivided act of justification. The words of the angel, He who is righteous, let him be justified still more, Apoc. XXII. 11 [ἔτι], do not support them at all, because by these words the justification of the sinner, which is what we are now discussing, is not distinguished from the justification of the sinner and of the righteous, which we have just mentioned. He who has been justified once and at the same time by faith, and absolved from sin, must be justified still more, that is, he must declare, demonstrate and manifest his justification, once accomplished through faith, by works. The same reasoning also overthrows what these men tell about the revival of sins once remitted, although their opinions on the manner of this revival disagree, as may be read in Becanus, de Sacram. cap. 33, q. 1. Some Orthodox writers also hold this opinion, which has a certain leaven in it, teaching that a remission of sins once made can be made void. The arguments adduced above prove quite otherwise, above all the covenant promise that God will not wish to remember our sins any more, Jerem. XXXI. 34. This promise has no tacit condition, if we do not sin again. Otherwise the promise would clearly be empty, since no one is certain that he will not sin again, and the promise speaks of all sins, and therefore also of future ones. My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. And if anyone sins, we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, 1. Joh. II. 1.
