Glorification is bound inseparably to the remission of sins: Whom he justified, them he also glorified, Rom. VIII. 30. But in whom do they assert that the remission of sins is made void? In the elect, or in the reprobate? Yet the elect obtain it, ibid. XI. 7; the seed of God remains in them, 1. Joh. III. 9; they are sealed with the Spirit of redemption, Ephes. IV. 30; they are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, 1. Pet. I. 5. But sins are never remitted to the reprobate, because they never have the faith which belongs to the elect, Tit. I. 1, and by which alone a man is justified. They vainly object to the parable of Christ, in which the creditor, who is compared with God remitting sins, after forgiving the debts of a cruel and ungrateful servant, revoked his sentence and handed him over to the torturers, Matth. XVIII. 27, etc. For not all the particulars and circumstances of that parable, but only its scope, must be applied to God the creditor. The scope is to persuade that the offences of brothers must be forgiven by those who wish their own sins to be remitted by God. So, says Christ in the conclusion, my heavenly Father will do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother his offences from your hearts, v. 35. Hence it is wrongly inferred that God wishes to impute again sins once remitted, since he intended only to show that those who do not forgive their brothers' offences will receive the most severe punishments, after the example of the cruel servant. This can happen even though sins once dismissed are not imputed.

units.la: LXXVIII. Sed justificatio licet in se actus indivisus, tamen ratione sensus acceptionis remissionis peccatorum, divisus & imperfectus est.
units.tr: LXXVIII. But justification, although in itself an undivided act, is nevertheless divided and imperfect when considered as the sense of the reception of the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: Nam justificatio duobus modis consideratur, tum quatenus est amor & judicium Dei de iis, quos per fidem in Christo existentes ἐνεχόντι invenit, Phil. III. 9. a peccato absolvit, & jure petendi vitam donat: tum quatenus est amoris & judicii illius Divini declaratio & sententia, qua ad animam & velut cor credentis pronunciata ipsi cognoscitur, & apud se sentiunt, quod a Deo in Christo Mediatore ut justi amentur, & haeredes vitae scribantur. Priore modo justificatio activa, posteriore passiva appellari solet. Nemo enim justificatur, quin a Deo ametur velut justus, & simul a Deo consolationem accipiat, quod sibi vita aeterna pro haereditate addicta sit, quodque jus eam speranti & petendi habeat.
units.tr: For justification is considered in two ways: first, as God's love and judgment concerning those whom He finds existing in Christ through faith [ἐνεχόντι], Phil. 3:9, by which He absolves them from sin and grants them a right to life by claim; and second, as the declaration and sentence of that Divine love and judgment, which is pronounced to the soul and, as it were, to the heart of the believer, so that he perceives it and feels within himself that he is loved by God as righteous in Christ the Mediator, and is enrolled as an heir of life. In the first way justification is usually called active, in the second passive. For no one is justified without being loved by God as righteous, and at the same time receiving from God the comfort that eternal life has been assigned to him as his inheritance, and that he has a right to claim it in hope.

units.la: LXXIX. Activa justificatio omnium fidelium justificatorum aequalis & plane indivisa, perfecta, & velut ὁν ἀπλῶ posita indivisibili est, nullamque omnino ante & post Christum justificatorum differentiam recipit.
units.tr: LXXIX. Active justification is equal for all justified believers, altogether undivided, perfect, and, as it were, set down as one indivisible thing, and it admits no difference at all between those justified before Christ and those after Him.

units.la: Neque illa proprie ab aeterno peragitur, quia Deus decretum justificandi aeternum non ante fidem exequitur, sed in tempore, partim in Coelo, post absolutas in cruce passiones Christi, quando Christus, Advocatus noster, Angelus ille unus ex mille, dicens: Redime ipsum, ne descendat in foveam; Lytrum inveni, Job. XXXIII. 23. 24. causam nostram agit, & Pater nos absolvit; partim in conscientia nostra, simul atque credimus in Christum, & sententia absolutionis velut ad fidem nostram pronuntiatur. Quis intentabit crimina adversus electos Dei? Deus est, qui justificat, Rom. VIII. 33. Passiva inaequalis, imperfecta, divisa, varia & differens est: tum respectu justificatorum Veteris & Novi Testamenti, uti Loc. XX. 42. ostendimus: tum respectu justificatorum singulorum. Consistit enim in sententiae pronuntiatae sensu, gustu & ob acceptam absolutionem gaudio; atque praecipue actu fidei consequente & consolatorio, quem supra fusius expositum, obsignante Spiritu S. absolvitur. In quo etiam credentes obsignati estis Spiritu promissionis Sancto, Ephes. I. 13. Licet enim justificatio activa & passiva quoad actum formaliter justificatorium tempore simul existant: tamen quoad animae sensum & consola-
units.tr: Nor is it properly carried out from eternity, since God does not execute His eternal decree of justifying before faith, but in time: partly in heaven, after Christ's sufferings on the cross have been completed, when Christ, our Advocate, that one angel out of a thousand, saying, "Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom," Job 33:23, 24, pleads our cause, and the Father absolves us; and partly in our conscience, as soon as we believe in Christ and the sentence of absolution is pronounced, as it were, to our faith. "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God that justifieth," Rom. 8:33. Passive justification is unequal, imperfect, divided, varied and differing: both with respect to the justified of the Old and New Testaments, as we showed in Locus 20, section 42, and with respect to individual justified persons. For it consists in the perception of the pronounced sentence, in the taste of it, and in the joy arising from the absolution received; and above all it is effected by the consequent and consoling act of faith, which we have set out more fully above, the Holy Spirit sealing it. "In whom also, after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that Holy Spirit of promise," Eph. 1:13. For although active and passive justification, as to the act that is formally justifying, exist at the same time, yet as to the sense and comfort of the soul,

units.la: tionem, praecipue autem actum fidei reflexum & ultimum, nec non penetrabilem illam animae dulcedinem ex justificatione ortam, posterior priorem longo saepe intervallo demum subsequitur, & haud raro inciditur atque interrumpitur. In peccatis enim gravioribus contra conscientiam; in tentationibus item difficilioribus aliquando non sentitur gratia Dei propitii, quae tamen vincente Spiritu, redit & innovatur, uti exempla Sanctorum idem faciunt. Atque eandem ob causam etiam imperfecta est. Quia enim sensus ille ex fide est, fides autem imperfecta est, in aliis magis, in aliis minus, prout Deus certam ejus mensuram singulis admetitur, Rom. XII. 3. fit, ut ipse quoque sensus plus minusve imperfectus sit, usque adeo, ut nullus unquam fuerit fidelis; ne Abrahamo quidem, Genes. XVII. 17. & Davide Psal. XLII. 6. 12. exceptis, cui non cum dubitatione de promissione gratiae luctandum fuerit. Unde credentes fide jam justificati, peccatorum suorum tum praeteritorum, ibid. XXV. 7. tum futurorum, Matth. VI. 12. remissionem quotidie, petere jubentur; nimirum ut magis magisque per Spiritum adoptionis, qui testatur Spiritui nostro, nos esse filios Dei, Rom. VIII. 16. de illorum remissione confirmentur, & pacata contra Sathanae criminationes conscientia fruantur.
units.tr: and especially the reflex and final act of faith, and that inward sweetness of the soul arising from justification, the latter often follows the former only after a long interval, and quite frequently it is interrupted and broken off. For in graver sins against conscience, and also in more difficult temptations, at times the grace of the propitious God is not felt; yet, with the Spirit prevailing, it returns and is renewed, as the examples of the saints likewise show. And for the same reason it is also imperfect. For since that sense arises from faith, and faith is imperfect, in some more and in others less, as God allots to each a certain measure of it, Rom. 12:3, it follows that this sense itself is more or less imperfect, to such an extent that no believer has ever been without it, not even Abraham, Gen. 17:17, or David, Ps. 42:6, 12, who had to struggle with doubt about the promise of grace. Hence believers, already justified by faith, are commanded to seek daily the remission of their sins, both past, Ps. 25:7, and future, Matt. 6:12; namely, so that they may be more and more confirmed concerning their remission by the Spirit of adoption, who testifies to our spirit that we are children of God, Rom. 8:16, and may enjoy a conscience at peace against the accusations of Satan.

units.la: LXXX. Fuit justificatio Peccatoris. Est & alterius generis justificatio; ejus videlicet, qui per fidem jam justus & justificatus est. Est autem justificatio illa justi demonstratio seu declaratio justitiae fidei acceptae, qua homo per fidem justificatus eandem justitiam fidei acceptam, adeoque ipsam fidei sinceritatem per opera demonstrans coram Deo, in conscientia & coram hominibus vere per fidem justificatus, vere fidelis, non hypocrita, sed integer & coram Deo ambulans declaratur & pronuntiatur. De qua passim Scriptura loquitur. Si Abraham ex operibus justificatus est, habet gloriationem, sed non ad Deum, Rom. IV. 2. Abraham Pater noster ex operibus justificatus est, offerens Isacum filium suum super altare. Vides, quod fides cooperata sit operibus, & ex operibus fides consummata sit, & impleta sit Scriptura, quae dicit: Credidit autem Abraham Deo, & imputatum est ei ad justitiam, & amicus Dei vocatus est. Videtis igitur, quod ex operibus justificetur homo, & non ex fide tantum, Jac. II. 21–24. Qui justus est, justificetur amplius, Apoc. XXII. 11. Qui mortuus est, justificatus est a peccato, Rom. VI. 7. Peccatoris justificatio est a priori ex causis: justificatio justi a posteriori, ex signis & effectibus illustribus. Illa peccatoris, haec justi est. Illa a causis ad effecta descendit: haec ab effectis ad causam ascendit. Illa accusationi Sathanae de violata lege operum per peccatum: haec ejusdem criminationi de violata per hypocrisin & infidelitatem conditione Evangelii opponitur. Illa causam imputationis justitiae: haec impletionem verbi de justificatione fidei facta, hoc est, stabilitionem & confirmationem ejus in cordibus nostris explicat. De illa potissimum S. Paulus Epistola ad Romanos: de hoc S. Jacobus Epistola sua Catholica agit. Conveniunt tamen hactenus, quod in utraque vox δικαιοῦν justificare sensum forensem, non faciendi, sed declarandi & pronuntiandi justum habet. Et in eadem pulchra ἀνδρικά est, dum pro diverso loquenloquentium scopo modo peccatoris, modo justi seu justificati absolutionem : modo donationem justitiæ Christi, modo ejusdem donatæ declarationem & demonstrationem multiplicem significat.
units.tr: LXXX. There is a justification of the sinner. There is also another kind of justification, namely that of one who is already righteous and justified through faith. This justification is the demonstration or declaration of the righteousness of accepted faith, by which a man justified through faith, demonstrating before God, in conscience and before men, that same accepted righteousness of faith, and thus the very sincerity of his faith, by works, is declared and pronounced truly justified through faith, truly a believer, not a hypocrite, but upright and walking before God. Scripture speaks of this everywhere. "If Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God," Rom. 4:2. "Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar? Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect? And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God. Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only," Jas. 2:21–24. "He that is righteous, let him be righteous still," Rev. 22:11. "He that is dead is freed from sin," Rom. 6:7. The justification of the sinner proceeds a priori from causes; the justification of the righteous proceeds a posteriori, from signs and conspicuous effects. The former is of the sinner, the latter of the righteous. The former descends from causes to effects; the latter ascends from effects to the cause. The former is opposed to Satan's accusation of the violated law of works through sin; the latter to his charge of violating the condition of the Gospel through hypocrisy and unbelief. The former explains the cause of the imputation of righteousness; the latter explains the fulfilment of the word concerning justification by faith, that is, its establishment and confirmation in our hearts. St. Paul treats chiefly of the former in his Epistle to the Romans; St. James treats of the latter in his Catholic Epistle. They agree thus far, however, that in both passages the word δικαιοῦν [dikaioun, to justify] has a forensic sense: it means to pronounce just, not to make just, but to declare and pronounce righteous. And in the same word there is a fine ambiguity, since, according to the differing aim of the speakers, it signifies now the absolution of the sinner, now the absolution of the righteous or justified person, now the bestowal of the righteousness of Christ, and now the many-sided declaration and demonstration of that bestowed righteousness.

units.la: LXXXI. Distinctam verò illam justificationem peccatoris & justi tum nexus utriusque, tum duplex Dei, cui homo subest judicium ; tum duplex, à qua justificatus absolvitur, condemnatio : tum duplex Sathanæ accusatio : tum duplex tribunal: postulat & illustrat. Nexus justificationis utriusque, quia qui peccatores fide justificati à peccato absoluti, & justi reputati sunt, iidem δικαιοῦσθαι ἐν justificari amplius, vel potiùs iterum, Apoc. XXII. 11. hoc est, ex conspicuis signis & lætis floribus atque fructibus fidei justificantis, fidem demonstrare, & demonstrantes per ἀνυπηξίλον fidem justificati pronuntiari & declarari debent.
units.tr: LXXXI. We distinguish that justification of the sinner and that of the righteous, both by the connection between them and by the twofold judgment of God to which man is subject; by the twofold condemnation from which the justified person is absolved; by the twofold accusation of Satan; and by the twofold tribunal. The connection between the two justifications is this: those who as sinners have been justified by faith, absolved from sin and reckoned righteous, are the same who must be justified further, or rather again, Rev. 22:11, that is, by the conspicuous signs and joyful flowers and fruits of justifying faith; they must demonstrate their faith, and being demonstrated, they must be pronounced and declared justified through a faith without hypocrisy.

units.la: Ne quid dicam de justificationis per fidem, & sanctimoniæ necessaria copulatione, & indissolubili vinculo, partim ob decretum Dei, partim ob necessariam affectionem fidei, per quam impossibile est, ut homo dilectionem Dei Patris & Filii, hujusque satisfactionem & meritum gratuitò pollideat, nisi Dei amore, mutua dilectione & charitate in proximum incalescat, & ad calcanda Christi vestigia incitetur. Nam fides corda purificat, Act. XV. 9. Qui ergo à priori per fidem justificati sunt, iidem a posteriori etiam ex operibus justificari, hoc est, fidem ex operibus demonstrantes verè per fidem ἀνυπηξίλον justificati declarari & pronuntiari debent. Duplex Dei, cui homo subest, judicium id ipsum postulat. Sicut enim homo salvandus consideratur sub duplici ἐκλογή, vel ut peccator, vel ut conversus & vocatus in statu gratiæ : ita etiam duplex juxta duplicem illum statum judicium ; unum rigidum & exactum Dei, qua judicis, ex lege ; alterum mitius & benignius ejusdem, velut indulgentis Patris, ex Evangelio instituitur. Priori justificatio peccatoris, propter unicam Christi obedientiam, sine ulla ἀνυπηξίλον & acceptilatione : posteriori justificatio justi respondet.
units.tr: Not to mention the necessary joining and indissoluble bond of justification through faith with holiness, partly by the decree of God, partly by the necessary affection of faith, through which it is impossible for a man to possess freely the love of God the Father and the Son, and their satisfaction and merit, unless he glows with love of God, mutual affection and charity toward his neighbour, and is stirred to tread in the footsteps of Christ. For faith purifies the hearts, Acts 15:9. Therefore those who have been justified by faith in the first sense must also be justified by works in the second sense; that is, by demonstrating their faith through works, they must be declared and pronounced truly justified through a faith without hypocrisy. The twofold judgment of God to which man is subject demands this very thing. For just as man, to be saved, is considered under a twofold election, either as a sinner or as one converted and called into the state of grace, so likewise, corresponding to these two states, there is a twofold judgment: one rigid and exact, that of God as judge, according to the law; the other milder and more gracious, that of God as an indulgent Father, established by the Gospel. To the former corresponds the justification of the sinner, on account of the single obedience of Christ, without any unaccountability [ἀνυπευθυνία] and acquittal; to the latter corresponds the justification of the righteous.

units.la: In illa quæritur, an homo perfectè legi satisfecerit, vel propter Sponsorem satisfacientem perfectè & ipse satisfecisse censeatur : in hac, an homo vocatus fidémque professus, sanctæ Evangelii professioni respondérit, & latentem fidem conspicuis charitatis operibus πίστις φανέρωσις omnibus manifestam fecerit. Accedit duplex Sathanæ accusatio, adéoque duplex etiam eidem oppositá justificatio. Accusat enim ille κατήγορος accusator fratrum eosdem, ut peccatores, cui accusationi opponitur justificatio per fidem Christi & meriti atque justitiæ ejus. Sed non desistit accusator traducere coram Deo infinceritatem fidei & professionis, adéoque hypocrisin ; cui accusationi justificatio ex operibus fidei & professionis γνησιότης sinceritatem demonstrantibus opponitur. Sed & tribunalis diversitas eandem differentiam probat. Nam justificationis peccatoris tribunal non aliud quàm Divinum est, in quo solo causa hæc disceptatur. At justificationis justi tribunal geminum est, alterum ἀμέσως Divinum & publicum, alterum conscientiæ, ἐμμέσως Divinum & privatum. Divinum ἀμέσως erigitur vel in hoc sæculo, quandó hora gravis tentationis pro arbitrio Dei accelleratur; vel in altero sæculo. Ita in hoc sæculo Abrahamus ex operibus justificatus est, de quo post editum in hora tentationis illustre obedientiæ specimen, Deus ipse pronuntiavit: Nunc cognovi (δοκιμὴν experimentum cepi) te timere Deum, &c. Genes. XXII. 12. qua sententia justificatum esse Patrem credentium Divus Jacobus innuit. Alterum publicum & magis solenne tribunal Divinum in extremo & universali judicio succedet. Posterius tribunal ἐμμέσως Divinum & privatum conscientiæ est. Ne diligamus verbis, neque lingua solùm, sed opere & veritate. Per hoc cognoscimus nos ex veritate esse, & coram ipso secura reddemus corda nostra. Nam si nos condemnet cor nostrum, Deus potentior est corde nostro, & novit omnia. Si cor nostrum nos non condemnet, habemus fiduciam apud Deum, 1. Joh. III. 18–22. Conscientia igitur hominis fidei suæ in Christum experimentum capiens, non aliunde, quàm ex operibus fidem demonstrantibus se ipso judice stat & cadit, adeóque vel δόκιμος vel ἀδόκιμος habetur, vel justificatur & absolvitur, vel condemnatur. Cùmque conscientia non aliud sit, quàm Deus ipse in corde loquens, absolvens vel convincens, hinc adeò tribunal hoc Divinum itidem, sed privatim & in cordis penetralibus hospitans censetur. Tertium tribunal, Humanum videlicet, non nulli addunt, ut ex operibus justificari dicantur, qui ab hominibus ex conspicuis operibus justi reputantur & declarantur. Sed tenendum est, non in foro humano, sed apud tribunal solius Dei causam tum peccatorum, tum fidelium agi. Nihilominus justificari etiam dici possunt, qui humano non tam decretorio judicio, quàm testimonio ad glorificationem Divinæ gratiæ justi declarantur & censentur. Tenentur enim omnes splendere ut lux coram hominibus, ut videant bona eorum opera, & glorificent Deum Patrem in Cœlis, Matth. V. 16.
units.tr: In the first, the question is whether a man has fully satisfied the law, or whether, on account of a Surety who satisfies fully, he is himself judged to have satisfied it. In the second, the question is whether a man who has been called and has professed faith has answered the holy profession of the Gospel, and by visible works of charity has made his hidden faith manifest to all [πίστις φανέρωσις]. There is also a twofold accusation of Satan, and therefore a corresponding twofold justification set against it. For that accuser (κατήγορος), the accuser of the brethren, charges these same men as sinners, and this accusation is met by justification through the faith of Christ and his merit and righteousness. But the accuser does not stop from charging before God the insincerity of faith and profession, and so hypocrisy; to this accusation is opposed justification by the works of faith and profession, which show sincerity [γνησιότης]. The diversity of the tribunal also proves the same difference. For the tribunal of the justification of the sinner is none other than the divine tribunal, the only court in which this cause is tried. But the tribunal of the justification of the righteous is twofold: one is immediately divine and public [ἀμέσως], the other is that of conscience, mediately divine and private [ἐμμέσως]. The immediate divine tribunal is set up either in this age, when, at God's pleasure, the hour of grave temptation is hastened, or in the age to come. So in this age Abraham was justified by works, concerning whom God himself pronounced, after the illustrious proof of obedience given in the hour of temptation: Now I know (I have taken proof of) that you fear God, etc., Gen. XXII. 12. By this sentence St James indicates that the father of believers was justified. The other, public and more solemn divine tribunal will follow at the final and universal judgment. The latter tribunal is mediately divine and private, that of conscience. Let us not love in word, neither in tongue, but in deed and in truth. And hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him. For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things. If our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God, 1 John III. 18–22. Therefore a man's conscience, taking proof of his faith in Christ, stands or falls by its own judgment, drawn from nothing but the works that demonstrate faith; and so he is held either approved [δόκιμος] or unapproved [ἀδόκιμος], either justified and absolved or condemned. And since conscience is nothing other than God himself speaking in the heart, absolving or convicting, this divine tribunal is likewise regarded as dwelling privately in the innermost recesses of the heart. Some add a third tribunal, the human one, so that men are said to be justified by works when they are reckoned and declared righteous by other men on the basis of visible works. But it must be held that the cause both of sinners and of the faithful is pleaded not in a human court but before the tribunal of God alone. Nevertheless, those also may be said to be justified who are declared and judged righteous by human testimony, not so much a decisive judgment, to the glory of divine grace. For all are bound to shine as a light before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father which is in heaven, Matt. V. 16.

units.la: LXXXII. Hæc sic explicata plenissimum S. Paulum & S. Jacobum inter de Justificatione consensum pandunt. Nam variantes quidem de eo Patrum, Primasii, Augustini, Oecumenii; nec non Tridentinorum, Socini, Volkelii, Oftorodi, Grotii, Piscatoris, Capelli, Johannis Vorstii sententias Differt. Tom. I. XH. 24–31. ad incudem fuisus revocavimus. Simplicillima & verissima conciliatio est, quòd S. Paulus de justificatione Peccatoris & à priori, seu causis. S. Jacobus de justificatione Justi, à posteriori & signis seu effectibus, hoc est, de justitiæ per fidem acceptæ ejusdem signis, testimoniis & effectibus demonstratione & declaratione agat. Præclarè enim Hilarius, intelligentiam dictorum ex causis dicentium sumendam esse, monuit. Manifestum autem est, S. Paulum cum infidelibus agere, & hoc unum satagere, quòd peccator sine operibus legis per solam obedientiam Christi, ceu unicam justitiæ causam justificetur. S. Jacobus verò prædicata jam diu in Ecclesia justitia fidei, & sero quidem cum iis agit, qui jam in fidelium cœtu habebantur, doctrinam Evangelii profitebantur, at professionem fidei non ita, uti par erat, exornabant; adeóque adversus hypocritas ejusmodi, Evangelio justitiam ex sola fide revelante, abutentes, id satagit, quòd fides sine operibus vera, sincera, & salutaris minimè
units.tr: LXXXII. These things, thus explained, reveal the fullest agreement between St Paul and St James concerning justification. For we have, at length, brought to the anvil the varying opinions on this subject of the Fathers, Primasius, Augustine and Oecumenius, and also of the Tridentines, Socinus, Volkelius, Ostorodt, Grotius, Piscator, Cappel and John Vorstius (Differt. Tom. I. XH. 24–31). The simplest and truest reconciliation is this: St Paul treats of the justification of the sinner from its causes, a priori, while St James treats of the justification of the righteous man, a posteriori, from its signs or effects; that is, he deals with the demonstration and declaration of the righteousness received through faith by its signs, testimonies and effects. For Hilary rightly warned that the meaning of sayings is to be taken from the causes of those who speak. It is plain that St Paul is dealing with unbelievers, and is concerned with this one thing: that the sinner is justified without works of the law, through the sole obedience of Christ as the only cause of righteousness. St James, however, although the righteousness of faith had long been preached in the Church, deals late with those who were already counted in the assembly of the faithful and professed the doctrine of the Gospel, but did not adorn their profession of faith as they ought. So, against such hypocrites who abused the Gospel's revelation of righteousness by faith alone, he takes pains to show that faith without works is by no means true, sincere and saving

units.la: Ex distinctione consensus S. Pauli inter & S. Jacobum ; quorum illa ex sola fide, hic ex operibus justificari asseris ; plenissimus expontur ; & illam de justificatione peccatoris, hunc de justificatione justi agere, ostenditur. nimè sit, eo inter alia argumento, quòd fides talis non justificet, sed ex operibus demum demonstrata vera fides justificans declaretur, atque ita opera justificent, hoc est, fidem ab omni hypocriseos accusatione & crimine absolvant, veráque & sinceram declarent. Non ergo Jacobus de causa, qua peccator coram tribunali Dei justificatur, sed tum de qualitate fidei illius, quae justificat & salvat; tum de qualitate illius, qui justificatus est, adeóque de fidei salvificæ, & ipsius justitiæ Christi per fidem acceptæ signis, fructibus & effectis agit. Diserte enim v. 18. sibi fidem ex operibus δεικνύειν demonstrari petit; adeóque de operibus δεικτικῶς τῆς πίστεως demonstrativis fidei, seu justitiæ fidei acceptæ loquitur: & Abrahamum ex obedientia immolationis filii suscepta justificatum asserit, cùm pridem ante ex fide justificatus, & à reatu peccati per imputationem alienæ justitiæ absolutus fuerit, & Dei gratia flagraverit, quod vel solum foedus cum eo initum Genes. XVII. 1. 2. &c. & acceptio sigilli justitiæ Rom. IV. 11. ostendit. Non igitur demum post opera quamvis insigni, ut causa meritoria, justificatus dici potest: at justificatus, hoc est, per veram fidem justitiæ particeps factus, ex opere, ceu signo & testimonio consequente declarari & pronuntiari potuit. Ideo Jacobus justificationem Abrahami priorem ex sola fide impletam esse tum, cùm ex operibus justificatus est, v. 23. testatur: & Deus Abrahami ejusdem obedientia explorata dixit: Nunc cognovi (experimentum cepi) quòd timeas Deum, &c. Genes. XXII. 12. Unde liquet, non ad id pertinuisse Abrahami obedientiam, ut propter illam justum redderet operantem, sed potiùs, ut hoc experimento liquidò constaret, scilicet & ἀνυποχείτως ipsum Deum timere, & verè fidem ei ad justitiam imputatam esse. Et ex eodem opere illustri justificatus Abrahamus dicitur φίλος Θεοῦ κλήτος amicus Dei vocatus, vers. 23. hoc est, declaratus, publicè coram omnibus, & ipsius etiam justificati conscientia solenniter & peculiari ratione manifestatus. Nam etiam ante Dei foederatus & amicus fuit. At nunc demum solennis publicatio secuta est. Unde non amicus γενητὸς factus, sed κλητὸς vocatus dicitur. Denique opera illa, quibus Apostolus justificationem tribuit, v. 26. cum πνεῦμα spiritu, hoc est, πνοὴ respiratione & κίνησις motu comparantur. Sicut igitur illa effectuum & signum viventis corporis: ita etiam opera fidei justificantis, ipsiúsque adeò justificationis documenta, signa & effecta statui, manifestò consequitur.
units.tr: From the distinction between the agreement of St Paul and that of St James, of whom the one asserts that we are justified by faith alone and the other by works, the matter is set out most fully, and it is shown that the one treats of the justification of the sinner and the other of the justification of the righteous. Such faith, he argues among other things, can in no way be justifying; rather, true justifying faith is only declared when it has been demonstrated by works. Thus works justify, that is, they absolve faith from every accusation and charge of hypocrisy and declare it true and sincere. So James is not speaking of the cause by which a sinner is justified before the tribunal of God, but of the quality of that faith which justifies and saves, and also of the quality of the one who has been justified. He is therefore speaking of the signs, fruits and effects of saving faith and of the righteousness of Christ itself received through faith. For he plainly asks, at v. 18, that faith be shown (δεικνύειν) from works, and so he speaks of works that demonstrate faith [δεικτικῶς τῆς πίστεως], that is, of the righteousness of faith received. He asserts that Abraham was justified by obedience in offering up his son, although he had earlier been justified by faith and absolved from the guilt of sin through the imputation of another's righteousness, and had burned with God's grace. This is shown both by the covenant made with him alone, Gen. XVII. 1, 2, etc., and by his receiving the seal of righteousness, Rom. IV. 11. Therefore he could not be called justified, as a meritorious cause, only after some outstanding work. Rather, one who was already justified, that is, made a partaker of righteousness through true faith, could be declared and pronounced so from the work that follows as sign and testimony. So at v. 23 James testifies that the justification of Abraham, which was fulfilled earlier by faith alone, was complete when he was justified by works. And God, having tested the obedience of Abraham, said: Now I know (I have taken proof) that you fear God, etc., Gen. XXII. 12. From this it is clear that Abraham's obedience did not serve to make him righteous by making his work meritorious, but rather that by this proof it might be plainly established both that he feared God without dissembling and that faith had truly been reckoned to him for righteousness. And from this same illustrious work Abraham is said to have been justified and called the friend of God [φίλος Θεοῦ κλήτος, friend of God, called], v. 23, that is, declared publicly before all and made known solemnly, and in a peculiar way, to the conscience of the justified man himself. For he was already God's covenant partner and friend before. But only now did the solemn publication follow. Hence he is said not to have been made a friend but to have been called. Finally, those works to which the Apostle ascribes justification, v. 26, are compared with spirit [πνεῦμα], that is, with breath [πνοή] and motion [κίνησις]. Just as breathing and motion are the signs and proofs of a living body, so it plainly follows that the works of justifying faith, and thus the evidences, signs and effects of justification itself, are established.

units.la: LXXXIII. Non igitur Jacobus fidem & opera ejusdem justificationis συναιτια concausas, seu causas socias fecit, uti Bellarminus aliiqué fingunt. Neque id evincunt eorum rationes. Dixit equidem Jacobus: Vides igitur, ὅτι πίστις συνηργεῖ τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ quòd fides (Abrahami) cooperata fit operibus ejus, Cap. II. 22. Sed cooperatio intelligitur non fidei & operum, ceu concausarum ad eundem justificationis effectum. Nam obedientia Abrahæ ejusdem fidei, ut causæ, Hebr. XI. 17. tribuitur. Et jam ante opera sola fide justificatum esse Abrahamum, Jacobus vers. 23. concessit. Συνέργεια igitur fidei cum operibus intelligitur, quatenus illa operibus Abrahami, ceu eorum causa id suppeditavit, ut Deo grata & accepta essent.
units.tr: LXXXIII. Therefore James did not make faith and works co-causes [συναιτια], or joint causes, of this justification, as Bellarmine and others pretend. Nor do their arguments prove it. James did indeed say: You see then, that faith cooperated with his works [Vides igitur, ὅτι πίστις συνηργεῖ τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ], that is, that (Abraham's) faith was worked together with his works, ch. II. 22. But this cooperation is to be understood not as faith and works being concauses of the same effect of justification. For the obedience of Abraham is attributed to his faith as its cause, Heb. XI. 17. And James, at v. 23, has already granted that Abraham was justified by faith alone before the works. The cooperation [Συνέργεια] of faith with works is therefore to be understood insofar as faith supplied to the works of Abraham, as their cause, that they should be pleasing and acceptable to God.

units.la: Nam συνεργεῖν authoritate veteris Glossarii, quod Cyrillo adscribitur, etiam suppeditare significat. Sicut nempe radix suppeditat, quæ necessaria sunt & plantæ conservandæ & fructibus generandis: ita fides operibus, tanquam eorum causa necessaria suppeditat. Sensus etiam esse potest, fidem Abrahami cum operibus ejus existentem justificationem operatam esse. Jacobum enim verbis compositis gaudere, Interpretes ejus observarunt. Sed si retineamus etiam cooperationis vocem, fides operibus cooperata rectè dicitur, tum quia non fuit otiosa, expers operum, & quidem operantium, sed potiùs per charitatem efficax: quod unum Jacobus probandum susceperat: tum quia opera, tanquam fidei fructus, bonitatem suam à fide habent, adeò ut sine ea immunda & peccata sint, Rom. XIV. 23. tum quia opera fidem integram, minimè fucatam, vel claudicantem; vivam, & veram, non mortuam & ἀνεμένειν demonstrant & declarant. Eadem Abrahami fides etiam ἐκ τῶν ἔργων τελειωθῆ ex operibus consummata est, v. 22: hoc est, vera, viva, ingenua, definitionem vocabuli, non solam λέξιν dictionem habens, verbo, πλέια perfecta demonstrata est. Quo sensu Dei potentia in infirmitate nostra πληροῦται perficitur, consummatur, 2. Cor. XII. 9. hoc est, perfecta, & vim suam in infirmitate nostra exerens, demonstratur & cognoscitur: & ædificium ornamentis, Sponsa mundo suo, architectus opere, arbor fructu, causa quælibet effectu suo, & habitus vel potentia actu suo perficitur, hoc est, perfecta cognoscitur, declaratur. Quia enim de causa ex effectis judicamus, causæ ipsius vis & perfectio ex effectorum proportione minui vel augeri quodammodo videtur. Eodem sensu Jacobus cap. III. 2. τέλειον ἀνδρα perfectum virum dixit, qui in sermone non impingit, quia hoc perfectionis indicium & χαλινὸν indubitabile merito habetur. Fide Abrahami ita cum operibus ejus cooperante, & ex iisdem consummata, idem Jacobus infert, Scriptnram impletam esse, quæ dicit: Credidit autem Abraham Deo, & reputatum ei est ad justitiam, v. 23. nempe quia grandi & illustri specimine edito apparuit, veram vivámque fidem fuisse, qua justificatus est. Sicut enim verbi de justificatione fidei πληρώσεως impletio est in glorificatione: ita ejusdem impletio est in continuata sanctificatione, quæ ad glorificationem perducit. Utrobique justificatio fidei, tanquam causa in effectu necessario consequente, & ab ea necessario & proximè emanante, impletur. Denique Jacobus disputationem hanc sic concludit. Videtis igitur, quòd ex operibus justificatur homo, ἐξ ἔργων ex operibus ἐκ πίστεως μόνον, & non ex sola fide, v. 24. Ubi nomine πίστεως fidei vel fides mortua & operum expers, quam Apostolus oppugnat, vel ea fides, quæ credenti ad justitiam imputatur, intelligi debet. Si prius, fides mortua justificationis συναίτιον causa socia nullo modo esse potest. Si posterius, uti relatio ad fidem Abrahamicam proximè descriptam arguere videtur, manifestum erit, non causas socias ejusdem justificationis, sed diversas justificationes, alteram peccatoris ex causa, alteram justi ex signis & effectibus distingui. Diversa enim plane justifica-tio
units.tr: For synergein [συνεργεῖν], on the authority of the old Glossary attributed to Cyril, also means to supply. Just as the root supplies what is needed both to keep the plant alive and to produce its fruit, so faith, as the necessary cause of works, supplies them. The sense may also be that the faith of Abraham, existing together with his works, brought about justification. The interpreters have observed that James delights in compound words. But if we also keep the word cooperation, faith may rightly be said to be co-operating with works: first, because it was not idle or without works, but rather working, and indeed effective through love, which is the one thing James had undertaken to prove; second, because works, as the fruits of faith, have their goodness from faith, so that without it they are unclean and sinful (Rom. 14:23); third, because works show and declare that faith is whole, not feigned or limping, but living and true, not dead and inert. The same faith of Abraham was also consummated by works [ἐκ τῶν ἔργων τελειωθῆ], v. 22: that is, it was shown to be true, living and genuine, having the real character of the word and not merely the term, and so was shown to be perfect [τέλεια]. In this sense the power of God is made perfect [πληροῦται] in our weakness, 2 Cor. 12:9: that is, it is shown and known as perfect, exerting its strength in our weakness. So a building is perfected by its ornaments, a bride by her adornment, an architect by his work, a tree by its fruit, any cause by its effect, and a habit or power by its act; that is, it is known and declared to be perfect. For since we judge a cause from its effects, the power and perfection of the cause seem in some measure to be diminished or increased according to the proportion of its effects. In the same sense James (3:2) called the man perfect [τέλειον ἄνδρα] who does not stumble in speech, because this is rightly regarded as an indubitable sign and bridle of perfection. With Abraham's faith thus co-operating with his works and consummated by them, James infers that the Scripture was fulfilled which says: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness, v. 23. This is because, by a great and illustrious example given, it appeared that the faith by which he was justified was true and living. For just as the fulfilment [πλήρωσις] of the word about justification by faith lies in glorification, so its fulfilment lies in continued sanctification, which leads to glorification. In both cases the justification by faith is fulfilled as a cause in its necessarily following effect, which emanates from it necessarily and immediately. Finally, James concludes this discussion thus: You see then that a man is justified by works [ἐξ ἔργων], and not by faith only [ἐκ πίστεως μόνον], v. 24. Here by faith [πίστεως] must be understood either dead faith, destitute of works, which the Apostle opposes, or that faith which is imputed to the believer for righteousness. If the former, dead faith can in no way be a joint cause [συναίτιον]. If the latter, as the reference to the Abrahamic faith described just before seems to show, it will be clear that they are not joint causes of the same justification, but that different justifications are distinguished: one of the sinner from a cause, the other of the righteous from signs and effects. For the justification

units.la: Argumentum eorum, qui S. Jacobum fidem & opera causas socias justificationis facere perhibent, occurrunt. tio ex fide, & ex operibus est. In illa-
units.tr: This is the argument of those who claim that St. James makes faith and works joint causes of justification, and it is met.

units.la: tio ex fide, & ex operibus est. In illa πίστις λογίζεται εις δικαιοσύνην fides imputatur ad justitiam: in hac non opera imputantur ad justitiam, sed impletur Scriptura, quæ dicit: fidem imputatam esse ad justitiam. Si Abrahamo opera ad justitiam imputata fuissent, non impleta, sed rescissa fuisset Scriptura, quæ dicit, fidem imputari ad justitiam.
units.tr: from faith and that from works is quite different. In the one, faith is imputed for righteousness [πίστις λογίζεται εἰς δικαιοσύνην]; in the other, works are not imputed for righteousness, but the Scripture is fulfilled which says that faith was imputed for righteousness. If works had been imputed to Abraham for righteousness, the Scripture which says that faith is imputed for righteousness would not have been fulfilled but annulled.

units.la: LXXXIV. Justificatio justi per gradus proficit; uti & ipsa sanctificatio, quæ in judicio Dei justificationis illius causa est, gradus habet.
units.tr: LXXXIV. The justification of the righteous advances by degrees, just as sanctification itself, which is the cause of that justification in the judgment of God, has degrees.

units.la: Nam in hac vita imperfecta cum peccato luctatur: in morte, quoad spiritum, & in resurrectione, quoad totum hominem, spiritum & corpus perficitur. Par ratio est justificationis justi. Nam in hac vita justificamur ex operibus, quibus cum peccato residuo Spiritu S. opitulante luctamur. Ita Abrahamus in hac vita ex operibus justificatus est, quando edito illustri specimine obedientiæ, ceu strenuus adversus carnem & sanguinem athleta, fidei, per quam pridem justificatus fuit, ἐλικῶς ἐνεργῶν potenter demonstravit. Sed magis justificamur, quando peccati lucta finitur, & spiritus in gloria consummatur. Nam qui mortuus est, justificatus est à peccato, Rom. VI. 7. Morte enim lucta peccati finitur, & spiritus in gloria consummatur. Quæ δικαιώσις justificatio quædam est, quia qui hic consummatur spiritus, consummatione sanctificationis, & liberatione plenaria à peccato per fidem justificatus ἐν δυνάμει θεΐζεται potenter definitur & declaratur. Consummatissimè justificamur, quando etiam corpus revivificens in gloriam assumitur, & in ultimo judicio ex operibus justitiæ fidei perfectio & integritas clarissimè patefiet. Venite benedicti Patris mei, hæreditate Regnum à fundatione mundi vobis præparatum. Nam esurivi, & cibâstis me. Sitivi & potâstis me. Peregrinus fui, & congregâstis me, Matth. XXV. 34. 35.
units.tr: For in this imperfect life the believer struggles with sin; in death, as to the spirit, and in the resurrection, as to the whole man, spirit and body are perfected. The same reasoning holds for the justification of the righteous. For in this life we are justified by works, in which, with the help of the Holy Spirit, we struggle against the sin that remains. Thus Abraham in this life was justified by works, when, having given an illustrious example of obedience, like a vigorous athlete against flesh and blood, he powerfully demonstrated the faith by which he had earlier been justified. But we are justified more fully when the struggle with sin ends and the spirit is consummated in glory. For he who has died is justified from sin, Rom. 6:7. By death the struggle with sin ends, and the spirit is consummated in glory. This is a kind of justification [δικαίωσις], because the spirit which is here consummated, by the consummation of sanctification and full liberation from sin, is powerfully defined and declared to be justified through faith. We are justified most completely when the body, too, is revived and taken up into glory, and at the last judgment the perfection and integrity of the works of faith will be most clearly revealed. Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you gathered me in, Matt. 25:34-35.

units.la: LXXXV. Justificationis per fidem effecta varia sunt.
units.tr: LXXXV. The effects of justification through faith are various.

units.la: Potiora sunt adoptio, libertas spiritualis, conscientiæ tranquillitas, accessus ad Deum, timor filialis, nova obedientia, & certitudo gratiæ præsentis & futuræ. Adoptio in universum in filium assumptio est. Filii enim duorum generum sunt; alii naturales, ex substantia parentum geniti, alii adoptivi, qui aliunde oriundi in familiam eorum, quorum filii dicuntur, asciscuntur & transeunt. Quæ adoptio duplex; Humana & Divina est. Humana, qua homines alios non à se genitos in familiam suam asciscunt. Cujus usus antiquissimus fuit, non tantum in populo Dei, uti Ephraimi & Manassis à Jacobo, & Esther à Mardochæo adoptatæ exempla docent; sed etiam apud gentes profanas, uti exemplum filiæ Pharaonis Mosen adoptantis comprobat. Inventa est, uti JCti monent, in solatium sterilitatis conjugii, & defectus filiorum naturalium, eorum quoque, qui naturales liberos, at imbelles, improbos, degeneres nacti, alios meliores quærere conati sunt. Arrogatio etiam dicitur, sed hoc cum discrimine, quòd adoptari dicuntur ii, qui parentibus adhuc subsunt, arrogari, qui sui juris sunt. Divina vel generalis & integri populi, vel specialis & singularum personarum. Illa cum vocatione externa, & fœdere externo, quod Deus cum populo suo pepigit, convenit.
units.tr: The more important are adoption, spiritual freedom, tranquillity of conscience, access to God, filial fear, new obedience, and certainty of present and future grace. Adoption in general is the taking of someone as a son. Sons are of two kinds: some are natural, born of the substance of their parents; others are adopted, who come from elsewhere and are received and admitted into the family of those whose sons they are called. Adoption is twofold, human and divine. Human adoption is that by which men take into their own family others not born of them. Its use is very ancient, and not only among the people of God, as the examples of Ephraim and Manasseh adopted by Jacob, and of Esther adopted by Mordecai, show; it is also found among the profane nations, as the example of Pharaoh's daughter adopting Moses confirms. It was devised, as the jurists point out, as a consolation for the barrenness of marriage and the lack of natural children, and also for those who had natural children but unwarlike, wicked, or degenerate, and who sought to find better ones. It is also called arrogation, but with this difference: those are said to be adopted who are still under their parents, and those are arrogated who are their own masters. Divine adoption is either general, of a whole people, or special, of individual persons. The former agrees with the external calling and the external covenant that God made with his people.

units.la: Hujusmodi filii primò fuerunt Israelitæ, quorum erat υἱοθεσία adoptio, Rom. IX. 4. qui propterea etiam Filii Dei, & בני אל Filius Dei primogenitus, Exod. IV. 22. appellantur; deinde Gentiles, qui in locum Judæorum succedentes, adoptati, & filiationis privilegio donati sunt. Non populus meus vos, ibi vocabuntur, υἱοὶ Θεοῦ ζῶντος filii Dei viventis, Rom. IX. 26. Non amplius estis peregrini & advenæ, sed concives Sanctorum & domestici Dei, Ephes. II. 19.
units.tr: Of this kind the first sons were the Israelites, to whom belonged adoption [υἱοθεσία], Rom. 9:4, and who for this reason are also called sons of God, and firstborn son of God [בני אל], Exod. 4:22. Then came the Gentiles, who, succeeding into the place of the Jews, were adopted and endowed with the privilege of sonship: "They shall be called there, Ye are not my people; there they shall be called sons of the living God" [υἱοὶ Θεοῦ ζῶντος], Rom. 9:26. "Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellow-citizens with the saints and of the household of God," Eph. 2:19.

units.la: LXXXVI. Divina specialis seu singulorum Adoptio est sententia Dei gratiosa, justificatoria sententiæ veluti appendix & coronis, qua per fidem justificati & Deo reconciliati per & propter eundem Christum insuper quoque in filios & hæredes, cohæredes autem Christi assumuntur.
units.tr: LXXXVI. Special or individual divine adoption is the gracious sentence of God, an appendix and crown, as it were, of the justifying sentence, by which those who are justified through faith and reconciled to God, through and on account of the same Christ, are further taken up as sons and heirs, and indeed as joint heirs with Christ.

units.la: De qua pallim Scripturæ loquuntur. Filii ejus (Jehovæ, Petræ) labes ipsorum sunt, ab infidelibus pro labe habentur, Deut. XXXII. 5. Propter ægritudinem filiorum meorum & filiarum mearum, v. 19. Qui acceperunt eum, iis potestatem dedit, ut fierent filii Dei, credentibus in nomen ejus, Joh. I. 12. Accepistis πνεῦμα υἱοθεσίας spiritum adoptionis, Rom. VIII. 15. Emisit Deus Filium suum, &c. ἵνα τὴν υἱοθεσίαν ἀπολάβωμεν, ut adoptionem acciperemus Gal. IV. 4. 5. Prædestinavit nos εἰς υἱοθεσίαν ad Filiationem, Ephes. I. 5. Omnes Filii Dei estis per fidem in Christo Jesu, Gal. III. 26. Etenim si Deus Pater noster est, oportet, ut nos ejus filii simus. Cumque Filius Dei primogenitus frater noster sit, Rom. VIII. 29. Heb. II. 11. &c. nos quoque Dei filii sumus, ille natura, nos ex gratia.
units.tr: Scripture speaks of this in many places. "His sons" (of Jehovah, the Rock) "are their blemish; they are held as a blemish by unbelievers," Deut. 32:5. "Because of the provocation of my sons and my daughters," v. 19. "But as many as received him, to them he gave power to become the sons of God, to those who believe in his name," John 1:12. "Ye have received the Spirit of adoption [πνεῦμα υἱοθεσίας]," Rom. 8:15. "God sent forth his Son," etc., "that we might receive the adoption" [ἵνα τὴν υἱοθεσίαν ἀπολάβωμεν], Gal. 4:4, 5. "He predestinated us unto adoption [εἰς υἱοθεσίαν] to sonship," Eph. 1:5. "Ye are all the sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus," Gal. 3:26. For if God is our Father, it is necessary that we should be his sons. And since the Son of God is our firstborn brother, Rom. 8:29; Heb. 2:11, etc., we too are sons of God: he by nature, we by grace.

units.la: LXXXVII. Qui nos in filios adoptat, Deus Triunus est, servata tamen, quæ personas inter est, œconomia, juxta quam Deo Patri ordinatio, Filio acquisitio, & Spiritui S. obsignatio tribuitur.
units.tr: LXXXVII. The God who adopts us as sons is the Triune God, yet the economy that distinguishes the persons is preserved, according to which the ordaining belongs to God the Father, the acquiring to the Son, and the sealing to the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, &c. qui prædestinavit nos ad Filiationem per Jesum Christum ad se secundum beneplacitum voluntatis suæ, Eph. I. 3. 5. Quotquot eum acceperunt, iis dedit jus, ut filii Dei fierent, (pro iis se gererent) Joh. I. 12. Ecce ego, & pueri quos dedit mihi Deus, Hebr. II. 13. Spiritus testatur, nos esse filios Dei, Rom. VIII. 16. Per eum scimus, quæ Deus nobis gratificatus est, 1. Cor. II. 12. & obsignati sumus in diem redemptionis, Eph. IV. 30. Deus ille Triunus nos adoptat ex mera gratia & beneplacito voluntatis; non ex defectu liberorum, quia Pater habet Filium ἴδιον proprium & unigenitum, atque naturalem, in quo plenissimè acquiescit, Matth. III. 17. XVII. 5. sed ex abundante bonitate & amore erga Filium, ut primogenitus esset inter multos fratres, Rom. VIII. 29. Quod planè infrequens est & insolitum. Videte, qualem charitatem nobis Pater dedit, ut filii Dei vocemur, 1. Joh. III. 1. In Christo autem solo filii sumus, tum quia ipse solus, nemo alius merito suo jus υἱοθεσίας seu filiationis dandæ adeptus, eandem dare potest: tum quia solus ille ex Regno tenebrarum, dominio peccati, & mortis, tyrannide Sathanæ, cujus vinculis constricti tenebamur, eripere potuit. Servus non manet in domo perpetuò; filius manet perpetuò. Itaque si vos Filius in libertatem vindicaverit, verè liberi eritis, Joh. VIII. 35. 36. Ideo S. Paulus Heb. II. 10–17. filiationem nostram pluribus exaggerata, ad Christi ceu fratris puerorum incarnationem descendit. Sed inpriinprimis Spiritus S. gratiosi istius nominis signaculum & arrhabo est, κατ' ἐξοχὴν πνεῦμα υἱοθεσίας adoptionis Rom. VIII. 15. dictus, quia interiore isto commercio, testimonio & affatu animam nostram permutat, & cum fiducia Deum, ut Patrem in Christo adire facit, ut sic eum appellemus אבא Pater; qua, velut naturae ipsius voce & sono, Patrem olim quaerebant, qui ex servitute liberati, alienae familiae accessuri erant. Illud tamen testimonium Spiritus S. a fide, aliisque Christianae animae affectibus scrupulosè distinguendum non est: quasi postquam credidimus, alio Spiritus actu, vel immediato ejus affatu motus, velut inani & fallaci quadam echo, insinuetur. Simul enim atque credimus, & eo ipso, quòd credimus, obsignamur; haecque ipsa Spiritus nota & character & fides, unieum ejus signaculum est. In quo etiam σπερμα- τικῶς credentes obsignati estis Spiritu promissionis Sancto, qui est arrhabo haereditatis nostrae, Ephes. I. 13. 14. Sunt enim illae ἀπαρχαὶ primitiae Spiritus S. Rom. VIII. 23. quas porrò filiorum affectus & indoles, reliquúmque virtutum Christianarum agmen comitatur, quae cuncta ejus in nobis habitantis testimonia & σφραγῖδες signacula sunt.
units.tr: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, etc., who predestinated us unto sonship through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will," Eph. 1:3, 5. "As many as received him, to them he gave the right to become the sons of God" (to act as such towards them), John 1:12. "Behold I, and the children whom God hath given me," Heb. 2:13. "The Spirit himself beareth witness that we are the children of God," Rom. 8:16. Through him we know the things that God has freely given us, 1 Cor. 2:12, and we are sealed unto the day of redemption, Eph. 4:30. That Triune God adopts us out of pure grace and the good pleasure of his will; not from a lack of children, for the Father has his own and only-begotten natural Son, in whom he fully rests, Matt. 3:17; 17:5; but from abundant goodness and love towards the Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers, Rom. 8:29. This is quite rare and unusual. "Behold what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God," 1 John 3:1. Yet we are sons in Christ alone, both because he alone, and no one else, has by his merit obtained the right of giving adoption or sonship, and because he alone could snatch us from the kingdom of darkness, the dominion of sin and death, and the tyranny of Satan, by whose bonds we were held fast. "The servant abideth not in the house for ever; the son abideth ever. If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed," John 8:35, 36. Therefore St Paul, Heb. 2:10–17, after magnifying our sonship in many ways, descends to the incarnation of Christ as brother of the children. But above all the Holy Spirit is the seal and pledge of this gracious name, called preeminently the Spirit of adoption [κατ' ἐξοχὴν πνεῦμα υἱοθεσίας], Rom. 8:15, because by that inward intercourse, testimony and speech he exchanges our soul, and makes us approach God with confidence as Father in Christ, so that we call him Abba, Father; by which cry, as it were the very voice and sound of nature, those who had been freed from servitude and were about to come into a strange household used to seek a father. Yet the testimony of the Holy Spirit is not to be carefully distinguished from faith and the other affections of the Christian soul, as if, after we have believed, we were moved by another act of the Spirit, or by his immediate speech, and it were insinuated as some empty and deceptive echo. For as soon as we believe, and by the very fact that we believe, we are sealed; and this very faith is the mark and character of the Spirit, and his only seal. "In whom also, having believed, ye were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the earnest of our inheritance," Eph. 1:13, 14. For these are the firstfruits of the Spirit [ἀπαρχαὶ], Rom. 8:23, which are further accompanied by the disposition and character of sons and the whole band of Christian virtues, all of which are testimonies and seals of his dwelling in us.

units.la: LXXXVIII. Filiorum adoptivorum augustus titulus in emphasi sua tum regenerationem ex Deo, tum cognitionem nominis Dei & eorum, quae Deus facit, tum fiduciam ad Deum sine metu mortis, & servitute elementorum mundi, significat. Qui eum acceperunt, iis dedit potestatem, ut filii Dei fierent, &c. qui non ex sanguinibus, nec ex voluntate carnis, nec ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo geniti sunt, Joh. I. 12. 13. Sicut nempe voluntate hominis juxta generationem naturalem nascuntur homines, ita voluntate Dei per semen ipsius alii sunt, quàm nati erant; hoc est, cor novum & animum novum habent, Ezech. XXXVI. 26. Sicut in filiis hominum est semen paternum: ita in filiis Dei est semen Dei, verbum veritatis & spiritus ejus, de quo in loco plura. De cognitione Nominis Dei sic ipse Christus: Non amplius vos dico servos, quia servus nescit, quid faciat ejus Dominus. Vos autem dixi amicos, quia omnia, quae audivi à Patre meo, vobis notificavi, Joh. XV. 15. Accedit haereditas mundi, sive gentium in Christo obtenta. Et ex duobus illis, fiducia & haereditate filii Dei dicuntur Sacerdotes & Reges, Apoc. V. 10. secundum promissionem illam: Et vos Sacerdotes Domini (ἱερεῖς τοῦ Θεοῦ appropinquantes ad Deum) vocabimini, ministri Dei nostri, copiam gentium comedetis, & gloriam ipsarum vestram asseretis, Esaj. LXI. 6. Etiam ex illis gentibus accipiam in Sacerdotes & Reges, ibid. LXVI. 21.
units.tr: LXXXVIII. The noble title of adoptive sons, in its emphasis, signifies both regeneration from God, and knowledge of the name of God and of what God does, and confidence towards God without fear of death and without servitude to the elements of the world. "As many as received him, to them he gave power to become the sons of God, etc., who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God," John 1:12, 13. For just as men are born by the will of man according to natural generation, so by the will of God, through his seed, they are other than they were born; that is, they have a new heart and a new spirit, Ezek. 36:26. As in the sons of men there is the paternal seed, so in the sons of God there is the seed of God, the word of truth and his Spirit, of which more in its place. Concerning knowledge of the name of God, Christ himself says thus: "Henceforth I call you not servants, for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth; but I have called you friends, for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you," John 15:15. To this is added the inheritance of the world, or of the nations, obtained in Christ. And from those two things, confidence and inheritance, the sons of God are called priests and kings, Rev. 5:10, according to that promise: "But ye shall be named the priests of the Lord (priests of God, drawing near to God), the ministers of our God; ye shall eat the wealth of the nations, and in their glory shall ye boast yourselves," Isa. 61:6. "Also from those nations I will take some for priests and Levites," ibid. 66:21.

units.la: LXXXIX. Filiatio illa latè, strictè & strictissimè accipitur. Latè in oppositione illorum, qui alieni sunt à Deo. Quo sensu filii sunt omnes omnium temporum fideles. Strictè in oppositione illorum, qui sub servitute sunt. Quo sensu filii sunt fideles Novi Testamenti. Strictissimè in oppositione illorum, qui nondum adepti sunt haereditatem nisi in spe. Quomodo filii illi sunt, qui coelesti gloria fruuntur. Sunt ergo omnes electi, vocati & justificati filii Dei quocunque tempore. Sed filiorum tamen Dei diversus status est; alius servilis, alius liber, alius gloriosus. De servili sic Apostolus: Hoc dico, quandiu haeres infans est; nihil differt à servo, quamvis omnium dominus sit; sed sub tutoribus & curatoribus est usque ad tempus à Patre praefitutum, Gal. IV. 1. &c. De libero promissio Dei extat. Ecce dixeram, quomodo ponam te inter filios, Jer. III. 19. Impletionem Apostolus explicat, dicens: Non accepistis Spiritum servitutis iterum ad metum, sed accepistis Spiritum filiationis, in quo clamamus, Abba, Pater: Rom. VIII. 15. De status hujus liberi discrimine à servili plura Loc. XX. 45. 46. diximus. De glorioso idem Apostolus: Nos ipsi, qui primitias Spiritus habemus, & intra nos gemimus, ἀπεκδεχόμενοι υἱοθεσίαν expectantes adoptionem, redemptionem corporis nostri, Rom. VIII. 23. Nam in redemptione, seu liberatione corporis ex pulvere resurgentis Filiatio consummatur, quia tum Deus erit omnia in omnibus, 1. Cor. XV. 28. & haereditas ipsa plenissima cum fruitione aditur.
units.tr: LXXXIX. That sonship is taken in a broad, a strict and a most strict sense. Broadly, in opposition to those who are alien from God; in this sense all the faithful of every age are sons. Strictly, in opposition to those who are under servitude; in this sense the faithful of the New Testament are sons. Most strictly, in opposition to those who have not yet obtained the inheritance except in hope; in this sense those are sons who enjoy heavenly glory. All the elect, called and justified, are therefore sons of God at whatever time they live. Yet the state of the sons of God is not the same: one is servile, another free, another glorious. Of the servile state the Apostle says: "I say that as long as the heir is a child, he differs nothing from a servant, though he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and governors until the time appointed by the Father" (Gal. 4:1, etc.). Of the free state there is God's promise: "Behold, I had said how I would set you among the sons" (Jer. 3:19). The Apostle explains its fulfilment, saying: "You have not received the spirit of bondage again unto fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba, Father" (Rom. 8:15). We have said more about the difference between this free state and the servile one at Loc. 20, sections 45 and 46. Of the glorious state the same Apostle says: "We ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, the redemption of our body" (Rom. 8:23). For sonship is completed in the redemption, or deliverance, of the body when it rises from the dust, because then God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28), and the inheritance itself is entered upon in its fullness, with full enjoyment.

units.la: XC. Magna certè dignatio est, Filium Dei nuncupari, adeò ut infideles, Gentiles & Muhammedani Christianos eo nomine jam olim irriserint; quasi homuncio Dei ipsius progenies appellari sine phrenesi quadam nequeat. Dixit tamen gentilis Poëta: Τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν. Ejus (Dei) progenies sumus; Act. XVII. 28. Et non nostra haec dignitas, sed Dei dignatio est, qui & creatos, & redemptos à se filiorum nomine dignatur, & ἐξουσίαν τέκνα γίνεσθαι jus, potestatem, privilegium se pro filiis gerendi, atque δόξαν τέκνων Θεοῦ gloriam filiorum Dei, Rom. VIII. 23. impartitur. Cùmque Filius sit imago Patris, idem Deus hominem ad imaginem suam creavit, atque sic filium esse voluit, justit. Sicut igitur infidelium characteres filiorum nullos in se invenientium, sannas nihil moramur: ita Dei bonitatem & dignationem summam erga nos miramur. Hoc enim illud ὄνομα καινὸν nomen novum calculo albo (absolutorio) inscriptum est, quod nemo novit, nisi qui accepit, Apoc. II. 17. Num leve in oculis vestris est, inquiebat David Saulis filiam ducturus, affinitate conjungi cum Rege, cùm ego sim pauper & vilis? 1. Sam. XVIII. 23. Perinde nos admirabundi: Num leve est transfire in familiam Regis Regum, & Domini dominantium, qui viles imò כלא חשבו sicut nihilum reputati. Dan. IV. 32. & ἐχθροὶ inimici secundum naturalem affectum Rom. V. 10. sumus?
units.tr: XC. Surely it is a great honour to be called Son of God, so much so that unbelievers, Gentiles and Muhammadans have long since mocked Christians on account of that name, as if a mere mortal could not be called the offspring of God without some kind of frenzy. Yet a Gentile poet said: [Τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν] "For we are also his offspring" (Acts 17:28). And this dignity is not ours but God's gift, who deigns to call those whom he has created and redeemed by the name of sons, and [ἐξουσίαν τέκνα γίνεσθαι] the right and power to act as sons, and imparts [δόξαν τέκνων Θεοῦ] the glory of the sons of God (Rom. 8:23). And since the Son is the image of the Father, the same God created man in his own image and so willed him to be a son, and commanded it. Therefore, just as we pay no attention to the sneers of unbelievers, who find no marks of sons in themselves, so we marvel at God's goodness and his supreme condescension towards us. For this is that [ὄνομα καινὸν] new name, written in the white stone (the absolving pebble), which no one knows except the one who receives it (Rev. 2:17). Is it a small thing in your eyes, said David when he was about to marry Saul's daughter, to be joined by marriage to the king, since I am poor and mean? (1 Sam. 18:23). In the same way we, marvelling, ask: is it a small thing to pass into the family of the King of kings and Lord of lords, we who are worthless, indeed [כלא חשבו] reckoned as nothing (Dan. 4:32), and [ἐχθροὶ] enemies by natural disposition (Rom. 5:10)?

units.la: XCI. Adoptionis fructus plurimi & amplissimi sunt. Filii enim Dei in ejusdem familiam & domum recipiuntur, & filiorum instar habentur. Charitate perpetua dilexi te, attraxi te misericordia, Jerem. XXXI. 3. Ac licèt eosdem castiget, tamen amare non definit, imò stimulante amore, castigat. Obliti estis consolationis, quae vobis tanquam filiis loquitur: Fili mi, ne parum cures disciplinam Domini, neque fatiscas ab eo redargutus. Quem enim diligit Dominus, castigat; flagellat verò omnem filium, quem recipit. Si disciplinam sustinetis, tanquam filiis vobis utitur. Quis enim filius est, quem non in disciplina pater retineat? Hebr. XII. 5. 6. 7. Ita verò castigat, ut etiam benignè alat, benedictionibus corporalibus & spiritualibus macket. Quis pater à filio panem rogatus lapidem, & piscem rogatus serpentem reddet? &c. Si vos mali nostis bona dona dare liberis vestris, multò magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum S. petentibus ipsum,
units.tr: XCI. The fruits of adoption are very many and very great. For the sons of God are received into the family and house of the same God, and are regarded as children. "With everlasting love have I loved you; therefore with loving-kindness have I drawn you" (Jer. 31:3). And although he chastens them, he does not cease to love them; indeed, it is love that urges him to chasten. "You have forgotten the exhortation which speaks to you as to children: My son, do not despise the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when you are rebuked by him. For whom the Lord loves he chastens, and he scourges every son whom he receives. If you endure chastening, God deals with you as with sons; for what son is there whom the father does not correct?" (Heb. 12:5–7). And he so chastens that he also kindly nourishes them, and blesses them with bodily and spiritual blessings. "Which of you, if his son asks bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks a fish, will he give him a serpent?" etc. "If you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him."

units.la: Ejusdem fructus.
units.tr: The fruits of the same.

units.la: Haec dicta adoptio omnium gentium: strictè dicta Ecclesiae N. T. strictissimè dicta caelestis gloriae.
units.tr: This adoption, so called, belongs to all nations; taken strictly it belongs to the Church of the New Testament; taken most strictly it belongs to heavenly glory.

units.la: Luc. XI. 11. 12. 13. Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, qui benedixit vobis omni benedictione spirituali in supercoelestibus, Eph. I. 3. Idem filiis suis scutum est contra hostes quosvis, Genes. XV. 1. & eorum, ceu filiorum miseretur, Psal. CIII. 13. Tum familiariter Deus cum filiis agit, & iis se ut paterfamilias familiae, manifestat. Qui me diligit, &c. ego diligam ipsum, & manifestabo me ipsum ei, Joh. XIV. 21. Et interioris admissionis eosdem facit. Habent enim accessum liberum ad eum, Ephes. III. 12. accedentes cum fiducia ad thronum gratiae, Heb. IV. 16. & clamantes, Abba, Pater, Rom. VIII. 15. Accedit coelestis eorundem cognatio. Non pudet enim Christum nos nominare fratres, Hebr. II. 11. & Deum Patrem uti suum, ita etiam nostrum, Joh. XX. 17. Etiam Angelos uti conservos, Apoc. XIX. 10. ita fratres in eodem Patre salutant. Sed & rerum omnium domini sunt. Omnia sunt vestra, sive Paulus, sive Apollo, sive Cephas, sive mundus, sive vita, sive mors, &c. 1. Cor. III. 21. Insuper, si filii, etiam haeredes, haeredes Dei, & coheredes Christi sunt, Rom. VIII. 17. Cujus proin consummata fruitio adoptionis nomine ibidem venit. Nunc filii Dei sumus. Sed nondum manifestum est, quod erimus; 1. Joh. III. 2. Cumque non omnes filii paternarum facultatum haeredes sint, uti Ismael, Genes. XXI. 10. diserte excluditur, sunt filii Dei omnes aequo jure & ex asse haeredes, Reges & Sacerdotes Deo, Apoc. V. 10. omnes primogeniti, Heb. XII. 23. declarantur. Denique adoptio spiritualis laetitiae omnis nutricula est. Nam Spiritus adoptionis tum testis internus adoptionis nostrae, Rom. VIII. 16. tum sigillum in diem redemptionis, Ephes. IV. 30. tum arrhabo haereditatis nostrae ibid. I. 14. est. Quae laetitia interrumpi & obnubilari haud raro potest, at abolleri & extingui penitus non potest. Manet enim causa laetificans, paternus Dei amor: manet fons perennis laetitiae gratia fidei, quae nunquam deficit, Luc. XXII. 32. spes, Rom. V. 5. charitas Dei; aestimatio portionis nobis destinatae, denique cordis fidelis, & bonae conscientiae interrogatio illa, 1. Pet. III. 21. qua Deum Patrem de lecutura post lachrymas consitas laetissima messe fidenter interrogare, & eandem certo expectare potest. Qui seminarunt cum lachrymis, cum exultatione metent, Psal. CXXVI. 5.
units.tr: Luc. 11:11, 12, 13. Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places (Eph. 1:3). He is also a shield to his sons against any enemies (Gen. 15:1), and has compassion on them as a father has compassion on his sons (Ps. 103:13). Then God deals familiarly with his sons, and reveals himself to them as a householder to his household. "He who loves me, etc., I will love him, and will manifest myself to him" (John 14:21). And he makes them admitted to the inner presence. For they have free access to him (Eph. 3:12), coming with confidence to the throne of grace (Heb. 4:16), and crying, Abba, Father (Rom. 8:15). Their heavenly kinship is also added. For Christ is not ashamed to call us brothers (Heb. 2:11), and calls God his Father and also our Father (John 20:17). They greet even the Angels as fellow-servants (Rev. 19:10), and as brothers in the same Father. They are also lords of all things: "All things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death", etc. (1 Cor. 3:21). Moreover, "if sons, then also heirs, heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ" (Rom. 8:17). The full enjoyment of this adoption is also referred to by that name in the same place. "Now we are the sons of God, but it does not yet appear what we shall be" (1 John 3:2). And since not all sons are heirs of their father's property, as Ishmael is expressly excluded (Gen. 21:10), all the sons of God are declared to be equal heirs by the same right and in full, kings and priests to God (Rev. 5:10), all firstborn (Heb. 12:23). Finally, spiritual adoption is the nurse of all joy. For the Spirit of adoption is both the inner witness of our adoption (Rom. 8:16), and the seal for the day of redemption (Eph. 4:30), and the pledge of our inheritance (Eph. 1:14). This joy can often be interrupted and clouded over, but it cannot be wholly destroyed or extinguished. For the cause of joy remains, the Father's love of God; there remains the perennial spring of joy, the grace of faith, which never fails (Luke 22:32); hope (Rom. 5:5); the love of God; the estimate of the portion destined for us; and finally, the faithful heart's and the good conscience's appeal (1 Pet. 3:21), by which it can confidently ask God the Father for the most joyful harvest that will follow the tears sown, and can surely await it. "They who sow in tears shall reap in joy" (Ps. 126:5).

units.la: XCII. Sicut Adoptio justificationis fructus: ita libertas spiritualis adoptionis comes est.
units.tr: XCII. Just as adoption is the fruit of justification, so spiritual liberty accompanies adoption.

units.la: Quae duplex est, essentialis & accidentalis. Essentialis libertas est immunitas a maledictione legis & servitute peccati. De qua Paulus: Nulla amplius est condemnatio in iis, qui sunt in Christo Jesu. Nam lex spiritus vitae, qui est in Jesu Christo liberavit me a lege peccati & mortis, Rom. VIII. 1. 2. Peccatum vobis non dominabitur, cap. VI. 12. 14. Justificati enim omnes liberantur a lege peccati & mortis hactenus, ut peccatum iis non dominetur, & ut in judicium non veniant. Id enim fit per legem spiritus vitae in Christo, hoc est, per vim & potentiam meriti Christi, propter quod jus habet nos postulandi ceu haereditatem suam, pretio sanguinis emptam, & per Spiritum suum nos occupandi, qui legem Dei cordibus inscribat, ut in ipsum credamus, & coram eo, ut filii & liberi ambulemus, atque habentes cor purum, veritate & justitia delectemur. Haec libertas omnium fidelium est, & in quovis Ecclesiae statu obtinet. Quotquot enim justificantur, a maledictione legis reatu & dominio peccati liberantur, & justitiae servi fiunt. Quae liberatio ipsa justificatio est.
units.tr: This liberty is twofold, essential and accidental. Essential liberty is immunity from the curse of the law and from the slavery of sin. Of this Paul says: There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death, Rom. 8.1, 2. Sin shall not have dominion over you, ch. 6.12, 14. For all who are justified are freed from the law of sin and death to the extent that sin does not have dominion over them and they do not come into judgment. This happens through the law of the Spirit of life in Christ, that is, through the power and efficacy of the merit of Christ. On account of this merit he has the right to claim us as his own inheritance, bought with the price of his blood, and to take possession of us through his Spirit, who writes the law of God on our hearts, so that we believe in him and walk before him as sons and free men, and, having a pure heart, delight in truth and righteousness. This liberty belongs to all the faithful and holds in every state of the Church. For all who are justified are freed from the curse of the law, from the guilt and dominion of sin, and become servants of righteousness. This liberation itself is justification.

units.la: XCIII. Libertas Accidentalis major ille libertatis gradus est, quae in Novo Testamento obtinet, & Christiana appellari solet.
units.tr: XCIII. Accidental liberty is that greater degree of liberty which obtains in the New Testament and is usually called Christian.

units.la: Est autem immunitas vel exemptio, ab omni praecepto carnali & legis, hominumque legis custodum imperio. De quo Christus: Si veritas vos liberaverit, vere liberi eritis, Joh. VIII. 36. Quando enim datur Spiritus Filii, simul cognitio veritatis illius, quod non tantum propter Christum a maledictione legis & peccati dominio, sed etiam a servitute legali, & oneribus iis, quibus Patres ad tempus correctionis usque constricti erant, immunes, adeoque vere & plene consummate liberi fimus, datur. Qua de libertate N. T. plura Loc. XX. 51. 52. 53. diximus.
units.tr: It is immunity or exemption from every carnal precept of the law and from the authority of men who guard the law. Of this Christ says: If the truth shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed, John 8.36. For when the Spirit of the Son is given, at the same time the knowledge of that truth is given: that we are free not only through Christ from the curse of the law and the dominion of sin, but also from legal servitude and from those burdens by which the Fathers were bound until the time of correction. So we are truly and fully free, and perfectly so. We have spoken more about this liberty of the New Testament at Loc. XX. 51, 52, 53.

units.la: XCIV. Libertas Christiana tribus maxime regulis dirigitur.
units.tr: XCIV. Christian liberty is directed by three main rules.

units.la: Prima est, quod libertas non libido vel licentia sit, & in bono, non in malo distringi debeat. Ignorant enim Christianam libertatem, & servi peccatis servi corruptionis sunt, qui cum Antinomis & Libertinis eam in libidinem convertunt. Licet enim Ecclesia non sub lege, sed sub gratia sit, non tamen sub gratia esset, si sanctificationis expers esset. Lex illa, quae olim damnavit, ad peccandum proritavit, & occidit, nunc iis, qui sub gratia sunt, fit lex spiritus vitae, Rom. VIII. 2. quae nos Spiritui Christi addicit ad vivificandum nos in Christo: sermo infusus, Jac. I. 21. quia ejus veritas & bonitas ad conscientiam omnem manifestatur, testem conscientiam habet, & verbum & lex conscientiae est: Praeceptum novum, quod verum est in vobis, 1. Joh. II. 8. hoc est, lex Regis Christi, quam faciendo subjicimur Regi Christo & Spiritui ejus, & ad quam cordi nostro inscribendam Christus nobis Rex datus est, & ipse nos in populum & peculium suum emit, ut in nobis condecoraretur. Ita Spiritus inscribens legem est Spiritus spontaneitatis, Psal. LI. 14. quem qui habet, is ingenuus, sua sponte, se ipsum magis magisque ad bonum impellens, superextendens & elargiens, Esaj. XXXII. 8. Non enim Christianus est ex lex Deo, licet lege, in conscientiam hominum solutus, sed legem habens Christi, 1. Cor. IX. 21. Illi enim Christus ipse: fides sua & amor salutis, justitia donata, vita, laetitia & certitudo salutis, quae bona in Christo acceperunt, lex sunt; & illa ipsa quidem lex, quam Moses protulit, & omnis Scriptura V. & N. T. explicat.
