units.tr: The first is that liberty is not lust or licence, and it ought to be restrained for good, not for evil. Those who do not know Christian liberty, and who are slaves of sins, are slaves of corruption; they turn it into lust together with the Antinomians and Libertines. For although the Church is not under the law but under grace, it would not be under grace if it were without sanctification. That law which once condemned, which provoked to sin and killed, now becomes for those who are under grace the law of the Spirit of life, Rom. 8.2. It binds us to the Spirit of Christ, to quicken us in Christ. It is the implanted word, James 1.21, because its truth and goodness are made manifest to every conscience; it has conscience as its witness, and it is the word and law of conscience: a new commandment, which is true in you, 1 John 2.8. That is, it is the law of Christ the King, by doing which we are subjected to Christ the King and to his Spirit. For the writing of this law on our hearts Christ was given to us as King, and he himself redeemed us as his people and peculiar possession, so that he might be adorned in us. Thus the Spirit who writes the law is the Spirit of willingness, Ps. 51.14, and whoever has him is free-born, of his own accord, impelling himself more and more to good, extending and enlarging himself, Isa. 32.8. For the Christian is not without law to God [ἄνομος θεοῦ], though he is released from the law in the conscience of men, but he is under the law of Christ, legem habens Christi, 1 Cor. 9.21. For Christ himself is his law: his faith and love of salvation, the righteousness given to him, life, joy and certainty of salvation, these blessings which they have received in Christ, are the law. And this is indeed the very law which Moses set forth and which all Scripture of the Old and New Testament explains.

units.la: XCV. Secunda libertatis regula est, ut eam in usu rerum indifferentium fides & charitas dirigat.
units.tr: XCV. The second rule of liberty is that in the use of indifferent things it be directed by faith and love.

units.la: Quicquid enim non ex fide est, peccatum est, Rom. XIV. 23. Et scientia inflat, charitas vero aedificat, 1. Cor. VIII. 1. Fieri igitur possunt, quaecunque licent, dummodo, ut fiant, expeexpediat, & fidei atque charitati Dei & proximi non obsint. Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν; ἀλλ' οὐ πάντα συμφέρει. Omnia mihi licent (indifferentia, quæ ad imaginem Dei non faciunt, ut vel si adsint, eam constituant, vel si absint, destruant, & de quibus nullum præceptum Dei extat) sed non omnia expediunt, ibid. VI. 12. Omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia ædificant, ibid. cap. X. 23. Cavendum ne libertas nostra vel nobis, vel proximo noceat. Nobis nocet, cùm in amorem Dei incurrit. Inutile autem nobis est, si abusu libertatis Deo dissimiles fiamus, & non omnibus votis, desideriis, studiis & factis nostris ad Deum & gloriam ejus contendermus. Ita si rem, quam liberè amare possumus, finem & bonum nostrum fecerimus, non hic usus, sed abusus libertatis est, quia sic Dei gloria, & pietas nostra violatur. Proximo nocet, quando ille non ædificatur, sed destruitur. Velut si infirmo fratri scandalum offeratur, quo ille propter nos contristetur, vel ædificetur ad faciendum aliquid δια σκανδαλον, vel non in fide, vel si propter nos blasphemetur nomen Dei, atque ita impediatur aliquis, quò minùs ad Regnum Dei accedat.
units.tr: Whatever is not of faith is sin, Rom. 14.23. And knowledge puffs up, but love edifies, 1 Cor. 8.1. Therefore whatever is lawful may be done, provided that, in doing it, it is expedient and does not hinder faith, or the love of God and of neighbour. "All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient" [Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν; ἀλλ' οὐ πάντα συμφέρει], 1 Cor. 6.12. Things are lawful for me (indifferent things, which do not bear on the image of God, so that they either constitute it if present or destroy it if absent, and concerning which no command of God exists), but not all things are expedient, ibid. "All things are lawful for me, but not all things edify", ibid. 10.23. Care must be taken lest our liberty harm either ourselves or our neighbour. It harms us when it lapses into an inordinate love. It is also useless to us if, by abusing our liberty, we become unlike God and do not direct all our vows, desires, pursuits and deeds to God and his glory. Thus if we make a thing, which we may freely love, our end and good, this is not a use but an abuse of liberty, because thereby the glory of God and our piety are violated. It harms our neighbour when he is not built up but torn down. For example, if a stumbling block is put before a weak brother, by which he is grieved on our account, or is built up to do something through stumbling [δια σκανδαλον], or not in faith, or if the name of God is blasphemed on our account, and so someone is hindered from coming closer to the kingdom of God.

units.la: XCVI. Tertia regula est, ne libertas Christiana fiat prætextus dominationis, quasi propterea, quia hoc vel illud facere, vel non facere licet, etiam leges conscientiam obligantes ferre & ad earum obedientiam alios compellere liceat; vel illi pati debeant, ut compellantur, & potestatem leges ferendi sibi arrogantibus parere teneantur. Omnia mihi licent, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος. sed ego non redigar sub ullius potestatem, 1. Cor. VI. 12. Libertas enim insigne bonum est, quod non debemus pati nobis eripi. In libertate, in quam Christus vos asserunt, στήκετε, & non iterum jugo servitutis constringimini, Gal. V. 1. Non enim liberum nobis est libertate uti vel non uti, quia Christus emendo nos uni soli que sibi Domino nos subjecit. Qui igitur in libertate non stat, & servus hominum fit, is à Christo deficit, eum dominum abnegat, ab hæreditate & domo ejus, tanquam non emptus ab eo se separat. Non in eo ξυλον libertas nostra consistit, quòd non circumcidimur, tempora non discernimus, elementa non tractamus, sed in eo, quòd Christum dominum agnoscimus, ei servimus, & jugum ejus libentes volentésque suscipimus. XCVII. Ejusdem justificationis fructus insignis etiam Conscientiæ tranquillitas est. Nam justificati ex fide pacem habemus apud Deum, per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, Rom. V. 1. Accedamus cum vero corde, in fiducia fidei, ῥαντισμένοι τας καρδιας ἀπὸ συνειδήσεως πονηρᾶς aspersione (sanguinis Christi) purgati à mala conscientia, Hebr. X. 22. Quæ & ipsa sic omnium credentium in quovis Ecclesiæ statu est, ut tamen quoad τελειωσιν consummationem solorum fidelium N. T. sit. Eandem liber ad Deum accessus comitatur. Justificati per Christum τῇ πίστει accessum habemus, qui fide fit, in gratiam hanc, in qua stamus, & gloriamur in spe gloriæ Dei, Rom. V. 2. In quo habemus libertatem loquendi, & aditum cum fiducia per fidem ejus, Ephes. III. 12. Accessus ille in confidentia ad Deum jus præbet ad petendum à Deo id omne, quod filiorum Dei est. Nam in Christo habemus justitiam & causam vitæ æternæ & benedictionum omnium. Qua libertate utimur, & ita accedimus ad Deum in confidentia, quando in ipsum credimus. Credentes quippe ut eum credimus, quòd in eo remissionem peccatorum, vitam æternam & omnem benedictionem habeamus. Is enim & peccata nostra expiavit, & regnum nobis acquisivit. Excipit filialis timor, juxta illud Davidis: Apud te est condonatio, ut timearis, reverenter cola ris, Psal. CXXX. 4. Quem nova obedientia comitatur. Justificati per fidem permanebimusne in peccato, ut gratia auctior fiat? Absit. Imò in nova vita ambulemus, Rom. VI. 1. 2. 4. Cùm enim justificati peccato moriamur, fieri nequit, quin justitiæ vivamus, quia mori peccato est vivere Deo & justitiæ. Revera enim non morimur peccato, neque peccare desinimus, nisi resipiscamus, hoc est, Deum amare, & eidem obedire incipiamus. Per primum actum amoris Dei, qui fides est, vetustum hominem mortificamus. Sicut tenebrae per lucem, color ruber & sanguineus per niveum: ita Regnum Sathanæ per Regnum Spiritus; mala voluntas per bonam, tum in initio, tum in profectu extirpatur. Fructus hos Certitudo gratiæ præsentis & futuræ claudit. Nam si, cùm inimici essemus, reconciliati fuimus Deo per mortem Filii ejus, multò magis reconciliati servabimur per vitam ipsius, Rom. V. 10. Persuasus sum, neque mortem, neque vitam, neque Angelos, neque Principatus, neque potestates, neque præsentia, neque futura posse nos separare à charitate Dei, quæ est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro, ibid. VIII. 38. 39.
units.tr: XCVI. The third rule is that Christian liberty must not become a pretext for domination, as if, because it is lawful to do or not to do this or that, it were therefore also permitted to enact laws binding the conscience and to compel others to obey them; or as if others must allow themselves to be compelled and be obliged to obey those who arrogate to themselves the power of making laws. "All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anyone" [ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος], 1 Cor. 6.12. For liberty is a remarkable good, which we ought not to allow to be taken from us. "Stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage", Gal. 5.1 [στήκετε]. For it is not for us to choose whether to use liberty or not, since Christ, by buying us, has subjected us to himself alone as Lord. Therefore whoever does not stand in liberty and becomes a slave of men, he falls away from Christ, denies him as Lord, and separates himself from his inheritance and house, as one not bought by him. Our liberty does not consist in this, that we are not circumcised, do not observe times, and do not handle the elements; it consists in this, that we acknowledge Christ as Lord, serve him, and take up his yoke willingly and gladly. XCVII. A notable fruit of the same justification is also tranquillity of conscience. For we who are justified by faith have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, Rom. 5.1. "Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience" [ῥαντισμένοι τας καρδιας ἀπὸ συνειδήσεως πονηρᾶς], that is, by the sprinkling (of the blood of Christ), "purged from an evil conscience", Heb. 10.22. This tranquillity belongs to all believers in every state of the Church, yet in its full consummation [τελειωσιν] it belongs only to the faithful of the New Testament. Free access to God accompanies this peace. Being justified through Christ, we have access by faith [τῇ πίστει] into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God, Rom. 5.2. In him we have boldness of speech and access with confidence through his faith, Eph. 3.12. This access in confidence to God gives the right to ask of God all that belongs to the sons of God. For in Christ we have righteousness, the cause of eternal life and of all blessings. We use this liberty, and so we approach God with confidence when we believe in him. For in believing we believe that in him we have remission of sins, eternal life and every blessing. For he both expiated our sins and acquired the kingdom for us. Filial fear accompanies this, according to that saying of David: "There is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared", Ps. 130.4; we reverently worship him. New obedience accompanies it. Justified by faith, shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound? God forbid. Rather let us walk in newness of life, Rom. 6.1, 2, 4. For since we, being justified, die to sin, it cannot be that we do not live to righteousness, because to die to sin is to live to God and to righteousness. Indeed we do not die to sin, nor cease to sin, unless we repent, that is, unless we begin to love God and to obey him. Through the first act of the love of God, which is faith, we mortify the old man. As darkness is driven out by light, and a red or blood colour by snow-white, so the kingdom of Satan is driven out by the kingdom of the Spirit, and evil will by good, both at the beginning and in progress. Certainty of present and future grace completes these fruits. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more shall we be saved by his life, Rom. 5.10. I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, can separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord, Rom. 8.38, 39.

units.la: LOCUS VICESIMUS TERTIUS. De GRATIA SANCTIFICATIONIS.
units.tr: LOCUS TWENTY-THIRD. On the GRACE OF SANCTIFICATION.

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: Justificationis & Sanctificationis nexus. 1. Vox קדוש secretum ab impuritate, & sanctificatio hoc loco renovationem ad imaginem Dei continuatam notat. 2. Sanctificationis definitio. 3. Ejusdem à vocatione & justificatione differentia. 4. Pontificiorum justificationem & sanctificationem confundentium elenchus. 5. Syncretistarum fucus, quod hic de vocibus, non de re Pontificios inter & Evangelicos dissensus sit, discutitur. 6. Sanctificationis necessitas. 7. Quæ non consolationem afflictorum minuit, sed ad gaudium fidelium, excitationem torpentium, hostium veritatis convictionem, & cognitionem causarum studii bonorum operum facit. 8. Neque per sanctificationis necessitatem homines legi Dei iterum subjiciuntur, vel gratiæ Dei jacturam faciunt. 9. Deus solus Spiritu suo sanctificat. 10. Et sanctificat hominem totum, spiritum, corpus & animam. 11. Exemplar sanctitatis hominum Dei sanctitas est. 12. Norma ejusdem verbum Dei est. 13. Atque illud tum legis, tum Evangelii, sed lato cum discrimine modi, finis & operationis. 14. Essentia ejusdem in renovatione, seu instauratione hominis ad imaginem Dei consistit. 15. Pelagianorum & Socinianorum in sola actuum emendatione eam collocantium, elenchus. 16. Argumentis eorum fit satis. 17. Sanctificatio continuam praxin & exercitationem, non tam corporalem, quàm spiritualem habet. 18. Quæ in resipiscentia & nova obedientia consistit. Resipiscentiæ & Pœnitentiæ voces. 19. Resipiscentiæ definitio. 20. Ejus partes agnitio peccatorum, confessio eorundem, dolor & tristitia, imploratio remissionis peccatorum, & emendationis vitæ serium propositum sunt. Agnitio peccatorum explicatur. 21. Eorundem humilis confessio, Deo facienda. 22. Etiam hominibus certa conditione confitenda sunt. 23. Confessio auricularis refellitur. 24. Argumenta, quibus eandem Pontificii confirmare conantur, ad partes vocata. 25. Dolor & tristitia resipiscentium. 26. Timor gehennæ, quem Pontificii Attritionem appellant, per se non est resipiscentiæ pars, vel ad eam dispositio. 27. Objectiones contrariæ diluuntur. 28. Tristitia secundum Deum salutaris est. 29. Non sic voluntarius dolor est, ut terrores à lege incussos excludat. 30. Contritio sine fide in Christum non est salutaris. 31. Neque tamen resipiscentiæ strictè sumptæ fides pars est. 32. Tristitia secundum Deum humilis remissionis peccatorum imploratio comitatur. 33. Serium emendandæ vitæ propositum resipiscentiam absolvit. 34. Non tamen tempore à reliquis resipiscentiæ partibus differt, 35. Resipiscentia non meretur salutem, sed cum hujus spe, ceu τεκμήριον[?] ejusdem, connexa est. 36. Resipiscendum est homini per totam vitam. 37. Etiam sera pœnitentia vera esse potest. 38. Ejus signa exteriora explicantur. 39. Circa resipiscentiam hæreses Judæorum, Libertinorum & Implacabilium, Montanistarum, Novatianorum & Novatianensium perstringuntur. 40. Ecclesiæ circa resipiscentiam sententia media est, & resipiscendum omnino esse, & resipiscentibus veniam apud Deum paratam esse. 41. Argumentis Novatianorum occurritur. 42. Pontificiorum circa pœnitentiam errores. 43. Socinianorum circa eandem hæreses. 44. Nova obedientia exercetur per bona opera, quæ definiuntur. 45. Operis bonitas concursum omnium causarum requirit. 46. Primò fluere debent ex rectâ voluntatis habitu, ceu principio. Quæ in homine integro à natura integra fluxit: in peccatore à sola gratia Dei fluit. 47. Bonum igitur opus edi jam nisi ab iis, qui in statu gratiæ sunt, nequit. 48. Secundo bonum opus legi Divinæ conformandum est. 49. Tertiò rectitudinem circumstantiarum requirit. 50. Quartò ex amore Dei fluere debet. 51. Quintò ex fide in Christum oritur. 52. Sextò cum intentione recti finis exerceri debet. 53. His notis bona opera Christianorum ab operibus Pharisæorum & gentilium discernenda sunt. 54. Irregenitorum opera licèt quoad officium, seu actum externum bona esse possint, quoad finem tamen & reliquas causas bona esse non possunt. 55. Argumenta contraria dissolvuntur, 56. Pontificiorum jactata bona opera perstringuntur. 57. Ne fidelium quidem bona opera, ad legis Divinæ rigorem exacta vitio omni carent. 58. Argumentis Pontificiorum pro perfectione operum quorundam bonorum occurritur. 59. Bonorum operum necessitas. 60. Ubi infamec scopuli Libertinorum & Antinomorum vitandi sunt. 61. Augustanorum Theologorum circa necessitatem bonorum operum scrupuli minuuntur. 62. Bona opera vitam æternam non efficiunt. 63. Ac multò minùs merentur. 64. Ne quidem per Dei gratiam, & Christi meritum, qui Tridentinorum fucus est. 65. Vocibus merendi & meriti, quo sensu veteres usi sint? 66. Meriti requisita septem à Bellarmino prodita ad examen revocantur. 67. Veriora meriti ✻ panduntur. 68. Quibus plane justificatorum opera destituuntur. 69. Aliis etiam argumentis merita operum profligantur. 70. Nec ex congruo, nec ex condigno, nec ex pacto gratiæ augmentum vel gloriam, ejusque augmentum merentur. 71. Argumenta Pontificiorum pro meritis operum diluuntur. 72. Vana igitur omnis in meritis operum collocata fiducia. 73. Argumenta ad studium bonorum operum inflammantia. 74. Eorum præcipuæ species, Vita Christiana & Precatio sunt. Vita Christiana definitur, ejusque exemplar Christus imitandus, explicatur. 75. In abnegatione sui, tolerantia crucis & functione vocationis industria potissimùm consistit. Abnegatio sui multiplex distinguitur. 76. Præcipua ejus species carnis suæ, seu corruptionis, quæ in carne est, abnegatio tum impietatis omnis. 77. Tum concupiscentiarum hujus seculi. 78. Incentiva ad abnegationem sui ipsius. 79. Crucis tolerantia. 80. Ejus necessitas. 81. Nec non utilitas multiplex. 82. In ea & sensus acerbitatis & lætitia spiritualis esse debet. 83. Quo nomine patientia Christiana à Philosophica distinguitur. 84. Vocationis propriæ functio industria Christianæ etiam vitæ pars est. 85. Quæ etiam aliud agentium excludit. 86. Precatio definitur, ejusque necessitas explicatur. 87. Cui non obstat, quòd non omnia precibus nostris adipiscimur, & Deo desideria & necessitates nostræ sine monitore notæ sunt; quia Deus precari nos jussit, & precum maxima utilitas est. 88. Precum piarum requisita sunt, ut solum Deum oremus, ut magna cum reverentia & meditatione Majestatis & gloriæ ejus oremus: ut in oratione desideria cordis nostri Deo exponamus. 89. Ut oremus nonnisi in nomine Christi, vera fide in Christum & charitate; in Spiritu & veritate; juxta verbum & voluntatem Dei; denique cum humilitate & sensu indigentiæ & miseriæ nostræ. 90. Precationis author in nobis Spiritus S. est. 91. Precantes Deus exaudit; & certa semper exauditio est ad salutem nostram. 92. Neque tamen precatio exauditionem Dei meretur. 93. Precationis species. 94. Gratiarum actio. 95. Precatio seu petitio bonorum. 96. Deprecatio malorum, seu petitio auxilii Divini in malis. 97. Intercessio pro aliis. 98. Cum precatione imprecatio pugnat, quia nec sibi, nec sine speciali Dei mandato, aliis imprecari licet. 99. Oratio quævis vel mentalis, vel vocalis est. 100. Vocali Cantus accidit, cujus usus exponitur. 101. Et abusus, in cantu inprimis Gregoriano, & Musica scenica & theatrica Papali, perstringitur. 102. Oratio igitur vel subitanea seu ejaculatoria, vel præmeditata & composita. 103. Vel privata, vel publica. 104. Vel ordinaria, quæ statis vicibus, & certa ac constanti ratione peragitur; ad quam Horarum Canonicarum usus minimè referri debet; 105. Vel extraordinaria, speciali gravique de causa, privatim vel publicè ultra consuetum ordinem suscepta est. 106. Orationis locus sub N.T. quivis esse potest, neque ullus alio sacratior est. 107. Omni tempore & semper orare jubemur, sed sensu congruo, non rei, quæ præcipitur, naturæ, vel vitæ humanæ conditioni & officiis repugnante. 108. Precandi ordo certus vix præscribi potest. 109. Precantium gestus certis regulis informantur. 110. Oratio Dominica & formula orandi, eo ordine, iisdemque verbis, quo Christus concepit, usurpanda, & exemplar precationum reliquarum omnium est. 111. Ejus partes tres sunt, compellatio ejus, ad quem dirigitur, corpus & clausula. Compellatur Pater noster, qui in Cœlis est. 112. Corpus sex petitionibus constat, quarum tres priores Deum, posteriores riores nos concernunt. 113. Petitio prima, ut sanctificetur nomen Dei, 114. Secunda, ut adveniat Regnum Dei, 115. Tertia, ut voluntas Dei Patris fiat in terra, sicut fit in Coelo. 116. Quarta, ut Deus nobis det panem nostrum ἐπιούσιον, quæ vox explicatur. 117. Petitionis illius sensus. 118. Quinta, ut Deus remittat nobis debita nostra, sicut nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. 119. Sexta, ne Deus nos inducat in tentationem. 120. Sed ut liberet nos à malo. 121. Orationis clausula, & γνησίως doxologiæ. 122. Doxologiæ explicatio. 123. Votum & fiducia precantis acclamatione particulæ Amen declaratur. 124. Oratione Dominica sic utendum nobis est, ut aliis etiam uti fas piumque sit. 125. Incentiva ad precandum. 126. Precibus extraordinariis jejunium & festivitas accidit. Jejunium definitur. 127. A Deo præceptum est, & exerceri debet, non ut virtus, vel bonum opus, vel cultus Dei in se, sed ut virtutis adjumentum & humiliationis signum. 128. In jejunio exercitatio duplex, corporalis & spiritualis distinguitur; quarum illa sine hac mera abominatio est. 129. Jejunii utilitas. 130. Vel legale, vel Evangelicum est. 131. In abstinentia à cibo, potu, lautitiis & vitæ solatiis, non in ciborum delectu consistit. 132. Argumenta pro Xerophagia & delectu ciborum discutiuntur. 133. Jejunii tempus in specie in Verbo Dei definitum non est, at in genere definitum illud est, quo Sponsus ab Ecclesia abesse. Nulla proin stata jejunandi tempora esse debent. 134. Argumenta pro jejuniis statis solvuntur. 135. Jejunium privatum vel publicum est. 136. Jejuna Pontificiorum de jejuniis doctrina nil pietatis vel religionis habet. 137. Sicut jejunium in luctu, ita in lætitia & gratiarum actione festivitas locum habet. 138. Festa alia Veteris, alia Novi Testamenti sunt. 139. Pontificiorum circa festa, velut necessario ob mysterium & sacratiore, atque ad cultum efficaciore tempore celebranda superstitio retunditur: 140. Objectiones eorundem elisæ. 141. Ad precationem etiam votum referri debet, quod definitur & explicatur. 142. Votum vel generale & commune, vel speciale & singulare est; & utrique etiam in N. T. locus est. 143. Vovendum soli Deo non ulli homini est. 144. Vota nonnisi legitima Deo placent, & qualia legitima sint, exponitur. 145. Neque quidvis voveri potest, sed solum illud, quod vel in genere præceptum est, & per votum determinari potest; vel in specie præceptum est. 146. Bellarmini assertio, quod nec utile, nec necessarium sit, vovere ea, quæ in præcepto sunt, refellitur. 147. Vota legitimè nuncupata religiosè exsolvi debent. 148. Non item ea, quæ honori Dei & saluti nostræ & proximi derogant. 149. Jus vota confirmandi & relaxandi iniquè sibi Papa arrogat. 150. Sanctificatio in hac vita imperfecta est, & ob diversa regenitorum principia, Spiritum & carnem luctæ eorundem spirituali cum carne locum relinquit. 151. Lucta spiritualis definitur & explicatur. 152. Luctator principalis Deus, inprimis Spiritus S. est. 153. Minus principales regeniti sunt, non irregeniti, quorum lucta multum ab ea, quam regeniti sustinent, differt. 154. Regenitorum luctatorum Antagonistæ alii amici, velut Deus; alii hostes professi sunt, velut Sathanas, caro & mundus sunt. 155. Luctatores utrique, regeniti & eorum hostes, suam panopliam habent, quarum illa ex Ephes. VI. 11–19. explicatur. 156. Armatura Sathanæ, carnis & mundi in vi & dolo consistit. 157. Modus luctandi cum Deo, qui amicus est, exponitur. 158. Modus luctandi cum professis hostibus, Sathana, carne & mundo tribus gradibus perficitur, quorum primus est, hosti aggressori primum aditum intercludere: secundus, cum eo gradum conferre, eique strenuè repugnare: tertius, eum in fugam dare & vincere. 159. Luctæ spiritualis causa & utilitas. 160.
units.tr: The bond between justification and sanctification. (1) The Hebrew word for holy [קדוש] denotes separation from impurity, and sanctification here denotes the continuing renewal into the image of God. (2) The definition of sanctification. (3) Its difference from calling and from justification. (4) A refutation of the Papists, who confuse justification and sanctification. (5) The Syncretists' pretence is examined: that the dispute between the Papists and the Evangelicals is about words and not about the thing itself. (6) The necessity of sanctification. (7) This does not diminish the consolation of the afflicted, but it produces joy for the faithful, arouses the sluggish, convicts the enemies of truth, and teaches the causes of zeal for good works. (8) Through the necessity of sanctification, people are not made subject again to the law of God, nor do they lose the grace of God. (9) God alone sanctifies by his Spirit. (10) And he sanctifies the whole man: spirit, body and soul. (11) The pattern of human holiness is the holiness of God. (12) Its rule is the Word of God. (13) And this Word is both of law and of Gospel, but with a wide difference in manner, end and operation. (14) Its essence consists in the renewal, or restoration, of man to the image of God. (15) A refutation of the Pelagians and Socinians, who place sanctification in the mere amendment of actions. (16) Their arguments are answered. (17) Sanctification has a continuing practice and exercise, not so much bodily as spiritual. (18) It consists in repentance and new obedience. The words for repentance [resipiscentia] and penance [poenitentia]. (19) The definition of repentance. (20) Its parts are the recognition of sins, confession of them, sorrow and grief, the entreaty for forgiveness of sins, and the earnest purpose of amending one's life. The recognition of sins is explained. (21) Their humble confession, to be made to God. (22) They are also to be confessed to men under certain conditions. (23) Auricular confession is refuted. (24) The arguments by which the Papists try to confirm it are brought to the point. (25) The sorrow and grief of those who repent. (26) The fear of hell, which the Papists call attrition, is not in itself a part of repentance, nor a disposition towards it. (27) Contrary objections are dissolved. (28) Sorrow according to God is salutary. (29) Sorrow that is voluntary is not such that it excludes the terrors struck by the law. (30) Contrition without faith in Christ is not salutary. (31) Yet faith is not strictly a part of repentance. (32) Sorrow according to God is accompanied by humble entreaty for the remission of sins. (33) The earnest purpose of amending one's life completes repentance. (34) Yet it does not differ in time from the other parts of repentance. (35) Repentance does not merit salvation, but is connected with the hope of it, as a token [τεκμήριον] of it. (36) A person must repent throughout the whole of life. (37) Even late repentance can be true. (38) Its outward signs are explained. (39) Concerning repentance, the heresies of the Jews, the Libertines and the Implacable, the Montanists, and the Novatians and Novatianists are censured. (40) The Church's position on repentance is a middle one: that repentance is altogether necessary, and that pardon is ready with God for those who repent. (41) The arguments of the Novatians are met. (42) The errors of the Papists concerning penance. (43) The Socinian heresies on the same subject. (44) New obedience is exercised through good works, which are defined. (45) The goodness of a work requires the concurrence of all causes. (46) First, good works ought to flow from a right habit of the will, as from a principle. Which, in man in his integrity flowed from an integral nature; in a sinner it flows from the grace of God alone. (47) Therefore a good work cannot now be done except by those who are in a state of grace. (48) Second, a good work must be conformed to the divine law. (49) Third, it requires the rightness of its circumstances. (50) Fourth, it ought to flow from the love of God. (51) Fifth, it arises from faith in Christ. (52) Sixth, it ought to be performed with the intention of a right end. (53) By these marks the good works of Christians must be distinguished from the works of the Pharisees and of the Gentiles. (54) The works of the unregenerate may be good as to their office, or outward act, but as to their end and their other causes they cannot be good. (55) Contrary arguments are dissolved. (56) The boasted good works of the Papists are censured. (57) Even the good works of the faithful, if judged by the strictness of the divine law, are not free from every fault. (58) The Papists' arguments for the perfection of certain good works are met. (59) The necessity of good works. (60) Here the notorious rocks of the Libertines and Antinomians must be avoided. (61) The scruples of the Augustana theologians concerning the necessity of good works are lessened. (62) Good works do not bring about eternal life. (63) And much less do they merit it. (64) Not even through the grace of God and the merit of Christ, which is a pretence of the Tridentines. (65) In what sense did the ancients use the words merit and to merit? (66) The seven requirements of merit set forth by Bellarmine are brought back to examination. (67) The truer account of merit is laid open. (68) By which the works of the justified are wholly deprived of merit. (69) By other arguments too the merits of works are overthrown. (70) They merit neither an increase nor glory, nor an increase of glory, either by congruity, or by condignity, or by the covenant of grace. (71) The Papists' arguments for the merits of works are answered. (72) Vain, therefore, is all trust placed in the merits of works. (73) Arguments that kindle zeal for good works. (74) Their chief kinds are the Christian life and prayer. The Christian life is defined, and its pattern, Christ to be imitated, is explained. (75) It consists chiefly in self-denial, endurance of the cross, and diligence in the duties of one's calling. Self-denial is distinguished in many ways. (76) Its chief kind is the denial of one's flesh, that is, of the corruption which is in the flesh, and of all impiety. (77) And of the lusts of this age. (78) Incentives to self-denial. (79) Endurance of the cross. (80) Its necessity. (81) And its manifold usefulness. (82) In it there ought to be both a sense of bitterness and spiritual joy. (83) By which title Christian patience is distinguished from philosophical patience. (84) Diligence in the proper calling is also a part of the Christian life. (85) Which also excludes busying oneself with other things. (86) Prayer is defined, and its necessity is explained. (87) This is not hindered by the fact that we do not obtain everything by our prayers, and that our desires and needs are known to God without any reminder; because God has commanded us to pray, and the greatest benefit comes from prayer. (88) The requirements of godly prayer are these: that we pray to God alone; that we pray with great reverence and meditation on his majesty and glory; that in prayer we lay the desires of our heart open before God. (89) That we pray only in the name of Christ, with true faith in Christ and love; in the Spirit and in truth; according to the Word and will of God; and finally with humility and a sense of our want and misery. (90) The author of prayer in us is the Holy Spirit. (91) God hears those who pray, and the hearing is always certain for our salvation. (92) Yet prayer does not merit God's hearing. (93) Kinds of prayer. (94) Thanksgiving. (95) Prayer, or request, for good things. (96) Entreaty against evils, or request for divine help in evils. (97) Intercession for others. (98) Cursing is at odds with prayer, because it is not permitted to curse either oneself or others, except by a special command of God. (99) Every prayer is either mental or vocal. (100) Singing is an accompaniment of vocal prayer, and its use is set out. (101) And its abuse, especially in Gregorian chant, and in the papal theatrical and stage music, is censured. (102) Prayer is therefore either sudden, or ejaculatory, or premeditated and composed. (103) Either private or public. (104) Either ordinary, which is performed at set times and in a fixed and constant manner, and to which the use of the canonical hours ought in no way to be referred; (105) or extraordinary, undertaken for a special and weighty cause, privately or publicly, beyond the usual order. (106) Under the New Testament the place of prayer may be any place, and none is more sacred than another. (107) We are commanded to pray at all times and always, but in a sense that is fitting, and not in a way that contradicts the thing commanded, nature, or the condition and duties of human life. (108) A fixed order of praying can scarcely be prescribed. (109) The gestures of those who pray are shaped by certain rules. (110) The Lord's Prayer, and the form of prayer in the order and with the very words in which Christ framed it, is to be used, and it is the pattern of all other prayers. (111) Its parts are three: the address to him to whom it is directed, the body, and the close. The Our Father, who art in heaven, is the address. (112) The body consists of six petitions, of which the first three concern God, and the last three concern us. (113) The first petition: that the name of God be hallowed. (114) The second: that the kingdom of God come. (115) The third: that the will of God the Father be done on earth, as it is done in heaven. (116) The fourth: that God give us our bread, epiousion [ἐπιούσιον], a word which is explained. (117) The sense of that petition. (118) The fifth: that God forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. (119) The sixth: that God not lead us into temptation. (120) But deliver us from evil. (121) The close of the prayer, and the genuine doxology [γνησίως]. (122) Explanation of the doxology. (123) The wish and confidence of the one who prays is declared by the exclamation Amen. (124) We must use the Lord's Prayer in such a way that it is also lawful and right for others to use it. (125) Incentives to prayer. (126) Fasting and festival days accompany extraordinary prayers. Fasting is defined. (127) It is commanded by God, and ought to be practised not as a virtue, or a good work, or worship of God in itself, but as an aid to virtue and a sign of humiliation. (128) In fasting, bodily and spiritual exercise are distinguished; of which the first without the second is mere abomination. (129) The usefulness of fasting. (130) It is either legal or evangelical. (131) It consists in abstinence from food, drink, delicacies and the comforts of life, not in a choice of foods. (132) Arguments for xerophagy and for a choice of foods are discussed. (133) The time of fasting is not defined in particular in the Word of God, but it is defined in general: it is the time when the Bridegroom is absent from the Church. Therefore there ought to be no fixed times for fasting. (134) Arguments for fixed fasts are solved. (135) Fasting is either private or public. (136) The Papists' doctrine of fasts has nothing of piety or religion in it. (137) Just as fasting has its place in mourning, so festivity has its place in joy and in thanksgiving. (138) Some festivals belong to the Old Testament, others to the New Testament. (139) The superstition of the Papists concerning festivals, as if they must necessarily be celebrated at a time set for the sake of the mystery, more sacred, and more effective for worship, is refuted. (140) Their objections are overthrown. (141) A vow must also be referred to prayer; it is defined and explained. (142) A vow is either general and common, or special and singular, and both have a place under the New Testament. (143) A vow is to be made to God alone, not to any man. (144) Only lawful vows please God, and what kinds of vows are lawful is set out. (145) Nor can just anything be vowed, but only what is either commanded in general and can be determined by a vow, or is commanded in particular. (146) Bellarmine's assertion, that it is neither useful nor necessary to vow those things which are in the command, is refuted. (147) Vows lawfully made must be paid religiously. (148) Not so with those which detract from the honour of God, from our salvation, or from our neighbour's. (149) The Pope unjustly arrogates to himself the right to confirm and to annul vows. (150) Sanctification in this life is imperfect, and because of the different principles of the regenerate, the Spirit and the flesh struggle against each other, leaving room for a spiritual struggle with the flesh. (151) The spiritual struggle is defined and explained. (152) The principal combatant is God, above all the Holy Spirit. (153) The regenerate are secondary combatants, not the unregenerate, whose struggle differs much from the struggle which the regenerate undergo. (154) Of the opponents of the regenerate combatants, some are friends, as God; others are professed enemies, as Satan, the flesh and the world. (155) Both the combatants, the regenerate and their enemies, have their own panoply, of which the former is explained from Ephesians 6:11–19. (156) The armour of Satan, of the flesh and of the world consists in force and deceit. (157) The manner of struggling with God, who is a friend, is set out. (158) The manner of struggling with professed enemies, Satan, the flesh and the world, is carried out in three degrees: the first is to cut off the enemy's first approach; the second is to close with him and resist him vigorously; the third is to put him to flight and conquer him. (159) The cause and usefulness of the spiritual struggle. (160)

units.la: I. GRATIAM Justificationis immediatè Gratia Sanctificationis sequitur.
units.tr: I. Sanctification immediately follows justification.

units.la: Quæ licèt in catena aurea salutis non exprimatur, tamen & ut continuatio quædam & progressus Vocationis; & ut fructus Justificationis, & ut inchoatio Glorificationis subintelligitur. Sicut enim vocatio prima hominis novi creatio: ita sanctificatio ejusdem conservatio, & continuata quædam spiritualis creatio est. Et Apostolus Christum nobis factum justitiam & sanctificationem 1. Cor. I. 30. dicens, eam justificationi subjungit. Et illam ab hac diserte derivat, cum post traditam de justificatione doctrinam objectionem adversariorum doctrinæ de justificatione movet & diluit, his verbis: Quid ergo dicemus? Permanebimus in peccato, ut gratia abundet? Neutiquam, Rom. VI. 1.2. &c. Sed & glorificatio imperfecta, perfectæ quædam inchoatio, in sanctificatione est. Nam gloriam Domini speculantes in ejus imaginem transformamur à gloria in gloriam, velut à Domini Spiritu, 2. Cor. III. 18. Est enim gloria hujus vitæ: est & alterius vitæ. Una alteram præcedit, & una alteram pollicetur & apportat. Et in hac quoque vita à gloria ad gloriam, per incrementa renovationis nostræ, progredimur.
units.tr: Although sanctification is not named in the golden chain of salvation, it is understood as a certain continuation and progress of vocation, as the fruit of justification, and as the beginning of glorification. For just as the first calling is the creation of a new man, so sanctification is the preservation of that new man and a continued spiritual creation. The Apostle, saying that Christ was made to us righteousness and sanctification (1 Cor. 1:30), joins sanctification to justification. He also derives the one clearly from the other when, after setting out the doctrine of justification, he raises and answers the objection of its opponents in these words: "What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid" (Rom. 6:1-2, etc.). Moreover, imperfect glorification, a kind of beginning of perfect glorification, is found in sanctification. For beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into his image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18). There is a glory of this life and there is a glory of another life. The one precedes the other, and the one promises and brings the other. In this life too we advance from glory to glory, through the increase of our renewal.

units.la: Justificatio-nis & San-ctificationis nexus.
units.tr: The bond between justification and sanctification.

units.la: II. Sanctus Hebraicè קדוש dicitur. Quæ vox ab impuritate & vilitate secretum notat. Quo sensu Deus absolutè קדוש passim appellatur, quia ab omni planè impuritate & vilitate natura sua separatus est; creatura vero nonnisi κατὰ 1 secundum quid, quatenus Deo in puritate, hoc est, amore & cultu veritatis similis est. Inde גוי קדוש gens sancta, Exod. XIX. 6. assumpta, ut sit Dei, libera à reatu & servitute peccati; Deo similis: Timete Dominum קדשי Sancti ejus, Psal. XXXIV. 10. Et קדש אנשי קדש Viri sanctitatis, hoc est, Sancti, Exod. XXII. 31. dicuntur. Idem Græci ἅγιος & ὅσιος (quæ vox cum חסיד convenit) dicitur, quia à communi & profana gente segregatus Deo & ejus cultui singulariter dicatus est. Utrumque de filiis Dei, factis in Christo verè justis, dicitur, quia procul separati à mundo, licèt in eo degant, profanis judicio, studio, affectibus vitâque dissimiles, Deo & cultui ejus se totos consecraverunt, & Deus eos, ceu peculium suum signavit. Proin etiam קדש & ἁγιότης Sanctitas studium enixum & perpetuum peccata omnia fugiendi, & honesta quæque faciendi ad testandum gratum erga Deum & Christum Redemptorem animum significat. Inde sumpta vox Sanctificationis; quæ πλυσμὸς, hoc loco nec sanctitatis & gloriæ Dei agnitionem, ut in prece Dominica, Sanctificetur nomen tuum: nec rerum ad usum sacrarum separationem; ut in illo: Recordare diei Sabbathi, ut sanctifices illum, Exod. XX. 8. nec redemptionem, ut Exod. XXXI. 13. Heb. II. 11--14. nec universum opus gratiæ, quod in hac vita in peccatore peragitur, & vocationem ac justificationem ipsam includit, ut Ezech. XX. 12. Ephes. V. 26. sed ἀνακαίνωσιν renovationem hominis per Spiritum S. ad imaginem Dei in omni bona cogitatione & opere, adeoque continuatam à vitiis repurgationem & virtutum instaurationem denotat.
units.tr: II. In Hebrew the holy one is called [קדוש]. This word denotes separation from impurity and baseness. In this sense God is commonly called [קדוש], because by his nature he is wholly separated from all impurity and baseness, whereas a creature is holy only in some respect [κατὰ], in a particular sense (secundum quid), insofar as it is like God in purity, that is, in love and worship of the truth. Hence "a holy nation" [גוי קדוש] (Exod. 19:6), taken up so that it may belong to God, free from the guilt and slavery of sin and like God. "Fear the Lord, you his holy ones [קדשי]" (Ps. 34:9). And "men of holiness" [אנשי קדש], that is, holy men (Exod. 22:31), are so called. The Greeks likewise call the same thing [ἅγιος] and [ὅσιος] (a word that corresponds to [חסיד]), because it has been set apart from the common and profane people and singularly dedicated to God and his worship. Both words are said of the sons of God who have been made truly righteous in Christ, because, although they are separated far from the world and dwell in it, they are unlike the profane in judgment, zeal, affections, and way of life, and have consecrated themselves wholly to God and his worship, and God has marked them as his own possession. Accordingly, [קדש] and [ἁγιότης], holiness, signify an earnest and constant zeal to flee all sins and to do all that is honourable, to attest a grateful mind toward God and Christ the Redeemer. Hence the word sanctification is taken; which here means a cleansing [πλυσμὸς], and denotes neither the acknowledgement of God's holiness and glory, as in the Lord's Prayer, "Hallowed be thy name"; nor the setting apart of things for sacred use, as in "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy" (Exod. 20:8); nor redemption, as in Exod. 31:13 and Heb. 2:11-14; nor the whole work of grace that is carried out in a sinner in this life and that includes calling and justification itself, as in Ezek. 20:12 and Eph. 5:26. Rather it denotes the renewal [ἀνακαίνωσιν] of man by the Holy Spirit to the image of God in every good thought and work, and so a continued cleansing from vices and restoration of virtues.

units.la: III. Est enim Gratia Sanctificationis gratiosus ille Dei favor, quo is propter Christum Redemptorem per Spiritum S. naturam corruptam hominis fide justificati secundum verbum Dei magis magisque ad imaginem suam renovat, ut deinceps peccatis moriatur, & vivat justitiæ ad gloriam Dei & salutem æternam hominis sanctificati. Passim eam Deus inculcat, exigit & promittit. Sancti estote, quia & ego sanctus sum. Levit. XIX. 2. Cor mundum crea mihi, Deus, & Spiritum rectum in visceribus meis innova, Psal. LI. 12. Spiritum meum dabo in medio vestri, efficiámque ut in præceptis meis ambuletis, & judicia mea servetis. Ezech. XXXVI. 27. Sanctifica eos in veritate tua. Verbum tuum veritas est, Joh. X VII. 17. Sistite vos Deo, ut ex mortuis viventes, & membra vestra arma justitiæ, Rom. VI. 13. Ne conformemini cum sæculo hoc, sed transformemini renovatione mentis vestræ, ibid. XII. 2. Abluti estis, ἡγιάσθητε sanctificati estis, I. Cor. VI. 11. Deus pacis ἁγιάσαι ὑμᾶς ὁλοτελεῖς sanctificet vos totos, 1. Thess. V. 23. Induistis novum hominem, qui innovatur ad cognitionem, juxta imaginem ejus, qui ipsum creavit, Col. III. 10. Qui sanctus est, sanctificetur adhuc, Apoc. XXII. 11.
units.tr: III. Sanctification is that gracious favour of God by which, for the sake of Christ the Redeemer, through the Holy Spirit, he renews more and more to his own image the corrupt nature of the man who has been justified by faith according to the word of God, so that thereafter he may die to sin and live to righteousness, to the glory of God and the eternal salvation of the sanctified man. God everywhere inculcates, requires, and promises it: "Be holy, for I am holy" (Lev. 19:2). "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me" (Ps. 51:12). "I will put my Spirit in the midst of you, and I will cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my judgments" (Ezek. 36:27). "Sanctify them through your truth; your word is truth" (John 17:17). "Present yourselves to God, as those who are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness" (Rom. 6:13). "Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind" (ibid. 12:2). "You were washed, you were sanctified [ἡγιάσθητε]" (1 Cor. 6:11). "May the God of peace sanctify you wholly [ἁγιάσαι ὑμᾶς ὁλοτελεῖς]" (1 Thess. 5:23). "You have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him" (Col. 3:10). "He who is holy, let him be sanctified still" (Rev. 22:11).

units.la: IV. Sanctificatio hæc à vocatione & justificatione differt. A' vocatione, quia hæc conversionis & regenerationis initium: illa progressus & continuatio; hæc prima spiritualis creatio, illa continuata spiritualis creatio, seu regeneratio nis conservatio, & vitæ spiritualis profectus ad consummationem usque est. A' justificatione non uno modo: Nam justificatio apprehensione & sensu posterior quidem sanctificatione, utpote quæ I. Cor. VI. 11. illi præponitur, & tempore simul cum hac existens; ordine naturæ eandem præcedit. Habentes has promissiones (quòd Deus nobis in Deum & Patrem esse velit, quod in justificatione fit) purificemus nos ab omni pollutione carnis & spiritus, 2. Cor. VII. 1. coll. cum VI. 16. 18. Nam peccatores & inimici justificamur, reconciliati verò sanctificamur. Illa peccatoris, hæc justificati & jam regeniti est: Illa extra nos in Dei judicio per justitiæ alienæ imputationem & peccatorum remissionem peragitur: hæc mortificatione hominis veteris, & vivificatione novi constans in nobis perficitur. Illa ἀπολύτρωσις à merito & redemptione Christi; hæc ab operatione mortis & vitæ Christi proficiscitur. Illius fides manus & instrumentum est, donum justitiæ Christi apprehendens: hujus causa, corda purificans, Act. XV. 9. per charitatem efficax, Gal. V. 6. Illa relatio est, absolutio quippe peccatoris à culpa & immunitas reatus, Actor. XIII. 39. Rom. VIII. 1. hæc alteratio qualitativa, spiritualis renovatio hominis ad imaginem Dei, 1. Thess. IV. 3. Ephes. IV. 24. Illa in hac vita plena datur, quippe in se actus indivisus, unus & æqualis tum in genere, tum respectu omnium & singulorum: hæc in hac vita inchoatur, & pro mensura donationis Christi in justificatis incrementa facit, at in morte demum perficitur. Illa denique causa Regni; hæc via regnandi est.
units.tr: IV. This sanctification differs from vocation and from justification. It differs from vocation, because vocation is the beginning of conversion and regeneration, whereas sanctification is progress and continuation; vocation is the first spiritual creation, sanctification is the continued spiritual creation, or the preservation of regeneration, and the advance of spiritual life until its consummation. It differs from justification in more than one way. For justification, as apprehended and felt, is indeed later than sanctification, since it is placed before it in 1 Cor. 6:11, and exists at the same time with it; in the order of nature, however, it precedes it. "Having these promises" (that God will be our God and Father, which happens in justification), "let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit" (2 Cor. 7:1, compared with 6:16, 18). For we are justified as sinners and enemies, but reconciled, we are sanctified. Justification belongs to the sinner, sanctification to the one who is already justified and regenerated. Justification is accomplished outside us, in God's judgment, through the imputation of another's righteousness and the remission of sins; sanctification is accomplished in us, consisting in the mortification of the old man and the quickening of the new. Justification proceeds from the merit and redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις] of Christ, sanctification from the working of the death and life of Christ. Faith is the hand and instrument of justification, apprehending the gift of Christ's righteousness; faith is the cause of sanctification, "purifying hearts" (Acts 15:9), "working through love" (Gal. 5:6). Justification is a relation, for it is the absolution of the sinner from guilt and the freedom from liability to punishment (Acts 13:39; Rom. 8:1); sanctification is a qualitative change, the spiritual renewal of man to the image of God (1 Thess. 4:3; Eph. 4:24). Justification is given in full in this life, since in itself it is an undivided act, one and equal both in kind and with respect to all and each; sanctification is begun in this life and makes progress in believers according to the measure of the gift of Christ, but is at last perfected in death. Justification is finally the cause of the kingdom; sanctification is the way of reigning.

units.la: V. Justificatio ergo & sanctificatio beneficia & conjunctissima & distinctissima, quippe toto genere & causis omnibus disparata sunt, neque una definitione explicari possunt. Vitandi enim hic duo infames scopuli sunt; ne vel separentur, quod Libertinismum induceret; vel confundantur, quod Pharisaismum inveheret. Posterioris erroris rei Pontificii ex justificatione & renovatione actum miscellum faciunt, & utramque simul corrumpunt. Justitia enim Christi capitis, & nostra membrorum omnino subordinata sunt, quia hæc ex illa promanat. At cùm justitiæ nostræ vel tantilla vis in justificatione nostri tribuitur, opposita fiunt: Perinde ut lex & Evangelium eodem respectu sibi opponuntur & ἀσύγκλωστα sunt. Dicere enim, nos justificari etiam per sanctificationem vel renovationem, perinde est, atque si dicamus, nos simul ex lege & Evangelio, simul per fidem & opera justificari. At hæc Apostolo maximè opposita sunt. Colligimus justificari hominem sine operibus legis, Rom. III. 28.
units.tr: V. Justification and sanctification, then, are benefits that are both most closely joined and most distinct; indeed they are wholly different in kind and in all their causes, and cannot be explained by one definition. For two infamous rocks are to be avoided here: that they should either be separated, which would lead to Libertinism, or be confused, which would introduce Pharisaism. The Papists, in the latter error, make a mixed thing out of justification and renewal, and corrupt both together. For the righteousness of Christ the Head and our righteousness as members are wholly subordinate, since the latter flows from the former. But when even the slightest power is attributed to our righteousness in justification, they become opposed, just as law and gospel are opposed to each other in the same respect and are not to be joined [ἀσύγκλωστα]. For to say that we are justified even through sanctification or renewal is just as if we said that we are justified at once by law and gospel, at once by faith and works. But these are most opposed to the Apostle: "We conclude that a man is justified without the works of the law" (Rom. 3:28).

units.la: VI. Neque juvat ille Syncretistarum fucus mentientium, quòd Pontificios inter & Evangelicos hac in controversia de vocibus, non de re contentio sit, eò quòd Pontificii voce justificationis latiùs utantur, ut etiam sanctificationem includat: at Evangelici strictiùs, ut sanctificatio vel renovatio ab ea excludatur. Nam res toto genere, & causis omnibus, ut vidimus, disparatæ, uno; eóque in argumento eodem, salutem hominis unicè concernente con-
units.tr: VI. The pretence of the Syncretists does not help either, when they claim that the controversy between the Papists and the Evangelicals on this point is about words and not about the thing itself, because the Papists use the word justification more broadly, so that it includes sanctification, whereas the Evangelicals use it more strictly, so that sanctification or renewal is excluded from it. For the matters are wholly different in kind and in all their causes, as we have seen, though they are contended over in one and the same argument, which concerns man's salvation alone. They could not be expressed by one constant name except by some oracular Loxias [λοξία].

units.la: Vox קדוש secretum ab impuritate, & Sanctificatio hoc loco renovationem ad imaginem Dei continuatam notat. constanti nomine exprimi nisi à Jove quo-piam λοξία non potuissent. Sed removeantur tantisper nomina, & res cum re, causa cum causa certet. Etenim nemo bonus adeò conscientiam ejeravit, quin subinde severum Dei tribunal cogitet, & Deum in eo peccatori maledicentem, & à salutis æternæ cupidis legis impletionem exigentem intueatur. Quid hic Pontificius decretis suis Tridentinis fretus tentabit? Nitetur scilicet ille justitia sua inhærente, seu renovatione interiore vel omnino, vel ex parte duntaxat. Hac, si Papæ placet, ille justificatur, sic ut justitiæ & sanctitatis ejusmodi ex merito Christi conciliatæ infusione peccata sibi remissum, imò penitus sublatum iri, sicut (qui Tridentinorum sensus est) infusione lucis tenebræ dispelluntur, confidat. Hujus justitiæ exercitio maledictionem ille evitabit, benedictionem & salutem impetrabit? Quid Evangelicus? Is nihil in se ipso inveniens vel habens, quod legis postulato & maledictioni opponat, ad solum Christum, ejusque justitiam & meritum confugit, atque in his solis tutum adversus iram Dei perfugium, animæ solatium, pacem & salutem quærit & reperit; cum Anselmo dicens: Domine, mortem Domini nostri Jesu Christi objicio inter me & judicium tuum. Aliter tecum non contendo. Et cum Bernhardo: Domine justitiæ tuæ solius memorabo. Ipsa est enim & mea. Numquid enim verendum mihi, ne ambobus sufficiat? Non est pallium breve, quod non potest operire duos. Justitia tua in æternum, & me, & te pariter operiet, largiter larga, & æterna justitia. Annon sic Pontificiorum & Evangelicorum de justificationis & sanctificationis differentia professio totis castris diffidet? Et Evangelicorum de justificatione professionem cum verbo Dei plane congruere amplissimè jam confirmavimus.
units.tr: The word qadosh [קדוש] means what is set apart from impurity, and sanctification here denotes the renewal after the image of God continued. Still, let the names be set aside for the moment, and let the thing contend with the thing and the cause with the cause. No good man has ever so shaken off his conscience that he does not from time to time think of God's stern judgment seat, and see God threatening the sinner and demanding from those who long for eternal salvation the fulfilment of the law. What will the Papist, relying on his Tridentine decrees, attempt here? He will evidently rely on his inherent righteousness, or on interior renewal, either wholly or in part only. By this, if it pleases the Pope, he is justified, trusting that by the infusion of such righteousness and holiness, procured by the merit of Christ, his sins will be remitted to him, or rather utterly removed, just as (which is the sense of the Tridentines) darkness is dispelled by the infusion of light. Will he avoid the curse and obtain the blessing and salvation by the exercise of this righteousness? What does the Evangelical say? He, finding or having nothing in himself that can oppose the demand and the curse of the law, takes refuge in Christ alone and in his righteousness and merit. In these alone he seeks and finds a safe refuge against the wrath of God, comfort for his soul, and peace and salvation, saying with Anselm: Lord, I set the death of our Lord Jesus Christ between me and your judgment. I do not contend with you otherwise. And with Bernard: Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone. For it is also mine. Am I to fear lest it should not suffice for both of us? The cloak is not too short to cover two. Your righteousness, eternal, will cover me and you alike, abundantly broad and eternal righteousness. Does not the profession of the difference between justification and sanctification, as held by the Papists and the Evangelicals, thus fall apart in the whole camp? And we have already most fully confirmed that the Evangelical profession of justification agrees plainly with the Word of God.

units.la: VII. Sanctificationis summa necessitas est.
units.tr: VII. The necessity of sanctification is very great.

units.la: Nam sine sanctificatione nemo videbit Dominum, Hebr. XII. 14. Beati sunt puri corde. Nam illi videbunt Dominum, Matth. V. 8. Omnis, qui hanc spem in ipso habet, sanctificat se ipsum, ut ipse sanctus est, 1. Joh. III. 3. Omnis, qui in ipso manet, non peccat, ibid. v. 6. Qui ex Deo natus est, non peccat, neque potest peccare, ibid. v. 9. Eandem æterna Dei electio, Christi gratia & redemptio, & Spiritus vocatio, justificatio, adoptio, Regnum Christi, fides & spes, conscientiæ consolatio, sinceritas & libertas hominis, vitæ æternæ initia, promissiones Dei, necessitas ambulandi cum Deo, via & cursus ad cœlestem gloriam, maximo concentu, omnia postulant. Æterna Dei electio, quia electi sumus in Christo, ut essemus sancti & inculpati coram ipso, Ephes. I. 4. Non enim electi sumus duntaxat, ut à peccatis purgemur per sanguinem Christi, & regeneremur ad fidem, & votum melioris vitæ, sed etiam ad serium propositum ex puro corde, studium in bona conscientia, & opus ipsum charitatis. Tales enim inculpati demum evadimus, ut ceu alieni à Christo & injusti culpari, reprehendi non possimus. Christi gratia Redemptio, quia gratia Dei non debet recipi in vanum, 2. Cor. VI. 1. ut videlicet sit sterilis, & non sit fructificans, Col. I. 10. Christus tum venit, ut opera Diaboli, peccata & iniquitatem solveret, 1. Joh. III. 8. tum seipsum tradidit pro nobis, ut redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, & purgaret sibi populum peculiarem, æmulatorem bonorum operum, Tit. II. 14. absque quo foret, minister peccati esset, nec peccatum auferens, & reatum stabiliens, Gal. II. 17. tum venit, ut nos ad Deum adduceret, 1. Pet. III. 18. quod sine conversione ad Deum, quæ non est amoris Dei expers, fieri nequit: tum eos, quos redemit morte sua, sibi assimilat & conformat, ne caput & corpus, affectus diligentis, & eorum, qui dilecti sunt, discordent.
units.tr: For without sanctification no one will see the Lord, Heb. 12:14. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God, Matt. 5:8. Everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, as he is pure, 1 John 3:3. Everyone who abides in him does not sin, ibid. v. 6. Whoever has been born of God does not sin, and cannot sin, ibid. v. 9. The eternal election of God, the grace and redemption of Christ, the calling of the Spirit, justification, adoption, the kingdom of Christ, faith and hope, the consolation of conscience, the sincerity and freedom of man, the beginnings of eternal life, the promises of God, the necessity of walking with God, and the way and course to heavenly glory all demand sanctification with the greatest unanimity. The eternal election of God, because we are chosen in Christ that we should be holy and blameless before him, Eph. 1:4. For we are not chosen merely so that we may be cleansed from sins through the blood of Christ and be regenerated to faith and to a desire for a better life, but also to a earnest purpose of a pure heart, zeal for a good conscience, and the work of love itself. For only so do we at last become blameless, such that we cannot be accused or reproached as strangers to Christ and unrighteous. The redemption of Christ's grace, because the grace of God must not be received in vain, 2 Cor. 6:1, that is, so that it may not be barren and unfruitful, Col. 1:10. Christ came, on the one hand, to destroy the works of the devil, sin and iniquity, 1 John 3:8, and, on the other, he gave himself for us to redeem us from all iniquity and to purify for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works, Titus 2:14; without this he would be a minister of sin, neither removing sin nor establishing guilt, Gal. 2:17. He came, moreover, to bring us to God, 1 Pet. 3:18, which cannot happen without conversion to God, a conversion that is not free of the love of God. Lastly, those whom he redeemed by his death he makes like himself and conforms to himself, so that head and body, the affection of the one who loves and of those who are loved, may not be at odds.

units.la: Sanctificationis necessitas. Matth. V. 45. 48. Regnum Christi, quod nonnisi in eo esse potest, qui Christo & Deo obedit. Nam in quibus Deus regnat, ii Deo subjiciuntur. Fides in Christum, tum quia est amor & testis, & testimonii Dei, sive ejus veritatis, quae per testimonium notificatur, & qui ut petra salutis proponitur, qui amor ἀκλαγτ sterilis esse non potest: tum quia credentes in Christo sunt, & Deum glorificant; qui non per mala, sed per bona opera glorificatur: tum quia fides corda purificat, Act. XV. 9. & charitatis mater est, 1. Tim. I. 5. Spes gloriae in nobis revelandae, quia illa neque absque desiderio & quaestione verorum bonorum, neque absque studio habendi & videndi in se signa & argumenta acquisitionis & haereditatis coelestis: neque denique absque ἀπολαυσεως & certitudine, studioque certitudinis illius confirmandae esse potest. Conscientiae consolatio, tum quia non aliter illa constare nisi per δοκιμὴν fidei, in serio proposito, patientia, odio vitiorum, & amore virtutum potest: tum quia bonam conscientiam a se repellentes, circa fidem naufragium faciunt, hoc est, ad fidei portum non perveniunt, 1. Tim. I. 19. Sinceritas fidei, quae nonnisi per opera sanctificationis innotescere potest. Libertas Christianorum, quia veritas nos liberat, & ea credita aeque a peccati servitute, atque a servitute elementorum mundi nos liberat. Vitae aeternae in nobis initia, quia haec vita aeterna (aeternae vitae inchoatio) est, ut cognoscamus unum verum Deum, Patrem & Christum, Joh. XVII. 3. Ubi cognoscere non solam notitiam, sed perpetuam & vigilantem intentionem, animi observationem & intuitionem significat. Unde omnis pietas notitiae Dei nomine venit, & impietas atque τὸ μὴ ἔχειν Θεὸν ἐν ἐπιγνώσει non habere Deum in cognitione, vocatur ἀγνωσία Θεοῦ ignorantia Dei, 1. Cor. XV. 34. Promissiones Dei, quia qui eas habent, se ipsos purificant ab omni pollutione carnis & Spiritus, 2. Cor. VII. 1. Necessitas ambulandi coram Deo, quia ambulare coram Deo est inprimis ambulare, vel agere, tanquam Deo teste & inspectore; ad lucem accedere, ut manifesta fiant opera tanquam in Deo facta; accedere ad Deum, eum quaerere; opus Dei facere, ipsi servire, & Regno Coelorum operam dare. Ita servi coram hero ambulant, ejus nutum observantes, & jussa exequentes. Via ad Coelum; quo nomine Vita Christiana venit; in eo consistens, quod quis quaerit gloriam per bonam actionem, Rom. II. 7. salutem operatur in timore & tremore, Phil. II. 12. diligenter expendit singulas actiones suas, an bonae & utiles, an cum periculo aberrandi a via conjunctae sint. Nam arcta via, & innumeri scopuli, laquei, infesta multa, quae blandiuntur & decipiunt. Certate intrare per angustam portam, quia multi, dico vobis, quaerent intrare, & non poterunt, Luc. XIII. 24. Denique in via illa ad Coelum cursus & certamen Divinitus impositum, Gal. V. 7. 2. Tim. IV. 7. Apocal. III. 11. quia magno progressu opus est, ubi multum mali deponendum, & multum boni parandum: magno labore, ubi in ardua nitendum; magna vigilantia & fortitudine, ubi de corona, cum hostibus potentibus, & serpentino astu praeditis (Ephes. VI. 12. &c.) dimicandum est.
units.tr: The necessity of sanctification. Matt. 5:45, 48. The kingdom of Christ, which can exist only in one who obeys Christ and God; for those in whom God reigns are subject to him. Faith in Christ, both because it is love and a witness, and a witness of God's testimony, or of his truth, which is made known through testimony, and which is set forth as the rock of salvation; and such love [ἄκαρπος] cannot be barren. Also because those who believe in Christ glorify God, and God is glorified not by evil but by good works. Also because faith purifies the heart, Acts 15:9, and is the mother of love, 1 Tim. 1:5. The hope of glory to be revealed in us, because that hope cannot exist without desire for and inquiry into the true goods, nor without zeal to have and see in oneself the signs and evidences of the acquisition and inheritance of heaven, nor finally without enjoyment [ἀπόλαυσις] and certainty, and zeal to confirm that certainty. The consolation of conscience, both because it cannot be established otherwise than through the proof [δοκιμή] of faith, in earnest purpose, patience, hatred of vice and love of virtue; and also because those who thrust away a good conscience make shipwreck of the faith, that is, they do not arrive at the harbour of faith, 1 Tim. 1:19. The sincerity of faith, which can be made known only through the works of sanctification. The freedom of Christians, because the truth sets us free, and that truth, once believed, frees us equally from the bondage of sin and from the bondage of the elements of the world. The beginnings of eternal life in us, because this is eternal life (the inchoation of eternal life), that we may know the one true God, the Father, and Christ, John 17:3. Here "to know" signifies not mere acquaintance but a constant and watchful attention, an observation and intuition of the mind. Hence all piety is called by the name of knowledge of God, and impiety, and τὸ μὴ ἔχειν Θεὸν ἐν ἐπιγνώσει [not having God in knowledge], is called ἀγνωσία Θεοῦ [ignorance of God], 1 Cor. 15:34. The promises of God, because those who have them purify themselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, 2 Cor. 7:1. The necessity of walking before God, because to walk before God is above all to act as one under God's witness and overseer; to come to the light so that works may be made manifest as having been done in God; to draw near to God and seek him; to do the work of God, serve him, and labour for the kingdom of heaven. Thus servants walk before their master, watching his nod and carrying out his commands. The way to heaven, a name by which the Christian life is known, consisting in this: that one seeks glory through good action, Rom. 2:7, works out salvation in fear and trembling, Phil. 2:12, and carefully weighs each of one's actions, whether they are good and useful, or whether they carry a danger of straying from the way. For the way is narrow, and there are countless snares, traps and many hostile things that flatter and deceive. Strive to enter through the narrow gate, for many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able, Luke 13:24. Finally, on that way to heaven there is a course and a contest laid upon us by God, Gal. 5:7, 2 Tim. 4:7, Rev. 3:11, because great progress is needed where much evil must be laid aside and much good prepared; great labour where one must strive uphill; great vigilance and fortitude where, for the crown, one must fight against powerful enemies endowed with serpentine cunning (Eph. 6:12 etc.).

units.la: VIII. Necessitas Sanctificationis tanta.
units.tr: VIII. The necessity of sanctification is so great.

units.la: & tam praegnantibus argumentis confirmata non consolationem conscientiarum afflictarum & ad sanctificationem anhelantium minuit, sed plurimum tum ad gaudium fidelium, tum ad παροξυσμὸν excitationem torpentium; tum ad ἐπισυμισμὸν obthurationem oris hostium veritatis; tum ad cognoscendas veras causas studii bonorum operum facit. Anhelatio enim ipsa ad sanctificationem plenum gaudium & consolationem afflictorum parit, quia delectari justitia, & odisse injustitiam non in aliis dunta xat, sed in se ipso cumprimis, Spiritus praesentis & operantis certum κεντήριον est. Tum & torpentes; qui peccatis suis indormiverunt; & consolatione Evangelii ad ἀσκλησιν abutuntur, dicentes se habere fidem, sed eam ex operibus segniter demonstrantes; argumentis ejusmodi ad sanctificationem extimulandi sunt, ut noscant indolem verae fidei; quae Christum non tantum ut peccati expiatorem, sed etiam ut sanctificatorem apprehendit. Eadem opera hostium veritatis calumniae retunduntur; mentientium, Evangelicos solius fidei justificantis obtentu bona opera & sanctificationis universae studium procul amandare, & ejusmodi resipiscentiam docere, quia cuique vivere liceat, ut velit: & deinde Ministro dicere: Nullum factum, & tum minime de salute dubitare, quae Sathanica Grotii adversus Evangelicos blasphemia est, quam in decretorio suo agone, Publicanum, non operibus suis, sed uni solique misericordiae Dei confidentem profitsus, deplorare visus est. Denique sic verae studii bonorum operum causae cognoscuntur, quae solae illud Deo gratum acceptumque facere, & a virtutibus Philosophicis, ex solo naturae lumine oriundis distinguere aptae natae sunt. Omnes enim aliae causae sanctificationis, quas superstitio finxit, velut meritum bonorum operum & fiducia in iisdem efficiunt, ut homines bonis operibus studentes non Deum glorificent, sed suae sagenae sacrificent, & mercede, sive fructu boni operis, ut & consolatione Evangelica penitus excidant.
units.tr: Confirmed by such weighty arguments, it does not diminish the consolation of afflicted consciences and of those who long for sanctification. It greatly serves the joy of the faithful, the stirring up [παροξυσμὸν] of the sluggish, the stopping [ἐπισυμισμὸν] of the mouths of the enemies of the truth, and the knowledge of the true causes of zeal for good works. For the very longing for sanctification brings full joy and consolation to the afflicted, because to delight in righteousness and to hate unrighteousness, not only in others but above all in oneself, is a sure goad [κεντήριον] of the present and working Spirit. The sluggish, who have fallen asleep in their sins and abuse the consolation of the Gospel for licence [ἀσκλησιν], saying they have faith while showing it lazily by their works, must be spurred to sanctification by arguments of this kind, so that they may recognise the nature of true faith, which apprehends Christ not only as the expiator of sin but also as the sanctifier. At the same time the slanders of the enemies of the truth are beaten back. These liars claim that Evangelicals, on the pretext that faith alone justifies, cast far away good works and all zeal for sanctification, and teach such repentance that each may live as he pleases, and then say to the minister, Nothing done, and at that point have no doubt about their salvation. This is the Satanic blasphemy of Grotius against the Evangelicals, which he seemed to lament in his decisive contest, professing himself the publican who trusts not in his works but in the mercy of God alone. Finally, in this way the true causes of zeal for good works are known. They alone make it pleasing and acceptable to God, and they are fitted to distinguish it from philosophical virtues arising from the light of nature alone. For all the other causes of sanctification that superstition has invented, such as the merit of good works and trust in them, bring it about that men zealous for good works do not glorify God but sacrifice to their own dragnet, and so fall away from the reward, that is, the fruit of the good work, and from evangelical consolation altogether.

units.la: IX. Inanis metus est, ne sic homines legi iterum subjiciantur, & gratiae Dei jacturam faciant. Quin potius, quia non sumus sub lege, sed sub gratia, ideo legi Dei & justitiae inservimus. Peccatum vobis non dominabitur. Non enim estis sub lege, sed sub gratia, Rom. VI. 14. Si igitur sub lege essemus, non justitiae, sed peccato serviremus. Lex enim hominem peccatorem non convertit vel sanat, sed in peccato relinquit, non vivificat, vel regenerat, sed occidit. Gratia autem Dei in Jesu Christo nos per Spiritum Dei vivificat & regenerat, ut in lege Dei ambulemus. Litera occidit: Spiritus vivificat, 2. Cor. III. 6. Aliud enim est, esse sub lege, conditionem justitiae & vitae praescribente: aliud esse sub lege Spiritus vitae in Christo Jesu, legem cordi hominis inscribentis, & cor hominis ad imaginem Dei renovantis.
units.tr: IX. There is no good reason to fear that in this way men will be made subject to the law again and lose the grace of God. Rather, because we are not under the law but under grace, we serve the law and righteousness of God. "Sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under the law but under grace," Rom. 6:14. If we were under the law, then we would serve sin, not righteousness. For the law does not convert or heal the sinful man but leaves him in sin; it does not quicken or regenerate but kills. The grace of God in Jesus Christ, however, quickens and regenerates us through the Spirit of God, so that we may walk in the law of God. "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life," 2 Cor. 3:6. For it is one thing to be under the law, which prescribes the condition of righteousness and life; it is another to be under the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus, which writes the law on the heart of man and renews the heart of man after the image of God.

units.la: X. Deus est, qui sanctificat. Ego Jehova, qui vos sanctifico, Ezech. XX. 12. Deus gentibus poenitentiam dedit ad vitam, Actor. XI. 18. Ipse Deus pacis ἁγιάσαι sanctificet vos totos, 1. Thess. V. 23. Singulariter Spiritus S. nos sanctificat; qui ab hoc apotelesmate ἁγίῳ Sanctus passim, & Πνεῦ-
units.tr: X. It is God who sanctifies. "I am the LORD who sanctify you," Ezek. 20:12. "God has granted repentance unto life to the Gentiles," Acts 11:18. "May the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly," 1 Thess. 5:23 [ἁγιάσαι]. The Holy Spirit in particular sanctifies us; from this office He is everywhere called Holy, and [Πνεῦ-

units.la: {y} Quae non consolationem afflictorum minuit, sed ad gaudium fidelium, excitationem torpentium, obthurationem oris hostium veritatis, citationem torpentium, hostium veritatis convictionem, & cognitionem causarum studii bonorum operum facit. & Πνεῦμα ἀνακαινώσεως Spiritus renovationis Tit. III. 5. appellatur. Sed Spiritum hunc Deus Pater nobis donat: Filius redemptione sua promeruit. Christus nos redemit ab execratione legis, &c. ut ad gentes benedictio Abrahami pertingeret in Christo Iesu,ut promissionem Spiritus accipere-mus per fidem, Gal. III. 13. 14. Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, & se ipsum pro ea tradidit,ut eam sanctificaret, Ephes. V. 25. 26. Spiritum renovationis opulenter super nos effudit (Pater) per Iesum Christum Servatorem nostrum, Tit. III. 5. 6. Spiritus S. sic a Patre donatus, a Filio nobis promeritus sanctificandi munere sibi eximio sic defungitur, ut bonas in mente cogitationes, in voluntate sanctam obedientiam, & in corpore rectos motus efficiat. Deus nos a principio elegit ad salutem, quae contingit per sanctificationem Spiritus, & fidem veritatis, 2. Thess. II. 13. Sicut nempe in principio novae vitae & regenerationis nostrae Deum amamus, quia Deus Pater, propter obedientiam Filii, per Spiritus S. operationem omnipotente voluntate sua vult, ut ipsum amemus: ita post principium regenerationis & vitae nostrae spiritualis eundem amare, & sanctitati studere pergimus, quia Deus efficacissime vult iubetque, ut ipsum amare, & amorem eum vita inculpata testificari nunquam desinamus.
units.tr: {y} That it diminishes not the consolation of the afflicted but serves the joy of the faithful, the stirring up of the sluggish, the stopping of the mouths of the enemies of the truth, the conviction of the enemies of the truth, and the knowledge of the causes of zeal for good works. He is also called the Spirit of renewal [Πνεῦμα ἀνακαινώσεως], Titus 3:5. But God the Father gives us this Spirit, and the Son has merited Him for us by his redemption. "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law," etc., "that the blessing of Abraham might come upon the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith," Gal. 3:13-14. Christ "loved the Church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her," Eph. 5:25-26. "He (the Father) poured out upon us richly the Spirit of renewal through Jesus Christ our Saviour," Titus 3:5-6. The Holy Spirit, given by the Father and merited for us by the Son, thus discharges his distinguished office of sanctifying, so that He produces good thoughts in the mind, holy obedience in the will, and right motions in the body. "God chose you from the beginning for salvation through the sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth," 2 Thess. 2:13. Just as at the beginning of our new life and regeneration we love God, because God the Father, on account of the obedience of the Son, through the working of the Holy Spirit, by his almighty will wills that we love him, so after the beginning of our regeneration and spiritual life we continue to love him and to strive for holiness, because God most effectively wills and commands that we love him, and we never cease to bear witness to this love by a blameless life.

units.la: XI. Deus sanctificat hominem, & naturam corruptam hominis, sed non cujusvis, verum electi duntaxat, vocati & justificati. Sanctus appellabitur omnis scriptus ad vitam in Hierosolyma, omnis electus, Esaj. IV. 3. Ideo fideles omnes nominantur Sancti, quia non alii sancti sunt, quam qui per fidem justificantur. Et sanctificat sic Deus hominem electum, justificatum ὁλοπλῆ totum & ὁλόκληρον πνεῦμα ἢ ψυχὴ ἢ σῶμα, integrum spiritum, & animam, & corpus, 1. Thess. V. 23.
