Omnes enim hae partes peccato corruptae sanctificatione indigent. Neque homo tantum corpus, sed etiam anima & spiritus est; quae totidem operandi principia sunt. Spiritus judicium, anima voluntatem concupiscentem, & corpus, organa significat. Haec principia sunt, quibus homo bene vel male agit. Diliges Iehovam Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & tota anima tua, Deut. VI. 5. Ubi לב cor id ipsum est, quod Apostolo πνεῦμα spiritus, quod vocabulum pro animo ponitur, Ezech. XXXVI. 27. & a corde, hoc est, mente distinguitur. Est enim in homine γνῶσις ἢ γνώμη cognitio & sententia seu judicium; nec non Ἠλπια, ἐπιθυμία ἢ πάθη voluntas, concupiscentia & exercitus labor. Ea per vocabula πνεῦμα ἢ ψυχὴ, vel καρδία, πνεῦμα, ψυχὴ significantur. Parum vero refert, quid cuique tribuamus, quia ea vocabula modo latius, quando pauciora pronuntur, modo strictius, quando plura a se invicem distinguenda, pronuntur; accipi solent, dummodo ne separentur a se invicem, & homo tum ὁλοπλὴς integer, tum ejusdem partes, illam ὁλοπλέων efficientes, sanctificationis subjectum statuantur. Sicut enim homo anima & corpore constat, ita utraque pars sanctificatione indiget: anima, ut recta cogitemus & velimus: corpus, ut motus nullos, nisi rectas in animo cogitationes producentes, & bene cogitata, iussa & volita exequentes producat. Et quia spiritus seu mens principium est actionum
units.tr: XI. God sanctifies the human being, and the corrupt nature of the human being, but not of just anyone: only of the elect, the called and the justified. "Every one who is written down for life in Jerusalem shall be called holy" (Isa. 4.3): every elect person. For this reason all believers are called saints, because none are saints except those who are justified through faith. And so God sanctifies the elect and justified human being wholly [holoplē] and entire [holoklēron] in spirit, or soul, or body: "the whole spirit, and soul, and body" (1 Thess. 5.23). For all these parts, corrupted by sin, need sanctification. Nor is a human being only body, but also soul and spirit; and these are as many principles of action. "Spirit" signifies judgment, "soul" the desiring will, and "body" the organs. These are the principles by which a human being acts well or badly. "You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart" and "with all your soul" (Deut. 6.5). Where the Hebrew lev (heart) is the very thing which the Apostle calls pneuma (spirit), a word which is used for mind (Ezek. 36.27), and is distinguished from heart, that is, from mind. For in a human being there is gnōsis or gnōmē, that is, knowledge and opinion or judgment; and likewise elpis, epithymia or pathē, that is, will, desire and the laboring effort. These are signified by the words pneuma or psychē, or kardia, pneuma, psychē. Yet it matters little which we assign to each, since these words are sometimes taken more broadly, when fewer things are named, and sometimes more narrowly, when several things are to be distinguished from one another; provided they are not separated from one another, and the human being, both whole [holoplēs] and the parts of him making up the whole, is set down as the subject of sanctification. For just as a human being consists of soul and body, so each part needs sanctification: the soul, that we may think and will rightly; the body, that it may produce no motions except those which bring forth right thoughts in the mind, and carry out what has been well thought, commanded and willed. And because the spirit or mind is the principle of our actions,

units.la: nostrarum, quae corpore, ceu instrumento perficiuntur, iccirco sanctimonia in mente incipit, quae ad imaginem Dei creatoris renovari debet. Transmutamini τῇ ἀνακαινώσει ἐ νοὸς ὑμῶν renovatione mentis vestrae, ut exploretis, quae sit voluntas Dei bona, accepta & perfecta, Rom. XII. 2. Crea in me, Deus, cor purum, Psal. LI. 12. Induentes novum hominem, renovatum ad cognitionem secundum imaginem ejus, qui condidit ipsum, Col. III. 10. Profligata ex mente caligine tenebrarum, in eandem lucem cognitionis & sapientiae infert, ut habeamus illuminatos oculos mentis nostrae, ad sciendum quae spes sit vocationis nostrae, Ephes. I. 18. Ex mente sanctificatio in voluntatem & concupiscentiam progreditur, quam ab odio Dei & pravis cupiditatibus purgatam ad delectationem & πόθον desiderium rerum bonarum & amorem illibatum & sincerum Dei ex toto corde, tota anima & omnibus viribus, nec non proximi flectit & inflammat. Denique & membra, quae hactenus injustitiae membra fuerunt, Deo arma justitiae sistit, Rom. VI. 12. 13. id efficiens, ut cum oculis faciamus foedus de malo & vanitate non videnda, Job. XXXI. 1. & aures circumcidamus, ut missis nugis, fabulis & mendaciis, ad solius Dei verbum attendant; manus in Coelum attollamus, ad pauperes extendamus, & iisdem ad victum nobis acquirendum utamur; denique ore nostro laudes Dei decantemus. Magna enim ratio est sanctificationis corporis & membrorum, quia in iis sedes concupiscentiae & legis peccati est, quae in ipsa etiam anima Spiritui Dei litem & pugnam facit. Neque tantum sic ὁλοπλῆς totos Deus sanctificat, sed etiam ὁλοκλήρως integros 1. Thess. V. 23. servat, quia omnes illas partes in sanctificatione integras occupat, ne varii, inconstantes Prothei, sed instar תוד עולם fundamenti perpetui Proverb. X. 25. simus, sine vacillatione & declinatione de via, ut ita Deus per Spiritum suum possessor noster ex asse, non ex semisse, & solus Dominus noster sit.
units.tr: which are carried out through the body as an instrument, sanctity therefore begins in the mind, which must be renewed after the image of God the Creator. "Be transformed by the renewing [anakainōsei] of your mind, that you may prove what is the good, acceptable and perfect will of God" (Rom. 12.2). "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Ps. 51.12). "Putting on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him who created him" (Col. 3.10). Having dispelled the darkness of shadows from the mind, he brings in the same light of knowledge and wisdom, so that we have "the eyes of our mind enlightened, to know what is the hope of our calling" (Eph. 1.18). From the mind sanctification advances into the will and desire, which it purges from hatred of God and wicked lusts, and bends and inflames toward delight and longing [pothos] for good things, and toward a pure and sincere love of God with the whole heart, the whole soul and all strength, and likewise of the neighbor. Finally, the members which until now were instruments of unrighteousness, he sets up as "weapons of righteousness to God" (Rom. 6.12–13), bringing it about that "we make a covenant with our eyes not to look upon evil and vanity" (Job 31.1); and that we circumcise our ears, so that, sending away trifles, fables and lies, they attend to the word of God alone; that we lift up our hands to heaven, stretch them out to the poor, and use them to earn our living; and finally that with our mouth we sing the praises of God. For there is a great reason for sanctifying the body and its members, because in them is the seat of concupiscence and the law of sin, which wages strife and battle even against the soul itself against the Spirit of God. Nor does God sanctify in this way only the whole [holoplōs], but he also preserves them entire [holoklērōs] (1 Thess. 5.23), because he occupies all those parts entire in sanctification, so that we may not be various, inconstant Proteuses, but, like "the everlasting foundation" (yesod olam, Prov. 10.25), without wavering or turning aside from the way; so that God, through his Spirit, may be our possessor entirely, not by half, and may be our sole Lord.

units.la: XII. Exemplar Sanctitatis nostrae Dei Sanctitas est. Estote sancti, sicut ego sanctus sum, Levit. XIX. 2. Estote perfecti, sicut Pater vester in Coelis perfectus est, Matth. V. 48. Sicut igitur Deus nihil non Θεοπρεπὲς, gloriam suam non decens facit; ita homini cavendum sedulo est, ne quicquam gloria Dei indignum committat, vel aliquid omittat, quo Deus Creator & Redemptor noster glorificari possit. Hac demum ratione ceu pulchra imago Dei coruscamus. Inprimis Christi Salvatoris nostri sanctitas nostrae sanctitatis ἀρχέτυπον est. Discite a me, quoniam ego mansuetus & humilis corde sum, Matth. XI. 29. Estote imitatores mei, sicut ego Christi sum, 1. Cor. XI. 1. Sic demum cum imagine Filii Dei συμμορφοι conformes evadimus, Rom. VIII. 29. Sed de creatae sanctitatis exemplari causa plura Loc. III. 88. diximus.
units.tr: XII. The pattern of our holiness is the holiness of God. Be holy, as I am holy, Lev. 19:2. Be perfect, as your Father in heaven is perfect, Matt. 5:48. Just as God does nothing unworthy of himself [Theoprepes] and nothing that does not befit his glory, so man must take diligent care not to commit anything unworthy of the glory of God, or to omit anything by which God our Creator and Redeemer may be glorified. Only in this way do we shine forth as the beautiful image of God. Above all, the holiness of Christ our Savior is the archetype [archetypon] of our holiness. Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, Matt. 11:29. Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ, 1 Cor. 11:1. Thus at last we become conformed to the image of the Son of God [symmorphoi], Rom. 8:29. But we have said more about the pattern of created holiness at Loc. III. 88.

units.la: XIII. Inprimis norma sanctitatis nostrae verbum Dei est; utpote quo voluntas Dei, proxima officii creaturae regula continetur. Sanctifica eos in veritate tua. Verbum tuum veritas est, Joh. XVII. 17. In quo mundabit puer semitam suam? Observando secundum verbum tuum, Psal. CXIX. 9. In eo enim solo continetur voluntas Dei bona, accepta & perfecta, Rom. XII. 2.
units.tr: XIII. Above all, the rule of our holiness is the Word of God, since in it is contained the will of God, the immediate rule of the creature's duty. Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth, John 17:17. In what way will a young man cleanse his path? By observing your word, Ps. 119:9. For in that Word alone is contained the good, acceptable and perfect will of God, Rom. 12:2.

units.la: Atqui
units.tr: But

units.la: Et sanctificat hominem totum, spiritum, corpus & animam.
units.tr: And it sanctifies the whole man: spirit, body and soul.

units.la: Atqui hæc est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio nostra, 1. Thess. IV. 3. Ideo legem Dei diu noctuque meditari, iubemur, Psal. I. 2. ut quid ea iussum vetitumque sit, intelligamus; & iuxta eam sanctificationem perficiamus. Omnis enim Scriptura Divinitus inspirata est, utilis non tantum ad doctrinam & redargutionem, sed etiam ad correctionem & disciplinam in iustitia, ut perfectus fiat homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum adaptatus, 2. Tim. III. 16. 17. Ideo verbum Dei comparatur cum via, in qua ambulandum, Jer. VI. 16. Marc. XII. 14. Actor. XVIII. 25. cum lucerna, in loco obscuro lucente, ad pedes nostros in via pacis dirigendos, Psal. CXIX. 105. Prov. VI. 23. 2. Pet. I. 19. 20. Luc. I. 78. 79. cum speculo, cum regula, linea, canone, mensura, ad cuius amussim res formatur, exigitur, appenditur, mensuratur, Esai. XXVIII. 17. Galat. VI. 16. Phil. III. 16. Neque profecto pro sancto, iusto & recto deputari quidquam potest; quod pro tali non Deus ipse prior deputaverit. Sicut enim ipse sanctus & iustus est, & quid sanctum iustumque sit, solus definit: ita quid illud sit, quod sanctum iustumque definivit, solum Dei verbum demonstrat. Unde verbum, Scriptura, lex appellatur.
units.tr: Now this is the will of God, your sanctification, 1 Thess. 4:3. Therefore we are commanded to meditate on the law of God day and night, Ps. 1:2, so that we may understand what it commands and forbids, and may perfect ourselves in accordance with that sanctification. For all Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable not only for teaching and reproof, but also for correction and instruction in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work, 2 Tim. 3:16, 17. Therefore the Word of God is compared with a way in which we must walk, Jer. 6:16; Mark 12:14; Acts 18:25; with a lamp shining in a dark place, to guide our feet in the way of peace, Ps. 119:105; Prov. 6:23; 2 Pet. 1:19, 20; Luke 1:78, 79; with a mirror, a rule, line, standard, measure, by whose exact pattern a thing is shaped, tested, weighed and measured, Isa. 28:17; Gal. 6:16; Phil. 3:16. Indeed, nothing can be counted holy, just and right which God himself has not first counted as such. For as he alone is holy and just, and alone defines what is holy and just, so only the Word of God shows what that is which he has defined as holy and just. Hence it is called the Word, the Scripture, the law.

units.la: XIV. Verbum Dei, sanctificationis nostrae regula, tum Evangelii, tum legis est.
units.tr: XIV. The Word of God, the rule of our sanctification, is both of the Gospel and of the law.

units.la: Accipe ex ore ejus legem, & pone eloquia ejus in corde tuo, Job. XXII. 22. Sanctifica eos in veritate tua, Verbum tuum veritas est, Joh. XVII. 17. Sicut enim lex obedientiam ab homine exigit: ita Evangelium hominem in praestanda obedientia illa dirigit. Discere enim Christum oportet, cum audire, & in ipso doceri, sicut veritas est in Jesu, ut deponamus vetustum hominem, &c. & renovemur spiritu mentis nostrae, & induamus novum hominem, &c. Ephes. IV. 20--24. Sed latum tamen hic Evangelii & legis discrimen est, sive utriusque modum, sive finem, sive operationem spectemus. Nam quoad modum, quo lex & Evangelium sanctificationem praecipiunt, illa Deum ceu Creatorem: hoc eundem insuper in Christo, ceu Redemptorem colendum proponit. Ut omnes honorent Filium, sicut honorant Patrem, qui misit ipsum, Joh. V. 23. Creditis in Deum, credite etiam in me, ibid. XIV. 1. Gratia autem & redemptio Christi & pretiosissimae Evangelii promissiones multo adhuc fortius hominem Deo ligant, quam sola creatio & communis. Habentes has promissiones, purificemus nos ipsos, &c. 2. Cor. VII. 1. Unde cum ea argumenta conscientiae obiiciuntur, & per ea ad agendum incitamur, ex fide agimus. Quoad finem, quia lex sanctificationem propter vitam acquirendam: Evangelium eandem, ceu officium gratitudinis propter vitam & salutem acquisitam praecipit. Gratias agite in omnibus. Haec enim voluntas Dei in Christo Jesu erga vos, 1. Thess. V. 18. Denique quoad operationem, quia lex obedientiam postulat, at vires obediendi non sufficit, cum hominem ut creaturam Dei, cui Deus principio obediendi vires dedit, simpliciter respiciat: Evangelium vero & sanctificationem praecipit, & eandem per Spiritum Dei in regenitis operatur. Absque quo est, etiam Evangelium irregenitis lex, seu litera occidens fit: & cum quo est, Evangelium regenitis lex illa regia & libertatis Jac. I. 25. II. 12. evadit. Sed de lege & Evangelio abunde in loco diximus.
units.tr: Receive the law from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart, Job 22:22. Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth, John 17:17. Just as the law requires obedience from man, so the Gospel directs man in rendering that obedience. For one must learn Christ, to hear him and be taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus, so that we put off the old man, and so on, and are renewed in the spirit of our mind, and put on the new man, and so on, Eph. 4:20–24. Yet there is a broad difference between the Gospel and the law, whether we look at their manner, their end, or their operation. For as to the manner in which the law and the Gospel enjoin sanctification: the law sets God before us to be worshipped as Creator, while the Gospel sets forth the same God, moreover in Christ, to be worshipped as Redeemer. That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father who sent him, John 5:23. You believe in God; believe also in me, ibid. 14:1. But the grace and redemption of Christ and the most precious promises of the Gospel bind man to God far more strongly than creation alone and common providence. Having these promises, let us cleanse ourselves, and so on, 2 Cor. 7:1. Hence when those arguments are set before the conscience, and through them we are spurred to act, we act from faith. As to the end: the law demands sanctification in order to acquire life, whereas the Gospel enjoins the same as a duty of gratitude for life and salvation already acquired. Give thanks in all things, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you, 1 Thess. 5:18. Finally, as to the operation: the law demands obedience, but does not supply the strength to obey, since it regards man simply as a creature of God, to whom God gave the power of obedience at the beginning. The Gospel, however, both enjoins sanctification and works it through the Spirit of God in the regenerate. Without the Gospel, even the Gospel becomes law to the unregenerate, or the letter that kills; but with the Gospel, the law becomes for the regenerate that royal law of liberty, Jas. 1:25; 2:12. But we have spoken fully of law and Gospel at the proper place.

units.la: XV. Sanctificationis essentia in renovatione, seu instauratione hominis ad imaginem Dei consistit. Ut renovemur spiritu mentis nostrae, & induamus novum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus est in iustitia & sanctitate veritatis, Ephes. IV. 23. 24. Quae renovatio respectu tenebrarum a quo & ad quem, conversio a tenebris ad lucem, & a potestate Sathanae ad Deum est. Mitto te ad aperiendos eorum oculos, & ad convertendos eos a tenebris ad lucem, & a potestate Sathanae ad Deum, Act. XXVI. 17. 18. Proin in ea tum malum removetur, tum bonum restituitur. Illa in vitiosarum qualitatum abolitione, seu, uti Scriptura loquitur, in crucifixione, depositione & mortificatione veteris hominis: haec in qualitatum bonarum infusione & exercitio, seu resurrectione & vivificatione novi hominis consistit. Utraque circa omnes partes hominis occupatur. Nam & in mente discussis nativae caecitatis tenebris lux nova oritur ad salutarem Dei Christique agnitionem: & in voluntate abolita nativa pravitate, iustitia, sanctitas & nova obedientia restituitur & in affectibus repressis pravis cupiditatibus conformatio eorundem cum facultatibus superioribus, inprimis autem cum lege Dei, succedit: & in corpore ejusque membris, ejusmodi mutatio incessit; ut ex mortuis viva, ex armis injustitiae, arma justitiae; ex servis impuritatis & iniquitatis ad patrandam iniquitatem, serva justitiae ad sanctimoniam fiant.
units.tr: XV. The essence of sanctification consists in the renewal, or restoration, of man to the image of God. That we be renewed in the spirit of our mind, and put on the new man, who after God has been created in righteousness and the holiness of truth, Eph. 4:23, 24. This renewal, with respect to the darkness from which and to which it moves, is a conversion from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God. I send you to open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God, Acts 26:17, 18. Thus in it both evil is removed and good is restored. The former consists in the abolition of vicious qualities, or, as Scripture speaks, in the crucifixion, laying aside and mortification of the old man; the latter in the infusion and exercise of good qualities, or the resurrection and quickening of the new man. Both work upon all parts of man. For in the mind, once the darkness of native blindness is dispelled, a new light rises for the saving knowledge of God and Christ; and in the will, once native depravity is abolished, righteousness, holiness and new obedience are restored; and in the affections, once wicked desires are restrained, they are brought into conformity with the higher faculties, above all with the law of God; and in the body and its members a change of this kind takes place, so that, from being dead they become living, and from being instruments of unrighteousness they become instruments of righteousness; and from being slaves of impurity and iniquity, bent on committing iniquity, they become slaves of righteousness unto holiness.

units.la: XVI. Perperam ergo Pelagianizantes & Socinianí eorumque simili Remonstrantes, Sanctificationem in sola actuum emendatione & vitae morumque mutatione collocant. Sicut enim illi peccatum originis, sive inhaerentem naturae corruptionem, impura generatione in nos propagatam negantes, quicquid vitii aut labis homini inest, id omne crebris peccati actibus, & peccandi quadam assuetudine contractum asserunt: ita hominem, utpote naturaliter non corruptum, nec pravis qualitatibus imbutum, innovatione naturae indigere pernegant, satis habere dictitantes, si peccandi consuetudinem omittat, & vitae morumque reformationem suscipiat. Quod dum per seriam poenitentiam & sinceram vitae, juxta mandatum Christi emendationem facit, tum vero eum regenerari & sanctificari pertendunt. Qui non simplex, sed complicatus error est. Quo rejecto, orthodoxi asserunt, per regenerationem quidem novam vitam spiritualem, novas qualitates spirituales, in homine generari, imo creari: per sanctificationem vero novos habitus spirituales eosque permanentes conferri, indies perfici, & ad actus secundos excitari atque applicari. De prima regeneratione in loco fusius egimus. Neque tantum vitam & facultates in regeneratione prima, sed etiam habitus permanentes in sanctificatione donari, passim Scripturae testantur. Dabo legem meam in medio eorum, & cordi eorum inscribam eam, &c. Non docebunt ultra unusquisque proximum suum, & fratrem suum, dicendo: Cognoscite Jehovam, &c. Jerem. XXXI. 33. 34. Spiritum meum dabo in medio vestri, efficiamque, ut in praeceptis meis ambuletis, judicia mea custodiatis, & illa faciatis, ciatis, Ezech. XXXVI. 27. Ideo minimè simulata fides dicitur habitasse in Loide; & persuasus fuit Paulus, fore etiam ut in Timotheo habitet, ad memoriam eidem revocans, ut exsuscitet donum, quod in ipso erat, per impositionem manuum. Non enim, inquit, dedit nobis Deus spiritum formidinis, sed roboris & charitatis, &c. 2. Timoth. I. 5. 6. 7. Similiter cùm Petrus à Sathana tritici instar ventilandus esset, dixit ad eum Christus: Ora vi pro te, ne fides tua deficiat, Luc. XXII. 32. Manset igitur in ipso habitus fidei, nec in gravissima tentatione & lapsu, in quo actuum secundorum notabilis defectus fuit, defecit. Et passim etiam virtutes habituales permanentes recensentur. Maxima nobis & pretiosa promissa donavit, ut per hæc efficeremur Divinæ naturæ consortes, &c. Ad hoc ipsum verò vos, omni collato studio, adjicite fidei vestræ virtutem, virtuti notitiam, notitiæ continentiam, continentiæ tolerantiam, tolerantiæ pietatem, pietati fraternum amorem, fraterno amori charitatem. Hæc si vobis adsint & abundent, non inertes, nec infructuosos vos efficient in Domini nostri Jesu Christi cognitione, 2. Pet. I. 4-8. En dona in fideles collata, Divinæ naturæ per illa participationem, adeóque imaginis restitutionem, habitus habitibus cumulatos, & ex habitibus pullulantes actus & fructus ex Divinæ gratiæ irriguo fonte fluentia omnia! Unde etiam gaudium, charitas, pax, longanimitas, benignitas, bonitas, fides, lenitas, continentia inter fructus Spiritus, Gal. V. 22. recensentur. Quæ virtutes Spiritu S. in nobis manente & ipsæ permanent. Charitas enim nunquam excidit, 1. Cor. XIII. 8. Nunc verò manet fides, spes, charitas, ibid. v. 13. Adultorum est solidus cibus, eorum, qui propter habitum sensus habent exercitatos ad discretionem boni & mali, Heb. V. 14. Persuasum habens hoc ipsum, fore, ut qui in vobis opus bonum incepit, perficiat usque ad diem Jesu Christi. Et hoc oro, ut vestra charitas adhuc magis & magis exundet in cognitione & omni sensu, Phil. I. 6. 9. En igitur habitum, ac porrò opus Dei, quod in nobis producitur permanet, augetur & perficitur. Ex habitibus illis actus, omnis generis exercitia pietatis & bona opera fluunt. Γύμναζε σεαυτὸν Exerce te ipsum ad pietatem, 1. Tim. IV. 7. Si qua virtus, si qua laus, ταῦτα λογίζεσθε hæc reputate, Phil. IV. 8. Christus enim purificavit sibi populum peculiarem, ζηλωτὴν καλῶν ἔργων, Tit. II. 14. Quo in genere praxis fidei & resipiscentiæ, à principio vitali per regenerationem indito, & habitibus infusis manans, & jugiter, cum incremento renovationis, exercita maxima illustris est. Propterea non segnescimus, sed etiamsi externus homo noster corrumpitur, internus tamen indies renovatur, 2. Cor. IV. 16. Gratias debemus Deo semper agere de vobis, fratres, uti par est, quòd vehementer augescat fides vestra, & abundet mutua uniuscujusque omnium vestrum charitas, 2. Thess. I. 3. Cùm ergo & in prima regeneratione nova homini ex spirituali morte vita restituatur; & in consequente sanctificatione habitus ex vita illa spirituali fluentes & permanentes donentur, & per exercitium, Spiritu Dei sanctificatore, exerceantur, crescant & augescant indies; planum est, nec regenerationem primam, nec consequentem sanctificationem in sola actuum emendatione, & vitæ mosúmque mutatione consistere.
units.tr: Therefore the Pelagianizers and the Socinians, and their like, the Remonstrants, wrongly place sanctification solely in the amendment of actions and in a change of life and conduct. For just as those men deny that original sin, or the inherent corruption of nature, is propagated into us by an impure generation, and assert that whatever vice or stain is in a man has been contracted by frequent sinful acts and a certain habit of sinning, so they flatly deny that man, since he is naturally uncorrupted and not imbued with depraved qualities, needs an inward renewal of nature. They keep insisting that it is enough if he gives up the habit of sinning and undertakes a reformation of life and conduct. When he does this through earnest repentance and a sincere amendment of life according to the command of Christ, they then maintain that he is regenerated and sanctified. This is not a simple error but a compound one. Rejecting it, the orthodox assert that through regeneration a new spiritual life and new spiritual qualities are indeed begotten, or rather created, in man; but through sanctification new and lasting spiritual habits are conferred, are perfected day by day, and are stirred up and brought into play as secondary acts. We have discussed the first regeneration more fully in its own place. That not only life and faculties are given in the first regeneration, but also lasting habits in sanctification, the Scriptures testify everywhere: I will put my law in the midst of them, and write it in their hearts, etc.; they shall not teach every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the LORD, etc. (Jer. 31:33, 34). I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them (Ezek. 36:27). For this reason it is said that faith without hypocrisy dwelt in Lois, and Paul was persuaded that it would also dwell in Timothy, reminding him to stir up the gift that was in him through the laying on of hands. For God, he says, has not given us the spirit of fear, but of power and love, etc. (2 Tim. 1:5, 6, 7). Similarly, when Peter was to be sifted by Satan like wheat, Christ said to him: I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not (Luke 22:32). The habit of faith therefore remained in him, and in his most grievous temptation and fall, in which there was a notable lack of the second acts, it did not fail. And everywhere lasting habitual virtues are also enumerated. He has given us exceedingly great and precious promises, that by these we might be partakers of the divine nature, etc. And for this very reason, giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue, to virtue knowledge, to knowledge temperance, to temperance patience, to patience godliness, to godliness brotherly kindness, to brotherly kindness charity. For if these things be in you, and abound, they make you that ye shall be neither barren nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Pet. 1:4–8). Behold the gifts bestowed on believers: by them they partake of the divine nature, and so the restoration of the image; habits piled upon habits; and from the habits sprout acts and fruits, all flowing from the irrigating fountain of divine grace! Hence also joy, love, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faith, meekness and temperance are listed among the fruits of the Spirit (Gal. 5:22). These virtues, while the Holy Spirit dwells in us, also remain. For charity never fails (1 Cor. 13:8). And now abideth faith, hope, charity (ibid. v. 13). Strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil (Heb. 5:14). Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. And this I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and in all judgment (Phil. 1:6, 9). Behold then, the habit, and further the work of God that is produced in us, remains, increases and is brought to completion. From those habits flow acts, every kind of exercise of godliness and good works. [Γύμναζε σεαυτὸν] Exercise thyself unto godliness (1 Tim. 4:7). If there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things [ταῦτα λογίζεσθε] (Phil. 4:8). For Christ purified for himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works [ζηλωτὴν καλῶν ἔργων] (Titus 2:14). In this class the practice of faith and repentance, flowing from the vital principle implanted by regeneration and from the infused habits, and exercised continually with the growth of renewal, is most conspicuous. Therefore we do not grow weary, but even though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4:16). We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brethren, as it is meet, because your faith grows exceedingly, and the charity of every one of you all toward each other abounds (2 Thess. 1:3). Since, then, in the first regeneration a new life is restored to man out of spiritual death, and in the consequent sanctification habits flowing from that spiritual life are given and are kept, and by exercise, with the Spirit of God sanctifying, are exercised, grow and increase day by day; it is plain that neither the first regeneration nor the consequent sanctification consists solely in the amendment of actions and a change of life and conduct.

units.la: XVII. Nihil roboris adversantium argumenta habent.
units.tr: XVII. The arguments of our opponents have no force.

units.la: Nam quòd regenerationem ex aqua & Spiritu, Joh. III. 5. sic explicant, ut dicant, per regenerationem sordes, velut per aquam, tantùm ablui, & quodammodo iterum nasci & regenerari, quem vitæ prioris malè transactæ pœnitet, quíque bonam sanctamque vitam inchoat & agit; dilutum nimis est. Nam depositio vitiorum, & vitæ morumque emendatio, regenerationem, ceu proprii ejus fructus, Gal. V. 22. 23. & opera novæ obedientiæ, Matth. III. 8. Col. III. 5. sequuntur, non constituunt. Neque enim regeneratio illa depositio, vel emendatio, sed naturæ corruptæ renovatio, & ad imaginem institutio est. Sicut enim per generationem homo vetus nascitur; ita per regenerationem novus renascitur. Aqua verò illa; per quam homo regeneratur, vel Spiritus Dei, vel obedientia Christi est; quarum utraque vitæ spiritualis, non emendationis actuum duntaxat causa est. Mortificatio veteris, & vivificatio novi hominis non tantùm regenerationis Rom. VI. 11. VII. 4. Eph. II. 4. 5. sed etiam novæ obedientiæ & sanctificationis, quæ regenerationi, ut effectum causæ suæ analogicè respondet, Ephes. IV. 22. 23. Col. III. 5. &c. partes sunt. Priori sensu non actuum vitæ restitutionem, & mortis abolitionem significant. Posteriore emendationem etiam vitæ, sed conformatam principiis vitæ & habitibus continent. Aliter etiam novæ creaturæ à priore, aliter à posteriore dicimur. A priori per regenerationem: à posteriori per mutationem actualem in vita & moribus conformiter vitæ spirituali & habitibus infusis. Qui actus differtè Jerem. XXXI. 39. Ezech. XXXVI. 26. Ephes. II. 10. distinguuntur. Denique nec ambulatio in novitate vitæ, Rom. VI. 4. ipsa regeneratio, sed ejus fructus & consequens est, quia ibidem diserte à resuscitatione nostra cum Christo distinguitur.
units.tr: For their explanation of regeneration by water and the Spirit (John 3:5) is too watered down. They say that through regeneration filth is only washed away, as if by water, and that in a sense a man is born again and regenerated when he repents of his former ill-spent life and begins and lives a good and holy life. But the putting off of vices, and the amendment of life and conduct, follow regeneration as its proper fruits (Gal. 5:22, 23) and as works of new obedience (Matt. 3:8; Col. 3:5). They do not constitute it. For that regeneration is not the putting off or amendment of anything, but the renewal of a corrupted nature and its restoration to the image of God. As through generation the old man is born, so through regeneration the new man is born again. The water by which a man is regenerated is either the Spirit of God or the obedience of Christ, and each of these is the cause of spiritual life, not merely of the amendment of actions. The mortification of the old man and the quickening of the new man (Rom. 6:11; 7:4; Eph. 2:4, 5) belong not only to regeneration but also to new obedience and sanctification, which answers to regeneration as its effect answers to its cause (Eph. 4:22, 23; Col. 3:5, etc.). In the former sense these words signify the restoration of life and the abolition of death; in the latter they also contain the amendment of life, but one shaped by the principles of life and by the infused habits. We are also called new creatures in one sense from the former and in another from the latter: from the former, through regeneration; from the latter, through an actual change in life and conduct conformed to the spiritual life and the infused habits. These acts are distinguished in Jeremiah 31:33, Ezekiel 36:26 and Ephesians 2:10. Finally, the walking in newness of life (Rom. 6:4) is not regeneration itself but its fruit and consequence, since the passage there expressly distinguishes it from our resurrection with Christ.

units.la: XVIII. Habet Sanctificatio continuam praxin & ἀσκησιν exercitationem.
units.tr: XVIII. Sanctification has continual practice and exercise (askesis).

units.la: Exerce te ipsum ad pietatem. Nam γυμνασία exercitatio corporalis parum utilis est. Sed pietas ad omnia utilis est, 1. Tim. IV. 7. 8. Quæ γυμνασία exercitatio in eo consistit, quòd fideles sibi ipsis attendunt, curam studiúmque omne ad ea, quæ pietatis sunt, facienda adhibent, & ab omni malo recedunt, atque ita habitum Dei gratia contrahunt, consuetudinem induunt, apti promptíque ad cogitandum, loquendum, faciendum ea, quæ optima, Deo gloriosissima & proximo utilissima sunt, fiunt. Quæ γυμνασία & ἀσκησις exercitatio non tam corporalis, quàm spiritualis est. Illa enim ab hac scilicet separata, Apostolo teste σωμ. ὀλίγον ωφέλιμος ad pauca vel parum utilis est. Præsagiebat ei animus, fore, ut in Ecclesiam ἀσκησις σωματικὴ exercitatio corporalis quædam, Monachismus, mandata vel consilia humana de vitando conjugio, delectu ciborum, &c. introducantur, & in exercitatione tali utraque pietatis pagina ponatur. Qua in re non hoc equidem Apostolus satagit, quòd corpus & membra ad pietatem non sint exercenda, sed quòd tanti non sit, ullum præceptum dare, vel quicquam commendare præter exercitationem ad pietatem, & quod ipsa etiam corporalis exercitatio sit & esse debeat exer-
units.tr: Exercise yourself unto godliness. For bodily exercise [gymnasia] profits little, but godliness is profitable for all things (1 Tim. 4:7, 8). This exercise [gymnasia] consists in this: that the faithful attend to themselves, apply all care and zeal to the things that belong to godliness, and withdraw from every evil; and so they acquire by the grace of God a habit, put on a custom, and become apt and ready to think, speak and do those things which are best, most glorious to God and most useful to the neighbour. This exercise and training [askesis] is not so much bodily as spiritual. For bodily exercise, separated from this, is, as the Apostle witnesses, profitable [sōmatikē gymnasia] for little, or profits little. His mind foresaw that in the Church a certain bodily training [askēsis sōmatikē], monasticism, human commands or counsels about avoiding marriage, the choice of foods, and so on would be introduced, and that in such exercise the whole page of piety would be placed. In this matter the Apostle is not concerned to say that the body and its members are not to be exercised for piety, but that it is of no account to give any precept or to commend anything except exercise toward piety, and that bodily exercise itself is and ought to be a exercise for piety.

units.la: Argumentis fatis. exercitatio ad pietatem : Proin omnes exercitationes corporales, quæ non sunt ad pietatem, vel in pietate, cujusmodi sunt χαμεύνια, nuditas, somni importuna interruptio, aliaque ejusmodi, quæ habent rationem sapientiæ ἐν ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ, ἡ φιλανθρωπία, ἡ ἀφθαρσία σώματος ἐν ἐν ὑμῖν ὑμεῖν in cultu voluntario & humilitate & vexatione corporis, non in honore quoquam, Coloss. III. 23. vili floccique faciendæ sunt. Licet enim talia πρὸς ὀλίγον ὠφέλιμα ad pauca utilia sint, hoc est, utilitatem quandam, quam homines concupiscunt, habeant, velut quòd ἀσκητιαὶ tales apud homines in admiratione sint, religiosi ἀκεσάς, σωφροσύνη, singulares videri velint & se habere, in quo supra vulgus gloriari liceat, contendant; tamen cùm in iis non sit solida ad pietatem exercitatio, ea inutilis & perniciosa utilitas est. In pietate enim omnis utilitas est; neque vel utile est, nisi quod justum piùmque est, vel justum piùmque est, nisi quod utile est, hoc est, quod operando homo beatus est, & quod sine lætitia operari non poterit. Ideo Christus Deum cognoscere, hoc est, amare & timere, vitam appellat æternam, quia in eo beatitudo hominis consistit, Joh. XVII. 3.
units.tr: Therefore all bodily exercises which are not for piety, or in piety, such as pallets of straw [chamaeunia], nakedness, the unwelcome interruption of sleep, and others of that kind, which have the appearance of wisdom in self-chosen worship, humility and mortification of the body, and not in any honour (Col. 3:23), are to be held of little value. For although such things are useful for a little [pros oligon ophelima], that is, have a certain usefulness which men desire (for such ascetic practices are admired among men, and men want to appear to have singular religious observance and self-control, and strive to have something in which they may boast above the common people), nevertheless, since there is no solid exercise of piety in them, that usefulness is useless and harmful. For all usefulness lies in piety, and nothing is useful unless it is also just and pious, nor just and pious unless it is useful, that is, because by acting a man is blessed, and because he cannot act without joy. Therefore Christ calls to know God, that is, to love and fear him, eternal life, because in this the blessedness of man consists (John 17:3).

units.la: XIX. Sanctificationis & Pietatis exercitatio in resipiscentia & nova obedientia consistit. Resipiscentia à resipiscendo, seu iterum sapiendo, vel mentem suam ab insania & insipientia recipienda dicta, שוב ἐπιστροφὴ conversionem à Sathana ad Deum, & suavius μετάνοιαν mentis conversionem, seu consilium emendationis, conjunctum cum מטח μεταμέλεια angore, cura & supplicio veluti quodam animi, ob admissum peccatum significat. Promiscuè quidem voces μετάνοια & μεταμέλεια interdum usurpantur, uti ex Matth. XI. 21. XXI. 29. Hebr. XII. 17. colligitur. Sed propriè tamen μετάνοια renovatio & mutatio mentis & consilii, recessio à κακία maleficio Actor. VIII. 22. est, & solis fidelibus competit: μεταμέλεια verò angor & cura ob admissum peccatum est, quæ cum fide conjuncta salutaris, ab ea separata etiam infidelibus & hypocritis competit. Latinus interpres Poenitentiæ vocem adhibet, quæ à poenitendo, sicut obedientia ab obediendo dicta est. Pœnitere verò à pœna dicitur, quia poenitentem operis sui piget tædetque & tædium illud, & præteritæ dementiæ castigatio apud poenitentem ipsum, pœnæ instar est. Simile verbum est ἀνανήφειν iterum sobrium fieri, velut ab ebrietate, mania ad sobrietatem & pristinum mentis statum redire. Ut ἀνανήψωσιν ἐκ τῆς παγίδος Διαβόλου, 2. Tim. II. 26. Patres etiam μετανοεῖν sententiæ mutationem. Latè totam hominis conversionem & primam regenerationem: strictè iteratam & quotidiè renovatam conversionem à gravioribus lapsibus notat. Qui posterior sensus hujus loci est.
units.tr: XIX. The exercise of sanctification and piety consists in repentance and new obedience. Repentance [resipiscentia], named from resipiscing, that is, becoming wise again, or recovering one's mind from madness and folly, signifies the Hebrew shub and the Greek epistrophē, the conversion from Satan to God, and more gently metanoia, a conversion of mind, or a resolve to amend, joined with metamelei, that is, anguish, care and a kind of torment of spirit on account of sin committed. The words metanoia and metamelei are sometimes used indiscriminately, as is gathered from Matthew 11:21, 21:29 and Hebrews 12:17. But properly metanoia is the renewal and change of mind and purpose, a turning away from wickedness (kakia) (Acts 8:22), and belongs only to the faithful; while metamelei is anguish and care on account of sin committed, which, when joined with faith, is saving, and when separated from it, belongs also to unbelievers and hypocrites. The Latin translator uses the word poenitentia, which is named from poenitere, as obedientia is from obedire. But poenitere is so called from poena, because the penitent is grieved and wearied by his own deed, and that weariness and the chastisement of his past madness is, for the penitent himself, like a punishment. A similar word is ananephein, to become sober again, as from drunkenness or madness, to return to sobriety and the former state of mind, as in "that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil" (2 Tim. 2:26). The Fathers also use metanoein for a change of opinion. Broadly it denotes the whole conversion of man and his first regeneration; strictly, a repeated and daily renewed conversion from grievous falls. This latter sense is the sense of this passage.

units.la: XX. Resipiscentia est dolor ex agnitione peccatorum conjunctus cum fiducia remissionis eorundem, mutationem animi à malo ad bonum producens. Pœnam eam Deus exigit, & Sancti omnes admissa peccata agnoverunt, cum sancto horrore & mœrore deplorarunt, & vitam emendarunt semper. Lavate vos, mundi estote, removete malitiam operum vestrorum à conspectu oculorum meorum. Desinite malè facere, discite bene facere, quærite judicium, &c. Esaj. I. 16. 17. Facite fructus dignos pœnitentia, Matth. III. 8. Exemplum simul & speculum resipiscentium David, Manasses, Petrus, Publicanus, Maria Magdalena, Paulus suppeditant. Cùm enim sanctissimorum illorum, aliorumque exempla clament, regenitos à peccato haud raro occupari & superari, per resipiscentiam, secundam veluti post naufragium tabulam, & ipsi peccatum vicissim vincunt, & de eo triumphant.
units.tr: XX. Repentance is sorrow arising from the acknowledgement of sins, joined with trust in their forgiveness, producing a change of mind from evil to good. God demands this penalty, and all the saints have acknowledged their sins committed, have lamented them with holy horror and grief, and have always amended their lives. "Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, put away the evil of your deeds from before my eyes. Cease to do evil, learn to do well, seek judgment," etc. (Isa. 1:16, 17). "Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance" (Matt. 3:8). The examples and mirrors of the repentant are David, Manasseh, Peter, the publican, Mary Magdalene and Paul. For since the examples of those most holy men, and of others, cry out that the regenerate are not rarely overcome and overpowered by sin, repentance is, as it were, a second plank after shipwreck, by which they in turn overcome sin and triumph over it.

units.la: XXI. Resipiscentiæ partes sunt peccatorum agnitio & confessio, dolor & tristitia ob offensam Numinis, remissionis peccatorum humilis imploratio & emendationis vitæ serium propositum. Pleraque illæ in Divina de poenitentiæ agendæ modo informatione, quæ Hos. XIV. 1. 2. 3. extat, comprehenduntur. Revertere Israel (inquit Deus) ad Jehovam Deum tuum, quia impegisti in pravitatibus tuis. Accipite vobiscum verba (peccatum deplorantia, confitentia, orationem & votum ex sincero corde provenientia, cum fide & πεποίθησις) & revertimini ad Jehovam. Dicite ipsi. Quicquid accipis, pravitas est: (nihil boni à nobis accipis, quo gratiam tuam promereamur. Nihil ad salutem nostram conferimus. Filium tuum accipis, qui onustus peccatis nostris in ipsum impactis, pro iisdem sanguinem suum effudit, illa portans in crucem.) Et accipe bonum, (seu dona in hominibus, tanquam membris tuis, Psal. LXVIII. 19.) & retribuemus juvencos labia nostra, (confitebimur labiis nostris, corde dictante, peccata, fidem in Servatorem, profitebimur obedientiam, narrabimus virtutes ejus.) Antè omnia enim resipiscens vitam suam in speculo legis intueri, & transgressiones suas agnoscere tenetur. Scrutemur vias nostras, ac inquiramus, & revertamur ad Jehovam, Thren. III. 40. Defectiones meas novi & peccatum meum semper coram me est, Psal. LI. 5. Singularium inprimis & atrociorum peccatorum scrutinium poenitentem decet. Attendi & audivi. Non loquuntur rectum coram me. Non est quisquam, quem poeniteat mali, dicendo: Quid feci? Jerem. VIII. 6. Omnia judicia ejus coram me. Et statuta ejus non submovi à me, Psal. XVIII. 23. Ad excitandam hanc peccatorum agnitionem cognitio Dei & legis ejus aprime necessaria est. Unde Prophetæ, Christus & Apostoli ad poenitentiam adhortantes, multum diùque in Dei natura, bonitate, justitia, veritate, nec non describendis vitæ legibus & officiis hominum; item in accusandis & exaggerandis peccatis hominum, hærent & laborant.
units.tr: XXI. The parts of repentance are the acknowledgement and confession of sins, sorrow and grief on account of offending the Deity, humble prayer for the forgiveness of sins, and the earnest purpose of amending one's life. Most of these are comprehended in God's own instruction on the manner of repenting, which stands in Hosea 14:1, 2, 3: "Return, Israel," says God, "to Jehovah your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquities. Take with you words (lamenting sin, confessing, prayer and vow arising from a sincere heart, with faith and trust) and return to Jehovah. Say to him: 'Whatever you receive is wickedness' (we bring nothing good from ourselves by which we may merit your grace; we contribute nothing to our salvation. You receive your Son, who, burdened with our sins laid upon him, poured out his blood for them, bearing them to the cross). 'And receive the good' (or the gifts in men, as your members, Ps. 68:19), 'and we will render the calves of our lips' (we will confess with our lips, as the heart dictates, our sins, our faith in the Saviour; we will profess obedience and tell of his virtues)." For before all things the penitent is bound to look upon his life in the mirror of the law and to acknowledge his transgressions. "Let us search out our ways, and turn again to Jehovah" (Lam. 3:40). "I know my defections, and my sin is always before me" (Ps. 51:3). Above all, the penitent ought to search out particular and very grievous sins. "I listened and heard; they do not speak what is right. There is no one who repents of his wickedness, saying, 'What have I done?'" (Jer. 8:6). "All his judgments are before me, and I have not put away his statutes from me" (Ps. 18:23). The knowledge of God and of his law is especially necessary to stir up this acknowledgement of sins. Hence the prophets, Christ and the apostles, in exhorting to repentance, labour long and hard on the nature of God, his goodness, justice and truth, and likewise on describing the laws of life and the duties of men, and on accusing and magnifying the sins of men.

units.la: XXII. Peccatorum agnitionem & scrutinium eorundem humilis confessio sequitur. Quæ duplex est, tum ea, quæ Deo; tum ea, quæ hominibus fieri debet. Quæ Deo fieri debet, necessaria planè & inevitabilis, & cum pudore faciei conjuncta est. Tibi soli peccavi (verbum & legem tuam spernens, uti Nathan ei exprobraverat) & in oculis tuis malum feci, Psal. LI. 6. Qui tegit scelera sua, nunquam agit prospere. Qui verò confitetur & derelinquit, misericordiam consequetur, Prov. XXVIII. 13. si confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis & justus est, ut remittat nobis peccata, &c. 1. Joh. I. 9. Estque confessio illa vel publica totius Ecclesiæ, vel privata singulorum. PubliPublicæ exemplum est populus Babylone captivus, dicens: Peccavimus, & impietatem fecimus, impiè egimus, rebellavimus, &c. Tibi Domine, justitia, nobis autem pudor faciei, &c. Dan. IX. 5. 6. 7. &c. Nec non illa populi Dei: Palpavimus sicut cæci parietem, &c. Multiplicatæ sunt prævaricationes nostræ coram te, & peccata nostra testantur contra nos. Prævaricati sumus Jehovæ, &c. Esaj. LIX. 10. 11. &c. similes illæ Esræ & Nehemiæ confessiones sunt, quarum imitatione & vetus Ecclesia publicam peccatorum exomologesin in publico coetu, præeunte Pastore, instituit; & eandem in Papatu, non sine piorum dolore obsoletam Ecclesia Evangelica restituit. De privata intelligenda sunt illa Davidis & Solomonis citata, nec non baptizatorum à Johanne, confitentium peccata sua, Matth. III. 6. Eodem modo privatim confitemur Deo, quando vias nostras scrutamur, corda nostra coram Deo excutimus, solique abscondita pectoris nostri recludimus, deplorantes humiliter peccata nostra nobis nota & ignota; & cum Publicano precantes, ut nostri Deus misereatur. Quæ confessio ad peccatorum remissionem consequendam necessaria est, quia nisi agnita & confessa corruptione & injustitia nostra Christum vera fide non apprehendimus. Et uni soli que Deo peccata hoc modo confitenda sunt. Ille enim solus peccata remittere & delere potest, solus medicus est, cui uni secretiora vulnera aperire & revelare convenit. Solus peccato, qua peccatum est, offensus pacem restituere potest. Solus corda renesque scrutatur. De iis verò, qui peccata palliant, dicitur: super malo sunt manus ad faciendum bonum, Mich. VII. 3. hoc est, omni studio id agunt ut malum videatur bonum id, ita fingunt & formant.
units.tr: XXII. Recognition of sins and a close examination of them is followed by humble confession. This is of two kinds: that which must be made to God, and that which must be made to people. The confession to God is absolutely necessary and unavoidable, and it is joined with shame of face. "Against you only have I sinned, and done this evil in your sight" (Ps. 51:4), rejecting your word and law, as Nathan had reproached David. "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" (Prov. 28:13). "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins," etc. (1 John 1:9). This confession is either public, of the whole Church, or private, of individuals. The example of the public kind is the people captive in Babylon, saying, "We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, we have done wickedly, and have rebelled," etc. "O Lord, righteousness belongs to you, but to us shame of face," etc. (Dan. 9:5–7). So too is that of God's people: "We grope for the wall like the blind," etc. "Our transgressions are multiplied before you, and our sins testify against us: for our transgressions are with us; and as for our iniquities, we know them: in transgressing and lying against the Lord," etc. (Isa. 59:10–13). Like these are the confessions of Ezra and Nehemiah, in imitation of which the ancient Church instituted public exomologesis [ἐξομολόγησις] of sins in the public assembly, with the pastor leading; and the Evangelical Church has restored the same practice, long since obsolete under the Papacy, not without the grief of the godly. The passages cited from David and Solomon, and the people baptized by John "confessing their sins" (Matt. 3:6), are to be understood of private confession. In the same way we confess privately to God when we examine our ways, search our hearts before God, and lay open to him alone the hidden things of our breast, humbly lamenting our sins, known and unknown, and praying with the tax collector that God would have mercy on us. This confession is necessary for obtaining the forgiveness of sins, because unless we acknowledge and confess our corruption and unrighteousness, we do not apprehend Christ by true faith. And sins are to be confessed in this way to God alone. For he alone can forgive and blot out sins; he alone is the physician to whom it belongs to open and reveal the deeper wounds. He alone, offended by sin as sin, can restore peace. He alone searches the hearts and reins. Of those who cover up their sins it is said, "Their hands are upon evil, to do it diligently" (Mic. 7:3), that is, they strive with all zeal to make evil appear good, and so they feign and shape it.

units.la: XXIII. Confessio quædam peccatorum etiam hominibus non absolutè, sed certa conditione, fieri debet. Ecclesiæ inprimis confitendum peccatum est, quo illam peccator graviter perculit. Quæ Canonicæ confessionis nomine venit, quia juxta Canones Ecclesiæ diversimodè præstatur. In veteri Ecclesia inprimis frequens illa, & rigore non vulgari pro disciplinæ totius rigore, exercita est. Est & aliud confessionis hominibus faciendæ genus, de quo Jacobus: confitemini vobis invicem lapsus, &c. Jac. V. 16. Quæ tum necessaria est, cùm alius in alium peccavit, ei scandalum & tristandi, & se redarguendi ansam dedit. Si peccaverit in te frater tuus, redargue ipsum te inter & ipsum solum, Matth. XVIII. 15. Tum enim necesse est confiteri offensam, & audire corripientem, eíque satisfacere & dicere: Poenitet me; Nollem factum; ut sic scandalum sanetur, fratres inter se reconcilientur, & qui contristatus est, fratri remittere, & super ipso exhilarari possit, ne peccatum sit impedimentum precum pro fratribus. Si stultè egisti, efferendo te, & si cogitasti, manum ad os, noli excusare delictum, & redarguenti responsare, Prov. XXX. 32. His duobus confessionis proximo faciendæ generibus à nonnullis illa adjicitur, quia presli scelere gravi vel à Pastore gregis dominici, vel ab alio legis Dei perito con-filium petunt. Cæterum illa consultatio potiùs quàm confessio est, quæ nullibi præcepta vel prohibita, adeóque libera esse debet. Nemo igitur ad illam cogi potest. Si verò frater à Ministro Ecclesiæ, vel privato quopiam consilium petierit, charitas jubet, si potlis, inservire fratri. Imò periclitanti, si maximè non petat opem, succurrere charitas jubet. Fratres etiamsi præoccupatus fuerit homo in lapsu quopiam, vos, qui spirituales estis, reconcinnate talem in spiritu mansuetudinis: considerans te ipsum, ne & tu tenteris, Gal. VI. 1.
units.tr: XXIII. A certain confession of sins must also be made to people, though not absolutely, but on a certain condition. Above all, the sin by which the sinner has gravely wounded the Church must be confessed to the Church. This is called "canonical confession," because it is performed in different ways according to the canons of the Church. In the ancient Church this was especially frequent and was practised with no common strictness, befitting the strictness of the whole discipline. There is another kind of confession to be made to people, of which James speaks: "Confess your faults one to another," etc. (Jas. 5:16). This is necessary when one has sinned against another and given him occasion of offence, sorrow, and reproof. "If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone" (Matt. 18:15). For then it is necessary to confess the offence, to listen to the one who rebukes, to make satisfaction to him, and to say, "I am sorry; I would not have done it." In this way the scandal is healed, brothers are reconciled to one another, and he who was grieved can forgive his brother and rejoice over him, so that sin may not hinder prayers for brothers. "If you have done foolishly in lifting yourself up, or if you have thought evil, lay your hand upon your mouth. Do not excuse the offence, and do not answer back to the one who reproves" (Prov. 30:32). To these two kinds of confession to a neighbour, some add a third: when, after a grave crime, people seek counsel either from the pastor of the Lord's flock or from some other man skilled in the law of God. Yet that is rather a consultation than a confession, and it ought to be free, since nothing is commanded or forbidden in it. No one, therefore, can be compelled to it. But if a brother seeks counsel from a minister of the Church or from some private person, charity bids us, if we can, to serve the brother. Indeed, charity bids us help a man in danger even if he does not ask for help. "Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, you which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted" (Gal. 6:1).

units.la: XXIV. Inprimis Confessionem secretam seu auricularem in Concilio demum Lateranensi ab Innocentio III. eo tempore, quo extincta pietate & doctrina sine delectu quidvis licentiæ Pastorum larvæ sibi sumpserunt, tancitam repudiamus. Nam severa lege Papalis Ecclesia sancivit, ut peccatores sub necessitate salutis Sacerdoti omnia peccata mortalia, quorum memoria cum diligenti & debita præmeditatione haberi potest, etiam occultissima, quin & cogitationis peccata, & cupiditates adversus ultimum Decalogi præceptum militantes, una cum circumstantiis delictum augentibus vel minuentibus, clanculum in aures mulitent; neque alia lege peccatorum remissionem sperare ausint. Nam peccatum non confessum, inquiunt, non remissum. Cæterùm nec Christus peccata remittens secretam hanc peccatorum enumerationem à peccatoribus exegit; nec Apostolis, ut exigerent, mandavit. Neque ullum secretæ ejusmodi confessionis exemplum ostendi potest. Estque illa & animæ carnificina & desperationis laqueus, quia conscientia confessionis de sufficiente & justo scrutinio, & ex eodem pendente remissione peccatorum nunquam certa esse potest. Nam etiam verecundia ingenuam secretorum confessionem impedit. Et quotusquisque vel cordis sui, quod pravum & inscrutabile est, penetralia exactè novit: vel peccatorum mortalium & venialium discrimen dextrè statuere potest, ut sibi ipsi confitendo satisfaciat, quòd peccatum nullum mortale omiserit? Et tot casus, quibus confessio invalida fiat, Deuterotæ illi excogitarunt, ut non pauci ingenuè confiteantur, difficile, imò impossibile esse, juxta deuterôses illas confiteri. Impium verò maximè est, ad proprium nescio quem Sacerdotem relegare peccatorem, cùm Christus Ecclesiæ suæ ministros tantùm & præcones dederit, ipse verò solus universalis, & cujusque proprius Sacerdos in Ecclesia ad finem usque seculi maneat; ad quem unum confitendum peccatores omnes fideles ministri relegant. Accedit, quòd recitatio peccatorum non aliud quàm exercitatio impudentiæ, ab Apostolo 2. Tim. III. 6. 7. damnata esse potest, quod spurci confessionalium libri ab ipso Petro Aurelio non ita pridem denso opere castigati & exagitati, aperte produnt. Præterea in confessione Sacerdos non scrutatur conscientiam poenitentis, an Deum amet ex toto corde? An credat in Christum? An promissiones Evangelii amplectatur? An Deo confidat, & curas suas in ipsum conjiciat? An Dei honori studeat, pauperes alat, Scripturam legat, verbum Dei audiat? A' confitente non alia quàm Catholicitatis Romana
units.tr: XXIV. We reject, above all, the secret or auricular confession, introduced at last by Innocent III in the Lateran Council, at the time when, piety and doctrine having been extinguished, the larvae of pastors without any discernment seized for themselves whatever licence they pleased. For the Papal Church has enacted by a severe law that sinners, under necessity of salvation, must whisper into the ear of the priest all mortal sins that can be remembered with diligent and due reflection, even the most secret, and moreover the sins of thought and the desires warring against the last commandment of the Decalogue, together with the circumstances that increase or diminish the offence; and they dare to hope for forgiveness of sins by no other law. For, they say, "a sin not confessed is not forgiven." But Christ, when he forgave sins, did not demand from sinners this secret enumeration of sins, nor did he command the apostles to demand it. Nor can any example of such secret confession be shown. And this confession is a torture of the soul and a snare of despair, because the conscience can never be certain about a sufficient and just examination, on which the forgiveness of sins depends. For even shame prevents a frank confession of secrets. And who knows exactly the innermost parts of his own heart, which is wicked and unsearchable? Or who can rightly determine the distinction between mortal and venial sins, so as to satisfy himself by confessing to himself that he has omitted no mortal sin? And those casuists have devised so many cases by which a confession is rendered invalid, that not a few honest penitents confess that it is difficult, indeed impossible, to confess according to those subtle distinctions. It is most impious to refer the sinner to some private priest of his own, since Christ has given his Church only ministers and heralds, while he himself alone remains the universal and everyone's own priest in the Church until the end of the age; to him alone all believers, the ministers too, refer sinners for confession. Moreover, the recital of sins can be condemned as nothing other than "an exercise of impudence," as the Apostle says (2 Tim. 3:6–7); and the filthy books of confessors, lately scourged and assailed in a dense volume by Peter Aurelius himself, openly reveal this. Besides, in confession the priest does not examine the conscience of the penitent: whether he loves God with his whole heart? whether he believes in Christ? whether he embraces the promises of the Gospel? whether he trusts in God and casts his cares upon him? whether he strives for the honour of God, feeds the poor, reads Scripture, hears the word of God? From the penitent, the surer signs of Roman

units.la: mana manè certiora indicia peti solent. Denique confessio hæc non aliud quàm Regni Papalis vinculum, & dominationis arcanum est. Nam hamus est Sacerdotum & Ecclesiæ, cujus hoc modo mirificè crescunt divitiæ, authoritas & formidabilis potestas. Sic enim
units.tr: Catholicity are commonly sought instead. Finally, this confession is nothing other than the bond of the Papal kingdom and the secret of its dominion. For it is the hook of the priests and of the Church, by which their riches, authority, and formidable power grow marvellously. For

units.la: Scire volunt secreta domus, atque inde timeri. Magistratus & imperia terrori Papæ subiguntur, qui hac via in secretissima quæque penetrat; & Reges atque Principes sibi, utpote peccatorum ipsorum secretissimorum conscio, nullo negotio subjicit. Prætextu sigilli confessionis Regum & Principum vita anceps in discrimen adducitur, uti palam facit illa Jesuitæ Bineti vox, præstare omnes Reges occidi, quàm vel semel sigillum confessionis revelari, nec non alterius Jesuitæ apophthegma à Petronio adv. Regem Jacobum cap. 6. 7. approbatum. Si Christus in terra adhuc versaretur, potiùs permittendum, ut trucidetur, quàm ut confessio reveletur. Casus majores Papæ, ceu supremo Hierarchæ, & Ecclesiæ Principi, reservantur. Et imperandis post Confessionem satisfactionibus totum mundum Papa libidini suæ subjicit.
units.tr: "They wish to know the secrets of the house, and thence to be feared." Magistrates and governments are subjected to the terror of the Pope, who penetrates into every most secret matter by this route, and he subjects kings and princes to himself with no trouble, as one who knows their most secret sins. Under the pretext of the seal of confession, the lives of kings and princes are brought into peril, as the saying of the Jesuit Binet openly shows: that "it is better that all kings be killed than that the seal of confession be revealed even once," and also the aphorism of another Jesuit, approved by Petronius, against King James, ch. 6–7: "If Christ were still on earth, it would be better to permit him to be slaughtered than that confession be revealed." The greater cases are reserved to the Pope, as to the supreme Hierarch and Prince of the Church. And, by imposing satisfactions after confession, the Pope subjects the whole world to his lust.

units.la: XXV. De Confessione tali in Scripturis
units.tr: XXV. On Such Confession in the Scriptures

units.la: ne jota quidem unum extat. Nam illa ἐξομολόγησις confessio peccatorum, Matth. III. 6. Johanni à poenitentibus baptizandis facta & baptismum præcelsit, & generalis, non specialis fuit. Quippe ἐξομολόγησις, non τῆς ἀμαρτίας confessi dicuntur. Et tot homines ab ipso baptizati, quomodo peccata sua, eorumque circumstantias omnes in aures Johannis ingerere potuerunt? De sensu verborum Jacobi. Confitemini vobis invicem lapsus, Jac. V. 16. modò vidimus. Nulla ibi fratres inter distinctio est, quasi aliorum sit audire, aliorum edere confessionem. Æquiparantur inter se omnes, ita ut etiam maximo secundum sententiam hanc incumbat satisfacere minimo. Sed & πεπιστευκότες fideles, seu qui crediderant; Actor. XIX. 18. ἐξομολογούμενοι τὰς πράξεις confessi actus suos dicuntur ante etiam, non post baptismum, quod non pauci ex adversariis fatentur, & publicè, indefinitè atque generatim, exceptis curiosis illis artibus, quæ inter atrociora eorum peccata fuerunt. Neque S. Johannes dicens: Si confiteamur peccata, fidelis & justus est, ut nobis peccata remittat, 1. Joh. I. 9. Sacerdoti, sed illi, qui fidelis & justus est, hoc est, Deo peccata confitenda non speciatim, sed generatim, sicut præcedentia: Si dicamus, nos peccatum non habere, v. 8. & sequentia: Si dixerimus, ὅτι οὐχ ἡμαρτήκαμεν quòd non peccaverimus, v. 10. generatim intelliguntur, innuit. Et habent præcones Evangelii claves Regni Cœlorum, & cum iisdem potestatem aperiendi & claudendi Cœlum, peccata remittendi & retinendi; Matth. XVI. 19. Joh. XX. 23. Sed non iccirco judices peccatorum sunt, ut necesse habeant peccata singula ἐπεξεργαστικῶς cognoscere, quia Deus in causa sua nullum unquam hominem judicem constituit. Neque enim nudi homines corda & internos affectus hominum, in quibus proprie ratio & natura peccati posita est, norunt. Proin potestas clavium & remittendi peccata ministris Christi collata, non judicialis est, neque in æstimatione quantitatis vel qualitatis peccatorum consistit; sed ministerialis; non qua sententia fertur; sed qua per Evangelii præconium & disciplinam Ecclesiæ illa non absolute sed cum conditione ad conscientiam peccatoris prædicatur. Ad exercitium potestatis hujus merè ἀπλῶς particularis confessio non requiritur: sufficit generalis confessio facta Ecclesiæ, quæ scandalum patitur; vel etiam ea, quæ uni solique Deo fit. Ita enim etiam præco sententiam promulgat, qui tamen crimina specialiter non cognovit. Apostoli certè optimi potestatis clavium, & remittendorum peccatorum sibi collatæ interpretes, nusquam speciale & secretam ejusmodi confessionem peccatorum à quoquam exegerunt. Quæ porrò de typis confessionis secretæ Adamo, Evæ, Caino, Israelitis peccata coram Sacerdote confitentibus; mussant; ἀποκρυπτόμενοι sunt. Nam Protoplastorum confessio Deo, non ulli homini facta est. Caini verò non tam confessio, quàm desperatio fuit. Neque Israelitarum coram sacerdote confessio typus confessionis secretæ; sed confessionis Deo per Christum peccata expiantem, faciendæ fuit. Sicut verò in N. T. una oblatione consummantur omnes, qui sanctificantur, Hebr. X. 14. adeóque non amplius distinctæ hostiæ, vel humana expiatio requiritur: ità nec specialis ejusmodi confessio uni sacerdoti aperienda amplius necessaria est. Denique nec disciplinæ Ecclesiæ custodiendæ necessitas confessionem auriculatem exigit; quasi sic futurum sit; ut erubescentes minùs peccent. Nam & Christus, Apostoli & Ecclesia ad sera usque Innocentii III. tempora sine confessione secreta disciplinæ Ecclesiæ satis consulerunt: & Ecclesia Innocentiana per confessionem ejusmodi pudorem omnem destruxit. Nam & confessionarii & confitens ex circumstantiarum discussione horrenda scelera didicerunt. Stupris & adulteriis causas & occasiones innumeras confessio suppeditavit. Cafuistarum confessionarios suos informantium chartæ, quæ sanctimoniæ & verecundiæ plenæ esse debuerant; prisci Elephantidos libellis, & nuperis perditorum Italorum voluminibus obscoeniores sunt; in quibus, velut lupanarium scriniis, omnes turpitudinum formæ & modi, etiam qui nullo apud flagitiosissimos in usu fortasse sunt, accuratissimè describuntur.
units.tr: Not even a single jot of it exists. The confession of sins (exomologēsis) that John made to those being baptized, Matt. 3.6, came before baptism, and it was general, not specific. For they are said to have confessed (exomologēsis) generally, not "of sin" (tēs hamartias). And how could so many people, baptized by him, have poured all their sins and every circumstance of them into John's ears? As we have already seen, the sense of James's words, Confess your faults to one another, Jas. 5.16, admits no distinction among brothers, as if some were to hear confessions and others to make them. All are made equal, so that on this view even the greatest must make satisfaction to the least. Moreover, those who had believed (pepisteukotes), those who had believed, Acts 19.18, are said to have confessed (exomologoumenoi) their deeds (praxeis) even before, not after, baptism. Many of the adversaries admit this, and that it was public, indefinite and general, apart from those curious arts that were among their more atrocious sins. Nor does St John, when he says, If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, 1 John 1.9, mean a priest, but him who is faithful and just, that is, God, to whom sins are to be confessed not specifically but generally, just as the preceding and following verses are to be understood generally: If we say that we have no sin, v. 8, and If we have said that we have not sinned (hoti ouk hēmartēkamen), v. 10. The heralds of the Gospel have the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and with them the power of opening and shutting heaven, of forgiving and retaining sins, Matt. 16.19; John 20.23. But they are not on that account judges of sins, so that they must examine each sin one by one (epexergastikōs), since God, in his own cause, has never appointed any man a judge. For bare men do not know the hearts and inner affections of men, in which the true reason and nature of sin lies. Therefore the power of the keys and of remitting sins, given to Christ's ministers, is not judicial, nor does it consist in estimating the quantity or quality of sins. It is ministerial: not a sentence that is pronounced, but a declaration that, through the proclamation of the Gospel and the discipline of the Church, is made to the conscience of the sinner, not absolutely but on condition. For the exercise of this power a particular confession is not required at all (haplōs). A general confession made to the Church, which suffers the scandal, or even one made to God alone, is enough. For so too the herald proclaims a sentence even though he has not specifically known the crimes. Certainly the Apostles, the best interpreters of the power of the keys and of the remission of sins given to them, nowhere demanded such a special and secret confession of sins from anyone. As for what is said about the types of secret confession, Adam, Eve, Cain, and the Israelites confessing their sins before the priest, these are mere mutterings and hiding (apokryptomenoi). For the confession of the first parents was made to God, not to any man. Cain's confession was not so much a confession as a despair. Nor was the confession of the Israelites before the priest a type of secret confession, but a confession to be made to God, who expiates sins through Christ. And just as in the New Testament by one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified, Heb. 10.14, so that no further distinct sacrifice or human expiation is required, so too a special confession of this kind, to be opened to one priest, is no longer necessary. Finally, the need to preserve church discipline does not demand auricular confession, as if people would sin less through shame. For Christ, the Apostles and the Church, down to the late times of Innocent III, had sufficiently cared for the discipline of the Church without secret confession. And the Church of Innocent, by means of this kind of confession, destroyed all shame. For both confessors and penitents learned horrible crimes from the discussion of circumstances. Confession supplied countless causes and occasions for debauchery and adultery. The writings of the casuists who instructed their confessors, which ought to have been full of holiness and modesty, are more obscene than the old books of the Elephantis and the recent volumes of the depraved Italians, in which, as in the chests of brothels, every form and manner of filthiness, even those perhaps not in use among the most shameless, is described with the greatest exactness.

units.la: XXVI. Resipiscentia cum peccatorum
units.tr: XXVI. Repentance, with the recognition and confession of sins

units.la: agnitione & confessione perculsæ & vulneratæ animæ dolorem, quæsitissimum peccatorum sensum, horrorem & odium conjungit. Sed duplex dolor & tristitia ex peccati sensu concipitur; una mundi, altera secundum Deum. Nam quæ secundum Deum est tristitia, ea resipiscentiam efficit ad salutem, cujus nunquam pœniteat. At mundi tristitia mortem efficit, 2. Cor. VII. 10. Tristitia mundi est hominum de mundo, in quibus nihil est, nisi quod natura habent; non ex amore boni & odio mali, sed ex concupiscentia oriunda. Tum enim mundus tristatur, cùm concupiscentia sua privatur. Πᾶν τὸ ἐπιθυμοῦν τῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ λυπεῖν, Quicquid concupiscentiæ adversatur, ei triste est. Sed & triste ei accidit, cùm peccati poenas dat, vel de Dei sanctitate & judicio cogitat. Hæc tristitia amore Dei, & vera in Christum fide destituta θάνατον κατεργάζεται mortem efficit, ibid. Nam contra Deum est, & legis solius, quæ iram operatur, non Evangelii
units.tr: A soul struck and wounded by the recognition and confession of sins joins sorrow, the most exquisite sense of sin, with horror and hatred. But a twofold sorrow and grief arises from the sense of sin: one of the world, the other according to God. For the grief that is according to God produces a repentance that leads to salvation and is never regretted. But the grief of the world produces death, 2 Cor. 7.10. The grief of the world belongs to men of the world, in whom there is nothing but what they have by nature. It arises not from love of good and hatred of evil but from concupiscence. For the world grieves only when it is deprived of its lusts. Whatever opposes concupiscence (pan to epithymoun tē epithymia lypein) is grievous to it. But it also becomes grievous to it when it pays the penalty of sin, or when it thinks of God's holiness and judgement. This grief, destitute of love for God and of true faith in Christ, works death (thanaton katergazetai), 2 Cor. 7.10. For it is against God, and it belongs to the Law alone, which works wrath, not to the Gospel.

units.la: Dolor & tristitia repisicentium gelii effectus est, adeoque mortem non potest non operari.
units.tr: Sorrow and grief are an effect of the Law upon the repentant, and so they cannot but work death.

units.la: XXVII. Errant proin graviter Pontificii, qui timorem gehennæ & horrores ex contemplatione judicii & pœnæ; qui illis Attritionis, seu imperfectæ contritionis nomine veniunt; partem conversionis, vel dispositionem ad eandem esse, perinde ut fides est, imò, accedente Sacramento absolutionis, justificare contendunt. Nam timor gehennæ & horror judicii Divini per se, sine succedanea fide & amore Dei, malus, vitiosus, imò lethalis & mortiferus est, tum quia actus est hominis infidelis & irregeniti, cujusmodi omnes actus peccatum sunt: tum quia non procedit ex speciali gratia Christi: tum quia sine charitate est, utpote quæ timorem ἐξω βάλλει foras ejicit, excludit, 1. Joh. IV. 18. tum quia trepidatio hominis dat laqueum, Prov. XXIX. 25. tum quia fiduciæ contrariatur, & quædam de gratia desperatio est: tum quia ex amore sui, commodi & tranquillitatis propriæ, non ex amore Dei super omnia diligendi oritur: tum denique quia timor solus voluntatem peccandi excludere non potest, quod Tridentini falsò definiverunt. Nam cogitatio de Divina sanctitate, justitia & judicio non potest peccatorem emendare, si Evangelium bonum illud Dei verbum, non audiat, & ex eo Deum amare non occipiat. Et quæ ex metu oriuntur, secundum se spectata, involuntaria sunt, manente semper repugnantia voluntatis, qua nollet aliquis facere, si pœnæ metus abesset. Continet timor ille manum, sed non animum; premit cupiditatem, sed non exhaurit. Animus autem eodem modo semper cupiditati affixus manet. Imò peccati consideratio, collectio & discussio tantum abest, ut ad gratiam disponat, vel justificet, ut magis etiam peccatum augeat, irritet, & inflammet, Rom. IV. 15. V. 20. VII. 7. 8. 9. Sed impietatis numeros omnes Jesuiticum de attritione cum absolutione conjuncta, & peccatorem justificante, dogma implet. Quasi videlicet attrito, uti illi explicant, absolutio conveniat. Quod est mutare Evangelium, & sacerdotalem absolutionem in magicum carmen convertere. Etenim attritio per se magis peccatorem & hypocritam facit, quia non oritur ex corde sincero & ὑπόκρισιν, quod charitate munitum sit oportet, 1. Cor. XIII. 1. 2. &c. 1. Tim. I. 5. Talem ergo qua ratione Sacerdos absolvet, nisi verbis suis operationem, uti magi solent, tribuendo? Sed nefarii dogmatis Jesuitici crypsin non itapridem Montaltius Epist. Provinc. X. prodidit; ostendens videlicet Jesuitis curæ cordique esse, ut quosvis hypocritas, omni fide & amore Dei vacuos, ad tribunal suum pœnitentiale invitent, & promissa iis etiam, qui per totius vitæ decursum nunquam Deum dilexerint, venia, libidini suæ eosdem subjiciant. Merito enim Montaltius exclamavit: Quid restat amplius, nisi ut non amandi Dei privilegium à Christo hominibus allatum prædicetur? Hoc etiam vestri (Jesuitæ) prædicarunt. Crescere jam non potest impietas. Ad summum pervenit.
units.tr: XXVII. The Papists therefore err gravely, who contend that the fear of hell and the horrors arising from the contemplation of judgement and punishment, which go by the name of attrition, or imperfect contrition, are a part of conversion, or a disposition to it, in the same way as faith is, and indeed that, with the sacrament of absolution added, they justify. For the fear of hell and the horror of divine judgement, considered in themselves, without a substitute faith and love of God, are evil, vicious, indeed deadly and lethal. This is so because it is an act of an unbelieving and unregenerate man, and all such acts are sin; because it does not proceed from the special grace of Christ; because it is without charity, since charity casts out fear, 1 John 4.18; because the trembling of man gives a snare, Prov. 29.25; because it is contrary to trust and is a kind of despair of grace; because it arises from love of self, of one's own advantage and tranquillity, and not from love of God above all things; and finally because fear alone cannot exclude the will to sin, which the Trent fathers falsely defined.
