For thought about divine holiness, justice and judgement cannot amend the sinner, if he does not hear the Gospel, that good word of God, and begin from it to love God. And things that arise from fear, considered in themselves, are involuntary, the will always remaining opposed, so that a man would not wish to do them if the fear of punishment were absent. That fear restrains the hand, but not the mind; it checks desire, but does not drain it. The mind, however, remains always fixed in the same way on desire. Indeed, the consideration, gathering and discussion of sin is so far from disposing one to grace or justifying one that it rather increases, stirs up and inflames sin, Rom. 4.15; 5.20; 7.7–9. But the Jesuitical doctrine of attrition, joined with absolution and justifying the sinner, fills up all the measures of impiety. As if, that is, absolution suits attrition as they explain it. This is to change the Gospel and to turn the priestly absolution into a magical incantation. For attrition by itself makes a sinner more of a hypocrite, because it does not arise from a sincere heart and an unfeigned faith, which ought to be armed with charity, 1 Cor. 13.1–2; 1 Tim. 1.5. How then will the priest absolve one who has such attrition, unless he attributes to his words an operation, as magicians are wont to do? But Montalte has lately revealed the hidden side of this impious Jesuitical doctrine in his Provincial Letter X, showing that the Jesuits are concerned and eager to invite to their penitential tribunal every kind of hypocrite, empty of all faith and love of God, and to subject them to their lust by promising pardon even to those who have never loved God throughout the course of their lives. Montalte rightly exclaimed: What remains, except that the privilege of not loving God, brought to men by Christ, should be proclaimed? This too your Jesuits have proclaimed. Impiety can no longer grow. It has reached its height.

units.la: XXVIII. Timor ille, quem Sapientiæ initium Solomon Prov. I. 7. dixit, non servilis & pœnæ, qui tormentum habet, & fuga Dei est, sed filialis & offensæ est; arca & custodia sapientiæ, scientiæ & salutis, Esaj. XXXIII. 6. Qui principium, hoc est, caput, summa sapientiæ, non ad justificationem dispositio est. Nam ex justificatione, qua ad Deum cum timore & fiducia accedimus, & Deum Patrem nostrum compellamus, oritur. Neque timorem, sed fidem initium & radicem justificationis esse ipsimet Tridentini asserverant. Unius enim rei unicum initium, unica radix est. Tantum verò abest, ut timor pœnæ accessum ad Deum muniat, ut potius per se consideratus Deum, ceu iratum judicem vindicémque peccatorum horreat. Neque vel Israelitarum, de quibus David, Psal. LXXVIII. 34. 35. loquitur, vel Ninevitarum timor ad justificationem eosdem disposuit. Nam de Israelitis ibid. vers. 36. sequitur: Blandiebantur ore suo, & lingua ei mentiebantur. Ninevitarum verò timor & contritio procul à justificatione eorundem abfuit. Sicut fœdus & Testamentum Dei, ex quo solo remissio peccatorum & salus contingit, iis nec prædicatum, nec cognitum omnino est: ita etiam vera cordis fiducia, se Deo, ut fideli ad servandum Creatori non commiserunt. Crediderunt Deo, Jon. III. 5. non uti justificanti peccatorem in Christo, sed ut revelanti judicium suum, nî resipiscerent. Converterunt se à via sua mala, ibid. v. 8. hoc est, à gravioribus sceleribus, quibus hactenus iram, & horrenda judicia Dei provocaverant, ex metu judicii à Jona intentati. Denique Deum pœnituit mali, quod loquutus erat, se facturum ipsis, & non fecit, ibid. v. 10. quia judicium temporale gravissimum executus non est, sed utcunque pœnitentibus pepercit. Exemplis ejusmodi Deus insinuare voluit, quid salutari resipiscentiæ ex fide in Christum procedenti, tandem exspectandum sit; argumento simili, quo Poëta quondam usus est, dicendo:
units.tr: XXVIII. That fear which Solomon calls the beginning of wisdom (Prov. 1:7) is not the servile fear of punishment, which carries torment and flees from God, but the filial fear of offence. It is the ark and guard of wisdom, knowledge and salvation (Isa. 33:6). The beginning, that is, the head and sum of wisdom, is not a disposition towards justification. For justification is what brings us to God with fear and trust, and lets us call God our Father. The Tridentine fathers themselves assert that it is not fear but faith is the beginning and root of justification. A single thing has one beginning and one root. Fear of punishment, far from opening the way to God, rather makes a man shrink from God considered in himself, as an angry judge and avenger of sins. Nor did the fear of the Israelites, of whom David speaks in Ps. 78:34–35, or the fear of the Ninevites, dispose them to justification. Of the Israelites it follows in the same psalm, v. 36: They flattered him with their mouth, and lied to him with their tongue. The fear and contrition of the Ninevites were far from their justification. Just as they had neither heard nor known the covenant and testament of God, from which alone forgiveness of sins and salvation come, so they had not truly committed their heart to the Creator as to a faithful one to keep. They believed God (Jonah 3:5), not as one who justifies the sinner in Christ, but as one who announced his judgment, unless they repented. They turned from their evil way (v. 8), that is, from the grave crimes by which they had hitherto provoked the wrath and dreadful judgments of God, out of fear of the judgment threatened by Jonah. Finally, God repented of the evil which he had said he would do to them, and did not do it (v. 10), because he did not carry out the most severe temporal judgment, but in some measure spared those who repented. By examples of this kind God wished to suggest what is finally to be expected from salutary repentance proceeding from faith in Christ, using a similar argument to that which a poet once used when he said: Nisa is given to Mopsus: what may we lovers not hope? Moreover, this is not the character of every kind of fear, that it flees evils and seeks remedies for escaping them; it is only salutary fear, joined with faith and love. For fear of punishment considered in itself is not a remedy for seeking God and fleeing sin, but the mother of despair. And if fear of this kind teaches us to seek those remedies, it does so as metanoia and aletheia [μετάνοια, ἀλήθεια], producing a vague and uncertain emotion of avoiding evils, whether present or impending, and not showing the true method by which those evils are avoided. But when that vague fear troubles the mind, it does not prepare it for justification in this way; rather it gives a sure sign of perdition. Just as in storms at sea, those tossed on the deep who see torn sails, a broken mast, oars snapped, the rudder gone, certainly fear greatly and bear witness to their fear with loud cries; yet that fear and those cries do not snatch them from danger. Hence John the Baptist rebuked this fear: Who taught you, he said, to flee from the coming wrath? Adding reproach for wickedness, he calls them a brood of vipers (Matt. 3:7), as if hinting that this servile fear produces nothing but hypocrites. Therefore the fear which both avoids evils and seeks remedies is filial, not servile: God instils a true hatred of evil and shows the true remedy, inviting the sinner to it. Likewise also the fear

units.la: Mopso Nisa datur: quid non speremus amantes?
units.tr: To Mopsus Nisa is given: what may we lovers not hope?

units.la: Præterea nec hæc cujusvis timoris indoles est, ut mala fugiat, & evadendi remedia quærat; sed salutaris duntaxat, & cum fide atque amore conjuncti. Per se enim timor pœnæ non quæstionis Dei & fugæ peccati remedium, sed desperationis mater est. Et si timor ejusmodi, & adversus illa remedia quærere docet, facit id μετανοίας & ἀληθείας, vagum incertúmque affectum elucidandi ex malis sive præsentibus, sive imminentibus generans, non veram rationem, qua illa evitentur demonstrans. Cùm verò vagus ille timor mentem agitat, non sic illam ad justificationem præparat, sed certum potius perditionis signum præbet. Quomodo in marinis tempestatibus qui jactati in alto vident lacera vela, succisum malum, remos fractos, clavum amotum, timent utique vehementer, & timorem altis clamoribus testantur. Sed timor & clamores illi à periculo non eripiunt. Unde Johannes Baptista timorem hunc increpans: Quis, inquit, docuit vos fugere ab ira ventura? Sed addens vituperationem nequitiæ, progeniem viperarum appellat Matth. III. 7. quasi innuens, quòd timor hic servilis nil nisi hypocritas efficiat. Qui igitur timor & mala vitat, & remedia quærit, filialis, non servilis est; Deo & verum mali odium instillante, & verum remedium ostendente, atque ad illud invitante. Pariter etiam timor
units.tr: Moreover, this fear is not of a kind that merely flees evils and seeks ways of escape, but is salutary only, and joined with faith and love. For fear of punishment, taken by itself, is not the remedy for seeking God and fleeing sin; it is the mother of despair. And if such fear teaches men to seek those remedies, it does so in the manner of repentance [μετανοίας] and truth [ἀληθείας], generating a vague and uncertain feeling that tries to escape present or impending evils, but not showing the true way by which they are avoided. When that vague fear troubles the mind, it does not thus prepare it for justification; rather, it gives a sure sign of perdition. It is like sailors tossed on the open sea in a storm: when they see torn sails, a broken mast, broken oars and a lost rudder, they are certainly terrified and show their fear by loud cries. But that fear and those cries do not rescue them from danger. So John the Baptist, rebuking this fear, said: Who taught you to flee from the wrath to come? and, adding reproach for their wickedness, he calls them a brood of vipers (Matth. III. 7), as if hinting that this servile fear produces nothing but hypocrites. Therefore the fear that both shuns evils and seeks remedies is filial, not servile, since God instills a true hatred of evil and shows the true remedy, inviting men to it. Likewise also fear

units.la: Objectiones contrariæ dilumuntur. timor ille ibid. X. 28. à Christo jubente timere eum, qui animam & corpus perdere in gehenna potest, commendatus, filialis, cum fide & amore Dei conjunctus intelligitur. Nam timor est Dei, qui sicut supra omnia amandus, ita etiam supra homines omnes timendus est vel ideo etiam, quia Dominus vitæ & mortis est, & non timentem anima & corpore perdere potest. Denique neque pœnitentia Sacramentum est; neque si esset, virtute tanta polleret, ut per absolutionem ex attrito contritum facere, atque ita sola attritum, accedente sola absolutione, justificare valeret. Quod etiam Thomas, Scotus, aliique negant, ratione hac inducti, quòd Sacramentum voluntati aliud objectum non constituat. Et supponit sententia illa Sacramentorum efficaciam ex opere operato, quam alibi configimus.
units.tr: The contrary objections are answered. That fear commended by Christ, when he bids us (ibid. X. 28) fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell, is understood as filial, joined with faith and the love of God. For the fear is of God, who, as he is to be loved above all things, so is he to be feared above all men; and this is so also for the reason that the Lord has power over life and death, and can destroy both soul and body in hell. Finally, neither is repentance a sacrament, nor, even if it were, would it have such power that through absolution it could make the attrite contrite, and so justify the attrite by absolution alone. Thomas, Scotus and others also deny this, led by the reasoning that a sacrament does not constitute any other object for the will. And that opinion presupposes the efficacy of the sacraments ex opere operato, which we have refuted elsewhere.

units.la: XXIX. Alia planè ratio λύπης κ) Θεοῦ tristitia secundum Deum est, quæ operatur μετάνοιαν ἀμεταμέλητον resipiscentiam, cujus neminem pœnitet, (in actu & studio, non in ejus forma secundum quam tristitia resipiscentiæ pars est) ad salutem, 2. Cor. VII. 9. 10. Est autem tristitia secundum Deum, qua homo tristatur non propter se, sed propter Deum, quem & suapte indole bonum, sanctum, justumque, & tot nos beneficiis mactantem nos offendisse dolemus. Oritur igitur ex odio Sathanæ & mali, nec non ex amore Dei & boni. Nemini enim malum displicet, nisi qui bonum cognoscit & diligit. Et tristitia hæc κ) Θεοῦ secundum Deum dicitur, quia in ea quædam similitudo Dei est, non quòd apud Deum sit tristitia, sed tum quia Deo displicet illud, propter quod tristatur homo, qui secundum Deum tristatur: tum quia apud Deum verum & justum est, ut peccator peccati causa tristetur. Hæc illa trepidatio propter verbum Jehovæ est, Esaj. LXVI. 2. scissio, laceratio cordis, Joel. II. 13. πενθῶ· luctus propter violationem nominis & gloriæ Dei, Matth. V. 4. Esaj. LXI. 2. κατανύξις compunctio, contritio, de qua dicitur: Audientes κατενύγησαν τῇ καρδίᾳ compuncti sunt corde, Actor. II. 37. Quæ salutaris compunctio & contritio est, opposita illi κατανύξει, cujus spiritum Deus reprobis, oculos habentibus, nec tamen videntibus, aures & non audientibus dedisse, Rom. XI. 8. dicitur. Ubi κατανύξις respondet Hebraeo תַּרְדֵּמָה, Esaj. XXIX. 10. quod est κῶμα, κάρος· sopor veternus, lethargus. Spiritus enim intelligitur, non affectus vel habitus voluntatis & mentis, qui hominem dormitare facit; sed spiritus seductionis, qui hominem captivum tenet, & laqueis adstringit, ut ἀναννήψειν sobrius fieri & evigilare non valeat, 2. Tim. II. 26. Qui status hominum indurator um est, quos Sathanas infatuat, & quocunque vult seducit.
units.tr: XXIX. There is quite a different account: The sorrow that is according to God [λύπη κατὰ Θεόν] is sorrow according to God, which works repentance [μετάνοια] without regret [ἀμεταμέλητον], of which no one repents (in the act and disposition, not in the form in accordance with which sorrow is a part of repentance) unto salvation, 2 Cor. 7:9–10. Now sorrow according to God is that by which a man grieves not for himself but for God, whom he grieves to have offended, since God is good, holy and just in his own nature, and has overwhelmed us with so many benefits. It therefore arises from hatred of Satan and of evil, and also from love of God and of good. For evil displeases no one except one who knows and loves the good. And this sorrow is called according to God [κατὰ Θεόν], secundum Deum, because there is a certain likeness of God in it, not because there is sorrow in God, but both because that at which the man grieves displeases God, so that he who grieves according to God grieves in accordance with God, and because it is true and just before God that the sinner should grieve on account of sin. This is the trembling at the word of Jehovah (Isa. 66:2), the rending, the laceration of the heart (Joel 2:13), mourning [πενθῶ] for the violation of the name and glory of God (Matt. 5:4; Isa. 61:2), and compunction [κατάνυξις], contrition, of which it is said: When they heard it, they were pricked [κατενύγησαν τῇ καρδίᾳ] in their heart (Acts 2:37). This is the salutary compunction and contrition, opposed to that compunction [κατάνυξις] of which God is said to have given to the reprobate a spirit, eyes that see not and ears that hear not (Rom. 11:8). Here katanyxis corresponds to the Hebrew tardemah [תַּרְדֵּמָה] (Isa. 29:10), which is koma, karos [κῶμα, κάρος]: deep sleep, drowsiness, lethargy. For a spirit is understood, not an affection or habit of the will and mind that makes a man drowsy; but the spirit of delusion, which holds man captive and binds him with snares, so that he cannot become sober and awake [ἀναννήψειν] (2 Tim. 2:26). This is the state that hardens men whom Satan blinds and leads wherever he wishes.

units.la: XXX. Contritio hæc non sic voluntarius & liberè assumptus dolor est, ut passiones, seu terrores à lege incussos excludat, quod Tridentinorum inficetum dogma est; ne videlicet passiones ejusmodi aliquid de merito contritionis ad gratiam disponentis, deterant. Licèt enim à regenitorum contritione voluntariæ & liberæ actiones non absint, non tamen passiones & terrores à lege incussi, ad resipiscentiam non externa aliqua vi, sed blanda & flexanima Spiritus S. operatione trahentes, ab eadem exulant. Nam & in corde timor futuri judicii, & in conscientia compunctio, horror angorque summus obtinet. Neque omnino sine passione vel κατανύξει compunctio locum habet: vel Spiritus S. cor lapideum aufert, & carneum restituit, vàsque novum ex fracto format virtute creandi, uti Prosper loquitur: vel co fusio, erubescentia, percussio, conturbatio animæ, tribulatio Spiritus, cordis scissio cogitari potest. Irregenitorum verò contritio mere passiva est. Nam quæ in externis gestibus & actibus consistit, & ex viribus arbitrii naturalis oriri potest, hypocritica, non salutaris est. Coactioni externæ & violentiæ nullum hic locum concedimus. Lex enim per Spiritum filiationis ita fideles terret, & sancta desperatione afficit, ut voluntati vim nullam faciat, sed eam potius vi blanda ad Christum salutis anchoram adducat. Denique non si peccatum per liberum voluntatis consensum admittitur, dimitti etiam sola assensus libertate potest, quæ princeps Thomæ Aquinatis ratio est. Nam peccator sponte in servitutem peccati, & mortem spiritualem se præcipitavit. At servus peccati, & in eodem mortuus nulla ad resurgendum libertate & potestate valet.
units.tr: XXX. This contrition is not a grief so voluntary and freely assumed that it excludes the passions or terrors inflicted by the law, which is the absurd dogma of the Tridentines; for fear that such passions would detract something from the merit of contrition that disposes to grace. For although voluntary and free actions are not absent from the contrition of the regenerate, yet the passions and terrors inflicted by the law, which draw them to repentance not by any external force but by the gentle and soul-bending operation of the Holy Spirit, are not excluded from it. For in the heart there is fear of the future judgment, and in the conscience compunction, horror and the greatest anguish. Nor does compunction take place altogether without passion or katanyxis: either the Holy Spirit takes away the stony heart and restores a fleshy one, and forms a new vessel from the broken one by the power of creating, as Prosper says; or confusion, blushing, stricken shame, troubling of the soul, tribulation of spirit and rending of the heart may be thought of. But the contrition of the unregenerate is merely passive. For that which consists in external gestures and acts, and can arise from the powers of natural free will, is hypocritical, not salutary. We allow no place here for external coercion or violence. For the law, through the Spirit of adoption, so terrifies the faithful and affects them with holy despair, that it does no violence to the will, but rather, by a gentle force, brings it to Christ, the anchor of salvation. Finally, if sin is admitted through free consent of the will, it cannot be pardoned by freedom of assent alone, which is the chief argument of Thomas Aquinas. For the sinner has of his own accord cast himself into the slavery of sin and spiritual death. But a slave of sin, who is dead in it, has no freedom or power to rise again.

units.la: XXXI. Contritio sine fide in Christum salutaris esse non potest. Nam fides sola, non historica, quam disponere ad justificationem Pontificii nugantur, & quæ Diabolorum etiam esse potest; sed justificans, seu fiducialis illa apprehensio Christi, eam à non salutari, quæ reproborum est, distinguit. Cùm enim salutaris sit κ) Θεοῦ secundum Deum, amore Dei destitui nequit. Et amor Dei à fide est, 1. Tim. I. 5. Etenim Petri resipiscentia salutaris fuit, quia ex fide & amore Christi processit: at Judæ pœnitentia exitialis fuit, quia sine fide & amore Christi desperationem mortemque operata est. Quicquid enim sine fide est, peccatum est, Rom. XIV. 23. & sine fide impossibile est Deo placere, aut ad eum accedere, Heb. XI. 6. Sola ea cor purificat, Act. XV. 9. Absque qua est, pœnitentia tota est opus legis, neque ullam conscientiis anxiis consolationem solidam affert. Per fidem solam testimonium Dei de ejus χρηστότητι bonitate, quam is in Christo ad justificandum peccatorem exercet, apprehendentem primò peccator Deum amare incipit. Fides proin conversionis initium est. Ut merito Pontificiis fidem à salutari pœnitentia removentibus sic Chemnitius insultaverit: Hac nota, hoc indicio, Dei judicio, coram toto mundo revelatur; qualis Ecclesia Pontificum cœtus sit. Ad perpetuam igitur rei memoriam notum sit verè Ecclesiæ Dei, Concilium Tridentinum promittere pœnitentiæ reconciliationem cum Deo, & remissionem peccatorum sine fide, quæ quidem ex Evangelio concepta sit, & qua quis credat per Christum sibi peccata remissa esse.
units.tr: XXXI. Contrition without faith in Christ cannot be saving. For faith alone, not the historical faith which the Papists foolishly claim prepares a man for justification (and which even devils can have), but the justifying or fiducial apprehension of Christ, distinguishes saving contrition from the non-saving kind, which belongs to the reprobate. For since it is saving according to God [κατὰ Θεόν], it cannot be deprived of the love of God. And the love of God is from faith, 1 Tim. 1:5. Peter's repentance was indeed saving, because it proceeded from faith and love of Christ; but Judas's repentance was destructive, because without faith and love of Christ it brought about despair and death. For whatever is not of faith is sin, Rom. 14:23, and without faith it is impossible to please God or to draw near to him, Heb. 11:6. Faith alone purifies the heart, Acts 15:9. Without faith, repentance is wholly a work of the law, and it brings no solid comfort to anxious consciences. Through faith alone, which grasps the testimony of God concerning his goodness [χρηστότης] which he exercises in Christ to justify the sinner, the sinner first begins to love God. Faith is therefore the beginning of conversion. Chemnitz rightly mocked the Papists, who remove faith from saving repentance, in these words: By this mark, by this sign, by the judgment of God, it is revealed before the whole world what kind of assembly the Church of the Pontiffs is. Let it therefore be known for the perpetual memory of the matter that the Council of Trent truly, as far as the Church of God is concerned, promises reconciliation with God and remission of sins in repentance without faith, which indeed is conceived from the Gospel, and by which one believes that his sins have been forgiven through Christ.

units.la: XXXII. Cum resipiscentia strictè sumpta fides conjunctissima est; at pars tamen ejus non est. Passim enim à fide distinguitur. Resipiscite, & credite Evangelio, Marc. I. 15. Paulus testificatus est Judæis & Gentibus τὸν εἰς τὸν Θεὸν μετάνοιαν, καὶ πίστιν resipiscentiam in Deum, & fidem in Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, Act. XX. 21. Fides enim proprie in Christum: Resipiscentia in Deum fertur, ejusque voluntati se conformat. Pro diversa resipiscentiæ notione, & diversis ejusdem partibus ordo utriusque variat. Nam resipiscentia quoad dolorem & peccatorum sensum fide prior est, & Marc. I. 15. Actor. XX.21. diserte huic praemittitur; quia vix peccatorum remissionem nobis suademus, quorum vulnera & aculeos nondum sensimus. Quoad reliquam vero vitae emendationem fides resipiscentia prior est; quia vitae spiritualis initium est: ut tamen dolor de peccato & tristitia secundum Deum, sancta, Deoque placens & salutaris sit, fides efficit. Quo respectu iterum fides refipiscentiam praecedit; quia sine fide nihil Deo placere, Hebr. XI. 6. vel boni quicquam in homine existere potest.
units.tr: XXXII. Although faith is most closely joined with repentance taken strictly, it is nevertheless not a part of it. For it is everywhere distinguished from faith. Repent and believe the Gospel, Mark 1:15. Paul testified to both Jews and Gentiles repentance toward God, and faith [τὴν εἰς τὸν Θεὸν μετάνοιαν, καὶ πίστιν] toward our Lord Jesus Christ, Acts 20:21. For faith is properly directed to Christ, while repentance is directed to God and conforms itself to his will. The order of the two varies according to the different notions of repentance and its different parts. For repentance, as regards sorrow and the sense of sin, comes before faith, and Mark 1:15 and Acts 20:21 clearly place it first; for we can hardly persuade ourselves of the remission of sins whose wounds and stings we have not yet felt. As regards the remaining amendment of life, however, faith comes before repentance, because it is the beginning of the spiritual life; yet it is faith that makes the sorrow for sin and the grief according to God holy, pleasing to God, and saving. In this respect again faith precedes repentance, because without faith nothing can be pleasing to God, Heb. 11:6, nor can anything good exist in a man.

units.la: XXXIII. Tristitiam secundum Deum ex fide & amore Dei profectam humilima remissionis peccatorum, & innovationis gratiae implioratio comitatur.
units.tr: XXXIII. Sorrow according to God, arising from faith and love of God, is accompanied by the most humble plea for the remission of sins and for the renewal of grace.

units.la: Ita David poenitens: Gratiosus esto, inquit, secundum bonitatem tuam, secundum amplitudinem miserocordiae tuae dele defectiones meas. Multum lava me a pravitate mea, & a peccato meo purifica me, Psal. LI. 3. 4. Et mox: Expia me hyssopo, & purus ero. Lava me, & prae nive albescam. Averte faciem tuam a peccatis meis, & omnes pravitates meas dele. Cor purum crea in me, & spiritum firmum innova in medio mei, ibid. v. 9. 11. 12. Faciunt huc etiam Psalmi poenitentiales reliqui, sextus, trigesimus secundus, trigesimus octavus, centesimus secundus, centesimus trigesimus, & centesimus quadragesimus tertius, in quibus poenitentis preces humilimae, gratiam Dei & remissionem peccatorum implorantes continentur. Publicanus quoque percussus corde suo, precatus est: O Θεός ιλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ. O Deus propitius esto mihi peccatori, Luc. XVIII. 13.
units.tr: So David, repenting: Be gracious, he says, according to your goodness; according to the greatness of your mercy blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin, Ps. 51:3, 4. And soon after: Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean. Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities. Create in me a clean heart, and renew a steadfast spirit within me, ibid. vv. 9, 11, 12. The remaining penitential Psalms also bear on this: the sixth, the thirty-second, the thirty-eighth, the one hundred and second, the one hundred and thirtieth, and the one hundred and forty-third, which contain the most humble prayers of the penitent imploring the grace of God and the remission of sins. The publican also, struck in his heart, prayed: O God, be merciful to me a sinner [ὁ Θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ]: O God, be propitious to me, a sinner, Luke 18:13.

units.la: XXXIV. Denique ferium vitae emendandae propositum refipiscentiam absolvit.
units.tr: XXXIV. Finally, a firm purpose of amending one's life completes repentance.

units.la: Nam in Christo Jesu valet nova creatura, Gal. VI. 15. Si cut Christus surrexit ex mortuis, per gloriam Patris, ita & nos in novitate vitae ambulemus, Rom. VI. 4. Haec illa condeleatio sive deliciatio in lege Dei, ibid. VII. 22. Psal. I. 2. fames & sitis justitiae, atque ita servitutis justitiae ad gloriam Dei, Matth. V. 6. cum voto, proposito & studio serio proficiendi ad ἐπίγνωσιν cognitionem vel agnitionem, quae digna sit imagine Dei creatoris, Col. III. 10. & ad ἀπληροφορίαν τῆς ἐλπίδος plenitudinem spei. Neque illud obstat, quod vitae emendationem refipiscentiae fructum, non partem fecit Johannes Baptista, dicens: Ferte fructus dignos poenitentia; de resipiscentia quippe strictissime, pro solo animi dolore, accepta intelligendum hoc est.
units.tr: For in Christ Jesus a new creation avails, Gal. 6:15. As Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so also we should walk in newness of life, Rom. 6:4. This is that delight in the law of God, Rom. 7:22; Ps. 1:2; hunger and thirst for righteousness, and so for the righteous service to the glory of God, Matt. 5:6, with the wish, purpose, and earnest zeal of advancing toward knowledge [ἐπίγνωσις], or recognition, which is worthy of the image of God the Creator, Col. 3:10, and toward the fullness [πληροφορία] of hope. Nor does it count against this that John the Baptist made the amendment of life not a part but a fruit of repentance, saying: Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance; for this must be understood of repentance taken most strictly, as sorrow of mind alone.

units.la: XXXV. Praeterea non sic vitae emendatio a tristitia secundum Deum, reliquisque partibus divellenda est, ut tempore diversa putetur.
units.tr: XXXV. Moreover, the amendment of life must not be torn away from sorrow according to God and the other parts, as if it belonged to a different time.

units.la: Praecipuae enim refipiscentiae partes, tristitia secundum Deum & vitae emendatio, quarum illa, juxta tritum illud Ambrosii, peccata commissa plangit, haec plangenda haud iterum committit: ejusdem actionis & mutationis diversi duntaxat termini sunt, quorum priore vetus homo mortificatur, posteriore novus vivificatur. Et qui convertitur, a malo ad bonum, a tenebris ad lucem, a servitute Sathanae ad Deum convertitur, quae simul fiunt. Quoad ordinem vero naturae, licet novitas sit posterior vetusta-te, & in profecta tristitia prior sit laetitia, tamen novitas amoris Dei est causa abolendi vetustatem odii Dei. Sicut enim non tolluntur tenebrae nisi per lucem, nec mors nisi per vitam, nec paupertas nisi per divitias, nec nuditas nisi per vestitum, nec vitium nisi per virtutem; ita nec odium peccati & mali nisi per amorem virtutis & boni minui tollique potest.
units.tr: For the chief parts of repentance are sorrow according to God and amendment of life. Of these, the former, in Ambrose's well-worn phrase, laments the sins committed, and the latter does not commit again what is to be lamented. They are only different termini of one action and one change: by the first the old man is put to death, by the second the new man is made alive. And whoever is converted is turned from evil to good, from darkness to light, from the slavery of Satan to God, and these happen together. As to the order of nature, although newness comes after oldness, and in sorrow once arisen joy comes first, nevertheless the newness of love for God is the cause of abolishing the oldness of hatred of God. For just as darkness is removed only by light, death only by life, poverty only by riches, nakedness only by clothing, and vice only by virtue, so the hatred of sin and evil cannot be diminished or removed except by the love of virtue and good.

units.la: XXXVI. Resipiscentia omnis est ad vitam, Act. XI. 18. Impius si aversus fuerit ab omnibus peccatis suis, &c. vivendo vivet, Ezech. XVIII. 21.
units.tr: XXXVI. All repentance leads to life, Acts 11:18. "If the wicked turns away from all his sins, etc., by living he shall live," Ezek. 18:21.

units.la: Tristitia secundum Deum operatur refipiscentiam ad salutem, cujus neminem poenitet, 2. Cor. VII. 10. Non quod vitam & salutem, ut causa meritoria operetur, sed quia ἐχόμεθα τῆς σωτηρίας, Hebr. VI. 9. cum vita & salute, ut certissimum acceptae gratiae & justitiae ἀπαρτισμόν conjuncta est. Infinitum enim est dogma Tridentinorum Sess. IV. cap. 4. definientium, contritionem cum fiducia Divinae misericordiae & voto praestandi reliqua conjunctam ad remissionem peccatorum disponere; & eandem charitate perfectam hominem Deo reconciliare. Et Scholasticorum alii, velut Lombardus, Thomas, Bonaventura, Scotus, contritionem de congruo, alii, velut Richardus, de condigno meritoriam esse contendunt. Sed non semel reconciliationem & remissionem peccatorum mere gratuitam esse, confirmavimus. Et poenitentia cum Dei donum fit, Act. V. 31. 2. Tim. II. 25. meritoria esse non potest. Et sicut aegrotantis dolor nunquam morbum sanat: ita nec contritio peccatoris eundem justificat. Estque dogma hoc desperationis laqueus, quia nunquam conscientia de justa & debita, uti vocant, contritione, & adjuncta charitatis perfectione certa reddi potest. Ut ita de peccatorum remissione perpetim dubitandum sit. Neque contritionem causam vitae facit Ezechiel, dicens; Si se converterit impius, & fecerit judicium & justitiam, ipse animam suam vivificabit; cap. XVIII. 27. Vivificationis enim animae causa meritoria solus Christus est, Joh. V. 25. non homo ullus ullo opere suo. Convertens tamen se vivificare animam suam dicitur, quia conversio est conditio, signum & ἀνάμνησις vitae. Ejusmodi enim descriptiones synecdochicae in sacris usitatae sunt, in quibus ex parte totum, ex signo significatum, ex consequente antecedens, ex fructu arbor cognoscitur, ibid. v. 31. convertendus iubetur sibi facere cor novum, quod solus tamen Deus facere potest. Qui jubens facere cor novum, simul illud per Spiritum S. & ministerium verbi facit, de quo supra pluribus. Et passim quidem Patres docent, poenitentia Deum mitigari & placari, lachrymis peccata abluii, contritionem veniam mereri. Sed loquuntur illi de poenitentia salutari, & adjuncta eidem fide, cujus objectum apprehensum, Christus ejusmodi effectus sanguine suo producit. Et talia iis in genere loquendi non didascalico, sed homiletico, & ad poenitentiam hortatorio versantibus exciderunt. Concionatorum autem verba non eo semper rigore accipienda esse, quo primum ad auditorum aures perveniunt, cum multa per hyperbolen enuntient, & affectionum impetu, vel orationis cursu saepe abripiantur; etiam Sixtus Senensis Biblioth. lib. IV. Annot. 152. agnoscit. Alibi vero iidem Patres mentem suam commodius explicant.
units.tr: Godly sorrow works repentance unto salvation, which no one regrets, 2 Cor. 7:10. Not that it works life and salvation as a meritorious cause, but because we "hold on to salvation" [ἐχόμεθα τῆς σωτηρίας], Heb. 6:9, and life and salvation are joined to it as the most certain completion [ἀπαρτισμόν] of grace received and righteousness. The doctrine of the Tridentines, Sess. IV, cap. 4, is an endless one: they define that contrition, joined with confidence in divine mercy and a vow to perform the rest, disposes a man to the remission of sins, and that the same contrition, perfected by charity, reconciles a man to God. Some of the Schoolmen, such as Lombard, Thomas, Bonaventure and Scotus, contend that contrition is meritorious de congruo; others, such as Richard, that it is meritorious de condigno. But we have confirmed more than once that reconciliation and the remission of sins are purely gratuitous. And since repentance is a gift of God, Acts 5:31, 2 Tim. 2:25, it cannot be meritorious. Just as the pain of a sick man never cures the disease, so the contrition of a sinner does not justify him. This doctrine is a snare of despair, because the conscience can never be made certain of a just and due contrition, as they call it, joined with perfect charity; so one must always doubt the remission of sins. Nor does Ezekiel make contrition the cause of life when he says: If the wicked turns himself, and does judgment and justice, he shall vivify his soul, ch. 18:27. For the meritorious cause of vivifying the soul is Christ alone, John 5:25, and no man by any work of his own. Yet one who turns himself is said to vivify his soul, because conversion is the condition, sign and reminder of life. Such synecdochic descriptions are common in Scripture: from part the whole, from sign the thing signified, from consequent the antecedent, from fruit the tree is known. In ibid. v. 31 the one to be converted is bidden to make himself a new heart, which yet God alone can make. He who bids a new heart be made at the same time makes it, through the Holy Spirit and the ministry of the Word, as discussed more fully above. And indeed the Fathers everywhere teach that by repentance God is softened and appeased, that sins are washed away by tears, and that contrition merits pardon. But they speak of saving repentance, with faith joined to it, whose object, Christ, apprehended by faith, produces such effects by his blood. Such expressions slipped from them in a general manner of speaking, not didactic but homiletic, addressed to those who were being exhorted to repentance. Nor are the words of preachers always to be taken with the rigour with which they first reach the hearers' ears, since they utter many things by hyperbole and are often carried away by the rush of emotion or the course of their speech; even Sixtus of Siena acknowledges this, Bibliotheca, lib. IV, Annot. 152. Elsewhere, however, the same Fathers explain their meaning more suitably.

units.la: XXXVII. Resipiscendum homini per totum vitae curriculum est.
units.tr: XXXVII. A man must repent throughout the whole course of his life.

units.la: Semper enim malum odio habendum, bono adhærendum est, Rom. XII.9. Cùm Christus passus sit pro nobis carne, & vos eadem cogitatione armate, quòd qui passus est in carne (mortuus est, vel aliquid in carne adversum passus est) desiit à peccato. (non mali aliquid patiatur, sed cesset peccare, & ad peccandum tentari) Ne amplius hominum concupiscentiis, sed voluntati Dei reliquum tempus in carne vivatis. Sufficit enim præteritum vitæ tempus, ut voluntatem gentium feceritis, cùm ambulastis in lasciviis, concupiscentiis, vinolentiis, &c. 1.Pet.IV.1.2.3. Nihilominus casus & tempora quædam singularem resipiscentiam & ejus velut quoddam exigunt, velut cùm vel fideles gravia in peccata, conscientiam vastantia inciderunt; vel judicia Dei singularia imminere videntur, imò jam ingruunt; vel cùm nos ipsos ad singularem quampiam gratiam & favorem Dei percipiendum præparamus. Ita enim David gravia in peccata lapsus singularem & inusitatam pœnitentiam exercuit, 2.Sam. XII.16. &c. Psal.LI.2.3. &c. Et ingruentibus judiciis Dei. Sic faciam tibi, Israel, inquit Deus, Eò quòd hoc faciam tibi ... præpara teipsum in occursum Dei tui, ô Israel! Amos IV.12. Denique etiam Jacobus jussus ascendere in Bethel, & ibi manere, & altare Deo facere, ut præsentia Dei adversus fratris insidias erigi posset, domesticis suis omnibus præcipit: Auferte Deos alienos, qui sunt in medio vestri, & mundamini, & mutate vestimenta vestra, &c. Genes.XXXV.2.3.&c.
units.tr: For always evil is to be hated, good is to be clung to, Rom. 12:9. Since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same mind, for he who has suffered in the flesh (has died, or has undergone something adverse in the flesh) has ceased from sin (not that he suffers some evil, but that he ceases to sin and to be tempted to sin); so that you no longer live the rest of your time in the flesh for the lusts of men, but for the will of God. For the past time of your life is sufficient for having done the will of the Gentiles, when you walked in lasciviousness, lusts, drunkenness, etc., 1 Pet. 4:1-3. Nevertheless certain occasions and times demand a singular repentance, and as it were a certain kind of it: for instance, when the faithful have fallen into grave sins that lay waste the conscience; or when singular judgments of God seem to hang over them, or indeed are already bearing down; or when we prepare ourselves to receive some singular grace and favour of God. So David, having fallen into grave sins, exercised a singular and unusual repentance, 2 Sam. 12:16 etc., Ps. 51:2-3 etc. And when the judgments of God were approaching: Thus will I do to you, Israel, says God, because I will do this to you ... prepare yourself to meet your God, O Israel! Amos 4:12. Finally, Jacob, bidden to go up to Bethel, to dwell there and to make an altar to God so that the presence of God might be raised against the treachery of his brother, commands all his household: Put away the strange gods that are among you, and be clean, and change your garments, etc., Gen. 35:2-3 etc.

units.la: XXXVIII. Nunquam sera resipiscentia est, quæ vera est. Vera autem est, quæ tum odium peccati ejusque fugam conjunctam habet, juxta illa Davidis: Omnem semitam mendacii odi, Psal.CXIX.128. tum amore boni, & studio officii implendi, sine ulla exceptione incalescit, juxta illa ejusdem Davidis: Non afficiar pudore, cùm omnia præcepta tua intuitus fuero, ibid. v.6. tum omnes resipiscentiæ numeros sic implet, ut & odium peccati lucta perpetua, & inimicitia inexpiabili cum carne & peccato testatur, & amorem justitiæ ejusdem fructificatione & studio bonorum operum demonstret. Neque tamen ex doctrina hac sequitur, pœnitentiam tutò differri posse. Nam & extrema pœnitentia inveteratis adeò habitibus; cùm mala per longas invaluere moras, difficilior longè, & raro sincera est: & peccator ignorat, an ostium pœnitentiæ semper apertum futurum sit. Multi enim inopinatò & talibus morbis implicantur, qui rationis usum intercipiunt. Multi etiam moribundi sui similes manent, nec horrorem judicii Divini sentiunt; & vix experimentum veræ fidei capiunt, vel consolationem ullam concipiunt. Qui tandiu Deo monitori aures clauserunt: iis, nisi singulari plane & inusitata gratia, subitò aures non aperiet. Serae lachrymæ ex horrore inferni potius, quàm amore Dei scaturire possunt. Habet etiam Dei patientia definitum tempus, Genes.VI.3. Cùm igitur homines peccatis finem modumque nullum imponunt, at Deus patientiæ suæ limites figit. Plumbei Dei pedes, at ferreæ manus sunt. Et ut pœnitentia sera & vera nonnullis contingat, tamen pœnitentes illi jacturam totius operis antegressi, mali quipe & vani, patientur, & servabuntur quidem, sed tanquam per ignem. Hæc qui serio pensitaverit, properabit ille agere pœnitentiam, & virtutes Dei annuntiare, sicut se gloria afficere Deum & Redemptorem suum, optimum bonæ conscientiæ & consolationis spei thesaurum, & gradum excellentiorem in retributione hæreditatis lucrari, & laborem suum in Domino etiam in hac vita, quoad fructum hæreditatis plurimum frustra non fore. Quam enim spem habere is potest, qui non omne studium ad plenitudinem spei affert? Qui non timet? Qui Spiritus S. signaculum non habet, & illud vivens recènsque in se non intuetur?
units.tr: XXXVIII. Repentance that is true is never too late. But that repentance is true which has joined with it both hatred of sin and flight from it, according to David's words: I hate every false way, Ps. 119:128; and which glows with love of good and zeal to fulfil duty without any exception, according to the same David's words: I shall not be put to shame, when I have regarded all your commandments, ibid. v. 6; and which fulfils all the marks of repentance, so that both its hatred of sin shows a perpetual struggle and implacable enmity with the flesh and sin, and its love of righteousness is demonstrated by fruitfulness and zeal for good works. Yet it does not follow from this doctrine that repentance can safely be deferred. For even last-minute repentance, when habits have grown so inveterate that evils have grown strong through long delays, is far more difficult and rarely sincere; and the sinner does not know whether the door of repentance will always be open. For many are unexpectedly caught by such sicknesses as take away the use of reason. Many also remain like the dying man here described, and do not feel the horror of divine judgment, and scarcely gain any experience of true faith or conceive any comfort. Those who have so long closed their ears to God warning them: unless by a singular and quite unusual grace, he will not suddenly open their ears to them. Late tears may well spring from horror of hell rather than from love of God. God's patience also has a set time, Gen. 6:3. So when men set no end or measure to their sins, God sets limits to his patience. God's feet are leaden, but his hands are iron. And though a late but true repentance may fall to some, yet those penitents will suffer the loss of the whole work that went before, which was evil and vain, and they will indeed be saved, but as through fire. Whoever has seriously weighed these things will hasten to perform repentance and to proclaim the virtues of God; he will want to glorify God and his Redeemer, to gain the best treasure of a good conscience and the consolation of hope, and a higher rank in the reward of the inheritance; and he will know that his labour in the Lord, even in this life, will not be in vain as regards the fruit of the inheritance. For what hope can he have who does not bring all his zeal to the fullness of hope? Who does not fear? Who does not have the seal of the Holy Spirit, and does not look upon it living and fresh within himself?

units.la: XXXIX. Habet etiam Pœnitentia exteriora quædam signa, quibus suam pœnitentes coram Deo humiliationem peccatique horrorem; præcipuè in luctu & castigationibus testantur. Talia in populo Dei inprimis fuerunt pectoris percussio, Nahum.II.8. Luc.XVIII.13. Vestium scissio, 1.Reg.XXI.27. Joel.I.13. Saccorum, ceu vestis vilioris, asperæ, sordidæ, durae, &c. indumenta: pulveris in capite sparsio, in cinere volutatio, & cineris unâ cum pane manducatio; fletus & lachrymæ, quales etiam S. Petrus fudit: jejunia, eleemosynæ aliáque ejusmodi, de quibus copiosè & erudite Clariss.Gejerus de Luctu Hebræorum scripsit. Cùm enim pœnitentia sit totius hominis, illa etiam in corpore se exerat oportet. Nam illud sine motu omni spiritualiter mortui speciem præfert. Sed simulari tamen signa ejusmodi possunt; imò in talibus homines naturales & profani haud raro spiritualibus, qui plus spiritu quàm corpore valent, vividiores se gerunt, quod falsarum religionum pœnitentia demonstrat. An tale est jejunium, quod elegi, per diem ut affligat homo animam suam? An ut incurvet sicut juncus caput suum, & saccum & cinerem sternat? Nonne hoc est jejunium, quod elegi, ut dissolvas colligationes impietatis, solvas fasciculos graves, & dimittas confractos liberos? &c. Esaj.LVIII.5.6. Convertimini ad me toto corde vestro, & cum jejunio & cum fletu, & cum planctu. Et lacerate corda vestra, & non vestes vestras, & redite ad Jehovam Deum vestrum, Joel.I.12.13. Non vult enim Deus se coli consuetudinibus præcepto humano subintroductis, & κατ' ἀφοσίωσιν usurpatis. Conversionis verae laus quaerenda est apud Deum; non apud homines, nisi quando ipsorum ædificatio id postulat. Quoties verò ea, quæ conjungenda sunt, ab hominibus separantur, solet Scriptura in separatione tali meliorem partem eligere, & minorem quasi absolutè rejicere. Pietatem volo, & non sacrificium, Hos.VI.6. Accipite disciplinam meam, & non argentum, Prov.VIII.10. Misit me ad prædicandum, non ad baptizandum, 1.Cor. I.17.
units.tr: XXXIX. Repentance also has certain outward signs by which penitents testify before God to their humiliation and their horror of sin, chiefly in mourning and in acts of self-punishment. Among the people of God the most common of these were beating the breast, Nah. 2:8; Luke 18:13; tearing the garments, 1 Kings 21:27; Joel 1:13; wearing sackcloth, that is, coarse, rough, dirty and hard clothing; sprinkling dust on the head and rolling in ashes; eating ashes with bread; weeping and tears, such as Saint Peter shed; fasting and almsgiving, and other things of this kind, on which the most distinguished Gejerus has written fully and learnedly in his book On the Mourning of the Hebrews. For since repentance belongs to the whole man, it ought also to show itself in the body. Yet the body without any movement presents the appearance of one spiritually dead. But such signs can be feigned, and indeed natural and worldly men, who are more lively in spirit than in body, often display more vigour in them, as the repentance of false religions shows. Is such the fast that I have chosen, that a man should afflict his soul for a day? Is it to bow down his head like a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Is not this the fast that I have chosen: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free and break every yoke? Isa. 58:5, 6. Turn to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping and with mourning. And rend your heart and not your garments, and return to the LORD your God, Joel 2:12, 13. For God does not wish to be worshipped with customs introduced by human precept and adopted as acts of devotion [κατ' ἀφοσίωσιν]. The praise of true conversion is to be sought from God, not from men, unless their edification requires it. Whenever those things that ought to be joined are separated by men, Scripture is wont in such a separation to choose the better part and to reject the lesser as if absolutely. I desire mercy and not sacrifice, Hos. 6:6. Receive my instruction and not silver, Prov. 8:10. Christ sent me to preach, not to baptize, 1 Cor. 1:17.

units.la: XL. Circa resipiscentiam in universum gravissimè Judæi & hæretici errarunt, & hodie que errant. Judæi enim eam in externis fere castigationibus constituunt. Levia peccata confessione, graviora castigationibus, ac mortis denique supplicio expiari statuentes. Inter Christianos Libertini boni malique discrimen confundentes pœnitentiam omnem falsè irridper dent, & febrile commentum appellant. Omnes enim actus hominis vitio carere dictitant, dumdummodo opinio & timor, qualis in pœnitentia est, absit. Alii Implacabiles dicti, resipiscentibus aditum ad Ecclesiam negarunt, imò veniam omnem inclementer negarunt. Montanistæ enim omni pœne delicto Ecclesiæ fores obserarunt. Quibus secundas Tertullianus fecit, scripto de pudicitia libro, quo ex Montani Schola crudele dogma, Non posse Ecclesiam baptizatis, & post baptismum in mœchiam, homicidium, idololatriam, abnegationem fidei, vel simile crimen lapsis, etiamsi postea pœnitentiam egerint, veniam & pacem concedere, deprompsit, & adversus Catholicos, quos Physicorum, seu animalium Psychicorum convitio aspersit, defendendum suscepit. Eundem errorem arripuerunt, latiúsque sparserunt hæretici Novatiani, authore Novato Africanæ Ecclesiæ Presbytero, qui post Baptismum lapsos in persecutione Deciana ad pœnitentiam, pacem & communionem admittere recusarunt. Catharorum seu Purorum nomen ipsi sibi imposuerunt. Contra quos non pauca Cyprianus erudite scripsit, & Synodus tum Romana, tum Nicæna Can. 8. καθαρισμὸν στrinxit. Eundem vero errorem, Augustino teste, Meletiani, authore Meletio, Episcopo Ægyptio, recoxerunt, recusantes orare cum conversis, seu iis, qui persecutionis tempore ceciderunt, & pœnitentia lapsum suum piarunt. Illi quoque hæretici, qui se Apostolicos arrogantissimè vocarunt, avulsio quædam Novatianorum, eundem errorem implacabilitatis adversus lapsos secuti, omnem iisdem veniam negarunt. Massaliani etiam se ab omni corruptione liberatos, sicque se à Spiritu S. gubernatos jactarunt, ut nec jejunio, nec pœnitentia ulla sibi opus esse deliberent. Veterum illorum hæreticorum vestigiis insistens Melchior Stengerus in Ecclesia Erfortensi, teste Hartnakio, compendii Læti continuatore, docuit, in eos, qui semel acta pœnitentia, secunda vice lapsi sunt, vix quicquam universalia conversionis remedia valere; tertium verò lapsos ut plurimum damnari. Oppositus olim error fuit Novatiani, Ecclesiæ Romanæ Presbyteri (quem perperam cum Novato confundi, Valesius Not. ad Eusteb. lib. VI. 45. ostendit) & asseclarum ejus, Privati & Felicissimi, perditissimorum hominum. Qui ut Episcopis Catholicis ægrè facerent, lapsos etiam sine pœnitentia prævia suscipiendos & in integrum restituendos esse, pertenderunt.
units.tr: XL. Concerning repentance in general, the Jews and the heretics have erred most gravely, and they still err today. For the Jews place it almost entirely in outward castigations, deciding that lighter sins are expiated by confession, graver ones by castigations, and the gravest by the penalty of death. Among Christians the Libertines, who confuse the difference between good and evil, falsely mock all repentance and call it a feverish invention. They assert that all human actions are free from sin, provided that the opinion and fear that belong to repentance are absent. Others, called the Implacable, denied access to the Church to those who repented, and indeed denied all forgiveness harshly. For the Montanists barred the doors of the Church against almost every sin. Tertullian gave them a sequel in his book On Modesty, in which he drew from the school of Montanus the cruel dogma that the Church cannot grant pardon and peace to those baptized who, after baptism, have fallen into adultery, murder, idolatry, denial of the faith, or some similar crime, even if they afterwards did penance; and he undertook to defend it against the Catholics, whom he branded with the insult of physical or animal, psychic people. The same error was seized upon and spread more widely by the heretics called Novatians, from Novatus, a presbyter of the African Church, who refused to admit to repentance, peace and communion those who had lapsed in the Decian persecution after baptism. They gave themselves the name of Cathari or Pure. Cyprian wrote learnedly against them, and the synod both at Rome and at Nicaea (canon 8) condemned [καθαρισμόν] their purity. Yet, according to Augustine, the same error was revived by the Meletians, from Meletius, an Egyptian bishop, who refused to pray with those who had been converted, that is, with those who had fallen in the time of persecution and had atoned for their lapse by repentance. Those heretics too who most arrogantly called themselves Apostolic, a offshoot of the Novatians, following the same error of implacability against the lapsed, denied them all forgiveness. The Massalians also boasted that they were freed from all corruption and so governed by the Holy Spirit that they judged they had no need of fasting or of any repentance. Following the footsteps of these ancient heretics, Melchior Stenger in the Church of Erfurt, according to Hartnack, the continuator of Læticus's compendium, taught that for those who, having once done penance, have fallen a second time, the universal remedies of conversion are of little avail, and that those who have fallen a third time are for the most part condemned. The error opposed to this was once held by Novatian, a presbyter of the Roman Church (whom Valesius, in his notes on Eusebius, book 6, chapter 45, shows is wrongly confused with Novatus), and by his followers Privatus and Felicissimus, most abandoned men. In order to vex the Catholic bishops, they insisted that the lapsed were to be received even without prior repentance and restored to full standing.

units.la: XLI. Infames hosce Novatianorum seu Catharorum, & Novatianensium scopulos inter medii Orthodoxi navigarunt. Illi enim in Concilio Romano, Eusebio Hist. Eccl. lib. VI. 43. commemorante, omnino lapsis resipiscendum esse, quod Novatianenses negarunt, & hodièque Libertini inficiantur; & resipiscentibus veniam apud Deum & Ecclesiam paratam esse, quod Novatiani pernegaverunt, asseruerunt. Et resipiscendum omnino esse supra ∫ X X. probavimus. At lapsos pœnitentiæ remedio curandos & fovendos esse, Scripturæ testimonia & exempla luculenter confirmant. Cùm improbus conversus ab omnibus peccatis suis, quæ fecit, observabit omnia statuta mea, & exercebit jus & justitiam, vivendo vivet, non morietur. Omnes defectiones ejus, quas commisit, non commemorabuntur ei, in sua justitia, quam exercet, vivet. An ullo pacto delector morte improbi, dictum Domini Jehovæ?
units.tr: XLI. Between these notorious rocks of the Novatians, or Cathari, and the Novatianists, the orthodox have steered their course. For the Roman council, as Eusebius records (Hist. Eccl. book 6, chapter 43), asserted that the lapsed must in every case repent, which the Novatianists denied and the Libertines deny even today; and it asserted that for those who repent, pardon is ready with God and the Church, which the Novatians utterly denied. And we have already shown above (§ 20) that repentance is wholly necessary. But that the lapsed are to be cured and cherished by the remedy of repentance is clearly confirmed by the testimonies and examples of Scripture: When the wicked turns from all his sins that he has committed, and keeps all my statutes, and does what is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die. None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him; in his righteousness that he has done he shall live. Have I any pleasure at all in the death of the wicked, says the Lord GOD?

units.la: Ezech. XVIII. 21. 22. 23. Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut resipiscat & vivat, ibid. cap. XXXIII. 11. Lavate vos, purificate vos, amovete malignitatem actionum vestrarum ex adverso oculorum meorum, &c. Esaj. I. 16. 17. Revertere, aversus Israel, non faciam, ut irruat facies mea irata in vos. Nam benignus sum, dictum Jehovæ, non asservo iram in seculum. Tantummodo agnosce iniquitatem tuam, te à Jehova Deo tuo defecisse. Revertimini, filii aversantes, dictum Jehovæ. Nam ego conjugio junctus sum vobis, & ego recipiam vos, Jerem. III. 12. 13. 14. Septies cadit justus, & (per resipiscentiam) resurgit. Impii autem corruunt in malum, Prov. XXIV. 16. Christus quoque Petro quærenti: Domine, quoties in me peccabit frater meus, & remittam ei? An usque septies? respondit: Non dico tibi, usque septies, sed usque septuagies septies, Matth. XVIII. 21. 22. Et itatim parabola Regis cum servis suis rationes putantis, non obscurè Divinam remissionem cum humana comparat, v. 23--f. Perspicuè imprimis S. Johannes: Filioli mei, inquit, hæc scribo vobis, ne peccetis. Quòd si quis peccârit, apud Patrem advocatum habemus Jesum Christum justum. Et ille est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris: non pro nostris solùm, sed etiam pro totius mundi peccatis, 1. Joh. II. 1. 2. Faciunt huc tum exempla lapsorum pœnitentiâ in gratiæ Divinæ sinum receptorum, Aharonis, Davidis, Solomonis, Petri, Thomæ, aliorum; tum similia, velut ovis perditæ, drachmæ amissæ, filii prodigi, filii in vineam ire renuentis, at mox resipiscentis: tum promissiones generales Evangelii; quæ singula comparata illud Novatianorum, quòd qui ex impiis pii fiunt, restaurari possint, at non æquè pii lapsi: quódque lapsi cum Deo, at non cum Ecclesia in gratiam redire possint, nullo negotio præcidunt.
units.tr: Ezek. 18:21, 22, 23. As I live, I have no pleasure in the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live, ibid. 33:11. Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean; put away the evil of your doings from before my eyes, etc. Isa. 1:16, 17. Return, O backsliding Israel, says the LORD; I will not cause my anger to fall upon you, for I am merciful, says the LORD; I will not keep my anger for ever. Only acknowledge your iniquity, that you have rebelled against the LORD your God. Return, O backsliding children, says the LORD, for I am married to you; and I will take you, Jer. 3:12, 13, 14. For a righteous man falls seven times and rises again [through repentance]; but the wicked fall into evil, Prov. 24:16. Christ too, when Peter asked, Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?, answered: I do not say to you, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven, Matt. 18:21, 22. And straightway the parable of the king reckoning with his servants compares, not obscurely, divine forgiveness with human forgiveness, vv. 23 ff. Most plainly, Saint John says: My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. And he is the propitiation for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world, 1 John 2:1, 2. To the same purpose are the examples of the lapsed who, through repentance, were received into the bosom of divine grace: Aaron, David, Solomon, Peter, Thomas and others; also similar examples: the lost sheep, the lost drachma, the prodigal son, the son who at first refused to go into the vineyard but soon repented; and the general promises of the Gospel. All these readily refute the Novatian view that those who from wicked become godly can be restored, but the lapsed, who are no less godly, cannot; and that the lapsed can be reconciled with God but not with the Church.

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: Nihil præsidii veteres & novi Novatiani in decantato illo S. Pauli, Heb. VI. 4. &c. loco habent; ubi eos, qui ἅπαξ φωτισθέντες semel illuminati sunt, παραπεσόντας πάλιν ἀνακαινίζειν εἰς μετάνοιαν prolapsos iterum renovari ad resipiscentiam posse, negat. Unde illi colligebant, homini φωτισθέντι illuminato, hoc est, baptizato, si labatur, nullam ad pœnitentiam & reconciliationem viam relictam esse. Sed ut φωτισμὸς baptismum denotet, ratio nulla est. Potiùs ea illuminatio intelligitur, qua quis doctore Spiritu S. doctrinam resipiscentiæ a mortuis operibus, & fidei in Deum ib. v. 1. cognovit. Tum nec παραπίπτοντες Apostolo quilibet lapsi, sed prolapsi, hoc est, universali & malitiosa apostasia in peccatum ad mortem, seu in Spiritum S. prolapsi sunt. Faciunt huc illa Solomonis: Septies יפול cadit justus, & resurgit. Sed impii יכשלו corruunt ad malum, Prov. XXIV. 16. Sicut Hebr. X. 26. 29. voluntariè peccantes; pro quibus nulla hostia reliqua est; dicuntur, Filium Dei conculcare, & sanguinem Testamenti profanum ducere, ita hic v. 6. prolapsi dicuntur iterum sibi Filium Dei crucifigere, & exemplum facere. Utrumque eorum est, qui in Spiritum S. peccant. Neque profectò sic relapsis veniam negare Apostolus voluit, qui totis capitibus VII. VIII. IX. X. probat, Christum unica oblatione non unicum tantùm, aut certa quædam peccata, sed omnia abstulisse; & cap. I V. 16. peccatores resipiscentes quosvis sic invitat: Acce-
units.tr: The ancients and the moderns who follow Novatian have no support in that much-discussed passage of St Paul, Hebrews 6:4 and following, where he denies that those who were ἅπαξ φωτισθέντες [once enlightened] and have fallen away (παραπεσόντας) can be renewed again to repentance (ἀνακαινίζειν εἰς μετάνοιαν) [renewed again to repentance]. From this they inferred that for a man who has been enlightened, that is, baptized, if he falls, no way is left open to repentance and reconciliation. But there is no reason to take φωτισμός [enlightenment] as meaning baptism. Rather, that enlightenment is to be understood by which a man, under the teaching of the Holy Spirit, has come to know the doctrine of repentance from dead works and of faith in God (ib. v. 1). Nor are those who have fallen away (παραπίπτοντες) every kind of lapsed person, but those who have fallen away completely, that is, who have lapsed by a universal and malicious apostasy into sin unto death, or into sin against the Holy Spirit. Solomon's words are relevant here: "A righteous man falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked [יכשלו] stumble into evil" (Prov. 24:16). Just as in Hebrews 10:26, 29, those who sin wilfully, for whom no sacrifice remains, are said to trample under foot the Son of God and to count the blood of the covenant unholy, so here in v. 6 those who have fallen away are said to crucify the Son of God again for themselves and to make an example of him. Both describe those who sin against the Holy Spirit. Certainly the Apostle did not mean to deny forgiveness to such as relapse in this way, since in chapters 7, 8, 9 and 10 throughout he proves that Christ by one offering has taken away not only one sin or certain sins but all of them; and in chapter 4, verse 16, he thus invites every repentant sinner: "Let us draw near-"

units.la: Argumentum Novatianorum occurrit.
units.tr: The argument of the Novatians is met.

units.la: Accedamus igitur cum fiducia ad thronum gratiæ, ut consequamur misericordiam, & gratiam in auxilium opportunum inveniamus. Idem S. Paulus dicens: Esavum μετανοίας τόπον refipiscentiæ locum non invenisse, licet eam cum lachrymis quæsiverit, ibid. XII. 17. non resipiscenti veniam negat, sed Esavum lachrymis fusis impetrare potuisse, ut parentem Isacum consilii, quo Jacobo benedixerat, poeniteret, inficiatur. Nihil etiam causæ est, cur pronomen αὐτὴν ad μετανοίαν referatur, cum ad remotius, nimirum τὴν εὐλογίαν benedictionem, quam Esavus cum lachrymis quæsitavit, commodius referatur.
units.tr: Let us therefore draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need. The same St Paul, saying that Esau found no place for repentance (μετανοίας τόπον) although he sought it with tears (Heb. 12:17), does not deny pardon to the penitent, nor does he deny that Esau could by his tears obtain that his father Isaac should change his mind about the blessing he had given to Jacob. Nor is there any reason why the pronoun αὐτήν should be referred to μετάνοια [repentance]; it refers more fitly to the more distant noun, namely τὴν εὐλογίαν [the blessing], which Esau sought with tears.

units.la: XLIII. Doctrinam de Resipiscentia Evangelicam plane Pontificii, Judæorum hac in doctrina æmuli, corrumpunt.
units.tr: XLIII. The Papists, rivals of the Jews in this matter, plainly corrupt the evangelical doctrine of repentance.

units.la: Nam vocabuli pœnitentiæ errore abducti, eam magnam partem in pœnis & castigationibus externis à Pœnitentiario impositis, collocant, & formalem ejus rationem nonnisi pœnalem faciunt. Qui error veteris Ecclesiæ disciplinæ, & pœnitentiæ publicæ atque Canonicæ, severæ admodum, & graduum nimio rigore distinctæ, cunabula sua debet. Ejus imaginem vel umbram quale-cunque retinentes externam illam pœnitentiam cum interna confuderunt. Carnalis enim Papatus totus in externis hæret, internorum, & verè spiritualium plane incuriosus. Ac non obstante eo pœnitentiam etiam virtutem faciunt. Quasi virtus ulla in externa poena, & non potius in habitu cum lege & sanctitate Dei congruente consisteret. Ac si internum dolorem, & emendationis propositum spectes, non tam specialis virtus, quàm commune aliquod virtutis studium ea appellari debet. Iidem errorem errore cumulantes, ex pœnitentia etiam Sacramentum faciunt, cujus partes pœnitentis & pœnitentiarii actibus absolvunt. Sic enim & actus pœnitentis, quos contritionem, confessionem & satisfactionem faciunt; & actum Pœnitentiarii, qui iis absolutio est, Divina quadam virtute & efficacia promerendi gratiam, & eandem ex opere operato conferendi, imprægnandos censuerunt. Adeò Diaboli astus eorum mentes à simplicitate in Christum corrupit, 2. Cor. XI. 3. Sed ea de re plura in loco.
units.tr: For, led astray by the ambiguity of the word poenitentia (penance), they place the greater part of it in the external punishments and chastisements imposed by the penitentiary, and they make its formal nature purely penal. This error owes its origin to the discipline of the ancient Church, to its public and canonical penance, which was very severe and divided into degrees with excessive rigour. Retaining some image or shadow of that discipline, they have confused that external penance with the internal. For carnal Papacy as a whole clings to externals and is wholly careless of the internal and truly spiritual. And despite this, they even make penance a virtue. As if any virtue consisted in external punishment, and not rather in a disposition agreeing with the law and holiness of God. And if you look at inward sorrow and the purpose of amendment, it is not so much a special virtue as a general pursuit of virtue that ought to be called by that name. The same men, piling error upon error, also make a sacrament out of repentance, whose parts they set down as the acts of the penitent and of the penitentiary. Thus they have held that the acts of the penitent, which they make contrition, confession and satisfaction, and the act of the penitentiary, which is absolution, are endowed with a divine power and efficacy to merit grace and to confer it ex opere operato [by the work worked]. So much has the Devil's cunning corrupted their minds from the simplicity that is in Christ (2 Cor. 11:3). But more on this matter in its place.

units.la: XLIV. Non simplex etiam Socinianorum de Resipiscentia error est.
units.tr: XLIV. The error of the Socinians concerning repentance is not a simple one either.

units.la: Nam eam non legis, sed solius Evangelii præceptum faciunt. Quasi sub tempus Vet. Test. & promissionis nullus pœnitentiæ ac veniæ locus, nec ulla spes salutis affulserit. Tum & seram pœnitentiam eorum, qui cum pridem occasionem sese Christo aggregandi, & vitam emendandi habuerint, in exitu demum vitæ actionum suarum pœnitudine ducuntur, veram esse pernegant. Et seram quidem pœnitentiam periculo haud vacare, supra nos quoque ostendimus. Non enim tempus inveniendi & acceptum, nec non dies salutis negligendus est. Esaj. XLIX. 8. 2. Cor. VI. 2. ne fortassis à nobis occultet faciem suam, & nos in angustiis nostris subsannet. Cogitandum jugiter illud S. Petri est: si justus vix servatur; ubi manebit improbus? 1. Pet. IV. 18. Sed illi ipsi, qui seram pœnitentiam veram esse negant, jactatione absolutissimæ facultatis & virium sufficientium, nec non abnegatione necessitatis interioris operationis Spiritus S. animam differendi auscultationem verbi præbent timorem Dei à peccatore recessuri tollunt, & cætera, quæ ad fidem necessaria sunt, integra relinquunt. Falsissimum præterea est, ulli verè pœnitenti, quia ei tempus ad fructus pœnitentiæ copiosos ferendum non suppetit, salutem negandam esse. Quisquis enim verè & sERIO in Christum credit, eum credendo amat & confitetur; mundum & concupiscentias ejus abdicat, peccatum odit, Christi consortium anhelat, is verè pœnitens & salutis consors est. Hæc Evangelii consentiens vox est. Et eodem sigilla, Baptismus & Cœna ducunt, quibus omni tempore communio Christi, justitia & salus obsignatur. Neque opera nostra, sed Christus justitia, salus & redemptio nostra est, qui nunquam peccatorem pœnitentem ab amplexu suo arcet, & vel extremo halitu testatam pœnitentiam accipit. Socinianum contrà dogma est, quòd homini opera & facta propria ad justitiam imputentur. Cujus doctrinæ germen est, verè credentibus, atque ita pœnitentibus quibusdam salutem negare, & secundum humanum atque Socinianum modum justis, hoc est, Christi abnegatoribus & hypocritis vitam æternam adjudicare. S. Petrus asserit, etiam mortuis Evangelium prædicatum esse, ut secundum homines quidem judicarentur carne, viverent autem Deo spiritu, 1. Pet. IV. 6. innuens ante diluvium Christum per Noachum in spiritu suo prædicasse, ut homines in ipso diluvio etiam salvari possent fide Noachi hæredis & præconis justitiæ Christi. Christus enim vera Rupes est. Beatus omnis, qui ad ipsum confugit, Psal. II. 12.
units.tr: For they make repentance a precept of the Gospel alone, not of the law. As if at the time of the Old Testament and of the promise there was no place for repentance or pardon, and no hope of salvation had shone forth. Further, they deny that the late repentance of those who, though they had long had the opportunity of joining themselves to Christ and of amending their lives, are at last brought to repentance for their actions only at the end of their lives, is true repentance. We have already shown above that late repentance is not free from danger. For the accepted time and the day of salvation must not be neglected (Isa. 49:8; 2 Cor. 6:2), lest perhaps he hide his face from us and mock us in our distress. We must constantly bear in mind that saying of St Peter: "If the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?" (1 Pet. 4:18). But those very men who deny that late repentance is true, by boasting of an absolutely full ability and sufficient powers, and by denying the necessity of the inward operation of the Holy Spirit, give the soul an excuse for deferring the hearing of the word; they remove from the sinner the fear of God by which he should depart from sin, and leave intact the other things that are necessary for faith. Moreover, it is utterly false that salvation should be denied to any truly penitent person merely because time is not given him to bring forth abundant fruits of repentance. For whoever truly and earnestly believes in Christ, loves and confesses him by believing; renounces the world and its lusts, hates sin, and longs for fellowship with Christ, is truly penitent and a partaker of salvation. This is the consistent voice of the Gospel. And Baptism and the Supper, the seals that lead to the same end, seal communion with Christ, righteousness and salvation at all times. Nor is it our works, but Christ, who is our righteousness, salvation and redemption, who never shuts out the penitent sinner from his embrace, and receives even a repentance attested by his last breath. The Socinian dogma, on the other hand, is that a man's own works and deeds are imputed to him for righteousness. The germ of this doctrine is to deny salvation to some who truly believe and are thus penitent, and to adjudge eternal life, in the human and Socinian manner, to the just, that is, to deniers of Christ and to hypocrites. St Peter asserts that the Gospel was preached "even to the dead, that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit" (1 Pet. 4:6), implying that before the flood Christ preached through Noah in his Spirit, so that men might even in the flood itself be saved by the faith of Noah, the heir and herald of the righteousness of Christ. For Christ is the true Rock. "Blessed is everyone who takes refuge in him" (Ps. 2:12).

units.la: XLV. Resipiscentiam sequitur Nova Obedientia; quæ per bona opera exercetur.
units.tr: XLV. New obedience follows repentance, and it is exercised through good works.

units.la: Sunt autem bona opera actiones sanctificatorum voluntarie, quæ ex puro corde, amore Dei, vera fide in Christum, secundum legem Dei, ad ejus gloriam, utilitatem proximi & salutem propriam fiunt. Augustinus passim bonum opus definit id, quod fit sicut oportet, imitatione Apostoli, Rom. VIII. 26. Varia ejus loca & locutiones æquipollentes Jansenius de Grat. Salv. lib. XV. 11. collegit. Augustinum secutum Concilium Arausicanum can. 6. definit; credere, velle, petere nos debere, sicut oportet. Sic bonum opus simpliciter ἀγαθὸν ἔργον est, sed generaliter nimis. De bonis operibus passim Scripturæ loquuntur. Ita splendeat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant τὰ καλὰ ὑμῶν ἔργα bona vestra opera, Matth. V. 16. Creati in Christo Jesu propter bona opera, Ephes. II. 10. Præbe te typum bonorum operum, Tit. II. 7. Dedit se ipsum pro nobis, ut purificaret sibi populum pecaliarem, æmulum bonorum operum, ibid. v. 14. Etiam ἀρετὴ virtutis nomine sed raro; veniunt. Si quæ virtus, si quæ laus, hæc animo reputate, Phil. IV. 8. Omni studio collato suppeditate in fide vestra virtutem, 2. Pet. I. 5.
units.tr: Good works are the voluntary actions of the sanctified, performed from a pure heart, from love of God, from true faith in Christ, according to the law of God, for his glory, for the benefit of our neighbour, and for our own salvation. Augustine, throughout his writings, defines a good work as that which is done as it ought to be done, following the Apostle at Rom. 8:26. Jansenius, in De Gratia Salvatoris lib. XV c. 11, gathered Augustine's various passages and equivalent expressions. The Council of Orange, following Augustine, in canon 6, defines that we ought to believe, to will and to ask as we ought. So a good work is simply a good work (ἀγαθὸν ἔργον), but this is too general a description. The Scriptures speak of good works throughout. So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works [τὰ καλὰ ὑμῶν ἔργα], Matt. 5:16. Created in Christ Jesus for good works, Eph. 2:10. Show yourself a pattern of good works, Titus 2:7. He gave himself for us, that he might purify for himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works, ibid. v. 14. Virtue (ἀρετή) also occurs under the name of virtue, though rarely: If there be any virtue, if any praise, think on these things, Phil. 4:8. Add to your faith, with all diligence, virtue, 2 Pet. 1:5.

units.la: XLVI. Sicut pulchritudo corporis non sola coloris specie, vel justa membrorum magnitudine verùm omnium, quæ in corpore cernuntur, ordine, consensu omnium partium cum quodam lepore & proportione absolvitur: ita τὸ καλόν, pulchritudo, rectitudo & bonitas operis in rerum variarum concentu quodam & suavissima harmonia conspicitur. Hinc DioDionysii Areopagitæ illud de Div. Nom. cap. 4. quod bonum sit ex integra causa, malum autem ex quovis defectu. Ut enim bonum opus aliquid dicatur, non tantùm requiritur, ut motus membrorum præceptus sit, quale est verum dicere, munus pauperi porrigere, aut ut usus rei per se licitus sit, qualis est vestitus, esus, potus; aut ut quis abstineat à factis quæ nemo non vituperat & damnat, sed ut dignum sit homine, & quidem ut imaginem Dei gerente, & sic Deum judicem habente. Κυριακα & palmaria bonitatis & rectitudinis operum requisita ejusmodi sex sunt, ut videlicet bonum opus fiat ex rectæ voluntatis habitu; ut conformatum sit Legi Dei; ut habeat rectitudinem circumstantiarum; ut fluat ex amore Dei; ut fiat ex fide; ut denique propositum rectum finem habeat. Vel uno horum deficiente, malum opus est; quanquam vix unum deficere potest, quin reliqua omnia deficiant.
units.tr: XLVI. Just as the beauty of a body is complete not merely from the appearance of its colour or from the proper size of its limbs, but from the order of all the parts visible in the body and their harmony together with a certain grace and proportion, so τὸ καλόν, the beauty, rectitude and goodness of a work, is seen in a certain concord and most sweet harmony of various things. Hence the saying of Dionysius the Areopagite in De Div. Nom. ch. 4, that the good comes from the whole cause, but evil from any defect. For a work to be called good, it is not enough that the movements of the limbs be controlled, as when one speaks the truth or gives alms to the poor, or that the use of a thing lawful in itself be made, such as clothing, eating or drinking, or that one abstain from deeds which everyone blames and condemns. It must also be worthy of a human being, indeed of one who bears the image of God, and so has God as judge. The chief and outstanding requirements of the goodness and rectitude of works are six: namely, that a good work arise from a habit of a right will; that it be conformed to the Law of God; that it have rectitude in its circumstances; that it flow from the love of God; that it be done from faith; and finally that the purpose have a right end. If any one of these is lacking, the work is evil; although scarcely one of them can be lacking without all the others being lacking too.

units.la: XLVII. Primò igitur ad bonitatem operis requiritur, ut ex rectæ voluntatis habitu, seu recto principio fluat.
units.tr: XLVII. First, then, for the goodness of a work it is required that it flow from a habit of a right will, that is, from a right principle.

units.la: Hoc principium thesauri boni cordis, arboris bonæ, puri cordis nomine venit. Bonus homo ex bono thesauro cordis bona profert, Matth. XII. 35. Omnis arbor bona bonos fert fructus. Putris autem arbor fructus malos profert, ibid. VII. 17. Charitas ex puro corde, conscientia bona, &c. 1. Tim. I. 5. Etiam ἀφθονίαν abundantiam cordis Christus appellat. Ex abundantia cordis loquitur os, Matth. XII. 34. Nam ut bonum opus edi possit, requiritur attentio, & talis quidem, quæ non fluctuet, verum in animo certum, fixum & immobile aliquid habeat. Debet igitur, qui rectè operatur, præditus esse & scientia, qua quid rectè fieri possit, cognoscat; & constantia, qua eadem constanter appetat. Scitè Seneca Epist. 95.
