Actio recta non erit, nisi recta sit voluntas. Ab hac enim est actio. Rursus voluntas non erit recta, nisi habitus animi rectus fuerit. Ab hac enim est voluntas. Habitus porro animi non erit in optimo, nisi res ad verum redegerit. Non contingit tranquillitas, nisi immutabile certumque judicium adeptis. Principium isthoc Stoici ... firmam, certámque animi persuasionem appellant. Et Aristot. Ethic. Nicom. II. 4. rectè operari eum ait, qui primò εἰδὼς sciens, deinde ... eligens, & eligens propter ipsa; tertiò βεβαίως ... firmiter & constanter affectus agit. Rectè enim negat, actiones bonas habere τὸ ἐν ... bonum in se ipsis, sed quàm fiat in artibus. In homine integro recta illa voluntatis dispositio à natura integra fluxit: at in homine lapso non à natura, sed à gratia fluit. Manete in me, & ego in vobis. Sicut palmes non potest ferre fructum a se ipso, si non manserit in vite: ita nec vos, nisi in me manseritis. Ego sum vitis: vos palmites. Sine me non potestis facere quicquam, Joh. XV. 4-5. Et voluntas igitur, ut rectè disponatur; & singuli ejus actus, ut fiant, sicut oportet, gratia Dei indigent, quia sine Christo ... nihil possumus. Sive igitur parum, sive multum, sine illo fieri non potest, sine quo nihil fieri potest: quia etsi parum attulerit palmes, eum purgat agricola, ut plus afferat, uti scitè Augustinus in Johann. tract. 81. loquitur. Naturæ certè vox, sensu Scripturæ accepta, nativam corruptionem omnibus Adami posteris
units.tr: This principle is called the good treasure of the heart, a good tree, a pure heart. A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things, Matt. 12:35. Every good tree bears good fruit, but a corrupt tree bears evil fruit, ibid. 7:17. The love that comes from a pure heart and a good conscience, etc., 1 Tim. 1:5. Christ also calls it the abundance of the heart: Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, Matt. 12:34. For a good work to be performed, attention is required, and not the kind that wavers, but one that has in the mind something certain, fixed and immovable. Therefore whoever works rightly ought to possess both knowledge, by which he recognises what can rightly be done, and steadfastness, by which he constantly desires the same thing. Seneca says well, Ep. 95: An action will not be right unless the will is right, for action comes from the will. Again, the will will not be right unless the habit of mind is right, for the will comes from that. Moreover the habit of mind will not be sound unless it has brought things back to the truth. Tranquillity is not attained unless one has gained an unchanging and certain judgment. The Stoics call this principle a firm and certain persuasion of the mind. And Aristotle, Nic. Ethics II.4, says that he acts rightly who first acts knowingly, then chooses, and chooses for the sake of the things themselves, and thirdly acts firmly [βεβαίως] and constantly disposed. He rightly denies that good actions have the good in themselves, as they do in the arts. In the integral man that right disposition of the will flowed from integral nature; but in fallen man it flows not from nature but from grace. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, unless it abide in the vine, so neither can you, unless you abide in me. I am the vine, you are the branches. Without me you can do nothing, John 15:4-5. So the will, if it is to be rightly disposed, and each of its acts, if they are to be done as they ought, both need the grace of God, since without Christ we can do nothing. Whether therefore little or much, it cannot be done without him without whom nothing can be done; for even if the branch has borne little fruit, the husbandman prunes it that it may bear more, as Augustine aptly says in Tract. 81 on John. Certainly the voice of nature, taken in the sense of Scripture, signifies the native corruption clinging to all the posterity of Adam.

units.la: hærentem significat, 1. Cor. II. 14. Ephes. II. 3. A qua proin tantum abest, ut ullum bono operi præsidium sit, ut potius ejus sensus & studium inimicitia esse contra Deum dicatur, Rom. VIII. 7. Si tamen etiam naturæ vox ad significandas naturales facultates animæ & corporis, velut lucem rationis, libertatem voluntatis, motiones corporis, adhibeatur; non jam natura causa boni operis, sed subjectum, quod à gratia in bene operando dirigente informatur, censeri debet.
units.tr: It signifies, 1 Cor. 2:14; Eph. 2:3. So far is this from being any help to a good work that rather its sense and striving is said to be enmity against God, Rom. 8:7. If, however, the word nature is also used to signify the natural faculties of soul and body, such as the light of reason, freedom of the will, and the motions of the body, then nature is not to be regarded as the cause of a good work, but as the subject which is shaped by grace directing it in doing good.

units.la: XLVIII. Nullum ergo bonum opus edi nisi ab iis, qui in statu gratiæ sunt, & Christo insiti sunt, & Spiritus S. Christo inhærentis primitias habent, potest. Nam fructus Spiritus sunt gaudium, charitas, pax, ira cohibitio, bonitas, fides, &c. Gal. V. 22. Et qui sancte vivunt ... secundum spiritum ambulare dicuntur, Rom. VIII. 1.
units.tr: XLVIII. Therefore no good work can be performed except by those who are in a state of grace, who are engrafted into Christ, and who have the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit dwelling in Christ. For the fruits of the Spirit are joy, love, peace, restraint of anger, goodness, faith, etc., Gal. 5:22. And those who live holily are said to walk according to the Spirit, Rom. 8:1.

units.la: Et sterilis plane, imò inanis est operum steriliter bonorum & frugiferorum distinctio, qua Scotistæ inprimis usi, naturæ hominis corruptæ lenocinantur, quasi homines extra Christum & gratiam Spiritus S. opera bona sterilia, at non frugifera edere valerent. Nullum enim opus vere bonum sterile & non frugiferum est, quia Deus bonorum omnium certissimus ... remunerator est. Deus non est injustus, ut obliviscatur operis, laboris & charitatis nostræ. Hebr. VI. 10. Neque frustra colitur is, qui omni bono opere colitur. Neque bona opera, sed peccata sunt ... opera infrugifera tenebrarum, Ephes. V. 11. quæ stipulirum instar igne consumuntur, ... jactura afficiunt, defraudant, 1. Cor. III. 12. 15. quaiia opera bona esse nequeunt. Neque bona dici possunt, quæ sunt infrugifera, hoc est, quæ nec utilitatem ullam, nec bonam conscientiam afferre, nec Deo grata esse possunt; & de quibus dici non potest, quod de bonis dicitur: Labor vester non est vanus in Domino, 1. Cor. XV. 58. & quæ gratiam nullam dant iis, qui ea vident. Distinctio illa Sophistarum non verbum Dei, sed Pelagium authorem habet, uti ex Augustino contra Julian. lib. IV. 1. 3. liquet, ubi sic ille fibras ejus elidit: Fieri non potest, ut steriliter boni simus: sed boni non sumus, quòd steriliter sumus. Nullo igitur modo homines sunt steriliter boni; sed qui boni non sunt, possunt esse alii magis, alii minus mali.
units.tr: The distinction of works into barren and fruitful good works, which the Scotists especially used, is plainly sterile, indeed empty, and it flatters corrupt human nature, as if men outside Christ and the grace of the Holy Spirit could produce good works that are barren but not fruitful. For no truly good work is sterile and unfruitful, because God is the most certain rewarder of all good things. God is not unjust, that he should forget your work and labour of love, Heb. 6:10. Nor is he worshipped in vain who is worshipped in every good work. Those things are not good works but sins, unfruitful works of darkness, Eph. 5:11, which are consumed by fire like stubble, suffer loss, are cheated of their reward, 1 Cor. 3:12, 15, and so cannot be good works. Nor can those be called good which are unfruitful, that is, which bring no usefulness and no good conscience, cannot be pleasing to God, and of which cannot be said what is said of good works: Your labour is not in vain in the Lord, 1 Cor. 15:58; and which give no grace to those who see them. That distinction of the Sophists has its author not in the word of God but in Pelagius, as is clear from Augustine against Julian, lib. IV, where he crushes its sinews in this way: It cannot happen that we are barren good men; but we are not good because we are barren. Therefore men are in no way barren good men; but those who are not good may be some more and some less evil.

units.la: XLIX. Secunda boni operis conditio est, ut legi Divinæ conformetur.
units.tr: XLIX. The second condition of a good work is that it be conformed to the divine law.

units.la: Quæ conformatio non tantùm de actu exteriore, sed inprimis etiam interioribus animæ motibus, sanctis cogitationibus & piis affectibus, intelligi debet. Facies quæcunque jubeo. Nihil addas, nihil detrahas, Deut. XII. 32. In præceptis meis ambulate, Ezech. XX. 19. Memineritis omnium mandatorum Dei, & ea facietis: nec sequentini cogitationes vestras, Num. XV. 39. Frustra enim Deus colitur per doctrinas, quæ sunt ... præceptum hominum condocefactum, Esaj. XXIX. 13. Quis talia à manibus vestris requisivit? ibid. I. 12. Unde peccatum, seu malum opus ἀνομίας defectionis à lege nomine venit, 1. Joh. III. 4. Neque alio quàm legis Divinæ sensu rectitudinem operis sui defendere operans potest. Atque ea nota à censu bonorum operum cuncta illa, quæ humanis inventionibus & traditionibus innituntur; nec non consilia, quæ appellant Evangelicæ perfectionis, opera. ra supererogationis, aliáque ejusmodi quæ se-quiorum temporum superstitio invexit, exi-muntur. Omnia enim opera bona, Deóque pla-centia, generali mandato charitatis præcipiun-tur, jubente scilicet Deum diligere ex toto cor-de, tota anima & viribus omnibus. Quibus ver-bis tanta amoris Divini perfectio imperatur, ut ad eam nulla omnino accessio fieri possit.
units.tr: This conformity must be understood not only of outward action but above all of the inward motions of the soul, holy thoughts and pious affections. Do whatever I command. Add nothing, take nothing away, Deut. 12:32. Walk in my statutes, Ezek. 20:19. Remember all the commandments of God and do them, and do not follow your own thoughts, Num. 15:39. In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the precepts of men, Isa. 29:13. Who required such things at your hands? Ibid. 1:12. Hence sin, or an evil work, is called lawlessness [ἀνομία], departure from the law, which is what the name means, 1 John 3:4. Nor can a person who works defend the uprightness of his work in any sense other than that of the divine law. By this mark are excluded from the reckoning of good works all those that rest on human inventions and traditions; likewise the counsels which they call works of evangelical perfection, works of supererogation, and other such things which the superstition of later times introduced. For all good works, pleasing to God, are enjoined by the general command of charity, since God commands us to love him with the whole heart, the whole soul and all our strength. In these words so great a perfection of divine love is commanded that no addition at all can be made to it.

units.la: LI. Tertia boni operis conditio rectitudo circumstantiarum est. Sicut enim in corporibus non tantùm succus, moles, compages & sinia laudatur, sed etiam color, proceritas, composi-tio, proportio membrorum inter se spectatur: ita in actionibus moralibus non tantùm cogi-tatum, dictum, factum, quæ sunt veluti prin-ceps materies operis, per se & nudum conside-rari solet: sed variæ etiam circumstantiæ, per-sonarum, loci, temporis, modi agendi &c. quæ sunt velut externa forma operi adnexa, in nu-merum perveniunt. Rectè Bernhardus: Oportet in virtutibus & tempus, & locum, & modum spectari, præter quæ virtus non est virtus. Si enim non quis seu persona; neque quid fecerit, neque quo instrumento oportet, neque quomodo, neque in quo tempore vel loco; neque cuius gratia; neque circa quid, seu circa quam materiam (totidem enim circumstantias Aristoteles Nicom. III. 1. requirit) factum aliquid sit, reputetur, boni operis palmam reportare non potest. Non tantùm bona agenda sunt, sed etiam bene agen-dum est. Deus adverbiis delectatur. Sed cùm circumstantiæ ejusmodi etiam principia agen-di, & finem ipsum complectantur; de quibus seorsim dicendum est: iis immorari diutiùs ni-hil attinet.
units.tr: LI. The third condition of a good work is the rightness of its circumstances. For just as in bodies we praise not only the juice, bulk, joints and sinews, but also the colour, stature, build and the proportion of the limbs to one another, so in moral actions we usually consider by themselves and bare the thought, the word and the deed, which are as it were the chief matter of the work; but the various circumstances of persons, place, time, manner of acting and so on, which are as it were the external form attached to the work, are also taken into account. Bernard rightly says: "In virtues one must consider both time and place and manner, without which virtue is not virtue." For if one does not consider who the person is, what he has done, with what instrument it ought to be done, how, at what time or place, for whose sake, and concerning what matter (for Aristotle, Nic. III.1, requires just so many circumstances), then the deed cannot win the palm of a good work. Not only good things are to be done, but they must be done well. God delights in adverbs. But since circumstances of this kind also embrace the principles of acting and the end itself, which must be discussed separately, there is no point in dwelling on them longer here.

units.la: LI. Quarto bonum opus ex amore Dei, seu voluntate se totum Deo consecrante, flue-re debet. Charitas enim πλήρωμα ⁊ νόμου pleni-tudo legis est, Rom. XIII. 10. Nam & omnia Dei præcepta ad charitatem reducenda sunt: & sola charitas Dei causa est, ut ei obediatur: & opus ex amore Dei non profectum non tam gloriæ Dei inservit, quàm concupiscentiæ propriæ velificatur. Unde charitatem bono-rum operum radicem Apostolus 1. Cor. XIII. inductione plurimorum operum facit. Nisi amor Dei in corde sit, & ex illo actiones exter-nae mandatæ proficiscantur, hæ bonæ esse nulla-tenus possunt. Si enim quis terrore, auctoritate & potestate id effecerit, ut alius vera dicat, insi-gnia mala non faciat, & bona externa faciat, næ ille non pietatem, sed ὑπόκρισιν voluntatem pla-cendi ei, qui vel terrorem incutere potuit, vel imperio utitur, & authoritate pollere videtur in iis, qui ipsi parent, effecerit. Qui igitur alios ad solidam pietatem formare & ad bona opera adducere statuit, is necesse est, ut veram fidem & charitatem ei instillet. Finis enim præcepti est charitas ex puro corde, conscientia bona, & fide non ficta, 1. Tim. I. 5. Opera ergo requirun-tur, quia dilectio nec solius cordis, nec solius oris, sed etiam operis est, sed præ cæteris chari-tas cordis, seu dilectio ex puro corde proma-nans, in eo fontem habens, & ex eodem, velut fonte in omnes facultates hominis promanans requiritur. Perperam verò Scholastici amorem illum Dei & justitiæ, ex quo bonum opus pro-tedere debet, amorem legis, seu virtutis secun-dum se, hoc est, voluntatem faciendi opus mo-raliter bonum ex omnibus circumstantiis, etiamsi de illo opere in Deum referendo nulla cogitatio suscipiatur, interpretantur. Nam sic Stoicismum imprudentes resuscitant, cùm vir-tutem colendam esse amore sui, non Dei, docent. Atqui opus veré bonum inconnivis oculis si-nem suum intuetur, & eum unicè amat & com-plectitur. Finis autem operis est gloria Dei, non amor virtutis vel operis.
units.tr: LIV. Fourthly, a good work must flow from the love of God, that is, from a will that consecrates the whole self to God. For love is the fulfilling [πλήρωμα] of the law, Rom. 13:10. All God's precepts are to be reduced to charity, and the love of God alone is the cause why he is obeyed; and a work not proceeding from the love of God serves not so much the glory of God as it is bent to one's own desire. Hence the Apostle, in 1 Cor. 13, by enumerating many works, makes charity the root of good works. Unless the love of God is in the heart, and the commanded outward actions proceed from it, these cannot be good at all. For if someone, by terror, authority and power, has brought it about that another tells the truth, does no gross evils and performs outward good works, he has produced not piety but hypocrisy [ὑπόκρισιν], a desire to please the one who could instil terror or who wields command and seems to hold authority over those who obey him. Therefore whoever resolves to form others to solid piety and lead them to good works must necessarily instil into them true faith and charity. For the end of the command is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience and unfeigned faith, 1 Tim. 1:5. Works are therefore required, because love is not of the heart alone, nor of the mouth alone, but also of the work; yet above all the charity of the heart is required, that is, love springing from a pure heart, having its source there and flowing from that source into all the faculties of man. The Schoolmen, however, wrongly interpret that love of God and of justice from which a good work ought to proceed as the love of law or of virtue in itself, that is, the will to do a morally good work in all its circumstances, even if no thought of referring that work to God is entertained. For in this way they unwittingly revive Stoicism, when they teach that virtue is to be cultivated for love of self, not of God. Yet a truly good work, with unclouded eyes, looks to its own end and loves and embraces that alone. But the end of the work is the glory of God, not the love of virtue or of the work.

units.la: LII. Quinto ad bonitatem operis vera si-dei requiritur. Nam quicquid non est ex fide (qua voluntatem Dei cognoscimus & credi-mus, Deum esse remuneratorem eorum, qui quæruntipsum) peccatum est, Rom. XIV. 23. Charitas est ἐκ πίστεως ἀνυπόκριτος ex fide non si-mulata, 1. Tim. I. 5. Fides non simulata charitatem gignit. Nam amor Dei in regenitis à fi-de incipit; & fidei consequente opere bono & charitate erga Deum & proximum operosa est, Gal. V. 6. & operibus præcipuè externis συνεργεῖ cooperatur, Jac. II. 22. hoc est, in iis vivacita-tem suam exerit, quatenus vera fides tum non est absque fame & siti justitiæ; & sic ad requi-renda & comparanda justitiæ argumenta im-pellit; tum est amor gloriæ Dei in peccatore per sanctificationem & glorificationem ejus ex misericordia manifestandæ, cujus amoris exer-citium quoddam studium bonorum operum est: tum est consummatio boni operis, Jac. II. 22. quia per illa, ut argumenta certissima, fides & justificatio fidei cognoscitur; & per tale sui ex-perimentum fides ad spem gloriæ Dei, in quo glo-riamur, Röm. V. 2. 4. proficit. Accedit, quòd cor per fidem purificatur, Act. XV. 9. Quo non purificato homo impurus est. At impuris & infidelibus nihil purum est, sed polluta est eorum mens & conscientia, Tit. I. 15. Ideo S. Paulus Patriarcharum κανηθωμάτων veræ fidei accepta refert; Hebr. XI. 4. &c. Denique justus ex fide vivit, Habac. II. 4. Quem locum sic Augusti-nus contr. Julian. lib. IV. 3. urget: Absit, ut in aliquo vera virtus sit, nisi fuerit justus: absit autem, ut sit justus verè, nisi vivat ex fide. Justus enim ex fide vivet. Quis verò justum dixerit in-fidelem, justum dixerit impium, justum dixerit Dia-bolo mancipatum?
units.tr: LII. Fifthly, true faith is required for the goodness of a work. For whatever is not of faith (by which we know and believe the will of God, that God is the rewarder of those who seek him) is sin, Rom. 14:23. Charity is from faith unfeigned [ἐκ πίστεως ἀνυπόκριτος], 1 Tim. 1:5. Unfeigned faith begets charity. For the love of God begins in those who have been regenerated by faith; and faith, with a good work following, is active in love toward God and neighbour, Gal. 5:6, and cooperates [συνεργεῖ] especially with outward works, Jas. 2:22. That is, faith exerts its vitality in them, insofar as true faith is not without hunger and thirst for righteousness; and so it impels one to seek and obtain the evidences of righteousness. It is also the love of God's glory in the sinner, to be manifested through his sanctification and glorification out of mercy, and the exercise of this love is a certain zeal for good works. It is the completion of a good work, Jas. 2:22, because through these works, as most certain evidences, faith and the justification of faith are known; and through such trial of itself faith advances to hope of the glory of God, in which we glory, Rom. 5:2, 4. Add that the heart is purified by faith, Acts 15:9; and while it is not purified, a man is impure. But nothing is pure to the impure and unbelieving; their mind and conscience are defiled, Titus 1:15. Therefore St Paul refers the testimonies of the patriarchs [μαρτυριῶν] to true faith, Heb. 11:4, etc. Finally, the just lives by faith, Hab. 2:4. Augustine presses this passage thus against Julian, bk. IV ch. 3: "Far be it that there is true virtue in anyone unless he is just; far be it that he is truly just unless he lives by faith. For the just shall live by faith. Who would call the unbeliever just? Who would call the impious man just? Who would call one given over to the devil just?"

units.la: LIII. Sextò denique propositum, seu in-tentio recti finis requiritur. Illa enim oculi in-star est, quem operans sequitur. Si oculus tuus simplex fuerit, totum corpus lucidum erit, Matth. VI. 22. Intentionis ille oculus non tantùm quid agendum sit, sed etiam quam ob causam opus suscipiatur, dispicit. Nam voluntas non magis recta esse debet volendo, quod debet, quàm volendo propter quod debet. Quapropter inquit Anshelmus, omnis voluntas habet quid & cur. Nam vera virtus, inquit Augusti-nus contr. Julian. lib. III. 4. ex fine, non ex actio-ne judicatur. Nam sæpe latrones multa tolerant, avari item: neque tamen in iis est fortitudo. Igi-tur non officiis, sed finibus à vitiis virtutes discer-nuntur. Hinc decantatum illud Ambrosii: Quantum intendis, tantum facis. Recta autem in-tentio verum finem actionum humanarum in-tendit, qui Dei gloria est. Quicquid agitis, omnia ad gloriam Dei agite, 1. Cor. X. 31. Deus enim finis est hominis & rerum omnium, quæ homi-nis gratia factæ sunt. Sicut aquila pullos suos pro-
units.tr: LIII. Sixthly and finally, the purpose or intention of the right end is required. For this is like the eye which the doer follows. "If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light," Matt. 6:22. This eye of intention looks not only to what must be done, but also to the cause for which the work is undertaken. For the will ought to be right not only in willing what it ought to will, but also in willing for the sake of what it ought. Wherefore, says Anselm, every will has a what and a why. For true virtue, says Augustine against Julian, bk. III ch. 4, is judged by its end, not by its action. Robbers often endure many things, and so do the avaricious, yet there is no fortitude in them. Therefore virtues are distinguished from vices not by their outward duties but by their ends. Hence that oft-repeated saying of Ambrose: "As much as you intend, so much you do." The right intention aims at the true end of human actions, which is the glory of God. "Whatever you do, do all to the glory of God," 1 Cor. 10:31. For God is the end of man and of all things that were made for the sake of man. Just as the eagle tries its young

units.la: {y} ... (Marginal notes are given under notes.) probat eo indicio, quòd solem irretortis oculis aspicere possunt: ita filii Dei eo argumento probantur, quòd Deum assiduo obtentu sic respicere possunt, ut omnes actus suos ad ejus gloriam & honorem unicè & sincerè referant. Cum intentione hac finis ultimi, gloriæ Dei, connexa est intentio salutis proximi & nostræ, sed illi subordinatæ. Neque tamen etiam omne illud, quod homo ad gloriam Dei se facere putat, etiam ad gloriam Dei facit; sed id, quod facit ut obediens servus & diligens Patris filius. Non enim facienda sunt mala, ut eveniant bona, Rom. III. 8. Peccatum enim in eorum genere est, quæ nec eligi, nec ordinari ad bonum finem possunt, & ex quibus nihil boni consequi potest. Nam nec mala arbor bonum fructum proferre, nec tenebræ lucem generare possunt. Bonum opus cum sit ex integra causa, ad ejus bonitatem intentio non sufficit. Illa demum bona & recta intentio est, quæ Dei verbo regitur & ad finem honestum & licitum per media similia honesta & licita tendunt. Præclarè iterum Augustinus in Psal. 31. Bonum opus, inquit, intentio facit, intentionem fides dirigit. Et currendum est, & non præter viam currendum est.
units.tr: ...proves it by this sign: they can look at the sun without blinking. So the sons of God are shown to be such by this, that they can gaze on God with unwavering attention, so as to refer all their actions solely and sincerely to his glory and honour. Joined with this intention of the ultimate end, the glory of God, is the intention of the salvation of our neighbour and of ourselves, but subordinate to it. Yet not everything that a man thinks he does for God's glory is in fact done for God's glory, but only what he does as an obedient servant and a dutiful son. Evil must not be done that good may come, Rom. 3:8. For sin belongs to the class of things that cannot be chosen or directed to a good end, and from which no good can follow. A bad tree cannot bear good fruit, nor can darkness generate light. Since a good work proceeds from a complete cause, intention alone is not enough for its goodness. Only that intention is good and right which is governed by the word of God, and which aims at an honourable and lawful end through means that are likewise honourable and lawful. Augustine again put it well on Psalm 31: The intention makes the good work, and faith directs the intention. We must run, and we must run on the right road, not off it.

units.la: LIV. His notis verè bona opera ab apertè malis & speciosis seu fucatis distinguimus. Posterioris enim generis sunt opera infidelium, irregenitorum, & veterum novorumque Pharisæorum, qui opera bona non illa, quæ in lege Dei mandantur, sed quæ voluntate & arbitrio proprio suscipiuntur, faciunt. Quoad infidelium, seu gentilium opera, de iis vetus Augustini cum Pelagianis contentio fuit. Hi enim Gentilium virtutes & opera tam vera fuisse, quàm verum, eorum corpus, oculi, frumentum in illorum agris nata fuerunt, pertenderant. Nam etiam carentia recta intentione, non ideo rectitudine sua caruisse, sed sterilia tantùm, seu infrugifera fuisse, asseruerunt. Contrà Augustinus gentilium virtutes, & quæ laudari solent, eorum {κατοφθώματα}, utut splendida, vera tamen peccata, virtutum & bonorum operum fallaces imagines & simulachra fuisse, verissimè asseruit. Licèt enim quod ab iis factum est, officio seu actu bonum videretur, at fine recto id omne caruisse, adeóque veri nominis peccatum fuisse, fusiùs contra Julianum lib. IV. 3. asseruit. Pelagianos Scholastici, Jesuitæ cumprimis, uti ex Bullis Pii V. & Gregorii XIII. liquet, frustra obnitentibus paucis fanioribus, quos inter Jansenius eminet, secuti sunt; quos inter non defuerunt, qui eò impudentiæ proveherentur, ut palam docerent, Gentilium bona opera meritoria fuisse. Quæ verò de Gentilium, eadem de irregenitorum quorumvis bonis operibus docent. De Socinianis & Remonstrantibus nihil attinet dicere. Nam illi Gentilium virtutes & bona opera æterna salute digna proclamare non erubescunt. Atque inter eos Curcellæus etrori huic operosa scriptione patrocinatus est.
units.tr: LIV. By these marks we distinguish truly good works from those that are plainly evil or only specious and painted over. To the latter class belong the works of unbelievers, of the unregenerate, and of the old and new Pharisees, who do not perform the good works commanded in the law of God, but those undertaken by their own will and choice. As regards the works of unbelievers, or of the Gentiles, there was the old dispute between Augustine and the Pelagians. For these men contended that the virtues and works of the Gentiles were as true as their body, eyes, and grain grown in their fields. They asserted that even though such works lacked right intention, they did not therefore lack rectitude, but were only barren or unfruitful. Augustine, on the contrary, most truly maintained that the virtues of the Gentiles, and what are usually praised in them, their {κατοφθώματα} [katorthômata], however splendid, were nevertheless real sins, false images and counterfeits of virtues and good works. For although what they did seemed good in its duty or outward act, it lacked every right end, and so was truly sin; he argued this more fully against Julian, book 4, chapter 3. The Scholastics, and especially the Jesuits, followed the Pelagians, as the bulls of Pius V and Gregory XIII make plain, while a few more sober men, among whom Jansenius stands out, struggled against them in vain. Among these Jesuits there were some who went so far in their shamelessness as to teach openly that the good works of the Gentiles were meritorious. What they teach about the good works of the Gentiles, they teach likewise about the good works of any unregenerate persons. There is no need to speak of the Socinians and Remonstrants. For they do not blush to proclaim the virtues and good works of the Gentiles worthy of eternal salvation. Among them Curcellaeus defended this error at length in writing.

units.la: LV. Tametsi verò præclara quædam gentilium & irregenitorum facinora videri possunt, si officium, seu factum nudum & exterio-rem, actum in conspectum hominum prodeuntem quem substantiam operis appellant, spectamus: tamen, quia officium illud cum fine conjunctum non fuit, & requisita reliqua boni operis, defecerunt, officium illud per se laudabile ipso hoc defectu vitii labem contraxit. Corticem illa, at non radicem bonitatis habuerunt. Lex enim Dei non solum officium & actum externum, sed conjunctum cum omnibus boni operis conditionibus postulat. Nullum proin gentilium & irregenitorum opus, quamcunque illud speciem habeat, sive Dei, sive hominum judicio vere & moraliter bonum censeri potest. Non enim ejusmodi opera procedunt vel ex rectæ voluntatis habitu, quia in irregenitis & infidelibus nulla recta voluntas, cùm non sint bona arbor, & vita spirituali, quæ per gratiam Christi à Spiritu S. inhabitante suppeditatur, penitus destituantur, imò in peccatis mortui sint: vel ex legis Divinæ perfecta notitia, quia qui verum Deum ignorant, ejus legem pariter ignorant, & lux illa naturæ, seu residuæ in Gentibus conscientiæ eò tantum profecit, ut id agerent, quò esse possent civitas, & societas eorum tum domestica, tum politica conservaretur, non omnia recte facta Deóque placentia, & modum ipsum recte faciendi cognoscerent: nec ex incentivo amoris Dei veri, quia verum Deum saltem gentiles ignoraunt; & irregenitus nemo unquam amavit, vel amare potuit: vel ex fide salvifica, qua infideles & irregeniti penitus destituuntur: vel ex intentione glorificandi Deum, quia cognoscentes Deum, non ut Deum glorificarunt, Rom. I. 21. Cùm enim omnia, quæ in mundo, & in ipsis adeò cubilibus & visceribus terræ sunt, requisiverint, uti Jobus cap. XXVIII. ostendit. Unam tamen hanc quæstionem gloriæ Divinæ, & verbi Divini, quo sanctitatis, justitiæ & misericordiæ Dei gloria manifestatur, omiserunt. Quo nomine eos {ἀναπολογήτως} esse Apostolus Rom. I. 20. demonstrat.
units.tr: LV. Although certain splendid deeds of Gentiles and unregenerate persons may seem so, if we look only at the duty, or the bare outward deed, the act that appears in the sight of men, which they call the substance of the work, nevertheless, because that duty was not joined with the end, and the other requisites of a good work were lacking, that duty, praiseworthy in itself, has by this very defect contracted the stain of vice. They had the bark of goodness, but not its root. For the law of God requires not only the duty and outward act, but the act joined with all the conditions of a good work. Therefore no work of the Gentiles or the unregenerate, whatever appearance it may have, can be judged truly and morally good, either by the judgment of God or of men. Such works do not proceed from a habit of right will, since in the unregenerate and unbelievers there is no right will, as they are not a good tree, and are wholly destitute of the spiritual life supplied through the grace of Christ by the indwelling Holy Spirit; indeed they are dead in sins. Nor do they proceed from a perfect knowledge of the divine law, since those who do not know the true God do not know his law either, and that light of nature, or the conscience remaining among the Gentiles, has gone only so far that they did what would preserve the state and their domestic and civil society, without knowing all that is rightly done and pleasing to God, nor the very manner of doing it rightly. Nor do they proceed from the incentive of love for the true God, since the Gentiles at least do not know the true God; and no unregenerate person has ever loved, or could love, him. Nor do they proceed from saving faith, of which unbelievers and the unregenerate are wholly destitute. Nor from the intention of glorifying God, since knowing God, they did not glorify him as God, Rom. 1:21. For although they sought out everything that is in the world, and even in the very dens and bowels of the earth, as Job chapter 28 shows, they neglected this one question: the glory of God and of the word of God, by which the glory of God's holiness, justice, and mercy is made manifest. For this reason the Apostle shows that they are without excuse {ἀναπολογήτως} [anapologêtôs], Rom. 1:20.

units.la: LVI. Haud plane incredibile est, posse homines malos tam exacta specie veras virtutes mentiri, & τὰ ἐκ νόμου quæ legis sunt, quoad officium & actum legis externum facere, Rom. II. 14. licèt non faciant illa {κατὰ δεῖ} sicut oportet, ibid. VIII. 26. Sicut enim interdum a calidis hominibus plumbi vel æris lamina tanta dexteritate tingitur, ut ad alia experimenta nobilitatem & fulgorem principis metalli, puta auri, constanter mentiatur: ita quidam intus & in cute improbi mira similitudine bonorum virorum simplicitatem & candorem imitantur. Sicut etiam quæ veram & fundatam bonitatem habent, non solo visu, sed reliquis etiam sensibus, gustu inprimis & tactu se commendant: ita splendida facta non tantum videre, sed verbi Divini sensu propius attingere & gustare convenit. Potest quis fingere verba, quæ etiam justus profert munera oblata repudiare, fortiter pro patria dimicare & sexcenta ejusmodi: ex quibus tamen solis justus non censebitur. Non putamus Regem qui persona m Regis in scena sæpiùs sustinet. Eodem modo qui virtutem histrionicam consequuntur, licèt externo actu speciosa expromant, ex iis tamen de vera eorum virtute judicium ferri non poterit. Ut Sponsæ gloria: ita præcipuus virtutis ornatus est מִנְּגֶד introrsum, Psal. XLV. 14. Cætera omnia oculis dari possunt. Ipse se dæmon in Dei & Angelorum lucis formam transferre potest. Neque ideo quia Gentilium
units.tr: LVI. It is by no means incredible that wicked men can counterfeit true virtues with so exact an appearance, and do the things of the law, as far as the duty and outward act of the law goes, Rom. 2:14, though they do not do them as they ought {κατὰ δεῖ} [kata dei], Rom. 8:26. For just as sometimes a thin plate of lead or bronze is coated by skilful craftsmen with such dexterity that under other tests it constantly passes for the nobility and lustre of the prince of metals, namely gold, so some wicked men, inwardly and in their skin, imitate with remarkable likeness the simplicity and candour of good men. And just as things that have true and well-founded goodness commend themselves not only to sight but to the other senses as well, above all to taste and touch, so splendid deeds must be approached and tasted more closely by the sense of the divine word. A man may feign words; a just man may refuse offered bribes, fight bravely for his country, and countless such things; yet by these alone the just man will not be judged just. We do not call a man a king who often plays the part of a king on the stage. In the same way, those who attain a stage-actor's virtue, though they display it in an outwardly splendid act, cannot therefore be judged on their true virtue. As the glory of the bride is inward, so the chief adornment of virtue is מִנְּגֶד [mineged] within, Ps. 45:14. All other things can be given to the eyes. The devil himself can transform himself into the form of God and the light of angels. Nor, because the virtues of the Gentiles were splendid sins,

units.la: {y} finem tamen & reliquas causas bona esse non posse. (Marginal, right.) tilium virtutes splendida peccata fuerunt, sequitur, rectius eos facturos fuisse, si iis plane abstinuissent; cum peccata non facienda, sed omittenda sint. Nam operam dare debuerant, ut cum externo officio notitiam & amorem veri Dei, veram fidem, & studium glorificandi Dei conjungerent, quibus deficientibus actum externum lege praeceptum implere potius quam omittere, vel peccata atrociora, in quibus & officium & reliqua omnia a lege ablude-rent, perpetrare debuerunt. Officium enim externum lege praeceptum non per se malum fuit, sed defectu tantum eorum, quae juxta legem cum officio concurrere debent. Non igitur omittendum, sed omnino faciendum fuit, non qua rationem peccati habuit, quod ei aliena vi adhaesit, sed quatenus actus lege mandatus fuit. Et quamvis quod sic fecerunt, per accidens verum peccatum fuit, tamen mitius leviusque fuit, quam si illud majore socordia & dedignatione parendi omisissent. Hinc eorum praeclare factis etiam in hac vita praemium quoddam Deus ex incredibili bonitate indulsit. Quod sic Augustinus Epist. 5. ad Marcell. explicat: Rempublicam primi Romani constituerunt, auxerúntque virtutibus, etsi non habentes veram pietatem erga verum Deum, quae ipsos etiam in aeternam civitatem posset salubri religione perducere, custodientes tamen quandam sui generis probitatem, quae posset terrenae civitati constituendae, augendae, conservandaeque sufficere. Deus enim ostendit in opulentissimo & praeclaro Imperio Romanorum, quantum valerent etiam civiles sine vera religione virtutes, ut intelligeretur, hac addita fieri homines cives alterius civitatis, cujus Rex veritas, cujus Lex charitas, cujus modus aeternitas. Neque in hac tantum vita gentilium ejusmodi facinora Deus praemiis exornavit, sed eorum etiam in altero seculo recordabitur, ut mitius puniat eos, qui fecerunt, quae legis sunt. Minus enim punietur Fabricius quam Catilina, non quia iste bonus, sed quia ille minus malus, & minus impius, quam Catilina; Fabricius, non veras virtutes habendo, sed a veris virtutibus non plurimum deviando. Athenienses porro dicti sunt colere Deum ignotum, Actor. XVII.23. non quod vero & salutari cultu Deum prosecuti fuerint, sed quia verum Deum, etiamsi ignotum, vero cultu se afficere putarunt. Sic enim Apostolus mira eos Christo lucrifacere studuit, dum reprehensionem laudatione lenivit. Sicut enim non simpliciter eos quasi superstitiosiores, ne durior videretur: ita non simpliciter dixit colitis, sed ignorantes colitis, ut vanitatem eorum argueret, ne iisdem adulari putaretur.
units.tr: {y} ...nor, because the end and the other causes cannot be good. (Marginal, right.) it follows that they would have done better had they abstained from them altogether, since sins must not be done but left undone. For they ought to have taken pains to join the outward duty with the knowledge and love of the true God, true faith, and zeal for glorifying God. When these were lacking, they ought rather to have performed the outward act commanded by the law than to omit it, or else to commit more atrocious sins in which both the duty and all the other things would have been alien to the law. For the outward duty commanded by the law was not evil in itself, but only lacking those things that by the law ought to concur with the duty. It was therefore not to be omitted but altogether to be done, not in respect of the character of sin, which adhered to it by an alien force, but as far as the act was commanded by the law. And although what they did in this way was accidentally a true sin, it was nonetheless milder and lighter than if they had omitted it out of greater sloth and contempt for obeying. Hence God, from his incredible goodness, has granted some reward even in this life for their praiseworthy deeds. Augustine explains this in Epistle 5 to Marcellinus: The first Romans founded and increased the commonwealth by their virtues, though they lacked true piety toward the true God, which could have led them to the eternal city by a saving religion, yet they kept a certain probity of their own kind, which was sufficient for founding, increasing, and preserving an earthly city. For God showed in the most wealthy and splendid Roman Empire how much even civil virtues without true religion could accomplish, so that it might be understood that, with this added, men become citizens of another city, whose king is truth, whose law is charity, whose measure is eternity. Nor has God adorned such deeds of the Gentiles only with rewards in this life; he will also remember them in the next age, so that he may punish more mildly those who did what the law requires. Fabricius will be punished less than Catiline, not because the former was good, but because he was less bad and less impious than Catiline; Fabricius did not have true virtues, but did not depart very far from them. Moreover, the Athenians are said to worship the unknown God, Acts 17:23, not because they served God with true and saving worship, but because they thought they were devoting true worship to the true God, though unknown. For the Apostle, in this way, wished to win them to Christ with admirable skill, softening his rebuke with praise. Just as he did not call them simply superstitious, lest he seem too harsh, so he did not simply say you worship, but you worship in ignorance, to expose their vanity without seeming to flatter them.

units.la: LVII. Bonorum operum norma destituuntur Pontificiorum etiam opera, in quibus religionis suae proram & puppim collocant. Non enim Divina lege illa definiri patiuntur, sed propria voluntate eligunt & constituunt. Proin mera cultus voluntarius ab Apostolo Col. II.23. damnatus, sunt, & cum humana praecepta sint, similia Pharisaeorum veterum praeceptis, frustra Deus illis colitur, Matth. XV.9. Sed operum vere bonorum normam esse legem Dei, supra fuse probavimus.
units.tr: LVII. The Papists' good works also lack a norm, and they place the prow and stern of their religion in them. They do not allow these works to be defined by the Divine law but choose and establish them by their own will. Therefore they are mere voluntary worship, which the Apostle condemns (Col. 2.23). Since they are human precepts, like the precepts of the old Pharisees, God is worshipped with them in vain (Matt. 15.9). But we have shown at length above that the norm of truly good works is the law of God.

units.la: Qui alium Dei cultum, quam verbum ejus definitum fingit, is aliam Dei voluntatem, quam revera est, & qua se in verbo suo patefecit, fingit. Neque Deus, sed idola callitie humanitus excogitata colunt. Sicut ipsa sunt, qui faciunt ea, ita omnis est, qui iis fidit, Psal. CXV.8. Neque illud operum ejusmodi vitium tollit, quod praeter, at non contra legem Divinam illa militare contendunt. Nam etiam quae praeter legem in religione & cultu Dei fiunt, Deut.IV.2. Matth.XV.2. &c. damnantur. Lotiones enim illae manuum a Pharisaeis frequentatae per se non contra, sed praeter legem Dei militabant. Sed quia ut pars cultus Divini exigebantur, & earum omissio peccato deputabatur, contra legem Dei fieri censebantur. Frustra per bonam intentionem tolli, si quid superstitionis sit, illi causantur; quia non sunt facienda mala, ut bona eveniant, Rom. III.8. Et bonam intentionem verbo Dei & fide regi supra probavimus. Neque Gedeonem ex spoliis Ephod facientem, Judic. VIII.27. neque Saulem ex Deo devotis sacrificantem, 1. Sam. XV.22. neque persecutores fidelium causa cultus Dei, Joh. XVI.2.3. intentio purgavit.
units.tr: Whoever invents a worship of God other than the one his Word defines also invents a different will of God from the one he really has and has revealed in his Word. Such people worship not God but idols devised by human vanity. As those things are, so are those who make them, and everyone who trusts in them (Ps. 115.8). Nor does it remove this fault of works that they contend such works are outside the Divine law rather than against it. For things done outside the law in religion and the worship of God are condemned too (Deut. 4.2; Matt. 15.2, etc.). The washings of hands frequently practised by the Pharisees were not against the law of God but outside it. But because they were required as part of divine worship, and their omission was counted as sin, they were judged to be against the law of God. In vain do they plead that whatever superstition there is may be removed by a good intention, since evil things are not to be done that good may come (Rom. 3.8). We have shown above that a good intention is ruled by the Word of God and by faith. Nor did the intention cleanse Gideon, who made an ephod from the spoils (Judg. 8.27), nor Saul, who sacrificed the things devoted to God (1 Sam. 15.22), nor the persecutors of the faithful who did so for the sake of the worship of God (John 16.2, 3).

units.la: LVIII. Ac ne fidelium quidem bona opera ad amussim legis Divinae exacta omnes bonitatis numeros ita implent, ut nihil vitii iis haerere dici possit. Licet enim expensa ad Evangelii tmkaev, qua defectus operum per Christi meritum condonantur, perinde ac si nulli unquam fuissent, Deus gratiose & paterne accepta habeat: tamen legaliter considerata, hoc est, in foro justitiae Divinae ad obrussam legis Divinae exacta, peccata sunt, non per se, quia quod iis boni inest, vitio deputari non debet, sed ex accidenti, quia defectibus cum legis Divinae rigore akrívemos tam in gradibus, quam in partibus & perseverantia, laborant. Peccant fideles non bene agendo, sed a perfecta legis regula deflectendo. Legis enim akribéstatos est, ut Deum diligamus ex toto corde, ex tota anima, omnibus viribus, puro corde, bona conscientia, Matth.XXII.37.38. 1.Tim.I.5. Atqui nemo justificatus in quocunque bono opere perfectionis isthoc fastigium attingit. Ipse autem defectus charitatis in vitio est. Atque id ipsum Ecclesia humiliter agnoscit & deplorat. Extitimus כטמא sicut impurus omnes nos & sicut vestis remotionum omnes justitiae nostrae, Esaj.LXIV.6. Ubi & de justitia, & de omnibus, & de omnium justitiis sermo est. Neque proin צדקה justitia vel solas ceremonias, vel ceremoniarum legalium observantiam per pravam intentionem corruptam significat, quia in talibus non est justitia, & omnium omnis justitia intelligitur. Ideo etiam renati, atque illi sanctissimi, velut Jobus & David judicium Dei deprecantur. An vir labiorum justificabitur? Job. XI.2. Ne venias in judicium cum servo tuo. Nam coram te non justificabitur ulla caro, Psal.CXLIII.2. Non deprecaturi illi judicium Dei fuerant, nisi rectitudinem operum suorum vitiis pluribus contaminatam & deformem deprehendissent. Accedit, quod operationum principia etiam apud sanctissimos quosque labem & carnem reliquam, quotidie mortificandam habent. Nam & in intellectu manent tenebrae, 1. Cor. III.1. & in voluntate resistentia carnis, Rom.
units.tr: LVIII. Nor do even the good works of the faithful, though measured by the rule of the Divine law, fulfil all the measures of goodness in such a way that it can be said nothing of fault clings to them. For although, when weighed by the indulgence of the Gospel [ἐπιείκεια], by which the defects of works are pardoned for Christ's merit, as if they had never existed, God accepts them graciously and fatherly, yet when they are considered legally, that is, in the court of Divine justice and tested by the standard of the Divine law, they are sins. They are not sins in themselves, because the good that is in them ought not to be counted as fault, but they are sins accidentally, because they suffer from defects in the strictness [ἀκριβῶς] of the Divine law, both in degrees and in parts and in perseverance. The faithful sin not by acting well but by departing from the perfect rule of the law. For the most exact [ἀκριβέστατος] requirement of the law is that we love God with the whole heart, with the whole soul, with all our strength, with a pure heart and a good conscience (Matt. 22.37, 38; 1 Tim. 1.5). But no justified person in any good work reaches this height of perfection. And the defect of love is itself a fault. The Church humbly acknowledges and laments this very thing: We have all become like one unclean [כטמא], and all our righteousness is like a filthy garment (Isa. 64.6). Here the discussion concerns justice, and all, and the justice of all. Therefore the word for righteousness [צדקה] does not signify, through a corrupt and perverse intention, either mere ceremonies or the observance of legal ceremonies, because in such things there is no righteousness, and the whole of righteousness of all is meant. For this reason even the regenerate, and the most holy men such as Job and David, pray that God will not judge them. Can a man of lips be justified? (Job 11.2). Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no flesh will be justified (Ps. 143.2). They would not have prayed against the judgment of God unless they had found the uprightness of their works stained and deformed by many faults. Moreover, the sources of their actions even in the most holy men have the remnant of corruption and flesh, to be mortified daily. For darkness remains in the understanding (1 Cor. 3.1), and resistance of the flesh remains in the will (Rom. 7.17; Gal. 5.17). The struggle of the flesh against the Spirit blunts the motion of the Spirit, hinders it by contrary suggestions, and as long as we carry about this prison of the body, it stains our good works with defilement. Sacrifices were a type of this matter, which were seasoned with such sweet spices that even the most foul galbanum was mixed in; and so was Aaron, who had to bear the iniquities which the children of Israel hallowed in all their gifts and offerings (Exod. 28.38). Perfection and sanctification free of all stain belong not to this life but to the fatherland, and are perfected only at death. For who here is so far that he does not sometimes stumble? We all stumble in many things (Jas. 3.2). And yet whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point is guilty of all (Jas. 2.10). Augustine rightly says in Epistle 29 to Jerome: Perfect love, which can no longer be increased, is in no one as long as this man lives. But as long as it can be increased, surely that which is less than it ought to be is from fault. From this fault there is no one just on earth who does good and does not sin.

units.la: Ne fidelium quidem bona opera ad legis Divinae rigorem exacta vitio omni carent.
units.tr: Even the good works of the faithful, though measured by the rigour of the Divine law, are not free of all fault.

units.la: Pontificiorum falsata bona opera perstringuntur.
units.tr: The good works of the Papists, falsified, are condemned.

units.la: VII. 17. Gal. V. 17. Lucta carnis cum spiritu motus spiritus retundit, contrariis suggestionibus retardat, & quandiu corporis hoc ergastulum circumferimus bonis operibus nostris labem affricat. Typus ejus rei quondam fuerunt tum sacrificia, quae sic suavissimis aromatis condiebantur, ut galbanum etiam foetidissimum admixtum fuerit: tum Aharon, qui iniquitates eorum, quae filii Israel in cunctis muneribus & donariis suis sanctificarunt, portare debuit, Exod. XXVIII. 38. Perfectio nempe & sanctificatio labis omnis expers non vitae, sed patriae est, atque in morte demum perficitur. Quotusquisque enim hic est, quin aliquando labatur. In multis impingimus omnes, Jac. III. 2. Atqui totam legem si quis impleverit, & in uno impegerit, reus est omnium, ibid. II. 10. Praeclare Augustinus Epist. 29. ad Hieronym. Plenissima, inquit, charitas, quae jam non possit augeri, quandiu hic homo vivit, in nemine est. Quandiu autem augeri potest, profecto illud, quod minus est, quam debet, ex vitio est. Ex quo vitio non est justus in terra, qui faciat bonum & non peccet.
units.tr: VII. 17; Gal. 5.17. The struggle of the flesh against the Spirit blunts the motion of the Spirit, hinders it with contrary suggestions, and as long as we carry about this prison of the body, it stains our good works. Sacrifices were a type of this matter; they were seasoned with such sweet spices that even the most foul galbanum was mixed in. Aaron too was a type, who had to bear the iniquities which the children of Israel hallowed in all their gifts and offerings (Exod. 28.38). Perfection and sanctification free of all stain belong not to this life but to the fatherland and are perfected only in death. For how few are there here who do not sometimes stumble? We all stumble in many things (Jas. 3.2). Yet whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point is guilty of all (ibid. 2.10). Augustine rightly says in Epistle 29 to Jerome: Perfect love, which can no longer be increased, is in no one as long as this man lives. But as long as it can be increased, surely that which is less than it ought to be is from fault. From this fault there is no one just on earth who does good and does not sin.

units.la: LIX. Scriptura equidem opera regenitorum bona passim Matth. V. 16. 1. Tim. VI. 18. Ephes. II. 10. &c. appellat; at non absolute, verum secundum quid, prout diversi sunt bonitatis gradus, quorum summus in hac vita attingi non potest. Neque ob defectum simpliciter mala fidelium opera dici debent, quia quod malum est, gratiose remittitur, quod bonum est, paterne acceptatur. Ita eadem corpora diverso respectu alba & nigra, magna & parva dicuntur. Crepuscula sunt & pars diei apud vulgus, & pars noctis apud astrologos. Nulla sic in eodem opere diversimode bono vel malo essentiarum confusio magis est, quam in justo operante, quem sic justum esse posse, ut tamen non careat peccato, ipsimet adversarii agnoscunt. Jobus in toto hoc non peccavit, & non dedit insulsitatem Deo, Job. I. 22. non secundum districtam judicii Divini sententiam, sed secundum indulgentis miseri cordiae testimonium, quo non peccare dicitur, qui ad non peccandum proxime accedit. Et non peccavit sic, ut Deo daret insulsitatem, uti statim sequitur. Non enim de Jobi omni integritate, sed de certa tantum causa sermo est; ut satis appareat, copulam ibi esse hoc sensu: In omni hoc non peccavit, ut Deo insulsitatem daret. Ita Jobus idem cap. XLII. 8. laudatur, quod recte locutus fuerit, cum tamen quaedam non recta idem locutus fuerit; & sunt fideles arbor bona, Psal. I. 3. XCII. 13. Matth. VII. 17. Omnis etiam arbor bona fert fructus bonos, neque malos ferre potest, ibid. v. 18. Sed non ideo vel perfecte bonos fert, vel malos ferre omnino nullos potest. Alias nunquam quisquam bonus peccaret, quod ipsi adversarii inficiantur. Sed fideles, ceu bona arbor, non sic malos fructus ferunt, peccant, ut peccato, ceu domino adhuc, more irregenitorum, serviant. Et provocant iidem ad justitiam suam, Psal. VII. 9. XVIII. 21. XXVI. 1. sed in causa speciali, quae cum hostibus eorundem iis intercessit; non in justitiae persona; seu universali; neque sic in causa speciali, ut in modo operandi summum justitiae gradum assecuti fuerint. Sed & S. Paulus opera fidelium bona fundamento superstructa, cum auro, argento & pretiosis lapidibus comparans, 1. Cor. III. 12. non tam operationem, quam effectum operationem consequens, quae pura & sana doctrina est, intelligit. Non sequitur autem, perfecte bona opera justorum esse, si perfecte bonae sunt doctrinae, quas ex verbo Dei praedicant. Lapides pretiosi esse possunt, licet structurae eorum intervenire vitium possit. Ita in opere nuptiarum cum nunquam desit peccatum ob concupiscentiam, operatio, quae ex accidenti mala esse potest, bonum opus, hominem, qui Dei creatura est, producere potest. Ubi filius est opus patris. Placent quoque fidelium opera Deo, Act. X. 35. Phil. IV. 18. 2. Pet. II. 5. Sed placent non tanquam judici, sed tanquam patri misericordi; & non in se simpliciter, sed in Christo Dilecto illo, in quo nos, χαριτωσε gratiosos reddidit, Ephes. I. 6. Hujus enim obedientia omnes operum defectus teguntur & condonantur. Denique bona opera sunt Dei & Spiritus S. opera, ibid. II. 10. Gal. V. 22. Et quatenus a Deo & Spiritu S. immediate proficiscuntur, perfecte bona sunt; sed quatenus etiam mediante carne eduntur, vitii labem contrahunt. Perfectio & ornamentum omne Dei & Spiritus S. imperfectio & deformitas agnata carnis est.
units.tr: LIX. Scripture indeed calls the works of the regenerate good throughout (Matt. 5.16; 1 Tim. 6.18; Eph. 2.10, etc.), but not absolutely; rather in a qualified sense, since there are different degrees of goodness, and the highest of these cannot be reached in this life. Nor are the faithful's works to be called evil simply because of their defects, since what is evil in them is pardoned graciously, and what is good is accepted fatherly. Thus the same bodies are called white and black, or large and small, in different respects. Twilight is part of the day according to common people, and part of the night according to astrologers. In the same work there is no confusion of essences, good and bad in different ways, greater than in the righteous man at work, whom our opponents themselves acknowledge can be just and yet not be without sin. Job did not sin in all this, nor did he charge God with folly (Job 1.22), not according to the strict sentence of Divine judgment, but according to the testimony of indulgent mercy, by which he is said not to sin who comes very near to not sinning. And he did not sin in such a way as to charge God with folly, as immediately follows. For the discussion is not about all of Job's integrity but only about one particular cause; so it sufficiently appears that the conjunction there has this sense: In all this he did not sin, so as to charge God with folly. So Job is praised in the same chapter (42.8) for speaking rightly, although he had also said some things that were not right; and the faithful are a good tree (Ps. 1.3; 92.13; Matt. 7.17). Every good tree also bears good fruit, and cannot bear bad fruit (ibid. v. 18). But it does not follow from this that it bears either perfectly good fruit or that it bears no bad fruit at all. Otherwise no good man would ever sin, which our opponents themselves deny. But the faithful, like a good tree, do not bear bad fruit in such a way that they sin as slaves of sin, as still under their Lord, after the manner of the unregenerate. And the same men appeal to their righteousness (Ps. 7.9; 18.21; 26.1), but in a particular cause, which arose between them and their enemies; not in the person of righteousness, or universal; nor in a particular cause in such a way that they had attained the highest degree of righteousness in their manner of acting. But St. Paul too, comparing the good works of the faithful built upon the foundation to gold, silver and precious stones (1 Cor. 3.12), understands not so much the operation as the effect that follows the operation, which is pure and sound doctrine. But it does not follow that the works of the just are perfectly good if the doctrines they preach from the Word of God are perfectly good. Stones may be precious even though a fault may intervene in their building. Thus in the work of marriage, where sin from concupiscence never fails, the act, which may be evil by accident, can yet produce a good work, namely a man, who is God's creature. Where a son is the work of his father. The works of the faithful also please God (Acts 10.35; Phil. 4.18; 1 Pet. 2.5). But they please not as to a judge but as to a merciful father; and not simply in themselves, but in Christ the Beloved, in whom he has made us graciously acceptable (Eph. 1.6). For by his obedience all defects of works are covered and pardoned. Finally, good works are the works of God and of the Holy Spirit (ibid. 2.10; Gal. 5.22). And insofar as they proceed immediately from God and the Holy Spirit, they are perfectly good; but insofar as they are also brought forth through the flesh, they contract the stain of fault. The perfection and every ornament is of God and the Holy Spirit; the imperfection and deformity is inborn in the flesh.

units.la: LX. Non minus necessaria bona opera sunt quam ipsa sanctificatio est. Et eadem utrorumque necessitatis causae sunt, quas supra fusissime deprompsimus. Sunt enim arboris bonae fructus, gratiae, electionis & justificationis per Christum testimonia, vocationis ornamenta, gratitudinis erga Deum & Christum, glorificationis Dei & charitatis erga proximum documenta, & proximi Christo lucrifaciendi media. Licet enim per solam gratiam Dei in Christo, ut causam justitiae & salutis nostrae unicam justificemur & salvemur, tamen non ideo ab aeterno electi, in tempore nati renatique, & per fidem in Christum justificati sumus, ut otiemur, & brachia decussemus, sed ut indesinenter bona & utilia faciamus. Bona arbor bonum fructum fert, Matth. VII. 17. Qui in me manet plurimum fructum fert, Joh. XV. 5. Dei creatura sumus, conditi in Christo ad bona opera, quae praeparavit Deus, ut in iis ambulemus, Ephes. II. 10. Tradidit semetipsum pro nobis, ut redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, & mundaret sibi populum peculiarem, aemulum bonorum operum, Tit. II. 14. In Jesu Christo valet fides per charitatem operosa, Gal. V. 6.
units.tr: LX. Good works are no less necessary than sanctification itself, and the causes of the necessity of both are the same, as we have set out at length above. They are the fruits of a good tree, the evidences of grace, election and justification through Christ, the ornaments of our calling, the proofs of our gratitude towards God and Christ, the testimonies of our glorifying God and of our love towards our neighbour, and the means of winning our neighbour to Christ. For although we are justified and saved by the grace of God in Christ alone, as the sole cause of our righteousness and salvation, we were not therefore chosen from eternity, born and reborn in time, and justified through faith in Christ, so that we might be idle and fold our arms, but so that we might constantly do good and useful things. A good tree bears good fruit, Matt. 7:17. He who abides in me bears much fruit, John 15:5. We are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them, Eph. 2:10. He gave himself for us, to redeem us from all iniquity and to purify for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works, Titus 2:14. In Jesus Christ faith working through love avails, Gal. 5:6.

units.la: LXI. Vitandi infames scopuli sunt tum eorum, qui bona opera contemnunt, non curanda & inutilia esse blaterant: tum eorum, qui nimium iisdem arrogant. In illorum censu Libertini & Antinomi inprimis sunt; quorum furores non semel notavimus. Ausus est Johannes Islebius Agricola eo blasphemiae erumpere, ut assereret; Bona opera ad salutem perniciosa esse. Cui Nicolaus Amsdorfius, Lutheri flabellum, astipulatus est. Etiam Bellarminus Evangelicis vellicatis, & alienum in sensum detortis eorum, Lutheri inprimis, dictis quibusdam, impingit, quod bonorum operum necessitatem infringunt. Quem confessiones publicae eorundem apertae calumniae convincunt. Sed necessitas bonorum operum vel ad justificationem, cationem, vel ad fidem, vel ad salutem refertur. Ad justificationem bona opera nullum causæ usum habent; nec proin hactenus ad actum illum necessaria sunt. Fidei verò comites & fructus sunt. Saluti denique non quidem promerendæ, sed adeundæ inserviunt, ejusque adjuncta antecedentia, uti fidei consequentia sunt. Gratia enim Dei, solíusque Christi merito servamur. Ac plane impropriè operibus salus tribuitur, quæ propriissimè gratiæ tribuitur. Si enim ex operibus, jam non ex gratia, Rom. XI. 6.
units.tr: LXI. We must avoid two notorious rocks: first, of those who despise good works, chattering that they are to be ignored and are useless; and second, of those who attribute too much to them. Among the first are the Libertines and Antinomians above all, whose madness we have noted more than once. Johann Agricola of Eisleben ventured to break out into such blasphemy as to assert: Good works are pernicious to salvation. Nicolaus Amsdorf, Luther's fan-bearer, supported him. Bellarmine too, by plucking at evangelical statements and twisting certain sayings of theirs, especially of Luther, into a foreign sense, charges them with weakening the necessity of good works; the public confessions of these same men refute this open calumny. But the necessity of good works is referred either to justification, or to calling, or to faith, or to salvation. Good works have no causal role in justification, and therefore are not necessary to that act. They are the companions and fruits of faith. Finally, they serve salvation, not indeed to earn it, but to reach it, and as its antecedent accompaniments they follow faith. For we are kept safe by the grace of God and the merit of Christ alone. And it is quite improper to attribute salvation to works, when it is most properly attributed to grace. For if it is by works, then it is no longer by grace, Rom. 11:6.

units.la: LXII. Negat etiam Confessio Helvetica cap. 16. bona opera ad salutem ita necessaria esse, ut absque illis nemo unquam servatus sit: perstringens tacitè errorem Georgii Majoris, Wittebergensis Theologi, qui ab Augustana Sphinge, seu Libro Interim inductus, absolutam bonorum operum necessitatem ad salutem docuit, neminémque sine iis salvari posse pertendit. Atqui & infantes absque bonis operibus servantur, & adulti inter ipsa regenerationis principia expirantes bonis operibus, quoad exteriorem saltem actum, edendis tempore & occasione destituti possunt, quibus Dei gratia sufficit. De cætero magno consensu docemus, adultis omnibus, quibus ad id tempus & occasio suppetit, sic necessaria esse bona opera, ut qui ea contemnunt, fastidiunt, & planè proterveque negligunt, spem salutis nullam habeant. Quo sensu non abhorremus à phrasi illa, quòd bona opera ad salutem necessaria sint, quam Augustani Theologi odio assertionis Majoristarum rejicere visi sunt. Diversissimi enim necessitatis gradus sunt: nec quicquid ad salutem necessarium est, ut causa salutis necessarium est. Nihilominus facilè patimur eos abundare suo sensu, & contra Majoristas æquè atque Amsdorfianos hac phrasi uti, quòd bona opera necessaria sint ad salutem per gratiam & fidem consequendam, quam doctiss. Hornejus in hac controversia adhibuit, eodem enim res recident; Inprimis arridet nobis illa Betnhardi lib. de Grat. & Lib. Arbit. aureola: Si proprie appellentur ea, quæ dicimus nostra merita, spei quædam sint seminaria, charitatis incentiva, occultæ prædestinationis indicia, futuræ felicitatis præsagia, via Regni, non causa regnandi. Quæ utinam ad animum sibi Pontifcii, propter nostrum cum iis consensum nos exagitantes, revocarent.
units.tr: LXII. The Helvetic Confession also denies, in chapter 16, that good works are so necessary to salvation that no one has ever been saved without them. It tacitly tackles the error of Georg Major, a theologian of Wittenberg, who, led by the Augsburg Sphinx, or the Interim book, taught an absolute necessity of good works for salvation and maintained that no one can be saved without them. And yet infants are saved without good works, and adults who die amid the very beginnings of regeneration, lacking the time and opportunity to perform good works in outward act at least, are saved by God's grace, which suffices for them. Otherwise, we teach with great agreement that for all adults who have the time and opportunity for it, good works are so necessary that those who despise them, shun them, and plainly and stubbornly neglect them have no hope of salvation. In this sense we do not shrink from that phrase, that good works are necessary to salvation, which the Augsburg theologians seemed to reject out of hatred for the assertion of the Majorists. For there are very different degrees of necessity, and not everything necessary to salvation is necessary as a cause of salvation. Nevertheless, we readily allow them to abound in their own sense, and, against the Majorists and the Amsdorfians alike, to use this phrase: that good works are necessary for obtaining salvation through grace and faith. The most learned Hornejus used this phrase in this controversy, for the matter comes to the same thing. Above all, that golden saying of Bernard's in On Grace and Free Choice delights us: If those things we call our merits are properly named, they are certain seedbeds of hope, incentives to love, hidden signs of predestination, forerunners of future happiness, the way to the kingdom, not the cause of reigning. Would that the Papists, who harass us because we agree with them on this point, would call this to mind!

units.la: LXIII. Sed illi, ad extremum alterum præcipitantes, operibus suis bonis, quæ maximam partem voluntarius Dei cultus sunt, dignitatem tantam tribuunt, ut bonorum suorum operum idololatræ jure meritóque dicantur. Nam bonorum operum ad salutem efficiendam necessitatem propugnant. Cùm tamen passim Scripturæ declarent, salutem & vitam æternam χάρισμα gratuitum Dei donum esse, Rom. VI. 23. & à solo Christo dependere, Joh. XVII. 3. Actor. IV. 12. Ephes. II. 9. & gratiam atque opera ἀνάξιος esse, Rom. XI. 6. & operum ad justitiam & vitam efficiendam nullum omnino momentum esse, ibid. III. 20. &c. Ephes. II. 8. 9. 2. Tim. I. 9. Tit. III. 5. Neque omnino bona opera causa salutis esse possunt, quæ non sunt nisi via, quam Deus præparavit, ut in ea ambulemus, Ephes. II. 10. Et fideles cum timore & tremore operantur salutem, Phil. II. 12. non
units.tr: LXIII. But they, rushing to the opposite extreme, attribute such great dignity to their good works, which for the most part are voluntary worship of God, that they may rightly and deservedly be called idolaters of their own good works. For they defend the necessity of good works for effecting salvation, although Scripture everywhere declares that salvation and eternal life are a free gift [χάρισμα] of God, Rom. 6:23, and depend on Christ alone, John 17:3, Acts 4:12, Eph. 2:9, and that grace and works are [ἀνάξιος, unworthy], Rom. 11:6, and that works have absolutely no weight for effecting righteousness and life, ibid. 3:20, etc., Eph. 2:8, 9, 2 Tim. 1:9, Titus 3:5. Nor can good works at all be the cause of salvation, since they are only the way which God prepared that we should walk in it, Eph. 2:10. And the faithful work out their salvation with fear and trembling, Phil. 2:12, not

units.la: bonis operibus, quæ non causam, sed κατὰ δικαιοσύνης fructus justitiæ cap. I. 11. appellaverat, salutem propriam efficiendo, sed ea faciendo, quæ is, qui salutem consecuturus facere debet. Debet autem is credere in Christum, resipiscere, Deum & proximum diligere, sanctimoniam colere, bona opera facere, in cursu pietatis progredi, procul omni arrogantia & securitate carnali cum timore & tremore. Quæ non causæ, sed adjunctorum antecedentium salutis rationem habent. Quo sensu etiam ὑπομονὴς χρέαν ἔχειν patientiam nobis necessariam esse, ad reportandam promissionem Apostolus Hebr. X. 36. dixit. Ordinavit enim Deus, ut vitam æternam per passiones adeamus, Luc. XXIV. 26. Actor. XIV. 22. Illa igitur χρεία necessitas non causæ, sed adjuncti est. Et μισθὸς & νόμος factor legis beatus est, Jac. I. 25. non quòd beatitudinem sua opera efficiat, sed quia in via piorum ambulat, Psal. I. 1. Facere legem adjunctum signum, non causa efficiens beatitudinis est. Denique Evangelium non promittit salutem sub conditione bonorum operum, velut causarum eam efficientium, sed sub conditione fidei, ut instrumenti accipiendæ remissionis peccatorum, nec non resipiscentiæ & obedientiæ non perfectæ, sed per gratiam inchoatæ, ut causæ sine qua non.
units.tr: by good works, which he had called not the cause but the fruits of righteousness [καρπὸν δικαιοσύνης], Phil. 1:11, effecting their own salvation, but by doing those things which one who is to obtain salvation must do. He must believe in Christ, repent, love God and neighbour, cultivate holiness, do good works, and advance in the course of piety, far from all arrogance and carnal security, with fear and trembling. These have the character not of a cause, but of antecedent accompaniments of salvation. In this sense the Apostle also said that we have need of patience [ὑπομονῆς χρείαν], Heb. 10:36, to obtain the promise. For God ordained that we should enter eternal life through sufferings, Luke 24:26, Acts 14:22. That necessity, therefore, is of an accompaniment, not of a cause. And the doer of the law is blessed [μακάριος], James 1:25, not because his works bring about blessedness, but because he walks in the way of the godly, Ps. 1:1. Doing the law is an accompanying sign, not the efficient cause of blessedness. Finally, the Gospel does not promise salvation on condition of good works, as causes that effect it, but on condition of faith, as the instrument of receiving forgiveness of sins, together with repentance and obedience, not perfect but begun through grace, as a cause without which it does not happen.

units.la: LXIV. Cæterùm gravius illud est, quòd bona opera non utcunque efficere, sed etiam mereri vitam æternam iidem contendunt. Nam Tridentini Sess. VI. can. 32. sic definiunt: Si quis dixerit, hominis justificati bona opera ita esse dona Dei, ut non sint etiam bona ipsius justificati merita, aut ipsum justificatum bonis operibus, quæ ab eo per Dei gratiam & Jesu Christi meritum, cuius membrum vivum est, fiunt, non verè mereri augmentum gratiæ, vitam æternam, & ipsius vitæ æternæ; si tamen in gratia decesserit, consecutionem atque etiam gloriæ augmentum, anathema sit. Ergo opera bona verè mereri gratiæ augmentum, vitam æternam, ejus consecutionem, & gloriæ augmentum, hoc est, aureolas, sub anathemate sanciunt. Sed quomodo mereantur, an ex congruo, an ex condigno, an ex pacto, de quo Scholæ doctores mirè conflictantur, definire non sustinuerunt. Satis enim habuerunt, vera merita definire, quorum definiendorum magnam illi causam habuerunt. Si enim unum Christi meritum valere, atque illud fidelibus donari constiterit, nullum erit Purgatorium quo repurgentur, qui non satis meritorum habent, ut iis peccata sua redimant: nullæ satisfactiones, nulla opera supererogatoria, vel superflua merita per indulgentias applicanda, nullum sacrificium, quod pro vivis & mortuis in Missa offeratur. Hæc humanorum meritorum crypsis est.
units.tr: LXIV. Moreover, it is more serious that these same men contend that good works merit eternal life, not merely effect it in some way. For the Council of Trent, Session 6, canon 32, defines thus: If anyone shall say that the good works of a justified man are so gifts of God that they are not also the good merits of the justified man himself, or that the justified man by his good works, which are done by him through the grace of God and the merit of Jesus Christ, of whom he is a living member, does not truly merit an increase of grace, eternal life, and the attaining of that eternal life, and also the increase of glory, if indeed he dies in grace, let him be anathema. Therefore they sanction under anathema that good works truly merit an increase of grace, eternal life, its attainment, and an increase of glory, that is, aureoles. But they did not venture to define how they merit, whether by congruity, by condignity, or by covenant, a question over which the teachers of the schools struggle wonderfully. For they were content to define true merits, and they had a great reason for defining these. For if it is established that the one merit of Christ is of value and is bestowed upon the faithful, there will be no Purgatory in which those are purged who do not have enough merits to redeem their sins by them; no satisfactions, no supererogatory works, no superfluous merits to be applied through indulgences, no sacrifice offered for the living and the dead in the Mass. This is the secret hiding-place of human merits.

units.la: LXV. Sed opera gratiam & vitam merentia per Dei gratiam & Jesu Christi meritum fieri, Tridentini, imò etiam mereri alii asserunt. Sicut enim olim Pseud-Apostoli Evangelium cum Lege conjunxerunt, vel potiùs confuderunt, & partim in gratia Dei, partim in operibus Legis quærendam justitiam esse statuerunt: ita hi operum humanorum merita cummeri-o Christi conjungunt; atque illa non sine hoc meritoria esse, imò Christum gratiam & vim merendi gloriam meruisse, opera verò nostra
units.tr: LXV. But some assert that works which earn grace and life are done through the grace of God and the merit of Jesus Christ, as the Council of Trent says, and indeed that they also merit. Just as the false apostles of old joined the Gospel to the Law, or rather confused the two, and decided that righteousness is to be sought partly in the grace of God and partly in the works of the Law, so these men join the merits of human works to the merit of Christ. They declare that those works are meritorious only through this, and that Christ merited grace and the power of meriting glory, while our works, endowed with this power of merit flowing from Christ's merit, merit glory and life.

units.la: hac vi merendi ex merito Christi fluente praedita gloriam & vitam mereri; atque sic humanis meritis gloriam meriti Christi non minui, sed augeri, declamant. Qui meretricius ex meritis conflatus fucus est, quem ante omnia abstergi operae pretium fuerit. Non parum enim merito Christi detrahi necesse est, si non ipsum, sed humanum meritum propria, immediata & proxima gloriae & vitae aeternae causa est. Nam & habitum & opera quisque sua immediatam & propriam causam gloriae putat, Christi vero merito remota tantum causalitas, & causae sine qua non, sive potius connexi, relinquitur. Atqui vis merendi & meritum ipsum solius Christi proprium est. Solus ille dedit & dare potuit animam suam λύτρον redemptionis pretium pro multis, Matth. XX.28. & Ecclesiam proprio sanguine acquisivit, Act. XX.28. Mereri vero, ut alius mereatur, non est mereri, sed alii merituro cedere. Et quod Christus jam meruit, id impetravit & consecutus est, idque ab ipso solo speramus, & in ipso obtinemus, id non demum meremur. Accedit, quod justitia in Christo nobis donata vitam nobis addicit, bona igitur opera consequentia non possunt esse causa regnandi, sed fructus justitiae, & Regni donandi pignora. Praeterea opera meritoria, etiam per meritum Christi, homini in negotio justificationis gloriationis materiem relinquunt, uti exempla contraria Pharisaei in operibus, quae etiam gratiae Divinae accepta tulit gloriantis, Luc. XVIII.11. & Abrahami, qui regenitus justificari per opera non potuit, ne gloriandi ansam haberet, Rom. IV.1. docent. Et immane profecto illud, atque loquelae Draconis simile est, quod non Christus gloriam & vitam aeternam nobis promeruerit, sed nos virtute merendi ex Christi merito accepta, illam promereamur. Ita enim Christus nobiliore parte sui meriti, videlicet donatione gloriae & vitae aeternae spoliatur, & infra hominem abjicitur, quem penes stat vis illa merendi recte uti, vel non. Sed disertanimis vox Christi, est: Ego vitam aeternam do ovibus meis, & non peribunt in aeternum, Joh. X.28. Ipse enim consummatus factus est obedientibus sibi omnibus causa salutis aeternae, ib. cap. II.10. Neque ullus unquam Sanctorum opera salutis & gloriae meritoria unquam sibi arrogavit.
