Quorum potius, omnia sibi mandata facientium, ingenua confessio est: Sumus δοῦλοι ἀχρεῖοι servi inutiles, quia quod debuimus facere, fecimus, Luc. XVII.10. Denique meritum unius nihil ad meritum alterius conferre, nec omnino causa meritoria esse, propter quam opera alterius eam dignitatem, & id pretium habeant, ut meritoria sint, potest; quia non potest esse causa, ut perfecte bona, legi conformia, indebita, & praemio adaequata, adeoque vitae causa sint. Potuit Christus merito suo efficere, & effecit, ut sanctificaremur, & bonis operibus ornaremur, atque in iis ambularemus, Ephes. II.10. Sed quae sic bona per meritum Christi in nobis sunt opera, non ita ille sanguine suo tinxit, ut mererentur id, quod solus ipse mereri potuit, meruitque, adeoque vitae causa existerent. Merito enim suo, non opera bona hominis, sed peccata tinxit, eorum καθαρισμὸν purificationem faciens per se ipsum, Heb. I.3.
units.tr: In this way they claim that the glory of Christ's merit is not diminished by human merits but increased. This is a harlot's paint made of merits, and it will be worth the effort to wash it off first. For a good deal of Christ's merit must necessarily be taken away if human merit, and not Christ himself, is the proper, immediate and proximate cause of glory and eternal life. For each person thinks his own habit and works are the immediate and proper cause of glory, and to Christ's merit there remains only a remote causality, a cause without which nothing happens, or rather a connection. Yet the power of merit and the merit itself belong to Christ alone. He alone gave, and was able to give, his soul as a ransom, the price of redemption for many (Matt. 20.28), and acquired the Church with his own blood (Acts 20.28). But to merit so that another may merit is not to merit at all, but to yield to one who is yet to merit. What Christ has already merited, he has obtained and attained, and we hope for it from him alone and possess it in him; we do not merit it afterwards. Moreover, since the righteousness given to us in Christ assigns us life, the good works that follow cannot be the cause of reigning, but the fruit of righteousness and pledges of the Kingdom to be given. Furthermore, meritorious works, even through Christ's merit, leave man matter for boasting in the business of justification. The example of the Pharisee, who boasted of his works, and took them as received from the grace of God (Luke 18.11), and of Abraham, who, not yet regenerate, could not be justified by works, so that he would not have an occasion for boasting (Rom. 4.1), teach this. And it is truly monstrous and like the speech of a dragon, that Christ did not merit glory and eternal life for us, but we merit it by the power of merit received from Christ's merit. For in this way Christ is robbed of the nobler part of his merit, namely the bestowal of glory and eternal life, and is cast down beneath man, in whose power it lies to use that power of merit rightly or not. But the voice of Christ is very clear: I give eternal life to my sheep, and they shall not perish forever (John 10.28). For he became perfect, and the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him (ib., ch. II.10). Nor has any of the saints ever claimed for himself works meritorious of salvation and glory. Rather, the frank confession of all who do everything commanded them is this: We are unprofitable servants; we have done only what we ought to have done [δοῦλοι ἀχρεῖοι] (Luke 17.10). Finally, the merit of one person can contribute nothing to the merit of another, nor be at all a meritorious cause by which the works of another have that dignity and worth to be meritorious; for it cannot be the cause that they are perfectly good, in conformity with the law, not owed, and equal to the reward, and so causes of life. Christ was able by his merit to bring it about, and did bring it about, that we should be sanctified and adorned with good works, and walk in them (Eph. 2.10). But the works that are good in us through Christ's merit are not so tinged with his blood that they merit what only he himself could merit, and did merit, and so become causes of life. For by his merit he has made purification [καθαρισμὸν purificationem faciens per se ipsum] not of the good works of man, but of sins (Heb. 1.3).

units.la: LXVI. Mereri Veteribus idem est, quod consequi aliquid: & meritum idem quod consecutio O felix culpa (sic illi) quae talem meruit (consecuta, adepta est) Redemptorem! Est enim ἀ μέρω, significante λαμβάνω, λαγχάνω, consequor, fortior, uti Hesychius interpretatur. Idem merita esse non justificandorum, sed justificatorum dixerunt; ostendentes sic, se per merita non intelligere opera, quae essent causa juris petendi vitam aeternam.
units.tr: LXVI. For the ancients, to merit is the same as to obtain something, and merit the same as attainment: "O happy fault" (so they say), which earned (obtained, gained) such a Redeemer! For the Greek word [ἀ μέρω] means receive, obtain [λαμβάνω, λαγχάνω], attain, get [consequor, fortior], as Hesychius explains. They also said that merits belong to the justified, not to those who are to be justified, thereby showing that by merits they did not mean works which would give a legal claim to eternal life.

units.la: LXVII. Meriti proprie dicti septem requisita Bellarminus de Justif. lib. 5. texit; nimirum, ut sit opus bonum, in obsequium Dei factum, viatoris, liberum, ut operans sit amicus Dei, ut intercedat promissio, ut ex charitate procedat. Non libet singula haec excutere.
units.tr: LXVII. Bellarmine, in De Justificatione, book 5, sets out seven requisites of merit properly so called: namely, that it be a good work, done in obedience to God, by a wayfarer, freely, that the one working be a friend of God, that a promise intervene, and that it proceed from charity. I do not wish to examine each of these.

units.la: Vocibus meconsummatæ Sanctitatis: at meritum sive ἀξίωμα in nobis non impleri nisi, quatenus illud ἐν δικαιώματι, quod in Christo est, nobis, in communione ipsius per fidem, separatur. Cùm ergo peccator non possit habere opera legis, adeóque nec meritum; & opera renovationis non sint causa justitiæ, sed effecta & ornamenta, blasphemè faciunt, qui illa merita vitæ, & quidem ex condigno faciunt.
units.tr: But merit, or worthiness [ἀξίωμα], is not fulfilled in us except insofar as the righteousness that is in Christ [ἐν δικαιώματι] is applied to us, by faith, in communion with him. Since therefore a sinner cannot have the works of the law, and so cannot have merit, and since the works of renewal are not the cause of righteousness but its effects and ornaments, those who make these works merits of life, and indeed merits in the strict sense, speak blasphemously.

units.la: LXVIII. Certiora meriti proprië dicti ξεἀτηεἀα ipse Thomas de Argentina Comp. Theol. lib. IV. 15. & V. 10. pandit. Nam meritum ille definit opus indebitum, de nostro præstitum, premium ex indebito debitum faciens. Plenius nos meritum dicimus opus perfectè legi conveniens, indebitum, proprium, & æquale præmio. Opus perfectè Legi conveniens, quia Lex vitam promittens opus, quoad partes, gradus & perseverantiam perfectam requirit, & quod imperfectum idémque debitum est, non tam meretur quicquam, quàm gratuita condonatione indiget. Indebitum, quia debitum qui solvit, nihil novi juris solvendo ille meretur. Quæ igitur opera homo Deo debet, sive ut creatura, sive ob gratiam faciendi àDeo acceptam ea mereri proprië non possunt; neque sic utilia sunt Deo, quasi prius ipsi dentur, & iccirco reddere aliquid debeat. Proprium, & planè nostrum, quia de alieno largiens proprium meritum non habet. Denique æquale præmio, quia dignitas intrinseca operis meritorii requirit ἰσότητα æqualitatem dati & accepti, quæ solà meriti & mercedis proprië dictæ relationem fundat, & absque, quo est, quod datur operi, non merces, sed gratia est. Hoc sensu verissimo meritum est actio personalis solius Christi membris ipsius planè incommunicabilis.
units.tr: LXVIII. Thomas of Argentina himself sets out more exact notions of merit properly so called, in Comp. Theol., book IV, ch. 15, and V, ch. 10. For he defines merit as a work not owed, done by us, making a reward owed out of what is not owed. We define merit more fully as a work perfectly agreeing with the Law, not owed, our own, and equal to the reward. A work perfectly agreeing with the Law, because the Law, which promises life, requires a work perfect in its parts, degrees and perseverance; and what is imperfect, and therefore owed, does not merit anything, but needs gratuitous pardon. Not owed, because one who pays what he owes merits nothing new by paying it. Therefore the works that man owes to God, whether as a creature or on account of the grace of doing received from God, cannot properly merit; nor are they useful to God in such a way that they are first given to him, so that he should owe something in return. Our own, and plainly ours, because one who gives out of what belongs to another does not have his own merit. Finally, equal to the reward, because the intrinsic dignity of a meritorious work requires equality [ἰσότης] of what is given and what is received, which alone founds the relation of merit and wage properly so called; and without it, what is given for the work is not a wage but grace. In this most true sense, merit is a personal action of Christ alone, wholly incommunicable to his members.

units.la: LXIX. Justificatorum certè opera requisitis hisce meritorum destituuntur penitus. Nam imperfecta sunt, quia in hac vita nunquam ad summum amoris gradum pertingunt, & in multis offendimus omnes, Jacob. III. 2. & qui in uno impingit, omnium reus est, ib. cap. II. 10. Cognitio nostra, adeóque etiam consequens amor ἐκ μέρους ex parte est, 1.Cor. XIII. 9. & operantes ipsi imperfecti sunt, habentes ἁμαρτίαν ἐνοικοῦσαν peccatum inhabitans, Rom. VII. 20. Neque imperfecta duntaxat, sed etiam debita sunt. Cùm omnia vobis mandata feceritis, dicite: "Οτι δοῦλοι ἀχρεῖοί, quia servi inutiles sumus, quia debemus facere, quod fecimus, Luc. XVII. 10. Ὀφειλέται debitores sumus non carni, sed spiritui, Rom. VIII. 12. Inutiles verò servi sumus non tantùm ex natura, sed etiam ex gratia, tum quia etiam, ex hypothesi, facientes omnia, quæ mandata nobis sunt, inutiles dicimur, cùm tamen ex natura omnia mandata facere non valeamus: tum quia hæc Apostolis servis ex gratia dicuntur. Et inutiles servi sumus non tantùm Deo, sed etiam nobis. Qui domino suo inutilis est, etiam sibi nihil lucratur, cùm lucrum sit ex opere, quod alteri impenditur. Et parabola illa v. 9. dicit: Numquid gratiam habet servo illi, qui omnia sibi mandata fecit? Non puto. Quæ non utilitatem à servo in herum, sed ab hero in servum redundantem significant. Præterea nec nostra, vel ex nostro sint, quæ facimus, bona opera, sed dona gratiæ & Spiritus S. Omnis donatio bona, omne donum perfectum est superne à Patre luminum, Jac. I. 17. Deus in nobis operatur velle & perficere, Phil. II.
units.tr: LXIX. The works of the justified are entirely without these requisites of merit. For they are imperfect, because in this life they never reach the highest degree of love, and we all offend in many things (James 3.2), and whoever stumbles in one point is guilty of all (ib., ch. II.10). Our knowledge, and consequently also our love, is in part [ἐκ μέρους] (1 Cor. 13.9), and the workers themselves are imperfect, having sin dwelling in them (Rom. 7.20). They are not only imperfect, but also owed. When you have done all things commanded you, say: "We are unprofitable servants, because we are servants who have done only what we ought to do" [ὅτι δοῦλοι ἀχρεῖοί] (Luke 17.10). We are debtors [ὀφειλέται] not to the flesh but to the Spirit (Rom. 8.12). Yet we are unprofitable servants not only by nature but also by grace: both because, even on the supposition that we are doing all things which are commanded us, we are called unprofitable, since by nature we are not able to do all that is commanded; and because these things are said of the apostles, who were servants by grace. And we are unprofitable servants not only to God but also to ourselves. One who is unprofitable to his lord gains nothing for himself either, since gain comes from work that is devoted to another. And that parable at v. 9 says: Does he have thanks from that servant who did all that was commanded him? I think not. These words signify a benefit flowing not from servant to master but from master to servant. Moreover, the good works we do are not ours, nor from us, but gifts of grace and of the Holy Spirit: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, from the Father of lights (James 1.17); God works in us to will and to do (Phil. II.13).

units.la: 13. Quid habes, quod non accepteris? 1.Cor. IV. 7. Ut quis ex eo, quod dono datum est, bene mereatur de alio, qui dono non dedit, fieri potest. At ut bene mereatur idem de eo, qui dono dedit, & prior nihil accepit, fieri non potest. Denique nec æqualia præmio opera sunt puto, quòd passiones hujus temporis non sint dignæ gloria, quæ erga nos revelabitur, Rom. VIII. 18. Dilutum est, quod in se indignas esse passiones cœlesti gloria fatentur, at dignas esse, prout à Spiritu S. per gratiam profiteuntur, pertendunt. Nam Apostolus de passionibus loquitur, quatenus Spiritus S. gratia sunt, uti ex v. 15. 16. &c. constat. Neque etiam Spiritus S. ejusmodi opera vel passiones in homine fragili peccatore, & carne adhuc circumdato, quæ cum cœlesti gloria ὑπερβολὴ esse possint, operatur. Nam qualiscunque passio vel afflictio illa est, quam Spiritus S. in nobis operatur, manet illa ελαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως leve afflictionis, seu levis afflictio maximè excellenter æternum pondus gloriæ operans, (non merito, sed ἀκαλύπτως) adeóque nullum unquam cum gloria illa commensum habens, 2.Cor. IV. 17. Nam ὀλίγον ἄρτι λυπούμεθα parum nunc contristamur, 1.Pet. I. 6. Denique quæcunque meritis præmia redduntur, illa pro inæqualitate operum & ipsa inæqualia sunt. At vita æterna non redditur inæqualiter pro operum inæqualitate, quia, juxta parabolam, Matth. XX. 1. &c. operariis in vineam, aliis citiùs, aliis serius missis ex æquo denarius redditur. Cui parabolæ simile Regnum Cœlorum dicitur. v. 1. Nam quòd in ea non operum, sed tantùm temporis inæqualitatem poni, & in temporibus inæqualibus operas æquales esse posse nugantur, planè a parabola abludit. Non enim primi denarium accipientes indignari potuissent, si pares operæ diverso tempore toleratæ fuissent. Neque sic paterfamilius murmuranibus gratiam obtendisset, dicens: Volo huic ultimo dare, ut & tibi. Annon licet mihi, quod volo, facere in rebus meis? An oculus tuus malus est, quia ego bonus sum? v. 14. 15.
units.tr: 13. "What have you that you did not receive?" 1 Cor. 4:7. A person may deserve well of another from what has been given to him as a gift, namely one who did not give it as a gift. But the same person cannot deserve well of the one who gave the gift, since the earlier giver received nothing beforehand. Finally, I do not think that works are equal to the reward, because "the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us," Rom. 8:18. It is one thing to confess that sufferings are unworthy of heavenly glory in themselves, but another to contend that they are worthy, as they profess them to be through grace by the Holy Spirit. For the Apostle speaks of sufferings insofar as they are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as is clear from vv. 15, 16, etc. Nor does the Holy Spirit work such works or sufferings in a frail sinner who is still clothed with flesh, works that could possibly be "beyond measure" [ὑπερβολὴ] compared with heavenly glory. For whatever kind of suffering or affliction it is that the Holy Spirit works in us, it remains "the light affliction" [ελαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως], or "a light affliction, which works for us, far beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory" (not by merit, but [ἀκαλύπτως]), and so it never has any proportion to that glory, 2 Cor. 4:17. For "now for a little while we are in heaviness," 1 Pet. 1:6. Finally, whatever rewards are given as the due of merits are unequal in proportion to the inequality of the works. But eternal life is not given unequally in proportion to the inequality of works, since, according to the parable in Matt. 20:1 etc., the same penny is paid to laborers sent into the vineyard, some earlier and some later. To this parable "the kingdom of heaven" is said to be like, v. 1. For it is trifling to assert that the parable sets out an inequality of time only and not of works, and that equal works can be done in unequal times; this is plainly foreign to the parable. For those who received the penny first would not have had grounds for indignation if equal labors had been endured at different times. Nor would the householder have answered the murmurers with grace in this way, saying: "I will give to this last even as unto you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?" vv. 14, 15.

units.la: LXX. Accedunt & alia argumenta, quibus operum merita profligantur. Etenim Deus nos gratis elegit in Christo, ut essemus sancti & inculpati in conspectu ejus, Ephes. I. 4. At gratis nos electos esse ad vitam, & in Christo electos esse sic, ut per ejus redemptionem & meritum ad vitam perducamur, & simul ipsi gloriam & vitam operibus nostris mereamur, ἀσυμπτον est. Qualis enim electio, talis respectu nostri executio est. Illa merè gratuita est. Ergo & hæc, Intentionis & executionis Divinæ suavis harmonia est. Si igitur Deus ab æterno ex mera gratia quosdam in tempore salvare intendit, hoc est, ex gratia quosdam ad salutem elegit, in tempore exequendo electionem, salutem ex eadem gratia sine meritis operum conferat oportet. Ideo vita æterna diserte vocatur χάρισμα donum Dei, sicut contra mors ὀψώνια stipendia peccati, ceu mortem promerentis, Rom. VI. 23. Donum autem, seu χάρισμα, & quidem ὀφείλημα debito oppositum, ibid. IV. 4. non æquè ac stipendium cadit sub meritum. Et salus ex mera Dei gratia & misericordia confertur. Qui secundum canonem hunc incedunt, pax super eos & misericordia, Gal. VI. 16. Gratia salvati estis per fidem. Et hoc non ex vobis. Dei donum est. Non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur, Ephes. II. 8. 9. Non ex operibus, sed secundum misericordiam ejus salvavit nos, Tit.III.5. Operanti vero imputatur merces non ex gratia, sed ex debito, Rom.IV.4. Frustra vero illi merita gratiae subordinant. Dare enim aliquid ex gratia, & simul ex merito proprie dicto, ὀφειλημα sunt, quia meritum facit rem debitam, at gratia supponit indebitam. Quicquid ergo datur ex gratia & misericordia pura puta, id non potest dari simul ex merito. Alias gratia non esset gratia, Rom XI.6. Gratia mera meritum proprie dictum; & vicissim meritum gratiam devorat. Solus vero Christus obedientia sua perfectissima cum sublimitate personae conjuncta aeternam vitam nobis promeruit; & uno hoc merito omnis benedictio spiritualis stat. Benedixit nobis omni benedictione spirituali in supercoelestibus in Christo, Ephes.I.3. Non est in alio quoquam salus. Neque aliud nomen sub Coelo datum est hominibus, in quo nos oporteat salvari, Act.IV.12. Neque proin ex merito Christi hominum merita nascuntur, vel haec illi subordinantur, quam male fartam stropham abunde supra discussimus. Si enim Christus sanguine suo non tam peccata, quam merita nostra tinxit, jam Christus solus non est Servator noster, qui in tanti operis societatem hominem ipsum servandum asciverit. Annon enim hac ratione servandi Servatores fiunt? Et tot Servatores, quot boni sunt? Sic vero humana merita gratiae, misericordiae Dei, & merito Christi subordinantur, & in eo fundantur, uti cerea domus ardentibus prunis, superaedificatur, vel domus ex sale in medio fluminis construitur. Accedit, quod vita aeterna nobis datur ut haereditas. Si filii, etiam haeredes. Haeredes quidem Dei, coharedes autem Christi, Rom. VIII.17. Qui est arrhabo haereditatis nostrae, Ephes.I.14. Venite benedicti Patris, κληρονομήσατε adite haereditate praeparatum vobis Regnum, Matth.XXV.34. Atqui nulla haereditas meritis acquiritur. Neque filii possunt dici mereri haereditatem a patre suo, cui sic omnia secundum naturam debent, ut nunquam satisfacere possint. At vita aeterna non tantum haereditas dicitur, sed diserte filiorum. Si filii, etiam haeredes, Rom. VIII.17. Inane est, quod etiam Christum sibi haereditatem meruisse regerunt. Dispar enim ratio est. Ille enim perfecta sua obedientia non meruit sibi vitam, ceu haereditatem, neque jure paternae & gratiosae haereditatis eam adiit (alias nihil proprie meruisset, nec legi nostro loco unquam satisfecisset) sed meruit sibi haereditatem, hoc est, semen, haeredes, filios, quibus justitiam & vitam merito suo acquisitam ex consilio Patris donaret. Fideles contra vitam aeternam accipiunt, ceu haereditatem, hoc est, jure hereditario, quia haeredes Dei & Christi, ex mera gratia adoptionis. An sic quoque Christus haeres Dei Patris est ex gratia adoptionis? Haec scilicet haeresis Felicis Urgelitani & Elipandi, in Concilii Francofortensi damnata, fuit. Denique si vita & salus ex merito operum contingit, tum in operibus nostris gloriari & confidere possumus, imo debemus. Quisque enim suis meritis niti & insistere potest. At in operibus suis gloriari, iisque confidere nemini licet. Ubi est gloriatio? Exclusa est. Per quam legem? Operum? Non; sed per legem fidei, ibid. III.27. Ipse Bellarminus, postquam de Justif. lib.V.
units.tr: LXX. There are also other arguments by which the merits of works are overthrown. For "God chose us in Christ freely, that we should be holy and without blame before him," Eph. 1:4. But to be chosen freely to life, and to be chosen in Christ in such a way that we are brought to life through his redemption and merit, and at the same time to merit glory and life by our own works, is [ἄσυμφωνον] inconsistent. For the execution is of the same kind as the election: the election is wholly gratuitous, so the execution is too. This is the sweet harmony of God's intention and execution. If therefore God from eternity intended, out of pure grace, to save some in time, that is, chose some to salvation out of grace, then in carrying out that election in time he must bestow salvation from the same grace, without the merits of works. So eternal life is expressly called a gift [χάρισμα] of God, just as, on the other hand, death is called the wages [ὀψώνια] of sin, as earning death, Rom. 6:23. But a gift, or [χάρισμα], and indeed one set against a debt [ὀφείλημα], Rom. 4:4, does not fall under merit in the way that wages do. And salvation is conferred by the pure grace and mercy of God. "As many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them and mercy," Gal. 6:16. "By grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God; not of works, lest any man should boast," Eph. 2:8, 9. "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us," Titus 3:5. "To him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt," Rom. 4:4. Those who subordinate merits to grace do so in vain. For to give something both out of grace and at the same time out of merit properly so called is contradictory, since merit makes the thing owed, whereas grace presupposes what is not owed. Whatever is given out of grace and pure mercy, therefore, cannot be given at the same time out of merit. "Otherwise grace is no more grace," Rom. 11:6. Pure grace is merit properly so called in reverse, and conversely merit devours grace. Christ alone, by his most perfect obedience joined with the dignity of his person, merited eternal life for us, and in this one merit every spiritual blessing stands. "He hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ," Eph. 1:3. "Neither is there salvation in any other; for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved," Acts 4:12. Nor, therefore, do the merits of men arise from the merit of Christ, nor are these subordinated to it, a badly stuffed stropha which we have already sufficiently discussed. For if Christ tinged with his blood not so much our sins as our merits, then Christ alone is not our Savior, since he would have taken man himself into partnership in so great a work to be saved. For are not saviors made in this way, and as many saviors as there are good men? In this way human merits are subordinated to the grace and mercy of God and to the merit of Christ, and are founded upon it, just as a house of wax is built over burning coals, or a house of salt is constructed in the middle of a river. Moreover, eternal life is given to us as an inheritance. "If children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ," Rom. 8:17. "Which is the earnest of our inheritance," Eph. 1:14. "Come, ye blessed of my Father, [κληρονομήσατε] inherit the kingdom prepared for you," Matt. 25:34. Yet no inheritance is acquired by merits. Nor can sons be said to merit an inheritance from their father, to whom they owe everything by nature in such a way that they can never make full satisfaction. But eternal life is called not merely an inheritance, but expressly the inheritance of sons: "If children, then heirs," Rom. 8:17. It is empty to say that Christ too merited an inheritance for himself. For the reasoning is different. He did not, by his perfect obedience, merit life for himself as an inheritance, nor did he enter upon it by the right of a paternal and gracious inheritance (otherwise he would have merited nothing properly and would never have satisfied the law in our place). Rather he merited for himself an inheritance, that is, a seed, heirs, sons, to whom by the counsel of the Father he would give the righteousness and life acquired by his merit. Believers, on the contrary, receive eternal life as an inheritance, that is, by hereditary right, because they are heirs of God and of Christ, by the pure grace of adoption. Or is Christ also the heir of God the Father by grace of adoption? This was certainly the heresy of Felix of Urgel and Elipand, condemned at the Council of Frankfurt. Finally, if life and salvation come by the merit of works, then we can glory and trust in our works, indeed we ought to. For each person can rely and rest on his own merits. But no one is permitted to glory in his own works or to trust in them. "Where is boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? Nay: but by the law of faith," ibid. 3:27. Bellarmine himself, after he had laboriously disputed in De Justificatione, book 5,

units.la: 7. operose disputavit; fiduciam Sanctorum, quam in Deo constituunt, non ex fide sola, sed etiam ex meritis nasci; &: In bonis meritis, quae vere talia sunt, fiduciam aliquam collocari posse, modo superbia caveatur (scilicet qui sibi arrogat, quod solius Christi est, meritum, & in eodem confidit, superbiam egregie cavet) concludit denique, propter incertitudinem justitiae propriae, & periculum inanis gloriae, tutissimum esse, fiduciam (NB) totam in sola Dei misericordia & benignitate reponere. Quibus verbis una veluti litura cuncta a se pro meritis operum disceptata induxit. Thomas Waldensis Tom. VI. de Sacram. tit. I. cap.7. Reputo, inquit, faniorem Theologum, fideliorem Catholicum & Scripturis Sacris magis concordem, qui tale meritum simpliciter abnegat, & cum modificatione Apostoli & Scripturarum concedit, quia simpliciter quis non meretur Regnum Coelorum, sed ex gratia Dei, aut voluntate largitoris. Meritorum nostrorum in articulo mortis minime Deus attendit rationem congrui vel condigni; sed gratiam suam, aut misericordiam suam. Quomodo igitur non ad injuriam Salvatoris & gratuiti coronatoris accedit, quod gratia ejus tacita tantum disputamus de meritis?
units.tr: 7. "the confidence which the saints place in God is born not from faith alone but also from merits"; and: "trust may be placed in good merits, which are truly such, provided that pride is avoided" (namely, the one who arrogates to himself what belongs to Christ alone, the merit, and trusts in it, very well avoids pride). He concludes at last that "on account of the uncertainty of one's own righteousness and the danger of vainglory, it is safest to place the whole of one's trust (NB) in the mercy and kindness of God alone." By these words he has, as it were, struck out at a single stroke everything he had argued about the merits of works. Thomas Waldensis, Tom. VI, De Sacramentis, tit. 1, cap. 7: "I judge him a saner theologian, a more faithful Catholic, and one more in agreement with the Holy Scriptures, who simply denies such merit and concedes it only with the qualification of the Apostle and the Scriptures, because a man does not simply merit the kingdom of heaven, but by the grace of God or the will of the giver. At the point of death God does not look at the reckoning of our merits, whether congruous or condign, but at his grace or his mercy. How then does it not amount to an injury to the Savior and the gratuitous crowner, that we dispute about merits as if his grace were silent?"

units.la: LXXI. Denique opera hominis nec ex congruo gratiam; nec ex condigno, nec ex pacto gratiae augmentum, gloriam ejusque augmentum mereri, paucis nunc etiam adstruemus. Et meritum quidem ex congruo definiri solet opus moraliter bonum, factum ex libero arbitrio, a gratia non adjuto. Nempe illi Divinae gratiae & bonitati congruum atque conveniens esse statuunt, ut moraliter bene dispositis & facientibus, quod in se est, gratiam justificationis infundat. Ita Thomas Aquinas Sum. I. 2. q. 114. c. 6. in c. Sed Bellarminus tamen gratiam liberum arbitrium praevenientem agnoscit. Neque pauci meritum de congruo a gratia praevenient non adjutum repudiant. Deus enim non est προσωπολήπτης acceptor personae, ut quicquam in homine aspiciat, ad praemium justitiae deputandum & dandum, quod sanctissimae ejus regulae non est consentaneum. Non est προσωπολημψία παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ personae acceptio apud Deum, Rom. II.11. Ideoque vel propria obedientia integra & perfecta Deo exhibenda est, secundum illud: Qui fecerit illa homo, vivet in iis, Levit. XVIII.5. vel obedientia illa, quae est perfectum δικαίωμα ἐκ πολλῶν παραπτωμάτων opus justum, seu justitiae causa, ex multis lapsibus, Rom.V.16. apprehendenda, & in fide Deo offerenda est, ut inveniamur in Christo non habentes nostram justitiam, sed Dei justitiam, quae ex fide est, Phil.III.9. Nam in eo solo Deus, Matth. III.17. acquiescit; & solum illum habenti datur, & non habenti etiam adimitur id quod habet, ibid. XIII.12. At nec merentur opera de condigno, quasi dignum sit ullum opus hominis, etiam integri, nedum peccatoris, mercede aeternae vitae propter intrinsecam bonitatem, sive aequalitatem inter opus & mercedem. Nam ne integri quidem hominis obedientia mereri vitam ex condigno potuit, quod pluribus Loc. IX. § 78.79. ostendimus. Et quanto minus hominis peccatoris obedientia ad tantam dignitatem assurgere potest? Non potest enim inter hominem merum & Deum ejusmodi meritum intercedere. In solo Christo dignitas personae
units.tr: LXXI. Finally, we shall now briefly show that man's works merit neither grace by congruity, nor grace by condignity, nor an increase of grace under the covenant, nor glory and its increase. Merit of congruity is usually defined as a morally good work, done by free will and not aided by grace. These writers hold that it is congruous and fitting for the divine grace and goodness to pour the grace of justification into those who are morally well disposed and who do what lies in them. So Thomas Aquinas, Sum. I. 2. q. 114. c. 6. in c. But Bellarmine nonetheless acknowledges a grace that goes before free will, and not a few reject merit of congruity apart from a grace that goes before and aids. For God is not a respecter of persons [προσωπολήπτης], so as to look upon something in a man and assign and give it as the reward of righteousness, which would not agree with his most holy rule. There is no respect of persons with God [προσωπολημψία παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ], Rom. 2.11. Therefore either complete and perfect obedience must be rendered to God, according to that word: The man who does these things shall live by them, Lev. 18.5; or else that obedience which is the perfect righteous act [δικαίωμα] arising from many trespasses, that is, a work of righteousness or done for the sake of righteousness, from many offences, Rom. 5.16, must be laid hold of and offered to God in faith, so that we may be found in Christ, not having our own righteousness, but the righteousness of God, which is by faith, Phil. 3.9. For God is pleased in him alone, Matt. 3.17, and is given only to the one who has him, and is taken away even from the one who does not have what he has, ibid. 13.12. Nor do works merit by condignity, as if any work of man, even of a man in a state of integrity, much less of a sinner, were worthy of the reward of eternal life because of intrinsic goodness, that is, equality between work and reward. For even the obedience of a man in integrity could not merit life by condignity, as we have shown in many places, Loc. IX. § 78.79. And how much less can the obedience of a sinful man rise to such dignity? For no merit of this kind can come between mere man and God. Only in Christ is the dignity of the person found together with the perfection of obedience, sufficient to claim and acquire glory by merit.

units.la: Nec ex congruo gratiam, nec ex condigno nec ex pacto gratiae, aut gloriae augmentum meremur. sonæ cum perfectione obedientiæ ad postulandam & acquirendam ex merito gloriam reperitur. Hominum verò opera universa & debita, & à Deo donata præmio neutiquam ἰσόψηφοι, & Deo inutilia sunt. Num quid Deo proderit vir, cùm sapiens sibi ipsi proderit? An ei גבר lucrum erit, cùm perfectas reddideris vias tuas? Job. XXII. 2. 3. Quis ei prior dedit, & retribuetur ei? Rom. XI. 35. Facit huc apertus ille μυ-στηριασμὸς, quo Deus ipse merita humana subsannat. Atque etiam quid vos mihi, Tyre & Sidon, & omnes terminí Palæstinæ? Numquid מחיר משלמים meritum rependitis mihi? Et numquid vos עלי גמליכם meremini de me? Ocyssimè reddam גמלכם meritum vestrum in caput vestrum, Joel. III. 4. Sed requisita omnia meriti proprie dicti, seu de condigno deesse operibus justificatorum jam probavimus. At nec ex pacto vitam mereri possunt. Nam pactum illud vel legale vel Evangelicum est. Legale pactum cum homine integro intercessit. Cum peccatore justificato nullum intercedit. Lex operum una est, quæ dicit: Qui fecerit ea, vivet in iis, Levit. XVIII. 5. Cùm igitur sub Evangelio lex operum alia non sit, non potest etiam aliud pactum dari, ex quo opera mereantur. Et meritum operum ex pacto, si Apostolo credimus, & demonstrationi Spiritus S. atque veritati paremus, cum justitia fidei conjungi non potest. Ubique Evangelium credenti, nuspiam per opera merenti promittit. Proin pactum ejusmodi sub Evangelio & gratia urgere, non aliud est, quàm fœdus gratiæ in novum fœdus operum commutare, & legem ipsam corrumpere, quæ non nisi perfectæ obedientiæ mercedem promittit. Ipse Vasquez meritum ex pacto argumentis prægnantibus rejicit, cujusmodi inprimis sunt, quòd per promissionem res non acquirat internam dignitatem: & quòd eleemosynæ remissio peccatorum promittatur, & Abrahamo adventus Christi promissus fuerit, neque tamen vel eleemosynæ remissionem peccatorum mereantur, nec Abrahamus adventum Christi meruerit. Si tamen bona opera justificatorum ex pacto vitam merentur, ex condigno eandem non merentur. Nam mereri ex pacto & promissione, & simul mereri ex intrinseca dignitate operis, seu ex condigno, quæ Bellarmini aliorumque inepta meriti commixtio, seu potius confusio est, ἀσυγχυτον est. Opus enim intrinsecam dignitatem habens mercedem non ex pacto, sed ex tenore justitiæ postulat.
units.tr: Nec ex congruo gratiam, nec ex condigno nec ex pacto gratiae, aut gloriae augmentum meremur. The dignity of the person together with the perfection of obedience is found for asking and acquiring glory by merit. But the whole works of men, both those owed and those given by God, are by no means equal in reward and are useless to God. Can a man be profitable to God, when he who is wise is profitable to himself? Or is it any gain to the Almighty [גבר] that you make your ways perfect? Job 22.2, 3. Who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? Rom. 11.35. To this point belongs that manifest mockery [μυστηριασμὸς] by which God himself scorns human merits: And what are you to me, Tyre and Sidon, and all the regions of Palestine? Do you render to me a reward [מחיר משלמים], or do you merit anything from me by your deeds [עלי גמליכם]? Swiftly I will return your reward [גמלכם] upon your own head, Joel 3.4. But we have already proved that all the requisites of merit properly so called, that is, of condignity, are lacking in the works of the justified. Nor can they merit life by covenant. For that covenant is either legal or evangelical. A legal covenant was made with man in integrity; none is made with the justified sinner. There is one law of works, which says: He who does these things shall live by them, Lev. 18.5. Since under the Gospel there is no other law of works, no other covenant can be given by which works might merit. And if we believe the Apostle, and submit to the demonstration of the Holy Spirit and to the truth, merit of works by covenant cannot be joined with the righteousness of faith. Everywhere the Gospel promises to the believer, and nowhere promises to one who merits by works. Therefore to press a covenant of this kind under the Gospel and grace is nothing else than to change the covenant of grace into a new covenant of works, and to corrupt the law itself, which promises the reward only of perfect obedience. Vasquez himself rejects merit by covenant with weighty arguments, of which the chief are these: that a thing does not acquire inner dignity through a promise; and that forgiveness of sins is promised for alms, and the coming of Christ was promised to Abraham, yet neither do alms merit forgiveness of sins, nor did Abraham merit the coming of Christ. Yet even if the good works of the justified merit life by covenant and promise, they do not merit it by condignity. For to merit by covenant and promise, and at the same time to merit by the intrinsic dignity of the work, that is, by condignity, is an absurd mixing or rather confusion of merit, as taught by Bellarmine and others, and is [ἀσυγχυτον] without confusion. For a work that has intrinsic dignity demands its reward not by covenant but by the tenor of justice.

units.la: LXXII. Equidem vita æterna μισθὸς mercedis nomine venit. Magna merces vestra erit in Cœlis, Matth. V. 12. Reddidit operariis mercedem, ibid. XX. 8. Sed non quævis merces meritum supponit; sed ea demum, quæ redditur operi indebito, proprio, utili ei, qui mercedem tribuit, & cum mercede commensum habenti. Quæ merces legalis, debita, proprie dicta est. Alia ratio est mercedis Evangelicæ, gratuitæ, improprie tali, quæ redditur ex gratia, non ex debito. Operanti non imputatur merces ex gratia, sed ex debito, Rom. IV. 4. Alia igitur merces ex debito, alia ex gratia imputatur: illa operanti, hæc non operanti, sed credenti. Ideo mercedem fidei etiam Deus assignat. Ne metuas. Ego clypeus tuus, & merces tua magna valde, nempe merces fiduciæ in me, ut clypeo tuo, & depo-nendi metus; Gen. XV. 1. At fidei merces nisi secundum gratiam, benevolentiam & misericordiam assignari & reputari non potest. Quid enim meretur is, qui confidit omnipotenti & mentiri nescio, profitenti, se ei clypeum esse, & se ei mercedem maximam parasse; & metum atque dubitationem ponere jubet? Quam igitur mercedem Christus Matth. V. 12. Luc. VI. 23. 35. appellavit, eandem χάριν gratiam, ibid. vers. 32. etiam appellat, utrobique de eodem amore, eadem benevolentia erga amicos agens. Denique vita æterna ad opera nostra relata merces est analogia quadam, quia sicut proprie dicta merces datur & operanti, & in fine operis: ita vita æterna non datur sine opere, vitam non efficiente, sed antecedente, & nonnisi in fine operis. Ideo merces שכר appellatur. In observandis iis (præceptis tuis רב שכר merces ampla, Psal. XIX. 12. Unde Græci ἀντιπόδωμα, ἀντιμισθίαν retributionem reddunt. Proprie autem שכר finem, extremum notat, à עקב calx, calcaneus, seu extremum corporis. Hoc igitur nomine merces quævis venit, quia in fine operis datur, & operis exitus est. Eadem verò vita æterna ad Christi opus seu obedientiam relata vera, legalis & proprie dicta merces est. Et datur hæc vitæ æternæ merces κατὰ τὰ ἔργα secundum opera, Rom. II. 6. & κατὰ πρᾶξιν secundum actum cujusque, Matth. XVI. 27. sed nusquam διὰ propter opera, vel actum hominis. Qualia opera, talis retributio erit. Proin illud κατὰ secundum qualitatem & testimonium, non æqualitatem & proportionem operum significat. Nam etiam secundum bona opera retributio fit ex gratia, quia vita æterna est χάρισμα gratia Rom. VI. 23. & donum, Eph. II. 8. non datur nisi ex animo veniam precantibus. Si iniquitatas observaveris, ô Jah, quis stabit coram te? Sed apud te est venia, ut timearis, Psal. CXXX. 3. 4. Præterea ratio quidem dandæ hujus mercedis, seu vitæ æternæ in operibus ponitur. Hæreditate adite Regnum &c. Esurivi enim, & dedistis mihi cibum, Sitivi, & potastis me, &c. Matth. XXV. 34. 35. &c. Hi venerunt ex afflictione magna &c. διὰ τοῦτο propterea sunt in conspectu throni Dei, Apoc. VII. 14. 15. Sed ratio illa, ob quam vita datur, non causam, sed consequentiam, seu nexum consequentis & antecedentis designat. Velut si quis dicat, noctem esse, quia stellæ apparent; ægrotare hominem, quia pallet: ratio illa non à causa noctis, vel ægrotantis, sed à signo petitur. Ita Paulus: Misericordiam consecutus sum, quia ignorans feci in infidelitate, 1. Tim. I. 13. Ubi nemo in ignorantia, vel incredulitate meritum condigni posuerit. Fideles certè Regnum ab æterno paratum, non in tempore operum merito impetratum, & ceu à Patre benediicti, non merito suo digni; & velut hæreditatem, quæ nulla ex merito datur, possidebunt; & stabunt in conspectu throni, quia stolas laverunt, & sanguine Agni dealbarunt, hoc est, unico sacrificio Christi purgati, non proprio operum sapone, vel Purgatorio Pontificio digni reddit sunt. Sed & ex justitia vita æterna retribuetur. Nam δίκαιον justum est iis, qui affliguntur, retribuere relaxationem, 2. Thess. I. 6. Et bonum certamen certantibus repositia dicitur justitiæ corona, quam Dominus justus judex in illo die reddet, 2. Tim. IV. 7. 8. Sed justitia illa Dei, non hominis est, & datur vita, quia Deus justus, hoc est, verax, fidelis est, & promissa implet, non quia homo justus est. Neque proin etiam justitia Dei stricta & aequalitatis intelligitur; quomodo severum Dei judicium bona opera neutiquam sustinent, Psal. CXLIII. 2. sed misericordia temperata, veracitatis & fidelitatis, quia justum Deo est, stare promissis, & justitia Dei non patitur, ut redemptio Christi cassa & inutilis sit illis, qui fide eam apprehendunt. Si peccata nostra confitemur πιστὸς καὶ δίκαιος fidelis & justus est, ut remittat nobis peccata, 1. Joh. I. 9. Etiam καταξιωθέντες digni habiti, & ἄξιοι digni aeterna vita fideles pronuntiantur. Οἱ καταξιωθέντες αἰῶνος ἐκεῖνον. Qui digni habebuntur, ut consequantur seculum illud, Luc. XX. 35. Ut digni habeamini Regno Dei, 2. Thess. I. 5. Mecum ambulabunt in albis, ἐν ἀξίοι εἰσὶ quia digni sunt, Apoc. III. 4. Sed ἀξιοῦ dignus est, tum qui in se, & propter dignitatem personae & operis sui; tum qui aliunde dignus est, vel habetur. ἀξιοῦσθαι modo dignationem, modo dignitatis propriae declarationem significat. Fideles vero vita aeterna digni sunt vel habentur, ex dignatione Divina, non dignitate personae & operis sui; ratione albae vestis, justitiae Christi imputatae, qua induuntur, Gal. III. 27. nec non Divinae adoptionis; non inhaerentis sanctitatis, quae in hac vita perfecta & meritoria nulla est. Ideo vulgatus Interpres ἀξιοῦσθαι semper dignum haberi, nusquam mereri reddit. Et qui Act. V. 41. καταξιωθῆναι digni haberi, iidem Phil. I. 29. χαρίζεσθαι gratia affici, ut pro nomine Christi pati possint, dicuntur. Praeclare Bernhardus in Dedic. Eccl. Serm. 5. Dignatio, inquit, locum non habet, ubi dignitatis praesumptio fuerit. Certe de operum dignitate ne unus quidem Scripturae apex loquitur. Personae vero dignitas praecipue & primario in fide, quae credentem Christo unit, consistit. Praeterea non sicut mala opera damnationem, ita bona vitam merentur, quia illa penitus mala, haec imperfecte bona, nec vitae coelesti adaequata sunt; & horum bonitas omnis non tam ab homine, quam a Spiritu S. proficiscitur. Quomodo non si Solis ardor terram indurat, eandem gelu mollit. Neque etiam ideo Deus προσωπολήμπτης est, quia dat praemium aeternae vitae sine meritis: quia illud dat non secundum justitiam legis, sed secundum gratiam. At προσωπολημψία personarum acceptio in gratuitis nulla est. Praeterea filii Dei aeternam vitam magna cum libertate adeunt & postulant. Sed προσηγορίας illius fulcrum non proprium, sed Christi meritum est. Accedunt enim cum libertate loquendi ad thronum gratiae, Hebr. IV. 16. Et cuncta bona sibi dari propter obedientiam Sponsoris, non propriam expetunt. Non in justitiis nostris, sed in miserationibus tuis nos coram te prosternimus, Dan. IX. 18. Denique nec meritorum haec exagitatio homines securos segnesque reddit, ne bonis operibus studeant; tum quia omnes Christo insiti bonis operibus necessario studient: tum quia opera bona non ad merendum, sed ad glorificandum Deum, aedificandum proximum, & salutem tranquillitatemque propriam conscientiae necessaria sunt.
units.tr: LXXII. Indeed, eternal life is called a reward (μισθός): "Great is your reward in heaven," Matth. 5:12; "he gave the workers their wages," ibid. 20:8. But not every reward presupposes merit. Only that reward which is paid for work that is owed, that is proper to the worker, that is useful to the one who pays it, and that is commensurate with the wage is a merit. This is a legal, due, and properly so-called reward. There is another kind of reward, evangelical and free, which is improperly so called, because it is given out of grace and not out of debt. "To the one who works, the wage is not reckoned as grace but as debt," Rom. 4:4. So one reward is reckoned as debt, another as grace: the first to the one who works, the second to the one who does not work but believes. For this reason God also assigns a reward to faith: "Do not fear. I am your shield, and your reward will be very great" (Gen. 15:1). That is, the reward of trust in me, as a shield for you, and the removal of fear. But the reward of faith can be assigned and reckoned only according to grace, favour and mercy. For what does the one merit who trusts the Almighty, and who is told by him, who cannot lie, that he is his shield and has prepared for him a very great reward, and who is bidden to lay aside fear and doubt? So the same thing Christ called reward in Matth. 5:12 and Luke 6:23, 35, he also calls grace (χάρις) in the same passage, verse 32, speaking in both places of the same love and the same goodwill towards friends. Finally, eternal life, when it is related to our works, is a reward by a certain analogy: just as a reward properly so called is given to the one who works, and at the end of the work, so eternal life is not given without the work, not as producing life but as preceding it, and only at the end of the work. For this reason it is called reward [שכר]: "In keeping them (your precepts) there is a great reward [רב שכר]," Ps. 19:12. Hence the Greeks render it ἀντιπόδωμα and ἀντιμισθία, a requital. Properly, however, שכר denotes the end, the extremity, from עקב, heel, heel-bone, or the extremity of the body. Thus any reward at all comes under this name, because it is given at the end of the work and is the outcome of the work. But the same eternal life, when it is related to the work or obedience of Christ, is a true, legal and properly so-called reward. And this reward of eternal life is given according to the works (κατὰ τὰ ἔργα), Rom. 2:6, and according to the deed (κατὰ πρᾶξιν) of each one, Matth. 16:27; but nowhere on account of (διά) the works or deed of man. Such as the works are, such will the recompense be. Therefore the word according to (κατὰ) signifies a quality and a witness, not an equality and proportion of works. For even according to good works the recompense is made by grace, because eternal life is a gift of grace (χάρισμα), Rom. 6:23, and a gift, Eph. 2:8, which is given only to those who ask for pardon from the heart: "If you, O Jah, should mark iniquities, who could stand before you? But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared," Ps. 130:3, 4. Moreover, the ground for giving this reward, or eternal life, is indeed placed in works: "Inherit the kingdom, etc. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink," etc., Matth. 25:34, 35. "They came out of great tribulation, etc., and therefore (διὰ τοῦτο) are before the throne of God," Rev. 7:14, 15. But that ground on account of which life is given does not indicate a cause, but a consequence, that is, the connection of the consequent with the antecedent. As when someone says that it is night because the stars appear, or that a man is sick because he is pale: that ground is taken not from the cause of the night or of the sickness, but from a sign. So Paul: "I obtained mercy, because I did it in ignorance, in unbelief," 1 Tim. 1:13. Where no one would have set down the merit of worthiness in ignorance or unbelief. Certainly the faithful will possess the kingdom prepared from eternity, obtained not by the merit of works in time, and blessed by the Father, not worthy through their own merit; and they will possess it as an inheritance, which is given by no merit; and they will stand before the throne, because they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb, that is, they have been made fit not by the soap of their own works, nor by the Popish Purgatory, but by the one sacrifice of Christ. But eternal life is also rendered in justice. For it is just (δίκαιον) to render relief to those who are afflicted, 2 Thess. 1:6. And the crown of justice is laid up for those who fight the good fight, which the Lord, the just judge, will give on that day, 2 Tim. 4:7, 8. But that justice is the justice of God, not of man, and life is given because God is just, that is, true and faithful, and fulfils his promises, not because man is just. Nor, for this reason, is the justice of God understood as strict and of equality, since good works in no way bear up under the severe judgment of God, Ps. 143:2; but as tempered mercy, of truthfulness and of faithfulness, because it is right for God to stand by his promises, and the justice of God does not allow the redemption of Christ to be empty and useless to those who lay hold of it by faith. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just (πιστὸς καὶ δίκαιος) to forgive us our sins," 1 John 1:9. Those who are counted worthy (καταξιωθέντες) and those who are worthy (ἄξιοι) of eternal life are also pronounced faithful. "Those who are counted worthy to attain that age," Luke 20:35; "that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God," 2 Thess. 1:5; "they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy" (ἄξιοί εἰσιν), Rev. 3:4. But the one who is ἀξιοῦ is worthy both in himself and on account of the dignity of his person and work, and also the one who is worthy or held worthy from another source. To be ἀξιοῦσθαι signifies at one time the act of deeming worthy, at another the declaration of one's own dignity. But the faithful are worthy of or held worthy of eternal life by the deeming of God, not by the dignity of their own person and work; on account of the white robe, the justice of Christ imputed to them, with which they are clothed, Gal. 3:27, and also of divine adoption; not of inherent holiness, which in this life is neither perfect nor meritorious. For this reason the Vulgate translator always renders ἀξιοῦσθαι as to be held worthy, and never as to merit. And in Acts 5:41, καταξιωθῆναι, to be held worthy, the same persons are said, in Phil. 1:29, to be χαρίζεσθαι, to be favoured with grace, so that they may be able to suffer for the name of Christ. Bernard admirably says in the Sermon on the Dedication of a Church, no. 5: Dignatio, he says, has no place where there is a presumption of dignity. Certainly not even one point of Scripture speaks of the dignity of works. The dignity of the person, however, consists chiefly and primarily in faith, which unites the believer to Christ. Moreover, good works do not merit life in the way that bad works merit condemnation, because bad works are altogether evil, whereas good works are imperfectly good, and are not equal to heavenly life; and all their goodness proceeds not so much from man as from the Holy Spirit. It is as when the heat of the sun hardens the earth, while the same earth is softened by frost. Nor is God a respecter of persons (προσωπολήμπτης) for this reason, that he gives the reward of eternal life without merits: because he gives it not according to the justice of the law, but according to grace. But acceptance of persons (προσωπολημψία) has no place in gratuitous gifts. Furthermore, the sons of God approach and ask for eternal life with great confidence. But the support of that confidence is not their own, but the merit of Christ. For they approach with boldness of speech to the throne of grace, Heb. 4:16, and they seek all good things to be given to them because of the obedience of their Surety, not their own. "We do not prostrate ourselves before you on account of our righteousnesses, but on account of your mercies," Dan. 9:18. Finally, this disputing about merits does not make men secure and sluggish, so that they do not strive after good works; both because all who are ingrafted in Christ necessarily strive after good works, and because good works are necessary not for merit, but for glorifying God, for edifying one's neighbour, and for one's own salvation and the tranquillity of conscience.

units.la: LXXIII. Cùm operum merita nulla plane sint, vana omnis de fiducia in iis, & de meritis augmenti gratiae & gloriae, ad quod posterius aureolas suas, Martyribus, Virginibus & doctoribus erogandas Sophistae, Coeli metatores, referunt, disputatio est.
units.tr: LXXIII. Since good works have no merit at all, the whole discussion of trust in them, and of merits that increase grace and glory, is empty. The Schoolmen, the measurers of heaven, make the second of these the ground on which they assign their aureoles to martyrs, virgins and teachers.

units.la: Ac ne operari quidem intuitu mercedis proprie dictae licet, quia talis nulla est. Et in universum amor hominis erga Deum non mercenarius, sed ingenuus, ex Spiritu spontaneo Psal. CXIX. 108. profectus esse debet. Non enim servi, sed filii Dei sumus. Pie Albertus M. Enchir. cap. I. Delicata anima quasi abominatur per modum commodi, vel praemii Deum diligere. Nihilominus salvo gloriae Divinae; quae in animis hominum βασιλεύειν dominari, & caeteris omnibus ita praeponderare debet, ut illi nihil ἀνθρώπων nedum inferiores statuatur; respectu secundario & minus principaliter etiam aeterna salus nostra, Dei gloriae subordinata, eique arctissime conjuncta, ceu merces gratuita, quae credenti, non operanti imputatur, respici potest & debet, secus quam Antigoni discipulis, Zadoko & Baithoso, Sadducaeorum Magistris visum est. Nam a dilectione Dei secludi non potest, ut pro bono nostro habeatur, quin a gloria bonitatis Dei, suavitatibus suis nos implentis, plurimum delibemus & decerpamus. Promissa enim nobis in verbo Dei vita aeterna est, quam certa spe in hac vita praecipimus. Non dixi domui Israel: Frustra quaerite me, Esai. XLV. 19. Ideo Moses ἀπελπίζειν respexit praemii retributionem, Hebr. XI. 26. Et fidei character est, Deum μισθαποδότην intueri, ibid. v. 6. Et quid alias de spe, quae praecipua & cardinalis Christianorum virtus est, fieret? Etiam Christus ἀντὶ προκειμένης χαρᾶς pro gaudio proposito crucem sustinuit, ibid. XII. 2. Pauli vero & Mosis ecstases cum singularis exempli fuerint, nec perpetuae in ipsis, sed raptus & excessus cujusdam instar fuerint, regulam non faciunt.
units.tr: Nor is it lawful to work for the sake of a reward properly so called, since there is no such reward. In general, a person's love for God should not be mercenary but free, springing from a willing spirit (Ps. 119:108). For we are not servants but sons of God. Albert the Great devoutly says in the Enchiridion, chapter 1: A refined soul almost abhors loving God for the sake of advantage or reward. Nevertheless, the glory of God must be preserved. It must reign [βασιλεύειν] in human hearts and outweigh everything else, so that nothing of men [ἀνθρώπων] is set beside it, let alone above it. In a secondary and less principal respect, our eternal salvation, which is subordinate to the glory of God and most closely bound to it, may and should be considered as a free reward, imputed to the believer and not to the doer. This is not how Zadok and Boethus, the disciples of Antigonus and teachers of the Sadducees, saw it. For the love of God cannot be separated from our good, so that we are not also drawing and gathering much from the glory of God's goodness, which fills us with its sweetness. For eternal life is promised to us in the Word of God, and in this life we anticipate it with a certain hope. I did not say to the house of Israel, Seek me in vain (Isa. 45:19). Thus Moses looked away to [ἀπέβλεπεν] the recompense of the reward (Heb. 11:26), and it is a mark of faith to look upon God as rewarder [μισθαποδότην] (ibid. v. 6). What would become of hope, the chief and cardinal virtue of Christians, otherwise? Christ also endured the cross for the joy set before him [ἀντὶ προκειμένης χαρᾶς] (ibid. 12:2). The ecstasies of Paul and Moses, however, were the examples of singular men. They were not continuous in them but were like a sort of rapture and excess, and so they do not make a rule.

units.la: LXXIV. Oportet fideles omnes esse ζηλωταὶ καλῶν ἔργων ἐμulatores bonorum operum, Tit. II. 14.
units.tr: LXXIV. All the faithful ought to be zealous of good works [ζηλωταὶ καλῶν ἔργων] (Titus 2:14).

units.la: Non convenit enim populum Dei non differre a populis aliis. Inprimis ii, qui ad Christum pertinent, ejus nomen nominare & invocare tenentur. Sed qui Christi nomen nominat, is necesse est ab injustitia recedat, 2. Tim. II. 19. alioquin nomen Christi blasphemabit, & efficiet, ut verbum Dei, & nomen bonum super nos invocatum, & via veritatis blasphemetur, Tit. II. 5. Jac. II. 7. 2. Pet. II. 2. Qui Christum Regem Dominumque suum agnoscit & invocat, facere quae ipsi, non quae hostibus placent, tenetur. Neque desunt προτρεπτικοί incitationes validae aliae ad prosequendum studium bonorum operum. Nam bene agentibus bene erit. Dicite justo quod bene ei futurum sit, quia studiorum suorum fructum comedet, Esai. III. 10. Non enim Deo servire vanum est, uti Diabolus & mundus insusurrant. Dixistis, vanum servire Deo; & quid emolumenti quod observavimus observantiam ejus? Et quod ambulavimus atrati propter Jehovam Deum exercituum? Igitur beatos praedicamus feroces. Et aedificati sunt facientes improbitatem, & explorarunt Deum & effugerunt. Tunc colloquuti sunt timentes Jehovam quisque ad proximum suum, & auscultavit Jehova & audivit. Et scriptus est liber memoriali coram ipso pro timentibus Jehovam & reputantibus nomen ejus. Et erunt mei, dixit Jehova, in
units.tr: For it is not fitting that the people of God should not differ from other peoples. Above all, those who belong to Christ are bound to name and invoke his name. But whoever names the name of Christ must depart from iniquity (2 Tim. 2:19), otherwise he will blaspheme the name of Christ and cause the word of God and the good name invoked upon us, and the way of truth, to be blasphemed (Titus 2:5; Jas. 2:7; 2 Pet. 2:2). Whoever acknowledges and calls upon Christ as his King and Lord is bound to do what pleases him, not what pleases his enemies. Nor are there lacking other powerful exhortations to pursue the zeal for good works. For it will go well with those who do well. Tell the righteous that it will be well with him, for he shall eat the fruit of his doings (Isa. 3:10). For it is not vain to serve God, as the devil and the world whisper: You have said, It is vain to serve God; and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the LORD of hosts? Therefore we count the proud blessed; yes, those who work wickedness are set up, and they who tempt God are even delivered. Then those who feared the LORD spoke often one to another, and the LORD hearkened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who feared the LORD and thought upon his name. And they shall be mine, saith the LORD, in

units.la: Vana igitur omnis in nè sint, vana omnis de fiducia in iis in die, quem ego facio peculium. Et clemens ero super ipsis, uti quis clemens est super filio suo, qui servit ipsi, & convertemini, & videbitis differentiam justi & improbi, qui colit Deum, & ejus, qui non colit Deum, Mal. III. 14-18. Idque experientia omnium temporum confirmat. Nam Deus bono, vel bonum vel malum rependit. Malum autem pro bono rependere optimus non potest; Bonum igitur rependit. Si enim nemo bonus humanitatem alterius odio remuneratur, quanto minus Deus Optimus, qui nos, cum ejus inimici adhuc essemus, dilexit. Ille enim ספר זכרון librum memorialem coram se ipso pro timentibus Jehovam scripsit, ibid. vers. 16. Piorum enim nomina, studia & passiones pro Deo in libro & commentario Dei scriptae sunt, ut nunquam oblivioni tradantur, non tantum, ut fructum suae pietatis reportent, sed etiam ut hostium blasphemia in ipsorum caput recidat & pii in illis vindicentur.
units.tr: Therefore, and they shall be mine, in the day that I make up my jewels. And I will spare them, as a man spares his own son that serveth him. Then shall ye return and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him that serveth God and him that serveth him not (Mal. 3:14–18). Experience of all times confirms this. For God repays good with good, for he cannot repay good with evil. Therefore he repays good. For if no good man repays another's hatred with hatred, how much less will God, the best of beings, who loved us when we were still his enemies. For he wrote a book of remembrance before him for those who feared the LORD [ספר זכרון] (ibid. v. 16). The names, zeal and sufferings of the pious for God are written in the book and record of God, so that they are never forgotten, not only that they may receive the fruit of their piety, but also that the blasphemy of their enemies may fall back upon their own heads, and that the godly may be vindicated against them.

units.la: LXXV. Bonorum operum variae sunt classes, ad varia Decalogi praecepta accommodatae. Generatim Vita Christiana & Precatione comprehendi possunt.
units.tr: LXXV. The classes of good works are various, adapted to the various precepts of the Decalogue. In general they may be comprehended under Christian life and prayer.

units.la: Vita Christiana est, qua sanctificati Christum imitantes, per eum Deo novam obedientiam praestare student, praecipue abnegando se ipsos, tolerando crucem, & quae vocationis propriae sunt, operando. Exemplar vitae hujus Christus est, a quo Christiana appellatur, oppositè ad moralem illam Philosophorum, quae intra metas luminis naturalis consistens, ad perfectionem illam vitae Christi, & eorum, qui Christi sunt, & eundem imitari tenentur, neutiquam assurgit. Cum enim non postrema vitae hujus pars crux sit, tantum abest, ut illam mundus amet, vel ejus tolerantiam inter virtutes praecipuas collocet, ut sermonem crucis μωρίαν stultitiam reputet, I. Cor. I. 18. Licet enim virtutes Christianae ab Ethicis Philosophicis quoad moderationem affectuum & gubernationem loco-motivae secundum externam disciplinam solo perfectionis gradu differant: tamen quoad interiorem cordis obedientiam, quae ex fide est, & cum filiali Dei timore conjuncta est, specie differunt, quia alia longè charitas, patientia, justitia, Christiana quàm Ethica est. Et vitae Christianae norma quidem in lege Dei perfectissima, at ὑπόδειγμα & ὑπογραμμὸς exemplar in Christo, qui legem Dei perfectissimè implevit, est. Hic ergo, & vita hujus universa, quoad actus communes, non Mediatorios, in quibus obedientiam non potestatem ille exercuit, non in faciendis miraculis, sed in custodienda humilitate & patientia, ad quae nos Christus exemplo suo invitavit, uti scitè Augustinus in sententiis; religiosissima imitatione exprimi debet. Μαθετε ἀπ' ἐμοῦ. Discite à me, quia mansuetus & humilis corde sum, Matth. XI. 29. Imitatores estote mei, sicut ego Christi, I. Cor. XI. 1. Τῦτο φρονεῖσθω ἐν ὑμῖν, ὃ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ. Hoc sentiatur in vobis, quod est in Christo Jesu, Phil. II. 5. Ad hoc vocati estis, quia & Christus passus est pro vobis, vobis relinquens ὑπογραμμὸν exemplar, ut sequamini ipsius vestigia, I. Petr. II. 21. Iterum novum praeceptum scribo vobis, quod est verum in ipso, (Christo) & vobis, I. Joh. II. 8. Veritas enim promissionis, quae in Christo est, & ejus obedientia nos, novo quasi jure ad amorem Dei & odium Diaboli obligat: & vescitiatio promissionis in nobis per sanctificationem nostri ad fidem non promissionis duntaxat, sed etiam veritatis fit nobis Lex Spiritus ad Deum amandum, & Sathanam odio habendum. In cognitione Christi cognitio voluntatis Dei est. Nam is venit, ut voluntatem Dei faceret, Psal. XL. 9. Diligendo Christum ejusdem obedientiam & justitiam diligimus.
units.tr: Christian life is that by which the sanctified, imitating Christ, strive through him to render new obedience to God, chiefly by denying themselves, bearing the cross, and doing the works of their own calling. Christ is the pattern of this life, and it is from him that it is called Christian. This is in contrast to that moral teaching of the philosophers, which remains within the bounds of natural light and by no means rises to that perfection of life which belongs to Christ and to those who are Christ's and are bound to imitate him. For since the cross is not the least part of this life, the world is so far from loving it, or from counting endurance of it among the chief virtues, that it regards the word of the cross as foolishness [μωρίαν], 1 Cor. 1:18. For although Christian virtues differ from the ethical virtues of the philosophers only in degree of perfection, as regards moderation of the passions and control of conduct according to outward discipline, nevertheless they differ in kind as regards the inward obedience of the heart, which comes from faith and is joined with the filial fear of God. For Christian love, patience and justice are far other than those of ethics. The norm of Christian life is indeed the law of God, most perfect; but the pattern [ὑπόδειγμα] and example [ὑπογραμμός] is Christ, who fulfilled the law of God most perfectly. Therefore he, and the whole of his life, in respect of ordinary actions, not mediatorial ones (in which he exercised obedience, not power, not in performing miracles but in keeping humility and patience, to which Christ invited us by his example, as Augustine rightly says in his sentences), ought to be expressed by the most devout imitation. Learn from me [Μάθετε ἀπ' ἐμοῦ], for I am meek and lowly in heart, Matt. 11:29. Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ, 1 Cor. 11:1. Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus [Τοῦτο φρονεῖσθω ἐν ὑμῖν, ὃ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ], Phil. 2:5. For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example [ὑπογραμμόν], that you should follow in his steps, 1 Pet. 2:21. Again I write to you a new commandment, which is true in him (Christ) and in you, 1 John 2:8. For the truth of the promise, which is in Christ, and his obedience bind us, as by a new right, to the love of God and the hatred of the devil; and the truth of the promise, made effective in us through the sanctification of our faith, becomes to us not only a promise but also a law of the Spirit, to love God and hate Satan. In the knowledge of Christ is the knowledge of the will of God, for he came to do the will of God, Ps. 40:9. By loving Christ we love his obedience and his righteousness.

units.la: Atque ita dilectio nostra nobis fit lex, vel lex nostra voluntas & dilectio fit. Quod igitur Christus sensit & voluit, id nos quoque sentire & velle debemus. Quod ipse passus est, ad id patiendum nos quoque parati esse debemus. Ille obedientiam in passionibus; nos fidei & charitatis constantiam in afflictionibus ostendere debemus. Verbo, Christus omnis justitiae, obedientiae, sanctitatis, misericordiae, veritatis speculum & imago est.
units.tr: And so our love becomes a law to us, or rather our law becomes love and will. What Christ felt and willed, we too ought to feel and will. What he himself suffered, we too ought to be prepared to suffer. He must show obedience in his sufferings; we must show constancy of faith and love in our afflictions. In a word, Christ is the mirror and image of all righteousness, obedience, holiness, mercy and truth.

units.la: LXXVI. Christi imitatio in abnegatione sui & crucis tolerantia, ceu jugo quodam sanctissimo, à Christo ipso constituitur.
units.tr: LXXVI. The imitation of Christ in self-denial and in bearing the cross, as under a most holy yoke, is laid down by Christ himself.

units.la: Si quis post me venire (me sequi, esse ubi ego sum, me imitari) vult, abneget se ipsum, & tollat crucem suam, & (sic) sequatur me, Matth. XVI. 24. Crucis tolerantiam abnegatio sui praecedit, quia quò minus homo eleganter crucem ferat, potissimum amor & aestimatio sui, justitiae suae fiducia, & dilectio seculi hujus obstat. Quae impedimenta abnegatio sui è medio tollit. Et ἀπαρνήσασθαι abnegare quidem est aliquid, cujus nos pudet, & quod nostrum esse non debet, abdicare, deponere, fugere, exinanire. Abnegatio igitur sui quaedam sui, seu ejus, cujus, si nostrum fit, nos pudere debet, quia confiteri debebimus, veluti abdicatio, depositio, exinanitio est. Habet autem quisque in se mundum, consanguineos, naturam & carnem. Haec qui abnegat, seipsum abnegat. Mundum verò abnegat, qui ea, quae in mundo sunt, divitias, potentiam propter Christum abdicat. Ecce nos ἀφήκαμεν πάντα reliquimus omnia, & te secuti sumus, ib. XIX. 27. Pereat pecunia una cum possessoribus suis, qui auri & argenti mundi vel unius horae cum Christo commercium cupiunt. Consanguineos abnegat, qui eos propter Christum tanti non facit, quin eos amori ejus obstantes praetervehi, vel calcare & paratus sit. Si quis venit ad me, & non odit patrem suum & matrem suam, & uxorem, & liberos, & fratres, & sorores, non potest discipulus meus esse, Luc. XIV. 26. Qui diligit patrem vel matrem supra me, non est me dignus, Matth. X. 37. Odisse igitur parentes est non diligere eos supra Christum; imò in contentione cum Christo eos aversari, fugere, nulla communione dignari. Nonne odio habentes te, Jehova, odi, & insurgentium in te taedet me? Profectò odi illos, & pro inimicis mihi sunt, Psal. CXXXIX. 21. 22. Neque enim consanguinei supra Christum pondus habere possunt, quin utrosque perdamus. Licet enim ut nos, ita etiam nostri amandi, atque ita quaerendi sunt, ut eos lucrifaciamus Deo, & ut Deus in illis glorificetur; tamen in parentibus, uxoribus, liberis, fratribus aliquid est, quod nobis displiceat, si verè Christus placet; quòdque, si ad illum accedere, eum sequi volumus, fugiendum est. Naturam suam abnegat, qui etiam ψυχὴν ἑαυτὸν animam suam propter Christum odit, Luc. XIV. 26. seu perdit, Matth. X. 39. non diligit usque ad mortem,
units.tr: If anyone wishes to come after me (to follow me, to be where I am, to imitate me), let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and (so) follow me, Matt. 16:24. Self-denial precedes the bearing of the cross, because the chief things that hinder a man from bearing the cross gracefully are love and esteem of self, confidence in one's own righteousness, and love of this age. Self-denial removes these hindrances. To deny [ἀπαρνήσασθαι] is indeed to renounce, put away, depose, flee from, and empty out something of which we are ashamed and which ought not to be ours. Self-denial, then, is a kind of renunciation of self, or of that which, if it is ours, ought to make us ashamed, since we must confess it to be a renunciation, a deposing, and an emptying. Now each person has within himself the world, kindred, nature and flesh. He who denies these denies himself. He denies the world who for Christ's sake gives up the things that are in the world, riches and power. Behold, we have left all things [ἀφήκαμεν πάντα], and have followed you, ibid. 19:27. Let money perish together with its possessors, who desire fellowship with Christ at the price of the gold and silver of the world, even for a single hour. He denies kindred who does not hold them so dear for Christ's sake that he is ready to pass by them, or even trample them underfoot, when they stand in the way of his love for Christ. If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, and wife, and children, and brothers, and sisters, he cannot be my disciple, Luke 14:26. He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, Matt. 10:37. To hate parents, then, is not to love them above Christ; indeed, in conflict with Christ, to turn away from them, to shun them, and to think them unworthy of fellowship. Do I not hate those who hate you, O Jehovah, and am I not grieved with those who rise up against you? I truly hate them; they are my enemies, Ps. 139:21, 22. For kindred cannot have more weight than Christ without our losing both. For although our own people are to be loved, and are to be sought in such a way that we may win them for God, and that God may be glorified in them, nevertheless there is something in parents, wives, children and brothers which displeases us, if Christ truly pleases us; and if we wish to come to him and follow him, that must be shunned. He denies his nature who even hates his own soul [ψυχὴν ἑαυτοῦ] for Christ's sake, Luke 14:26, or loses it, Matt. 10:39, does not love even unto death,

units.la: Apoc. XII. 11. paratus adeò se ipsum offerre Deo, ut Christi corona etiam in cinere & pulvere floreat. Christi enim amor sui ipsius amorem vincere & infinitis post se parasangis relinquere debet. Denique carnem suam abnegat, qui carnis φθορὰν corruptionem deponit & exuit. Quæ præcipua abnegationis sui, à Christo præceptæ, species est.
units.tr: Rev. 12:11, being so ready to offer himself to God that the crown of Christ may flourish even in ashes and dust. For the love of Christ ought to overcome the love of self and leave it behind at infinite parasangs. Finally, he denies his flesh who lays aside and strips off the corruption [φθορὰν] of the flesh. This is the chief kind of self-denial prescribed by Christ.

units.la: LXXVII. De Abnegationis sui postrema hac specie ita S. Paulus.
units.tr: LXXVII. Concerning this last form of self-denial, St. Paul writes thus:

units.la: Illuxit gratia Dei salutifera omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos, ut ἀρνησάμενοι τὴν ἀσέβειαν καὶ τὰς κοσμικὰς ἐπιθυμίας, abnegata impietate, & mundanis cupiditatibus, temperanter, juste & pie vivamus in hoc seculo, Tit. II. 11. 12. Ubi abnegare impietatem & mundanas cupiditates, hoc est, tædium ex iis capere, pudori & probrohabere, non suas putare, à se alienissimas exististimare jubet. Et naturâ quidem homo impietatem & cupiditates mundanas non abnegat, sed potiùs injustitiam bibit instar aquæ, Job. XV. 16. hoc est, illas pro deliciis habet, & avidè se illis, tanquam sitim explere gestiens, ingurgitat. Sicut enim aquam bibere jucundum est: ita homo naturâ impietate & concupiscentiis delectatur. In quo misero statu homo duo nativa & propria habet, impietatem & mundanas cupiditates. Impietas Deum spectat. Nam naturâ homo Deum non cognoscit, non amat, de eo libenter non cogitat, vellet eum talem esse, qualis ipse est; hoc agit, ut sibi persuadeat Deum sibi similem esse, non offendi peccatis, in consiliis & factis hominum acquiescere, eos justificare ex eo quod ipsi faciunt, vel saltem sine justitia eos justificare. Qui affectus in Scriptura odium Dei appellatur. Quod illorum etiam est, qui sibi δῆθεν θεοσεβεῖς & σοφοὶ sapientes videntur, quia religionem ex consilio suo constituunt; & quibus sapientia Dei stultitia est, 1. Cor. II. 14. Ex quo impietatis fonte omnis amor sui, elatio animi, ferocia, ignorantia, error, superstitio, idololatria, atheismus pullulat. Sed gratia, quæ illuxit, sanans & erudiens nos efficit, ut abnegata hac impietate in hoc seculo εὐσεβῶς pie vivamus, hoc est, amore nostri, typho & sapientia carnali, terrestri, animali, diabolica, cogitationibus propriis, & fiducia in nobis, viribus & operibus nostris abdicatis, nos ipsos evacuemus planè & exinaniamus, Dei verbo totos nos subjiciamus, Idem verum & virtutes ejus, inprimis justitiam & sanctitatem in Christo demonstratam agnoscamus, & diligamus, eum, ut summum & potentissimum Dominum, Salvatorem nostrum timeamus, ei uni soli que confidamus, in eoditescere maximi faciamus, dona ejus non negligamus, iram & judicium ejus expavescamus, in eo amore atque timore ipsi grata facere, bonam conscientiam habere, & in eo solo deliciari studeamus; denique nos ipsi totos ad mortem usque pro nomine ejus sustinendam impendamus.
units.tr: The saving grace of God has appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness [ἀρνησάμενοι τὴν ἀσέβειαν] and worldly lusts [τὰς κοσμικὰς ἐπιθυμίας], we should live soberly, righteously and godly in this present age, Tit. 2:11-12. Here he bids us deny ungodliness and worldly lusts, that is, to take weariness of them, to regard them with shame and reproach, to think them not our own, and to judge them utterly foreign to us. By nature, however, man does not deny ungodliness and worldly lusts, but rather drinks iniquity like water, Job 15:16, that is, he counts them as delights and gulps them down eagerly, as one longing to quench a thirst. For just as drinking water is pleasant, so by nature man takes delight in impiety and in his desires. In this wretched state man has two things that are native and his own: impiety and worldly lusts. Impiety concerns God. For by nature man does not know God, does not love him, gladly does not think of him, and would wish him to be such as he himself is. He labours to persuade himself that God is like himself, that he is not offended by sins, that he acquiesces in the counsels and deeds of men, that he justifies them on account of what they do, or at least justifies them without righteousness. This disposition is called in Scripture the hatred of God. It belongs also to those who seem to themselves to be pious and wise (supposedly god-fearing, δῆθεν θεοσεβεῖς), because they set up their religion by their own counsel, and to whom the wisdom of God is foolishness, 1 Cor. 2:14. From this fountain of impiety spring all self-love, arrogance of spirit, ferocity, ignorance, error, superstition, idolatry and atheism. But the grace that has appeared, healing and teaching us, makes us, with this impiety denied, to live piously [εὐσεβῶς] in this age. That is, with self-love, pride, and carnal, earthly, animal and diabolical wisdom, our own thoughts, and confidence in ourselves, our strength and our works abandoned, we should utterly empty and emptify ourselves, wholly submit ourselves to the word of God, acknowledge and love the truth and virtues of God shown in Christ, above all his justice and holiness, and fear him as our supreme and most powerful Lord and Saviour.
