We should trust in him alone, hold him in highest esteem in knowledge, not neglect his gifts, dread his wrath and judgment, strive in love and fear to please him, keep a good conscience, and take our delight in him alone. Finally, we should devote ourselves wholly, even to death, to bear suffering for his name.

units.la: LXXVIII. Sunt etiam naturâ in homine κοσμικαὶ ἐπιθυμίαι mundanæ cupiditates.
units.tr: LXXVIII. Worldly desires [κοσμικαὶ ἐπιθυμίαι] also exist in man by nature.

units.la: Ubi enim impietas est, ibi dilectio Dei nulla est. Ubi nulla Dei dilectio est, ibi omnis appetitus & voluntas hominis est ἐπιθυμία concupiscentia, seu amor non veri boni, tanquam veri boni, vel amor mali, tanquam boni, quæ φθορὰ corruptio 2. Pet. I. 4. appellatur, tum quia concupiscen-tia talis est rerum pereuntium & φθαρτῶν corruptibilium, quæ satiare non possunt, & delectatio in iis, vel tristitia propter eas: tum quia in ea est aversio à Deo summo bono, & à viis ejus, & conversio ad malum, peccatum, atque in eodem delectatio, quibus voluntas hominis, quoad moralem rectitudinem suam planè corrumpitur. Quæ etiam mundana concupiscentia vocatur, quia mundus ei servit. Omne quod in mundo est, concupiscentia carnis, & concupiscentia oculorum, & superbia vitæ, non est ex Patre, sed ex mundo est, 1. Joh. II. 16.
units.tr: Where there is impiety, there is no love of God. Where there is no love of God, every appetite and will of man is epithymia [ἐπιθυμία], that is, desire, or love of what is not the true good as though it were the true good, or love of evil as though it were good. This is called corruption [φθορά], 2 Pet. 1:4, both because such desire is for things that perish and are corruptible [φθαρτῶν], which cannot satisfy, and because delight in them, or sorrow over them, follows; and also because in it there is aversion from God, the supreme good, and from his ways, and a turning to evil and sin, and delight in these. By this the will of man is wholly corrupted as to its moral uprightness. It is also called worldly desire, because the world serves it. All that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life, is not of the Father but is of the world, 1 John 2:16.

units.la: Pertinent huc omnes mali affectus, qui in homine sunt, amor nostri, odium proximi, inimici inprimis, φιλανδρία amor voluptatum & luxuria, ambitio, avaritia, & quicquid non ex Deo, sed ex mundo est. Sed gratia Dei erudit nos, ut etiam has concupiscentias abnegare, exuere, deponere, ceu non nostras, sed Sathanæ & mundi, abdicare, fugere, oculos manus & cuncta membra, quæ scandalizant, seu ad peccandum imperio suo seducunt, exscindere, mortificare studeamus; & contra vivamus tum σωφρόνως temperanter, εὐσεβῶς pie & δικαίως juste. Nam amori non vere boni, & ejus abusui temperantia: amori & actioni mali, velut boni, justitia opponitur. Hoc enim ante omnia fides gratiæ Dei in homine operatur, ut non appetat ea, quæ in mundo sunt, & circa quæ, ceu vera bona, mundus insanit, & patitur (unde concupiscentiæ πάθημα & φρόνημα σαρκὸς studium carni satisfaciendi ad insaniam usque, appellantur) sed sanas castásque circa ea cogitationes, & integros non corruptos sensus atque affectus habeat; denique circa utramque legis tabulam proprium ingenium exuat, & abneget id omne, quod non lex Dei, sed ratio & voluntas dictat.
units.tr: All the evil affections that are in man belong here: self-love, hatred of one's neighbour, above all of enemies, love of pleasures and luxury, ambition, avarice, and whatever is not from God but from the world. But the grace of God teaches us to deny, cast off and put away these desires as not ours but Satan's and the world's; to renounce and flee them, and to strive to cut off and mortify the eyes, hands and all members which cause offence or which, under their rule, lead us into sin; and on the contrary to live soberly [σωφρόνως], piously [εὐσεβῶς] and justly [δικαίως]. For temperance is opposed to love of what is not truly good and to its abuse, while justice is opposed to love of evil and to acting on it as though it were good. For faith in the grace of God first of all works this in a man: that he does not desire the things that are in the world, and about which the world rages and suffers as if they were true goods (whence these desires are called the passion [πάθημα] and mind of the flesh [φρόνημα σαρκὸς], zeal to satisfy the flesh even to madness). Rather, he has sane and chaste thoughts about them, and whole, uncorrupted senses and affections. Finally, with regard to both tables of the law, he should strip off his own disposition and renounce all that is dictated not by the law of God but by reason and will.

units.la: LXXIX. Res difficilima omnium & maximè exercita sui abnegatio est.
units.tr: LXXIX. Self-denial is the most difficult of all things and the one that is most often practised.

units.la: Nam sui ipsius mortificatio, abdicatio, altarium quædam destructio & membrorum scandalizantium, seu affectuum in iis regnantium excidium est. Ideo Apostolus, ut animos nostros ab omnibus laqueis extricet, ad spem beatæ immortalitatis nos revocat. Προσδεχόμενοι, inquit, expectantes beatam illam spem, & affulgentiam gloriæ magni illius Dei & Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi, Tit. II. 13. Magnum ergo abnegatio sui præmium habet, expectationem beatitudinis & hæreditatis cœlestis. Nam ipsa illa gratia, quæ nos erudit, ut nos ipsos abnegemus, etiam nos erudit, ut abnegantes nos ipsos beatitudinem expectemus. Quæ considerratio impedimenta & illecebras, quæ nos obnubilant, ne uti decet, ad cœlestem gloriam aspiremus, omnes discutit. Neque enim jubet sperare & gloriari sine effectu gratiæ in hoc seculo, sed cum eo, ita nempe, ut effectus hujus gratiæ ὁ ἁγιασμὸς sanctificatio & abnegatio nostri, in hoc seculo ἀρραβὼν pignus sit. Accedunt alia quoque abnegandi sui incentiva. Nam idem in fidelibus sensus esse debet, qui fuit in Christo, Phil. II. 5. Atqui ille propter nos ἐκένωσεν ἑαυτὸν seipsum exinanivit, ibid. v. 7. Propterea propositâ sustinuit crucem, & probrum contempsit, Hebr. XII. 2. Cùm dives esset, propter nos pauper factus est, 2. Cor. VIII. 9. Etiam nobilibus sui eum renes erudiverunt, Psal. XVI. 7. Idem Sanctorum omnium studium fuit, uti Abrahami qui vocatus patriam ultrò deseruit, ignarus,quò iret,Hebr. XI. 7. Et Mosis, qui unà cum populo Dei male haberi, quàm peccati temporariam fruitionem habere maluit, ibid. v. 25. Apostolorum, qui propter Christum omnia reliquerunt,Matth. XIX. 27. aliorúmque exempla probant. Praeterea abnegatio sui certissimum veri & sinceri Christiani χαρακτήρ est. Cùm hypocritae & Sathanas,in Angelum lucis se transformans,plurima simulare possint,at propter Christum se abnegare non possunt. Regenitorum solorum ἀπλοΐχτμα & lydius lapis sui abnegatio est.
units.tr: For the mortification and renunciation of oneself is a kind of destruction of the altars and a cutting out of the scandalous members, that is, of the affections that reign in them. Therefore the Apostle, to free our minds from all snares, calls us back to the hope of blessed immortality. Looking for that blessed hope, he says, and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, Tit. II. 13 [Προσδεχόμενοι, prosdechomenoi]. Self-denial therefore has a great reward: the expectation of blessedness and of a heavenly inheritance. For the very grace that teaches us to deny ourselves also teaches us, in denying ourselves, to look for blessedness. This consideration dispels all the hindrances and allurements that cloud us, so that we do not aspire to heavenly glory as we ought. Nor does it bid us hope and glory without the effect of grace in this age, but along with that effect, so that sanctification [ἁγιασμὸς] and the denial of ourselves, which are the effect of this grace, are in this age the earnest [ἀρραβὼν] or pledge. There are other incentives to self-denial as well. For the same mind should be in believers that was in Christ, Phil. II. 5. Yet he for our sake emptied himself [ἐκένωσεν ἑαυτὸν], ibid. v. 7. For the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, and despised the shame, Heb. XII. 2. Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, 2 Cor. VIII. 9. My reins also have instructed me, even in the nights, Ps. XVI. 7. Such was the aim of all the saints: as Abraham, when he was called, went out of his own country, not knowing whither he went, Heb. XI. 7; and Moses, who chose rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season, ibid. v. 25; and the apostles, who for Christ's sake left all things, Matt. XIX. 27, together with other examples, prove the point. Moreover, self-denial is the most certain mark [χαρακτήρ] of the true and sincere Christian. Hypocrites and Satan, who transforms himself into an angel of light, can feign many things, but they cannot deny themselves for Christ's sake. Self-denial is the sure sign [ἀπλοΐχτμα] and the touchstone of the regenerate alone.

units.la: LXXX. Post abnegationem sui crucis tolerantiam Christus praecipit. Tollat crucem meam,Matth.XVI.24. hoc est, exemplo meo crucem & ipse ferat,crucifigatur,moriatur mecum, atque sic me imitetur, sequatur,conformis mihi fiat. Fidus sermo est: Si unà mortui sumus,etiam unà vivemus. Si toleramus,etiam conregnabimus, 2. Tim. II. 11. 12. Si unà patimur, etiam unà glorificabimur,Rom. VIII. 17. Oportet ut per multas afflictiones in Regnum Coelorum intremus,Actor.XIV. 22. In mundo afflictionem habebitis. Sed estote bono animo. Ego vici mundum,Joh.XVI. 33. Omnes qui volent pie vivere in Christo Jesu, persecutionem patientur, 2. Tim. III. 12. Quoscunque igitur Dominus coeptavit, & suo consortio dignatus est, ii se ad duram,laboriosam,inquietam,plurimis variisque malorum generibus refertam vitam praeparare debent. Haec enim ejus voluntas est, talem in modum eos exercere, ut certum de fide & obedientia eorum experimentum capiat. Ita Christus ipse,primogenitus ejus Filius perpetua cruce exercitatus est,verè ut tota ejus vita nihil aliud quàm perpetuae crucis species fuerit. Nam Filius licèt,obedientiam ex iis,quae passus est,didicit,Hebr. V. 8. Quae capitis conditio fuit, eadem membrorum esse debet, inprimis cùm nostri causa passus fuerit , ut inter alia ✱tiam nobis in se ipso patientiae exemplar exhiberet,quò in passionibus etiam conformes ei reddamur,Rom. VIII. 29. Nec levis ea Christianorum consolatio est, quòd sic cum passionibus Christi communicant,ut sicut ipse à malorum omnium labyrinthis in coelestem gloriam enixus est, ita in eandem per varias tribulationes deducantur. Propter Christum jacturam omnium facio,&c. ut cognoscam ipsum,& potentiam resurrectionis ejus,& communionem passionum ejus,& conformatus morti ejus, Phil. III. 8. 10. Insuper passiones fidelium ab efficacia mortis Christi proficiscuntur. Mors Christi in nobis operatur,vita autem Christi in vobis,2.Cor. IV. 12. Nam à morte & passionibus Christi coercitio, humiliatio & mortificatio carnis & corporis nostri oritur, atque sic morti Christi assimilamur, & rursus à vita Christi consolatio, refrigerium, & tranquillatio nostra sequitur. Quo igitur magis rebus adversis afflictamur, hoc certiùs nostra cum Christo societas & conformitas confirmatur. Cujus communione passiones ipsae non modò benedictae nobis fiunt,sed etiam ad promovendam salutem nostram plurimùm adjumenti afferunt.
units.tr: LXXX. After self-denial Christ commands the bearing of the cross: Let him take up his cross, Matt. XVI. 24. That is, by my example let him bear the cross himself, be crucified, die with me, and so imitate me, follow me, and be made conformable to me. It is a faithful saying: If we be dead with him, we shall also live with him. If we suffer, we shall also reign with him, 2 Tim. II. 11, 12. If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified together, Rom. VIII. 17. We must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God, Acts XIV. 22. In the world ye shall have tribulation; but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world, John XVI. 33. All that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution, 2 Tim. III. 12. Therefore, all whom the Lord has begun to call and has deigned to make his companions must prepare themselves for a hard, laborious, restless life, filled with very many and varied kinds of evils. For this is his will: to exercise them in such a way that he may obtain a sure proof of their faith and obedience. So Christ himself, his firstborn Son, was exercised by a continual cross, so that truly his whole life was nothing but a kind of continual cross. For though he was a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered, Heb. V. 8. What was the condition of the Head should be the condition of the members as well, especially since he suffered for our sake, so that among other things he might set before us in himself a pattern of patience, that we might be made conformable to him in his sufferings, Rom. VIII. 29. This is no small comfort to Christians, that they share in the sufferings of Christ in such a way that, just as he himself struggled out of the labyrinths of all evils into heavenly glory, so they are led into the same glory through various tribulations. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things, etc., that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable to his death, Phil. III. 8, 10. Moreover, the sufferings of believers proceed from the efficacy of Christ's death. Death works in us, but life in you, 2 Cor. IV. 12. For from the death and sufferings of Christ arise the restraint, humbling and mortification of our flesh and body, and so we are made like to the death of Christ; and again, from the life of Christ follow our consolation, refreshment and tranquillity. Therefore the more we are afflicted by adversity, the more surely our fellowship and conformity with Christ is confirmed. By this communion the sufferings themselves are not only made blessed to us, but also bring very great help to the furthering of our salvation.

units.la: LXXXI. Summa igitur crucis & necessitas & utilitas est. Necessitas, tum ut superbia nostra retundatur: tum ut humiliati discamus invocare auxilium Dei: tum ut virtutis Divinae praesentiam experiamur. Nam natura homo propensus est ad omnia carni suae tribuenda,& nisi ei imbecillitas sua ob oculos ponatur, facile virtutem suam supra justum modum aestimat,& adversus Deum ipsum contumaciter superbit. Hanc superbiam ut retundat Deus, ignominia, paupertate,orbitate,morbo,calamitatibus affligit,& experimentis his comprobat, quanta ille fragilitate laboret. Ita humiliatus, & malis illis sustinendis impar,Dei gratiam & virtutem, quae sola sub pondere afflictionum sustentat,implorat. Ego dixi in quiete mea: Non movebor in aeternum. Jehova,quem per benevolentiam tuam constituerac in monte roboris , simul abscondisti faciem tuam,perculsus sum. Ad te,Jehova, clamabam , & ad Jehovam supplicabam, Psal. XXX. 7. 8. 9. Ad Deum ubi se in angustiis convertit, Divinae virtutis praesentiam, in qua satis superque praesidii est,experitur.
units.tr: LXXXI. The sum, then, is that the cross is both necessary and useful. It is necessary: first, so that our pride may be broken; second, so that, being humbled, we may learn to call upon the help of God; third, so that we may experience the presence of divine power. For by nature man is inclined to ascribe everything to his own flesh, and unless his weakness is set before his eyes, he easily esteems his own power beyond what is just and proudly rebels against God himself. To break this pride God afflicts with disgrace, poverty, bereavement, sickness and calamities, and by these trials he proves how great is the frailty under which man labours. Thus humbled, and unequal to bearing these evils, he implores the grace and power of God, which alone sustains under the weight of afflictions. I said in my prosperity, I shall never be moved. Lord, by thy favour thou hast made my mountain to stand strong; thou didst hide thy face, and I was troubled. I cried to thee, O Lord; and unto the Lord I made supplication, Ps. XXX. 7, 8, 9. When in distress a man turns to God, he experiences the presence of divine power, in which there is help enough and more.

units.la: LXXXII. Utilitatem etiam multiplicem crux habet. Nam ex afflictionibus pacificum fructum justitiae percipere est,Heb. XII. 11. Non tantum verò , sed & gloriamur in afflictionibus, scientes,quòd afflictio patientiam operetur,patientia verò experimentum,experimentum verò spem, spes autem non confundat, Rom. V. 3. 4. 5. Spes dulcissimum vitae condimentum est. Ea in afflictionibus nascitur. Nam in afflictionibus datur patientia,cujus usus rebus adversis, non secundis obtinet. In patientia autem fidei & charitatis δοκιμὴ, experimentum est; numquid scilicet possimus Deum solum amare , mundo huic valedicere , proximo injuriam facienti condonare,inimicum diligere. Quae experientia arrhabonem spiritus in suo nitore & claritudine exhibet ; qui facit spem , eámque non languidam,quae per forsan absolvatur, sed quae non frustretur,pudefaciat, sed expectationem pariat, quippe cùm charitas Dei in cordibus nostris effusa sit per Spiritum Dei, hoc est,dùm sentimus nos à Spiritu Dei sanctificari & recreari, etiam à Deo diligi nos sentiamus. Ideo etiam in afflictionibus gloriamur. Omnes enim afflictiones pudore & probro carent , iis exceptis, quas suo vitio & jumento homo sibi concivit. Ad obediendum quoque Deo cruce erudimur; quia sic non ad proprium votum,sed ad Dei arbitrium vivere jubemur. Si ex sententia animi cuncta fluerent, nesciret homo, quid sit ἀκολουθεῖν sequi Christum, & ἐπεσθω τῷ Θεῷ Deo obsequi. Nam & Seneca commemorat,vetere adagio receptum fuisse,ut ad res adversas tolerandas hortaturi quempiam, occlamarent: Deum sequere. Si igitur aequissimum est , ut coelesti Patri nos per omnia obsequentes esse approbemus,detrectandum non est,ut ad reddendam sibi obedientiam omnibus modis assuefaciat. Accedit,quòd per crucem carnis nostra lascivia domatur. Accidit enim hominí,quod equo refractario,qui aliquot dies per otium saginatus, vix postea praे ferocitate domari potest,& aegrè sessorem patitur. Et impinguatus est Jeschurun & recalcitravit, (impinguatus es, incrassatus es, texisti te adipe) & omisit Deum, qui fecit eum, & proscelerato tractavit rupem salutis suae,Deut. XXXII. 15. Cùm igitur tanta hominis malignitas fit , ut indulgentia Dei corrumpatur, disciplina crucis cohiberi debet,ne in talem petulantiam exultet , idque variis modis, quantum tum unicuique salubre est. Ad hæc imposita cruce Deus infirmitates nostras prævenit, & præterita delicta corrigit, ut nos in legitima erga se obedientia contineat. Si nos discerneremus, non judicaremur. Judicati vero castigamur, ne cum mundo condemnemur, 1. Cor. XI. 31. 32. Affligit enim Deus, non ut perdat, vel occidat, sed ut à damnatione liberet. Fili mi, ne respuas correctionem Domini, neque afficiaris tædio, cum ab eo argueris. Quem enim diligit Deus, corripit, & eum, velut pater filium, amplectitur, Prov. III. 11. 12. Hoc inter incredulos & fideles interest, quòd illi, ceu in nequitia inveterati, flagellis deteriores & obstinatiores fiunt; hi ceu filii ingenui ad pœnitentiam proficiunt: quòdque illi nullam sub cruce spem habent; hi quoad statum in hoc sæculo miseriores, quoad spem longè feliciores sunt, quod inprimis Jobi Liber totus comprobat. Denique crucis haud postrema utilitas est, quòd ea presli vitæ præsentis contemptui assuescunt, & ad futuræ meditationem excitantur. Novit enim Deus, hominem mundi hujus belluini amore insanire. Ideo amorem hunc variis afflictionum variarum pharmacis extinguit, ut sub crucis disciplina bona hujus mundi incerta, fluida, vana, multùsque malis admixtis vitiata cernentes, & certamina vitæ hujus continuare putantes, oculos in Cœlum attollamus, & de corona cogitemus.
units.tr: LXXXII. The cross also has many uses. For from afflictions we receive the peaceable fruit of righteousness, Heb. XII. 11. And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also, knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope; and hope maketh not ashamed, Rom. V. 3, 4, 5. Hope is the sweetest seasoning of life, and it is born in afflictions. For in afflictions patience is given, whose use is found in adversity rather than in prosperity. Now in the patience of faith and love there is a proof [δοκιμὴ], that is, an experience: whether we can indeed love God alone, bid farewell to this world, forgive an injury done to us by our neighbour, and love an enemy. This experience displays the earnest of the Spirit in its own brightness and clarity; it produces hope, and not a languid hope that may perhaps be dissolved, but one that does not disappoint and does not put to shame, but brings forth expectation; since the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Spirit of God, that is, while we feel ourselves sanctified and renewed by the Spirit of God, we also feel ourselves loved by God. Therefore we also glory in tribulations. For all afflictions are free from shame and reproach, except those which a man has brought upon himself by his own fault and folly. We are also trained by the cross to obey God, since in this way we are commanded to live not according to our own will but according to the decision of God. If everything went according to our own mind, man would not know what it is to follow Christ [ἀκολουθεῖν], and to obey God [ἕπεσθαι τῷ Θεῷ]. For Seneca also records that by an old proverb it was customary, when exhorting someone to bear adversity, to cry out: Follow God. If, therefore, it is most just that we should approve ourselves obedient to our heavenly Father in all things, we should not shrink from being accustomed in every way to render obedience to him. Besides, through the cross the wantonness of our flesh is tamed. For it happens to a man as to an unbroken horse, which, fattened in idleness for some days, can scarcely afterwards be tamed for its ferocity, and endures its rider with difficulty. But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked (thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness), and he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation, Deut. XXXII. 15. Since, then, man's malice is so great that the indulgence of God is corrupted, the discipline of the cross must restrain him, lest he exult in such wantonness; and this in various ways, as far as is useful to each one. Moreover, by laying the cross upon us God anticipates our infirmities and corrects past offences, so as to keep us in lawful obedience to himself. For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged. But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world, 1 Cor. XI. 31, 32. For God afflicts not in order to destroy or kill, but to deliver from condemnation. My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, neither be weary of his correction. For whom the Lord loveth he correcteth, even as a father the son in whom he delighteth, Prov. III. 11, 12. This is the difference between unbelievers and believers: the former, like men hardened in wickedness, become worse and more obstinate under the lash; the latter, like free-born sons, advance to repentance. And while the former have no hope under the cross, the latter, though more wretched in their present state in this age, are far happier in their hope, as the whole Book of Job especially proves. Finally, not the least use of the cross is that through it men become accustomed to despise the present life and are roused to meditate upon the future. For God knows that man is driven mad by a brutish love of this world. Therefore he extinguishes this love with various remedies of various afflictions, so that, under the discipline of the cross, we may see the goods of this world to be uncertain, fleeting, empty, and corrupted by many evils mingled with them, and, supposing that the struggles of this life must continue, we may lift our eyes to heaven and think upon the crown.

units.la: LXXXIII. Afflictiones fidelium non esse pœnas proprie dictas, fusius Loc. X. 92. 93, probavimus. Ubi etiam earundem species, παιδείαν, δοκιμασίαν & μαρτύριον explicatas, §94. dedimus. Unum igitur addimus, sic crucem, inprimis per Christi causam impositam animo hilari sustinendam esse, exemplo Apostolorum, qui χαίροντες gaudentes à facie Synedrii discesserunt, eò quòd digni habiti sunt, qui pro nomine Christi contumelia afficerentur, Act. V. 41. & S. Jacobi monitu: πᾶσαν χαρὰν ἡγήσασθε omnem laetitiam reputate, cùm varias in tentationes incideritis, Jac. I. 2. ut tamen ab ejus patientia omnis acerbitatis & doloris naturalis sensus non exulet. Ideo Petro Christus dixit: Cùm esses junior, cingebas te, & ambulabas, quò libebat. Cùm autem senueris, præcinget te alius, & ducet, quò non vules, Joh. XXI. 18. Nulla enim in cruce Sanctorum patientia esset, nisi & dolore torquerentur, & molestiæ sensum perciperent. Si nulla esset in egestate asperitas, nullus in morbis cruciatus, nulla in ignominia punctio, nullus in morte horror, cujus vel fortitudinis, vel moderationis foret, ea susque deque habere? At cùm unumquodque eorum ingenita sibi amaritudine mordet, in eo se hominis fidelis fortitudo profert, si timore Dei refrænatus in intemperiem nullam erumpat, neque sic tristatur, ut in spirituali Dei consolatione non simul lætetur & acquiescat. Quem conflictum patientiæ fidelis adversus naturalem doloris sensum sic Apostolus describit: In omnibus affligimur, sed non coarctamur: ambigui, sed non prorsus hæsitantes: Persecutionem patimur, sed non derelinquimur: Prosternimur, sed non perdimur. Semper mortificationem Christi in corpore circumferentes, ut etiam vita Jesu in corpore nostro manifestetur, 2. Cor. IV. 8. 9. 10. Non ergo patienter ferre crucem est obstupescere, & omni doloris sensu privari; uti Stoici magnanimum hominem stulte olim descripserunt, qui exuta humanitate rebus adversis perinde ac prosperis, tristibus perinde ac lætis afficeretur. Simulachrum patientiæ illi depinxerunt, quod nec repertum unquam inter homines est, nec extare potest. Nihilominus inter Christianos novi Stoici sunt, quibus non modò gemere & flere, sed etiam tristari & solicitum esse vitiosum est. Sed ferream Philosophiam istam Christus ipse verbo & exemplo suo damnavit. Mundus gaudebit, vos autem flebitis & lugebitis, Joh. XVI. 20. Et beatos etiam πενθοῦντας lugentes prædicavit, Matth. V. 4. Lazarum resuscitaturus idem ἐδάκρυσε lachrymatus est, Joh. XI. 35. Et sanguineæ lachrymæ è corpore ejus destillarunt, Luc. XXII. 44. denique ejus anima περίλυπος tristis fuit usque ad mortem, Matth. XXVI. 38. Sed hanc patientiæ laudem Scriptura defert, quòd cruciati ita malorum duritie afflictantur, ut non frangantur, vel concidant; ita amaritudine punguntur, ut simul spirituali gaudio perfundantur; ita anxietate premuntur, ut Dei consolatione exhilarati respirent; ita turbantur, ut non perturbentur. Hoc ergo, si post Christum venire, & ejus discipuli esse volumus, operam dandum est, ut animi Dei observantia & obedientia sic imbuantur, ut omnes affectiones contrarias domare, & sub voluntatis Divinæ jugum mittere valeant. Hoc solo modo in summis angustiis infractam patientiam constanter retinere licet. LXXXIV. Permultum ergo Christianam inter & Philosophicam patientiam interest. Pauci enim Philosophi eò assurrexerunt, ut manu Dei nos exerceri per afflictiones intelligerent, & Deo sic obtemperandum esse agnoscerent. Nam non aliam fere patientiæ rationem, quàm duræ necessitatis telum afferunt, quasi dicerent, cedendum esse Deo, quia frustra oblucta ri contendas. Sed si Deo paremus ideo tantùm, quia necesse est parere, si evadere licuerit, desinemus. Aliud longè Scriptura in voluntate Dei considerare jubet, nempe justitiam primùm & æquitatem, deinde salutis curam. Hujusmodi ergo ad crucis patientiam Christiana disciplina exhortatur. Non cedere jubet, quia necesse est, sed obtemperare, quia resistere nefas est, & id omne saluti & bono patientis cedit. Quæ cogitationes faciunt, ut quantum animi nostri in crue naturali acerbitatis sensu contrahuntur, tantum spirituali lætitia diffundantur. Unde & gratiarum actio sequitur, quæ nulla sine gaudio esse potest. LXXXV. Ad Christianam vitam etiam Vocationis cujusque industria functio pertinet. Obtestamur vos, fratres, φιλοτιμεῖσθαι ἡσυχάζειν καὶ πράσσειν τὰ ἴδια, ut studeatis quiescere, & propria agere, & opus facere vestris manibus propriis, quemadmodum vobis denuntiavimus, 1. Thess. IV. 10. 11. Audimus, quosdam ambulare inter vos inordinate nihil operantes, sed περιεργαζομένους aliud agentes. Talibus vero denuntiamus, & rogamus per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, ut quiete opus suum facientes panem suum comedant, 2. Thess. III. 11. 12. Et quieta igitur cum industria hoc agendum; & aliena non agenda sunt. Non enim vita Christiana vel otium, vel turbidam & negotiorum appetentem industriam, vel ἀπεργίαν ἀπεργίαν: legible Greek word read with uncertainty at line end. {a} curiositatem, & rerum aliarum præposte- ram curam probat. Sed oportet ἡσυχίας cum quiete seu tranquillitate opus facere, puta ἀγαθὸν bonum, Eph.IV.28. utile, laudabile, etiam manuum, quæ organa organorum sunt, quamvis non minor labor animi & ingenii excolendi, & alieni etiam formandi sit. Unde S. Paulus duplici honore dignos esse presbyteros inprimis κοπιῶντας laborantes in sermone & doctrina, ait, 1.Tim.V.17. eadem voce κοπιῶν utens, qua de labore manuum, Ephes.IV.28. usus est. Habent enim etiam Principes & Magistratus suum opus: habent docentes: habent opifices: habent milites: habent servi τὰ ἴδια propria, quæ agant. Multa animo & corpore per hominem administrari ad propriam & aliorum utilitatem possunt. Quod quis facere novit, quod faciendi facultatem habet, ad quod vocatus est, id facere debet. Unusquisque in vocatione, in qua vocatus est, ambulet, 1. Cor.VII. 17.20. Vocatio enim ad fidem nullam necessitatem affert mutandi status civilis, quasi ullus status honestus & vitii expers vocationi illi incommodet. Charitatis etiam est, suum talentum exercere, domum, civitatem augere, exornare, rerum utilium copiam præstare. Non frustra Deus occasiones & media ad plurium utilitatem accommodata offert. Villici sumus bonorum & donorum Dei, quæ Deus uni impertiendo pluribus dedit. Ideo etiam rationem, ingenium, vires, occasiones discendi bonas artes Deus dedit, ut aptos nos reddamus ad opus, quod utilissimum facere possumus, quod faciendo nemini simus incommodi; & vitam sustentemus, ne cuiquam graves simus, & τὴν χρείαν ἔχουσι μεταδιδόναι opus habenti impertiri, Ephes.IV.28. possimus. Nam & proprium panem comedere Apostolus jubet, quia alienum comedere injustum est. Qui vero laborare potest, & non laborat, proprium panem non comedit, quales inprimis Monachi sunt, qui se voto ad nihil habendum proprium, adeoque panem alienum comedendum obstringunt, atque sic orationum & jejuniorum, quæ ἐργων χειρῶν opus manuum non esse recte Chrysostomus observat; & communia Christianis omnibus esse debent; prætextu, aliorum opes intervertunt, & crumenas exenterant; atque ita fures sunt, & charitate carent.
units.tr: LXXXIII. That the afflictions of believers are not punishments properly so called, we proved at greater length in Loc. X, §§92–93. There, in §94, we also explained their kinds: discipline (παιδεία), testing (δοκιμασία) and martyrdom (μαρτύριον). So we add only this: the cross laid upon us, especially for Christ's cause, must be borne with a cheerful mind, after the example of the Apostles, who "departed from the presence of the council rejoicing [χαίροντες], because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Christ" (Acts 5:41). Also in accordance with the admonition of St James: "Count it all joy when you fall into various temptations" (Jas. 1:2). Yet this patience does not banish all bitterness and natural sense of pain. Hence Christ said to Peter: "When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished. But when you are old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go" (John 21:18). For there would be no patience in the cross of the saints if they were not tormented by pain and did not feel the sting of suffering. If there were no harshness in poverty, no torment in sickness, no sting in disgrace, no horror in death, what would be the courage or the moderation of someone who treats these things with indifference? But since each of these bites with its own inborn bitterness, the strength of the faithful man shows itself in this: restrained by the fear of God, he breaks out into no intemperance, and he is not so saddened that he fails to rejoice and find rest at the same time in the spiritual consolation of God. The Apostle describes this struggle of faithful patience against the natural sense of pain in this way: "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed; always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our body" (2 Cor. 4:8–10). Therefore to bear the cross patiently is not to be numb and deprived of every sense of pain, as the Stoics foolishly once described the magnanimous man: stripped of human feeling, he would be affected by adversity just as by prosperity, by sorrow just as by joy. They painted a picture of patience that has never been found among men and cannot exist. Nevertheless, among Christians there are new Stoics, for whom to groan and weep, and not only that but also to be saddened and anxious, is sinful. But Christ himself, by his word and his example, condemned this iron philosophy: "The world will rejoice, but you will weep and mourn" (John 16:20). He also pronounced blessed those who mourn [πενθοῦντας] (Matt. 5:4). About to raise Lazarus, he himself wept [ἐδάκρυσε] (John 11:35). And "his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground" (Luke 22:44). Finally, his soul was sorrowful [περίλυπος] "even unto death" (Matt. 26:38). But Scripture gives this praise to patience: those who are tormented are so beaten by the hardness of evils that they are not broken or cast down; they are so pricked by bitterness that they are at the same time bathed in spiritual joy; they are so pressed by anxiety that, cheered by God's consolation, they breathe again; they are so troubled that they are not thrown into confusion. Therefore, if we wish to come after Christ and be his disciples, we must take care that our minds be so steeped in the observance and obedience of God that they are able to tame all contrary affections and put them under the yoke of the Divine will. Only in this way can one constantly keep patience unbroken in the greatest distress. LXXXIV. There is therefore a very great difference between Christian and philosophical patience. For few philosophers rose so far as to understand that we are exercised by the hand of God through afflictions, and to acknowledge that God must thus be obeyed. For they offer almost no other ground of patience than the weapon of hard necessity, as if they were saying that one must yield to God because it is vain to struggle against him. But if we obey God only because we must obey, we shall stop obeying as soon as we can escape. Scripture bids us consider something quite different in the will of God, namely first justice and equity, then the care of our salvation. It is to such patience under the cross that Christian discipline exhorts us. It does not bid us yield because we must, but obey because it is wrong to resist, and all this turns to the salvation and good of the one who is patient. These thoughts bring it about that, as much as our mind is contracted by the natural sense of bitterness in the cross, so much is it spread abroad with spiritual gladness. Hence there follows also thanksgiving, which can exist only with joy. LXXXV. The diligent performance of each one's calling also belongs to the Christian life. "We exhort you, brothers, to make it your ambition to be quiet [φιλοτιμεῖσθαι ἡσυχάζειν], to mind your own affairs [πράσσειν τὰ ἴδια], and to work with your hands, as we charged you" (1 Thess. 4:10–11). "We hear that some among you walk in idleness, doing no work but busy-bodies [περιεργαζομένους], doing other people's business. Now such persons we command and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ to work in quietness and eat their own bread" (2 Thess. 3:11–12). Therefore this must be done with quiet diligence, and the affairs of others must not be undertaken. For the Christian life approves neither idleness [ἀπεργίαν], nor a restless and busy zeal that seeks business, nor curiosity, nor a preposterous care for other matters. But one must do work "with quietness" [ἡσυχίας], that is, "with calm and tranquillity," namely work that is "good" [ἀγαθὸν] (Eph. 4:28), useful and praiseworthy, even manual work, which are the instruments of instruments, although the labour of cultivating the mind and intellect, and of forming others, is no less. Hence St Paul says that elders who labour [κοπιῶντας] in preaching and teaching are especially worthy of double honour (1 Tim. 5:17), using the same word for labour [κοπιῶν] that he used of manual labour (Eph. 4:28). For princes and magistrates also have their work; teachers have theirs; craftsmen have theirs; soldiers have theirs; servants have "their own affairs" [τὰ ἴδια] to carry out. Many things can be administered by a man, in body and mind, for his own benefit and that of others. Whatever a man knows how to do, whatever he has the ability to do, and to which he is called, that he ought to do. "Let each one walk in the calling in which he was called" (1 Cor. 7:17, 20). For the call to faith imposes no necessity of changing one's civil station, as if any honest station free of vice would hinder that calling. It is also an act of charity to exercise one's talent, to increase and adorn one's household and city, and to provide an abundance of useful things. God does not offer opportunities and means suited to the benefit of many in vain. We are stewards of the goods and gifts of God, which God gave to be shared among many by giving them to one. Therefore God also gave reason, talent, strength, and opportunities for learning the good arts, so that we might make ourselves fit for the work which we can do most usefully, and by doing which we harm no one; and so that we might sustain our life, not being a burden to anyone, and be able to share with one who has need (Eph. 4:28). For the Apostle bids us eat our own bread, because it is unjust to eat another's. But whoever is able to labour and does not labour does not eat his own bread; this is especially true of monks, who by vow bind themselves to have nothing of their own, and therefore to eat the bread of others, and thus, under the pretext of prayers and fasts, which, as Chrysostom rightly observes, are not "the work of hands" [ἐργων χειρῶν], and things that ought to be common to all Christians, they overturn the wealth of others and empty their purses. And so they are thieves, and lack charity.

units.la: LXXXVI.
units.tr: LXXXVI.

units.la: Qui otiosi nihil operantur, illi ut plurimum <bl>περιεργάζεσθαι</bl> aliud agunt, & <bl>ἀτάκτως περιπατοῦσιν</bl> inordinatè ambulant, quod ibidem Apostolus vetat. Non ita enim spiritus hominis desesotiari potest, quin aliquid agat. Qui bonum non agit, is malum agit, & majori quidem labore. Unde <bl>πονηρὸν</bl> improbum <bl>ἀπὸ τοῦ πόνου</bl> à labore dictum, quòd plus ille in malis patrandis, quàm probus in bonis faciendis laboris operæque sumat, ajunt. Qui nihil eorum, quæ familiæ vel civitati prosunt, operatur, & tamen quiescere nec vult, nec potest, is <bl>περιεργία</bl> curiositati, rerum alienarum explorationi, rebus novis & suspiriis indulget. Nam <bl>περιεργία</bl> indoles est, velle nosse aliena secreta, venditare proximi existimationem, velle videri necessarium multis, faciem pædagogicam assumere, suspirare & ingemiscere super aliorum peccatis, quiritari de omnibus, accurationem & <bl>ἀκρίβειαν</bl> exigere, & sub eo prætextu aliquid facere, quod vulgus non facit, in gestu, habitu, abstinentia, voto paupertatem profiteri, propter orationes (scilicet, meditationes, humiliationem carnis, <bl>σιωπὴν</bl> & similia multa, per quæ simplicioribus imponi potest; ut <bl>ἐπίσκοποι</bl> illi sancti, singulariter Deo chari, conscientiæ directores, propter orationes aliis necessarii æstimentur. Ejusmodi <bl>ἐπίσκοποι</bl> & <bl>ἀλαζονεῖα</bl> specie zeli & charitatis ad seducendum, factiones colligendas, seditiones suscitandas, pædagogicum supercilium erigendum, potestatem malis artibus occupandam & pejoribus exercendam aptissimi sunt.
units.tr: Those who are idle and do no work usually busy themselves with other people's affairs (periergazesthai) [περιεργάζεσθαι] and walk about disorderly (ataktôs peripatousin) [ἀτάκτως περιπατοῦσιν], which the Apostle forbids in the same place. For the human spirit cannot be idle; it must do something. Whoever does not do good does evil, and with greater effort. Hence they say that the word for wicked (ponēron) [πονηρὸν] is derived from toil (apo tou ponou) [ἀπὸ τοῦ πόνου], because the wicked person spends more labour and effort on doing harm than the upright person spends on doing good. Whoever does nothing that benefits the household or the state, yet neither wants nor is able to rest, gives himself over to busybody curiosity (periergia) [περιεργία], to prying into other people's affairs, and to novelties and sighing. For busybodying is a disposition to wish to know other people's secrets, to peddle a neighbour's reputation, to want to seem indispensable to many, to assume the manner of a schoolmaster, to sigh and groan over the sins of others, to complain about everyone, and to demand exactness and precision (akribeian) [ἀκρίβειαν]; and under that pretext to do something that the common people do not do: in bearing, dress and abstinence, to profess poverty by a vow, on account of prayers (that is, meditations, mortification of the flesh, silence (sigēn) [σιωπὴν] and many similar things, by which the simpler folk can be deceived), so that those holy overseers (episkopoi) [ἐπίσκοποι], singularly dear to God, directors of conscience, are judged necessary to others on account of their prayers. Such overseers, under the appearance of zeal and charity, are most fit for seducing people, gathering factions, stirring up sedition, raising a schoolmasterly haughtiness (alazoneia) [ἀλαζονεῖα], seizing power by wicked arts and exercising it more wickedly.

units.la: LXXXVII.
units.tr: LXXXVII.

units.la: Cum vita Christiana conjungi Precatio religiosa debet, qua scilicet pii uniusque, folique Deo καρδιογνώστη desideria cordis sui recte cumque eo, quo par est, affectu patefaciunt, profesque aliis Deo gratias agunt, bona necessaria petunt, & mala deprecantur. Hanc Scripturæ præprimis commendant, & ad eam amplis promissionibus invitant. Amen, Amen dico vobis, quæcunque petieritis à Patre meo in nomine meo, dabit vobis, Joh.XVI.23. Quicquid petieritis in nomine meo, id faciam, ib.c.XIV.13. De nulla re solliciti estote, sed omni in re precibus & deprecatione cum gratiarum actione petitiones vestræ apud Deum innotescant, Phil.IV.6. Adhortor vos, ut primò omnium fiant petitiones, orationes, intercessiones, gratiarum actiones pro omnibus hominibus, 1.Tim.II.1. Indesinenter orate. In omni re gratias agite. Hoc enim est voluntas Dei in Christo Jesu erga vos, 1.Thess. V.17.18. Si cui vestrum desit sapientia, petat a Deo, qui dat omnibus simpliciter, & non exprobrat, & dabitur ei; Petat autem in fide nihil disceptans, Jac.I.5.6. Quandoquidem enim Jehova Deus noster est, qui nobis peccata condonat, nos sanctificat, conservat, obsignat, & æternum salvat, necesse est, non tantum eum Deum nostrum apud alios confiteamur, & in eo, ut Deo nostro, gloriemur, sed etiam ut ipsi gloriam demus, & dicamus. Tu es Jehova Deus noster, hoc est, ei confiteri peccata & miseriam nostram, ei gratias agere, ab eo petere, & pro aliis etiam, ut hæredes gloriæ fiant, intercedere.
units.tr: Religious prayer ought to be joined with the Christian life, by which the pious person, and he alone, and to God alone, who knows the heart (kardiognōsté) [καρδιογνώστη], lays open the desires of his heart rightly and with the affection that is fitting, and gives thanks to God before others, asks for the good things he needs, and entreats to be spared from evils. Scripture especially commends this and invites us to it with ample promises. Truly, truly I say to you, whatever you ask of my Father in my name, he will give you, John 16:23. Whatever you ask in my name, I will do it, ibid. 14:13. Be anxious about nothing, but in everything, by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God, Phil. 4:6. I exhort you that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings be made for all men, 1 Tim. 2:1. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you, 1 Thess. 5:17–18. If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to him; but let him ask in faith, doubting nothing, James 1:5–6. For since Jehovah God is our God, who forgives us our sins, sanctifies us, preserves us, seals us and saves us eternally, it is necessary not only that we confess him as our God before others and glory in him as our God, but also that we give him glory and say: You are Jehovah our God. That is, we are to confess to him our sins and our misery, to give thanks to him, to ask of him, and to intercede also for others, that they may become heirs of glory.

units.la: LXXXVIII.
units.tr: LXXXVIII.

units.la: Ac licet non omnia precibus nostris adipiscamur, cum Deus prævenit nos, dando nobis Filium suum, Salvatorem mundi, & inveniatur etiam à non quærentibus ipsum, Esaj.LXV.1. Rom.X.20. atque insuper cordis nostri desideria, & universæ necessitates nostræ Deo, sine monitore, & certiùs longè quàm nobis innotescant, quia tamen æternæ ejus sapientiæ visum est hoc omnis boni donique salutaris à munificentia ejus impetrandi medium statuere, par est, voluntati & mandato ejus, in quo ἰσχυρὰ προσκλησις fortis instigatio ad petendum ea, quæ per Christum nobis parata sunt; humiliter obsecundare. Nam Spiritus, qui in nos effusus est, est Spiritus gratiæ & precum, Zach.XII.10. Et Deus multa dona, & eorum amplitudinem non vult dare nisi petentibus, ita ut preces nostras illis coordinaverit: Aperi os tuum, & satiabo illud, Psal.LXXXI.11. Petite & dabitur vobis. Quærite & invenietis. Pulsate & aperietur vobis, Matth.VII.7. Atque id imprimis ad utilitatem nostram, & Dei gloriam impensè conducit. Nam & nos precando miseriam nostram nos agnoscere, ejus sensu afficì, omnem in Dei bonitate spem & fiduciam repositam habere, ad eum velut sacram anchoram
units.tr: Although we do not obtain everything by our prayers, since God anticipates us by giving us his Son, the Saviour of the world, and he is found even by those who do not seek him (Isa. 65:1; Rom. 10:20), and although God knows the desires of our hearts and all our needs without any prompting, and far better than we ourselves do, it has nonetheless seemed good to his eternal wisdom to appoint prayer as the means of obtaining every good and saving gift from his bounty. It is therefore fitting that we humbly obey his will and command, in which [ἰσχυρὰ πρόσκλησις] a strong summons to ask for those things which have been prepared for us through Christ is given. For the Spirit who has been poured out upon us is the Spirit of grace and of supplication (Zech. 12:10). God also does not wish to give many gifts, and great ones, except to those who ask, so that he has bound our prayers to them: Open your mouth, and I will fill it (Ps. 81:10). Ask, and it will be given you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you (Matt. 7:7). This contributes greatly, above all, to our own benefit and to the glory of God. For by praying we acknowledge our misery, we are moved by a sense of it, we place all our hope and trust in the goodness of God, and we flee to him as to a sacred anchor,

units.la: Quæ etiam περιεργίαν aliud agen- tium excitan- tur. ram confugere, ab ipsius verbo, promissione & providentia totos pendere testamur; quin & resipiscentiam, fidem, in Deo fiduciam, zelum & charitatem, peccati odium & amorem justitiae rite precando excitamus, accendimus, fovemus, augemus, à coeno ad Coelum nos convertimus,& per hoc velut familiare animae cum Deo colloquium seu soliloquium propius nos ipsi unimus, & cum imagine ejus conformamur. In qua unione summa beatitudo hominis consistit. Sed maxime precatio gloriam Dei illustrat, quia per eam Divina ejus attributa & virtutes sonora velut voce praedicantur, & in immensum extolluntur. Nam qui precatur, Deum profitetur ubique praesentem, qui undecunque locorum ad se suspirantes exaudiat; Omniscium, qui etiam cordis desideria scrutetur; Omnipotentem, qui quicquid vult, ad salutem nostram praestare, & nos ab omni malo liberare potest; & boni omnis fontem, quia ab eo benedictiones quaevis temporales & coelestes expectantur; & summe misericordem, qui misereri nostri, peccata nobis remittere, & aeternam vitam nobis donare velit; denique fidelem & veracem, cujus promissiones omnes in Christo nae & Amen sint. Quam igitur chara nobis Dei glorificatio, & multiplex adeo utilitas nostra est, tam charae preces esse debent.
units.tr: which also rouses curiosity [περιεργίαν] in those who are busy with other things. We testify that we depend entirely on his word, promise and providence. Indeed, by praying rightly we stir up, kindle, foster and increase repentance, faith, trust in God, zeal and love, hatred of sin and love of righteousness. We turn from the mire to heaven, and through this we unite ourselves more closely to God, as in a familiar conversation or soliloquy of the soul with God, and we are conformed to his image. In this union the highest blessedness of man consists. But prayer above all displays the glory of God, because through it his divine attributes and virtues are proclaimed, as it were with a resounding voice, and are exalted beyond measure. For he who prays confesses that God is present everywhere, who hears those who sigh to him from whatever place; that he is all-knowing, who searches even the desires of the heart; that he is almighty, who can provide whatever he wills for our salvation and free us from every evil; and that he is the fountain of every good, since from him are expected all blessings, temporal and heavenly; and that he is supremely merciful, who wishes to have mercy on us, to forgive us our sins and to give us eternal life; and finally that he is faithful and true, in whom all his promises are Yes and Amen (2 Cor. 1:20). Therefore, as dear to us as the glorifying of God is, and as manifold as our benefit is, so dear ought prayers to be.

units.la: LXXXIX. Non omnis precatio religiosa, vel Deo grata & accepta est. Quiritabantur, & non erat Salvator. Ad Jehovam, & non respondebat ipsis, Psal.XVIII.42. Tunc vocabunt me, & non respondebo, palpantes quaerent me, & non invenient me, Prov.I.28. Precandum igitur est, καθ' ὁ δεῖ sicut oportet, Rom.VIII.26. Et primo quidem precandus solus Deus est, qui in verbo suo se patefecit. Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & illi soli servies, Deut.VI.13. Matth.IV.10. Invoca me in die angustiae, liberabo te, & glorificabis me, Psal.L.15. Solus enim Deus καταλογωσης, omnipotens, Salvator est. Pertinet huc adoratio soli Deo debita, de qua fusè Loc.XV. Sect.2. §23.24. seq. diximus. Secundò, ad thronum gratiae solius Dei accedendum est cum seria meditatione tum Majestatis & gloriae ejus, qua super omnes creaturas infinitis parasangis eminet, & quae sola timorem & reverentiam in nobis operatur; tum misericordiae, gratiae & bonitatis, quam verbo, promissione & opere constantissimè exerit, quae fiduciam in nobis efficere potest. Precandum enim est tanta reverentia, ut si Deo, tanta fiducia, ut si amico loquamur, quomodo Lutherum orasse, vitae ejus scriptor refert. Tertiò, cordis desideria Deo exponenda sunt. Non enim precatio proprie labiorum, sed primum & praecipuè cordis opus est. Unde sic Anna ad Heli: Mulier aegra animo sum, & vinum aut siceram non bibi, sed effundo desiderium cordis mei coram Jehova, I.Sam.I.15. Quae etiam loquebatur in corde suo. Tantum labia ejus movebantur, vox autem ejus non audiebatur, ib. v. 13. Etiam David: Confidite ei omni tempore o populemi. Effundite coram eo cor vestrum, Psal.LXII.9. Effundo coram eo meditationem meam, & angustias meas coram ipso indico, ibid.CXLII.3. Quae cordis desideria non tantùm per verba & gestus corporis externos, sed inprimis per cogitationes internas, per gemitus & suspiria, quae Deo non minùs quàm sermo quivis ... patent, quia omnia corda exquirit Jehova, & omne figmentum cogitationum intelligit, I.Chronic. XXVIII.9. exponenda sunt. Ita Deus ad Mosen: Quid clamas ad me? Exod.XIV.15. cùm tamen nihil ore loqueretur, sed intimo tantùm cordis affectu ad Deum clamaret.
units.tr: LXXXIX. Not every prayer is religious, or pleasing and acceptable to God. "They cried out, but there was no Saviour; they cried to the LORD, but he did not answer them" (Ps. 18:42). "Then they shall call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me" (Prov. 1:28). Therefore we must pray as it is fitting [καθ' ὃ δεῖ] (Rom. 8:26). First, indeed, God alone is to be prayed to, he who has revealed himself in his word: "You shall worship the LORD your God, and serve him alone" (Deut. 6:13; Matt. 4:10). "Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me" (Ps. 50:15). For God alone is [καταλογωσης] almighty, the Saviour. To this belongs the worship owed to God alone, of which we have spoken at length in Loc. XV, sect. 2, §§23, 24 and following. Secondly, we must approach the throne of grace of God alone, with serious meditation both on his majesty and glory, by which he surpasses all creatures by infinite parasangs, and which alone works fear and reverence in us, and on his mercy, grace and goodness, which he most constantly displays in his word, promise and work, and which can produce trust in us. For we must pray with such reverence as if we were speaking to God, and with such trust as if we were speaking to a friend; so, as the writer of his life reports, Luther prayed. Thirdly, the desires of the heart must be laid open before God. For prayer is not properly the work of the lips, but first and chiefly of the heart. Hence Hannah says to Eli: "I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit; I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the LORD" (1 Sam. 1:15). She was also speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard (ibid., v. 13). So also David: "Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him" (Ps. 62:8). "I pour out my meditation before him, and I declare my troubles before him" (ibid., 142:2). These desires of the heart must be laid open not only by words and outward bodily gestures, but above all by inward thoughts, groans and sighs, which are no less manifest to God than any speech, because the LORD searches all hearts and understands every imagination of the thoughts (1 Chron. 28:9). Thus God said to Moses: "Why do you cry to me?" (Exod. 14:15), although he was speaking nothing with his mouth, but crying to God only with the inward affection of his heart.

units.la: XC. Quartò, cordis desideria soli Deo exponenda sunt, sed non nisi in Christo. Quicquid petieritis in nomine meo, hoc faciam, ut glorificetur Pater in Filio. Si quid in nomine meo petieritis, ego faciam, Joh.XIV.13.14. Nam ad Patrem sine Filio Sacerdote accedere non licet. Quis ille est, qui ב in fidem suam recepit cor suum, ut ad me accedat? quis sibi spopondit, cor suum tranquillavit, ut ad me, ceu ignem consumentem accedat sine Christo, Jerem.XXX.21. per illum (Pontificem sanctum &c.) accedimus ad Deum, Hebr. VII.25.26. Habemus fiduciam ad introitum Sancti in sanguine ejus; quem velut recentem & vivam viam dedicavit, ibid.X.19.20. Neque enim Deus nisi in Christo Mediatore tum satisfactionis, tum intercessionis, Sacerdote & Sponsore unico gratiosus & propitius invenitur. Cùm & in illo solo omnia nobis gratificatur, Rom.VIII.32. Et preces nostrae tot infirmitatibus obnoxiae Deo, nisi in Christo acceptae esse non possunt, in quo solo filiorum Dei haec balbuties placet. Et sic Pater in Filio compellandus est, ut intentio sit Patrem in Filio glorificandi; scilicet, ut agnoscamus, Patrem Filio dedisse, ut credentes in ipsum credamus in Deum, I.Pet. I.21. & per ipsum gratias agamus Deo, & gloriantes in eo gloriemur velut in Deo. Unde Quintò precationi necesse est, adsit fides in Christum, utpote qui merito suo omnem potestatem in Coelo & in terra consecutus est, Matth. XXVIII.18. & accepit dona in hominibus, Psal.LXVIII.19. atque ita nitamur promissione hac, quod quaecunque in nomine ejus, hoc est, ipso authore, & in fiducia meriti ejus, petierimus, acceptu-ri simus. Petat autem in fide, nihil dubitans, quin in fide Christi supplex desiderata consecuturus sit, Jac.I.6. Pie Hieronymus: Non orarem nisi crederem. Oratio sine fide Dei irrisio est. Cum fide charitas erga Divinam gloriam & proximi salutem conjungi debet. Sextò, precandum est in Spiritu & veritate. Nam Deus Spiritus est: & adorantes eum, in spiritu & veritate adorare debent, Joh.IV.24. In spiritu, non in carne, vel concupiscentia & ritibus carnalibus sine spiritu & pio cordis affectu; & veritate, non amplius in umbris, figuris, nedum in solis, sed in fide veritatis, Christi praestiti, cultu vero, sincero, recto, qualis Deum, qui Spiritus & veritas immutabilis est, decet. Septimò, sic precandum est, ne in iis, quae precamur à verbo & voluntate Dei aberremus. Precatio enim ex fide & bona voluntate, non ex concupiscentia proficisci debet. Non igitur petenda sunt non necessaria, inutilia, noxia, quae bonum nostrum & aliorum non sunt, & per quae Deus non glorificatur: Ea petenda sunt, quae Deus peti jussit, Atqui ille omnia peti jussit, quae à Deo ut Deo & Patre nostro, cum laude sapientiae Divinae & bono nostro atque aliorum dari possunt. Licet ergo nobis petere omnia bona, imò licet etiam petere perfectionem, & omnia, quorum defectus imperfectionis est; sic tamen, ut Deo arbitrium distridistributionis gratiarum suarum permittamus; & in universum quidem sic petamus sanctificationem, salutem & liberationem ab omni malo, ut tamen viam nostram in eum reiiciamus, securi, ipsum facturum esse, Psal. XXXVII. 5. Non enim ordinem distribuendæ gratiæ nobis vindicare possumus, quasi pro sapientia & ingenio nostro de œconomia gratiæ Deo gloriosa & nobis salutari decidere aliquid possemus. Nam etiam quid precemur, sicut oportet, ignoramus, Rom. VIII. 26. Octavo, etiam precanti humilitas & sensus indigentiæ atque miseriæ suæ apprimè necessarius est, ne petat quicquam cum superbia, & opinione meriti, tanquam si Deum debitorem habeat. Quid vobis mihi, Tyre & Sidon? Numquid meritum rependitis mihi? Et numquid vos meremini de me? Ocyssimè reddam meritum vestrum super caput vestrum, Joel. III. 4. Superbiæ ejusdem, non humilitatis est; pauca petere; cum rerum omnium indigeamus, & non precanti nihil eorum quibus fideles indigent, detur; & officii nostri sit, illa diligenter, serio & indesinenter petere, quæ Deus promisit. Nam cum talis promissio extet, ingratitudo extrema foret, non requirere, quid Deus promiserit, & ea non expetere, vel tanti non facere, sive cum Ecclesia iis potiamur, sive non.
units.tr: XC. Fourthly, the desires of the heart are to be laid before God alone, but only in Christ. "Whatever you ask in my name, I will do it, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask anything in my name, I will do it" (John 14:13-14). For no one may come to the Father without the Son as Priest. "Who is he that has pledged his heart to come to me? Who has promised himself and calmed his heart to approach me, as a consuming fire, without Christ?" (Jer. 30:21). "Through him (the holy High Priest, etc.) we draw near to God" (Heb. 7:25-26). "We have confidence to enter the sanctuary by his blood, which he has dedicated for us as a new and living way" (Heb. 10:19-20). For God is not found gracious and propitious except in Christ the Mediator, both of satisfaction and of intercession, the one Priest and Surety; and it is in him alone that he gives us all things graciously (Rom. 8:32). Nor can our prayers, so beset by so many weaknesses, be accepted by God except in Christ, in whom alone this stammering of the sons of God is pleasing. So the Father is to be addressed in the Son, with the aim of glorifying the Father in the Son; that is, that we acknowledge that the Father has given the Son, so that through believing in him we believe in God (1 Pet. 1:21), and through him give thanks to God, and in him glory as in God. Hence, fifthly, faith in Christ must be present in prayer, since by his merit he has obtained all power in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28:18), and has "received gifts among men" (Ps. 68:19). And so we rest on this promise, that whatever we ask in his name, that is, with him as author and in confidence in his merit, we shall receive. Let him ask in faith, doubting nothing, since he who asks in the faith of Christ will obtain what he desires (Jas. 1:6). Jerome piously says: "I would not pray unless I believed. Prayer without faith is mockery of God." Love for the divine glory and for the salvation of one's neighbour ought to be joined with faith. Sixthly, one must pray in Spirit and in truth. For God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth (John 4:24). In spirit, not in the flesh, or in lust and carnal rites without the Spirit and a devout affection of the heart; and in truth, no longer in shadows and figures, much less in these alone, but in faith in the truth of the Christ who has been given, with a worship that is true, sincere, and upright, such as befits God, who is Spirit and unchangeable truth. Seventhly, one must so pray that we do not go astray from the Word and will of God in what we ask. For prayer ought to proceed from faith and good will, not from desire. Therefore we must not ask for things that are unnecessary, useless, or harmful, which are not for our good or the good of others, and through which God is not glorified. We must ask for the things that God has commanded us to ask. Now he has commanded us to ask for all things that can be given by God as our God and Father, with praise of divine wisdom and for our good and that of others. It is lawful, then, for us to ask for all good things, indeed it is lawful also to ask for perfection and all things whose lack is imperfection; yet in such a way that we leave to God the decision about the distribution of his graces; and in general we so ask for sanctification, salvation, and deliverance from every evil that we nevertheless cast our way upon him, confident that he will act (Ps. 37:5). For we cannot claim for ourselves the order of the distribution of grace, as if, by our own wisdom and ingenuity, we could decide anything about the economy of grace, which is glorious to God and salutary to us. For we do not know what we ought to pray for as we ought (Rom. 8:26). Eighthly, humility and a sense of one's own need and misery are also most necessary for the one who prays, lest he ask for anything with pride and a notion of merit, as if he held God as a debtor. What have you to do with me, Tyre and Sidon? Are you repaying me something? And do you deserve anything from me? I will most swiftly return your deserving upon your own head (Joel 3:4). It is a sign of the same pride, not of humility, to ask for little, since we need all things, and nothing that the faithful need is given to one who does not ask; and it is our duty to ask diligently, earnestly, and unceasingly for those things that God has promised. For since such a promise stands, it would be the utmost ingratitude not to seek what God has promised, and not to desire it or to value it little, whether or not we obtain it with the Church.

units.la: XCI. Sed fidelis precationis numeros hoc ce omnes sine Spiritu S. non implemus.
units.tr: XCI. But we cannot fulfil any of the requirements of faithful prayer without the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Is enim Spiritus precationum est, Zach. XII. 10. Idque Apostolus eo argumento probat, quod nesciamus nos, quid oremus, sicut oportet, Rom. VIII. 26. Quæ scientiæ infirmitas ad multa se extendit, tum bona, quæ necessaria, quæve utilia sint; tum mala, pericula spiritualia, scandala, carnis nostræ affectiones, cordis lamas & profunditates, quæ expurgandæ & evacuandæ omnes sunt. Quid ergo oremus, sicut oportet, non cognoscimus, uti id cognosci meretur, atque cognoscibile est, si ad illud animum intendamus. Nec bona nostra, vel proximi; nec malorum averruncationem desideramus vel petimus sicut oportet, quia ne quidem cognoscimus, sicut oportet, vel cognoscere avemus. Neque ideo non in fide oramus, quia etiam, quæ non novimus, in fide petere possumus; tum quia quæ petere jussi sumus, ut ea petere jussi sumus, non dubitamus esse bona, & petimus secundum voluntatem ejus, 1. Joh. V. 14. tum quia Deo, qui, quæ re indigeamus, novit, Matth. VI. 32. confidimus: tum quia promissioni Dei inhæremus, neque dubitamus fore, ut, quæ petimus, accipiamus. Sed inprimis hic Spiritus S. infirmitati huic cognitionis & orationis nostræ opitulatur, interpellans pro nobis gemitibus, quos effari non licet. Sicut enim in ipso clamamus, v. 15. ita in eodem ingemiscimus, quia utrumque in nobis, ut paracletus clientum suorum causam agens, operatur, ceu signum studii & voluntatis suæ erga nos, quæ intercessionis instar habet. Infans matermo utero inclusus non clamat, nec nisi natus clamat. Sic & homo in naturali statu suo decumbens clamare ad Deum & ingemiscere non potest. Sed per Spiritum S. regenitus illico clamat: Abba, Pater. Quamprimum ille cor ingreditur, ad precandum movet. De Paulo primùm converso Christus ipse ad Ananiam: Ecce precatur, Act. IX. 11. Quia filii estis, Deus Spiritum Filii sui in corda vestra misit, qui clamat Abba, Pater, Gal. IV. 6. Scitè Prosper: Implet Spiritus S. organum suum, & tanquam fila chordarum, tangit digitus Dei corda Sanctorum. Nemo enim potest nominare Dominum Jesum nisi in Spiritu S. 1. Cor. XII. 3. Ideo etiam donum precandi, quod Spiritus S. in fidelibus citra sapientiam & intellectum eorum operatur, spiritus nomine venit; quia in spiritu hominis, & à Spiritu S. est. Quid igitur? Orabo Spiritu, sed & mente orabo. Psallam spiritu. Sed & psallam mente, seu intellectu, ib. XIV. 15.
units.tr: For He is the Spirit of prayers, Zach. XII. 10. The Apostle proves this from the fact that we do not know what we should pray for, as we ought, Rom. VIII. 26. This ignorance extends to many things: to what is good and needful, and what is useful; and to what is evil, to spiritual dangers, to stumbling-blocks, to the affections of our flesh, and to the shallows and depths of our heart, all of which must be cleansed and emptied out. So we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, though it deserves to be known, and is knowable, if we give our minds to it. Nor do we desire or ask, as we ought, for the averting of evils, either for our own good or our neighbour's, because we do not even know as we ought, nor are we eager to know. Yet we do not therefore fail to pray in faith, for we can ask in faith even for things we do not know: first, because we do not doubt that the things we have been commanded to ask for are good, and we ask according to his will, 1 John V. 14; second, because we trust God, who knows what we need, Matth. VI. 32; third, because we cling to the promise of God and do not doubt that we shall receive what we ask. But here above all the Holy Spirit helps this weakness of our knowing and praying, interceding for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. For as we cry out in him, v. 15, so in him we groan, since he works both in us, as an advocate pleading the cause of his clients, a sign of his zeal and goodwill toward us, which has the force of intercession. An infant enclosed in the mother's womb does not cry out, and cries out only once born. So too a man lying in his natural state cannot cry out to God or groan. But the one born again through the Holy Spirit at once cries out: Abba, Father. As soon as he enters the heart, he moves it to pray. Of Paul, just converted, Christ himself said to Ananias: Behold, he prays, Acts IX. 11. Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father, Gal. IV. 6. Prosper wisely says: The Holy Spirit fills his instrument, and as the finger of God touches the strings, so it touches the hearts of the saints. For no one can name the Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. XII. 3. Therefore also the gift of prayer, which the Holy Spirit works in believers apart from their wisdom and understanding, is called by the name of spirit, because it is in the spirit of man and is from the Holy Spirit. What then? I will pray with the spirit, but I will also pray with the mind. I will sing with the spirit, but I will also sing with the mind, that is, with the understanding, ibid. XIV. 15.

units.la: XCII. Sic precantes Deus exaudit. Invoca me in die angustiæ. Liberabo te, Psalm. L. 15. O auditor precum, ad te omnis caro accedet, Psal. LXV. 3. Petenti dabitur, &c. Omnis enim orans accipit, & quærens invenit, & pulsanti aperietur, Matth. VII. 7. 8. Nam remunerator est eorum, qui ipsum quærunt, Heb. XI. 6. De qua exauditione cum Jobo adversus hostes sic gratulari licet. Deridiculum me ero, invocans Deum, cui is respondet? Job. XII. 4. Cum enim in Christi nomine preces ad Deum fundantur, non potest non Deus aures vacivas iis præbere. Ego novi, quod semper me exaudias, Joh. XI. 42. Licet enim aliquando Deus, qui Spiritus sui vocem in nobis haud illiberiter audit, & constantia nostra, seu fructu justitiæ delectatur, auxilium differat, & pii quiritari necesse habeant: Numquid in seculum defecit misericordia ejus? Numquid oblitus est Deus misereri? Psal. LXXVII. 3. 9. 10. quin & cupita ipsa non semper Deus faciat, subinde simpliciter jubens in sua gratia acquiescere, 2. Cor. XII. 9. tamen exauditio certa est, & gratificatur Deus vel citò, vel tardius, prout saluti & explorationi constantiæ nostræ conducit; & vel ea, quæ petimus, vel majora illis. Nam potest supra omnia facere, ex superfluo eorum, quæ petimus, vel cogitamus, Ephes. III. 20. Sic ergo precibus, studio & & patientia nobis opus est, ut tamen à Dei, qui multò plura potest, quàm petimus & intelligimus, maxima quæque expectemus. Nam quod Evangelium ad nos pervenit, & id purè nobis prædicatur, & credimus, ab Antichristi jugo liberati sumus, à tot malis custodimur, in tot peccatis nostris non deserimur, quo studio, quibus cogitationibus, quibus precibus nostris impetravimus?
units.tr: XCII. God hears those who pray in this way. Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, Psalm L. 15. O you who hear prayers, all flesh shall come to you, Psalm LXV. 3. To him who asks it shall be given, etc. For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it shall be opened, Matth. VII. 7, 8. For he is the rewarder of those who seek him, Heb. XI. 6. Concerning this hearing we may rejoice over our enemies with Job: I am made a laughingstock, calling upon God, who answers me? Job XII. 4. For when prayers are poured out to God in the name of Christ, God cannot but give ear to them. I know that you always hear me, John XI. 42. For although God sometimes delays help, and the godly must perforce cry out, while God gladly hears the voice of his Spirit within us and takes delight in our constancy, or the fruit of righteousness: Has his mercy ceased forever? Has God forgotten to be merciful? Psalm LXXVII. 9, 10. Indeed God does not always grant what we desire, but at times simply bids us rest content in his grace, 2 Cor. XII. 9. Yet the answer is certain, and God grants our requests either soon or later, as is good for our salvation and for the testing of our constancy, and grants either what we ask or something greater. For he is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, Eph. III. 20. So we need prayer, zeal and patience, yet while we wait we should expect the greatest things from God, who can do far more than we ask or understand. For consider: that the Gospel has come to us and is preached to us in its purity, and that we believe it; that we have been freed from the yoke of Antichrist; that we are guarded from so many evils and are not forsaken in so many sins: by what zeal, what thoughts, what prayers of ours did we obtain these things?

units.la: XCIII. Qualiscunque ergo precum nostrarum exauditio est, nunquam illa ex earum merito contingit. Nam & ipsæ preces nostræ sunt effecta gratiæ, Spiritus sanctificantis, justitiæ nobis donatæ, & meriti Christi; nec non signa, quòd nobis à Deo in Christo omnia bona parata sint, Rom. VIII. 32. Sicut suspiria, ita etiam orationes nostræ sunt quasi voces Spiritus S. quibus pro nobis intercedit, & suum studium, quod nostri causa habet, significat. Spiritus coopitulatur nostris infirmitatibus. Nam quid precemur, sicut oportet, ignoramus. Sed idem ille Spiritus maximè intercedit pro nobis suspiriis ineffabilibus. Qui verò scrutatur corda, novit, quodnam sit studium Spiritus, quòd secundum Deum intercedat pro Sanctis, ibid. VIII. 26. 27. Ipsæ adeò preces sunt dona Dei. Quid enim majus est, quàm habere accessum ad Patrem cum fiducia, certàque persuasione, quòd quæ petis
units.tr: XCIII. Whatever the answer to our prayers is, it never comes on account of their merit. For our prayers themselves are the effects of grace, of the sanctifying Spirit, of the righteousness given to us, and of the merit of Christ; and they are also signs that all good things are prepared for us by God in Christ, Rom. VIII. 32. Like our sighs, so also our prayers are as it were the voices of the Holy Spirit, by which he intercedes for us and signifies the zeal he has on our behalf. The Spirit helps our weaknesses. For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought. But that same Spirit himself intercedes for us most of all with unspeakable sighs. And he who searches the hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because he intercedes for the saints according to God, ibid. VIII. 26, 27. Prayers themselves, then, are gifts of God. For what is greater than to have access to the Father with confidence and the sure persuasion that what you ask

units.la: Precationis author in nobis Spiritus S. est. petimus, secundum promissionem ejus accepturi simus? Quid gloriosius, quàm clamare, Abba, Pater? Quid beatius, quàm scire, quæ petimus, non nostra desideria, sed Spiritus S. studium esse? Quæ omnia multum à merito & satisfactione, quam Pontificii precibus, ceu operi poenali, tribuunt, absunt. Quæ opinio ab humana, ut diximus, superbia provenit: cùm tamen preces humanæ tenuitatis certissimum argumentum sint. Et S. Paulus ibid. precum nostrarum tantam imperfectionem declaret, ut homo ignoret, quid oret, sicut oportet, & gemitu, velut gravatus suam infirmitatem profiteatur. Nam quòd preces Cornelii ad memoriam Dei ascendisse Actor. X. 4. dicuntur, probat, eas Deo gratas & acceptas esse, & ab eodem exaudiri, sed non propter nostrum, verùm propter Christi meritum.
units.tr: The author of prayer within us is the Holy Spirit. we shall receive according to his promise? What is more glorious than to cry out, Abba, Father? What is more blessed than to know that what we ask is not our own desires but the zeal of the Holy Spirit? All of this is far removed from the merit and satisfaction which the Papists ascribe to prayers as a penal work. That opinion arises from human pride, as we have said, although human prayers are the most certain evidence of human frailty. And St Paul in the same place declares such great imperfection in our prayers that a man does not know what he should pray for as he ought, and, as if burdened, confesses his weakness with groaning. For that the prayers of Cornelius are said to have ascended into the memory of God, Acts X. 4, proves that they were pleasing and acceptable to God and were heard by him, yet not on account of our worth, but on account of the merit of Christ.

units.la: XCIV. Dona Dei alia jam accepimus: alia nobis desunt. Quæ jam accepimus, per εὐχαριστίαν gratiarum actionem recognoscenda sunt. Quæ nobis aliisque desunt petenda, & mala, cum quibus conflictamur, deprecanda sunt. Ideo S. Paulus Ephes. I. II. III. de bonis jam acceptis loquens, ferè ea per recitationem suæ gratiarum actionis commemorat: de nondum acceptis, velut augmento, perseverantia & amplificatione Regni Dei agens, ea per recitationem precum explicat. Et 1. Tim. II. 1. diserte quatuor orationis species, δεήσεις petitiones auxilii in malis: προσευχὰς precationes, quibus bona communia petimus: ἐντεύξεις intercessiones, quibus aliorum mala deprecamur: & εὐχαριστίας gratiarum actiones pro beneficiis à nobis aliisque acceptis, enumerat. Alibi 1. Thess. V. 17. 18. has species ad duas, gratiarum actionem, & προσευχὰς preces, sub quibus deprecationes malorum, petitiones bonorum, & intercessionem pro aliis intelligit, revocat.
units.tr: XCIV. Some of God's gifts we have already received; others are still lacking to us. What we have already received must be acknowledged with thanksgiving [εὐχαριστίαν]. What is lacking to us and to others must be asked for, and the evils with which we struggle must be deprecated. So St Paul, in Eph. I, II, III, speaking of the good things already received, recalls them mostly by the recitation of his thanksgiving; and speaking of what is not yet received, such as the increase, perseverance and enlargement of the kingdom of God, he sets them out by the recitation of prayers. And in 1 Tim. II. 1 he plainly enumerates four kinds of prayer: entreaties [δεήσεις], petitions for help in evils; prayers [προσευχὰς], by which we ask for common goods; intercessions [ἐντεύξεις], by which we deprecate the evils of others; and thanksgivings [εὐχαριστίας] for benefits received by us and by others. Elsewhere, 1 Thess. V. 17, 18, he reduces these kinds to two, thanksgiving and prayers [προσευχὰς], under which he understands the deprecation of evils, the petition for goods, and intercession for others.

units.la: XCV. Præcedit species reliquas εὐχαριστία gratiarum actio pro bonis, quæ ipsi à Deo jam exauditi accepimus, & acceperunt alii. Par enim est, ut nova beneficia rogaturus vetera grata mente prius recolat & commemoret, quia gratiarum actio novi beneficii invitatio est. Estque illa gratiarum actio oratio fidelium, qua illi gratiæ & bonitatis Divinæ sensu in conferendis bonis & averruncandis malis exhilarati, nomen Dei invocant, ejus gratiæ cuncta accepta humiliter ferunt, sapientiam, bonitatem, misericordiam & potentiam ejus laudibus amplissimis extollunt, & ex cunctis illis gloriam Dei celebrant, atque sic se dignos Dei amore, hoc est, tales, quales sunt, quos Deus amat, exhibent. Sacrifica Deo confessionem, Psal. L. 14. Tibi sacrificabo sacrificia confessionis, ibid. CXVI. 17. Solvemus juvencos, labia nostra, Hos. XIV. 2. Heb. XIII. 16. Gratias agentes semper de omnibus, in nomine Domini nostri Jesu Christi, Deo & Patri, Ephes. V. 20. In omnibus gratias agite. Hæc enim est voluntas Dei in Christo Jesu erga vos, 1. Thess. V. 18. Gratiæ agendæ sunt ἐν παντὶ in omni, seu de omnibus rebus, bonis & malis. Qualis εὐχαριστία etiam ob res malas hominis Christiani proprium opus est.
