Solus enim ille novit, omnia fidelibus cooperari ad bonum, Rom. VIII. 28. nos Christo vivere & mori, ibid. XIV. 7. 8. Etiam cùm labimur, Deo sacrificium confessionis & gratiarum actionis offerendum est, non quòd peccata gratiarum actionis materia sint, sed quia habemus apud Deum Paracletum Jesum Christum, justum illum, 1. Joh. II. 1. & certi sumus, quòd potentia Dei in nostra infirmitate consummetur, 2. Cor. XII. 9. nobisque bonum esse humiliari, ne nobis confidamus, & supra alios peccatores nos efferamus; quin potius corda nostra, ne quid mali in iis lateat, scrutemur. Gratias agimus chirurgo brachium secanti, medico pharmacum amarum propinanti, dummodo uterque sic sanitati inserviat. Et quanto ampliores gratiæ cœlesti medico persolvendæ sunt, cùm nos per mala & mortem ipsam sanat, atque cœlestem ad vitam traducit? Et si pro malis gratiæ Deo referendæ sunt, multò magis pro bonis, pro Christo & justitia ejus, pro spe gloriæ, & benedictionibus, quæ in superceelestibus sunt, persolvendæ sunt? Et persolvendæ illæ sunt tum sincerè, in veritate, non dolo labiorum, quia propinquus Jehova est omnibus, qui eum invocant באמת in veritate, Psal. CXLV. 18. tum perfectè, pro modulo persolventis, ne pro imbribus gratiæ guttas orationis reddat: tum hilares; quia hilarem datorem, adeóque etiam gratiarum actorem, diligit, 2. Cor. IX. 7. & omnibus dat ἁπλῶς simpliciter, Jac. I. 5. & ἁπλῶς opulenter; tum prægnantes, non modio, nec trimodio, sed toto horreo, quod ajunt, adhibito membro nobilissimo, lingua cum corde connexa: tum artificiosè compositæ, repræsentantes inprimis virtutes illas Dei, à quibus præsens benedictio manavit; quarum exemplum est in illis Mosis: Fortitudo mea & laus est Jah. Fuit enim mihi in salutem. Ipse Deus meus: propterea tabernaculum ei faciam. Ipse Deus patris mei; propterea exaltabo illum. Jehova vir belli, Jehova nomen ejus, Exod. XV. 2. 3. Tum denique perseverantes, quandiu ipsa Dei gratia manet, quæ in æternum manet. Laudabo Jehovam in vita mea. Psallam Deo meo, quamdiu ero, Psal. CXLVI. 2.
units.tr: XCV. Thanksgiving (εὐχαριστία) comes before the other kinds of prayer, giving thanks for the good things we have already received from God when our prayers were heard, and that others have received. For one who is about to ask for new benefits should first recall and remember the old ones with a grateful mind, since thanksgiving is an invitation to a new benefit. This thanksgiving is the prayer of the faithful, by which they, cheered by a sense of God's grace and goodness in bestowing good things and averting evils, call upon the name of God, humbly receive all things as gifts of his grace, extol his wisdom, goodness, mercy and power with the highest praises, and from all these celebrate the glory of God. In this way they show themselves worthy of God's love, that is, such as God loves. Offer to God a sacrifice of confession, Ps. 50:14. I will offer to you the sacrifices of confession, ibid. 116:17. We will render the calves of our lips, Hos. 14:2; Heb. 13:16. Giving thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God and the Father, Eph. 5:20. In everything give thanks; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you, 1 Thess. 5:18. Thanks are to be given ἐν παντὶ [en panti], in everything, or for all things, good and bad. Such thanksgiving, even for evil things, is the proper work of a Christian. For he alone knows that all things work together for good for the faithful, Rom. 8:28, and that we live and die to Christ, ibid. 14:7-8. Even when we fall, a sacrifice of confession and thanksgiving is to be offered to God. This is not because sins are a matter for thanksgiving, but because we have with the Father an advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous, 1 John 2:1, and we are certain that the power of God is made perfect in our weakness, 2 Cor. 12:9. It is good for us to be humbled, so that we do not trust in ourselves and raise ourselves above other sinners; rather we should search our hearts, so that nothing evil lies hidden in them. We thank the surgeon who cuts our arm and the physician who gives us a bitter draught, provided that each serves our health. How much greater thanks must be paid to the heavenly physician, who heals us through evils and even through death, and leads us to heavenly life! And if thanks must be given to God for evils, how much more must they be given for good things: for Christ and his righteousness, for the hope of glory, and for the blessings which are in the heavens above? These thanks must be rendered sincerely, in truth, not with deceit of the lips, because Jehovah is near to all who call upon him in truth [בֶּאֱמֶת], Ps. 145:18. They must be rendered perfectly, in proportion to the one giving thanks, lest in return for showers of grace he give back only drops of prayer. They must be rendered cheerfully, because God loves a cheerful giver, and so also a cheerful thanker, 2 Cor. 9:7, and gives to all simply [ἁπλῶς], Jas. 1:5, and liberally [ἁπλῶς]. They must be rendered fruitfully, not with a peck or three pecks, but with the whole granary, as they say, employing that most noble member, the tongue, joined with the heart. They must be skilfully composed, representing above all those virtues of God from which the present blessing flowed. An example of this is in the words of Moses: The Lord is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation. This is my God, and I will prepare him a dwelling; the God of my father, and I will exalt him. Jehovah is a man of war; Jehovah is his name, Exod. 15:2-3. Lastly, they must be rendered perseveringly, as long as God's grace itself remains, which remains forever. I will praise Jehovah in my life. I will sing psalms to my God as long as I am, Ps. 146:2.

units.la: XCVI. Proxima huic est προσευχὴ precatio, seu αἴτησις Jac. I. 5. petitio bonorum, quæ nobis desunt, & quæ abundare atque florere impensè cupimus. Quæ in universum tum Regnum & gloria Dei, tum salus & commodum proprium sunt. Gloriam Dei primore, salutem nostram posteriore loco petimus. Atque ubi in contentionem veniunt, illam huic non tantùm præferimus, sed etiam cum hujus dispendio optamus, exemplo Mosis petentis potius deleri è libro vitæ, quàm ut gloria promissionis Divinæ detrimentum patiatur, Exod. XXXII. 32. Et bona nostra petenda alia spiritualia & æterna, alia corporalia & temporalia sunt. Quorum illa primò & præcipuè, hæc ut libera accessio; illa quatenus simpliciter necessaria, absolutè, hæc cum conditione petenda sunt. Quærite primò Regnum Dei & justitiam ejus, & hæc omnia vobis adjicientur, Matth. VI. 33. Domine, si voluerиc, poteris me purificare, ibid. VIII. 2. Si invenero gratiam in oculis Jehovæ, reducet me. Sin vero dixerit: Non est mihi in eo beneplacitum; Ecce ego: Faciat mihi, quod bonum est in oculis suis, 2. Sam. XV. 25. 26. Nihil enim obstat, quòd in Oratione Domini prius panem quotidianum, quàm remissionem peccatorum petimus, tum quia utrumque petitio bonorum spiritualium, sub petitione sanctificandi Nominis nis Dei, Regni ejus accelerandi, & voluntatis Dei in terra religiose implendæ, comprehensa, præceßit: tum quia licet spiritualia & æterna voto atque intentione nostra primò quærenda sunt, tamen temporis ordine terrena ad vitam neceßaria, ceu minora & leviora, sic primò peti possunt, ut ea petitione simul semelque defuncti in potioribus diutius immoremur. Petenda ergo sunt, quæcunque animæ & corpori neceßaria sunt. Sed neceßitas illa tamen non unius generis est. Quædam enim ad statum animæ & corporis absolutè neceßaria sunt; quomodo etiam corpori neceßaria sunt, quæ ad concupiscentiæ in eo Regnum abolendum pertinent, ut sanctificationis particeps fiat. Alia ad majorem lætitiam, vel ad uberiorem fructum & claritatem nominis ac Regni Dei, ejúsque propagationem, & pleniorem Regni Sathanæ destructionem: nonnulla etiam ad exercendam charitatem, & opus Dei faciendum, inprimis illud, quod singulari vocatione cuique commendatum est; neceßaria sunt. Circa hæc quidem omnia affectus, appetitus & desiderium nostrum versari debet, sic tamen, ut fides nostra absolutè neceßaria, & promissa sine dubitatione & conditione petat; ad cætera autem seriò anhelemus, & sic delectatio animæ nostræ sit, ut illa fiant, ut tamen horam Divinæ gratiæ & benedictionis cum patientia præstolemur, & cuncta ejus arbitrio permittamus. Ac licet verbum Dei, & promissiones ejus, quæ bonorum petendorum regula sunt, omnibus & singulis, rudibus inprimis & ἀναλ-φαβήτως non æquè omnes notæ & exploratæ sint, tamen universalis promissio extat, quòd Deus in omnibus, quæ κατὰ τὸ θέλημα secundum voluntatem ejus petierimus, nos exaudire velit, 1. Joh. V. 14. Quicquid etiam Sanctos à Deo petiisse, sine Dei reprehensione, & extra specialis officii limites, legimus vel audimus, illud ipsum etiam juste à Deo peti potest.
units.tr: XCVI. Next to this is prayer (προσευχή), or petition (αἴτησις, Jas. 1:5), asking for the good things which we lack and which we eagerly desire to abound and flourish. In general these concern both the kingdom and glory of God and our own salvation and advantage. We ask for the glory of God first, and for our salvation in the second place. When the two come into conflict, we not only prefer the former to the latter, but even wish for the loss of the latter, following the example of Moses, who asked to be blotted out of the book of life rather than that the glory of the divine promise should suffer harm, Exod. 32:32. Our goods to be sought are partly spiritual and eternal, and partly bodily and temporal. The former are to be asked first and chiefly, the latter as a free addition. The former, insofar as they are simply necessary, are to be asked absolutely; the latter are to be asked with a condition. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you, Matt. 6:33. Lord, if you will, you can make me clean, ibid. 8:2. If I find favour in the eyes of Jehovah, he will bring me back. But if he says: I have no pleasure in you; behold, here I am; let him do to me what is good in his eyes, 2 Sam. 15:25-26. Nothing stands in the way of the fact that in the Lord's Prayer we ask for daily bread before the forgiveness of sins. This is both because the request for spiritual goods, contained under the petitions to hallow God's name, to hasten his kingdom, and to fulfil God's will religiously on earth, came first; and because, although spiritual and eternal things are to be sought first in our vow and intention, yet in the order of time the earthly things necessary for life, as lesser and lighter, may be asked first, so that by one petition we may be dispatched at once and linger longer over the weightier matters. Therefore whatever is necessary for soul and body is to be asked. But this necessity is not of one kind. Some things are absolutely necessary for the state of soul and body; and so also are those things necessary for the body which pertain to the abolishing of the kingdom of concupiscence in it, so that it may become a partaker of sanctification. Others are necessary for greater joy, or for more abundant fruit and brightness of the name and kingdom of God, its propagation, and the fuller destruction of Satan's kingdom. Some are also necessary for exercising love and doing the work of God, above all that which has been entrusted to each by a singular calling. Around all these things our affections, appetites and desire should indeed be occupied; yet in such a way that our faith asks absolutely, and without doubt or condition, for what is necessary and promised. For the rest we are to long earnestly, so that our soul's delight is in their being done; yet we must await the hour of divine grace and blessing with patience, and commit everything to his will. And although the word of God and his promises, which are the rule of the goods to be asked, are not equally known and tested to all and each, especially to the unlearned and the illiterate [ἀναλφαβήτως], yet there stands a universal promise, that God wishes to hear us in all things which we ask according to his will [κατὰ τὸ θέλημα], 1 John 5:14. Whatever we read or hear that the saints asked of God, without rebuke from God and beyond the limits of a special office, that very thing too can justly be asked of God.

units.la: XCVII. Cum περισσὸν bonorum petitione, δέησις deprecatio malorum, seu potius supplex petitio (hoc enim δέησις proprie notat) auxilii Dei in malis cohæret.
units.tr: XCVII. The petition for good things [περισσὸν] is joined with the deprecation of evils [δέησις], or rather with a humble petition for God's help in evils, since δέησις properly signifies this.

units.la: Nam & ipsa mali averruncatio bonum aliquod est. Cùmque aliud malum culpæ, aliud pœnæ sit, utrumque legitimè deprecamur, sed conveniente modo utrobique servato. Et adversus peccati quidem reatum & dominium totis viribus jugiter precandum nobis est, quia hæc à communione Dei excludunt, & abominandos ipsi reddunt. Etiam tentationes externas ad peccatum impellentes juste deprecamur, quia licet non ejusdem cum peccato generis sint, cùm & ipse Christus iis obnoxius fuerit, nostri tamen respectu periculo non vacant, quia fomitis & pulveris pyrii instar ad tentationum Sathanicarum scintillas excipiendas proclives nimium sumus. Malum verò pœnæ vel æternum, vel internum & spirituale, vel externum & temporale est. Adversus malum æternum, quod æterna damnatio est, indesinenter nobis orandum est. Adversus interna & spiritualia mala, seu pœnas, quæ peccatoribus obstinatis justo Dei judicio infliguntur; cujusmodi sunt, traditio in manum Sathanæ & mentem reprobam, desertio à Deo, mentis excæcatio, cordis obduratio, conscientia κεκαυτηριασμένη, non minùs
units.tr: For averting evil is itself some good. Since one evil is of guilt and another of punishment, we may rightly pray against both, though in a suitable manner in each case. Against the guilt and dominion of sin we must pray continually and with all our strength, because these cut us off from communion with God and make us abominable to him. We also rightly pray against external temptations that drive us to sin. Although they are not of the same kind as sin, since Christ himself was subject to them, they are not without danger for us, because we are far too prone, like tinder and gunpowder, to catch the sparks of Satanic temptation. The evil of punishment is either eternal, or internal and spiritual, or external and temporal. We must pray without ceasing against eternal evil, which is eternal damnation. Against internal and spiritual evils, that is, the punishments which the just judgment of God inflicts on obstinate sinners (such as being handed over into Satan's hand, a reprobate mind, desertion by God, blindness of mind, hardening of heart, and a conscience seared [κεκαυτηριασμένη]), we must pray no less

units.la: obnixè, quàm adversus æternam damnationem; cujus illæ limen & vestibulum sunt; orandum nobis est. Alia externorum & temporalium malorum, cujusmodi morbi, afflictiones, exilia, orbitas, paupertas, ignominia, mors corporalis aliáque ejus generis sunt, ratio est. Cùm enim hæc electis in pharmaca & remedia salutaria convertantur, non absolutè ea deprecanda, sed Deus rogandus est, ut ea vel auferre, vel moderari, vel nobis ita sanctificare, nósque ad patientiam eorum præparare dignetur, ut per ea simul Deus glorificetur, simul animarum nostrarum salus promoveatur. Modus verò deprecandorum malorum idem, qui petendorum bonorum est, quia ipsa malorum remotio, quam à Deo petimus, boni rationem habet.
units.tr: earnestly than against eternal damnation, of which these are the threshold and vestibule. Other external and temporal evils, such as diseases, afflictions, exile, bereavement, poverty, disgrace, bodily death, and the like, call for a different treatment. Since these are turned into healing medicines for the elect, they are not to be prayed against absolutely. Rather, we must ask God that he would deign either to remove them, or to moderate them, or to sanctify them to us and prepare us to bear them patiently, so that through them God may be glorified and the salvation of our souls advanced at the same time. The manner of praying against evils is the same as that of praying for good things, since the very removal of evil, which we seek from God, has the character of a good.

units.la: XCVIII. Superest ἐντευξις intercessio pro aliis, quæ ex charitate proximi proficiscitur, quomodo in tota Oratione Dominica non oramus soli. Dicimus enim: Pater noster: Da nobis: Remitte nobis. Et in petitione tertia pro omnibus hominibus petimus. Fiat voluntas tua ut in Cœlo, sic etiam in terra. Vigilandum nempe est δεήσεσι καὶ πάντων ἁγίων oratione pro omnibus sanctis, Ephes. VI. 18. Hoc enim concordiæ, charitatis, conspirationis est. Et vult Deus χαρίσματα ἐκ πολλῶν πρεσβευόντων ἐυχαριστηθῆ διὰ πολλῶν donum nobis collatum ex multis respectibus per multos gratiarum actione celebrari, 2. Cor. I. 11. ut ita fructus laudis Dei ad plures perveniat, & illorum charitas in mutua congratulatione exerceatur. Et orandum est pro omnibus, non vel defunctis, utpote quorum immutabilis status est; vel viventibus, qui peccatum in Spiritum S. committunt, quia illud remitti non potest; vel pro omnibus & singulis collectivè, ut salventur, quia voluntas Dei non est, ut in universum omnes homines salventur; sed ὑπὲρ πάντων pro omnibus hominibus, 1. Tim. II. 1. cujuscunque demum conditionis sint, sive intra, sive extra Ecclesiam; sive fideles, sive infideles, sive nobiles, sive ignobiles; sive amici, sive inimici sint; dummodo eo in statu sint, ut precibus nostris juvari possint. Cujus rei has rationes ibidem Apostolus affert: velut quòd hoc bonum & acceptum sit coram Deo Salvatore nostro, v. 3. qui cùm Salvator sit, ei allimilari, precibus salvando alios suo modo, debemus: quòd Deus omnes (quosvis) salvari, & ad agnitionem veritatis pervenire velit, v. 4. omnibus proin media salutis, quæ inter etiam preces mutuæ sunt, applicanda sint, inprimis cùm charitatis judicium secutis de nemine desperandum sit: quòd unus sit Deus, unus Mediator Dei & hominum, v. 5. qui proin in N. T. inimicitiam inter gentes abolere, populos unire, & non Judæorum duntaxat, sed etiam Gentium Deus & Salvator esse voluit. Deus non amplius populos distinguit, sed omnium Deus & Salvator est. Nec precantes igitur distinguere debent. Dei gratia non est parca. Nec vota nostra restricta esse debent. Neque obstat, quòd precari περὶ πάντων τῶν ἁγίων pro omnibus Sanctis, Ephes. VI. 18. jubemur. Nam intercedendm inprimis pro sanctis est, non exclusis reliquis, qui sanctificari possunt. Qui enim charitatis ordo est, à nobis in loco expositus, idem intercessionis, quæ à charitate est, esse Deprecatio malorum, seu petitio auxilii Dei in malis. Intercessio pro aliis. esse debet. Atque charitas jam conversos & sanctos ante omnes reliquos respicit. Dum tempus opportunum habemus, fimus benefici erga omnes, maxime autem erga domesticos fidei, Gal. VI. 10. Pari ratione pro omnibus precandum est; sed inprimis pro Sanctis, pro Ecclesia Christi militante, fidis Ecclesiae Dei ministris, domesticis, patria, & civitatis ejusdem, quam incolimus, membris. Denique sicut pro nobis gratias Deo agimus, bona precamur, mala deprecamur: ita pro aliis faciendum idem est.
units.tr: XCVIII. There remains ἐντευξις, intercession for others, which springs from love of neighbour; this is why in the whole Lord's Prayer we do not pray alone. For we say: Our Father; give us; forgive us. And in the third petition we pray for all men: Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. We must, indeed, be watchful in "supplication and prayer for all the saints" (Eph. 6.18). For this belongs to concord, to charity, and to unity of spirit. God wills that the gift bestowed on us, obtained through the prayers of many [χαρίσματα ἐκ πολλῶν πρεσβευόντων ἐυχαριστηθῆ διὰ πολλῶν], be celebrated with thanksgiving by many (2 Cor. 1.11), so that the fruit of praise to God may reach more people and their love may be exercised in mutual rejoicing. We must pray for all: not for the dead, whose state is unchangeable; nor for the living who have committed the sin against the Holy Spirit, since that cannot be forgiven; nor for all and each collectively, that they may be saved, since it is not God's will that all men without exception be saved; but "for all men" (1 Tim. 2.1) [ὑπὲρ πάντων], of whatever condition they are, whether within or outside the Church, whether faithful or unbelieving, noble or base, friends or enemies, provided they are in such a state that they can be helped by our prayers. The Apostle gives these reasons for this in the same place: that it is good and acceptable before God our Saviour (v. 3), and since he is Saviour, we ought to be made like him by praying, in our own way, for the salvation of others; that God wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (v. 4), so the means of salvation, which include mutual prayers, must be applied to all, especially since, following the judgment of charity, no one should be despaired of; that there is one God and one Mediator between God and men (v. 5), who therefore in the New Testament wished to abolish enmity between the nations, to unite the peoples, and to be God and Saviour not of the Jews alone but of the Gentiles too. God no longer distinguishes peoples; he is the God and Saviour of all. Those who pray, therefore, ought not to distinguish either. The grace of God is not niggardly, and our vows ought not to be restricted. Nor does it stand in the way that we are commanded to pray "for all the saints" (περὶ πάντων τῶν ἁγίων, Eph. 6.18). For intercession is to be made above all for the saints, without excluding the rest who can be sanctified. The order of charity, which we have set out in its place, is also the order of the intercession that springs from charity: intercession for others ought to be made. Charity looks first to those who are converted and holy, before all others: "As we have opportunity, let us do good to all, and especially to the household of faith" (Gal. 6.10). By the same reasoning we must pray for all, but above all for the saints, for the militant Church of Christ, for the faithful ministers of God's Church, for our household, our country, and the members of the city we inhabit. Finally, just as we give thanks to God for ourselves, pray for good things, and pray against evils, so the same must be done for others.

units.la: XCIX. Cum precationis his speciebus imprecatio pugnat. Nam nec sibi, nec aliis, sine speciali Dei mandato, imprecari licet. Non sibi, quia quisque seipsum amare tenetur, & nemo carnem suam odio habet, sed eam nutrit & fovet, Ephes. V.29. Jobus diei nativitatis suae maledixit, neque probatus tamen a Deo, neque imitandus: at sibi non maledixit. Neque jurantes teste & vindice Deo invocato sibi imprecantur, quia imprecandi illa formula jurata non adhibetur directe ad sibi imprecandum, sed ad veritati attestandum fortius, & ut sit vinculum speciale, quo jurans se ultro & certius firmiusque ad juramenti fidem exolvendam obstringit. At nec mulier adulterii suspecta sibi imprecari tenebatur. Sive enim illa innocens fuit, hausto zelotypiae poculo, diras adversus se nullas protulit, sed fidem innocentiae suae fecit; sive nocens fuit, ingenua confessione zelotypiae poculum, & cum eodem diras omnes vitare debuit potuitque. Praeterea nec mulier ejusmodi imprecationes illas proferre, sed tantum Sacerdoti eas proferenti, Amen dicendo, subscribere debuit, Num. V.12. &c. Tanta in juramentis etiam legitimis cautio & religio fuit. At nec aliis, citra speciale Dei mandatum, quale Prophetae habuerunt, imprecari licet. Nam proximum sicut se ipsum diligere quisque tenetur. Causa impia, & veritati Divinae adversans damnari, dirisque omnibus defigi semper meretur: at non personae, quae eam sustinent; nisi quatenus salus spiritus eorum requirit, ut corpus dometur, 1. Cor. V.5. 1. Tim. I. 20. Adversus Paganismum, Judaismum, Turcismum, Antichristianismum, consilia & molimina eorum precari semper licet: adversus Paganos, Judaeos, Turcas, Papistas nunquam. Hostes porro nostri vel privati, vel publici & Ecclesiae sunt. Privatis imprecari nunquam licet, quia etiam inimicos diligere jubemur, & tenemur. Publici curabiles vel incurabiles sunt. Curabiles intercessione nostra juvari debent. Incurabiles soli Deo, & quibus ille revelat, noti sunt. Quibus ille revelat, illos eadem revelatione singulari ad imprecandum iis movet. Tales Prophetae erant, a Spiritu Dei lati, 2. Pet. I. 21. qui tamen & ipsi non tam imprecati sunt, quam obventura hostibus Ecclesiae deploratis mala praedixerunt. Quos eodem Spiritu non praeditis imitari haud licet. Nam & discipulis suis Eliae exemplo Samaritanis imprecatoris Christus dixit: Nescitis cujus spiritus fitis vos, Luc. IX. 55. Nobis adversus homines impios, obstinatos, Ecclesiae persecutores diros, ... & pertinaces indefinite precari, sine speciali ad personas, quas Dei judicio relinquere praestat, applicatione, sufficiat, formula tali, quae olim procedente Arca usurpari suevit.
units.tr: XCIX. Cursing is incompatible with these kinds of prayer. Neither for oneself nor for others may one curse without a special command of God. Not for oneself, because each is bound to love himself, and no one hates his own flesh but nourishes and cherishes it (Eph. 5.29). Job cursed the day of his birth, yet he was neither approved by God nor to be imitated, and he did not curse himself. Nor do those who swear, calling God to witness and avenger, curse themselves, because that formula of an oath is not used directly to curse oneself, but to attest the truth more strongly and as a special bond by which the one swearing binds himself more readily and firmly to keep the faith of his oath. Nor was the woman suspected of adultery bound to curse herself. For if she was innocent, after drinking the cup of jealousy she uttered no dire curses against herself but gave proof of her innocence; and if she was guilty, by an open confession she ought and could avoid the cup of jealousy and all the curses that go with it. Moreover, the woman was not to utter those imprecations herself, but only to assent to the priest who pronounced them, by saying Amen (Num. 5.12 etc.). Such was the caution and reverence observed even in lawful oaths. Nor may one curse others without a special command of God, such as the prophets had. For each is bound to love his neighbour as himself. An impious cause, opposed to divine truth, always deserves to be condemned and pierced with every curse; but not the persons who maintain it, unless the salvation of their spirit requires it, so that the flesh may be subdued (1 Cor. 5.5; 1 Tim. 1.20). It is always lawful to pray against the schemes and enterprises of Paganism, Judaism, Turkism, and Antichristianism; but never against pagans, Jews, Turks, or Papists as persons. Our enemies are either private or public, and public enemies are of the Church. We may never curse private enemies, since we are commanded and bound to love even our enemies. Public enemies are either curable or incurable. The curable ones ought to be helped by our intercession. The incurable are known only to God and to those to whom he reveals them. Those to whom he reveals them, he moves by the same special revelation to curse them. Such were the prophets, moved by the Spirit of God (2 Pet. 1.21), who nevertheless did not so much curse as foretell the evils that were to come upon the hopeless enemies of the Church. Those not endowed with the same Spirit may not imitate them. For Christ also said to his disciples, when they wanted to call down fire on the Samaritans as Elijah had done, You do not know what spirit you are of (Luke 9.55). For us, it is enough against impious and obstinate men and violent persecutors of the Church to pray in an indefinite way that they be cursed, without applying the curse to particular persons whom it is better to leave to God's judgment, using the formula that was customarily used of old when the Ark went forward.

units.la: Surge, Jehova, & dispergantur inimici tui, fugiantque osores tui a facie tua, Num. X.35. & qua usus David est: Pudefiant, qui perfide agunt, Psal. XXV. 3. Imprecationes vero Prophetarum, velut Mosis, Num. XVI.15. Davidis, Psal. XXXV. 4. XL.15. CIX.6. &c. Jeremiae cap. XVIII. 21. Pauli, 2. Tim. IV.14. tum ut Prophetiae, quibus Deus patefecit, quam horrenda Dei judicia perfidos, obstinatos, Ecclesiae inprimis hostes diros & perseverantes maneant: tum ut preces, sed non adversus has vel illas personas, sed indefinite adversus incurabiles Dei & Ecclesiae hostes applicandae, servire nobis debent.
units.tr: Arise, O LORD, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee before your face (Num. 10:35). David also used the words: Let those be put to shame who act treacherously (Ps. 25:3). The imprecations of the prophets, such as Moses (Num. 16:15), David (Ps. 35:4; 40:15; 109:6, etc.), Jeremiah (ch. 18:21), and Paul (2 Tim. 4:14), should serve us in two ways: as prophecies, by which God has revealed how dreadful his judgments will be upon the faithless, the obstinate, and above all the enemies of the Church who persevere in their hostility; and as prayers, to be applied not against this or that particular person, but in general against the incurable enemies of God and the Church.

units.la: C. Variae insuper etiam precum, pro varietate accidentium & circumstantiarum, species sunt. Nam primo aliae mentales, aliae vocales sunt. Mentales extra mentem & cor seu spiritum non egrediuntur. Exempla sic precantium, Moses, Exod. XIV.15. David, Psal. XXXVIII.10. LXXIX.11. Christus ipse, qui nullis ad Deum verbis fusis pro exauditione ejus gratias egit, Joh. XI.41. sunt. Earum usus ubique & semper esse potest. Nihil enim spiritum hominis impedire potest, si non ipse se impediat. Vocales mentis desideria voce exprimunt. Tollite vobiscum verba, & dicite: Omnem iniquitatem aufer, & reddemus vitulos labiorum nostrorum, Hos. XIV.2.3. Non tantum enim spiritu, sed etiam corpore Deus glorificandus est. Inter corporis autem organa praecipuum lingua est, per quam Deo & Patri benedicimus, Jac. III. 9. & cujus usus ex corde proveniens, vicissim internum cordis affectum fovet; sicut ignis in foco accensus ipsum focum frigentem calefacit, qui calefactus mox ignis ipsius calorem geminat. Facundia earum in eo consistit, quod & supinitatem orationis & curiosam phrasium affectationem ex aequo vitamus, & orationis lumina a Spiritu S. & verbo ejus mutuamur; & Spiritum contritum, qui dissertos inprimis facit, & animam coram Deo velut aquam effundit, ad linguae precantis usum afferimus. Sic ergo lingua precante ad mentem & interiorem animi affectum, cujus lingua adminiculum est, attendendum est, ut non omnino nulla verborum cura sit, ne videlicet non decentia, & Deo digna sint.
units.tr: C. Moreover, there are various kinds of prayer, according to the variety of occasions and circumstances. First, some prayers are mental and some are vocal. Mental prayers do not go beyond the mind and heart, or spirit. Examples of such prayers are Moses (Exod. 14:15), David (Ps. 38:10; 79:11), and Christ himself, who, without uttering any words to God, gave thanks for being heard (John 11:41). Such prayer can be used everywhere and at all times, for nothing can hinder the spirit of a man unless he himself hinders it. Vocal prayers express the desires of the mind by the voice: Take with you words, and say: Take away all iniquity, and we will render the calves of our lips (Hos. 14:2, 3). For God is to be glorified not only in spirit but also in body. Among the organs of the body, the tongue is the chief, by which we bless God and the Father (James 3:9); and its use, when it proceeds from the heart, in turn fosters the inner affection of the heart, just as a fire kindled on a hearth warms the cold hearth itself, and the hearth, once warmed, doubles the heat of the fire. Its eloquence consists in this: that we avoid alike both careless slackness in prayer and a fussy affectation of phrases, and borrow the lights of prayer from the Holy Spirit and his Word; and that we bring to the use of the praying tongue a contrite spirit, which above all makes men eloquent, and pour out the soul before God like water. Thus, while the tongue prays, attention must be given to the mind and the inner affection of the soul, of which the tongue is the aid; yet there must be some care for the words, lest they be unseemly and unworthy of God.

units.la: CI. Orationi vocali etiam Cantus accidit. Ejus usus non contemnendus est, si ex pio corde proficiscatur, ut non Musica chordula, sed cor, non clamor, sed amor psallat in aure Dei, juxta Davidis illud: Paratum est cor meum, Deus, paratum est cor meum, canam & psallam. Gloria mea evigila, nablium & cithara, excitabo auroram, Psal. LVII.8.9. Si ad audientium & canentium edificationem, 1. Cor. XIV.26. Spiritus inprimis languentis suscitationem instituatur, & non voluptati aurium, sed glorificationi Dei, & deliciationi in solo ipso inserviat: denique in gratia, Col. IV.6. Ephes. IV.29. ita exerceatur, ut venustatem, decus, gravitatem comitem habeat, & laetitia canentis a gratia Dei procedat. Male quis habet in vobis? Oret: bono animo quispiam est? psallat, Jac. V.13. Ubi non est carere omni molestia, sed in ipsis etiam afflictionibus spem & bonum animum habere. Nam & talibus, adeoque omnibus canere, vel laetitiae tiæ signa quovis sermone, sive is rythmo, numeris & poëtica elegantia prædितus sit, sive pedestri gradu incedat, edere convenit. Implemini spiritu, loquentes invicem ψαλμοῖς καὶ ὕμνοις καὶ ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς, Psalmis, hymnis, & canticis spiritualibus (Spiritum Dei authorem referentibus, qualia inprimis ab eo inspirata sunt) ᾄδοντες καὶ ψάλλοντες canentes & psallentes in corde vestro Domino, Ephes. V. 19. Sermo Christi habitet in vobis copiosè in omni sapientia: docentes & monentes vos invicem Psalmis & hymnis & cantilenis spiritualibus, in gratia canentes in corde vestro Domino vestro, Col. III. 16. Ubi ψαλμοὶ Psalmi cantica illa sunt, quibus Musica organa conveniunt, ἀπὸ ψάλλειν tangere, pulsare, levi motu quatere; Hebræis מזמור , quam vocem ψαλμὸν Græci reddunt: ὕμνοι hymni idem quod תהלה & שיר cantica quævis: ᾠδαί cantica, idem quod נגינה cantica modulis constantia, sicut & ψάλλειν fidibus canere est. Est enim vel ligata oratio & carmen; vel etiam modulata voce canitur: vel instrumentum additur. Quomodo autem vocabula hæc invicem respondeant, anxiè inquirendum non putamus, quia Apostolus omnes species conjungere voluit. In omnibus verò est cantus. Nam Apostolus, Col. III. 16. jubet ᾄδειν canere Psalmis, hymnis & canticis spiritualibus. Et commendat ille cantum tum privatum, tum Ecclesiasticum. Cùm enim dicit: Ἐνοικείτω ἐν ὑμῖν. Habitet in vobis; non de privato dunt. xat sermone, sed de eo inprimis, qui in cœtu fratrum fit, loquitur. In Mose extant carmina Miriam, Exod. XV. & Mosis, Deut. XXXII. In Libro Judicum, Deborae, Jud. V. In Numeris carmen Israelitarum, Num. XXI. 17. &c. Dein David fuit נעים זמירות ישראל suavis cantilenis Israelis, 2. Sam. XXIII. 1. Tempore Davidis & Asaphi populo Psalmi à Spiritu S. commendati sunt. Et sæpe Scriptura adhortatur ad canendum Deo, etiam novum canticum Mosis & Agni, hoc est, Promissioni & Evangelio conveniens, Apoc. XIV. 3. XV. 3. Et Christianos Christo ut Deo hymnos cecinisse, jam sua ætate Plinius Epistola ad Trajanum notavit. Denique etiam instrumentorum usum in ipsa Ecclesia esse posse, Pauli adhortatio docet: Licèt jàm olim Justinus Martyr. Quæst. & Resp. ad Orthod. q. 10. Musicam Organicam ceu νηπιώδη infantilem, infantibus in V. T. inservientem, perstrinxerit. Dicamus igitur, & Davidem & Elisæum νήπιον infantem fuisse. Sed nos illis ὁμοπαθεῖς sumus, & illi nobis fuerunt. Si quæ in organis typica significatio fuit, illa desiit. At organa ipsa spiritualis lætitiæ adjumenta esse non desinunt. Libere igitur iis Ecclesia privatim, vel publicè etiam utitur, prout eorum usum æ-dificatio ejusdem postulat, vel abnuit. Serò tamen illam in Ecclesiam Occidentalem inprimis, introductam esse, satis constat. Nam & Thomas Aquinas in 2.2. q. 91. art. 2. Ecclesiam suo tempore instrumenta Musica assumpsisse negat. Neque Apostolus commendans ψαλμὸς Psalmos, organicam Musicam mandato Apostolico in Ecclesiam introduci simpliciter voluit, quia alibi, 1. Cor. XIV. 26. οἰκοδομὴς ædificationis conditionem apposuit, & res ipsa per se indifferens est, neque aliter quàm utilitate ad finem suum definiri potest.
units.tr: CI. Singing also belongs to vocal prayer. Its use is not to be despised, if it proceeds from a pious heart, so that it is not the musical string but the heart, not the shout but the love, that sings in the ear of God, according to David's words: My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and psalm. Awake, my glory; awake, lute and harp; I will awaken the dawn (Ps. 57:8, 9). If it is undertaken for the edification of the hearers and singers (1 Cor. 14:26), chiefly for the reviving of a languishing spirit, and serves not the delight of the ears but the glorification of God and the delight that is found in God alone; and if, finally, it is performed in grace (Col. 4:6; Eph. 4:29) in such a way that it has loveliness, dignity and gravity as its companions, and the joy of the singer proceeds from the grace of God. Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing psalms (James 5:13). This does not mean being free from all trouble, but having hope and a cheerful spirit even in afflictions. For it is fitting to sing, and to show signs of joy in any kind of speech, whether it be bound in rhythm, measures and poetic elegance, or moves on in plain prose, both for such persons and indeed for all. Be filled with the Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs (ψαλμοῖς καὶ ὕμνοις καὶ ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς) (Eph. 5:18, 19; here the songs are said to refer to the Spirit of God as their author, as those inspired by him above all are), singing and psalming in your heart to the Lord (ᾄδοντες καὶ ψάλλοντες). Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to your Lord (Col. 3:16). Here ψαλμοί (psalms) are those songs to which musical instruments are suited, from ψάλλειν, to touch, to pluck, to shake with a light motion; for the Hebrews it is מזמור, which the Greeks render ψαλμός. ὕμνοι (hymns) is the same as תהלה and שיר, songs of any kind; ᾠδαί (songs) is the same as נגינה, songs consisting of melodies, just as ψάλλειν means to sing to the lyre. For either it is bound speech and verse, or it is sung in a modulated voice, or an instrument is added. We do not think it necessary to inquire anxiously how these words correspond to one another, since the Apostle wished to combine all the kinds. In all of them there is singing. For the Apostle, Col. 3:16, bids them ᾄδειν (to sing) with psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. And he commends singing both private and ecclesiastical. For when he says: Ἐνοικείτω ἐν ὑμῖν (let it dwell in you), he speaks not of private discourse, but chiefly of that which takes place in the assembly of the brethren. In Moses there are the songs of Miriam (Exod. 15) and of Moses (Deut. 32). In the Book of Judges, the song of Deborah (Judg. 5). In Numbers, the song of the Israelites (Num. 21:17, etc.). Then David was the נעים זמירות ישראל, the sweet singer of Israel (2 Sam. 23:1). In the time of David and Asaph the Holy Spirit commended psalms to the people. And often Scripture exhorts us to sing to God, even the new song of Moses and the Lamb, that is, a song fitting the promise and the gospel (Rev. 14:3; 15:3). And that Christians sang hymns to Christ as to God was already noted in his own time by Pliny in his letter to Trajan. Finally, Paul's exhortation teaches that the use of instruments also may be permitted in the Church. Although Justin Martyr long ago, in Quaest. & Resp. ad Orthod. q. 10, disparaged organ music as infantile (νηπιώδη), serving infants in the Old Testament, let us say that David and Elisha were infants (νήπιον). But we are of like passions with them (ὁμοπαθεῖς), and they were with us. If the organs had some typical meaning, that has ceased; but the organs themselves do not cease to be aids of spiritual joy. Therefore the Church may use them freely, both privately and publicly, as the edification of the Church requires their use, or may refrain from them. It is nevertheless quite certain that they were introduced into the Western Church rather late. For Thomas Aquinas, in 2.2 q. 91 art. 2, denies that in his time the Church had adopted musical instruments. Nor did the Apostle, in commending psalms (ψαλμός), wish organ music simply to be introduced into the Church by apostolic command, since elsewhere, 1 Cor. 14:26, he added the condition of edification (οἰκοδομή); and the thing itself is indifferent in itself and cannot be defined except by its usefulness for its end.

units.la: CII. Abusus tantùm cantus utriusque, vo-calis & organici cavendus est. Nam & in populo Dei notantur delicatuli, qui Davidis Nabliorum æmulatione Deo displicuerunt: הפרשים על פי הנבל Qui minuriunt ad Nablium, ut David, sibi instrumenta excogitarunt, Amos. VI. 5. Nam quod Musices studium David ad laudem Dei contulit, illi ad pruritum aurium, & effœminandum auditum contulerunt. Etiam in Babylone Mystica vox citharœdorum, Musicorum, tibicinum & tubicinum, Apoc. XVIII. 22. perstringitur. Atqui in Papatu non plateæ, conclavia & cubilia duntaxat, sed Templa cumprimis & Basilicæ instrumentis Musicis exquisitissimis ad insaniam usque perstrepunt, atque Jesuitæ inprimis id operam dant, ut hac suavitate, auriumque, ne dicam, Veneris etiam, illecebra, homines animales & φιλήδονες capti seductique sacra sua amplectantur. Et illi ipsi in suis fornicibus, ad spiritualem fornicationem comparatis, hymnos & cantica sua, quamvis subinde sancta & pia, non tam canendo, quàm reboando & mugiendo, adeóque non ἐν χαρᾷ in gratia, & plerunque nec in spiritu, nec ἐν νοῒ in intelligentia (quæ Apostolus in omni oratione & cantu, 1. Cor. XIV. 15. requirit) decantant. Non in spiritu, cùm vel sibi ignota, vel sine pio cordis affectu, luscitiarum more, cantillant. Non in intelligentia, quia lingua peregrina canentes à populo non intelliguntur. Non pauca igitur in Cantu illorum, quem Gregorianum (non à Gregorio I. qui cantui non admodum favebat, sed à Gregorio V. seculi decimi exeuntis Papa) appellant, desideramus. Nam & pleraque illorum cantica non ex Scripturis, nisi detortis & corruptis, ut parum vel nihil genii Divini adsit, pleraque ex Legendis nescio qualibus petita sunt: & pro defunctis etiam cantatur, pro quibus orandum non est: & præcipitur ille cantus, non sponte & liberali spiritu peragitur: & cantatur pro pretio, potiundi beneficii Ecclesiastici gratia: & à clericis solis ad hoc conductis, non à tota Ecclesia Christi; & cantatur dies noctésque sine fine & modo: & impio atque inepto ejusmodi cantui, ceu Divino & meritorio operi tribuitur plus quàm vera fides admittat: & cantatur peregrina lingua paucisque nota, sine fructu omni Ecclesiæ, quæ canenti non potest dicere, Amen: & auditur diu sonus sine verbis significantibus, suspensus; sursum deorsumque flexus: & cantores vocibus sic inter se certant, ut totum Templum rauco boatu detonet, & per vocum contentiones nihil auditores intelligant. Ne quid dicam de intervenientibus scenicæ & theatralis; uti Bernhardus vocat; Musicæ organis; cujus usus in Horis Canonicis, nominatim Vesperis solennibus, in celebratione festorum, & solennis Missæ obtinet. De qua querelas Erasmi, & Guilhelmi Lindani, Episcopi Ruremundani, a-libi consignavimus. Denique cùm omnis carminis, quali & cantica constant, & ipsius cantionis, hic usus sit, ut quæ vera, recta, sancta, pulchra, Deo decora sunt, suavius dulciúsque, nec sine ἐνεργεία verborum & arte, quæ in carmine plurimùm valet, in animum influant; nequissimum ejusdem abusum esse consequitur, cùm vel Dii impuri, vel fabulæ stultæ, vel ἀκαθαρσία & ἀλεχπλία, impura & scurrilia carmine can-
units.tr: CII. Only the abuse of singing, both vocal and instrumental, is to be avoided. For among the people of God there are noted those effeminate men who displeased God by imitating the harps of David: הפרשים על פי הנבל (Who sing idly to the harp, like David, and devise instruments for themselves) (Amos 6:5). For the zeal for music which David devoted to the praise of God, they devoted to tickling the ears and softening the hearing. Also in Babylon the mystical voice of harpers, musicians, flute-players and trumpeters is denounced (Rev. 18:22). But in Papacy the squares, rooms and bedchambers are not the only places resounding; the temples and basilicas above all ring with the most exquisite musical instruments to the point of madness, and the Jesuits in particular take pains that men, being animal and φιλήδονες (lovers of pleasure), may be captured and seduced by this sweetness and by the allurement of the ears, not to mention that of Venus, and so embrace their rites. And they themselves, in their vaults prepared for spiritual fornication, sing their hymns and canticles, though often holy and pious, not so much by singing as by bellowing and roaring, and thus not ἐν χαρᾷ (in joy) in grace, and mostly neither ἐν πνεύματι (in spirit) nor ἐν νοῒ (in understanding), which the Apostle requires in every prayer and song (1 Cor. 14:15). Not in spirit, since they warble things either unknown to themselves or without any pious affection of the heart, in the manner of mourners. Not in understanding, since they sing in a foreign tongue and are not understood by the people. Therefore we miss a good deal in their chant, which they call Gregorian (not from Gregory I, who was not very favourable to singing, but from Gregory V, Pope at the close of the tenth century). For most of their songs are taken not from Scripture, except in distorted and corrupted form, so that there is little or nothing of the divine spirit in them, and most are drawn from I know not what legends; and they sing also for the dead, for whom we are not to pray; and this singing is enjoined and not performed of free will and a willing spirit; and it is sung for a fee, for the sake of obtaining an ecclesiastical benefice; and it is performed by clergy alone hired for the purpose, not by the whole Church of Christ; and it is sung day and night without end or measure; and to such impious and foolish singing is attributed, as a divine and meritorious work, more than true faith can admit; and it is sung in a foreign language known to few, with no profit to the Church at all, which cannot say Amen to the one singing; and a sound without meaningful words is heard for a long time, drawn out, bent up and down; and the singers compete with one another in their voices so that the whole temple thunders with a hoarse roar, and through the contention of voices the hearers understand nothing. Not to mention the scenic and theatrical music of the organs, as Bernard calls it, which is in use in the canonical hours, especially at solemn vespers, in the celebration of feasts, and at the solemn Mass. We have set down elsewhere the complaints of Erasmus and of William Lindanus, Bishop of Roermond, about this. Finally, since all poems, and songs too, and singing itself, have this purpose: that what is true, right, holy, beautiful and becoming to God should flow into the mind more sweetly and pleasantly, and not without the energy of words and the art which counts for much in poetry; it follows that the most wicked abuse of this is that impure gods, foolish fables, or ἀκαθαρσία and ἀλεχπλία (uncleanness and buffoonery), impure and scurrilous things sung in song

units.la: Et abusus, tûque celebrantur, ut ita nequitia gratior dul-ciórque evadat.
units.tr: And such abuses are celebrated in this way, so that wickedness becomes more pleasing and sweeter.

units.la: CIII. Secundò Preces vel subitaneæ, vel præmeditatæ & compositæ sunt. Subitaneæ cordis quædam ejaculatio sunt, qua pro occasione præsente subitò mens ad Deum elevatur, ejúsque præsentia & gratia imploratur. Sicut sale cibus, ita his omne otium, omne negotium, omnis labor noster velut condiri & sanctificari debet. Præmeditatæ & Compositæ sunt, quæ partibus & membris congruo ordine digestæ, plenum integrúmque corpus exhibent. Súntque hæ vel conceptæ, vel præscriptæ. Conceptæ à precante ipso, Spiritu S. intus movente, docente & dirigente componuntur. Nam Spiritus S. est Spiritus precationum, Zach. XII. 10. qui in nobis clamat, Abba, Pater, Rom. VIII. 15. & coopitulatur infirmitatibus nostris. Quid enim precemur, sicut oportet, non novimus, sed idem ille Spiritus intercedit pro nobis suspiriis ineffabilibus, ibid. v. 26. Ille ergo preces in nobis concipit, sed singulari dono, quod eorum est, qui perfecti, provectiores & firmiores sunt. Cum enim quotidie nova precum materies, variæque occasiones & argumenta se offerant, precum etiam tenor novo conceptu variandus & occasioni præsenti aptandus est. Præscriptæ sunt, quæ ab aliis dictatæ, & ad usum publicum vel privatum digestæ sunt. Tales sunt Oratio Dominica, Psalmi Davidis, Orationes, quas Scriptores alii suppeditant. Multa enim in sacro Codice exempla precationum sunt, quas Sancti ad Deum fuderunt, & quas in eodem Spiritu, in simili statu constituti, nostras facere possumus. Sunt etiam Prophetiæ, quibus conceptis verbis vota & desideria Ecclesiæ N.T. repræsentantur; quas negligere non decet. Etiam statæ precum formulæ juxta exemplar & typum Orationis Dominicæ, aliarumque Orationum à viris piis formatæ privatim adhiberi, & publicum in Ecclesiæ usum introduci possunt. Non enim in Schola Christi eò usque omnes profecerunt, ut sine formularum præsidio necessitates suas, vel totius etiam Ecclesiæ concinnè satis & coram Deo effundere possint, qui tamen alios verba præeuntes & formantes promptissimo affectu sequuntur. Spiritus enim Dei, quo authore illæ formatæ sunt, in utrisque, etsi non pari mensura, operatur. Nam quòd nonnulli libertatem Spiritus sic restringi, imò motus ejus extingui causantur, inane est. An enim, si Paterfamilias preces familiæ suæ præeat, spiritus libertas periclitatur? Neque etiam fideles formulis ejusmodi præscriptis adstringuntur, sed earum duntaxat usus, ceu licitus defenditur hactenus, ut infirmioribus & rudioribus pietatis & devotionis administrandis. Interea qui infirmi & pueri sunt, tales manere, vel ex alieno semper ore pendere non debent. Conentur & ipsi aliquando suis se alis humo tollere.
units.tr: CIII. Secondly, prayers are either extempore or premeditated and composed. Extempore prayers are a certain ejaculation of the heart, by which, on a present occasion, the mind is suddenly raised to God, and his presence and grace are implored. As food is seasoned with salt, so all our leisure, all our business and all our labour ought to be, as it were, seasoned and sanctified by such prayer. Premeditated and composed prayers are those which, arranged in parts and members in due order, present a full and complete body. These are either conceived or prescribed. Conceived prayers are composed by the one praying, the Holy Spirit moving, teaching and directing him within. For the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of supplications, Zech. XII. 10, who cries within us, Abba, Father, Rom. VIII. 15, and helps our infirmities. For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the same Spirit intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered, ibid. v. 26. He therefore conceives prayers in us, but this is a singular gift, belonging to those who are perfect, more advanced and stronger. For since every day new matter for prayer and varied occasions and subjects present themselves, the tenor of prayer must also be varied by fresh conception and fitted to the present occasion. Prescribed prayers are those dictated by others and arranged for public or private use. Such are the Lord's Prayer, the Psalms of David, and the prayers which other writers supply. For the sacred Code contains many examples of prayers which the saints poured out to God, and which we, placed in a similar condition, can make our own in the same Spirit. There are also prophecies, in which the vows and desires of the Church of the New Testament are represented in express words; these it is not proper to neglect. Also, fixed forms of prayer, framed after the pattern and type of the Lord's Prayer and of other prayers composed by pious men, may be used privately and introduced into the public use of the Church. For not all have advanced so far in the school of Christ that they can pour out their needs, or the needs of the whole Church, fittingly and before God without the support of set forms; yet they follow with the most ready affection those who go before them and shape the words. For the Spirit of God, by whose authorship those forms were framed, works in both, though not in equal measure. That some claim that the liberty of the Spirit is thus restricted, or rather that its motions are quenched, is empty. For if the head of a household leads the prayers of his family, is the liberty of the Spirit endangered? Nor are the faithful bound by such prescribed forms; their use is defended only as lawful, so far as it serves the weaker and more untutored in piety and devotion. Meanwhile, those who are weak and childish ought not to remain so, nor always depend on another's mouth. Let them also try at some time to lift themselves from the ground on their own wings.

units.la: CIV. Tertiò Preces privatæ vel publicæ sunt. Privatæ vel solitariæ, seu secretæ; vel domesticæ sunt. Solitariæ seu secretæ sunt, quas precantes soli & secreti instituunt. De quibus Christus. Tu precaturus ingredere cubiculum tuum, & clauso ostio precare Patrem tuum in occulto. Et Pater tuus videns te in occulto, reddet tibi in propatulo, Matth. VI. 6. Ipse Christus precaturus loca solitaria & turbis inaccessa, edita montium cacumina, hortorum secessus adiit. Neque enim preces privatæ in Templis fuisse efficaciores iis sunt, quæ in secretioribus adytis funduntur, quæ Pontificiorum superstitio est. Nullus enim locus in N.T. ex singulari institutione Divina alio sacratior est. Et qui cum aliis in eodem Templo precantur, non soli illi, vel secreti precantur. Sunt autem preces secretæ reliquarum omnium veluti nutricula & fomentum, & ad easdem sancta paraseceva, quin & occasio remotis omnibus arbitris totam animam sine ulla coram Deo effundendi, omnes sinus coram eo excutiendi, quod pari libertate coram nullo Mortalium facere sustineremus; utpote quorum conscientiam in multis reformidare necesse est. Domesticæ sunt, quæ coram & cum familia, vel paucis amicis in loco privato funduntur. Ita cum famulo suo Elisa: cum Petro, Johanne & Jacobo assumptis Christus oravit. Per has preces familiæ in totidem velut Ecclesias particulares commutantur. Cujusmodi in domo Philemonis, Aquilæ & Priscillæ fuerunt. Publicæ à sacro fidelium coetu per personam ad munus illud selectam in loco publico obiri solent. Ubi fratres habitant in unum, vel simul, illuc præcepit Jehova benedictionem & vitam usque in seculum, Psal. CXXXIII. 1. 3. Non deserentes congregationem, Hebr. X. 25. Habentque preces illæ efficaciam apud Deum omnium maximam. Sicut enim plura ligna seu cremia in unum congesta & succensa flammam validiorem & vehementiorem efficiunt: ita multorum uno humero Deum colentium Zephon. III. 9. preces Dei aures sanctissimas potentius longè feriunt, & cœlestis sacrarii fores majore vi pulsant: Ideo Joel: Congregate populum, sanctificare congregationem, cogite senes, parvulos & jugentes ubera, &c. Et dicant: Parce Jehova populo tuo, &c. Et tunc zelabit Jehova pro terra sua, & parcet populo suo, Joel. II. 16. 17. 18. Personæ has preces celebrantes Pastor & populus sunt. Ille os Dei erga populum, & os populi erga Deum est. Populus precanti ipsi interno cordis affectu & assensu suffragatur, dicens sive corde, sive, quod in V. & N.T. factitatum legimus, ore etiam Amen, Nehem. VIII. 7. &c. 1. Cor. XIV. 16. In modo precum publicarum inprimis conformitas, in gestus & actus externi decentia, ordinis & vitandæ confusionis gratia, ibid. v. 33. & unanimitas, qualis in primis Christianis extitit, Actor. II. 46. & usum vernaculum linguæ plane postulat, requiritur.
units.tr: CIV. Thirdly, prayers are private or public. Private prayers are either solitary or secret, or domestic. Solitary or secret prayers are those which the one praying offers alone and in secret. Of these Christ spoke: But you, when you pray, enter into your chamber, and having shut your door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly, Matt. VI. 6. Christ himself, when he was to pray, went to solitary places inaccessible to crowds, to the high peaks of mountains and the retreats of gardens. For private prayers offered in temples are no more effective than those poured out in the more secluded sanctuaries, which is the superstition of the Papists. For no place in the New Testament is holier by singular divine appointment than another. And one who prays with others in the same temple does not pray alone or in secret. Secret prayers, however, are as it were the nurse and fostering-care of all the rest, and a holy preparation for them; indeed they are also an opportunity, with all witnesses removed, to pour out the whole soul without reserve before God and to search every corner of the heart before him, something we could not do with the same freedom before any mortal, since we must greatly fear their judgment of our conscience. Domestic prayers are those poured out in a private place before and with the family, or a few friends. So Christ prayed with his servant Elisha, and with Peter, John and James taken along. Through such prayers a family is turned into a kind of particular Church. Such were the prayers in the house of Philemon, Aquila and Priscilla. Public prayers are customarily offered by the sacred assembly of the faithful, in a public place, through a person chosen for that office. Where brethren dwell together, in unity, there Jehovah has commanded the blessing and life for evermore, Ps. CXXXIII. 1, 3. Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, Heb. X. 25. Such prayers have the greatest efficacy with God. For as several logs or pieces of wood gathered into one and set alight make a stronger and fiercer flame, so the prayers of many who worship God with one shoulder, Zeph. III. 9, strike the most holy ears of God much more powerfully and knock at the gates of the heavenly sanctuary with greater force. Hence Joel: Gather the people, sanctify the congregation, assemble the elders, the little ones and those who suck the breasts, etc. And let them say: Spare, Jehovah, your people, etc. Then Jehovah will be jealous for his land, and will spare his people, Joel II. 16, 17, 18. The persons celebrating these public prayers are the minister and the people. He is the mouth of God towards the people, and the mouth of the people towards God. The people join in the prayer by inward affection and assent of the heart, saying, either in the heart or, as we read was customary in the Old and New Testaments, also with the mouth, Amen, Neh. VIII. 7, etc.; 1 Cor. XIV. 16. In the manner of public prayers, above all conformity is required, decency in gesture and external action, for the sake of order and of avoiding confusion, ibid. v. 33, and unanimity, such as existed among the first Christians, Acts II. 46; and it plainly demands the use of the vernacular tongue.

units.la: CV. Denique Preces ordinariæ vel extraordinariæ sunt. Ordinariæ sunt, quæ statis vicibus, & certa quadam atque constanti ratione sive privatim, sive publicè funduntur. Et publicæ quidem preces tempore ab Ecclesia pro ratione & loci & personarum liberè definito frequentantur; Privatarum verò tempus privatus quisque liberè definit. Neque enim necessitate quadam ad tempus certum statásque vices obeundas privati compelli possunt, quæ Horarum Canonicarum in Papatu superstitio est. Quas communis sententia septem matutinas, primam, tertiam, sextam, nonam, vesperam completoriam numerat; ad quarum exercitium Monachi & Moniales ex voto, Ecclesiasticæ personæ ex necessitate, & pretio quidem, qui non sunt in sacris, sine pretio, qui sunt in sacris majorum ordinum; qui verò minorum ordinum sunt, ex consilio obligantur. De quarum mysteriis multa multi disputant. Quæ inter & illud est, quòd Sacerdos una hora suas horas omnes implere potest, dummodo tam bene se expediat, ut tenorem recitandorum septem intra horas una vice recitet. Reliquum tempus in popina, & ubicunque libet, exigere potest. Sed mera Dei irrisio, & humanum hoc inventum est, quo laceræ & corruptæ veteris Prophetiæ reliquiæ, quibus fabulæ & ineptiæ multæ attextæ sunt, comprehenduntur. Cujusmodi mixtura nova admodum, cum opinione necessitatis, meriti, operis operati, sanctitatis loci & temporis, seu numeri septenarii idololatria, ignotæ pluribus linguæ usu, inextricabili vexatione spiritus, à qua sexcentis dubiis & scrupulis se expedire non possunt; ineptiis pluribus, quibus precandi zelus & devotio extinguitur potius quàm fovetur; denique mercenaria pietate, seu impietate potius conjuncta, indignissima est, quæ in Ecclesia Christi usurpetur vel toleretur, nisi otiosis potius ventribus quibusdam, quàm toti Ecclesiæ consultum malumus. Licet enim & David media nocte ad Deum celebrandum surrexerit, Psal. CXIX. 62. & Petrus ac Johannes Templum hora nona, quæ precum erat, ingressi, Act. III. 1. denique Paulus & Silas sub mediam noctem in carcere Deum laudasse ibid. XVI. 25. legantur, abfuit tamen ab hac eorum pietate omnis necessitatis & meriti opinio: abfuit superstitio palis. Neque illi, qui temporibus illis orarunt, horas eas præcisè & ordinarie servasse leguntur. Et media nox adeò officio huic obeundo idonea non est, ut Pontificii ipsi illud tempus in matutinum transtulerint. David quoque septies quotidie Deum laudavit, Psal. CXIX. 164. non numero præciso, uti Genebrardus ipse observat, sed numero definito pro indefinito posito, quia sæpissime precatus est. Instituerunt etiam Hieronymo Epist. ad Læt. teste, Patres horas officio huic destinatas, sed non pro solis Ascetis, vel Clero, verum Christianis omnibus. Hieronymus idem quinque vel sex; Basilius septem horarum meminit. Sed quicquid de rigore præscripti temporis vix probando fiat, procul tamen superstitionis fœx ab eorum cultu abfuit.
units.tr: CV. Finally, prayers are ordinary or extraordinary. Ordinary prayers are those which are poured out at set intervals, and in a certain fixed and constant manner, either privately or publicly. Public prayers are repeated at times freely determined by the Church according to the place and the persons; private individuals freely determine the time for their own private prayers. For private persons cannot be compelled by any necessity to perform these at a fixed time and set intervals, which is the superstition of the Canonical Hours in the Papacy. The common opinion counts them as seven: Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers and Compline; for the performance of which monks and nuns are bound by vow, ecclesiastical persons by necessity, and indeed for a fee if they are not in holy orders, without a fee if they are in the higher orders, and those in the lower orders are bound by counsel. Many dispute at length about their mysteries. Among these is the claim that a priest can fulfil all his hours in one go, provided he manages so well that he recites the whole series of seven within the hours in a single sitting. The rest of the time he may spend in a tavern, or wherever he likes. But this is a mere mockery of God and a human invention, in which the torn and corrupted remnants of the old prophecy are gathered together, with many fables and follies woven into them. Such a very new mixture, with the notion of necessity, of merit, of the opus operatum, of the holiness of place and time, or the idolatry of the number seven, with a language unknown to most people, with an inextricable harassment of the spirit, from which they cannot free themselves from countless doubts and scruples, with many trifles by which zeal and devotion in prayer are extinguished rather than fostered, and finally joined with a mercenary piety, or rather impiety, is most unworthy to be used or tolerated in the Church of Christ, unless we prefer to consult certain idle bellies rather than the whole Church. For although David is said to have risen at midnight to praise God, Ps. CXIX. 62, and Peter and John entered the Temple at the ninth hour, which was the hour of prayer, Acts III. 1, and finally Paul and Silas are read to have praised God in prison at midnight, ibid. XVI. 25, yet the opinion of necessity and of merit was far from their piety; superstition with its fixed rules was absent. Nor are those who prayed in those times read to have kept those hours precisely and regularly. Nor is midnight so suitable a time for this duty that the Papists themselves have transferred it to Matins. David also praised God seven times a day, Ps. CXIX. 164, not as a precise number, as Genebrard himself observes, but a definite number put for an indefinite one, because he prayed very often. The Fathers also appointed hours for this duty, as Jerome testifies in his letter to Laeta, but not only for ascetics or the clergy, rather for all Christians. The same Jerome mentions five or six hours; Basil mentions seven. But whatever is done about the rigour of a prescribed time, which can hardly be approved, nevertheless the dregs of superstition were far from their worship.

units.la: CVI. Preces Extraordinariæ
units.tr: CVI. Extraordinary Prayers

units.la: CVI. Preces Extraordinariæ speciali gratia, privatim vel publicè ultra consuetum ordinem, sive temporis moram, sive affectus vehementiam, sive adminicula alia, jejunia cumprimis & eleemosynas, adhibita spectamus, instituuntur. Tales fuerunt Jacobi Esavo occurrentis, Genes. XXXII. 11. Mosis pro Israele, Deut. IX. 18. Annæ, 1. Sam. I. 12. Davidis, 2. Sam. XII. 16. Estheræ & popularium, Esth. IV. 6. Dan. X. 2. ipsius Christi in horto cum valido clamore, lachrymis & sudore sanguineo fusæ, Matth. XXVI. 39. Hebr. V. 7. In iis enixior longè, quàm in ordinariis contentio & affectus major desiderii & doloris vehementia, non sine rugitu, Psal. XXII. 2. XXXII. 3. clamore horrido, gemitibus, suspiriis & lachrymis Tesse profert.
units.tr: CVI. We consider extraordinary prayers, which are instituted privately or publicly beyond the usual order, by special grace, whether through a longer duration, the intensity of feeling, or other aids, especially fasting and almsgiving. Examples are Jacob's prayer when he met Esau (Gen. 32:11), Moses' prayer for Israel (Deut. 9:18), Hannah's (1 Sam. 1:12), David's (2 Sam. 12:16), Esther's and her people's (Esth. 4:16), Daniel's (Dan. 10:2), and that of Christ himself in the garden, poured out with strong crying, tears and bloody sweat (Matt. 26:39; Heb. 5:7). In these the effort is far more earnest than in ordinary prayer, and the intensity of desire and the vehemence of grief are greater, not without groaning (Ps. 22:2; 32:3), and they express themselves in a dreadful cry, in sighs, sobs and tears.

units.la: Sicut enim igneum semen in densa & humida nube conclusum in claustro suo contineri non potest, sed protinus in tonitrua, fulgura & imbres erumpit: ita intentior cordis affectus cohiberi non potest, quin in rugitus, clamores & lachrymas prorumpat. Et lachrymæ quidem tanti apud Deum ponderis sunt, ut eas in utre suo reponere dicatur, Psal. LVI. 9. Non enim ab horrore poenæ, quæ ἀναλγησίαν induc it, sed à quæsitissimo sensu ingratitudinis erga Deum benignissimum Parrem, adeòque amore ejusdem promanant.
units.tr: For just as a fiery seed enclosed in a thick and damp cloud cannot be contained in its prison but at once breaks out into thunder, lightning and rain, so a more intense feeling of the heart cannot be restrained but bursts out into groans, cries and tears. Tears indeed have such weight with God that he is said to store them in his bottle (Ps. 56:8). For they do not flow from the horror of punishment, which brings insensibility [ἀναλγησίαν], but from a keen sense of ingratitude toward God, the most kind Father, and therefore from love for him.

units.la: CVII. Orationi cuivis locus, tempus, ordo & gestus accidunt. De Loco S. Paulus: Volo orare viros in omni loco, 1. Tim. II. 8. Nullus enim sub N. T. locus alio sacratior est, ut in eo potius, quàm alio Deus adesse, & preces exaudire velit, quasi in terra quicquam sit, propter quod, & cujus intuitu Deus preces nostras exaudire velit. Pessimè proin faciunt, qui homines, vel ad certam mundi partem converti, vel ad templa, memorias Martyrum, imagines, tanquam loca precibus aptiora & sanctiora adorare, & orationum fundendarum causa peregrinari, vel ab uno ad alium locum vagari jubent. Aliud longè habet promissio. Ab ortu Solis usque ad occasum ejus magnum est nomen meum in gentibus, & in omni loco hostia offeretur nomini meo, & munus purum, Mal. I. 11. Olim enim cultus ceremonialis non in omni loco celebrabatur, sed in loco, quem Deus elegit, Deut. XII. 5. 6. Nunc figuris abolitis, & libertate restituta in omni loco æquè efficaciter colitur. Nullum enim præ alio locum Divina institutio sacrat. Ubi fides, ubi charitas est, ibi locus precum est: Non ubi locus, ibi fides & charitas. Ecclesia verò certa cultui locum deputat, non loci sacrationis, vel ad orandum efficacioris, quæ Pontificiorum, à præsentia imaginum, reliquiarum, altarium, precum efficaciam suspendentium insana superstitio est, sed propter ordinem, quo cultus externus carere nequit.
units.tr: CVII. Place, time, order and posture belong to every prayer. Concerning place, St. Paul says: I will that men pray in every place (1 Tim. 2:8). For under the New Testament no place is holier than another, so that God should wish to be present and to hear prayers in one place rather than another, as if there were anything on earth on account of which, or for whose sake, God would wish to hear our prayers. Therefore those do very badly who bid people turn to a certain part of the world, or worship temples, memorials of martyrs and images as places more suitable and holier for prayer, or who order pilgrimages for the sake of pouring out prayers, or who send people wandering from one place to another. The promise has quite a different meaning: From the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense shall be offered to my name, and a pure offering (Mal. 1:11). For formerly ceremonial worship was not celebrated in every place, but in the place which God chose (Deut. 12:5-6). Now, with the figures abolished and liberty restored, he is worshipped equally effectively in every place. For divine institution consecrates no place above another. Where there is faith and love, there is a place for prayer; not where there is a place, there faith and love are. The Church, however, assigns a place for public worship, not because a place is consecrated or more effective for prayer, which is the mad superstition of the Papists, who make the efficacy of prayer depend on the presence of images, relics and altars, but on account of the order which external worship cannot do without.

units.la: CVIII. De Tempore sic idem Paulus: Precamini omni tempore, Ephes. VI. 18. Adiaλείπτως προσευχόμενοι indesinenter orate, 1. Thess. V. 17. Christus quoque in parabola ostendit δεῖ πάντοτε προσεύχεσθαι oportere semper precari, Luc. VIII. 1. Conveniunt semper, indesinenter, omni tempore orare. Tempus autem accipi de καιρῷ opportunitate, tempestivitate potest. Orandum, quoties opportunum, tempestivum est: tum die, tum nocte, adeòque jugiter; sicut sacrificium matutinum & vespertinum tamid juge, seu ἐνδελεχισμὸς continuum dictum est: tum in angustia, Psal. L. 15. ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ πονηρᾷ in die malo, Ephes. VI. 13. tum in pace & rebus secundis, ut Deo gratias agamus, & ejus nunquam oblivisceamur, Deut. VIII. 10. 11. 14. & vel ad quietem nos componentes de certamine & militia ad Regnum Sathanæ destruendum cogitemus. Cum enim nullum tempus sit, quo non aliquid nobis desit, quo non possimus tentari, vel donum aliquod Divinum accipere; omne certè precandi tempus occupare, omnia orandi tempora captare, etiam inter labores & occupationes nostras ejaculando identidem suspiria, orare, saltem
units.tr: CVIII. Concerning time, the same Paul says: Pray at all times (Eph. 6:18). Praying without ceasing (1 Thess. 5:17). Christ also shows in a parable that it is necessary always to pray (Luke 18:1). They agree always, constantly, at all times, to pray. The word time may be taken in the sense of the opportune moment [καιρῷ], of fitness. We must pray whenever it is opportune and fitting, by day and by night, and so continually; just as the morning and evening sacrifice was called tamid, continual, or continuum [ἐνδελεχισμὸς]. We must pray in distress (Ps. 50:15), in the evil day [ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ πονηρᾷ] (Eph. 6:13), and in peace and prosperity, that we may give thanks to God and never forget him (Deut. 8:10, 11, 14). And even when we compose ourselves to rest we should think of the struggle and warfare for destroying the kingdom of Satan. For since there is no time when something is not lacking to us, when we cannot be tempted or receive some divine gift, certainly we should occupy every time for prayer and seize every opportunity for praying, even among our labours and occupations, by sending up sighs from time to time, at least praying.

units.la: Vel extraordinaria speciali gratiaque de causa, primum, vel publicè, ultra consuetum ordinem suscepta est. tem semper ἀπαύστως parati ad orandum esse debemus. Et ad hoc ipsum Apostolus jubet vigilare in omni perseverantia, Ephes. VI. 18. Nam & homo occasionibus orandi semper invigilare, & somno atque recreationibus aliquid demere, atque id meditationi gratiae Dei, luctae nos circumstantis, bonorum, quae Deus petere justit, & periculi atque miseriae, in qua Ecclesia vel mundus versatur, impendere: & vigilantes in stratis nostris easdem cogitationes, desideria, vota volvere oportet. Ipsae etiam preces non somnolentae, frigidae, socordes, sed ἐνεργούμεναι efficaces, Jac. V. 16. esse debent. Quomodo enim Deus nos exaudiet, si nos ipsi nos non audiemus? Quanquam ubi sincerus affectus est, Deus infirmitati precantis succurrit, exaudiens, ante quam is clamet, Esaj. LXV. 24. Cum enim nos ἑτοίμως paratos & accensos ad clamandum videt, jam exaudit & respondet, non expectans dum ornate & composite loquamur, & turbationem animi, cui reluctamur, condonans. Denique vigilandum ad preces in omni perseverantia est; ne segnescamus, Luc. XVIII. 1. vel silentium demus Deo, donec stabilitat, & Hierosolymam laudem ponat in terra, Esaj. LXII. 7. Nam quae speramus & petimus, cum patientia expectare debemus, Rom. VIII. 25. Ex quibus liquet, praeceptum omni tempore & semper orandi capiendum esse sensu congruo, non absurdo, & rei, quae praecipitur, naturae, vel vitae humanae conditioni & officiis repugnante, quod esset cum veteribus & novis Messalianis & Euchetis praecepti hujus obtentu solis precibus, abdicatis reliquae pietatis & vocationis officiis, vacantibus, Scripturae uber nimium premendo, pro lacte sanguinem elicere.
units.tr: Extraordinary prayer, undertaken for some special grace and a particular cause, privately or publicly, beyond the usual order, has been taken up. We ought always to be ready without ceasing [ἀπαύστως] to pray. And the Apostle commands us to this very thing: to watch in all perseverance (Eph. 6:18). For a man must always be on watch for occasions of prayer, and must take something away from sleep and recreation and devote it to meditating on the grace of God, the struggle that surrounds us, the goods which God bids us seek, and the danger and misery in which the Church or the world is engaged. Lying awake in our beds, we ought to turn over these same thoughts, desires and vows. Prayers themselves should not be sleepy, cold or careless, but effective [ἐνεργούμεναι] (Jas. 5:16). For how will God hear us if we ourselves do not hear ourselves? Yet where there is sincere feeling, God helps the weakness of the one praying, answering before he calls (Isa. 65:24). For when he sees us ready [ἑτοίμως] and kindled to cry out, he already hears and answers, not waiting until we speak in an elaborate and composed way, and pardoning the disturbance of mind against which we struggle. Finally, we must watch for prayer in all perseverance, lest we grow slack (Luke 18:1), or give God no rest until he establishes and makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth (Isa. 62:7). For what we hope for and seek we must wait for with patience (Rom. 8:25). From these things it is clear that the command to pray at all times and always must be understood in a fitting sense, not an absurd one, nor one contrary to the nature of the thing commanded or to the condition of human life and its duties. Otherwise, with the old and new Messalians and Euchites, by pretext of this precept, withdrawing from the duties of the rest of piety and calling, and devoting themselves to prayer alone, they would squeeze too hard the abundant breast of Scripture and draw blood instead of milk.

units.la: CIX. De Ordine instituendae precationis
units.tr: CIX. On the Order to Be Observed in Prayer

units.la: praeceptum nullum extat. Nam in re arbitraria, & Spiritus intus docentis & ducentis motui relicta praeceptum intervenire non potuit; neque proin nos anxios & scrupulosos nimium esse convenit. Varia precantium conditio, fines varii esse possunt. Cum enim precationum genera sejungenda non sint; sed cum peccatorum confessione doxologia, cum precatione, deprecatione & intercessione gratiarum actio conjungenda sit, prout animo laetiore ob res secundas, vel maestiore, & peccati conscientia turbatione sumus, alius atque alius orandi ordo observandus est. In universum hic ordo servandus videtur, ut a Deo prius exauditi gratias ei ante omnia persolvamus, inde peccatorum exomologesin instituamus, bona petamus, mala deprecemur, pro aliis intercedamus, & in doxologia desinamus. Cujus ordinis rationem ipsa Oratio Dominica suppeditare videtur. Nam Patrem appellantes, tacite pro jure accedendi ad ipsum in Christo, & adoptione nostra gratias agimus; tum bona precamur, & glorificantes Deum, claudimus.
units.tr: There is no command on this point. Since the matter is left to our judgment and to the movement of the Spirit who teaches and leads within us, no command could be laid down; so we ought not to be overly anxious or scrupulous about it. The condition of those who pray varies, and their aims can vary. For the kinds of prayer are not to be kept apart: confession of sins must be joined with doxology, and thanksgiving with petition, deprecation and intercession. Depending on whether our mind is more cheerful because of prosperity, or more sad and troubled by a sense of sin, a different order of prayer must be observed. In general, this order seems to be the one to keep: first, having been heard by God, we render thanks to him before all else; then we make confession of our sins; then we ask for good things, pray against evils, intercede for others, and end in doxology. The Lord's Prayer itself seems to supply the reason for this order. For when we address the Father, we tacitly give thanks for the right of access to him in Christ and for our adoption; then we ask for good things, and closing with the glorifying of God, we end.

units.la: CX. Denique de Gestibus etiam orantium speciale mandatum Dei nullum extat.
