Neque illi in quavis oratione necessarii sunt. certe non in mentali, neque etiam vocali quavis, velut ejaculatoria, aegrotantium. Ubi vero adhibendi sunt, cavendum est, ne vel precatio gesticulatio fiat, vel inusitati gestus adhibeantur, vel necessitatis opinio adsit, vel oculis hominum quicquam detur. Sunt quidam gestus, quos natura ipsa precibus accommodatas esse docet, quales sunt, aperire caput, spirituali nuditati & subjectioni testandae: oculos ad Coelum, velut solium Dei attollere: tollere manus; quomodo manus porrigentes ostendunt, totum animum quasi ire ad eum, cui ex porriguntur; vel porrigi eas apprehendendas, ut qui aquis mergun-tur. Stare etiam reverentiae; ingeniculare humiliationis & abjectionis coram Deo signum est. Sed non omnes ritus omni loco & tempori conveniunt. Neque etiam ullus status corporis a precibus alienus est. Si enim semper precandum, in omni corporis statu precandum est. S. Paulus sanctas manus ἐπαίροντες levare jubet, 1. Tim. II. 8. praecipiens, ut cum eas levamus, sanctae, puras, innocentia lotae, Psal. LXXIII. 14. in opere virtutis & justitiae exercitae sint, sicut ipsa oratio תפלה oratio pura esse debet, Job. XVI. 17. Sed possunt tamen, qui inter precandum manus non elevant, oculos in Coelum non attollunt, genua inflectunt, in terram se non prosternunt, eum animum gerere, qui manuum & oculorum in Coelum elevatione, genuum flexione, & sui in terram abjectione significatur. Et in universum circa gestus hae regulae figi possunt; ut seligantur tales, qui notitiae erga Majestatem Dei devotioni, venerationi, humilitati, zelo & fiduciae, quae in corde orantis flagrare debent, exprimendae quam maxime idonei sunt: ut in precibus publicis quisque Ecclesiae particularis, in qua degit, ritum, si absurdus & indecens non sit, sequatur; quia omnis dissensio schisma parit: ut in privatis quisque sequatur, quod animi affectum inflammare pote est; quia gestus non adhibentur, ut Deo acceptior oratio sit, sed ut per eum homo ad orandum gemendumque humilius & ferventius excitetur: ut in utrisque potior animi quam corporis ratio habeatur, quia Deus cor intuetur, 1. Sam. XVI. 7. Denique ut exempla gestuum, quos Christus & Sancti in verbo Dei adhibuisse leguntur, potius quam aliorum quorumvis, libera & conducibili imitatione exprimantur.
units.tr: CX. Finally, there is no special command of God about the gestures of those who pray. Nor are they necessary in every prayer: certainly not in mental prayer, nor in any vocal prayer, such as ejaculatory prayer made by the sick. Where they are to be used, care must be taken that prayer does not become a mere gesturing, that unusual gestures are not adopted, that there is no belief that they are necessary, and that nothing is offered to the eyes of men. There are some gestures which nature itself teaches to be fitting for prayer, such as uncovering the head, to show spiritual nakedness and submission; lifting the eyes to heaven, as to the throne of God; lifting up the hands, as those stretching out their hands show that their whole mind goes out to him to whom they are stretched; or stretching them out to be grasped, as those who are drowning in water do. Standing is also a sign of reverence; kneeling is a sign of humiliation and abasement before God. But not all rites suit every place and time. Nor is any bodily posture foreign to prayer. For if we must always pray, we must pray in every bodily posture. St Paul bids us lift up holy hands [sanctas manus ἐπαίροντες], 1 Tim. 2:8, instructing that when we lift them, they should be holy, pure, washed in innocence [innocentia lotae], Ps. 73:14, in the exercise of virtue and righteousness, just as prayer itself [תפלה] ought to be pure, Job 16:17. Yet those who do not lift their hands while praying, who do not raise their eyes to heaven, who bend their knees, or who do not prostrate themselves on the ground, may still bear the attitude that is signified by lifting hands and eyes to heaven, bending the knees, and casting oneself down to the earth. And in general, the following rules can be fixed concerning gestures: such gestures should be chosen as are most suitable for expressing the devotion, reverence, humility, zeal and trust which ought to burn in the heart of the one praying, in regard to the majesty of God. In public prayer, each person should follow the rite of the particular congregation in which he lives, provided it is not absurd or indecent, because all dissent gives birth to schism. In private prayer, each person should follow whatever can inflame the affection of his mind, because gestures are not used to make prayer more acceptable to God, but so that through them a man may be stirred to pray and sigh more humbly and fervently. In both, a greater regard should be had for the mind than for the body, because God looks at the heart [Deus cor intuetur], 1 Sam. 16:7. Finally, examples of gestures which Christ and the saints are read to have used in the Word of God should be expressed by free and fitting imitation, rather than by those of any others whatsoever.

units.la: CXI. Non pauca in V. & N. T. precationum exempla occurrunt. Sed praecipue commendata nobis esse Oratio, quam Dominus discipulos suos docuit, debet; de qua frequentanda ipsius Christi praeceptum extat. Cum oratis, dicite: Pater noster, &c. Luc. XI. 2. Matth. VI. 9. In ea professio fidei & charitatis erga Deum & proximum includitur, simulque exploratio nostri quotidiana nobis commendatur, ut si cor nostrum nos non condemnet, cum fiducia ad Deum accedamus, scientes, eum Patrem nostrum esse, & nos habere, quae ab eo petimus, 1. Joh. III. 21, 22, 23. Et oratio igitur in ea continetur, quam fundere omnes tenentur, juxta illa Christi: sic igitur orate vos; Matth. VI. 9. & orationum omnium canon, regula & amussis, ad quam preces omnes ab hominibus compositae exigendae sunt, juxta illa ejusdem Christi: Cum oratis, dicite, Luc. XI. 2. Canon enim ille ceu modum & materiam orandi praescribit, ut juxta exemplar ejus omnis oratio nostra ad solum Deum, & in lingua omnibus cognita fundatur, & petantur; quae ad Dei gloriam, & salutem nostram pertinent, ut gloria beneficiorum omnium ad unum solumque Deum referatur. Sed simul, ceu precationis formula eo ordine, iisdémque verbis nobis recitanda & usurpanda est, quod temerè Brounistæ inficiantur. Licèt enim non ita formulæ huic nos Christus adstrinxerit, ut aliis ad ejus amussim compositis uti nefas sit; & recitantes eam neutiquam ea superstitione laborare debeant, quasi in literis & syllabis efficacia lateat, atque illa potiùs cum intelligentia, gratia & spiritu 1. Cor. XIV. 14. 15. usurpari debeat: tamen ejus usus pius omnino est, & omitti non potest. Nam formulam precandi Apostoli petierunt, & Christus iis gratificaturus formulam eam accuratissimè dispositam tradidit: & Evangelistæ iisdem pœne verbis eam repetierunt: & par ejus, atque formulæ Decalogi, Baptismi, S. Cœnæ ratio est: & accommodata illa omnibus omni loco ac tempore orantibus est: & fiduciam exauditionis nostræ inprimis confirmat, quia ejus author respectu Dei Filius Dei, respectu nostri Filius hominis, nosterque frater similiter, ut nos, sed absque peccato, tentatus fuit. Unum addo, videri Viris doctissimis, Christum in contexenda Oratione hac secutum esse λειψανα quædam præstantissimorum cimeliorum, quæ in Ecclesiæ Judaicæ thesauro supererant. Cui rei probandæ formulas Orationis hujus pleraque in libris & Euchologiis Hebræorum veterum Drusius, Capellus, Ligthfootus, alii ostendere satagunt. Et potest sanè Christus æquè ac novus Elias, Johannes, hac ratione cor filiorum ad patres eorum convertere, Mal. IV. 6. & φρόνησιν δικαιων sensum patrum justorum eorundem animis instillare, Luc. I. 17. atque ita sicut in doctrina, ita etiam in oratione fidelium V. & N. T. ὁμόνοιαν manifestam facere, atque id denique apud suos efficere, ut neque nimiæ & affectatæ novitatis cupidus videri posset, & facilius oratio intelligeretur, atque in animos orantium influeret. Sed compages tamen Orationis sapientissimo pulcherrimóque ordine disposita solum Jesum authorem habet, ejúsque Divinam sapientiam commendat.
units.tr: CXI. Not a few examples of prayer occur in the Old and New Testaments. But above all, the Prayer which the Lord taught his disciples ought to be commended to us; and there is a command of Christ himself to use it frequently: When you pray, say: Our Father [Cum oratis, dicite: Pater noster], etc., Luke 11:2; Matt. 6:9. In it is included a profession of faith and of love towards God and neighbour, and at the same time a daily self-examination is commended to us, so that, if our heart does not condemn us [si cor nostrum nos non condemnet], we may approach God with confidence, knowing that he is our Father and that we have what we ask from him, 1 John 3:21-23. Therefore, the prayer which all are bound to pour forth is contained in it, according to those words of Christ: So pray you [sic igitur orate vos], Matt. 6:9; and it is the canon, rule and standard of all prayers, to which all prayers composed by men must be measured, according to those same words of Christ: When you pray, say [Cum oratis, dicite], Luke 11:2. For that canon prescribes, as it were, the manner and the matter of praying, so that according to its pattern every prayer of ours is founded upon God alone, and is made in a language known to all, and asks for those things which pertain to the glory of God and our salvation, so that the glory of all benefits is referred to the one God alone. But at the same time, it is to be recited and used by us as a formula of prayer, in the same order and with the same words, which the Brownists rashly deny. For although Christ has not bound us to this formula in such a way that it would be wrong to use others composed according to its pattern, and those who recite it ought not to labour under the superstition that efficacy lies hidden in the letters and syllables, but rather that it should be used with understanding, grace and spirit, 1 Cor. 14:14-15, nevertheless its pious use is altogether proper and cannot be omitted. For the apostles asked for a formula of prayer, and Christ, granting their request, handed down a formula most carefully arranged; and the Evangelists repeated it in almost the same words; and the case of it is like that of the formula of the Decalogue, of Baptism and of the Lord's Supper; and it is suited to all who pray in every place and at every time; and it especially strengthens our confidence of being heard, because its author, with respect to God, is the Son of God, and with respect to us, the Son of Man, and our brother, likewise tempted as we are, but without sin. I add one thing: learned men think that in composing this Prayer Christ followed some remnants [λειψανα] of most excellent treasures which survived in the treasury of the Jewish Church. To prove this, Drusius, Capellus, Lightfoot and others labour to show that most of the formulas of this Prayer are found in the books and prayer-books of the ancient Hebrews. And certainly Christ, like the new Elijah, John, could in this way turn the hearts of the children to their fathers, Mal. 4:6, and instil into their minds the wisdom of the righteous [φρόνησιν δικαίων] of those righteous fathers, Luke 1:17; and so, just as in doctrine, so also in the prayer of the faithful of the Old and New Testaments, he might make manifest harmony [ὁμόνοιαν], and finally bring it about among his own people that he could not seem to be a man who desired excessive and affected novelty, and that the prayer might be more easily understood and might flow into the minds of those praying. But nevertheless the structure of the Prayer, arranged in the wisest and most beautiful order, has Jesus alone as its author, and it commends his divine wisdom.

units.la: CXII. Tres Orationis illius partes sunt, compellatio ejus, ad quem illa dirigitur, corpus, seu materia ejusdem, & clausula. Compellatio est ejus, ad quem oratio dirigitur: Πατερ ἡμῶν, ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς. Pater noster, qui es in Coelis. Quæ verba maxima emphasi paucis multa complectuntur. Nam & Patrem compellantes, affectum filiorum, jus ad eum accedendi habentium, non mercenariorum, fiduciámque exauditionis non in nobis & operibus nostris, sed in Deo per Christum in communione Spiritus S. conciliato Patre testamur: & nostrum cientes, tum fidei indolem, applicantis sibi promissionem, velut ad se pertinentem; tum charitatem erga proximum, cum quo, ceu nostro in Christo fratre, condonatis ei offensis omnibus, in gratiam nos rediisse; & pro quo, æquè ac pro nobis ipsis coram facie Dei nos comparere, atque ita accedentium ad Deum agmen facere, fraternitatem amplexari, charitatem promittere, profitemur: & compellantes eum, qui in Coelis est, confitemur, non quòd Coelis inclusus sit is, quem coeli coelorum non capiunt; sed quòd tum se ipsum & gloriam suam in Coelo, ceu domo sua, quam demonstrandæ gloriæ suæ πολυπικιλω fecit, omnia ibi in omnibus im-
units.tr: CXII. There are three parts of that Prayer: the address to him to whom it is directed; its body, or matter; and its conclusion. The address [Compellatio] is to him to whom the prayer is directed: Our Father, who art in heaven [Πατερ ἡμῶν, ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς]. Our Father, who art in the heavens [Pater noster, qui es in Coelis]. These words, with the greatest emphasis, comprise many things in few. For in addressing the Father [Patrem], we bear witness that we have the affection of children, who have the right to approach him, not of hired servants, and that our trust of being heard rests not in ourselves and our works, but in God, the Father reconciled through Christ in the communion of the Holy Spirit. And in calling him our [nostrum] Father, we profess both the nature of faith, which applies the promise to itself as belonging to it, and love towards our neighbour, with whom, as our brother in Christ, we have been restored to favour, all offences being forgiven, and for whom, equally as for ourselves, we stand before the face of God, and thus we profess that we form a company of those who approach God, embrace brotherhood and promise love. And in addressing him who is in heaven [qui in Coelis est], we confess that he, whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain, is not shut up in heaven; but that he has made both himself and his glory manifest in heaven, as in his own house, which he has made of very various [πολυποικίλῳ] display of his glory, and there, in all things, im-

units.la: Ejus partes tres sunt, compellatio ejus, ad quem dirigitur, corpus & clausula.
units.tr: Its parts are three: the address to the one to whom it is directed, the body, and the closing clause.

units.la: plendo immediatè & efficaciùs longè, quàm in terra, manifestet, atque ibi, velut in patria nostra, mansio nobis à Christo, qui & ipse, ceu Angelus & Mediator Testamenti illuc ascendit, & Majestatem suam supra Coelos posuit, Psal. VIII. 2. parata sit: tum ad eum, ceu Patrem, sic liber nobis accessus pateat, ut nihilominus eum tam sublimi Majestate verendum, ceu vermiculi humi repentes humilimè colamus & suspiciamus: tum precum nostrarum ardor & vociferatio tam vehemens esse debeat, ut ad Coelum usque pertingat: tum denique magnam in coelesti Patre, coelorum ipsorum regendorum arbitrium habente, fiduciam collocemus, quòd, qui in Coelis est, & facere potest, quicquid vult, ibid. CXV. 3. ceu Pater noster, nostri causa omnia velit & possit, ut certam exauditionis spem concipere valeamus.
units.tr: filling all things, immediately and far more effectively than on earth, and there, as in our homeland, a dwelling be prepared for us by Christ, who himself ascended there as the Angel and Mediator of the covenant and set his majesty above the heavens (Ps. 8:2). Then may such free access to him as Father be open to us, that we nonetheless revere him with so lofty a majesty and worship and look up to him in the deepest humility, like little worms crawling on the ground. Then the fervour and outcry of our prayers ought to be so vehement that they reach even to heaven. Finally, let us place a great trust in the heavenly Father, who has the disposal of the heavens themselves, that, since he who is in heaven can do whatever he wills (Ps. 115:3), he will will and be able to do all things for our sake as our Father, so that we may conceive a sure hope of being heard.

units.la: CXIII. Corpus ipsum Orationis sex petitionibus constat; quarum tres priores Deum ejúsque gloriam, tres posteriores proximi & nostram salutem concernunt. Planè enim ut Decalogus duabus tabulis, quarum priore amor Dei, posteriore amor proximi præcipitur, constat, etiam Orationem hanc Christus ipse duabus velut tabulis inclusit, quarum priore suæ gloriæ, posteriore nostræ saluti consuluit. Sicut etiam Decalogi summam paucis verbis Deus ipse constrinxit, mandans amare Deum ex toto corde, tota anima, & tota cogitatione, proximum verò sicut seipsum, Deut. VI. 5. ita Christus Orationis à le præscriptæ petitiones in hanc summam contraxit: Quærite primò Regnum Dei & justitiam ejus, & omnia hæc vobis addentur, Matth. VI. 32. Præcedit enim jure meriòque Deus & gloria ejus, cujus nobis cura præcipua cum zelo, & cum periculo etiam salutis nostræ, temporalis inprimis, commendata esse debet: & sequitur cura salutis nostræ. Neque ordo ille per amorem nostri potiùs, quàm Dei, sine manifesta hypocrisi, turbari, vel invertì potest. Nam & pronomen illud Tuum Nomen, Regnum, Voluntas: Nostrum panem, debitorum remissionem à prioribus secludit, & posteriore loco amandat. Quo non obstante anima fidelis pro Deo orare vísa, pro se ipsa orat, quia pro Deo orando, non eum beatiorem vel perfectiorem facit, sed in Dei gloria suam gloriam, in Dei felicitate suam felicitatem invenit. Cùm enim Dei gloriam obnixà prece poscit, id ipsum simul poscit, ut in se gloriosus & admirabilis fieri velit, qui beatitudinis nostræ apex est.
units.tr: CXIII. The body of the Prayer consists of six petitions. The first three concern God and his glory, the last three concern our neighbour and our salvation. Just as the Decalogue consists of two tables, the first commanding love of God and the second love of neighbour, so Christ himself enclosed this Prayer within two tables, as it were, of which the first provides for his glory and the second for our salvation. Likewise God himself summed up the Decalogue in a few words, commanding us to love God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind, and the neighbour as oneself (Deut. 6:5). So Christ drew the petitions prescribed in the Prayer into this summary: Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matt. 6:33). For God and his glory rightly and justly come first, and our care, with zeal and even with danger to our salvation, and above all our temporal welfare, ought to be commended to us, and the care of our salvation follows. Nor can that order be disturbed or inverted, through love of ourselves rather than of God, without manifest hypocrisy. For those pronouns, Thy name, kingdom, will, and our bread and the remission of debts, shut out the first and relegate them to a later place. Nevertheless, the faithful soul, though it seems to pray for God, prays for itself. For in praying for God, it does not make him more blessed or more perfect, but finds its own glory in the glory of God and its own happiness in the happiness of God. For when it earnestly asks for the glory of God, it at the same time asks that he, who is the summit of our blessedness, be glorious and admirable in himself.

units.la: CXIV. PRIMA Petitio est de Sanctificatione Nominis Dei: Ἁγιασθήτω τὸ ὄνομά σου, Sanctificetur Nomen tuum. Per Nomen Dei, Majestas Dei & Deus ipse intelligitur. Psallam Nomini Domini Altissimo, Psal. VII. 18. Benedictum Nomen gloriæ ejus in seculum, & replebitur gloria ejus omnis terra, ibid. LXXII. 19. Ecce ego cogitavi ædificare domum לשם יהוה Nomini Jehovæ, 1. Reg. V. 5. לשמך Ad Nomen tuum, & ad memoriam tuam est desiderium animæ tuæ, Esaj. XXVI. 8. Neque Deum simpliciter significat, sed illud inprimis, per quod gloria ejus innotescit, quo in censu sunt Dei nomina, virtutes, monumenta, seu opera & cultus, per quæ nobis innotescit. Nominis hujus Dei sanctificatio ejusdem, ceu absolutè sanéti celebratio, glori-
units.tr: CXIV. The FIRST petition concerns the sanctification of God's Name: Ἁγιασθήτω τὸ ὄνομά σου [Let your name be sanctified]. By the Name of God is understood the majesty of God and God himself: I will sing to the name of the Lord Most High (Ps. 7:18); Blessed be his glorious name for ever, and let the whole earth be filled with his glory (Ps. 72:19); Behold, I purpose to build a house for the name of Jehovah [לשם יהוה] (1 Kings 5:5); To your name, and to your remembrance, is the desire of the soul [לשמך] (Isa. 26:8). It does not signify God simply, but chiefly that by which his glory is made known, which includes the names, virtues, monuments, or works and worship of God by which he is made known to us. The sanctification of this Name of God, that is, the celebration of it as absolutely holy, glorifies it.

units.la: Corpus sex petitionibus constat, quarum tres priores Deum, posteriores nos concernunt.
units.tr: The body consists of six petitions, of which the first three concern God and the latter three concern us.

units.la: Prima petitio, ut sanctificetur Nomen Dei. glorificatio, ab omni usu profano segregatio est. Non enim Nomen Dei à nobis sanctum fieri, sed agnosci, celebrari, prædicari potest & debet. Sicut nec profanari sic Deus potest, ut profanus fiat, sed ut ceu profanus habeatur, proclametur, quod profanantis scelus est; sed Deo ipsi labem affricare non potest. Perinde ut matronæ castæ pudicitia lascivis oculis limata adulterium est, Matth. V. 28. Neque tamen de matronæ pudicitia quicquam delibat. Et sanctificationem potius quàm glorificationem Nominis Dei petere jubemur, tum quia sanctitas Dei gloriæ basis est, Exod. XV. 11. tum quia magnitudo Dei in ejusdem sanctitate maximè conspicua est, Esaj. XII. 6. adeò ut regiam etiam Majestatem sacratissimam appellare mos sit: tum quia sanctitas Dei ejusdem decus, status est, Psal. XCVI. 9. CX. 3. tum quia Angelus selectissimam Dei virtutem expressurus Sanctum, Sanctum, Sanctum appellat, Esaj. VI. 3. tum denique, quia glorificari nisi à sanctis, Sanctissimus & ipse, non potest. Sic petentes ut sanctificetur Nomen Dei, petimus, tum ut Nomen Dei, justitia inprimis & misericordia in Christo ejusque merito reveletur, agnoscatur, celebretur, quod precandum inprimis eo tempore fuit, quo sanctificatio & glorificatio Nominis Dei per mortem Christi proximè instabat: tum ut Deum rectè cognoscamus, & lucentem in omnibus operibus ejus, præcipuè autem gratia electionis & redemptionis atque salutis æternæ, nec non gubernationis Ecclesiæ & totius mundi omnipotentiam, sapientiam, bonitatem, justitiam, misericordiam, veritatem, & reliquas virtutes omnes devotè veneremur, prædicemus, celebremus: tum gratiæ illius, per quam Nomen Dei sic celebrandum & sanctificandum est, lætiora indies incrementa capiamus; tum denique, ut universam vitam nostram, cogitationes, sermones & actiones, sic instituamus, ne sanctissimum Nomen Dei, quod super nos invocatum est, propter nos contumelia afficiatur, sed honore potius laudibusque illustretur. Ita orantes sanctificationem Nominis Dei à Deo simul veram & salutarem Dei, Christi, verbi & operum ejus notitiam, fidem in Deum & verbum ejus, utcunque ejus revelatio carni & sanguini adversetur, quomodo etiam Abrahamus credendo gloriam Deo dedisse, Rom. IV. 20. dicitur: timorem Dei solius: humilitatem, ut cum Davide dicamus. Non nobis, non nobis, sed Nomini tuo da gloriam propter misericordiam tuam, Psal. CXV. 1. patientiam, ut in adversis etiam Nomen Dei laudemus; gratitudinem pro beneficiis innumeris; aperta corda & linguas sonoras ad confitendum, invocandum, gratias agendum, ut erudiet cor verbum bonum, & lingua sit ut stylus scribæ velocis, ibid. XLV. 2. & laudem Dei prædicet, ibid. LI. 17. denique vitam exactam, & professione Nominis Dei dignam, exuberantésque fidei fructus, ut qui eos vident, Patrem nostrum in Cœlis glorificent, Matth. V. 16. petimus.
units.tr: The first petition, that the Name of God be sanctified, is the glorification of it, its separation from every profane use. For the Name of God cannot and ought not to be made holy by us, but to be acknowledged, celebrated, and proclaimed. Just as God cannot be profaned so as to become profane, but can be treated as profane, which is the crime of the one who profanes him, yet cannot be stained in himself, so too the chastity of a chaste matron is violated by lascivious eyes, which is adultery (Matt. 5:28), yet nothing is taken from the matron's chastity. We are commanded to ask for the sanctification rather than the glorification of God's Name, both because God's holiness is the basis of his glory (Exod. 15:11), and because the greatness of God is most conspicuous in his holiness (Isa. 12:6), so that it is even customary to call a king's majesty most sacred; and because the holiness of God is his adornment and state (Ps. 96:9; 110:3); and because the angel, wishing to express God's most excellent power, calls him Holy, Holy, Holy (Isa. 6:3); and finally, because he cannot be glorified except by holy ones, being himself most holy. Thus in asking that the Name of God be sanctified, we ask first that the Name of God, chiefly his justice and mercy in Christ and by his merit, be revealed, acknowledged, and celebrated, which ought especially to be prayed for at the time when the sanctification and glorification of God's Name through the death of Christ was immediately at hand. Then we ask that we may rightly know God and devoutly venerate, proclaim, and celebrate him as he shines in all his works, especially in the grace of election, redemption, and eternal salvation, and also in the government of the Church and the whole world, and in his omnipotence, wisdom, goodness, justice, mercy, truth, and all his other virtues. Then that we may receive ever happier increases of that grace by which the Name of God is to be so celebrated and sanctified. Finally, that we so order our whole life, thoughts, words, and deeds, that the most holy Name of God, which has been invoked over us, may not be treated with contumely on our account, but rather be illustrated with honour and praise. Praying thus, we ask of God at the same time for true and saving knowledge of God, Christ, the Word, and his works; for faith in God and his Word, however his revelation may be opposed by flesh and blood, just as Abraham is said to have given glory to God by believing (Rom. 4:20); for the fear of God alone; for humility, so that with David we may say, Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your mercy's sake (Ps. 115:1); for patience, so that we may praise the Name of God even in adversity; for gratitude for countless benefits; for open hearts and resonant tongues to confess, invoke, and give thanks, so that my heart overflows with a good word, and my tongue is like the pen of a swift scribe (Ps. 45:1), and may proclaim the praise of God (Ps. 51:15). Finally, we ask for a holy life worthy of the profession of the Name of God, and abundant fruits of faith, so that those who see them may glorify our Father in heaven (Matt. 5:16).

units.la: CXV. Secunda Petitio Adventum Regni Dei orat.
units.tr: CXV. The Second Petition: It Prays for the Coming of God's Kingdom

units.la: Ελθάτω ἡ βασιλεία σου, Veniat Regnum tuum. Est autem Regnum Dei vel hujus vel alterius vitæ. Hujus vitæ aliud naturale & universale, quo Deus omnes creaturas suas regit & moderatur; aliud spirituale, quo Christus Ecclesiam suam in hoc mundo Spiritu suo & sceptro verbi regit, usque dum hostes ejus pedum ejus scabellum ponantur, 1. Cor. XV. 25. In quo Regno Christus Rex, Psal. II. 6. Hos. III. 5. Sancti subditi, Apoc. XV. 3. Verbum ejus Lex, Job. XXII. 22. Angeli ut creaturæ omnes Ministri, Hebr. I. 6. 14. præcones verbi Legati, 2. Cor. V. 20. Diabolus & Regnum ejus, damnati omnes, hostes, adversarii, Luc. XIX. 27. & scabellum pedum Christi sunt, Psal. CX. 1. Atque aliter Deus illud in V. T. sub servitute elementorum mundi gubernavit; aliter in Novo, sub libertate gubernat. Posterius illud κατ' ἐξοχὴν Regni Dei & Cœlorum nomine venit, quia & Dei est sine sociis, & Regem habet in Cœlo tanquam throno suo sedentem, ad quem, Cœlis apertis, accedimus, habentes communionem cum iis, qui in Cœlo sunt, ratione consummationis, in communi redemptione, pace & justitia. Alterius vitæ Regnum Gloriæ est. Adventum Regni Dei orantes, inprimis Regnum Gratiæ per Gloriam consummandum intelligimus, quod appropinquaverat tum, cùm Christus adventum ejus petere jussit; & mox venit violenter, & quotidie venit, tum intra cor hominum, tum in perfectione sua per amplificationem Ecclesiæ, & abolitione hostium Regni ejus, Diaboli, Bestiæ, Antichristi, donec Christus inter hostes regnare desinet, & omnia in omnibus erit, omnésque suos cœlesti gloria implebit. Summa igitur voti est, ut Deus non tantùm creaturas omnes in cursu naturæ & societatis externæ civilis & domesticæ, quin & ipsum Diabolum, ut Ecclesiæ præter voluntatem suam inservire cogatur, potenter regat, sed inprimis Ecclesiam Verbo & Spiritu suo sic moderetur, ut & in hac vita virtute & potentia Christi; unici Ecclesiæ capitis, salutem suorum promovenus, & hostes atque perduelles ejus omnes domantis, crescat & amplificetur, & in altera vita æterna gloria impleatur. Et media quidem amplificandæ Ecclesiæ, pro quibus precamur, adventum Regni Gratiæ precantes, interna vel externa sunt. Internum Spiritus S. est, cujus virtute Christus Ecclesiam colligit, conservat & propagat, effundens eum cum donis & motibus suis necessariis in omnes salvandos. Externa sunt Verbum Dei, Sacramenta & Disciplina Ecclesiæ, quibus Spiritus S. ad conversionem & salutem nostram utitur. Orandum igitur jugiter est, ut Deus & Verbum suum, ceu sceptrum roboris Regni Christi, Psal. CX. 2. Evangelium Regni Dei, Marc. I. 14. emittat in Sionem, quò illud inoffenso pede τρέχη currat, 2. Thess. III. 1. Omniáque verbo huic contraria, humanas inventiones, Diaboli & Antichristi adversus illud machinas potenter destruat, & Sacramenta, verbi gratiæ sigilla, in legitimo usu, ad confirmationem fidei confervet, oppositaque ei spuria Sacramenta & Missæ sacrificium aboleat: & Disciplinam singulorum atque totius Ecclesiæ ad sanctificationem ejus per verbum & Spiritum suum moderetur, omnémque teporem discutiat, & in conscientias tyrannidem refrœnet; denique ut Ecclesiam per pios Magistratus, Meretricis Babylonicæ non amasios, sed ofores, & impietatis omnis hostes, nec non fidos ministros & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei, quosque in competente sibi cura & officio gubernet. Et quæ Ecclesiæ totius, eadem singulorum etiam ratio est. Nam singuli etiam pro se orant, ut Regnum Dei ad se veniat, hoc est, ut liberati à Regno Sathanæ Christi Regnum subeant; in communionem bonorum cœlestium vocati, per veram fidem & pœnitentiam, verbo & Spiritu Dei regantur, & se Deo magis magisque subjiciant, Regni Christi bonis, justitia, pace & lætitia in Spiritu S. potiantur, atque ita & ipsi spirituales Reges evadant. Neque tantùm Regni Gratiæ, sed etiam Regni Gloriæ, quod à Regno Gratiæ non reipsa, sed administrandi duntaxat modo & duratione differt, adventum precamur, ut Deus Ecclesiam & singulos nos, per medios veluti hostes, à Deo pacis sub pedibus nostris contritos profligatosque in cœlestis gloriæ possessionem immittat, atque eundem in finem adventum secundum Filii sui promoveat. Cujus desiderio tot infirmitatibus onerati, identidem Christo testificanti:Ναὶ ἔρχομαι ταχὺ Etiam, venio citò, acclamemus, Ναὶ ἔρχου Κύριε Ἰησοῦ Etiam, veni Domine Jesu, Apoc. XXII. 20.
units.tr: Let your kingdom come [Ελθάτω ἡ βασιλεία σου], Let your kingdom come. The Kingdom of God belongs either to this life or to the next. In this life there is one kind that is natural and universal, by which God rules and governs all his creatures. There is another, spiritual kingdom, by which Christ in this world rules his Church by his Spirit and the sceptre of his Word, ruling until his enemies are made the footstool of his feet, 1 Cor. 15:25. In this Kingdom Christ is the King, Ps. 2:6; Hos. 3:5. The saints are his subjects, Rev. 15:3. His Word is the law, Job 22:22. The angels, as all creatures, are his ministers, Heb. 1:6, 14; the preachers of the Word are his ambassadors, 2 Cor. 5:20. The devil and his kingdom, and all the damned, are his enemies and adversaries, Luke 19:27, and they are the footstool of Christ's feet, Ps. 110:1. God has governed this kingdom in one way under the Old Testament, under the bondage of the elements of the world, and in another way under the New, in liberty. The latter is called, par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], the Kingdom of God and of heaven, because it belongs to God alone without partners, and because it has its King in heaven, seated as on his throne. To him we draw near, with heaven opened, having fellowship with those who are in heaven, by reason of the consummation, in common redemption, peace and righteousness. The kingdom of the other life is the kingdom of glory. When we pray for the coming of God's kingdom, we understand first the Kingdom of Grace, to be consummated through glory. This kingdom had drawn near when Christ bade us ask for its coming, and soon it came violently, and it comes every day, both within the hearts of men and in its perfection through the enlargement of the Church and the overthrow of the enemies of its kingdom: the devil, the beast, and Antichrist. It will continue until Christ ceases to reign among his enemies, and God is all in all, and he fills all his people with heavenly glory. The sum of our prayer, therefore, is that God should powerfully rule not only all creatures in the course of nature and in external civil and domestic society, but even the devil himself, so that he is compelled to serve the Church against his own will. Above all, we pray that he would so govern the Church by his Word and Spirit that it may grow and be enlarged in this life, by the virtue and power of Christ, the only Head of the Church, who promotes the salvation of his own and subdues all his enemies and rebels, and that it may be filled with eternal glory in the life to come. The means of enlarging the Church, for which we pray as we ask for the coming of the Kingdom of Grace, are either inward or outward. The inward means is the Spirit of God, by whose power Christ gathers, preserves and propagates the Church, pouring his Spirit with his necessary gifts and motions into all who are to be saved. The outward means are the Word of God, the Sacraments, and the discipline of the Church, by which the Holy Spirit works for our conversion and salvation. We must therefore constantly pray that God would send out his Word, like the sceptre of strength of Christ's Kingdom, Ps. 110:2, the gospel of the Kingdom of God, Mark 1:14, into Zion, so that it may run [τρέχη] with unhindered foot, 2 Thess. 3:1. May he powerfully destroy everything contrary to this Word, human inventions, and the machinations of the devil and Antichrist against it. May he preserve the Sacraments, the seals of the Word, in their lawful use, for the confirmation of faith, and abolish the spurious sacraments opposed to them, and the sacrifice of the Mass. May he govern the discipline of each person and of the whole Church, for its sanctification through his Word and Spirit, shake off all lukewarmness, and restrain tyranny over consciences. Finally, may he govern the Church through pious magistrates, who are not lovers of the Babylonian harlot but her enemies, and enemies of all impiety, and through faithful ministers and stewards of the mysteries of God, each in the care and office that belongs to him. What holds for the whole Church holds also for each individual. Each of us prays for himself that the Kingdom of God may come to him, that is, that, freed from the kingdom of Satan, he may come under the kingdom of Christ. Called into fellowship with heavenly goods through true faith and repentance, he may be ruled by the Word and Spirit of God, submit himself more and more to God, and possess the blessings of Christ's kingdom: righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Thus he too may become a spiritual king. We pray for the coming not only of the Kingdom of Grace but also of the Kingdom of Glory, which differs from the Kingdom of Grace not in substance but only in the manner of its administration and in its duration. We pray that God would bring the Church and each of us, through what are as it were enemies, into possession of heavenly glory, having crushed and routed them under our feet, the God of peace. To this end we pray that he would hasten the second coming of his Son. Burdened by so many infirmities, and longing for that day, let us, as Christ repeatedly testifies, cry out: Yes, I come quickly [Ναὶ ἔρχομαι ταχὺ], Yes, I come quickly; and let us answer: Yes, come, Lord Jesus [Ναὶ ἔρχου Κύριε Ἰησοῦ], Yes, come, Lord Jesus, Rev. 22:20.

units.la: CXVI. Tertia Petitio promovendæ in Regno hoc voluntati Dei unicè inservit. Γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου ὡς ἐν οὐρανῷ, ἡ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Fiat voluntas tua sicut in Cœlo, ita etiam in terra. Quò potentius Dei Regnum est, hoc severiùs voluntatem suam fieri vult. Et cujus voluntatem facimus, eum Regem & Dominum nostrum eadem ratione testamur. Doce me facere voluntatem tuam, quia tu Deus meus, Psal. CXLIII. 10. Denique & facientes voluntatem Dei Patris in Cœlis, ingredimur Regnum Cœlorum, Matth. VII. 21. Duplex verò Dei voluntas est, decernens, seu efficiens, quæ priusquam Deus decreta sua exequitur, occulta est; & præcipiens seu approbans, quæ in verbo ejusdem revelata est. Illa de nobis, hæc à nobis fit. Utramque fieri petimus, sed diversimodè. Illam petentes, declaramus, tum nos acquiescere in omnibus, quæ Deus de nobis statuit, dicentes cum Maria: Ecce, ancilla Domini, fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum, Luc. I. 38. tum promptos nos esse ad inserviendum consilio Dei, alacrésque ad propositi Divini executionem nos offerre, tum cupere nos, ut non aliud in nobis alìsque fiat, quàm quod æterno Dei decreto semel fixum est, exemplo Cæsareensium, aliorúmque Pauli amicorum, qui auditis Pauli vinculis, denique acquieverunt, ut non obstantibus iis Hierosolymam ascendat, dicentes: Fiat voluntas Domini, Actor. XXI. 12. 13. 14. Quicquid proin facere intendimus, ea conditione, si Dominus voluerit, Jac. IV. 15. eàque vel implicita, vel explicita facere intendimus; neque nimium severè & operosè intendimus, ne Dei decreto præjudicemus, providentes inprimis maturè, ne quid propositio nostro exequendo adversetur. Voluntas Dei omnium affectuum fraenum est in iis, qui gloriam Dei serió quærunt. Nam & ipsum cor Regis est in manu Jehovæ, Prov. XXI. 1. Et hominis sunt præparationes cordis, sed à Jehova est responsio linguæ, ibid. XVI. 1. Inprimis Voluntatem Dei præcipientem & revelatam à nobis fieri oramus, & orandi magnas causas habemus, quia aliter subditi Regni Dei esse non possumus. Est autem aliquid in nobis, quod ex Regno Dei non est, nempe caro, & malum nobis adjacens, lex contraria legi Dei, captivans nos sub legem peccati, quæ in membris nostris est, Rom. VII. 17-24. Φρόνημα σαρκὸς sensus carnis, qui inimicitia adversus Deum est, & legi Dei non subjicitur, nec subjici potest, ibid. VIII. 7. Neque potest nobis Regnum Dei amantibus & mente Deo servientibus, non difficultas, quam ex reluctatione carnis nostræ, spiritus fraenum mordentis, experimur, Gal. V. 17. Ideo enixè oramus, ut Dei voluntas etiam à nobis fiat, ut in Christum credamus, & sanctificationi studeamus, & concupiscentiæ per Spiritum resistamus. Hæc enim voluntas Dei, sanctificatio nostra, 1. Thess. IV. 3. quæ abnegatione nostri, piæ vitæ studio, crucis patiente tolerantia & gloriæ cœlestis desiderio constat, ut videlicet abnegata impietate & mundanis concupiscentiis temperanter, justè & piè vivamus in præsenti seculo, expectantes beatam illam spem & illustrem adventum gloriæ magni illius Dei & Servatoris nostri Jesu Christi, Tit. II. 12. 13. Ne configuramini seculo huic, sed transformamini per renovationem mentis vestræ ad hoc, ut probetis quæ sit voluntas Dei bona illa, accepta & perfecta, Rom. XII. 1. 2. Petimus porro voluntatem Dei à nobis fieri, sicut illa in Cœlo fit. In Cœlo enim est pax, sanctitas, justitia. Et in Regno Dei admittimur ad consortium cœlestium, ut civitas nostra sit in Cœlo, Ephes. I. 10. Phil. III. 20. Hebr. XIII. 20. Ut ergo civitate illa digni simus, cupimus voluntatem Dei à nobis fieri, sicut in Cœlo fit. Tum in Cœlo est ipse Filius Dei, qui facit omnem voluntatem Patris sui, Psal. XL. 9. Sunt Angeli, valentissimi robore, facientes voluntatem Dei, auscultantes voci verbi ejus, ibid. CIII. 20. Sunt animæ beatæ, quæ sequuntur Agnum quocunque iverit, Ap. XIV. 4. Christum ergo, caput nostrum, Angelos & beatos Cœlites humana imbecillitas imitari habet, pro modulo gratiæ, qua in hac vita potitur, & non sine studio proficiendi ad perfectionem, quæ in stadio hoc velut cum impetu τρέχομεν, currentibus meta proponitur. Ut verò petitio hæc accommodata sit regulæ charitatis proximi, petimus, non ut quisque pro se voluntatem Dei faciat, sicut in Cœlo illa fit; sed ut fiat sicut in Cœlo, ita etiam in terra, hoc est, in tota terra, ne sint in ea, qui Deo rebellent, & Regem illum pati renuant. Qualis petitio charitatem sic exercens etiam fit in fide; tum quia novimus, hoc bonum & acceptum sacrificium, quippe boni odoris, Deo esse: tum quia promissiones de Regno Christi extant, nunquam fore, ut mundus Ecclesiam vincat, ut voluntatem mundi illa faciat, cùm potiùs fides nostra vicerit mundum, 1. Joh. V. 4. 5. & Christum victurum omnes hostes suos, & Diabolum sub pedes Ecclesiæ contriturum, Rom. XVI. 20. denique, si infirmitas apud nos reliqua sit, eam potiùs futuram reliquam esse, ut potentia Dei in ea consummetur, & ut appareat, gratiam Dei nobis sufficere, 2. Cor. XII. 9. neque adeò eam impedituram, quò minùs fiamus compotes hæreditatis, quam Pater noster in Cœlo, ubi nil nisi justitia habitat, præparavit, 2. Pet. III. 13.
units.tr: CXVI. The third petition serves solely to advance the will of God in this Kingdom. Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven [Γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου ὡς ἐν οὐρανῷ, ἡ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς]. The more powerful God's Kingdom is, the more earnestly he wills that his own will be done. And by the same reasoning, we bear witness that the one whose will we do is our King and Lord. Teach me to do your will, for you are my God, Ps. 143:10. Finally, those who do the will of the Father in heaven enter the Kingdom of heaven, Matt. 7:21. The will of God is twofold. There is the will that decrees or effects, which is hidden until God carries out his decrees, and the will that commands or approves, which is revealed in his Word. The former is done concerning us, the latter is done by us. We pray that both be done, but in different ways. In praying for the former, we declare both that we acquiesce in all that God has determined concerning us, saying with Mary: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word, Luke 1:38; and that we are ready to serve the counsel of God, and offer ourselves eager to carry out the divine purpose; and that we desire that nothing be done in us or in others except what has once been fixed by the eternal decree of God. So did the Caesareans and the other friends of Paul, who, when they heard of Paul's chains, finally acquiesced, so that, despite these things, he should go up to Jerusalem, saying: The will of the Lord be done, Acts 21:12-14. Whatever we intend to do, therefore, we intend it on the condition if the Lord wills, James 4:15, and we intend it either implicitly or explicitly. Nor do we intend it too severely or laboriously, lest we prejudge the decree of God, and above all we take care in advance that nothing in our proposal conflicts with its execution. The will of God is the bridle of all the affections in those who seriously seek God's glory. For the very heart of the king is in the hand of Jehovah, Prov. 21:1; and the preparations of the heart belong to man, but the answer of the tongue is from Jehovah, ibid. 16:1. Above all, we pray that the will of God, as commanded and revealed, be done by us. We have great reasons for praying so, for otherwise we cannot be subjects of the Kingdom of God. There is, however, something in us that is not of the Kingdom of God, namely the flesh, and the evil that clings to us, a law contrary to the law of God, taking us captive under the law of sin, which is in our members, Rom. 7:17-24. The mind of the flesh [Φρόνημα σαρκὸς], which is enmity against God, and which is not subject to the law of God, nor can be, ibid. 8:7. Nor can the difficulty we experience from the resistance of our flesh, which bites against the bridle of the spirit, Gal. 5:17, fail to trouble us who love the Kingdom of God and serve God in mind. Therefore we earnestly pray that God's will be done also by us: that we believe in Christ, strive for sanctification, and resist concupiscence through the Spirit. For this is the will of God, your sanctification, 1 Thess. 4:3. It consists in self-denial, in zeal for a godly life, in patient endurance of the cross, and in desire for heavenly glory. That is, denying impiety and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously and godly in the present age, looking for that blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, Titus 2:12-13. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is that good, acceptable and perfect will of God, Rom. 12:1-2. We further pray that the will of God be done by us as it is done in heaven. For in heaven there is peace, holiness and righteousness. And in the Kingdom of God we are admitted to fellowship with the heavenly ones, so that our citizenship is in heaven, Eph. 1:10; Phil. 3:20; Heb. 13:20. So, to be worthy of that citizenship, we desire the will of God to be done by us as it is done in heaven. Moreover, the Son of God himself is in heaven, who does all the will of his Father, Ps. 40:9. There are the angels, mighty in strength, doing the will of God, obeying the voice of his word, ibid. 103:20. There are the blessed souls, who follow the Lamb wherever he goes, Rev. 14:4. Human weakness has therefore Christ, our head, and the angels and the blessed inhabitants of heaven to imitate, according to the measure of grace which it enjoys in this life, and not without zeal to advance toward perfection, which is set before those who run [τρέχομεν] in this race as a goal. But so that this petition may agree with the rule of love for our neighbour, we pray not that each man do God's will for himself as it is done in heaven, but that it be done on earth as it is in heaven, that is, throughout the whole earth, so that there may be none in it who rebel against God and refuse to submit to that King. Such a petition, exercising love in this way, is also made in faith. For we know that this is a good and acceptable sacrifice, indeed a sweet-smelling one, to God. And we know that the promises concerning the Kingdom of Christ stand firm: the world will never overcome the Church so as to make it do the world's will, since rather our faith has overcome the world, 1 John 5:4-5, and Christ will conquer all his enemies and will crush Satan under the feet of the Church, Rom. 16:20. Finally, if any weakness remains in us, we believe it will rather remain so that the power of God may be made perfect in it, and so that it may appear that the grace of God is sufficient for us, 2 Cor. 12:9. Nor will it hinder us from becoming partakers of the inheritance which our Father in heaven has prepared, where nothing dwells but righteousness, 2 Pet. 3:13.

units.la: CXVII. Quarta Petitio est Panis τὸν ἐπιούσιον. Τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον δὸς ἡμῖν σήμερον, Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie, Matth. VI, 11. Apud Lucam: Da nobis τὸ καθ'
units.tr: CXVII. The fourth petition is for bread: "Give us this day our daily bread" (τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον δὸς ἡμῖν σήμερον), Matt. 6:11. In Luke it reads "Give us day by day" (τὸ καθ' [τὸ καθ'])

units.la: ἡμέραν in diem, Luc. XI. 3. seu quantum in hunc diem opus est, quomodo Quintilianus Declam. 19. feras & volucres praesentis modò cibi memores in diem vivere dixit. Hebraeis est דבר יום ביומו res diei in die suo, seu quantum ad unumquemque diem pro necessario victu requiritur, demensum quotidianum, Jerem. L II. 34. Dan. I. 5. quod Sapiens פן כמנה panem demensi appellat, Prov. XXX. 8. Sed in explicatione vocis ἐπιούσιος discors doctorum sensus est. Alii enim ἐπὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἡμετέραν ἀρμόζουσαν substantiae nostrae convenientem: alii καθημέραν quotidianum: alii cum Vulgato supersubstantialem interpretati sunt. Nempe iis ἐπιούσιος est panis ἐπὶ οὐσίαν adveniens essentiae vel substantiae, sicut ἐπιμετρον dicitur, quod supra mensuram est. Alii ἐπισιον ab ἐπιών, quod est ἐπερχόμενον ventu-rus, sicut ἀεὶ ὤν est ἀεὶών quod abundat; derivant. Atque horum alii cum Cypriano & Cyrillo de Christi, coelestis panis, adventu ultimo: alii de pane naturali, qui instat, sive subsequitur, explicant. Non puto tamen obstare quicquam, quò minus vox ex ἐπὶ & οὐσία composita censeatur, sicut ex ὤν & ἐξουσία, ὑπερ-ούσιος derivatur. Neque analogia compositionis impedit, cùm ea non sit sola haec ut vocis ἐπὶ Jota ante vocalem compositae vocis, detrahatur, sicut ὑπερούσιος dicitur, non ἐπιουσιος: sed etiam altera ut interdum maneat, sicut ex ἐπὶ & ὀρος, ἐπιορκος & ἐπιορκία: ex ἐπὶ & ὀπλομαι ἐπιόπλομαι. Ita panis ἐφήμερος erit καθημερινὸς quotidianus, diurnus, seu interprete etiam Basilio, ὡς πρὸς τὸν ἐφημερον ζωὴν τῆς οὐσίας ἡμῶν προσηκοῦσαν ad quotidianam vitae sustentationem substantiae nostrae conducens. Neque tamen πλεονασμος erit, si precemur: Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis σήμερον hodie; quin potius conveniet cum phrasi Hebraea דבר יום ביומו rem diei, seu victum demensum cujusque diei, in die suo, id est quotidie, Jerem. L II. 34. Dan. I. 5. Ex qua phrasi verba Christi expressa videntur, adeoque sensu γνησιον non panem mysticum, de quo secunda petitio egit, sed naturalem significat. Cùm enim homo anima & corpore constet, & sine corpore anima in hac vita nihil operari, neque omnino Deo, sibi & proximo inservire possit, utrique Deus consulere, utramque suis benedictionibus mactare vult. Pro utriusque igitur ἐνεξία precari nos Christus voluit, jussit. Pium nihilominus est, ut panem naturalem rogantes, de supernaturali & mystico etiam cogitent, quia homo non ex pane solo, sed ex quovis verbo, quod ex ore Dei prodit, vivit, Matth. IV. 4.
units.tr: day by day, Luke 11:3, or as much as is needed for the present day. Quintilian, in Declamation 19, says that wild beasts and birds, which remember only their present food, live from day to day. The Hebrews have דבר יום ביומו [davar yom beyomo], the thing of the day in its day, meaning what is required for each day's necessary sustenance, the daily measure, Jer. 52:34; Dan. 1:5. The Wise Man calls this פן כמנה [pan kemanah], bread of measure, Prov. 30:8. But the learned disagree about the meaning of the word ἐπιούσιος. Some interpret it as ἐπὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἡμετέραν ἀρμόζουσαν [suited to our substance], suited to our substance; others as καθημέραν [daily]; others, with the Vulgate, as supersubstantial. For these interpreters, ἐπιούσιος is bread ἐπὶ οὐσίαν [coming upon the substance], coming to the essence or substance, just as ἐπιμετρον is said of what is beyond measure. Others derive it from ἐπιών, which is ἐπερχόμενον [coming on], about to come, just as ἀεὶ ὤν becomes ἀεὶών, that which abounds. Of these, some with Cyprian and Cyril explain it of the last coming of Christ, the heavenly bread; others explain it of natural bread, which is at hand or follows. I do not think, however, that anything prevents the word from being regarded as compounded of ἐπὶ and οὐσία, just as ὑπερούσιος is derived from ὤν and ἐξουσία. Nor does the analogy of composition stand in the way, since it is not the only rule: the iota of ἐπὶ is dropped before a vowel in compounds, as in ὑπερούσιος (not ἐπιουσιος), but in other cases it is kept, as in ἐπιορκος and ἐπιορκία from ἐπὶ and ὄρκος, and ἐπιόπλομαι from ἐπὶ and ὀπλομαι. So the bread that is ἐφήμερος will be καθημερινὸς [daily], of the day, or, as Basil also renders it, bread ὡς πρὸς τὸν ἐφημερον ζωὴν τῆς οὐσίας ἡμῶν προσηκοῦσαν [suited to the daily sustaining of our substance and life]. Nor will the petition be a pleonasm if we pray: Give us our daily bread today ("σήμερον" [today]), for it rather agrees with the Hebrew phrase דבר יום ביומו, the thing of the day, or the measured food of each day, in its day, that is, daily, Jer. 52:34; Dan. 1:5. Christ's words seem to be expressed from this phrase, and so in the genuine sense they mean not the mystical bread, of which the second petition spoke, but natural bread. For since a man consists of soul and body, and without the body the soul can do nothing in this life, and cannot serve God, itself and its neighbour at all, God wishes to provide for both and to bless both with his gifts. Christ therefore bade us pray for the good of both. Nevertheless it is pious, when we ask for natural bread, to think also of the supernatural and mystical, because man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God, Matt. 4:4.

units.la: CXVIII. Panis, quem petere Christus nos jussit, per synecdochen Hebraeis usitatam, omnia ad vitam tolerandam, & recreationem etiam qualemcunque adminicula necessaria significat, quae S. Paulus ad duo capita, διατροφάς alimenta vitam in posterum prorogantia, & σκεπάσματα integumenta revocat. Habentes alimenta & tegumenta, his contenti erimus, 1. Tim. VI. 8.
units.tr: CXVIII. The bread which Christ bade us ask for, by a synecdoche common among the Hebrews, signifies everything needed to sustain life and whatever aids to refreshment there are. St. Paul refers these to two heads: διατροφάς [food], foods which prolong life into the future, and σκεπάσματα [coverings], clothing. Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content, 1 Tim. 6:8.

units.la: Non enim delicias, coturnices, non thesauros supervacuos orare jubet, quasi aliquid ex mundo hoc asportaturi essemus, ibid. v. 7.8. Nihil enim in hoc mundo habere possumus, nisi quo utimur. Nemini vita est ἐν τῷ ἀφθονίᾳ in eo quod abundat, Luc. XII. 15. Imò quod abundat, in Coelum tendentes onerat, ut difficulter progrediantur, Matth. XIX. 24. sicut tunica non longa, sed concinna probatur: ita victus & amictus necessarius, non superfluus juvat. Ἀρκούμενοι τοῖς παροῦσι contenti simus praesentibus. Dixit enim: Non te deseram, neque te derelinquam. Hebr. XIII. 5. Coeli enim cives, & in terra hospites sumus. Omnia supervacua ἀντίτυπα, saltem non nostra sunt. Vetat Christus solicitos esse, quid esuri, quid bibituri, quid induturi simus, Matth. VI. 31. nempe velut diffidentes Deo, velut delicati, & non vulgaria quaerentes, quod gentiles faciunt. Atqui nihil in mundum intulimus, quod nostrum sit. Necesse est omnia nos accipere ut dona Dei sine murmure. Necessaria porro sigillatim sunt, tum quae sufficiunt naturae, quae limites posuit, non esurire, non sitire, non algere, tum quae cujusque vocationis & officio inevitabilia sunt: tum quae aliquatenus etiam in futurum necessaria sunt, quomodo parentes filiis thesauros colligere, Paulus 2. Cor. XII. 14. asserit. Haec à Deo precari, non viribus nostris sine Deo quaerere, Christus jussit; quia à Deo impetrata sanctificantur, 1. Tim. IV. 5. atque seductionis periculum avertunt, & honestissimum est, ea habere ex Coelo, sicut ad honorem Christi pertinuit, quòd ceu panis Dei ex Coelo descendit, & vitam mundo dedit, Joh. VI. 33. Et denique iis destituti non aeque promptè Deo inservire, & cum labore atque studio pari, & cum plurimorum fructu, possumus. Non enim in hac vita sustentamur miraculosè sine pane, quemadmodum in altera vita fiet, ubi σῶμα πνευματικὸν corpus spirituale habebimus. Hac donatione etiam ἄρτος ἡμῶν panis noster fit, quia tum jure spirituali in Christo, haerede omnium, per fidem omnia nostra sunt, 1. Cor. III. 22. tum externa nostra sunt, quae labore nostro & bonis artibus quaesivimus; & quaerenda semper sunt, quo sensu etiam nostra sunt non κυρίως proprietario respectu Dei, sed χρήσει usufructuario; sed non sine Deo, à quo precamur, ut noster sit, & noster maneat, & necessitati atque delectationi nostrae, accedente benedictione ejus, quae scipionis instar est, & ψωμο fulcimentum est, quo cor hominis sustentatur & fulcitur, & absque qua est, non panis, sed venenum est, Psal. CIV. 15. Esaj. III. 1. Prov. X. 22. Dan. I. 13. 14. 15. inserviat. Et panem sic nostrum petimus non simul semelque pro tota vita, non annuum, menstruum, hebdomadarium, sed ἡμερήσιον diurnum, qui sit פן demensum, seu דבר יום ביומו res demensum diei in die suo, & qui detur σήμερον hodie, ne Deo & providentiae ejus diffidentes, anxii simus pro crastino, quia crastino diei sua cura erunt, & unicuique diei malum suum sufficit, Matth. VI. 34. & ut tanto fortiori animo praesentibus malis occurramus, & in sequens tempus curam nostri Deo committamus. Deus enim dat escam ביומו in tempore suo praesente, Psal. CXLV. 15. Crastino die, priusquam venerit, non indigemus, &, an venturus sit, ignoramus. Qualis enim vita nostra est? Vapor est, qui parumper apparet, & postea disparet, Jac. IV. 14. Hodie mori possumus, & si crastino à nobis provisum sit, aegriore animo crastina mori contingat. Fidei est, vivere à manu ad os: infidelitatis, pro crastino anxias curas volvere. Possumus quidem pro crastino, si Deus
units.tr: For he does not bid us pray for delicacies, quails, or superfluous treasures, as if we were going to carry something out of this world, ibid. vv. 7–8. For we can have nothing in this world except what we use. No one's life consists in ἐν τῷ ἀφθονίᾳ [the abundance] of what he has, Luke 12:15. Indeed, what is superfluous weighs down those who are heading for heaven, so that they make slow progress, Matt. 19:24, just as a tunic is approved for being not long but neat; so necessary food and clothing, not superfluous, are helpful. Ἀρκούμενοι τοῖς παροῦσι [Be content with what you have]; for he has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you, Heb. 13:5. For we are citizens of heaven and sojourners on earth. Everything superfluous is ἀντίτυπα [a counterfeit], at least not ours. Christ forbids us to be anxious what we shall eat, what we shall drink, or what we shall put on, Matt. 6:31; that is, as if we distrusted God, as if we were fastidious and sought uncommon things, which the Gentiles do. Yet we have brought nothing into the world that is our own. We must receive everything as gifts of God, without grumbling. Necessities, moreover, are of several kinds: first, what suffices for nature, which has set its limits, so that we do not hunger, thirst, or freeze; second, what is unavoidable for each one's calling and office; third, what is in some measure needed for the future, as Paul asserts that parents ought to lay up treasure for their children, 2 Cor. 12:14. Christ bade us ask these things of God, not seek them by our own powers without God, because things obtained from God are sanctified, 1 Tim. 4:5, and they ward off the danger of deception. It is most honourable to have them from heaven, as it befits the honour of Christ that, as the bread of God came down from heaven and gave life to the world, John 6:33. Lastly, being destitute of them, we cannot serve God with equal readiness, with equal labour and zeal, and with equal fruit for many. For in this life we are not sustained miraculously without bread, as will happen in the other life, where we shall have a σῶμα πνευματικὸν [spiritual body], a spiritual body. By this gift the bread also becomes ἄρτος ἡμῶν [our bread]: for by spiritual right in Christ, the heir of all, through faith, all things are ours, 1 Cor. 3:22; and our external possessions, which we have sought by our labour and honest arts, are ours, and must always be sought. In this sense they are ours not κυρίως [properly], in the owner's respect toward God, but χρήσει [by use], in the respect of usufruct. Yet this is not without God, from whom we pray that they may be ours and remain ours, and that, with his blessing added, they may serve our need and delight. That blessing is like a staff, and is ψωμο [a support], the support by which the heart of man is sustained and strengthened, and without which bread is not bread but poison, Ps. 104:15; Isa. 3:1; Prov. 10:22; Dan. 1:13–15. So we ask for our bread, not all at once for the whole of life, not yearly, monthly, or weekly, but ἡμερήσιον [daily], day by day, which is פן [the measure], that is, דבר יום ביומו [the thing of the day in its day]; and which is given σήμερον [today], today, lest we, distrusting God and his providence, be anxious about tomorrow, since tomorrow will be anxious for itself, and each day's trouble is enough for it, Matt. 6:34; and that we may meet present evils with a braver spirit, committing our care for the time to come to God. For God gives food in its season (בעתו), Ps. 145:15. We do not need tomorrow's bread before tomorrow comes, and we do not know whether it will come. For what is our life? It is a vapour which appears for a little while and then vanishes, James 4:14. We may die today, and even if tomorrow's provision were made for us, it would be a sadder thing to die tomorrow with a troubled mind. It is a mark of faith to live from hand to mouth; of unbelief, to turn anxious cares over in one's mind for tomorrow. We may indeed be concerned for tomorrow, if God...

units.la: Petitionis illius sensus. Deus pro eo aliquid largiri velit, προνοῶν providere, atque id fidei esse Apostolus, 1. Tim. V. 8. declarat; sed sine ærumna & anxietate, qua hodierno diei prospicimus. Precandum igitur est omnibus & singulis diebus, pro pane singulis diebus sufficiente, quia Dei dona non simul semelque ex Coelo destillant, sed torrentis instar aquarum, Psal. XXXVI. 9. quarum aliæ hodie, aliæ cras defluunt. Principalis cura & anxietas nostra pro Coelo & coelesti gloria, quæ non ἀιώνια diurna, sed æterna, incorruptibilis, immarcescibilis, impolluta hæreditas est, 1. Pet. I. 4. desudare debet. Denique petitio hæc etiam pacem, bonum regimen, conservationem parentum, amicorum, Præsidum Reipublicæ, doctorum & rectorum, omniumque adeo, qui donum acceperunt, quod in publicum utile esse possit, comprehendit. Non enim pro se quisque panem petit, sed pro aliis etiam, orando: Panem, &c. da nobis. Summa voti est, tum ut Deus nobis aliisque suppeditet omnia ad vitam pie & tranquille transigendam necessaria; ut per ea agnoscamus, eum unicum & irriguum illum fontem esse, ex quo omnia bona icaturiunt, ac nisi ipse benedicat, omnem curam & industriam nostram, quin & ipsa Dei dona nihil proficere, imo officere, infelicia & noxia esse: tum ut largiatur clementer, quo fiduciam nostram ab omnibus creaturis aversam, in solo ipso collocemus.
units.tr: The sense of this petition: God is willing to bestow something on us, to provide [προνοῶν], and the Apostle declares that this belongs to faith (1 Tim. 5:8). But it is to be asked without the distress and anxiety with which we look ahead to the coming day. We must therefore pray every day, and each day, for bread sufficient for that day, since God's gifts do not drip down from heaven all at once, but flow like a torrent of waters (Ps. 36:9), some of which run down today and others tomorrow. Our principal care and anxiety should be for heaven and heavenly glory, which is not short-lived [ἀιώνια] but eternal, an incorruptible, unfading, undefiled inheritance (1 Pet. 1:4). Finally, this petition also embraces peace, good government, the preservation of parents, friends, the rulers of the commonwealth, teachers and magistrates, and indeed all who have received a gift that may be of public use. For in praying we do not ask for bread for ourselves alone, but for others also: Give us bread, etc. The sum of our prayer is this: that God would supply us and others with everything needed to live our lives piously and peacefully; that through these gifts we may acknowledge him as the one and only fountain from which all good things flow; and that unless he himself blesses, all our care and effort, and even God's own gifts, achieve nothing, or rather harm us, becoming unhappy and hurtful. And we pray that he would graciously grant these things, so that, turning our trust away from all creatures, we may place it in him alone.

units.la: CXIX. Quinta Petitio Remissionem debitorum solicitat.
units.tr: CXIX. The Fifth Petition seeks the remission of debts.

units.la: Καὶ ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν, ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀφίεμεν τοῖς ὀφειλέταις ἡμῶν. Et remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Dubitari non potest, quin ὀφειλημάτων debitorum nomine, ex Hebraeorum loquendi consuetudine, peccata intelligantur, quia ipse Lucas sic interpretatur, Luc. XI. 4. non eo quidem sensu, quo bona opera debita etiam appellantur, ibid. XVII. 10. Rom. XIII. 8. quæ persolvere Deo tenemur, cum peccata, quia talia, nec debita, nec solvenda sint, sed quia reos faciunt Deo & strictæ justitiæ ejus debendi poenam, quæ ad ultimum usque quadrantem a peccatore, vel ejus sponsore exsolvi debet. Eorum remissionem petentes ante omnia confitemur peccata nostra, ne dicamus, nos peccatum non habere, vel non peccasse, 1. Joh. I. 8. 9. 10. hoc est, peccatum non esse in nobis, vel, quod in carne nostra deprehendimus, peccatum non esse; vel etiam quicquam egisse absque peccato, & ita, uti oportet. Semper igitur peccatum confitendum nobis est, neque unquam cum propriæ justitiæ ostentatione coram Deo comparere nobis licet. Sed ita confitenda nobis peccata sunt, ut eorum remissionem imploremus, hoc est, consolationem de remissione peccatorum per fidem accepta desideremus, & in fide Christi ad Deum accedamus, ut cum remissione eorum, & absolutione conscientiæ ab ipso dimittamur. Quam consolationem & accessum ad Deum per fidem in Christum creberrimi lapsus nostri requirunt. Proin petitio hæc fidem in Christum, sanguine suo a peccatis nos purificantem, & studium accedendi ad ipsum, ut in ipso inveniamur, non habentes nostram justitiam, sed eam, quæ ex Deo est, involvit. Si quis enim, gentilis adinstar, non agnoscens Christi sacrificium, vel proprio sacrificio fretus, ad Deum clamet: Remitte mihi debita mea; is nec in fide orabit, nec exauditionis spem ullam habebit, imo Deo injuriam faciens, quasi sine satisfactione peccata remittere possit, culpam suam augebit etiam. Argumentum & signum verae fidei in Christum, per quam consolatio de remissione debitorum habetur, minimus ille charitatis proximi modus est, quo & nos debitoribus nostris peccata, quibus nos offenderunt, adeoque non uti sunt ἀνομία, & iniquitas in Deum, quo sensu solus ipse peccata remittit, Marc. II. 7. sed quatenus injuria & damnum nobis datum sunt, condonamus. Oramus enim remissionem debitorum, sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris, quod latius itatim Christus explicat, dicens: Si remiseritis hominibus peccata sua, etiam vobis remittet Pater vester coelestis. Si vero non remiseritis hominibus peccata sua, neque Pater vester remittet vobis peccata vestra, Matth. VI. 14. 15. Tum vero proximo debita seu peccata remittimus, cum & vindictam propter offensas eorum, atque iram permanentem cohibemus, atque ita non vincimur a malo, sed malum per bonum vincimus, Rom. XII. 21. imo & nos ipsos vincimus, quod majus quid est, quam urbem capere, Prov. XVI. 32. & radicem vindictæ & odii adversus ipsum ex corde nostro omnem evellimus, ἐκ τῶν καρδιῶν ex cordibus, Matth. XVIII. 35. & ex corde puro, 1. Tim. I. 5. non sine commiseratione intima & fletu, exemplo Josephi, Genes. L. 17. condonantes, & parati sumus pro malo bonum rependere, ejus bono gaudere, & benedicere imprecantibus nobis, Matth. V. 44. & oramus pro eo, ne Deus peccatum ei imputet, Actor. VII. 60. & ut a peccato convertatur. Absque hac debitorum remissione remissionem peccatorum petens, testimonium bonae conscientiae habere non potest, quod tanquam justus petat, & fiduciam secundum verbum Dei ad petendam peccatorum remissionem habeat, quia charitatem signum verae fidei, in se non reperit. Ubi enim charitas non est, ibi nec fides est. Qui proximum non diligit, Deum non diligit. Qui Deum non diligit, non credit in Deum. Inter remissionem porro Dei & nostram proportio intercedit similitudinis, quia petimus, ut Deus remittat nobis debita nostra, ὡς sicut & nos debitoribus nostris remittimus: non æqualitatis, quia non eodem plane modo, nec perfecte remittimus, sicut Deus. Non eodem modo, quia Deus remittit ut judex, nec sine λύτρῳ & satisfactione: nos ut servi & sine satisfactione, nisi quatenus per Rectores Reipublicæ debitores ad faciendum id, quod justum est, adigi pro re nata possunt. Non perfecte, quia eadem remissionis nostrae offensionum proximi ratio est, quae reliquorum nostrorum operum est, quae imperfecta omnia sunt. In conditione ergo hac implenda cum infirmis, morientibus inprimis, caute agendum est, ne propter infirmitatem suam de remissione peccatorum incerti relinquantur. Alia enim malitiosorum & obstinatorum, alia infirmorum ratio est.
units.tr: And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors [Καὶ ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν, ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀφίεμεν τοῖς ὀφειλέταις ἡμῶν]. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. There can be no doubt that by the name of debts [ὀφειλήματα] sins are meant, according to the Hebrew manner of speaking, since Luke himself so interprets it (Luke 11:4). This is not in the sense in which good works are also called debts (Luke 17:10; Rom. 13:8), which we are bound to render to God; sins are not debts to be paid, because they are such, but because they make us guilty before God and liable to the penalty required by his strict justice, which must be paid by the sinner or his surety down to the last farthing. In asking for their remission, we first of all confess our sins, lest we say that we have no sin, or have not sinned (1 John 1:8–10); that is, that sin is not in us, or that what we find in our flesh is not sin, or even that we have done anything without sin and so as we ought. Therefore we must always confess our sin, and we may never come before God with a display of our own righteousness. But our sins are to be confessed in such a way that we implore their remission, that is, we long for the comfort of forgiveness of sins received through faith, and approach God in faith in Christ, that we may be dismissed by him with forgiveness of them and with the absolution of conscience. Our most frequent falls demand this comfort and this access to God through faith in Christ. Hence this petition involves faith in Christ, who cleanses us from sins by his blood, and the eagerness to come to him, that we may be found in him, not having our own righteousness, but that which is from God. For if anyone, like a Gentile, not acknowledging the sacrifice of Christ, or relying on his own sacrifice, cries out to God, Remit my debts, he will neither pray in faith nor have any hope of being heard; indeed, by doing injury to God, as if he could remit sins without satisfaction, he will even increase his guilt. The argument and sign of true faith in Christ, through which comfort concerning the remission of debts is obtained, is that least measure of love for our neighbour by which we also forgive our debtors the sins by which they have offended us, which are not, of course, lawlessness [ἀνομία] and iniquity against God, in which sense God alone forgives sins (Mark 2:7), but insofar as they have done us injury and harm. For we pray for the remission of debts, as we also forgive our debtors, which Christ explains more fully at once, saying: If you forgive men their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive men their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins (Matt. 6:14–15). Then indeed we forgive our neighbour his debts or sins, when we restrain both the vengeance for their offences and lasting anger, and thus are not overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good (Rom. 12:21). We even overcome ourselves, which is a greater thing than to take a city (Prov. 16:32), and we tear out from our heart every root of vengeance and hatred against him, from the hearts [ἐκ τῶν καρδιῶν] (Matt. 18:35), and from a pure heart (1 Tim. 1:5), not without inward compassion and weeping, after the example of Joseph (Gen. 50:17), forgiving; and we are ready to repay evil with good, to rejoice in his good, and to bless those who curse us (Matt. 5:44), and we pray for him, that God would not impute sin to him (Acts 7:60), and that he may be turned from sin. Without this remission of debts, one who asks for the remission of sins cannot have the testimony of a good conscience that he asks as a righteous person, nor have confidence, according to the word of God, to ask for the forgiveness of sins, because he does not find in himself the love which is the sign of true faith. For where love is not, there faith is not either. He who does not love his neighbour does not love God; he who does not love God does not believe in God. Moreover, a relation of likeness [similitudinis], not of equality [æqualitatis], lies between God's remission and ours, because we ask that God forgive us our debts, as [ὡς] we also forgive our debtors. It is not equality, because we do not forgive in exactly the same way, nor perfectly, as God does. Not in the same way [eodem modo], because God forgives as judge, and not without a ransom [λύτρῳ] and satisfaction; we forgive as servants and without satisfaction, except insofar as, when the case requires, the rulers of the commonwealth can compel debtors to do what is just. Not perfectly, because the same account of our remission of our neighbour's offences applies to our remaining works, which are all imperfect. Therefore, in dealing with the weak, and especially the dying, in securing this condition caution must be exercised, lest because of their weakness they be left uncertain about the remission of their sins. For the case of the malicious and obstinate is one thing, and the case of the weak is another.

units.la: CXX. Sexta, eaque ultima Petitio Tentationem deprecatur, & a malo liberationem implorat. Καὶ μὴ εἰσενέγκῃς ἡμᾶς εἰς πειρασμόν, ἀλλὰ ῥῦσαι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ. Et ne nos induc
units.tr: CXX. The sixth and last Petition asks to be kept from temptation and implores deliverance from evil. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. [Καὶ μὴ εἰσενέγκῃς ἡμᾶς εἰς πειρασμόν, ἀλλὰ ῥῦσαι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ.]

units.la: Et ne nos induinducas in tentationem, sed libera nos à malo. Petitio haec cum superiore connectitur, tum quia remissio peccatorum, & tentatio Sathanae ad malum individuo nexu cohaerent, cum non eos Sathanas tentet, qui in potestate ejus adhuc sunt, & qui remissionis peccatorum suorum conspicua criteria non offendunt, sed eos potius, quibus remissa peccata esse suspicatur, quos, ceu desertores & profugos cribrare conatur, ut triticum, Luc. XXII. 31. tum quia remissio peccatorum, & animus tentationum oneri succumbens ἀσνρξω sunt. Exui tunicam meam, quomodo induam eam? Lavi pedes meos, quomodo eos fædabo? Cant. V. 3. Gratia enim Dei erudit nos abnegare impietatem, Tit. II. 11. 12. & condonantur peccata, ut timeatur Deus, Psal. CXXX. 4. & diligatur multùm, Luc. VII. 42. 43. non ut per tentationem ab eo divellamur. Scitè Tertullianus de orat. Adjecit, inquit, ad plenitudinem tam expeditæ Orationis, ut non de remittendis tantùm, sed etiam de evertendis in totum delictis supplicaremus. Est autem πειράζειν tentare gultum, experimentum de alicujus animo & opere capere, explorare, ad aliquid solicitare. Estque tentatio vel Divina, vel Humana, vel Diabolica. Divina, qua Deus ipse tentat, non ad malum solicitando, quia sicut ipse ἀπείραστος κακῶν à malis tentari, seu titillari non potest, ita neminem tentat, seu ad malum pellicit, Jac. I. 13. sed probando, explorando, & certum animi vel operis experimentum, non propter se, quia πανταπτήμων est, & ceu supremus opifex, operis sui penitiorem notitiam, quàm ipsum opus, habet, sed propter alios, tentatum præprimis, capiendo, atque ita bonum vel malum, quod in homine est, eliciendo, non ad illud alliciendo בחנני יהוה ונסני צרופה Proba me, Domine, & tenta me, consli renes & cor meum, Psal. XXVI. 2. Humana est, qua homines tentant vel se ipsos, quales sint conditione naturæ, vel beneficio gratiæ, 1. Cor. XI. 28. 2. Cor. XIII. 5. 6. nec non per concupiscentiam propriam, qua se extrahi & inescari patiuntur, Jac. I. 14. vel alios, Apoc. II. 2. vel Deum ipsum, cujus potentiam & veracitatem in dubium temerè revocant, providentiam, neglectis mediis, lacessunt, Majestatem minuunt; Diabolica est, qua Sathanas fideles ad peccatum solicitat, ut Dei iram & offensam adversus se peccando provocantes in ditionem & potestatem suam redigat. Pertinent huc στρατάγματα (στρατηγήματα, στρατηγήματα stratagemata) πνευματικὰ ἐν ἐπουρανίοις spiritualia nequitiæ in supercœlestibus, subtiles, ingeniosæ nequitiæ circa cœlestia, Ephes. VI. 12. & μεθοδίαι & Διαβόλου artes, versutiæ Diaboli, in quibus sunt נתיבות μεθόδοι viæ devia, non aggeratæ, vel munitæ, ibid. v. 11. Tentationis hujus exempla notoria in tentatione Evæ & Christi ipsius sunt, quarum exemplo fideles omnes, & proprie solos illos tentat. Non enim, uti scitè Hieronymus, quærit Diabolus homines infideles, non eos, qui foris sunt, & quorum carnes Rex Assyrius in olla succendit. De Ecclesia Christi rapere festinat. Escæ ejus selectæ sunt. Actus tentationis ipsius in solicitatione, suasione & incitatione ad peccatum, fidei, spei & charitatis oppositum, consistit. Etiam Deus quodammodo in tentationem inducit, tum res nimium secundas, vel adversas, quibus facilè
units.tr: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. This petition is connected with the previous one in two ways: because the forgiveness of sins and Satan's temptation to evil are bound together in a single chain, since Satan does not tempt those who are still in his power and who do not show any clear marks of forgiveness of their sins, but rather those whom he suspects of having been forgiven, whom he tries to sift like deserters and fugitives, as wheat, Luke 22:31; and because forgiveness of sins and a mind that yields under the burden of temptations are ἀσυνρξω (incompatible). I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? Song 5:3. For the grace of God teaches us to deny ungodliness, Titus 2:11-12, and sins are forgiven so that God may be feared, Ps. 130:4, and loved much, Luke 7:42-43, not so that we may be torn away from him by temptation. Tertullian, in his work on prayer, wisely says: "He added, to complete so brief a prayer, that we should ask not only for the remission of sins but also for their complete overthrow." Now πειράζειν means to test, to make trial of someone's mind and work, to examine, to provoke to something. Temptation is either divine, human, or diabolical.
