Divine temptation is that by which God himself tests, not by soliciting to evil (for, as he is ἀπείραστος κακῶν, untempted by evils, he cannot himself be tempted or enticed by evil, and so he tempts no one to evil, James 1:13), but by proving and examining, and taking a sure trial of the mind or work; not for his own sake, since he is omniscient and, like a supreme craftsman, knows his work more intimately than the work itself, but for the sake of others, chiefly of the one tempted, by drawing out the good or evil that is in a man, not by enticing him to it: Prove me, O Lord, and try me; test my reins and my heart, Ps. 26:2. Human temptation is that by which men test either themselves, what they are by the condition of nature or by the benefit of grace, 1 Cor. 11:28, 2 Cor. 13:5-6; or, through their own lust, by which they allow themselves to be drawn away and enticed, James 1:14; or others, Rev. 2:2; or God himself, whose power and truthfulness they rashly call into doubt, whose providence they provoke by neglecting means, and whose majesty they diminish. Diabolical temptation is that by which Satan entices the faithful to sin, so that by sinning they provoke the wrath and offence of God against themselves and reduce them under his dominion and power. To this belong the στρατάγματα (stratagems) spiritual wickednesses in high places, subtle and ingenious wickednesses concerning heavenly things, Eph. 6:12, and the μεθοδίαι (methods) and wiles of the devil, in which there are devious ways, not paved or fortified, ibid. v. 11. The well-known examples of this temptation are in the temptation of Eve and of Christ himself, and by their example he tempts all the faithful, and properly only them. For, as Jerome wisely says, the devil does not seek unbelieving men, nor those who are outside, whose flesh the king of Assyria burned in a pot. He hastens to snatch from the Church of Christ. His food is the chosen ones. The act of temptation itself consists in soliciting, persuading and inciting to sin, which is opposed to faith, hope and charity. God too in some sense leads us into temptation, both by sending things too prosperous or too adverse, by which a man can easily

units.la: homo ad malum induci potest, immittendo, tum tentationem admittendo, & circa eam efficaciter operando. Ideo Christus nos precari Deum Patrem jubet, ne in tentationem nos inducat, hoc est, non, ut ipse nullo modo nos tentet, cùm quædam tentatio etiam precanda sit, Psal. XXVI. 2. sed ut vel omnes mundi, carnis concupiscentiæ propriæ, & Diaboli, imò suas etiam cum periculo tentatorum conjunctas tentationes avertat, vel, si eas justo judicio permittere decreverit, tum tolerabiles, nec viribus nostris majores immittat, 1. Cor. X. 13. tum in iis ne nos deserat, & quid in nobis sit, cum pudore nostro, ne manifestet, quomodo Regem Ezechiam, pium licèt, deseruit, ויתנסה ad tentandum eum, ut sciret quid sit in corde ejus, 2. Paralip. XXXII. 31. tum ut auxilium præsens ad resistendum carni & Diabolo ministret: tum ut maturè ex certamine isto nos liberet, neque nos oneri ejus succumbere sinat, quin potius panoplia, seu universali armatura illa, quam S. Paulus, Ephes. VI. 11. assumere nos jubet, nos instruat, & adversus Sathanam invictos reddat. Sicut nempe ingredi in tentationem, Matth. XXVI. 41. significat, ita involvi tentationum illecebris & periculis, ut ex iis extricari non possimus: ita inducere in tentationem, hoc est, uti Hebraeos loqui Grotius notavit בידנסיון in manum, potestatem, dominium tentationis; significat ita hominem tentationi carnis propriæ & Sathanæ, omnes artes suas adversus fideles excutientis, permittere, ut excussa armatura spirituali omni, ab ea vincatur, & cœlesti brabeo defraudetur. Hanc in tentationem ne Deus nos, ne Ecclesiam, cui innumerae à Pseudo-Prophetis, Pseudo-Christis, seductoribus, persecutoribus certamina, & non unam tentationis horam, Apoc III. 10. imminere Spiritus Dei praedixit, inducat, precamur merito. Quia natura adeò fragiles & infirmi sumus, ut nobis & hostibus nostris relicti ne momento quidem subsistere possimus; infensissimi autem hostes nostri, Sathanas, mundus, caro continenter & πανσεχῶς nos oppugnant, nisi Deus nos sustentet, & Spiritus sui robore firmet, facile in spirituali hoc certamine succumbimus, hostibúsque nostris palmam relinquimus.
units.tr: be led to evil, and by allowing temptation and working effectually around it. Therefore Christ bids us pray to God the Father that he not lead us into temptation, that is, not that he himself should in no way tempt us (since some temptation is to be prayed for, Ps. 26:2), but that he should turn away all the temptations of the world, of the flesh, of our own lust, and of the devil, and even those of his own that are joined with danger to the tempted; or, if he has decided by just judgment to permit them, that he send them as tolerable and not greater than our strength, 1 Cor. 10:13; that he not forsake us in them, and not expose to our shame what is in us, as he forsook King Hezekiah, though pious, to test him, that he might know what was in his heart (ויתנסה), 2 Chron. 32:31; and that he supply present help to resist the flesh and the devil; and that he free us quickly from this struggle and not let us yield under its burden, but rather that he instruct us in the panoply, that is, the complete armour which St Paul bids us take up, Eph. 6:11, and make us invincible against Satan. For just as to enter into temptation, Matt. 26:41, means to be entangled in the allurements and dangers of temptations so that we cannot extricate ourselves from them, so to lead into temptation, that is, as Grotius observed the Hebrews speak, בידנסיון (into the hand), into the power and dominion of temptation, means to permit a man to be given over to the temptation of his own flesh and of Satan, who shakes all his arts against the faithful, so that, with all his spiritual armour stripped away, he is conquered by it and defrauded of the heavenly prize. We rightly pray that God not lead us, nor his Church, into this temptation, to which, the Spirit of God foretold, there would be impending countless struggles from false prophets, false Christs, seducers and persecutors, and not only one hour of temptation, Rev. 3:10. For we are by nature so frail and weak that, left to ourselves and our enemies, we could not hold out even for a moment; and our most hostile enemies, Satan, the world and the flesh, assail us continually and unceasingly, so that unless God sustain us and strengthen us with the vigour of his Spirit, we would easily succumb in this spiritual struggle and yield the palm to our enemies.

units.la: CXXI. Eadem Petitione liberari ῥύσαι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ à Malo expetimus.
units.tr: CXXI. By the same petition we ask to be delivered from the Evil One [ῥύσαι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ], from evil.

units.la: Ejusdem enim petitionis hæ partes sunt, quas sic alibi Christus contraxit. Rogo ἵνα τηρήσῃς αὐτοὺς ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ ut serves eos à malo, Joh. XVII. 15. Prior negativa, posterior affirmativa est, quæ duæ unam propositionem quandoque efficiunt, velut in illis Dei, Morieris, & non vives, Esa. XXXVIII. 1. Ideo Christus partes illas non per copulam disjungit, sed per particulam disjunctivam ἀλλὰ sed conjungit. Et prior petitionis pars gratiam malum praevenientem, posterior ab eodem jam hominem occupante liberantem implorat. Planè igitur intempestiva Pontificiorum crisis est, qui sicut Decalogi praeceptum ultimum, ita ultimam etiam Orationis Dominicæ petitionem in duas diiitrahunt, septémque adeò petitiones, pro septemplici videlicet Spiritus S. gratia faciunt. Non enim septuplex duntaxat Spiritus S. gratia est, sed χάρις πολυποίκιλος gratia multiplex 1. Petr. IV. 10. Πονηρὸς Malus ille, à quo liberari petimus, ille ipse est, qui nos ad
units.tr: For the parts of this same petition are those which Christ elsewhere expressed in this way: "I ask that you keep them from the evil one [ἵνα τηρήσῃς αὐτοὺς ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ], that you keep them from evil," John 17:15. The first clause is negative and the second affirmative, and the two together sometimes form one proposition, as in God's words: "You shall die, and not live," Isa. 38:1. So Christ does not separate those parts by a copula, but joins them with the disjunctive particle ἀλλὰ [but]. The first part of the petition begs for grace that goes before evil, and the second begs for deliverance from evil already laying hold of the man. Therefore the Papists' division is plainly out of place: just as they split the last commandment of the Decalogue into two, they split the last petition of the Lord's Prayer as well, and so make seven petitions, corresponding to the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. But the grace of the Holy Spirit is not merely sevenfold; it is "the manifold grace of God" [χάρις πολυποίκιλος], 1 Pet. 4:10. The Evil One [Πονηρὸς] from whom we ask to be delivered is the very one who tempts us to evil

units.la: Sed ut libe-ret nos à malo. ad malum tentat, & cui haud raro tentati succumbimus. Capitalis ille Malus Sathanas est, ille πονηρὸς Malus, quem adolescentes illi fortes vincisse dicuntur, 1. Joh. II. 14. qui tanquam leo rugiens obambulat, quaerens, quem devoret, 1. Pet. V. 8. quique bellum fidelibus inexpiabile cum odio & inimicitia indixit; cui caro & concupiscentia nostra, ceu fomes incendii ab eodem suscitati, mundus & in eo squamae omnes Sathanae alacriter & addictissimè inserviunt, tentationibus suis fideles in omni eorum vita, vocatione externa & interna, rebus secundis & adversis, esu & potu, curis omnibus & remissionibus ab iisdem, solitudine & cum aliis conversatione institutA, pietatis exercitiis, aliisque, si qua pote, implicaturi, & implicantes haud raro, ut cadant & succumbant. Cùm ergo solus Deus sit ille ῥύστης Liberator, Salvator noster, qui ῥύεται ἀπὸ πάντος ἔργα πονηρὰ liberabit ab omni opere malo, & servabit ad Regnum coeleste, 2. Tim. IV. 18. ῥύσατο ἢ ῥύεται, ἢ ῥύσεται liberavit, liberat & liberabit, 2. Cor. I. 10. & qui petra, arx & liberator noster solus est, 2. Sam. XXII. 2. ab illo supplici voto & voce contendimus, ut & malum omne praevertat, & citò illud avertat, efficiatque, ut in bonum nobis cooperetur, & propter malum futurum ad se nos congreget, Esaj. LVII. 1. & à cogitatione, dicto & facto malo, à dissidiis, schismatibus, persecutionibus nos liberet; & ipsos hostes nostros illuminet atque convertat. Exlegem illum spiritu oris sui magis magisque conficiat & aboleat; Denique nos exantlata militia nostra in Regnum suum suscipiat, & Ecclesiam laboribus suis defunctam consoletur, ipsum verò illum insignitè πονηρὸν improbum & nequam spiritum, qui omnium malorum author est, cum Pseudo-propheta & Bestia in stagnum ardens igne & sulphure conjiciat. Novit Deus pios ex tentatione liberare, injustos in diem judicii puniendos servare, 2. Pet. II. 9. Ac licèt liberationis una via septa videatur, aliam tamen fides intuetur. Si silendo silueris tempore hoc, respiratio & evasio stabit Judaeis ex alio loco, Esth. IV. 14. Fides enim indifferentem se gerit, cogitando semper, forte Deum nobiscum fore in angustiis, Psal. XCI. 15. forte custoditurum animam nostram & liberaturum, ibid. XXV. 20. forte erepturum nos è luto ne demergamur: erepturum ab osoribus, & à profundis aquarum, ibid. LXIX. 15. quae singula liberationis à malo vice reputat.
units.tr: (but that he may deliver us from evil), and to whom we who are tempted all too often succumb. That chief Evil One is Satan, the Evil One [πονηρὸς] whom those "young men" are said to have overcome, "the strong," 1 John 2:14, who "as a roaring lion walks about, seeking whom he may devour," 1 Pet. 5:8, and who has declared an unending war against the faithful with hatred and enmity. To him our flesh and concupiscence, like the tinder of a fire kindled by him, serve as fuel, and the world, with all the scales of Satan, serves him eagerly and most devotedly. They will entangle the faithful in their temptations throughout their whole life: in their external and internal calling, in prosperity and adversity, in food and drink, in all the cares and relaxations that come from these, in solitude and in association with others, in the exercises of piety, and in whatever else they can use to entangle them; and once they have entangled them, they often make them fall and succumb. Since God alone is the Deliverer [ῥύστης], our Saviour, who "will deliver us from every evil work [ῥύεται ἀπὸ πάντος ἔργα πονηρὰ] and will preserve us for his heavenly kingdom," 2 Tim. 4:18; who "has delivered, delivers and will deliver" us [ῥύσατο, ῥύεται, ῥύσεται], 2 Cor. 1:10; and who alone is our rock, fortress and deliverer, 2 Sam. 22:2, we contend with him in a prayer and cry of supplication, that he would both turn away every evil and quickly avert it, and bring it about that it works together for good for us, and gathers us to himself because of the evil to come, Isa. 57:1; that he would deliver us from evil thought, word and deed, from dissensions, schisms and persecutions; and that he would enlighten and convert our very enemies. May he more and more consume and abolish that lawless one with the breath of his mouth. Finally, after our warfare is finished, may he receive us into his kingdom and comfort the Church, which has been worn out by its labours, while he casts that wicked and worthless spirit, the author of all evils, with the false prophet and the beast into the burning lake of fire and brimstone [πονηρὸν]. "The Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment," 2 Pet. 2:9. And although the way of deliverance seems closed, faith nevertheless looks to another. "If you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place," Esth. 4:14. For faith does not stand idle: it always thinks that perhaps "God will be with us in trouble," Ps. 91:15; perhaps he "will keep our soul and deliver it," ibid. 25:20; perhaps he "will rescue us from the mire, lest we sink; he will rescue us from those who hate us, and from the deep waters," ibid. 69:15. Each of these considers deliverance from evil in its turn.

units.la: CXXII. Clausula Orationis tum Doxologia
units.tr: CXXII. The closing clause of the prayer, the doxology

units.la: Dei, tum precantis votum & fiduciam continet. ὅτι σοῦ ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία, ἡ δύναμις, ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας. Ἀμήν. Quia tuum est Regnum, & potentia & gloria in secula, Amen, Matth. VI. 13. Clausulam hanc Lucas omisit, & in vetustissimis Codicibus Latinis Matthaei eadem desideratur. Legunt nihilominus eam Syrus vetustissimus, Graeci codices uno Parisiensi excepto. Patres Graeci, & Hebraeorum Euchologia, ex quibus Christum partes Orationis hujus collegisse eruditi conjectant. Nam & in Sepher Hammusar 9:12. legere est: כי המלכות שלך היא ועולמים עד בכבוד quia tuum est Regnum, & in secula seculorum regnabis gloriosè. Apud Lucianum etiam in Philopatore Triphon ad Critiam dicit: Precationem recita, quae incipit à Patre, & ad finem ejus adde πο-
units.tr: of God, and it contains both the petitioner's vow and his confidence: "For yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen" [ὅτι σοῦ ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία, ἡ δύναμις, ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας. Ἀμήν]; "For yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever, Amen," Matt. 6:13. Luke omitted this clause, and it is missing from the oldest Latin manuscripts of Matthew. Nevertheless, the most ancient Syriac version reads it, and so do the Greek manuscripts, with the single exception of one Parisian manuscript. So do the Greek Fathers and the Hebrew prayer books, from which learned men conjecture that Christ gathered the parts of this prayer. For in the Sepher Hammusar 9:12 one can read: "For yours is the kingdom, and forever and ever you shall reign in glory" [כי המלכות שלך היא ועולמים עד בכבוד]. Also in Lucian's Philopatris, Triphon says to Critias: "Recite the prayer which begins with the Father, and add to its end..."

units.la: CXXIII. Connectitur porrò Doxologia hæc cum superioribus, ceu petendorum omnium causa, per causalem ὅτι quia.
units.tr: CXXIII. The doxology is further joined to what precedes, as the reason for all the petitions, by the causal ὅτι [hoti], "because."

units.la: Oratio enim omnis ad Deum etiam argumentis munini & confirmari debet, uti etiam Moses, Exod. XXXII. 11. 12. 13. Asa, 2. Chron. XIV. 11. firmarunt. Ego cum Deo omnipotente loquor, & cum Deo argumenta disceptare volo, Job. XIII. 3. Os meum implebo argumentis, ibid. XXIII. 4. Est enim cultus noster, cujus pars oratio est, λογικὴ λατρεία cultus rationalis, Rom. XII. 1. Neque Deo bene placitum est in stultis, Eccl. V. 3. Neque aliam ob causam David orationem suam meditationem, Psal. V. 2. appellat. Argumentum verò ipsum à Regno, potentia & gloria Dei arcesslitur. Quia enim Deus Regnum habet, ideo ceu Rex Coeli & terrae, habens clavim Davidis, quo aperiente nemo claudit, claudente nemo aperit, Ap. III. 7. thesaurorum suorum aperiendorum, & dispensandorum plenum arbitrium habet: quia δύναμιν potentiam habet. Potens est facere super omnia ex abundanti eorum quae petimus vel cogitamus; Ephes. III. 20. Quia δόξαν gloriam habet, ejus interest, ut fideles, gloriae hujus praecones, exaudiat, & promissionum suarum veritatem impleat. Ceu Rex subditos juvat, ceu peculium & haereditatem suam conservat, eos implet: ceu potens juvare potest; & sibi inniti jubet, nihil reveritos impotentiam suam & potentiam Sathanae: ceu Rex potens gloriosus in aeternum, gloriae suae patefaciendae causa faciet propter nomen suum, Jerem. XIV. 7. ut in ipso solo gloriemur, ei gratias agamus, & ad hoc anhelemus, ut ipse in nobis glorificetur, hic in certamine, ibi in gloria, cùm admirabilis & gloriosus in omnibus sanctis fiet, 2. Thess. I. 10. Testamur insuper fiduciam nostram, fore, ut Deus manifestum faciat, se solum esse Regem, sibi soli debere obedientiam, se habere peculium, pro quo, ceu pupilla oculi sui vigilet & zelet; & se habere potentiam, qua facere supra illa, quae petimus & cogitamus, possit: denique se debere & velle glorificari, ceu magnum, divitem bonum & rectum, ita ut gloria ipsius in laude nostra consummetur.
units.tr: Every prayer to God ought to be fortified and confirmed by arguments, as Moses did (Exod. 32:11-13) and Asa did (2 Chron. 14:11). I will speak with Almighty God, and I desire to argue my case with God (Job 13:3). I will fill my mouth with arguments (Job 23:4). Our worship, of which prayer is a part, is λογικὴ λατρεία [logikē latreia], a reasonable service (Rom. 12:1). God is not pleased with fools (Eccl. 5:3). David, for his part, calls his prayer a meditation (Ps. 5:2) for no other reason. The argument itself is drawn from the kingdom, power and glory of God. Because God has a kingdom, he holds, as King of heaven and earth, the key of David, so that when he opens no one shuts, and when he shuts no one opens (Rev. 3:7), and he has full freedom to open and distribute his treasures. Because he has power [δύναμις, dynamis], he is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think (Eph. 3:20). Because he has glory [δόξα, doxa], it is his concern to hear the faithful, the heralds of this glory, and to fulfil the truth of his promises. As King he helps his subjects; as the guardian of his own peculiar people and inheritance he fulfils them; as one who is able to help, he can do so, and he bids them rely on him, having no fear of his own weakness or of the power of Satan. As the King who is mighty and glorious for ever, he will act for his name's sake (Jer. 14:7), so that we may glory in him alone, give him thanks, and strive that he may be glorified in us: here in the struggle, there in glory, when he shall be marvelled at and glorified in all his saints (2 Thess. 1:10). We further declare our confidence that God will make it plain that he alone is King, that obedience is owed to him alone, that he has a peculiar people for whom he watches and is jealous as over the apple of his eye, that he has power to do above all that we ask or think; and, finally, that he ought and wills to be glorified, as great, rich, good and upright, so that his glory is perfected in our praise.

units.la: CXXIV. Votum & fiducia precantis ejusdem acclamatione particulae Ἀμήν Amen declaratur, quae sigilli instar est.
units.tr: CXXIV. The wish and confidence of the one praying is declared by the acclamation of the particle Ἀμήν [Amēn], Amen, which is like a seal.

units.la: Est autem particula illa tum optantis, tum affirmantis. Cùm optan-
units.tr: The particle is used both by one who wishes and by one who affirms. When it is used by one who wishes, it signifies the same as Γένοιτο [genoito], "let it be."

units.la: Doxologiae explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation of the doxology.

units.la: Orationis Clausula, & Doxologiae.
units.tr: The clause of the prayer, and the doxology.

units.la: Votum & fiducia precantis acclamatione particulae.
units.tr: The wish and confidence of the one praying by the acclamation of the particle.

units.la: optantis est, idem quod Γένοιτο Fiat, significat. Ita Mulier illa zelotypiæ potum bibens dicere debuit אמן אמן Amen, Amen, hoc est, uti Græci reddunt, γένοιτο, γένοιτο: fiat, fiat, Num. V. 22. Confer Deut.XXVII.15. Alibi Jer.XXVIII. 6. אמן Amen explicatur per יעשה יהוה כן sic faciat Dominus. Affirmantis, rem certo ratam, significat ἀληθῶς verè. Quomodo cum Christus dixit: Amen dico vobis, Matth. XVI. 18. alibi id ipsum explicat ἀληθῶς verè. Luc. I X. 27. Idem Lucas cap. XI.51. Amen illud, quod Matth. XXIII.36. extat, perναί etiam explicat. Utramque significationem jungentes illi, qui orant, tum optant fieri, quæ orant, testificantes sinceritatem, bonam conscientiam, fidem non fictam & charitatem; quódque non sint ambigui, Jac. I. 6. 8. vel διψύχοι duplicis viæ, sed serio quærant Regnum Dei & justitiam ejus, & quæ additurum ie Deus promisit, Matth.VI. 32. tum affirmant rem, ceu apud Deum ratam, & quæ juxta ejus promissionem aliter habere non possit. Oratio enim & ardens desiderium precando precantis, Jac. V. 17. & fidem ibid. I. 6. involvit. Fides autem est substantia rerum sperarum, & demonstratio eorum, quæ non videntur, Hebr. XI. 1. Nam Deo pulsanti per clavim precum aperiente, Matth.VII. 7. & prædivites gratiæ suæ thesauros pandente, fides acclamans Amen, obsignat, quòd Deus ἀληθὴς verax sit, Joh. III. 33. & preces nostras certò exaudiat, atque exaudire cœperit. Quotquot enim sunt promissiones Dei in Christo, tunt etiam, & in ipso sunt Amen, ad Dei gloriam per nos, 2. Cor. I. 20.
units.tr: ...so that it signifies, "Let it be done." Thus the woman accused of jealousy, drinking the potion, ought to have said אמן אמן [amen amen], Amen, Amen, which the Greeks render γένοιτο, γένοιτο, let it be, let it be (Num. 5:22). Compare Deut. 27:15. Elsewhere (Jer. 28:6), Amen is explained by יעשה יהוה כן [ya'aseh YHWH ken], "so may the Lord do." When it is used by one who affirms, it signifies that a thing is certainly settled, ἀληθῶς [alēthōs], truly. So when Christ said, "Amen I say to you" (Matt. 16:28), elsewhere he explains it by ἀληθῶς, truly (Luke 9:27). Luke, in chapter 11:51, also explains that Amen, which stands in Matthew 23:36, by ναί [nai], yes. Those who pray, combining both senses, both wish that what they pray for may come to pass, bearing witness to their sincerity, good conscience, unfeigned faith and love; and so that they are not wavering (Jas. 1:6, 8), double-minded [διψύχοι, dipsychoi], but seriously seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and what God has promised to add (Matt. 6:32); and they affirm the thing as settled before God, and one which, according to his promise, cannot be otherwise. For prayer involves the fervent desire of the one praying (Jas. 5:17), and also faith (Jas. 1:6). Faith is the substance of things hoped for and the evidence of things not seen (Heb. 11:1). For when God knocks by the key of prayer and opens (Matt. 7:7), and spreads abroad the treasures of his most abundant grace, faith, crying Amen, seals that God is ἀληθὴς [alēthēs], true (John 3:33), and that he certainly hears our prayers and has begun to hear them. For however many the promises of God are, in Christ they are Yea, and in him Amen, to the glory of God through us (2 Cor. 1:20).

units.la: CXXV. Oratione hac Dominica verborum numeris brevissima, at sententiarum pondere longissima ita utendum est unica, ut fas piùmque sit aliis etiam formulis & verbis uti, dummodo ne sensu ab hac, ceu unica, & numeris omnibus absoluta precandi forma discrepent. Est enim Oratio Dominica series seu catenatio certarum classium, seu generum, ad quæ res omnes petendæ referri debent. Qui ergo possit petere generalia, is etiam specialia petere possit. Si cui deest sapientia, is petat eam à Deo, & dabitur ei, Jac. I. 5. Orate, ne fuga vestra fiat in hiemé, Matth. XXIV. 20. Quæ in Oratione Dominica ἀνωλέξει non extant. Idem ostendunt multa precum exempla V. & N. T. Christi ipsius Joh. XVII. & Apostolorum, Actor. IV.24. quæ verbis ab hac formula discrepant. Christiana quoque libertas non ita contrahi & constringi debet, quò minùs Deum in omnibus linguis, quibusvis verborum formulis, cum regula Orationis Dominicæ congruentibus, oremus, dummodo in eodem spiritu, eadem fide, cordis affectu, charitate & intelligentia fiat. Ipsa quin etiam cordium nostrorum coram Deo effusio requirit, ut tollamus nobiscum verba, & vitulos labiorum pro renata offeramus, Hos. XIV. 2. Orationem ergo Dominicam ad speciales necessitates applicare per preces Ecclesiasticas, domesticas, secretas, ad indigentiam nostram accommodatas licet. Quandoquidem enim, uti pulchrè Tertullianus lib. de Orat. cap. 9. loquitur: Dominus prospexit humanarum necessitatum feorsim, post traditam orandi disciplinam: Petite, inquit, & accipietis, & sunt, quæ petantur, pro circumstantia cujusque præmissa legitima & ordinaria oratione, quasi
units.tr: CXXV. This Prayer of the Lord, the shortest in words but the longest in the weight of its sentences, is to be used as a single form, though it is generally permitted to use other formulas and words, provided they do not differ in sense from this form, which is one and complete in all its parts. For the Lord's Prayer is a series or chaining together of certain classes or kinds, to which all things to be asked ought to be referred. Whoever can ask for general things can also ask for particular things. If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask it of God, and it will be given him (Jas. 1:5). "Pray that your flight may not be in winter" (Matt. 24:20), things which are not expressly in the Lord's Prayer. Many examples of prayer in the Old and New Testaments show the same, including Christ's own (John 17) and the Apostles' (Acts 4:24), which differ in words from this formula. Christian liberty ought not to be so restricted and bound that we may not pray to God in all tongues and in any verbal formulas agreeing with the rule of the Lord's Prayer, provided it is done in the same Spirit, the same faith, with the same disposition of heart, love and understanding. Indeed, the pouring out of our hearts before God itself requires that we take words with us and offer the calves of our lips as a renewed offering (Hos. 14:2). It is therefore permitted to apply the Lord's Prayer to particular needs, through ecclesiastical, domestic and private prayers, adapted to our necessity. For, as Tertullian speaks well in his book On Prayer, chapter 9: the Lord looked to human needs separately, after he had delivered the discipline of praying: "Ask," he says, "and you shall receive" (Matt. 7:7); and there are things to be asked for according to the circumstances of each, the legitimate and ordinary prayer having been set down beforehand as a

units.la: fundamento, accidentium jus est desideriorum, jus est superstruendi extrinsecas petitiones, cum memoria tamen præceptorum, ne quantum à præceptis, tantùm ab auribus Dei longè simus.
units.tr: foundation. There is a right to accidental desires, a right to build external petitions upon it, yet with the remembrance of the precepts, lest we be as far from God's ears as we are from his precepts.

units.la: CXXVI. Nec pauca, nec exigua incentiva ad precandum sunt. Necessario enim propter Dei præceptum & religionis per preces exercitium precandum esse, jam supra attruximus. Tum precatio vox Spiritus S. in nobis clamantis, & studium atque patrocinium suum pro nobis probantis, Rom. VIII.26. manus fidei, clavis ad referandos Dei thesauros, animæ advocatus, cordis armiger, animi interpres, Matth. VII.7. Ephef. VI.18. bonorum spiritualium & terrestrium conciliatrix, 2. Chron. VII. 14. est. Eadem creaturas sanctificat, ut nobis utiles sint, 1. Tim. IV. 5. Crucem suavem facilémque reddit, & ab eadem novam omnem avertit, 2. Cor. XII. 18. Cor ad humilitatem, vitam ad sobrietatem componit, Dei gratias omnes corroborat, tentationes vincit, corruptionem subigit, desideria defœcatiora reddit, officia & universa opera nostra Deo acceptiora, & vitam nostram proximo proficuam, & nobis vitam juxta atque mentem jucundam salutarémque reddit, Actor. IV.24. VII. 59. IX. 11. Ephef. VI. 18. Nam oratio, uti scite Augustinus, oranti est subsidium, Deo sacrificium, dæmoni flagellum. Nihil magis aversatur Sathan, quàm preces, quibus & spicula ejus præcaventur, & quæ jam animo inhærent, franguntur.
units.tr: CXXVI. The incentives to prayer are neither few nor small. For we have already shown above that prayer must be offered because of God's command and the exercise of religion. Prayer is the voice of the Holy Spirit crying in us and proving his zeal and advocacy for us (Rom. 8:26); the hand of faith; the key to unlocking God's treasures; the advocate of the soul; the armour-bearer of the heart; the interpreter of the mind (Matt. 7:7; Eph. 6:18); the reconciler of spiritual and earthly goods (2 Chron. 7:14). The same prayer sanctifies creatures so that they become useful to us (1 Tim. 4:5); it makes the cross sweet and easy to bear and turns away every new one (2 Cor. 12:8). It composes the heart to humility and life to sobriety, strengthens all the graces of God, overcomes temptations, subdues corruption, renders desires purer, makes all our duties and works more acceptable to God, makes our life profitable to our neighbour and makes life and mind joyful and healthful for us (Acts 4:24; 7:59; 9:11; Eph. 6:18). For prayer, as Augustine wisely says, is a help to the one who prays, a sacrifice to God, and a scourge to the devil. Satan shrinks from nothing more than prayers, by which his darts are warded off and those already lodged in the mind are broken.

units.la: CXXVII. Precibus extraordinariis Jejunium & Festivitas, illud in luctu & suppli catione; hæc in lætitia & gratiarum actione accidit. Jejunium intelligimus non quamvis abstinentiam, qualis & metaphorica est, à peccatis & injustitia, & propria eaque vel naturalis, vel coacta, vel ob negotium urgens, & sanitatis aliásque causas suscepta esse potest, sed religiosam, seu religioni inservientem à cibo, potu aliisque vitæ temporalis adjumentis & solatiis quantum humana fragilitas permittit, abstinentiam, à Deo ipso præceptum eum in finem, ut carne subacta ad enixius orandum, affixius vigilantiùsque meditandum, & nos ipsos abjectius coram Deo humiliandum aptiores evadamus. Hebræis כנעה cœarctatio & שחיקה subbatio, afflictio animæ, Græcis νηστεία, hoc est, ἀλιγοπάθια cibi parsimonia & paucitas appellatur. צום קדש Sanctificate jejunium, vocate cœtum, &c. Joel. I. 14. Convertimini ad me toto corde vestro, & cum jejunio, & cum fletu, & cum planctu. cap. II. 12. Non possunt filii Sponsi lugere, quandiu Sponsus cum iis est. Venient autem dies, quando Sponsus ab iis auferetur τότε νηστεύσουσι & tum jejunabunt, Matth. IX. 15. Luc. V. 34. 35. Hoc genus non egreditur, nisi per precationem & νηστείας jejunium, Matth. XVII. 21. Extant etiam jejunantium exempla in utroque, Vetere & Novo Testamento.
units.tr: CXXVII. Fasting and festivity accompany extraordinary prayers: fasting belongs to mourning and supplication, festivity to joy and thanksgiving. By fasting we mean not any abstinence from sins and injustice, which is metaphorical, nor the private abstinence that may be undertaken for natural or compelled reasons, for some pressing business, for health, or for other causes. We mean a religious abstinence, or one serving religion, from food, drink, and the other supports and comforts of temporal life, as far as human frailty allows. God himself has commanded it, so that by subduing the flesh we may become more fit for praying earnestly, meditating attentively and watchfully, and humbling ourselves more deeply before God. In Hebrew it is called kin'ah [כנעה] (affliction) and shechiqah [שחיקה] (bruising), affliction of the soul; in Greek it is called nēsteia, that is, [ἀλιγοπάθια] restriction and scantiness of food. "Sanctify a fast [צום קדש], call a solemn assembly," etc. (Joel 1:14). "Turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning" (Joel 2:12). "The children of the bridechamber cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them. But the days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then they shall fast" [τότε νηστεύσουσι] (Matt. 9:15; Luke 5:34–35). "This kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting" (Matt. 17:21). Examples of fasting are found in both Testaments, the Old and the New.

units.la: CXXVIII. Licet enim Regnum Dei non consistat in esca & potu, sive ille assumatur, sive omittatur, Rom. XIV. 17. quia tamen jejunium humiliationi nostræ sub manu potentis Dei, & afflictioni animæ propter conscientiam peccati inservit, eatenus à Deo præcipi potuit, & à piis exerceri debet, non ut virtus vel bonum opus in se, sed ut virtutis adjumentum, impedimenta, quæ à carne turgida, humohumoribus & spiritibus provenire possunt, subtrahens, & ut significatio humiliationis, quālis etiam est jacere in terra, sedere in pulvere, cinerem capiti injicere, lacerare vestem, flere, plangere & similia. In quibus omnibus excessus δεισιδαιμονίαν superstitionem, Col. II. 23. ostentatio hypocrisin, Matth. VI. 16. arguit. Sic ergo jejunium eodem praecepto, quo oratio & humiliatio, ceu utriusque adjumentum & signum, praecipitur, ut tamen per se, ceu bonum opus, & cultus Dei non praecipiatur, nec ut talis sine superstitione exerceri possit. Non enim jejunium alimentum, sed medicamentum animae est, & Joel. II. 12. cum fletu & planctu, re per se nec bona, nec mala conjungitur. Nullum enim res ejusmodi momentum nisi a fine iuo, propter quem instituuntur, habent; & χρυσᾶ σωματικὴ mere corporalis exercitatio sunt, quae ad pauca utilis est, 1. Tim. IV. 8. Hinc etiam Christus neglectum jejunii in discipulis suis excusavit, Matth. IX. 14. 15. non excusaturus, si in eo cultus per se Deo placens esset. Haec enim praetextum sapientiae in delectu voluntario, humilitate & vexatione corporis habent, non in honore alterius, ad impletionem carnis, Col. II. 23. In Pontificios igitur in jejunio per se cultum Dei collocantes, quadrant verba Dei, veteribus hypocritis oppositae. Quando jejunatis numquid propter me jejunatis? Et quando editis, nonne vos estis illi, qui comeditis? Zach. VII. 5. 6. quasi diceret: Nihil mihi per jejunium & esum vestrum accedit, vel decedit, feritur vel metitur. Non ergo in eo, ceu re per se bona beneplacitum habeo. An tale erit jejunium, quod eligam, quo debilitet homo animam suam? Annon hoc est jejunium, quod eligam, solvere nodos improbitatis, & laxare colligationes vestis, & dimittere calumniam passos liberos, & omnem vectem rumpere? Annon ut frangas esurienti panem tuum, & inopes, qui persecutionem patiuntur, domum deducas? Cum videris nudum, ut illum operias, & carnem tuam non negligas? Esaj. LVIII. 5-8. Neque obstat, quod jejunium a Deo praecipitur, & pro re nata a superioribus etiam praecipi potest; & in obsequio per se bono honor erga praecipientem per se etiam bonus exercetur, quia non ut virtus, aut opus bonum morale, cultus Dei, sed horum adminiculum duntaxat & signum praecipitur, vel praecipi potest; & obsequium erga Deum & superiores bonum esse potest, etiamsi res quae praecipitur per se nec bona, nec mala sit.
units.tr: CXXVIII. For although the kingdom of God does not consist in food and drink, whether these are taken or omitted (Rom. 14:17), fasting nonetheless serves our humbling under the hand of the mighty God and our affliction of soul on account of consciousness of sin. So far it may be commanded by God and should be practised by the godly, not as a virtue or good work in itself, but as an aid to virtue, removing the hindrances that can arise from a swollen flesh, from humours and spirits. It is also a sign of humbling, as are lying on the ground, sitting in dust, putting ashes on the head, tearing one's clothes, weeping, and beating the breast, and similar things. In all of these, excess argues superstition [δεισιδαιμονίαν] (Col. 2:23), and display argues hypocrisy (Matt. 6:16). Thus fasting is commanded by the same precept as prayer and humbling, as a support and sign of both, yet it is not commanded in itself, as a good work and worship of God, nor can it be practised as such without superstition. For fasting is not food for the soul but its medicine, and it is joined with weeping and mourning (Joel 2:12), things which are in themselves neither good nor evil. Such things have no weight except from the end for which they are instituted, and bodily exercise is of little profit [σωματικὴ γυμνασία] (1 Tim. 4:8). Hence also Christ excused the neglect of fasting in his disciples (Matt. 9:14–15), and he would not have excused it if fasting were in itself a worship pleasing to God. For such things "have indeed a shew of wisdom in will-worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body, not in any honour, to the satisfying of the flesh" (Col. 2:23). Therefore the words of God, set against the hypocrites of old, fit the Papists who place the worship of God in fasting itself: "When ye fasted and mourned, did ye at all fast unto me? And when ye did eat and drink, did ye not eat for yourselves?" (Zech. 7:5–6), as if he said: nothing accrues to me or is lost to me through your fasting or eating, nor is it weighed or measured by me. I therefore have no pleasure in it as a thing good in itself. Is it such a fast that I have chosen, a day for a man to afflict his soul? Is not this the fast that I have chosen: to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? When thou seest the naked, that thou cover him, and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh? (Isa. 58:5–8). Nor does it stand in the way that fasting is commanded by God, and may also be commanded by superiors as occasion requires. In obedience to what is good in itself, honour towards the one who commands, which is also good in itself, is practised; for fasting is commanded, or may be commanded, not as a virtue, or moral good work, or worship of God, but only as the aid and sign of these. And obedience towards God and superiors may be good even if the thing commanded is in itself neither good nor evil.

units.la: CXXIX. Jejunium legitimum duabus rebus, exercitatione corporali, spirituali inserviente & analoga: & exercitatione spirituali, quae corporalem sanctificat & salutarem reddit, absolvitur. Prior tamen proprie jejunii nomine venit; posterior vero ei, ut res per jejunium adjuta & significata sic respondet, ut sine ea jejunium religiosi jejunii rationem habere non possit, imo aeque ac oratio & sacrificia iis carentia abominatio sit, Joel. II. 13. Prov. XXVIII. 9. Exercitatio corporalis in abstinentia rerum licitarum, vel in universum, vel maximam earum partem, & ad tempus, quantum humana fragilitas finit, ut natura castigetur, sed non perdatur, & sensuum delectatio, sine eorum detrimento ad tempus leponatur; consistit. Res a quibus abstinendum, variae
units.tr: CXXIX. Lawful fasting is completed by two things: a bodily exercise, serving and analogous to the spiritual, and a spiritual exercise, which sanctifies the bodily one and makes it wholesome. The former properly comes under the name of fasting, but the latter corresponds to it as the thing aided and signified by fasting, so that without it fasting cannot have the character of religious fasting. Indeed, like prayer and sacrifices without these things, it is an abomination (Joel 2:13; Prov. 28:9). Bodily exercise consists in abstaining, either entirely or for the greater part, from lawful things, and for a time, as far as human frailty allows, so that nature may be chastened but not destroyed, and so that the pleasure of the senses may for a time be put aside without harm to them.

units.la: sunt, puta alimentum, Esth. IV. 16. Jon. III. 7. esus & potus, Luc. V. 33. Opera & curae vocationis ordinariae, Num. XXIX. 7. ad vacandum unice exercitiis sacris, quo tempus jejunii tempus etiam Sabbathi nomine venit, Levit. XXIII. 32. Vestimentorum diversicolorum & ornamentorum quorumvis sepositio, Exod. XXXIII. 4. 5. Jon. III. 5. 6. Somni, recreationum cohibitio, Dan. VI. 18. X. 2. 3. defraudatio tori ad tempus, 1. Cor. VII. 5. Corporalis haec exercitatio jejunantibus ad animum revocat, quod propter peccata vitae hujus muneribus & commodis prorsus indigni sint, imo digniores sint, qui infra terram subsidant, & in infernum conjiciantur, quam qui supra terram spiritum trahant, quod veteres sparsione pulveris & terrae supra caput indigetatur, ex Job. II. 12. Esth. IV. 3. Jer. VI. 26. Ezech. XXVII. 30. constat. Spiritualis exercitatio in studio & contentione singulari, nos ipsos coram Deo humiliandi; & faciem gratiamque ejus impetrandi consistit. Tunc indixi jejunium ut affligeremus nos coram Deo nostro, ut quaereremus ab eo viam rectam nobis & parvulis nostris, &c. Esr. VIII. 21. Pertinent huc scissio cordium noltrorum Joel. II. 13. scrutinium, confessio & deploratio humilima peccatorum nostrorum & alienorum, Esr. IX. 3. &c. Neh. IX. 1. &c. approximatio ad Deum per fidem, Luc. XV. 18. 21. & invocatio auxilii nominis Dei, Jon. III. 8. Esaj. LVIII. 4. Humiliatio ipsa afflictionem & tristitiam cordium nostrorum ex horrore peccatorum & poenarum iisdem debitarum oriundam exigit, quam mire speculum legis Dei & comminationum ejus, exempla judiciorum Dei adversus μετανοοῦντες, judicia praesentia & imminentia, contemplatio spiritualis Salvatoris nostri in cruce pendentis, vulnerum & vibicum, mortisque ejus maledictae, promovent. Approximatio vero ad Deum per fidem, tum seriam & importunam velut pulsationem ostii misericordiae Dei ad impetrandam remissionem peccatorum, judiciorum Dei aversionem, & gratiae benedictionisque Divinae consecutionem, Psal. LI. 1. 2. 14. tum redintegrationem foederis cum Deo, Nehem. IX. 38. Esr. X. 3. 5. tum renovationem resipiscentiae in posterum per amorem sincerum justitiae & odium peccati, Esaj. LV. 7. postulat.
units.tr: These things from which one must abstain are various: for example, food (Esth. 4:16; Jonah 3:7); eating and drinking (Luke 5:33); the works and cares of one's ordinary calling (Num. 29:7), so that one may devote oneself solely to sacred exercises, a time which in the case of fasting is also called the Sabbath (Lev. 23:32); the putting aside of coloured garments and all ornaments (Exod. 33:4–5; Jonah 3:5–6); the restraint of sleep and recreation (Dan. 6:18; 10:2–3); the withholding of marital intercourse for a time (1 Cor. 7:5). This bodily exercise recalls to fasting people's minds that, because of the sins of this life, they are wholly unworthy of its gifts and comforts; indeed, those who sink under the earth and are cast into hell are more worthy than those who draw breath above the earth. This the ancients signified by sprinkling dust and earth on the head, as is clear from Job 2:12; Esth. 4:3; Jer. 6:26; Ezek. 27:30. Spiritual exercise consists in a particular zeal and striving to humble ourselves before God, and to obtain his face and grace. "Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river Ahava, that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones," etc. (Ezra 8:21). To this belong the rending of our hearts (Joel 2:13); self-examination; confession and most humble lamentation of our sins and of others' (Ezra 9:3, etc.; Neh. 9:1, etc.); approach to God by faith (Luke 15:18, 21); and the invocation of help in the name of God (Jonah 3:8; Isa. 58:4). Humbling itself requires that the affliction and sorrow of our hearts arise from horror at sins and at the punishments owed to them. This is wonderfully promoted by the mirror of God's law and its threats, by examples of God's judgements against the penitent, by present and impending judgements, and by the spiritual contemplation of our Saviour hanging on the cross, of his wounds and bruises and his cursed death. But approach to God by faith requires both a serious and importunate knocking, as it were, at the door of God's mercy to obtain forgiveness of sins, the turning away of God's judgements, and the attaining of divine grace and blessing (Ps. 51:1–2, 14); and also the renewal of the covenant with God (Neh. 9:38; Ezra 10:3, 5); and, for the future, the renewal of repentance through sincere love of righteousness and hatred of sin (Isa. 55:7).

units.la: CXXX. Tale jejunium maxima quaeque Dei beneficia provocat, qualia sunt, quod sic in irruptione veluti stantibus nobis Deum poenitet mali, quod inflicturus videbatur, & populo parcit, Joel. II. 14. 18. quod jejunantes ipsi pro se signum gratiae gementibus propter abominationes populi promissae accipiunt, Ezechiel. IX. 4. 6. salutis suae, retributionis Dei in aperto, & amoris Dei certiores reddentur, Matth. VI. 18. spirituali robore adversus tentationes, patientia & consolatione in afflictionibus, variisque gratiis mactantur. Deus enim remunerator eorum est, qui ipsum quaerunt, Hebr. XI. 6. Qui seminarunt cum lachrymis, cum exultatione metent, Psal. CXXVI. 5. Sed tam nullum jejunii, quam precum ipsarum, quarum adjumentum, & humiliationis nostrae, cujus signum illud est, meritum est, satisfactio, qualem male jejunantes Papicolae somniant, nulla. Institutur enim non adquaeitum
units.tr: CXXX. Such fasting provokes the greatest blessings of God. These include this: while we stand in the breach, God repents of the evil he was about to inflict and spares the people (Joel 2:14, 18). Fasting people receive for themselves the sign of grace, the promise made to those groaning over the abominations of the people (Ezek. 9:4, 6). They are made more certain of their salvation, of God's rewarding of them openly, and of his love (Matt. 6:18). They are strengthened spiritually against temptations, and they are enriched with patience, consolation in afflictions, and various other graces. For God is the rewarder of those who seek him (Heb. 11:6), and those who sowed in tears will reap with joy (Ps. 126:5). But fasting, like the prayers themselves, whose help and sign of our humiliation it is, has no merit or satisfaction, such as the foolish followers of the Papists dream of when they fast. For it is instituted not for the acquisition of salvation, but for obtaining grace, which freely pardons sins; not to make satisfaction for sin, but to testify to repentance and a contrite heart.

units.la: {*} Jejunii utilitas. stum salutis, sed ad impetrationem gratiæ, gratis peccata condonantis non ad satisfaciendum pro peccato, sed ad resipiscentiam & cor contritum testandum. Placatur autem Deus jejunio non proprie, seu interna vi sua, & propria dignitate, quia sic solus Christus ἱλασμὸς placamen nostrum est, 1. Joh. II. 1. sed improprie, quatenus internæ pœnitentiæ externum signum & testimonium est.
units.tr: Benefit of fasting. God is appeased by fasting not properly, that is, by its own internal power and intrinsic worth, for in that sense Christ alone is our propitiation [ἱλασμός] (1 John 2:1). It is appeased improperly, insofar as fasting is the outward sign and testimony of inward repentance.

units.la: CXXXI. Jejunium vel Legale vel Evangelicum est. Legale est, quod sub Lege obtinuit. Ordinarium autem sub Lege jejunium fuit dies Kippurim decimus septimi mensis, Levit. XVI. 29. 30. 31. XXIII. 32. Num. XXIX. 7. Νηστεία appellatur, Act. XXVII. 9. In eo confessio & remissio peccati ceremonialiter facta est. Ei Judæi alia diversis occasionibus adjunxerunt, de quibus Zach. VII. 3. 5. VIII. 19. Quod lege impositum erat, commemorationem peccati, ut nec dum per Christi sacrificium expiati, habuisse, in loco vidimus. Cætera sponte suscipiebantur, secundum generalem Legem orandi instanter, meditandi diligenter, & se coram Deo demississime humiliandi, seu cor sunm dandi להבין ולהתענות ad intelligendum & se affligendum coram Deo, Dan. X. 12. Quod in eo ceremoniale erat, per Christum abrogatum, & credentibus in diem lætitiæ conversum est. Quod quasi morale, spirituale, seu cultui spirituali & morali perpetuo inserviebat, sub N. T. manet. Proin Evangelicum jejunium à Legali differt, quatenus ab eo typus rei futuræ, qui in hoc obtinuit, abest, manente eo, quod orationis, meditationis, humiliationis singularis perpetuum adjumentum & signum est. Licet enim discipuli Christi non jejunaverint, nempe πολλὰ multum, sicut Pharisæi, & juxta ritum sub lege usitatum, Matth. IX. 14. atque adventante N. T. gaudio, ad quod animi eorum præparandi erant, & eatenus illos non jejunantes Christus defenderit: tamen idem prædixit, venturos esse dies, quibus Sponsus ab illis auferendus sit; atque tum eos jejunaturos, ibid. v. 15.
units.tr: CXXXI. Fasting is either legal or evangelical. Legal fasting is what held under the Law. The ordinary fast under the Law was the day of Kippurim, the tenth day of the seventh month (Lev. 16:29–31; 23:32; Num. 29:7). It is called nēsteia [νηστεία] (Acts 27:9). On that day confession and forgiveness of sin were made in a ceremonial way. The Jews added other fasts on various occasions, about which see Zech. 7:3, 5; 8:19. We have seen in its place that what was imposed by the Law was a remembrance of sin, as sins were not yet expiated by Christ's sacrifice. Other things were undertaken voluntarily, in keeping with the general law of praying earnestly, meditating diligently, and humbling oneself most deeply before God, that is, to give one's heart להבין ולהתענות [lehavin velehit'anot] to understand and to afflict oneself before God (Dan. 10:12). What was ceremonial in it has been abrogated through Christ and turned into a day of joy for believers. What was, as it were, moral and spiritual, serving perpetually the spiritual and moral worship, remains under the New Testament. Thus evangelical fasting differs from legal fasting insofar as the type of a future thing, which held in the legal fast, is absent from it, while what remains is the perpetual help and sign of prayer, meditation and special humiliation. For although the disciples of Christ did not fast πολλά [polla] much, as the Pharisees did, and according to the rite customary under the Law (Matt. 9:14), and although Christ defended them for not fasting, since the joy of the New Testament was approaching, for which their minds had to be prepared, nevertheless he also foretold the same thing: that days would come when the Bridegroom would be taken away from them; and then they would fast (ibid., v. 15).

units.la: CXXXII. Jejunium Evangelicum abstinentia religiosa ab omni cibo, potu, lautiitiis, vitæ adjumentis & solatiis est; quatenus scilicet naturæ imbecillitas id finit. Neque proin in ciborum delectu jejunium est, sed helluatio, compotatio, sybariticus luxus esse, æque atque extra jejunium potest. Quomodo Pontificii in ciborum, nominatim piscium, herbarum, leguminum delectu, non exclusò etiam quovis potu, condimentis & deliciis & quidem per prandium etiam & cœnas exactum jejunium pro legitimo & Evangelico venditare, & illud non probantibus, ceu helluonibus & potatoribus insultare non erubescunt; Pharisæorum Christo, ceu φάγω ἡ οἰνοπότης helluoni & potatori impie insultantium, malitiam strenuè secuti. Atqui vox ipsa νηστεία, quod ἄοιτον impastum Suidas reddit, ciborum delectum tollit. Neque ulli unquam Sancti in ciborum delectu jejunasse, sed ab omni cibo abstinuisse omnes leguntur, 1. Sam. XIV. 24. 2. Sam. III. 35. Dan. X. 3. 4. Luc. V. 33. VII. 33. Jejunii enim ratio in afflictione, humiliatione, castigatione corporis, ut spiritui humiliando obsequentius sit, consistit, qui nonnisi ciborum & deliciarum corporis, quibus caro ferocior redditur, & spiritui impedimentum objicitur, abdicatione obtinetur. Neque sine causa præceptum ἡ ἀπέχεσθαι βρωμάτων abstinendi à cibis certis, quale illud Ecclesiæ est; ciborum delectum, ceu rem in jejunio necessariam, & conscientiam obligantem præcipiens, nigerrimo carbone notatur, ceu διδασκαλία δαιμονίων doctrina dæmoniorum, quæ eorum est, qui ἐν ὑποκρίσει ψευδολόγῳ ἐν συνειδήσει ἰδίᾳ κεκαυτηριασμένην ἔχοντες in hypocrisi mendaciloqua, & conscientiam propriam cauteriatam habent, 1. Tim. IV. 1. 2. Non enim gravi illa censura notantur soli Manichæi, qui cibos quosdam, ut malos damnaverant; sed quotquot certos cibos prohibent, etiam religionis gratiâ. Utriq; enim diversas licet ob causas, à cibis abstinere jubentur. Nam & Montanistæ damnantur haud dubiè, qui tamen abstinentiam à cibis non ut malis, sed solius temperantiæ causa, præceperunt. Neque etiam verba illa, quos Deus creavit, ut assumantur cum gratiarum actione, sententiam jubentium à certis cibis abstinere, quia à Deo conditi non sint, exprimunt, (quia aliâs dicendum fuisset, jubentium abstinere à cibis à Deo non conditis, vel affirmantium, quòd Deus eos non condiderit) sed potius argumentum, seu demonstrationem, quòd certis cibis, sive in jejunio, sive extra illud, prohibendi non sint; quia videlicet sic prohibentes præcepta dant de rebus bonis, licitis, à Deo conditis, sanctificatis, explicant. Ne dicam cum Manichæis facere Pontifices Zachariam & Gregorium II. nec non Alex. Alensem & Durandum, quorum illi quorundam animalium, hi carnium, ceu unâ cum terra maledictarum, esum prohibitum esse statuerunt. Idem S. Paulus alibi: Ne quis vos damnet ob cibum, vel potum. Si cum Christo mortui estis, cur, ut viventes in mundo, decreta sustinetis? (qualia sunt) Ne tangas, ne gustes, ne contrectes. Quæ rationem habent sapientiæ in cultu voluntario, & submissione animi, & in eo, quod corpori non parcunt; & tamen nullius pretii sunt, Coloss. II. 16–20. Non potuisset Papistarum oculum impetere & ferire rectius. Colligit enim omnes causas, quibus superstitiosi ciborum quorundam abstinentiam commendant & palliant, quales sunt, quòd præscripta sit ab hominibus, Papa, Ecclesia: quod rationem habeat sapientiæ, quippe non sine justis causis institura: quòd hæc ratio sapientiæ sit in cultu voluntario, summissione animi in eo, quod corpori non parcitur, quæ singula perpetim in ore Papistarum sunt. Vetat S. Paulus quemquam damnare ob cibum vel potum. Illi damnant dicentes, peccare mortaliter, qui certis temporibus à carnibus non abstinent. Vetat eos, qui cum Christo mortui sunt, δογματίζεσθαι decretis (libertatem Christi morte partam infringentibus) onerari. Illi onerant. Frustra erga clamant, agi de Cerinthianis, vel Platonicis, qui ex superstitioso Angelorum cultu, abstinentiam à certis cibis præceperunt. Esto enim. An ideo Papistæ non æquè taxantur? Scilicet si toto genere hi ab illis differunt. Qui eadem peccata peccant, eadem lege continentur. Imò nec Cerinthiani, nec Platonici causas illas, quòd abstinentia sit cultus voluntarius, & ἀφειδία σώματος urgebant. At urgent Papistæ. Accedit, quòd ciborum quodvis genus & usus pars uniuniversalis dominii à Deo humano generi conceßi est, Gen. I. 26. 27. 29. IX. 3. 4. Quòd dominium sub V. T. ab ipso Deo legibus quibusdam positivis restrictum, sub N. T. in solidum restituitur. Quod in os ingreditur, non inquinat hominem, Matth. XV. 11. Quæ Deus purificavit, ne profana ducito, Actor. X. 15. Omnia munda sunt mundis, Tit. I. 15. Neque Ecclesia eam potestatem habet, ut libertatem hominibus concessam Divino jure, stricta lege abroget, & observationem electus actum obedientiæ & cultus Divini faciat. Nam ne ipsi quidem Spiritui S. visum est, discipulis imponere onus, Actor. XV. 28. Atqui ciborum discrimen revera onus est: Et qui tali præcepto paret, is peregrinum Deum colit, eum, qui se pro Deo collocat in Templo. Præterea nec cibi in jejunio electi, nec potus mortificationi spiritus conducunt. In potu enim inflammatio concupiscentiæ, & ἀσωλία Ephes. V. 18. esse potest. Facilius enim potu quàm cibo satiamur. Neque ichtyophagia & xerophagia magis quàm esus carnium spiritum contundere apta nata est. Perditissimi luxu ex salsamentis, conchis aliisque piscibus convivia instruunt. Qui igitur potu generoso, piscibus Eois, dapibus intonatis, leguminibus, herbis delicatè apparatis, aliisque ejusmodi aromatibus probè conditis cibis ingluviem, stomachúmque oblectat, eumne quisquam mortificare carnem, jejunare dixerit? Inprimis cùm Alensis aliique statuant, excessum in quantitate cibi & potus meritum jejunii minuere, at illud non solvere, quia, inquit, Ecclesia non determinavit, quantum in communi sumi debeat. Et olim quidem jejunium plenaria abstinentia, neque nisi una refectione, cœnæ puta, post occidentem solem, non prandii definitum esse, Bellarminus haud dissitetur. Qui mos adhuc Thomæ Aquinatis tempore obtinuit; mutatus tamen est ante seculum XVI. ut posthac non cœnare duntaxat, sed etiam prandere licuerit. Neque etiam ovum ovo similius esse, quàm Montanistarum & Papistarum jejunia sunt, liquidò Celeb. Dallæus probavit. Si qui verò ante sextum septimumve seculum à certo ciborum genere abstinuerunt, illi tamen nec nudam abstinentiam à carnibus pro vero jejunio habuerunt, nec delectum illum nisi in quadragesima in more habuerunt, nec lautè in cæterorum ciborum apparatu victitarunt, nec ulla lege Ecclesiæ, sed liberè certum ciborum genus delegerunt. Primi cœlibes, splendorem apud mundum affectantes, à carnium solidiorúmque ciborum usu abstinuerunt, quod continentiæ suæ graves reputarent. Secuti sunt Ascetæ; donec ex voluntaria quorundam disciplina lex publica hominum, aliorum libera voluntate, aliorum tyrannide facta est. Sed ipsam hanc legem cudendi non postrema hæc ratio Papæ fuit, ut dispensationum suarum licentia, ambitioni & quæstui suo velificaretur. Cujus rei fidem Taxa Cancellariæ Romanæ, in qua dispensationes ejusmodi certo pretio addicuntur, facit.
units.tr: CXXXII. Evangelical fasting is the religious abstinence from all food, drink, delicacies, and the comforts and solaces of life, insofar as the weakness of nature allows. Therefore fasting does not consist in choosing foods, but in gluttony, drinking bouts, and Sybaritic luxury, which can also happen outside fasting. In this way the Papists do not blush to pass off, as lawful and evangelical, a fast that consists in choosing foods, especially fish, herbs, and pulses, without excluding any drink, seasonings, or delicacies, and indeed a fast observed even at lunch and dinner. And they insult those who do not approve of it as gluttons and drunkards, closely following the malice of the Pharisees, who impiously insulted Christ as a glutton and a drunkard, φάγος καὶ οἰνοπότης [phagos kai oinopotēs]. Yet the word νηστεία [nēsteia] itself, which Suidas renders as unfed [ἄοιτος], excludes the choice of foods. Nor is it ever read that any of the saints fasted by choosing foods; rather, all are read to have abstained from all food (1 Sam. 14:24; 2 Sam. 3:35; Dan. 10:3; Luke 5:33; 7:33). For the principle of fasting consists in affliction, humiliation, and the chastisement of the body, so that the spirit may be more obedient in being humbled, and this is obtained only by renouncing food and the delicacies by which the flesh is made wilder and an obstacle is placed before the spirit. Nor without reason is the precept ἀπέχεσθαι βρωμάτων [apechesthai brōmatōn] abstaining from certain foods, such as the Church's precept is, marked with the blackest charcoal. The Church's precept, which prescribes the choice of foods as something necessary in fasting and binding on conscience, is called διδασκαλία δαιμονίων [didaskalia daimoniōn] a doctrine of demons, which belongs to those who, speaking lies in hypocrisy and having their own conscience seared (1 Tim. 4:1–2). For it is not only the Manichaeans, who condemned certain foods as evil, who are branded with that grave censure, but all who prohibit certain foods, even for the sake of religion. For both are commanded to abstain from foods, though for different reasons. Indeed the Montanists are undoubtedly condemned, who nevertheless enjoined abstinence from foods not as evil, but solely for the sake of temperance. Nor do the words which God created to be received with thanksgiving express the opinion of those who command abstinence from certain foods because they were not created by God (for otherwise it would have had to be said either that those commanding abstinence hold that they were not created by God, or that they affirm that God did not create them). Rather, they express an argument or demonstration that they are not to be prohibited as certain foods, whether in fasting or outside it; because those who prohibit them in this way lay down precepts about things that are good, lawful, created and sanctified by God. I will not mention that the Pontiffs, along with the Manichaeans, Zachariah and Gregory II, and also Alexander of Hales and Durandus, have acted in the same way, for some of them declared that the eating of certain animals was forbidden, and others the eating of flesh, as if it were cursed along with the earth. The same St. Paul elsewhere says: Let no one judge you in food or drink. If you have died with Christ, why, as though living in the world, do you submit to decrees? (of the kind) Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle. These things have an appearance of wisdom in voluntary worship, and humility, and in not sparing the body; yet they are of no value (Col. 2:16–20). He could not have struck the eye and wounded the Papists more accurately. For he gathers together all the reasons by which superstitious people commend and cover up the abstinence from certain foods: that it is prescribed by men, by the Pope and the Church; that it has the appearance of wisdom, since it is instituted not without just causes; and that this appearance of wisdom lies in voluntary worship, humility of mind, and in not sparing the body. These points are constantly on the lips of the Papists. St. Paul forbids anyone to judge in food or drink. They condemn, saying that those who do not abstain from flesh at certain times sin mortally. He forbids those who have died with Christ to be burdened by decrees, which undo the liberty won by Christ's death. They burden. In vain do they cry out that this concerns the Cerinthians or the Platonists, who enjoined abstinence from certain foods out of a superstitious worship of angels. Granted. But are the Papists not equally charged? Surely not if they differ from those in every respect? Those who commit the same sins are bound by the same law. Indeed, neither the Cerinthians nor the Platonists urged those reasons, that abstinence is voluntary worship and a severity toward the body. But the Papists do urge them. Add to this that every kind and use of food is part of the universal dominion granted by God to the human race (Gen. 1:26–29; 9:3–4). Under the Old Testament that dominion was restricted by God himself through certain positive laws, but under the New Testament it is restored in full. What enters the mouth does not defile a man (Matt. 15:11). What God has cleansed, do not call common (Acts 10:15). To the pure all things are pure (Titus 1:15). Nor does the Church have the power to abrogate, by a strict law, a liberty granted to men by divine right, and to make the observance of a chosen food an act of obedience and divine worship. For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden (Acts 15:28). Yet the distinction of foods is in truth a burden. Whoever obeys such a precept worships a foreign God, namely the one who sets himself up in God's place in the Temple. Moreover, neither the foods chosen in fasting nor the drinks help the mortification of the spirit. For drink can cause the inflaming of lust and excess (Eph. 5:18). We are more easily sated by drink than by food. Nor is a diet of fish or of dry food any better suited to crushing the spirit than eating meat. The most wanton men furnish their feasts with salted fish, shellfish, and other fish. Who, then, would say that a man who delights his belly and gullet with generous wine, Eastern fish, rich dishes, pulses, herbs elegantly prepared, and other foods seasoned with such spices is mortifying the flesh or fasting? Especially since Alensis and others hold that excess in the quantity of food and drink diminishes the merit of fasting, though it does not dissolve it, because, they say, the Church has not determined how much may be taken in general. And Bellarmine does not deny that once fasting was defined as complete abstinence, with only one meal, namely supper, after sunset, and not lunch. This custom still prevailed in the time of Thomas Aquinas, but it was changed before the sixteenth century, so that it became lawful thereafter to lunch as well as to dine. Nor are the fasts of the Montanists and the Papists any more alike than one egg is to another, as the learned Dallaeus has clearly shown. If any before the sixth or seventh century abstained from a certain kind of food, they did not regard bare abstinence from flesh as true fasting, nor did they observe that choice except in Lent, nor did they live sumptuously in the preparation of their other foods, nor did they do so by any law of the Church, but freely chose a certain kind of food. The first to do so were celibates, seeking splendor before the world, who abstained from the use of flesh and more solid foods, because they considered this a burden to their continence. The ascetics followed; until, from the voluntary discipline of some, a public law was made, by the free will of some and the tyranny of others. But the Pope's not least reason for making this very law was to let his ambition and profit sail with the license of his dispensations. The Taxa of the Roman Chancery, in which such dispensations are assigned at a fixed price, bears witness to this fact.

units.la: CXXXIII. Imbelles pro xerophagia & electu ciborum ratiunculæ sunt.
units.tr: CXXXIII. The trivial arguments for xerophagy and the choice of foods are weak.

units.la: Divinum enim interdictum certorum ciborum, velut arboris scientiæ boni & mali in Paradiso, animalium, quæ immunda lex declaravit, sanguinis & suffocati, &c. nec in jejunio locum habuit; & hominibus religionis causa interdicendi ea, quæ Dominus non interdixit, nullum facit. Non enim hi perinde rerum domini sunt, atque ille est. In Novo certè Testamento Deus omnes promiscuè indulsit, & remoto repagulo usibus nostris omnes liberaliter dedicavit. Danielis verò à carne & vino, & מנחת לחם pane desiderabili seu delicato per tres hebdomadas abstinentia cap. X. 2. 3. laudabilis illa certè, at jejunium in electu ciborum minimè constituit. Carnibus abstinuit; an & piscibus indulsit? Etiam pane desideriorum abstinuit. At illi in piscibus & oleribus nullas מנחת delicias fugiunt. Daniel ergo tribus hebdomadis jejunavit; prolixius quàm ut posset natura durare, nullo prorsus cibo sumpto. Necesse igitur habuit singulis diebus jejunium solvere. Sed cùm solvit, tum omne genus lautitias & delicias vitavit, verè ut se lugere, in doloribus esse, ostenderet. Verbo, exemplum Danielis ad abstinentiam pertinet, non ad electum: & voluntatis propriæ, non legis fuit. Et par ferè Johannis Baptistæ ratio est, qui locustas & mel sylvestre esitavit, Matth. III. 4. non lege ulla, sed libera voluntate, ad faciendam austeræ vitæ exemplo vocationi extraordinariæ fidem; & quia cibus ille in deserto obvius maximè fuit; neque in jejunio, sed ordinariè hoc cibo usus est. Quamquam nec aliud eum non edisse, Matthæus testatur. Nam & Israelitæ mannam, Sacerdotes res sanctas comederunt. At aliud ipsos non comedisse, non sequitur. Ad similem etiam temperantiam neminem Johannes adegit, quod mitrati faciunt, qui verè saliaribus & pontificalibus cœnis se saginantes, reliquis abstinentiæ legem figunt. Sed & Timotheus vino abstinuit, 1. Tim. V. 23. at nec in jejunio duntaxat, nec religionis & merendi gratia, sed quia ita à puero assuevit. Sacrificuli contra, authores hujus legis, nec in jejunio, nec extra illud vino abstinent, sed plenis cyathis bibunt. Petrum lupinis, Matthæum oleribus & baccis vesci solitos, Jacobum vino & carne abstinuisse, vetus, sed incerta traditio est, falsæque similis, quia ex Ebionitarum lacunis hausta, uti Epiphanius & Eusebius testantur. Sed esto vera traditio; delecti fuerint ab Apostolis cibi non religiosi jejunii & meriti gratia, nec ad tempus, sed in omni vita & sponte. Denique neque regula aliqua circa ciborum discrimen opus est, quia jejunium in abstinentia ciborum consistit, & Christus atque Apostoli, neque circa quantitatem, neque circa qualitatem ciborum in jejunio quicquam definiverunt. Satis est, quòd in genere omnis in victu immoderatia & intemperantia vetita est. Unde quisque sibi facilè consulere poterit. Neque enim oves Christi pecudes sui nescias sunt, quarum pastum omnem & victum aliena manus regere debeat. Si igitur tenuiorem victum quorundam infirmitas in jejunio postulat, ciborum tenuiorum nec qualitas nec quantitas definiri potest. De quantitate fatentur οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας. At nec qualitas lege certa determinari potest, quia non eadem omnium complexio est, nec eadem voluptas omnes capit.
units.tr: The divine prohibition of certain foods, such as the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in Paradise, the unclean animals that the law declared unclean, blood, and what is strangled, etc., had no place in fasting. And to forbid people, for the sake of religion, things the Lord did not forbid creates no such obligation. For these men are not in the same position as the Lord who owns all things. In the New Testament, God has certainly granted everything to all without distinction, and, with the barrier removed, has freely given all things to our use. Daniel's abstinence "from flesh and wine, and from delicate bread [מנחת לחם]" for three weeks (Dan. 10:2, 3) is certainly praiseworthy, but it does not establish a fast in the choice of foods. He abstained from meat. Did he also refrain from fish? He abstained from "bread of desires" too. But those who fast on fish and vegetables avoid no "delicacies" [מנחת] at all. Daniel therefore fasted for three weeks, for longer than nature could endure without taking any food whatever. So he necessarily had to break his fast each day. But when he broke it, he avoided every kind of luxury and delicacy, truly showing that he was mourning and in distress. In short, the example of Daniel pertains to abstinence, not to a choice of food, and it was a matter of his own will, not of law. The case of John the Baptist is nearly similar: he "ate locusts and wild honey" (Matt. 3:4), not by any law, but by his free will, to give credibility by the example of a severe life to his extraordinary calling; and because that food was most readily available to him in the desert. He did not use this food in fasting but ordinarily. Yet Matthew testifies that he did not eat anything else. For the Israelites ate manna, and the priests ate holy things; but it does not follow that they did not eat anything else. John did not compel anyone to a similar temperance, which the mitred men do not do, who, gorging themselves on sumptuous and pontifical feasts, impose a law of abstinence on others. But Timothy also abstained from wine (1 Tim. 5:23), and not only during a fast, nor for the sake of religion or merit, but because he had been accustomed to it from boyhood. The little priests, on the contrary, the authors of this law, abstain from wine neither during a fast nor outside it, but drink full cups. The old but uncertain tradition that Peter was accustomed to eat lupins, Matthew vegetables and berries, and James abstained from wine and meat, is like a falsehood, because it was drawn from the pools of the Ebionites, as Epiphanius and Eusebius testify. But suppose the tradition is true: those foods were chosen by the Apostles not for the sake of a religious fast or merit, not for a time, but freely throughout their whole lives. Finally, no rule about the distinction of foods is needed, because fasting consists in abstinence from food, and Christ and the Apostles defined nothing in fasting either about the quantity or the quality of food. It is enough that, in general, all immoderation and intemperance in diet is forbidden. By this each person can easily look after himself. For the sheep of Christ are not ignorant of their own flock, whose whole pasture and food ought not to be governed by another's hand. If therefore the weakness of some demands a lighter diet in fasting, neither the quality nor the quantity of lighter food can be defined. Our opponents [οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας] concede the point about quantity. But neither can quality be determined by a fixed law, because the constitution of all is not the same, and not all find the same pleasure in food.

units.la: CXXXIV. Jejunii tempus in specie verbo Dei definitum non est.
units.tr: CXXXIV. The time of fasting is not defined in particular by the Word of God.

units.la: In universum verò definitum illud est, quo singulares, extraordinariæ
units.tr: In general, however, that time is defined, in which singular and extraordinary

units.la: Argumenta pro xerophagia & electu ciborum exeuntur.
units.tr: Arguments for xerophagy and the choice of foods are exhausted.

units.la: Jejunii tempus in specie in verbo Dei
units.tr: The time of fasting in particular in the Word of God

units.la: nariæ & prægnantes causæ preces extra ordinem, & humiliationem coram Deo, quarum jejunium adjumentum est, exposcere videntur. Veluti cùm judicia Dei præsentia, vel imminentia iræ Divinæ deprecationem singularem suadent: vel insignis Dei gratia, & ingens aliquod beneficium à manu Dei expectamus. Christus enim tum jejunandum esse, quando Sponsus ablatus fuerit, hoc est, quando lætitia in tristitiam luctum (uti Christus vocat) commutatur, & Deus paterna abscondita facie, se vertere in crudelem videtur Job. XXX. 21. definivit, Matth. IX. 15. Luc. V. 34. Et Cornelius jejunavit, futurus primitiæ eorum, qui ex Gentibus converti debuerunt, Actor. X. 30. Antiocheni quoque illi Prophetæ & Doctores jejunarunt, cùm & seorsim quosdam ad opus Domini petierunt, & separatis manus imponere statuerunt, ibid. XIII. 2. 3. Quæ ratio plane evincit, jejunandum esse pro rebus, non pro diebus: adeóque & ilata jejunia evertit, & Papæ jejunia tum hebdomadaria, velut quartæ, sextæ & inprimis septimæ feriæ; tum menstrua, velut quatuor temporum, quæ in Januarium, Majum, Septembrem & Decembrem incidunt; tum anniversaria Quadragesimæ, nec non vigiliarum Apostolorum & Martyrum, sub peccato mortali pleraque illa sanctientis, & lege quadam Ecclesiæ obtrudentis, tyrannidem in conscientiam & superstitionem apricatur. Neque enim tempora luctus ob absentiam Sponsi, vel expectandæ à Deo singularis gratiæ, statu, fixa sunt, sed pro occasionibus mutabilibus accommodata sunt. Dies observationis, & menses, & tempora, & annos. Vereor ne frustra circa vos laboraverim, Galat. IV. 10. 11. Ethnicam, juxta Augustinum, Judaicam, juxta Chrysostomum, dierum observantiam vetari, regerunt. Sed si Ethnica, an propterea non Judaica? Si Judaica, an propterea non Ethnica? Si utraque, annon propterea etiam Papistica, quæ cum utraque illa paria facit? Nimis absurdè Apostolicæ doctrinæ vim illi luxant, quia ex ea particulare de ritibus ethnicis, vel Judaicis enuntiatum eliciunt. Longè saniores sunt, qui universale axioma retinentes, Christianos non debere dies, menses, tempora, annos ceu aliis sanctiores, observare. At universale axioma æquè Papistas atque quoscunque alios stringit, nisi forte nova illi arte docere possunt, non observare dies, qui dicunt: Cras erit septima hebdomadæ; peccabis mortaliter, si carnes comedes: non menses, qui mensium quatuor jejunia; non annos, qui anniversaria sub peccato mortali indicunt. Præterea in Scripturis æquipollentia sunt jejunare, animam affligere, jejunium, afflictio, Lev. XVI. 29. Psal. XXXV. 13. Matth. IX. 15. Et jejunium actu lugentis ipsimet adversarii definiunt. Cùm igitur non sint stata luctus & moeroris Ecclesiæ tempora, nec stata jejunii esse possunt. Ac licèt Nunquam bella piis, nunquam certamina desint; tamen jejunandi necessitatem non quævis, sed extraordinaria calamitas gravis imponit. Dantur enim Ecclesiæ etiam tempora refrigerii, Actor. III. 19. Deus vulnerat, & sanat, occidit & vivificat, Deut. XXXII. 39. Hos. VI. 2. Primus Montanus jejunia legibus sanxit, Eusebio Hist. Eccles.
units.tr: and pressing causes seem to call for extraordinary prayers and humiliation before God, of which fasting is an aid. For example, when the presence of God's judgments or the imminence of divine wrath urges a special supplication, or when we expect some remarkable grace of God and some great benefit from his hand. For Christ defined that they should fast when "the bridegroom was taken away," that is, when joy is turned into sorrow, "mourning" (as Christ calls it), and God, with his fatherly face hidden, seems to turn himself "into a cruel one" (Job 30:21) (Matt. 9:15; Luke 5:34). Cornelius fasted, about to be the first-fruits of those from the Gentiles who were to be converted (Acts 10:30). Those Antiochene "prophets and teachers fasted" when they both set apart certain men for the work of the Lord and resolved to lay hands on them, having been separated (Acts 13:2, 3). This reasoning plainly proves that one should fast for occasions, not for days; and so it overthrows the fasts that were already established, and the Pope's fasts: weekly, such as on the fourth, sixth and especially the seventh days of the week; monthly, such as the Ember days, which fall in January, May, September and December; and annual, such as Lent, and also the vigils of the Apostles and Martyrs. Those fasts, which set up a tyranny over conscience and superstition, impose many things under mortal sin and thrust them on by a certain law of the Church. For times of mourning, because of the absence of the bridegroom, or because of a special grace expected from God, are not fixed by status; they are adapted to changing occasions. "You observe days, and months, and times, and years. I am afraid that I have laboured over you in vain" (Gal. 4:10, 11). They argue that the observance of days is forbidden, the heathen observance according to Augustine and the Jewish observance according to Chrysostom. But if it is heathen, is it therefore not Jewish? If it is Jewish, is it therefore not heathen? If both, is it not therefore also Papistical, which makes the same as both of those? They wrongly twist the force of apostolic doctrine too absurdly, because they draw from it a particular statement about heathen or Jewish rites. Much more sound are those who, retaining the universal principle, teach that Christians ought not to observe days, months, times and years as if holier than others.
