But the universal principle binds the Papists equally with all others, unless perhaps they can teach by some new art that they need not observe "days" when they say: "Tomorrow will be the seventh day of the week; you will sin mortally if you eat meat"; nor "months," when they prescribe the four fasts of the months; nor "years," when they announce annual observances under mortal sin. Moreover, in the Scriptures "to fast, to afflict the soul, fasting, affliction" are equivalent (Lev. 16:29; Ps. 35:13; Matt. 9:15). And our opponents themselves define fasting as the act of one who mourns. Since therefore the times of mourning and sorrow of the Church are not fixed, neither can the times of fasting be fixed. And although "wars and contests never fail the godly," yet it is not any kind of calamity, but a grave and extraordinary one, that imposes the necessity of fasting. For there are also times of refreshing for the Church (Acts 3:19). "God wounds and heals, he kills and makes alive" (Deut. 32:39; Hos. 6:2). Montanus was the first to enact fasts by law, according to Eusebius, Hist. Eccles.

units.la: V. 17. ex Apollonio teste. Quadragesimæ jejunium jejunatricis disciplinæ Papatus acropolis ex Antepaschali jejunio, maturè, ex arbitrio, non imperio, usitato ortum seriùs habuit. Primò enim unius Paraseeves; mox Sabbathi, post, glisccente hominum studio, aliarum ejusdem hebdomadæ feriarum, demum quadraginta diebus ante Pascha jejunium fuit. Sabbathicum primum in Hispania circa A. 305. invitis & reclamantibus Græcis; reliqua omnia seriùs invaluerunt.
units.tr: 5:17, on the testimony of Apollonius. The fast of Lent, the citadel of the Papacy's fasting discipline, arose later than the fast before Easter, which was used early on by choice, not by command. For at first there was the fast of only one Preparation Day (Friday); soon after, of the Sabbath; later, as men's zeal grew, of the other days of the same week; and at last there was a fast of forty days before Easter. The first Sabbath fast was in Spain around the year 305, against the wishes and protests of the Greeks; all the others prevailed later.

units.la: CXXXV. In V. T. statum jejunandi tempus dies Kippurim, Deus ipse instituit. Sed qui dierum discrimen sub pædagogia Legis, ad tempus usque correctionis instituit, idem adventante correctionis tempore, illud abolevit. Placuit enim Deo anniversario die peccatum & ejusdem poenas commemorari. Sed peccati nunc commemoratio cessat, quando uno die illud ablatum est. Par ratio est statorum temporum, quibus Judæi certos menses jejuniis sacrarunt. Jejunium quarti, quinti, septimi & decimi (mensis) fiet domui Judæ in hilaritatem, Zach. VIII. 19. Non enim illa in perpetuum, sed ad tempus ex ipsarum populi rerum statu & qualitate statuta fuerunt, hac videlicet lege, ut perseverante eorum calamitate observarentur, definente verò, tristibusque in lætiora mutatis abrogarentur, uti ex Zachar. VII. 3. & VIII. 19. ipse Sanctius aliique colligunt. Quæ quidem ipsissima jejuniorum N. T. ex nostra etiam sententia, ratio est. Incertum porro est, an Ecclesia Judaica ex constitutione Mardochæi, festum Purim quotannis per jejunium etiam exegerit. Nihil de eo literæ Estheris & Mardochæi habent. Constituunt enim observari dies fortium, & suo tempore cum gaudio, epulis & conviviis celebrari, Esth. IX. 18. 21. 22. Quid jejunio cum epulis & festiva solennitate? Quòd verò v. 31. dicitur, Judæos suscepisse dies Purim, sicut receperunt super animam suam, & super semen suum jejunia & clamorem suum, non aliud significat, quam quòd Judæi istos dies Purim, quos ex Mardochæi literis se observaturos constituunt, monumento futuros ejus salutis, quam jejunio & clamoribus suis à Deo consecuti fuerant. Et Pharisæi quidem, imò & Johannis discipuli olim stata jejunia habuerunt, bis jejunantes in Sabbatho, Luc. XVIII. 12. coll. cum Matth. IX. 14. Et Johannis discipulis ex Christo quæ-rentibus, cur discipuli sui non jejunent, respondit Christus, aliquando eos jejunaturos esse, sed eo modo jejunaturos, quo ipsi statis temporibus jejunaverant, non respondit. Imò jejunium ad tempus auferendi Sponsi, quod statum minimè erit, restrinxit: & simul propositæ v. 16. de panno rudi inveterata vesti non assuendo, vel vino novo in veteres uteres non infundendo, non obscurè docuit, aliam se à Judaica jejunii disciplinam instituere, puta Evangelicam sub cruce, salutaris moeroris plenissimam, quæ perpetui instar jejunii est, & extraordinarium etiam luctum jejuniumque includit. Præterea nec Christi quadragesimale jejunium imitatione exprimi potest, quia miraculosum fuit, & non quotannis repetitum, & dierum noctiumque fuit, excepto eo, quod morale in eo fuit. Ita Christus jejunavit, jejunando Tentatori Satanæ
units.tr: CXXXV. Under the Old Testament, God himself instituted the set time for fasting, the day of Kippurim. But he who established a distinction of days under the schooling of the Law, until the time of correction, also abolished it when the time of correction arrived. For it pleased God that on that annual day sin and its punishments should be remembered. But the remembrance of sin now ceases, since it has been taken away in one day. The same reasoning applies to the fixed times on which the Jews consecrated certain months with fasts: "The fast of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth (month) shall be to the house of Judah for joy" (Zech. 8:19). For those fasts were established not for ever, but for a time, from the state and condition of the people's own affairs, namely on this condition, that they should be observed while their calamity continued, but should cease when it ended and their sorrows were changed into joys; as Sanchez and others gather from Zech. 7:3 and 8:19. This is in fact the very reason for the fasts of the New Testament, even by our own opinion. Moreover, it is uncertain whether the Jewish Church, by the constitution of Mordecai, also required the feast of Purim to be kept each year with a fast. The books of Esther and Mordecai say nothing of this. For they ordain that the days of "the brave" be observed, and celebrated "in their season with gladness, feasts and banquets" (Esth. 9:18, 21, 22). What has fasting to do with feasts and festive solemnity? But when it is said in verse 31 that the Jews "undertook the days of Purim, as they had undertaken upon themselves and upon their seed the fasts and their cry," it means nothing other than that the Jews, who resolved to observe those days of Purim according to the letters of Mordecai, would make them a memorial of the salvation which they had obtained from God by their fasting and cries. The Pharisees indeed, and even the disciples of John, once had fixed fasts, "fasting twice in the Sabbath" (Luke 18:12, compared with Matt. 9:14). And when the disciples of John asked Christ why his disciples did not fast, Christ answered that they would fast at some time, but he did not answer that they would fast in the same way in which the others had fasted at fixed times. Indeed, he restricted fasting to the time when the bridegroom would be taken away, which would by no means be a fixed time. At the same time, by the parables of verse 16, of the new patch not sewn on an old garment, and of new wine not poured into old wineskins, he taught not obscurely that he was establishing a different discipline of fasting from the Jewish one, namely the Gospel discipline under the cross, full of saving sorrow, which is like a perpetual fast and includes even extraordinary mourning and fasting. Moreover, Christ's forty-day fast cannot be expressed by imitation, because it was miraculous, was not repeated every year, and was of days and nights; except for what was moral in it. Thus Christ fasted, and by fasting he resisted Satan the Tempter. These things are to be imitated, not that manner of fasting.

units.la: {y} Quædam menses, et tempora. Sabbathi, etc. thanæ restitit. Hæc imitanda sunt, non jejunii illius modus. Denique veteres stata quædam jejunia habuerunt, sed alieni tamen à reliquis Pontificiorum jejunantium erroribus fuerunt, & nondum eventus experimento institutionis statorum temporum periculum cognoverunt, adeóque imprudentes, at de cætero innocentes ejusmodi nonnulla jejunia obiverunt. Præstat autem Christi, quàm hominum aberrantium instituta sequi.
units.tr: {y} Certain months and times. Sabbaths, etc. He resisted Satan. These are things to be imitated, but not the manner of that fast. Finally, the ancients did keep certain fixed fasts, but they were free of the errors of the Papists who fast, and since they had not yet learned from experience the danger of instituting fixed times, they observed some such fasts without realising the risk, though innocently. It is better, however, to follow the practice of Christ than the institutions of men who go astray.

units.la: CXXXVI. Jejunium privatum vel publicum est. Privatum quisque sibi vel familiæ suæ ob causas & necessitates privatas indicit. Tale fuit Danielis cap. IX. 3. & esse potest fidelium quorumvis, 1. Cor. VII. 5. Publicum authoritate & consensu publico à tota Ecclesia suscipitur, non tamen ad placitum, quia nihil religiosum est, quod ex voluntate humana pendet, sed ob causas extraordinarias & occasiones publicas, cujusmodi peccata publica, Nehem. IX. 1. calamitates publicæ, Jon. III. 7. 8. susceptio negotiorum magni momenti, aliáque ejusmodi esse possunt. Differentia utrumque inter in eo etiam consistit, quòd in publico luctus & mœror palam ostendi, in privato occultari magis, quanto exploratio sinceritatis & ipses benedictionis major est, debet. Cùm jejunatis, ne hypocritarum instar tetrici estote. Abscondunt enim facies suas, ut videantur hominibus jejunantes. Amen dico vobis, mercede sua excidunt. Tu verò cùm jejunaveris, unge caput tuum, & lava faciem tuam, ne videaris hominibus jejunans, sed Patri tuo in occulto. Et Pater tuus videns in occulto, reddet tibi in propatulo, Matth. VI. 16. 17. 18. Indicto legitimè jejunio publico, obire illud omnes, qui jejunare possunt, tenentur, tum propter generale Dei mandatum, tum propter obedientiam Potestati legitimè illud indicenti, &c. generale mandatum Dei applicanti debitam. Excipiuntur tum ii, qui corporis infirmitate laborant, ut sine valetudinis dispendio jejunare non possint: tum qui jejunii disciplinam & finem non cognoscunt, nec cognoscere possunt, cujusmodi infantes lactentes sunt.
units.tr: CXXXVI. A fast is either private or public. A private fast is appointed by each person for himself or his household, for private causes and needs. Such was the fast of Daniel, ch. IX. 3, and it may be the practice of any of the faithful, 1 Cor. VII. 5. A public fast is undertaken by the whole Church, by public authority and common consent, not at pleasure, since nothing is religious that depends on human will, but on account of extraordinary causes and public occasions: such as public sins, Neh. IX. 1; public calamities, Jonah III. 7, 8; the undertaking of matters of great moment, and other such things. The difference between the two lies also in this, that in a public fast grief and mourning are shown openly, while in a private fast they should be more hidden, the more the test of sincerity and the blessing itself is at stake. When you fast, do not be gloomy like the hypocrites. For they disfigure their faces, so that they may appear to men to be fasting. Truly I say to you, they have their reward. But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you do not appear to men to be fasting, but to your Father in secret. And your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you openly, Matt. VI. 16, 17, 18. When a public fast has been lawfully appointed, all who are able to fast are bound to keep it, both because of God's general command and because of obedience to the authority that lawfully appoints it, and so on, the general command of God being applied to it as is due. Excepted are those who labour under bodily weakness, so that they cannot fast without loss of health; and those who do not know, and cannot know, the purpose and discipline of fasting, such as nursing infants.

units.la: CXXXVII. Jejuna Pontificiorum de jejuniis doctrina est; nec pietatis & religionis quicquam habet, licet in ea pietatis & induciæ suæ arcem collocent, & jejuniorum talium contemptores justos, perinde ut Pharisæi olim Christum, helluones & potatores, & perinde etiam ut olim Urbicus ille Romanus ab Augustino Epist. ad Casul. gravi propterea censura notatus, omnes Sabbatho prandentes ceu carnales & ventricolas stultissimè & insolentissimè convitiantur. Cùm enim jejunium humiliationi & afflictioni animæ inprimis inserviat, illi simulato jejunio adeò turpiter inflantur & insolescunt, ut se jejunando mereri contendant. Quæ horrenda abominatio est. Tum diebus illis, quibus jejunant, non plus vel ardentiûs, quàm quovis alio die orant, vel cultui Dei vacant. Ut jejunium eorum merè corporalis exercitatio sit, omissa exercitatione spirituali, sine qua iterum jejunium abominatio est. Præterea in ipsa exercitatione corporali nihil pro vero jejunio faciunt. Non enim à cibo & potu, non à prandio & cœna abstinent, sed carne abstinentes, piscibus, cupediis & vino utun-
units.tr: CXXXVII. The fasting of the Papists is a doctrine of fasts; it has nothing of piety or religion, although they place in it the citadel of their piety and their security, and, just as the Pharisees once called Christ gluttons and drunkards, so they, with the utmost folly and insolence, abuse as fleshly and gluttonous all who dine on the Sabbath, as that Roman Urbicus once was, severely rebuked for it by Augustine, Epist. ad Casulan. Since fasting serves above all for the humbling and affliction of the soul, they are so shamefully puffed up and grow arrogant by their pretended fasting that they contend they merit salvation by fasting. This is a horrible abomination. Moreover, on those days on which they fast they pray no more, or more fervently, or devote themselves to the worship of God, than on any other day. So their fasting is merely a bodily exercise, with the spiritual exercise omitted, and without that spiritual exercise fasting is again an abomination. Besides, in the bodily exercise itself they do nothing that belongs to true fasting. For they do not abstain from food and drink, from lunch and supper, but while abstaining from meat, they use fish, dainties and wine,

units.la: tur, quod jejunium tale est, quale helluonum, potatorum & ventricolarum est: & carne abstinent, ceu illo saltem tempore immunda; quæ dæmoniorum doctrina est. Et exercitationem ejusmodi merè corporalem, nil veri jejunii habentem, sub peccato mortali præcipiunt; ejus observationem sine alio fine actum obedientiæ & cultus, omissionem actum inobedientiæ & mortalis peccati faciunt, quæ in conscientiam hominum sævissima tyrannis est. Accedit, quòd dispensationibus suis etiam exercitationem corporalem, qua nil frigidius esse potest, laxant & resolvunt, nec sine pretio subinde; quæ ambitionem & avaritiam illorum demonstrant. Denique formam jejunii, sine vi & potestate ejus introducunt, stata quædam tempora ordine recurrentia jejuniis dicantes, quod naturæ exercitii extraordinarii planè repugnat. Et ut formam jejunii magis inanem reddant, etiam tempora jejuniis dicata ultra spatium exercitio extraordinario, vel abstinentiæ jejunii congruens, producunt. Velut in quadragesima. In tota igitur jejunii Pontificii textura ne filum quidem tenuissimum est, quod scabie & lepra obductum, fœdéque corruptum non sit.
units.tr: which is a fast such as gluttons, drinkers and bellies practise; and they abstain from meat as if it were unclean at least at that time, which is a doctrine of demons. And this merely bodily exercise, having nothing of true fasting in it, they enjoin under pain of mortal sin; they make its observance, without any other purpose, an act of obedience and worship, and its omission an act of disobedience and mortal sin, which is the most cruel tyranny over men's consciences. Add to this that by their dispensations they relax and dissolve even this bodily exercise, which can be no more trivial, and that not without payment; which shows their ambition and avarice. Finally, they introduce the form of fasting without its force and power, assigning certain fixed times recurring in order to fasts, which is plainly contrary to the nature of an extraordinary exercise. And to make the form of fasting still more empty, they extend the times dedicated to fasts beyond the space that fits an extraordinary exercise or the abstinence of a fast. As in Lent. In the whole fabric of the Papist fast, therefore, there is not even the finest thread that is not covered with scab and leprosy and foully corrupted.

units.la: CXXXVIII. In lætitia & gratiarum actione Festivitas locum habet. Quæ publica pro beneficio singulari à Deo extra ordinem accepto gratiarum actio, & lætitia spiritualis testificatio est. Hebræis שמח dicitur à שמח quod proprie motum, & quidem in circum significat, ut ita cum שמח orbis, circulus, conveniat. Talis motus est choreas ducentium. Plerunque festivam concursationem & πανήγυρις lætitiæ causa institutam significat. Græcis ἑορτὴ est, quæ vox ferias & diem solennem, ejúsque celebrationem notat. Scopus Festivitatis est, lætari coram Domino, & gratias agere pro beneficiis, iis cumprimis, quæ per preces & jejunium impetravimus. Habet verò & illa exercitationem geminam, corporalem & spiritualem. Corporalis in lætitia singulari, & liberiore creaturarum, sive quoad victum, sive quoad amictum, usu consistit. Dies sanctus est Jehovæ Deo nostro. Ne lugeatis, neque fleatis. Dixit præterea: Ite, comedite pinguia, & bibite dulcia, & mittite partes ei, cui nihil paratum est, quia sanctus dies Domino nostro. Neque contristemini, quia gaudium Jehovæ est fortitudo vestra, Nehem. VIII. 9. 10. Ubi tamen & modus lætitiæ indicendus, & in esu atque potu non tam circa quantitatem, quàm circa qualitatem ejus à communi diæta recedendum, & in amictu omnis vanitas vitanda atque cavenda, & cuncta hæc, utpote in quibus per se Regnum Dei non consistit ad finem religiosum, seu exercitationem spiritualem referenda sunt. Quæ in eo consistit, ut & vocem nostram in gratiarum actione pro beneficiis præstitis & præstandis, ad Deum attollamus; & recordemur afflictionum & malorum, à quibus Deus nos liberavit, eáque cum præsente liberationis beneficio comparemus, & præsentis gratiæ & beneficii meditatione nostram in Deo, beneficiorum & gratiæ omnis authore fiduciam, & futuræ etiam liberationis spem confirmemus: & eleemosynis atque muneribus pauperibus erogandis, nostram erga Deum gratitudinem testificemur.
units.tr: CXXXVIII. Festivity has its place in joy and thanksgiving. It is a public thanksgiving for a singular benefit received from God beyond the ordinary course, and a testimony of spiritual joy. To the Hebrews it is called [šāmaḥ] from [šāmaḥ], which properly signifies motion, and indeed motion in a circle, so that it agrees with [šāmaḥ] orb, circle. Such is the motion of those who lead dances. Generally it signifies a festive gathering, and a [panēgyris] instituted for the sake of joy. To the Greeks it is [heortē], which word denotes a holiday and a solemn day, and its celebration. The aim of the Festivity is to rejoice before the Lord and to give thanks for benefits, especially those we have obtained through prayer and fasting. But it also has a twofold exercise, bodily and spiritual. The bodily consists in a singular joy and a freer use of created things, both as to food and as to clothing. The day is holy to Jehovah our God. Do not mourn nor weep. He said moreover: Go, eat fat things, and drink sweet things, and send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared, because the day is holy to our Lord. Neither be sorrowful, for the joy of Jehovah is your strength, Neh. VIII. 9, 10. Yet here the measure of joy must be prescribed, and in eating and drinking one must depart from the common diet not so much as to quantity as to quality, and in clothing all vanity must be avoided and guarded against; and all these things, since the Kingdom of God does not in itself consist in them, must be referred to a religious end or spiritual exercise. This consists in raising our voice to God in thanksgiving for benefits bestowed and to be bestowed; in remembering the afflictions and evils from which God has freed us, and comparing them with the present benefit of deliverance; in confirming, by meditation on present grace and benefit, our trust in God, the author of all benefits and grace, and our hope of future deliverance too; and in testifying our gratitude towards God by giving alms and gifts to the poor.

units.la: CXXXIX. Festa alia Veteris Testamenti fuerunt, alia Novi sunt.
units.tr: CXXXIX. Some festivals belonged to the Old Testament, and others belong to the New.

units.la: De Festis V. T. in loco plura diximus. In Novo Testamento festum quoddam perpetuum est, sine distinctione dierum, otio, vel carnalibus exercitiis, sola laetitia spirituali & gratiarum actione perpetua pro beneficiis acceptis agitandum. Ἑορτάζωμεν Festum agamus, non in fermento veteri, neque in fermento vitii & nequitiae, sed in azymis sinceritatis (vitio & nequitiae oppositae) & veritatis, (figurae veteri & literae oppositae) 1.Cor.V.8. De caetero Ecclesiae libertati relictum est, an velit vel singularia beneficia recens praestita festivitate singulari & extraordinaria celebrare & recolere: vel anniversarios etiam dies festivos, quibus Christi Nativitas, Circumcisio, Passio, Resurrectio, Ascensio in Coelum, Missio Spiritus S. in discipulos, religiose celebretur, deligere. Ac in eo etiam Evangelici jure Christianae libertatis variant, alios dies quosdam festivitati tali deputantibus, aliis solam diem Dominicam celebrantibus. Priores illi non ex necessitate fidei, cum de celebratione festorum mandatum non extet, sed ex dictamine prudentiae, quae aedificationi invigilat, & arbitrio charitatis Dei, generale de congregationibus instituendis mandatum ad solennes inter alia etiam festosque dies applicant. Quos nec posteriores metu abusuum, qui festorum occasione in Papatu invaluerunt & grassantur, festis ejusmodi abstinentes, damnant, sed ita utrinque statuunt, sub diversis ritibus eandem fidem latitare posse, &, juxta Augustini illud, rituum dissonantiam non tollere fidei consonantiam. Optimum videtur, ut celebrentur dies aliqui festi, ad excitandam & augendam devotionem, & more Ecclesiae veteris, ne fit ἀπλξία: ut pauci, ne onerentur fideles: ut in memoriam Christi & beneficiorum ejus, non Sanctorum, instituantur; ne periculum idololatriae subsit: ut superstitiosa & scrupulosa necessitas tollatur, ne Christiana libertas in discrimen veniat, & conscientiae vis inferatur: ut cultus opinio absit, ne ἐθελοθρησκεία introducatur: ut habeatur ratio decori & ordinis in Ecclesia, in qua cuncta ordine & decenter fieri debent: denique ne ejusdem Ecclesiae membrum in rei hujus indifferentis usu morosum se gerat, ut scandalum & dissidium non necessarium vitetur.
units.tr: We have said much about the festivals of the Old Testament in its proper place. In the New Testament there is one festival that is perpetual, not tied to particular days, to be kept without idleness or carnal observances, with spiritual joy alone and with constant thanksgiving for the benefits received. Let us keep the feast [Ἑορτάζωμεν], not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of vice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity (opposed to vice and wickedness) and of truth (opposed to the old figure and to the letter), 1 Cor. 5:8. For the rest, it is left to the liberty of the Church whether it wishes to celebrate and commemorate with a special and extraordinary festivity the particular benefits recently bestowed, or to choose annual festival days on which the Nativity, Circumcision, Passion, Resurrection, Ascension into heaven and the sending of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples of Christ are religiously observed. In this matter also, those who live under the Evangelical law of Christian liberty differ: some assign certain days to such a festivity, while others observe only the Lord's Day. The former do not do so from any necessity of faith, since there is no command for the observance of festivals, but from the judgement of prudence, which watches over edification, and from the discretion of love; and they apply the general command concerning the gathering of congregations to solemn and also festal days among other occasions. Nor do the latter, from fear of the abuses which grew up and still flourish under the Papacy on the occasion of festivals, condemn those who keep such festivals or abstain from them; instead, both sides maintain that under different rites the same faith can lie hidden, and, in accordance with Augustine's saying, the dissimilarity of rites does not destroy the harmony of faith. It seems best that some festal days be observed: to stir up and increase devotion; following the custom of the ancient Church; lest there be idleness [ἀπραξία]; that there be few, so that the faithful are not burdened; that they be instituted in memory of Christ and his benefits, not of the saints; so that there is no danger of idolatry; that a superstitious and scrupulous necessity be removed, lest Christian liberty be endangered and force be done to conscience; that the opinion of worship be absent, lest will-worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία] be introduced; that regard be had for decency and order in the Church, in which all things ought to be done in order and decently; and finally, that a member of the same Church not behave perversely in the use of this indifferent matter, so that an unnecessary scandal and division be avoided.

units.la: CXL. Sed abhorremus tamen merito ab insania Pontificiorum circa festos dies solemnia delirantium, dum festa Christianorum, etiam indubitato ab hominibus instituta non solum ratione ordinis & politiae, sed necessitate praecepti Divini conscientiam obligantis, & ratione mysterii, celebranda esse, & dies festos aliis sacratiores, ex peculiari quadam sanctitate, ob quam gratia Dei uberiore mensura istis, quam aliis diebus offeratur, & dispensetur; quin & partem Divini cultus esse, scribunt, qui merus Judaismus est. Ἡμέρας παρατηρεῖτε Dies observatis, & menses, & annos. Vereor ne frustra circa vos laboraverim, Gal.IV.10. Ne quis vos judicet ἐν μέρει ἑορτῆς in parte festi, vel neomeniae, vel Sabbathorum. Quae sunt umbra futurorum. Corpus autem Christi est, Col.II.16.17. Nulla in his exceptio, nulla distinctio, ne sola Judaica festa feriri putemus. Damnantur, quotquot dies, tempora observant, sic ut in observantia illa cultum & sanctificationem singularem, mysteriumque ponant. Hactenus enim Judaica & Pontificia festa conveniunt, nisi quod illa sanctitatem & mysterium singulare ex institutione Divina habuerunt; haec per κατ' ἐντολὴν humana lege impossita, simile habere finguntur. Omnis autem discretio, sive formaliter Judaica, sive analogica & Judaicae imitatrix, ex aequo prohibetur. Non enim confirmata libertate Christiana, & Evangelio plene patefacto oportet κρίνειν ἡμέραν παρ' ἡμέραν judicare diem prae die, hoc est, alium alio sacratiorem aestimare, Rom.XIV.5. Cumque ad necessitatem cultus & conscientiae obligationem speciale mandatum Dei requiratur; nullum tale in N.T. uspiam occurrit. Nam Christus & Apostoli festa Judaica aboleverunt, at nova speciali mandato nulla surrogarunt. Quod & Bellarminus fatetur, & in universum patet, quia ipsi Papistae annotarunt, quod festum, quo authore homine procedente tempore institutum sit. Sicut autem in V.T. Deus & festa, & τὰ μέρη ἑορτῆς partes festi ipse Deus speciali mandato imposuit: ita etiam in N.T. Christus & Apostoli speciali mandato illa injunxissent, si par eorum sub N.T. necessitas, par cultus foret. Accedit, quod festum proprie dictum mysticam beneficii in tempus ejus incidentis repraesentationem & cum peculiari gaudio commemorationem, nec non singularem cultus & officii Divini in eo celebrandi modum & ceremoniam habet: uti ex analogia festorum V.T. colligere est. Atqui in festis ab hominibus institutis singula haec deficiunt: tum quia commemoratio beneficiorum Christi nusquam certo tempori, seu sacratiori, adstricta ita est, ut non liceat eodem tempore alia beneficia Dei commemorare: tum quia sic festi dies ab aliis per relativam sanctitatem, per verbum mandati & promissionis, distingui deberent; sicut aqua Baptismi a profana per simile verbum distinguitur: tum quia aliās festa alia addi iis temporibus, in quae etiam magna beneficia Dei inciderunt, alia aboleri, in quae grandia mysteria non inciderunt, deberent: tum quia nulli festorum dierum horum ceremonia solennis Divina authoritate mandata est. Et si non alias ob causas, at certe ob superstitionem & idololatriam non simplex vitium festa Papalia contrahunt. Non enim dies festivos tantum caeteris sanctiores fingunt, sed etiam operis operati opinionem fovent, spiritualem exercitationem pensi non habent, in vacatione sola a servilibus operibus & auditione Missae, quae, fatente ipso Valentia sine actuali & expressa Dei dilectione fieri possunt, acquiescunt; iis meritum, sanctificationem, & peccatorum expiationem tribuunt, eos Sanctis consecrant, adeoq; latriae cultu eos afficiunt, cum judice ipso Durando, Festivitates ad latriam pertineant; tot festos dies instituunt, & tam difficilibus nugis, scrupulis, labyrinthaeis circulationibus animos distrahunt, ut magni in Papatu viri, nominatim Nicolaus de Clemangis, Petrus de Aliaco, Felix Malleolus, Polydorus Vergilius, ipse Urbanus VIII. alibi a nobis citati, graves de iis querelas consignaverint, denique festa non pauca, velut Corporis Christi, conceptionis & assumptionis Mariae, Georgii, Christophori, aliorum chimericorum SanctoSanctorum ex narrationibus apocryphis dubiis, incertis in Ecclesiæ orchestram introduxerunt.
units.tr: CXL. Yet we rightly shrink from the madness of the Papists, who rave about festal days with solemnities, while they teach that the festivals of Christians, even those instituted by men beyond doubt, must be celebrated not only for reasons of order and policy but by the necessity of a Divine precept binding the conscience, and also on account of a mystery; that some festival days are holier than others, by a particular sanctity, on account of which the grace of God is offered and dispensed on those days in a more abundant measure than on other days; and they even write that such observance is a part of Divine worship, which is pure Judaism. You observe days, and months, and years. I am afraid that I have laboured in vain among you, Gal. 4:10. Let no one judge you in respect of a part of a feast [ἐν μέρει ἑορτῆς], or of a new moon, or of the Sabbaths. These are a shadow of things to come; but the body is Christ's, Col. 2:16–17. There is no exception here, no distinction, so that we might think only the Jewish festivals are struck. All who observe days and seasons are condemned, insofar as they place in that observance a special worship and sanctification and mystery. For Jewish and Papal festivals agree in this, except that the former had holiness and a singular mystery from Divine institution, while the latter, imposed by human law by commandment [κατ' ἐντολὴν], are feigned to have a similar character. Moreover, every distinction, whether formally Jewish or analogous to and imitating the Jewish, is equally prohibited. For after Christian liberty has been established and the Gospel fully revealed, one ought not to judge one day above another, that is, to esteem one day holier than another, Rom. 14:5. And since for the necessity of worship and the obligation of conscience a special command of God is required, no such command occurs anywhere in the New Testament. For Christ and the Apostles abolished the Jewish festivals, but they substituted no new ones by any special command. Bellarmine also admits this, and it is plain in general, because the Papists themselves have recorded by what human author and at what point in time each festival was instituted. Just as in the Old Testament God imposed both the festivals and the parts of a festival [τὰ μέρη ἑορτῆς] by a special command of his own, so too in the New Testament Christ and the Apostles would have enjoined those things by a special command, if their necessity under the New Testament were equal, and their worship equal. Add to this that a festival properly so called has a mystical representation of the benefit that falls in its time, and a commemoration with a peculiar joy, and also a singular mode and ceremony of performing the Divine worship and duty in it; as may be gathered from the analogy of the festivals of the Old Testament. But in festivals instituted by men each of these is lacking: first, because the commemoration of the benefits of Christ is nowhere bound to a certain time, or to a holier time, so that it would not be lawful at the same time to commemorate other benefits of God; second, because such festal days would have to be distinguished from others by a relative sanctity, through a word of command and promise, just as the water of Baptism is distinguished from ordinary water by a similar word; third, because otherwise other festivals would have to be added at those times when great benefits of God also fell, and others abolished in which no great mysteries fell; fourth, because no solemn ceremony of these festal days has been commanded by Divine authority. And if for no other reason, certainly on account of superstition and idolatry the Papal festivals contract no mere vice. For they not only imagine festal days to be holier than others, but also foster the opinion of a work done (ex opere operato); they take no account of spiritual exercise, and rest content with mere abstinence from servile works and with hearing Mass, which, as Valentia himself admits, can be done without actual and express love of God; they attribute merit, sanctification and the expiation of sins to these things, they consecrate them to the saints, and so honour them with the worship of latria, although, by the judgement of Durandus himself, festivities pertain to latria; they institute so many festal days, and distract minds with such difficult trifles, scruples and labyrinthine circuits, that great men within the Papacy, namely Nicholas of Clamanges, Pierre d'Ailly, Felix Hemmerlin, Polydore Vergil, and Urban VIII himself (cited by us elsewhere), have recorded grave complaints about them. Finally, they have introduced into the Church's dance not a few festivals, such as those of the Body of Christ, of the conception and assumption of Mary, of George, of Christopher, and of other chimerical saints, drawn from doubtful and uncertain apocryphal narratives.

units.la: CXLI. Infirma nimis fulcra sunt, quibus superstitionem suam festivam ὀι ἐξ εὐαγγελίας sustinere conantur. Nam Judæos quidem festa quædam, velut Purim, Encæniorum liberè instituisse, ἀνεξαγώνιον est. Et eadem ratione Christiana etiam Ecclesia festa quædam liberè instituere & observare potest, dummodo opinio necessitatis, mysterii & cultus, nec non idolatria absit. Dies Dominica nec festum proprie magis est, quàm fuit Sabbathum V. T. nec dies distinguit, vel diei, ceu cæteris sacratioris observatio est, nec mysterium in tempore ipso habet, sed tempus illud est, ad quod cultus Dei generatim mandatus ab Ecclesia Apostolico exemplo celebratur. Nam cultus Dei sine tempore obiri non potest. Neque tamen in tempore ipso mysterium vel sanctitas est, quæ cultum ipsum sanctificet. Quod verò idem dies resurrectionis Dominicæ memoriale factus est, κατὰ ζυμβεβηκὸς & secundario factum est, quia eodem die Christus è mortuis resurrexit. Neque etiam Christus nascendo, patiendo, resurgendo, in Cœlum ascendendo dies illos, quibus natus, passus est, resurrexit, in Cœlum ascendit, proprie consecravit. Aliàs omnia etiam loca & tempora, quibus docuit, vel miracula patravit, consecrasse dicendus fuerit. Sed consecratio rei alicujus mandatum & institutionem Divinam specialem requirit, uti analogia festorum V. T. ostendit. Nec ad eam qualiscunque sive loci, sive temporis connotatio sufficit, utpote quæ rerum omnium creatarum circumstantiæ sunt. Et quid hoc ad dies Nativitatis & Paschatis, quos præcisè eosdem esse, quibus Christus natus est, & resurrexit, minimè constat. S. Paulus porrò festinavit, ut die Pentecostes Hierosolymis esset, Actor. XX. 16. non ut festum illud cum Judæis, vel cum Christianis Christiano more necessariò celebraret, (nam nec Ἰουδαΐζειν voluit, nec Pentecostes festum Christianum jam tum viguit) sed ut occasione festi confluentibus ibi Judæis Evangelium prædicaret. Habent & Christiani Pascha suum, Christum, 1. Cor. V. 7. non externum & ceremoniale, de quo quæstio, sed spirituale, toto vitæ tempore celebrandum. Præterea nec abolenda festa sunt, si nulla iis sanctitas, significatio, mysterium inest. Cùm enim non dies, seu tempus, quo mysteria illa recoluntur, sed verbum Dei, quod illo tempore prædicatur, & cultus Dei, qui exercetur, nos de nativitate, passione, resurrectione, ascensione Christi admoneat, omnis illa significatio & mysterium non tempori, sed verbo Dei inerit. Non tamen propterea tempus ipsum prædicationi illi destinatum tolli necessariò debet. Quomodo non quia præceptor, non tempus discipulum erudit, iccirco nullum tempus, quo ille erudiatur, constitui debet. Sed & Patres dies festos sanctos, sacros, mysticos quandoque appellant, non per se, sed per accidens, respectu mysterii & cultus, qui eo tempore celebrari suevit. Denique fucus, non res est, quòd festa Sanctis consecrata Deo in Sanctis dicaverint. Nam sic dicarunt citra Dei institutionem & jussum, adeóque non sine ἐπιλοδηγοσεια. Et in festis illis
units.tr: CXLI. The props on which they try to sustain their superstition of festal days [ὀι ἐξ εὐαγγελίας, those from the Gospel] are far too weak. For that the Jews freely instituted certain festivals, such as Purim and the Feast of Dedication, is indisputable [ἀνεξαγώνιον]. And by the same reasoning the Christian Church too can freely institute and observe certain festivals, provided that the opinion of necessity, of mystery and of worship is absent, and idolatry too. The Lord's Day is no more a festival properly so called than the Sabbath of the Old Testament was; nor does it distinguish a day, nor is its observance holier than that of other days, nor does it have a mystery in the time itself; rather, it is that time at which the worship of God, commanded in general, is celebrated by the Church by apostolic example. For the worship of God cannot be performed without time. Nor, however, is there in the time itself any mystery or sanctity that sanctifies the worship itself. That the same day has become a memorial of the Lord's resurrection is by accident [κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς] and secondary, because on that same day Christ rose from the dead. Nor did Christ, by being born, suffering, rising and ascending into heaven, properly consecrate those days on which he was born, suffered, rose and ascended. Otherwise all the places and times in which he taught or worked miracles would have to be said to have been consecrated. But the consecration of anything requires a special Divine command and institution, as the analogy of the festivals of the Old Testament shows. Nor is any mere connotation of place or time sufficient for this, since these are the circumstances of all created things. And what has this to do with the days of Christmas and Easter, which it is by no means certain are exactly the days on which Christ was born and rose? Moreover, St Paul hastened to be at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, Acts 20:16; not so that he would necessarily keep that festival with the Jews, or with Christians in the Christian manner (for he wished neither to Judaize, nor did the Christian festival of Pentecost yet flourish), but so that, on the occasion of the festival, when Jews were gathering there, he might preach the Gospel. Christians too have their Passover, Christ, 1 Cor. 5:7; not an external and ceremonial one, which is the question here, but a spiritual one, to be celebrated through the whole time of life. Besides, festivals are not to be abolished if they have no holiness, significance or mystery in them. For since it is not the day or time on which those mysteries are recalled, but the Word of God preached at that time and the worship of God exercised, that reminds us of the nativity, passion, resurrection and ascension of Christ, all that significance and mystery lies in the Word of God, not in the time. Nevertheless, the time set aside for that preaching need not on that account necessarily be removed. Just as a teacher does not instruct a pupil by the time, yet no time need be fixed on which he is taught. Furthermore, the Fathers sometimes call festal days holy, sacred, mystical, not in themselves but incidentally, with respect to the mystery and worship which were customarily celebrated at that time. Finally, it is a pretence, not a reality, that they dedicated festivals to God in the saints, consecrating them to the saints. For they dedicated them thus without the institution and command of God, and therefore not without [ἐπιλοδηγοσεια, unwarranted leading]. And in those festivals

units.la: ipsos etiam Sanctos religiosè colunt & invocant, & quidem uti Bellarminus lib. III. 16. loquitur, ita ut honor festorum dierum immediatè & terminativè ad Sanctos pertineat, quæ profligata idololatria cùm sit, à Deo ratus & acceptus ille cultus esse non potest.
units.tr: They also religiously worship and invoke the saints themselves, and indeed, as Bellarminus says in lib. III. 16., in such a way that the honour of festal days pertains immediately and terminatively to the saints. Since that is plainly idolatry, the worship cannot be regarded as approved and accepted by God.

units.la: CXLII. Ad Precationem etiam Votum refertur. Nam & una eademque voce ἐυχὴς tum precatio, Jac. V. 15. tum votum, Act. XVIII. 18. XXI. 23. significatur. Est autem votum religiosa, spontanea & solennis promissio Deo legitimè dedito animo & firmo cordis proposito facta de re vel actu aliquo ad honorem ejusdem, & bonum proximi, vel voventis ipsius faciente. Hebraeis נדר appellatur, quod ευχλω fere semper, rarissimè ὁμολογίαν LXX. interpretantur. Graecorum autem ευχεσθαι tum sacris, tum profanis etiam authoribus tria communiter significat, optare, precari, vovere. Latinis verò votum vehemens voluntatis desiderium significat. Scriptura etiam ad ὅρκως juramenta refert. Quia juravit Jehovae, vovit Potenti Jacob, Psal. CXXXII. 2. Nam & in juramento quædam solennis promissio fit, adeóque votum Deo nuncupatur. Cúmque omne votum in timore Dei, ut sinceritatem amantis, & hypocrisin detestantis, concipiatur, juramenti rationem habet. Sicut porro in pœnitente propositum obedientiæ omnis, & glorificandi Deum in genere necessarium est: ita & votum. Vovete & reddite Jehovae Deo vestro; quicunque circa ipsum sunt, offerant munus timendo, Psal. LXXVI. 12. Nulla enim recta oratio sine voto est. Nam qui aliquid à Deo petit, etiam spondet, se Deum amaturum, ei gratias acturum, eum glorificaturum, ab eo se non recessurum, & eum omni honore culturum, maximè in charitate proximi. Deus hominum moribus συγκατάβασιν quadam se accommodans, sicut homines sibi aliquid mutuò dant, vel daturos se pollicentur: ita ipse hominibus tum dat, tum daturum se pollicetur beneficia corporalia & spiritualia; & vicissim patitur ab hominibus, & postulat interdum sibi aliquid dari, & per anathema sibi consecrari, vel in futurum etiam promitti: non quòd re ulla indigeat, ipse ἀντιέχεις, sed ad testificandam nostram ergo ipsum gratitudinem, & ad beneficia ab eodem impetranda.
units.tr: CXLII. A vow is also related to prayer. The one Greek word εὐχή [euchē] signifies both prayer (Jas. V. 15.) and vow (Acts XVIII. 18., XXI. 23.). A vow is a religious, voluntary and solemn promise made to God by a mind rightly disposed and a firm resolve of the heart, concerning some thing or act that tends to God's honour, or to the good of a neighbour, or of the one vowing. The Hebrews call it נדר [nedher], which the Seventy almost always render by εὐχή [euchē], and very rarely by ὁμολογία [homologia]. Among the Greeks, εὐχεσθαι [euchesthai], in both sacred and profane authors, commonly means three things: to wish, to pray, and to vow. For the Latins, votum means an intense desire of the will. Scripture also relates it to oaths [ὅρκους]: Because he swore to Jehovah, he vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob, Psal. CXXXII. 2. For in an oath too a solemn promise is made, and so an oath is also called a vow to God. Since every vow is conceived in the fear of God, as the lover of sincerity and the hater of hypocrisy, it has the character of an oath. Just as a purpose of obedience to all of God's commands, and of glorifying God in general, is necessary in the penitent, so too is a vow. Vow and pay to Jehovah your God; let all who are around him bring gifts in fear, Psal. LXXVI. 12. For no right prayer is without a vow. Whoever asks something of God also promises that he will love God, give him thanks, glorify him, not turn away from him, and worship him with all honour, above all in love of neighbour. God, condescending [συγκατάβασις, synkatabasis] to human ways, just as men lend each other things or promise to give them, himself both gives and promises to give bodily and spiritual benefits to men; and in turn he suffers things from men, and sometimes demands that something be given to him, or be consecrated to him under anathema, or even promised for the future. This is not because he needs anything, being in want of nothing [ἀνενδεής], but to bear witness to our gratitude to him, and to obtain benefits from him.

units.la: CXLIII. Votum vel generale & commune, vel singulare & proprium est. Generale, quo nos nosstraque omnia Deo ejúsque cultui vovemus & devovemus. Tale Jacobi illud fuit: Si Deus mecum fuerit, méque in itinere isto servaverit והיה יהוה לי לאלהים & erit mihi Jehova in Deum, Genes. XXVIII. 20. 21. Simile omnium Christianorum in Baptismo nuncupatum, & in Coena Domini frequentatum votum est, frustra tricantibus Pontificiis, non esse hoc votum, quia in Baptismo spondeatur id, quod debitum & necessarium est. Nam & Jacobo necessarium fuit, ut Dominum pro Deo suo haberet. Singulare & proprium est, quo singulare quid singulariter Deo vovemus sanctéque promittimus; sive ob accepta à Deo beneficia, sive ad impetranda illa. Ejusmodi vota plura ab Israelitis sub lege Mosis Deo nuncupabantur. Inprimis Nazirætus votum, cujus modum & ritum Deus ipse præscripsit. Et de suis bonis ad cultum, sacrificia inprimis, singuli vovevovere poterant. Ejusmodi vota duum generum erant, puta נדר votum simpliciter, in quo res devota redimi potuit, & חרם anathema, in quo rem devotam redimere nefas fuit, de quo in loco. Vota ejusmodi singularia etiam in N. T. licita sunt; frustra nonnullis fastidio & odio votorum Pontificiorum in dubium revocantibus. Nam in omni oratione & juramento votum quodammodo implicari jam diximus. Et perpetuum illud Dei mandatum est: Vovete, & reddite Jehovæ Deo vestro, Psal. LXXVI. 12. Et Christiani omnes se ipsos Deo offerre vivam hostiam, sanctam &c. tenentur, Rom. XII. 1. Sive etiam sermo est de moralibus officiis, velut de observantia mandatorum Dei, & fuga peccatorum, ea voventur in Baptismo & S. Cœna, & extra illa etiam voveri possunt: sive de exercitiis corporalibus: velut de jejunio, eleemosyna, &c. solenniter illa promitti ad Dei honorem & charitatem proximi facit: sive de facto aliquo, velut consecratione sui vel suorum ad peculiare ministerium Ecclesiæ, etiam illud ad honorem Dei & Ecclesiæ utilitatem facere, adeóque voveri potest. Absit modò superstitio, opinio cultus & meriti; & Christiana libertas constet, cunctáque ad veram fidem, pœnitentiam, sobrietatem, charitatem aliásque virtutes Christianas alendas ex serio pii Deóque devoti animi proposito dirigantur. Neque obstat, quòd ex necessitate Divini præcepti cuncta nostra Deo debemus, quia etiam socordia nostra ad debitum illud promptiús solvendum excitari debet. Præterea nec libertati voventis necessitas præcepti, sed sola vis & coactio officit. Et ne periculo se voventes exponant, tum prudentia, quæ cautionem voventibus præscribit, tum pietas, quæ fidem fallere vetat, efficit. Ac licet etiam vota specialia, quatenus Legis ceremonialis appendices sunt, per Christum abrogata sint, nullaque propterea de iis præceptio in N. T. extet: quatenus tamen juris naturalis, & vincula quædam, quibus omnes homines ad opera moralia Deo naturaliter & per se debita arctiús adstringuntur, sunt, non minùs nobis, quàm Patribus ante Legem de iis latam, licita sunt.
units.tr: CXLIII. A vow is either general and common, or singular and proper. A general vow is one by which we vow and dedicate ourselves and all that is ours to God and his worship. Such was Jacob's: If God will be with me and keep me on this journey, והיה יהוה לי לאלהים [vehayah YHWH li le'elohim], then Jehovah shall be my God, Gen. XXVIII. 20. 21. A similar vow of all Christians, made at Baptism and repeated at the Lord's Supper, is not idle, though the Papists wrongly object that it is not a vow, because in Baptism what is due and necessary is promised. For Jacob too needed to have the Lord as his God. A singular and proper vow is one by which we vow something particular to God in a particular way and promise it solemnly, either because of benefits received from God or to obtain them. Under the law of Moses the Israelites made many vows of this kind to God. Above all, the vow of the Nazirite, whose manner and rite God himself prescribed. Each person could also vow some of his goods to the worship of God, especially sacrifices. Vows of this kind were of two sorts: נדר [nedher], a vow simply made, in which the devoted thing could be redeemed; and חרם [kherem], a ban, in which it was unlawful to redeem the devoted thing, as will be discussed in its place. Singular vows of this kind are also lawful in the New Testament, though some call them into question in vain out of distaste and hatred for the vows of the Papists. For we have already said that a vow is in some way bound up in every prayer and oath. And there is the perpetual command of God: Vow, and pay to Jehovah your God, Psal. LXXVI. 12. And all Christians are bound to offer themselves to God as a living sacrifice, holy, etc., Rom. XII. 1. Whether the matter is moral duties, such as keeping God's commandments and fleeing sin, which are vowed at Baptism and the Lord's Supper and may also be vowed outside those occasions; or bodily exercises, such as fasting or almsgiving, which one makes it a solemn promise to perform for God's honour and love of neighbour; or some deed, such as consecrating oneself or one's own to the particular ministry of the Church, which also serves God's honour and the Church's benefit, and so may be vowed. Provided only that superstition, the notion of worship and merit, is absent, and Christian liberty is preserved, and all things are directed by a serious purpose of a pious and God-devoted mind toward nourishing true faith, repentance, sobriety, love and the other Christian virtues. Nor does it stand in the way that we owe God everything by the necessity of a divine precept, because even our laziness ought to be roused to pay that debt more readily. Moreover, the necessity of a precept does not hinder the freedom of the one vowing; only force and compulsion do. And prudence, which prescribes caution to those who vow, and piety, which forbids breaking faith, keep those who vow from exposing themselves to danger. And although special vows, insofar as they are appendages of the ceremonial law, have been abrogated through Christ, and there is therefore no precept about them in the New Testament, nevertheless, insofar as they belong to natural law and are certain bonds by which all men are more tightly bound to the moral works that are due to God by nature and in themselves, they are lawful for us no less than they were for the Fathers before the Law, of whom they were required.

units.la: CXLIV. Vovendum soli Deo est. Nam
units.tr: CXLIV. A vow is to be made to God alone. For

units.la: quæ orationis, eadem voti ratio est. Si voveris votum Jehovæ Deo tuo, Deut. XXIII. 21. Vovete & solvite Jehovæ Deo vestro, Psal. LXXVI. 12. Solus verò Jehova Deus noster est. Cùm voveris votum Deo, ne tardes illud solvere, Eccles. V. 3. In voto enim tum spontanea & ingenua voluntas Deo serviendi: tum invocatio ejus cui vovetur, est. Et omnipotens atque omniscius esse debet, cui aliquid vovetur. Nam & voventis cor scire, & potestatem habere vindicandi transgressionem debet: Hinc ipse Thomas 2. 2. q. 88. a. 5. Votum esse actum latriæ, sive religionis proprie, asserit. Cùm tamen Sanctis & Cœnobiarchis voveri in Papatu, viderit, ad inane κενοφωνίαν se convertit, ajens, promissionem Sanctis factam sub votum cadere tantùm materialiter, quia homo vovet Deo se impleturum, quod Sanctis promisit. Quod non est Sanctis vovere, quod illi faciunt, sed in Sanctorum gratiam aliquid vovere. Non enim sic Sancti Deo in voti objecto, sed in materia junguntur, quomodo & alii homines superstitites jungi possunt. Ideo Cajetanus in Thom. 2. 2. q. 88. a. 5. eadem ratione Deo & Sanctis fieri vota asserit, addita ratione, quòd considerentur Sancti, uti sunt Dii participative, & in iis Deus honoretur. Cui sententiæ Bellarminus de Monach. c. 14. calculum suum his verbis adjicit. Vota verè fiunt Sanctis, sed ut sancti sunt, id est, ut excellentissimo modo participant Dei naturam & gloriam. Sed sic votum nuncuparetur Deo, & impleretur in persona Sancti, non autem Sancto proprie. Sed ille vota Sanctis proprie & formaliter nuncupari, & ad eos, ceu terminum referri, statuit, & ut idololatriæ maculam diluat, de Sanct. Beat. lib. III. 9. respondet, non eadem ratione fieri votum Deo & Sanctis. Nam Deo promitti in signum gratitudinis erga primum principium, & proinde illam promissionem esse actum latriæ; at Sanctis promitti in signum gratitudinis erga Mediatores & Intercessores, per quos à Deo beneficia accipimus. Quæ ratio si valeret, etiam proprie dictum sacrificium Sanctis formaliter, & tanquam proprio termino, offerri posset; quod illi negant. Verùm voti æquè atque sacrificii hæc forma est, ut nulli alii, quàm primo principio offerri possit; ita ut vovere proprie & formaliter, sed non tanquam Deo, vel primæ causæ, sit contradictio in adjecto, quasi quis diceret, vovere proprie, & non vovere proprie. Idem Bellarminus ingenuè fatetur; In Scriptura nomen voti semper pro promissione Deo facta accipi, addita ratione, quòd cùm scriberentur Scriptura, nondum cœperit usus vovendi Sanctis. Cujus confessionis cùm puderet alios, repererunt illi, quod pueri in faba. Nam abusi errore Codicum quorundam Vulgatæ versionis, qui Prov. XX. 25. legunt: Ruina est homini devotare Sanctos, & post vota retractare. Hic ergo vota Sanctis nuncupata ostendunt. Sed vitiosam lectionem Papæ Sixtus IV. & Clemens VIII. in nova Bibliorum editione correxerunt; pro barbaro devotare scribentes devorare. Nam in Hebraeo קדש יהוה devorare, deglutire sanctificatum, non devotare, seu votum Sanctis nuncupare significat.
units.tr: The reasoning for a vow is the same as for prayer. "When you make a vow to Jehovah your God" (Deut. 23:21). "Make vows to Jehovah your God and fulfil them" (Ps. 76:12). Jehovah God alone is ours. "When you make a vow to God, do not delay to pay it" (Eccl. 5:3). For a vow includes both a free and sincere will to serve God and an invocation of the one to whom the vow is made. The one to whom anything is vowed must also be almighty and omniscient, for he must know the heart of the one who vows and have the power to avenge a breach. Hence Thomas himself (2.2 q. 88 a. 5) asserts that a vow is an act of latria, or religion properly so called. Yet when he saw that vows were being made to saints and abbots in the papacy, he turned to empty talk, saying that a promise made to the saints falls under a vow only materially, because a man vows to God that he will fulfil what he promised to the saints. On this view, one does not vow to the saints what they do, but vows something for the saints' benefit. For the saints are not joined to God as the object of the vow, but only as its matter, in the way that other men, even superstitious ones, may be joined. Therefore Cajetan (on Thomas 2.2 q. 88 a. 5) asserts that vows are made to God and the saints for the same reason, adding the ground that the saints are considered as they are gods by participation and that God is honoured in them. Bellarmine adds his own verdict to this opinion in these words (De monachis c. 14): "Vows are truly made to the saints, but as they are saints, that is, as they participate in the nature and glory of God in the most excellent way." But on this view a vow would be declared to God and fulfilled in the person of a saint, and not properly made to the saint. Yet Bellarmine (De sanctorum beatitudine III. 9) lays down that vows are properly and formally declared to the saints and referred to them as their terminus, and to wipe away the stain of idolatry he answers that a vow is not made to God and the saints for the same reason. For a promise is made to God as a sign of gratitude toward the first principle, and so that promise is an act of latria; but a promise is made to the saints as a sign of gratitude toward the mediators and intercessors through whom we receive benefits from God. If this reasoning held, a sacrifice properly so called could also be formally offered to the saints, as to their proper terminus, and they deny this. But the form of a vow, just as of a sacrifice, is that it can be offered to no one but the first principle. So to vow "properly and formally," yet not "as to God" or the first cause, is a contradiction in terms, as if someone said to vow properly and not to vow properly. Bellarmine himself frankly admits the same: "In Scripture the name of vow is always taken for a promise made to God," adding the reason that when Scripture was written the practice of vowing to saints had not yet begun. Since others were ashamed of this confession, they found what boys find in a bean. For, through the error of some codices of the Vulgate version, which at Prov. 20:25 read, "It is a ruin for a man to devote the saints and afterwards to reconsider the vows," they show vows made to saints. But the Papal editors Sixtus IV and Clement VIII corrected this faulty reading in the new edition of the Bible, writing devorare ("to devour") for the barbarous devotare ("to devote"). For in the Hebrew קדש יהוה [qadash Yahweh] means "to devour, to swallow up what is sanctified," not "to devote," that is, to declare a vow to the saints.

units.la: CXLV. Vota nonnisi legitima Deo placent. Ut verò legitima sint, temeritas, præcipitatio & inconsideratio vitanda est; ne temerè, inconsultò, præpropere nimis, sed ut prudenter & maturo cum judicio & consilio nuncupentur; & nuncupaturus se ipsum, & quid sibi datum sit, probè consideret, non sibi confidat, sed se suspensum habeat, precibus invigilet, ut augeantur sibi dona Dei & vires, quibus Deo grata peragere possit. Satius enim est non vovere, quàm voto semel nuncupato animo angi, & in prompta exsolutione voti ancipitem animi hærere. Aurea illa Sapientis regula est; quam voventes præ oculis semper habeant oportet: Cùm voveris votum Deo, ne tardes illud solvere. Non enim voluptas in stultis est. Quod voveris, solve. Melius est, ut non voveas, quàm ut voveas & non solvas. Ne des os tuum ad peccati ream faciendam carnem tuam; neque dicas coram Angelo, quòd error sit. Cur Deus effervescere ob vocem tuam, & corrumperet opus manuum tuarum? Nam ut plurimùm somnia, & vanitates, & verba multa. Nam Deum time. Eccl. V. 3–7. Non quivis igitur ad vota specialia (alia enim generalis ratio est) prosiliere, vel admitti debent. Vovendum soli Deo, non ulli homini est. Vota nonnisi legitima Deo placent, & qualia legitima sint, exponitur. bent, non pueri, mares, vel fœminæ, quia inconsulta & imprudens adolescentia est: non mulieres, maritis insciis, Num. XXX. 6. non servi heris insciis; sed soli, qui vota, eorumque indolem & officia probè discernere & dijudicare valent, & potestati alienæ, cujus est conscientiam voti habere, non subsunt. Impiè profin Pontificii impuberes pœne ad emittenda vota Monastica admittunt, imò, cauponantes animas, alliciunt; quorum pondus, momentum, & persolvendi difficultatem, judicio & ætate deficiente, pensitare nequeunt. Ac ne adultiores quidem & sapientes omnes vovere tenentur. Nam si desieris vovere, non erit in te peccatum, Deut. XXIII. 22. Sed ii demum vovere possunt, qui vel cum calamitate præsente conflictantur, & Divinæ gratiæ & præsidii ad vincendam eam sensu destituuntur, ad corroborandam fidem gratiæ: vel à gravissimo malo liberati, vel maximo bono mactati sunt; pro quo religiosa boni pollicitatione gratitudo erga Deum testanda est.
units.tr: CXLV. Only lawful vows please God. For vows to be lawful, rashness, haste and thoughtlessness must be avoided: they must not be made rashly, carelessly or too hastily, but prudently, with mature judgment and deliberation. The one who is about to make a vow must consider carefully both himself and what has been given to him. He must not trust in himself but keep himself in suspense, and watch in prayer that the gifts and strength of God may be increased in him, so that he may be able to do what is pleasing to God. For it is better not to vow than, once a vow has been spoken, to be troubled in mind and to hang in doubt about the ready performance of the vow. That golden rule of the Wise Man is one that those who vow must always keep before their eyes: "When you make a vow to God, do not delay to pay it. For there is no pleasure in fools. Pay what you have vowed. It is better that you not vow than that you vow and not pay. Do not let your mouth bring your flesh into sin, and do not say before the angel that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands? For in most cases dreams, vanities and many words come; but fear God" (Eccl. 5:3–7). Therefore not everyone should rush into special vows (for the general reason is different), nor should they be admitted to them. A vow is to be made to God alone, not to any man. Only lawful vows please God, and what makes a vow lawful is set out here. Children, males or females, should not be admitted to vows, because youth is unadvised and imprudent. Nor should wives make vows without the knowledge of their husbands (Num. 30:6), nor servants without the knowledge of their masters. Only those who are able to judge and distinguish properly what a vow is, its nature and its duties, and who are not subject to another's authority, which has the right to know of the vow, should make vows. The Papists impiously allow even those below puberty to take monastic vows; indeed, bargaining for souls, they entice them, though these children cannot weigh the burden, the gravity and the difficulty of fulfilling such vows, their judgment and age being deficient. Nor are all adults and wise men bound to vow. For "if you refrain from vowing, there will be no sin in you" (Deut. 23:22). Those alone can vow who are struggling with a present calamity and lack a sense of divine grace and help to overcome it, in order to strengthen faith in grace; or who have been freed from some very grave evil or have been blessed with some very great good, and for which religious gratitude toward God is to be shown by a pledge of good.

units.la: CXLVI. Neque etiam quidvis voveri potest.
units.tr: CXLVI. Nor can just anything be vowed.

units.la: Certè non mala, & cum lege Dei pugnantia, vel in potestate nostra non posita. Nam Deo non est beneplacitum in stultis, Eccles. V. 3. imò stolidis, qui sibi confidunt, Prov. XXVIII. 26. qui vovent, quod præstare suæ potestatis non est; quod levicu-lum, stultum, ridiculum, imò malum & periculosum est; quod pro cultu eligunt, cum opinione meriti, & superba professione, in quo inutiliter occupantur; & quo se ab officio debito abstrahunt. Non enim vinculum, quo Divinæ legi homo obligatur, vovendo rumpere licet, quod esset se ipsum sibi Deum facere. Etiam stultitia est, promittere quædam fidentius & levius, quàm petere gratiam humiliùs, quia hoc est gloriationis & præsumptionis, quæ mala est, Jac. IV. 16. Ejusdem enim vota nec Deo placent, & nuncupata temerè non servanda, sed fideli pœnitudine expianda sunt. Neque etiam indifferentia, nec bona nec mala, per se & propter se vovere licet. Nam Deo vovere non bona, qualia cuculla sunt, habitus, tonsura, habitatio, certum opus, nec in genere, nec in specie præceptum, regula, &c. Deum subsannare est. Et votum semper est de re meliori, quàm ejus oppositum est. At res indifferens re sibi oppositia melior esse non potest. Sed vovenda in universum sunt, quæ ad Dei honorem, & proximi nostramque salutem faciunt. Talia verò sunt, quæ lege Dei, saltem generali, præcepta sunt, & in quibus Deum habere beneplacitum posse, certò persuasi sumus. Exempli causa. Lex generalis Deum colere, & proximum ex opibus suis sublevare jubet: Sed modus ejus rei definitus non est, quia alias charitatis ingenuitas explorari, 2. Cor. VIII. 8. non potuisset. Hic genuina charitas determinat, se velle decimas dare, & sibi hanc veluti legem imponens, firmúmque animi propositum concipiens, decimas sanctificat, & suopte judicio damnationem mendacis & sacrilegi, si promissa fefellerit, subit. Ita vovens secundum legem generalem propósito suo actum ex se indifferentem & quodammodo liberum, determinatum & necessarium facit. Ergo voti ma-
units.tr: Certainly not evil things, nor things contrary to the law of God, nor things not within our power. For "God is not pleased with fools" (Eccles. 5.3), indeed with foolish men who trust in themselves (Prov. 28.26), who vow what is not within their power to perform. Such vows are trivial, foolish and ridiculous, indeed evil and dangerous. Men choose them as a form of worship, with the notion of merit and a proud profession, and in them they are uselessly occupied, and by them they draw themselves away from the duty they owe. For a man may not break by vowing the bond by which he is bound to the divine law, since that would be to make himself a god to himself. It is also folly to promise certain things more confidently and lightly than to ask for grace more humbly, because this belongs to boasting and presumption, which is evil (Jas. 4.16). Such vows are displeasing to God, and vows made rashly are not to be kept but expiated by faithful repentance. Nor may we vow things that are indifferent, neither good nor evil, in themselves and for their own sake. To vow to God things that are not good, such as hoods, habits, tonsure, a dwelling, a particular work not commanded either in kind or in species, a rule, and the like, is to mock God. A vow is always about something better than its opposite, but an indifferent thing cannot be better than the thing opposed to it. Rather, the things to be vowed in general are those which serve the honour of God and the salvation of our neighbour and of ourselves. These are the things which are commanded by the law of God, at least in general, and in which we are firmly persuaded that God can take pleasure. For example, the general law bids us worship God and relieve our neighbour from our wealth. But the manner of this is not defined, since otherwise the genuineness of charity could not be tested (2 Cor. 8.8). Here genuine charity determines that it wishes to give tithes; imposing this on itself as a kind of law, and conceiving a firm purpose of mind, it sanctifies the tithes, and by its own judgement incurs the condemnation of a liar and a sacrilegious person if it fails the promise. Thus by vowing in accordance with the general law, one makes by one's purpose an act that is in itself indifferent and in some sense free, determined and necessary. Therefore the subject-matter of a vow

units.la: teria non alia esse potest, quàm res præcepta, vel in specie, vel saltem in genere & ex certa causa, quatenus illa per gratiam Dei absque speciali privilegio præstari & impleri potest. Talis est promissio ambulandi in præceptis Dei, desistendi à vitiis, eleemosynam dandi, fidem conjugalem obstringendi, jejunium & abstinentiam ad preces, vel edomandam carnem suf-cipiendi. In V. T. erat locus spontaneis oblationibus, quæ ut exercitia fidei, in genere præcepta erant. In N. T. iis locus non est, sed solis sacrificiis justitiæ, ideóque & horum votis. Et talia vovenda sunt cum Christiana modestia, ut præsens cordis propositum sincerum declarent. Dei autem subsidium in futurum enixo suspirio petant.
units.tr: can be nothing other than a thing commanded, either in species or at least in genus and for a certain cause, insofar as it can be performed and fulfilled through the grace of God without any special privilege. Such is the promise to walk in the commandments of God, to desist from vices, to give alms, to bind oneself to conjugal faithfulness, to undertake fasting and abstinence for prayer or for subduing the flesh. Under the Old Testament there was room for spontaneous offerings, which, being exercises of faith, were commanded in genus. Under the New Testament there is no room for these, but only for the sacrifices of righteousness, and therefore for vows of these. Such things are to be vowed with Christian modesty, so that they declare the present sincere purpose of the heart; but for help from God in the future, they should seek it with a fervent sigh.

units.la: CXLVII. Impiè Bellarminus de Mon. lib. II. 19. Thomæ Aquinati suffragatus, ut Baptismi votum oppugnet, negat, ullo modo necessarium, vel utile admodum esse de iis rebus, quæ in præcepto sunt, vota nuncupare. Præterquam enim, quòd sic omnia vota, in quibus ipsi tamen religionum suarum proram & pupim collocant, tollit, cùm in religione nihil non à Deo vel generaliter, vel specialiter præceptum facere, adeóque nec faciendum vovere liceat; etiam enervat sanctum pietatis propositum in Christianis, & negat utile vel necessarium esse, nos ipsos Deo hostiam vivam offerre, Rom. XII. 1. Ideo etiam Gregorius de Valentia oppositam Thomæ sententiam scandalosum errorem in Ecclesia appellare non veretur. Neque enim obstat, quòd vota נדבות spontanea, Deut. XXIII. 23. esse debent, & de re indebita vulgò censentur, & de iisdem lex dicit: Si desieris vovere, non erit in te peccatum, ib. v. 22. cùm non facientes præcepta Dei peccent. Sed hæc cum grano salis accipienda sunt. Nam simpliciter Deo gratum indebitum nihil est; & omnis obedientia spontanea, atque voluntati & præceptis Dei conformis esse debet; & peccant, qui vota omittunt, quæ circumstantiæ postulare videntur. Sunt ergo vota in materia indebita ratione supervenientis obligationis, quæ per illa obligationi rerum præceptarum accedit; & ratione determinationis præcepti generalis in re indebita per se, at debita ratione circumstantiæ & singularis causæ, per quas generale præceptum à vovente sic determinatur, ut ex actu libero & indifferente necessarius & debitus reddatur. Non ergo juxta illa Deut. XXIII. 22. peccant, rem sive in genere, sive in specie præceptam non voventes, nisi id circumstantiæ & prægnantes causæ; cujusmodi excitatio socordiæ, memoriæ officii nostri refricatio, malorum singularium averruncatio, bonorum provocatio, gratitudinis Deo præstandæ necessitas sunt, postulent. Hæ verò ubi vota postulant, tum verò non tam obligationis novatio, uti Bellarminus asserit, quàm justæ obligationis voluntaria accessio per ejus agnitionem & receptionem promptiorem fit. Pluribus enim vinculis ad cognoscendum & præstandum id, ad quod semel obligati sumus, nos constringi nihil vetat. Etsi ergo Divino & naturali jure Deo honorem, cultum, reverentiam & obsequium debemus; possumus nihilominus ad illud præstandum novo vinculo ad id nos ipsos adstringere, cùm singulares causæ id poscunt. Filum enim triplicatum simplici fortius est. Atque id etiam in civilibus contractibus obtinet, in quibus ad majorem rei confirmationem, pluribus vinculis ad praestandum aliquid haud raro homines se obligant.
units.tr: CXLVII. Bellarmine impiously, following Thomas Aquinas in attacking baptismal vows, denies that it is in any way necessary or very useful to make vows concerning things that are commanded (De Monachis, II. 19). For apart from the fact that in this way he removes all those vows in which men nevertheless place the prow and stern of their religious orders, since in religion nothing is commanded by God either generally or specially, and so it is not lawful even to vow what is to be done, he also weakens the holy purpose of piety among Christians, and denies that it is useful or necessary for us to offer ourselves to God as a living sacrifice (Rom. 12.1). Hence Gregory of Valencia does not hesitate to call the opinion opposed to Thomas's "a scandalous error in the Church." For it is no obstacle that vows must be נדבות [nedaboth], spontaneous (Deut. 23.23), and are commonly held to concern something not owed, and that the law says of them: "If you cease to vow, there will be no sin in you" (ibid. v. 22), since those who do not do what God commands do sin. But these words must be taken with a grain of salt. For nothing undue is simply pleasing to God; all spontaneous obedience ought to be conformed to the will and precepts of God; and those sin who omit the vows which circumstances seem to require. Vows therefore concern matter that is not owed, by reason of the obligation that supervenes, which through the vow is added to the obligation of things commanded; and by reason of the determination of a general precept concerning a thing not owed in itself but owed by reason of circumstance and a particular cause, by which the general precept is so determined by the one vowing that from a free and indifferent act it becomes necessary and owed. Therefore those who do not vow a thing commanded, either in genus or in species, do not sin according to Deut. 23.22, unless circumstances and pressing causes demand it: such as the arousing of sloth, the refreshing of the memory of our duty, the averting of particular evils, the provoking of goods, and the necessity of rendering gratitude to God. But where these demand vows, the vow is not so much a renewal of obligation, as Bellarmine asserts, but a voluntary addition of a just obligation, which comes about through its acknowledgement and more ready acceptance. For nothing forbids us being bound by several bonds to know and to perform what we were once obliged to. Thus, although by divine and natural right we owe God honour, worship, reverence and obedience, we can nevertheless bind ourselves to perform it by a new bond, when particular causes require it. For a threefold cord is stronger than a single one. And this holds also in civil contracts, in which, for the greater confirmation of a matter, men not infrequently bind themselves by several bonds to do something.

units.la: CXLVIII. Vota semel legitimè nuncupata religiosè & sine cunctatione exsolvi debent. Cùm votum voveris Jehovæ Deo tuo לא תאחר לשלמו non differes solvere illud ei,quia requirendo requiret illud Jehova Deus tuus à te,& erit in te peccatum,Deut.XXIII. 21. Solve Altissimo vota tua,Psal. L. 14. Cùm voveris votum, non differes solvere illud,Eccles. V. 3. Ubi Solomon praeceptum vota sine mora solvendi pluribus argumentis confirmat. Cujusmodi sunt, quòd voluptas Dei non fit in stultis, v. 3. quales sunt, qui non serió vovent, & cùm voverunt, irritam fidem suam faciunt.1. Tim. V. 12. quòd melius (minus peccatum,& minor poena) sit non vovere, omittere bonum aliquod, vel non tam ardentem esse in bono opere quàm possis,cùm in voto accedat praesumptio, legis dictio & veniae renuntiatio,v. 4. quòd os suum dans,concipiens praepropere vovendi decretum, & velut apud se promulgans, carnem suam peccati ream faciat, citò & crebrò vovendo & cunctanter solvendo,facilè corpus suum poenae subjiciat, & pronitatem carnis ad malum irritet,in tentationes se praecipitet,& differens solutionem voti ansam sibi διαλογισμῶν καὶ γογυσμῶν ratiocinationum & murmurationum det, v. 5. quòd frustra coram Angelo, custode vitae,castigationisDei ministro,& teste obsequii & patientiae in ea castigatione , dicturus fit כי רמו quòd erratum fit, nequicam infirmitatem & ignorantiam obtendens, cùm semel se innodaverit,illud,quòd Deus se non solventibus vota irasciturus ob vocem voventis,& destructurus fit opus manuum ejus, non habiturus pro insonte, qui nomen ejus temerè usurpaverit, ibid. quòd vota ob vanas spes,& vanos metus concepta non aliud sint quàm multitudo somniorum, vanitates & verba multa, v. 6. quòd denique Deus timendus, adeóque non temerè ejus nomen vovendo usurpandum sit, & cùm rite vovimus,votum Deo ipsi nuncupatum, timore ejusdem promptè exsolvendum sit, ibid.
units.tr: CXLVIII. Vows once lawfully made must be paid religiously and without hesitation. When you make a vow to the LORD your God, you shall not delay to pay it, for the LORD your God will surely require it of you, and it will be sin in you (Deut. 23.21) [לא תאחר לשלמו]. Pay your vows to the Most High (Ps. 50.14). When you vow a vow, do not delay to pay it (Eccles. 5.3). Here Solomon confirms by several arguments the precept that vows must be paid without delay. Such are these: that the pleasure of God is not in fools (v. 3), such as those who do not vow seriously, and when they have vowed, make their faith void (1 Tim. 5.12); that it is better (less sin and less punishment) not to vow, and to omit some good, or not to be as fervent in a good work as you could, since in a vow there is added presumption, a dictating of the law and a renunciation of pardon (v. 4); that by giving his mouth, conceiving hastily a decree of vowing and as it were promulgating it to himself, one makes his flesh guilty of sin; by vowing quickly and often and paying hesitantly, he easily subjects his body to punishment, provokes the proneness of the flesh to evil, throws himself into temptations, and by deferring the payment of the vow gives himself occasion for [διαλογισμῶν καὶ γογυσμῶν] reasonings and murmurings (v. 5); that he will say in vain before the angel, the guardian of life, the minister of God's chastisement and the witness of obedience and patience under that chastisement, [כי רמו] "that it was an error," pleading weakness and ignorance, since once he has bound himself, God, being about to be angry at the voice of the one vowing and to destroy the work of his hands, will not hold him guiltless who has rashly used his name (ibid.); that vows made from vain hopes and vain fears are nothing else than a multitude of dreams, vanities and many words (v. 6); and finally that God is to be feared, and therefore his name is not to be rashly used in vowing, and when we have vowed properly, the vow made to God himself is to be promptly paid out of fear of him (ibid.).

units.la: CXLIX. Sed vota tamen honori Dei vel saluti nostrae & proximi derogantia exsolvi non debent,quia legitima non sunt. Peccat sic vovens,sed votum non reddens,& errorem deplorans, poenitentiam agit. Etiam differri solutio voti potest, si expedita solutione majus bonum,vel praestatio officii melioris impediatur. Nam & Rechabitas voventes, quòd domos pro habitatione aedificaturi non sint, voti violati reos Deus non peregit, quando ascendente Hierosolymam Nebucadnezare, in urbem Hierosolymam vitae confervandae gratiâ, se contulerunt,& in ea habitarunt ad tempus, Jerem. XXXV. 5. 10. 11. Pari ratione si nostra & proximi salus,& honor Dei inprimis postulaverit, à solutione voti ad tempus abstinere fas piúmque est.
