Omnia enim de rebus futuris inprimis,quae in potestate nostra non sunt, vota conditionata sunt,& conditionem vel expressam, ( uti pleraque veterum voventium exempla docent) vel tacitam innexam implicatámque habent. Pietatis enim & amoris Dei & proximi adminicula, non impedimenta esse debent. Deus misericordiam, non sacrificium vult; & plus pietate & charitate, quàm donariis & anathematis delectatur.
units.tr: CXLIX. Vows, however, that detract from the honour of God or from our own salvation or our neighbour's should not be paid, because they are not lawful. Whoever makes such a vow sins; but if he does not fulfil it, and laments his error, he does penance. The payment of a vow may also be deferred if paying it at once would hinder a greater good or the performance of a better duty. Thus the Rechabites, who vowed that they would not build houses for dwelling, were not held by God to be guilty of breaking the vow when Nebuchadnezzar came up against Jerusalem, and they went into the city to preserve their lives and lived there for a time (Jer. 35:5, 10, 11). By the same reasoning, if our salvation and the honour of God above all demand it, it is right and lawful to refrain for a time from paying a vow. For all vows concerning future things, especially those that are not in our power, are conditional, and contain a condition, either expressed (as most examples of ancient vowers show) or tacit, bound up and implied in them. For the aids of piety and of the love of God and neighbour ought to be aids, not hindrances. God desires mercy, not sacrifice, and he delights more in piety and charity than in gifts and offerings.

units.la: CL. Iniquè verò Papa Romanus jus & potestatem vota pro arbitrio suo recipiendi, confirmandi & dissolvendi rapturit. Nam vota vel legitima sunt,vel non sunt. Quae legitima sunt, nec confirmatione humana indigent, cùm in verbo Dei, & judice Deo, ad conscientiam hominis satis confirmata sint,nec dissolvi fine impietate & injuria adversus Deum & praeceptum ejus , nec non Antichristiana supra Deum ἐπάρσῃ elatione, possunt. Quae illegitima sunt, in iis vel impossibile, vel legi Dei repugnans aliquid votum vel devotum est. Impossibile promissum ipso jure & facto nullum est. Non ergo alio, qui dissolvat opus est, quàm propria voventis conscientia , qui si hac in re sibi suffenus sit; & Deo fucum facere instituat, Deum impietatis & fraudis suae vindicem habebit. Neque proin humana in terris ad dissolvenda ejusmodi vota potestas vel authoritas, sed sola doctrina & institutio ex Dei verbo requiritur. Si quid legi Dei repugnans homo vovit , sola etiam voventis conscientia rectiora edocta cum dolore & poenitentia conjuncta ad solvendum à voti nexu,qui in tali voto proprie nullus est,sufficit. Si denique votum προπετῶς praecipitanter & inconsultò , imò etiam in metu à Deo ipso, vel homine etiam, sed ex justa causa, incusso, nec non in perturbatione tali,quae usum rationis reliquit ; in re tamen nec impossibili, nec mala, omissum est, timor Dei solus , cui votum tale nuncupatum est, ejusdem observantiam flagitat. Habitabit in monte sanctitatis tuae נשבע להרע ולא ימיר qui juravit ad malum (cum malo & incommodo jurantis conjunctum) & non mutat.Psal.XV.4.
units.tr: CL. The Roman Pope, however, unjustly seizes the right and power of receiving, confirming and dissolving vows at his own discretion. For vows are either lawful or not. Those that are lawful need no human confirmation, since in God's Word, and before God as judge, they are sufficiently confirmed to a man's conscience; nor can they be dissolved without impiety and injury against God and his command, and without Antichristian arrogance [ἐπάρσῃ] elation above God. Those that are unlawful are vows or devotions of something either impossible or repugnant to the law of God. An impossible promise is null by law and in fact. No one else is therefore needed to dissolve it except the conscience of the one who vowed it; if he is over-confident in this matter and sets out to deceive God, he will have God as the avenger of his impiety and fraud. Nor, therefore, is any human power or authority on earth required to dissolve such vows, but only the teaching and instruction of God's Word. If a man has vowed something repugnant to the law of God, the conscience of the vower alone, once more rightly taught, joined with sorrow and repentance, suffices to release him from the bond of the vow, which in such a case is properly no bond at all. Finally, if a vow was made rashly [προπετῶς] thoughtlessly and without deliberation, indeed even under fear inflicted by God himself or by a man, though for a just cause, and in such agitation as has taken away the use of reason; yet if the matter was neither impossible nor evil and the vow was left unfulfilled, the fear of God alone, to whom the vow was made, demands its observance. "He who dwells on your holy hill... who swears to his own hurt and does not change" (Ps. 15:4) [נשבע להרע ולא ימיר].

units.la: CLI. Hactenus de Bonis Operibus,Sanctificationis effecto. Ejusdem & haec proprietas est, quòd in hac vita imperfecta est; gradibus tamen augescens & ad perfectionem contendens. Imperfecta est,quia nemo Mortalium in hac vita ad ἀναμαρτησίαν , seu sanctitatem omnis peccati & tentationis ejusdem internae expertem pertingere potis est. Nam ex parte cognoscimus,& ex parte prophetamus. Postquam autem advenerit,quod perfectum est, tunc quod ex parte est,abolebitur,1.Cor. XIII. 9 10. Si dixerimus nos peccatum non habere,nos ipsos fallimus,& veritas in nobis non est,1. Joh. I. 8. Sanctificatus enim ex duobus principiis,carne&spiritu,Gal. V. 16. 17. constat; & juxta illa principia in duos quasi homines, internum & externum,2. Cor.IV. 16. veterem & novum,Ephes. IV.22.24. distinguitur. Cùmque principiorum contraria sit ratio , perpetua inter duo illa principia lucta est. Caro concupiscit adversus spiritum , spiritus antem adversus carnem. Haec vero sibi invicem contrariantur,Gal. V. 17. Ipse enim homo sibi concors, secum pugnat,habens inimicos οἰκιακὰς domesticos,Matth.X. 36. Quod graphicè suo exemplo Apostolus Rom.VII.14. &c. ostendit. Hinc à diversis principiis procedentes actiones & ipsae mixtae sunt,partim bonae partim malae, non ex consensu, sed ex conflictu; quatenus non quicquid caro vult, spiritus permittit, sed ut oppositus,resistit,& vicissim. cissim. Sed in hoc tamen conflictu sanctifica-tio augescit, & incrementa laetiora capit. Non elanguescimus ; sed etiamsi exterior homo noster corrumpitur, interior tamen de die in diem renovatur,2.Cor. IV. 16. Sic ἐπιτείνομεν ... perficimus sanctitatem in timore Dei, veritatem amantes, meliora explorantes, & in studio sanctitatis proficientes, 2. Cor. VII. 1. Non quod jam apprehenderim, vel perfectus sim, sed persequor, an quoque apprehendam. Unum autem ago, eorum, quae à tergo sunt, oblivisçens, ad ea, quae à fronte sunt, contendens, scopum versus feror ad palmam supernae vocationis Dei in Christo Jesu,Phil.III. 12. 14. Sed de imperfectione & profectu regenerationis & sanctificationis amplissimè dicta Loc. XXI. 72. &c. heic ad compendium ponimus, & de lucta spirituali fidelium, seu spiritus eorum cum carne residua, indicta hactenus, edisserimus.
units.tr: CLI. So far concerning good works, the effect of sanctification. It is also a property of sanctification that in this life it is imperfect, yet growing by degrees and striving towards perfection. It is imperfect because no mortal in this life can attain to sinlessness [ἀναμαρτησίαν], that is, to holiness free from all sin and from the inward temptation to it. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect comes, then that which is in part will be done away (1 Cor. 13:9–10). If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (1 John 1:8). For the sanctified man is made up of two principles, flesh and spirit (Gal. 5:16–17), and according to those principles is distinguished into two men, as it were, inner and outer (2 Cor. 4:16), old and new (Eph. 4:22, 24). And since the principles have opposite tendencies, there is a perpetual struggle between those two principles. The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another (Gal. 5:17). For man, though he is one, is at odds with himself, having enemies of his own household (Matt. 10:36)[οἰκιακὰς], as the Apostle vividly shows by his own example (Rom. 7:14 ff.). Hence the actions that proceed from the different principles are themselves mixed, partly good, partly evil, arising not from agreement but from conflict; inasmuch as whatever the flesh wills, the spirit does not permit, but resists as its opponent, and vice versa. Yet in this conflict sanctification grows and gains happier increase. We do not lose heart; but even if our outward man is wasting away, yet the inward man is renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4:16). Thus we perfect holiness in the fear of God, loving truth, seeking out better things, and making progress in the pursuit of holiness (2 Cor. 7:1)[ἐπιτείνομεν]. Not that I have already attained, or am already perfect; but I press on, if I may apprehend that for which I was apprehended. One thing I do: forgetting what lies behind, and straining towards what lies ahead, I press on towards the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus (Phil. 3:12–14). But we have treated the imperfection and progress of regeneration and sanctification at length in Loc. XXI. 72. &c.; here we set it down briefly, and proceed to explain the spiritual struggle of believers, that is, of their spirit against the remaining flesh, which has not been discussed until now.

units.la: CLII. Lucta spiritualis regenitorum cum carne est Certamen illud, quo fideles duce & auspice Deo, inprimis Spiritu Christi contra carnem, seu peccatum post regenerationem permanens, ejusque promachos mundum & Sathanam vera fide in Christum, & panoplia spirituali muniti sic belligerantur, ut volentes bonum secundum interiorem hominem, secundum exteriorem tamen ita subinde succumbant, ut tamen spiritu Dei victore vera fide sanctitatem in timore Dei perficiant, & in die Domini salventur. Nam homo regenitus, quamdiu in hoc saeculo agitat, corpus peccati & mortis,Rom. VI. 6. VII. 24. corpus peccatorum carnis, Col. II. 11. carnem seu concupiscentiam, cujus corruptio se in membris carnis scandalizantibus potissimum exerit, peccatum, malum circumfert, non tamen ut dominentur, vel perdant & condemnent, sed ut ad luctam existant. Non enim tota haec deponit, prius quam corpus deponat. Manet vitiositas & pravitas quasi habitualis, qua fit, ut homo, cùm cogitat & desiderat, mala etiam cogitet & desideret, atque etiam bonum volens facere, non inveniat, Rom. VII. 18. Cum hoc malo per totam vitam luctatur, quia perfectio non est in corpore mortali. Cur enim alias corpus propter peccatum deponendum mori necesse haberet? ibid. VIII. 10. Primitias enim spiritus habentes suspiramus & redemptionem corporis ab omni miseria & malo, à redemptione Christi provenientem expectamus, adeóque nec dum possidemus, ibid. v. 23. Quis potest dicere: Purificavi cor meum, purus sum à peccato meo? Prov. XX. 9. Solus enim Christus ... separatus à peccatoribus est,Heb. VII. 26. Et habet etiam caro, peccatum suos promachos, mundum ejusque illecebras, inprimis Sathanam, ... malum illum ... qui nihil reliqui facit, ut hominem ad peccandum seducat, & à Deo abstrahat. Non enim nobis ... cum sanguine & carne, sed cum Principatibus, Potestatibus,&c. est, Ephes. VI. 12. Hic ergo pugnandum est. Nemini veniunt sine Marte triumphi. Ad hoc enim nati, ad hoc renati sumus, ... annon militia est vita hominis super terra? Job. VII. 1. Huic militiae in Baptismo voti & Sacramenti religione nomen dedimus. Ad hanc in Paradiso ipso suos Deus, inimicitia cum serpente posita, auctoravit, Genes. III. 15.
units.tr: CLII. The spiritual struggle of the regenerate with the flesh is that contest in which the faithful, with God as their leader and guide, and chiefly by the Spirit of Christ, fight against the flesh, or the sin remaining after regeneration, and its champions, the world and Satan, armed with true faith in Christ and the spiritual armour; so that, while they will what is good according to the inner man, yet according to the outer man they sometimes give way; nevertheless, with the Spirit of God as victor, through true faith they perfect holiness in the fear of God and are saved on the day of the Lord. For the regenerate man, as long as he lives in this age, carries about the body of sin and death (Rom. 6:6; 7:24), the body of the sins of the flesh (Col. 2:11), the flesh or concupiscence, whose corruption shows itself chiefly in the members of the flesh that cause stumbling: sin and evil. Yet they do not rule, nor destroy and condemn him, but are there for the struggle. For he does not put off all of this before he puts off the body. A vitiosity and perversity remain, as it were habitual, by which it happens that when man thinks and desires, he also thinks and desires evil things, and even while willing to do good, he does not find it (Rom. 7:18). He wrestles with this evil through the whole of life, because there is no perfection in the mortal body. For why otherwise would the body have to die because of sin? (Rom. 8:10). For having the firstfruits of the Spirit, we groan within ourselves, waiting for the redemption of the body, from all misery and evil, which comes from the redemption of Christ; and so we do not yet possess it (Rom. 8:23). Who can say, "I have cleansed my heart, I am pure from my sin"? (Prov. 20:9). For Christ alone is separated from sinners (Heb. 7:26). The flesh also has sin, its champions the world and its allurements, and especially Satan, that evil one who leaves nothing undone to seduce man to sin and to draw him away from God. For our struggle is not with flesh and blood, but with principalities and powers, and so on (Eph. 6:12). Here, then, we must fight. No triumph comes to anyone without battle. For to this we are born, and to this we are reborn; is not the life of man upon the earth a warfare? (Job 7:1). We gave our name to this warfare at baptism, through the vow and the sacred obligation of the sacrament. To this warfare God enlisted his own in Paradise itself, enmity being set between the serpent and the woman (Gen. 3:15).

units.la: CLIII. In lucta hac spirituali cum peccato & ejus promachis principalis ... Luctator Deus est. Nam solus ille resistendi vires suppeditat, & in congressu illo, ceu dux & fortissimus heros in prima acie stat. Jehova fortitudo mea, Jehova Petra mea & arx mea ... liberator meus, in eo sperabo,&c. Psal. XVIII. 2.3. &c. Sufficit tibi gratia mea. Potentia enim mea in infirmitate consummatur, 2.Cor. XII. 9. Sine Deo enim bonum nec velle nec operari,Phil.II. 13. nec loqui,Prov. XVI. 1. nec cogitare, 2.Cor. III. 5. multò minus obedire possumus, Rom. VIII. 7. Singulariter Spiritus Christi sanctificationis, in oeconomia salutis, ... author luctæ huic praeest, quem idem Tertullianus Xystarchen, athletarum Praesidem, sicut Deum Patrem Agonotheten; & Christum Epistaten appellat. Spiritu ambulate, & concupiscentiam carnis non perficite. Nam caro concupiscit adversus Spiritum, & Spiritus adversus carnem. Haec autem inter se opposita sunt, Galat. V. 16. 17. Ubi Spiritus non tam vim & efficaciam Divinam, quae Christianis inest, & eos ad vitae pietatem impellit, uti Sociniani explicant, quàm Personam ipsam Spiritus S. significat. Ille enim nos Christo complantat & vivificat, ibid. v. 25. Charismata donat prout vult, 1. Cor. XII. 11. nos ungit, (uti athletae ungi solebant) confirmat & obsignat, velut arrhabo nostler, 2. Cor. I. 21. 22. cui, ad certitudinem spei nostrae, sanctificatio tribuitur, & qui in lucta cum carne efficit ... ut velimus, & ut concupiscentiam carnis non perficiamus, sed ei pro viribus resistamus, tandemque praevaleamus, Gal. V. 16. 17. Contra invidiam desiderat Spiritus, qui habitationem in nobis cepit, Jac. IV. 5. Est enim Spiritus Zelotes, & non minus pro gloria Dei & Christi justitia, quàm Diabolus ex adverso zelat. Si igitur zelat, etiam ad zelum & amorem flagrantissimum excitat, & pugnat adversus carnem in regenitis residuam, quae efficit, ut non faciamus, quod volumus,Gal. V. 17. hoc est, reluctando bonum opus fidelium saepe impedit, ut concupiscentiae spiritus non pareat, & ut nunquam tam bene, prompte, perfecte, jucunde, sine omni imprudentia, & carnali metu bonum opus faciant, atque ipsi bonum opus à se aliisque fieri magno opere vellent, & ut nunquam veniam precari erratorum & sphalmatum suorum, sine quibus ipsum bonum opus non faciunt, cogantur.
units.tr: CLIII. In this spiritual struggle against sin and its chief champions... God is the chief wrestler. For he alone supplies the strength to resist, and in that contest he stands like a leader and most valiant hero at the front of the battle line: Jehovah is my strength, Jehovah is my rock and my fortress... my deliverer, in whom I will trust, etc., Ps. 18:2–3, etc. My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness, 2 Cor. 12:9. For without God we are able neither to will nor to do the good, Phil. 2:13; nor to speak, Prov. 16:1; nor to think, 2 Cor. 3:5; much less can we obey, Rom. 8:7. The Spirit of Christ, the author of sanctification in the economy of salvation, presides over this struggle in a unique way. Tertullian calls him the Xystarches [Ξυστάρχης], the president of the athletes, just as he calls God the Father the Agonothetes [ἀγωνοθέτης], and Christ the Epistates [ἐπιστάτης]. Walk in the Spirit, and do not fulfil the desire of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are opposed to one another, Gal. 5:16–17. Here "Spirit" signifies not so much the divine power and efficacy that is in Christians and impels them to a godly life, as the Sociniens explain it, but the Person of the Holy Spirit himself. For he grafts us into Christ and gives us life, ibid. v. 25. He distributes gifts as he wills, 1 Cor. 12:11. He anoints us (as athletes were accustomed to be anointed), confirms and seals us, and is like our pledge, 2 Cor. 1:21–22. To him, for the certainty of our hope, sanctification is ascribed; and he, in the struggle with the flesh, brings it about that we should will, and that we should not fulfil the desire of the flesh, but resist it with our strength and at last prevail, Gal. 5:16–17. The Spirit who dwells in us desires envy, Jas. 4:5. For the Spirit is a zealot, and no less zealous for the glory of God and the righteousness of Christ than the Devil is zealous against them. If therefore he is zealous, he also stirs up zeal and most ardent love, and he fights against the flesh that remains in the regenerate, which brings it about that we do not do what we want, Gal. 5:17. That is, by resisting, it often hinders the good work of believers, so that the spirit does not obey its desires, and so that they never do the good work so well, promptly, perfectly, joyfully, and without all imprudence and carnal fear, and so that they are never compelled, though they greatly wish the good work to be done by themselves and by others, to beg pardon for their errors and lapses, without which they do not do the good work itself.

units.la: CLIV. Deo duce & Spiritu S. Xystarche, luctam hanc regeniti sustinent, & qua regeniti per Spiritum S. cujus athletae & ... boni milites Jesu Christi,2. Tim. II. 3. sunt; & qua fideles, quippe interveniente fide. Esto ... fidelis usque ad mortem, & dabo tibi coronam vitae,Apoc. II. 10. Luctantur etiam irregeniti. Sed toto Caelo regenitorum & irregenitorum lucta distat. Illa enim Spiritus S. & mentis, seu rationis illuminatae adversus carnem, seu prava judicia, consilia, inclinationes corruptae naturae consentaneas, ipsúmque Diabolum : haec affectuum seu affectus unius adversus affectum alium, velut spiritus superbi, gloriam coram hominibus aucupantis, adversus affectum intemperantiae ; vel ad summum rationis utcunque illustratae, at non sanctificatae adversus affectuum cohortem conflictatio est.
units.tr: CLIV. With God as leader and the Holy Spirit as Xystarches, the regenerate sustain this struggle, as they are good soldiers of Jesus Christ, 2 Tim. 2:3, and athletes of the Holy Spirit; and as believers, since faith intervenes. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life, Rev. 2:10. The unregenerate also struggle. But the struggle of the regenerate and of the unregenerate differs by the whole heaven. For the former is a conflict of the Holy Spirit and of the enlightened mind, or reason, against the flesh, that is, against depraved judgments, counsels and inclinations consonant with corrupt nature, and against the Devil himself. The latter is a conflict of affections, or of one affection against another: for example, the spirit of pride, seeking glory before men, against the affection of intemperance; or, at most, a conflict of reason, however enlightened, but not sanctified, against the troop of the affections.

units.la: {y} Minus pr n.ipalis regeniti sunt, non irregeniti, quorum lucta n.ultum ab ea, quam regeniti sustinent, differt. est. Nonnunquam enim apertissima vitia aliis vitiis occultis vincuntur. Non enim omnis impetus & desiderium carnis vel rationis est concupiscentia Spiritus S. Potest concupiscentia una, velut honoris, potentiæ, ad tempus aliam, velut voluptatis, impedire & supprimere, sicut unus fluctus alium frangit. Ita non audent peccare mali formidine poenæ. Et qui radicem non habent, atque se commendare aliis volunt, quædam vera & bona dicere & facere, Deo & hominibus mentiri, & cum Sathana in Angelos lucis se transformare, labio blando, & in duplici corde loqui, eligunt. Sed concupiscentia Spiritus, quæ carni contrariatur, ex illis virtutibus, quas Apostolus fructus Spiritus appellat, æstimari debet; quæ in animo sunt, & maximam præcipuámque partem in eo includuntur, & sentiuntur. Tum regenitorum lucta ex nova natura & filiali Dei amore oritur: irregenitorum ex servili affectu & metu poenæ. Illa sanctis rationibus armata, dignoscitur ex rationibus, quibus luctantes concitantur & foventur; hæc argumentis merè carnalibus excitatur & geritur. Illa adversus peccata omnia, leviora etiam: hæc adversus atrociora duntaxat belligeratur. In illa Spiritus carne potentior, denique victor existit, & carnis tumultum æstúmque extinguit: in hac peccata reprimuntur ad tempus, sed demum rupto obice, flammæ instar exitum invenientis, acriúsque exardescunt & concupiscentia succumbit.
units.tr: {y} Less principal in this struggle are the unregenerate, not the regenerate, whose struggle differs little from that which the regenerate endure. For sometimes the most open vices are overcome by other hidden vices. For not every impulse and desire of the flesh or of reason is the concupiscence of the Holy Spirit. One lust, such as that for honour or power, can for a time hinder and suppress another, such as that for pleasure, just as one wave breaks another. So they do not dare to sin for fear of punishment. And those who have no root, and wish to commend themselves to others, choose to say and do certain things that are true and good, to lie to God and men, to transform themselves with Satan into angels of light, and to speak with a smooth lip and a double heart. But the concupiscence of the Spirit, which is opposed to the flesh, must be judged by those virtues which the Apostle calls the fruit of the Spirit; these are in the mind, and are for the most part included and felt within it. Then the struggle of the regenerate arises from a new nature and from filial love of God; that of the unregenerate from a servile affection and fear of punishment. The former, armed with holy reasons, is recognised by the reasons with which the combatants are stirred up and nourished; the latter is aroused and waged by purely carnal arguments. The former wages war against all sins, even the lighter ones; the latter only against the more atrocious. In the former the Spirit, being more powerful than the flesh, at last emerges as victor and quenches the tumult and heat of the flesh; in the latter sins are restrained for a time, but at length, the barrier broken, they blaze up more fiercely, like a flame finding an outlet, and concupiscence gives way.

units.la: CLV. Sed habent regeniti in lucta hac antagonistas non unius generis. Alii enim amici sunt eorum constantiam & fidem explorantes: alii inimici professi, eosdem seducere & perdere annitentes. Amicus antagonista Deus est. Is enim licet ad malum neminem tentet vel provocet, sicut & ipse malis tentari non potest, Jacob. I. 13. tamen ceu Agonothetes & Epistates, ad certamen suos provocat, cum iis luctatur tum immediate; vel præcipiens talia, quæ naturæ nostræ adversantur, & viribus majora sunt, sicut Abrahamum tentavit, Gen. XXII. 1. vel se ipsum, ceu adversarium, sensibus eorum offerentem in apparitionibus, sicut Angelus Jehova cum Jacobo luctatus est, velut excitato in campo pulvere, ibid. XXXII. 24. tum mediate, sive per immissos cordi terrores Dei, qui eos velut acie instructa adoriuntur, Job. VI. 4. dum gratiæ suæ sensum minuit vel adimit, Psal. LXXVII. 7. 8. vel eos derelinquit, ad tentandum eos, ut quid in corde eorum sit, sciat, 2. Chron. XXXII. 31. ut infirmitates suas agnoscant, & in solo Deo salutis suæ præsidium quærant; sive per temporalem felicitatem, pacem longam & res omnes secundas, quibus affluentes facilè in securitatem incidunt, dicentes in tranquillitate sua; Non movebimur in æternum, Psal. XXX. 7. sive per crucem & afflictiones, quibus suos castigat & exercet, Hebr. XII. 5. Inimici professi antagonistæ caro & ejus promachi mundus & Sathanas, seculi hujus Deus, 2. Cor. IV. 4. & in certamine hoc archistrategus; sunt. Et caro quidem se habet fomitis instar ignem concipientis, mundus & Sathanas ignem suum in fomitem jacientium, atque ita concupiscentiæ adversus Spiritum & affectuum incendium excitantium.
units.tr: CLV. But the regenerate have antagonists in this struggle of more than one kind. For some are friends, testing their constancy and faith; others are open enemies, striving to seduce and destroy them. The friendly antagonist is God. For although he tempts no one to evil nor provokes anyone to it, just as he cannot be tempted with evil, Jas. 1:13, nevertheless, as the Agonothetes and Epistates, he challenges his people to the contest, wrestling with them both immediately, by commanding such things as are contrary to our nature and beyond our strength, as he tempted Abraham, Gen. 22:1, or by presenting himself to their senses as an adversary in appearances, as the angel of Jehovah wrestled with Jacob, as if dust were raised in the field, ibid. 32:24; and mediately, either by sending terrors of God into the heart, which assail them as if in battle array, Job 6:4, while he diminishes or takes away the sense of his grace, Ps. 77:7–8, or leaves them to test them, that he might know what was in their heart, 2 Chron. 32:31, so that they may recognise their weaknesses and seek the protection of their salvation in God alone; or by temporal happiness, long peace and all prosperous circumstances, by which those who abound easily fall into security, saying in their tranquillity, We shall never be moved, Ps. 30:7; or by the cross and afflictions, with which he chastens and exercises his own, Heb. 12:5. The open enemies and antagonists are the flesh and its champions, the world and Satan, the god of this age, 2 Cor. 4:4, and in this contest the chief strategist. The flesh, indeed, is like tinder that catches fire, while the world and Satan are those who throw their fire into the tinder, and so stir up the lusts against the Spirit and the blaze of the affections.

units.la: Horum omnium Spiritui repugnantium scopus architectonicus est, vi & dolo omni fideles ad peccatum impellere, à gratia & favore Dei abstrahere, & in æternum exitium præcipitare.
units.tr: The architectonic aim of all these enemies of the Spirit is to drive the faithful into sin by every force and fraud, to draw them away from the grace and favour of God, and to hurl them headlong into eternal ruin.

units.la: CLVI. Hæ ex adverso compositæ luctantium acies sunt. Sed habent utraque παταλιαν, seu חלוצה, 2. Sam. II. 21. plenam armaturam suam, seu arma impetum sustinentia & ferentia, quibus se ad ἀγωνίαν hanc comparant. De fidelium armatura sic Apostolus: Induite armaturam Dei, ut possitis stare adversus stratagemata Diaboli, &c. State igitur cinctos lumbos habentes in veritate, & induti thoracem justitiæ, & calceati pedibus promptitudine annuntiationis pacis. Super omnia assumpto scuto fidei, in quo poteritis omnia jacula nequam illius ignita extinguere. Et galeam Salutaris accipite, & gladium Spiritus, qui est verbum Dei. Omni oratione & petitione orantes in Spiritu, & ad hoc ipsum vigilantes in omni perseverantia & oratione pro omnibus sanctis, Ephes. VI. 11–19. Talis hæc militis spiritualis panoplia est, ut totum eum protegat, & ad certamen feliciter cernendum instruat. Nam lumbos cingit, pectus munit, pedes calceat, totum hominem protegit, caput armat, latus succingit, & manus implet. Sed tergo tamen non providet armatura hæc; innuente Apostolo, nunquam hosti vertenda terga esse. Et lumbos quidem cingit ζωνη αληθειας baltheo veritatis, seu agnitionis veritatis de Deo & rebus Divinis, quæ cum amore Dei, & bona conscientia conjuncta hominis cogitationes coercet, constringit, continet, ne luxentur, laxentur, & evagentur ad mendacium; & in cordibus fidelium efficit, סתר יר cogitationes fixas, Esaj. XXVI. 3. prohibet, ne simus ancipites, leves, laxi, Psal. CXIX. 114. 2. Cor. I. 17. ne fluctuemus, & circumagamur omni vento doctrinæ, in alea & versutia hominum, juxta viam erroris, Ephes. IV. 14. Pectus munit θωρακα δικαιοσυνης thorace justitiæ, non hominis, sed Dei ipsius, Christi, qui justitiam pro lorica induere, Esaj. LIX. 17. dicitur, & eandem, ceu loricam fidelibus suis donat. Thorax enim pectus munit, à quo egressus vitæ & vita ipsa est. Est autem justitia Christi per fidem nobis donata δικαιωσις ζωης justificatio vitæ, Rom. V. 18. quia justitia legis à Christo præstita vitæ nobis causa est. Pedes ἐν ἑτοιμασια & Εὐαγγελίῳ τῆς εἰρήνης promptitudine Evangelii pacis, hoc est, præconio nostræ cum Deo reconciliationis, nec non abolitæ gentes inter Diaboli imperio hactenus subjectas, & populum Dei calceat; ut ita liber ad Deum, velut in Christo placatum, accessus nobis sit, & pax iis, qui μακραν και εγγυς propè & procul sunt, evangelizari possit, Ephes. II. 14–18. Totum hominem θυρεὸν τῆς πίστεως scuto fidei ad extinguenda tela ignita Mali illius, protegit. Pro scuto enim fides justificans est, non quatenus actus hominis credentis est, sed quatenus Christo fœta & gravida est, eúmque unâ cum justitia & meritis suis fide apprehendit. Habet enim Deus clypeum & Regem, Christum, quem Ecclesiæ & credentibus omnib* donat. Domini est מגן clypeus noster, & Sancti Israelis Rex noster, Psal. LXXXIX. 19. Sicut enim scutum extra corpus militis est, sed manu militis apprehenditur, & munitur, atque que ita universale quoddam corporis munimentum est: ita φυλαξ velut militari quodam praesidio totum hominem protegit & custodit, & reliquorum etiam armorum omnium commune velut φυλακτηριον est. Inprimis vero fides Mali illius tela πεπυρωμένα ignita seu a gehenna inflammata, Jac. III. 6. qualia sunt, quae tanta vehementia adiguntur, ut ipso motu ignem concipiant, & hominem inflamment; non tantum retundit, sed etiam extinguit, quia scutum illud sanguine Christi, quo ipse infernalis ignis extinctus est, tinctum vim ignita quaeque extinguendi habet. Caput κεφαλαια της Σωτηριας galea Salutaris Christi, qui & caput nostrum est, quia nos, ceu corpus suum tegit & protegit; & Salus nostra est, quia corporis sui Σωτηρ Salvator, adeoque nobis retentus, Col. II. 19. galea fit, armat. Retento hoc capite retinetur Σωτηριον Salutare, Jesus Christus, quem Pater ex morte salvavit; qui pro corpore suo oravit, & orans a Patre exauditus est, qui & potentiam ad nos salvandum, & potestatem ad nos decore salvandum habet: & caput nobis datus est, ut nos salvaret; qui corpori suo dat spiritum, & injurias corpori suo factas suas reputat atque ulciscitur. Denique latus succingit, & manus implet μαχαιρα πνευματος Θεου, ὁ εστι ῥημα Θεου gladio Spiritus, qui est verbum Dei, quod & quoad rem, & quoad λεξιν est Dei, quia ab ipso, & de ipso, inprimis in Christo peccatori gratioso est; & quo omnis veritas & sapientia Dei ad salutem peccatoris comprehenditur.
units.tr: CLVI. These are the battle lines drawn up by the two sides wrestling against each other. But each side has its full armour, παταλιαν [παράταξις, battle array], or חלוצה (2 Sam. 2:21), that is, weapons able to withstand and bear the force of an attack, with which they prepare themselves for this contest. The Apostle speaks thus of the believers' armour: Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil, etc. Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness; and your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace; above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked. And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God: praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints (Eph. 6:11–19). Such is the spiritual soldier's panoply, so that it protects the whole man and equips him to fight the battle successfully. For it girds the loins, guards the breast, shoes the feet, protects the whole man, arms the head, girds the side and fills the hands. Yet this armour makes no provision for the back, for the Apostle indicates that one must never turn one's back on the enemy. The belt of truth, ζωνη αληθειας, girds the loins, that is, the knowledge of the truth about God and divine things; joined with the love of God and a good conscience, it restrains, binds and holds the thoughts of man, so that they do not become loose, slack and wander off into falsehood. In the hearts of believers it produces fixed thoughts (Isa. 26:3), and it prevents us from being double-minded, fickle, slack (Ps. 119:113; 2 Cor. 1:17), so that we are not tossed about, and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by the sleight and cunning of men, in the way of error (Eph. 4:14). It guards the breast with the breastplate of righteousness, θωρακα δικαιοσυνης, not man's but God's own, that of Christ, who is said to put on righteousness as a breastplate (Isa. 59:17), and who gives the same to his believers as a breastplate. For the breastplate protects the breast, from which the issues of life and life itself come. Now the righteousness of Christ is given to us through faith, δικαιωσις ζωης, the justification of life (Rom. 5:18), because the righteousness of the law performed by Christ is for us the cause of life. The feet, ἐν ἑτοιμασια & Εὐαγγελίῳ τῆς εἰρήνης, with the readiness of the gospel of peace, that is, with the proclamation of our reconciliation with God, and of the nations, hitherto under the dominion of the devil, now abolished, shoes the feet of God's people; so that free access to God, as one reconciled in Christ, is open to us, and peace may be preached to those who are afar off and near (Eph. 2:14–18). It protects the whole man with the θυρεὸν τῆς πίστεως, the shield of faith, for quenching the fiery darts of that evil one. For faith that justifies serves as the shield, not insofar as it is an act of the believing man, but insofar as it is pregnant and big with Christ, and by faith apprehends him together with his righteousness and merits. For God has a shield and a King, Christ, whom he gives to the Church and to all believers. The Lord is our shield (מגן), and the Holy One of Israel is our King (Ps. 89:18). For just as a shield lies outside the soldier's body, yet is grasped and held by the soldier's hand, and is thus a general protection of the body, so the φυλαξ, as a kind of military guard, protects and keeps the whole man, and is, as it were, a common φυλακτηριον for all the other armour too. Above all, faith quenches and not merely blunts the fiery darts of that evil one, πεπυρωμένα, that is, set on fire from hell (Jas. 3:6), such as those which are hurled with such violence that by their very motion they catch fire and set the man ablaze; for that shield, dyed with the blood of Christ, by which the infernal fire itself was quenched, has the power to quench any fiery missile. The helmet of salvation, κεφαλαια της Σωτηριας, is the head, Christ, who is also our head, because he covers and protects us as his body, and is our salvation, because he is the Saviour of his body, and so, being held by us (Col. 2:19), becomes a helmet and arms us. By holding fast to this head we hold fast the Σωτηριον, the salvation, Jesus Christ, whom the Father saved from death; who prayed for his body, and who, being heard by the Father in his prayer, has both the power to save us and the authority to save us fittingly. He was given to us as head, so that he might save us; he gives his Spirit to his body, and regards the wrongs done to his body as done to himself, and avenges them. Finally, he girds the side and fills the hands with the μαχαιρα πνευματος Θεου, which is ὁ εστι ῥημα Θεου, the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; which is God's both in substance and in word, because it comes from him and speaks of him, above all of Christ, who is gracious to the sinner; and in which all the truth and wisdom of God for the salvation of the sinner is comprehended.

units.la: Verbum Dei vivum est & efficax, secantius omni bicipiti gladio, & penetrans usque ad divisionem animae & spiritus, (ut spiritus & mens hominis animae irrationali, seu cupiditati, conscientia concupiscentiae adversetur) compagum & medullarum,&c. Hebr. IV. 12. quin & omni ense chalybeo μαχαιρα secantius, omni βεβαιωτικη penetrantius, ad ratiocinationem omnem, omnemque sublimitatem, quae adversus Dei cognitionem se attollit, evertendam, omnemque cogitationem ad obsequium Christi subigendam, 2. Cor. X. 5. Gladius vero Spiritus est, quia in Spiritus S. officina cusus, ab illo traditus, per illum efficax, neque ab aliis quam a spiritualibus, & contra spiritualia nequitiae cognosci, stringi, vibrari idoneus est. Medium porro, quo spiritualia haec arma luctator spiritualis adversus hostes suos feliciter abhiberi potest, προσευχη και δεησις orationem & petitionem, & in eadem vigilantiam & perseverantiam Apostolus v. 18. facit. Cujus & necessitatem arguit, quod miles spiritualis non propriis, sed alienis & Divinis tum armis, tum viribus pugnat; quae ceu mere gratuita, nisi precibus a Deo, earum authore & datore unico, impetrari non possunt: & utilitatem propalat, quod petens accipit, quaerens invenit, pulsanti aperitur, Matth. VII. 8. Hae enim argenteae illae tubae sunt, quarum in hoc conflictu clangor ab omnibus praelium inituris, in Christo Sacerdotibus spiritualibus factis, miceri debet. Panopliae porro hujus totius ad luctam spiritualem ικανοτης aptitudinem & usum maximum fusius alibi expositum.
units.tr: The word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, (so that the spirit and mind of man are opposed to the irrational soul, or lust, and the conscience to concupiscence), of the joints and marrow, etc. (Heb. 4:12). Indeed it is sharper than any steel sword, μαχαιρα, and more penetrating, βεβαιωτικη, for overthrowing every reasoning and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and for bringing every thought into obedience to Christ (2 Cor. 10:5). The sword is that of the Spirit, because it is forged in the workshop of the Holy Spirit, given by him, effective through him, and fit to be known, drawn and brandished not by anyone but spiritual people, and against spiritual wickedness. Now the means by which this spiritual weapon can be used successfully by the spiritual combatant against his enemies is prayer and supplication, προσευχη και δεησις, and in the same, watchfulness and perseverance, as the Apostle says (v. 18). The necessity of this is shown by the fact that the spiritual soldier fights not with his own weapons and strength but with alien, divine ones, which, being purely gratuitous, cannot be obtained except by prayer to God, their unique author and giver. Its usefulness is shown by the fact that he who asks receives, he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it is opened (Matt. 7:8). For these are the silver trumpets, whose sound in this conflict, by all who are about to engage in battle, having been made spiritual priests in Christ, ought to be heard. The aptitude and very great usefulness of this whole panoply for spiritual struggle has been set out more fully elsewhere.

units.la: CLVII. De Armatura hostium spiritualium dicere nihil attinet. Paucis Diaboli archistrategi hostium armaturam Lutherus in nobili illo Cantico in Psal. XLVI. expressit.
units.tr: CLVII. There is no need to say anything about the armour of the spiritual enemies. Luther, in that noble hymn on Psalm 46, has expressed in a few words the armour of the archstrategist of the devil and his enemies.

units.la: Armatura Sathanae, carnis & mundi in carnalia non æquè atque adversus carnem & sanguinem proficiunt.
units.tr: The armour of Satan, of the flesh and of the world, is not equally effective against spiritual things as against flesh and blood.

units.la: CLVIII. Modus luctandi alius cum Deo Antagonista amico: alius cum antagonistis hostibus profeßis est. Cum Deo luctandum est per obedientiam, fidem, humilitatem, patientiam, preces ardentes ad Deum,qui solus vires ita luctandi, imò etiam benedictione sua donata,vincendi confert. Ita Jacobus fortitudine sua שרה את אלהים tanquam dux exercitus, pugnavit cum Deo; וישר & certavit cum Angelo Fœderis ויכל & superior eo fuit. Ploravit & supplicavit ei,Hos. XII. 4. 5. Ploratu & supplici prece extorsit Deo benedictionem, dicens: Non dimittam,nisi benedixeris mihi,Gen. XXXII. 26. atque ita cum Deo pugnans vicit, experimentum nactus,quòd multò magis homines, fratrem Esavum insidias sibi struentem, superaturus sit. Hoc modo Sancti omnes cum Deo luctantur, & sic vincunt, ut quæ à Deo vera fide & obnixè orant, consequantur.
units.tr: CLVIII. The manner of wrestling is one way with God as an friendly antagonist, and another with professed hostile antagonists. One must wrestle with God through obedience, faith, humility, patience, and fervent prayers to God, who alone grants the strength to wrestle thus, and, indeed, to conquer by the blessing he bestows. So Jacob, with his strength, [שרה את אלהים], as a commander of an army, contended with God; [וישר] and struggled with the Angel of the covenant, [ויכל] and prevailed over him. He wept and made supplication to him (Hos. 12:4–5). By weeping and humble prayer he wrung a blessing from God, saying: I will not let thee go, except thou bless me (Gen. 32:26). And so, wrestling with God, he conquered, having the experience that he would much more overcome men, his brother Esau who was plotting against him. In this way all the saints wrestle with God, and thus they conquer, so that they obtain what they ask of God with true faith and earnest prayer.

units.la: CLIX. Modus luctandi cum antagonistis hostibus professis, carne, mundo & Sathana tribus gradibus absolvitur. Primus est, ut luctator hosti aggressori primum aditum intercludat. Non enim hoste conspecto fugere,sed intrepido animo obviam ire, & ad pugnam se offerre debet. Inprimis id in principio luctæ faciendum est. Ne date locum Diabolo, Ephes. IV. 27. Ideo Christus primo limine Sathanam repulit. Nam ad Petrum à Sathana seductum infit: Abi post me Sathan. Non enim sapis, quæ sunt Dei,sed quæ hominum sunt,Matth. XVI. 13. Præclarè Hieronymus Epist. 22. Noli sinas cogitationem crescere. Nihil in te Babylonium, nihil confusionis adolescat. Dum parvus est hostis, interfice. Nequitia, ne zizania crescat, in semine. Et Cyprianus de Jejun. Diaboli, inquit, titillationibus obviandum est, nec coluber foveri debet, donec in serpentem formetur. Ille enim in primo aditu Siren est, qui admissus vipera evadit. Ubi claustra hostis perfregit,& aditum sibi patefecit, secundus luctandi gradus excipit, qui est cum hoste gradum conferre,strenuéque repugnare. Resistite Diabolo, & fugiet à vobis, Jac. IV. 7. 1. Pet. V. 9. State, cincti lumbos veritate,&c. Ephes. VI. 14. State in fide, viriliter agite,fortes estote, 1. Cor. XVI. 13. Quæ statio non corporis, sed animi actus, isque hominis ex morte spirituali resuscitati primus est,& contentionem virium omnium Spiritus ad resistendum Sathanæ & carni,eum oppugnandum, fraudulentiam ejus eludendam, violentiam frangendam,hostémque vincendum notat. Ita Christus Salvator Tentatoris tribus aggressioni
units.tr: CLIX. The manner of wrestling with the professed adversaries, the flesh, the world and Satan, is completed in three stages. The first is that the wrestler cut off the enemy's first approach to him. For when the enemy is in sight, one must not flee but must meet him with an undaunted spirit and offer oneself for battle. This must be done especially at the very beginning of the struggle. Give no place to the devil, Eph. 4:27. For this reason Christ drove Satan back at the very threshold. When Satan had led Peter astray, Christ began: Get behind me, Satan. For you do not mind the things that are of God, but the things that are of men, Matt. 16:23. Jerome admirably says, Letter 22: Do not allow the thought to grow. Let nothing Babylonian, nothing of confusion, grow up in you. While the enemy is small, kill him. Destroy the vice before the tares grow up; nip them in the seed. And Cyprian, On Fasting: One must meet the enticements of the devil, and the serpent must not be nursed until it has been formed into a snake. For he who is admitted at the first approach is a siren, who, once admitted, escapes as a viper. When the enemy has broken through the barriers and opened an approach for himself, the second stage of wrestling follows, which is to stand foot to foot with the enemy and resist him vigorously. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you, Jas. 4:7; 1 Pet. 5:9. Stand, having your loins girded with truth, etc., Eph. 6:14. Stand fast in the faith, act like men, be strong, 1 Cor. 16:13. This standing is an act not of the body but of the soul, and it is the first act of a man raised from spiritual death. It signifies the straining of all the powers of the Spirit to resist Satan and the flesh, to attack them, to frustrate their deceit, to break their violence and to conquer the enemy. Thus Christ the Saviour resisted the threefold assault of the Tempter

units.la: nibus strenuè repugnavit,& pugnando stetit, & Michael atque Angeli ejus cum Dracone & Angelis ejus fortiter pugnárunt, non prævalentibus Dracone & Angelis ejus,ut in Cœlo locum invenirent,Apoc. XII. 7. 8. ὑπαγεσμὸν lucta-toribus relinquentes,ut insuperabili illa armatura Dei freti in pugna hac non languescant, sed sub ducis Christi signis, & Spiritu S. Archistratego hostem potenter feriant. Tertius gradus est, hostem vincere, & postquam periculum nostri fecit,& quæ in rem suam faciebant,molitus est,extremis viribus suis, confundere, turpémque in fugam dare. Quæ victoria fidei est. Hæc est victoria,quæ vincit mundum,fides vestra. Quis est victor mundi,nisi qui credit,quòd Jesus sit Filius Dei? 1. Joh. V. 4. 5. Vincit enim fides carnem, mundum & Sathanam non virtute & dignitate sua,sed Christi efficacitate,à quo solo victoria pendet & patratur. In mundo afflictionem habebitis. Sed confidite. Ego vici mundum,Joh.XVI. 33. In omnibus his ὑπερνικῶμεν plus quàm victores sumus per eum,qui nos dilexit,Rom.VIII.37. Gratia sit Deo, τῷ νῦν Θεῷ ἀμεταβλήτως ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ qui semper in Christo nos triumphare facit, 2. Cor. II. 14. Sed victoria illa, quamdiu in carne sumus, perinde ac fides ipsa, ejus causa, imperfecta est,nec ante mortem luctatoris numeris omnibus consummatur. Utut ergo victores aliquando simus, fieri tamen potest,ut, Sathana prælium instaurante iterum succumbamus,uti tristissimi Sanctorum lapsus oste-ndunt. Et si vel maximè novam victoriam reportamus,non tamen id sine vulnere quodam & cicatrice obtingit. Denique licèt hostes iterum iterúmque vincantur,tamen indefessi semper ad pugnam redeunt,ut luctæ hujus finis in exercita mortalitate sperari nullus possit. Nam & Christi lucta cum hostibus ejus ad mortem usque duravit. Quantò minùs fideles, qui in carne,peccato necdum soluta degunt,& in tabernaculo hoc στενάζοντες βαρούμενοι suspirant onerati, 2. Cor. V. 4. plenam in carne & à carne victoriam sibi polliceri ausint?
units.tr: vigorously, and by standing and fighting he stood firm; and Michael and his angels fought bravely with the Dragon and his angels, the Dragon and his angels not prevailing, so that they found no place in heaven, Rev. 12:7, 8. They leave no way of retreat [ὑπαγεσμὸν] to the wrestlers, so that, relying on that invincible armour of God, they may not grow weary in this battle, but under the banners of Christ the captain and by the Holy Spirit, the Archistrategus, may strike the enemy powerfully. The third stage is to overcome the enemy: after he has tested our strength and has laboured by his utmost powers to bring about what served his own purpose, to confound him and put him to shameful flight. This is the victory of faith. This is the victory that overcomes the world, your faith. Who is the victor over the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? 1 John 5:4, 5. For faith overcomes the flesh, the world and Satan not by its own strength and dignity, but by the efficacy of Christ, from whom alone the victory depends and is achieved. In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage, I have overcome the world, John 16:33. In all these things we more than conquer [ὑπερνικῶμεν] through him who loved us, Rom. 8:37. Thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ [τῷ νῦν Θεῷ ἀμεταβλήτως ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ], 2 Cor. 2:14. But that victory, as long as we are in the flesh, is imperfect, just as faith itself, of which it is the fruit, is imperfect; and it is not fully completed before the death of the wrestler. Therefore, however often we may at some time be victors, it can nevertheless happen that, when Satan renews the battle, we again give way, as the most sorrowful falls of the saints show. And even if we win a new victory, it does not come without some wound and scar. Finally, although the enemies are conquered again and again, they always return to the fight untiring, so that no end of this struggle can be hoped for in our mortal life. For Christ's own wrestling with his enemies lasted even to death. How much less should the faithful, who live in the flesh, not yet freed from sin, and groaning, being burdened [στενάζοντες βαρούμενοι] in this tabernacle, 2 Cor. 5:4, dare to promise themselves a victory complete in the flesh and from the flesh?

units.la: CLX. De causis & utilitate luctæ spiritualis cum carne, mundo & Sathana, pluscula Loc. XXI. 7. diximus. Cuncta ad humilitatem & studium faciunt. Ad humilitatem, ne nobis placeamus, si quid boni cogitasse, dixisse, vel fecisse videamur. Ad studium, quia Spiritus ad resistendum carni mensura uberior non sine studio & precibus datur,& lucta atque tentatio multiplex in hac vita & via nostra nobis parata est, ad quam armaturæ Dei omnis usus, & summa contentio requiritur.
units.tr: CLX. We have said a good deal about the causes and usefulness of spiritual wrestling with the flesh, the world and Satan at Loc. XXI. 7. All of it serves humility and diligence. It serves humility, so that we may not please ourselves if we seem to have thought, said or done anything good. It serves diligence, because a fuller measure of the Spirit for resisting the flesh is not given without diligence and prayer, and because manifold struggle and temptation are prepared for us in this life and on our way, for which the whole use of the armour of God and the utmost exertion are required.

units.la: LOCUS VICESIMUS QUARTUS. De CONSTANTIA FOEDERIS GRATIÆ. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: LOCUS VICESIMUS QUARTUS. On the CONSTANCY OF THE COVENANT OF GRACE. A SUMMARY.

units.la: Fœderis Gratiæ constantia in Perseverantia Sanctorum, & certitudine salutis consistit. 1. Utriusque nexus indivulsus, & ad salutem necessitas. 2. Utriusque quædam firmitas est; at prior objecti, posterior subjecti firmitas est. 3. Perseverantiæ Sanctorum definitio. 4. Non quorumvis hominum, nec quævis est, sed militans hujus vitæ. 5. Liberale Dei donum, non habitus moralis, crebris actionibus acquisitus est. 6. Pontificiorum & Remonstrantium, ab usu liberi arbitrii illud suspendentium elenchus. 7. In dono hoc producendo tota S.S. Trinitas, & singulæ personæ distincta operatione œconomica, Deus Pater eligendo, Filius redimendo, & Spiritus S. obsignando (quæ totidem principalia perseverantiæ fundamenta sunt) laborant. 8. Dei PATRIS ad vitam æternam electio, Perseverantiæ præcipua basis est. 9. Exceptiones elisæ. 10. Electionis æternæ efficacia, & cum cæteris gratiæ beneficiis eodem electionis decreto definitis, nexus perseverantiam potenter evincit. 11. Dei FILII operatio œconomica, Fœdere Gratiæ se Mediatore, inito, redimentis, altera Perseverantiæ basis est. Nam Fœdus illud Gratiæ promissionem fidei & obedientiæ, secus quàm fœdus operum includit. 12. Et quidem fidei atque obedientiæ perseverantis. 13. Quam ob causam Fœdus Gratiæ etiam æternum appellatur. 14. Modus ille, quo Deus fidem conservat, & perennem reddit, tum in continuo influxu gratiæ in fœderatos. 15. Tum in protectione eorundem adversus hostes, ceu causas destruentes, consistit. 16. Quæ protectio etiam Ecclesiæ & fidelium super petra ædificationis similitudine. 17. Nec non præsidii & potentis custodiæ promissione insinuatur. 18. Promissionum fœderalium confirmatio perseverantiam docet; quæ gemina est, unà consistens in modo comparativo, quo illa cum rebus maximè stabilibus comparatur. 19. Velut cum conjugio. 20. Cum Testamento. 21. Cum statutis æternæ Providentiæ. 22. Altera consistens in factis & signis. Facta sunt ejusmodi, qualia homines ad promissionum fœderalium inprimis, corroborationem adhibent; cujusmodi sunt acta publica, libri, tabulæ, quibus promissiones inscribuntur. 23. Juramenta, quibus eædem confirmantur. 24. Testes Personæ Trinitatis in Cœlo, & nubes hominum in terra. 25. Sacrificium Christi; 26. Monumenta, cujusmodi in terra sunt cultus Dei publicus; in Cœlo arcus ille circa thronum Christi, & Christus ipse, statua & altare. 27. Signa constantia promissionum earundem sunt convivia spiritualia cum fidelibus, arrhabo & sigillum Spiritus S. Sacramenta, ceu sigilla gratiæ. 28. Accedunt his preces pro dono perseverantiæ, & gratiarum actio pro eodem accepto. 29. Causa impulsiva fœderis Gratiæ, amor summus erga fœderatos, & in æternum perseverans; nec non ejusdem causa finalis, manifestatio gloriæ gratiæ; eandem perseverantiam postulant. 30. Inprimis fundamentum ejus est Christus Sponsor & Mediator. Qui in susceptione officii Mediatorii Deo Patri obedientiam ad colligendum sibi peculiarem populum promisit. 31. Tum ut servus Dei factus, certissimam adducendorum ad Deum illorum, in quorum gratiam servi munus suscepit, promissionem accepit. 32. Tum ut Sponsor & Mediator eorum, pro quibus spopondit, & Mediatoris officium suscepit, salutem in tuta arce collocavit. 33. Vicissim Deus Christo, Servo, Sponsori & Mediatori hæreditatem & peculium, cujus ille hæres, Rex, caput & Dominus esset, promittens, mittens, eorum, qui ei hæreditas & peculium dati sunt, salutem certissimam reddidit. 34. Non enim Deus Pater Filio Semen & hæreditatem promisit ex prævisione eorum, qui gratiam Dei liberè amplexuri erant. 35. Christus Ecclesiæ suæ propter obedientiam præstitam Caput factus, corporis sui salutem in tuto collocavit. 36. Executio Muneris Mediatorii Christi in eo consistit, quòd populum suum redemit & salvavit, & hostes suos vicit. 37. Ut Redemptor & Salvator redemptorum à se & salvatorum salutem certissimam reddidit. 38. Inprimis intercessio Christi pro suis, eorundem salutem extra aleam omnem incertitudinis ponit. 39. Idem fecit ut Victor & Triumphator Sathanæ. 40. Victoriæ Sathanæ, & fructus atque applicationis ejus distinctio inanis est. 41. Verissima in utroque foro, poli & soli, seu cordis, eâque perfectissima victoria est. 42. Quam hostes perseverantiæ mirum in modum extenuant. 43. Dei Spiritus S. operatio œconomica, obsignatio & sanctificatio electorum & redemptorum, Tertia Perseverantiæ basis est. Nam ille datus fidelibus Spiritus veritatis & spei, in iisdem manet. 44. Ceu sigillum & arrhabo incertam eorum, quibus talis datus est, salutem esse non finit. 45. Ceu Spiritus potentiæ, potenter operatur novam creationem, conservat, & efficit, ut beneficia per Christum acquisita iis, qui Christi sunt, conferantur, & in iis maneant. Quæ constantia gratiarum à Spiritu S. collatarum probatur tum generatim, ex immutabilitate donorum Dei. 46. Nec non ex nexu indivulso beneficiorum Dei. 47. Beneficia Gratiæ à Spiritu S. collata singula perennant; veluti unio nostri cum Christo per fidem; 48. Justificatio. 49. Adoptio. 50. Sanctificatio. 51. Nec non per eandem producta in cordibus fidelium sanctitas, consistens partim in novitate vitæ. 52. Partim in triga illa virtutum, puta Fide, Spe & Charitate, quæ & conjunctæ stabiles sunt. 53. Et singulæ. 54. Juxta operationes has œconomicas trium personarum S. S. Trinitatis fidelium & regenitorum status immotus & illabefactabilis est. Nam electi à Patre certò salvantur. 55. Et redempti à Christo certò perseverant. 56. Et obsignati & sanctificati à Spiritu S. ad finem usque vitæ durant. 57. Ecclesiæ veteris de Perseverantia consensus ad seculum usque nonum, & confictatio deinceps oborta. 58. Post Reformationem palam Tridentini Perseverantiam Sanctorum proscripserunt. Lutherani ita intercidi, ut fideles totaliter, at non finaliter deficere possint, asserunt. Remonstrantes denuo eam exploserunt. 59. Argumenta Perseverantiæ opposita diluuntur petita ex verbis Ezechielis cap. XVIII. 24. 25. 60. Ex parabola Christi, Matth. XIII. 20. 21. 61. Limborchii instantiis fit satis. 62. Ex verbis S. Pauli Hebr. VI. 4. ş. 6. 63. Ex verbis S. Petri, 2. Petr. II. 18. &c. 64. Limborchii instantiæ expenduntur. 65. Ex Exemplis Davidis, Solomonis, Petri. 66. Nec non Hymenæi, Phileti, Alexandri & Demæ. 67. Ex eo, quòd Perseverantia cum adhortationibus, promissionibus & comminationibus Dei ἀσφαλῶς fit. 68. Perseverantiæ comes Certitudo fidei perseverantis & salutis est. 69. Certitudo in genere definitur & distinguitur. 70. Certitudo fidei alia via & luctans, alia Patriæ, & eluctans est. 71. Certitudo Gratiæ & salutis definitur, & fundamenta ejusdem panduntur. 72. Cujusmodi sunt ipsa Perseverantia Sanctorum, quæ certitudinem salutis necessario infert. 73. Fœderis Gratiæ & promissionum ejus stipulatio, cujus obedientia est, non timere, sed Deum habere pro suo clypeo, atque ei confidere. 74. Mutua Deum inter & fideles oppigneratio, qua fideles Deo se ipsos & salutem suam, ceu sacrum depositum oppignorant; 75. Et vicissim Deus fidelibus Spiritum suum, ceu arrhabonem & primitias, pignoris loco, confert, & eodem illos obsignat. 76. Cujus in fidelibus operatio & testimonium, quo unà cum Spiritu nostro testatur, certitudinem salutis potenter evincit. 77. Exceptio adversantium, quòd testimonium Spiritus S. secundum se, at non secundum nos certum fit, plane testimonium illud evertit. 78. Promissiones Dei generales, & speciales ipsius certitudinis. 79. Fidei salvificæ nativa indoles, quæ assensus & fiduciæ suæ certa est. 80. Mandatum probandæ & explorandæ fidei, absque qua homo reprobus est. 81. Fiducia remissionis peccatorum, quæ fidem justificantem consequitur, ut actus consolatorius, ipsa gratiæ certitudo est. 82. Fidei objectum & fructus eandem certitudinem gratiæ ostendunt. 83. Spei natura eandem confirmat. 84. Bellarmini spei certitudinem oppugnantis tricæ. 85. Charitatis indoles non patitur amantem Dei incertum esse de mutuo amore Dei erga se, qui in cor ejus per Spiritum S. diffusus est. 86. Unio, communio & familiare nostrum cum Deo commercium certitudinis Gratiæ ejusdem index est. 87. Nec non electionis & vocationis nostræ firmandæ studium. 88. Precum efficacia & privilegium. 89. Denique Sacramentorum obsignatio. 90. Fundamentis ejusmodi freti Sancti certitudi-nem nem gratiæ præ se firmiter tulerunt. Veluti Abrahamus, David, Paulus, non ullo speciali privilegio vel revelatione, sed fide & revelatione omnibus credentibus communi. 91. Singuli proin fideles studium ad plenitudinem spei in finem usque demonstrare debent. 92. Methodus, qua de Gratia & salute fideles se certos reddere possunt. 93. Non in præsens duntaxat, sed in futurum etiam fideles de Gratia Dei & salute certi esse possunt. 94. Non ex facultate, & integritate potestatis suæ, sed ex eo, quòd Spiritum & fidem habent. 95. Neque tamen fideles in hac vita eum certitudinis gradum consequuntur, qui omnem contrarii formidinem perpetuò excludat; quia indiciorum experimentalium certitudo subinde non parum à carnis reliquiis. 96. Inprimis à tentationibus labefactatur. 97. Neque tamen ita evertitur; 98. Sed resuscitatur tandem, & confirmatur magis. 99. Ecclesiæ veteris & Scholasticorum de certitudine Gratiæ sensus. 100. Post Reformationem eam palam oppugnant Pontificii. 101. Et reduces in eorum castra Remonstrantes. 102. Eorum conspirantium argumenta certitudini Gratiæ opposita refelluntur. Velut, quòd nemo dicere possit, corsiuum purum esse, & nesciat homo, amore an odio dignus sit; 103. Quòd perfectissimi quique certitudinem gratiæ sibi vindicare ausi non fuerint. 104. Quòd Scriptura varias conditiones, quoad impletionem hominis incertas, præscribat. 105. Quòd post peractam etiam pœnitentiam dubia sit gratia Dei, & remissio peccatorum. 106. Quòd Scriptura diserte timorem commendet. 107. Quòd in Syllogismo practico Propositio Minor, qua fideles se credere & resipiscere assumunt, prorsus incerta, non revelata, adeòque nec fidei sit. 108. Certum esse certitudine fidei potest, quod immediatè in Verbo Dei non continetur. 109. Bellarmini ratiunculæ, quòd de sua fide & resipiscentia nemo certitudine fidei certus esse possit, eliduntur. 110. Doctrina de certitudine Gratiæ & Salutis non est pulvinar carnis, nec pietati, bonis moribus & precibus inimica. 111. Ceu pretiosus Sponsæ Christi thesaurus firmiter retinepi debet. 112.
units.tr: The constancy of the covenant of grace consists in the perseverance of the saints and the certainty of salvation. (1) The bond between the two is indissoluble, and both are necessary to salvation. (2) Each has a certain firmness: the firmness of the first lies in its object, that of the second in its subject. (3) A definition of the perseverance of the saints. (4) It is not the perseverance of any men, nor of every kind, but that of those fighting in this life. (5) It is a liberal gift of God, not a moral habit acquired by repeated acts. (6) A refutation of the Papists and Remonstrants, who make it depend on the exercise of free will. (7) In producing this gift the whole Holy Trinity works, each person with a distinct economic operation: God the Father by choosing, the Son by redeeming, and the Holy Spirit by sealing. These are the three principal foundations of perseverance. (8) The election of God the Father to eternal life is the chief basis of perseverance. (9) The exceptions are overthrown. (10) The efficacy of eternal election, and its connection with the other benefits of grace, which are determined by the same decree of election, powerfully proves perseverance. (11) The economic operation of God the Son, who redeems by entering as Mediator into the covenant of grace, is the second basis of perseverance. For that covenant of grace includes a promise of faith and obedience, unlike the covenant of works. (12) And indeed of persevering faith and obedience. (13) For this reason the covenant of grace is also called eternal. (14) The manner in which God preserves faith and keeps it lasting consists in a continual inflow of grace into those in covenant. (15) It also consists in their protection against enemies, as destroying causes. (16) This protection is also suggested to the Church and the faithful by the similitude of building upon a rock. (17) It is likewise implied in the promise of defence and a mighty guardianship. (18) The confirmation of the covenant promises teaches perseverance. It is twofold: one part consists in the comparative mode, by which those promises are compared with the most stable things. (19) As with marriage. (20) As with a testament. (21) As with the decrees of eternal providence. (22) The other consists in deeds and signs. These are such deeds as men chiefly use to strengthen covenant promises: public acts, books, and tablets on which promises are inscribed. (23) Oaths, by which the same promises are confirmed. (24) The witnesses are the Persons of the Trinity in heaven and the clouds of men on earth. (25) The sacrifice of Christ. (26) Monuments: on earth, the public worship of God; in heaven, that rainbow around the throne of Christ, and Christ himself, the statue and the altar. (27) The signs of the constancy of these promises are the spiritual banquets with the faithful, the earnest and seal of the Holy Spirit, and the sacraments as seals of grace. (28) To these are added prayers for the gift of perseverance, and thanksgiving for it once received. (29) The impulsive cause of the covenant of grace is the highest love toward those in covenant, a love that endures for ever; its final cause is the manifestation of the glory of grace. Both demand perseverance. (30) Chiefly, its foundation is Christ, the Surety and Mediator, who in undertaking the office of Mediator promised obedience to God the Father, to gather for himself a peculiar people. (31) Then, having become the servant of God, he received the most certain promise that those for whose sake he took up the servant's task would be brought to God. (32) Then, as Surety and Mediator of those for whom he gave his pledge and took up the office of Mediator, he placed their salvation in a safe stronghold. (33) In turn, God, promising to Christ the Servant, Surety and Mediator an inheritance and a people of whom he would be heir, King, head and Lord, gave most certain salvation to those who were given to him as his inheritance and people, by sending them. (34) For God the Father did not promise the Son a seed and an inheritance on the foresight of those who were going to embrace the grace of God freely. (35) Christ, made Head of his Church on account of the obedience he rendered, placed the salvation of his body in safety. (36) The execution of Christ's office as Mediator consists in this: that he redeemed and saved his people, and conquered his enemies. (37) As Redeemer and Saviour he gave most certain salvation to those whom he redeemed and saved. (38) Chiefly, the intercession of Christ for his own places their salvation beyond all hazard of uncertainty. (39) He did the same as Conqueror and Triumphant over Satan. (40) The distinction between the victory over Satan and the fruits and application of that victory is an empty one. (41) It is a most true victory in both courts, of heaven and of earth, or of the heart, and a most perfect victory. (42) Enemies of perseverance wonderfully diminish it. (43) The economic operation of the Holy Spirit, the sealing and sanctification of the elect and redeemed, is the third basis of perseverance. For that Spirit of truth and hope, given to the faithful, remains in them. (44) As seal and earnest, he does not allow the salvation of those to whom he is given in such a way to be uncertain. (45) As Spirit of power, he powerfully works the new creation, preserves it, and brings it about that the benefits acquired through Christ are conferred upon those who belong to Christ and remain in them. This constancy of the graces conferred by the Holy Spirit is proved both generally, from the immutability of God's gifts. (46) And from the indissoluble connection of God's benefits. (47) Each of the benefits of grace conferred by the Holy Spirit endures; for example, our union with Christ through faith; (48) justification; (49) adoption; (50) sanctification; (51) and likewise the holiness produced by the same Spirit in the hearts of the faithful, consisting partly in newness of life, (52) partly in that triad of virtues, namely Faith, Hope and Charity, which, joined together, are stable. (53) And each one singly. (54) According to these economic operations of the three Persons of the Holy Trinity, the state of the faithful and regenerate is unmoved and unshakeable. For the elect are surely saved by the Father. (55) And the redeemed surely persevere by Christ. (56) And the sealed and sanctified last until the end of life by the Holy Spirit. (57) The consensus of the ancient Church on perseverance lasted until the ninth century, and the wrangling that arose afterward. (58) After the Reformation the Tridentine fathers openly rejected the perseverance of the saints. The Lutherans assert that the faithful can fall away totally, but not finally. The Remonstrants have again cast it out. (59) The arguments against perseverance are answered, drawn from the words of Ezekiel ch. XVIII. 24, 25. (60) From the parable of Christ, Matth. XIII. 20, 21. (61) The instances of Limborch are satisfied. (62) From the words of St Paul, Heb. VI. 4-6. (63) From the words of St Peter, 2 Pet. II. 18, etc. (64) The instances of Limborch are weighed. (65) From the examples of David, Solomon, and Peter. (66) Likewise of Hymenaeus, Philetus, Alexander, and Demas. (67) From the fact that perseverance comes about [ἀσφαλῶς] with the exhortations, promises and threats of God. (68) Accompanying perseverance is the certainty of the persevering faith and of salvation. (69) Certainty is defined and distinguished in general. (70) The certainty of faith is one thing in the way of struggle, another that of the homeland, which is attained by struggling through. (71) The certainty of grace and of salvation is defined, and its foundations are laid open. (72) Such is the perseverance of the saints itself, which necessarily brings certainty of salvation. (73) The stipulation of the covenant of grace and of its promises, whose obedience is not to fear but to have God as one's shield and to trust in him. (74) The mutual pledge between God and the faithful, by which the faithful pledge themselves and their salvation to God as a sacred deposit; (75) and in turn God gives his Spirit to the faithful, as earnest and firstfruits, in place of a pledge, and seals them by him. (76) The operation of this Spirit in the faithful, and his testimony by which he bears witness together with our spirit, powerfully proves the certainty of salvation. (77) The objection of opponents, that the testimony of the Holy Spirit is certain in itself but not certain to us, utterly overthrows that testimony. (78) The general and special promises of God concern this certainty. (79) The native character of saving faith, which is certain of its assent and its trust. (80) The command to test and examine faith, without which a man is reprobate. (81) The trust in the forgiveness of sins, which follows justifying faith as a consoling act, is itself the certainty of grace. (82) The object and fruit of faith show the same certainty of grace. (83) The nature of hope confirms the same. (84) The wretched arguments of Bellarmine, who attacks the certainty of hope. (85) The nature of charity does not allow the one who loves God to be uncertain of God's mutual love toward him, which has been poured into his heart by the Holy Spirit. (86) The union, communion and familiar intercourse of ours with God is the index of this certainty of grace. (87) Likewise the zeal for confirming our election and calling. (88) The efficacy and privilege of prayers. (89) Lastly, the sealing of the sacraments. (90) Relying on such foundations, the saints have firmly borne the certainty of grace before themselves, as Abraham, David and Paul did, not by any special privilege or revelation, but by faith and by a revelation common to all believers. (91) Therefore each of the faithful ought to show zeal for the fullness of hope until the end. (92) The method by which the faithful can make themselves certain of grace and salvation. (93) The faithful can be certain of the grace and salvation of God not only for the present, but also for the future. (94) Not from the faculty and integrity of their own power, but from the fact that they have the Spirit and faith. (95) Yet in this life the faithful do not attain such a degree of certainty as perpetually excludes all fear of the contrary; for the certainty of experimental evidences is at times not a little weakened by the remnants of the flesh. (96) Chiefly it is shaken by temptations. (97) Yet it is not thus overthrown; (98) but it is at length revived and confirmed the more. (99) The sense of the ancient Church and of the Schoolmen concerning the certainty of grace. (100) After the Reformation the Papists openly attack it. (101) And the Remonstrants, returning to their camp. (102) The arguments of these conspirators against the certainty of grace are refuted. For example, that no one can say his heart is pure, and that a man does not know whether he is worthy of love or of hatred; (103) that the most perfect men have not dared to claim for themselves the certainty of grace; (104) that Scripture prescribes various conditions, uncertain as to their fulfilment by man; (105) that even after repentance has been completed, the grace of God and the forgiveness of sins remain doubtful; (106) that Scripture expressly commends fear; (107) that in the practical syllogism the minor proposition, by which the faithful assume that they believe and repent, is wholly uncertain, not revealed, and therefore not of faith. (108) Something not immediately contained in the Word of God can be certain with the certainty of faith. (109) Bellarmine's petty arguments, that no one can be certain by the certainty of faith of his own faith and repentance, are overthrown. (110) The doctrine of the certainty of grace and of salvation is no pillow for the flesh, nor hostile to piety, good morals and prayers. (111) Like the precious treasure of the Bride of Christ, it must be firmly retained. (112)

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: NON postrema Constantiæ Fœderis Gratiæ Gratia est. Quæ in eo potissimùm consistit, quòd non tantùm Deus à fœdere semel inito nunquam discedit, sed etiam foederati homines per Dei fœdus contrahentis singularem & eximiam gratiam non solùm in fœdere eo ad finem usque vitæ perseverant, & æternùm salvantur; sed etiam Gratiæ fœderalis sensum ad consolationem suam in vita & morte percipiunt, adeòque de gratia Dei & consecutione salutis certi sunt. Duo ergo Constantiæ Fœderis Gratiæ capita sunt, Gratia Perseverantiæ Sanctorum in Gratia semel collata, ad finem usque: & Gratia Certitudinis Gratiæ, qua fœderati de amore & gratia Dei atque consecutione salutis suæ certi sunt.
units.tr: The last of the gifts of the Covenant of Grace is not the least. It consists chiefly in this: God never withdraws from the covenant once entered, and the men who are party to it not only persevere in that covenant to the end of life and are saved for ever, but also perceive, for their consolation in life and death, the sense of the covenanted grace, and so are certain of the grace of God and of attaining salvation. There are therefore two chief parts of the Covenant of Grace: the Grace of the Perseverance of the Saints, once bestowed in grace, to the end; and the Grace of the Certainty of Grace, by which the covenanted are certain of the love and grace of God and of the attainment of their salvation.

units.la: II. Etenim absque Perseverantia Sanctorum est, reliqua omnis gratia, quantacunque illa est, irrita est, neque ad salutem proficit. Nam ὁ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος, οὗτος σωθήσεται Qui sustinuerit, perseveraverit ad finem usque, ille salvabitur, Matth. XXIV. 13. Qui vincit, ille induetur vestimentis albis, Apoc. III. 5. Esto fidelis usque ad mortem, & dabo tibi coronam vitæ, ibid. II. 10. Neque electus, neque fidelis, neque sanctus est, qui non perseverat. Non electus, quia electio assequitur, Rom. XI. 7. Non fidelis, quia vera fides & Deum glorificat, & peccatorem justificat & salvat. Quod non faceret, si non ad finem usque perseveraret. Non sanctus, quia קדוש יאמר הכתוב לחיים Sanctus appellabitur, qui scriptus est ad vitam in Hierosolyma, Esaj. IV. 3. At nemo non perseverans ad vitam scriptus est. Et par Certitudinis Gratiæ & salutis ratio est, qua ad finem perseverantes certam utrius-que fiduciam & spem habent.
units.tr: II. Indeed, without the Perseverance of the Saints, all the rest of grace, however great it is, is vain and does nothing for salvation. For "he who endures to the end, the same shall be saved" (Matt. 24:13); "he who overcomes shall be clothed in white garments" (Rev. 3:5); "be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life" (ibid. 2:10). He is neither elect, nor faithful, nor holy, who does not persevere. Not elect, because election obtains its end (Rom. 11:7). Not faithful, because true faith glorifies God and justifies and saves the sinner; it would not do this if it did not persevere to the end. Not holy, because "he shall be called holy who is written unto life in Jerusalem" (Isa. 4:3) [קדוש יאמר הכתוב לחיים]. But no one is written unto life who does not persevere. The same reasoning holds for the Certainty of Grace and of salvation, which those who persevere to the end have as a sure confidence and hope in each.

units.la: Nam qui ad Deum accedit, ante omnia scire debet, quòd accedentes de gratia Dei & salute certi esse possint, tum quia aliàs certitudinem, quæ πληροφορία τῆς ἐλπίδος plenitudo spei Hebr. VI. 11. est, non quæret: tum quia sine ea homo Deum diligere, eíque gratias agere, non potest, imò Deum, quem extra certam salutis & gratiæ spem non potest non considerare ut judicem, odit: tum quia jubemur vocationem & electionem nostram βεβαίαν firmam, certam, nobis exploratam intimè facere, 2. Pet. I. 10. tum quia sine ea homo spem nullam habet, qui statu eorum est, qui in mundo ἄθεοι sine Deo sunt, Eph. II. 12. tum quia sine spe & certitudine hac facile λήθην λαμβάνομεν oblivisci mur purificationis peccatorum τῶν πάλαι olim admissorum, 2. Pet. I. 9. tum denique, quia doctrina illa pietatis nutricula est. Nam efficit timorem Dei, non illum, quo Deum fugimus & horremus, sed quo eum, ceu Patrem, unicè amabilem & desiderabilem, æstimamus, caventes enixè, ne gratiam Dei εἰς κενὸν in vanum receperimus, 2. Cor. VI. 1. & operam dantes, ut lucem faciei ejus, ceu Patris nostri, semper in nobis resplendentem habeamus. Qui Dei timor tantum abest, ut incertos dubiósque de gratia & salute reddat, ut potiùs אוצר ישועות thesaurus & veluti arca custos salutum & sapientiæ, Esaj. XXXIII. 6. & מקור חיים fons vitæ, Prov. XIV. 27. sit.
units.tr: For whoever approaches God must first know that those who draw near can be certain of God's grace and salvation. Otherwise they would not seek the certainty that is "the fullness of hope" (Heb. 6:11). Without it, a person cannot love God or give him thanks. Indeed, someone who lacks a sure hope of grace and salvation cannot help regarding God as a judge, and so hates him. We are also commanded to make our calling and election firm [βεβαίαν], certain, and thoroughly known to us (2 Pet. 1:10).
