To him he said: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession, Ps. II. 8. Who shall declare his generation? If he shall make his soul

units.la: Tum ut Sponsor & Mediator eorum, pro quibus spopondit, & Mediatoris officium suscepit, salutem in tuta arce collocarit. mam suam sacrificium, videbit Semen, Esaj. LIII. 8. Populus tuus spontaneitatum in die strenuitatis tuæ. In ornamentis sanctitatis tuæ. Ros generationis tuæ tibi est præ rore uteri auroræ, Psal. CX. 3. Et illi ipsi, pro quibus Christus Patri servivit, ei in populum promissi sunt. Tui erant, & tu mihi eos dedisti, Joh. XVII. 6. Mea omnia tua sunt, & tua mea sunt, & glorificatus sum in iis, ibid. v. 10. Posuit Deus Pater Filium κληρονόμον πάντων hæredem omnium, Hebr. I. 2. Dedit ipsi ἀδελφὸς fratres, παιδία pueros, ibid. II. 12. 14. Fecit eum κύριον Dominum, Actor. II. 36. Unxit eum Regem super montem Sion, Psal. II. 6. Venit principatus in humerum ipsius, ad amplificationem principatus, & pacem sine fine super throno Davidis, & super Regno ipsius, &c. Esaj. IX. 6. 7. Omnia subjecit pedibus ipsius, & dedit ipsum Caput super omnia Ecclesiæ, quæ est corpus ejus, Ephes. I. 22. 23. Taceo innumera ejusmodi, quæ intelligi non possunt, si fides ex voluntate hominum pendet, & semel credentes & Sancti deficere possunt. Si enim singuli deficere possunt, omnes deficere possunt. Si omnes deficere possunt, contingere potest, ut Christus mercedem operæ suæ amittat, hæreditate destituatur, semine, fratribus careat, Dominus sine populo, Rex sine Regno, Caput sine corpore existat. Promittitur ei Semen, promittuntur pueri. An ex voluntate eorum pendet, ut nascantur Christo, & ipse eorum Pater fiat? Promittitur hæreditas, Regnum, populus. An in potestate hominum est, ut fiant fundus possessionis ejus, vel non; Verbo & Spiritu suo eos sibi subjiciat, vel non? Et si hoc est, quomodo sine fine Regnum ejus est? Esaj. IX. 7. principatus ejus in æternum stat, Dan. II. 44?
units.tr: Then, as Surety and Mediator, he placed in a secure stronghold the salvation of those for whom he stood surety and undertook the office of Mediator: an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, Isa. LIII. 8. Your people shall offer themselves willingly in the day of your power, in the beauty of holiness; the dew of your youth is yours, like dew from the womb of the dawn, Ps. CX. 3. And those very people for whom Christ served the Father were promised to him as a people. They were yours, and you gave them to me, John XVII. 6. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them, ibid. v. 10. God the Father appointed the Son heir of all things [Greek: κληρονόμον πάντων], Heb. I. 2. He gave him brothers [Greek: ἀδελφούς] and children [Greek: παιδία], ibid. II. 12, 14. He made him Lord [Greek: κύριον], Acts II. 36. He anointed him King over Mount Zion, Ps. II. 6. The government shall be upon his shoulder, for the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, etc., Isa. IX. 6, 7. He put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, Eph. I. 22, 23. I pass over countless such things, which cannot be understood if faith depends on the will of men, and believers and saints, once they have believed, could fall away. For if individuals can fall away, all can fall away. If all can fall away, it may happen that Christ loses the reward of his labour, is deprived of his inheritance, lacks seed and brothers, is Lord without a people, King without a kingdom, Head without a body. The Seed is promised to him, children are promised. Does it depend on the will of these people that they are born to Christ and he becomes their Father? An inheritance, a kingdom, a people are promised. Is it in the power of men whether they become the estate of his possession or not; whether he subjects them to himself by his Word and Spirit or not? And if so, how is his kingdom without end, Isa. IX. 7; how does his dominion stand for ever, Dan. II. 44?

units.la: XXXV. Sed forte certum Christo Semen, certa hæreditas, certum Regnum est, sed ex prævisione eorum, qui gratiam libera voluntate amplexuri erant. Ita dicis causa Remonstrantes; sed revera omnem promissionem, quin & prævisionis certitudinem sustollentes. Promissionem, quia ea erit vel ipsa prævisio, vel aliqua alia promissio Christo ab æterno facta. At non prævisio, quia prævisio & promissio toto cœlo differunt; illa intellectus, hæc voluntatis: illa rei ex arbitrio humano suspensæ; hæc rerum, quæ in arbitrio promittentis sunt. Neque Deus promittere potest, quæ ab alieno arbitrio pendent, nisi fingatur, μεγαλαυχῶν instar loquens elata, 1. Sam. II. 3. Non alia promissio quæpiam Christo ab æterno facta, quia talis prævisionem obsequii vel antecessit, vel secuta est. Si antecessit, obsequium non amplius ab arbitrio humano, sed a promissione Divina pendet. Si secuta est, ridicula promissio evadit. Pater enim Filio promitteret imperium in homines postquam Christum illud ab hominibus impetrandum prævidit. Certitudinem quoque prævisionis tollunt, quia obsequium illud ex eorum mente ad summum possibile foret, quatenus voluntas a Deo creanda potestatem illud præstandi haberet. At certò & determinatè futurum vel non futurum dici nequit. Nulla enim futuritionis determinatio vel a parte Dei, vel a parte rei est. Non a parte Dei, quem decreto aliquo obsequium prædeterminasse negant. Non a parte rei, seu voluntatis humanæ, utpote quæ nondum extitit, neque determinare
units.tr: XXXV. But perhaps the Semen, the inheritance and the Kingdom are certain for Christ, yet only from the foreseen will of those who were going to embrace grace by their free will. So the Remonstrants say, for the sake of argument; but in truth they overthrow every promise, and even the certainty of foreknowledge itself. Promise, because that would be either the foreknowledge itself or some other promise made to Christ from eternity. But it is not foreknowledge, because foreknowledge and promise differ as heaven from earth: the one belongs to the intellect, the other to the will; the one concerns a thing hanging on the human choice, the other concerns things that lie in the power of the one who promises. Nor can God promise what depends on another's will, unless we pretend that He is boasting [μεγαλαυχῶν], speaking loftily like the one in 1 Sam. 2.3. Nor is it some other promise made to Christ from eternity, for such a promise either preceded or followed the foreseen obedience. If it preceded, the obedience no longer depends on human choice but on the divine promise. If it followed, the promise turns out ridiculous. For the Father would promise the Son dominion over men after the Son had foreseen that He would obtain it from men. They also take away the certainty of foreknowledge, because that obedience, from their point of view, would be at most possible, insofar as the will to be created by God had the power to perform it. But it cannot be said with certainty and determinately that something will or will not be future. For there is no determination of future events either on God's side or on the side of the thing. Not on God's side, for they deny that He predetermined the obedience by any decree. Not on the side of the thing, that is, of the human will, since that does not yet exist and so could determine

units.la: quicquam potuit. Præterea Scriptura κρίσεως ejusmodi penitus incidit, utpote quæ docet, Semen, hæreditatem, Regnum Christo promissum & collatum non ex prævisa determinatione humanæ voluntatis, sed tum vi pacti, Testamenti & voluntatis absolutæ Patris & Filii; Psal. II. 8. Esaj. LIII. 10. Luc. XXII. 29. tum vi juris Filii ipsius, Regnum in eos, quos sanguine proprio sibi emit, non ut precarium, & ab iis, qui subditi ejus sunt, pendens, sed ceu sibi debitum duplici jure, tum mercedis, ob laborem Deo navatum, tum emptionis ob pretium pro hominibus solutum, petentis. De jure mercedis sic ipse Christus. Atqui ego dixeram: In vanum laboravi, in cassum & frustra vim meam consumpsi. Certè judicium meum est apud Dominum, & opera pretium meum cum Deo meo, Esaj. XLIX. 4. Et Deus Pater: Si posuerit animam suam sacrificium, videbit Semen: Propter laborem animæ suæ videbit fructum, ibid. LIII. 10. 11. De jure emptionis Paulus: Acquisivit Ecclesiam proprio sanguine, Actor. XX. 28. Empti estis pretio, 1. Cor. VII. 23. Dedit eum pro nobis, ut redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, & purificaret sibi populum peculiarem, æmulum bonorum operum, Tit. II. 14.
units.tr: nothing. Moreover, Scripture falls utterly into a judgement [κρίσεως] of this kind, since it teaches that the Semen, the inheritance and the Kingdom were promised and conferred on Christ not from a foreseen determination of the human will, but by the power of the covenant, testament and absolute will of the Father and the Son: Ps. 2.8; Isa. 53.10; Luke 22.29. And by the power of the Son's own right, He seeks the Kingdom over those whom He bought for Himself with His own blood, not as something precarious and dependent on those who are His subjects, but as owed to Him by a twofold right: the right of wages, for the labour undertaken for God, and the right of purchase, for the price paid for men. Christ Himself speaks of the right of wages thus: "But I had said: I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing and in vain. Surely my judgement is with the Lord, and my reward with my God," Isa. 49.4. And God the Father: "If He shall make His soul an offering for sin, He shall see His Seed… for the travail of His soul He shall see fruit," ibid. 53.10, 11. Of the right of purchase, Paul: "He obtained the Church with His own blood," Acts 20.28. "You were bought with a price," 1 Cor. 7.23. "He gave Himself for us, that He might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for Himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works," Titus 2.14.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: At nec illud leve est, quòd Christus Ecclesiæ & fidelibus promissus & datus Caput est. Caput autem cum corpore unitum sit oportet; neque uniri sine spiritu ex capite in corpus vim exerente potest. Christus ergo Ecclesiæ caput, eidem Spiritum suum, & Spiritus sui dona, justitiam & vitam donat. Veri in charitate crescamus in ipsum quoad omnia, qui est caput, Christus. Ex quo omne corpus coagmentatum & compactum per omnem junczuram suppeditationis secundum operationem in mensura uniuscujusque partis incrementum corporis facit ad ædificationem sui in charitate, Eph. IV. 15. 16. Vanissimum verò est, quòd adversarii Christum omnium hominum caput esse ratione repræsentationis & meriti, solorum verò fidelium, quandiu tales perseverant, ratione influxus vitæ, & applicationis meriti, quippe ab arbitrio hominis suspensæ, pertendunt. Quæ mera durities præfracti animi, & inanis speculatio cerebri humani est. Scriptura enim Christum non omnium hominum, sed solius Ecclesiæ, & illius Ecclesiæ, quæ ejus corpus est, caput facit. Et sic caput facit, ut etiam Patrem, fratrem, amicum, sponsum faciat, qualis omnium respectu non est. Tum infelix Christi meritum inter & influxum divortium cum natura unionis caput inter & corpus, titulorum, quibus Scriptura unionem hanc declarat, ἐμφάσει, oppositione primi & secundi Adami, sapientia atque Majestate tanti capitis, & unitate corporis ejus pugnat. Cum natura unionis caput inter & corpus, cujus duo gradus sunt, prior in consilio & judicio Dei, in quo Christus ex sua & Patris voluntate eos, pro quibus mortuus est, repræsentat, quibus proin unitus est unione moraliter dicta, & per repræsentationem; posterior in hominibus ipsis, quibus unione spirituali, per Spiritum S. unitur. Vi prioris illi, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, in ipso moriente esse censebantur; vi posterioris ipse vivit in fidelibus, Gal. II. 20. & in ipsorum cordibus dibus habitat, Ephes. III. 17. Prior posteriorem infert, imò in Christo voluntatem absolutè promerendi salutem iis, quos moriendo repræsentavit, in Patre verò voluntatem absolutam iisdem justitiam & vitam adjudicandi includit. Non potest enim Christus concipi ut ferens pœnas, tanquam caput illorum, & pro illis, quin & illi censeantur tulisse pœnas. Hoc judicamus, quòd si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, igitur illi omnes mortui sunt, 2. Cor. V. 15. Neque etiam in Christo censeri possunt tulisse pœnas peccatorum, & vitam adipisci, nisi quibus Deus illam adjudicat. Nam quæ propter repræsentationem uniuntur, illorum extrema non aliter uniuntur, quàm quatenus ejusmodi voluntas & placitum est, cujus vi fructus æquè reales ab uno ad alterum derivantur, ac si physicè unita essent. Ubi enim extrema realiter unita non sunt, neque ulli fructus communicantur, unio nec realis, nec moralis obtinere potest. Quamobrem si adjudicatio justitiæ, & applicatio meriti Christi & fructuum ejus à libera voluntate hominis pendet, unio Christi morientis cum iis, pro quibus mortuus est, & quos moriendo repræsentavit, tollitur; imò nec Christus mori potuit, ut caput repræsentans cujusquam hominis. Fructus enim mortis Christi, seu adjudicatio vitæ non ex repræsentatione capitis, sed ex sententia & arbitrio hominum pendebit. Quod crudum dogma est, & pugnans è diametro cum Scriptura, quæ realem ἀντιμισθίαν bonorum & malorum inter Christum, & eos, pro quibus mortuus est, toties inculcat. Dum enim factus est peccatum pro nobis, nos facti sumus justitia Dei in ipso, 2. Cor. V. 21. & dum ipse maledictio pro nobis factus est, nos à maledictione redempti sumus, Gal. III. 13. Ex hac porro unione morali necessariò unio spiritualis & fidei fluit. Si enim Christus non pro se, sed pro nobis mortuus est, & quidem ex voluntate absoluta, non à conditione ulla suspensa, necessariò sequitur, voluisse eum quoque voluntate absoluta, tum suo, tum Patris illis per communicationem fidei & Spiritus sui uniri. Aliàs ii, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, simul justificarentur & non justificarentur. Justificarentur, quia Christus non posset eos repræsentare in morte sua, nec Pater repræsentationem eam acceptare, nisi justitiam Christi pro justitia eorum, quos repræsentat, haberet. Non justificarentur, quia illis Christus fidem, sine qua nemo justificatur, non communicaret. Quòd si fides non donaretur iis, pro quibus Christus mortuus est; judicium Patris à seipso dissentiret, & voluntas Filii secum ipsa luctaretur. Pater enim Christo Sponsori affirmasset, se acceptasse satisfactionem Filii nomine eorum, pro quibus mortuus est; & tamen fidem non donans hominibus, sed eam à libero eorum arbitrio suspendens, negaret, eos satisfecisse in Christo: Christus voluisset mori ut caput hominum, & tamen mortuus non foret, ut caput hominum, quia homines in ipso mortui non essent. Pugnat etiam divortium illud capitis promerentis & influentis tum cum emphasi titulorum Christi, cujusmodi sunt, quòd Pater, frater, amicus, Sponsus, caput appellatur, adeòque in mystico illo patre, fratre, amico, sponso, capite reperiri debet, quicquid officii pater erga liberos, frater erga fra-
units.tr: Nor is this a slight matter: that Christ was promised and given to the Church and to believers as their Head. But the head must be united with the body, and it cannot be united without the Spirit exercising its power from the head into the body. Christ therefore, as Head of the Church, gives to it His Spirit, and the gifts of His Spirit, righteousness and life. "Let us grow up in love into Him in all things, who is the head, Christ; from whom the whole body, fitted and joined together through every joint of supply, according to the working of each part, makes the increase of the body for the building up of itself in love," Eph. 4.15, 16. It is most empty, however, that our opponents insist that Christ is the head of all men by reason of representation and merit, but of believers alone, as long as they persevere, by reason of the influx of life and the application of merit, which of course depends on human choice. This is mere hardness of a stubborn mind, and empty speculation of the human brain. For Scripture makes Christ the head not of all men, but of the Church alone, and of that Church which is His body. And it makes Him head in such a way that it also makes Him Father, brother, friend and bridegroom, which is not the case with respect to all. Then, the unhappy divorce between Christ's merit and influx, and between the head and body, fights against the nature of the union, against the titles by which Scripture declares this union, by emphasis [ἐμφάσει], by the opposition of the first and second Adam, and against the wisdom and majesty of so great a head and the unity of His body. The nature of the union between head and body has two degrees: the first is in the counsel and judgement of God, in which Christ, by His own and the Father's will, represents those for whom He died, and with whom He is therefore united by a union called moral, and by representation; the second is in the men themselves, with whom He is united by a spiritual union, through the Holy Spirit. By virtue of the first, those for whom Christ died were regarded as being in Him when He died; by virtue of the second, He Himself lives in believers, Gal. 2.20, and dwells in their hearts, Eph. 3.17. The first implies the second; indeed, in Christ it includes an absolute will to procure salvation for those whom He represented in dying, and in the Father it includes an absolute will to adjudge righteousness and life to the same. For Christ cannot be conceived as bearing punishments as head of those and for them without those also being regarded as having borne punishments. "We judge that if one died for all, then all have died," 2 Cor. 5.15. Nor can they be regarded as having borne the punishments of sins in Christ, and as having obtained life, unless God adjudges it to them. For those who are united on account of representation are not united at their extremities except insofar as such is the will and pleasure, by whose power the fruits, equally real, pass from one to the other, as if they were physically united. For where the extremes are not really united, and no fruits are communicated, a union can obtain neither real nor moral existence. Therefore, if the adjudication of righteousness and the application of the merit of Christ and its fruits depend on the free will of man, the union of Christ dying with those for whom He died, and whom in dying He represented, is taken away; indeed Christ could not even have died as head representing anyone. For the fruit of Christ's death, that is, the adjudication of life, would depend not on the representation of the head but on the opinion and choice of men. This is a crude dogma, and diametrically opposed to Scripture, which so often inculcates the real reciprocal exchange [ἀντιμισθίαν] of good and evil between Christ and those for whom He died. For while He was made sin for us, we were made the righteousness of God in Him, 2 Cor. 5.21; and while He was made a curse for us, we were redeemed from the curse, Gal. 3.13. Moreover, from this moral union the spiritual and faith union necessarily flows. For if Christ died not for Himself but for us, and indeed by an absolute will not suspended on any condition, it necessarily follows that He also willed, by an absolute will, both on His own part and on the Father's, that they should be united to Him through the communication of faith and of His Spirit. Otherwise those for whom Christ died would at the same time be justified and not justified. Justified, because Christ could not represent them in His death, nor could the Father accept that representation, unless He had the righteousness of Christ in place of the righteousness of those whom He represents. Not justified, because Christ would not communicate to them faith, without which no one is justified. And if faith were not given to those for whom Christ died, the Father's judgement would dissent from itself, and the will of the Son would struggle against itself. For the Father would have declared to Christ the Surety that He had accepted the Son's satisfaction in the name of those for whom He died; yet by not giving faith to men, but making it depend on their free choice, He would deny that they had been satisfied in Christ. Christ would have willed to die as the head of men, and yet He would not have died as the head of men, because men would not have died in Him. That divorce of the head that merits and influences also clashes with the emphasis on the titles of Christ, such as that He is called Father, brother, friend, Bridegroom, Head, and therefore whatever duty a father owes his children, a brother his brother, a friend his friend, a bridegroom his bride, and the economic, political and physical head owes to the body of which it is a part, must be found in that mystical father, brother, friend, bridegroom and head, not without influence, certainly, especially of the head upon the body; and it clashes also with the comparison of the first and second Adam, both of whom are called heads of their own not by representation alone,

units.la: trem, amicus erga amicum, sponsus erga sponsam & caput œconomicum, politicum & physicum erga congener corpus præstat, non sine influxu certè, inprimis capitis in corpus; tum cum collatione Adam primi & secundi, qui uterque caput suorum dicitur non repræsentatione sola, & merito vel demerito, sed etiam communicatione reali, quia primus peccatum & mortem communicat, adeòque etiam secundus justitiam & vitam communicare debet, & communicat, Rom. V. 12. 17. 19. tum cum Sapientia & Majestate Christi Capitis, quæ pati non potuit, ut caput esset in noxa, at incertus esse de gloria: ut sanguinem funderet pro sponsa, incertus de ejus fide: ut se per sponsionem & mortem uniret iis, quorum dubium esset, Pater an hostis, Rex gratiæ, an judex & vindex foret: denique cum unitate Corporis Christi, quia sic foret Caput omnium merito suo in cruce, paucorum in applicatione gratiæ per resurrectionem; omnibus vitam acquirens, nemini absoluta voluntate conferens; & membra diversissimæ sortis habens, alia, cum quibus nil commercii haberet, velut eos, quibus Evangelium non prædicatur; alia, quæ cum ipso idem Christus sunt, 1. Cor. XII. 12. alia modò in corporis sui unitatem adscita, alia mox deficientia ab eodem resecta; alia, quæ perpetuò animat; alia, quæ animare definit; alia, quæ Regno æterno donat; alia, quæ æternum in inferis torquentur.
units.tr: ...of a wife, the husband of his bride, and the head in economy, politics and nature toward the body of the same kind, not without some influence, certainly, of the head upon the body; then with the comparison of the first and second Adam, both of whom are called heads of their own people, not by representation alone and by merit or demerit, but also by real communication, because the first communicates sin and death, and so the second too ought to communicate righteousness and life, and does so, Rom. 5:12, 17, 19; then with the wisdom and majesty of Christ the Head, who could not suffer to be the head in guilt but uncertain of the glory, to shed his blood for his bride but uncertain of her faith, to unite himself by pledge and death to those of whom it was doubtful whether he would be Father or enemy, King of grace or judge and avenger; and finally with the unity of the body of Christ, because in this way he would be the Head of all, by his merit on the cross, of a few by the application of grace through the resurrection; acquiring life for all, conferring absolute will on none; and having members of the most diverse lot: some with whom he would have no fellowship, such as those to whom the Gospel is not preached; others who are the same Christ with him, 1 Cor. 12:12; some taken into the unity of his body only for a time, others soon falling away and cut off from the same; some whom he quickens forever, some whom he ceases to quicken, some whom he gives to his eternal kingdom, and some who are tormented eternally in hell.

units.la: XXXVII. Hactenus ex susceptione officii Christi Mediatorii perseverantiam fidei probavimus. Eandem nunc executione ejusdem comprobemus. Executus autem est morte sua redimendo & salvando eos, quos Deus Pater ipsi dedit; hostésque suos debellando, & de iis triumphando. Hinc enim Redemptoris & Salvatoris, nec non Victoris & Triumphatoris nomine venit.
units.tr: XXXVII. Thus far, from the undertaking of the office of Christ as Mediator, we have proved the perseverance of faith. Now let us prove the same from its execution. He executed it by dying, redeeming and saving those whom God the Father gave to him, and by conquering his enemies and triumphing over them. For from this he came by the names of Redeemer and Saviour, and also of Victor and Triumphant.

units.la: XXXVIII. Nam in V. T. יהוה, Vindex & Liberator, Job. XIX. 25. Esaj. LIX. 20. nec non ישוע Salvator, ibid. XIX. 20. Et in N. T. λυτρωτὴς & Σωτὴρ frequentissimè appellatur, imò proprio etiam nomine Ἰησοῦ Jesu, quod Salvatorem à peccatis notat, venit. Qui tituli si magni nominis sui mensuram implent, uti planè implent, verè igitur redimuntur, salvantur illi, quos redimendos & salvandos Christus suscepit, adeòque certa fidelium salus est. Non enim, quæ adversantium anchora est, Christus Redemptor & Salvator noster ob solam impetrationem salutis, non applicationem ejusdem nobis promeruit. Tituli enim illi applicationem salutis manifestè includunt. Non enim Redemptor vel Salvator is dicitur, qui liberare vult, meretur, vel inceptum nonnihil promovet, pendente salute, sed qui reipsa salvat & liberat. Christum igitur fingere Salvatorem eorum, qui non salvantur, est relatum sine correlato concipere, & Salvatorem dicere sine salvatis, quod oppidò absurdum est. Scitè Augustinus cont. Jul. lib. III. 2. Quomodo, inquit, putabim redemptos, quos videmus permanere captivos? Redimuntur, sed non liberantur? Hæc sunt sententiarum portenta vestrarum! Inprimis verò tituli illi ἀντινομασικῶς Christo tributi, adeò ut etiam proprium inde nomen Ἰησοῦ Jesu, Salvatoris ei impositum sit, augustiores sunt, quàm ut eum SalSalvatorem sine salvatis indigetare possint. Cicero certè indignatus Verri, quòd se Siciliæ non Patronum, sed Σωτῆρ inscripsisset, tantum esse bunc Σωτῆρ titulum dixit, ut Latino uno verbo Servatoris exprimi non posset. Is, inquit, Σωτὴρ est, qui salutem dedit. An Christus alios vocabit יְשׁוּעִים redemptos suos, Esaj. LXIII. 4. vel de iis, ceu redemptis suis gloriabitur, nisi quibus salutem applicaverit? Cur igitur præter mentem ejus redemptorem eum dicemus illorum, quos redemptos suos non agnoscit? Etiam typici illi Jehosuæ seu Salvatores & λυτρωτὴς Redemptores V. T. actu salvarunt, liberarunt, redemerunt; & non salvaret, liberaret actu antitypus illorum κατ' ἐξοχὴν dictus non tantùm in concreto 'Ιησοῦς, Σωτὴρ, sed etiam in abstracto יְשׁוּעָה & יְשׁוּעָה Salus, Gen. XLIX. 18. Esaj. LXII. 11. Σωτήριον Salutare, Luc. II. 30. Ephes. VI. 17. Inprimis cùm id tum status redimendorum, tum modus redemptionis, tum fructus ejusdem, tum distincta beneficia postulent. Et status quidem redimendorum, quorum fundus calamitatis non in eo duntaxat positus est, quòd ceu constricti reatu peccati, salutem sibi promereri non potuerunt, sed in eo etiam, quòd ceu presli dira servitute peccati & legis, promeritam constanti fide applicare sibi non potuerunt, ut omnino perfectus Redemptor, seu רב להושיע magnus seu potentissimus ad salvandum, Esaj. LXIII. 1. qui & reatum peccati solveret, & animam à regno ejus liberaret; iis necessarius fuerit. Modus etiam Redemptionis is fuit, quòd redemit partim pretio sanguinis, Act. XX. 28. 1. Petr. I. 19. ad impetrationem respectu justitiæ Dei, cui λύτρον debebatur; partim robore seu רב כוחו magnitudine potentiæ suæ, Esaj. LXIII. 1. ad potentissimam applicationem & destructionem Regni peccati & Sathanæ in nobis. Quomodo etiam in Lege גאל vindices cognationis non tantùm servituti mancipatos suos oblato pretio redemerunt, Levit. XXV. 25. sed etiam sanguinis vindices, de homicida vindictam expetierunt. Ideo Christo tribuuntur nomina Agni & Leonis: Agni, quia sanguine suo nos liberavit ab Angelo vastatore. Leonis e tribu Juda, quia robore suo nos e faucibus Leonis rugientis infernalis eripuit. Non tantùm enim Christus justitiam ut loricam induxit, Esaj. LIX. 17. sed etiam galeam salutis in capite suo habet, Ephes. VI. 17. non tantùm mortuus est propter peccata nostra, sed etiam resurrexit propter justitiam nostram, seu in signum perfectæ justificationis nostræ, Rom. IV. 25. non tantùm reconciliavit nos per mortem, sed etiam servat per vitam, ibid. V. 10. Neque tantùm in sanguine ejus est ἱλαστήριον propitiatorium, ibid. III. 25. sed etiam vetus homo cum eo crucifixus est, ut aboleatur corpus peccati, ibid. VI. 6. Fructus redemptionis est, quòd פדויי יהוה Redempti à Jehova veniunt in Sion cum laude & Lætitia perpetua super caput eorum, Esaj. XXXV. 10. Hinc eadem ἀπολύτρωσις redemptionis voce etiam redemptio corporis in novissimo die venit, Rom. VIII. 23. quæ est ἀπολύτρωσις τῆς πληρώσεως redemptio plenæ possessionis, seu vindicationis, Eph. I. 14. Æternitas redemptionis idem comprobat. Nam Christus in sancta intravit αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν æternam redemptionem inveniens, Hebr. IX. 12. & αἰώνιος ζωῆς ...
units.tr: XXXVIII. For in the Old Testament he is called יהוה, Avenger and Deliverer [Jehovah], Job 19:25; Isa. 59:20, and also ישוע, Saviour [Yeshua], ibid. 19:20. And in the New Testament he is most frequently called λυτρωτὴς and Σωτὴρ [Redeemer and Saviour], and he comes also by the proper name Ἰησοῦς, Jesus [Iesous], which signifies the Saviour from sins. If these titles fill out the measure of their great name, as they plainly do, then truly those whom Christ undertook to redeem and save are redeemed and saved, and so the salvation of believers is certain. For Christ our Redeemer and Saviour did not merit for us, as the anchor of our opponents has it, merely the impetration of salvation, but not the application of it to us. For those titles manifestly include the application of salvation. For he is not called Redeemer or Saviour who wishes to deliver, or merits it, or somewhat advances a undertaking while salvation hangs in the balance, but he who actually saves and delivers. To imagine Christ as Saviour of those who are not saved is therefore to conceive a relative without its correlate, and to call him Saviour without the saved, which is utterly absurd. Augustine rightly says, against Julian, book 3, chapter 2: How, he says, shall I think of the redeemed whom we see remaining captives? They are redeemed, but not set free? These are the monstrosities of your opinions! Above all, those titles ascribed to Christ by antonomasia, so that even the proper name Jesus, Saviour, was given to him, are too lofty to be called by him Saviour without the saved. Cicero, indeed, indignant at Verres for having inscribed himself on Sicily not as Patron but as Σωτήρ [Soter], said that this title Soter is so great that it cannot be expressed in the single Latin word Servator. He is, he said, Soter who has given salvation. Will Christ call others יְשׁוּעִים [yeshu'im], his redeemed, Isa. 63:4, or will he glory in them as his redeemed, unless those to whom he has applied salvation? Why then, against his intention, shall we call him Redeemer of those whom he does not acknowledge as his redeemed? Also those typical Joshuas or Saviours and λυτρωταί [redeemers] of the Old Testament actually saved, delivered and redeemed; and their antitype, called so pre-eminently, would not actually save and deliver, he who is named not only concretely Ἰησοῦς, Σωτήρ, but also abstractly יְשׁוּעָה [yeshu'ah] and יְשׁוּעָה, Salvation, Gen. 49:18; Isa. 62:11; Σωτήριον [Soterion], salvation, Luke 2:30; Eph. 6:17. Above all, since both the condition of those to be redeemed, and the manner of redemption, and its fruit, and the distinct benefits, demand it. And indeed the condition of those to be redeemed, whose basis of calamity lies not only in this, that, bound by the guilt of sin, they could not merit salvation for themselves, but also in this, that, pressed by the dire servitude of sin and the law, they could not apply to themselves what was merited by a steadfast faith, requires that he be altogether a perfect Redeemer, or רב להושיע [rav lehoshia], mighty, or most powerful to save, Isa. 63:1, who both dissolves the guilt of sin and frees the soul from its kingdom. The manner of redemption also was this: he redeemed partly by the price of blood, Acts 20:28; 1 Pet. 1:19, for the impetration with respect to the justice of God, to whom the λύτρον [ransom] was owed; partly by strength, or רב כוחו [rav kocho], by the greatness of his power, Isa. 63:1, for the most powerful application and destruction of the kingdom of sin and of Satan in us. Just as also in the Law the גאל [go'el], avengers of kinship, not only redeemed their kinsmen sold into slavery by a price paid, Lev. 25:25, but also as avengers of blood sought vengeance upon the murderer. Therefore the names of Lamb and Lion are given to Christ: Lamb, because by his blood he freed us from the destroying Angel; Lion of the tribe of Judah, because by his strength he snatched us from the jaws of the roaring infernal Lion. For Christ did not only put on righteousness as a breastplate, Isa. 59:17, but also has the helmet of salvation on his head, Eph. 6:17; he did not only die for our sins, but also rose again for our justification, or as a sign of our perfect justification, Rom. 4:25; he did not only reconcile us by his death, but also saves us by his life, ibid. 5:10. Nor is he the ἱλαστήριον [propitiatory] only in his blood, ibid. 3:25, but also our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, ibid. 6:6. The fruit of redemption is that פדויי יהוה [redeemed of Jehovah] come to Zion with praise and everlasting joy upon their heads, Isa. 35:10. Hence the same word ἀπολύτρωσις [redemption] is used for the redemption of the body at the last day, Rom. 8:23, which is the ἀπολύτρωσις τῆς πληρώσεως [redemption of full possession], that is, the vindication, Eph. 1:14. The eternity of redemption proves the same. For Christ entered into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption [αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν], Heb. 9:12, and he is called the eternal cause of salvation [αἰώνιος ζωῆς], ibid. 5:9, and by one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified, ibid. 10:14. Finally, the chain of all benefits in Christ has a great weight that cannot be pulled apart. For he is not only the ἀρχηγὸς [author], that is, the beginning, but also the τελειωτὴς [perfecter] of faith, ibid. 12:2; not only the Alpha and beginning [ἀρχή], but also the Omega and end [τέλος], Rev. 1:8; not only he who begins a good work but also who completes it, Phil. 1:6. He is the Way, as Priest opening heaven by the merit of his death; the Truth, as Prophet illuminating the eyes with the light of the Gospel; and the Life, as King quickening the will by the efficacy of the Spirit, John 14:6. Made to us by God wisdom through the gift of faith, righteousness through the imputation of satisfaction, sanctification through regeneration, and redemption through the power of death and resurrection, 1 Cor. 1:30. But we have also demonstrated at greater length, in Locus 19, §88, that the Holy Spirit merited and obtained regeneration and faith for those for whom Christ died.

units.la: caus̈a salutis æterna dicitur, ibid. V. 9. & una oblatione πεπλεώκε consummavit sanctificatos, ibid. X. 14. Denique ingens pondus nexus omnium beneficiorum in Christo indivulsus habet. Non tantùm enim ἀρχηγὸς princeps, seu principium, sed etiam τελειωτὴς consummator fidei est, ibid. XII. 2. non tantùm Alpha & ἀρχή principium, sed etiam Omega & τέλος finis, Apoc. I. 8. non tantùm incipiens bonum opus, sed etiam perficiens, Phil. I. 6. Via, ut Sacerdos Cœlum aperiens mortis merito, Veritas, ut Propheta oculos Evangelii luce illustrans, & Vita, ut Rex voluntatem Spiritus efficacia vivificans, Joh. XIV. 6. Factus nobis à Deo sapientia per donum fidei, justitia per imputationem satisfactionis, sanctificatio per regenerationem, redemptio per mortis & resurrectionis vim, 1. Cor. I. 30. sed pluribus etiam Christum iis, pro quibus mortuus est Spiritum S. regenerationem & fidem meruisse & impetrasse Loc. XIX. 88. demonstravimus.
units.tr: is the eternal cause of salvation, ibid. 5:9; and by one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified, ibid. 10:14. Finally, the chain of all benefits in Christ has a great weight that cannot be pulled apart. For he is not only the ἀρχηγὸς [author], that is, the beginning, but also the τελειωτὴς [perfecter] of faith, ibid. 12:2; not only the Alpha and beginning [ἀρχή], but also the Omega and end [τέλος], Rev. 1:8; not only he who begins a good work but also who completes it, Phil. 1:6. He is the Way, as Priest opening heaven by the merit of his death; the Truth, as Prophet illuminating the eyes with the light of the Gospel; and the Life, as King quickening the will by the efficacy of the Spirit, John 14:6. Made to us by God wisdom through the gift of faith, righteousness through the imputation of satisfaction, sanctification through regeneration, and redemption through the power of death and resurrection, 1 Cor. 1:30. But we have also demonstrated at greater length, in Locus 19, §88, that the Holy Spirit merited and obtained regeneration and faith for those for whom Christ died.

units.la: XXXIX. Maximi verò momenti est efficacia intercessionis Christi, à qua fidei perseverantia fluit. Rogavi pro te, ne deficiat fides tua, Luc. XXII. 32. Cùm igitur intercessio Christi pars meriti ejus sit, & ab eadem perseverantia fidei efficiatur, manifestum est, & perseverare fidem, & perseverare vi meriti Christi. Intercessio enim in morte Christi fundatur; quia non alius ὁ παράκλητος Advocatus noster est, quàm qui idem propitiatio pro peccatis nostris est, 1. Joh. II. 1. Pro quibus ergo Christus intercedit, illi non deficiunt à fide, ne quidem ad tempus & totaliter. Non enim Christus rogavit, ut fides Petri, postquam is defecerit, iterum accendatur, sed ne deficiat. Et scopus Christi pro Petro intercedentis idem flagitat. Id enim Sathanas egit, ut per tentationem mox suscitandam cribrans Petrum, fidem ex ejus corde excuteret. Si totaliter fidem amisisset, conatus Sathanæ successisset, & irrita Christi intercessio fuisset, petentis à Deo, ne fides ejus in corde deficeret, etiam quando ob metum mortis in ore defecit. Ac multò minùs finaliter. Quomodo enim non deficit, qui finaliter perit? Nam quòd singularem hanc erga Petrum gratiam fuisse tricantur, frigidum nimis est. Id ipsum enim Christus pro reliquis Apostolis, & pro omnibus fidelibus oravit. Pater sancte, serva eos, (discipulos) in nomine tuo, Joh. XVII. 11. Non rogo, ut eos ex mundo tollas, sed ut eos serves à malo, ibid. v. 15. Non pro iis duntaxat rogo, sed pro credentibus per sermonem eorum in me, ut omnes unum sint, unione videlicet indissolubili; sicut tu Pater in me, & ego in te, ibid. v. 20.21. Pater, quos dedisti mihi (redimendos) volo, ut ubi ego sum, etiam illi mecum sint, in Cœlo, ibid. v. 24. Vel igitur Christus orans non exauditur, quod falsum esse ipse ibid. XI. 42. docet: vel credentes in ipsum non deficiunt, sed salvantur. Neque frustra pro iis orat, si deficere non possunt, quia non sibi relicti, sed per gratiam Dei, quam jugi intercessione sua Christus impetrat, imò postulat, deficere non possunt.
units.tr: XXXIX. The efficacy of Christ's intercession, from which the perseverance of faith flows, is of the greatest importance. I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail, Luke 22:32. Since, then, Christ's intercession is part of his merit and is what brings about the perseverance of faith, it is clear that faith persists by the power of Christ's merit. Intercession is grounded in Christ's death, since our advocate [ὁ παράκλητος] is none other than the one who is himself the propitiation for our sins, 1 John 2:1. Therefore, those for whom Christ intercedes do not fall away from faith, not even for a time and not wholly. Christ did not ask that Peter's faith be kindled again after it had failed, but that it may not fail. And the aim of Christ's intercession for Peter demands the same thing. For Satan's purpose was to shake Peter through a temptation that was about to arise and to shake faith out of his heart. If Peter had wholly lost faith, Satan's attempt would have succeeded, and Christ's intercession, which asked God that Peter's faith might not fail in his heart, even when it failed in his mouth through fear of death, would have been in vain. And it is far less likely that faith fails finally. For how can someone not fail who perishes finally? As for those who claim that this grace was a special favour to Peter alone, the claim is too cold. For Christ prayed the same thing for the other apostles and for all the faithful. Holy Father, keep them (the disciples) in your name, John 17:11. I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil, ibid. v. 15. I pray not only for these, but for those who believe in me through their word, that they all may be one, that is, with an indissoluble union; as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, ibid. vv. 20, 21. Father, those whom you have given me (to be redeemed) I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, in heaven, ibid. v. 24. Either, then, Christ praying is not heard, which Christ himself says is false, ibid. 11:42; or those who believe in him do not fail, but are saved. Nor is he praying for them in vain, if they cannot fail, because they are not left to themselves but are kept by the grace of God, which Christ obtains, indeed demands, by his continual intercession.

units.la: XL. In executione muneris Mediatorii Christus non tantùm Redemptor, Salvator, sed etiam Victor Sathanæ & Triumphator est, quod perseverantiam Sanctorum mire confirmat. Nam statim post lapsum promissum est Semen Mulie-
units.tr: XL. In carrying out his office as Mediator, Christ is not only Redeemer and Saviour but also Conqueror of Satan and Triumphant, and this wonderfully confirms the perseverance of the saints. For immediately after the fall it was promised that the Seed of the Woman

units.la: Imprimis Intercessio Christi pro suis eorum demum salutem extra eam omnem intercessionis pœnis.
units.tr: First, the intercession of Christ for his own secures their salvation at last, outside of which there is no salvation, by any penalty of intercession.

units.la: Idem efficit Victor & Triumphator Sathanæ. Mulieris contriturum caput serpentis, Genef.III. 15. Deus pacis brevi συντρίψει conteret Sathanam sub pedibus vestris, Rom.XVI.20. Absorpta est mors εἰς νῖκος ad victoriam. Ubi tuus, mors, aculeus? Ubi tua, inferne νῖκος victoria? Deo gratia, qui dedit nobis victoriam per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, 1.Cor.XV.54.55.57. Per mortem abolevit eum, qui potestatem mortis habet, Diabolum, Hebr:II.14.
units.tr: The Conqueror and Triumphant One of Satan does the same. He shall crush the head of the serpent, Gen. 3:15. The God of peace will shortly crush [συντρίψει] Satan under your feet, Rom. 16:20. Death is swallowed up [εἰς νῖκος] in victory. Where, death, is your sting? Where, grave, is your victory? But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 15:54, 55, 57. Through death he destroyed him who has the power of death, that is, the devil, Heb. 2:14.

units.la: XLI. Qui victoriam hanc & debellationem Sathanæ ab ejusdem fructu & applicatione distinguunt, asserentes, victum à Christo esse Sathanam, sed fructum victoriæ ad solos eos pertingere, qui libera voluntate eum carpunt; næ illi nomen Victoris Sathanæ, nescio quo tropo illusorio, Christo concedunt, at victoriam negant. Nam imperium Sathanæ in homines in potestate eos excæcandi, & mortem iisdem infligendi constitit, quæ permissio Divina illegitime usurpati imperii, & laxatio fraenorum furoris est. Ut ita Sathanas respectu justitiæ Divinæ, carnificis, respectu modi, quo imperium illud invasit & exercet, tyranni similitudinem habeat. Ad imperium illud evertendum, & victoriam de eodem reportandam, duplex Christus certamen sustinuit, unum in se, ignita Sathanæ tela in vita & morte excipiens & extinguens, ne technis serpentis hujus succumberet: alterum extra se, atque illud iterum tum in judicio & foro Poli, ubi id obtinere debuit, ut à Deo sibi imperium in credentes, ceu legitimum, adjudicaretur, & Sathanæ, ceu usurpatori abjudicaretur, & quidem per sententiam judicis absolutam, non à conditione pendentem, quia alias æquè Sathanas imperium sibi retinere, atque illud ei eripere Christus potuisset: tum in arce cordis humani, ubi id satagendum Christo fuit, ut sceptrum fortitudinis suæ ad subjiciendum sibi cor indomitum hominis, & virgam ferream ad conterendum caput serpentis, qui suum in corde hominis thronum habet, exerceret. Nil citra certamen prius illud posterius; neq; citra posterius prius illud ad victoriam à Sathana reportandam valuit. Facenim in judicio Dei condemnationem Sathanæ & abrogationem Imperii ejus Christus certans obtinuerit. At quandiu in corde non obtinet, victor evadere non potest, sed vel Diabolus victor & princeps manet, vel eum debellare & vincere fideles libera voluntate sua Sathanam ex cordibus suis profligantes, debent. Neque proin Christus victor, neque victoria Christi est, si fructus & applicatio redemptionis non abejus potestate, sed à libera hominis voluntate, pendet. Christo enim solum victoriæ possibilis meritum cedit: at victoria vel nulla est, vel non Christi, sed fidelium est. Atque ita verè Serpens calcaneum Christi momorderit: at non æquè verè Semen Mulieris caput Serpentis contriverit.
units.tr: XLI. Those who distinguish this victory and the overthrow of Satan from the fruit and application of it, asserting that Satan has been conquered by Christ, but that the fruit of the victory reaches only those who take hold of it by free will, grant Christ the name of Conqueror of Satan by some illusory figure of speech, but deny him the victory itself. For Satan's dominion over men consists in his power to blind them and to inflict death upon them, and this is the permission of God, a loosing of the reins of a power illegitimately seized and a fury given free rein. Thus Satan, with respect to divine justice, has the likeness of an executioner, and with respect to the manner in which he seized and exercises that dominion, the likeness of a tyrant. To overthrow that dominion and win the victory over it, Christ waged a twofold conflict: one in himself, catching and quenching the fiery darts of Satan in life and death, lest he succumb to the wiles of this serpent; the other outside himself. This second conflict was itself twofold: first in the judgment and court of heaven, where he had to obtain that the dominion over believers be adjudged to him by God as lawful, and be taken from Satan as a usurper, and this by an absolute sentence of the judge, not dependent on any condition, since otherwise Satan could have kept his dominion just as well, and Christ could have snatched it from him. And second, in the citadel of the human heart, where Christ had to labour to exercise his sceptre of strength to subdue the unbroken heart of man, and his rod of iron to crush the head of the serpent, who has his throne in the human heart. The latter conflict has no value without the former, and the former has no value for winning the victory from Satan without the latter. For Christ, contending in the judgment of God, has obtained the condemnation of Satan and the abrogation of his dominion. But as long as the victory is not won in the heart, it cannot be complete; either the devil remains victor and prince, or the faithful, by their free will, must overcome and conquer him, driving Satan out of their hearts. Therefore Christ is not victor, nor is his victory a victory, if the fruit and application of redemption depend not on his power but on the free will of man. For to Christ is ascribed only the merit of a possible victory, but the victory is either no victory at all, or it is not Christ's but the faithful's. And so the serpent may truly have bitten the heel of Christ, but the Seed of the Woman has not equally truly crushed the head of the serpent.

units.la: XLII. Atqui & verissima in utroque illo foro, & certissima, nec ab ulla conditione suspensa, & perfectissima Christi victoria est. Verissima in utroque illo foro, quia non tantum libera rationem eorum, pro quibus mortuus est, à potestate Sathanæ accusatoris & carnificis justitiæ suæ merito impetravit, juxta Apostoli illud: Quis intentabit crimina adversus electos Dei? Quis condemnabit? Christus mortuus est, & excitatus est, & sedet ad dextram Patris, atque intercedit pro nobis, Rom.VIII.33. Nec non Jesajæ illud de Christo: Calamum quassatum non franget, &c. ad veritatem, vel (interprete Christo Matth. XII.20.) εἰς νῖκος ad victoriam proferet judicium (sententia enim pro veritate in judicio veritatis victoria est), Esaj.XLII.3. sed etiam, tanquam Rex & potens armatus ἰσχυρότερος validior ex aula cordis humani potentem armatum Diabolum, aulam illam obsidentem, & totam ejus armaturam ejecit, Luc.XI.21.22. Nam μείζων major est ὁ ἐν ἡμῖν, qui in nobis (in corde nostro) est, quàm qui in mundo est, 1.Joh.IV.4. Certissima etiam est, quia vi mortis & meriti ejus impetrata. Nam per mortem καταργησε abolevit, destruxit eum, qui mortis imperium habet, Hebr.II.14. Nunc adest judicium. Nunc princeps hujus mundi ejicietur foras, Joh. XII.31. Sedibus igitur suis excussus, possessione sua exturbatus, certam Christo morienti, & morte sua eum excutienti, exturbanti victoriam, certam cordis occupationem & infessionem reliquit. Ego si (per mortem) sublatus fuero, omnes (Sathanæ ereptos) traham ad me, ibid. 32. Non suspensa ab ulla conditione, quia tum Deus Filio suo dominium in hostes absolutè adjudicavit, dicens: Dominare in medio hostium tuorum, Psal.CX.2. imò in se sententiæ suæ executionem recepit, dicens: Sede ad dextram meam, donec hostes tuos posuero scabellum pedum tuorum, ibid. v. 1. tum ipsa voluntas hominis hostis vincendus, & præmium victoriæ Christi est. Nam cor hominis & intestinus Dei hostis est, caro inimicitia adversus Deum, Rom.VIII. 7. cujus non subjicientis se Deo pertinaciam, ceu opus Diaboli Christus fregit & dissolvit, 1.Joh.III.8. & aula illa est, quam custodit Diabolus, Luc. XI.21. Thronus, in quo superbit, arx, in qua munitiones suas extruit, 2.Cor.X.4. Hunc igitur hostem domare, hanc aulam, thronum, arcem, ceu victoriæ suæ præmium, Christus morte sua occupare debuit; non domiturus, non occupaturus, si sibi & arbitrio suo cor relictum, & à conditione mutabili cordis suspensa victoria fuisset. Denique perfectissima est, tum quoad hostes victos, quia & Sathanæ, & satellitum ejus, peccati, legis maledicentis, mortis ipsius victoria est: tum quoad gradus omnes, quia & vincula, quibus Sathan homines sub imperio mortis detinet, puta reatum & dominium peccati; illum in cruce, hoc per Spiritum suum simul semelque abrupit, & peccati luctantis reliquias ἡμέρα καὶ ἡμέρα de die in diem 2.Cor.IV. 16. abolet, donec mortem, ultimum hostem, destruet, 1.Cor.XV.26. Tum denique quoad sequelas omnes, seu fructus debellatorum hostium, quorum in victoria hac Christi Scriptura meminit. Nam Christus, perinde ut heros alius Victor & Triumphator hostium, fideles etiam suos victoriæ hujus participes reddit, ut & ipsi Sathanam sub pedibus conculcent & vincant, Rom. XVI.20. 1.Joh.II.13. idque virtute Dei, & per sanguinem Agni, Apoc.XII.11. & hostibus infernalibus spolia eripuit, eósque ἐν παρρησίᾳ ἐδειγμάτισεν palàm traduxit tum in cruce, Col.II.15. tum in ascensione sua in Cœlum, captivam ducens captivitatem, Ephes.IV.8. & caput hostium suorum percusit, Psal.LXVIII.22. CX.6. Caput Serpentis contrivit, Gen.III.15. & prædam partitus est, Esaj.LIII,12, amplissimum victoriæ suæ frufructum hominibus tribuens, & in signum ejus rei dona hominibus conferens, Ephes.IV.8. & redemptos à Jehova ad cantum & laetitiam perpetuam vocat, Esaj. XXXV.10. & denique ad laudes victori & triumphatori sibi decantandas solenniter invitat. Cantate Domino canticum novum. Egressus est via bellorum. Certavit & praevaluit in hostes, ibid. XLIX.15.
units.tr: XLII. Yet Christ's victory is most true in both courts, most certain, not suspended on any condition, and most complete. It is most true in both courts, because he has obtained, by the merit of his death, not only the deliverance of those for whom he died from the power of Satan, the accuser and executioner of justice, according to the Apostle's words: Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? Who is the one who condemns? Christ died, and was raised, and sits at the right hand of the Father, and intercedes for us, Rom. 8:33. And there is Isaiah's word about Christ: He will not break a bruised reed, etc., and he will bring forth judgment to truth, or, as Christ interprets it, Matt. 12:20, to victory [εἰς νῖκος], for a sentence in favour of the truth is a victory in the court of truth, Isa. 42:3. But he has also cast out, as a king and a stronger one [ἰσχυρότερος], from the hall of the human heart, the strong armed man, the devil who occupies that hall, together with all his armour, Luke 11:21, 22. For greater [μείζων] is he who is in you (in your heart) than he who is in the world, 1 John 4:4. The victory is also most certain, because it was won by the power of his death and merit. For through death he destroyed [καταργήσῃ] and brought to nothing him who has the power of death, Heb. 2:14. Now is the judgment. Now the prince of this world will be cast out, John 12:31. Thus, thrown from his seat and driven from his possession, he left to Christ, dying and by his death casting out and driving away, a certain victory and a certain occupation and possession of the heart. If I am lifted up (through death) I will draw all (who have been snatched from Satan) to myself, ibid. 32. It is not suspended on any condition, because God then adjudged the dominion over his enemies to his Son absolutely, saying: Rule in the midst of your enemies, Ps. 110:2; indeed he took upon himself the execution of his sentence, saying: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet, ibid. v. 1. Then the very will of man, the enemy to be conquered, is the prize of Christ's victory. For the heart of man is an inner enemy of God: the flesh is hostile to God, Rom. 8:7. Christ broke and dissolved its obstinacy in refusing to submit to God, as the work of the devil, 1 John 3:8; and this is the hall which the devil guards, Luke 11:21. It is the throne in which he exalts himself, the citadel in which he builds his strongholds, 2 Cor. 10:4. Christ, therefore, had to occupy this enemy, this hall, throne and citadel by his death, as the prize of his victory; he would not have subdued them or occupied them if the victory had been left to the heart and to its own choice, and had been suspended on a changeable condition of the heart. Finally, it is most complete, both as regards the enemies conquered, since it is a victory over Satan, his attendants, sin, the accusing law, and death itself; and as regards all the degrees, since the bonds by which Satan holds men under the dominion of death, namely the guilt and dominion of sin, he has broken at once, once for all, the one on the cross and the other through his Spirit, and he destroys the remnants of struggling sin day by day [ἡμέρα καὶ ἡμέρα], 2 Cor. 4:16, until he destroys death, the last enemy, 1 Cor. 15:26. Finally, it is complete as regards all the consequences, or fruits, of the defeated enemies, of which the Scripture makes mention in this victory of Christ. For Christ, just like another hero, a conqueror and triumphant over enemies, makes his faithful partakers of this victory as well, so that they too trample Satan under their feet and conquer him, Rom. 16:20; 1 John 2:13, and this by the power of God, and through the blood of the Lamb, Rev. 12:11. He has snatched spoils from the infernal enemies and led them openly in triumph [ἐν παρρησίᾳ ἐδειγμάτισεν], both on the cross, Col. 2:15, and in his ascension into heaven, leading captivity captive, Eph. 4:8; and he has struck the head of his enemies, Ps. 68:22; 110:6. He has crushed the head of the serpent, Gen. 3:15, and divided the spoil, Isa. 53:12, bestowing the most ample fruit of his victory on men, and as a sign of this he is giving gifts to men, Eph. 4:8; he calls those redeemed by Jehovah to song and everlasting joy, Isa. 35:10; and finally he solemnly invites them to sing praises to him as victor and triumphant. Sing to the Lord a new song. He has gone forth by the way of wars. He has fought and prevailed against his enemies, ibid. 49:15.

units.la: XLIII. Viderint ergo Perseverantiae Sanctorum hostes, qualem Victorem Triumphatoremque Christum, gloriosissimum omnium Nicetam, faciant, & qualem eidem victoriam tribuant. Talem videlicet tribuunt, quae quoad omnes ab omnium voluntate mutabili suspensa & ipsi Christo incerta est, ita ut proprie Christus sub nullius pedibus Sathanam conterat, neque aliam omnino vim exerat, quam illam, qua posita Sathan illaesus evadere, & imperium integrum in omnes homines servare potest; quoad innumeros nullam sequelam, fructum nullum habet, nisi quod velamen super cordibus eorum manet, & miseram servitutem Sathanae per omnem vitam, tandemque ejulatus aeternos in inferno patiuntur, & blasphemias horribiles adversus Christum evomunt: quoad quosdam vero, fideles & salvandos, precaria est, & aliena vi, arbitraria eorum voluntate a Christo obtinetur; ita ut proprie & non tam Christus quam fideles sub pedibus suis Sathanam conterant. An igitur sic Christus Poena cecinit ante victoriam, vel sibi arrogavit, quod a voluntate humana se obtenturum praevidit, quando sic triumphabundus hostibus suis insultavit: E manu inferni redimam eos, a morte vindicabo eos: Ubi peste tua (aculei tui) o Mors? Ubi venenum tuum, o inferne? Hos. XIII.14. Ubi tuus, mors, aculeus est? Ubi tua, inferne, victoria? 1.Cor. XV.54. Si quos Christus morte sua clementer redemit, nunquam ille potenter asserit, pereunt illi certe; at nec sic Sathanas de Christo triumphat. Si Christus patitur, ut quos semel asseruit, iterum ex manibus ejus a Diabolo surripiantur, pereunt etiam illi; at Sathanas de Christo triumphat. Quanto rectius, pie magis, & ad consolationem efficacius ejusmodi Christo victoriam tribuimus, in qua indubitata salus eorum; qui Christi sunt, includatur, & fiducia atque consolatio fidelium securè quiescat?
units.tr: XLIII. Let the enemies of the perseverance of the saints consider what kind of Victor and Triumphant Christ, most glorious of all, they make him, and what kind of victory they assign to him. They assign one that, with respect to all, hangs on the changeable will of everyone and is uncertain even to Christ himself, so that Christ does not really crush Satan under anyone's feet, and exerts no power except that by which, Satan being set in place, he can escape unharmed and keep his dominion intact over all men. With respect to countless people it has no sequel and no fruit, except that the veil remains over their hearts, and they suffer miserable slavery to Satan throughout their lives, and at last eternal wailing in hell, and they vomit horrible blasphemies against Christ. With respect to certain people, however, the faithful and those who are to be saved, it is precarious: it is obtained from Christ by another's power, by their arbitrary will, so that it is really the faithful, and not so much Christ, who crush Satan under their feet. Did Christ, then, sing thus before the victory, or did he claim for himself that he would obtain it from the human will, when he exulted over his enemies in triumph: From the hand of hell I will ransom them, I will deliver them from death. O death, where is your plague (your sting)? O hell, where is your poison? Hos. 13.14. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O hell, is your victory? 1 Cor. 15.54. If Christ mercifully redeemed some by his death, he never asserted powerfully that they would perish; yet Satan does not triumph over Christ in this way. If Christ suffers that those whom he has once claimed should be snatched again from his hands by the Devil, they too perish, and Satan triumphs over Christ. How much more rightly, more piously, and more effectively for consolation do we ascribe to Christ such a victory, in which the undoubted salvation of those who belong to Christ is included, and the trust and consolation of the faithful rest securely?

units.la: XLIV. Superest ut Perseverantiam Sanctorum etiam ex tertiae Personae Divinitatis, Spiritus S. operatione oeconomica demonstremus. Sicut enim electio Patris & Filii, quo Mediatore Foedus Gratiae coaluit, redemptio perseverantiae illius immota firmamenta sunt: ita iisdem accedens Spiritus S. cuncta gubernantis, consummantis & obsignantis operatio & sanctificatio eandem potenter confirmat. De quo sic Christus ipse: Ego rogabo Patrem & alium Paracletum dabit vobis, ut maneat vobiscum in aeternum; Spiritum veritatis, quem mundus non potest accipere, quia non videt illum, neque cognoscit illum. Vos autem cognoscitis illum, quia apud vos manet, & in vobis erit, Joh. XIV.16.17. Hic enim ille est index alter, pro Christo in Coelum sublato, datus, Zach. IX.12. & quidem, ut maneat nobiscum in seculum, & in nobis fit. Quae promissio illis, qui Christi sunt, facta absoluta est; neque ullam conditionem implicat, uti superbi nugatores, Spiritus veritatis, spei, amoris & laetitiae fidelium inimici, omnia conditionibus alligantes, pertendunt. Nam Christus verbis illis aut nihil promisit, aut promisit, quod Spiritus mansurus sit in credentibus ad sanctificationem ipsorum, & quod mansurus sit in ipsis ut paracletus, intercedens filialibus precibus & suspiriis. Ideo Spiritus veritatis appellatur, quia in ejus datione promissio vera cernitur; qui facit ὁμολογεῖν τῷ Θεῷ, quod sit ἀληθὴς verus: quem dare Deo dignum est; quem petere possunt fideles & Deus dare potest, & quia ipsum ita decet, vult; per quem Deus vere fit Deus peccatoris; & qui fideles non amplius sub umbris, figuris & servitute continet, sed in veritate, luce & libertate exhilarat.
units.tr: XLIV. It remains to show the perseverance of the saints also from the economic operation of the third Person of the Divinity, the Holy Spirit. For just as the election of the Father and the Son, by which the covenant of grace was made with the Mediator, are the immovable foundations of that perseverance, so the operation and sanctification of the Holy Spirit, who comes alongside them, governing, completing and sealing all things, powerfully confirms the same. Christ himself speaks of him thus: I will pray the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may abide with you for ever; the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you know him, for he abides with you and will be in you, John 14.16-17. For this is that other Advocate, given in place of Christ taken up into heaven, Zech. 9.12, and indeed, that he may remain with us for ever and be in us. The promise made to those who belong to Christ is unconditional; it does not imply any condition, as proud triflers, enemies of the Spirit of truth, of the hope, love and joy of the faithful, who bind everything to conditions, maintain. For in those words Christ either promised nothing, or promised that the Spirit would remain in believers for their sanctification, and that he would remain in them as Paraclete, interceding with filial prayers and sighs. He is called Spirit of truth because in his giving the promise is seen to be true; he makes us ὁμολογεῖν τῷ Θεῷ [to confess to God], that he is ἀληθὴς [true]. He is the one whom it is worthy of God to give, whom the faithful can ask for and God can give, and because it befits him so, he wills it; through him God truly becomes the God of the sinner; and he does not keep the faithful any longer under shadows, figures and slavery, but cheers them in truth, light and liberty.

units.la: XLV. Idem Spiritus S. credentium sigillum & arrhabo est. In quo credentes obsignati estis Spiritu promissionis Sancto, qui est arrhabo hereditatis nostrae, ad redemptionem acquisitionis, ut ceu acquisiti & empti pretio, redimamur; hoc est, plene liberemur, seu pleno redemptionis effectu tandem donemur; ad laudem gloriae ejus, Ephes. I.13.14. Qui nos vobiscum confirmat in Christum, & unxit nos, qui etiam obsignavit nos, & dedit nobis arrhabonem Spiritus in cordibus nostris, 2.Cor. I.21.22. Signare & obsignare homines solent, quae non negligere, jactare, sed custodire, conservare, retinere, afferere constituerunt. Ita pater familias rebus suis, pastor ovibus suis signum imponit. Pari ratione, quos Deus fide donavit & Christo inserviet, illos curare, custodire, retinere, ceu caros pretiososque in oculis suis, non ceu viles in miseria relinquere, sed ceu redemptos & pretio emptos apud se ornamenti sui causa retinere, ut in iis glorificetur, certum habet. Signat ergo eosdem & obsignat Spiritus S. promisso, qui Spiritus filiationis est, & tum datur, cum fidem Evangelii accipimus, Gal. III.14. ut signati sic a Deo noscantur, & oculis ejus pateant; ut eos, tanquam suos, pro quibus lytron datum est, curet, ut ab omni malo liberentur. Neque fas cuiquam est sigillum hoc violare & perfringere, quia ipsius Dei sigillum est, quo is rem suam, ceu sibi eximiam, munit, & munitam vindicat; imo sigillum hoc ipse Spiritus S. est, qui se ipsum adversus violatores omnes tueri potens satis superque est. Imo Deus suos sigillo hoc munit ad redemptionem acquisitionis hoc est, εἰς ἡμέραν ἀπολυτρώσεως ad diem usque redemptionis, quo, pretio empti, plenissimè a morte ipsa liberabimur, & aeternum glorificabimur; & εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης ad laudem gloriae ejus, ut hac ex re nomen, virtutes & divitias atque posteritas... Populus, quem formavi mihi, תהלתי laudem meam narrabunt, Esaj. XLIII.21. Neque signantur vel obsignantur a Deo, qui ipsius res, & peculium inviolabile non sunt: neque obsignantur ipso Spiritu S. qui sigillum hoc perfringere ipsi possunt, vel quorum sigillum perfringere alii possunt; neque obsignantur Spiritus S. ad redemptionem acquisitionis, qui ante plenariam redemtionem & liberationem perire aeternum possunt: neque obsignantur Spiritus S. ad laudem gloriae Dei, ex quorum seductione & interitu id evenit, ut populus a Deo formatus ejusdem laudem narrare, & eundem glorificare non possit. Accedit, quod idem ille Spiritus propromissionis, quo credentes obsignantur ad diem usque redemptionis, etiam ἀρραβὼν τῆς κληρονομίας arrhabo hæreditatis nostræ appellatur. Est autem arrhabo μέρος τῆς πάντως pars totius, quæ ערבון (unde ἀρραβὼν seu ערבון nomen) ceu pignus spondet pro toto, & securitatis atque certitudinis causa datur, fidejussorisque loco est. Spiritus S. igitur ita credentibus hæreditatem spondet & obsignat, ut eo, ceu arrhabone freti certò sibi hæreditatem polliceri possint. Et quomodo polliceri arrhabone hoc freti, possunt, quorum incerta & fluxa salus est, qui in diem vivunt, incerti, quid volvendo dies afferat? Nulla hic conditio, quæ mutabilem obsignationem & arrhabonem reddat. Nam πιστεύοντες credentes, hoc est, semel Christum fide amplexi, & per fidem cum eodem uniti obsignantur, & impresso velut sigillo muniuntur, ut fidem donatam, & cum eadem spem hæreditatis amittere non possint.
units.tr: XLV. The same Holy Spirit is the seal and the pledge of believers. In him you who believed were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, for the redemption of what is acquired, so that, as acquired and bought at a price, we are redeemed; that is, we are fully freed, or at last given the full effect of redemption, to the praise of his glory, Eph. 1.13-14. He who establishes us with you in Christ and anointed us is God, who also sealed us and gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts, 2 Cor. 1.21-22. People are accustomed to sign and seal those things which they have decided not to neglect, to cast away, but to guard, keep, retain and assert. Thus a householder sets a mark on his goods, a shepherd on his sheep. By the same reasoning, God is confident that he will care for, guard and keep those whom he has given to Christ by faith, as dear and precious in his eyes; he will not leave them as worthless in misery, but will keep them with himself, as redeemed and bought with a price, for the sake of his own adornment, so that he may be glorified in them. Therefore the Holy Spirit signs and seals these same people by the promise, who is the Spirit of adoption, and is given when we receive the faith of the Gospel, Gal. 3.14, so that, marked in this way, they are known by God and lie open to his eyes, and so that he may care for them as his own, for whom a ransom has been given, and free them from every evil. Nor is it lawful for anyone to violate and break this seal, because it is God's own seal, by which he secures his property as especially his own, and claims it as secured. Indeed, the Holy Spirit himself is this seal, who is more than able to defend himself against all violators. Indeed God marks his own with this seal for the redemption of what is acquired, that is, εἰς ἡμέραν ἀπολυτρώσεως [unto the day of redemption], until the day of redemption, on which, bought at a price, we shall be most fully freed even from death itself and shall be glorified for ever; and εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης [unto the praise of his glory], to the praise of his glory, so that from this his name, virtues and riches, and posterity... The people whom I have formed for myself, תהלתי [my praise], shall declare my praise, Isa. 43.21. Nor are those sealed or marked by God who are not his property and inviolable treasure; nor are those sealed by the Holy Spirit who can themselves break this seal, or whose seal others can break; nor are those sealed by the Holy Spirit for the redemption of what is acquired who can perish eternally before full redemption and liberation; nor are those sealed by the Holy Spirit for the praise of God's glory, through whose seduction and destruction it comes about that the people formed by God cannot declare his praise and glorify him. Moreover, that same Spirit of promise, by whom believers are sealed until the day of redemption, is also called ἀρραβὼν τῆς κληρονομίας, the pledge of our inheritance [arrabon tes klēronomias]. Now a pledge is part of the whole (μέρος τοῦ πάντος), which, as an ערבון [arabon] (whence the name ἀρραβὼν or ערבון), stands surety for the whole as a pledge, and is given as a guarantee of security and certainty, and takes the place of a guarantor. The Holy Spirit therefore promises and seals the inheritance to believers in such a way that, relying on him as a pledge, they can certainly promise themselves the inheritance. And how can those promise themselves anything relying on this pledge whose salvation is uncertain and unstable, who live from day to day, uncertain what the turning day will bring? There is no condition here that would make the sealing and the pledge changeable. For believers, πιστεύοντες, that is, those who have once embraced Christ by faith and been united with him through faith, are sealed and secured, as if a seal had been impressed, so that they cannot lose the faith given them, and with it the hope of the inheritance.

units.la: XLVI. Sed Spiritus qui
units.tr: XLVI. But the Spirit who

units.la: XLVI. Sed Spiritus qui σφραγὶς καὶ ἀρραβὼν sigillum seu nota Dei & arrhabo seu pignus est, idem etiam πνεῦμα δυνάμεως Spiritus potentiæ, seu potenter operans est, 2.Tim.1.7. Est enim creator noster, & potens creator novi hominis, per quem inserimur Christo, qui nos conservat, & gratiæ Dei omnis nos participes reddit, atque id denique efficit, ut beneficia Dei per Christum acquisita fidelibus conferantur, neque conferantur duntaxat, sed etiam ad finem usque permaneant. Nam constantiam illam beneficiorum gratiæ à Spiritu S. collatorum Scriptura tum generatim, tum sigillatim declarat. Generatim, quando & חסד דוד gratias Davidis, vel Davidi typico, & ὁμοίως omnibus, vel à Davide antitypico, Christo collatas נאמנה fideles, stabiles, permanentes, non fluxas, vel humanis casibus obnoxias, Esaj.L V. 3. & dona Dei ἀμετα μέλητα seu talia, quorum nunquam Deum ita pœniteat, ut ea revocet, Rom. XI.29. appellat. Jejunum enim planè est, quòd gratias & dona Dei constantia & ἀμετάμελητα esse per se, si homines ex vitio suo iis indignos non reddant, & respectu Dei, fidem iis, qui mediis ad eam ordinatis utuntur, conservantis; non respectu hominum, fidem sæpiusculè excutientium, regerunt. Licèt enim ad conservationem fidei rectus mediorum usus requiratur, tamen ipse etiam ille usus rectus inter gratias Dei fideles & dona ἀμετα μέλητα referri debet. Tum gratiæ Dei fideles promittuntur ex fœdere, eóque æterno, quod irritum nec à parte Dei, nec à parte hominum reddi poterit; atque præterea etiam ברית נאמנה fœdus fidele, & tali quidem tantaque fidelitate & constantia, ut ne propter peccata quidem filiorum Davidis mystici rescindatur, Psal.LXXXIX.29.31. appellatur. Apostolus verò dona ἀμεταμέλητα ab ἐκλογὴ electione Divina, v.28. arcessit, & electionem asseque justitiam & salutem, v.7. docet. Pertendit enim totum Israelem electum salvatum iri, v.26. eo argumento fretus, quòd dona & vocatio Dei ἀμεταμέλητα sint. Ex donis verò amissibilibus & vocatione suspensæ efficaciæ certitudinem salutis totius Israelis astruere non potuit. Denique si fideles suo vitio privari donis semel collatis possunt, eo ipso ἀμεταμέλητα esse desinerent. Non aliam enim ob causam ἀμεταμέλητα dicuntur, quàm quia Deus eos, quibus illa impertitur, nunquam eò usque deserit, ut ad
units.tr: XLVI. But the Spirit who is the seal and pledge [σφραγὶς καὶ ἀρραβὼν], that is, the mark of God and the earnest or pledge, is also the Spirit of power [πνεῦμα δυνάμεως], that is, the one who works powerfully, 2 Tim. 1.7. For he is our Creator and the mighty creator of the new man, by whom we are engrafted into Christ. He preserves us, makes us partakers of all the grace of God, and finally brings it about that the benefits of God acquired through Christ are conferred on believers, and not merely conferred but also remain to the end. Scripture declares this constancy of the benefits of grace bestowed by the Holy Spirit, both in general and in particular. It does so in general when it calls the graces of David [חסד דוד], that is, those bestowed on the typical David, and alike [ὁμοίως] on all, or those bestowed by the antitypical David, Christ, faithful [נאמנה], stable, enduring, not fleeting or subject to human chances, Isa. 55.3; and it calls the gifts of God [ἀμετα μέλητα], that is, of such a kind that God never so regrets them as to recall them, Rom. 11.29. It is quite pointless to say that the grace and gifts of God are constant and irrevocable [ἀμεταμέλητα] in themselves, yet, when people make themselves unworthy of them through their own fault, and with respect to God, who preserves faith in those who use the means ordained for it, while not with respect to men, who often shake faith, they are lost. For although the right use of means is required for the preservation of faith, that right use itself must also be counted among the faithful graces of God and the gifts [ἀμετα μέλητα]. Then the graces of God are promised as faithful by a covenant, and an eternal one, which can be annulled neither on God's side nor on man's; and besides, it is called a faithful covenant [ברית נאמנה], and indeed of such faithfulness and constancy that it is not rescinded even because of the sins of the sons of David, that is, the mystical David's, Ps. 89.29, 31. The Apostle, moreover, derives the irrevocable [ἀμεταμέλητα] gifts from the election [ἐκλογὴ] of God, v. 28, and teaches that election brings righteousness and salvation, v. 7. For he maintains that all Israel, being elect, shall be saved, v. 26, relying on the argument that the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable [ἀμεταμέλητα]. But from gifts that can be lost, and from a calling whose efficacy is suspended, he could not have established the certainty of the salvation of all Israel. Finally, if believers can, through their own fault, be deprived of gifts once bestowed, then by that very fact these gifts would cease to be irrevocable [ἀμεταμέλητα]. For they are called irrevocable [ἀμεταμέλητα] for no other reason than that God never deserts those to whom they are given to the point that they reach that degree of wickedness which could move God to deprive them of these gifts, and so to regret [pœnitudo] them.

units.la: eum malitiæ gradum perveniant, qui Deum ad illos donis his privandi, adeóque ad pœnitudinem adigere possit.
units.tr: to that degree of wickedness which could move God to deprive them of these gifts, and so to regret them.

units.la: XLVII. Etiam beneficiorum gratiæ nexus indivulsus perennitatem eorundem comprobat. Nam in universum ex plenitudine Christi χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος gratiam pro gratia, seu unam gratiam supra aliam, vel gratiam gratiæ succedentem, adeóque continuum gratiarum fluxum accipimus, Joh.I.16. Deus enim ex amore operis sui illud imperfectum non relinquit. Habenti dabitur, καὶ περισσευθήσεται & abundabit, Matth.XIII. 12. Qui etiam beneficiorum nexus inde liquet, quòd Scriptura illa non tantum à Divina electione Patris, & à redemptione Filii, ceu fonte suo derivat, & passim unionem nostram cum Christo, cum justificatione & adoptione, atque cum his sanctificationem connectit; sed etiam illa copulat cum Divina conservatione velut, Judæ v.1. ubi fideles κλητοὶ ἠγαπημένοι καὶ τετηρημένοι vocati, sanctificati, & conservati in Christo Jesu dicuntur; Quin & vocatio & complementum salutis velut connexa proponit. Nemo potest ad me venire, nisi Pater eum traxerit, & ego resuscitabo eum in ultimo die, Joh. VI. 44. Persuasum habeo hoc ipsum, fore, ut qui cœpit in vobis opus bonum, illud perficiat usque ad diem Jesu Christi, Phil.I.6. Quod Pauli de certis personis, quas pro fidelibus habuit, charitatis equidem & æquitatis judicium fuit, sed fundatum tamen in judicio fidei, quod in iis in genere, in quibus opus cœpit, illud, ob fidelitatem promissionum suarum, omnino perfecturus sit; juxta 1.Cor.X.13. 2.Thess.III.3. Alias persuasio ejus vana præsumptio rei à Deo non promissæ fuisset. Neque solidius illud est, quod iidem respondent: Deum bonum hoc opus perfecturum, modò fideles sibi ipsi non desint. Nam ne sibi desint, hoc ipsum illud ἔργον ἀγαθὸν opus bonum est, quod Deus perficit, ut videlicet in communione Evangelii Phil.I.5. perstent. Et si efficacia operationis Divinæ ab hominis operatione suspenderetur; Apostolus suæ persuasionis rationem non ab operatione Divina, sed à cooperatione humana Philippensium petiisset; neque dixisset, se ideo persuasum esse de perfectione operis hujus, quia Deus operaturus erat, sed quia spem concipiebat, fore ut operationi Divinæ respondeant, atque sic operationem Divinam incertæ juxta adversarios efficaciæ cooperatio in libertate hominis relicta certam reddat. Neque sic Deus bonum opus perficeret, sed perficeret homo. Denique hanc salutis consummationem Apostolus non tantùm ut nexum cum ejus impetratione & initio habentem, sed etiam ut necessariò fluentem ex dono tum Filii tum reconciliationis nostræ per eum proponit. Qui proprio Filio suo non pepercit, &c. quomodo non cum eo omnia nobis gratificabitur? Rom.VIII.32. Si cùm inimici essemus, reconciliati fuimus Deo per mortem Filii ejus, multò magis reconciliati servabimur per vitam ejus, ib.V.10.
units.tr: XLVII. The unbroken chain of the benefits of grace also proves their perpetuity.
