For in general we receive, from the fullness of Christ, grace for grace [χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος], that is, one grace upon another, or a grace succeeding a grace, and so a continuous flow of graces, John 1.16. For God, out of love for his work, does not leave it imperfect. To him that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance [καὶ περισσευθήσεται], Matt. 13.12. This connection of benefits is also clear from the fact that Scripture derives them not only from the divine election of the Father and the redemption of the Son, as from their source, and everywhere joins our union with Christ to justification and adoption, and with these to sanctification; it also links them with divine preservation, as in Jude v. 1, where believers are said to be called, beloved and kept [κλητοὶ ἠγαπημένοι καὶ τετηρημένοι], sanctified and preserved in Christ Jesus. Indeed, it sets forth the calling and the completion of salvation as if they were linked together: No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day, John 6.44. I am confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ, Phil. 1.6. This was Paul's judgment about certain persons whom he regarded as believers; it was a judgment of charity and fairness, yet it was grounded in a judgment of faith, that in those in whom he had begun the work, he would certainly complete it, on account of the faithfulness of his promises, according to 1 Cor. 10.13 and 2 Thess. 3.3. Otherwise his confidence would have been an empty presumption of a thing not promised by God. Nor is it any firmer when the same people reply that God will perfect this good work, provided only that believers do not fail themselves. For that they do not fail themselves is itself the good work [ἔργον ἀγαθὸν] that God performs, namely that they persevere in the fellowship of the gospel, Phil. 1.5. And if the efficacy of the divine operation were suspended on the operation of man, the Apostle would have sought the ground of his confidence not in the divine operation but in the cooperation of the Philippians, and would not have said that he was confident of the completion of this work because God would work it, but because he hoped that they would respond to the divine operation; and so, according to our opponents, the cooperation left to human freedom would make certain an operation whose efficacy is uncertain. Nor would God then be the one who perfects the good work, but man. Finally, the Apostle sets forth this completion of salvation not merely as connected with its obtaining and beginning, but as necessarily flowing from the gift both of the Son and of our reconciliation through him: He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? Rom. 8.32. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved by his life, Rom. 5.10.

units.la: XLVIII. Beneficia Gratiæ à Spiritu S. collata singula æquè atque universa perennant. Eorum veluti truncus quidam unio nostri cum Christo per fidem; rami verò justificatio, adoptio & sanctificatio sunt. Unionem nostri cum Christo non tantùm natura sua, & respectu Dei, sed etiam respectu hominis semel Christo uniti
units.tr: XLVIII. The benefits of grace conferred by the Holy Spirit endure, each one as much as all together. Of these, our union with Christ through faith is, as it were, the trunk; justification, adoption and sanctification are the branches. Our union with Christ is indissoluble, not only by its nature and with respect to God, but also with respect to man, once he has been united to Christ.

units.la: {a} Ceu Spiritus potentiæ, potenter operatur, mauam creationem conservat & efficit, ut beneficia per Christum acquisita iis qui Christi sunt, conferantur, & in iis manent. Quæ constantia gratiarum à Spiritu S. collatarum probatur tum generatim, ex immutabilitate donorum Dei. uniti, indissolubilem esse, emphasis terminorum, quibus ea exprimitur, proprietates, similitudines, vincula, fundamenta, efficacia & fructus ejus comprobant. Emphasis terminorum, cujusmodi sunt, quòd Christus dicitur habitare in cordibus nostris, Ephes. III. 17. & manere in nobis, Joh. VI. 56. Habitat in cordibus fidelium ut paterfamilias, non ut hospes & peregrinans divertit. Et manet apud fideles non ad tempus, sed in aeternum, ibid. XIV. 16. Proprietates ejusdem sunt, quòd & reciproca & arctissima est. Reciproca, juxta illa Christi: Qui comedit carnem, & bibit sanguinem meum, is in me manet, & ego in ipso, ibid. VI. 56. Arctissima, quia non qualiscunque unio, sed unitio est. O qui agglutinatus est Domino, unus Spiritus est, I. Cor. VI. 17. Imò etiam unitas est. Unum enim corpus est, Ephes. IV. 4. Corpus Christi, I. Cor. XII. 27. unus Spiritus cum eo, ibid. VI. 17. Imò corpus hoc mysticum constans Christo & nobis Christi nomine venit, ibid. XII. 12. Similitudines quoque seu comparatio unionis mysticæ cum omni genere unionum, naturalis, moralis, politicæ, œconomicæ, artificialis eandem indissolubilitatem potenter astruunt. Naturalis eaque arctissima unio vitis & palmitum; cibi & corporis, capitis & membrorum in corpore humano est. Christus vitis, nos palmites sumus, Joh. XV. 1. non emorientes utique, sed viventes semper; nisi forte Christo eam imperfectionem tribuere libet, quæ in terrena vite est, quæ palmites non semper vivificat, quia & ipsa emori, vel saltem marcescere poterit. Idem panis est ex Cœlo descendens, & vitam dans mundo, Joh. VI. 33. & quidem permanens ad vitam æternam, quem qui semel comedit, vivit in æternum, & non moritur, ib. v. 27. 50. 58. Sed & caput est corporis, quod Ecclesia est, Ephes. I. 22. 23. & tale quidem, quod membra sua vivificat, I. Cor. XV. 22. format primùm ex gleba inepta, quibus mox Spiritum vitæ inspirat, cujus continuo fluxu ea conservat, & quæ tandem in ultimo die resuscitat, Rom. VIII. 11. I. Cor. XV. 16. Moralis unio amicos inter intercedit. Christus quoque amicus suorum, eos amat usque ad finem, Joh. XIII. 1. amicitiæ illius author trahit homines funiculis humanis & funibus amoris, Hos. XI. 4. & in eo amorem suum commendat, quòd ex inimicis amicos facit, Rom. V. 8. & quoties hi periclitantur, pro iis intercedit, ne fides deficiat, Luc. XXII. 32. atque ita arcana vi exorbitantes in gyrum revocat. Politica unio Regis & subditorum est. Christus Rex, nos subditi ejus sumus; & Regnum ille non terrenum, vel precarium, sed æternum & promeritum debitumque habet, adeóque plane indissolubile, uti supra ostendimus. Oeconomica unio conjuges inter, nec non parentes & liberos obtinet. De conjugio Christi & Ecclesiæ ejúsque constantia multa superius diximus. Æternum enim est, Hos. II. 19. & formator Sponsæ suæ Christus est, Esaj. XLIII. 21. Ephes. II. 10 quam magnetica quadam vi ad se trahit, ut currat ad eum, & cujus ἐρως ei ἀνπρως inspirat, Cant. I. 4. quam sanctificat & lavacro aquæ purgat, Ephes. V. 26. Etiam Pater noster Christus est, quia nos genuit, Deut. XXXII. 18. Psal. LXXXVII. 4. Esaj. LXVI. 9. & frater noster idémque primogenitus, Rom.
units.tr: {a} Like the Spirit of power, he works powerfully, preserves the new creation and brings it about that the benefits acquired through Christ are conferred on those who are Christ's and remain in them. This constancy of the graces conferred by the Holy Spirit is proved in general from the immutability of God's gifts: united, it is indissoluble. The emphasis of the terms by which it is expressed, its properties, similitudes, bonds, foundations, efficacy and fruits confirm this. Consider the emphasis of the terms, such as that Christ is said to dwell in our hearts, Eph. 3.17, and to abide in us, John 6.56. He dwells in the hearts of believers as a master of the house, not as a guest who lodges and passes on; and he abides with believers not for a time but for ever, John 14.16. Its properties are that it is both reciprocal and very close. It is reciprocal, according to those words of Christ: He that eateth my flesh and drinketh my blood dwelleth in me, and I in him, John 6.56. It is very close, because it is not any sort of union but a joining together: He that is joined to the Lord is one spirit, 1 Cor. 6.17. Indeed it is also a unity: There is one body, Eph. 4.4; the body of Christ, 1 Cor. 12.27; one spirit with him, ibid. 6.17. Indeed this mystical body, consisting of Christ and of us, is called by the name of Christ, ibid. 12.12. The similitudes, too, that is, the comparisons of the mystical union with every kind of union, natural, moral, political, domestic and artificial, powerfully confirm the same indissolubility. The natural union, which is most close, is that of the vine and its branches, and of food and the body, and of the head and the members in the human body. Christ is the vine, we are the branches, John 15.1; branches that do not indeed die, but always live; unless perhaps one chooses to attribute to Christ that imperfection which belongs to an earthly vine, which does not always keep its branches alive, since it too may die or at least wither. He is the same bread that comes down from heaven and gives life to the world, John 6.33; and indeed the bread that remains to eternal life, so that whoever eats it once lives for ever and does not die, ibid. vv. 27, 50, 58. He is also the head of the body, which is the Church, Eph. 1.22, 23; and he is such a head that he quickens his members, 1 Cor. 15.22; he first forms them out of unfit clay and then breathes into them the spirit of life, by whose continual flow he preserves them, and at last on the last day he raises them up, Rom. 8.11; 1 Cor. 15.16. The moral union is that between friends. Christ too is the friend of his own; he loves them to the end, John 13.1; the author of this friendship draws men with cords of a man and with bands of love, Hos. 11.4; and in this he commends his love, that from enemies he makes friends, Rom. 5.8; and whenever they are in danger he intercedes for them, that their faith may not fail, Luke 22.32, and so by a hidden power he brings back those who have strayed into the right course. The political union is that of a king and his subjects. Christ is King, and we are his subjects; and he holds a kingdom that is not earthly or precarious, but eternal, merited and due, and therefore plainly indissoluble, as we have shown above. The domestic union holds between spouses, and likewise between parents and children. We have said much above about the marriage of Christ and the Church and its constancy. For it is eternal, Hos. 2.19; and Christ is the former of his bride, Isa. 43.21; Eph. 2.10, whom he draws to himself with a certain magnetic power, so that she runs to him, and in whom he breathes love [ἔρως], that is, desire for him, Song 1.4; whom he sanctifies and cleanses with the washing of water, Eph. 5.26. Christ is also our Father, because he begot us, Deut. 32.18; Ps. 87.4; Isa. 66.9; and our brother, and likewise the firstborn, Rom.

units.la: VIII. 29. & quidem talis prædestinatus, ib. adeóque perseverans; quin & author hujus relationis, quia in ipso Deus nos adoptavit, Ephes. I. 5. & Deus prædestinavit nos, ut conformes ipsi efficiamus, Rom. VIII. 29. Quomodo ergo non constanter conservaret, quos ipse sibi in fratres dari voluit, & quos idem Pater ipsi conformes dat? Unio denique artificialis fundamentum & petram inter atque domum, vestem inter & corpus est. Christus fundamentum & Petra Ecclesiæ est, Esaj. XXVIII. 16. Psal. XCV. 1. Matth. XVI. 18. I. Cor. III. 11. Super eo fundamento ædificamur, & super eo ædificium illud augescit in Templum sanctum in Domino, Ephes. II. 20 21. Neque tantùm ædificii hujus spiritualis fundamentum, sed etiam architectus Christus est. Super petram hanc ego ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, & portæ inferorum non prævalebunt, Matth. XVI. 18. Etiam vestis Christus est, qua induimur. Induite Dominum Jesum Christum, Rom. XIII. 14. Quotquot in Christum baptizati estis, Christum induistis, Gal. III. 27. Ipse verò hanc vestem, se ipsum, & justitiam suam donat, & eadem donatos adversus hostiles injurias munit; quæ etiam induta sui amorem imprimit, & ne unquam eam exuere velimus, efficit. Ecclesia amicta Sole justitiæ est, qui non tantum illustrat, sed etiam curationem in aliis suis affert, Malach. IV. 2. Apoc. XII. 1. Hac ceu veste desiderium Genes. XXXVII. 3. induti Deo Patri placent, & ab eodem benedictionem ἀμετάμελητον & irrevocabilem impetramus. Arctissima proin & constantissima hæc Christi & fidelium unio sit oportet, cui effigiandæ Spiritus S. omnium, quæ uspiam occurrunt, rerum συγγένεια & uniones adumbravit. Et uniones quidem mundanæ vitio hominum haud raró dissolvuntur & dispalescunt. At spiritualis hæc ne hominum vitio dissolvi possit, vel dissolvatur unquam, Christus efficit, qui non tantùm unionis hujus author & conservator, defectus, qui in terrenis illis emblematibus occurrunt, supplet & emendat, in singulis illis allusionibus ad res terrenas addens aliquid, quo unionis hujus mysticæ perpetuitas signanter notatur, uti ex iis, quæ attulimus, liquet; sed etiam in Divina illa sua oratione ἀπολύτως precatus est, ut credituri in ipsum unum sint in Patre & Filio, uti Pater est in Filio, & Filius in Patre, Joh. XVII. 22. Quid unitate Personarum S. S. Trinitatis indissolubile magis? Non enim unitæ sunt, sed ἓν εἰσι unum sunt, I. Joh. V. 7. Cùm igitur nec natura, nec mos, nec politia, nec œconomia, nec ars constantiam unionis nostræ cum Christo plenè adumbrare potuerit, Scriptura ineffabilem non tam unionem, quàm unitatem personarum S. S. Triados, ceu augustissimum quoddam exemplar insinuat. Accedunt ejusdem unionis tum vincula Spiritus S. quo Christus se fidelibus unit, & fides, qua fideles Christo se uniunt: tum fundamentum non hominis, sed Dei voluntas, qui prior nos dilexit, I. Joh. IV. 10. neque illa à consensu hominis dubio suspensa, sed consensum efficiens, & rata, seu veritas, firmitas, hoc est, firmissima, Esaj. XXV. 1. quippe morte Christi confirmata: tum denique ejusdem sequelæ & effectus, cujusmodi sunt, I. Cor. II. 22. Omnia ad bonum Deum diligentibus cooperantur, Rom. VIII. 28, & quòd vi unionis illius non modò Deus nos unà vivificavit spiritualiter, sed etiam unà suscitavit, & in cœlis collocavit,in Christo Iesu: (ubi de re futura, velut de re præterita loquitur, certitudinis insinuandæ gratia,) Ephes.II.6. Quomodo verò id, si unio hæc dissolubilis est, & ex putri paxillo humani arbitrii pendet?
units.tr: VIII. 29. And indeed such a person is predestined (ibid.), and therefore persevering. Moreover, the author of this relationship is himself, since God adopted us in him (Eph. I. 5), and God predestined us that we should be made conformed to him (Rom. VIII. 29). How then would he not constantly preserve those whom he himself willed to be given to him as brothers, and whom the same Father gives to be conformed to him? Finally, the union is pictured by images: artificial unions lie between foundation and rock and house, between garment and body. Christ is the foundation and Rock of the Church (Isa. XXVIII. 16; Ps. XCV. 1; Matt. XVI. 18; I Cor. III. 11). We are built upon that foundation, and upon it the building grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Eph. II. 20, 21). Christ is not only the foundation of this spiritual building but also its architect: upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail (Matt. XVI. 18). Christ is also the garment with which we are clothed: put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. XIII. 14); as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ (Gal. III. 27). He gives this garment, namely himself and his righteousness, and protects those who are so given against hostile injuries; and once clothed in it they are imprinted with his love and made unwilling ever to take it off. The Church is clothed with the Sun of righteousness, who not only illumines but also brings healing in his wings (Mal. IV. 2; Rev. XII. 1). Clothed in this garment of desire (Gen. XXXVII. 3), we please God the Father and obtain from him a blessing [ἀμετάμελητον], irrevocable. This union of Christ and believers therefore ought to be most close and most constant, and the Holy Spirit has shadowed it forth in the kinship [συγγένεια] and unions of all things found anywhere. Earthly unions are indeed often dissolved and fall apart through human fault. But this spiritual union cannot be dissolved through human fault, nor will it ever be dissolved, because Christ effects it. He is not only the author and preserver of this union; he also supplies and corrects the defects that occur in those earthly emblems, adding in each of those allusions to earthly things something by which the perpetuity of this mystical union is expressly marked, as is clear from what we have brought forward. He also, in his divine prayer, prayed absolutely [ἀπολύτως] that those who believe in him may be one in the Father and the Son, as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father (John XVII. 22). What could be more indissoluble than the unity of the Persons of the Holy Trinity? For they are not merely united, but are one [ἓν εἰσι] (I John V. 7). Since, therefore, neither nature, custom, civil order, economy, nor art could fully represent the constancy of our union with Christ, Scripture suggests the ineffable unity, rather than mere union, of the Persons of the Holy Triad as a most august model. To this union there also belong the bonds of the Holy Spirit, by which Christ unites himself to believers, and the faith by which believers unite themselves to Christ; also the foundation, which is not the will of man but the will of God, who loved us first (I John IV. 10). That will is not suspended on the doubtful consent of man, but effects consent and is firm, that is, the truth and firmness, most firm (Isa. XXV. 1), as it has been confirmed by the death of Christ. Finally, there are its consequences and effects, such as: all things work together for good for those who love God (Rom. VIII. 28); and that by the power of that union God not only made us alive together with him spiritually, but also raised us up together and seated us in the heavens in Christ Jesus (where he speaks of a future thing as though past, to convey certainty), Eph. II. 6. But how could this be so, if this union is dissoluble and hangs on the rotten peg of human choice?

units.la: XLIX. Ex unione cum Christo inprimis justificatio peccatoris fluit. Eam irrevocabilem esse, jam supra Loc.XVIII.77. obiter probare occupavimus. Scriptura certè ejus, quoad actum justificantem immutabilitatem diserte asserit. Nulla condemnatio in iis est, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, Rom.VIII.1. Qui credit, non venit in condemnationem, Joh.V.24. non morietur, ib.VI.50. imò translatus est à morte in vitam, ib.V.24. beatus est, Rom IV.6.7. & glorificatur, ibid.VIII.30. Tum justificationis causa seu fundamentum est פְּרָא צִדְקַת עוֹלָמִים justitia seculorum, sempiterna, ipsius Christi, Dan.IX.24. qui αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν æternam redemptionem invenit, Hebr. IX.12. sub conditione quidem, sed quam ipse quoque, ut applicaretur nobis, meruit. Non tantùm enim justitia illa promissa, sed etiam repræsentata, & à Patre in judicio pro nostra acceptata est, ut imputatio ejus dubia, vel ab incerta conditione suspensa dici nullo modo possit. Justificatio certè fidelium manifestatio, argumentum & complementum est justificationis ipsius Sponsoris; & negatio fructuum mortis & resurrectionis Christi negationem ipsius mortis & resurrectionis Christi involvit. Si mortui non suscitantur, neque Christus suscitatus est, 1.Cor.XV.16. Suscitatus enim est tanquam caput, in quo fideles vivificantur, ibid.v.22. Si igitur omnes illi, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, non sunt mortui: aut non justificantur, neque unus mortuus, justificatus & vivificatus est pro omnibus; quod falsum esse, Apostolus, 2. Cor.V.21. docuit. Certè Christus eos, qui sanctificantur, unica oblatione τετελείωκε, consummavit, hoc est, perfectè sanctificavit, Hebr.X.14. Quæ τελείωσις consummatio, si durationem perpetuam non includit, consummatio non est. Quod Apostolus ostendit, addens statim, εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς in perpetuum, citra interruptionem & finem, quomodo etiam Christus, ib.v.12. ad dextram Dei consedisse εἰς διηνεκὲς in perpetuum dicitur. Id ipsum etiam unitas justificationis seu τὸ ἐφάπαξ confirmat. Semel enim in Dei judicio lata sententia absolutionis perpetuum vigorem habet. Si unius lapsu multi mortui sunt, multò magis gratia Dei, & donum in gratia unius hominis Iesu Christi in multos abundavit; & qui abundantiam gratiæ & doni justitiæ acceperunt in vita regnabunt per unum Iesum Christum, Rom.V.15.17. Accedit tempus, quo Deus hominem justificat, illud ipsum videlicet, quo credere incipit. Si ambigua hominis obedientia & in fide perseverantia esset; Deus justificationem ad tempus usque consummatæ fidei & perseverantiæ differret. Nam justificatus κληρονόμος γίνεται hæres fit secundum spem vitæ æternæ, Tit.III.7. Neque hic juvat cum Remonstrantibus distinguere justificationem semiplenam, conditionatam & revocabilem hujus vitæ, & plenam, absolutam, irrevocabilem alterius vitæ. Nuspiam enim ita Scripturæ distinguunt, & præmaturè nimis Deus sic tribunal conscenderet. Neque ullam
units.tr: XLIX. From union with Christ, first of all, the justification of the sinner flows. We have already set out above, in passing, at Loc. XVIII.77, that it is irrevocable. Scripture certainly asserts its immutability expressly, as regards the justifying act: there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom. VIII. 1); he who believes does not come into condemnation (John V. 24); he shall not die (ibid. VI. 50); indeed he has passed from death to life (ibid. V. 24); he is blessed (Rom. IV. 6, 7), and is glorified (ibid. VIII. 30). Moreover, the cause or foundation of justification is the everlasting righteousness [פְּרָא צִדְקַת עוֹלָמִים], that is, the eternal righteousness of Christ himself (Dan. IX. 24), who obtained eternal redemption [αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν] (Heb. IX. 12). This is indeed under a condition, but a condition that he himself also merited, so that it might be applied to us. For that righteousness was not only promised but also presented, and was accepted by the Father in judgment on our behalf, so that its imputation cannot in any way be called doubtful or suspended on an uncertain condition. Certainly the justification of believers is the manifestation, the evidence and the completion of the justification of their Surety; and to deny the fruits of Christ's death and resurrection involves denying Christ's own death and resurrection. If the dead do not rise, then Christ has not been raised (I Cor. XV. 16). For he has been raised as the head, in whom believers are made alive (ibid. v. 22). If therefore all those for whom Christ died are not dead, then either they are not justified, or one who died, and was justified and made alive, was not dead for all; and the Apostle taught that this is false (II Cor. V. 21). Certainly by one offering he has perfected [τετελείωκε], that is, has consummated, those who are sanctified, that is, he has sanctified them perfectly (Heb. X. 14). But that perfecting or consummation is not a consummation if it does not include perpetual duration. The Apostle shows this, adding at once for ever [εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς], without interruption or end; just as Christ too is said to have sat at the right hand of God for ever [εἰς διηνεκὲς] (ibid. v. 12). The unity of justification, or once for all [τὸ ἐφάπαξ], likewise confirms this. For once the sentence of absolution has been pronounced in God's judgment, it has perpetual force. If through one man's fall many died, much more the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded to many; and those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life through the one Jesus Christ (Rom. V. 15, 17). Add to this the time at which God justifies a man, namely the very moment at which he begins to believe. If man's obedience were uncertain and his perseverance in faith doubtful, God would defer justification until faith and perseverance were brought to completion. For the justified person becomes an heir according to the hope of eternal life (Titus III. 7). Nor does it help here to distinguish with the Remonstrants a justification of this life that is half-complete, conditional and revocable, from another life's justification that is full, absolute and irrevocable. For Scripture nowhere makes such a distinction, and God would thus be mounting the tribunal much too early. Nor would any

units.la: sic justificationis vel prioris vel posterioris promissio consolatio :m haberet : & respectu Dei justificatio revocabilis ejus Majestate & Sapientia indigna foret, quia ne humano quidem judici sententiam talem quisquam tribueret. Quis enim judex gravis & prudens sedebit ad judicium, in quo ferat sententias non necessarias, quibus se hominum ludibrio exponat, hodie absolvens, cras condemnans, & toties mutans dictum, quoties reus mores mutat. Sed irrevocabilis gratiæ sententia non humanæ obedientiæ, sed Christi ἀνυπέρβατα innititur, sapientia Dei judicis digna, & cum laude summæ benignitatis Dei hominem de salute sua certum, non funambulum reddentis, conjuncta est. Præterea fructus justificationis nostræ, quoad statum præsentem pax conscientiæ, tentationi de ira Dei opposita: quoad statum fururum gloriatiu sub spe gloriæ Dei, Rom.V.1.2. opposita tentationi de mutabilitate statūs nostri præsentis statuitur. Quis intentabit crimina adversus electos Dei? Deus est, qui justificat. Quis condemnabit? Christus is est, qui mortuus est, Rom. VIII. 33.34. Qui triumphus planè inanis esset, si Deus justificationem suam unquam revocaret. Denique Scriptura justificatos pœnam omnium peccatorum suorum luituros testatur. Faciet judicium de omnibus, & redarguet omnes impios eorum de omnibus operibus impietatis eorum, quæ impiè egerunt, Jud.v.15. An ergo Deus semel in hac vita remissa peccata in inferno puniet? Nam quæ de peccatorum ante remissorum reviviscentia Scholastici garriunt, ἀνοσια plane sunt, quia pœna reviviscere non potest, nisi culpa reviviscat, neque hæc reviviscere potest, nisi iidem actus ante patrati & habitus peccati per justitiam deleti, individualiter reproducantur, & eo quidem momento, quo fidelis gratia excidit. Et par delirarium est remissionem peccatorum conditionatam statuentium, quia conditionata ejusmodi remissio non remissio, sed suspensio remissionis, vel spes data remissionis purae, imò quodammodo retentio pœnæ, dum conditio impleatur, est. Et remissionis peccatorum descriptioni è diametro repugnat. Nam Deus peccata delere, eorum non recordari, ea in profundissimum maris projicere, faciem ab iis avertere, &c. dicitur. Et absolute Nathan Davidi dixit: Iehova peccatum tuum transtulit, 2. Sam. XII. 13. Christus Paralytico; Remissa tibi sunt peccata tua, Matth.IX.2.
units.tr: promise of justification, either earlier or later, afford such consolation: and with respect to God, a revocable justification would be unworthy of his majesty and wisdom, since no one would attribute such a sentence even to a human judge. For what grave and prudent judge would sit down to a judgment in which he pronounced sentences that were unnecessary, by which he exposed himself to the mockery of men, absolving today, condemning tomorrow, and changing his verdict as often as the accused changes his conduct? But the sentence of irrevocable grace rests not on human obedience but on the unbreakable [ἀνυπέρβατα] ground of Christ; it is worthy of the wisdom of God as judge, and joined with praise of the supreme goodness of God, rendering a man certain of his salvation, not a tightrope walker. Moreover, the fruits of our justification are set against temptation: as regards the present state, peace of conscience, set against the temptation concerning the wrath of God; as regards the future state, boasting in hope of the glory of God, set against the temptation concerning the mutability of our present state (Rom. V. 1, 2). Who will bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? It is Christ Jesus, who died (Rom. VIII. 33, 34). That triumph would be utterly empty if God ever revoked his justification. Finally, Scripture testifies that the justified will pay the penalty for all their sins: he will execute judgment on all, and convict all the ungodly of all their ungodly deeds, which they have committed ungodly (Jude v. 15). Will God then, having once remitted sins in this life, punish them in hell? For what the Scholastics babble about the revival of sins previously remitted is utterly impious [ἀνοσια], because punishment cannot revive unless guilt revives, and guilt cannot revive unless the same acts committed before, and the habits of sin that were destroyed by righteousness, are reproduced individually, and at the very moment when the believer falls from grace. And it is equally absurd to hold a conditional remission of sins, because a remission of that kind is not a remission but a suspension of remission, or a hope given of pure remission; indeed it is in some way a retention of punishment while the condition is being fulfilled. It is also diametrically opposed to the description of the remission of sins. For God is said to blot out sins, not to remember them, to cast them into the depths of the sea, to turn his face away from them, and so on. And Nathan spoke absolutely to David: the LORD has put away your sin (II Sam. XII. 13); and Christ to the paralytic: your sins are forgiven you (Matt. IX. 2).

units.la: L. Justificationem adoptio sequitur. Cujus beneficium non minùs atque illius durabile, imò perpetuum est. Ideo enim Deus justificatos adoptat in filios, ut certissimam salutem iis redderet, utpote ad quam duplex in Christo jus & titulum iis contulit. Christus enim suis se uniens simul caput & frater noster esse voluit. Et quatenus ille ceu caput nostrum pro nobis satisfecit, Deus, qua judex æternam vitam nobis adjudicat: quatenus verò nos fratres suos fecit, Deus, qua Pater. Testamento suo nobis salutem, ceu hæreditatem promittit. Facti enim sumus Dei hæredes & cohæredes Christi, Rom. VIII.17. Cujus hæreditatis certitudinem ipsa adoptionis natura ostendit. Nam nec Deus adoptans certas personas sibi deligere hæredes voluit, cum consilio & periculo mutandi Testamenti: & adoptio ipsa tanta dignitas, gnitas, & tam sublimis honor est, ut cogitari sine stabilitate & certitudine possessionis non possit. Adamus equidem creatus mutabilis est, sed servus Dei, in statu merendi vitam positus, nondum jus ad illam habens. At fideles in Christo filii Dei jus habent ad vitam à Christo illis acquisitam, & Testamento donatam. Licet ergo minus luminis & sanctitatis in hac vita habeant, quàm Adamus integer habuit, plus tamen in statu suo firmamenti habent. Nam illis secus ac Adamo hæreditas salutis non ut contingens & possibilis, sed ut futura & certa tribuitur. Designantur enim hæredes, ceu μέλλοντες κληρονομεῖν τὴν σωτηρίαν salutem hæreditate accepturi, seu futuri hæredes salutis, Hebr. I. 14. utpote hæreditate adituri Regnum iis à fundatione mundi præparatum, Matth. XXV. 34. Imò Scriptura diserte verbis adoptionis constantiam declarat. Dabo (cunctis retinentibus fœdus meum) in domo mea, & in muris meis manum & nomen melius nomine filiorum & filiarum. Nomen æternum dabo ipsis, quod non exscindetur, Esaj. LVI. 5. quæ illa ἐξουσία γίνεσθαι τέκνα Θεοῦ potestas, ut fiant filii Dei, Joh. I. 12. est. Et servus, inquit Christus ipse, non manet in domo in seculum, Filius manet in seculum, Joh. VIII. 35. Ubi autem Filius Christus est, ibi etiam fratres ejus sunt. Ubi ego sum, etiam vos eritis, ibid. XIV. 3. Cúmque ad hæreditatem Regni Cœlorum duo requirantur, titulus juris, & aptitudo ad possidendam eam, juris titulum adoptio, aptitudinem ad possidendum regeneratio præstat. Qui duo filiationis modi in filiatione naturali, in qua nec genitus adoptatur, nec adoptivus gignitur, ἀνυιοθεσία, in spirituali concurrunt, quia generatio spiritualis seorsim spectata communicat quidem fidelibus θείας φύσεως Divinam naturam, 2. Petr. I. 4. sed jus hæreditatis non confert, quia improprie dicta generatio est, quæ non essentiam gignentis, sed imaginem duntaxat, eámque imperfectam & labe peccati in hac vita infectam communicat. Ideo generationi spirituali adoptio accedit, jus & possessionem hæreditatis conferens, eóque certius, quia Divina adoptio & regeneratio iis imperfectionibus, quæ inter homines exhæredationi locum dant, obnoxia non est. Nam qui adoptant, quærunt virtute præditos & morigeros; & qui generant, pietatem genitis optant, at non communicant. Sed Deus adoptans & regenerans probos piósque facit, non quærit vel optat. Ac licèt adoptati & regeniti identidem in peccata incidant, atque exhæredationem mereantur, tamen Deus semel adoptatos & regenitos non exhæredat. Corripit virga hominem, sed benignitatem suam non amovet, 2. Sam. VII. 14. Quæ promissio, Psal. LXXXIX. 31. ad omnes filios Davidis spirituales extenditur, asseverante ibidem Deo, se contra veritatem, fœdus & juramentum suum acturum, si aliter ageret, ibid. v. 34. 35. 36. Quin etiam Deus adoptionis hujus firmitatem & æternitatem per scripta & facta atque symbola confirmat. Per scripta, quia non tantùm fidelis quisque sua manu, quasi dato chirographo, ad perpetuitatem transitionis suæ in familiam Dei consignandam, scribit, יהוה Jehovæ sum, Esaj. XLIV. 5. sed etiam Deus ipse nomen fidelium tum in Cœlis scribit, Luc. X. 20. & quidem in libro Agni, Apoc. XIII. 6. tum & in, vel super nobis,
units.tr: Adoption follows justification. Its benefit is no less lasting than justification itself; indeed it is perpetual. God adopts the justified as sons so that he may give them the most certain salvation, since in Christ he has granted them a double right and title to it. For Christ, uniting himself with his own, wished to be both our head and our brother. Insofar as he, as our head, has made satisfaction for us, God, as judge, adjudges eternal life to us; insofar as he has made us his brothers, God acts as our Father. By his testament he promises us salvation as an inheritance. For we have become heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ [Rom. 8.17]. The very nature of adoption shows the certainty of this inheritance. For God, adopting certain persons, did not wish to choose heirs for himself, since that would involve a plan and the risk of changing the testament; and adoption itself is such great dignity and so sublime an honour that it cannot be conceived without stability and certainty of possession. Adam, indeed, was created mutable, but as a servant of God, placed in a state of earning life, he did not yet have a right to it. But the faithful, as sons of God in Christ, have a right to the life acquired for them by Christ and bequeathed by the testament. Although they have less light and holiness in this life than Adam had in his integrity, they have more firmness in their state. For the inheritance of salvation is given to them, unlike Adam, not as contingent and possible, but as future and certain. They are designated heirs, as those who are about to inherit salvation [μέλλοντες κληρονομεῖν τὴν σωτηρίαν], to receive salvation by inheritance, or future heirs of salvation (Heb. 1.14), since they are to enter upon the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world (Matt. 25.34). Indeed, Scripture plainly declares the constancy of adoption in the very words of adoption: To those who keep my covenant I will give in my house and within my walls a hand and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off (Isa. 56.5). This is that power to become the children of God [ἐξουσία γίνεσθαι τέκνα Θεοῦ] (John 1.12). And Christ himself says: The servant does not remain in the house for ever; the son remains for ever (John 8.35). Where the Son Christ is, there his brothers are also: Where I am, there you also will be (ibid. 14.3). Since two things are required for the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven, a title of right and fitness to possess it, adoption supplies the title of right, and regeneration supplies the fitness to possess. These two modes of sonship meet in spiritual sonship, whereas in natural sonship, in which the begotten is not adopted and the adopted is not begotten, there is no such union. Spiritual generation, considered by itself, indeed communicates to the faithful the divine nature [θείας φύσεως] (2 Pet. 1.4), but it does not confer the right of inheritance, because it is improperly called generation: it communicates not the essence of the begetter but only an image, and that an imperfect one, tainted in this life by the stain of sin. Therefore adoption is added to spiritual generation, conferring the right and possession of the inheritance, and all the more surely because divine adoption and regeneration are not subject to those imperfections which, among men, give occasion for disinheritance. For those who adopt look for men endowed with virtue and obedient; and those who beget wish their offspring to be pious, but cannot bring this about. But God, in adopting and regenerating, makes men upright and pious; he does not look for or wish for this. And although the adopted and regenerated fall into sin from time to time and deserve disinheritance, God does not disinherit those whom he has once adopted and regenerated. The rod corrects a man, but he does not take away his kindness (2 Sam. 7.14). This promise, Ps. 89.31, extends to all David's spiritual sons, God solemnly declaring there that, if he acted otherwise, he would act against his truth, covenant and oath (ibid. vv. 34–36). Indeed God confirms the firmness and eternity of this adoption by writings, deeds and symbols. By writings: for not only does each believer write with his own hand, as if by a handwritten deed, to seal the permanence of his transfer into God's family, I am Jehovah's (Isa. 44.5); but God himself also writes the names of the faithful in heaven (Luke 10.20), and indeed in the Lamb's book (Rev. 13.8), and in us or upon us,

units.la: juxta illa Christi: Qui vicerit, faciam eum columnam in populo Dei mei, & scribam super ipso nomen Dei mei, & nomen civitatis Dei mei, novæ Hierusalem, & nomen meum novum, ibid. III. 12. & intra nos in cordibus nostris, ad sensum ejus nobis ingenerandum, dans calculum album, & in calculo eo novum nomen inscriptum, nempe filiorum Dei, quod nemo novit, nisi qui accipit, ibid. II. 7. & denique extra nos, in fronte, ad significandam protectionem Dei adversus omnes hostes, ibid. VII. 3. Accedit, quòd etiam de nomine Dei vocandi fideles, Esaj. LXV. 1. dicuntur. Quorsum hæc omnia, nisi ad significandam constantiam adoptionis? Per facta etiam & symbola, cujusmodi plurima supra § XXI. &c. cumulavimus.
units.tr: according to those words of Christ: He who overcomes, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, and my new name (Rev. 3.12); and within us, in our hearts, to engrave this sense in us, giving a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, namely that of the sons of God, which no one knows except him who receives it (ibid. 2.17); and finally outside us, on the forehead, to signify God's protection against all enemies (ibid. 7.3). To this is added that the faithful are said to be called by the name of God (Isa. 65.1). To what end are all these things, if not to signify the constancy of adoption? Through deeds and symbols also, of which very many we have heaped up above, §XXI, etc.

units.la: LI. Cum justificatione & adoptione sanctificatio cohæret. Ejus τὸ ἁγιασμὸν non tantùm in universum Apostolus confirmat, asserens, Christum unica oblatione consummasse eos, qui sanctificantur, Hebr. X. 14. sed etiam ejusdem denominationes, sacramentum, & sanctitatis ipsius descriptio comprobant. Quoad denominationes, passim illa glorificationis, resurrectionis & regenerationis nomine venit. Glorificationis nomine Apostolus subintelligit, dicens: Quos justificavit, eos glorificavit, Rom. VIII. 30. Ubi sanctificatio in terra inchoata, & in Cœlo gloriosè consummanda intelligitur. Nam hæc justificationi succedit; ideò etiam loquitur in praeterito, dicens; ὡς ἐδόξασεν quos glorificavit, quia videlicet ejus in hac vita initium quoddam est, & glorificationis consummatæ certitudinem conjunctam habet. Resurrectionis sanctificationem significantis vox, distinctio & cum resurrectione Christi collatio eandem sanctificationis perpetuitatem statuminat. Vox, quia Scriptura sanctificationem resurrectionis, seu vivificationis mortuorum nomine Joh. V. 25. indigetans, ad resurrectionem corporum universalem v. 28. alludit, quæ cùm unica & constans sit, etiam animæ resurrectio unica & constans sit oportet. Distinctio, quia sicut respectu reproborum unica resurrectio, nempe corporum est: ita fidelium respectu gemina duntaxat, spiritualis & corporalis resurrectio commemoratur. Beatus & sanctus, qui partem habet in resurrectione prima. In tales mors secunda potestatem non habet, Apoc. XX. 6. Præterea etiam collatio resurrectionis nostræ spiritualis & corporalis Christi id ipsum mirè confirmat. Sicut enim Christus ex mortuis suscitatus non amplius moritur, sed vivit in æternum: ita nos cum Christo mortui, & credentes, quòd cum eodem viduri simus, semel resuscitati spiritualiter cum eodem non morimur amplius, sed in æternum vivimus, Rom. VI. 8. 9. Nam quòd mortuus Christus est, peccato semel mortuus est. Quòd verò vivit, vivit Deo. Sic & vos reputate, vos quidem mortuos esse peccato, viventes verò Deo in Jesu Christo, Domino nostro, in perpetuum videlicet, & sensu augustiore, quo & Christus non moritur, sed in æternum vivere dicitur, ibid. v. 10. 11. Etiam denominatio ἀναγέννησις & παλιγγενεσίας regenerationis, qua voce sanctificatio, Tit. III. 5. 1. Petr. I. 3. venit, quia in regeneratione confertur, ejusdem σεμνότητα firmitudinem comprobat. Nam si sanctificatio spiritualis regeneratio est, totalis & essentialis, ratione status spirispiritualis, mutatio sit oportet. Sicut enim per generationem à non esse ad esse transimus, nec bis in mundo nascimur, sed semel nati ad mortem usque corpore, & spiritu in æternum duramus; ita regeniti, seu spiritualiter geniti semel, non bis pluriésve in novo Ecclesiæ mundo nascimur, & vitam spiritualem perpetuam traducimus. Sacramentum sanctificationis nostræ, in V.T. Circumcisio, in Novo Baptismus eandem constantiam luculenter etiam comprobat. Neutrum enim illud iterari potuit, vel potest. Vel ergo perseverantiæ adversarii Novatianorum, veniam lapsis negantium, errorem refodere; vel, si sæpius homo regenerari potest, Sacramenti ejusdem repetitionem admittere debent; inprimis cùm iidem Baptismum non tantùm sigillum, sed etiam causam regenerationis esse pertendant.
units.tr: LI. With justification and adoption sanctification is joined. The Apostle confirms this in general, asserting that Christ by one offering has perfected those who are sanctified (Heb. 10.14) [τὸ ἁγιασμὸν]; but the names given to it, the sacrament, and the description of holiness itself confirm the same. As to the names, it is everywhere designated by the names of glorification, resurrection and regeneration. The Apostle implies glorification when he says: Whom he justified, them he also glorified (Rom. 8.30). Here sanctification is understood as begun on earth and to be gloriously consummated in heaven. For it follows justification; therefore he also speaks in the past tense, saying whom he glorified [ὡς ἐδόξασεν quos glorificavit], because it has in this life a certain beginning and carries with it the certainty of consummated glorification. The word resurrection, signifying sanctification, together with the distinction and comparison with the resurrection of Christ, establishes the same perpetuity of sanctification. The word: because Scripture, calling sanctification by the name of resurrection, or the quickening of the dead (John 5.25), alludes to the universal resurrection of bodies (v. 28); and since this is single and constant, the resurrection of the soul must also be single and constant. The distinction: because, just as with the reprobate there is only one resurrection, namely of the body, so with the faithful only a twofold resurrection, spiritual and bodily, is mentioned. Blessed and holy is he who has a part in the first resurrection. Over such the second death has no power (Rev. 20.6). Moreover, the comparison of our spiritual and bodily resurrection with that of Christ confirms this very thing remarkably. For just as Christ, raised from the dead, dies no more, but lives for ever, so we, dead with Christ and believing that we shall live with him, once spiritually raised do not die with him any more, but live for ever (Rom. 6.8–9). For in that Christ died, he died once to sin; but in that he lives, he lives to God. So also you reckon yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Jesus Christ our Lord (ibid. vv. 10–11), that is, for ever, and in a fuller sense, in which Christ is also said not to die but to live for ever. The name of regeneration also, anagennēsis and palingenesia [ἀναγέννησις & παλιγγενεσίας], by which sanctification is designated (Titus 3.5; 1 Pet. 1.3), since it is conferred in regeneration, confirms the same firmness of it. For if spiritual sanctification is regeneration, it must be total and essential, a change in the condition of the spirit. For just as by generation we pass from non-being to being, and are not born twice in the world, but once born we endure in body until death and in spirit for ever, so the regenerate, or those spiritually begotten once, are not born twice or more in the new world of the Church, but lead a perpetual spiritual life. The sacrament of our sanctification, circumcision in the Old Testament and baptism in the New, also clearly proves the same constancy. For neither of these could or can be repeated. Therefore, either they must dig up the error of the Novatians, who deny pardon to the lapsed, in the very perseverance of their opponents; or, if a man can be regenerated often, they must admit a repetition of the same sacrament, especially since they contend that baptism is not only the seal but also the cause of regeneration.

units.la: LII.
units.tr: LII.

units.la: Res per sanctificationem in cordibus nostris producta Sanctitas, ejusdem perpetuitatem amplius demonstrat. Quæ in genere nova vita, in specie singulis virtutibus constat. Quæ si perpetuæ & indeclinabiles sunt, ipsa quoque sanctificatio perpetua & indeclinabilis sit oportet. Atqui nova vita æterna est. Nam Christus ovibus suis dat ζωὴν αἰώνιον vitam æternam, Joh. X. 28. non si perseveret in fide, sed absolutè, quia ipsa fides vita spiritualis animæ nostræ, vel ejus magna pars est. Et Christus diserte dicit, credentem ἔχειν ζωὴν αἰώνιον habere jam vitam æternam, & in judicium non venire, sed transivisse ex morte in vitam, Joh. V. 24. Nempe vita illa non fidelium, sed ipsius Christi est. Vivo non amplius ego, sed vivit in me Christus: Quod verò nunc vivo in carne, in fide vivo Filii Dei, Gal. II. 20. Non ergo vita hæc humanæ voluntatis arbitrio subjacet, sed simpliciter æterna est, quia Christus factus est Sacerdos non secundum legem mandati carnalis, sed κατὰ δύναμιν ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτου secundum potentiam vitæ indissolubilis, Heb. VII. 16. Neque enim secundus Adamus perinde ut primus, factus est in animam viventem, sed εἰς πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν in spiritum vivificantem, 1. Cor. XV. 45. Adami primi vita æterna esse potuit; sed æternam ille vitam non habuit, quia vitæ conservatio non in fœdere operum, sed gratiæ promissa est. Etiam novus homo & nova creatura, quales fideles sunt, 2. Cor. V. 17. Gal. VI. 15. Eph. IV. 24. perennat utique. Nam τὸ παλαιούμενον καὶ γηράσκον quod antiquatur & senescit, prope est ut evanescat, Hebr. VIII. 13. At nova, quale novum Cœlum, nova terra est, durant. Ideo novus homo non perinde ut vetus, destrui, evanescere, sed crescere in Domino, Eph. II. 21. & αὐξεῖν τῷ αὐξήσιν ἐν Θεῷ crescere incrementum Dei, Col. II. 19. transformari de gloria in gloriam, 2. Cor. III. 18. dicitur. Imò Christus ipse in nobis μορφοῦται formatur, Gal. IV. 19. & nos participes naturæ Divinæ nulli corruptioni & caducitati obnoxiæ, simus, 2. Petr. I. 4.
units.tr: The holiness produced in our hearts through sanctification further demonstrates its perpetuity. In general it consists of a new life, and in particular of the individual virtues. If these are perpetual and unchangeable, sanctification itself must also be perpetual and unchangeable. But the new life is eternal. For Christ gives to his sheep eternal life [ζωὴν αἰώνιον], John 10:28, not on condition that they persevere in faith, but absolutely, because faith itself is the spiritual life of our soul, or a large part of it. Christ also plainly says that the one who believes has eternal life [ἔχειν ζωὴν αἰώνιον] already, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life, John 5:24. Indeed that life belongs not to the faithful but to Christ himself: "I no longer live, but Christ lives in me; and the life I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God," Gal. 2:20. Therefore this life is not subject to the choice of the human will, but is simply eternal, because Christ was made priest not according to the law of a carnal commandment, but according to the power of an indissoluble life [κατὰ δύναμιν ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτου], Heb. 7:16. For the second Adam was not made, as the first was, a living soul, but a life-giving spirit [εἰς πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν], 1 Cor. 15:45. The life of the first Adam could have been eternal; but he did not have it eternally, because the preservation of life was promised not in the covenant of works but in the covenant of grace. The new man and new creature, which believers are, 2 Cor. 5:17; Gal. 6:15; Eph. 4:24, certainly endures. For what is growing old and aging [τὸ παλαιούμενον καὶ γηράσκον] is close to vanishing, Heb. 8:13. But the new, like a new heaven and a new earth, lasts. Therefore the new man does not, as the old man does, get destroyed and vanish, but is said to grow in the Lord, Eph. 2:21, and to increase with the increase of God [αὐξεῖν τῷ αὐξήσιν ἐν Θεῷ], Col. 2:19, and to be transformed from glory to glory, 2 Cor. 3:18. Indeed Christ himself is formed in us [μορφοῦται], Gal. 4:19, and we are partakers of the divine nature, subject to no corruption or decay, 2 Pet. 1:4.

units.la: LIII.
units.tr: LIII.

units.la: In specie Sanctitas illa θαυμαστὴ τελεωτάτη admirabili triga virtutum Christianismi, fidei, spei & charitatis absolvitur. Et conjunctæ illæ & singulæ statum, efficaciam & firmitatem maximam habent. Efficacia illarum in eo consistit, quòd fidelem ad officium impellant, & adversus molimina hostium custodiant, quæ duo firmitatis etiam & stabilitatis eorundem certissima argumenta sunt. Priorem efficaciam Apostolus docet, fidei τὸ ἔργον ὁ ὁπus, charitati τῶν κόπων laborem, & spei τῶν ὑπομονὴν patientiam tribuens, 1. Thess. I. 3. Singulæ ergo sunt ἐνεργούμεναι efficaces, operantes, quod fidei Apostolus, Gal. V. 6. tribuit. Fides enim ad exercitium bonorum operum: charitas ad difficultates & molestias in iis superandas: Spes afflictiones tolerandas valet. Posteriorem efficaciam commendat, quòd hæ virtutes, ceu præstantissima fidelis armatura, caput & pectus, ne vitæ ejus spiritualis sedes lædatur, muniens, laudantur. Nos autem cùm simus lucis, vigilemus, induti thoracem fidei & charitatis, & galeam, spem salutis, 1. Thess. V. 8. Earundem perennitatem Apostolus docet: Tria hæc, inquiens, fides, spes & charitas manent, 1. Cor. XIII. 13. Et manent non ad breve tempus, cùm hæc nec vera mansio sit; sed usque dum perfectio in Cœlis advenerit. Cùm venerit τὸ τέλειον perfectum, abolebitur τὸ ἐκ μέρους quod ex parte est, hoc est, fidei & spei, qualis in hac vita est, imperfectio; at his major charitas in altera etiam vita durabit, ibid. v. 9. 10. 12. 13. Fides enim & spes ad Cœlum perducunt, sed in Cœlum non ingrediuntur, quia illa in visionem Dei, hæc in fruitionem gloriæ ejus convertitur: Charitas autem in cœlum ingreditur, æternúmque durat.
units.tr: Holiness is perfected in particular in the admirable and most perfect triad of Christian virtues: faith, hope and charity. These, both joined together and each on its own, have the greatest state, efficacy and firmness. Their efficacy consists in this: they drive the believer to duty and guard against the schemes of enemies, and these two things are the most certain proofs of their firmness and stability. The Apostle teaches the first kind of efficacy, ascribing to faith the work [τὸ ἔργον], to charity the labour [τοῦ κόπου], and to hope the patience [τῆς ὑπομονῆς], 1 Thess. 1:3. Each of them is therefore energetic, working [ἐνεργούμενα], which the Apostle ascribes to faith, Gal. 5:6. For faith serves the practice of good works; charity serves to overcome the difficulties and troubles in them; hope serves to endure afflictions. The second kind of efficacy is commended in that these virtues, like the most excellent armour of the believer, are praised for protecting the head and breast, so that the seat of his spiritual life is not harmed. But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation, 1 Thess. 5:8. The Apostle teaches their perpetuity: These three, he says, faith, hope and charity remain, 1 Cor. 13:13. And they remain not for a short time, since this is not their true abode, but until perfection comes in heaven. When that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be done away [τὸ ἐκ μέρους], that is, the imperfection of faith and hope, such as it is in this life; but charity, which is greater than these, will last even in the other life, ibid. vv. 9, 10, 12, 13. For faith and hope lead to heaven, but do not enter heaven, because faith is turned into the vision of God and hope into the enjoyment of his glory. But charity enters heaven and lasts for ever.

units.la: LIV.
units.tr: LIV.

units.la: Fidei scorsim Scriptura στερέωμα soliditatem, firmitatem tribuit. Gaudeo videns τὸ στερέωμα τῆς εἰς Χριστὸν πίστεως ὑμῶν, firmitatem fidei vestræ in Christum, Col. II. 5. Oppositè ad fidem temporariam eidem ῥίζα radix Matth. XIII. 21. tribuitur. Fide stamus, 2. Cor. I. 24. Fides ὑπόστασις subsistentia eorum, quæ speratur, est, Hebr. XI. 1. credentem corroborat, Rom. IV. 20. dubitationem, ἀκαταστασίαν inconstantiam excludit, Jac. I. 6. 7. 8. Φυλάσσει custodit, 1. Pet. I. 5. ὀπλὸς scutum est quo ignita Sathanæ tela extinguuntur, Ephes. VI. 16. Vincit mundum, 1. Joh. V. 4. promissionem ζωῆς αἰωνίου vitæ æternæ habet, Joh. V. 24. & quòd credens non esuriturus vel bibiturus sit, ibid. VI. 35. Ejusdem excellentiam & proprietates Scriptura emblemate rerum, quæ sua pulchritudine & pretio se commendant, quibus tamen ipsis in eo quòd fluxæ & caducæ sunt, eandem opponit. Nam plantæ Matth XIII. 8. comparatur, & simul opponitur, quia non æquè atque illa torrefit & exarescit, ibid. v. 6. Auro etiam per ignem explorato sic comparatur, ut tamen pretiosior χρυσίου χρυσωμένῳ auro pereunte, adeóque non perire ipsa statuatur, Apoc. III. 18. 1. Petr. I. 7. Denique & lumini comparatur, Esaj. LX. 1. Ephes. V. 14. sed σβέννυμι, quod non extinguitur, quia lychnum fumigantem Christus non extinguit, Esaj. XLII. 3. neque permittit, ut fides deficiat, sicut lumen terrestre deficit & extinguitur. Ejusmodi enim lux est, quæ erumpit sicut aurora, ibid. LVIII. 8. & perpetuò usque ad plenum meridiem progreditur. Quæ fidei, eadem spei ratio est. Est enim ζῶσα viva, 1. Petr. I. 3. quia & fructus vitæ edit, & spes vitæ est, & permanet: uti vivere dicuntur, quæ perennia sunt. Deus enim nobis dat παράκλησιν ἀγαθὴν consolationem æternam & spem bonam, adeóque etiam spem æternam, quia consolatio nonnisi spei, in qua fundatur, respectu,
units.tr: Scripture ascribes to faith by itself firmness and solidity [στερέωμα]. I rejoice, seeing your firmness [τὸ στερέωμα] of faith in Christ, Col. 2:5. In contrast to temporary faith, a root [ῥίζα] is ascribed to it, Matt. 13:21. By faith we stand, 2 Cor. 1:24. Faith is the substance [ὑπόστασις] of the things hoped for, Heb. 11:1; it strengthens the believer, Rom. 4:20; it excludes doubt and inconstancy [ἀκαταστασίαν], Jas. 1:6–8. It guards [φυλάσσει], 1 Pet. 1:5. It is a shield [ὁπλὸν] by which the fiery darts of Satan are quenched, Eph. 6:16. It overcomes the world, 1 John 5:4; it has the promise of eternal life, John 5:24; and that the one who believes will not hunger or thirst, ibid. 6:35. Scripture sets forth its excellence and properties by means of images of things which commend themselves by their beauty and worth, and yet sets faith over against them in that they are fleeting and perishable. For faith is compared to a plant, Matt. 13:8, and at the same time contrasted with it, because it does not wither and dry up as that does, ibid. v. 6. It is also compared to gold tested by fire, yet in such a way that it is set up as more precious than perishing gold, and so as not to perish itself, Rev. 3:18; 1 Pet. 1:7. Finally it is compared to light, Isa. 60:1; Eph. 5:14, but a light that is not put out [σβέννυμι], because Christ does not quench the smoking flax, Isa. 42:3, and does not allow faith to fail as earthly light fails and goes out. For this is the kind of light that breaks forth like the dawn, ibid. 58:8, and advances constantly until full noon. What holds for faith also holds for hope. For it is living [ζῶσα], 1 Pet. 1:3, because it both produces the fruits of life and is the hope of life, and it abides, as things are said to live when they are perennial. For God gives us good consolation [παράκλησιν ἀγαθὴν], eternal consolation and good hope, and so also an eternal hope, because consolation is eternal only with respect to the hope on which it is founded.

units.la: Et singulæ respectu, æterna est, 2. Thess. II. 16. Qui hanc spem habet, is purificat se, ne unquam ea excidat, 1. Joh. III. 3. Est enim anchora animæ, eaque ἀσφαλὴς καὶ βεβαία tuta & firma, Heb. VI. 19. Anchora ut tuta & firma sit, duo requirit; ut loco solido infigatur, & navi firmiter alligata sit. Utrumque spes habet: Nam penetrat εἰς ἐσώτερον τὸ καταπέτασμα in interius velum, seu sanctuarium cœleste, ubi rupi æternitatis adhæret; & quam dein ἔχομεν habemus, digito Dei animæ nostræ implantatam, ut inde evelli nequeat. Accedit, quòd spes gloriationem in sperante efficit. Nam καυχώμεθα in' ἐλπίδι gloriamur in, super, vel sub spe gloriæ Dei, in ipsis etiam afflictionibus, Rom. V. 3. Impiorum enim spes perit, at תוחלת צדיקים expectatio justorum lætitia est, quia spes illorum certum eventum habens in lætitiam convertitur, Prov. X. 28. Solida enim est, non spei instar hypocritarum, quæ succiditur, & בית עכביש instar domus aranea est, Job. VIII. 14. Si incerta perseverantia est, simul vana spes est, vana gloriatio, utpote quæ confundit. At spes non confundit, quia charitas Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum S. qui nobis datus est, Rom. V. 5. Dilectio Dei & Spiritus S. donatio, certissima spei fundamenta, impediunt, ne ullo modo irrita spes evadat. Ideo fidelis sperans velut exerto capite ambulat, κατὰ τὸν ὑπόκαιρον ... secundum præstolationem (qualis ejus est, qui ... capite quasi exerto observat & prospicit id, quod certò expectat) & spem, quòd in nulla re pudefaciendus sit, Phil. I. 20. Non enim erubescet Jacob, neque expallescet facies ejus, Esaj. XXIX. 22. idque עד עולמי usque in secula seculi, ibid. XLV. 17. Denique etiam Charitati Scriptura τὸ ἀνεκλιπὲς & ἀσθεσον, quòd nunquam futurum sit, ut vel excidat, vel extinguatur, tribuit. Nam charitas οὐδέποτε ἐκπίπτει nunquam excidit, 1. Cor. XIII. 8. neque in hac vita, in qua semper quoad dispositionem & habitum manet, & se in actibus, quando animus sedata tentationum procella ad se redit, profert; neque in altera, utpote in qua manet, & perfectionem suam adipiscitur, ibid. v. 13. Et mutuus ille Christi & Ecclesiæ amor invictus est, ut mors (quæ πανδαμάτωρ omnia vincit) zelus ejus durus, ut orcus (qui omnia devorat) scintillæ ejus sunt scintillæ ignis, שלהבתיה flamma Dei. (hoc est, vehementissima, vel à Deo accensa & in æternum duratura) Aquæ multæ non possunt extinguere amorem, & fluvii non inundabunt ipsum, Cant. VIII. 6. 7. Similis enim charitas est igni cœlitus delapso, quem aquæ altari ab Elia structo affusæ, & aquæ ductum implentes adeò non extinxerunt, ut ipsæ potius una cum holocausto ab igne eo absumptæ fuerint, 1. Reg. XVIII. 38. Neque etiam charitas nisi perennans σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος vinculum perfectionis, Col. III. 14. dici potest, quia vinculum tale est non tantùm quatenus virtutum omnium officia inter se copulat, & in amore; uti scitè Cyprianus; omnium Scripturarum volumina coarctantur; Sed etiam respectu corporis mystici, Christi & Ecclesiæ, quod charitas tum ratione modi suaviter simul & arctissimè, tum ratione durationis ἀδιαλύτως & indissolubiliter, adeóque perfectissimè unit.
units.tr: And each of them is eternal with respect to its object, 2 Thess. 2:16. Whoever has this hope purifies himself, so that he never loses it, 1 John 3:3. For it is an anchor of the soul, and it is sure and steadfast [ἀσφαλὴς καὶ βεβαία], Heb. 6:19. For an anchor to be sure and steadfast, two things are required: that it be fixed in a solid place, and that it be firmly attached to the ship. Hope has both. For it enters into the inner veil [εἰς ἐσώτερον τὸ καταπέτασμα], that is, the heavenly sanctuary, where it clings to the rock of eternity; and we have it [ἔχομεν] implanted in our soul by the finger of God, so that it cannot be torn out from there. Moreover, hope produces boasting in the one who hopes. For we boast [καυχώμεθα] in hope, that is, we glory in, above, or under the hope of the glory of God, even in afflictions, Rom. 5:3. For the hope of the wicked perishes, but the expectation of the righteous [תוחלת צדיקים] is joy, because their hope, having a certain outcome, is turned into joy, Prov. 10:28. For it is solid, not like the hope of hypocrites, which is cut off, and which is like a spider's house [בית עכביש], Job 8:14. If perseverance is uncertain, then hope is also vain, and the boasting is vain, since it puts to shame. But hope does not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, Rom. 5:5. The love of God and the gift of the Holy Spirit, the most certain foundations of hope, prevent it from ever turning out in vain. Therefore the believer who hopes walks with head held high, waiting eagerly [κατὰ τὸν ἀποκαραδοκίαν] (in the manner of one who, with head raised, watches and looks out for what he certainly expects), and with the hope that he will not be put to shame in anything, Phil. 1:20. For Jacob shall not be ashamed, nor shall his face grow pale, Isa. 29:22, and this for ever and ever [עד עולמי], ibid. 45:17. Finally, Scripture ascribes to charity that it never fails and never goes out, that it can never either fall away or be extinguished. For charity never fails [οὐδέποτε ἐκπίπτει], 1 Cor. 13:8; it neither does so in this life, in which it always remains in disposition and habit, and shows itself in acts when the soul, once the storm of temptations has calmed, returns to itself; nor in the other life, since in it it abides and attains its perfection, ibid. v. 13. And that mutual love of Christ and the Church is invincible, so that death, which conquers all [πανδαμάτωρ], cannot overcome it; its zeal is as hard as the grave, which devours everything; its sparks are sparks of fire, a flame of the Lord [שלהבתיה] (that is, most vehement, or kindled by God and to endure for ever). Many waters cannot quench love, and rivers will not overflow it, Song 8:6–7. For charity is like fire that has fallen from heaven, which the waters poured over the altar built by Elijah, and the water filling the trench, did not so much quench as rather were themselves consumed together with the burnt offering by that fire, 1 Kings 18:38. Nor can charity be called the bond of perfection [σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος], Col. 3:14, unless it endures, because it is such a bond not only in so far as it joins together the duties of all the virtues, and it is in love, as Cyprian aptly says: the whole volumes of Scripture are summed up; but also with respect to the mystical body of Christ and the Church, since charity unites most sweetly and most closely in its manner, and indissolubly [ἀδιαλύτως] in its duration, and so most perfectly.

units.la: LV. Hactenus ex operationibus œconomicis trium S. Trinitatis Personarum Perseverantiam Sanctorum & constantiam gratiæ immota in veritatis arce collocavimus.
units.tr: LV. Hitherto, from the economical works of the three Persons of the Holy Trinity, we have set the perseverance of the saints and the unchanging constancy of grace upon the fortress of truth.

units.la: Unum addimus, juxta easdem fideles tanquam immotum etiam & ἀσάλευτον illabefactabilem statum habentes, passim in Scripturis describi: Pauca in medium proferemus. Quantum igitur ad operationem Dei Patris, quæ electio est, attinet, electio assequitur, Rom. XI. 7. prædestinati glorificantur, ibid. VIII. 29. 30. & electi in tam firmo statu sunt, ut seduci non possint. Surgent Pseudo-Christi & Pseudo-Prophetæ, & dabunt signa magna & prodigia ὥστε πλανᾶσθαι, εἰ δυνατὸν, καὶ οὐχ ἐκλεκτούς, adeò ut, si possibile foret, etiam electos seducerent, Matth. XXIV. 24. Marcus cap. XIII. 20. signanter vocat ἐκλεκτοὺς ὧς ἐξελέξατο electos, quos elegit, indicans discrimen eorum, qui putant se electos esse & non sunt. Ubi frustra Perseverantiæ hostes εἰ δυνατὸν fi possibile esset, convertunt in εἰ ῥᾳδίως si facile esset quali non absoluta impossibilitas, sed difficultas, vel impossibilitas non ex parte rei, sed conantium solummodo indicaretur, quod tum est Scripturam ... tum consolationem adversus Pseudoprophetarum tentationem nimiùm labefactat: & prorsus scopo Christi repugnat.
units.tr: We add one thing: that the faithful, who have this same fixed and unshakeable, indestructible state, are described everywhere in the Scriptures. We will bring forward a few instances. So, as far as the work of God the Father is concerned, which is election, election obtains the goal: those predestined are glorified (Rom. 11:7; Rom. 8:29-30), and the elect are in so firm a state that they cannot be seduced. Pseudo-Christs and pseudo-prophets will arise, and will give great signs and wonders, ὥστε πλανᾶσθαι, εἰ δυνατὸν, καὶ οὐχ ἐκλεκτούς [so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect], so that, if it were possible, they would seduce even the elect (Matt. 24:24). Mark (ch. 13:20) pointedly calls them ἐκλεκτοὺς ὧς ἐξελέξατο [the elect whom he chose], indicating the difference between those who think they are elect and are not. Here the enemies of perseverance vainly change εἰ δυνατὸν [if possible] into εἰ ῥᾳδίως [if easily], as if it meant not absolute impossibility but difficulty; or as if the impossibility were indicated not on the part of the thing but only of those attempting it. This both does violence to Scripture and weakens too much the comfort against the temptation of false prophets, and it is wholly opposed to the aim of Christ.

units.la: Christus enim summum discrimen ultimorum temporum à Pseudochristis & Pseudoprophetis imminens, exaggerans, simul suos adversus tam horrendam tentationis procellam munire voluit. Si igitur εἰ δυνατὸν difficultatem tantummodò notaret, & impossibilitas non ex parte rei, sed consilii & conatus humani intelligeretur, vel difficultas illa superabilis est, vel non. Si superabilis est, quid magni vel novi talibus est, difficultates omnes aggredi, & semper electos superare, cùm nil plerumque, quod in se est, illi inausum relinquant. Et quid opus fuit, talia dici, vel prædici? Si superabilis non est, obstaculum igitur non ab impotentia vel socordia hominum, sed à superiori causa, hoc est, à decreto Dei, quod frustra illi oppugnant, provenit. Ita non difficultas, sed impossibilitas, & quidem ex parte rei, indicatur, & summi momenti Christi exhortatio est. Perinde enim est, ac si dixisset: Licèt ab æterno obsignata sit electorum perseverantia, vobis tamen vigilandum & orandum est, quia per ista media ex eodem Dei decreto vobis eluctandum est. Ne igitur neglectis his securi estote, quia non constat à priori, quid Deus decreverit, & immunes ab aliorum scandalo esse debetis.
units.tr: For Christ, foreseeing and stressing the very great danger from pseudo-Christs and pseudo-prophets that threatens in the last times, wished at the same time to fortify his people against so dreadful a storm of temptation. If, therefore, εἰ δυνατὸν [if possible] marked only a difficulty, and the impossibility were understood not on the part of the thing but of human plan and effort, then that difficulty is either surmountable or it is not. If it is surmountable, what great or new thing is there in such people attacking every difficulty and always overcoming the elect, since for the most part they leave nothing untried that lies within them? And what need was there to say or foretell such things? If it is not surmountable, then the obstacle arises not from the weakness or carelessness of men but from a higher cause, namely the decree of God, which they assail in vain. Thus it is not difficulty but impossibility that is indicated, and indeed impossibility on the part of the thing, and this is Christ's exhortation of the highest importance. For it is as if he had said: Although the perseverance of the elect has been sealed from eternity, yet you must watch and pray, because by these means, according to the same decree of God, you must struggle through. Therefore do not be secure while neglecting these things, since it is not known a priori what God has decreed, and you ought to be free from the stumbling-block of others.

units.la: LVI. Certum etiam & inconcussus fidelium ex operatione Filii, fœdere gratiæ, Christi sponsione, redemptione, intercessione & victoria status ubique describitur. Si fuerit apud eum Angelus Advocatus, unus ex mille, ut annuntiet homini rectitudinem ejus, miserebitur ejus, & dicet: Redime illum, ne descendat in foveam. Inveni redemptionem. Revirescens augescit caro ejus præ pueritia, redit ad dies adolescentiæ suæ. Supplicat Deo, & gratum ipsum habet, & videt faciem ejus cum jubilo, & reddit homini justitiam suam, Job. XXXIII. 23-27. Montes recedent, & colles dimovebuntur. Attamen benignitas mea à te non recedet; & fœdus pacis meæ non dimovebitur, ait Jehova miserator tuus, Esaj. LIV. 10. Sic dixit Jehova creator tuus, & Jacob, & formator mator tuus, ô Israel, ne timeas, כי גאלתיך quia redemi te, vocavi nomen tuum: לי אתה Meus es tu. Cùm transieris per aquas, tecum ero, & flumina non operient te. Cùm ambulaveris per ignem, non combureris, neque flamma ardebit in te. Quia ego Jehova Deus tuus, Sanctus Israelis, מושיע Servator tuus, ibid. XLIII. 1. 2. 3. Audite me domus Jacob, & omnes reliquiæ domus Israelis, qui portamini ab utero, & gestamini à vulva, & usque ad senectam. Ego sum. Ego feci, & ego feram, ego quoque portabo & eruam, ibid. XLVI. 3. 4. Qui biberit ex aqua, quam ego dabo illi, non sitiet in æternum. Sed aqua quam ego dabo illi, fiet in ipso πηγή ὕδατος ἀλλομένου εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam, Joh. IV. 14. Quicquid dederit mihi Pater, ad me veniet, & venientem ad me non ejiciam foras, ibid. VI. 37. Cùmque Fœdus Gratiæ perpetuum, sponsio Christi certa & irrevocabilis, hæreditas indubia, ejus, ceu capitis, cum corpore unio indivulsa, Redemptio Christi certissimi effectus, intercessio efficacissima, & victoria hostium planè pleneque patrata sit, fœderatorum sponsione in fidem receptorum hæredum, redemptorum, & eorum, pro quibus intercessit, & quorum hostes vicit, & qui membra atque corpus ejus sunt, status lubricus esse non potest.
units.tr: LVI. The certain and unshaken state of the faithful is also described everywhere in the work of the Son: in the covenant of grace, in Christ's promise, redemption, intercession and victory. If there be with him an Angel, an Advocate, one among a thousand, to declare to man his uprightness, he will have mercy on him and say: Redeem him, that he go not down into the pit. I have found a ransom. His flesh shall be fresher than a child's; he shall return to the days of his youth. He shall pray to God, and he will be favourable to him, and he shall see his face with joy, and he will restore to man his righteousness (Job 33:23-27). The mountains shall depart and the hills be removed. But my kindness shall not depart from you, and the covenant of my peace shall not be removed, says Jehovah your merciful one (Isa. 54:10). Thus says Jehovah your creator, and Jacob, and your former, O Israel: Fear not, for כי גאלתיך [I have redeemed you], I have called you by name: לי אתה [you are mine]. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you, and the rivers shall not overwhelm you. When you walk through the fire, you shall not be burned, nor shall the flame burn in you. For I am Jehovah your God, the Holy One of Israel, מושיע [your Saviour] (ibid. 43:1-3). Hear me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, who are carried from the womb and borne from the belly and even to old age. I am he. I made, and I will bear; I also will carry and deliver (ibid. 46:3-4). Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst. But the water that I shall give him shall become in him a πηγή ὕδατος ἀλλομένου εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον [a fountain of water springing up into eternal life] (John 4:14). Whatever the Father has given me shall come to me, and him who comes to me I will by no means cast out (ibid. 6:37). Since the covenant of grace is perpetual, Christ's promise certain and irrevocable, the inheritance indubitable, the union of his members with him, as their head, indissoluble, the redemption of Christ most certain in its effect, his intercession most efficacious, and the victory over his enemies wholly and completely achieved; and since the heirs, the redeemed, and those for whom he interceded, and whose enemies he conquered, and who are his members and body, have been received into faith by the promise of the parties to the covenant, their state cannot be slippery.

units.la: LVII. Et par fidelium ex operatione Spiritus S. cuncta conservantis, gubernantis & obsignantis, & unionem cum Christo, justitiam & sanctitatem conferentis, status describitur. Quomodo enim perire, Diaboli prædà fieri possunt, qui à Spiritu S. conservantur, & quos ipse se ipso, ceu sigillo & arrhabone munit, obsignat, inviolabiles reddit? Cum Christo indissolubiliter uniti non perseverant? Quomodo perire illi, qui habent χαρίσματα ἀμεταμέλητα, gratias perennes & irrevocabiles, possunt? Quomodo justitia Christi, quæ seculorum, Dan. IX. 24. & in seculum, Psal. CXIX. 142. est, induti, eadem iterum exui, & remissio peccatorum semel in Dei judicio peremptorie facta irrita reddi, adeóque justificatus perire potest? Atqui in justitia fideles stabiliuntur, Esaj. LIV. 14. Justus est יסוד עולם fundamentum seculi, Prov. X. 25. in seculum non nutans, columna in domo Dei, Apoc. III. 12. Justitia hæc est servorum Dei ab ipso, ut omnem linguam condemnent, & omne telum contra ipsos factum non prosperetur, Esaj. LIV. 17. Jam & regenitorum status prorsus immutabilis est, quia regeneratio unica est, & semen ejus in regenitis sic manet, ut peccare, seu peccata semen regenerationis excutientia, & condemnantia committere, adeóque finaliter, vel etiam totaliter deficere non possint. Omnis ex Deo genitus peccatum non facit, quia semen ejus in ipso manet, & non potest peccare, quia ex Deo genitus est, 1. Joh. III. 9. Non possunt ex Deo geniti peccatum condemnans ipsos facere, tum quia ex Deo geniti sunt, hoc est, ex Dei proposito & promissione facti sunt filii ipsius, & in regeneratione fidem & Christum acceperunt; tum quia Semen Dei, hoc est, Spiritus S. qui ut semen regenerationis est; ita etiam regenitis fit arrhabo, spem in posterum faciens, at ejusdem causa organica, verbum Dei, non per se, sed quatenus est potentia Dei ad salutem, in iis manet. Quæ insulsè adversarii in sensu composito sic explicant, ut dicant, ex Deo genitum, hoc est, quà ex Deo genitus est, & quandiu Semen in eo, seu, uti explicant, charitas, peccatis lethalibus contraria manet, non peccare lethaliter. Nam hæc explicatio particulam causalem on quia, in conditionalem, si geniti sint, si semen maneat, commutat. Qui ex Deo natus est, non tantùm quà ex Deo natus est, & Semen Dei in eo manet, non peccat. Semen enim illud Dei in genito constanter manens, & nativitas ex Deo, quæ aboleri nequit, causa est, cur regeniti ne quidem peccare possint. Tantum abest, ut peccando semen illud excutiant. Hoc enim criterio regeniti ab irregenitis discernuntur. Illi ex Diabolo cùm sint, dant operam peccato, securo impetu & pruriente desiderio. Sed qui ex Deo natus est, peccatum non facit, quia semen ejus in eo manet, hoc est, quia in regenito semper aliquid latet, quod manum injicit, ut à peccando retrahat. Semen igitur hoc indelebilis character, & hæreditatis arrhabo est, quo renati ad redemptionem obsignantur. Unde autem contractus nisi à sigillo vim habet? Unde fructus nisi ex semine in radice efflorescit? Neque adeò impossibilitas peccandi se tenet ex parte hominis, sed tum seminis, fidelem à tali lapsu præservantis, tum genituræ spiritualis, quæ causa perseverantiæ est, & apostasiam excludit. Nam τὸ ex Deo natum esse, & Semen Dei manens habere, & τὸ non posse peccare, habent se ut causa & effectus. Desino ex perseverante in fidelibus fide, spe & charitate, statum immobilem credentium, sperantium & diligentium demonstrare amplius. Cùm enim fidei justitia, salus, vita, satietas omnis: Spei soliditas & gloriatio: amori perpetua duratio tribuatur, quomodo credentes non justificari, salvari, vivere, satiari: sperantes spe sua defraudari: diligentes ab amore deficere & odium Dei contrahere dici possunt?
units.tr: LVII. A similar state of the faithful is also described in the work of the Holy Spirit, who preserves, governs and seals all things, and who confers union with Christ, righteousness and holiness. For how can those perish and become the prey of the devil who are preserved by the Holy Spirit, and whom he himself fortifies, seals and renders inviolable, as with a seal and a pledge? How can those who are united indissolubly to Christ not persevere? How can those who have χαρίσματα ἀμεταμέλητα [gifts without regret], perennial and irrevocable graces, perish? How can one who has put on the righteousness of Christ, which is everlasting (Dan. 9:24) and for ever (Ps. 119:142), be stripped of it again, and the forgiveness of sins, once and for all pronounced peremptorily in God's judgment, be made void, so that one who has been justified can perish? Yet the faithful are established in righteousness (Isa. 54:14). The righteous man is יסוד עולם [the foundation of the world] (Prov. 10:25), not wavering for ever, a pillar in the house of God (Rev. 3:12). This righteousness is such that God's servants are protected by him, so that every tongue that accuses them is condemned, and every weapon formed against them does not prosper (Isa. 54:17). Moreover, the state of the regenerate is altogether unchangeable, because regeneration is one, and its seed remains in the regenerate in such a way that they cannot sin, or commit sins which would shake out the seed of regeneration and condemn them, and so cannot finally or even totally fall away.
