Everyone born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin, because he is born of God (1 John 3:9). Those born of God cannot make sin condemn them: partly because they are born of God, that is, they have been made his sons by God's purpose and promise, and in regeneration they received faith and Christ; partly because the Seed of God, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is as the seed of regeneration, also becomes a pledge to the regenerate, giving hope for the future, and his organic cause, the Word of God, remains in them, not in itself but insofar as it is the power of God unto salvation. The adversaries foolishly explain this in a composite sense, so as to say that one born of God, that is, insofar as he is born of God, and as long as the seed remains in him, or, as they explain it, love, which is contrary to deadly sins, remains, does not sin deadly. For this explanation changes the causal particle "because" into a conditional, "if they are born, if the seed remains." But whoever is born of God not only insofar as he is born of God and the Seed of God remains in him does not sin. For that seed of God constantly remaining in the one born again, and the birth from God, which cannot be abolished, is the cause why the regenerate cannot even sin; so far is it from being the case that by sinning they shake out that seed. For by this criterion the regenerate are distinguished from the unregenerate. The latter, since they are of the devil, devote themselves to sin with secure impetus and burning desire; but he who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him, that is, because in the regenerate something always lies hidden which lays a hand upon him to draw him back from sinning. This seed, therefore, is the indelible character and the pledge of the inheritance, by which the reborn are sealed for redemption. For from what does a contract derive its force, unless from the seal? From what does fruit blossom, unless from the seed in the root? Nor, indeed, does the impossibility of sinning lie on the part of the man, but on the part of the seed, which preserves the believer from such a fall, and of the spiritual begetting, which is the cause of perseverance and excludes apostasy. For to have been born of God and to have the Seed of God remaining, and not to be able to sin, stand to each other as cause and effect. I shall not go on to show further, from the perseverance of the faithful in faith, hope and love, the immovable state of believers, those who hope and those who love. For since justice, salvation, life and every satisfaction are ascribed to faith, steadfastness and boasting to hope, and perpetual duration to love, how can it be said that believers are not justified, saved, live, or are satisfied; that those who hope are cheated of their hope; that those who love fall away from love and contract hatred of God?

units.la: LVIII. Tot & tam solidis munimentis insistens de Perseverantia Sanctorum doctrina diu satis in Ecclesia viguit.
units.tr: LVIII. Resting on so many and such solid bulwarks, the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints has for a long time flourished in the Church.

units.la: Licèt enim Patres nonnulli ante Augustinum lubricè satis de ea philosophati sint, Philosophiæ paganæ fermento fidemque Christianam inficientes, peccatoris conversionem ab ancipiti voluntatis humanæ flexu arcessentes, tamen, fatente ipso Cumel. in primam partem, & primam secundæ Aquinatis, non defuerunt, qui efficaciam gratiæ non ad acceptantis facilitatem, sed ad energeticum vocantis propositum referentes, perseverantiam à salvo conservantis Dei conductu, non à vacillante conservati progressu æstimandam judicarent. Hòs inter Cyprianus Epist. 55. diserté scribit, Ecclesiam, quæ in Christum credit, & quæ semel id, quod cognovit, tenet, nunquam ab eo omnino discedere, & eos esse Ecclesiam, qui in domo Dei permanent, plantationem verò à Deo Patre plantatam non esse, quos videmus non frumenti stabilitate solidari, sed tanquam paleas dissipantis inimici spiritu ventilari. Inprimis Augustinus duobus de Prædestinatione Sanctorum, & bono Perseverantiæ libris adversus Pelagianos & Semipelagianos, homini & perfistendi & desistendi à gratia libertatem vindicantes, editis, ita initium, progressum & successum fidei asseruit, ut licèt Sathanas nunquam zizania sua superseminare desierit, triticum tamen hoc penitus, ne revireceret, suffocari non potuerit. Nam Fulgentius tius ad Maxim. de Prædest. diserte asseruit gratiam non solum errantem justificando in viam revocare, sed etiam bene ambulantem custodire & adjuvare, ut ad donum glorificationis æternæ perveniat. Et Prosper Aquitanicus de Vocat. Gent. lib. II. 11. docet; Charitatem, quæ ipse Deus est, stabiles & perseverantes atque insuperabiles facere, quos flumine suo voluptatis impleverit. Qui autem, inquit, aquarum istarum dulcedinem nesciunt, & adhuc de torrentibus mundi hujus bibunt, aut etiam si aliquid primoribus labris de vitæ fonte gustaverunt, inebriati tamen aureo (NB) Babylonis calice delectantur, suo prorsus decipiuntur arbitrio, sua voluntate labuntur, etsi in hac desidia perseverant, ipsi se his, quæ accepere, dispoliant. Eandem in rem cum plura Patrum testimonia Gratianus de Pœnit. de 2. cap. 12. collegisset, concludit tamen: Ex his præmissis apparet, quod charitas semel habita, ulterius non amittitur. Seculo adhuc nono Godeschalcus docuit: Eos qui pereunt, etsi prius crediderint & baptizati fuerint, nonnisi signotenus redemptos fuisse a Christo, nec unquam a perditionis massa secretos. Qua in doctrina Moguntinam Synodum, & post Rhemenses sub Hincmaro adversantes habuit. Cautius tamen deinceps Lugdunenses, Viennenses & Arelatenses in Lugdunensi & Valentino Concilio gratiam, a qua quis excidere posset, non a proposito Dei immutabili, sed ab externo Baptismi lavacro, & cæteris hujusmodi φαῦνομένοις fluere asseruerunt. Augustini doctrinam adhuc Bernhardus retinuit; sed ejus coætaneus Abælardus ad Pelagii castra deflectens corrupit. Succedanei his Scholastici ad 3. Sent. d. 31. & Aquinatis 2.2. q.24. a. 11. quærunt: An charitas semel habita amitti possit? Affirmant illi communiter de quibusdam charitatis gradibus, sed non de omnibus: idque ex parte subjecti, cuivis mutabilitati obnoxii non decreti Divini, ad felicem exitum perducentis, quod gratiose contulit. Sed Guido tamen ordinis Heremitani S. Augustini a Parisiensibus Sorbonistis thesin hanc, quod charitas, quæ habetur & deperditur, nunquam vera charitas fuerit, tanquam falsam & hæreticam revocare coactus est. Nihilominus VViclefus & Bradvvardinus aliisque etiam Augustini, Godeschalki & Guidonis sententiam defendere nulli dubitarunt.
units.tr: Although some Fathers before Augustine philosophized about it rather loosely, mixing pagan philosophy into the Christian faith and deriving the conversion of the sinner from the wavering turn of the human will, nonetheless, as Cumel. in the first part and the first of the second part of Aquinas himself admits, there were those who referred the efficacy of grace not to the readiness of the one who accepts it but to the powerful purpose of the one who calls, and who judged that perseverance must be measured by the safe escort of God preserving the one kept, not by the wavering progress of the one preserved. Among these, Cyprian clearly writes in Epist. 55 that the Church, which believes in Christ and holds once and for all what it has known, never wholly departs from him, and that those are the Church who remain in the house of God, whereas those whom we see are not made firm by the steadfastness of the wheat but are winnowed like chaff by the spirit of the enemy who scatters them, are not a planting planted by God the Father. Above all, Augustine, in his two books On the Predestination of the Saints and On the Gift of Perseverance, published against the Pelagians and Semipelagians, who vindicated for man the freedom both to persevere and to fall away from grace, so asserted the beginning, progress and completion of faith that, although Satan never ceased to sow his tares over it, that wheat could not be wholly suffocated so as to fail to revive. For Fulgentius, in his ad Maxim. de Prædest., clearly asserted that grace not only recalls the one who has gone astray to the way by justifying him, but also keeps and helps the one who walks well, so that he may reach the gift of eternal glorification. And Prosper of Aquitaine, de Vocat. Gent. lib. II. 11, teaches: Charity, which is God himself, makes stable, persevering and unconquerable those whom he has filled with his river of delight. But those who, he says, do not know the sweetness of those waters, and still drink from the torrents of this world, or even if they have tasted something from the fountain of life with the lips' first touch, yet are delighted, drunk from the golden (NB) cup of Babylon, are utterly deceived by their own judgment; they slip by their own will, and even if they persist in this sloth, they strip themselves of what they have received. When Gratian, de Pœnit. de 2. cap. 12, had gathered many testimonies of the Fathers to the same effect, he nevertheless concludes: From the premises it appears that charity once possessed is not lost afterwards. Still in the ninth century Godeschalk taught that those who perish, even if they had believed earlier and been baptized, had been redeemed by Christ only in name and were never set apart from the mass of perdition. The Synod of Mainz, and afterwards the Rheims council under Hincmar, opposed this doctrine. More cautiously thereafter, however, the councils of Lyons, Vienne and Arles, at the Council of Lyons and of Valence, asserted that grace, from which one could fall away, flows not from God's immutable purpose but from the external washing of baptism and other such φαῦνομένοις [phainomenois, appearances]. Bernhardus still retained Augustine's doctrine, but his contemporary Abælardus corrupted it by turning aside into the camp of Pelagius. The Scholastics who came after them, on the Third Sentences dist. 31 and Aquinas, 2.2 q. 24 a. 11, ask: Can charity once possessed be lost? They commonly affirm this of certain degrees of charity, but not of all; and they say it arises from the side of the subject, which is liable to every mutability, not from the decree of God, which brings to a happy end what it has graciously bestowed. But Guido of the Hermit Order of St. Augustine was nonetheless compelled by the Parisian Sorbonnists to retract, as false and heretical, his thesis that charity which is had and then lost was never true charity. Nevertheless, Wycliffe and Bradwardine, and others as well, did not hesitate to defend the opinion of Augustine, Godeschalk and Guido.

units.la: LIX. Post Reformationis tempora ante omnes Tridentini Perseverantiæ Sanctorum assertores diris devoverunt.
units.tr: LIX. After the times of the Reformation, the Tridentine council cursed with dire anathemas all the defenders of the perseverance of the saints.

units.la: Si quis ita Sess. VI. Can. 23. illi definiunt, hominem semel justificatum dixerit amplius peccare non posse, nec gratiam amittere, atque ideo eum, qui labitur & peccat, nunquam vere fuisse justificatum, anathema sit. Illi ergo & totalem & finalem apostasiam Sanctorum defendunt, eum in finem, ut non tantum miseros proselytos suos, a fiducia in Christum abductos, arundineis ipsorum supplementis addictiores habeant, sed etiam proficuum adeo sibi de opere operato Sacramentorum commentum firmius stabiliant, incautioresque speciosius emungant. Ne de liberi arbitrii idolo dicam. Cujus religione inducti Socinians docent, uti liberum est credere, ita a fide deficere liberum pariter esse. At Lutheri discipuli sanioreS electos & fideles ad finem usque perseverare, in cursu vero pietatis Spiritum S. penitus amittere, totaliterque adeo ad tempus saltem, at non in perpetuum, deficere posse docent. Cujus dissensus momentum alibi expendimus.
units.tr: If anyone says, as they define in Session VI, canon 23, that a man once justified can no longer sin or lose grace, and that therefore the one who falls and sins was never truly justified, let him be anathema. They therefore defend both a total and a final apostasy of the saints, with this aim: that they may hold their wretched proselytes, led away from trust in Christ, more devoted to their own reed-like props, and may more firmly establish the profit they gain from the fiction of the sacraments working ex opere operato, and more splendidly drain the purses of the more careless. I say nothing of the idol of free will, by whose religion the Socinians are led to teach that just as it is free to believe, so it is equally free to fall away from faith. But the more sensible disciples of Luther teach that the elect and the faithful persevere to the end, while in the course of piety they may wholly lose the Holy Spirit, and so may fall away completely, at least for a time, though not forever. We have weighed the force of this disagreement elsewhere.

units.la: Alii etiam finalem apostasiam non electorum quidem, sed fidelium & renatorum tamen, tuentur, ne errorem de Sacramentorum efficacia ejerare cogantur. Si enim Sacramenta gratiam, ut causæ operantur, quod illi pertendunt, omnes baptizati gratiam adipiscantur necesse est; a qua tamen deficere ad finem usque plerosque, notorium est. Sed præcipua de Perseverantia Sanctorum cum Remonstrantibus lis est; qui cum eandem cum liberi arbitrii idolo suo conciliare non possent, nodum secare quam solvere maluerunt. Prætextus enim, non res est, quod asserta Sanctorum apostasia nostram de Prædestinatione doctrinam Stoicam, uti appellant, sic corrigi, & Deum a peccati causalitate liberari debere, illi nugantur; cum non aliud satagant magis, quam ut in contumeliam gratiæ Dei & constantiæ ejusdem Pelagianismum, Dei consilia ex arbitrii humani vertigine suspendentem, ex orco resuscitent.
units.tr: Others also defend a final apostasy, not of the elect indeed, but of believers and the regenerate, lest they be forced to renounce their error about the efficacy of the sacraments. For if the sacraments work grace as causes, as they maintain, then all who are baptized must necessarily obtain grace; yet that most of them fall away before the end is notorious. But the chief dispute about the perseverance of the saints is with the Remonstrants, who, being unable to reconcile it with their idol of free will, preferred to cut the knot rather than untie it. For the pretext, not the reality, is that once the apostasy of the saints is asserted, our doctrine of predestination, which they call Stoic, must be corrected in this way, and God must be freed from being the cause of sin. Those men trifle; for they are concerned with nothing more than to raise up again from hell, to the insult of the grace of God and of its constancy, a Pelagianism that makes the counsels of God hang on the whirling of human choice.

units.la: Illi ergo in medio relinquunt, an Deus quosdam, diu exercitatos & probatos, extra ordinem, & singulari gratia, indefectibili perseverantiæ dono remuneretur. Cæterum potentiam deficiendi talem statuunt, ut positis illis omnibus, quæ ad perseverandum in fide necessaria & sufficientia sunt, quæque Deus ad conservandum adhibere vult, fieri tamen posse dicant, ut homo non perseveret. Quippe neminem Deum ad perseverantiam elegisse, Christum perseverantiam certam nemini meruisse, omnem gratiæ efficaciam resistibilem esse, ita ut fidem neque certo procreet, neque conservando faciat, ut certo perseveret. Defectionem porro asserunt fieri gradatim, homine per negligentiam suam principium suæ in Christo suitentationis deserente, idque voluntate vel directa, ut homo nolit perseverare, & ad vitam profanam se convertat; sive indirecta & interpretativa, cum debitam ad perseverandum diligentiam non adhibeat. Neque enim Deum fidem nostram vi omnipotente, quæ liberam obedientiam, & deficiendi potentiam tollat, conservare velle statuunt. Denique fideles incipientes, proficientes & adultos distinguentes, illos facile; istos difficilius, hos difficilime, ut deficiant, induci, sed omnes tamen illos deficere posse, scisciunt. Hæc illorum gratiæ hostium, & propriæ potestatis atque libertatis palponum de Perseverantia fidelium arrogantia ψευδο φισματα sunt.
units.tr: They therefore leave it open whether God rewards some, who have been long exercised and proved, beyond the ordinary course and by a singular grace, with the gift of indefectible perseverance. Furthermore, they lay down such a possibility of falling away that, though all those things are set in place which are necessary and sufficient for persevering in faith, and which God wills to employ for preserving them, yet they say it may still come about that a man does not persevere. Indeed, they assert that no one has been elected by God to perseverance, that Christ has merited certain perseverance for no one, and that all efficacy of grace is resistible, so that it neither surely begets faith nor, by preserving it, makes a man surely persevere. They further assert that defection happens gradually, when a man through his own negligence abandons the principle of his support in Christ; and this happens either by a direct will, so that the man does not wish to persevere and turns to a profane life, or by an indirect and interpretive will, when he does not apply the diligence due for perseverance. For they do not hold that God wills to preserve our faith by an omnipotent force that would take away free obedience and the power of falling away. Lastly, distinguishing believers who are beginners, advancing and mature, they decree that the first are easily, the second with more difficulty, and the third with the greatest difficulty induced to fall away, yet that all of them can fall away. These pseudophantasmata [ψευδοφάσματα, false phantoms] are the arrogant fancies of these enemies of grace, these flatterers of their own power, liberty, and their doctrine of the perseverance of the faithful.

units.la: LX. Argumentis similibus pœne omnes Perseverantiæ adversarii decernunt.
units.tr: LX. Almost all the opponents of perseverance rely on similar arguments.

units.la: Alia enim ex Scripturæ testimoniis; alia ex deficientium exemplis, alia ex rationibus depromunt. Scripturæ testimoniis aliisque argumentis ante omnia electionis æternæ τὸ ἀμετάπτωτον impetunt, quæ alibi Loc. V. 49. diluimus. At nec cætera, quibus insistunt, Scripturæ testimonia iis patrocinantur. Decantatus enim ille, qui eorum Achilles est, Ezechielis locus, quo asseritur; justum, si se averterit a sua justitia & fecerit iniquitatem secundum omnes abominationes, quas operari solet impius, non vivere, imo futurum, ut omnium justitiarum, quas fecerit, Deus non recordetur, sed in prævaricatione & peccato, quod peccavit, moriatur, Ezech. XVIII. 24. 25. 26. nullum
units.tr: They draw some arguments from the testimonies of Scripture, others from the examples of those who fall away, and others from reasoning. Before all else, they attack the eternal election, the unchangeableness [τὸ ἀμετάπτωτον], with testimonies of Scripture and other arguments, which we have refuted elsewhere (Loc. V. 49). But the other Scripture testimonies on which they rely do not support them either. For that much-trumpeted passage of Ezekiel, which is their Achilles and by which they assert that if the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and does iniquity according to all the abominations which the wicked man is wont to do, he shall not live; indeed, it will come about that none of the righteousnesses which he has done will be remembered by God, but in the trespass and sin which he has committed he shall die (Ezek. 18:24, 25, 26),

units.la: Argumenta Perseverantiæ opposita diluuntur: petita ex verbis Ezechielis cap. XVIII. 24. 25. 26.
units.tr: Arguments opposed to perseverance are refuted, those drawn from the words of Ezekiel, chapter 18, verses 24, 25, 26.

units.la: nullum errori præsidium commodat. Non enim ibi יצדיק justum per fidem in Christum justificatum, de quo solo quæstio est, sed eum, qui inquinamenta mundi effugit in cognitione Dei, & justis connumeratus est, & cujus nomen scriptum & in catalogo populi Dei, & qui nomen habet, quòd vivat, 2. Petr. II. 20. Apoc. III. 1. significat. Nam & talis impietati & justitiæ suæ renuntiare, amorem Dei, & recessionem à via sua mala profiteri, verba justorum loqui, facta eorum assumere, atque ita & sibi justus videri, & ab aliis justus judicari potest. Non aliud certè Ezechiel justo tali tribuit, quàm צדקה עשות facere justitias, v. 24. hoc est, quædam vera dicta & facta assumere & usurpare, qualis secundum judicium charitatis, quæ omnia sperat, pro justo haberi debet. Neque v. 24. de judicio Dei agitur, sicut v. 9. ubi mentio est ambulantis in statutis Dei, & judicia ejus observantis לעשות אמת ut faciat veritatem; de quali diserte ibi dicitur צדיק הוא justus ille est. Aliud certè est justum esse, Dei etiam judicio, aliud justum apparere, propter dicta & facta externa: aliud veritatem facere, aliud apparentiam habere. Nam qui veritatem non facit, non revertitur à defectionibus suis, & ab improbitate sua, sed peccat adhuc, licèt multa, quæ vera sunt, loquatur; & quæ recta, bona & mandata sunt, externè faciat. Tales erant Judæi, adversus Deum & æquitatem viarum ejus murmurantes, & justitiis suis, seu rectis factis suis confidentes, Ezech. XXXIII. 13. atque ita se innocios mala sua luere, patres labrusscam comedisse, sibi dentes stupere, ibid. XVIII. 2. jactantes. Ideo Ezechiel idem v. 31. ad veram justitiam & resipiscentiam requirit, ut sibi faciant cor novum & spiritum novum. Non enim in dictis & factis externis solis imago Dei & operum bonitas & rectitudo consistit. Neque obstat, quòd justus, si non fecisset injustitiam, victurus fuerit, juxta verba Prophetæ: Justus si fecerit iniquitatem, an vivet? v. 24. &: Cùm dixero de justo: vivendo vivet, & ille confisus sua justitiæ fecerit injustitiam, morietur, Ezech. XXXIII. 13. Nam verba illa, cùm dico de justo, intelligi possunt de genere, ut non indigeretur hic vel ille, qui justitias fecerit, & in iis confidat. Ita Ezech. XVIII. v. 9. Propheta dicens: Vir si fuerit justus, &c. vivendo vivet. Hoc modo intelligitur, non debere quemquam inflari propter promissionem vitæ, ut suæ justitiæ confidat. Si tamen verba illa in specie etiam de hoc vel illo justo intelliguntur, sub conditione intelligenda sunt, sicut verba: Cùm dixero improbo, moriendo morieris; sub conditione accipienda sunt. Sensus igitur foret, si justus fecerit justitiam non qualemcunque vel externam duntaxat, quæ sola non vivificat, sed veram, quæ veritas est, v. 9. & in cordis circumcisione, & spiritus novi formatione consistit, v. 31. victurum eum, non moriturum esse. Hic enim Prophetiæ scopus est, ne Judæi confidant suis rectis factis, quæ facientes distinguebantur à gentibus peccatoribus, sed cor novum & spiritum novum sibi parent. Sine quo nulla vitæ spes est, etiamsi quis multa bona mandata dixerit, & secundum literam vixerit. Ubi autem cor novum & spiritus novus est, ibi fides est, qua stamus, Rom. XI. 20. ibi radix est, Matth. XIII. 21. ibi deni-
units.tr: gives no protection to error. For there the word the righteous [יצדיק] does not mean a man justified through faith in Christ, which alone is the question, but signifies one who has escaped the pollutions of the world in the knowledge of God, who is counted among the righteous, whose name is written also in the catalogue of the people of God, and who has the name that he lives (2 Pet. 2:20; Rev. 3:1). For such a person can also renounce his impiety and his unrighteousness, profess love of God and turning from his evil way, speak the words of the righteous, take up their deeds, and so both seem righteous to himself and can be judged righteous by others. Certainly Ezekiel attributes to such a righteous man nothing other than doing righteousnesses [צדקה עשות] (v. 24), that is, to take up and appropriate certain true sayings and deeds, which by the judgment of charity, which hopes all things, ought to be held righteous. Nor does v. 24 speak of God's judgment, as v. 9 does, where mention is made of one walking in God's statutes and keeping his judgments, to do truth [לעשות אמת]; of such a person it is expressly said there: he is righteous [צדיק הוא]. It is one thing to be righteous, even by God's judgment, and another to appear righteous on account of external words and deeds; one thing to do truth, another to have the appearance. For he who does not do truth does not turn back from his defections and his wickedness, but still sins, though he may speak many things that are true and outwardly do what is right, good and commanded. Such were the Jews, murmuring against God and the equity of his ways, and trusting in their righteousnesses, that is, in their right deeds (Ezek. 33:13), and so boasting, that they have eaten a sour grape, and their teeth are set on edge (ibid. 18:2), that is, that they were innocent and that their evils were paid for by their fathers. Therefore Ezekiel, at v. 31, requires true righteousness and repentance, that they make for themselves a new heart and a new spirit. For the image of God and the goodness and uprightness of works do not consist in external words and deeds alone. Nor does it stand in the way that the righteous man, had he not done iniquity, would live, according to the words of the prophet: If the righteous man does iniquity, shall he live? (v. 24), and: When I say of the righteous man that he shall surely live, and he, trusting in his righteousness, does iniquity, he shall die (Ezek. 33:13). For those words, when I say of the righteous, can be understood as a general statement, so that it would not be necessary to refer to this or that man who does righteousnesses and trusts in them. So too Ezekiel 18:9, where the prophet says: If a man is righteous, etc., he shall surely live. In this way it is understood that no one should be puffed up by the promise of life so as to trust in his righteousness. If, however, those words are understood of this or that particular righteous man, they must be understood under a condition, just as the words: When I say to the wicked, you shall surely die, are to be taken under a condition. The sense, therefore, would be: if the righteous man does righteousness, not any kind or merely external, which alone does not give life, but true righteousness, which is truth (v. 9), and consists in circumcision of the heart and formation of a new spirit (v. 31), he will live and not die. For this is the scope of the prophecy: that the Jews should not trust in their right deeds, by which they were distinguished from the sinful nations, but should prepare for themselves a new heart and a new spirit. Without these there is no hope of life, even if someone has spoken many good commandments and lived according to the letter. But where there is a new heart and a new spirit, there is faith, by which we stand (Rom. 11:20); there is the root (Matt. 13:21); there

units.la: que gratia est, in qua stamus, & gloriamur in spe gloriæ Dei, Rom. V. 2. Sic ergo doctrina de Gratia Dei conservante, & justitia hæreditatem aferente diligenter retinenda est, ut tamen non transferatur ad lasciviam, ut cùm Deus de justo dicit: vivet. Judæorum more, confidamus verbis & factis nostris, quæ non justitiæ, יין injustitiæ patratio est, Ezech. XXXIII. 13.
units.tr: finally is grace, in which we stand, and we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God (Rom. 5:2). Thus the doctrine of God's preserving grace, and of justification bestowing the inheritance, is to be carefully retained, yet so that it is not turned into licentiousness, as when God says of the righteous man: he shall live. In the manner of the Jews, let us not trust in our words and deeds, which is not the practice of righteousness but of iniquity (Ezek. 33:13).

units.la: LXI.
units.tr: LXI.

units.la: Neque etiam Sanctorum apostasiam Christus docuit in parabola dicens: Quod in terram petrosam seminatum est, hic est, qui verbum audit, & statim cum gaudio accipit, non habet autem in se radicem, sed temporarius est: orta verò afflictione, aut persecutione propter sermonem illum, statim offenditur, Matth. XIII. 20. 21. Quid enim fideli & per fidem justificato cum terra petrosa, hoc est, homine irregenito, lapideum cor habente; & cum terra radicem non habente, neque adeò fructificante? Terra enim, quæ bibit sæpius in eam venientem pluviam, & parit herbam commodam iis, propter quos colitur, accipit benedictionem à Deo. Quæ autem fert spinas & tribulos, reproba est, & prope execrationem, cujus finis est crematio, Hebr. VI. 7. 8. Herba bona signum est agri à Deo benedicti: tribulus & spina maledicti. Quis credentem in Christum, & fide hac justificatum, imò & salvandum, agrum ejusmodi maledictum dixerit? Nempe ad veram fidem in Christum non satis est sermonem Dei audire, & audito eo repentinum gaudium, concipere, & cum tali gaudio sermonem λαμβάνει accipere, sed absque radice. Est enim quædam jucunditas subitanea ex auditione verbi, cum curiositate, atque etiam zelo & gloriatione, & magna phantasia conjuncta; quæ à carne & concupiscentia, non ab amore Dei & fide proficiscitur. Statim enim lætari malum signum est, quia non potest non verbum Dei, si rectè percipiatur in homine operari displicentiam sui, ἀγωνίαν, angustias, cor contritum, spiritum fractum, famem & sitim, denique luctum, Matth. V. 4. 6. Tum repentinum gaudium indicat arrogantiam, quasi jam statim omnia perdiderideris, cùm opus sit plurima investigatione, & via pietatis ad dextram & sinistram multas tentationes & insidias Sathanæ conjunctas habeat. Non ergo fides hæc πεῖσμα, quod supra etiam ostendimus, vera justificans fides est, sed convictio de Divinitate Scripturæ, & nominis Christi, atque quarundam veritatum assumptio, & cum concupiscentia atque opinionibus propriis, ad gloriandum coram Deo & hominibus copulatio; denique hypocrisis quædam, quæ illos ipsos, qui eam habent, latet. Deest enim illis radix, cognitio & amor fundamenti, in quo omnis ratio Divinæ sapientiæ fundatur, quo solo cognito ἀναλογία omnium veritatum salutarium, & Dei nomen cognoscitur & glorificatur. Cúmque terra bona, oppositá petrosæ sit cor à Domino præparatum, à Spiritu S. apertum, carneum, circumcisum, spiritus novus, cui tribuitur, patienter audire & ζυνιέναι intelligere, hoc est, propter amorem gloriæ Dei, & sitim justitiæ considerare, meditari, componere, atque ita ad radicem ipsam & fundamentum ac cognitionem Divinæ sapientiæ in mysterio pietatis pervenire, qui bonæ illius terræ fructus sunt: manifestum est, fidem illam, quæ terræ petropetrosæ tribuitur, & radice atque fructibus his omnibus destituitur, nil minùs esse, quàm fidem illam, cui justificatio, unio cum Christo & salus tribuitur.
units.tr: Nor did Christ teach the apostasy of the saints in the parable when he said: "That which was sown on stony ground is the one who hears the word and at once receives it with joy, but has no root in himself and is temporary. When affliction or persecution arises because of the word, he is immediately offended," Matth. XIII. 20. 21. For what has a faithful man, justified through faith, to do with stony ground, that is, a man unregenerate with a heart of stone; or with ground not having a root, and so not even bearing fruit? "For the earth which drinks the rain that often falls on it, and brings forth herbage useful to those for whose sake it is tilled, receives blessing from God. But that which bears thorns and briers is worthless and close to being cursed, and its end is burning," Hebr. VI. 7. 8. A good herb is the sign of a field blessed by God; briers and thorns, of one cursed. Who would call a field of this kind cursed when it is a man believing in Christ, justified by this faith, and indeed to be saved? Certainly, for true faith in Christ it is not enough to hear the word of God, to conceive a sudden joy on hearing it, and to receive the word with such joy [λαμβάνει], but without a root. For there is a certain sudden delight that comes from hearing the word, joined with curiosity, even zeal and boasting, and a great deal of fancy. This comes from the flesh and concupiscence, not from the love of God and faith. For to rejoice at once is a bad sign, because the word of God, if it is rightly perceived in a man, cannot but produce displeasure with oneself, [ἀγωνίαν] anguish, straitness, a contrite heart, a broken spirit, hunger and thirst, and finally mourning, Matth. V. 4. 6. Then a sudden joy indicates arrogance, as if you had already at once obtained everything, when there is need of much searching, and the way of piety, to right and left, has many temptations and snares of Satan joined to it. Therefore this faith, the anchor (πεῖσμα) which we also showed above, is not the true justifying faith, but a conviction about the divinity of Scripture and the name of Christ, and an acceptance of certain truths, joined with concupiscence and one's own opinions, for boasting before God and men; in short, a certain hypocrisy, which lies hidden even from those who have it. For they lack the root, the knowledge and love of the foundation on which every reason of divine wisdom is built, by knowing which alone the analogy of all saving truths is known, and the name of God is known and glorified. And since the good ground, opposed to the stony, is the heart prepared by the Lord and opened by the Holy Spirit, fleshy and circumcised, the new spirit to which is given the power to hear patiently and to understand [συνιέναι], that is, for the love of God's glory and thirst for righteousness, to consider, meditate, and compose, and so to reach the root itself, the foundation and knowledge of divine wisdom in the mystery of godliness, which are the fruits of that good ground: it is manifest that that faith which is attributed to stony ground, and is destitute of this root and all these fruits, is nothing less than that faith to which justification, union with Christ and salvation are attributed.

units.la: LXII. Insulsæ Limborchii exceptiones sunt, quòd non fides, sed homines dicantur ἀπόστατοι: quòd perseverantia non sit de essentia fidei, sed ejus consequens, sine quo fidei essentia eadem constet: quòd Christus similitudine hac ejusdem præconii Evangelici diversum eventum, non cordium differentiam explicaverit: quòd seminati in terra petrosa à seminatis in terra bona differant, non respectu fidei, sed respectu mercedis, solis perseverantibus promissæ: quòd etiam fides temporalis comparetur cum herba, quæ ex terra petrosa φυέντα subitò exurgit, mox æstu solis exarescit, vers. 5. & Luc. VIII. 6. & similia. Cùm enim qui deficit homo, cessét credere, non potest homo ἀπόστατος esse, quin etiam talis fides sit. Quid enim homo ἀπόστατος aliud est, quàm verbo Dei cum gaudio ex levibus, non solidis causis orto assentiens, credens, atque illud etiam profitens ad tempus? Ita improbus ab improbitate, apostata ab apostasia, homicida ab homicidio dicitur. Ac licèt perseverantia non sit de essentia fidei, ex gratia tamen & voluntate Dei eandem necessariò consequitur, eo ipso, quòd in bona terra, seu bono corde est & radicatur. Diversam porro fidei temporariæ & justificantis essentiam, etiam extra perseverantiæ consequentis respectum esse, satis constat, quia fiducialis illa apprehensio & amor, qui in justificante est, in temporaria non est. Quæ enim erga Deum fiducia, quis Christi genuinus amor ex terra petrosa, nec radicem habente, nec fructum ferente pullulare potis est? Præterea terra petrosa & bona illud est, quod semen verbi Dei cum dispositione ad conservandum idonea vel non idonea recipit. Atqui illud cor hominis est, quod petrosum & irregenitum ad retinendum dispositum non est, bonum & carneum ad retinendum illud per gratiam regenerationis dispositum est. Quod etiam Lyranus, Glossa ordinaria & Didacus de la Vega, aliíque agnoscunt. Sed quid multis? Ipse Christus, Malum rapere τὸ ἐσπαρμένον ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ seminatum in corde vers. 19. dixit. Illud quoque frivolum est, quòd seminati in terra petrosa à seminatis in terra bona non respectu fidei, sed respectu promissæ mercedis differant; cùm manifestè adeò discrimen in causa διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν βάθος γῆς, quòd semen in terram petrosam projectum non habeat profunditatem terræ, neque radicem, vers. 5. 6. & in eo, quòd fructum non ferat per patientiam collocetur. Præterea, qui rei cardo est, fides temporaria à justificante non sola duratione, sed essentia & causis, effectis, subjecto & adjunctis differt. Nam fidei justificantis causa æterna electio, Actor. XIII. 48. Rom. VIII. 29. 30. nec non Spiritus S. renovatio, Tit. III. 5. regeneratio, Joh. III. 5. Temporalis causa gratia communis, & Spiritus S. φωτισμὸς illuminatio, qualis etiam in blasphemos cadit, Hebr. VI. 4. est. Illius essentia in συνέσει intelligentia, Matth. XIII. 23. πληροφορίᾳ τῆς πίστεως fiduciali apprehensione, Rom. IV. 21. per quam credens in Christo radicatur & confirmatur, Ephes. III. 17. Col. II. 7,
units.tr: LXII. Limborch's objections are insipid: that it is not faith but men that are called apostates; that perseverance is not of the essence of faith but its consequence, without which the essence of faith remains the same; that by this likeness of the same evangelical preaching Christ explained a different outcome, not a difference of hearts; that the seeds sown on stony ground differ from those sown on good ground not with respect to faith but with respect to the reward promised only to the persevering; that temporary faith is also compared with the herb which from stony ground [φυέντα] springs up at once and is soon scorched by the heat of the sun, v. 5, and Luke VIII. 6, and similar things. For when a man who falls away ceases to believe, he cannot be an apostate unless such faith existed. For what else is an apostate man than one who, for a time, assents to, believes, and even professes the word of God, rejoicing in it from light and not solid causes? Thus a wicked man is called wicked from wickedness, an apostate from apostasy, a murderer from murder. And although perseverance is not of the essence of faith, it necessarily follows from the grace and will of God, by the very fact that faith is in good ground, a good heart, and is rooted there. Moreover, that temporary faith differs in essence from justifying faith, even apart from the consideration of its consequence, perseverance, is quite clear, because that trustful apprehension and love which are in justifying faith are not in temporary faith. For what trust in God, what genuine love of Christ, can spring up from stony ground that has neither root nor bears fruit? Moreover, stony and good ground is that which receives the seed of the word of God with a disposition suited or unsuited to keeping it. But it is the heart of man that is stony and unregenerate and so not disposed to retain it; good and fleshy, it is disposed to retain it through the grace of regeneration. Lyra, the Glossa ordinaria, Diego de la Vega and others also acknowledge this. But why say more? Christ himself said that the evil one snatches away what was sown in the heart [τὸ ἐσπαρμένον ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ], v. 19. This too is trifling: that those sown on stony ground differ from those sown on good ground not with respect to faith but with respect to the promised reward. For the difference is manifestly placed in the cause, "because it had no depth of earth" [διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν βάθος γῆς], because the seed cast on stony ground does not have depth of soil or a root, vv. 5. 6, and in the fact that it does not bear fruit with patience. Moreover, which is the crux of the matter: temporary faith differs from justifying faith not only in duration but in essence, causes, effects, subject and adjuncts. For the cause of justifying faith is eternal election, Act. XIII. 48, Rom. VIII. 29. 30, and also the renewal of the Holy Spirit, Tit. III. 5, and regeneration, John III. 5. The temporal cause is common grace and the enlightening [φωτισμὸς] of the Holy Spirit, such as falls even on blasphemers, Hebr. VI. 4. The essence of the former is in understanding [συνέσει], Matth. XIII. 23, and in fiducial apprehension [πληροφορίᾳ τῆς πίστεως], Rom. IV. 21, by which the believer is rooted and confirmed, Eph. III. 17, Col. II. 7.

units.la: hujus qualiscunque assensus, sine intelligentia, fiducia, amore & radicatione ulla est, Luc. VIII. 13. Illius finis salus animarum, Hebr. X. 39. 1. Petr. I. 5. 9. hujus perditio, Hebr. X. 27. 2. Petr. II. 20. nec non ἀναπολογήτως Joh. XIV. 22. est. Illa purificationem cordis, Actor. XV. 9. pacem conscientiæ, Rom. V. 1. καρποφορίαν fructificationem, Matth. XIII. 23. charitatem inprimis, Gal. V. 6. gaudium solidum & constans, Joh. XVI. 22. hæc alia omnia operatur. Illa electorum & regenitorum: hæc reproborum est. Illa sincera, 1. Tim. I. 5. & radicata, Luc. VIII. 13. 15. perseverans, ibid. XXII. 32. hæc simulata, 1. Joh. II. 19. & deciduo quovis folio levior est, Luc. VIII. 13. Denique similitudo fidei temporalis & herbæ ex petrosa terra ἐνθέως ἐξανατελλόντος subitò exurgentis, Matth. XIII. 5. non in essentia utriusque, sed in modo generationis & durationis collocatur. Sicut semine in terram petrosam projecto oritur citò herba; sed citò etiam perit: ita semine verbi Dei in cor hominis petrosi sparso citò oritur quædam fides; sed citò etiam evanescit. At non quæ in universum ratio herbæ, etiam fidei est, nisi quòd variæ herbarum species sunt, & præter frumentum etiam zizania succrescunt.
units.tr: Of this kind of faith, whatever assent it may be, there is no understanding, trust, love or rooting at all, Luke VIII. 13. The end of the one is the salvation of souls, Hebr. X. 39, 1 Pet. I. 5. 9; the end of the other is perdition, Hebr. X. 27, 2 Pet. II. 20, and also [ἀναπολογήτως] being without excuse, John XIV. 22. The one works purification of the heart, Act. XV. 9, peace of conscience, Rom. V. 1, fruitfulness [καρποφορίαν], Matth. XIII. 23, above all love, Gal. V. 6, and solid and constant joy, John XVI. 22; the other works all things else. The one belongs to the elect and regenerate; the other to the reprobate. The one is sincere, 1 Tim. I. 5, and rooted, Luke VIII. 13. 15, persevering, ibid. XXII. 32; the other is feigned, 1 John II. 19, and lighter than any falling leaf, Luke VIII. 13. Finally, the comparison of temporary faith with the herb that springs up at once [ἐνθέως ἐξανατελλόντος] from stony ground, Matth. XIII. 5, lies not in the essence of either, but in the manner of their origin and duration. Just as when seed is cast on stony ground the herb springs up quickly but also quickly perishes, so when the seed of the word of God is sown in the heart of a stony man some faith springs up quickly, but quickly also vanishes. But this is not the nature of herbs in general, even of faith, except that there are various kinds of herbs, and besides the wheat, tares also grow up.

units.la: LXIII. Nullum etiam adversariis præsidium est in verbis Apostoli dicentis, impossibile esse, ut, qui illuminati sunt, & gustaverunt donum illud cœleste, & participes facti sunt Spiritus S. & bonum Dei verbum gustaverunt, & virtutes futuri seculi, & prolapsi fuerunt, rursus ad resipiscentiam renoventur, Hebr. VI. 4–7. Clarum enim est, Apostolum non loqui de iis, qui verè resipuerunt, & fide justificati sunt, sed de iis, qui infra perfectionem filiorum Dei substiterunt. Jubet enim missis initiis sermonis Christi φέρεσθαι εἰς τελειότητα ferri ad perfectionem, v. 1. eo potissimum argumento, quod citra illam perfectionem filiorum Dei, principiis inhærentes prolabi possint, & prolapsi ad pœnitentiam renovari non possint. Quos mox v. 8. cum terra spinas & tribulos ferente, reproba & execrationi propinqua, cujus finis est εἰς καῦσιν ad cremationem, comparat, sicut contra v. 7. verè fideles cum terra, quæ bibit sæpius in se venientem pluviam, & parit herbam commodam iis, propter quos colitur, & benedictionem accipit, contendit, & de iisdem v. 9. dicit: Persuasi sumus de vobis dilecti, κρείττονα meliora, ἃ ἔχομεν σωτηρίας saluti conjuncta, oppositè ad omne illud, quod de iis, qui παραπεσόντες prolabi possunt, dixerat. Ejusmodi meliora & saluti conjuncta sunt fides vera, justificans, ad quam refertur ἔργον opus & κόπος ἀγάπης labor charitatis, v. 10. Non cohæret cum salute, quod ab ea divelli potest. Possunt verò apostatæ hactenus proficere, ut illuminentur, hoc est, cognoscant doctrinam resipiscentiæ à mortuis operibus, & fidei in Deum, (non ut regenerentur & sanctificentur) ut gustent donum illud cœleste, Christum, qui de Cœlo venit, & ex mortuis resurrexit, & de eo convincantur, (non ut donum illud & panem cœlestem vera fide accipiant, & in sanguinem succúmque spiritualem convertant) ut participes fiant Spiritus S. quatenus donorum illorum, quæ in effusione Spiritus S. post ascensionem Christi in cœlos in multos per impositionem manuum redundarunt, nec non ἐλέγχως & convictionis ejus participes cipes facti sunt; non ut Spiritus S. iis Paracletus & arrhabo, & Spiritus gratiæ & precum essent, vel in unum corpus uno Spiritu baptizarentur, ut gustarent bonum Dei verbum, Evangelium cum convictione conscientiæ & gaudio atque exultatione nonnulla audiant, & virtutes futuri seculi, seu prærogativas Ecclesiæ Christianæ seu bona N. T. libertatem inprimis & gaudium Christianorum, admirabundi suspiciant. Quæ cuncta tamen ad perfectionem filiorum Dei, qui in Christum credunt & justificantur, neutiquam proficiunt. Cuncta enim hæc non sunt ἐχόμενα ζωῆς conjuncta saluti, & in hypocritis, & irregenitis locum habere possunt. Neque illud obstat, quòd tales πάλιν iterum ad pœnitentiam renovari posse Apostolus negat. Non enim id arguit, semel jam renovatos illos fuisse, quia secunda renovatio ad pœnitentiam intelligi potest non post veram resipiscentiam, sed post similitudinem resipiscentiæ in gaudio. Sicut enim secunda mors dicitur illorum, qui tamen non sunt participes primæ resurrectionis, Apoc. XX. 6. ita secunda renovatio, quæ possibilis esse negatur, dici potest ejus, qui non verè renovatus & vivificatus fuerat, sed sibi visus fuerat renovatus & vivificatus, & eo usque illuminatus fuerat, uti v. 4. 5. descriptum est.
units.tr: LXIII. Nor do our opponents find any support in the words of the Apostle: it is impossible that those who were once enlightened, and have tasted that heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, should be renewed again to repentance, Heb. 6:4–7. For it is clear that the Apostle is not speaking of those who truly repented and were justified by faith, but of those who remained below the perfection of the sons of God. He bids them, leaving the beginnings of the doctrine of Christ, be carried on to perfection [φέρεσθαι εἰς τελειότητα], v. 1, and chiefly on this ground: that without that perfection of the sons of God men, clinging to the first principles, can fall away, and once fallen, cannot be renewed to repentance. Soon afterwards, at v. 8, he compares these men to land bearing thorns and briars, worthless and near to being cursed, whose end is burning [εἰς καῦσιν]. On the other hand, at v. 7, he contends that truly faithful people are like land that drinks in the rain that often falls on it, and bears herbage useful to those for whose sake it is tilled, and receives blessing; and of these same people he says at v. 9: We are persuaded of you, beloved, better things [κρείττονα], and things that accompany salvation [ἃ ἔχομεν σωτηρίας], in contrast to everything he had said about those who could fall away [παραπεσόντες]. Such better things that accompany salvation are true, justifying faith, to which belong work [ἔργον] and labour of love [κόπος ἀγάπης], v. 10. What can be taken away from a man cannot be bound up with his salvation. Those who apostatize may, however, advance so far as to be enlightened, that is, to know the doctrine of repentance from dead works and of faith in God (though not to be regenerated and sanctified); to taste that heavenly gift, namely Christ, who came down from heaven and rose from the dead, and to be convinced of it (though not to receive that gift and heavenly bread in true faith and turn it into spiritual blood and food); to be made partakers of the Holy Spirit, in so far as they share in those gifts which after Christ's ascension into heaven overflowed upon many through the laying on of hands at the outpouring of the Spirit, and in the Spirit's convicting and convincing [ἐλέγχως] work; not in the sense that the Spirit would be to them Paraclete and pledge, and the Spirit of grace and of prayer, or that they would be baptized into one body by one Spirit; to taste the good word of God, so that they hear the Gospel with some sense of conscience convicted and with joy and exultation, and to look on with wonder at the powers of the age to come, that is, the privileges of the Christian Church, or the goods of the New Testament, above all the liberty and joy of Christians. Yet none of these things contributes in any way to the perfection of the sons of God, who believe in Christ and are justified. For none of these things are things that hold to life and are bound up with salvation [ἐχόμενα ζωῆς]; they can exist in hypocrites and the unregenerate. Nor does it stand in the way that the Apostle denies that such men can be renewed again [πάλιν] to repentance. For this does not prove that they had already been renewed once, since a second renewal to repentance can be understood not as following true repentance but as following a mere likeness of repentance in joy. Just as the second death is spoken of those who nevertheless do not share in the first resurrection, Rev. 20:6, so the second renewal, which is said to be impossible, can be spoken of one who was never truly renewed and made alive, but seemed to himself to be renewed and made alive, and had been enlightened to the point described in vv. 4 and 5.

units.la: LXIV. At nec S. Petrus errori patrocinatur scribens: Prætumida vanitatis pronuntiantes inescant in cupiditatibus carnis, in lasciviis, eos, qui ὄντως verè effugerunt in errore versantes, &c. Si enim, cùm effugerint inquinamenta mundi in cognitione Domini & Servatoris Jesu Christi, his verò rursus impliciti vincuntur, facta sunt iis postrema deteriora prioribus. Melius enim ipsis erat, non cognovisse viam justitiæ, quàm, cùm cognoverint, a præcepto sancto ipsis tradito converti, 2. Petr. II. 18-22. Cuncta enim illa πάθη seu effecta, prout à Petro enuntiantur, non fidei justificantis vel regenitorum propria, sed fidei temporariæ & irregenitis communia sunt. Agit quippe de ψυχὰς ἀστηρίκτους animabus instabilibus, v. 14. de iis, qui sunt fontes sine aqua, nubes à turbine circumactæ, v. 17. qui ὑπεροχικὰ μεγάλως ματαιότητος Φθέγγονται prætumida vanitatis pronuntiant, & inescant in lasciviis eos, qui verè effugerunt in errore versantes; libertatem promittentes, cùm ipsi servi corruptionis sint, v. 18. 19. Tribuit iisdem, quòd μιάσματα τῆς κόσμου inquinamenta mundi (errores fœdos, in quibus mundus jacet, ignorantiam, idololatriam, infidelitatem) effugerint, in cognitione Domini & Servatoris Jesu Christi, cujusmodi est, quòd Christus sit Dominus & Servator, ex Virgine natus, pro credentibus mortuus, habens gloriam, magnitudinem, potentiam, nec non hæreditatem sibi ex Testamento datam, quam morte sua emerit, & quæ Spiritu ipsius eidem uniatur; cujus solius gratia & merito homines credentes salventur: quòdque cognoverint viam justitiæ, doctrinam de justificatione, & sanctum præceptum credendi in Christum & resipiscendi accepisse, v. 20. 21. An verò omnes, qui cognito Domino & Servatore Jesu Christo inquinamenta mundi effugiunt, & doctrinam de justificatione per fidem cognoscunt, fideles, justificatos, regenitos esse dicemus? Nempe si sola cognitio Christi Salvatoris & Domini, sine fiducia & amore; nec non errorum, & infidelitatis, quæ in mun-
units.tr: LXIV. Nor does St Peter lend any support to this error when he writes: For when they speak great swelling words of vanity, they allure through the lusts of the flesh, through lasciviousness, those who have truly escaped from those who live in error, etc. For if, after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their latter end is worse than the beginning. For it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, having known it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them, 2 Pet. 2:18–22. For all those passions or effects, as Peter describes them, belong not to justifying faith or to the regenerate, but are common to temporary faith and to the unregenerate. He is speaking indeed of unstable souls [ψυχὰς ἀστηρίκτους], v. 14, of those who are springs without water, clouds driven by a whirlwind, v. 17, who speak great swelling words of vanity [ὑπεροχικὰ μεγάλως ματαιότητος φθέγγονται], and allure through lasciviousness those who have truly escaped from those who live in error, promising liberty while they themselves are slaves of corruption, vv. 18, 19. He grants to these same men that they have escaped the pollutions of the world [μιάσματα τοῦ κόσμου] (the foul errors in which the world lies: ignorance, idolatry, unbelief) through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, which includes knowing that Christ is Lord and Saviour, born of the Virgin, dead for believers, possessing glory, greatness and power, and the inheritance given to him by the testament, which he obtained by his death and which is joined to him by his Spirit; and that by his grace and merit alone believing men are saved; and they have known the way of righteousness, the doctrine of justification, and have received the holy commandment of believing in Christ and repenting, vv. 20, 21. But shall we say that all who escape the pollutions of the world through knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ and come to know the doctrine of justification by faith are believers, justified and regenerate? Indeed, if mere knowledge of Christ as Saviour and Lord, without trust and love, and mere renunciation of the errors and unbelief that are in the world, together with bare knowledge of the chief heads of orthodox religion, made a man truly faithful, justified and regenerate,

units.la: do est, abdicatio, & nuda præcipuorum religionis orthodoxæ capitum notitia verè fidelem, justificatum, regenitum faciunt; & verè fideles, justificati & regeniti omnes sunt, qui Christum Salvatorem & Dominum esse nôrunt, & talem ore profitentur. Sed aliud est agnoscere veritatem & justitiam juxta sanctum mandatum, aliud viam veritatis, justitiæ & sancti mandati ingredi. Sic etiam fatui & leves non aberraturi dicuntur, cùm via sanctitatis patefacta fuerit, Esaj. XXXV. 8. Alia enim est cognitio superficiaria, quæ est absque ζωὴ intelligentia, Matth. XIII. 23. ἄκαρπος sine fructu, 2. Pet. I. 8. inflans, non ædificans, 1. Cor. VIII. 1. alia cognitio, quæ est ex virtute, & in qua habetur ἐγκράτεια temperantia, quæ suppetens & abundans non otiosos, nec infrugiferos constituit, 2. Pet. I. 5. 6. 8. Sicut non ille Judæus est, qui in aperto est, sed qui in occulto est, Rom. II. 28. 29. ita nec ille Christianus verus, fidelis, justificatus est, qui palam id præ se fert, & cognitionem habet, sed non κατ' ἐνστάσεων secundum pietatem habet, Tit. I. 1.
units.tr: then all would be truly faithful, justified and regenerate who know Christ to be Saviour and Lord and profess it with their mouth. But it is one thing to acknowledge the truth and righteousness according to the holy commandment, and another to walk in the way of truth, righteousness and the holy commandment. So too the foolish and light-minded are said not to go astray once the way of holiness has been opened, Isa. 35:8. For there is a superficial knowledge, which is without understanding [συνιείς], Matt. 13:23, unfruitful [ἄκαρπος], without fruit, 2 Pet. 1:8, puffing up, not building up, 1 Cor. 8:1; and there is another knowledge, which comes from virtue and in which there is self-control [ἐγκράτεια], which, when present and abundant, makes men neither idle nor unfruitful, 2 Pet. 1:5, 6, 8. Just as he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, but he who is one inwardly, Rom. 2:28, 29, so he is not a true, faithful, justified Christian who carries the outward profession and possesses knowledge, but does not have it according to godliness [κατ' εὐσέβειαν], Titus 1:1.

units.la: LXV. Sed præposteram Theologiam hanc vocat Limborchius, docere, eos, qui semel crediderunt, in adulterium, homicidium, aliâque enormia peccata prolapsos semper, etiam dum ista peccata committunt, & in illis perseverant, verè fideles, Deique filios manere; eos verò, qui verè effugiunt eos, qui in errore versantur, quique per agnitionem Jesu Christi inquinamenta mundi effugerunt, etiam quamdiu in illo statu sunt, verè fidelium numero excludere. Sed affingit ille nobis Theologiam, quæ nostræ non est. Nam in gravia & atrocia peccata prolapsos, & in iis perseverantes, verè fideles & Dei filios manere, nulli docemus; sed eos qui cadunt, & resurgunt; qui faciunt, quod factum nollent, & quo non delectantur; qui peccant ex infirmitate, non studio & elata manu. Tales David, Petrus, alii Sancti & fideles fuerunt, qui sic peccarunt, ut Spiritum S. tristitiam secundum Deum pro tempore in iis operantem, non amiserint, Psal. LI. 8. 13. 2. Cor. VII. 20. & quorum etiam peccantium gravissimè veritas in renibus, & sapientia in corde, Psal. LI. 8. nec non fides in corde non defecit, Luc. XXII. 32. qui denique secundum exteriorem hominem à Domini pascuis, sed non à Pastoris protectione recesserunt, & in naufragio tabulam retinuerunt. Non enim cum actu habitus semper perit, vel marcescente folio radix marcescit & moritur. Alia planè ratio apostatarum illorum est, quos S. Petrus graphicè adeò describit ceu animas ἀστηρίκτους instabiles, fontes sine aqua, nubes à turbine actas, servos corruptionis, & lotos quidem, sed ut sues, neque ultra cognitionem Christi, ut Salvatoris & Domini. & fugam inquinamentorum mundi, seu abdicationem errorum & infidelitatis mundi, nec non sancti præcepti professionem progrediuntur. Cuncta enim isthæc sine Spiritu S. & fide cor purificante haberi & ad tempus retineri possunt. Impius ille nimis est, qui Sanctos, quorum de caetero comperta fides & sanctitas est, in gravissima peccata prolapsos, at seriò resipiscentes, cum ejusmodi strumis & vomicis comparare audet. Viderit verò Limborchius, viderint alii sectæ ejusdem assectæ, annon S. Petrus apostatas illos ἀλλοτρίωσιν ἐπαγγελιάν libertatem promittentes vers. 19. notans, fatidico Spiritu digitum intenderit in eos, qui ab Ecclesia vera secedentes, libertatem arbitrii, qua homo liber sit ad faciendum bonum, & non indigeat gratia Dei, quæ in ipso cor bonum & purum creet, eum sanctificet, & ad finem usque conservet, inter præcipuas secessionis suæ causas numerant; idque eo magis, quia doctrina illorum de libertate hominis, gangrænæ instar, νομὴν pastum habentis, in universum religionis ipsorum corpus serpit. Hi profecto illi sunt, qui postquam per cognitionem Christi, Domini & Salvatoris effugerunt in errore versantes, & inquinamenta mundi, errores Pelagianorum, Pontificiorum, denuo iis implicantur, & canis instar ad vomitum, porci loti ad volutabrum revertuntur, quorum postrema prioribus deteriora facta esse, vers. 20. satis illud comprobat, quod ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἀσεβείας ad ampliorem seu per impietatem proficientes, 2. Tim. II. 16. Socini castris magis magisque appropinquant. Denique non magis mirum est, inter vere fideles numerari in gravissima peccata prolapsos, sed resipiscentes, & ab eorundem numero excludi apostatas, quales Petrus describsit, quam mirum illud est, inter vivos censeri illum, qui gravissimo vulnere sauciatus est, inter mortuos vero, qui non ita fœdatus vulneribus, vivere tamen videtur, cum mortuus sit. Nam quod apostatas illos actiones vitæ spiritualis edere Limborchius regerit, sine ratione regerit. Non magis certe illi actiones, quam edidit Angelus Ecclesiæ Sardensis, quem mortuum esse Christus dixit, licet & ille viam justitiæ & sanctum præceptum audiverit & acceperit, atque ita per cognitionem Christi, Salvatoris & Domini inquinamenta mundi fugerit, & nomen habuerit, quod vivat, Apoc. III. 1. 3. Potest ergo Evangelium audiri, potest recipi etiam à mortuis, qui nomen habent, quod vivant, Christiani veri sint, & tamen mortui sunt. Non enim in eo consistit vita, ut quis dicat: Domine, Domine, Matth. VII. 22. nec etiam in eo, ut errantes redarguat, vel etiam irrideat, & ad eos non accedat. Quomodo primis Ecclesiæ temporibus, non ii veri Christiani fuerunt, qui Judæos & gentium idololatriam reliquerunt, & Jesum Salvatorem ac Dominum dixerunt, quod etiam Pseudapostoli fecerunt. Novit etiam Diabolus se multis & miris modis præconem justitiæ simulare.
units.tr: LXV. But Limborch calls this a perverse theology: that those who have once believed, having fallen into adultery, murder and other enormous sins, always remain, even while they commit these sins and persist in them, true believers and sons of God, while he excludes from the number of true believers those who truly escape from those who are in error and who, through the knowledge of Jesus Christ, have fled the pollutions of the world, even for as long as they are in that state. But he fabricates for us a theology that is not ours. For we teach that no one who has fallen into grave and atrocious sins, and persists in them, remains a true believer and son of God. We teach instead that those who fall and rise again, who do what they would not wish to have done and take no pleasure in it, who sin from weakness and not from zeal and a high hand, are such. David, Peter and other saints and believers were such, who so sinned that they did not lose the Holy Spirit, who for the time was working in them godly sorrow (Ps. 51:8, 13; 2 Cor. 7:10), and in whose most grievous sins truth in the inward parts and wisdom in the heart remained (Ps. 51:8), and whose faith did not fail (Luke 22:32). They departed, at last, according to the outward man, from the pasture of the Lord, but not from the protection of the Shepherd, and they kept hold of a plank in the shipwreck. For the habit does not perish with the act, nor does the root wither and die when the leaf withers. The case of those apostates whom St. Peter describes so vividly is quite different: unstable souls [ἀστηρίκτους], wells without water, clouds driven by a whirlwind, servants of corruption, and washed, indeed, but like swine. They do not go on to the knowledge of Christ as Saviour and Lord, nor to escape from the pollutions of the world, that is, the renunciation of the errors and unbelief of the world, nor to the profession of the holy commandment. For all these things can be had and retained for a time without the Holy Spirit and a faith that purifies the heart. That man is too impious who dares to compare with such scrofulous and festering sores those saints whose faith and holiness are otherwise established, who fell into the gravest sins but truly repented. Let Limborch see to it, and let the other adherents of that same sect see to it, whether St. Peter, marking those apostates promising liberty [ἐλευθερίαν ἐπαγγελλόμενοι] (v. 19), did not point with a prophetic Spirit at those who, separating from the true Church, number among the chief causes of their secession freedom of the will, by which man is free to do good and has no need of the grace of God, which creates in him a good and pure heart, sanctifies him, and preserves him to the end. And they do so all the more because their doctrine of human freedom, like a gangrene having pasture [νομὴν], creeps through the whole body of their religion. These are surely the ones who, after they have escaped through the knowledge of Christ, Lord and Saviour, are again entangled in the pollutions of the world, the errors of the Pelagians and Papists, and like a dog returning to its vomit, the washed sow returns to the wallowing-place. That their last state has become worse than the first (v. 20) is sufficiently proved by the fact that they are advancing to more ungodliness [ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἀσεβείας] (2 Tim. 2:16) and draw ever nearer to the camp of Socinus. Finally, it is no more surprising that those who have fallen into the gravest sins but repent should be numbered among true believers, and apostates, such as Peter describes, excluded from their number, than it would be surprising to count among the living one who is grievously wounded, and among the dead one who, though not so disfigured by wounds, nevertheless seems to live while he is dead. For when Limborch objects that those apostates perform the actions of the spiritual life, he objects without reason. Certainly they do not perform those actions any more than the Angel of the Church of Sardis did, whom Christ said was dead, although he too had heard and received the way of righteousness and the holy commandment, and thus through the knowledge of Christ, Saviour and Lord, had fled the pollutions of the world, and had the name that he lives (Rev. 3:1, 3). The Gospel, therefore, can be heard, and can be received, even from the dead, by those who have the name that they live, and who are yet dead. For life does not consist in saying: Lord, Lord (Matt. 7:22), nor in rebuking those who err, or even mocking them, while not approaching them. How, in the earliest times of the Church, were not those true Christians who forsook Jewish and Gentile idolatry and called Jesus Saviour and Lord, which even the false apostles did? The Devil also knows how to pretend, in many wonderful ways, to be a herald of righteousness.

units.la: LXVI. Neque plus exempla eorum, quos defecisse à fide & justitia clamitant, efficiunt. Davidis enim, Solomonis, Petri apostasiam non sine blasphemia Sanctorum Dei tuentur. Retinuit enim David gravissimè peccans Spiritum Dei, Psal. LI. 13. & Deus ipsi veritatem in præcordiis, fidem & amorem veritatis conservavit, & in occulto sapientiam notificavit, v. 8. ut à Nathane increpitus peccatum agnosceret, atque illud à se transferri sentiret, & vera fide sapientiam Dei ampleCteretur, misericordiam imploraret. Qui etiam Sanctorum suspiria cum bona conscientia conjuncta suo exemplo adumbrat: Erravi ut ovis perdita, quære servum tuum. Nam legis tuæ non sum oblitus, Psal. CXIX. 176. Iniquus ei est Limborchius, asserens, eum ex malitia & deliberatione consilii perfecta peccasse, quia deliberandi spatium habuerit, & circumstantias facti sui noverit, & alia quandiu
units.tr: LXVI. Nor do the examples of those whom they cry out have fallen away from faith and righteousness prove more. For they defend the apostasy of David, Solomon and Peter only by blaspheming the saints of God. For David, sinning most grievously, retained the Spirit of God (Ps. 51:13), and God preserved for him truth in the inward parts, faith and love of the truth, and made known wisdom in the hidden part (v. 8), so that, rebuked by Nathan, he might acknowledge his sin, and feel that it was transferred from himself, and with true faith might magnify the wisdom of God and implore mercy. His own example also portrays the sighs of the saints joined with a good conscience: I have erred like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I have not forgotten your law (Ps. 119:176). Limborch is unjust to him, asserting that he sinned from malice and a fully deliberate purpose, because he had time to deliberate, knew the circumstances of his deed, and, for as long as

units.la: absque ullo resipiscentiæ motu perseveraverit non subito æstu cupiditatis abreptus fuerit. Licet enim graviter & contra conscientiam peccaverit, & caro ejus spiritui prævalens sua ἀπάτῃ seductione peccati vias & rationes quæsiverit, atque in peccato homicidii & adulterii, velut spirituali deliquio aliquandiu obtorpuerit; non tamen ex malitia, perfecta consilii deliberatione, & contemptu Dei peccavit, sicut Saul; sed semen filialis amoris & timoris Dei retinuit. Reprehensus enim à Nathane ita peccatum suum agnovit & confessus est, ut simul ad gratiam Dei in Christo confugerit. Et seriam illam atque fidelem confessionem & resipiscentiam fuisse, constat, quia ei Nathan Dei nomine ilico dixit: Jehova transtulit peccatum tuum, 2. Sam. XII. 13. Etsi igitur in deliquio illo fides & vita spiritualis Davidis ad tempus sopita fuerit, atque in eo etiam intervallo sensum gratiæ Dei non perceperit, tamen nec vita spiritualis & fides ejus extincta est, nec à gratia Dei plane is destertus est. Neque etiam Solomonem inter apostatas & reprobos pie Bellarminus numeravit. Lapsus est in idololatriam indirectam, cæco erga uxores affectu eandem in iis tolerans, non abjurans Dei cultum, vel idola in Templum inferens. Qua in re cor ejus non fuit שלם perfectum coram Deo, sicut fuit cor Davidis, patris sui, 1. Reg. XI. 4. & non implevit ire post Jehovam, sicut David Pater ejus, ibid. v. 6. Gradus integritatis & perfectionis, non integritas & perfectio negatur. Ideo cum Davide etiam jungitur, 2. Paralip. XI. 17. ubi Rehabeam, quandiu Dei cultum integrum servavit, ambulasse בדרך דוד ושלמה in via Davidis & Solomonis dicitur. Pœnitentia vero & salus ejus in dubium revocari non potest. Nam Deus ipsi etiam peccanti gratiæ suæ constantiam promisit, dicens: Cum impie egerit, arguam eum virgis hominum. Sed חסדי לא יסור misericordia mea non recedet ab illo, 2. Sam. VII. 14. 15. Ubi חסד non est gratia המלכות Regni ei collati, sed omnis illa gratia, quam ante peccatum habuit, adeoque etiam fidei, precum sanctitatis. Quomodo etiam gratia illa, quam Deus à Saule abstulisse ibidem dicitur, non tam gratia Regni, quam Spiritus Prophetiæ, sapientiæ, fortitudinis, quam prius habuit, intelligitur. Quamquam etiam verba illa, כאשר הסרתי non necessario in eo ponunt חסד משאול gratiam vel misericordiam eam, cujus continuatio Solomoni promittitur, cum הסרתי non tantum reddi possit abstuli, sed etiam non contuli, non feci ad illum accedere. Sed Solomon profecto fuit ידידיה Dilectus Domini, ibid. XII. 25. qualis non fuit Saul. Est autem omne Dei אהבת עולם amor seculi, æternus, Jer. XXXI. 3. Et Deus illi fuit in Patrem, ipse ei in filium, 2. Sam. VII. 14. Resipiscentiæ vero ejusdem testis omni exceptione major, post lapsum scriptus ab eodem קהלת Ecclesiastes seu ἐπαυλαγὼν aggregans se iterum Ecclesiæ, & se cum eadem reconcilians, adeoque pœnitens, quo libro, inprimis cap. VII. 23-27. peccatum suum confitetur, detestatur, gratiam Dei liberantis ab eodem agnoscit, & fideles, ne similem in stultitiam ruant, informat. Mitto alia in loco fusius expositia. Nec illud obstat, quod Solomon excelsa ipsi Ashteroth, Chamos & Milcom erecta non sustulisse videtur, quia ea demum Josias sustulisse 2. Reg. XXIII. 13. dicitur. Certum enim est Ezechiam pridem ante Josiam excelsa & altaria ex universa Jehuda & Benjamin sustulisse, 2. Paralip. XXXI. 1. &c. Quod ergo in loco Regum dicitur, vel de RegibusSolomonem imitantibus, & excelsis similibus illis, quæ Solomon erexit, vel de ruderibus relictis intelligendum est. Potuerunt etiam excelsa ipsa relinquí, sed ad cultum veri Dei Israelis traduci, uti populus immolasse in excelsis [Hebrew] tantummodò Domino Deo suo, ibid. XXXIII. 17. dicitur, quod peccatum quandiu in idololatriam non degeneravit, Deus singulari bonitate & [Greek] quibusdam saltem temporibus dissimulavit & toleravit, donec Josias præ cæteris Regibus flagrantioris zeli illa diruit extirpavitque penitus. De Petri lapsu nihil dicam, cùm ipse Christus pro eo, ne fides ejus deficeret, intercesserit, Luc. XXII. 32. Et par fidelium omnium lapsorum, at non prolapsorum ratio est; qui pro tempore à fidei & virtutis tramite, sed non penitus à scopo defecerunt, in naufragio tabulam, in hieme semen, in paroxysmo lymphatico rationis principium retinuerunt. Non enim cum actu habitus, cum affectu seducto redeundi propositum periit. Quod in Petro clarissimum est, qui utcunque per Servatorem obtinuerit, ne fides ejus deficeret, non tamen id consecutus est, ut cum non abnegaret. Proin actus abnegationis fidei ejus habitum non extinxit, sed turbavit tamen. Unde Salvator eum respiciendo non novum infudit habitum, sed conservatum resuscitavit; & recordatus est Petrus, hoc est, ad se rediit, quem timor ante distraxerat, Luc. XXII. 61.
units.tr: he persisted without any movement of repentance, and was not suddenly carried away by a sudden surge of desire. For although he sinned grievously and against conscience, and though his flesh, prevailing over his spirit, sought the ways and reasons of sin by the deceit [ἀπάτῃ] of seduction, and for a while grew numb in the sins of murder and adultery, as if in a spiritual swoon, yet he did not sin from malice, by a fully deliberate purpose and contempt of God, as Saul did; he retained the seed of filial love and fear of God. For when rebuked by Nathan he so acknowledged and confessed his sin that at the same time he fled to the grace of God in Christ. That this was a serious and faithful confession and repentance is clear, because Nathan at once said to him in God's name: Jehovah has transferred your sin (2 Sam. 12:13). Therefore, even if in that lapse the faith and spiritual life of David were for a time dormant, and even if in that interval he did not perceive the sense of God's grace, nevertheless neither his spiritual life nor his faith was extinguished, nor was he utterly cut off from the grace of God. Nor did Bellarmine rightly number Solomon among apostates and reprobates. He fell into indirect idolatry, tolerating it through a blind affection for his wives, not renouncing the worship of God, nor bringing idols into the Temple. In this matter his heart was not שלם perfect before God, as the heart of David his father was (1 Kings 11:4), and he did not fully follow the Lord, as David his father did (ibid. v. 6). A degree of integrity and perfection is not denied; therefore he is also joined with David (2 Chron. 11:17), where Rehoboam, as long as he kept the worship of God whole, is said to have walked בדרך דוד ושלמה in the way of David and Solomon. But his repentance and salvation cannot be called into doubt. For God promised him the constancy of his grace even when he sinned, saying: When he does wrong, I will chasten him with the rod of men. But חסדי לא יסור my mercy shall not depart from him (2 Sam. 7:14, 15). Here חסד does not mean the grace of the kingdom given to him, but all that grace which he had before the sin, and so also faith, prayers and holiness. In the same way, that grace which God is said there to have taken away from Saul is understood not so much as the grace of the kingdom but as the Spirit of prophecy, wisdom and fortitude, which he had earlier. Although the words כאשר הסרתי do not necessarily imply that חסד was taken from Saul, that is, the grace or mercy whose continuation is promised to Solomon, since הסרתי can mean not only I took away but also I did not bestow, I did not allow him to approach. But Solomon was surely ידידיה Beloved of the Lord (2 Sam. 12:25), which Saul was not. Moreover, all of God's אהבת עולם love is everlasting, eternal (Jer. 31:3). And God was a Father to him, and he a son to God (2 Sam. 7:14). Of his repentance there is a witness beyond all exception: the book written by himself after his fall, קהלת Ecclesiastes, or ἐπαυλαγὼν aggregating himself again to the Church and reconciling himself with it, and so repenting. In that book, especially chapter 7:23-27, he confesses and detests his sin, acknowledges the grace of God that delivered him from it, and instructs the faithful not to fall into a similar folly. I pass over other matters explained more fully elsewhere. Nor does it stand in the way that Solomon seems not to have removed the high places erected to Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom, since it is said that Josiah removed them only (2 Kings 23:13). For it is certain that Hezekiah had long before Josiah removed the high places and altars from all Judah and Benjamin (2 Chron. 31:1, etc.). What is said in the passage of Kings must therefore be understood either of kings imitating Solomon, and of high places like those which Solomon erected, or of ruins left behind. The high places themselves could also have been left standing but turned to the worship of the true God of Israel, just as the people are said to have sacrificed in the high places [במה] only to the Lord their God (2 Chron. 33:17). As long as this sin had not degenerated into idolatry, God, by singular goodness and [Greek] at least for certain times, overlooked and tolerated it, until Josiah, of more fervent zeal than the other kings, utterly destroyed and rooted it out. I will say nothing of the fall of Peter, since Christ himself interceded for him, that his faith might not fail (Luke 22:32). The case of all the faithful who have fallen, but not fallen away, is similar: for a time they departed from the path of faith and virtue, but not utterly from the goal, and they retained, in the shipwreck a plank, in winter the seed, and in the frenzy of fever the principle of reason. For the habit does not perish with the act, nor the purpose of returning perish with an affection that has been led astray. This is clearest in Peter, who, though he obtained through the Saviour that his faith should not fail, did not thereby obtain that he should not deny. Thus the act of denying did not extinguish his habit of faith, but it did disturb it. Hence the Saviour, by looking at him, did not pour in a new habit but revived the one preserved; and Peter remembered, that is, came back to himself, whom fear had before distracted (Luke 22:61).

units.la: LXVII. Minoris momenti exempla Hymenæi & Phileti, Alexandri & Demæ sunt.
units.tr: LXVII. The examples of Hymenaeus and Philetus, and of Alexander and Demas, are of lesser weight.

units.la: Nunquam enim illi verè fideles, regeniti & justificati fuerunt. Egressi sunt ex nobis, sed non erant ex nobis. Si enim fuissent ex nobis, mansissent utique nobiscum, 1. Joh. II. 19. Stella cadens nunquam vera stella fuit. Hymenæus & Philetus [Greek] à veritate aberraverunt, vel circa illam non collinearunt, dicentes, resurrectionem jam factam esse, 2. Tim. II. 17. 18. Qui aberrarunt à veritate, ad eam ceu scopum non pertigerunt, illos in numero fidelium & regenitorum quis sanus reposuerit? A' tota veritate aberrant, qui partem mysterii, cui cætera connexa & consentanea sunt, abnegant. Neque veritatem recepisse dici possunt, qui ejus partem principalem, qualis resurrectio mortuorum in fine mundi est, negant. Quomodo nec Evangelio unquam credidisse dici possunt, qui Christum verum Deum esse, vel ejus justitiam imputari negant. Quomodo nec Judæi dici possunt credere Mosi & Prophetis, negantes, quæ Moses & Prophetæ de Christo & Regno ejus scripserunt. Idem Hymenæus & Alexander [Greek] repulsa (non expulsa, aliud enim est à se pellere, rejicere, quod quis nondum habuit; aliud expellere, quod quis jam habuit) fide & bona conscientia, circa fidem naufragium fecerunt, 1. Tim. I. 20. Tum verò bona conscientia repellitur, cùm cogitatio de rebus Divinis à vero scopo & certa regula averti-tur, & temerè, atque ex concupiscentia potiùs, quàm conscientia sine amore veritatis & Dei, aliquid admittitur. Qui sic conscientiam bonam repellunt, nunquam illi eam habuerunt, & ad fidem pervenire non possunt, sed potiùs circa eam naufragium faciunt; hoc est, pereunt circa fidem, quatenus id de eo dici potest, qui videri fidelis vult, vel auditor verbi Divini est, & se Regni Dei sectatorem profitetur, qui videtur in via esse ad vitam, & frustra est, quia tantum abest, ut ad vitam perveniat, ut ne quidem ad fidem pervenire possit.
