Non habet enim bonam conscientiam, quæ ad fidem salvificam requiritur. Si enim ex fide est charitas, & charitas ex puro corde & conscientia bona, 1. Tim. I. 5. utique fides sine conscientia bona esse non potest. Alias posset homo credere, & nescire, quid credat, & an hoc sit à Deo, vel Deo decorum & gloriosum sit? Similes locutiones Apostolus in hac epistola usurpat, velut [Greek] aberrare à re aliqua, cap. I. 6. [Greek] aberrare à fide, cap. VI. 10. [Greek] circa fidem non collineare, quod ibid. v. 20. 21. iis tribuitur, qui falsò nominatam cognitionem sectantur. Frustra ergo Limborchius est, qui Hymenæum & Alexandrum bonam conscientiam expulsse, adeóque habuisse; iisdem fidem tribui, & fidem talem, qualem Timotheus habuit, tribui pertendit, quæ falsa esse, ex iis, quæ diximus, liquet. Verè igitur & ipse [Greek]. Demæ exemplum [Greek] est. Reliquit ille Paulum, 2. Tim. IV. 10. Non ei nuntium remittens, vel ab eo ad Gentilismum vel Judaismum deficiens, sed non assistens ipsi in periculo. Quo sensu S. Paulus v. 16. dicit: In prima mea defensione nemo mihi adfuit, sed omnes me [Greek] deseruerunt. Idem dicitur [Greek] diligens, vel, qui vocum [Greek] & [Greek] etiam significatus est, boni consulens (non admodum appetens, vel plus quàm oportet, diligens) hoc seculum, hoc est, amore mundi mortem formidans, & metu mortis Paulum relinquens, quod etiam Apostolos fecisse Christo comprehenso constat. Non enim etiam verè fidelibus eadem semper animi præsentia & constantia adest. Infirmitas hæc Demæ, qualem optimi etiam, malentes in hoc seculo Divina longanimitate uti, quàm ad judicium ire, quandoque experiuntur; non à fide defectio fuit. Cùm enim cum aliis [Greek] cooperariis Pauli in libro vitæ scriptus dicatur, Phil. IV. 3. potius est, & inter [Greek] referendum, ut de eo benignius judicemus, quàm intempestivo studio & judicio eum, sine Dei sententia, ex libro vitæ deleamus. Neque obstant illa Johannis: Si quis diligit mundum, in eo non est dilectio Patris, 1. Joh. II. 15. & illa Jacobi: Qui amicus vult esse mundi, inimicus fit Deo, Jac. IV. 4. Aliud enim est sic diligere mundum, ut propter bona terrestria Deo, Christo, Cœlo prorsus renuntiemus; aliud, ut amore vitæ, quæ in mundo est, victi mortem pro Christo oppetere formidemus. In illis dilectio Patris esse non potest: in his esse potest, uti Apostolorum exemplum docet.
units.tr: They never were truly faithful, regenerate and justified. They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us, 1 John 2:19. A falling star was never a true star. Hymenaeus and Philetus [ἠστόχησαν] went astray from the truth, or did not aim at it, saying that the resurrection is already past, 2 Tim. 2:17, 18. Who in his right mind would count among the faithful and regenerate those who have gone astray from the truth and not reached it as their goal? They wander wholly from the truth who deny a part of the mystery, to which the rest is joined and with which it agrees. Nor can those be said to have received the truth who deny its principal part, such as the resurrection of the dead at the end of the world. Likewise, those who deny that Christ is true God, or that his righteousness is imputed to us, cannot be said ever to have believed the Gospel. Nor can the Jews be said to believe Moses and the Prophets if they deny what Moses and the Prophets wrote about Christ and his kingdom. The same Hymenaeus and Alexander [ἀπωσάμενοι] thrust away (not expelled; for it is one thing to push away from oneself, to reject, which a man has not yet had, and another to expel, which he has already had) faith and a good conscience, and made shipwreck concerning the faith, 1 Tim. 1:20. A good conscience is indeed rejected when thought about divine things is turned away from the true aim and certain rule, and something is admitted rashly, out of lust rather than conscience, without love of truth and of God. Those who thus reject a good conscience never had it, and cannot come to faith, but rather make shipwreck concerning it; that is, they perish as regards the faith, insofar as this can be said of one who wishes to seem faithful, or is a hearer of the divine Word, and professes himself a follower of the kingdom of God, who seems to be on the way to life, and is in vain. For he is so far from reaching life that he cannot even attain to faith. He does not have the good conscience that is required for saving faith. For if love springs from faith, and love from a pure heart and a good conscience, 1 Tim. 1:5, then faith certainly cannot exist without a good conscience. Otherwise a man could believe and yet not know what he believes, or whether it is from God, or whether it is fitting and glorious to God. The Apostle uses similar expressions in this letter: to go astray from a thing, aberrare à re aliqua, ch. 1:6; to go astray from the faith, aberrare à fide, ch. 6:10; and not to aim at the faith [circa fidem non collineare], which in v. 20, 21 is attributed to those who pursue knowledge falsely so called. Therefore Limborch is wrong when he contends that Hymenaeus and Alexander expelled a good conscience, and so had it, and that faith, and such faith as Timothy had, is attributed to them. From what we have said, this is plainly false. Thus Demas is truly [ἐγκατέλιπέν] an example of the same kind. He forsook Paul, 2 Tim. 4:10, not by sending him away or by falling away from him to Gentilism or Judaism, but by not standing by him in danger. In this sense St Paul says in v. 16: No one stood with me at my first defence, but all forsook me [ἐγκατέλιπον]. The same man is called diligent [ἀγαπήσας], a word which also carries the sense of being content with this age, that is, fearing death out of love of the world, and through fear of death abandoning Paul, as it is well known the Apostles also did when Christ was seized. Not even true believers always have the same presence of mind and steadfastness. Demas's weakness, of which even the best sometimes have experience, preferring to use the divine long-suffering in this world rather than to go to judgment, was not a defection from the faith. For since he is said to be written in the book of life with the other fellow-workers of Paul, Phil. 4:3, it is rather to be recorded among them, and we ought to judge him more kindly than to blot him from the book of life by an ill-timed zeal and judgment, without God's sentence. Nor do those words of John stand in the way: If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, 1 John 2:15; or that of James: Whoever wishes to be a friend of the world becomes an enemy of God, James 4:4. For it is one thing so to love the world that for the sake of earthly goods we utterly renounce God, Christ and heaven; it is another to be afraid to face death for Christ because we are overcome by love of the life that is in the world. In the former the love of the Father cannot be; in the latter it can be, as the example of the Apostles teaches.

units.la: LXVIII. Rationibus etiam apostasiam Sanctorum suffulcire conantur. Negant enim perseverantiam cum adhortationibus ad soli-citudinem
units.tr: LXVIII. They also try to support the apostasy of the saints with arguments. For they deny that perseverance can coexist with exhortations to carefulness

units.la: citudinem & perseverantiam, nec non cum promissionibus & comminationibus Dei, quae perseverantibus vel non perseverantibus proponuntur, consistere posse. Scriptura enim jubet vigilare, stare in fide, viriliter agere, 1. Corinth. XVI. 13. Gratiam Dei non in vanum accipere, 2. Corinth. VI. 1. non deficere a Deo, Hebr. III. 12. 13. tum perseveranti ad finem usque salutem, Matth. XXIV. 13. & fideli ad mortem coronam vitae, Apoc. II. 10. promittit; denique cadentibus severitatem & excidium, Rom. XI. 20. &c. & excidenti, ac non resipiscenti adventum hostilem, Apoc. II. 4. 5. comminatur. Atqui ubi ex vi Decreti Divini, & providentiae illi innixae, certa & necessaria fidelium perseverantia est, adeo ut Deus ipsos sit praeservaturus, ne in gravia peccata incidant, aut licet in gravia peccata incidant, certi sint tamen, respectu ipsorum esse infirmitates, Deumque illis non obstantibus perseverantiam, & a lapsibus resipiscentiam operaturum; ibi nullum fidei amittendae & a salute excidendi periculum, adeoque nec adhortationibus, promissionibus, comminationibus locum esse, tricantur. Sed aranearum haec tela est. Nam adhortationes, promissiones & comminationes ex ejusdem aeterni decreti dispositione media & acres instigationes perseverandi, & a tentationibus eluctandi sunt; sine quibus Christus in Sathanae insultu victoriam non spondet; & quibus Deus uti voluit, ut convenienter nostrae naturae, & suaviter, non violenter nos ad vitam aeternam perduceret. Cum enim creaturae rationales simus, suasiones & hortationes nobis ducendis ad vitam Deus adhibet, cum quibus tamen efficaciam internam Spiritus S. incrementum plantationi & rigationi addentis, conjungit, qua, ut sponte obediamus & curramus, efficit. Praedestinatio enim non supinis & oscitantibus, sed vigilantibus, nec sine mediis, salutem decrevit, quae tamen media in foedere Gratiae Deus ipse operatur. Per patientiam propositum nobis stadium decurramus, Hebr. XII. 1. Et justificatio post se trahit demonstrationem diligentiae ad fiduciam spei usque ad finem, ne simus socordes, imitatores vero magis simus per fidem eorum, qui promissionum haereditatem adeunt, Hebr. VI. 11. 12. Neque adeo media ejusmodi perseverantiae opponenda, sed subordinanda sunt, quia Deus donum perseverantiae non absolute sine mediis, sed per media, inprimis verbum ejusque usum conferendum promisit, Esaj. LIX. 21. Neque, quod illi urgent, adhortationes & promissiones periculum & metum contrarii eventus simpliciter tollunt, sed tollunt duntaxat, ubi rectus mediorum usus est, & respectu non naturae, sed gratiae, a qua ipse etiam mediorum usus provenit. Ita Paulus certus utique ex Divina promissione nulli omnino conditioni mutabili subjecta, nullius animae navigantium secum jacturam fore, nihilominus militibus dixit: Nisi hi in navi manserint, salvi non eritis, Act. XXVII. 22. 31. Cumque Christus probe noverit, nullum sibi datorum periturum, solo excepto Juda, nihilominus passim eosdem ad vigilantiam & perseverantiam exhortatus est, quin & Deum Patrem, ut eos custodiat, rogavit, Joh. XVII. 11. Praeceptiones enim, promissiones
units.tr: and perseverance, or with the promises and threats of God, which are set before those who persevere and those who do not. For Scripture commands us to watch, stand fast in the faith, act like men, 1 Cor. XVI. 13; not to receive the grace of God in vain, 2 Cor. VI. 1; not to fall away from God, Heb. III. 12, 13. It promises salvation to him who perseveres to the end, Matt. XXIV. 13, and the crown of life to the faithful unto death, Rev. II. 10. Finally, it threatens severity and ruin to those who fall, Rom. XI. 20, etc., and threatens a hostile coming upon the one who falls and does not repent, Rev. II. 4, 5. But where, by the force of the divine decree and the providence resting upon it, the perseverance of the faithful is certain and necessary, so that God will preserve them from falling into grave sins, or, even if they fall into grave sins, they are nevertheless certain that those are mere infirmities as far as they are concerned, and that God will work perseverance and recovery from their lapses notwithstanding them: there, they say, there is no danger of losing faith and falling from salvation, and so no place for exhortations, promises or threats. But this is a spider's web. For exhortations, promises and threats are, by the arrangement of the same eternal decree, the means and sharp incitements to persevere and to struggle through temptations; without them Christ does not promise victory in Satan's assault, and God chose to use them so that he might lead us to eternal life in a manner fitting our nature, gently and not by force. For since we are rational creatures, God employs persuasions and exhortations to lead us to life, and joins to them the inward efficacy of the Holy Spirit, who gives increase to the planting and the watering. By this he brings it about that we obey and run willingly. For predestination decreed salvation not for the sluggish and the drowsy, but for the watchful, and not without means; and God himself works these means in the covenant of grace. Let us run with patience the race set before us, Heb. XII. 1. And justification draws after it the showing of the same diligence unto the full assurance of hope to the end, that you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith inherit the promises, Heb. VI. 11, 12. Nor, therefore, are such means to be set against perseverance, but subordinated to it, because God promised the gift of perseverance not absolutely without means, but through means, above all by bestowing the word and its use, Isa. LIX. 21. Nor do exhortations and promises, as they urge, simply remove the danger and fear of the contrary outcome; they remove it only where there is right use of the means, and with respect not to nature but to grace, from which the very use of the means also comes. So Paul, certain indeed from the divine promise, which was subject to no changeable condition, that not one soul of those sailing with him would be lost, nevertheless said to the soldiers: Unless these remain in the ship, you cannot be saved, Acts XXVII. 22, 31. And since Christ knew perfectly well that none of those given to him would perish, except Judas alone, he nevertheless everywhere exhorted the same men to watchfulness and perseverance, and even asked the Father to keep them, John XVII. 11. For precepts, promises

units.la: & comminationes animant fideles, & iisdem verbum Dei in mentem revocant. Nec praeceptiones & adhortationes, nec ipse amor & fiducia in Deo adjutore, nec invocatio Dei, nec spes ex promissione Dei concepta, nec promissio, vel testamentum res inanes & otiosae sunt. Sed nefas tamen est, ut adhortationes facias potentes potentiam gratiae Dei, justitiae Dei, spiritus ejus, & vim precum tollere. Non obstante Perseverantia Sanctorum comminatur Christus a non habente ablatum iri id, quod habet, Matth. XIII. 12. Luc. VIII. 18. nempe cognitionem aliquam, gaudium ex ea, recte dicta & facta, nomen viventium, pellem ovium. Imo etiam deletionem ex libro vitae Deus comminatur; non quod Deus ex libro suo & Testamento suo quemquam deleat eorum, quos ipse heredes vitae scripsit, sed quod cum justis non scribantur; Psal. LXIX. 29. Ezech. XIII. 9. Et Deus nomina illorum non sumat in os, Psal. XVI. 4. eos abneget, Matth. VII. 23. 2. Tim. II. 12. & cum ipsi nomina sua inter fideles scripserint, Esaj. XLIV. 5. per defectionem inde nomen suum tollant, & se abscindant, Gal. V. 12. denique Deus illos inter alumnos suos, vocandos, solicitandos, tolerandos non amplius ferat, Exod. XXXII. 33. sed regnum suum ab iis auferat, Matth. XXI. 43. Praeterea neque fideles, quia possunt opera carnis patrare, pariter a fide totaliter & finaliter deficere possunt, quia non plena voluntate & data opera; neque in iisdem sibi placent, vel perseverant; imo hoc sensu peccare non possint, 1. Joh. III. 9. Neque adeo fidelis integer, vel mens regenita, qua talis, peccat, sed peccatum, Lex ejus in membris, Rom. VII. 23. peccatum inhabitans, ibid. v. 17. reliquiae scilicet hominis & corruptionis naturalis, mentem sive invitam, sive insciam, sive oscitantem, improvidam, & ad legem Dei non attendentem, certe nolentem a recto tramite abripientes. Homo interim internus, lege Dei delectatur, & quod facit, quatenns caro & carnalis est, ipse non vult, imo odit, ibid. v. 14. 15. 22. Porro etiam Sancti gravia in peccata lapsi viri mortis sunt, 2. Sam. XII. 5. 7. quibus graviter Deus irascitur, 1. Reg. XI. 9. quia id peccatum per se & natura sua meretur. Ex quo tamen perperam convellitur id, quod peccatori, ex immutabili Dei gratia, per accidens tribuitur. Nam etiam dum Deus virga hominum punit, gratia ejusdem a fidelibus non recedit, neque Deus pater esse desinit, 2. Sam. VII. 14. 15. [Hebrew] Cum ceciderit justus non prosternitur, quia Jehova sustentat manum ejus, Psal. XXXVII. 24. Etiam fideles justi & regeniti ob atrox scandalum juste excommunicari, imo & Sathanae tradi ad carnis perniciem possunt, sed ut spiritus salvetur in die Domini Jesu, 1. Cor. V. 5. non ut cum epulone a Sathana aeternum crucientur. Excommunicatio enim non evellit fidei fibras, sed impietatis sarmenta amputat. Unde excommunicatus talis definens esse membrum communionis externae, internae membrum in occulto esse non definit. Denique doctrina de perseverantia Sanctorum securitatem carnalem inducere, & excuti fidelibus solicitam illam curam, passim iis ad resistendum Diabolo praescriptam, clamitant. Viderint vero perseverantiae inimici, an minus apud suos carnalis securisecuritas regnet, & an per doctrinam suam, qua sibi & libertati suæ confidentes, vim suam faciunt Deum suum, & sagenæ suæ sacrificant, atque reti suo suffire non desinunt, Habac.I. 11.16. aptiores ad resistendum Diabolo evadant. Davidis certè curam & industriam adversus æstus Saulis Divina promissio Regni in humeros ejus devolvendi non minuit, nedum extinxit, sed acuit etiam. Et par fidelium ratio, quibus Cœlestis Regni hæreditas promissa est. Illi contrà, qui perseverantiam negant, tollunt spem, incentivum & nutriculam pietatis, & homines faciunt vel desperare, vel saltem cum desperatione semper luctari, vel salutem securè negligere; & necesse habent fidem perseverantem facere non omnino donum Dei, perpetuis precibus ambiendum, ne integrum maneat: Qui gloriatur, glorietur in Domino, 1.Cor.I.31. Fides verò, quæ radicem non habet, & ideo deficere poterit, etiamsi ad finem perseveret, servare non poterit, quia mera hypocrisis est. Claudimus verbis Apostoli verè fidelium & regenitorum omnium statum sic describentis: Nos non sumus ὑποστολῆς subductionis ad interitum, sed fidei εἰς περιποίησιν ψυχῆς ad acquisitionem lucrifactionem animæ, Hebr. X. 39.
units.tr: and threats animate the faithful, and by them the word of God is brought back to mind. Neither precepts and exhortations, nor love itself and trust in God as helper, nor the invocation of God, nor hope conceived from the promise of God, nor the promise or covenant are empty and idle things. But it is wrong to make exhortations powerless, and to take away the power of the grace of God, the justice of God, his Spirit, and the force of prayers. Notwithstanding the perseverance of the saints, Christ threatens that from him who has not, what he has shall be taken away, Matt. XIII. 12; Luke VIII. 18: namely, some knowledge, joy in it, things rightly said and done, the name of the living, the sheepskin. Indeed God even threatens blotting out from the book of life, not because God blots out from his own book and his own covenant any of those whom he has written as heirs of life, but because they are not written with the just, Ps. LXIX. 29; Ezek. XIII. 9. And God does not take their names upon his lips, Ps. XVI. 4; he disowns them, Matt. VII. 23; 2 Tim. II. 12; and when they have written their names among the faithful, Isa. XLIV. 5, through defection they take away their name from there and cut themselves off, Gal. V. 12; finally God no longer bears them among his pupils, to be called, urged and tolerated, Exod. XXXII. 33, but takes away his kingdom from them, Matt. XXI. 43. Moreover, the faithful, because they can commit the works of the flesh, cannot in the same way fall away totally and finally from faith, since they do not do it with full will and deliberate effort; nor do they take pleasure in those works or persist in them. Indeed, in this sense they cannot sin, 1 John III. 9. Nor, then, does the whole believer, or the regenerate mind as such, sin; but sin does, his law in my members, Rom. VII. 23; sin dwelling in me, ibid. v. 17, namely the remnants of man and of natural corruption, which drag the mind, whether unwilling or unaware, drowsy, heedless, and not attending to the law of God, certainly against its will, away from the straight path. Meanwhile the inner man delights in the law of God, and what he does, insofar as he is flesh and fleshly, he himself does not will, nay hates, ibid. vv. 14, 15, 22. Furthermore, even saints who have fallen into grave sins are men of death, 2 Sam. XII. 5, 7, with whom God is angry in earnest, 1 Kings XI. 9, because that sin deserves it by its own nature. From this, however, what is granted to the sinner by the accident of the immutable grace of God is wrongly torn away. For even while God punishes with the rod of men, his grace does not depart from the faithful, nor does God cease to be a Father, 2 Sam. VII. 14, 15. Though the righteous fall, he shall not be cast down, for the LORD upholds his hand, Ps. XXXVII. 24. Even faithful, justified and regenerate persons may justly be excommunicated for a grave scandal, and indeed may be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, but that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus, 1 Cor. V. 5; not that they should be tormented eternally by Satan along with the glutton. For excommunication does not tear out the fibres of faith, but cuts off the shoots of impiety. Hence an excommunicated person who ceases to be a member of external communion does not cease to be a member of the inward communion, which is hidden. Finally, they cry out that the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints induces carnal security, and that the anxious care which is everywhere prescribed to the faithful for resisting the Devil is shaken off. But let the enemies of perseverance see whether carnal security reigns less among their own people, and whether, by their doctrine, by which they trust in themselves and in their freedom, they make their own strength their god, and sacrifice to their net, and do not cease to burn incense to their drag-net, Hab. I. 11, 16, they become more fit to resist the Devil. Certainly the divine promise that the kingdom would be transferred to David's shoulders did not lessen David's care and diligence against the fury of Saul, let alone extinguish it; it even sharpened it. And the same reasoning holds for the faithful, to whom the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom is promised. On the other hand, those who deny perseverance remove hope, the incentive and nourishment of piety, and make men either despair, or at least always struggle with despair, or carelessly neglect salvation. And they are obliged to make persevering faith not wholly a gift of God, to be sought by perpetual prayers, lest it remain whole: He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord, 1 Cor. I. 31. But faith that has no root, and so may fail, though it persevere to the end, will not be able to save, because it is mere hypocrisy. We conclude with the words of the Apostle, who thus describes the state of all true believers and the regenerate: We are not of those who draw back [ὑποστολῆς] to perdition, but of faith unto the saving [εἰς περιποίησιν] of the soul, Heb. X. 39.

units.la: LXIX. Perseverantiæ Sanctorum Certitudo salutis, qua credens in Christum, & justificatus per fidem certam de consecutione salutis suæ persuasionem habere potest, & habet, individua comes est. Si enim Deus certam, & immutabili causarum & effectuum nexu stabilitatem, firmámque fidem & salutem nostram esse voluit justitque, eandem etiam credenti, ad cujus inprimis consolationem illa pertinet, innotescere voluit. Duo enim sunt, quæ religionem veram supra cæteras immensum quantum evehunt, infallibilis veritas, & inexhausti fructus consolationis. Sicut nempe erroneæ doctrinæ hominum, quas Christus σκότος tenebras Joh. III. 19. appellat, hinc caligine sua mentem obnubilant, & à recto salutis tramite avertunt; isthinc animum terrore implent, & conscientias anxietate constringunt: ita doctrina cœlestis & rectam Cœli viam aperit, & animam certa beatitudinis futuræ fiducia sustentat. Hoc enim sapientiæ & bonitati Dei quàm maximè consentaneum est. Ideo Christus non tantùm viam ad Cœlum ostendit, sed etiam omnibus oneratis & laborantibus ad se accitis ἀνάπαυσιν quietem promisit, Matth. XI. 28. Qualis quies est, quæ perpetuos conscientiarum angores & perturbationes conjunctas habet? Atque inde est, quòd Evangelium non tantùm φῶς lumen à Christo vocatur, Joh. III. 19. quia nativas mentis tenebras discutit, sed etiam ut φῶς τῆς ζωῆς lumen vitæ ibidem VIII. 12. commendatur; quia spirituali lætitia, quæ vera anima vitæ est, pectora perfundit. Et author illius Christus in fidelibus oritur non tantùm ut Sol, qui in cordibus nostris splendescit ad illuminationem scientiæ gloriæ Dei, 2.Cor. IV. 6. sed etiam ut Sol justitiæ, sanitatem in alis suis afferens, Mal.IV.2. Neque Deus tantùm ut Deus veritatis, sed etiam ut Princeps pacis, Esaj. IX. 6. & Deus omnis consolationis, Rom. XV. 5. nec tantùm ut vera via, sed etiam ut vita ipsa, Joh. XIV. 6. se ipsum offert. Non ergo Evangelium integrum illi retinent, imò vim ejus ignorant, qui ita illud annuntiant, ut nolint conscientias ejus ope spirituali tranquillitate frui, sed cum perpetua dubitatione conflictari jubeant. Qui certè legem cum Evangelio, fœdus operum cum fœdere gratiæ, montem Sinai cum monte Sion, & æquabilem atque exhilarantem sonum cornu, quo accessus ad Deum annuntiatur, Exod. XIX. 13. cum vehementi & terribili tubæ sonitu confundunt. Cùm verò Evangelium eorum, qui credunt, respectu, omni ex parte lætum nuntium fit, neque tantùm Evangelium veritatis, sed etiam pacis & salutis Eph.I.13. VI.15. fit, certitudo salutis, ceu præcipua ejusdem doctrina, & consolationis omnis, in ærumnosæ hujus vitæ fluctibus, basis & fulcrum maximum, & verissimus portus voluptatis & tranquillitatis, Psal. CVII. 30. ex Scripturis demonstrari, & undique tuta in arce cœlesti veritatis collocari debet.
units.tr: LXIX. The certainty of salvation, by which the believer who is justified through faith in Christ can have, and does have, a sure persuasion that he will attain his salvation, is inseparable from the perseverance of the saints. For if God has willed and ordained that our faith and salvation be something firm and stable, bound by an unchangeable chain of causes and effects, he has also willed that this certainty be made known to the believer, since it chiefly concerns his comfort. There are two things which raise true religion immeasurably above all others: infallible truth and an inexhaustible fruit of consolation. Just as the erroneous doctrines of men, which Christ calls darkness [σκότος] (John 3:19), cloud the mind with their fog and turn it from the right path to salvation, and likewise fill the soul with terror and bind consciences with anxiety, so the heavenly doctrine opens the right way to heaven and sustains the soul with the sure confidence of future blessedness. For this is most consonant with the wisdom and goodness of God. Hence Christ not only shows the way to heaven, but also promises rest [ἀνάπαυσιν] to all who are burdened and labouring and come to him (Matt. 11:28). What kind of rest is it that has perpetual anguish and disturbance of conscience attached to it? And this is why the Gospel is called by Christ not only light [φῶς] (John 3:19), because it dispels the innate darkness of the mind, but is also commended as light of life [φῶς τῆς ζωῆς] in the same place (8:12), because it fills the heart with spiritual joy, which is the true life of the soul. And Christ, the author of this, arises in the faithful not only as the Sun which shines in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God (2 Cor. 4:6), but also as the Sun of righteousness, bringing healing in its wings (Mal. 4:2). Nor does God offer himself only as the God of truth, but also as the Prince of peace (Isa. 9:6) and the God of all consolation (Rom. 15:5); nor only as the true way, but also as life itself (John 14:6). Therefore those who announce the Gospel in such a way that they do not want consciences to enjoy spiritual tranquillity through its help, but bid them struggle in perpetual doubt, do not hold the whole Gospel, indeed they do not know its power. They certainly confound the law with the Gospel, the covenant of works with the covenant of grace, Mount Sinai with Mount Zion, and the even and cheering sound of the trumpet, by which access to God is announced (Exod. 19:13), with the violent and terrible blast of a trumpet. But since the Gospel, with respect to believers, is in every way a joyful message, and is not only the Gospel of truth but also of peace and salvation (Eph. 1:13; 6:15), the certainty of salvation must be demonstrated from the Scriptures, as the chief doctrine of the Gospel and the greatest basis and support of all consolation amid the waves of this troubled life, and the most true harbour of delight and tranquillity (Ps. 107:30), and it must be set firmly in the heavenly stronghold of truth on every side.

units.la: LXX. Certum idem est quòd cretum à cernendo, quia res certa, velut creta & decreta oculis corporis vel animi quasi cernitur & perspicitur. Inde & eventus rei certus dicitur, qui cretus & decretus veluti cernitur; & notitia atque assensus animi certus dicitur, quando πληροφορεῖται, atque indubitatus est, & argumento quasi creto, viso & perspecto nititur. Posterior hujus loci est. Estque illa vel experientiæ, puta sensus vel corporalis, vel spiritualis, quorum neuter circa objectum proprium fallitur; vel scientiæ, qua res naturalis per causas naturales indubitatas cognoscitur; scire enim est rem per causam cognoscere; vel intelligentiæ, qua principia rerum cognoscendarum & agendarum apprehenduntur: vel fidei in revelatis. Quæ non tantùm est assensus in mente, sed etiam fiduciæ in corde, promissionem revelatam applicantis, & in firmitudine creditorum acquiescentis. Fides enim duplex est, quæ creditur, quæ Catholica doctrina in Scripturis revelata est; & qua creditur, sive speciatim, quia fidelis revelatis non tantùm assentitur, sed etiam res in revelatione promissas sibi applicat, iisdémque firmiter innititur, ut salutem inde consequatur. Quam verò alii addunt certitudinem moralem, quæ dubitationem & formidinem oppositi non excludit, illa nomen certitudinis non sustinet, quia per eam nihil certò cognoscitur, vel sive corpore, sive spiritu clarè videtur & perspicitur. Certitudo salutis quam fidelis habet, nec experientiæ sensus naturalis, nec scientiæ, nec intelligentiæ, sed mixta ex certitudine fidei, qua ex Scriptura credunt, omnes Christo ad salutem confidentes certò salvatum iri, & experientiæ sensus spiritualis, quæ ex proprio animi sensu & conscientia, ac impresso Spiritus S. arrhabone & charactere, quem intus fidelis deprehendit, est. Sicut enim primò subnixi testimonio Dei per fidem credimus revelationi: ita deinceps per actum fiduciæ & sensum experientiæ illam obsignamus. LXXI. Tum & certitudo alia viæ & imperfecta atque luctans, alia patriæ & perfecta atque eluctans est. Illa fidelium in hac vita est. Hi enim cùm ex principiis duobus, carne & spiritu, constent, & spiritus adversus carnem, atque caro adversus spiritum concupiscat, & utraque sibi contrarientur atque colluctentur continuè, certitudo, carne obstrepente, & nonnunquam, ddd nunquam, seu πεῖς κατέχον spiritui prævalente, ita perfecta esse, ut quoad sensum gratiæ nunquam interrumpatur, nequit. Fiducia proin illa, innatæ imbecillitatis respectu, sæpiuscule concutitur & fluctuat, præsertim in vocationis tyrocinio, cum fidelis νεόφυτος est, sub cruce & tentationis æstu, quando spiritus solatii sic nonnunquam intercluditur, & lumen Divinæ faciei abscond() ut fideles in festinatione dicant & quiritentur נאָתִי מִנֶּךָּ פָנֶיךָ Excisus sum ab oculis tuis, Psal. XXXI. 23. Sagittæ omnipotentis apud me sunt, quare venenum ebibit spiritus meus, terrores Dei oppugnant me, Job. VI. 4. Deus mi, Deus mi, quare dereliquisti me? Matth. XXVII. 46. Neque tamen in certamine hoc ita succumbunt, quin elucentur, & ad vividum gratiæ & salutis sensum redeant, tandemque soluti carne, quæ morosæ fœminæ instar responsitare & obniti non desinit, in cœlesti patria ad plenissimum salutis & gloriæ in æternum perseveraturæ sensum enitantur.
units.tr: LXX. The word certum (certain) is the same as cretum, from cernere (to discern), because a certain thing is, as it were, sifted and seen clearly by the eyes of body or mind. Hence also the outcome of a thing is called certain when it is, as it were, discerned and determined; and the knowledge and assent of the mind is called certain when it is fully assured [πληροφορεῖται], is beyond doubt, and rests on a proof, as it were sifted, seen and examined. The latter is of this kind: it is either of experience, namely of the senses, whether bodily or spiritual, neither of which is deceived about its proper object; or of science, by which a natural thing is known through indubitable natural causes, for to know a thing is to know it through its cause; or of understanding, by which the first principles of things to be known and done are grasped; or of faith in matters revealed. Faith is not merely assent in the mind, but also trust in the heart, applying to itself the revealed promise and resting firmly on the strength of what is believed. For faith is twofold: that which is believed, which is the Catholic doctrine revealed in the Scriptures; and that by which it is believed, which is specifically the faith by which the faithful not only assent to what is revealed, but also apply to themselves the things promised in the revelation and rest firmly upon them, so as to obtain salvation thereby. As for the so-called moral certainty, which does not exclude doubt and fear of the opposite, that does not deserve the name of certainty, because through it nothing is known for sure, nor is it clearly seen and perceived either by body or by spirit. The certainty of salvation which the faithful have is neither of natural sense-experience, nor of science, nor of understanding, but is compounded of the certainty of faith, by which all who trust in Christ for salvation believe from Scripture that they will certainly be saved, and of the experience of the spiritual sense, which comes from the believer's own inner sense and conscience, and from the impressed pledge and seal of the Holy Spirit, which the believer perceives within. For just as we first, supported by the testimony of God, believe the revelation through faith, so afterwards by an act of trust and by the sense of experience we seal it. LXXI. Moreover, there is one certainty that is of the way and imperfect and struggling, and another that is of the homeland and perfect and triumphant. The former belongs to the faithful in this life. For since they consist of two principles, flesh and spirit, and the spirit lusts against the flesh and the flesh against the spirit, and both continually oppose and wrestle with each other, the certainty cannot be so perfect that, with the flesh clamouring, and sometimes, never, or when the flesh prevails over the spirit [πεῖς κατέχον], it is never interrupted as far as the sense of grace is concerned. Therefore that trust, on account of innate weakness, is often shaken and wavers, especially in the apprenticeship of calling, when the believer is newly planted [νεόφυτος], under the cross and in the heat of temptation, when the comfort of the Spirit is sometimes cut off in this way, and the light of the Divine face is hidden, so that the faithful in their haste say and complain: I am cut off from before your eyes [נִגְרַזְתִּי מִנֶּגֶד עֵינֶיךָ] (Ps. 31:23); The arrows of the Almighty are within me; my spirit drinks up their poison; the terrors of God assail me (Job 6:4); My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt. 27:46). Yet they do not so yield in this struggle as to be overcome, but return to a living sense of grace and salvation, and at last, released from the flesh, which like a tiresome woman never ceases to talk back and resist, they strive in the heavenly homeland toward the fullest sense of salvation and glory, which they will persevere in for ever.

units.la: LXXII. Est ergo Certitudo Gratiæ & Salutis perfuasio illa electorum & fidelium, qua illi subnixi fide Divina, testimonio Spiritus S. & sensu atque experientia gratiæ in se operantis, non quoad actum continuatum, sed quoad fundamentum & habitum fiduciæ, pro mensura fidei suæ & Spiritus certo confidere possunt, & confidunt, se non ex dignitatis propriæ, sed dignationis Divinæ & custodiæ ejusdem deliberato intuitu, non tantum in præsentiarum in statu gratiæ esse, sed in eodem etiam, licet non sine certamine cum dubitatione & tentatione, quam Sathanas, mundus & caro suggerunt, ad finem usque vitæ perseveraturos, atque ita infallibiliter salvandos esse, ad laudem gloriæ gratiæ Dei, & eorundem in vitæ hujus perpetuis ærumnis, consolationem. Ejusmodi certitudinem quosdam Sanctos adeptos esse, in confesso est. Nam S. Paulus diserte eam sibi aliisque vendicat, dicens: Persuasus sum, quod neque vita, neque mors, &c. ἡμᾶς Nos separare possit a charitate Dei, quæ est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro, Rom. VIII. 38. 39. Illi vero ἡμῖς nos qui alii esse possunt, quàm qui eandem fidem & Spiritum habent, quam S. Paulus habet? Qui fideles & credentes omnes sunt, quos cap. I. 7. ἀγαπητοὺς Θεοῦ, κλητοὺς, ἁγίους dilectos Dei, vocatos, sanctos appellat; & de quibus 1. Cor. II. 10.12. dicit: Nobis revelavit per Spiritum suum: Nos accepimus Spiritum, qui ex Deo est, ut cognoscamus, quæ Deus nobis gratificatus est. Neque enim S. Paulus fiduciam hanc suam & aliorum petiit ex revelatione extraordinaria, sed à rationibus illis, quæ ipsi cum omnibus fidelibus communes erant. Qui proprio, inquit, Filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus illum tradidit, quomodo non etiam cum illo nobis omnia gratificabitur? Quis accusabit electos Dei? Deus est, qui justificat. Christus est, qui interpellat pro nobis, Rom. VIII. 32. 33. 34. Atqui omnibus fidelibus Christus datus est: omnes illi justificantur, pro omnibus Christus interpellat. Cùm ergo ex ejusmodi præmissis Apostolus fiduciales illam conclusionem: Persuasus sum, &c. inferat, constat, omnes fideles, quibus ad salutaria hæc media jus est, πληροφορίαν de salute & perseverantia sua sibi applicare posse. Accedit, quòd omnibus fidelibus communia sunt certitudinis hujus fundamenta, cujusmodi præter indigetata jam
units.tr: LXXII. The certainty of grace and salvation is therefore that persuasion of the elect and faithful, by which, supported by divine faith, by the testimony of the Holy Spirit, and by the sense and experience of grace working in them, they are able to trust, and do trust, according to the measure of their faith and of the Spirit, not in a continuous act but as to the foundation and habit of trust, that they are not only at present in the state of grace, not from their own worth but from the divine favour and from the deliberate regard of its custody, but that they will also persevere in the same state until the end of life, though not without struggle, with doubt and temptation, which Satan, the world and the flesh suggest, and so are infallibly to be saved, to the praise of the glory of God's grace and to the consolation of these same faithful in the perpetual troubles of this life. That some saints have attained such a certainty is beyond dispute. For St Paul expressly claims it for himself and for others, saying: I am persuaded that neither life nor death, etc., shall be able to separate us [ἡμᾶς] from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom. 8:38–39). But who else could the us [ἡμῖν] be, than those who have the same faith and Spirit that St Paul has? These are all the faithful and believers, whom he calls in chapter 1:7 beloved of God, called, holy; and of whom he says (1 Cor. 2:10, 12): God has revealed them to us through his Spirit. We have received the Spirit, who is from God, that we may know the things which God has freely given us. For St Paul did not seek this confidence of his own and of others from extraordinary revelation, but from those grounds which were common to him with all the faithful. He who did not spare his own Son, he says, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? Who shall accuse God's elect? It is God who justifies. It is Christ who intercedes for us (Rom. 8:32–34). But Christ has been given to all the faithful; all of them are justified; for all Christ intercedes. Since therefore the Apostle draws that confident conclusion, I am persuaded, etc., from such premises, it is clear that all the faithful, who have a right to these saving means, can apply to themselves full assurance [πληροφορίαν] of their salvation and perseverance. Besides, the foundations of this certainty are common to all the faithful, and of this kind, apart from the things already mentioned, are also the benefits of God and Christ common to all the faithful, from which St Paul concluded for himself and others. These include the perseverance of the saints itself, the stipulation of the covenant of grace, the mutual pledge between God and the faithful, the divine promise, the innate character of faith, hope and love, union and

units.la: communia fidelibus omnibus Dei & Christi beneficia, ex quibus S. Paulus pro se & aliis conclusit, etiam sunt. Ipsa Sanctorum perseverantia, Fœderis Gratiæ stipulatio, mutua Deum inter & fideles oppigneratio, Divina promissio, fidei, spei & charitatis nativa indoles, unio & communio cum Deo, necessitas studii confirmandæ electionis & vocationis nostræ, precum nostrarum efficacia, & Sacramentorum obsignatio. Quæ fundamenta pluribus nunc aperienda sunt.
units.tr: The benefits of God and Christ that are common to all believers, and from which St Paul drew his conclusions for himself and others, are these as well: the perseverance of the saints itself, the stipulation of the covenant of grace, the mutual pledge between God and believers, the divine promise, the innate character of faith, hope and love, union and communion with God, the necessity of striving to confirm our election and calling, the efficacy of our prayers, and the sealing of the sacraments. These foundations must now be set out more fully.

units.la: LXXIII. Et Perseverantia quidem Sanctorum & certitudinis salutis nexum non semel jam asseruimus. Illam enim S. Paulus diserte præstruit, & hanc illi inædificat. Quos præcognovit, &c. hos etiam glorificavit, &c. Persuasum habeo, quòd neque mors, neque vita, &c. nos possit separare à dilectione Dei, Rom. VIII. 29. 30. 38. 39. Non enim Deus satis habet nos propter gloriam suam conservare, nisi propter eandem & consolationem nostram conservationis ejusdem certiores nos redderet. Benedictus Deus, &c. cujus potentia custodimur per fidem ad salutem, 1. Petr. I. 3. Non autem benedicimus Deo de iis, quæ nobis ad salutem paravit, & quæ nobis occultat. Ideo Christus non tantum pro Petro oravit, ne ejus fides deficeret; sed id ipsum etiam ipsi significavit: dicens ad Petrum: Oravi pro te, ne deficiat fides tua, Luc. XXII. 32. Neque etiam ad consolationem & studium fidelium sufficit, ut in Ecclesiæ navi positi ad salutis portum velis remisque contendant, nisi firmiter etiam persuasum habeant, non posse a portu optato secludi, & non in cassum se laborare. Cùmque id, quod Deus ab æterno paravit fidelibus, à libera voluntate Dei pendeat, adeòque eatenus סוד arcanum sit, Deus illud fidelibus, ad quos pertinet, & quorum amorem & studium acuit, revelat. Nam סוד יהוה ליראיו arcanum Domini est pro timentibus ipsum, & fœdus suum, adeòque etiam bona fœderis sui, iis notificat, Psal. XXV. 14. Perseverantia Sanctorum infinita Dei potentia, & Divinis planè sulcris, æterna electione Patris, redemptione & intercessione Filii, & obsignatione Spiritus & nititur. Atque ea ipsa etiam apud credentes certis πληροφορίαν se patefaciunt. Quæ ergo de perseverantia eorum ad finem usque vitæ residua dubitatio esse potest?
units.tr: LXXIII. The connection between the perseverance of the saints and the certainty of salvation we have already asserted more than once. For St Paul expressly lays down the one and builds the other upon it: Whom he foreknew, them he also glorified ... I am persuaded that neither death nor life ... can separate us from the love of God, Rom. 8:29, 30, 38, 39. God does not think it enough to preserve us for his own glory unless he also makes us more certain of that preservation for our own comfort. Blessed be God ... by whose power we are kept through faith unto salvation, 1 Pet. 1:3. But we do not bless God for what he has prepared for our salvation while concealing it from us. So Christ did not merely pray for Peter that his faith would not fail; he also made this known to him, saying to Peter: I have prayed for you, that your faith fail not, Luke 22:32. Nor is it enough for the comfort and zeal of believers that, placed in the ship of the Church, they strive with sails and oars for the harbour of salvation, unless they also firmly believe that they cannot be shut out from the desired harbour and that they are not labouring in vain. And since what God has prepared from eternity for believers depends on the free will of God, and so is in that respect a secret [סוד], God reveals it to those to whom it belongs and whose love and zeal he sharpens. For the secret [סוד] of the LORD is with those who fear him, and he will show them his covenant, Ps. 25:14; so the good things of his covenant also he makes known to them. The perseverance of the saints rests on the infinite power of God and on wholly divine grounds: the eternal election of the Father, the redemption and intercession of the Son, and the sealing of the Spirit. These very things reveal themselves to believers with full assurance [πληροφορίαν]. What doubt, then, can remain about their perseverance to the end of life?

units.la: LXXIV. Fœderis Gratiæ & promissionum ejus stipulatio eandem certitudinem salutis includit. Sic enim stipulatur: Noli metuere. Ego clypeus tuus, & merces tua magna valde, Genes. XV. 1. Cujus insinuationis sive stipulationis, & ὁμολογίας mandati fœderalis obedientia est. Nihil metuere, neque in præsens, neque in futurum, sed Deum pro clypeo & justitia sua habere, & ab eo maximam mercedem expectare, nempe ut pro Deo propter hæc gratias agamus, eum ex corde diligamus, & in eodem gloriemur. Quod cùm facimus, ὁμολογοῦμεν τῷ Θεῷ consentimus Deo, & ipsi sacrificium confessionis & gratiarum actionis persolvimus simul-que viam munimus, qua Jehova nos salutem Dei videre, sentire, cognoscere, & de ea πληροφορίας certiores nos reddi facit. Et ne nostra nos imbecillitas terreat, etiam cum juramento consilium suum immutabile nobis indicavit, ut confugientes validam instigationem ad arripiendam spem habere.
units.tr: LXXIV. The stipulation of the covenant of grace and of its promises includes the same certainty of salvation. For it stipulates thus: Fear not; I am your shield, and your reward shall be exceedingly great, Gen. 15:1. The obedience of the covenant mandate is the response to this declaration or stipulation, and its confession [ὁμολογίας]. To fear nothing, neither now nor in the future, but to have God as our shield and righteousness, and to look to him for the greatest reward, namely that on account of these things we give thanks to God, love him from the heart, and glory in him. When we do this, we confess to God [ὁμολογοῦμεν τῷ Θεῷ], that is, agree with God, and offer him the sacrifice of confession and thanksgiving, and at the same time prepare the way by which Jehovah makes us see, feel and know the salvation of God, and makes us more certain of it in full assurance [πληροφορίας]. And lest our weakness terrify us, he has also declared his unchangeable purpose to us with an oath, so that we who flee for refuge may have a strong incentive to take hold of the hope.

units.la: Ipsius haberemus, Hebr. VI.18. Dictum enim est: Beati qui ad ipsum (Filium) confugiunt, Psal. II.12. Ad Filium autem confugiunt, quotquot certo judicio statuunt, in eo justitiam & vitam esse, atque ideo in ipso inveniri desiderant. Neque aliter fœdus gratiæ, in quo fides ad justitiam exigitur, iniri potest. Ubi enim opus ad mercedis redditionem imputari non potest, ibi fides ad justitiam imputatur. Fides autem, quæ ad justitiam imputatur, illa est, qua quis credit in eum, qui justificat impium, sciens, se credentem in eum justificari & vivere, Rom. IV.5.
units.tr: Of this we have it in him, Heb. 6:18. For it is said: Blessed are all who take refuge in him (the Son), Ps. 2:12. Now those flee to the Son who with a settled judgement hold that righteousness and life are in him, and therefore desire to be found in him. Nor can a covenant of grace, in which faith is required for righteousness, be made in any other way. For where a work cannot be credited as the payment of wages, there faith is imputed for righteousness. The faith, however, which is imputed for righteousness, is that by which someone believes in him who justifies the ungodly, knowing that in believing in him he is justified and lives, Rom. 4:5.

units.la: LXXV. Pertinet huc inprimis mutua illa Deum inter & fideles oppignoratio, illic depositi nostri in Dei manu custoditi, hinc arrhæ Divinæ cordibus nostris inditæ. Utrumque pignus non ad utriusque, sed ad unius duntaxat partis securitatem datur, nempe nostri. Utrumque licet utrinque possideatur, tamen unius tantùm partis Dei fidelitate custoditur. De priori sic S. Paulus. Non confundar. Novi enim, ᾧ πεπίστευκα, cui credidi, & persuasus sum, quòd potens sit depositum meum custodire in diem illum, 2. Tim. I. 12. Depositum ibi pignus salutis nostræ & nos ipsi: Potens custodire, ibi custos firmus: Persuasus sum, ibi fides: Non confundar, ibi fiducia. Sic enim fidem suam Apostolus explicat, ut dicat, se salutem suam & seipsum Deo commisisse & tradidisse custodiendum, ceu παραθήκην depositum εἰς ἐκεῖνον τὸν ἡμέραν in diem illum, hoc est, quòd crediderit Deo, ut conservaturo, eíque credens salutem suam, ut pignus, commiserit, & Deum invocaverit, ut se conservet in diem adventus Christi, si scilicet ad illum usque superstes sit, vel ad diem finiendæ militiæ, ut in die Christi coram ipso stare ἀμεμπτῶς possit. Qui regerunt, confidendum esse potentiæ Dei & Christi, quòd possit vitam æternam dare iis, qui obediunt ex se, aut ex adjutorio communi, & qui permissi suæ mutabilitati à fide non deficiunt, nec promissionem, nec potentiam Dei, quæ utraque ratio talis fidei, & tradendi Deo hujus depositi est pensitant. Non promissionem, qua Deus promisit, se clypeum nostrum, rupem salutis, & arcem, ad quam confugimus, nec non servatorem & custodem futurum: se nos in angustiis exauditurum, nobiscum futurum, &c. Non potentiam, secundum quam Deus nos ad se vocans, & Deum nostrum se fore dicens, vult nos sibi credere & confidere, quia potens est custodire depositum. Cùm igitur sciamus, Deum posse, & secundum promissionem velle depositum nostrum, salutem & nos ipsos ad diem usque Christi custodire, perfidi & infideles erimus, nisi ipsi animas & salutem nostram custodiendam commiserimus.
units.tr: LXXV. Here above all belongs the mutual pledge between God and believers: on the one side our deposit, kept in the hand of God; on the other the divine earnest placed in our hearts. Each pledge is given not for the security of both parties but of one only, namely ours. Each, although held on both sides, is guarded only by the faithfulness of one party, God. Of the former St Paul says: I am not ashamed. For I know whom I have believed [ᾧ πεπίστευκα], and I am persuaded that he is able to keep my deposit until that day, 2 Tim. 1:12. There the deposit is the pledge of our salvation and of ourselves; able to keep names the firm guardian; I am persuaded names the faith; I am not ashamed names the confidence. For this is how the Apostle explains his faith: he had committed and handed over his salvation and himself to God to be kept as a deposit [παραθήκην] unto that day [εἰς ἐκεῖνον τὸν ἡμέραν]. That is, he believed God would keep it, and believing him he committed his salvation to him as a pledge, and called upon God to preserve him until the day of Christ's coming, if indeed he should survive to that time, or until the day of ending his warfare, so that he might stand before Christ on that day blamelessly [ἀμεμπτῶς]. Those who argue that we must trust in the power of God and Christ, that he is able to give eternal life to those who obey of themselves or by common help, and who through their own changeability do not fall from faith, weigh neither the promise nor the power of God, which are the two grounds of such faith and of committing this deposit to God. Not the promise, by which God promised that he would be our shield, the rock of salvation and the fortress to which we flee, and also our saviour and keeper; that he would hear us in distress and be with us, and so on. Not the power, by which God, calling us to himself and saying that he will be our God, wills that we believe and trust him, because he is able to keep the deposit. Since therefore we know that God can, and according to his promise will, keep our deposit, our salvation and ourselves until the day of Christ, we shall be treacherous and faithless unless we commit our souls and our salvation to him to be kept.

units.la: LXXVI. De posteriore pignore penes fideles ipsos locato sic Apostolus: Credentes obsignati estis Spiritu promissionis Sancto, qui est arrhabo hæreditatis nostræ, ad redemptionem perculii, ad laudem gloriæ ejus, Ephes. I. 13. 14. IV.30. Qui nos vobiscum confirmavit in Christum, & unxit nos, Deus. Qui etiam nos obsignavit, & dedit nobis arrhabonem Spiritus in cordibus nostris, 2. Cor. I. 22. Ipsi primitias Spiritus S. accepimus, Rom. VIII.23. Datur ergo Spiritus S. omnibus credentibus, ut sigillum, arrhabo, primitiæ. Quæ tam magnificè sonantia, inane nomen sunt, si fidelibus salutis suæ certitudo & salus non constat. Quomodo enim σφραγὶς sigillum est credentium, quo illi tanquam res & peculium Dei, ad solum eum pertinens, signantur & obsignantur, quod fit per renovationem eorum, quæ confessionem fidei, exercitium charitatis & patientiæ operatur, si horum conscii non sunt? Non enim ut oves irrationales signantur, sicut olim circumcisi & hodie baptizati, qui sigillo hoc collato certum habent, se fœderatos, & militiæ Christianæ adscriptos esse. His externis sigillis internum Spiritus S. sigillum respondet, quo obsignantur credentes, ut sciant, se esse filios, peculium & proprietatem Dei. Infert igitur obsignatio hæc tum peculiarem applicationem, tum applicationis certitudinem, non ex levi conjectura, sed ex authoritate Divina, Dei obsignantis, & sigilli Spiritus Dei, qua nulla major esse potest.
units.tr: LXXVI. Concerning the latter pledge, which is lodged with believers themselves, the Apostle says: In him you also, having believed, were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the earnest of our inheritance, for the redemption of the purchased possession, to the praise of his glory, Eph. 1:13, 14; 4:30. He who confirms us with you in Christ and anointed us is God; he also sealed us and gave us the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts, 2 Cor. 1:22. We have the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit, Rom. 8:23. The Holy Spirit is therefore given to all believers as seal, earnest, firstfruits. These words sound so grand, yet they would be empty names if the certainty of salvation did not belong to believers. For how is the seal [σφραγὶς] of believers, by which they are marked and sealed as the property and possession of God, belonging to him alone, done through the renewal of those things that produce the confession of faith and the exercise of love and patience, if they are not aware of these things? For they are not marked as irrational sheep are marked, as the circumcised were formerly and the baptized are today; those who have received this seal hold it certain that they are bound by covenant and enrolled in Christian warfare. To these external seals the internal seal of the Holy Spirit corresponds, by which believers are sealed, so that they know they are sons, the possession and property of God. This sealing therefore brings both a particular application and certainty of that application, not from slight conjecture but from divine authority: of God who seals, and of the seal of the Spirit of God, than which none can be greater.

units.la: Quomodo etiam Spiritus S. arrhabo est, spondens & certos reddens de tota hæreditate, si certitudinem totius hæreditatis consequentis & spem vivam non præstat? Nam arrhabonis apud omnes is usus est, ut semel acceptus & visus promissionibus momentum addat, & pignus ac repræsentatio quædam sit rei futuræ, in cujus locum datur. Sic Deus maxima quæque fidelibus spondens, Spiritum S. arrhabonem dat ut certissimi sint, non tantùm certis hæredibus vitam æternam dandam esse, sed etiam se ipsos in eorum numero esse, quibus illa conferenda sit, adeò ut fide Divina, quippe Dei arrhabonem dantis, & arrhabonis Spiritus S. certè statuere debeant, sibi vitam æternam collatum iri. Quomodo denique Spiritus S. ἀπαρχὴ primitiæ hæreditatis est, si qui eas acceperunt, totius massæ certitudine destituuntur? Si Deus hac arrha priùs nobis data, his primitiis concessis, reliquæ hæreditatis & massæ certò adipiscendæ fidem non facit, & dubitare accipientes arrham & primitias de hæreditate & massa tota tenentur, imò hæreditas & massa tota interverti potest, non tantùm nihil arrha & primitiæ hæ significant, sed etiam Deus arrhæ & primitiarum suarum perditarum damnum pati potest. Scitè enim Chrysostomus Homil. in 2. Cor. I. οὐ γὰρ, εἰ μὴ ἐμέλλε τὸ πᾶν δίδοναι, ἄλλο ἂν ἀρραβῶνα ἀπαιτεῖν ... Non enim, si totum dare noluit, præbere arrhabonem, & frustra eum perdere elegit.
units.tr: Likewise, is the Holy Spirit not an earnest, guaranteeing and making us certain of the whole inheritance, if he does not provide certainty of obtaining the whole inheritance and a living hope? For the use of an earnest among everyone is this: once received and seen, it adds weight to the promises, and it is a pledge and a kind of representation of the future thing, in whose place it is given. So God, promising the greatest things to the faithful, gives the Holy Spirit as an earnest, so that they may be most certain not only that eternal life will be given to the certain heirs, but also that they themselves are among those to whom it is to be conferred. Thus, by divine faith, since it is God who gives the earnest, and the earnest is the Holy Spirit, they must surely determine that eternal life will be conferred on them. Lastly, how is the Holy Spirit the ἀπαρχὴ [first-fruits] of the inheritance, if those who have received them lack certainty of the whole mass? If God, having first given us this earnest and granted these first-fruits, does not make us sure of the rest of the inheritance and mass to be surely obtained, and if those who receive the earnest and first-fruits are bound to doubt about the inheritance and the whole mass, then indeed the inheritance and the whole mass could be overturned. In that case, not only do earnest and first-fruits signify nothing, but God himself may suffer the loss of his earnest and first-fruits. For Chrysostom aptly says in his Homily on 2 Cor. I: For if he did not intend to give the whole, he would not offer an earnest and then foolishly lose it [οὐ γὰρ, εἰ μὴ ἐμέλλε τὸ πᾶν δίδοναι, ἄλλο ἂν ἀρραβῶνα ἀπαιτεῖν].

units.la: LXXVII. Sed Spiritus S. dati credentibus sigilli, arrhabonis & primitiarum operatio in iis, quibus, ut tali datur, certitudinem salutis potenter demonstrat. Operatio enim inter alias hæc est, quòd datus ut spiritus adoptionis, in quo clamamus, Abba, Pater, Συμμαρτυρεῖ τῷ πνεύματι ἡμῶν, ὅτι ἐσμὲν τέκνα & Θεοῦ contestificatur Spiritui nostro; quòd sumus filii Dei; si autem filii, etiam hæredes, &c. Rom. VIII. 15. 16. 17. Duo ergo Spiritus S. in iis, quibus ut sigillum & arrhabo datur, facit. Nam primò facit, ut clament, Abba, Pater, non nescii utique, vel ambigui, an ipsi filii, & Deus illorum Pater sit. Deinde spiritui nostro contestificatur, quòd sumus filii & hæredes. Ubi duo adoptionis nostræ testimonia citantur, unum spiritus nostri, alterum Συμμαρτυρεῖ& contestificantis Spiritus S. Et spiritus quidem noster, seu anima nostra testatur, quòd sumus filii Dei, dum clamamus in Spiritu Dei, Abba Pater. Clamamus enim fide, spe, amore, invocatione, desiderio, confessione, gratiarum actione. Sicut credendo obsignamus, quòd Deus sit verus: ita credendo obsignamus, quòd filii Dei simus, & is Pater in Christo amabilis nobis sit. Amamus enim ut patrem, glorificamus, ut filii. Nemo se filii instar gerit, quin judicet, & certò statuat, se esse filium Dei; & Deo pro amore paterno gratias se agere debere. Huic testimonio, quod in se certum est, quia sensu & conscientia nititur, succenturiatur alterum Spiritus S. qui clamantibus Abba ană testificatur, quòd sint filii Dei & hæredes. Testificatur autem Spiritus S. nostro spiritui, quòd simus filii Dei, duobus modis, puta tum donis suis, tum verbo suo. Donis suis, quia fides, spes, charitas, confessio, &c. quas in filiis Dei operatur, sunt testimonium φρονήματος voluntatis & studii ipsius, quod pro nobis habet; usque ad ipsos gemitus & suspiria nostra. Verbo suo, eóque scripto, quia testans spiritui nostro, non aliud testatur, quàm quod scriptum est, sed ea docet, suggerit, & cordibus inscribit, quæ ab omnibus audita sunt. Quæ autem scripta sunt, quia à Spiritu S. dictata sunt, verè testimonium Spiritus S. sunt. In his verò, quæ scripta sunt, testimonium illud Spiritus S. est, quo conte stificatur, nos esse filios Dei. Nam Spiritus S. in Scripturis non tantum revelat Dei propositum, quòd velit quosdam salvare in Christo, sed etiam peccatores jubet confugere ad Christum & ad Deum, sedentem in throno gratiæ cum fiducia accedere; neque hoc tantum, sed etiam fidei naturam depingit, & credentem in Christum μακάριον beatum praedicat, & fideles seipsos excutere jubet, & docet, esse sensum fidei & amoris in iis, qui credunt; & eos ἰσχυρῶς παρακαλεῖ valide instigat, ut arripiant spem expositam, eámque teneant; & jubet eos confidere, sperare, lætari, gratias agere, in Deo gloriari; affirmans, sitim & famem justitiæ; atque amorem Dei non esse à carne, sed à sua efficacia & vita Christi in ipsis; séque in credentibus esse ut donum, quo uncti sunt in Sacerdotes & Reges; quo, ceu sigillo, obsignillo, ut res Dei, obsignentur, quòd in ipsis fit, ut arrhabo, ut suæ redemptionis certi sint, & spem habeant non fallacem gloriæ Dei, in quo glorientur; denique ut Paracletus, qui pro ipsis apud Deum tanquam patrem ipsorum, interpellet: Denique Christum accipientibus ipsum dedisse potestatem & jus se gerendi pro filiis Dei, Joh. I. 12. Consequens hinc est, certitudinem fidelium de sua adoptione non esse tantum λογισμὸν minimè fallacem, juxta illud Apostoli: Οὕτω λογίζεσθε, sic colligite, vos mortuos quidem esse peccato, vivos autem Deo in Christo Iesu Domino nostro, Rom. VI. 11. sed etiam fidem testimonii Spiritus S. in Scripturis revelati.
units.tr: 77. But the operation of the Holy Spirit, given to believers as seal, earnest and first-fruits, powerfully demonstrates certainty of salvation in those to whom he is given as such. For among his other operations this is one: that, given as the spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, Abba, Father, he bears witness with our spirit [Συμμαρτυρεῖ τῷ πνεύματι ἡμῶν] that we are children of God [ὅτι ἐσμὲν τέκνα θεοῦ]; and if children, then also heirs, etc., Rom. VIII. 15. 16. 17. So the Holy Spirit does two things in those to whom he is given as seal and earnest. First, he makes them cry, Abba, Father, not being at all unaware or doubtful whether they are sons and whether God is their Father. Then he bears witness with our spirit that we are sons and heirs. Here two testimonies of our adoption are cited: one of our spirit, the other of the Holy Spirit, who bears witness with it. Our spirit, that is our soul, testifies that we are children of God, while we cry out in the Spirit of God, Abba, Father. For we cry out in faith, hope, love, invocation, desire, confession and thanksgiving. Just as by believing we attest that God is true, so by believing we attest that we are children of God, and that this Father is lovable to us in Christ. For we love him as a father and glorify him as children. No one behaves as a son without judging, and firmly determining, that he is a son of God, and that he ought to give thanks to God for his fatherly love. To this testimony, which is certain in itself because it rests on feeling and conscience, the other testimony of the Holy Spirit is added, who testifies to those crying Abba that they are children of God and heirs. Now the Holy Spirit testifies to our spirit that we are children of God in two ways: by his gifts and by his word. By his gifts, because faith, hope, charity, confession, etc., which he works in the children of God, are a testimony of the disposition [φρονήματος] of his will and zeal, which he has toward us, even to our groans and sighs. By his word, and that written, because in bearing witness to our spirit he does not testify to anything other than what is written, but teaches these things, suggests them, and inscribes them on hearts, things which have been heard by all. Those things which are written, since they were dictated by the Holy Spirit, are truly the testimony of the Holy Spirit. In those things which are written, that testimony of the Holy Spirit is there, by which he bears witness that we are children of God. For the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures not only reveals God's purpose, that he wishes certain people to be saved in Christ, but also commands sinners to flee to Christ, and to approach with confidence God sitting on the throne of grace. And not only this, but he also depicts the nature of faith, and declares the believer in Christ blessed [μακάριον], and bids the faithful to examine themselves, and teaches that there is a sense of faith and love in those who believe. He strongly exhorts [ἰσχυρῶς παρακαλεῖ] them to seize the hope set before them and to hold it fast, and bids them trust, hope, rejoice, give thanks and glory in God, affirming that there is a thirst and hunger for righteousness, and that the love of God is not from the flesh but from his own efficacy and the life of Christ in them. He also declares that he himself is in believers as a gift with which they are anointed as priests and kings; with which, as with a seal, the things of God are sealed, since in them it comes about, as an earnest, that they may be certain of their redemption and have a hope not deceptive of the glory of God, in whom they may glory; and finally, as Paraclete, who intercedes for them before God as their Father. Finally, he gave to those who received Christ power and the right to act as children of God, John I. 12. It follows from this that the certainty of believers concerning their adoption is not merely a reasoning [λογισμὸν] least liable to deceit, according to the saying of the Apostle: Thus reckon, that you are dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord [Οὕτω λογίζεσθε], Rom. VI. 11, but is also the faith of the testimony of the Holy Spirit revealed in the Scriptures.

units.la: LXXVIII. Planè testimonium illud Spiritus S. spiritui nostro conte stificantis evertunt, qui illud secundum se certum, ἀλλ' ἡμᾶς secundum nos incertum esse, quia nobis non constat, illud esse à Spiritu S. & non à Diabolo, asserunt.
units.tr: 78. Indeed, those who assert that this testimony of the Holy Spirit bearing witness to our spirit is certain in itself, but uncertain for us, because it is not clear to us that it comes from the Holy Spirit and not from the devil, overturn it altogether.

units.la: Quomodo enim contestificatur spiritui nostro, si spiritus noster de testimonio eo certus esse non potest? Sed tam certus haud dubiè Spiritus noster de testimonio Spiritus S. est, quàm certus esse potest de veritate eorum, quæ testatur Scriptura, utpote per quam Spiritus S. testatur. Neque profecto idem testimonium potest esse à Spiritu S. & Diabolo; vel inter Dei & Spiritus S. testificationem dicentis animæ piæ: Ego sum salus tua, Psal. XXXV. 3. & Diaboli illusionem mentientis: Pax, pax, ubi non est pax, Ezech. XIII. 10. 16. nihil interest.
units.tr: For how does it bear witness to our spirit, if our spirit cannot be certain of that testimony? But our spirit is undoubtedly as certain of the testimony of the Holy Spirit as it can be of the truth of those things which Scripture attests, since it is through Scripture that the Holy Spirit testifies. Certainly the same testimony cannot come from both the Holy Spirit and the devil. Nor does it make any difference whether it is the testimony of God and the Holy Spirit saying to the pious soul, I am your salvation, Ps. XXXV. 3, or the devil's delusion, lying, Peace, peace, where there is no peace, Ezek. XIII. 10. 16.

units.la: Exceptio adversantium, quòd testimonium Spiritus S. fecundum se, at non secundum nos certum fit, plane testimonium illud evertit. que is, qui ignem sentiens, calidum esse negat. Sicut enim ignis per calorem agit, & per eundem se manifestat: ita Spiritus S. motus in credentibus excitat, & per eosdem se illis declarat. Licet ergo, quod idem Becanus objicit, etiam Spiritus malus in Angelum lucis sese transfiguret.
units.tr: The objection of opponents, that the testimony of the Holy Spirit is certain in itself but not for us, plainly overturns that testimony; it is like one who, feeling fire, denies that it is hot. For just as fire acts by heat and manifests itself through the same, so the Holy Spirit stirs up movements in believers and declares himself to them through those same movements. Let it be granted, then, as Becanus also objects, that even an evil spirit may transform himself into an angel of light.

units.la: LXXIX. Accedunt oppignerationi Divinae promissiones. Quæ vel generales sunt, vel speciales ipsius certitudinis. Generales illæ sunt, quibus credentibus omnibus in verbo Dei remissio peccatorum, gratia perseverans, & salus æterna promittitur. Qui credit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur, Marc. XVI. 16. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, &c. ut quisquis in Christum credit, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam, Joh. III. 16. Justitia Dei per fidem Jesu Christi in omnes, & super omnes, qui credunt, Rom. III. 22. Faciunt huc argumenta omnia, quæ pro Perseverantia Sanctorum ex Divinis promissionibus attulimus. Quicquid Deus omnibus credentibus promittit, id singulis etiam promittit, quia singularia sub universali stant. Et quicquid singulis promittit, de eo singuli certi esse possunt, quia Deus promissionum author verax est, & promissiones certissimæ & juratæ sunt, & earum finis est, ut fideles de Dei bona erga se voluntate certi reddantur. Et ut singuli tanto sibi confidentius generales promissiones applicent, Scriptura quandoq; in singulari numero & persona secunda loquitur. Si confessus fueris ore tuo Dominum Jesum, &c. salvaberis, Rom. X. 9. Ego, ego deleo defectiones tuas, Esaj. XLIII. 25. Et requiritur quidem ad applicationem fidei; sed illa in fœdere gratiæ promissa est, & donum Dei est. Etiam speciales & disertæ certitudinis hujus promissiones extant. Sic enim S. Paulus: Nullo dono destituti estis in ulla re, expectantes revelationem Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Qui etiam vmᾶς βεβαιώσει ἕως τέλος vos firmabit usque ad finem irreprehensibiles in die Domini nostri Jesu Christi, 1. Cor. I. 7. 8. Nulla βεβαίωσις confirmatio, stabilitio usque ad finem, & quidem ἀνεγκλήτων irreprehensibilium eorum est, qui de gratia & salute ad finem usque vitæ dubitare tenentur. Tales enim nec βεβαίοι firmi esse possunt, quia dubitans vel disceptans omnis similis est fluctui maris ventis agitato, vir duplicis animi, ἀκατάστατος & inconstabilis in omnibus viis suis, Jacob. I. 6. 8. nec ἀνέγκλητοι irreprehensibiles sunt, quia dubitatio perpetua de salute, faciens hominem funambulum & δειλὸν meticulosum, reprehensionem certè illa meretur. Idem S. Paulus: Fidelis est, inquit, Dominus, qui nos στηρίξει confirmabit, & custodiet à malo, 2. Thessal. III. 3. Non ergo Dominus noster, qui fidelis est, & nos fallere & frustrari non potest, cum quo fœdus habemus, ex quo Deus & Pater noster est, pati vult, ut agitemur instar arundinis. Promisit enim suis στηριγμὸν confirmationem, ut sint velut quercus justitiæ, Esaj. LXI. 3. & fundamentum seculi, Prov. X. 25. ne moveantur in æternum, Psal. XV. 5. Facit enim στερεῖς τῇ πίστει firmos fide, 1. Pet. V. 9. Fides enim Dei donum est non initioduntaxat suo & tenella ætate, sed etiam in incrementis & stabilitate sua.
units.tr: 79. To this assurance are added Divine promises. These are either general or special as to this very certainty. The general promises are those in which, in the Word of God, forgiveness of sins, perseverance in grace and eternal salvation are promised to all believers: He who believes and is baptized will be saved, Mark XVI. 16. God so loved the world, etc., that whoever believes in Christ should not perish but have eternal life, John III. 16. The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ comes to all and upon all who believe, Rom. III. 22. All the arguments which we brought from the divine promises for the perseverance of the saints belong here. Whatever God promises to all believers, he also promises to each one, because singulars stand under the universal. And whatever he promises to each one, each can be certain of, because God is the truthful author of the promises, the promises are most certain and sworn, and their purpose is that the faithful be made certain of God's good will toward them. And so that individuals may apply the general promises to themselves the more confidently, Scripture sometimes speaks in the singular number and the second person: If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, etc., you will be saved, Rom. X. 9. I, I am he who blots out your transgressions, Isa. XLIII. 25. Indeed, it is required for the application of faith; but that faith is promised in the covenant of grace and is the gift of God. There are also special and explicit promises of this certainty. Thus St Paul: You lack no gift in any matter, while waiting for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. He also says that God will confirm you to the end [βεβαιώσει ἕως τέλος], blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. I. 7. 8. But no confirmation (βεβαίωσις), stability to the end, belongs to the blameless [ἀνεγκλήτων], that is, to those who are bound to doubt about grace and salvation until the end of life. For such people cannot be firm [βεβαίοι], because every doubter or disputer is like a wave of the sea driven by the winds, a man of two minds, unstable [ἀκατάστατος] and inconstant in all his ways, Jas. I. 6. 8. Nor are they blameless [ἀνέγκλητοι], because perpetual doubt about salvation, making a man a tightrope walker and fearful [δειλὸν], certainly deserves reproof. The same St Paul says: Faithful is the Lord, who will establish [στηρίξει] and guard you from evil, 2 Thess. III. 3. Therefore our Lord, who is faithful, and who cannot deceive or frustrate us, with whom we have a covenant, and from whom God is our Father, does not wish us to be tossed about like a reed. For he has promised his people steadfastness [στηριγμὸν] and confirmation, so that they may be like oaks of righteousness, Isa. LXI. 3, and the foundation of the age, Prov. X. 25, that they may not be moved for ever, Ps. XV. 5. For he makes them firm in faith [στερεῖς τῇ πίστει], 1 Pet. V. 9. Faith is a gift of God not only in its first and tender age, but also in its growth and steadfastness.

units.la: LXXX. Natura inprimis fidei salvificæ certitudinem hanc confirmat. Nam illa assensus & fiduciæ suæ certa est. Qui credit in Filium Dei, habet testimonium in se ipso, 1. Joh. V. 10.
units.tr: LXXX. First of all, the nature of saving faith confirms this certainty. For faith is certain of its own assent and trust. "He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself" (1 John 5:10).

units.la: Qui confidit Filio Dei ad salutem, is testimonium, quod Deus vitam æternam dederit nobis, & dederit in Filio, non ante oculos duntaxat, vel in auribus, sed in se ipso, in corde suo obsignatum habet, adeoque eundem dictatum cordis habet, qui est dictatus vocis Dei. Pro te (vice tua) dicit cor meum, Psal. XXVII. 8. Qui verò non credit Deo, ei, ut Domino suo, ad gloriam ipsius, se non committit, is mendacem fecit Deum, quia non credidit in testimonium, quod Deus de Filio suo testatus est, 1. Joh. V. 10. Ideo S. Paulus: Novi, inquit, cui crediderim, & persuasum sum, quod potens sit depositum meum custodire in diem illum, 2. Tim. I. 12. Ἡμεῖς οἴδαμεν Nos novimus quod ex morte in vitam transiverimus, quia diligimus fratres, 1. Joh. III. 14. Diligere autem nos fratres certè conscii sumus, sicut S. Petrus Christo interroganti, Simon diligis me? sincerè respondere potuit: Domine, tu omnia nosti, tu nosti quod diligam te, Joh. XXI. 17. Quæ notitia non moralis, sed fidei est, quia amor fraternus proficiscitur ex fide, 1. Tim. I. 5. & Scriptura testatur, amantes fratrum nosse, quod ex morte ad vitam transiverint: & fideles ex sensu charitatis juxta Divinam revelationem notitiæ suæ fidem fundare possunt. Idem S. Johannes: In hoc cognovimus, quod maneat in nobis, ex Spiritu, quem nobis dedit, 1. Joh. III. 24. Cujus scilicet tum interna revelatio certitudinem fidei apud omnes fideles generat; tum operatio continua fidei & charitatis ad sensum hominis spiritualis patet. Clarissimè verò, & sine ullius conditionis circuitu sic idem S. Johannes: Scimus, quoniam ex Deo sumus, ibid. V. 19. Hanc verò notitiam fidei esse, in loco ostendimus. Cùmque dici posset, & dicant hodie multi, fidem pretiosam esse, & debere hominem præsumere, se esse in fide, jussit Deus etiam fidem confiteri, Rom. X. 9. Atqui non jussit nos mentiri, vel dicere id, quod scire non possumus.
units.tr: He who trusts in the Son of God for salvation has the testimony that God has given us eternal life, and has given it in his Son. He holds this sealed, not merely before his eyes or in his ears, but in himself, in his own heart. So he has the same dictate of the heart that is the dictate of the voice of God: "My heart says on your behalf" (Ps. 27:8). But he who does not believe God does not commit himself to him as to his Lord, for his glory; he has made God a liar, because he has not believed the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son (1 John 5:10). Hence St Paul: "I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to keep what I have committed to him until that day" (2 Tim. 1:12). "We know [Ἡμεῖς οἴδαμεν] that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers" (1 John 3:14). We are certainly conscious that we love the brothers, just as St Peter could sincerely answer Christ when asked, "Simon, do you love me?": "Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you" (John 21:17). This knowledge is not moral but of faith, because brotherly love proceeds from faith (1 Tim. 1:5). Scripture testifies that those who love the brothers know that they have passed from death to life, and believers, from the sense of charity and according to divine revelation, can ground the faith of this knowledge. The same St John says: "By this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit which he gave us" (1 John 3:24). The inward revelation of this Spirit produces the certainty of faith among all believers, and the continual operation of faith and charity is evident to the sense of the spiritual man. Most clearly, and without any conditional circuit, the same St John says: "We know that we are of God" (ibid. 5:19). We have shown in its place that this knowledge is of faith.
