And although it could be said, and many today do say, that faith is a precious thing and that a man ought not presume that he is in the faith, God has commanded us even to confess the faith (Rom. 10:9). But he has not commanded us to lie, or to say what we cannot know.

units.la: LXXXI. Tam verò certa fides nostra est, ut ejus etiam experimentum capere, & cognoscere, quòd Jesus Christus in nobis sit; ita Scriptura jubeat, ut sine eo nos ἀδόκιμοι reprobos esse pronuntiet. Vos ipsos tentate (experimentum capite, faciendo omnia, quæ ad emendationem & boni conservationem pertinent) si quidem estis in fide (in ea conditione & statu, quem fides conciliat, qui justitiæ, potentiæ, sanctificationis vitæ, Regni Dei est) vos ipsos probate, (affectus, cor, ratiocinationes, studia, curas, metus, amores, odia, actiones, totam vitam ad certam regulam & normam revocate, atque ita de vobis ipsis judicate) Annon recognoscitis vos ipsos, quòd Jesus Christus sit in vobis (credentibus, in quibus Jesus Christus habitat, & qui cognoscendo se ipsos inveniunt in se ipsis viventem Christum, qui in ipsis glorificari vult.) Nisi forte reprobi estis (si de fide vestra non estis certi, in fide non estis, vos recognoscendo in vobis Christum non invenistis, ἀδόκιμοι reprobi estis, similes hominibus mente corruptis ἀδόκιμοις περὶ τὴν πίστιν reprobis quoad fidem, 2. Tim. III. 8 nomine, non re Christiani) Spero saltem vos cognituros, quòd nos non sim° reprobi (sed veri Christi discipuli, ministri justitiæ, & Apostoli irreprehensibiles; atq; eo ipso etiam animum sumptuosi, cogituros vos ipsos, quòd sitis in fide, & Christus in vobis sit) 2. Cor. XIII. 5. 6. Si credentes dentes sunt in fide, & fidei hujus experimentum capere possunt, & se ipsos recognoscentes in se ipsis Christum inveniunt,& qui tales non sunt, reprobi sunt, quid statuendum de iis videtur,qui credentes de fide sua, gratia Christi, & salute sua certos esse posse inficiantur,adeoque & ipsi profitentur,incertum sibi esse,an in fide sint,& an Christus in se habitet? Quod ἀδόκιμων reproborum est. Agnoscit Aquinas hunc locum explicans, certò nos cognoscere,quòd Christus in nobis sit. Sed inepte addit: secundum intellectum, non effectum, quasi Apostolus excitaret ad examen intellectus tantum, aut Christus in intellectu tantum,non etiam in corde fidelium, imò toto homine regenito habitaret, & eum vivificaret. Dilutum & illud est, quod Bellarminus, aliíque regerunt, Apostolum loqui non de praesentia vel inhabitatione Christi secundum gratiam gratum facientem, sed secundum potentiam, providentiam & miracula,quae apud Corinthios faciebat. Quod audax,ad eludendam veritatis vim,commentum est. Non enim Apostolus Corinthios extra se potentiae & miraculorum experimentum circumspicere, sed probare se ipsos, hoc est,proprii cordis recessus inspicere,& in iis hospitantem fidem,Christum requirere jubet. Apostolus quoque non recognoscentes, quòd Christus in ipsis sit, reprobos appellat. Sed multi fideles Christum per miracula in se habitantem non habent; quos tamen in reproborum numerum rejicere pietas vetat. Denique exploratio sui ipsius omnino opus humanae industriae est, sed secundum certam regulam testimonium spiritus credentis, & fidem per ejus πιστώσεως in se investigantis, nec non Spiritus sancti una testificantis. Est igitur opus & exercitatio fidei, quae in cognitionem fidei inexistentis,& Christi inhabitantis ducit,& certitudinem internam non demum gignit, sed existentem exerit, manifestat & declarat.
units.tr: LXXXI. Our faith is so certain that we can also take proof of it and know that Jesus Christ is in us. So Scripture commands us to examine ourselves, and pronounces us reprobate without this. "Test yourselves (make trial, doing all that pertains to the amendment and preservation of the good), whether you are in the faith (in that condition and state which faith brings, which belongs to righteousness, power, the sanctification of life, and the Kingdom of God). Prove yourselves" (examine your affections, heart, reasonings, pursuits, cares, fears, loves, hatreds, actions; refer your whole life to a sure rule and norm, and so judge yourselves). "Do you not recognise yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?" (believers, in whom Jesus Christ dwells, and who, knowing themselves, find within themselves Christ living, who wishes to be glorified in them). "Unless perhaps you are reprobate" (if you are not certain of your faith, you are not in the faith; not recognising Christ in yourselves, you are reprobate [ἀδόκιμοι], like men corrupt in mind, reprobate concerning the faith [ἀδόκιμοι περὶ τὴν πίστιν], 2 Tim. 3:8, Christians in name but not in reality). "I hope at least that you will recognise that we are not reprobate" (but true disciples of Christ, ministers of righteousness and irreproachable apostles; and by that very fact you will also think, with confidence, that you are in the faith and that Christ is in you) (2 Cor. 13:5–6). If believers are in the faith, and can take proof of this faith, and recognising themselves find Christ in themselves, and those who are not such are reprobate, what is to be determined concerning those who deny that believers can be certain of their faith, of the grace of Christ and of their salvation, and so themselves profess that it is uncertain to them whether they are in the faith and whether Christ dwells in them? That is the state of the reprobate [ἀδόκιμων]. Aquinas, explaining this passage, acknowledges that "we know with certainty that Christ is in us." But he foolishly adds, "according to the understanding, not the effect," as if the Apostle were urging an examination of the intellect alone, or as if Christ dwelt only in the intellect and not also in the heart of the faithful, indeed in the whole regenerate man, enlivening him. Also weak is what Bellarmine and others reply, that the Apostle speaks not of the presence or indwelling of Christ according to grace that makes acceptable, but of his power, providence and the miracles he worked among the Corinthians. This is a bold invention to evade the force of the truth. The Apostle does not bid the Corinthians look about outside themselves for proof of power and miracles, but to prove themselves, that is, to look into the recesses of their own heart and seek Christ, who lodges there by faith. The Apostle also calls those who do not recognise that Christ is in them reprobate. But many believers do not have Christ dwelling in them through miracles, and yet piety forbids us to number them among the reprobate. Finally, self-examination is altogether a work of human diligence, but it is carried out according to a sure rule: the testimony of the believing spirit, and faith investigating itself through its assurance [πιστώσεως], together with the Holy Spirit testifying along with it. It is therefore a work and exercise of faith, which leads to knowledge of the faith that exists and of Christ who dwells within; and it does not so much produce inward certainty as bring to light, manifest and declare the certainty that already exists.

units.la: LXXXII. Fides justificans fiduciam involvit, eámque triplicem, assensus practici, apprehensionis Christi, ceu Salvatoris nostri & confidentiae,seu acquiescentiae & consolationis ex animae ad Christum καταφυγὴ oriundae. Priores illae sunt actus fidei formalis justificantes: postrema est actus fidei justificantis, prioris consequens,sed infallibiliter. De qua fiduciae distinctione plura Loco XVIII.107.108.109. diximus. Postrema illa fidem consequens, & super eam reflectens fiducia ipsa certa & fiducialis de remissione peccatorum & salute omnium,qui ad Christum confugerunt, & eum, ceu arcem salutis, apprehenderunt, perfuasio est. Quid enim Christus fide apprehensus,ut Salvator, justitia, arx salutis, portus tranquillitatis apprehendentibus se, & ei uni solique innitentibus non praestat? Quomodo in sinu suo quiescentes perpetuae diffidentiae & anxietati exponit? Ipsae voces משׁען, מִבְטָח fiduciam includunt. Et fidei ὑπόστασις subsistentia,seu pollicitatio, repraesentatio sperandorum, Hebr. XI.1. παρρησία libera,aperta & confidens professio, πεποίθησις fiducia, Ephes. III.12. ἀπληροφορία perfuasio plena,certioratio,1.Thess. I.5. Hebr. XI.6. καύχησις gloriatio,Rom.V.17. ὑπόστασις καύχησις subsistentia gloriationis, 2.Cor.IX.14. ἐπερώτημα interrogatio seu stipulatio bonae con-
units.tr: LXXXII. Justifying faith involves trust, and this is threefold: the practical assent, the apprehension of Christ as our Saviour, and confidence, that is, the acquiescence and consolation that arise from the soul's refuge [καταφυγὴ] to Christ. The first two are the acts of formal, justifying faith; the last is the act of justifying trust, which follows the first infallibly. We have said more about this distinction of trust at Locus XVIII, 107–109. That last trust, which follows faith and reflects upon it, is the certain and confident persuasion of the remission of sins and of salvation for all who have fled to Christ and laid hold of him as the citadel of salvation. For what does Christ, apprehended by faith as Saviour, righteousness, citadel of salvation and harbour of tranquillity, not provide to those who commit themselves to him and rest on him alone? How does he expose to perpetual distrust and anxiety those who rest in his bosom? The very words [משען] and [מִבְטָח] include trust. Faith's [ὑπόστασις], substance, is also a promise, a "representation of things hoped for" (Heb. 11:1); its [παρρησία] is a free, open and confident profession; its [πεποίθησις] is confidence (Eph. 3:12); its [ἀπληροφορία] is full persuasion and assurance (1 Thess. 1:5; Heb. 11:6 as printed). Its [καύχησις] is glorying (Rom. 5:17 as printed), and [ὑπόστασις καύχησις] is the substance of glorying (2 Cor. 9:14 as printed). Its [ἐπερώτημα] is a question or pledge of a good conscience toward God (1 Pet. 3:21), and [διάκρισις] doubt or hesitation is opposed to it (Matt. 21:21; James 1:6). Its proper affections are therefore set against doubt,

units.la: scientiae apud Deum, 1.Petr.III.21. & eidem διαχείσις dubitatio, sive haesitantia, Matth. XXI.21. Jac.I.6. opponitur. Quomodo haec fidei affectiones propriae cum incertitudine salutis & dubitatione consistere possunt? Fatetur Bellarminus, haec fidei inesse, & propterea fidem certissimam esse. Sed remissionem peccatorum & salutem, atque de eadem certitudinem ad fidem pertinere negat. Quod delirare potius, quàm disputare est. Nam peccatorum remissio & salus utique tum ad articulos fidei,& articuli fidei ad fidem proprie dictam pertinent: tum fides remissionem peccatorum & salutem in Christo apprehendit & sibi applicat. Quotquot eum receperunt,dedit iis potestatem segerendi pro filiis Dei, nempe iis, qui credunt in nomine ejus, Joh.I.12. Ubi credere in Christum & recipere Christum aequipollent. Qui igitur vere in Christum credunt, eundem recipiunt, & sibi applicant, exclamantes cum Thoma,Domine mi, & Deus mi,Joh.XX.28. Denique cui fides competit, eidem fidei forma & proprietates atque consequentia inseparabilia, cujusmodi illa sunt,quae diximus;competunt. Non enim ista de re concludunt,& non de persona,quia sicut fides illa in se, vel à se habet; ita eadem necessario iis personis, in quibus illa existit, confert. Quo minus vero illa humana imbecillitas,vel indispositio,ne minus debitum effectum sortiantur, intercipit vel disturbat, & Spiritus S. credentes obsignans & testimonio suo muniens,efficit.
units.tr: and against them stands doubt, or hesitation (Matt. 21:21; James 1:6). How can these proper affections of faith consist with uncertainty of salvation and with doubt? Bellarmine admits that these belong to faith, and that for this reason faith is most certain. But he denies that the remission of sins and salvation, and certainty concerning them, pertain to faith. That is less an argument than a raving. For the remission of sins and salvation do pertain to the articles of faith, and the articles of faith pertain to faith properly so called; and faith apprehends the remission of sins and salvation in Christ and applies them to itself. "As many as received him, to them he gave the power to become children of God, namely to those who believe in his name" (John 1:12). Here "to believe in Christ" and "to receive Christ" are equivalent. Those, therefore, who truly believe in Christ receive him and apply him to themselves, crying out with Thomas, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28). Finally, to whomever faith belongs, to them belong its form, properties and inseparable consequences, of the kind we have described. For these do not conclude concerning the thing and not the person, because just as that faith has what it has from itself, so it necessarily confers the same on the persons in whom it exists. Human weakness or indisposition does not so intercept or disturb this that it fails to produce its due effect; the Holy Spirit brings this about, sealing believers and confirming them by his testimony.

units.la: LXXXIII. Id ipsum etiam fidei causa, objectum & fructus demonstrant. Causa enim est Spiritus Christi,qui estSpiritus vitae in Christo, sive Spiritus, per quem Christus in nobis vivit, Rom. VIII.2. Gal.II.20. Et est fructus meriti Christi. Ego per legem legi mortuus sum ut Deo vivam,ibid. II.19. Per legem enim Christi Salvatoris credentibus perseverans sanctificatio, & ejusdem sensus, ceu fructus donatae justitiae, addicitur. Objectum fidei est Christus ipse,seu promissio gratiae in Christo. Nam Deus Christum per fidem propositum propitiatorium in sanguine ejus,Rom. III.25. Huic omnes Prophetae attestantur, quod remissionem peccatorum in nomine ejus accepturus sit omnis credens in ipsum, Actor. X.43. Ad accipiendam remissionem peccatorum, & fortem in sanctificatis, per fidem in me, ibid. XXVI.18. Qui ergo Christum & remissionem peccatorum,& mediantibus his etiam salutem per fidem accipiunt,illi de Christo,remissione peccatorum & salute per fidem πληροφορηθέντες certi reddunntur. Quod enim quis habet & possidet, de eo incertus esse nequit. Fructus vero fidei est pax apud Deum, & persuasio de ejusdem charitate & gratia, ut de gloria coelesti,imò Deo ipso, tanquam Patre nostro in Christo,sanctè gloriari, & in ipsis afflictionibus exultare possimus. Justificati ex fide habemus pacem apud Deum per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, per quem accessum habemus in fide ad gratiam hanc,in qua stetimus, & gloriamur in spe gloriae Dei,&c. Quia charitas Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum S. donatum nobis, Rom. V.1-5. Atqui pax illa apud Deum est tranquillitas conscientiae in Deo per Christum sibi reconciliato fiducialiter conquiescentis,& spiritualiter securae. Et
units.tr: LXXXIII. The cause, object and fruit of faith also show the same thing. The cause is the Spirit of Christ, who is the Spirit of life in Christ, or the Spirit by whom Christ lives in us, Rom. 8.2; Gal. 2.20. And faith is the fruit of Christ's merit: I through the law died to the law, that I might live to God, ibid. 2.19. For through the law of Christ the Saviour, a lasting sanctification and its sense are assigned to believers as the fruit of the righteousness given to them. The object of faith is Christ himself, or the promise of grace in Christ. For God set forth Christ through faith as a propitiation in his blood, Rom. 3.25. To him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins through his name, Acts 10.43. To receive remission of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified, through faith in me, ibid. 26.18. Therefore those who through faith receive Christ and the remission of sins, and through these also salvation, are made fully assured [πληροφορηθέντες] of Christ, of remission of sins and of salvation. For what a man has and possesses, he cannot be uncertain about. But the fruit of faith is peace with God and the persuasion of his love and grace, so that we can boast devoutly of heavenly glory, indeed of God himself as our Father in Christ, and exult even in afflictions. Being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have access by faith to this grace in which we stand, and we boast in the hope of the glory of God, etc. Because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit given to us, Rom. 5.1-5. Now that peace with God is the tranquillity of conscience, confidently resting in God, reconciled to us through Christ, and spiritually secure. And

units.la: Fiducia remissionis peccatorum, quae fidem justificantem consequitur, ut actus consolatorius ipsa gratiae certitudo est. Et persuasio de charitate Dei, qua nos in Christo complectitur est sensus hujus charitatis, in cordibus nostris per Spiritum S. diffusus; unde cætera fidei effecta pullulant.
units.tr: The confidence of forgiveness of sins, which follows justifying faith, is, as a consoling act, the very certainty of grace. And the persuasion of God's love, by which he embraces us in Christ, is the sense of this love, poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit; from this the other effects of faith spring forth.

units.la: LXXXIV. Tum etiam Spes, ejusque natura certitudinem hanc confirmat. Nam Christianorum professionem totam ἐλπιστικὴν ex ipse constantem esse, scite jam olim Chrysostomus monuit. Etenim τῇ ἐλπίδι εσωθημεν ipse salvati sumus, Rom. VIII.24. quia sperantes jam salvi esse incipimus, & salus nobis ita data est, ut eam expectare possimus & debeamus. Gloriamur in afflictionibus, scientes, quòd afflictio patientiam operetur, patientia autem experientiam, experientia autem spem; spes autem non pudefacit, Rom. V. 3.4. 5. Spei objectum gloria Dei, ipse Deus, æternum bonum nostrum est, quod promissum à Deo expectamus, certi, futurum, ut Deus se in nobis, ceu divitem, potentem, misericordem, justum, veracem glorificet. Cùm igitur id, quod fideles sperant, sit gloria Dei, rectè & securè id sperant & in ea spe gloriantur. Nam Deus gloriam suam non abnegat, sed pro ea zelat. Qualis igitur spes Christianorum est? Numquid ea tantùm, quod judicant, possibile esse, ut gloriæ Dei compotes fiant, atque ita desperare non debeant? Imò verò spes est gloriæ Dei, & quæ ipsa parit gloriationem, in ipsis etiam afflictionibus, quæ aliàs spem minuere possunt. Fidelis certè ad Christum confugiens cùm sperat, & in spe gloriatur, Deo obsequitur, & ὁμολογίαν assensum & astipulationem ei præstat, Hebr. X.23. Nititur illa spes verbo Dei & potentia ejus. Omnes qui expectant te, non pudefient, Psal. XXV.3. In te confisi sunt patres nostri, confisi sunt, & fecisti eos evadere, ibid. XXII. 5. Si igitur spes temeraria est, erit in mendacio. Atqui Deus non mentitur, nec quemquam fallit. Si quis persuasus, se à Deo vitam æternam consecuturum, nullas afflictiones metuat, persecutiones contemnat, Deo gratias agat, eum dictis & factis glorificet, concupiscentiis & justitiæ suæ renuntiet, & ad vitam æternam anhelet, an ille vel temerarius audiet, vel contumeliam Deo faciet, & non glorificabit potiùs? Si hoc, quare id non licebit? Quomodo non fidelis erit ea persuasio cùm Deus ipse passim testatus sit, se velle, ut toto corde simus בטחים cum securitate confidentes, קיים expectantes, מיחלים operientes Domini & operatio justitiæ sit ובטח tranquillitas & securitas in seculum, Esaj. XXXII.17. & spes talis non pudefaciat, Rom. V. 5. Si pudefacere, frustrari spes sua Christianos posset, Deus fieret non--Deus, non--rupes, non--perfugium, non מבטח arx roboris, Prov. XIV.26. in qua securi esse possimus. Sed spes, ad quam vocamur & gloriationem habet, & non pudefacit, adeòque non conjectura humana, sola non desperatio, languida præsumptio, quæ dicat fortassis, est, sed fidelem affirmationem futuri eventus continet, & non minùs securum, quàm studiosum & timentem Dei efficit. Ideò etiam ἐλπὶς ζῶσα spes viva, 1. Pet. I. 3. appellatur; quia non languida, infirma est, sed παρρησίαν & παυχημα habet; & perpetua simul, semperque exhilarans est, neque unquam intermoritur, sed semper renovatur & refocillatur, in eo, qui eam habet, manet, neque unquam eum deserit. Nam
units.tr: LXXXIV. Hope, too, and its nature confirm this certainty. For Chrysostom long ago wisely observed that the whole profession of Christians consists of hope [ἐλπιστικὴν]. For by hope we have been saved [τῇ ἐλπίδι ἐσώθημεν], Rom. 8.24, because by hoping we already begin to be saved, and salvation has been given to us in such a way that we can and ought to await it. We boast in afflictions, knowing that affliction works patience, patience experience, and experience hope; and hope does not put us to shame, Rom. 5.3-5. The object of hope is the glory of God, God himself, our eternal good, which we await as promised by God, certain that it will come, so that God may glorify himself in us as rich, powerful, merciful, just and true. Since, then, what the faithful hope for is the glory of God, they hope for it rightly and securely, and boast in that hope. For God does not deny his glory but is zealous for it. What kind of hope, then, do Christians have? Is it only that they judge it possible that they may become partakers of the glory of God, and so ought not to despair? Indeed, hope is of the glory of God, and it itself produces boasting, even in afflictions, which otherwise might diminish hope. Certainly the believer who flees to Christ, when he hopes and boasts in hope, obeys God and gives him assent and agreement, Heb. 10.23. That hope rests on the word of God and his power. All who wait for you will not be put to shame, Ps. 25.3. Our fathers trusted in you; they trusted, and you delivered them, ibid. 22.5. If, therefore, hope is rash, it will be in falsehood. But God does not lie, nor deceive anyone. If someone, persuaded that he will obtain eternal life from God, fears no afflictions, despises persecutions, gives thanks to God, glorifies him by word and deed, renounces his lusts and his own righteousness, and longs for eternal life, will that man be heard as rash, or will he do an insult to God rather than glorify him? If this is so, why should it not be permitted? How could that persuasion not be faithful, since God himself has testified everywhere that he wishes us to be with our whole heart בטחים confidently trusting with security, קיים waiting, מיחלים looking for the Lord, and the work of righteousness will be ובטח tranquillity and security for ever, Isa. 32.17; and such hope does not put to shame, Rom. 5.5. If hope could put Christians to shame, and its expectation be frustrated, God would become not-God, not-rock, not-refuge, not מבטח a fortress of strength, Prov. 14.26, in which we could be secure. But the hope to which we are called has boasting, and does not put to shame; so it is not human conjecture, nor mere non-despair, a languid presumption that says perhaps, but contains a faithful affirmation of the future outcome, and makes a man no less secure than eager and fearing God. Therefore it is also called a living hope [ἐλπὶς ζῶσα], 1 Pet. 1.3, because it is not languid or weak, but has boldness [παρρησίαν] and boasting [καύχημα]; and it is at once continual and always gladdening, never dies out, but is always renewed and revived, remains in the one who has it, and never abandons him. For

units.la: qui participes Christi facti sunt it, παρρησίαν καὶ καύχημα τῆς ἐλπίδος fiduciam & gloriationem spei, & ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποστάσεως principium fiduciæ, gloriationis, seu pollicitationis, ad finem usque firmam retinent, Hebr. III.6.14. Denique ipes vita hominis regeniti est, per quam vivit; sicut enim ad fidem; ita etiam ad ipsam vivificamur. Quæ causa est, quòd studium πληροφορίας τῆς ἐλπίδος plenitudinis spei enixè adeò Scriptura commendat. Cupimus unumquemque verum idem præstare studium ad plenitudinem spei usque in finem, ibid. VI. 11.
units.tr: those who have become partakers of Christ hold fast to the end the boldness [παρρησίαν] and boasting [καύχημα] of hope, and the beginning [ἀρχὴν] of the confidence, boasting, or promise, firm to the end, Heb. 3.6, 14. Finally, hope is the life of the regenerate man, by which he lives; for as we are made alive to faith, so also are we made alive to hope itself. This is why Scripture so earnestly commends the zeal for the fullness [πληροφορίας] of hope. We desire each one of you to show the same diligence for the full assurance of hope until the end, ibid. 6.11.

units.la: LXXXV. Operæ pretium heic est excutere tricas Bellarmini, quibus ille spei certitudinem oppugnat. Ait ille de justif. c.11. Certitudinem spei considerari ex parte intellectus, & ex parte voluntatis. Ex parte voluntatis illam esse firmam adhæsionem voluntatis ad rem speratam, quæ maxima esse possit, etsi ex parte intellectus homo non sit certus, se rem illam esse consecuturum. Imò videri spem non solum non exigere, sed nec ferre posse certitudinem absolutam ex parte intellectus, quia quod certò nos habituros scimus, non sperare, sed expectare dicamur. Habere tamen spem etiam ex parte intellectus duplicem certitudinem, unam ex fundamento primario, quod est promissio Dei, alteram ex charitate. Cùm tamen præter promissionem alia, dum hic peregrinamur, ad justificationem requirantur, fieri posse, ut qui amicus Dei est, iterum fiat inimicus, adeòque sine timore vivere non possit. Hactenus ille. Sed pro more ἀνεξεμμένα perversa loquens. Ante omnia enim desiderium & spem confundit. Illius, non hujus firmitas à voluntate pendet. Firma voluntatis ad rem speratam adhæsio, ubi homo ex parte intellectus de ejus adoptione persuasus non est, firmitas desiderii est, quod spes præsupponit, non certitudo spei, cùm nihil speremus, de cujus consecutione persuasi nullo modo sumus. Et humana quidem spes rationibus humanis, certis vel probabilibus nititur. Divina à Spiritu S. infusa, promissionum Divinarum veritate nititur; quam nisi fides apprehendat & applicet, spes præsidium nullum habet. Vanissimum igitur est, quòd spes certitudinem ex parte intellectus non exigat, ac neferat quidem. Nam speravit, Paulus resurrectionem mortuorum, Actor. XXIV. 15. cujus tamen ex parte intellectus maximam certitudinem habuit. Ratio ejusdem, quòd, quæ certò nos adepturos scimus, non sperare, sed expectare dicamur, apud ethnicos, quibus incerti boni nomen est, aliquid valeret, sed apud Christianos nullius momenti est. In Scriptura enim V.T. spes & expectatio ne vocibus quidem distinguuntur, cùm utraque מחלה & מקוה nomine veniat. In Novo verò Testamento re ipsa confunduntur. Ἀπολύτρωσιν adoptionem expectantes. Nam ἐλπίδι εσωθημεν spe salvati sumus; Si quod non cernimus, speramus, per tolerantiam ἀπεκδεχόμεθα expectamus, Rom. VIII.23. 24.25. Καπὰ τὴν ἀποκαραδοκίαν ἡ ἐλπίδα μου, secundum expectationem & spem meam, Phil. I.20. Quin & Lombardus atque Thomas spem certam expectationem futuræ beatitudinis definiunt. Etiam Christus in terris degens absolutam certitudinem ex parte intellectus de gloria corporis futura habuit, quem tamen spem respectu immor-
units.tr: LXXXV. It is worth the effort here to shake out the trifles of Bellarmine, by which he attacks the certainty of hope. In De justificatione c. 11 he says that the certainty of hope is to be considered from the side of the intellect and from the side of the will. On the part of the will, it is a firm adherence of the will to the thing hoped for, which can be very great, even though on the part of the intellect a man is not certain that he will obtain that thing. Indeed, hope seems not only not to require, but not even to be able to bear, absolute certainty on the part of the intellect, because we are said not to hope for what we know we will surely have, but to expect it. Yet hope has a double certainty even on the part of the intellect: one from its primary ground, which is the promise of God, and the other from charity. Since, however, besides the promise, other things are required for justification while we are wayfarers here, it can happen that one who is a friend of God becomes an enemy again, and so cannot live without fear. So far he. But, in his usual manner, he speaks perversely. For first of all he confuses desire and hope. The firmness of the one depends on the will, not the firmness of the other. The firm adherence of the will to the thing hoped for, where a man on the part of the intellect is not persuaded of its attainment, is the firmness of desire, which hope presupposes, not the certainty of hope, since we hope for nothing of whose attainment we are in no way persuaded. Human hope indeed rests on human reasons, certain or probable. Divine hope, infused by the Holy Spirit, rests on the truth of the divine promises; unless faith grasps and applies these, hope has no support. It is therefore most vain that hope does not require certainty on the part of the intellect, and cannot even bear it. For Paul hoped for the resurrection of the dead, Acts 24.15, of which nevertheless he had the greatest certainty on the part of the intellect. The reason that we are said not to hope but to expect what we know we will certainly attain may carry some weight among the heathen, for whom the name of good is uncertain, but among Christians it is of no moment. For in the Old Testament hope and expectation are not even distinguished by words, since both are signified by the terms מחלה and מקוה. In the New Testament they are really confused: awaiting adoption [ἀπολύτρωσιν]. For by hope we were saved [ἐλπίδι ἐσώθημεν]; if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience [ἀπεκδεχόμεθα], Rom. 8.23-25. According to my eager expectation and hope [ἀποκαραδοκίαν], Phil. 1.20. Indeed Lombard and Thomas define hope as a certain expectation of future blessedness. Even Christ, living on earth, had absolute certainty on the part of the intellect about the future glory of his body, yet he had it as hope with respect to immor-

units.la: {y} Bellarmini spei certitudinem oppugnantia. immortalitatis & gloriæ corporis habuisse, Thomas 3. q. 7. a. 4. asserit. Præter promissionem gratiæ Dei alia quoque ad justificationem & salutem requiri, certum est; quæ infirmitatis quidem humanæ respectu immutabilia & certa sunt, quia ab eadem promissione Dei αψ&-δῆ pendent. Denique amici Dei sibi relicti inimici ejusdem fieri possunt; sed ne fiant, gratia Dei æterna, Christi intercessio, & Spiritus S. obsignatio efficiunt.
units.tr: Bellarmine's objections against the certainty of hope. He asserts (Thomas, 3, q. 7, a. 4) that Christ on earth had certainty of immortality and of the glory of his body. It is certain that, besides the promise of God's grace, other things are also required for justification and salvation. With respect to human weakness these are unchangeable and certain, because they depend on that same promise of God, which is unfailing [ἀψευδῆ]. Finally, the friends of God, if left to themselves, can become his enemies. But they do not become so, because the eternal grace of God, Christ's intercession and the sealing of the Holy Spirit bring this about.

units.la: LXXXVI. Spei non pudefacientis veluti tibicen quidam charitas est, quam excidere numquam Apostolus, 1. Cor. XIII. 8. dicit.
units.tr: LXXXVI. Love is, as it were, a flute-player for a hope that does not disappoint; the Apostle says it never fails (1 Cor. 13:8).

units.la: Est autem amoris nostri erga Deum hæc indoles, ut sine sensu & certitudine non tantùm sui amantis, sed etiam mutui amoris, seu amoris Dei, qui amatur, & amantes vicissim amat, neque omnino frustra amari potest, imò iis, quos amat, sui etiam amorem instillat, esse non possit. Ideo S. Paulus charitatem Dei in cordibus nostris effusam esse per Spiritum S. nobis datum, Rom. V. 5. scribit. Postquam enim dixit, spem non pudefacere, ne nostris id meritis vel dignitati tribueremus, veram causam, charitatem Dei in cordibus nostris per Spiritum S. diffusam allegat. Effusam vel diffusam dicit, tum propter τὸ δαψιλὲς largitatem ejus: tum, quia ejus sensus in cordibus nostris est. Cor nostrum dilatatum est, &c. Dilatamini etiam vos, 2. Cor. VI. 11. 12. 13. Est autem amor Dei in dilatato amantis corde diffusissimus, quia ita credentes & amantes à Deo diliguntur, ut is amor totum eorum cor impleat, & ad Deum, ac quicquid in Deo est, rapiat & convertat, tanquam ad unicum Solem, cibum & gaudium. Quem proin amorem tam certum, & tam præsentem in corde nostro habemus, atque si eum in corde Dei cerneremus. Qui ergo negant, nos certam habere spem, in eorum cordibus Dei dilectio diffusa non est; atque ii non habent fiduciam in Deo, sed in suis consiliis; neque habent spem pudefacientem; neque amant Deum, quem non glorificant, in quo non requiescunt, & non vident amorem Dei, neque ad eam spem anhelant, imò Deum, ceu adversantem sibi, fugiunt & oderunt. Neque amoris nostri imbecillitas terrere nos debet, quia etiam imperfectus amor, dummodo sincerus sit, & crescere contendat, Spiritus S. effectus, & amoris Dei proxissimi testis & argumentum est.
units.tr: Our love towards God is of such a nature that it cannot exist without a sense and certainty not only of our own love but also of mutual love, that is, of the love of God, who is loved and who in turn loves those who love him. Nor can it be that he is loved in vain; indeed, he instils his love into those whom he loves. So St Paul writes that the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit given to us (Rom. 5:5). For after he has said that hope does not disappoint, lest we attribute this to our merits or worth, he names the true cause: the love of God shed abroad in our hearts through the Holy Spirit. He says it is poured out or shed abroad, partly because of its abundance [τὸ δαψιλὲς], its generosity, and partly because it is felt in our hearts. Our heart is enlarged, etc.; you also be enlarged (2 Cor. 6:11–13). Now the love of God is most fully poured out in the enlarged heart of the one who loves, because believers and lovers are so loved by God that this love fills their whole heart and draws and turns them to God and to everything in God, as to the one sun, food and joy. Therefore we have this love so certain and so present in our heart as if we saw it in the heart of God. Those who deny that we have a certain hope do not have the love of God shed abroad in their hearts. They do not have confidence in God but in their own plans; they do not have a hope that does not disappoint; they do not love God, whom they do not glorify, in whom they do not rest, and they do not see the love of God, nor do they long for that hope. Indeed, they flee from God and hate him as one opposed to them. Nor should the weakness of our love terrify us, because even imperfect love, provided it is sincere and strives to grow, is the effect of the Holy Spirit and a witness and proof of the nearest love of God.

units.la: LXXXVII. Jam & unio ac communio cum Deo, sanctùsque ille cum eo consensus & familiare commercium certitudinis hujus testis omni exceptione major est.
units.tr: LXXXVII. Furthermore, union and communion with God, that holy agreement with him and familiar intercourse, is a witness to this certainty that is greater than any objection.

units.la: Nam fidem nos cum Christo unire, supra fusiùs ostendimus, & similitudinibus multifariis declaravimus. Fidelis Deus, per quem vocati estis ad communionem Filii ejus Jesu Christi, Domini nostri, 1. Cor. I. 9. Neque tantùm Christo unimur, in eo fumus, & cum eo communionem habemus, sed etiam in eo manemus. Nam in Christo esse, & in illo μένειν manere, alternant, 1. Joh. II. 5. 6. Etiam Abrahamus φίλος Θεοῦ amicus Dei vocatus est, 2. Chron. XX. 7. Jacob. II. 23. Et tanta Deo cum fidelibus familiaritas intercedit, ut propterea Deus timentibus ipsum etiam סוד arcanum suum revelet, Psal. XXV. 14. Vos estis φίλοι amici mei, si feceritis, quæ vobis præcipio. Vos dixi amicos; quoniam omnia, quæ audivi à Patre meo, notificavi vobis, Joh. XV. 14. 15. Neque tantùm amici, sed etiam filii Dei fideles sunt, Gal. IV. 7. Hæc omnia, si gratiæ Dei & salutis certitudo absunt, vana & inania sunt, nec verus Dei amor, nec amicitia, nec communio ulla cum Deo locum habere potest; quando ne in humana quidem amicitia diffidentiæ & dubitationi de mutuo favore & amore locus jure esse potest, utpote in qua animorum, voluntatem, studiorum summa conjunctio esse debet.
units.tr: For we have shown above at greater length that faith unites us with Christ, and we have explained this by many similitudes. Faithful is God, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord (1 Cor. 1:9). We are not only united to Christ, in him and having communion with him, but we also abide in him. For to be in Christ and to abide [μένειν] in him are interchangeable (1 John 2:5, 6). Abraham too was called friend of God [φίλος Θεοῦ] (2 Chron. 20:7; James 2:23). And there is such familiarity between God and the faithful that God reveals his secret [סוד] to those who fear him (Ps. 25:14). You are friends [φίλοι], my friends, if you do what I command you. I have called you friends, because all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you (John 15:14, 15). The faithful are not only friends but also sons of God (Gal. 4:7). If the certainty of God's grace and salvation is absent, all these things are vain and empty; neither true love of God, nor friendship, nor any communion with God can have a place. For even in human friendship there can rightly be no room for distrust and doubt about mutual favour and love, since there ought to be in it the highest union of minds, wills and pursuits.

units.la: LXXXVIII. Sed & firmandæ electionis atque vocationis nostræ studium certitudinem gratiæ & salutis ostendit.
units.tr: LXXXVIII. Moreover, the earnest effort to make our election and calling sure shows certainty of grace and salvation.

units.la: Jubet enim S. Petrus vocationem & electionem nostram βεβαίαν firmam facere, 2. Petr. I. 10. Vocatio nostra est ad communionem Christi, 1. Cor. I. 9. & electio ad vitam æternam. Si vocatio & electio nostra semper est ἀβέβαιος infirma, instabilis, nutans, & de ea certi esse nunquam possumus, quomodo illam βεβαίαν firmam facere jubemur? Quomodo vocationem in se firmam facere possumus, si ea nobis firma & certa esse nunquam potest? Nam in vocatione bona Dei voluntas de salute nostra nobis significatur. Et si electionem & vocationem suam certam reddunt fideles, vel intelligunt se hoc facere, vel non intelligunt. Si non intelligunt, cæco feruntur impetu, absque fidei notitia, sine quâ nemo salvatur. Si intelligunt, certi igitur de electione & vocatione sua sunt. Verum est, per signa vocationis & electionis eandem firmari, stabiliri, sed sic stabiliuntur non apud Deum, apud quem gratia æterna est, & ἀμετάθετον βουλὴ immutabile consilium, sed apud vocatos & electos, ut signis his confirmati de vocatione & electione sua nulli dubitent. Neque signa illa, quæ vocati & electi in se vident, conjecturam duntaxat, non fidei certitudinem pariunt, quia Spiritus S. in scripturis & conscientiis nostris testando obsignat, quòd fallacia non sint.
units.tr: For St Peter bids us make our calling and election sure [βεβαίαν] (2 Pet. 1:10). Our calling is to communion with Christ (1 Cor. 1:9), and our election is to eternal life. If our calling and election are always unstable [ἀβέβαιος], wavering and uncertain, and we can never be certain of them, how are we commanded to make them sure [βεβαίαν]? How can we make our calling sure in itself, if it can never be sure and certain to us? For in the calling the good will of God concerning our salvation is made known to us. And if the faithful make their election and calling certain, either they understand that they are doing so or they do not. If they do not understand, they are carried on by a blind impulse, without knowledge of faith, without which no one is saved. If they understand, then they are certain of their election and calling. It is true that the calling and election are confirmed and established by their signs, but they are not established in God's sight, with whom grace is eternal and his unchangeable counsel [ἀμετάθετον βουλὴ]. They are established in the sight of those who are called and elect, so that, confirmed by these signs, they doubt nothing about their calling and election. Nor do those signs which the called and elect see in themselves produce mere conjecture rather than certainty of faith, because the Holy Spirit seals, bearing witness in the Scriptures and in our consciences, that they are not deceptive.

units.la: LXXXIX. Accedit precum efficacia & privilegium.
units.tr: 89. The efficacy and privilege of prayer also.

units.la: Nam quod precibus à Deo expetimus, & expetere tenemur, illud ad nos pertinere merito confidimus: & de eo impetrando vel impetrato certiores nos reddi, dubitari nequit. Quæcunque orantes petieritis, credite accepturos vos, & evenient vobis, Marc. XI. 24. Hæc est fiducia, quam apud Deum habemus, ipsum, si quid secundum voluntatem ejus petierimus, nos audire. Et si novimus, quòd exaudiat nos in iis, quæ petierimus, scimus nos habere petitiones, quas ab eo expetierimus, 1. Joh. V. 14. 15. Atqui singuli remissionem peccatorum & vitam æternam ex speciali Dei in Christo misericordia petere tenemur, juxta mandatum Christi: Vos ita orate: Adveniat Regnum tuum. Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris, Matth. VI. 9. &c. Luc. XI. 2. &c. Propter hoc oraturus est te, quemcunque benignitate prosequeris tempore opportuno, Psal. XXXII. 6. Et vetat hic omnem dubitationem Deus. Postulet cum fide, nihil disceptans, Jac. I. 6. Neque profecto oratio in fide sine hæsitatione cum incertitudine rei, quæ petitur spiritualis & ad salutem æternam pertinentis, vel impetrandæ, vel impetratæ consistere potest. Alia temporalium beneficiorum ratio est, de quibus definita promissio nulla extat, sed conditionalis duntaxat, quaquatenus Dei gloriæ & saluti nostræ convenit. Neque ideo certitudo nutat, quia orare tenemur, ut salutem consequamur, cùm nemo sanus, uti illi argutantur, petat id, quod possidet, & de quo jam certus est. Non enim salutem re, sed spe sola possidemus, & precatio, ceu præcipuum ad consequendum medium intervenit. Orare autem in fide, nisi eadem fides nobis sponderet, fore, ut compotes voti Deus nos reddat, neque liceret, neque attineret multùm. Cùmque certitudo nostra non precum perfectione, sed Christi intercessione, & pia cordis affectione nitatur, circumstantiæ in oratione neglectæ nec preces inanes, nec irritam certitudinem reddere possunt. Deus enim non oran-tis meritum, sed sinceritatem respicit; & qui interpellare nos facit, interpellandi & gemendi affectum nobis inspirat, uti scitè Augustinus. Quid quòd fideles pro remissione peccatorum impetrata gratias etiam Deo agunt? Benedic, anima mea, Jehovæ, & ne oblivisearis ullius beneficiorum ejus. Qui condonat omnes iniquitates tuas, qui medetur omnibus morbis tuis, Psal. CIII. 2. 3. Ineptum & ludicrum est, agnoscere beneficium, quod non acceperis. Quo argumento Catharinus & Marinarus ipsi in Concilio Tridentino certitudinem gratiæ statuminarunt.
units.tr: For we confidently trust that what we ask of God in prayer, and are bound to ask, pertains to us, and it cannot be doubted that we are assured of obtaining it or of having obtained it. Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it will be yours, Mark 11:24. This is the confidence we have before God, that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him, 1 John 5:14, 15. Yet, according to Christ's command, each of us is bound to ask for the forgiveness of sins and eternal life from God's special mercy in Christ: Pray in this way: Your kingdom come. Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors, Matt. 6:9ff.; Luke 11:2ff. For this reason everyone who is faithful will pray to you at a time when you may be found, Ps. 32:6. Here God forbids all doubt: Let him ask in faith, with no wavering, James 1:6. Certainly prayer cannot stand in faith with hesitation and uncertainty about a thing that is sought, whether to be obtained or already obtained, if that thing is spiritual and pertains to eternal salvation. The case of temporal benefits is different: there is no definite promise concerning them, but only a conditional one, insofar as they agree with God's glory and our salvation. Nor does our certainty waver for this reason, that we are bound to pray in order to obtain salvation, since (as they quibble) no sane person asks for what he already possesses and is already certain of. For we do not possess salvation in reality but in hope alone, and prayer intervenes as the chief means of obtaining it. Yet to pray in faith would neither be permitted nor be of much use, unless that same faith assured us that God will grant our request. And since our certainty rests not on the perfection of our prayers but on the intercession of Christ and the pious affection of the heart, neglected circumstances in prayer can make neither prayers empty nor certainty void. For God regards not the merit of the one praying but his sincerity, and he who causes us to intercede inspires in us the desire to intercede and to groan, as Augustine rightly says. What of the fact that the faithful also give thanks to God for the forgiveness of sins obtained? Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his benefits. He forgives all your iniquities; he heals all your diseases, Ps. 103:2, 3. It is foolish and absurd to acknowledge a benefit that you have not received. By this argument Catharinus and Marinarus themselves, at the Council of Trent, established the certainty of grace.

units.la: XC. Denique & Sacramentorum obsignatio certitudinem hanc evincit.
units.tr: 90. Finally, the sealing of the sacraments also proves this certainty.

units.la: Sunt enim signa & sigilla fœderis, justitiæ & salutis. Abraham signum accepit circumcisionis, sigillum justitiæ fidei, Rom. IV. 11. Baptismus salvat, ceu stipulatio bonæ conscientiæ in Deum, 1. Pet. III. 21. Et Eucharistia est Sacramentum communionis cum corpore & sanguine Christi, 1. Cor. X. 16. Uno Spiritu (non aqua) omnes in unum corpus (Christi) baptizati sumus: & omnes in unum Spiritum (communionem Spiritus ejusdem) potati sumus, ibid. XII. 13. Sacramenta Deus credentibus, confugientibus, trepidis, pavidis, esurientibus & sitientibus propositit, atque iis uti fideniter jussit. Datur igitur sensus fidei: datur libertas profitendi fidem, & in ea gloriandi, & nomen Dei ut nostri, & fœdus ejus; atque sigilla justitiæ assumendi. Si humana sigilla certitudinem muniunt, Divina Dei omnipotentis, fallere nescii & veracis illius testis sigilla munire apta nata non sunt? Quæ igitur ex usu Sacramentorum consolatio? Et tantò certitudo major ex eorum usu sequatur oportet, si, quòd οἱ ἐξ εὐαγγελίας sustinent, Sacramenta gratiam & salutem ex opere operato conferunt.
units.tr: For they are signs and seals of the covenant, of righteousness and of salvation. Abraham received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4:11. Baptism saves us, as the pledge of a good conscience toward God, 1 Pet. 3:21. And the Eucharist is a sacrament of communion with the body and blood of Christ, 1 Cor. 10:16. By one Spirit (not by water) we were all baptized into one body (of Christ), and we were all given to drink of one Spirit (the fellowship of the same Spirit), ibid. 12:13. God has offered the sacraments to believers, to those who flee for refuge, to the trembling, the fearful, the hungry and the thirsty, and has commanded them to use them with confidence. Therefore there is a sense of faith; there is freedom to profess the faith, to glory in it, and to take up God's name as ours, and his covenant, and the seals of righteousness. If human seals confirm certainty, shall not the seals of the almighty God, who cannot deceive and who is a true witness, be fitted to confirm it? What consolation, then, comes from the use of the sacraments? And greater certainty must surely follow from their use, if, as those of the Gospel [οἱ ἐξ εὐαγγελίας] maintain, the sacraments confer grace and salvation by the work worked.

units.la: XCI. Hæc illa certitudinis Gratiæ perseverantis & salutis fundamenta sunt.
units.tr: 91. These are the foundations of certainty of persevering grace and salvation.

units.la: Quibus inducti Sancti eandem præ se firmiter tulerunt: Nam Abrahamus, Pater credentium contra spem sub spe (הוּא שׁ לָךְ secure, sine dubitatione) credidit, non infirmus fide, sed πληροφορηθεὶς plenissimè persuasus, quòd ille, qui promisit posset (recte, laudabiliter, cum justitia & gloria summa) efficere, ut sit pater gentium, & fide sua præeat, & promissionem ratificet, Rom. IV. 18. 21. David quoque: Quando eo in valle umbræ mortis, non timeo malum, quia tu mecum es: Certè bonum & gratia persequentur me (non lentè vel sensim, sed celeriter & affatim me circumvallabunt) in omnes dies vitæ meæ, & versabor in domo Jehovæ in longitudine dierum, Psal. XXIII. 4. 6. Ad te recepi me; Jehova, non confundar in seculum, Psal. XXXI. 2. S. Paulus: Persuasus sum, quòd nec vita, nec mors, &c. possit nos separare à dilectione Dei, quæ est in Christo Jesu, Rom. VIII. 38. 39.
units.tr: Moved by these things, the saints firmly displayed the same certainty. For Abraham, the father of believers, against hope, in hope, believed (secure, without doubt [הוּא שׁ לָךְ]), not weak in faith, but fully persuaded [πληροφορηθεὶς] that he who had promised was able (rightly, praiseworthily, with justice and the highest glory) to make him the father of nations, and would both keep his faith and ratify the promise, Rom. 4:18, 21. David also: When I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I fear no evil, for you are with me. Surely goodness and grace will follow me (not slowly or gradually, but swiftly and abundantly they will surround me) all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days, Ps. 23:4, 6. I have taken refuge in you, O Lord; let me never be put to shame, Ps. 31:2. Paul: I am persuaded that neither life nor death, etc., will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus, Rom. 8:38, 39.

units.la: Quæ persuasio non moralis, vel conjecturalis, sed fidei est, quia tum materia persuasionis est de certitudine prædestinationis, quæ nulla conjecturalis est: tum incertitudinis vel formidinis impedimenta omnia removentur. Idem S. Paulus: Certamen bonum certavi, cursum absolvi, fidem retinui. Quod reliquum est, repositâ mihi est justitiæ corona, quam dabit Dominus in die illa non tantùm mihi, sed omnibus diligentibus adventum ejus, 2. Tim. IV. 7. 8. Vanum est dicere, quòd singulari privilegio, & speciali revelatione paucis his certitudo hæc obrigerit.
units.tr: This persuasion is not moral or conjectural but of faith, because the matter of the persuasion is the certainty of predestination, which is in no way conjectural, and because all the hindrances of uncertainty or fear are removed. The same Paul: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord will give to me on that day, and not only to me but to all who have loved his appearing, 2 Tim. 4:7, 8. It is vain to say that this certainty was granted to these few by a singular privilege and special revelation.

units.la: Nam S. Paulum suam persuasionem ex donatione Christi, justificatione credentium, & intercessione Christi; quæ omnibus credentibus communis est, arcessentem, & ἡμᾶς nos vocatos & justificatos omnes includentem, supra vidimus. Præterea omnibus illis, qui Christi sunt, data est eadem, variante licèt mensura, fides, eadem gratia, idem Spiritus, idem testis, eadem arrha, eadem consolatio. Nam quid habent peculiare hic & ille, quod non idem credentibus omnibus sit promulgatum. Tum & Fidelium exemplum & praxis nostra institutio est. Illi de salute certi fuerunt. Qui verò ex fide sunt, benedicuntur cum fideli Abrahamo, Gal. III. 8. 9. 14. Non scriptum est propter illum solum (Abrahamum) quòd ipsi imputatum sit, sed etiam propter nos, quibus credentibus in eum, qui Jesum Dominum ex mortuis resuscitavit, imputare vult, Rom. IV. 23. 24. Omnibus fidelibus remissio peccatorum & vita promittitur. Eadem ergo ratione mihi, tibi, illi credenti, & tam certò, ac si Deus id è Cœlo proclamaret. Singularia enim sub universali stant. Præterea Paulus non tantùm, Rom. VIII. capite toto universalem doctrinam tractat, neque fundamentum singulari privilegio ulpiam repetit, sed etiam Abrahami illam certitudinem non speciali revelationi, sed fidei accepam retulit, Hebr. XI. 9. &c. Et de omnibus fidelibus S. Johannes: Nos scimus, quòd translati sumus à morte in vitam, quia diligimus fratres, 1. Joh. III. 14. Signum quidem certitudinis, dilectio fratrum, humanum est; sed verbum Dei, signum hoc cum re signata connectens, Spiritus S. illud conscientiis obsignans, Divinam certitudinem efficit. Si enim cor nostrum nos non condemnat, fiduciam habemus apud Deum, ibid. v. 21. Et per hoc cognoscimus eum (Christum) habitare in nobis, ex Spiritu, quem nobis dedit, ibid. v. 24.
units.tr: For above we have seen that Paul drew his persuasion from the gift of Christ, from the justification of believers, and from the intercession of Christ, which is common to all believers, and which includes all of us who are called and justified. Moreover, the same faith, though varying in measure, the same grace, the same Spirit, the same witness, the same pledge, and the same consolation have been given to all who belong to Christ. For what is there peculiar to this man or that which has not been proclaimed alike to all believers? Further, the example and practice of the faithful is our instruction. They were certain of their salvation. Those who are of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham, Gal. 3:8, 9, 14. It is not written for his sake alone that it was credited to him, but also for our sake, to whom it will be credited if we believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, Rom. 4:23, 24. Forgiveness of sins and life are promised to all the faithful. Therefore, for the same reason, they are promised to me, to you, and to that believer, and as surely as if God proclaimed it from heaven. For singular cases rest under the universal. Moreover, Paul does not merely treat the universal doctrine throughout the whole of Romans 8, nor does he anywhere derive the foundation from a singular privilege; he also referred Abraham's certainty not to a special revelation but to faith, Heb. 11:9ff. And St John speaks of all the faithful: We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers, 1 John 3:14. The love of the brothers is indeed a human sign of certainty; but the word of God, connecting this sign with the thing signified, and the Holy Spirit sealing it in our consciences, makes it a divine certainty. For if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God, ibid. v. 21. And by this we know that he (Christ) dwells in us, by the Spirit which he has given us, ibid. v. 24.

units.la: Si denique Abraham, David, Paulus, alii de salute sua certi fuerunt ex speciali privilegio & revelatione, illa certitudo non fuit certitudo fidei. Sic enim Bannes ipse in 2. 2. quæst. a. 1. dub. 3. scribit: Revelata particularibus personis quamvis supernaturalia sint, non pertinent ad assensum fidei Catholicæ, aut virtutis Theologicæ, sed illa tantùm, quæ nota sunt Ecclesiæ, & ab illa proponuntur. At verò de Abrahamo & Davide palam est, quòd de gratia Dei certi fuerint per fidem: Ergo non per revelationem specialem, sed per revelationem talem, qualis se ad omnes fideles extendit. Omnium enim fidelium certitudo omnis, quam pro mensura fidei habent, non ex peculiari revelatione præter aut extra verbum bum facta, sed ex fide promissionum Dei, quas in verbo suo ad solatium nostrum copiosissimè revelavit, ex testimonio Spiritus S. testantis cum spiritu nostro, nos esse filios Dei & haeredes, denique ex serio & sancto bonae conscientiae & bonorum studio, fluit.
units.tr: If Abraham, David, Paul and others were certain of their salvation only through a special privilege and revelation, that certainty was not the certainty of faith. Bannes himself writes in this way in 2. 2. quæst. a. 1. dub. 3: Revelations made to particular persons, although they are supernatural, do not belong to the assent of Catholic faith or to the theological virtue, but only those things which are known to the Church and proposed by her. But it is plain that Abraham and David were certain of the grace of God through faith. Therefore they were certain not by a special revelation but by a revelation of the kind that extends to all the faithful. For all the certainty that believers have, in proportion to the measure of their faith, arises not from some private revelation made apart from or beyond the Word, but from faith in the promises of God, which he has revealed in his Word most abundantly for our comfort; from the testimony of the Holy Spirit bearing witness with our spirit that we are the sons and heirs of God; and finally from the earnest and holy pursuit of a good conscience and of good works.

units.la: XCII. Haec cum ita sint, satisfaciendum est desiderio Apostoli, ut singuli credentes idem studium demonstrent ad plenitudinem spei usque ad finem, Hebr. VI. 11. 12. Spes enim illa non est sine signaculo, sine arrhabone. Neque arrhabo spem facit, nisi visus. Nam quod evanidum est, solidum non est. Et Spiritus idem, qui in nobis manet, etiam in nobis operatur, & ubi operatur, sentitur. Occultat quidem aliquando se in suis, ut in Ezechia, quem Deus dereliquit, ut tentaret eum, ad cognoscendum id omne, quod in corde ejus erat, 2. Chron. XXXII. 31. sed occultat se, ut requiratur studiosius. Et per peccata tristitia afficitur, Ephes. IV. 30. dum à nobis ei praebetur causa operandi tristitiam secundum Deum, 2. Cor. VII. 10. 11. ut per eam demum nobis laetitia salutis restituatur, Psal. LI. 14. Si igitur mercatores mercaturae, & Pater familias familiae suae rationes frequenter ineunt, etiam Christianis omnibus incumbit, ut diligenter & juxta atque prudenter inquirant, quo in statu versentur; tentent se ipsos, explorent, an sint in fide, 2. Cor. XIII. 5. requirant in se sigillum & arrhabonem, & ejusdem operationem atque sensum, vocationem & electionem suam firmam reddant, 2. Petr. I. 10. fiduciam & gloriationem spei ad finem usque firmam retineant, Hebr. III. 6. 14. Absque hoc enim studio, ejusque successu Christiani omnium hominum miserrimi, & reprobi 2. Cor. XIII. 5. sunt. Neque ullum contra vitae calamitates & mortis terrores solatium suppetit, nisi omni cura & studio in id incumbimus, ut salutis aeternae non modo olim participes, sed etiam in hac vita certi reddamur, & post tentationes plusquam victores evadamus, Rom. VIII. 37.
units.tr: XCII. Since this is so, the Apostle's desire must be satisfied, that each one of the believers should show the same diligence to the full assurance of hope until the end, Heb. VI. 11, 12. For that hope is not without a seal or an earnest. Nor does an earnest produce hope unless it is seen. For what is fading is not solid. And the same Spirit who dwells in us also works in us, and where he works he is felt. Indeed he sometimes hides himself in his people, as in Hezekiah, whom God left, that he might test him, that he might know all that was in his heart, 2 Chron. XXXII. 31; but he hides himself so that he may be sought more eagerly. And through sins he is grieved, Eph. IV. 30, when we give him occasion for working sorrow according to God, 2 Cor. VII. 10, 11, so that through that sorrow the joy of salvation may at last be restored to us, Ps. LI. 14. If therefore merchants often make up the accounts of their trade, and the head of a household the accounts of his household, it lies upon all Christians also to inquire diligently and wisely into the state in which they stand; to test themselves, to examine whether they are in the faith, 2 Cor. XIII. 5; to seek in themselves the seal and the earnest, and its working and sense; to make their calling and election sure, 2 Pet. I. 10; to hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of hope to the end, Heb. III. 6, 14. For without this diligence, and its success, Christians are the most wretched of all men, and reprobate, 2 Cor. XIII. 5. Nor is there any comfort against the calamities of life and the terrors of death, unless we apply ourselves with all care and zeal to become certain not only that we shall one day share in eternal salvation, but also in this life, and so that after temptations we emerge more than conquerors, Rom. VIII. 37.

units.la: XCIII. Possunt autem fideles de gratia in Christo parta & salute certiores reddi, non tantum, quia acceperunt Spiritum S. arrham salutis & liberationis suae, sed etiam quia charitas Dei in illorum cordibus per Spiritum S. diffusa, & alabastri instar illius unguenti nardi liquidae, vel fidelis multi pretii fracti, & super caput Christi effusi, Marc. XIV. 3. velut aperta, fracta, & varias in gratias, ut suaviorem odorem spiret, & sensum penitiorem efficiat, super corpus Christi, & singula ejus membra velut distribuitur, 1. Cor. XII. 11. Inprimis Spiritus S. credentibus datus, & charitas Dei in eorum cordibus sic diffusa id efficit, ut peccata agnoscamus, ex animo propter admissa ea doleamus, in posterum vehementi odio illa persequamur; credamus, Deum habere Filium, qui morte sua veniam scelerum omnibus in eum credentibus, & gratiam ejus desiderantibus, & eum, ceu unicum & sufficientissimum Salvatorem supra omnia diligentibus promeruerit, ad eum, ceu arcem salutis nostrae confugiamus, remissionem peccatorum propter meritum ejus desideremus, in eo invenia-mur, ei uni solique confidamus, gratias agamus; nos ipsos abnegemus, crucem ejus toleremus, Deum ex toto corde, & proximum sincerè diligamus. Haec operationes Spiritus S. & gratiae Dei in cordibus diffusae tam flagrantem sui odorem spirant, tam quaesitum Spiritus S. & gratiae Dei sensum ingenerant, ut qui isthaec in se inveniunt, non minus de gratia Dei & Spiritus S. inhabitatione certi esse possint, quam odorem rei odoriferae, suavitatem unguenti percipientes rei ipsius odoriferae sibi collatae, & unguenti supra se effusi certi sunt. Neque profecto nos latere potest, an vel serio ob peccata nostra doleamus, vel credamus, Deum habere Filium placamentum pro peccatis mundi, vel ad eum confugerimus, ut Salvatorem, & ei uni soliqué ad salutem confidamus, vel nos ipsos abnegemus, vel Deum & proximum diligamus.
units.tr: XCIII. Moreover the faithful can be made more certain of the grace obtained in Christ and of their salvation, not only because they have received the Holy Spirit as the earnest of their salvation and deliverance, but also because the love of God, poured out in their hearts through the Holy Spirit, is spread over the body of Christ and each of his members, as though it were like the alabaster flask of liquid spikenard ointment, or the precious ointment that was broken and poured over the head of Christ, Mark XIV. 3, opened and broken and distributed in various graces, so that it breathes a sweeter fragrance and produces a deeper sense, 1 Cor. XII. 11. Above all, the Holy Spirit given to believers, and the love of God so poured out in their hearts, bring it about that we recognise our sins, grieve for them from the heart on account of the sins we have committed, and pursue them with a strong hatred from now on; that we believe God has a Son who by his death has merited pardon of sins for all who believe in him and desire his grace, and who is loved above all things by those who love him as the one and most sufficient Saviour; that we flee to him as the citadel of our salvation, desire the forgiveness of sins for the sake of his merit, are found in him, trust in him alone, give thanks; that we deny ourselves, bear his cross, and love God with the whole heart and our neighbour sincerely. These operations of the Holy Spirit and the grace of God poured out in hearts breathe so strong a fragrance of themselves, and produce so keen a sense of the Spirit and of the grace of God, that those who find these things in themselves can be no less certain of the grace of God and of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit than those who perceive the fragrance of a sweet-smelling thing, or the sweetness of ointment poured over them, are certain of the fragrant thing itself that is brought to them and of the ointment poured upon them. Indeed it cannot escape us whether we truly grieve for our sins, or believe that God has a Son as the propitiation for the sins of the world, or have fled to him as Saviour and trust in him alone for salvation, or have denied ourselves, or love God and our neighbour.

units.la: Nam dolorem sentimus conscii, sicut & laetitiam, quia uterque cogitandi modus in mente miseriam vel felicitatem producit; & recte nos dolere novimus, quando propter Deum benignum & supremum Dominum peccatis offensum dolemus; & fidei nostrae, quod Deus habeat Filium, qui justitia nostra esse potest, & quod ei ad salutem confidamus, conscii sumus, quin qui credit in Filium, in se ipso testimonium habet, 1. Joh. V. 10. & abnegationis nostri conscientiam habemus ex abnegatione impietatis & concupiscentiarum hujus seculi, Tit. II. 12. & amoris, quo Deum & proximum prosequimur, sensu destituì nullo modo possumus, quia omnis amor in amante, qui se amato unit, suavitatem efficit: & fidei nostrae incerti esse non possumus, quia charitatem illa operatur, & facta bonorum operum mater est; quorum etiam a nobis editorum nescii esse non possumus, quia amoris Dei & proximi fructus sunt. Qui porro certi sunt, se peccatorum seria & sincera poenitentia duci, & vera fide Christo liberatore niti, ii tuto credunt, & persuadentur, se tum accepisse Spiritum S. ejusque primitias, quia serius de peccatis dolor est fructus Spiritus S. corda nostra à peccatorum sordibus purgantis: tum habere justitiam in Christo, quia eam esurientes & sitientes satiantur, & beati sunt, Matth. V. 6. Psal. II. 12. tum se esse filios Dei, membra & fratres Christi, quia quotquot Spiritu Dei ducuntur, filii Dei sunt, Rom. VIII. 14. & qui Spiritum Christi habet, Christi est, ibid. v. 9. tum vivere in communione Dei, secundum promissionem Christi: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit: & Pater meus diliget eum, & ad eum veniet, & cum eo manebimus, Joh. XIV. 23. tum esse electos ad vitam coelestem, quia fides, studium sanctitatis, justitia Christi, communio Dei electionis infallibilia sunt, Rom. VIII. 30. Ephes. I. 4. 2. Thess. II. 13.
units.tr: For we feel sorrow with consciousness, as also joy, because each mode of thought produces misery or happiness in the mind; and we know that we grieve rightly when we grieve for having offended by sins a gracious God and supreme Lord; and we are conscious that we believe that God has a Son who can be our righteousness, and that we trust in him for salvation; indeed he who believes in the Son has the testimony in himself, 1 John V. 10. And we have a consciousness of self-denial from denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, Titus II. 12. And we can in no way be destitute of the sense of love by which we pursue God and our neighbour, because all love in the lover who unites himself to the beloved produces sweetness; and we cannot be uncertain of our faith, because love is its work and the mother of good works; and we cannot be ignorant of the good works done by us, because they are the fruits of love towards God and neighbour. Moreover those who are certain that they are led by serious and sincere repentance and rest in Christ the Liberator by true faith, they confidently believe and are persuaded that they have received the Holy Spirit and his first-fruits, because sorrow for sins is a fruit of the Spirit cleansing our hearts from the filth of sin; that they have righteousness in Christ, because those who hunger and thirst are satisfied, and are blessed, Matt. V. 6; Ps. II. 12; that they are sons of God, members and brothers of Christ, because as many as are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God, Rom. VIII. 14, and he who has the Spirit of Christ is Christ's, ibid. v. 9; that they live in communion with God, according to the promise of Christ: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him, John XIV. 23; that they are elect to heavenly life, because faith, the pursuit of holiness, the righteousness of Christ and communion with God are infallible signs of election, Rom. VIII. 30; Eph. I. 4; 2 Thess. II. 13.

units.la: XCIV. Non ergo fideles in praesens quidem certi esse possunt, at de futuro incerti, nutabundi haerent. Satis enim ex iis, quae attulimus, certitudinis fundamentis, & collectione gratiae atque salutis ex iisdem, liquet, etiam perseverantis ad finem usque gratiae certitudinem promitti & conferri. Etenim Scriptura filiationem & haereditatem haereditatem individuo nexu conjungit. Si filii, etiam haeredes, Rom. VIII. 17. Neque intervertendae haereditatis periculum est, quia Deus ipse fustem
units.tr: XCIV. Therefore the faithful cannot be certain of the present only, while they hang wavering and uncertain about the future. For it is sufficiently clear from the foundations of certainty we have set out, and from the collection of grace and salvation drawn from them, that certainty of grace persevering to the end is also promised and conferred. Indeed Scripture joins sonship and inheritance in an indivisible bond: if sons, then also heirs, Rom. VIII. 17. Nor is there any danger that the inheritance will be lost, because God himself sustains

units.la: Hebr. VI. 11. 12. sustentat fortem, hæreditatem nostram, Psal. XVI. 5. Et Spiritus S. arrhabo, primitiæ de secutura hæreditate & redemptione spondet; & quorum arrhabo, primitiæ est, ii id ignorare non possunt. Non enim arrha esset, nisi nossemus. Jam ergo per arrham Spiritus habemus æternam beatitudinem, jam possidemus, & novimus, neminem eam intervertere posse, Rom. VIII. 35. 38. 39. Ita hæres, etiam dum puer est, κυρίῳ πάντων Dominus omnium est, Gal. IV. 1. Spiritus illius fidelibus conferendi eximia promissio extat, Zach. XII. 10. Effundam super domum David, & super habitantem Hierosolymis רוח חן תחנונים Spiritum gratiæ. (consentaneum & convenientem gratiæ & immensò favori Dei erga nos, & gratiam Dei nostram facientem) & implorationis (qua clementiam Dei precibus adimus, ad impetranda omnia nobis salutaria, quod primum fidei opus est.) Quomodo sic effusus Spiritus gratiæ ejúsque Deo decoræ & precum destituere eum, in quem semel effusus est, potest? Ejusdem Spiritus S. fructus ἐλπὶς σπες, παρρησία confidentia de futuro, ἀπολαυσις καυχησεως susceptio gloriationis certitudinem futurorum etiam bonorum confirmat.
units.tr: Heb. 6:11, 12. God himself sustains the strong one, our inheritance (Ps. 16:5). The Holy Spirit also gives us a pledge and firstfruits of the inheritance and redemption to come. Those whose pledge and firstfruit it is cannot be ignorant of this, for it would not be a pledge unless we knew it. So through the pledge of the Spirit we already have eternal blessedness, we already possess it, and we know that no one can cut us off from it (Rom. 8:35, 38, 39). Thus the heir, even while still a child, is lord of all [κυρίῳ πάντων] (Gal. 4:1). There is an outstanding promise that this Spirit will be given to believers (Zech. 12:10): "I will pour out upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace [רוח חן] and of supplications [תחנונים]." This is fitting and consistent with the grace and the boundless favour of God toward us, and it makes us gracious to God; and the spirit of supplication is the means by which we approach God's mercy with prayers to obtain everything salutary for us, which is the first work of faith. How could God withdraw the Spirit thus poured out, the Spirit of grace and of prayer that becomes God, from the one upon whom he was once poured out? The fruits of the same Holy Spirit are hope [ἐλπὶς], confidence [παρρησία] about the future, and the enjoyment [ἀπόλαυσις] of boasting [καυχήσεως], which confirms the certainty of even the good things to come.

units.la: XCV. Unde verò, inquias, scio, me in fide, in bonis operibus perseveraturum? Non ex facultate tua, ô pia anima, non ex integritate potestatis vel libertatis tuæ; multò minùs ex indifferentia & mutabilitate tua, quam solam ob oculos sibi statuentes circa fidem certitudinis hujus & salutis suæ naufragium faciunt; sed ex eo ipso, quòd Spiritum Dei, quòd fidem habes, siquidem ex animo credis.
units.tr: XCV. But whence, you will say, do I know that I shall persevere in faith and in good works? Not from your own ability, O pious soul, not from the integrity of your power or freedom; still less from your indifference and changeableness, which alone are set before the eyes of those who make shipwreck of this certainty and of their salvation with regard to faith. Rather, you know it from this very fact, that you have the Spirit of God, that you have faith, if indeed you believe from the heart.

units.la: Quod te scrutari, explorare, sine præjudicio & φιλαυτίᾳ ad veram cotem experiri, & ad quem omni studio precibusque contendere decet. Si fidem habes, arrham habes, donum habes, quod ut tuum non fuit ab initio habere, ita nec tuum est, servare, sed ejusdem ac solius est, illud conservare, augere & coronare, ejus etiam dare est. Quod soli illi ignorant, vel præfractè etiam negant, qui vel fidem veram & radicatam ignorant, atque sibi persuadent, fidem non aliud esse quàm assensum veritati habitum, quo quis convictus fatetur, verbum Dei verum esse, & leve illud gaudium, cum quo temporarii sermonem excipiunt, de cætero autem de acceptatione gratiæ, apprehensione Christi, fame & siti justitiæ, pauper tate spirituali, abnegatione cupiditatum, inscriptione legis Dei in corda, fiducia & timore Dei ne somniant quidem unquam: vel fidei victoriam à mutabilitate voluntatis suspendentes, certitudinem ei afferere, consolationem inde haurire, & tentatis impertiri non audent, & sic quod dari negant, ne quærendum quidem vel precandum ostendunt, faciúntque in præsens superbos, quos volunt ex fide, arbitrii sui sobole, de gratia persuasos esse; in futurum verò vel desperabundos & vacillantes, si certitudinem desiderent, vel supinos languidósque, si eam spernant.
units.tr: You should examine yourself and test yourself, without prejudice and without self-love, by the true touchstone, and you ought to strive for this with all your zeal and prayers. If you have faith, you have the pledge, you have the gift. Just as it was not yours to have it at the beginning, so it is not yours to keep it; it belongs to him alone to preserve it, increase it and crown it, and it is his to give it as well. Those alone are ignorant of this, or even stubbornly deny it, who either do not know true and rooted faith, and persuade themselves that faith is nothing other than an assent to the truth, by which a person, once convinced, confesses that the word of God is true, together with that light joy with which they receive the word for a time; but as for the acceptance of grace, the apprehension of Christ, hunger and thirst for righteousness, spiritual poverty, the renunciation of desires, the writing of the law of God on the heart, and trust in and fear of God, they never even dream of these. Or else, making the victory of faith depend on the changeableness of the will, they do not dare to assert certainty for it, to draw consolation from it, or to impart it to the tempted; and thus, by denying what is to be given, they show that it need not even be sought or prayed for. They make people proud for the present, persuaded of grace from faith, the offspring of their own free will, and for the future either despairing and wavering, if they desire certainty, or sluggish and listless, if they despise it.

units.la: XCVI. Sed persuasio tamen illa fidei in hac vita non eum certitudinis gradum assequitur, qui omnem contrarii formidinem perpetuò excludat.
units.tr: XCVI. But that persuasion of faith does not, in this life, reach that degree of certainty which utterly excludes all fear of the contrary.

units.la: Nam quod supra dicere occupavimus, fides optimorum etiam, imò & heroum, quales Abrahamus, David, Paulus, alii fuerunt, hic luctatur, in Cœlo demum elucta-tur. Aliquando vivida est, aliquando languida, aliquando, ut in tentationibus, nulla. In donis enim spiritualibus, quibus in hac vita imbuimur, sinceritas, non graduum perfectio speclatur. Nam & fides, spiritualis illa manus, quæ reliqua omnia arripit & tractat, suos morbos & debilitates pati potest, quæ non parum certitudinem minuere & de ea delibare possunt. Ipsa quidem promissionum Divinarum veritas immoto semper talo stat, nec concuti unquam potest. Sed applicatio & assumptio illarum experimentalibus indiciis, per privatam hominis conscientiam pensitatis nititur. Ubi cor humanum altos nimis recessus habens & adeò ידע כפש supplantans, lamosum præ omni re, & incurabiliter ægrum, ut solus Deus illud cognoscere perfectè possit, Jerem. XVII. 9. 10. haud raro sibi ipsi diffidit, & experimentalia indicia in dubium revocat.
units.tr: For what we have already undertaken to say above is that the faith even of the best, indeed of heroes such as Abraham, David, Paul, and others, struggles here and only in heaven is it finally victorious. At times it is lively, at times languid, and at times, as in temptations, it is absent altogether. For in the spiritual gifts with which we are endowed in this life, sincerity is looked for, not perfection of degree. For faith too, that spiritual hand which grasps and handles all other things, can suffer its own diseases and weaknesses, which can considerably diminish certainty and take something away from it. The truth of the divine promises itself stands always on an unmoving heel and can never be shaken. But the application and assumption of those promises rests on experiential signs weighed by the private conscience of a person. Where the human heart, having deep and too hidden recesses, and supplanting so that it knows [ידע] no one, is more crooked than all things and incurably sick, so that only God can know it perfectly (Jer. 17:9, 10), it very often distrusts itself and calls the experiential signs into doubt.

units.la: Unde non æqualiter semper vegeta & valida consolatio, & de gratia Dei atque æterna salute persuasio in promptu est. Nam & ipsa fidei Catholicæ principia, utcunque ex revelatione in se clara, cùm tamen per certitudinem non evidentiæ, sed adhæsionis nobis innotescant, non ejusmodi æquabilem assensus firmitatem, qualem mathematicæ demonstrationes & communes notiones habent, apud fideles sortiuntur. In intuendis enim illis, ex carnalis nostræ diffidentiæ reliquiis vapores subinde oboriuntur, per quos Divinæ, immutabilis veritatis lumen quodammodo refringi, vel obscurari nobis videtur. Quantò igitur crebrior & diuturnior in personali sua fiducia intuenda singulorum fidelium, eorum inprimis, qui in secundis adhuc consistunt, hallucinatio est. Quorum quidem oculi semper caligarent, nisi & hanc communem fidei Catholicæ revelationem, & illam propriam subsumentis conscientiæ applicationem Spiritus Dei, qui ... infirmitatibus nostris coopitulatur, Rom. VIII. 26. & spiritui nostro contestificatur, quòd sumus filii Dei & hæredes, ibid. v. 16. 17. firmaret, & cordibus applicaret. Hoc autem ipsum Spiritus S. testimonium, etsi quoad testem, & semen ipsum in corde credentis nunquam extinguatur, quoad fructum tamen vel sensum vel se subducit, ut nobis infirmitas nostra pateat: vel ad tempus ingratitudine & securitate nostra tantùm non obruitur.
