units.tr: Hence a consolation that is not always equally vigorous and robust, and a persuasion about the grace of God and eternal salvation, is not always at hand. For even the principles of the Catholic faith, however clear they may be in themselves from revelation, since they are known to us not by evidence but by adherence, do not obtain among the faithful that even firmness of assent which mathematical demonstrations and common notions have. For when they look upon those truths, vapours arise from the remnants of our carnal distrust, through which the light of the divine and unchangeable truth seems in some way to be refracted or obscured for us. Therefore the more frequent and the more lasting is the hallucination when individual believers look upon their own personal confidence, especially those who still stand among the beginners. Their eyes would indeed always be dim, unless the Spirit of God, who helps our weakness (Rom. 8:26), and who bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God and heirs (ibid. vv. 16, 17), strengthened that common revelation of the Catholic faith as well as that proper application of the assuming conscience, and applied both to the hearts. This testimony of the Holy Spirit itself, although as to the witness and the seed itself in the heart of the believer it is never extinguished, nevertheless as to its fruit or its sense it withdraws itself, so that our weakness may be laid open to us; or for a time it is scarcely overwhelmed by our ingratitude and our complacency.

units.la: XCVII. Inprimis indiciorum experimentalium certitudo & gratiæ Dei persuasio, tentationum velut nube quadam occultatur & oppugnatur.
units.tr: XCVII. First, the certainty of experiential signs and the persuasion of God's grace are, as if by some cloud of temptations, hidden and assailed.

units.la: Eæ sunt partim afflictiones, quæ malum poenæ intentare videntur; partim perversæ concupiscentiæ nostræ, quæ malum culpæ & reatum imprimunt; partim Diaboli laquei & insultus, quibus nos utroque in genere illo infestat. Præcipua verò palæstra in carnis & spiritus collutatione est. In qua lucta cùm spiritus carnem vincit, tum verò vivificit fides, & triumphum canit. Quis nos separabit à charitate Christi? Rom. VIII. 35. Sin, quod crebrò fit, spiritus delassatus & fractus ad tempus succumbit, vel afflictionum malo nimiùm premitur, vel graviorum peccatorum maculis fœdatur, facilè tum spiritualis consolatio intercluditur; & Divini vultus lumen abscondi-tur. tur. Jobus certè de sagittis & terroribus Domini contra se militantibus quiritari cap. VI. 4. necesse habuit. Et Ecclesia Dei : Iniquè, inquit, egimus, & ad iracundiam provocavimus. Texisti te ira, & persecutus es nos. Occidisti, non usus es misericordia. Tegmen nube fecisti,ne transeat oratio,Thren. III. 42-45. Ubi altius tentationum fluctus surgunt, non tantùm suavis hæc persuasio exulat,sed contraria etiam succedit,qua turbati sancti Deum ceu crudelem aspiciunt, & in inferorum portas sibi ruituri videntur. Unde Jobi illæ desperabundæ voces : Pereat dies ,in qua natus sum, cap.III.2. Verteris mihi לאכזר in hostem immanem; valore manus tuæ infestas me, cap.XXX.21. Et Davidis illa vox: Dixi in præcipitatione mea; Excisus sum ab oculis tuis, Psal.XXXI.23.
units.tr: These temptations are partly afflictions, which seem to threaten the evil of punishment; partly our perverse lusts, which impress the evil of guilt and liability; and partly the snares and assaults of the Devil, with which he harasses us in both of those ways. The chief arena, however, is the wrestling of flesh and spirit. In this struggle, when the spirit overcomes the flesh, faith then quickens and sings of triumph: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?" (Rom. 8:35). But if, as often happens, the spirit is weary and broken and for a time gives way, either pressed down by the weight of afflictions or defiled by the stains of graver sins, then spiritual consolation is easily cut off, and the light of the divine countenance is hidden. Job certainly had to complain "of the arrows and terrors of the Lord fighting against him" (Job 6:4). And the Church of God says: "We have acted wickedly and provoked anger. You have covered yourself with anger and pursued us. You have slain and not spared. You have covered yourself with a cloud, so that prayer cannot pass through" (Lam. 3:42–44). When the waves of temptation rise higher, not only does this sweet persuasion vanish, but its opposite takes its place, so that the troubled saints look upon God as cruel and seem to themselves about to rush into the gates of hell. Hence those despairing words of Job: "Let the day perish on which I was born" (Job 3:2); "You have turned against me into a cruel enemy [לאכזר]; with the might of your hand you oppose me" (Job 30:21). And that cry of David: "I said in my haste, I am cut off from your eyes" (Ps. 31:22).

units.la: XCVIII. Neque tamen anxia ista & fere desperabunda tristitia cum certitudine & salute filiorum Dei pugnat. Nam afficiuntur illa, non ut perdantur, sed ut salventur. Placet enim sapientiæ Dei hoc modo illos in notitiam sui perducere, eorum fidem, patientiam,humilitatem,desiderium gratiæ exercere & probare; atque eadem etiam opera memorandi hujus fati gnaris exemplum proponere,quod intuentes discant tela omnipotentis Dei metuere, peccata horrescere , ad gratiam & amicitiam Dei suspirare, & credere illa, quæ in Scripturis de æterno impiorum angore leguntur. Tum etiam ipsi sic tentati medios inter angores fidei, patientiæ , & tenerrimi erga Deum amoris, quandoque etiam spei testimonia edunt. Dicam Deo, petræ meæ : Ut quid oblitus es mei? Cur dejecta es anima mea ? Expecta Deum, quia adhuc eum confitebor, Psal.XLII.10.12. Ac licèt ad salutem necessaria sit fames & sitis justitiæ,remissionis peccatorum desiderium , consolatio fidei salutaris effectus , non tamen homogeneus perpetuus& æquabiliter vividus æquè necessarius est,quia pia mens simul Deum & Salvatorem suum vehementer amare , gratiam Dei fervidissimè optare, & fiduciam in Christo ponere; simul horum omnium conscientiam & sensum vividum ad tempus amittere potest. Atqui esurientibus & sitientibus justitiam beatitudo,pauperibus spiritu Regnum Cœlorum,lugentibus consolatio,fatigatis & oneratis refocillatio, plangentibus justitia,contritis,confractis & trepidantibus gratiosus Dei intuitus promittitur,Matth.V. 3.4.6. XI.28. Luc.XVIII.13.14. Psal.LI. 19. Esaj.LXVI.5. Cùmque salutis nostræ fulcrum non sit robur humanum , sed gratia Dei in infirmitate hominum potens,& quæ ideo sufficere nobis debet,2. Cor.XII.9. non est,quòd ob infirmitatem nostram desperemus & hastam abjiciamus.
units.tr: XCVIII. Yet this anxious and almost despairing sorrow does not conflict with the certainty and salvation of the sons of God. For these things are inflicted not so that they may perish, but so that they may be saved. For it pleases the wisdom of God to lead them in this way to the knowledge of themselves, to exercise and prove their faith, patience, humility, and desire for grace; and also, by the same work, to set before those who know this experience an example to be remembered, so that, looking upon it, they may learn to fear the arrows of almighty God, to shudder at sin, to long for the grace and friendship of God, and to believe those things which are read in the Scriptures about the eternal anguish of the wicked. Then also those who are so tempted, in the midst of anguish, bear witnesses of faith, patience, and most tender love toward God, and sometimes also of hope: "I will say to God, my rock: Why have you forgotten me? Why is my soul cast down? Wait for God, for I shall yet praise him" (Ps. 42:10–12). And although hunger and thirst for righteousness, the desire for forgiveness of sins, and the comfort of saving faith are necessary for salvation, a constant and evenly lively sense of these is not equally necessary, because a pious mind can at the same time love God and its Saviour most ardently, desire the grace of God most fervently, and place its trust in Christ, yet for a time lose the consciousness and lively feeling of all these things. And yet "blessedness is promised to those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the kingdom of heaven to the poor in spirit, comfort to those who mourn, refreshment to the weary and burdened, justice to those who lament, and a gracious look of God to the contrite, the broken, and the trembling" (Matt. 5:3, 4, 6; 11:28; Luke 18:13, 14; Ps. 51:19; Isa. 66:5). And since the support of our salvation is not human strength, but "the grace of God, which is powerful in the weakness" of men, and which therefore ought to be sufficient for us (2 Cor. 12:9), there is no reason for us to despair because of our weakness and to throw away the spear.

units.la: XCIX. Sicut verò in natura , ita etiam in gratia,nube pulsa,clarior dies it,& morbi in posterum salutares sunt. Fideles enim denique è gravium tentationum fluctibus emergentes non tantùm eandem,quæ pœne suffocata erat, fiduciam resuscitant, sed majorem etiam ejus gradum acquirunt,ab exercitio fortiores, à victoria lætiores evadunt. Quorum etiam ossa in lucta confracta firmiorem in modum consolidantur. Facies me audire hilaritatem & laetitiam. Gaudebunt ossa, quæ contrivisti, Psal.LI. 10. Quia enim hominis regeniti vita & status spiritualis est , & cum peccati vel tentationis vi abripitur, quasi contra naturam distinetur, spiritus facilè ad ingenium suum redit,& priorem suam de paterna misericordia Dei fiduciam recognoscit. Quod Sanctorum exempla probant, qui certamina sua vehementiora denique in vivæ fidei testificatione definentia expresserunt. Ita Jonas in utero ceti. Abjectus sum è conspectu oculorum tuorum ; veruntamen rursus videbo sanctum Templum tuum, Jon. II. 5. Paulus : Miser ego homo, quis me liberabit à corpore mortis hujus? Gratias ago Deo per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum,Rom. VII.24.25. Anima enim anhela,& reconciliationem paternam sitiens,ad aquæ vivæ fontem avidius accurrit, & qua fruitione Dei placati aliquantum se privari gemebunda sensit , eam posthac avidius suaviùsque degustat. Inde fidei semen in se agnoscit, cujus vi ad ipsos fidei ruinas resarciendas exsurgit. Cujus quidem radix ipsa concussione crescit, & novas fibras emittit: Unde majoris certitudinis propagines succrescunt. Nam ex hac collu&tatione & afflictione patientiam discit,qua donatur;patientia probationem, qua se explorat ; probatio spem non pudefacientem efficit , Rom. V. 3.4.5. Qua fretus animum ad futuras tentationes fortiùs superandas munit. Qui de tantis periculis nos eripuit & eruit ; in quem speramus,quòd adhuc eripiet , 2. Cor. I. 10. Hæc ergo Dei sapientia & bonitas est,quòd peccatorem non finit perire,sed se in eo glorificare volens,id agit,ut cognoscatur & misericors maximè,& potentissimus & sanctissimus , & justissimus , & in sua sanctitate & justitia,quam naturaliter peccator horret,peccatori ipsi amabilissimus. Atque eundem in finem peccatori dat testimonium justitiæ & ἐλπίδος spei de æterna beatitudine , ut cum gaudio perpetuo omnes cruces & afflictiones sustineat,Deum glorificet,eíque in vita & morte gratias agat.
units.tr: XCIX. But just as in nature, so also in grace, when the cloud is driven away, the day comes brighter, and the illnesses are in the future healthful. For the faithful, emerging at last from the waves of grave temptations, not only revive the same confidence which had nearly been suffocated, but also acquire a greater degree of it, and come out stronger from the exercise and more joyful from the victory. Their bones, broken in the struggle, are also knit together more firmly: "You will make me hear joy and gladness; the bones which you have crushed will rejoice" (Ps. 51:8 [Vulg. 51:10]). For since the life and spiritual state of a regenerate man is such that, when it is carried away by the force of sin or temptation, it is drawn away as if contrary to its nature, the spirit easily returns to its own disposition and recognises its earlier confidence in the Father's mercy of God. This the examples of the saints prove, who, having expressed their most vehement struggles, at last ended them in the testimony of a living faith. So Jonah in the belly of the whale: "I am cast out from before your eyes; yet I shall again look upon your holy temple" (Jonah 2:4 [Vulg. 2:5]). Paul: "Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death? I thank God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom. 7:24, 25). For the panting soul, thirsting for the Father's reconciliation, runs more eagerly to the fountain of living water, and, having felt with groaning that it was somewhat deprived of the enjoyment of God's favour, tastes it more eagerly and sweetly afterwards. Hence it recognises in itself the seed of faith, by whose power it rises up to repair the very ruins of faith. Indeed, the root of this faith grows by the very shaking and puts forth new fibres, from which shoots of greater certainty spring up. For from this wrestling and affliction it learns "patience," by which it is endowed; "patience" produces "proof," by which it tests itself; and "proof" produces "hope that does not put to shame" (Rom. 5:3, 4, 5). Relying on this, it fortifies its mind to overcome future temptations more bravely. "He who has delivered us from so great dangers, and does deliver us, in whom we hope that he will yet deliver us" (2 Cor. 1:10). This, then, is the wisdom and goodness of God: that he does not allow the sinner to perish, but, wishing to glorify himself in him, he works so that he may be known as most merciful, most powerful, most holy, and most just, and, in his holiness and justice, which the sinner by nature shudders at, most lovable to the sinner himself. And to the same end he gives the sinner a testimony of righteousness and of hope [ἐλπίδος] of eternal blessedness, so that with perpetual joy he may bear all crosses and afflictions, glorify God, and give him thanks in life and in death.

units.la: C. De certitudine hac gratiæ & salutis veteres non æquè clarè & diserte involutam animi sui notionem explicarunt. Negat Augustinus de Doctr. Christ. lib. III. 32. revera esse de corpore Christi, qui non sunt in æternum cum ipso mansuri. Idem de Verb. Dom. serm. 28. Non est arrogantia ,sed fides, prædicare ea , quæ accepisti. Et in Psal.32. conc. 3. An temerè dicimus faciendo Deum nobis in possessionem ? Dicat anima secura,dicat, Deus meus es tu; quia dicit animæ nostræ : Salus tua ego sum. Idem in Joh. tract. 5. Nemo interroget hominem. Redeat ad cor suum. Si ibi inveniat charitatem,securus sit, quia transiit à morte ad vitam. Et de Trin. lib. XIII. 1. Fidem ipsam videt quisque esse in corde suo , si credit , vel non esse, si non credit. Et decantata illa aureola Chrysostomi in Rom. 14. sunt: Quando spiritus testatur, quænam relinquitur ambiguitas? Nec non ejusdem illa Homil. 1. in 2. Cor. Si Deus hac arrha nobis prius data reliquam hereditatis possessionem non adjiceret , ipse arrhæ perditæ damnum pateretur. Cyprianus de Immort. Deus , inquit , tibi è mundo discedenti immortalitatem pollicetur ,& tu dubitas ? Hoc est Deum omnino non nosse, hoc est Christum credentium magistrum peccato incredulitatis offendere, hoc est in Ecclesia constitutam fidem in domo fidei non habere. Et paulò post. Ejus est mortem timere,
units.tr: C. Concerning this certainty of grace and salvation, the ancients did not explain the notion, involved in their minds, as clearly and plainly as they might have. Augustine denies that those who are not going to remain with him for ever are really of the body of Christ (On Christian Doctrine, bk. 3, ch. 32). The same author, in his sermon on the Lord's words (serm. 28): "It is not arrogance but faith to proclaim those things which you have received." And in Ps. 32, sermon 3: "Do we rashly say that God is ours in possession? Let the secure soul say, let it say: You are my God; for he says to our soul: I am your salvation." The same, in his Tractate 5 on John: "Let no one question a man. Let him return to his own heart. If he finds charity there, let him be secure, because he has passed from death to life." And in On the Trinity, bk. 13, ch. 1: "Each one sees faith itself in his own heart, that it is there if he believes, or that it is not there if he does not believe." And the famous little golden saying of Chrysostom on Romans 14: "When the Spirit bears witness, what ambiguity remains?" Nor is that other saying of his in the first homily on 2 Corinthians: "If God, having first given this earnest to us, did not add the remaining possession of the inheritance, he himself would suffer the loss of the lost earnest." Cyprian, in On Mortality: "God, you say, promises you immortality as you depart from the world, and do you doubt? This is to not know God at all; this is to offend Christ, the teacher of believers, by the sin of unbelief; this is to not have, in the house of faith, the faith established in the Church." And a little later: "It belongs to him to fear death."

units.la: Neque tamen ita evertitur.
units.tr: Yet it is not overturned in this way.

units.la: Sed resuscitatur tandem & confirmatur magis.
units.tr: Rather, it is at last restored and made firmer.

units.la: Ecclesiæ veteris & Scholasticorum de certitudine Gratiæ sensus. mere, qui ad Christum transire nolit: ejus ad Christum nolle ire, qui non se credit cum Christo regnare incipere. Ambrosius de Sacr. lib. IV. 5. Præsume non de operatione tua, sed de Christi gratia. Gregorius M. Moral. lib. XXXI. 23. juīti viri securitatem cum Leone comparat, quia cum contra se quoslibet insurgere conspicit, ad mentis suæ confidentiam redit, & scit, quod cunctos adversantes superet, quia illum solum diligit, quem invitus nullo modo amittit. Ex his aliisque similibus interpretanda sunt, quæ iisdem incautius dicta exciderunt. Quale illud Chrysostomi in Rom. 8: 33. promiscuè dictum: Ἐν ἀδήλω τῷ ἡμέτερῳ ἐπηκεῖ ἑως ἐαυτῆς ἀναπνοῆς Incertus est status noster usque ad extremum halitum. q. d. Vulgò sic agimus, ut nec nobis, nec alii certò appareat, an revera simus filii Dei. Loquitur de σωσυνδεσμοῖς temporariis, qui claudicant in fide, neque fodiunt usque ad radicem, ut in ea fundamentum ponant. Qui habentes initium qualecunque, ad perfectionem non perveniunt, sed deficiunt. Alii Divina miseratione jam jam morituri hoc consequuntur, ut spes bona non in arena, sed in rupe fundata in ipsis exoriatur. Hi ante ultimum certamen, quo terrorem mortis bona spe superant, de fide sua certi esse non possunt. Qui Patrum ætatem secuti sunt, Scholastici, sic fluctuant illi, ut tamen ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ ἀλλά σωτηρίας salutis certitudinem non ex principiis innatis, sed ex revelatis in Scriptura colligi, asserant. Nota est regula illa vetus Scoti, quam retinuerunt recentiores etiam Vega, Medina, Canus, alii sequuntur, quòd Conclusio ex una propositione credita, & altera evidenti ex fide certa fit. Jam propositio illa: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur; ipsius Christi, adeóque credenda. Atqui ego credo & baptizatus sum, propositio evidens est, & Spiritus S. atque conscientiæ testimonio nititur. Ergo ego salvabor, conclusio ex fide certa erit. Etiam Eisengremius ex Scholasticis æquè ac ex Patribus certitudinem salutis demonstravit. Fatendum nihilominus, Scholasticos suo more omnia commiscere, & vix sibi ipsis constare satis.
units.tr: The view of the ancient Church and the Schoolmen on the certainty of grace. ...he who is unwilling to pass over to Christ; and to be unwilling to go to Christ is the mark of one who does not believe that he has begun to reign with Christ. Ambrose, On the Sacraments IV.5: "Presume not on your own works, but on the grace of Christ." Gregory the Great, Morals XXXI.23, compares the security of the righteous man to that of a lion, because when he sees himself attacked on every side, he returns to the confidence of his mind and knows that he overcomes all his adversaries, since he loves only the one whom he never loses against his will. Passages of this kind, and others like them, must be interpreted in the light of those statements which were carelessly let slip by the same writers. Such is that remark of Chrysostom on Romans 8:33, made in passing: "Our state is uncertain until our last breath" [Ἐν ἀδήλῳ τῷ ἡμετέρῳ ... ἕως ἐσχάτης ἀναπνοῆς]. That is, as a rule we live in such a way that neither we nor others can clearly see whether we are really children of God. He is speaking of temporary believers, who limp in faith and do not dig down to the root so as to lay a foundation in it. Having some beginning of whatever kind, they do not come to perfection but fail. Others, by the divine mercy, are about to die, and through this obtain that a good hope is founded not on sand but on rock within themselves. These people, before the final struggle in which they overcome the terror of death by good hope, cannot be certain of their faith. Those who followed the age of the Fathers, the Schoolmen, waver in such a way that nevertheless, as a rule [ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ], they assert that the certainty of salvation is gathered not from innate principles but from what is revealed in Scripture. That old rule of Scotus is well known, which the more recent writers also retained: Vega, Medina, Canus and others follow it, namely that "a conclusion is made certain by faith from one proposition believed and another evident." Now that proposition, "He who believes and is baptized will be saved" (Mark 16:16), is Christ's own and therefore to be believed. But "I believe and I am baptized" is an evident proposition, resting on the testimony of the Holy Spirit and of conscience. Therefore "I shall be saved" will be a conclusion certain from faith. Eisengrein also, among the Schoolmen no less than among the Fathers, demonstrated the certainty of salvation. Nevertheless it must be admitted that the Schoolmen, after their manner, mix everything together and scarcely agree with themselves.

units.la: CI. Post Reformationem Pontificii & Remonstrantes in diversum abierunt tum à veritate, tum inter se.
units.tr: CI. After the Reformation the Papists and the Remonstrants have departed in different directions, both from the truth and from one another.

units.la: In Concilio Tridentino Ambrosius Catharinus & Marinarus pro certitudine gratiæ gravissimis argumentis pugnarunt. Inde natus ille Concilii cothurnus est, quo Sess. VI. can. 13. sic Patres illi sanxerunt: Si quis dixerit, omni homini ad remissionem peccatorum assequendam necessarium esse, ut credat certò, & absque ulla hæsitatione propriæ infirmitatis & indispositionis peccata sibi esse remissa, anathema sit. Quo de canonis sensu ipsimet adversarii disceptant. Ibidem verò cap. 9. disertius negant, quemquam valere scire certitudine fidei, cui non possit subesse falsum, se gratiam Dei esse consecutum. Sed sensum decretorum illorum adversarii ipsi etiam post Concilium sibi discordes quique ad sensum suum detorquent. Ac nominatim ad suum etiam detorquent Catharinus, Marinarus, Eisengremius, certitudinem salutis etiam post Concilium propugnantes, quasi Concilii definientis, neminem valere certitudine fidei, cui non possit subesse falsum, scire se gratiam Dei consecutum esse, verba non omnem fidei de propria gratia & justitia certitudinem fidei Catholicæ tollunt: De eo quicquid fiat, frustra certè Walenburgii Pontificios inter & nos, detortis utrorumque sententiis instituere consensum satagunt. Non potest enim Ecclesia Romana, quæ fidem in ignorantia, & fiduciam justificationis in justitiæ propriæ habitu, adeóque dispositione hominis reponit, certitudinem gratiæ & salutis non oppugnare, & perpetuæ dubitationi atque timori locum cedere. Stabilita etiam semel hac de salute fiducia protinus Missa, invocatio Sanctorum, peregrinationes, purgatorium, supererogatio, indulgentiæ & cæteræ ejusdem ἀιἀγέοντεδίας menses numulariæ, velut Dagon coram arca, concideren. Ideo Gregorius de Valentia Tom. II. disp. 8. q. 4. punct. 4. triplicem certitudinem distinguit, quarum prima non tantùm actum formidandi, sed etiam potentiam, quandiu quis deliberato de re substrata cogitat, & eadem deliberanti argumenta succurrunt: Secunda actum formidandi, non potentiam; excludit. Si tamen, ut raro vel nunquam accidat, ut quis moraliter prudens vacillet, quin inveniat aliquid, quo ad se redeat: Tertia probabilis tantùm sit ex signis & conjecturis, quibus cùm satis confirmatus videatur fidelis, facilè meritóque dubitare possit, an id, quod credit, an oppositum verius sit. Primam extraordinariè illuminatis, B. Mariæ & Angelis: Secundam iis, qui à mundo longiùs se summoverunt, & Dei amori & familiaritati arctiùs innexi sunt: Tertiam promiscuæ fidelium sorti tribuit. Graviter certè Lutherus in Genes. XLI. definivit: Etiamsi nihil præterea peccatum fuisset in doctrina Pontificia quam quod docuerunt, nos debere vagari & fluctuare ambigentes & dubios de remissione peccatorum, gratia & salute nostra, justas tamen haberemus causas, cur ab Ecclesia infideli nos sejungeremus. Cujus tamen discipuli nonnulli licèt ipsialem fiduciam adversus fluctuantem Tridentinorum hæsitationem ex firmissimis in Christo promissionibus optimè muniunt, non plenè tamen fermentum Pontificium expurgant, dum eam ad præsentem fidelium conditionem restringunt, nec certi aliquid de futura perseverantia spondere audent.
units.tr: At the Council of Trent Ambrose Catharinus and Marinarus fought for the certainty of grace with the weightiest arguments. From this arose that buskin of the Council by which those Fathers decreed in Session VI, canon 13: "If anyone shall say that it is necessary for every man, in order to obtain the remission of sins, that he believe with certainty, and without any doubt whatever, that his sins have been forgiven him, let him be anathema." The adversaries themselves dispute about the sense of this canon. In the same place, chapter 9, they deny more plainly "that anyone can know with the certainty of faith, in which there can be no falsehood, that he has obtained the grace of God." But even after the Council the adversaries themselves, who are not in agreement with one another, twist the sense of those decrees to suit their own. Catharinus, Marinarus and Eisengrein in particular, who even after the Council defended the certainty of salvation, twist them to their own sense, as if the words of the Council, defining that "no one can know with the certainty of faith, in which there can be no falsehood, that he has obtained the grace of God," did not remove all certainty of faith concerning one's own grace and righteousness. Whatever be the case here, Walenburch and others strive in vain to establish an agreement between the Papists and us by twisting the opinions of both sides. For the Roman Church, which places faith in ignorance and confidence of justification in a habit of one's own righteousness, and so in man's own disposition, cannot fail to attack the certainty of grace and salvation, and must give place to perpetual doubt and fear. Once this confidence of salvation is established, the Mass, the invocation of the saints, pilgrimages, purgatory, works of supererogation, indulgences and all the other money-changers' trades of the same kind would straightway fall, like Dagon before the ark. Therefore Gregory of Valentia, Tome II, disputation 8, question 4, point 4, distinguishes three kinds of certainty. The first excludes not only the act of fearing but also the power of fearing, as long as a man thinks deliberately about the matter in question and arguments come to him as he deliberates. The second excludes the act of fearing but not the power; this happens if, as rarely or never occurs, a morally prudent man should waver without finding something by which he returns to himself. The third is merely probable, resting on signs and conjectures, by which, although a believer seems sufficiently confirmed, he can easily and rightly doubt whether what he believes or its opposite is the truer. He assigns the first to those who are enlightened in an extraordinary way, to the Blessed Virgin and the angels; the second to those who have withdrawn far from the world and are more closely bound to the love and familiarity of God; the third he assigns to the common lot of the faithful. Luther certainly defined the matter gravely in his commentary on Genesis 41: "Even if nothing else had been sinful in Papist doctrine than what they taught, we ought to wander and waver, doubting and uncertain about the forgiveness of sins, our grace and our salvation; yet we would have just grounds for separating ourselves from the unfaithful Church." Some of his disciples, although they fortify this confidence well against the wavering hesitation of the Tridentines from the most firm promises in Christ, do not fully purge out the Papist leaven, since they restrict it to the present condition of the faithful and dare not promise anything certain about future perseverance.

units.la: CII. Neque minùs certitudinem gratiæ & salutis Remonstrantes exagitant. Nam Arminius, quòd fideles esse possint certi, se à fide non defecturos, unquam pro Catholico dogmate, vel ejus contrarium pro hæretico habitum esse pernegat. Ajunt iidem tum posse hominem certum esse de salute, at non absolutè, verùm sub conditione, si perseveret ad finem usque: tum posse eundem absolutè certum esse, quòd in gratia sit, utpote de quo dubitari ex natura fidei & efficacia Spiritus obsignantis nequeat; quòd verò in gratia perseveraturus sit usque ad finem vitæ, nemini certum esse posse sine speciali revelatione, asserunt. Addunt, doctrinam de absoluta salutis & perseverantiæ certitudine ex natura & indole sua esse carnis pulvinar, pietati, bonis moribus, precibus, aliisque sanctis exercitiis noxiam, contra de ea dubitare, esse laudabile. Ita sublata solida consolatione in hac vita omni, Pontificiorum dubitationem inducere in Ecclesiam religioni non duxerunt. CIII. Nul Post Reformationem palam eam oppugnant Pontificii. Et reducto in eorum castra Remonstrantes. lium eos condemnat, credentes in Christum, in quo justificati conscientiae tranquillitatem habent. Et tunc, uti scite Augustinus, nos in ista vita, in qua eorde creditur ad justitiam, non reprehendit cor nostrum, si eadem fides non negligit reprehendere peccatum nostrum. Sed certitudinem gratiae maximos inter Sathanae insultus non depositu Jobus, dicens: Si occidere me Dominus voluerit, tamen in eo sperabo, cap. XIII. 15. Scio, quod redemptor meus vivat: In carne mea eum videbo, cap. XI. 25. David quoque: Non moriar sed vivam, et narrabo opera Domini, Psal. CXVIII. 17. De Pauli certitudine supra. Quosdam etiam perfectissimos, quales hi fuerunt, certitudinem gratiae ex speciali revelatione habuisse, ipsi etiam adversarii asserunt. Argumentari ab inhaerentis puritatis conscientia ad diffidentiam de superveniente Dei misericordia hoc modo: Quia ipse mihi diffido; ergo de promissis Dei in Christo nil certi mihi polliceri possum; perinde est absurdum, ac si ex altera parte quis nugaretur: Nullius rei mala mihi conscius sum in hac vel illa causa, ob quam juste me homines reprehendere possent: Ergo ἀναμάρτητος sum.
units.tr: CII. The Remonstrants likewise harass the certainty of grace and salvation no less. For Arminius denies outright that the faithful can be certain that they will never fall away from the faith, and he holds that the opposite of this has been regarded as a heretical dogma, while the Catholic dogma is that it is certain. The same men also claim that a man can be certain of his salvation, but not absolutely; rather under the condition that he persevere to the end. They also claim that the same man can be absolutely certain that he is in grace, since this cannot be doubted from the nature of faith and the efficacy of the sealing Spirit; but that he will persevere in grace to the end of his life, they assert, no one can be certain without a special revelation. They add that the doctrine of the absolute certainty of salvation and perseverance is, by its nature and character, a pillow for the flesh, harmful to piety, good morals, prayers and other holy exercises; and that on the contrary it is laudable to doubt it. Thus, by removing all solid consolation in this life, they did not think it wrong to bring the Papists' doubt into the Church. CIII. Since the Reformation the Papists openly attack it, and the Remonstrants have gone back into their camp. Scripture condemns none of those who believe in Christ, in whom the justified have tranquillity of conscience. And then, as Augustine rightly says, "in this life, in which the heart believes unto righteousness, our heart does not reproach us if that same faith does not neglect to reproach our sin." But Job did not lay down the certainty of grace amid the greatest assaults of Satan, saying: "Though the Lord should wish to slay me, yet I will hope in him" (Job 13:15); "I know that my redeemer lives; I shall see him in my flesh" (Job 19:25). So also David: "I shall not die but live, and shall declare the works of the Lord" (Psalm 118:17). Concerning the certainty of Paul we have spoken above. Even the adversaries themselves assert that certain most perfect men, such as these were, had the certainty of grace through a special revelation. To argue from the conscience of inherent purity to distrust of the mercy of God that is coming, in this way: "Because I distrust myself, therefore I can promise myself nothing certain from God's promises in Christ"; this is just as absurd as if, on the other side, someone should trifle thus: "I am conscious of no evil in this or that matter for which men could justly reproach me: therefore I am sinless [ἀναμάρτητος]."

units.la: CV. Tertia classis ex iis Scripturae testimoniis conflatur, quae ex parte nostri varias conditiones, sed quas incertas, quoad impletionem nostram esse pertendunt, ad firmitatem certitudinis requirunt. Invenies Dominum, si toto corde eum quaesiveris, Deut. IV. 29. Si impius poenitentiam egerit ab omnibus peccatis suis, vivendo vivet, Ezech. XVIII. 27. Vos amici mei eritis, si feceritis, quae vobis praecipio, Joh. XV. 14. Passim similia occurrunt; sed aliena prorsus, quia de conditionum impletione licet non numeris omnibus absoluta, at vera tamen, seria et sincera certi esse possumus. Quomodo Eunuchus interroganti Apostolo: Credis ex toto corde? Respondit: Credo Jesum Christum esse Filium illum Dei, Actor. VIII. 37. et Petrus Christo quaerenti; Diligis me? respondit: Domine tu nosti omnia. Tu nosti, quod te diligam, Joh. XXI. 17. Intellexerunt igitur, quod crediderint et dilexerint; et conditionem intellectam observarunt. Norunt enim, fidelem esse, qui promisit, eumque subventurum, ut impleat, quod promisit; et linum fumigans eundem non extinguere, nec calamum quassatum confringere, Esaj. XLII. 3. Dat enim cor novum, et Spiritum ponit in praecordiis, etc. ut ambulemus in statutis ejus, et judicia ejus faciamus, Ezech. XXXVI. 26. 27. Cur vero dubitemus de eo, quod Spiritum S. in nobis operari sentimus, videmus, experimur ipsi? Nos credidimus, inquiunt Apostoli, et scimus, te esse Christum, Filium Dei viventis, Joh. VI. 69. Accepimus, ita fideles omnes, Spiritum, qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus, quae Deus nobis gratificatus est, 1. Cor. II. 12. Scite Barnesius, Monachus Benedictinus: Cum fides sit scientia salutis, et credere sit quoddam scire, sequitur, quod quemadmodum sciens sit, se scire, ita quisquis ad salutem credit, credit se credere salutari fide. Ex quo efficitur; pie in Christum credentes certos esse de sua fide justificante, qua justi sunt. CVI. Non majus pondus quarta testimoniorum classis habet, qua quae post peractam poenitentiam incertam remissionem peccatorum facere videntur, dubitandi particulis, quales sunt: Quis scit, si forte, fortasse, &c. expressis. Scin- Nullum conspirantibus in hoc errore in Scripturis praesidium est. Quinque fere testimoniorum classes illi in aciem producunt. Prima Solomonis illa continet: Quis potest dicere: Mundum est cor meum? Prov. XX. 9. Nescit homo, amore an odio dignus sit, sed omnia in futurum incerta servantur, Eccles. IX. 1. Uti Vulgatus reddit. Sed prior ille textus ἀσφαλής est, quia certitudo salutis non a justitiae inhaerentis puritate, sed a justitia Christi imputata, nec ab exacto respicentiae rigore, sed ab ejus humili sinceritate pendet. Quisquis ergo dicit; Mundum est cor meum ab impuritate inhaerente, atque ideo certus sum de Gratia Dei et salute, Pharisaeismi veneno turget. Sed dicere tamen fideles possunt, cor suum mundum esse per fidem in Christum, adeoque Christi justitia; qua lapsus et impuritas omnis tegitur et condonatur: purificatum, sincerum et ab hypocrisi purgatum, Act. XV. 9. Nam spes beatitudinis sine munditie cordis non constat, Matth. V. 8. Posterior textus et versione mala et sensu praepostero corruptus est. Nam et justi et improbi sciunt, se amore non esse dignos, et odio dignos esse. Sic autem Sapiens dicit hoc est, ad verbum: Et amorem, et odium non novit homo. Omnia sunt ante ipsos. Sensus est, hominem non habere exploratum, quam bene appetat vel averset quicquam, et quomodo id cum rationibus Divinae ordinationis conveniat: neque eum amorem et odium suum explorata scientia moderari, Deo fingente corda omnium, Psal. XXXIII. 15. Nam et amor et odium hominis in manu Dei est. Si ad Dei amorem vel odium verba referantur, sensus erit, hominem ex beneficiis Dei externis, quae et improbis communia sunt, amorem et odium Dei non cognoscere. Nam ex externo fortunae vultu Dei vultus non agnoscitur. Unde non cum fortuna, sed cum Deo sentiendum, et bonae conscientiae standum. Potest enim amor Dei ex aliis argumentis et interno statu hominis colligi. Neque etiam omnia in futurum servari incerta, Solomon dixit; sed omnia ante ipsos homines esse; hoc est, decreta esse priusquam nati sunt. Et omnia ut omnibus, hoc est, tam mala, quam bona externa simili ratione et modo bonis et malis eveniunt. CIV. Secunda classis ea testimonia comprehendit, ex quibus perfectissimos etiam certitudinem salutis sibi arrogare non sustinuisse, colligere conantur. Dixit enim, juxta Vulgatam versionem Jobus: Non reprehendit me cor meum in tota vita mea, cap. XXVII. 6. David: Judica me, Domine, quia in innocentia ingressus sum, Psal. XXVI. 1. Paulus: Nil mihi conscius sum, 1. Cor. IV. 4. Sed aliud scilicet est propriae justitiae typho inflari, aliud gratuitae reconciliationis fiducia erigi; aliud justitiam personae sibi vindicare: aliud justitiam causae. Hoc non illud sibi perfectissimi et optimi vindicarunt et jure vendicarunt: Jobi tamen verba mala iterum versione corrupta sunt. Dixit enim: Non reprehendit. Quae verba non gloriationem de ἀναμαρτησία sonant, sed hoc sibi volunt, quod cor Jobi nulla die convitiaturum, vel blasphematurum sit. Quanquam nec cor fideScindite cor vestrum, &c. Quis scit, an convertatur & poeniteat eum mali, Joel. II. 14. Odio habete malum & diligite bonum [Hebrew] forte miserebitur Jehova Deus exercituum reliquiis Josephi, Amos. V. 15. Quærite Jehovam, [Hebrew] forte abscondemini in die furoris Jehovæ, Zeph. II. 3. Respipisce, &c. [Greek] si forte remittatur tibi cogitatio cordis tui, Actor. VIII. 22. sed particulæ ejusmodi non semper dubitantium, sed excitantium, confirmantium, bona sperantium, & eventum Deo committentium sunt. Exempla 2. Reg. XIX. 4. Prov. XXIV. 18. Eccles. V. 5. Joh. V. 46. VIII. 19. Rom. XI. 21. videri possunt. Tum potissimum Scriptura particulas ejusmodi usurpat, quando peccantes retinere vult, ne se per desperationem in præcipitium abjiciant, & eosdem excitat, ut saltem cogitent de pœnitentia reputantes, fortassis illud utile iis fore in hoc & altero seculo. Fideles autem incitat ad quærendum Deum, & operam dandam justitiæ & judicio, quia fortasse id profuturum sit ipsis, ut tegantur in die iræ Domini. Ita qui agrum colit, negotiatur, piscatur, omni tempore laborat, nesciens, quando fructum laboris reportaturus sit, sed de eo non desperans. In loco Act. VIII. 22. [Greek] idem est, quod ἵνα ut remittatur: plane sicut, Phil. III. 11. [Greek] si forte perveniam, idem est quod ἵνα ut perveniam ad resurrectionem mortuorum. Quo sensu sæpe sumi Eustathius in Homerum observat. Quis enim dubitat, quin peccata pœnitentibus remittantur?
units.tr: CV. The third class is made up of those passages of Scripture which, on our side, require certain conditions for the firmness of certainty, conditions that they say are uncertain as to whether we will fulfil them. You will find the Lord if you seek him with your whole heart, Deut. 4:29. If the wicked man turns from all his sins and lives by keeping them, he shall live, Ezek. 18:27. You are my friends if you do what I command you, John 15:14. Similar passages occur everywhere. But they are wholly beside the point, because we can be certain, truly, seriously and sincerely, that the conditions have been met, even if not in every respect perfectly. So the eunuch answered the Apostle who asked, Do you believe with all your heart?: I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, Acts 8:37. And Peter, when Christ asked him, Do you love me?, answered: Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you, John 21:17. They understood, therefore, that they believed and loved, and they observed the condition they understood. For they know that he is faithful who promised, and that he will come to help them fulfil what he promised, and that he will not quench the smoking flax nor break the bruised reed, Isa. 42:3. For he gives a new heart and puts a spirit within the inward parts, etc., so that we may walk in his statutes and do his judgments, Ezek. 36:26, 27. Why then should we doubt concerning that which we ourselves feel, see and experience: that the Holy Spirit works in us? We have believed, say the Apostles, and we know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, John 6:69. We have received, says every believer, the Spirit who is from God, that we may know the things that have been freely given us by God, 1 Cor. 2:12. The Benedictine monk Barnes writes well: Since faith is the knowledge of salvation, and to believe is a kind of knowing, it follows that just as one who knows knows that he knows, so whoever believes unto salvation believes that he believes with saving faith. From this it follows that those who believe in Christ with devotion are certain of their justifying faith, by which they are righteous. CVI. The fourth class of testimonies carries no greater weight; these seem to make the remission of sins after repentance uncertain, by means of expressions of doubt, such as: Who knows, if perhaps, peradventure, etc. Those who conspire in this error have no support in the Scriptures. They bring forward nearly five classes of testimonies. The first contains that saying of Solomon: Who can say, My heart is clean? Prov. 20:9. No man knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things are kept uncertain for the future, Eccles. 9:1, as the Vulgate renders it. But that first text is secure [ἀσφαλής], because the certainty of salvation depends not on the purity of inherent righteousness but on the righteousness of Christ imputed, and not on the strictness of a completed repentance but on its humble sincerity. Whoever therefore says, My heart is clean, from inherent impurity, and so is certain of God's grace and salvation, swells with the poison of Pharisaism. Yet believers can say that their heart is clean through faith in Christ, and so through the righteousness of Christ, by which every fall and impurity is covered and forgiven: purified, sincere, and cleansed from hypocrisy, Acts 15:9. For the hope of blessedness does not stand without purity of heart, Matt. 5:8. The second text is corrupted both by a bad translation and by a perverse sense. For both the righteous and the wicked know that they are not worthy of love and that they are worthy of hatred. But the Wise Man says this, word for word: Man knows neither love nor hatred; all things are before them. The sense is that man does not have a clear knowledge of how well he likes or dislikes anything, or how this fits with the reasons of the divine ordering; nor does he govern his love and hatred by any clear knowledge, God forming the hearts of all, Ps. 33:15. For both the love and the hatred of man are in the hand of God. If the words are referred to the love or hatred of God, the sense will be that man does not recognise the love or hatred of God from the external benefits of God, which are common even to the wicked. For the face of God is not recognised from the external face of fortune. Hence one must judge not by fortune but by God, and stand by a good conscience. For the love of God can be gathered from other arguments and from the inward state of a man. Nor did Solomon say that all things are kept uncertain for the future; he said that all things are before them, that is, that they were decreed before men were born. And all things come alike to all, that is, evils and external goods alike befall good and bad by the same reason and manner. CIV. The second class comprises those testimonies from which they try to gather that even the most perfect men did not presume to claim for themselves certainty of salvation. For Job, according to the Vulgate version, said: My heart has not reproached me in all my life, ch. 27:6. David: Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my integrity, Ps. 26:1. Paul: I am conscious of nothing against myself, 1 Cor. 4:4. But clearly it is one thing to be puffed up with the pride of one's own righteousness, another to be lifted up by the confidence of gratuitous reconciliation; one thing to claim righteousness for the person, another for the cause. The most perfect and best men did not claim the former for themselves, and rightly so; but the words of Job are again corrupted by a faulty version. For he said: has not reproached. These words do not sound of boasting about [ἀναμαρτησία] sinlessness, but mean that the heart of Job would never on any day rail or blaspheme. Although not even the heart of the faithful... Rend your heart, etc. Who knows whether he will turn and repent, and the evil man?, Joel 2:14. Hate evil and love good [Hebrew], perhaps the Lord God of hosts will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph, Amos 5:15. Seek the Lord [Hebrew], perhaps you will be hidden in the day of the Lord's anger, Zeph. 2:3. Repent, etc. [Greek], if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you, Acts 8:22. But particles of this kind are not used by those who doubt, but by those who stir up, confirm, hope for good things, and commit the outcome to God. Examples may be seen at 2 Kings 19:4, Prov. 24:18, Eccles. 5:5, John 5:46, 8:19, Rom. 11:21. Scripture uses such particles chiefly when it wishes to hold back sinners, lest they throw themselves headlong into destruction through despair, and when it stirs them up to at least think about repentance, considering that perhaps this will be useful to them in this age and the next. It urges the faithful to seek God and to labour for righteousness and judgment, because perhaps it will profit them, so that they may be hidden in the day of the Lord's wrath. So too the man who tills the field, trades, fishes, labours at all times, not knowing when he will reap the fruit of his labour, yet does not despair of it. In the passage Acts 8:22 [Greek] means the same as [ἵνα] that it may be forgiven; just as in Phil. 3:11 [Greek], if perhaps I may attain, means the same as [ἵνα] that I may attain to the resurrection of the dead. Eustathius in his commentary on Homer observes that the word is often used in this sense. For who doubts that sins are forgiven to those who repent?

units.la: CVII. Ultima classis illa testimonia repræsentat, quibus confidentiam hanc, qua de loquimur, diserte concuti asseverant.
units.tr: CVII. That last class sets out the testimonies which, they assert, plainly shake the confidence we are discussing.

units.la: Beatus est homo [Hebrew] qui semper pavet, Prov. XXVIII. 14. Cum timore & tremore salutem vestram operamini, Phil. II. 12. In timore incolatus vestri tempore conversamini, I. Pet. I. 17. Sed duplex timor est, bonus & malus. Malus ille est, qui cor hominis dejicit, & spe omni defraudat. Qualis eorum est, qui Deum fugiunt, ceu crudelem & sibi infensum; nec non eorum, qui Deo blandiuntur, & malam conscientiam habent, diligentes ea, quæ in mundo sunt, propter quæ anxii sunt, & se ipsos animi discruciant. Bonus, qui Dei altitudinem & bonum ejus pavet, Hos. III. 5. & Deo rugiente timet, ibid. XI. 10. 11. & periculum considerat, in quo omnis homo constitutus est. Qui partim solicitudinem de mediis, non dubitationem & hæsitantiam de fine inculcat: partim [Greek], [Greek], præsumtionem carnalem de propriis viribus, & propriam prudentiam excludit: partim industriam, studium, curam omnem acuit, solicitos & salutis suæ studiosos Deus adjuvat, & viribus suis diffisos Divina potentia erigit. Quomodo olim icti serpentibus cum nihil in se auxilii reperirent, diffisi sibi, & auxilium solicite circumspectantes in exaltati serpentis aspectu confusi non abierunt. Ideo etiam timor talis cum gaudio conjunctus est, juxta illud Davidis: Servite Jehovæ cum timore, Psal. II. 11. & bonam conscientiam atque fiduciam parit, juxta illud ejusdem: Pavete, & ne peccetis, Psal. IV. 5. & est arca, qua conservatur omnis salus & sapientia: Erit fides temporis tui possessio salutum, sapientia & cognitionis, cujus arca est timor Domini, Esaj. XXXIII. 6. Timor enim Domini est animi perpetua humilitas, qua homo studet
units.tr: "Blessed is the man [Hebrew] who always fears," Prov. 28:14. "With fear and trembling work out your own salvation," Phil. 2:12. "Pass the time of your sojourning in fear," 1 Pet. 1:17. But there are two kinds of fear, good and bad. The bad fear is the kind that casts down a man's heart and deprives him of all hope. It belongs to those who flee from God as from a cruel enemy hostile to them, and also to those who flatter God yet have an evil conscience, who love the things of the world, on account of which they are anxious and torment their own souls. The good fear is that of the one who reveres God's height and goodness, Hos. 3:5, and who "trembles at the Lord's roaring," ibid. 11:10, 11, and who considers the peril in which every man stands. This fear urges anxious care about the means, not doubt or hesitation about the end. Partly it excludes carnal presumption about one's own strength and one's own prudence [Greek], [Greek]; partly it sharpens diligence, zeal and every care, and God helps those who are anxious and eager for their salvation, while divine power raises up those who distrust their own strength. Just as those once bitten by serpents, finding in themselves no help, and distrusting themselves, looked anxiously about for aid and were not turned away, confused, from the sight of the lifted-up serpent. For this reason such fear is also joined with joy, according to David's words: "Serve the Lord with fear," Ps. 2:11; and it produces a good conscience and confidence, according to his words again: "Tremble, and do not sin," Ps. 4:5; and it is the chest in which all salvation and wisdom is kept: "The faithfulness of your times shall be the possession of salvation, wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord is its treasure," Isa. 33:6. For the fear of the Lord is a constant humility of spirit, by which a man takes pains

units.la: spem vitæ æternam sartam tectamque habere, quæ proin tantum abest, ut hominem dubium de salute reddat, ut potius arca sit, in qua omnes thesauri Dei asservantur. Et per quod salutem operamur, illud nos de salute dubios non reddit, sed potius in spe salutis confirmat.
units.tr: to keep the hope of eternal life safe and sheltered. This fear is so far from making a man doubtful of his salvation that it is rather the chest in which all the treasures of God are kept. And that by which we work out our salvation does not make us doubtful of it, but rather confirms us in the hope of salvation.

units.la: CVIII. Neque ratio solida, sed levis argutatio est, certitudinem salutis vellicantium eo argumento, quod propositio hæc v. 9. Augustinus vere justificatus est, & salvabitur; nec immediate in verbo Dei contineatur, nec per bonam consequentiam ex eodem colligatur, adeóque certæ fidei Catholicæ certitudine esse non posset. Non contineri immediate, dubitatione caret, quia nuspiam Augustinus in verbo Dei nominatur. At nec per consequentiam ex verbo Dei colligi, probare illi contendunt, quia in Syllogismo Practico, quo illam colligi assertimus, qualis est: Omnes credentes & resipiscentes certum habent, se justificatos esse, & salvatum iri. At ego Augustinus credo & resipisco. Ergo ego Augustinus, certum habeo, me justificatum esse & salvatum iri; Minor propositio vel falsa, vel saltem fidei non sit. Falsa, quia cor hominis imperscrutabile est, Jerem. XVII. 9. multi, qui se habere putant, quod non habent, falluntur, & fidei & resipiscentiæ signa unica, opera charitatis, fallacia esse possunt, cum etiam experientia doceat, hæreticos pro defensione perfidiæ suæ mortem libenter oppetere, & possit aliquis omnia sua pauperibus largiri, qui tamen charitatem non habeat, I. Cor. XIII. 2. 3. Fidei non esse, quia fides revelatione nititur; nuspiam autem revelatum, hunc vel illum hominem vere credere & resipiscere. Cumque propositio illa minor saltem fidei non sit; Conclusionem, quæ fidei sit, exire non posse, quia Conclusio præmissam debiliorem sequatur.
units.tr: CVIII. The argument by which they try to undermine the certainty of salvation is not solid reasoning but light sophistry: namely, that the proposition "Augustine is truly justified and will be saved" is not contained in the Word of God immediately, nor can it be drawn from it by good consequence, and so could not have the certainty of Catholic faith. That it is not contained immediately is beyond dispute, because Augustine is nowhere named in the Word of God. But they contend that it cannot be inferred from the Word of God by consequence, because in the practical syllogism by which we assert it is inferred, which runs: "All who believe and repent are certain that they are justified and will be saved. But I, Augustine, believe and repent. Therefore I, Augustine, am certain that I am justified and will be saved," the minor premise is either false or at least not an article of faith. It is false, because the heart of man is unsearchable, Jer. 17:9; many who think they have what they do not have are deceived, and the single signs of faith and repentance, works of charity, can be deceptive; experience also teaches that heretics willingly face death in defence of their perfidy, and someone may "give all his goods to the poor" yet "not have charity," 1 Cor. 13:2, 3. Nor is it an article of faith, because faith rests on revelation, and nowhere has it been revealed that this or that man truly believes and repents. And since that minor premise is at least not an article of faith, the conclusion, which would be of faith, cannot follow, because the conclusion follows the weaker premise.

units.la: CIX. Sed aranearum hæc tela evanescens acumen est. Nam propositio illa; quod nihil certum sit certitudine fidei catholicæ, quin idem in verbo Dei immediate comprehendatur, vel ex eodem per consequentiam colligatur, vera est de generalibus, at non de singulatibus, quia Scriptura in hujusmodi rebus aliud principium certitudinis, internam Spiritus S. una cum spiritu nostro testificantis, efficaciam, commonstrat. At certitudo salutis credentium non universale quid, sed singulare, non excedens personam uniuscujusque fidelis est. Fides igitur, quæ creditur, revelationem externam desiderat. At fides, qua creditur, internam conscientiæ, visionis Spiritus S. revelationem, secundum Dei verbum, non aliud quicquam ad sui certitudinem desiderat. Igitur nihilominus propositio illa; quod Augustinus vere justificatus, & salvandus sit, licet non immediate in Scriptura legatur, tamen necessario deducitur per evidentem consequentiam, quomodo omnia particularia non tantum deducuntur, sed etiam evidenter ab universalibus deducuntur. Ita eundem Augustinum à Deo per Filium creatum esse, evidentissime ex propositione illa universali, quod Deus in Christo omnia creaverit, Col. I. 16. colligitur; Etsi Scriptura nomen Augustini immediate non habeat. Ut ergo certitudo gratiæ Dei & salutis, eáque non probabilis duntaxat, sed fidei, constet, sufficit, ut generalis propositio in Scriptura contineatur, atque
units.tr: CIX. But this cobweb of theirs is a vanishing subtlety. For that proposition, that nothing is certain with the certainty of Catholic faith unless it is comprehended in the Word of God immediately, or inferred from it by consequence, is true of general matters, but not of particular ones, because Scripture shows in such matters another principle of certainty: the inward efficacy of the Holy Spirit bearing witness together with our spirit. But the certainty of the salvation of believers is not something universal but particular, not exceeding the person of each faithful individual. Faith as "what is believed" therefore requires external revelation. But faith as "that by which one believes" requires, according to God's Word, nothing else for its certainty than the inward revelation of the conscience, the witness of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, nonetheless, that proposition, that "Augustine is truly justified and is to be saved," though it is not read immediately in Scripture, is still necessarily deduced by evident consequence, just as all particulars are not only deduced but are evidently deduced from universals. Thus that Augustine was created by God through the Son is most evidently inferred from the universal proposition "that God created all things in Christ," Col. 1:16, even though Scripture does not have Augustine's name immediately. So, for the certainty of God's grace and of salvation, and that not merely probable but of faith, it suffices that a general proposition is contained in Scripture, and

units.la: {a} Quod in Syllogismo Practico propositio minor, quia fideles se credere & resipiscere assumunt, prorsus incerta, non revelata, adeoque nec fidei sit. atque eam singuli credentes per δοκιμασία explo- rationem, atque diligens & sincerum sui exa-men, in eadem Scriptura mandatum, Spiritu S. adjuvante & unâ testificante, sibi applicent. Fides enim nunquam sine peculiari applicatione est; qua negata ipsa fides tollitur. Et insani-ret haud dubiè ille, qui cognito objecto suo, tamen se nihil cognoscere diceret. Qui verò credunt & resipiscunt, credere se & resipiscere nõrunt. Nam sensus & cognitio omnis obiecti, & sui ipsius simul sensus & cognitio est. Qui verò nullum fidei & resipiscentiæ suæ sensum habent, illi vera & salvifica fide destituuntur. Nam pacem illam conscientiæ, quæ superat omnem intellectum, & שלום gaudium illud salutis, quod David Psal. LI. 19. expetit, non percipiunt. Non enim fides generalis illa professio & persuasio est, quòd Christus passus, mortuus, sepultus, resuscitatus sit; qualem etiam Diabolus cum omnibus reprobis habet. Nisi pronomina illa Me & Meus ad usum revocare, & cum Thoma: Dominus meus, ac Deus meus, Joh. XX. 28. cum Paulo: Vivo ego, vivit autem in me Christus. Quod verò nunc vivo in carne, in fide vivo Filii Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit se ipsum pro me, Gal. II. 20. vera cum fiducia ingeminare didicerimus, de salute nostra actum est. Quid denique Papæ fiet, si hæc adversantium methodus recipitur? Esto enim Syllogismus: Quicunque est vicarius Christi, is potestatem habet præcipiendi, judicandi, peccata remittendi. At ego (Paulus Innocentius Papa) sum vicarius Christi. Ergo. Ubi assumptio scripta est? Unde per necessariam consequentiam colligitur? Qua fide divina fidem propositioni illi Hierarchici facient?
units.tr: {a} That the minor premise in the practical syllogism, because the faithful assume that they believe and repent, is wholly uncertain, not revealed, and therefore not even an article of faith. and that individual believers apply it to themselves, through examination [δοκιμασία], through diligent and sincere self-scrutiny, with the Holy Spirit helping and bearing witness with them, under the command contained in that same Scripture. For faith is never without a personal application; when this is denied, faith itself is destroyed. And he would surely be mad who, knowing his object, yet said he knew nothing. Those who truly believe and repent know that they believe and repent. For the sense and knowledge of every object is at the same time the sense and knowledge of oneself. But those who have no sense of their own faith and repentance are deprived of true and saving faith. For they do not perceive that peace of conscience which surpasses all understanding, and that "shalom" [שלום] joy of salvation for which David longs, Ps. 51:19. For faith is not that general profession and persuasion that Christ suffered, died, was buried and rose again, which even the devil and all the reprobate have. Unless we have learned to bring back into use the pronouns "me" and "my," and with Thomas to repeat with true confidence, "My Lord and my God," John 20:28, and with Paul, "I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me," Gal. 2:20, then our salvation is undone. And what will become of the Pope, finally, if this method of our opponents is accepted? Let there be the syllogism: "Whoever is Christ's vicar has the power to command, to judge, and to forgive sins. But I (Pope Paul Innocent) am Christ's vicar. Therefore..." Where is the minor premise written? From what is it inferred by necessary consequence? With what divine faith will the Hierarchs make us believe that proposition?

units.la: CX. Neque solidæ adversantium ἐνστάσεις, quibus propositionis assumentis & applicantis certitudinem illi sugillant, sunt. Licèt enim pravum & imperscrutabile cor hominis sit, ut ab aliis investigari non possit; tamen quisque adhibito studio & cura, sui cordis & fiduciæ, quæ in corde est, sensum habere potest. Quis hominum novit, quæ hominis sunt, nisi spiritus hominis, qui in ipso est? 1. Cor. II. 11. Quæstio autem nostra de certitudine fidei propriæ, non alienæ est. Verum est, cor hominis altos adeò recessus habere, ut ne ipse homo suos omnes pervestigare possit, & solus Deus possit. Sed adjuvat hîc hominem Spiritus Dei, clamans, Abba, Pater, & unâ cum spiritu nostro testificans, infirmitatibus nostris coopitulans, 1. Rom. VIII. 15. 16. 26. Neque illud obstat, quòd multi falsa præsumptione se ipsos decipiunt. Sic enim multi quoque scioli sibi docti videntur. ἡ ἀπειρία Ἰεσσαῖα ... Imperitia audaciam parit. At verè docti modesti sunt, & verè fideles humiles, qui cum timore & tremore salutem operantur. Equidem & Paulus Christianos persequens putavit, se verè Deum diligere: & Petrus satis constantiæ ad tolerandam mortem sibi promisit. Sed nos hîc & verè fidelem supponimus, quem impossibile est decipi posse, cùm se fidelem esse sentit & cogitat: & de habitu fidei, non de ejus operationibus, in quibus fides ipsa variis infirmitatibus, quæ defectum humanum testantur, at gratiam Dei non evacuant, frequenter concutitur, loquimur. Porrò fidei & resipiscentiæ signa unica esse o-
units.tr: CX. Nor are the objections of our opponents [ἐνστάσεις], by which they try to cast doubt on the certainty of the applying premise, solid. For although the heart of man is perverse and unsearchable, so that it cannot be investigated by others, yet each person, by applying study and care, can have a sense of his own heart and of the trust that is in his heart. "Who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of man which is in him?" 1 Cor. 2:11. But our question concerns the certainty of one's own faith, not another's. It is true that the heart of man has such deep recesses that man himself cannot search out all of them, and only God can. But the Spirit of God helps man here, "crying, Abba, Father," and "bearing witness with our spirit, helping our infirmities," Rom. 8:15, 16, 26. Nor does it stand in the way that many deceive themselves by false presumption. For in this way many smatterers also seem learned to themselves. [ἡ ἀπειρία] Inexperience breeds boldness. But truly learned people are modest, and truly faithful people are humble, who work out their salvation with fear and trembling. Indeed Paul, persecuting Christians, thought that he truly loved God, and Peter promised himself enough steadfastness to endure death. But here we assume a truly faithful man, whom it is impossible to deceive, since he feels and thinks that he is faithful; and we speak of the habit of faith, not of its operations, in which faith itself is frequently shaken by various infirmities, which testify to human weakness but do not nullify the grace of God. Moreover, those who pronounce that the single signs of faith and repentance are

units.la: pera charitatis, falsò illi pronuntiant, quia ipsa charitas longè certior est, quam Apostolus in cordibus nostris per Spiritum S. diffusam esse Rom. V. 5. dixit. Et quæ de operibus à charitate separatis Apostolus, 1. Cor. XIII. 2. dixit, perperam illi iisdem operibus cum charitate conjunctis applicant. Ac ut concedamus, in operibus aliquid imperfectionis certitudinis esse, tamen superest testimonium Spiritus, altius non tantùm operibus, sed etiam charitate ipsa, quia cùm opera sint à charitate, ipsa charitas à Spiritu S. est. Denique assumptio atque applicatio partim conscientiæ, partim Spiritus S. testimonio nititur. Conscientia, quia cuique conscientia actuum suorum mille initar testium est. Gloriatio hæc nostra est testimonium conscientiæ nostræ, 2. Cor. I. 12. Nam lucerna Jehovæ est anima hominis perscrutans omnia penetralia ventris, Prov. XX. 27. Ejus igitur נר יהוה lucerna Jehovæ ipsius, testificatio omni exceptione major est. Nam quod digito suo ipse Deus conscientiæ inscripsit, incertitudine laborare non potest. Spiritus S. utpote, qui & obsignat credentes, ceu arrhabo Ephes. I. 13. & unâ cum spiritu nostro testatur, Rom. VIII. 16. & quidem per testimonium non ἀδηλον, sed apertum ipsius S. Scripturæ, in qua sinceritatis fidei & resipiscentiæ notas & criteria revelavit, quæ ex eadem per internam etiam revelationem spiritui credentis ostendit. Nihil ergo ad fidem propositionis assumentis, & conditionem promissioni annexam applicantis deest, quando eam revelatio & testificatio conscientiæ & Spiritus S. fidei, imò & visionis argumenta certissima fundant. Conclusio ergo & ipsa, præmissarum, quæ fidei sunt, certitudini innixa, tota fidei est.
units.tr: The signs of faith and repentance are the works of charity, as they wrongly claim. For charity itself is far more certain than the Apostle's statement that it is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, Rom. 5:5. What the Apostle said about works separated from charity, 1 Cor. 13:2, they wrongly apply to works joined with charity. Even if we grant that works carry some imperfection of certainty, the testimony of the Spirit remains, which is higher not only than works but than charity itself, since works come from charity and charity comes from the Holy Spirit. Finally, the assumption and its application rest partly on conscience and partly on the testimony of the Holy Spirit. Conscience, because for each person the conscience of his own actions is like a thousand witnesses. Our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, 2 Cor. 1:12. For the lamp of Jehovah is the human spirit, searching all the inner chambers of the belly, Prov. 20:27. So the testimony of his lamp of Jehovah [נר יהוה] is greater than any objection. For what God himself has written with his own finger on the conscience cannot suffer uncertainty. The Holy Spirit, who both seals believers as an earnest, Eph. 1:13, and bears witness with our spirit, Rom. 8:16, gives this testimony not as something unclear [ἄδηλον] but as the open testimony of Holy Scripture itself, in which he has revealed the marks and criteria of sincere faith and repentance, and which he also shows to the spirit of the believer by inner revelation. Nothing is therefore lacking to the faith that accepts the proposition and applies the condition attached to the promise, when revelation, the testimony of conscience and of the Holy Spirit, and the most certain arguments of sight establish it. The conclusion itself, therefore, which rests on the certainty of the premises that belong to faith, is wholly a matter of faith.

units.la: CXI.
units.tr: CXI.

units.la: Ultimus, quem adversus certitudinem salutis intorquent, aries est, quòd doctrina de certitudine salutis æquè ac doctrina de Perseverantia ex natura & indole sua pulvinar carnis, pietati, bonis moribus, precibus aliisque sanctioribus exercitiis noxia, dubitatio contra iisdem proficua sit. Sed qui metum hunc cient, & ut hypothesi suæ fortiùs ancillentur, confingunt, næ illi demonstrant, se efficaciam Divinæ gratiæ, & operationem ignorare, & contradicunt Apostolo distertis verbis affirmanti: Dilecti mei, nunc filii Dei sumus, sed nondum patefactum id est, quod erimus. Scimus autem fore, ut cùm ipse patefactus fuerit, nos ei similes erimus, quoniam videbimus eum, sicuti est. Et quisquis hanc spem in eo habet, purificat se ipsum, sicut ipse purus est, 1. Joh. III. 2. 3. Calumniam ergo hanc & Divina veritas, & humana experientia retundit, quia perseverantiæ & salutis certitudo non tantùm quoad rei naturam, sed etiam quoad ipsum eventum in Ecclesia effectus, Deo benedicente, prorsus contrarios producit. Nam quoad rei naturam finis infallibilitas mediorum usum non tollit, sed stabilit. Qui igitur & constantiam in via, & fruitionem in patria sibi spondent, simul norunt, certíque sunt, intermediis sanctimoniæ officiis opus esse, & eadem per gratiam Dei & inhabitantem in se Spiritus S. se præstituros. Non ergo illi valedicunt mediis istis, sed sedulò magis incumbunt, in veritatis, pietatis, charitatis & gratitudinis via omni collato studio incedunt, opera carnis & mem-
units.tr: The last ram they drive against the certainty of salvation is this: that the doctrine of the certainty of salvation, like the doctrine of perseverance, is by its nature and character a pillow for the flesh, harmful to piety, good morals, prayers and other holier exercises, whereas doubt is useful for these. But those who raise this fear, and invent it so that their hypothesis may be defended more strongly, clearly show that they are ignorant of the efficacy and operation of divine grace, and they contradict the Apostle, who affirms in plain words: Beloved, now we are children of God, but it has not yet been revealed what we shall be. We know, however, that when he is revealed we shall be like him, since we shall see him as he is. And everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, as he is pure, 1 John 3:2, 3. Divine truth and human experience both refute this calumny, because the certainty of perseverance and of salvation produces, by God's blessing, effects entirely contrary to one another, not only as regards the nature of the thing but also as regards the actual outcome in the Church. For as regards the nature of the thing, the infallibility of the end does not abolish the use of means but establishes it. Those therefore who promise themselves both constancy on the way and enjoyment in the homeland at the same time know, and are certain, that the duties of holiness are needed as means, and that they will perform those same duties through the grace of God and the Holy Spirit dwelling in them. So they do not bid farewell to these means, but apply themselves all the more diligently, and press forward with all zeal in the way of truth, piety, love and gratitude, mortifying the works of the flesh and their members

units.la: Doctrina de certitudine gratia & salutis non est pulvinar carnis, nec pietati, bonis moribus & precibus inimica. & membra sua terrestria mortificant, Deum timent, à peccatis cavent, cum timore & tremore salutem operantur. Dat enim Deus iis, juxta tenorem fœderis cor novum & spiritum novum, efficitque, ut in statutis suis ambulent, & jura sua faciant, Ezech. XXXVI. 26. & fiant ut arbor plantata ad rivos aquarum, quæ fructum edit tempore suo, Psal. I. 3. Revera enim, qui ex Deo natus est, peccatum non facit, quia semen ejus manet in ipso, nec peccare potest, quia ex Deo natus est, I. Joh. III. 9. Quod ipsa etiam eorum, qui de favore Dei & salute certi fuerunt exempla demonstrant. Caput ipsum fidelium, Jesus Christus, qui de Patris favore & gloria sua certissimus fuit, simul in precibus dies noctesque assiduus fuit. Neque S. Paulo in precibus & pietatis exercitio Mortalium quisquam frequentior & studiosior fuit, quo tamen de salute & corona sua vix alius certior extitit. Sicut enim nihilo segnius agebant Moses, Gedeon, David, alii populi sancti duces, Judices, Reges propterea quod Divinis oraculis certi fuerunt, traditum iri hostes in manus suas: sic verè fideles de consequenda salute sua non dubii, alacriùs etiam suam salutem operari, & adversus tentationes omnes pugnare non dubitant. Tantum ergo abest, ut doctrina hæc mater securitatis & impietatis sit, ut potius non solidæ consolationis duntaxat, sed etiam filialis, spontaneæ & ingenuæ pietatis fœta mater, & magistra existat. Sensus enim gratiæ gignit amorem & timorem Dei, & gratiarum actionem facitque, ut Deum rebus omnibus longè anteferamus, &, ceu unicum salutis nostræ auctorem diligamus, celebremus, & offendere magnopere caveamus, ne vel consolatione primi vemur, vel à facie ejus repellamur. Quæ animi dispositio procul à securitate, superbia & fluctuatione abest. Quod ad experientiam & eventum attinet, verum quidem est, posse veritatem saluberrimam quamvis hominum abusu in perversum rapi. At ex doctrina certitudinis nullum plane hujusmodi incommodum hactenus Ecclesiæ nostræ senserunt; in quibus non magis ob inviolabilem adoptionis fiduciam & solatii specialis plenam consolationem, quàm apud adversarios certitudinem salutis nostræ à firmitate Divini propositi ad humani arbitrii fragilitatem & arundinem revocantes, atque in Pyrrhoniam dubitationem convertentes, vel fraena concupiscentiis laxari, vel pietatem omnem pessumdari, rebus ipsis & experiundo novimus, Deoque per Christum gratias agimus.
units.tr: The doctrine of the certainty of grace and salvation is not a pillow for the flesh, nor hostile to piety, good morals and prayers: and they mortify their earthly members, fear God, guard against sins, and work out their salvation with fear and trembling. For God gives them, according to the tenor of the covenant, a new heart and a new spirit, and brings it about that they walk in his statutes and keep his judgments, Ezek. 36:26, and become like a tree planted by the rivers of water, which brings forth its fruit in its season, Ps. 1:3. Indeed, whoever is born of God does not sin, because his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin, because he is born of God, 1 John 3:9. The examples of those who were certain of God's favour and salvation also demonstrate this: they demonstrate it. The very head of the faithful, Jesus Christ, who was most certain of the Father's favour and glory, was at the same time day and night constant in prayer. Nor was any of mortals more frequent and diligent than St Paul in prayer and the exercise of piety, and yet no one was more certain of his salvation and crown. For just as Moses, Gideon, David, and other holy leaders of the people, judges and kings, were none the less diligent because they were certain by divine oracles that their enemies would be delivered into their hands, so truly believers, not doubting of attaining their salvation, do not hesitate to work out their salvation more eagerly and to fight against all temptations. So far is this doctrine from being the mother of security and impiety, that it is rather the mother and teacher not only of solid consolation but also of filial, spontaneous and sincere piety. For the sense of grace begets love and fear of God, and thanksgiving, and makes us prefer God far above all things, and love and celebrate him as the sole author of our salvation, and take great care not to offend him, lest we be either lifted up by consolation or repelled from his face. This disposition of mind is far from security, pride and wavering. As for experience and outcome, it is true that the most wholesome truth can be twisted into perversion by human abuse. But from the doctrine of certainty our Church has hitherto felt no harm of this kind at all; among us there is no more an inviolable confidence of adoption and the full comfort of special consolation than there is among our adversaries, who, turning the certainty of our salvation from the firmness of the divine purpose to the frailty and reed-like weakness of the human will, and converting it into Pyrrhonian doubt, either loosen the reins to the lusts or utterly destroy all piety. We know this from the things themselves and from experience, and we give thanks to God through Christ.

units.la: CXII. Hanc de Perseverantia credentium & Sanctorum, ejusque Certitudine doctrinam (liceat Theologorum Synodi Dordracenæ de Perseverantia sanct. art. 15. verbis gravibus colophonem tractationi imponere) quam Deus ad nominis sui gloriam, & piarum animarum solatium in verbo suo abundantissimè revelavit, & cordibus fidelium imprimit; caro quidem non capit, Sathanas odit, mundus ridet, qui novum illud nomen calculo albo inscriptum, non accepit, adeoque nec nosse potest, Apoc. II. 17. & hypocritæ in abusum rapiunt, spiritusque erronei oppugnant; sed Sponsa Christi, ut inæstimabilis pretii thesaurum tenerrimè semper dilexit, & constanter propugnavit. Quod ut porrò faciat, procurabit Deus, adversus quem nec consilium valere, nec robur ullum prævalere potest.
units.tr: CXII. This doctrine of the perseverance of believers and saints, and of its certainty (let me close this treatment with the weighty words of the Synod of Dort's Theologians on the Perseverance of the Saints, art. 15), which God has most abundantly revealed in his word for the glory of his name and the comfort of pious souls, and imprints on the hearts of the faithful, the flesh indeed does not grasp, Satan hates, the world laughs at, and those who have not received that new name written on the white stone, and so cannot know it, Rev. 2:17, twist to abuse, and erring spirits attack; but the Bride of Christ, as a treasure of inestimable worth, has always loved most tenderly and defended constantly. That she may continue to do so, God will provide, against whom neither counsel can avail nor any strength prevail.

units.la: LOCUS VICESIMUS QUINTUS. De Cultu Externo; Inprimis de Sacramentis Novi Testamenti. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWENTY-FIVE. On External Worship, and especially on the Sacraments of the New Testament. A SUMMARY.

units.la: Fœderis Gratiæ sub Oeconomia N. T. Ritus & cultus externus. 1. Cultus Dei naturalis & instituti differentia. 2. Cultus Dei institutus externus N. T. Mal. I. 10. 11. prædictus est. 3. Externus licet, spiritualis tamen & rationalis etiam est. 4. Semper nos & nostra Divinæ gloriæ consecrare, & velut mactare tenemur. 5. Nihilominus exercitia quædam singulari ratione ad cultum Dei publicè celebrandum pertinent. 6. Eò prædicatio verbi, preces, hymni, eleemosynæ, & Sacramentorum usus referri debent. Prædicatio verbi qualis sub Evangelio obtineat? 7. Liturgiarum in cultu publico usus. 8. Pro quibus alii Directoria quædam obtrudunt, quorum adversus Liturgias argumenta diluuntur. 9. Liturgiæ Apostolicæ simplicitas paulapaulatim obsolevit: Scripturæ translatione & lectione prohibita, & linguæ barbaræ usu in Liturgiam invecto. 10. Bellarmini fucus obductus abstergitur. 11. Argumenta S. Pauli adversus usum linguæ peregrinæ in cultu publico repetuntur. 12. Et suffragio Cajetani & Johannis VIII. confirmantur. 13.
