Bellarmini adversus usum linguæ vulgaris in Missa argumenta discutiuntur. 14. Origo peregrinæ linguæ usus in Ecclesiam introducti. 15. Non veræ Ecclesiæ, sed infidelium & hæreticorum mos est sacra celare. 16. Argumentis Mysticorum occurritur. 17. Sacramenta Oeconomiæ Fœderis Gratiæ sub Evangelio à Sacramentis V. T. quodammodo differunt. 18. Sacramenta N. T. duo sunt, Baptismus & S. Cœna. 19. Argumenta pro numero septenario Sacramentorum N.T. refelluntur. 20. Baptismi definitio & nomina. 21. Baptismi Proselytorum ante Christum usus institutioni ejus ansam dedit. 22. Baptismus Johannis. 23. Ejus à Baptismo Christi differentia, & in præcipuis cum eodem convenientia. 24. Objectiones Pontificiorum adversus convenientiam utriusque elisæ. 25. Baptismus discipulorum Christi. 26. Ministerium ejus vocationem requirit. 27. Laicorum & mulierum Baptismus rejicitur. 28. Argumenta pro eodem ad incudem revocantur. 29. Requisita Baptistæ; & quatenus hæreticorum Baptismus probari possit? 30. Baptismi elementum aqua est, idonea maximè ad significandam regenerationem per obedientiam Christi, & sanctificationem Spiritus. 31. Socinianorum Baptismum aquæ pro indifferente venditantium elenchus. 32. Argumenta eorundem diluuntur. 33. Cum elemento aquæ Verbum Evangelii conjungitur. 34. Ritus baptismalis in aquam immersio, vel ejusdem asperso est. Asperionis numerus. 35. Formula Baptismi. 36. Ejusdem sensus. 37. Res significata Baptismi in universum Evangelium, sigillatim regeneratio per meritum Christi, & Spiritum S. est. 38. Rei hujus cum signo analogia exponitur. 39. Nec non cum ritu immersionis & asperionis. 40. Beneficiorum Evangelicorum in Baptismo significatio & potens obsignatio peragitur. 41. Simul sigillum & causa gratiæ esse non potest. 42. Neque enim Baptismus gratia, ut causa, virtute sive inhærente, sive assistente, operatur. 43. Circa efficaciam Baptismi recentiorum quorundam opinio expenditur. 44. Baptismus remissionem peccatorum etiam post Baptismum commissorum obsignat. 45. Objectiones Pontificiorum dissolvuntur. 46. Baptismus efficaciam nonnisi in legitimo usu exerit. 47. Neque omnibus regenerationem potentialem & vitam novam, sed in quibusdam suffocabilem illam obsignat. 48. Nihilominus nonnulla baptizatorum non electorum supra non baptizatos prærogativa est. 49. Baptismus adultorum & infantum est: & adultis, atque infantibus in infantia morientibus, vel vitam ad rationis usum provehentibus quatenus prosit, disquiritur. 50. Respectu infantum, sive in infantia morientium, sive vitam prorogantium non inanis ceremonia vel figura ludicra est. 51. Baptismi effecta. 52. & subjectum. 53. Pædobaptismus demonstratur. 54. Socinianorum & Anabaptistarum adversus illum argumenta ad partes vocata. 55. Baptismus spuriorum, expositititorum, eorum qui excommunicati, hæretici, infideles sunt, liberorum, & monstrosorum, &c. 56. Mortuorum, rerum irrationalium & inanimatarum, inprimis campanarum. 57. Baptismi tempus. 58. Et locus. 59. De necessitate Baptismi error Quintillianorum, Manichæorum, Socinianorum & Anabaptistarum. 60. Necessitatis rerum ad salutem distinctio. 61. Baptismi necessitas non absoluta & medii, sed secundum quid & præcepti est. 62. Quod pluribus demonstratur. 63. Augustini ea in re hallucinatio, & Tridentinorum hæresis. 64. Christus Joh. III. 5. absolutam Baptismi necessitatem non docuit. 65. Reliqua pro absoluta ea necessitate argumenta excussa. 66. Baptismus non tollit id omne, quod peccati rationem habet. 67. Baptismus unus genere, & unus numero est. 68. Quæ unitas & irreiterabilitas non charactere fictitio, sed verioribus argumentis nititur. 69. Baptismi ceremoniæ ascititiæ utiles, in Baptismo adultorum olim usitatæ, deinceps nimia negligentia in Baptismo infantum retentæ sunt. Velut Catechismus, Professio nominis, susceptores & scrutinium. 70. Ceremoniæ ascititiæ superstitiosæ. 71. Coenæ Domini definitio & nomina. 72. Partes ejus sunt ministerium externum & mysterium. In externo ministerio personæ, signa & actiones considerantur. Personæ administrantes explicantur. 73. Personæ communicantes in prima Cœna fuerunt Christus & Apostoli, non excepto Juda. 74. Post Cœnam primam communicantes sunt fideles omnes, qui se explorarunt; non infantes, furiosi, scelerati, catechumeni, &c. 75. Symbolum geminum est, panis & vinum; non sine sapientia singulari Christi instituentis ad convivium hoc delectum. 76. Panis ejusmodi fuit, qualis in usu erat, azymus; de quo Græcos inter & Latinos inutilis contentio diu duravit. 77. Et fermentati & azymi panis liber in Ecclesia usus est. 78. Non item hostiarum numulariarum, quas Transsubstantiationis dogma invexit. 79. Ritus circa panem à Christo adhibiti, 80. quam non in pronuntiatione verborum, Hoc enim est corpus meum, constituisse, probatur. 81. Argumentis contrariis fit satis. 82. Fractio panis, & ejusdem ad Sacramenti integritatem necessitas. 83. Fractionis modus indifferens est. 84. Panis datio, seu distributio non in os communicantis facta est. 85. Ei Missæ privatæ, in quibus solus sacerdos communicat, 86. nec non panis assservatio, & in pixide inclusio, repugnant. 87. Rationes pro assservatione panis refelluntur. 88. Alterum Cœnæ symbolum vinum est; sive illud merum, sive aqua dilutum. 89. Iisdem circa vinum ritibus Christus usus est, quibus circa panem. 90. Communionem calicis per sacrilegium immane Ecclesia Romana populo negat. 91. Communio calicis à Christo mandata est. 92. Æquè ac communio panis. 93. Causa distinctæ obsignationis corporis & sanguinis Christi per distincta symbola ex mysterio redemptionis animæ & corporis, in Eucharistia obsignato, arcessitur. 94. Argumenta alia pro communione calicis. 95. Ecclesiæ veteris Orientalis & Occidentalis consensus. 96. Pontificiorum, calicem suffurantium, objectionibus occurritur. 97. Argumento ex antiquitate petito fit satis. 98. Locus celebrandæ Eucharistiæ. 99. Ad mensam, non apud altare celebranda est. 100. Tempus primæ & consequentium cœnarum. 101. Eucharistia mysterium habet, sine quo nil externum ejus ministerium prodest. 102. Consistit illud in gaudio convivii spiritualis & interni, per convivium externum & symbolicum adumbrato, cujus dapes sunt corpus & sanguis Christi, panis & vini symbolis repræsentatus, seu communio corporis & sanguinis Christi. 103. Quæ communio non corporalis, sed spiritualis est. 104. Totius Evangelii summam mysterium illud complectitur. 105. Symbolorum & actionum circa symbola cum mysterio hoc collatio. 106. In verbis promissionis, Hoc est corpus meum, panis pro subjecto ponitur, de quo corpus improprie, seu metonymice prædicatur. 107. Cœna Domini ad recordationem ejus, & annuntiationem mortis ejus, ceu aptissimum utriusque medium, institutum est. 108. Finis Cœnæ principalis & subordinatus. 109. Usum ejus exploratio sui præcedat oportet. 110. Præsentia & communio corporis & sanguinis Christi in Eucharistia non imaginaria & intentionalis, sed vera & realis est. 111. Præsentiæ & communionis ejusdem modus duplex est, unus relativus seu sacramentalis, 112. alter spiritualis. 113. Duplex ille modus præsentiæ & communionis ad salutarem Cœnæ Domini usum sufficit. 114. Et pro sufficiente & vera in Ecclesia judicata semper est, quandiu in ea Evangelii doctrina integra permansit; qua corrupta paulatim corporalis præsentia, Transsubstantiationis dogma & Missa in Ecclesiam invecta est. 115. Missa centrum mysterii iniquitatis est. 116. Mater Missæ Transsubstantiatio est, quæ refellitur. 117. Argumenta pro Transsubstantiatione configuntur. 118. Ruente Transsubstantiatione præsentia corporalis Christi in Eucharistia corruit. 119. Objectionibus pro eadem occurritur. 120. Transsubstantiatione & præsentia corporali elisa Missæ sacrificium perit, quod pluribus argumentis refellitur. 121. Rationes Missam confirmantes solvuntur. 122. Cadente Missa, Missæ pro defunctis, in honorem sanctorum. 123. Et adoratio hostiæ, verissima idololatria, cadit. 124. Argumenta pro adoratione hostiæ discussa. 125. Confubstantiatio refellitur. 126. Manducatio corporis & potus sanguinis Christi in Cœna non oralis, sed spiritualis est. 127. Proin infideles & indigni corporis & sanguinis Christi non fiunt participes. 128. Argumenta contraria diluuntur. 129. Momentum controversiæ Lutheranos inter & Reformatos de præsentia corporali Christi in Eucharistia & manducatione orali, infidelium etiam expenditur. 130. In Cœna Domini corporis & sanguinis Christi conjunctio non cum solo spiritu, sed etiam cum corporibus nostris fit, sed non per contactum superficierum. 131. Sententia Socinianorum Cœnam in fidei & obedientiæ tesseram convertentium cryptis. 132. & elenchus. 133. Verborum Christi; Hoc est corpus meum, Sociniana exegesis refellitur. 134. Impietas eorundem manducationem spiritualem ex ea eliminantium. 135. Grotii de communicatione sine symbolis novella hypothesis perstringitur. 136. Sacramenta supernumeraria Pontificiorum. 137. Confirmationis Sacramentum refutatur. 138. Argumentis pro eodem occurritur. 139. Pœnitentiæ Sacramentum rejectum. 140. Solutis pro eodem argumentis adversantium. 141. Unctio extrema; 142. Ordinatio. 143. Et Matrimonium ex numero sacramentorum expunguntur. 144.
units.tr: The rite and external worship under the economy of the New Testament, the covenant of grace. (1) The difference between natural worship of God and instituted worship. (2) The instituted external worship of the New Testament is foretold in Mal. 1. 10, 11. (3) Although it is external, it is also spiritual and rational. (4) We are always bound to consecrate ourselves and our possessions to the glory of God, and as it were to offer them in sacrifice. (5) Nevertheless, certain practices belong in a special way to the public celebration of worship. (6) To these belong the preaching of the Word, prayers, hymns, almsgiving, and the use of the sacraments. What kind of preaching of the Word holds under the Gospel? (7) The use of liturgies in public worship. (8) For these some others thrust upon us certain directories, and the arguments against liturgies are dissolved. (9) The simplicity of the apostolic liturgy gradually fell into disuse, when Scripture was forbidden to be translated and read, and the use of a barbarous language was introduced into the liturgy. (10) Bellarmine's veneer is wiped away. (11) The arguments of St. Paul against the use of a foreign tongue in public worship are repeated. (12) And they are confirmed by the authority of Cajetan and John VIII. (13) Bellarmine's arguments against the use of the vernacular in the Mass are examined. (14) The origin of the use of a foreign tongue introduced into the Church. (15) It is not the custom of a true Church but of unbelievers and heretics to conceal sacred things. (16) The arguments of the Mystics are met. (17) The sacraments of the economy of the covenant of grace under the Gospel differ in some respects from the sacraments of the Old Testament. (18) There are two sacraments of the New Testament, Baptism and the Lord's Supper. (19) The arguments for a septenary number of sacraments of the New Testament are refuted. (20) The definition and names of Baptism. (21) The use of baptism of proselytes before Christ gave occasion to its institution. (22) The baptism of John. (23) The difference between his baptism and the baptism of Christ, and their agreement in the main points. (24) The objections of the Papists against the agreement of both are overturned. (25) The baptism of the disciples of Christ. (26) Its ministry requires a lawful calling. (27) The baptism of laymen and women is rejected. (28) The arguments for the same are brought back to the anvil. (29) The qualifications of the baptizer; and to what extent the baptism of heretics can be approved. (30) The element of baptism is water, most suitable above all for signifying regeneration through the obedience of Christ and the sanctification of the Spirit. (31) A refutation of the Socinians, who make the baptism of water a matter of indifference. (32) Their arguments are dissolved. (33) The Word of the Gospel is joined with the element of water. (34) The rite of baptism is immersion in water or sprinkling with it. The number of sprinklings. (35) The formula of Baptism. (36) Its sense. (37) The thing signified by Baptism, in the Gospel generally and in particular, is regeneration through the merit of Christ and the Holy Spirit. (38) The analogy of this thing with the sign is set out. (39) And likewise with the rite of immersion and sprinkling. (40) The signification of the Gospel benefits in Baptism and the powerful sealing of them is carried through. (41) A seal and a cause of grace cannot be the same thing at once. (42) For Baptism does not work grace as a cause, by an inherent or an assisting power. (43) The opinion of some recent writers concerning the efficacy of Baptism is examined. (44) Baptism seals the remission of sins, even of those committed after Baptism. (45) The objections of the Papists are resolved. (46) Baptism exerts its efficacy only in lawful use. (47) It seals regeneration in potential form and new life not to all, but in some it can be suffocated. (48) Nevertheless, the advantage of the baptized, even of the non-elect, over the unbaptized is something. (49) Baptism belongs to adults and to infants; and it is inquired how far it benefits adults, and infants dying in infancy, or those who bring their life on to the use of reason. (50) With respect to infants, whether dying in infancy or prolonging their life, it is not an empty ceremony or a childish figure. (51) The effects of Baptism. (52) And its subject. (53) Infant baptism is demonstrated. (54) The arguments of the Socinians and Anabaptists against it are brought into the field. (55) The baptism of bastards, foundlings, those who are excommunicate, heretics, unbelievers, children of such, monstrous births, etc. (56) The dead, irrational and inanimate things, especially bells. (57) The time of Baptism. (58) And the place. (59) The error of the Quintillianists, Manichaeans, Socinians and Anabaptists concerning the necessity of Baptism. (60) The distinction of the necessity of things for salvation. (61) The necessity of Baptism is not absolute and of means, but relative and of precept. (62) This is shown by many arguments. (63) Augustine's mistake in this matter, and the heresy of the Council of Trent. (64) Christ did not teach an absolute necessity of Baptism in John 3. 5. (65) The remaining arguments for that absolute necessity are shaken. (66) Baptism does not remove everything that has the character of sin. (67) Baptism is one in kind and one in number. (68) This unity and non-repeatability rests not on a fictitious character but on truer arguments. (69) The ceremonies of Baptism added from outside, useful, once customary in the baptism of adults, were afterwards retained in the baptism of infants with excessive carelessness: such as the catechism, the profession of the name, sponsors, and the scrutiny. (70) Superstitious ceremonies added from outside. (71) The definition and names of the Lord's Supper. (72) Its parts are the external ministry and the mystery. In the external ministry the persons, signs and actions are considered. The administering persons are explained. (73) The persons communicating at the first Supper were Christ and the Apostles, not excepting Judas. (74) After the first Supper, those who communicate are all the faithful who have examined themselves; not infants, the insane, the wicked, catechumens, etc. (75) There are two elements, bread and wine; this choice for the feast was not made without the singular wisdom of Christ who instituted it. (76) The bread was of the kind in use, unleavened; over this a useless dispute between the Greeks and the Latins lasted a long time. (77) The use of leavened and unleavened bread is free in the Church. (78) Not so with the coin-shaped hosts, which the dogma of transubstantiation introduced. (79) The rites with regard to the bread used by Christ, (80) which are shown not to have been established in the pronouncing of the words, This is my body. (81) Enough is said in answer to the contrary arguments. (82) The breaking of the bread, and the necessity of it for the integrity of the sacrament. (83) The manner of breaking is a matter of indifference. (84) The giving or distribution of the bread was not done into the mouth of the communicant. (85) Private Masses, in which only the priest communicates, (86) and likewise the keeping of the bread and its enclosure in a pyx, are repugnant. (87) The reasons for keeping the bread are refuted. (88) The other symbol of the Supper is wine, whether it be pure or diluted with water. (89) Christ used the same rites with regard to the wine as with regard to the bread. (90) The Roman Church denies the communion of the cup to the people by an enormous sacrilege. (91) Communion of the cup was commanded by Christ. (92) Just as much as communion of the bread. (93) The reason for the distinct sealing of the body and blood of Christ through distinct symbols is drawn from the mystery of the redemption of soul and body, sealed in the Eucharist. (94) Other arguments for communion of the cup. (95) The consensus of the ancient Eastern and Western Church. (96) The objections of the Papists, who purloin the cup, are met. (97) The argument from antiquity is answered. (98) The place of celebrating the Eucharist. (99) It is to be celebrated at the table, not at the altar. (100) The time of the first and subsequent suppers. (101) The Eucharist has a mystery, without which its external ministry avails nothing. (102) That mystery consists in the joy of a spiritual and inward feast, foreshadowed by the external and symbolic feast, whose dainties are the body and blood of Christ, represented by the symbols of bread and wine; that is, the communion of the body and blood of Christ. (103) This communion is not bodily but spiritual. (104) That mystery embraces the sum of the whole Gospel. (105) A comparison of the symbols and of the actions concerning the symbols with this mystery. (106) In the words of promise, This is my body, bread is put for the subject, of which body is improperly, or metonymically, predicated. (107) The Lord's Supper was instituted for the remembrance of him and the proclamation of his death, as the most fitting means of both. (108) The principal and subordinate end of the Supper. (109) Self-examination ought to precede its use. (110) The presence and communion of the body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist is not imaginary and intentional, but true and real. (111) The mode of this presence and communion is twofold: one relative or sacramental, (112) the other spiritual. (113) This twofold mode of presence and communion is sufficient for the saving use of the Lord's Supper. (114) And it has always been judged in the Church to be sufficient and true, as long as the doctrine of the Gospel remained whole in it; when that was corrupted, little by little bodily presence, the dogma of transubstantiation and the Mass were introduced into the Church. (115) The Mass is the centre of the mystery of iniquity. (116) Transubstantiation is the mother of the Mass, and it is refuted. (117) Arguments for transubstantiation are put together. (118) With transubstantiation overthrown, the bodily presence of Christ in the Eucharist falls. (119) The objections for the same are met. (120) With transubstantiation and bodily presence destroyed, the sacrifice of the Mass perishes, which is refuted by many arguments. (121) The arguments confirming the Mass are resolved. (122) With the Mass fallen, the Masses for the dead, and those in honour of the saints, fall. (123) And the adoration of the host, the most true idolatry, falls. (124) The arguments for the adoration of the host are discussed. (125) Consubstantiation is refuted. (126) The eating of the body and drinking of the blood of Christ in the Supper is not oral but spiritual. (127) Therefore unbelievers and the unworthy do not become partakers of the body and blood of Christ. (128) The contrary arguments are dissolved. (129) The weight of the controversy between the Lutherans and the Reformed concerning the bodily presence of Christ in the Eucharist and oral manducation, even of unbelievers, is also weighed. (130) In the Lord's Supper the conjunction of the body and blood of Christ is made not with the spirit alone but also with our bodies, yet not through contact of surfaces. (131) The opinion of the Socinians who turn the Supper into a token of faith and obedience, and into a mere sign. (132) And its refutation. (133) The Socinian exegesis of the words of Christ, This is my body, is refuted. (134) The impiety of those who eliminate spiritual manducation from it. (135) The novel hypothesis of Grotius concerning communication without symbols is condemned. (136) The supernumerary sacraments of the Papists. (137) The sacrament of Confirmation is refuted. (138) The arguments for it are met. (139) The sacrament of Penance is rejected. (140) The arguments of its opponents for it having been answered. (141) Extreme unction; (142) Ordination. (143) And Matrimony are struck off the number of sacraments. (144)

units.la: I. EOEDUS Gratiæ præceptis, promissionibus & ritibus Divinitus præscriptis absolvitur.
units.tr: I. The covenant of grace is completed by the precepts, promises and rites prescribed by God.

units.la: Illa obedientiæ, ista fidei, hæc cultus externi canon & norma sunt. Quæ cum in prioribus œconomiis Fœderis Gratiæ occurrerint, in ultima hac œconomia ejusdem sub Evangelio locum pariter habent. Præcepta enim vitæ omnia ab Evangelio adoptata, & ab humanis scoriis sordibúsque defœcata, perfectissima plenitudine & latitudine à Servatore Christo nobis proposita, non semel explicavimus. Fidei verò, omnibus figuris & ænigmatibus evolutæ canonem in suavissimis & pretiosissimis promissis suis, Evangelium nobis exhibuit. Supererat rituum ceremoniarúmque sub Evangelio minimè operosus apparatus, in verbi, quod sub N.T. revelatum est, prædicatione, precum spiritualium simplicissimis ritibus, & Sacramentorum administratione; quibus cultus externus Novi Testamenti absolvitur.
units.tr: The first of these is the canon and norm of obedience, the second of faith, and the third of external worship. Since these already appeared in the earlier dispensations of the covenant of grace, they likewise have their place in this last dispensation of the same covenant under the Gospel. For we have already explained that Christ our Saviour has set before us all the precepts of life, taken up from the Gospel and purged of human dross and filth, in the most perfect fullness and breadth. And the Gospel has presented to us the canon of faith, unfolded from all figures and enigmas, in its most sweet and precious promises. There remained under the Gospel a very simple apparatus of rites and ceremonies: the preaching of the Word, which has been revealed under the New Testament, the most simple rites of spiritual prayer, and the administration of the sacraments. By these the external worship of the New Testament is completed.

units.la: II. Duplex Dei cultus est, naturalis & institutus. Naturalis ex ipsa Dei natura pendet, ita ut licèt nullam legem Divinitus revelatam haberemus, si tamen Dei naturam rectè perspectam haberemus, uti Adamus integer habuit, ex illius idonea contemplatione omnia illa, quæ hac in parte ad officium nostrum pertinent, Dei gratia auxiliante, percipere possemus. Nemo enim est, qui rectè Dei naturam intelligens, non simul in eum credendum, sperandum, eúmque amandum, invocandum, & in omnibus audiendum esse, necessario agnoscat. Hic proin cultus simpliciter necessarius ad salutem; & unus idémque atque immutabilis est. Institutus est medium ex Dei voluntate ad cultum naturalem exercendum & promovendum ordinatum. Sicut igitur naturalis à Dei natura, ita institutus ab ejusdem voluntate liberrima pendet, & pro eadem varius est, pro varia Ecclesiæ ante & post Christum exhibitum constitutione. Neque tamen legitimus est, nisi Deum authorem habeat. Nam quis mentem Dei novit? Esaj. XL.13. Rom.XI.34. 1.Cor. II.16. Ne sequamini cor vestrum, & oculos vestros, quæ sequentes scortamini post eos, Num.XV.39. Ideóque quod facit homo ex propria inventione, vel ex hominum præcepto, tanquam honorans Deum, eo ipso post cor & oculos suos scortatur, & Deum blasphemat, non sanctificat. Cúmque simul cultus Deo placens oriatur à sanctificatione Spiritus, juxta illud Pauli, quòd oblatio gentium Deo accepta tum fit, cùm sanctificata in Spiritu S. est, Rom. XV.16. manifestum est, opus operatum Deo non placere, neque omnino obtinendæ gratiæ & justitiæ causam esse posse.
units.tr: II. There are two kinds of worship of God, natural and instituted. Natural worship depends on the very nature of God, so that even if we had no law revealed by God, yet if we had a right perception of the nature of God, as Adam had it in his integrity, we could, by God's helping grace, perceive from a fitting contemplation of him all those things that pertain to our duty in this matter. For there is no one who rightly understands the nature of God and does not at the same time necessarily acknowledge that he must be believed in, hoped in, loved, invoked, and obeyed in all things. This worship is therefore simply necessary for salvation, and it is one and the same and unchangeable. Instituted worship is a means, ordained by the will of God, for exercising and promoting natural worship. Just as natural worship depends on the nature of God, so instituted worship depends on his most free will, and it varies according to his will, in accordance with the varying constitution of the Church before and after the manifestation of Christ. Yet it is not lawful unless it has God as its author. For "who has known the mind of God?" (Isa. 40:13; Rom. 11:34; 1 Cor. 2:16). "Do not follow your heart and your eyes, which lead you to whore after them" (Num. 15:39). Therefore whatever a man does from his own invention, or from the precept of men, as if honouring God, by that very fact he whores after his own heart and eyes, and blasphemes God rather than sanctifying him. And since worship pleasing to God arises at the same time from the sanctification of the Spirit, according to Paul's saying that the "offering of the Gentiles" is then acceptable to God when it is sanctified in the Holy Spirit (Rom. 15:16), it is clear that a work done (merely) as a work does not please God, and cannot be any cause of obtaining grace and righteousness.

units.la: III. Nobis hic de cultu Dei non naturali, sed institute; eóque non interno, sed externo, quatenus ille sub N.T. obtinet, sermo est. Eum Deus ipse in V.T. prædixit; Ab ortu solis, inquiens, usque ad occasum ejus magnum est nomen meum in gentibus; & in omni loco incensum seu hostia offertur Nomini meo, & munus purum. Nam magnum est Nomen meum in gentibus, dixit Jehova exercituum, Mal.I.11. Ante dixerat: Non est mihi voluptas in vobis. Munus non accepta ex manibus vestris, v.10. Rejecto igitur quandoque munere seu oblatione sacerdotum, sibi acceptum fore incensum seu adolitum & munus atque utrumque; purum nomini suo in omni loco, ab ortu solis usque ad occasum ejus, ubi magnum Dei nomen in gentibus esse debuit, offerendum, testatur. Duplex sacrificium est, unum, quod figura est, alterum, quod veritas est. Illud ante Christum obtinuit; hoc post Christum natum obtinet. Et hilasticum quidem non in omni loco, sed in eo, in quo pax per hoc sacrificium danda erat, offerri debuit. In loco hoc (domo posteriore) dabo pacem, ait Jehova, Deus exercituum, Hagg.II.9. Hierosolyma is locus est, ubi Christus crucifixus, peccatum terræ illius uno die abster sit, Zach. III.9. Eucharisticum verò, de quo Deus apud Malachiam loquitur, in omni loco. De quo etiam David: Sacrificate sacrificia justitiæ, Psal. IV.6. Immola Deo laudem, Psal.L.14. Sacrificium non vis, &c. Sacrificia Dei spiritus contritus; cor fractum & contritum, ô Deus, non despicies. Tunc voles sacrificia justitiæ, ibid. LI.18.19.21. Populus Dei: Quicquid accipis, pravitas est, & accipe bonum. Et solvemus, retribuemus juvencos, labia nostra, Hos. XIV. 2. hoc est, non mutam & brutam victimam, sed rationalem, nimirum fidem cordis, & confessionem oris, seu labiorum confitentium nomen ejus, Heb. XIII.15. Nam talibus victimis delectatur Deus, ibid. v.16. Distinguit tamen Deus apud Malachiam incensum seu adolitum, & munus; illo corporum, hoc bonorum, utroque totius nostri & nostrorum oblationem spiritualem significans. Convenit expositio ipsius Christi: Venit hora, & nunc est, cùm veri adoratores adorabunt in Spiritu & veritate. Etenim Pater tales quærit adorantes ipsum. Spiritus est Deus. Et adorantes ipsum in spiritu & veritate adorare debent, Joh. IV.23.24.
units.tr: III. Here our discussion concerns not natural but instituted worship of God, and not internal but external worship, as far as it holds under the New Testament. God himself foretold this in the Old Testament: "From the rising of the sun, he says, even to its setting, my name is great among the nations; and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering. For my name is great among the nations, says the LORD of hosts" (Mal. 1:11). Earlier he had said: "I have no pleasure in you, nor will I accept an offering from your hands" (v. 10). Thus, having at some point rejected the offering or sacrifice of the priests, he testifies that the incense or burnt offering and the offering, both pure, will be acceptable to him, to be offered to his name in every place, from the rising of the sun to its setting, where "the name of God is great among the nations." There are two sacrifices: one, which is a figure, and the other, which is the truth. The former held sway before Christ; the latter holds sway since Christ was born. The propitiatory sacrifice was to be offered not in every place, but in that place where peace was to be given through this sacrifice: "In this place (the later house) I will give peace, says the LORD of hosts" (Hag. 2:9). Jerusalem is the place where Christ was crucified, when "the sin of that land was removed in one day" (Zech. 3:9). But the eucharistic sacrifice, of which God speaks through Malachi, is in every place. David also speaks of it: "Offer the sacrifices of righteousness" (Ps. 4:5). "Offer to God praise" (Ps. 50:14). "You do not desire sacrifice," etc. "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise. Then you will desire the sacrifices of righteousness" (Ps. 51:18–19, 21). The people of God say: "Whatever you receive is wickedness; take what is good. And we will render the bullocks, our lips" (Hos. 14:2). That is, the victim is not a dumb and brutish one, but a rational one, namely the faith of the heart and the confession of the mouth, or of the lips confessing his name (Heb. 13:15). For God is pleased with such victims (v. 16). Yet through Malachi God distinguishes incense or burnt offering from gift, the former signifying the offering of bodies, the latter of goods, and both together signifying the spiritual offering of all that we are and have. The exposition of Christ himself agrees: "The hour comes, and now is, when true worshippers will worship in spirit and truth. For the Father seeks such to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth" (John 4:23–24).

units.la: IV. Et spiritualis igitur & rationalis Novi Testamenti cultus etiam externus est; in oppositione literæ & præcepti carnalis, quale nullum amplius in cultu N.T. obtinet. Et spiritualis quidem est, quia eum Spiritus non servitutis, sed promissionis & adoptionis exhibitus sanctificando operatur, & sedem suam præcipuè non in membris corporis, sed in mente & voluntate, quæ & ipsa spiritus est, habet. Nam exercitatio corporalis ad pauca utilis est, 1.Tim.IV.8. Neque aliter, quæ per membra fiunt, Deo placent, quàm quatenus secundum verbum Dei spiritus hominis, rectum judicium, & dictatus charitatis ad gloriam Dei facienda illa esse decernit. Etiam rationalis N.T. cultus est. Rogo vos per miserationes Dei, ut exhibeatis corpora vestra hostiam viventem, sanctam, placentem Deo, rationalem cultum vestrum, Rom. XII.1. Sacrificium offerre sacerdotis est. Nos autem per misericordiam Dei & purificationem Christi facti sumus Sacerdotes Deo, Apoc.I.v.6. V.9.10. Nam à Christo ad Deum adducimur, & in eodem ad Deum accedimus, quod Sacerdotis est. Omnis porrò cultus noster, quo Deum ex toto corde, tota anima, & omnibus viribus amamus, Θυσία sacrificium est. Ita & Sacerdotes & sacrificium sumus. Sacerdotes, quatenus,ut personæ,agimus & offerimus: Sacrificium, quatenus ut res,& facultatibus præditi, & partes habentes, quæ à nobis ita adhibentur & exhibentur, ut Deo ad honorem & gloriam misericordiæ sint, Deo offerimus & consecramur toti. Et Apostolus quidem jubet τὰ σώματα corpora Deo hostiam exhibere, non excludens animas. Sed corpora nominavit, quia sic evidentius distinguitur pars, qua magis sumus Sacerdotes ab ea, qua magis sacrificium sumus; & corpus ad sacrificium requiritur, quatenus per illud Deus apud alios honoratur. Præterea sicut animam Deo offerre, nisi oblato corpore, non possumus, quia corpus sine spiritu mortuum est, Jac. II. 26. ita neque corpus sine anima offerre possumus. Ideo mox corpora nostra appellat hostiam ζῶσαν, ἁγίαν, εὐάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ vivam, sanctam, placentem Deo; & vivam quidem, quia & in vita & in morte, sive aliquid agamus, sive in pulverem descendamus, charitate animatur: & quando spiritus membra bene movet & regit, ita ut homo in bono opere ex amore boni se exerceat, & ex odio mali à malo abstineat, tum corpus vivum fit: Sanctam propter inhabitationem Spiritus S. qui eam vivificat; quomodo etiam sacrificii caro sancta, sed typicè dici suevit: Deo placentem, quia sicut sacrificium Filii, ita fructus ejus, libamina & dapalia fidelium munera, quibus Christi satisfactio honoratur, in eodem Christo, ceu altari, per intercessionem Christi & Spiritus, Deo impensè placent: denique rationalem cultum, oppositè ad carnalem, quia Christianorum cultus in fide ejusque confessione & glorificatione Dei consistens merè rationalis est; sine quo ne ipsorum quidem Sacramentorum à Christo institutorum usus Deo placere potest.
units.tr: IV. The spiritual and rational worship of the New Testament is therefore also external, in contrast to the letter and to carnal precept, which holds no further place in New Testament worship. It is spiritual indeed because it is brought about by the Spirit, not of bondage but of promise and adoption, who works sanctification, and it has its seat chiefly not in the members of the body but in the mind and will, which are themselves spiritual. For "bodily exercise profits little" (1 Tim. 4:8). Nor do the things done through the members please God otherwise than insofar as the spirit of man, according to the Word of God, decides that they are to be done for the glory of God, by sound judgement and the dictate of charity. The New Testament worship is also rational: "I beseech you through the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, your rational service" (Rom. 12:1). To offer a sacrifice belongs to a priest. But we, through the mercy of God and the purification of Christ, have been made "priests to God" (Rev. 1:6; 5:9–10). For we are brought to God through Christ, and in him we approach God, which is the office of a priest. Moreover, all our worship, by which we love God with the whole heart, the whole soul and all our strength, is a sacrifice [θυσία]. Thus we are both priests and sacrifice. We are priests insofar as, as persons, we act and offer; we are a sacrifice insofar as, as things and endowed with faculties, and having parts which are used and employed by us in such a way that they serve God's honour and glory of mercy, we offer and consecrate ourselves wholly to God. And the Apostle indeed bids us present our bodies [τὰ σώματα] to God as a victim, not excluding our souls. But he named the bodies because in this way the part by which we are more priests is more clearly distinguished from the part by which we are more the sacrifice; and the body is required for sacrifice insofar as God is honoured among others through it. Moreover, just as we cannot offer the soul to God without the body offered, because "the body without the spirit is dead" (Jas. 2:26), so we cannot offer the body without the soul. Therefore he at once calls our bodies a victim "living, holy, pleasing to God" [ζῶσαν, ἁγίαν, εὐάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ]. They are "living" because, both in life and in death, whether we do something or go down into the dust, they are animated by charity; and when the spirit moves and rules the members well, so that a man exercises himself in a good work out of love of the good, and abstains from evil out of hatred of evil, then the body is alive. They are "holy" on account of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, who quickens it; in the same way the flesh of the sacrifice was customarily called "holy", but in a typical sense. They are "pleasing to God" because, just as the sacrifice of the Son is, so its fruit, the libations and feast offerings, the gifts of the faithful by which the satisfaction of Christ is honoured, are most acceptable to God in that same Christ, as on an altar, through the intercession of Christ and the Spirit. Finally, they are "rational worship", in contrast to carnal worship, because the worship of Christians, consisting in faith, its confession and the glorification of God, is purely rational; without it not even the use of the sacraments instituted by Christ can please God.

units.la: V. Per omnem quidem vitæ nostræ decursum nos & nostra omnia, vivæ fidei & charitatis actibus, Divinæ gloriæ consecrare, & velut mactare debemus. Per eum (Christum) offeramus hostiam laudis semper Deo, hoc est, fructum labiorum confitentium nomini ejus. Beneficentiæ autem & communionis ne oblivisciminí. Talibus enim hostiis Deus colitur, Hebr. XIII. 15. 16. Ubi hostia αἰνέσεως laudis & ὁμολογίας confessionis ipsam laudem & confessionem, hoc est, pro peccato condonato gratiarum actionem notat, quam διὰ παντὸς semper Deo offerri jubet, quia sacrificium hoc nulli loco, tempori, personæ astrictum, publicè & privatim à quovis Christiano peragi potest & debet; omnes enim sacerdotes sunt. Habet alius aliud donum; sed nulli sacrificium laudis deest. Omnis enim actio nostra ad celebrationem nominis Dei & Christi tendere debet, adeóque sacrificium est, quod διὰ παντὸς jugiter (תמיד) ἐνδελεχῶς jugis instar sacrificii, Exod. XXIX. 42.) Deo offerri ab omnibus debet. Et cum celebratione nominis Dei conjungenda est communio cum fratribus, in ipsorum etiam afflictionibus & necessitatibus: nec non ξυνωνία beneficentia erga omnes. Nam θρησκεία καθαρὰ ἡ ἀμίαντος religio, vel cultus purus & impollutus apud Deum & Patrem hic est, visitare orphanos & viduas in afflictione sua; immaculatum se servare à mundo, Jac. I. 27. Quorum illud charitatis, hoc sanctificationis & timoris, ne cum peccatis mundi communicemus, cum mundo scortemur, ei in peccato assimilemur, & facta ejus approbemus, est.
units.tr: V. Throughout the whole course of our life we ought to consecrate ourselves and all that we have to the divine glory, and as it were offer ourselves in sacrifice, by the acts of a living faith and charity. Through him (Christ) let us always offer to God the sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name. But do not forget beneficence and fellowship; for with such sacrifices God is worshipped, Heb. 13:15, 16. Here the sacrifice of "praise [αἰνέσεως]" and of "confession [ὁμολογίας]" denotes praise itself and confession, that is, thanksgiving for sin forgiven, which the apostle bids be offered to God "continually [διὰ παντὸς]." This sacrifice is bound to no place, time or person, and it can and ought to be performed by every Christian, both publicly and privately, for all are priests. One has one gift and another has another, but no one lacks the sacrifice of praise. Every action of ours ought to aim at the celebration of the name of God and Christ, and so it is a sacrifice which all ought to offer to God "continually [ἐνδελεχῶς]," like the continual sacrifice [תמיד], Exod. 29:42. With the celebration of God's name must be joined fellowship with the brethren, including sharing in their afflictions and needs, and "beneficence [ξυνωνία]" towards all. For "pure and undefiled religion [θρησκεία καθαρὰ ἡ ἀμίαντος]" before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world, James 1:27. The former belongs to charity, the latter to sanctification and fear, lest we share in the sins of the world, commit fornication with the world, be made like it in sin, and approve its deeds.

units.la: VI. Sed sunt tamen exercitia quædam singulari quadam ratione ad cultum Dei, inprimis publicè celebrandum pertinentia. Quæ partim actus & fructus fidei atque charitatis, partim media atque adminicula ad παροξυσμὸν seu exstimulationem mutuam sunt. Consideremus alii alios εἰς παροξυσμὸν ἀγάπης καὶ καλῶν ἔργων ad exstimulationem charitatis & bonorum operum. Non deserentes congregationem, sed adhortantes, Heb. X. 24. 25. Nam propter infirmitatem carnis, malum nobis adjacens & tentationes charitatis exstimulatione indigemus. Et necessaria est fidelibus mutua observatio, non ad noscenda aliorum secreta, sed ad charitatis exstimulationem. Quem in finem etiam ἐπισυναγωγὰς congregationes frequentandæ sunt. Nam Deus justus est, & justitias diligit. Ideo rectum (rectorum multitudinem) quod attinet; videbunt (recti) faciem suam invicem, Psal. XI. 7. Non in angulum & ad oras amplius depellentur doctores tui, & oculi tui erunt videntes doctores tuos, & aures tuæ audient verbum pone te, dicendo: Hæc est via, ambulate in ea, cum ad dextram vel sinistram flexeritis, Esaj. XXX. 20. 21. Non simplex enim congregationum bonum est, quia in iis consensum testamur in eandem legem, ad Deum uno humero colendum contessteramur, preces conjungimus, communi gratiarum actione Deum colimus, exempla piorum ante oculos habemus, pudore & verecundia à malo abstinemus, & invicem nos ad pietatem & charitatem acri stimulo incitamus.
units.tr: VI. There are, however, certain exercises belonging in a special way to the worship of God, above all to be celebrated publicly. Some of these are acts and fruits of faith and charity, and others are means and aids to mutual "provocation [παροξυσμὸν]," that is, stirring up one another. Let us consider one another to provoke [εἰς παροξυσμὸν] to love and good works, not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, but exhorting one another, Heb. 10:24, 25. For on account of the weakness of the flesh, the evil that clings to us, we need the stirring up of charity against temptations. Mutual watchfulness is also necessary for believers, not to learn each other's secrets, but to stir up charity. To this end the "assemblies [ἐπισυναγωγὰς]" are also to be frequented. For God is just and loves justice; therefore, as to the upright multitude, the upright shall see his face, Psal. XI. 7. Your teachers shall no longer be driven into a corner, but your eyes shall see your teachers, and your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying: This is the way, walk in it, when you turn to the right hand or to the left, Isa. XXX. 20, 21. For the good of congregations is not a simple one, since in them we testify our consent in the same law, confess that we worship God with one mind and one shoulder, join our prayers, worship God by common thanksgiving, have the examples of the pious before our eyes, abstain from evil through shame and modesty, and urge one another to godliness and charity with a sharp goad.

units.la: VII. Pertinent ergo huc prædicatio verbi, preces, hymni, eleemosynæ & Sacramentorum usus. De verbi Dei auditu Loc. XIV. §II. 32. &c. de precibus & hymnis, Loc. XXIII. 87. &c. de Eleemosynis, Loc. XIV. 36. &c. plurscula diximus. Singulare illud œconomia Fœderis Gratiæ sub Evangelio habet, quòd verbum Dei Christianos inter aliud auditi non debet, quàm Evangelii, sine mangonio legis, nisi quatenus illud Evangelio inservit, atque ita lex Spiritus vitæ Christi Rom. VIII. 2. evadit. Cúmque illud ad omnes pervenerit eodem revelationis & certitudinis genere, 1. Cor. XIV. 36. at non eodem illuminationis gradu; iccirco ii, qui χαρισμα διδασκαλίας donum docendi Rom. XII. 7. acceperunt, verbum Dei publicè repetunt, sensum ejus per comparationem spiritualium demonstrant, & per παράκλησιν adhortationem, ceu fidelos & prudentes servi, quos Dominus huic διακονία procurationi præfecit, Matth. XXIV. 45. cum omni prudentia ad auditorum ædificationem applicant. Eorum sermo non imperiosus, velut ad servos, sed suavis & velut ad liberos & ingenuos potissimum παράκλησις & δέησις rogatio est. Pro Christo legatione fungimur, tanquam Deo rogante per nos, petimus Christi causa; Reconciliamini Deo, 2. Cor. V. 20. Atque pars hæc cultus ad fidei professionem simul & exsuscitationem plurimum valet. Nam fides est ex auditu, & auditus per verbum Dei, Rom. X. 17. Et ministerium hoc universum versum sub N. T. spiritus, non amplius literæ esse fusius supra Loc. XX.63.&c. exposuimus. Quoad precationem id Evangelium ἴδιον proprium habet, quòd & formam precum ab ipso Christo artificiosissimè contextam habet: & nunc sublata populorum inimicitia, pro omnibus hominibus, 1. Tim. II. 1. etiam pro gravifimis peccatoribus, quin & Judæis ipsis, ut salvum Deus faciat populum Israel, Jerem. XXXI.7. fundendæ sunt. Quoad cantum, is in N. T. inprimis rationalis, argumenti perspicui, ad puerorum etiam in Christo captum accommodati, esse debet.
units.tr: VII. To this therefore belong the preaching of the word, prayers, hymns, alms and the use of the sacraments. We have said much about the hearing of the word of God, Loc. XIV §II 32 etc.; about prayers and hymns, Loc. XXIII 87 etc.; and about alms, Loc. XIV 36 etc. The peculiar feature of the economy of the covenant of grace under the Gospel is that Christians ought to hear the word of God as nothing other than the Gospel, without the admixture of the law, except insofar as the law serves the Gospel; and so the law of the Spirit of life in Christ comes forth, Rom. VIII. 2. Since the word "has come to all" with the same kind of revelation and certainty, 1 Cor. XIV. 36, but not with the same degree of illumination, those who have received the gift of teaching [χαρισμα διδασκαλίας], Rom. XII. 7, publicly repeat the word of God, show its sense by comparing spiritual things with one another, and apply it with all prudence to the edification of the hearers by "exhortation [παράκλησιν]," as faithful and wise servants whom the Lord has set over his household to give them their portion of food [διακονία], Matth. XXIV. 45. Their speech is not domineering, as to slaves, but gentle, as to free and well-born men above all: exhortation and entreaty [παράκλησις & δέησις]. We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you through us; we pray you in Christ's stead, be reconciled to God, 2 Cor. V. 20. This part of worship contributes greatly both to the profession of faith and to its arousing, for faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God, Rom. X. 17. That this whole ministry under the New Testament is of the Spirit and not of the letter, we have explained more fully above, Loc. XX. 63 etc. As to prayer, the Gospel has its own peculiarity: Christ himself framed the form of prayer most skilfully. And now, with the enmity of peoples removed, prayers are to be poured out for all men, 1 Tim. II. 1, even for the most grievous sinners, and indeed for the Jews themselves, that God may save his people Israel, Jer. XXXI. 7. As to singing, it under the New Testament ought above all to be rational, of clear subject matter, and adapted even to the understanding of children in Christ.

units.la: VIII. Cultui publico Ecclesiarum Liturgia inserviunt. Et Liturgia quasi λειτουργία publicum opus, vel publica functio, administratio, hic ad ἱερουργίαν sacram administrationem, quæ publicè peragitur, restringitur. Ejus pars Litania, à λιτανεύω supplico, atque hoc à λιτὴ precibus seu supplicatione, est. In universum Liturgiæ sunt διατάξεις Ordinationes & Agenda Ecclesiastica, quibus ratio & modus sacrorum conventuum definitur, formæ precum publicarum & privatarum, administrationis Sacramentorum, consecrationis conjugii, visitationis ægrotantium ex verbo Dei præscribuntur, & summa doctrinæ Christianæ in usum catechumenorum, κατ' ἐπιτομὴν proponitur. Quarum finis est, ut tum conformitas in doctrina, cultu externo & ritibus, quoad ejus fieri potest, retineatur, tum ruditati auditorum, ut & assequi orantem, &hinc formulas mutuari queant, consulatur. Tametsi verò indifferens esse, five libero sermone preces recitentur, five ex libro & præscripto prælegantur; imò plus gratiæ & spiritus esse in precibus liberè formatis, fi donum adsit, ultrò fateamur; nihilominus statæ ejusmodi Liturgiæ, dummodo verbo Dei conformes preces contineant, & necessitatis atque cultus opinio absit, exemplo non carent, & usum non contemnendum habent. Nam & Aharoni atque filiis ejus benedicendi forma, Num. VI.23. præscripta est; & David passim formulas precum publicarum concepit; uti ex Psalmis, nec non exemplo Ecclesiæ, 2. Chron. XXIX.27.30. liquet: Et in N. T. Christus orationem Dominicam, & typum & orandi formulam, uti supra ostendimus; quam etiam Apostolos in suis conventibus retinuisse, Juftinus Martyr Apolog. 2. Tertullianus Apolog. c. 30. & alii apud Caffandrum in Liturgicis testantur. Extant etiam Liturgiæ publicæ non paucæ Græcorum & Latinorum, quæ Apostolorum & Patrum nomina ferunt, non quòd ab iis compositæ, sed quòd in iis Ecclesiis, quæ ab illis plantatæ sunt, vel quibus illi præfuerunt, quæque interpolatæ licèt non parum, antiquæ tamen maximam partem sunt, & praxin Ecclesiæ veteris repræsentant, de quibus Pammelius, Caffander, Hoornbekius, alii fufiùs. Nihil enim inter verba concepta & libera interest, dummodo affectu orantis pio nunquam destituantur. Neque etiam facultas concipiendi preces, donum memoriæ, cognitionis, elocutionis omnibus datum, vel spiritus precum pari mensura concessus omnibus est. Denique fi spiritus cujusvis dictamini publicæ preces promiscuè permitterentur, tot fere in publico cultu distractiones, quot convenientium enthusiasmi existerent, & ad incertum αὐτοσχεδιασμόν orantis, vel gratias agentis exitum ne periores quidem, nedum idiotæ tutò Amen dicerent; & εὐχαριστία atque εὐφημία in delectu eorum, quæ ex verbo Dei cœtui præire oportet, non parum labasceret.
units.tr: VIII. Liturgies serve the public worship of the churches. "Liturgy," as a public work or public function, here means administration, and is restricted to the sacred administration [ἱερουργία] that is performed publicly. Part of it is the litany, from "litaneuō [λιτανεύω]," I supplicate, and this from "litē [λιτὴ]," prayers or supplication. In general, the liturgies are the "ordinances [διατάξεις]," the ecclesiastical orders and agendas, by which the manner and mode of sacred assemblies is defined. In them the forms of public and private prayers, the administration of the sacraments, the consecration of marriage and the visitation of the sick are prescribed from the word of God, and the sum of Christian doctrine is set forth briefly for the use of catechumens. Their purpose is that both conformity in doctrine, external worship and rites be retained as far as possible, and that the rudeness of the hearers be provided for, so that they can follow the one praying and so borrow the formulas. Although it is indeed indifferent whether prayers are recited in free speech or read out from a book and prescribed text, and although we freely admit that there is more grace and spirit in freely formed prayers where the gift is present, nevertheless fixed liturgies of this kind are not without example and have a use not to be despised, provided they contain prayers conformed to the word of God and the opinion of necessity and of worship is absent. For the form of blessing was prescribed to Aaron and his sons, Num. VI. 23; David composed formulas of public prayer in many places, as is clear from the Psalms and from the example of the Church, 2 Chron. XXIX. 27, 30. In the New Testament Christ gave the Lord's Prayer both as a type and as a form of praying, as we showed above, and the apostles retained it in their assemblies, as Justin Martyr (Apology 2), Tertullian (Apology c. 30) and others testify, cited by Cassander in his Liturgica. There also exist not a few public liturgies of Greeks and Latins which bear the names of apostles and Fathers; not because these were composed by them, but because they belong to those churches which were planted by them or over which they presided. Although greatly interpolated, they are for the most part ancient and represent the practice of the early Church, concerning which Pamelius, Cassander, Hoornbeeck and others speak at greater length. For there is no difference between set and free words, provided the prayer is never lacking the pious affection of the one praying. Nor is the faculty of composing prayers, a gift of memory, knowledge and eloquence, given to all, nor is the spirit of prayer granted in equal measure to all. Finally, if public prayers were permitted indiscriminately to the dictate of every spirit, there would be almost as many distractions in public worship as there were enthusiasms among those assembled; and with the uncertain extemporising of the one praying or giving thanks, not even the learned, much less the unlearned, could safely say Amen. "Thanksgiving [εὐχαριστία]" and "good speech [εὐφημία]" in the choice of those things which ought to precede the assembly from the word of God would not a little totter.

units.la: IX. Inventi tamen sunt in Ecclesia, Anglicana inprimis, morosi, scrupulosi & delicatuli nimis, qui rejectis Liturgiis nescio quæ Directoria fine ullis conceptis formulis, invexerunt, quos ad id novandi studium, ut sub specioso libertatis orandi & prophetandi velo omni generi sectarum in Ecclesiam introitus pateret; nec non affectatio spiritus Apostolici ad id impulisse videtur. Frustra illi statas liturgias, ceu inventa hominum, ad ἐλλοφήμιον seducentia, sugillant. Cur enim statæ preces magis, quàm extemporaneæ & publicæ à tota Ecclesia compositæ vel approbatæ magis quàm privatæ periculum ejusmodi foverent? Et doctrina quidem fidei & charitatis eadem ubique & semper esse debet, neque mutationem ullam subire debet. Sed qui doctrinæ ancillatur, ordo, & doctrinæ ipsius ad varios usque applicatio variare potest. Neque lectio precum vel idolum, vel similitudo veræ precationis, locum verbi & spiritus supplentis, est, quia preces etiam lectæ cum pia attentione & mentis devotione, absque qua est, quævis precatio, ceu sonus fine mente, idolum est, fundi possunt. Præterea neque preces ejusmodi statæ Spiritum precationum fidelibus, Zach. XII. 10. & ineffabilibus suspiriis intercedentem pro nobis Rom. VIII. 26. intercluduntnedum extinguunt. Est enim Spiritus dictans, quid de novo petendum fit, & Spiritus assistens, quem imploramus, ut publicis supplicationibus nostris subveniat. Tam privatim quàm publicè oranti adest Spiritus, dummodo cuncta privata privatim, publica publicè juxta dictamen ejus fiant. Et Spiritus S. est adminiculum orantium internum, formulæ orandi externum, illi fubordinatum, non oppositum. At nec formulæ ejusmodi derogant honori Christi, quia ascendens in cœlum dona dedit hominibus necessaria ad opus ministerii, Ephef. IV. 8.11. cujus partes docere & orare sunt, Actor. VI. 4. Nam & distributio donorum illorum inæqualis est, & differente mensura datur: & rudiorum etiam atque infantum in Ecclesia ratio haberi debet. Quod hostiæ carnalis nomine preces statas traducunt, convitium, non res est. Preces enim cum spiritu & devotione lectæ æquè spirituales sunt, ac ex tempore fusæ; & utræque hostiæ carnales sunt, à carnalibus fusæ; spirituales, cùm à Spiritu S. & corde sanctificato proficiscuntur. Et Liturgiæ quidem in genere omnes necessitates comprehendunt; sed variari tamen, authoritate publica, cùm id res & occasio atque necessitas singularis tulerit, possunt. Neque enim accessoria statas ejusmodi formulas tollunt, sed præfenti occasioni accommodant. Denique alia concionum, quæ ex libro statæ non leguntur, alia precum ratio est. Explicationes enim & applicationes, quæ in concionibus proponuntur, variæ & differentes sunt. At orationum materies, saltem in plerisque semper sibi constat.
units.tr: IX. Yet in the Church, especially the English Church, there have been fastidious, scrupulous and over-delicate people who, having rejected the liturgies, introduced I know not what Directories without any set forms. Their zeal for innovation seems to have been driven by the desire to open a way into the Church for every kind of sect under the specious veil of freedom to pray and prophesy, and also by an affected imitation of the Apostolic Spirit. Their attacks on set liturgies, as human inventions leading to blasphemy [βλασφήμιον], are in vain. For why should set prayers carry more danger of this kind than extempore prayers, or public prayers composed or approved by the whole Church more than private ones? Doctrine of faith and love must everywhere and always be the same and must undergo no change. But the order that serves doctrine, and the varied application of that doctrine, can vary. Nor is reading prayers an idol or a likeness of true prayer that takes the place of the word and the Spirit, since prayers read with pious attention and devotion of mind may be offered, and without that devotion any prayer is an idol, like a sound without a mind. Moreover, set prayers of this kind do not shut out, much less extinguish, the Spirit of prayers to believers (Zech. 12:10) or the Spirit interceding for us with unutterable groanings (Rom. 8:26). For the Spirit is both dictating what is to be newly sought and assisting, whom we implore to help our public supplications. The Spirit is present to the one praying privately as much as publicly, provided that all private matters are done privately and public matters publicly, according to his dictate. The Holy Spirit is the inward helper of those who pray, and the form of prayer is the outward helper, subordinate to him and not opposed to him. Nor do such forms detract from the honour of Christ, for ascending into heaven he gave gifts to men, needed for the work of the ministry (Eph. 4:8, 11), whose parts are to teach and to pray (Acts 6:4). For the distribution of those gifts is unequal, and given in differing measure, and the case of the weaker and of infants in the Church must also be taken into account. That they call set prayers by the name of carnal sacrifice is an insult, not an argument. For prayers read with the Spirit and devotion are as spiritual as those poured out extempore; and both are carnal sacrifices when offered by carnal men, and spiritual when they proceed from the Holy Spirit and a sanctified heart. Liturgies, in general, cover all needs; yet they may be varied by public authority whenever the matter, occasion and particular necessity require. For set forms of this kind do not exclude additions, but adapt themselves to the present occasion. Finally, the method for sermons, which are not read from a book, is one thing, and the method for prayers is another. For the explanations and applications set out in sermons are various and different, whereas the subject matter of prayers, at least in most cases, always remains the same.

units.la: X. Liturgiæ quàm fimpliciffimæ & verbo
units.tr: X. Liturgies should be as simple as possible and, above all, conformed to the Word of God.

units.la: Dei conformes inprimis eſſe debent. Talis Apoſtolica fuit, ſola verbi leſtione & prædicatione, Sacramentorum pura administratione & precatione conſtans. Primi illi Christiani liberrimi ...
units.tr: Such was the apostolic liturgy, consisting solely of the reading and preaching of the Word, the pure administration of the sacraments and prayer. Those first Christians, most free ...

units.la: Bellarmini focus obductus abstergitur. peregrino idiomate poenæ loco ab ipso Deo Esaj.XXVIII.11.12. intentetur, vers.21. quòd linguæ in signum datæ sint non credentibus, sed infidelibus, v.22. quòd & denique percepto sermone loquentis etiam infideles in Ecclesia converti possint, v.23-26. Hæc argumenta disertissima omnium ab Apostolo futuræ Antichristi perfidiæ præscio contexta sunt, eum haud dubiè in finem, ne Ecclesiæ subsidium pestilentissimum, & Ecclesiæ totius devoratorium errorem redarguendi desit; & ut inde Tridentinos suum anathema adversus ipsum S. Paulum, imò Dominum, Christum, inter cujus præcepta Paulus suum illud v.37. refert, quia mandatum Domini est, Matth.XXVIII.20. ut doceamus ea, quæ ipse præcepit (peregrinæ autem linguæ in sacris usum non præcepit, sed exemplo etiam suo vernacula lingua docentis, precantis, & Sacramenta instituentis atque administrantis condemnavit) vibrasse, & adversus Deum ipsum insano molimine belligerari constet.
units.tr: The smoke-blackened hearth of Bellarmine is wiped clean. A foreign idiom is threatened by God himself as a punishment, Isa. 28:11–12; verse 21 says the tongues were given as a sign not to believers but to unbelievers; verse 22 says that, the message once received, even unbelievers can be converted in the Church (verses 23–26). These most explicit arguments were woven together by the Apostle, who foresaw the future faithlessness of Antichrist, no doubt to this end: that the Church should not lack a most pestilential remedy, and a refutation of the error that devours the whole Church; and it is plain that the Tridentines have thereby hurled their anathema against St Paul himself, indeed against the Lord Christ, among whose precepts Paul counts his statement in verse 37, because it is the commandment of the Lord (Matt. 28:20), that we should teach those things which he commanded. (He did not command the use of a foreign tongue in sacred matters, but by his own example condemned it, teaching, praying and instituting and administering the sacraments in the vernacular.) They have made war against God himself with a mad enterprise.

units.la: XIII. Adeò diserta Apostoli adversus linguæ peregrinæ in sacris usum argumenta sunt, ut Cajetano in 1. Cor. XIV. hanc confessionem extorserint: Ex hac doctrina habetur, quòd Melius ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ est, orationes publicas, quæ audiente populo dicuntur, dici lingua communi clericis & populo, quàm dici Latinè. Ante ipsum Lyranus eundem in locum dixerat: Ostendit, quòd si in oratione publica populus intelligat orationem, seu benedictionem Sacerdotis, melius reducitur in Deum & devotius respondet Amen. Addit: Quid proficit populus simplex & non intelligens, quasi diceret, nihil, aut modicum, quia nescit se conformare tibi, qui es minister Ecclesiæ, respondendo Amen. Propter quod in primitiva Ecclesia benedictiones & cætera communia fiebant in vulgari. Ante utrumque Johannes VIII. Papa Epist. 247. ad Sfentorem Moraviæ Principem (quem Baronius ad A. 880. § 19. recitat) iisdem Apostoli argumentis usus jubet Moravos in lingua sua sacris defungi, satis & manifestè admoneri nos ab Apostolo dictitans, quatenus linguis (vulgaribus) utentes Ecclesiam ædificemus. Scenæ equidem Johannes inservivit licentiam sacra vulgari lingua celebrandi Sclavis impertiens, veritus, ne, si præfractè negaret, illi Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani dictioni, Bulgarorum exemplo, se submitterent. Nam Græcis Sacerdotibus converși jure Constantinopolitano Patriarchæ se subjicere debuerant. Verùm ille astu accersito ad se Methodio cum eo sic transfegit, ut universum Evangelium Latinè priùs, dein Sclavonicè legeretur, sed Pauli tamen verbis pro usu linguæ vulgaris pugnans, invitus forte, & asinæ Bileami adinstar. Et quod Sclavis dedit, mox Gregorius VII. iisdem eripuit.
units.tr: XIII. The Apostle's arguments against using a foreign tongue in worship are so clear that even Cajetan was forced to confess, on 1 Cor. 14: From this teaching it follows that it is better for the edification of the Church that public prayers, which are said while the people listen, be said by the clergy and people in a common language than in Latin. Before him Lyra had said of the same passage: It shows that if the people in public prayer understand the prayer, or the priest's blessing, they are led more fully to God and answer Amen more devoutly. He adds: What good does the simple people do, which does not understand? That is, nothing or very little, because it does not know how to conform itself to you, who are the minister of the Church, by answering Amen. For this reason in the primitive Church blessings and other common prayers were said in the vernacular. Before both of them, Pope John VIII, in Epistle 247 to Sfentopulcrus, Prince of Moravia (which Baronius recounts at A.D. 880, § 19), used the same arguments of the Apostle and ordered the Moravians to perform the sacred rites in their own language, declaring that we are plainly and sufficiently admonished by the Apostle that by using the (vernacular) tongues we build up the Church. Indeed John yielded to the situation when he granted the Slavs permission to celebrate sacred rites in their vernacular, fearing that if he refused flatly they would submit to the authority of the Patriarch of Constantinople, as the Bulgarians had done. For the Greek priests who had been converted were bound by Constantinopolitan law to submit to the Patriarch. But he summoned Methodius to himself and came to terms with him so that the whole Gospel was read first in Latin and then in Slavonic. Yet in doing so he was fighting against the words of Paul about the use of the vernacular tongue, perhaps unwillingly, like Balaam's ass. And what he gave to the Slavs, Gregory VII soon took away from them.

units.la: XIV. Sed Bellarminus S. Paulo velut in os contradicens: Nulla, inquit, est necessitas, quæ cogat vulgari lingua Sacramenta administrare. Quid ita verò, cùm Apostolo contra visum fuerit? Sacrificii, inquit, oblatio magis in re, quàm in verbis consistit. Verba non diriguntur ad auditores instruendos, sed primò ad elementum consecrandum, &c. Elementum autem nullam linguam intelligit; secundò ad Deum, qui omnes linguas intelligit. Ut nihil de falsa sacrificii exter-
units.tr: XIV. But Bellarmine contradicts St. Paul, as it were to his face: There is no necessity, he says, that compels the sacraments to be administered in the vernacular. Why so, since the Apostle has ruled otherwise? The offering of the sacrifice, he says, consists more in the thing than in the words. The words are not directed to instructing the hearers, but first to consecrating the element, etc. But the element understands no language; secondly, they are directed to God, who understands all languages. To say nothing of the false hypothesis of an external sacrifice, and of the shameless clash with the sayings of St. Paul,

units.la: ni hypothesi, nec non de pugna effronti cum S. Pauli effatis, dicam, aperte etiam à Tridentinis Mystagogis diffidet. Si enim, quod illi censuerunt, Missa magnam populi fidelis eruditionem continet; atque iccirco frequenter aliquid de mysterio eo populo declarandum est, ne panem petenti desit, qui frangat: quomodo in Missa nihil est, quod ad auditores dirigatur, nullaque necessitas vernaculum idioma postulat? Quinimo cùm Missam multis verbis celebrari placuerit, & talibus quidem plerisque quæ non ad Deum, sed ad fideles communicantes diriguntur; & quæ ad Deum diriguntur non pauca nomine populi totius ad eum dirigantur, quis furor sacrificulos agitavit, ut non ea saltem verba, preces, hymnos; nec non reliqua, preces & benedictiones vernacula & intelligibili lingua pronuntiarent? Cùm tamen Apostolus dilertis adeò verbis peregrinæ in cultu publico linguæ usum sustulerit? Sed negat ille, Apostolum agere de lectione Scripturarum, vel officiis Divinis, & de exhortatione duntaxat spirituali, collatione & canticis spiritualibus, quæ Christiani ad laudandum Deum, & gratias ei agendas, & simul ad suam, simul ad aliorum ædificationem composuerant, agi pertendit. Esto ita: Sed manet ratio interdicti Apostolici, quo eum, qui linguis loquitur, tacere jubet, nisi adsit interpres, quia sermo talis futurus sit infructuosus, omni ædificatione, adhortatione & consolatione destitutus. Sed finis, inquit ille, præcipuus illorum canticorum erat instructio, vel consolatio populi: at Divinorum officiorum finis præcipuus non est instructio vel consolatio populi, sed cultus Dei. Quæ autem populum scire oportet ex Divinis officiis, à Pastoribus explicantur. Quæ vanissima sunt. Si enim Divinorum officiorum finis non est instructio vel consolatio populi, cur S. Paulus idem omnia (quæ in cœtu fiunt convenientibus fratribus) ad ædificationem fieri, vers.26. jussit? Qualis ædificatio est, ubi nulla instructio, nulla populi consolatio? Ubi nemo, vel pauci intelligunt, quod dicitur? Ubi auditur, v.8. sermo non significans, v.9.? Ubi alter alteri barbarus est, & qui loquuntur, furere videntur? Ubi tacere, si nullus interpres sit, vers.28. jubentur? Et cujusmodi Dei cultus est, quem officiorum præcipuum finem esse dicit, in quo nulla colentis intelligentia est? Nam preculas sine intellectu demurmurare, mussitare non gratus certè Deo cultus, sed manifesta ejus irrisio est. Est hoc opus operatum, sed hypocriticum, quo labiis ad Deum appropinquantes corde longè ab eo absunt: est devotio, sed stupida suíque ignara: est affectus cordis, sed cæcus & άλογος. Nam quod per frequentissimas conciones satis populum instrui regerit, dilutum esse, jam ostendimus. Et rarè extra Quadragesimæ & Adventus tempus sacerdotum conciones sunt: & ipsæ conciones lectionem Scripturæ in lingua vulgari postulant, ut ad Jydium ejus lapidem exigantur.
units.tr: it is plainly also at odds with the Tridentine mystagogues. For if, as they have judged, the Mass contains great instruction of the faithful people, and therefore something about that mystery must often be explained to the people, lest there be no one to break bread for those who ask for it: how is it that in the Mass there is nothing directed to the hearers, and no necessity demands the vernacular language? Indeed, since they have resolved that the Mass be celebrated with many words, and most of them not directed to God but to the faithful communicants, and since not a few of those directed to God are offered to him in the name of the whole people, what madness drove these little priests to refrain from pronouncing at least those words, prayers and hymns, and the remaining prayers and blessings, in a vernacular and intelligible language, when the Apostle has so clearly removed the use of a foreign tongue in public worship? But he denies that the Apostle is speaking of the reading of Scripture or of the divine offices, and insists that he is speaking only of spiritual exhortation, conference, and spiritual songs, which Christians composed to praise God and give thanks to him, and at the same time for their own edification and that of others. Granted it be so: yet the rule of the Apostle remains, by which he bids the one who speaks in a tongue to keep silent unless an interpreter is present, because such speech would be unfruitful, destitute of all edification, exhortation and consolation. But, he says, the chief aim of those songs was the instruction or consolation of the people; whereas the chief aim of the divine offices is not the instruction or consolation of the people but the worship of God. What the people ought to know from the divine offices is explained by the ministers. These claims are most empty. For if the chief aim of the divine offices is not the instruction or consolation of the people, why did St. Paul in 1 Cor. 14:26 order that all things done in the assembly of the brethren be done for edification? What kind of edification is there where there is no instruction and no consolation of the people? Where no one, or few, understand what is said? Where, in v. 8, the speech is not clear? Where one is a barbarian to another, and those who speak seem to be mad? Where, in v. 28, they are commanded to keep silent if there is no interpreter? And what sort of worship of God is it, which he says has the chief aim of the offices, in which the worshipper has no understanding? For to mumble prayers without understanding, to mutter them, is not worship pleasing to God, but a plain mockery of him. It is an opus operatum, but hypocritical, by which people draw near to God with their lips while being far from him in their hearts: it is devotion, but stupid and unaware of itself: it is an affection of the heart, but blind and unreasoning [ἄλογος]. For we have already shown that the claim that the people is sufficiently instructed by very frequent sermons is refuted. And sermons are rare outside the seasons of Lent and Advent, and the sermons themselves require the reading of Scripture in the vernacular, so that they may be tested by its touchstone.

units.la: XV. Negari non potest, & Scripturas vernaculas & sacra vernacula Ecclesiam veterem saniorem adhuc perpetuo in usu habuisse. Quod Celeb. Ussherius Armachanus, nec non eidem suppetias ferens Henricus Warton in novissimè
units.tr: It cannot be denied that the ancient Church, sounder than ours, always kept in constant use both Scriptures in the vernacular and sacred services in the vernacular. The celebrated Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, and Henry Warton, who lent him support, have shown this, in the most recently published

units.la: Origo peregrinæ linguæ usus in Ecclesiam introducti. vissimè excusa Historia dogmatica de Scripturis & Sacris vernaculis, tum testimoniis Patrum Græcorum & Latinorum ad A. DC. usque, tum Decretis Ecclesiasticis & Regalibus: tum praxi Ecclesiæ veteris,qua & Scripturæ vernaculæ versiones cusæ sunt, & earum lectio promiscua fuit; & commune officium vulgari lingua celebratum fuit, & variarum gentium liturgiæ vernaculæ hodiéque extantes conscriptæ sunt; inductis amplissimè & irrefragabiliter demonstrarunt. Demum nascente Antichristo,qui potestatem septicollis Bestiæ,& urbis magnæ, habentis Regnum super Reges terræ, Apoc. XVII. 18. in conspectu ejus exercituru†rus,& effecturus erat, ut omnes characterem, nomen & numerum Bestiæ haberent, & Romanæ potestatis subditos se profiterentur; Pontifices Romani id operam dederunt,ut Latina lingua, quantumvis incognita,& non intellecta,ubique in ditione sua obtineret. Qua in re potestatem Romæ veteris ethnicæ imitati sunt, operam dantis, uti Augustinus de Civit. D. lib. XIX. 7. observavit; ut imperiosa civitas non solùm jugum, verùm etiam linguam suam domitis gentibus per pacem societatis (socialis legendum censet Lipsius) imponeret, de quo egregia Pauli Merulæ Cosmogr. p. 795. 796, dissertatio extat. Ita nempe, uti Laurentius Valla Præfat. in Lib. eleg. scribit,Romanum Imperium videbatur, ubicunque lingua Romana dominabatur. Barbaris Italiam vastantibus & possidentibus evenit, ut Galli & Hispani,quibus Latinus sermo vernaculus erat, alium ex Romano & Barbarico varie commixtum paulatim reciperent. Linguas enim Italicam, Hispanicam & Gallicam Latini sermonis propagines esse, in confesso est. Et sub Carolo M. ita corrupta est Romana lingua,quæ apud vulgus tum temporis obtinebat, ut prisca & purior illa vix intelligeretur ampliùs. Cúmque Carolus in votis maximis haberet, ut Latina lingua nondum plane apud populum plane obsoleta restitueretur,& ubique retineretur,id etiam,dissonantia Ecclesiastici cantus inter Romanos & Gallos suos offensus, & judicans (uti Sigebertus Gemblacensis ad A. 774. scribit) justius esse de puro fonte, quàm de turbato rivo bibere; operam navavit, ut Ordo Romanus in lingua Latina, quantumvis non intellecta, à posteris retineretur. Qua re non parum,at nec opinans tamen Romani Antichristi conatum promovit. Nam procedente tempore Latinæ linguæ usus in Sacra omnium Papæ clientum inductus,& lectio Scripturæ vernaculæ modis omnibus, horrendis etiam adversus legentes suppliciis repræsentatis,sufflaminata est, donec & Tridentini anathema adversus dissentientes Evangelicos vibrarunt; & in Regula 4. per Patres in Synodo Tridentina delectos confecta,& A. M D LXIV. in Indice librorum prohibitorum à Pio IV. edito, conclusum est; ut hac in parte judicio Episcopi aut Inquisitoris stetur,ut cum consilio Parochi vel Confessarii,Bibliorum à Catholicis authoribus versorum lectionem in vulgari lingua eis concedere possint,quos intelle-xerint ex hujusmodi lectione non damnum, sed fidei atque pietatis augmentum capere posse, quam facultatem in scriptis habeant. Qui autem, inquiunt, absque tali facultate ea legere,sen habere
units.tr: The origin of the use of a foreign tongue introduced into the Church. work, Dogmatic History of the Scriptures and the Sacred Vernacular, both from the testimonies of the Greek and Latin Fathers down to A.D. 600, and from ecclesiastical and royal decrees, and from the practice of the ancient Church, by which vernacular versions of Scripture were printed and their reading was open to all, the common service was celebrated in the vernacular, and the vernacular liturgies of various peoples, still extant today, were written. They have demonstrated this very fully and irrefutably. Finally, when Antichrist was about to arise, who would exercise the power of the seven-hilled Beast and bring it about before his eyes that the great city, which reigns over the kings of the earth, Apoc. XVII. 18, and make everyone bear the mark, name and number of the Beast and profess themselves subjects of Roman power, the Roman pontiffs took pains that the Latin tongue, however unknown and unintelligible, should prevail everywhere in their dominion. In this they imitated the power of ancient pagan Rome, bent on this, as Augustine observed in De Civitate Dei XIX. 7, so that the imperious city would impose upon subdued nations not only its yoke but also its language, through the peace of society (socialis, Lipsius thinks should be read). On this there is an excellent discussion in Paulus Merula, Cosmographia pp. 795–796. Indeed, as Lorenzo Valla writes in his preface to the Elegies, the Roman Empire seemed to exist wherever the Roman language prevailed. When the barbarians ravaged and occupied Italy, it came about that the Gauls and Spaniards, for whom Latin had been their vernacular speech, gradually adopted another, mixed variously from Roman and barbarian. For it is agreed that the Italian, Spanish and French languages are offshoots of the Latin tongue. Under Charles the Great the Roman language then current among the common people was so corrupted that the old and purer form was scarcely understood any longer. Since Charles greatly wished that Latin, not yet wholly obsolete among the people, should be restored and retained everywhere, and was also offended by the discord of ecclesiastical chant between his Romans and Gauls, and judging (as Sigebert of Gembloux writes at 774) that it is more right to drink from a pure spring than from a muddied stream, he took pains that the Roman Order should be retained by posterity in Latin, however unintelligible. In this, though he did not intend it, he advanced not a little the attempt of the Roman Antichrist. For as time went on, the use of Latin in the sacred services of all the clients of the Pope was introduced, and the reading of Scripture in the vernacular was hindered in every way, with horrible punishments set before readers, until the anathemas of Trent were hurled against dissenting Evangelicals.
