In Rule 4, drawn up by Fathers chosen at the Council of Trent, and in the Index of prohibited books published by Pius IV in 1564, it was concluded that in this matter the judgment of the bishop or inquisitor shall stand, so that with the advice of the parish priest or confessor they may grant to those whom they have understood can gain from such reading not harm but an increase of faith and piety, the reading of the Bible translated into the vernacular by Catholic authors, which permission they shall have in writing. Those who, they say, read or have these without such permission

units.la: præsumpserint, nisi priùs Bibliis ordinario redditis peccatorum absolutionem percipere non possint. Sed Clemens VIII. A. M D XCV. Indicem librorum prohibitorum recognitum edi jubens, hanc Regulæ illi Pii IV. animadversionem addidit; quòd per Indicis illius novam editionem,nulla de novo tribuatur facultas Episcopis vel Inquisitoribus, aut Regularium Superioribus concedendi licentiam emendi,legendi aut retinendi Biblia vulgari lingua edita, cùm hactenus mandato & usu Sanctæ Romanæ & universalis Inquisitionis sublata iis fuerit facultas concedendi hujusmodi licentias legendi aut retinendi Biblia vulgaria, aut alias S. Scripturæ tam Novi quàm Veteris Testamenti partes quavis vulgari lingua editas, ac insuper Summaria etiam & Compendia historica eorundem Bibliorum, seu librorum S. Scripturæ, quocunque vulgari idiomate conscripta; quod quidem inviolatè servandum est.
units.tr: presume to do so, cannot obtain absolution of their sins unless first they return the Bibles to the ordinary. But Clement VIII, in 1595, ordering that a revised Index of prohibited books be published, added this comment to that rule of Pius IV: that through the new edition of that Index, no new faculty is to be granted to bishops or inquisitors, or to superiors of religious orders, to concede licence to buy, read or keep Bibles printed in the vernacular, since hitherto, by the command and practice of the Holy Roman and Universal Inquisition, the faculty of granting such licences to read or keep vernacular Bibles, or other parts of Holy Scripture of both Testaments printed in any vernacular, and moreover summaries and historical compendia of these same Bibles or books of Holy Scripture written in any vernacular idiom, has been withdrawn; which indeed must be inviolably observed.

units.la: XVI. Si ulla, hac certè in re Ecclesia Romana ab Ecclesia Apostolica & Christiana saniore omni discessionem fecit,& in infidelium atque hæreticorum castra palam ingressa est. His enim non illis sacra sua celare mos semper fuit. Opera & instinctu malorum dæmonum mortis supplicium adversus librorum Hystaspis, aut Sibyllæ, aut Prophetarum lectores à gentilibus constitutum esse, Justinus Martyr Apol. 2. pro Christ. prodidit, ut ita per timorem ab illis homines, quò minùs scripta ea legentes rerum bonarum notitiam percipere-rent, sed in servitute eorum manerent,absterrerentur. An eadem opera,& instinctu malorum dæmonum Christiano populo librorum Propheticorum lectione à Romanis Præsulibus interdictum sit,atque iidem horrendis supplicis in lectores Scripturæ sæviant,& S. Scripturæ Volumina flammis tradant,quæ flagitiosorum semper Ecclesiæ hostium, velut Jehojakimi,Diocletiani, Donatistarum, Georgii Cappadocis consuetudo fuit, alii judicent. Hoc certè constat, à sacrilegii hujus patronis, Ledesma de Script. quavis lingua non legendis cap. 22. §17. Peresio de Tradit. aliis hoc ipso argumento interdictum hoc defendi,quòd antiqui illi Romani Sibyllina carmina legendi facultatem certis tantùm Magistratibus,viris prudentissimis concesserint. Ut eodem spiritu agitatos utrosque esse appareat. At verò nos,sic Justinus loc. cit. loquitur, absque timore non tantùm hujusmodi scripta legimus, verùm etiam vobis ad inspiciendum, quæ eis traduntur, offerimus, grata acceptáque omnibus fore scientes. Ægyptios Sacerdotes mysteria sua paucis, futuris Regibus & Sacerdotibus compertæ fidei atque prudentiæ, commisse Diodorus Siculus, Lucianus, alii testantur. Hoc ipsum, ne ignari essemus à quibus magistris disciplinam hanc Pontificii hauserint,diligenter Ledesma loc. cit. inculcat. Addere ille poterat ex Orphei sacris illa: φθέγξομαι οἷς Θέμις ἐςὶ θύρας δ' ἐπιθέσθαι βεβήλοις, Dignis sanctâ loquor: procul hinc arcete profanos; nec non ex Bacchi mysteriis: Odi profanum vulgus,& arceo. Pythagoræ etiam & Lysidis,sectatoris ejus, nec non Eleusiniorum sacrorum abscondita mysteria idem Ledesma laudat. In universum fida silentia, sic Lactantius Inst. lib. V. 20. scribit, sacris instituta sunt ab hominibus, ut nesciat populus, quid colat. Tantum abest
units.tr: XVI. If ever the Roman Church has departed from the apostolic and Christian Church, which was sounder in every respect, certainly it is in this matter, and it has openly gone over into the camps of unbelievers and heretics. For it was always their custom to hide their sacred things from those, not from these. By the work and instigation of evil demons, Justin Martyr, in Apology II for the Christians, reports that the penalty of death was established by the Gentiles against readers of the books of Hystaspes, or the Sibyl, or the Prophets, so that men would be frightened by fear from reading those writings and gaining knowledge of good things, and so would remain in their servitude. Whether by the same work and instigation of evil demons the reading of the prophetic books has been forbidden to the Christian people by the Roman prelates, and whether these same men rage with horrible punishments against readers of Scripture and hand the volumes of Holy Scripture to the flames, which was always the custom of the wicked enemies of the Church, such as Jehoiakim, Diocletian, the Donatists and George of Cappadocia, others may judge. This at least is certain: the defenders of this sacrilege, Ledesma, On Scriptures not to be read in any language, ch. 22 §17, and Peresius, On Tradition, and others, have defended this prohibition by this very argument, that the ancient Romans granted the right to read the Sibylline verses only to certain magistrates, the most prudent men. So both sides appear to be stirred by the same spirit. But we, so Justin speaks in the passage cited, read such writings without fear, and we offer them to you to inspect, knowing that they will be welcome and acceptable to all. Diodorus Siculus, Lucian and others testify that the Egyptian priests committed their mysteries to a few, to future kings and priests of proven faith and prudence. Ledesma, cited above, diligently insists on this very point, so that we may not be ignorant from which teachers the Papists have drawn this discipline. He could have added from the rites of Orpheus: I will speak to those for whom it is lawful; close the doors against the profane; I speak to the worthy; keep the profane far away [φθέγξομαι οἷς Θέμις ἐστὶ θύρας δ' ἐπιθέσθαι βεβήλοις]; and from the mysteries of Bacchus: I hate the profane crowd and keep it off. The same Ledesma also praises the hidden mysteries of Pythagoras and of his follower Lysis, and of the Eleusinian rites. In general, Lactantius writes, Inst. V. 20, faithful silences have been instituted by men for sacred rites, so that the people may not know what they worship. So far is it

units.la: ggg abest, ut Ethnicorum exemplum Ecclesiæ imitandum cum Jesuitis commendaverit. Non enim Christiani, sed hæretici veteres illud imitati sunt, qui Irenæo lib. III. 2. teste, ex Scripturis reprehensi in accusationem ipsarum Scripturarum conversi sunt; quasi varie essent dicta, & non posset ex his inveniri veritas ab his, qui Traditionem nescuint. Non enim, inquiebant, per literas tradita illa est, sed per vivam vocem, ob quam causam & Paulus dixit: Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, sapientiam autem non mundi hujus, & (hoc etiam textu eos usos fuisse, Tertullianus confirmat) O Timothee, depositum custodi. Iisdem Scripturæ textibus Pontificii etiam militant. Promptum foret in impietate hac conspirantes Carpocratianos, Basilidianos, Marci (hæretici Valentiniani) discipulos, Messalianos, Psellianos sive Euchitas, Ossenos & Helcesaitas, Theodotum, Gnosimachos, Apollinaristas, alios producere, nisi idem, qui supra, Usserius Histor. Dogm. cap. 9. consensum illum luculenter jam demonstrasset. Sed & cum Judæis atque Turcis paria faciunt. Usque ad hunc diem, sic Bellarminus de Verbo Dei lib. II. 15. argutatur, in Synagogis Judæi Scripturas Hebraicè legunt, cùm nulli nationi hoc tempore lingua Hebræa vulgaris sit. Quasi Judæorum & Antichristianorum conjuratio adversus Dominum & Ecclesiam ejus maximo nobis argumento ad socia cum illis arma conjungenda esse deberet, A' Judæis interim, quorum adhuc cordibus velamen cæcitatis hæret, Biblia sanéta perlegi fere ab incunabilis, Possevinus Histor. Eccles. lib. IV. 6. fatetur. Quidni igitur hic eos Bellarminus sequatur, qui in sacris peragendis sequendos sibi proposuit. Turcas Bellarminus omisit; sed Reginaldus & Giffordus, Turco-Papistæ, uti author Calvino-Turc. Saltivius lib. IV. 7. prodidit, non omiserunt. Nam illos lingua Arabica, quam pauci inter illos intelligunt, preces fundere, & Alcoranum eadem lingua conscriptum legere, non intelle&tum licet, nisi à Sacerdotibus, constat. Legem, sic Christophorus Richerius de moribus Turc. lib. II. scribit, Arabicè conscriptam habent, & in omnibus publicis privatisque rebus Arabicis literis utuntur. His similibúsque Patriarchis Pontificii sacra sua peregrinæ linguæ beneficio occultantes gaudent. Addo velut in cumulum, jam olim Solomonem mulieri malæ seu meretrici linguam peregrinam Prov. VI. 24. 26. tribuisse: & Deum, ceu poenam comminatum esse, quòd in sannis labii & lingua peregrina ad populum locuturus sit, Esaj. XXVIII. 11. 12. 1. Cor. XIV. 21. 22.
units.tr: from the truth that he has commended to the Church, together with the Jesuits, the example of the Gentiles to be imitated. For it was not Christians but ancient heretics who imitated that practice, who, as Irenaeus, Book III. 2, testifies, when refuted from the Scriptures, turned to accusing the Scriptures themselves, as if they had been variously stated and the truth could not be found in them by those who did not know tradition. For it was not handed down in writing, they said, but by the living voice; for which reason Paul also said, We speak wisdom among the perfect, but wisdom not of this world, and (Tertullian confirms that they used this text too) O Timothy, keep the deposit. The Papists also fight with the same texts of Scripture. It would be easy to name, as conspirators with them in this impiety, the Carpocratians, Basilidians, the disciples of Marcus (a Valentinian heretic), Messalians, Psellians or Euchites, Ossenes and Elcesaites, Theodotus, the Gnosimachi, Apollinarists, and others, were it not that Ussher, cited above, had already clearly demonstrated that agreement in his Dogmatic History, ch. 9. But they also do the same with the Jews and the Turks. Up to this day, Bellarmine argues in On the Word of God II. 15, in the synagogues the Jews read the Scriptures in Hebrew, although Hebrew is the vernacular of no nation at this time. As if the conspiracy of Jews and Antichristians against the Lord and his Church ought to be a very great argument for us to join arms with them! Meanwhile Possevinus, Ecclesiastical History IV. 6, admits that the Jews, in whose hearts the veil of blindness still clings, have read the holy Bibles almost from the cradle. Why, then, should Bellarmine not follow them, since he has proposed to follow them in performing sacred rites? Bellarmine omitted the Turks; but Reginald and Gifford, Turco-Papists, as the author of Calvino-Turcismus, Saltivius, IV. 7, has revealed, did not omit them. For it is established that they pour out prayers in Arabic, which few of them understand, and read the Koran written in the same language, which cannot be understood except by the priests. They have the law, so Christoph Richer writes in On the Customs of the Turks II, written in Arabic, and in all public and private affairs they use Arabic letters. With such patriarchs as these the Papists rejoice, hiding their sacred things by the benefit of a foreign tongue. I add, as if to crown it all, that long ago Solomon ascribed a foreign tongue to a wicked woman, or harlot, Prov. VI. 24, 26; and God threatened, as a punishment, that with stammering lips and a foreign tongue he would speak to this people, Esaj. XXVIII. 11, 12; 1 Cor. XIV. 21, 22.

units.la: XVII. Habent tamen mystici colores, quibus Sibyllina folia sua fucant potiùs, quàm exornant.
units.tr: XVII. Yet the mystical colours with which they dye their Sibylline leaves serve rather to disguise them than to adorn them.

units.la: Clamant enim; Pontifices, Pius IV. & Clemens VIII. plus detrimenti quàm utilitatis inde hauriri; alii, Vulgus Scripturas non intelligere, & iis le&tis, vel vulgari lingua auditis, facilè in hæreses prolabi. Quasi verò, liceat fucum eum Erasmi, ante exortum Lutheri liberius differentis verbis, quæ in Enarrat. Psal. I. Operum Tom. V. p. 153. extant, abstergere, ea sit doctrina Christi, ut nonnisi à paucis Theologis possit intelligi. Imò ut ipso Christo nihil fuit commu-nius, ita doctrina ejus nihil popularius. Legat arator, erit qui pascatur: legat eruditissimus; erit quod discat. Verùm enimverò vereor, ne isti, qui velint populum nihil attingere, non tam periculo commoveantur illorum, quam sui respe&u; videlicet ut ab ipsis so*is, velut ab oraculis petantur omnia. Quid hac de re scriptum est? Hoc scriptum est. Quem habet sensum quod scriptum est? Sic intellige, sic senti, sic loquere. Atque isthuc est bubalum esse, non hominem. Fortasse movet & hoc nonnullos, quoniam animadvertunt, Divinas Scripturas parum quadrare ad vitam suam, malunt eas antiquari, aut certè nesciri, ne quid hinc jaciatur in os. Et ad humanas traditiunculas populum avocant, quas ipsi ad suam commoditatem probè commenti sunt. Idem Præfat. Paraphr. in Matth. Cur indecorum videtur, si quisquam sonet Evangelium ea lingua, qua natus est, & quam intelligit, Gallus Gallica, Britannus Britannica, Germanus Germanica, Indus Indica? Mihi indecorum vel ridiculum potiùs videtur, quòd idiotæ & mulierculæ psittaci exemplo, Psalmos suos & precationem Dominicam Latinè murmurant; quum ipsæ, quod sonant, non intelligant. Ego cum Divo Hieronymo sentiens, citiùs gratuler gloriæ crucis, magnificúmque ac triumphale dixerim, si linguis omnibus ab omni hominum genere celebretur. Si stivam tenens arator aliquid sua lingua decantat è Psalmis mysticis. Si textor assidens telæ nonnihil ex Evangelio modulans, soletur laborem. Hinc nauclerus assixus clavo cantillet aliquid; denique ad colum sedenti matronæ sodalis aut cognata hinc recitet aliquid. Quam sententiam verè Christianam idem Erasmus adversus Nicolaum Ecmondanum, Natalem Beddam, Petrum Sutorem, Theologos Parisienses, aliósque strenuè tutatus est. Reliquas pro interdicto Scripturarum in vernaculo idiomate legendarum ratiunculas Loc. II. 103. discussimus. Neque melioris commatis sunt, quæ adversus vernaculæ in precibus & Sacramentorum administratione linguæ usum movent. Quale illud est, quòd Spiritui S. authori tribuendum sit, quòd, cùm per mille annos Latina lingua vernacula esse desierit, nihilominùs Liturgia Romana intemerata manserit. Nam eo ipso tempore, quo Latina lingua passim vernacula fuit, Græci, Syri, aliíque sacra sua idiomate vulgari celebrarunt. Quidni ergo desita etiam usurpari Latina lingua vernaculo idiomate sacra obire fas sit? Neque Spiritui S. authori, quòd per plura secula Liturgia Latina retenta est, sed potiùs socordiæ Episcoporum, Ecclesiis suis non aliter providentium, & mysterio impietatis indies invalescenti, ferendum acceptum est. De Sacerdotum socordia sic Johannes Beleth, qui A. MCXC. vixit in principio Summæ de Divinis Officiis; In primitiva Ecclesia prohibitum erat, ne quis loqueretur linguis, nisi esset, qui interpretaretur. Quid enim prodesset loqui, nisi intelligeretur? Inde etiam inolevit usus, vel laudabilis consuetudo in Ecclesia in quibusdam partibus, ut pronuntiato literaliter Evangelio statim in vulgari populo exponeretur. Quid autem in nostris temporibus agendum est, ubi nullus vel rarus invenitur vel legens vel audiens, qui intelligat? Videns vel agens, qui animadvertat? Jam videtur esse completum, quod à Propheta dicitur: Et erit Sacerdos quasi unus de populo. Videtur ergo potiùs esse tacendum, quam psallendum, potiùs silendum, quàm tripudiandum. Quòd in Missa sacrificium Deo offerri, & nullis ad Deum verbis, multò minùs talibus,
units.tr: For they cry out that Popes Pius IV and Clement VIII drew more harm than benefit from it; and others cry that the common people do not understand the Scriptures, and that by reading them, or hearing them in the vernacular, they easily slip into heresies. As if indeed it were allowed to wipe away that dye of Erasmus, whose words, spoken more freely before Luther arose, are found in in Enarrat. Psal. I. Operum Tom. V. p. 153.: The doctrine of Christ is such that it can be understood by only a few theologians. Indeed, just as nothing was more common than Christ himself, so nothing is more popular than his doctrine. Let the ploughman read it, and there will be something to feed him; let the most learned read it, and there will be something for him to learn. But I fear that those who want the people to get nothing from it are moved not so much by danger to them as by regard for themselves, namely that everything should be sought from them alone, as from oracles. What has been written on this matter? This has been written. What sense has what is written? Understand it so, feel it so, speak it so. And that is to be an ox, not a man. Perhaps this also moves some people: they notice that the divine Scriptures do not fit well with their way of life, and so they prefer that they be made old-fashioned, or at least left unknown, lest anything be hurled back in their faces. And they call the people away to human little traditions, which they have cleverly devised for their own convenience. The same Erasmus, in the Preface to the Paraphrase on Matthew: Why does it seem unseemly if anyone proclaims the gospel in the language in which he was born and which he understands: the Frenchman in French, the Briton in British, the German in German, the Indian in Indian? To me it seems rather unseemly, even ridiculous, that unlearned men and silly women mutter their psalms and the Lord's Prayer in Latin like parrots, since they do not understand what they are saying. I, agreeing with the divine Jerome, would more readily congratulate the glory of the cross, and would call it magnificent and triumphal, if it were celebrated in all languages by every kind of man. Let the ploughman, holding his plough, sing something from the mystical Psalms in his own tongue. Let the weaver, sitting at his loom, relieve his labour by singing something from the Gospel. Let the sailor, fixed to his tiller, chant something; finally, let a friend or kinswoman recite something to the matron sitting at her distaff. This truly Christian opinion the same Erasmus has vigorously defended against Nicolaus Ecmondanus, Natalis Beda, Petrus Sutor, the Parisian theologians, and others. We have discussed the remaining little arguments against the prohibition of reading the Scriptures in the vernacular tongue in Loc. II. 103. Nor are those of better quality which they bring against the use of the vernacular language in prayers and in the administration of the sacraments. Such is that claim that it must be attributed to the Holy Spirit, the author, that although for a thousand years Latin has ceased to be the vernacular, the Roman liturgy has nevertheless remained unchanged. For at the very time when Latin was everywhere the vernacular, the Greeks, the Syrians, and others celebrated their sacred rites in their common idiom. Why then should it not be permitted to stop using Latin in the sacred rites now that it is no longer the vernacular? Nor is it to the Holy Spirit, the author, that the retention of the Latin liturgy for many centuries must be credited; rather it must be put down to the carelessness of bishops who provided for their churches in no other way, and to the mystery of iniquity, which grows stronger every day. On the carelessness of the priests, John Beleth, who lived in 1190, says at the beginning of his Summa de Divinis Officiis: In the primitive Church it was forbidden that anyone speak in tongues unless there was someone who would interpret. For what would it profit to speak if it were not understood? Hence also grew the custom, or laudable practice, in some parts of the Church, that when the Gospel had been read aloud, it was at once explained to the common people in the vernacular. But what must be done in our times, when there is none, or hardly anyone, who either reads or hears and understands? Who sees or acts and takes notice? Now it seems to be fulfilled what the Prophet says: And the priest will be as one of the people. It seems, therefore, that one should keep silent rather than sing psalms, and be still rather than dance. That in the Mass a sacrifice is offered to God, and that there is no need of any words to God, much less of such words as are intelligible to the people who regard that oblation, and moreover that the words of consecration in the same are said to be addressed not to men but to the elements, all this is built on the Mass-sacrifice as its base, and when that falls, this futile reasoning falls with it. Yet the Council of Trent admits that the great Mass contains the instruction of the faithful people. If this is true, whether a sacrifice is offered in it or not, it certainly ought to have been celebrated in the popular tongue, so that the people could be properly instructed through the Mass. Furthermore, it is plain that the Mass is celebrated with many words, both to God, but in the name of the people, and to the communicating people, and these ought to be understood, not kept secret. Moreover, all the Eastern liturgies are in the vernacular idiom. The Western liturgies were in Latin even at the time when Latin was the vernacular, which itself is proof that sacred rites were once customarily celebrated in the vernacular idiom. But after Latin fell into disuse, the Latin liturgy remained, I admit; but this is through the fault of ill-advised bishops, as we have said, and not by any right. For it was the task of the bishops to adapt the liturgy to the new languages, because divine worship is not to be adapted to languages, but languages, which ought to serve the understanding of the mysteries, are to be adapted to worship. As for the inconveniences which those who grumble attach to the use of the vernacular in sacred rites, such as that the fellowship of the Churches is thereby impeded, since it cannot happen that Latins also meet in an Italian church; that the reverence and majesty of the sacred rites is diminished; that there is danger of change and corruption if all do not use the same language; and finally that a door is opened to ignorance and to the forgetting of Latin among the ministers of the Church: the shallow-minded do not consider that inconveniences of this kind are objected not so much to us as to Christ, the Apostles, and the ancient Church, which agreed in using the vernacular in sacred rites. The building up of the Church, rather than such invented inconveniences, ought to have been the concern, so that the unity of the faith may be kept, not by the use of a foreign language, but by the Word of God read and understood, and by the unity of his Spirit. Nor did St Paul think that the majesty of the sacred rites is turned into a matter of foreign speech, when he noted in 1 Cor. 14.23 that there is madness [μανίαν] in it. Nor is there any such danger of change and corruption to be feared, because even the Apostles celebrated the sacred rites among different peoples in different languages, and corruption lies not in the words but in the sense, which by evildoers can be clothed in the same words in one way or another. But nor ought the ignorance of the clergy to be so much dreaded, both because the Fathers, who used the vernacular language, were far more learned than today's little priests, and because today the Roman priests, who celebrate the sacred rites in a foreign language, are for the most part stupid and rude to good letters.

units.la: Argumentis Mysticorum occurrunt. bus, quæ hominibus oblationem illam spectan-tibus intelligibilia sunt, opus esse; quin & verba consecrationis in eadem non ad homines, sed ad elementa dirigi caussantur, omne id sacrificio Missatico, ceu basi suæ, inædificatur, quo ruente, futilis etiam ratiocinatio corruit. Sed fatetur tamen Tridentina Synodus, Missam magnam populi fidelis eruditionem continere. Id si verum est, sive in ea sacrificium offertur, sive non, populari certè lingua utendum fuerat, ut populus per Missam commodè erudiri posset. Præterea Missam pluribus verbis tum ad Deum, sed nomine populi, tum ad homines communicantes celebrari palam est, quæ noscibilia esse, non secreta oportuit. Porrò Orientales Liturgiæ vernaculo idiomate omnes constant. Occidentales Latinæ fuerunt eo etiam tempore, quo lingua Latina vernacula fuit, quod ipsum argumento est, sacra vernaculo idiomate celebrari olim consuêsse. At postquam lingua Latina in desuetudinem venit, mansit, fateor, Liturgia Latina; sed Episcoporum malè consultorum, uti diximus, culpa, non jure ullo. Episcoporum enim partes erant, Liturgiam novis idiomatis accommodare, quia non cultus Divinus linguis, sed linguæ, quæ intelligentiæ mysteriorum ancillari debent, cultui accommodandæ fuerant. Quæ verò incommoda cum vulgaris in sacris linguæ usu conjuncta illi mussant, velut, quòd sic commercium Ecclesiarum impediatur, cùm fieri non possit, ut in Ecclesia Italorum conveniant etiam Latini: quòd reverentia & majestas sacrorum minuatur: quòd periculum sit mutationis & depravationis, si non eadem lingua omnes utantur: quòd denique porta ignorantiæ & oblivioni linguæ Latinæ apud ministros Ecclesiæ aperiatur; non cogitant scioli, incommoda ejusmodi non tam nobis, quàm Christo, Apostolis & consentienti veteri Ecclesiæ vernacula lingua in sacris utentibus objici. Ædificatio potiùs Ecclesiæ quàm conficta ejusmodi incommoda curæ esse debuit, ut fidei unitas retineatur, non peregrinæ linguæ usu, sed verbo Dei lecto & intellecto, atque spiritus ejus unitate opus est. Neque S. Paulo visum est, sacrorum majestatem in usu linguæ peregrinæ verti, qui 1. Cor. XIV. 23. non obscurè μανίαν furorem in eo notavit. Neque ullum sic mutationis & depravationis periculum timendum est, quia etiam Apostoli apud diversos populos diversis linguis sacra celebrarunt, & depravatio non in verbis, sed in sensu, qui iisdem etiam verbis alius atque alius à malefariis indui potest, sita est. At nec ignorantia cleri sic extimescenda fuit, tum quia olim vernacula licèt lingua usi Patres longè sacrificulis hodiernis doctiores fuerunt: tum quia hodie peregrina lingua sacra celebrantes Romani flamines plerique tamen stupidi & rudes bonarum literarum sunt.
units.tr: Sacred rites are opposed by the arguments of the mystics, which are intelligible to men who look upon that oblation; and indeed they allege that the words of consecration in the Mass are directed not to men but to the elements. All this is built on the Mass-sacrifice as its foundation, and when that falls, this futile reasoning falls too. Yet the Council of Trent admits that the great Mass contains the instruction of the faithful people. If this is true, whether a sacrifice is offered in it or not, it certainly ought to have been celebrated in the popular tongue, so that the people could be properly instructed through the Mass. Furthermore, it is plain that the Mass is celebrated with many words, both to God, but in the name of the people, and to the communicating people, and these ought to be understood, not kept secret. Moreover, all the Eastern liturgies are in the vernacular idiom. The Western liturgies were in Latin even at the time when Latin was the vernacular, which itself is proof that sacred rites were once customarily celebrated in the vernacular idiom. But after Latin fell into disuse, the Latin liturgy remained, I admit; but this is through the fault of ill-advised bishops, as we have said, and not by any right. For it was the task of the bishops to adapt the liturgy to the new languages, because divine worship is not to be adapted to languages, but languages, which ought to serve the understanding of the mysteries, are to be adapted to worship. As for the inconveniences which those who grumble attach to the use of the vernacular in sacred rites, such as that the fellowship of the Churches is thereby impeded, since it cannot happen that Latins also meet in an Italian church; that the reverence and majesty of the sacred rites is diminished; that there is danger of change and corruption if all do not use the same language; and finally that a door is opened to ignorance and to the forgetting of Latin among the ministers of the Church: the shallow-minded do not consider that inconveniences of this kind are objected not so much to us as to Christ, the Apostles, and the ancient Church, which agreed in using the vernacular in sacred rites. The building up of the Church, rather than such invented inconveniences, ought to have been the concern, so that the unity of the faith may be kept, not by the use of a foreign language, but by the Word of God read and understood, and by the unity of his Spirit. Nor did St Paul think that the majesty of the sacred rites is turned into a matter of foreign speech, when he noted in 1 Cor. 14.23 that there is madness [μανίαν] in it. Nor is there any such danger of change and corruption to be feared, because even the Apostles celebrated the sacred rites among different peoples in different languages, and corruption lies not in the words but in the sense, which by evildoers can be clothed in the same words in one way or another. But nor ought the ignorance of the clergy to be so much dreaded, both because the Fathers, who used the vernacular language, were far more learned than today's little priests, and because today the Roman priests, who celebrate the sacred rites in a foreign language, are for the most part stupid and rude to good letters.

units.la: XVIII. De Sacramentis in universum Loc. XI. 4–69. & de Sacramentis V. T. velut de Iride & Circumcisione, Loc. XII. 75–88. de Paschate, Baptismo in nube & mari, potu & aqua Petræ, Serpente æneo, Loc. XIII. 80–108. fusiùs egimus. Supersunt Sacramenta Fœderis Gratiæ sub Evangelio. Sicut enim Deus antiquis temporibus non solo verbo, sed etiam
units.tr: XVIII. We have treated fully of the sacraments in general in Loc. XI. 4–69, and of the sacraments of the Old Testament, such as the rainbow and circumcision in Loc. XII. 75–88, and of the Passover, baptism in the cloud and the sea, the drink and the water from the rock, and the bronze serpent in Loc. XIII. 80–108. There remain the sacraments of the covenant of grace under the Gospel.

units.la: symbolis Ecclesiam docuit, & sigillis credentes certiores fecit: ita etiam in plenitudine temporum fecit. Atque ut status Ecclesiæ sub Evangelio consummatior est: ita etiam Sacramenta sub Evangelio τελείωσιν consummationem ejusdem significantia & obsignantia, non iterum καταδυλεῖν in servitutem redigere, sed de communione cum Christo, ejúsque morte, & in eodem adoptione, justificatione, aliisque N. T. bonis ἀληθοφορεῖν certiores reddere debuerunt, de quo etiam Loc. XX. 68. pluribus. Neque tamen causæ gratiæ efficientes sive per inhærentem, sive per assistentem efficaciam, sunt, vel ex opere operato eandem operantur, uti Tridentinis, ea in re Sacramenta N. T. à Sacramentis V. T. disparantibus, aliisque visum est, quod fusius etiam Loc. XI. 60. 61. nec non Loc. XIII. 99. 100. demonstravimus.
units.tr: For just as God in ancient times taught the Church not only by the word but also by symbols, and made believers more certain by seals, so he has also done in the fullness of time. And just as the state of the Church under the Gospel is more perfect, so also the sacraments under the Gospel, signifying and sealing the consummation [τελείωσιν] of it, ought not to reduce us again to slavery [καταδυλεῖν], but to assure us [ἀληθοφορεῖν] of communion with Christ and his death, and in him of adoption, justification, and the other goods of the New Testament, on which we have also spoken at greater length in Loc. XX. 68. Yet the sacraments are not efficient causes of grace, whether through inherent or assisting efficacy, nor do they work it ex opere operato, as the Tridentines and others have thought, who on this point set the sacraments of the New Testament apart from those of the Old; this too we have demonstrated more fully in Loc. XI. 60, 61, and also in Loc. XIII. 99, 100.

units.la: XIX. Duo N. T. Sacramenta sunt, Baptismus & Cœna Domini. Cùm enim Sacramentum sit signum elementare à Christo institutum, gratiam redemptionis Christi Ecclesiæ perpetim significans & obsignans: præter hæc duo nulla alia, definitionis illius perfectionem sustinent. Respondent enim Sacramentis V. T. ordinariis, Baptismus Circumcisioni, Sacramento initiationis: Cœna Domini Paschati, Sacramento progressus & nutritionis. Habentes alimenta & tegumenta, his contenti erimus, 1. Tim. VI. 8. Atqui per Baptismum Christum induimus, Gal. III. 27. per Cœnam participes fimus alimenti spiritualis, corporis & sanguinis Domini, 1. Cor. X. 16. Quia & Apostolus symbola Sacramentalia V. T. extraordinaria etiam Ecclesiæ Christianæ accommodans, duo tantum N. T. Sacramenta, Baptismum & Cœnam Domini designavit. Nolo vos ignorare, quòd Patres nostri omnes fuerint sub nube, & omnes per mare transierunt: & omnes in Mosen baptizati sunt in nube & mari: Et omnes eundem cibum spiritualem comederunt, & omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberunt. Biberunt enim ex spirituali sequente petra. Petra autem erat Christus, 1. Cor. X. 1–5. Ubi Baptismo in nube & mari Baptismum aquæ N. T. & mannæ, nec non potui ex petra Eucharistiam non obscurè ἀντίτυπα. Deus etiam communionis nostræ cum Christo testeras, Baptismum & Cœnam, idem Paulus disertè facit. Uno Spiritu omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus, sive Judæi, sive Græci, sive servi, sive liberi. Et omnes in unum Spiritum potati estis, 1. Cor. XII. 13. Sicut enim in vita naturali generatione & conservatione vitæ per alimentum indigemus: ita in spirituali regeneratione seu insitione nostri in Christo, & incremento atque perseverantia in eodem indigemus. Tot verò Sacramenta sunt, quot res sunt, quibus planè indigemus; quia per Sacramenta res nobis ad justificationem & salutem nostram necessariæ obsignantur; regeneratio per Baptismum, conservatio & incrementum per Eucharistiam. Et totidem Sacramenta, non plura, Christus instituit, & in se ipso usurpavit & sanctificavit. Neque plura proprie dicta Vetus Ecclesia agnovit. Primi Hugo de S. Victore & Lombardus, qui seculo XII. floruerunt, sine ratione septem Sacramenta numerarunt; atque eum numerum Eugenius IV. post Concilium Florentinum, in decreto super unione Arme- Sacramenta œconomiæ Fœderis Gratiæ sub Evangelio & Sacramentis V. T. quodammodo differunt. Armeniorum confirmavit. Nondum tamen vel Scholastici, vel ipse Eugenius omnia haec septem vere & propriissime d'ita Sacramenta esse definiverant. Primi Tridentini Seff. VII. can.2. sine ullo Scripturae praesidio hoc determinarunt, Bellarminus certe de Effectu Sacr. lib. II. 27. fatetur, duo tantum Sacramenta ex latere Christi profluentia, Graecis fere omnibus ut magis communia & principalia poni, quamvis distinctio principalium & non principalium Graecis veteribus ne quidem in mentem unquam venit. Unde Arcudius Corcyraeus de Concord. Eccles. Or. & Occid. in Sacr. administr. lib. I. 2. Graecorum consensum jactans, nullum tamen ex veteribus pro septenario numero adducere potuit, contentus recentiorum quorundam, Simeonis Archiepiscopi Thessalonicensis, Jeremiae Patriarchae Constantinopolitani, Gregorii Protosincelli, & nescio cujus Monachi Jobi suffragiis. Caeterum Latini Sacramenta multiplicandi non unam occasionem non pretio, sed vi abstulerunt. Nam quae per metaphoram singularem dicta in Scripturis repererunt, illi ad ceremonias traduxerunt. Hinc Confirmatio. Tum signa ad patrationem miraculi instituta, cessante miraculorum dono, retinuerunt, & ad significandam spiritualem gratiam detorserunt. Hinc Extrema Unctio. Praeterea quae in personae coram Ecclesia praesentatione, & peccatoris absolutione fieri consueverunt, ad ministrorum dignitatem, & potestatem exaggerandam, in mysterium & Sacramentum converterunt. Hinc Sacramenta illa, quae manuum impositione peragunt, Poenitentia & Ordo. Denique & ipsa vox Sacramenti alicubi usurpata, & utilitas inde ad clerum redundans numerum locupletavit. Hinc Matrimonium.
units.tr: XIX. The New Testament has two sacraments, Baptism and the Lord's Supper. For since a sacrament is an outward sign instituted by Christ, continually signifying and sealing to the Church the grace of Christ's redemption, no other rite besides these two can meet the full requirements of that definition. For they correspond to the ordinary sacraments of the Old Testament: Baptism to circumcision, the sacrament of initiation, and the Lord's Supper to the Passover, the sacrament of progress and nourishment. "Having food and covering, we shall be content with these" (1 Tim. 6:8). Yet through Baptism we put on Christ (Gal. 3:27), and through the Supper we become partakers of spiritual food, the body and blood of the Lord (1 Cor. 10:16). Paul also, applying the extraordinary sacramental symbols of the Old Testament to the Christian Church, named only two New Testament sacraments, Baptism and the Lord's Supper. "I would not have you ignorant, brethren, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea; and were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and did all eat the same spiritual meat; and did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ" (1 Cor. 10:1–5). Here, in the cloud and the sea, the baptism of New Testament water, and in the manna and the water from the rock, the Eucharist, are clearly foreshadowed [antitypa]. Paul also plainly makes Baptism and the Supper the testimonies of our communion with Christ: "For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, whether bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit" (1 Cor. 12:13). For just as in natural life we need food for generation and for the preservation of life, so in spiritual regeneration, or our engrafting into Christ, and in growth and perseverance in him, we need nourishment. Now there are as many sacraments as there are things of which we truly have need, since through the sacraments the things necessary for our justification and salvation are sealed to us: regeneration through Baptism, and preservation and growth through the Eucharist. Christ instituted exactly these sacraments, no more, and himself used and sanctified them. The ancient Church likewise recognised no more that are properly so called. Hugh of St Victor and Lombard, who flourished in the twelfth century, first numbered seven sacraments without good reason; and Eugenius IV, after the Council of Florence, confirmed that number in his decree on the union of the Armenians (the sacraments of the economy of the covenant of grace under the Gospel and the sacraments of the Old Testament differ to some extent). Yet neither the Schoolmen nor Eugenius himself had yet defined that all seven were truly and most properly sacraments. The Council of Trent first determined this, in Session VII, canon 2, without any support from Scripture. Bellarmine certainly admits (On the Effect of the Sacraments, book II, ch. 27) that almost all the Greeks set down only two sacraments, which flowed from the side of Christ, as more common and principal; yet the distinction between principal and non-principal never once occurred to the ancient Greeks. Hence Arcudius of Corfu (On the Concord of the Eastern and Western Church in the Administration of the Sacraments, book I, ch. 2), boasting of the consensus of the Greeks, could nevertheless cite none of the ancients for the number seven, and was content with the support of certain more recent writers: Simeon, archbishop of Thessalonica, Jeremiah, patriarch of Constantinople, Gregory Protosyncellus, and some monk named Job. Moreover, the Latins did not take their occasion for multiplying sacraments from any single source, but by force. For whatever they found expressed by a single metaphor in the Scriptures, they transferred to ceremonies. Hence Confirmation. Then they retained signs instituted for the working of a miracle, after the gift of miracles had ceased, and turned them to signify spiritual grace. Hence Extreme Unction. Besides, what customarily happened in the presenting of a person before the Church and in the absolution of a sinner, they turned into a mystery and sacrament, to magnify the dignity and power of the ministers. Hence those sacraments which are performed by the laying on of hands: Repentance and Orders. Finally, the word sacrament, used somewhere else, and the profit flowing from it to the clergy, swelled the number. Hence Matrimony.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Quae pro septenario numero Sacramentorum adversus binarium Pontificii obducunt, ficulnea folia sunt. Nam quod definitionem & requisita Sacramenti suis etiam supernumerariis, Confirmationi, Poenitentiae, Extremae Unctioni, Ordini & Matrimonio competere ajunt, fidem facere non possunt. Nam de essentia & definitione Sacramenti nihil certi habent, & mire invicem conflictantur. Haud dubie vero requisita genuina Sacramenti illa sunt, quae Baptismus & Coena habent; ex quibus Sacramenti definitionem supra posuimus. Sed nullum supernumerariorum est, quod a Christo institutum sit, & elementare signum habeat, & gratiam spiritualem justificantem obsignet, & perpetuum in Ecclesia statum habeat, adeoque singula illa junctim possideat, uti singula expendenti liquebit. Frivolum dein est, quod septem vitae spiritualis & salutis remedia, & totidem iis accommodata Sacramenta, puta pro regeneratione Baptismum: pro augmentatione Confirmationem; pro nutritione Eucharistiam: pro peccatis postbaptismalibus Poenitentiam: pro reliquiarum peccati abolitione Unctionem extremam: pro Ecclesiae propagatione Matrimonium: pro gubernatione ejusdem Ordinem institutum nugantur. Nam nec necesse est, tot Sacramenta esse, quot salutis remedia sunt, quia caetera paria esse debent, & institutio Christi inprimis Sacramentum facit: neque difficile esset, salutis remedia arctiorem in numerum cogere, vel in latiorem extendere. Christus enim ἐν unum necessarium esse, Luc. X.41. docet, sub quo uno pro diversis necessitatis gradibus plura vel pauciora continentur. Cumque salutis remedia omnibus conveniant, supernumeraria quaedam non omnibus convenire, ipsimet fatentur. Par figmenti septem virtutum & peccatorum totidemque illis adjuvandis, his repellendis accommodatorum Sacramentorum ratio est. Nullum enim ex controversis vel Papali ambitioni occurrit, vel fidem ad justificationem promovet. Tum septenarium virtutum numerum Spiritus S. ipse infringit, fidem, spem & charitatem 1. Cor. XIII. 13. numerans. Et Sacramentum quodvis virtutibus adjuvandis omnibus, & vitiis repellendis omnibus, quoad gratiae sanctificantis obsignationem, accommodatum est. Sacramenta vero ex institutione Christi: non congruentiis ab hominibus confectis metiri par est. Quod numerum septenarium in sacris celebrem esse commemorant, plus quam puerilis pro septenario Sacramentorum numero ratiocinatio est. Nam ita etiam in V. T. Sacramenta septem institui debuissent; inprimis cum constet, numerum septenarium ex creatione ἑπταμέρω celebritatem suam habere. Jocularis inprimis a septem sigillis Apocalypticis petita ratio est, quia nec ex symbolis argumentari licet, & liber iste septem sigilla complexus non sacramentalis, sed praescientiae & Decretorum Divinorum est.
units.tr: The arguments the Papists bring forward for the number seven against the two are fig-leaves. For their claim that the definition and requisites of a sacrament belong to their additional supernumerary rites, Confirmation, Penance, Extreme Unction, Orders and Matrimony, they cannot make good. For they have nothing certain concerning the essence and definition of a sacrament, and they wildly contradict one another. The genuine requisites of a sacrament are undoubtedly those which Baptism and the Supper possess, and from these we set down the definition of a sacrament above. But none of the supernumeraries was instituted by Christ, has an outward element, seals spiritual justifying grace, and has a perpetual standing in the Church; and so they do not possess all these together, as will become clear to anyone who examines each one. Next, it is trifling to invent that seven remedies of spiritual life and salvation, and as many sacraments fitted to them, namely: for regeneration, Baptism; for growth, Confirmation; for nourishment, the Eucharist; for post-baptismal sins, Penance; for the removal of the remnants of sin, Extreme Unction; for the propagation of the Church, Matrimony; for its government, the institution of Orders. For it is not necessary that there be as many sacraments as there are remedies of salvation, since the rest ought to be equal, and the institution of Christ above all makes a sacrament. Nor would it be difficult to compress the remedies of salvation into a narrower number, or to extend them into a wider one. For Christ teaches that there is one thing needful (Luke 10:41, hen), under which one thing, for different degrees of need, more or fewer things are contained. And since the remedies of salvation suit all, the supernumeraries, they themselves admit, do not suit all. The reasoning behind the sacraments fitted to seven virtues and seven vices, and to as many things to help the former and repel the latter, is of the same fabricated kind. For none of the disputed rites either serves Papal ambition or advances faith toward justification. Moreover, the Holy Spirit himself overturns the number seven of the virtues, when he counts faith, hope and charity (1 Cor. 13:13). And any sacrament whatever is suited to help all virtues and repel all vices, as far as the sealing of sanctifying grace is concerned. But sacraments must be measured by the institution of Christ, not by congruities devised by men. As for their claim that the number seven is celebrated in sacred things, the reasoning that this makes the number of sacraments seven is more than childish. For in that case seven sacraments ought also to have been instituted under the Old Testament, especially since it is established that the number seven has its celebrity from the creation of the seven-part [hepta­mer] week. The reasoning drawn from the seven Apocalyptic seals is especially jocular, since one may not argue from symbols, and that book, which comprises the seven seals, concerns not sacraments but foreknowledge and the decrees of God.

units.la: XXI. BAPTISMUS est Sacramentum regenerationis, quo per aspersionem & ablutionem aquae omnibus & singulis Dei foederatis interna ablutio a peccatis per sanguinem & Spiritum Christi declaratur & obsignatur.
units.tr: XXI. BAPTISM is the sacrament of regeneration, by which an inward washing from sins through the blood and Spirit of Christ is declared and sealed to all and each of those who are in covenant with God, by the sprinkling and washing of water.

units.la: Vox ipsa βάπτισμα & βαπτισμός à βάπτειν mergere, intingere, proprie immersionem; improprie modo per metonymiam finis καθαρισμόν purificationem, Joh. III. 25.26. lotionem Marc. VII. 4. modo per metonymiam adjuncti doctrinam illo ritu confirmatam, uti quidam in verbis illis, Act. XVIII. 25. sciens tantum Baptisma Johannis, doctrinam ejus notari putant; rectius tamen & praedicatio & Baptismus, & testimonium Johannis de Christo junctim intelligitur: modo per metaphoram afflictiones & martyria piorum, velut in verbis Christi ad discipulos: Potestis baptizari baptismate, quo ego baptizor? Quibus annuentibus Christus respondit: Poculum meum bibetis, & baptismate, quo ego baptizor, baptizabimini, Matth. XX. 22.23. nec non effusionem donorum Spiritus S. velut in verbis Johannis. Ipse (Christus) baptizabit vos in Spiritu S. & igne, Matth. III. 11. & Christi ipsius: Vos baptizabimini Spiritu S. post dies non multos, Act. I. 5. modo per synecdochen Sacramentum N. T. prius, seu lavacrum aquae & regenerationis, Eph. V. 26. Tit. III. 5. quo de in praesentiarum agimus, significat. Diversa illa vocis usurpatio distinctionem Baptismi Fluminis, Flaminis, Sanguinis, & quem alii addunt Luminis peperit, quae vocis potius homonymae in sua significata, quam rei seu definiti in suas species divisio est.
units.tr: The word itself, baptisma and baptismos [βάπτισμα, βαπτισμός], from baptein [βάπτειν], to dip, to steep, properly means immersion. Improperly, it means by metonymy of the effect purification [καθαρισμόν], as in John 3:25–26, or a washing, as in Mark 7:4; or by metonymy of the adjunct, the teaching confirmed by that rite. Some think that this is meant in the words of Acts 18:25, "knowing only the baptism of John," since they take it to mean his teaching; yet it is more rightly understood as preaching and Baptism together with John's testimony about Christ. It is used by metaphor for the afflictions and martyrdoms of the godly, as in Christ's words to the disciples: "Can ye be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?" To which they assented, and Christ answered: "Ye shall drink indeed of my cup, and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with" (Matt. 20:22–23). It is also used for the outpouring of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as in John's words: "He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire" (Matt. 3:11), and in Christ's own: "Ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence" (Acts 1:5). By synecdoche it signifies the first New Testament sacrament, or the washing of water and regeneration (Eph. 5:26; Titus 3:5), which is what we are discussing at present. This varied use of the word has given rise to the distinction of Baptism into water, Spirit, blood, and what some add, light. That division concerns the various meanings of a homonymous word rather than a division of the thing or definition into its kinds.

units.la: XXII. Frequentes apud Judaeos Βαπτισμοὶ Lotiones, purificationes Divinitus institutae fuerunt; quarum & ritum seu βαπτισμὸς καθάρσεως lotiones varias, Hebr. IX. 10. Loc. XV. 63. & mytuiioni ejus & mysterium ibid. § 93. 94. exposuimus. Ubi etiam de מטבילי עלימת βαπτισμῷ υπὲρ νεκρῶν baptismo pro mortuis dictum est. Hæ lotiones טבילת נדה baptismi seu lotionis à fœditate nomine veniunt. A quo distinctus est, qui apud eosdem טבילת הגרות Baptismus Proselytorum appellatur. Cujus prima vestigia apparent in Sichemitidis fœmellis, aliisque gentilibus illis, quas Jacobus in familiam & Ecclesiam suam cooptavit. Dixit Jacobus familiæ suæ, omnibusque, qui cum eo erant. Amovete à vobis Deos alienos והטברו & mundamini, hoc est, uti rectè Abenezra רחצו הצוף lavate corpus, baptizamini. Dein totam gentem Israeliticam במילה בטבילה ובקרבן per Circumcisionem, Baptismum & Sacrificium in fœdus Dei transiisse; per Circumcisionem, sicut dicitur: Nullus incircumcisus comedet de Pascha te; per Baptismum paulò ante datam legem, quando iussit Deus populum se sanctificare & vestimenta lavare: per Sacrificium, post legem datam: Majmonides, magnus juris Hebraici interpres, in Issure Biah cap. 13. notavit. Hinc proselytos omnes deinceps tribus illis consecratos asserunt, juxta tritum axioma: אין גר עד שימול וטבול Non est quis proselytus, usque dum circumcidatur & baptizetur. Etiam parvulos baptizari mos erat, uti habetur in Bab. Cherubb. sol. 11. 1. גר קטן מטבילין אותו Proselytum parvulum baptizant secundum sententiam Synedrii. Simul enim cum patre baptizabantur liberi. Incertum autem est, quando & quo authore Baptismus Circumcisioni proselytorum adjunctus, ceu inseparabilis fuerit, sed adjunctum tamen esse, ambigi non potest. Nec simplicem hæc observata usum habent.
units.tr: XXII. Among the Jews, frequent baptisms, that is, washings for purification, were instituted by God. We have already set out their rite, the baptism of purification [βαπτισμὸς καθάρσεως] with its various washings, Heb. 9:10, and its mystery, at Loc. XV. 63, and at §§ 93 and 94 of the same place. There we also spoke of those who are baptized for the dead [βαπτισμῷ ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν], that is, baptism for the dead. These washings come under the name of baptism or washing from uncleanness [טבילת נדה]. Distinct from them is what the same writers call the baptism of proselytes [טבילת הגרות]. Its first traces appear in the Shechemite women and other Gentiles whom Jacob admitted into his household and Church. "Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him: Put away the strange gods from among you, and be clean [והטברו]," that is, as Abenezra rightly explains it, "wash the body," be baptized. Afterwards the whole Israelite nation passed into the covenant of God [במילה בטבילה ובקרבן] by circumcision, baptism and sacrifice: by circumcision, as it is said, "No uncircumcised person shall eat of the Passover"; by baptism shortly before the law was given, when God commanded the people to sanctify themselves and wash their garments; by sacrifice after the law was given. Maimonides, the great interpreter of Hebrew law, noted this in Issure Biah, chapter 13. Hence they assert that all proselytes thereafter were consecrated to those tribes, according to the common axiom: "No one is a proselyte until he is circumcised and baptized" [אין גר עד שימול וטבול]. It was also customary to baptize little children, as is found in Bab. Cherubb. sol. 11, 1: "They baptize a little proselyte according to the opinion of the Sanhedrin" [גר קטן מטבילין אותו]. Children were baptized together with their father. It is uncertain when and by whose authority baptism was joined to the circumcision of proselytes so as to be inseparable from it, but that it was joined to it cannot be doubted. Nor did these observances have a merely simple use.

units.la: XXIII. Primus sub Evangelio Johannes baptizavit.
units.tr: XXIII. John was the first to baptize under the Gospel.

units.la: Cui inde Baπτιςτὴς Baptista nomen inditum Evangelistæ frequentant. Ita equidem morem proselytos baptizandi receptum secutus est, ut tamen singularis vocatio, eadem, qua ad ministerium suum universum, vocatus est, Divina planè à Prophetis prædicta, & ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ex Cœlo Matth. XXI. 25. intercesserit. Qui misit me baptizare, ille dixit,&c. Joh. I. 33. Factum est verbum Dei ad Johannem in deserto, & venit in omnem regionem Jordanis, & prædicavit Baptismum pœnitentiæ, Luc. III. 2. 3. Ideo Pharisæi spernentes ejus Baptismum, consilium Dei sprevisse ibid. VII. 30. dicuntur. Baptizavit & prædicavit ille Baptisma pœnitentiæ, dicens populo, ut crederent εἰς τὸν ἐρχόμενον μετ' αὐτὸν in eum, qui post ipsum venturus erat, hoc est, in Jesum Christum, Actor. XIX. 4. Prædicavit Baptismum resipiscentiæ in remissionem peccatorum, Marc. I. 4. Plura de eo Loc. XX. 79. diximus.
units.tr: From this the Evangelists regularly give him the name John the Baptist [Βαπτιστὴς]. Indeed he followed the custom of baptizing received for proselytes, but his calling was singular, the same by which he was called to his whole ministry, plainly foretold by the prophets and "from heaven" [ἐξ οὐρανοῦ], Matt. 21:25. "He who sent me to baptize, he said..." John 1:33. "The word of God came to John in the wilderness, and he went into all the region of the Jordan and preached the baptism of repentance," Luke 3:2, 3. Therefore the Pharisees, despising his baptism, are said to have "rejected the counsel of God," ibid. 7:30. He baptized and preached "the baptism of repentance, telling the people that they should believe in him who was coming after him [εἰς τὸν ἐρχόμενον μετ' αὐτὸν], that is, in Jesus Christ," Acts 19:4. "He preached the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins," Mark 1:4. We have said more about him at Loc. XX. 79.

units.la: XXIV. Licet ergo ejus Baptismus à Baptismo Christi diversus fuerit, tum modo patefactionis, quia Christum nec procul absentem, nec præsentem mortuum, sed mox passurum; Christi verò Baptismus, quem post ejus ascensionem in Cœlum discipuli ejus administrarunt, Christum jam passum, mortuum & consummatum significavit: tum collatione donorum, quia Johannis Baptismus, nondum glorificato Christo, adeóque nec dum effuso Spiritu S. tantam copiam donorum spiritualium, visibilium & invisibilium præsentem, quantam Baptismus discipulorum Christi, obsignare non potuit; tamen in rei substantia & obsignatione gratiæ regenerantis & remissionis peccatorum, quæ Sacramenti illius nucleus est; adeóque in præcipuis eadem vis utriusque extitit. Ne dicam, Johannem baptizantem aqua, obsignasse etiam Baptismum Christi futurum, quo is in Spiritu S. & igne Pentecostes die, credentes baptizaturus, & iisdem Spiritum adoptionis & charismatum collaturus erat. Nequicquam ergo Tridentini Seff. VII. can. 1. anathema tonant in eos, qui eandem vim utriusque esse statuunt. Nam Scholastici Johannis Baptismum mundando corpora, at non à peccatis, rudimentarium, ad pœnitentiam deduxisse, & gratiæ præludium fuisse, contendunt. Sed quæ præconii Baptismi Johannis, eadem Baptismi præconium obsignantis ratio fuit. Atqui præconium fuit approximationis Regni Cœlorum, Matth. III. 2. Salutis in remissione peccatorum, Luc. I. 77. Christi, ceu Agni tollentis peccata mundi, Joh. I. 29. quo de præconio & testimonio Johannis plura Loc. XX. 77. 78. diximus. Conveniunt utriusque Baptismi causæ & effecta. Nam Johannis æquè ac Christi Baptismi causa Efficiens Deus instituens, & vocans: Materia externa aqua, interna promissio gratiæ remissionis peccatorum & regenerationis Spiritus, Matth. III. 11. 12. Luc. III. 3. Act. XVIII. 25. XIX. 5. Forma testificatio & obsignatio gratiæ ejusdem per aquam & ritum ablutionis, nec non promissionis cum hoc elemento & ritu ejus copulatio, Marc. I. 4. Luc. VII. 30. Finis, confirmatio baptizatorum de gratia Dei, eorum segregatio à Pharisæis, hypocritis, & in Ecclesiæ cœtum receptio. Effecta tum resipiscentia, Marc. I. 4. tum remissio peccatorum, Luc. III. 3. tum fides in Christum, Actor. XIX. 4. 5. tum Spiritus Dei quoad dona ordinaria præsens, quomodo Apollo sciens tantùm baptisma Johannis ζέων πνεύματι fervens spiritu fuisse ibid. XVIII. 25. dicitur. Quoad extraordinaria verò & adoptionem post ascensionem Christi futurus; quæ omnia Baptismus Johannis obsignavit. Dilutum est, quòd Baptismum Johannis talia contulisse excitando moraliter ad fidem in Christum, & mediante ea ad pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum; Christi verò Baptismum per se & immediatè, regerunt. Totum enim illud operis operati Baptismi Christi figmento innititur. Atqui nec Baptismus Christi cuiquam nisi pœnitenti gratiam promittit, vel confert: Et Baptismus Johannis eadem suppositâ gratiam & promisit, & pro ratione Sacramenti contulit. Accedit, quòd etiam Christus à Johanne baptizatus est, ut & baptismum nostrum sanctificaret, & in ipso, ut capite nostro, remissio peccatorum nobis per sanguinem ejus parta obsignaretur. Non potest autem baptismus, quo Caput baptizatum est, à baptismo, quo membra ejus baptizantur, tota essentia differre, quia baptismus est symbolum unitatis fidelium in uno corpore mystico, non tantùm inter se, sed etiam cum Christo, capite, Galat. III. 27. Neque malè Patres Baptismum nostrum vim & efficaciam suam à contactu Christi à Johanne baptizati, accepisse, dixerunt. Verisimile etiam est, Apostolos ipsos non alio baptismo, quàm quo etiam Christus, baptizatos fuisse. Accedit, quòd Baptismus Evangelii licet ἀδαχῆς βαπτισμῶν doctrinæ baptismatum nomine Apostolo, Hebr. VI. 2. veniens: quia ggg 3 quia duplex baptismus fuit, Johannis & Christi, uterque adventus Christi firmamentum, nihilominus ἐν Βάπτισμα unum Baptisma, Ephes. IV. §. diserte dicitur. Atqui etiam Johannis Baptismus Evangelii Baptismus fuit; quia omnes Prophetæ & Lex usque ad Johannem prophetarunt, Matth. XI. 13.
units.tr: XXIV. Although his baptism differed from the baptism of Christ, first in the manner of revelation, since he proclaimed Christ not as far away, nor as present and dead, but as about to suffer soon, whereas the baptism of Christ, which his disciples administered after his ascent into heaven, signified Christ already suffered, dead and consummated; and second in the bestowal of gifts, since John's baptism, before Christ was glorified and so before the Holy Spirit was poured out, could not seal the abundance of spiritual gifts, visible and invisible, that the baptism of Christ's disciples sealed; yet in the substance of the thing, and in the sealing of regenerating grace and the remission of sins, which is the kernel of that sacrament, the power of both was the same, at least in essentials. Not to mention that John, baptizing with water, also sealed the future baptism of Christ, by which he would baptize believers in the Holy Spirit and fire on the day of Pentecost and bestow on them the Spirit of adoption and gifts. In vain, therefore, the Council of Trent (Sess. VII, can. 1) thunders anathema against those who hold that the power of both is the same. For the Scholastics contend that John's baptism, cleansing bodies but not from sins, led to repentance as a rudimentary thing and was a prelude to grace. But the reason for the proclamation of John's baptism was the same as the reason for the proclamation of the baptism that seals. And that proclamation was of the approach of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 3:2), of salvation in the remission of sins (Luke 1:77), and of Christ as the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (John 1:29). About this proclamation and testimony of John we have said more at Loc. XX. 77, 78. The causes and effects of the two baptisms agree. For the efficient cause of both the baptism of John and that of Christ is God, instituting and calling. The external matter is water; the internal matter is the promise of the grace of remission of sins and of regeneration by the Spirit (Matt. 3:11, 12; Luke 3:3; Acts 18:25; 19:5). The form is the testimony and sealing of the same grace through water and the rite of washing, and the joining of the promise to this element and rite (Mark 1:4; Luke 7:30). The end is the confirmation of the baptized concerning the grace of God, their separation from the Pharisees and hypocrites, and their reception into the assembly of the Church. The effects are repentance (Mark 1:4), remission of sins (Luke 3:3), faith in Christ (Acts 19:4, 5), and the Spirit, present as to ordinary gifts; so Apollos, knowing only the baptism of John and fervent in spirit [ζέων τῷ πνεύματι], is said to have been (Acts 18:25). As to extraordinary gifts and adoption, these were to come after Christ's ascension; all these things John's baptism sealed. It is refuted that John's baptism conferred such things only by morally stirring men to faith in Christ and, through faith, to repentance and the remission of sins, while Christ's baptism works through itself and immediately. For all that rests on the fiction of the work worked (opus operatum) of Christ's baptism. But neither does Christ's baptism promise or confer grace on anyone except the penitent; and John's baptism, on the same supposition, both promised grace and conferred it according to the nature of a sacrament. Add that Christ himself was baptized by John, both to sanctify our baptism and so that, in him as our head, the remission of sins obtained for us through his blood might be sealed. But the baptism by which the Head was baptized cannot differ in its whole essence from the baptism by which his members are baptized, since baptism is the symbol of the unity of the faithful in one mystical body, not only with one another but also with Christ the head (Gal. 3:27). Nor did the Fathers speak amiss when they said that our baptism received its power and efficacy from the contact of Christ, who was baptized by John. It is also probable that the Apostles themselves were baptized with no other baptism than the one by which Christ was baptized. Add that the baptism of the Gospel, though it is called by the Apostle the doctrine of baptisms [ἀδαχῆς βαπτισμῶν] (Heb. 6:2), since there were two baptisms, John's and Christ's, each supporting the coming of Christ, is nevertheless expressly called one baptism [ἓν βάπτισμα] (Eph. 4:5). But John's baptism too was a baptism of the Gospel, since all the prophets and the Law prophesied until John (Matt. 11:13).

units.la: XXV. Vocatur equidem Baptismus hic Βάπτισμα Ἰωάννου Baptisma Johannis tum absolutè, quia is primus sub N. T. Baptismi administer fuit, Joh. I. 33. tum relatè ad Baptismum discipulorum Christi, quatenus non eadem, quia hic, donorum ubertate abundavit. Neque tamen ideo Divina institutione caruit, quam supra probavimus. Ac licet etiam à Johanne in nomine Domini Jesu, Actor. XIX. §. non diserte Trinitatis nomine administratus dicatur, implicitè tamen etiam in Trinitatis nomine administratus est, quia obsignavit doctrinam ejus, qua, in Baptismo inprimis Christi, S. Trinitatem conspicuis documentis praedicavit. Baptizavit ille certè in nomine non idoli, sed veri Dei, qui Triunus, seu essentia unus, persona trinus est. Sed quid multis? Ipsi etiam Apostoli jussi à Christo baptizare in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. tamen baptizasse ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ in nomine Jesu Christi, Actor. II. 38. X. 48. leguntur. Baptizantes tamen utrique Johannes & Apostoli in nomine Christi simul baptizarunt in nomine S. Trinitatis sive explicitè, sive implicitè, quia, uti scitè Ambrosius, Christi nomen complectitur tum Patrem, qui unxit Filium oleo lætitiæ: tum Filium, cui Pater dedit Spiritum non ad mensuram: tum Spiritum S. qui ipsa unctio est. Legitimus igitur etiam Christi Baptismus in solius Christi nomine administratus est, quia, uti rectè Papa Nicolaus I. Institutio Christi non de vocibus, sed de rebus intelligenda est. Non remisit Baptismus Johannis peccata ex opere operato, fateor. At nec sic remittit Baptismus Christi. At nec nudè idem Johannis Baptismus ad poenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum dispositus, sed æquè ac hic poenitentibus remissionem peccatorum obsignavit. Dicta porrò, quibus Johannes suum Baptisma à Christi Baptismo disparavit, velut, cùm dixit: Ego baptizo aqua ad poenitentiam. At qui post me venit, baptizabit vos Spiritu S. & igne, Matth. III. 11. non derogant Baptismo Johannis efficaciam, sed partim personas in ordine causarum efficientium discernunt, & Christum authorem gratiæ, Johannem ministrum esse, docent: partim verbum baptizandi Christo & Johanni alio atque alio significatu tribuunt. Johanni administro Baptismi, proprie; Christo, authori gratiæ & Spiritus S. metaphoricè; quia nunquam is proprie aquâ baptizavit. Denique nec Ephesii discipuli à Johanne baptizati, denuo baptizati à Paulo, commemorante prius, quòd audientes Baptismum Johannis, baptizati sint in nomine Jesu, adeóque alio baptismo in nomine Jesu non indigeant, sed impositæ iis tantùm manus sunt, ut Spiritus S. in eos veniret, Actor. XIX. 4. §. 6. nec si denuo baptizati essent, id efficaciæ Baptismi Johannis quoad speciem, sed tantùm quoad gradum derogaret.
units.tr: XXV. This baptism is indeed called the baptism of John, both absolutely, because he was the first administrator of baptism under the New Testament (John 1:33), and relatively to the baptism of Christ's disciples, inasmuch as it was not the same, because the latter abounded in richness of gifts. Yet for that reason it did not lack divine institution, which we proved above. And although it is said that John administered it in the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 19), and not expressly in the name of the Trinity, nevertheless it was implicitly administered in the name of the Trinity too, because he sealed his doctrine, which, especially in the baptism of Christ, proclaimed the holy Trinity by clear evidence. He certainly baptized in the name not of an idol but of the true God, who is triune, one in essence and three in persons. But why say more? The Apostles themselves, commanded by Christ to baptize in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, are read to have baptized in the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 2:38; 10:48). Yet both John and the Apostles, baptizing in the name of Christ, baptized at the same time in the name of the holy Trinity, either expressly or implicitly, because, as Ambrose wisely says, the name of Christ embraces the Father, who anointed the Son with the oil of gladness; the Son, to whom the Father gave the Spirit not by measure; and the Holy Spirit, who is the anointing itself. Therefore the baptism of Christ too, administered in the name of Christ alone, is lawful, because, as Pope Nicholas I rightly says, the institution of Christ is to be understood not in words but in things. John's baptism did not remit sins by the work worked, I grant. But neither does Christ's baptism remit them in that way. Nor was John's baptism bare and merely disposing men to repentance and the remission of sins; like the baptism of Christ, it sealed the remission of sins to the penitent. Moreover, the sayings by which John distinguished his baptism from that of Christ, as when he said, I baptize you with water unto repentance, but he who comes after me will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire (Matt. 3:11), do not take away the efficacy of John's baptism. Rather, they partly distinguish the persons in the order of efficient causes, teaching that Christ is the author of grace and John the minister; and partly attribute the verb to baptize to Christ and to John in different senses: to John, as administrator of baptism, properly; to Christ, as author of grace and of the Holy Spirit, metaphorically, since he never properly baptized with water. Finally, the Ephesian disciples, baptized by John and afterwards baptized again by Paul, who recalled that, having heard John's baptism, they had been baptized in the name of Jesus, did not need another baptism in the name of Jesus; only hands were laid on them, so that the Holy Spirit came upon them (Acts 19:4–6). Nor, even if they had been baptized again, would that detract from the efficacy of John's baptism as to its kind, but only as to its degree.

units.la: XXVI. Post Johannem Baptistam baptizarunt Apostoli tum ante, tum post resurrectionem Christi. Ante eam Jesus ipse non baptizavit (aqua; quia Spiritu baptizare potius ipsius fuit, & falsam persuasionem baptizandorum, qua ab ipso immediatè baptizati aliis se præferre potuissent, amoliri voluit.) sed discipuli ejus, Joh. IV. 2. authoritate tamen magistri sui Christi, non demum in colloquio cum Nicodemo Baptismum discipulorum suorum instituentis, uti novissimè antagonista meus Sfondrati; tum Sanctogallensis Abbas, & nunc Cardinalis purpuratus; nugatus est, reperisse sibi visus, quod pueri in faba; sed statim atque eos ad ministerium vocavit, unà cum præconio & verbo audibili iis etiam obsignationem præconii & verbum visibile injungens, sive, quod Bellarmino aliisque veteribus visum probabilius est, quando Dominus ipse in Jordane baptizatus est; & juxta illud veterum, aquæ contactu Baptismo discipulorum suorum vim & efficaciam contulit. Sed cùm hactenus solos Judæos baptizaverint; post resurrectionem Christi ex mortuis, jussi proficisci, facere discipulos omnes gentes, & baptizare eos in nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Matth. XXVIII. 19. baptizarunt in nomine Jesu Christi, Judæos æquè ac gentes, Actor. II. 38. 41. XVI. 33. XVIII. 8. 1. Cor I. 14. 16. institutis etiam ad muneris illius χαρισματων Evangelistis, uti ex Act. VIII. 12. IX. 18. X. 48. liquet. Nam Apostolis præcipua evangelizandi cura fuit, adeò ut tempus & opportunitatem evangelizandi nulla alia occupatione, ac ne baptizandi quidem, perdendam putaverint. Non misit me Christus (potissimum, præcipuè, ante omnia) ad baptizandum, sed ad evangelizandum, 1. Cor. I. 17. Comparativa enim, non simplex negatio est. Nam quosdam & ipse Paulus & alii Apostoli baptizarunt, malè facturi, si ad baptizandum planè missi non essent.
units.tr: XXVI. After John the Baptist, the apostles baptized both before and after Christ's resurrection. Before the resurrection Jesus himself did not baptize with water. This was because baptizing with the Spirit was rather his own work, and he wished to remove the false notion among those being baptized that they could set themselves above others if they had been baptized directly by him. But his disciples did, John 4:2, nonetheless by the authority of their master Christ. Nor was it only in conversation with Nicodemus that he instituted the baptism of his disciples, as my recent opponent Sfondrati, then the Abbot of St Gall and now a purple-robed Cardinal, trifled, thinking he had found it, as children play with a bean in a cake. Rather, as soon as he called them to the ministry, he enjoined on them, together with the proclamation and the audible word, the sealing of that proclamation, a visible word. Or, as seems more probable to Bellarmine and other ancients, this happened when the Lord himself was baptized in the Jordan, and, according to the saying of the ancients, by contact with the water he gave to the baptism of his disciples its force and efficacy. But since they had baptized only Jews until then, after Christ's resurrection from the dead, having been ordered to go, make disciples of all nations, and baptize them in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, Matt. 28:19, they baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, Jews and Gentiles alike, Acts 2:38, 41; 16:33; 18:8; 1 Cor. 1:14, 16. They were also appointed as evangelists for the gift of that office [χαρισμάτων], as is clear from Acts 8:12; 9:18; 10:48. For the apostles' chief care was preaching the gospel, so much so that they thought the time and opportunity for evangelizing should not be lost to any other occupation, not even to baptizing. Christ did not send me (chiefly, above all) to baptize, but to preach the gospel, 1 Cor. 1:17. For this is a comparative, not a simple, negation. Indeed Paul himself and other apostles did baptize some, and would have done wrong had they not been sent expressly to baptize.

units.la: XXVII. Baptismi proin administratio missionem & vocationem postulat; neque aliis competit quàm iis, qui & ipsi ad praedicandum & evangelizandum vocati sunt. Nemo in universum, nemo sibi sumit honorem, sed qui vocatus est à Deo, sicut & Aharon, Hebr. V. 4. Si nec Aharon, nec Christus non vocati munus suum obire potuerunt, nulli alii non vocati publicum Ecclesiæ munus, quod totius Ecclesiæ nomine obeundum est, involare & occupare audent. Tum munus baptizandi cum munere Evangelium prædicandi manifestè Christus conjunxit, jubens eosdem μαθητεύειν docere, κηρύσσειν prædicare Evangelium, & βαπτίζειν baptizare, Matth. XXVIII. 19. Marc. XVI. 16. Nemini autem nisi vocato & misso prædicare licet. Quomodo prædicabunt nisi missi? Rom. X. 15. Magna enim inter verbum Dei & Sacramenta διαφορα est. Illud audibile, hæc visibilia signa sunt. Inane κενοσφυγέιον est, quòd viri & fœminæ, non quidem publicè & cum solennitate, at sine solennitate tamen & privatim docere, adeóque etiam baptizare possint. Christus enim potestatem baptizandi cum munere publico prædicandi Evangelium, non cum quovis actu docendi conjunxit. Sicut autem Evangelium prædicare cum authoritate pastoris & præconis Evangelici privatim vel publicè nonnisi vocato convenit: ita baptizare sive privatim, sive publicè, & quovis casu non convenit nisi
units.tr: XXVII. The administration of baptism therefore requires a mission and a calling, and it belongs to none but those who are themselves called to preach and to evangelize. No one at all takes this honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was, Heb. 5:4. If neither Aaron nor Christ could discharge his office unless called, do any others dare to seize and occupy the public office of the Church, which must be discharged in the name of the whole Church, without being called? Christ also manifestly joined the office of baptizing with the office of preaching the gospel, commanding the same men to teach [μαθητεύειν], to proclaim the gospel [κηρύσσειν], and to baptize [βαπτίζειν], Matt. 28:19; Mark 16:16. But no one may preach unless he is called and sent. How shall they preach unless they are sent? Rom. 10:15. For there is a great difference between the Word of God and the sacraments. The one is audible; the others are visible signs. It is an empty [κενοσφυγέιον] notion that men and women may teach, not indeed publicly and with solemnity, but without solemnity and privately, and so may also baptize. For Christ joined the power of baptizing to the public office of preaching the gospel, not to every act of teaching. Just as to preach the gospel, whether privately or publicly, with the authority of a pastor and a herald of the gospel belongs only to one who is called, so to baptize, whether privately or publicly, and in any case, belongs only to

units.la: {a} Baptismus discipulorum Christi. nisi illi, qui cum authoritate Pastoris & praeconis Evangelici ad praedicandum Evangelium simul & ad baptizandum vocatus est. Nam quae Deus conjunxit, homini separare non licet. Potest enim munus aliquod privatim exerceri, licet & munus & persona exercens publica & authoritate praedita esse debeat, & absque muneris & personae authoritate publica exerceri non posset. Quomodo & sacrificuli Unctionis extremae Sacramentum privatim administrant, neque tamen sine munere publico, & publicae personae respectu sic administrare possunt. Baptismus enim Evangelii Christi nomine & authoritate praedicati sigillum est. Sicut autem diplomati Regio sigillum non nisi a Rege vocatus & auctoratus sine piaculo apponere audsit: ita nec Evangelium Christi, Regis Coelorum diploma, Baptismo obsignare nisi vocatus a Christo & authoritate ejus nemo potest. Cumque Sacramenta inter mysteria censeri debeant, non nisi ab oeconomis mysteriorum, hoc est, ὑπηρέται & Χρισ̄ ministris Christi 1. Cor. IV. 1. tractari possunt. Denique per Baptismum membra Ecclesiae visibilis & externae fiunt. At tam non Ecclesiae & Civitati Dei civem & membrum privatus, non pollens authoritate publica addere potest: quam non privato civitatem externo jure civitatis donato cive augere fas est.
units.tr: {a} The baptism of the disciples of Christ. only to one who has been called, with the authority of a pastor and herald of the gospel, to preach the gospel and at the same time to baptize. For it is not lawful for man to separate what God has joined. A private person may indeed exercise some office privately, although both the office and the person exercising it ought to be public and invested with authority, and it could not be exercised without the public authority of the office and the person. So too priests administer the Sacrament of Extreme Unction privately, yet they cannot administer it in this way without a public office and in respect of a public person. For Baptism is the seal of the gospel proclaimed in the name and by the authority of Christ. Just as no one may affix the seal to a royal diploma without being called and authorized by the King, and without sin, so no one can seal the gospel of Christ, the diploma of the King of heaven, with Baptism unless he is called by Christ and acts under his authority.
