And since the sacraments must be counted among the mysteries, they can be handled only by the stewards of the mysteries, that is, by the servants [ὑπηρέται] and ministers of Christ, 1 Cor. 4:1. Finally, through Baptism men become members of the visible and external Church. But a private person, not possessing public authority, cannot add a citizen and member to the Church and City of God, just as it is not right for a private person to enlarge a state by admitting a citizen who has been granted the external rights of citizenship.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Diversi abeunt Pontificii, postquam inprimis Eugenius IV. in Concilio Florentino, seu potius in decreto super Unione Armenorum ita definivit: Minister hujus Sacramenti (Baptismi) est Sacerdos, cui ex officio competit baptizare. In casu ergo necessitatis non solum Sacerdos, vel Diaconus, sed etiam Laicus, vel mulier, imo etiam paganus, vel haereticus baptizare potest, dummodo formam servet Ecclesiae; & facere intendat, quod facit Ecclesia. Ubi illud ridiculum est, quod laicis, mulieribus, paganis & haereticis concedunt, quod in hac administratione praecipuum & solum Divino jure institutum est, puta baptizare, at iisdem ceremoniarum per homines inventarum apparatu, quasi per ludibrium interdicunt; quasi in humanis ejusmodi assumentis, & non potius in ipso Divinitus instituto baptismate opus sacerdotale & Apostolicum situm esset. Cum tamen juxta illud etiam juris Canonici, accessorium naturam principalis sequi congruat. Neque quidquam vel Scripturae, vel Veteri Ecclesiae inauditum magis est, quam Baptismus per mulieres etiam & haereticos administratus. Mulieri enim ne loqui quidem in Ecclesia, 1. Cor. XIV. 34. nedum munere Ecclesiastico, quod natura sua publicum est, defungi licet. Cumque Baptismum salutis aeternae causam necessariam illi faciunt, salutem hominis ex potestate & actu mulieris, pagani, haeretici suspendere oppido absurdum est. Gynaeco-baptismum vero a Marcione introductum Concilium Carthaginense IV. cujus pars Augustinus fuit, can. 100. sic definivit: Mulier baptizare non praesumat. Ita in omnibus Conciliorum editionibus legitur. Sed Lombardus 4. Sent. Dist. 6. & Gratianus de Consecr. Dist. 4. Can. Mulier, de suo adjecerunt, quasi explicationis ergo, nisi necessitate cogente, quod assumentum ita artificiose illi attexuerunt, ut incauto lectori genuinum videri possit. Si casum necessitatis Carthaginenses excipere voluerunt, cur eum non enuntiant, sicut de laicis fidelibus in suo canone Eliberitani Patres fecerant? In opere constitutionum Apostolicarum, quod Clementi Romano falso tributum licet, non tamen seculo quinto vel sexto recentius est, lib. III. cap. 9. haec constitutio habetur: quod non oporteat mulieres baptizare; esse enim id impium, & a doctrina Christi alienum. Atque illud & esse probat author ille, quia caput mulieris sit vir, & praeter naturam sit, ut mulier Sacerdotali munere fungatur, quia mulieri non concessum sit docere, adeoque nec baptizare, quia id atheismum gentilium, qui foeminis deabus, foeminas Sacerdotes constituerint, respiciat: quia non conveniat cum Christi institutione: quia, si mulierum esset baptizare, Christus a sua matre, non a Johanne baptizatus esset, quia Christus Apostolos ad baptizandum mittens non miserit cum iis mulieres ad hoc etiam faciendum, quia nemo sibi sumit honorem, nisi qui vocatus est. Et cap. II. aliis clericis exclusis, solis Episcopis & Presbyteris administrationem Baptismi, sub Coritarum poena vendicat. Quin & laicis omnibus absolute illicitam esse Baptismi administrationem, Cyprianus & Firmilianus, eorumque collegae, Africani & Asiatici reste Basilio ad Amphil. Episc. can. 1. judicarunt.
units.tr: Many Papists have departed from this view, especially since Eugenius IV first defined in the Council of Florence, or rather in the decree on the union of the Armenians, as follows: "The minister of this sacrament (of Baptism) is the priest, to whom it belongs by office to baptize. In a case of necessity, therefore, not only a priest or deacon but also a layman, or a woman, or even a pagan or heretic, can baptize, provided that he keeps the form of the Church and intends to do what the Church does." Here what is ridiculous is this: they grant to laymen, women, pagans and heretics the chief and only part of this administration that was instituted by divine right, namely to baptize, yet they forbid them, as if in mockery, the same display of ceremonies invented by men. As if the priestly and apostolic work lay in such human additions, and not rather in baptism itself, which God instituted. Yet according to that saying of canon law also, "an accessory ought to follow the nature of the principal." Nor is anything more unheard of in Scripture or in the ancient Church than baptism administered even by women and heretics. For "let a woman not even speak in the church," 1 Cor. XIV. 34, much less may she discharge an ecclesiastical office, which by its nature is public. And since they make baptism a necessary cause of eternal salvation, it is utterly absurd to make a man's salvation depend on the power and act of a woman, a pagan, or a heretic. The Council of Carthage IV, of which Augustine was a part, can. 100, defined the gynaecobaptism introduced by Marcion as follows: "Let a woman not presume to baptize." So it is read in all editions of the councils. But Lombard, 4 Sent. dist. 6, and Gratian, de Consecr. dist. 4, can. Mulier, added of their own, as if by way of explanation, "unless compelled by necessity." They wove this addition in so artfully that it might seem genuine to an unwary reader. If the Carthaginians wanted to except the case of necessity, why do they not state it, as the Fathers of Elvira did in their canon about lay faithful? In the work of the Apostolic Constitutions, which is falsely attributed to Clement of Rome but is nonetheless no more recent than the fifth or sixth century, book III chapter 9, this constitution is found: that "it is not right for women to baptize; for this is impious," and foreign to the teaching of Christ. That author proves this too: because the man is the head of the woman; because it is against nature for a woman to perform a priestly office, since it is not granted to a woman to teach, and so not to baptize either; because it resembles the atheism of the Gentiles, who made women priests of goddesses; because it does not agree with Christ's institution; because, if it were for women to baptize, Christ would have been baptized by his mother, not by John; because Christ, in sending the apostles to baptize, did not send women with them to do this too; because no one takes honour to himself unless he is called. And in chapter II, excluding the other clergy, he claims the administration of baptism for bishops and presbyters alone, under penalty of the Coritae. Indeed Cyprian and Firmilian, with their colleagues, the Africans and Asians, rightly judged, as Basil says in his letter to Amphilochius, can. 1, that the administration of baptism by laymen is absolutely unlawful.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Unicum fere in necessitate absoluta Baptismi praesidium adversarii collocant. Nos autem infra non absolutam esse, confirmabimus. Si tamen absoluta esset, quae temeritas foret, propterea ordinem Divinum turbare, & nolente atque invito Deo homines humana prudentia & οἰκονομίᾳ salvare velle? An ita mulier, paganus, haereticus consilium Dei irritum faciet? Circumcidit Zippora filium, Exod. IV. 25. 26. sed circumcidit praesente Mose, Propheta, duce populi, & sacerdote tanto. At Pontificii negant, mulieri licere baptizare praesente viro laico, nedum sacerdote. Nam quod ita ab Angelo vexatum & perculsum esse, ut necesse habuerit munus circumdendi mulieri committere, Bellarminus regerit, dilutum est. Nam qui vexabat negligentem, non vexasset, sed potius solatus esset obedientem. Deinde si jussu Prophetae id fecit, salvares est. Expectant etiam nostrae mulieres jussionem Prophetae. Tum dispar circumcisionis & Baptismi ratio est. Illius enim administratio certo Ministrorum ordini injuncta non fuit. Secus se habere de Baptismo, jam ostendimus. Poterant etiam laici Agnum Paschalem macta-re. An iccirco etiam laico in casu necessitatis Eucharistiam consecrare fas erit? Quod die Pentecostes solos Apostolos tria hominum millia, Act. II. 41. baptizare non potuisse, adeoque etiam laicos iis operam navasse, quin & septuaginta discipulos laicos fuisse, Ananiam laicum Paulum, ibid. IX. 18. & Cornelii familiam non solum Petrum, sed fratres, qui cum ipso venerant, laicos utique, ibid. X. 48. Denique Philippum Diaconum Samaritanos & Eunuchum Aethiopem, ibid. VIII. 12. 38. baptizasse, objiciunt, infirmo cuncta talo nituntur. Nam Xavierus, si Salmeroni fides est, apud Indos uno die quindecim millia baptizavit. Et duo-
units.tr: Our opponents place almost their only defence in the absolute necessity of baptism. But we will show below that it is not absolute. Yet even if it were absolute, what rashness would it be to disturb the divine order for that reason, and to wish to save men by human prudence and οἰκονομία, against the will of God and unwilling? Will a woman, a pagan, or a heretic make the counsel of God void? Zipporah circumcised her son, Exod. IV. 25, 26, but she did so in the presence of Moses, the prophet, leader of the people, and so great a priest. Yet the Papists deny that a woman may baptize in the presence of a lay man, let alone a priest. As for Bellarmine's reply, that she was harassed and struck by the angel so that she had to commit the office of circumcising to another, this has been refuted. For he who harassed the negligent would not also have harassed the obedient, but would rather have comforted her. Next, if she did it by the command of the prophet, it was safe. Our women also await a command from a prophet. Then the case of circumcision is unlike that of baptism, for the administration of circumcision was not enjoined on any fixed order of ministers. It is otherwise with baptism, as we have already shown. Laymen too could slaughter the paschal lamb. Will it therefore be lawful for a layman also to consecrate the Eucharist in a case of necessity? They object that on the day of Pentecost the apostles alone could not baptize "three thousand men," Acts II. 41, and so laymen helped them; moreover, that the seventy disciples were laymen; that Ananias the layman baptized Paul, ibid. IX. 18; and that Peter baptized the household of Cornelius, and the brothers who had come with him, surely laymen, ibid. X. 48; finally, that Philip the deacon baptized the Samaritans and the Ethiopian eunuch, ibid. VIII. 12, 38. They rest all of this on a weak heel. For Xavier, if Salmeron is to be believed, baptized fifteen thousand among the Indians in one day. And that the twelve-

units.la: Laicorum & mulierum Baptismus rejicitur.
units.tr: The baptism of laymen and women is rejected.

units.la: Argumenta pro eodem ad incudem revocantur.
units.tr: The arguments in favour of the same are put back on the anvil.

units.la: duodecim Apostoli tria millia baptizare non potuerint ? Neque septuaginta discipuli eo tempore laici fuerunt, quos jam ante Christus ipse ad ministerium vocaverat, publicos in messe sua operarios constituerat, publica commissione instructos miserat, & quibus dixerat: Qui vos audit, me audit, Luc. X. 16. Ananiæ etiam immediata Christi revelatio & præceptio vocationis instar fuit, atque fuit ille sic Propheta cœlesti oraculo auctoratus. Philippus etiam & Evangelista, & immediatis revelationibus ductus fuit, Actor. VIII. 29. Cornelium deinque & domesticos ejus Petrus mandavit baptizari in nomine Domini, ibid. X. 48. hoc est, jussit aquam adferri, & ex ipsius Petri manu Sacramentum accipere. Et fratres, qui cum eo venerunt laicos fuisse, vel ab iis domesticos Cornelii baptizatos esse, non liquet. Circumspectant denique à veteribus Patribus auxilium. Tertullianus enim de Bapt. c. 17. etiam laicis jus esse baptizandi ait, eo argumento, quòd ex æquo dari possit id, quod ex æquo accipitur. Concors huic Hieronymus Dial. adv. Lucifer. Ubi sic ille: Si necessitas coegerit, scimus etiam licere laicis (baptizare) ut enim accipit quis, ita & dare potest. Quæ ratio & solis laicis baptizatis, non paganis, Judæis, hæreticis quibusvis jus tingendi eximium facit: & prorsus infirma est, quia ea stante, quivis solenniter baptizatus etiam extra necessitatis casum, præsentibus clericis, publicè & solenniter baptizare; & qui Eucharistiam accepit, eandem dare poterit. Augustinum fateor, aliósque præpositera opinio necessitatis impulit, ut à laico, sed baptizato non infideli & hæretico, datum baptisma probarent. Nam baptisma, quod administratur ab eo, qui potestatem non habet, ideo ratum esse veteres, imò etiam incauti recentiores Wittakerus aliísque nonnulli asseruerunt, quia juxta Innocentii III. Ext. de Regal. cap. 16. tritum illud, multa fieri prohibentur, quæ si facta fuerint, firmitatem obtinent. Sed loquitur tamen ibi Innocentius de iis, quæ legibus humanis prohibita sunt. Aliàs Gregorius apud Gratianum C. 25. q. 2. Can. Imperiale. constitutum esse Imperiali sanctione ait, ut ea, quæ contra leges fiunt, non solùm inutilia, sed etiam pro infectis habeantur. Ubi videlicet perpetua prohibitionis causa est. Hic verò perpetua prohibitionis causa est, lex Dei stans, nuspiam à Deo mutata, & in qua Deus ipse non dispensavit. Denique non valet illa Augustini contr. Parm. lib. II. 13. ratio. Quod datum est, non potest dici non datum, quamvis recte possit dici illicitè datum. Nam quod datum est, haud dubiè datum illud est. At à laico datum est baptisma, seu lotio externa, cum quibusdam ritibus externis, sed non Sacramentum, quod nonnisi à vocato dari potest. Quomodo si laicus Eucharistiam consecret, vel ordinet iisdem ritibus, quibus sacerdotes ordinant & consecrant Ordinis & Eucharistiæ Sacramentum, ab eodem datum esse nemo agnoscet.
units.tr: dozen Apostles could not baptize three thousand? Nor were the seventy disciples laymen at that time: Christ had already called them to the ministry, had appointed them public workers in his harvest, sent them out with public commission, and had said to them, "He who hears you hears me," Luke X. 16. For Ananias too, the immediate revelation and command of Christ served in place of a call, and so he was authorised as a prophet by a heavenly oracle. Philip too was an evangelist, and was led by immediate revelations, Acts VIII. 29. Peter "commanded" Cornelius and his household to be baptized in the name of the Lord, ibid. X. 48, that is, he ordered water to be brought and the sacrament to be received from Peter's own hand. Whether the brothers who came with him were laymen, or whether they baptized Cornelius's household, is not clear. Finally, they look about for help from the ancient Fathers. For Tertullian, de Bapt. c. 17, says that laymen too have the right to baptize, on the argument that what is received on equal terms can be given on equal terms. Jerome agrees, Dial. adv. Lucifer: "If necessity compels, we know that it is lawful for laymen to baptize too; for as one receives, so one can give." This reasoning makes the right of baptizing a special privilege of baptized laymen alone, not of pagans, Jews, or any heretics whatever; and it is utterly weak, because on this principle any solemnly baptized person could solemnly baptize, even outside a case of necessity, publicly, in the presence of clergy; and one who has received the Eucharist could give it too. I admit that Augustine and others were driven by a perverse opinion of necessity to approve baptism given by a layman, though not by an unbeliever or heretic, but by one who was baptized. For the older writers, and even the careless later ones such as Whitaker and some others, have asserted that baptism administered by one who lacks authority is valid, because of the well-worn saying of Innocent III, Ext. de Regal. cap. 16: "Many things are forbidden which, if they are done, obtain firmness." But Innocent there speaks of things forbidden by human laws. Otherwise Gregory, in Gratian, C. 25 q. 2, Can. Imperiale, says that it was established by imperial sanction that things done against the laws are held not only invalid but even as if they had never been done. Here, clearly, the cause of the prohibition is perpetual. Here too the cause of the prohibition is perpetual: the law of God stands, nowhere changed by God, and God himself has not dispensed from it. Finally, that argument of Augustine against Parmenian, II. 13, does not hold: "What has been given cannot be said not to have been given, although it can rightly be said to have been given unlawfully." For what has been given is without doubt given. But baptism, or an external washing with certain external rites, was given by a layman, not the sacrament, which can be given only by one who has been called. Just as no one will acknowledge that the sacrament of Orders or of the Eucharist was given by a layman who consecrated the Eucharist or ordained with the same rites by which priests ordain and consecrate.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: In baptizante legitima vocatio, retæ de Baptismo fides & vitæ integritas requiritur. Legitima ad Ministerium Vocatio, quia, uti diximus, nemini nisi ad ministerium vocato baptizare fas est. Recta de Baptismo, quoad essentialia saltem ejus fides, quia qui essentiam Baptismi negat, pro ministro verbi & Sacramentorum Dei haberi nequit. Vitæ integritas, quia quivis verbi Dei, adeóque etiam sacramentorum minister & dispensator integer vitæ scelerisque purus esse debet, 1. Tim. III. 2. 3. &c. Priora & ad personam, & ad Sacramenti efficaciam & validitatem; ultimum ad personam baptizantis, non ad Sacramenti efficaciam, uti veteres Donatistæ, nominatim Petilianus, & hodieque Anabaptistæ pertendunt, requiruntur. Neque obstat quòd quidam etiam hæretici, nominatim Pontificii, institutionem Baptismi retinentes, Baptismi ministri legitimi censentur, neque adeò ab iis juxta institutionem Christi baptizati, rebaptizari debent, quod de quibusvis hæreticis baptizantibus incautè satis Cyprianus, ejúsque collegæ, in Epistola Synodali ad Stephanum Episcopum Romanum, & post eosdem maligné & præfractè Donatistæ negarunt. Licèt enim hæretici, Pontificii nominatim, nec vocationem habeant ad prædicandas hæreses suas, & Baptismum accessoriis ceremoniis collutulent; eorum tamen & vocatio ad præconium fundamenti salutis, quod verbis saltem profitentur, licèt obliqua ratione illud destruant; legitima: & de Baptismo in præcipuis, essentia puta, in administratione ejus juxta institutionem, cum invocatione S. Trinitatis conjuncta, fides recta est. Proin nec eorum Baptismus invalidus magis censeri debet, quàm invalida fuit circumcisio Ecclesiæ Israeliticæ, quæ corruptissima licèt & repudio digna per circumcisionem Deo filios filiásque genuit, Ezech. XVI. 20. XXIII. 37. Neque etiam Christus ipse Circumcisionem repudiavit, licèt Scribæ & Pharisæi gravissimè erraverint, & ipsum atrociter persecuti fuerint. Vis enim & efficacia Sacramenti non à Ministro errante vel hæretico, sed à Christo pendet, quia non hæreticus, sed Christus hæretici manu baptizat, uti Augustinus alicubi loquitur. Præterea nec hæretici censendi sunt in iis, in quibus cum Catholicis conjuncti, sed in quibus ab iis separati sunt, uti non semel Augustinus Donatistis respondit. Alia hæreticorum, institutionem Baptismi & fundamentum salutis directè rejicientium ratio est, quales olim Arriani, hodie Socinian, & invocationem S. Trinitatis, & fundamentum salutis, Christi Deitatem & satisfactionem tollentes, sunt. Quam ob causam etiam Synodus Nicena Can. 21. non quosvis hæreticos, sed Paulianistas, hoc est, Samosathenianos: Et Synodus Laodicena Can. 8. Cataphrygæs, Montani discipulos, rebaptizandos statuit.
units.tr: A person who baptizes must have a legitimate call and a correct belief about Baptism, and must have an upright life. A legitimate call to the ministry is required because, as we have said, no one may baptize except one who has been called to the ministry. A correct belief about Baptism is required at least as to its essentials, because someone who denies the essence of Baptism cannot be regarded as a minister of the Word and the sacraments of God. Integrity of life is required because whoever is a minister and dispenser of the Word of God, and therefore also of the sacraments, ought to be blameless in life and free from wickedness (1 Tim. 3:2, 3, etc.). The first two requirements concern both the person and the validity and efficacy of the sacrament. The last concerns the person who baptizes, not the efficacy of the sacrament, as the ancient Donatists, especially Petilianus, contended, and as the Anabaptists still do today. Nor is it an objection that some heretics, especially the Papists, who retain the institution of Baptism, are considered legitimate ministers of Baptism, and that those they baptize according to Christ's institution must not be rebaptized. Cyprian and his colleagues rashly said this of all heretics who baptize, in their synodal letter to Stephen, Bishop of Rome, and afterwards the Donatists denied it maliciously and obstinately. For although heretics, the Papists especially, have no call to proclaim their heresies, and although they contaminate Baptism with added ceremonies, nevertheless their call to proclaim the foundation of salvation, which they at least profess in words, though they undermine it indirectly, is legitimate; and their belief about Baptism is correct in its principal points, namely its essence and its administration according to the institution, joined with invocation of the Holy Trinity. Therefore their Baptism ought no more to be considered invalid than the circumcision of the Israelite Church was invalid. Although that Church was most corrupt and worthy of rejection, through circumcision it nevertheless begot sons and daughters for God (Ezek. 16:20; 23:37). Nor did Christ himself reject circumcision, although the scribes and Pharisees erred most gravely and persecuted him savagely. For the force and efficacy of a sacrament depends not on an erring or heretical minister but on Christ, since, as Augustine says somewhere, it is not the heretic but Christ who baptizes by the heretic's hand. Moreover, heretics are not to be regarded as such in those things in which they agree with Catholics, but in those in which they are separated from them, as Augustine answered the Donatists more than once. There is another kind of heretic, who directly rejects the institution of Baptism and the foundation of salvation, such as the Arians formerly and the Socinians today, who deny the invocation of the Holy Trinity and the foundation of salvation, namely Christ's deity and satisfaction. For this reason the Council of Nicaea (Can. 21) decreed that not all heretics but the Paulianists, that is, the Samosatenes, should be rebaptized, and the Council of Laodicea (Can. 8) decreed the same for the Cataphrygians, the followers of Montanus.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Baptismi elementum, seu materia externa ὕδωρ Aqua est, qualis erat illa Jordanis, quo Johannes baptizavit, Matth. III. 6. 16. Cùm Philippus & Eunuchus ascendissent ex aquâ, Act. VIII. 39. Num quis aquam prohibere potest, quo minus baptizentur isti? ibid. X. 47. Purificavit Ecclesiam λουτρῷ ἐν ῥήματι. Nam & βαπτίζειν proprie aqua tingere, improprie lavare, abluere aqua significat. Nulla verò, ut cum Tertulliano de Bapt. c. 4. loquamur, distinctio est, mari quis, an stagno, flumine, an fonte, lacu an alveo diluatur: nec quicquam refert inter eos, quos Johannes in Jordane, & Petrus in Tiberi tinxit. Nisi & ille spado, quem Philippus intervius fortuita aqua tinxit plus salutis aut minus retulit. Atque
units.tr: The element, or outward matter, of Baptism is water [ὕδωρ], such as that of the Jordan in which John baptized (Matt. 3:6, 16); when Philip and the eunuch had come up out of the water (Acts 8:39); Can anyone forbid water, that these should not be baptized? (ibid. 10:47). He cleansed the Church by the washing of water with the word [λουτρῷ ἐν ῥήματι] (Eph. 5:26). For baptizein [βαπτίζειν] properly means to dip in water, and figuratively to wash or cleanse with water. Yet, to use Tertullian's words (de Bapt. c. 4), there is no distinction as to whether one is washed in the sea, a pond, a river, a spring, a lake or a pool; nor does it matter whether they were dipped by John in the Jordan or by Peter in the Tiber. Nor did the eunuch, whom Philip baptized in whatever water he happened upon along the road, gain more or less salvation by it. And so

units.la: Requisita Baptisfa, et quatenus hæretico-rum baptismus probari possit? Atque aquæ Baptismi etiam typus aquæ diluvii, per quas octo animæ salvatæ sunt, 1.Pet.III.20. & aquæ nubis & maris rubri 1. Cor. X.1.2. fuerunt. Nihil enim significandæ regenerationi hominis per & propter obedientiam Christi & sanctificationem Spiritus aptius est. Habet enim aqua vim & suffocandi atque mortificandi mersos; & vim abluendi sordes corporis. Ita & morti Christi, & sanctificationi atque justificationi nostræ figurandæ maximè idonea est. Nam id quod in sermone ad significandam rem spiritualem metaphoram præbet, communioni cum eadem significandæ & obsignandæ, ceu signum & sigillum commodè adhibetur. Atqui passiones, afflictiones & mors ipsa figurat βαπτισμὸς lotio dicitur. Accedamus cum vero corde in fiducia fidei, aspersi corda à conscientia mala, & abluti corpus ὕδατι καθαρῷ aqua pura, Hebr. X. 22. 23. Id quod in se sanctum, etiam vim sanctificandi & purificandi habet, aquam spiritualiter etiam Deus ipse dixit. Spargam super vos aquam puram, & purificabimini ab omnibus pollutionibus vestris, Ezech. XXXVI. 25. Et Christus: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest intrare in Regnum Dei, Joh. III.5. Alibi tamen, 1. Joh. V. 6. aqua à sanguine distinguitur, & per illam Christi ὁσιότης pietas & sancta studiositas; per hunc ejusdem mors significatur.
units.tr: The requisites of Baptism, and how far the baptism of heretics can be proved. The water of Baptism is also a type of the waters of the flood, through which eight souls were saved (1 Pet. 3:20), and of the cloud and the sea of the Red Sea (1 Cor. 10:1, 2). For nothing is more fitting to signify the regeneration of man through and because of the obedience of Christ and the sanctification of the Spirit. Water has the power both to suffocate and kill those who are submerged, and the power to wash away the filth of the body. Thus it is most suitable to figure both the death of Christ and our sanctification and justification. For what provides a metaphor in speech for signifying a spiritual thing is conveniently used, as a sign and seal, to signify and confirm communion with that thing. Now the sufferings, afflictions and death itself are figured by baptism [βαπτισμός], which is called washing. Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water [ὕδατι καθαρῷ] (Heb. 10:22, 23). That which is holy in itself also has the power to sanctify and purify, and God himself spoke of water in a spiritual sense: I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be clean from all your filthiness (Ezek. 36:25). And Christ: Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God (John 3:5). Elsewhere, however, water is distinguished from blood (1 John 5:6), and through the former is signified Christ's holiness [ὁσιότης], that is, piety and holy zeal, while through the latter is signified his death.

units.la: XXXII. Baptismum in aqua nec à Christo mandatum esse, & sine mandato ab Apostolis usurpatum, ad tempus duntaxat durare debuisse; eum vero Baptismum, qui à Christo, ceu perpetim duraturus Matth. XXVIII.19. institutus est, non aquæ, sed luminis seu doctrinæ esse, Socini ichola, tam Sacramentis Christi, quàm ipsi Christo infensa, sine omni ratione & pudore comminiscitur. Etenim Christum mandantem Apostolis, & unà toti Ecclesiæ Christianæ omnium temporum, ut baptizarent, non Baptismum doctrinæ, insolenti ænigmate, sed Baptismum potiùs aquæ intellexisse ipsa Baptismum inter & doctrinam antithesis probat. Dicit enim βαπτίζοντες & διδάσκοντες, baptizantes & docentes, Matth. XXVIII. 19.20. Et testatur id ipsum tum Baptismus Johannis, qui aquæ fuit, à discipulis Christi continuatus: tum promulgatio Baptismi aquæ deinceps facta ab Apostolis Christi, per effusum in ipsos Spiritum S. illuminatis, ipso die Pentecostes, Actor. II. 38. 41. & imperata in nomine Christi deinceps, ac religiosissimè observata praxis, ibid. VIII.12. 16. 36. X. 33. 47. 48. XV. 13. 14. 33. XVIII. 8. Adeò quidem ut ipse S. Paulus Christianismo æquè atque Apostolatui suo per Baptismum ex Christi ipsius Ananiam mittentis mandato initiari debuerit, ibid. IX. 18. coll. cum XXII. 16. Frustra verò glossæ suæ obtendunt phrasin istam ἐπίστασθαι βαπτισμα scire Baptismum, cap. XVIII. 25. Ubi Apollo tantùm scivisse Baptismum Johannis dicitur. Licet enim phrasis illa per synecdochen scientiam doctrinæ Johannis comprehendat, ipsa tamen synecdoche illa evincit, Baptismum ejus non excludi, sed præsupponi. Baptismi enim nomine expresso, doctrinæ significatio suppressa est propter necessariam in ministerio Johannis connexionem verbi cum ritu sacro. Quin si vel doctrina Johannis tantùm expresse nomi-
units.tr: XXXII. That Baptism in water was not commanded by Christ, and was used by the Apostles without command, and was meant to last only for a time; and that the Baptism which Christ instituted as if it were to last forever (Matt. 28:19) is not of water but of light or doctrine: this is the invention of the Socinian school, hostile to the sacraments of Christ and to Christ himself, devised without any reason or shame. For that Christ, in commanding the Apostles and with them the whole Christian Church of all times to baptize, meant not a baptism of doctrine, in a strange riddle, but rather a baptism of water, is proved by the very antithesis between Baptism and doctrine. For he says baptizing and teaching [βαπτίζοντες & διδάσκοντες] (Matt. 28:19, 20). The baptism of John, which was of water, was continued by the disciples of Christ, and this is attested as well by the proclamation of water Baptism made afterwards by the Apostles of Christ, who were enlightened by the Holy Spirit poured out upon them on the very day of Pentecost (Acts 2:38, 41), and by the practice, commanded in the name of Christ and most religiously observed thereafter (ibid. 8:12, 16, 36; 10:33, 47, 48; 15:13, 14, 33; 18:8). So much so that Saint Paul himself had to be initiated into Christianity, as well as into his apostolate, by Baptism, according to the command of Christ himself sending Ananias (ibid. 9:18; compare 22:16). In vain do they try to support their gloss with the phrase to know the baptism [ἐπίστασθαι βάπτισμα] (Acts 18:25), where Apollos is said to have known only the baptism of John. For although that phrase, by synecdoche, comprehends the knowledge of John's doctrine, that very synecdoche shows that his Baptism is not excluded but presupposed. For when the name Baptism is expressed, the meaning of doctrine is implied, because of the necessary connection in John's ministry between the word and the sacred rite. Indeed, even if only the doctrine of John were expressly named,

units.la: nata esset, unà tamen etiam Baptisma ab ipso ministratum intelligi deberet, quia Baptismi promulgatio pars doctrinæ fuit. Unde Baptismum prædicasse, Marc. I. 4. Act. X. 37. XIII. 24. dicitur. Neque aqua baptizandi ritum illum temporarium, & circa initium Ecclesiæ colligendæ tantùm necessariò adhibendum fuisse, sed ad finem usque mundi ex Christi mandato frequentandum esse, cum praxi Apostolorum collata illa verba Christi: Docentes eos servare omnia, quæ mandavi vobis; & ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi, Matth. XXVIII. 20. confirmant. Quæ clausula ab excessu Apostolorum deinceps ad consummationem seculi prorogata est institutio S. Ministerii & Sacramentorum, nominatim Baptismi aquæ; definita Christi imperio & mandato cum promissione assistentiæ perpetuæ, qua sui mandati observantiæ præsidio & auxilio suo defuturus nunquam sit. Quomodo aliàs erit unum Baptisma, Ephes. IV. 5. si non est unum omnibus fidelibus omnium temporum commune signaculum? At nec illi Sacramentum hoc conati essent supprimere, nisi priùs doctrinam mysterii salutis ita sustulissent, ut stante illorum doctrina sigillum hoc eluforium futurum sit.
units.tr: Baptism administered by him would also have to be understood along with it, because the proclamation of Baptism was part of his doctrine. Hence it is said that he preached the baptism (Mark 1:4; Acts 10:37; 13:24). Nor was water needed only for that temporary rite, necessary at the beginning of gathering the Church; rather, by Christ's command it is to be practised until the end of the world. The words of Christ, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you; and behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age (Matt. 28:20), when compared with the practice of the Apostles, confirm this. This clause, extended after the death of the Apostles to the end of the age, is the institution of the holy ministry and of the sacraments, especially of water Baptism, established by the command and charge of Christ together with the promise of his perpetual presence, by which he will never fail to help and support those who observe his command. Otherwise how could there be one Baptism (Eph. 4:5) if it were not one seal common to all believers of all times? Indeed, they would not have tried to suppress this sacrament unless they had first so destroyed the doctrine of the mystery of salvation that, while their doctrine stood, this seal would be made of no account.

units.la: XXXIII. Non obstant institutioni Baptismi aquæ perpetuæ verba Pauli: Non misit me Christus ad baptizandum, sed ad evangelizandum, 1. Cor. I. 17. Nam & antecedentia, uti supra ostendimus, & collatio historiæ Act. XVIII. 8. non absolutam, sed comparatam negationem, negotii puta principalis, non minùs principalis, intelligi evincunt. Paulo enim, Sila & Timotheo prædicantibus Corinthii plures crediderunt & baptizati sunt, ibid. vers. 8. adeò ut Baptismum unanimiter singuli prædicaverint, & hoc tantùm sibi Paulus 1. Cor. I. 14-17. gratulatus sit, quòd ἵνα μή τις εἴπῃ, seu, ut manu sua plures baptizaret, solicitè non affectavit ratus id, non interesse ad muneris bene gesti rationem Deo reddendam, plures an pauciores manu sua quis baptizaverit, dummodo baptismum resipiscentiæ ore suo fideliter docuerit & ejusdem observationem persuaserit. Nam communi cooperariorum consensu Baptismi αὐτεργίᾳ uni mandari poterat, ut quod per manum unius factum est, omnes fecisse viderentur; secus quàm fas est in munere docendi, quod singuli suo ore obire tenentur. At nec illud, quòd Apostoli non in nomine S. Trinitatis diserte, sed in nomine Christi baptizasse leguntur, obstare, ex iis, quæ supra eam in rem diximus, liquet. Quòd verò & Apostolos & LXX. discipulos, Act. I. 15. & quingentos fratres, 1. Cor. XV. 6. Baptismo aquæ caruisse illi asserunt, mera ariolatio est. Licèt enim Scriptura baptismum eorum sigillatim non commemoret, tamen duo fuisse genera discipulorum Christi docet; unum eorum, qui ex schola Johannis ad Christum transierunt, ab illo jam ante baptizati, Joh. I. III. alterum eorum, quos ipse Christus in cœtum suum cooptavit, quos ab Apostolis ipsis baptizatos fuisse Johannes Evangelista saltem in genere testatur, cap. IV. 1. 2. Alterutro Baptismo tinctos fuisse illos, quibus utrumque adversarii negant, authoritate Scripturæ, & ipsius Christi baptizati, Matth. III. 15. 16. exemplo statuimus. Et est doctrina Christi tota quidem spiritualis secundum internam virtutem & efficaciam quia verba Christi spiritus & vita sunt, Joh. VI. 63. sed secundum dispensationem externam, captui humano accommodatam, secundum quam Christus etiam σύμβολα terrestria, ibid. III. 12. & multa ἀνθρωπίνα humanitus propter infirmitatem carnis, Rom. VI. 19. locutus est, nec verba, nec similia humana, nec symbola visibilia rerum non futurarum τεσοσυμβολικά, sed praeteritarum μνημονικά respuit. Denique nec pro jugo habendus est tantae consolationis interpres ritus. Nulla enim hic obumbratio gratiae, sed mera illustratio; non corporis futuri praemonstratio; non peccati necdum expiati accusatio, vel commemoratio, sed fontis aperti pro peccato & menstruo Zach. XIII. 1. commonstratio.
units.tr: XXXIII. The words of Paul, Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, 1 Cor. 1:17, do not stand in the way of the perpetual institution of water baptism. For both what precedes, as we have shown above, and the comparison with the history in Acts 18:8, prove that this is not an absolute denial but a comparative one, concerning a principal business that is nonetheless not less principal. For when Paul, Silas and Timothy were preaching, many Corinthians believed and were baptized, ibid. v. 8, so that each of them preached baptism alike. Paul rejoiced only in this, in 1 Cor. 1:14-17, that lest anyone should say [ἵνα μή τις εἴπῃ], or, that he did not earnestly seek to baptize more people with his own hand, thinking that it made no difference to the account of his office, which he must render to God, whether more or fewer were baptized by his hand, provided that he faithfully taught baptism as a sign of repentance by his mouth and persuaded people to observe it. For by the common agreement of fellow workers the administration [αὐτεργίᾳ] of baptism could be committed to one man, so that what was done by one hand would seem to have been done by all; this is not so in the office of teaching, which each must discharge with his own mouth. Nor does it stand in the way that the Apostles are read as having baptized not expressly in the name of the Holy Trinity but in the name of Christ; this is clear from what we have said above on that point. As for the claim that the Apostles and the seventy disciples, Acts 1:15, and the five hundred brethren, 1 Cor. 15:6, lacked water baptism, this is mere guesswork. For although Scripture does not mention their baptism one by one, it teaches that there were two kinds of disciples of Christ: one kind, who passed from the school of John to Christ, having already been baptized by him, John 1:35-37; and the other kind, whom Christ himself enrolled in his company, and of whom the Evangelist John testifies at least in general terms that they were baptized by the Apostles themselves, John 4:1-2. We hold, on the authority of Scripture and on the example of Christ himself being baptized, Matt. 3:15-16, that they were marked by one or the other baptism, and the adversaries deny both. And the teaching of Christ is wholly spiritual in its inner power and efficacy, since the words of Christ are spirit and life, John 6:63; but in its outward dispensation, adapted to human capacity, Christ also spoke of earthly signs [σύμβολα], John 3:12, and of many human things [ἀνθρωπίνα], because of the weakness of the flesh, Rom. 6:19. Nor does he reject human words, or similar human things, or visible symbols of things not yet future [τεσοσυμβολικά], but of things past [μνημονικά]. Finally, the rite of so great a consolation is not to be regarded as a yoke. For there is here no overshadowing of grace, but plain illumination; no prefiguring of a body yet to come; no accusation or reminder of sin not yet expiated, but a showing of a fountain opened for sin and for uncleanness, Zech. 13:1.

units.la: XXXIV. Cum elemento aquae Scriptura Verbum jungit.
units.tr: XXXIV. Scripture joins the Word to the element of water.

units.la: Christus tradidit se pro Ecclesia, ut eam sanctificaret mundatam lavacro aquae in verbo, Eph. V. 26. Nam lavacrum aquae fundatum est in verbo institutionis Christi, Matth. XXVIII. 19. Accedit hoc verbum ad elementum, & fit Sacramentum. A baptizante igitur repetenda sunt verba institutionis Christi, & doctrina de mysterio Baptismi, & requam obsignat. Quomodo Johannes Baptista praedicavit resipiscentiam, & populum de re interna per aquam externam significata docuit. Ego baptizo vos aqua ad resipiscentiam. Qui vero post me venit, fortior me est. Is baptizabit vos Spiritu S. & igne, ibid. III. 11. Eodem verbo tum indigentiam Baptismi, seu ablutionis spiritualis propter haereditariam impuritatem & pollutionem nostram ad animum revocare; tum Deo gratias agere, quod Filium suum placamentum pro peccatis nostris & sanguinem ejus, ceu fontem apertum Israeli, ad abluendas in eo sordes peccati donavit, & Baptismum ablutionis ejus Sacramentum & sigillum instituit: tum fidem mortis Christi & promissionum Divinarum confiteri: tum pro eo, qui baptizandus est, ut Deus Spiritu suo eum baptizare, & eundem internum baptismum externo efficaciter obsignare dignetur, precari convenit. Sicut enim quaevis res alia verbo & oratione sanctificatur, 1. Tim. IV. 5. ita speciali ratione aqua haec Sacramentum futura per verbum institutionis & orationem ad Deum, ut institutioni & sancto ordini suo benedicat, sanctificatur & consecratur. Praeterea ipse etiam Baptismus visibile quoddam ῥῆμα verbum Dei est, quatenus & impuritatem hominis, & ablutionem ejus per aquas puras, seu sanguinem Jesu Christi, & communionem nostram cum eodem per Spiritum ejus, & velut baptismum in unum corpus cum Christo per Spiritum ejus corda nostra purificantem, & Spiritum atque corporea sanctificantem visibili ratione docet, atque ita fidem quodammodo operatur. Unde doctrina baptismatum eam doctrinam, quae cum baptismo, & per doctrinam Johannis Christi praedicata & tradita est, Hebr. VI. 1. significat.
units.tr: Christ gave himself for the Church, that he might sanctify it, cleansing it by the washing of water in the word, Eph. 5:26. For the washing of water is grounded in the word of Christ's institution, Matt. 28:19. The word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament. Therefore the words of Christ's institution, and the teaching concerning the mystery of baptism, must be repeated by the one baptizing, and the thing itself, which is sealed. Thus John the Baptist preached repentance, and taught the people about the inward matter signified by the outward water: I baptize you with water unto repentance. But he who comes after me is mightier than I. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire, ibid. 3:11. By the same word, it is fitting to call to mind the need of baptism, that is, of spiritual washing, on account of our inherited impurity and pollution; to give thanks to God that he has given his Son as the propitiation for our sins and his blood, as an open fountain for Israel, to wash away the filth of sin in it, and has instituted baptism as the sacrament and seal of that washing; to confess the faith in the death of Christ and in the divine promises; and to pray for the one to be baptized, that God may deign to baptize him with his Spirit and effectively seal that inward baptism with the outward. For just as any other thing is sanctified by the word and prayer, 1 Tim. 4:5, so this water, which is to become a sacrament, is sanctified and consecrated by the word of institution and prayer to God, in a special way, so that God may bless his institution and holy ordinance. Moreover, baptism itself is a certain visible word [ῥῆμα] of God, in that it teaches in a visible manner both the impurity of man and his cleansing through pure water, that is, the blood of Jesus Christ, and our communion with him through his Spirit, and, as it were, our baptism into one body with Christ through his Spirit, which purifies our hearts, and sanctifies body and soul; and thus it in some measure works faith. Hence the doctrine of baptisms, Heb. 6:1, signifies the teaching that was proclaimed and handed down with baptism, and through the teaching of John and of Christ.

units.la: XXXV. Aqua verbo sanctificata applicatur per ritum βαπτισμόν, hoc est, καθαρισμόν purificationem, Johann. III. 25. 26. quae fit vel per mersionem seu immersionem, qualem Johannes Baptista & plerunque Apostoli usurparunt, more Judaeorum, qui abluentes omnem carnem, Levit. XV. 16. se a ceremoniali inquinatione purificabant: vel per aspersionem & affusionem aquae, qualis etiam in lege usurpata est, idem mysterium significantem. Nam & mysterium ipsum aeque voce ῥαντισμός aspersionis, Hebr. X. 22. 1. Petr. I. 2. atque λουτρόν lavacri 1. Cor. VI. 11. Tit. III. 5. insinuatur. Expiabis me hyssopo, id est, aspergine hyssopi, Psal. LI. 9. ubi res seu mysterium per vocabulum elementi & ritus denotatur. Quam rem S. Paulus cum praecedente figura sic comparat: Si sanguis taurorum & hircorum, & cinis vaccae aspergens pollutos sanctificat ad carnis puritatem, quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per aeternum Spiritum se ipsum obtulit vitio carentem Deo, purificabit conscientiam vestram a mortuis operibus ad serviendum Deo vivo? Hebr. IX. 13. 14. Non refert igitur Baptismus immersione in aquam, qualis olim in orientalibus calidioribus regionibus obtinuit, & hodieque obtinet; an aspersione, qualis deinceps in frigidioribus locis introducta est, peragatur. Utroque enim usu Scripturae βαπτισμός baptismus est; immersio proprie & stricte, aspersio vero notione generali & metaphorica. Generali, velut in βαπτισμῷ λιναν baptismo lectorum, Marc. VII. 4. διαφόρους βαπτισμοῖς diversis baptismis Judaeorum, Hebr. IX. 10. & βαπτισμῷ baptismo ante prandium, seu lotione manuum, Luc. XI. 38. qui baptismi nonnisi aspersione constabant. Metaphorica, velut cum baptismus Spiritus S. Matth. III. 11. Actor. I. 5. & baptismus sanguinis Matth. XX. 22. memoratur. Ille enim, cum per effusionem dandus promissus fuerit, Joel. II. 28. non tam immersionem, quam aspersionem significat: hic vero, seu tolerantia persecutionum aspersionis etiam potius quam immersionis similitudinem habet. Forte etiam baptizati ter mille, & quidem in urbe Hierosolyma, ubi non erat flumen, & statim post admonitionem Petri, Act. II. 41. 42. nec non Lydia & Commentariensis cum tota familia, ibid. XVI. 15. aspersi potius quam immersi sunt. Accedit quod Baptismus est Sacramentum ablutionis a peccatis, ibid. XXII. 16. Heb. X. 23. Ablutio vero spiritualis etiam per ῥαντισμὸν aspersionem fit, quia & ipse sanguis Christi a peccatis purgans, αἷμα ῥαντισμοῦ sanguis aspersionis, Hebr. XII. 24. appellatur. Sicut porro immersio non cessat esse signum vel mortificationis, Rom. VI. 4. etiamsi eam non sequatur suffocatio; vel purificationis, etiamsi eam non sequeretur λόυτρα, depositio sordium carnis, quia immersi tantum descendebant in aquam, & ascendebant inde: ita aqua aspersa & affusa omnia illa, quae significat baptismus, pariter significat. Quin & capiti aspersa unda aliquatenus immersionem, in qua aquae ad caput usque baptizati a pedibus super omnia membra corporis ascendebant, repraesentat. Cumque in locis frigidioribus periculum valetudinis tenellorum infantum, si immergantur frigidae, subsit, valet hic illud Dei: Misericordiam volo, & non sacrificium, Hos. VI. 6. Matth. IX. 13. Ob eandem forte causam in veteri etiam Ecclesia orientali baptismus tempore Paschatis & Pentecostes plerunque administratus fuit, non hyberno, quod tum tenerorum Cum elemento aquae Verbum Evangelii conjungitur. Ritus baptismalis in aquam immersio, vel ejusdem aspersio. rorum corporum in fluvium immersorum valetudo periclitari posset. Eadem clinicorum seu in lectis decumbentium Baptismum non tam immersione quàm aspersione administravit. Quem morem Cyprianus Epist. 76. ad Magnum probavit ajens, aspersionem quoque aquae salutaris lavacri instar obtinere; & quando haec in Ecclesia fiunt, ubi dantis & accipientis fides integra est, stare omnia, & consummari ac perfici posse Majestate Domini, & veritate fidei. Licet ergo immersionis ritus & vetustior & propter significantiorem mortis & sepulturae Rom. VI. 4. repraesentationem, illustrior sit, aspersionem tamen in essentia & mysterio Baptismi nihil immutare, ex iis, quae diximus, liquet. Nihil etiam interest, quoties aspersio fiat, semel, bis vel ter, dummodo non ceremoniae novae, ceu necessario observandae introducantur. Nam & una immersione usi sunt, qui Trinitatem abnegarunt, & trina qui Deitatem dividebant, Ariani. Non contendendum igitur de eo pertinaciter est, dummodo superstitio & haeresis absit. Qui unicam aspersionem adhibent, essentiae Divinae unitatem, qui trinam Personarum Trinitatem figurarunt. Trinam tamen Tertullianî jam aetate receptam, & à Patribus confirmatam Ecclesia praetulit, tum propter formulam Baptismi Matth. XXVIII. 19. Ubi Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. distincte ponuntur: tum quia in fidem Trinitatis baptizamur, adeóque & actus Baptismi distingui convenit, tum propter haereticos unâ immersione S. Trinitatem abnegantes. In universum tamen mos receptus, & mysterio congruens nonnisi malè & seditiosè mutatur.
units.tr: XXXV. Water sanctified by the word is applied by the rite of baptism [βαπτισμόν], that is, purification [καθαρισμόν], John 3:25-26. This is done either by immersion, the sort which John the Baptist and generally the Apostles used, after the manner of the Jews, who purified themselves from ceremonial defilement by washing all their flesh, Lev. 15:16; or by sprinkling and pouring of water, which was also used in the law, signifying the same mystery. For the mystery itself is alike hinted at by the word sprinkling [ῥαντισμός], Heb. 10:22; 1 Pet. 1:2, and by washing [λουτρόν], 1 Cor. 6:11; Titus 3:5. You shall purge me with hyssop, that is, with the sprinkling of hyssop, Ps. 51:9, where the thing or mystery is denoted by the word of the element and the rite. St. Paul compares this matter with the preceding figure in this way: If the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctify to the purity of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? Heb. 9:13-14. It does not matter, therefore, whether baptism is performed by immersion into water, as it once prevailed in the warmer regions of the East, and still prevails today, or by sprinkling, as was later introduced in the colder places. For in either practice of Scripture it is baptism [βαπτισμός]: immersion properly and strictly, but sprinkling in a general and metaphorical sense. In a general sense, as in the baptism of couches [βαπτισμῷ λιναν], Mark 7:4; diverse baptisms [διαφόρους βαπτισμοῖς] of the Jews, Heb. 9:10; and baptism before dinner [βαπτισμῷ], that is, washing of the hands, Luke 11:38, which baptisms consisted of nothing but sprinkling. In a metaphorical sense, as when the baptism of the Holy Spirit, Matt. 3:11; Acts 1:5, and the baptism of blood, Matt. 20:22, are mentioned. For the former, since it was promised to be given by pouring out, Joel 2:28, signifies not so much immersion as sprinkling; and the latter, that is, enduring persecutions, has the likeness of sprinkling rather than of immersion. Perhaps also the three thousand who were baptized, and indeed in the city of Jerusalem, where there was no river, and immediately after Peter's exhortation, Acts 2:41-42, and likewise Lydia and the jailer with his whole household, ibid. 16:15, were sprinkled rather than immersed. Add to this that baptism is the sacrament of washing away of sins, Acts 22:16; Heb. 10:22. Yet spiritual washing also takes place by sprinkling [ῥαντισμὸν], since the very blood of Christ, which cleanses from sins, is called the blood of sprinkling [αἷμα ῥαντισμοῦ], Heb. 12:24. Again, just as immersion does not cease to be a sign either of mortification, Rom. 6:4, even if suffocation does not follow it, or of purification, even if washing [λόυτρα], the putting away of the filth of the flesh, did not follow it, since those immersed only went down into the water and came up out of it; so water sprinkled and poured signifies equally all those things which baptism signifies. Indeed, water sprinkled on the head represents to some extent the immersion in which those baptized rose in the water from their feet up over all the members of the body, to the head. And since in colder places there is a danger to the health of tender infants if they are immersed in cold water, the saying of God applies here: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice, Hos. 6:6; Matt. 9:13. For the same reason, perhaps, in the ancient Eastern Church baptism was generally administered at the time of Easter and Pentecost, and not in winter, when the health of tender bodies immersed in a river could be endangered. By the same custom, baptism was administered to the sick, that is, to those lying in bed, not so much by immersion as by sprinkling. Cyprian approved this custom in Epistle 76 to Magnus, saying: the sprinkling of the water of saving washing also holds the place of the other; and when these things are done in the Church, where the faith of the giver and of the receiver is whole, all things can stand, be completed and be perfected by the majesty of the Lord and the truth of the faith. So although the rite of immersion is both older and more illustrious, because of its more significant representation of death and burial, Rom. 6:4, it is clear from what we have said that sprinkling changes nothing in the essence and mystery of baptism. Nor does it matter how often the sprinkling is done, once, twice or three times, provided that no new ceremonies are introduced as if they must necessarily be observed. For those who denied the Trinity used a single immersion, and the Arians, who divided the Deity, used a threefold one. Therefore one should not contend stubbornly about this, provided that superstition and heresy are absent. Those who use a single sprinkling express the unity of the divine essence; those who use a threefold one represent the Trinity of Persons. Yet the Church has preferred the threefold practice, which was already received in the time of Tertullian and confirmed by the Fathers, both because of the formula of baptism, Matt. 28:19, where Father, Son and Holy Spirit are set down distinctly; and because we are baptized into faith in the Trinity, and so it is fitting that the act of baptism be distinguished; and because of the heretics who deny the Holy Trinity by one immersion. In general, however, the accepted custom, which accords with the mystery, is changed only wrongly and seditiously.

units.la: XXXVI. Formula baptizandi illa est, qua baptizans testatur, se baptizare in nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Matth. XXVIII. 19.
units.tr: XXXVI. The formula of baptizing is that by which the one baptizing declares that he baptizes into the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, Matt. 28:19.

units.la: Quae formula pro scripta utique, non pro traditâ ore tantum haberi debet, uti Bellarminus nugatur. Licet enim verba: Ego baptizo te in nomen Patris, & Filii & Spiritus S. quibus Occidentalis Ecclesia utitur: nec non illa: Baptizetur servus Domini in nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. quibus Graeci utuntur, in verbis Domini & explicitè non continentur: implicitè tamen & per consequentiam, sicut species sub genere, individuum sub specie, in iis continentur. Neque haec mutatio, sed applicatio est, pro natura Sacramentorum. Baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomine Jesu Christi, Act. II. 38. Neque etiam à Christo praescriptam non esse formulam baptizandi sequitur, quia Apostoli in nomine Jesu Christi baptizarunt; tum quia in verbis illis docetur, non qua formula Apostoli baptizaverint, sed quae efficiens & finalis causa baptismi sit; hoc est, quòd authoritate Christi, Messiae, & in ejus fidem atque doctrinam baptizaverint, cùm probabile non sit, quòd Apostoli in Magistri sui verbis quicquam innovaverint: tum quia in nomen Jesu Christi baptizare ibid. VIII. 16. XIX. 5. synecdoche est, qua unâ cum Christo Pater ungens, & Filius unctio intelligitur; & in nomine Christi baptizare, ibid. II. 38. X. 48. est Christi jussu & authoritate, in nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. uti ipse jussit, baptizare. De caetero formula Occidentalium. Ego baptizo, &c. haud dubiè formulae Graecorum: Baptizetur servus Domini, &c.
units.tr: This formula must certainly be held to be written, not merely handed down by word of mouth, as Bellarmine trifles. For although the words "I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit", which the Western Church uses, and "Let the servant of the Lord be baptized in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit", which the Greeks use, are not explicitly contained in the words of the Lord, they are contained in them implicitly and by consequence, as a species is contained under a genus and an individual under a species. Nor is this a change but an application, according to the nature of the sacraments. "Let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ", Acts 2:38. Nor does it follow that the formula was not prescribed by Christ because the apostles baptized "in the name of Jesus Christ". First, those words do not teach what formula the apostles used, but what is the efficient and final cause of baptism: namely, that they baptized by the authority of Christ, the Messiah, and into his faith and doctrine. It is not probable that the apostles changed anything in their Master's words. Second, "to baptize in the name of Jesus Christ", ibid. 8:16, 19:5, is a synecdoche, by which the Father, who anoints, and the Son, who is the anointing, are understood together with Christ. And "to baptize in the name of Christ", ibid. 2:38, 10:48, means to baptize by the command and authority of Christ, into the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, as he himself commanded. For the rest, the Western formula "I baptize", etc., is undoubtedly equivalent to the Greek formula "Let the servant of the Lord be baptized", etc.

units.la: praeferenda est, tum quoad baptizantem, cui sicut Christus dicens: Baptizate, docete, &c. authoritatem baptizandi contulit: ita eam ipso actu, dicens: Ego baptizo, authoritate legationis, (2. Cor. V. 20.) cujus hic actus est, ostendere debet; tum quoad baptizatum, quia Sacramenta speciatim unicuique applicanda sunt. Baptizetur unusquisque vestrûm, Act. II. 38. Denique dummodo sensus integer sit, & de industria nihil corrumpatur, etsi formula ista quoad λέξιν praecisè non observetur, baptisma pro legitimo haberi debet.
units.tr: It is to be preferred, both with regard to the one baptizing and with regard to the one baptized. As Christ, saying "Baptize, teach", etc., conferred on them the authority to baptize, so the one baptizing, by the very act of saying "I baptize", must show that he acts by the authority of his commission (2 Cor. 5:20), of which this act is the sign. And with regard to the one baptized, because sacraments are to be applied to each person individually: "Let each of you be baptized", Acts 2:38. Finally, provided the sense is whole and nothing is deliberately corrupted, baptism must be held valid even if the formula is not observed exactly in its wording.

units.la: XXXVII. Formula illa, qua mandante Christo, in nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. baptizamur, hunc sensum habet, quòd baptizati in Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S. tanquam tres testes in caelo & terra testantes, qui unum & in unum sunt, 1. Joh. V. 7. 8.
units.tr: XXXVII. That formula by which, at Christ's command, we are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit has this meaning: that those baptized are baptized into the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, as three witnesses in heaven and on earth, who are one and agree in one (1 John 5:7, 8).

units.la: Patrem Deum, ac Patrem Filii & nostrum; Filium redemptorem; Spiritum S. sanctificatorem, Paracletum & arrhabonem nominant, in omni gloriatione, glorificatione & gratiarum actione; & Personis his se consecrant, ut populum peculiarem, & omne nomen in Coelo & in terra nominatum longè infra hoc nomen habeant; neque ullum aliud nomen, quasi datum ad salutem, recognoscant, vel ei obediant. Cui proin formulae aequipollet Baptismus εἰς ὄνομα Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ in nomen Jesu Christi, Filii Dei, Act. VIII. 16. 37. XIX. 5. nec non βαπτίζεσθαι εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν baptizari in Christum Jesum, Rom. VI. 3. Galat. III. 27. Id enim significat, Filium Dei esse datum Jesum, seu Deum in carne manifestatum, Salvatorem à peccatis; eúmque Christum, unctum in Regem & Dominum, & unctionis suae participes facientem eos, qui peculium ejus sunt. Unde Act. XIX 4. 5. demonstrans, Johannem baptizasse in Jesum Dominum & Christum, inquit, in Johannis baptismo fuisse obsignationem promissionis de effundendo Spiritu S. juxta illa Petri: Dextra igitur Dei exaltatus (Christus) cùm accepisset promissionem (impetrasset executionem promissionis) Spiritus S. (effundendi) effudit hoc, quod nunc videtis & auditis. Pro certo igitur cognoscat omnis domus Israel, quòd Dominum & Christum ipsum Deus fecerit (declaraverit, & ad dominium suum exercendum, atque Regnum per effusionem Spiritus S. administrandum admiserit) hunc Jesum, quem vos crucifixistis, ibid. II. 33-36. Et sanè Jesum esse Christum, Evangelii summa & fundamentalis veritas est; ut baptizari in nomen Jesu Christi perinde sit, atque Evangelii stipulationi subjici: & promissionibus omnibus matari.
units.tr: They name the Father God, and the Father of the Son and of us; the Son the Redeemer; the Holy Spirit the Sanctifier, the Paraclete and the earnest; and in all boasting, glorifying and thanksgiving they dedicate themselves to these Persons, to be a peculiar people, and they hold every name named in heaven and on earth far below this name, and acknowledge or obey no other name as given for salvation. Therefore baptism into the name of Jesus Christ, the Son of God [εἰς ὄνομα Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ], Acts 8:16, 37, 19:5, and being baptized into Christ Jesus [βαπτίζεσθαι εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν], Rom. 6:3, Gal. 3:27, is equivalent to this formula. For this means that Jesus, the Son of God, is given, namely God manifested in the flesh, the Saviour from sins; and that he is Christ, anointed as King and Lord, and makes those who are his own partakers of his anointing. Hence Acts 19:4, 5, where it is shown that John baptized into Jesus as Lord and Christ, says that in John's baptism there was a sealing of the promise concerning the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, according to Peter's words: "Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God, Christ, having received the promise of the Spirit (having obtained the fulfilment of the promise), poured out what you now see and hear. Let therefore all the house of Israel know for certain that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ (has declared him, and admitted him to exercise his dominion and to administer his kingdom through the outpouring of the Spirit)", ibid. 2:33–36. Indeed, that Jesus is the Christ is the sum and fundamental truth of the Gospel, so that to be baptized into the name of Jesus Christ is the same as to be subjected to the covenant of the Gospel and to be furnished with all its promises.

units.la: XXXVIII. Ita res per elementum aquae, ejusque per ministrum baptizantem aspersae significata & obsignata in universum quidem totum Evangelium est; at sigillatim regeneratio per Christum & Spiritum S. est. Nam in baptismo est λουτρὸν παλιγγενεσίας lavacrum regenerationis, Tit. III. 5. Ubi παλιγγενεσία regeneratio nova nativitas, novus ortus est ipsa vivificatio & ἀνάστασις resurrectio ex morte peccati & corporis. Nam regeneratio nostra in vivificatione & resurrectione ex morte peccati per vocem Filii Dei Joh. V. 25. incipit, & in vivificatione, seu resurrectione corporis, qua incipimus esse in amore perfecto, & cognitione Dei, quemadmodum cogniti sumus, & in satie-tate ac plenitudine lætitiæ perficitur. Unde posterior etiam παλιγγενεσία regenerationis, seu novi ortus nomine venit. Amen dico vobis, quòd vos sequentes me ἐν τῇ παλιγγενεσίᾳ in regenera-tione, quando Filius hominis sedebit in throno glo-riæ, sedebitis super duodecim thronis, &c. Matth. XIX. 28. Atque ita lavacarum, quod sua natu-ra depositio sordium peccati est, credentibus σφραγὶς signaculum, & pignus vitæ novæ, & resurrectionis ex mortuis fit.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Thus the thing signified and sealed through the element of water, and applied through the minister who baptizes, is in general the whole Gospel; but particularly it is regeneration through Christ and the Holy Spirit. For in baptism there is "the washing of regeneration" [λουτρὸν παλιγγενεσίας], Titus 3:5. Here regeneration [παλιγγενεσία] means a new birth, a new origin, and is the quickening itself and the resurrection [ἀνάστασις] from the death of sin and of the body. For our regeneration begins in quickening and resurrection from the death of sin through the voice of the Son of God, John 5:25, and is brought to completion in the quickening or resurrection of the body, by which we begin to be in perfect love and in the knowledge of God, as we have been known, and in the satiety and fullness of joy. Hence the later regeneration [παλιγγενεσία] also comes under the name of regeneration, or new origin: "Truly I tell you, that you who follow me, in the regeneration [ἐν τῇ παλιγγενεσίᾳ], when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his glory, you also shall sit on twelve thrones, etc.", Matt. 19:28. And so the washing, which by its nature is the removal of the filth of sin, becomes for believers a seal [σφραγίς] and a pledge of new life and of resurrection from the dead.

units.la: XXXIX. Cùm porro Regeneratio nostra Christi merito & Spiritus sanctificatione peragatur, manifestissima cum utroque aquæ & ritus baptizantis circa aquam analogia est. Nam Aqua meriti seu sanguinis Christi pulcher-rimum emblema est non tantùm naturali sua aptitudine, sed inprimis Divina institutione, sine qua nihil naturalis aptitudo & congruen-tia valet. Illa elementum ad vitam hominis corporalem, hic res ad vitam hominis spiritua-lem adeò necessaria est, ut sine eo vivere non detur. Illa hominem recreat, sitis ardorem ex-tinguit; hic spiritualem sitim εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα in æternum extinguit, Joh. IV. 14. Illa facilè, nul-lo pretio acquiritur: hic מחיר בלא sine pretio acquiritur à sitientibus, quibus non est argentum, Esaj. LV. 1, 2. Illa elementum commune omni-bus est, quod omnium æquè usui patet: hic nemini sitienti, credenti, recipere Christum, Joh. I. 12. gestienti negatur. Illa elementum super-fluum & abundans adeò est, ut exhauriri à bi-bentibus non possit: hic sufficit omnibus, neque unquam deficere, vel exarescere potest, & ex ejus plenitudine sic omnes hauriunt, ut tamen nihil ei decedat. Illa denique purificat, & sor-des cunctas abstergere potis est; hic ceu aqua illa, ex qua regeneramur, Joh. III. 5. ab omni-bus peccatis nos purificat, 1. Joh. I. 7. Ipsa quo-que applicatio aquæ per baptizantem applica-tionem sanguinis & meriti Christi non obscu-rè figurat. Sicut enim aqua non applicatur nisi corpori sordibus deformi: ita nec sanguis Christi nisi ei, qui pollutus & impurus est, ab impuro genitus, & peccatorum maculis fœda-tus totus est, quíque pollutionem suam con-fitetur & deplorat, exemplo eorum, qui apud Jordanem à Johanne baptizabantur, ἐξομολο-γούμενοι τὰς ἁμαρτίας confitens peccata, Matth. III. 6. Sicut aqua nonnisi applicata sordes corporis eluit: ita sanguis Christi nonnisi ap-plicatus peccatori per gratiam Spiritus S. fidem operantis, à peccatis purificat. Tales eratis. Sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, sed justificati estis in nomine Domini Jesu, & in Spiritu Dei vestri, 1. Cor. VI. 11. In uno Spiritu omnes vos in unum corpus baptizati estis, ibid. XII. 13.
units.tr: XXXIX. Since our regeneration is accomplished by the merit of Christ and by the sanctification of the Spirit, there is a most evident analogy between both and water and the rite of the one baptizing with water. For water is a most beautiful emblem of the merit or blood of Christ, not only by its natural aptness but above all by divine institution, without which natural aptness and fittingness would avail nothing. Water is so necessary for the corporeal life of man, and this thing for the spiritual life of man, that one cannot live without it. Water refreshes a man and quenches the burning of thirst; this quenches spiritual thirst "for ever" [εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα in æternum], John 4:14. Water is acquired easily and at no price; this is acquired "without price" [מחיר בלא sine pretio] "by the thirsty, who have no money", Isa. 55:1, 2. Water is a common element for all, open equally to the use of all; this is denied to no one who thirsts, who believes, who desires to "receive Christ", John 1:12. Water is so plentiful and abundant that it cannot be exhausted by those who drink; this suffices for all, and can never fail or dry up, and all draw from its fullness in such a way that nothing is diminished. Finally, water cleanses and is able to wipe away all filth; this, like that water from which we are regenerated, John 3:5, "cleanses us from all sins", 1 John 1:7. The very application of water by the one baptizing also clearly figures the application of the blood and merit of Christ. For just as water is applied only to a body deformed by filth, so the blood of Christ is applied only to one who is polluted and impure, wholly born of impurity and defiled with the stains of sins, and who confesses and laments his pollution, after the example of those who were baptized by John at the Jordan, "confessing their sins" [ἐξομολογούμενοι τὰς ἁμαρτίας], Matt. 3:6. Just as water cleanses the filth of the body only when applied, so the blood of Christ, applied to the sinner through the grace of the Holy Spirit who works faith, purifies from sins. "Such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and in the Spirit of our God", 1 Cor. 6:11. "For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body", ibid. 12:13.

units.la: XL. Accedit ritus immersionis in aquam, vel aspersionis, qua baptizans aspergit baptizan-dum, mortis, sepulturæ & resurrectionis Chri-sti & nostræ non obscurum hieroglyphicon. Habet enim aqua non tantùm ρυπτικὸν δύναμιν vim sordes corporis auferendi, sed etiam vim suf-focandi, mergendi, mortificandi. Sicut igitur qui immergitur vel aspergitur aquis in immer-sione quoad totum corpus, in aspersione quo-ad caput, tectus & obrutus, quodammodo mortificatur, in eo statu est, in quo is est, qui suffocatur & sepelitur, atque ex eo statu aquis in immersione per ascensum ex illis, in aspersio-ne, per diffluxum & exiccationem corpus de-ferentibus, velut resurgit & revivisci: ita Christus mori atque ita metaphoricè baptizari Matth. XX. 22. sepeliri, & ex morte resurgere atque vivificari debuit; & cum eodem etiam fideles in abolitione veteris hominis tum ini-tiati in hac vita, & perficienda in depositione corporis peccatorum carnis mori & sepeliri, atque in vivificatione novi hominis, initiati in hac vita, & perficienda in altera ex mortuis re-surgere ad novitatem vitæ debent. Quem ty-pum sic Apostolus explicat: An ignoratis, nos, quotquot baptizati sumus in Christum Jesum, in mortem ejus (communionem cum morte ejus, immersione in aquas, vel aspersione earum ad-umbrata) baptizatos esse? Consepulti sumus igi-tur ipsi per Baptismum in mortem (accepimus Baptismum, ut sigillum communionis sepul-turæ Christi, & finitæ maledictionis, quæ nobis incumbebat, per mortem ejus, ad hoc, ut & nos moreremur) ut, sicuti Christus resurrexit ex mor-tuis per gloriam Patris: ita & nos in novitate vitæ ambulemus. Si enim σύμφυτοι coaliti (connati, seu unâ testamento Patris, & sponsione Filii facti unum, ut caput & membra per Spiritum Christi in ipso existentes & viventes) facti su-mus similitudine mortis ipsius (ut & ipse more-retur, & nos similiter moreremur) non tantùm, sed etiam resurrectionis erimus. (ejus similitudi-ne σύμφυτοι connati, unum erimus, ut sicut ipse resurrexit, nos quoque resurgamus, & renove-mur ea renovatione, quæ unioni Christi & membrorum ejus consentanea erit) Hoc scien-tes, veterem nostrum hominem unà crucifixum es-se, ut aboleatur corpus peccati (quia dum Chri-stus crucifixus est, hoc simul actum & impetra-tum est, ut vetus noster homo, seu vitiositas carnis omnis etiam crucifigatur, & simul cor-pus peccati per mortem exuatur) ut non am-plius serviamus peccato. Nam qui mortuus est, justificatus est à peccato, Rom. VI. 3-8. Idem S. Paulus: In Christo circumcisi estis circumcisione non manu facta, in depositione corporis peccato-rum carnis, in circumcisione Christi: Consepulti ipsi in Baptismo (in quo nobis communio mortis & sepulturæ Christi obsignatur) in quo etiam unâ excitati estis per fidem operationis Dei, Col. II. 11, 12. Ita Baptismus ἀντίτυπον similis & vi-carius velut typus est veteris typi aquarum di-luvii, quibus arca Noæ mersa, at nunquam submersa est. Cui rei arcæ respondens antitypon Baptismi, nos salvat, &c. 1. Petr. III. 20. sed & aspersio aquæ manifestum ῥαντισμὸς aspersionis sanguinis Christi, quo corda nostra à mala con-scientia purificanda asperguntur, Hebr. X. 22. XII. 24. significationem habet. Denique etiam ἐκχυσις effusio aquæ in caput baptizandi simili-tudinem tantum cum effusione Spiritus S. in eos, qui baptizantur, habet, ut metaphora luci-dissima Baptismi Spiritus S. nomine veniat. Ille (Christus) est ὁ βαπτίζων ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ bap-tizans Spiritu S. Joh. I. 33. Baptizabimini Spi-ritu S. Actor. I. 5.
units.tr: 40. To this is added the rite of immersion in water, or of sprinkling, in which the one baptizing sprinkles the one to be baptized. It is a plain picture of the death, burial and resurrection of Christ and of our own. For water has not only the power of cleansing [ῥυπτικὸν δύναμιν], the power to remove the filth of the body, but also the power to suffocate, to drown and to mortify. Therefore, just as one who is immersed in water, or who is sprinkled with water (in sprinkling, as to the head), and is covered and overwhelmed, is in a way mortified, being in the condition of one who is suffocated and buried, and then, as the water in immersion lifts him up again, or in sprinkling, as it drips and dries off the body, he rises and is brought back to life, so Christ had to die, and so be metaphorically baptized (Matth. XX. 22.), be buried, and rise from death and be made alive. Along with him, the faithful ought to die and be buried, those who are initiated in this life, in the abolition of the old man, and to complete this in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh; and to rise again to newness of life, in the making alive of the new man, those initiated in this life, and to complete this in the other life after rising from the dead. The Apostle explains this type thus: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death (shadowed forth by communion with his death, by immersion in the waters or sprinkling with them)? Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death (we have received baptism as the seal of communion with Christ's burial, and of the ended curse that lay upon us, through his death, so that we too might die), so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have become [σύμφυτοι] united (grown together, or made one by the Father's testament and the Son's pledge, as head and members, existing and living in him through the Spirit of Christ) with the likeness of his death (so that he too died, and we likewise die), we shall also be [united] in the likeness of his resurrection (we shall be one [σύμφυτοι] grown together in his likeness, so that just as he rose, we too shall rise and be renewed by that renewal which will agree with the union of Christ and his members). Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed (because when Christ was crucified, this was done and obtained at the same time, that our old man, or all the sinfulness of the flesh, should also be crucified, and the body of sin should be stripped off through his death), so that we should no longer be slaves to sin. For he who has died has been justified from sin (Rom. VI. 3-8.). The same St. Paul: In Christ you were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ. Buried with him in baptism (in which the communion with Christ's death and burial is sealed to us), in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God (Col. II. 11, 12.). Thus Baptism, as the [ἀντίτυπον] antitype, is like and corresponds to the old type of the waters of the flood, in which the ark of Noah was lifted up but never sunk. To which the antitype of baptism corresponds, and it now saves us, etc. (1 Pet. III. 20.). Also the sprinkling of water clearly has the meaning of sprinkling [ῥαντισμὸς] of the blood of Christ, by which our hearts are sprinkled to be purified from an evil conscience (Heb. X. 22.; XII. 24.). Finally, the effusion [ἐκχυσις] of water on the head of the one to be baptized has a likeness only to the effusion of the Holy Spirit upon those who are baptized, so that, as a most clear metaphor, it comes under the name of Baptism of the Holy Spirit. He is the one who baptizes [ὁ βαπτίζων ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ] with the Holy Spirit (John I. 33.). You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit (Acts I. 5.).

units.la: XLI. Manifesta igitur regenerationis no-stræ per sanguinem Christi pro nobis mortui & resuscitati à Spiritu S. cordibus nostris ad vi-vificationem spiritualem aspersum, nec non beneficiorum Evangelicorum maximorum in Baptis-
units.tr: 41. The clear meaning and sealing, therefore, of our regeneration through the blood of Christ, who died for us and was raised by the Holy Spirit, sprinkled on our hearts for spiritual life, and also of the greatest evangelical benefits, is in Baptism.

units.la: Baptismo significatio & obsignatio est. Nam illo tum naturalis pravitatis nostrae,quae in Scriptura vetus homo & caro appellari solet, quam deponere,& cui mori debemus,& cujus sordes per puram aquam abstergendae sunt,Rom. VI. 3.4. Col. II. 11. 12. tum aquae illius purae, per quam sordes peccati expiantur & eluuntur,obedientiae puta purissimae & sanguinis Christi,Joh. III. 5. Hebr. X.23. Ezech. XXXVI.25. tum mortis sepulturae & resurrectionis Christi,ad consummandam redemptionem,abolendum peccatum & reatum ejus,Rom. VI.4.5. tum justitiae Christi nobis sanguine ejusdem per Spiritum S. aspersis imputatae per fidem, remissionis peccatorum & adoptionis,ibid. IV. 11. Actor. II.38. XXII.16. tum communionis nostrae cum Christi morte, sepultura & resurrectione,quae nobis in justificatione per imputationem, in sanctificatione per conformationem nostram cum Christo,ejusque imagine; per quam utramque etiam ipsi ut Domino & Salvatori nostro unico,ceu populus peculii ejus,subjicimur,obtingit: tum Spiritus S. per quem Christo inserimur, ejus mors nobis applicatur,& in unum cum eo corpus baptizamur: tum glorificationis nostrae , quam in Christo mortui cum eodem etiam certo reviviscemus , a lucta peccati in morte,& a morte corporis,ultimo hoste,in resurrectione liberandi, Rom. VI.4.5.&c. tum arrhabonis & pignoris horum omnium ab ipso Deo in aquis dati,adeoque sigilli,fiduciae nostrae in Deo & Christo, quae interrogatio illa conscientiae bonae in Deum per resurrectionem Jesu Christi,(firmamentum bonae conscientiae per fidem purificatae, ad liberè petenda à Deo, ad quae accipienda & donanda Christus à mortuis resurrexit) est,1. Petr. III.21. mysterium continetur. Scitè igitur Baptismus à Theodoreto arrhabo futurorum bonorum, & resurrectionis paratae figura,& communio Dominicarum passionum,& participatio Dominicae resurrectionis appellatur.
units.tr: Baptism.
