Further, the Israelites, who once were near, and the believers from the Gentiles, who once were far off (μακρὰν), are under the New Testament regarded without any distinction: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus, Gal. 3:28. Hence also the children of a believing Gentile parent, the other spouse's unbelief not standing in the way, are holy (ἅγιοι), 1 Cor. 7:14. This holiness is no less than that of which St. Paul says: If the firstfruit is holy, so is the lump; if the root is holy, so are the branches, Rom. 11:16. Hence also the seed of Israel is called holy, Isa. 6:13; Ezra 9:2, and in the same way the Gentiles taken into the covenant with the Israelites are on an equal footing, because they too are the spiritual seed of Abraham. Since, then, baptism no less than circumcision seals to believers that covenant into which, once received, they have holy children, by the same right the Church bestows baptism on infants by which circumcision was once bestowed on them. Nor does it stand in the way that the command of circumcision had an added threat of excision, which baptism does not have, and that circumcision was administered only to males on the eighth day, whereas baptism is also administered to females. For the analogy of each sacrament, and also their succession to one another, holds not in all circumstances but in the principal conditions, which relate to the confirmation of the gratuitous covenant and are declared in the New Testament. The threat of excision, however, was a circumstance adapted to the polity of Israel. Of the same kind is the fixing of a time, and the exclusion of the female sex as unfit for that sacrament's sign. Then Christ commanded his disciples, μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, "make all nations disciples and baptize them," Matt. 28:19. Those who are born and received into the bosom of the Church, and for whom the instruction of the father [אב מוסר] and the teaching of the mother [אם תורה] is the word of God, as it was also for the children of the patriarchs, and who are capable of instruction, which ought to begin even in infancy, who could deny that these, together with their parents, belong to the discipleship of Christ? To such Christ also promises the kingdom of heaven, Matt. 19:14; Mark 10:13. But to exclude from the symbols of the communion of the saints those who are disciples of Christ, who exist in the bosom of the Church, and who are holy and not ἀκάθαρτοι, "unclean," 1 Cor. 7:14; whom, just as the children of the Israelites, as sharers in his covenant, God does not cut off, Gen. 17:10, 11, but even admits in express words, and in whom he sometimes also carries on the sanctification of the Spirit: truly that is too monstrous. Nor is it surely for nothing that, although the Apostles were commanded to baptize the Gentile nations, if they should believe entire, and it is read more than once that they baptized entire households, in exactly the same manner of speaking in which the nation of Abraham's descendants was commanded to be circumcised, and entire households were circumcised, yet no restriction to adults alone is found either in the indefinite command or in the record of the sacred practice, so that a like sealing of the same promise, which was under the Old Testament, should be understood to be made to like persons. Moreover, since baptism is the seal of the covenant of God's grace and of the promise of the covenant, Acts 2:39, no cause can be given why it should not be impressed on infants. For even on inanimate things a seal of the covenant was once impressed: the rainbow in the cloud was a seal of the covenant, Gen. 9:13; the law engraved on the altar likewise was a seal of the covenant, Josh. 8:30, 31; blood sprinkled on twelve upright pillars representing the twelve tribes of Israel was a seal and bond of the covenant, Exod. 24:4, etc. And how much more can the seal be impressed on infants, who are animate, endowed with reason and capable of the covenant? It was once the case with circumcision, and our infants lack no equal capacity. It is not the disposition of the recipient but the will of the one who institutes that is required. And since in baptism we are bound to obedience to the Holy Trinity, it is clear that infants, indeed even those not yet born, are bound as heirs, Deut. 29:15. For the thing to which someone is bound has its right of obligation from the equity of the matter, not from the capacity of the one who is bound.

units.la: quis obligatur, jus obligationis ex aequitate rei, non ex captu ejus, qui obligatur, habet. Praeterea privilegii aequè infans ac senex capax est. Coronatus enim aliquando in cunis infans Rex est; & in libertatem cooptatus infans est, qui servus natus est. Unde Proselytos etiam parvulos Hebraei baptizarunt, eò quòd Baptismus iis cedat in privilegium ובן לאר שלא בבני & privilegio etiam absentem donent, uti habetur in Bab. Cethub. sol. 11. Frustra ergo Paedobaptismi hostes eum oppugnant eo argumento, quòd ejus nec praeceptum, nec exemplum extet. Licèt enim praeceptum & exempla ejus ἐν τῷ ἑντῷ nulla extent, tamen ἐν διαθήκῃ extare, satis ex iis, quae diximus, liquet. Ut verò ἐν τῷ ἑντῷ praeciperetur, necesse non fuit. Quomodo nec ἐν τῷ ἑντῷ usquam exprimitur, ne foeminabus Eucharistia administretur; & exemplum nullum extat, quo foeminae Eucharistiam datam esse, disertis verbis affirmetur. Imò satis fuit, quòd à Christo non prohibitus est. Cùm enim Paedobaptismus in Ecclesia Judaica Proselytos per Baptismum in coetum suum cooptante notissimus, usitatissimus & frequentissimus fuerit, non opus erat, ut novo praecepto roboraretur. Christus enim Baptismum in manus suas & usum Evangelicum suscepit, qualem invenit, hoc solo eundem locupletans, quòd eum ad finem longè digniorem, & usum sanctiorem nobiliorémque promovit. Noverant enim omnes, parvulos Ecclesiae in gremium per Baptismum recipi. Id verò, quod communi usu invaluerat, praecepto non indiguit. Imò si infantes baptizandos Servator nollet, plana & aperta prohibitione opus fuit, ne omnino baptizarentur, qualis nulla usquam occurrit. Silentium ergo Scripturae hac in re, in qua declaratio nova necessaria fuisset, paedobaptismum potiùs confirmat. Quòd verò infantes nec μαθητεύσαι, nec servare mandata Dei, Matth. XXVIII. 19. 20. nec credere, nec fidem profiteri posse, objiciunt, pondus nullum habet. Nam μαθητεύεσθαι, uti diximus, discipulum fieri significat; idque locutione Hebraica, qua תלמיד est μαθητής discipulus; unde iidem Hebraei תלמוד μαθητεῦσαι facere discipulum, & התלמוד μαθητεύεσθαι fieri discipulum, formant. Sed gemina ratione homines discipuli Christi fiunt, alii sententia & optione propria, discendo & credendo Evangelium annuntiatum: alii voluntate & cura aliena, parentum puta, vel eorum, qui parentum vicibus funguntur. Subsunt enim infantes potestati patriae, eóque obligantur confirmare institutum parentum per se bonum & rectum, quo ad serviendum Deo & Christo tota vita destinati fuerunt. Tametsi verò per aetatem teneraм Praeceptoris Divini mandata nondum intelligunt, adultorum instar, tamen & infantili aetate ad discipulatum hunc velut inaugurationem quandam consecrari, & consecrati jam crescentibus annis de voluntate Dei erudiri possunt ac debent. Sed praeterea mandatum Baptismi, ibid. XXVIII. 19. 20. formatum est, & enuntiatur pro statu primaevae Ecclesiae primariò & immediatè ex adultis gentilibus per praeconium Evangelii & Baptismum constituendae. De infantibus verò analogicè & consequenter explicandum est ex natura foederis, nexu infan-tum tum cum parentibus fidelibus, juxta quem, si radix sancta est, etiam rami sancti sunt, Rom. XI. 16. eodemque adeò fœderis & sanctitatis sigillo donandi; juxta perpetuum Ecclesiæ, inde ab Abrahamo, usum. Quod ergo in præsentiarum nec doceri, nec credere, nec fidem profiteri possunt, rem principaliter Baptismo significatam non aufert, utpote cujus obsignatio ipsis utilis, & ubi adoleverint, usui futura est. Obsignatur enim iis arcana in Ecclesiæ invisibilis corpus mysticum insitio, & communio Spiritus S. eos custodientis, donec vel in hac vita, vel in mortis articulo infantilis ætas finem accipiat: ut vel hîc in carne, vel quando carnem exuunt, vel per fidem, vel per visionem agnoscant, quæ ipsis inde à matris utero Deus secundum electionis suæ æternæ propositum gratificatus est. Præterea etiam Christus parvulos appellat credentes in se, Matth. XVIII. 6. Habent enim fidem fœderis, etsi non habeant fidem fœderatorum. Durum enim foret, illos infideles appellare. Fideles ergo appellare eos haud durum est; inprimis cùm non tantùm fides parentum, vel eorum, qui eos Baptismo offerunt, ipsorum hactenus fit, ut iis jus ad externam fœderis communionem conferat; sed etiam Spiritus S. applicans iisdem immediatè meritum Christi, fidei vicem suppleat, & paulatim fidem in iis operetur. Arcana autem illa Spiritus S. operatio est, cujus modum certò definire non licet. Neque regenerationis initia ac novæ vitæ semina minùs in ipsos cadere possunt, quàm corruptæ naturæ languor, & labes, quam ex Adamo hauserunt. Ac ut maximè de pædobaptismo nihil in Conciliis definitum fuerit, & Patres de tempore administrandi Baptismi sententiis variaverint, nonnullis ad ætatem provectiorem eum differentibus, non tamen Patrum aliorum, Origenis, Cypriani, Augustini inprimis pro pædobaptismo suffragia desunt. Et de hoc quicquid fiat, & Scripturæ authoritate & Ecclesiæ, seu, uti Augustinus cont. Donat. lib. IV. 23. loquitur, universitatis Ecclesiæ more invaluit.
units.tr: Whoever is bound by an obligation has a right to that obligation grounded in the justice of the matter, not in the capacity of the one who is bound. Moreover, an infant is as capable of a privilege as an old man is. An infant is sometimes made king while still in the cradle, and an infant who was born a slave is admitted to freedom. Hence the Hebrews baptized even little proselytes, because Baptism is to them a privilege [ובן לאר שלא בבני], and they grant a privilege even to one who is absent, as is found in Bab. Cethub. sol. 11. It is therefore in vain that the enemies of infant baptism attack it on the ground that no command or example of it exists. For although no command or example of it stands in the commandment [ἐν τῷ ἐντῷ, i.e. ἐντολῇ] at all, it is clear enough from what we have said that it stands in the covenant [ἐν διαθήκῃ]. Nor was it necessary that it be commanded in express terms. In the same way, the commandment nowhere expresses that the Eucharist is not to be given to women, and there is no example in which it is stated in plain words that women were given the Eucharist. Indeed, it was enough that Christ did not forbid it. For since infant baptism, by which proselytes were admitted into the Jewish assembly, was very well known, very customary and very frequent in the Jewish Church, there was no need for it to be strengthened by a new command. Christ took up baptism into his own hands and into evangelical use in the form he found it, enriching it only in this, that he advanced it to a far worthier end and a holier and nobler use. For everyone knew that little children were received into the bosom of the Church through baptism. What had prevailed by common use did not need a command. Indeed, if the Saviour had wished infants not to be baptized, there would have been need of a plain and open prohibition that they should not be baptized at all, and no such prohibition is anywhere to be found. The silence of Scripture in this matter, where a new declaration would have been necessary, therefore rather confirms paedobaptism. As for the objection that infants cannot make disciples [μαθητεῦσαι], observe the commands of God, Matth. XXVIII. 19. 20, believe, or profess faith, it carries no weight. For to be made a disciple [μαθητεύεσθαι], as we have said, means to become a disciple, and this in the Hebrew idiom, in which talmid [תלמיד] is a disciple, the same Hebrews form talmud [תלמוד] for to make a disciple [μαθητεῦσαι], and hatalmud [התלמוד] for to become a disciple [μαθητεύεσθαι]. But people become disciples of Christ in two ways: some by their own judgement and choice, by learning and believing the announced Gospel; others by the will and care of another, namely of parents, or of those who take the place of parents. For infants are subject to the authority of the father, and are therefore bound to confirm the institution of their parents, which is good and right in itself, by which they were destined from their whole life to serve God and Christ. Although, by reason of their tender age, they do not yet understand the commands of the Divine Teacher, as adults do, nevertheless in infancy they can and ought to be consecrated to this discipleship as to a kind of initiation, and once consecrated, as their years grow, they can and ought to be instructed in the will of God. But further, the command of baptism, Matth. XXVIII. 19. 20, is framed and stated primarily and immediately for the condition of the primitive Church, which was to be established chiefly from adult Gentiles through the proclamation of the Gospel and baptism. But concerning infants it must be explained by analogy and by consequence from the nature of the covenant, from the bond of infants with believing parents, according to which if the root is holy, so are the branches, Rom. XI. 16, and they are therefore to be given the seal of that covenant and holiness, in accordance with the perpetual practice of the Church from Abraham onward. Therefore, that they cannot for the present be taught, believe, or profess faith does not remove the thing principally signified by baptism, since its sealing is useful to them, and will be of use to them when they have grown up. For there is sealed to them that hidden ingrafting into the invisible mystical body of the Church and that communion of the Holy Spirit which keeps them, until their infant age comes to an end either in this life or at the point of death, so that they may come to know, either here in the flesh or when they put off the flesh, either by faith or by sight, the things which God from the womb onward has graciously bestowed upon them according to the eternal purpose of his election. Furthermore, Christ also calls little ones believers in himself, Matth. XVIII. 6. For they have the faith of the covenant, even if they do not have the faith of those who are in covenant. For it would be harsh to call them unbelievers. It is therefore not harsh to call them believers; especially since the faith not only of the parents, or of those who offer them to baptism, becomes theirs so far as to give them a right to external communion in the covenant, but also since the Holy Spirit, applying to them immediately the merit of Christ, supplies the place of faith and gradually works faith in them. That hidden working of the Holy Spirit is, however, a matter whose manner cannot be defined with certainty. Nor can the beginnings of regeneration and the seeds of new life fall upon them any less than the languor and stain of corrupt nature, which they have drawn from Adam. And although nothing about paedobaptism was defined in the Councils, and the Fathers varied in their opinions about the time for administering baptism, some deferring it to a more advanced age, nevertheless the votes of other Fathers, of Origen, Cyprian and Augustine especially, in favour of paedobaptism are not lacking. And whatever may be the case about this, the practice has prevailed both by the authority of Scripture and by the custom of the Church universal, as Augustine, against the Donatists, book IV, 23, calls it.

units.la: LVI. Baptizandi omnes fœderati sunt.
units.tr: LVI. All those in covenant are to be baptized.

units.la: Sub iis etiam Spurii & Nothi aliive natalium labe, vel parentum vitiis notabiles. Distinctio enim personarum, quoad externa, sub N. T. sublata est; ubi jam non est Judæus, neque Græcus, neque servus, neque liber; neque mas, neque fœmina, omnes unus sunt in Christo Jesu, Gal. III. 28. Non enim sicut in V. T. ita etiam in N. T. personarum acceptor Deus est; sed in omni gente ὁ φοβούμενος αὐτὸν qui timet ipsum, & justitiam operatur, gratus ipsi est, Act. X. 34. 35. Spurii tamen in Ecclesiis bene constitutis non ante pœnitentiam parentum, & reconciliationem cum Ecclesia baptizantur; quia Ecclesia sancta est, & communio est sanctorum, distincta à publicè flagitiosis; & oblatio liberorum, quæ fit in Baptismo, ante pœnitentiam & reconciliationem cum Deo offerentium, Deo grata non est, Matt. V. 23. &c. Si tamen parentum pœnitentia desit, communis & pia omnium mater Ecclesia suo sinu eos recipit & fovet. Neque Expositititii à Baptismo arcendi sunt, dummodo constet parentibus Christianis editos esse. Diligenter igitur in parentes inquirendum est; atque ubi inveniri non possunt, in re dubia sententia favorabilis eligi, atque sponsores & curatores, qui eorum curam gerant, authoritate publica constituendi sunt. Excommunicatorum etiam liberi à Baptismo arcendi non sunt, quia excommunicatio non simpliciter ab Ecclesia separat, sed salutaris animæ medicina est, & liberi eorum non minus, quàm parentes gratia fœderis comprehenduntur, neque personalem parentum culpam luere debent. Sed & liberi Hæreticorum illorum, qui fidem S. Trinitatis non abnegant, & dociles sunt, atque se liberos in fide orthodoxa instituturos, vel saltem ne id ab aliis fiat, intercessuros promittunt, baptizandi sunt. Neque tamen vi illis, & aliis etiam, infidelibus puta, Judæis vel Muhammedanis eripiendi & tingendi sunt, quod animarum tortores & conscientiarum carnifices faciunt. Nil tale Johannes Baptista & Apostoli fecerunt, baptizantes non quosvis, sed ἀσμένως πιστεύοντας libenter credentes, Act. II. 41. Nil vetus Ecclesia Apostolica, in qua Gregorius I. improbavit, quòd Chilpericus Judæos baptizari coegit; & Synodus Toletana IV. can. 55. id fieri prohibuit; & Alcuinus Carolum M. Saxonibus baptismum imperantem, liberè monuit, ut Christianam institutionem præmitti pateretur, quia ad fidem cogi nemo possit. Proxima autem liberorum cura jure naturæ & politiæ, quod Evangelium non abolet, parentibus incumbit, quam non temerè publica potestas involare debet; quibus id potiùs satagendum, ut & hæretici & infideles legitimis mediis convertantur, atque conversione ea liberi sanctificentur, & ad Baptismum idonei evadant. Qui enim nec sui, nec parentum respectu in fœdere sunt, citra sacrilegium baptizari non possunt. Licèt enim Deus adducat μαχέσθαι ὄντας eos, qui procul sunt, Act. II. 39. hoc est, gentiles Ephes. II. 13. tamen certo ordine adducit, ut instituti credant & baptizentur, qui ordo Act. II. 38. &c. & alibi observatus est. Abrahamus etiam servos suos circumcidit, Genes. XVII. 23. sed ad Deum conversos. Fidelis enim fuit cum tota domo sua, quam timorem Dei docuit, ibid. XVIII. 19. De monstrosis partubus, daemoniacis, maniacis prudenter judicandum, neque à baptismo depellendus quisquam est, in quo aliquid Christi reperitur. Favores utique ampliandi & odia restringenda sunt, sic tamen, ne quid temerè fiat, & opportuna tempora melioresque vicissitudines ad opus isthoc peragendum eligantur. Denique infantes fidelium baptizandi sunt, sed non vel in lucem nondum editi, secundum partem corporis, non totum corpus nati, quæ superstitio Pontificiorum est, inter pariendum baptizantium quodcunque membrum. Nam juxta illud Augustini, renascitur, qui natus est, non qui natus nondum est.
units.tr: Under this heading belong also bastards and illegitimate children, and others marked by a stain of birth or by the sins of their parents. For under the New Testament the distinction of persons, as far as outward matters go, has been removed. Here there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female; for all are one in Christ Jesus, Gal. III. 28. For God does not, as under the Old Testament, show partiality among persons, but in every nation the one who fears him [ὁ φοβούμενος αὐτὸν] and works righteousness is acceptable to him, Acts X. 34, 35. Nevertheless, in well-ordered churches, the children of illegitimate birth are not baptized before the repentance of their parents and their reconciliation with the Church, because the Church is holy and is the communion of saints, distinct from those who are publicly given to scandal. An offering of children made in baptism by parents who have not yet repented and been reconciled to God is not pleasing to God, Matt. V. 23, etc. If, however, the parents' repentance is lacking, the common and pious mother of all, the Church, receives and cherishes such children in her bosom. Nor are foundlings to be shut out from baptism, provided it is established that they were born of Christian parents. Therefore the parents must be sought out with care; and where they cannot be found, the more favourable opinion is to be chosen in a doubtful matter, and sponsors and guardians, who will take care of them, are to be appointed by public authority. The children of the excommunicated also are not to be excluded from baptism, because excommunication does not simply cut off from the Church but is a medicine for the saving of the soul, and their children are included in the grace of the covenant no less than their parents, and ought not to bear the personal guilt of their parents. Also the children of those heretics who do not deny the faith of the Holy Trinity, and who are teachable, and who promise that they will bring up their children in the orthodox faith, or at least that they will intercede to prevent others from doing otherwise, are to be baptized. Yet they are not to be seized by force and dipped, as is done by the torturers of souls and the executioners of consciences, nor should this be done to others who are unbelievers, such as Jews or Muslims. John the Baptist and the Apostles did nothing of this kind; they baptized not just anyone but those who gladly believed [ἀσμένως πιστεύοντας], Acts II. 41. The ancient Apostolic Church did nothing of this kind either. Gregory I disapproved of Chilperic for compelling the Jews to be baptized; the Fourth Council of Toledo, can. 55, forbade this; and Alcuin, when Charlemagne was ordering the Saxons to be baptized, freely advised him to allow Christian instruction to come first, since no one can be compelled to faith. The immediate care of children, however, belongs to parents by the law of nature and of civil order, which the Gospel does not abolish, and public authority ought not rashly to usurp it. Parents should rather take pains that both heretics and unbelievers be converted by lawful means, and that through that conversion their children be sanctified and become fit for baptism. For those who are not in the covenant, either in their own person or through their parents, cannot be baptized without sacrilege. For although God brings in those who are far off [μαχέσθαι ὄντας], Acts II. 39, that is, the Gentiles, Eph. II. 13, nevertheless he brings them in by a fixed order, so that they are instructed, believe and are baptized; this order is observed in Acts II. 38, etc., and elsewhere. Abraham also circumcised his servants, Gen. XVII. 23, but they had been converted to God. For he was faithful with his whole household, which he taught the fear of God, ibid. XVIII. 19. Concerning monstrous births, demoniacs, and madmen, judgment is to be made prudently, and no one is to be driven away from baptism in whom anything of Christ is found. Favours certainly are to be enlarged and hatreds restricted, yet in such a way that nothing is done rashly, and suitable times and better opportunities are chosen for carrying out this work. Finally, the infants of believers are to be baptized, but not those who have not yet been brought to light, or who are born only in part, not with the whole body, a superstition of the Papists, who baptize any member whatever of the child during delivery. For according to Augustine's saying, he is born again who has been born, not he who is not yet born.

units.la: LVII. Improbandus inprimis est Nexromantia Baptismus mortuorum, quem Corinthiani frequentarunt. Quod nihil aliud esse, quàm sancta in terra projicere Chrysostomus monuit, quod etiam Pontificii mortuos & sepulchra aqua lustrali aspergentes faciunt. Similis Marcionitarum error fuit, mortuorum vice vivos in eorum locum substitutos baptizantium. Utrisque προεξεργασία textus, I, Cor. XV. 29. de BaptifBaptismo ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ansam errandi dedit. Sed non mortuos baptizandos, sed vivos quosdam propter mortuos contrectatos, adeoque impuros juxta legem ablui, Apostolus docuit. Ac multò minùs res sua natura vel irrationales, velut bestiae; vel inanimae, velut naves bellicae, urbium propugnacula, vexilla ipsumque aes campanarum baptizari debent, quae sacrilega Pontificiorum consuetudo, seu incantatio potius est. Nam aquae sacrae usus in aliud, adeoque sacrilegium illud est: & eidem tributa vis pellendi à rebus inanimatis & bestiis daemonem, nec non avertendi fulmina, tonitrua, tempestates, & victorias accelerandi, similiaque, quae Pontificale Romanum plurima & maxima recenset, efficiendi, quam nec à natura, nec à gratia habent, quid aliud quàm φαρμακεία est? Nam quod Stanislaus Hosius campanas à suis non baptizari, sed benedici & consecrari caussatur, dilutum est, quia & Baptismi nomine actio haec apud illos venit, & nihil in Baptismo hominum fit, quin in campanarum tinctione pariter fiat. Nam veri Baptismi ritus, forma & verba in pudendis istis Baptismis usurpantur, uti ex Pontificali illo liquet. Neque benedictio & consecratio ejusmodi φαρμακεία crimen expiat, quia ei miraculosi effectus tribuuntur, quorum producendorum vim nec à natura, nec à promissione & revelatione Divina habent. Imperator certè Maximilianus I. & Status Imperii in centum Gravaminibus A. MDXXII. legato Pontificio Norimbergae exhibitis de campanarum hoc Baptismo, ceu re nefanda, non jolum superstitiosa, sed etiam religioni Christianae contraria, simplicium seductione, & mera (sacrificulorum) exactione graviter quiritati sunt.
units.tr: LVII. Above all, necromantic baptism of the dead, which the Corinthians practised, must be condemned. Chrysostom warned that this is nothing other than casting holy things on the ground. The Papists do the same when they sprinkle the dead and their tombs with holy water. The error of the Marcionites was similar, who baptized living persons as substitutes in place of the dead. For both groups a preconceived pretext [προεξεργασία] for error was given by the text of 1 Cor. XV. 29 about baptism on behalf of the dead [ἀπὸ νεκρῶν]. But the Apostle taught that it is not the dead who are to be baptized, but certain living persons who had touched the dead and were therefore unclean according to the law, and so were to be washed. Much less should things which are by their nature either irrational, like beasts, or inanimate, like warships, the bulwarks of cities, banners, and even the bronze of bells, be baptized; this is rather an incantation than the sacrilegious custom of the Papists. For to put the holy water to another use is sacrilege. And the power ascribed to it of driving out demons from inanimate things and beasts, and of averting lightning, thunder and storms, and of hastening victories, and similar effects, which the Roman Pontifical lists in great number, which they do not have either from nature or from grace, what else is it but witchcraft [φαρμακεία]? As for the claim of Stanislaus Hosius that the bells are not baptized by his people but blessed and consecrated, this is refuted, because the action among them goes by the name of baptism, and nothing is done in the baptism of men that is not equally done in the dipping of the bells. For the true rite, form and words of Baptism are used in these shameful baptisms, as is clear from that Pontifical. Nor does the blessing and consecration of this kind expiate the crime of witchcraft, since miraculous effects are attributed to them, the power of producing which they have neither from nature nor from divine promise and revelation. Certainly the Emperor Maximilian I and the Estates of the Empire, in their one hundred Grievances presented at Nuremberg in 1522 to the Papal legate, loudly complained about this baptism of bells as an unspeakable thing, not only superstitious but also contrary to the Christian religion, a seduction of the simple, and a mere extortion (of the priests).

units.la: LVIII. De Tempore Baptismi administrandi mandatum Dei non extat, quale olim in Circumcisionis Sacramento definitum est.
units.tr: LVIII. There is no command of God concerning the time for administering Baptism, such as was once laid down in the Sacrament of Circumcision.

units.la: Meritò enim Cyprianus Fidum Episcopum definientem, quòd octavo die infantes baptizandi sint, improbavit, & quantocyùs baptizandos statuit. Non enim illorum Baptismum necessitas institutionis remoratur; nec quidquam aliud terrestre & mundanum remorari debet. Et Baptismi dignitas atque utilitas ingens, & Ecclesiae atque parentum consolatio postulat, ne nimiùm differatur, sed ut proxima opportunitate, dum valetudo tenellae prolis sinat, peragatur; absit modò superstitio absolutae necessitatis. Improbata igitur meritò & paulatim abolita est veteris Ecclesiae consuetudo à Siricio Papa, & Leone M. laudata ceu legitima, bis in anno, Paschate & Pentecoste baptizandi. Omne enim tempus habile Baptismo esse rectè Tertullianus monuit; licèt perperam idem de Bapt. Inf. cap. 18. cunctationem Baptismi infantum pro conditione, dispositione, aetate personae, praecipuè circa parvulos utiliorem esse, dixerit, nisi forte de fidelium infantibus loquitur, quorum aequè atque adultorum infidelium Baptismus praecedaneam institutionem requirit. At nec ille ultra tempus justae κατηχήσεως, qua fidei fundamenta posita sunt, protolli debet. Non enim operiri tempus, quo Christus baptizatus est, tricesimum annum necesse est, quia Christus & circumcisus jam fuit, & Baptismo pro se nullo indiguit, & Baptismate etiam ad munus suum consecrari voluit; quae cuncta singularia sunt. Neque laudanda vel imitanda pietas, sed potiùs superstitio fuit Constantini M. Nicomediae sub extremum vitae tempus baptizati, teste Eusebio, & Oratione ejusdem Constantini ad Episcopos Nicomedienses, quam Eusebius de vita Const. M. lib. ult. cap. 62. retulit; & cui major fides, quàm Nicephoro, illi μυθῶν καὶ λεγῶν ψευδῶν scribenti, quòd Romae à Sylvestro baptizatus sit, debetur.
units.tr: Rightly, then, Cyprian rejected Bishop Fidus, who held that infants must be baptised on the eighth day, and he ordered that they be baptised as soon as possible. The necessity of the institution does not delay their Baptism, and nothing earthly or worldly ought to delay it. The dignity and great usefulness of Baptism, and the comfort of the Church and of parents, demand that it not be postponed too long, but that it be performed at the nearest opportunity, while the health of the tender offspring allows; provided only that the superstition of absolute necessity is absent. The custom of the ancient Church, of baptising twice a year, at Easter and at Pentecost, which Pope Siricius rejected and Leo the Great praised as lawful, was therefore rightly rejected and gradually abolished. Tertullian rightly warned that every time is suitable for Baptism, although he wrongly said in his book On Baptism, chapter 18, that the delay of infant Baptism is more useful according to the condition, disposition and age of the person, especially with regard to little children, unless perhaps he is speaking of the infants of believers, whose Baptism, just like that of adult unbelievers, requires preceding instruction. But neither should that period be extended beyond the time of the proper catechesis [κατηχήσεως], by which the foundations of faith are laid. For it is not necessary to wait until the thirtieth year, the time when Christ was baptised, because Christ was already circumcised, had no need of Baptism for himself, and chose to be consecrated to his office even by Baptism; all these things are unique to him. Nor was the piety of Constantine the Great, who was baptised at Nicomedia near the end of his life, to be praised or imitated, as Eusebius testifies, both in the oration of the same Constantine to the bishops of Nicomedia, which Eusebius reported in On the Life of Constantine the Great, last book, chapter 62; it was rather superstition. And greater credence is due to him than to Nicephorus, who wrote false stories [μυθῶν καὶ λεγῶν ψευδῶν] that he was baptised at Rome by Sylvester.

units.la: Cùm enim ille Nicaenae Synodo interfuerit, imò & praefuerit, & cum eadem fidem Christianam jam confessus fuerit, nihil amplius aquam, quo minùs baptizaretur, impedire debuit. Sed Constantini ἀναβολὴ dilatio intempestiva desiderio aquarum Jordanis adscribi debet, quasi fluenta illa majore efficacia praedita fuerint, ad rite peragendum Baptisma, quàm aliae quaecunque in rerum natura aquae mundae. Sed desiderium etiam illud propter incerta vitae humanae, eventu caruit.
units.tr: For since he was present at the Council of Nicaea, indeed presided over it, and had already confessed the Christian faith along with it, nothing more should have prevented water from being applied to him. But Constantine's delay [ἀναβολὴ], an untimely postponement, must be ascribed to a longing for the waters of the Jordan, as if those streams were endowed with greater efficacy for duly performing baptism than any other clean waters in nature. Yet that longing too lacked its outcome, because of the uncertainties of human life.

units.la: LIX. At nec Locus Baptismi in Verbo Dei definitus est.
units.tr: LIX. Nor is the place of baptism defined in the Word of God.

units.la: Rectè tamen ordinarius ejus locus idem, qui praeconii Evangelii, cujus obsignatio est, statuitur. Neque tamen loco illi ita alligatur, quin alibi etiam legitimè administretur; modò ne absit Ecclesia, & desit superstitio. Quibus evitandis scopulis non peccant Ecclesiae, quae ordini se adstringunt. Licèt enim ordo Ecclesiae servire, non imperare debeat, & Apostoli etiam in via, aedibus privatis, & carcere baptizaverint; ubi tamen ordo servatus periculum atque incommodum nullum fovet, rectius ille custoditur, quàm confusio invehitur, & erroris atque superstitionis periculum alitur.
units.tr: Nevertheless, its ordinary place is rightly fixed as the same as that of the proclamation of the Gospel, of which baptism is the seal. Yet it is not so tied to that place that it may not also be lawfully administered elsewhere, provided the Church is not absent and superstition is absent. Churches that bind themselves to order do not stumble on these rocks, since they avoid them. For although the order of the Church ought to serve, not rule, and the Apostles baptized on the road, in private houses and in prison, yet where order is kept and does not foster danger or inconvenience, it is more rightly observed than confusion is introduced and the danger of error and superstition is nourished.

units.la: LX. De Necessitate Baptismi sobriè inprimis loquendum, & piè credendum est, ne vel creaturae accepta referatur salus, quae soli Creatori referri accepta debet: vel ordo à Deo constitutus & voluntas Evangelii perturbetur.
units.tr: LX. On the necessity of baptism we must speak soberly above all, and believe devoutly, lest salvation be attributed to the creature, which ought to be attributed to the Creator alone, or the order established by God and the will of the Gospel be thrown into confusion.

units.la: Posterius veteres & novi haeretici non unius generis fecerunt, & faciunt. Jam olim enim Quintilla & ejus sectatores Quintilliani Baptismum contempserunt & abstulerunt. Contrà quos ex professo Tertullianus libro de Baptismo disputavit. Eodem furore Manichaei, Messaliani & Pelagiani Baptismi necessitatem & utilitatem sustulerunt. Quintillianorum ratio erat, quòd ad salutem fides sufficiat, & Abrahamus nullius aquae nisi fidei Sacramento Deo placuerit. Cui sententiae Tertullianus respondit: quòd licèt fides integra de salute secura sit; tamen lex tingendi nunc à Domino imposita sit; quae salva fide negligi non posset; & Abrahamus jam fide justificatus Deo circumcisionem imponenti imparens non fuerit, sed signum circumcisionis, sigillum justitiae fidei, quam in praeputio habuit, acceperit. Tum Quintilliani verba Apostoli: Non misit me Christus ad baptizandum 1. Cor. I. 17. urierunt. Quibus sic Tertullianus cap. 14. respondit: Cur igitur tinxit Cajum & Crispum & Stephanae domum? Verùm haec pro conditione illius temporis ad Corinthios scripta sunt, quoniam schismata & dissensiones inter illos movebantur, dum alius Paulo deputat, alius Apollo. Propter quod pacificus Apostolus, ne sibi omnia deferre videretur, non ad tingendum ait se missum, sed praedicandum. Nam & prius est praedicare? dicare, & posterius est tingere. Idem Quintiliani aliique simplicitatem Baptismi, & aquæ vilitatem, nihil proficientem ad munditiem animæ, ad ejusdem contemptum induxerunt. Quibus pia antiquitas respondit, non esse de Divinis mysteriis judicandum κατ' ὄψιν, secundum externam faciem, sed mentes ad Deum omnipotentem & veracem, qui lavacrum hoc aquæ instituit, adjecta promissione invisibilis gratiæ, attollendas, & Deo præcipienti obediendum, promittenti credendum esse. Stultum enim Dei sapientius esse hominibus, & quod infirmum Dei est, validius esse hominibus. Sed enim, inquit Tertullianus cap. 2. quanta vis est perversitatis ad fidem labefactandam, vel in totum non recipiendam, ut ex his eam impugnet, ex quibus constat? Nihil adeo est, quod obduret mentes hominum, quàm simplicitas Divinorum operum, quæ actu videntur, & magnificentia, quæ in actu repromittitur? Ut hic quoniam tanta simplicitate, sine pompa, sine apparatu novo aliquo, & denique sine sumptu, homo in aqua demissus, & inter pauca verba tinctus, non multo, vel nihilo mundior resurgit, eò incredibilis existimetur consecutio æternitatis. Mentior, si non è contrario idolorum solennia vel arcana de suggestu & apparatu, déque sumptu fidem & authoritatem sibi exstruunt. Prob? Misera incredulitas, quæ denegas Deo proprietates suas, simplicitatem & potestatem! &c. Hæc commemorare placuit, ut quibus Sociniani & Anabaptistæ, Baptismum vili pendentes, & inter ceremonias cassas amandantes, Patriarchis gaudeant, constet. Quanquam veteribus illis forte deteriores sunt, quia non tantùm Baptismi visibilis, seu sigilli necessitatem tollunt, sed etiam Baptismi invisibilis, seu rei obsignatæ, justitiæ fidei, & redemptionis Christi, veritatem abnegant.
units.tr: Later ancient and new heretics have done, and still do, this in more than one way. Long ago Quintilla and her followers, the Quintillians, despised and rejected baptism, and against them Tertullian disputed expressly in his book On Baptism. With the same frenzy the Manichaeans, Messalians and Pelagians removed the necessity and usefulness of baptism. The reasoning of the Quintillians was that faith is sufficient for salvation, and Abraham pleased God by no water, but only by the sacrament of faith. Tertullian replied to this opinion that, although faith intact is secure about salvation, nevertheless the law of washing has now been imposed by the Lord, and it could not be neglected while faith remained intact; and Abraham, already justified by faith, was not disobedient to God imposing circumcision, but received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith, which he had while still uncircumcised. Then the words of the Apostle, Christ did not send me to baptize 1 Cor. 1.17, troubled the Quintillians. Tertullian answered these in chapter 14 thus: Why then did he baptize Gaius and Crispus and the household of Stephanas? But these things were written to the Corinthians according to the conditions of that time, since schisms and dissensions were being stirred up among them, while one assigned himself to Paul, another to Apollos. On account of this the peacemaking Apostle, lest he seem to claim everything for himself, says that he was sent not to baptize but to preach. For preaching comes first, and baptizing afterwards. The same Quintillians and others, moved by the simplicity of baptism and the cheapness of water, which contributes nothing to the cleanness of the soul, were led to despise it. To these the pious antiquity replied that Divine mysteries are not to be judged according to appearance [κατ' ὄψιν], by the outward face, but minds must be raised to God, almighty and true, who instituted this washing with water, with the promise of invisible grace added; and that one must obey God commanding and believe God promising. For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and what is weak in God is stronger than men. But indeed, says Tertullian in chapter 2, what a great force of perversity there is in undermining faith, or not receiving it at all, by attacking it from the very things by which it consists! Is there anything that hardens the minds of men more than the simplicity of the Divine works, which are seen in action, and the magnificence which is promised in the action? So when a man, plunged into water with such simplicity, without pomp, without any new apparatus, and finally without expense, and dipped with a few words, rises not much cleaner or not cleaner at all, the attainment of eternity is thought incredible. I lie, if on the contrary the solemnities or mysteries of idols, from their platform and apparatus, and from their expense, do not build up faith and authority for themselves. Wretched unbelief, which denies to God his own properties, simplicity and power! etc. It has pleased to recall these things, so that it may be clear to those who, Socinians and Anabaptists, valuing baptism cheaply and dismissing it among empty ceremonies, take comfort in the Patriarchs. Yet they are perhaps worse than those ancients, because they not only remove the necessity of visible baptism, or of the seal, but also deny the truth of invisible baptism, that is, of the thing sealed: the righteousness of faith and the redemption of Christ.

units.la: LXI.
units.tr: LXI.

units.la: Sed duplex eorum, quæ ad salutem credenda vel facienda sunt, necessitas est; una absoluta & medii, sine quo salus non datur, simul atque præcepti; altera secundum quid,& præcepti duntaxat. Illo modo necessaria sunt notitia Christi, ut Principis vitæ & causæ salutis; fides in Christum, & vitæ sanctitas, quæ & præcepta sunt & simul media salutis sunt: hoc modo, quæ præcepta & salutis nostræ promovendæ causa à Deo instituta sunt, velut olim sacrificia; nunc Sacramenta; sed media salutis efficiendæ, absque quibus salus non contingit, non sunt; utpote quorum necessitati Deus ipse limites ponit, juxta illud: Misericordiam volo & non sacrificium, Hos. VI. 6. Matth. XII. 7. Illa simpliciter ἀναγκαῖα necessaria, hæc τὸ ἐπάναγκες subnecessaria Actor. XV. 28. sunt, quia res suâ naturâ liberæ, nec bonæ nec malæ, omnem à præcepto & institutione Divina necessitatem habent.
units.tr: But there are two kinds of necessity for what must be believed or done for salvation. One is absolute and of the means, absoluta & medii, so that without it salvation is not given, and it is at the same time a precept. The other is necessary in a certain respect, & of precept only. In the first sense, the knowledge of Christ as the Prince of life and the cause of salvation is necessary; so are faith in Christ and holiness of life, which are both precepts and at the same time means of salvation. In the second sense are the things that God has instituted for the sake of promoting our salvation, as sacrifices once were and sacraments now are. But they are not means of attaining salvation, without which salvation does not come, since God himself sets limits to their necessity, according to the words: I desire mercy and not sacrifice, Hos. 6:6; Matt. 12:7. The former are simply necessary [ἀναγκαῖα]; the latter are necessary to a degree [τὸ ἐπάναγκες], Acts 15:28, because things which are by their nature free, neither good nor evil, have whatever necessity they have only from the divine precept and institution.

units.la: LXII.
units.tr: LXII.

units.la: Posteriore illo, non priore modo Baptismus necessarius est. Nam non jus ad Christum & gratiam ejus primò fundat & impartitur, sed jus nobis Christi merito quæsitum, & fide applicatum, ceu sigillum ejusdem confirmat & obsignat. Sicut enim in Fœdere operum, Deus Adamo obedienti vitam promisit, & arborem vitæ promissionis Sacramentum & sigillum instituit; atque non arbor vitæ, sed promissio obedienti facta vitæ causa & medium fuit, cui soli etiam, sine arbore vitæ, vita promitti potuisset, cùm ad fructum conferendæ vitæ promissio sine arbore vitæ, at arbor vitæ sine promissione efficax esse non potuerit: ita in fœdere gratiæ Deus fidelibus & semini illorum Christum & beneficia ejus promisit, ac demum Baptismum, promissioni illi obsignandæ Sacramentum instituit. Non Baptismus, seu ablutio sordium carnis, quatenus Sacramentum est, salvat, sed promissio: neque aqua à peccatis purificat, sed sanguis Jesu Christi. Promissio, sanguis Christi simpliciter ad salutem necessaria erat: Sacramentum secundum quid, propter fidei nostræ infirmitatem, cui corroborandæ hoc modo succollare gratia voluit.
units.tr: Baptism is necessary in the latter sense, not the former. For it does not first found and impart the right to Christ and his grace, but it confirms and seals to us the right acquired by Christ's merit and applied by faith, as a seal of it. For just as in the covenant of works God promised life to Adam if he obeyed, and instituted the tree of life as a sacrament and seal of the promise, and it was not the tree of life but the promise made to the obedient man that was the cause and means of life, since life could have been promised to him alone even without the tree of life (the promise could be effective for bearing fruit of life without the tree, but the tree could not be effective without the promise), so in the covenant of grace God promised Christ and his benefits to believers and to their seed, and at last instituted Baptism as the sacrament sealing that promise. It is not Baptism, or the washing away of the filth of the flesh, insofar as it is a sacrament, that saves, but the promise; nor does water cleanse from sins, but the blood of Jesus Christ. The promise and the blood of Christ were simply necessary to salvation; the sacrament is necessary in a certain respect, on account of the weakness of our faith, which God willed to support in this way and to strengthen.

units.la: Non enim fœderi gratiæ, promissioni & sanguini Christi quidquam firmitudinis ex Sacramento accedit; sed fidei gratiam & meritum Christi apprehendenti Sacramentum suppetias fert. Quotiescunque ergo Deus Baptismum homini confert, ingens gratiæ & amoris Dei ἐνέχυρον & pignus, nec non fidei fulcimentum est, quod nisi contempta gratia & fide & consolatione, & sanctissima significatione, quà præpollere hoc Sacramentum scitè Augustinus dixit, contemni non potest. Quotiescunque contra Deus Baptismum, sive præcoce baptizandi fato, cujus ipse solus vitæ & necis Dominus, causa est, sive interveniente alieno, non proprio baptizandi, vitio, negat, ἀρκεῖ ἡ χάρις sufficit gratia Dei, & in privatione hac innoxia potentia Dei multò magis, quàm in infirmitate hominis consummatur, 2. Cor. XII. 9. Sicut enim absolutæ potestatis Domino liberum est, an clienti sola voluntate, an addita voluntati promissione, an utrique addito sigillo beneficium conferre velit; & cùm beneficium uni hoc modo confert, facultatem alii alio modo idem conferendi sibi non præripit: ita multò magis Deus clientibus, imò filiis suis gratiam & hæreditatem vel sola voluntate, vel voluntati juncta promissione, vel utrque conjuncto sigillo conferre & confirmare potest; atque cùm uni hoc modo illam confert, facultatem alii alio modo eandem conferendi neutiquam sibi præripit. Optimus enim, sapientissimus, potentissimus & liberrimus est, & in Cœlis cùm sit, facit quicquid vult, Psal. CXV. 3.
units.tr: For nothing of firmness is added to the covenant of grace, to the promise, or to the blood of Christ from the sacrament; but the sacrament brings help to the faith that lays hold of the grace and merit of Christ. Therefore, whenever God confers Baptism on a man, it is a great pledge [ἐνέχυρον] of God's grace and love, and a support of faith, which cannot be despised unless grace, faith, consolation and that most holy signification, by which this sacrament excels (as Augustine rightly said), are despised. On the other hand, whenever God denies Baptism, whether because of an early death, of which the Lord alone is master of life and death, or through the fault of another and not of the one to be baptized, the grace is sufficient [ἀρκεῖ ἡ χάρις] for him, and God's power is made perfect all the more in this harmless privation than in human weakness, 2 Cor. 12:9. For just as it is free to the Lord of absolute power to confer a benefit on a client by his will alone, or by his will with a promise added, or with a seal added to both, and when he confers a benefit on one in this way he does not take from himself the freedom to confer the same benefit on another in another way, so much more can God confer and confirm grace and inheritance on his clients, indeed on his sons, by his will alone, or by his will joined to a promise, or by both joined to a seal; and when he confers it on one in this way, he by no means takes from himself the freedom to confer the same on another in another way. For he is best, wisest, most powerful and most free, and since he is in the heavens, he does whatever he pleases, Ps. 115:3.

units.la: LXIII.
units.tr: LXIII.

units.la: Sed velle Deum quandoque sola voluntate & Spiritu, vel utrique etiam juncta promissione sine Sacramento & sigillo utrisque conjuncto gratiam & hæreditatem conferre, neque adeò voluntatem nulli unquam eam sine Sacramento & sigillo conferendi declarasse, testatissimum in scripturis est. Nam olim circumcisio sigillum fœderis fuit, magna severitate injunctum, per comminationem excidii, si quis sua culpa incircumcisus mansisset. Incircumcisus & masculus, qui non circumciderit (circumcidi curaverit; de adulto enim, qui curare potest, sermo est) carnem præputii sui, excidetur anima ejus de populo suo; quia fœdus meum irritum fecit, Genes. XVII. 14. Neque tamen sine sua culpa non circumcisi à vita æterna exclusi sunt. Nam in verbis illis excidium intentatur iis, qui fœdus irritum faciunt; quod de infantibus dici non potest. Tum Davidi filius ex Bathsheba natus obiit die septimo, absque circumcisione; de cujus salute David minimè dubitavit. Dixit enim: Ego sum abiturus ad ipsum: ast ipse non est reversurus ad me, 2. Sam. XII. 18. 23.
units.tr: But that God sometimes confers grace and inheritance by his will and Spirit alone, or by his will joined with a promise, without a sacrament and a seal joined to both, and that he has never declared his will to confer it on anyone without a sacrament and seal, is most clearly attested in the Scriptures. For formerly circumcision was the seal of the covenant, enjoined with great severity under threat of cutting off, if anyone remained uncircumcised through his own fault. The uncircumcised male who has not circumcised (that is, who has not had himself circumcised; for the discussion concerns an adult, who can take care of it) the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant, Gen. 17:14. Yet those who were uncircumcised were not excluded from eternal life without their own fault. For in those words excision is threatened to those who break the covenant, which cannot be said of infants. Again, the son of David born of Bathsheba died on the seventh day without circumcision, and David did not doubt for a moment about his salvation. For he said: I shall go to him, but he will not return to me, 2 Sam. 12:18, 23.

units.la: Ergo nec Baptismo sine culpa sua carentes damnantur. Nam paria paribus conveniunt. Circumcisio enim & Baptismus in signis differunt, in re significata conveniunt. Circumcisio veteribus fuit Baptismus, & Baptismus vice versa Christianis Circumcisio est, Col. II. 11. Utrumque vero Sacramentum foederis & justitiæ fidei sigillum est, Gen. XVII. 11. Rom. IV. 11. Act. II. 39. Filii Davidis incircumcisi & salvati argumento Ambrosius Imp. Valentiniano sine Baptismo decedenti salutem asseruit. Dolendum est, ita in concione in obitum Valent. loquitur; quòd nobis cito raptus sit: consolandum, quòd ad meliora transierit. David filium morituorum flebat, mortuum non dolebat. Flebat, ne sibi eriperetur: sed flere desiit ereptum, quem sciebat esse cum Christo. Quam vero illud crudele & absurdum est, dicere, Cœlum jam clausum esse infantibus Christianorum, quod patuit infantibus Israelitarum, & insuperabili necessitate pereundi constringi tot myriadas infantum, qui si nati fuissent in vetere illo populo, sub lege V. T. salvi fuissent; quamvis par utrorumque culpa, par innocentia sit. Tum Sacramentorum omnium, adeóque etiam Baptismi, necessitas omnis est à præcepto Divino positivo, non naturali. Est enim earum rerum, quæ per se non pertinent ad imaginem Dei, & sine quibus homo salvaretur; nisi positivum mandatum interveniret. Talia verò quæ sunt, illorum carentia nemini exitialis esse, nisi transgredienti potest. At infantes Sacramento privati, præcepta ejusmodi positiva non transgrediuntur, ac ne transgredi quidem possunt, quia nec præcepti intimatio iis fieri potest, nec per naturam obedientiæ, vel transgressionis actualis capaces sunt. Nam quòd eos perire non propter transgressionem præcepti, sed propter defectum remedii pro remissione peccati originalis obtinenda regerunt, nullius momenti est, quia licet durante præcepto de Baptismo nullum sit aliud remedium sacramentale, seu regenerationis visibile Sacramentum, non tamen sequitur, nullum aliud esse simpliciter. Non deerat remedium remittendo peccato originali ante institutionem ullius Sacramenti; & Sacramenta instituta nec præcipua, nec sola vel unice efficax, ac ne efficiens quidem, sed tantum obsignans causa remissionis peccatorum sunt. Ac ne quidem Sacramentum infallibile, nedum præcipuum, & simpliciter necessarium applicationis medium est; quia omnia Sacramenta ex fide efficaciam habent; nec sine fide Sacramentum, sed sine Sacramento non contempto fides prodest. Et aggregantur etiam Ecclesiæ parvuli per Baptismum, sed quoad sacramentalem significationem & obsignationem, non quoad participationem fœderis. Nam hæc illius conditio prærequisita est. Alias baptizandi essent omnes omnium infidelium infantes, & invitis etiam parentibus. Ac licet etiam in potestate illius, qui ex sua liberalitate & beneficentia aliquid largitur, sit præscribere, quamcunque libuerit, conditionem, sine qua beneficium non sit daturus: tamen nemo bonus & sapiens positivo præcepto unquam conditionem simpliciter impossibilem, nec naturaliter necessariam cuiquam præscripsit. Præterea Baptismum non habere necessitatem medii ad sa-
units.tr: Therefore those who lack Baptism without their own fault are not condemned either. For like agrees with like. Circumcision and Baptism differ in their signs but agree in the thing signified. Circumcision was Baptism to the ancients, and Baptism in turn is Circumcision to Christians, Col. 2:11. Both sacraments are a seal of the covenant and of the justification of faith, Gen. 17:11; Rom. 4:11; Acts 2:39. Ambrose, using the argument of the uncircumcised sons of David who were saved, asserted the salvation of the Emperor Valentinian, who died without Baptism. In a sermon on the death of Valentinian he says: It is to be grieved, that he was snatched quickly from us; but to be consoled, that he has passed to better things. David wept for his son who was dying; he did not grieve for him when dead. He wept lest the boy be taken from him; but he ceased to weep for him when taken, because he knew he was with Christ. How cruel and absurd, however, it is to say that heaven is now closed to the infants of Christians, when it was open to the infants of Israel, and that so many myriads of infants are bound by an insuperable necessity of perishing, who, had they been born in that ancient people under the law of the Old Testament, would have been saved, although the guilt and innocence of both are equal. Moreover, all the necessity of all sacraments, and so also of Baptism, comes from a positive divine precept, not from natural law. For these are things which do not of themselves pertain to the image of God, and without which a man would be saved, unless a positive command intervened. Now, the lack of such things can be fatal to no one except one who transgresses. But infants deprived of the sacrament do not transgress such positive precepts, nor can they even transgress them, since neither can the precept be intimated to them nor are they capable of actual obedience or transgression by nature. For that they are said to perish not on account of a transgression of the precept but on account of the lack of a remedy for obtaining the remission of original sin, is of no weight, since although, while the precept about Baptism holds, there is no other sacramental remedy, that is, no visible sacrament of regeneration, it does not follow that there is no other remedy at all. There was no remedy for the remission of original sin before the institution of any sacrament; and the sacraments instituted are neither the principal nor the sole or uniquely efficacious means, nor even the efficient cause of the remission of sins, but only a sealing cause. Nor is a sacrament the infallible or, much less, the principal and simply necessary means of application; for all sacraments have their efficacy from faith, and faith profits without a sacrament, but a sacrament does not profit without faith that is not despised. Children are also added to the Church through Baptism, but with respect to sacramental signification and sealing, not with respect to participation in the covenant; for the latter is its prerequisite condition. Otherwise all the infants of all unbelievers would have to be baptized, even against the wishes of their parents. And although it is within the power of one who bestows something from his own generosity and kindness to prescribe whatever condition he pleases, without which he will not give the benefit, yet no good and wise person has ever prescribed by a positive precept to anyone a condition that is simply impossible or naturally necessary. units.la: lutem, sine quo impossibile sit placere Deo, vel videre Deum; satis illud evincit, quòd nec ad cultum Dei internum pertinet, nec cultus interni fidei & sanctitatis causa procreans est, utpote qui dona illa jam procreata obsignat & confirmat, quod pluribus supra confirmavimus; nec ad omnia Ecclesiæ tempora pertinet; cùm media salutis propriè dicta ad omnia tempora pertineant, & fidelibus omnibus communia sint; uti Christi, meriti ejus, fœderis gratiæ; fidei, resipiscentiæ, sanctitatis exemplis liquet; & indignè aliquando & ad perniciem accipi potest, quod de mediis salutis propriè talibus dici non potest. Non ergo externa ablutio medii ad salutem, sed præcepti necessitatem habet. Quæ necessitas non absoluta, sed conditionata & limitata est, quia Deus certos ei limites posuit, ut graviori casu imminente & urgente locum non habeat. Tunc enim ceremoniæ quæcunque mediis ad salutem magis necessariis posthabendæ sunt; uti Christi discipulos Sabbatho facientes quod non liceret, excusantis, Matth. XII. 1. &c. Luc. VI. 1. &c. sententia docet. Præterea nec infantes ante Baptismum decedentes à prædestinatione ad vitam æternam & regeneratione excludendi sunt. Nam fœderati Dei cùm sint, ex formula fœderis: Ero Deus tuus & Seminis tui, Genes. XVII. 7: gratiæ foederalis capaces sunt: Ideo Deus Jacobum in utero matris dilexit, Rom. IX. 13. & Davidem in utero adhuc delitescentem gratia sua texit, Psal. CXXXIX. 13. 16. Jeremiam & Johannem Baptistam in utero sanctificavit, Jerem. I. 5; Luc. I. 15. Neque id singulare quorundam privilegium fuit; quia S. Paulus Rom. IX. 10. &c. Jacobi exemplo universalem doctrinam ad filios promissionis omnes pertinentem probat. Quos ergo Deus purificavit, homo polluere non debet, Actor. X. 10. &c. Hinc ad prædestinationem eorundem facilis ascensus est. Nam quos Deus dilectione, favore & gratia sua prosequitur, & ad cœlestem hæreditatem mox adeundam pro modulo ipsorum regenerat; illi vasa misericordiæ, adeóque ad vitam æternam prædestinati sunt. Ideo Christus, paucis omnia complexus, infantum esse Regnum Cœlorum, puta gratiæ & gloriæ, Matth. XIX. 14. dixit. Sancto igitur & veraci illo, qui clavem Davidis habet; Apocal. III. 7: parvulis Regnum Cœlorum aperiente, quis ab eo illos excludat? Nam quòd Bellarminus de Bapt. c. 4. opinatur, cùm Deus prædestinatis ad salutem remedia ad salutem efficacissimè providerit, omnes, qui in infantia moriuntur, si prædestinati sunt, certò baptizari, & contra, si reprobi sunt, non baptizari, inclemens & crudelis ariolatio, non res est, quia & reprobi multi baptizantur; & contra electi quidam sive parvuli, sive adulti, velut latro in cruce, non baptizantur, quibus Deus absque Baptismo externo, cui gratiam suam non alligavit, media ad salutem alia efficacissimè providit. Neque enim Spiritus S. qui ubi vult, spirat, & parvulos in utero materno sanctificat, tarda Sacramentorum auxilia expectare necesse habet. Sed & Christus infantes fidelium ante Baptismum decedentes, utpote fœderatos suos, morte sua à peccato & morte æterna redemit. Ipse enim fœdus gratiæ cum electis initum, ceu testamentum, mentum, morte sua sanci vit. Unde Mediator fœderis & testator, Hebr. IX. 15.16.17. dicitur. Et quòd infantum quoque nondum sacro flumine tinctorum, imò nondum in lucem editorum, nominatim Redemptor & Salvator sit, S. Paulus dilucide probat, ajens: Quoniam igitur pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis, ipse quoque consimiliter particeps factus est eorundem, ut per mortem aboleret eum, penes quem mortis robur est, hoc est, Diabolum, ibid. II. 14. Potuisset Christus statim ab ortu suo virilem justámque staturam suscipere, virúmque agere: at voluit infans prius nasci atque puer esse, imò virtute Spiritus S. in utero Virginis concipi, in eóque velut alii pueri, carnem & sanguinem assumere, ut hac ratione se infantum quoque in utero delitescentium Salvatorem & Redemptorem ostenderet, & conceptionem nostram labe peccati infectam, sua conceptione & incarnatione sanctificaret & purgaret, atque morte sua tam parvulos quàm adultos à potestate Diaboli & metu mortis liberaret. Scriptura quinetiam dicens, Christum esse propitiationem pro peccatis totius mundi, 1. Joh. II. 2. universalitas illa infantes quoque, in utero materno adhuc latentes, quorum Deus præcipuè curam gerit, comprehendit. Et quomodo Christus in cœlesti sua gloria infantes sanguine suo redemptos, quos vel in ipso utero materno, vel post, repentino subitóque casu sine Baptismo hinc migrare, contingit, excipiat ac tractet, ex historia parvulorum, qui ad ipsum his in terris portati fuerunt, ut illis benedictionem impertiretur, collectu proclive est. Sicut enim illos, increpata discipulorum morositate, ad se venire jussit, ratione addita observatu dignissima, quòd illorum sit Regnum Cœlorum: ita, cùm voluntas ejus sit immutabilis, sibique in omni æternitate constans, nunc in Cœlis sedens ad dextram Patris sui omnipotentis, vult parentum fidelium infantes, ad quos Regnum Cœlorum jure tum electionis, tum redemptionis pertinet, ad se venire, eósque ex hoc mundo immundo, ne pestiferis ejus illecebris & lenociniis corrumpantur, non immaturè, uti vulgi opinio fert, sed maturè ad cœlestes illas suas sedes atque domicilia evocat & accersit. Et sicut in terra parvulis illis suis manus impo suit, & fausta precatus est: ita multò magis in Cœlis ad se venientes, imò Angelorum manibus ad se portatos, obviis ùnis & paterno sinu atque gremio excipit, & perpetua benedictione prosequitur. Viderint ergo μισάν... illi, qui mortis Christi meritum, peccati originalis remissionem & vitam æternam infantibus sacro flumine non tinctis adjudicant, quid responsuri quandoque sint Domino, quando ineptam illorum morositatem, imò crudelem ἀσπργίαν, & importunitatem judicandi alios increpabit. Cúmque infantes ante Baptismum decedentes sint in statu ad martyrium idoneo, uti constat de parvulis Israelitarum in Ægypto, quos Pharao recentes à partu in flumen projici jussit, Exod. I. 22. & de Bethlehemiticis Herodis jussu interfectis, Matth. II. 16. quos inter sine dubio quidam etiam nondum circumcisi fuerunt; déque aliis multis, qui Baptismo fluminis nondum suscepto, sanguine propter Christum baptizati, martyrii coronam reportarunt; à vita æterna exeludi illi non possunt; quia martyrii corona vita æterna est, Apoc. II. 10. Licèt enim martyres omnes non sint, at moriuntur tamen in statu ad martyrium idoneo; adeóque à vita æterna excludi non possunt. Alias enim excluderentur & damnarentur propter culpam simpliciter alienam, puta parentum Baptismum negligentium, vel ob necessitatem fati, cujus culpam non sustinent. Atqui anima quæ peccaverit, morietur. Filius non portabit miquitatem patris, Ezech. XVIII. 20. Si maximè, quod illi regerunt, infantes morerentur ob peccatum originale baptismo non expiatum, tamen aliena adhuc, non propria culpa expiatione illa privarentur, atque ita damnarentur, quod & textui illi, & justitiæ Dei adversatur. Ideo Jehova non Mosis filium non circumcisum, sed Mosen circumcisionem filii negligentem ad mortem popos cit, Exod. IV. 24. Taceo, quòd non Baptismus, quà est ablutio sordium carnis, adeóque Sacramentum, sed fiducia in Deo salvat, 1. Pet. III. 21. quódque obsignatio gratiæ Christi, quam solam Baptismus efficit, necessaria est non tam ad consequendam vitam æternam, quàm ad consolationem, lætitiam & tranquillitatem baptizati in hac vita, qua non ita plena potientes nihilominus salvantur. Nam etiam hæredes Dei sigillis rectè utentes æterna vita potiuntur, etiamsi subinde angantur in hac vita, metuántque infernum, & se ob peccata à Deo desertos quiritentur. Saturantur enim esurientes & sitientes justitiam Christi, licèt se saturatum iri quandoque diffidant, & communio sanguinis & Spiritus Christi ad obtinendum jus vitæ æternæ, & instaurandam in nobis imaginem Dei, interdum sensu communionis illius destituuntur. Est tamen fateor, hæredum Christi major in hac vita felicitas sensu illo Baptismi etiam pignore excitato & confirmato abundantium, sed non minor tamen gloria erit hæredum in altera vita, qui pleniorem consolationis & lætitiæ mensuram in hac vita non habuerunt. Ii ipsi quoque qui pro absoluta Baptismi necessitate, ceu pro aris & focis pugnant, martyrium, seu Baptismum sanguinis, contritionem, seu Baptismum Flaminis, & votum Baptismi, Baptismum Fluminis supplere asserunt, atque id disputationibus suis latius diffundunt. Non ergo etiam gratia Dei & Spiritus S. operatio supplebunt? Si illis martyrii, contritionis & voti casus excipere, nullibi diserte excipiente Scriptura, licuit, nobis privationis casum in infantibus, propitia Scriptura, excipere nefas erit? Inprimis cùm martyrium etiam quoddam charitate destitui posiit, 1. Cor. XIII. 3. Sed de eo quicquid sit, Baptismi necessitas absoluta esse non potest, si voto & Baptismo Flaminis atque sanguinis supplari poterit. Denique qui Baptismo, uti is est depositio sordium carnis, adeóque Sacramentum, salutis causalitatem tribuunt, & gratiam atque salutem elemento, seu inhærente, seu assistente virtute prædito alligant, parùm illi ab idololatria absunt, id creaturis asserentes, quod solius Dei est. Creatura enim quævis, cui salutis efficientia tribuitur, idolum est, & qui huic inservit, idololatra est.
units.tr: "...lation, nor is it necessary for salvation, without which it is impossible to please God or to see God. This is shown well enough by the fact that baptism belongs neither to the inward worship of God nor is it the cause that produces inward worship, faith, and holiness, since it rather seals and confirms those gifts already produced, as we have shown at length above. Nor does it belong to all times of the Church, since the means of salvation properly so called belong to all times and are common to all the faithful, such as Christ, his merit, the covenant of grace; as the examples of faith, repentance, and holiness make clear. And what cannot be said properly of the means of salvation can sometimes be received unworthily and to destruction. Therefore it is not the external washing that has the necessity of a means to salvation, but the necessity of a precept. This necessity is not absolute but conditional and limited, because God has set certain limits to it, so that it has no place when a greater case is pressing and urgent. For then any ceremonies must be set aside in favour of means that are more necessary to salvation, as the teaching of the saying excusing Christ's disciples for doing what was not lawful on the Sabbath shows, Matt. 12:1 etc., Luke 6:1 etc. Moreover, infants who die before baptism are not to be excluded from predestination to eternal life and from regeneration. For since they are the covenanted of God, by the formula of the covenant, 'I will be your God and the God of your seed,' Gen. 17:7, they are capable of covenant grace. Thus God 'loved Jacob' in the womb, Rom. 9:13, and covered David with his grace while he was still hidden in the womb, Ps. 139:13, 16, and sanctified Jeremiah and John the Baptist in the womb, Jer. 1:5; Luke 1:15. Nor was this a peculiar privilege of certain individuals, since St Paul, Rom. 9:10 etc., by the example of Jacob proves a universal doctrine pertaining to all the children of promise. 'Whom God has cleansed, let not man call common,' Acts 10:15 etc. From this there is an easy step to their predestination. For those whom God pursues with his love, favour, and grace, and whom he soon regenerates, according to their measure, for the heavenly inheritance soon to be entered, are vessels of mercy and so predestined to eternal life. Therefore Christ, summing up everything in few words, said that of such infants is the kingdom of heaven, that is, of grace and of glory, Matt. 19:14. Since, then, that holy and true one, who has the key of David, Rev. 3:7, opens the kingdom of heaven to little ones, who can exclude them from it? For as to what Bellarmine, On Baptism, ch. 4, holds, that since God has most effectively provided the remedies for salvation to the predestined, all who die in infancy, if they are predestined, are surely baptized, and conversely, if they are reprobate, are not baptized, this is a merciless and cruel guess, and not a fact. For many reprobate are baptized, and conversely some elect, whether little ones or adults, like the thief on the cross, are not baptized; for God, to whom he has not bound his grace to external baptism, has most effectively provided other means of salvation without it. Indeed the Holy Spirit, who blows where he wills and sanctifies little ones in the maternal womb, does not need to wait for the slow aid of the sacraments. But Christ also redeemed, by his death, from sin and eternal death the infants of believers who die before baptism, as being his covenanted ones. For he himself, having entered the covenant of grace with the elect, ratified it by his death as a testament. Hence he is called the Mediator of the covenant and its testator, Heb. 9:15-17. And that Redeemer and Saviour is named specifically for infants not yet washed in the holy stream, indeed not yet born into the light, St Paul clearly proves, saying: 'Since therefore the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same, that through death he might destroy him who has the power of death, that is, the devil,' ibid. 2:14. Christ could have taken up a grown and just stature from his birth and acted as a man; but he willed to be born an infant first and to be a child, indeed to be conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin, and in that state, like other children, to assume flesh and blood, so that in this way he might show himself the Saviour and Redeemer of infants also who lie hidden in the womb, and might sanctify and cleanse by his conception and incarnation our conception, which is infected by the stain of sin, and by his death free little ones no less than adults from the power of the devil and the fear of death. Moreover, Scripture, saying that Christ is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world, 1 John 2:2, that universality embraces infants also, still hidden in the maternal womb, whom God especially takes care of. And how Christ in his heavenly glory receives and cares for infants redeemed by his blood, who, whether in the very womb or after birth, by a sudden and unexpected accident, without baptism happen to depart hence, may easily be gathered from the history of the little children who were brought to him on earth so that he might bestow a blessing upon them. For just as, rebuking the peevishness of the disciples, he bade them come to him, adding a reason most worthy of notice, that of such is the kingdom of heaven, so, since his will is unchangeable and constant to himself through all eternity, now sitting in heaven at the right hand of his almighty Father, he wills the infants of believing parents, to whom the kingdom of heaven belongs by right both of election and of redemption, to come to him; and he calls and summons them out of this unclean world, lest they be corrupted by its deadly allurements and enticements, not prematurely, as the opinion of the common people has it, but at the proper time, to those heavenly seats and dwellings of his. And just as on earth he laid his hands on those little ones and prayed good blessings over them, so much more in heaven he receives with open arms and a fatherly bosom those who come to him, indeed who are carried to him by the hands of angels, and attends them with everlasting blessing. Let those see to it, then, who adjudge the merit of Christ's death, the remission of original sin, and eternal life to infants not washed in the holy stream [μισάν...], for they will one day have to answer to the Lord, when he rebukes their foolish peevishness, indeed their cruel [ἀσπλαγχνίαν] lack of compassion and their presumption in judging others. And since infants who die before baptism are in a state fit for martyrdom, as is clear of the little children of the Israelites in Egypt, whom Pharaoh ordered to be cast into the river as soon as they were born, Exod. 1:22, and of the children of Bethlehem slain by Herod's order, Matt. 2:16, among whom without doubt some were not yet circumcised, and of many others who, not yet having received the baptism of water, were baptized in blood for Christ and won the crown of martyrdom, they cannot be excluded from eternal life, because the crown of martyrdom is eternal life, Rev. 2:10. For although they are not all martyrs, yet they die in a state fit for martyrdom, and so they cannot be excluded from eternal life. Otherwise they would be excluded and condemned on account of a fault that is wholly another's, namely that of parents who neglected baptism, or by the necessity of fate, whose fault they do not bear. But 'the soul that sins, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father,' Ezek. 18:20. Even if, as they argue, infants died on account of original sin not expiated by baptism, yet they would be deprived of that expiation on account of another's fault, not their own, and so would be condemned; and this is contrary both to that text and to the justice of God. Therefore Jehovah sought the death not of Moses' son, who was uncircumcised, but of Moses, who had neglected the circumcision of his son, Exod. 4:24. I say nothing of the fact that it is not baptism, as it is 'the washing away of the filth of the flesh,' and so a sacrament, that saves, but the confidence placed in God, 1 Pet. 3:21; nor that the sealing of the grace of Christ, which baptism alone effects, is necessary not so much for obtaining eternal life as for the consolation, joy, and tranquillity of the baptized in this life, those who do not possess it so fully are nonetheless saved. For even the heirs of God who rightly use the seals obtain eternal life, even though at times they are troubled in this life, fear hell, and complain that they have been forsaken by God on account of their sins. For those who hunger and thirst after the righteousness of Christ are filled, though they sometimes distrust that they will be filled, and the fellowship of Christ's blood and Spirit, which gives the right to eternal life and restores the image of God in us, is sometimes lacking to them in sense. Yet I admit that the heirs of Christ have greater happiness in this life, when that sense of baptism is roused and confirmed by its pledge, but the heirs who did not have the fuller measure of consolation and joy in this life will have no less glory in the other life. Those too who, arguing for the absolute necessity of baptism, fight as for their altars and hearths, assert that martyrdom, or the baptism of blood, contrition, or the baptism of the Spirit, and the vow of baptism, supply for the baptism of water, and spread this more widely in their disputations. Will not then the grace of God and the working of the Holy Spirit supply? If it was lawful for them to except the cases of martyrdom, contrition, and vow, though Scripture nowhere expressly excepts them, will it be an impious thing for us to except the case of infants who are deprived of baptism, Scripture being favourable? Especially since even a kind of martyrdom may be wanting in charity, 1 Cor. 13:3. But whatever be the case of that, the necessity of baptism cannot be absolute if it can be supplied by the vow and by the baptism of the Spirit and of blood. Finally, those who attribute the causality of salvation to baptism, insofar as it is the putting off of the filth of the flesh and so a sacrament, and who bind grace and salvation to an element endowed with a power either inherent or assisting, are not far from idolatry, since they ascribe to creatures what belongs only to God. For any creature to which the efficacy of salvation is attributed is an idol, and whoever serves it is an idolater."

units.la: LXIV. Augustinum, fateor, aliósque veteres pro peccato originali ex Baptismo, ceu illud tollente, argumentum depromentes, fervor disputationis, & bonæ causæ fiducia eò abripuit, ut alicubi de necessitate Baptismi æquo incautiùs, dubitanter tamen passim, loquerentur. Quod ut illis condonetur, odio hæreseos Pelagianæ in errorem inductis, at Baptismi tamen non salutis insita quadam vi efficientiam, sed significationem necessariam tribuentibus, non tamen, post tantam veritatis manifestationem, Papistarum crassa elementorum superstitione laborantium pertinacia excusari potest. Hi in Concilio Tridentino de necessitate Baptismi disceptarunt. Nam Marinarus rigidam illam non tantùm Baptismi, sed etiam voti ejus necessitatem, adductis exemplis Cornelii, Centurionis, familiæ ejus, latronis in cruce, & Martyrum in persecutionis æstu ad Christum conversorum, & solius Christi virtute, sine Sacramentorum notitia, illuminatorum, & pro Christo sic morientium, cordatè sapienterque oppugnaverat. Pondus argumentorum ejus Tridentinos Patres movit, ut Sess. VII. de Sacrament. in gen. Canonem 4. ambiguum hunc cuderent: anathema esse, qui dixerit, sacramenta novæ legis non esse necessaria, & ad salutem superflua, & sine iis, aut eorum voto per solam fidem homines à Deo gratiam justificationis adipisci, licèt omnia singulis necessaria non sint. Addunt Can. 5. etiam eum anathema esse, qui dixerit, Baptismum liberum esse, hoc est, non necessarium ad salutem.
