Sed anathematis ambigui sensum sic Catechismus Romanus explicat: Nihil magis necessarium videri potest, quàm ut doceamur, omnibus hominibus Baptismi legem à Domino præscriptam esse, ita ut nisi per Baptismi gratiam Deo renascantur, in sempiternam miseriam & interitum à parentibus, sive fideles, sive infideles sint, procreentur. Clementiores, sed non saniores, Augustino & veteribus, qui non baptizatos nil miserantis Orci igne ustulatum iri crediderunt, videri iidem volunt, sempiternam illam miseriam non de inferni flammis, seu pœna sensus, sed de limbi exilio, & pœna damni, explicantes. Saniores omnino veteres, austeriores licèt, fuerunt hactenus, quòd simplici de necessitate Baptismi errore constricti, limbi figmentum omiserunt, cujus nulla in Scriptura uspiam mentio est. Etiam in Ecclesiis nostris popularis error, ignorantiæ passivæ fœtus, de necessitate Baptismi multos afflavit, vel operi operato ceremoniæ nimiùm arrogantes, vel ordinem Ecclesiæ circa tempus & locum Baptismi constitutum turbare gestientes, & ob innoxiam quandoque Baptismi infantum suorum carentiam nimiùm tristantes. Qui error recta de necessitate Baptismi haud peremptoria institutione corrigi debet.
units.tr: LXIV. I admit that Augustine and other ancient writers, who drew on baptism as an argument for original sin, on the ground that it removes it, were carried away by the heat of debate and confidence in their good cause. In consequence they sometimes spoke about the necessity of baptism rather too carelessly, though doubtfully and not throughout. These men may be pardoned, since they were led into error by their hatred of the Pelagian heresy, yet they ascribed to baptism not an inherent power of effecting salvation but a necessary significance. After so great a manifestation of the truth, however, the stubborn obstinacy of the Papists, who labour under the gross superstition of the elements, cannot be excused. These men disputed about the necessity of baptism at the Council of Trent. Marinarus had vigorously and wisely opposed that rigid necessity, not only of baptism but also of the desire for it. He adduced the examples of Cornelius, the centurion, and his household, the thief on the cross, and the martyrs who were converted to Christ in the heat of persecution and were enlightened by the power of Christ alone, without knowledge of the sacraments, and who so died for Christ. The weight of his arguments moved the Tridentine Fathers to frame the ambiguous Canon 4 of Session VII, On the Sacraments in general: anathema be to him who says that the sacraments of the new law are not necessary for salvation and are superfluous, and that without them, or without the desire for them, men obtain from God the grace of justification through faith alone, although not all of them are necessary for each individual. In Canon 5 they add that he is also anathema who says that baptism is free, that is, not necessary for salvation. The Roman Catechism explains the sense of this ambiguous anathema as follows: Nothing can seem more necessary than that we be taught that the law of baptism has been prescribed by the Lord for all men, so that unless they are born again to God through the grace of baptism, they are begotten by their parents, whether faithful or unbelieving, to everlasting misery and destruction. Those who are more lenient, but not more sound, than Augustine and the ancients, who believed that the unbaptized would be burned by the fire of the nether Orcus, wish it to be thought that this eternal misery is explained not as the flames of hell or the pain of sense, but as exile in limbo and the pain of loss. The ancients, though stricter, have hitherto been altogether saner, because, bound by a simple error about the necessity of baptism, they omitted the fiction of limbo, of which there is no mention anywhere in Scripture. In our own churches also, a popular error, the offspring of passive ignorance, has breathed upon many concerning the necessity of baptism. Some attribute too much to the ceremony through the work done (ex opere operato); others are eager to disturb the order of the Church established concerning the time and place of baptism; and some grieve excessively when their innocent infants are without baptism. This error ought to be corrected by a sound teaching that the necessity of baptism is not absolute.

units.la: LXV. Errorem de peremptoria Baptismi necessitate inprimis παρεξεμνεια verborum Christi ad Nicodemum peperit. Amen, Amen, sic ille; nisi quis ex aqua & Spiritu genitus fuerit, non potest intrare in Regnum Dei, Joh. III. 5. Verùm errori non patrocinantur verba, si maximè per ὕδωρ aquam Baptismus intelligatur. Nam etiam Lombardus 4. Sent. D. 4. tum dictum illum intelligendum esse monet de illis, qui baptizari possunt; & contemnunt baptizari quantum ad visibile Sacramentum; quamvis, inquit, absolutè intelligendum sit, quantum ad spiritualem regenerationem. Eodem modo Bonaventura in 4. Sent. D. 4. p. 2. art. 1. q. v. dictum illud de eo, qui facultatem habet, & non præpeditur necessitate, explicandum dicit. Qui etiam Baptismum Sacramentum necessitatis dici statuit, non quia sine eo non possit homo salvari, sed quia ad hoc tenetur; si potest; & hoc neglecto non potest salvari. Non desunt, qui per βασιλείαν Θεοῦ Regnum Dei intelligi, ut sæpe aliàs, putent Ecclesiam externam, quam nisi per Baptismum aquæ intrare nemini licet. Sed tum multi per Baptismum aquæ intrant, qui Spiritum Dei non habent. Velut Simon Magus; Christus autem aquam & Spiritum copulavit. Nobis certum est, Christum per aquam non intellexisse Baptismum, tum quia eam aquam intellexit, sine qua nemo intrare Regnum Dei δύναται potest, adeóque ceu in propositione non affirmativa, sed negativa, absolutam impossibilitatem sine aqua illa vitam consequendi notavit, quod de Baptismo intellectum & Evangelio repugnat, & hypothesibus adversariorum, statuentium, quòd multi sine Baptismo aquæ, solo ejus voto, vel Baptismo Sanguinis & Flaminis in Regnum Dei intrent, quódque eo tempore, quò Christus ad Nicodemum illa locutus est, Baptismus aquæ absolutè necessarius non fuerit: tum quia par ad introitum in Regnum Dei necessitas aquæ & Spiritus à Christo statuitur, cùm aquæ Baptismi & Spiritus S. par ad salutem necessitas, juxta ipsos etiam adversantes, qui solo Spiritu sine aqua multos salvari fatentur, non fit: tum quia illius per aquam regenerationis necessitatem Christus astruit, quæ debuit, potuit, cùm Baptismi ad regenerationem necessitatem Christus pro Israele sub V.T. non instituerit, adeóque doctor Israelis eam cognoscere nec potuerit, nec debuerit: tum quia Christus principia illa regenerationis, aquam & Spiritum, procedente ad Nicodemum sermone explicans, Baptismi nec explicitè, nec implicitè meminit: tum quia aliàs etiam Eucharistiæ participatio etiam absolutè necessaria ipsis etiam infantibus erit, quia verba Christi: Amen, Amen dico vobis, nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis, & biberitis sanguinem ejus, non habebitis vitam in vobis, Joh. VI. 53. (quæ verba adversarii de Eucharistia interpretantur) similiter plane; uti illa Christi ad Nicodemum concepta sunt: tum denique, quia Deus ipse regenerationem per aquam & Spiritum futuram, qualis doctori Israelis ex ejus verbis innotescere debuit, & ad quam Christus in sermone ad Nicodemum allusit, talem prædixit, qualis de Baptismo aquæ intelligi non potest. Sic autem ille: Spargam super vos aquas puras & mundabimini ab omnibus inquinamentis vestris: & dabo vobis (per aquas illas puras) cor novum, & spiritum novum dabo in medio vestri, Ezech. XXXVI. 25. 26. Similia his verba Dei sunt: Effundam aquas super sitientem; effundam Spiritum meum super semen tuum; Esaj. XLIV. 3. Quibus verbis & de regeneratione agitur; quia promittitur datio cordis novi & principia eadem regenerationis ponuntur, aquæ puræ & Spiritus. Atqui per aquas puras non intelligitur Baptismus; tum quia ejus aquam homo, non Deus affundit: tum quia ad illum aquæ puræ non requiruntur,neque omnimoda illarum puritas necessaria est : tum quia aqua Baptismi,etiam quà Baptismi est,abluit sordes carnis,at ab inquinamentis peccatorum,& idolis non purificat, sed aquæ mysticæ,sanguis Christi , qui solus unà cum Spiritu regenerationis principium est. De qua idem Deus: Omnes sitientes venite ad aquas, venite, emite, &c. Esaj. LV. 1. Et Christus ipse in colloquio cum Samaritana muliere aquas illas disertius explicans : Si scires donum Dei, & quis sit, qui tecum loquitur, petiisses ex ipso, & dedisset tibi, ὕδωρ ζῶν aquam vivam. Omnis qui bibit ex hac aqua, quam ego dabo ipsi,non sitiet in æternum, sed aqua, quam dabo ipsi, in ipso erit fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam,Joh.IV.10.14. Neque profectò per aquam & Spiritum, regenerationis principia alia, quàm quæ ipse mox Christus exposuit,intelligere convenit. Atqui ille tum Spiritum S. vers. 6-13. tum Christum in cruce exaltandum & in Cœlum ascensurum,v. 13-22. velut illius regenerationis principia explicat. Christus ergo,ejus obedientia purissima,& sanguis effusus, atque conscientiis nostris aspersus illa aqua est,ex qua æquè ac ex Spiritu S. & utroque solo, regeneramur.
units.tr: LXV. The error of an absolute necessity of baptism was above all brought about by the misinterpretation [παρερμηνεία] of Christ's words to Nicodemus. "Verily, verily," so he says, "unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God" (John 3:5). But the words do not support this error, even if by "water" [ὕδωρ] baptism is understood. For Lombard, in the Fourth Book of the Sentences, Distinction 4, also warns that this saying is to be understood of those who can be baptized and despise baptism as to the visible sacrament; although, he says, it must be understood absolutely as to spiritual regeneration. In the same way Bonaventure, in the Fourth Book of the Sentences, Distinction 4, Part 2, Article 1, Question 5, says that the saying is to be explained of one who has the opportunity and is not hindered by necessity. He also holds that baptism is called a sacrament of necessity, not because a man cannot be saved without it, but because he is bound to it, if he can; and if he neglects it, he cannot be saved. There are some who think that by "the kingdom of God" [βασιλεία τοῦ Θεοῦ], as often elsewhere, the external Church is meant, which no one may enter except through the baptism of water. But then many enter through the baptism of water who do not have the Spirit of God, as Simon Magus did; whereas Christ joined water and the Spirit together. It is certain to us that Christ did not by "water" mean baptism. First, because the water he meant is that without which no one can [δύναται] enter the kingdom of God, and so, as in a proposition that is not affirmative but negative, he noted an absolute impossibility of obtaining life without that water. This is inconsistent with baptism understood in this way, with the Gospel, and with the hypotheses of our opponents, who hold that many enter the kingdom of God without the baptism of water, by the desire for it alone, or by the baptism of blood and of the Spirit; and that at the time when Christ spoke these words to Nicodemus, the baptism of water was not absolutely necessary. Second, because Christ asserts an equal necessity of water and of the Spirit for entering the kingdom of God, whereas the necessity of the baptism of water and of the Holy Spirit for salvation is not equal, even according to our opponents themselves, who confess that many are saved by the Spirit alone without water. Third, because Christ asserts the necessity of regeneration through water, which he ought to have known and could have known, since Christ did not institute the necessity of baptism for regeneration for Israel under the Old Testament, and so the teacher of Israel could neither know it nor ought to have known it. Fourth, because Christ, in explaining the principles of regeneration, water and the Spirit, in the course of his discourse with Nicodemus, makes no explicit or implicit mention of baptism. Fifth, because otherwise the participation in the Eucharist would also be absolutely necessary even for infants, since the words of Christ, "Verily, verily I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you have no life in you" (John 6:53), which our opponents interpret of the Eucharist, are framed in exactly the same way as those words of Christ to Nicodemus. Finally, because God himself foretold a regeneration through water and the Spirit that was to come, of such a kind as ought to have been known to the teacher of Israel from his words, and to which Christ alluded in his discourse with Nicodemus, one of such a kind that it cannot be understood of the baptism of water. God speaks thus: "I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be clean from all your filthiness; and I will give you (through those clean waters) a new heart, and a new spirit will I put within you" (Ezek. 36:25, 26). Similar to these are the words of God: "I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my Spirit upon thy seed" (Isa. 44:3). In these words regeneration is also in view, because the giving of a new heart is promised and the same principles of regeneration are set down, clean water and the Spirit. But by clean waters the baptism is not understood: first, because it is man, not God, who pours the water of baptism; second, because clean water is not required for baptism, nor is complete purity of it necessary; third, because the water of baptism, even as it is the baptism of water, cleanses the filth of the flesh, but does not purify from the filthiness of sins and idols; rather, the mystical water is the blood of Christ, which alone, together with the Spirit, is the principle of regeneration. Of this same God speaks: "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, come, buy, etc." (Isa. 55:1). And Christ himself, explaining those waters more clearly in his conversation with the Samaritan woman: "If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that speaks to thee, thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water [ὕδωρ ζῶν]. Whoever drinks of this water that I shall give him will never thirst for ever, but the water that I shall give him will be in him a fountain of water springing up into everlasting life" (John 4:10, 14). Nor indeed is it fitting to understand by water and the Spirit any principles of regeneration other than those Christ himself expounded immediately afterwards. He there explains the Holy Spirit (vv. 6–13) and Christ to be lifted up on the cross and to ascend into heaven (vv. 13–22) as the principles of that regeneration. Christ, therefore, with his most pure obedience and his shed blood, sprinkled upon our consciences, is that water, by which we are regenerated equally with the Holy Spirit, and by both alone.

units.la: LXVI. Haud majorem reliqua pro absoluta necessitate Baptismi argumenta vim habent. Nam quòd S. Paulus Deum Ecclesiam sanctificare & purificare lavacro aquæ in verbo Ephes. V. 25. 26. testatur, & Baptismum lavacrum regenerationis,Tit.III.5. appellat,non eam vim habet,ut sine Baptismo neminem sanctificari, purificari & regenerari arguat. Propositiones enim ejusmodi universales affirmativæ non reciprocantur. Licet ergo verissimum sit, per Baptismum nos sanctificari, purificari & regenerari, non proprie, sed phrasi sacramentali, qua per metonymiam signo, quod rei signatæ est, tribuitur ; quia Baptismus circa sanctificationem, purificationem & regenerationem nostram aliquid omnino agit,non illam efficiendo,& ex opere operato producendo,uti supra ostendimus, sed obsignando,& unà cum πίστις verbo fidem excitando : tamen nonnisi per Baptismum nos sanctificari, purificari & regenerari , non sequitur. Quomodo non quia qui credit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur, etiam qui non crediderit,& non baptizatus fuerit,sed qui non crediderit, damnabitur, Marc. XVI. 16. Similia argumenta Loc.XI.61. fusius diluimus. Neque etiam Baptismi necessitas ex peccati originalis infantum necessaria remissione,rectè concluditur. Alias nemini sine Baptismo peccatum originale remitteretur,quod ipsi adversarii, Baptismum Flaminis, vel Sanguinis Baptismo Fluminis quandoque substituentes,negant. Etiam Circumcisio peccato originali tollendo fuit, neque tamen omnibus absolutè necessaria fuit. Est sanè Baptismus,æquè atque Circumcisio fuit , remedium adversus peccatum originale, verùm non proprie & per se, sed improprie & per aliud. Non enim medetur peccato nisi per gratiam, & medetur non efficiendo, sed obsignando, cujusmodi remedia non absolutè necessaria sunt. Inane & illud est,quòd non baptizatos non pertinere ad Ecclesiam & extra Ecclesiam neminem salvari objectant. Aliter enim salvandi ad Ecclesiam
units.tr: LXVI. The other arguments have no greater force in support of the absolute necessity of Baptism. For when St Paul testifies that God sanctifies the Church and cleanses it by the washing of water with the word (Eph. 5:25-26), and calls Baptism the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5), this does not prove that no one is sanctified, cleansed or regenerated without Baptism. Universal affirmative propositions of this kind are not convertible. So although it is entirely true that we are sanctified, cleansed and regenerated through Baptism, this is said not properly but in sacramental language, in which, by metonymy, the sign is given the name of the thing signified. Baptism does indeed do something entirely real in respect of our sanctification, purification and regeneration. It does not effect these by working ex opere operato, as we have shown above, but by sealing them and, together with the word, [πίστις] stirring up faith. Yet it does not follow that we are sanctified, cleansed and regenerated only through Baptism. In the same way, it does not follow from the fact that he who believes and is baptized shall be saved that he who has not believed and has not been baptized will not be saved. Rather, he who does not believe shall be damned (Mark 16:16). We have refuted similar arguments at greater length in Locus XI, section 61. Nor is the necessity of Baptism rightly inferred from the necessary remission of original sin in infants. Otherwise original sin would be forgiven to no one without Baptism, which the opponents themselves deny, since they sometimes substitute Baptism of the Spirit or Baptism of blood for water Baptism. Circumcision too was for the removal of original sin, and yet it was not absolutely necessary for everyone. Baptism is certainly, just as circumcision was, a remedy against original sin, but not properly and in itself; it is a remedy improperly and through something else. For it heals sin only through grace, and it heals not by effecting but by sealing, and remedies of this kind are not absolutely necessary. Equally empty is the objection that the unbaptized do not belong to the Church and that no one is saved outside the Church. For those who are to be saved belong to the Church in one way according to its unity,

units.la: pertinent secundum ejus unitatem ; aliter secundum ejus ordinem. Ad unitatem Ecclesiæ omnia membra Christi pertinent ; & qui ad eam non pertinent,non salvantur. Ad ordinem ii duntaxat, quibus Deus salutem per ministerium hominum conferre vult ; ad quem qui non pertinent non ideo non salvantur, uti exempla Martyrum,& latronis in cruce comprobant. Deus enim salutem huic ordini nuspiam alligavit ; neque qui eo sine culpa sua caret,damnabilis est. Denique neque Augustini aliorúmque veterum errori patrocinatur consentientium sententia : tum quia testimonium humanum est : tum quia diversa, uti ostendimus,errantium facies fuit : tum quia Augustinus aliíque veteres non Baptismi solius , sed Eucharistiæ etiam infantibus conferendæ necessitatem ex tenore dictorum similium, Joh. III. 5. & VI. 53. collegerunt, quorum consensum cùm Ecclesia propter Scripturæ authoritatem in posteriore deseruerit , in priori propter eandem jure meritòque deserit.
units.tr: and in another way according to its order. All the members of Christ belong to the unity of the Church, and those who do not belong to it are not saved. They belong to its order only in so far as God wills to confer salvation through the ministry of men. Those who do not belong to this order are not for that reason not saved, as the examples of the martyrs and of the thief on the cross prove. For God has nowhere tied salvation to this order, and whoever lacks it without fault of his own is not condemned. Finally, the opinion of those who agree with it does not defend the error of Augustine and other ancients. First, because it is a human testimony. Second, because, as we have shown, the error of those who erred was of a different kind. Third, because Augustine and the other ancients drew the necessity not only of Baptism but also of the Eucharist for infants from the tenor of similar sayings, John 3:5 and 6:53. Since the Church has abandoned their consensus on the latter point because of the authority of Scripture, it rightly and justly abandons it on the former for the same reason.

units.la: LXVII. Affinis eorundem error est asseverantium, quòd per Baptismum tollatur id omne,quod peccati veram & propriam rationem habet; & quæ reliquia in regenitis concupiscentia,& fomes peccati est,non verè & proprie peccatum sit,sed tale dicatur, quia ex peccato est,& ad peccatum inclinat, quæ Tridentinorum Sess. V. can. 5. definitio est. Dum enim sic Baptismum extollere conantur,hominem,& concupiscentiam in illo reliquam , ceu rem puram, extollunt,& sanctitatem Dei deprimunt. Sed dimittitur peccatum in Baptismo non ut non fit,sed ut non objit, seu non imputetur, licet infit,uti passim Augustinus. Quamvis enim peccatum & concupiscentia baptizatis regenitis non ita insit,sicut inest irregenitis,nempe tam forte & regnans , peccatum tamen verum & proprium est,atque dicitur,quia est peccati regnantis λεῖμμα residuum,& rebellando nos trahere nititur ad reatum,& peccandi delectatione movetur nobis invitis,eique consentire peccatum esse idem Augustinus loquitur. Clarius verò Paulus ἁμαρτίαν peccatum vocat,quia κακὸν malum est , & legi Dei contrariatur,Rom. VII.7.18.21.23. & ex Deo non est,Jac.I.13. 1.Joh.II.16. Quam in rem plura Loc.X.55. 58.59. diximus.
units.tr: LXVII. Closely related to this error is that of those who assert that through Baptism everything is removed that has the true and proper character of sin, and that the concupiscence remaining in the regenerate, which is the tinder of sin, is not truly and properly sin but is called sin because it comes from sin and inclines to sin. This is the definition of the Tridentine Session V, canon 5. For in trying thus to exalt Baptism, they exalt the man and the concupiscence remaining in him as if they were something pure, and they depress the holiness of God. But sin is forgiven in Baptism not so that it does not come into being, but so that it does not harm, or is not imputed, although it does exist, as Augustine says everywhere. For although sin and concupiscence do not dwell in the baptized and regenerate as they dwell in the unregenerate, namely as strong and reigning, sin is nonetheless true and proper sin, and it is called so because it is the remnant [λεῖμμα] of reigning sin. It strives to draw us by rebellion into guilt, and it is moved by the delight of sin against our will; Augustine says that to consent to it is sin. More clearly still, Paul calls it [ἁμαρτίαν] sin, because it is [κακὸν] evil and opposed to the law of God (Rom. 7:7, 18, 21, 23), and it is not from God (James 1:13; 1 John 2:16). We have said more on this point in Locus X, sections 55, 58 and 59.

units.la: LXVIII. Baptismus unus genere,& unus numero est. Unus genere, quia unus omnium est. "Ἓν βάπτισμα unus Baptismus est,Eph. IV. 5. Uno Spiritu omnes εἰς ἓν σῶμα in unum corpus baptizati sumus, sive Judæi, sive Græci,sive servi, sive liberi, 1.Cor. XII.13. Unus numero respectu singulorum fidelium, quia semel,non iterum , vel sæpe tinguntur. Quæ unitas non characteri in Baptismo impresso, & indelebili, sed voluntati Dei accepta referri debet. Non characteri, uti Tridentini Sess.VII. can. 9. statuunt,quia is fictitius plane est, & solius Ecclesiæ (Papalis) authoritate invaluit , uti ipse Scotus fatetur. Nam nec ad signum Baptismi pertinet,cum elementaris & sensibilis non sit: nec ad rem signatam, cùm juxta eosdem à gratia distinguatur. Nihil autem in Baptismo præter signum & rem signatam occurrit. Cumque characteris sit discernere, character Baptismo addi-
units.tr: LXVIII. Baptism is one in kind and one in number. It is one in kind because it is one for all: one Baptism [Ἓν βάπτισμα] (Eph. 4:5); by one Spirit we were all baptized into one body [εἰς ἓν σῶμα], whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free (1 Cor. 12:13). It is one in number with respect to individual believers, because they are washed once and not again or often. This unity should be ascribed not to a character impressed and indelible in Baptism but to the acceptable will of God. Not to a character, as the Tridentine Session VII, canon 9 decrees, because such a character is entirely fictitious and gained strength only by the authority of the (Papal) Church alone, as Scotus himself admits. For it belongs neither to the sign of Baptism, since it is not elemental and sensible, nor to the thing signified, since according to the same authorities it is distinct from grace. Yet nothing in Baptism occurs apart from the sign and the thing signified. And since it is the function of a character to distinguish,

units.la: Reliqua pro absoluta ea necessitate argumenta exemplfa. additus baptizatos nec apud Deum, nec apud homines discernit. Non apud Deum, quia is scrutator cordis & renum characteris nota non indiget. Non apud homines, quia spiritualis esse fingitur. Neque aliam ob causam character sequioribus temporibus post Gratianum & Lombardum inductus est, quàm ut Sacramenti certitudo fluxæ arenæ inædificetur, & consolatio vera, quæ ex Sacramentis hauriri debet, tollatur. Gabriel Biel in 4. sent. D. 6. q. 2. dub. 16. non tantùm fatetur, magis ignotum esse Baptismum imprimere characterem, quàm iterari non posse; sed etiam in toto canone Bibliæ non inveniri characterem nisi, Apoc. XIII. &c. Ubi fiat mentio de charactere Bestiæ. Profectò ex tripode. Nam Roma, ubi Bestia & Babylon est, imprimit fronti characterem per exorcismum baptismalem & Confirmationis Sacramentum, aliaque hujusmodi præstigiarum Pontificiarum amuleta: dextrè verò characterem indelebilem per Sacramentum ordinationis, in quo ordinandi omnes manu dextra signantur. Vis characteris est, ut sic signati Domino Romæ obnoxii toti sint, & jus emptionis ac venditionis acquirant. Roma enim tota emporium est, ubi fere non aliud agitur, quàm quòd emitur & venditur; Hinc adeò baptizatos omnes obligari ad obedientiam Papæ, & ejus judiciis obnoxios esse, pertendunt. Si quis dixerit, ita Concil. Tridentini Sess. VII. de Bapt. can. 8. sonat, baptizatos liberos esse ab omnibus sanctæ Ecclesiæ: (Papalis, quæ Romæ se magistram fidei jactat) præceptis, quæ vel scripta vel tradita sunt, ita ut ea observare non teneantur, nisi sua sponte illis submittere se voluerint (quæ verba obelo notanda ex Lutheri scriptis excerpta sunt.) anathema sit. Imò jus illud characteristicum, sic illi interdum urgent, ut præ se aperte ferant; Infantem, dum à Romano Sacerdote baptizatur, Pontifici Romano sic obligari, ut contra talem, si deinceps deficiat, actio perjurii sit.
units.tr: the other arguments for that absolute necessity are likewise refuted by examples. A character added to the baptized distinguishes them neither before God nor before men. Not before God, because he who searches the heart and reins has no need of a mark on the character. Not before men, because it is pretended to be spiritual. Nor was the character introduced in later times, after Gratian and Lombard, for any other reason than that the certainty of the sacrament might be built on shifting sand and the true consolation that ought to be drawn from the sacraments might be taken away. Gabriel Biel, In 4 Sent., D. 6, q. 2, dub. 16, not only admits that it is less known that Baptism imprints a character than that it cannot be repeated, but also that in the whole canon of the Bible the character is not found, except in Revelation 13, etc., where mention is made of the character of the Beast. Certainly this is from the tripod. For Rome, where the Beast and Babylon is, impresses a mark on the forehead through the baptismal exorcism and the sacrament of Confirmation, and other such amulets of Papal sorcery; but it impresses an indelible character on the right hand through the sacrament of ordination, in which all who are ordained are signed on the right hand. The force of the character is that those so marked are wholly bound to the Lord of Rome and acquire the right of buying and selling. For Rome is an entire marketplace, where scarcely anything else is done than buying and selling. Hence they maintain that all the baptized are bound to obedience to the Pope and are subject to his judgments. The canon of the Council of Trent, Session VII, on Baptism, canon 8, sounds thus: If anyone shall say that the baptized are free from all the precepts of the holy Church (that is, the Papal Church, which boasts itself the teacher of the faith at Rome), whether written or handed down, so that they are not bound to observe them unless they have of their own will chosen to submit to them (words to be marked with an obelus, taken from the writings of Luther), let him be anathema. Indeed they press that characteristic right so far that they openly declare: An infant, while he is baptized by a Roman priest, is so bound to the Roman Pontiff that if he should afterwards fall away, it would be an action for perjury.

units.la: LXIX. Non ergo charactèri impressò, sed voluntati Dei Baptismi Unitas referenda accepta est; uti etiam Scotus & Gabriel Biel agnoscunt. Voluit enim Deus, ut legitimè non nisi semel baptizemur. Quæ ejus voluntas non uno indicio & argumento colligitur. Nec in loco proprio, in quo Baptismus instituitur, nec alibi uspiam Baptismum repetere jubemur; sicut Eucharistiam repetere non obscurè 1. Cor. XI. 25. jubemur. Et tot baptizatorum exempla in Scripturis cùm legamus, neminem tamen post Baptismum (Christi saltem) in gravissimum peccatum lapsum, tinctum denuo legimus. Quo argumento etiam Hieronymus adv. Lucif. pugnat. Tum nec circumcisio, cui Baptismus successit, iterari debuit, vel potuit. At nec fideles Christum, quem semel in Baptismo induerunt, exuunt iterum, sed semel in Christo nascuntur, seu renascuntur; neque nati, uti scite Augustinus Tract. 11. in Joh. loquitur, uterum repetunt. Nam Dei dona, vocatio imprimis, quæ per regenerationem, cujus Baptismus Sacramentum est, fit, ἀμεταμέλητα pœnitudinis expertia sunt, Rom. XI. 29. Præterea ea fœderis gratiæ, quod Baptismus, ceu sigillum ejusdem, obsignat, natura est, cùm æternum sit, per peccata hominis succedanea caducum non fiat, utpote quod peccatorum quotidianorum
units.tr: LXIX. Therefore the unity of Baptism is to be ascribed to the will of God, not to an impressed character, as Scotus and Gabriel Biel also acknowledge. For God willed that we should be baptized lawfully only once. This will of his is gathered from more than one indication and argument. Nowhere in the place where Baptism is instituted, nor anywhere else, are we commanded to repeat Baptism, as we are clearly commanded to repeat the Eucharist (1 Cor. 11:25). And although we read of so many baptized persons in the Scriptures, we nowhere read that anyone (at least of Christ's) who fell into grievous sin after Baptism was washed again. Jerome also argues against Lucifer with this argument. Moreover, circumcision, which Baptism succeeded, ought not and could not be repeated. Nor do believers strip off Christ, whom they have once put on in Baptism, and put him on again; rather they are born once in Christ, or reborn, and, as Augustine rightly says in Tractate 11 on John, those who have been born do not return to the womb. For God's gifts, above all the calling, which comes through regeneration, of which Baptism is the sacrament, are [ἀμεταμέλητα] free from repentance (Rom. 11:29). Furthermore, the covenant of grace, which Baptism seals as its sign, is by its nature eternal, and it does not become void through the substitute remedies for human sins, since it promises forgiveness of daily sins to believers and penitents, who return to the memory of the forgiveness of sins sealed in Baptism, and it does not promise this to those who are baptized again. Likewise a husband is reconciled to an adulterous wife not by joining her to himself in a new marriage but by calling her back to the former covenant. Add to this that the blood of Christ, whose…

units.la: remissionem credentibus & pœnitentibus, atque in Baptismi remissionem peccatorum obsignantis memoriam redeuntibus, non denuo baptizatis, promittit. Quomodo etiam maritus conjugi adulteræ reconciliatur, non novo matrimonio sibi eam copulans, sed ad prius fœdus eam revocans. Accedit, quòd & sanguis Christi, cujus baptismalis lympha symbolum est, ab omni peccato nos mundat, 1. Joh. I. 7. & Spiritus S. opus semel cœptum, regenerationis opus in iis, consummat, Phil. I. 6. & Baptismus gratiam regenerantem significat per modum mortis, qua peccato morimur, quæ cùm non non repetatur, nec signum ejus repeti convenit: & Baptismo iterato abnegaretur is, cui ut Domino, semel per Baptismum consecrati sumus, Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. Has similésque ob causas gravissimas Ecclesia Catholica Hemerobaptismum & Anabaptismum constanter rejicit.
units.tr: He promises forgiveness to believers and penitents, and to those who return to the memory of the forgiveness of sins sealed in baptism, and he promises that they need not be baptized again. So also a husband is reconciled to an adulterous wife, not by joining her to himself in a new marriage, but by calling her back to the former covenant. Moreover, the blood of Christ, of which the water of baptism is the symbol, cleanses us from every sin, 1 John 1:7; the Holy Spirit completes in such people the work of regeneration once begun, Phil. 1:6; and baptism signifies regenerating grace by way of the death by which we die to sin. Since that death is not repeated, its sign ought not to be repeated either. Moreover, by repeating baptism one would deny him to whom, as Lord, we were consecrated once through baptism: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. For these and similar very weighty reasons the Catholic Church constantly rejects Hemerobaptism and Anabaptism.

units.la: LXX. Baptismi à Christo instituti simplicitas paulatim ascititiis ceremoniis mutationem subiit. Sed sunt tamen ceremoniæ ascititiæ aliæ utiles, aliæ superstitiosæ. Utiles dico, quæ à natura Sacramenti pro statu Ecclesiæ introductæ sunt. Ubi tamen ex antiqua Ecclesia nullas ferè nisi in Baptismo adultorum usitatas habemus; quæ deinceps nimia negligentia in infantibus baptizandis retentæ sunt. Tales sunt Catechismus, Professio nominis, susceptores & scrutinium. Catechismus fuit institutio eorum, qui à gentilitate ad Ecclesiam accederent; Unde ipsis Catechumenis Græcè, Audientibus & Competentibus, quòd Baptismum postulârent, Latinè nomen fuit. Quanquam alii Catechumenos à Competentibus distinxerunt; illos appellantes, quandiu ad Baptismum non accederent; hos, qui exacta legitima institutione Baptismum tandem sibi repræsentari postularent. In competentium talium gradu erat Professio nominis. Nam Antistiti hoc significabatur, à quo ἐν δέλτοις ἀγίοις in pugillaribus sacris scribebatur. Unde postea in ipso baptizandi actu ἐνεκηρύξωσ inclamabantur. Quod tamen tum demum in usu fuisse videtur, cùm celebratio facta ordinaria est. Nam cùm extra ordinem multa millia simul accurrebant, vix illud observari potuit. Susceptores (ita Dionysius insignit) baptizando aderant, imò baptizandum ad Antistitem adducebant. Tertulliano de Bapt. c. 18. Sponsorum, Dionysio Areopagitæ de Eccles. Hierar. cap. 7. ἀναδέχων susceptorum, παιδαγωγῶν Pædagogorum καθηγεμόνων ducum & χειραγωγῶν manuductorum, Concilio Arelatensi IV. c. 19. Patrinorum & fidejussorum nomine veniunt. Quos idem Dionysius, quisquis ille est, & infantibus & adultis datos commendatósque testatur. Concilium illud Arelatense A. 813. sub Carolo M. celebratum l. cit. sic definit: ut parentes filios suos, & patrini eos, quos de fonte suscipiunt, erudire summopere studeant: illi, quia eos genuerunt, & eis à Domino dati sunt; isti, quia pro eis fidejussores exstiterunt. Denique Scrutinium recens est nomen, sed res ipsa vetus. Nam moris erat venientes ad Baptismum scrutari, an fidem radicitus corde defixissent, nec ne. Cujus ritus duæ partes erant, Renuntiatio seu ἀπόταξις, & Confessio fidei. In Renuntiatione competens profitebatur, se renuntiare Diabolo, pomppompæ ejus & operibus; Verba solennia erant: ἈΠΟΤΑΣΣΟΜΑΙ σοι, Σατανᾶ, καὶ πᾶσαι τῆς ἐργοις σου, καὶ πᾶσῃ τῇ πομπῇ σου Renuntio tibi, Sathana, & omnibus operibus tuis, & omni pompæ tuæ. Cui addita professio fidei, quæ, uti Augustinus Confess. lib. VIII. 2. loquitur, verbis certis conceptis retentisque memoriæ de loco eminentiore in conspectu populi fidelis Romæ reddi solet ab iis, qui ad gratiam accessuri sunt. Quod reddere symbolum appellabant. Quandoque perpetua oratione, frequentius per dialogismum & certos articulos id peragi suevit. Hos ritus omnes primitus in Baptismo adultorum usurpari moris erat: at Professionem fidei, & susceptorum ministerium etiam in Baptismo Infantum. Sed Catechismus quoque & scrutinium, scenica affectatione ad Baptismum infantum translatum etiam est. Et in Baptismo adultorum ritus illi omnes, in Baptismo vero infantum etiam impositio nominis & susceptorum ministerium, utiles erant, atque retineri etiam potuerunt, sed liberè, & procul superstitione. Nam & susceptorum ministerium, propter testimonium de baptizato, usum habere poterat. Quanquam illud grave est, quòd anxiæ de educando infante curæ præterea involvuntur & onerantur, quod officium Ecclesiæ promissum pauci obeunt, & nonnulli obire non possunt. Turpe verò illud est, quòd ubique fere officium illud argento redimitur, & susceptores potentes & divites quæruntur, qui id præstare valeant. Denique superstitioni illud deputandum, quòd Pontificii ex sponsione illa cognationem spiritualem, matrimonium impedientem, conflarunt. Neque enim arbitrio humano delecti compatres spirituales consanguinei fieri possunt: & spirituales consanguinei cùm simus omnes, unum Patrem in Cœlis, & unam matrem in terris habentes, verè spiritualis tamen cognatio illa matrimonium non impedit. Et quanto minùs fictitia illa impedire poterit? Unde figmentum illud cognationis spiritualis Episcopi nonnulli in Concilio Tridentino tolli expetierunt, sed surdis fabulam canentes.
units.tr: LXX. The simplicity of the baptism instituted by Christ gradually underwent change through added ceremonies. But some added ceremonies are useful and others superstitious. I call useful those that were introduced from the nature of the sacrament to suit the state of the Church. Yet from the ancient Church we have almost none that were in use except in the baptism of adults; these were afterwards retained through great carelessness in baptizing infants. Such are the catechism, the profession of name, the sponsors and the scrutiny. The catechism was the instruction of those who came to the Church from heathenism; hence the catechumens themselves were called in Greek Audientes and Competentes, and in Latin, from their asking for baptism, the name was Competentes. Although some distinguished catechumens from competents, calling the former those who had not yet come to baptism, and the latter those who, after the full and lawful instruction, asked that baptism be finally offered them. In the rank of such competents stood the profession of name. For this was signified to the bishop, in whose holy tablets [ἐν δέλτοις ἀγίοις] the name was written. Hence afterwards, in the very act of baptizing, they were called out [ἐνεκηρύξωσ]. This seems to have been in use only when the celebration had become ordinary; for when many thousands came together outside the ordinary order, this could hardly be observed. The sponsors (so Dionysius names them) were present at the baptism, and indeed brought the one to be baptized to the bishop. In Tertullian (On Baptism, ch. 18) they are called sponsores; in Dionysius the Areopagite (On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, ch. 7) receivers [ἀναδέχων], instructors [παιδαγωγῶν], guides [καθηγεμόνων] and leaders by the hand [χειραγωγῶν]; in the Council of Arles IV (ch. 19) they come under the name of godparents and sureties. The same Dionysius, whoever he was, testifies that they were given and commended both to infants and to adults. That Council of Arles, held in 813 under Charlemagne, defines in the place cited as follows: Let parents earnestly strive to instruct their sons, and godparents those whom they receive from the font: the former because they begot them and were given them by the Lord; the latter because they became sureties for them. Finally, scrutiny is a recent name, but the thing itself is ancient. For it was the custom to examine those coming to baptism, whether they had fixed the faith firmly in their heart or not. This rite had two parts: the renunciation, or apotaxis, and the confession of faith. In the renunciation the competent declared that he renounced the Devil, his pomp and his works. The solemn words were: I renounce you, Satan, and all your works, and all your pomp [ΑΠΟΤΑΣΣΟΜΑΙ σοι, Σατανᾶ, καὶ πᾶσαι τῆς ἐργοις σου, καὶ πᾶσῃ τῇ πομπῇ σου]. To this was added the profession of faith, which, as Augustine says (Confessions, Book VIII, ch. 2), was usually given back, in fixed words conceived and held in memory, from a more elevated place in view of the faithful people at Rome, by those who were about to come to grace. They called this giving back the creed. Sometimes it was done by a continuous speech, more often by question and answer on certain articles. All these rites were at first customary in the baptism of adults; but the profession of faith and the ministry of sponsors were also used in the baptism of infants. Yet the catechism too and the scrutiny were carried over to the baptism of infants, with theatrical affectation. And in the baptism of adults all those rites, and in the baptism of infants also the giving of a name and the ministry of sponsors, were useful and could also have been retained, but freely and far from superstition. For the ministry of sponsors could be of use as testimony concerning the one baptized. Yet this is burdensome, because anxious cares about bringing up the infant are further involved and laid on them, a duty which few undertake as promised to the Church and some cannot undertake at all. It is truly shameful that almost everywhere this office is bought with money, and powerful and rich sponsors are sought who are able to provide it. Finally, the following must be counted as superstition: the Papists from that sponsorship have forged a spiritual kinship which impedes marriage. For chosen co-parents cannot become spiritual relatives by human choice; and since we are all spiritual kin, having one Father in heaven and one mother on earth, that spiritual kinship truly does not impede marriage. And how much less could that fictitious kinship impede it? Hence some bishops at the Council of Trent sought that this fiction of spiritual kinship be abolished, but they were singing a tale to deaf ears.

units.la: LXXI. Ceremoniæ superstitiosæ, Baptismi ludibria & ... non pauca eundem procedente tempore fœdarunt.
units.tr: LXXI. Superstitious ceremonies, the mockeries of Baptism, and ... which in the course of time defiled it in no small measure.

units.la: LXXI. Ceremoniæ superstitiosæ, Baptismi ludibria & non pauca eundem procedente tempore fœdarunt. Velut signum crucis in fronte & pectore: Exorcismus: Exsufflatio: Narium & aurium ex saliva contactus, cum Ephata: salis gustatio: Unctio ex oleo in pectore & scapulis: Consecratio aquæ baptismalis: Unctio chrismatis in fronte: Cereus accensus à neophytis gestandus: Vestis candidæ indumentum. Quas ceremonias nequicquam ab Apostolica traditione Pontificii derivant. Nam & cum Christianismi simplicitate, Mosaicorum rituum multiplicitati opposita pugnant, & vel ob materiæ raritatem atque pretium, vel ob indecorum à Christianismi genio abludunt: & frustra Divinæ atque absolutissimæ institutioni adjectæ sunt: & rituum eorum in actibus Apostolicis atque historia veteris Ecclesiæ nulla uspiam mentio extat: & multitudine nimia essentialem Baptismi ritum obscurant: & mysterio quodam imprægnati, & in partem cultus conversi vero pietatis mysterio obsunt: & nonnulli denique ex iis inimici, sordidi & profani sunt, velut cùm ad pellendum dæmonium Sacerdos ter in faciem baptizandi exsufflat, & accipiens de saliva oris sui tangit ejus nares & aures, quam ceremoniam à Messalianis seu Euchetis mutuati sunt, perinde ac si Diaboli scorpiones, saliva extinguendi essent. Signi quidem crucis plurima apud veteres mentio est. Sed oleo vel chrismate illud pictum antiquitus esse, nemo veterum testis est: & signo crucis idem, non ut operativa ex opere operato, uti Bellarminus appellat, sed ut externa professionis tessera, ceu cum infidelibus commixti, usi sunt. Taceo, quòd Baptismi aquam incantamento quodam lustrant: & non sine populi Christiani contumelia, quasi fidelium infantes Diaboli mancipia essent, Exorcismo defunguntur, quod Lutheri affectæ nonnulli de Romanæ Ecclesiæ pompa in Baptismo suo cacozelia quadam retinuerunt. Neque enim vel sacrificuli donum exorcizandi habent: vel exorcismus verus est, Sathanam ex animabus pellere: vel infantes fidelium baptizandi promiscuè sub Diaboli imperio agitant. Sed cessante in Ecclesia gratia extraordinaria, Exorcistarum nomen retinere, & catechesin eo significare veteribus placuit, uti pluribus Justellus Not. ad Can. Eccl. Univ. p. 168. comprobavit; donec adjurationibus additis in magicum ritum sequiore ætate actio illa degeneravit. Neque quæsitarum significationum, vel mysterii alicujus color sufficit. Nam & plus quàm simplicem rerum spiritualium picturam Pontificii in iis collocant; & prætextu illo superstitiosos cultus introducunt, & Ecclesiam gravi jugo onerant: & Scripturæ testimonia non pauca ad ritus illos, velut necessarios, detorquent, cùm non ritus illi in testimoniis illis extent, sed eorum occasione illi olim efficti, & obtorto collo in Ecclesiam introducti sunt. Etiam adversarii eos oderunt, qui Baptismo ignem addunt; licèt Christus Spiritu & igne baptizaturus Matth. III. 11. dicatur. Quanto minùs tolerandi ii sunt, qui longè leviori prætextu ex Scripturis quidvis corradunt? Neque proin insipienter Catharina Medicæa, Franciæ Regina, Regni pro filio Carolo IX. rectrix, literis A. MDLXI. ad Pium IV. exaratis, ex Johannis Monlucii Valentini Episcopi, uti creditur, consilio, inter alia Reformationis capita petiit, ut in Baptismo exorcismi, & certæ precum formulæ, quæ extra ejus institutionem sunt, omittantur, ac sufficiat, ut aquæ & verbum duntaxat, juxta Dei præscriptum adhibeantur, addens: Sputi in os injectionem non solum non necessariam videri, sed etiam periculo non carere. Quam Catharinæ epistolam ex Thuano Hispani Bibliomastiges deleri, jusserunt.
units.tr: LXXI. Superstitious ceremonies, the mockeries of Baptism, which in the course of time defiled it in no small measure. Such as the sign of the cross on the forehead and breast; exorcism; breathing upon the candidate; touching the nostrils and ears with saliva, with the word Ephphatha; tasting salt; anointing with oil on the breast and shoulders; consecrating the water of baptism; anointing with chrism on the forehead; the lighted candle carried by the neophytes; and the clothing in a white garment. The Papists derive these ceremonies in vain from apostolic tradition. For they fight against the simplicity of Christianity, setting themselves against the multiplicity of Mosaic rites; they are either rare and costly in their material, or out of keeping with the spirit of Christianity as unbecoming; they are added in vain to a divine and most complete institution; no mention of these rites is found anywhere in the Acts of the Apostles or in the history of the ancient Church; by their excessive number they obscure the essential rite of Baptism; and, steeped in a certain mystery and turned into a part of worship, they harm the true mystery of piety. Finally, some of them are offensive, filthy and profane. For example, when the priest, to drive out the demon, breathes three times in the face of the one to be baptized, and, taking saliva from his own mouth, touches his nostrils and ears. They borrowed this ceremony from the Messalians or Euchites, as if the scorpions of the devil were to be extinguished with saliva. Indeed, there is much mention of the sign of the cross among the ancients. But that it was painted on with oil or chrism in antiquity, no ancient witness attests; and the same sign of the cross they used, not as operative from the work worked (operativa ex opere operato), as Bellarmine calls it, but as an external token of profession, as those who were mixed with unbelievers used it. I say nothing of the fact that they purify the water of baptism with a certain incantation, and that, to the disgrace of the Christian people, as if the infants of the faithful were slaves of the devil, they are made to undergo exorcism. Some of Luther's admirers, out of a certain misguided zeal, retained this pomp of the Roman Church in their own Baptism. For neither does a mere priest have the gift of exorcising, nor is exorcism a true expelling of Satan from souls, nor do they indiscriminately drive the infants of the faithful, when baptized, under the rule of the devil. But when the extraordinary grace in the Church had ceased, it pleased the ancients to retain the name of exorcists and to signify by it catechesis, as Justellus has shown at length in his Notes on the Canons of the Universal Church, p. 168; until, with the addition of adjurations, that action degenerated into a magical rite in a later age. Nor is a colour of some sought-after meaning or mystery enough. For the Papists place in these rites more than a simple picture of spiritual things; under that pretext they introduce superstitious worship and burden the Church with a heavy yoke; and they twist not a few testimonies of Scripture to those rites as if they were necessary, when those rites do not appear in those testimonies, but were devised in later times on the occasion of them and were forced into the Church against the grain. Even opponents hate those who add fire to Baptism, although Christ is said to be going to baptize with the Spirit and fire (Matth. 3.11). How much less tolerable are those who scrape together anything whatever from Scripture on a much lighter pretext? Not unwisely, therefore, Catherine de' Medici, Queen of France, ruling the kingdom for her son Charles IX, in a letter written in the year 1561 to Pius IV, presumably at the advice of John of Monluc, Bishop of Valence, asked among other heads of reformation that in Baptism exorcisms and certain formulas of prayer, which are outside its institution, be omitted, and that it suffice that only water and the word be used according to God's prescription, adding: the injection of spittle into the mouth seems not only unnecessary but also not free from danger. The Spanish Bibliomastiges, as Thuanus relates, ordered this letter of Catherine to be erased.

units.la: LXXII. Coena Domini est alterum N. T. Sacramentum, quo per panis fracti, & vini effusi distributionem & perceptionem fidelibus communio corporis Christi pro iis in cruce fracti, & sanguinis pro ipsis effusi ad remissionem peccatorum & salutem æternam declaratur & obsignatur.
units.tr: LXXII. The Lord's Supper is the second sacrament of the New Testament, by which, through the distribution and reception of broken bread and poured-out wine, the communion of the body of Christ, broken for us on the cross, and of his blood, poured out for us, is declared and sealed to the faithful, for the forgiveness of sins and eternal salvation.

units.la: Sacramentum hoc aliis atque aliis nominibus à Christo, Apostolis & Patribus notatur. Christus enim Corpus & Sanguinem suum propter communionem utriusque externis symbolis distincte obsignatum, Matth. XXVI. 26. 28. & alibi; nec non Novum Testamentum in suo sanguine, Luc. XXII. 20. quia Sacramentum est sanguinis Christi, quo Novum TestaTestamentum dedicari & consecrari debuit, appellavit. Apostoli Δεῖπνον Κυριακὸν Cœnam Dominicam, 1. Cor. XI. 20. quia & vesperi pro more Cœnæ, celebrata erat, & instituente Domino, quo authore, fine & scopo nititur, cùm morti ejus perpetim celebrandæ inserviat: Frustra nomen illud Pontificiis nonnullis ad agapas detorquentibus, quia ibidem Apostolus jubet insisti institutioni Domini, cùm agapæ à Christo institutæ non fuerint: κλάσιν ἄρτου fractionem panis, Actor. II. 42. XX. 7. à symbolo altero cœnæ, per synecdochen usitatam cœnam totam significante: Κοινωνία Communionem corporis & sanguinis Christi, 1. Cor. X. 16. quia communionis illius sacramentum & pignus est: Τραπέζα Κυρίου mensam Domini, ibid. v. 21. quia Dominus instituens Sacramentum hoc cum discipulis suis eadem in mensa accubuit: Ἄρτον καὶ ποτήριον Κυρίου Panem & poculum Domini, ibid. XI. 27. quia symbola & dapes externæ panis & poculum sunt; insigniverunt. Patres denique Græci & Latini in nominibus, quibus mysterium hoc appellavere, tantum non luxuriarunt. Singula apponere nihil attinet. Potiora sunt Σύναξις Congregatio & Συνέλευσις Conventus, præeunte Scriptura, Actor. XX. 7. 1. Cor. XI. 20. 26. 27. 33. Εὐχαριστία Gratiarum actio, quia Christus Cœnam instituens etiam εὐχαριστήσας gratias egisse Matth. XXVI. 27. & benedixisse v. 26. & Marc. XIV. 22. dicitur: à cujus etiam εὐχαριστίας solenni formula semper apud Christianos veteres Sacramenti hujus formula inchoata est, uti ex veteribus Liturgiis colligere est; nempe cùm gratias agerent Deo fideles pro omnibus ab eo in humanum genus collatis beneficiis, repetito initio à creatione, aut deducto per omnes historiæ Ecclesiasticæ partes, donec ad redemptionis ipsius œconomiam in Jesu Christo, à quo Sacramentum hoc peculiariter institutum fuit. Λειτουργία Cultus, voce totius cultus pro parte ejus accepta: Προσφορὰ Oblatio, & Θυσία Victima, propter ejus in Sacramento hoc institutam ἀνάμνησιν recordationem, nec non laudum & gratiarum actionem pro perecta salute oblationem: Sacramentum corporis & sanguinis Domini: inprimis Missa, non à הנה, quæ vox Deut. XVI. 10. juxta quosdam oblationem, juxta alios indictionem significat, uti plerique Pontificii nugantur, sed à Catechumenorum & fidelium communicantium dimissione. Nam & initio catechumenos, & in fide communicantes voce ἄφεσις dimissio, Missa, (uti collecta pro collectione, & remissa pro remissione dici suevit) &: ite, missa est, proclamata, dimittere moris erat. Nullum tamen nomen tanto mysterio magis ineptum excogitari potuit, quod tantum abest, ut Cœnæ essentiam exprimat, ut ne ullam quidem partem actionis saltem externæ, exprimat. Nam profectò finis actionis nulla pars actionis est. Neque inter Ethnicos olim pars ulla sacrificii illud Ilicet fuit. Sed placuit inane nomen retinere iis, qui rem ipsam pridem sustulerunt.
units.tr: This sacrament is named by Christ, the Apostles and the Fathers by various names. For Christ called his body and blood, distinctly sealed by external symbols for the sake of the communion of both, (Matth. 26.26, 28, and elsewhere), and the New Testament in his blood (Luke 22.20), because it is the sacrament of Christ's blood by which the New Testament was to be dedicated and consecrated. The Apostles called it the Lord's Supper [Δεῖπνον Κυριακὸν] (1 Cor. 11.20), because it was celebrated in the evening in the manner of a supper, and because, by the Lord's institution, it rests on him as its author, its end and its aim, since it serves to be celebrated continually in remembrance of his death. That name is vainly twisted by some Papists to refer to the agapae, since the Apostle there bids them to adhere to the institution of the Lord, whereas the agapae were not instituted by Christ. The breaking of bread [κλάσιν ἄρτου] (Acts 2.42; 20.7), from the other symbol of the supper, by the usual figure of synecdoche signifying the whole supper. The communion [Κοινωνία] of the body and blood of Christ (1 Cor. 10.16), because it is the sacrament and pledge of that communion. The table of the Lord [Τραπέζα Κυρίου] (ibid. v. 21), because the Lord, instituting this sacrament, reclined at the same table with his disciples. The bread and cup of the Lord [Ἄρτον καὶ ποτήριον Κυρίου] (ibid. 11.27), because the external symbols and the feast are bread and cup. Finally, the Greek and Latin Fathers, in the names by which they called this mystery, were almost extravagant. It is pointless to list each one. The more important are Synaxis [Σύναξις], Congregation, and Synelusis [Συνέλευσις], Assembly, following Scripture (Acts 20.7; 1 Cor. 11.20, 26, 27, 33). Eucharist [Εὐχαριστία], Thanksgiving, because Christ, instituting the Supper, is said to have given thanks [εὐχαριστήσας] (Matth. 26.27), and to have blessed (v. 26; Mark 14.22). From this word eucharistia the solemn formula of this sacrament was always begun among the ancient Christians, as can be gathered from the ancient liturgies: namely, when the faithful gave thanks to God for all the benefits conferred by him on the human race, beginning again from the creation, or leading through all parts of ecclesiastical history, until they came to the economy of redemption itself in Jesus Christ, by whom this sacrament was specially instituted. Liturgy [Λειτουργία], worship, the word for the whole worship taken for a part of it. Oblation [Προσφορὰ] and Sacrifice [Θυσία], victim, on account of its remembrance [ἀνάμνησιν], that is recollection, instituted in this sacrament, as also the offering of praise and thanksgiving for a perfected salvation. The sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord. Above all Mass (Missa), which does not come from the Hebrew word that in Deut. 16.10 signifies, according to some, an offering, according to others a festal assembly, as most Papists trifle, but from the dismissal of the catechumens and of the communicants of the faith. For at first it was customary to dismiss the catechumens and the communicants of the faith with the word apheses [ἄφεσις], dismissal, Mass (just as collecta was used for collection and remissa for remission), and the proclamation ite, missa est was the custom for dismissing. Yet no name could have been devised more unfitting for so great a mystery, which is so far from expressing the essence of the Supper that it does not even express any part of the action, at least the external action. For surely the end of an action is no part of the action. Nor among the Gentiles was that Ilicet formerly any part of the sacrifice. But they have chosen to retain the empty name, though they had long since abolished the thing itself.

units.la: LXXIII. Cœna hæc Domini duabus partibus, externo ministerio, cunctisque ejus partibus & circumstantiis; & mysterio absolvitur. In externo ministerio personæ, signa exter-
units.tr: LXXIII. This Supper of the Lord consists of two parts: the external ministry, with all its parts and circumstances, and the mystery.

units.la: na, & circa eadem ritus atque actiones considerandæ sunt. Personæ vel administrantes, vel communicantes sunt. Primus eam administrat idem, qui eam instituit, Christus. Dominus Jesus ea nocte, qua proditus est, panem accepit & gratias agens fregit, &c. 1. Cor. XI. 23. 24. Unde Dominicæ Cœnæ nomen ibid. &c. obtinuit. Instituit autem & administravit Christus Cœnam non in altera Cœna Azymorum à Cœna Paschali seu agni distincta, seu in mensis secundis & ספרא Cœna Σοταλική, uti Scaligero visum; quia Cœnarum illa differentia non obtinuit, & post Cœnam Agni addito solo poculo, gratiarum actionis, convivium finiri suevit; sed immediatè post Cœnam Paschalem; sic tamen, ut ei continuò non sublatis mensis, subjuncta fuerit, quod pluribus argumentis Cel. Buxtorfius convicit. Christi authoritate & jussu eandem deinceps Apostoli, & qui illos secuti sunt, Ecclesiæ Pastores & rectores administrarunt atque administrant. Non enim à privatis etiam & quovis privato in epulo, administrari magis quàm Baptismus, & verbi Dei præconium potest, quæ Socinianorum & Episcopii, Cœnam æquè atque Baptismum; & utriusque mysterium flocci facientium, & in nuda signa quædam, à quovis Christiano tractabilia convertentium, sententia est. Nam nec omnes οἰκονόμοι τῶν μυστηρίων dispensatores mysteriorum sunt, sed pauci & iidem, qui ὑπηρέται Χριστοῦ ministri Christi sunt, 1. Cor. IV. 1. Non alii quàm Apostoli panem sacrum fregisse & distribuisse in eorundem actibus legunntur. Nam quòd fideles promiscuè dicuntur persevèrasse in fractione panis, Act. II. 42. non alium sensum habet, quàm quòd Cœnam Domini frequenter celebraverint, sed eo ordine, qui à Christo institutus est. Cùmque amoris Dei certissima symbola & pignora in convivio eò dispensentur, nonnisi à Christi ministris, & publica ejus authoritate dispensari possunt, ne promiscuo usu contaminentur, & inter tractantium quorumvis manus vilescant. Ideo etiam in veteri Ecclesia S. Cœnam Episcopi & Presbyteri dederunt; quanquam ministerio Diaconorum auxiliante. Neque promiscuam hanc administrationem fecit Apostolus dicens: Panis, quem frangimus: Poculum, cui benedicimus, &c. 1. Cor. X. 16. sed universa Ecclesia facere censetur; quod ejus nomine cœtus minister atque præses facit; & universi partes suas in sacro illo actu habent, esitantes de pane, & hymnis laudibusque sacris actionem hanc prosequentes.
units.tr: In the external ministry we must consider the persons, the external signs, and the rites and actions connected with them. The persons are either administrators or communicants. The first to administer it was the one who instituted it, Christ: "The Lord Jesus, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread, and when he had given thanks, broke it," etc., 1 Cor. 11.23, 24. Hence the name "Supper of the Lord" in the same passage, etc. Christ instituted and administered the Supper not in a separate Supper of Unleavened Bread distinct from the Paschal or Lamb Supper, nor in the second courses and the ספרא [Sifra], the "Sotalic Supper" [Σοταλική], as Scaliger thought. That distinction of suppers did not hold, and after the Lamb Supper, with only the cup of thanksgiving added, the feast was customarily brought to an end. Rather, Christ instituted it immediately after the Paschal Supper, yet in such a way that the tables were not at once removed and it was added to that meal, as the learned Buxtorf has proved by many arguments. By the authority and command of Christ, the Apostles and those who followed them, the ministers and rulers of the Church, administered it then and still administer it now. For it cannot be administered by private persons, or by any private individual at a banquet, any more than Baptism and the proclamation of God's Word can be. That is the view of the Socinians and Episcopius, who make the Supper as worthless as Baptism, who regard both mysteries as nothing, and who turn them into bare signs that any Christian may handle. For not all are "stewards of the mysteries" [οἰκονόμοι τῶν μυστηρίων], but only a few, and these are the same who are "ministers of Christ" [ὑπηρέται Χριστοῦ], 1 Cor. 4.1. Only the Apostles are read as having broken and distributed the sacred bread in their own acts. For the statement that the faithful indiscriminately "persevered in the breaking of bread," Acts 2.42, has no other sense than that they frequently celebrated the Lord's Supper, but in the order instituted by Christ. Since the most certain symbols and pledges of God's love are dispensed in this banquet, they can be dispensed only by Christ's ministers and by his public authority, lest they be contaminated by promiscuous use and cheapened in the hands of anyone whatever. For this reason, in the ancient Church too, the Bishops and Presbyters gave the Holy Supper, though with the assistance of the Deacons' ministry. Nor did the Apostle make this administration promiscuous when he said: "The bread which we break, the cup which we bless," etc., 1 Cor. 10.16. Rather, the whole Church is considered to do it, because the minister and president of the assembly does it in its name, and all have their parts in that sacred action, eating of the bread and accompanying the act with hymns and sacred praises.

units.la: LXXIV. Personæ communicantes in prima Cœna fuerunt Christus & Apostoli. Nam & Christum familiæ Apostolicæ parentem, ut convivatorem cum convivis Cœnam sacram percepisse, satis illud arguit, quòd post poculum inter discipulos distributum dixerit: Amen dico vobis, non bibam amplius ex fructu vitis; usque ad diem illum, cùm bibam novum in Regno Dei, Marc. XIV. 25. Et tam Cœna sacra in Postcœnio Paschali, quàm ipsa Paschali Cœna haud dubiè Christus usus est. Sicut enim circumcisus est, & Pascha comedit, ut promissiones pluribus factas confirmaret: ita baptizatus & Cœna usus est; ut Evangelium, acceptis sigillis justitiæ suæ, quæ ex fide nostra esset, obsignarEt. Partes ejus sunt ministerium externum & mysterium. signaret. Ac ne Judas quidem proditor ab ea exclusus videtur. Nam Christus Coena à se jam instituta & celebrata dixit: Ecce manus prodentis me mecum est in mensa, Luc. XXII. 21. Quod igitur Joh. XIII. 30. dicitur, Judam accepto ψωμίῳ seu buccella ὑιῆως mox exivisse, ita accipiendum est, ut vel ψωμίον notet buccellam panis Eucharistici, qualem Hebraei מרוסה particulam divisam appellant, vel ὑιῆως illud cum ἀλλάτῃ latitudine quadam intelligatur, & sensus sit, quod mox post offam acceptam, & introitum in eum Sathanae, sed nonnisi finito convivio, quando iter ad montem oliveti Christus cum discipulis suscepit, discesserit. Sic enim Evangelistarum narratio constabit. Neq; tamen ille accepit corpus Domini, sed jussus accipere panem ut corpus Domini, non accepit illud nisi ut panem. Non enim verba Christi, quibus ille panem loco corporis substituebat, fide miscuit. Ideo Christus Judam è numero comedentium panem ut corpus Domini, & bibentium ex poculo ceu sanguinis pro ipsis effusi Sacramento, diserte excipit, dicens: ἀλλ᾽ ἰδοὺ, veruntamen ecce, manus prodentis me, Luc. XXII.21. Cyprianus de Coena Dom. Sceleratum, inquit, os panis sanctificatus intrat. Et de illo pane & Judam accepisse, Augustinus tract. 50. in Joh. dixit. Neque enim jam tum Christus judicem egerat. Et aliud est in Ecclesia tempus tolerandi indignos monitos, ne indigne comedant: aliud tempus judicandi & vitandi τὸ ζυνεδιεν.
units.tr: LXXIV. The communicants at the first Supper were Christ and the Apostles. That Christ, the parent of the Apostolic family, received the sacred Supper as host among his guests is sufficiently shown by his saying, after the cup was distributed among the disciples: "Verily I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the Kingdom of God," Mark 14.25. Christ undoubtedly used the sacred Supper both in the after-meal of the Passover and in the Paschal Supper itself. For just as he was circumcised and ate the Passover to confirm the promises made in many ways, so he was baptized and used the Supper, so that the Gospel, having received the seals of his righteousness, which is by our faith, might seal it. Its parts are the external ministry and the mystery. Nor does Judas the betrayer seem to have been excluded from it. For Christ, speaking of the Supper now instituted and celebrated by himself, said: "Behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table," Luke 22.21. What is said at John 13.30, that Judas, having received the morsel [ψωμίον] or piece of bread, went out immediately [εὐθέως], must therefore be understood in this way: either the morsel denotes a piece of the Eucharistic bread, such as the Hebrews call a divided portion [מרוסה], or the word "immediately" is taken with some latitude, and the sense is that he departed soon after receiving the morsel and Satan's entry into him, but only when the supper was finished, when Christ set out with the disciples on the way to the Mount of Olives. For that is how the account of the Evangelists will stand. Yet Judas did not receive the body of the Lord. Bidden to take the bread as the body of the Lord, he took it only as bread, for he did not mix the words of Christ, by which Christ substituted bread for his body, with faith. So Christ expressly excludes Judas from the number of those who eat the bread as the body of the Lord and drink from the cup as the sacrament of the blood poured out for them, saying: "But behold, nevertheless, the hand of him who betrays me," Luke 22.21. Cyprian, On the Lord's Supper: "The wicked mouth," he says, "enters the sanctified bread." And Augustine, in Tractate 50 on John, said that Judas received of that bread. For Christ had not yet acted as judge then. There is one time in the Church for tolerating the unworthy after admonition, lest they eat unworthily, and another time for judging and avoiding those who would eat together [συνεσθίειν].

units.la: LXXV. Post primam Coenam in numerum Communicantium veniunt omnes fideles & veri Christiani, qui rite se explorarunt, & mysteria illa didicerunt, atque vita puros integrosque se praestant. Exploret quisque seipsum, & ita de pane illo edat, & de poculo illo bibat, 1. Cor. XI. 28. Quorum in numero non sunt infantes, quibus diu vetus Ecclesia περιεχομένοις verborum Christi, Joh. VI. 53. cum verbis ejusdem Christi, ibid. III. 5. collatorum inducta, sacra Coenae symbola impertita est. Non enim illi seipsos explorare possunt. Ita carnem victimarum soli adulti Israelitae, sacrificiorum usum intelligentes manducarunt; nec Patres familias liberis offerebant portionem Agni comedendam prius, quam liberationem ex Aegypto cognoscerent. Neque obstat, quod sacra unda abluantur, quia hoc ritu à parentibus, vel parentum vicariis servitio Dei consecrantur, quod à prima aetate fieri debet. Sed epuli sacri usu testificamur, nos credere, Jesum Christum pro remissione peccatorum nostrorum in crucem actum esse, quale testimonium infantes nec intelligunt, nec perhibere possunt. Ac licet illi etiam lacte & nutrimento vitae in Deo indigeant; tamen illud iis non sacra Coena, sed summa religionis Christianae est, qua crescentibus annis imbuendi sedulo sunt, donec mysteriorum salutarium periti sacro huic epulo idonei evadant. Ab eodem convivio arcendi sunt tum furiosi, quandiu tales sunt: tum aperte facinorosi & ἀμεταγνώστοι; quibus cum peccata non remitti possint, sed retineri debeant, remissionis pignora offerri nec fas, nec prium est: tum Catechumeni, qui mysteriorum rudes nondum fidem profiteri idonea ratione possunt. De surdis & amentibus ex emicantibus
units.tr: LXXV. After the first Supper, all the faithful and true Christians come into the number of communicants: those who have duly examined themselves, learned those mysteries, and show themselves pure and blameless in life. "Let each man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup," 1 Cor. 11.28. Among those are not infants, to whom the ancient Church for a long time gave the sacred symbols of the Supper, bringing together the words of Christ at John 6.53 with the same Christ's words at John 3.5. For infants cannot examine themselves. So only grown Israelites, understanding the use of the sacrifices, ate the flesh of the victims. Nor did heads of families offer their children a portion of the Lamb to eat before the children knew of the deliverance from Egypt. Nor does it stand in the way that infants are washed with sacred water, for by this rite they are consecrated to the service of God by their parents or by those who act in their parents' place, which ought to be done from the earliest age. But by the use of the sacred feast we testify that we believe Jesus Christ was nailed to the cross for the remission of our sins, a testimony that infants neither understand nor can give. And although they too need milk and the nourishment of life in God, that is for them not the Sacred Supper but the highest part of the Christian religion, in which they must be diligently instructed as they grow, until, skilled in the saving mysteries, they become fit for this sacred feast. The insane must be kept from the same banquet as long as they are such. Also kept away are those who are openly wicked and unrepentant [ἀμεταγνώστοι]: since their sins cannot be remitted but must be retained, it is neither lawful nor proper to offer them pledges of remission. Catechumens, who are still ignorant of the mysteries and cannot yet profess faith in a sound manner, must be kept away as well.

units.la: fidei indiciis, & intervallis melioribus, ex charitatis regula, judicandum est, nec omnino favores contrahendi, sed ampliandi etiam sunt. Abstemiis quoque vel potus consuetus, si ita mos ferat, concedi, vel fides signorum expers sufficere potest, quia propter paucos regula infringi, & communis mos temere mutari non debet. Sicubi vero symbolum, velut vini, uti apud Americanos, copia plane deest, usitato potionis genere uti, quam prorsus Sacramentum omittere cum Calvino & Melanchthone tutius, & consilio atque sensui Christi convenientius arbitramur. Etiam moribundis Synodus Nicena Can. 13. Carthaginensis IV. can. 76. & Agathensis cap. 11. hoc velut ἐφόδιον viaticum praeberi jussit. Sed libertate heic sua Ecclesia gaudet, ut periculo erroris & superstitionis signorum atque operis operati, aliisque incommodis, quae in populosis & dissipatis coetibus, quibus unus pastor praeest, emergere possunt; praevertendis, moribundis fidem solam puramque, nec non spiritualem, qua se oblectant, communionem, & toties peractae externae communionis fidelem recordationem commendare possit.
units.tr: Concerning the deaf and the mentally impaired, judgment must be made from the clear signs of faith that shine forth and from their better intervals, by the rule of charity. They must not be wholly excluded but rather admitted more widely. For teetotallers, a customary drink may be granted if custom allows, or faith free of signs may suffice, since the rule should not be broken for the sake of a few, and common custom should not be rashly changed. Where indeed the symbol of wine is wholly lacking, as among the Americans, we judge it safer, and more in keeping with the counsel and mind of Christ, to use the usual kind of drink, rather than to omit the Sacrament altogether as Calvin and Melanchthon did. The Council of Nicaea, canon 13, the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 76, and the Council of Agde, chapter 11, also ordered that this be given to the dying as a provision for the journey [ἐφόδιον], the viaticum. But here the Church enjoys its freedom, so that it may commend to the dying faith alone and pure, together with the spiritual communion in which they delight, and the faithful remembrance of the external communion so often celebrated. In this way it guards against the danger of error and of superstition about signs and about the work done, and against other inconveniences that can arise in crowded and scattered assemblies over which a single minister presides.

units.la: LXXVI. Symbolum sacri hujus convivii geminum est, Panis & Vinum. Utrumque enim convivii, quod instituere Christus paraverat, ratio, & spiritualis alimoniae mysterium requirebat. Neque parum sapientiam institutionis coelestium horum pignorum commendat, quod ejusmodi illa instituit, quae ad Sacramentum universale Ecclesiae, & ad finem usque seculi duraturum, ubique fere, & exiguo sumptu parabilia & obvia sunt: quodque non illustriora illa, qualia olim Israelitis in deserto exhibuit, praescribere visum est; quia non parum externus ille splendor spiritualium fidelium visui offecisset, qui non tam externo signo, quam re significata jam pasci & satiari, atque Servatorem suum quotidiana in imagine adspicere potius & amplecti, quam in illustri aliquo signo stupere, atque isto velut idolo se oblectare debuerunt. Accedebat periculum superstitionis, quod in simplicioribus & humilioribus illis signis evitari cum non potuerit, gravius longe immiscuisset. At nec mysterio carent, quod non animalium carnes & cruentas atque sanguine manantes dapes, uti in V.T. factum, ad sacrum hoc convivium instituit, sed pane & vino solo mensam hanc oneravit. Nam post sanguinem Christi effusum nulli amplius sanguini in sacris locus esse potest. Adeo quidem, ut cum olim sanguis altari ad expiationem faciendam servatus sine piaculo attrectari & comedi non potuerit, in N.T. ubi expiatione consummata nihil amplius expiare potest, promiscuus ille omniumque usibus expositus sit. Nihil ergo efficacius ad significandum tum consummatum sacrificium per effusum sanguinem Christi, tum spiritualem nutritionem instituisse potuit. Nam vinum laetificat cor hominis, & faciem nitere facit pre oleo: & panis cor hominis fulcit, Psal. CIV. 15.
units.tr: LXXVI. The sign of this sacred feast is twofold: bread and wine. The nature of the meal Christ had prepared to institute, and the mystery of spiritual nourishment, both required this. The institution also commends no little wisdom in that he appointed such things as are almost everywhere available and easily obtained at small cost, and which will last for the universal sacrament of the Church until the end of the age. He thought it fitting not to prescribe more splendid things, such as he once gave the Israelites in the desert. That outward splendour would have been no small hindrance to the sight of the spiritual faithful, who ought to be fed and satisfied not so much by the outward sign as by the thing signified, and who should look upon and embrace their Saviour in the daily image rather than gape at some striking sign and delight in it as in an idol. There was also the danger of superstition. Since this could not be avoided even with those simpler and humbler signs, it would have crept in far more seriously with more splendid ones. Nor is there lack of mystery in the fact that he did not load this sacred feast with the flesh of animals and dishes dripping with blood, as was done in the Old Testament, but furnished this table with bread and wine alone. For after the blood of Christ was shed, no further place for blood can be in the sacred rites. So much so that whereas once the blood kept for the altar to make atonement could not be touched or eaten without sacrilege, in the New Testament, where the atonement is complete and can atone no further, that blood has become common and open to all uses. Therefore he could have instituted nothing more effective for signifying both the sacrifice accomplished through the shed blood of Christ and the spiritual nourishment. For "wine gladdens the heart of man, and makes the face shine with oil, and bread strengthens the heart of man," Ps. 104.15.

units.la: LXXVII. Panis à Christo adhibitus fuit talis, qualis in communi usu eo tempore, quo Coenam instituit, extitit. Azymus autem ille ex lege illa, qua fermentum omne Paschatis tempore expurgandum fuit, adhibitus est. De quo Graeci quo frustra Græci litem movent, pertendentes, Christum Pascha Judaicum anticipasse, atque ita fermentato pane usum esse. Sed pane fermentato sine transgressione legis uti non poterat.
