Licet igitur Pascha Judaicum, celebratum non νομίμως juxta legem, sed ἀνομίως, juxta consuetudinem & traditionem sive canonis Badu, vetantis die sexto hebdomadis Pascha celebrare, ne populus biduum ab opere cessare cogeretur: sive edicti, quo non tam ζνοδον quàm φάσιν luminarium in Paschate indicendo sequi jubebantur; omnino anticiparunt; tamen & die XIV. Nisam, ἡ εἰς quo oportuit, Luc. XXII. 7. & τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῶν ἀζύμων die azymorum, uti ibidem dicitur, Pascha suum celebravit. Et azymo igitur pane omnino usus est; & fermentato si maximè usus fuisset, non inde necessitatem fermentato utendi imposuisset, quia panis esse potest, qui fermentatus non est. At nec saniores vel minùs obstinati Latini sunt, qui ex facto Christi in pane azymo Coenam instituentis legem necessariò utendi pane azymo cudunt. Cùm enim ea res merè accessoria fuerit, & ex lege ceremoniali, quæ nunc sublata est, petita sit, ad ὑσίαν essentiam Sacramenti non pertinet, ut pane azymo utamur. Ut dolendum, mirandúmque simul sit, quòd de re levi adeò Latini & Græci annos jam quingentos & amplius, inde nempe ab A. MLIII. quo controversiam coepisse ex Epistola Leonis IX. ad Michaelem Episcopum Constantinopolitanum liquet; rixari religioni non duxerint. Nam ne nunc quidem contendendi finis est, quando hoc etiam seculo Jeremias Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus necessitatem utendi pane fermentato propugnavit, frivola inter alias ratione usus, quòd ἀέλ descendat ab αἴρω τῶ κᾱφίζω, attollo, cùm farina non attollatur nisi per fermentum: quasi non verisimilius Eustathius ἄζυμον ab αἴρω, quod est πεσσοφίζω, quia aliquid substantiæ corpori affert, derivaverit; inprimis cùm Græci interpretes, Exod. XXIX. 2. Judic. VI. 20. etiam panem azymum ἄζυμα nomine expresserint. Et Bellarminus, ejusque sequaces pro pane azymo, ceu aris & focis propugnant, licèt etiam Eugenius IV. in Concilio Florentino Græcis pane fermentato utendi gratiam fecerit. Certè post primam Coenam Apostoli ubique ἄζυμον panem vocant, nullo fermentati vel non fermentati discrimine.
units.tr: LXXVII. The bread Christ used was of the kind customary at the time when he instituted the Supper. It was unleavened, in accordance with that law by which all leaven had to be removed at the time of the Passover. The Greeks wrangle over this in vain, contending that Christ anticipated the Jewish Passover and so used leavened bread. But he could not have used leavened bread without transgressing the law. Granted, the Jews sometimes celebrated the Passover not lawfully according to the law but unlawfully according to custom and tradition, namely the canon of Badu, which forbade celebrating the Passover on the sixth day of the week lest the people be forced to abstain from work for two days; or according to the edict by which, in fixing the Passover, they were ordered to follow not so much the course as the appearance of the heavenly luminaries. They did indeed anticipate it altogether. Yet Christ celebrated his Passover on the fourteenth day of Nisan, when it ought to be, Luke 22.7, and "on the day of unleavened bread," as it is said there. So he certainly used unleavened bread. And even if he had used leavened bread, that would not have imposed any necessity of using leavened bread, since there can be bread that is not leavened. Nor are the Latins any more sensible or less obstinate, who from Christ's act of instituting the Supper with unleavened bread forge a law that unleavened bread must necessarily be used. For since that matter was purely incidental, and taken from the ceremonial law, which is now abolished, the use of unleavened bread does not belong to the essence [οὐσία] of the sacrament. It is lamentable, and at the same time astonishing, that the Latins and Greeks have not thought it wrong to quarrel over religion for more than five hundred years about such a trivial matter, namely from A.D. 1053, when the controversy began, as is clear from the epistle of Leo IX to Michael, Bishop of Constantinople. Even now there is no end to the contention, for in this century also Jeremiah, Patriarch of Constantinople, defended the necessity of using leavened bread, among other frivolous arguments, namely that ἄζυμον [azymon] derives from ἀέλ, from αἴρω, to raise up, since flour does not rise except through leaven. As if Eustathius had not more plausibly derived azymon from another root, because it brings some substance to the body. Especially since the Greek translators, at Exod. 29.2 and Judg. 6.20, also rendered unleavened bread by the word ἄζυμα [azyma]. Bellarmine and his followers defend unleavened bread as if it were their altars and hearths, although Eugenius IV, at the Council of Florence, granted the Greeks the favour of using leavened bread. Certainly after the first Supper the Apostles everywhere call it azymon bread, with no distinction between leavened and unleavened.

units.la: LXXVIII. Fermentati igitur æquè ac azymi panis in Eucharistia liber usus est, dummodo ne alteruter ceu necessarius, & nullo casu mutabilis præscribatur. Uterque analogiam quandam fundit: ille nutritionis plenioris, hic sinceritatis & sanctitatis, ad quam Eucharistia obligat, majoris. Nostræ Ecclesiæ usum azymi à Zwinglio externorum ejusmodi planè incuriosò, & interiorum atque spiritualium tenacissimo, retentum, ceu fractioni & distributioni opportuniorem, ut mutarent, hactenus inducì non potuerunt, novandi periculum metuentes. At nec Ecclesiis fermentato utentibus nimium succensent; nec legem sibi nunquam mutandi, vel mutabilis usus dixerunt; & unà cum reliquis Ecclesiis minutias oblatarum, seu, uti vocant, hostiarum nummulariarum, quæ non panis, sed quisquiliarum panis similitudinem habent, unanimiter rejiciunt. LXXIX. Non enim nummulariis ejusmodi hostiis usus Christus est, neque ex panis, sed glutinis potiùs nomenclaturam merentur & inter signum & rem signatam analogiam vel planè nullam, vel obscuram certè habent; & fractionis ritum simul atque mysterium tollunt, & unitatis plurium significationem, quam Apostolus 1. Cor. X. 17. urget, abolent; & non priùs earum usus in Ecclesiam irrepsit, quàm Transubstantiationis dogma, cui monstro alendo non parùm ancillari visæ sunt, invalescaret. Nam & invisibili corpori continendo minimè palpabilis hostia idonea magis visa est, & ad accidentium quàm substantiæ similitudinem propiùs accedunt; & cavere sic placuit pani in Numen conversò, seu novo huic Numini Panaceo, cujus, si panis non totus atque integer, sed frangenda daretur particula aliquà jam Deificata, solvi & dilabi facilè potuisset. Agnoscunt Honorius Augustodunensis Gemm. anim. lib. I. 60. & Durandus Rat. tract. 4. olim in Ecclesia magnum panem & omnibus sufficientem distribui consuesse; sed nunc, ita Durandi verba habent, formantur in modum denarii, tum quòd panis vitæ pro denariis traditus est: item, quia idem denarius in vinea laborantibus in præmium dandus est. Sirmondus de Azym. c. 4. integros solidósque panes olim consecratos, & in partes ad distribuendum comminutos esse fatetur; at morem illum circa seculum sextum immutatum pertendit, quo primùm ad corporis Dominici Sacramentum panes non vulgares & oblatitios, sed peculiares, studiòque ad id paratos adhiberi placuerit. Sed nullam ille tam maturæ mutationis argumentum aliud affert, quàm ex Concilio Toletano A. DCCXXXI. celebrato, quo cautum erat, ut non aliter panis in altari benedictione sacerdotali sanctificandus proponatur, nisi qui studio præparatus fuerit. Circa seculum igitur octavum panis communis usurpari desiit, & ejus loco peculiaris, isque azymus, sed adhuc integer & fractioni idoneus, adhiberi coepit; donec seculo XI. Leonis IX. Nicolai II. & Gregorii VII. authoritate admissum à Latinis Transubstantiationis dogma, eos ad formam oblatarum nummulariarum comminiscendam impulit; Quibus jam inductis minutiis, non defuerunt tamen, qui consuetudinem hanc improbarent. Nam Bernoldus Presbyter Constantiensis, qui circa A. MLX. vixit, lib. de Ord. Rom. sic scripsit: Si nihil omnino intra vel extra Templum Domini fieri absque mensura & ratione debet, videntur oblatarum minutiæ ad Christum & Ecclesiam nihil pertinere, quia sunt absque ratione & mensura. LXXX. Ritus circa panem sunt ejusdem in manus acceptio, benedictio seu sanctificatio, fractio, distributio, acceptio & manducatio. Nam ante omnia Christus ἔλαβε τὸν ἄρτον accepit panem, Matth. XXVI. 26. Marc. XIV. 22. Luc. XXII. 19. 1. Cor. XI. 23. Factum id more Hebræorum veterum, qui benedicturi cibis, pani, in manus eum sumebant. Quomodo in Schylcham Aruch dicitur: שלחן ערוך קודש שיתפוס הלחם Non est benedicendum nisi apprehenso pane. Acceptum sic panem Christus à pane communi segregavit: Factum autem illud est ἐσθίοντων αὐτῶν comedentibus illis Matth. XXVI. 26. seu, uti Lucas cap. XXII. 20. habet, μετὰ μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι; postquam cœnassent: & Johannes cap. XIII. 2. Δείπνου γινομένου Cœna (Paschali) facta. Sed mox ita accepto & segregato atque in manu sustentato pani benedixit,& benedicendo eundem sanctificavit. Nam accepto pane εὐλογήσας benedicens eidem,&c. Matth. XXVI. 26. Marc. XIV. 22. εὐχαριστήσας gratias agens, Luc. XXII. 19. Idem enim εὐλογίαν & εὐχαριστίαν sonare, satis probat, quòd Evangelistæ illa verba alternant; & passim, velut Marc. VIII. 6. 7. 1. Cor. XIV. 16. pro eodem ponuntur; Hebræorum idiotismo, quo ברך & benedictionem, & gratiarum actionem significat. Sicut enim Christus alias benedicendo, gratias agendo panes aliósque cibos ad usum naturalem sanctificavit, Matth. XIV. 19. Luc. IX. 16. & Paulus cibum quemvis precibus & gratiarum actione sanctificari 1. Tim. IV. 4. 5. docuit: & olim Judæus pater familias sumpta in Paschali epulo placenta Deum hac benedictionis formula: Benedictus tu Domine Deus noster, mundi Domine, qui panem e terra producis, laudavit: ita Christus hac benedictione & gratiarum actione panem à naturali ad sacrum usum segregavit, ut Sacramentum corporis sui existeret. Benedictionis & gratiarum actionis illius expressa formula licet descripta non sit, tamen ejusdem sensus ex re ipsa proclivis collectu est. Non potuit enim Christus pani benedicere, & Deo gratias agere, quin & usum panis supernaturalem commemoraret, & Deo Patri gratias ageret, quòd sic mundum dilexerit, ut Filium suum unigenitum pro eo morti exponeret, eùmque sibi hæreditatem decerneret; atque ei rei Sacramentum, panem simili modo frangendum & comedendum instituerit; & denique (gratiarum actione, parte orationis præcipua, pro quavis oratione tropicè accepta) eundem quæsitissimis precibus oraret, ut & mortem suam fidelibus & electis omnibus proficuam, & externa signa ad eandem iisdem obsignandam efficacia esse velit, jubeat.
units.tr: LXXVIII. Therefore the use of leavened as well as unleavened bread is free in the Eucharist, provided that neither is prescribed as necessary and unchangeable in any case. Each carries a certain analogy: leavened bread of fuller nourishment, unleavened of the sincerity and holiness to which the Eucharist binds us, in greater measure. Our Church's use of unleavened bread, retained from Zwingli, who was entirely careless of such outward things and most tenacious of the inward and spiritual, as more suitable for breaking and distribution, has so far not been induced to change, for fear of the danger of innovation. Yet they are not greatly angry with churches that use leavened bread, nor have they said that there is a law of never changing or of a changeable custom. Together with the other Churches, they unanimously reject the small wafers of the oblations, or, as they call them, coin-like hosts, which have the likeness not of bread but of crumbs. LXXIX. Christ did not use such coin-like hosts. They deserve the name not of bread but rather of paste. They have either no analogy at all between sign and thing signified, or certainly an obscure one. They remove both the rite and the mystery of breaking, and abolish the signification of the unity of many, which the Apostle urges at 1 Cor. 10.17. Their use did not creep into the Church until the dogma of transubstantiation, to which they seemed no small handmaid in feeding that monster, had grown strong. For a very unpalpable host seemed more fitting for containing an invisible body, and such hosts come closer to the likeness of the accidents than of the substance. Thus it pleased them to guard against the bread being turned into a deity, or into this new panacea-god, which, if bread were given whole and entire rather than a fragment to be broken, already deified, could easily be dissolved and fall apart. Honorius of Autun, Gemma animae, book 1, ch. 60, and Durandus, Rationale, tract 4, acknowledge that in the Church formerly a large loaf sufficient for all was distributed. "But now," the words of Durandus are, "they are formed in the manner of a coin, both because the bread of life was handed over in exchange for coins, and because the same coin is to be given as the reward to those labouring in the vineyard." Sirmond, On Azymes, ch. 4, admits that whole and solid loaves were once consecrated and broken into pieces for distribution. But he maintains that this custom was changed around the sixth century, when it first pleased that for the sacrament of the Lord's body not common and ordinary loaves but special ones, prepared with care for this purpose, should be used. Yet he offers no other argument for so early a change than the Council of Toledo, held in A.D. 731, which provided that bread should not be put forward to be sanctified on the altar by the priestly blessing unless it had been prepared with care. Around the eighth century, therefore, common bread ceased to be used, and in its place a "special" bread, unleavened but still whole and fit for breaking, began to be employed. Then in the eleventh century, under the authority of Leo IX, Nicholas II and Gregory VII, the Latins admitted the dogma of transubstantiation, which drove them to devise the form of coin-like wafers. Once these crumbs had been introduced, there were nevertheless not lacking those who disapproved of the custom. For Bernold, presbyter of Constance, who lived around A.D. 1060, wrote thus in his book On the Roman Order: "If nothing at all is to be done inside or outside the house of the Lord without measure and reason, the crumbs of the oblations seem to have nothing to do with Christ and the Church, because they are without reason and measure." LXXX. The rites concerning the bread are: taking it into the hands, blessing or sanctifying, breaking, distributing, receiving and eating. For above all, Christ "took the bread," Matt. 26.26; Mark 14.22; Luke 22.19; 1 Cor. 11.23. This was done in the manner of the ancient Hebrews, who, about to bless their food, took the bread into their hands. So it is said in the Shulchan Aruch: "One should not bless unless the bread has first been taken in hand" [לא יברך אלא אחר שתפס הלחם]. Having taken the bread thus, Christ set it apart from common bread. This happened "while they were eating," Matt. 26.26, or, as Luke 22.20 has it, "after they had supped," and John 13.2, "supper (of the Passover) being made." But soon, with the bread so taken and set apart and held in his hand, he "blessed" it, and by blessing it he sanctified it. For, the bread taken, he "blessed" (εὐλογήσας [eulogesas]) it, Matt. 26.26; Mark 14.22, and "giving thanks" (εὐχαριστήσας [eucharistesas]), Luke 22.19. That both "blessing" and "giving thanks" have the same sense is sufficiently proved by the fact that the Evangelists alternate these words, and they are used for the same thing throughout, as at Mark 8.6-7 and 1 Cor. 14.16. This is due to the Hebrew idiom, by which ברך [barak] signifies both blessing and giving of thanks. For just as Christ at other times, by blessing and giving thanks, sanctified loaves and other food for natural use, Matt. 14.19; Luke 9.16, and Paul taught that every food is sanctified "by the word of God and prayer," 1 Tim. 4.4-5; and once the Jewish head of a household, taking a cake at the Passover meal, praised God with this formula of blessing: "Blessed are you, Lord our God, Lord of the world, who bring forth bread from the earth"; so Christ, by this blessing and giving of thanks, set the bread apart from natural to sacred use, so that it might become the sacrament of his body. Although the express formula of that blessing and thanksgiving is not recorded, its sense is readily gathered from the thing itself. For Christ could not bless the bread and give thanks to God without also recalling the supernatural use of bread, and giving thanks to God the Father that he so loved the world as to expose his only-begotten Son to death for it, and to appoint him heir; and for this he instituted the sacrament, bread to be broken and eaten in a similar manner. And finally (thanksgiving being the principal part of prayer, taken figuratively for any prayer), he prayed most earnestly that his death might be profitable to all the faithful and elect, and that the external signs might be effective for sealing it to them.

units.la: LXXXI. Hæc illa primæva panis (& similis etiam calicis) benedictio & sanctificatio à Christo, Eucharistiæ Domino & authore facta, tanti ponderis est, ut per eam Eucharistia juxta institutionem ejusdem ubivis celebrata, ad finem usque mundi efficax sit. A' qua immane quantum consecratio illa sacerdotum Missæ, verborum Christi; Hoc enim est corpus meum, super pane recitatione peracta, & quatum propter occultam verborum illorum vim, tum propter peculiarem virtutem ordinis Sacerdotalis, panem in corpus Christi realiter & substantialiter transmutari asserunt, distat. Nam Christum verbis illis benedixisse & consecrasse, oppidò absurdum est, cùm antequam verba illa enuntiasset, jam benedixerit, gratias egerit, & benedicendo & gratias agendo elementa consecraverit. Benedicens enim pani & calici haud dubiè exauditus est, adeóque panem benedictione benedictum, similiterque calicem effecit, antea quàm verba illa: Hoc est corpus meum, enuntiasset. Et verba illa pronuntiante eo, jam panis corpus erat, non factum est, quia non dixit: Hoc fiat, sed Hoc est corpus meum; & adversarii ipsi per pronomen Hoc corpus Christi intelligunt. Cùmque benedictio & consecratio quædam precatio sit, in verbis: Hoc enim est corpus meum, nulla certe precationis species est. Præterea certa verba, & syllabarum apices numerare, & iis arcano susurro demurmuratis operationem tribuere, parum equidem à Magorum mysteriis & profana verborum potentia abest. Quò & illud pertinet, quòd eodem susurro tacito nec Deum, nec populum, sed sacra signa affari solent, atque illa imperiosis ejusmodi verbis ex crusta in corpus Christi transmutari asserunt. Christus autem verba illa: Hoc enim est corpus meum, non ad elementa, sed ad Apostolos, & quidem clara, atque ab iisdem probè intellecta, non arcana, uti illi appellant, hoc est, ad aures populi non pertingente, voce dixit. Nam cùm Christus in Coena adsit, non ut pani, rei inanimæ, sed homini, pane utenti verba isthæc dici debent. Cùmque consecratio non unius Sacerdotis, sed totius Ecclesiæ causa fiat, atque omnes fideles in ea Deo gratias agere debeant (unde & εὐχαριστία appellatur) etiam quæcunque in hoc mysterio dicuntur, à fidelibus cunctis audiri oportet.
units.tr: LXXXI. This original blessing and consecration of the bread (and likewise of the cup), made by Christ, the Lord and author of the Eucharist, is of such weight that the Eucharist, celebrated anywhere according to his institution, remains effective until the end of the world. From it, the consecration in the Mass that the priests perform by reciting over the bread the words of Christ, "This is my body," differs immensely. They assert that the bread is changed really and substantially into the body of Christ, both by the hidden power of those words and by the special virtue of the priestly order. For it is utterly absurd to say that Christ blessed and consecrated by those words, since before he uttered them he had already blessed, given thanks, and by blessing and giving thanks consecrated the elements. Indeed, when he blessed the bread and the cup, he was undoubtedly heard, so the bread was blessed by the blessing and likewise the cup was made holy, before he had spoken the words "This is my body." And when he pronounced those words, the bread was already his body, not made so by them, because he did not say "Let this become," but "This is my body." Even the opponents themselves understand the body of Christ by the pronoun "this." Since blessing and consecration are a kind of prayer, there is certainly no form of prayer in the words "This is my body." Moreover, to count out certain words and the marks of syllables, and to ascribe an effect to them when they have been muttered in a secret whisper, is surely not far from the mysteries of the magicians and the profane power of words. To this also belongs the fact that with this same silent whisper they are accustomed to address not God or the people but the sacred signs, and they assert that by such commanding words those things are changed from bread into the body of Christ. Christ, however, spoke those words, "This is my body," not to the elements but to the Apostles, and aloud, and clearly understood by them; they were not "secret," as the Papists call them, that is, not spoken so as to fail to reach the ears of the people. For since Christ is present at the Supper, these words ought to be spoken not to the bread, an inanimate thing, but to the man who is eating the bread. And since the consecration is made not for one priest but for the whole Church, and all the faithful ought to give thanks to God in it (whence it is also called the eucharist [εὐχαριστία]), all that is said in this mystery must be heard by all the faithful.

units.la: LXXXII. Frivolæ adversantium rationes sunt.
units.tr: LXXXII. The objections of our opponents are trivial.

units.la: Nam cùm Sacramenti confectio certa esse debeat, negant illi eam, quæ benedictione & precibus solis fit, certam esse, quia incertum sit, an Deus exaudiat, nec ne. Verùm sic Baptismi etiam consecratio, quæ benedictione & precibus fit, incerta semper erit, & nemini de eo, an legitimè baptizatus sit, constare poterit. Sed preces, quibus promissio facta est, semper Deo acceptæ sunt. Tales autem sunt, quibus symbola consecrantur, quia verba Christi, quibus jussit hoc facere, adeóque etiam benedicere, tantam promissionem futuri in posterum effecti, includunt. Accedit, quòd Eucharistiæ consecratio efficaciam à benedictione & sanctificatione semel à Christo facta habet; neque eam perdit, si administrans eam non oret in fide, dummodo faciat, quod Christus facere jussit. Licèt tamen S. Coenæ consecratio à sola Divina virtute, invisibili Spiritus S. operatione, & Christi institutione vim omnem habeat, non iccirco preces & benedictio administrantis inutilis est, quia ea ex institutione Christi interveniente consecratio peragitur. Eadem institutio jubens facere, quod Christus fecit, postulat, ut administrantes Eucharistiam verba illa: Hoc enim est corpus meum pronuntient. Sed non ideo consecrationem illa operantur, nisi forte & reliqua omnia operantur. Præceptum verò hoc faciendi non pertinet ad verba illa: H. E. E. C. M. nisi ut recitetur id, quod jam est, non ut per ea conficiens Sacramentum operetur id, quod non est. Denique gerræ Siculæ & meræ nugæ sunt, cùm verba Christi practica esse, hoc est, facere, quod Christus dicit, argutantur. Si enim sic practica sunt, imperativè, non enuntiativè prolata fuissent. Atqui Christus dixit: Hoc est, non Hoc fiat, vel erit. Facit sanè Christus, quod dicit, nempe cùm, ut fiat aliquid, dicit, vel imperat, non cùm ceu jam factum pronuntiat. Quomodo cùm Herodem vulpem esse dixit, non vulpem fecit, sed patefecit.
units.tr: For since the making of a sacrament ought to be certain, they deny that the consecration that is done by blessing and prayer alone is certain, because it is uncertain whether God hears or not. But in that case the consecration of Baptism too, which is done by blessing and prayer, would always be uncertain, and no one could be sure whether he had been validly baptized. Yet prayers to which a promise has been attached are always acceptable to God. Such are the prayers by which the elements are consecrated, because the words of Christ, by which he commanded us to "do this," and therefore also to bless, include the promise of an effect to come in the future. Moreover, the consecration of the Eucharist has its efficacy from the blessing and sanctification once made by Christ, and does not lose it if the minister who administers it does not pray in faith, provided he does what Christ commanded him to do. Although the consecration of the Lord's Supper derives all its force from divine power alone, from the invisible operation of the Holy Spirit and from Christ's institution, the prayers and blessing of the minister are not for that reason useless, because that consecration is accomplished by the intervention of Christ's institution. The same institution, commanding us to do what Christ did, requires that those who administer the Eucharist pronounce the words "This is my body." But they do not therefore effect the consecration, unless perhaps they effect everything else as well. Moreover, the command "do this" does not apply to the words "This is my body" except in the sense that what already exists is recited, not that the minister by those words effects what does not exist. Finally, they chatter Sicilian trifles and mere nonsense when they argue that the words of Christ are practical, that is, that they make what Christ says happen. For if they were practical in that way, they would have been uttered in the imperative, not the indicative. But Christ said "This is," not "Let this be," or "it will be." Christ certainly does what he says, namely when he says something in order that it may come to be, or commands it, not when he declares it as if already done. Thus when he said of Herod, "Go and tell that fox," he did not make him a fox, but exposed him.

units.la: LXXXIII. Sequitur Fractio panis.
units.tr: LXXXIII. Follows the breaking of bread.

units.la: Nam Christus benedicens εὐλογεῖ fregit, Matth. XXVI. 26. Marc. XIV. 22. Luc. XXII. 19. 1. Cor. XI. 24. Et Ecclesia Apostolica Coenam ab hoc ritu necessitatem integritatem...
units.tr: For Christ, when he had blessed [εὐλογεῖ], broke it (Matt. 26:26; Mark 14:22; Luke 22:19; 1 Cor. 11:24). And the Apostolic Church [regarded] the Lord's Supper as lacking nothing of its necessity and integrity without this rite.

units.la: quàm non in pronunciatione verborum, Hoc enim est corpus meum, constituisse, probatur.
units.tr: That this rite was established not in the pronouncing of the words, "This is my body," is proved.

units.la: Argumentum contrarium sit falsum.
units.tr: The contrary argument is false.

units.la: Fractio panis, & ejusdem ad Sacramenti integritatem necessitate. ritu κλάσιν τὴ ἄρτ fractionem panis appellavit, Actor. 11. 42. XX. 7. Et S. Paulus: Panis, quem frangimus, nonne est communio corporis Christi? 1. Cor. X. 16. Hebræi in libris ritualibus id יצא appellant. In Thalmud Berach. sol. 9. מברך ואחר כן ברוך Pater familias benedicit, & postea frangit. Qui ritus & à Christo atque Apostolis adhibitus fuerit, & fractionem corporis Christi, & κοινωνίαν communionem multorum velut divisorum cum uno corpore 1. Cor. X. 16. significet, necessarius est, non quidem ut pars Sacramenti essentialis, vel integrans præcipua, qualis in homine cor & caput est; sine quo alterutro homo non est; sed ejusmodi tamen, quæ ad rei integritatem pertineat; uti sunt oculus, auris, brachium, pes. Neque fractionem nummulariorum panum asserores tuentur, qui eam vel in massæ totius in multarum oblatarum minutias, vel in distributionem convertunt. Nam discerptio ejusmodi coquinaria, non mystica est, atque in culina, non in Templo, ante Sacramentum, non in usu Sacramenti peragitur. Ac licèt alicubi שבר & פרס frangere pro distribuere dicatur, velut cum dicitur. Frange esurienti panem, Esaj. L VIII. 7. Parvuli petebant panem, & non erat, qui frangeret; Thren. I V. 4. quibus locis frangere κατα μετάλημψιν accipitur, pro ea distributione, quæ fractionem sequitur, ita ut frange tantundem sit atque frange & divide: tamen in Cœnæ verbis hæc μετάλημψιν locum non habet, uti de Christo distinctè dicitur, ἐκλασε καὶ ἐδωκε fregit & dedit, seu distribuit. Panis enim ut distribui posset, frangi debuit. Etiam probandum erat, Christum & Apostolos, qui non Hebræo, sed Syro sermone usi sunt, vocem usurpasse, quæ non minùs distribuere quàm frangere significet: Nam verbum ܦܪܣ quod apud Syrum Interpretem est, non distribuere, sed frangere κνεῖσ est. Neque obstat, quòd Christo, ceu vero Agno, ossa fracta non sunt; quia corpus ejus mortificatum, adeóque etiam fractum est. Frangun-tur enim membra, quando per mortem spiritu, qui continet, privantur, atque itá luxantur; desinunt esse unum; neque amplius organa sunt, quia illis anima, quæ in sanguine & nervis viventis est, & sine qua nec motus, nec sensus fit, deest. Ideo corpus Christi pro nobis fractum 1. Cor. XI. 24. disertè dicitur, & in Scripturis שבר mortem significat. Præterea fractio de pane proprie, de corpore Christi improprie per metonymiam puta signi dicitur, quia panis signum corporis Christi, proprie frangitur: Inter signum verò & signatum, nec tantùm inter panem & corpus, sed etiam inter panis fractionem, & corporis Christi crucifixionem analogia & similitudo intercedit, quæ analogia ad usus ritus hujus in cœna necessitatem demonstrandam sufficit.
units.tr: The breaking of the bread, and its necessity for the integrity of the sacrament. Luke called this rite "the breaking of the bread" [κλάσιν τοῦ ἄρτου], Acts 11.42, 20.7. And St Paul says: "The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" 1 Cor. 10.16. The Hebrews call it by the word [יצא] in their ritual books. In the Talmud (Berachot, fol. 9) we read: "The head of the household blesses, and afterwards breaks" [מברך ואחר כן פורס]. This rite, which was used by Christ and the apostles, signifies both the breaking of Christ's body and the "communion" [κοινωνία] of many, as if divided, with the one body (1 Cor. 10.16). It is necessary, not indeed as an essential part of the sacrament or its chief integral part, as the heart and head are of a man, without either of which a man does not exist, but as something that belongs to the completeness of the thing, like the eye, the ear, the arm, or the foot. Nor do the defenders of the breaking of wafers, who turn it either into the cutting of a whole mass into many small pieces or into distribution, make good their case. For such kitchen cutting is not mystical, and it is performed in the kitchen, not in the temple, before the sacrament, and not in its use. And although in some places the words [שבר] and [פרס], "to break", are used for "to distribute", as when it is said, "Break your bread to the hungry" (Isa. 58.7), and "The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it" (Lam. 4.4), where "to break" is taken by metalepsis for the distribution that follows the breaking, so that "break" means the same as "break and divide", yet in the words of the Supper this metalepsis has no place. Of Christ it is said distinctly, "he broke and gave" [ἐκλασε καὶ ἐδωκε], that is, he distributed. For the bread could be distributed only if it was first broken. It also had to be shown that Christ and the apostles, who spoke not Hebrew but Syriac, used a word that means "to distribute" no less than "to break". For the Syriac word [prs] in the Syriac translator means not "to distribute" but "to break" [κνεῖν]. Nor is there any objection in the fact that no bone of Christ was broken, as of the true Lamb; for his body was put to death, and so it was also broken. Limbs are broken when, through death, they are deprived of the spirit that sustains them and so are put out of joint; they cease to be one, and they are no longer organs, because the life is gone from them, the life that lives in the blood and nerves and without which there is no motion or sensation. So it is expressly said that Christ's "body was broken for us" (1 Cor. 11.24), and in the Scriptures [שבר] signifies death. Moreover, the breaking is properly said of the bread and only improperly, by metonymy, of the body of Christ, because the bread, which is the sign of Christ's body, is what is properly broken. Between the sign and the thing signified, and not only between the bread and the body but also between the breaking of the bread and the crucifixion of Christ's body, there is an analogy and likeness, and this analogy is enough to show the necessity of this rite in the Supper.

units.la: LXXXIV. Dum porrò fractio retinea-tur, de fractionis modo contendendum non putamus. Potuit Christus panem in duas partes confringere, earumque alteram dare illi, qui ei proximus ad dextram accumbebat; alteram verò illi, qui ad sinistram, ut isti deinceps proximè accumbentibus porrigerent, donec singuli particulam sibi decerpsissent, qui mos in Ecclesia nostra obtinet. Forte etiam Christus digito fregit, non cultro scidit, quia Judæi utebantur pane lato, at non admodum spisso; ac præterea sulcis quibusdam decussatim incisô, ut commodè in quadratas quasdam buccellas manu frangeretur. Quomodo incisos panes Græci βλωμίλιας vocabant, uti Athenæus lib. III. scribit, nempe à βλωμὸς, quod Hevchiò teste ἰχῦν ψωμὸν tenuem seu exiguam buccam notat. Martialis quadram, non quartam panis partem; sed placentæ ψωμὸν buccellam appellat. Talis Judaica fractio fuit. Sed Orientales panem Eucharisticum non frangebant, sed instrumento scindebant, uti Nicol. Casobilas Expos. Liturg. c. 7. testatur. Eundem morem apud Æthiopas obtinere Sanctius in Act. II. 42. aliique scribunt.
units.tr: LXXXIV. Moreover, while the breaking is retained, we do not think that we must dispute about the manner of breaking. Christ could have broken the bread into two parts, and given one part to the one who reclined next to him on the right, and the other to the one on the left, so that these in turn might pass them to those reclining next to them, until each had plucked off a little piece for himself; which custom prevails in our Church. Perhaps also Christ broke it with his finger rather than cutting it with a knife, because the Jews used a bread that was broad but not very thick, and moreover scored with certain furrows crosswise, so that it could be conveniently broken by hand into square little morsels. As the Greeks called such scored breads blōmilias, as Athenaeus writes in book III, namely from blōmos, which according to Hesychius means a thin or small mouthful [ἰχῦν ψωμὸν]. Martial calls a square not a quarter part of the bread, but a little morsel [ψωμὸν] of a cake. Such was the Jewish breaking. But the Orientals did not break the Eucharistic bread, but cut it with an instrument, as Nicolaus Caseobilas attests in his Exposition of the Liturgy, ch. 7. That the same custom prevails among the Ethiopians, Sanctius on Acts 2:42 and others write.

units.la: LXXXV. Fractionem Distributio ad mandu-candum excipit.
units.tr: LXXXV. The distribution comes after the breaking, for eating.

units.la: Nam Christus fregit κατὰ ἰδιαν ... dedit discipulis; & dixit: Accipite; manducate, Matth. XXVI. 26. Marc. XIV. 22. Luc. X XII. 19. Iterum secundum priscam Hebræorum consuetudinem, quorum ea de re canon est: הבורא גוית פרוסה לפני אחר ואחר Frangens dat particulam coram unoquoque; & alter tollit, vel accipit eam manu sua. Datio igitur illa Christi distributio panis fracti, adeóque à fractione diversus ritus erat. Datio autem erat פרוסה seu ψωμὸς particulæ defractæ, divisæ; adeóque buccellæ, non ingestio vel in manum, nedum in os, qualis sequiore ætate usu recepta est. Neque enim Christus, qui cum pluribus discumbebat, facere id potuisse videtur, nisi de loco surgens ire ad singulos vellet. Quod satis intelligunt, qui veterum discumbendi morem; ab eruditis Philologis in iis, quæ de Triclinio scripserunt; expressum norunt. In veteri certè Ecclesia mos manibus panem sumendi diutissime viguit; sed paulatim mos ille mutatus est; neque id aliunde, quàm à superstitione signorum, quæ in ψελλάπηνα tandem evasit: Primò enim circa tempus Gregorii M. in Concilio Antisiodorensi can. 42. mulieribus interdictum est, ne nuda manu sua Eucharistiam sumerent. Acceperunt ergo manu, sed linteo, cui Dominicalis nomen erat, velata. Paulò post in vasculis accipi suevit, quam consuetudinem Patres Concilii Constantinopolitani in Trullo habiti aboleverunt. Demum seculo nono Eucharistia, in os communicantis immitti cœpit. Nam Batherius Veronensis Episcopus, qui A. CMLXXIV. ad plures migravit Serm. 2. de Pasch. morem hunc panem in os ingerendi se vivente jam receptum fuisse, significat. Burchardus verò, qui seculo XI. ineunte vixit, Decr. lib. III. 76. à Synodo quadam Rhotomagensi conditum in hæc verba decretum exhibet: Nulli laico aut fœminæ Eucharistiam in manibus ponat; sed tantum in os ejus cum his verbis ponat: Corpus & sanguis Domini prosit tibi ad remissionem peccatorum ad vitam æternam. Quæ lex circa A. DCCCXIV. post Caroli M. mortem sancita putatur. Ita paulatim pulso, tandemque antiquato veteri tradendæ in communicantium manus Eucharistiæ ritu, obtinuit apud Latinos ejus in ora fidelium immittendæ mos, iis temporibus, quibus panis sacri per Transsubstantiationis fidem ... hominum in novum Numen religionem in immensum promovit. Cùm tamen analogia Sacramenti non ...
units.tr: For Christ broke the bread κατὰ ἰδίαν ... and gave it to the disciples, and said: Take, eat, Matth. XXVI. 26; Marc. XIV. 22; Luc. XXII. 19. Again, following the ancient custom of the Hebrews, whose rule on this point is: הבורא גוית פרוסה לפני אחר ואחר [The one who breaks gives a piece before each person, and the other takes it in his own hand.] The giving by Christ, then, was a distribution of the broken bread, and so a rite different from the breaking itself. The giving was of a פרוסה, or ψωμός [a piece, a morsel], of bread that had been broken and divided, and so a morsel, not a placing into the hand, still less into the mouth, which became the practice in a later age. For Christ, who was reclining with several others, does not seem able to have done this unless he rose from his place and went to each of them. Those who know the ancient manner of reclining, as learned philologists have described it in their writings on the triclinium, understand this well enough. In the ancient Church, certainly, the custom of taking the bread in the hands lasted for a very long time. But gradually that custom changed, and this came about for no other reason than superstition about signs, which in the end turned into a ψελλάπηνα [a mere trifle]. For first, around the time of Gregory the Great, at the Council of Auxerre (canon 42) it was forbidden to women that they should receive the Eucharist with a bare hand. So they received it in the hand but covered with a linen cloth, which was called the dominicale. Shortly afterwards it was customary to receive it in small vessels, a practice which the fathers of the Council of Constantinople held in the Trullo abolished. Finally, in the ninth century, the Eucharist began to be put into the mouth of the communicant. For Ratherius, bishop of Verona, who died in the year 974, in Sermon 2 on Easter, shows that this custom of putting the bread into the mouth had already been received in his lifetime. Burchard, who lived at the beginning of the eleventh century, in Decretum book III, 76, gives a decree drawn up by a certain Synod of Rouen in these words: Let no one place the Eucharist in the hands of a layman or a woman; but let him place it only in the mouth, with these words: May the body and blood of the Lord profit you for the forgiveness of sins and for eternal life. This law is thought to have been enacted around the year 814, after the death of Charlemagne. Thus, as the old rite of delivering the Eucharist into the hands of communicants was gradually driven out and at last abolished, the custom of placing it into the mouths of the faithful prevailed among the Latins, at a time when, through faith in transubstantiation, ... the religion of a new deity of men spread enormously. Yet since the analogy of the sacrament does not ...

units.la: Fractionis modus indifferens est. in modo sumendi, sed in sumptione ipsa consistat, atque sumptio permaneat, sive manibus symbola prehendas, sive ore à ministro percipias, consuetudo absque manuum ministerio cibum ore sumendi, dummodo absque superstitione id fiat, tanti non erit, ut iccirco Ecclesia turbari debeat.
units.tr: The manner of breaking is a matter of indifference. The sacrament consists in the taking itself, and the taking remains the same whether you grasp the symbols with your hands or receive them into your mouth from the minister. The custom of eating the food with the mouth, without the help of the hands, provided it is done without superstition, is not so important that the Church should on that account be thrown into confusion.

units.la: LXXXVI. Distributio panis manducationis gratia facta est. Christus enim dedit & dixit: Accipite, manducate, Matth. XXVI. 26. Ab institutionis igitur Christi lineis Sacerdos Pontificius deflectit, qui in Missis, quas vocant, privatis, panem nec distribuit, nec aliis manducandum præbet, sed solus manducat. Christus enim non solus edit & bibit, aliis vel absentibus, vel nudè spectantibus, sed panem distribuit, manducare eos, quibus distribuit, & hoc facere iussit. Nam quod Missas ejusmodi publicas esse nugantur, quia populus in iis spiritualiter communicet, & Sacerdos, ceu persona publica, non pro se solo, sed pro omnibus fidelibus sacrificet, parum ad rem facit, quia quocunque nomine Missæ ejusmodi venditentur, institutioni & exemplo Christi Eucharistiam ad manducandum distribuentis contrariari non desinunt. Non enim de nomine, sed de re quæstio est. Et quid si etiam Sacerdos celebrans spiritualiter communicet, an sic institutioni satisfaciet, & si nec sumat ipse, nec aliis consecrata dispensat? Est etiam is, qui Eucharistiam celebrat, publicus Ecclesiæ Minister, sed non ut contra institutionem Christi solus Cœna utatur, & hoc toti Ecclesiæ proficiat. Sed quam Christus Cœnæ ad manducandum distribuendæ rationem instituit, eandem Apostoli & eorundem discipuli religiosè retinuerunt. Perseverarunt enim discipuli eorum in doctrina Apostolorum & κοινωνίᾳ communicatione & fractione panis, Actor. II. 42. de discipulis Apostolorum Lucas: Συνηγμένων τῶν μαθητῶν congregatis discipulis ad frangendum panem, ibid. XX. 7. Paulus quoque: Συνεχομένων ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ Convenientibus vobis in unum, non est hoc Cœnam Dominicam manducare, I. Cor. XI. 20. Συνεχόμενοι εἰς τὸ φαγεῖν Convenientes ad manducandum, ibid. v. 33. Licet enim eo in conventu etiam agapæ factæ sint, tales tamen factæ sunt, ut in communionem desinerent. Quorsum alias Apostolus institutionem Eucharistiæ Corinthiis suis repetitam ob oculos statueret? Ideo etiam Eucharistiam Κυριακὸν δεῖπνον Cœnam Dominicam appellat, quod communicationem cœnantium omnium, non unius Patris familias significat. Omnes enim hoc cibo indigent, adeoque ad pascendum se liberaliter invitare debent. Cumque Eucharistia etiam typus unitatis plurium sit, I. Corinth. X. 17. in privatis Missis mysterium unitatis ejusmodi repræsentari nequit. In veteri certè Ecclesia privatæ Missæ inauditæ fuerunt. Nam illi Eucharistiæ nominibus συνάξεως, συνελεύσεως Collectæ, Cœnæ Domini, Convivii, quæ solitarias Missas evertunt, venit. Et in Liturgiis omnibus non tantum altum de iisdem silentium est, sed etiam plures cum sacerdote communicantes occurrunt. Quin & Concilii Nannetensis canon. 30. quem ex Regione, qui decimo sæculo vixit, Cassander exhibet, nec non in Synodo Moguntiaca Carolo M. superstite habita, cavetur, ne ullus Presbyter solus LXXXVII. Eadem verò imperata panis ad manducandum distributio etiam asservationem, inclusionem in pixide, & ad alios usus accommodationem ejusdem in Papatu receptam, evertit. Christus enim discipulis panem non asservandum, sed illico manducandum obtulit. Et quod ipse fecit, Ecclesiam facere iussit. Neque aliud Apostoli fecisse ullo piam commemorantur. Falsò autem illi manducationem ad Sacramenti essentiam requiri negant, quia Eucharistia cibus est. Omnis autem cibi, quà cibi, relatio ad manducationem simpliciter necessaria est. Et tum symbola consecrata veri Sacramenti rationem habent, cùm omnes Divinæ institutionis Divinæ partes implentur. Tum verò implentur, cùm symbola benedicta franguntur, distribuuntur, accipiuntur, & in commemorationem Christi manducantur, Matth. XXVI. 26. 27. 28. Atqui nec ante, nec post usum hæ Divinæ institutionis partes servantur. Et par Eucharistiæ & Baptismi ratio est. Sicut igitur aqua Baptismi ante & post usum rationem Sacramenti nullam habet: Ita nec panis in Eucharistia habet. Sacramenti enim eujuslibet essentiam in usu consistere etiam Gabriel Biel dixit. Cùmq; Eucharistia Paschati successerit, satis constat, Pascha nisi manducatis Agni carnib° Sacramenti nullam rationem habuisse. Impii verò etiam & peregrini Eucharistiæ asservandæ fines sunt; puta adoratio hostiæ, etiam extra Synaxeos tempus; usus ejusdem ad consecrationes varias, festorum pompam, circumgestationem, custodiam & præsidium Papæ, aliáq; ejusmodi, quibus Eucharistia à Christo neutiquam destinata est. Denique asservatio & repositio hæc nec Apostolica traditione, nec vetustissimo Ecclesiæ universalis more recepta est. Nam veteres, uti ex Clementis Romani, Hieronymi, Hesychii Hierosolymitani testimoniis constat, reliquias panis non manducati cremarunt. CúmqueGræcis in usu esset Liturgia προηγιασμένων Præsanctificatorum, acerrimè Humbertus,
units.tr: LXXXVI. The distribution was made for the sake of eating. For Christ gave and said: Take, eat, Matth. XXVI. 26. Therefore the Papist priest departs from the lines of Christ's institution, who in the so-called private Masses neither distributes the bread nor offers it to others to eat, but eats it alone. For Christ did not eat and drink alone, with others either absent or merely watching, but distributed the bread, and bade those to whom he distributed it to eat it, and to do this. As for their babbling that such Masses are public because the people communicate in them spiritually, and the priest, as a public person, sacrifices not for himself alone but for all the faithful, this has little to do with the matter, because whatever name such Masses are sold under, they do not stop being contrary to the institution and example of Christ, who distributed the Eucharist to be eaten. For the question is not about the name but about the thing. And what if the celebrating priest communicates spiritually: would he thereby satisfy the institution, if he neither takes it himself nor dispenses the consecrated elements to others? The one who celebrates the Eucharist is indeed a public minister of the Church, but not in such a way that he alone uses the Supper against the institution of Christ, and that this benefits the whole Church. But the manner in which Christ instituted the Supper to be distributed for eating, the Apostles and their disciples religiously retained. For they persevered (Acts II. 42), "in the teaching of the Apostles and in κοινωνία, communion, and the breaking of bread." Luke also says of the disciples of the Apostles: Συνηγμένων τῶν μαθητῶν [when the disciples were gathered together to break bread], ibid. XX. 7. Paul too: Συνεχομένων ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ [when you come together in one place], this is not to eat the Lord's Supper, I Cor. XI. 20; Συνεχόμενοι εἰς τὸ φαγεῖν [coming together to eat], ibid. v. 33. For although agape-feasts were also held at that gathering, they were held in such a way that they ended in communion. Why else would the Apostle set before the eyes of his Corinthians the institution of the Eucharist, which he had repeated to them? For this reason he also calls the Eucharist Κυριακὸν δεῖπνον [the Lord's Supper], because it signifies the communion of all who dine, not of one head of a household. For all need this food, and so they ought to invite one another generously to feed on it. And since the Eucharist is also a type of the unity of many, I Cor. X. 17, the mystery of such unity cannot be represented in private Masses. Certainly in the ancient Church private Masses were unheard of. For the names of the Eucharist, συνάξεως, συνελεύσεως [of gathering, of assembly], collecta, the Lord's Supper, the banquet, which overturn solitary Masses, belong to that time. And in all the Liturgies there is not only a deep silence about such Masses, but also several people are found communicating with the priest. Indeed, canon 30 of the Council of Nantes, which Cassander gives from the Regino who lived in the tenth century, and also what was laid down at the Synod of Mainz held while Charlemagne was still alive, provide that no priest alone ... LXXXVII. The same distribution of bread commanded for eating also overturns the keeping of it, its enclosure in a pyx, and its adaptation to other uses, which were received in the papacy. For Christ offered the bread to the disciples not to be kept, but to be eaten at once. And what he himself did, he commanded the Church to do. Nor is any other practice recorded as having been followed by the Apostles or by pious people. The Papists falsely deny that eating is required for the essence of the sacrament, because the Eucharist is food. But every food, as food, is necessarily related to eating. And the consecrated elements then have the character of a true sacrament when all the parts of the divine institution are fulfilled. They are fulfilled when the blessed elements are broken, distributed, received, and eaten in remembrance of Christ, Matth. XXVI. 26-28. Yet these parts of the divine institution are kept neither before nor after the use. And the case of the Eucharist and of Baptism is the same. Just as the water of Baptism has no character of a sacrament before or after its use, so the bread in the Eucharist has none. Gabriel Biel also said that the essence of any sacrament consists in its use. And since the Eucharist succeeded the Passover, it is quite clear that the Passover had no character of a sacrament apart from the eating of the flesh of the lamb. The impious and foreign ends of keeping the Eucharist are indeed these: for example, adoration of the host even outside the time of the synaxis; its use for various consecrations, the pomp of festivals, carrying it in procession, the guard and protection of the Pope, and other such things, for which Christ never intended the Eucharist at all. Finally, this keeping and reservation was received neither by Apostolic tradition nor by the most ancient custom of the universal Church. For the ancients, as is clear from the testimonies of Clement of Rome, Jerome, and Hesychius of Jerusalem, burned the remnants of bread that had not been eaten. And since the Liturgy of the Greeks, that of the Presanctified, was in use, Humbert,

units.la: Episcopus sylvæ candidæ, se ei opposuit; frustra à Leone Allatio eam ob causam sugillatus. Pixidis verò usum nemo ante Burchardum, hominem XI. seculi memoravit. Neque ipse Bellarminus instituti hujus authorem antiquiorem prodere potuit. Nam Pseudo-clementis illa πυξὶς ... non ejusmodi pixides, ciboria, sed לשכה (quam vocem πυξὶς LXX. Interpp. Ezech. XLII.1. reddunt) conclavia, cellas, qualia Sacerdotum & Levitarum apud Templum erant, notat. In oratoriis nempe & Basilicis veterum ex utroque latere exstructa cubilia fuerunt, in quorum altero sacra ministeria, in altero sacri libri reponebantur. Eò etiam synaxeos residua, à religiosis consumenda, inferebantur. De cætero asservationem quandam in veteri Ecclesia usitatam fuisse, nulli diffitemur, eámque tum privatam, ob persecutiones imminentes; tum publicam, propter ægrotantes vel hospites. Sed neutra asservationi pontificiæ favet. Non illa, quia cessante persecutione ejusdem usus cessavit, & à Concilis Cæsaraugustano & Toletano abrogata est. Non hæc, quia & libero more, non lege ulla, uti Tridentina illa, introducta est, neque ubique, vel semper obtinuit. Quin & utriusque illius finis manducatio fuit. At in Romana Ecclesia circumgestatio fit ad ostentationem & pompam; ad incendia; ad cultum adorationis hostiæ, quæ commenta majorem partem magica, idololatrica & ethnica Ecclesiæ veteris sapientiam fugerunt.
units.tr: The Bishop of Silva Candida opposed him, and Leo Allatius reviled him for it, to no avail. Nobody mentioned the use of the pyx before Burchard, a man of the eleventh century. Nor could Bellarmine himself name an older author of this practice. For that pyx of the Pseudo-Clement does not denote pyxes or ciboria of this kind, but chambers, cells [לשכה], such as the priests and Levites had in the Temple (a word the Septuagint translators render πυξὶς in Ezekiel 42:1). In the oratories and basilicas of the ancients there were chambers built on either side, in one of which the sacred vessels were kept and in the other the sacred books. Leftovers of the communion, to be consumed by the devout, were also carried there. We do not deny that some reservation of the elements was practised in the ancient Church, both private, on account of impending persecutions, and public, for the sick or for travellers. But neither supports the papal reservation. The former ceased because the practice ceased with the persecution, and it was abolished by the Councils of Saragossa and Toledo. The latter was introduced by free custom, not by any law such as the Tridentine one, and it did not prevail everywhere or always. Indeed, the purpose of both was eating. But in the Roman Church the host is carried about for display and pomp, to ward off fires, and for the adoration of the victim. These inventions, for the most part magical, idolatrous and heathen, are foreign to the wisdom of the ancient Church.

units.la: LXXXVIII. Frivolæ rationes sunt, quibus asservationem ejusmodi suffulciunt.
units.tr: LXXXVIII. The reasons by which they prop up this reservation are flimsy.

units.la: Nam verba quidem illa Christi: Hoc enim est corpus meum, ante manducationem & usum, fateor; prolata sunt; sed non de pane quovis, verùm de accepto, benedicto, fracto, & ad manducandum jam distributo; atque ita quidem, ut præceptum manducandi, cui statim Apostoli satis facere debuerunt, jam præcesserit. Asservatio proin institutioni Christi repugnat; neque panis corpus Christi est, vel Sacramenti rationem habet, nisi quando fractus distribuitur, manducandus porrigitur, & actu statim manducatur. Accedente quinetiam verbo ad elementum fit Sacramentum, sed non extra actionem, uti ex aqua Baptismi liquet, quæ extra actionem Sacramentum non est. Verba porrò illa: Hoc enim est corpus meum, ante manducationem vera esse potuerunt, sed non absolutè, sive manducarent Apostoli, sive non; verùm κατὰ λ, si præcepto manducandi id, quod jam acceperant, satisfacerent. Quomodo in ordinatione etiam verbum institutionis extra actionem veritatem habere, ipsimet inficiantur. Sensus igitur verborum Christi hic est; quòd Hoc, id est, panis juxta præceptum Christi, acceptus, benedictus, fractus & manducatus, sit corpus Christi. Denique manducatio est hominis suscipientis, non Dei, vel ministri conferentis. Sed non ideo ad integritatem Sacramenti non requiritur, quia ejus objectum est panis consecratus; cujus distributio ex natura relationum præsupponitur. Ipsi quoque adversarii in pœnitentia actiones pœnitentis, seu Sacramentum suscipientis, materiam Sacramenti, & unâ cum forma ejusdem Sacramentum esse asserunt. Nec ulla ratio cogit, non posse à Deo ullam partem Sacramenti constitui actionem suscipientis æquè atque Ministri celebrantis. Nam æquè utraque partes sunt hominis, cujus non est Sacramentum conficere, sed administrare & accipere. Solus Deus efficit, ut hæc vel illa actio, vel susceptio Sacramentum, vel Sacramenti pars sit.
units.tr: For I grant that the words of Christ, For this is my body, were spoken before the eating and use of the bread. But they were not spoken of any bread whatever, but of bread taken, blessed, broken and already distributed for eating. And so the command to eat, which the apostles were bound to obey at once, had already gone before. Reservation therefore conflicts with the institution of Christ. Nor is the bread the body of Christ, or has the character of a sacrament, unless it is broken, distributed, offered to be eaten and eaten at once. Moreover, the word is added to the element and so makes a sacrament, but not outside the action, as is plain from the water of baptism, which is not a sacrament outside the action. Again, those words, For this is my body, could have been true before the eating, but not absolutely, whether the apostles ate or not; rather, they were true only in this sense, that if they ate, they would satisfy the command to eat what they had already received. In the same way, our opponents themselves admit that the words of institution are not true outside the action in ordination. So the sense of Christ's words is this: that this, that is, the bread taken, blessed, broken and eaten according to Christ's command, is his body. Finally, the eating is the act of the person receiving, not of God or of the minister who gives. Yet it is not for that reason excluded from the integrity of the sacrament, because its object is the consecrated bread, whose distribution is presupposed by the nature of the relations. Our opponents also assert that in penance the acts of the penitent, that is, of the one receiving the sacrament, are the matter of the sacrament and, together with the form, constitute it. Nor does any reason compel us to deny that God can make the action of the recipient a part of the sacrament just as much as the action of the minister who celebrates. For both are acts of the man, whose task is not to make the sacrament but to administer and receive it. God alone makes this or that act or reception a sacrament, or a part of one.

units.la: LXXXIX. Alterum convivii hujus symbolum vinum est.
units.tr: LXXXIX. The other symbol of this feast is wine.

units.la: Nam quod in poculo à Christo benedicto & distributo fuit; γενημα ἀμπέλου genimen vitis, quod vinum est; diserte Matth. XXVI. 29. Luc. XXII. 18. appellatur; ut nec cum Bellarmino ex traditione sola id discere, nec cum Tatianis sive Encratitis & Hydroparastatis, seu Aquariis temperantiæ prætextu vinum refugere; ac loco ejus aquam in Sacramento hoc usurpare necesse habeamus. Ac licèt vinum illud, quod Christus cum discipulis bibit; forte aqua dilutum fuerit, pro more gentis, generosa & calida vina sua aqua temperantis; & Ecclesia vetus vino mixto usa sit; quia post Cœnam eodem vino Agapas suas celebrantes, ansam dare gentilibus, quasi mero ad satietatem vel ebrietatem uterentur, noluerunt: tamen præcepti Divini necessitate vini aquâ diluti usus injungi non potest, quod ab Ecclesia Papali factum. Institutio enim aquæ nuspiam meminit, & mixtura veterum, si qua obtinuit; per accidens, ob regionis indolem, obtinuit. Sublata autem indole illa, accidens cessat. Mutatæ circumstantiæ factum ipsum, quatenus ab illis pendet, mutant. Præter mandatum autem & institutionem Christi mixturam ejusmodi, ceu partem cultus, præscribentibus dici potest: יין כמים מזוג vinum tuum aqua mixtum est; Esaj. I. 22. Non parum enim Ecclesiæ libertatem Tridentini læserunt, Sess. XXII. can. 9. anathema iis dicentes; qui aquam vino miscendam ex Christi institutione inficiantur. Tyrannis enim est rem per se adiaphoram sub anathematis & peccati mortalis pœna injungere. Inprimis cum jam ante Concilium Florentinum Armenios, vini meri usum ceu necessarium asserentes; non Divini; sed Ecclesiastici mandati authoritate pesserit. At Ecclesiæ nulla potestas competit; ex rebus liberis necessarias ad cultum, & mysticas cudendi; inprimis cum non desint; qui mixturam hanc non ad esse, sed ad bene esse requiri asserant, quo in numero Thomas, Bonaventura, Richardus; alii sunt. Ipsa Glossa Juris Canonici sciscit, aquam vino admiscendam esse de honestate tantum, quæ verba post Concilium Tridentinum Pii V. jussu expurgata sunt. Jure igitur Richerius, vir suo tempore doctissimus Villagagnoni, necessitatem præcepti urgenti, & de eo jussu Cardinalis Lotharingi controversiam Reformatis moventi; oppositum; & sacrilegium esse; addere quicquam Christi præcepto non sancitum: & blasphemium, dicere; non sine grandi peccato in Cœna omitti, quod juxta Christi institutionem nec ad materiam, nec ad formam Sacramenti pertinet; & hæreticum, affirmare post Aquarios non posse Cœnam sine aqua celebrari, cùm tamen Innocentius VIII. Saxonibus; & alius Pontifex Norvvegis concessisse dicatur, ut sine vino celebrarent, quod, addita Volaterrani authoritate. Puteanus ad 3. Th. q. 47. dub. 2. refert. Quod verò in calice mysterium aquæ & sanguinis ex latere Christi fluentis repræsentari ajunt, frivolum satis videtur. Duo Sacramenta repræsentari veteres nonnulli putarunt; non unum Eucharistiæ, quod sanguinis, non aquæ Sacramentum est. Tum nec quicquid in Passione Domini cernere erat, necesse est in Sacramento aliquid habeat, per quod significetur. Neque magis ad rem facit, quòd unionem aquæ cum vino unionem Ecclesiæ, seu populi cum Christo figurari pertendunt. Licet enim aquæ quandoque populum significent, non tamen id ad ritum extruendum sufficit, quia Theologia symbolica non est argumentativa. Ficulnea igitur hæc machæra est, qua & Tridentinos, & ante ipsos Cæsarium, Rabanum, Paschasium uti non puduit.
units.tr: For what was in the cup blessed and distributed by Christ is the fruit of the vine, which is wine, as Matthew 26:29 and Luke 22:18 expressly call it. So we cannot learn from tradition alone, as Bellarmine does, nor under the pretext of temperance flee the wine with the Tatians, or Encratites and Hydroparastatae, that is, the Aquarians, and must needs use water in this sacrament instead. Although that wine which Christ drank with his disciples may have been diluted with water, according to the custom of the nation, which tempered its strong and hot wines with water, and although the ancient Church used mixed wine, yet it refused to do so because, celebrating its agapes after the supper with the same wine, it gave the Gentiles occasion to think they drank wine to satiety or drunkenness. Nevertheless, the use of wine diluted with water cannot be enjoined by the necessity of a divine precept, as the Papal Church has done. For the institution nowhere mentions water, and such mixture as the ancients observed, if any, prevailed only by accident, on account of the character of the region. When that character is removed, the accident ceases; changed circumstances change the thing itself, insofar as it depends on them. Apart from the command and institution of Christ, such a mixture, as a part of worship, may be enjoined by those who say: your wine is mixed with water (Isaiah 1:22). The Tridentine fathers did no little harm to the liberty of the Church when they pronounced an anathema on those who deny that water is to be mixed with wine by the institution of Christ (Session 22, canon 9). For it is tyranny to impose under pain of anathema and mortal sin a thing that is in itself indifferent, especially since before the Council of Florence the Armenians, who asserted that the use of pure wine was necessary, had been condemned not by divine but by ecclesiastical authority. Yet the Church has no power to make necessary for worship, and mystically to stamp, things that are free, especially since there are those who say that this mixture is required not for being but for well-being, among whom are Thomas, Bonaventure, Richard and others. The Gloss of the Canon Law itself decides that water is to be mixed with wine only for decency, and those words were expunged by order of Pius V after the Council of Trent. Rightly, therefore, Richerius, the most learned man of his time, opposed Villegagnon, who, urging the necessity of the precept, and at the command of the Cardinal of Lorraine, raised the controversy against the Reformed. He argued that it is sacrilege to add anything to Christ's precept that he did not sanction, that it is blasphemy to say that the Lord's Supper may be omitted without great sin when it is not part of the matter or form of the sacrament according to Christ's institution, and that it is heretical to affirm, after the Aquarians, that the supper cannot be celebrated without water. Yet it is said that Innocent VIII granted the Saxons, and another pontiff the Norwegians, leave to celebrate without wine; Puteanus reports this on the third part of Thomas, question 47, doubt 2, on the authority of Volaterranus. As for the claim that the mystery of the water and blood flowing from the side of Christ is represented in the cup, this seems quite frivolous. Some of the ancients thought that two sacraments were represented, not one, for the Eucharist is a sacrament of blood, not of water. Nor is it necessary that everything seen in the passion of the Lord should have something in the sacrament by which it is signified. Nor does it help the case much that they contend that the union of water with wine figures the union of the Church, or of the people, with Christ. For although water sometimes signifies the people, that is not enough to build a rite upon, since symbolic theology is not argumentative. This, then, is a fig-leaf sword, which the Tridentines, and before them Caesarius, Rabanus and Paschasius, were not ashamed to wield.

units.la: XC. Iisdem circa vinum,quibus circa panem ritibus Christus usus est. Nam ante omnia τὸ ποτήριον ἔλαβε poculum accepit, Matth. XXVI.27. Lucas cap.XXII.17.20. bis poculi meminit; ad v.17. Paschale, v.20. Eucharisticum indigetans. Solennis apud Hebræos poculi acceptio erat,qua Paterfamilias illud consecraturus מקבלו בשתי ידיו accepit ambabus manibus & consecrare incipiens נותלו בימינו dextera sua sustulit. Accepto poculo benedixit & gratias egit,Matth.XXVI.27. Marc.XIV.23. Unde ποτήριον εὐλογίας poculum benedictionis 1.Cor. X.16. appellatur. Quomodo iidem Hebræi seorsim etiam poculo benedicere sueverunt,& quidem duplice formula,una ante, altera post sumptum cibum. Prioris formula erat: ברוך אתה יהוה אלהינו מלך העולם בורא פרי הגפן Benedictus sis, Domine Deus noster, Rex mundi, creans fructum vitis. Posterior: נברך שאכלנו משלו ובשובו חיינו Benedicamus ei, qui cibavit nos de suo,cujus bonitate vivimus. An alterutra, & qua formula benedicendi Christus usus sit, incertum est. Cùm tamen ad sublimiorem longè usum, quàm vulgò fiebat,vini usum in Eucharistia provexerit, sublimiore etiam formula uti potuit. De quo inBenedictionis panis ritu dicta huc se vocari debent. Infusionis vini, quæ fractioni panis respondebat,expressa mentio non est, quia nulla peculiari ceremonia peragebatur. In mystica tamen explicatione uti expressa sanguinis Christi fusi mentio est, ita ad eam manifeste alluditur. Inde Christus poculum benedictum ἔδωκε dedit,diserto cum mandato : πίετε ἐξ αὐτοῦ πάντες. Bibite ex eo omnes, Matth.XXVI.27. Et olim quidem fideles calicem simpliciter,atque convivantium in morem acciperent; tum venerabundi & corpore inclinato; demum ori admotum, ut perinde manus à vino,atque à pane abstinerent. Augescente superstitione fistulæ argenteæ adhibitæ sunt,ne quid calicem inter supremáque labra de sanguine Christi periret. Quæ signorum reverentia transubstantiationi incunabula dedit.
units.tr: XC. Christ used the same rites for the wine as for the bread. For first of all he took the cup (Matthew 26:27); Luke 22:17, 20 mentions the cup twice, calling it at verse 17 the Passover cup and at verse 20 the Eucharistic cup. Among the Hebrews the taking of the cup was a solemn act, by which the father of the household, about to consecrate it, took it with both hands [מקבלו בשתי ידיו] and, beginning to consecrate, lifted it in his right hand [נותלו בימינו]. Having taken the cup, he blessed and gave thanks (Matthew 26:27; Mark 14:23). Hence it is called the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16). The same Hebrews were accustomed to bless the cup separately, with a twofold formula, one before and one after the meal. The first formula was: Blessed art thou, O Lord our God, King of the world, creator of the fruit of the vine [ברוך אתה יהוה אלהינו מלך העולם בורא פרי הגפן]. The second: Let us bless him who fed us of his own, by whose goodness we live [נברך שאכלנו משלו ובשובו חיינו]. It is uncertain which of these formulas Christ used, or whether he used either. But since he introduced the use of wine in the Eucharist to a far higher purpose than was common, he may also have used a more exalted formula. On this matter, what has been said on the rite of blessing the bread should be called to mind here. The pouring out of the wine, which corresponded to the breaking of the bread, is not expressly mentioned, because no special ceremony was performed. Yet in the mystical explanation the pouring out of Christ's blood is expressly mentioned, and there is a clear allusion to it. Hence Christ gave the blessed cup, with the express command: Drink ye all of it (Matthew 26:27). Formerly the faithful took the cup simply, in the manner of banqueters, then reverently, with the body bowed, and finally with the cup raised to the mouth, so that they abstained from the wine as they did from the bread. As superstition grew, silver tubes were introduced, lest anything of the blood of Christ be lost from the cup between the lips. This reverence for the signs gave birth to transubstantiation.

units.la: XCI. Immane & non ferendum sacrilegium est Pontificiorum; laicos calicis benedicti usu defraudantium. Nam in Concilio Constantiensi Sess. XIII. sic definitum est: Licet Christus sub utraque specie panis & vini hoc venerabile Sacramentum administraverit: Licet in primitiva Ecclesia idem Sacramentum reciperetur sub utraque specie. TAMEN HOC NON OBSTANTE (ita impia Constantiensium) seu potius Non-obstantiensium ora) illud à conscientibus sub utraque & à laicis tantummodo sub specie panis suscipi debet, atque id habendum pro lege,quam non liceat reprobare, sub poena excommunicationis; statuit. Eadem Concilii Basileensis Sess. XXX. & Tridentini Sess. XXI. cap.1. & can.1. sententia est. Hi enim nequicquam orbe Christiano, Principum oratoribus non paucis, hoc velut beneficium calicis à se instantissimè petentibus,susque deque habitis omnium quæsitissimis precibus & supplicationibus, definiverunt, nullo Divino præcepto laicos & clericos non conscientes obligari ad Eucharistiæ Sacramentum sub utraque specie sumendum; neque ullo pacto salva fide, dubitari posse, quin illis alterius speciei communio ad salutem sufficiat. Eo ipso,quo hæc Tridentini definiverunt, tempore Cresl aus Epis copus Vladislavien sis, Adamum Presbyterum quendam,speciem utramque laicis porrigentem,comburi jussit: Neque obscura sacrilegii causa est; ut potestate & excellentia Sacerdotum amplificata authoritas pro lubitu conscientiis dominandi crescceret, verba promissionis de remissione peccatorum ad Missam facilius transferantur, passimque homines ad eam pretio emendam invitarentur, & Conciliorum atque Pontificum præcedentium nefariæ mutilationis authorum,infallibilitas firmiore talo staret. Quæ Antichristiana sunt, à Spiritu Dei prædicta, præsagiente, quòd futurum sit, ut non occisi in plagis,non resipiscant ἐκ τῶν χλεμμάτων de furtis suis, Apoc. IX.21.
units.tr: XCI. The Papists are guilty of an immense and intolerable sacrilege in depriving the laity of the use of the blessed cup. For the Council of Constance, Session XIII, defined as follows: Although Christ administered this venerable Sacrament under both kinds of bread and wine; although in the primitive Church the same Sacrament was received under both kinds. NEVERTHELESS, NOTWITHSTANDING THIS (so say the impious mouths of the Constantians, or rather the Non-obstantians), it ought to be received by those who are communicants under both kinds, and by the laity only under the kind of bread, and this is to be held as a law which it is not lawful to reject, under pain of excommunication. The Council of Basel, Session XXX, and the Council of Trent, Session XXI, chapter 1 and canon 1, hold the same opinion. For these men, though the Christian world was full of ambassadors of princes who most urgently sought this favour of the cup, and though the most earnest prayers and supplications were made to them, treated them as nothing and cared nothing for them; they defined that by no divine precept are the laity and the non-communicating clergy bound to receive the Sacrament of the Eucharist under both kinds; nor can it be doubted in any way, without loss of faith, that communion in one kind is sufficient for their salvation. At the very time when the Council of Trent made these definitions, Kreslaus, bishop of Wladislaw, ordered a certain priest, Adam, who gave both kinds to the laity, to be burned. Nor is the cause of this sacrilege obscure: the authority of priests, increased by their power and eminence, might grow so as to lord it over consciences at will; the words of promise concerning the remission of sins might more easily be transferred to the Mass; men might everywhere be invited to buy it for a price; and the infallibility of the Councils and of the earlier Popes, the authors of this wicked mutilation, might stand on firmer ground. These things are Antichristian, foretold by the Spirit of God, who foresaw that it would come to pass that they did not repent of their murders, nor of their sorceries, nor of their fornication, nor of their thefts [ἐκ τῶν κλεμμάτων], Rev. IX.21.

units.la: XCII. Sed vera Christi Ecclesia à Christi Testamento,& signaculis ejus ab eodem fidelibus sine discrimine omnibus liberaliter concessis,quæ inter calicis etiam usus est,adeò neminem secludit,ut potius sicut esurientes, ita sitientes omnes Christi Domini ipsius authoritate freta, prolixè invitet. Compellit ad id institutio ejusdem, qui, quos manducare jusserat,eosdem etiam bibere jussit. Bibite, ajens, ex hoc omnes, Matth. XXVI.27. Quo audito præcepto, ἔπιον ἐξ αὐτοῦ biberunt ex eo poculo omnes, Marc.XIV.23. Hoc autem etiam in posterum sacram Domini Coenam celebrantibus faciundum imitandúmque esse,liquet ex præcepto Christi: Hoc facite ad mei commemorationem, Luc.XXII.19. Quæ necessitas est administrandi & manducandi panem, eadem est porrigendi calicem,& ex eo bibendi,quia Christus ὡσαύτως similiter (sicut panem) accepit calicem, ei benedixit, & ex eo bibere jussit. Par ergo utriusque necessitas est,ut vel utrumque symbolum,adeóque Sacramentum totum, negligere fas sit, vel alterutrum negligere nefas sit. Dicta hæc sunt, fateor, ad Apostolos, sed non ut Apostolos, nedum ut conficientes (solus enim Christus confecerat) verùm ut μαθητὰς discipulos, uti diserte Evangelista Matth. XXVI.26. appellat,hoc est,& fideles,& fideles deinceps universos repræsentantes. Ideo sanguis ejus,cujus symbolum vinum Christus instituit ὑπὲρ πολλῶν pro multis, hoc est,fidelibus universis effusus dicitur, ibid. vers.28. Ergo τὸ πᾶντες omnes universè ad omnes fideles pertinet,ad quos Sacramentum pertinet. Illi enim omnes sicut edere, ita bibere jubentur. Unde Paschasius de corp. & sang. Dom. c.15. sic· πα-ντες ἐπεὶ φηση: Accipite,& bibite ex hoc omnes,tam miniministri, quàm reliqui credentes. Hic est calix sanguinis mei, novi & æterni Testamenti. Licèt ergo soli Apostoli adfuerint, tamen finis Christi fuit, præscribere Ecclesiæ rationem administrandi Cœnam, quam servari vellet, usque dum venerit ad judicandum. Quod nisi nobiscum adversarii fatentur, unde comprobabunt priorem Cœnæ partem, hoc est, manducationem panis, ad laicos pertinere? Præsertim cùm in ea signum universale OMNES non æquè ac in calicis præcepto legatur. Neque obstat, quòd Lucas dicit, Christum accepisse poculum μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι post cœnandum, cap. XXII. 20. Quod eodem ordine Paulus 1. Cor. XI. 25. repetit, quasi Christus in Cœna panem comederit, & comedi jusserit: at post Cœnam, adeóque finito jam Sacramento calicem demum propinaverit, & ex eo bibere Apostolos jusserit, rem scilicet indifferentem indicans. Nam illud μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι post cœnandum manifestam habet rationem, ad alterum poculum in Cœna Paschali propinatum, & ab eodem Luca cap. XXII. 17. commemoratum, adeóque non poculum à pane Eucharistico, sed à poculo Paschali, ceu ab eo diversum disterminat. Quod etiam Lucas Burgensis observat. Et de hoc quicquid sit, standum Christianis est mandato Christi, jubentis sicut edere, ita etiam bibere; sive ipse cum discipulis in Cœna, sive sub finem Cœnæ bibit. Inprimis cùm ὡσαύτως similiter uti panem, sic calicem accepisse, ei benedixisse, ex eo bibere jussisse omnes dicatur. Neque ullum error colorem in eo habet, quòd Christus τοῦτο ποιεῖν hoc facere ad sui commemorationem tantùm post institutionem panis, non post institutionem calicis jussit, Luc. XXII. 19. quasi, qui nuper benigni Bossueti, Meldensis & Condomensis Episcopi, triumphus est, mirabili Dei providentia id factum sit, ut intelligant omnes, vinum non dandum esse omnibus. Sed nos vicissim miramur Dei providentiam, & Spiritus S. sapientissimam libertatem, quais Paulo, etiamsi is Lucam ante oculos habuisse inprimis videatur, ea verba post mentionem poculi quoque suggerere 1. Cor. XI. 25. voluit. Prævidit enim Spiritus S. fore, ut ordine verborum Lucæ Sophistæ ad erroris sui patrocinium abutantur.
units.tr: XCII. But the true Church of Christ, from the Testament of Christ and its seals, which are freely given without distinction to all the faithful, and among which is the use of the cup, does not shut out anyone at all; rather, relying on the authority of the Lord Christ himself, it invites all who thirst, just as it invites those who hunger, most abundantly. The institution of the same Christ compels this, for he who had ordered them to eat also ordered them to drink. Saying, Drink ye all of this, Matt. XXVI.27. When this command was heard, they all drank of it [ἔπιον ἐξ αὐτοῦ], that is, of the cup, Mark XIV.23. It is clear from the command of Christ that this too is to be done and imitated by those who celebrate the holy Supper of the Lord in future: Do this in remembrance of me, Luke XXII.19. The necessity of administering and eating the bread is the same as the necessity of offering the cup and drinking from it, because Christ likewise [ὡσαύτως] took the cup, and gave thanks over it, and ordered them to drink from it. There is therefore an equal necessity for both: it is either permissible to neglect both symbols, and thus the whole Sacrament, or it is wrong to neglect either of them. I admit that these words were spoken to the Apostles, but not as Apostles, still less as those who celebrate (for Christ alone had celebrated), but as disciples [μαθηταί], as the Evangelist expressly calls them, Matt. XXVI.26; that is, as believers, and as representing all believers thereafter. Therefore his blood, whose symbol Christ instituted as wine, is said to be poured out for many [ὑπὲρ πολλῶν], that is, for all the faithful, ibid., verse 28. Therefore all [τὸ πάντες] pertains universally to all the faithful, to whom the Sacrament pertains. For all of them are commanded to drink just as they are commanded to eat. Hence Paschasius, On the Body and Blood of the Lord, chapter 15, says: Take and drink of this, all of you, both ministers and the rest of the believers. This is the cup of my blood, of the new and eternal Testament. Although only the Apostles were present, nevertheless it was Christ's purpose to prescribe to the Church the manner of administering the Supper which he wished to be kept until he comes to judge. Unless our opponents agree with us in this, how will they prove that the first part of the Supper, that is, the eating of the bread, pertains to the laity? Especially since in that passage the universal sign all is not read as it is in the command concerning the cup.
