Nor is it an obstacle that Luke says Christ took the cup after supper [μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι], chapter XXII.20. Paul repeats this in the same order, 1 Cor. XI.25, as if Christ had eaten the bread at the Supper and ordered it to be eaten, but then, after the Supper, and so with the Sacrament now finished, at last offered the cup and ordered the Apostles to drink from it, clearly indicating a matter of no consequence. For the phrase after supper [μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι] has a plain reason: it refers to the other cup offered during the Passover meal, which the same Luke mentions in chapter XXII.17, and so it distinguishes the cup not from the Eucharistic bread but from the Passover cup, as something different from it. Lucas Burgensis also observes this. Whatever the case about this, Christians must abide by the command of Christ, who orders them to drink just as they eat, whether he himself drank with the disciples during the Supper or at the end of it. Especially since it is said that he likewise [ὡσαύτως] took the cup just as he took the bread, gave thanks over it, and ordered all to drink from it. Nor does any error gain colour from the fact that Christ ordered this do [τοῦτο ποιεῖν], to do in remembrance of him, only after the institution of the bread and not after the institution of the cup, Luke XXII.19, as if, by a wonderful providence of God, it was done so that all might understand that wine is not to be given to everyone. This is the recent triumph of the kindly Bossuet, Bishop of Meaux and Condom. But in turn we marvel at the providence of God and the most wise freedom of the Holy Spirit, who wished that Paul, even though he seems chiefly to have had Luke before his eyes, should add those words after mention of the cup as well, 1 Cor. XI.25. For the Holy Spirit foresaw that the sophists would abuse the order of Luke's words in defence of their error.

units.la: XCIII. Hic ergo veritatis triumphus est, quòd collatis Evangelistarum & Pauli de pane & vino verbis adeò nullum; quoad mandatum edendi & bibendi, personarum communicantium respectu, discrimen occurrat, ut nemo, qui Scripturæ credit, & veritatem fideíque certitudinem quærit, de eo vel tantillum ambigere possit. Nam Christus juxta consonam narrationem omnium, in eadem Cœna pane & vino usus est: utrumque dedit, unum post alterum: idem circa utrumque egit, data opera, accipiendo, benedicendo, distribuendo, jubendo comedere, bibere, & ne ullum discrimen fingi posset, addidit, ὡσαύτως similiter, similiter plane modo, hoc est, eodem animo, eodem fine: circa utrumque, quantum ad modum sanctificationis, consecrationis, seu applicationis ad usum gratiæ & religionis, idem egit: iisdem convivis utrumque dedit, ne minimo quidem personarum & officiorum discrimine: Apostolos simpliciter consideravit ut μαθητὰς discipulos, quæ appellatio erat omnium in Christum credentium, à quibus, ut & LXX. illis, aliás characterè Apostolorum distingui solebant: Poculum porrexit αὐτοῖς illis ipsis, ut nemo unquam de duplici ipsorum persona, quasi in ipsa scena, mutata, gregariorum fidelium altera, cùm panis sumeretur; Sacerdotum altera, cùm biberetur, vel per somnium cogitaturus fuerit, nisi invalescens error quidvis confingere subegisset, ne sacrilegium pelluceret: utrumque symbolum, eodem actus genere dedit: utrumque pari usu externo adhiberi, illud manducari, hoc bibi jussit: bibere jussit omnes, qui bibere in commemorationem Christi, & mortem ejus annuntiare possunt, cùm manducare omnes expressis verbis non jusserit, haud obscure futurum illud sacrilegium ad perpetuam memoriam notans, & velut stigmate compungens: utrumque facere in sui recordationem jussit: calici non minùs quàm pani mysticam relationem, qua usus & fructus ejus indigetatur, addit; huic, quòd sit corpus pro nobis datum, illi, quòd sit sanguis N. T. pro multis effusus, ad remissionem peccatorum, non pani, quòd sit sanguis, vel poculo, quòd sit corpus; ut clarissimè inde constet, neminem corpus & sanguinem Christi sacramentaliter accipere posse, nisi, quantum in se est, utendo simul utroque symbolo. Fides enim in Sacramentis se verbis adstringit, & juxta ea meditationem in illis, quæ sensus feriunt, instituit. Ut jam figmentum illud concomitantiæ corporis & sanguinis Christi suppetias ferre non posset. Licèt enim nemo cum parte Christi sensum communionem habere posset, quia Christus non est divisus, 1. Cor. I. 13. & nemo, qui Christi particeps fit, communionem nisi cum toto Christo ἀνθρώπῳ accipiat; tamen ad fruendum communione Christi, diversa media, quæ Christus sapienter instituit & præcepit; adhibeanda sunt. Idem enim Christus fidei aliter atque aliter secundum diversa beneficia objici, & communionis ejus gradus fructúsque diversi dari possunt. Ideo Alensis Summ. p. IV. q. 60. m. 3. art. 2. Totus, inquit, Christus non continetur sub utraque specie sacramentaliter, sed caro tantùm sub specie panis, sanguis tantùm sub specie vini. Accipitur Christus totus per fidem; extra omne etiam Sacramentum. Nihilominus sapientissimus optimusque salvator Sacramentum, fidei sub distinctis symbolis subsidium & exercitium præscripsit, quod nisi Christo & fide ipsa contempta contemni nequit. XCIV. Sed mysterium vini æquè bibendi atque panis manducandi pensitemus. Juslit enim Christus discipulos bibere, addita ratione τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι τὸ αἷμά μου, Hoc enim est sanguis meus pro vobis effusus, Matth. XXVI. 28. Sicut igitur panem, corpus quippe suum quod, ceu victimam piacularem, in mortem pro nobis tradidit, comedere; ita vinum, ceu sanguinem suum pro ipsis effusum, bibere eosdem jussit. In V. T. prohibuit Deus, ne quisquam vescretur carne sacrificii piacularis pro suis peccatis oblati. Sive enim pro privato Israelita immolatum esset, Sacerdos solus eas partes comedebat, quæ combustæ non essent: sive pro ipso summo Sacerdote, aut toto cœtu filiorum Israel, non exclusò Sacerdote, integrum sacrificium igni erat absumendum. Nemo enim proprio corpore pro se ipso peccati expiationem facere potest. Qui verò partem sacrificii in suam carnem vescendo convertebat, reliquam partem quasi sui corporis immolare censebatur. Sacerdos autem pro aliis offerens typum gerebat veri illius Sacerdotis, se ipsum pro aliis oblaturi, ad quam rem adumbrandam ipse in communionem victimæ, quæ pro aliis offerretur, veniebat. Cùm tamen ipse sibi sufficere non potuerit, hinc ex eadem ratione, qua gregario Israelitæ ipsi etiam de sacrificio pro se ipso oblato comedere nefas fuit, ne se ipsum pro peccato suo obtulisse putaretur. Cúmque Sanctificator & sanctificati esse ex uno, Heb.II.11. adeoq; communionem intimam ad sanctificationem & vivificationem invicem habere debeant, liquere poterat, nondum veram sanctificationem & vivificationem peractam esse, quandiu carnem sacrificii piacularis comedendo in vitæ suæ spiritualis partem convertere nondum licuit. Imò quoties absumi illud igne & in fumum abire viderunt, colligendum illis fuit, sacrificia ejusmodi non esse paria iræ Divinæ ferendæ & extinguendæ; neque ex illis flammis salva emergere, & quasi rediviva vivere in iis, pro quibus oblata essent, posse. Ne ergo veram expiationem in sacrificiis talibus veteres sperarent, vetitum iis gravissimè est, ne carnes eorum comederent. Sed quando Christus venit, & carnem suam pro vita mundi dedit, & eandem ad gloriam Patris vivificavit, jam idem ille carnem suam omnibus fidelibus manducandam offerre debuit, ut vitam in se haberent, & æternùm per eam vivèrent, Joh. VI.51--58. Neque hoc tantùm, sed etiam illius rei symbolum, panem, omnibus manducandum dedit, & manducantibus fidem fecit, quòd communionem habeant cum corpore Christi pro se crucifixo, & ex morte resuscitato, quæ consummata illorum consolatio est, qua veteres à carnis piacularis typicæ esu abstenti non ita fruebantur. Neque tantùm carnis illius esus, sed etiam sanguinis potus, & striẞiore quidem interdicto prohibitus est: Si quis comederit sanguinem, ponam faciem meam contra animam illam, &c. quia anima carnis in sanguine est. Ego autem dedi illum vobis super altari, ad expiationem faciendam super animabus vestris, si quidem sanguis expiat animam; Levit. XVII. 10-14. Per peccatum enim non vita duntaxat corporis, sed anima etiam reatum mortis contraxit. Totus verò homo corpore & anima constans redimi, corpus per destructionem corporis vicarii: anima per substitutionem animæ vicariæ, inprimis animæ Pontificis veri, qui Christus est, in quam ira Dei desæviret, & quæ legi satisfaceret, debuit. Hæc in elementis mundi adumbrare placuit. Ideo corporis mors in morte carnis bestiæ clarè expressa est. At bestiæ animam, qualis hominis est, non habent. Habent tamen analogum quid, sanguinem, & in eodem motum spirituum, qui animæ loco est. Sanguis ergo sacrificii in altari respersus, & ad pedem ejus effusus, animæ peccatoris, simúlque Christi, veræ victimæ piacularis conspicuus typus fuit. Illè Deo devotus, effusus perditus est. Hæc Deo devota puniri non per destructionem substantiæ, sed per privationem communionis cum Deo, quæ animæ peccantis
units.tr: XCIII. Here, then, is the triumph of truth: when the words of the Evangelists and of Paul about the bread and the wine are compared, there is no difference at all with respect to the command to eat and drink or to the persons who communicate. So no one who believes Scripture and seeks the truth and the certainty of faith could have the slightest doubt about it. For, according to the agreeing account of all of them, Christ used both bread and wine in the same Supper. He gave both, one after the other. He did the same thing with each, deliberately: taking, blessing, distributing, and commanding them to eat and to drink. And, so that no difference could be invented, he added ὡσαύτως [hōsautōs], "likewise" (in just the same way), that is, with the same intention and the same purpose. With regard to both, he did the same thing as to the manner of sanctifying, consecrating, or applying them to the use of grace and of religion. He gave both to the same guests, with no difference at all in persons or in offices. He regarded the Apostles simply as μαθηταί [mathētai], disciples, a name shared by all who believe in Christ, by which they were usually distinguished, as also by the Seventy, from other characters of the Apostles. He handed the cup to those very same men, so that no one could ever think, as if the scene had changed, that when the bread was taken they were ordinary believers, and when the wine was drunk they were priests. Nor would anyone have thought this even in a dream, unless a growing error had compelled people to invent something, so that the sacrilege would not show through. He gave both symbols in the same kind of action. He ordered both to be used in the same outward way: he ordered the one to be eaten and the other to be drunk. He ordered all who can drink in remembrance of Christ and proclaim his death to drink, though he did not expressly order all to eat. Clearly he was marking that future sacrilege for perpetual memory, as if pricking it with a brand. He commanded them to do both in remembrance of himself. To the cup, no less than to the bread, he attaches a mystical account of its use and fruit: to the bread, that it is his body given for us; to the cup, that it is the blood of the New Testament poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. The bread is not said to be the blood, nor the cup to be the body. From this it is most clearly established that no one can receive the body and blood of Christ sacramentally unless, so far as lies in him, he uses both symbols together. For faith is bound to the words in the Sacraments, and according to them it establishes its meditation upon the things that strike the senses. So that fiction about the concomitance of Christ's body and blood cannot come to its aid. For although no one could have communion with a part of Christ, since Christ is not divided (1 Cor. 1:13), and no one who becomes a partaker of Christ receives communion except with the whole Christ as ἀνθρώπῳ [anthrōpō] (as man), nevertheless, to enjoy communion with Christ, different means must be used, which Christ wisely instituted and commanded. For the same Christ can be set before faith in different ways according to different benefits, and different degrees and fruits of his communion can be given. Therefore Alensis, in his Summa, part IV, question 60, member 3, article 2, says: "The whole Christ is not contained sacramentally under both kinds, but only his flesh under the species of bread and only his blood under the species of wine. Christ is received whole through faith, even outside any Sacrament." Nevertheless, the most wise and best Saviour prescribed the Sacrament, with distinct symbols, as an aid and exercise for faith. This cannot be despised except by despising Christ and faith itself. XCIV. But let us weigh the mystery of drinking the wine equally with eating the bread. Christ ordered the disciples to drink, adding the reason: τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι τὸ αἷμά μου [touto gar estin to haima mou], "For this is my blood, which is shed for you" (Matt. 26:28). Just as he gave them the bread, which is his body given up to death for us like a sin-offering, to eat, so he ordered them to drink the wine, as his blood poured out for them. In the Old Testament God forbade anyone to eat the flesh of a sin-offering offered for his own sins. For if it was offered for a private Israelite, the priest alone ate those parts that were not burned. If it was offered for the high priest himself, or for the whole assembly of the sons of Israel, the priest not being excluded, the whole sacrifice had to be consumed by fire. For no one can make atonement for sin for himself by his own body. But whoever, by eating, turned part of the sacrifice into his own flesh was considered to have offered the remainder as his own body. The priest, however, offering for others, bore the type of that true Priest who would offer himself for others, and to shadow forth this he himself entered into communion with the victim that was offered for others. Yet since he could not suffice for himself, for the same reason it was unlawful even for an ordinary Israelite to eat of the sacrifice offered for himself, lest he be thought to have offered himself for his own sin. And since "the Sanctifier and those who are sanctified are all of one" (Heb. 2:11), and therefore ought to have intimate communion with one another for sanctification and quickening, it could be made clear that true sanctification and quickening had not yet been accomplished, as long as it was not yet lawful to turn the flesh of the sin-offering, by eating it, into a part of their spiritual life. Indeed, whenever they saw that it was consumed by fire and went up in smoke, they had to conclude that such sacrifices were not equal to bearing and quenching the wrath of God, nor could they emerge safe from those flames and live as if restored to life in those for whom they were offered. So, lest the ancients hope for true atonement in such sacrifices, it was most strictly forbidden to them to eat their flesh. But when Christ came, and gave his flesh for the life of the world, and quickened the same flesh to the glory of the Father, then he himself ought to offer that same flesh for all believers to eat, so that they might have life in themselves and live for ever through it (John 6:51–58). And not only this, but he also gave the symbol of that thing, bread, to be eaten by all, and made it certain to those who eat that they have communion with the body of Christ crucified for them and raised from death. This is the consummate consolation of their faith, which the ancients did not enjoy in the same way when they abstained from eating the flesh of the typical sin-offering. Nor is only the eating of that flesh forbidden, but the drinking of the blood also, and with an even stricter prohibition: "If anyone eats blood, I will set my face against that soul, etc., because the life of the flesh is in the blood. But I have given it to you upon the altar, to make atonement upon your souls; for it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul" (Lev. 17:10–14). For through sin not only the life of the body but also the soul has incurred the guilt of death. Yet the whole man, consisting of body and soul, had to be redeemed: the body through the destruction of a substitute body, the soul through the substitution of a substitute soul, above all the soul of the true High Priest, who is Christ, upon whom the wrath of God would rage and who would satisfy the law. It pleased God to shadow forth these things in the elements of the world. Therefore the death of the body is clearly expressed in the death of the flesh of the beast. But beasts do not have a soul such as man has. Yet they have something analogous, the blood, and in it the motion of the spirits, which takes the place of the soul. So the blood of the sacrifice, sprinkled on the altar and poured out at its foot, was a visible type both of the soul of the sinner and of Christ, the true sin-offering. That blood, devoted to God, was poured out and lost. These things devoted to God ought to be punished not by the destruction of their substance, but by the privation of communion with God, which is the punishment of the sinning soul.

units.la: poena est, debuit. Unde sanguis Christi à corpore ejus distinctus non tam materialem corporis liquorem, quàm animam ejus notat, quod pluribus Loc. XII. 74. ostendimus. Ne verò ante Christum quisquam eam in cogitationem incideret, quasi anima bestiæ redimendis animabus sufficeret, Deus sanguinem totum perire, & nihil ex eo in communionem ejus, pro cujus anima typicè expianda sanguis oblatus & effusus est, per ejus esum venire voluit, secus quàm in N.T. ubi sanguis veri Pontificis animas nostras expians ex mandato ejusdem manducari, in signo, vino symbolicè, in re verò ipsa etiam spiritualiter, atque ita in communionem ejus, pro quo effusus est, venire debet. Qui manducat carnem meam, & bibit sanguinem meum, habet vitam æternam, &c. Joh. VI.54. Sicut igitur Deus in V.T. redemptionem corporis & animæ peccatoris perChristum præstandam distinctis typis, victimæ piacularis carnis & sanguinis figurare: ita Christus in N.T. eandem præstitam distinctis symbolis panis & vini, illius comedendi, hujus bibendi, ut redemptionem per Christum consummatam esse, & credentes in ipsum perfectam cum eodem communionem habere constare possit, repræsentare voluit. Quæ plane ostendunt, quantæ consolationis & lætitiæ spiritualis momentum in eo vertatur, quòd nunc calicem, quo tam arcta, tam salutaris cum sanguine illo salutifero communio offertur, bibere jubemur: & quanta impietas sit hominum, calicis usu interdicentium, & simul mysterium tantum, de quo nec ipsi cogitant, nec alios cogitare sinunt, intervertentium. Neque mirum est, symbolum negare eos, qui mysterium, vicarias animæ Christi pro nostris animabus passiones, & consummatam redemptionem ejusdem abnegant.
units.tr: was owed. Hence the blood of Christ, distinguished from his body, signifies not so much the material liquid of the body as his soul, as we have shown in several places (Loc. XII. 74.). Lest anyone before Christ should suppose that the soul of a beast was sufficient to redeem souls, God willed that the whole blood should perish and that none of it should come, by being eaten, into communion with him for whose soul the blood was offered and poured out as a typical expiation. It was otherwise in the New Testament, where the blood of the true High Priest, which expiates our souls, is to be eaten by command of the same Priest: in the sign, sacramentally in the wine, but in the thing itself, spiritually, and so it must come into communion with him for whom it was poured out. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, etc. (Joh. VI.54.). Therefore, just as God in the Old Testament willed to represent by distinct types, the flesh and blood of the sacrificial victim, the redemption of the body and soul of the sinner to be accomplished through Christ, so Christ in the New Testament willed to represent, by the distinct symbols of bread and wine, the same redemption accomplished: the eating of the one and the drinking of the other, so that it may be clear that redemption through Christ is consummated and that believers have perfect communion with him. These things plainly show how great a matter of consolation and spiritual joy it is that we are now commanded to drink from the cup, by which so close and so saving a communion with that life-giving blood is offered; and how great is the impiety of those men who forbid the use of the cup and at the same time subvert the mystery, which they themselves do not think about and do not allow others to think about. Nor is it surprising that they deny the symbol who deny the mystery of the vicarious sufferings of Christ's soul for our souls and of the consummated redemption.

units.la: XCV. Institutioni Christi & mysterio calicis alia accedunt, ex quibus calicis communio confirmatur. Ante omnia enim Christi institutionem & mandatum Apostoli & Christiani primi religiosè secuti sunt. Nam S. Paulus secutus traditionem Domini Ecclesiam Corinthiacam ad communionem utriusque symboli obligavit, repetitis pœne iisdem verbis Lucæ 1.Cor.XI.23.24. ubi etiam manducationem & bibitionem, velut duas essentiales ejusdem mysterii partes per particulam ὡσαύτως similiter connectit, & in consectarius ex verbis institutionis Domini deductis, tanquam inseparabiles, perpetuò conjungit. Neque obstat, quòd panis usum absolutè ab eo præscribi, dicente: Hoc facite ad recordationem mei, v.24. Calicis autem cum conditione, quia dicit: Hoc facite, ὁσάκις quoties bibitis, &c. v.25. Nam statim v.26. illud ὁσάκις de utroque symbolo usurpat, dicens: Ὁσάκις quoties ederitis panem hunc, & calicem hunc biberitis, mortem Domini annuntiate. Tum calicem vocat Christus Καινὴ Διαθήκη Novum Testamentum in suo sanguine, hoc est, sanguinem N.T. seu symbolum sanguinis illius, quo Novum Testamentum ratificatum est, Luc. XXII.20. Ad quos igitur Testamentum, ejusque ratificatio pertinet, ad eosdem calicis usus pertinet. Atqui ad fideles universos Testamentum pertinet, utpote qui in eo scripti hæredes sunt. Et sicut nefas est Testamento mento humano, nedum Divino ἐπιλαπικῶς ἐπιθυμ supra disponere, Gal. III. 15. ita supra Testamenti Sacramentum disponere nefas pariter est. Praeterea sublato calice repraesentatio Christi, velut sanguine fuso mortui, nec non solidae integraeque nutritionis per corpus & sanguinem Christi repraesentatio, & cum eodem viva & perfecta consolatio de remissione peccatorum, quae bibitioni aeque ac manducationi annexa est, tollitur. Sacramenta enim eum in finem instituuntur, ut de promissionum Divinarum veritate certiores reddant. Sed & Christus bibere aeque ac comedere εἰς ἀνάμνησιν ad recordationem sui & mortis suae jussit, Luc. XXII. 19. 1. Cor. XI. 26. Non caret enim mysterio, quod sanguis Christi effusus ad remissionem peccatorum, & ejusdem ἀνάμνησις commemoratio seu recordatio per symbolum non panis duntaxat, sed etiam calicis facta dicitur. Nam haec ἀνάμνησις recordatio Christi & mortis ejus directe opponitur illi ἀνάμνησιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν recordationi peccatorum, quae in sacrificiis veterum, non peccata vere expiantibus, sed non expiata commemorantibus, erat, Heb. X. 3. ut jam absque piaculo illud Christianorum privilegium violari, & a calice salutis repelli isti non possint. Denique & vinum potius, quam quivis potus alius, laetitiae quippe & consolationis signum, adhibitum est. Olim enim a vini libamine, utpote altari infundendo, Num. XV. 10. fideles arcebantur. Contra saepissime Prophetiae promittunt vinum novum, atque illud abundantissimum, & sine pretio. Omnes sitientes venite, &c. Emite absque argento, & absque pretio vinum, Esaj. LV. 1. Mox autem post porrectum calicem N. T. dixit: Non bibam ex hoc tempore ex hoc fructu vitis, usque ad diem illum, cum ipsum bibam vobiscum καινὸν novum in Regno Patris mei, Matth. XXVI. 29. Ego Testamento lego vobis Regnum, sicut mihi legavit Pater meus, ut edatis & bibatis in mensa mea in Regno meo, Luc. XXII. 29. Novum illud vinum consummata ejus justitia, pax & gaudium in Spiritu S. est. Hoc nos πιστεύω potat, 1. Cor. XII. 13. ubi non obscure ad calicem Eucharisticum digitus intenditur.
units.tr: XCV. Other matters are added to the institution of Christ and to the mystery of the cup, by which the communion of the cup is confirmed. First of all, the Apostles and the first Christians faithfully followed the institution and command of Christ. For St Paul, following the tradition of the Lord, bound the Corinthian Church to the communion of both symbols, repeating almost the same words as Luke (1 Cor. XI.23.24.). There too he joins eating and drinking, as two essential parts of the same mystery, by the particle likewise [ὡσαύτως], and as consequences drawn from the words of the Lord's institution he always joins them together as inseparable. Nor is it an objection that he prescribes the use of the bread absolutely, saying: Do this in remembrance of me (v.24.), while the cup is given with a condition, since he says: Do this, as often as [ὁσάκις] you drink, etc. (v.25.). For immediately at v.26 he applies that as often as to both symbols, saying: As often as [ὁσάκις] you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord. Then Christ calls the cup the New Testament in his blood [Καινὴ Διαθήκη], that is, the blood of the New Testament or the symbol of that blood by which the New Testament was ratified (Luk. XXII.20.). Therefore, the use of the cup belongs to those to whom the Testament and its ratification belong. But the Testament belongs to all the faithful, since they are written heirs in it. And just as it is unlawful to add to or set aside [ἐπιδιατάσσεται] a human testament, much less a divine one (Gal. III.15.), so it is equally unlawful to dispose of the sacrament of the Testament. Moreover, if the cup is removed, the representation of Christ as one dead by the shedding of blood is removed, as is the representation of solid and complete nourishment through the body and blood of Christ, together with the living and perfect consolation of the remission of sins, which is joined to drinking as much as to eating. For sacraments are instituted for this end, that they may make us more certain of the truth of the divine promises. But Christ also commanded us to drink as well as to eat for the remembrance [εἰς ἀνάμνησιν] of himself and of his death (Luk. XXII.19.; 1 Cor. XI.26.). For there is a mystery in the fact that the blood of Christ was poured out for the remission of sins, and that its remembrance [ἀνάμνησις], recollection, is said to be made by a symbol not of bread only but also of the cup. For this remembrance [ἀνάμνησις] of Christ and of his death is directly opposed to that remembrance of sins [ἀνάμνησιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν], which in the sacrifices of the ancients, which did not truly expiate sins but only recalled unexpiated ones, was made (Heb. X.3.). So these men cannot now violate that privilege of Christians without sin, nor exclude them from the cup of salvation. Finally, wine rather than any other drink has been used, as a sign of joy and consolation indeed. For in former times the faithful were kept from the libation of wine, since it was poured out on the altar (Num. XV.10.). On the contrary, the prophecies very often promise new wine, and that in great abundance and without price: All you who thirst, come, etc., Buy wine without money and without price (Isa. LV.1.). Soon after he had handed the cup of the New Testament, he said: From now on I will not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new [καινὸν] with you in the Kingdom of my Father (Matth. XXVI.29.). I bequeath to you a kingdom, as my Father bequeathed to me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom (Luk. XXII.29.). That new wine is his consummated righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. By this we are all made to drink [ἐποτίσθημεν] (1 Cor. XII.13.), where the finger is plainly pointed at the Eucharistic cup.

units.la: XCVI. Has etiam ob causas praegnantissimas Ecclesia vetus Orientalis & Occidentalis in Sacramento Eucharistiae sicut panem ad manducandum, ita vinum ad bibendum distribuit.
units.tr: 96. For these very weighty reasons, the ancient Church, both Eastern and Western, distributed bread to be eaten and wine to be drunk in the sacrament of the Eucharist.

units.la: Quod viri Ecclesiastice antiquitatis petitissimi, Mornaeus, Hospinianus, Calixtus & Daillaeus amplissime confirmarunt. Fatetur id ipsum quoque Concilium Constantiense; Licet, inquiens; in primitiva Ecclesia hujusmodi Sacramentum receptum fit a fidelibus sub utraque specie, &c. Et de Orientali Ecclesia diserte id ipsum Cassander fatetur; neque inficiari ausus est Leo Allatius, paucis casibus exceptis. In Ecclesia vero Latina mille ultra annos communionem sub utraque integram mansisse, & eo ipso tempore, quo dimidiata in locis quibusdam incessit, in aliis, Monasteriis inprimis ad MCD. usque integram retentam esse idem Cassander probavit. Adeo vero institutionis Christi tenax Ecclesia fuit, uti qui Leonis M. tempore solum panem acceperunt, pro Manichaeis, qui vinum fel Draconis appellarunt, habiti fuerint; ipso Leone M. Sermone 4. de quadragesima teste. Tantum abest, ut liberè, non ulla necessitatis opinione, sub utraque specie Eucharistiam veteres distribuerint, quod audacter adversarii fingunt, nullo teste idoneo. Neque enim eo licentiae progressi sunt, ut crederent, licet Christus sub utraque specie Sacramentum hoc administraverit, &c. tamen hoc non obstante illud à laicis sub una specie suscipi debere. Nondum πνεῦμα καταψυξεως spiritus soporis & vertiginis ita illas religiosiores longè institutionis & mandati Christi aestimatores, dementaverat. Quantopere vero in ipsa Tridentina Synodo Germani, Galli, Bohemi alii in id incubuerint, ut Ecclesiae calix restitueretur, eo usque negotium promovientes, ut quinquaginta ampliùs Praesules in partes suas pertraxerint, alibi narravimus.
units.tr: The most learned scholars of ancient Church history, Mornaeus, Hospinianus, Calixtus and Daillé, have confirmed this at length. The Council of Constance admits the same thing: "Although," it says, "in the primitive Church this sacrament was received by the faithful under both kinds," and so on. Cassander plainly admits the same for the Eastern Church, and Leo Allatius did not dare to deny it, apart from a few exceptions. In the Latin Church, communion under both kinds remained whole for more than a thousand years, and Cassander has also shown that even at the time when it began to be halved in some places, it was still kept whole in others, especially in monasteries, until about 1400. The Church was so faithful to Christ's institution that those who in the time of Leo the Great received only bread were regarded as Manichaeans, who called wine the gall of the dragon; Leo the Great himself is the witness, in Sermon 4 on Lent. So far were the ancients from distributing the Eucharist under both kinds freely, without any sense of necessity, as our opponents boldly pretend without any reliable witness, that they did not go so far as to believe that "although Christ administered this sacrament under both kinds, etc., nevertheless, notwithstanding this, it ought to be received by the laity under one kind only." The "spirit of stupor and dizziness" [πνεῦμα καταψυξεως] had not yet so driven mad those more scrupulous men who valued Christ's institution and command so highly. How greatly the Germans, French and Bohemians, and others, strove in the Council of Trent itself to have the cup restored to the Church, pressing the matter so far that they drew more than fifty prelates to their side, we have related elsewhere.

units.la: XCVII. Inconsultum est, quòd Christum Joh. VI. 51. dicentem: Si quis manducet ex hoc pane, vivet in aeternum, insinuasse communionem sub una panis specie, Tridentini affirmant.
units.tr: 97. The Tridentine fathers affirm that it is not to be inferred that Christ, saying in John 6:51, "If anyone eats of this bread, he will live for ever," hinted at communion under one kind of bread.

units.la: Nam nec de Eucharistiae Sacramento, sed de sola manducatione spirituali eo capite Christus loquitur; & si maximè de Eucharistiae Sacramento Christus ibi concionatus esset, communionem sub utraque confirmasset, gravissimè edicens: Amen, Amen dico vobis (ne de re indifferenti eum loqui putemus) nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis, & biberitis ejus sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis ipsis, v. 53. Supra vero vers. 51. non mandatum, sed promissio vitae manducanti panem extat. Neque etiam verba illa: Bibite ex hoc omnes, invitantis, & liberum obsequium permittentis, non praecipientis sunt; quia simile etiam esset: Edite; atque totum Sacramentum optionis & arbitrii utentium esset. Divina vero invitatio spiritualiter esurientium & sitientium non liberum certè obsequium edendi & bibendi sicut carnem & sanguinem; ita etiam utriusque symbola facit, inprimis cùm adversarii sustineant, sub specie vini ipsum Christi sanguinem contineri. An enim liberum est, sanguine Christi vesci, vel non? Communionem cum eo habere, vel non? At nec in verbis Christi: Qui edit panem hunc, aut bibit poculum Domini indigne, reus est corporis & sanguinis Domini, 1. Cor. XI. 27. particula ἢ sic membra disjungit, ut alterius omittendi gratiam faciat; quae Methodistarum recentium λεπτολογία veteribus inaudita est. Nam sic etiam Sacerdoti conficienti liberum erit, sub una specie celebrare: & sumenti liberum erit vel edere vel bibere. Sed quod dicitur in sententia condemnante, perperam plane ad traditionem symboli, & ἀνάληψιν ipsam transfertur. Reus enim corporis & sanguinis Christi fieri potest, sive edendo, sive bibendo, qui non celebrat S. Coenam tantùm comedendo. Quanquam nec reus fieri potest edendo, qui reus non fiat bibendo, si explorans se ipsum aliquis ad Coenam accesserit: Pontificii tamen laici tantùm édentes, non bibentes, indignè edere, atque ita corporis & sanguinis Christi rei fieri haud dubiè possunt. Et fieri potuit, ut S. Paulus perfidiae πονηρ-εἰσαγωγῆς praescius sic disjunxerit. In ἀνάληψη verò ipsa, v. 28. conjunguntur copulativè per ἰσθίετω καὶ πινέτω edat & bibat. Quin saepe etiam particulam ἢ aut sensu copulativo scriptores sacros & profanos accipere, eruditi probarunt. Ex multis locum Rom.IV.13. coll. cum Gal.III. 16. consulere licet. Quæ de potestate Ecclesiæ in mutandis ritibus Sacramentorum,ad substantiam eorundem non pertinentibus, Tridentini & eosdem secutus novissimè Benignus Bossuet°, garriunt, ἀπεγσιδιοντα sunt. Nam elementum seu materia Sacramenti ad substantiam profectò Sacramenti,non mutabilem ejus ritum, pertinet. Neq; etiam à Christo disertis adeò verbis mandatumEcclesia mutandi potestatem habet: & quæ mutat,non Christianam,sed Antichristianam Ecclesiam, & coetum τὸ Ἀντίμα se esse prodit. Dispar plane immersionis Baptismi in aspersionem ab Ecclesia conversæ ratio est, quia per utrumque ritum institutio servatur. Uterque enim βαπτισμὸς purificatio & lotio est, quomodo βαπτισμὸς & κατηγετισμὸς Joh.III.25. 26. æquipollent. At μετανοεῖν non ritum liberum,sed & substantiam Sacramenti, & ritum ejusdem essentialem abolet. Porrò ευχαριστία nomine κλασις ἄρτου fractionis panis venit,Actor. II.42. & XX. 7. Sed tám non synecdochica illa Hebræis,quibus שבר לחם frangere panem est אכל comedere, convivari, usitata locutio potum ex sacro hoc convivio eliminat,quàm non vox Hebræa משתה & Græca συμπόσιον à bibendo nomen utraque habens,ab eodem convivio panem summovet. Neque illi disputant, sed nugantur, cùm synecdochen illam explosuri objiciunt, fractioni panis primorum Christianorum etiam Nazaraeos adfuisse,quos vini potum voto sibi interdixisse constet. An enim majorem fuisse obligationem Nazaraeorum non bibendi vinum putamus,quàm Judaeorum omnium non bibendi sanguinem ? Et tamen Christum & Apostolos. Judaeos utrosque,bibisse sanguinem illi pertendunt. Et semel in Actis mentio est quatuor virorum,capita certo die ex voto radentium. Hinc statim iis nati sunt Nazaraeorum manipuli, qui abstemii Apostolos cogerent in sui gratiam calicem de manibus plebis excutere,& institutioni Christi fraudem facere,ne scilicet Nazaraei præter votum suum vinum biberent. Neque tamen ullo authore idoneo probant, Nazaraeos fractioni panis interfuisse, & propter eos dictum esse, discipulos in fractione panis perdurasse,nisi forte propter eosdem, Esaj. LVIII.7. dictum est. Frange esurienti panem. Sed sub altera specie panis æquè ac sub utraque totum & integrum Christum sumi,neque quoad fructum ulla gratia defraudari eos,qui unam duntaxat speciem accipiunt, Tridentini asseverant. Addunt alii,totum Christum sub una specie contineri, non vi sacramentalium verborum,sed per concomitantiam, quia vi consecrationis corpus Christi sub pane exi-stat,& existat vivum, adeóque minimè exsangue. Sed concomitantiæ illud figmentum jam supra elidere coepimus. Quicquid enim de concomitantia corporis & sanguinis Christi in re significata fiat, insignis certè significantibus illa obtinere non potest, quia Christus in institutione sic illa distinxit,ut cum pane corpus, cum vino sanguinem Christi, non cum pane per concomitantiam utrumque sumi,declaraverit. Tum in Eucharistia panis corporis Christi fracti & traditi,vinum sanguinis effusi Sacramentum est. Nam in annuntiationem mortis suæ Christus illud instituit. Et eo modo ille panem Ϲῶμα corpus suum vocavit, quo in Paschate Agnus corpus Paschatis, seu Agni Paschalis appellabatur. Atqui Agni corpus, & Christi σῶμα à sanguine sejunctum corpus exsangue notat. Non ergo etiam in re per panem fractum,& sanguinem effusum significata corpus & sanguis concomitantur invicem,sed separantur, quia sanguis effusus extra venas est. Quo argumento invicto in Concilio etiam Tridentino Amans Servita Brixianus concomitantiam oppugnavit. Aliâs ne Sacerdos quidem calice opus haberet. Universa quinetiam Eucharistia sic aboleri posset, quia aliis etiam modis Christi participes fimus,per fidem , Spiritum inhabitantem,Baptismum. Sed & ipsam Transubstantiationem concomitantia evertit , quia si sanguis concomitatur corpus,tum verbis illis. Hoc poculum est sanguis meus; vinum non transubstantiatur in sanguinem, quippe jam ante sub specie panis per concomitantiam contentum. Taceo fructus distinctos corporis & sanguinis, distinctis etiam symbolis repræsentatos; de quibus supra fusius. Denique frustra justas gravesque causas Coenæ mutilandæ Ecclesiam habuisse causantur. Quas enim illi allegare potuerunt, non communes Coenæ Christi, Apostolorum & Ecclesiæ ad seculum XII. usque ? Si igitur illæ nec Christum,quò minus sub utraque Coenam instituteret, neque Ecclesiam,quò minus mandato Christi oblequens sub utraque tamdiu celebraret, remorari potuerunt ; cur Papalem Innocentii III. sub quo Coena mutilari coepit, remorari debuerunt, quò minus institutionem Christi & praxin Ecclesiæ retineret? Sed nova Transubstantiationis superstitio nova incommoda peperit. Tollatur modò superstitio, & prava persuasio, quæ imaginaria incommoda vanissimo terrore auget, & salvares erit.
units.tr: Christ does not speak of the Sacrament of the Eucharist in that chapter, but of spiritual eating alone. Even if Christ had been preaching there about the Sacrament of the Eucharist, he would have confirmed communion under both kinds, since he solemnly declares: "Verily, verily, I say unto you" (lest we think he is speaking of a matter of indifference), "Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you" (v. 53). In verse 51, however, there is no command but a promise of life to the one who eats the bread. Nor are the words "Drink ye all of this" a command. They invite and leave the act of obedience free; otherwise "Eat" would be the same, and the whole Sacrament would be a matter of choice and of the will of those who use it. The divine invitation to those who are spiritually hungry and thirsty does not make eating and drinking the flesh and blood optional in the way the words suggest, and it does not make the two kinds equally optional either. This is especially so since our opponents maintain that the very blood of Christ is contained under the species of wine. Is it optional to feed on the blood of Christ or not? To have communion with him or not? Nor, in the words of Christ, "Whosoever shall eat this bread, or drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord" (1 Cor. 11:27), does the particle [ἢ] separate the members in such a way as to grant the freedom of omitting one of them. That hair-splitting [λεπτολογία] of the recent Methodists was unknown to the ancients. For on this reading it would also be free for the priest who consecrates to celebrate under one kind only, and for the communicant to eat or to drink as he pleases. What is said in the condemnatory sentence is plainly and wrongly transferred to the tradition of the symbol and to the reception itself. For a man can become guilty of the body and blood of Christ whether by eating or by drinking, and he who does not celebrate the Holy Supper by eating alone. Yet no one can become guilty by eating who does not also become guilty by drinking, if he examines himself before coming to the Supper. Nevertheless the Papist laity, eating but not drinking, may certainly eat unworthily and so undoubtedly become guilty of the body and blood of Christ. It is possible that St. Paul, foreseeing the wicked introduction of perfidy, wrote the disjunction in this way. But in the reception itself, v. 28, the words "let him eat and let him drink" [ἰσθίετω καὶ πινέτω] are joined by a copulative. Learned men have shown that sacred and profane writers often take the particle [ἢ] in a copulative sense; of the many examples one may consult Rom. 4:13 compared with Gal. 3:16. As to what the Tridentines, and Benignus Bossuet, who most recently followed them, babble about the power of the Church to change the rites of the Sacraments which do not belong to their substance, these are empty trifles [ἀπεγσιδιοντα]. For the element or matter of the Sacrament certainly belongs to the substance of the Sacrament, and its rite is not changeable. Nor does the Church have power to change what Christ commanded in such clear words. A church that changes these things shows itself to be not a Christian but an Antichristian church, and an assembly of the Antichrist [τὸ Ἀντίμα]. The case of baptism by immersion changed by the Church into sprinkling is plainly different, because the institution is preserved under either rite. For each is a [βαπτισμὸς] purification and washing, just as [βαπτισμὸς] and [καθαρισμὸς] are equivalent in John 3:25-26. But repentance [μετανοεῖν] does away not with a free rite but with the substance of the Sacrament and its essential rite. Moreover, the name "breaking of bread" [κλάσις ἄρτου], Acts 2:42 and 20:7, stands for the Eucharist. But that figurative use is not the common Hebrew idiom by which [שבר לחם], "to break bread," means [אכל], "to eat," "to feast together," and thus it does not exclude the drink from this sacred feast any more than the Hebrew word [משתה] and the Greek [συμπόσιον], both named from drinking, remove bread from the same feast. Nor do they argue well but trifle when, in order to overthrow this figure, they object that Nazarites, who are known to have abstained from wine by vow, were present at the breaking of bread of the first Christians. Do we think the obligation of the Nazarites not to drink wine was greater than the obligation of all the Jews not to drink blood? Yet they insist that Christ and the apostles, both being Jews, drank the blood. Once in the Acts there is mention of four men who shaved their heads on a certain day in fulfilment of a vow. Straightaway there arose from them bands of Nazarites, teetotallers, who would compel the apostles, for their sake, to snatch the cup from the hands of the people, and so commit a fraud against the institution of Christ, namely, that the Nazarites might not drink wine contrary to their vow. Yet they prove by no trustworthy author that the Nazarites were present at the breaking of bread, or that the words "they continued in the breaking of bread" were said on their account, unless perhaps it was said on their account in Isaiah 58:7, "Break thy bread to the hungry." But the Tridentines assert that Christ is received whole and entire under one kind of bread just as under both, and that those who receive only one species are not in any way defrauded of its fruit. Others add that the whole Christ is contained under one kind, not by the power of the sacramental words, but by concomitance, because by the power of consecration the body of Christ exists under the bread, and exists living, and so is by no means bloodless. But we have already begun to refute that fiction of concomitance above. For whatever happens with the concomitance of the body and blood of Christ in the thing signified, it certainly cannot hold good for the signs, because in the institution Christ so distinguished them, declaring that with the bread the body and with the wine the blood of Christ, not that both are received together with the bread by concomitance. Furthermore, in the Eucharist the bread is the sacrament of the body of Christ broken and given, and the wine of his blood poured out. For Christ instituted it in remembrance of his death. And in the same way that he called the bread his [σῶμα] body, so at the Passover the lamb was called the body of the Passover, or the paschal lamb. But the body of the lamb, and the [σῶμα] body of Christ separated from the blood, signify a bloodless body. Therefore in the thing signified, by the bread broken and the blood poured out, the body and blood do not accompany one another but are separated, since the blood poured out is outside the veins. By this unanswerable argument Amans the Servite of Brescia also attacked concomitance at the Council of Trent. Otherwise not even the priest would need the cup. The whole Eucharist could even be abolished in this way, since we partake of Christ in other ways too: by faith, by the indwelling Spirit, and by baptism. But concomitance also overthrows transubstantiation itself. For if the blood accompanies the body, then at those words, "This cup is my blood," the wine is not transubstantiated into blood, since it is already contained beforehand under the species of bread by concomitance. I say nothing of the distinct fruits of the body and blood, represented also by distinct signs, of which we have spoken more fully above. Finally, they vainly allege that the Church had just and grave reasons for mutilating the Supper. For what reasons could they have alleged, given that the Supper of Christ, of the apostles and of the Church was common until the twelfth century? If, then, those reasons could not hinder Christ from instituting the Supper under both kinds, nor the Church, obeying the command of Christ, from celebrating it under both kinds for so long, why ought they to have hindered the Papal decree of Innocent III, under which the Supper began to be mutilated, from retaining the institution of Christ and the practice of the Church? But the new superstition of transubstantiation has brought new inconveniences. Let the superstition be removed, and the perverse persuasion which increases imaginary inconveniences with most vain terror, and there will be salvation.

units.la: XCVIII. Etiam Ecclesiam veterem obtorto collo ad partes suas, & rapinæ hujus sacræ , trahere niituntur, sed non sine ingratiis ipsius Concilii Tridentini, quod fatetur ingenuè, primitivam Ecclesiam sub utraque specie Sacramentum hoc recepisse , Manichaeos sub una specie communicasse,neque tamen eo nomine reprehensos esse ; imò Romæ latuisse, neque latere potuisse , nisi Ecclesia Romana communionem sub una specie probasset vel usurpasset, Bellarminus arguit. Egregium vero argumentum à Syncretismo cumManichaeis petitum ! Romæ eos latuisse,ad tegendam infidelitatem suam Catholicorum mysterio interfuisse, ita tamen ut panem manducarent,at vino ex Sectæ instituto abstinerent , Leo M. testis est. Sed alibi, & ubique ita fecisse non constat. Et pauci illi Romæ erant , universæ Catholicorum multitudini permixti; ac forte ne omnes quidem illi communicarunt , raro ad Communionem venientes,ac cùm venirent, fraudem Ecclesiæ facientes, ut à Presbytero panem accipientes mox furtim ante Diaconi calicem porrecturi adventum se proriperent,neque adeò à non suspicantibus vel observantibus facilè deprehendi possent. Infirmis verò & moribundis quinto seculo Eucharistiam data tam Argumenta ex antiquitate petita sit satis. tam esse fatemur, sed non sub una specie. Scrapion enim à puero per Presbyterum misso buceliam, sed vino madefactam accepit. Neque id quaeritur, quomodo pauci nonnulli necessitate quadam constricti in privatis inprimis locis communicaverint; sed an ministri Eucharistiam communicantibus apud mensam rite & solenniter sub una specie ex communi aevi sui more porrexerint. At nec infantibus Eucharistiam sub una specie porrectam constat. Quin Cyprianus, qui ejus rei testis citatur alibi, eos sic loquentes inducit: Nos nihil fecimus, nec derelicto cibo & potu ad profana contagia sponte properavimus. Hodieque Aethiopes & Graecos ex veteri consuetudine infantibus panem multa aqua maceratum praebere, idonei testes Alvarezius, Allatius & Thomas Schmit comprobant. Figmentum etiam esse, quod olim fideles particulas Eucharistiae servatas domi siccas comedisse ajunt; ipse Albaspinaeus Observat. lib. I. 4. docet, & post Dallaeus & Calixtus fusius confirmant. Et par ratio est Missae προηγιασμένων praesanctificatorum, quae & recentior est, & apud Graecos, teste Cabasila Eupost. cap. 24. Dona πλήρα ἡ ἡγιασμένα ἡ Ϛωμα καὶ αἷμα Χριστοῦ perfecta & sanctificata & corpus & sanguinem Christi habet. Et de eadem Latinorum communione Ordo Romanus Bibl. Pat. T. X. 75. habet, quod Subdiaconus repositio à Presbyteris in patina corpore Domini, ante ipsos calicem cum vino non consecrato teneat, & utrumque, id est, corpus Christi, & vini calix super altare à Presbyteris deferatur, & panis sancti particula in calicem ponatur; atque sic vinum non consecratum per sanctificatum panem sanctificetur. Quod etiam Ordo Romanus à Cassandro descriptus docet. Cumque ipsi adversarii Missam Praesanctificatorum imperfectam & aequivocè talem appellent, & in ea nihil amplius Sacerdos quam populus accipiat, infirmum à Sacramento aequivoco ad univocum argumentum est. Denique & laicam communionem non de alio communicandi genere, sed de gradu, ordine & loco communicantium, quoties clerici ob delictum aliquod non cum clero, sed inter laicos extra cancellos communicare debuerunt; veteres intellexisse doctissimi quique, etiam Pammelius, Albaspinaeus, Morinus confitentur. Nam, uti Concilium Toletanum I. habet, Sacerdotes & Levitae ante altare communicabant, in choro clerus, extra chorum populus. Sed si è Clero quispiam grave crimen admisisset, is clericatus ordine movebatur, & poenitentiae causa inter laicos communicabat, quod Concilium Neocaesariense can. 1. vocat ad poenitentiam inter laicos redigi. Et triplex ejusmodi excle-ricorum poena erat, pro ratione delictorum. Nam in delictis gravibus inter laicos communicabant: in gravioribus nonnisi moribundis communicare licebat: in gravissimis etiam extrema agentibus communio negabatur. Eodem etiam communio Peregrina referri debet, quae praeter statos dies peregrinantium causa fiebat. Quam inter clericorum etiam poenas fuisse, ex Concilii Agathensis can. 1. liquet.
units.tr: Our opponents also strive to drag the ancient Church, by force, onto their side in this matter of sacred plunder, but not without embarrassment from the Council of Trent itself, which frankly admits that the primitive Church received this Sacrament under both kinds, and that the Manichaeans communicated under one kind without being rebuked for it. Bellarmine argues that the Manichaeans lay hidden at Rome and could not have remained hidden unless the Roman Church had approved or practised communion under one kind. What a remarkable argument, drawn from the syncretism of the Manichaeans! That they lay hidden at Rome, taking part in the Catholic mystery to conceal their unbelief, but only eating the bread and abstaining from the wine by the rule of their sect, Leo the Great bears witness. But that they did this everywhere, and elsewhere, is not established. Those few at Rome were mixed into the whole multitude of Catholics, and perhaps not all of them even communicated. They came to communion rarely, and when they did come they deceived the Church: receiving bread from the presbyter, they slipped away quietly before the deacon arrived with the cup, so that they could not easily be detected by those who neither suspected nor watched them. To the sick and the dying, the Eucharist was given in the fifth century, we admit, but not under one kind. Scrapion, for when he was a boy, was sent a morsel by a presbyter, but it was soaked in wine. Nor is the question how a few people, constrained by some necessity, communicated in private places, especially; the question is whether the ministers, following the common custom of their own age, handed the Eucharist to communicants at the table, rightly and solemnly, under one kind alone. Yet it is not established that the Eucharist was given under one kind even to infants. Indeed Cyprian, who is cited as a witness on this point elsewhere, introduces them speaking thus: We have done nothing, nor, leaving behind food and drink, have we hastened of our own accord to profane contagions. Even today the Ethiopians and the Greeks, from ancient custom, give infants bread soaked in much water, as the reliable witnesses Alvarez, Allatius and Thomas Schmit confirm. It is also a fiction that the faithful of old ate dry particles of the Eucharist kept at home; Albaspinaeus himself teaches this in Observat. lib. I. 4, and afterwards Dallaeus and Calixtus confirm it at greater length. The same reasoning applies to the Mass of the προηγιασμένων [pre-sanctified], which is also more recent, and which among the Greeks, as Cabasilas witnesses in Eupost. cap. 24, has Dona πλήρα ἡ ἡγιασμένα ἡ σῶμα καὶ αἷμα Χριστοῦ [perfecta & sanctificata & corpus & sanguinem Christi, i.e. the perfected and sanctified gifts, the body and blood of Christ]. And the Roman Ordo, in Bibl. Pat. T. X, p. 75, says of the same communion among the Latins that the subdeacon, holding the body of the Lord laid in a paten by the presbyters, holds before them the cup with unconsecrated wine, and both, that is the body of Christ and the cup of wine, are carried by the presbyters to the altar, and a particle of the holy bread is put into the cup; and thus the unconsecrated wine is sanctified through the sanctified bread. The Roman Ordo described by Cassander teaches the same. And since our opponents themselves call the Mass of the pre-sanctified imperfect and equivocally so named, and in it the priest receives nothing more than the people do, the argument from an equivocal sacrament to a univocal one is weak. Finally, that the ancients understood lay communion not as a different way of communicating but as a matter of the rank, order and place of the communicants, whenever clergy, on account of some offence, had to communicate not with the clergy but among the laity outside the chancel, is acknowledged by all the most learned men, including Pamelius, Albaspinaeus and Morinus. For, as the First Council of Toledo states, the priests and Levites communicated before the altar, the clergy in the choir, the people outside the choir. But if any of the clergy had committed a grave crime, he was removed from the order of the clergy and, for the sake of repentance, communicated among the laity, which the Council of Neocaesarea (can. 1) calls being reduced to repentance among the laity. There were three kinds of such penalties for clergy, according to the nature of their offences. For in serious offences they communicated among the laity; in more serious ones they were allowed to communicate only when dying; in the most serious cases, communion was denied even to those at the point of death. The communion called Peregrina [foreign or pilgrim communion] should also be placed here, which took place outside the appointed days for the sake of those travelling. That this too was among the penalties of the clergy is clear from the Council of Agde, can. 1.

units.la: XCIX. Fuerunt in externo Coenae ministerio Personae, symbola externa, & circa eadem ritus atque actiones. Supersunt Circumstantiae ejusdem Locus & Tempus. Locum
units.tr: XCIX. In the external ministry of the Supper there were persons, outward signs, and rites and actions connected with them. There remain the circumstances of the same: place and time.

units.la: quod attinet, satis constat, primam Coenam in aedibus privatis τὰ δεῖνα à Christo institutam & celebratam esse, Matth. XXVI. 18. Marc. XIV. 13. Festorum enim solennium tempora Judaeis advenis aedes etiam privatae Hierosolymis patebant; Christus proin Paschate in privatis aedibus cum suis vescens, in iisdem S. Coenam Paschati surrogavit. Frangebant deinceps Apostoli panem κατ' οἶκον domatim, Actor. II. 46. Et prisca Ecclesia sine locorum discrimine, ubicunque cogebatur, sacro epulo fruí suevit. Templis vero erectis privatae & domesticae coenae expirarunt. Quanquam neque unquam sic privatae fuerunt, quin in fratrum conventu celebrarentur, & fidei atque communionis testandae gratia plures accumberent. Neque adeo probandus mos est aegris Eucharistiam administrandi, quia is & praeter Sacrae Coenae, quae Συνάξις congregatio est, & Συνελ-θόν in τὸ αὐτὸ conventum in unum atque Ἐκκλησίαν Ecclesiam I. Cor. XI. 18.20. postulat, institutus est: & cum superstitione necessitatis atque operis operati conjungi potest: & si omnibus aegris porrigenda sit, vix ejus profanatio vitari, vel unus minister sufficere, pestilentiae inprimis tempore, poterit; si quibusdam, συμ-παρα-φθιάς vitium à Jacobo Apostolo cap. II. 9. damnatum incurretur. Sed alia ratio erit, si tempore persecutionis Ecclesia in privatis aedibus colligatur, & minister legitime vocatus, qui Coenam administret, adsit. Ubique verò τάξις ordo Ecclesiae canonibus sancitus custodiri debet. Omnia decenter & secundum ordinem fiant, I. Cor. XIV. 33.40. Multa enim licent, quae nec ubique, nec omnibus expediunt. Dabunt inprimis operam sani, ut frequenter Sacram Coenam usurpent: aegri, ut fideli memoria praecedentem communionem & Baptismum etiam suum; in quo etiam memoria mortis Christi fit, recolant: omnes, ut, quoties necessitate vel ordine Sacramento privantur, in spiritua-li communione acquiescant, juxta Augustini illud: Crede, & manducasti.
units.tr: As regards place, it is quite certain that the first Supper was instituted and celebrated by Christ in a private house (τὰ δεῖνα), Matt. 26:18; Mark 14:13. For at the time of the great festivals, private houses in Jerusalem were open to Jewish strangers, so Christ, eating with his disciples at the Passover in a private house, substituted the holy Supper for the Passover in the same house. Afterwards the apostles broke bread κατ' οἶκον [from house to house], house by house, Acts 2:46. And the early Church, without distinction of places, enjoyed the sacred feast wherever it was gathered. But once temples were built, private and domestic suppers ceased. Yet they were never so private that they were not celebrated in an assembly of the brethren, and several took their places at table to bear witness to faith and communion. Nor, indeed, is the custom of administering the Eucharist to the sick to be approved, because it is instituted apart from the Lord's Supper, which requires a συνάξις [gathering], a συνελθόντων [coming together] into τὸ αὐτό [the same place], into one assembly, ἐκκλησία [Church], 1 Cor. 11:18–20; and it may be joined with the superstition of necessity and of the work done (opus operatum). And if it is to be given to all the sick, the profanation of it can hardly be avoided, nor could one minister suffice, especially in time of plague; if it is given to some, the fault of συμπαραφθορά [mutual corruption] condemned by the apostle James (2:9) will be incurred. But the case will be different if, in a time of persecution, the Church is gathered in private houses and a lawfully called minister is present to administer the Supper. Everywhere, however, the order (τάξις) of the Church established by the canons ought to be kept. Let all things be done decently and in order, 1 Cor. 14:33, 40. For many things are permissible which are neither expedient everywhere nor for everyone. Those in health should take care to use the Holy Supper frequently; the sick should recall, with faithful memory, the preceding communion and their own baptism, in which also the memory of Christ's death is renewed; all should, whenever they are deprived of the sacrament by necessity or by church order, rest content with spiritual communion, according to Augustine's saying: Believe, and you have eaten.

units.la: C. Prima Coena ad mensam peracta est. Nam Christus ἀνίκειτο accubuit cum duodecim, Matth. XXVI. 20. Non potestis participes esse mensae Domini & mensae Daemoniorum. I. Cor. X. 21. Ubi illud per τράπεζαν mensam intelligitur, in quo peracto sacrificio convivium, seu μέθοχη participatio convivii instituitur. Quod mensa, non altare est; utpote in quo comessari nec mos, nec fas fuit. Comedentes quidem victimas facti sunt κοινωνοὶ & ἰνοκοινεῖς participes altaris, seu victimae in altari oblatae, ibid. v. 18. Sed non ideo non in mensa, verum in altari victimas illi comederunt. Neque nos symbolorum corporis & sanguinis Christi in ara prius oblati, in eadem ara participes reddimur; sed cibi spiritualis in ara oblati participes in mensa fimus. Quomodo etiam Eusebius Demonst. Evang. lib. I. 10. scribit; nos ἀναμιμνήσκομεν... sacrificii hujus memoriam super mensa per symbola corporis ejus, & salvifici sanguinis. Mensas enim, non altaria Christiani veteres habuerunt, quibus id etiam Celsus apud Originem, & Caecilius apud Minutium, omnes vulgo apud Arnobium, Julianus apud Cyrillum exprobrarunt. runt, quòd nullas aras, nulla altaria habeant. Erantque mensæ veterum non vel lapideæ vel fixæ,sed ligneæ & portatiles, sicut calices atque patinæ illorum ligneæ fuerunt. Ut immeritò vitio detur Ecclesiis nostris, quòd mensis, patinis & calicibus similiter ligneis utuntur. Nam & veteres in eo imitantur, & memores sunt, quòd rituum simplicitas doctrinæ puritatem alat. Mutatio etiam mensarum lignearum in lapideas & fixas, nec non calicum & patinarum lignearum in aureas & argenteas, inprimis verò mensarum ipsarum in altaria proprie dicta,non parum Missatici sacrificii opinionem auxit.
units.tr: C. The first Supper was celebrated at a table. For Christ reclined with the twelve, Matt. 26:20. You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons, 1 Cor. 10:21. Here the table (τράπεζα) is understood as that at which, once the sacrifice was completed, a feast, or μέθεξις [participation] in the feast, was instituted. It is a table, not an altar, since eating (comessari) was neither customary nor lawful at an altar. Those who ate the sacrifices became κοινωνοί [partners] and ἰσοκοινεῖς [sharers] of the altar, that is, of the victim offered on the altar, ibid. v. 18. But they did not eat the victims on the altar for that reason rather than at the table. Nor do we, who have been offered the symbols of the body and blood of Christ previously on the altar, become partakers at that same altar; rather we become partakers of the spiritual food offered on the altar at the table. Eusebius also writes in this way, Demonst. Evang. lib. I. 10: we ἀναμιμνήσκομεν [call to mind] the memory of this sacrifice upon the table by the symbols of his body and of his saving blood. For the ancient Christians had tables, not altars; Celsus, as cited by Origen, and Caecilius, in Minucius, reproached them with this, and generally Arnobius, and Julian, in Cyril, objected that they had no altars, no altars at all. The tables of the ancients were not stone or fixed, but of wood and movable, just as their cups and patens were wooden. So our churches are unjustly faulted for using wooden tables, patens and cups similarly. For the ancients are imitated in this, and we remember that the simplicity of rites nourishes the purity of doctrine. The change of wooden tables into stone and fixed ones, and of wooden cups and patens into golden and silver ones, and above all the turning of the tables themselves into altars properly so called, has greatly increased the notion of a Masses sacrifice.

units.la: C I. Tempus primæ Cœnæ feria quinta hebdomadæ, Pascha præcedens fuit. Quem diem anniversarium vetus Ecclesia celebrandæ Cœnæ,in primæ memoriam,destinavit; sic tamen, ut & aliis etiam diebus, præsertim Dominico frequenter communicaverint. Primo die hebdomadæ congregatis Apostolis ad frangendum panem,Paulus disseruit, Actor. XX. 7. Celebravit autem Christus sub vesperam, seu inter duas vesperas,quas inter Pascha comedi debuit. Dominus ea nocte,qua proditus est, panem accepit, 1. Cor. XI. 23. Præcedere enim Cœna immediatè Christi passionem debuit, utpote cujus Sacramentum destinatum erat. Cujus imitatione etiam veteres primò noctur-nas,ac deinceps etiam persecutionum metu antelucanas Cœnas frequentarunt. Conveniens autem celebrationi mysterii hujus matutinum inprimis tempus est,quo animi & sensuum vigor inprimis constat. Cùm tamen Christus nullum certum tempus celebrando sacro huic epulo definiverit, Ecclesiæ cuique illud definire liberum est, id solum dum caveatur, ne nimis infrequens communio sit; quia & memoria mortis Christi symbolorum usu acuitur, & fides atque charitas erga Deum & Salvatorem firmiùs sic fulcitur, atque vehementiùs incenditur. Ὁσάκις quotiès ederitis panem hunc, & biberitis poculum hoc, mortem Domini annuntiate, usque dum venerit, ibid. vers. 26. Ubi particula ὁσάκις quotiescunque ex traditione Dominica repetita, Paschati semel quotannis duntaxat celebrando non obscurè opponitur. Atque ita Ecclesiam Apostolicam, in doctrina Apostolorum & communione & fractione panis & precibus κατὰ ἡμέραν quotidie perseverasse prima Ecclesiæ acta confirmant,Actor. II. 42. 46. Duravit diu satis ille fervor; & Dominica præ cæteris ad obeundum solennius hoc sacrum placuit; donec refrigescente zelo nonnulli tertia quaque Dominica, alii vix bis terve,imò & semel duntaxat in anno,exemplo eremitarum,qui Chrysostomo in 1. Cor. X. hom. 17. notante, tantùm semel in anno,vel post biennium ad communionem progressi sunt,communicarant. Quam supinam negligentiam & Eucharistia in sacrificium atque otiosum spectaculum conversa,& privatæ Missæ; & Monachorum audacia verba Christi Edite,Bibite in verbum spectate commutantium; & tribunitiæ sacrificulorum de periculo communicantium conciones,& crescens cleri dignitas & laicorum contemptus post Concilium Lateranense Tridentini Sess. XIII. can. 9. anathema vibrantes adversus eum, qui negaverit,omnes & singulos Christi fideles utrius-que sexus, cùm ad annos discretionis pervenerint, teneri singulis annis, saltem semel in Paschate, ad communicandum juxta præceptum sanctæ matris Ecclesiæ; non parum foverunt. Ita sicut Christus adventu suo Judaicas, ita Antichristus adventu suo Christianas ceremonias paulatim abolevit. Neque sine causa Arnoldus Sorbonista libro de frequente communione veterum edito gravem de neglecta in Papatu communione querelam conlignavit. Sed servandus sicut in rebus omnibus,ita hic etiam modus est,ut nec nimis frequens communio fit, ne, quæ humana infirmitas est, quotidiano vel nimis crebro usu mysterii dignitas vilescat,& præparationis necessariæ ardor defervescat: nec raro nimis esca illa carpatur,ne sacrificium Domini,quod tanquam juge nostrum, perpetuò colendum & celebrandum est, neglectim habere deprehendamur.
units.tr: C I. The time of the first Supper was the Thursday of the week before Easter. The ancient Church set this anniversary day aside for celebrating the Supper in memory of the first one. Yet they also communicated frequently on other days, especially on the Lord's Day. On the first day of the week, when the Apostles had gathered to break bread, Paul preached, Acts 20:7. Christ celebrated it in the evening, or between the two evenings, during which the Passover had to be eaten. On the night in which he was betrayed, the Lord took bread, 1 Cor. 11:23. The Supper had to come immediately before Christ's passion, since it was instituted to represent that passion. Imitating this, the ancients first celebrated it at night, and later, from fear of persecution, before dawn. The morning is especially suitable for celebrating this mystery, because the vigour of mind and senses is greatest then. Since Christ did not fix any certain time for celebrating this sacred feast, each Church is free to fix it, provided only that communion is not made too infrequent. For the memory of Christ's death is sharpened by the use of the symbols, and faith and love towards God and the Saviour are thus more firmly supported and more vehemently kindled. As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes, ibid. v. 26. Here the particle as often as [ὁσάκις], repeated from the Lord's tradition, plainly opposes the celebration only once a year at Passover. So the first acts of the Church confirm that the Apostolic Church persevered in the teaching of the Apostles, in the fellowship, in the breaking of bread and in prayers, daily [κατὰ ἡμέραν], Acts 2:42, 46. That fervour lasted long enough, and the Lord's Day was preferred above the rest for celebrating this sacred rite more solemnly. But when zeal cooled, some communicated every third Sunday, others hardly twice or three times, and even only once a year, after the example of the hermits, who, as Chrysostom observes on 1 Cor. 10, homily 17, went to communion only once a year or after two years. This sluggish negligence, the conversion of the Eucharist into a sacrifice and an idle spectacle, private masses, the audacity of monks who changed Christ's words Eat, drink into the word look, the tribunician sermons of the priestlings on the danger of communicating, and the growing dignity of the clergy and contempt of the laity, did not a little to foster all this. After the Council of Lateran, the Council of Trent, Session 13, canon 9, brandished its anathema against anyone who denies that all and each of the faithful of Christ, of either sex, when they have reached the years of discretion, are bound each year, at least once at Easter, to communicate according to the precept of holy Mother Church. Just as Christ by his coming gradually abolished the Jewish ceremonies, so Antichrist by his coming gradually abolished the Christian ones. Nor without cause did Arnold the Sorbonist, in his book On the frequent communion of the ancients, bring forward a grave complaint about the neglect of communion under the Papacy. But this measure must be observed here, as in all things: communion must not be too frequent, lest, since human weakness is what it is, the dignity of the mystery grow cheap through daily or too frequent use, and the ardour of the necessary preparation cool. Nor should that food be taken too rarely, lest we be found to treat carelessly the Lord's sacrifice, which, as our perpetual yoke, must always be honoured and celebrated.

units.la: C II. Explicato externo S. Cœnæ quoad Personas, symbola, ritus & circumstantias Ministerio,ejusdem Mysterium perpendendum est. Non enim vulgare hoc, sed planè mysticum convivium est,cujus omne decus, pretium,solatium & gaudium non corporis, sed fidei oculis cernitur,& à Christi solius revelatione unicè petendum est. Cùm convenitis in unum, non hoc est Cœnam Dominicam comedere. Quisque enim propriam Cœnam præoccupat, dum edit: & hic quidem esurit, ille verò ebrius est. Numquid privatas ædes non habetis ad comedendum & bibendum? Ego enim accepi à Domino,&c. 1. Cor. XI. 20-23. Non ergo edere & bibere; ac ne convenire quidem ad Cœnam Domini comedendam est Cœnam Domini ἀξίως digne comedere, si id fiat sine fide mysterii, quod Cœna occultat. Neque simpliciter hic vel panis, ut panis,sed ut corpus Domini; vel vinum ut vinum, sed ut sanguis Domini,& communio utriusque comedi & bibi debet; neque id sine fide mysterii illius, & annuntiatione mortis Christi digne fieri potest. Sicut enim aqua in Baptismo mysterium regenerationis conjunctum habet, neque sine eo Baptismus est: ita panis & vinum in Cœna mysterii expers non est. Regeneratio per Baptismum obsignatur: gaudia Regni Cœlorum sacri convivii Sacramento adumbrantur,& ad firmitudinem spei quasi repræsentantur; quatenus autem in hac vita percipiuntur, quasi aluntur & sustentantur. Neque præter Scripturæ analogiam primi & secundi Sacramenti ille αἰνιγμὸς est. Ad hoc enim lavamur,& in fidem Dei recipimur, ut cum Christo discumbamus,coram Deo edamus & bibamus, & specie ipsius saturemur. Gustate & videte quòd bonus sit Jehova, Psal. XXXIV. 9. Comedent & adorabunt omnes pingues terræ, Psal. XXII. 30: Præparas coram me mensam, è regione hostium meorum; impinguasti oleo caput meum; calix meus exuberat, ibid. XXIII. ç. Veni in hortum meum Soror mea sponsa. Comedi favum meum cum melle meo; bibi vinum meum cum lacte meo. Comedite, amici, bibite & inebriamini,charissimi, Cant. V. 1. Omnes sitientes, venite ad aquas; Venite, emite absque argento,& absque pretio vinum & lac; Comedite bonum, & delectabitur in pinguedine anima vestra, Esaj. LV. 1.2. Propterea sic dixit Dominus. Ecce servi mei comedent,& vos esurietis. Ecce, servi mei bibent, & vos sitietis. Ecce servi mei lætabuntur præ jucunditate cunditate cordis, Esaj. LXV. 13. 14. Dico vobis, venient multi ab Oriente & Occidente, & accumbent cum Abrahamo, Isaaco & Jacobo in Regno Coelorum, Matth. VIII. 11. Assimulatum est Regnum Coelorum homini Regi, qui nuptias instruxit Filio suo, &c. ibid. XXII. 2. &c.
units.tr: C II. Having explained the external side of the holy Supper, as regards the persons, symbols, rites and circumstances, we must now weigh its mystery, which is the ministry and mystery of the same. For this is not an ordinary banquet but a plainly mystical feast, whose whole glory, value, comfort and joy is seen not with the eyes of the body but of faith, and must be sought solely from Christ's revelation. When you come together, it is not to eat the Lord's Supper. For each one takes his own supper beforehand as he eats: one is hungry, another is drunk. Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? For I received from the Lord, etc. 1 Cor. 11:20–23. So it is not only eating and drinking, nor even coming together, to eat the Lord's Supper. To eat the Lord's Supper worthily [ἀξίως] is not possible if it is done without faith in the mystery which the Supper hides. Nor is it here simply bread as bread, or wine as wine, but bread as the body of the Lord, and wine as the blood of the Lord; the communion of both must be eaten and drunk, and this cannot be done worthily without faith in that mystery and the proclamation of Christ's death. For just as water in Baptism has the mystery of regeneration joined to it, and Baptism is not without it, so bread and wine in the Supper are not without a mystery. Regeneration is sealed through Baptism; the joys of the Kingdom of Heaven are foreshadowed by the sacrament of the sacred banquet, and are, as it were, represented for the firmness of hope; and as far as they are received in this life, they are, as it were, nourished and sustained. Nor is that enigma [αἰνιγμὸς] of the first and second sacrament contrary to the analogy of Scripture. For we are washed for this purpose, and received into the faith of God, that we may recline with Christ, eat and drink before God, and be satisfied with his very presence. Taste and see that the LORD is good, Ps. 34:9. All the fat ones of the earth shall eat and worship, Ps. 22:30. You prepare a table before me, in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows, ibid. 23:5. Come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, friends; drink, and be drunk, beloved, Song 5:1. Everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; come, buy without money and without price wine and milk; eat what is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness, Isa. 55:1, 2. Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry. Behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty. Behold, my servants shall rejoice for joy of heart, Isa. 65:13, 14. I tell you, many will come from east and west, and sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the Kingdom of Heaven, Matt. 8:11. The Kingdom of Heaven is likened to a king who prepared a wedding feast for his son, etc., ibid. 22:2, etc.

units.la: CIII. Convivii ergo Eucharistici externi mysterium in convivio spirituali & interno per externum illud declarato juxta atque obsignato consistit. Cujus convivii spiritualis partes & apparatum ipse Christus corpus suum & sanguinem suum promisit. Hoc (panis a Christo acceptus, benedictus, fractus, distributus ad manducandum) est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur. Hoc (poculum) est sanguis meus ille Novi Testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur ad remissionem peccatorum, Matth. XXVI. 26 28. Marc. XIV. 22. 23. Luc. XXII. 19. 20. Quae verba S. Paulus explicatiora sic reddidit: Poculum benedictionis, cui benedicimus, nonne est communio sanguinis Christi? Panis quem frangimus, nonne est communio corporis Christi? 1. Cor. X. 16. Manifestum autem est, proprie nec panem corpus Christi pro nobis traditum; nec poculum sanguinem Christi pro multis effusum: nec panem & poculum communionem corporis Christi fracti, & sanguinis ejus effusi esse. Nam haec omnia disparata cum sint; de se invicem proprie praedicari nequeunt. Neque etiam panis causa est corporis Christi; quia Spiritus vita est, & ne quidem caro Christi, oraliter manducata; nedum panis, ad vitam, prodest, Joh. VI. 63. Alias similiter verba Coenae, Hoc est corpus, explicanda essent: Hoc est causa corporis, quod absurdum certe erit. Cum ergo panis & poculum non sint causa communionis corporis & sanguinis Christi; sequitur, esse signaculum, pignus, arrhabonem, seu, uti 1. Cor. XI. 25. Paulus appellat, commemorationem Christi; adeoque etiam communionis corporis & sanguinis Christi. Ideo cap. X. 17. sic se statim explicat: quoniam unus panis unum corpus multi sumus. Ubi particula causalis quia ostendit, Apostolum verba sua; quibus panem communionem corporis, & poculum communionem sanguinis Christi dixerat; explicare. Panis autem unus non utique causa est, quod plures unum corpus sint, sed signum, testimonium & memoriale. Ergo pari ratione panis est communio corporis Christi, hoc est, sigillum, pignus, testimonium Sacramentum corporis Christi. Emphaticus plane & usitatissimus ille modus loquendi est; quo dicitur Hoc esse aliud; ut doceatur, non modo aliud per hoc significari, sed etiam hoc substitui pro illa re alia, tum ad commemorationem rei in similitudine & figura: tum ad commemorationem verbi; quo illud datur. Non enim tantum signum est rei proprietatem similitudine quadam ad animum revocans, sed etiam sigillum, de eadem certitudinem efficiens. Quomodo in pane fracto omnes quidem fractionem corporis Christi, ut in figura intuentur; sed fideles dum panem fractum comedunt per fidem, pro sigillo illum habent Christi in se habitantis, & cuncta beneficia mortis suae sibi impartientis, quae invisibilis illa communio corporis fracti est.
