units.tr: CIII. The mystery of the external Eucharistic banquet therefore consists in the spiritual and inward banquet, declared through that external one and at the same time sealed by it. Christ himself promised his body and his blood as the parts and furnishing of this spiritual banquet. This (the bread, taken, blessed, broken and distributed by Christ to be eaten) is my body, which is given for you. This (the cup) is my blood of the New Testament, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins, Matt. 26:26–28; Mark 14:22, 23; Luke 22:19, 20. St Paul explained these words more fully thus: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? 1 Cor. 10:16. It is clear, however, that properly speaking the bread is not the body of Christ given for us, nor the cup the blood of Christ poured out for many; nor are the bread and the cup the communion of the body of Christ broken and of his blood poured out. For since these things are different, they cannot be properly predicated of one another. Nor is the bread the cause of Christ's body, since the Spirit is life, and not even the flesh of Christ, eaten orally, profits for life, let alone bread, John 6:63. Otherwise the words of the Supper, This is the body, would similarly have to be explained: this is the cause of the body, which would certainly be absurd. Since then the bread and the cup are not the cause of the communion of Christ's body and blood, it follows that they are a seal, pledge, earnest, or, as St Paul calls them in 1 Cor. 11:25, a commemoration of Christ, and so also of the communion of Christ's body and blood. So in chapter 10, verse 17, he at once explains himself thus: because we, being many, are one bread, one body. Here the causal particle because shows that the Apostle is explaining his words in which he had called the bread the communion of the body and the cup the communion of the blood of Christ. But one bread is certainly not the cause of the many being one body; it is a sign, a testimony and a memorial. By the same reasoning, then, the bread is the communion of Christ's body, that is, the seal, pledge and testimony of the sacrament of Christ's body. That mode of speaking is quite emphatic and very common, by which one says this is another, to teach that not only something else is signified by this, but that this is also substituted for that other thing: both for the commemoration of a thing in likeness and figure, and for the commemoration of the word by which it is given. For it is not merely a sign which by a certain likeness calls the property of the thing to mind, but also a seal which produces certainty about the same thing. In the same way, in the broken bread, all indeed see the breaking of Christ's body as in a figure; but the faithful, while they eat the broken bread by faith, have it as a seal of Christ dwelling in them and imparting to them all the benefits of his death; and this invisible communion is the communion of the broken body.

units.la: CIV. Jam ergo duplex convivii Eucharistici cibus & potus est, unus symbolicus, corporalis & visibilis, panis & vinum, alter realis, spiritualis & invisibilis, corpus Christi pro nobis fractum, & sanguis ejusdem pro nobis effusus ad remissionem peccatorum.
units.tr: CIV. The food and drink of the Eucharistic feast are therefore twofold: one is symbolic, bodily and visible, namely bread and wine; the other is real, spiritual and invisible, namely the body of Christ broken for us and his blood poured out for us for the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: Quae comedentes & bibentes viva & vera fide, communionem cum corpore & sanguine Christi habemus; perinde ut comedentes panem & bibentes vinum cum eodem communionem habemus. Sicut autem non qualiscunque panis comesti, & vini hausti cum comedente & hauriente, sed vitalis maxime atque ejusmodi communio est; ut corpus & sanguis vivificetur, conservetur, pascatur ad vitam, reficiatur & laetificetur: ita corporis Christi manducati & sanguinis ejusdem bibiti cum manducante & bibente non levis aliqua communio est, qualis esse potuit Judae, militum corpus Christi contrectantium, crucifigentium, imo etiam Mariae Magdalenae Christum tangere gestientis, sed maxime vitalis, vitam spiritualem peccato amissam, & cum eodem remissionem peccatorum; justitiam, pacem, laetitiam; spem gloriae & beatitudinis coelestis restituens, & quidem nobiliore atque perfectiore longe ratione post mortem Christi, quam ante eam. Licet enim mortis Christi futurae efficacia etiam Patres fideles vivificati, cibati, potati, pasti, neque spirituali laetitia, qualem cibus & potus praebent; omnino destituti fuerint, adeoque per fidem, auxiliantibus symbolis suis, cum corpore Christi frangendo, & sanguine ejus effundendo communionem habuerint tantam, quanta ad salutem eorum sufficiebat: tamen corpore jam fracto, sanguine effuso, atque consummatis ita omnibus, cibus ille corporis fracti, & potus sanguinis fusi vitam spiritualem vitaliorem, fortiorem efficit, & gaudium plenius; omniaque consummatiora, pro statu praesentis vitae reddit. Et corpus quidem Christi semel fractum, sanguis semel fusus est; sed mox corpus resuscitatum, vivificatum, sanguis in venas refusus est. Neque a quoquam corpus fractum, & sanguis fusus corporaliter manducatum vel bibitum est; ne ab ipsis quidem discipulis Christi, utpote qui plerique fuga vitae suae consulentes mortuum eum ne viderunt quidem, sed demum vivificatum amplexi sunt. Quo argumento ad liquidum perducimus communionem illam corporis fracti & sanguinis effusi non corporalem, sed spiritualem esse; neque aliud esse quam communionem cum ipsius morte, satisfactione, merito, justitia, vita, quae perinde carnem Christi comedentes & sanguinem bibentes communia, & intima habent, atque illi, qui panem comedunt, & vinum bibunt, illa sibi communia & intima habent; imo in substantiam, succum & sanguinem suum convertunt. Est ergo communio corporis Christi fracti; atque sanguinis ejus effusi communio cum Christo toto, quoad fundum & fructum, & quidem cum mortificato, etiam cum vivificato, sedente ad dextram Dei, qua ceu membra & corpus ejus mortis, meriti, justitiae & vitae ejus participes in hac vita reneriti vivificamur magis magisque, conservamur, ad vitam aeternam pascimur, & in ipso unice deliciamur. Haec illa unice necessaria & salutaris cum Christo communio est; absque qua est, nihil nobis caro Christi fracta, nihil sanguis effusus prodest, imò obest magis, quia quorum, ceu corporis sui, Christus Salvator non est, illorum, propter spretam ejus mortem & communionem, severus judex erit.
units.tr: Those who eat and drink with a living and true faith have communion with the body and blood of Christ, just as those who eat bread and drink wine have communion with that bread and wine. But just as the communion between the one who eats and drinks and the bread eaten and wine drunk is not some slight or ordinary one, but a most vital kind, so that the body is quickened, preserved, nourished to life, refreshed and gladdened, so too the communion between the one who eats and drinks and the body of Christ eaten and the blood of Christ drunk is no slight communion, such as Judas could have had, or the soldiers who handled the body of Christ and crucified him, or even Mary Magdalene, who longed to touch Christ. It is rather the most vital communion, restoring the spiritual life lost through sin, and with it the forgiveness of sins, righteousness, peace and joy, and the hope of heavenly glory and blessedness. And this communion is far nobler and more perfect after the death of Christ than before it. For although the faithful of the Fathers, though they were made alive by the efficacy of Christ's future death, were fed and watered and nourished, they were nevertheless wholly without that spiritual joy which food and drink provide. Thus, by faith, with the help of their symbols, they had communion with the body of Christ as it was to be broken and his blood as it was to be poured out, and that communion was as great as their salvation required. But now that the body has been broken, the blood poured out, and all things thus accomplished, that food of the broken body and that drink of the poured-out blood make the spiritual life more living and stronger and the joy fuller, and render all things more complete for the state of the present life. The body of Christ was broken once and his blood was poured out once; but soon his body was raised up and quickened, and his blood was poured back into his veins. Nor was the broken body or the poured-out blood ever eaten or drunk bodily by anyone, not even by the disciples of Christ themselves, most of whom, seeking safety for their own lives in flight, did not even see him dead, but embraced him only after he had been made alive. By this argument we make it clear that this communion with the broken body and poured-out blood is not bodily but spiritual; and it is nothing other than communion with his death, satisfaction, merit, righteousness and life. Those who eat the flesh and drink the blood of Christ have these things in common and intimately, just as those who eat bread and drink wine have these things in common and intimately with them; indeed, they are converted into their own substance, juice and blood. So there is a communion with the broken body of Christ, and a communion with Christ as a whole through his poured-out blood, both as to foundation and fruit, and indeed with him as crucified and also with him as made alive, sitting at the right hand of God. As members of his body, we are sharers in his death, merit, righteousness and life, and in this life we are quickened more and more, preserved, nourished to eternal life, and find our delight in him alone. This is the one necessary and saving communion with Christ. Without it, the broken flesh of Christ and the poured-out blood profit us nothing; indeed they harm us more, for those whose Saviour Christ is not, as of his body, will have him as a stern judge, because of their scorning of his death and of this communion.

units.la: C V. Maximum ergo & unicè salutare Eucharistici hujus convivii mysterium est, & totius Evangelii atque Fœderis gratiæ sub Evangelio œconomiæ summam, quæ æquè Sacramentorum Christi, atque verbi ejus indoles est, complectitur. Docet enim convivium isthoc per visibilia & corporalia repræsentans invisibilia, spiritualia & cœlestia, Jesum Christum, Filium Dei, venisse in mundum, tanquam panem cœlitus missum, qui vitam dat mundo. Eum verò, ut fieret nobis cibus & potus satians, hoc est, ut cum ipso habeamus communionem ad vitam & lætitiam, quemadmodum necesse erat, corpus suum frangendum, & sanguinem effundendum pro mundi vita dedisse. Itaque corpus ipsius revera esse escam, & sanguinem ejus revera esse potum, hoc est, mortem ipsius ad expiationem & vivificationem multorum, qui in ipso mortui sint, comparatam esse. Et nisi quis carnem ejus edat, & sanguinem ejus bibat, hoc est, per fidem in ipsum crucifixum particeps mortis ipsius fiat, non habere vitam in se; eum verò, qui ejus carnem edit, & sanguinem bibit, hoc est, qui in ipsum credit, non tantum ut de Cœlo datum, sed etiam ut mortuum, habere vitam æternam, cum & ipse in Christo maneat, & vicissim Christus in illo. Proin etiam cessare Vetus Testamentum, & omnia per πλήρωσιν consummationem eorum, quæ per mortem Christi consummari debuerant, nova facta, & Testamentum ipsum gratiæ æternum fuso Christi sanguine dedicatum, ejusque bona eximia in promptu credentibus omnibus esse; quia Christo mortuo, figuræ per veritatem abolitæ, accusatio peccati & servitus legis sublata, πλήρωσις per justitiæ & libertatis adductionem Ecclesiæ donata sit; atque etiam, sublato intergerino pariete, hæreditas gentium sic à filiis Abrahami cernatur, ut ex Novo Testamento ipsæ quoque gentes jam hæredes sint. Sicut enim gentes ad Baptismum, ita etiam ad Cœnam vocantur, & de eodem pane participant, ut, qui credunt, unum corpus Christi esse intelligantur. Neque nudè hæc declarari & recentari, sed etiam institutione usus symbolorum, manducationis panis, & potus vini, velut in sacro epulo, offerri & obsignari credentibus, atque sic eorundem fidem non parùm corroborari voluit. Quæ apertissimis verbis tum institutionis Cœnæ, Matth. XXVI. 26. &c. tum concionis, Joh. VI. 32. &c. ubi Christus analogiam symboli locutione metaphorica de communione mortis suæ per fidem fundat: tum declarationis S. Pauli 1. Cor. X. 16. 17. tradita sunt.
units.tr: CV. The greatest and only saving mystery of this Eucharistic feast is therefore the sum of the whole Gospel and of the economy of the covenant of grace under the Gospel, which is equally the character of the sacraments of Christ and of his Word. For this feast, representing invisible, spiritual and heavenly things through visible and bodily ones, teaches that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, came into the world as bread sent down from heaven, which gives life to the world. He gave his body to be broken and his blood to be poured out for the life of the world, as was necessary, so that he might become for us food and satisfying drink, that is, so that we might have communion with him unto life and joy. Thus his body is truly food, and his blood is truly drink; that is, his death has been provided for the atonement and quickening of many who have died in him. And unless one eats his flesh and drinks his blood, that is, becomes by faith a partaker of his death, one does not have life in oneself. But whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood, that is, whoever believes in him not only as given from heaven but also as dead, has eternal life, since he himself abides in Christ and Christ in him in turn. Therefore also the Old Testament has ceased, and all things have been made new by the fulfilment [πλήρωσιν] of those things which had to be accomplished through the death of Christ, and the Testament of grace itself, dedicated by the poured-out blood of Christ, and its excellent blessings are ready for all believers. For since Christ died, the figures have been abolished by the reality, the accusation of sin and the bondage of the law have been removed, and the fulfilment [πλήρωσις] has been given to the Church through the bringing in of righteousness and liberty. Moreover, with the dividing wall taken away, the inheritance of the Gentiles is so regarded by the sons of Abraham that, according to the New Testament, the Gentiles themselves are now heirs. For just as the Gentiles are called to Baptism, so they are also called to the Supper, and partake of the same bread, so that those who believe may be understood to be one body of Christ. Nor did he wish these things merely to be declared and recounted, but by the institution of the use of the symbols, the eating of the bread and the drinking of the wine, to be offered and sealed to believers as at a sacred feast, and thus their faith to be not a little strengthened. These things have been delivered in the most manifest words: both in the institution of the Supper, Matth. 26. 26 etc., and in the sermon, John 6. 32 etc., where Christ, by a metaphorical expression, grounds the analogy of the symbol on communion through faith with his death; and also in the declaration of St. Paul, 1 Cor. 10. 16. 17.

units.la: C VI. Sed symbola æquè ac ritus Eucharistici convivii ad mysterium quæque suum referenda sunt. Non simplex, sed duplex symbolum, Panem & Vinum Christus instituit, quia ita & perfecta redemptio corporis atque animæ nostræ, illius per fractionem corporis, hujus per effusionem sanguinis, cujus typus, sanguis animalium, animæ eorundem hospitium præcessit, (quod pluribus jam supra explicare occupavimus) & plenâ nutritio atque vivificatio spiritualis requirebat; & communio sanguinis communionem mortis & quidem violentæ, quæ fusionem sanguinis connexam habet, communio verò corporis non tantùm communionem ejus ut fracti, sed etiam ut resuscitati ad vitam significat. Nam multi dicimur ἐν Σῶμα unum corpus, 1. Cor. X. 17. quod & fractum & mortificatum fuit, & nunc vivum est. Ita cum Christo & mortuo & vivo communionem justitiæ & meriti morte acquisiti, & per resuscitationem atque vivificationem demonstrati; Rom. IV. 25. & cum eodem mortuo communionem mortis veteris hominis, vivo communionem novitatis vitæ habemus. Conformamur enim per manducationem corporis & sanguinis Christi cum toto Christo; neque tantùm in nobis ille moritur, sed etiam vivit, & vivit non tantùm in lætitia, sed etiam in cognitione & amore Dei, & sanctitate vitæ. Sicut panis & vinum sufficientissima & efficacissima vitæ corporalis sustentandæ & conservandæ media sunt: ita corpus & sanguis Christi vitæ spiritualis inchoandæ, conservandæ & consummandæ media efficacissima sunt. Ante omnia Christus panem & vinum accepit, & accipiendo à pane & vino vulgari discrevit. Sic plane Deus Pater in æterno consilio Christum accepit, & à reliqua massa humani generis, futurum Salvatorem populi, segregavit. Panis & vino Christus benedixit, & benedictione utrumque consecravit. Ita Deus Pater Filium suum in plenitudine temporis misit, & ad munus Mediatoris obeundum unxit atque sanctificavit. Panis fractio & vini effusio corporis Christi mortem & sanguinis effusionem, omnesque corporis & animæ cruciatus & πάθηματα ejusdem conspicua maximè similitudine expressit. Nec panis integer & non fractus, nec vinum non fusum pascit & nutrit. Ita Christus non fractus & mortuus vitam restituere non potuit. Utrumque panem & vinum Christus distribuit, panem edendum, vinum bibendum discipulis suis sigillatim obtulit, quo singuli credentes Christum acciperent, Joh. I. 12. & cum eo consummato communionem, quam hactenus habere non licuit, haberent, atque signaculum & testimonium Divinum justitiæ & remissionis peccatorum suorum consummatæ, crucifixione quippe corporis & effusione sanguinis Christi, adeoque testatoris consummationis acquisitæ haberent. Hoc sibi volunt verba promissionis de pane. Hoc enim est corpus meum (non amplius םשא ש׳ נף corpus Paschatis, sed) Σῶμά μου corpus meum, sacrificium verum, quod Deo Patri pro vobis offero, & quod pro vobis frangitur; & de poculo: Hoc est sanguis meus; ille Novi Testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur ad remissionem peccatorum, Matth. XXVI. 26.28. 1. Cor. XI. 24. Quibus in verbis εὐλογήσας jussio & denominatio rei, panis & vini accipienda est, qua ipsi certum officium & ministerium assignatur, ut licet non desinant esse panis & vinum, nihilominus recipiantur potiùs ut corpus & sanguis Domini, quàm ut panis & vinum. Panem enim corpus suum, & poculum sanguinem suum appellans, significat, se ea loco corporis, in Cœlum mox subvehendi, tanquam ἐνίχυσον pignus & sigillum substituere atque relinquere, & non minùs certum habeant, quòd corporis sui per fidem & Spiritum suum participes effecti sint, quam si oculis corporis videre possent unionem nostri cum ipsius corpore, æquè ac unionem nostrorum membrorum inter ipsa cernimus, aut ea, quæ comedimus & bibimus ad saturitatem & lætitiam, visceribus nostris misceri sentimus. Singulari quinetiam emphasi [?] Novum Testamentum in sanguine Christi appellatur, Luc. XXII. 20. quia Christus discipulis poculum tradidit velut instrumentum sive diploma manu & sigillo suo munitum, cujus fide nixi ipsum [?] interrogare, & in fiducia semper convenire potlint de eo, quod ipsis promiserat, quòd sicut sibi Pater; ita ipse illis Regnum Testamento donet, ibid. v. 29. Est enim Novum Testamentum æterni consilii ac propositi, quo Deus Pater & Filius constituerunt, ut Filius morte sua victa morte & peccato in mundo Regnum haberet, & Ecclesiam ad libertatem atque lætitiam per fidem in ipsum, nova ac recens veteri servituti succedens executio; quæ per [?] fidei Evangelii, & resipiscentiæ cum promissionibus ei propositò convenientibus peragitur. Id Testamentum in sanguine Christi consistit, quia eo fuso nihil amplius obstat, quò minùs animo etiam in hac vita adeatur, & percursis vitæ hujus spatiis, actu possideatur. Panem igitur corpus suum & poculum sanguinem suum, seu Testamentum Novum in sanguine suo accipere jussi Apostoli mandato obsequentes acceperunt. Quæ [?] acceptionis Christi & beneficium ejus per fidem nostræ figura est. Non aliis enim ad Christum & beneficia ejus jus est; quàm vera & viva fide eundem [?] accipientibus, Joh. I. 12. Denique jussi edere & bibere, ederunt & biberunt ex poculo omnes, Marc. XIV. 23. Cujus hæc [?] spiritualis significatio est, quòd nulla nobis sine unione & communione cum Christo & beneficiis ejus vita constet, adeòque Christus unà cum merito & beneficiis ejus cunctis necessitatibus & defectibus animæ nostræ alacri cum lætitia applicandus, imò totus Christus induendus, & in vitæ spiritualis succum & sanguinem convertendus sit, sicut enim Deus elementis externis acceptis benedicit ad vitæ temporalis sustentationem & robur: ita Christus fide apprehensus, Deo benedicente, corpus & animam nostram ad æternam vitam servat. Hic est ille panis, qui ex cælo descendit, ut quisquis ex eo comedit non moriatur. Ego sum panis vitæ, qui ex Cœlo descendit. Si quis comederit ex hoc pane, vivet in æternum. Et panis, quem ego dabo, caro mea est, quam dabo pro vita mundi, Joh. VI. 50. 51.
units.tr: CVI. But the symbols, just like the ritual of the Eucharistic feast, must each be referred to its own mystery. Christ instituted not a single symbol but a double one, bread and wine, because the perfect redemption of our body and soul required it in this way: of the one by the breaking of his body, of the other by the outpouring of his blood. The blood of animals, whose lodging of the soul preceded this as its type (as we have already undertaken to explain at length above), and full spiritual nourishment and quickening required it. Communion in the blood signifies communion in death, and indeed violent death, which has the shedding of blood joined to it. Communion in the body signifies communion not only in his body as broken but also in it as raised to life. For we, being many, are "one body" [ἓν σῶμα], 1 Cor. 10:17, which was both broken and put to death and is now alive. Thus we have communion with Christ both dead and living: with the dead Christ, communion in the righteousness and merit acquired by his death, and shown through his resurrection and quickening (Rom. 4:25); and with the same Christ, communion in the death of the old man, and, as living, communion in the newness of life. For by eating the body and blood of Christ we are conformed to the whole Christ. Not only does he die in us, but he also lives, and lives not only in joy but also in the knowledge and love of God and in holiness of life. Just as bread and wine are the most sufficient and effective means for sustaining and preserving bodily life, so the body and blood of Christ are the most effective means for beginning, preserving and bringing to completion spiritual life. First of all, Christ took bread and wine, and by taking them he distinguished them from common bread and wine. Thus God the Father, in his eternal counsel, took Christ and set him apart from the rest of the mass of mankind as the future Saviour of the people. Christ blessed the bread and the wine, and by the blessing he consecrated both. So God the Father sent his Son in the fullness of time, and anointed and sanctified him to undertake the office of Mediator. The breaking of the bread and the pouring out of the wine expressed, with a most conspicuous likeness, the death of Christ's body and the effusion of his blood, and all the torments of body and soul and his sufferings [παθήματα]. Neither whole unbroken bread nor unpoured wine feeds and nourishes; so Christ, unbroken and dead, could not restore life. Christ distributed both bread and wine. He offered the bread to be eaten and the wine to be drunk, to each of his disciples separately, so that each believer might receive Christ (John 1:12), and with him, now that it was accomplished, might have the communion which had not hitherto been permitted. They would have the seal and divine testimony of the righteousness and forgiveness of their sins now fulfilled, namely by the crucifixion of Christ's body and the outpouring of his blood, and so of the testator's accomplished consummation. This is what the words of promise over the bread mean: "This is my body" (not the body of the Passover [גוף פסח] any longer, but) "my body" [Σῶμά μου], the true sacrifice which I offer to God the Father for you, and which is broken for you. And over the cup: "This is my blood, the blood of the New Testament, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Matt. 26:26–28; 1 Cor. 11:24). In these words the "blessing" [εὐλογήσας] and the naming of the bread and wine must be taken as a command and a designation of the thing, by which a definite office and ministry is assigned to them. So although they do not cease to be bread and wine, they are received rather as the body and blood of the Lord than as bread and wine. For in calling the bread his body and the cup his blood, he signifies that in place of his body, soon to be carried up into heaven, he substitutes and leaves these as a pledge [ἐνέχυρον] and seal. And believers are no less certain that they have been made partakers of his body through faith and his Spirit than if they could see with bodily eyes our union with his body, just as we see the union of our members with one another, or feel what we eat and drink, for satisfaction and joy, being mixed into our inward parts. Moreover, with a singular emphasis the New Testament is called "in the blood of Christ" (Luke 22:20), because Christ handed the cup to the disciples as an instrument or charter, confirmed by his hand and seal. Relying on this, they might ask him and always confidently claim what he had promised them: that "as my Father has appointed to me, so I appoint to you a kingdom" by testament (ibid. v. 29). For the New Testament is the execution of the eternal counsel and purpose by which God the Father and the Son determined that the Son, by his death having overcome death and sin, should have the kingdom in the world, and that the Church should come to liberty and joy through faith in him. This is a new and recent execution, succeeding the old servitude, and it is carried out through faith in the Gospel and repentance, in agreement with the promises set forth to it. This Testament consists in the blood of Christ, because once that blood was poured out nothing more stands in the way of approaching him in mind even in this life, and, having run through the span of this life, of actually possessing him. Therefore the apostles, obeying the command, received the bread as his body and the cup as his blood, that is, the New Testament in his blood. This "receiving" of Christ and his benefit through faith is the figure of our own. For no one has a right to Christ and his benefits except those who receive him by true and living faith (John 1:12). Finally, as they were commanded to eat and drink, they all ate and drank from the cup (Mark 14:23). The spiritual significance of this is that there is no life for us apart from union and communion with Christ and his benefits. Christ, together with his merit and benefits, is therefore to be applied with cheerful joy to all the needs and defects of our soul; indeed, all of Christ is to be put on and turned into the juice and blood of spiritual life. For just as God, blessing external elements when they are taken, sustains and strengthens temporal life, so Christ, apprehended by faith, with God blessing, preserves our body and soul to eternal life. "This is the bread which came down from heaven, that whoever eats of it should not die. I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world" (John 6:50–51).

units.la: CVII. In verbis promissionis Christi, Hoc est corpus meum, Matth. XXVI. 26. 27. panem pro subjecto poni, & series institutionis atque [?] & pronomen Τοῦτο Hoc; quod corpus ipsum sine [?] insicta non tare non potest, & [?] alterius signi, poculi, quod diserte Novum Testamentum in sanguine Christi Luc. XXII. 20. appellatur, & Apostoli explicatio omni exceptione major, quia is [?] panem dixit communionem corporis Christi, 1. Cor. X. 16. manifestè arguunt. Neque panem corpus, vel communionem corporis poculum sanguinem, vel communionem sanguinis proprie dici, supra jam ostendimus. Maxima enim locutionum ejusmodi sacramentalium impropriarum ratio est, substitutio scilicet signi in locum rei signatæ, ad [?] fidei signendam majorem. Neque tamen propterea locutiones illæ insolentes vel obscuræ haberi debent, quia artis rhetoricæ authores disceptant, quisnam in iis tropus sit. Quorum [?] sicut aliquando judicium & memoriam discentium adjuvant; ita prudentes nulla lege adstringunt, & intelligentiam eorum, qui in Scripturis sensus exercitatos habent, remorari non possunt. Satis est, quòd locutio improprie, at in Sacramentis tamen usitata est, atque ad propriam nullo negotio revocari potest, dummodo [?] & sophistice absit. Et in subjecto quidem proprius & naturalis panis; in prædicato verum & naturale corpus Christi intelligitur. Sed modus prædicationis, quem copula [?] est indicat, non proprius & substantialis est, quia panis proprie non est corpus Christi, nec substantia corporis Christi est substantia panis. At nec synecdochicus est, quasi corpus Christi in pane, sanguis in poculo contineatur, quia Christus non docuit, ubi suum corpus, vel suus sanguis sit, quibusque ambo receptaculis continentur, sed quod officium, quemve usum panis & vinum hoc in Sacramento habeant. Est verò modus ille prædicationis sacramentalis & metonymicus, in omnibus Sacramentis usitatus, quo nomen rei signatæ de signo prædicatur. Atque ita panis est corpus Christi tum per [?] , tum per [?] sive vicariam substitutionem, qualis est sigilli & pignoris pro se promissa, integra hæreditate, fundo, regno; & similibus, quæ tradito symbolo tradi dicuntur: & poculum est Testamentum per [?] significationem & confirmationem: & panis est communio corporis Christi; poculum communio sanguinis Christi per [?] obsignationem. In quibus singulis ratio significandi, obsignandi, vices obeundi in copula subauditur. Quæ etiam in propria nullo negotio revocantur, & quidem plenissimè & universo mysterio exprimendo sic, ut panis à Christo acceptus, benedictus, fractus, distributus, acceptus à communicantibus, & manducatus, atque ita in substantiam manducantis, non sine sensu lætitiæ & vitæ conversus esse signum, sigillum, pignus, arrhabo corporis Christi à Deo Patre accepti seu segregati & sanctificati ad hoc ut frangatur, seu moriatur pro peccatore, eidem offeratur, ab eodem vera & viva fide apprehendatur & applicetur, atque ita manducatus secundum meritum; justitiam & vitam in communionem manducantis intimam, ad ejusdem justitiam, lætitiam, sanctitatem & vitam perennem perveniat; prædicetur. Et de poculo similiter. Quam analysin propositionum sacramentalium ipsum mysterium symbolorum & rituum circa symbola superius erutum amplissimè confirmat.
units.tr: CVII. In the words of Christ's promise, "This is my body" (Matt. 26:26–27), the bread is put as the subject, and the sequence of the institution clearly shows this, as does the pronoun Τοῦτο ("this"), which cannot refer to anything but the body itself. The other sign, the cup, is expressly called the New Testament in the blood of Christ (Luke 22:20), and the Apostle's explanation, greater than any objection, clearly proves it, since he called the bread the communion of the body of Christ (1 Cor. 10:16). As we have already shown above, the bread is not properly called the body, nor the cup the blood, nor is the communion of the body properly the body. For the chief ground of such sacramental and improper expressions is the substitution of the sign for the thing signified, so as to strengthen the faith. Nor, on that account, ought these unusual or obscure expressions to be regarded as obscure, merely because writers on the art of rhetoric dispute which trope they are. Such discussions sometimes help the judgement and memory of learners, but the wise do not bind them by any rule, nor can they hinder the understanding of those who have trained senses in the Scriptures. It is enough that the expression is improper, yet customary in the Sacraments, and can be restored to its proper sense without any difficulty, provided that there is no trickery or sophistry. In the subject, indeed, the bread is understood as proper and natural bread; in the predicate, the true and natural body of Christ. But the mode of predication which the copula is indicates is not proper and substantial, because bread is not properly the body of Christ, nor is the substance of the body of Christ the substance of bread. Nor is it synecdochical, as if the body of Christ were contained in the bread and the blood in the cup; for Christ did not teach where his body or his blood is, or in what receptacles both are contained, but what office and use bread and wine have in this Sacrament. Rather, that mode of predication is sacramental and metonymical, used in all the Sacraments, by which the name of the thing signified is predicated of the sign. Thus "the bread is the body of Christ" by a figure of signification and by a vicarious substitution, such as is the seal and pledge promised in place of the whole inheritance, the estate or the kingdom, and similar things, which are said to be delivered when the symbol is delivered. "The cup is the Testament" by a figure of signification and confirmation; "the bread is the communion of the body of Christ," and "the cup the communion of the blood of Christ," by a figure of sealing. In each of these the sense of signifying, sealing, and taking the place of, is understood in the copula. These too are easily restored to the proper sense, and indeed fully, so as to express the whole mystery: that the bread, taken by Christ, blessed, broken, distributed, and received by those communicating, and eaten, and thus, not without a sense of joy and life, converted into the substance of the eater, is a sign, seal, pledge and earnest of the body of Christ, taken by God the Father, or set apart and sanctified, that it might be broken, or die for the sinner, and offered to him; apprehended and applied by him with true and living faith; and so, eaten, it attains, according to its merit, to the inward communion of the eater with justice and life, to his righteousness, joy, holiness and everlasting life. The same is said of the cup. This analysis of the sacramental propositions is amply confirmed by the very mystery of the symbols and rites, as brought out above concerning the symbols.

units.la: CVIII. Verbum Christi, quo usum Cœnæ à se institutæ in posterum etiam commendat, illud est; [?] Hoc facite ad mei recordationem, Luc. XXII. 19. 1. Cor. XI. 24. Et quoties ederitis, &c. annuntiate mortem Domini donec venerit, vers. 26. Id testatestatur fidelem recordationem Christi, amoris, obedientiæ, sacrificii & mortis ejus sufficere tentatis ad consolationem. In V. T. erat recordatio peccati in sacrificiorum celebratione à Deo instituta, Hebr. X. 3. Hic instituitur non monimentum peccati, flagitans repetitionem sacrificii, sed memoriale unici sacrificii, quod est in morte Christi, quo sanctificati in perpetuum consummantur, ibid. v. 14. 17. 18. Et verbum illud secutus Apostolus tradidit Corinthiis, quod à Domino acceperat, 1. Cor. XI. 23. nec tantùm Corinthiis, sed omni etiam homini, qui se ipsum exploraverit, ut non indignè comedat & bibat, ibid. 23. 26. 29. Ex quo clarum est; hoc verbo Christi potestatem fieri omnibus fidelibus, ubi se exploraverint, cum ἀγγελ ... accipiendi panem & vinum benedictum, edendíque & bibendi sæpius, donec ipsi ex hac vita discedant, & Christus veniat ad judicium, ad recordationem Christi, hoc est, ut recordentur, corpus ejus pro ipsis datum fractumque esse, & sanguinem ipsius pro ipsis fusum esse ad remissionem peccatorum, ut hæredes justitiæ & vitæ ex N. T. fierent. Est autem Cœna Domini aptissimum medium conservandæ memoriæ dictorum & factorum Christi, inprimis mortis & resurrectionis ejus; non tantum ut cogitatio illius in mentem veniat, u-tenti, sed etiam ut ille in Ecclesia custoditus faciat fidem, quòd ea, quæ in Evangelio de Christo scripta sunt, sic dicta, facta, prædicata, credita sint, & vera sint, si enim vera non essent, Christiani primi induci non potuissent, ut, repugnantibus Judæis & Gentibus, ea crederent, & in memoriam eorum Cœnam celebrarent. Neque ulla arte vel potentia Sathanæ effici potuit, ut hic ritus ab Ecclesia tolleretur. Et quia is apud Ecclesiam ita conservatus est, secundum substantiam, ut à Christo usurpatus & traditus est, cognoscimus veritatem historiæ apparitionis Christi, quæ in libris Evangeliorum testata est. Neque enim hic ritus recipi nisi à recipientibus libros Evangelicos potuit. Nec potuerunt recipi libri Evangelici, nisi ab iis, qui ista sic geri dicique vidissent & audivissent, aut ad quos à videntibus & audientibus ea ad certitudinem confirmata fuissent. Denique & ipsa summa doctrinæ Christianæ verbis institutionis continetur, quibus animo evidentius insculpendis symbolum ipsum, si mens læva non sit, accommodatissimum est.
units.tr: The words of Christ, by which he further commends the use of the Supper he instituted, are these: Do this in remembrance of me, Luke 22:19; 1 Cor. 11:24. And as often as you eat, &c., proclaim the Lord's death until he comes, v. 26. This testifies that the faithful remembrance of Christ, of his love, obedience, sacrifice and death, is enough for consolation in temptations. In the Old Testament, the sacrifices instituted by God brought a remembrance of sin, Heb. 10:3. Here, by contrast, is instituted not a memorial of sin demanding the repetition of a sacrifice, but a memorial of the one sacrifice made in the death of Christ, by which those who are sanctified are perfected for ever, ibid. vv. 14, 17, 18. Following these words, the Apostle delivered to the Corinthians what he had received from the Lord, 1 Cor. 11:23, and not only to the Corinthians but to every person who examines himself, so that he does not eat and drink unworthily, ibid. vv. 23, 26, 29. From this it is clear that by these words of Christ all the faithful are given the power, when they have examined themselves, to receive the blessed bread and wine [angelia] and to eat and drink them often, until they depart from this life and Christ comes to judgment, in remembrance of Christ; that is, so that they may remember that his body was given and broken for them, and his blood was shed for them for the forgiveness of sins, so that they might become heirs of righteousness and life through the New Testament. The Lord's Supper is indeed the most fitting means of preserving the memory of the sayings and deeds of Christ, above all of his death and resurrection; not only so that thought of them comes to mind, but also so that, being kept in the Church, it makes faith certain that what the Gospel writes about Christ was said, done, preached and believed as it is related, and is true. For if it were not true, the first Christians could not have been induced, against the opposition of Jews and Gentiles, to believe these things and to celebrate the Supper in their memory. Nor could this rite have been removed from the Church by any art or power of Satan. And because it has been so preserved in the Church, in substance, as it was used and handed down by Christ, we recognise the truth of the history of Christ's appearance, which is attested in the books of the Gospels. For this rite could not have been received except by those who received the Gospel books; nor could the Gospel books have been received except by those who had seen and heard these things so done and said, or to whom they had been confirmed as certain by those who saw and heard. Finally, the very sum of Christian doctrine is contained in the words of institution, and the symbol itself is most suitable for impressing them more vividly on the mind, if the mind is not perverse.

units.la: CIX. Finis ergo S. Cœnæ præcipuus est recordatio mortis Christi, & ejusdem annuntiatio; eáque non tenuiter accepta, sed prægnans; non theoretica tantùm, sed etiam practica, qua is, qui mortis Christi recordatur & eandem annuntiat, beneficia omnia morte ejus parta grata mente recolit, fide per symbola confirmata sibi applicat, & communionem cum Christi morte & vita habet. Sicut enim peregrè proficiscens aliquod pignus ei, quem diligit quandoque relinquit, ut quotiescunque illud viderit, amoris & beneficiorum ejus suaviter recordari, grata mente recolere, & eo ipso delicias sibi facere possit: ita Christus in cœlum mox profectu-rus dilectis suis symbola hæc, velut amoris sui pignus, reliquit, ut illa intuentes vera fide, mortis & beneficiorum ejus jucundam memoriam animo suo agitent. Cùmque commemoratio illa inferat communionem corporis & sanguinis Christi, nudè theoretica esse non potest. Tali enim commemoratione, uti scitè Wesselus Groningensis de Euchar. cap. 5. dixit, reficimur, & ab omnibus debitis absolvimur. Hæc enim (corpus & sanguis Domini) hausta & sumpta faciunt ut nos in Christo, & Christus in nobis maneat. Qui igitur Christi recordatur & ejus mortem annuntiat, is etiam recordatur & annuntiat, se credere mortem Christi in fide juxta dictum Christi: Hoc enim est corpus meum, &c. Nam nec κατ' ἀγγελία annuntiatio illa est sine ἐπικλήσει & ὀνόματος & Κυρίου invocatione nominis Domini, qua ipsum Dominum nostrum dicimus cum gloriatione & gratiarum actione ob beneficia morte Christi nobis parta, & solenniter in hac ipsa mensa denuo confirmata, ob quæ vicissim ad eum amandum & colendum obligamur. Principali igitur subordinatus & secundarius finis est tum confirmatio fidei nostræ de remissione peccatorum per sanguinem Christi effusum εἰς ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ad remissionem peccatorum, Matth. XXVI. 28. ejusque publica professio: tum incrementum charitatis & lætitiæ in Spiritu S. pacis conscientiæ, spei vitæ æternæ, & gratiarum Dei omnium, inprimis etiam promptitudinis nostræ ad præstanda alacriter officia, ad quæ Christi Domini voluntas, & debita pro tantis beneficiis gratitudo nos obligat: tum conservatio publici cultus verbi Dei & precum in publico coetu: tum denique conjunctio fidelium, non tantùm cum capite Christo, sed etiam inter se. Unus panis, unum corpus multi sumus. Nam omnes ex uno pane participamus, 1. Cor. X. 17. Omnes in unum Spiritum potati sumus, ibid. XII. 13. Ideo in Veteri Ecclesia nemo nisi ὁμόψυχοι in sacris ad mensam Dominicam admittebatur; hereticorum excommunicabantur, & unitas fidei per missitationem reciprocam Eucharistiæ inter illos obstringebatur. CX. Usum Cœnæ sedula & diligens δοκιμασία exploratio seu probatio uniuscujusque fidelis præcedat oportet. Δοκιμαζέτω ἄνθρωπος ἑαυτόν, Probet homo se ipsum & sic de pane edat, & de poculo bibat, 1. Cor. X. 28. Nam qui se ipsum non δοκιμάζει probat, is ἀδόκιμός est. Est autem se ipsum explorare cogitationes suas, judicium suum de mysterio Cœnæ & de se ipso, famem & sitim justitiæ, propositum cordis, notitiam, amorem, studium, fiduciam, vitam suam omnem & resipiscentiam cum Divino verbo, ceu regula & lydio lapide hujus examinis comparare. In verbo enim Dei veræ fidei & resipiscentiæ typus extat. Non enim hic aliorum de se judicium operiri, vel se, quòd ab aliis dignus judicatur, dignum existimare, sed se ipsum quivis probare juxta regulam illam debet. Neque etiam præparatio ad Cœnam perfectionem operis nostri, velut contritionis, confessionis & satisfactionis postulat, uti Tridentini definiverunt. In Eucharistia enim nobis offeruntur ea, quæ Filius Dei nobis corporis sui traditione, & sanguinis sui effusione promeruit, & promissioni Evangelii pignus & obsignatio additur. Quæ gratuita promissio non opere nostro, nedum merito contritionis & satisfactionis nostræ, sed fide, ad quam solam promissio relationem habet, appreapprehenditur. Ipsa vero praestantiae hujus cibi & potus, nec indigentiae nostrae antithesis, per se conscientias nostras terrere apta nata est. Ex quo terrore non contritionis & satisfactionis nostrae fiducia, sed abnegatione meriti nostri, & fiducia in Christi solius merito elucidamur. Sed & fructus Coenae Dominicae hoc modo nobis inutilis redditur. Semper enim conscientia anceps haerebit, an contritio & satisfactio sufficiens, qualem illi exigunt, a nobis praestita sit. Denique praeparationis illum rigorem praescribere iis placuit, ad publicam communionem obliterandam, & Missas privatas stabiliendas. Nam has sine ullo periculo meritorias esse ad delenda quaevis peccata mortalia contendunt.
units.tr: CIX. The principal end of the Holy Supper is therefore the remembrance of the death of Christ and the proclamation of it; and this not taken in a thin sense, but in a full and fruitful one, not merely theoretical but also practical, whereby the one who remembers the death of Christ and proclaims it gratefully recalls all the benefits won by his death, applies them to himself by faith confirmed through the signs, and has communion with the death and life of Christ. For just as a man setting out on a journey sometimes leaves behind some pledge for the one he loves, so that whenever he sees it he may sweetly remember that love and its benefits, recall them with a grateful mind, and so find delight for himself, so Christ, about to depart at once into heaven, left these signs to his beloved as a pledge of his love, so that, looking upon them with true faith, they might stir in their minds a pleasant memory of his death and benefits. And since that remembrance brings with it communion with the body and blood of Christ, it cannot be merely theoretical. For by such remembrance, as Wessel of Groningen rightly says in his book on the Eucharist, chapter 5, we are refreshed and absolved from all our debts. For these things (the body and blood of the Lord), when drunk and eaten, cause us to abide in Christ and Christ in us. Therefore whoever remembers Christ and proclaims his death, also remembers and proclaims that he believes in the death of Christ by faith, according to the saying of Christ: For this is my body, &c. For that proclamation [katangelia] is not without the invocation [epiklesis] and calling upon the name of the Lord [onomatos kai Kyriou], by which we call him our Lord with rejoicing and thanksgiving for the benefits won for us by the death of Christ, and solemnly confirmed anew at this very table, and by which in turn we are bound to love and worship him. The principal end, therefore, and a subordinate and secondary end, is both the confirmation of our faith in the forgiveness of sins through the blood of Christ shed for the forgiveness of sins [eis aphesin tōn hamartiōn], Matt. 26:28, and its public profession; and the increase of love and joy in the Holy Spirit, of peace of conscience, of hope of eternal life, and of all the grace of God; above all also of our readiness to perform duties eagerly, to which the will of the Lord Christ and the gratitude we owe for such great benefits bind us; and the preservation of the public worship of God's Word and of prayer in the public assembly; and finally the union of the faithful, not only with Christ their head but also with one another. We, being many, are one bread, one body; for we all partake of one bread, 1 Cor. 10:17. For we were all made to drink into one Spirit, ibid. 12:13. Therefore in the ancient Church no one was admitted to the Lord's table in the sacred rites except those of one mind [homopsychoi]; heretics were excluded, and the unity of faith was bound among them by the mutual sending of the Eucharist. CX. The use of the Supper ought to be preceded by a diligent and careful examination [dokimasia], that is, the testing of each believer. Let a man examine himself [dokimazetō anthrōpos heauton], and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup, 1 Cor. 11:28. For whoever does not test himself is unapproved [adokimos]. To examine oneself is to compare one's thoughts, one's judgment about the mystery of the Supper and about oneself, one's hunger and thirst for righteousness, the purpose of the heart, knowledge, love, zeal, trust, one's whole life and repentance, with the Word of God, as with a rule and touchstone of this examination. For in the Word of God there is the pattern of true faith and repentance. Nor is it for one to wait for the judgment of others about oneself, or to regard oneself as worthy because one is judged worthy by others; each person ought to test himself by that rule. Nor does the preparation for the Supper require, as the Tridentine fathers defined, the perfection of our own work, as of contrition, confession and satisfaction. For in the Eucharist are offered to us those things which the Son of God merited by the giving of his body and the shedding of his blood, and a pledge and seal are added to the promise of the Gospel. This free promise is apprehended not by our work, much less by the merit of our contrition and satisfaction, but by faith, to which alone the promise has relation. Moreover, the very excellence of this food and drink, set against our neediness, is by its nature fitted to terrify our consciences. From this terror we are freed not by confidence in our contrition and satisfaction, but by renouncing our own merit and trusting in the merit of Christ alone. But also the fruit of the Lord's Supper is made useless to us in this way: the conscience will always remain in doubt whether the contrition and satisfaction we have offered are sufficient, of the kind they demand. Finally, those men were pleased to prescribe that rigour of preparation in order to wipe out public communion and to establish private Masses; for they contend that these are meritorious without any danger for blotting out any mortal sins.

units.la: CXI. Sed de praesentia & communione corporis & sanguinis Domini in Eucharistia ejusque modo amplius etiam dicendum. Et initio quidem non imaginaria & intentionalis duntaxat, uti loquuntur, in Eucharistia corporis & sanguinis Christi praesentia & communio est, quia non corporalis est. Neque meros corticcs sine nucleo, hoc est, nuda & vacua signa absque Christo convivium hoc mysticum promittit. Nam nec V. T. Sacramenta, in quibus corporalis Christi praesentia ne cogitari quidem potest, Christo vacua fuerunt. Omnes enim Patres ederunt eandem (inter se & nobiscum) escam spiritualem, & biberunt eundem potum spiritualem. Biberunt enim ex sequente spirituali petra, Petra autem erat Christus, 1. Cor. X. 3. 4. 5. Et quanto minus nostra Sacramenta Christo vacua sunt? Veteres enim umbram futurorum bonorum habuerunt, nos autem habemus αὐτὴν τὴν εἰκόνα τῶν πραγμάτων ipsam expressam formam rerum, Hebr. X. 1. Sicut enim pictores, quorum ars ex umbris inventa dicitur, cum imaginis summas lineas ducunt, eam adumbrare; cum pingendo easdem illustrant, expressam rei formam repraesentare dicuntur. Ita V. T. Patres umbram & adumbrationem corporis & sanguinis Christi: nos imaginem vivis Evangelicae historiae coloribus illustratam habemus. Christus enim in Evangelio & Sacramentis ejusdem ob oculos nobis depingitur, Gal. III. 1. Tum Evangelium corpus & sanguinem Christi nobis proponit; quia haec praecipuum Evangelii objectum sunt, uti ex Joh. VI. & ipsa Eucharistiae institutione liquet. Eadem ergo Eucharistia quoque nobis praesentia sistit. Eucharistia enim Evangelii objectum non mutat, sed magis confirmat, externa symbola adjiciens, ut Evangelium, quod auditus proprie objectum est, Rom. X. 17. ad fidem magis excitandam, visibile quodammodo reddatur. Unde S. Augustinus Tract. 80. in Joh. Sacramentum visibile verbum scite appellat. Ubi etiam Sacramenti hanc [?] tradit. Accedit verbum ad elementum & fit Sacramentum. Accedente igitur ad aquam verbo, Baptismus; ad panem & vinum, Eucharistia fit. Quod verbum promissionis verbum est. Sacramentorum simul anima atque nucleus, & Evangelii summa. Praeterea fides nostra Spiritus S. virtute corpus & sanguinem Domini in Coena amplectitur. Idem enim Evangelii & fidei objectum est, corpus & sanguis Domini. Quod Evangelium proponit, id fides amplectitur;
units.tr: CXI. But we must also say more about the presence and communion of the body and blood of the Lord in the Eucharist, and about its manner. First, the presence and communion of the body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist is not merely imaginary and intentional, as they put it, since it is not bodily. Nor does this mystical feast offer mere husks without the kernel, that is, bare and empty signs without Christ. For the sacraments of the Old Testament were not empty of Christ either, although the bodily presence of Christ cannot even be conceived in them. For all the Fathers ate the same spiritual food (among themselves and with us), and drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ, 1 Cor. X. 3. 4. 5. And how much less are our sacraments empty of Christ? For the ancients had a shadow of the good things to come, but we have the very image of the things [αὐτὴν τὴν εἰκόνα τῶν πραγμάτων], the very expressed form of the things, Heb. X. 1. For painters, whose art is said to have been discovered from shadows, when they draw the outermost lines of an image are said to shadow it forth, but when by painting they bring out its colours they are said to represent the expressed form of the thing. So the Fathers of the Old Testament had the shadow and adumbration of the body and blood of Christ; we have the image brought out in the living colours of the Evangelical history. For Christ is painted before our eyes in the Gospel and in its sacraments, Gal. III. 1. Then, the Gospel sets forth the body and blood of Christ before us, because these are the chief object of the Gospel, as is clear from John VI. and from the very institution of the Eucharist. The same Eucharist therefore also presents them to us. For the Eucharist does not change the object of the Gospel but rather confirms it, adding outward symbols, so that the Gospel, whose proper object is what is heard, Rom. X. 17., is in a way made visible to excite faith more strongly. Hence St. Augustine, Tract. 80 on John, aptly calls the sacrament a visible word. There, too, he gives this definition [?]: The word comes to the element and it becomes a sacrament. So when the word is added to the water, there is Baptism; when it is added to the bread and wine, there is the Eucharist. This word is the word of promise, the soul and kernel of the sacraments at once, and the sum of the Gospel. Moreover, by the power of the Holy Spirit our faith embraces the body and blood of the Lord in the Supper. For the body and blood of the Lord are one and the same object of the Gospel and of faith. What the Gospel sets forth, faith embraces.

units.la: Ideo Evangelium dicitur potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I. 16. Lex fidei, ibid. III. 27. Verbum fidei, ibid. X. 8. At fides in Coena corpus & sanguinem Christi amplectitur, utpote in qua Evangelii haec summa, quod Christi corpus pro nobis traditum, & sanguis pro nobis effusus sit ad remissionem peccatorum. Matth. XXVI. 28. proponitur. Haec in Coena vera fide ruminamus, utpote quam in sui recordationem Christus instituit, Luc. XXII. 19. Quae recordatio una cum fide conjuncta corpus Domini traditum, jam licet gloriosum, & sanguinem ejus effusum, dudum licet exaruerit, praesentissima nobis sistit. Fides enim efficit, ut quae sperantur, extent, & demonstrat quae non videntur, Heb. XI. 1. sive illa praesentia, sive praeterita, sive futura sint, ut ex symbolo constat. Ac licet etiam extra Coenam id quotidie fieri debeat; tamen misericordiae Dei memoriam nostram per externa symbola, oculis fidelibus subjecta, excitare, atque ita fidem confirmare visum est. Ipsa symbolorum distributio & sumptio credentibus singulis facta significat, & obsignat, Christum pro credentibus singulis passum esse. Sicut enim verbum Dei beneficia Christi non in genere tantum proponit, & velut e longinquo fidelibus ostentat, sed fidelium singulis applicat, Psal. CIII. 3. Esaj. XLIII. 25. Gal. II. 20. ita Sacramenta, quae verbi Dei sigilla sunt, eadem Christi beneficia singulis fidelibus obsignat. Usus igitur Eucharistiae fidei salvificae exercitium & gymnasium est, in quo non tantum corporis & sanguinis Christi symbola ore corporeo sumimus, sed ipsum etiam corpus & sanguinem Christi fide percipimus; sed id totum Spiritus S. virtute fit: is enim est, qui vivificat, Joh. VI. 63. 2. Cor. III. 6. & vivam in nobis fidem, qua corpus Domini fractum comedimus, & sanguinem ejus fusum bibimus, ut per illa alamur, & ad vitam aeternam conservemur, excitat, Joh. VI. 53. &c. Communio vero illa corporis & sanguinis Christi, quam fides Spiritus S. virtute in Coena Domini amplectitur, praesentiam illorum necessario postulat.
units.tr: Hence the Gospel is called the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, Rom. I. 16.; the law of faith, ibid. III. 27.; the word of faith, ibid. X. 8. But in the Supper faith embraces the body and blood of Christ, since in it is set forth the sum of the Gospel, namely that the body of Christ was given for us and his blood shed for us for the remission of sins, Matt. XXVI. 28. In the Supper we chew this over with true faith, since Christ instituted it in remembrance of himself, Luke XXII. 19. This remembrance, joined with faith, presents to us most vividly the body of the Lord given up, though now glorious, and his blood shed, though it dried up long ago. For faith causes the things hoped for to be real, and demonstrates the things not seen, Heb. XI. 1., whether they are present, past or future, as is clear from the creed. And although this ought to be done daily even outside the Supper, it has nonetheless seemed good to stir up our memory of God's mercy through outward symbols placed before the eyes of the faithful, and so to confirm faith. The very distribution and eating of the symbols, done for each believer, signifies and seals that Christ suffered for each believer. For just as the word of God sets forth the benefits of Christ not only in general, and displays them from afar to the faithful, but applies them to each of the faithful, Ps. CIII. 3., Isa. XLIII. 25., Gal. II. 20., so the sacraments, which are the seals of the word of God, seal the same benefits of Christ to each of the faithful. The use of the Eucharist is therefore an exercise and training ground of saving faith, in which we not only take the symbols of the body and blood of Christ with our bodily mouth, but also perceive the body and blood of Christ themselves by faith. This whole thing, however, is done by the power of the Holy Spirit, for he is the one who gives life, John VI. 63., 2 Cor. III. 6., and he stirs up in us a living faith by which we eat the broken body of the Lord and drink his shed blood, so that we are nourished by them and preserved to eternal life, John VI. 53. etc. But that communion with the body and blood of Christ, which faith embraces by the power of the Holy Spirit in the Lord's Supper, necessarily requires their presence.

units.la: CXII. Duplex igitur praesentiae & communionis corporis & sanguinis Christi in Eucharistia modus est, relativus & spiritualis. Relativus qui idem etiam symbolicus & sacramentalis vocatur, est, quo juxta Domini institutionem panis & vinum, & illius simul fractio & comestio, hujus fusio & bibitio, ad verbum promissionis obsignandum, & bona promissa, corpus Domini pro nobis traditum, & sanguinem ejus pro nobis fusum, significanda & exhibenda ordinantur atque consecrantur. Relativum dicitur, quia in relatione consistit, qua tum pani & vino, tum ritibus a Deo institutis, tanquam signis ad res signatas repraesentandas & obsignandas adhaeret. Quanta vero vis sit relationum in asserenda & confirmanda rerum acquisitione & possessione, non Sacramenta duntaxat, sed etiam Testamenta, literae, sigilla, arrhae, pignora, & alia id genus testantur, quae propter relationem, quae illis vel authoritate publica, vel eorum, quorum interest, consensu adhaeret, in rerum instrumentis illis comprehensorum possessionem, non utique [?] imaginariam & dubiam, sed realem & certam, quas oportet, mittunt. Panis ergo vinum, juxta institutionem Domini sumpta, corpus & sanguinem Domini, & verbum promissionis nobis exhibent & obsignant relative quidem, sed pro relatorum à Deo inprimis ipso, institutorum indole adeo potenter, ut Sacramentum hoc longe certius bona promissa, corpus & sanguinem Domini, in manus nobis tradat, quam Testamentum res legatas, & literae ac sigilla reditus annuos haeredibus & possessoribus, exhibeant & obsignent. Nam si contractus humani suam firmitatem habent, institutio & promissio Divina infinito certior erit. Fidus quippe Dei sermo est, & omni omnium receptione dignus, 1. Tim. I. 15. Idem vero modus etiam symbolicus & sacramentalis dicitur, quia talis relatorum unio, id est, signorum & rerum signatarum conjunctio relativa in omnibus Sacramentis locum habet; quam etiam analogia, quae inter Sacramenta, & res earum, quarum Sacramenta sunt, intercedit, & propter quam Sacramenta plerunque rerum ipsarum nomen accipiunt; nec non substitutio signorum in locum rerum signatarum, commendat.
units.tr: CXII. There is therefore a twofold manner of the presence and communion of the body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist: the relative and the spiritual. The relative manner, which is also called symbolic and sacramental, is that by which, according to the Lord's institution, the bread and wine, together with the breaking and eating of the one and the pouring out and drinking of the other, are ordained and consecrated to seal the word of promise, and to signify and exhibit the promised goods, the body of the Lord given for us and his blood shed for us. It is called relative because it consists in a relation, by which it attaches to the bread and wine, and to the rites instituted by God, as signs to represent and seal the things signified. How great the power of relations is in asserting and confirming the acquisition and possession of things is attested not only by sacraments but also by testaments, letters, seals, earnests, pledges and other things of this kind. Because of the relation which attaches to these, either by public authority or by the consent of those concerned, they convey possession of the things contained in those instruments, not an imaginary and doubtful possession, but a real and certain one, as they ought to. So the bread and wine, taken according to the institution of the Lord, present to us and seal the body and blood of the Lord and the word of promise, relatively indeed, but so powerfully by the nature of the relations instituted by God, above all by God himself, that this sacrament hands over to us the promised goods, the body and blood of the Lord, far more certainly than a testament presents and seals the legacies, or letters and seals present and seal annual revenues to heirs and possessors. For if human contracts have their firmness, the institution and promise of God will be infinitely more certain. For God's word is faithful, and worthy of all acceptance by all, 1 Tim. I. 15. This same manner is also called symbolic and sacramental, because such a union of relata, that is, the relative conjunction of signs and the things signified, holds a place in all sacraments. It is also commended by the analogy that exists between the sacraments and the things of which they are sacraments, on account of which sacraments mostly receive the names of the things themselves, and by the substitution of signs in the place of the things signified.

units.la: CXIII. Neque tamen relativus & sacramentalis ille praesentiae & communionis corporis & sanguinis Domini modus sufficit, quia per hunc modum corpus Domini in mortem traditum, & sanguis effusus nobis offeruntur quidem & traduntur, promissionibus additis dulcissimis, quibus ad amplectendum illa allicimur: sed frustra omnia nisi manu & ore fidei instructi praesentia Dei munera apprehendamus, iisque fruamur. Sicut enim Testamentum non ad quosvis, sed ad haeredes tantum pertinet: ita Sacramenta fidelibus tantum prosunt, Actor. VIII. 37. 1. Cor. XI. 28. Ipse enim Dominus Eucharistiam Testamentum in sanguine suo, seu sanguine suo pro multis effuso sanctitum, Matth. XXVI. 28. Luc. XXII. 20. Hebr. IX 16, 17. vocat. Atqui in Testamento illo non omnes, sed soli secundum propositum vocati aeternae promissionis haereditatem accipiunt, ibid. vers. 15. Rom. VIII. 28. Addendus igitur in gratiam fidelium praesentiae & communionis modus spiritualis, quo Spiritus S. fundum & fructus, id est, corpus Domini traditum & sanguinem ejus pro nobis effusum, beneficia item omnia, quae is morte sua nobis peperit, per externa symbola & verbum promissionis fidelibus offert, donat & applicat, & propria ipsis dicat, ut in fide indies robustiores, Christo magis magisque uniantur. Sicut enim modus sacramentalis & relativus ab institutione Divina tantum: ita spiritualis a peculiari praeterea Spiritus S. operatione dependet. Neque tamen per hanc Spiritus S. operationem corpus & sanguis Christi externis elementis, pani & vino, conjunguntur, quibus illa sacramentaliter uniri sufficit: sed animabus nostris, quae per spiritualem hunc cibum & potum vera fide assumptum, Christo vicissim uniuntur, & tanquam viva illius membra, reficiuntur, & ad vitam aeternam aluntur. De qua spirituali alimonia Christus Joh. VI. concionatur, & quam concionem in institutione S. Coenae repetit. Quorum locorum harmonia id aperte docet. Nam Joh. VI. 51. dicit Dominus: Panis, quem ego dabo, caro mea est. In institutione: Hoc (pa-nis) est corpus meum, Matth. XXVI. 26. Ibi Dominus carnem suam comedi, & sanguinem suum bibi jubet, addita promissione vitae aeternae, & conjunctionis nostrae cum Christo, v. 54. 55. 56. hic eadem verba repetit, addita promissione testamentaria remissionis peccatorum, Matth. XXVI. 28. Ibi phrasibus minus claris de carnis suae manducatione, & sanguinis bibitione clariorem aspergit, dicens: Qui ad me venit, non esuriet: qui in me credit, non sitiet unquam, Joh. VI. 35. Amen dico vobis, qui in me credit, habet vitam aeternam, v. 47. imo clavim addit, qua universus concionis sensus referatur, dicens: Hoc (quod de carne mea edenda & sanguine meo bibendo dixi) vos scandalizat? Cum igitur videritis Filium hominis ascendentem, ubi erat prius? Spiritus est, qui vivificat. Caro mea nihil prodest. Verba, quae ego loquor vobis, Spiritus & vita sunt, hoc est, instrumentum Spiritus S. nos baptizantis in unum corpus, & Christo unientis ad convertendam animam, ut Spiritus Dei per fidem habitet in cordibus nostris, eaque vivificet & purificet, atque ad aeternam vitam sanctificet, v. 61. 62. 63. Hic similiter se explicat, sui recordari nos jubens, Luc. XXII. 19. quod cordis est: & annuntiare mortem suam, 1. Cor. XI. 26. quod oris est. Corde enim creditur ad justitiam, & ore fit confessio ad salutem, Rom. X. 10. Hic vivae fidei gymnasium Dominus instituit, quo meritum ejus celebremus, nobisque applicemus. Eandem locorum horum harmoniam S. Augustinus de Doctr. Christ. lib. III. 16. vidit, concionem Domini ex verbis institutionis, in quibus memoria Christi commendatur, fideliter exponens: Nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis, & sanguinem ejus biberitis, non habebitis vitam in vobis. Flagitium videtur jubere. Figura est ergo, praecipiens, passioni Domini esse communicandum, & suaviter atque utiliter recondendum in memoria, quod pro nobis caro ejus crucifixa & vulnerata fit. CXIV. Duplex ille praesentiae & communionis corporis & sanguinis Domini modus ad usum Coenae Dominicae salutarem sufficit. Nam & duae tantum Coenae Dominicae partes: duo sumendi organa: duo administrantium & communicantium genera, & duo fines adaequati Eucharistiae sunt. Ergo totidem etiam communionis modi sunt, quod de singulis demonstramus. Tot ergo primo praesentiae & communionis istius modi sunt, quot Coenae Dominicae partes, natura disparatae, sunt, terrena panis & vinum, & coelestis, promissiones Evangelii, & res promissae, corpus & sanguis Domini. Atqui partes istae duos etiam nec plures nec pauciores praesentiae & communionis corporis & sanguinis Christi modos postulant. Nam signa res signatas, Divinam juxta institutionem nobis offerunt, & praesentes sistunt; qui modus sacramentalis est. Tum duplicis illius cibi sumendi duo tantum sunt organa, os corporis & os animae. Sicut enim duae tantum sunt hominis partes, corpus & anima; & duplex tantum alimonia: ita duo tantum illa ora corporis & animae sunt, per quae quaelibet pars convenientem sibi alimoniam assumit. Os corporis sacramentale: os animae, vel os fidei spiritualem cibum & potum appetens. Ergo duobus alter spiritualis duobus tantùm modis cibus ille accipitur. Nam ora singula singulos communionis modos necessario inferunt. Spiritualis enim modus nonnisi spirituali; & sacramentalis nonnisi sacramentali ori aptari potest. Externo homini externum signum; & interno homini res & veritas ipsa exhibetur; pulchra scilicet dispensatione,ut externus homo externa sua cognata, & spiritualis interna sibi convenientia habeat. Præterea duo sunt administrantium genera, puta ministri & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei, exterius panem & vinum: & Spiritus S. corpus & sanguinem Domini interius dispensans,& cordibus,verbi & Sacramentorum ministerio, inscribens. Ideo enim ministerium Spiritus & Justitiæ 2. Cor. III. 8. 9. dicitur,quia corda justitiam esurientia & sitientia carne & sanguine Domini saturantur,Matth. V. 6. Joh. VI. 35. Ergo duo etiam, non plures communionis modi sunt. Nam duo illi communionis modi, sacramentalis & spiritualis utrique administrantium generi, externo & interno, tam aptè respondent, ut communionis modi nec esse plures debeant, nec esse possint. Sed & communicantes duplici tantùm communionis modo indigent. Communicantes enim vel digni vel indigni sunt. Digni probantes se ipsos,sive jam firmiores,sive infirmiores in fide, & Sacramentum, & rem Sacramenti percipiunt; illud sacramentaliter,hanc spiritualiter. Indigni Sacramenti tantùm participes fiunt. Suntque illi vel fidelium nonnulli, vel infideles. Nam & fideles aliquando mundanis curis præpediti, ad S. Cœnam se negligenter parant; ideóque fine ejus primario, ob explorationis defectum, excidunt. Tales Corinthii fuerunt,qui corpus Domini non discernentes,nec debito in pretio illud habentes, judicium πα-ραc seu castigationis paternæ sibi ipsis ederunt & biberunt,rei facti corporis & sanguinis Domini, 1. Cor. XI. 27. quia symbola eorum non debita cum reverentia susceperunt. Alia infidelium,coetibus fidelium permixtorum,& impietatem suam hypocrisi tegentium, ratio est. Nam si fideles etiam ob mysterii tanti abusum rei fiunt corporis & sanguinis Domini,gravesque pœnas dant,quid illis fiet, qui sanguinem fœderis profanum ducunt, & pertinaci incredulitate corpus Domini aspernantur? Si lapsibus fidelium non ignoscitur,quis erit finis eorum, qui non parent Evangelio? Qui similes Judæ sunt,de quo Augustinus Tract. 59. in Joh. dixit: Cùm reliqui discipuli manducaverint Dominum; Judas manducavit panem Domini: illi vitam, hic pœnam. Cùm ergo duplici tantùm modo communionis ipsi communicantes indigeant, duplex ille modus ejusdem abundè sufficit. Digni enim nihil amplius requirunt; & indigni nihil salutare accipiunt. Neque digni quidquam ultra requirunt, quia quod per signa illis offertur, id per Spiritum S. ipsis datur. Indigni nihil amplius accipiunt,quia fideles carni pro tempore succumbentes fidei exercitio: infideles & reprobi fide salvifica; qua sola promissiones Evangelii; & res promissas amplecti licet, prorsus carent. Denique finis Eucharistiæ adæquati modos præsentiæ & communionis alios non requirunt. Nam sufficientia mediorum à finibus dependet,& media ordinem atque mensuram à finibus accipiunt. Duplex Eucharistiæ finis adæquatus,primarius & secundarius est. Ille mortis Christi recordatio & annuntiatio; hic fidei nostræ per communionem cum Christo capite, & ejusdem corpore, fidelibus omnibus, per symbolorum fidelem usum confirmatio,de quo plura superiùs diximus. Ad fines hos non aliis mediis, quàm utroque illo, sacramentali & spirituali, communionis modo pertingimus.
units.tr: CXIII. Yet that relative and sacramental mode of the presence and communion of the body and blood of the Lord is not sufficient. By this mode the body of the Lord given to death and the blood shed are indeed offered and delivered to us, with the sweetest promises added by which we are drawn to embrace them. But all of it is in vain unless we, equipped with the hand and mouth of faith, lay hold of the gifts of God that are present and enjoy them. For just as a testament pertains not to anyone at all but only to heirs, so the sacraments profit only believers (Acts 8:37; 1 Cor. 11:28). Indeed the Lord himself calls the Eucharist a testament sanctified in his own blood, or in his blood poured out for many (Matt. 26:28; Luke 22:20; Heb. 9:16, 17). But in that testament not all receive the inheritance of the eternal promise, but only those who are called according to purpose (ibid. v. 15; Rom. 8:28). For the sake of believers, therefore, there must be added a spiritual mode of presence and communion, by which the Holy Spirit, who is the ground and fruit, that is, the body of the Lord given and his blood shed for us, and likewise all the benefits that he has obtained for us by his death, offers, bestows and applies through the external signs and the word of promise to believers, and makes them their own, so that in faith they may grow stronger day by day and be more and more united to Christ. For just as the sacramental and relative mode depends only on divine institution, so the spiritual mode depends further on a peculiar operation of the Holy Spirit. Yet by this operation of the Spirit the body and blood of Christ are not joined to the external elements, bread and wine, to which the sacramental union suffices. Rather they are joined to our souls, which, receiving this spiritual food and drink with true faith, are in turn united to Christ, are refreshed as his living members, and are nourished unto eternal life. Christ preaches about this spiritual nourishment in John 6, and he repeats this sermon in the institution of the Holy Supper. The harmony of these passages clearly teaches this. For in John 6:51 the Lord says: The bread which I will give is my flesh. In the institution: This (bread) is my body (Matt. 26:26). There the Lord commands us to eat his flesh and drink his blood, with the promise of eternal life and of our union with Christ added (vv. 54, 55, 56). Here he repeats the same words, with the testamentary promise of the remission of sins added (Matt. 26:28). There, in less clear phrases about eating his flesh and drinking his blood, he sheds a clearer light, saying: He who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst (John 6:35); Verily, verily, I say unto you, he who believes in me has eternal life (v. 47). Indeed he adds the key by which the whole sense of the sermon is referred back, saying: Does this (what I have said about eating my flesh and drinking my blood) offend you? What then if you see the Son of man ascending where he was before? It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are Spirit and life. That is, the instrument of the Holy Spirit, who baptizes us into one body and unites us to Christ, is for the converting of the soul, so that the Spirit of God dwells in our hearts through faith, and quickens and purifies them, and sanctifies them to eternal life (vv. 61, 62, 63). Here too he explains himself in a similar way, bidding us remember him, which belongs to the heart (Luke 22:19), and proclaim his death, which belongs to the mouth (1 Cor. 11:26). For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation (Rom. 10:10). Here the Lord has established the school of living faith, in which we celebrate his merit and apply it to ourselves. St. Augustine also saw this same harmony of these passages, faithfully expounding the Lord's sermon from the words of the institution, in which the remembrance of Christ is commended: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you. It seems a crime to command this. It is therefore a figure, commanding us to share in the Lord's passion and to store up sweetly and profitably in memory that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us (De doctrina Christiana, III. 16). CXIV. This twofold mode of the presence and communion of the body and blood of the Lord is sufficient for the saving use of the Lord's Supper. For there are only two parts of the Lord's Supper, two organs of receiving, two kinds of those who administer and those who communicate, and two adequate ends of the Eucharist. Therefore there are also just as many modes of communion, which we demonstrate for each one. First, then, there are as many modes of this presence and communion as there are parts of the Lord's Supper that are naturally distinct: the earthly bread and wine, and the heavenly promises of the Gospel and the things promised, the body and blood of the Lord. Yet these parts require two modes of the presence and communion of the body and blood of Christ, neither more nor fewer. For the signs offer the things signified to us according to Divine institution, and set them before us as present; this is the sacramental mode. Then there are only two organs for receiving this twofold food: the mouth of the body and the mouth of the soul. For just as there are only two parts of man, body and soul, and only a twofold nourishment, so there are only these two mouths, of body and of soul, through which each part takes up the nourishment suited to it: the sacramental mouth of the body, and the mouth of the soul, or the mouth of faith, which seeks spiritual food and drink. Therefore that spiritual food is received in only two ways by the two mouths. For each mouth necessarily brings with it its own mode of communion. For the spiritual mode can be fitted only to the spiritual mouth, and the sacramental mode only to the sacramental mouth. To the outward man an outward sign is given; and to the inward man the thing and the truth itself is exhibited; with a fine arrangement, namely, that the outward man has his outward kindred things, and the spiritual man his inward things that suit him. Moreover there are two kinds of administrants, namely the ministers and dispensers of the mysteries of God, who outwardly dispense bread and wine, and the Holy Spirit, who inwardly dispenses the body and blood of the Lord, and inscribes them on hearts by the ministry of the word and the sacraments. For this reason the ministry is called the ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness (2 Cor. 3:8, 9), because hearts that hunger and thirst after righteousness are satisfied with the flesh and blood of the Lord (Matt. 5:6; John 6:35). Therefore there are also two modes of communion, and not more. For those two modes of communion, sacramental and spiritual, correspond so aptly to both kinds of administrants, the outward and the inward, that there ought not to be more modes of communion, nor can there be. But also the communicants need only a twofold mode of communion. For those who communicate are either worthy or unworthy. The worthy, examining themselves, whether they are already stronger or weaker in faith, receive both the sacrament and the thing of the sacrament: the former sacramentally, the latter spiritually. The unworthy become participants only in the sacrament. And these are either some of the faithful or unbelievers.
