For even believers are sometimes hindered by worldly cares and prepare themselves negligently for the Holy Supper; and therefore, through lack of self-examination, they fall away from its primary end. Such were the Corinthians, who, not discerning the body of the Lord, and not holding it in due esteem, ate and drank judgment [κρίμα], that is, fatherly chastisement, upon themselves, and became guilty of the body and blood of the Lord (1 Cor. 11:27), because they received their symbols without due reverence. The second cause is for unbelievers, who mix with assemblies of the faithful and cover their impiety with hypocrisy. For if believers too become guilty of the body and blood of the Lord through the abuse of so great a mystery, and suffer grievous punishments, what will happen to those who count the blood of the covenant as profane, and who despise the body of the Lord with stubborn unbelief? If the lapses of believers are not forgiven, what will be the end of those who do not obey the Gospel? They are like Judas, of whom Augustine said in Tract. 59 on John: When the other disciples ate the Lord, Judas ate the bread of the Lord: they received life, he received punishment. Since, then, those who communicate need only a twofold mode of communion, that twofold mode is abundantly sufficient. For the worthy require nothing more, and the unworthy receive nothing saving. Nor do the worthy require anything beyond this, because what is offered to them through the signs is given to them through the Holy Spirit. The unworthy receive nothing more, because the faithful, yielding to the flesh for a time, lack the exercise of faith, and unbelievers and reprobates altogether lack saving faith, by which alone it is lawful to embrace the promises of the Gospel and the things promised. Finally, the adequate ends of the Eucharist do not require other modes of presence and communion. For the sufficiency of means depends on the ends, and means receive their order and measure from their ends. The adequate end of the Eucharist is twofold, primary and secondary. The former is the remembrance and proclamation of the death of Christ; the latter is the confirmation of our faith, through communion with Christ the head and with his body, for all the faithful, through the faithful use of the symbols, concerning which we have said more above. We attain these ends by no other means than by both modes of communion, the sacramental and the spiritual.

units.la: CXV.
units.tr: CXV.

units.la: Hæc de præsentia & communione corporis & sanguinis Domini, ejusque modo doctrina verè & unicè salutaris; Evangelii gratuitam remissionem peccatorum per sanguinis Christi meritum promittentis nucleum in mysterio Cœnæ implicitum habens,& plena Evangelicæ consolationis,lætitiæ & instigationis ad fiduciam in morte Christi,& gratitudinem pro ea atque Christianam conversationem Evangelio dignam, tandiu in Ecclesia Christiana, ceu Evangelium,& Christus qui-dam typicus, illibata mansit,quàndiu Evangelium & Christus ipse intemeratus mansit. Ubi verò doctrinæ Evangelii & gratuitæ per solius Christi meritum remissionis peccatorum oblivio incessit, atque illa ab hominibus,ambitioni & avaritiæ obnoxiis fœdè sic interpolata est; ut remissio peccatorum & salus non amplius uni solíque merito & obedientiæ Christi, sed humanis meritis,ritibus & operibus,quod ajebant, operatis accepta referretur: atque ita morti Christi cruentæ mors incruenta; sacrificio crucis, sacrificium adulterinum & pretiò addictum sacrificium Missæ; & mysterio pietatis mysterium iniquitatis substitueretur; tum demum præsentia vera sacramentali & spirituali abolita, nova quædam monstrosa carnalis & corporalis confingi cœpit. Non poterat enim vel sacerdotium proprie dictum, cujus honorem, firmamentum potentiæ suæ Papatum maximè,cùm Monarchiam suam absolutam in spiritualibus & temporalibus flagrantissimè appetiit, hoc est, tempore Innocentii III. seu Concilii Lateranensis assumpsit; sine sacrificio proprie dicto; vel sacrificium proprie dictum sine hostia proprie dicta; vel hostia proprie dicta sine præsente corpore Christi hostiæ materia: vel corpus Christi præsens sine miraculosa quadam ejusdem productione; humanæ credulitati propinari. Hinc natum, Antichristo parturiente,& obstetricante Sathana, prodigiosum illud dogma Translibstantiationis, præsentiæ corporalis Christi, & Missæ; in quo מִרְאֶה Mirabilia Regni Antichristiani Mysteria universa abscondita sunt. Qua in re mirari subit Sathanæ fraudes & παντεργια; quà admirabilem de credulitate hominum triumphum egit. Non enim,si ad unum omnes phreneticos coegisset, magis ille genus humanum ludificari potuisset, quàm cùm pro articulo fidei propudiosum adeò; sensuum testimonio omni,intellectui & fidei repugnans dogma obtrufit; quo velut pro veritate capitali & mysterio catholico sancitum est; vi quinque illorum verborum; Hoc enim est corpus meum à Sacerdote prolatorum, & secreto mussitatorum panem & vinum; abolita ejus substantia, & remanentibus solis accidentibus,in verum & naturale corpus & sanguinem Christi transsubstantiari.
units.tr: This is the doctrine of the presence and communion of the body and blood of the Lord, and of its manner, which is truly and uniquely saving. It holds within the mystery of the Supper the kernel of the Gospel, which promises the free forgiveness of sins through the merit of Christ's blood. It is full of the Gospel's consolation, joy and encouragement to trust in Christ's death, to give thanks for it, and to live a Christian life worthy of the Gospel. So long as the Gospel and Christ himself remained uncorrupted, this doctrine remained unimpaired in the Christian Church, as a kind of Gospel and a typical Christ. But when the Gospel was forgotten, and the teaching that forgiveness of sins comes through Christ's merit alone was foully corrupted by men given over to ambition and greed, so that forgiveness of sins and salvation were no longer ascribed to the merit and obedience of Christ alone, but to human merits, rites and works, as they called them, then the bloodless death was substituted for Christ's bloody death, a counterfeit sacrifice and a sacrifice sold for money (the Mass) for the sacrifice of the cross, and a mystery of iniquity for the mystery of godliness. Then, at last, once the true sacramental and spiritual presence had been abolished, a new and monstrous carnal and corporal presence began to be invented. For the priesthood properly so called could not be offered to human credulity, nor could a sacrifice properly so called be offered without a sacrifice properly so called, nor a sacrifice properly so called without a victim properly so called, nor a victim properly so called without the body of Christ present as the matter of the victim, nor the body of Christ present without some miraculous production of it. Papacy, which most ardently sought the honour of the priesthood as the foundation of its power, and which took it up in the time of Innocent III, that is, at the Lateran Council, when it most eagerly aspired to its absolute monarchy in spiritual and temporal affairs, could not do otherwise. From this, with Antichrist in labour and Satan acting as midwife, was born that monstrous dogma of transubstantiation, of the corporal presence of Christ, and of the Mass, in which all the hidden mysteries of the kingdom of Antichrist, the wonders (Hebrew: מִרְאֶה [mar'eh]), lie concealed. In this matter one marvels at the frauds and all-working [παντέργεια] of Satan, and at the admirable triumph he gained over human credulity. For had he forced all men into one frenzy, he could not have mocked the human race more than when he thrust upon them, as an article of faith, a shameless dogma so wholly opposed to the testimony of the senses, to the intellect and to faith. By it, as though it were the chief truth and a Catholic mystery, it was decreed that, by the force of those five words, This is my body, spoken by the priest and murmured in secret, the bread and wine, their substance abolished and only the accidents remaining, are transubstantiated into the true and natural body and blood of Christ.

units.la: Et pro sufficiente & vera in Ecclesia judicatus semper est, quando in ea Evangelii doctrina integra permansit; qua corrupta paulatim corporalis præsentia, transsubstantiationis dogma & Missa in Ecclesiam invecta est. stantiari; atque ita quidem, ut quod videtur, tangitur, gustatur, odore percipitur, intellectu concipitur, nil aliud quàm panis & vinum appareat; at de cætero credatur non esse panis & vinum, sed illorum accidentia, sub quorum involucro corpus & sanguis Domini delitescat. Quod licèt prima fronte adeò stolidum videatur, ut mirandum sit, tale quid hominibus, qui pecora non sunt, persuaderi potuisse, ejusmodi tamen est, ut in eo universæ Regni Antichristiani mystici artes se prodant, nihil ut Sathanas evertendo Regno Christi, & stabiliendæ idololatriæ aptius excogitare potuerit. Cùm enim in animo haberet, profligato Evangelio Christi, Judaismum & Ethnicismum postliminio reducere, & Christianismo utcunque conglutinare, juge sacrificium introduxit, Missæ & incruenti sacrificii nomine incrustatum. Rursus cùm id solo pane & vino conficere non posset deducendus ex alto Filius Dei, ceu Jupiter quidam Elicius, fuit, ut, qui in Cœlos ascendit, rursus novo artificio in terram descenderet, & hominum libidini obsequeretur.
units.tr: And this has always been judged a sufficient and true sign of a Church in which the doctrine of the Gospel has remained whole; when that doctrine was corrupted, bit by bit the corporal presence, the dogma of transubstantiation and the Mass were brought into the Church. So that what is seen, touched, tasted, perceived by smell and grasped by the intellect appears to be nothing but bread and wine; yet one is to believe for the rest that it is not bread and wine, but their accidents, under whose covering the body and blood of the Lord lie hidden. Although at first sight this seems so foolish that one may wonder that such a thing could have been persuaded upon men who are not beasts, nevertheless it is of such a kind that in it all the mystical arts of the kingdom of Antichrist betray themselves. Satan could not have devised anything better suited to overthrowing the kingdom of Christ and establishing idolatry. For since he intended, once the Gospel of Christ was crushed, to bring back Judaism and heathenism by the right of return, and to cement them somehow with Christianity, he introduced a perpetual sacrifice, encrusted with the name of the Mass and an unbloody sacrifice. Again, since he could not accomplish this with bread and wine alone, the Son of God had to be brought down from on high, like some Jupiter Elicius, so that he who had ascended into heaven would descend again to earth by a new contrivance and submit to men's lust.

units.la: CXVI. Sicut juge sacrificium apud Judæos nucleus mysterii Christi erat: ita apud hos centrum mysterii iniquitatis Missa est. Ex hoc enim gurgite foedissima abominationum colluvies in Ecclesiæ corpus redundat, & ex hoc in illud regurgitat. Missa enim, uti ejus mysta nonnemo, tot repleta est mysteriis, quot mare guttis, Cœlum Empyræum Angelis, firmamentum stellis, Sol atomis, & terra arenulis. Sub hoc enim Deo Peregrino arcium seu munimentorum (revera enim his velut arcibus & munimentis Regnum Antichristianum superstruitur) quicquid usquam superstitionis & idololatriæ invaluit, dogmata propudiosissima quæque Transubstantiatio, adoratio spumæ, Ignis purgatorius, Indulgentiarum thesaurus, cum omni suppellectile sua culinaria, sacrificium pro vivis & mortuis, &c. & nundinatio sacra flagitiosissima omnium exercetur. Hæc enim & similia ad Dei illius genealogiam spectant, & velut quædam sunt, qua Missalis monstri partum partum promoverunt, partim insecuta sunt. Ne tamen Deus ille peregrinus videretur, & non Divina facie in scenam prodiret, Filium ipsum Dei in partes vocarunt, atque in idolum, sub panis, seu spumæ potius, specie, commutarunt, è throno Majestatis dextræ Dei detractum, & iterum crucifigendum ostentuique habendum, Hebr. VI. 6. Ut enim Christum corpore præsentem haberent, atque populo ostendere, & dicier, Hic est Christus: illic est Christus, possent, neque tamen, quod in eorum potestate non fuit, vivum, spirantem, loquentem, nedum Divina facientem repræsentare possent, quo modo iis licuit, præsentem stiterunt; ne cadaver quidem vel idolum mutum, de quo dici posset: os habet, sed non loquitur; manus, & non tangit, pedes, & non ambulat; sed inanem Christi larvam, adeò impotentem, ut se ne adversus fures quidem tueri, & à vermibus & muribus custodire, naufragii periculis eripere, vel ab hominum contumeliis & injuriis vindicare posset. Talis enim Christus placuit, qui ad nutum Sacerdotis impii etiam sordidique staret atque rigeret, deprimeretur, elevaretur, adoraretur, manducaretur, atque in corporis humani infernum descenderet, & denique in minimas partes resolveretur, non resuscitandus prius quàm & ipsa corpora manducantium mortua resuscitentur. Noluerunt enim Sacerdotes hi Christum, qui ipsis dominaretur, sed cui dominarentur ipsi: non talem, qui cum flagello ingredi eorum templa, & mentes evertere posset; sed quem ipsi, velut arcta in custodia, ceu colonum carceris, haberent: non qui viva voce doceret, abusus taxaret, hypocrisin propalaret; sed cui populus illum colens similis fieret. Arcanum hoc prodidit Gabriel Biel Lect. II. in Can. Missæ, asserens, non voluisse Dominum aliquam habere potestatem solvendi & ligandi super corpus mysticum, seu Ecclesiam, nisi haberet potestatem super corpus Christi; & Sacerdotes digniores esse Regibus, Angelis, B. Virgine Maria, quia Christum creant. & Lect. 4. ita exclamat: Quis unquam vidit talia? Qui creavit me, dedit mihi creare se, & qui creavit me sine me, creatur mediante me. Eandem Christi sub manu Sacerdotis humiliationem Franciscus Conformit. lib. I. p. 2. pag. 277. sic asserit: Ut quid non cognoscitis veritatem, & creditis in Filium Dei, qui quotidie se humiliat, sicut quando è Regalibus sedibus venit in uterum Virginis, quotidie venit ad nos ipse humilis apparens, quotidie descendit de sinu Patris supra altare in manu Sacerdotis.
units.tr: CXVI. As the perpetual sacrifice was the kernel of the mystery of Christ among the Jews, so the Mass is the centre of the mystery of iniquity among these people. For from this whirlpool a most foul sewer of abominations overflows into the body of the Church, and from it flows back again. For the Mass, as one of its initiates has said, is as full of mysteries as the sea is of drops, the highest heaven of angels, the firmament of stars, the sun of atoms, and the earth of grains of sand. Under this foreign God are the fortresses or bulwarks (for indeed the kingdom of Antichrist is built upon these as upon fortresses and bulwarks), and whatever superstition and idolatry has anywhere gained strength: the most shameful dogmas of every kind, transubstantiation, adoration of froth, purgatorial fire, the treasury of indulgences with all its kitchen furniture, the sacrifice for the living and the dead, and so on; and the most scandalous sacred trade of all is carried on. For these things and similar ones concern that god's genealogy, and are like those things which, partly, have promoted the birth of the Missal monster and, partly, have followed it. Yet lest that foreign god should seem to be no god, and should not appear on the stage in divine form, they summoned the Son of God himself into the play, and changed him into an idol under the appearance of bread, or rather of froth, drawn down from the throne of the majesty at God's right hand, and crucified again and held up for display (Heb. 6:6). For to have Christ bodily present and to be able to show him to the people, and to say, Here is Christ, there is Christ, they set him there. Yet they could not, as was not in their power, represent him living, breathing, speaking, much less doing divine works, as they had been able to make him present. Rather they set up a dead body or dumb idol of whom one could say: he has a mouth but does not speak; hands but does not touch; feet but does not walk. They produced instead an empty mask of Christ, so powerless that it could not even defend itself against thieves, guard itself from worms and mice, rescue itself from the perils of shipwreck, or avenge itself on men's insults and injuries. For such a Christ pleased them: one who would stand, stiffen, be lowered, raised up, adored and eaten at the nod of a wicked and even filthy priest, and descend into the hell of the human body, and finally be dissolved into the smallest particles, not to be raised again before the very bodies of those who eat him are raised from the dead. For these priests did not want a Christ who would rule over them, but one over whom they themselves would rule: not one who could enter their temples with a whip and overturn their minds, but one whom they could hold, as in a narrow prison, like a jailer of a dungeon; not one who taught by living voice, censured abuses and exposed hypocrisy, but one by whose worship the people would become like him. Gabriel Biel revealed this secret in Lect. II on the Canon of the Mass, asserting that the Lord did not wish to have any power of loosing and binding over the mystical body, or the Church, unless he had power over the body of Christ; and that priests are more worthy than kings, angels, the Blessed Virgin Mary, because they create Christ. And in Lect. 4 he cries out thus: Who has ever seen such things? He who created me gave me to create him, and he who created me without me is created through me. Francis (Conformit. lib. I, p. 2, p. 277) asserts the same humbling of Christ under the priest's hand in these words: Why do you not know the truth, and believe in the Son of God, who humbles himself every day, just as when he came from the royal seat into the womb of the Virgin? Every day he comes to us, appearing lowly; every day he descends from the bosom of the Father upon the altar, into the hand of the priest.

units.la: CXVII. Mater Missæ, Helena illa, Transubstantiatio est; quam non Christi institutio, sed hominum recentiorum audacia commendat. Christus equidem pani & poculo benedixit, & benedicendo symbola illa ita mutavit, ut, quæ ante communia erant, sacra fierent, & mysterio huic inservirent. Sed prolatis illis verbis Τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά μου Hoc est corpus meum, nec substantiam panis abolevit, nec corpus suum naturale recens sive adductum, sive productum accidentia relicta subire justit. In verbis enim illis: Hoc enim est corpus meum, Pronomen Hoc non aliud notare poterit, quàm panem, ejusque substantiam, quod constat tum ex integra serie verborum Christi: tum quia ex hypothesi adversariorum per verba H. E. E. C. M. Transubstantiatio fit. Quod autem corpus Christi demum fit verbis ius pronuntiatis, illud nondum pronuntiatis verbis corpus nondum erat. Vel igitur panis erat, vel aliud quid erat, quod quale fuerit, illi exponere non possunt. Addo, verba illa censeri conversiva. In omni autem conversione duo termini sunt, unus à quo, alter ad quem. Cùm igitur terminus ad quem sit in prædicato, terminus à quo, qui substantia panis est, in subjecto sit oportet. Ideo Apostolus: Panis, inquit, quem frangimus, est communio corporis Christi, 1. Cor. X. 16. Atqui nec accidentia, nec panis cœlestis, nec aliud quid, quàm substantia panis in Eucharistia frangitur. Et in altera convivii parte, poculo, id de quo Christus dixit: Hoc est sanguis meus, etiam post prolata illa verba γεννημα ἀμπελ ge-nimen vitis appellatur. Si igitur quod Christus discipulis dedit, de quo etiam dixit: Hoc est corpus meum, & hoc est sanguis meus, substantia panis & vini fuit, transubstantiata illa esse, dici non potest. At nec pronuntiatis verbis illis substantiam panis in substantiam corporis sui vel substantiam vini in substantiam sangui-nis nis sui commutavit; tum quia non dixit: Hoc fiat corpus, sanguis meus; sed, Hoc est, &c. enuntians, quod jam erat, non quod fieri debebat: tum quia dici praesupponit esse, ac proin propositio illa vera non fuit, nisi corpus jam fuit, prius quam diceretur corpus: tum quia substantia panis mutata est nec in corpus Christi integrum, quia integrum pro nobis datum non est; nec in fractum, quia cum Christus verba ea pronuntiavit, corpus non fractum, sed frangendum erat. Si ergo pronuntiatis verbis illis Christus substantiam panis & vini in substantiam corporis & sanguinis sui non convertit, multo minus sacerdotes verba illa Christi repetentes id efficere possunt. Inprimis cum non dicant illi: Hoc est corpus Christi; sed, hoc est corpus meum. Proin si verbis illis a Sacerdote pronuntiatis omnino transubstantiatio fieret, panis non in substantiam corporis Christi, sed sacrificuli converteretur. Et quale in corpus Christi panem illi convertunt? Passibile, an gloriosum? Atqui passibile non amplius est, & gloriosum pro nobis non amplius dari, vel frangi potest. Praeterea Transubstantiatio cum institutione Coenae, & articulis fidei pluribus pugnat. Cum institutione Coenae, quoad ejus tum circumstantias, quia Christus mensae accumbens panem in substantiam corporis sui, & quidem pro nobis dati convertere, & corpus suum pro nobis datum ipse vivens spiransque dare manducandum discipulis non potuit: tum facta, quia id quod distribuit, ipse quoque comedit; at corpus suum ipse comedere non potuit: tum dicta, quae usurpavit, uti vidimus: tum finem, qui est anamnesis recordatio Christi. Cum praecipuis articulis fidei; inprimis Christi conceptione, nativitate, resurrectione, ascensione in Coelum, sessione ad dextram Dei, reditu ad judicium & communione Sanctorum. Sed & Coenae Dominicae essentiam Transubstantiatio penitus destruit, quia ex ea tum signa, tum rem signatam, tum analogiam sacramentalem tollit. Signa, quia panis & vini substantiam, relictis speciebus, abolet. Species autem seu accidentia absque subjecto suo spectra potius fallacia, quam rerum Divinarum testimonia sunt. Res signatas, quia corpus Christi spoliat sua quantitate & dimensionibus; pro uno multiplex inducit, & pro nucleo Eucharistiae ejusmodi carnem substituit, quam Christus ipse prodesse vel vivificare negat. Analogiam sacramentalem, quia relationis sacramentalis fundamentum tollit; & ubi signum in rem signatam convertitur, omnis inter illa similitudo definit. Accedit, quod dogma hoc non tam miracula, quam paralogismata, sanae rationi; & fidei, quae sanam rationem non destruit, sed perficit, repugnantia involvit, cujusmodi inprimis illud est, quod salvis accidentibus panis & vini, substantia eorum in substantiam toto genere distinctam, & prius jam existentem convertatur, cum tamen nec individuum praeexistens substantialiter converti quidpiam possit; & in miraculosis conversionibus, quas Scripturae memorant, omnibus non tantum, mutatio facta judicio sensuum deprehendi possit; quod hic non fit, sed una cum substantia etiam accidentia mutata sint, manente communi mutationis subjecto; nec mens humana
units.tr: CXVII. The mother of the Mass, that Helena, is transubstantiation. It is commended not by Christ's institution but by the audacity of recent men. Christ indeed blessed the bread and the cup, and by blessing them changed those symbols so that what had been common became sacred and served this mystery. But when he had uttered the words Τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά μου [This is my body], he neither abolished the substance of the bread nor commanded his natural body, either newly brought in or produced, to undergo the accidents left behind. For in those words, Hoc enim est corpus meum [For this is my body], the pronoun Hoc [This] can denote nothing other than the bread and its substance. This is clear from the whole sequence of Christ's words, and also because, on the opponents' own hypothesis, transubstantiation takes place through the words H. E. E. C. M. (Hoc enim est corpus meum). But the body of Christ comes to be when the words are spoken, and what was not yet a body before the words were pronounced was not yet a body. So it was either bread or something else, and they cannot explain what it was. I add that these words are judged to be conversive. In every conversion there are two terms, one from which and one to which. Since the term to which is in the predicate, the term from which, which is the substance of the bread, must be in the subject. Hence the Apostle: The bread, he says, which we break, is the communion of the body of Christ (1 Cor. 10:16). But in the Eucharist it is neither the accidents, nor a heavenly bread, nor anything other than the substance of the bread that is broken. Likewise on the other side of the meal, the cup, that of which Christ said This is my blood, even after those words is called γέννημα ἀμπέλου [the fruit of the vine], genimen vitis. If, then, what Christ gave the disciples, of which he also said This is my body and this is my blood, was the substance of bread and wine, it cannot be said that it was transubstantiated. Nor did he, by pronouncing those words, change the substance of the bread into the substance of his body, or the substance of the wine into the substance of his blood. This is because he did not say Let this become body, my blood, but This is, etc., declaring what already was, not what ought to be made. It is also because is presupposes existence, so that the proposition would not have been true unless the body already was before it was called a body. And it is because the substance of the bread was changed neither into the whole body of Christ, since the whole body was not given for us, nor into a broken body, since when Christ uttered those words his body was not yet broken but was to be broken. If, then, by pronouncing those words Christ did not convert the substance of the bread and wine into the substance of his body and blood, much less can priests, repeating those words of Christ, effect this. Above all, they do not say This is the body of Christ, but This is my body. Therefore, if transubstantiation were truly effected by those words pronounced by the priest, the bread would be converted not into the body of Christ but into the body of the little priest. And what kind of body of Christ do they make of the bread? A passible one or a glorified one? But a passible body is no longer, and a glorified body cannot be given or broken again for us. Moreover, transubstantiation conflicts with the institution of the Lord's Supper and with several articles of faith. It conflicts with the institution of the Supper as to its circumstances, since Christ, reclining at the table, could not convert the bread into the substance of his body, given for us, nor, living and breathing, could he give his body given for us to be eaten by the disciples. It conflicts as to what was done, since what he distributed he himself also ate, yet he could not eat his own body. It conflicts as to what was said, which they have usurped, as we have seen. And it conflicts as to its end, which is anamnesis, the remembrance of Christ. It conflicts with the chief articles of faith: above all the conception, birth, resurrection, ascension into heaven, sitting at the right hand of God, return to judgment, and the communion of saints. Transubstantiation also utterly destroys the essence of the Lord's Supper, since it takes away the signs, the thing signified, and the sacramental analogy. It takes away the signs, since it abolishes the substance of the bread and wine while leaving the species behind. But species or accidents without their subject are rather deceptive phantoms than testimonies of divine things. It takes away the things signified, since it strips the body of Christ of its quantity and dimensions, introduces many where there was one, and substitutes for the kernel of the Eucharist a flesh of such a kind that Christ himself denies it profits or gives life. It takes away the sacramental analogy, since it removes the foundation of the sacramental relation, and where the sign is converted into the thing signified, all likeness between them ceases. Besides, this dogma involves contradictions not so much miracles as paralogisms, contrary to sound reason and to faith, which does not destroy sound reason but perfects it. Chief among these is that, with the accidents of bread and wine remaining, their substance is converted into a substance wholly different in kind and already existing. Yet no individual pre-existing substance can be substantially converted into anything. In the miraculous conversions that Scripture records, the change could be detected by the judgment of all the senses, which is not the case here. Rather, the accidents too are changed along with the substance, the common subject of the change remaining. Nor can the human mind even think of real accidents of bread and wine existing without a subject, without thinking of them as substance, and so thinking of accidents as non-accidents. Moreover, in the consecrated host there remain such accidents as solidity, impenetrability, extension, and the position of parts outside parts. Since these are the very essence of corporeal substance, or its primary and radical property, when the essence is changed these cannot but change too. Then after the consecration of the symbols, their shape, colours, odours and flavours, which indicate the presence of corporeal substance, remain. And what so remains nourishes like bread and wine, withers, decays, is touched, is broken, and is soaked in poison. I say nothing of the countless such prodigies of transubstantiation, among which none yields to that portent which thrusts upon us not only the accidents of bread and wine stripped of their substance, but also the substance of Christ stripped of the accidents naturally emanating from it. For is the human body something neither coloured nor shaped, and having no relation to any category except substance? Or is the soul, deprived of all its accidents, something that thinks or wills? Nor do the opponents agree about the manner in which the bread becomes the body of the Lord. For some, such as the Dominicans, maintain a productive change of the body of Christ; others, like the Franciscans, maintain an adductive change, but in an instant and momentary motion, so that the later place is acquired without losing the earlier. Yet the body of Christ is not produced in the place where it comes to be. The Franciscans prove this against the Dominicans, because what is produced did not previously exist actually, whereas the body of Christ actually existed even before the consecration. And a body to be produced would either exist out of nothing by the infinite power of God, or be formed from the substance of the Eucharistic bread. Neither way would it be the same as the body of Christ existing in heaven, since it is formed neither from nothing nor from Eucharistic bread. Nor can it be shown how not only the body but also the soul of Christ is produced from the substance of Eucharistic bread. But neither can the body of Christ be brought down from heaven, as the Dominicans prove against the Franciscans with equally weighty arguments. Among these are these: in any conversion properly so called, not only does the term from which cease to be, but the term to which begins to be, which is impossible; the body of Christ would be brought from heaven in an instant without leaving its place, since the words from heaven denote a term from which a progress is made to another; the adduction of a substance, whose term is not a substance but local presence, is not a conversion of substance into substance, and so not transubstantiation; and this mode explains the obscure by the more obscure, since it can still be asked what that adduction is, and whether the body of Christ is brought from heaven to the altar by passing through the whole intervening space or without passing through it, neither of which can be said. Thus the Sophists perish, pierced by their own weapons. Nor are those any wiser who maintain a change that is neither productive nor, according to Gabriel Biel, conservative, by which the body of Christ is preserved in its former being; or, according to others, constitutive, by which a new body comes to be under these species with the connotation of the substantial defection of the bread; or, according to others, initiative, by which the substance of the body and blood of Christ is united to the accidents of bread and wine and sustained by them in the manner of an efficient cause. For those modes labour under the same and many other absurdities, since whatever is changed and is conserved, constituted or united somewhere must have been previously produced or brought to that place. Further, what becomes of the substance of the bread? Some say it is annihilated; others, with Bellarmine, say it is not conserved, as if what is not conserved were nothing, and so annihilated. Yet what is converted into something else cannot properly be said to be annihilated. Finally, both the word and the thing transubstantiation are wholly unknown to sound and hoary antiquity. For the word was first used, around 1106, by Stephen, bishop of Autun, and soon after by Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Blois, and by the archdeacon of Bath around 1160, and by Innocent III in the Lateran Council of 1215. Yet, as the most learned men have observed after Blondel, they did not use it in the sense of the bread's substance having ceased and the body of Christ being newly produced or brought in, but rather in the sense of one substance being substituted for another, which is also the sense of the Greek word μεταστοιχείωσις, transelementation. But by the occasion of the word, and as the soundness of words is always removed when the soundness of things is removed, first consubstantiation was asserted, namely the coexistence of the body of Christ with the bread, by Gerson, Peter of Ailly, the Cameracensian, and others. Indeed, in 1059 Nicholas II himself (whom Berengar called a maker of pomp and a maker of dust) asserted that the bread and wine are on the altar after the consecration. At last came the cessation of the substance of the bread and the substitution in its place of the substance of the body of Christ, assumed privately, though it was not defined before the Council of Trent. Indeed, the unanimous testimonies of the older Fathers, Irenaeus, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Epiphanius, Cyprian, Facundus of Hermiane, Fulgentius, were quite recently yielded up to us of their own accord by Peter de Marca, first archbishop of Toulouse and then of Paris, in his book on the Eucharist.

units.la: vel cogitare possit accidentia panis & vini realia, sine subjecto existentia, quin illa cogitet ut substantiam, adeoque accidentia non-accidentia cogitet; quin & tum in consecrata hostia remaneant ejusmodi accidentia, velut soliditas, impenetrabilitas, extensio, partium extra partes positio, quae cum sint ipsa substantiae corporeae essentia, seu primaria & radicalis proprietas; mutata essentia, ipsa quoque non possunt non mutari: tum post consecrationem symbolorum, eorundem figura, colores, odores, sapores; praesentiam substantiae corporeae arguentes, remanent; & quod sic remanet, instar panis & vini nutrit, marcescit, corrumpitur, tangitur, frangitur, veneno imbuitur. Taceo Transubstantiationis prodigia ejusmodi innumera, quae inter & illud nulli portento cedit, quod non tantum panis & vini accidentia substantia sua spoliata, sed etiam substantiam Christi accidentibus naturaliter ab ea emanantibus exutam obtrudunt. An enim corpus humanum est, quod nec coloratum, nec configuratum est, neque ullum ad ullam categoriam; praeterquam substantiam, respectum habet? an anima, quae destituta omnibus accidentibus suis nihil cogitat, vult? Neque etiam adversarii de modo, quo panis fit corpus Domini, consentiunt. Alii enim, puta Dominicani, mutationem corporis Christi productivam: alii, velut Franciscani, adductivam, sed in instanti & motu momentaneo, ut non amisso priore posteriorem locum acquirat; tuentur. Atqui corpus Christi non produci in loco; ubi fit, contra Dominicanos Franciscani probant, quia quod producitur, ante actu non erat, cum corpus Christi, etiam ante consecrationem actu fuerit; & corpus producendum vel existeret ex nihilo infinita Dei potentia; vel e substantia panis Eucharistici formaretur; atque neutro modo idem esset cum corpore Christi in coelo existente, utpote quod nec ex nihilo, nec ex pane Eucharistico formatum est. Neque etiam ostendi potest, quomodo ex substantia panis Eucharistici non corpus tantum, sed etiam anima Christi producatur. At nec adduci corpus Christi e Coelo contra Franciscanos Dominicani aeque praegnantibus argumentis probant. Cujusmodi sunt, quod in quavis proprie dicta conversione non tantum terminus a quo esse desinat, sed etiam terminus ad quem esse incipiat: quod impossibile sit; corpus Christi e Coelo adduci in momento, & non deserto loco, quia illud e Coelo denotet terminum, a quo alio fit progressio: quod adductio substantiae, cujus terminus non substantia, sed praesentia localis est, non sit conversio substantiae in substantiam; adeoque nec Transubstantiatio: quod hic modus obscurum per obscurius probet; cum quaeri adhuc possit, quid sit illa adductio, & an corpus Christi e Coelo ad altare adducatur, transeundo per totum medium; vel non transeundo; quorum neutrum dici possit. Sic Sophistae suis ipsi telis confossi pereunt. Neque magis sapiunt; qui mutationem nec productivam; sed, juxta Gabrielem Biel, conservativam; qua corpus Christi in antiquo suo esse conservetur; vel juxta alios constitutivam; quatenus novum corpus sub his speciebus cum connotatione defectionis substantialis panis, vel, juxta alios, initiativam. vam, qua corporis & sanguinis Christi substan- tia uniatur accidentibus panis & vini, eáque per modum causæ efficientis sustentet ; esse pertendunt. Nam modi illi iisdem & pluribus etiam absurdis laborant, quia id omne, quod mutatum alicubi conservatur vel constituitur, vel unitur, ibidem ante productum, vel adduc- ctum sit oportet. Quid porro de substantia panis fit ? Alii eam annihilari dicunt: alii cum Bellarmino non conservari, quasi non, quod non conservatur, nihil esset, adeóque annihilaretur. Et quod in aliud convertitur, annihilari equidem dici non potest. Denique Transsubstantiationis & vox, & res sanæ & canæ antiquitati prorsus ignota est. Vocem enim primus sive Stephanus Æduensis Episcopus circa A. MCVI. eúmque mox secuti Petrus Blesensis, Archidiaconus Blesensis, Archidiaconus Bathonensis A. MCLX. & Innocentius III. in Concilio Lateranensi, A. MCCXV. usurparunt, neque tamen, quod viri doctissimi, post Blondellum, observarunt, usurparunt eo sensu, ut desitam substantiam panis, & corpus Christi recens productum vel adductum, sed potius substantiæ pro substantia substitutionem significet, qui sensus etiam vocis Græcæ μεταστοιχήσεως seu transelementationis, est. Sed occasione vocis, uti semper vocum sanitate sublata rerum sanitas tollitur, primò consubstantiatio, seu corporis Christi cum pane coexistentia, à Gersone, Petro de Alliaco, Cameracensi, aliisque, quin & A. MLIX. ipso Nicolao II. (quem Pompificem & Pulvificem Berengarius vocavit) asserente, quòd panis & vinum post consecrationem in altari sint, asserta: demum desitio substantiæ panis, & in ejusdem locum succedanea corporis Christi substantia privatim assumpta, neque tamen ante Tridentinum Concilium definita est. Vetustiorum certè Patrum, Irenæi, Theodoreti, Chrysostomi, Epiphanii, Cypriani, Facundi Hermianensis, Fulgentii nobis plane ὁμοψηφων suffragia non ita pridem Petrus de Marca, primò Tholosensis, dein Parisiensis Archiepiscopus, libro de Eucharistia edito, ultro nobis cessit.
units.tr: Nor can anyone think of the real accidents of bread and wine as existing without a subject without thinking of them as substance, and so thinking of non-accidents as accidents. Moreover, in the consecrated host there remain such accidents as solidity, impenetrability, extension, and the position of parts outside parts, which are the very essence of corporeal substance, or its primary and radical property. When the essence is changed, these too cannot but be changed. Then, after the consecration of the elements, their shape, colours, odours and flavours, which indicate the presence of corporeal substance, remain. And what so remains nourishes, withers, decays, is touched, is broken, and is soaked with poison, just like bread and wine. I say nothing of the countless such prodigies of transubstantiation. Among them is one that yields to no other marvel: they thrust forward not only that the accidents of bread and wine are stripped of their substance, but also that the substance of Christ is stripped of the accidents that naturally flow from it. For does a human body have any relation to any category except substance, when it is neither coloured nor shaped? Or does a soul, deprived of all its accidents, think or will anything? Nor do our opponents agree about the manner in which bread becomes the body of the Lord. For some, namely the Dominicans, maintain that the change of Christ's body is productive; others, such as the Franciscans, maintain that it is adductive, but in an instant and by a momentary motion, so that it acquires its later place without losing the earlier one. Yet the body of Christ is not produced in the place where the change occurs. The Franciscans prove this against the Dominicans, because what is produced did not previously exist, whereas the body of Christ actually existed even before the consecration. And a body to be produced would either come into being out of nothing by the infinite power of God, or be formed out of the substance of the eucharistic bread. Either way it would not be the same as the body of Christ existing in heaven, since it was formed neither from nothing nor from the eucharistic bread. Nor can it be shown how the body and also the soul of Christ are produced from the substance of the eucharistic bread. But neither do the Dominicans prove, against the Franciscans, that the body of Christ is brought down from heaven, with arguments that are equally pregnant. Such arguments are these: that in any change properly so called, the term from which not only ceases to be, but the term to which also begins to be; that this is impossible; that the body of Christ is brought down from heaven in a moment and without leaving its place, because the phrase from heaven denotes a term from which the movement proceeds; that the bringing of a substance, whose term is not a substance but local presence, is not a conversion of substance into substance, and so not transubstantiation; and that this mode proves the obscure by the more obscure, since it can still be asked what that bringing is, and whether the body of Christ is brought down from heaven to the altar by passing through the whole intervening space, or without passing through it. Neither of these can be affirmed. Thus the Sophists perish, pierced by their own weapons. Nor are those any wiser who maintain that the change is neither productive, but, according to Gabriel Biel, conservative, by which the body of Christ is preserved in its former being; nor, according to others, constitutive, insofar as a new body comes to be under these species with the connotation of the substantial defect of the bread; nor, according to still others, initiative, by which the substance of the body and blood of Christ is united with the accidents of bread and wine and sustains them by way of an efficient cause. For those modes labour under the same and several further absurdities, because everything that is changed and is conserved, constituted or united somewhere must have been previously produced or brought there. What then becomes of the substance of the bread? Some say that it is annihilated. Others, with Bellarmine, say that it is not conserved, as if what is not conserved were nothing, and so would be annihilated. Yet what is converted into something else cannot indeed be said to be annihilated. Finally, both the word transubstantiation and the thing itself are wholly unknown to sound and hoary antiquity. For the word was first used by Stephen, bishop of Autun, about 1106, and was soon followed by Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Blois, the archdeacon of Bath around 1160, and Innocent III at the Lateran Council in 1215. Yet, as the most learned men have observed after Blondel, they did not use it in the sense of the substance of bread having ceased and the body of Christ newly produced or brought in its place, but rather to signify the substitution of one substance for another. This sense is also that of the Greek word [μεταστοιχήσεως], that is, transelementation. But on the occasion of the word, as always when soundness of words is lost, soundness of things is lost too. First, consubstantiation, that is, the coexistence of the body of Christ with the bread, was asserted by Gerson, Pierre d'Ailly, of Cambrai, and others. Indeed in 1059 Nicholas II himself (whom Berengar called Pompifex and Pulvifex) asserted that bread and wine are on the altar after the consecration. Finally came the cessation of the substance of bread, and in its place the substance of the body of Christ was taken up as a substitute. This was not defined, however, before the Council of Trent. Indeed the unanimous support of the older Fathers, Irenaeus, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Epiphanius, Cyprian, Facundus of Hermiane and Fulgentius, was not long ago freely ceded to us by Pierre de Marca, first archbishop of Toulouse and then of Paris, in his book on the Eucharist. [ὁμοψήφων]

units.la: CXVIII.
units.tr: CXVIII.

units.la: Sed verba Cœnæ: Hoc enim est corpus meum, mutationem inferre, atque illam non metaphoricam, sed realem & substantialem, quia proprie illa ceu verba Testamenti, pacti, legis, dogmatis: & quidem Apostolis rudibus adhuc dicta certámque sententiam, quæ fidem in πληροφορία immota stabilire queat, postulantia, accipienda sint ad nauseam usque Transsubstantiatores declamant. Mutationem agnoscimus, sed relativam, non substantialem, vel essentialem. Tropica verò, non propria esse verba institutionis, non semel confirmavimus.
units.tr: But the words of the Supper, This is my body, introduce a change, and not a metaphorical one but a real and substantial one, because the transubstantiators declare, to the point of nausea, that these words must be taken properly, as the words of a testament, covenant, law and doctrine, and especially as words spoken to the Apostles, who were still untutored and who needed a definite sense that could fix faith in full assurance [πληροφορία]. We acknowledge a change, but a relative one, not a substantial or essential one. We have already confirmed more than once that the words of institution are tropical and not proper.

units.la: Manifeste enim id docent tum verba promissionis sive feorsim sumpta, velut cùm poculum pro vino: Novum Testamentum seu fœdus pro ejus instrumento metonymicè, sanguis pro sacrificio cruento, & remissio peccatorum pro tota redemptione synecdochicè; verba datur, frangitur, effunditur, pro dabitur, frangetur, effundetur, per enallagen temporis dicuntur; sive conjunctim, quia panis corpus pro nobis datum. & vinum sanguis pro nobis effusus proprie esse non potest; tum scopus instituendi Sacramenti, cùm omnium Sacramentorum ea ratio sit, ut de rebus significatis impropriè prædicentur: tum circumstantiæ eæque partim antecedentes, velut quod Christus cum corpore vivo mensæ accubuit, panem ex farina pistum, vinum ex uvis expressum accepit, iis benedixit, ea fregit, distribuit; & de iisdem dixit: Hoc est corpus meum, sanguis meus; partim consequentes, quibus testatus Christus est, se Cœnam instituisse in recordationem sui & ad annuntiationem mortis suæ, & quidem usque dum venerit, adeóque abientis: tum denique analogia articulorum fidei plurium, quos sensus proprius conturbaret. Sed ipsi quoque adversarii in hoc mysterio ludunt tropis, verùm audacibus illis, quibus nulla Rhetorice nomen dedit.
units.tr: For this is plainly taught, first by the words of promise, whether taken separately, as when the cup stands for the wine; the New Testament or covenant stands metonymically for its instrument; blood stands for a bloody sacrifice; and the forgiveness of sins stands synecdochically for the whole redemption; and the words is given, is broken, is poured out are used for will be given, will be broken, will be poured out by an enallage of tense; or taken together, because bread cannot properly be the body given for us, nor wine the blood poured out for us. Second, by the purpose of instituting the sacrament, since the nature of all sacraments is that the things signified are predicated of them improperly. Third, by the circumstances, some preceding and some following. Preceding: that Christ reclined at table with his living body, took bread made of ground flour and wine pressed from grapes, blessed them, broke them, distributed them, and said of them: This is my body, this is my blood. Following: that Christ testified that he had instituted the Supper in remembrance of himself and to proclaim his death, and indeed until he comes, and so while he is absent. Fourth, and finally, by the analogy of several articles of faith, which a literal sense would throw into confusion. But the adversaries themselves also play with tropes in this mystery, though with those bold ones to which rhetoric has given no name.

units.la: Nam in verbis illis H.E.E.C.M. Hoc iis rem vagam & indeterminatam, quæ nec panis nec corporis substantia sit, cùm panis substantiam designari ipsi negent, & corpus non fiat nisi in ultimo instanti verborum à Sacerdote prolatorum; nec accidentia panis, cùm iis nec panis, nec corporis, quippe tum nondum producti subjectum subsitet, adeóque merum nihil notat: Est continetur sub eo, vel in illud transsubstantiatur: corpus meum, non quale ex B. Virgine accepi, sed invisibile, impalpabile, inextensum, in Eucharistia productum, licet ante existens: genimen vitis sanguis: facere sacrificare: panis id quod ante consecrationem panis fuit, & per eam corpus Christi factum fuit, &c. significat.
units.tr: For in those words H.E.E.C.M. they signify a vague and indeterminate thing, which is neither the substance of bread nor of the body, since they deny that the substance of bread is designated, and the body does not come into being until the last instant of the words spoken by the priest. Nor do they signify the accidents of bread, since with those accidents neither the subject of bread nor of the body subsists, for the body has not yet been produced, and so the phrase signifies mere nothing. Is means is contained under, or is transubstantiated into. My body means not the body received from the Blessed Virgin, but an invisible, impalpable, unextended body, produced in the Eucharist, although it existed before. The fruit of the vine means blood. Do means sacrifice. Bread means what was bread before consecration and by it has been made the body of Christ, and so on.

units.la: Qua igitur fronte aliis leges præscribunt, quas ipsi non sequuntur? Testamenta porrò, leges, pacta, dogmata haud raro verbis impropriis exprimuntur, & satis est, si locutiones ejusmodi usitatæ, obviæ sint, & certum sensum gignant. Tropi enim orationis non tenebræ, sed lumina sunt. Sed verba Christi H.E.E.C.M. practica sunt, inquiunt. Ergo efficiunt, quod significant. Quasi non practica esse possint, significando duntaxat, non efficiendo etiam. Significant enim quod enuntiant & prædicant, non efficiunt; quia jam ante corpus fuit per benedictionem; & dici supponit esse; & panis dicitur esse, non fieri corpus Christi, & nullum imperium, jussio nulla in verbis illis continetur. Sunto tamen verba illa practica etiam efficiendo & mutando. At praxis erit non chymica, vel physica, sed moralis & mystica, ostendens, non quò elementa per substantiæ mutationem transeant, sed cui usui per Christi institutionem & sanctionem inserviant.
units.tr: With what face, then, do they prescribe laws for others which they themselves do not follow? Moreover, testaments, laws, covenants and doctrines are not seldom expressed in improper words, and it is enough if such locutions are in common use and are obvious and produce a definite sense. For the tropes of speech are not darkness but light. But, they say, the words of Christ, This is my body, are practical. Therefore they effect what they signify. As if words could not be practical by signifying only, and not also by effecting. For they signify what they state and declare, and do not effect it, since it was already the body before, through the blessing; and the statement presupposes that it is, and bread is said to be, not to become, the body of Christ; and no command, no injunction, is contained in those words. Yet let those words be granted to be practical also in effecting and changing. But the practice will be not chemical or physical, but moral and mystical, showing not by what change of substance the elements pass over, but to what use they are subservient through the institution and sanction of Christ.

units.la: Frustra verò sic in Eucharistiam inanes figuras, vacua signa & cortices sine nucleo introduci clamitant. Non enim vacua signa sunt, quæ rem non nudè significant, sed obsignant, & in legitimo usu exhibent, de quo plura superius. Ipsi contra in Eucharistia nec signa, nec veritatem habent. Panem enim & corpus comica licentia ex Eucharistia exterminant, nuda pro pane significante accidentia substituunt, & sub accidentium illorum larva non corpus Christi, sed substantiam quandam invisibilem, corpus non-corpus, id est, Nihilum sub Nihilo ostentant, perinde ac si spectatoribus suis ludicrum illud occinerent: Ἀλλὰ μηδέν, καὶ καλῶς. Accipe nihil, & bene tene. Veteres equidem mutationem symbolorum passim μεταβολὴν, μετατύπησιν, μεταχειώσιν, μετατροπὴν, μεταρρυθμισιν, conversionem, transelementationem, permutationem &c. appellant. Sed similibus etiam vocar vocabulis mutationem, quæ in Sacramento obtinet, quæque iis substantialis minimè est, enuntiant. Ita enim juxta eos panis & vinum, mutantur & transelementantur, ut tamen juxta Ambrosium de Sacram. lib. IV. 4. sint, quæ erant: juxta Theodoretum Dial. I. II. in priore essentia, specie, figura permaneant: juxta Epiphanium in Anachor. sint ut antea, inanimata & insensibilia: juxta Augustinum Serm. ad recens baptizatos, verus panis, quod oculi renuntiant, verum in poculo genimen vitis, quæ fiant corpus quodammodo, nempe per signum, & juxta Tertullianum, adv. Marc. lib. IV. 40. figuram corporis. Non enim sic Augustinus contr. Adim. cap. 12. clarissimè loquitur, Dominus dubitavit dicere, Hoc est corpus meum, cùm signum daret corporis sui.
units.tr: In vain, then, do they cry out that empty figures, void signs and husks without a kernel are thus introduced into the Eucharist. For those are not void signs which do not merely signify a thing but seal it, and in lawful use exhibit it, concerning which more was said above. But they themselves, on the contrary, have in the Eucharist neither signs nor truth. For by comical licence they banish bread and body from the Eucharist, substitute bare accidents in place of the bread which signifies, and under the mask of those accidents display not the body of Christ but a certain invisible substance, a non-body, that is, Nothing under Nothing, just as if they were singing that little jingle to their spectators: But nothing, and well done [Ἀλλὰ μηδέν, καὶ καλῶς]. Take nothing, and hold it well. The ancients indeed commonly call the change of the symbols metabolē [μεταβολή], metatypēsis [μετατύπησις], metacheiōsis [μεταχείωσις], metatropē [μετατροπή], metarrhythmisis [μεταρρύθμισις], conversion, transelementation, permutation, and so on. But by similar words they also state the change that takes place in the sacrament, and which is in no way substantial. For according to them bread and wine are changed and transelemented, and yet, according to Ambrose, De Sacramentis book 4, chapter 4, they remain what they were; according to Theodoret, Dialogue 1 and 2, they remain in their former essence, species and figure; according to Epiphanius, On the Anchored Man, they remain as before, lifeless and insensible; according to Augustine, in his sermon to the newly baptized, true bread, which the eyes report, and true in the cup the fruit of the vine, which become the body in a certain manner, namely through the sign; and according to Tertullian, Against Marcion book 4, chapter 40, the figure of the body. For Augustine does not speak so plainly in Against Adimantus chapter 12: The Lord hesitated to say, This is my body, when he was giving the sign of his body.

units.la: CXIX. Jugulata matre perit fœtus. Sublata Transubstantiatione pariter præsentia corporalis Christi in Eucharistia corruit.
units.tr: CXIX. When the mother is slaughtered, the fetus perishes. With transubstantiation removed, the bodily presence of Christ in the Eucharist likewise falls.

units.la: Nam per illam hanc effici contendunt. Sed disertissimis etiam verbis Christus illam jugulavit, prædicens & præcavens: Tunc, si quis dixerit vobis: Ecce hic est Christus, aut illic, ne credite. Suscitabuntur enim Pseudo-Christi & Pseudo-Prophetæ, & dabunt signa magna & prodigia, adeò ut si fieri posset, etiam electos seducerent. Ecce prædixi vobis. Si igitur dixerint vobis: Ecce in deserto est, ne egredimini. Ecce ἐν ταμείοις penetralibus, ciboriis est, ne credite. Sicut enim fulgur exit ab Oriente, & apparet usque in Occidentem: ita erit præsentia Filii hominis, Matth. XXIV. 23-27. Qui igitur non amplius in terris est (juxta humanam naturam) ὧδε ἢ ὧδε hic aut illic, non in eremo (ubi sunt monasteria Eremitarum, Anachoretarum) ἐν ταμείοις in conclavibus, penetralibus, ciboriis, (monstrantiis in quibus Missifices Pseudo-prophetæ Christum monstrant) & cujus adventus in terram non erit posthac ullus nisi fulgidus, clarus & illustris, similis adventui fulguris ab Oriente in Occidentem: is non est in ciboriis Eucharisticis sub speciebus symbolorum invisibili modo præsens.
units.tr: For the Papists contend that the bodily presence is effected by transubstantiation. But Christ destroyed this doctrine in the plainest words, foretelling and warning: Then if anyone says to you, "Look, here is Christ, or there," do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise, and will show great signs and wonders, so as to deceive even the elect, if that were possible. See, I have told you beforehand. So if they say to you, "Look, he is in the desert," do not go out; "look, he is in the inner rooms [ἐν ταμείοις], in the sanctuaries, in the ciboria," do not believe it. For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man (Matt. 24:23–27). Therefore he who is no longer on earth in his human nature, here or there [ὧδε ἢ ὧδε], not in the desert (where the monasteries of the hermits and anchorites are), in the inner rooms [ἐν ταμείοις], in the sanctuaries, in the ciboria (the monstrances in which the Mass-priests, the false prophets, display Christ), and whose coming to earth from now on will be only bright, clear and manifest, like the coming of lightning from east to west: he is not present in the Eucharistic ciboria, invisibly, under the appearances of the signs.

units.la: Quomodo enim invisibili modo venit, vel præsens est, qui non aliter venit; vel præsens est, quàm sicut venit fulgur ex oriente in occidentem? Frustra ergo illi occultam & invisibilem à manifesta & invisibili præsentia corporali distinguunt; & illam quotidie obtinere, alteram in judicio extremo successuram asserunt. Non ita Christus, qui non aliam quàm manifestam & visibilem agnoscit, at occultæ atque invisibilis assertionem Pseudo-christis & Pseudo-prophetis tribuit, & refutat.
units.tr: For how can he be present in an invisible manner who does not come in any other way, or how can he be present otherwise than as lightning comes from east to west? In vain, then, do they distinguish a hidden and invisible presence from a manifest and visible bodily presence, and claim that the one they obtain every day, while the other is to follow at the final judgment. Christ does not do this. He acknowledges only a manifest and visible presence, and he attributes to the false christs and false prophets the assertion of a hidden and invisible presence, and refutes it.

units.la: Accedit, quòd Christus assertionem invisibilis præsentiæ tribuit Pseudo-prophetis, eam per jactata miracula confirmantibus, planè ut adversarii præsentiam Christi invisibilem jactatis prodigiis & miraculis confirmare solent. Tum corpus & sanguis Domini in Eucharistia præsens est, illud quà datum, fractum, hic quà effusus; Matth. XXVI. 26.27: Luc. XXII. 19. Non ergo præsens est secundum indistantiam loci, quia post resurrectionem ejus corpus non amplius datur, frangitur; sanguis ejus non amplius effunditur.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ attributes the assertion of an invisible presence to the false prophets who confirm it by boasted miracles, just as our opponents are wont to confirm their invisible presence of Christ by boasted prodigies and miracles. Again, the body and blood of the Lord are present in the Eucharist: the body as given and broken, the blood here as poured out (Matt. 26:26–27; Luke 22:19). Therefore he is not present by the nearness of place, because after his resurrection his body is no longer given or broken, and his blood is no longer poured out.

units.la: Non entis nulla accidentia sunt. Ineptè regerunt, dari, frangi, effundi non in se, sed in alio, puta specie panis & vini. Hoccine enim verba Christi proprie interpretari est? Sed si in se corpus Christi non frangitur, sanguis in se non effunditur, quomodo in specie panis frangi, sanguis in specie vini effundi dicetur, cùm tamen frangi, effundi nisi corpus non posset? Et quod solatium fideli animæ ex fractione speciei panis, effusione speciei vini affulgebit? Quid est Evangelii nucleum perdere, & populo misello mederi velle נקלה ע"י re levicula, nihili, titivillitio, Jerem. VIII. 11. si hoc non est? An species panis pro peccatis nostris crucifixa, species vini effusa est?
units.tr: Non-being has no accidents. They absurdly reply that to be given, broken and poured out belongs not to the thing in itself but to another, namely the appearance of bread and wine. Is this what it means to interpret Christ's words properly? But if the body of Christ is not broken in itself, and the blood is not poured out in itself, how can it be said that it is broken in the appearance of bread, and poured out in the appearance of wine, when yet it could only be broken or poured out if it were body or blood? And what comfort would shine on the faithful soul from the breaking of the appearance of bread and the pouring out of the appearance of wine? What is this but to lose the kernel of the Gospel, and to wish to heal the poor people lightly [נקלה ע"י], by a trifle of nothing, a bagatelle (Jer. 8:11)? Or was the appearance of bread crucified for our sins, and the appearance of wine poured out?

units.la: Accedit, quòd Christus docet, corpus & sanguinem suum in Cœna ita adesse, quatenus panis corpus, sanguis genimen vitis est: quòd panis ita corpus est, sicut calix Novum Testamentum est, atque hic ita Novum Testamentum est, ut Novum Testamentum sub specie calicis non contineatur: quòd id, quod in Eucharistia localiter præsens est, diserte ἄρτος & genimen vitis, Matth. XXVI. 29. quódque Christus in Cœna edere panem corpus suum, bibere vinum sanguinem suum jussit εἰς ἀνάμνησιν ad recordationem sui, Luc. XXII. 19. atque ita, ut annuntietur ceu mortuus, & quidem, donec venerit, adeóque absens, nec prius præsens futurus, quàm ad universale judicium redibit: 1. Cor. XI. 26.
units.tr: Furthermore, Christ teaches that his body and blood are present at the Supper in such a way that the bread is his body and the wine the fruit of the vine: that the bread is his body as the cup is the New Testament, and yet the New Testament is not so contained under the appearance of the cup; that what is locally present in the Eucharist is expressly called bread and the fruit of the vine (Matt. 26:29); and that Christ commanded at the Supper that the bread be eaten as his body and the wine drunk as his blood, in remembrance [εἰς ἀνάμνησιν] of him (Luke 22:19), and so that his death is to be proclaimed as one who is dead, and indeed until he comes, and therefore absent, and not to be present until he returns to the universal judgment (1 Cor. 11:26).

units.la: Et recordationem tum sui, tum actionis suæ Christus præscripsit, quia & sui, ceu absentis recordari, & mortem suam annuntiari jussit. Nam quòd corpus Christi invisibile, sub speciebus panis & vini delitescens, signum μνημονικόν, seu monumentum ejusdem in mortem olim traditi, & traditionis ipsius in cruce factæ nugantur, næ absurdi nimis sunt.
units.tr: Christ prescribed the remembrance both of himself and of his action, because he commanded us to remember him as one absent, and to proclaim his death. For the claim that the invisible body of Christ, lying hidden under the appearances of bread and wine, is a memorial sign, or a monument of the one once delivered to death, and of the betrayal itself made on the cross, is trifling, and indeed exceedingly absurd.

units.la: Quomodo enim id, quod corpus esse supponitur, & tamen in sensus non incurrit, adeóque & indivisibile, & invisibile est, atomi Democriteæ instar, monumentum, signum, monumentum rei & actionis corporeæ & sensibilis esse potest, cùm omne signum & μνημόσυνον, Augustino finitore, sub sensus cadere, & aliud menti subjicere debeat; atque res viva, invisibilis & indivisibilis, impassibilis, monumentum rei mortuæ, visibilis, passibilis esse nequeat; atque Paulus monumentum illud esse rei absentis innuerit, jubens in Cœna prædicare mortem Christi, usque dum venerit.
units.tr: For how can that which is supposed to be a body, and yet does not fall under the senses, and is therefore indivisible and invisible, like the atoms of Democritus, be a monument, a sign, a memorial of a bodily and sensible thing and action? Since every sign and memorial, as Augustine defines it, must fall under the senses and present something else to the mind; and since a living thing, invisible, indivisible and impassible, cannot be a monument of a dead thing that is visible and passible. And Paul indicated that this is a monument of an absent thing, when he bids us proclaim the death of Christ in the Supper until he comes.

units.la: Præterea panis in Eucharistia vocatur communio corporis Christi, 1. Corinth. X. 16. non utique per localem corporis sub speciebus alienis latentis præsentiam, sed per solam sacramentalem significationem & obsignationem, quæ jus ad corpus Christi, & cum illo, ejúsque merito & justitia consortium, tanquam ejus pignus & arrhabo, præstat.
units.tr: Besides, in the Eucharist the bread is called the communion of the body of Christ (1 Cor. 10:16). This is certainly not through the local presence of the body hidden under alien appearances, but through the sacramental signification and sealing alone, which gives the right to the body of Christ, and fellowship with him, and with his merit and righteousness, as a pledge and earnest of it.

units.la: Non enim hæc κοινωνία est μετάδοσις communicatio corporis, per porrectas panis species in hunc vel illum locum venientis; sicut cùm Apostolus statim se explicans dixit: Unus panis, unum corpus multi sumus, non hoc sibi voluit, quòd multi corpus Christi sint sub speciebus panis latens, sed quòd multi de eodem pane comedentes jus habeant ad corpus & sanguinem Christi, hoc est, ad meritum mortis ejus, justitiam & vitam.
units.tr: For this koinonia is not a metadosis, a communication of the body by the bread's appearances being extended to this or that place. Just as when the Apostle, explaining himself at once, said: One bread, we who are many are one body (1 Cor. 10:17), he did not mean that we who are many are the body of Christ hidden under the appearances of bread, but that we who are many, eating of the same bread, have a right to the body and blood of Christ, that is, to his merit, righteousness and life.

units.la: Sic enim communionem corporis Christi habemus, & sic unum corpus sumus; sicut Israelitæ victimas comedentes erant κοινωνοὶ & θυσιαστηρίου participes altaris, ibid. v. 18. Atqui illi victimas comedentes non intra se localiter altare habuerunt; sed communionem cum vera victima; Christo. sto, per altare typicum adumbrato habuerunt. Præterea quicunque sine motu locali descendit in terram, & simul manet in Cœlo, is verus Deus est, juxta illa Christi: Nemo ascendit in Cœlum, nisi qui descendit de Cœlo, Filius hominis, qui est in Cœlo, Joh. III. 13. Atqui Christus secundum naturam humanam non est Deus. Non ergo secundum naturam humanam sine motu locali in terram descendit, & in terra simul & in Cœlo præsens est, quod de eo propugnatores corporalis præsentiæ affirmant. Sed & illud in Eucharistia præsens est, quod recta fide utentibus prodest. Nam Eucharistia ad fidelium utilitatem instituta est. Atqui caro Christi oraliter manducata, adeóque sic corporaliter præsens, nihil prodest, Joh. VI. 63. Vanum est quod voce carnis non carnis Christi substantiam, sed carnale aliquid, & Spiritui S. resistens, seu carnalem & Capernaiticam verborum Christi intelligentiam, significari regerunt. Nam & series verborum Christi evincit, per carnem substantiam carnis ejus, non aliud intelligi, quia de carne, quam comedendam obtulit, manifestè agitur: & manducatio carnis, qualem illi tuentur, Capernaitica est, quia est manducatio substantiæ carnis per instrumenta corporis, qualem solam Capernaitæ aversabantur. Parum enim refert de laceranda Christi carne, an de carne sub speciebus panis integra, indivisibili, spirituali, sed ore corporis manducanda, qualis Pontificia manducatio est, sententiam eorum interpretemur. Manducationis hi diversi modi, æquè absurdi utrique: at manducatio substantiæ carnis eadem est. Et in responsione sua Christus ejusmodi argumentis utitur, quæ quamlibet oralem manducationem carnis, seu corporis ipsius in solidum excludunt. Opponit enim ascensionem suam in locum, ubi ante erat, v. 62. & Spiritum oppositè ad carnem ore comestam, vivificare, quia qui Christi Spiritum habet, is in Christo est, & vitam habet, & quidem per verbum, non per deglutitionem carnis indivisibilis, v. 63. docet. Insuper Christus corpore suo, relicta terra, in Cœlum ascendit, ad dextram Dei consedit, mansurus ibi usque ad consummationem seculorum, ibid. v. 61. 62. Actor. I. 9. 11. III. 21. Non ergo post ascensionem suam corpore suo in Eucharistia localiter præsens est. Neque enim unum idémque numero corpus simul terram relinquere, & in Cœlo fixam sedem statuere, atque ibi manere ad consummationem usque seculi: simul in terra, eodem intervallo temporum præsens localiter & ἀδιαςάτως esse potest. Nebulæ meræ sunt, quibus argumentum hoc obscurare conantur, asserentes, corpus Christi in Cœlo circumscriptivè, in terra definitivè simul existere. Nam corpus in loco nisi circumscriptivè esse non potest. Neque definitivè, seu, ut illi loquuntur, spirituum more in loco corpora esse possunt, nisi simul in spiritum substantiam abeant, adeóque corpora esse desinant. Si Deus per miraculum efficere potest, ut corpus Christi corporaliter, substantialiter, penetrativè, definitivè & indivisibiliter in pluribus simul locis sit circumscriptivè, fatentibus id Scotistis, quia ubi Deus facere potest substantiam naturalem sub modo suo non naturali, sed opposito, ibi eandem facere potest sub modo natu-
units.tr: For thus we have the communion of the body of Christ, and thus we are one body, just as the Israelites who ate the sacrifices were koinonoi and partakers of the altar (v. 18). Yet those who ate the sacrifices did not have the altar locally within themselves, but they had communion with the true sacrifice, Christ, prefigured by the typical altar. Moreover, whoever descends to earth without local motion, and at the same time remains in heaven, is true God, according to those words of Christ: No one has ascended into heaven, except him who came down from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven (John 3:13). But Christ according to his human nature is not God. Therefore he does not, according to his human nature, descend to earth without local motion, and is present on earth and in heaven at once, which the advocates of the bodily presence affirm of him. But that is present in the Eucharist which benefits those who use it with true faith, for the Eucharist was instituted for the profit of the faithful. Yet the flesh of Christ, eaten with the mouth, and so bodily present, profits nothing (John 6:63). It is vain to reply that by the word flesh is signified not the substance of Christ's flesh but something fleshly, resisting the Holy Spirit, that is, a carnal and Capernaitic understanding of the words of Christ. For the sequence of Christ's words proves that by flesh nothing else is understood than the substance of his flesh, since it is clearly spoken of the flesh which he offered to be eaten; and the eating of the flesh, such as they defend, is Capernaitic, because it is the eating of the substance of the flesh by the instruments of the body, which alone the Capernaites abhorred. For it matters little whether we interpret their opinion as concerning the flesh of Christ to be torn, or the flesh under the appearance of bread, whole, indivisible, spiritual, but to be eaten by the mouth of the body, which is the Papist eating. These different modes of eating are equally absurd on either view, but the eating of the substance of the flesh is the same. And in his reply Christ uses arguments of such a kind that they exclude every oral eating of his flesh, or of his body entire. For he sets against it his ascension to the place where he was before (v. 62), and teaches that the Spirit quickens, as opposed to the flesh eaten with the mouth (v. 63), because whoever has the Spirit of Christ is in Christ and has life, and indeed through the word, not through the swallowing of indivisible flesh. Moreover, Christ, leaving the earth, ascended into heaven with his body, sat at the right hand of God, and will remain there until the consummation of the ages (ibid. vv. 61–62; Acts 1:9, 11; 3:21). Therefore after his ascension he is not locally present in the Eucharist in his body. For one and the same body, numerically, cannot at the same time leave the earth and take up a fixed seat in heaven and remain there until the end of the age, and at the same time be locally present on earth, and without separation [ἀδιαςάτως] in the same interval of time. Mere clouds are those with which they try to obscure this argument, asserting that the body of Christ exists simultaneously in heaven circumscriptively and on earth definitively. For a body in a place cannot be there except circumscriptively. Nor can bodies be in a place definitively, or, as they say, in the manner of spirits, unless they pass at the same time into the substance of spirit, and so cease to be bodies. If God can by miracle bring it about that the body of Christ is, bodily, substantially, penetratively, definitively and indivisibly, in several places at once, circumscriptively (the Scotists admitting this), because where God can make a natural substance under a non-natural mode, which is opposite to its own, there he can make the same substance under a natural mode, that is, one congruent with its nature, since this is equally easy, or indeed easier, than that; and for the former two miracles would have to concur, for the latter only one. But the Thomists, affirming and maintaining against the Scotists, hold that the body of Christ cannot by miracle be at once in…

units.la: rali, seu naturæ suæ congruente, cùm hoc æquè facile, imò facilius sit, quàm illud; & ad illud duo miracula, ad hoc unicum concurrere debeat. Atqui fatentibus & pertendentibus adversus Scotistas Thomistis, corpus Christi non potest per miraculum simul esse in pluribus locis circumscriptivè, quia corpus localiter esse in loco nihil aliud est, quàm circumscribi & comprehendi à loco secundum commensurationem propriarum dimensionum; quod autem comprehenditur à loco aliquo, ita in loco illo est, ut extra eum nihil ejus sit; ac proin ponere, quòd Christi corpus circumscriptivè & localiter sit in hoc loco, & eodem modo sit in alio, est contradictoria ponere. Ergo corpus Christi non potest esse simul in pluribus locis, in uno circumscriptivè, in aliis definitivè, penetrativè & indivisibiliter. Cùmque Christus assumpserit corpus humanum, simile nostro, excepto peccato, adeóque extensum, finitum, circumscriptum, habens carnem & ossa, non potest simul in Cœlo esse circumscriptivè, simul in terra non circumscriptivè, sed definitivè, indivisibiliter & invisibiliter. Ejusmodi enim corpus non est simile nostro. Neque obstat, quòd Christus nunc spirituale, incorruptibile & gloriosum est, quia gloria, incorruptibilitas & spiritualitas illa proprietates essentiales corporis Christi non tollit aut mutat, uti in loco ostendimus. At nec omnino corpus humanum in pluribus locis simul actu & substantialiter, quocunque variante modo, præsens esse potest. Tale enim si quod daretur corpus πολύτοπον, nec unum illud esset, quippe à seipso divisum: & simul esset actu & potestate, atque ad se ipsum relatione reali referri posset. Ideo Angelus: Non est hic, inquit, surrexit enim, Matth. XXVIII. 6. non obscurè à positione unius loci, alterius negationem concludens. Quin & post ascensionem Christum Cœlo δέχεσθαι recipi usque ad tempora restitutionis omnium, Apostolus Actor. III. 21. testatur. Ἀπεξεσθιόμενον vero exemplum animæ est, quam in toto corpore, singulisque ejus partibus totam esse Scholastici tuentur. Ubi enim de πολυλοπία corporis extensi & circumscripti, quod proprie & positivè totum dicitur, quia partes habet, agitur, nulla ratione locatio spiritus toto genere diversa, obscura & perceptu difficilima ingeritur. Cùmque quæstio nostra agat de locis adæquatis, ad quæ requiritur æqualitas inter superficiem concavam corporis continentis, & convexam contenti, nec non de locis pluribus & disjunctis; anima sicut superficiem & extremitates non habet, ita nec à corpore contineri, nec cum eo commensurari potest; & si tota in toto corpore & singulis ejus partibus est (quod ipsum tamen ambiguè admodum dicitur) simul in omnibus membris intermediis seu interpositis existit. Toto igitur Cœlo hæc differunt. Denique corporalis præsentiæ Christi dogma puriori antiquitati ne fando quidem auditum est. Primi in Ecclesia Orientali Anastasius Sinaita, & mox Damascenus & Theophylactus errorem invexerunt & aluerunt. In Ecclesia verò Occidentali seculi noni anno decimo octavo Paschasius Ratbertus, Monachus Corbejensis, libro de Corpore & Sanguine Domini edito, primus novitiam de corporali præsentia doctrinam in Ecclesiæ proscenium protulit, asserere ausus, Eucharistiam simul corporis Christi figuram & ejus veritatem esse, cùm tamen, uti olim Gaudentius dixit, figura non fit veritas, sed veritatis imitatio. Sed veterem de præsentia Christi in Eucharistia doctrinam orthodoxam Bertramus, seu Batramnus Corbejensis Monachus & Presbyter, jussu Caroli Calvi Regis, scripto de Corpore & Sanguine Domini libello, novissimè à Claudio, Parisiensi Theologo, vernaculum in idioma translato, & solidè vindicato adversus Paschasium masculè defendit.
