Certantibus pro veritate Prudentio, Tricassino, sive Trecensi Episcopo, Drutmaro, Remigio Altisiodorensi, Bernone Augiensi, sive Brunone, Berengario Turonensi, aliis, error homines oscitantes & indoctos paulatim invaluit, & post Berengarium diu res non disputationibus & styIo, sed persecutionibus & pilo acta, & corporalis præsentia demum in Concilio Tridentino definita est, de quo in loco plura diximus.
units.tr: Those who hold, and who maintain against the Scotists, that the Thomists are right, deny that the body of Christ can by miracle be circumscriptively present in several places at once, because to be locally present in a place is nothing other than to be circumscribed and contained by that place, in proportion to one's own dimensions. Whatever is contained by some place is in that place in such a way that none of it is outside it. So to posit that Christ's body is circumscriptively and locally in this place, and is in the same way in another place, is to posit a contradiction. Therefore the body of Christ cannot be in several places at once, circumscriptively in one and definitively, penetratively and indivisibly in others. Since Christ assumed a human body like ours, apart from sin, and so extended, finite, circumscribed, having flesh and bones, it cannot be in heaven circumscriptively and at the same time on earth not circumscriptively but definitively, indivisibly and invisibly. For such a body would not be like ours. Nor does it count against this that Christ is now spiritual, incorruptible and glorious, because glory, incorruptibility and spirituality do not remove or alter the essential properties of Christ's body, as we have shown in the proper place. Nor can a human body in fact be present in several places at once, actually and substantially, in any varying manner whatever. For if there were such a body [πολύτοπον, in many places], it would not be one body, since it would be divided from itself, and it would at the same time be actual and potential, and could be related to itself by a real relation. Therefore the angel said: He is not here, he says, for he is risen, Matt. 28:6, obviously concluding the denial of the other place from the affirmation of one place. Indeed, the Apostle also testifies, Acts 3:21, that after the ascension Christ is received in heaven [δέχεσθαι] until the times of the restoration of all things. The example of the soul, which the Scholastics maintain is whole in the whole body and in each of its parts, is in fact a case of being apportioned [ἀπεξεσθιόμενον]. For where we are dealing with the multi-placed character [πολυλοπία] of an extended and circumscribed body, which is properly and positively called whole because it has parts, there is no reason to introduce a manner of location of spirit that is wholly different in kind, obscure and very hard to grasp. And since our question concerns adequate places, which require equality between the concave surface of the containing body and the convex surface of the contained, and also concerns several separated places, the soul, which has neither surface nor extremities, cannot be contained by a body nor measured against it. And if it is whole in the whole body and in each of its parts (a phrase which is itself quite ambiguous), it exists at the same time in all the intervening or interposed members. These things therefore differ by the whole heaven. Finally, the dogma of Christ's corporal presence was never heard of even in the purer antiquity. In the Eastern Church Anastasius of Sinai first introduced and fostered the error, and soon after him Damascene and Theophylact. In the Western Church, in the eighteenth year of the ninth century, Paschasius Radbertus, a monk of Corbie, published his book On the Body and Blood of the Lord, and was the first to bring the new doctrine of corporal presence onto the stage of the Church, daring to assert that the Eucharist is at once a figure of Christ's body and its truth, although, as Gaudentius once said, a figure does not become the truth, but an imitation of the truth. But Bertram, or Ratramnus, a monk and presbyter of Corbie, by command of King Charles the Bald, wrote a little book On the Body and Blood of the Lord, which was lately translated into the vernacular by Claude, a Parisian theologian, and solidly vindicated, and he defended the old orthodox doctrine of Christ's presence in the Eucharist manfully against Paschasius. With Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, Drutmar, Remigius of Auxerre, Bernon of Reichenau (or Bruno), Berengar of Tours and others contending for the truth, the error gradually gained strength among dozing and unlearned men. After Berengar, the matter was for a long time decided not by disputations and writing but by persecutions and the stake, and at length corporal presence was defined by the Council of Trent, on which we have said more in the proper place.

units.la: CXX. Levia sunt, quibus præsentiam Christi corporalem in Eucharistia οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας propugnant, argumenta.
units.tr: CXX. The arguments by which the opponents [οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας] defend Christ's corporal presence in the Eucharist are weak.

units.la: Nam infirmo illo tibicine proprietatis verborum institutionis H.E. E.C.M. pleraque innituntur. Nos autem tropica esse verba, supra demonstravimus. Dixit Christus de poculo: Hoc Poculum, Novum Testamentum ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου in sanguine meo, τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυννόμενον, qui (sanguis non quod poculum) pro nobis effusus est, Luc. XXII. 20. Nam sanguis propinquius, poculum remotius subjectum est; & non poculum, sed sanguis Christi pro nobis effusus est. In verbis igitur illis est enallage casus recti pro obliquo, Hebraeis inprimis nomini præcedenti obliqui casus signum habenti adjectivum & participium in primo casu adjungentibus familiaris. Similia exempla sunt, Joh. I. 14. XXI. 12. 2. Cor. XII. 5. Eph. III. 7. IV. 1.2. Apoc. I. 5. Unde Basilius in Moral. reg. 21.3. habet: Τῷ αἵματι τῷ ἐκχυνομένῳ Sanguine, qui effunditur. Et Lucæ phrasis ex reliquorum Evangelistarum phrasi, analogia Sacramentorum & mysterii sive Testamenti explicanda est. Testamentum enim ratificatur per sanguinem Christi Testatoris in cruce effusum, sive per mortem ipsius, Hebr. IX. 16. 17. 18. Quid verò ad ratificationem Testamenti faceret, si sanguis ex poculo invisibiliter effunderetur? Et si hoc fit, & quidem pro nobis effunditur, nempe ad remissionem peccatorum, quare Christus pro nobis mortuus est, & quid moriens impetravit, & quæ est illa ἄφεσις, quæ ἀπογραφὴν excludit? ibid. X. 18. Quo sensu panis κοινωνία communio corporis, & poculum communio sanguinis ejusdem dicatur, sæpiusculè ostendimus. Et Christus Joh. VI. 51. 52. &c. carnem Christi edendam, & sanguinem ejus bibendum esse, multis comprobat, agens de manducatione spirituali, non de sacramentali, nedum corporali, uti supra probavimus. Plures certè Pontificii, & ex iis duo Summi Pontifices, Innocentius III. & Pius II. eo capite de Sacramento agi, pernegant. Patres alii verba Christi de propria carne & proprio sanguine ut ad mortem datis: alii de pane & vino interpretantur. Neutri corporali præsentiæ favent. Non illi, quia ad manducationem spiritualem
units.tr: For most of their case rests on that feeble prop, the literal sense of the words of institution. We have shown above that these words are tropical. Christ said of the cup: This cup is the New Testament in my blood [ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου], which is poured out [τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυννόμενον] for you, that is, which (the blood, not the cup) was poured out for us, Luke 22:20. For the blood is the nearer subject and the cup the more remote, and it is not the cup but the blood of Christ that was poured out for us. In those words, then, there is an enallage of the nominative for the oblique case, a usage familiar especially to Hebrews, who add an adjective or participle in the nominative to a preceding noun that has the sign of an oblique case. There are similar examples at John 1:14, 21:12; 2 Cor. 12:5; Eph. 3:7, 4:1–2; Rev. 1:5. Hence Basil, in Moral. reg. 21.3, has: To the blood which is poured out [Τῷ αἵματι τῷ ἐκχυνομένῳ], the blood which is poured out. And Luke's phrasing must be explained from the phrasing of the other Evangelists, and from the analogy of the sacraments and of the mystery or testament. For the testament is ratified by the blood of Christ the testator shed on the cross, or by his death, Heb. 9:16–18. But what would contribute to the ratification of the testament if the blood were invisibly poured out from the cup? And if this happens, and indeed is poured out for us, namely for the remission of sins, why did Christ die for us, what did he obtain by dying, and what is that remission which excludes an annual remembrance [ἀπογραφή], Heb. 10:18? In what sense the bread is called the communion [κοινωνία] of the body and the cup the communion of the same blood, we have shown more than once. And Christ, John 6:51–52 etc., proves in many ways that his flesh is to be eaten and his blood drunk, speaking of spiritual eating, not of sacramental, still less of corporal eating, as we have proved above. Certainly many Papists, and among them two supreme pontiffs, Innocent III and Pius II, flatly deny that this chapter is about the Sacrament. Other Fathers interpret Christ's words about his own flesh and his own blood as given to death; others interpret them of bread and wine. Neither interpretation favours corporal presence. The former does not, because spiritual eating does not require the presence of the thing to be eaten. The latter does not either, because the flesh and blood of the Lord are one thing and the sacrament of his flesh and blood another.

units.la: non requiritur præsentia subjecti, quod comedendum est. Non hi, quia aliud caro & sanguis Domini, aliud Sacramentum carnis & sanguinis ejus. Dixit Christus, carnem suam ἀληθῶς βρῶσιν vere cibum esse, Joh. VI. 55. sed, quod Cajetanus etiam observat, non cibum corporis, sed animæ; ad significandum, quod caro sua non falsò, non opinione, sed secundum veritatem cibat animam. Venit etiam ad nos Christus δι' αἵματος & per sanguinem, & per eundem testatur in terra, I. Joh. V. 6. 8. Sed non per sanguinem sub speciebus vini latentem, quomodo nec per aquam, per quam etiam venisse dicitur, sub elemento aliquo latentem venit. Sed venit per sanguinem, qui ex latere Christi in cruce pendentis fluxit, Joh. XIX. 34. 35. non tantùm cum aqua, seu perfecta sanctitate, sed etiam cum sanguine, pretio perfecto, quo à reatu liberamur, & à peccato purificamur, I. Joh. I. 7. Sanguis verò ille in terra testans ille est, quem pro Christi nomine credentes effundunt. Typi porrò seu figuræ, quales fuerunt Manna, Agnus Paschalis, sanguis vituli &c. non arguunt corporalem præsentiam in Eucharistia, eò quòd aliàs illi nobilius, quam hæc Christum figurassent. Non enim Eucharistiæ, sed Christi typi fuerunt. Augustior verò & nobilior significandi ratio non in ritibus, sed in modo significandi, qui in Eucharistiæ Sacramento, clarior, facilior, evidentior est, poni debet. Posse corpus aliquod pluribus simul in locis esse frustra illi probare conantur; quia de voluntate Sacramentum instituentis, non de potentia Dei quæstio est. At nec potentia πολυομία Christi Paulo apparentis, Act. IX. 5. &c. rite confirmat. Visio enim illa spiritualis & mentalis potiùs, quàm corporalis. Et si corporalis maximè fuisset, non Christum in Cœlo & terra vel aëre simul existentem, sed in solo Cœlo vel oculorum acie elevata, ut illuc pertingeret, vel fulgore Majestatis Christi in terram diffuso, vidisset. Reliqua pro omnipræsentia vel πολυομία carnis Christi argumenta superius discussimus.
units.tr: Christ said that his flesh is truly food [ἀληθῶς βρῶσιν], John 6:55, but, as Cajetan also observes, not food of the body but of the soul; to signify that his flesh does not feed the soul falsely, nor by opinion, but according to truth. Christ also comes to us by water and blood [δι' αἵματος], and bears witness to this on earth through the same, 1 John 5:6, 8. But not through blood hidden under the species of wine, any more than he comes through water, which is also said to be the means of his coming, hidden under some element. Rather he comes by the blood which flowed from the side of Christ hanging on the cross, John 19:34–35, not only with the water, that is, perfect holiness, but also with the blood, the perfect price by which we are freed from guilt and purified from sin, 1 John 1:7. That blood which bears witness on earth is the blood which believers shed for the name of Christ. Moreover, the types or figures, such as the manna, the paschal lamb, the blood of the calf, etc., do not prove corporal presence in the Eucharist, because otherwise they would have represented Christ more nobly than this rite does. For they were types of Christ, not of the Eucharist. The more august and noble way of signifying lies not in the rites but in the mode of signifying, which in the Sacrament of the Eucharist is clearer, easier and more evident, and should be put first. They try in vain to prove that one body can be in several places at once, since the question concerns the will of the one who instituted the Sacrament, not the power of God. Nor does the power of Christ's multi-presence [πολυομία] appearing to Paul, Acts 9:5 etc., properly confirm it, for that vision was spiritual and mental rather than corporal. And if it had been chiefly corporal, Paul would not have seen Christ existing at once in heaven, on earth and in the air, but only in heaven, or by lifting up the sight of his eyes to reach there, or in the splendour of Christ's majesty spread over the earth. We have discussed the remaining arguments for the omnipresence or multi-presence [πολυομία] of Christ's flesh above.

units.la: CXXI. Transubstantiatione & præsentia corporali cadente, Missæ sacrificium ultro cadit & evanescit penitus.
units.tr: CXXI. With transubstantiation and the bodily presence overthrown, the sacrifice of the Mass falls with them and vanishes altogether.

units.la: Si enim corpus & sanguis Christi in Coenam non adducuntur, & in ea corporaliter non exist​unt, victima externa proprie dicta, & pro peccatis hominum propitiatoria in Cœna nulla alia ostendi poterit. Licèt enim Eucharistia etiam à veteribus sacrificii nomine veneat, symbolice, propter communicationem, repræsentationem, applicationem, recordationem, laudem & gratiarum actionem, tamen Christum in Eucharistia sub speciebus panis & vini offerri Deo Patri, adeoque in Cœna sacrificium proprie dictum ἱλαστήριον propitiatorium pro peccatis vivorum & mortuorum à Sacerdote proprie dicto immolari, nullo apice Eucharistiæ institutio docet. Nam in ea Christus Cœnam & Sacramentum, ceu sigillum corporis & sanguinis sui, instituit, cum quo sacrificium prorsus ἀναίμακτον est; quia illud accipitur ab hominibus, hoc Deo datur: ipse mensæ accubuit, non Sacerdotis instar altari astitit: panem & vinum benedictione sua sanctificavit, fregit, distribuit, comedendum, bibendum, non immolandum, circumgestandum, adorandum dedit: facere discipulos id jussit εἰς ἀνάμνησιν ad recordationem sui, non ad ἱλασμὸν expiationem, propitiationem pro peccatis: facere iussit id, quod ipse fecit, qui in prima Coena non sacrificavit, sed post eam ad sacrificandum se accinxit. Cùm igitur institutione Divina Missaticum sacrificium careat, in Missificibus impletur querela illa Dei: Ædificarunt excelsa Baalim, quæ ego nec præcepi, nec locutus sum, nec ascenderat in cor meum, Jerem. XIX. ƒ. Tum sacrificium proprie dictum Sacerdotem externum & altare requirit. Atqui in Coenæ Domini institutione nec altare uspiam apparet: nec Sacerdos proprie dictus. Christus enim non ut Sacerdos cum discipulis Coenam celebravit; sed demum post Coenam Sacerdotium obiit: nec Sacerdotes proprie dictos instituit, sed suo Sacerdotio omne sacerdotium externum abolevit. Nam ἅπαξ semel duntaxat eum offerri Apostolus Hebr. IX. 26-f. X. 1-19. gravissimis argumentis convicit, sufficientiam unicì illius παρασφορᾶς oblationis amplissimè confirmans, tum quia omnia peccata priscorum seculorum Christi sanguis semel effusus tollere & abolere potuit, cap. IX. 25.26. tum quia convenit ordini Divino, ut sicut omnis homo moritur semel, & mortem hanc ejus judicium sequitur: ita Christus semel mori, & deinceps sine peccato conspici debuit, v. 27. tum quia ratio repetendi sacrificii non convenit sacrificio Christi, sicut conveniebat sacrificiis V. T. quæ nec accedentes consummare poterant, cùm commemorationem duntaxat peccatorum effecerint; nec peccata omnino auferre valuerant, quia taurorum duntaxat & hircorum sanguine constiterant, cap. X. 1-10. tum quia Christus oblatione defunctus non mansit in terra, ut Sacerdotes Aharonici, sed consedit ad dextram Patris εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς in perpetuum, v. 11. 12. tum quia Christus jam nihil aliud expectat, quàm ut ponantur hostes ejus scabellum pedum ejus, v. 13. 14. tum denique quia Christi oblatione vera, solida & perfecta remissio peccatorum impetrata est, v. 16-19. Quæ omnia liquidò demonstrant, unicam oblationem Christi in cruce consummatam adeò perfectam & sufficientem esse, ut aliud sacrificium citra blasphemiam statui nullum possit. Neque aliud adversarii reponunt, quàm quòd in sacrificio crucis & Missæ unum numero sacrificium offeratur. Quod deploratum κενοφυλέον est, & eadem ratione rejicitur, qua asseritur. Et in eo conspicua Dei providentia est, quòd Antichristus unitatem sacrificii Christi, saltem externa professione, abnegare non debuit. Quomodo verò unum sacrificium est, oblatum & offerendum, factum & faciendum, præteritum, præsens & futurum, in Oriente & Occidente, eodem & diversis temporibus oblatum? Atqui Apostolus unitatem & Sacerdotii & sacrificii asserens, eo ipso sacrificia proprie dicta reliqua omnia quocunque nomine veniant, jugulat. Sed de eo pluribus infra. Præterea in tota Missæ celebratione nihil inveniri poterit, in quo essentia, seu formalis ratio sacrificii collocari possit. Vel enim ea in fractione, vel in oblatione hostiæ, quæ Deo fit, vel in consecratione, vel in benedictione collocari deberet. Atqui in nulla harum collocari poterit. Non in fractione, quia corpus Christi ἀπαθὲς impassibile est, & juxta
units.tr: For if the body and blood of Christ are not brought into the Supper and do not exist there bodily, then no external victim, properly so called, and no sacrifice propitiatory for the sins of men, can be shown in the Supper. For although the Eucharist too has been called a sacrifice by the ancients, symbolically, on account of its communion, representation, application, remembrance, praise and thanksgiving, yet the institution of the Eucharist does not teach in any way that Christ is offered to God the Father under the species of bread and wine, and so that in the Supper a sacrifice properly so called, a propitiatory [ἱλαστήριον] for the sins of the living and the dead, is immolated by a priest properly so called. For in it Christ instituted the Supper and the Sacrament, as a seal of his body and blood, and with this sacrifice is altogether unbloody [ἀναίμακτον], because the one is received by men, the other is given to God. He himself reclined at the table; he did not stand at the altar like a priest. He sanctified the bread and wine by his blessing, broke them, and distributed them to be eaten and drunk, not to be immolated, carried about or adored. He bade his disciples do this for the remembrance [εἰς ἀνάμνησιν] of himself, not for expiation [ἱλασμὸν], the propitiation for sins. He bade them do what he himself did, who in the first Supper did not sacrifice, but afterwards girded himself to sacrifice. Since, then, the Mass-sacrifice lacks divine institution, that complaint of God is fulfilled in the Mass-mongers: "They have built the high places of Baal, which I neither commanded, nor spoke, nor did it come into my heart," Jer. 19. Moreover, a sacrifice properly so called requires an external priest and an altar. But in the institution of the Lord's Supper no altar appears anywhere, nor a priest properly so called. Christ did not celebrate the Supper with his disciples as a priest; he only afterwards laid down his priesthood. Nor did he institute priests properly so called, but by his own priesthood he abolished all external priesthood. For the Apostle, in Heb. 9.26 – 10.1–19, proves with the weightiest arguments that he was offered only once [ἅπαξ], amply confirming the sufficiency of that single oblation [παρασφορᾶς]: first, because the blood of Christ, shed once, could take away and abolish all the sins of former ages, ch. 9.25–26; second, because it accords with the divine order that, as every man dies once and after death comes judgment, so Christ was to die once and thereafter be seen without sin, v. 27; third, because the reason for repeating a sacrifice does not fit the sacrifice of Christ, as it did the sacrifices of the Old Testament, which could not perfect those who drew near, since they effected only a remembrance of sins, and could not wholly take away sins, since they consisted only of the blood of bulls and goats, ch. 10.1–10; fourth, because Christ, having finished his offering, did not remain on earth as the Aaronic priests did, but sat down at the right hand of the Father for ever [εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς], v. 11–12; fifth, because Christ now awaits nothing else than that his enemies be made the footstool of his feet, v. 13–14; and finally, because by the true, solid and perfect offering of Christ the remission of sins has been obtained, v. 16–19. All these things clearly demonstrate that the single offering of Christ on the cross, once accomplished, is so perfect and sufficient that no other sacrifice can be set up without blasphemy. Nor do our adversaries reply anything else than that in the sacrifice of the cross and in the Mass one and the same sacrifice is offered in number. This is a deplorable and empty fancy, and it is rejected on the same ground on which it is asserted. In this the providence of God is conspicuous, that Antichrist ought not to have denied the unity of Christ's sacrifice, at least in outward profession. But how is it one sacrifice, offered and to be offered, done and to be done, past, present and future, offered in the East and the West, at the same and at different times? Now the Apostle, asserting the unity both of priesthood and of sacrifice, thereby slays all other sacrifices properly so called, by whatever name they come. But more on this below. Furthermore, in the whole celebration of the Mass nothing can be found in which the essence, or formal reason, of a sacrifice could be placed. For it would have to be placed either in the breaking, or in the offering of the victim made to God, or in the consecration, or in the blessing. But it can be placed in none of these. Not in the breaking, because the body of Christ is impassible [ἀπαθὲς], and according to

units.la: adversantes sub quavis hostiæ particula integrum manet: atque iidem fractionem ad essentiam sacrificii & Coenæ pertinere negant. Non in oblatione, quæ Deo fit, qua sacerdos hostiam attollens à Deo petit, ut hanc oblationem prono affectu suscipiat; quod ipse Bellarminus negat, quia eam oblationem nec Christus, nec Apostoli principiò adhibuerint; & verba hujus oblationis non in persona Christi, sed Sacerdotis & Ecclesiæ dicantur, sacrificium autem in persona Christi præcipuè offeratur. Neque Sacerdos Christum, sed bona hæc, quæ Deus creat, sanctificat, benedicit & præstat. Non in benedictione, quia benedicere panem non est sacrificare panem, vel offerre Deo sacrificium propitiatorium pro peccatis. Non in consecratione, quam in verbis, H. E. E. C. M. ponunt, quia aliud est hostiæ consecratio, aliud ejusdem immolatio, quæ duo non minùs quàm media à fine distant; & verbis illis, H. ƒ. E. C. M. nihil à Christo Deo Patri oblatum, sed discipulis aliquid collatum & donatum fuit, atque insuper in Missa nihil, quod consecratum sit, Deo offertur. Nam quòd Bellarminus ait, consecratione rem profanam fieri sacram, atque talem in altari collocari, atque ita Deo offerri, & ad veram, realem & externam mutationem & destructionem ordinari, nihil pro vero sacrificio ille dicit, quia ordinare ad destructionem & destruere & occidere, atque ita sacrificare realiter differunt. Et quæ illa ordinatio ad sacrificium est? Ordinatio, inquit, ad cibum, qui & ipse ad destructionem, puta τῶ esse sacramentalis, ordinatur. Sic essentia sacrificii consistit in duabus rebus, ordinatione ad destructionem, & destructione ipsa τῶ esse sacramentalis. Quæ mera Christianorum ludificatio est. Hæc igitur sacrificatio erit, quod in altari ponitur corpus, ut fiat cibus Sacerdotis, & ita fiat cibus, ut corruptis ejus speciebus, seu τῶ esse sacramentali, desinat in ipso esse. Totum ergo mysterium, totus apex religionis, quæ tanta cum pompa & honore peragitur, in eo est, quòd ad vocem sacrificuli incipit corpus esse in altari, & eo species in os ingerente, definit esse in altari, atque incipit esse in ore & ventriculo, & mox consumptis speciebus, definit etiam ibi esse. Hoc illud sacrificium N. T. hæc commu-nio corporis Christi; hic cibus manens in seculum, & vitam dans mundo, est. O cæcas hominum mentes! Non denique in manducatione, quia aliàs singuli de plebe forent Sacerdotes, & quot plebis & Sacerdotum ora, tot altaria forent; neque manducare est offerre Deo, sed oblatum à Deo accipere à Deo, & in rem suam vertere. Neque planè in Missa offerri Christi corpus & sanguis potest, quia Christi sacrificium non est nisi obedientia & passio ejus usque ad mortem & destructionem ejus, eâmque cruentam, quia sine effusione sanguinis nulla fit remissio, Hebr. IX. 22. Non potest enim esse θυσία absque θυσιν, neque occisio victimæ animatæ absque sanguine. Neque Christus remissionem peccatorum aliter impetrat, quàm quatenus Mediator N. T. est. Ubi autem Testamentum est, ibi mors testatoris intercedat necesse est, ibid. v. 16. Atqui in Missa nulla Christi mors & destructio cruenta est. Quid enim in ea destruitur? Panis? At negant illi pro prolatis verbis, H. E. E. C. M. substantiam panis superesse. Et panis substantia destructa non potest cluere sacrificium λογικὸν. An Christus sub hostia latens? Atqui ille semel mortuus & destructus, mox resuscitatus ascendit in Coelum, & consedit ad dextram Dei, ubi ἀπαθὴς impassibilis plane, gloriosè regnat. An τὸ esse sacramentale, hoc est, esse sub speciebus definens in stomacho, & sic esse cibum visibilem? Quod perinde est, ac si diceret, destrui hominem, cùm tunicam exuit. Ita ad rationem sacrificii satis fuisset, si Christus vestem suam ex lana, lino, imò accidentibus confectam cruci affigi passus esset, modò ille tamdiu vivus spiransque lateret sub illa veste, spectator ridiculi dramatis, donec crucifixio perageretur, ipse interea illaesus, nullóque mali sensu percitus. Quid futilius, & majori cum ignominia de ejus sacrificio dici posset? Haec scilicet impia Gnosticorum & Aphtardocetarum deliramenta sunt. Etenim Christus per passiones consummatus est, ut princeps salutis nostrae, Heb. II. 10. V. 7. 8. At his si creditur, semper consummatur sine passionibus, per destructionem non realem, non τὸ esse, sed χρῆσιν, seu τὸ esse sacramentalis, hoc est, per desinere esse in stomacho Sacerdotis; & tamen nunquam est consummatus, nisi quando in Missa offerri desierit, quod demum in fine mundi futurum illi sperant. Sed produnt in universum Missificos, se in illorum censu esse, quos Apostolus Filium Dei sibimet ipsis ἀναστανρόω iterum crucifigere ἐν παραδείγματι & ostentui habere dicit, ibid. VI. 6. Quid enim Filium Dei iterum crucifigere sibi ipsis, & ostentui facere est, si eundem infinitis vicibus in Missa sacrificare, theatrica cum pompa offerre, & adorandum ostentare; atque id omne quaestus sui gratia, non est? Denique Missae sacrificium Ecclesiae veteri plane incognitum, incunabula sua ab ipsa Transubstantiatione & praesentia corporali, cujus seram originem supra eruimus; sortitum est. Intervallo enim illo temporum, quod Lateranense inter sub Innocentio III. celebratum & Tridentinum Concilium fluxit, obstetricantibus variis erroribus, miraculis etiam fictitiis, conceptum, formatum, natum, exclusum, & in Concilio Tridentino bruto anathemate firmatum & roboratum est. In ipso Tridentino Concilio adhuc Georgius Ataides, Lusitanus Theologus, negavit, ex Dei verbo Missam probari posse, & argumenta ex eo petita diluit: Et Episcopus Vegliensis in Missa non esse sacrificium proprie dictum, solidis rationibus convicit: Dissensuntt adversariorum circa Missam, quae totius Papatus arx & acropolis est, nec non contradictiones, quibus ipsum sacrificium Missaticum scatet, alibi ad vivum repraesentatas, hic commemorare supersedemus.
units.tr: those who oppose this, it remains whole under any particle of the host; and the same people deny that the breaking pertains to the essence of sacrifice and of the Supper. Not in the offering made to God, in which the priest, lifting up the host, asks God to accept this offering with a gracious disposition; Bellarmine himself denies this, because neither Christ nor the Apostles used such an offering in the beginning, and the words of this offering are spoken not in the person of Christ but of the priest and the Church, whereas the sacrifice is offered chiefly in the person of Christ. Nor does the priest offer Christ, but these goods which God creates, sanctifies, blesses and bestows. Not in the blessing, because to bless bread is not to sacrifice bread, or to offer to God a sacrifice propitiatory for sins. Not in the consecration, which they place in the words, Hoc est enim corpus meum, because the consecration of the host is one thing and its immolation another, and these two are no less distant than means from end; and by those words, Hoc est enim corpus meum, nothing was offered by Christ to God the Father, but something was conferred and given to the disciples; moreover, in the Mass nothing that has been consecrated is offered to God. For as to Bellarmine's saying that by consecration a profane thing is made sacred, and placed thus on the altar, and so offered to God, and ordered to a true, real and external change and destruction, he says nothing for a true sacrifice, because to be ordered to destruction, and to destroy, and to kill, and thus to sacrifice really, differ. And what is this ordering to sacrifice? It is, he says, an ordering to food, which itself is ordered to destruction, namely as to its sacramental being [τῶ esse sacramentalis]. Thus the essence of sacrifice consists of two things: an ordering to destruction, and the destruction itself of the sacramental being. This is mere mockery of Christians. This, then, will be the sacrificing: that the body is placed on the altar, so that it becomes food for the priest, and becomes food in such a way that, when its species are corrupted, or its sacramental being, it ceases to be in its own being. The whole mystery, then, the whole height of religion, which is carried on with such pomp and honour, consists in this: at the voice of the little priest the body begins to be on the altar, and when the priest puts the species into his mouth it ceases to be on the altar, and begins to be in the mouth and stomach, and soon, when the species are consumed, it ceases to be there too. This is that sacrifice of the New Testament, this communion of the body of Christ; this is the food that remains unto eternal life and gives life to the world. O blind minds of men! Finally, the sacrifice does not consist in the eating, because otherwise each single man of the common people would be a priest, and there would be as many altars as mouths of the people and priests; nor is to eat to offer to God, but to receive from God what has been offered by God, and to turn it to one's own use. Nor can the body and blood of Christ truly be offered in the Mass, because the sacrifice of Christ is nothing but his obedience and passion, even to death and his destruction, and that a bloody one, since "without shedding of blood there is no remission," Heb. 9.22. For there cannot be a sacrifice [θυσία] without a slaying [θυσιν], nor the killing of a living victim without blood. Nor does Christ obtain the remission of sins otherwise than insofar as he is Mediator of the New Testament. "Where a testament is, there must of necessity be the death of the testator," ibid. v. 16. But in the Mass there is no death and bloody destruction of Christ. For what is destroyed in it? Bread? But they deny that the substance of the bread remains after the words, Hoc est enim corpus meum have been spoken. And a bread whose substance has been destroyed cannot constitute a rational [λογικὸν] sacrifice. Is it Christ lying hidden under the host? But he, once dead and destroyed, soon raised up, ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of God, where, altogether impassible, he reigns in glory. Or is it the sacramental being, that is, being under the species, ceasing in the stomach, and so being visible food? That is just as if one were to say that a man is destroyed when he takes off his coat. Thus for the nature of a sacrifice it would have sufficed if Christ had suffered his garment made of wool or linen, or indeed made of accidents, to be nailed to the cross, provided he lay hidden under that garment, alive and breathing, a spectator of a ridiculous drama, until the crucifixion was carried out, himself meanwhile unharmed and stirred by no sense of evil. What could be more trifling, and said with greater disgrace, about his sacrifice? These are surely the impious ravings of the Gnostics and the Aphthartodocetae. For Christ was made perfect through sufferings, as the author of our salvation, Heb. 2.10; 5.7–8. But if one believes these men, he is always made perfect without sufferings, through a destruction that is not real, not a being but a use, or sacramental being, that is, by ceasing to be in the stomach of the priest; and yet he is never perfected, unless when he has ceased to be offered in the Mass, which they hope will happen at last at the end of the world. But they show in general that the Mass-mongers are among those whom the Apostle says crucify again to themselves the Son of God [ἀναστανρόω] and hold him up to open shame [ἐν παραδείγματι], ibid. 6.6. For what is it to crucify the Son of God again to oneself, and to make him a public spectacle, if one sacrifices him again in the Mass in endless repetitions, offers him with theatrical pomp, and displays him for adoration; and all this for the sake of gain? Finally, the sacrifice of the Mass, altogether unknown to the ancient Church, received its beginnings from transubstantiation itself and the bodily presence, whose late origin we have brought to light above. For in that interval of time which passed between the Lateran Council celebrated under Innocent III and the Council of Trent, with various errors acting as midwives, even with fictitious miracles, it was conceived, formed, born, brought forth, and at the Council of Trent was confirmed and strengthened with a brutal anathema. Even at the Council of Trent itself, Georgius Ataides, a Portuguese theologian, denied that the Mass could be proved from the Word of God, and refuted the arguments drawn from it; and the Bishop of Vence convicted by solid reasons that in the Mass there is no sacrifice properly so called. We pass over here the disagreements of our adversaries concerning the Mass, which is the citadel and acropolis of the whole Papacy, as well as the contradictions with which the Mass-sacrifice itself abounds, which have been set forth to the life elsewhere.

units.la: CXXII. Non rationes, sed merae praestigiae sunt, quibus Missifices Missae suae sacrificium confirmare satagunt. Tale illud est, quòd Christum, ceu Sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, aequè sub speciebus panis & vini sacrificium Deo offerre debere, atque Melchisedecus Deo panem & vinum obtulerit; Genes. XIV. 18. nugantur. Nam Melchisedecus nec Christi typus in eo fuit, quòd panem & vinum obtulerit, sed in aliis omnibus, quae S. Paulus Hebr. VII. 1. &c. diserte admodum & ἀνάμεσον exposuit, panis & vini oblationem altissimo silentio involvens; nec panem & vinum ceu sacrificium Deo obtulit, sed, fatentibus etiam adversariis non paucis, ceu xenia, ad reficiendum Abrahami exercitum protulit, similem enim simili in causa morem finitimis regionibus fuisse, non obscurè Historia sacra pandit. Ita enim Ammonitis & Moabitis vitio datur, quòd Israelitas in via, cùm exirent ex Aegypto non anticiparunt (exceperunt) cum pane & aqua, Deut. XXIII. 4. Et Gedeon Jordanem transiturus cum trecentis viris fatigatis ad cives Suchot dixit: Date quaeso populo, qui comitatur me tortas panis, lassi enim sunt. Responderunt primores urbis Suchot & Zalmunah: Num palma Sebah & Zalmunah jam in manu tua est, ut demus exercitui tuo panem? Judic. VIII. 5-15. Neque etiam Abrahami, ceu Sacerdotis, sacrificium pro materia panem & vinum, sed decimas ex omnibus, Gen. XIV. 20. habuit, & si maximè etiam panem & vinum habuisset, non illa panis & vini oblatio principale sacrificium fuisset, sed ἐπιμιστέον duntaxat, & ἀπεσφηκαν, qualis olim fuit panis & vini oblatio Levitis praescripta, quam non principale sacrificium, sed accessoriam ejus partem & condimentum fuisse, Bellarminus fatetur. Neque obstant verba illa Et ipse fuit Sacerdos Dei altissimi, v. 18. utpote quibus nec causa actus allegatur, nec si exponeretur, oblati panis & vini, ceu sacrificii proprie dicti, sed benedictionis potius sacerdotalis, de qua statim v. 19: dicitur: et benedixit ei &c. exponeretur. Benedictionis enim hujus apud Mosen & Paulum expressa mentio est: oblationis nulla. Patres vero nonnulli ad hoc Melchisedeci factum alludentes, non sacrificium Missaticum, quale nullum agnoscunt, inde concludunt, sed Melchisedeci donaria cum Coenae symbolis contendunt. Et quae tandem sacrificium inter Melchisedeci & Missaticum similitudo est? An sicut in hoc fingunt, in illo etiam rei oblatae substantialis mutatio, remanentibus accidentibus facta est? An etiam Melchisedecus Sacerdotes habuit, sicut Christum habere fingunt? Et tamen ille mortalis fuit, hic potentia vitae indissolubilis praeditus; ut sacerdotium ejus morte interrumpi nequiret. Et est Christus Sacerdos in saeculum; secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, Psal. CX 4. sed non ideo sacrificium perpetuum, seu à ministris Sacerdotibus in terra continuandum usque ad finem mundi, habere debet. Nam id ipsum Apostolus refellit; conferens Christum cum Aharonidis, qui non manebant, sed morte intercedente, successoribus indigebant, Hebr. VII. 23. 24. Nec Sacerdotum minorum & ministrorum color juvat, cùm illi non minùs quàm minores Mediatores, Salvatores, Sponsores & Testatores excludantur. Est igitur Sacerdos aeternus, quia aeterna ejus voluntas est, per quam salutem & vitam accipimus, indissolubilis vitae ejus potentia, secus quàm Sacerdotum Aharonidarum, est, & tum oblationis fructus, tum intercessio sacerdotalis aeterna est. Grave profecto Christianae pietati illud est, quod sacrificium crucis, ceu formaliter non perpetuum, sine sacrificio Missae Missatico perpetuum, & cum perpetuo Eccle-siæ statu connexum illi negant. Quomodo e-nim una eadémque numero utriusque sacrifi-cii hostia esse potest,quod illi asserunt? Etenim si sacrificium Christi sic formaliter perpetuum esse debet,ut identidem à Sacerdotibus Christi Ministris illud repetatur, an etiam in Cœlo,in quo Sacerdos esse non definit, quippe Sacerdos לעולם in seculum, sic repeti illud necesse habe-bit? Et quomodo sacrificium crucis sic πλεω-ικὸν erit ? Cúmque illud semel peractum ad delenda etiam peccata præterita omnia value-rit,quomodo non ad delenda etiam futura va-let ? Potuit Melchisedecus sine ullis vicariis vel ministris sacerdotium continuantibus in typo esse sine initio & sine dierum, adeóque æ-ternus esse. Cur Christus,in quo illud in veri-tate rei impletum est,non posset? Neque etiam illud תמיד juge sacrificium , quod abolitum iri Dan.XII.11. prædictum est,Missaticum sacri-ficium sub Antichristo interrumpendum, no-tat; sed vel proprie dictum juge sacrificium ab Antiocho Epiphane , & in Hierosolymæ exci-dio abolitum: sive id,quod per juge illud sa-crificium Leviticum adumbratum fuit, hoc est,jugis, seu quotidianus & perpetuus valor sacrificii Christi , qui pro Ecclesia apud Deum comparet εις διηνεκες jugiter , seu in perpetuum, Hebr. VII.3. IX.24. & quod in Ecclesia jugi-ter Deo in fide repræsentatur. Quando igitur invalescente Antichristo, fides ea mutata est in opinionem sacrificii alterius,quale Missaticum est,nec non in opinionem operis operati, & ea opinio prævaluit, tum vero juge sacrificium, fides & confessio Sanctorum, qui latere coacti sunt, ablatum est. Agno Paschali verum Pa-scha, Christus per eum figuratus successit, in cruce semel,non iterum iterúmque per Sacer-dotes vicarios & ministros mactatus & obla-tus,vera fide in Cœna & extra eam comeditur. Non enim Agnus ille mysticus Eucharistiæ,vel sacrificii incruenti in Eucharistia , sed Christi & mortis ejus in Eucharistia , & cujusvis con-vivii spiritualis,in quo caro & sanguis ejus per fidem manducatur,typum gessit. Fuit Pascha verè פסח זבח victima transitus , ratione aspersi sanguinis,non ratione manducationis Agni,cui spiritualis carnis & sanguinis Christi mandu-catio in Eucharistia , & extra eam respondet. Sed & prædictum est,fore ut ab ortu solis us-que ad occasum ejus magnum sit nomen Dei inter gentes, & in omni loco מקטר incensum offeratur nomini ejus, & מנחה טהורה oblatio pura, Mal.I. II. quod impletum est non in sacrificio Missæ, quia in eo nec incensum , seu holocaustum , nec oblatio pura obtinet,& nec incensum,nec obla-tio pura, quatenus ab incenso distinguitur, sa-crificium ιλαστικὸν propitiatorium, quale solum illi in Missa agnoscunt, obtinet ; sed in cultu spirituali,thure precum,& oblatione sui in ho-stiam viventem,atque fructu labiorum confi-tentium nomen ejus consistens, in quo Deus, qui in Cœlis est, in spiritu & veritate adora-tur. Venit hora & nunc est,cùm veri adoratores adorabunt Patrem in Spiritu & veritate. Nam & Pater tales adoratores quærit, Joh.IV.23. Qui cultus Spiritus, typico & externo illi respon-dens,quoad rem in utroque Testamento idem fuit; at modo, efficacia, gradu & adorantium extensione differt. Et appellatur oblatio illa טהורה munda, non simpliciter, sed quatenus à corde per fidem purificato proficiscitur , quo-modo etiam fideles omnes καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ mundi corde, Matth. V.8. appellantur. Figura igitur exprimitur , sed res, seu veritas figurata intelligitur. Rectius longè Judæus, Paraphra-stes Chaldæus, quàm adversarii Christiani λε-γόμενοι, sic verba Malachiæ reddidit; אנא אקרב צלותיכם ושמי יקדש וצלותיכם כקרבן כי קרמי Ego recipiam preces vestras,& nomen meum sanctificabitur,& oratio vestra erit sicut oblatio mun-da coram me. Ita David: Dirigatur oratio mea קטרת sicut incensum in conspectu tuo , manuum mearum munus מנחה ערב sicut oblatio vespertina, Psal.CXLI.2. Dilutum porrò est & illud, quòd Christum in ultima Cœna corpus & san-guinem suum sub speciebus panis & vini ob-tulisse, & jubentem hoc facere, Apostolos Sa-cerdotes,similiter corpus & sanguinem Christi offerentes instituisse, pertendunt. Nam in ipso Tridentino Concilio non pauci , Christum se ipsum in ultima Cœna obtulisse,negarunt,eò quòd alias oblatio ejus in cruce supervacanea fuisset,& Christus Cœnam in commemoratio-nem sui in cruce offerendi instituerit,& neque Scriptura, nec canon Missæ, nec Concilium ul-lum ejus rei meminerit. Sed nihil argumenta ejus profecerunt apud eos , quorum suffragia astutus Jesuita Salmeron impudentissimè in Concilio ipso prensavit. Neque obstant verba illa temporis præsentis,datur, frangitur,effundi-tur , in quibus conspicua & Hebræis usitata enallage temporis præsentis pro futuro,utpo-te proximè imminente est. Neque enim ver-ba institutionis Deum Patrem , sed discipulos respiciunt, quibus symbola data sunt non of-ferenda,sed utenda,fruenda,non ut sacrificium corporis & sanguinis , sed ut Sacramentum utriusque. Quod ergo ποιεῖν facere discipulos jussit, non ad oblationem , quæ nulla in prima Cœna fuit,sed ad id,quod Christus externè fe-cit,& à discipulis fieri potuit,referendum est. Ideo S. Paulus illud ποιεῖν facere per πίνειν , ἐυ-λογεῖν, κλᾶν , κυριακὸν δεῖπνον φαγεῖν, bibere, be-nedicere, frangere, Cœnam Dominicam edere, I. Cor. X. 16. 20. XI.25.26. interpretatur. De institutione Sacerdotii ne apicem quidem ha-bet. Inepta verò illa grammaticatio est, qua facere pro sacrificare positum afferunt : Licèt enim apud Latinos facere cum ablativo casu construetum,& addita victimæ,nec non apud Hebræos עשה facere, addita etiam victimæ sa-crificare significet , tamen nunquam eo sensu vox Græca ποιεῖν usurpatur. Matthæus autem Græcè verba hæc descripsit,nec victimæ ullum in sermone ejus vestigium extat. Et quales quæso Sacerdotes à Christo instituti sunt ? Aharonidæ? At illos abolevit. An secundum or-dinem Melchisedeci ? Atqui Sacerdotium hoc ἀπαρχὴν describitur. Neque alii in Scriptu-ra Sacerdotes , quàm Baalis memorantur. Sed & Lucas de Barnaba & Nigro verba faciens,di-cit , λειτουργούντων αὐτῶν, Actor. XIII.2. quod perperam Missifices interpretantur,sacrificanti-bus illis. Nam etiam vetus Interpres reddit: Ministrantibus illis. Et de plebejis etiam vox il-la,2.Cor.IX.12. Rom.XV.27. de Regibus, ibid.XIII.16. de Angelis,Hebr.I.7.14. usur-patur, patùr, quos Missifices nunquam illi fecerint. Si tamen cum Erasmo sacrificandi notio placet, in Eucharistia sacrificium symbolicum, at non reale est. Æquè enim panis & vinum locutione sacramentali, seu metonymia signi, sacrificium, atque ipsum corpus & sanguis Christi appellari possunt. Ficulnea verò & illa folia sunt, cùm in sacrificio Missæ eundem Christum contineri & immolari, qui se in ara crucis pro nobis obtulit; & in eodem sacrificium crucis applicari & repræsentari pronuntiant. Dictatorie enim nimis asserunt, non ex Scripturis probant, quòd Christus, eadem numero victima, duobus modis cruento & incruento modo sacrificetur. Diversas verò esse numero actiones, eam, quæ à Christo in cruce facta est, & quæ quotidie in Missa fit, facilè probatur, quia definitione differunt. Sacrificium enim crucis cruentum, asperum, visibile, uno in loco oblatum, irreiterabile fuit. Sacrificium Missæ contra est. In illo Christus satisfecit, & fuit in statu merendi: in hoc contra. Præterea Christus moriens & non moriens una victima esse non possunt, cùm ne victima esse quidem possit, nisi cùm moritur. Imò semel duntaxat Christum oblatum esse, Apostolus Heb. IX. 25. &c. affirmat, & pluribus argumentis demonstrat. Ipsa quoque adversantium assertio, quòd sacrificium crucis in Missa repræsentetur & applicetur, id ipsum confirmat. Nam quo sacrificio aliud repræsentatur & applicatur, illud aliud illud sacrificium esse non potest. Repræsentare verò & applicare rem gestam, est agnoscere, nos non facere, quod factum est, sed tantùm recolere, repetere, ne excidat, & ut nobis prosit. Qualis applicatio non potest esse oblatio, cùm hæc oblatio facienda illam oblationem factam præsupponat, ut applicatio hominibus, oblatio Deo fiat. Insulsum etiam est, sacrificium comminisci, quod tantùm commemoratorium & repræsentativum alterius sacrificii, & simul expiatorium sit; Hoc enim de qualicunque sacrificii expiatorii imagine dici non potest, cùm ibi demum expiatio sit, ubi realis oblatio est. Quòd porrò Christianam religionem sacrificio externo carere non posse tricantur, non cogitant, in Cœlo, ubi religio consummabitur, nulli oblationi novæ locum futurum esse. At nec Christiana religio sacrificio destituitur, Christi nimirum in cruce perac̄ti, cujus cùm æternus & infinitus valor sit, repræsentatio & recordatio, at non iteratio, vel distincta oblatio, locum habere potest. Patres denique unum sacrificium propitiatorium in cruce peractum agnovisse, irrefragabilibus argumentis nostri, Mornæus inprimis, Hospinianus & Albertinus demonstrarunt. Ubi hæc veluti κλεῖς τῆς γνώσεως clavis intelligentiæ tenenda est, quòd dicta eorum non ex verborum sono, sed ex loquentium sensu æstimanda sit. Non enim quia subinde Missæ, altaris, mensæ, sacrificii, Sacerdotum meminerunt, Pontificiam illi Missam somniarunt. Sacrificium inprimis illi vel oblationem elementorum à populo factam, vel sacrificium corporis Christi, sed improprie & metonymicè, signo nomen rei signatæ induentes, ut disertissimè Augustinus Epist. 23. explicavit; vel sacrificium spirituale, intuitu tum ipsius actionis in Eucharistia, quæ pars cultus soli
units.tr: These are not arguments but mere tricks, by which the makers of the Mass labour to confirm the sacrifice of their Mass. Of this kind is the claim that Christ, as priest according to the order of Melchisedec, ought to offer sacrifice to God under the species of bread and wine just as Melchisedec offered bread and wine to God (Gen. 14:18). They trifle. For Melchisedec was a type of Christ not in that he offered bread and wine, but in all the other respects which St Paul set out very clearly in Heb. 7:1 and following, [ἀνάμεσον], passing over the offering of bread and wine in deep silence. Nor did he offer bread and wine to God as a sacrifice; rather, as many of the opponents themselves admit, he brought them as gifts to refresh Abraham's army, for sacred history makes plain that a similar custom prevailed in neighbouring regions in similar circumstances. Thus the Ammonites and Moabites are blamed because they did not meet the Israelites on the way with bread and water when they came out of Egypt (Deut. 23:4). And Gideon, about to cross the Jordan with three hundred weary men, said to the men of Succoth: "Please give bread to the people who follow me, for they are faint." The leaders of the city of Succoth and of Zalmunna answered: "Is the hand of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?" (Judg. 8:5-15). Nor did Abraham, as priest, make bread and wine the matter of his sacrifice, but tithes of all things (Gen. 14:20); and even if he had offered bread and wine, that offering would not have been the principal sacrifice, but merely ἐπιμιστέον and ἀπεσφηκαν, like the offering of bread and wine once prescribed for the Levites, which Bellarmine admits was not the principal sacrifice but an accessory part and seasoning of it. Nor do the words And he was the priest of God Most High (v. 18) stand in the way, since no cause of the act is given there, and even if they were explained, they would refer not to an offering of bread and wine as a sacrifice properly so called, but to the priestly blessing, of which v. 19 goes on: and he blessed him, and so on. For Moses and Paul expressly mention this blessing; they mention no offering. Some of the Fathers, alluding to this deed of Melchisedec, do not draw from it a Mass-sacrifice, which they do not acknowledge at all, but compare Melchisedec's gifts with the symbols of the Lord's Supper. And what resemblance, after all, is there between the sacrifice of Melchisedec and the Mass? Do they imagine, as in the Mass, a change of the substance of the offered thing with the accidents remaining? Did Melchisedec have priests, as they imagine Christ has? Yet he was mortal, while Christ is endowed with the power of an indissoluble life, so that his priesthood cannot be interrupted by death. Christ is a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedec (Ps. 110:4), but he does not therefore have to have a perpetual sacrifice, or one to be continued on earth by ministers and priests until the end of the world. For the Apostle himself refutes this, comparing Christ with the sons of Aaron, who did not remain but, through death, needed successors (Heb. 7:23-24). Nor does the pretext of lesser priests and ministers help them, since these are excluded no less than lesser mediators, saviours, sureties and testators. Christ is therefore an eternal priest, because his will is eternal, through which we receive salvation and life, and the power of his life is indissoluble, unlike that of the sons of Aaron; both the fruit of his offering and his priestly intercession are eternal. It is truly a grievous thing for Christian devotion that they deny that the sacrifice of the cross is perpetual in the formal sense, and claim that it is made perpetual, and connected with the perpetual state of the Church, only by the Mass-sacrifice. For how can one and the same victim in number be present in both sacrifices, as they assert? For if the sacrifice of Christ must be formally perpetual, so that it is repeated again and again by Christ's priestly ministers, will it also be necessary for it to be repeated in this way in heaven, where he does not cease to be a priest, since he is priest [לעולם] for ever? And how will the sacrifice of the cross thus be πλεω-ικὸν? And since it, once accomplished, was sufficient to blot out all past sins, how is it not sufficient to blot out also future ones? Melchisedec, without any vicars or ministers continuing the priesthood, could in the type be without beginning and without end of days, and so be eternal. Why could Christ, in whom this was fulfilled in the truth of the thing, not be so? Nor does the word [תמיד] continual sacrifice, which Dan. 12:11 foretold would be abolished, signify the Mass-sacrifice to be interrupted under Antichrist. It means either the continual sacrifice properly so called, abolished by Antiochus Epiphanes and at the destruction of Jerusalem; or that which was foreshadowed by that Levitical continual sacrifice, namely the continual and perpetual value of the sacrifice of Christ, who appears before God for the Church [εις διηνεκες], that is, continually, or for ever (Heb. 7:3; 9:24), and which is represented to God in the Church continually by faith. Therefore, when Antichrist gained strength, that faith was changed into the opinion of another sacrifice, such as the Mass is, and into the opinion of the work wrought (opus operatum), and when that opinion prevailed, then the continual sacrifice, the faith and confession of the saints, who were compelled to go into hiding, was taken away. The true Passover, Christ, who was prefigured by the Paschal Lamb, was sacrificed once on the cross, not again and again by priests as vicars and ministers; he is eaten in true faith both in the Supper and outside it. For that mystical Lamb did not prefigure the Eucharist, or an unbloody sacrifice in the Eucharist, but the death of Christ in the Eucharist, and in every spiritual feast in which his flesh and blood are eaten by faith. The Passover was truly [פסח זבח], the victim of the passing over, by reason of the sprinkled blood, not by reason of the eating of the lamb, to which the spiritual eating of the flesh and blood of Christ in the Eucharist, and outside it, corresponds. But it was also foretold that from the rising of the sun to its setting, my name shall be great among the nations, and in every place incense [מקטר] shall be offered to my name, and a pure offering [מנחה טהורה] (Mal. 1:11). This was fulfilled not in the sacrifice of the Mass, for in it there is neither incense, that is, burnt offering, nor pure offering, nor, as far as the pure offering is distinguished from incense, the ἱλαστικὸν, propitiatory sacrifice, which alone they acknowledge in the Mass. It was fulfilled rather in spiritual worship, in the incense of prayers, in the offering of oneself as a living sacrifice, and in the fruit of the lips confessing his name; in this God, who is in heaven, is worshipped in spirit and truth. The hour comes, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such worshippers (John 4:23). This spiritual worship, answering to the typical and external worship, was the same in substance in both Testaments; but it differs in efficacy, in degree, and in the extent of those who worship. That offering is called pure [טהורה] not simply, but because it proceeds from a heart purified by faith; in the same way all the faithful are called pure in heart [καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ] (Matt. 5:8). Thus the figure is expressed, but the thing figured, or the truth, is understood. Far more correctly than the Christian sophists did, the Jew, the Chaldee paraphrast, rendered the words of Malachi thus: Ana akrab tzelotaykhon ve-shmi yitqaddash ve-tzelotaykhon kakorban kedami, that is, "I will receive your prayers, and my name shall be sanctified, and your prayer shall be as an offering pure before me." So David: Let my prayer be directed as incense [qetoret] in your sight, the lifting up of my hands as the evening offering [minkha] (Ps. 141:2). It is also false that Christ offered his body and blood under the species of bread and wine at the last supper, and that, commanding them to do this, he instituted the apostles as priests who likewise offered the body and blood of Christ. For in the Council of Trent itself, not a few denied that Christ offered himself at the last supper, because otherwise his offering on the cross would have been superfluous, and because Christ instituted the Supper in commemoration of what he would offer on the cross; and neither Scripture, nor the canon of the Mass, nor any council mentions this matter. But their arguments availed nothing with those whose votes the crafty Jesuit Salmeron most shamelessly snatched in the Council itself. Nor do the words of the present tense, is given, is broken, is poured out, stand in the way, in which there is the clear and Hebrew-customary use of the present tense for the future, as it is imminent. For the words of institution do not look to God the Father, but to the disciples, to whom the symbols were given not to be offered, but to be used and enjoyed, not as a sacrifice of body and blood, but as a sacrament of both. What he bade the disciples to do [ποιεῖν], therefore, is to be referred not to an offering, for there was none at the first supper, but to what Christ did outwardly and what the disciples could do. Hence St Paul explains that doing as drinking, blessing, breaking, eating the Lord's Supper (1 Cor. 10:16, 20; 11:25-26). Of the institution of a priesthood it does not have even a trace. That grammatical trick, by which they claim that to do is used for to sacrifice, is absurd. For although among the Latins facere, construed with the ablative case and with the addition of the victim, and among the Hebrews עשה to do, with the addition of the victim, can mean to sacrifice, the Greek word ποιεῖν is never used in that sense. Moreover, Matthew wrote these words in Greek, and no trace of a victim appears in his account. And what sort of priests, I ask, were instituted by Christ? The sons of Aaron? But he abolished them. A priesthood according to the order of Melchisedec? But that priesthood is described as without beginning. Nor do the Scriptures mention any priests other than those of Baal. And Luke, speaking of Barnabas and Niger, says λειτουργούντων αὐτῶν (Acts 13:2), which the makers of the Mass wrongly translate sacrificing to them. For even the old translator renders it: ministering to them. And this word is used also of ordinary people (2 Cor. 9:12; Rom. 15:27), of kings (Rom. 13:16), and of angels (Heb. 1:7, 14), none of whom the makers of the Mass would ever have called priests. If, however, with Erasmus, the notion of sacrificing pleases them, then in the Eucharist there is a symbolic sacrifice, but not a real one. For bread and wine, by sacramental language, that is by metonymy of the sign, may be called a sacrifice just as the body and blood of Christ themselves may be. But those fig leaves are also too thin, since they affirm that in the sacrifice of the Mass the same Christ is contained and immolated who offered himself for us on the altar of the cross, and that the sacrifice of the cross is applied and represented in the same sacrifice. For they assert this too dogmatically, and do not prove from Scripture that Christ, the same victim in number, is sacrificed in two ways, bloodily and unbloodily. That the actions are different in number, however, the action done by Christ on the cross and that done daily in the Mass, is easily proved, since they differ in definition. The sacrifice of the cross was bloody, painful, visible, offered in one place, and not to be repeated. The Mass-sacrifice is the reverse. In the former Christ made satisfaction, and was in a state of meriting; in the latter, the contrary. Furthermore, Christ dying and Christ not dying cannot be one victim, since he cannot even be a victim except when he dies. Indeed the Apostle affirms that Christ was offered once only (Heb. 9:25 and following), and demonstrates it by many arguments. The very assertion of the opponents, that the sacrifice of the cross is represented and applied in the Mass, confirms this same point. For that sacrifice to which another is represented and applied cannot itself be that other. To represent and apply a past deed, moreover, is to acknowledge that we do not do what has been done, but only recall it, repeat it, lest it fall into oblivion, and so that it may benefit us. Such an application cannot be an offering, since the offering to be made presupposes that offering which was made, the application being made to men and the offering to God. It is also foolish to invent a sacrifice which is merely commemorative and representative of another sacrifice, and at the same time expiatory; for this cannot be said of any sort of expiatory sacrifice, since expiation exists only where there is a real offering. Moreover, when they insist that the Christian religion cannot be without an external sacrifice, they do not consider that in heaven, where religion will be consummated, there will be no place for any new offering. Yet the Christian religion is not without a sacrifice, namely that of Christ accomplished on the cross, whose value is eternal and infinite, so that a representation and remembrance of it, but not a repetition or a separate offering, can have a place. Finally, that the Fathers acknowledged one propitiatory sacrifice accomplished on the cross has been demonstrated by irrefutable arguments by our writers, above all Mornay, Hospinian and Albertinus. Here this should be held as the clavis intelligentiae, the key to understanding: that their sayings are to be judged not by the sound of the words but by the sense of those who speak them. For it is not because they sometimes mention Mass, altar, table, sacrifice and priests that they dreamed up the Papist Mass. Chiefly they called it a sacrifice either the offering of the elements made by the people, or the sacrifice of the body of Christ, but improperly and metonymically, giving the name of the thing signified to the sign, as Augustine most clearly explained in Epist. 23; or a spiritual sacrifice, with regard both to the action itself in the Eucharist, which is a part of the worship due to God alone, and to the invocation of the Lord from a contrite heart and sincere faith, and to the offering of oneself, by which the faithful, approaching the Lord's table, professed that they were redeemed by the blood of the Lord and were servants of the Lord, and vowed faithful service. Such were the sacrifices of the ancients. But far…

units.la: Deo debiti, est; tum invocationis Domini ex corde contrito & sincera fide, tum oblationis sui ipsius, qua fideles ad mensam Domini accedentes se sanguine Domini redemptos, servos Domini profitebantur, & fidele servitium vovebant; appellarunt. Talia veterum sacrificia fuerunt. Sed longè alio sensu sacrificantes Papistæ Christum de iis sic loquentem: Non libabo libamina eorum de sanguine; neque assumam nomina eorum in labiis meis, Psal. XVI. 4. audire coguntur. Hi enim illi sunt, qui instruunt Turmæ mensam, & implent numero crama, Esaj. LXV. 11. Ut verè in illos quadrent verba Pauli: Quæ immolant gentes dæmoniis immolant, & non Deo. Nolo autem vos consortes dæmoniorum esse, 1. Cor. X. 20.
units.tr: is the sacrifice owed to God. Then there is the invocation of the Lord from a contrite heart and sincere faith, and the offering of oneself, by which the faithful, coming to the Lord's table, professed that they were redeemed by the blood of the Lord and were servants of the Lord, and vowed faithful service. They called these sacrifices. Such were the sacrifices of the ancients. But the sacrificing Papists are forced to hear Christ speaking of these in a very different sense: I will not offer their drink offerings of blood, nor take up their names into my lips, Ps. 16.4. For these are the ones who prepare a table for that troop and fill the mixed cup for that number, Isa. 65.11. The words of Paul fit them exactly: The things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils and not to God; and I would not that you should have fellowship with devils, 1 Cor. 10.20.

units.la: CXXIII. Cadente sic sacrificio Missali, Missæ pro peccatis alienis, seu viventium, seu defunctorum, & in honorem Sanctorum institutæ; Canon Missæ; Ceremoniæ Missales; & adoratio hostiæ concidunt. Christus enim Cœnam instituit in usum eorum, qui ipsi manducant & bibunt, non eorum, qui non manducant, nec bibunt, sive viventes, sive mortui. Pro iis enim instituit, quibus dictum est: Accipite, edite, hoc enim est corpus meum, &c. Qui accipientes, edentes & bibentes sunt. Et defuncti vel beati vel damnati sunt. Neutris Cœna Dominica convenit. Non illis, quia saturati & consummati sunt. Non his, quia ex inferno liberari non possunt. Neque ullius sacrificii pro defunctis oblati Scriptura vel Veteris vel Novi Testamenti meminit. Ne Judas quidem Macchabæus pro defunctis offerri jussit, sed pro viventibus, ne iis defunctorum peccatum imputaretur, 2. Macchab. XII. 43-f. idque juxta legem, Levit. IV. 13. 14. Et gravior etiam abusus est, quòd Missam in honorem Sanctorum, & pro intercessione eorum obtinenda celebrant. Nam offerre alicui corpus Christi pro patrocinio & intercessione obtinenda, Divinus honor est, & ad latriæ cultum pertinet. At nec Divino honore, nec latriæ cultu affici debent. Neque refert, Sancto cuipiam ut primo principio & absolutè, an ut instrumento, & respectivè, latriæ cultus deferatur, quia hic non intentio offerentis, sed actus ipse spectatur; & distinctio illa hypocritica, & ad meretriciam impietatem, seu idololatriam fucandam inventa est. Canon verò Missæ & novus est, authore nescio quo, Scholastico dicto, Gregorii M. coævo, cuius: & multa à veteribus rectè dicta in pessimum sensum detorquet: & absurda non pauca continet, velut, quòd intercedens pro Papa & Regibus, illius supra hos eminentiam astruit; meritis & precibus Sanctorum defunctorum nos protegi asserit; institutionemChristi verbis ascititiis corrumpit; in eo Sacerdos peccator Deum orat, ut Filium suum acceptum habere velit, & quidem eo modo, quo dignatus est munera pueri sui justi Abel, & Abrahæ sacrificium acceptum habere; sacrificia pro defunctis stabilit, & Sacerdos sine præfatione dicit: Hoc enim est corpus meum; quasi Christi corpus suum corpus sit: & denique sub anathemate obtrusa conscientiis ejus formula, libertati Christianæ & praxi veteris Ecclesiæ repugnat. Nam olim uti quacunque forma, analogiæ fidei consentanea, licuit. Quod Liturgiarum
units.tr: CXXIII. With the Missal sacrifice thus falling, the Masses offered for the sins of others, whether of the living or of the dead, and those instituted in honour of the saints, fall too; likewise the Canon of the Mass, the Missal ceremonies, and the adoration of the host. For Christ instituted the Supper for the use of those who themselves eat and drink, not of those who neither eat nor drink, whether living or dead. For he instituted it for those to whom it was said: Take, eat; for this is my body, etc. Those who take, eat and drink. The dead, whether blessed or damned, are neither of these. The Lord's Supper suits neither group: not the dead in bliss, because they are satisfied and perfected; not the damned, because they cannot be freed from hell. Nor does Scripture, of the Old or the New Testament, mention any sacrifice offered for the dead. Not even Judas Maccabeus ordered offerings for the dead, but for the living, so that the sin of the dead would not be imputed to them, 2 Macc. 12.43 ff., and this according to the law, Lev. 4.13, 14. And there is a more serious abuse in that they celebrate the Mass in honour of the saints, and to obtain their intercession. For to offer the body of Christ to anyone in order to obtain his patronage and intercession is divine honour, and belongs to the worship of latria. But neither divine honour nor the worship of latria ought to be paid to any saint. Nor does it matter whether the worship of latria is given to a saint as a first and absolute principle, or as an instrument and in a relative sense, since here the intention of the offerer is not looked at but the act itself; and that hypocritical distinction was devised to disguise a harlot's impiety, or idolatry. The Canon of the Mass is also new, put together by I know not what author called a Scholastic, a contemporary of Gregory the Great, and it twists many things rightly said by the ancients into the worst sense, and contains not a few absurdities. For example, it claims the eminence of the Pope and kings above others while interceding for them; it asserts that we are protected by the merits and prayers of the dead saints; it corrupts the institution of Christ with added words; in it the priest, a sinner, prays God to be willing to have his Son accepted, and indeed in the way that he deigned to accept the gifts of his righteous servant Abel and the sacrifice of Abraham; it establishes sacrifices for the dead; and the priest says without a preface: For this is my body, as if his body were the body of Christ. Finally, the formula, forced upon consciences under anathema, is opposed to Christian liberty and to the practice of the ancient Church. For formerly it was permitted to use any form consistent with the analogy of faith, which the variety of liturgies proves.

units.la: {ɸ} giarum varietas comprobat. Ceremonia vero Missales, vestes & externa illa signa, quibus Missifex ex Ecclesiæ præscripto utitur, non pietatis officia, sed impietatis & idololatriæ incitabula sunt. Pleraque enim in tanta rituum multitudine, quibus tantos effectus pollicentur, fatentibus etiam adversariis, authoritate merè humana, non Christi institutione, vel Apostolorum praxi invaluerunt; & Sacerdos ante consensum altaris gradum peccata non soli Deo, sed etiam Sanctis confitetur, atque superstitiosas preculas pro mortuorum salute fundit; & pro defunctis bis canit Agnus Dei; & secreto silentio atque murmure defungitur, & peregrinæ linguæ usu mysteria occultat; & demurmuratis le Creatoris sui creatorem facit. Pleraque etiam ceremoniæ pravæ Judaismi vel gentilismi imitationi debentur; &, si quæ veterum in usu fuerunt, mirificè nunc corruptæ sunt; & si non aliter, at nimia multitudine peccant; & cùm vanissimæ atque superstitiosissimæ pleraque sint atque meram histrioniam sapiant, non verentur tamen mirificam vim & meritum solis etiam spectatoribus ex opere operato obventurum iisdem tribuere.
units.tr: Ceremonies of the Mass, the vestments and those external signs which the celebrant uses by the prescription of the Church, are not duties of piety but incitements to impiety and idolatry. For most of them, in such a great multitude of rites, to which they promise such great effects, have prevailed by purely human authority, not by the institution of Christ or the practice of the Apostles, even as the adversaries themselves confess. The priest, before the consent of the altar, confesses his sins not only to God but also to the saints, and pours out superstitious little prayers for the salvation of the dead; for the dead he sings the Agnus Dei twice; he performs the rite in secret silence and a murmur, and hides the mysteries by using a foreign tongue; and, having murmured, he makes the Creator of his Creator. Most of the ceremonies, too, are owed to the imitation of the perverse Judaism or paganism; and if any of the ancient ones were in use, they are now wonderfully corrupted; and if not otherwise, they sin by their excessive multitude. And since most of them are very vain and most superstitious, and smack of pure stage-play, they nonetheless do not hesitate to attribute to them a wonderful power and merit, to be gained ex opere operato even by the mere spectators.

units.la: CXXIV. Denique adoratio hostiæ omnem impietatem & idololatriam superat.
units.tr: CXXIV. Finally, the adoration of the host surpasses all impiety and idolatry.

units.la: Nam Tridentini Sess. XIII. cap. 5. diserte definiunt, non tantùm Christum in Sacramento adorandum esse, sed etiam Sacramento, in quo Christus præsens est, cultum latriæ exhibendum esse. Quæ verba non sine Numine in calamum Scriptoris venerunt, ne desit, ex quo idololatriæ turpissimæ manifestè convinci possint, qui verbis illam amoliuntur, at reâpse illam σφηλμοφανεγως committunt. Cùm enim aliud sit Sacramentum, aliud Christus in Sacramento, ut illi definiunt, præsens; &, à Christo si discesseris, ex adversariorum hypothesi non aliud in Eucharistiæ Sacramento sit, quàm visibilia panis & vini accidentia, rei tam tenui & levi, qua vix quicquam in omni rerum natura longius à Deo distat, Divinissimum latriæ cultum, aliàs soli Deo debitum, decernunt.
units.tr: For the Council of Trent, Session XIII, chapter 5, expressly defines that Christ is to be adored not only in the sacrament, but that "worship of latria is to be offered to the sacrament in which Christ is present." These words did not come to the writer's pen without the guidance of the Deity, so that those who try to remove idolatry by words, while in fact committing it [σφαλμοφανῶς, manifestly and erroneously], may be plainly convicted of the most shameful idolatry. For the sacrament is one thing, and Christ present in the sacrament, as they define, is another. If you take Christ away, then on the adversaries' hypothesis there is in the sacrament of the Eucharist nothing but the visible accidents of bread and wine. Yet they decree to a thing so thin and light, from which scarcely anything in all of nature is further removed from God, the most divine worship of latria, which otherwise is owed to God alone.

units.la: Nam quòd Pallavicinus Hist. Conc. Trid. p. 1. lib. XII. 7:6. ad purgandam Synodi impietatem profert, Christum in Sacramento esse dici, non ut aquam in vasculo, sed ut partem in toto, cujus pars est; frigidum nimis est, quia Tridentini Christum in Sacramento non simpliciter esse, sed præsentem adesse dixerunt, quæ verba non partis in toto, sed contenti in continente præsentiam notant. Sed Christus symbola manducare & bibere, non Sacramentum adorare jussit. Neque Apostoli Sacramentum adorarunt, Bellarmino ipso fatente, & cur id neglexerint, frivolas rationes allegante. Accubuerunt illi mensæ, non genubus flexis orationes ad hostiam fuderunt.
units.tr: As for Pallavicini (History of the Council of Trent, part 1, book XII, chapter 7), who puts forward, to clear the Synod of impiety, that "Christ is said to be in the sacrament not as water is in a vessel, but as a part is in the whole of which it is a part," this is far too feeble. For the Tridentine fathers did not say that Christ is simply in the sacrament, but that he is "present", and such words denote the presence of a container in what contains it, not of a part in a whole. But Christ bade us eat and drink the symbols, not adore the sacrament. Nor did the Apostles adore the sacrament, as Bellarmine himself admits, while alleging trivial reasons why they neglected to do so. They reclined at the table; they did not kneel and pour out prayers to a host.

units.la: Unus enim solúsque Deus adorandus est, Deut. VI. 13. Matth. IV. 10. Sive autem Sacramenti ratio formalis ponatur in solis speciebus consecratis, quod Vasquez, Soto, alii faciunt: sive in compositione ex speciebus & corpore Christi, quod Suarezio, Becano, Bellarmino placet, nunquam efficietur, ut totum Sacramentum sit solus summus Deus adorandus. Et qui Christum adorat, oportet infallibili fide statuat, Deum & Christum esse, quem adorat. At de certa fide Pontificios credere, quòd Christus in Eucharistia præsens sit, vetant domestica principia, juxta quæ, ut Transsubstantiatio fiat, conditiones ratione panis, vini, pronuntiationis consecrativæ, Sacerdotis consecrantis, exigunt, de quibus nunquam πλεοφοριοσω possunt.
units.tr: For "the Lord thy God only shalt thou worship" (Deut. 6:13; Matt. 4:10). Whether the formal nature of the sacrament is placed in the consecrated species alone, as Vasquez and Soto do, or in the compound of the species and the body of Christ, as Suarez, Becanus and Bellarmine prefer, it can never be made that the whole sacrament is to be adored as the one supreme God alone. And whoever adores Christ must hold with infallible faith that the one he adores is God and Christ. But the principles of the Papists themselves forbid them to believe with certain faith that Christ is present in the Eucharist. For according to those principles, in order that transubstantiation may take place, they require conditions concerning the nature of the bread and wine, the words of consecration, and the consecrating priest, and of these they can never be fully assured.

units.la: {a} Et adoratio hostiæ, veneratissima idololatria, cadit. idololatriam via foret. Quid enim vetaret etiam Ethnicos unctum in trivio lapidem adorantes, ita excipere, non saxum, vel statuam, sed vim Divinam in ea hospitantem Deumque ipsum in corpore isto praesentem sese adorare? Sed Christus jam in Coelo est, atque ibi, non uspiam alibi quaerendus est. Nulli enim in N.T. loco vel symbolo memoriale suum, ac Numinis velut praesentiam affixit. Accedit, quod Christus in Eucharistia praesens est ut mortuus. Corpus autem vel cadaver Christi, quod mera creatura est, Divino honore coli, religio vetat. Neque quia totus Christus Mediator adorandus est, totum etiam Sacramentum ex symbolis & Christo compositum adorandum esse, sequitur. Christus enim cum symbolis benedictis unione mere parastatica & sacramentali, cum carne hypostatica & personali conjungitur. Denique elevatio hostiae nec primaevae Ecclesiae usitata fuit, sed seculo demum sexto apud Graecos usu recepta est, non ut hostia sic elevata a plebe adoraretur, sed ut Christi in cruce elevatio, & in Coelum ascensio adumbraretur. Apud Latinos vero non ante seculum XII. elevari coepta est adorationis causa, quod fusissime Cl. Daillaeus de Cult. Relig. lib. III. 20. 21. &c. demonstravit. Ineptissime vero ritus ille ex Divino jure arcessitur; vocatis ad patrocinium erroris verbis illis Davidis: Erit pugillus frumenti in terra in vertice montium, Psal. LXXII. 16. Nihil ibi de Eucharistia, ad quam neoterici locum detorserunt, sed de fertilitate summa verbi Dei, & credentium in Ecclesia. Neque poni in vertice montium elevationem necessario notat. Nec sacrificia olim super caput Sacerdotum elevata sunt. Ut vero elevarentur praeceptum erat. At ut hostia elevetur, & quidem adorationis gratia praeceptum nuspiam est.
units.tr: {a} And the adoration of the host, the most venerated idolatry, falls. Indeed, it would be a short road to idolatry. For what would prevent even the heathens, adoring an anointed stone at a crossroads, from taking it in this way: that they adore not the stone or the statue, but the divine power dwelling in it, and God himself present in that body? But Christ is now in heaven, and there he is to be sought, not anywhere else. For in no place or symbol of the New Testament has he attached his memorial, or as it were the presence of the Deity. Moreover, Christ is present in the Eucharist as dead. But religion forbids the body or corpse of Christ, which is a mere creature, to be worshipped with divine honour.
