Nor does it follow, because the whole Christ as Mediator is to be adored, that the whole sacrament, composed of the symbols and Christ, is to be adored. For Christ is joined to the blessed symbols by a union that is merely parastatic and sacramental, but to his hypostatic and personal flesh by a union of another kind. Finally, the elevation of the host was not in use in the primitive Church. It was first received among the Greeks in the sixth century, not so that the host thus raised should be adored by the people, but so that the lifting up of Christ on the cross and his ascension into heaven might be represented. Among the Latins it did not begin to be elevated for the sake of adoration before the twelfth century, as the distinguished Daillé has demonstrated at great length (On the Cult of Religious Worship, book III, chapters 20 and 21, etc.). But that rite is most absurdly derived from divine law, the words of David being called in to support the error: "There shall be an handful of corn in the earth upon the top of the mountains" (Ps. 72:16). Nothing there concerns the Eucharist, to which the moderns have twisted the place, but the abundant fertility of the word of God and of believers in the Church. Nor does "set upon the top of the mountains" necessarily denote elevation. Nor were sacrifices formerly lifted up above the heads of priests. Indeed, it was commanded that they be lifted up; but that the host be raised, and indeed for the sake of adoration, is commanded nowhere.

units.la: CXXVI. Alia facies erroris est, quando pro Transsubstantiatione Κυνωσια, seu ut alii loquuntur Διαστασια, Κυνωπαξις, Consubstantiatio adoptatur.
units.tr: CXXVI. Another form of error is when, instead of transubstantiation, what is adopted is Synousia [συνουσία], or as others put it Diastasis [διάστασις], Synopaxis [συνπάξις], that is, consubstantiation.

units.la: Quae quidem Transsubstantiatione antiquior, a Joh. Damasceno, Paschasio, Rutperto Tuitiense olim asserta; ac post introductam Transsubstantiationem, ad incommoda ejus evitanda, per Scholasticos quosdam, inprimis Cardinalem Cameracensem rursus renovata, tandem Luthero ejusque assecl is placuit, & tristi atque funesto illi Ecclesiarum divortio ansam dedit. Sentiunt enim illi, per Τουτο Hoc duas res simul praesentes, visibilem panem & invisibile Christi corpus monstrari; & occultae atque invisibili illi duarum substantiarum coexistentiae asserendae, tres vocu-las in, cum & sub pane addunt. Cumque corpus Christi ita cum pane conjungi arbitrantur, corporis Christi participes fieri omnes, qui panem manducant, adeoque etiam indignos & infideles, nulli dubitant. Sed haec opinio, dum vitat vitia, in contraria currit. Duo enim corpora ponit in eodem loco, & a verbis institutionis longissime discedit. Cum enim Dominus dixerit: Hoc, seu hic panis, quem Christus discipulos accipere & comedere jussit, est corpus meum; vel, corpus in hoc pane invisibiliter latens est corpus meum. Adde, quod ex unione hypostatica perperam intellecta ubiquitatem corporis Christi derivant. Absurda igitur
units.tr: This view is older than transubstantiation. It was formerly asserted by John of Damascus, Paschasius and Rupert of Deutz, and after transubstantiation was introduced, it was renewed again by certain Scholastics, above all the Cardinal of Cambrai, in order to avoid its drawbacks. At last it pleased Luther and his followers, and gave occasion for that sad and deadly division of the churches. For they hold that by the word "This" two things are shown at once, which are present together: the visible bread and the invisible body of Christ. And in order to assert that hidden and invisible coexistence of the two substances, they add three little words: in, with and under the bread. And since they think that the body of Christ is so joined with the bread, they do not hesitate to say that all who eat the bread become partakers of the body of Christ, and so also the unworthy and unbelieving. But this opinion, while it avoids those faults, runs into the opposite ones. For it places two bodies in the same place, and departs very far from the words of institution. For when the Lord said "This", that is, this bread, which Christ bade the disciples take and eat, "is my body", the meaning is "the body hidden invisibly in this bread is my body." Add to this that from a wrongly understood hypostatic union they derive the ubiquity of Christ's body. Absurd, therefore,

units.la: Pontificiae de conversione unius substantiae in aliam, & subsistentiae accidentium sine subjecto vitantes, alia absurda reponunt, nempe coexistentiam duorum corporum, unius visibilis, alterius invisibilis, eodem in loco, & ubiquitatem carnis Christi. Et corpus etiam hoc Christi invisibile cum variis fidei articulis, praesertim de humana Christi natura ex Maria Virgine naturae nostrae per omnia, excepto peccato, simili, nec non praesenti ejus statu atque gloria conciliari nequit; atque insuper tum Sacramentorum analogiae, quae rem significatam non substantialiter continent, sed obsignant; uti quidem nec in Baptismo sanguis Christi in, cum & sub aqua continetur; cum tamen Baptismus cum Coena analogice conveniat non tantum ratione ενεργειας, uti illi pertendunt, sed etiam ratione σεσαν, quae non in orali manducatione, sed obsignatione rei promissae utrobique consistit: tum primâ Christi Coenâ, in qua ipse Christus accubuit, & panem benedictum & fractum, non corpus mortuum, vel sanguinem effusum distribuit: tum ipsis verbis Coenae, manifeste adversantur. Nam hoc, id est, panis & corpus conjuncta, non est corpus Christi, quia panis non venit in partem corporis Christi. Neque profecto propria, sed insolenter impropria erit propositio, si per Hoc, in, cum & sub hoc; per Est, continetur vel includitur: per corpus meum, aliquid quod nec quantum, nec visibile, nec locale, nec omnino tale, quale Christus ex utero Beatae Virginis attulit, intelligatur. Cumque in Eucharistia corpus Christi ut datum, sanguis ut fusus fidei offerantur, non possunt illa, ceu talia, in, cum & sub pane & vino contineri; quia corpus & sanguis Christi non amplius separantur, frangun-tur, vel effunduntur. Nam quod simul physice unita at hyperphysice separata dicunt, non magis a contradictione liberari potest; quam si quis dicat, ferrum hyperphysice actu e fundo ascendere, & in superficie aquae natare, 2. Reg. VI. 6. & simul eodem actu & tempore ad fundum a superficie descendere, & in fundo quiescere. Simul actu corpus a sanguine separari & non separari, contradictoria ejusmodi sunt, ut nulla fides illa conciliare possit.
units.tr: The Papists, avoiding the absurdity of the conversion of one substance into another and of accidents subsisting without a subject, put forward other absurdities in their place: namely, the coexistence of two bodies, one visible and the other invisible, in the same place, and the ubiquity of the flesh of Christ. Nor can this invisible body of Christ be reconciled with the various articles of faith, especially with the true human nature of Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, like ours in all things except sin, nor with his present state and glory. Moreover, it is at odds with the analogy of the sacraments, which do not contain the thing signified substantially but seal it. For in Baptism, indeed, the blood of Christ is not contained in, with and under the water. Yet Baptism agrees analogously with the Supper, not only in respect of the [energeias, action] as they contend, but also in respect of the [sphragis, seal], which consists not in oral eating but in the sealing of the promised thing in both. They are also plainly opposed to the first Supper of Christ, at which Christ himself reclined and distributed bread blessed and broken, not a dead body or blood poured out. And they are opposed to the very words of the Supper. For "this, that is", bread and body joined together, is not the body of Christ, because bread does not come into the part of the body of Christ. Nor indeed will the proposition be proper, but unusually improper, if by "This" we understand "in, with and under this"; by "is", "is contained or included"; and by "my body", something that is neither quantitative, nor visible, nor local, nor in any way such as Christ brought from the womb of the Blessed Virgin. And since in the Eucharist the body of Christ is offered as given, and the blood as poured out, for faith, they cannot be contained as such "in, with and under bread and wine", because the body and blood of Christ are no longer separated, broken or poured out. For what they say, that things are physically united yet hyperphysically separated, cannot be freed from contradiction any more than if someone said that iron rises hyperphysically from the bottom in act and floats on the surface of the water (2 Kings 6:6), and at the same moment and in the same act descends from the surface to the bottom and rests on the bottom. To be actually separated from the blood and not separated at the same time are contradictories of such a kind that no faith can reconcile them.

units.la: CXXVII. Praesentiam corporalem Christi in Coena supra, asserta spirituali & sacramentali, refutavimus. Sublata illa etiam oralis manducatio tollitur. Revera enim qualis cibus & potus in Eucharistia est; talis edendi ac bibendi modus est.
units.tr: CXXVII. We have refuted the corporeal presence of Christ in the Supper, which we asserted above to be spiritual and sacramental. With that removed, oral eating is also removed. For the manner of eating and drinking is of the same kind as the food and drink in the Eucharist really are.

units.la: Corpus autem Christi cibus non corporalis, sed spiritualis; & sanguis ejus potus non corporalis, sed spiritualis est. Nam illa & animae, non corporis nutrimentum sunt; Johann. VI. & instrumento non oris corporis, Matth. XV. 17. I. Cor. VI. 13. sed oris fidei, Joh. VI. 35. 47-54. sumuntur; & non intra ventrem corporis, utpote cui βρωμα & εσκα corporales destinantur; I. Cor. VI. 13. sed intra animam fidelem, & cor, in quo solo Christus per fidem habitat, Ephes. III. 17. recipiuntur; & remissionem peccatorum, unionem cum Christo, gloriosam resurrectionem & vitam aeternam operantur, Joh. VI. 47. 48. quae corporalis cibus nullo modo operari potest. Nam oralis perceptio corporis & sanguinis Christi & impossibilis & inutilis est. Impossibilis, quia Chri
units.tr: The body of Christ is not bodily food but spiritual food, and his blood is not bodily drink but spiritual drink. For these are nourishment of the soul, not of the body (John VI.), and they are received not by the instrument of the bodily mouth (Matth. XV. 17; I Cor. VI. 13) but by the mouth of faith (John VI. 35, 47-54). They are not received within the belly of the body, for which food [βρῶμα] and bodily meat [ἔσκα] are appointed (I Cor. VI. 13), but within the faithful soul and the heart, in which alone Christ dwells through faith (Ephes. III. 17). They work the remission of sins, union with Christ, glorious resurrection and eternal life (John VI. 47, 48), which bodily food can in no way work. For oral reception of the body and blood of Christ is both impossible and useless. Impossible, because Chri[st]

units.la: Manducatio corporis & potus sanguinis Christi in Coena non oralis, sed spiritualis est. Christus corpus suum in Cœlum evexit. Quid si igitur spectaveritis Filium hominis ascendentem eò, ubi erat prius, Joh. VI. 62. In Cœlum igitur evectum corpus Christi in terra corporaliter existere & manducari non potest. Nam quòd Christum mysterio ascensionis suæ in Cœlum fidem mysterio manducationis carnis, & bibitionis sanguinis sui in terra, fecisse regerunt, nil soliditatis habet. Probavit enim Christus argumento ascensionis suæ in Cœlum non manducationem corporalem vel oralem, sed sensum genuinum verborum suorum de carne sua manducanda, & sanguine bibendo, quòd nimirum spiritualis illa, non corporalis sit. Statim enim subjicit: Spiritus est, qui vivificat, v. 63. q. d. Spiritus S. efficiens in vobis fidem, ut credatis in Christum carne sua data & sanguine fuso remissionem peccatorum & vitam vobis promeriturum, non caro mea oraliter manducata, vos vivificabit. Alias enim localis Christi in Cœlum ascensio haud creditu difficilior est, quàm ipsa manducatio carnis & bibitio sanguinis Christi, ut per illam huic fidem Christus facere voluerit. Nam & ante Christum alii corporibus suis in Cœlum ascenderunt; sed aliorum tamen caro manducata non est, nec ut manducaretur, præceptum est. Capernaitis certè tam absurda Christi in Cœlum ascensio, quàm manducatio carnis ejus videri non potuit, quia hanc flagitium continere suspicabantur, illam verò sine flagitio contingere posse, facilè, ut crederent, animum induxerunt. Inutilis verò etiam est, teste ipso Christo, statim dicente: Caro mea (oraliter, Capernaitice manducata) nihil prodest. Verba, quæ ego loquor vobis, Spiritus & vita sunt, v. 63. Non enim ibi Christus de cogitationibus crassis & carnalibus oppositè ad carnem, quatenus illa oraliter manducatur, loquitur, quia ipsæ de carne oraliter manducanda cogitationes Capernaitarum crassæ & carnales fuerunt. Et si Capernaitica carnis Christi manducatio à Christo inutilis declaratur, vel manducatio carnis Christi, quam sacramentalem illi appellant, improprie dicta manducatio erit; vel si proprie dicta est, æquè inutilis atque Capernaitica illa erit. Nam manducatio proprie dicta & oralis à Capernaitica realiter non differt. Neque profectò alias Christus supersedisset distinguere modos manducationis oralis, quasi alia sit corporis Christi lacerati & Capernaitica, alia corporis Christi integri & indivisibilis, quæ sacramentalis & spiritualis. Inprimis cùm posterior illa non minùs, si non magis, absurda videri posset, quàm prior, quia corpus humanum indivisibile & spirituale omnem rationis captum superat: ut corporis humani laceratio cruda equidem & crudelis videri posset, at rationis captum minimè superat. Nam & Cannibales, aliósque dari, nemini fere ignotum est.
units.tr: The eating of the body and the drinking of the blood of Christ in the Supper is not oral but spiritual. Christ has raised his body into heaven. What then if you should see the Son of man ascending thither, where he was before? (John VI. 62). Therefore a body taken up into heaven cannot exist and be eaten bodily on earth. As for their claim that Christ, by the mystery of his ascension into heaven, has made faith the mystery of eating his flesh and drinking his blood on earth, this has no solidity. For by the argument of his ascension into heaven Christ proved not bodily or oral eating but the true sense of his words about eating his flesh and drinking his blood, namely that it is spiritual and not bodily. For he immediately adds: It is the Spirit that quickens (v. 63), as if to say: the Holy Spirit, working faith in you, so that you believe in Christ, who gave his flesh and shed his blood to merit for you the remission of sins and life, quickens you, not my flesh eaten orally. For otherwise the local ascension of Christ into heaven is no harder to believe than the very eating of Christ's flesh and drinking of his blood, by which Christ wished to produce faith in him. For before Christ others also ascended into heaven in their bodies, yet their flesh was not eaten, nor was it commanded that it be eaten. Certainly the Capernaites could not regard his ascension into heaven as absurd in the way they regarded the eating of his flesh; for they suspected the latter contained a crime, while they readily persuaded themselves that the former could happen without crime. Moreover it is useless, as Christ himself testifies, immediately saying: My flesh (eaten orally, in the Capernaite manner) profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit and life (v. 63). For Christ is not there speaking against crass and carnal thoughts about the flesh insofar as it is eaten orally, since the Capernaites' own thoughts about eating the flesh orally were crass and carnal. And if the Capernaitic eating of Christ's flesh is declared useless by Christ, then either the eating of Christ's flesh, which they call sacramental, will be an eating improperly so called, or, if it is properly so called, it will be just as useless as the Capernaitic eating. For proper and oral eating does not really differ from the Capernaitic. Nor, certainly, would Christ otherwise have bothered to distinguish modes of oral eating, as if the eating of Christ's torn body is one thing and Capernaitic, while the eating of Christ's whole and indivisible body, which is sacramental and spiritual, is another. This is especially so since the latter could appear no less, if not more, absurd than the former, because a human body that is indivisible and spiritual surpasses every grasp of reason; whereas the laceration of a human body may indeed seem raw and cruel, yet it does not at all surpass the grasp of reason. For that there are cannibals, and others like them, is known to almost everyone.

units.la: CXXVIII.
units.tr: CXXVIII.

units.la: Cùm ergo nec Christi corpus in, cum & sub substantia panis continea-tur, nec manducatio ejus oralis sit, corpus & sanguinem ejus ab infidelibus & indignis, pa-nem manducantibus non percipi, ultro conse-quitur. Non enim aliud illi, quàm panem manducant, & vinum bibunt, nuda itaque symbola, non rem symbolis signatam percipientes. Ipsa enim symbola indignè percipi pos-sunt, 1. Cor. XI. 29. At res signatas indignè sumi, nusquam profectò reperitur. Nemo enim indignè in Christum credit. Atqui manducare carnem Christi, & bibere ejus sanguinem, est in Christum pro nobis mortuum credere. Qui ad me venit, non esuriet: & qui in me credit, non sitiet unquam, Joh. VI. 35. Amen dico vobis, qui in me credit, habet vitam æternam, v. 47. Quibus verbis, quæ de manducatione carnis, & bibitione sanguinis dixerat, interpretatur. Tum qui Christi carnem manducat, & sanguinem ejus bibit, habet vitam æternam & resuscitabit eum Christus in novissimo die, ibid. v. 54. & in me manet, & ego in ipso, v. 56. Atqui nemo infidelis habet vitam æternam, vel in novissimo die resuscitatur, vel in Christo manet. Non enim infideles, quà tales, Christi membra sunt. Inanis igitur est salutarem inter & non salutarem manducationem corporis & sanguinis Christi, distinctio quia juxta Christi sententiam, omnis manducatio carnis & bibitio sanguinis Christi salutaris, nulla non salutaris est. Præterea quib nihil Evangelium promittit, iis nihil sacramenta obsignant; quia Sacramenta Evangelii, seu Novi Testamenti, quod diploma gratiæ est, sigilla sunt. Atqui infidelibus nihil Evangelium promittit, quia promissiones ejus omnes conditionem fidei implicitam habent, & infidelibus minæ iræ Dei & damnationis proponuntur, Joh. III. 16. Marc. XVI. 16. Denique gloriosissimo corpore Christi indignum est, ut ore impuro mancipiorum Sathanæ hauriatur & polluatur. Licet enim caro Christi carni sceleratissimorum etiam hominum ὁμοούσιος sit, quatenus specie eadem est; tamen Christus naturam humanam numero diversam, & talem quidem assumpsit, quæ à peccatoribus planè separata est, Hebr. VII. 26.
units.tr: Since, then, the body of Christ is contained neither in, with, nor under the substance of the bread, and his eating is not oral, it follows of its own accord that his body and blood are not received by unbelievers and the unworthy who eat the bread. For such people eat only bread and drink only wine, thus receiving only bare symbols and not the thing signified by the symbols. For the symbols themselves can be received unworthily (I Cor. XI. 29), but that the things signified are received unworthily is nowhere found. For no one believes unworthily in Christ. Yet to eat the flesh of Christ and to drink his blood is to believe in Christ who died for us. He who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst (John VI. 35). Verily I say to you, he who believes in me has eternal life (v. 47). By these words he interprets what he had said about eating the flesh and drinking the blood. Then: he who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and Christ will raise him up on the last day (ibid. v. 54), and he abides in me, and I in him (v. 56). Yet no unbeliever has eternal life, or is raised up on the last day, or abides in Christ. For unbelievers, as such, are not members of Christ. Therefore the distinction between a saving and a non-saving eating of the body and blood of Christ is empty, since according to the sentence of Christ every eating of the flesh and drinking of the blood of Christ is saving, and none is non-saving. Moreover, to those to whom the Gospel promises nothing, the sacraments seal nothing; for the sacraments of the Gospel, or of the New Testament, which is the diploma of grace, are seals. Yet the Gospel promises nothing to unbelievers, because all its promises have faith implicitly as a condition, and to unbelievers are set forth the threats of God's wrath and damnation (John III. 16; Mark XVI. 16). Finally, it is unworthy of the most glorious body of Christ to be swallowed up and polluted by the impure mouths of the servants of Satan. For although the flesh of Christ is consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] with the flesh of even the most wicked men, insofar as it is of the same species, yet Christ assumed a human nature numerically different, and indeed one that is entirely separated from sinners (Hebr. VII. 26).

units.la: CXXIX.
units.tr: CXXIX.

units.la: Nil adversantium rationes momenti habent. Nam quòd manducationem in Eucharistia non spiritualem, sed oralem, adeóque ipsum etiam instrumentum manducationis non spirituale, sed orale esse eo argumento pertendunt, quia fit distinctis actibus, etiam ab indignis, non tantùm ad salutem, verùm etiam interdum ad damnationem, fallax est. In S. enim Cœna non est equidem manducatio spiritualis signorum, panis & vini: at est rei signatæ, corporis & sanguinis Domini. Signa distinctis actibus à fidelibus ad salutem, & ab infidelibus ad damnnationem percipiuntur. Sed res signata uno actu fidei, qui modò manducatio, modò bibitio appellatur, à solis fidelibus, & ad salutem tantùm percipitur. Neque proin quo instrumento panis & vinum percipiuntur, eodem corpus & sanguis Christi percipiuntur. Nam id ex professo Christus Joh. VI. refutavit. Non enim sic panis & vinum cum corpore & sanguine Christi unitur, ut hæc sub illis contineantur: neque unio Sacramentalis, quæ καταχρηστικῶς appellatur, in hujusmodi signi & signati conjunctione consistit. Ac licèt Christus simpliciter dixerit: Edite, hoc est corpus meum, tamen non eodem instrumento edi corpus, quo panem jussit. Imò panem edi non in alimentum, corporis nostri, sed in Sacramentum corporis sui jussit. Non adhibuit equidem Christus, manducare jubens, distinctionem manducationis corporalis & spiritualis,
units.tr: The arguments of our opponents carry no weight. They contend that the eating in the Eucharist is oral and not spiritual, and that the instrument of eating is therefore also oral and not spiritual, because it is done by distinct acts, and even by the unworthy, who eat not only to salvation but sometimes to damnation. This argument is fallacious. In the Holy Supper there is indeed no spiritual eating of the signs, the bread and wine, but there is eating of the thing signified, the body and blood of the Lord. The signs are received by distinct acts: by the faithful to salvation, and by unbelievers to damnation. But the thing signified is received by one act of faith, which is called now eating, now drinking, and it is received only by the faithful and only to salvation. Therefore the body and blood of Christ are not received by the same instrument by which the bread and wine are received. For Christ expressly refuted this in John 6. The bread and wine are not so joined with the body and blood of Christ that these are contained under them, nor does the sacramental union, which is called catachrestically, consist in such a conjunction of sign and thing signified. And although Christ simply said, Eat, this is my body, the body was not to be eaten by the same instrument by which he bade them take the bread. Indeed he bade them eat the bread not as nourishment for our body but as a sacrament of his body. Christ, in bidding them eat, did not use the distinction between corporal and spiritual eating,

units.la: Proin infideles & indigni corporis & sanguinis Christi non fiunt participes. ritualis, quia de solo pane locutus est, quod dissentientium ipsorum causam non parum laedit. Si enim de una eademque manducatione citra omnem distinctionem locutus est, equidem non praecepit, ut panis physicè, corpus sub pane hyperphysicè comederetur. Sed manducationem corporis Christi, quae mandatur ut actio formalis in Coena, fieri ad memoriam; at manducationem spiritualem non fieri ad memoriam, objiciunt. Verùm non quaevis manducatio corporis Christi praecepta fit ad memoriam, sed sola sacramentalis. At praeter eam etiam spiritualem praecipi, neque tamen ad memoriam eam fieri, ipsimet fatentur. Viderint ergo ipsi, quo jure inter actiones Coenae formales referant tantùm externas, qui tamen Sacramentum proprie dictum pro composito ex re terrestri & coelesti habent. Cur ergo non etiam actiones internae & spirituales à Christo praeceptae inter formales referantur? Quos porro oralis manducationis usus exaggerant, cujusmodi sunt consolatio conjunctionis nostrae cum Christo, apprehensionis Dei & hominis, quae ad conjunctionem mutuam Christi & nostri requiratur; sanctificationis, ablutionis & applicationis, & resurrectionis, illi omnes sine orali manducatione, per solam sacramentalem & spiritualem, constant. Nam nec unio cum Christo corporalis est, quia alias etiam Judas & carnifices illa potiti essent, & illa impossibilis aequè atque inutilis, uti vidimus, est: & Christum ἀνθρώπων sola fide apprehendimus: & corda nostra per solam etiam fidem, & Christi spiritualem in nobis inhabitationem sanctificantur: & Redemptor in verbo & Sacramentis offertur non ore corporis, sed fidei apprehendendus & applicandus: & beatam corporibus nostris resurrectionem caro Christi vivifica pro mundi vita data, & fide excepta confert. Non caruerunt etiam Patres V. T. omnium horum consolatione; qui tamen corporali Christi manducatione procul omni dubio caruerunt. Et in Novo Testamento oralem manducationem infidelibus consolationem ejusmodi nullam afferre, ipsimet οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας fatentur. Denique neque ideo, quia indignè manducantes fiunt rei corporis Christi, & non dijudicant, seu discernunt corpus Christi, 1. Cor. XI. 27.29. corpus Christi oraliter comedi, & sanguinem ejus oraliter bibi ab indignis & infidelibus etiam, sequitur. Nam Apostolus non corpus Christi, sed τὸν ἄρτον τοῦτον panem hunc eos ἀναξίως indignè manducare, & non sanguinem, sed τὸ ποτήριον calicem Domini indignè bibere v. 27. dicit. Et reum fieri corporis & sanguinis Christi, atque simul illud accipere, contraria sunt. Nam qui reus fit, ideo reus fit, quia non curat id habere, quod habere oportet, & id contemnit, aut putat, se id habere, quod non habet, cùm non ostendat se talem, qualem esse dignum est eum, qui habet. Imò rei possunt esse mortis Christi, qui tamen non habent communionem mortis ejus; sicut Christum sibi, in necem suam, crucifigunt, qui animum habent crucifigendi eum, & in illorum societatem veniunt, & iterum crucifigunt, quia quoad animum & voluntatem suam non desinunt crucifigere crucifixum. Et infideles rei corporis & sanguinis Domini etiam extra Coenam sunt. Sunt autem qui indignè sic panem manducant, & calicem bibunt, rei corporis & sanguinis Domini, quia manducantes & bibentes illi, qui Christo non sunt digni, vel non cum illa decentia & emendatione, quae Christo digna est, in corpus & sanguinem Christi manifestò peccant. Contemnunt enim vocationem coelestem, qua panis corpus suum, & vinum sanguinem suum appellavit. Propter quam coelestem vocationem non amplius panem & vinum ut panem & vinum, sed ut corpus & sanguinem Domini, & ipsum Dominum, cujus μελογίω nobis vendicamus & asserimus, quoties de pane manducamus, considerare oportet. Propter quam causam veteres φρικτὰ μυστήρια tremenda mysteria appellarunt. Nihil enim φρικλότερον tremendum magis est, quam cum mala conscientia ad Deum accedere, & se servum, imò filium ejus coram ipso, & vi, non pretio, ablatis symbolis ejus, jactare. Non igitur perceptio corporis Christi, sed partim contemptus Christi, partim signi ipsius profanatio & abusus causa illius reatus est. Neque ideo, quia indignè manducantes non dijudicant, seu discernunt corpus Domini, corpus Domini indignè manducare censendi sunt; quia corpus Domini indignè manducari non potest; sed non distinguunt panem, corporis Christi Sacramentum, à pane communi, neque majori reverentia & religione illum, quàm hunc tractant. Vocat equidem Apostolus id, quod discernendum est corpus Domini, sed sacramentaliter & metonymicè. Qui sic indignè edit, quod datum est ad recordationem Domini, & ad annuntiationem mortis ejus, is non recordatur Domini, non annuntiat mortem ejus cum glorificatione ejus; atque ita nec panem, nec corpus Domini, vel ipsum Dominum distinguit, quasi Dominum gloriae, rupem salutis, contemnere, probris afficere, crucifigere non magis piaculare sit, quàm nebulonem, vel vulgarem hominem contemnere & occidere, quod S. Paulus τὸ αἷμα τῆς Διαθήκης κοινὸν ἡγήσατο sanguinem Testamenti profanum ducere, Hebr. X. 29. vocat. Ita Deus Sacerdotes in altari Dei cibum inquinatum, aegrum, caecum, claudum offerentes, mensam Jehovae contemptibilem dicere, atque ea re nomen Domini contemnere, Mal. I. 7.8.9. queritur. Similiter is, qui ad mensam Domini indignè accedit, is mensam Domini atque symbola ejus contemnit, & ipsum Dominum, & nomen ejus, à quo se cognominat, contemnit; & ad Christum altare nostrum, accedit, ut ei caecum, claudum & aegrum offerat. Licèt enim in Coena hoc agamus, ut de communione corporis & sanguinis Christi certiores reddamur, tamen in eadem etiam Deo aliquid offerimus, nempe recordationem Christi in corde, & annuntiationem mortis ejus in ore, quod decantatum illud sacrificium laudis, Psal. L. 14.23. Hebr. XIII. 15. est.
units.tr: Therefore unbelievers and the unworthy do not become partakers of the body and blood of Christ: ritual, because he spoke only of bread, which does no small harm to the cause of these dissenters themselves. For if he spoke of one and the same eating without any distinction, he did not command that bread be eaten physically and the body under the bread be eaten hyperphysically. But they object that the eating of the body of Christ, which is commanded as a formal action in the Supper, is to be done in remembrance, whereas spiritual eating is not done in remembrance. Yet not every eating of the body of Christ is commanded to be done in remembrance, but only the sacramental eating. They themselves admit that, besides this, spiritual eating is also commanded, and yet it is not done in remembrance. Let them see for themselves by what right they count among the formal actions of the Supper only the external ones, although they hold that the sacrament properly so called is composed of an earthly and a heavenly thing. Why then are the internal and spiritual actions commanded by Christ not also counted among the formal ones? Moreover, those who magnify the oral use of eating, such as the comfort of our conjunction with Christ, the apprehension of God and of man which is required for the mutual conjunction of Christ and us, sanctification, cleansing and application, and resurrection, all of these subsist without oral eating, through sacramental and spiritual eating alone. For the union with Christ is not corporal, since otherwise Judas and the executioners would have possessed it, and such a union is as impossible as it is useless, as we have seen. We apprehend Christ, the Man, by faith alone; our hearts are sanctified by faith alone and by Christ's spiritual indwelling in us; the Redeemer is offered in the Word and the sacraments to be apprehended and applied not by the mouth of the body but by faith; and the life-giving flesh of Christ, given for the life of the world, confers the blessed resurrection of our bodies and is received by faith. The Fathers of the Old Testament also did not lack all this comfort, and yet without doubt they lacked the corporal eating of Christ. Even our opponents themselves admit that in the New Testament oral eating brings no such comfort to unbelievers. Finally, it does not follow that because those who eat unworthily become guilty of the body of Christ, and do not discern the body of Christ, 1 Cor. 11.27, 29, the body of Christ is eaten orally, and his blood is drunk orally, by the unworthy and even by unbelievers. For the Apostle does not say that they eat the body of Christ unworthily, but that they eat this bread (τὸν ἄρτον τοῦτον) unworthily, and not that they drink the blood, but that they drink the cup of the Lord unworthily, v. 27. Also, to be guilty of the body and blood of Christ and at the same time to receive it are contrary things. For whoever is guilty is guilty because he does not care to have what he ought to have, and despises it, or thinks he has what he does not have, since he does not show himself such as he ought to be who has it. Indeed, people may be guilty of the death of Christ who nevertheless have no fellowship in his death; just as those who have the purpose of crucifying him, and join themselves to those who do so, crucify Christ to their own destruction, and crucify him again, because in their mind and will they do not cease to crucify the crucified. Unbelievers are also guilty of the body and blood of the Lord outside the Supper. But there are those who eat this bread and drink this cup unworthily, guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, because those who eat and drink who are not worthy of Christ, or who do not do so with that reverence and amendment of life which is worthy of Christ, manifestly sin against the body and blood of Christ. For they despise the heavenly calling, by which he called the bread his body and the wine his blood. On account of this heavenly calling, whenever we eat of the bread, we must consider it no longer as bread and wine but as the body and blood of the Lord, and the Lord himself, whose benefits we claim and assert for ourselves. For this reason the ancients called them tremendous mysteries (φρικτὰ μυστήρια). For nothing is more tremendous than to approach God with an evil conscience, and to boast of being his servant, or rather his son, in his presence, while having seized his tokens by force and not bought them. Therefore it is not the reception of the body of Christ, but partly contempt of Christ and partly the profanation and abuse of the sign itself, that is the cause of this guilt. Nor, because those who eat unworthily do not discern, that is, do not discern the body of the Lord, are they to be judged as eating the body of the Lord unworthily, since the body of the Lord cannot be eaten unworthily; rather, they do not distinguish the bread, the sacrament of the body of Christ, from common bread, nor do they treat it with greater reverence and devotion than ordinary bread. The Apostle indeed calls that which must be discerned the body of the Lord, but sacramentally and metonymically. Whoever eats unworthily that which is given for the remembrance of the Lord and for the proclamation of his death does not remember the Lord, does not proclaim his death with glorification of him; and thus he distinguishes neither the bread nor the body of the Lord, nor the Lord himself, as the Lord of glory, the rock of salvation. To despise, reproach or crucify him is no more sinful than to despise and kill a scoundrel or a common man. This is what St. Paul calls to count the blood of the covenant a common thing, Heb. 10.29. So God complains that the priests who offer on the altar of God polluted, sick, blind and lame food call the table of Jehovah contemptible, and by that act despise the name of the Lord, Mal. 1.7, 8, 9. Similarly, whoever comes unworthily to the table of the Lord despises the table of the Lord and its tokens, and despises the Lord himself and his name, from which he takes his own name, and comes to Christ's altar to offer him the blind, the lame and the sick. For although in the Supper we do this so that we may be assured of the communion of the body and blood of Christ, yet in the same Supper we also offer something to God, namely the remembrance of Christ in the heart and the proclamation of his death with the mouth, which is that well-known sacrifice of praise, Ps. 50.14, 23; Heb. 13.15.

units.la: CXXX. Hactenus ergo in argumento hoc à Lutheranis dissensum profitemur, sed propter eum dissensum, discordiam non alimus. Aliud enim dissensus, aliud discordia est: sicut aliud est consensus, aliud concordia. Haec enim charitate, pace & sacrorum communione constat: illa opinionum consonantia. Quae ubi per-
units.tr: CXXX. Thus far we profess dissent from the Lutherans on this question, but on account of that dissent we do not foster discord. For dissent is one thing and discord another, just as agreement is one thing and concord another. Concord consists in charity, peace and communion in sacred things; agreement is a harmony of opinions. Where this agreement is found

units.la: perfecta & numeris omnibus absoluta invenitur, nullus ad discordiam aditus, nisi consensione prius labefactata, patet. Perfecta vero in opinionibus omnibus apud pios etiam consensio in militante Ecclesia optanda potius, quam sperauda est. Sed cum imperfecta etiam judiciorum consensione vera, & pro vitae hujus modulo perfecta concordia esse potest. Quotquot perfecti sumus, hoc sentiamus. Et si quid aliter sentitis, & hoc Deus vobis revelabit. Tantum, ad quod pervenimus eadem regula incedamus, Phil. III. 15. 16. Non pauca vero sunt, in quibus Evangelici circa Sacramentum Coenae Domini consentiunt, quae numero capitum triginta & unius Forbesius Instruct. Hist. Theol. lib. XIV. 7. constrinxit. Quicquid in eo salutare est, & ad consolationem conscientiae, ex institutione Divina, pertinet, id omne pars utraque sartum tectumque retinet. Controversa autem de orali manducatione corporis & sanguinis Christi, eaque fidelibus & infidelibus communi, quaestio, sive negata, sive affirmata, salutis fundamentum non evertit, quia utrinque in confesso est, in utriusque partis Ecclesiis, non obstante illo dissensu, usum Sacramenti, secundum Christi institutionem, sine substantialium additione vel detractione, integrum & illibatum manere. Esto autem falsa sententia, quae oralem manducationem & corporalem praesentiam negat; non ideo non celebrabimus Eucharistiam ex institutione Christi, quia praesentia corporis Christi in Eucharistia non ab hominum opera, nec a persuasione & fide communicantium, sed, utcunque verbis negata, a veritate Christi pendet, qui cum id, quod in Eucharistia datur, corpus suum esse dixerit, nobis, quantumvis corporalem praesentiam non credentibus, faciet esse corpus suum. Neque obstat, quod promissio ea est, & promissio, nisi fide suscepta, non impletur. Duo enim genera promissionum sunt; aliud credentibus solis, aliud credentibus & infidelibus factarum. Ita enim etiam infidelibus Judaeis Messias promissus & datus est. Ejusmodi foret promissio praesentiae substantialis corporis Christi in Eucharistia, quae vel ideo non posset non esse communis, fidelibus & infidelibus facta, quia corpus Christi in panis substantia comprehensum ab omnibus panis substantiam manducantibus, adeoque fidelibus & infidelibus, perciperetur. Unde Rintelenses Theologi in Colloquio Cassellensi confessi ingenue sunt, neminem inter suos reperiri, qui Reformatos habere verum Sacramentum, ambigat. Nos quoque opinionem Lutheranorum, quod in Coena Domini corpus Christi organo oris a dignis & indignis comedatur, pro stipula fundamento salvo perperam superstructa, habemus, quia in examine conscientiae, & probatione nostri, & legitimo Coenae Dominicae usu, protinus exoritur & evanescit; quando videlicet pia & fidelis anima non, quid alii sumant, cogitat, sed ut ipsa digne, mystico videlicet & spirituali modo, per veram fidem corpus & sanguinem Christi percipiat, allaborat. Otiosam ergo speculationem quandam de reprobarum communione opinio illa continet, quae fidei praxin in communione salutari, quam ipsis etiam Lutheranis concedimus, non impedit, & de qua
units.tr: perfect and complete in every point, it is plain that there is no access to discord unless agreement has first been overthrown. Indeed, a perfect agreement of opinions among all the godly in the militant Church is to be wished for rather than hoped for. But even with an imperfect agreement of judgments, a true concord, and a concord perfect to the measure of this present life, can exist. "As many of us as are perfect, let us think this; and if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal this to you also. Only, let us walk by the same rule to which we have attained" (Phil. 3:15-16). Yet there are not a few points on which the Evangelicals agree concerning the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper, which Forbesius Instruct. Hist. Theol. lib. XIV. 7. has reduced to thirty-one heads. Whatever is saving in it, and pertains by divine institution to the comfort of conscience, each side retains whole and intact. The controverted question of the oral eating of the body and blood of Christ, and that this eating is common to believers and unbelievers, whether denied or affirmed, does not overturn the foundation of salvation, because it is admitted on both sides that in the Churches of each party, despite that dissent, the use of the Sacrament remains whole and unimpaired according to Christ's institution, without addition or subtraction of essentials. Even if the opinion that denies oral eating and corporeal presence were false, we would not therefore cease to celebrate the Eucharist according to Christ's institution, because the presence of Christ's body in the Eucharist depends not on human works, nor on the persuasion and faith of the communicants, but, however it is denied in words, on the truth of Christ, who, when he said that what is given in the Eucharist is his body, will make it his body for us even though we do not believe in a corporeal presence. Nor does it stand in the way that this is a promise, and a promise is not fulfilled unless it is received by faith. For there are two kinds of promises: one made to believers alone, and another made to believers and unbelievers alike. Thus the Messiah was also promised to, and given to, the unbelieving Jews. A promise of the substantial presence of Christ's body in the Eucharist would be of the second kind, which could not fail to be common, made to believers and unbelievers alike, because the body of Christ, contained in the substance of the bread, would be perceived by all who eat the substance of the bread, and so by believers and unbelievers alike. Hence the Rinteln theologians at the Colloquy of Kassel frankly confessed that no one among their own people could be found who doubted that the Reformed have a true Sacrament. We too hold the opinion of the Lutherans, that the body of Christ is eaten with the mouth's organ by the worthy and the unworthy in the Lord's Supper, to be a stubble wrongly built upon the foundation, which remains safe; for in the examination of conscience, in the testing of oneself, and in the lawful use of the Lord's Supper, it straightway arises and vanishes, namely when a devout and faithful soul does not think about what others take, but labours that it may itself worthily receive the body and blood of Christ, in a mystical and spiritual manner, through true faith. That opinion therefore contains an idle speculation about the communion of the reprobate, which does not hinder the practice of faith in the saving communion that we even concede to the Lutherans themselves, and about which

units.la: qui morosius disputant, perinde faciunt, atque Medici de homine mortuo disceptantes, an epotum pharmacum in eo vim habeat, nec ne? Nucleum certe Sacramenti utraque pars, non obstante illo de modo praesentiae dissensu, integrum illibatumque retinet, in eo consistentem, quod per signa Divinitus instituta, ceu ἀρραβῶν, pignora, sigilla, arrhabonem, in legitimo usu credentibus significatur, obsignatur & exhibetur communio cum corpore & sanguine Christi, quatenus videlicet corpus Christi pro nobis datum, sanguis ejus pro nobis effusus est ad justitiam coram Deo, remissionem peccatorum & vitam aeternam nobis acquirendam. Quae communio cum corpore & sanguine Christi non qualiscunque intelligitur, sed prout corpus ejus, ceu Sponsoris & Salvatoris nostri pro nobis traditum, sanguis pro nobis ad justitiam & vitam nostram effusus est, hoc est, prout Christus cum toto merito & justitia sua, adeoque fundus & fructus, noster est, & nobis per fidem imputatur. Quid vero ad communionem ejusmodi refert, sine corpus & sanguis Christi vicinum nobis secundum indistantiam loci, an remotum? Quid refert ejus, qui pro vita alterius spopondit, corpus & sanguis ipsi loco conjunctum, an disjunctum sit? Satis est, quod Sponsor propter vitam ejus mortuus est, mors ejus a judice acceptatur, cum eodem communionem habet, & propterea vivit & spirat, ubicunque locorum Sponsor, corpus & sanguis ejus existat.
units.tr: those who dispute more fussily act just as physicians do who argue over a dead man, whether the medicine he has swallowed has any effect in him or not. Both sides certainly retain whole and unimpaired the kernel of the Sacrament, despite that dissent about the mode of presence. It consists in this: through the signs divinely instituted, as an earnest [ἀρραβῶν], pledges, seals and a pledge deposit, communion with the body and blood of Christ is signified, sealed and exhibited to believers in the lawful use, insofar as the body of Christ given for us and the blood of Christ shed for us are for our acquiring righteousness before God, forgiveness of sins and eternal life. This communion with the body and blood of Christ is not understood as any kind of communion, but as the communion in which his body, given for us as our Surety and Saviour, and his blood, shed for us for our righteousness and life, are ours; that is, in which Christ, with his whole merit and righteousness, and so his foundation and fruit, is ours and is imputed to us through faith. What does it matter for communion of this kind whether the body and blood of Christ are near us in respect of nearness of place, or far off? What does it matter to one who has stood surety for another's life whether the body and blood of the surety are joined to him in place or separated? It is enough that the Surety died on account of his life, that his death is accepted by the Judge, that he has communion with him, and therefore lives and breathes, wherever in the world the Surety's body and blood exist.

units.la: CXXXI. Neque illud harmoniam Evangelicorum turbare debet, quod corporis & sanguinis Christi conjunctio arctissima non cum anima duntaxat, sed cum corpore etiam nostro requiritur.
units.tr: CXXXI. Nor should it disturb the harmony of the Gospels that the closest union with the body and blood of Christ is required not only with the soul but also with our body.

units.la: Nam neque hoc inficias imus. Sed conjunctionem illam cum corpore etiam Christi non corporis, sed animae ope fieri credimus. Quando enim mens nostra cum corpore & sanguine Christi arcte colligari gestit, & eo desiderio reapse cum Christo colligatur, tum vita Dei a mente in corpus etiam derivatur. Meritum enim Christi carnem in crucem figendam tradentis & sanguinem fundentis, per animam fide cum Christo conjunctam etiam in corpore rectos motus producit, & legem peccati in membris abolet. Sanctas enim cogitationes animae recti corporis motus sequuntur. Atque ita corpus aeque atque anima nostra cum Christi corpore & sanguine, adeoque cum toto Christo conjungitur, eique conformatur. Neque enim ad id requiritur, ut corpus & sanguis Christi superficie sua superficiem corporis nostri attingat, quia talis superficierum conjunctio inter absentes impossibilis, & inter praesentes inutilis est, cum caro sic conjuncta nihil prosit, & in pluribus non vitae, sed mortis & condemnationis causa foret, saltem durabilis & perpetua, qualis nostra cum Christo communio esse debet, non existeret. Sufficit autem praesentia corporis Christi tum per meritum Filii Dei, propter quod & mens & caro nostra vitam in Deo vivit: tum per signa & pignora, quae substituta in locum corporis & sanguinis Christi maximam communionis cum iisdem certitudinem praestant: tum per fidem & cogitationes mentis, quae mortis Christi perpetuo recordatur, & fructum illius ardenter expeexpetit : Hæc enim si communionem illam cum Christi corpore & sanguine non efficiunt, quid contactus superficierum præstabit? Nam quòd corpus Christi partem pignoris & sigilli facere videntur, neque illud sic necessarium est, ut, qui id non credunt, pignore & sigillo carere putandi sint. Negari enim non potest, quin panis solus pignoris illius locum sustinere possit, quia à Deo institutus est sigillum atque pignus, & sigillum atq; pignus omne vim & efficaciam suam à Divina institutione habet. Salva igitur utrinque & communio corporis & sanguinis Christi non cum anima duntaxat, sed etiam cum corpore nostro, & sigilli atq; pignoris ratio est.
units.tr: We do not deny this. But we believe that union with the body of Christ is brought about not by the body but by the soul. For when our mind longs to be closely bound to the body and blood of Christ, and in that desire is truly joined to Christ, then the life of God flows from the mind into the body as well. For the merit of Christ, who delivered his flesh to be nailed to the cross and poured out his blood, works through the soul, joined to Christ by faith, and produces right motions even in the body, and abolishes the law of sin in our members. For right bodily motions follow holy thoughts of the soul. And so our body, just as much as our soul, is joined to the body and blood of Christ, and so to the whole Christ, and is conformed to him. Nor is it required for this that the body and blood of Christ touch our body by their surface, because such a contact of surfaces is impossible between those who are absent, and useless between those who are present, since flesh so joined would profit nothing, and in most cases would be a cause not of life but of death and condemnation, and in any case would not be lasting and perpetual, as our communion with Christ ought to be. But the presence of the body of Christ is sufficient: first through the merit of the Son of God, on account of which both our mind and our flesh live the life in God; second through the signs and pledges, which, put in the place of the body and blood of Christ, give the greatest certainty of communion with them; third through faith and the thoughts of the mind, which constantly remembers the death of Christ and eagerly seeks its fruit. For if these do not bring about that communion with the body and blood of Christ, what will contact of surfaces accomplish? For that the body of Christ seems to make up part of the pledge and seal, this is not so necessary that those who do not believe it are to be thought to lack the pledge and seal. For it cannot be denied that bread alone can take the place of that pledge, since it was instituted by God as seal and pledge, and every seal and pledge has its force and efficacy from divine institution. Therefore the communion both of the body and of the blood of Christ, not only with the soul but also with our body, and the nature of the seal and pledge, remain safe on both sides.

units.la: CXXXII. Habet denique Sacramentum Cœnæ hostes inprimis capitales Socinianos, qui Christi merito & satisfactione profligatis, ceremoniam quidem S. Cœnæ se retinere, expuncto Baptismo, profitentur, sed sola fidei & obedientiæ professione eam fieri & absolvi, neque in ea quicquam novi accipi, vel nobis obsignari, pertendunt. Quid enim acciperemus, & quid Cœna nobis obsignaret, si Christus vicaria morte sua remissionem peccatorum nobis non impetravit? Sublatis his dapibus convivium perit. Nihil enim dari, nihil obsignari, nihil accipi potest. Cùmque ad manducationem corporis Christi necessaria sit præsens existentia corporis Christi naturalis in Cœlis, vel saltem in rerum natura, illi veram existentiam corporis Christi naturalis nullam aliam, quàm præteriti temporis credunt. Nam Christum in Cœlum ascendentem desiisse habere carnem & sanguinem, asserunt; adeóque pariter corporalem & spiritualem præsentiam & perceptionem, præsentis temporis aut loci, in Cœlo vel in terra ἀδύνατον censent. Unum ergo hoc per mataeologiam eorum superest, ut jussers Christus post suam in Cœlum ascensionem celebrari S. Cœnæ ritum, vel ceremoniam, ad repræsentandam crucifixionem carnis, & effusionem sanguinis illius, qui olim fuit, nunc vero est Non-Ens, & illa repræsentatione Non-Entis, quod olim fuit, contesserari corpus Christi mysticum; quæ corporis mystici contesseratio per ceremoniam S. Cœnæ, totàque adeò mandati istius ceremonialis obedientia, potus & cibus noster spiritualis sit.
units.tr: CXXXII. Finally, the Sacrament of the Supper has as its chief enemies the Socinians, who, having destroyed the merit and satisfaction of Christ, profess that they retain the ceremony of the Holy Supper while Baptism is removed, but maintain that it is performed and completed by the mere profession of faith and obedience, and that nothing new is received in it or sealed to us. For what would we receive, and what would the Supper seal to us, if Christ had not obtained for us the forgiveness of sins by his vicarious death? Take away these dainties and the banquet perishes. For nothing can be given, nothing sealed, nothing received. And since the present existence of the natural body of Christ in heaven, or at least in the nature of things, is necessary for the eating of the body of Christ, they believe that the true existence of the natural body of Christ is nothing but past time. For they assert that Christ ceased to have flesh and blood when he ascended into heaven; and so they consider a bodily and spiritual presence and perception of the present time or place, in heaven or on earth, to be impossible [ἀδύνατον]. Therefore this one thing remains of their vain speculation, that Christ commanded the rite or ceremony of the Holy Supper to be celebrated after his ascension into heaven, to represent the crucifixion of the flesh and the outpouring of the blood of him who once was, but now is a non-being; and by that representation of a non-being, which once was, the mystical body of Christ is knit together; and this knitting together of the mystical body, through the ceremony of the Holy Supper, and indeed the whole obedience to this ceremonial command, is our spiritual food and drink.

units.la: CXXXIII. Verùm aliquid omnino credentibus in mystico hoc convivio à Christo datur : non convivæ duntaxat in ea Christo hospiti liberalissimo charisteria persolvunt. Nulla enim sine beneficio gratitudo est. Ideo Christus dicens; Edite, hoc enim est corpus meum: Bibite, hoc est sanguis meus, &c. edendum corpus suum, & bibendum sanguinem suum dedit, & comedentes atque bibentes illa acceperunt. Verba dat Volkelius lib. IV. 22. speciosè asserens, non modò pane fracto corpus Christi fractum, potu autem, qui poculo continetur, sanguinem Christi pro nobis fusum adumbrari, omnibusque ante oculos mortem Christi cruentam poni; verum etiam panem illum edendo, atque è poculo bibendo, palam nos testari & profiteri, nos corpus Christi fractum atque crucifixum pro animæ cibo, sanguinem fusum pro potu habere, quo ad vitam spiritualem & sempiternam perinde alamur & confirmemur, ac cibo potúque corpora nostra ad vitam terrenam ac temporalem sustentantur. Quæ mere hypocritica sunt.
units.tr: CXXXIII. But in this mystical banquet something is truly given by Christ to those who believe: the guests do not merely pay thanks to Christ, the generous host, with their gifts. For there is no gratitude without a benefit. Therefore Christ, saying: Eat, for this is my body: Drink, this is my blood, etc., gave his body to be eaten and his blood to be drunk, and those who eat and drink have received these things. Volkelius (book IV, chapter 22) gives words to this, speciously asserting that not only is the body of Christ broken depicted by the broken bread, and the blood of Christ poured out for us by the drink contained in the cup, and the bloody death of Christ set before everyone's eyes; but also that by eating that bread and drinking from the cup we openly testify and profess that we hold the broken and crucified body of Christ as food for the soul, and the poured-out blood as drink, by which we are nourished and strengthened for spiritual and eternal life, just as our bodies are sustained by food and drink for earthly and temporal life. These things are purely hypocritical.

units.la: Quicquid enim orthodoxi similibus verbis morti Christi, seu obedientiæ illius, qua crucem sustinuit, & sanguinem suum fudit, merito tribuunt, id totum illi de martyrii constantis exemplo, cujus meditatione ipsi nos alamus, & in similis obedientiæ propositio confirmemus, intelligunt. Vitam enim spiritualem nostro officio, non Dei beneficio, & vitam sempiternam nostri operis mercede, quam expectamus, definiunt. Ideo etiam per κοινωνίαν communionem illam corporis & sanguinis Christi, quam panem & poculum esse Apostolus dixit; & quod idem, unum panem, unum corpus multos esse, dixit, 1. Cor. X. 16. 17. professionem & declarationem nostram, per quam religionis & cultus illius, qui in Cœna peragitur, participes fimus, hoc est, professionem ceremonialem officii nostri, quo Deo & Christo religionem & cultum, proximo charitatem debemus, sine ulla communione, quæ sit à Christo carnem suam edendam & sanguinem bibendum nobis communicante, quam harmonia verborum Apostoli cum harmonia Evangelica verborum Cœnæ Dominicæ institutæ & à Christo celebratæ Matth. XXVI. 26. &c. Marc. XIV. Luc. XXII. postulat; intelligi statuunt. Cùm verò in Cœnæ Dominicæ usu non edamus τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα propriam Cœnam, sed τὸ Κυριακὸν σῶμα Cœnam Dominicam, 1. Cor. XI. 20. 21. in qua assidemus non propriæ, sed Domini mensæ, & bibimus non nostrum, sed Domini poculum, ibid. X. 21. XI. 27. ut censeamur invitati convivæ, qui poculo excipimur; seu à Domino potamur, manifestum est, in ea non ceremonialem duntaxat officii nostri, quo mortem Domini commemoramus; & ad ejus exemplum nos componimus, sed etiam beneficii, quo à Christo Domino nostro mactamur; commemorationem præcipi. Unde passiva illa verba, in utriusque Sacramenti mysterio significando adhibita : ἐσταυρώθη, ἐποτίσθη; baptizati sumus, potati sumus, ibid. XII. 13.
units.tr: For whatever the orthodox rightly attribute with similar words to the death of Christ, or to that obedience by which he bore the cross and shed his blood, all this they understand of the example of constant martyrdom, by meditation on which we nourish ourselves and are strengthened by the proposal of similar obedience. For they define spiritual life as the result of our duty, not of God's benefit, and eternal life as the wage of our work, which we expect. Therefore they also hold that the communion [κοινωνία] of the body and blood of Christ, which the Apostle called the bread and the cup, and which he likewise called one bread and one body, saying that we are many, in 1 Cor. 10:16-17, is our profession and declaration, by which we become partakers of the religion and worship that is carried out in the Supper; that is, a ceremonial profession of our duty, by which we owe religion and worship to God and Christ, and charity to our neighbour, without any communion in which Christ gives us his flesh to eat and his blood to drink, which the harmony of the Apostle's words demands along with the harmony of the Gospel words of the Lord's Supper instituted and celebrated by Christ, Matt. 26:26 etc., Mark 14, Luke 22. But since in the use of the Lord's Supper we do not eat the own body [τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα], that is, our own supper, but the Lord's body [τὸ Κυριακὸν σῶμα], the Lord's Supper, 1 Cor. 11:20-21, in which we sit not at our own table but at the Lord's table, and drink not our own but the Lord's cup, ibid. 10:21, 11:27, so that we are reckoned as invited guests who are received at the cup, or are given drink by the Lord; it is clear that in it is commanded not only the ceremonial remembrance of our duty, by which we recall the death of the Lord and conform ourselves to his example, but also the remembrance of the benefit by which we are nourished by Christ our Lord. Hence those passive verbs used in signifying the mystery of both sacraments: [ἐσταυρώθη] he was crucified, [ἐποτίσθη] he was given drink; we have been baptized, we have been given drink, ibid. 12:13.

units.la: CXXXIV. Verba porrò Cœnæ: Hoc est corpus meum sic Sociniani intricant potiùs quàm explicant: Hoc, id est, hæc actio, quæ circa elementum panis peragitur, est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur, Sanguis meus, &c. seu est commemoratio, & quædam adumbratio ejus, quod de corpore meo futurum est. Et similiter de propositione: Hoc est sanguis meus. Ita explicare debuerunt, ne victimam expiatoriam agnoscere necesse haberent. Verùm & subjectum & prædicatum fœdè depravant: Subjectum, quia hoc ad panem & poculum distributum adeò manifestè refertur, ut Lucas & Paulus in altera propositione, pronomini Τοῦτο diserte opposuerint substantivum ποτήριον poculum; Luc. XXII. 20. 1. Cor. XI. 25. & Paulus pluribus finem atque usum Cœnæ S. explicans, utrumque subjectum non semel aut bis; sed tertium exponat; ibid. v. 26. 27. 28. Prædicatum, quia corpus & sanguis Christi non aliter in Cœna Domini proponuntur; quàm quatenus illud datum seu fractum in cruce, hic pro nobis ad remissionem peccatorum effusus est, Luc. XXII. 19. 20. 1. Corinth. XI. 24. 25. & panis insuper corpus Christi, vinum verò ejus sanguis vocatur metonymia sacramentali, qua nomen rei signatæ de signo prædicatur, non propter solam celebrationem, vel externæ professionis symbolum cum ea conjunctum, sed propter illius per alterum declarationem, testificationem & obsignationem. Idem Paulus Τὸ Hoc ad panem, qui frangitur, & poculum, cui benedicitur, refert, & panem fractum & poculi effusionem communionem corporis & sanguinis Christi, non qualemcunque, sed eam demum, quæ est Divinum testimonium, & efficax symbolum, seu pignus beatæ illius communionis, quam omnes & singuli fideles in Christo & beneficiis ejus obtinent, per quam etiam in unum corpus mysticum, & cum Christo, tanquam capite, & inter se, velut membra corporis, revera coalescunt & continentur, 1. Cor. X.16.17. Quam communionem Sociniani in celebratione mortis Christi ad confirmationem doctrinæ ejus, & externam testificationem communis professionis, qua fideles ab infidelibus, Christiani à Judæis & Gentibus discriminantur, convertentes, evertunt. Neque obstat, quòd utrique propositioni apud Paulum, alteri apud Lucam additur : Hoc facite ad mei commemorationem; ubi Hoc ad actionem refertur. Non enim propositiones illæ : Hoc est corpus meum : Hoc est sanguis meus; &: Hoc facite ad mei commemorationem, æquipollentes sunt, cùm illæ angustiores, hæc latior: illæ finem sacræ Cœnæ distincte in divisis symbolis, hæc conjunctim declarent.
units.tr: CXXXIV. Moreover, the words of the Supper, This is my body, the Socinians entangle rather than explain: This, that is, this action which is performed concerning the element of bread, is my body, which is delivered for you, my blood, etc.; or it is a commemoration and a kind of representation of what is to happen to my body. And similarly with the proposition This is my blood. They ought to explain it thus, so that they would not be obliged to acknowledge a sin-offering. But they foully distort both subject and predicate. The subject, because this is referred so plainly to the bread and cup that Luke and Paul, in the second proposition, expressly set the substantive cup [ποτήριον] against the pronoun This [Τοῦτο], Luke 22:20, 1 Cor. 11:25; and Paul, explaining the end and use of the Holy Supper at more length, sets out both subjects not once or twice but as a third, ibid. vv. 26-28. The predicate, because the body and blood of Christ are presented in the Lord's Supper only insofar as that body was given or broken on the cross and that blood was poured out here for us for the forgiveness of sins, Luke 22:19-20, 1 Cor. 11:24-25. Moreover, the bread is called the body of Christ and the wine his blood by sacramental metonymy, by which the name of the thing signified is predicated of the sign, not merely on account of the celebration, or because a symbol of external profession is joined with it, but on account of its declaration, testimony and sealing of that thing through the other. The same Paul refers This [Τὸ] to the bread, which is broken, and the cup, over which thanks is given, and the broken bread and the pouring out of the cup to the communion of the body and blood of Christ; not just any communion, but that which is the divine testimony and efficacious symbol, or pledge, of that blessed communion which all and each of the faithful obtain in Christ and his benefits, through which also they are truly united and contained in one mystical body, and with Christ as head, and among themselves as members of the body, 1 Cor. 10:16-17. The Socinians, turning this communion into a mere confirmation of his doctrine in the celebration of the death of Christ, and an external testimony of the common profession by which the faithful are distinguished from unbelievers, Christians from Jews and Gentiles, overturn it. Nor does it stand in the way that to both propositions in Paul, and to the second in Luke, is added: Do this in remembrance of me; where This refers to the action. For those propositions, This is my body; This is my blood, and Do this in remembrance of me, are not equivalent, since the former are narrower and the latter broader: the former declare distinctly the end of the Holy Supper in the separate symbols, the latter jointly.

units.la: CXXXV. Impiè iidem spiritualem Christi manducationem, qua corpus Christi, tanquam panis, sive cibus vitæ, verbo promissionis nobis oblatum, ad animæ nutritionem apprehenditur & fide accipitur, ex Cœna Domini tollunt. Nam in S. Cœna est manducatio fidei, tum quia est Sacramentum N. T. fidem requirentis, 1. Cor. XI.25. sicut ablutio spiritualis à peccatis in Baptismo fit per fidem, Marc. XVI. 16. ita manducatio corporis Christi, & bibitio sanguinis ejus in Cœna nonnisi fide peragitur : tum quia communio absque fide est eorum, qui ἀναξίως indignè comedunt, 1. Cor. XI.27.28. 2. Cor. XIII. 5. adeóque communio dignorum fide perficitur. Fides porro in Cœna Domini intuetur & apprehendit in verbo promissionis corpus Christi pro nobis crucifixum, quod disertè elemento panis additur, Matth. XXVI. 26. &c. & intuetur illud ut panem seu cibum vitæ, Joh. VI.35.52. Nam S. Cœna efficaciam mortis Christi per lætum epulum nobis adumbrat & obsignat. Et ut cibum vitæ ad animæ famelicæ sufficientem & salutarem alimoniam intuetur, uti tum ex analogia cibi & potus spiritualis, quibus similes effectus necessariò respondent : tum ex concione Christi, Joh. VI. 35. 50. 51. &c. inprimis colligitur. Non enim, uti adversarii contendunt, Christus in concione illa de pane vitæ, manducatione carnis, & potu sanguinis, sic de fide in Christum collocanda simpliciter loquitur, ut metaphoricè tantùm fidei nostræ opus illustret, ejúsque necessitatem & vim energeticam, seu obedientiæ nostræ zelum ostendat, eliminata ex fidei objecto obedientia Christi nobis imputata, qua carnem suam crucifigendam dedit, & sanguinis sui effusione expiationem pro nobis fecit. Sic enim, inaudita catachresi, manducatio carnis Christi, & potus sanguinis ejus dicebatur sola ruminatio martyrii à Christo obiti, ad consummationem promissionis vitæ æternæ, & in exemplum opere & obedientia fidei nostræ imitandum, sine ullo mysterio gratiæ illius efficaciter operantis, qua Christus mortis suæ merito nos sibi, ut membra capiti, agglutinat, quod mysterium Apostolus Ephes. IV. 15.16. V.32. tradit. Absque ea enim nullum foret corpus Christi mysticum ; & inanis etiam confessio, & confessionis tessera foret. Præterea etiam manducationem corporis Christi spiritualem & signum & res signata Cœnæ Domini confirmat. Signum, quia similitudine quadam naturam rei signatæ declarat. At signum est cibus terrenus & corporeus. Res igitur signata cœlestis & spiritualis cibus sit oportet. Spirituale autem solo spiritu ac fide percipitur, Joh. VI. 63. Res signata, quia in verbo promissionis illa nobis offertur, ut cibus vitalis, 1. Cor. XI.24. Joh. VI.51. Proinde nec aliter quàm fide percipitur. Accedit, quòd omnium Sacramentorum res signata est spirituale quiddam, fide percipiendum; Circumcisionis carnis, circumcisio cordis, Deut. XXX.6. Col. II. 11. Paschatis, Agnus Dei peccata mundi auferens, & fide comedendus, 1. Cor. V.7. Baptismi, interna ablutio à peccatis per sanguinem & Spiritum, ibid. VI.11. Tit. III.5. Quorum omnium spiritualis duntaxat fructus & perceptio est, Rom. II.28.29. 1. Cor. V.7. Col. II.11. 1. Petr. III.21. Ergo par etiam Sacramenti Cœnæ Domini ratio est. Neque obstat, quòd manducatio spiritualis corporis Christi etiam extra Cœnam fit. Res enim utrobique eadem est, sed modus variat. Extra Cœnam fide Christus percipitur in verbo nudæ promissionis ; in Cœnæ usu in verbo promissionis Sacramento vestitæ & obsignatæ. Denique falsa est definitio manducationis spiritualis, quam illi obtrudunt, & cujus prætextu eam ex Cœna eliminant. Nam illam cogitationE potestatis illius, quam Christus per crucifixionem corporis sui consecutus est ad salutem nostram, & meditatione atque imitatione doctrinæ ipsius, ut ea ceu animæ pabulo, nutriamur & sustentemur, absolvant. Nam talem spiritualem manducationem in Cœna non reperiri fatemur, quia ne vera quidem manducatio spiritualis est, sive actus, sive objectum, sive effecta ejus spectamus. Actus enim dicuntur cogitatio potestatis Christi, & imitatio doctrinæ ejus, qui non magis naturam hujus manducationis, quàm ipsius fidei, cum qua illa convenit, Joh. VI. 35. 47. declarant. Objectum partim potestas Christi Dominica, morte acquisita, pro qua vitam æternam donat : partim doctrina ejus, vitæ exemplo ad imitationem Christi prælucanda. Scriptura verò hoc objectum ignorat, & non aliud quàm corpus Christi pro nobis fractum, sanguinem effusum, Luc. XXII. 19. 1. Cor. XI.24. sive carnem ipsius, quatenus in morte Christi pro mundi vita data est, Joh. VI. 51. docet. Effecta denique manducationis illius non bona opera, tanquam imitationis Christi exempla, sed illa, quæ Salvator, Joh. VI. 35. &c. ex illa deducit, sunt.
units.tr: CXXXV. The same people impiously remove from the Lord's Supper the spiritual eating of Christ, by which the body of Christ, as bread or food of life offered to us in the promise of the Word, is apprehended for the nourishment of the soul and received by faith. For there is a eating by faith in the Holy Supper, first because it is a sacrament of the New Testament that requires faith (1 Cor. 11:25). Just as spiritual washing from sins takes place in Baptism through faith (Mark 16:16), so the eating of Christ's body and the drinking of his blood in the Supper are accomplished only by faith. Second, because communion without faith belongs to those who eat unworthily [ἀναξίως] (1 Cor. 11:27, 28; 2 Cor. 13:5), and therefore the communion of the worthy is completed by faith. Moreover, in the Lord's Supper faith looks upon and apprehends in the word of promise the body of Christ crucified for us, which is expressly added to the element of bread (Matt. 26:26, etc.), and looks upon it as bread or food of life (John 6:35, 52). For the Holy Supper sets before us and seals the efficacy of Christ's death through a joyful feast. And that the Supper looks upon this as the food of life, a sufficient and saving nourishment for the hungry soul, is chiefly gathered both from the analogy of spiritual food and drink, to which similar effects necessarily correspond, and from Christ's discourse in John 6:35, 50, 51, etc. For, as our opponents contend, Christ in that discourse about the bread of life, the eating of flesh and the drinking of blood, does not speak simply of placing faith in Christ, so as only metaphorically to illustrate the work of our faith, its necessity and energetic power, or to show the zeal of our obedience, with the obedience of Christ imputed to us removed from the object of faith, by which he gave his flesh to be crucified and made atonement for us by the shedding of his blood. For in that way, by an unheard-of catachresis, the eating of Christ's flesh and the drinking of his blood would be called merely the rumination on the martyrdom undergone by Christ, for the fulfilment of the promise of eternal life, and as an example to be imitated in the work and obedience of our faith, without any mystery of that grace which effectively works, by which Christ, through the merit of his death, joins us to himself as members to the head, a mystery which the Apostle sets forth in Eph. 4:15, 16; 5:32. For without this there would be no mystical body of Christ, and the confession would be empty, and a mere token of confession. Furthermore, the spiritual eating of Christ's body is also confirmed by the sign and the thing signified in the Lord's Supper. The sign, because by a certain likeness it declares the nature of the thing signified. But the sign is earthly and bodily food. The thing signified must therefore be heavenly and spiritual food. Now the spiritual is perceived by the Spirit and faith alone (John 6:63). The thing signified, because in the word of promise it is offered to us as vital food (1 Cor. 11:24; John 6:51). Therefore it is perceived in no other way than by faith. Besides, the thing signified in all the sacraments is something spiritual, to be received by faith: of circumcision, the circumcision of the heart (Deut. 30:6; Col. 2:11); of the Passover, the Lamb of God taking away the sins of the world, to be eaten by faith (1 Cor. 5:7); of Baptism, the inward washing from sins through the blood and the Spirit (ibid. 6:11; Titus 3:5). The fruit and the perception of all these is purely spiritual (Rom. 2:28, 29; 1 Cor. 5:7; Col. 2:11; 1 Pet. 3:21). Therefore the case is the same also for the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper. Nor does it stand in the way that the spiritual eating of Christ's body also takes place outside the Supper. For the thing is the same in both cases, but the mode differs. Outside the Supper Christ is perceived by faith in the word of bare promise; in the use of the Supper, in the word of promise clothed and sealed by the sacrament. Finally, the definition of spiritual eating which they force upon us, and under the pretext of which they remove it from the Supper, is false. For they reduce it to the thought of that power which Christ obtained through the crucifixion of his body for our salvation, and to the meditation and imitation of his teaching, so that we are nourished and sustained by these as by food for the soul. For we confess that such a spiritual eating is not found in the Supper, because it is not even a true spiritual eating, whether we consider its act, its object or its effects. For they call the act the thought of Christ's power and the imitation of his teaching, which declare the nature of this eating no more than of faith itself, with which it agrees (John 6:35, 47). The object is partly the Lord's power of Christ, acquired by death, for which he grants eternal life; partly his teaching, which is to be set before us as an example for the imitation of Christ. But Scripture knows nothing of this object, and teaches only the body of Christ broken for us, the blood shed (Luke 22:19; 1 Cor. 11:24), or his flesh as given for the life of the world (John 6:51). Finally, the effects of that eating are not good works, as examples of imitating Christ, but those which the Saviour derives from it (John 6:35, etc.).

units.la: CXXXVI. Vicinus Sociniano error est ille Hugonis Grotii, qui Dissertatione sua. An semper communicandum sit per symbola ? hominibus
units.tr: CXXXVI. Close to the Socinian error is that of Hugo Grotius, who in his dissertation "Whether the Lord's Supper must always be communicated by symbols?"

units.la: Grotii de communicatione symbolis
units.tr: Grotius on communion by symbols

units.la: nibus ejusdem secum furfuris persuadere laboravit, non necessarium esse post Christi & Apostolorum tempora Eucharistiæ usum, & cum nulla partium Christianarum participandam esse Eucharistiam, ne cum ulla speciale Religionis communionem profiteri necesse habeant. Quod etiam Episcopius Resp. ad 64. Quæstiones adoptavit. Cœnam enim Domini illi ex traduce post-cœniorum apud Hebræos diebus festis usu receptorum vel more etiam illo, quo gentiles sacrificantes extorum partem ei reddebant, qui conviva vocabatur, derivant. Abolitis igitur festis Judæorum & Gentilium simul Cœnam à Christo institutam cessare, asserunt. Pauli enim Christi verba explicantis verba: Hoc facite ... intelligenda esse, quasi dixisset: Quando feceritis, hoc est, festas Cœnas celebraveritis, & postcœnio eas clauseritis. Quæ foeda verborum Apostoli detorsio est, jussit enim Christus discipulos hoc facere ad sui commemorationem, usque dum ipse de Cœlo rediturus & præsens Ecclesiam beaturus est; seu usque dum venerit, 1. Cor. XI.26. Etenim nec religio, nec pietas sine externo cultu constat. Unde Deus Sacramentorum usum ante lapsum, sub promissione & lege instituit. Atque abolitis signis, quæ omne religionis Christianæ mysterium continent, & in omne ævum eam conservant, ipsa quoque religio Christiana paulatim extingueretur & periret. Neque ulla erroris ἀποφασις est in verbis S. Pauli: Παρέλαβον, ὃ καὶ παρέδωκα, Accepi, quod & tradidi vobis, 1. Cor. XI.23. Non enim his verbis liberum institutum, nullo præcepto, seu definito imperio nixum, quod facile ex causa probabili omitti posset, innuitur. Nam similiter etiam de fide mortis, sepulturæ & resurrectionis Christi loquitur, dicens: Παρέδωκα Tradidi vobis primis, quod & accepi, quod Christus mortuus sit pro peccatis nostris, & sepultus sit, &c. ibid.XV.3.4. Corruet hac verborum detorsione omnis Divina auctoritas traditionis Apostolicæ scriptæ, quæ maximam partem Scripturæ Novi Testamenti facit.
units.tr: ...of the same kind as himself, sought to persuade men that after the time of Christ and the Apostles the use of the Eucharist was not necessary, and that it is not to be shared with any Christian party, since they need not profess a special communion with any religion. Episcopius also adopted this in his Responsio ad 64 Quaestiones. They derive the Lord's Supper from the custom, received among the Hebrews, of holding post-supper gatherings on festal days, or from that practice by which the Gentiles, when sacrificing, gave a portion of the entrails to the man called the convive. Therefore, they assert, with the feasts of the Jews and Gentiles abolished, the Supper instituted by Christ also ceased. They hold that the words of Paul explaining Christ's words, "Do this", are to be understood as though he had said, "When you have done it", that is, when you have celebrated the festal suppers and closed them with an after-meal. This is a foul twisting of the Apostle's words. For Christ commanded the disciples "to do this in remembrance of me" until he himself returns from heaven and blesses the Church in his presence, or "until he comes", 1 Cor. 11.26. Indeed, neither religion nor piety exists without outward worship. Hence God instituted the use of sacraments before the fall, under promise and law.
