And if the signs which contain the whole mystery of the Christian religion were abolished, and which preserve it for all ages, the Christian religion itself would gradually be extinguished and perish. Nor is there any denial of error in the words of St Paul: "I received" [Παρέλαβον], "what I also delivered to you" [ὃ καὶ παρέδωκα], 1 Cor. 11.23. For these words do not imply a free institution, resting on no precept or defined command, which could easily be omitted for some probable cause. For he speaks in the same way of the faith concerning the death, burial and resurrection of Christ, saying: "I delivered to you first of all what I also received, that Christ died for our sins, and was buried", etc., ibid. 15.3, 4 [Παρέδωκα]. All divine authority of the written apostolic tradition, which makes up the greater part of the Scripture of the New Testament, would collapse by this twisting of the words.

units.la: CXXXVII.
units.tr: CXXXVII.

units.la: Fuerunt genuina N. T. Sacramenta. Illis Tridentini quinque alia, Confirmationem, Pœnitentiam, Extremam Unctionem, Ordinem & Matrimonium accensent, quæ Sacramenta veri nominis, seu sigilla justitiæ non sunt, quia Sacramenti proprietatibus destituuntur. Quod de singulis confirmabimus.
units.tr: There were two genuine sacraments of the New Testament. To these the Tridentines add five others: Confirmation, Penance, Extreme Unction, Orders and Matrimony. These are not sacraments in the true sense, or seals of righteousness, because they lack the properties of a sacrament. This we shall confirm for each one.

units.la: CXXXVIII. Confirmationem sic Petrus de Aliaco, Cardinalis Cameracensis in 4. q. 4.
units.tr: CXXXVIII. Confirmation is thus defined by Peter of Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, in 4. q. 4.

units.la: definit; quod sit unctio hominis viatoris, viri scilicet & mulieris, nec actualiter, nec habitualiter dissentientis, facta in fronte, in figura crucis, cum chrismate sanctificato, & hoc à ministro idoneo, simul cum intentione debita in ungente, certa verba proferente ex institutione Dei, significans untonem animæ per gratiam roboratam, ad confitendum cum fiducia fidem Christi. Constat ergo signo crucis & chrismate ex oleo olivarum & balsamo, inflicta confirmando alapa; neque ab alio, quàm Episcopo vel Suffraganeo ejus conferri potest, & confertur his verbis: Signo te signo crucis, & confirmo te chrismate salutis in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Ejusmodi verò Sacramentum Christus nec mandato, nec actu usquam instituit.
units.tr: as an anointing of a human wayfarer, that is, of a man or a woman who neither actually nor habitually dissents, made on the forehead in the figure of a cross, with sanctified chrism, and this by a suitable minister, together with due intention in the one anointing, pronouncing certain words from the institution of God, signifying the anointing of the soul through strengthened grace, to confess the faith of Christ with confidence. It therefore consists of the sign of the cross and chrism made from olive oil and balsam, with a blow on the cheek being given to the person to be confirmed; and it can be conferred only by a bishop or his suffragan, and is conferred with these words: I sign you with the sign of the cross, and I confirm you with the chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. But Christ nowhere instituted such a sacrament, either by command or by action.

units.la: Neque ut instituereret, ulla ratio fuit, quia spirituale robur & augmentum, quod hic prætexitur, Baptismo, Eucharistiæ, precibus, fide & Spiritus S. gratia acquiritur. Et non à Christo, sed in Concilio demum Meldensi institutum esse Alexander Alensis, aliique fatentur. Ubi enim vestigia sunt chrismatis ex oleo & balsamo conficiendi, atque eodem cujusquam inungendi? Ideo Jesuitæ & Canonistæ deserto chrismate, materiam hujus Sacramenti impositionem manuum faciunt, asserentes, quòd Apostoli demum ritum impositionis manuum indeterminatum in chrisma commutaverint. ritum S. corroborantem; nec inserat Christo; nec in eo, ut proprio hæreditas Dei ab eo curanda & conservanda signemur. Baptizatus non tenetur se persecutoribus objicere, nisi inquisitio fiat; confirmatus tenetur. In duobus, ita Jesuita Costerus Augment. Enchir. de Sac. Conf. loquitur; Confirmatio præfertur Baptismo, tum in dignitate Ministri, qui solus Episcopus est, tum in perfectione effectus. Denique piæ antiquitati incognitum hoc Sacramentum fuit. Primus Tertullianus unctionis cum Baptismo conjunctæ meminit, ad ejus solennitatem, non substantiam, uti diserte Pammelius; & eo consilio, ut mysteria simplicissima, & proin à multis fastidita ad conciliandos hominum animos pompam & ornatum acciperent. Paulatim circa Baptismum ritus incrementa acceperunt. Sed unctio illa paulatim à Baptismo coepit, cùm vel ab hæresi venientes non novo Baptismo, sed unctione, vel manuum impositione in Ecclesiæ sinum reciperentur, vel qui urgente necessitate à laicis, vel alioquin à Diacono vel Presbytero baptizati erant, post ab Episcopo, cui soli novos Christo milites legere fas erat, ungerentur, vel imposita manu confirmarentur. Ita chrismatio Pontificia ex veteri unctionis Judaicæ ritu desumpta, seculo demum XII. circa tempora Arnoldi Bonævillensis, Lombardi, Hugonis de S. Victore effecta, & postà Concilio Florentino in Sacramentorum numerum recepta est. Proin etiam antiquissimæ, & rituum tenacissimæ Ecclesiæ Orientales, Græcæ, Æthiopicæ, Armenicæ, Chaldaicæ ritum hunc penitus ignorant; nisi quatenus iis chrismatio Baptismalis ritus est.
units.tr: Nor was there any reason for him to institute it, since the spiritual strength and increase that is here put forward is obtained through Baptism, the Eucharist, prayers, faith and the grace of the Holy Spirit. And Alexander of Hales and others admit that it was instituted not by Christ but at last in the Council of Meaux. For where are there traces of making chrism from oil and balsam, and of anointing anyone with it? Therefore the Jesuits and the canonists, having abandoned the chrism, make the matter of this sacrament the imposition of hands, asserting that the Apostles at last changed the indeterminate rite of the imposition of hands into chrism. The rite strengthens; nor does it implant anyone in Christ, nor are we sealed in him so that we may be cared for and preserved by him as the inheritance of God. A baptized person is not bound to expose himself to persecutors unless an inquiry is made; a confirmed person is bound. In two respects, so the Jesuit Costerus speaks in his Augment. Enchir. de Sac. Conf.: Confirmation is preferred to Baptism, both in the dignity of the minister, who is only the bishop, and in the perfection of its effect. Finally, this sacrament was unknown to pious antiquity. Tertullian was the first to mention an anointing joined with Baptism, for its solemnity, not its substance, as Pamelius clearly says; and with the purpose that the most simple mysteries, and therefore despised by many, might receive pomp and ornament to win over the minds of men. Gradually rites grew up around Baptism. But that anointing gradually began to be separated from Baptism, when those coming from heresy were received into the bosom of the Church not with a new Baptism but with anointing or the imposition of hands, or when those who had been baptized in urgent necessity by laymen, or otherwise by a deacon or a presbyter, were afterwards anointed by the bishop, to whom alone it was lawful to enrol new soldiers for Christ, or were confirmed by the imposition of hands. Thus the Papist chrismation, taken from the ancient Jewish rite of anointing, was finally brought into being in the twelfth century, around the time of Arnold of Bonneval, Lombard and Hugh of Saint Victor, and was received into the number of the sacraments after the Council of Florence. Therefore even the most ancient Eastern Churches, which are most tenacious of their rites, namely the Greek, Ethiopian, Armenian and Chaldean, know nothing at all of this rite, except insofar as chrismation is for them a part of the rite of Baptism.

units.la: CXXXIX. Sed mandatum Confirmationis illi executione, seu facto Apostolorum manus imponentium; Signum visibile ex ipsa impositione manuum, ab Apostolis usurpata, Act. VIII. 17. 18. 19. XIX. 6. rem signatam, seu promissionem ex promissione Spiritus S. Luc. XXIV. 49. Joh. XV. 16. XVI. 23. 24. extundere nequicquam conantur. Quid enim cuncta hæc ad unctionem hominis viatoris in fronte factam, in figura crucis cum chrismate sanctificato? Quid impositioni manuum cum unctione frontis per chrisma, seu oleum balsamatum? Quid est in rebus fidei mutare quadrata rotundis, si hoc non est? Neque enim, quod Bellarminus nugatur, extensionem manus Episcopi erga illum, quem ungit, nec non signationem & unctionem, quæ manu fit, rectè manuum impositionem appellari, frivolum nimis est: quia nec extendere super aliquem manum, nec signare, vel ungere, manus imponere est; cùm manuum impositio Divino & Ecclesiastico sermone sit certus & definitus actus, quo expansa super alicujus capite manus ita statuitur, ut in ejus vertice recumbat. Unde Græcis χειροθεσία, Hebræis סמיכת ידים à סמך quod inniti, fulcire, conjungere significat, nomine venit. Qualis manuum impositio ab Apostolis ad conferenda extraordinaria Spiritus S. dona, liberè usurpata est. Nobis verò nunc sufficit, quòd omnes Spiritum filiationis per fidem accipimus, Gal. III. 14. IV. 6. Neque de Sacramento Confirmationis Papali loquitur S. Paulus, dicens: Qui confirmat nos vobiscum in Christo, & qui unxit nos, Deus, qui & signavit nos, & dedit
units.tr: CXXXIX. But they try in vain to extract the command of Confirmation from the practice, or the deed, of the Apostles laying on hands; the visible sign, from the imposition of hands itself, used by the Apostles, Acts 8:17, 18, 19; 19:6; the thing signified, or the promise, from the promise of the Holy Spirit, Luke 24:49; John 15:16; 16:23, 24. For what do all these have to do with the anointing of a human wayfarer on the forehead, made in the figure of a cross, with sanctified chrism? What has the imposition of hands to do with an anointing of the forehead with chrism, or balsamed oil? What is it in matters of faith to change square into round, if this is not so? For it is not too trivial, as Bellarmine trifles, to say that the stretching out of the bishop's hand over the one he anoints, and also the signing and anointing done by the hand, are rightly called the imposition of hands; because to stretch a hand over someone, or to sign or anoint, is not to lay on hands; since in the language of Scripture and of the Church the imposition of hands is a definite and specific act, by which a hand, stretched out, is so placed upon someone's head that it rests on the crown. Hence it is named in Greek cheirothesia [χειροθεσία], and in Hebrew smikhat yadayim [סמיכת ידים], from samakh [סמך], which means to lean upon, to prop up, to join. Such an imposition of hands was freely used by the Apostles for conferring the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit. For us now it is enough that we all receive the Spirit of adoption through faith, Galatians 3:14; 4:6. Nor does St. Paul speak of the Papal sacrament of Confirmation when he says: Now he who establishes us with you in Christ, and who anointed us, is God, who also sealed us and gave

units.la: pignus Spiritus in cordibus nostris, 2. Cor. I. 21. Nisi enim aliunde de eo constet, dubiis & improprriis verbis probari non potest. Sed hoc sibi vult, Deum nos unire Christo per fidem, & quidem, ut nos in eum firmet; simúlque nos unxisse, quando nos fecit esse in Christo, & cum eo Reges & Sacerdotes, atque nos signasse & notasse ceu rem & hæreditatem sibi propriam, & ad spem nostram nobis Spiritum pro arrhabone dedisse. Hæc ex Scripturis nota sunt: Chrismatio verò papalis ignota est. Certè non homini cuipiam, sed Deo soli authori confirmatio, unctio & obsignatio isthæc accepta fertur. Quomodo etiam χεῖρμα unctio illa, 1. Joh. II. 20. 27. non homini, sed τῷ Ἁγίῳ Sancto illi tribuitur, quæ & hoc præstat, ut noverimus omnia, & non habeamus opus, ut quisquam nos doceat, quod chrismatio papalis quomodo præstet, ipsi viderint. Et post Baptismum, quo τὸ esse spirituale nobis obsignatur, Christus non Confirmationis, sed Eucharistiæ, quo illius vitæ spiritualis confirmatio & augmentum obsignetur, instituit.
units.tr: the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts, 2 Cor. 1.21. For unless it is established from elsewhere that this refers to it, it cannot be proved from doubtful and improper words. But this means that God unites us to Christ through faith, and indeed that he establishes us in him; and at the same time that he anointed us when he made us to be in Christ, and with him kings and priests; and that he sealed and marked us as a thing and inheritance proper to himself, and gave us the Spirit as an earnest for our hope. These things are known from the Scriptures; but papal chrismation is unknown. Certainly this confirmation, anointing and sealing is ascribed to no man, but to God alone as author. Likewise that anointing, 1 John 2.20, 27, is attributed not to a man but to the Holy One [τῷ Ἁγίῳ], who also brings about this result, that we know all things, and have no need that anyone should teach us. How papal chrismation brings this about, let them see for themselves. And after Baptism, by which our spiritual being is sealed to us, Christ instituted not Confirmation but the Eucharist, by which the confirmation and increase of that spiritual life is sealed.

units.la: CXL. Alterum Pœnitentiæ Sacramentum Christus pariter nec instituit, nec exercuit. Non ad aliam enim poenitentiam nos vocavit, quàm eam, quæ à Prophetis & Johanne prædicata est. At nec Apostoli de poenitentia, & ratione consequendi remissionem peccatorum aliter docuerant, quàm Prophetæ V. T. Quæ tamen poenitentia Sacramenti rationem, fatentibus adversariis, non habuit. Absurdè verò iidem signum ejus externum contritionem, confessionem & satisfactionem faciunt; quas sensu eorum acceptas, ne quidem poenitentiæ in Evangelio requisitæ partes esse, supra probavimus. At nec signum esse Sacramenti actus illi possunt. Nam contritio in sensus non incurrit nisi per fallacia operum testimonia. Nec confessio morbi signum sanationis est. Satisfacere verò pro debito non signum gratiæ est, sed gratiæ repugnat. Ubi autem materia non est, ibi nec forma locum habet, de qua ipsi vehementer diffidunt; plerisque eam in verbis absolutionis: Ego absolvo te, &c. monstrantibus; quæ tamen nec in Scriptura, nec in omni antiquitate reperitur; adeóque & novitium inventum est, & non in poenitente, sed in non-poenitente, qui Sacerdos absolvens est, obtinet. Quomodo ergo poenitentiæ forma esse potest? Etenim forma id est, per quod res est id quod est; & essentiam rei constituit. Atqui absolutio à peccatis essentiam poenitentiæ & actuum ejus, contritionis, confessionis & satisfactionis non constituit: Et quænam in actibus poenitentis, & ministri absolutione analogia talis, qualis inter elementum terrestre, & rem coelestem esse debet, ostendi potest? Satis denique illud constat, quòd poenitentia sacramentalis ortum à corruptione disciplinæ Ecclesiæ veteris habeat. Nam in ea contritionis signa, confessio publica, & satisfactio, seu reparatio scandali per atrociora crimina publicè dati exigebantur. Multa de his in libris veterum, Tertulliani inprimis, Cypriani & Ambrosii. Etiam Concilia vetera Canonibus poenitentialibus perspersa sunt, quibus poenitentiæ gradus, tempus & similia. At Sacramenti nulla apud eos mentio est. Neque post poenitentiam absolutio his verbis: Ego
units.tr: CXL. Christ likewise neither instituted nor practised the second sacrament, that of Repentance. He did not call us to any other repentance than the one preached by the Prophets and John. Nor did the Apostles teach about repentance, or about the way of obtaining the forgiveness of sins, differently from the Prophets of the Old Testament. Yet that repentance, as our opponents admit, did not have the character of a sacrament. Absurdly, they make the external sign of it to be contrition, confession and satisfaction; and we have already proved above that these, taken in their sense, are not even parts of the repentance required in the Gospel. Nor can those acts be signs of a sacrament. For contrition does not fall under the senses except through the deceptive testimony of works. Nor is confession a sign of healing from a disease. And to satisfy for a debt is not a sign of grace, but is opposed to grace. Where there is no matter, there is no place for form either, and about this form they themselves are deeply uncertain; most of them point to the words of absolution, I absolve you, etc. Yet these words are found neither in Scripture nor in all antiquity, and so this is a novelty, and it holds not in the penitent but in the non-penitent, namely the priest who absolves. How then can it be the form of repentance? For a form is that through which a thing is what it is, and it constitutes the essence of the thing. But absolution from sins does not constitute the essence of repentance and of its acts, contrition, confession and satisfaction. And what analogy, of the kind that ought to exist between an earthly element and a heavenly thing, can be shown between the acts of the penitent and the absolution of the minister? Finally, it is well established that sacramental repentance has its origin in the corruption of the discipline of the ancient Church. For in that discipline, signs of contrition, public confession, and satisfaction, or the repair of scandal caused by publicly known more atrocious crimes, were required. Much about this is found in the books of the ancients, especially Tertullian, Cyprian and Ambrose. Also the ancient Councils are interspersed with penitential Canons, which concern degrees of repentance, its duration and similar matters. But there is no mention of a sacrament among them. Nor after repentance was the absolution with these words: I

units.la: Argumentis pro eodem occurrunt. Ego absolvo te, &c. fieri, sed poenitens impositione manuum Episcopi, & precibus Ecclesiae reconciliari suevit. Poenae reconciliationem peccatoris praecedebant, non, uti nunc ridicule fit, sequebantur. Neque etiam Sacerdos stipem a poenitente accepit, absolutionis mercedem; nec populus docebatur, defectum poenarum Purgatorii flammis suppleri. Haec & similia novitiorum seculorum foecis inventa sunt: Veteres vero Canones poenitentiales Ecclesia Romana posterioris aevi abrogavit, & novam poenitentiae formam invexit.
units.tr: Arguments for the same point occur. I absolve you, etc., was not used, but the penitent was wont to be reconciled by the laying on of the bishop's hands and by the prayers of the Church. The penances preceded the reconciliation of the sinner; they did not, as now happens ridiculously, follow it. Nor did the priest receive an offering from the penitent as the wage of absolution, nor was the people taught that the lack of penalties is made up by the flames of Purgatory. These and similar things are the dregs of later centuries' inventions. But the Roman Church of a later age abrogated the ancient penitential Canons and introduced a new form of repentance.

units.la: CXLI.
units.tr: CXLI.

units.la: Christus equidem Apostolis & universis Evangelii praeconibus potestatem peccata remittendi, & retinendi dedit; Accipite, inquiens, Spiritum S. Quorum peccata remiseritis, remittentur iis, & quorum retinueritis, retenta erunt, Joh. XX. 23. Sed verba illa generalia cum sint, neque vel ritum vel signum sacramentale determinent, Sacramentum nullum ex iis confici potest. Nam etiam in praeconio verbi poenitentibus peccata remittuntur, seu remissa in Christi nomine declarantur. Christus enim in nomine suo poenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum praedicari jussit, Luc. XXIV. 47. neque tamen praeconium illud Sacramentum declaravit. Promissio gratiae agit quidem de remissione peccatorum, sed nuda ac simplex, non vestita aut confirmata externis symbolis est; cujusmodi in promulgatione Evangelii perpetua est. Deficiente vero signo, tanquam relato, signatum, quod correlatum sit, salvum esse nequit. Mandatum quoque remittendi peccata nihil ad Poenitentiae Sacramentum in specie, sed ad ministerium Evangelii, clavium que potestatem in genere pertinet. Quod argumento a pari sic Christus confirmat: Sicut me misit Pater, ita & Ego mitto vos, Joh. XX. 21. At ille misit Filium ad evangelizandum, Luc. XIV. 18. Sic ergo Apostoli quoque missi fuerunt. Cum que fideles V. T. de remissione peccatorum absque externo aliquo symbolo in ejusmodi Poenitentiae Sacramento certi esse potuerint, cur similiter fideles N. T. certi esse non possunt? Et quid vetat, quo minus vel externum illud signum sit verbum Dei, etiam extra Sacramentum praedicatum, & peccatori idonee applicatum: vel peccator sibi peccata remissa esse sine externo signo, solo interno Spiritus S. motu, intelligat? Vanum, imo impium est, quod Sacerdotes & Prophetae V. T. & Ministri N. T. extra Sacramentum Poenitentiae praedicaverint, & praedicent poenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum, sed sine potestate ponendi signum remissionis practicum, remissionem infallibiliter operans. Sola enim voluntas Dei practica, seu effectiva remissionis peccatorum est. Verba vero hominum practica sunt, remissionem non efficiendo, sed certa conditione significando & declarando. Peccantes proin post Baptismum non novo Sacramento poenitentiae ad remissionem peccatorum indigent; utpote quibus fides, foederis gratiae in Baptismo obsignati pia recordatio, & poenitentia, qualis in Evangelio describitur, sufficit. Neque secunda post naufragium tabula requiritur, quia fidei & justitiae semel acceptae naufragium nemo facit. Nam potentia Dei per fidem custodimur, 1. Pet. I. 5. Denique poenitentia peccata tollit, at nec
units.tr: Christ indeed gave to the Apostles and to all heralds of the Gospel the power of remitting and retaining sins: Receive, he says, the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them, and whose you retain, they are retained, John 20:23. But since those words are general, and determine neither a rite nor a sacramental sign, no sacrament can be made from them. For even in the proclamation of the Word, sins are remitted to penitents, or are declared remitted in the name of Christ. For Christ ordered that repentance and the remission of sins be preached in his name, Luke 24:47, yet that proclamation did not declare a sacrament. The promise of grace indeed deals with the remission of sins, but it is bare and simple, not clothed or confirmed by external symbols; such is its character always in the promulgation of the Gospel. And when the sign, as the thing referred to, is lacking, the thing signified, which is correlated to it, cannot be safe. The command to remit sins also pertains not to the sacrament of Repentance in particular, but to the ministry of the Gospel and to the power of the keys in general. Christ confirms this by an argument from like to like: As the Father sent me, so I also send you, John 20:21. But he sent the Son to evangelize, Luke 14:18 [sic]. So the Apostles too were sent in this way. And since the faithful of the Old Testament could be certain of the remission of sins, without any external symbol, in such a sacrament of Repentance, why can the faithful of the New Testament not likewise be certain? And what forbids that either the external sign be the Word of God, even when preached apart from a sacrament and suitably applied to the sinner, or the sinner understand that his sins are remitted to him without an external sign, by the inward motion of the Holy Spirit alone? It is vain, indeed impious, to think that the priests and prophets of the Old Testament and the ministers of the New, when they preached repentance and the remission of sins outside the sacrament of Repentance, and still preach them, do so without the power of placing a practical sign of remission, which infallibly effects remission. For the practical, that is, effective, will of God alone is the cause of the remission of sins. But the words of men are practical, not by effecting remission, but by signifying and declaring it under a certain condition. Therefore sinners after Baptism do not need a new sacrament of repentance for the remission of sins; for faith, the pious remembrance of the covenant of grace sealed in Baptism, and repentance such as is described in the Gospel, suffice for them. Nor is a second plank after shipwreck required, because no one suffers shipwreck of the faith and righteousness once received. For we are kept by the power of God through faith, 1 Peter 1:5. Finally, repentance takes away sins, but not

units.la: efficienter, quia id soli gratiae Dei convenit; nec significative, quod Sacramentorum est, sed formaliter, quatenus per gratiam Dei ex malis mutat in bonos; haud secus ac reliquae virtutes vitia sibi oppositá tollunt, neque tamen Sacramentis annumerantur.
units.tr: efficiently, since that belongs to the grace of God alone; nor significatively, which is the mark of the sacraments, but formally, insofar as by the grace of God it changes evil into good. In no other way do the remaining virtues remove the vices opposed to them, yet they are not counted among the sacraments.

units.la: CXLII. Unctionis extrema Sacramentum aeque fictitium est.
units.tr: CXLII. The sacrament of Extreme Unction is equally fictitious.

units.la: Ejus vi, Sacerdote oleo ab Episcopo consecrato exteriores sensus & renes agonizantis inungente, peccatorum reliquias abstergi, morbos leviuss ferri, tentationibus Sathanae facile resisti, & sanitatem corporis interdum recuperari, afferunt. Caeterum Sacramenti proprietates nullas habet. Nuspiam enim a Christo institutus in Sacramentum Ecclesiae ordinarium & perpetuum est. Apostoli quidem aegros oleo unxerunt, Marc. VI. 13. Quo facto Sacramentum hoc non quidem institutum, sed insinuatum tamen Tridentini nequicquam asserunt. Nam miraculosa tota fuit, & ad curationem morborum pertinuit. Christus enim Apostolis potestatem daemonia ejiciendi, & morbos curandi, Matth. X. 1. Marc. VI. 7. impertitus est. Qua potestate accepta olei unctione illico morbos sanarunt, & daemonia ejecerunt, Marc. VI. 13. utrumque non sine miraculo, nec potestate ordinaria, sed extraordinaria. Neque gravissimorum morborum curatio, oleo potius quam miraculo tribui poterat. Ex hoc loco explicandus est ille, Jac. V. 14. 15. Ubi presbyteri ab infirmo accersiti super eum precari, & ungere eum oleo in nomine Domini jubentur, addita promissione: Et fidelis precatio servabit laborantem, & si peccata fecerit remittentur ei. Eadem utrobique res, eadem rei causa, materia, finis, effectum. Si igitur unctio Apostolorum non fuit ordinaria & sacramentalis, neque a Jacobo imperata haec talis est. Est quidem in utroque loco elementum oleum, cum ritu unctionis, atque illud symbolicum, non medicinale. Sed symbolum est non sacramentalis significationis, vel obsignationis gratiae, sed miraculosae sanationis, cujus donum vigebat in Ecclesia. Adhibebatur circa aegrotos, valetudinis recuperandae gratia, non circa moribundos, desperata jam valetudine. Administri vero erant Presbyteri, iisque plures, charismate hoc praediti, ut circumstantias reliquas taceam; quarum nulla in papali unctione servatur vel deprehenditur. Promissio quinetiam gratiae symbolo addita, de gratia sanationum manifeste loquitur, quae plane diversa est a gratia salutis, in foedere promissa. Meminit quidem Jacobus etiam remissionis peccatorum, sed promissionem ejus intelligit non absolutam, nec quorumvis peccatorum, sed eorum duntaxat, quae morbi peculiaris causa videri poterant; de quali peccato quaerebant discipuli Christi: Rabbi, quis peccavit, hic, an parentes ejus, quod caecus natus est? Joh. IX. 2. Nec promissio illa unctioni, sed orationi fideli facta est, nec si unctioni facta esset, duratura erat ultra signum & mandatum, quod temporarium fuit, eos solos spectans, qui charisma illud sanationum tum acceperant, ejusque sibi conscii erant. Facete autem illi Sacramentum illud constitutum dicunt ad egressum ab Ecclesia; oppositè ad Baptismum, quem Sacramentum esse ingredientium in Ecclesiam scisciunt. Quomodo & Baptismi efficaciam enervant, quasi ejus ad ἐνσφράγισιν nulla vis esset, & mortem piorum egressum ab Ecclesia fingunt, cùm tamen sit introitus ad Dominum, non ἐκδυσις exutio, sed ἐπένδυσις superindutio, 2. Cor. V.4. Longè alia praesidia, quàm aliptica ejusmodi, sunt, quibus Deus finem vitae fidelium munivit, nimirum Spiritus ejus, unctio in iis manens, verbum Dei solatiis refertissimum, armatura tota spiritualis, solatium firmissimum ex foedere Dei, semel in Baptismo, & toties in Eucharistia obsignatum; verbo dicam, Jesus Christus pro nobis crucifixus. Manet equidem miraculosa illa unctio diu satis in Ecclesia; ex cujus καταζηλία demum seculo XII. Bernhardus & Lombardus visi sunt docere, extremam unctionem praecisè necessariam esse, & gratiam remissionis peccatorum egredientibus ex Ecclesia conferre. Eam Scholastici amplificarunt & expoliverunt, & Concilia sequentia definiverunt.
units.tr: By its power, when a priest anoints the outer senses and the loins of a dying man with oil consecrated by a bishop, they claim that the remnants of sins are wiped away, illnesses are more lightly borne, the temptations of Satan are easily resisted, and bodily health is sometimes recovered. Otherwise it has no properties of a sacrament. For Christ nowhere instituted it as an ordinary and perpetual sacrament of the Church. The apostles indeed "anointed the sick with oil", Marc. VI. 13. By doing this, the Tridentine fathers assert in vain, they did not institute this sacrament but at least hinted at it. For that whole thing was miraculous and pertained to the healing of diseases. Christ bestowed on the apostles the power "of casting out demons and of curing diseases", Matth. X. 1. Marc. VI. 7. Having received this power, they immediately healed the sick and cast out demons with the anointing of oil, Marc. VI. 13. Both were done not without a miracle, and by extraordinary, not ordinary, power. Nor could the cure of very grave diseases be attributed to the oil rather than to the miracle. From this passage that one in Jac. V. 14. 15. must be explained, where the presbyters, summoned by the sick man, are ordered "to pray over him and to anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord", with the added promise: "And the prayer of faith will save the one who is suffering, and if he has committed sins, they will be forgiven him." The thing is the same in both places, with the same cause, matter, end, and effect. If, therefore, the anointing of the apostles was not ordinary and sacramental, neither is this one, enjoined by James, sacramental. In both places there is indeed the element of oil with the rite of anointing, and it is symbolic, not medicinal. But it is a symbol not of sacramental signification or sealing of grace, but of miraculous healing, a gift which flourished in the Church. It was applied to the sick to recover their health, not to the dying whose health was already despaired of. The ministers were presbyters, and several of them, endowed with this charisma, not to mention the other circumstances, none of which is kept or found in the papal anointing. The promise attached to the sign of grace also speaks plainly of the grace of healings, which is quite different from the grace of salvation promised in the covenant. James indeed also mentions "remission of sins", but he understands the promise not as absolute, nor as applying to any sins whatever, but only to those which could seem to be the particular cause of the illness. The disciples of Christ asked about such a sin: "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?" Joh. IX. 2. Nor was that promise made to the anointing but to the prayer of faith. Nor, even if it had been made to the anointing, would it have lasted beyond the sign and command, which was temporary, looking only to those who had then received that charisma of healings and were conscious of it. They wittily call this sacrament instituted "for the departure from the Church", in contrast to Baptism, which they hold to be the sacrament of those "entering the Church". In this way they also weaken the efficacy of Baptism, as if it had no force for sealing [ἐνσφράγισιν], and they imagine the death of the pious to be a departure from the Church, when it is an entrance to the Lord: not unclothing [ἐκδυσις] but putting on over [ἐπένδυσις], 2. Cor. V. 4. Quite different protections from such anointing are those with which God has fortified the end of the lives of the faithful: namely, his Spirit, the anointing remaining in them, the word of God most full of consolations, the whole spiritual armour, the firmest comfort from God's covenant, sealed once in Baptism and so often in the Eucharist; in a word, Jesus Christ crucified for us. That miraculous anointing indeed remained in the Church long enough. From its excess [καταζηλία] at last, in the twelfth century, Bernard and Lombard seemed to teach that extreme unction is strictly necessary, and confers the grace of remission of sins on those departing from the Church. The Scholastics amplified and polished it, and the following councils defined it.

units.la: CXLIII. Proximum huic Sacramentum Ordinem, seu Ordinationem, & vel χειροθεσία impositione manuum, vel porrectione instrumentorum (dubitant enim) collatum gradum eminentiorem in Ecclesia, gratiam gratum facientem conferentem, & ad actum sacramentalem rite & legitimè exercendum, disponentem faciunt. Sed ejusmodi Ordo & institutione, & elemento, & verbo promissionis, & usu ordinario caret; adeóque Sacramentum proprie dictum non est. Institutione, quia ut ordinatio Ministrorum Ecclesiae Sacramentum sit, nusquam Christus instituit. Nam quod illi mandatum allegant, vel expressum, vel speciale est, velut id, quo Spiritus S. dixit: Separate mihi Barnabam & Saulum ad opus, ad quos eos vocavi; quo accepto, jejunantes & orantes manus iis imposuerunt, Actor. XIII.2.3. quod ab instituto planè alienum est, quia Paulus & Barnabas ibi nec Ordinem, nec Sacramentum acceperunt, vel generale & implicitum, quale ex Actor. XX.28. ubi Spiritus S. Episcopos posuisse dicitur, ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei, nec non Ephes. IV.11. uti Christus alios Apostolos, &c. alios Pastores dedisse dicitur, colligunt; ex quo Divina Ministerii Ecclesiastici institutio convenienter asseritur; at Ordo sacramentalis nihilo rectius concluditur, quàm Apostolatus & Prophetia Sacramentis N. T. accensentur. Elemento, quia nec impositio manuum, nec traditio instrumentorum, calicis, patinae, libri Evangeliorum, baculi pastoralis, & aliorum, signa Divinitus mandata sunt. Nam impositio manuum, ritus ex V. T. petitus, Ordinationi cum multis aliis, etiam Confirmationi communis est, & non tam signum vel elementum, quàm actio est; & à Christo Apostolos solo verbo, mandato & deputatione simplici, adhibita etiam insufflatione, quem sacramentalem fuisse adversarii negant, ordinante usurpata non est. Neque etiam sacramentale quicquam traditio instrumentorum habet, humano consilio ordinationi addita, de qua altum in Scripturis S. silentium est. Promissione gratiae; quia verbum illud promissionis, quo Episcopus utitur, dicens: Accipe potestatem in nomine Domini, &c. in Scripturis non habetur, nec ad promissionem gratiae propriè pertinet. Promissio verò gratiae, quae ordinandis juxta institutionem Christi fit, duplex est; una de sufficiendis donis, ut idonei N. T. ministri sint, 1. Cor. III.5.6. altera de largiendo salutari successu, ne opera ministerii inanis sit, 1. Cor. XV.58. Neutra gratia foederalis & justificans est, qualis sola in Sacramentis obsignatur. Nam etiam Bellarminus de Sacr. lib. I.26. authoritatem Sacramenta conferendi negat esse gratiam gratum facientem, & asserit esse gratiam gratis datam; eò quòd non pugnet cum improbitate vitae, ut simul cum ea esse nequeat, quod exemplo Cajaphae, & aliorum virtutes in nomine Christi edentium comprobat. Denique usu ordinario, omnibus Ecclesiae membris, tanquam ejusdem foederis sociis, communi, cùm ritus iste, antiqua consuetudine, ministerii Ecclesiastici proprius sit. Accedit, quòd verum Sacramentum characterem imprimens, quale Ordinem faciunt, iterari non posse, & in quocunque, quantumvis fictè & indignè accedat, suum & proximum effectum sortiri Scholastici constanter asserunt. At Ordinatio non semper effectum suum habet; Simoniaci nihil accipiunt, & haeretici nihil conferunt; quin & Ordo ipse amissibilis & iterabilis est.
units.tr: CXLIII. Next to this is the sacrament of Order, or Ordination, which they make a higher rank in the Church, conferred either by the laying on of hands [χειροθεσία] or by the handing over of instruments (they hesitate between the two), conferring sanctifying grace and disposing the recipient to perform the sacramental act rightly and lawfully. But such an Order lacks, both in its institution, in its element, in the word of promise, and in ordinary use, and so it is not a sacrament properly so called. It lacks institution, because Christ nowhere instituted ordination of the ministers of the Church as a sacrament. For what they allege as a command is either express and special, such as that in which the Holy Spirit said: "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them"; and, having received this, fasting and praying, they laid hands on them, Actor. XIII. 2. 3. which is quite foreign to the institution, since Paul and Barnabas there received neither Order nor sacrament; or it is general and implicit, such as they gather from Actor. XX. 28., where the Holy Spirit is said to have placed bishops "to feed the Church of God", and from Ephes. IV. 11., where Christ is said to have given some apostles, etc., and some pastors. From this the divine institution of the ecclesiastical ministry is fairly asserted; but a sacramental Order is concluded no more rightly than apostleship and prophecy are counted among the sacraments of the New Testament. It lacks an element, because neither the laying on of hands nor the handing over of instruments, the chalice, the paten, the book of the Gospels, the pastoral staff, and the rest, are signs commanded by God. For the laying on of hands, a rite taken from the Old Testament, is common to ordination, and to many other things, even to confirmation; it is an action rather than a sign or element; and Christ did not use it when ordaining the apostles, who were appointed by his word, mandate and simple designation alone, with the addition of a breathing upon them, which the adversaries deny was sacramental. Nor does the handing over of instruments, added to ordination by human counsel, have anything sacramental, and of it there is a deep silence in the Holy Scriptures. It lacks the word of promise, because that formula of promise which the bishop uses, saying "Receive the power in the name of the Lord", etc., is not found in Scripture, and does not properly pertain to a promise of grace. But the promise of grace which is made to those being ordained, according to the institution of Christ, is twofold: one concerns the furnishing of gifts so that they may be fit ministers of the New Testament, 1. Cor. III. 5. 6.; the other concerns the bestowal of a saving success, so that the work of the ministry may not be in vain, 1. Cor. XV. 58. Neither is a covenant or justifying grace, such as alone is sealed in the sacraments. For Bellarmine also, De Sacr. lib. I. 26., denies that the authority of conferring sacraments is sanctifying grace, and asserts that it is a grace freely given; because it is not incompatible with wickedness of life, so that it cannot be present along with it, which he proves by the example of Caiaphas and of others who performed miracles in the name of Christ. Finally, it lacks ordinary use, being common to all members of the Church as partners of the same covenant, since that rite, by ancient custom, belongs to the ecclesiastical ministry. Moreover, the Scholastics consistently assert that a true sacrament imprints a character, as Order is said to do, cannot be repeated, and that whoever approaches it, however feignedly and unworthily, obtains its own and its proper effect. But Ordination does not always have its effect: the simoniacs receive nothing, and heretics confer nothing; indeed Order itself can be lost and repeated.

units.la: CXLIV. Eadem causa Matrimonium ex Sacramentorum numero summovent.
units.tr: CXLIV. For the same reason, marriage is removed from the number of the sacraments.

units.la: Licet enim à Deo institutum sit, non tamen in Novo demum Testamento, ceu Sacramentum institutum est. Non aliud enim Nov. Test. matrimonium esse, quàm Veteris Testamenti fuit, luculenter Christus ipse, Matth. XIX.4.5. ad primam institutionem provocans, docuit. Atqui in Veteri Testamento institutum non fuisse, ut Sacramentum, adversarii fatentur. Neque institutionem ejus ut Sacramenti ex verbo Apostoli, Ephes. V.32. generatim & ambiguè à veteri Interprete redditis, & à Scholasticis ad constituendum detortis, rite exsculpunt. Si enim Apostolus loquitur: Adhaerebit vir uxori suae, & erunt duo in unam carnem. Τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν· Λέγω δὲ εἰς Χριστὸν, καὶ εἰς τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν. Mysterium hoc magnum est, Dico autem in Christum & Ecclesiam. Neque mysterium magnum quodvis proprie dictum Sacramentum est. Latius enim μυστήριον mysterii quàm Sacramenti proprie dicti vox patet. Neque vox illa signum, sed rem signatam spiritualem in Scriptura & Ecclesia usitatè declarat, uti ex Matth. XIII.11. Ephes. I.9. III.3. Col. I.26. 1. Tim. III.16. liquet. Ac ne conjugium quidem, sed arcanam conjunctionem Christi cum Ecclesia mysterium nuncupat, disertè ajens: Ego autem dico εἰς Χριστὸν, καὶ εἰς τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν in Christum & Ecclesiam, quod tum forma exclamationis, habens παθῶ admirationis, tum series antecedentium, inde à v.25.26. evincit. Hujus conjunctionis mysterio plenissimae signum matrimonium est, quia illud similitudine quadam repraesentat, sed non illum in finem sanctificatum & institutum, nec efficax ejusdem sigillum, quia viri cum muliere conjunctio non per se, sed per accidens id significat, quia Christus Ecclesiae Sponsus dictus est. Fuit autem matrimonium prius, quàm Christus Ecclesiae Sponsus factus est. Imò ne quidem Apostolus constitutum habuit demonstrare unitatem Christi & Ecclesiae per unionem viri & uxoris, sed potiùs unitatem viri & uxoris per unitatem Christi & Ecclesiæ, uti ex v. 29. manifestè colligitur. His fulcris subversis, tota Sacramenti hujus structura corruit. Ritus enim sacramentalis nullus apparet; & quem ipsi comminiscuntur, is nullo modo quadrat. Nam nec personæ matrimonium contrahentes, eorumque corpora sacramentale signum esse possunt, quia subjectum recipiens sunt: nec copula carnalis, quia eam necessariam esse, adversarii plures negant; & Mariam inter atque Josephum sine copula carnali sanctum conjugium fuit. Neque etiam verba & ritus, quibus matrimonium contrahitur, & consensus declaratur, signum sacramentale statui possunt. Verba enim sensibilia quidem, sed non permanentia sunt. Neutra etiam de essentia matrimonii sunt, quia verba possunt abesse à conjugio muto, & nutus à loquaci, utraque à conjugiis, quæ inter absentes per procuratores contrahuntur. Sed & tum verba, tum nutus jam occupatas operas habent. Nam consensus verbis vel nutibus expressus nihil aliud est, quàm significatio consensus per verborum & nutuum signa. Novo ergo anfractu in Sacramento hoc instituta essent signa signorum, quod nemini sano in mentem venire potest. Denique cùm materia externa cum interna analogiam habere debeat, quam analogiam verba & nutus cum gratia justificante habent? Præterea nec promissio gratiæ, qualis in Sacramento proprië dicto est, matrimonio addita est. Dixit olim Eckius, matrimonium dare gratiam avariter minimam & exiguam, qualis non est illa, quæ in Sacramentis obsignatur. Etiam Canonistæ & Lombardus Sacramentum hoc gratiam adjutricem conferre negant. Quale igitur Sacramentum est? Si Deus conjugibus quibusdam id largitur, ut spiritualiter animi eorum conjungantur, & Divinam benedictionem experiantur; non tamen id omnibus conjugibus promissum est, vel confertur. Nihil enim infidelium conjugio Deus promittit, vel confert, si à beneficio multiplicationis generis humani discesseris. Et salvatur mulier διὰ τεκνογονίας per generationem liberorum, 1. Tim. II. 15. non virtute generationis liberorum, quæ communis infidelibus esse potest; sed non obstante ea, & virtute fidei, charitatis, sanctificationis & modestiæ, uti statim Apostolus subjicit. Denique matrimonium Sacramentum esse, jam olim etiam Durandus, aliique eum secuti, prægnantibus argumentis allatis negarunt. Et qui Sacramentum faciunt, se ipsos condemnant, dum matrimonium & fœdè traducunt; & in clericis, tanquam opus carnis, damnant, eíque concubinatum, scortationem, πορνείας & lupanaria, velut minùs malum, ad evitandum majus, præferunt; & matrimonii votum ac juramentum, fœdúsque Dei, quod inter virum & uxorem est, Mal. II. 14. per votum phanaticæ religionis solvunt; & de gradibus in lege prohibitis dispensare non verecundantur.
units.tr: Although marriage was instituted by God, it was not instituted as a sacrament in the New Testament. Christ himself plainly taught that marriage under the New Testament is no different from marriage under the Old, when he appealed to its first institution, Matt. 19:4-5. Our opponents admit that it was not instituted as a sacrament under the Old Testament. Nor do they correctly draw its institution as a sacrament from the words of the Apostle, Eph. 5:32, which the old translator rendered in a general and ambiguous way, and which the Scholastics twisted to suit their purpose. For when the Apostle says, "A man shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh," and then adds, "This mystery is great [τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν]. But I speak concerning Christ and the Church" (Latin: "Mysterium hoc magnum est, Dico autem in Christum & Ecclesiam"), a great mystery is not on that account strictly speaking a sacrament. The word μυστήριον has a wider meaning than the strict sense of sacrament. Nor does that word in Scripture and in the Church commonly denote a sign rather than the spiritual thing signified, as is clear from Matt. 13:11, Eph. 1:9, 3:3, Col. 1:26 and 1 Tim. 3:16. Moreover, the word "mystery" does not refer to marriage at all, but to the hidden union of Christ with the Church. The Apostle says this expressly: "But I speak concerning Christ and the Church [Λέγω δὲ εἰς Χριστὸν, καὶ εἰς τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν]," and the form of the exclamation, with its note of wonder, together with the sequence of what precedes from v. 25 and 26 onward, proves it. Marriage is a sign of this union, and a very full one, because it represents it by a certain likeness; but it was not sanctified and instituted for that purpose, nor is it an effective seal of it. The union of a man and a woman signifies this not in itself but by accident, because Christ is called the Bridegroom of the Church. Moreover, marriage existed before Christ was made the Bridegroom of the Church. Indeed, the Apostle did not even intend to demonstrate the unity of Christ and the Church through the union of husband and wife; rather he shows the unity of husband and wife through the unity of Christ and the Church, as is plainly gathered from v. 29. With these supports overthrown, the whole structure of this sacrament collapses. No sacramental rite appears, and the rite they invent does not fit at all. The persons contracting marriage and their bodies cannot be a sacramental sign, since they are the recipients of the sacrament; nor can carnal intercourse be one, since many of our opponents deny that it is necessary, and holy wedlock existed between Mary and Joseph without carnal intercourse. Nor can the words and rites by which marriage is contracted and consent declared be established as a sacramental sign. For spoken words are indeed sensible, but they are not lasting. Neither is part of the essence of marriage, since words may be absent from a marriage of a mute person, and nods from a marriage of a talkative one, and both from marriages contracted between absent parties through proxies. Moreover, both words and nods have their own work already assigned to them. For consent expressed by words or nods is nothing other than the signification of consent through the signs of words and nods. Thus, by a new roundabout route, signs of signs would be instituted in this sacrament, which no sane person could conceive. Finally, since the outward matter ought to have an analogy with the inward, what analogy do words and nods have with justifying grace? Besides, no promise of grace, such as belongs to what is strictly called a sacrament, has been added to marriage. Eck once said that marriage confers a grace that is, in his words, most meagre and slight, not such as is sealed in the sacraments. The canonists and Lombard also deny that this sacrament confers any helping grace. What sort of sacrament, then, is it? If God bestows on some spouses that their minds may be spiritually joined and that they may experience the divine blessing, yet this is not promised or conferred on all spouses. For God promises or confers nothing on the marriage of unbelievers, if you set aside the blessing of the increase of the human race. And the woman "shall be saved through childbearing [διὰ τεκνογονίας]," 1 Tim. 2:15, through the generation of children, not through the power of begetting children, which can be common even to unbelievers; but notwithstanding that, and through the power of faith, love, sanctification and modesty, as the Apostle immediately adds. Finally, that marriage is not a sacrament was long ago denied, with weighty arguments, by Durandus and others who followed him. And those who make it a sacrament condemn themselves: while they vilify marriage, and in the clergy condemn it as a work of the flesh, they prefer concubinage, fornication, [πορνείας] and brothels, as a lesser evil to avoid a greater; they dissolve the vow and oath of marriage, and the covenant of God that exists between husband and wife (Mal. 2:14), through the vow of a fanatical religion; and they are not ashamed to dispense from the degrees forbidden by the law.

units.la: LOCUS VICESIMUS SEXTUS. De ECCLESIA. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: LOCUS TWENTY-SIXTH. Concerning the CHURCH. A SUMMARY.

units.la: Fœderis Gratiæ subjectum Ecclesia est. 1. Ecclesiæ nomen, & ejusdem cum קהל & ירה convenientia. 2. Nusquam in Scripturis locum seu ædem sacram notat. 3. In voce Ecclesiæ est notio κλήσεως vocationis, cujus terminus fides in Christum est. 4. Interest Ecclesiæ veræ & falsæ ideam exploratam habere. 5. Ecclesia vera proprië & augustè, vel improprië & latè accipitur. Proprië dicta definitur. 6. Vocatorum tria genera distinguuntur. 7. Ecclesiæ causa efficiens Deus, eam verbo & Spiritu vocat. 8. Ecclesiam hanc proprië dictam Scriptura intelligit, ubi illustria Ecclesiæ elogia, & promissiones eximias eidem factas commemorat. 9. Ecclesia cœtus est non Angelorum, sed hominum; nec unius hominis, sed plurium, eorumque ex genere humano maledictioni subjecto ab æterno electorum, & in tempore vocatorum, & nunquam deficientium est. 10. Eam internè fides in Christum, & ab eodem manantes virtutes constituunt. 11. Per fidem Ecclesia cum Christo Capite suo unitur, tum subjectione, tum communione cum eodem; quam sequitur unio membrorum corporis inter se. 12. Ecclesia communio Sanctorum est. 13. Ecclesia hæc proprië dicta invisibilis est. 14. Argumenta invisibilitati huic objecta diluuntur. 15. Ecclesia Una est, non ut Regnum mundanum, sed spirituali & catholica ratione; extra quam nemini salus contingit. 16. Sancta quoque est, imputatione, & renovationis internæ inchoatione; neque tamen in terris erroris & vitii omnis expers. 17. Profectu correctione in hac vita semper indiget. 18. Argumentis pro perfectione & absoluta infallibilitate Ecclesiæ in doctrina satisfit. 19. Ecclesia Catholica est; tum absolutè, tum oppositè ad Ecclesiam V. T. conventicula hæreticorum, & imperia mundana. 20. Idque tum universè, tum particulariter, in Cœlo vel in terra; non actu, sed potentia. 21. Pontificiorum Ecclesiam Romanam Catholicam facientium elenchus. 22. Ecclesiæ perpetuitas adversus Socinianos asseritur. 23. Eorundem argumentis contrariis occurritur. 24. Ecclesiæ veræ membra desiderio communionis & congregationis etiam externæ flagrant. 25. Congregationem fidelium fides, charitas, & prudentia dirigunt. 26. Necessitas congregationis fidelium ad salutem non absoluta, sed limitata. 27. In externa communione & congregatione illa fideles etiam hypocritarum & infidelium occultorum mixturam patiuntur. 28. Hinc emergit notio Ecclesiæ improprie & latius dictæ, quæ definitur. 29. Non omnis multitudo nomen Christi profitentium Ecclesia ejusmodi est; & Ecclesiæ nomine illa improprie venit, secundum opinionem, complexionem & debitam charitatem. 30. Ecclesia proprie & improprie dicta non duplex, sed una est. 31. Ecclesia externa & improprie dicta, secus quàm proprie dicta certis notis infallibiliter dignoscitur, & propter congregationis cum Ecclesia aliqua particulari necessitatem, dignosci sic debet. 32. Notarum Ecclesiæ notæ genuinæ disquirendæ sunt. 33. Pontificii notas notarum falsas perhibent. 34. Veræ & genuinæ notarum notæ. 35. Notæ Ecclesiæ visibilis ex eadem forma, quæ confessio fidei in Christum est, arcessuntur, eæque tres, doctrinæ seu confessionis verbo Dei conformatæ veritas, cultus externus in prædicatione verbi & Sacramentorum administratione consistens, & ordo seu regimen Ecclesiæ; quibus notis & Ecclesiæ natura declaratur, 36. & vera Ecclesia à falsa discernitur. 37. Triplex circa notas has animadversio. 38. Objectiones adversus notas Ecclesiæ veras discussæ. 39. Ecclesia externa visibilis est, at non μὴ συνδρομὴ, nec omnibus. 40. Visibilis est tum in personis singulis, tum in cœtibus, sed lato discrimine puritatis interioris, status exterioris, loci & operationis. 41. Non ideo Ecclesia non visibilis est, quia minor numerus Christum in veritate confitentium, quàm ore & corde, vel alterutro abnegantium est. 42. Ecclesia externa non est erroris & vitii expers. 43. Prædictiones de Antichristi & apostasiæ mixtura cum fidelibus in eadem communione Ecclesiæ. 44. Semper in Ecclesiæ externæ communione mixtura tritici & zizaniorum atque palearum fuit, & maturè mysterium iniquitatis operari cœpit. 45. Communio fidelium cum Ecclesia errante & inordinata quatenus licita, & non exitialis sit? 46. Judicium de colenda cum errantibus & inordinatis communione ex erroribus, ritibus & disciplinæ ratione petendum est. 47. Abrupta cum Ecclesia communio schisma facit, quod aliquando pium & laudabile, aliquando vituperabile est. 48. Non separatio, sed separationis causa schisma facit; quæ aliquando injusta. 49. Aliquando justa & necessaria est. 50. Emissariorum, quamvis separationem damnantium, impietas & argumenta ad incudem revocata. 51. Ecclesia quævis particularis visibilis deficere potest. 52. Argumenta contraria diluuntur. 53. Ecclesia quævis particularis purgari & reformari potest & debet, idque vel ordinariè; 54. vel subinde etiam extraordinariè. 55. Emissariorum objectiones, quibus possibilem Ecclesiæ reformationem oppugnant, refelluntur. 56. Idea falsæ Ecclesiæ exponitur; eáque tum ex mente Fanaticorum & Socinianorum visibilem Ecclesiam destruentium; 57. quorum argumentis occurritur. 58. Tum Pontificiorum, Ecclesiam invisibilem destruentium; quibus Ecclesiæ vox Papatum, seu visibilem Monarchiam notat. 59. Definitio Ecclesiæ ex mente Bellarmini. 60. Quæ non Ecclesiæ veræ, sed falsæ ideam exhibet. 61. Convenientia Ecclesiæ talis cum Babylone magnâ explicatur. 62. Argumenta, quibus definitio Ecclesiæ à Pontificiis exhibita suffulcitur, & Ecclesia inprimis invisibilis, electorum, vocatorum & fidelium, oppugnatur, discussa. 63. Ecclesia etiam externa & visibilis non gloriosè visibilis, Regni mundani instar; nec uni loco & cathedræ alligata est. 64. Argumenta pro Cathedræ & Regni perpetua & illustri visibilitate obducta solvuntur. 65. Ecclesiam in mundo vicissitudines lucis & umbræ habere, & ex commixto Antichristi Regno & zizaniis gravem subinde jacturam pati, nec tamen interire debuisse, ex prædictionibus Divinis confirmatur. 66. Modus, quo Ecclesia ab agnatis hostibus, Antichristo inprimis, pressa, conservari debuit, Divinitus etiam prædictus est. 67. Ecclesiæ sub Antichristo pressæ & conservatæ historia. 68. Mediorum, per quæ Ecclesia sub Antichristo pressa conservata est, recensio. 69. Ecclesia sub Antichristo non sic obscurata est, quin semper se per confessionem & opus commune Christianismi, nec non manifestationem probórum borum videndam præbuerit, inprimis per distinctas emicationes suas, quæ explicantur. 70. Unde de Ecclesia ante Reformationem ὑποδοχὴ judicium promptius est. 71. Adversariorum objectio, quòd Ecclesia nostra ante Reformationem cum nulla alia visibili vera se univerit, & conformaverit, retunditur. 72. Ecclesia à Papatu se separans, à vera Ecclesia se non separavit. 73. Notæ, quibus veram Ecclesiam agnosci, Pontificii asserunt, non unius generis ab illis proponuntur. 74. Epitheta Ecclesiæ in Symbolo Nicæno-Constantinopolitana extantia, quòd sit Una, Sancta, Catholica & Apostolica, non sunt totidem ejusdem notæ. 75. Bellarmini quindecim notæ, quibus Ecclesiam investigant, ad examen revocantur. 76. Velut nomen Catholici & Christiani. 77. Antiquitas. 78. Duratio. 79. Amplitudo, seu multitudo credentium. 80. Successio Episcoporum ab Apostolis usque, sine interruptione in Ecclesia Romana hunc usque in diem continuata. 81. Consensus in doctrina cum Ecclesia antiqua & Patribus. 82. Unio membrorum inter se & cum capite. 83. Sanctitas doctrinæ. 84. Efficacia doctrinæ. 85. Sanctitas vitæ auctorum & Patrum religionis. 86. Miraculorum gloria. 87. Lumen Propheticum. 88. Confessio Adversariorum. 89. Infelix exitus hostium Ecclesiæ. 90. Felicitas temporalis. 91. Notas præcedentes Scriptura non obscurè Antichristo & Synagogæ Sathanæ tribuit. Ut ejus potiùs quàm veræ Ecclesiæ notæ sint. 92.
units.tr: The Church is the subject of the covenant of grace. 1. The name Church, and its agreement with the Hebrew [קהל] and [ירה]. 2. Nowhere in Scripture does it denote a place or a sacred building. 3. The word Church carries the notion of calling [κλήσεως], whose terminus is faith in Christ. 4. It matters to have a carefully examined idea of the true and the false Church. 5. The true Church is taken properly and strictly, or improperly and broadly. The Church properly so called is defined. 6. Three kinds of the called are distinguished. 7. The efficient cause of the Church is God, who calls it by the Word and the Spirit. 8. Scripture means the Church properly so called where it recounts the illustrious praises of the Church and the remarkable promises made to it. 9. The Church is an assembly not of angels but of men; not of one man but of many, and these drawn from the human race, which is subject to the curse, chosen from eternity, called in time, and never failing. 10. Inwardly, the Church is constituted by faith in Christ and the virtues flowing from him. 11. Through faith the Church is united to Christ its Head, both by subjection and by communion with him, and this is followed by the union of the members of the body with one another. 12. The Church is the communion of saints. 13. The Church properly so called is invisible. 14. The arguments raised against this invisibility are answered. 15. The Church is one, not in the manner of a worldly kingdom but in a spiritual and catholic way; outside it salvation comes to no one. 16. It is also holy, by imputation and by the beginning of inward renewal; yet on earth it is not free from all error and vice. 17. In this life it always needs progress and correction. 18. The arguments for the perfection and absolute infallibility of the Church in doctrine are satisfied. 19. The Church is Catholic, both absolutely and in contrast to the Church of the Old Testament, to heretical conventicles and to worldly empires. 20. And this both universally and particularly, in heaven or on earth; not actually but potentially. 21. A refutation of the Papists, who make the Roman Church the Catholic Church. 22. The perpetuity of the Church is asserted against the Socinians. 23. Their contrary arguments are met. 24. The true members of the Church burn with desire for communion and also for external congregation. 25. Faith, charity and prudence direct the congregation of the faithful. 26. The necessity of the congregation of the faithful for salvation is not absolute but limited. 27. In that external communion and congregation the faithful also suffer a mixture of hypocrites and hidden unbelievers. 28. Hence emerges the notion of the Church improperly and more broadly called, which is defined as follows. 29. Not every multitude professing the name of Christ is such a Church; the name Church is applied to it improperly, according to outward profession, association and due charity. 30. The Church, taken properly and improperly, is not twofold but one. 31. The external Church, taken improperly, unlike the Church taken properly, is recognised infallibly by certain marks, and because of the necessity of congregation with some particular church it ought to be recognised in this way. 32. Among the marks, the genuine marks of the Church must be sought. 33. The Papists put forward false marks as the marks. 34. The true and genuine marks. 35. The marks of the visible Church are drawn from the same form which is the confession of faith in Christ, and they are three: the truth of doctrine, or confession, conformed to the Word of God; external worship, consisting in the preaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments; and the order or government of the Church. By these marks the nature of the Church is also declared, 36. and the true Church is distinguished from the false. 37. A threefold observation concerning these marks. 38. Objections against the true marks of the Church are discussed. 39. The external Church is visible, but not a mere gathering [μὴ συνδρομὴ], nor visible to all. 40. It is visible both in single persons and in assemblies, but with a wide difference in inward purity, outward state, place and operation. 41. The Church is not invisible for this reason: that the number of those who confess Christ in truth is smaller than the number of those who deny him with mouth and heart, or with either. 42. The external Church is not free from error and vice. 43. Predictions concerning Antichrist and the mixture of apostasy with the faithful in the same communion of the Church. 44. In the communion of the external Church there has always been a mixture of wheat, tares and chaff, and the mystery of iniquity began early to work. 45. Is communion of the faithful with an erring and disorderly Church lawful, in so far as it is not destructive? 46. The judgment about cultivating communion with the erring and disorderly must be drawn from their errors, rites and church discipline. 47. A broken communion with the Church makes a schism, which is sometimes pious and praiseworthy, and sometimes blameworthy. 48. It is not separation but the cause of separation that makes a schism, and this cause is sometimes unjust. 49. Sometimes it is just and necessary. 50. The impiety and arguments of the emissaries, who condemn separation, are brought back to the anvil. 51. Any particular visible Church can fail. 52. The contrary arguments are refuted. 53. Any particular Church can and ought to be purged and reformed, ordinarily; 54. or, at times, even extraordinarily. 55. The objections by which the emissaries oppose the possible reformation of the Church are refuted. 56. The idea of the false Church is set out, both according to the mind of the Fanatics and Socinians, who destroy the visible Church, 57. whose arguments are met. 58. And according to the Papists, who destroy the invisible Church, for whom the word Church denotes the Papacy, or visible monarchy. 59. The definition of the Church according to Bellarmine. 60. This presents the idea not of the true Church but of the false. 61. The agreement of such a Church with Babylon the Great is explained. 62. The arguments by which the Papists' definition of the Church is supported, and by which the invisible Church, that of the elect, the called and the faithful, is especially attacked, are discussed. 63. The Church, even external and visible, is not gloriously visible in the manner of a worldly kingdom, nor is it bound to one place and one chair. 64. The arguments for the perpetual and illustrious visibility of the Chair and the Kingdom are answered. 65. The Church in the world has its vicissitudes of light and shadow, and from its mixture with the kingdom of Antichrist and with tares it sometimes suffers grave loss; yet it ought not to have perished, as divine predictions confirm. 66. The manner in which the Church, pressed by its hostile kin, above all by Antichrist, was to be preserved, was also divinely foretold. 67. The history of the Church pressed and preserved under Antichrist. 68. A survey of the means by which the Church, pressed under Antichrist, was preserved. 69. The Church under Antichrist was not so obscured that it did not always show itself to be seen, through the confession and common work of Christianity, and also through the manifestation of good men, above all through its distinct outbursts, which are explained. 70. Hence a more ready judgment of reception [ὑποδοχὴ] is possible concerning the Church before the Reformation. 71. The objection of our adversaries, that our Church before the Reformation did not unite and conform itself with any other true visible Church, is refuted. 72. The Church separating itself from the Papacy did not separate itself from the true Church. 73. The marks by which the Papists claim the true Church is recognised are not proposed as all of one kind. 74. The epithets of the Church found in the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed, that it is One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic, are not all of the same mark. 75. Bellarmine's fifteen marks, by which they investigate the Church, are brought to examination. 76. Such as the name Catholic and Christian. 77. Antiquity. 78. Duration. 79. Extent, or the multitude of believers. 80. An uninterrupted succession of bishops from the Apostles, continued in the Roman Church down to this day. 81. Agreement in doctrine with the ancient Church and the Fathers. 82. Union of the members with one another and with the head. 83. Holiness of doctrine. 84. Efficacy of doctrine. 85. Holiness of life among the authors and Fathers of the religion. 86. The glory of miracles. 87. Prophetic light. 88. The confession of the adversaries. 89. The unhappy end of the enemies of the Church. 90. Temporal felicity. 91. Scripture does not obscurely ascribe the preceding marks to Antichrist and the synagogue of Satan, so that they are rather marks of those than of the true Church. 92.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: OEDERIS Gratiæ, & beneficiorum ejus sub quolibet œconomia Fœderis Gratiæ, nec non obsignationis eorundem, singuli quidem electi, vocati & fideles, sed arcta communione invicem colligati, subjectum sunt. Quibus ita colligatis Ecclesiæ nomen in Scripturis impositum est. Sicut enim Christus dilexit ἐκκλησίαν Ecclesiam, & se pro ea exposuit, Ephes. V. 25. acquisivit Ecclesiam proprio suo sanguine, Actor. XX. 28. sic Ecclesiæ, ceu corpori suo salutem dat, Ephes. V. 23. eam lavacro aquæ per verbum sanctificat, ut tandem eam sistat gloriosam, absque macula & ruga, sanctam & inculpatam, ibid. v. 26. 27. atque ita eam in hac vita conservat, ut ne portæ quidem inferorum ei prævaleant, Matth. XVI. 18. Non enim vel Deus ab æterno singulos à se divulsos, sed conjunctos, ἡμᾶς nos omnes junctos, ceu corpus unum in Christo capite elegit, Ephes. I. 4. vel Christus fidelium singulorum dissipatorum, & membrorum luxatorum atque fluitantium, sed corporis sui, cujus membra nos sumus ex carne ejus, & ex ossibus ejus, Caput & Salvator est, Ephes. V. 23. 30. vel Spiritus S. fideles singulos seorsim tantùm, sed πάντας εἰς ἓν σῶμα omnes in unum corpus baptizari curat, 1. Cor. XII. 13. Hoc corpus quippe ex variis membris compositum & coagmentatum, Eph. IV. 16. Ecclesia est, Semen, Regnum, hæreditas, peculium, populus Christi, palmarium S. S. Trinitatis opus, in quo universa Dei sapientia, potentia & gratia ab initio mundi, ad extremum ejus finem usque, laborat, & per partes se spectandam præbet: vellus illud Gedeonis, in quod unum solúmque omnis cœlestium benedictionum ros affatim depluit. Absque quo esset, frustra mysterium Patris atque Filii, & unctionis ejus revelatum esset; neque Christus vel Propheta, vel Sacerdos, vel Rex esse posset sine populo, cui voluntatem Patris exponeret, pro quo se offerret, & cui, tanquam peculio suo dominaretur.
units.tr: The covenant of grace, and its benefits under whatever economy of the covenant of grace, together with the seals of these, belong to individual persons who are elect, called and believers, but who are also bound together in close communion with one another. It is to these persons, so bound, that the name Church is given in the Scriptures. For just as Christ loved the Church (ἐκκλησία) and gave himself up for her (Eph. 5:25), and acquired the Church with his own blood (Acts 20:28), so he gives salvation to the Church as to his own body (Eph. 5:23), sanctifies her by the washing of water through the word, so that at last he may present her glorious, without spot or wrinkle, holy and blameless (ibid. vv. 26, 27), and so preserves her in this life that the gates of hell shall not prevail against her (Matt. 16:18). For God did not from eternity choose individuals separated from one another, but chose us all joined together (ἡμᾶς, us all) as one body in Christ the head (Eph. 1:4). Nor is Christ the head and Saviour of scattered believers, and of dislocated and floating members, but of his body, of which we are members, from his flesh and from his bones (Eph. 5:23, 30). Nor does the Holy Spirit baptise individual believers apart from one another, but takes care that all (πάντας) are baptised into one body (1 Cor. 12:13). Indeed, this body, composed and joined together from various members (Eph. 4:16), is the Church: the seed, the kingdom, the inheritance, the peculiar people, the people of Christ, the chief work of the Holy Trinity, in which the whole wisdom, power and grace of God labours from the beginning of the world to its very end, and displays itself to be seen piece by piece. It is that fleece of Gideon, upon which alone the dew of all heavenly blessings falls abundantly. Without it the mystery of the Father and the Son and of his anointing would have been revealed in vain; nor could Christ be prophet, priest or king without a people, to whom he would declare the will of the Father, for whom he would offer himself, and over whom, as his own peculiar people, he would rule.

units.la: II. Ecclesiæ vox Græca, ἀπὸ τῆς ἐκκαλέων evocando dicta, id ipsum notat, quod aliás ἀγορά, & Latinis concio. Ecclesia enim profanis Scriptoribus concio est, hoc est, non optimatum coetus tantùm, sed eorum etiam, qui è plebe sunt; à con & ciere, hoc est, convocare, quia singuli edicto publico proposito in concionem evocabantur. Etiam in lingua Latina vestigia ejus vocis extant, dum quædam comitia calata seu convocata vocant. Itaque inde primitus dicta Ecclesia videri potest, quòd sit multitudo hominum evocatorum, qui jussi sunt ponere curam rei domesticæ ad tempus, egredi domo, & curare Rempublicam, ídque ut fieri posset, unum in locum convenire. Sed in Scripturis alio sensu Ecclesia dicitur, ad designandam multitudinem quandam hominum. Nam in V. T. sæpe קהל occurrit, quod ἐκκλησίαν Græci reddunt, eo sensu ut significet coetum, seu multitudinem hominum quacunque de causa consociatorum & in unum locum coactorum, adeò ut etiam legamus in Vulgato Interprete: Odi (קהל) Ecclesiam malignantium, Psal. XXVI. 5. & passim populus Israelis non per familias dispersus, sed unum in locum congregatus, profanorum more, ἐκκλησίας Ecclesiæ nomine veniat. Unde היום הקהל Deut. IX. 10. XVIII. 16. in N.T. dicitur ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ in Ecclesia, seu Divinis comitiis, Actor. VII. 38. Ubi verò de coetu, qui stato tempore & loco convenit, adeóque de coetu lege quadam evocato, sermo est, tum non קהל ἐκκλησίας, sed עדה, quod Græci συναγωγὴν synagogam interpretantur, & multitudinem concitorum ex condicto notat, nomine venit; à יעד condicere, seu convenire facere. Est verò etiam ubi duo illa conjunguntur ἐπαλλήλως ישראל כל קהל עדת συναγωγῆς omnis concio vel coetus congregatorum, Exod. XII. 6. Et Solomon: Parvo momento extiti in omni malo בתוך קהל ועדה ἐν μέσῳ ἐκκλησίας καὶ συναγωγῆς in medio comitii & coetus delecti, Prov. V. 14. q. d. in medio comitii & concionis populi, præsidentibus iis, qui ad hoc σεσημειωμένοι sunt. Unde הקבל העדה facere ut totus coetus in concionem coeat, Lev. VIII. 3. quod ἐκκλησιάζεσθαι congregare coetum in unum locum est. Sed vocem tamen קהל Græci modò ἐκκλησίαν, modò συναγωγὴν, adeóque inconstanter reddunt. De eo quicquid sit, manifeste in locis citatis קהל & עדה distinguuntur: atque
units.tr: II. The Greek word ἐκκλησία, said to be derived from ἐκκαλεῖν (to call out), means the same thing as ἀγορά elsewhere, and concio in Latin. For among profane writers ἐκκλησία is a sermon or assembly, that is, not only a gathering of the nobles, but also of those who are of the common people; from con- and ciere, that is, to convoke, because each person was called out to the assembly by a public proclamation. Traces of this word also survive in the Latin language, when we speak of certain comitia calata or convoked assemblies. So the Church may be seen to have been named first from this, that it is a multitude of called-out men, who were ordered to set aside the care of their household affairs for the time being, to go out of their homes, and to attend to the commonwealth; and so that this could happen, they were to meet in one place. But in the Scriptures the Church is spoken of in another sense, to designate a certain multitude of men. For in the Old Testament the word קהל often occurs, which the Greeks render ἐκκλησία, in the sense that it signifies an assembly, or multitude of men joined together and gathered into one place for whatever reason; so that we even read in the Vulgate translator: "I have hated the Church (קהל) of evildoers" (Ps. 26:5). And everywhere the people of Israel, not dispersed by families but gathered into one place, is, after the manner of profane writers, called by the name ἐκκλησία, Church. Hence היום הקהל (Deut. 9:10; 18:16) is in the New Testament called ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, in the Church, or divine assembly (Acts 7:38). But where the discussion is of an assembly which meets at a fixed time and place, and so of an assembly called together by some rule, the word is not קהל (ἐκκλησία) but עדה, which the Greeks translate συναγωγή, synagogue, and which signifies a multitude of those summoned by agreement; it comes from יעד, to agree or bring about a meeting. There are also places where both words are joined together alternately: ישראל כל קהל עדת (συναγωγῆς), all the assembly or congregation of the gathered Israel (Exod. 12:6). And Solomon says: "I was almost in all evil in the midst of the assembly and congregation" (בתוך קהל ועדה, ἐν μέσῳ ἐκκλησίας καὶ συναγωγῆς) (Prov. 5:14), that is, in the midst of the assembly and gathering of the people, with those presiding who have been appointed for this purpose. Hence הקבל העדה, to make the whole congregation assemble into the sermon (Lev. 8:3), which is ἐκκλησιάζεσθαι, to gather the congregation into one place. But the Greeks render the word קהל sometimes ἐκκλησία, sometimes συναγωγή, and so inconsistently. Whatever be the case with that, in the places cited קהל and עדה are clearly distinguished; and

units.la: קהל & עדה con-venientia. atque ita distingui possunt, ut קהל multitudinem collectam, seu confusaneam illam, seu ἐννομον legitimam, Actor. XIX. 39. at עדה multitudinem, cui ex condicto convenire fas est, significet. Perperam proin Augustinus, Linguæ Hebraicæ imperitia, Ecclesiam hominum, synagogam belluarum, quæ non vocantur, sed in unum coguntur, congregationem dixit, inde factum putans, quòd Ecclesia Christiana ποίμνη gregis, seu ovilis nomine Luc. XII. 32. venit. Et συνάγεσθαι congregari etiam Christiani dicuntur, Matth. XIII. 2. XVIII. 20. Joh. XI. 52. Et Ecclesia etiam confusanea concio esse potest: Synagoga verò non item. Omnis עדה synagoga etiam קהל ἐκκλησία est; sed non vicissim. Sed alia tamen notio est vocis ἐκκλησία in Novo Testamento, ubi non tantùm multitudinem hominum in unum locum coactorum, sed etiam multitudinem seorsim habitantium & viventium, quam Deus iisdem oculis intuetur, ac si unum in locum convenissent, quia, ubicunque sit, tota velut in unum locum coacta oculis Dei subjicitur, significat. Unde obiter Bellarmini, qui ex eo, quod in V. T. Ecclesiæ nomen semper visibilem coetum significat, Ecclesiam in N. T. coetum semper visibilem esse conclusit, ἀσυλλογίστως cernere est. Nam & ipsi Judæi hodie קהל Ἐκκλησίαν non coetus suos, qui in synagogis congregantur, qui iis nomine כנסת & כנישה Συναγωγῆς congregationis in unum locum veniunt; sed religiosam societatem, quæ inter eos est, sive convenientes unum in locum, sive non; appellant; quomodo nos Ecclesias dicimus plurali numero non Ecclesiam universalem, sed eas societates particulares, ex quibus Ecclesia universalis conflatur; Velut cùm Anglicanas, Germanicas dicimus. Sed Apostoli refugerunt vocabulum כנישה Συναγωγῆς collectionis, quod Judæi suum fecerunt; nullo eorum odio, superstitione nulla, sed tum ut fidelium præcipuè ex gentibus coetus à synagogis Judæorum, quæ magna pertinacia Christum rejecerunt, hoc nomine distinguerentur: tum quia nomen Ecclesiæ, utpote de νομίμοις legitimis, Actor. XIX. 39. honestis & ordinatis inter ipsas conventibus usitatum, uti ex Aristotele, Demosthene, Thucydide constat, notius erat: tum quia declarandæ naturæ multitudinis credentium aprimè accommodatum est.
units.tr: קהל and עדה agree, and yet can be so distinguished that קהל signifies a gathered multitude, or that confused crowd, or ἔννομον lawful assembly (Acts 19:39), whereas עדה signifies a multitude to which it is right to come together by agreement. Therefore Augustine wrongly, through ignorance of the Hebrew language, called the Church the gathering of men and the synagogue the gathering of beasts, which are not called but driven together into one place, thinking this came about because the Christian Church is named ποίμνη, flock, or ovilis, sheepfold, in Luke 12:32. And Christians are also said to be συνάγεσθαι, gathered together (Matt. 13:2; 18:20; John 11:52). And the Church can also be a confused assembly; but the synagogue cannot be so. Every עדה synagogue is also a קהל ἐκκλησία, but not conversely. But the word ἐκκλησία has another meaning in the New Testament, where it signifies not only a multitude of men gathered into one place, but also a multitude living and dwelling separately, which God regards with the same eyes as if they had come together into one place, because wherever it is, the whole is, as it were, gathered into one place and placed before the eyes of God. Hence it is evident how inconsequently Bellarmine concluded, from the fact that in the Old Testament the name Church always signifies a visible assembly, that the Church in the New Testament is always a visible assembly.
