For even the Jews today do not call their Ἐκκλησίαν the assemblies which gather in their synagogues, and which come together into one place under the names כנסת and כנישה, συναγωγῆς congregationis; they call it the religious society which exists among them, whether they meet in one place or not. In the same way we say Churches in the plural, not the universal Church, meaning those particular societies out of which the universal Church is put together; as when we speak of the English or German churches. But the Apostles avoided the word כנישה, συναγωγῆς collectionis, which the Jews had made their own; not from any hatred of it, nor from any superstition, but so that the assembly of believers, chiefly from the Gentiles, might be distinguished by this name from the synagogues of the Jews, who with great obstinacy rejected Christ; and also because the name Church, customary for lawful and orderly assemblies (as is clear from Aristotle, Demosthenes and Thucydides), and drawn from νομίμοις legitimis (Acts 19:39), was better known; and also because it was most suitable for declaring the nature of the multitude of believers.

units.la: III. Vox Ἐκκλησίας Ecclesiæ nuspiam sive in Veteri, sive in Novo Testamento ædem sacram notat. Frustra enim Bellarminus ex V. T. locum Judith, cap. VI. 10. ubi Bethulienses εἰς τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν in Ecclesiam convenisse dicuntur, allegat, quia non sic author libri scripsit, sed verba illa ἐν τῳ ἱερῳ adjecta videntur. Sed de eo quicquid sit, in Novo certè Testamento nuspiam vocis ἐκκλησίας ille usus occurrit, quicquid etiam Doctissimo Fullero placuerit. Nam Apostolus I. Cor. XI. 18. dicens: Συνερχομένων ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, cùm convenitis in Ecclesia, audio inter vos esse schismata, &c. non ædem sacram, sed conventus religiosi, ubicunque ille instituatur, sanctitatem significat. Et quòd convenire ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ idem v. 20. dixit, non tam locum, quàm personarum conjunctionem notat, ut sensus sit, convenire simul, nulla habita ratione loci, licèt impossibile sit simul convenire, qui non sunt eodem loco. Sed horum tamen alterum prius, alterum posterius est. Appetitur enim locus propter conjunctionem, non conjunctio propter locum. Idem enim est ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό, & Hebræum יחד, quæ vox, cùm de conventu agitur, respectum notat, non personarum ad locum, sed personarum inter se. Sensus igitur est, convenisse ἅμα simul, ὁμοθυμαδὸν unanimiter. Idem Apostolus interrogans, vers. 22. An domus non habetis ad edendum & bibendum? non tam locum privatum publico, seu Ecclesiæ, quàm conventum plurium inspectantium loco, in quo nemo inspectat, opponit. Quomodo S. Paulus I. Cor. XIV. 34. 35. jubens mulieres ἐν Ἐκκλησίαις in Ecclesiis tacere, & ἐν οἴκῳ domi maritos interrogare, non tam loco locum opponit, quia nefas non est mulierem interrogare virum, vel loqui in eo loco, ubi publicè convenitur; sed in conventu publico & Ecclesiastico mulierem loqui vetat. Ibidem v. 40. omnia εὐσχημόνως decenter & ordine fieri jubet. Sed decorum & ordo non à loco pendet, quia aliàs decorum & ordo nullus in conventibus primorum Christianorum antelucanis fuisset. Nam ut in publico semper loco conveniatur, sola pacis & tranquillitatis publicæ tempora permittunt. Tenendum igitur est, Ecclesiæ nomen in N. T. neque conventum proprie, neque locum, in quo convenitur, significare, licèt junctum nomini aut verbo significet conventum, ut cùm dicitur, convenire in Ecclesiam; loqui in Ecclesia.
units.tr: III. The word Ἐκκλησίας (Church) signifies nowhere, either in the Old or the New Testament, a sacred building. Bellarmine is wrong to cite from the Old Testament the passage of Judith 6:10, where the men of Bethulia are said to have come together εἰς τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν, into the Church; for the author of the book did not write thus, but those words ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ, in the temple, seem to have been added. But whatever be the case with that, in the New Testament certainly that usage of the word ἐκκλησίας nowhere occurs, whatever may have pleased the most learned Fuller. For the Apostle, saying Συνερχομένων ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, "when you come together in the Church" (1 Cor. 11:18), I hear that there are schisms among you, etc., signifies not a sacred building but a religious assembly, wherever it is held. And when in v. 20 he said that they come together ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό, into the same place, he signifies not so much a place as the joining of persons, so that the sense is to come together at the same time, without regard to place, although it is impossible to come together at the same time if they are not in the same place. Yet of these two, the one is first and the other second: for the place is sought on account of the union, not the union on account of the place. For ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό is the same as the Hebrew יחד, a word which, when an assembly is in question, denotes a relation not of persons to a place but of persons to one another. The sense, therefore, is that they came together ἅμα, at the same time, ὁμοθυμαδόν, with one accord. The same Apostle, asking in v. 22, An domus non habetis ad edendum & bibendum? "Have you not houses for eating and drinking?", sets against the public place, that is the Church, not so much a private place as a gathering of several people looking on, in a place where no one is looking. In the same way St. Paul, in 1 Cor. 14:34-35, bidding women ἐν Ἐκκλησίαις, "keep silent in the Churches", and ἐν οἴκῳ, "ask their husbands at home", sets place against place not so much because it is wrong for a woman to question a man, or to speak in that place where a public gathering is held, but because he forbids a woman to speak in a public and ecclesiastical assembly. In the same passage (v. 40) he orders that all things be done εὐσχημόνως, "decently and in order". But decency and order do not depend on the place, for otherwise there would have been no decency or order in the assemblies of the first Christians, which were held before dawn. For only periods of peace and public tranquillity permit one always to meet in a public place. It must therefore be held that the name Church in the New Testament signifies neither the assembly properly, nor the place in which one meets, although when joined to the name or verb it signifies an assembly, as when it is said convenire in Ecclesiam, to come together into the Church, loqui in Ecclesia, to speak in the Church.

units.la: IV. Ecclesiæ ergo vox in N. T. coetum sacrum hominum ἐκκλησίαν evocatorum notat. Nam omnino in voce ἐκκλησίας est notio κλήσεως vocationis. Quod ex Actor. II. 47. liquet, ubi σῳζομένους τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν addi eos, qui salvantur. Ecclesiæ, respondet ei, quod v. 39. dictum est: ὅσους προσκαλέσηται ὁ Κύριος quos advocaverit Dominus. Est ergo Ecclesia coetus advocatorum à Domino. Quæ etiam ἡ κλῆσις, οἱ κλητοὶ, οἱ κεκλημένοι, vocatio & vocati I. Cor. I. 24. 26. appellatur. Nam qui ibi v. 24. κλητοὶ Ἰουδαῖοι καὶ Ἕλληνες vocati Judæi & Græci dicuntur, iidem cap. X. 32. Judæi, Græci καὶ Ἐκκλησία θεοῦ & Ecclesia Dei vocantur. Quia verò vocationis terminus est fides, & fidei opus est insitio in Christum, & unio hæc cum Christo communionem secum infert, hinc eodem planè sensu coetus fidelium, vel coetus eorum, qui sunt in Christo, vel coetus eorum, qui habent communionem cum Christo, definitur. Proin vox Ecclesiæ etiam unionem notat. Nam Ἐκκλησία sive sit קהל multitudinem congregatam; sive עדה multitudinem conscriptam, & ad conveniendum paratam significat. Coetus enim talium est, quia in multitudine consociata, vel communitate multorum non in uno aliquo vocato proprie consistit. Unde etiam corporis, domus, familiæ, civitatis, Regni, gregis &c. nominibus, unionem & communionem quandam implicantibus passim venit. Et sicut fides ita Christum respicit, ut per Christum etiam Deum respiciat: ita Ecclesia illa, quæ per fidem existit, ut ad Christum, tanquam ad caput, & per Christum ad Deum refertur. Unde Ecclesia σῶμα Χριστοῦ Corpus Christi, Col. I. 24. & Ecclesia etiam Dei, I. Cor. X. 32. Regnum Christi, Col. I. 13. & Regnum Dei, Rom. XIV. 17. dicitur.
units.tr: IV. The word Ecclesia in the New Testament therefore denotes a holy assembly of men called out [ἐκκλησίαν, evocatorum]. For the notion of calling [κλήσεως, vocationis] is entirely contained in the word ἐκκλησίας. This is clear from Acts 2:47, where those who are being saved [σῳζομένους] are added to the Church [τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν]. This corresponds to what is said in verse 39: whomever the Lord shall call [ὅσους προσκαλέσηται ὁ Κύριος]. The Church is therefore the assembly of those called by the Lord. It is also named ἡ κλῆσις, οἱ κλητοὶ, οἱ κεκλημένοι, that is, the calling and the called (1 Cor. 1:24, 26). For in verse 24 those who are called [κλητοὶ] Jews and Greeks are the same people who in 1 Cor. 10:32 are called Jews, Greeks, and the Church of God [καὶ Ἐκκλησία θεοῦ]. Since the goal of calling is faith, and the work of faith is engrafting into Christ, and this union with Christ brings communion with him, the assembly of believers is defined in exactly the same sense: either as the assembly of those who are in Christ, or as the assembly of those who have communion with Christ. Hence the word Ecclesia also signifies union. For Ἐκκλησία, whether it stands for קהל, a gathered multitude, or for עדה, a multitude that has been enrolled and is ready to assemble, means the same. For such an assembly is not properly located in one person who is called, but in a united multitude or fellowship of many. Therefore the Church is also frequently named by terms that imply union and a certain communion, such as body, house, family, city, kingdom, and flock. And just as faith looks to Christ, and through Christ also looks to God, so the Church, which exists through faith, is referred to Christ as its head, and through Christ to God. Hence the Church is called the body of Christ [σῶμα Χριστοῦ, Corpus Christi] (Col. 1:24), and also the Church of God (1 Cor. 10:32), the kingdom of Christ (Col. 1:13), and the kingdom of God (Rom. 14:17).

units.la: V. Sed haec ἐκ τῶν ἐιζῶν à radicibus, quod ajunt, imisque stirpibus eruere, & verae falsaeque Ecclesiae ideam ex Dei verbo omni fide studiósque repraesentare juvabit. Vix enim satis diversa, imò contraria illa idea inculcari infigíque potest, hoc inprimis tempore, quo Jesuitae, aliíque Papatus Atlantes Ecclesio-latrae palmarium hoc artificium struunt, ut deserta Scriptura nihil nisi Ecclesiam jactent, & Ecclesiam nominantes, vel unum Papam, Aristotele chorago, qui Ethic. IX. 9. civitatem id maximè esse docet, quod in ea ἀεχον principale seu dominans est; vel certè Monarchiam Ecclesiasticam, seu universitatem Praelatorum in Conciliis, sub uno capite Papa congregatorum, intelligant; fuco veteratorio, ut ex Ecclesia dominante ficta doctrinam obtrudant, non ex doctrina Ecclesiam unam formen t. Revera enim iis Ecclesia non aliud, quàm Monarchia temporalis, mysterii & religionis praetextu quaesita, terrenum & summum in Imperatores, Reges & principes populúmque Christianum universum, quin & infideles ipsos partim actu proferens, partim jure confi-cto, praetendens. Haec enim illa larva est, sub qua Methodistae prodeuntes, & terram atque maria, ad proselytos lucrandos pervagantes, pro virgine cervam, & pro flore Floram, non imperitis duntaxat & jam subjugatis clientibus suis, sed oculatioribus etiam audacter obtrudere conantur. Animadvertunt enim probè, primò ipsum nomen Ecclesiae, seu dominantis Monarchiae omnibus terrorem incutere & obedientiam imperare; & dein ita triticum paleae immixtum esse, ut non cuivis illa secernere datum sit.
units.tr: V. But it will be helpful to uproot, as they say, this idea from its very roots and deepest stock, and to set forth with all faith and diligence the true and false idea of the Church from the Word of God. For that idea, so different and indeed contrary, can hardly be impressed and fixed firmly enough, especially at this time, when the Jesuits and other Atlases of the Papacy, the idolaters of the Church, are devising this supreme trick: that, Scripture being neglected, they boast of nothing but the Church, and by naming the Church they mean either the one Pope, with Aristotle as their guide, who teaches in Ethics IX.9 that a city is most of all that in which the principal or ruling element lies; or certainly they mean the ecclesiastical monarchy, that is, the body of prelates gathered in councils under one head, the Pope. They use this deceitful trickery so that from a feigned dominating Church they may force doctrine on people, instead of forming one Church from doctrine. For in truth the Church, for them, is nothing other than a temporal monarchy, sought under the pretext of mystery and religion, which puts forward its earthly and supreme power over emperors, kings, princes, and the whole Christian people, and even partly exercises it over unbelievers in fact and partly claims it by fabricated right. For this is the mask under which the Methodists come forward, wandering over land and sea to win proselytes, and they boldly try to foist upon their more discerning clients, not just the unskilled and already subjugated, a stag for a virgin and Flora for a flower. For they clearly perceive that, first, the very name of the Church, or of a dominating monarchy, strikes terror into all and commands obedience; and second, that the wheat is so mixed with chaff that it is not given to everyone to separate them.

units.la: VI. Ecclesia vera in S. Literis duobus modis, vel propriè, emphaticè & augustè, vel minùs propriè & paulò latius accipitur. Propriè & augustè Ecclesia est coetus seu collectio hominum electorum, vocatorum & fidelium, quos Deus per verbum & Spiritum è statu peccati in statum gratiae ad aeternam gloriam vocat. Ita finit ipse Angelus, Ecclesiam indigetans eos, qui cum Agno, ceu Domino Dominorum & Rege regum, militantes, sunt κλητοὶ καὶ ἐκλεκτοὶ, καὶ πιστοὶ vocati, electi & fideles, Apoc. XVII. 14. Qui cum Agno, Domino Dominorum & Rege Regum Christo sunt, & ab ejus partibus stant, haud dubiè illi vera Christi Ecclesia, Christi populus & exercitus sunt. Hi autem, finitore Angelo, vocati, electi & fideles sunt. Sunt autem quidam vocati, at non electi, Matth. XX. 16. XXII. 14. Ab his Angelus eos, qui cum Christo sunt, sic discernit, quòd sint κλητοὶ vocati, sed non quovis modo, vel quivis quovis modo, sed sic vocati, ut etiam sint electi, adeóque κλητοὶ κατὰ πρόθεσιν vocati secundum propositum, Rom. VIII. 28. & πιστοὶ fideles, quia vocationis secundum propositum terminus est fides, sicut fidei opus est insitio in Christum & unio atque communio cum Christo. Non ergo Ecclesia simpliciter coetus vocatorum & electorum est, quia nec externè tantùm, & non etiam internè vocati, nec electi, at nondum vocati & fideles Ecclesia, vel ejus membra sunt; sed coetus est vocatorum, electorum, hoc est, secundum electionem in tempore vocatorum per verbum & Spiritum Dei, & simul fidelium, seu per fidem Christo, ut membra capiti, insitorum. Omnes Ecclesiae ci-ves electi sunt: sed non omnes electi Ecclesiae cives sunt, nisi destinatione & datione Testamenti, quo scripti sunt haereditas Christi; & postulatione Redemptoris. Quo sensu definitio illa Johannis Hus-si, quòd universalis Ecclesia fit praedestinatorum universitas in Concilio Constantiensi haereseos damnata, intelligenda est. Sed electi tamen prius quam regenerantur per sanctificationem Spiritus ad fidem veritatis, sicut actu extra Christum, ita etiam actu extra Ecclesiam, sub ira, & in eo statu sunt, in quo si manerent, Ecclesiae aggregari & servari non possent. Sed vocatio electionis Rom. IX. 11. efficit, ut in illo statu non maneant, sed per verbum invitationis & potentiam Spiritus vocentur, sive adducantur, ut in Christo sint. Ita Paulus electus destinatione erat membrum Ecclesiae, etiam in Pharisaismo, cùm Ecclesiam persequeretur, actu vero membrum ejus per gratiam vocationis factus est, Gal. I. 15.
units.tr: VI. In Holy Scripture the true Church is understood in two ways: either properly, emphatically and in its noblest sense, or less properly and more broadly. Properly and in its noblest sense, the Church is the assembly or collection of chosen, called and faithful men, whom God calls by the Word and the Spirit from the state of sin into the state of grace to eternal glory. So the Angel himself defines it, naming the Church as those who, fighting with the Lamb, as Lord of lords and King of kings, are called, chosen and faithful (Rev. 17:14). Those who are with the Lamb, the Lord of lords and King of kings Christ, and stand on his side, are without doubt the true Church of Christ, the people and army of Christ. Now, according to the Angel's definition, they are called, chosen and faithful. But some are called and not chosen (Matt. 20:16; 22:14). The Angel distinguishes from these those who are with Christ in this way: they are called, but not in any manner or by just any manner, but so called that they are also chosen, and so are κλητοὶ κατὰ πρόθεσιν, called according to purpose (Rom. 8:28), and πιστοὶ, faithful. For the goal of calling according to purpose is faith, just as the work of faith is engrafting into Christ and union and communion with Christ. Therefore the Church is not simply an assembly of called and chosen people, because those who are called only outwardly, and not inwardly, and those who are not yet called and faithful, are not the Church or members of it. Rather, it is an assembly of called, chosen people, that is, of those called in time according to election through the Word and Spirit of God, and at the same time faithful, that is, grafted through faith into Christ as members into the head. All the citizens of the Church are chosen, but not all the chosen are citizens of the Church, except by the destination and bestowal of the Testament, by which they are written as the heirs of Christ, and by the appointment of the Redeemer. In this sense the definition of John Hus, that the universal Church is the universality of the predestinate, which was condemned as heresy at the Council of Constance, must be understood. But the elect, before they are regenerated by the sanctification of the Spirit to the faith of truth, are, just as they are actually outside Christ, so also actually outside the Church, under wrath, and in that state in which, if they remained, they could not be joined to the Church or preserved. But the calling of election (Rom. 9:11) brings it about that they do not remain in that state, but are called, or brought, through the word of invitation and the power of the Spirit, so that they are in Christ. Thus Paul, elect by destination, was a member of the Church even while in Pharisaism, when he was persecuting the Church; but he was made a member of it in fact by the grace of calling (Gal. 1:15).

units.la: VII. Triplicem omnino vocati differentiam recipiunt. Vel enim ii sunt, qui vocationem, seu invitationem simpliciter audiunt; vel ii, qui ita se componunt, ut vocanti parere, & ad eum jam adducti videantur: vel ii, qui revera per verbum Dei, & vocationem aeterni propositi, ac potentiae Spiritus Dei adducti sunt, & per fidem in Christo existunt, quomodo Deus vocat ea, quae non sunt, Rom. IV. 17. & קרא הדורות מראש vocat generationes ab initio, Esaj. XLI. 4. quae ipsa jussio, imperium Dei, ut res sint, est; Psal. XXXIII. 9. Nam per verbum promissionis, tanquam declarationem Testamenti, nascuntur Abrahamo filii, Rom. IX. 8. Gal. IV. 28. Cujus verbi specimen est: In Isaco vocabitur tibi Semen, Rom. IX. 7. Quod verbum ab ipso Deo immediatè profectum in aeternum stat, & potens est omnia efficere, quae per id jubentur; etiam regenerationem mortuorum in peccatis, imò excitationem filiorum Abrahami ex lapidibus, 1. Petr. I. 23. 24. 25. Matth. III. 9. Haec ergo illa vocatio sancta, secundum propositum, & gratiam datam in Christo Jesu ante tempora saecularia, 2. Timoth. I. 9. est, à qua Ecclesia coetus vocatorum appellatur.
units.tr: VII. The called receive altogether a threefold difference. For either they are those who simply hear the calling or invitation; or those who so dispose themselves that they seem to obey the one calling and have already been brought to him; or those who in truth are drawn by the Word of God and the calling of eternal purpose and the power of the Spirit of God, and exist in faith in Christ. This is how God calls those things that are not (Rom. 4:17), and קרא הדורות מראש, calls the generations from the beginning (Isa. 41:4). That calling is itself the command and authority of God, that things may be (Ps. 33:9). For through the Word of promise, as a declaration of the Testament, children are born to Abraham (Rom. 9:8; Gal. 4:28). An example of this word is: In Isaac shall your seed be called (Rom. 9:7). This Word, proceeding immediately from God himself, stands for ever and is able to bring about all that is commanded by it, even the regeneration of the dead in sins, and indeed the raising up of children of Abraham from stones (1 Pet. 1:23–25; Matt. 3:9). This, then, is that holy calling, according to purpose and the grace given in Christ Jesus before the world began (2 Tim. 1:9), and from it the Church is called the assembly of the called.

units.la: VIII. Vocationis Ecclesiae causa Deus est, qui per verbum & Spiritum S. vocat. Principalis enim causa Ecclesiae est Deus omnis gratiae, quae vocavit nos ad aeternam gloriam in Christo Jesu, 1. Petr. V. 10. Fidelis enim est, per quem vocati estis in communionem Filii ipsius, 1. Cor. I. 9. Singulariter verò Jesus Christus, qui Ecclesiam sanguine suo acquisivit, Act. XX. 28. eamque purificat & aeterna salute donat, Ephes. V. 26. &c. Est enim caput super omnia Ecclesiae, quae corpus ipsius est, ibid. I. 22. Col. II. 19. Nam quae in capite physico spectari solent, dignitas ordinis, perfectionum omnium amplitudo, virtus movendi & vivificandi; & quae in capite mystico insuper requiritur, durationis perpetuitas; illa universa in Christo Ecclesiae capite; & solo illo repetiuntur. Ac licet vocatio Dei sit potens imperium & jussio, ut existant, seu adducantur, qui vocati sunt, tamen ordinariè adductio illa non fit sine vocatione, quae promiscuè secundum imperium immortalis Dei per homines verbi praecones proponitur; Quomodo enim credent, si non audiverint? Quomodo audient audient sine praedicante? Rom. X. 14. Volens genuit nos verbo veritatis, ut simus primitiæ creaturarum ejus, Jac. I. 18. Regeniti sumus διὰ λόγου ζῶντος per sermonem viventem Dei & manentem in seculum, 1. Petr. I. 23. Vocavit nos per Evangelium suum,ad acquisitionem gloriæ Domini nostri Jesu Christi, 2. Thess. II. 14. Et sicut Deus vocationem illam secundum electionem gratiæ procurat ἰδίοις καιροῖς propriis suis temporibus, 1. Tim. II. 6. ita etiam, quibus ipsi videtur, locis. Tum etiam non omnes electi jam quoque fideles vel vocati sunt; sed qui & præconii κατηχούμενοι vocati, & ab æterno electi in Christo, ut essent sancti, Eph. I. 4. & jam verbum ἀκοῆς in bono corde, quod Dominus præparat cum fide, qua Spiritus S. corda purificat, Actor. XV. 9. exceperunt, adeóque electi, seu opere ipso à pereuntibus secreti sunt ἐν ἁγιασμῷ Πνεύματος εἰς ὑπακοὴν καὶ ῥαντισμὸν τοῦ αἵματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ κατὰ πρόγνωσιν Θεοῦ Πατρὸς in vel per sanctificationem Spiritus regenerantis ad obedientiam fidei, & in fide ad aspersionem sanguinis Jesu Christi, hoc est, justificationem, secundum præcognitionem Dei Patris, seu electionem ante jacta mundi fundamenta factam, 1. Petr. I. 1. 2. illi proprie & κυριολεκτῶς Ecclesia Dei sunt, & à vocatis, hoc est, vel invitatis tantum, vel etiam ad suscipiendum ac profitendum nomen Christi, sed non in veritate adductis distinguuntur.
units.tr: VIII. God is the cause of the calling of the Church: he calls through the Word and the Holy Spirit. The principal cause of the Church is God of all grace, who has called us to his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, 1 Pet. 5:10. For he is faithful, through whom you have been called into the fellowship of his Son, 1 Cor. 1:9. But especially Jesus Christ, who acquired the Church with his own blood, Acts 20:28, and cleanses it and grants it eternal salvation, Eph. 5:26, etc. For he is head over all things to the Church, which is his body, ibid. 1:22; Col. 2:19. What is usually looked for in a physical head, namely the dignity of rank, the fullness of all perfections, and the power to move and quicken, and what is additionally required in a mystical head, namely the perpetuity of endurance, all of these are found together in Christ, the head of the Church, and in him alone. Although God's calling is a powerful command and decree, bringing into existence or drawing near those who are called, that drawing near ordinarily does not happen without a calling, which is proclaimed indiscriminately through men, the heralds of the Word, according to the command of the immortal God: For how will they believe if they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher? Rom. 10:14. Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we might be the firstfruits of his creatures, Jas. 1:18. We have been born again through the living word [διὰ λόγου ζῶντος] of God, which abides forever, 1 Pet. 1:23. He called us through his Gospel to obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, 2 Thess. 2:14. And just as God brings about that calling according to the election of grace in its own times [ἰδίοις καιροῖς], 1 Tim. 2:6, so also he does it in the places that seem good to him. Moreover, not all the elect are yet believers or called; but those who have been called to the catechumenate, and who were chosen from eternity in Christ that they should be holy, Eph. 1:4, and who have now received the word of hearing [ἀκοῆς] in a good heart, which the Lord prepares together with the faith by which the Holy Spirit purifies the hearts, Acts 15:9, these are elect, or are set apart from those who perish by the work itself, in sanctification of the Spirit unto obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ [ἐν ἁγιασμῷ Πνεύματος εἰς ὑπακοὴν καὶ ῥαντισμὸν τοῦ αἵματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ κατὰ πρόγνωσιν Θεοῦ Πατρός], that is, by the sanctification of the Spirit who regenerates to obedience of faith, and by faith to the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ, that is, to justification, according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, or the election made before the foundation of the world, 1 Pet. 1:1-2. These are properly and strictly the Church of God, and they are distinguished from those who are merely invited, or who are brought in only in name to profess the name of Christ, but not in truth.

units.la: IX. Dubitari enim non potest, in Scriptura Ecclesiam veram proprie φεψωνύμως & augustiore sensu describi, quando עדת צריקים coetum justorum, Psal. I. 5. גוי צדיק שמר אמנים gentem, justam, quæ veritatem servat, Esaj. XXVI. 2. יהוה כלם צדיקים populum Domini, omnes justos, ibid. LX. 21. memorat. Et Apostoli ad Ecclesias scribentes, fideles, sanctos, vocatos sæpius insigniunt; & S. Petrus Ecclesiam, ceu electos à pereuntibus secretos & assumptos, secundum præcognitionem Dei per sanctificationem Spiritus, ad obedientiam & aspersionem sanguinis Jesu Christi, 1. Petr. I. 1. 2. circumscribit, quin & privilegia ejus edisserens eandem γένος ἐκλεκτὸν, βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα, ἔθνος ἅγιον, λαὸν περιποίησιν, genus electum, regale Sacerdotium, gentem sanctam, populum peculiarem, cap. II. 9. appellat. Neque profecto nisi vere & proprie dicta Ecclesia cogitari potest illa, quam Christus se petræ inædificare, & cui inferorum portas non prævalituras, Matth. XVI. 18. dixit; quæque domus Dei viventis, 1. Tim. III. 15. seu קהל אלהים Ecclesia Dei, Nehem. XIII. 1. & Ecclesia Χριστοῦ Christi, Matth. XVI. 18. habita relatione peculii ad Dominum, Regni ad Regem, consociatorum ad auctorem societatis, convenientium ad vocantem Christum; nec non indicato fine, nempe ut cum Christo sint, & ipsius aspectu ἐμφανισμῷ & alloquio fruantur; cujus caput Christus, Ephes. I. 22. quæ à Christo diligi, ibid. v. 25. & ejus ceu capitis corpus esse Col. I. 18. 24. dicitur. Talia enim elogia non alii quam Ecclesiæ proprie & augustiore sensu talis competere, prædicata illa testantur. Nam ædificari in petra, est Christo inædificari, & cum eo communionem per fidem, & in eo ac per eum robur & firmitudinem ad salutem habere: non superari à portis inferorum, est non manere in morte, non venire in judicium, non
units.tr: IX. For it cannot be doubted that Scripture describes the true Church properly, in a figurative and more exalted sense, when it speaks of the assembly of the righteous [עדת צדיקים], Ps. 1:5; a righteous nation that keeps the truth [גוי צדיק שמר אמנים], Isa. 26:2; the people of the Lord, all righteous [יהוה כלם צדיקים], ibid. 60:21. And the Apostles, writing to the churches, very often designate them as faithful, holy, called; and St. Peter defines the Church as the elect, set apart from those who perish and taken up, according to the foreknowledge of God, by the sanctification of the Spirit, to obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ, 1 Pet. 1:1-2. Indeed, unfolding its privileges, he calls it the same thing: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession [γένος ἐκλεκτὸν, βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα, ἔθνος ἅγιον, λαὸν περιποίησιν], ch. 2:9. Surely that Church which Christ said he would build on himself as the rock, and against which the gates of hell shall not prevail, Matt. 16:18, cannot be conceived except as truly and properly the Church. It is also the house of the living God, 1 Tim. 3:15; or the Church of God [קהל אלהים], Neh. 13:1; and the Church of Christ, Matt. 16:18. These names express the relation of a people to the Lord, of a kingdom to the King, of companions to the founder of the society, of those who assemble to Christ who calls them; and they indicate the end, namely that they may be with Christ and enjoy his presence [ἐμφανισμῷ] and speech; of this Church Christ is the head, Eph. 1:22; she is loved by Christ, ibid. v. 25; and she is said to be the body of him as its head, Col. 1:18, 24. For these praises testify that such titles belong to no other than the Church, properly and in the higher sense. For to be built on the rock is to be built into Christ, and to have communion with him through faith, and to have in him and through him strength and firmness for salvation. Not to be overcome by the gates of hell is not to remain in death, not to come into judgment, not to

units.la: rapi è manibus Christi, non fieri prædam Sathanæ. Domum Dei esse, est inhabitari à Deo, nos sibi in Templum & domum ornante, ut in nobis opus suum, hoc est, opus gratiæ moliatur, & nobis ceu filiis-familias, se ipsum cum omni affectu Patris-familias ἐμφανίζῃ manifestet & ostentet: Corpus Christi capitis esse, est Christo dari, cum eo conjungi, ab eo vivificari, per ejus spiritum, velut ex capite in corpus defluentem, penetrantem, atque illud donis implentem, vivere. Hæc, similiaque Ecclesiæ veræ ἀπολυτρωμένα non aliis, quàm vocatis, electis & fidelibus competere, meridiano sole clarius est. Unde etiam Ecclesiam proprie & emphatice dictam non aliam esse, quàm coetum vocatorum, electorum & fidelium, seu corpus Christi mysticum, ipsi, ceu capiti suo, juxta æternam electionem & temporalem vocationem constanter & intimè unitum, manifestè colligitur. Hæc enim illa מלכה Βασίλισσα Regina & Augusta, Psal. XLV. 10. Sponsa Christi, Cant. I. 1. &c. Filia Regis, cœlestis Patris, propter regenerationem, adeóque etiam Soror Regis Christi, ibid. V. 1. quam sibi Christus asciivit sociam, ut esset os ex ossibus ejus, caro ex carne ejus, Domina & hæres Regni ejus, summo post summum Dei honorem, honore decorata.
units.tr: be snatched out of the hands of Christ, not to become the prey of Satan. To be the house of God is to be inhabited by God, who adorns us for himself as a temple and house, so that he may work his work in us, that is, the work of grace, and so that he may show and display himself to us as children of the household, with all the affection of a father of the household. To be the body of Christ the head is to be given to Christ, to be joined to him, to be quickened by him, and to live by his Spirit, flowing from the head into the body, penetrating it and filling it with gifts. That these and similar things belong to the true Church, the redeemed [ἀπολυτρωμένα], and to none but the called, the elect and the faithful, is clearer than the noonday sun. Hence it is also plainly gathered that the Church properly and emphatically so called is nothing other than the assembly of the called, the elect and the faithful, or the mystical body of Christ, constantly and intimately united to him as to its head, according to eternal election and temporal calling. For this is that queen [מלכה] and Basilissa [Βασίλισσα], queen and empress, Ps. 45:10; the bride of Christ, Song 1:1, etc.; the daughter of the King, of the heavenly Father, by regeneration; and therefore also the sister of the King Christ, ibid. 5:1, whom Christ has taken as his partner, so that she is bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh, the mistress and heir of his kingdom, adorned with the highest honour after the highest honour of God.

units.la: X. Ecclesia cœtus hominum, non Angelorum est. Licet enim Angeli boni ratione aliqua ad Ecclesiam pertineant, propter unionem illam, quam cum Christo habent, conservationis gratiam ab illo communicatam, & ministerium, quod Ecclesiæ Divinitus ad illud missi navant, non tamen Ecclesiæ à Christo redemptæ membra homogenea sunt. Neque etiam illi, ut homines, vocati & fideles dici possunt. Cumque cœtus hominum, seu multitudo hominum unita sit, in uno consistere non potest, uti olim Elias 1. Reg. XIX. 10. opinabatur, & Pontificii de B. Virgine Maria & Papa, idolo suo, delirant. Nam unus non est populus Dei, grex, multitudo credentium, gens sancta, civitas Dei, corpus Christi, congregatio justorum, quibus nominibus passim Ecclesia venit. Neque quivis quorumvis hominum cœtus Ecclesia est; quia non omnes, sed pauci electi sunt, Matth. XX. 16. & fides non est omnium, 2. Thess. III. 2. sed eorum, quos Deus ab æterno electos in tempore separat, & ex genere humano maledictioni obnoxio καλεῖ vocat, atque fide donat. Ego vos elegi ex mundo, Joh. XV. 19. Notificavi nomen tuum hominibus, quos dedisti mihi ex mundo, ibid. XVII. 6. Quomodo etiam Israel ex Amorrhæis esse dicitur: Pater tuus est Amorrhæus, & mater tua Hittհæa, Ezech. XVI. 3. Quos ab æterno electos in tempore sic Deus vocat & salvat, illi soli Ecclesiæ veræ membra sunt. Non enim Scripturæ nota est illa Lutheranorum quorundam distinctio electorum & vocatorum specificè & proprie, & generaliter atque improprie sic dictorum, quorum illi gratia non excidant, hi excidere possint, & quandiu non excidunt, æquè ac illi Ecclesiæ membra sint. Nuspiam enim, qui deficiunt, electorum vocatorum nomine veniunt. Neque Ecclesiæ sic ὀνοματοποιεῖν, hoc est, nomina Scripturæ nominibus, imò & rei repugnantia cudere licet. Ecclesia autem illa, cui portæ inferorum prævalere non possunt, Matth. XVI. 18. cujus membra sic
units.tr: X. The Church is an assembly of men, not of angels. For although good angels in some respects belong to the Church, because of that union which they have with Christ, the grace of preservation communicated by him, and the ministry which they perform for the Church when sent by God for that purpose, nevertheless they are not members of the same kind as the Church redeemed by Christ. Nor can they, as men, be called called and faithful. And since an assembly of men, or a multitude of men united, cannot exist in one person, as Elijah once supposed, 1 Kings 19:10, and as the Papists rave about the Blessed Virgin Mary and about the Pope, their idol. For one is not the people of God, the flock, the multitude of believers, the holy nation, the city of God, the body of Christ, the congregation of the righteous, which are the names by which the Church is everywhere called. Nor is every gathering of any men whatever the Church; for not all but few are chosen, Matt. 20:16, and faith is not of all, 2 Thess. 3:2, but of those whom God, chosen from eternity, separates in time and calls out of the human race, which is liable to the curse [καλεῖ], and bestows faith upon. I have chosen you out of the world, John 15:19; I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world, ibid. 17:6. In the same way Israel is said to be of the Amorites: Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite, Ezek. 16:3. Those whom God thus calls and saves in time, chosen from eternity, are alone the members of the true Church. For the distinction of certain Lutherans, between those who are elect and called specifically and properly, and those who are so named generally and improperly, of whom the former cannot fall from grace while the latter can fall, and who are members of the Church as long as they do not fall away, is not known to Scripture. For nowhere do those who fall away come under the name of elect and called. Nor is it permissible to coin names by which the Church would name things [ὀνοματοποιεῖν] in a way that is contrary to the names of Scripture, or even contrary to the reality. But that Church against which the gates of hell cannot prevail, Matt. 16:18, whose members are thus

units.la: Ecclesiam hanc proprie dictam Scriptura intelligit, ubi illustria Ecclesiæ elogia, & promissiones eximias eidem factas commemorat. sic vocantur,ut ex femine incorruptibili renascan-tur, 1. Petr. I. 23. & quæ communio Sanctorum in remissione peccatorum, resurrectione carnis & vita æterna est,electos vocatos,à gratia electionis & vocationis descisce volentes, adeóque ambiguarum partium & funambulos in sanctum contubernium suum haud recipit. Excommunicati & catechumeni nondum baptizati,cùm electi & vocati esse possint,uti exemplo excommunicatorum ab Ecclesia Judaica, Joh. IX. 22. & catechumenorum, Latronis, Luc. XXIII. 43. & Cornelii Actor. X. 2. 3. 4. liquet, possunt membra Ecclesiæ esse,& revera sunt, quotquot vera fide præditi sunt. Infantes & amentes Ecclesiæ accensentur foris, ex conditione nativitatis, à qua sancti dicuntur, qui ex parente fideli uno vel utroque nati sunt, 1. Cor. VII. 14. intus autem ex vocationis internæ dono, Rom. XI. 29. per quod novit Dominus eos,qui sui sunt, 2. Tim. II. 19. Surdorum alia ratio est, qui non vocationis internæ duntaxat, sed, experientia teste, externæ etiam,non per auditum,sed per visum,quo etiam audienda percipi possunt, participes fieri possunt. Denique ab Ecclesia hac proprie & augustius dicta soli reprobi exulant,utpote qui nec destinatione, nec actu Ecclesiæ membra unquam sunt, vel fieri possunt, de quo infra in idea Ecclesiæ falsæ.
units.tr: Scripture means the Church in the proper sense when it recalls the Church's illustrious praises and the remarkable promises made to it. Its members are called so that they are born again from incorruptible seed, 1 Pet. 1:23. The communion of saints in the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh and eternal life does not admit into its holy fellowship those who are chosen and called but wish to fall away from the grace of election and calling, nor those who play a double game and tread the tightrope between two sides. Excommunicated persons and catechumens who are not yet baptized can be chosen and called, as is clear from the example of those excommunicated by the Jewish Church, John 9:22, from the catechumen who was the thief, Luke 23:43, and from Cornelius, Acts 10:2-4. Such people can be members of the Church, and in fact are, as many as possess true faith. Infants and the mentally impaired are counted as members of the Church outwardly, by reason of their birth, by which they are called holy, since they were born of one or both believing parents, 1 Cor. 7:14. They are counted inwardly, however, by the gift of internal calling, Rom. 11:29, by which the Lord knows those who are his, 2 Tim. 2:19. The case of the deaf is different: they can become sharers in the Church not only by internal calling but, as experience shows, by external calling too, not through hearing but through sight, by which things to be heard can also be perceived. Finally, the reprobate alone are excluded from this Church in the proper and stricter sense, since they neither are nor can ever become members of it, either by divine appointment or in fact. This will be discussed below in the idea of the false Church.

units.la: XI. Ecclesiam seu coetum electorum vocatorum non vel vocatio ipsa, vel unio & communio membrorum cum Christo & inter se, quàm fides in Christum constituit. Nam vocatio Ecclesiam facit; unio & communio ostendit, fides constituit, utpote quæ Ecclesiæ τὸ εἶναι esse suum impartitur. Id enim Ecclesiæ essentiam constituit, quod æquè in omnibus vocatis reperitur. Hoc autem relatio est, habens vim illam, quæ in prima & intima affectione ad Christum consistit. Talis in homine nulla datur præter fidem. Sicut enim fides singulorum vocatorum, ita etiam eorundem collectorum forma & essentia est. Iidem enim homines fideles, qui prout seorsim & sigillatim considerantur,vocati Dei sunt: sunt etiam Ecclesia Dei, prout conjunctim in coetu considerantur. Hinc omnes promissiones Dei,quæ Ecclesiæ in Scripturis factæ sunt,& præcipuas benedictiones continent,ad singulos etiam fideles pertinent. Et tam hæc ad Christum per fidem relatio Ecclesiæ propria & eximia est, ut ejus ratione non tantum Christus Ecclesiæ sit, & Ecclesia Christi; juxta illud Sponsæ Christi: דודי לי ואני לו Dilectus meus est meus, & ego sum illius, Cant. VI. 2. Sed etiam Christus in Ecclesia, & Ecclesia in Christo est. Manete in me, sicut ego in vobis. Non potestis fructum ferre, nisi in me manseritis, Joh. XV. 4. Qui servat mandata ejus,in eo manet Christus,& ipse in eo Christo,ibid. XV. 4. Neque aliam ob causam Ecclesia mysticè dicitur Χριστὸς Christus, 1. Cor. XII. 12. & πλήρωμα τὸ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι πληρουμένου. Plenitudo (qualis in corpore requiritur, quæ מלא קומה plenitudo staturæ, 1. Sam. XXVIII. 20. vocatur.) ejus,qui omnia in omnibus implet, Eph. I. 23. Christus enim sibi corpus suum format, perficit, & donis implet, & omnia in omnibus implet, non quòd omnes corpus suum faciat, quia nemo corpus ejus fit,vel donis impletur sine ipso: quomodo solem omnia illustrare dicimus,quia sine eo nihil illustratur. Et Ecclesia metaphoricè Christi Sponsa, civitas,domus, palmites,corpus: Christus Ecclesiæ Sponsus,Rex,Paterfamilias, vitis & caput appellatur. Quibus similitudinibus non unio duntaxat & communio illa, quæ Christum inter & Ecclesiam intercedit; sed etiam ordinis ratio,qua Christus Ecclesiæ est omnis vitæ, virtutis, dignitatis & perfectionis principium, significatur.
units.tr: XI. The Church, or the assembly of the elect and called, is constituted not by the calling itself, nor by the union and communion of the members with Christ and with one another, but by faith in Christ. For calling makes the Church; union and communion show it; faith constitutes it, since faith imparts to the Church its being [τὸ εἶναι]. For that which is found equally in all who are called constitutes the essence of the Church. This, however, is a relation, which has that force which consists in the first and innermost disposition towards Christ. In a human being there is no such relation apart from faith. For just as faith is the form and essence of each called person, so it is also of those gathered together. The same men who are believers, considered separately and one by one, are the called of God; they are also the Church of God, when considered together in an assembly. Hence all the promises of God made to the Church in the Scriptures, which contain the chief blessings, also pertain to each individual believer. And this relation of the Church to Christ through faith is so proper and remarkable that by it Christ is not only the Church's and the Church is not only Christ's, according to the saying of the Bride of Christ: My beloved is mine, and I am his [דודי לי ואני לו], Song 6:2. Christ is also in the Church, and the Church in Christ: Abide in me, as I abide in you. You cannot bear fruit unless you abide in me, John 15:4. He who keeps his commandments abides in him, Christ, and he in him, ibid. 15:4. For this reason the Church is mystically called Christ [Χριστός], 1 Cor. 12:12, and the fullness [πλήρωμα] of him who fills all things in all [τὸ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι πληρουμένου]. The fullness (which in a body is required, and is called the fullness of stature [מלא קומה], 1 Sam. 28:20) of him who fills all in all, Eph. 1:23. For Christ forms his body for himself, perfects it and fills it with gifts, and fills all things in all. Not that he makes everyone his body, since no one becomes his body or is filled with gifts without him; we say the sun illuminates all things in the same way, because nothing is illuminated without it. Metaphorically the Church is called Christ's bride, city, house, branches, body, and Christ is called the Church's bridegroom, king, master of the household, vine and head. By these likenesses is signified not only the union and communion that lies between Christ and the Church, but also the order by which Christ is the source of all the Church's life, power, dignity and perfection.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: XII. Per fidem hanc sicut singuli fideles, ita collecti etiam, seu Ecclesia, cum Christo capite suo unionem habet. Quæ unio duobus capitibus, subjectione & communione absolvitur. Subjicitur enim Ecclesia Christo capiti suo, Ephes. V. 24. Et propter subjectionem illam Christus caput Ecclesiæ corpori suo bona sua communicat. Sumus enim membra corporis ejus,ex sanguine ejus & ex ossibus ejus,ibid. v. 30. Insiti sumus Christo,sicut palmes vitis: Ego sum vitis; vos estis palmites. Qui manet in me, sicut ego in ipso, is fructum multum fert, quia sine me nihil potestis facere, Joh. XV. 5. Quæ illa Συμφυτις complantatio cum Christo,Rom. VI. 5. est; qua sicut surculi arbori insiti in unam naturam coalescunt; ita nos Christo insiti unctionis & beneficiorum ejus omnium μέτοχοι participes reddimur; cum eo Prophetæ, Sacerdotes & Reges efficimur,atque ex ejus plenitudine gratiam pro gratia accipimus, Joh. I. 16. Neque sine tali unione Christus Ecclesiæ caput,Sponsus, Rex, Pastor, Dominus, hæres esse potest. Nam χωρὶς sine ipso (seorsim ab ipso seu uti Hebraei dicunt, לבד ממנו) nihil potestis facere; sicut palmes seorsim à vite nec vivit,nec facere quicquam potest,ibid. XV. 5. Et unione illa,quæ per fidem in Christum est,sublata,omne malum ponitur. Nam qui non credit in Filium,ira Dei manet super ipsum, non ignis instar,leviter afflans & lambens, sed non destruens, verùm expoliens & purgans, transit; sed ita manet,ut perdens non disperdat,crucians nunquam perimat, vel cruciare desinat, Joh. III. 36. Qui Filium habet,vitam habet: qui non habet Filium Dei, non habet vitam, 1. Joh. V. 12. Nihil hac unione jucundius suaviùsque est, quia affert pacem,quæ omnem intellectum superat,Phil. IV. 7. Neque tantùm unio illa est Ecclesiæ ceu corporis cum Christo,ceu capite, per fidem; sed etiam corporis, seu membrorum corporis sibi arctè unitorum per charitatem; seu mutua dilectionis officia, per quæ varia Spiritus S. dona ad communem usum conferuntur, ut nullum in corpore schisma, sed summa membrorum omnium rebus secundis simul atque adversis consensio glisceat. Sive patitur unum membrum,compatiuntur reliqua: sive glorificatur unum membrum, reliqua omnia simul lætantur, 1. Cor. XII. 26. Ne sua quisque spectetis; sed unusquisque etiam, quæ sunt aliorum, Phil. II. 4. Ut quisque accepit donum, ita alius alii subministrantes, ut boni dispensatores variæ gratiæ Dei, 1. Pet. IV. 10. Sicut porro membra corporis cum capite & inter se vinculo spiritus: ita Ecclesia cum Christo,& singula ejus membra inter se vinculo Spiritus S. conjunguntur. Is enim electos per fidem cum Christo capite, & per charitatem inter se, ceu corporis unius membra unit atque conjungit, & unitos conjunctosque regit atque confervat. Per hoc enim cognoscimus, nos in eo manere, & ipsum in nobis, quia nobis de Spiritu suo dedit, 1. Joh. IV. 13.
units.tr: XII. Through this faith, the Church as a whole, just as each individual believer, has union with Christ its head. This union is completed in two respects: subjection and communion. For the Church is subject to Christ its head, Eph. 5:24. And because of that subjection, Christ the head communicates his goods to the Church, his body. For we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones, ibid. 5:30. We are grafted into Christ, like branches into a vine: I am the vine, you are the branches. He who abides in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing, John 15:5. This is that grafting together [Συμφυτις] with Christ, Rom. 6:5, by which, just as shoots grafted into a tree grow together into one nature, so we, grafted into Christ, become sharers [μέτοχοι] in his anointing and in all his benefits; with him we are made prophets, priests and kings, and from his fullness we receive grace upon grace, John 1:16. Without such union Christ cannot be the head, bridegroom, king, shepherd, Lord and heir of the Church. For apart from him [χωρὶς] you can do nothing (separately from him, or as the Hebrews say, apart from him [לבד ממנו]); just as a branch separated from the vine neither lives nor can do anything, ibid. 15:5. And when the union that comes through faith in Christ is removed, every evil is set in place. For he who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God abides upon him. It does not pass over like a fire that gently breathes and licks without destroying, but rather refines and cleanses. It abides in such a way that, destroying, it does not utterly destroy, and tormenting, it never kills or ceases to torment, John 3:36. He who has the Son has life; he who does not have the Son of God does not have life, 1 John 5:12. Nothing is more joyful or sweeter than this union, for it brings a peace which surpasses all understanding, Phil. 4:7. Nor is this union merely that of the Church, as a body, with Christ as its head, through faith; it is also that of the body, or of the members of the body, closely joined to one another through love, that is, through the mutual duties of love by which the various gifts of the Holy Spirit are shared for common use, so that no schism arises in the body, but the complete agreement of all the members grows, in prosperity and adversity alike. If one member suffers, all the others suffer with it; if one member is honoured, all the others rejoice together, 1 Cor. 12:26. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others, Phil. 2:4. As each has received a gift, so use it to serve one another, as good stewards of the varied grace of God, 1 Pet. 4:10. Just as the members of the body are joined to the head and to one another by the bond of the Spirit, so the Church is joined to Christ, and each of its members to one another, by the bond of the Holy Spirit. For he unites and joins the elect, through faith, to Christ the head, and through love to one another, as members of one body, and having united and joined them, he rules and preserves them. For by this we know that we abide in him, and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit, 1 John 4:13.

units.la: XIII. Ita Ecclesia, juxta Symbolum Apostolicum, Communio Sanctorum est. Quae verba cum in prisci symbolis non occurrant, declarandae Ecclesiae gratia adjecta videntur. Ecclesia enim omnino Sanctorum communio est, quia est unio, societas, coetus omnium fidelium, qui commune quid invicem habent. Est autem res illa communis Christus, Ecclesiae caput unicum; nec non dona, quae ex Christo capite per Spiritum S. in singula ejus membra defluunt, unguenti instar illius optimi, quod super caput Christum est, & descendit super barbam Aaronis, & fimbrias vestimentorum ejus, seu subjecta Ecclesiae membra, Psal. CXXXIII. 2. Bipertita etiam illa est, cum Christo capite, & membrorum inter se. In illa Christus Ecclesiae praestantissima quaeque, se ipsum videlicet, utpote qui totus sors & portio ejus evadit, justitiam inprimis & vitam: Ecclesia vicissim Christo dona in ea accipienti amorem, cultum, laudem, gratiarum actionem impartitur. In hac vel Sancti viventes cum viventibus, vel viventes cum mortuis communicant. Viventium cum viventibus communio partim in mutuo vel aequali affectu, atque φιλαδελφίᾳ, quam unus idemque in omnibus Spiritus format, efficit & fovet in omnibus iis, qui animas suas in obsequio veritatis sanctificarunt, 1. Petr. I. 21. partim in donis Spiritus, fide, spe, charitate, timore Dei aliisque, quae ejusdem corporis membra in mutuum usum commodumque per exempla Matth. V. 14. 1. Cor. XI. 1. exhortationes, Hebr. XIII. 22. παρακλήσεις seu instigationes, ibid. X. 24. consolationes, Rom. XII. 8. orationes & preces, 1. Tim. II. 1. 2. sic convertunt, ut singuli fideles jus habeant ad omnia charismata, quae Deus corpori suo ad aedificationem communem dispensat, utpote quae non uni, sed toti ἀδελφότητι fraternitati & corpori data censentur: partim denique in donis etiam corporalibus, quae ad usum & honorem totius corporis impertienda sunt, ita ut ὑμετιδότοι, κοινωνικοὶ libenter impertientes, communicabiles &c. sint, 1. Tim. VI. 18. & commune fortunae utriusque sensum habeant, consistit. Mortuorum etiam cum viventibus, & vicissim, communio flagrat, quia nec mortui sic viventium curam in universum abjiciunt, quin militantis Ecclesiae liberationem jugiter Deo commendent, Ap. VI. 10. & viventes, cum quantum ad cordis θερμότητα, cum coelitibus πνεῦμα suum in Coelis habeant, conjunctionem cum illis flagranter semper expetunt, eorum fidem laudant, & pro virili imitari contendunt. Imo secundum communionem hanc Ecclesia illa, quae in coelis est, cum ea quae in terra est, conjungitur. Nam quorum Deus est Jehova, illi Deo vivunt, & mansiones in Coelo habent, in gloriam introducti, & secundum Spiritum consummati sunt, Matth. XXII. 32. Luc. XX. 38. Joh. XIV. 2. Hebr. II. 10. XII. 23. neque adeo a fratribus suis, qui in terra sunt, dividuntur. Haec ergo decantata illa Sanctorum communio est, qua nulla inter homines arctior & sanctior conjunctio & contesseratio est, utpote quam unum corpus, unus Spiritus, una spes vocationis, unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma, unus Deus & Pater omnium, qui est super omnes, & per omnes, & in omnibus, ceu totidem δεσμοὶ σύνδεσμοι vincula pacis & charitatis Ephes. IV. 3. &c. potentissima, adamantino & indissolubili nexu adstringunt.
units.tr: XIII. Thus the Church, according to the Apostles' Creed, is the communion of saints. These words do not occur in the older creeds, and seem to have been added for the sake of explaining the Church. For the Church is wholly the communion of saints, because it is the union, fellowship and assembly of all believers, who have something common to them. The common thing is Christ, the sole head of the Church, and also the gifts that flow from Christ the head through the Holy Spirit into each of his members, like that precious ointment which is upon the head of Christ, and runs down upon the beard of Aaron, and the skirts of his garments, that is, the members of the Church subject to him, Ps. 133:2. This communion is twofold: that with Christ the head, and that among the members themselves. In the first, Christ gives the Church his most excellent things, namely himself, since he becomes wholly the lot and portion of the Church, and above all his righteousness and life. The Church in turn gives to Christ, who gives gifts to it, love, worship, praise and thanksgiving. In the second, either the saints who are living share with the living, or the living share with the dead. The communion of the living with the living consists partly in mutual and equal affection and brotherly love [φιλαδελφία], which one and the same Spirit forms, produces and fosters in all those who have purified their souls in obedience to the truth, 1 Pet. 1:21. It consists partly in the gifts of the Spirit, faith, hope, love, the fear of God and others, which the members of the same body so turn to mutual use and benefit: through examples, Matt. 5:14; 1 Cor. 11:1; through exhortations, Heb. 13:22; through encouragements or incitements [παρακλήσεις], ibid. 10:24; through consolations, Rom. 12:8; through prayers and supplications, 1 Tim. 2:1-2. In such a way that each believer has a right to all the gifts of grace which God dispenses to his body for the common edification, since these are considered given not to one person but to the whole brotherhood [ἀδελφότης] and body. Finally, it consists partly in bodily gifts as well, which must be shared for the use and honour of the whole body, so that people are generous, ready to share [ὑμεταδότοι, κοινωνικοί], willing to give and to share, 1 Tim. 6:18, and have a common feeling for each other's fortunes. The communion of the dead with the living, and in turn of the living with the dead, also burns brightly. For the dead do not so completely cast off care for the living that they cease to commend the liberation of the militant Church continually to God, Rev. 6:10; and the living, as far as the warmth of their hearts is concerned, while they have their own spirit [πνεῦμα] in heaven with the heavenly ones, always eagerly seek fellowship with them, praise their faith, and strive, as far as they can, to imitate it. Indeed, according to this communion, the Church that is in heaven is joined with the Church that is on earth. For those whose God is Jehovah live to God, and have dwellings in heaven; they have been brought into glory and made perfect in the Spirit, Matt. 22:32; Luke 20:38; John 14:2; Heb. 2:10; 12:23; and so they are not separated from their brothers who are on earth. This, then, is that much-celebrated communion of saints, than which there is no closer or holier bond and joining among men, since one body, one Spirit, one hope of calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in all, as so many bonds [δεσμοί], binding [σύνδεσμοι], bonds of peace and love, Eph. 4:3 etc., bind together with the most powerful, adamantine and indissoluble tie.

units.la: XIV. Ex iis, quae diximus, liquet, Ecclesiam illam, cujus Christus Rex & caput est, non esse de mundo, neque Regni mundani aspectabilis & pomposi rationem habere. Non enim illam videmus & palpamus, sicut Regnum aliquod terrestre; sed credimus. Quae autem credimus, τῶν ἃ βλεπομένων, eorum, quae non videmus, sunt, Hebr. XI. 1. Nam & ipsa electio, quae Ecclesiam destinat, vocatio, quae eam efficit, & fides, quae eam constituit, nonnisi mentis & fidei nostrae oculis usurpantur. Sicut enim Christus, Ecclesiae caput, cum in terris his peregrinaretur, nonnisi purgatis fidei oculis conspici potuit: ita quoque corpus Domini, quod Ecclesia est, solis fidelibus innotescit. Tota gloriosa filia Regis est פנימה introrsum, Psal. XLV. 14. Intus enim in justitia, Spiritu ipsi donato, charismatis πολυποικίλοις, novo homine & virtutibus novi hominis, ipso denique Christo, qui in ea per fidem vivit, Galat. II. 20. se prodit. Ideo Christus de Sponsa sua: Una est columba mea, Sincera mea. Una matri suae: chara genitrici suae בנות ראו viderent eam filiae, beatam praedicarent! Reginae & pellices celebrarent eam! Cant. VI. 8. Neque vel cantilenam illam novam, quam canunt fideles, nisi ipsi intelligunt, Apoc. XIV. 3. vel calculum illum album, & ei inscriptum nomen novum quisquam cognoscit, nisi qui eum accipit, ibid. II. 17. Iccirco membra Ecclesiae germana, genuinas Christi oves, solus Deus certo novit. Ego bonus Pastor sum, καὶ γινώσκω τὰ ἐμά & novi mea, & cognoscor a meis, Joh. X. 14. Deus novit, qui sui sunt, 2. Tim. II. 19. Ecclesia enim vera est corpus mysticum, Ephes. V. 23. 32. per Spiritum & fidem coadunatum, 1. Cor. XII. 13. Ephes. IV. 5. & οἶκος τῶν πνευματικῶν domus spirituales, 1. Petr. II. 5.
units.tr: XIV. From what we have said it is clear that the Church, whose King and head is Christ, is not "of this world," and does not have the outward and showy character of a worldly kingdom. For we do not see and handle it as we would some earthly kingdom; we believe in it. Now the things we believe are "the evidence of things not seen" (Heb. 11:1). Even the election that destines the Church, the calling that brings it into being, and the faith that establishes it are apprehended only by the eyes of our mind and faith. For just as Christ, the head of the Church, while he went about on earth, could be seen only by purified eyes of faith, so also the body of the Lord, which is the Church, is known only to believers. "The king's daughter is all glorious within" [פנימה] (Ps. 45:14). For within, in righteousness, by the Spirit given to her, through manifold gifts [πολυποικίλοις], by the new man and the virtues of the new man, and finally by Christ himself, who lives in her through faith, she shows herself (Gal. 2:20). Therefore Christ says of his bride: "My dove, my undefiled, is but one; she is the only one of her mother, the darling of her who bore her. The daughters saw her and called her blessed; the queens and concubines praised her" (Song 6:8). Nor does anyone know the "new song" that the faithful sing, unless they themselves understand it (Rev. 14:3), nor the white stone with the "new name" written on it, unless he who receives it (Rev. 2:17). Therefore God alone knows with certainty the true members of the Church, the genuine sheep of Christ. "I am the good Shepherd, and I know my own, and am known by mine" (John 10:14). "The Lord knows those who are his" (2 Tim. 2:19). For the true Church is the mystical body (Eph. 5:23, 32), joined together by the Spirit and faith (1 Cor. 12:13; Eph. 4:5), and "a spiritual house" (1 Pet. 2:5).

units.la: XV. Fideles quidem ξένοι συμπολῖται se invicem & norunt, sed non infallibilis fidei lumine, verum charitatis ex probabilibus signis probabiliter inferentis, & cuncta sperantis judicio. Licet ibi esse Ecclesiam, ubi electorum, vocatorum & fidelium operationes gliscunt, tuto credere possint. Ac licet Ecclesia ratione vocationis, congregationis & professionis externae ita visibilis sit, ut per fidem cognosci possit, hunc vel illum coetum Ecclesiae membrum esse; tamen quinam in visibili coetu verae Ecclesiae membra sint, solus Deus certo & infallibiliter novit. Et quam non ortus & progressus Ecclesiae in utroque Testamento conspicuus sit, Christus ostendit, dicens: Non venit Regnum Dei μετὰ παρατηρήσεως cum observatione, pompa, qualis Regnum venientium & incedentium est, Luc. XVII. 20. Neque omnis societas hominum in externis & visibilibus signis, ex quibus socii se mutuo agnoscant & videant, consistit. Licet enim id in societate naturali civili & Ecclesiastica externa obtineat, in spirituali tamen non aeque obtinet; quia ejus vinculum, Spiritus, fides, charitas ἀνυπόκριτος solius Dei oculis patent, & πλεγχνλισμὸς refupinata Heb. IV. 13. sunt. Est sane ubi Ecclesiae vox visibilem lem & externam notat. Sed ubi de proprie dicta Ecclesia agitur,velut Matth. XVI. 18. Eph. V.23. 32. Heb. XII. 23. aliisque supra citatis locis, invisibilis tantum intelligitur. Denique Ecclesiae verae sub periculo mortis aeternae nos adjungere tenemur; sed quoad internam communionem simpliciter,quia Christus sui tantum corporis Salvator est,Ephes.V.23. quoad externam vero communionem secundum quid, quatenus per temporis, aliarumque circumstantiarum ratione id fieri potest. Non igitur quoad internam communionem visibilis sit necesse est,quia communio per fidem in Christum,& cum eodem non est visibilis. Satis est, si quoad externam communionem certis gradibus suis visibilis sit, ut ei certo investigatae conjungere nos valeamus. Nullum tamen etiam salutis amittendae periculum est, si sine culpa externam communionem colere non licet,quia simpliciter necessaria ad salutem non est,& externam illam communionem interna supplet.
units.tr: XV. Believers indeed know one another as "strangers and fellow citizens" [ξένοι συμπολῖται], but not by the light of infallible faith; rather by charity, which infers probably from probable signs, and by the judgment of one who hopes all things. They may confidently believe that the Church is where the operations of the elect, the called and the faithful flourish. And although the Church, by reason of its calling, its gathering and its outward profession, is so visible that by faith one may recognise this or that assembly as a member of the Church, nevertheless God alone knows with certainty and infallibility who in the visible assembly are the true members of the Church. That the rise and progress of the Church are not conspicuous in either Testament, Christ shows when he says: "The kingdom of God does not come with observation" [μετὰ παρατηρήσεως], that is, with the pomp that belongs to kingdoms that come and advance (Luke 17:20). Nor does every fellowship of men consist in outward and visible signs by which its members recognise and see one another. For although this holds in natural, civil and outward ecclesiastical fellowship, it does not hold equally in the spiritual; because its bond, the Spirit, faith and charity [ἀνυπόκριτος], lies open to the eyes of God alone, and all things are "naked and laid bare" [τετραχηλισμένα] (Heb. 4:13). Certainly there are places where the word "Church" denotes something visible and external. But where the Church properly so called is meant, as in Matt. 16:18; Eph. 5:23, 32; Heb. 12:23, and the other passages cited above, it is understood as invisible only. Finally, we are bound to join ourselves to the true Church under pain of eternal death; but with regard to internal communion, simply, because Christ is the Saviour of his body alone (Eph. 5:23); with regard to external communion, however, in a qualified sense, so far as this can be done in view of time and other circumstances. Therefore visibility is not necessary in respect of internal communion, because communion through faith in Christ and with him is not visible. It is enough if the Church is visible, in its certain degrees, with respect to external communion, so that we may be able to join ourselves to it when it has been surely found. Nor is there any danger of losing salvation if, without fault, it is not permitted to keep external communion, because it is not simply necessary for salvation, and internal communion supplies for that external communion.

units.la: XVI. Est autem Ecclesia Una, Sancta & Catholica. Una est non ut Regnum mundanum , quod una externa societate imperantis & parentium contentum, certis locis & limitibus arctatur, & humanis,non Divinis consiliis regitur; sed spirituali & catholica ratione, qua sub Christo capite Coelesti fideles omnes in Coelo & terra,ceu unius corporis membra, Spiritu, fide & charitate eadem in unum coalescunt. Et unitate non generica , vel specifica,sed numerica, adeoque sic una,ut etiam sit unica, אחת היא יונתי תמתי אחת לאמה Una est columba mea, integra mea,unica matri suae,Cant. VI.8. Unum enim corpus mysticum Christus habet,cui omnes salvandos ipse aggregat,Actor. II.47. Unum corpus, unus Spiritus (Ecclesiam ceu Templum suum vivificans & regenerans) Unus Dominus, (Christus,Ecclesiam,ceu Sponsam,corpus,gregem suum unicum redimens) Una fides, (quoad rerum promissarum & credendarum substantiam) unum baptisma, (unitatis illius signaculum) unus Deus & Pater omnium,(qui Ecclesiam ab aeterno elegit, ceu domum, familiam & peculium suum,& in tempore per verbum & Spiritum vocat.) Ephes. IV.4.5.6. Multi unum corpus sumus in Christo, singuli vero aliorum membra sumus; Rom. XII. 5. Multiplex corpus etiam πολυκέφαλον est,seu multiplex caput requirit. Atqui unum est Ecclesiae caput, Christus. Cumque sic una sit Ecclesia, nemini extra eam salus contingere potest. Nemo enim salvatur nisi electus, vocatus,fidelis. Atqui Ecclesia est coetus electorum,vocatorum & fidelium,uti vidimus. Scite proin Cyprianus lib. de unit. Eccl. dixit : Non habet Deum Patrem, qui non Ecclesiam matrem. Ecclesia instar arcae Noae est; sicut diluvio submersi sunt, qui extra eam fuerunt : ita salute excidunt, quotquot extra Ecclesiam sunt, 1. Petr.III.20.21. Sed intelligimus id de Ecclesia Catholica,non particulari illa,qualis etiam Romana est, quia non perinde in Novo, ut in Veteri Testamento Ecclesia uni genti vel loco alligata est. Neque enim qui coetus particulares, pro rerum suarum conditione, mutant, salutis dispendium patiuntur. Cum tamen bifariam extra Ecclesiam Catholicam esse possimus, puta separatione fidei, vel separatione loci; qui priore sensu ab ea separatus est, & ἀσυνδετον πίστιν æque pretiosam fidem non habet, salvari non potest, quia impossibile est Deo placere, adeoque etiam salvari, absque fide, Hebr. XI.6. Posteriore vero sensu extra Ecclesiam salus est,vel non est. Est, ubi ob persecutiones, morbum,vel alias causas,cum nullo coetu Ecclesiastico conjunctio impossibilis est ; quia externam communionem interna per fidem & ἀναφυμίαν animi compensat. Non est,si quis se ipsum separet, & conventus Ecclesiasticos negligat & contemnat; quia contemptus ille cum fide consistere non potest. Observemus alii alios ad institutionem charitatis & bonorum operum, non deserentes congregationem eorum,sicut quibusdam mos est, Hebr.X.24.25.
units.tr: XVI. The Church is one, holy and catholic. It is "one," not as a worldly kingdom is one, which is bound by one outward society of ruler and subjects, confined to certain places and limits, and governed by human rather than divine counsels; but in a spiritual and catholic manner, by which all believers in heaven and on earth, under Christ the heavenly head, as members of one body, coalesce into one by the same Spirit, faith and charity. And it is one not in kind or species, but in number, and so one that it is also unique: "My dove, my undefiled, is one" [אחת היא יונתי תמתי אחת לאמה], "my undefiled is but one, the only one of her mother" (Song 6:8). For Christ has one mystical body, to which he himself gathers all who are to be saved (Acts 2:47): "one body, one Spirit" (who quickens and regenerates the Church as his temple), "one Lord" (Christ, who redeems the Church as his bride, body and flock, his only one), "one faith" (as to the substance of the promised and believed things), "one baptism" (the seal of that unity), "one God and Father of all" (who chose the Church from eternity as his house, family and peculiar people, and calls it in time through the Word and the Spirit) (Eph. 4:4–6). "We, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another" (Rom. 12:5). A body with many heads, a polycephalous body, is also a body that requires a multiplicity of heads. But the Church has one head, Christ. And since the Church is thus one, salvation can come to no one outside it. For no one is saved except the elect, the called and the faithful. But the Church is the assembly of the elect, the called and the faithful, as we have seen. Therefore Cyprian rightly said in his book On the Unity of the Church: "He does not have God as Father who does not have the Church as mother." The Church is like Noah's ark; as those who were outside it were drowned in the flood, so all who are outside the Church perish from salvation (1 Pet. 3:20–21). But we understand this of the catholic Church, not of that particular Church, such as the Roman one is, because in the New Testament the Church is not tied to one nation or place as it was in the Old. Nor do those who change particular assemblies, according to the circumstances of their affairs, suffer any loss of salvation. Yet we can be outside the catholic Church in two ways, namely by separation of faith or by separation of place. He who is separated from it in the former sense, and has a faith unconnected [ἀσύνδετον πίστιν], which is not equally precious, does not have faith and cannot be saved, because it is impossible to please God, and so to be saved without faith (Heb. 11:6). In the latter sense, however, salvation is or is not outside the Church. It is possible where, because of persecution, sickness or other causes, union with no ecclesiastical assembly is impossible; because internal communion through faith and the solace of the mind makes up for external communion. It is not possible if anyone separates himself, and neglects and despises the ecclesiastical assemblies; for that contempt cannot consist with faith. Let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works, not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is (Heb. 10:24–25).

units.la: XVII. Etiam Sancta Ecclesia est.
units.tr: XVII. The Holy Church is also holy.

units.la: Nam ἐν ἅγιον gens sancta est, 1. Petr. II.9. πόλις ἁγία urbs sancta, Apoc. XI.2. quae tota est illud קדש הקדשים Sanctum Sanctorum, typico illi respondens, Dan. IX.24. Ezech. XLIII.21. Ad sanctitatem enim ab aeterno electa,Ephes.I.4. in tempore redempta & regenita est. Sancta autem est tum imputatione, quia sanctificata est per oblationem corporis Jesu Christi semel factam, Hebr. X.10. tum inchoatione per renovationem Spiritus S. eam regenerantis, Tit. III.5. nec non quotidianum in pietate profectum, Phil. III.12.13.14. tum separatione, quia est populus ille περιούσιος peculiaris; Tit.II.14. Genus electum, Regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis, 1. Petr.II.9. Sic igitur sancta est, quoad sanctitatem inhaerentem, ut tamen, quandiu illa in terra militat, à Domino peregrinatur,& ἀμαρτίαν illam εὐπερίστατον peccatum facile circumstans Hebr. XII. 1. circumfert,non omnino expers sit, vel ignorantiae vel erroris in mente, vel defectus & vitii in voluntate. Cum enim ex electis & fidelibus singulis illa componatur, singulorum defectus recipit. Et quod singuli fideles & electi non habent,universi collecti possidere non possunt, quomodo si hospites singuli δανιμέοι sunt, universi symbolum solvere non possunt. Singuli autem nec ignorantiae & erroris, nec vitii omnis expertes sunt. Non ignorantiae & erroris in mente, quia ex parte cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus, 1. Cor. XIII. 9. & sanctissimi quique non plane ab errore immunes fuerunt. Ideo Apostolus ad Corinthios scribens monet eos, se non potuisse iis loqui,ut spiritualibus,sed ut carnalibus,& pueris in Christo, ibid. III. 1. Qui ergo Evangelium & veritatis amorem accipiunt, atque ita in Christo sunt ; possunt tamen in multis esse puerorum instar,multa ignorare,de multis vanas & erroneas opiniones habere,& in multis offendere, Jac.III.2. Est quidem in Ecclesia perpetuus canon & norma doctrinae arctissima , sed ejus ἀκρίβεια non plane capit Ecclesia, quae in terrestri coeno reptat. Neque id affirmare potest nisi is,qui principium cum fine,sationem cum messe, infantem cum viro, carceres cum meta, praelium cum triumpho,& coenum cum Coelo confundit. Ecclesia igitur quatenus credit verbo Dei,non errat : at quia imperfecte credit,humanaeque doctrinae vento circumagitur, errat. Non vitii in voluntate, quia semper,regenitorum etiam,caro concupiscit adversus adversus spiritum, Gal. V. 17. & lex membrorum belligeratur adversus legem mentis, Rom. VII. 23. propterea etiam illi peccatorum remissionem quotidie à Deo expetunt, Matth. VI. 12.
units.tr: For it is a holy nation [ἔθνος ἅγιον], 1 Pet. 2:9; a holy city [πόλις ἁγία], Rev. 11:2; and as a whole it is the Holy of Holies [קדש הקדשים], answering to that type, Dan. 9:24; Ezek. 43:21. For it was chosen out of eternity unto holiness, Eph. 1:4, and in time it has been redeemed and regenerated. It is holy in three ways: by imputation, because it has been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once made, Heb. 10:10; by inchoation, through the renewal of the Holy Spirit who regenerates it, Titus 3:5, and also through its daily progress in godliness, Phil. 3:12–14; and by separation, because it is that people [περιούσιος] peculiar, Titus 2:14, a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, 1 Pet. 2:9. Thus it is holy with regard to inherent holiness, yet, while it wages war on earth and is a pilgrim from the Lord, it carries about that sin which easily besets it [εὐπερίστατον ἁμαρτίαν], Heb. 12:1, and it is not wholly free from ignorance or error in mind, or from defect and vice in will. For since it is made up of the individual elect and faithful, it receives the defects of each. And what the individual faithful and elect do not possess, all of them gathered together cannot possess; just as if individual guests are in debt, they cannot all together pay the bill. Yet individuals are not free from ignorance and error, nor from every vice. Not from ignorance and error in mind, because we know in part and we prophesy in part, 1 Cor. 13:9; and the most holy men have never been wholly free from error. Therefore the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, warns them that he could not speak to them as to spiritual people, but as to carnal people and as to infants in Christ, ibid. 3:1. Those, then, who receive the Gospel and love of truth, and so are in Christ, may nevertheless in many things be like children, be ignorant of much, hold many vain and erroneous opinions, and offend in many things, James 3:2. There is indeed in the Church a perpetual canon and a most strict norm of doctrine, but the Church, which crawls in earthly mire, does not fully grasp its exactness [ἀκρίβεια]. Nobody can affirm this except one who confuses the beginning with the end, sowing with harvest, the infant with the man, the starting-gates with the goal, battle with triumph, and mud with heaven. Therefore the Church, insofar as it believes the Word of God, does not err; but because it believes imperfectly and is tossed about by the wind of human doctrine, it does err. Nor is there not vice in will, because always, even in the regenerate, the flesh lusts against the Spirit, Gal. 5:17, and the law of the members wars against the law of the mind, Rom. 7:23; for this reason they also daily seek forgiveness of sins from God, Matt. 6:12.

units.la: XVIII. Non ergo Ecclesia in terris militans omnibus numeris consummata est. Licet enim Divinitus custodita à justitia Christi, & veritate fundamenti nunquam deficiat, ac ne quidem, obstante Dei & Christi amore, ac praesidio potentiae Dei per fidem custodita deficere possit, quia inferorum portae nunquam ei praevalent, Matth. XVI. 18. neque ullum peccatum exitiale & ἑκούσιον voluntarium in eam cadat, quia regenitus ex Deo non peccat, quia semen Dei in eo manet, & peccare non potest, quia ex Deo genitus est, 1. Joh. III. 9. tamen sicut in vita labi in singulis, atque peccatorum gravissimorum nexibus alligari potest, & de die in diem, adeoque magis magisque renovari debet: ita in doctrina proficere indies tenetur, & ignorare multa, impingere in multis, errores non lethales admittere potest. Est equidem Ecclesia coetus electorum, vocatorum & fidelium. Sed nondum relicta, in optimis etiam quibusque carne, erroris, peccati & concupiscentiae fomite ac rubigine, electio, vocatio & fides universam in iis vim & efficaciam in hoc mundo exerunt. Caro enim adversus Spiritum concupiscens, cujus fructus haud laetabiles sunt, animae totius in intellectu pariter atque voluntate perfectionem non parum minuit. Iccirco internus homo non simul semel que perfectionem suam adipiscitur, sed ἀνακαινοῦται ἡμέρᾳ ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ renovatur de die in diem, 2. Cor. IV. 16. donec omne veteris hominis fermentum reliquum mors expurgaverit, Rom. VII. 24. Alias militiae nullus in terra campus foret; at foret amplissimus triumphi, qui Coelum, non terram decet. Neque verbi Divini testimonio quisquam Mortalium à conditione hac excipitur. Cumque Ecclesia non sit idea, vel Reipublicae instar Platonicae, extra singularia subsistentis; sed in singularibus suis, electis, vocatis & fidelibus, quorum collectio est, subsistat, aliam certe & perfectiorem naturam habere non potest, quam singuli etiam optimi habent.
