Ideo S. Paulus monet, ut, si sedenti aliquid reveletur, qui antea locutus est, si leat, & ei locuturo locum cedat, 1. Cor. XIV. 29. 30. Unde constat, posse sedenti aliquid revelari, hoc est, posse sedentem aliquid discere ex Scripturis, quod prius loquenti non fit revelatum; ita ut in sermone praecedentis sit si non error, vel lapsus, qui ἐπανορθωσιν correctionem requirat, saltem defectus sit, qui ἀναπλήρωσιν exigat. Nunquam ergo Ecclesia eo usque in terris proficit, ut in eo, quod hucusque auditum est, nihil omnino corrigendum, vel ad perfectionem majorem proficiendum non videatur. Neque etiam δικαιῶσαι facere censendus est, qui quod sibi revelatum est, loquitur, sive ad illustrationem & confirmationem eorum, quae audita sunt, sive ad correctionem, sive ad ἀναπλήρωσιν, sive ad καταρτισμὸν ὑστερημάτων resarciendos defectus, qui supersunt. Quomodo etiam S. Paulus videre faciem Thessalonicensium, καὶ καταρτίσαι τὰ ὑστερήματα τῆς πίστεως consolidare defectus fidei eorum optavit, 1. Thess. III. 10. Ad id igitur Ecclesia pervenisse
units.tr: XVIII. Therefore the Church militant on earth is not finished in every respect. For although, divinely guarded by the righteousness of Christ and by the truth of the foundation, it never fails, and indeed, despite the love of God and Christ and the protection of God's power, it cannot fail, since it is kept by faith, because the gates of hell shall never prevail against it, Matt. 16:18; and although no deadly and voluntary sin falls upon it, since whoever is born of God does not sin, for his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin, because he has been born of God, 1 John 3:9; nevertheless, just as in life it can slip in individuals and be bound by the chains of the gravest sins, and must be renewed from day to day and so more and more, so in doctrine it is bound to make progress daily, and it can be ignorant of many things, stumble in many things, and admit errors that are not deadly. Indeed the Church is an assembly of the elect, called and faithful. But election, calling and faith have not yet exerted their full force and efficacy in this world, since even in the best people the flesh, with the fomes of error, sin and concupiscence and its rust, remains. For the flesh lusting against the Spirit, whose fruits are not very joyful, diminishes not a little the perfection of the whole soul, in intellect as well as in will. Hence the inner man does not attain his perfection all at once, but is renewed day by day, 2 Cor. 4:16, until death purges away all the remaining leaven of the old man, Rom. 7:24. Otherwise there would be no field of battle for the soldier on earth, but only a great triumph, which befits heaven, not earth. Nor is any mortal excepted from this condition by the testimony of the Divine Word. And since the Church is not an idea or a Platonic commonwealth subsisting apart from individuals, but subsists in its individuals, the elect, called and faithful, of whom it is the collection, it cannot have another and more perfect nature than even the best individuals have. Therefore St. Paul advises that, if something is revealed to one who is sitting, the one who spoke before should be silent and yield his place to the one about to speak, 1 Cor. 14:29–30. From this it is clear that something can be revealed to one who is sitting, that is, the one sitting can learn from the Scriptures something that was not revealed to the one who spoke before; so that in the earlier speech there is, if not an error or lapse which requires correction [ἐπανόρθωσιν], at least a defect which requires supplying [ἀναπλήρωσιν]. Therefore the Church never advances so far on earth that nothing at all seems to need correcting in what has been heard so far, or that there is no greater perfection to be pursued. Nor is anyone to be considered as claiming perfection [δικαιῶσαι] who speaks what has been revealed to him, whether for the illustration and confirmation of what has been heard, or for correction, or for supplying, or for the fulfilment [καταρτισμὸν] of the deficiencies [ὑστερημάτων] that still remain to be made good. So also St. Paul wished to see the face of the Thessalonians and to complete what was lacking in their faith, 1 Thess. 3:10 [καὶ καταρτίσαι τὰ ὑστερήματα τῆς πίστεως]. The Church is said to have attained to that

units.la: dicitur, quod omnibus, qui in Ecclesia sunt, demonstratum est ad fidem. Et in eo, ceu regula, sic ambulandum est, Phil. III. 16. ut tamen non putemus, nos divites & faturos esse atque regnare, 1. Cor. IV. 8. neque posse vel accessionem fieri sapientiae & prudentiae, sive ad pleniorem & clariorem cognitionem; sive ad στηριγμὸν firmitudinem fidei; vel nihil omnino in nobis reprehendi, sive in modo loquendi, sive in modo probandi, sive in eo, quod non satis firmis ex causis statuimus, posse. Papa vero sine suffragio sibi privilegium infallibilitatis vindicans, quia ita Regno ejus conducere videtur, eo deterior est, quo melior, & à communi sorte exemptus magis haberi vult. Saltem veteres quosdam Pontifices, multum recentioribus, horrendam metamorphosin passos, meliores, haeresin contraxisse, historica veritas est, longe certior illa, quod Petrus Romae fuerit, vel Papa Petro successerit, in qua Regni Papalis cardo volvitur. Sed denuntiatio & comminatio Regni alicujus mundani, infallibilitatem & cum eadem seposita Scriptura, magisterium assumentis, in toto quidem codice sacro reperitur; sed sub elogio sceptri improbitatis, throni nequitiae, apostasiae, Antichristi, Bestiae & Babylonis.
units.tr: which has been demonstrated to all who are in the Church as belonging to faith. And in it, as a rule, we must walk, Phil. 3:16; yet we must not think that we are rich and full and already reigning, 1 Cor. 4:8, nor that any addition can be made to our wisdom and prudence, whether to a fuller and clearer knowledge, or to the firmness [στηριγμόν] of faith; or that nothing at all in us is open to rebuke, whether in our manner of speaking, or in our manner of proving, or in the fact that we settle matters on grounds that are not firm enough. The Pope, however, claiming for himself without any vote the privilege of infallibility, because it seems to serve his kingdom, is the worse for it, the better he is, and the more he wishes to be held exempt from the common lot. At least it is historical truth that certain earlier Pontiffs, who suffered a horrible metamorphosis, much more than the recent ones, the better ones, contracted heresy; that truth is far more certain than the claim that Peter was at Rome, or that the Pope succeeded Peter, on which the hinge of the Papal kingdom turns. But the denunciation and threat of some worldly kingdom that assumes infallibility, and with it sets aside Scripture and takes up the magisterium, is found throughout the sacred code, under the titles scepter of wickedness, throne of iniquity, apostasy, Antichrist, Beast and Babylon.

units.la: XIX. Timendum non est, ne non satis consultum sit Ecclesiae, vel illa deficiat etiam, si infallibilis non statuatur. Hic enim metus non veram Ecclesiam, quae se verbo Dei subjicit, sed eam, quae mundani instar Regni, dominari fidei gestit, idque ad τὰ πληρωμα̃ impletionem carnis, Col. II. 23. discruciat. Vera autem Ecclesia in norma infallibili verbi Dei, & donatione Spiritus legem fidei cordi inscribentis, nec non ministerio illorum, qui, ut rigent & plantent, atque ceu sapientes architecti, fundamentum collocant, eique rite superaedificant, 1. Cor. III. 6–13. acquiescit, securae, abundae sibi ita prospici, ne in haereses exitiales incidat, vel erroneas, si quibus implicatur, opiniones pro fundamento ponat, eas in idolum erigat, principium, justitiam, Evangelium aliud constituat, atque aeternam damnationem incurrat, quod futurum nunquam esse, Divinae promissiones spondent. Ac multo minus propterea Ecclesia deficere potest, quod plane cum Christi jure, Regno & promissione, fore scilicet, ne portae inferorum Ecclesiae praevaleant, Matth. XVI. 18. vel electi seducantur, ibid. XXIV. 24. pugnaret. Ex quo illud consequitur, fieri non posse, ut totam Ecclesiam ejusmodi haereses invadant, quae cum verbis & fide fundamenti sic pugnent, ut veritas fundamenti non possit ab ignorantibus simul cum haeresi tenerí, qualis haeresis est, Christum non esse Deum & hominem, vel non esse justitiam credentis. Nam ut Ecclesia, ceu credentium numerus aliquis, fit, necesse est esse tales in mundo, qui credant, Evangelium esse à Deo; in Mose, Prophetis & Evangelio contineri viam ad vitam aeternam, Christum esse Filium Dei unigenitum, verum Deum, causam justitiae & vitae nostrae; quique ex verbo Dei, & testimonio Jesu ad sapientiam & prudentiam proficere parati sint & studeant. Caeterum haec fides excludit quidem positionem alius fundamenti & legis, nec non voluntatem obediendi hominibus; at Profectu & correctione in hac vita semper indiget. at ἐπλήμματα quævis, ignorantias & errores omnes non excludit. Potest enim in fidelibus ex infirmitate carnis debita attentio ad omnia deficere, atque inde evenire facile, ut, salva, in præcipuis, fide & charitate, multiplex in Ecclesiam abusus, magna tristisque verborum inanium & errorum futilium in Ecclesiam incessat; denique fundamento recte posito, fœnum & stipulæ superstruantur, igni comburendæ, salvis, velut per ignem, iis, qui superstruunt, 1. Cor. III. 12. 13. &c. Neque illud Ecclesiæ infallibilitatem omnimodam arguit, quod illa ceu domus Dei viventis στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας columna & stabilimentum veritatis appellari videtur; 1. Tim. III. 15. Non enim verba illa cum Ecclesia Dei viventis, quæ domus Dei est, construenda videntur, quia sic oratio Apostoli nimis hiulca & suspensa reddinitur; neque satis verba cohærent, & nunquam Apostolus novam orationem a copula inchoat; sed potius cum sequentibus, ut mysterium illud pietatis omnium confessione magnum dicatur columna & stabilimentum veritatis. Hebræi enim præcipua fidei dogmata sic appellant. Quomodo Majmonides initio libri de Fundamentis legis sic scribit: Fundamentum fundamentorum & columna sapientiæ est, cognoscere isthic primum ens. Neque aliter etiam Irenæum construxisse, ex lib. III. initio colligere est. Sed non ideo Ecclesiæ hoc elogium invidemus, quæ recte etiam ritéque dicitur στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας. Nam & quivis etiam justus יסוד עולם fundamentum seculi, Prov. X. 25. & Ecclesia disertè etiam מוסד מוסד fundamentum fundatum, Esaj. XXVIII. 16. & omnes fideles τῇ πίστει πεφεμελιωμένοι καὶ ἑδραῖοι fide fundati & stabiles, Col. I. 23. & Ecclesia super petram ædificata, Matth. XVI. 18. dicuntur. Estque Ecclesia & columna, quia Scripturam sermonem vitæ supra se fert, adeoque per sermonem vitæ, ut luminare in mundo lucet, Phil. II. 15. qualis certè non est, quæ se dominam & authorem veritatis, & Scripturam, veritate, Christo prius cognitam mentitur: & stabilimentum veritatis, tum passivè τὸ ἑδραιωμένον ὑπ' ἀληθείας quod a veritate cœlesti stabilitur (quo sensu voces στήριμα, ζέβασμα, ζήτημα, ἕδραμα, ἑδραίωμα accipiuntur) tum activè, quia ministerio suo veritatem ἑδραιοῖ stabilit, quatenus & veritatis sedes est, utpote in qua veritas sedet, & velut in throno suo regnat; & veritatis eorum, quæ in Scripturis narrantur, testis & præconiatrix est. Sed non propterea vel veritas sine Ecclesia στῦλος & obscura est: vel Ecclesia omnimodè infallibilis est. Nam columnis atque fundamentis contingit, ut aliquando nutent & concutiantur, quomodo & Petrus στῦλος columna non parum nutavit, Gal. II. 9. 11. 12. & satis est ad Ecclesiæ stabilitatem, quòd fidei fundamento inædificata manet, & verbum infallibile veritatis omnis normam, habet, custodit, & ceu vexillum in mundo præfert, attollit & ostentat, licet in hac vita nunquam ad perfectionem tantam assurgat, ut nihil ignoret, & subinde in iis, quæ ad salutem necessaria sunt, cespitet. Nam & Moses tabulas legis manu gestavit, licet legem non perfectè servaverit, & quandoque incredulitate sua Deum offenderit. Porrò Ecclesia à Christo ceu Sponso & capite per Spiritum S. perinde ut corpus ab anima regitur. Qui proin Ecclesiæ semper rector adfuit, & ad consummationem seculi usque aderit. Sed non propterea omnis erroris magis, quam omnis peccati expers est. Nam & experientia testatur, & adversarii attestantur, Ecclesiam graviter errare in moribus posse. Atqui Christus non magis solicitus est de cognitione veritatis per Spiritum S. in Ecclesia conservanda, quam de conservanda morum sanctimonia & integritate. Cognitio enim medium; integritas & sanctimonia finis est. Multò igitur commendatior est sanctimonia, tanquam finis, quàm cognitio, tanquam medium ad finem. Est enim cognitio veritatis secundum pietatem, 1. Tim. VI. 3. Tit. I. 1. ac proin non theoretica, sed practica. Est igitur Christus Sponsus & caput Ecclesiæ, & Spiritus S. ejusdem doctor & rector, qui discipulos suos natura hebetes & obtusos reddit doctos atque ingeniosos. Sed neuter tamen in hac vita vim suam plenè & perfectè exerit. Alias enim omnes pariter sancti paritérque docti forent. Atqui mensura donorum Spiritus S. non æqualis est. Æqualis autem esset, si Spiritus S. perfectè ageret. Et Spiritus veritatis quidem ὁδηγεῖ ducit in omnem veritatem, Joh. XVI. 13. Sed Apostolos, qui omnem veritatem scribere infallibiliter singulari Divina inspiratione debuerunt; & ἀναλογικῶς Ecclesiam, at non simpliciter in omnem veritatem, sed in eam, sine qua salus non constat. Non enim illi ad salutem magis infallibilitas in doctrina, quàm ἀναμαρτησία necessaria est. Quo sensu etiam verba Johannis: Accepistis unctionem & nostis omnia, 1. Joh. II. 20. accipienda sunt. Hyperbolicæ enim locutiones sunt, quibus id significatur, quòd Spiritu Dei præditi iis, quæ ad salutem pertinent, instructissimi sint. Etiam Ecclesiam audire Christus suos jussit, Matth. XVIII. 17. Sed corripientem, & quidem elencho instituto per demonstrationem ex Dei verbo. Nam & parentes audiendi sunt, juxta illa Salomonis: Conserva præceptum patris tui, & ne relinquas legem matris tuæ. Alliga eam cordi tuo, & annecte gutturi tuo. Cùm deambulaveris, deducet, cùm dormiveris, custodiet te; cùm expergefactus fueris colloquetur tecum, Prov. VI. 20. 21. 22. & Pharisæos ipsos audire, at juxta opera eorum non facere, Matth. XXIII. 3. & Paulus ductoribus quibusvis obsequi Heb. XIII. 17. jussit. Quisquamne inde concluserit, parentes, Pharisæos, ductores quosvis infallibiles esse? Audienda est Ecclesia, audiendi sunt homines in rebus fidei, si ex Deo, & cum Deo loquantur, sin, repudiandi sunt. Denique ne illud quidem, quòd Scriptura Ecclesiæ testimonium perhibet, eam infallibilem reddit. Nam Ecclesiæ testanti, quòd Scriptura sit Dei verbum, non credimus propter authoritatem & infallibilitatem ejus, sed propter fidelitatem, qua testimonii sui documenta affert, quomodo in foro tum demum testium fides certa est, cùm testando aperiunt ea, quæ clausa fuerunt, quæque postmodum judices experiendo vera esse deprehenderunt, haud deprehensuri, nisi testes ea documenta aperuissent.
units.tr: XIX. There is no need to fear that the Church will be inadequately provided for, or even perish, if it is not declared infallible. This fear torments not the true Church, which submits itself to the Word of God, but the Church that, like a worldly kingdom, longs to rule over faith, and so is racked by the "fullness of the flesh" [τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς σαρκός] (Col. 2:23). The true Church rests in the infallible norm of the Word of God and in the gift of the Spirit who writes the law of faith on the heart, and also in the ministry of those who, as wise architects, plant and water, lay the foundation and rightly build upon it (1 Cor. 3:6–13). It is secure, and it is assured that it will be so provided for that it does not fall into deadly heresies, or hold erroneous opinions as its foundation, raise them into an idol, or set up another principle, another righteousness, another gospel, and so incur eternal damnation. The divine promises assure us that this will never happen. Still less can the Church fail on account of the fact that such a view would plainly conflict with the right, kingdom and promise of Christ, namely that the gates of hell will not prevail against the Church (Matt. 16:18), and that the elect will not be led astray (ibid. 24:24). From this it follows that it is impossible for all the Church to be overtaken by heresies of such a kind that they so conflict with the words and faith of the foundation that the truth of the foundation cannot be held together with the heresy by those who are ignorant of it. Such a heresy is the denial that Christ is God and man, or that he is the righteousness of the believer. For the Church, as a number of believers, can exist only if there are in the world people who believe that the Gospel is from God; that the way to eternal life is contained in Moses, the Prophets and the Gospel; that Christ is the only-begotten Son of God, true God, and the cause of our righteousness and life; and who are ready and eager to grow in wisdom and prudence from the Word of God and the testimony of Jesus. Moreover, this faith excludes indeed the positing of another foundation and law, and the will to obey men, but it always needs progress and correction in this life. It does not exclude every slip [ἐπλήμματα], every ignorance and every error. For in believers, because of the weakness of the flesh, due attention may fail in all things, and so it may easily happen that, while faith and love remain sound in the chief matters, there arise in the Church manifold abuses, and a great and sad crop of empty words and trivial errors. Finally, when the foundation has been rightly laid, hay and stubble may be built upon it, to be burned in the fire, while those who build are saved, as through fire (1 Cor. 3:12–13), and so on. Nor does it prove the unlimited infallibility of the Church that it seems to be called the house of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth [στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας] (1 Tim. 3:15). For those words do not seem to be joined with the Church of the living God, which is the house of God, since in that case the Apostle's sentence would be too broken and suspended, and the words would not cohere well; and the Apostle never begins a new sentence with a conjunction. Rather, the words belong to what follows, so that that mystery of godliness, great by the confession of all, is called the pillar and ground of the truth. The Hebrews indeed call the chief dogmas of faith in this way. Thus Maimonides at the beginning of his book on the Foundations of the Law writes: The foundation of foundations and the pillar of wisdom is to know that there is a first being. And one may gather from the beginning of the third book that Irenaeus also understood it in the same way. But we do not begrudge the Church this title, which is also rightly and properly said to be the pillar and ground of the truth. For every just man is called "the foundation of the world" (יסוד עולם) (Prov. 10:25), the Church is expressly called "a founded foundation" (מוסד מוסד) (Isa. 28:16), all believers are founded and steadfast in faith [τῇ πίστει πεφεμελιωμένοι καὶ ἑδραῖοι] (Col. 1:23), and the Church is built upon the rock (Matt. 16:18). The Church is also a pillar, because it holds forth the word of life above itself, and so, through the word of life, shines as a light in the world (Phil. 2:15). Certainly the Church is not a pillar if it claims to be the mistress and author of the truth, and claims that Scripture is to be known by the truth, which was known to it before Christ. And it is the ground of the truth both passively, in that it is established [τὸ ἑδραιωμένον ὑπ᾽ ἀληθείας] by the heavenly truth (in which sense the words στήριμα, ζέβασμα, ζήτημα, ἕδραμα, ἑδραίωμα are understood), and actively, because by its ministry it establishes [ἑδραιοῖ] the truth, inasmuch as it is also the seat of the truth, since the truth sits in it and reigns as on its throne, and it is the witness and herald of the truth of those things which are recounted in the Scriptures. But this does not mean that the truth is without the Church as pillar and is obscure, or that the Church is altogether infallible. For it happens to pillars and foundations that at times they totter and are shaken, as Peter, the pillar, also tottered not a little (Gal. 2:9, 11, 12). It is enough for the stability of the Church that it remains built upon the foundation of faith, and that it holds, guards and, as a banner in the world, bears aloft and displays the infallible Word of truth as the rule of all things, even though in this life it never rises to such perfection that it knows nothing, and at times stumbles in those things which are necessary for salvation. For Moses too carried the tables of the law in his hand, although he did not keep the law perfectly, and sometimes by his unbelief offended God. Moreover, the Church is ruled by Christ as its Bridegroom and Head through the Holy Spirit, just as the body is ruled by the soul. Therefore he has always been present as the ruler of the Church, and will be present until the end of the age. Yet it does not follow that the Church is free from error any more than from sin. For experience bears witness to this, and opponents too attest that the Church can err grievously in morals. But Christ is no more concerned to preserve knowledge of the truth in the Church through the Holy Spirit than to preserve the holiness and integrity of morals. For knowledge is the means, while integrity and holiness are the end. Holiness, therefore, as the end, is much more to be commended than knowledge, as the means to the end. For it is the knowledge of the truth which accords with godliness (1 Tim. 6:3; Titus 1:1), and so is not theoretical but practical. Christ, then, is the Bridegroom and Head of the Church, and the Holy Spirit is its teacher and ruler, who makes disciples that are by nature dull and obtuse learned and clever. But neither of them in this life exerts his power fully and perfectly. For otherwise all would equally be holy and equally learned. But the measure of the gifts of the Holy Spirit is not equal, and it would be equal if the Holy Spirit acted perfectly. And indeed the Spirit of truth leads [ὁδηγεῖ] into all truth (John 16:13); but this was said of the Apostles, who were to write all truth infallibly by singular divine inspiration; and the Church, analogically, is led not simply into all truth, but into that without which salvation does not stand. For infallibility in doctrine is no more necessary for salvation than sinlessness [ἀναμαρτησία]. In this sense also the words of John, You have the anointing and know all things (1 John 2:20), are to be understood. For these are hyperbolical expressions, by which it is signified that those endued with the Spirit of God are most thoroughly instructed in those things which pertain to salvation. Christ also commanded his followers to hear the Church (Matt. 18:17). But it is to hear one who rebukes, and indeed by an elenchus instituted through demonstration from the Word of God. For parents too are to be heard, according to the words of Solomon: Keep the commandment of your father, and do not forsake the law of your mother. Bind them upon your heart, and tie them about your neck. When you walk, they will lead you; when you sleep, they will keep you; and when you awake, they will talk with you (Prov. 6:20–22). The Pharisees themselves are to be heard, though not to be imitated in their works (Matt. 23:3); and Paul commanded that one should obey any leaders (Heb. 13:17). Would anyone therefore conclude that parents, Pharisees, or any leaders are infallible? The Church is to be heard, and men are to be heard in matters of faith if they speak from God and with God; but if not, they are to be rejected. Finally, even the fact that Scripture bears witness to the Church does not make it infallible. For we do not believe the Church when it testifies that Scripture is the Word of God because of its authority and infallibility, but because of the faithfulness with which it sets forth the evidence of its testimony. It is just so in a court of law, where the testimony of witnesses is at last certain only when, in giving evidence, they open up what was closed, and what the judges afterwards discover by experience to be true, which they would not have discovered unless the witnesses had opened up that evidence.

units.la: XX. Sed & Καθολικὴν Catholicam Ecclesiam profitemur. Quæ vox licet ἀγεσφῶν, ab Eccle-
units.tr: XX. But we also profess the Catholic [Καθολικὴν] Church. Although this word [ἀγεσφῶν] is not from Scripture, it was taken up from the Eccle-

units.la: Ecclesia Catholica dicta. Ecclesia, ad distinguendam se à conventiculis haereticorum, qui per loca & suas quaque provincias continebantur, assumpta ; orthodoxa tamen est, quia convenit cum dictione Scriptu-rae, in qua ΠΠuna dicitur esse columba, Cant. VI. 8. & ejus μία πίστις una fides, Ephes. IV. 5. Duobus autem modis Catholica dicitur, absolute & oppositè. Absolute, quia amplectitur doctrinam de Christo Servatore Θεανθρώπῳ, cui testimonium dant omnes Prophetae quòd in nomine ejus remissionem peccatorum accipiat quivis, qui in eum credit, Actor. X. 43. & per cujus gratiam æquè Patres V. T. salvati sunt, atque nos salvamur, ibid. XV. 11. Oppositè Catholica N.T. Ecclesia est, partim ad Cathedram Mosis, seu Ecclesiam V. T. angustis Judææ finibus inclusam; partim ad conventicula haereticorum, secundum proprias concupiscentias sibi doctores coacervantia, & ex eorum nominibus se discernentia, quales Antitrinitarii & Donatistæ fuerunt; partim ad imperia mundana, quæ non possunt esse extensa per totum mundum, vel sparsa per omnes terras, sed in certo quodam terræ climate congregata ab uno, paucis vel multis hominibus le regi patiuntur, & pro Dei nutu ortum & occasum temporarium habent. Catholica enim sic Ecclesia est, non angularis, vel temporaria, ad angulum, vel unum aliquod orbis clima, & tempus certum restricta, uni loco populóque affixa, uni genti elocata, ac velut in servitutem tradita; sed una & universalis, ex universo genere humano per totum terrarum orbem, sub diversissimis imperiis sparsa, collecta, soli Deo legislatori & Christo capiti affixa, idem ex Dei verbo scripto omni tempore tenens fundamentum fidei, impietati & concupiscentiis omnibus renuntians, adeóque uni capiti suo Jesu Christo vinculo Spiritus S. sic unita, ut ejus per Christum vivificatæ unus sit Deus, unus Dominus, unus Spiritus, una fides & spes, unum baptisma, &c. Ephes. IV. 4. 5. talisque sine ulla ἐπροδιδασκαλία, haeresi, schismate maneat usque ad consummationem seculi. Scitè enim plane Hieronymus Dial. adv. Lucif. Si, inquit, Ecclesiam per totum orbem diffusam non habet Christus, aut si in Sardinia tantùm habet, nimis pauper factus est. Et Vincentius Lirinensis adversus haereses cap. 3. In ipsa, inquit, Catholica Ecclesia maximopere curandum est, ut id teneatur, quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est. Hoc est enim verè proprieque catholicum, quod ipsa vis nominis ratioque declarat, qua omnia verè universaliter comprehendit.
units.tr: siastical writers and is called Catholic. The Church adopted the name to distinguish itself from the conventicles of heretics, which were confined to particular places and provinces. Yet it is orthodox, because it agrees with the usage of Scripture, in which the dove is called "one" (Song 6:8), and in which there is "one faith" (Eph. 4:5). The Church is called Catholic in two ways, absolutely and in opposition. Absolutely, because it embraces the doctrine of Christ the Saviour, the God-man, to whom "all the prophets bear witness that through his name everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins" (Acts 10:43), and through whose grace the fathers of the Old Testament "were saved in the same way as we are" (Acts 15:11). In opposition, the Catholic Church of the New Testament is set against, partly, the "seat of Moses," or the Church of the Old Testament enclosed within the narrow limits of Judea; partly, the conventicles of heretics, which gather teachers for themselves according to their own lusts and take their names from their leaders, as the Antitrinitarians and Donatists did; and partly, worldly empires, which cannot be extended throughout the whole world or spread over all lands, but are gathered in a certain climate of the earth, ruled by one or a few men, and by God's will have a temporary rise and fall. The Catholic Church is not a Church confined to a corner, or to one region of the world and a particular time, fixed to one place and people, handed over to one nation and as it were enslaved. It is "one and universal," gathered and scattered from the whole human race throughout the entire earth, under the most diverse empires, joined to God alone as lawmaker and to Christ as head, always holding to the same foundation of faith from the written Word of God, renouncing impiety and all lusts. It is so united to its one head, Jesus Christ, by the bond of the Holy Spirit, that in those quickened through Christ there is "one God, one Lord, one Spirit, one faith and hope, one baptism," etc. (Eph. 4:4–5). It remains so, without any false teaching, heresy or schism, until the end of the age. Jerome rightly says in the Dialogue against the Luciferians: "If Christ does not have a Church spread through the whole world, or if he has it only in Sardinia, he has become too poor." And Vincentius of Lérins, Against Heresies, chapter 3: "In the Catholic Church itself, great care must be taken to hold what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. For that is truly and properly Catholic, which the very force of the name and its meaning declares, since it embraces all things truly and universally."

units.la: XXI. Catholica Ecclesia spectatur vel universè, ratione totius multitudinis fidelium, ex quibus illa constituitur, cujuscunque sint loci & temporis (eatenus enim à terreno certæ gentis Regno distinguitur) vel particulariter, & κατὰ μέρος, nunc in ea, quæ in Cœlis cum Christo gloriosè regnat; nunc in ea quæ sive in coetus particulares collecta, sive extra eos palabunda, in terra laborat, militat & luctatur. Sicut autem catholicum Latinis universale, Philosophi non ex actu, sed ex potentia definiunt, illud statuentes καθόλου, quod pluribus inesse aptum natum est: Sic Ecclesia, fides, religio dicitur, non quam uno tempore multi sequuntur, vel profitentur; sed profiteri multi quocunque loco & tempore possunt, seu quia multi profiteri deberent. Pariter Catholica Ecclesia non est, quæ multos uno tempore vocatos, electos & fideles complectitur, sed quæ multos complecti potest. Genus humanum in Paradiso in uno primùm, dein in duobus individuis subsistitit: in arca Noæ ad octo individua redactum est. Ita Ecclesia Catholica ad μικρὸν ποίμνιον parvum gregem, Luc. XII. 32. statim cùm Christus in mundo creditus est; & procedente tempore ad duos testes, Apoc. XI. 3. hoc est, comparatos cum ingenti multitudine Bestiae adhaerente, paucos, redacta, numero, non fide & zelo, vel studio veritatis orthodoxae defendendae, defecit, neque iccirco Catholica esse desiit.
units.tr: XXI. The Catholic Church is considered either universally, with respect to the whole multitude of believers of whatever place and time of which it is made up (for in this sense it is distinguished from the earthly kingdom of a particular nation), or particularly, and in part: now the part that reigns gloriously with Christ in heaven, now the part that, gathered into particular assemblies or wandering outside them, labours, fights and struggles on earth. Just as the Latins define "catholic" as "universal," the philosophers define it not by actual existence but by potential existence, holding that the universal is that which is naturally fit to be in many. So the Church, or faith, or religion is called catholic not because many follow or profess it at one time, but because many can profess it in any place and time, or because many ought to profess it. Likewise, the Catholic Church is not the one that embraces many who are called, chosen and believing at one time, but the one that can embrace many. The human race subsisted first in one individual in Paradise, then in two; in Noah's ark it was reduced to eight individuals. So the Catholic Church, reduced to a "little flock" (Luke 12:32) as soon as Christ was believed in the world, and as time went on to "two witnesses" (Rev. 11:3), that is, few in number compared with the vast multitude adhering to the Beast, did not fail in faith, zeal, or the desire to defend orthodox truth, and therefore did not cease to be Catholic.

units.la: XXII. Sed Pontificii ἐκκλησίαν Καθολικὴν Ecclesiam Catholicam faciunt diversissimo sensu, quàm Symbolum Apostolicum, Scripturæ convenienter, fecit.
units.tr: XXII. But the Papists understand "the Catholic Church" in a very different sense from that which the Apostles' Creed gives, in agreement with Scripture.

units.la: Cùm enim Catholici vox Ecclesiam nullo discrimine ex Judæis & gentibus ad eandem sortem, sine affixione ad locum & cathedram certam, Mosaicæ similem, significet, illi Catholicæ fidei desertores, hoc tempore, spreta vocabuli notione, Ecclesiam Catholicam faciunt, Romanam, seu coetum affixum Romanæ sedi. Quod plane ἀσυνέδον est; cùm Catholicum, & ad certum locum atque sedem affixum esse è diametro pugnet. Nempe illi sicut rerum, ita nominum transsubstantiatores sunt. Apud eos enim fere omnia Scripturæ & Ecclesiæ nomina vim suam perdidere, & jam præter nativam indolem & intentionem Spiritus S. aliud significant. Ita enim iis Regnum Dei est Regnum hominis; spirituale Respublica aspectabilis, serviens elementis; Petrus Papa; & quis singula enumeret? Non potuit enim meretrix magna sine hac vocabulorum etiam interemptorum persona in proscenium prodire. Cùmque καθολικὸν etiam unitatem, divisioni illi, quam olim lex dividens Israelitas à gentibus, mares à foeminis, servos à liberis, seniores à subditis, Israelitas à Levitis, Levitas à Sacerdotibus, Sacerdotes à summo Sacerdote, & eos, qui in terra erant, à coelitibus, faciebat, quæque in N.T. aboleri, atque cum pace, libertate & πλεονεξία communi commutari debuit, oppositam notet; novi hi Catholici in unitate gloriantes, veram hanc unitatem quàm maximè oppugnant. Cathedra enim Romana, & spiritus ejus privatus, & cleri prærogativæ illam unitatem, ἰσότιμον τῆς πίστεως libertatem atque communem πλεονεξίαν planè interimunt. Quæ enim unitas apud eos esse potest, qui falsi capitis & legis introductione Ecclesiam scindunt; anathema iis, qui omnia de Deo, foedere, justitia Christi & Sacramentis in Scripturis revelata credunt, denuntiant, & apud quos nulla cum φρονήσει δικαίων, qui ante illos fuerunt, consensio est?
units.tr: For while the word Catholic signifies the Church without distinction from Jews and Gentiles, on equal terms and not fixed to a particular place or seat like the Mosaic, these deserters of the Catholic faith, in this age, disregarding the meaning of the word, make the Catholic Church the Roman one, that is, the assembly attached to the Roman see. This is plainly absurd, since to be Catholic and to be fixed to a certain place and seat are diametrically opposed. Indeed, they transubstantiate names as well as things. For among them almost all the names of Scripture and of the Church have lost their force, and now mean something other than their native character and the intention of the Holy Spirit. Thus for them "the kingdom of God" is the kingdom of man; "spiritual" means an outward commonwealth serving the elements; "Peter" means the Pope; and who could list them all? For the great harlot could not come forward on stage without the persona of these words also being destroyed. And since catholic also denotes unity, which is opposed to that division which the dividing law once made between Israelites and Gentiles, males and females, slaves and free, elders and subjects, Israelites and Levites, Levites and priests, the priests and the high priest, and those on earth and those in heaven, a division which was to be abolished in the New Testament and replaced by peace, liberty and common privilege, these new Catholics who boast of unity most fiercely attack this true unity. For the Roman see, its private spirit, and the prerogatives of the clergy utterly destroy that unity, that equal honour of faith, that liberty and common privilege. What unity can there be among those who, by introducing a false head and law, split the Church, and who pronounce anathema on those who believe all things about God, the covenant, the righteousness of Christ and the sacraments revealed in Scripture, and with whom there is no agreement in the wisdom of the righteous who were before them?

units.la: XXIII. Ecclesia Christi vera & propriè dicta existentiam in mundo perpetuam habet, eámque non contingentem, ut posset etiam deficere & non existere, sed planè necessariam, necessitate illa, quæ ex hypothesi dicitur; maximè causæ efficientis tum primæ, quæ voluntas Dei immutabilis est, Rom. IX. 11. 29. tum secundæ, sive proximæ, quæ verbum Dei, & Spiritus S. per illud efficax est, Esaj. LIX. 21. Quod Sociniani, aliíque liberi arbitrii, & apostasiæ ftasiæ Sanctorum assertores inficiantur, neque non inficiari possunt. Etenim perpetuam ejus existentiam Deus in verbo suo veraciter promisit. Ponam in seculum semen ejus, & thronum ejus, sicut dies cæli, &c. Psal. LXXXIX. 30. Spiritus meus, qui est super te, & verba mea, quæ posui in ore tuo,non recedent de ore tuo, & de ore seminis tui, & de ore Seminis seminis tui, ex hoc tempore, & usque in seculum, Esaj. LIX. 21. Super hac Petra ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, & portæ inferorum non prævalebunt ei, Matth. XVI. 18. Quibus verbis promissio fit Ecclesiæ, non quà Ecclesia est, seu quandiu talis manet, sed etiam, ut perpetuò sit Ecclesia. Nam portæ inferorum non prævalebunt Ecclesiæ, sic ut eam opprimant vel destruant. Et promittitur Ecclesiæ beneficium non post mortem, si eò usque perseveret, sed in hac vita. Cùm enim oppugnatio ejus in hac vita fiat, etiam defensio & conservatio ejus in hac vita, ei promittitur. Ideo Christus promisit: Ego ero vobiscum usque ad consummationem seculi, Matth. XXVIII. 20. Quæ promissio Apostolis data non minùs ad Ecclesiam juxta naturam relatorum, pertinet. Est enim Ecclesia Regnum & corpus Christi. Atqui nunquam ille vel Regno suo caret, quia ejus finis nullus erit, Luc. I. 32: 33. vel corpore, quod crescere, augescere usque ad sui perfectionem, ultimo demum die futuram, debet, Eph. IV. 15. 16. V. 26. 27. Apoc. VI. 11. destituitur. Neque sine vocationis Divinæ certo successu vel obedientia Christi usque ad mortem coronari, gloria & honore Regni illius, quod ipsi Pater disposuit, Lucæ XXII. 29. vel ipse unctus Rex super Sion montem sanctum Dei, Psal. II. 6: vel Pater ipsi servasse promissionem juratam æterni Sacerdotii, ibid. CX. 4. censeri potuisset. Si enim ex hypothesi, sic totus terrarum orbis illi adversaretur, ut nullus efficaci vocatione, secundum Dei vocantis propositum, efficeretur ex non-populo populus Dei, I. Petr. II. 9: 10. Hos. II. 23. nullum esset Christo Sacerdotium, nullum Regnum in Monte sancto, sed regnandum ipsi foret in monte Sinai, sola hostili dominatione, & tandem rebellium triumphatione. Atque ita fieri potuisset, ut Christus in cassum laboraret, & vires suas consumeret, neque omnino haberet opera sua mercedem, Esaj. XLIX. 4. & pro eo, quòd animam suam posuit sacrificium, non videret Semen; ibid. LIII. 10. 11. Denique Scriptura de Ecclesia tum omnes causas defectionis negat, ajens, eam nec à portis inferorum vinci, Matth. XVI. 18. nec à Pseudo-Prophetis seduci, ibid. XXIV. 24. nec à carne ad peccatum regnans præcipitari posse, I. Joh. III. 9. tum omnes actu causas perseverationis ejus affirmat, asserens, eandem ex immutabili Dei proposito, 2. Tim. II. 19. quod in Christo redemptore & advocato nostro est, I. Joh. II. 1. 2. Rom. VIII. 33. 34. Spiritus S. virtute ac præsidio ad salutem custodiri per fidem, Joh. XIV. 16. 17. I. Petr. I. 5.
units.tr: XXIII. The Church of Christ, truly and properly so called, has a perpetual existence in the world, and not a contingent one, such that it might also fail and cease to exist. Its existence is absolutely necessary, with the necessity that is said to arise from hypothesis; this is so chiefly because of the first efficient cause, which is the immutable will of God (Rom. 9:11, 29), and because of the second, or proximate, cause, which is the Word of God and the Holy Spirit working efficaciously through it (Isa. 59:21). The Socinians and others who assert free will and the apostasy of the saints deny this, and indeed cannot help denying it. For God has truly promised its perpetual existence in his Word: "I will establish his seed for ever, and his throne as the days of heaven" (Ps. 89:30); "My Spirit that is upon you, and my words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart out of your mouth, nor out of the mouth of your seed, nor out of the mouth of your seed's seed, from henceforth and for ever" (Isa. 59:21); "Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" (Matt. 16:18). By these words a promise is made to the Church not only as long as it is the Church, or for as long as it remains such, but that it shall be the Church for ever. For the gates of hell shall not prevail against the Church so as to overwhelm or destroy it. And the benefit is promised to the Church not after death, if it perseveres to that point, but in this life. For since its assault happens in this life, its defence and preservation in this life are also promised to it. Therefore Christ promised: "I am with you always, even to the end of the age" (Matt. 28:20). This promise, given to the Apostles, pertains no less to the Church, according to the nature of what is related. For the Church is the kingdom and body of Christ. Now he is never deprived of his kingdom, since "of his kingdom there shall be no end" (Luke 1:32–33), nor of his body, which must grow and increase until it reaches its perfection on the last day (Eph. 4:15–16; 5:26–27; Rev. 6:11). Nor could it be said that he is crowned, without the sure success of the divine calling or the obedience of Christ unto death, with the glory and honour of that kingdom which "the Father has appointed to him" (Luke 22:29), or that he is the one "anointed king upon Zion, my holy mountain" (Ps. 2:6), or that the Father has kept for him the promise "sworn of the eternal priesthood" (Ps. 110:4). For if, by hypothesis, the whole world were so hostile to him that no one was made, by the effectual calling according to the purpose of God who calls, from "not a people" into "the people of God" (1 Pet. 2:9–10; Hos. 2:23), there would be no priesthood for Christ, no kingdom on the holy mountain, but he would have to reign on Mount Sinai, by hostile domination alone, and at last by the triumph over rebels. And so it could come about that Christ laboured in vain and wore out his strength, and did not in fact have "his reward for his work" (Isa. 49:4), and instead of having "given his soul as a sacrifice," would not see his seed (Isa. 53:10–11). Finally, Scripture denies all causes of the Church's defection, saying that it cannot be overcome "by the gates of hell" (Matt. 16:18), nor be led astray by false prophets (Matt. 24:24), nor be cast down by the flesh reigning in sin (1 John 3:9). And it asserts all the actual causes of its perseverance, declaring that it is kept from the immutable purpose of God (2 Tim. 2:19), which is in Christ our Redeemer and Advocate (1 John 2:1–2; Rom. 8:33–34), and kept by the power and protection of the Holy Spirit unto salvation through faith (John 14:16–17; 1 Pet. 1:5).

units.la: XXIV. Est equidem Christus Rex illius Regni, cujus subditi sponte ac liberè mandanti obtemperant, non vi quadam in obedientia continentur & perseverant. Sunt enim populus spontaneitatum, Psal. CX. 3. Sed non ideo sic liberè obediunt, ut omnes simul non obedire; atque ita Ecclesia penitus defice-re possit. Neque enim vel motus ille gratiæ, qua homines ad obedientiam adducuntur, & in ea retinentur, violenta coactio, sed efficax in cordibus hominum operatio est, quamente & voluntate renovantur, & ex nolentibus volentes, ex immorigeris morigeri redduntur, Tit. III. 3. 4. 5. vel libertas obedientiæ, quæ Christo præstatur, indifferentia ad bonum & malum, sed spontanea inclinatio animi per Spiritum S. renovati, ad parendum Deo & legi ejus est; ut licet per reliquam carnis pravitatem repugnare possit, tamen per Spiritus prævalentis & vincentis virtutem nolit, atque sic Deo perseverantes, & libenter Actor. II. 41. adhæreat.
units.tr: XXIV. Christ is indeed the King of that kingdom whose subjects obey his command willingly and freely. They are not held in obedience and kept there by some kind of force. They are a people of free will, Ps. 110:3. But they do not obey so freely that all of them together could fail to obey, so that the Church could utterly fall away. For that movement of grace by which people are brought to obedience and kept in it is not a violent compulsion but an effective working in human hearts, by which they are renewed in mind and will, and from unwilling become willing and from disobedient become obedient, Titus 3:3-5. Nor is the freedom of obedience given to Christ an indifference between good and evil. It is a spontaneous inclination of a mind renewed by the Holy Spirit to obey God and his law. So although the remaining corruption of the flesh can resist, nevertheless, by the power and victory of the Spirit, the renewed mind does not will to resist, and so it persists in God and gladly cleaves to him, Acts 2:41.

units.la: XXV. Habet verò & hoc Ecclesia Dei, ut singuli, qui in ea sunt, mutuo communiones.
units.tr: XXV. The Church of God also has this feature: that the individuals who are in it mutually desire communion and congregation, even external congregation.

units.la: Eorundem argumentis contrariis occurrunt. nis & congregationis etiam externæ desiderio flagrent, exemplo Davidis, profitentis: Ego sum socius omnium, qui te timent, חבר כל אשר ירא״ך Psal. CXIX. 63. Quod necessarium esse impiè Libertini & Schwenkfeldiani aliíque seculi nostri fanatici & enthusiastæ, spiritualis cum Ecclesia communionis prætextu, externam vellicantes, & meditationum privatarum obtentu, publicos conventus negligentes, inficiantur. Qui enim credit, Ecclesiam esse, etiam credit, eam esse communionem Sanctorum. Qua in κοινωνία communione primi Christiani perseverasse, Actor. II.42. dicuntur. Nam κοινωνίαν μετ' ἀλλήλων communionem inter nos invicem habere, in luce ambulantes debemus, 1. Joh. I. 7. Hanc qui credit, simul credit, Deum varia corpori suo dona distribuisse, & constituisse, ut alius alio indigeat, & ut, qui in Christo adolescere cupit, is se ad fideles quoque alios applicet, ut per illos ad Dei & Christi amorem proficiat: Deum sic dona sua hominibus distribuere, ut non det omnia omnibus, quò sic dona nostra invicem promptiores impendamus, fidelium villicorum instar, per quos Deus plurimos lucrari vult, à quibus ipse glorificetur & admirabilis fiat: deberi fratribus charitatem ob amorem ejus, ex quo illi geniti sunt, adeóque requirendos esse, quos diligant, quibus prosint, quorum fide ad salutem lætentur, & à quibus vicissim diligantur, & ad salutem ædificentur: Christo promissam esse hæreditatem eorum, qui ipsum diligunt; & sicut Abrahamo; ita etiam fidelibus promissum esse Semen, cui in ipso, sive cum ipso benedicatur; suúmque adeò esse, gignere filios Dei, & cernere hæreditatem Christi, velut suam, eámque locupletare. Cúmque non possit homo, ceu natura ζῷον πολιτικὸν animal sociale in mundo seorsim solus agere; vel jam fidelis conversabitur cum infidelibus & peccatoribus notoriis, & cogetur eos redarguere, ne cum malis eorum operibus communicet; saltem cum illis, ceu fratribus lætari non poterit: vel communicabit cum fidelibus, & cum iis communem bonorum malorúmque sensum habebit, quam ob rem ipsa mundi ἀνλωσίας fideles in mundo conjungit & contesserat. Quis enim non amicos & socios quærit, quibuscum συμφυτευθῆναι possit? Et eodem etiam pertinent ἐπισυναγωγαὶ congregationes fidelium publicæ ad loquendum, audiendum, meditandum, mutuúmque ad usum revocandum Dei verbum, & usurpanda signa gratiæ, eo ordine, quem Deus in verbo suo instituit. Has enim, ut & considerationem mutuam ad instigationem charitatis & bonorum operum relinquere, Lex Dei sanctificationem nominis ejus in publico etiam coetu, in quarto Decalogi præcepto, mandans, Apostolus, Hebr. X. 25. quin & ipsa communio cum ἡγου-μένοις, iis, qui præsunt, pastoribus & doctoribus à Christo datis, ut per eos vera fides & pietas vitæ excitetur, augeatur & confirmetur, Ephes. IV. 11. &c. adeóque & charitas, & mutua ædificatio, & Dei gloria prohibent. Neque enim fideles ἑαυτὸς ἀποδιορίζουσι se ipsos separant, Jud. vers. 19. vel dissensiones, schismata faciunt, Rom. XVI. 17. adeóque segreges vivunt, ceu homines animales, spiritum non habentes, Jud. v. 19. memores, se unum corpus, & invicem mem-
units.tr: They meet the contrary arguments of the same men. David professes the example: I am a companion of all who fear you, [חבר כל אשר ירא״ך] Ps. 119:63. That this is necessary is denied impiously by the Libertines, the Schwenkfeldians, and other fanatics and enthusiasts of our age, who, under the pretext of a spiritual communion with the Church, disparage external communion, and, on the pretext of private meditations, neglect public assemblies. For whoever believes that there is a Church also believes that it is the communion of saints. In this communion [κοινωνία] the first Christians are said to have persevered, Acts 2:42. For we ought to have communion with one another [κοινωνίαν μετ' ἀλλήλων], walking in the light, 1 John 1:7. Whoever believes this also believes that God has distributed various gifts to his body and has ordained that one should need another, and that whoever desires to grow in Christ should attach himself to other believers, so that through them he may advance in the love of God and Christ. God distributes his gifts to people in such a way that he does not give all things to all, so that we may more readily spend our gifts for one another, like faithful stewards through whom God wishes to gain many, by whom he is glorified and made wonderful. Brotherly love is owed to brothers on account of the love of him from whom they were born. Therefore they are to be sought out whom we love, whom we may help, in whose faith we rejoice for salvation, and by whom in turn we are loved and built up unto salvation. The inheritance is promised to Christ's own who love him; and just as to Abraham, so also to believers is the Seed promised, in whom or with whom they are blessed; and it is their own to beget children of God and to see the inheritance of Christ as their own and to enrich it. And since a human being, as a social animal [ζῷον πολιτικὸν], cannot act alone and separately in the world, either a believer will already be living with unbelievers and notorious sinners, and will be compelled to rebuke them, lest he share in their evil works; at the least he will not be able to rejoice with them as brothers. Or he will share with believers, and have a common sense of good and evil with them. For this reason the very world's [ἀνλωσίας] (?) joins and weaves believers together in the world. For who does not seek friends and companions with whom he may be planted together [συμφυτευθῆναι]? To the same end belong the public congregations [ἐπισυναγωγαὶ] of believers for speaking, hearing, meditating, and mutually recalling the Word of God, and for using the signs of grace in the order that God has instituted in his word. For these, as well as the mutual consideration that stirs up love and good works, the law of God commands in the fourth commandment the sanctifying of his name even in public assembly, and the Apostle, Heb. 10:25, commands the same. Indeed, communion itself with those who lead [ἡγουμένοις], those who preside, the ministers and teachers given by Christ, so that through them true faith and godliness of life may be stirred up, increased and confirmed, Eph. 4:11 and following. Thus charity, mutual edification, and the glory of God forbid us to do otherwise. For believers do not separate themselves [ἑαυτὸς ἀποδιορίζουσι], Jude v. 19, nor do they make dissensions, schisms, Rom. 16:17, and so they do not live apart like sensual people, not having the Spirit, Jude v. 19. Mindful that they are one body, and members one of another, and that as such they ought to be grown together [ςυμφυτεῦσαι] with Christ.

units.la: bra esse, & ut talia Christo ςυμφυτεῦσαι complantari debere. Ideo Sancti omnes, velut in V. T. Patriarchæ, Israelitæ, erectis passim altaribus, Tabernaculo, Templo, Synagogis, & in N. T. Christiani in cœtus suos coaluerunt, & optimi quique Ecclesiæ adjungi & domestici ejus fieri enixè desiderarunt, Psal. XXVI. 8. XXVII. 4. XLII. 1.&c. XLVII. 10. LXIII. 2. 3. LXXXIV. 2. CXXII. 6. 7. Denique & Ecclesia invisibilis in visibili est, atque adeo qui visiblilem deserit, is nec invisibilis membrum esse potest.
units.tr: For this reason all the saints, as in the Old Testament the patriarchs and Israelites, with altars erected everywhere, in the Tabernacle, the Temple, and the synagogues, and in the New Testament Christians, gathered into their assemblies, and the best of them earnestly desired to be joined to the Church and to become its members of the household, Ps. 26:8; 27:4; 42:1 etc.; 47:10; 63:2-3; 84:2; 122:6-7. Finally, the invisible Church is in the visible, and therefore whoever deserts the visible cannot be a member of the invisible.

units.la: XXVI. Ut verò & communio atque congregatio illa, & libertas filiorum Dei unâ consistere, & amicè conspirare possint, fides, charitas & prudentia efficiunt. Fides, ne communicet fidelis cum iis, qui abdicato Dei verbo, authoritatem, verbum & fabulas hominum consectantur; sed cùm iis potiùs, apud quos verbum Dei, sermo ille Propheticus, prædicatur, ἐλεγχῶ, Spiritus & vocatio non rejicitur, atque scandala non nimiùm & passivè grassantur. Charitas quæ de singulis fundamentum retinentibus, & quas ei superstruunt, stipulas in idolum non erigentibus, bene sperat, cum illis fraternitatem colit, congregationem frequentat, atque id sedulò operam navat, ut docendo, hortando, facem pietatis præferendo, sequendo, sibi & aliis prosit. Prudentia denique, ut φρόνησις ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ ψευδοπροφητῶν attendat ad homines & Pseudo-prophetas, Matth. VII. 15. X. 17. observet probè hominum dicta, de illis ex Dei verbo judicet, omnia exploret, bonum retineat, fidei suæ dominari patiatur neminem; perpetim memor sit, justum sua, non aliena fide vivere, suis, non alienis oculis videre debere; & prædictum esse, fore ut Ecclesiæ communioni se quandoque zizania, Pseudo-Prophetæ, Antichristus, apostatæ, Bestia & Babylon commisceat, & veritatem Evangelii mirè corrumpat, propter quos summa vigilantia & prudentia opus est, ne non cum sponsa Christi, sed cum adultera & meretrice communicet.
units.tr: XXVI. So that this communion and congregation and the freedom of the children of God may stand together and agree in friendship, faith, love and prudence bring this about. Faith does not share with those who, having renounced the Word of God, pursue their own authority and the fables of men, but rather with those among whom the Word of God, that prophetic speech, is preached, and the reproof [ἐλεγχῶ], the Spirit and the calling are not rejected, and offenses do not spread too much or go unchecked. Charity, which hopes well of those who hold the foundation, and do not raise up on the idol the straw that others build on it, cultivates brotherhood with them, frequents the congregation with them, and takes care diligently to benefit both itself and others by teaching, exhorting, holding forth and following the torch of godliness. Finally prudence, so that it may attend to men and false prophets [ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ ψευδοπροφητῶν] (Matt. 7:15; 10:17), carefully observes the words of men, judges them by the Word of God, tests all things, holds fast to what is good, and allows no one to lord it over its faith. It always remembers that the righteous lives by his own faith, not another's, and must see with his own eyes, not others'. It also knows that it has been foretold that tares, false prophets, the Antichrist, apostates, the Beast and Babylon will at some point mingle with the communion of the Church and wonderfully corrupt the truth of the gospel. Because of these, the greatest vigilance and prudence are needed, lest one share communion not with the bride of Christ but with the adulteress and harlot.

units.la: XXVII. Neque tamen hæc externa cum fidelibus communio simpliciter ad salutem necessaria est; ut vera Ecclesiæ membra, salutem æternam consecutura, non amplius censeantur ii, qui non ulla culpa sua, sed temporum calamitate & injuria communione hac suavissima & salutari privantur. Sublato enim aliena vi communionis actu, manet animi affectus, voluntas & propensio. Manet communio interior animorum, qua Christo capiti vera fide, & sanctis omnibus sincera charitate, quæ etiam extra communionem externam efficax esse potest, arctissimè uniuntur. Neque enim desinunt esse cœtus & congregatio, ratione vinculi & communionis, quam per fidem in Deo cum Christo, atque inter se per charitatis pium affectum habent, etiamsi in mundo dislipentur, & mundus iis dicat, ut fugiat instar avicula à monte, Psal. XI. 1. atque columbæ instar, in fissuris petrarum delitescere Cant. II. 14. cogantur. Non enim congregatio παντικὴ localis & visibilis semper necessaria est, sed tum demum, cùm absque violentia, & sine fidei periculo instituta potest; atque pascua vel in universum salubriai sunt, vel in universum venenq infecta non sunt.
units.tr: XXVII. Yet this external communion with believers is not simply necessary for salvation, so that those who are deprived of this most sweet and salutary communion, not through any fault of their own but through the calamity and injury of the times, should no longer be counted true members of the Church destined to obtain eternal salvation. For when the act of communion is removed by another's force, the affection of the mind, the will and the disposition remain. The inner communion of souls remains, by which they are most closely united to Christ the head by true faith, and to all the saints by sincere love, which can be effective even outside external communion. For they do not cease to be an assembly and congregation by reason of the bond and communion which they have through faith in God with Christ and among themselves through the pious affection of love, even if they are scattered in the world, and the world says to them that they should flee like a little bird from the mountain, Ps. 11:1, and be forced to hide like doves in the clefts of the rocks, Song 2:14. For a local and visible congregation [παντικὴ] is not always necessary, but only when it can be instituted without violence and without danger to faith. And pastures are either wholesome in general or not infected with poison in general.

units.la: Desiderio communionis & congregationis etiam externæ flagrant. sunt. Communio enim externa non ad destructionem sed ad aedificationem instituta est, & tum demum obligat, cum sine salutis dispendio haberi potest. Ex earum enim rerum genere est, quarum non privatio, sed contemptus damnat. Alias non foret Ecclesia, cum duo vel tres in distinctis locis, at in nomine tamen Christi conveniunt, Matth. XVIII. 20. & ad Ecclesiam atque sortem Sanctorum in luce, coelestemque Hierosolymam non pertinerent, qui in carceribus, claustris, triremibus detenti, vel in sylvis, montibus, cavernis terrae, propter metum hominum, latitantes, integram erga Christum fidem, integrumque erga Sanctos charitatis affectum retinent. Neque vel Elias in deserto solitudinem suam deplorans, vel duo illi testes Apocalyptici, saccis amicti, ad Ecclesiam pertinuissent. Et quid alias facient illi, qui relicta Ecclesia, parentibus, conjugibus, liberis, pastoribus, fratribus ὁμοπνεύς profitentur, se exire ex mundo, imo & in eremum abeunt, atque ibi non cum hominibus, sed cum feris agitant? Forte illi habent communionem externam cum Ecclesia per caput suum Papam, vel per eadem Sacramenta, sed ut coetus in coetu, & a coetu separatus. Quanto magis, qui cum hoc vel illo coetu externam communionem habere non possunt, internam cum electis fidelibus per Christum, verum illud commune & unicum caput retentum, colere possunt?
units.tr: Men also burn with desire for communion and for an external assembly. External communion was instituted not for destruction but for edification, and it binds only when it can be had without loss to salvation. It belongs to the class of things whose privation does not condemn but whose contempt does. Otherwise there would be no Church when two or three gather in separate places yet in the name of Christ (Matt. 18:20). Nor would the saints held in prisons, cloisters and galleys, or hiding in woods, mountains and caves of the earth for fear of men, yet keeping whole faith toward Christ and whole affection of charity toward the saints, belong to the Church, to the lot of the saints in light, and to the heavenly Jerusalem. Nor would Elijah lamenting his solitude in the desert, or the two Apocalyptic witnesses clothed in sackcloth, have belonged to the Church. And what will those do who, leaving the Church, parents, spouses, children, ministers and brothers, profess with one spirit that they are going out of the world, and even withdraw into the wilderness, where they live not with men but with wild beasts? Perhaps they have external communion with the Church through their head, the Pope, or through the same sacraments, but only as a group within a group, separated from the group. How much more, then, can those who cannot have external communion with this or that assembly cultivate internal communion with the elect faithful through Christ, the true common and only head being retained?

units.la: XXVIII. Sed accidit tamen aliena vi & fere semper, ut fideles cum fidelibus sibique similibus societatem inire & colere instituentes, non cum solis illis, etiam cum permixtis iisdem occultis infidelibus, hypocritis eandem fidem, saltem quoad fundamentum, profitentibus, eadem symbola gratiae usurpantibus, eadem Templorum limina calcantibus, externam communionem ineant colantque. Cum enim καρδιογνώστης non sint, & solas externas fidei & charitatis operationes, quae cum vera & ἀνυπο κρίτῳ fide & charitate necessarium nexum, nec apud omnes, nec semper habent; cognoscant, vere fideles ab infidelibus in hac vita, in qua paleae cum tritico commixtae jacent, discernere non possunt. Sed charitas tamen χρηστεύεται, οὐ περπερεύεται, οὐ λογίζεται τὸ κακόν, πάντα στέγει, πάντα πιστεύει, πάντα ἐλπίζει, benigna est, non procax, non cogitat malum, cuncta credit, cuncta sperat, 1. Cor. XIII. 4. 5. 6. Hac ergo charitate instigante vere fideles, verae Ecclesiae membra, quamdiu in mundo exi-stunt, se non possunt non congregare cum iis etiam, qui apud Deum fideles non sunt, sed apud homines, quorum communioni forte nascendi, vel alias ob causas miscentur, ut Deo & hominibus mentiantur, propter communes operationes externas, quae vel a fide & Spiritu Dei, vel ab utriusque simulatione pululare possunt, pro fidelibus habentur. Et hic quidem homo spectat ad oculos, Jehova spectat ad cor, 1. Sam. XVI. 7.
units.tr: XXVIII. But it happens, by an alien force and almost always, that the faithful, in setting about and cultivating fellowship with the faithful and those like themselves, enter into and cultivate external communion not only with those but also with hypocrites mixed among them, secret unbelievers who profess the same faith at least as to its foundation, who use the same signs of grace and tread the same threshold of the temples. For since men are not heart-knowers and can know only the external operations of faith and charity, which do not have a necessary connection with true and unfeigned [anypokritos] faith and charity, neither among all men nor always, they cannot truly distinguish the faithful from unbelievers in this life, in which the chaff lies mixed with the wheat. But charity is kind, is not puffed up, does not behave itself unseemly, does not seek its own, is not provoked, thinks no evil, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things (1 Cor. 13:4–7) [chrēsteuetai, ou perpereuetai, ou logizetai to kakon, panta stegei, panta pisteuei, panta elpizei]. Therefore, with this charity urging them on, the truly faithful, the true members of the Church, as long as they exist in the world, cannot but gather together also with those who are not faithful before God but only before men, whom perhaps the accident of birth or other causes mingle with them, so that they lie to God and men; because of common external operations, which may spring either from faith and the Spirit of God or from the pretence of both, they are held to be faithful. And here indeed man looks to the eyes, but Jehovah looks to the heart (1 Sam. 16:7).

units.la: XXIX. Hinc emergit altera notio Ecclesiae, in Scripturis etiam usitata, qua illa non proprie, stricte & emphatice, sed improprie, paulo latius & minus potenter accipitur, & coetus, seu congregatio externa eorum, qui Christum Dominum suum profitentur, & verbi Divini praedicati ac Sacramentorum communione sociantur; definitur. Hoc sensu passim etiam in Scriptura Ecclesiae nomen adhibetur; velut cum Christus Ecclesiae dicere jubet, Matth. XVIII. 17. Ecclesia quotidie crevisse, Actor. XVI. 5. & Paulus & Barnabas Seniores in Ecclesiis constituisse, ib. XIV. 23. dicuntur; & Ecclesiae Romanorum, Corinthiorum, Ephesiorum, septem Asiaticarum, &c. ad quas Apostoli scripserunt, memorantur. Faciunt huc parabolae Evangelicae, velut areae, in qua triticum & paleae, Matth. III. 12. agri, in quo triticum & zizania, ibid. XIII. 24. verriculi, in quo pisces salubres & putres, ibid. v. 47. nuptiarum, in quibus alii cum veste nuptiali, alii sine ea comparent, ib. XXII. 10. 11. Virginum, quarum aliae prudentes, aliae fatuae sunt, ibid. XXV. 1. &c. Ovilis, in quo oves & haedi sunt, Joh. X. 1. Vitis, in qua palmites frugiferi & aridi sunt, ibid. XV. 1. domus magnae, in qua vasa ad decus & dedecus sunt, 2. Tim. II. 20. Et duplices sunt filii Abrahami, vocati, carnales, atque electi & spirituales, duplices Judaei, carne & spiritu; Rom. II. 28. 29. IX. 6. Joh. VIII. 39.
units.tr: XXIX. Hence emerges a second notion of the Church, also in use in the Scriptures, by which it is taken not properly, strictly and emphatically, but improperly, somewhat more broadly and less powerfully, and is defined as the assembly or external congregation of those who profess Christ as their Lord and are joined by communion in the preaching of the divine Word and the sacraments. In this sense the name Church is used everywhere in Scripture: as when Christ bids that it be told to the Church (Matt. 18:17); the Church is said to have grown daily (Acts 16:5); Paul and Barnabas are said to have appointed elders in the churches (Acts 14:23); and the churches of the Romans, the Corinthians, the Ephesians, the seven churches of Asia, and so on, to whom the apostles wrote, are mentioned. The Gospel parables bear on this: the threshing floor, in which wheat and chaff are (Matt. 3:12); the field, in which wheat and tares are (Matt. 13:24); the dragnet, in which good and bad fish are (Matt. 13:47); the marriage, in which some appear with the wedding garment and others without it (Matt. 22:10–11); the virgins, of whom some are wise and some foolish (Matt. 25:1, etc.); the sheepfold, in which there are sheep and goats (John 10:1); the vine, in which there are fruitful and withered branches (John 15:1); the great house, in which there are vessels for honour and dishonour (2 Tim. 2:20). And there are two kinds of sons of Abraham, called and chosen, fleshly and spiritual; two kinds of Jews, in the flesh and in the spirit (Rom. 2:28–29; 9:6; John 8:39).

units.la: XXX. Non omnis equidem multitudo nomen Christi profitentium Ecclesia talis etiam nominatur, sed ea demum, in qua verae fideles & sancti continentur, vel saltem contineri possunt; in qua scilicet verbum Dei ita praedicatur, & Sacramenta ita administrantur, ut fundamentum fidei, & Salvatoris institutio salva & inconcussa maneant, neque obliqua etiam ratione aliqua evertantur, quicquid de admixtis erroribus & scandalis fiat. Est autem Ecclesiae fidelium ἐπικαλεῖσθαι ὄνομα τῷ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ nominare nomen Domini nostri Jesu Christi, 1. Cor. I. 2. Quisquis enim nominaverit nomen Domini, salvabitur, Rom. X. 13. Sed sunt in externo coetu, qui Christum ἐπικαλοῦνται nominant & praedicant τῇ ἀληθείᾳ vere, sunt, qui σχημάτι prætextu & obtextu, nomen Christi cupiditatibus suis obtendentes, Phil. I. 18. Ea ergo multitudo hominum profitentium nomen Christi, in qua sunt, vel esse possunt, qui Christum nominant non vere, sed obtentu, dummodo ita loquantur, ut fideles cum iis miscerí possint, hoc est, fundamentum fidei, nec directe, nec indirecte evertant; Ecclesiae etiam nomine veniat, non proprie & ἐνεργολικῶς, sed latius paulo & minus proprie, tum τῇ δόξαν secundum opinionem, quia ita se nominant, & ejus singula membra pro verae Ecclesiae membris habent, tum τῇ συνεκδοχῇ secundum complexionem, quia coetus talis Ecclesiam justorum & sanctorum gremio suo includit, tum denique τῇ τῶν ὀφειλομένων ἀγάπῃ secundum debitam charitatem, quia eam multitudinem, quae sic Christum nominat; ut in ea Ecclesia, hoc est, fideles nidulari possint; diligere, ut Ecclesiam, & cum ea, quamdiu talis est, ceu multitudine fratrum, communicare tenemur.
units.tr: XXX. Not every multitude that professes the name of Christ is called the Church in this sense, but only that in which true believers and saints are contained, or at least can be contained: that is, a community in which the word of God is so preached and the sacraments so administered that the foundation of faith and the Saviour's institution remain safe and unshaken, and are not overturned in any indirect way, whatever mixed errors and scandals there may be. It belongs to the Church of believers to call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ [ἐπικαλεῖσθαι ὄνομα τῷ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ], 1 Cor. 1.2. For whoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved, Rom. 10.13. But in the outward assembly there are some who truly name and confess Christ [ἐπικαλοῦνται], and others who do so in outward show and pretence, using the name of Christ as a cover for their lusts, Phil. 1.18. So the multitude of men professing the name of Christ, among whom are, or may be, those who name Christ not truly but as a pretext, provided only that they speak in such a way that believers can mix with them, that is, they do not overturn the foundation of faith, either directly or indirectly, is also called the Church. It is so called not strictly and properly, but in a somewhat wider and less proper sense: first, by opinion, because they so name themselves and regard each of their members as members of the true Church; second, by synecdoche, according to the whole, because such an assembly encloses the Church of the righteous and saints within its bosom; and finally, by due charity, because we are bound to love that multitude which so names Christ, in which the Church, that is, believers, may nest, and to share with it, as long as it is such, as with a multitude of brothers.

units.la: XXXI. Neque tamen sic duplicem Ecclesiam facimus; quia Ecclesia improprie & latius dicta ab Ecclesia proprie & augustius dicta, non modo exi-stendi in mundo, sed modo considerandi differt. Neque enim proprie dicta, quamdiu in mundo militat, seorsim congregata existit, sed ut plurimum in externa communione illa, in qua etiam hypocritae degunt, vel degere possunt. Sed variat tamen considerandi modus, quia aliter consideratur Ecclesia
units.tr: XXXI. Yet we do not thereby make the Church double; for the Church spoken of improperly and in a wider sense differs from the Church spoken of properly and in a more dignified sense not only in mode of existence in the world but also in mode of consideration. For the Church properly so called, while it fights in the world, does not exist as a separately gathered body, but for the most part in that outward communion in which hypocrites also live, or can live. Yet the mode of consideration varies, because the Church is considered in one way when it consists of the elect, called and believers alone, separately, and known to God alone distinctly, and in another way when it exists in the outward congregation and suffers the mixture of evil men and hypocrites.

units.la: {f} Hinc emergit notio Ecclesiae improprie & latius dicta, quae definitur. sia ex solis electis, vocatis & fidelibus seorsim constans, & soli Deo distinctè nota; aliter cùm eadem in externa congregatione existens mixturam etiam malorum & hypocritarum patitur. Qui enim in communione illa externa vere fideles sunt, proprie dicta Ecclesia esse non desinunt, licèt communio illa externa, quae eodem sinu bonos & malos, viva & mortua, sed viventium speciem habentia, recipit, respectu malorum admixtorum non proprie, sed improprie Ecclesia dicatur. Licet enim hypocritae Deum, Christum labiis suis honorent, professionem fundamenti fidei & salutis non ejurent, & externos etiam ritus & observantias subinde majore, quàm electi zelo obeant, non ideo tamen in fide & vita à Christo non aberrant, quin potiùs sunt in agapis macula unâ comessantes, & sine timore semet ipsos pascentes, Jud. v.12. hoc est, iisdem verbis & signis sacris utentes, bonis externis Ecclesiae secure vescentes, at de caetero non loquentes nisi in fraude, signis gratiae abutentes, adeóque carcinomata mera in agapis, seu congressibus fidelium, sic olim dictis, quia merè charitativi esse debent, juxta illa: Edite, bibite amici, inebriamini charitatibus ac suavitatibus, Cant. V.1. Horum solorum respectu externa illa communio Ecclesia propriè non est, sed dicitur; quae fidelium & electorum respectu Ecclesia propriè est & dicitur. Neque adeò Ecclesiam propriè & improprie dictam distinguentes, plures Ecclesias facimus, sed nominis duntaxat ambiguitatem notamus, & diversas ejusdem Ecclesiae veras, prout illa vel seorsim consideratur, vel unâ cum hypocritis commixta est, distinguimus. Sicut enim una Christi Ecclesia, non duplex fuit, licèt ille modò cum discipulis suis fidelibus solis, modò etiam cum Juda proditore communicans consideretur, atque unum idémque triticum est, sive illud seorsim spectetur, sive, prout cum palea mixtum & ea tectum est: ita una vera & propriè dicta Ecclesia est, licèt illa vel seorsim, quà talis, vel mixta cum membris heterogeneis, quae verae Ecclesiae membra dicuntur, at non sunt, consideretur.
units.tr: Hence emerges the notion of the Church spoken of improperly and in a wider sense, which is defined thus: the Church consisting of the elect, the called and believers alone, taken separately, and known distinctly to God alone. Those who are truly believers in that outward communion do not cease to be the Church properly so called, although that outward communion, which receives within the same bosom good and bad, living and dead, but having the appearance of the living, is said to be the Church not properly but improperly with respect to the mixed evil men. For although hypocrites honour God and Christ with their lips, do not renounce the profession of the foundation of faith and salvation, and sometimes perform external rites and observances with greater zeal than the elect, they do not on that account stray from Christ in faith and life. Rather, they are feasting together with you in your love-feasts without fear, feeding themselves, Jude 12, that is, using the same words and sacred signs, securely feeding on the outward goods of the Church, but otherwise speaking only in deceit, abusing the signs of grace, and thus are mere cankers in your love-feasts, or gatherings of believers, so called of old, because they ought to be purely of charity, according to those words: Eat, drink, friends; be drunk with loves and delights, Song 5.1. With respect to these only, that outward communion is not the Church properly, but is so called; whereas with respect to believers and the elect it is properly the Church and is so called. Nor, in distinguishing the Church properly and improperly so called, do we make several Churches; we only note the ambiguity of the name, and distinguish the different true aspects of the same Church, according as it is considered either separately or as mixed with hypocrites. For just as there was one Church of Christ, not two, although he is considered sometimes communing with his faithful disciples alone, and sometimes also with Judas the betrayer, and it is one and the same wheat whether it is viewed separately or as mixed with chaff and covered by it, so there is one true Church, properly so called, whether it is considered separately as such, or mixed with heterogeneous members, which are called members of the true Church but are not.

units.la: XXXII. Ecclesia externa & improprie dicta certis notis dignosci, & à falsa Ecclesia discerni potest & debet.
units.tr: XXXII. The external Church, improperly so called, can and must be recognised by certain marks and distinguished from a false Church.

units.la: Alia enim hactenus propriè dictae & invisibilis, alia improprie dictae & visibilis Ecclesiae ratio est. Nam illius notae certae & infallibiles apud homines quidem nullae sunt, quia solus Deus electos, qui sui sunt, novit, 2. Tim. II. 19. Is enim electos spiritu adoptionis obsignat, quam notam is solus sentit, qui habet, solus videt, qui impressit. Estque haec nota non coetus universi, sed singulorum, quorum unusquisque tenetur se ipsum per notas fidei efficacis, spei patientis, & charitatis laboriosae explorare, sitne verum & vivum ejus membrum. De proximo vero non aliud quàm charitatis judicium, quod certitudinem probabilem reddit, Matth. V. 16. Jac. II. 18. &c. ei relictum est. Neque Ecclesia universalis visibilis notas requirere necesse est, quia illae evidentes, non controversae sunt, Baptismus & externa fidei professio, atque cum universali Ecclesia congregatio externa non datur. Sed Ecclesiae particularis, qua cum in hac vita con-
units.tr: There is one account of the properly so called and invisible Church, and another of the improperly so called and visible Church. For the certain and infallible marks of the former are in fact none among men, because God alone knows the elect, who are his own, 2 Tim. 2:19. He seals the elect with the Spirit of adoption, a mark that only the one who has it feels and only the one who impressed it sees. This mark belongs not to the whole assembly but to individuals, each of whom is bound to examine by the marks of effectual faith, patient hope and laborious love whether he is a true and living member. Concerning a neighbour, however, only a judgement of charity is left to him, which makes certainty probable, Matt. 5:16; James 2:18, etc. Nor is it necessary for the universal visible Church to require marks, since these are evident and not disputed: baptism and external profession of faith; and an external congregation of the universal Church is not given. But for the particular Church, in which in this life we

units.la: gregari gestimus & studemus certae notae requirendae sunt, ex quibus constare possit, sitne ἐκκλησία ἔννομος Ecclesia legitima, Actor. XIX. 39. ex qua iis, qui ex mandato Dei congregari debent, benedictio Divina expectanda sit, an ἀνόμως illegitima, & malignantium, ex qua exitium provenit.
