Licèt autem ad legitimae Ecclesiae μόρφωσιν formationem & discretionem judicium charitatis, quale in discretione Ecclesiae invisibilis solum obtinet, excludi non debeat: tamen necessario praeit judicium veritatis, absque quo judicium charitatis caecum, vel nullum est. Nam οἱ δίκαιοι probi manifestari debent, 1.Cor. XI.19. Latent igitur natura, adeóque certis criteriis manifestandi sunt. Atque judicium isthoc ex certis notis, secus quàm Socinians & fanatici pertendunt, necessarium est, quia, uti supra demonstravimus, fideles necessariò congregari in eadem Ecclesia, adeóque quae vera Ecclesia sit, dignoscere debent. Licèt enim extra ordinem contingere possit, ut quis μεμονωμένος segrex, sine verbo praedicato, privata lectione verbi Dei, adeóque extra omnem coetum Ecclesiae visibilis, Divina benedictione ad fidem perducatur, & membrum Ecclesiae invisibilis efficiatur, tamen ordinarie fides est ex auditu, non sine praedicante, Rom. X.14. Cùm igitur Ecclesiae visibiles & particulares in mundo aliae puriores, aliae impuriores sint, & idem Ecclesiae nomine vera Christi Sponsa, & adulterae atque meretricantes sibi vendicent, notis certis & infallibilibus opus est, quibus Sponsa Christi à lupanarum grege, & castus ejus thalamus à meretricum sellis & stabulis dignoscatur.
units.tr: wish and strive to be gathered, certain marks must be required, by which it may be established whether it is a lawful church [ἐκκλησία ἔννομος], Acts 19:39, from which the blessing of God is to be expected by those who ought to be gathered by God's command, or an unlawful church [ἀνόμως], that of the wicked, from which ruin proceeds. Although the judgement of charity, which alone holds in discerning the invisible Church, ought not to be excluded from the formation [μόρφωσιν] and discernment of a lawful Church, nevertheless a judgement of truth necessarily goes before it, without which the judgement of charity is blind or nonexistent. For the righteous must be made manifest [οἱ δίκαιοι], 1 Cor. 11:19. They are therefore hidden by nature, and so must be made manifest by certain criteria. And this judgement from certain marks is necessary, contrary to what the Socinians and fanatics contend, because, as we have shown above, the faithful must necessarily be gathered into the same Church and so ought to recognise which is the true Church. For although it may happen out of order that someone, a solitary [μεμονωμένος], without the preached word, by private reading of the word of God, and so outside every assembly of the visible Church, is brought to faith by divine blessing and made a member of the invisible Church, nevertheless ordinarily faith comes from hearing, not without a preacher, Rom. 10:14. Since therefore the visible and particular Churches in the world are some purer and others less pure, and the same name of Church is claimed both by the true bride of Christ and by adulteresses and harlots, certain and infallible marks are needed by which the bride of Christ may be distinguished from the herd of brothels and her chaste bridal chamber from the stalls and stables of harlots.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Sed ipsarum Ecclesiae notarum notae requirendae etiam sunt, quia hodie fere nothae & fallaces, atque falsa γνωσίματα obtruduntur, quae ignium fatuorum instar in errorem inducunt, & homines Ecclesiam veram quaerentes transversos abripiunt, ut pro Sponsa Christi meretricem prensent. In universum Nota signum vel argumentum est, quo aliquid declarari potest. Sed notarum & signorum ejusmodi duo genera sunt; alia εἰκότα, alia πεκμήρια. Illa communi quadam & probabili, sed minimè necessaria ratione: haec ratione singulari & certissima rem, quae investigatur, notant & declarant. Posterioris generis notae hic requiruntur, quia res investiganda ad salutem hominis, quodammodo requiritur, qua in re ne fallamur, certissimae notae sint oportet. Ejusmodi vero essentiales & internae sint oportet, quibus positis certò rem poni, sublatis certò tolli necesse est. Ac licèt in entibus per accidens & aggregationem forma non sit nisi accidentalis, nihil tamen impedit, quò minùs essentiales & necessariae notae illae dicantur, quae in re illa, quam designant, verè, simul, constanter, & perpetuò observantur. Quomodo si de exercitu Turcico & Christiano discernendo agatur, castrorum ratio, vexilla, tessera militaris, Dux, militiae institutum, signum buccina datum, tympanorum clangor & similia certò & evidenter discernunt, si verè & semper talia adsint, cujusmodi ex certa notitia Christianorum aut Turcarum esse constat; Licèt omnia haec per stratagemata ad tempus mutari, aut fingi ad imponendum aliis, possint.
units.tr: But the marks of the Church's marks also need to be investigated, because today nearly spurious and deceptive ones are thrust forward, and false signs [γνωσίματα] which, like will-o'-the-wisps, lead men into error and sweep aside those seeking the true Church, so that they grasp a harlot in place of Christ's bride. In general, a mark is a sign or argument by which something can be declared. But there are two kinds of such marks and signs: some are probable [εἰκότα], others demonstrative [τεκμήρια]. The former denote and declare the thing under investigation by a common and probable, but by no means necessary, reasoning; the latter by a singular and most certain reasoning. Marks of the latter kind are required here, because the thing to be investigated concerns human salvation, and in such a matter, so that we may not be deceived, the marks must be most certain. Such marks must be essential and internal, so that when they are posited the thing is certainly posited, and when they are removed it is certainly removed. And although in beings by accident and aggregation the form is only accidental, nothing prevents those marks from being called essential and necessary which are truly, simultaneously, constantly and perpetually observed in the thing they designate. So if a Turkish and a Christian army are to be distinguished, the arrangement of camps, the standards, the military password, the commander, the military order, the signal given by trumpet, the clash of drums and the like distinguish them certainly and evidently, if such things are truly and always present, of the kind which is known from certain knowledge to belong to Christians or Turks; although all these can be changed for a time or feigned to deceive others by stratagems.

units.la: XXXIIII. Tres
units.tr: XXXIV. Three

units.la: XXXIV. Tres Notarum notas Bellarminus posuit; ut sint propriæ rei discernendæ, non communes, ne quidem opinione aliorum: ut sint notiores ea re, cujus notæ sunt: ut sint insepara-biles. Ubi in prima nota præterquam quod multa sunt, quæ à notis, quibus insigniuntur, reapse non differunt, velut lux & similia, in quibus notæ reipsa notiores non sunt, sophisticè etiam additur, ne quidem opinione aliorum; quia si ad opinionem hujus vel illius exigendæ rerum proprietates essent, nihil de iis certum unquam haberemus: in secunda verò ambigue dicitur, notas notiores ea re, cujus notæ sunt, esse debere; quia huic aut illi homini, hoc vel illo modo, notitia distincta vel confusa magis, vel minus notæ esse possunt. Alii in hoc uno subsistunt; Notas Ecclesiæ esse debere signa sensibilia & magis nota, quàm sit ipsa Ecclesia, quia omnis generis hominibus ad discernendam veram Ecclesiam à falsa inservire debeant. Alias, inquiunt, homines gentiles & simplices ab Ecclesia & salute excluderentur. Sed notas omnes sensibiles esse, necesse non est; quia quædam esse possunt; quæ sola mente concipiuntur, quorum tamen cognitio ad rei alicujus minus notæ cognitionem viam aperiat; cujusmodi tamen notæ non sensibiles effecta sensibilia producunt. Quomodo pax diuturna, & prosperitas civium nota Reipublicæ bene constitutæ est, quæ etsi non usurpantur oculis, effecta tamen visibilia producunt. Et si maximè notæ sic evidentes & sensibiles esse deberent, tamen, si ex iisdem evidenter concludi deberet, hanc, vel illam veram Ecclesiam esse, cui secundum istas aggregari debeamus, in antecessum constare deberet, has vel illas sensibiles notas esse veras notas Ecclesiæ, quarum indicio tutò huic potius, quàm alii Ecclesiæ nomen dandum sit. Quod ipsum infideli & idiotæ judicatu haud proclive esset, & tamen, nisi periculo se exponere vellet, omnino dijudicandum esset. Adduntque Methodistæ, quærendas esse notas Ecclesiæ, non ejus, quæ Christi & Apostolorum ætate fuit, adeòque Ecclesiæ non incipientis & adolescentis, quando infans, & grani sinapi instar fuit; sed hodiernæ & senescentis, quando in arborem magnam excrevit. Quia animadversione hypothesi suæ strenuè vehicantur, declinantes argumentum firmissimum, quod à statu Ecclesiæ Apostolicæ adversus nothas eorundem notas depromimus. Quasi Ecclesia vel ab externa ejus specie, & non ab intrinseca & essentiali constitutione, quam nulla ætas, nullæ rugæ mutant, penderet; vel Ecclesia, quæ talis, perinde ut homo, oculis corporeis conspiceretur; vel eadem seculis Apostolicam Ecclesiam sequentibus fidei robore, puritate doctrinæ, sanctitate vitæ, confessorum multitudine creverit, inprimis tum, cum Antichristus Ecclesiæ se commiscuit, & apostasia in eandem incessit; à quibus procedente tempore repurgari necesse habuit. Denique iidem Ecclesiæ notas anxiè investigantes non parum vineta sua cæduntur. Si enim, quod illi pertendunt, Ecclesia aspectabilis instar Regni, hostibus æquè atque domesticis visibilis est, & antiquissima atque αὐτοπιστῷ Ecclesiæ auctoritas est, à qua pendent, nullus omnino notarum Ecclesiæ usus esse poterit, quia notæ rei ignotæ, non notæ sunt, & aliunde notæ esse debent, quàm à re, cujus notæ sunt. Illi autem notarum fidem omnem ab Ecclesia, cujus notæ sunt, suspendunt.
units.tr: XXXIV. Bellarmine laid down three marks of marks: that they should be proper to the thing to be distinguished and not common, not even in the opinion of others; that they should be better known than the thing of which they are marks; and that they should be inseparable. In the first, apart from the fact that many things are not really different from the marks by which they are distinguished, such as light and the like, in which the marks are not really better known, it is also sophistically added "not even in the opinion of others"; for if the properties of things were to be judged by the opinion of this or that person, we would never have anything certain about them. In the second he speaks ambiguously when he says the marks ought to be better known than the thing of which they are marks, since distinct or confused knowledge may be more or less known to this or that man, in this or that way. Others rest on this one point: that the marks of the Church ought to be sensible signs and better known than the Church itself, because they ought to serve all kinds of men in distinguishing the true Church from the false. Otherwise, they say, Gentiles and simple people would be excluded from the Church and salvation. But it is not necessary that all marks be sensible, since there can be some which are conceived by the mind alone, yet whose knowledge opens a way to the knowledge of a less known thing; and yet such non-sensible marks produce sensible effects. Thus lasting peace and the prosperity of citizens is a mark of a well-ordered commonwealth, which, though not grasped by the eyes, produces visible effects. And even if marks ought to be so evident and sensible, still, if from them it were to be evidently concluded that this or that is the true Church with which we ought to assemble according to them, it would have to be established beforehand that these or those sensible marks are the true marks of the Church, by whose indication this Church rather than another may safely be given the name. This very thing would not be easy to judge even for an unbeliever or an unlearned person, and yet, unless he wished to expose himself to danger, it would altogether have to be decided. The Methodists add that the marks to be sought are not those of the Church which existed in the time of Christ and the Apostles, and so not of the Church when it was beginning and growing up, when it was like an infant and like the grain of mustard seed, but of the present and ageing Church, when it has grown into a great tree. They vigorously carry this hypothesis by their own assumption, avoiding the most firm argument which we draw from the state of the Apostolic Church against the spurious marks of the same. As if the Church depended on its external appearance and not on its intrinsic and essential constitution, which no age and no wrinkles change; or as if the Church as such were seen with bodily eyes like a man; or as if the same Church, following the Apostolic Church over the centuries, had grown in strength of faith, purity of doctrine, sanctity of life and multitude of confessors, especially when Antichrist mingled himself with the Church and apostasy crept into it, from which, as time went on, it had to be purged again. Finally, those who anxiously investigate the marks of the Church are not a little cutting down their own vineyards. For if, as they contend, the visible Church is like a kingdom, visible to enemies as well as to its own members, and if its authority is most ancient and self-trusting, on which everything depends, then no use of the marks of the Church could be possible at all, since marks of an unknown thing are not marks, and they must be known from elsewhere than from the thing of which they are marks. But they make all faith in the marks depend on the Church of which they are marks.

units.la: XXXV. Veræ & infallibiles Notarum Ecclesiæ notæ sunt, quòd Ecclesiæ, cujus veritatem notant, essentiales, propriæ & ab eadem inseparabiles sunt. Quod ex natura rei, notarum illarum usu, & adversariorum confessione liquet. Ex natura rei, quia notarum munus est, ut specificam subjecti naturam, sive ipsam Ecclesiæ essentiam declarent: eòque non modo omni & soli, sed & semper convenire debent, & salvo integróque manente subjecto ab eadem separari non possunt. Sicut enim singuli fideles, quâ membra Ecclesiæ externæ, ex iis cognoscuntur, quæ membris Ecclesiæ externæ essentialia, propria & ab iisdem inseparabilia sunt: ita Ecclesia externa, quæ membrorum talium collectio est, non aliunde certius cognoscitur. Quomodo si quis acervi tritici notas quæreret, deberet prius perspectas habere notas, quibus singula tritici grana à reliquis seminibus secernuntur: & quæ notæ singulorum granorum sunt, eadem acervi granorum est. Essentiales notas dicimus, quæ essentiam Ecclesiæ declarant, sive ex iis, quæ eam constituunt, sive ex iis, quæ eam necessariò comitantur vel sequuntur. Neque enim obstat, quòd in iis, per quæ essentia rei constituitur, ipsa res consistit, neque adeò idem per se ipsum notari posse videtur. Multæ enim aliæ etiam res non aliis rebus cognoscuntur, quàm quibus earum ipsa natura constituta est. Qua enim nota lucem agnoscimus, quæ ab ipsa lucis natura discrepet? Quæ ἀναλογίας denotant; in quibus ὁ λόγος τῆς ἐσίας elementi illius non consistat? Quibus notis aciem ad pugnam instructam cognoscimus, nisi iis; quæ aciem formant & constituunt? Tum aliter res ejusmodi considerantur, cùm sumuntur pro notis; aliter, cùm ad rei ipsius definitionem & naturam explicandam adhibentur. Cùm enim pro notis sumuntur, seorsim ad certiorem rei notitiam comparandam, considerantur; cùm ad definitionem rei afferuntur in unum componuntur & junctim considerantur. Ex notarum usu, quia per ejusmodi γνώσεως Ecclesiæ naturam intimam declarantia, & infideles & de Ecclesiæ suæ veritate dubitantes, & de ejusdem falsitate convicti, veram Ecclesiam agnoscent; neque certius recognoscere poterunt. Veritas enim & falsitas cujusque rei ex ejus essentia & proprietate apud omnes rectè diiudicatur. Denique ex confessione adversariorum, qui ex his ipsis principiis & canonibus notas nostras examinant & oppugnant.
units.tr: XXXV. The true and infallible marks of the Church are those which are essential to the Church whose truth they indicate, proper to it, and inseparable from it. This is clear from the nature of the thing, from the use of these marks, and from the admission of our opponents. It follows from the nature of the thing because the office of marks is to declare the specific nature of their subject, that is, the very essence of the Church. Therefore they must belong not only to every case and to the only case, but to it always, and while the subject remains whole and unchanged they cannot be separated from it. Just as individual believers are known as members of the external Church by those things which are essential to, proper to, and inseparable from the external members of the Church, so the external Church, which is the collection of such members, is not known more certainly by anything else. If someone sought the marks of a heap of wheat, he would first have to know the marks by which each grain of wheat is distinguished from other seeds, and the marks of the individual grains are the same as the marks of the heap of grains. We call essential marks those which declare the essence of the Church, whether they are taken from what constitutes it or from what necessarily accompanies or follows it. Nor is it an objection that the thing itself consists in those things through which its essence is constituted, and so it seems the same thing cannot be noted through itself. For many other things too are known not by other things than those by which their own nature is constituted. By what mark do we recognize light, if the mark differs from the very nature of light? What things denote proportions [ἀναλογίας], in which the ratio of essence [ὁ λόγος τῆς ἐσίας] of that element does not consist? By what marks do we recognize an army drawn up for battle, except by those things which form and constitute the battle line? Moreover, such things are considered one way when they are taken as marks, and another way when they are used to define and explain the nature of the thing itself. For when they are taken as marks, they are considered separately, to obtain a more certain knowledge of the thing; when they are brought forward for its definition, they are put together and considered jointly. It follows from the use of marks that, through such knowledge [γνώσεως] declaring the inner nature of the Church, both unbelievers and those who doubt the truth of their own church, and those convicted of its falsehood, will recognize the true Church, and they will not be able to recognize it more certainly. For the truth or falsehood of anything is rightly judged by all from its essence and property. Finally, it follows from the admission of our opponents, who examine and attack our marks from these very principles and rules.

units.la: XXXVI. His suppositis, quærendæ sunt Notæ; quæ veræ Ecclesiæ essentiam demonstrant, eique sic propriæ sunt, ut eam ab aliis omnibus distinguant, & ab eadem separari nequeant. Cumque Ecclesiæ essentia in ejusdem materia & forma consistat; materia quidem nullam nobis notam, in qua ullum tale ἐστίν sit, suppeditat. Vel enim materia Ecclesiæ in hominibus, vel in communione & societate eorum certis legibus colligata consideratur. At nec homines Ecclesiæ notam suppeditant, quia homines etiam Athei, Pagani & Turcæ sunt, ab Ecclesia longissimè remoti; nec communio munio & societas hominum certis legibus colligatorum, quia talis societas citra ullam religionis causam existere potest. Quae Ecclesiae formam constituunt vel sequuntur, & notae naturam habere possunt, partim verae Ecclesiae essentiam declarant, partim eandem ab aliis discernunt. Quoad prius, sicut Ecclesiae invisibilis forma propriè in fide in Jesum Christum consistit: ita visibilis & externae Ecclesiae, quà talis, forma fidei ejusdem professio est. Sicut enim illa duo inter se reciprocantur: Ille in Christum credit: Ergo ad Ecclesiam invisibilem pertinet; Et: Pertinet ille ad Ecclesiam invisibilem; Ergo credit in Christum: ita duo haec pariter inter se convertuntur: Ille fidem in Christum profitetur: Ergo pertinet ad Ecclesiam visibilem; &: Pertinet ille ad Ecclesiam visibilem; Ergo profitetur fidem in Christum. Sicut ergo singulos eos, qui fidem in Christum profitentur, ex ea nota cognoscimus, ad Ecclesiam aliquam visibilem pertinere; ita consequens est, ut illam ipsam societatem, ad quam eos, tanquam partem pertinere videmus, ex eo Ecclesiam esse noscamus, quòd professionem illam fidei in Christum prae se ferunt. Sed professio fidei in Christum non una ratione declaratur. Primò enim cùm fides sit persuasio alicujus rei, quam pro vera agnoscimus, necesse est, ut, qui fidem in Christum profitetur, eadem opera profiteatur, sese veritatem Christi amplecti. Christi autem veritas est verbum Dei, & inprimis doctrina illa verbi Dei, quam Christus & Apostoli docuerunt, quòd in morte & resurrectione Christi spes unica salutis repositta sit. Quae igitur societas Christum profitetur juxta verbum Dei, & doctrinam Christi & Apostolorum de Jesu Christo Salvatore unico, vera Ecclesia est. Proin professio fidei in Christum conformata verbo Dei de Christo, Salvatore mundi, prima & maximè propria Ecclesiae nota est. Nam & essentialis est, quia ex ipsa Ecclesiae forma petita; juxta quam Ecclesia externa est coetus hominum per verbum Dei ad profitendum fidem in Christum vocatorum: & propria, quia Ecclesiae externae verae, uni, soli & semper convenit: & ab eadem inseparabilis, quia cum ea incipit & desinit. Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit. Propterea vos non auditis, quia ex Deo non estis, Joh. VIII. 47. Si manseritis in sermone meo, verè discipuli mei eritis, ibid. v. 31. Oves meae vocem meam audiunt, vocem alienorum non audiunt, ibid. X. 5. 27. Ecclesia enim sicut ex verbo Dei, ceu semine incorruptibili, & per Evangelium Jesu Christi nascitur, 1. Corinth. IV. 15. Jac. I. 18. 1. Petr. I. 23. ita ex eodem noscitur. Deinde sicut fides, habitus non theoreticus, sed practicus, in actiones etiam erumpit: ita ejusdem juxta verbum Dei professio in actiones pariter erumpit, quae sitae sunt in externo Dei cultu, praedicatione publica verbi, precibus, & administratione Sacramentorum. Quae nota Ecclesiae externae pariter tum essentialis est, quia, quatenus externa est, & congregatur, atque congregari potest, ex mandato verbi Dei ad cultum externum, praeconium verbi & administrationem Sacramentorum obligatur, Matth. XXVIII. 19. 20. atque ea obligatio ex forma Ecclesiae, professione fidei in Christum, tum quoad propositum animi, tum, quoties licet, etiam quoad actum, sequitur: tum propria, quia cultus talis externus verbo Dei conformatus quoad animi saltem propositum, si non quoad actum, uni Ecclesiae verae, soli & semper convenit: tum, quoad eandem praeparationem animi ab eadem inseparabilis est, quia nunquam animi propositum deest; & actus adest, quoties aliunde, sine Ecclesiae culpa non impeditur. Denique cùm societas quaevis ordine aliquo contineatur, qui certarum legum constitutione & observatione custoditur, ad plenam Ecclesiae notificationem quodam etiam Ecclesiae regimine, seu disciplina, cum Ecclesiae natura consentanea opus est. Quae nota Ecclesiae etiam & essentialis est, quia naturam Ecclesiae in societate ordinata consistentem, comitatur: & propria, quia regimen ejusmodi verbo Dei conformatum, & reliquis notis conjunctum Ecclesiae uni, soli & semper convenit: & ab eadem inseparabilis, quia societas ἀνομία non societas, sed factio & conspiratio quaedam est.
units.tr: XXXVI. With these things assumed, we must seek the marks which demonstrate the essence of the true Church, which are so proper to it that they distinguish it from all others and cannot be separated from it. Since the essence of the Church consists in its matter and form, the matter does not offer us any mark by which some such essence [ἐστίν] might be found. For the matter of the Church is considered either in human beings or in their fellowship bound together by certain laws. But human beings do not supply a mark of the Church, because human beings include atheists, pagans and Turks, who are very far removed from the Church; nor does the fellowship of human beings bound by certain laws, because such a society can exist without any cause of religion. Those things which constitute or follow the form of the Church, and can have the nature of a mark, partly declare the essence of the true Church and partly distinguish it from others. As to the former: just as the form of the invisible Church properly consists in faith in Jesus Christ, so the form of the visible and external Church, as such, is the profession of that same faith. For just as those two propositions reciprocate with each other: He believes in Christ; therefore he belongs to the invisible Church; and: He belongs to the invisible Church; therefore he believes in Christ; so these two likewise convert into each other: He professes faith in Christ; therefore he belongs to the visible Church; and: He belongs to the visible Church; therefore he professes faith in Christ. Therefore, just as we recognize from this mark that each person who professes faith in Christ belongs to some visible Church, so it follows that we know that very fellowship to which we see them belong as a part to be the Church, because they display that profession of faith in Christ. But the profession of faith in Christ is declared in more than one way. First, since faith is the persuasion of something which we acknowledge as true, it is necessary that whoever professes faith in Christ at the same time professes that he embraces the truth of Christ. But the truth of Christ is the word of God, and especially that doctrine of the word of God which Christ and the Apostles taught, that the sole hope of salvation rests in the death and resurrection of Christ. Therefore that fellowship which professes Christ according to the word of God, and the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles concerning Jesus Christ the only Saviour, is the true Church. Hence the profession of faith in Christ conformed to the word of God concerning Christ, the Saviour of the world, is the first and most proper mark of the Church. For it is both essential, because it is drawn from the very form of the Church, according to which the external Church is an assembly of men called through the word of God to profess faith in Christ; and proper, because it belongs to the one true external Church alone, and always; and inseparable from it, because it begins and ends with it. He who is of God hears the words of God. Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God, John 8:47. If you abide in my word, you will be truly my disciples, ibid. v. 31. My sheep hear my voice, and they do not hear the voice of strangers, ibid. 10:5, 27. For the Church is born from the word of God, as from an incorruptible seed, and through the Gospel of Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 4:15; James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:23; and it is known from the same source. Next, just as faith, which is not a theoretical but a practical habit, also breaks out into actions, so likewise the profession of it according to the word of God breaks out into actions, which are placed in the external worship of God, in the public preaching of the word, in prayers, and in the administration of the sacraments. This mark of the external Church is likewise essential both then, because, insofar as it is external and gathers, and can gather, it is bound by the command of the word of God to external worship, the proclamation of the word and the administration of the sacraments, Matt. 28:19, 20; and this obligation follows from the form of the Church, the profession of faith in Christ, both as to the purpose of the mind and, whenever it is permitted, also as to the act. Then it is proper, because such external worship, conformed to the word of God at least as to the purpose of the mind, if not as to the act, belongs to the one true Church alone, and always. Then, as to the same preparation of the mind, it is inseparable from it, because the purpose of the mind is never lacking, and the act is present whenever it is not otherwise hindered without fault of the Church. Finally, since every society is held together by some order, which is maintained by the establishment and observance of certain laws, a certain government, or discipline, consistent with the nature of the Church, is also needed for the full indication of the Church. This mark of the Church is also both essential, because it accompanies the nature of the Church consisting in an ordered society; and proper, because such government, conformed to the word of God and joined with the other marks, belongs to the one Church alone, and always; and inseparable from it, because a society in lawlessness [ἀνομία] is not a society but a faction and a certain conspiracy.

units.la: XXXVII. Neque tantùm notae hae veram Ecclesiam constituunt, sed etiam, quod alterum earum munus est, Ecclesiam veram à falsa, quae fidem in Christum solo nomine profitetur, discernunt.
units.tr: XXXVII. Nor do these marks only constitute the true Church; they also, which is their other function, distinguish the true Church from the false one, which professes faith in Christ in name only.

units.la: Nam fidei Christi confessio ea demum vera est, quae veritatem, qualis à Christo & Apostolis tradita est, retinet, & Sacramenta in eodem verbo Dei instituta conservat, & ordinem in eodem sancitum custodit. Quae societas vel omnia ista egerit, vel ex iis aliqua aut funditus evertit, aut penitus corrumpit & violat, dum Ecclesiae Christianae nomen sibi vendicat, perinde facit, ac si Italus ortu & animo, ementito Germani nomine, Germanos inter versaretur. Sicut enim sua cum loquela, & vitae institutum, & gestus corporis, & color atque habitus facile arguit: ita talem societatem mendacium, quod amplectitur, alieni à Christianismo ritus, & tyrannica gubernandi ratio, ementitae nomenclaturae convincit. Et mendacium quidem veritati vel directa ejus abnegatione & contradictione, vel indirecta, per appositionem rerum heterogenearum veritatem mentientium, opponitur. Prius, ubi circa fundamentum veritatis versatur, & publicè sancitur, Ecclesiam planè subruit quale Socinianorum Christi Deitatem & satisfactionem negantium mendacium est. Posterius Ecclesiam non subruit, quandiu veritatem mendacio oppositam profiteri liberum est. Sicut enim convivium appellari potest, in quo cibi salubres & venenati apponuntur, quandiu illa secernere, & venenum abstergere & abradere licet: ita Ecclesia, in qua mendacium fuco veritatis tectum cum veritate commiscetur, Ecclesia esse non definit, quandiu falsum dogma à veritate salutari in coetu ecclesiastico separare liberum est. Quatenus enim veritatem participat, Ecclesia est, licèt superinducto mendacio aegra & sic obscurata, ut quia Ecclesia naturam nonnisi aegrè retinet, ejus appellationem difficulter tueatur. Sed simpliciter & absolutè Ecclesia est, quae veritatem sic profitetur, ut ne partem ejus ullam ad salutem necessariam rejiciat, neque ullum mendacium, vim salvificae veritatis corrumpens, admittat. Sicut autem Ecclesiae, quae veritatem mendaciis permiscent, miscent, non unius modi sunt, & aliarum labes & plures & majores sunt,& altius in Ecclesiae penetralia descendunt,aliarum verò maculae rariores sunt,& magis in extimis earum partibus ἐπιπλάζει: sic nota illa veritatis absolutè veram Ecclesiam ab illis diversimodè secernit. Quomodo si prorsus sanum hominem cum alio valde leproso conferas,sanæ cutis vividus nitidúsque color in ea comparatione splendescit; qui si comparetur cum eo,qui lepra laborat quidem,sed mitius, nec cutem nisi leviter maculosam habet, offuscatur nonnihil, & de splendore suo deperdit. Quando igitur Ecclesiæ valde impuræ cum purissima comparantur,hæc veritatis charactere adeò facile innotescit,ut judicium de illarum impuritate & sordibus arduum & difficile non sit. Cùm verò comparatio inter eam,& Ecclesias maculis, sed non æquè multis vel periculosis laborantes,instituitur, proclivior in dijudicandis iis error est.
units.tr: For the confession of faith in Christ is true only if it holds to the truth as it was handed down by Christ and the Apostles, preserves the sacraments instituted in the same Word of God, and keeps the order sanctioned in that Word. A society which either does none of these things, or utterly overturns or thoroughly corrupts and violates some of them, while claiming for itself the name of the Christian Church, acts just as if an Italian by birth and disposition, under the false name of a German, were living among Germans. For just as his speech, his way of life, his gestures, his complexion and dress easily betray him, so such a society is exposed by the lie it embraces, by its rites foreign to Christianity, and by its tyrannical manner of governing, which contradict its borrowed name. A lie is opposed to truth either directly, by outright denial and contradiction, or indirectly, by placing alongside it things foreign to it that pass themselves off as truth. The former, when it concerns the foundation of the truth and is publicly sanctioned, utterly overthrows the Church; this is the case with the lie of the Socinians, who deny the deity and the satisfaction of Christ. The latter does not overthrow the Church, so long as it is lawful to profess the truth opposed to the lie. For just as a banquet may be called such even when wholesome and poisonous food is set out on it, provided it is lawful to separate the one from the other and to wipe away and scrape off the poison, so a Church in which a lie hidden under the colour of truth is mixed with the truth does not cease to be a Church, so long as it is lawful to separate a false doctrine from the saving truth within the ecclesiastical assembly. For insofar as it partakes of the truth, it is a Church, although it is sick and so obscured by the lie laid over it that, since it retains its nature only with difficulty, it can hardly sustain its name. But that is simply and absolutely a Church which professes the truth in such a way that it rejects no part of it necessary to salvation, and admits no lie that corrupts the power of the saving truth. Now, Churches which mix lies with the truth are not all of one kind: the stains of some are both more numerous and greater, and reach more deeply into the inner sanctuary of the Church, while the blemishes of others are rarer and lie more on its outer parts, where they epiplazei [ἐπιπλάζει]. So that mark of truth distinguishes the Church which is absolutely true from the others in differing degrees. It is as when you compare a perfectly healthy man with another who is badly diseased with leprosy: the lively and bright colour of healthy skin shines out in that comparison; but if it is compared with one who suffers from leprosy, yet more mildly, and has skin only lightly spotted, it is somewhat dimmed and loses some of its brightness. Therefore, when very impure Churches are compared with the purest, the Church is so easily recognised by the mark of truth that a judgment about the impurity and filth of the others is not difficult or hard to make. But when the comparison is made between it and Churches afflicted with blemishes that are not so numerous or dangerous, the error in judging them is more likely.

units.la: Quoad cultum Divinum, præsertim in Sacramentis error multifarius contingere potest. Nam vel cultus ipse Divinus tollitur,dogmate,quod ei pro fundamento est, planè surrepto; obliterant; & tum sic surripientes & extincta veritate etiam Sacramenta obliterantes,Ecclesia esse desinunt: Vel relinquitur dogma,ex quo cultus enascitur,sed variis mendaciis vim veri dogmatis obliterantibus, & cultum ex eo enascentem, non modò obscurantibus,sed evertentibus,& in superstitionem atque idololatriam commutantibus,obrutum,& tum Ecclesiæ nomen coetus talis non meretur, nisi quatenus, vigente dogmate, quo cultus Dei purus, & legitimus Sacramentorum usus nititur, integro, nonnulli, iisque non pauci numero sunt,qui id à corruptione secernunt; atque sic coetus ille Ecclesia perinde dici potest, ut homo, quem pestis invasit,quíque jam occupatis veneno præcordiis, ægrè spiritum languentem,& frequentibus syncopis intercisum, trahit, adeóque homo vivus, sed vitæ quàm morti propior est: vel denique & dogma verum relinquitur,& cultus ex eo emergens non præfocatur,sed rituum inutilium & falsorum, licèt non exitialium doctrinarum additamentis obscuratur; & tum coetus talis Ecclesiæ, licèt non puræ,axioma non amittit. Primum in Socinianis,secundum in Pontificiis ante, vel post Reformationem diversimodè; tertium in Lutheranis conspicuum est. Denique Regimen & Disciplina Ecclesiæ,sicut minus ad salutem obtinendam momentum habet, quàm fides veritatis & cultus Divini atque Sacramentorum puritas; sic nota in eo sita minùs certò quàm priores veram Ecclesiam à falsa discernit. Duo tamen vitia extrema sunt, quæ Ecclesiæ interitum machinantur,Anarchia & Tyrannis. Illa enim,uti dissoluta est, ἀναξία continuò generat,quam sicut Deus graviter aversatur, 1.Cor. XIV. 33. ita societatis exitium illa post se trahit. Omnia enim ordine continentur. Hæc non minùs Ecclesiæ conservationi inimica est, quia libertatem opprimit,& Christum, quantum potest, è folio suo deturbat. Ad priorem scopulorum illorum navim Fanatici, Libertini & Enthusiastæ; ad posteriorem Hierarchici Papæ jurati allidunt.
units.tr: With regard to divine worship, and especially in the sacraments, many kinds of error can occur. For either divine worship itself is abolished, the dogma which underlies it being utterly snatched away, and then those who snatch it away, having extinguished the truth, also obliterate the sacraments, and cease to be a Church; or the dogma from which worship arises is left, but is buried under various lies which obliterate the force of the true dogma, and the worship arising from it is not only obscured but overturned and changed into superstition and idolatry. In that case such an assembly does not deserve the name of Church, except insofar as, while the dogma on which the pure worship of God and the lawful use of the sacraments rests remains intact, some, and not a few in number, separate it from the corruption; and so that assembly may be called a Church in the same way as a man whom the plague has attacked, whose vital organs are already occupied by poison, and who drags along a failing breath, interrupted by frequent fainting spells: he is a living man, but nearer to death than to life. Or finally, the true dogma is left and the worship arising from it is not suffocated but is obscured by additions of useless and false rites, though not of deadly doctrines; and then such an assembly, though not pure, does not lose the name of Church. The first case is seen among the Socinians, the second among the Papists, before and after the Reformation in different ways, and the third is conspicuous among the Lutherans. Finally, the government and discipline of the Church, as it has less weight for obtaining salvation than the faith of the truth and the purity of worship and of the sacraments, so the mark located in it distinguishes the true Church from the false less certainly than the former ones. There are, however, two extreme vices which plot the ruin of the Church: anarchy and tyranny. The former, being dissolute, continually generates disorder [ἀναξία], which God abhors greatly (1 Cor. 14:33), and it drags the destruction of the society after it, for all things are held together by order. The latter is no less hostile to the preservation of the Church, because it oppresses liberty and casts Christ, as far as it can, down from his throne. The Fanatics, Libertines and Enthusiasts dash their ship against the former of these rocks; the hierarchical Popes, sworn to it, against the latter.

units.la: XXXVIII. Tria insuper animadversio-
units.tr: XXXVIII. Three further observations deserve attention here.

units.la: nem heic merentur. Primum, quòd manifestatio Ecclesiæ per notas has non ejusmodi sit,ut per eam certò cuivis constet, quinam verè fideles sint; sed ut in genere constet,Deum adhuc habere populum in mundo,& Ecclesiam, quam ab erroribus & scandalis purgare velit; quivis autem fidelis apud se ex arrhabone Spiritus, quo obsignatur, & qui est calculus albus, cui inscriptum nomen est, quod nemo novit, nisi qui accipit,Apoc.II.17. coetus esse possit de communione Sanctorum; & ut in bona conscientia confessionem, patientiam, laborem&opera tanquam testimonia fidei suæ, allegare possit ad hoc, ut apud homines sit ἀκατάληπτος & ἀκατάγνωστος. Neque aliud in mundo quæri opus est,quàm coetum vocatorum fidem Christi profitentium, ut cum illis, ceu fratres,conjungamur,ad mutuam ædificationem & glorificationem Dei: & quò magis in fratribus abundent fructus Spiritus,eò magis lætemur; ubi autem scandala glisc unt, ut cum δοκίμοις faciamus. Neque aliud invenien-di ejus medium est,quàm ἡ κλῆσις ἀρία, sancta per verbum & Sacramenta vocatio, & ἀναστροφὴ ἀξία τῆς κλήσεως conversatio vocationi illi conveniens, quæ notæ illæ Ecclesiæ sunt. Secundum, quòd notæ illæ Ecclesiæ propriæ necessitate,ejúsque gradibus distinguantur. Summo enim gradu verbum, ejúsque, saltem quoad fundamentum,pura prædicatio necessaria est; absque qua Ecclesia visibilis nec est, nec dici potest. Medio necessaria est legitima Sacramentorum administratio,quæ ex priore dependet, at abesse tamen ad tempus,quoad actum, non quoad propositum & desiderium, potest, uti exemplo Ecclesiæ Israeliticæ in deserto circumcisione sine salutis dispendio carentis, liquet. Non eadem obsignationis, quæ promissionis ipsius necessitas est. Tertio gradu necessarius sanctæ disciplinæ & regiminis usus est, qui ad tuendum Ecclesiæ statum sic pertinet, ut absque eo, absit modò anarchia & tyrannis,verbum Dei legitimè prædicatum consistere possit. Eadem nempe distinctio graduum necessitatis in notificanda Ecclesia, quæ in constituenda obtinet. Atqui Ecclesiam visibilem primò verbum fidem ingenerans,ejúsque prædicatio,Rom.X.16.17: inde Sacramentorum administratio , doctrinam verbi obsignans; ac demum utriusque auxiliatrix disciplina,quæ sic utriusque custos & vindex est,ut tamen ad fidem immediatè non faciat, constituunt. Tertium,quòd notæ illæ non apud solos fideles,sed etiam apud infideles valeant; secus ac Sociniani & Novatores, ut rudibus & incautis hæreseos suæ virus tantò facilius instillent, eas ad solos fideles contrahentes, afferunt. Apud utrosque enim valent, sed diverso modo. Apud fideles, ut confirmentur, & in communione ejus constanter perseverent. Apud infideles, ut in notitiam veræ Ecclesiæ perducantur, ejúsque communioni adhæreant. Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona opera vestra,& glorificent Patrem vestrum,qui in Coelis est,Matth.V.16. Si omnes prophetaverint,& ingressus fuerit infidelis, vel idiota aliquis, reprehenditur ab omnibus,dijudicatur ab omnibus. Et sic occulta cordis ejus manifesta fient, & ita prolapsus in faciem adorabit Deum, annuntians, quòd quòd Deus verè in vobis sit, 1. Cor. XIV. 24. 25. Nam per quod Ecclesia colligitur & constituitur, per id quoque ab infidelibus cognoscitur,quia cognitio fit per causas. Per verbum autem ejusque prædicationem Ecclesia constituitur; quia per illa μαθητευσατε discipuli fiunt, Matth. XXVIII. 19. Neque pura prædicatio ab infidelibus,dum convertuntur,aliunde quàm ex verbo Dei cognoscitur; uti exemplo Berrhoensium Actor. XVII. 11. liquet. Et si notarum nullus apud infideles usus esset,nulli omnino per prædicationem verbi, ejus ministerium converterentur; cùm tamen finis prædicationis & ministerii hominum conversio sit. Ideo enim Deus S. Paulum ad prædicandum gentibus infidelibus misit, ut aperirentur eorum oculi, & reverterentur ex tenebris ad lucem, ex potestate Sathanæ ad Deum,&c. ibid. XXVI. 17. 18.
units.tr: First, the manifestation of the Church through these marks is not of such a kind that, by means of it, it is certain to everyone who the truly faithful are. Rather, it is established in general that God still has a people in the world, and a Church which he wishes to purge of errors and scandals. Yet every believer, within himself, from the earnest of the Spirit by which he is sealed, which is the white stone on which a name is written that no one knows except the one who receives it (Rev. 2:17), can be a member of the communion of the saints. And in a good conscience he can offer his confession, patience, labour and works as evidence of his faith, so that before men he is incomprehensible [ἀκατάληπτος] and unaccused [ἀκατάγνωστος]. Nor is anything more needed in the world than to seek out the assembly of those called who profess faith in Christ, so that we may join ourselves to them as brothers, for mutual edification and the glorification of God. And the more the fruits of the Spirit abound among the brothers, the more we rejoice; but where scandals grow, we are to act with the approved ones [δοκίμοις]. Nor is there any other means of finding them than the holy calling [ἡ κλῆσις ἁγία], the calling through the Word and the sacraments, and a manner of life worthy of the calling [ἀναστροφὴ ἀξία τῆς κλήσεως], a conduct suited to that calling. These are the marks of the Church. Secondly, these marks of the Church are distinguished by the proper necessity of each and by their degrees. For at the highest degree stands the Word, and the pure preaching of it, at least as to its foundation, is necessary; without it the visible Church neither exists nor can be called such. At the middle degree, the lawful administration of the sacraments is necessary; it depends on the former, yet it can for a time be absent in act, though not in purpose and desire, as the example of the Israelite Church in the desert, which lacked circumcision without loss of salvation, makes clear. The sealing is not necessary in the same way as the promise itself. At the third degree, the use of holy discipline and government is necessary; it so pertains to preserving the state of the Church that, without it, the Word lawfully preached could still stand, provided that anarchy and tyranny are absent. There is, of course, the same distinction of degrees of necessity in making the Church known as there is in constituting it. Now, the visible Church is constituted first by the Word, which begets faith, and its preaching (Rom. 10:16, 17); then by the administration of the sacraments, which seals the doctrine of the Word; and finally by discipline, which helps both, and so is their guardian and defender, yet does not directly produce faith. Thirdly, these marks are valid not only among the faithful but also among unbelievers. The Socinians and Novatians, on the contrary, assert that they belong only to the faithful, so that they may more easily instil the poison of their heresy into the simple and the unwary. For these marks are valid among both, but in different ways. Among the faithful, they serve to confirm them and to keep them steadfast in its communion. Among unbelievers, they lead them to knowledge of the true Church and cause them to cleave to its communion. So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven (Matt. 5:16). If all prophesy, and there come in one that believeth not, or one unlearned, he is convinced of all, he is judged of all: and thus are the secrets of his heart made manifest; and so falling down on his face he will worship God, and report that God is in you of a truth (1 Cor. 14:24, 25). For by that by which the Church is gathered and constituted, it is also known to unbelievers, because knowledge comes through causes. Now the Church is constituted through the Word and its preaching, because by these disciples are made [μαθητεύσατε] (Matt. 28:19). Nor is the pure preaching known to unbelievers, as they are converted, from any source other than the Word of God, as the example of the Bereans makes clear (Acts 17:11). And if these marks had no use among unbelievers, none at all would be converted through the preaching of the Word and its ministry, although the conversion of men is the end of preaching and of the ministry. For God sent St Paul to preach to the unbelieving Gentiles to open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, etc. (Acts 26:17, 18).

units.la: XXXIX. Vana Pontificiorum adversus notas Ecclesiæ à nobis assertas objectamenta sunt.
units.tr: XXXIX. The vain objections of the Papists against the marks of the Church which we have asserted.

units.la: Falsum enim & blasphemum est,quòd verbum Dei, seu Scripturam, & sinceram ejus prædicationem non aliunde nobis innotescere, quàm ex testimonio Ecclesiæ, ac proin prius Ecclesiam noscendam esse, quàm verbum Dei, asserunt. Nam Spiritus veritatis est,qui primò, per se & efficaciter id docet, Ecclesia autem nonnisi secundariò, instrumentaliter, neque aliter quàm ex ipsa Scriptura docet, quicquid rectè docet. Cùm enim Ecclesia ex verbo Dei nascatur,& nascatur, Ecclesia verbo Dei prior vel notior esse non potest. Neque veritatem notarum insolens hæreticorum, easdem coetibus suis vindicantium gloriatio minuit. Mentiuntur enim, non rectè ritéque gloriantur. Ostendant illi doctrinam suam ex verbo Dei, & vel ipsi hæretici esse desinent,vel notæ non amplius propriæ erunt. Non ex ægrorum somniis, vel temulenta opinione, sed rei veritate de nobis judicandum est. Veritas hæc ex communibus principiis arcessenda est. Est autem Scriptura Christianorum principium αὐτόπιστον; quod qui defugit, Christiani nomine indignus est. Sed nec disputandum est de principio, ex quo controversiæ definiendæ sunt. Cùm ergo quæratur inter Christianos, non quæ & qualis Scriptura sit,quam Divinam esse omnes fatentur: sed quæ qualisve sit Ecclesia, necesse est hoc problema per principium illud demonstrari. Estque principium hoc tesseræ & vexilli instar,ex quo milites dignoscuntur. Quicunque coetus signum præfert,Christi auspiciis pugnare intelligitur. Ex vexillo legionem, non ex legione vexillum agnoscimus. Non obscurè Pontificii ostendunt, malle se Scripturæ auctoritatem & fundamenta everti,quàm pati,ut quæstio de Ecclesia,ejusque notis ex Scriptura definiatur. Quæ non obscura spiritus tenebrarum,quo lucifugæ illi impelluntur,nota est. Neque etiam propterea verbi & Sacramentorum dispensatio non sunt Ecclesiæ notæ, quia ejus bona & dotes sunt. Non enim hæc ἀσυμπτωτα sunt: siquidem etiam in rebus terrenis possessio & usus earum est nota translati dominii, neque propterea fructus seu bonum ejus esse definit. Sic Fœderis à Deo cum Ecclesia sanciti nota est verbum, sive Scriptura, tanquam instrumentum ejus authenticum, Sacramentorum sigillis obsignatum & munitum: ex quorum legitima dispensatione & usu fructus uberrimi ad possessores redeunt. Denique verbi Dei prædicatio adeò ab Ecclesia externa inseparabilis est,ut cum ea oriatur vel occidat, corrupta vel incorrupta habeatur,uti particularium Ecclesiarum exempla docent. Sunt tamen etiam sinceritatis & puritatis gradus; nec statim Ecclesia cessat,ubi secundum gradus aliquot cessat,dummodo ne plané cessét.
units.tr: For it is false and blasphemous when they assert that the Word of God, or Scripture, and its sincere preaching, are known to us from no other source than the testimony of the Church, and that therefore the Church must be known before the Word of God. For it is the Spirit of truth who teaches this first, through himself and effectually; the Church teaches only secondarily and instrumentally, and it teaches whatever it teaches rightly only from Scripture itself. Since the Church is born of the Word of God, and is born by it, the Church cannot be prior to or better known than the Word of God. Nor does the boast of heretics, who claim these marks for their own assemblies, diminish the truth of the marks. For they lie; they do not boast rightly and properly. Let them show their doctrine from the Word of God, and either the heretics themselves will cease to be heretics, or the marks will no longer be proper to them. We must judge of us not by the dreams of the sick or by drunken opinion, but by the truth of the matter. This truth must be drawn from common principles. Now Scripture is the self-credible principle [αὐτόπιστον] of Christians; whoever shuns this is unworthy of the name of Christian. But neither should one dispute about the principle from which controversies are to be settled. Since, therefore, the question among Christians is not what sort of Scripture it is, which all confess to be divine, but what sort of Church it is, this problem must necessarily be demonstrated by that principle. And this principle is like a token and a banner by which soldiers are recognised. Whatever assembly bears the sign is understood to fight under Christ's auspices. We recognise the legion by its banner, not the banner by the legion. The Papists show clearly that they would rather have the authority and foundations of Scripture overthrown than suffer the question of the Church and its marks to be settled from Scripture. The spirit of darkness, by which those light-shunners are driven, is no obscure sign. Nor, for that reason, are the administration of the Word and the sacraments not marks of the Church, merely because they are its goods and endowments. For these are not inseparable [ἀσύμπτωτα]: even in earthly affairs, possession and use of things are a mark of transferred ownership, yet they do not thereby cease to be its fruit or its good. Thus the Word, or Scripture, is the mark of the covenant sanctioned by God with the Church, as its authentic instrument, sealed and secured by the seals of the sacraments; from their lawful administration and use the richest fruits return to the possessors. Finally, the preaching of the Word of God is so inseparable from the external Church that, rising or falling with it, it is held to be corrupt or incorrupt, as the examples of particular Churches teach. Yet there are also degrees of sincerity and purity; nor does the Church immediately cease where it ceases in some degrees, provided it does not cease altogether.

units.la: XL. Sicut Ecclesia proprie dicta invisibilis; ita externa hæc improprie & latius dicta, atque notis suis conspicua,credens simul & loquens,Psal. CXVI. 10. 2. Cor. IV. 13. visibilis est; quatenus id, quod fideles congregati in nomine Christi verbum Dei profitendo & prædicando, eique doctrinam & conversationem suam conformando,faciunt,videri & cognosci ab aliis & à se invicem etiam, atque inde judicium capi potest, quod ita facientes vera Christi Ecclesia, cui se aggregare salvandi debent,censeri possint & debeant. Sed non omnibus tamen Ecclesia Dei visibilis est,sed iis demum, qui possunt audire verba Christi,& qui possunt videre ea,quæ discipuli Christi dicunt & faciunt erga omnes, & potissimum fratres suos, atque etiam patiuntur, ex charitate. A nemine ergo videtur & cognoscitur nisi ab eo, qui videt & cognoscit doctrinam Christi, & eam discit amando, sive cupiendo fratribus amorem impendere. Non enim quicquid visibile est actu videtur ab omnibus, quia non omnes habent oculos ad videndum,quod vident cum judicio. Etiam discipuli, qui cum Christo Emauntem proficiscebantur, eum videntes non videbant,quia nesciebant,se Jesum videre. Sacerdotes Judæorum nesciebant, se Christum crucifigere. Ita Ecclesia videtur,& id videtur, per quod Ecclesia cognoscitur; sed non videtur, hoc est, cognoscitur Ecclesia,nisi ab iis,qui cognoscunt id,per quod cognoscitur. Ideo Christus: In hoc, inquit, cognoscent omnes, quòd discipuli mei sitis, si charitatem habeatis invicem, Joh. XIII. 35. Amor enim fratrum ad id comparatus est,ut omnes homines, saltem, qui salvi futuri sunt,cognoscant discipulos Christi,& in iis vitam Christi; & ut extranei etiam à Regno Christi ad doctrinam Christi rectè intelligendam,approbandam, & ut salventur, faciendam, attendant. Fratres enim non prius cognoscuntur,quàm doctrina Christi: certè sine doctrina Christi non possunt cognosci discipuli Christi: neque prius doctrina Christi cognosci potest,quàm cognoscitur debitum charitatis,& charitas,sive voluntas se cum fratre aggregandi & communionem habendi adeñt. At demum frater ad lætitiam fratris cognoscitur,quando is cognoscitur diligere fratres secundum doctrinam Christi. Licèt ergo Ecclesia visibilis sit & cognoscatur,tamen Regnum Christi non est μετὰ παρατηρήσεως cum observatione, Luc. XVII. 20. hoc est, cum ea evidentia, quæ & animos stupentes & errore imbutos latere non potest, qualis παρατήρησις observatio & evidentia est mundanæ civitatis, quæ ne invitos quidem latere potest,& splendore suo etiam hostium & non amantium oculos præstringit,qualem Ecclesiæ visibilitatem Hierar-
units.tr: XL. Just as the Church properly so called is invisible, so this external Church, called improperly and more broadly, and conspicuous by its marks, believing and speaking together (Ps. 116:10; 2 Cor. 4:13), is visible. For the faithful, gathered in the name of Christ, profess and preach the Word of God, and conform their doctrine and conduct to it; these things can be seen and known by others and by one another, and from them a judgement can be formed that those who so act may and ought to be regarded as the true Church of Christ, to which those who are to be saved must join themselves. Yet the Church of God is not visible to all, but only to those who can hear the words of Christ and who can see what the disciples of Christ say and do towards all, and especially towards their brothers, and also suffer, out of love. Therefore it is seen and known by no one except him who sees and knows the doctrine of Christ and learns it by loving, that is, by desiring to show love to the brothers. For not everything that is visible is actually seen by all, since not all have eyes to see with judgement what they see. The disciples who were travelling with Christ to Emmaus, seeing him, did not see him, because they did not know that they were seeing Jesus. The priests of the Jews did not know that they were crucifying Christ. So the Church is seen, and that by which the Church is known is seen; but the Church is not seen, that is, known, except by those who know that by which it is known. Hence Christ said: By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another (John 13:35). For love of the brothers is so ordered that all men, at least those who are to be saved, may know the disciples of Christ, and in them the life of Christ; and that strangers also to the kingdom of Christ may attend to the doctrine of Christ, so as to understand it rightly, approve it, and do it, that they may be saved. For brothers are not known before the doctrine of Christ; certainly without the doctrine of Christ the disciples of Christ cannot be known, nor can the doctrine of Christ be known before the duty of love is known, and love, that is, the will to join oneself with a brother and to have fellowship with him, is present. But at last a brother is recognised by the gladness of the brother, when he is known to love the brothers according to the doctrine of Christ. Although, therefore, the visible Church is visible and can be known, nevertheless the Kingdom of Christ does not come with observation [μετὰ παρατηρήσεως] (Luke 17:20), that is, with that evidence which cannot be hidden even from stupefied minds and minds steeped in error. Such observation and evidence belong to the earthly city, which cannot be hidden even from those who do not wish to see it, and dazzles with its splendour even the eyes of enemies and of those who do not love it. This is the kind of visibility that the Hierar-

units.la: Objectiones adversus notas Ecclesiæ veras discussæ. Hierarchia Papalis, quæ pro Ecclesia Regnum humanum extruit, fingit.
units.tr: Objections against the true marks of the Church discussed. The Papal hierarchy, which builds a human kingdom and passes it off as the Church, is a fiction.

units.la: XLI. Ecclesia externa sic visibilis est tum in personis singulis, tum in cœtibus. In personis singulis, quia fideles per fidem Christo uniti, per confessionem fidei, & conversationem charitatis lucem suam coram hominibus sic lucere sinunt, ut homines videant eorum bona opera, & Patrem, qui in Cœlis est, glorificent, Matth. V. 16. In cœtibus, particularibus puta, non uno aliquo universali, utpote qui in sua amplitudine & universitate non videtur, sed creditur, juxta Symbolum: Credo Ecclesiam Catholicam. Sed in particularibus tamen cœtibus visibilis est, quia Deus semper in mundo habet Regnum distinctum societatibus seu cœtibus particularibus illorum, qui Christum Salvatorem suum agnoscunt, eúmque vel ore & corde, vel ore saltem, colunt & profitentur juxta regulam Divini verbi; atque ita videri & ab aliis per judicium fidei & charitatis discerni possunt; licet lato cum discrimine puritatis interioris, status exterioris, loci & operationis. Puritatis interioris, quia modo purior & defæcatior, atque à fermento errorum & scandalorum liberior clariorque: modo erroribus, abusibus & scandalis implicatior, obscurior & decolor magis videtur. Status exterioris, quia neque statum Regni humani visibilis & pomposi habet, & extra statum ejusmodi mundanum, modo pace, tranquillitate & καιρὸς ἀναψυξεως temporibus refrigerii florentior, illustrior, & gloriosior; modo persecutionum nube & nocte præsfa deformior, obscurior & minus mundo nosci bilis & gloriosa est. Loci, quia non sic ulli loco mundi alligata, & velut matri seu metropoli, uti in V. T. obtinuit, affixa est, quin fidelibus hujus vel illius cœtus, vel ad Dominum evocatis, vel alió migrantibus, ipsi desinere, & candelabrum loco suo motum alibi sedem invenire & figere possit. Denique operationis, quia licet Ecclesiæ hic fulgor Christi gloriam mire illustrat, cui etiam hostes ejus, qui ut plurimum externæ Ecclesiæ atrium majore numero calcant, mentiri coguntur, & quem Jesum Christum ad gloriam Dei Patris esse, omnes lingua confiteri debent, Phil. II. 11. tamen de cætero visibilis illa conditio non plus Regno Christi, quàm Sathanæ & Antichristi commodi vel honoris conciliat, quia hoc non minus quàm illud in mundo aspectabile & visibile est. Non enim hic tam visibilitas cœtus cujuspiam, quàm modus visibilitatis, quo homines per præconium verbi Dei & manifestationem veritatis ad conscientiam ad fidem Christi convertuntur, spectari debet. Inde enim visibilitati pretium omne constat; & absque eo est, Ecclesiam non esse visibilem præstaret.
units.tr: XLI. The external Church is visible both in individual persons and in assemblies. It is visible in individual persons because the faithful, united to Christ through faith, let their light shine before men through the confession of faith and the practice of love, so that men see their good works and glorify the Father who is in heaven, Matt. 5:16. It is visible in assemblies, meaning particular assemblies and not some one universal assembly, which in its full extent and universality is not seen but believed, according to the Creed: "I believe the Catholic Church." Yet in particular assemblies it is visible, because God always has in the world a kingdom distinct in societies or particular assemblies of those who acknowledge Christ as their Saviour and worship and profess him, with mouth and heart or at least with the mouth, according to the rule of the divine Word. In this way they can be seen by others and distinguished through the judgment of faith and love, though with a wide variation in inner purity, outer state, place and activity. As to inner purity, it sometimes appears purer, more refined, freer from the leaven of errors and scandals, and brighter; sometimes, entangled in errors, abuses and scandals, it appears more obscure and dull. As to outer state, it does not have the form of a visible and splendid human kingdom; apart from such worldly state, it is sometimes more flourishing, illustrious and glorious in times of peace, tranquillity and "seasons of refreshing"; sometimes, under the cloud and night of persecution, it is more deformed, obscure and less known and glorious to the world. As to place, it is not bound to any place in the world, nor fixed, as it was under the Old Testament, to a mother or metropolis. Rather, when the faithful of this or that assembly are called to the Lord or move elsewhere, the assembly itself can cease there, and the lampstand, moved from its place, can find and fix its seat elsewhere. Finally, as to activity: although the brightness of the Church wonderfully displays the glory of Christ, before which his enemies, who for the most part trample the outer court of the Church in greater numbers, are compelled to lie, and whom every tongue must confess to be Jesus Christ, to the glory of God the Father, Phil. 2:11, nevertheless that visible condition brings no more advantage or honour to the kingdom of Christ than to that of Satan and Antichrist, since the latter is no less conspicuous and visible in the world than the former. For here one must look not so much at the visibility of any assembly as at the manner of visibility by which men are converted in conscience to the faith of Christ through the proclamation of God's Word and the manifestation of truth. For all the worth of visibility arises from this, and without it, it would be better that the Church were not visible.

units.la: XLII. At nec visibilis esse vera Ecclesia cessat, licet minor longè numerus eorum, qui Christi nomen in veritate confitentur, quàm eorum, qui illud ore & corde, vel alterutro abnegant, glisçat. Nam dum Bestiæ Regnum paulatim incrementa sumit, & ὁ Ἀνομος ἐν πάντα ... in astutia & seductione surgit, ipsi fideles inter hostes Christi ipsi mentes multiplicantur, & eo ipso fideles esse cognoscuntur, quia plurimi non ex fide eadem, quæ ipsi in fide, loquuntur. Interim congregationes τοπικαὶ locales eorum, qui profitentur Christum Dominum, quò major Bestiam adorantium, & charagma illius suscipientium numerus est; quò plures etiam sunt fideles, qui Sathanæ profunditates ignorant, & servi Dei errantes, scortantes, & idolothyta comedentes; eò magis sinceræ, puræ & incontaminatæ esse desinunt. Qui autem prudentes sunt, & Sathanæ dolos intelligunt & gemunt atque indignantur, aliquando palam audiuntur, aliquando non, sed victi oppressive videntur. Aliud vero est, Ecclesiam visibilem esse; aliud eam conspicuam & publicam se exhibere. Habet enim diversa lucis tempora, prout à Sole justitiæ suo magis minúsve illustratur, adeóque purior vel impurior apparet; atque pro temporum iniquitate vel felicitate majore in cœtus coeundi, & se orbi ostendendi facultatem habet; aut tyrannorum furore dissipata, simul & congregari & conspici desinit. Quanquam & ii, qui impuritatem doctrinæ contrahunt, atque victi videntur, in Ecclesiis corruptis & depravatis permanent, & Divinitus à corruptelis, saltem quoad fundamenta salutaris doctrinæ præservantur; & qui persecutionum tempore dissipati in cœtus coire vetantur, vel de petrarum fissuris columbæ instar, Cant. II. 14. gemitum planctúmque edere non cessant, & vel clamore atque martyrio suo se non solum notos, sed illustres etiam reddere gestiunt. Sed eam in rem infra plura dicenda sunt.
units.tr: XLII. Nor does the true Church cease to be visible, even though the number of those who confess the name of Christ in truth is far smaller than the number of those who deny it, with mouth and heart or with either of them, and that number grows. For while the kingdom of the Beast gradually increases, and the [ἄνομος] lawless one rises up in deceit and seduction, the faithful themselves are multiplied among the enemies of Christ, and by that very fact they are known to be faithful, because very many speak not from the same faith that they themselves hold. Meanwhile, the local [τοπικαί] congregations of those who profess Christ the Lord are, the greater the number of those who worship the Beast and receive its mark, and the more there are faithful who do not know the depths of Satan, and servants of God who err, commit fornication and eat things sacrificed to idols, the less they remain sincere, pure and uncontaminated. But those who are prudent, who understand the wiles of Satan and groan and are indignant, are sometimes heard openly and sometimes not, but are seen to be overcome and oppressed. It is one thing for the Church to be visible, and another for it to present itself as conspicuous and public. For it has different times of light, according as it is more or less illuminated by the Sun of righteousness, and so appears more or less pure; and according to the iniquity or greater happiness of the times, it has the opportunity to assemble and to show itself to the world; or, when scattered by the fury of tyrants, it ceases both to be gathered and to be seen. Yet those who contract impurity of doctrine and seem overcome remain in corrupted and depraved churches, and are divinely preserved from corruptions, at least as to the foundations of saving doctrine. And those who, scattered in time of persecution and forbidden to assemble, like doves in the clefts of the rocks, Cant. 2:14, do not cease to utter groaning and lamentation, and seek by their outcry and martyrdom to make themselves not only known but even illustrious. But more on this matter must be said below.

units.la: XLIII. Cùm Ecclesiam proprie dictam electorum fidelium non omnis erroris vitiique expertem esse, supra fidem fecerimus, multò minùs Ecclesia externa, non electorum, vocatorum duntaxat, sed etiam vocatorum non electorum cœtus, erroris vitiíque omnis expers est. Nam qui in eodem cœtu sunt, electi vocati, licet potentia Dei conservati à fundamento fidei descisçere, & in specie χαρακτῆρα & θηρίου signaturam Bestiæ in manum vel frontem recipere, vel ἑκουσίως voluntarie peccare non possunt; at possunt tamen erroribus fundamentum non evertentibus implicari, & in multis impingere; vocati verò non electi erroribus ipsum etiam fundamentum fidei sucutientibus pollui, & gravissimis atque exitialibus scandalis nocere sibi aliisque possunt. Nam juxta prædictiones Divinas fieri potuit, imò debuit, ut verae Ecclesiae Christi in externa communione se magno numero reprobi, scandalosi, hypocritæ, infideles, athei, Diotrephes, fidei aliorum dominantes, illustres cathedras occupantes, & brachio seculari ad stabiliendum dominium suum succincti sese immiscerent; pellem Ecclesiæ, sicut olim alinus leonis, ad incutiendum terrorem, induerent, & veram lic Ecclesiam, velut fumo quodam, implerent, obscurarent, & tantùm non obruerent, denique in laxiore quadam custodia, illecebris instructissima, velut captivam attinerent, eo plane modo, quo olim Babylon Chaldaica Ecclesiam Dei captivam conclusit. Id Christus ipse parabolis zizaniorum agrum dominicum replentium, & triticum ipsum non parum affligentium & obruentium, Matth. XIII. 24–31. Sagenæ, quæ in mare missa putres æquè atque bonos pisces attrahit, ibid. v. 47. Convivii nuptialis, cui se velte nuptiali induti,
units.tr: XLIII. Since we have shown above that the Church properly so called, of the elect faithful, is not free from every error and vice, much less is the external Church free from all error and vice. This external Church is the assembly not only of the called elect but also of the called non-elect. For those who are in the same assembly, the called elect, although preserved by the power of God from falling away from the foundation of faith, and specifically from receiving the character or the mark of the Beast on hand or forehead, or from sinning wilfully [ἑκουσίως], cannot do so; yet they can be entangled in errors which do not overturn the foundation, and stumble in many things. The called non-elect, on the other hand, can be polluted with errors that shake the foundation of faith itself, and can harm themselves and others with most grave and deadly scandals. For according to the divine predictions it was possible, indeed it was necessary, that the reprobate, the scandalous, hypocrites, unbelievers, atheists, and Diotrephes, lording it over the faith of others, occupying illustrious chairs and girding themselves with the secular arm to establish their dominion, should mix themselves in great numbers into the external communion of the true Churches of Christ; that they should put on the skin of the Church, as once the ass put on the lion's skin to strike terror; that they should fill and obscure this true Church as with a kind of smoke, and all but overwhelm it; and that finally, in a somewhat looser custody, most richly furnished with allurements, they should hold it as a captive, in just the way that Chaldean Babylon once shut up the Church of God in captivity. Christ himself teaches this in his parables: of the tares filling the Lord's field and greatly afflicting and overwhelming the wheat itself, Matt. 13:24–31; of the net cast into the sea, which draws in rotten fish as well as good ones, ibid. v. 47; of the wedding feast, to which those who are clothed in a wedding garment and those who lack it are admitted together, ibid.

units.la: Visibilis est tum in personis singulis, tum in cœtibus, sed lato discrimine puritatis interioris, status exterioris, loci & operationis. duti, & eadem carentes, miscent, ibid. XXII. 11. Virginum prudentium & fatuarum, ibid. XXIV. 1. &c. Ovilis, oves & hœdos, Joh. X. 1. Vitis, palmites vivos & aridos, ibid. XV. 1. includentis; nec non Johannes Baptista area, in qua triticum & paleæ simul coacervantur, Matth. III. 12. luculenter docent. Nam cum talibus Regnum Cœlorum, hoc est, Ecclesiam externam illi contendunt.
units.tr: It is visible both in individual persons and in assemblies, but with a wide variation in inner purity, outer state, place and activity. ...are mixed together, ibid. 22:11; of the virgins, wise and foolish, ibid. 25:1, etc.; of the sheepfold, sheep and goats, John 10:1; of the vine, living and dried branches, ibid. 15:1, enclosing them; and John the Baptist likewise, with the threshing floor in which wheat and chaff are heaped together, Matt. 3:12, clearly teach this. For they maintain that the kingdom of heaven, that is the external Church, is made up of such people.

units.la: XLIV. Et ne communionem illam externam in solis moribus corrumpi, at in fide neque errare, & gravissimè etiam, quoad commixtam inprimis illam hypocritarum partem posse putemus, obstat, non tantum prædictio Pauli, fore ut post discessum suum intrent lupi graves, non parcentes gregi, & (ἐξ ὑμῶν ex vobis) adeóque ex ipsius Ecclesiæ visceribus surgant viri λαλοῦντες διεστραμμένα loquentes perversa, & discipulos post se abstrahentes, Actor. XX. 29. 30. & oportere, ut sint hæreses, ut qui probi sunt, manifesti fiant, 1. Cor. XI. 19. Sed inprimis & omnium instar disertissima illa Prophetia de apostasia per filium perditionis in Ecclesiam invehenda; nec non de Adversario, se supra omne id, quod vocatur Deus, aut venerabile, efferente, adeò ut sedeat etiam in Templo, ut Deus, demonstrans se ipsum, quòd Deus sit, 2. Thess. II. 4. Debuit ergo quandoque Adversarius ille Christi, "Ανομος Exlex, seu Antichristus, in ipso Templo Dei, seu Ecclesia Dei, erigere suum principatum, & ἀνομίαν illegalitatem exercere, adeóque mendacia sua per seductionem in hypocrisi docere, 1. Tim. IV. 1. 2. Neque enim ibi ναὸς Templum proprie Hierosolymitanum Templum esse potest, quia eo tempore S. Pauli stante nullus "Ανομος in eo sedens, & se super omne Numen efferens, & demonstrans se, quòd Deus sit, ostendi potest; & Templum illud, ejus populi, cujus ἀποστασία defectio v. 3. notatur, & propter quam "Ανομος Exlex, seu Antichristus missus est, esse debuit. Hæc autem ἀποστασία non Judæorum, sed Gentium ad Christum accedentium, sed non ea fide studioque, quo par erat, eum colentium, esse debuit. Neque id ullo modo in Judæos competit, quia ante destructum Templum nunquam illi Regni hujus cives scribi gestiverunt; & post destructum illud aliud Templum Hierosolymitanum expectandum non erat, quod ναὸς Θεοῦ Templi Dei nomine venire posset. Si maximè Hierosolymæ Judæi vel Turcæ Templum, quale Solomonicum erat, extruerent, tamen illud Templum Dei non esset, quin potius Deus illud, ceu fundatum & stabilitum non suo, sed Antichristi nomine, detestaretur. Prophetia verò illa S. Pauli parallela est illi, in qua de Filio Aurorae dicitur; Confidebo in monte conventus, in lateribus Aquilonis, Esaj. XIV. 13. Id Apostolus explicat de 'Ανόμω Exlege in Ecclesia Dei confessuro, perinde ac si in latere Aquilonis, in Templo Dei, tanquam Deus sederet. In Templo enim Solomonis juxta altare ad latus Aquilonis mactabantur victimæ coram Deo, ut habitante in Templo Dei, Levit. I. 5. 15. Illud Prophetæ ænigma sic Apostolus explicat: Sedebit in Ecclesia, quæ verè Templum Dei est, ut Deus. Neque illud obstat, quòd sic in Templo sedens vocatur 'Ανλκεμένω Adversarius Christi, Exlex, Homo peccati, quia Ecclesiæ do-
units.tr: XLIV. And lest we think that this external communion is corrupted only in morals and not in faith, nor can err very gravely, especially as to the mixed-in part of hypocrites, the following stands in the way: not only Paul's prediction that after my departure grievous wolves will enter in, not sparing the flock, and (ἐξ ὑμῶν, from among you), so that from the very bowels of the Church men will arise speaking perverse things [λαλοῦντες διεστραμμένα] and draw disciples away after them, Acts 20:29–30; and that there must be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest, 1 Cor. 11:19. But above all, and most clearly of all, that prophecy about the apostasy to be brought into the Church by the son of perdition, and about the Adversary, who exalts himself above everything that is called God or is worshipped, so that he sits even in the Temple, showing himself as God, 2 Thess. 2:4. Therefore that Adversary of Christ, the [Ἄνομος] Lawless One or Antichrist, had to set up his rule in the Temple of God, that is in the Church of God, and to practise lawlessness [ἀνομίαν], and so to teach his lies by hypocritical deception, 1 Tim. 4:1–2. For the temple [ναὸς] cannot properly be the temple at Jerusalem, because in St Paul's time no Lawless One could be shown sitting in it, exalting himself above every divinity and showing himself to be God; and that temple belonged to the people whose apostasy is noted in v. 3, and on account of which the Lawless One, or Antichrist, had to be sent. But this apostasy had to be not of the Jews but of the Gentiles who come to Christ, yet not with that faith and zeal with which they ought to worship him. Nor does this apply in any way to the Jews, because before the temple was destroyed they never wanted to be enrolled as citizens of this kingdom; and after it was destroyed, no other Jerusalem temple was to be expected that could be called the Temple of God. Even if the Jews or the Turks were to build a temple at Jerusalem such as Solomon's, it would still not be the Temple of God; rather God would detest it as founded and established not in his name but in Antichrist's. But that prophecy of St Paul is parallel to the one in which it is said of the Son of the Dawn: I will sit on the mount of assembly, in the sides of the north, Isa. 14:13. The Apostle explains this as referring to the [Ἄνομος] Lawless One who will sit in the Church of God, just as if he sat on the side of the north, in the Temple of God, as God. For in Solomon's temple, beside the altar on the north side, victims were slain before the Lord, as one who dwells in the Temple of God, Lev. 1:5, 15. The Apostle thus explains the prophet's riddle: he will sit in the Church, which is truly the Temple of God, as God. Nor does it stand in the way that the Adversary of Christ, the Lawless, the man of sin, is called so while sitting in the temple, because he has crept into the Church, which he is about to rule over.

units.la: minaturus obrepsit per nomen Christiani, habens eadem verba fundamenti, professionem Symboli Apostolici in ore & Scripturas in manu.
