XI. 22. durat in verae Ecclesiae Catholicae, quae Deum ex verbo ejus recte agnoscit, & rite colit, gremio: seque adeo, illi fundamento, cujus lapis angularis Christus est, aggluti-nata, conformavit Ecclesiae Christi & Apostolorum, omniumque succedentium, & Reformationis sequentium temporum aetate existentium, quatenus & illa vel captiva in media Babylone, vel in libertate, sive in Oriente, sive in Occidente doctrinam suam, saltem in fidei praecipuae & unice salutaris compage, Christi & Apostolorum doctrinae cum qua sola doctrinae Ecclesiae conformatio necessaria est, conformavit, & conformare non definit. Cumque corporalem non potuerit, Reformationis inprimis tempore, quo Ecclesia Occidentalis externa, paucis hinc inde Ecclesiis particularibus exceptis, sub Papae jugo prope modum collapsa fuit, nec hodieque possit; spiritualem communionem, sanctificans animas suas in obedientia veritatis, per Spiritum, ad amorem fraternum minime fucatum, I. Pet. I. 22. coluit, colit & colet semper cum omnibus fidelibus, qui per totum terrarum orbem fuerunt; sunt & erunt, in uno solóque Christo spem suam omnem collocantes, Scripturam pro regula fidei & poenitentiae retinentes sequentesque; licet de caetero non pauci illorum infirmi, pueri in Christo, in multis caespitaverint, & hodieque caespitent. Praedictionibus enim Divinis innixi credimus, & historia irrefragabili teste, scimus, fideles ejusmodi, sive collectos, sive sparsos, in omnibus mundi partibus, tum ante Reformationem, tum ipso Reformationis temtempore, (quod tot myriadum data porta ad amplectendam Evangelii doctrinam, subitaneus confluxus luculentissimè probavit) tum maximè post illam, in Oriente & Occidente, ipsius etiam Ecclesiæ Romanæ visceribus, non recipientes legem Papæ, neque castra Bestiæ, sed Agni secutos innumeros fuisse, & futuros esse. Verè ut Ecclesia Catholica in mundo diffusa credatur.
units.tr: LXXIII. Yet the Evangelical Church, when it shook off the terrible yoke of the Roman Church, which clearly defied the command of the lording Christ, and separated itself from that Italian faction that sat upon the body of the Church and offered poison instead of wholesome food, a stone instead of bread, a serpent instead of fish, a scorpion instead of an egg, did not therefore separate itself from the true Church of Christ existing in the world. For it remains and abides in the goodness of God (Rom. 11.22), it dwells in the bosom of the true Catholic Church, which rightly knows God from his Word and duly worships him; and thus, joined to that foundation whose cornerstone is Christ, it has conformed itself to the Church of Christ and the Apostles, and of all who succeeded them, and to those living in the age following the Reformation, insofar as that Church, whether captive in the midst of Babylon or in liberty, whether in the East or in the West, has conformed and does not cease to conform its doctrine, at least in the structure of the chief and alone saving faith, to the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles, with which alone the conformity of the Church's doctrine is necessary. And since it could not, and cannot even now, cultivate a bodily communion, especially at the time of the Reformation, when the external Western Church, with few particular Churches excepted here and there, had almost collapsed under the yoke of the Pope, it has cultivated, cultivates and will always cultivate a spiritual communion, "sanctifying its souls in obedience to the truth through the Spirit, for brotherly love unfeigned" (1 Pet. 1.22), with all the faithful who have been, are and will be throughout the whole world, placing all their hope in Christ alone and retaining and following Scripture as the rule of faith and repentance. Although many of them, weak children in Christ, have stumbled in many things, and still stumble today. For relying on the divine predictions, and on the testimony of irrefutable history, we know that such faithful people, whether gathered or scattered, existed in all parts of the world, both before the Reformation and at the very time of the Reformation (as the sudden flocking of so many myriads, the door opened for embracing the doctrine of the Gospel, has most clearly proved), and especially after it, in the East and in the West, even in the very bowels of the Roman Church, not receiving the law of the Pope nor the camp of the Beast, but following the Lamb, and that countless such people have been and will be. Thus the Catholic Church is truly believed to be spread throughout the world.

units.la: LXXIV. Sed habet insuper & jactat Ecclesia Papalis notas, quibus & veram Ecclesiam à falsa discerni, & suam solam veram nosci pertendit. Rejectis enim genuinis Ecclesiæ notis, quas supra asseruimus, alias illa ad Ecclesiæ suæ, qualem illi terrestri civitati, seu civili Monarchiæ similem finxerunt, amussim factas fictasque tradit. Non enim curæ habet ejusmodi Ecclesiæ notas tradere, quibus vel conscientia tranquilletur coram Deo, vel agnoscatur, & recipiatur aliquis in nomine discipuli Christi, sive ut frater, quo cum sine peccato communicare liceat; sed quibus inveniri possit Ecclesia, in qua regnent tales, qui summam & primam quoad nos authoritatem habent. Unde clarum est, non habere eos verum principium credendi, sed ἰδίον βέλημα consilium & voluntatem propriam partim seducendi mundum, ut in Ecclesiam illam, ceu Regnum terrestre ingrediatur: partim se tradendi in obedientiam hominum propter commoda terrestria, & vim conscientiæ faciendam. Neque tamen de numero & ordine notarum illarum inter ipsos satis convenit, dum alii cum Harantio unam duntaxat, continuatam videlicet Sacerdotum, & præcipuè Romanorum Pontificum successionem: alii ex Catechismo Tridentino duas, τὸ Catholicum & Apostolicum: alii ex Catechismo Canisiano totidem, sed paulò diversas, Romanum Pontificem & Cathedram Romanam: alii cum Stapletono tres, Multitudinem, Visibilitatem & Perpetuitatem: alii cum Costero & Tirino quatuor, ex totidem epithetis Ecclesiæ, qua Sancta, Catholica, Una & Apostolica est: alii deinde plures, velut Jesuitæ Postnanienses septem, Medina undecim; Pistorius duodecim. Ex quibus omnibus quindecim Bellarminus conflavit, numero strepentes, at nec virtute pugnantes, nec pollentes robore. Tales illi sunt Nomen Ecclesiæ Catholicæ & Christianorum, Antiquitas, Duratio diuturna & nunquam interrupta; Amplitudo, sive multitudo & varietas credentium. Successio Episcoporum; Conspiratio in doctrina cum Ecclesia antiqua & Patribus; Unio membrorum inter se & cum capite; Sanctitas doctrinæ; Efficacia Doctrinæ; Sanctitas vitæ primorum authorum; Gloria miraculorum: Lumen Propheticum; Confessio adversariorum; Infelix exitus eorum, qui Ecclesiam oppugnant; & Felicitas temporalis.
units.tr: LXXIV. But the Papal Church also has and boasts marks by which it claims that the true Church is distinguished from the false, and that only its own is known to be true. Having rejected the genuine marks of the Church, which we asserted above, it puts forward instead marks made and shaped to fit its own Church, which they have modelled on an earthly city or civil monarchy. For it does not care to set out marks of the Church by which conscience may be calmed before God, or by which someone may be recognized and received in the name of a disciple of Christ, as a brother with whom it is lawful to communicate without sin. Its concern is rather to find the Church in which those rule who hold the supreme and first authority over us. Whence it is clear that they do not have a true principle of believing, but ἰδίον βέλημα, counsel and their own will: partly to seduce the world so that it enters that Church as an earthly kingdom, and partly to surrender themselves to obedience to men for earthly advantages and to do violence to conscience. Nor do they agree well among themselves on the number and order of those marks. Some, with Harantius, count only one, namely the continuous succession of priests, and above all of the Roman Pontiffs. Others, from the Tridentine Catechism, count two: the Catholic and the Apostolic. Others, from the Canisian Catechism, count the same number but slightly different ones: the Roman Pontiff and the Roman Chair. Others with Stapleton count three: multitude, visibility and perpetuity. Others with Costerus and Tirinus count four, taken from the four epithets of the Church, which is holy, catholic, one and apostolic. Others count more: the Jesuits of Postnania seven, Medina eleven, Pistorius twelve. From all of these Bellarmine assembled fifteen, noisy in number but not powerful in strength, nor strong in force. Such are: the name of the Catholic Church and of Christians; antiquity; long duration, never interrupted; amplitude, that is, the multitude and variety of believers; succession of bishops; agreement in doctrine with the ancient Church and the Fathers; union of the members with one another and with the head; holiness of doctrine; efficacy of doctrine; holiness of life in the first authors; glory of miracles; prophetic light; confession of adversaries; unhappy end of those who attack the Church; and temporal happiness.

units.la: LXXV. Qui cum Costero & Tirino, quos Waleuburgii sequuntur, epitheta illa Ecclesiæ in Symbolo Nicæno-Constantinopolitano expressa, quod sit μία, ἁγία, καθολικὴ ἡ Ἀποστολικὴ, Una, Sancta, Catholica & Apostolica, in totidem Ecclesiæ notas convertunt, illi & à ratione verarum Ecclesiæ notarum discedunt, & Ecclesiæ suæ veritatem evertunt. A ratione verarum Ecclesiæ notarum discedunt, quia credentes Ecclesiam Unam, Sanctam, Catholicam & Apostolicam Ecclesiam, cujus hæc epitheta sunt, supponunt, & circa rem hanc præsuppositam, & palam notam postulatur fides illa, quòd verbum illud, quod credentes profitentur, sit verbum Apostolorum; quòd Apostoli à Christo sint missi; quòd sit Divina vocatio, quæ per verbum hoc peragitur, & quòd ejus verbi prædicatio cum astipulatione multorum ex Judæis & Gentibus sit testimonium veritatis Dei promittentis ædificationem Ecclesiæ in Christo. Nihil enim aliud in verbis illis, quibus profitemur nos credere Sanctam, Unam Catholicam & Apostolicam Ecclesiam, continetur, quàm confessio fidei habitæ verbo Dei de Ecclesia, quòd illa sit, & quòd Sancta, sive Coetus sanctorum, seu sanctificatorum per Spiritum Dei ad fidem in Christum, & justitiam in eo, & ad omne opus bonum: Una, Catholica, hoc est, sublato pariete intergerino, ex Judæis & Gentibus καθολικῶς catholicè collecta, non astricta ulli in mundo Cathedræ; Apostolica, hoc est, quòd ad eam colligendam missi sint Apostoli; & quòd futurum sit, ut per verbum eorum, secundum Prophetias, in perpetuum colligatur, sit. Atque hæc maximè pertinent ad ea, quæ proprie & in se non videntur, sed creduntur; quale est sanctificatio regenerationis & justificationis, fidei unitas, remissio peccatorum & communio Sanctorum. In ipsa voce Ecclesiæ continetur κλήσεως vocatio, & κλητοὶ vocati, intellige per verbum Dei & Spiritum ejus, ut in Christo per fidem fiant unum quid & Catholicum ex toto mundo. Ecclesia igitur plane & omnino à vocatione pendet, & nonnisi à vocationis illius receptione, conversione ad Deum, accessu ad Christum, & ὁμολογία τῆς κλήσεως astipulatione in vocationem in verbis & factis, hoc est, ipsius fœderis receptione & observatione æstimari debet. Et vocatio illa Apostolica est, hoc est, Apostolorum omnium, & ab iis in totum mundum egressa, sive scriptis, sive sermone uniformiter, ut sic nulla vocatio Apostolica; adeóque nulla propositio authentica cujuscunque, vel quorumcunque admitti debeat; quia aliàs non maneret Ecclesia Apostolica. Si igitur Una & quidem Apostolica Ecclesia est, & erit usque ad finem mundi, & hoc credo, simul credo, scripta Apostolorum eam potentiam habere, ut Divinæ κλήσεως vocationis authentiam semper conscientiæ approbare possint, neque ulla authoritate visibilis in mundo Cathedræ ad id indigeat. Hoc enim ipsa terminorum æquivalentia luculenter testatur. Sed adversariis Apostolica vocatio dicitur, quæ est Papæ, multitudinem sibi obnoxiam jubentis quidem audire verbum Dei, sed quatenus ille legere illud permittit, & in eo sensu, quem ipse, sine demonstratione veritatis, dictat. Unde mira anomalia Ecclesiæ has notas cudunt. Cùm enim quæratur, utrum in Scripturis contineatur sancta vocatio, & quæ illa sit, non tantùm quoad verba, sed etiam quoad sensum, ut ita pateat, quam multitudinem Ecclesiam Sanctam, hoc est, sanctæ vocationis sequacem reputare debeamus, illi mera fraude sic hæc duo separant, ut vocationem Papalem pro Apostolica substituentes ex ea vocationem sanctam & veram Ecclesiam demonstrare velint, quod symboli Nicæno-Constantinopolitani ni ni authoribus & confessoribus nunquam in mentem venit. Pura enim hæc & puta decep- tio,& vocationis Apostolicæ in jussionem Papalem per fascinum successionis non doctrinæ, sed Paparum in Cathedra,de qua nihil in Symbolo eo legimus,transubstantiatio est. Atque ita non obscurè etiam Ecclesiæ suæ veritatem οἱ ἐξ ἐκκλησίας evertunt; quippe quæ non in doctrina verbi Dei cum omnibus Sanctis conveniens, neque Apostolorum Scripturas, quoad verba & sensum recipiens, sed in mendaciis conspirans,& fidem Monarchiæ Papæ consentaneam, detortis ad eam Scripturis, fraude & vi obtrudens,non Sancta,Una,Catholica & Apostolica, sed Profana,Apostatica, Idololatrica & Tyrannica est,quos titulos pro furtivis illis titulis ipsis reddere æquum est.
units.tr: LXXV. Those who follow Costerus and Tirinus, whom the Walenburgii follow, turn the epithets of the Church expressed in the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed, namely that it is μία, ἁγία, καθολικὴ ἡ Ἀποστολικὴ (Una, Sancta, Catholica & Apostolica), into as many marks of the Church. In doing so they depart from the principle of the true marks of the Church and overthrow the truth of their own Church. They depart from the principle of the true marks of the Church, because those who believe the Church to be one, holy, catholic and apostolic, of which these are the epithets, presuppose it. And concerning this presupposed and plainly known matter, that faith requires that the word which believers profess is the word of the Apostles; that the Apostles were sent by Christ; that there is a divine calling which is carried out through this word; and that the preaching of this word, with the agreement of many from among Jews and Gentiles, is a testimony to the truth of God, who promises the building up of the Church in Christ. For nothing else is contained in those words by which we profess that we believe the Holy, One, Catholic and Apostolic Church than the confession of the faith we hold, on the basis of God's word, concerning the Church: that it is, and that it is Holy, that is, the assembly of saints, or of those sanctified by the Spirit of God to faith in Christ, to righteousness in him, and to every good work; One, Catholic, that is, with the dividing wall removed, gathered καθολικῶς catholicè from Jews and Gentiles, and bound to no chair in the world; Apostolic, that is, that the Apostles were sent to gather it, and that it will be gathered through their word, according to the prophecies, for ever. And these things pertain chiefly to those matters which are not seen as such in themselves but are believed: such as the sanctification of regeneration and justification, unity of faith, forgiveness of sins and the communion of saints. In the very word Ecclesia is contained κλήσεως vocatio, the calling, and κλητοὶ, the called, understood through the word of God and his Spirit, so that in Christ, through faith, they become one thing and catholic from the whole world. The Church therefore depends entirely and wholly on the calling, and must be judged only by the reception of that calling, by conversion to God, by approach to Christ, and by ὁμολογία τῆς κλήσεως, agreement with the calling in words and deeds, that is, by the reception and observance of the covenant itself. That calling is Apostolic, that is, of all the Apostles, and has gone out from them into the whole world, whether in writing or in speech, uniformly; so that no Apostolic calling, and therefore no authentic proposition of any person or persons, ought to be admitted; otherwise the Church would not remain Apostolic. If therefore the Church is one and indeed Apostolic, and will be so until the end of the world, and I believe this and at the same time believe that the writings of the Apostles have the power to let the authenticity of the divine κλήσεως vocationis always be approved by conscience, and that no authority of a visible chair in the world needs this. The equivalence of the terms themselves clearly attests this. But by our adversaries the Apostolic calling is called that of the Pope, who indeed commands the multitude subject to him to hear the word of God, but only insofar as he permits it to read it and in the sense which he dictates without any demonstration of truth. Whence these people coin these marks of the Church with strange inconsistency. For when it is asked whether a holy calling is contained in the Scriptures, and what that calling is, not only as to words but also as to sense, so that it may appear which multitude we ought to regard as the holy Church, that is, the followers of the holy calling, they separate these two things by sheer fraud. Substituting the Papal calling for the Apostolic, they wish to demonstrate from it a holy calling and a true Church, which never came into the minds of the authors and confessors of the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed ni ni. For this is pure and sheer deception, a transubstantiation of the Apostolic calling into the Papal command, by the magic of a succession not of doctrine but of popes in the chair, of which we read nothing in that Creed. And so they no less clearly overthrow the truth of their own Church, οἱ ἐξ ἐκκλησίας, those who are from the Church. For it does not agree with the doctrine of the word of God shared by all the saints, nor does it receive the Scriptures of the Apostles in words and sense. Rather it conspires in lies and forces upon people, by fraud and violence, a faith suited to the monarchy of the Pope, with Scriptures twisted to fit it. Such a Church is not holy, one, catholic and apostolic, but profane, apostate, idolatrous and tyrannical, and it is right to return these titles to it in place of those stolen titles.

units.la: LXXVI. At nec melioris metalli quindecim illæ Bellarminianæ notæ sunt. Non enim illæ ab Ecclesia inseparabiles, eique essentiales & propriæ sunt,quas notarum notas esse, supra confirmavimus; ac ne notæ quidem sunt; &,siquid veri quoad verba saltem (nam alium sensum iis induunt) habent, illud omne ad primariam Ecclesiæ notam,quæ conformatio cum Dei verbo est,vel prærogativas potius & epitheta, quàm notas Ecclesiæ reducitur; & denique non paucæ illarum genuino sensu explicatæ, ne quidem Ecclesiæ Papali examuslim conveniunt, & verius Ecclesiæ nostræ conveniunt, quod de singulis ζητήματος demonstrabimus.
units.tr: LXXVI. Nor are those fifteen Bellarminian marks of better metal. For they are not inseparable from the Church, nor essential and proper to it; we have already shown above that these are the marks of marks, and they are not even marks. And if they contain anything true, at least as to the words (for they put another sense on them), all of it is reduced to the primary mark of the Church, which is conformity with the word of God, or rather to privileges and epithets, not marks of the Church. Finally, not a few of them, when explained in their genuine sense, do not even agree with the Papal Church, but agree more truly with our Church. We will demonstrate this concerning each one [ζητήματος, question].

units.la: LXXVII. Et nomen quidem Ecclesiæ Catholicæ & Christianorum subdolè Bellarminus conjunxit, cùm distincta sint,& diversa ratione subjecto attribuantur. Tum nota illa ambigua est. Nam aut sensus hujusmodi est, notam Ecclesiæ esse,quòd Catholica & Christiana sit, prout nominatur,aut ipsum nomen & appellationem illius notam esse. Priore sensu falsum id est, quia, uti Bellarminus ipse arguit, omnis nota videtur,aut cadit in sensus. At τὸ καθόλου universale non cadit sub sensus; neque ulla forma interior, qualis Christianitas est,videri potest. Sin formam externam intelligit, cum decima & sequentibus convenit, de quibus post. Posteriore sensu neutrum nomen, vel ullum etiam nomen Ecclesiæ essentiale, quia multi habent nomen quòd vivant, & mortui sunt, Apoc. III. 1. & πᾶν τὸ λεγόμενον omne dici est tum à συνθήκη impositione voluntaria; omnis autem impositio arbitraria & contingens est. At nec proprium Ecclesiæ hoc nomen est,quia etiam ab aliis, qui extra Ecclesiam degunt,& se ab ea scindunt,communiter usurpari potest. Nam & Lactantius Instit. IV. 4. affirmat; quosque hæreticorum cœtus se potissimum Christianos, & suam Ecclesiam Catholicam putare. De Donatistis & Arianis res manifesta est. Nostra quoque memoria à Pontificiis convitio Lutheranorum,Calvinistarum,hæreticorum proscilli, se Catholicos,se Christianos esse regesserunt. Denique nec inseparabile ab Ecclesia hoc nomen, quia Ecclesia in V. & N. T. fuit,quando nec Catholicæ,nec Christianæ nomine venit. Tum nomen Catholicum Ecclesiæ impositum est ex consuetudine, ad significandum quid sit Ecclesia, non quæ sit. Nemo autem virum bonum dixit,quòd bonus vocatur, sed quòd est. Nam vir bonus rem in genere significat, non cui res illa conveniat,ostendit. Par ratio illorum nominum est. Et nomen Catholicæ Ecclesiæ in schismate sive justo, quo οἱ δόκιμοι manifesti per tyrannidem expulsi sunt, sive injusto, quo veri hæretici ab Ecclesia discesserunt, remansit, vel jure in schismate injusto, vel injuria in justo. Ita Israel mansit nomenclatura majoris partis, & Judæi, ceu major pars populi à vero Dei populo se separantes,abolita etiam politia,nomen Judæorum retinuerunt. Neque tamen hoc tempore Judæum nominari gloriosum est. Et nomen quidem Catholici non licuit Evangelicis initio usurpare,quia occupatum ab iis fuit,à quibus minimè debebat; & si nos illud usurpassemus, multitudine oppressi jacuissemus. Nam hæretici dicuntur,non qui reapse sunt,sed qui vulgò putantur; & Catholici, quorum authoritas & potentia summa est. Nomen ergo hoc partim usurpatione , partim admiratione omnis terræ Apoc. XIII. 3. obtinuit. Et Patres quidam olim Orthodoxos ab hæreticis nomine Catholici distinxerunt, propter doctrinam Catholicam, quam constanter retinuerunt, non quòd larva inani nominis illius se ab his discriminari putaverint. Alia quoque fuit Ecclesiæ Antichristi tempora præcedentis,alia sequentis ratio. Ante ejus tempora merito Ecclesia ab hæreticis veris, se ipsos temerè separantibus, divulsa, Catholicæ nomen sibi vendicavit. Sed post ea tempora sicut Antichristus Christi munus involavit, atque se vice Christi regnare mentitus est: ita elogia & titulos Ecclesiæ rapturivit,& vi,non pretio abstulit. Nunc qui Reformatam Ecclesiam dicit,dicit partem Catholicæ Ecclesiæ Reformationi studentem: qui Catholicam Romanam Papalem, significat partem multitudinis ejus,quæ olim vocabatur Ecclesia Catholica , reformationi obstrepentem & in errore suo obduratam. Hæc gloriatio non est bona, quia est gloriatio de fermento, 1. Cor. V. 6. Denique vim nominis Catholici pridem illi decoxerunt, qui Ecclesiam τοπικῶς localem cathedralem, cœtui particulari Romano καταχυ-ευούσῃ prædominanti alligarunt.
units.tr: LXXVII. Bellarmine has craftily joined the name Catholic Church with that of Christians, although these are distinct and are attributed to a subject in different ways. Moreover, this mark is ambiguous. For the sense is either that it is a mark of the Church that it is Catholic and Christian, as it is called, or that the name and appellation itself is a mark. In the first sense the claim is false, because, as Bellarmine himself argues, every mark is or falls under the senses. But τὸ καθόλου, the universal, does not fall under the senses, nor can any inner form, such as Christianity is, be seen. If he means the outward form, it agrees with the tenth and following marks, which we will discuss later. In the second sense neither name, nor any name at all, is essential to the Church, because many have a name that they are alive, and are dead, Rev. 3:1; and πᾶν τὸ λεγόμενον, everything that is said, is named by an agreement which is voluntary, and every imposition is arbitrary and contingent. Nor is this name proper to the Church, because it can be commonly used also by others who live outside the Church and separate themselves from it. For Lactantius, Institutes IV. 4., also affirms that the most of the heretical sects think that they are above all Christians, and that their own Church is Catholic. The case of the Donatists and Arians is clear. In our own memory too, the Papists, in reproach against the Lutherans, Calvinists and the scattered heretics, have answered that they are Catholics and Christians. Finally, this name is not inseparable from the Church, because the Church existed in the Old and New Testament without being called by the name Catholic or Christian. Then the name Catholic was imposed on the Church by custom, to signify what the Church is, not what it is like. Nobody has called a good man good because he is called so, but because he is so. For a good man signifies the thing in general; it does not show to whom that thing belongs. The case of these names is similar. The name Catholic Church remained both in the just schism, in which the approved, manifest were driven out by tyranny, and in the unjust schism, from which the true heretics departed from the Church; it remained rightly in the unjust schism, and wrongly in the just one. So Israel kept its name through the greater part of the nation, and the Jews, as the greater part of the people separating themselves from the true people of God, retained the name of Jews even after their polity was abolished. Yet it is not glorious to be called a Jew at this time. And the name Catholic was not lawful for the Evangelicals to use at the beginning, because it was occupied by those by whom it ought least to have been; and if we had used it, we would have lain oppressed by the multitude. For heretics are called not those who really are such, but those who are commonly thought to be; and Catholics are those whose authority and power are supreme. This name therefore obtained its place partly by usurpation and partly by the admiration of the whole earth, Rev. 13:3. And some of the Fathers of old distinguished the Orthodox from the heretics by the name Catholic, because of the Catholic doctrine which they constantly retained, not because they thought themselves to be distinguished from these by the empty mask of that name. The reasoning was also different for the times before and after the Antichrist. Before his time the Church, rightly torn away from the true heretics who rashly separated themselves, claimed the name Catholic for itself. But after that time, just as Antichrist stole Christ's office and falsely claimed to reign in the place of Christ, so he has seized the praises and titles of the Church, taking them by force, not by price. Now whoever says Reformed Church means the part of the Catholic Church that strives for reformation; whoever says Roman Papal Catholic Church means the part of that multitude which was once called the Catholic Church, which opposes reformation and is hardened in its error. This boasting is not good, because it is boasting in leaven, 1 Cor. 5:6. Finally, those who bound the Church, which is τοπικῶς, local and cathedral, to the particular Roman assembly that dominates καταχυ-ευούσῃ, have long since exhausted the force of the name Catholic for themselves.

units.la: LXXVIII. Antiquitas nec essentialis Ecclesiæ nota est, quia rerum quarumlibet duration aliquam existentiæ habentium accidens est ; nec propria, quia antiqua etiam antiqui Serpentis synagoga est , inde à Caino huc usque,propagata: antiquissimum post fœdus operum peccatum Regnum concupiscentiæ & error est: nec inseparabilis, quia Ecclesia vera & optima fuit, quando recens,non antiqua fuit ; & tum etiam vera & optima est, quando cum prima & recentissima se conformat; Et multæ Ecclesiæ ab Apostolis conditæ interciderunt, priusquàm mediocrem ætatem attigerunt. Nam doctrina salutaris illa est,quæ statim post peccatum edita Patres salvavit; in qua fundamentum fidei Ecclesiæ continetur. Cum hac doctrina variat οἰκονομία τῶν καιρῶν. In ultimis temporibus vera antiquitas est Apostolica: quæ nonnisi ex scriptis Apostolicis probatur. Quæ Ecclesia fundamentum in Paradiso positum,& Mosen ac Prophetas & Evangelium, ut principium credendi retinet in vero sensu,& eas tentationes subiit, quas Scriptura præprædixit, easque superavit, vera Ecclesia est. Est ergo antiquitas Ecclesiæ prærogativa, quia Deus & ejus verbum Sathanam & hujus verbum præcedit; at nota non est; tum quia oportet hanc notam prius cognosci in doctrina, quàm in Ecclesia: tum quia uniformitas doctrinæ infallibilis extra Scripturam in Ecclesia qualicunque per omnes ætates falsò supponitur: tum quia extra Scripturam illa difficilimè cognoscitur. Mutatio quidem omnis designari potest, nempe quæ fit in melius, sed non quæ fit in deterius. Nam mutationi in melius renituntur omnes, quia mundus veritatem odit, & ea patefacta tumultuatur. Mendacium furti instar veritatis est, & mendaces fures sunt, qui ubi caute agunt, obrepunt latenter: at ita tamen, ut deprehendi possint, non quidem ut, quod fures postulant, demonstretur, qua hora, quibus præsentibus, & quo loco furtum fecerint, sed ita tamen ut fures demonstrentur, eò quòd rem alienam pertinaciter detinent. Sic satis nobis est demonstrasse errorem, qui novus est, & à veritate devius, quocunque tempore cœperit: sicut contra veritas non potest non esse antiquissima, quia error à veritate deflexio est. Quod Ecclesiæ Papalis novitati demonstrandæ sufficiat.
units.tr: LXXVIII. Antiquity is neither an essential mark of the Church nor a proper one, nor is it inseparable. It is not essential, because the duration of any thing that has existence is merely an accident of its existence. It is not proper, because the ancient synagogue of the old Serpent has been propagated from Cain down to the present, and sin and the kingdom of concupiscence and error are the most ancient things after the covenant of works. Nor is it inseparable, because the Church was true and best when it was new rather than ancient, and it is still true and best whenever it conforms itself to the first and most recent age. Many churches founded by the Apostles perished before they reached middle age. The saving doctrine is the one published immediately after the fall, which saved the Fathers, and in it is contained the foundation of the Church's faith. The economy of the times [οἰκονομία τῶν καιρῶν] varies along with this doctrine. In the last times the true antiquity is Apostolic, and it is proved only from the Apostolic writings. The Church that holds the foundation laid in Paradise, and Moses, the Prophets and the Gospel as the principle of belief in their true sense, and that undergoes and overcomes the temptations which Scripture foretold, is the true Church. Antiquity is therefore a prerogative of the Church, since God and his Word precede Satan and his word; but it is not a mark, for several reasons: first, because this mark must be known in doctrine before it can be known in the Church; second, because an infallible uniformity of doctrine outside Scripture is falsely presupposed in the Church, in whatever condition it may be, through all ages; third, because outside Scripture antiquity is very hard to recognise. Change of any kind can indeed be pointed out, namely that which takes place for the better, but not that which takes place for the worse. For all men resist change for the better, because the world hates the truth and rages when it is revealed. Falsehood is like theft, and liars are thieves who, when they act cautiously, creep in unnoticed; yet they can be caught, not indeed by demonstrating what the thieves demand, namely at what hour, in whose presence and in what place they committed the theft, but by pointing them out as thieves because they stubbornly keep what belongs to another. So it is enough for us to have shown that the error which is new, and which has deviated from the truth, is such, whatever time it began; just as, on the contrary, the truth cannot but be most ancient, because error is a deflection from the truth. Let this suffice to demonstrate the novelty of the Papal Church.

units.la: LXXIX. Quæ antiquitatis, eadem Durationis perpetuæ Ecclesiæ ratio est, quia re ipsa ab antiquitate non differt.
units.tr: LXXIX. The reason for the perpetual duration of the Church is the same as the reason for its antiquity, since in fact it does not differ from antiquity.

units.la: Iisdem igitur rationibus conficitur, illam Ecclesiæ notam essentialem, propriam & inseparabilem non esse. Et Ecclesiæ quidem particulari uli: duratio perpetua promissa non est. Universæ verò illa tribuitur vel ratione fidei, ut ea Ecclesiæ natura sit, ut semper in ea fuerint, sint & futuri sint, qui verè in Deum credant, vel ratione doctrinæ, ut ea ratio sit doctrinæ, qua fides in hominum cordibus gignitur, ut semper tradita fuerit, tradatur, & tradenda sit. Utroque modo Ecclesiæ universæ duratio competit, sed neutro ejus nota est. Non priore, quia sic necesse foret scire, quinam verè credant, & in vera fide perseverent, quod solus Deus novit. Non posteriore, quia necesse erit scire, quæ doctrina ab initio mundi authoritatem obtinuerit, & ad finem usque mundi obtentura sit, quod sciri non potest, nisi duobus modis; puta vel ex historia, quæ, si verbum Dei excipias, nulla est, quæ hoc demonstrare possit; vel ex doctrina, atque ita prius doctrinam scire oportet. Et durare Ecclesiam alterutro, vel utroque modo, potiùs fide ex Dei promissione cognoscimus, quàm sensu percipimus. Est igitur Ecclesia æterna, quia est Regnum illud, quod æternum est, semper fuit, est, & erit, Dan. II. 44. Luc. I. 32. 33. sed non particularis quævis certæ sedi, vel successioni alligata, verum Catholica absolutè, cujus æternitas hæc prærogativa, non nota est. Denique Papalis Ecclesia, & diu post Ecclesiam veram esse cœpit, & ante Ecclesiam veram etiam in hoc mundo, nedum in altera vita, desinet.
units.tr: By the same reasons it follows that duration is not an essential, proper and inseparable mark of the Church. Perpetual duration is promised neither to a particular church, nor to any one of them. It is ascribed to the universal Church either on the ground of faith, so that it is the nature of the Church that those who truly believe in God have always been in it, are in it now, and will be in it in the future; or on the ground of doctrine, so that it is the character of doctrine, by which faith is begotten in human hearts, that it has always been handed down, is handed down, and is to be handed down. In either way perpetual duration belongs to the universal Church, but neither way is a mark of it. Not the former, because then it would be necessary to know who truly believe and persevere in true faith, which God alone knows. Not the latter, because it would be necessary to know which doctrine from the beginning of the world has held authority and is to hold it until the end of the world; and this cannot be known except in two ways: either from history, which, if you except the Word of God, is none that can show this; or from doctrine, and so one must first know the doctrine. We know by faith, from God's promise, rather than perceive by sense, that the Church endures in one way or the other, or in both. The Church is therefore eternal, because it is that kingdom which is eternal, has always been, is, and will be (Dan. 2:44; Luke 1:32, 33); but not any particular church bound to a certain see or succession, rather the Catholic Church absolutely, whose eternity is this prerogative and is not a known mark. Finally, the Papal Church both began to be the true Church long after, and will cease to be the true Church in this world, not to mention the next life, before the true Church does.

units.la: LXXX. Amplitudo seu Multitudo credentium non est nota Ecclesiæ vel essentialis, quia Ecclesia cum impiorum multitudine comparata est pusillus grex, Luc. XII. 32. cœtus paucorum electorum, cùm multi vocati sint, Matth. XXII, 14. paucorum angustam illam viam, qua Cœlum aditur, ingredientium, ibid. VII. 13.
units.tr: LXXX. The amplitude or multitude of believers is not an essential mark of the Church, because compared with the mass of the wicked the Church is a little flock (Luke 12:32), a company of few chosen, since many are called (Matt. 22:14), and those few enter by the narrow way by which heaven is reached (ibid. VII. 13).

units.la: Plane sicut numerus stultorum, malorum & ignavorum major multùm est numero sapientum, bonorum & fortium virorum: nec propria, quia aliquando convenit errori, veluti cùm, uti olim Hieronymus questus est; ingemuit orbis, & se factum Arianum miratus est; & Antichristi Synagoga amplissima esse debuit, Apoc. XIII. XVII. 1. 15. & semper plures aperti & occulti infideles, Christo mentientes, & Templum Dei velut fumo quodam implentes & obnubilantes, ibid. XV. 8. quàm verè fideles fuerunt: nec inseparabilis, quia Ecclesia tempore Noæ, Abrahæ & Christi ampla certè non erat. Tribuitur quidem multitudo Ecclesiæ, ubi cum semetipsa comparatur. Nam multò amplior est in Novo, quàm in V. T. Licèt tamen gentium vocatio in magna multitudine suo tempore evidens testimonium veræ Ecclesiæ sit; quia Divinitus prædicta & impleta est, & complebitur adhuc; non tamen omni tempore major multitudo purioris conditionis præsumptionem habet. Et diversæ Ecclesiæ periodi sunt, juxta quas numerus credentium crescit, vel decrescit, & fideles manifestantur, vel occultantur. Nam modò persecutionem patitur, modò regnat, modò captiva, modò libera est, modò vincitur & succumbit, modò triumphat. Non ergo hæc veræ Ecclesiæ nota esse potest, quia Ecclesia interdum se ipsa major, interdum se ipsa minor esse potest. Si comparetur cum V. T. vel cum certis periodis N. T. multitudo ei tribuetur ex institutio Dei constituentis Ecclesiam nulli certo loco, cathedræ certæ amplius alligare, & modò numero florentiorem, modò contractiorem exhibere. Ac ne sic quidem nota erit Ecclesiæ, quia præcedere debet notitia doctrinæ & verbi Dei, sine quibus nec verè credentes, nec dispensatio temporum Ecclesiæ cognoscitur. Ideo Bellarminus ipse lib. IV. 7. hanc notam delet, sic scribens: Nota hæc non hoc requirit, ut hoc fiat simul, ita ut uno tempore, in omnibus provinciis necessariò esse oporteat aliquos fideles. Satis enim est, si fiat successivè. Ex quo id sequitur, quòd si sola una provincia retineret veram fidem, adhuc proprie & verè diceretur Ecclesia Catholica, dummodo clarè ostenderetur, eam esse unam & eandem cum Ecclesia illa, quæ fuit aliquo tempore, vel diversis in toto mundo. Neque minùs notanda illa Bannes in 2. q. 1. a. 10. p. 109. verba sunt: Universalitas Ecclesiæ potest considerari dupliciter, ratione materiæ, quæ sunt fideles, ex quibus congregatur: & ratione formæ, scilicet fidei. Ratione materiæ est Catholica, non quia actu extenditur ad omnes angulos terræ, sed quia nullam excludit, omnes indifferenter vocat, & omnes suis præceptis, quæ Dei sunt, obligat, & fortasse, quia successivè se ad omnes nationes extendit. Ratione formæ, vel fidei universalis est, quia fides ad omnia se extendit. Ordinat homines quoad omnes suos actus interiores & exteriores, remedium proponit contra omne genus peccatorum, & purificat totum hominem. Quæ posterior etiam rationis hujus explicatio, argutior quàm solidior licet, ostendit, posse Ecclesiam quamvis particularem vocari Catholicam, quamvis una parœcia contineatur, dummodo fidem illam profiteatur, quæ ab Apostolis per totum fere mundum prædicata fuit. Non igitur obstat, quod Apostoli & Prophetæ prædixerunt, Evangelium per totum terrarum orbem diffundendum esse. Nam & diffusum est, non obstante Antichristo, & fuerunt 140000. signati ex omni mundo. Sed id non obstat, quo minus maximus numerus hypocritarum, & in multis doctrinæ capitibus errantium esset. Nam sic Ecclesia diffundi debuit, ut etiam seductio & apostasia invalescere debuerit. Quando ex prædictionibus Divinis argumenta petuntur, omnes de eodem subjecto prædictiones conjungendæ, non divellendæ sunt, uti Judæi divellunt, qui sic prædictiones de Christi Regno & vita æterna observant, ut eas, quæ de ejus humilitate & morte agunt, non agnoscant; & easdem de felicitate Israelis & Hierosolymæ & Templi illustratione decantantes, conjunctas illis de carnalis Israelis rejectione, & Templi desolatione negligant. Denique nec Adversarii amplitudinem illam credentium jure sibi vendicare prius possunt, quàm veram suorum fidem & doctrinam ex verbo Dei demonstraverint, qua non demonstrata non tantùm non ampla eorum Ecclesia, sed nulla est, quocunque demum fumo se venditet. Cùmque multitudo credentium unionem habere cum capite Christo & inter se debeat; illorum cum peregrino capite conjunctorum & dominantis, ac servientium, velut in terrestri Monarchia, multitudo, non Ecclesiæ vera multitudo sed Antichristiana turba & conspiratio est.
units.tr: Plainly, as the number of fools, wicked and lazy people is far greater than the number of wise, good and brave men, so it is not a proper mark, because sometimes it agrees with error. Thus, as Jerome once lamented, "the world groaned and marvelled that it had become Arian"; and the synagogue of Antichrist must have been very large (Rev. 13; 17:1, 15). There have always been more open and hidden unbelievers, lying to Christ and filling and clouding the temple of God as with a certain smoke (ibid. 15:8), than there were truly faithful. Nor is it an inseparable mark, because the Church in the time of Noah, Abraham and Christ was certainly not large. Multitude is indeed attributed to the Church when it is compared with itself, for it is much greater in the New Testament than in the Old. Yet although the calling of the Gentiles in great numbers is in its time clear testimony to the true Church, since it was foretold and fulfilled by God and will yet be fulfilled, still a greater multitude does not always carry a presumption of a purer condition. There are different periods of the Church, according to which the number of believers increases or decreases, and the faithful are made manifest or hidden. For now it suffers persecution, now it reigns; now it is captive, now free; now it is conquered and succumbs, now it triumphs. Therefore this cannot be a mark of the true Church, because the Church can at one time be greater than itself and at another time less than itself. If it is compared with the Old Testament or with certain periods of the New, a multitude will be ascribed to it according to the institution of God, who established the Church not to be bound to any fixed place or certain see, and who now presents it flourishing in number, now more contracted. Nor even so will it be a mark of the Church, because knowledge of the doctrine and Word of God must come first, without which neither true believers nor the dispensation of the times of the Church is known. Therefore Bellarmine himself, in Book IV, chapter 7, deletes this mark, writing thus: This mark does not require that it happen at the same time, so that at one time there must necessarily be some faithful in all provinces. For it is enough if it happens successively. From which it follows that if only one province retained the true faith, it would still properly and truly be called the Catholic Church, provided it were clearly shown to be one and the same with that Church which existed at some time, or in various places throughout the whole world. Nor are the words of Bañez (on 2 q. 1 a. 10, p. 109) less worth noting: The universality of the Church can be considered in two ways, by reason of matter, which are the faithful from whom it is gathered, and by reason of form, namely faith. By reason of matter it is Catholic, not because it actually extends to every corner of the earth, but because it excludes no one, calls all indifferently, and binds all by its precepts, which are God's, and perhaps because it extends successively to all nations. By reason of form, or of faith, it is universal, because faith extends itself to all things. It orders men in regard to all their interior and exterior acts, offers a remedy against every kind of sin, and purifies the whole man. This latter explanation of the reason, though more subtle than solid, shows that a church, however particular, can be called Catholic even if it is contained in one parish, provided it professes that faith which was preached by the Apostles through nearly the whole world. Therefore it is no obstacle that the Apostles and Prophets foretold that the Gospel would be spread throughout the whole circle of the earth. For it has been spread, despite Antichrist, and 144,000 were sealed from every part of the world. But this does not prevent the largest number of hypocrites, and of those erring in many points of doctrine, from being there. For the Church had to spread in such a way that seduction and apostasy would also grow strong. When arguments are drawn from divine predictions, all predictions about the same subject must be joined together, not separated, as the Jews separate them. They observe the predictions about Christ's kingdom and eternal life, but do not acknowledge those that speak of his humility and death; and while singing the predictions about Israel's happiness and the glory of Jerusalem and the Temple, they neglect those joined with them about the rejection of carnal Israel and the desolation of the Temple. Finally, the Adversaries cannot rightly claim that amplitude of believers for themselves before they have demonstrated from the Word of God the true faith and doctrine of their own. Without that demonstration their Church is not only not ample, it is nothing, whatever smoke it puffs itself up with. And since the multitude of believers ought to be united with Christ the head and with one another, the multitude of those joined to an alien head, and ruled and serving it as in an earthly monarchy, is not the true multitude of the Church but an Antichristian crowd and conspiracy.

units.la: LXXXI. Sed inprimis illi Successionem Episcoporum ab Apostolis usque sine ulla interruptione in hunc usque diem in Ecclesia Romana continuatam, ceu victricem quandam Ecclesiæ notam, sine fine & modo jactant, dicentes cum principibus illis Ægyptiis ad Pharaonem suum. Ego sum filius sapientum, בן מלך קדם ô fili regum priscorum, Esaj. XIX. 11. Cæterùm nec essentialis, nec propria, nec inseparabilis hæc Ecclesiæ veræ nota est. Non essentialis, quia successio Episcoporum localis & personalis merè contingens, & præter Ecclesiæ naturam est, nisi in unitate sanæ doctrinæ & veræ fidei fundetur. Nam Episcopi veri à Pseudo-Episcopo distincti forma veræ fidei & doctrinæ professio, atque humilis ejusdem prædicatio est. Neque jus vel fas est Ave dicere iis, qui non afferunt, quod ab initio audivimus, 2. Johann. 10. Prius ergo doctrina fidei & veritas probanda est, quàm de successione doctorum judicari quicquam possit. At ipsum Dei verbum tantum abest, ut ad Ecclesiæ veritatem Episcoporum successionem localem & personalem requirat, ut eam potiùs ab Ecclesia removeat; quia Ecclesiam non uni loco vel cathedræ affixam, sed ambulatoriam facit. Talis ergo ipsa quoque successio esse debet. At nec propria est, quia etiam Annas & Cajaphas Aaroni in cathedra Mosis successerunt, Christo verò & Apostolis in eadem sede haud interrupta serie nulli successerunt. Sed & in Ecclesia Constantinopolitana, Antiochena, Alexandrina, Anglicana, quas ipsi pro veris Ecclesiis non habent, Episcoporum successio est. Sed Episcopos illos non colere communionem cum Ecclesia Romana causantur. Ergo sola successio non est Ecclesiæ nota. Imò verò, quod gravissimum est, priùs sciri oportet, quòd communio cum Ecclesia Romana requiratur. Sed requiri communionem cum Romana, præter Romanos, quorum auctoritas in dubium vocatur, omnes hodie Christiani inficiantur. Denique nec inseparabilis illa nota est, quia in primordiis Ecclesiarum nascentium successioni non fuit locus, & in fine eorum cum ipsis, integra manente Ecclesia Catholica, deficit. Supponit præterea nota hæc id, quod absurditatis omnes numeros implet, nimirum, in quavis successione manere statum eum, qui erat tempore illius, qui in successione illa primus fuit, quasi nulla rerum humanarum conversio locum habere, & non Episcopi fieri hæretici, atque aures plebis puriores, quàm lingua Sacerdotis fieri pollint. Annon verò sicut super Ægyptum quandam novus Rex exortus est, qui Josephum non noverat, & callidè populum Dei circumvenien dum esse statuerat, ne augesceret: ita in Ecclesia exoriri Pharaones mystici, qui Christum & Apostolorum doctrinam non nõssent, & populum Dei callidè circumventum summum in discrimen adducerent, potuerunt? Patres quidem argumento à successione petito adversus hæreticos usos esse, nulli dissimulamus. Cæterùm illi non de sola personarum successione, sed de perpetua ejusdem doctrinæ & fidei quasi per manus succedentium sibi Episcoporum traditione loquuntur, aliàs ne audiendi quidem. Primi argumento eo Irenæus & Tertullianus adversus hæreticos: Optatus & Augustinus adversus Manichæos & Donatistas usi sunt. Erat illud tempus ab ævo Apostolorum minùs remotum, sanctius, doctrinæ Apostolicæ observantius, neque usque adeò magnis & variis mutationibus obnoxium, quales prævalente tandem summa Episcoporum insciitia & improbitate, longus seculorum ordo inducere potuit, & verè induxit. Sed ex tripode Ambrosius de Pœnit. lib. I. 6. dixit: Non habet Petri hæreditatem, qui non habet Petri fidem. Et juxta illud Nazianzeni Orat. in Anthasium: Τὸ ὁμόγνωμον ἢ ὁμόδοξον· Τὸ δὲ ἀντίδοξον καὶ ἀντίδοξον: Qui eandem fidem profitetur, ejusdem throni particeps est: qui contrariam fidem amplectitur, adversarius quoque in throno censeri debet. Successio fidei vera successio est. Nisi quis forte itaque successorem dicat, quemadmodum mortem sanitati, tempestatem tranquillitati, dementiam prudentiæ succedere dicimus. Et de Petri cathedra Bernhardus Epist. 125. Bestia illa de Apocalypsi, cui datum os loquens blasphemias, & bellum gerere cum Sanctis, Petri cathedram occupat, tanquam leo paratus ad prædam. Personalem verò & externam successionem iidem secundario tantùm allegant, & iis opponunt, qui sua commenta pro Apostolicis institutis per successionem acceptis venditabant, sed à doctrinali minimè aveliebant. Præscribit ergo nota hæc novitatibus Papismi, à fide Christi & Apostolorum deficientis. Præterquam enim quòd successionis perpetuitas haud parum per Inter-Pontificia & schismata pertinacissima interrupta est, haud dubiè in Episcoporum succedentium censu computandi sunt, non qui nominetenus tales sunt, carnalibus statuis similes, sed qui verorum Episcoporum numeros implent, hoc est, qui, finitore Apostolo, potentes sunt exhortari in doctrina sana, & eos, qui contradicunt arguere: ἀντιλέγοντας. ἀνέγκλητοι inculpati, Tit.I.9. exemplaria gregis fidelium in sermone, conversatione, charitate, spiritu, fide & castitate, 1.Tim.IV.12. Non dominantes cleris, nec turpe lucrum affectantes, 1. Petr. V.2.3. legitimè vocati, non sumentes sibi honorem, sicut Aharon, Hebr. V.4. Hæccine verò in Episcopis Romanis continuata serie succedentibus quisquam, etiam addictissimus partibus, præstare ausit? Quando potentes exhortari in doctrina aliquot seculis vix denos; ad populum qui verba in æde sacra faceret, vix unum, & à quingentis annis sacrarum rerum peritos nullos, causidicos, mercatores, astutos Politicos, milites plerosque omnes reperias. Hæreticos nonnullos jam olim fuisse, constat: & in hæresin prolabi posse, ante Albertum Pighium Theologi Pontificii plerique omnes ingenuè fassi sunt. Quotusquisque verò exemplar fidelium in sermone, conversatione, castitate est? Quotusquisque talem se gerit, ut de eo veri nominis ἀποστολικῆς successio illa, quam S. Paulus in Timotheo commendat, prædicari possit: Σὺ δὲ παρηκολούθηκάς μοι τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ Tu verò assecutus es meam doctrinam, sectam vitæ, propositum, fidem, longanimitatem, charitatem, patientiam, persecutiones, &c. 2. Tim. III.10.11. Quotusquisque à dominio in cleros abstinet? Quotusquisque non per Simoniam intrat, non idololatriæ, tyrannidis, capitalium errorum author, patronus & defensor est? Talis ergo jactata illa successio est, qualis illa est, qua tyrannus Regi, lupus pastori, nox diei, morbus sanitati, mors vitæ succedere dicitur. Neque in urbe Romana perpetuus thronus veritatis, sed thronus Draconis à Bestia occupatus est, Apoc. II.13. XII.XIII.
units.tr: LXXXI. But above all they boast of the succession of bishops from the Apostles, continued without any interruption down to this day in the Roman Church, as a kind of conquering mark of the Church, without end or measure, saying with those Egyptian princes to their Pharaoh: I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings [בן מלך קדם, ben melek qedem], Isaiah 19:11. Yet this is neither an essential, nor a proper, nor an inseparable mark of the true Church. Not essential, because a succession of bishops that is merely local and personal, and happens by chance, lies outside the nature of the Church, unless it is founded on unity in sound doctrine and true faith. For the form of a true bishop, distinguished from a pseudo-bishop, is the profession of true faith and doctrine, and the humble preaching of the same. Nor is it lawful or right to say "Hail" to those who do not bring what we have heard from the beginning, 2 John 10. So doctrine and the truth of the faith must be tested first, before anything can be judged about the succession of teachers. But the Word of God itself is so far from requiring a local and personal succession of bishops for the truth of the Church that it rather removes it from the Church, because it makes the Church not fixed to one place or chair but wandering. Such, then, must the succession itself be. Nor is it proper, because Annas and Caiaphas also succeeded Aaron in the seat of Moses, whereas no one succeeded Christ and the Apostles in that same seat in an unbroken line. Yet there is also a succession of bishops in the Churches of Constantinople, Antioch, Alexandria and England, which they themselves do not count as true Churches. But they allege that those bishops do not keep communion with the Roman Church. So succession alone is not the mark of the Church. Indeed, and this is most serious, it must first be known that communion with the Roman Church is required. But that communion with the Roman Church is required, apart from the Romans themselves, whose authority is called into doubt, is denied by all Christians today. Lastly, this is not an inseparable mark, because in the beginnings of the Churches there was no place for succession, and at their end it fails, while the Catholic Church remains intact. Moreover, this mark presupposes something absurd in every respect, namely that in any succession the state of affairs remains what it was at the time of the first in that succession, as if no change in human affairs could take place, and bishops could not become heretics, and the ears of the people could not become purer than the tongue of the priest. Indeed, just as a new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph, and who decided to deal craftily with the people of God so that they would not increase, could not mystical Pharaohs likewise arise in the Church, who did not know Christ and the doctrine of the Apostles, and who could bring the people of God, craftily deceived, into the greatest peril? We do not deny that the Fathers used the argument drawn from succession against heretics. But they did not speak of succession of persons alone, but of the perpetual handing down of the same doctrine and faith, as it were by hand, from bishop to succeeding bishop; otherwise they would not even be worth hearing. Irenaeus and Tertullian were the first to use this argument against heretics; Optatus and Augustine used it against the Manichaeans and the Donatists. That time was less remote from the age of the Apostles, holier, more observant of apostolic doctrine, and not so exposed to great and varied changes as the long course of centuries could bring about, and did indeed bring about, once the great ignorance and wickedness of the bishops had at last prevailed. But Ambrose, from his tripod, said in On Repentance, book 1, chapter 6: He does not have the inheritance of Peter who does not have the faith of Peter. And in line with that saying of Nazianzen in his oration against Athanasius: [Τὸ ὁμόγνωμον ἢ ὁμόδοξον· Τὸ δὲ ἀντίδοξον καὶ ἀντίδοξον] He who professes the same faith is a sharer in the same throne; he who embraces a contrary faith ought also to be counted an adversary on the throne. The succession of faith is the true succession. Unless perhaps someone should say that one succeeds to another in the way that we say death succeeds health, a storm succeeds calm, madness succeeds prudence. And Bernard, concerning the chair of Peter, Epistle 125: That beast of the Apocalypse, to whom was given a mouth speaking blasphemies and making war with the saints, occupies the chair of Peter, like a lion ready for prey. But these same writers adduce personal and external succession only as a secondary matter, and set it against those who used to hawk their own inventions as apostolic institutions received by succession, while not separating them from doctrine. This mark therefore excludes the novelties of Papism, which has fallen away from the faith of Christ and the Apostles. For, apart from the fact that the perpetuity of the succession has been broken not a little by interpapal schisms and most obstinate divisions, those are without doubt to be counted among the successors who are not such merely by name, like carved statues, but who fill the number of true bishops, that is, who, as the Apostle prescribes, are able to exhort in sound doctrine, and to convict those who contradict [ἀντιλέγοντας], blameless [ἀνέγκλητοι], Titus 1:9; examples of the flock of the faithful in speech, conduct, love, spirit, faith and chastity, 1 Timothy 4:12; not lording it over the clergy, nor seeking shameful gain, 1 Peter 5:2-3; lawfully called, not taking honour to themselves, just as Aaron did, Hebrews 5:4. But who would dare to claim that these qualities are found in the Roman bishops succeeding one another in unbroken order, even if he were most devoted to their cause? When will you find the men who are able to exhort in doctrine in a few centuries, hardly ten; hardly one who would speak to the people in a sacred building; and, for five hundred years, no one skilled in sacred things, but lawyers, merchants, crafty politicians and almost all soldiers. That some heretics existed long ago is established; and that teachers can fall into heresy, almost all the Papist theologians have openly confessed, before Albert Pighius. But how few are an example of the faithful in speech, conduct and chastity? How few behave in such a way that that true apostolic succession, which St Paul commends in Timothy, could be claimed for them: [Σὺ δὲ παρηκολούθηκάς μοι τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ] But you have followed my doctrine, my manner of life, purpose, faith, patience, love, endurance, persecutions, etc., 2 Timothy 3:10-11. How few refrain from lordship over the clergy? How few do not enter by simony, and are not authors, patrons and defenders of idolatry, tyranny and mortal errors? Therefore that boasted succession is of the same kind as that by which a tyrant is said to succeed a king, a wolf a shepherd, night the day, sickness health, death life. Nor is there a perpetual throne of truth in the city of Rome, but the throne of the Dragon, occupied by the Beast, Revelation 2:13; 12-13.

units.la: LXXXII. Consensus in doctrina cum Ecclesia antiqua & Patribus post Apostolos
units.tr: LXXXII. Agreement in doctrine with the ancient Church and the Fathers after the Apostles

units.la: etiamsi Ecclesia illa, & Patres, præter, ne dicam, contra Scripturam aliquid statuerint, quæ revera mens Bellarmini est, multum à veris & genuinis Ecclesiæ notis dissidet. Nam nec essentialis est, quia Ecclesia tantum fundamento Prophetarum & Apostolorum superstruitur, Ephes.II.20. non fundamento seniorum, Matth.V.21.27. vel Patrum, Ezech.XX.18.19. nec propria, quia consensum illum etiam hæretici jactant, & saltem in quibusdam docere possunt, cum non eadem semper Ecclesiæ puritas & integritas fuerit: nec inseparabilis, quia Ecclesiæ Patriarchali primæ & Apostolicæ aptari nequit. Si tamen de Ecclesiæ veteris doctrina puriore, & verbo Dei consentanea, non quavis, notam intellexerint, jam doctrina illa ad verbi Dei amussim exigenda est, & nota illa ad veram Ecclesiæ notam, quæ conformatio doctrinæ cum verbo Dei est, revocanda fuerit. Sin Ecclesiæ veteris & Patrum dicta & doctrinam ἀκαταλήπτως receptam pro nota tali venditant, quid nota ea ignobilius esse potest? Nam fidem, quæ ex auditu verbi Dei est, hominum dictis & placitis subjicit, & post Deum & verbum ejus scortari facit. Et notam talem præcedere aliud debet, nempe ut teneamus, qui Patres fuerint, & quæ eorum doctrina fuerit. Quod & operosum est, & non aliis cognitu facile, quàm doctissimis, qui in Ecclesia pauci sunt. At cùm afferuntur notæ ad illustrandam rem ignotam, non ejusmodi afferendæ sunt,
units.tr: Even if that Church and the Fathers laid down something beyond Scripture, or, to say no more, against it (which is in fact Bellarmine's view), this mark still differs much from the true and genuine marks of the Church. For it is not essential, because the Church is built only on the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, Eph. 2.20, not on the foundation of the elders, Matt. 5.21, 27, or the Fathers, Ezek. 20.18, 19. Nor is it proper, because heretics also boast of this consent, and can teach at least some of the same things, since the Church has not always had the same purity and integrity. Nor is it inseparable, because it cannot be applied to the first and Apostolic Patriarchal Church. If, however, they understand by this mark not any consensus but the purer doctrine of the ancient Church, which agrees with the Word of God, then that doctrine must be measured by the rule of God's Word, and the mark must be referred back to the true mark of the Church, which is the conformity of doctrine with the Word of God. But if they peddle the sayings and the doctrine of the ancient Church and the Fathers as a mark, received ἀκαταλήπτως [without examination], what could be more base than such a mark? For it subjects faith, which comes from hearing the Word of God, to the sayings and opinions of men, and makes it play the harlot after God and his Word. Such a mark must also be preceded by another, namely that we know who the Fathers were and what their doctrine was. This is both laborious and not easily known to anyone except the most learned, of whom there are few in the Church. But when marks are brought forward to illustrate a thing that is unknown, they should not be of such a kind,

units.la: quæ nonnisi ab iis cognosci possunt, qui notis non indigent. Ac licet Ecclesiam antiquam veram Christi Ecclesiam fuisse ultro fateamur, tamen id non omnibus iis, quorum interest Ecclesiam veram cognoscere, æquè certum est; & nemini certum est, nullam omnino variationem in ulla doctrinæ parte in Ecclesiam tot seculis irrepsisse. Cæterum quàm aptè hæc nota Ecclesiæ Papali conveniat, clamant novitas Papatus, integris voluminibus demonstrata; calumniæ nostris aspersæ dilutæ, nec non ejus censuræ, & quos quotidie concinnat, Indices expurgatorii, quibus consensum suum cum Ecclesia prisca egregiè testatur, ut multa alia taceam.
units.tr: which can be known only by those who do not need marks. Although we freely confess that the ancient Church was the true Church of Christ, this is not equally certain to all those who have an interest in knowing the true Church; and no one can be certain that no variation at all in any part of doctrine crept into the Church over so many centuries. Moreover, how aptly this mark fits the Papal Church is shown by the novelty of the Papacy, demonstrated in whole volumes; by our calumnies refuted; by its censures; and by the Indexes of expurgation which it draws up every day, by which it so clearly attests its agreement with the ancient Church, not to mention many other things.

units.la: LXXXIII. Neque magis unio membrorum inter se & cum capite extra Scripturæ veritatem, & Christum, unicum Ecclesiæ caput, Ecclesiæ nota est.
units.tr: LXXXIII. Nor is the union of the members with one another and with the head, apart from the truth of Scripture and Christ the sole head of the Church, a mark of the Church either.

units.la: Nam nec essentialis Ecclesiæ est, quia Apostolus unitatem & firmamenta unitatis, recensens, Ephes.IV.4.5.6. Unum Dominum, Christum, ceu caput Ecclesiæ, non alium Dominum vel caput, quocum Ecclesia uniri possit, commemorat, neque Ecclesia aliud caput, cum quo uniri possit vel debeat, quàm Christum agnoscit, & unio Ecclesiæ propria spiritualis & mystica est, quæ in sensus incurrere non potest: nec propria, quia unio etiam inter hæreticos & impios esse potest; sicut revera commune attributum omnium eorum, quæ in se sunt indivisa, & ab aliis divisa, est: nec inseparabilis, quia inter Christianos Catholicos sæpe dissensio fuit, & esse potest, salva veritate, Actor. XI.2. XV.39. Phil.III.15.16. Cùmque unio Ecclesiæ, etiam vera cum capite Christo duplex sit, interna vel externa, neutra Ecclesiæ nota esse potest. Non interna, quia invisibilis est; Non externa, quia caput verum Ecclesiæ Christus, licèt aliquando in terra visibilis fuerit, & nunc in Cœlo visibilis sit, tamen unio, quæ Christum inter & Ecclesiam intercedit, in terris nunquam fuit visibilis, quamvis in Cœlis visibilis futura sit; externa verò communio membrorum Ecclesiæ inter se Ecclesiæ nota esse non potest, quia etiam profanis coetibus convenit, neque ob distantiam locorum, diversitatem & dissensionem Rerumpublicarum & Regnorum, quæ Ecclesiæ hospitia sunt, schismata, persecutiones, semper locum habet. Est quidem Ecclesia unum corpus, Ephes.IV.4.5. Unum ovile, Joh. X.16. Sed non ideo unitas seorsim sumpta Ecclesiæ nota est; & varii unitatis modi sunt, ex quibus sola verbi & vocationis, itémque Sacramentorum unitas Ecclesiæ nota est. Et Ecclesiæ quidem cum Christo, ut corporis cum capite, unionem agnoscimus: cum Papa verò non aliam, quàm qualis post Concilium Tridentinum inprimis, per nomen Bestiæ, & ejus χάραγμα est; & corporis cum struma & carcinomate, coactam insuper & servilem, qualis est miscellanei exercitus, militum variè animatorum sub uno duce & Imperatore, conjunctionem esse, asserimus. Non possunt aliter sentire, inquit Bellarminus, quia sensum suum sensui unius subjiciunt. Et qualis sit illa unio membrorum inter se, res ipsa loquitur. Canonistæ ab una parte, & Sorboniæ ab altera Jesuitas habent pro falsis Prophetis, circa ipsam auctoritatem Papæ. Dominicani eosdem propter ptet doctrinam de Gratia & libero arbitrio Semipelagianis annumerant. Becani & Bellarmini ipsius libri quidam Parisiis publicè damnati & combusti sunt. Neque Ecclesia illa, quæ ex Papa uno pendet (quamvis non raro Pontifices multi fuerunt) Ecclesiam facit unam, sed sub uno prout Regna varia sunt, sub uno Rege, uti Cajetanus in 2. 2. q. 39. a. 1. 9. observat. Talis unitas est, qualis vulpium Simsonis caudis colligatarum, & capitibus liberiùs grassantium, fuit; cum maxima quippe dissormitate religiosorum dogmatum, inprimis de potestate Papæ.
units.tr: For it is not essential to the Church, because the Apostle, in listing the unity and the supports of unity, Eph. 4.4, 5, 6, mentions one Lord, Christ, as the head of the Church, not another Lord or head with whom the Church could be united; nor does the Church acknowledge any head with whom it can or must be united other than Christ. The proper union of the Church is spiritual and mystical, and cannot fall under the senses. Nor is it proper, because union can also exist among heretics and the impious; indeed it is a common attribute of all things that are undivided in themselves and divided from others. Nor is it inseparable, because dissension has often arisen among Catholic Christians, and can arise, while the truth remains intact: Acts 11.2, 15.39; Phil. 3.15, 16. And since the union of the Church with Christ, its true head, is twofold, internal or external, neither can be a mark of the Church. Not the internal, because it is invisible. Not the external, because Christ is the true head of the Church, and although he was visible on earth once and is now visible in heaven, the union that lies between Christ and the Church has never been visible on earth, although it will be visible in heaven. The external communion of the members of the Church with one another cannot be a mark of the Church either, because it also belongs to profane assemblies; and it is not always present, since distance of places, the diversity and dissension of commonwealths and kingdoms (which are the lodgings of the Church), schisms and persecutions always intervene. The Church is indeed one body, Eph. 4.4, 5, one fold, John 10.16. But unity taken by itself is not for that reason a mark of the Church. There are various modes of unity, of which only the unity of the Word and of the calling, and likewise of the Sacraments, is a mark of the Church. We acknowledge the union of the Church with Christ as that of a body with its head; but with the Pope we assert there is no other union than such as, after the Council of Trent especially, is marked by the name of the Beast and its χάραγμα [mark]: a union of a body with a tumour and a cancer, moreover forced and servile, like that of a mixed army, of soldiers variously disposed, under one leader and one emperor. They cannot think otherwise, says Bellarmine, because they submit their own opinion to the opinion of one man. What such a union of members with one another is, the thing itself makes plain. Canonists on one side, and the Sorbonne on the other, hold the Jesuits to be false prophets concerning the very authority of the Pope. The Dominicans count the same men among the Semipelagians on account of their doctrine of grace and free will. Some books of Becanus and of Bellarmine himself were publicly condemned and burned at Paris. Nor does that Church, which depends on one Pope (although there have often been many Popes), make the Church one, but under one, as various kingdoms are under one king, as Cajetan observes in 2. 2. q. 39. a. 1. 9. Such a unity is like that of the foxes of Samson, tied together by their tails and running more freely with their heads, since there was the greatest dissimilarity of religious dogmas, especially concerning the power of the Pope.

units.la: LXXXIV. Quoad sanctitatem doctrinæ,
units.tr: LXXXIV. As to the sanctity of doctrine,

units.la: cùm ex revelatione Divina illa derivetur, & ex ea sola æstimari debeat, eatenus nota hæc à nostra non differt. Neque enim sanctitas doctrinæ, quæ est secundum pietatem, nisi perceptā doctrina, intelligi potest. Unde enim sanctitas doctrinæ colligatur, quàm ex consideratione omnium partium verbi Dei & dogmatum fidei? Unde ὁσιότης ἀληθείας sanctitas veritatis, seu doctrinæ veræ, appellatur, Ephes. IV. 24. quia voluntas sancta non delectatur nisi eo, quod verum est; neque verum est, quod ad sanctitatem non ducit. Non ergo hîc adversus nos, sed nobiscum adversus semetipsos pugnant, & quidem acerrimè. Si enim Sanctitas doctrinæ nota Ecclesiæ est, apud nos certè, non apud Pontificios ea est. Doctrina enim nostra hominem admonet suæ miseriæ, fastum humani ingenii dejicit, gratiam & misericordiam in Christo commendat, nihil homini, omnia Deo tribuit, ejus nominis gloriam unicè prædicat, homines ad veram pietatem hortatur; quæ nulla est, ubi hominum authoritas regnat, & homines se Deum sibi demereri putant; rectà homines ad Christum ducit, languentes consolatur, afflictos & jacentes erigit. Et ii ipsi, qui Sanctitatem doctrinæ notam Ecclesiæ faciunt, nullam sanctitatem requiri, ut quis Ecclesiæ & corporis Christi mysticì membrum sit; afferunt. Si tamen Sanctitatem doctrinæ cum Walemburgiis aliisque Sanctitatem vitæ, & opera regenerationis, per quæ doctrina ornatur, vel ipsam sanctitatis professionem interpretari lubet, Ecclesiæ nota non esse potest, quia nec essentialis est, cùm Ecclesia sancta proprie dicatur non ob sanctitatis professionem, sed ob sanctitatem Christi imputatam, & ex eadem derivatam inhærentem, quæ ipsa tamen utraque simulari ab hostibus Deo adulantibus potest; & posterior etiam imperfecta est, cùm optimi quique nævis maximis laborent, & in piis quandoque nihil præter innocentiam cernatur: nec propria, quia professio sanctitatis doctrinæ, & species sanctimoniæ in moribus etiam infidelibus & hæreticis communis est, & pro zelo pietatis aliquando superstitio se venditat, tantò pietate fervidior, quantò illa magis opus carnis, hæc spiritus est, illa prono impetu fertur, ut opera Indorum idololatrarum testantur; hæc luctam patitur; illa se superbè jactat; hæc humiliter cum Deo ambulat: nec inseparabilis, quia tandem evanescit, quando Christus detrahere larvam Ecclesiæ, ejúsque hypocrisin revelare & damnare decrevit. Denique sanctitas externæ professionis, qualis in Papatu laudatur, resolvitur
units.tr: Since that doctrine is derived from divine revelation and must be judged by that revelation alone, this mark does not differ from ours in that respect. Indeed, the sanctity of doctrine, which is according to godliness, cannot be understood unless the doctrine has been perceived. For where else is the sanctity of doctrine gathered from, if not from the consideration of all parts of the Word of God and of the articles of faith? Hence it is called ὁσιότης ἀληθείας [holiness of truth], that is, the holiness of truth or of sound doctrine, Eph. 4:24, because a holy will takes delight only in what is true; and that is not true which does not lead to holiness. So these men do not fight against us here, but with us, and against themselves, and very fiercely. For if the sanctity of doctrine is a mark of the Church, then certainly it is so among us, but not among the Papists. Our doctrine reminds a man of his misery, casts down the pride of human wit, commends grace and mercy in Christ, ascribes nothing to man but everything to God, preaches the glory of his name alone, and exhorts men to true godliness. That godliness is nowhere to be found where the authority of men reigns and men think they can earn God's favour for themselves. Our doctrine leads men straight to Christ, comforts the faint, and raises up the afflicted and the fallen. And those who make the sanctity of doctrine a mark of the Church also assert that no sanctity is required for someone to be a member of the Church and of the mystical body of Christ. Yet if they wish to interpret the sanctity of doctrine, with Walenburg and others, as the sanctity of life and the works of regeneration by which doctrine is adorned, or even the profession of sanctity itself, it cannot be a mark of the Church. It is not essential, since the Church is properly called holy not because of a profession of sanctity but because of the sanctity of Christ imputed and the inherent sanctity derived from it; and both of these can be feigned by enemies who flatter God. The latter is also imperfect, since the best of men labour under very great blemishes, and in the godly sometimes nothing but innocence can be seen. Nor is it proper, since a profession of sanctity of doctrine and an appearance of holiness in conduct are common even to unbelievers and heretics, and under the pretext of zeal for piety superstition sometimes puts itself on sale, all the more fervent in piety the more it is a work of the flesh rather than of the spirit. The former is carried along with headlong impetus, as the works of the idolatrous Indians bear witness; the latter struggles; the former boasts proudly, the latter walks humbly with God. Nor is it inseparable, since it finally vanishes when Christ has decided to tear away the mask of the Church and to reveal and condemn its hypocrisy. Finally, the sanctity of external profession, such as is praised in Papacy, is reduced

units.la: juxta Bellarminum in nihil, docere absurdum & contra rationem, quasi vel ratio, non verbum Dei rationem sanans, sit principium fidei, vel rationi consentaneum sit, credere & obedire Prælatis, sine ratione loquentibus, ut taceam innumeras Papatus absurditates ἀλόγως. Præterea superstitiosa & hypocritica tota est. Nam ταπεινοφροσύνη humilitas quædam, θρησκεία 'Αγγέλων cultus Angelorum & beatorum spirituum, ἀφεσία ἐ(ωμα)τ vexatio proprii corporis, ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων præcepta hominum, ἐθελοθρησκεία electitii cultus, non sunt boni commatis, nec in bona conscientia fieri, Col. II. 23. nedum pro fructibus pietatis venditari possunt. Inprimis bonum ostentatio corrumpit; velut eleemosynas, preces, jejunia, Matth. VI. 3. 5. 7. 16. ut spes sit, apud Reformatos meliùs erogari, orari, jejunari in occulto, quàm apud Pontificios in propatulo. Neque vel vota, vel status perfectionis, vel erogationes, vel regulæ ordinum & fraternitatum, vel confessiones, vel Sanctorum cultus, vel peregrinationes, & similia, quorum exercitio sanctitas eorum intumescit, & quæ à bonis æquè atque à malis præstantur, ac ne quidem bona, sed verbo Dei damnata sunt, veram solidámque pietatem redolere possunt. Inprimis Theologia casuistica & moralis Jesuitarum hodierna, quavis disciplina Cynica deterior, cujusmodi in Papatu Sanctitas, vel Sanctitatis professio regnet, demonstrat.
units.tr: by Bellarmine to nothing: to teach what is absurd and contrary to reason, as if reason, not the Word of God healing reason, were the principle of faith, or as if it were consonant with reason to believe and obey prelates who speak without reason, not to mention the countless absurdities of Papacy, ἀλόγως [unreasonably]. Moreover, the whole of it is superstitious and hypocritical. For ταπεινοφροσύνη [humility] of a sort, θρησκεία 'Αγγέλων [worship of angels], the worship of angels and blessed spirits, ἀφεσία ἐ(ωμα)τ [severe treatment of the body], the mistreatment of one's own body, ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων [commandments of men], the precepts of men, ἐθελοθρησκεία [self-chosen worship], the worship of one's own choosing, are not of good report, nor are they done in a good conscience, Col. 2:23, much less can they be put on sale as fruits of godliness. Above all, ostentation corrupts a good work, as with alms, prayers and fasts, Matt. 6:3, 5, 7, 16. So there is hope that among the Reformed alms are given, prayers are offered and fasts are kept more properly in secret than among the Papists in public. Nor can vows, states of perfection, works of supererogation, the rules of orders and brotherhoods, confessions, the cult of the saints, pilgrimages, and the like, whose practice makes their doers swell with pride, and which are performed alike by good and bad men, and indeed are not good but condemned by the Word of God, give off the scent of true and solid piety. Above all, the present-day casuistical and moral theology of the Jesuits shows what sanctity, or the profession of sanctity, reigns in Papacy, a discipline worse than any Cynic one.

units.la: LXXXV. Haud certior Ecclesiæ nota Efficacia doctrinæ est. Nam illa vel à doctrina ita sejungitur, ut vera ea doctrina dicatur, quæ efficax est; vel cum ea conjungitur. Neutro modo nota hæc Ecclesiæ immediatè convenit, sed interveniente doctrina, de qua priùs constare debet. Neque enim efficacia à doctrina sejuncta Ecclesiæ nota esse potest, quia propter ingenii humani perversitatem, mendacium subinde veritate efficacius est.
