Deus enim ἐνέργειαν πλάνης efficaciam erroris non raro immittit hominibus, ut credant mendacio, 2. Thess. II. 9. Mali homines proficient in pejus, decipientes & decepti, 2. Tim. III. 13. Efficacia verò doctrinæ veræ juncta, convenit Ecclesiæ, sed non ut ejus nota; tum quia id Ecclesiæ nec essentiale est, quia non Ecclesiæ, sed Dei in ea opus est, cooperantis & sermonem confirmantis, Marc. XVI. 16. nec pro prium est, quia etiam falsam doctrinam efficacia quadam pollere jam diximus; & Babylon vino concupiscentiæ & fornicationis suæ omnes gentes potare, & propterea cum ea Reges terræ fornicari debuerunt, Apoc. XVIII. 3. nec denique inseparabile, quia Deus nec semper, nec ubique, nec æquali gradu efficaciæ verbo Evangelii cooperatur, sed quando, ubi & quantum ei placet, Matth. XI. 26. 27. XIII. 11. Ideo testes duo quandoque etiam à Bestia vinci, & eorum cadavera in foro civitatis magnæ jacere debuerunt, quando verbum Dei per falsas interpretationes velut interfectum est; donec post dies tres & dimidium spiritus vitæ ex Deo iterum super ipsos intravit, & in pedes suos illi constiterunt, ibid. XI. 7–12. Et interdum pauci, interdum multi Evangelio credunt. Nam humana quidem, seu ingenio humano accommodata, cujusmodi sunt cultus superstitiosi in rebus externis positi, nec non præcepta vitæ degendæ, quæ Sanctitas doctrinæ. Efficacia doctrinæ. quæ caro facilè præstare potest, itèm ratio satisfaciendi Deo facilis, hominibus placent. Sed doctrina, quæ ab humano ingenio abhorret, quæ patientiam sub cruce suadet, & hominem à peccato ad veram pietatem, quæ interna est, revocat, apud malos efficaciam suam, nisi quando supereminens magnitudo illa potentiæ Dei, Eph. I. 19. accedit, non exerit. Licèt ergo verbum Dei sit λόγος ἐνεργὴς sermo efficax, Hebr. IV. 12. tamen non semper efficaciam suam exerit; & quando exerit, non per se efficacia doctrinæ, sed ipsa doctrina verbi, comitem habens efficaciam Ecclesiæ nota est. Nam efficacia, seu suada Spiritus Dei ab efficacia erroris sæpe discerni non potest, nisi per veritatem doctrinæ. Denique pontificiæ doctrinæ, quà talis, efficacia omnis, non in Spiritus, sed in carnificis gladio; non in fidei persuasione, sed in fidelium persecutione posita: nec doctores ejus animas Christo lucrifacere, sed opes, corpora & animas Pontifici suo mancipare & mactare satagunt.
units.tr: LXXXV. The mark of the efficacy of doctrine is no more certain. For this either is separated from doctrine, so that the doctrine that is efficacious is called true, or it is joined to doctrine. In neither way does this mark belong to the Church immediately, but only through the intervening doctrine, whose truth must first be established. For efficacy separated from doctrine cannot be a mark of the Church, because on account of the perversity of the human mind a lie is sometimes more efficacious than the truth. For God often sends upon men ἐνέργειαν πλάνης [the working of error], the efficacy of error, so that they believe the lie, 2 Thess. 2:9. Evil men will proceed from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived, 2 Tim. 3:13. But efficacy joined to true doctrine belongs to the Church, yet not as its mark; first because this is not essential to the Church, since it is God's work in it, cooperating and confirming the word, Mark 16:16; nor is it proper, since we have already said that even false doctrine is powerful with a certain efficacy; and Babylon makes all nations drink of the wine of her lust and fornication, and therefore the kings of the earth were bound to commit fornication with her, Rev. 18:3. Finally, it is not inseparable, since God does not cooperate with the word of the gospel always, everywhere, or to an equal degree of efficacy, but when, where and as much as it pleases him, Matt. 11:26, 27; 13:11. So two witnesses were at times conquered by the Beast, and their corpses were bound to lie in the street of the great city, when the Word of God was as it were killed by false interpretations; until after three days and a half the spirit of life from God entered into them again, and they stood upon their feet, ibid. 11:7–12. And at times few, at times many believe the gospel. For human things, or things suited to the human mind, such as superstitious worship consisting in external matters, and also precepts for living, which are the sanctity of doctrine, please men. The efficacy of doctrine, which the flesh can easily supply, and the way of satisfying God that is easy, please men. But doctrine that shrinks from human wit, that urges patience under the cross, and that calls a man back from sin to true piety, which is inward, does not exert its efficacy among the wicked, unless that surpassing greatness of the power of God, Eph. 1:19, comes upon them. Therefore, although the word of God is λόγος ἐνεργὴς [a living word], an efficacious word, Heb. 4:12, nevertheless it does not always exert its efficacy; and when it does exert it, the efficacy is a mark of the Church not in itself, as efficacy of doctrine, but because the doctrine of the word, having efficacy as its companion, is the mark. For the efficacy, or the persuasive power, of the Spirit of God can often not be distinguished from the efficacy of error except by the truth of the doctrine. Finally, all the efficacy of Papist doctrine, as such, lies not in the sword of the Spirit but in the executioner's sword, not in the persuasion of faith but in the persecution of the faithful. Nor do its teachers strive to win souls for Christ, but to hand over and slaughter wealth, bodies and souls to their Pontiff.

units.la: LXXXVI. Jam & Sanctitas vitæ auctorum & Patrum religionis, cujusmodi scilicet Pontifices Romani, & ab iis creati per aureaam Canonizationis scalam Sanctuli, Benedictus, Franciscus, Dominicus, Lojola, fallax inprimis Ecclesiæ nota est.
units.tr: LXXXVI. Now also the sanctity of life of the authors and fathers of religion, namely the Roman Pontiffs and those whom they created Saints by the golden ladder of canonization, such as Benedict, Francis, Dominic, Loyola, is above all a deceptive mark of the Church.

units.la: Non enim vel essentialis est; quia Ecclesia Catholica non soli Episcopi, Præsules & ordinum Monachalium authores sunt; & vera sanctitas vitæ ex solo Dei verbo cognoscitur, atque simulari etiam externis factis potest; quin & hæc non Ecclesiæ vel doctrinæ, sed personarum duntaxat, per hoc seculum transeuntium, dum Ecclesia ipsa permanet, est: vel propria, quia etiam Sathanas in angelum lucis se transfigurat, 2. Cor. XI. 14. quod solenne inprimis est hæreticis, ritus varios pro arbitrio, sive per ἐθελοθρησκείαν constitutos, ad speciem sanctimoniæ assumendam, observantibus; cùm interim vera sanctitas interna sit, nec in oculos incurrat; vel ab ea inseparabilis, quia absque ejusmodi Patribus diu Ecclesia stetit, floruitque, & stabit florebítque diu. Ad quos primitus verbum Dei factum est, illi, antequam vocarentur, aliis sanctiores non fuerunt, & postquam vocati sunt, peccarunt. Deus autem eos sanctificavit, castigavit, & iis condonavit. Qualis vero Pontificum & Sanctulorum ejusmodi sanctitas fuerit, scriptores vitarum Pontificum Romanorum, Legendæ & Vitæ Sanctorum testantur. Nam ne quidem illa ad Sanctitatem Pharisæorum assurgit.
units.tr: For it is not essential, since the Catholic Church is not made up only of bishops, prelates and the founders of monastic orders; and true sanctity of life is known from the Word of God alone, and can be counterfeited even by external deeds. Indeed, this sanctity belongs not to the Church or to doctrine but only to persons passing through this age, while the Church itself remains. Nor is it proper, since Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, 2 Cor. 11:14, which is especially customary for heretics, who adopt various rites established at their own pleasure, or by ἐθελοθρησκεία [self-chosen worship], to assume the appearance of holiness; whereas true sanctity is inward and does not come under the eyes. Nor is it inseparable from the Church, since the Church has stood and flourished for a long time without such Fathers, and will stand and flourish for a long time. Those to whom the Word of God was first given were no holier than others before they were called, and after they were called they sinned. But God sanctified them, chastised them, and forgave them. What sort of sanctity such Pontiffs and Saints had, the writers of the lives of the Roman Pontiffs, the legends and the lives of the Saints bear witness. For not even that sanctity rises to the level of the holiness of the Pharisees.

units.la: LXXXVII. At nec Miraculorum gloria veram Ecclesiam infallibiliter notat.
units.tr: LXXXVII. Yet neither does the glory of miracles infallibly mark the true Church.

units.la: Non enim illa Ecclesiæ essentialis est, quia miracula ex Ecclesiæ doctrina, non Ecclesiæ doctrina ex miraculis dijudicanda est; & extra ordinem, non ordinariè illa fiunt. Regula certè illa, quæ credere miracula facientibus, sive extra Scripturam loquantur, sive cum ea, non veritatis, sed apostasiæ regula est. Cui contraria illa à Mose præcipitur: Si frater tuus ediderit signum, atque id signum evenerit, & is dicat: Eamus, colamus Deos alienos (Bestiam & ejus imaginem) ne auscultes verbis illius Prophetæ. Nam Dominus Deus tuus te tentat, an diligatis Dominum Deum vestrum ex toto corde. Dominum Deum vestrum sequemini, ipsum metuetis, & voci ejus auscultabitis, & ei servietis, & ipsi affixi eritis, Deut. XIII. 1-4. Neque tantùm Moses, sed etiam Christus vetuit credere miracula facientibus, & præter illa, quæ ipse dixerat, factuns.
units.tr: For this glory is not essential to the Church, because miracles are to be judged by the Church's doctrine, not the Church's doctrine by miracles; and such works happen outside the ordinary course, not ordinarily. Surely the rule that one should believe those who work miracles, whether they speak outside Scripture or with it, is a rule not of truth but of apostasy. Moses gives the contrary command: If thy brother shall show a sign, and the sign come to pass, and he say, Let us go and serve other gods (the beast and its image), thou shalt not hearken to the words of that prophet. For the Lord thy God tempteth you, that he may know whether ye love the Lord your God with all your heart. Ye shall walk after the Lord your God, and fear him, and keep his commandments, and obey his voice, and ye shall serve him, and cleave unto him, Deut. XIII. 1-4. Nor did Moses alone forbid believing those who work miracles; Christ too forbade it, and foretold that such would come besides those things which he himself had said.

units.la: Pseudo-Christi & Pseudoprophetæ dabunt signa magna, & portenta, ut, si possibile sit, etiam electos seducant. Si igitur (ii ipsi) dixerint: Ecce in deserto est, ne exeatis: ecce in cubiculis, ne credatis, Matth. XXIV. 24. 26. Ipse Christus ea simul dixit & fecit, quæ de eo prædicta erant; nec solis miraculis fidem nostram niti voluit. Non ergo etiam miraculorum gloria Ecclesiæ propria est, quia etiam Pseudo-prophetæ & Pseudochristi ea faciunt: & Antichristus inprimis miraculis patrandis famosus esse debuit, utpote cujus adventus esse debuit secundum efficaciam Sathanæ, cum omni potentia & signis & prodigiis mendacibus, 2. Thess. II. 10. 11. & Bestia atque Pseudo-propheta facere ... signa magna debuit, Apoc. XIII. 13. Nam per tales etiam Deus miracula edere voluit, ad tentandos eos, qui veritatem diu manifestatam non diligunt. Miracula igitur, quæ in nomine Christi fiunt, si vera sunt, Christi & Christianæ Ecclesiæ sunt, & confirmant fidem in Scripturis traditam: & quæ fiunt in Ecclesia falsa, seu apud eos, qui extra Scripturam loquuntur, etiam sic confirmant veritatem dicti Christi, atque Regnum, & fidelibus luculentæ admonitiones sunt, ut attendant doctrinæ, quam audiunt, ne à veritate ad mendacium seducantur: Denique nec miraculorum patratio ab Ecclesia inseparabilis est. Fatetur enim Bellarminus, non semper necessarium esse ad Ecclesiæ existentiam, ut patrentur miracula, sed illa tantùm ad novam fidem, vel extraordinariam missionem requiri. Et sanè Ecclesia à multis Pseudo-prophetis, & Johanne Baptista collecta nullis miraculis claruit. Neque deficientibus miraculis Ecclesia defecit. Et novissimorum temporum miracula tantùm abest, ut veritatem Ecclesiæ illius, in qua eduntur, notent, ut eam potiùs suspectam quàm maximè reddant, quia Deus per illa justo judicio homines tentat, eò quòd veritatem pridem patefactam non dilexerunt, ut salvarentur, 2. Thess. II. 10. Ac ne Reformatio quidem doctrinæ miracula poscit, quia non doctrina formatur, sed vetus Christi & Apostolorum miraculis confirmata reducitur. Qui sic reformant, sine miraculis explorari possunt, quia non aliud ab iis requiritur, quàm ut rem suam ad verbum Dei, ceu amussim unicam, exigant. Nihil enim se facere profitentur, quod miraculum requirat. Quid enim æquius est, quàm ut audiatur Deus in Scriptura loquens ab iis, qui Deum verum agnoscunt, & in Scriptura loqui profitentur? Non possunt quidem vera miracula nisi Dei virtute edi. Sed non ideo doctrinæ veritas ex iis æstimari debet, quia inter verbum & miracula Divina mutua affectio est; ut sicut illud horum veritatem; ita hæc illius Divinitatem illustrent. Nemo talia signa, qualia tu facis, edere potest, nisi Deus cum ipso sit, Joh. III. 2. Hæc (signa) scripta sunt, ut credatis, quòd Jesus sit Christus, Filius Dei, ibid. XX. 31. Et Patrum ætate, Paganismo vigente, & inter Paganos Ecclesia habitante, miracula edita sunt, sed minùs clara, minùs nota, nec talia, ut cum Christi & Apostolorum miraculis comparari potuerint. Quæ crecredito & confirmato Evangelio, & fide principii ac fundamenti, necessaria amplius non sunt, quia nova sine fine signacula iisdem tabulis adhibenda, requirere nihil attinet. Denique qualia sint miracula, quibus Pontificii Ecclesiae suae veritatem demonstrare nituntur, alibi ostendimus. Spiritus Dei illa φαρμακιῶν incantationum, Apoc. IX.21. XVIII.23. & prodigiorum mendacii, 2. Thess. II.9.10. nomine perstringit. Si revera Monachi miracula faciunt, quare non ad nos accedunt, linguis loquuntur, de futuris vaticinantur, mortuos resuscitant, &c. ? Cur non ostendunt nobis in verbo Dei prima & consequentia ? Esaj. XLI. 21.22.23. Longè vero certiora & potentiora sunt Dei μεγαλεῖα magnalia, opera maxima & verè θαυμάσια mirabilia, quibus Deus Reformationi Ecclesiae institutae & propagatae evidenter cooperatus est, & cooperari non definit, de quibus in loco copiosissimè diximus.
units.tr: False Christs and false prophets shall arise, and shall shew great signs and wonders, insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect. Wherefore if they shall say unto you, Behold, he is in the desert; go not forth: behold, he is in the secret chambers; believe it not, Matth. XXIV. 24, 26. Christ himself spoke and did at the same time the things foretold about him, and he did not wish our faith to rest on miracles alone. Therefore the glory of miracles is not proper to the Church either, since false prophets and false Christs also perform them; and Antichrist above all ought to be famous for working miracles, since his coming was to be after the working of Satan, with all power and signs and lying wonders, 2 Thess. II. 9, 10; and the Beast and the false prophet were to do great signs, Rev. XIII. 13. For God too wished to work miracles through such people, to test those who do not love the truth that has long been made manifest. Miracles therefore that are wrought in the name of Christ, if they are true, belong to Christ and to the Christian Church, and they confirm the faith handed down in Scripture; and those that happen in a false Church, or among those who speak outside Scripture, likewise confirm the truth of Christ's saying and of his Kingdom, and they are plain warnings to the faithful to attend closely to the doctrine they hear, lest they be led from truth into falsehood. Finally, the working of miracles is not inseparable from the Church. Bellarmine concedes that miracles are not always necessary for the existence of the Church, but that they are required only for a new faith or an extraordinary mission. And indeed the Church, gathered by many false prophets and by John the Baptist, shone without any miracles; and when miracles failed, the Church did not fail. As for the miracles of the latest times, they are so far from marking the truth of the Church in which they occur that they rather make it highly suspect, because by them God, in just judgment, tempts men, since they did not love the truth revealed long before, that they might be saved (2 Thess. II. 10). Nor does the Reformation of doctrine demand miracles, for doctrine is not being newly devised; rather the old doctrine, confirmed by the miracles of Christ and the Apostles, is being brought back. Those who reform in this way can be tested without miracles, since nothing more is required of them than that they measure their cause by the Word of God, as by the one true rule. For they profess that they do nothing that would call for a miracle. For what is more fair than that God speaking in Scripture should be heard by those who acknowledge the true God and profess to speak from Scripture? True miracles can indeed be wrought only by the power of God; yet the truth of a doctrine is not to be judged by them merely because there is a mutual bond between the Word and divine miracles, so that, just as the Word vouches for their truth, so they illustrate its divinity. No one can do these signs that thou doest, except God be with him, John III. 2. These (signs) are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, ibid. XX. 31. In the time of the Fathers too, while paganism flourished and the Church dwelt among the pagans, miracles were wrought, but they were less clear, less known, and not such as could be compared with the miracles of Christ and the Apostles. Once the Gospel has been believed and confirmed, and the faith in the principle and foundation, such miracles are no longer necessary, since it is pointless to demand new seals without end to be applied to the same tablets. Finally, as to what sorts of miracles the Papists strive to use to demonstrate the truth of their Church, we have shown elsewhere. The Spirit of God brands them with the name of sorceries [φαρμακιῶν], Rev. IX. 21, XVIII. 23, and lying wonders, 2 Thess. II. 9, 10. If the monks really work miracles, why do they not come to us, speak in tongues, foretell the future, raise the dead, and so on? Why do they not show us the first things and the things that follow in the Word of God? Isaiah XLI. 21-23. Far more certain and mighty are God's great works [μεγαλεῖα], his greatest works and truly marvellous [θαυμάσια] deeds, by which God has evidently cooperated in the Reformation of the Church, and continues to cooperate, about which we have spoken at great length in the proper place.

units.la: LXXXVIII. Ejusdem ferè commatis & notae Lumen Propheticum est.
units.tr: LXXXVIII. Of nearly the same class and mark is the Prophetic Light.

units.la: Si enim Prophetia strictè sumatur pro dono praedictionis futurorum, species quaedam miraculi est, adeòque nec essentialis nota Ecclesiae, quia ad charismata miraculosa pertinet: nec propria, quia etiam daemonibus, Pseudoprophetis, & impostoribus tribuitur, Deut. XIII.2. Num. XXIII.7. XXIV.3. Joh. XI.51. & tam verus Propheta fuit Savanarola, ab adversariis combustus, quem hoc dono claruisse, Mirandula & Cominaeus testantur, quàm vel Malachias ille Hibernus, vel Martinus Stredonius, quem hoc nomine Jesuitae hodie celebrant, fuit: nec insepara-bilis, quia non semper in Ecclesia coruscat, sed ξῇ τῇ δοξῇ, sicut & quando videtur & placet Deo, qui abscondita revelat. Etiam in Israele Prophetae fuerunt, sed non ideo rectores Israelis illi, qui Prophetas occiderunt, vera Dei Ecclesia fuerunt. Sin latiùs pro intelligentia & interpretatione Scripturarum Propheticum lumen illi interpretantur, hoc illud habet, ut omnis prophetia dijudicari debeat, 1. Cor. XIV.29. neque aliunde quàm ex verbo Dei dijudicari possit. Unde res illa ad verbum Dei, ejusque sensus demonstrationem ex verbo Dei, redit.
units.tr: If Prophecy is taken strictly as the gift of foretelling future things, it is a kind of miracle, and so it is not an essential mark of the Church, since it belongs to miraculous charisms. Nor is it a proper mark, since it is also attributed to demons, false prophets and impostors (Deut. 13.2; Num. 23.7; 24.3; John 11.51). Savonarola was as true a prophet as the Irish Malachy, or Martin of Strido, whom the Jesuits celebrate today under that name, though Savonarola was burned by his adversaries; Mirandola and Commines bear witness that he was renowned for this gift. Nor is it inseparable, since it does not always shine forth in the Church, but comes and goes [ζῇ τῇ δόξῃ], as and when it seems good and pleasing to God, who reveals hidden things. There were prophets in Israel too, yet those rulers of Israel who killed the prophets were not therefore the true Church of God. But if the prophetic light is interpreted more broadly, as the power to understand and interpret the Scriptures, it has this consequence: every prophecy ought to be judged (1 Cor. 14.29), and it can be judged only by the Word of God and nothing else. So the matter comes back to the Word of God, and to the demonstration of its sense from the Word of God.

units.la: Si in Papa & Cardinalibus spiritus Propheticus est, quare hucusque in consiliis suis, quae ad opprimendam Ecclesiam susceperunt, decepti & confusi sunt, & laborarunt populi pro igne, & nationes pro nihilo fatigatae sunt ? Habac. II. 13.14. Quare non impediverunt, ne terra cognitione Dei impleretur ? Veraciùs certè Lutherus prophetavit, invitis illis verbum Dei staturum. Per Dei gratiam nos eum ex verbo Dei fructum percipimus, ut, fatentibus & furentibus adversariis, in omni afflictione spem habeamus, scientes, nihil haetenus in mundo accidisse, quin praedictum sit, & praedictum esse, fore, ut nunquam Ecclesia opprimatur, at hostes Ecclesiae confundantur. Ibi Prophetia est, ubi vera doctrina, & Prophetiae in bona conscientia applicatio est. At Papa Pseudo-Propheta est, quia sine authoritate loquitur. Quin ne Prophetiam quidem interpretari & ad nostra tempora deducere potest sine contorsione, quin se ipsum & Ecclesiam suam damnet. At in nostris Ecclesiis explicatio Prophetiae in substantialibus concors, Ecclesiae nostrae veritati miré suffragatur.
units.tr: If the prophetic spirit is in the Pope and the cardinals, why until now have they been deceived and confounded in the counsels they have undertaken for the suppression of the Church, and the peoples have labored for the fire, and the nations have wearied themselves for nothing? (Hab. 2.13-14). Why have they not prevented the earth from being filled with the knowledge of God? Luther prophesied more truly when he said that the Word of God would stand in spite of them. By the grace of God we receive this fruit from the Word of God: that, even while our adversaries rage and admit nothing, we may have hope in every affliction, knowing that nothing has so far happened in the world that was not foretold, and that it has been foretold that the Church will never be crushed while her enemies are confounded. Prophecy is where there is true doctrine and the application of prophecy with a good conscience. But the Pope is a false prophet, because he speaks without authority. Indeed he cannot even interpret the prophecy and bring it down to our times without distortion, without condemning himself and his Church. In our Churches, on the other hand, the interpretation of prophecy agrees in its substantial points and wonderfully supports the truth of our Church.

units.la: LXXXIX. Par fallacia est notae illius, pro qua Confessionem adversariorum venditant.
units.tr: LXXXIX. The fallacy of the next mark is equal, for which they vaunt the confession of adversaries.

units.la: Tanta enim, inquiunt, vis est veritatis, ut etiam ex invitis pectoribus erumpat, juxta illa populi Dei: Non est Deus noster, ut sunt dii illorum. Et inimici nostri sunt judices, Deut. XXXII. 31. Neque nullum vel contemnendum est testimonium ex sinu hostium petitum. Sed non quicquid aliquando Ecclesiae, provido singulariter Numine, accidit, Ecclesiae nota perpetua est. Confessio certè hostium veritatis neque Ecclesiae essentialis est, quia testimonium illud externum, & ab extraneis profectum, per se nullam vim habet, neque quicquam arguit, nisi aliunde de veritate constet: neque propria, quia Christiani pro candore Christiano, virtutem etiam in hostibus laudant, & gentilibus aequè atque haereticis haud inviti tribuunt, si quid doctrinae, virtutis, vel laudis habent: impii contra etsi tacitè apud se testimonium bonis perhibent, aegrè tamen odii & invidiae faci-bus praepediti, ab se impetrant, ut id palam profiteantur: neque inseparabilis, quia Christo, Matth. V.11. praedicente, saepius Ecclesiam convitiis proscindunt; quo in genere Jesuitae, ex calumniis & mendaciis toti consuti, primas obtinent. Et sic Ecclesia, quae adversarios strenuè mendaces, malignos, virulentos, maledicos, Diabolos habet, vera Ecclesia non erit. Etiam Bestiam laudarunt & adorarunt homines dicentes: Quis similis est Bestiae ? Quis belligerari cum ea potest ? Et adorabunt Bestiam habitantes super terram, quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitae, Apoc. XIII. 4.8. Sed fallit nimis judicium incolarum terrae de Bestia. Inimici vero Ecclesiae judices, juxta illud Deut. XXXII. 31. tum fiunt, cùm, hostili licèt animo praediti, vel certè Christo mentientes, ibid. XXXIII. 29. Psal. XVIII. 45. LXVI. 3. patrocinium tamen Ecclesiae suscipiunt, edictis publicis ejus securitati providen t, atque ita Ecclesiae judices fiunt. Quod non semel à Pseudo-christianis & infidelibus, Turcis, aliisque factum. Sed nusquam, inquiunt illi, Catholici doctrinam vel vitam Ethnicorum vel haereticorum laudasse inveniuntur. Deteriores ergo illi sunt hostibus suis, qui, quae bona illis videntur, laudant, si ipsi commerita laude defraudant, si quid boni in Ethnicis & haereticis residuum est; uti quidem in horum doctrina & vita non omnia rejicienda, sed quaedam segreganda sunt. Attamen Augustinus Tychonium Donatistam; Basilius Libanium; Ausonius Symmachum magnificè laudarunt. Non enim qui laudentur, sed quid laudetur, spectandum est. Si qui porrò nostrùm vel Pontifices, vel Pontificios quosdam laudarunt, non in eo, in quo adversarii fuerunt, sed in eo, in quo consenserunt, & laudem commeriti sunt, laudarunt. Qualis confessio sicut adversariorum confessio dici non potest: ita ne religio eorum falsa in caeteris sit, non efficit. Non enim qui pretiosum quid laudat, etiam vile cum pretioso conjunctum laudat. Nos in Pontificiis damnamus, quae damnanda sunt, agnoscimus, quae agnoscenda sunt. Hoc si facere in nobis vellent, non tantùm nihilo pejores, sed etiam potiores illis essemus.
units.tr: For they say there is such force in truth that it bursts forth even from unwilling breasts, according to that saying about the people of God: Our God is not as their gods are, and our enemies are the judges (Deut. 32.31). Nor is any testimony to be despised that is drawn from the bosom of enemies. But not everything that happens to the Church, by the peculiar providence of God, is a perpetual mark of the Church. The confession of enemies to the truth is certainly not an essential mark of the Church, because that testimony is external and comes from outsiders, and of itself has no force and proves nothing unless the truth is established from elsewhere. Nor is it a proper mark, because Christians, out of Christian candor, praise virtue even in their enemies, and are quite willing to grant it to pagans and heretics alike, if they have anything of doctrine, virtue or merit. The impious, on the other hand, though they silently bear witness to the good in their own hearts, can hardly bring themselves to profess it openly, held back by the torches of hatred and envy. Nor is it inseparable, because, as Christ foretold (Matt. 5.11), they very often tear the Church to pieces with abuse; and in this kind the Jesuits, sewn wholly together out of calumnies and lies, hold the first place. And so a Church that has adversaries who are fiercely lying, malicious, venomous, slanderous, devils, would not be the true Church. Men have also praised and worshipped the Beast, saying: Who is like the Beast? Who can make war with it? And all who dwell on the earth will worship the Beast, whose names are not written in the book of life (Rev. 13.4, 8). But the judgment of the inhabitants of the earth about the Beast is greatly deceived. Indeed, the enemies of the Church become its judges, according to Deut. 32.31, when, though they are endowed with a hostile mind, or at least lie to Christ (ibid. 33.29; Ps. 18.45; 66.3), they nevertheless take up the protection of the Church and provide for its safety by public edicts, and so become judges of the Church. This has been done more than once by pseudo-Christians and unbelievers, Turks and others. But, they say, Catholics are never found to have praised the doctrine or life of pagans or heretics. Those men, then, are worse than their enemies, who, if they defraud the deserving of praise, do not praise what seems good to them, if there is anything good left in pagans and heretics. Indeed, in their doctrine and life not everything is to be rejected, but some things must be separated out. Yet Augustine praised Tyconius the Donatist magnificently, and Basil praised Libanius, and Ausonius praised Symmachus. For what matters is not who is praised, but what is praised. If any of ours, whether bishops or some Papists, have praised anything, they did not praise it in the respect in which the adversaries were wrong, but in the respect in which they agreed with them and deserved praise. Such a confession cannot be called the confession of adversaries, just as their religion is not made any less false in other respects. For whoever praises a precious thing does not thereby praise a cheap thing joined to it. We condemn in the Papists what is to be condemned, and we acknowledge what is to be acknowledged. If they would do the same toward us, we would not only be no worse than they, but even better than they.

units.la: XC. Ecclesiam veram leviter etiam infelix exitus hostium ejus notat.
units.tr: XC. The unhappy end of its enemies only weakly marks out the true Church.

units.la: Non enim Ecclesiae clesiæ id vel essentiale est, quia illi extra Ecclesiam sunt, & pereunt: & an hostes Ecclesiæ sint, nec ne, aliunde & prius constare debet, vel proprium, quia etiam Ecclesia & membra ejus tristissimum subinde exitum habent, uti Christi, Apostolorum & S. Martyrum exemplis liquet: vel ab ea inseparabile, quia etiam hostes & persecutores Ecclesiæ quandoque sicca & placida morte pereunt, ut gravius in altera vita luant. Præterea infelix exitus ex hac vita eorum est, qui non obdormiunt in fide Christi. Qui verò sic feliciter, vel infeliciter ex hac vita migrent, certò cerni, vel discerni non potest. Tu quis es judicans alienum servum? Stat & cadit Domino suo, Rom. XIV. 4. Congruit equidem cum regula justitiæ Divinæ, ut hostes Dei puniantur. Sed tam incertum est, an hostes maneant, & hostilem animum retineant, qui moriuntur: tum in hac vita puniri hostes Dei contingens est, & arbitraria Dei justitia haud raro eidem judicio bonos malosque involvit. Licet ergo infelix exitus tyrannorum ipsorum scelus probet, & Christus etiam tandem vincat, quin & Sancti, dum vincuntur, vincant; denique Deus electos suos die & nocte ad ipsum clamantes vindicet, Luc. XVIII. 7. 8. tamen tempus est, cum meretrix gloriatur: Sedeo Regina, & luctum non videbo, Apoc. XVIII. 7. Poenæ enim Ψευδαλοι in hac vita arbitrariæ sunt. Si tamen adversariis insultare & suppeditare, quod iis non inutilem notam, documentum & admonitionem præbeat, liberet, nostra & Patrum memoria paucis Ecclesiam vexantibus feliciter cessisse, at feliciter cessisse plerisque, quorum opera Deo in reformanda Ecclesia uti placuit; qui fere pie in Domino abdormiverunt, demonstrare nullo negotio possemus, & demonstravimus alibi. Intueantur modo exitum Crescentii Cardinalis, Francisci Spiræ, Henrici II. & filiorum ejus, Philippi II. Mariæ Scoticæ, Jacobi II. & aliorum. Quidni verò etiam Zwinglium, non hostem, sed vigilantissimum Pastorem Ecclesiæ, pie in Domino obdormivisse confidamus, cum pro Patriæ salute & libertate occubuerit, obsecutus patriis legibus, quæ jubent, ut qui sacris præest, idem militiæ comes sit.
units.tr: For this is not essential to the Church, because those outside the Church also perish; and whether they are enemies of the Church must be established from elsewhere and beforehand. Nor is it a property of the Church, because the Church and its members also sometimes have a most sorrowful end, as the examples of Christ, the Apostles and the holy martyrs make clear. Nor is it inseparable from the Church, because the enemies and persecutors of the Church sometimes also die a dry and peaceful death, so that they may pay the heavier penalty in the next life. Moreover, an unhappy departure from this life belongs to those who do not fall asleep in the faith of Christ. But whether someone departs this life happily or unhappily cannot be seen or discerned with certainty. Who are you to judge another's servant? To his own master he stands or falls, Rom. 14.4. It is indeed consistent with the rule of divine justice that the enemies of God should be punished. But it is so uncertain whether those who die remain enemies and retain a hostile mind; and the enemies of God may be punished in this life, while divine justice, being arbitrary, not seldom involves good and bad in the same judgment. Therefore, although the unhappy end of tyrants proves their wickedness, and Christ at last conquers, and indeed the saints, while they are being conquered, conquer; and finally God will avenge his elect, who cry to him day and night, Luke 18.7, 8, yet there is a time when the harlot boasts: I sit a queen, and shall see no sorrow, Rev. 18.7. For punishments in this life are arbitrary (ψευδαλοι). If, however, it pleases them to insult their opponents and to supply them with something, since it gives them no useless mark, lesson and warning, we could easily show, from our own memory and that of the Fathers, that a few who have harassed the Church have ended happily, but that most of those through whose work God was pleased to reform the Church have ended happily and fallen asleep piously in the Lord; and we have demonstrated this elsewhere. Let them look at the end of Cardinal Crescentius, Francis Spira, Henry II and his sons, Philip II, Mary of Scotland, James II and others. Why, then, should we not confidently believe that Zwingli, not an enemy but a most vigilant minister of the Church, fell asleep piously in the Lord, since he fell for the safety and liberty of his country, obeying the laws of his homeland, which order that whoever presides over sacred things should also accompany the army?

units.la: XCI. Claudit agmen notarum Felicitas temporalis, purpuratæ Babylonis, quàm castæ Christi Sponsæ expressior nota. Non enim veræ Ecclesiæ nota temporalis felicitas est. Sed crux, quia prædestinati sumus, ut reddamur conformes imagini Filii Dei, Rom. VIII. 29. 30. cum quo patientes etiam glorificabimur & regnabimus, ibid. v. 17. 2. Tim. II. 11. 12. Omnes qui volent pie vivere in Christo Jesu, persecutionem patientur, ibid. III. 12. Reprobi hæc gloriatio est: Non nutabo. In generationem omnem est, qui non in malo est, Psal. X. 6. q. d. Hæc illa Ecclesia, cui non prævalebunt portæ inferorum, est, quæ felix est in mundo, & prospero semper fortunæ flatu utitur, & per cujus numerosos pauper & honestus quisque conteritur, enervatur & cadit, ibid. v. 11. Nihil ergo Ecclesiæ minus essentiale est, quàm temporalis felicitas, quia ejus potius tessera crux est. Nihil proprium minus, quia Babyloni, Antichristo & mundo gaudia & commoda temporalia congruunt. Eorum enim est καταςρηνιαν lascivire, Apoc.
units.tr: XCI. The last of the marks is temporal felicity, a mark more fitting to the purple-clad Babylon than to the chaste Bride of Christ. For temporal happiness is not a mark of the true Church. Rather the cross is: we are predestined to be made conformable to the image of the Son of God, Rom. 8:29-30, with whom if we suffer, we shall also be glorified and reign, ibid. v. 17; 2 Tim. 2:11-12. All who will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution, ibid. 3:12. This boast belongs to the reprobate: I shall not be moved. He is in every generation who is not in evil, Ps. 10:6, as if to say: this is that Church against which the gates of hell shall not prevail, which is happy in the world and always enjoys the prosperous breeze of fortune, and through whose numerous ranks every poor and honest man is crushed, weakened and falls, ibid. v. 11. Nothing, therefore, is less essential to the Church than temporal felicity, since its badge is rather the cross. Nothing is less proper to it, since joys and temporal advantages suit Babylon, Antichrist and the world. For it is theirs to live wantonly [καταστρηνιᾶν], Rev. 18:7, to rejoice, John 16:20. Nothing is more separable from it, since, as the experience of all times attests, the Church obtains either no peace at all, or a peace that is unfaithful and slippery.

units.la: XVIII. 7. gaudere, Joh. XVI. 20. Nihil separabile magis, quia, teste experientia omnium temporum, Ecclesiæ aut nulla, aut infida & lubrica pax obtingit. Licet enim pietas promissionem etiam habeat ζωὴν τῆς νῦν vitæ præsentis, 1. Tim. IV. 8. tamen id non de felicitate externa, evanida, fluxa, & impiis quoque communi, sed de vera & solida, idque cum exceptione castigationis & crucis, quam Scriptura Psal. XCIX. 8. Esaj. XXX. 20. Marc. X. 30. exprimit, intelligi debet. Sed hoc tamen Ecclesia habet, quod ex malis suis tandem emergit & triumphat, & sub cruce, ut lilium inter spinas, floret, palmæ instar, sub pondere surgit, & cum vincitur maximè, vincit. Huc denique ergo felicitatis & victoriarum Babylonicarum magnitudo exit, ut Ecclesiæ incrementis & veræ felicitati inserviat.
units.tr: Apoc. XVIII. 7, "rejoice"; Joh. XVI. 20. Nothing is more separable from it, since, as the experience of every age attests, the Church obtains either no peace at all or a peace that is unsafe and slippery. For although godliness has the promise of "the life that now is" [ζωὴν τῆς νῦν] (1. Tim. IV. 8), this must be understood not of outward happiness, which is fleeting, transient and common even to the impious, but of true and solid happiness, and that with the exception of chastisement and the cross, which Scripture expresses in Psal. XCIX. 8, Esaj. XXX. 20 and Marc. X. 30. Yet the Church has this at least: out of its evils it at last emerges and triumphs, and under the cross, like the lily among thorns, it flourishes; like a palm it rises under the weight, and when it is most overcome, it conquers. To this end, finally, the greatness of Babylonian happiness and victories comes, that it serves the increase of the Church and true happiness.

units.la: XCII. Hæc vana illa terriculamenta Romanæ Synagogæ sunt; hi adulteri illi fuci, quibus rugosa illa meretrix, postquam ætatis suæ lenocinium amisit, sese pingere adhuc solet, ut si novos amasios adhuc allicere amplius non possit, veteres saltem vi consuetudinis retineat. Sed occulto Dei judicio evenit, ut instituentes Ecclesiæ veræ notas tradere, repudiatis veris & genuinis, ipsoque, proh pudor! Dei verbo, quod Ecclesiæ, seu Papæ, ceu ignotius, Ψευδομαχοῦντες illi subjicere audent; eas ferè sine ullo Scripturarum præsidio (ubi enim Scriptura tanta pompa & ornatu Ecclesiam instruit, adornat, & velut theatralem in scenam adducit, & quomodo pompa illa notarum cum Ecclesiæ natura, qualem Scriptura depingit, convenit?) traderent, quas Scriptura Antichristo non obscure vendicat: ut Antichristi quàm Christi, synagogæ Sathanæ quàm Dei notas verius longè dixeris. Scriptura enim Antichristo tribuit tum Catholicismum & Successionem, quia cum in Templo Dei sedentem, 2. Thess. II. 4. & Bestiam ex terra, hoc est, verae Ecclesiæ gremio, ascendentem, velut in thronum suum, & in throno hoc dominantem in subjectum terrarum orbem, velut throno & cathedræ huic affixum & obnoxium, Apoc. XIII. 14. docet: tum Antiquitatem, asserens, jam tempore Apostolorum operari cœpisse mysterium iniquitatis, 2. Thess. II. 7. tum Durationem longam, quia gentes civitatem sanctam calcaturas mensēs quadraginta duos, Apoc. XI. 2. 3. seu dies Prophecticos 1260. ibid. XIII. 5. docet, tum Multitudinem & Unitatem profitentium unum caput, eique arctissimè adhærentium, quando omnes incolas terræ, quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitæ, Bestiam adoraturos, ib. XIII. 8. & cum Meretrice magna Reges terræ fortaturos, & ex vino fornicationis ejus inebriandos omnes incolas terræ, ibid. XVII. 2. prædicit; tum Miraculorum gloriam, quando adventum ejus futurum secundum operationem Sathanæ in potentia omni, & signis, & prodigiis mendacii, 2. Thess. II. 9. & Bestiam editurām miracula magna, Apoc. XIII. 13. vaticinatur: tum Doctrinæ efficaciam, hoc est, ἐνέργειαν πλάνης efficaciam doctrinæ seductricis, 2. Thess. II. 11. tum sanctitatem authorum religionis, seu Monachatus, quia Bestia habere cornua similia cornibus Agni, Apocal. XIII. 11. & venire in veste ovilla, Matth. VII. 15. debuit: tum felicitatem temporalem & victovictorias adversus hæreticos, quos vocat, quia futurum, ut Bestia Sanctos vincere, Apoc. XIII. 7. & Mulier Meretrix inebriari sanguine sanctorum, & sanguine testium Jesu, ibid. XVII. 6. debuerit. Frustra ergo Ecclesiam suam tali notarum choragio & fuco pingere atque exornare satagunt, quo cautioribus & cordatis omnibus turpitudinem suam produnt. Tu autem, quid facis, quòd induis te dibapho (rebus externis, quasi Deo imponere possis, qui non externa pompa, sed cordis puritate delectatur) quòd ornas te ornatu aureo, quòd laceras fuco oculos tuos? In vanum reddis te pulchram, respuunt te עבריים amasii tui, Jerem. IV. 30.
units.tr: XCII. These are the empty bugbears of the Roman synagogue. They are the adulterers' paints with which that wrinkled whore, having lost the allure of her youth, still likes to make herself up, so that if she can no longer attract new lovers, she may at least hold on to the old ones by force of habit. But by the hidden judgment of God it has come about that these men, who undertake to set out the marks of the true Church, have rejected the true and genuine marks, and, shame to say, God's own Word. Those fighters against the truth [Ψευδομαχοῦντες] dare to subject that Word to the Church, or to the Pope, as though it were the less known of the two. They offer marks almost without any support from the Scriptures. For where does Scripture furnish and adorn the Church with such pomp, and bring her out as if onto a theatre stage? And how does that display of marks agree with the nature of the Church as Scripture paints it? The marks that Scripture plainly assigns to Antichrist are far more truly the marks of Antichrist than of Christ, and of the synagogue of Satan rather than of God. For Scripture attributes to Antichrist (1) catholicity and succession, since it teaches that he will sit in the temple of God (2 Thess. 2:4) and that the beast will rise out of the earth, that is, out of the bosom of the true Church (Rev. 13:14), and rule from that throne over the subject world, as though fixed to and bound to that throne and seat; (2) antiquity, asserting that the mystery of iniquity was already at work in the time of the Apostles (2 Thess. 2:7); (3) long duration, since it foretells that the nations will trample the holy city for forty-two months (Rev. 11:2, 3), or 1260 prophetic days (ibid.; cf. 13:5); (4) the multitude and unity of those professing one head and clinging to him most closely, since it predicts that all the inhabitants of the earth, whose names are not written in the book of life, will worship the beast (ibid. 13:8), and that the kings of the earth will commit fornication with the great whore, and that all the inhabitants of the earth will be made drunk with the wine of her fornication (ibid. 17:2); (5) the glory of miracles, since it prophesies that his coming will be according to the working of Satan, with all power, and signs, and lying wonders (2 Thess. 2:9), and that the beast will perform great miracles (Rev. 13:13); (6) the efficacy of doctrine, that is, the working of error [ἐνέργειαν πλάνης], the efficacy of a seductive teaching (2 Thess. 2:11); (7) the holiness of the authors of the religion, or of monasticism, since the beast was to have horns like a lamb's (Rev. 13:11) and to come in sheep's clothing (Matt. 7:15); (8) temporal happiness and victories over those whom they call heretics, since it was to be that the beast would overcome the saints (Rev. 13:7) and the harlot would be made drunk with the blood of the saints and the blood of the witnesses of Jesus (ibid. 17:6). In vain, therefore, do they labour to paint and adorn their Church with such a troupe of marks and such cosmetics, by which they betray their own foulness to all the more cautious and sensible people. But you, what are you doing, when you clothe yourself in fine linen (external things, as if you could impose on God, who delights not in external pomp but in purity of heart), when you adorn yourself with golden ornaments, when you paint your eyes with cosmetics? In vain you make yourself beautiful; your lovers [מאהביך] despise you (Jer. 4:30).

units.la: LOCI VICESIMI SEPTIMI De REGIMINE ECCLESIÆ SECTIO PRIOR. De REGIMINE ECCLESIÆ CHRISTIANO. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: TOPIC TWENTY-SEVEN: On the Government of the Church, Section One. On the Christian Government of the Church. A SHORT SUMMARY.

units.la: Ecclesia regimine & politia sua carere non potest: quod aliud Divinum & Christianum, aliud Antichristianum est, atque illud vel internum & invisibile, vel externum atque visibile est. 1. Regimen Ecclesiæ externum principale penes solum Deum, inprimis Christum, Ecclesiæ caput, est. 2. Variis capitis notio. 3. Christus Ecclesiæ caput respectu dignitatis communionis, conjunctionis, dependentiæ & regiminis est. 4. Quod pluribus asseritur. 5. Similitudinis capitis gradus Christo applicantur. 6. Regimen Ecclesiæ Ministeriale describitur. 7. Duplex illud est, vel Ecclesiasticum, vel Civile. Ecclesiasticum Ecclesiæ quædam politia est. 8. Non propria, sed Christi authoritate administratur, juxta charismata, quæ distribuit. 9. Charismatum distinctio. 10. Ministeriorum juxta eadem charismata distinctio. 11. Charismata alia extraordinaria, alia ordinaria sunt. 12. Ministeriorum similis ratio est; 13. Ministeriorum ordinariorum necessitas. 14. Enthusiastarum, Libertinorum, &c. rationes contrariæ refelluntur. 15. Ministri ordinarii Ecclesiæ V.T. 16. Ordinarii N.T. distribuuntur. Pastorum nomina. 17. Eorundem officium. 18. Gregem pascere, & eidem invigilare debent. 19. Officii eorundem partes. 20. Incentiva ad defungendum officii illius partibus. 21. Vocationis Ministrorum Ecclesiæ necessitas. 22. Author ejus Christus est. 23. Vocatio interna extraordinaria, vel ordinaria est. 24. Externa immediata, vel mediata est; & hæc mediante tota Ecclesia, adeóque etiam populo, peragi debet. 25. Argumentis contrariis occurritur. 26. Jus vocandi toti Ecclesiæ, & singulis ejus membris competit. 27. Variante exercitio ejusdem, 28. Vocandi ad minsterium explorari debent. 29. Exploratio illa in voluntatis & facultatis illius disquisitione consistit. 30. Voluntatis & facultatis hujus dotes ex S. Paulo & Christi ipsius ad Petrum voce explicantur. 31. Veteris Ecclesiæ in præparandis Ecclesiæ Ministris praxis. 32. Ordinationis ad ministerium tempus. 33. Vocationis & ordinationis complementum in ejusdem confirmatione, & libero usu impositionis manuum consistit. 34. Quæ Divino jure Presbyteris competens, procedente tempore Episcopo demandata est. 35. Legitima vocatio & ordinatio est, quæ ab Episcopo uno, à Presbyteris distincto non peragitur. 36. Vocatio Reformatorum Ecclesiæ legitima fuit. 37. Successio Pastorum Ecclesiæ vel in corpus, vel in caput est. 38. Electioni Pastorum tum personarum acceptio. 39. Tum Simonia adversatur. 40. Ecclesiæ Ministris stipendia debentur. 41. Anabaptistarum objectiones diluuntur. 42. Modus, quo Ecclesiæ Ministris de sustentatione providendum est, est, exponitur. 43. Ministris Ecclesiæ præter stipendia ab Ecclesiis collata, alia bona possidere licet. 44. Stipendia Ecclesiæ Ministris, etiam ex reditibus, quibus sacrificuli ante hac sustentati sunt, destinari possunt. 45. Seniorum Ecclesiæ à Pastoribus docentibus distinctorum peculiaris ordo est. 46. Vindicatur ab exceptionibus Hierarchicorum. 47. Et à Presbyterio Ecclesiæ Judaicæ distinguitur. 48. Officium Seniorum. 49. Doctorum Ecclesiæ Divina institutio. 50. Eorum perpetuus in Ecclesia usus. 51. Nec non officium. 52. Et requisita, linguarum inprimis originalium & artium peritiæ necessitas. 53. Doctorum vocatio & inauguratio. 54. Eorundem examen. 55. Veritatis & charitatis iis præcipua cura esse debet. 56. Diaconorum, seu bonorum Ecclesiæ curatorum institutio. 57. Eorundem ad munus obeundum vocatio. 58. Gubernatio Ecclesiæ per ministeria in eorundem officio & potestate consistit. 59. Potestas distinguitur. 60. Ecclesiæ potestas clavium potestatis nomine venit. 61. Duplex clavium Regni Cœlorum potestas berilis & œconomica distinguitur. 62. Potestas clavium Petro data in potestate peccata remittendi & retinendi consistit. 63. Non uni Petro, sed in persona ejus Ecclesiæ collata est. 64. Ecclesiæ ministris omnibus una & æqualis potestas à Christo data est. 65. Forma regiminis Ecclesiæ Ministerialis analogicè aristocratica, seu potius œconomica est. 66. Regimen Ecclesiæ in generalibus uniforme & immutabile, in particularibus varium & mutabile est. 67. Disceptatio de regimine per Episcopos an presbyteros administrari debeat, conciliari potest. 68. Regimen Ecclesiæ circa personas & res versatur. Personæ omnes Ecclesiæ cives, varie inter se distincti sunt. 69. Res sunt doctrina verbi Dei, Sacramenta, ceremoniæ, disciplina & bona Ecclesiæ. Doctrina qualis esse debeat. 70. Ejus argumentum & norma verbum Dei est. 71. Cujus prædicatio Ecclesiæ ministris incumbit, & prædicta in V.T. & à Christo. 72. Et impleta, variante licet methodo, puritate & successu. 73. Præconis verbi Dei proprium munus. 74. Ædificatio Ecclesiæ scopus ejus præcipuus esse debet; in declaratione & applicatione Scripturæ consistens. 75. Privata singulorum institutio præconi commendata esse debet. 76. Juventutis institutio domestica vel ecclesiastica est. 77. Utriusque necessitas. 78. Ordo & methodus institutionis catechetica. 79. Ministrorum Ecclesiæ officium circa ceremonias. 80. In quibus non pars cultus Divini, sed ordinis Ecclesiastici externi exercitium consistit. 81. Regulæ circa ceremoniarum observantiam tenendæ. 82. Disciplinæ Ecclesiæ necessitas. 83. Ejusdem Divina institutio. 84. Rationes disciplinam Ecclesiæ confirmantes. 85. Peccata disciplinam Ecclesiæ subeuntia distinguuntur. 86. Modus exercendæ disciplinæ spiritualis, non corporalis est. 87. Correptionis occultorum peccatorum gradus primus, quo peccator solus à solo redarguitur. 88. Secundus, quo coram testibus redarguitur. 89. Succedit his gradus, quo ab Ecclesia, apud quam delatio peccatoris fit, & peccatum manifestatur, redarguitur. 90. Delatio peccatoris ad Ecclesiam, mediata vel immediata, & censura Presbyterialis, vel Ecclesiastica est. 91. Judicium Ecclesiæ adversus refractarios. 92. Erasti, aliorumque disciplinam Ecclesiæ oppugnantium, elenchus. 93. A judicio Ecclesiæ ad Magistratum quatenus provocatio detur. 94. Circa excommunicationem Ecclesiæ sensus & praxis variat. 95. Ecclesiarum quarundam Helveticarum circa excommunicationem sententia & praxis. 96. Argumenta ejusdem ex Aretio, aliisque narrata. 97. Ἐπιχείσις circa eandem. 98. Praxeos patriæ circa excommunicationem singularis ratio excusatur. 99. Reformandæ vitæ necessitas. 100. Circa Reformationem vitæ prudens συγκατάθεσις & charitas requiritur. 101. Bonorum Ecclesiæ temporalium necessitas. 102. Eorundem usus. 103. Et administratio religiosa. 104. Regulæ circa eorum possessionem, administrationem, usum & abusum observandæ. 105. Ecclesiarum plurium in Synodis & Conciliis congregatio. 106. Independentium eam oppugnantium elenchus. 107. Modus controversias in Synodis & Conciliis definiendi exponitur. 108. Objectio tyrannidis diluitur. 109. Conciliorum distributio. 110. Eorundem membra quænam esse possint. 111. Ordo in Conciliis servandus. 112. Gubernatio Ecclesiæ civilis definitur. 113. Magistratus origo Divina est. 114. Potestas ejusdem omnis à Deo est. 115. Progressus potestatis illius inde à principio suo. 116. Reipublicæ forma, modus & personæ magistratum gerentes hominum electioni subsunt. 117. Magistratui non competit absoluta potestas quidvis faciendi. 118. Pontificiorum & Anabaptistarum adversus Magistratus blasphemiæ. 119. Objectionibus eorundem occurritur. 120. Pseudo-politicorum, Machiavelli, Hobbesii tyrannidem & cæcam obedientiam propugnantium elenchus. 121. Argumenta eorum rum ad partes vocata. 122. Ecclesiæ Reformatæ apologia adversus improperium genii singularis regnantibus infensi. 123. Potestas Magistratus in Legislatione, 124. nec non judiciorum, etiam capitalium, administratione consistit. 125. Contraria Anabaptistarum argumenta refelluntur. 126. Ad judicia Magistratus etiam belli jus pertinet. 127. Magistratui inprimis Ecclesiæ & religionis cura incumbit. 128. In definienda Magistratus circa religionem cura & potestate in defectu peccant Pontificii & Anabaptistæ. 129. In excessu Pseudo-Politici, Erastiani & Remonstrantes. 130. Ecclesia mediam viam init, prævis eam in rem animadversionibus. 131. Potestas formaliter & proprie Ecclesiastica Magistratui non competit. 132. Objectiones contrariæ diluuntur. 133. Neque Magistratus circa religionem potestas & Ecclesiam, quâ talis est, proprie architectonica est. 134. Plura etiam Ecclesia habet, in quæ nihil Magistratui licet. 135. Quæ specialius enarrantur. 136. Cura Ecclesiæ Magistratui incumbens generaliter exponitur. 137. Ejusdem partes præcipuè edisseruntur. 138. Officium Magistratus circa conversionem errantium & prophetandi libertatem. 139. In judicio adversus errantes proprio judicio uti debet. 140. In judicio adversus errantes ferendo errores & errantes ipsi distinguendi sunt. 141. Alia status Reipublicæ liberi, alia perturbati est; & utrique judicium Magistratus circa errantes accommodari debet. 142. Gubernationis Ecclesiæ civilis & Ecclesiasticæ harmonia beatam Ecclesiam reddit. 143. Mutua Ecclesiæ & Magistratus subjectio cum temperamento conjuncta esse debet. 144.
units.tr: The Church cannot do without government and polity of its own. There is a divine and Christian polity and an Antichristian one, and the government is either internal and invisible or external and visible. 1. The principal external government of the Church rests with God alone, above all with Christ, the Head of the Church. 2. The various senses of "head." 3. Christ is the Head of the Church with respect to dignity, communion, conjunction, dependence and government. 4. This is asserted by many. 5. The degrees of the likeness of the head are applied to Christ. 6. The ministerial government of the Church is described. 7. It is twofold, either ecclesiastical or civil. Ecclesiastical government is a certain polity of the Church. 8. It is administered not by its own authority but by the authority of Christ, according to the gifts (charismata) that he distributes. 9. The distinction of gifts. 10. The distinction of ministries according to these same gifts. 11. Some gifts are extraordinary, others ordinary. 12. The same reasoning holds for ministries. 13. The necessity of ordinary ministries. 14. The contrary arguments of the enthusiasts, the Libertines, etc. are refuted. 15. The ordinary ministers of the Church of the Old Testament. 16. The ordinary ministers of the New Testament are distinguished; the names of pastors. 17. Their office. 18. They ought to feed the flock and watch over it. 19. The parts of their office. 20. Incentives to discharge the parts of that office. 21. The necessity of the calling of ministers of the Church. 22. Christ is its author. 23. The internal calling is either extraordinary or ordinary. 24. The external calling is either immediate or mediate, and the latter must be carried out through the whole Church, and so also through the people. 25. Arguments to the contrary are met. 26. The right to call belongs to the whole Church and to each of its members. 27. The exercise of this right varies. 28. Those who are to be called to the ministry must be tested. 29. This testing consists in an inquiry into their willingness and ability. 30. The qualities of this willingness and ability are explained from St. Paul and from the words of Christ himself to Peter. 31. The practice of the early Church in preparing ministers of the Church. 32. The time of ordination to the ministry. 33. The completion of calling and ordination consists in its confirmation and in the free use of the laying on of hands. 34. What belonged to the elders by divine right was in the course of time committed to a bishop. 35. A lawful calling and ordination is one that is not carried out by one bishop distinct from the elders. 36. The calling of the ministers of the Reformed Church was lawful. 37. The succession of the pastors of the Church is either to the body or to the head. 38. In the election of pastors, acceptance of persons is opposed. 39. Simony is also opposed. 40. Stipends are owed to the ministers of the Church. 41. The objections of the Anabaptists are dissolved. 42. The manner in which provision must be made for the maintenance of the ministers of the Church is set out. 43. Ministers of the Church may possess other goods besides the stipends contributed by the Churches. 44. Stipends may be assigned to the ministers of the Church even from the revenues by which the priests were formerly supported. 45. The order of elders, distinct from the teaching pastors, is a peculiar order of the Church. 46. It is defended against the objections of the hierarchists. 47. And it is distinguished from the presbytery of the Jewish Church. 48. The office of elders. 49. The divine institution of the teachers of the Church. 50. Their perpetual use in the Church. 51. And likewise their office. 52. And the requirements, above all the necessity of skill in the original languages and the arts. 53. The calling and inauguration of teachers. 54. Their examination. 55. Care for truth and charity should above all be theirs. 56. The institution of deacons, or stewards of the goods of the Church. 57. The calling of these to discharge their duty. 58. The governing of the Church through the ministries consists in the office and power of these. 59. Power is distinguished. 60. The power of the Church comes under the name of the power of the keys. 61. The twofold power of the keys of the kingdom of heaven is distinguished, the lordly and the economic. 62. The power of the keys given to Peter consists in the power of remitting and retaining sins. 63. It was conferred not on Peter alone but on the Church in his person. 64. One and the same power was given by Christ to all the ministers of the Church. 65. The form of the ministerial government of the Church is analogically aristocratic, or rather economic. 66. The government of the Church is uniform and unchangeable in general matters, but varied and changeable in particular matters. 67. The dispute whether government should be administered by bishops or by presbyters can be reconciled. 68. The government of the Church concerns persons and things. All persons are citizens of the Church, variously distinguished among themselves. 69. The things are the doctrine of the Word of God, the sacraments, ceremonies, discipline and the goods of the Church. What the doctrine ought to be like. 70. Its subject and rule is the Word of God. 71. Its preaching falls to the ministers of the Church, and it was foretold in the Old Testament and by Christ. 72. And it was fulfilled, with varying method, purity and success. 73. The proper task of the herald of the Word of God. 74. The edification of the Church should be its chief aim, consisting in the declaration and application of Scripture. 75. Private instruction of individuals should be commended to the preacher. 76. The instruction of youth is either domestic or ecclesiastical. 77. The necessity of each. 78. The order and method of catechetical instruction. 79. The duty of the ministers of the Church concerning ceremonies. 80. Those in which consists not part of the divine worship but the exercise of external ecclesiastical order. 81. Rules to be observed concerning the keeping of ceremonies. 82. The necessity of church discipline. 83. Its divine institution. 84. Reasons confirming the discipline of the Church. 85. Sins liable to church discipline are distinguished. 86. The manner of exercising spiritual, not bodily, discipline. 87. The first degree of correction of secret sins, in which the sinner is rebuked by one alone. 88. The second, in which he is rebuked before witnesses. 89. There follows this degree, in which he is rebuked by the Church before which the sinner is reported and the sin made manifest. 90. The reporting of the sinner to the Church, whether mediate or immediate, and the censure is either by the presbytery or by the Church. 91. The judgment of the Church against the refractory. 92. An refutation of Erastus and of others who attack the discipline of the Church. 93. In what measure an appeal from the judgment of the Church to the magistrate is allowed. 94. The opinion and practice concerning excommunication vary in the Church. 95. The opinion and practice concerning excommunication in certain Swiss Churches. 96. The arguments of the same, as related from Aretius and others. 97. An attempt [Ἐπιχείσις] concerning the same. 98. The particular reason for the practice of our country concerning excommunication is excused. 99. The necessity of reforming one's life. 100. In the reformation of life, prudent condescension [συγκατάθεσις] and charity are required. 101. The necessity of temporal goods of the Church. 102. Their use. 103. And their religious administration. 104. Rules to be observed concerning their possession, administration, use and abuse. 105. The gathering of several Churches in synods and councils. 106. A refutation of the Independents who oppose it. 107. The manner of settling controversies in synods and councils is set out. 108. The objection of tyranny is dissolved. 109. The distribution of councils. 110. What their members may be. 111. The order to be observed in councils. 112. Civil government of the Church is defined. 113. The origin of the magistrate is divine. 114. All his power is from God. 115. The progress of that power from its beginning. 116. The form of the commonwealth, the manner, and the persons who hold the magistracy are subject to human choice. 117. Absolute power to do anything whatever does not belong to the magistrate. 118. The blasphemies of the Papists and Anabaptists against the magistrates. 119. Their objections are met. 120. A refutation of the pseudo-politicians, of Machiavelli and of Hobbes, who champion tyranny and blind obedience. 121. Their arguments are called to account. 122. An apology of the Reformed Church against the reproach of a single genius hostile to rulers. 123. The power of the magistrate consists in legislation, 124. and likewise in the administration of judgments, even capital ones. 125. The contrary arguments of the Anabaptists are refuted. 126. The right of war also belongs to the magistrate's judgments. 127. Above all, the care of the Church and of religion rests upon the magistrate. 128. The Papists and Anabaptists err by defect in defining the magistrate's care and power concerning religion. 129. The Pseudo-Politicians, Erastians and Remonstrants err by excess. 130. The Church takes the middle way, with the following remarks on this matter. 131. Power formally and properly ecclesiastical does not belong to the magistrate. 132. Contrary objections are dissolved. 133. Nor is the magistrate's power over religion, or over the Church as such, properly architectonic. 134. The Church also has many matters in which the magistrate has no right. 135. Which are narrated more specifically. 136. The care of the Church incumbent on the magistrate is set out in general. 137. Its parts are chiefly discussed. 138. The office of the magistrate concerning the conversion of those in error and the freedom of prophesying. 139. In judgment against those in error he must use his own judgment. 140. In passing judgment against those in error, errors and the erring themselves must be distinguished. 141. The state of a commonwealth may be free or disturbed, and the magistrate's judgment concerning those in error must be adapted to each. 142. The harmony of civil and ecclesiastical government makes the Church blessed. 143. Mutual subjection of Church and magistrate must be joined with moderation. 144.

units.la: I. NULLA sine regimine & politia quadam societas consistere potest. Proin & Ecclesia, quæ religiosa societas est, regimen & politiam habet. Sicut autem Ecclesiæ veræ & falsæ ideam supra, ob πτιδείας τέλην, distinximus: ita in regimine ejusdem explicando duplicis illius ideæ distinctio pariter adhibenda nobis est. Aliud enim regimen Ecclesiæ verae, aliud falsæ est. Illud Divinum, Christianum, authore Deo & Christo institutum: Hoc humanum & Antichristianum hominibus, Antichristo inprimis Ecclesiam in Regnum terrestre convertente, authoribus introductum est. Et Divinum quidem atque Christianum, perinde ut Ecclesia ipsa, vel internum & invisibile, vel externum & visibile est. Illud Deus arcano, merè spirituali & incomprehensibili modo, per verbum & Spiritum gerit. Hoc vel αὐτοκεφάλοιμον principale & dominans, vel ministeriale, principali illi, per Ministros à Deo ad id selectos, inserviens est.
units.tr: I. No society can exist without some government and polity, and so the Church, which is a religious society, also has government and polity. But just as we distinguished the true and false Church above, on account of its end (τέλος), so in explaining its government we must apply the same distinction. The government of the true Church is one thing, and that of the false Church is another. The former is divine and Christian, instituted by God and Christ; the latter is human and Antichristian, introduced by men, above all by Antichrist, who turned the Church into an earthly kingdom. And just as the Church itself is either internal and invisible or external and visible, so the divine and Christian government is likewise either internal or external. God governs the internal government by a secret, purely spiritual and incomprehensible means, through the Word and the Spirit. The external government is either principal and ruling, or ministerial, serving that principal government through ministers chosen by God for this purpose.

units.la: II. Regimen Ecclesiæ externæ Divinum & Christianum principale & αὐτοκεφάλοιμον pen es solum Deum & Christum est. Ille enim Ecclesiam non secundum formam ejus invisibilem, hoc est, donum fidei, spei & charitatis duntaxat, sed etiam secundum conditionem ejus exteriorem & visibilem principali authoritate & potestate regit atque moderatur. Ei enim omnis potestas in Cœlo & terra data est, Matth. XXVIII. 18. De quo plura in doctrina de Officio Christi, Regio inprimis, diximus. Pertinet huc maximè, quòd Christus in Scripturis passim Κεφαλὴς Capitis Ecclesiæ nomine venit. Et ipsum (Christum, non alium) dedit Caput supra omnia Ecclesiæ; quæ est Corpus ipsius, impletio (seu id, quod impletur) ejus, qui omnia in omnibus implet (se ipso omnia in suis omnibus implet) Eph. I. 22. 23. Sicut enim Ecclesia corpus Christi dicitur, quod Christus implet ita, ut sit in ipso, & in omnibus ejus membris omnia, Coloss. II. 9. 10. 19. ita Christus Ecclesiæ caput dicitur, quia Ecclesiam, velut corpus suum, & omnia ejus membra implet, Ephes. V. 23. Αὐτὸς Ipse, qui est imago Dei, primogenitus, in quo omnia condita sunt, est caput illud corporis illius Ecclesiæ, &c. Col. I. 18. Οὐδεὶς ὑμᾶς καταβραβευέτω Nemo vos (ceu arbiter & judex) obnoxios faciat; vel (ceu victor) præmio spoliet, volens (ex motu proprio) in humilitate & cultu Angelorum, quæ non videt, ingrediens, temerè inflatus à mente carnis suæ, καὶ οὐ κρατῶν τὴν κεφαλὴν non retinens caput illud, ex quo omne corpus per commissuras & vincula suppeditationem habens, & coagmentatum crescit in incrementum Dei, ibid. II. 18. 19.
units.tr: II. The divine and Christian principal and self-governing (αὐτοκεφάλοιμον) government of the external Church rests with God and Christ alone. For he rules and directs the Church not only according to its invisible form, that is, the gift of faith, hope and love alone, but also according to its external and visible condition, by principal authority and power. "All power in heaven and on earth has been given to him" (Matt. 28:18). We have said more on this in the doctrine of the Office of Christ, especially the kingly office. What chiefly pertains here is that in the Scriptures Christ everywhere comes under the name of Head (κεφαλή) of the Church. And God himself gave him, and no other, as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the fullness (or that which is filled) of him who fills all things in all (who fills all things in all his own) (Eph. 1:22–23). For just as the Church is called the body of Christ, which Christ fills so that he is in it and all things are in all its members (Col. 2:9–10, 19), so Christ is called the head of the Church, because he fills the Church as his own body and all its members (Eph. 5:23). He himself, who is the image of God, the firstborn, in whom all things were created, is the head of that body, the Church, etc. (Col. 1:18). "Let no one condemn you" (as arbiter and judge) or deprive you of the prize (as a victor), by insisting, of his own accord, on humility and the worship of angels, entering into things he has not seen, rashly puffed up by the mind of his flesh, "and not holding fast to the Head" (καὶ οὐ κρατῶν τὴν κεφαλήν), from whom the whole body, supplied and knit together through joints and ligaments, grows with the increase of God (Col. 2:18–19).

units.la: III. Varia in Capitis nomine allegoria est, pro diverso genere & gradu similitudinis. Quandoque enim Caput tantummodo ut corporis organici pars dignior & honoratior spectatur. Adeóque in allimilatione, Christo Nomen Capitis tribuitur in corpore Ecclesiæ κατ' ἐξοχὴν, prout sub Deo membrum reliqui corporis (σωματικὸν) primum & principale est. Sed salvâ ἐξοχὴ seu eminentia illa, alia etiam capita Christo subordinata censentur. Ejusmodi subordinata Christo capita, vir respectu mulieris, & Ecclesiæ visibilis membra honoratiora respectu ignobilium, dicuntur. Omnis viri caput Christus est, (quia solum Christum pro capite recognoscit, ex quo est, quicquid est) Caput autem mulieris vir est, (non quòd non etiam Christus mulieris caput sit, sed quia vir solum Christum caput habet, mulier verò etiam virum pro capite agnoscit, utpote qui eam in matrimonio præcedit) Caput autem Christi (non secundum formam Dei, sed hominis) Deus (Pater) est, 1. Cor. XI. 3. Quo argumento Apostolus conficit, non debere velari virum, quia ante se nihil in terra habet, quod illum præcedat; at debere velari mulierem, quia aliquid in terra habet, quod illam præcedit, scilicet virum, qui mulieris, propter ἐξοχὴν, seu præcedentiam illam caput est. Sicut autem hoc loco Christus omnis viri caput, subordinatum sibi caput mulieris virum habet: ita subordinata in Christo capita in Ecclesia idem Apostolus intellexit, dicens : Non potest oculus dicere manui : Non indigeo te, aut iterum caput pedibus : Non indigeo vobis, ibid. XII. 21. Quibus verbis S. Paulus non indigetat vel Christum, vel quodcunque tandem unum individuum, sed quævis Ecclesiæ visibilis membra honoratiora, & viros in Ecclesia eximios, juxta illud: Senex & honorabilis vultu הוא הראש ipse caput est : & Propheta, qui docet mendacium הוא הזנב ipse cauda est, Esaj.IX.15. Ita olim primogeniti ראשי בית אבות Capita familiarum paternarum, Exod. VI.14. Levitæ primarii ראשי הלויים capita Levitarum; Nehem. XI. 16. Patriarchæ ראשי אבות capita Patrum, seu Patres summi: denique Principes populi ראשי עם capita populi, sive πρεσβύτεροι τῆς λαοῦ Seniorum populi collegium, Deut. XXXIII. 5. dicti sunt.
units.tr: III. The allegory of the name Head is varied, according to the different kind and degree of likeness. Sometimes the head is regarded merely as the more worthy and honourable part of an organic body. Thus in this likeness the name Head is given to Christ in the body of the Church pre-eminently (κατ' ἐξοχήν), since under God he is the first and principal member of the rest of the body (σωματικόν). But without prejudice to that pre-eminence or eminence, other heads subordinate to Christ are also recognised. Such subordinate heads are said to be: the husband with respect to the wife, and the more honourable members of the visible Church with respect to the lowly. "The head of every man is Christ" (because he acknowledges only Christ as head, from whom comes whatever he is). "But the head of the woman is the man" (not that Christ is not also the head of the woman, but because the man has only Christ as his head, while the woman also acknowledges the man as head, since he precedes her in marriage). "But the head of Christ (not according to the form of God, but of man) is God (the Father)" (1 Cor. 11:3). By this argument the Apostle concludes that a man ought not to cover his head, because he has nothing on earth before him that precedes him; but a woman ought to cover hers, because she has something on earth that precedes her, namely the man, who is her head by pre-eminence, or by precedence. Just as in this passage Christ is the head of every man, and the man has a subordinate head in the woman, so the same Apostle understood subordinate heads in Christ's Church, saying: "The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you; or again the head to the feet, I have no need of you" (1 Cor. 12:21). By these words St Paul does not point to Christ, or to any single individual whatever, but to the more honourable members of the visible Church and to the eminent men in the Church, according to that saying: "The elder and honourable of countenance, he is the head [הוּא הָרֹאשׁ]; and the prophet who teaches lies, he is the tail [הוּא הַזָּנָב]" (Isa. 9:15). So in former times the firstborn were called "heads of the paternal houses" [רָאשֵׁי בֵית אָבוֹת] (Exod. 6:14); the chief Levites "heads of the Levites" [רָאשֵׁי הַלְוִיִּם] (Neh. 11:16); the patriarchs "heads of the fathers" [רָאשֵׁי אָבוֹת], that is, the chief fathers; and finally the princes of the people "heads of the people" [רָאשֵׁי עָם], or "the college of the elders of the people" (πρεσβύτεροι τοῦ λαοῦ) (Deut. 33:5).

units.la: IV. Christus Caput quinque potissimum modis, respectu tum dignitatis supra membra reliqua corporis; tum communionis naturæ; tum conjunctionis cum Ecclesia, tum dependentiæ Ecclesiæ à Christo capite; tum regiminis corporis totius, seu Ecclesiæ dicitur. Non tantum enim in his similitudo Christi cum capite naturali consistit, siquidem & illud dignissimum corporis membrum est, & ejusdem cum corpore naturæ est; cum humano corpori humanum, non cervinum caput jungatur, & arctissimam cum corpore necessitudinem habet, & reliquorum corporis organici membrorum functiones varias dirigit atque gubernat, & in officio continet : sed etiam singula illa Christo convenire, & ad Ecclesiæ salutem pertinere, Scriptura testatur.
units.tr: IV. Christ is called Head in five principal ways: with respect to his dignity above the other members of the body; with respect to communion of nature; with respect to conjunction with the Church; with respect to the dependence of the Church on Christ the head; and with respect to the government of the whole body, or the Church. For the likeness between Christ and the natural head does not consist only in these points, namely that the head is the most worthy member of the body and of the same nature as the body (since a human head, not a deer's head, is joined to a human body), that it has the closest connection with the body, and that it directs and governs the various functions of the other organic members of the body and keeps them in order. Scripture also testifies that each of these things belongs to Christ and pertains to the salvation of the Church.

units.la: V. Caput igitur Christus est respectu dignitatis supra membra reliqua corporis, quia omnibus Ecclesiæ membris prælatus, supra μετόχους consortes suos oleo lætitiæ unctus, Psal. XLV. 7. Hebr. I. 8. 9. major Angelis factus, ibid. vers. 4. primogenitus inter multos fratres, Rom. VIII. 29. & πάσης κτίσεως omnis creaturæ, Col. I. 15. hoc est, Filius unigenitus, & sic primus omnium, cum cæteri sint κτίσεις creaturæ ipsius, πρὸ πάντων ante omnes, & πρωτεύων ἐν πᾶσι primas tenens in omnibus, ibid. v. 17. 18. Hoc sensu Christus dicitur caput viri, 1. Cor. XI. 3. Respectu communionis naturæ Caput dicitur, quia μέτοχοί Capros καὶ αἵματος particeps est carnis & sanguinis, sicut & pueri, membra corporis ejus, Hebr. II. 14. qui propterea etiam ἀδελφοί fratres ejus, Rom. VIII. 29. appellantur. Quam naturæ communionem Apostolus ex datione ילדים παιδίων puerorum, seu filiorum hominis, Esaj. VIII. 18. conficit, nempe ut eos, ceu suos asseret, & liberaret, Hebr. II. 13. 14. Sanctificans enim & sanctificati ex uno sunt, ibid. v. 11. quomodo etiam ἀπαρχή de eodem φυράματι, eadem massa sunt, 1. Cor. XV. 20. Ex hac naturæ communione in Christo est jus & officium Ecclesiam dirigendi, ceu corpus suum, redimendi, in membris vero ejus jus & competentia recipiendi ea, quæ capitis sunt. Et propter eandem communionem Christus ceu Caput, & Adamus secundus, Sponsor, Sacerdos &c. totum corpus repræsentat. Respectu conjunctionis cum Ecclesia, quæ ex communione naturæ sequitur, Caput Christus dicitur, quia sicut capitis naturalis, membri illius primarii & principis, cum membris infirmioribus omnibus &
units.tr: V. Christ is therefore the Head with respect to his dignity above the other members of the body, because he is set above all the members of the Church, anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions (μέτοχοι) (Ps. 45:7; Heb. 1:8–9), made greater than the angels (ibid. v. 4), the firstborn among many brethren (Rom. 8:29), and firstborn of every creature (πάσης κτίσεως) (Col. 1:15), that is, the only-begotten Son, and thus first of all, since the others are creatures of his; "before all things" (πρὸ πάντων), and "holding the first place in all things" (πρωτεύων ἐν πᾶσι) (ibid. vv. 17–18). In this sense Christ is called the head of the man (1 Cor. 11:3). He is called Head with respect to communion of nature, because he is a partaker (μέτοχος) of flesh and blood, as are the children, who are members of his body (Heb. 2:14); for this reason they are also called his brethren (ἀδελφοί) (Rom. 8:29). The Apostle proves this communion of nature from the giving of the "children" (παιδία) or sons of men, "the children" [יְלָדִים] (Isa. 8:18), namely that he might claim them and deliver them as his own (Heb. 2:13–14). For "he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one" (Heb. 2:11). Likewise they are of the same lump (ἀπαρχή from the same φύραμα), the same mass (1 Cor. 15:20).
