From this communion of nature in Christ comes the right and duty of directing the Church as his own body and of redeeming it, and, in his members, the right and authority to receive what belongs to the head. And because of this same communion, Christ as Head, and as the second Adam, Surety, Priest, etc., represents the whole body.

units.la: singulis corpus integrantibus arctissima necessitudo intercedit, propter quam vita à capite tanquam fonte in reliqua membra derivatur, & caput corpori vitam, sensum & motum impertitur : ita Christus, caput Ecclesiæ suæ arctissimè cum eadem conjungitur, ut nec Filius Dei sine Ecclesia, nec Ecclesia sine Filio Dei sit, neque vel Christus Ecclesiam abnegare, membra sua abjicere vel calcare, vel Ecclesia Christo carere, vel sine eo vitam sperare posset. Nam vivit Christus in Ecclesia, & Ecclesia in fide Christi capitis sui vivit, Gal. II. 20. Et frequenter in Christo esse, vivere, manere, cum eo pati, resurgere, vivificari, glorificari dicimur. Sicut enim caput sine corpore, & corpus sine capite mutilum, & nec corpus, nec caput est : ita Christus sine Ecclesia Christus, & Ecclesia sine Christo Ecclesia esse non potest. Ideo Deus Pater dedit nos Filio, & ipsi conjunxit tum propositio gratiæ ante jacta mundi fundamenta, ut primogenitus inter multos fratres esset, Rom. VIII. 29. tum uno spiritu, 1. Cor. XII. 13. qui fidem operatur, ut in ipso simus, ibid. I. 30. & Ipse in nobis, Ephes. III. 17. Ex qua conjunctione & unione Christi & Ecclesiæ, bonorum etiam & donorum Christi communio sequitur. Ideo etiam Christus Ecclesiæ caput est respectu dependentiæ Ecclesiæ, ceu corporis, à se, ceu capite. Nempe caput in hominibus radicis instar habet. Christus autem est radix Jesse & Davidis, Esaj. XI. 10. Apoc. V. 5. & sic omnium Sanctorum, Joh. XV. 1. Membra porro mystici corporis à Christo capite suo dependent, tum quatenus sunt, & ad ipsum, & propter ipsum, ceu ejus populus peculiaris, semen & hæreditas promissa & postulanti data, sunt, atque in ipsum vocantur & colliguntur : tum quatenus membra Ecclesiæ per varia charismata, ministeria & operationes distinguit, & cuique mensuram fidei, operationis & gloriæ admetitur, atque ita καταρτισμὸν & Σωμάτων concinnationem corporis per multas partes molitur, Ephes. IV. 12. tum quatenus membra corporis συναρμολογεῖ coaptat, & velut εἰς ἁρμογὴν compagem colligit, ut velut membra ad invicem, 1. Cor. XII. 27. utilitatem sibi mutuò impertiantur & recipiant : tum quatenus totum corpus συμβιβάζει compingit & coagmentat, ne pars à parte secedat, & sic corpus diffluat, sed ut sit unum; unde κεφαλὴ γωνίας caput anguli, & summus lapis angularis, qui ædificium totum continet, Psal. CXVIII. 22. Matth. XXI. 42. Ephes. II. 20. appellatur : tum quatenus, ceu fons irriguus, & semper saliens corpori suo subjecto ἐπιχορηγεῖ suppeditat Spiritum & operationem, & quidem διὰ τῶν ἁφῶν καὶ συνδέσμων per junctiuras & vincula, non quòd alii immediatè, alii mediatè à Christo dependeant, sed quia, sicut omnia membra Spiritum per nervos ex capite accipiunt, ita membra Ecclesiæ sibi invicem spiritualia charismata communicant, ut bonis Christi abundent, ita ut Christi sit ἐπιχορηγία suppeditatio omnis, at membrorum ad se invicem διακονία ministerium; Ephes. IV. 15. 16. Col. II. 19. tum denique quatenus sic Ecclesiam, ceu ædificium, Templum & corpus suum αὐξάνει crescere facit, & velut summus angularis lapis corpus suum εἰς πᾶν πλήρωμα Θεοῦ ad omnem plenitudinem Dei educit, Eph. II. 21. IV. 16. Col. II. 19. Denique Christus Ecclesiæ caput est respectu regiminis & dominii, quod ceu Rex & Dominus erga Ecclesiam gerit. Ideo caput Ecclesiæ datus dicitur super omnia, Ephes. I. 22. & post resurrectionem & ascensionem in Cælum, velut Regali in solio collocatus, & universo mundo, ceu summus Ecclesiæ dux, rector & caput, ostensus, omnem potestatem in Cælo & in terra accepit, Matth. XXVIII. 18. qua sibi efficaciter omnia subjicere, Phil. III. 21. & in communi gubernatione universi omnia ad bonum Ecclesiæ ordinare I. Cor. III. 21. 22. 23. potest.
units.tr: Between Christ and the individual members that make up his body there is a most intimate bond. By it life flows from the head, as from a fountain, into the remaining members, and the head gives the body life, sensation and motion. So Christ, the head of his Church, is joined to it most closely, so that the Son of God cannot be without the Church, nor the Church without the Son of God. Christ could not deny his Church, cast off or trample on his members, and the Church could not lack Christ or hope for life without him. For Christ lives in the Church, and the Church lives by the faith of Christ its head, Gal. 2:20. And we are often said to be in Christ, to live, remain, and suffer with him, to rise, be quickened and be glorified in him. For as a head without a body, or a body without a head, is maimed and is neither body nor head, so Christ cannot be Christ without the Church, nor the Church be the Church without Christ. Therefore God the Father gave us to the Son and joined us to him, both by the grace purposed before the foundation of the world, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers, Rom. 8:29, and by one Spirit, 1 Cor. 12:13, who works faith, so that we may be in him, ibid. 1:30, and he in us, Eph. 3:17. From this conjunction and union of Christ and the Church there follows also the communion of Christ's goods and gifts. Christ is therefore the head of the Church also with respect to the dependence of the Church, as body, upon him as head. Indeed, in human beings the head takes the place of a root, and Christ is the root of Jesse and David, Isa. 11:10; Rev. 5:5, and so of all the saints, John 15:1. The members of the mystical body depend on Christ their head in several ways: first, insofar as they belong to him and are for him, being his peculiar people, the seed and promised inheritance given to whoever asks, and are called and gathered into him; second, insofar as he distinguishes the members of the Church by various gifts, ministries and operations, assigns to each a measure of faith, of working and of glory, and so brings about the [katartismon] equipping and the [sōmatōn] building up of the body through its many parts, Eph. 4:12; third, insofar as he [synarmologei] fits the members of the body together and gathers them [eis harmogēn] into a joint, so that the members mutually share and receive help from one another, 1 Cor. 12:27; fourth, insofar as he [symbibazei] knits and binds the whole body together, so that no part separates from another and the body dissolves, but it remains one; whence he is called [kephalē gōnias], the head of the corner, and the chief cornerstone which holds the whole building together, Ps. 118:22; Matt. 21:42; Eph. 2:20; fifth, insofar as, like a fountain that waters and always flows, he [epichorēgei] supplies the Spirit and working to his body, and indeed [dia tōn haphōn kai syndesmōn], through joints and ligaments. This is not because some members depend on Christ immediately and others mediately, but because, just as all members receive the Spirit from the head through the nerves, so the members of the Church communicate spiritual gifts to one another, so that they abound in the goods of Christ; thus all supply comes from Christ, but the [diakonia] service is the ministry of the members to one another, Eph. 4:15–16; Col. 2:19. Finally, insofar as he so makes the Church, as building, temple and his own body, to [auxanei] grow, and as the chief cornerstone he leads his body [eis pan plērōma Theou] to the full measure of God, Eph. 2:21; 4:16; Col. 2:19. Lastly, Christ is the head of the Church with respect to the rule and dominion which he exercises over the Church as King and Lord. Therefore he is said to be given as head of the Church [super omnia], over all things, Eph. 1:22; and after his resurrection and ascension into heaven, set upon a royal throne and shown to the whole world as the supreme leader, ruler and head of the Church, he has received all power in heaven and on earth, Matt. 28:18, by which he can effectively subject all things to himself, Phil. 3:21, and in the general government of the universe order all things for the good of the Church, 1 Cor. 3:21–23.

units.la: VI. Christus ergo caput est, quia & prior atque dignior omnibus creaturis, fratribus inprimis, quorum primogenitus est: & corpori Ecclesiæ (σώματι) seu ejusdem naturæ participes, ac proin etiam redemptor, vindex, salvator ejusdem, æquè illud repræsentans, ceu Adamus secundus, atque Adamus primus totum genus humanum repræsentavit, ut quæcunque ei, ceu capiti, competunt, etiam corporis sint, & esse reputentur: & Ecclesiæ conjunctissimus, atque ab ea in vita & morte individuus, vivens in corpore, & , ceu fons vitæ, eidem vitam impertiens: & in corpus suum sic influens, ut ei Spiritum suum, & Spiritus sui charismata impertiatur, & per charismata atque ministeria membris Ecclesiæ πολυποικίλως distributa, Ecclesiam, ejusque membra ad usus mutuos aptet, totúmque corpus in unitatem spiritus & fidei compingat, lætisque indies incrementis, ad consummationem usque beet: & denique, ceu Dominus & Rex Ecclesiæ, membrorum Ecclesiæ functiones omnes dirigat, gubernet, & in officio contineat. Qua postrema assimilatione maximè Ecclesiæ visibilis politia & gubernatio in terris attenditur, utpote qua sedens ad dextram Patris illam militantem in terris defendit & protegit, per (συμπαθείαν) illam, qua caput corpori condolet. Ecclesiæ salutem sacerdotali intercessione procurat, Hebr. II. 17. IV. 15. 16. in Regii muneris functione Angelos bonos, ceu spiritus ministrantes, ad salutis Ecclesiæ ministerium adhibet, Hebr. I. 14. malos sub pedibus Ecclesiæ conterit, Rom. XVI. 20. & Ecclesiæ ipsi de operariis illam ædificantibus prospicit, Ephes. IV. 11. 12. &c. In primo similitudinis gradu ipsi, ceu capiti, τὰ πρωτεῖα primatus dignitatis supra consortes: in secundo primatus atque prærogativa amoris, meriti & beneficentiæ erga Ecclesiam: in tertio & quarto primatus seu influxus, velut fontis vitæ spiritualis in Ecclesiam universam, omniúmque donorum spiritualium five ad vitam & gloriam singulorum membrorum, sive ad officii privati & publici uniuscujusque ad salutem totius corporis (ἐπιχορηγία) suppeditatio: in quinto denique primatus seu potius principatus supra omnia, ad salutem Ecclesiæ, & gloriæ suæ amplificationem, asseritur. Quæ omnia cùm in Christum cadant, longè perfectiùs Ecclesiæ, tanquam comparis sibi corporis, caput est, quàm naturali in corpore primatus & principatus capiti datus est. Unde non naturali duntaxat Capitis, sed etiam œconomica Sponsi, Viri, Patris, Domini, politica Regis, denique artificiali Petræ, Vitis, Fundamenti, Lapidis angularis similitudine in Scripturis repræsentatur. Quæ omnia unitatem Capitis Ecclesiæ clarissimè demonstrant, quia nec naturale caput, nisi monstrosum, multiplex est; & quæ Christo capiti, Sponso, Regi, Domino, &c. competunt, merè Divina, uni soli que Christo conveniunt. Et S. Paulus dicens: Sicut corpus unum est, & præditum multis membris, omnia autem membra corporis unius, multa cùm sint, unum corpus sunt: sic & Christus, I. Cor. XII. 12. Christum vocat hoc totum, quod Christi est, sicut Regem visum à nobis dicimus, cùm faciem ejus vidimus, cui vestitum accensemus. Ut sic totum illud corpus mysticum Christo solo capite & membris ejus absolvatur. De quo plura inferius.
units.tr: VI. Christ is therefore the head: first, because he is prior to and more worthy than all creatures, and especially than the brothers, of whom he is the firstborn; second, because he shares the nature of the body of the Church [sōma], and so is also its redeemer, avenger and saviour, representing it just as the second Adam, as the first Adam represented the whole human race, so that whatever belongs to him as head belongs to the body too and is accounted to be its own; third, because he is most intimately joined to the Church and is inseparable from it in life and death, living in the body and, as the fountain of life, imparting life to it; fourth, because he so flows into his body that he gives it his Spirit and the gifts of his Spirit, and through the gifts and ministries distributed in manifold ways among the members of the Church, he fits the Church and its members for mutual service, binds the whole body into unity of Spirit and faith, and brings it on, with joyful increase day by day, to its consummation; and finally, as Lord and King of the Church, he directs and governs all the functions of the Church's members and keeps them in their duty. By this last comparison the visible polity and government of the Church on earth is especially noted, since, sitting at the right hand of the Father, he defends and protects the militant Church on earth through that [sympatheia], that fellow feeling by which the head suffers with the body. He secures the salvation of the Church by his priestly intercession, Heb. 2:17; 4:15–16; in the exercise of his kingly office he employs good angels, as ministering spirits, for the ministry of the Church's salvation, Heb. 1:14; he crushes evil powers under the feet of the Church, Rom. 16:20; and he provides for the Church in respect of the workers who build it, Eph. 4:11–12, etc. In the first degree of likeness, the [prōteia], the primacy of dignity, belongs to him as head above his fellows; in the second, the primacy and pre-eminence of love, merit and beneficence towards the Church; in the third and fourth, the primacy or influence, as of a fountain of spiritual life into the whole Church, and the supply [epichorēgia] of all spiritual gifts, both for the life and glory of individual members and for the salvation of the whole body through each one's private and public office; and in the fifth and last, primacy, or rather principate, over all things is claimed for the salvation of the Church and the enlargement of his own glory. All these things, since they fall upon Christ, belong to him far more perfectly as head of the Church, his fellow body, than the primacy and principate given to the head in the natural body. Hence he is represented in the Scriptures not only by the likeness of a natural head, but also by that of a household Bridegroom, Husband, Father and Lord, a political King, and finally by the artificial images of Rock, Vine, Foundation and Cornerstone. All of these clearly demonstrate the unity of the head of the Church, because a natural head, unless it is a monstrosity, is not multiple; and what belongs to Christ as head, Bridegroom, King, Lord and so on, is purely divine and belongs to Christ alone. St. Paul, saying, "As the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the one body, though many, are one body: so also is Christ," 1 Cor. 12:12, calls this whole, which belongs to Christ, by Christ's name, just as we say that we have seen the king when we have seen his face, to which we add his clothing. So the whole mystical body is completed by Christ alone as head, together with his members. More on this below.

units.la: VII. Regimen Ecclesiæ Ministeriale illud est, quo Deus Ecclesiam suam è mundo collectam, hominum ministerio regit & tuetur. Nam Deus alios quidem constituit in Ecclesia primùm Apostolos, deinde Prophetas, tertiò doctores, postea virtutes, deinde dona sanationum, item opitulationes, gubernationes, genera linguarum, I. Cor. XII. 28. Ubi κυβερνήσεις gubernationes, seu directiones, ποιμένες Pastores aliósque, qui constituti sunt propter eos, qui se ipsos regere non possunt, adeóque παιδαγωγούς in Christo, & παιδεύτας in justitia exercentibus opus habent, significant. Quæ sic alibi Apostolus exprimit: Ipse dedit quidem alios Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, alios Evangelistas, alios vero Pastores & doctores, ad concinnationem Sanctorum, ad opus ministerii, ad ædificationem corporis Christi, donec perveniamus omnes ad unitatem fidei & cognitionem Filii Dei, ad virum perfectum, ad mensuram staturæ ejus, quod completur à Christo, Ephes. IV. 11. 12. 13. Sunt etiam ἐξουσίαι ὑπὸ Θεοῦ πεπυγμέναι potestates à Deo ordinatæ, Rom. XIII. 1. quæ quandoque etiam Ecclesiæ non tantum hospitia, sed etiam nutritiæ sunt, Esaj. XLIX. 23.
units.tr: VII. The ministerial government of the Church is that by which God rules and protects his Church, gathered out of the world, through the ministry of men. For God has indeed set some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, also helps, governments [κυβερνήσεις], kinds of tongues, 1 Cor. 12:28. Here "governments" or "directions" [κυβερνήσεις], "pastors" [ποιμένες], and others appointed for those who cannot govern themselves, and so need "guides" [παιδαγωγούς] in Christ and "instructors" [παιδεύτας] in righteousness, are meant. The Apostle expresses this elsewhere: "He himself gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ; until we all come to the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ," Eph. 4:11-13. There are also powers ordained by God [ἐξουσίαι ὑπὸ Θεοῦ τεταγμέναι], Rom. 13:1, which are sometimes not only guests but also nurses of the Church, Isa. 49:23.

units.la: VIII. Emergit hinc distinctio regiminis seu gubernationis Ecclesiæ externæ. Nam aliud Ecclesiasticum, aliud Civile & Politicum est. Regimen Ecclesiæ Ecclesiasticum est, quo Dei Ecclesia per personas Ecclesiasticas, Dei Christiq, ceu Capitis Ecclesiæ unici, ministras, juxta verbum ejus & canones Ecclesiasticos ei congruentes, docetur, curatur, & gubernatur. Dari verò ejusmodi regimen, seu, uti alii vocant, politiam Ecclesiæ, ab interno & spirituali, nec non externo, Divino, principali & civili disparatum, perperam nonnulli sive rerum imperiti, sive pravo adversus Ecclesiam affectu imbuti inficiantur. Nam Deus ipse in V. T. accuratissimam & operosissimam Ecclesiasticî regiminis formam definivit & descripsit. Christus quoque & Apostoli in N. T. Ecclesiam certis legibus, certóque ordine gubernationis constituerunt, uti historiæ Evangelistarum & Apostolorum, nec non Epistolæ Apostolicæ testificantur. Nam in iis & Deus perhibetur author ordinis in omnibus Ecclesiis, I. Cor. XIV. 33. 40. & εὐταξία ubique præcipitur & urgetur, I. Tim. III. 14. 15. Tit. I. 5. & passim quicquid ἄταξον inordinatum est, damnatur. Ecclesia quoque vocatur Regnum Dei & Cœlorum, Matth. XIII. 24. &c. XXV. 1. &c. Domus Dei, I. Tim. III. 14. 15. Ejus Rex & Caput Christus est, Psal. II. 6. Matth. XXI. 5. Joh. XVIII. 36. Ministri œconomi, Apostoli, Pastores, Doctores, Eph.IV. 11. Et in eadem Ecclesia alii præsunt, alii subsunt, alii κυβερνῶσι gubernant, 1.Cor. XII.28. προϊστάμενοι præsunt, Rom.XII.8. 1.Thess. V.12. 1.Tim.V.17. ἡγούμενοι ducunt, Heb. XIII.7. 17. alii πείθονται obediunt & ὑπείκουσιν cedunt, ibid. XIII.17. Utrosque autem certis legum vinculis & nervis connecti necesse est. Quid verò multis? Omnes regiminis & politiæ cujusdam causæ adsunt. Adest Rex & Dominus Ecclesiæ Christus, cum plenissima potestate actu regnans, Psal. CX. 1.2. Matth. XXVIII. 18. 19. Adsunt Ministri ejus Apostoli, Pastores, alii. Adsunt leges regiminis, verbum Dei, atque illud Legis & Evangelii. Adsunt personæ Ecclesiasticæ communione comprehensæ, sive præsint, sive subsint, nec non res, doctrina, cæremoniæ, disciplina; & rerum illarum ad certas personas, earundemque ad destinata officia adaptatio, ut inde Ecclesiæ ordo & gubernatio legitima, verbo Dei consentanea emergat, Exod. XXV.40. 1.Tim.III.15. Tit.I.5. Denique nulla societas sine legibus, politia, & certa gubernationis forma consistere potest. Proin neque Ecclesia, tot in mundo periculis exposita, ea carere potest. Inanis verò metus est, ne sic Ecclesia vel in statum civilem commutetur, vel periculosè cum eo confundatur, vel jus Magistratus civilis per Ecclesiasticos imminuatur. Disparata enim Ecclesia & Politia, atque gubernatio utriusque est, quorum tantum abest, ut altera alteri noxam afferat, ut potius amicè conspirent, & auxiliatrices invicem manus porrigant.
units.tr: VIII. Hence arises the distinction between the government, or administration, of the external Church. For one is ecclesiastical, the other civil and political. The ecclesiastical government of the Church is that by which the Church of God is taught, cared for and governed through ecclesiastical persons, ministers of God and of Christ, the sole Head of the Church, according to his word and the ecclesiastical canons agreeing with it. That such a government exists, or, as others call it, the polity of the Church, distinct from the internal and spiritual, and also from the external, divine, principal and civil, some wrongly deny, either being ignorant of affairs or imbued with a perverse attitude against the Church. For God himself in the Old Testament defined and described the most exact and laborious form of ecclesiastical government. Christ also and the Apostles in the New Testament established the Church under fixed laws and a certain order of government, as the histories of the Evangelists and Apostles and the Apostolic Epistles bear witness. For in them God is also declared to be the author of order in all churches, 1 Cor. 14:33, 40, and good order [εὐταξία] is everywhere commanded and urged, 1 Tim. 3:14-15; Tit. 1:5, and whatever is disorderly [ἄταξον] is everywhere condemned. The Church is also called the Kingdom of God and of heaven, Matt. 13:24 etc.; 25:1 etc. It is the house of God, 1 Tim. 3:14-15. Its King and Head is Christ, Ps. 2:6; Matt. 21:5; John 18:36. Its ministers are stewards, Apostles, Pastors, Teachers, Eph. 4:11. And in the same Church some preside, others are subject, and others govern [κυβερνῶσι], 1 Cor. 12:28; some preside [προϊστάμενοι], Rom. 12:8; 1 Thess. 5:12; 1 Tim. 5:17; some lead [ἡγούμενοι], Heb. 13:7, 17; and others obey [πείθονται] and yield [ὑπείκουσιν], ibid. 13:17. Both must be bound together by fixed bonds and sinews of law. But why say more? All the causes of a government and of a certain polity are present. Christ, the King and Lord of the Church, is present, reigning in fact with the fullest power, Ps. 110:1-2; Matt. 28:18-19. His ministers are present: Apostles, Pastors and others. The laws of government are present: the word of God, that is, Law and Gospel. Ecclesiastical persons, held together in communion, whether ruling or subject, are present, as are the matters, doctrine, ceremonies and discipline; and the adaptation of those things to particular persons, and of those persons to their appointed offices, so that from this the orderly and lawful government of the Church, consonant with the word of God, emerges, Exod. 25:40; 1 Tim. 3:15; Tit. 1:5. Finally, no society can exist without laws, a polity and a fixed form of government. Therefore the Church, exposed to so many dangers in the world, cannot do without it. It is an empty fear that in this way the Church would either be changed into the civil state, or dangerously be confused with it, or the right of the civil magistrate be diminished by ecclesiastical men. For Church and polity, and the government of each, are distinct; and so far is one from harming the other that they rather agree amicably and extend helping hands to one another.

units.la: IX. Regimen Ministeriale Ecclesiæ Ministri ejus non authoritate vel potestate propria, sed Dei Christique, cujus ministri & legati sunt, administrant. Christus enim Ecclesiæ caput unicum, eam κυρίως non tantùm secundum formam ejus spiritualem, quæ in se invisibilis est, sed etiam secundum ejus conditionem externam & visibilem regit. Ab eo quippe est verbum & vocatio, qua Ecclesia colligitur. Ipse distribuit charismata Spiritus sui ad utilitatem totius corporis. Ipse unicuique membro operationem suam assignat, & efficit, ut per charismata & dona à se variè distributa Ecclesiæ structura συναρμολογουμένη coagmentata καταρτισμὸν concinnationem & αὔξησιν incrementum capiat, atque ita crescat in Templum sanctum in Domino, donec perveniamus omnes ad unitatem fidei, &c. Ephes.II.21. IV. 12-16. Charismata illa διακονίας ministeria pariunt; imò ministeria ipsa etiam charismata sunt. Et qualia charismata, talia etiam ministeria sunt. Extraordinaria charismata extraordinaria ministeria: ordinaria verò ordinaria pariunt. Ubi circa charismata duo in universum tenenda sunt. Prius est, quòd qualiscunque ordo sit ministeriorum in Ecclesia, opera enixè danda sit, ne velulla charismata sint εἰς κενὸν in vanum recipiantur, 2.Cor. VI.1. adeóque infrugifera sint, vel varietas & jactatio charismatum ἀκαταστασίαν confusionem vel conturbationem afferat. Non enim omnia, nec omnium dona sunt omnis loci & temporis. Posterius est, quod charismatum ejusmodi, quæ gratiæ gratis datæ vulgò appellantur, diversa ratio sit ab iis, quæ fidelium quorumvis sunt, & gratiarum gratos facientium nomine veniunt. Illa enim non tam ad peculiarem eorum, quibus dantur, salutem, quàm ad communem totius Ecclesiæ usum & ædificationem pertinent. Hæc ad singulorum, quibus dantur, salutem propriam faciunt.
units.tr: IX. Ministers administer the ministerial government of the Church not by their own authority or power, but by the authority of God and Christ, whose ministers and envoys they are. For Christ, the sole Head of the Church, rules it properly [κυρίως], not only according to its spiritual form, which is invisible in itself, but also according to its external and visible condition. From him indeed come the word and the calling by which the Church is gathered. He distributes the gifts of his Spirit for the benefit of the whole body. He assigns his own working to each member, and brings it about that, through the gifts and endowments variously distributed by him, the structure of the Church, fitly joined together [συναρμολογουμένη], receives perfecting [καταρτισμόν] and growth [αὔξησιν], and so "grows into a holy temple in the Lord, until we all come to the unity of faith," etc., Eph. 2:21; 4:12-16. These gifts [charismata] produce ministries [διακονίας]; indeed the ministries themselves are also gifts. And as the gifts are, so are the ministries. Extraordinary gifts produce extraordinary ministries; ordinary gifts produce ordinary ones. Here two points about gifts must be held in general. The first is that, whatever the order of ministries in the Church, care must be taken earnestly that the gifts are not received in vain [εἰς κενὸν], 2 Cor. 6:1, and so remain unfruitful, or that the variety and tossing about of gifts does not bring disorder [ἀκαταστασίαν] or confusion. For not all gifts, nor the gifts of all, belong to every place and time. The second is that gifts of this kind, which are commonly called "graces freely given" (gratiae gratis datae), are of a different nature from those which belong to any of the faithful and go under the name of "graces that make one acceptable" (gratiae gratum facientes). For the former pertain not so much to the personal salvation of those to whom they are given as to the common use and edification of the whole Church; the latter bring about the individual salvation of those to whom they are given.

units.la: X. Charismata juxta atque Ministeria S. Paulus 1.Cor. XII.8-31. distinxit. De charismatis distinctis sic loquitur: Huic per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ (quo sapientia verbi Dei, & fundamenti, atque omnium veritatum cum fundamento coagmentatarum exponitur, idque modò extraordinariè, modò ordinariè, pro ratione revelationis, quæ modò per alloquium, & extraordinariè per inspirationem Divinam, modò ordinariè per studium verbi Dei accipitur) alteri verò sermo cognitionis, (qualis tum φρόνησις prudentia, tum omnis eruditio est) per eundem Spiritum: alii verò fides in eodem Spiritu (assensus omni veritati Divinæ, sive ea per revelationem, sive per naturam, sed non sine fide revelationis, cognoscitur, habitus; quæ fides omnium Christianorum est, vera quippe demonstratio Spiritus S. in mundo, sine qua nec animadverterentur opera Dei, & ex iis Divinitas, & mundus ad idola muta abduceretur) alii verò charismata sanationum in eodem Spiritu (quæ ordinariè, vel extraordinariè dantur) alii verò operationes virtutum (quales sunt resuscitare mortuos, occidere refractarios, &c. quæ nonnisi extra ordinem dantur) alii verò prophetia (intelligentia & sagax explicatio sermonis prophetici, & futurorum etiam explicatio, hoc est, revelatio operum Divinæ providentiæ, quæ in verbo Dei definitè & distinctè revelata non sunt) alii verò discretiones spirituum (prudentia spiritus discernendi, & profunditates Sathanæ penetrandi, idque per verbum Dei ad homines & tempora applicatum, tum per exempla, quæ in Scripturis occurrunt) alii genera linguarum (per quas ab hominibus illiteratis cognitas, uno velut momento Evangelium tot gentibus prædicari potuit, & quarum peritia etiam studio comparari potest, sed non sine Deo, qui ingenium, memoriam, eloquium, præceptores & commoditates largitur, idque inprimis ad usum prophetiæ) alii verò interpretatio linguarum (qualis eorum est, qui populari lingua commodè explicant, quæ incognitis & barbaris linguis scripta vel dicta sunt, licèt linguis iis loqui non possint; & quæ etiam Prophetiæ inservit) 1.Cor. XII. 8.9.10. Quibus addi possunt ἀντλήψεως opitulationes, quales sunt τῶν μεταδιδόντων distribuentium, & quovis modo alios adjuvantium, & velut cum aliis aliquid apprehendentium ad opitulandum invicem; nec non κυβερνήσεως gubernationes, ibid. v.28. & donum illud, quod Apostoli præcipuum habuerunt, ut essent testes resurrectionis Domini.
units.tr: X. St Paul distinguished gifts just as he distinguished ministries, 1 Cor. 12:8-31. He speaks of the distinct gifts thus: "To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom" (by which is set forth the wisdom of the word of God and of the foundation, and of all truths joined together with the foundation; and this is received sometimes extraordinarily, sometimes ordinarily, according to the manner of revelation: extraordinarily by divine inspiration, through speech, and ordinarily through the study of the word of God); "to another the word of knowledge" (such as is both prudence [φρόνησις] and all learning); "by the same Spirit; to others faith in the same Spirit" (a habit of assent to all divine truth, whether it is known by revelation or by nature, but not without faith in revelation. This faith belongs to all Christians, for it is the true demonstration of the Holy Spirit in the world, without which the works of God would not be noticed, and from which the Divinity would be recognised, and the world would be led away to dumb idols); "to others gifts of healings in the same Spirit" (which are given ordinarily or extraordinarily); "to others the working of miracles" (such as raising the dead, striking down the obstinate, and so on, which are given only beyond the ordinary course); "to others prophecy" (understanding and shrewd explanation of prophetic speech, and also explanation of future events, that is, revelation of the works of divine providence which are not definitely and distinctly revealed in the word of God); "to others the discerning of spirits" (the prudence to discern spirits and to penetrate the depths of Satan, and this through the word of God applied to men and times, and also through the examples that occur in the Scriptures); "to others kinds of tongues" (by which the Gospel could be preached to so many nations, in a single moment, in languages known to unlettered men; the skill in which can also be acquired by study, but not without God, who bestows talent, memory, eloquence, teachers and opportunities; and this especially for the use of prophecy); "to others the interpretation of tongues" (such as belongs to those who suitably explain in the common language what has been written or spoken in unknown and barbarous tongues, even though they cannot speak those tongues; and this too serves prophecy), 1 Cor. 12:8-10. To these may be added helps [ἀντλήψεως], such as those of distributors and of those who in any way assist others, and as it were take hold together with others to help one another; also governments [κυβερνήσεως], ibid. v. 28; and that gift which the Apostles held in special measure, that they should be witnesses of the Lord's resurrection.

units.la: XI. Juxta charismata hæc etiam διακονίας ministeria sic Apostolus distinguit. Vos autem estis corpus Christi, & membra invicem (quorum singula privum & singulare aliquid habent, quo aliis prosint, Christum glorificent, ut per aliorum operam & ζωοποιεῖν, Dei autem ἐνεργεια omnes & singuli gratiam aliquam accipiant, atque sic ἀνθ' ὧν χαρισμάτων mutua gratiarum communicatio, Rom.I.11. obtineat) Et alios quidem posuit Deus in Ecclesia πρῶτον primò (propter pter ordinem necessitatis & utilitatis) quidem Apostolos (testes resurrectionis Domini ad omnes homines, sub quibus etiam Evangelistæ intelliguntur, quod ministerium directè & primò ordinatum est ad fidem, quæ per Spiritum filiationis omnibus membris datur) secundò Prophetas (interpretes Prophetiarum V. T. Ephes. II. 20. quorum donum necessarium erat, ut prædicatio de Christo & justitia in promissione & prophetia præcedente fundamentum haberet) tertiò Doctores (qui sermonem sapientiæ & cognitionis habent) postea virtutes, (Thaumaturgos, quia prædicatio Evangelii propter infideles omnibus signis & potentiis comitata procedere debuit) deinde dona sanationum, opitulationes, gubernationes, genera linguarum, 1. Cor. XII.28. Quæ ministeria divisa esse, statim sic probat: An omnes Apostoli? An omnes Prophetæ? (sic ut & donum & ministerium explicandæ & applicandæ Prophetiæ acceperint) An omnes doctores? An omnes virtutes? An omnes dona habent sanationum? An omnes linguis loquuntur? An omnes interpretantur? ibid. vers. 29. 30. Idem verò S. Paulus alibi ministeria, quæ δόματα dona appellat, quia sine charismate nullum ministerium est, & illa ad completionem totius corporis nonnisi Christi donantis voluntate obtingere possunt; recensens, sic illa distinguit: Et ipse dedit alios quidem Apostolos, alios autem Prophetas, alios verò Evangelistas, alios verò Pastores (pascentes sive curantes gregem, vel regendo tantùm, vel regendo atque docendo) & doctores (qui ab omnibus audita narrant, indicant, in memoriam revocant, & ex iis veritates demonstrant) Ephes. IV. 11. Ubi priora ministeria posteriora includunt; sed non vicissim. Nam Apostoli etiam, Prophetæ, Evangelistæ, Pastores & Doctores fuerunt; sed non quivis Prophetæ, Evangelistæ, Pastores & Doctores Apostoli sunt. Ita Prophetæ possunt esse Evangelistæ, Pastores & Doctores, sed non vicissim quivis Doctores, Pastores, etiam Prophetæ iunt, quatenus Propheta is est, qui ea, quæ facta prædicantur, fieri sic debuisse & facta esse, ex Prophetiis & eventu demonstrat. Evangelistæ etiam, seu scriptores historiæ Christi per singularem assistentiam & gratiam Spiritus S. nec non comites & cooperarii Apostolorum Pastores etiam & Doctores esse potuerunt. Denique Pastores, saltem qui laborant in verbo, etiam Doctores sunt. Vicissim nec Doctores, quà tales, vel Pastores, vel Evangelistæ, vel Prophetæ, vel Apostoli: nec Pastores, quà tales, etiam Evangelistæ, Prophetæ & Apostoli: nec Evangelistæ, quà tales, Prophetæ & Apostoli: nec Prophetæ, quà tales, etiam Apostoli sunt & fuerunt.
units.tr: XI. In keeping with these gifts, the Apostle also distinguishes the ministries [διακονίας] in this way: You, however, are the body of Christ, and members of one another (each of which has its own particular and individual gift, by which it may benefit others and glorify Christ, so that through the work of others they may give life [ζωοποιεῖν], and by the operation [ἐνεργεια] of God all and each receive some grace, and thus a mutual sharing of gifts [ἀνθ' ὧν χαρισμάτων] is obtained, Rom. 1.11). And God has set some in the Church, first [πρῶτον] (first, in the order of necessity and usefulness) apostles (witnesses of the resurrection of the Lord to all men, under whom the evangelists are also understood, a ministry directly and primarily ordained for faith, which is given to all the members through the Spirit of adoption); secondly, prophets (interpreters of the prophecies of the Old Testament, Eph. 2.20, whose gift was necessary so that the preaching about Christ and righteousness might have a foundation in the promise and in the prior prophecy); thirdly, teachers (who have the word of wisdom and of knowledge); after these, powers (wonder-workers, because the preaching of the Gospel, on account of unbelievers, ought to proceed accompanied by signs and powers in all things); then the gifts of healings, helps, governments, kinds of tongues, 1 Cor. 12.28. He immediately proves that these ministries are distinct, saying: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? (so that they received both the gift and the ministry of explaining and applying prophecy) Are all teachers? Are all workers of miracles? Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret? ibid. verses 29, 30. But the same St. Paul elsewhere, enumerating the ministries, which he calls gifts [δόματα], because there is no ministry without a gift, and these can come to the completion of the whole body only by the will of Christ who gives them, distinguishes them thus: And he himself gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, some pastors (feeding or caring for the flock, either by ruling only, or by ruling and teaching) and teachers (who recount what has been heard by all, point out, call back to memory, and from these demonstrate truths), Eph. 4.11. Here the earlier ministries include the later ones, but not conversely. For apostles were also prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers; but not every prophet, evangelist, pastor and teacher is an apostle. Thus prophets can be evangelists, pastors and teachers, but not conversely is every teacher or pastor also a prophet, insofar as a prophet is one who demonstrates from the prophecies and the outcome that the things which are predicted as done ought so to have been done and have been done. Evangelists, that is, the writers of the history of Christ, through the singular assistance and grace of the Holy Spirit, and also the companions and co-workers of the apostles, could also be pastors and teachers. Finally, pastors, at least those who labour in the Word, are also teachers. Conversely, teachers as such are not pastors, evangelists, prophets or apostles; nor are pastors as such evangelists, prophets and apostles; nor are evangelists as such prophets and apostles; nor are prophets as such apostles, though they may be and have been.

units.la: XII. Refert autem cognoscere, quæ charismata & ministeria in Ecclesia extraordinaria & temporaria: quæ ordinaria & perpetua esse debuerint. Charismata extraordinaria seu temporaria alia ad cognitionem, alia ad sermonem, alia ad operationem referuntur. Ad cognitionem refertur tum Prophetia, quatenus futurorum prædictionem, & infallibilem prophetiarum explicationem continet: tum infallibilis spiritum discretio, qua spiritus singulari perspicacia & ἀγχινοία prompté & infalliblier discernuntur. Ad sermonem dona linguarum, quatenus illæ sine studio & industria cognoscuntur, & interpretationis infallibilis referuntur. Ad operationem dona sanationum & virtutum pertinent. Cùm enim quæ humanæ mentis cognitionem superant, humana ratione confirmari nequeant, adhibenda ejusmodi opera sunt, quæ vires humanas, totiúsque naturæ transcendentia, prophetias, tanquam Divina quadam demonstratione, confirment. Atque hæc charismata ad Ecclesiæ inchoationem & plantationem distribuere Deo placuit. Reliqua charismata ordinaria & perpetua sunt, cujusmodi sunt tum Prophetia, quatenus prophetiarum explicatio per demonstrationem sensus earum est: tum sermo sapientiæ & cognitionis, sive prudentiæ, quo sapientia Divina explicatur, veritas demonstratur, via vitæ indicatur, bonum eligitur, malum vitatur, tum fides, qua testimonio de rebus Divinis, veritate operum Dei, Christo & justitia assentimur: tum genera linguarum, quatenus earum cognitio arte, studio & disciplina acquiritur: tum interpretatio linguarum, quatenus peregrinæ linguæ studio & usu cognitæ populari sermone exponuntur: discretiones spirituum, quatenus illi singulari studio & sagacitate juxta verbum Dei & exempla in Scripturis extantia, sine dono infallibilitatis, discernuntur: Ἀντλήψεις opitulationes mutuæ: denique gubernationes, quibus ii, qui Ecclesiæ præsunt, eandem gubernant & dirigunt. Differentiam illam donorum tum experientia & usus, tum ratio ædificandæ Ecclesiæ, cui dona inservire debuerunt, demonstrat. Cessarunt enim diu in Ecclesia prophetia infallibilis, dona linguarum, sanationum, virtutum & infallibilis discretionis spirituum, quæ Evangelium primitus prædicatum mundo commendare, & velut sigillis quibusdam munire debuerunt, ut sic Christus in mundo crederetur. Reliqua perennant, & perennare debuerunt, quia sine iis homines verbo Dei conservando, propagando, prædicando & applicando ministrare non potuissent.
units.tr: XII. It is worth knowing which gifts and ministries in the Church were extraordinary and temporary, and which ought to be ordinary and perpetual. The extraordinary or temporary gifts relate some to knowledge, some to speech, some to action. To knowledge belong prophecy, insofar as it contains the prediction of future things and the infallible explanation of prophecies, and the infallible discerning of spirits, by which spirits are discerned promptly and infallibly by singular perspicacity and quickness of judgement. To speech belong the gifts of tongues, insofar as these are known without study and effort, and the infallible gift of interpretation. To action belong the gifts of healing and miracles. For since those things which exceed the knowledge of the human mind cannot be confirmed by human reason, works of this kind must be employed which transcend human powers and the whole of nature, to confirm the prophecies as a kind of divine demonstration. And God was pleased to distribute these gifts for the beginning and planting of the Church. The remaining gifts are ordinary and perpetual, and of this kind are: prophecy, insofar as the explanation of prophecies is their demonstration of meaning; the word of wisdom and of knowledge, or prudence, by which divine wisdom is explained, truth is demonstrated, the way of life is pointed out, good is chosen and evil avoided; faith, by which we assent to the testimony concerning divine things, the truth of God's works, Christ and righteousness; the kinds of tongues, insofar as their knowledge is acquired by art, study and discipline; the interpretation of tongues, insofar as a foreign language known by study and practice is expounded in the common speech; the discernings of spirits, insofar as these are distinguished by singular diligence and sagacity according to the Word of God and the examples extant in Scripture, without the gift of infallibility; mutual helps [ἀντλήψεις]; and finally governments, by which those who preside over the Church govern and direct it. The experience and practice, and the purpose of building up the Church, which the gifts ought to serve, demonstrate this distinction of gifts. For the infallible prophecy, the gifts of tongues, of healing, of miracles, and of infallible discernment of spirits, which were to commend the Gospel when first preached to the world and to fortify it as with certain seals, so that Christ might thus be believed in the world, ceased in the Church long ago. The rest remain, and ought to remain, because without them men could not minister to the preservation, propagation, preaching and application of the Word of God.

units.la: XIII. Charismatum differentia ministeriorum etiam differentiam pandit. Nam extraordinaria ministeria sunt, quæ & quatenus charismata extraordinaria requirunt. Ejusmodi ministeria sunt Prophetarum, Apostolorum & Evangelistarum. De Prophetis & Prophetia alibi Loc. XII. 46-60. plusculà diximus. Apostoli, testes resurrectionis Christi, Divino suffragio designati, virtute ex alto induti, signis & distributione Spiritus S. comitati, ad verbum Dei sine errore in omnibus gentibus, sermone vel etiam scripto, ad perpetuum Ecclesiæ N. T. usum in prophetando, prædicando, & ad fideles ubique in cœtum colligendos, & eum cœtum ordinandum missi sunt. Quorum ministerium quoad effectum in perpetuum durat, at quoad functionem cessat, quia Christus & Evangelium per eos annuntiatum, Lex Dei in medio Israelis totius sic posita est, ut voluntas Dei ignorari amplius non possit. De iisdem & temporario eorundem ministerio Loc. XX. 83-98. fusius etiam egimus. Sed & de Prophetis N. T. & quatenus eorum munus ordinarium, vel extraordinarium fuerit, ibid. § 99. nec non de Evangelistis, ibid. § 100. quantum satis est, diximus. Ordinaria verò ministeria
units.tr: XIII. The difference of gifts also reveals the difference of ministries. For the extraordinary ministries are those which require, and insofar as they require, extraordinary gifts. Such ministries are those of the prophets, apostles and evangelists. We have spoken at some length about prophets and prophecy elsewhere, Loc. 12, §§ 46–60. The apostles, witnesses of the resurrection of Christ, designated by divine suffrage, clothed with power from on high, accompanied by signs and by the distribution of the Holy Spirit, were sent to proclaim the Word of God without error to all nations, by speech or also in writing, for the perpetual use of the Church of the New Testament in prophesying and preaching, and to gather the faithful everywhere into an assembly and to order that assembly. Their ministry endures perpetually as to its effect, but as to its function it has ceased, because Christ and the Gospel announced through them, and the Law of God, have been so set in the midst of all Israel that the will of God can no longer be unknown. We have also treated these things, and their temporary ministry, more fully, Loc. 20, §§ 83–98. And concerning the prophets of the New Testament, and whether their office was ordinary or extraordinary, ibid. § 99, and concerning the evangelists, ibid. § 100, we have spoken as far as is sufficient. But the ordinary ministries

units.la: Charismata alia extraordinaria, alia ordinaria sunt. fteria sunt, quæ & quatenus ordinaria charismata requirunt; & in annuntiando, promovendo & applicando verbo gratiæ & reconciliationis, consilio Dei specialiter inserviunt. Qui illa obeunt, in genere διάκονοι Χριστοῦ ministri Christi, homines per verbum Christi ad Christum & fidem ejus adducentes: nec non œconomi mysteriorum Dei, quibus, ceu œconomis & dispensatoribus mysteria Dei credita sunt, 1. Cor. IV. 1. appellantur. Ita enim Dominus in terram longinquam proficiscens servis suis talenta distribuit, quibus negotientur, & fructum atque fœnus parent, Matth. XXV. 15. Quod fœnus in eo est, ut mysteria ipsis credita plurimis communicentur, atque per ea Christus multos servos, Deus multos filios lucretur.
units.tr: Gifts are partly extraordinary, partly ordinary. Those ministries are ordinary which require ordinary gifts, and which, insofar as they do so, specially serve the counsel of God in announcing, promoting and applying the word of grace and reconciliation. Those who discharge them are, in general, called ministers of Christ [διάκονοι Χριστοῦ], men who through the word of Christ bring people to Christ and to faith in him; and also stewards of the mysteries of God, since the mysteries of God have been entrusted to them as stewards and dispensers, 1 Cor. 4.1. For the Lord, setting out for a distant land, distributed talents to his servants, with which they should trade and acquire fruit and interest, Matt. 25.15. This interest consists in this: that the mysteries entrusted to them are communicated to many, and through them Christ gains many servants and God gains many sons.

units.la: XIV. Necessitatem ministrorum ordinariorum Ecclesiæ Scripturæ passim docent.
units.tr: XIV. The Scriptures teach everywhere the necessity of ordinary ministers of the Church.

units.la: Fidem enim ex auditu esse, neque vel auditum sine prædicante, vel prædicantem sine missione contingere S. Paulus Rom. X. 15. confirmat. Et ne id ad Apostolorum duntaxat tempora pertinere putemus, idem intercedit, dicens, Christum in Cælum ascendentem dedisse alios Apostolos, alios Prophetas, alios Evangelistas, alios Pastores & Doctores, & quidem ad concinnationem Sanctorum, ad opus ministerii, ad ædificationem corporis Christi, donec perveniemus omnes ad unitatem fidei, & cognitionis Filii Dei, in virum perfectum, ad mensuram staturæ plenitudinis Christi, Ephes. IV. 11. 12. Cum ergo ministerio Apostolorum, Prophetarum, Evangelistarum, Pastorum & Doctorum πάντες omnes sancti, adeóque ad finem mundi usque crescere & proficere debeant, in viros perfectos, juxta mensuram staturæ plenitudinis Christi; quæ statura non moles corporis, sed animi magnitudo, digna plenitudine Christi, intelligitur; manifestum est, non tantum apud Ecclesiam perseverare, infallibile verbum & testimonium Apostolorum, Prophetarum & Evangelistarum, sed etiam Pastores & Doctores ab Apostolis, Prophetis & Evangelistis illis distinctos juxta eorundem verbum & testimonium infallibile Ecclesiam ad finem usque mundi pascere & docere debere. Nulla aliás ratio Pastores & Doctores ab Apostolis, Prophetis & Evangelistis distinguendi fuisset. Licuit enim Deo per stultitiam prædicationis servare credentes, 1. Cor. I. 21. Eandem ob causam & S. Paulus atque Barnabas per suffragia (Ecclesiæ adeóque non immediatè) crearunt Presbyteros per Ecclesias, Actor. XIV. 23. & S. Paulus Tito mandatum dedit in Creta oppidatim constituendi Presbyteros, seu Seniores, Tit. I. 5. qui videlicet idonei sint ad alios quoque docendos, 2. Tim. II. 2. adeóque publicè & privatim docerent, admonerent & inclamarent: Hæc est via, ambulate in ea, Esaj. XXX. 20. 21. non utique infallibiles, quales Apostoli & Evangelistæ fuerunt, sed ab iis distinctos, qui juxta canonem verbi ab illis Ecclesiæ dati pascerent & docerent. Quamobrem idem etiam Senioribus, Episcopis, Pastoribus & Doctoribus ejusmodi leges, juxta quas ἐπισκοπὴ & vitam suam componerent, præscripsit, 1. Tim. III. 1. &c. Tit. I. 6. &c. & Ephesiis Episcopis seu Presbyteris hanc legem dixit: Attendite vobis ipsis, & toti gregi vestro, cui vos Spiritus S. Episcopos præfecit, ad pascendum Ecclesiam Dei, quam proprio sanguine suo acquisivit, Actor. XX. 28. Ratio igitur pascendi & docendi publicè Ecclesiam Dei est, quia Deus eam sanguine suo acquisivit, quod de quavis, & cujusvis temporis Ecclesia particulari valet. Et talibus obedire jubemur. Obedite præpositis vestris. Illi enim sunt, qui pro vobis vigilant, tanquam rationem reddituri, ut cum gaudio id faciant, Hebr. XIII. 17. Rogamus vos fratres, ut agnoscatis eos, qui laborant inter vos, & qui vobis præsunt in Domino, & admonent vos, & eos supra modum charos habeatis propter opus ipsorum, 1. Thess. V. 12. 13. Non enim minor Ecclesiæ per Pastores & Ministros Christi conservandæ, quàm per Apostolos instituendæ necessitas est. Et Christus potestatem clavium in persona Petri toti Ecclesiæ, & perseverantem in ejus collegiandæ, & supra Petro Christo ædificandæ usum dedit, Matth. XVI. 18. 19. XVIII. 18. Joh. XX. 23. Promisit enim quòd Apostolis adeóque eorum etiam in communi munere successoribus adesse velit ad consummationem usque seculi, Matth. XXVIII. 19. 20. Neque infima judicii Divini erga populum pars est, cùm Pastorum & Doctorum ministerio privatur. Nam cùm visio deest, nudatur populus, Prov. XXIX. 18. Ideo Christus maxima commiseratione motus est; quando Israelitas dissipatos & disjectos, quasi oves non habentes Pastorem, intuitus est, & exclamavit: Messis magna est, sed operarii pauci sunt. Rogate autem Dominum messis, ut operarios in messem suam emittat, Matth. IX. 36. 37. 38. Denique S. Paulus Timotheo dicens: Manus ne citò cuiquam imponito, nec cum alienis peccatis communicato, 1. Tim. V. 22. non obscurè impositionem manuum, & mediante eadem ordinationem & vocationem ad ministerium comprobat.
units.tr: St Paul confirms that faith comes by hearing, and that neither hearing comes without a preacher nor preaching without a sending (Rom. 10.15). Lest we think this pertains only to the times of the Apostles, the same Paul adds that Christ, ascending into heaven, gave some apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers, and this for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all come to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (Eph. 4.11, 12). Since, then, all the saints, by the ministry of apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, ought to grow and advance until the end of the world into perfect men, according to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (and this stature is understood not as bulk of body but as greatness of soul, worthy of the fullness of Christ), it is clear that not only does the infallible word and testimony of the Apostles, Prophets and Evangelists remain in the Church, but also that pastors and teachers, distinct from those Apostles, Prophets and Evangelists, ought to feed and teach the Church until the end of the world, according to that same word and infallible testimony. Otherwise there would be no reason for distinguishing pastors and teachers from apostles, prophets and evangelists. For it has pleased God "by the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe" (1 Cor. 1.21). For this same reason St Paul and Barnabas, "by the vote of the Church" (and so not immediately), "appointed elders in every church" (Acts 14.23); and St Paul gave Titus the command to appoint elders, or seniors, in every town in Crete (Titus 1.5), namely such as are fit "to teach others also" (2 Tim. 2.2), and so to teach, admonish and cry out both publicly and privately: "This is the way, walk in it" (Isa. 30.21). These were not, of course, infallible as the Apostles and Evangelists were, but were distinct from them, feeding and teaching according to the rule of the word which the Apostles had given to the Church. Therefore the same Paul also prescribed to the elders, bishops, pastors and teachers rules of this kind, by which they should order their office and life (1 Tim. 3.1ff.; Titus 1.6ff.). And to the bishops, that is the elders, of Ephesus he gave this charge: "Take heed to yourselves, and to all the flock over which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood" (Acts 20.28). The ground, then, for feeding and teaching the Church of God publicly is that God purchased it with his own blood; and this holds good of every particular church of any time. And we are commanded to obey such men: "Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls, as those who will have to give account, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning" (Heb. 13.17). "We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labour among you and have charge over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work" (1 Thess. 5.12, 13). For the need to preserve the Church through the pastors and ministers of Christ is no less than the need to found it through the Apostles. Christ also gave the power of the keys, in the person of Peter, to the whole Church, and to the perpetual gathering of it and building of it upon Peter (Matt. 16.18, 19; 18.18; John 20.23). For he promised that he would be present with the Apostles, and so with their successors in the common office, "to the end of the age" (Matt. 28.19, 20). Nor is it the least part of the judgment of God upon a people when it is deprived of the ministry of pastors and teachers: "Where there is no vision, the people is unrestrained" (Prov. 29.18). Hence Christ, moved by the greatest compassion when he saw the Israelites scattered and dispersed, "as sheep having no shepherd", cried out: "The harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few. Therefore pray the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers into his harvest" (Matt. 9.36–38). Finally, when St Paul says to Timothy, "Lay hands on no one hastily, and do not share in the sins of others" (1 Tim. 5.22), he clearly attests the imposition of hands, and through it the ordination and calling to the ministry.

units.la: XV. Vanæ sunt rationes, quibus Enthusiastæ, Libertini, Weigeliani, aliique Ministerii Ecclesiastici hostes in contrarium nituntur.
units.tr: XV. The arguments by which Enthusiasts, Libertines, Weigelians and other enemies of the ecclesiastical ministry strive to the contrary are empty.

units.la: Promittit Deus, se velle quærere gregem suum, ut eum pascat, Ezech. XXXIV. 12-17. Et Christus bonus ille Pastor, Joh. X. 11. Ἀρχιποίμην princeps pastor gregis etiam homines quosdam jussit ποιμαίνειν pascere Ecclesiam, gregem suum, Actor. XX. 28. & quosdam ποιμένας Pastores dedit. Ephes. IV. 11. Pascit ergo Deus, Christus, pascunt homines. Ille ut Dominus gregis sui, Spiritu & gratia oves proprias: hi ut ejusdem ministri & villici, externo apud homines præconio, & disciplinæ pedo, oves alienas. Et nunc in N. T. nemo amplius docet proximum suum, Jerem. XXXI. 34. Sed omnes θεοδίδακτοι à Deo docti sunt, Esaj. LIV. 13. Joh. VI. 45. quia revelatio omnis, norma institutionis & doctrinæ hominum, consummata, & verbum Dei in publico omnium est, ut nemini docere quenquam novo adducto verbo, & non per verbum quod commune omnium est ad consentiam hominis demonstratum liceat. Regit equidem Christus post ascensionem suam in Cœlum Ecclesiam Spiritu suo, & eodem in omnem veritatem ducit, Joh. XVI. 13. Sed ipse Spiritus Dei utitur etiam organis, quibus operationi suæ ministrantibus Ecclesiam regit. Ministrantibus illis Domino, &c. dixit Spiritus S. Separate mihi Barnabam & Saulum ad opus, ad quod eos adadvocavi, Actor. XIII. 2. Quis est Paulus, quis est Apollo,nisi ministri, per quos credidistis, 1. Cor. III. 5. Dei sumus administri, Dei arvum, Dei ædificium estis, ibid. vers. 9. Συνεργοῦντες cooperantes hortamur, ne frustra gratiam Dei receperitis, 2. Cor. VI. 1. Sed & manifeste Christus Spiritum S. & ministros conjungit, dicens: Spiritus illè veritatis, qui à Patre emanat,illè testabitur de me. Sed & vos testabimini, Joh. XV. 26. 27. Convitium igitur, non ratio est,quòd Fanatici N. T. Ministros γεαμματ literæ,non πνευματ Spiritus ministros, velut juxta 2. Cor. III. 6. appellant. Nam N. T. ministri Spiritus, non literæ ministri sunt,quia non amplius inserviunt literæ legis,seu pædagogiæ veteri legis,quæ per se sola occidit, sed merè Spiritui S. qui per verbum Evangelii & consummationis omnium vivificat. Si sub N.T. sunt διάκονοι καινῆς Διαθήκης ministri Novi Testamenti, non literæ, sed Spiritus, sunt igitur ministri,qui Novo Testamento & Spiritui S. inserviunt. Dantur ergo N. T. ministri,quod ipsum τὸ κεχωρισμένον est. Ideo v. 3. fideles omnes vocat Epistolam Christi διακονηθεισαν administratam per ministros illos N. T. scriptam non atramento, sed Spiritu Dei viventis, ubi est ζυγία Spiritus Dei, & ministrorum Spiritus. Ideo Evangelium etiam à Ministris Spiritus S. prædicatum potentia Dei ad salutem, Rom. I. 16. & brachium Domini, Esaj. LIII. 1. insignitur, quia est organon Spiritus S. per quod potenter operatur. Non enim, uti Fanatici somniant,Evangelium Christum in corda hominum se infundentem, sed Scripturam & præconium ex Scriptura Christi notat. Evangelium enim à Christo, ceu actus ab objecto, signum à signato,continens à contento,& ministerium ab utroque, uti etiam à fide, qua Evangelium recipitur, distinguitur. Evangelium enim Dei est, & de Filio Dei Jesu Christo, Domino nostro, per quem quidem gratiam & Apostolatum ad obedientiam fidei accipiunt, est, Rom. I. 1-6. Neque verbum Dei πνευματικὸν spirituale duntaxat, & in Deo est, sed quatenus salutarem doctrinam, variis modis revelatam, & externè calamo humano scriptam,voce humana prædicatam notat,non in Deo, sed à Deo est,& corporale quippiam est,sicut omnes aliæ voces hominum scriptæ vel prædicatæ. Et ad tale verbum corporale, in tempore à Mose, Prophetis, Christo & Apostolis scriptum & prædicatum Deus nos amandat, per illud electos convertit,in fide conservat,& ad actus fidei & charitatis excitat. Habent Mosen & Prophetas, Luc. XVI. 29. Animas vestr.as purificastis, auscultando veritati per Spiritum, &c. per sermonem Dei vivi. Hoc autem est verbum illud, quod vobis evangelizatum est, 1. Petr. I. 22. 23. 25. Impiæ verò tricæ illæ sunt, quòd soni verbi Dei pro externo duntaxat homine sint,& ad instituendum hominem nihil valeant, quia aliud soni materiale, aliud formale,in significatione consistens est. Illud externum hominem, ejúsque aures ferit; hoc ad cor hominis pertingit,& ab homine spirituali dijudicatur, 1. Cor. II. 14. Si voces pronunciatæ vel scriptæ merè corporales soni, adeóque repudiandi sunt,cur Fanatici ipsi famulis, liberis suis loquuntur? cur scripturis & paratragoediationibus suis hominas seducere conantur? Atqui hæc scripta
units.tr: God promises that he himself will "seek out his flock to feed it" (Ezek. 34.12–17). And Christ, that good Shepherd (John 10.11), the chief shepherd [ἀρχιποίμην], also commanded certain men "to shepherd [ποιμαίνειν] the Church, his flock" (Acts 20.28), and gave some as shepherds [ποιμένας] (Eph. 4.11). God therefore feeds, Christ feeds, and men feed. He feeds as Lord of his flock, feeding his own sheep by his Spirit and grace; they feed as his ministers and stewards, feeding other men's sheep by an outward proclamation among men and by the staff of discipline. And now in the New Testament "no one shall any longer teach his neighbour" (Jer. 31.34), but "all shall be taught of God" (Isa. 54.13; John 6.45). This is because all revelation, the rule of instruction and teaching for men, is complete, and the word of God lies open to all, so that it is not lawful for anyone to teach another by bringing in a new word, and not by demonstrating from the word common to all, to the conscience of man. Indeed, after his ascension into heaven Christ rules the Church by his Spirit, and by the same Spirit "leads it into all truth" (John 16.13). But the Spirit of God also uses organs, by which the Church is governed, they ministering to his operation. "As they were ministering to the Lord, etc., the Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them" (Acts 13.2). "What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Only ministers, through whom you believed" (1 Cor. 3.5). "We are God's fellow workers; you are God's field, God's building" (ibid., v. 9). "Working together with him, we urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain" (2 Cor. 6.1). And Christ plainly joins the Holy Spirit and the ministers together, saying: "The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness to me; and you also will bear witness" (John 15.26, 27). It is therefore a reproach, not an argument, that the Fanatics call the ministers of the New Testament ministers "of the letter" [γράμματος], not "of the Spirit" [πνεύματος], as if according to 2 Cor. 3.6. For the ministers of the New Testament are ministers of the Spirit, not of the letter, since they no longer serve the letter of the law, or the pedagogy of the old law, which of itself alone kills, but serve purely the Holy Spirit, who through the word of the Gospel and of the completed revelation gives life. If under the New Testament there are "ministers [διάκονοι] of the new covenant", not of the letter but of the Spirit, then there are ministers who serve the New Testament and the Holy Spirit. Therefore ministers of the New Testament are given, which is itself the thing set apart [τὸ κεχωρισμένον]. Hence in v. 3 he calls all the faithful "the letter of Christ" [ἐπιστολή], "ministered" [διακονηθεῖσα] by those ministers of the New Testament, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, where there is the yoking together [συζυγία] of the Spirit of God and the ministers of the Spirit. Hence the Gospel, also preached by the ministers of the Holy Spirit, is marked as "the power of God unto salvation" (Rom. 1.16) and "the arm of the Lord" (Isa. 53.1), because it is the instrument [ὄργανον] of the Holy Spirit through which he works powerfully. For the Gospel does not mean, as the Fanatics dream, Christ pouring himself into the hearts of men, but the Scripture and the proclamation from the Scripture of Christ. For the Gospel is distinguished from Christ as the act from its object, the sign from the thing signified, the container from the thing contained, and the ministry from both, and also from the faith by which the Gospel is received. "The Gospel of God, concerning his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom we received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith" (Rom. 1.1–6). Nor is the word of God only spiritual and "in God", but insofar as it signifies the saving doctrine, revealed in various ways, written outwardly with a human pen and preached with a human voice, it is not in God but from God, and is something bodily, just as all other human words written or spoken. It is through such a bodily word, written and preached in time by Moses, the Prophets, Christ and the Apostles, that God sends us to himself, converts the elect through it, preserves them in faith, and stirs them to acts of faith and love. "They have Moses and the Prophets" (Luke 16.29). "Having purified your souls by obeying the truth through the Spirit… through the word of the living God. Now this is the word which was preached to you as the Gospel" (1 Pet. 1.22, 23, 25). Those are impious quibbles which say that the sounds of the word of God are only for the outward man and avail nothing to instruct the man, because the material sound is one thing and the formal sound, consisting in its meaning, another. The former strikes the outward man and his ears; the latter reaches the heart of man and "is judged by the spiritual man" (1 Cor. 2.14). If spoken or written words are merely bodily sounds and so to be rejected, why do the Fanatics themselves speak to their servants and their children? Why do they try to seduce men with their writings and their paratragedies? And yet "these things are written" [hæc scripta] sunt…

units.la: sunt, est vox Christi ipsius, ut credatis, & ut credentes vitam habeatis, Joh. XX. 31. Dilutum & illud est,quòd ministerium Apostolicum,& reliquorum ministrorum non immediatè à Deo vocatorum,distinguentes, illius ministerium efficax & vivum fuisse,horum inefficax & mortuum esse, occlamant. Fuit Apostolorum præconium efficacius communi, quia & majorem ἀπόδειξιν πνεύματος & δυνάμεως demonstrationem Spiritus & potentiæ conjunctam habuit, 1. Cor. II. 4. & pluribus hominibus convertendis,& Ecclesiis plantandis inservivit. Omnibus illis περισσοτέρως abundantius laboravi, ibid. XV. 10. Non tamen nulla communis ministerii efficacia est. Nam qui in uno operatur, etiam in alio operatur, Galat. II. 8. Sic erit verbum meum,&c. non revertetur ad me vacuum, &c. Esaj. LV. 11. Quæ promissio extendi ad omnia tempora debet,quia & Christi Regnum perpetuum est, Luc. I. 33. & Christus suam cum ministris verbi Dei præsentiam ad consummationem seculi usque promisit, Matth. XXVIII. 20. Idem Dei verbum,quod vivum semper & efficax est,Hebr. IV. 12. eadem arma, quæ Apostoli habuerunt & tractarunt, Ecclesiæ ministri omnes habent & tractant,1. Petr. I. 25. 2. Petr. I. 19. 2. Tim. III. 15. quæ spiritualia & Deo potentia sunt, 2. Cor. X. 3. 4. Non ergo Ministerium N. T. & præconium verbi Dei inter egena mundi elementa, vel umbras deputandum est,Gal. IV. 3. Col. II. 17. Nam illa præsente corpore, Christo, nauci sunt. At Evangelium prædicatum potentia Dei ad salutem, & brachium Domini est. Sed & præposterum illud est,quòd Ecclesiæ Ministros ordinarios, non à Deo, Christo, sed ab hominibus vocatos,adeóque non Dei,sed hominum legatos, imò mercenarios, qui non missi currunt, Jerem. XXIII. 21. iidem criminantur. Nam Prophetæ damnant eos, qui non missi à Deo currunt,hoc est,immediatam vocationem sine tabulis mentiuntur. Sed non propterea Ecclesiæ suffragiis delecti currunt, & mercenarii sunt, quia Christus Ecclesiæ in persona Petri jus clavium, sub quo jus vocandi quosdam, qui claves habeant & administrent, continetur,dedit. Quomodo nec Timotheus, Titus, Presbyteri à Paulo & Barnaba, adeóque omnes illi ab hominibus, delecti vel cucurrerunt, vel in censu mercenariorum fuerunt. Christus enim non minus Pastores & Doctores, quàm Apostolos,Prophetas & Evangelistas ἔδωκε dedit, Ephes. IV. 11. Licet illi ab hominibus immediatè vocentur, hi à Christo immediatè vocati fuerint. Non enim Pastores & Doctores propterea ἀνθρώπινοι κλήσεις humanæ creaturæ sunt. Nam Reges quidem leguntur, accipiuntur,nascuntur. Non item ii, per quos Regnum Cœlorum erigi & concinnari debet. In Pastoribus & Doctoribus charismata λόγῳ· σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως sermo sapientiæ & cognitionis ad officium faciendum necessaria: Charitas ad libenter serviendum Ecclesiæ: & occasio dono suo in certo loco vel coetu utendi, distingui debent. Licet verò Pastores & Doctores ab hominibus,sed in nomine Christi, Matth. XVIII. 20. adeóque in fide & charitate convenientibus & deliberantibus,& velut fœdus de mutuis officiis illinc cura & ἀπαρχὴ, hinc obedientia in nominomine eodem, pangentibus, vocentur, tamen eorum legitima constitutio à solo Christo & Spiritu ejus pendet, atque ita omnis διακονία omne ministerium etiam χάρις gratia est, & Christus se ἀκρογωνιαῖον λίθον οἰκοδομῆς summum angularem lapidem œdificii demonstrat. Denique non ideo Pastores & Doctores Dei & Ecclesiæ ministri non esse possunt, quia fallere & falli possunt. Nam etiam V. T. Ecclesiæ ministri esse potuerunt, qui infallibiles non fuerunt, nisi quatenus juxta מורה juxta os legis docuerunt, Deut. XVII. 11. Labia Sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, & legem requirunt ex ore ejus, quia legatus Jehovæ est. Sed vos recessistis de via. Offendiculo fuistis multis in lege. Corrupistis fœdus Levi, dixit Jehova exercituum, Malach. II. 7. 8. Satis ad ministerii efficaciam est, quòd Deus infallibile verbum, ministerii ejusdem normam dedit, & Spiritu suo sic ministros regit, ut nunquam in mundo desint, qui officio suo rite defungantur, & saltem fundamentum aliud non ponant præter illud, quod ab Apostolis, sapientibus illis architectis, positum est; Licèt ei fundamento etiam fœnum & stipulas superstruere possint, 1. Cor. III. 10. 11. &c. Non enim, quia ministri Dei falli possunt, semper eos falli sequitur, quia custodem Spiritum Dei Christus iis promisit. Quomodo nec semper medici, jurisperiti; actuarii publici, testes in judicio & extra illud doctores, &c. falluntur, quia infallibiles & ἀναμάρτητοι nulli sunt, & alii creberrimè falluntur. Qui scopulorum signa observant, ad eos navim non appellunt; at allidunt illi, qui incauti & temulenti non observant.
units.tr: are the very voice of Christ himself, that you may believe, and that believing you may have life, John 20:31. Nor is it sound to contrast the ministry of the apostles, and of the other ministers who were not called immediately by God, and to cry out that the former was effective and living while the latter is ineffective and dead. The preaching of the apostles was indeed more effective than the ordinary kind, since it was accompanied by a greater demonstration of the Spirit and of power, 1 Cor. 2:4, and it served to convert more people and plant more churches. I laboured more abundantly than all of them, 1 Cor. 15:10. Yet the common ministry is not without effect. For he who works in one also works in another, Gal. 2:8. So shall my word be, etc., it shall not return to me empty, etc., Isa. 55:11. This promise must extend to all times, because Christ's kingdom is everlasting, Luke 1:33, and Christ promised his presence with the ministers of the Word of God until the end of the age, Matt. 28:20. The same word of God, which is living and always effective, Heb. 4:12, and the same weapons which the apostles had and handled, all ministers of the Church have and handle, 1 Pet. 1:25; 2 Pet. 1:19; 2 Tim. 3:15. These weapons are spiritual and mighty through God, 2 Cor. 10:3-4. Therefore the ministry of the New Testament and the preaching of the Word of God must not be counted among the weak and beggarly elements of the world, or among the shadows, Gal. 4:3; Col. 2:17. For those shadows, once the body, that is Christ, is present, are worth nothing. But the gospel preached is the power of God unto salvation, and the arm of the Lord. It is also absurd that the same men accuse the ordinary ministers of the Church of being sent not by God or Christ but by men, and therefore as envoys not of God but of men, indeed as hired hands who run without being sent, Jer. 23:21. For the prophets condemn those who run without being sent by God, that is, who lie about an immediate call without any credentials. But ministers chosen by the votes of the Church are not for that reason running without being sent and are not hired hands, because Christ gave to the Church, in the person of Peter, the right of the keys, and under that right is contained the right to call certain men who are to hold and administer the keys. In the same way Timothy, Titus, and the elders were chosen by Paul and Barnabas, and so all those were chosen by men; they were neither running without being sent nor counted among the hired hands. For Christ gave pastors and teachers no less than apostles, prophets and evangelists, Eph. 4:11. Although the former are called immediately by men, the latter were called immediately by Christ. Pastors and teachers are not for that reason human creatures, a human calling. For we read of kings being chosen, accepted and born; but not so of those through whom the kingdom of heaven is to be raised up and built. In pastors and teachers, the gifts needed to perform the office, namely the word of wisdom and of knowledge, must be distinguished from the charity to serve the Church willingly and from the opportunity to use one's gift in a certain place or assembly. Although pastors and teachers are called by men, yet they are called in the name of Christ, Matt. 18:20, and therefore by those who gather in faith and charity and deliberate, and who, as it were, make a covenant of mutual duties, on one side care and on the other obedience, in the same name. Still, their lawful appointment depends on Christ and his Spirit alone; and thus every service, every ministry, is also a grace, and Christ shows himself to be the chief cornerstone of the building. Finally, pastors and teachers cannot be ministers of God and of the Church merely because they can deceive and be deceived. For even in the Old Testament there could be ministers of the Church who were not infallible, except insofar as they taught according to the mouth of the law, Deut. 17:11. The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and men seek the law from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the LORD. But you have turned aside from the way; you have caused many to stumble at the law; you have corrupted the covenant of Levi, says the LORD of hosts, Mal. 2:7-8. It is enough for the effectiveness of the ministry that God gave an infallible Word as the rule of that ministry, and that by his Spirit he so governs the ministers that there are never lacking in the world those who rightly perform their office, and who at least do not lay any other foundation than that laid by the apostles, those wise architects, although upon that foundation they may build hay and stubble, 1 Cor. 3:10-11. For it does not follow that, because ministers of God can err, they always err, since Christ promised them the Spirit of God as guardian. Nor do physicians, lawyers, notaries, witnesses in court and teachers outside court, and so on, always err, although none of them is infallible or sinless, and others err very often. Those who watch for the signs of the rocks do not steer their ship toward them; but those who are careless and drunken, who do not watch, run aground on them.

units.la: XVI. Habuit Ecclesia Ministros ordinarios sub quavis œconomia. Post lapsum primùm Patres liberorum doctores & rectores fuerunt. Lex Dei fuit præceptum patris, & lex matris, Prov. VI. 20. Multiplicato humano genere, fideles se separarunt, & nomen Jehovæ nuncuparunt, Genes. IV. 26. Qui etiam institutis cœtibus publicis Patriarchis vetustioribus pastoribus & doctoribus usi sunt. Post diluvium, lapsis ad idololatriam gentibus, Patriarchæ domi promissionem suis inculcarunt. Quam in rem plura Loc. XII. 40. &c. diximus. Cùm Moses & populus in Ægypto essent, Seniores ei præfuerunt, & Sacerdotium primogeniti, vel ad hoc electi habuerunt, Exod. XIX. 22. 24. XXIV. 5. donec Levitæ pro primogenitis, altaris ministerio admoverentur, Num. VIII. 16. 17. Quorum officium fuit docere populum, Mal. II. 6. quod & Seniores in omnibus portis fecerunt, illi præsertim, qui præsente Pontifice, vel Judice in eo loco, quem Deus elegerat, sederent, Deut. XVII. 9. 12. Quorum mos fuit per χειροτονίαν ordinare magistros, qui nonnullam jurisdictionem habebant etiam priùs, quàm summo Principum collegio adscriberentur. Eorundem fuit, omnem transgressionem non tantùm contra legem, judiciis à Deo præscriptis, sed etiam contra instituta majorum, legis violationem caventia, non sancientia, verberatione, aliisque poenis arbitrariis vindicare, Ezr. VII. 25. 26. X. 8. De quibus in loco etiam plusculà diximus.
units.tr: XVI. The Church has had ordinary ministers under every economy. After the fall, the fathers were first the teachers and rulers of their children. The law of God was the commandment of the father and the teaching of the mother, Prov. 6:20. When the human race had multiplied, the faithful separated themselves and called upon the name of the LORD, Gen. 4:26. Even when public assemblies had been instituted, they used the older patriarchs as pastors and teachers. After the flood, when the nations had fallen into idolatry, the patriarchs inculcated the promise in their own households. On this matter we have said more in Locus 12, paragraphs 40 and following. When Moses and the people were in Egypt, the elders presided over them, and the priesthood belonged to the firstborn or to those chosen for this purpose, Exod. 19:22, 24; 24:5, until the Levites were brought near to the ministry of the altar in place of the firstborn, Num. 8:16-17. Their office was to teach the people, Mal. 2:6. The elders also did this at all the gates, especially those who sat in the place God had chosen, in the presence of the high priest or the judge, Deut. 17:9, 12. It was their custom to appoint magistrates by election (cheirotonia), who had some jurisdiction even before they were enrolled in the supreme council of princes. It was also their task to punish with flogging and other arbitrary penalties every transgression, not only against the law and the judgments prescribed by God, but also against the institutions of the elders that guard against violations of the law without themselves having the force of law, Ezra 7:25-26; 10:8. We have also said a little more about these men in the place cited.

units.la: XVII. Ordinarii N. T. Ministri sunt Pastores tum docentes, tum gubernantes; Seniores gubernantes, at non docentes: Doctores, Ecclesiam docentes, at non gubernantes, & Diaconi, stricte sic dicti, necessitatibus Sanctorum inservientes. Pastores sunt, qui Ecclesiam docendo voluntatem Dei, & curando atque gubernando pascunt. Dabo vobis Pastores secundum cor meum, & pascent vos scientia & intelligentia, Jerem. III. 15.
