Ipsi Pastores non norunt intelligere, Esaj. LVI. 10. 11. Attendite vobis ipsis, & toti gregi vestro, cui vos Spiritus S. præfecit Episcopos ad pascendam Ecclesiam, &c. Act. XX. 28. Christus dedit alios Pastores, &c. Eph. IV. 11. Pascite gregem, qui penes vos est inspectioni ejus vacantes, 1. Pet. V. 2. Idem insigniuntur nominibus inspectorum, seu rei divinæ curandæ præfectorum, Esaj. LVI. 10. Act. XX. 28. 1. Tim. III. 1. 2. Seniorum, quatenus non tantùm Ecclesiam curant & gubernant, sed etiam in sermone & doctrina laborant, 1. Tim. V. 17. quo sensu nomen Episcopi & Senioris alternant, Actor. XX. 17. 28. Tit. I. 5. 7. 1. Petr. V. 1. 2. ἡγουμένων ductorum, Heb. XIII. 7. 17. πρὸ προϊστάμενων præsidum, seu primo loco stantium, 1. Thess. V. 12. Οἰκονόμων dispensatorum mysteriorum Dei, 1. Cor. IV. 1. Tit. I. 7. Ecclesiastica vocabula sunt Ecclesiastarum, Præconum, Prædicantium παροίκων Parochorum (vel à παροικεῖν præbere, exhibere Sacramenta; vel à παροικία conventu vicinorum, unde corrupta vox Parochi) Curatorum & curionum, &c. Etiam πάππας, πάππα, Papa olim Ecclesiæ Pastor appellatus est. Quæ vox Hesychio ὑπέρπατρος blandam Patris appellationem innat; & Pastoribus atque Episcopis Ecclesiæ olim eximia fuit, uti ex Cypriano, Ambrosio, Augustino, Sidonio, &c. liquet. Abusus vocabuli est, cùm iidem Sacerdotum nomine veniunt; qui externi Sacerdotes sub N. T. nulli sunt, & spirituales Sacerdotes omnes sunt.
units.tr: XVII. The ordinary ministers of the New Testament are pastors, who both teach and govern; elders, who govern but do not teach; teachers, who teach the Church but do not govern; and deacons, strictly so called, who serve the needs of the saints. Pastors are those who feed the Church by teaching the will of God and by caring for and governing it. I will give you pastors after my own heart, and they shall feed you with knowledge and understanding, Jer. 3:15. The pastors themselves have no understanding, Isa. 56:10-11. Take heed to yourselves, and to all the flock over which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God, etc., Acts 20:28. Christ gave some as pastors, etc., Eph. 4:11. Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising oversight, 1 Pet. 5:2. The same men are designated by the names of overseers, that is, those set over the care of divine things, Isa. 56:10; Acts 20:28; 1 Tim. 3:1-2. And elders, insofar as they not only care for and govern the Church but also labour in word and doctrine, 1 Tim. 5:17. In this sense the names of bishop and elder are interchanged, Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5, 7; 1 Pet. 5:1-2. Leaders, Heb. 13:7, 17. Those who preside, that is, those who stand in the first place, 1 Thess. 5:12. Stewards of the mysteries of God, 1 Cor. 4:1; Titus 1:7. Ecclesiastical terms are ecclesiastes, heralds, preachers, parochi (either from paroikein, to provide or administer the sacraments, or from paroikia, a gathering of neighbours, whence the corrupted word parish), curates and parsons, and so on. Also pappas, pappa, papa was once used as the title of a pastor of the Church. This word, as Hesychius shows, carries the affectionate sense of a father above father, and it was once a distinguished title of pastors and bishops of the Church, as is clear from Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, Sidonius and others. The use of the word is an abuse when the same men are called priests; for under the New Testament there are no external priests, and all are spiritual priests.

units.la: XVIII. Officium Pastorum Ecclesiæ paucis S. Paulus constrinxit, Ephesios Presbyteros & Episcopos sic admonens: Προσέχετε ἑαυτοῖς, καὶ παντὶ τῷ ποιμνίῳ, Attendite vobis ipsis & toti gregi, cui vos Spiritus S. præfecit Episcopos ad pascendum Ecclesiam Dei; quam proprio sanguine acquisivit, Actor. XX. 28. Sibi ipsis attendumi studio cœlestis sapientiæ, ut veram sapientiam illam, quæ ἄνωθεν superne est, & casta (ne cum operibus tenebrarum, mendacio, blasphemia, idolis, Regno Diaboli communicet) pacifica (studens concordiæ, ut omnes idem loquantur, & invicem in opere Domini conjungantur, omnes Deo & Patri benedicant; sint tanquam vir unus, & uno humero Deo serviant) æqua (non efficiens sapientem importunum, ἄσπονδον, odiosum, stolidum, sed officiosum, offensas timentem, cupientem placere proximo in omni possibili bono) morigera (quæ alios libenter audit, ad rationes ejus attendit, veritati cedit, non cavillatur, tergiversatur, vitilitigat) plena misericordiæ & bonorum fructuum (quia errantes & offendentes miseratur, iis parcit, benignè succurrit, & ad bonos fructus ferendos idoneos efficit) sine disceptatione (non disceptans, murmurans, ratiocinans contra Deum & verbum ejus) & simu-
units.tr: XVIII. St Paul summed up the duty of the Church's pastors in a few words, when he admonished the elders and bishops of Ephesus thus: "Take heed to yourselves, and to all the flock over which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood" (Acts 20:28). Take heed to yourselves with zeal for heavenly wisdom, so that you hold to that true wisdom which is from above, and which is pure (so that it has no fellowship with the works of darkness, lies, blasphemy, idols, or the kingdom of the devil), peaceable (eager for concord, so that all speak the same thing, are joined together in the work of the Lord, all bless God the Father, and serve him as one man with one shoulder), gentle (not making a man troublesome, quarrelsome, hateful or foolish, but dutiful, fearing offence, desiring to please one's neighbour in every good way), compliant (willing to listen to others, to attend to their reasons, to yield to the truth, not to quibble, evade or wrangle), full of mercy and good fruits (pitying those who err and offend, sparing them, kindly helping them, and making them fit to bear good fruits), without partiality (not disputing, murmuring, or reasoning against God and his word), and without pre-

units.la: Ministri ordinarii Ecclesiæ V. T. simulatione (non per ostentationem quicquam agens, sed ex corde) est, Jac. II. 17. & precibus assiduis à Deo expetant, quia à Patre luminum, Christi merito & regeneratione est, & rerum terrestrium sphæram omnem egreditur : eámque in omni ministerio suo sectantur & exerunt. Faciunt huc monita S. Pauli: Tu verò permane in iis, quæ didicisti, 2. Tim. III. 14. Interim dum venio, προσέχε τῇ ἀναγνώσει intentus esto lectioni, exhortationi, doctrinæ. Ne neglige donum, quod tibi datum est per prophetiam (accedente prophetia, seu jussu & promissione Spiritus S. monentis Paulum, ut Timotheum assumeret; vel virtute & efficacia prophetiæ Pauli, quæ in Timotheo efficax fuit ad excitandum in ipso animum, alacritatem & promptitudinem ad legationem ad Gentes cum Paulo obeundam) cum impositione manuum Presbyterii: Hæc meditare, in his esto, ut profectus tuus manifestus sit in omnibus. Insta tibi & doctrinæ, seu institutioni. (per quam fides & charitas ædificetur) Mane in iisdem. Hoc enim faciens, & te ipsum salvabis, & qui te audiunt, 1. Tim. IV. 13-f. Puro pietatis erga Deum zelo & exercitatione continua, ut Dei timore cor muniant, amore imbuant, nec quicquam nisi ejus auspiciis suscipiant, bonæ conscientiæ studeant, nihil temere, vel pudendum faciant, denique totos se Deo devoveant, & gloriæ ejus sacrificent; qui præ cæteris gloriæ Dei, & Regno ejus amplificando inservire debent. Denique sanctæ conversationis cum proximo exemplo. Nam minister Ecclesiæ oportet sit τύπος τῶν πιστῶν exemplar fidelium (ποιμνίου gregis, 1. Pet. V. 3. ut sint quasi אדירי הצאן duces ovium, Jerem. XXV. 34. qui se ipsos prius quàm alios doceant. Rom. II. 21. ut ostendant, se id credere, quod docent; quomodo etiam Christus passus nobis reliquit ὑπογραμμὸν exemplar, & Apostoli Christum imitati sunt, 1. Corinth. XI. 1.) in sermone (ut sanctus, ad glorificandum Deum, & ædificandum proximum comparatus sit) in conversatione (ratione vivendi & agendi inter homines honesta, Ecclesiæ, civitati, familiæ utili, habitum animi bonum & virtutes omnes resipiente, modesta inprimis, venusta & amabili) in charitate, in spiritu (zelo pro bono adversus malum, suspiriis ad Deum, revelatione per verbum Dei, desiderio spiritualium, discretione spirituum, &c.) in fide (fiducia, fortitudine, constantia) in castitate (fuga impuritatis omnis, & communionis cum omni peccato) 1. Tim. IV. 12. Sed fusius idem Ministrorum Ecclesiæ necessarias dotes passim & ex professo 1. Tim. III. 1. &c. describit. Quorum etiam vivum in se ipso exemplum statuit, dicens: Σὺ δὲ παρηκολούθηκάς μου τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ Tu assecutus es, (didicisti, cognovisti,) doctrinam meam, ἀγωγὴν vitæ sectam, propositum, fidem, longanimitatem, charitatem, patientiam, 2. Tim. III. 10.
units.tr: tence (doing nothing for show, but from the heart) (James 2:17). Ministers of the ordinary Church of the Old Testament ask God for this by constant prayer, since it comes from the Father of lights, through Christ's merit and regeneration, and it goes beyond the whole sphere of earthly things; and they pursue and exercise it in all their ministry. St Paul's admonitions bear on this: "But you, continue in the things you have learned" (2 Tim. 3:14). Meanwhile, until I come, give attention to reading, exhortation and doctrine. Do not neglect the gift that was given you through prophecy (prophecy coming with it, that is, by the command and promise of the Holy Spirit, who moved Paul to take Timothy along; or by the power and efficacy of Paul's prophecy, which was effective in Timothy to rouse in him courage, eagerness and readiness to undertake with Paul the mission to the Gentiles) with the laying on of the hands of the eldership. Meditate on these things, be in them, so that your progress may be evident to all. Attend to yourself and to doctrine, or teaching (through which faith and love are built up). Continue in these things. For in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you (1 Tim. 4:13 f.). With pure zeal for piety towards God and continual practice, so that they fortify their hearts with the fear of God, imbue them with his love, and undertake nothing except under his guidance; that they strive for a good conscience, do nothing rashly or shameful; and finally devote themselves wholly to God and sacrifice themselves to his glory, since they above all others ought to serve the glory of God and the enlarging of his kingdom. Lastly, by the example of holy conversation with one's neighbour. For a minister of the Church ought to be a pattern of the faithful (of the flock, 1 Pet. 5:3), so that they may be as the leaders of the flock [אדירי הצאן] (Jer. 25:34), who teach themselves before they teach others (Rom. 2:21), so that they show that they believe what they teach. In the same way Christ, who suffered, left us an example [ὑπογραμμὸν], and the Apostles imitated Christ (1 Cor. 11:1). In speech (so that he is holy, prepared to glorify God and edify his neighbour); in conduct (honest in his manner of living and acting among men, useful to the Church, the state and the household, showing a good disposition of mind and all the virtues, above all modest, graceful and lovable); in love, in spirit (zeal for good against evil, sighs to God, revelation through the word of God, desire for spiritual things, discernment of spirits, etc.); in faith (trust, fortitude, constancy); in chastity (flight from all impurity and from fellowship with every sin) (1 Tim. 4:12). But the same apostle describes at length, and expressly, the necessary gifts of the Church's ministers, at 1 Tim. 3:1 and following. He also set up a living example of these in himself, saying: "But you have followed my teaching" (you have learned and known it), my way of life, purpose, faith, longsuffering, love, patience (2 Tim. 3:10).

units.la: XIX. Gregi verò attendunt Pastores, eundem pascendo, & pro eo vigilando. Nam Episcopos attendere gregi sic Apostolus jubet, ut Ecclesiam pascant, & vigilent, Actor. XX. 28. 30. Vigilare Pastorum, & eorum, qui pro salute civium excubant, est. Ideo vigilare doctores pro animabus suis sibi creditis, Apostolus Hebr. XIII. 17. asserit. Vigilandum autem illis est, tum ne quid gregi, vel ulli gregis membro desit, tum ne quid ei, cui semper hostes imminent, noceat. Ad quam curam pertinet studium meditationis Scripturarum ad parandum necessaria institutioni Ecclesiæ, 1. Tim. IV. 13. 16. 2. Tim. I. 13. & enixa atque perpetua oratio, & diligens visitatio atque admonitio. Neque defunctorie, sed magno cum labore, magna cum contentione officio hoc defungi debent. Est enim ἐπισκοπὴ ἔργον inspectio opus, 1. Tim. III. 1. Et qui Ecclesiæ sic præest, idem etiam bonus miles Jesu Christi, & similis γεωργῷ laboranti agricolæ est, 2. Tim. II. 3. 6. Oportet enim κοπιᾶν laborare in sermone & doctrina, 1. Tim. V. 17. Ideo Solomon suadet, ut sapientiam quæramus, velut aurum, quod ex visceribus terræ eruitur, Prov. II. 4. Non igitur Pastores sedere ut Dominos, judices & legislatores, sed laborare & suadere in institutione Ecclesiæ tum publicè, tum privatim convenit. Omnis enim ministerii regula est διακονεῖν ministrare, non ministerium in principatum & dominationem convertere. Porro si quis ministrat ὡς ἐξ ἰσχύος, ut ex virtute, quam suppeditat Deus, ut in omnibus glorificetur Deus per Jesum Christum, 1. Pet. IV. 11. Præceptum amoris Dei est, ut eum amemus ἐξ ὅλης διανοίας, καὶ ὅλης ἰσχύος ex omni cogitatione, & omni content one, Marc. XII. 30. Quod in omni charitate, adeòque etiam διακονία ministerio, quod charitatis actus est, obtinet. Si enim Dei amor exercetur etiam amore proximi, ab eo τὸ ἐξ ἰσχύος ex virtute, & robore, quod Deus suppeditat, sejungi non potest. Virtutis illius est, μὴ ὑποστέλλεσθαι, μὴ ἐκκακεῖν se non subducere, non segnescere, Actor. XX. 27. 2. Cor. IV. 1. 16. Maledictus enim est, qui facit opus Domini רמיה fraudulenter, Jerem. XLVIII. 10. Talis enim non impendit se Ecclesiæ, sicut æquum est, & ipse spopondit, & per ipsum stat, quò minùs χάρισμα Dei fructificet. Quam diligentiam inprimis parabola talentorum, & in ea judicium de illo, qui videri voluit satisfacere hero, si talentum suum sine ullo fœnore ipsi restituereret, commendat.
units.tr: XIX. Pastors attend to the flock by feeding it and watching over it for its sake. For the Apostle commands the bishops to attend to the flock in such a way that they feed and watch over the Church (Acts 20:28, 30). Watching is the task of pastors, and of those who keep guard for the safety of citizens. So the Apostle declares that teachers watch over the souls entrusted to them (Heb. 13:17). They must watch, both lest anything be lacking to the flock or to any member of it, and lest anything harm it, since enemies are always threatening it. To this care belongs the study of meditating on the Scriptures in order to prepare what is needed for the instruction of the Church (1 Tim. 4:13, 16; 2 Tim. 1:13), and earnest and continual prayer, and diligent visitation and admonition. They must discharge this duty not in a perfunctory way, but with great labour and great effort. For oversight is a work [ἐπισκοπὴ ἔργον], inspection, work (1 Tim. 3:1). And whoever thus presides over the Church is also a good soldier of Jesus Christ, and like a labouring farmer [γεωργῷ] (2 Tim. 2:3, 6). For it is necessary to labour [κοπιᾶν] in preaching and teaching (1 Tim. 5:17). So Solomon urges us to seek wisdom like gold, which is dug out of the bowels of the earth (Prov. 2:4). Pastors ought therefore not to sit as lords, judges and lawgivers, but to labour and persuade in the instruction of the Church, both publicly and privately. For the rule of every ministry is to serve [διακονεῖν], not to turn the ministry into principality and domination. Moreover, if anyone ministers, as of the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ (1 Pet. 4:11). The command of the love of God is that we love him with all our mind and all our strength [ἐξ ὅλης διανοίας, καὶ ὅλης ἰσχύος] (Mark 12:30). This holds in every charity, and so also in service [διακονία], which is an act of charity. For if the love of God is exercised also by love of neighbour, then strength [τὸ ἐξ ἰσχύος], that is, the vigour and strength which God supplies, cannot be separated from it. It belongs to this strength not to shrink back [μὴ ὑποστέλλεσθαι], not to faint [μὴ ἐκκακεῖν], not to draw back, not to grow slack (Acts 20:27; 2 Cor. 4:1, 16). For cursed is he who does the work of the Lord deceitfully [רמיה] (Jer. 48:10). Such a man does not give himself to the Church as is fitting, as he himself promised, and through him it stands, so that the gift [χάρισμα] of God does not bear fruit. The parable of the talents especially commends this diligence, and in it the judgment on the man who wished to appear to satisfy his master by returning his talent to him without any interest.

units.la: XX. Officii & procurationis, quam Pastoribus Ecclesiæ Christus ejusdem Dominus, imposuit, partes sunt, ut doctrinam verbi Divini ex limpidissimis Israelis fontibus ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ publicè & privatim, adultis & catechumenis, sanis, ægrotis & moribundis, juxta normam Legis & Evangelii, prout id gregis salus & necessitas postulat, proponant; idemque in Scholis à præceptoribus etiam ut fiat, solicitè curent. Sacramenta juxta Christi institutionem purè administrent: in Ecclesiasticis ritibus adiaphoris ordine & decenter omnia componant: disciplinæ rationem habeant, & subsidiaria Presbyterorum Ecclesiæ & Magistratus opera id enixè satagant, ut expurgato scelerum & scandalorum fermento, in pietate, sinceritate, veritate omnes vitam traducant, Deúmque purè colant: pauperum necessitatibus, adjutoribus eleemosynariis subveniant: ægrotos visitent, illòsque sive doctrina, sive exhortationibus, sive eleemosynarum subsidiis opus sit, quàm commendatissimos sibi habeant. Sic enim Christus Apostolis adeóque omnibus Ecclesiæ pastoribus præcepit: Docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus Officii eorundem partes. ritus S. docentes eos servare omnia, quæ mandavi vobis, Matth. XXVIII. 19. 20. Justit idem Cœna S. uti ad sui memoriam, & annuntiationem mortis suæ, adeóque eandem administrare & dispensare, Luc. XXII. 19. 1. Cor. XI. 24. 25. Et S. Paulus hortatur: Seniorem ne increpes, sed adhortare ut Patrem: juniores ut fratres; mulieres natu grandiores ut matres: juniores ut sorores, cum omni castitate, 1. Tim. V. 1. 2. Et quantam idem curam pauperum habuerit, & quàm sæpe ad eandem Timotheum & Titum adegerit, ex 2. Cor. VIII. & IX. maximè elucescit. Sed de his officii Pastorum partibus infra pluribus.
units.tr: XX. The duties and the charge which Christ, the Lord of the Church, has laid upon its pastors are these: they are to set forth the doctrine of the Divine word, from the purest springs of Israel, for the edification of the Church, publicly and privately, to adults and catechumens, to the healthy, the sick and the dying, according to the rule of Law and Gospel, as the salvation and need of the flock require; and they are to take care that the same is also done in the schools by the teachers. They are to administer the sacraments purely according to Christ's institution; to arrange all matters of indifferent ecclesiastical ritual in good order and decently; to attend to discipline, and with the help of the elders of the Church and the work of the magistrate to strive earnestly that, with the leaven of sins and scandals purged out, all live in piety, sincerity and truth, and worship God purely. They are to help the poor in their needs, with the aid of almoners; to visit the sick, and to hold them most highly in regard, whether they need teaching, exhortation or the support of alms. For Christ thus charged the Apostles, and so all the pastors of the Church: "Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit" (duties of the same office), "teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you" (Matt. 28:19, 20). The Supper of the Lord likewise bade them use it in remembrance of him and in proclaiming his death, and so to administer and dispense it (Luke 22:19; 1 Cor. 11:24, 25). And St Paul exhorts: "Do not rebuke an elder, but exhort him as a father; the younger men as brothers; the older women as mothers; the younger women as sisters, with all purity" (1 Tim. 5:1, 2). And how great a care for the poor the same apostle had, and how often he urged Timothy and Titus to it, is shown most clearly from 2 Cor. 8 and 9. But of these duties of the pastors' office, more below.

units.la: XXI. Non una ratione Scripturæ Pastores ad fideliter defungendum ministerii sui partib* stimulant. Nam S. Paulus attendere eos gregi jubet, tum quia à Spiritu S. ipso constituti Ecclesiæ Episcopi sunt: tum quia ab eo pascendæ Ecclesiæ Dei; quam sibi proprio sanguine suo Deus (non nudus homo aliquis) acquisivit, atque ita sibi vendicavit, ut ab omni creaturarum servitute liberam voluerit; cura eis impositia est, tum quia immineat Ecclesiæ huic tentatio post ἀφι- ξιν discessum suum, quando intraturi sint homines, loquentes perversa, ut post se discipulos abstrahant; quorum ingenium amplius denudat, prædicens, quòd futuri sint lupi graves, non parcentes gregi, adeoq; pios graviter persecuturi etiam; adversus quos γρηγορεῖν vigilare eos jubet, suo etiam exemplo monitos, utpote qui triennio integro diu noctúque non cessaverit cum lachrymis unumquemque illorum hortari, Actor. XX. 28-32. Ibid. v. 18. 22. sic exemplum suum urget: Vos nostis, quemadmodum à primo die, quo in Asiam perveni, per omne tempus vobiscum extiterim, serviens Domino cum omni humilitate, & multis lachrymis & tentationibus, quæ mihi exinsidiis Judæorum obvenerunt, quemadmodum nihil conducibilium subduxerim, quò minùs annuntiarem vobis & docerem vos δημοσίᾳ καὶ κατ' οἴκους publicè & domatim, testificatus Judæis & Græcis resipiscentiam in Deum, & fidem, quæ est in Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum; Acris verò ille stimulus est, quòd iis ratio reddenda est pro animabus sibi creditis. Fili hominis, σκοπὸν ἐπίσκοπον inspectorem, speculatorem dedi te domui Israel. Audies igitur ex ore meo verbum, & admonebis eos nomine meo. Cùm dixero improbo: Moriendo morieris, & non admonueris illum, & locutus fueris, ut admonitione adducas improbum à via sua improba ad vitam ei conciliandam, ipse improbus in iniquitate sua morietur, & sanguinem ipsius ex manu tua requiram. Et tu cùm admonueris improbum, & non conversus fuerit ab improbitate sua, & à via sua improba, ipse in pravitate sua morietur, tu autem animam tuam eripuisti, Ezech. III. 17. 20. Et S. Paulus: Ductores vestri vigilant pro animabus vestris, tanquam rationem reddituri, ut cum gaudio faciant & non suspirantes, Hebr. XIII. 17. Nam iis œconomia & villicatio credita est, quibus proin curandum, ut vera & recta doceant, & nemini desint. Imò qui ministerium curandi vel docendi Ecclesiam in se suscipit, eam in fidem suam recipit, & pro ea spondet, saltem quòd per se staturum non sit, quò minùs amplissimi fructus justitiæ ad honorem Dei in illa proveniant, aut quò minùs omnes salventur. Qui eam sponsionem fecit, haud dubiè de ea etiam rationem in judicio Dei reddet. Unde Jacobus cavens veluti nobis admonet: Ne multi doctores fiatis, scientes, quòd majus judicium accipiemus, Jac. III. 1. Graviter Augustinus Suppl. p. 328. Serm. var. 1. Misericordem, inquit, Dominum habeo, sed rigidum computatorem: Oviculas suas quotidie numerat, has in manibus descriptas habet, exigit numerum, quem si non reddiderim, ingenti capiti meo periculum creabitur. Nam maledictus est, qui opus Domini fraudulenter facit, Jerem. XLVIII. 10. Ille quoque fortis admodum ad excitandam diligentiam, & acuendum studium ministris verbi Dei stimulus esse debet, quòd stant in eo loco, quem Apostoli tenuerunt. Tu autem, sic Paulus ad Timotheum, sobrius esto in omnibus, mala perpetere, fac opus Evangelistæ, τὸ ἔργον ... simple ministerium tuum. Ego enim jam libor, & tempus discessus mei instat, 1. Tim. IV. 5. 6. Hanc ergo charitatem Deo & Ecclesiæ debent, quam Apostoli præstiterunt. Verbum, quod loquuntur, à Prophetis & Apostolis traditum habent. Labor, industria, timor, fides præstanda sunt. Quod post Apostolos non ita laboratum est, ab imminuta charitate esse, Spiritus Dei innuit: Novi opera tua, & κόπον laborem tuum, & patientiam, &c. Sed habeo contra te, quòd primam charitatem reliqueris, Apoc. II. 4. Accedit, quòd fidelis ministrorum labor fructu & mercede sua minimè defraudatur. Dictum enim iis est: Laboranten agricolam oportet πρῶτον primum de fructibus percipere, 2. Tim. II. 6. Ita ergo, quibus officium docendi, & auditorum animos, ceu arvum vel Paradisum Dei colendi demandatum est, seminare, plantare, rigare debent, ut fructum sperare possint, & primi illi percipient in illuminatione oculorum mentis, amore veritatis, amore mutuo fratrum, præsertim in amore ipsorum docentium. Qui colit agrum suum satiabitur pane; & qui sequitur vacuos, satiabitur paupertate, Prov. XXVIII. 19. Si quis igitur, ceu sedulus agricola, omnem laborem & curam impenderit agro Domini sibi commendato, eúmque frugiferum reddere contenderit, non tantùm Deus proventu justitiæ delectabitur, sed etiam ipse fructu laboris sui satiabitur. Et qui bene præsunt, Presbyteri, duplici honore afficiuntur, maximè qui laborant in sermone & doctrina, 1. Tim. V. 17. Quem honorem Apostolus de stipendii honore statim v. 18. interpretatur. Si enim bovi triturandi de tritura pabulum præberi debet, multò magis homini debetur cibus ex opere suo, & quidem opere suo dignus, quemadmodum bos comedit de ipso cibo, quem homini parat. Sed hoc leve est. Permittit enim Deus fidelibus servis suis, gnaviter officio suo fungentibus, non tantùm in hac vita incrementa charismatum, juxta illa Christi: Habenti dabitur, Matth. XIII. 12. Sed etiam æternæ gloriæ amplissimam mercedem. Euge, serve frugi & fidelis. In exiguo fidelis fuisti, super multa te constituam. Ingredere in gaudium Domini, ibid. XXV. 21. Qui alios erudiunt ad justitiam, ut stellæ lucebunt in saeculum, Dan. XII. 3. Pascite gregem non coacte, &c. Et cùm manifestus factus fuerit ille Pastorum princeps, reportabitis illam ἀμαράντινον immarcescibilem gloriæ coronam, 1. Pet. V. 2. &c. Ac licet in mundo do contemnantur, exagitentur, irrideantur ab impuro illo Epicuri grege, tamen Deo multò magis quàm Reges curæ sunt. In omnibus afflìguntur, sed non coarctantur; ambigui sunt, sed non prorsus hæsitant; persecutionem patiuntur; sed non derelinquuntur; prosternuntur, sed non perduntur, 2. Cor. IV. 8. 9. Nemo impunè unctos hos tangit, 1. Paral. XVI. 22. Jacent Lazari instar, ulceribus lacerati, in vestibulo divitum, à quibus negliguntur, sed Deus Angelico præsidio missô eos sibi curæ esse testatur. Quæ non exigua fidelium Pastorum & Doctorum consolatio est, quòd pro gloria hujus seculi, quam ministerio suo, ex quo nil nisi ignominiam mundi reportant; perdunt, & quæ non est ἀμαράντ-ος, nec necessaria vel obses ei, qui hæres æternæ gloriæ futurus est; immarcescibilem gloriæ coronam certo sibi recipere possunt.
units.tr: XXI. Scripture urges pastors to discharge the duties of their ministry faithfully for more than one reason. First, St. Paul bids them take heed to the flock, because they have been appointed bishops of the Church by the Holy Spirit himself, and because they are to feed the Church of God, which God acquired for himself with his own blood (not any mere man), and so claimed for himself that he willed it to be free from all servitude to creatures, and the care of it has been laid upon them. Second, because a temptation threatens this Church after his departure [ἀφιξιν], when men will arise speaking perverse things to draw disciples away after themselves. Paul lays bare their nature more fully, foretelling that grievous wolves will come in, not sparing the flock, and that they will indeed severely persecute the godly. Against them he bids the elders keep watch [γρηγορεῖν], and he backs this with his own example, since for three whole years, night and day, he did not cease to admonish each one of them with tears (Acts 20:28-32). In Acts 20:18, 22 he presses his example thus: "You know how, from the first day that I came into Asia, I was with you the whole time, serving the Lord with all humility and with many tears and trials, which came upon me through the plots of the Jews; how I kept back nothing profitable from you, but declared to you and taught you publicly and from house to house [δημοσίᾳ καὶ κατ' οἴκους], testifying to Jews and Greeks repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ." The goad is sharper still, because they must render an account for the souls entrusted to them. "Son of man, I have made you a watchman [σκοπὸν] and overseer [ἐπίσκοπον] to the house of Israel. You shall hear the word from my mouth and warn them in my name. When I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you do not warn him, nor speak to warn the wicked from his evil way that he may live, the wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood at your hand. But if you warn the wicked and he does not turn from his wickedness and his evil way, he shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul" (Ezek. 3:17, 20). St. Paul also says: "Your leaders watch over your souls, as those who will give an account, so that they may do it with joy and not with groaning" (Heb. 13:17). For stewardship and management have been committed to them, so they must take care to teach what is true and right, and to be lacking to no one. Indeed, whoever takes upon himself the ministry of caring for or teaching the Church receives it into his trust and stands surety for it, at least in that he will not be the reason why the most abundant fruits of righteousness do not arise in it to the honour of God, or why all are not saved. Whoever has given that pledge will undoubtedly also render an account of it at the judgment of God. Hence James, warning us as it were, admonishes: "Do not become many teachers, knowing that we shall receive a greater judgment" (James 3:1). Augustine speaks weightily: "I have a merciful Lord, but a strict reckoner. He counts his little sheep every day; he has them written down in his hands; he demands the number, and if I do not render it, a great danger will be created for my head." For "cursed is he who does the work of the Lord deceitfully" (Jer. 48:10). That too ought to be a very strong goad to stir up diligence and sharpen the zeal of the ministers of God's Word, because they stand in the place which the apostles held. "But you," Paul says to Timothy, "be sober in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist [τὸ ἔργον], fulfil your ministry. For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand" (2 Tim. 4:5-6). They owe God and the Church the same love that the apostles showed. The word they speak they have received as handed down by the prophets and apostles. Labour, diligence, fear, and faith must be rendered. That after the apostles the work was not carried on in the same way is a sign of diminished love, as the Spirit of God intimates: "I know your works, and your toil [κόπον] and patience, etc. But I have this against you, that you have left your first love" (Rev. 2:2, 4). Moreover, the faithful labour of ministers is not at all defrauded of its fruit and reward. For it is said to them: "The hardworking farmer ought to be the first [πρῶτον] to receive a share of the fruits" (2 Tim. 2:6). Thus those to whom the duty of teaching has been committed, and of cultivating the minds of hearers as a field or paradise of God, must sow, plant, and water, so that they may hope for fruit, and they will be the first to receive it in the enlightening of the eyes of the mind, in love of the truth, in mutual love of the brethren, and especially in love of the teachers themselves. "He who tills his land will be satisfied with bread, but he who follows idle pursuits will be satisfied with poverty" (Prov. 28:19). So if anyone, like a diligent farmer, has bestowed all his labour and care upon the field of the Lord entrusted to him, and has striven to make it fruitful, God will not only be delighted with the harvest of righteousness, but he himself will also be satisfied with the fruit of his labour. And "those who rule well, the elders, are counted worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in the word and teaching" (1 Tim. 5:17). The apostle explains this honour as a stipend in the very next verse, 5:18. For if the ox treading the grain must be given food from the threshing, much more is food owed to a man from his work, and indeed to one who is worthy of his work, just as the ox eats of the very food he prepares for the man. But this is a small matter. For God grants to his faithful servants, who discharge their office diligently, not only increases of gifts in this life, according to that saying of Christ, "To him who has, more will be given" (Matt. 13:12), but also the most ample reward of eternal glory: "Well done, good and faithful servant. You were faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord" (Matt. 25:21). "Those who turn many to righteousness shall shine like the stars forever" (Dan. 12:3). "Feed the flock, not under compulsion," etc. And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading [ἀμαράντινον] crown of glory (1 Pet. 5:2, etc.). And although in the world they are despised, harassed, and mocked by that impure herd of Epicurus, yet they are of far greater concern to God than kings are. They are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; they are perplexed, but not in despair; they are persecuted, but not forsaken; they are cast down, but not destroyed (2 Cor. 4:8-9). No one touches these anointed ones with impunity (1 Chron. 16:22). Like Lazarus, they lie covered with sores in the vestibule of the rich, by whom they are neglected, but God testifies by sending angelic protection that they are of concern to him. This is no small consolation for the faithful pastors and teachers: that they lose the glory of this age, which in their ministry brings them nothing but the world's shame, and what is not unfading [ἀμαράντ-ος], nor necessary, nor a pledge to him who is to be heir of eternal glory, yet they can with certainty receive for themselves the unfading crown of glory.

units.la: XXII. Ad ministerium Ecclesiæ obeundum vocatio requiritur. Nemo sibi sumit honorem hunc, sed qui vocatur à Deo, ut Aharon, Heb. V. 4. Ubi in hypothesi de Aharone, in thesi de omnibus, qui ministerio funguntur, adeóque de iis etiam, qui πρεσβείαν legationem pro Christo habent, sermo est. Quomodo enim prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Quemadmodum scriptum est: Quàm speciosi sunt pedes evangelizantium? Rom. X. 15. Non misi Prophetas, & illi cucurrerunt, non locutus sum ad ipsos, & illi vaticinati sunt, Jerem. XXIII. 21. Neque enim omnes docere possunt. Num omnes Apostoli, num omnes Prophetæ, num omnes doctores, num omnes potestates? 1. Cor. XII. 29. Negat id, dum interrogat, Apostolus. Licèt enim omnium sit fratrem & proximum verbo & exemplo docere, hortari, dehortari, consolari, redarguere, instigante tum charitate proximi, quæ legis impletio est, Rom. XIII. 10. tum diserta lege Dei, ne feramus peccatum in fratre & proximo, Levit. XIX. 17. & ut observemus alii alios ad instigationem charitatis & bonorum operum, Hebr. X. 24. Et sub initio Ecclesiæ Prophetæ multi, habentes donum linguarum & Prophetiæ, promiscuè in coetu surrexerint, & ordine dijudicantibus aliis, de rebus Divinis disseruerint, 1. Cor. XIV. 29. &c. quin & disperși illi post mortem Stephani prædicaverint, Act. VIII. 4. XI. 19. tamen & commune illud charitatis officium, & peculiaris mos ille prophetandi temporarius, vigentibus donis extraordinariis ad fidem doctrinæ Christianæ mundo recens illatæ eò magis conciliandam, usitatus, & interior ille afflatus Spiritus S. qui nonnullis nascentis inprimis Ecclesiæ tempore, pro vocatione fuit; certorum & delectorum quorundam hominum Ecclesiis vel omnibus, vel quibusdam præpositorum ministerium non excludit. Nam eodem tempore apud Corinthios etiam Paulus plantavit & Apollo rigavit, & ministri illi fuerunt, per quos Corinthii crediderunt, 1. Cor. III. 5. 6. & præter ejusmodi Prophetas & ipsos Apostolos immediatè vocatos fuerunt πρεσβύτεροι κατ' Ἐκκλησίαν Presbyteri in Ecclesiis, & Episcopi iidem, Act. XX. 17. 28. idque ex institutione Christi, de qua supra. Citò etiam in Ecclesia cùm ipsis donis extraordinariis, quæ vocationis vicem fungebantur, promiscuæ illæ Prophetarum, immediata Spiritus S. inspiratione ad docendum agitatorum, institutiones cef-sarunt; & qui primitus sine labore, præparatione & tempore, subitò ἀδαχτοι apti ad docendum facti sunt, deinceps non sine labore, præparatione & tempore tales fuerunt. Neque Ecclesia cessantibus nunc donis extraordinariis, & singulari illa directione, qua cum iisdem Spiritus S. Ecclesiam moderatus est, sine extrema confusione quosvis non exploratos, non vocatos ordine, & Spiritus S. afflatum temerè mentientes recipere & audire ausit. Nullus enim sic turbarum, schismatum, ἀπαξλιας finis vel modus in Ecclesia, in qua tamen omnia ordine & decenter fieri debent, esset, quod Enthusiastarum, Reformationis tempore, væsano impetu Ecclesiam sic turbantium nefarii furores docuerunt. Denique nec Christus, Ecclesiæ Princeps, nec Apostoli, nec Presbyteri, ac ne Diaconi quidem in Ecclesia Apostolica & primitiva sine Divina immediata vel mediata vocatione munus Ecclesiasticum capessiverunt, vel gesserunt. Et si ἀδιδακτος doctor vocatus majus judicium accipiet, non per omnia muneri satisfaciens, Jac. III. 1. quomodo evadet judicium, qui non vocatus ad docendum, & nescius, quid doceat, tamen docet? Cùmque Ecclesiæ ministri non amplius, uti sub lege factum est, natalium conditione distinguantur, necesse est illos conditione vocationis distingui. Quæ Socinianis & Fanaticis quibusdam, mediatam imprimis vocationem fastidientibus, & ædilitatem hanc sacram sine suffragio, quod ajunt, gerentibus, retundendis sunt.
units.tr: XXII. A call is required for the discharge of the ministry of the Church. "No one takes this honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was" (Heb. 5:4). Here the statement about Aaron is the hypothesis, and the thesis concerns all who hold ministerial office, and so also those who hold the embassy [πρεσβείαν] on behalf of Christ. "For how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the gospel!" (Rom. 10:15). "I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied" (Jer. 23:21). For not all can teach: "Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all workers of miracles?" (1 Cor. 12:29). The Apostle denies it by asking. For although it is the duty of everyone to teach, exhort, dissuade, console and rebuke his brother and neighbour by word and example, prompted both by love of neighbour, which is the fulfilment of the law (Rom. 13:10), and by the plain law of God that we must not bear sin in our brother and neighbour (Lev. 19:17), and so that we may consider one another to provoke to love and good works (Heb. 10:24), still that common duty of love, and that particular and temporary custom of prophesying, which was in use while the extraordinary gifts flourished so that the Christian doctrine, newly brought into the world, might be the more readily believed, and that inward inspiration of the Holy Spirit which for some was a call especially at the time of the first beginnings of the Church, do not exclude the ministry of certain chosen men, either over the churches as a whole or over some of them. For at the same time among the Corinthians Paul planted and Apollos watered, and they were ministers through whom the Corinthians believed (1 Cor. 3:5, 6). Besides such prophets, and besides the apostles themselves who were called immediately, there were also elders in the congregations [πρεσβύτεροι κατ' Ἐκκλησίαν], and the same men were bishops (Acts 20:17, 28), and this came from the institution of Christ, of which we spoke above. Soon also in the Church, once those extraordinary gifts, which took the place of a call, had ceased, those promiscuous institutions of prophets, moved to teach by the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, came to an end; and those who at first became untaught [ἄδιδακτοι] yet apt to teach, without labour, preparation and time, afterwards became such only with labour, preparation and time. Nor, now that the extraordinary gifts and that singular direction by which the Holy Spirit governed the Church along with them have ceased, does the Church dare to receive and hear without the utmost confusion any men who are untested, not called in due order, and who falsely pretend to the inspiration of the Spirit. For there would be no end or measure to such disturbances, schisms and lawlessness [ἀπαξλιας] in the Church, in which, nevertheless, all things ought to be done in order and decently, as the wicked frenzies of the Enthusiasts, who in the time of the Reformation disturbed the Church with raging fury, have taught. Finally, neither Christ, the Prince of the Church, nor the apostles, nor the elders, nor even the deacons in the apostolic and primitive Church took up or discharged any ecclesiastical office without a divine call, whether immediate or mediate. And if an untaught [ἀδίδακτος] teacher who has been called will receive the greater judgment, not satisfying the office in every respect (Jas. 3:1), how will he escape judgment who, not called to teach and ignorant of what he teaches, nevertheless teaches? And since the ministers of the Church are no longer distinguished by birth, as was done under the law, it is necessary that they be distinguished by the condition of their call. This must be pressed against the Socinians and certain Fanatics, who above all despise a mediate call and who carry on this sacred office without, as they say, a vote.

units.la: XXIII. Auctor vocationis Pastorum Ecclesiæ princeps Christus Ecclesiæ caput, & ministrorum Dominus, est. Ille enim quosdam Pastores & Doctores dat, Ephes. IV. 11. Distributiones διακονιῶν ministeriorum sunt; & idem Dominus, Christus eorum author, 1. Cor. XII. 5. Rogate Dominum messis, ut emittat operarios in messem suam, Matth. IX. 38. Ejusdem est ministros legere, & in Ecclesiæ arvum immittere, à quo muneris ipsius potestas & authoritas est. Cùmque Ecclesia Dei peculium & Sponsa sit, solus Deus indicare potest, quinam peculiò huic ministrare, fideles præparare, & ut virginem puram uni viro, Christo, sistere debeant, 2. Cor. XI. 2. Ipse est ὁ αὐξάνων ille, qui incrementum dat, 1. Cor. III. 7. Solus ille dona ministerio necessaria conferre potest; neque homines vel aliter eligere possunt, quàm ipse in verbo suo præscripsit, vel alios eligere possunt, quàm quos à Deo per charismata sua aptatos & idoneos inveniunt.
units.tr: XXIII. The author of the call of ministers of the Church is Christ, the Head of the Church and the Lord of the ministers. For he gives ministers and teachers (Eph. 4:11). There are distributions of ministries [διακονιῶν]; and the same Lord, Christ, is their author (1 Cor. 12:5). Pray the Lord of the harvest that he send out labourers into his harvest (Matt. 9:38). It belongs to him to choose ministers and to send them into the field of the Church, and from him comes the power and authority of their office. And since the Church of God is his own possession and his bride, God alone can indicate who are to minister to this possession, to prepare the faithful, and to present them as a pure virgin to one husband, Christ (2 Cor. 11:2). He is the one who gives the increase (1 Cor. 3:7). He alone can bestow the gifts necessary for the ministry; nor can men choose otherwise than as he has prescribed in his Word, nor can they choose others than those whom they find fitted and qualified by God through his gifts.

units.la: XXIV. Vocatio illa Divina vel interna, vel externa est. Interna vel extraordinaria, vel ordinaria. Illa per solum afflatum & inspirationem internam specialem & extraordinariam, quæ vocationis instar est, quomodo olim Deus Prophetas vocavit. Hæc per collatam tum ἱκανότητα aptitudinem ad officium obeundum, tum charitatem Dei & proximi ad illud concupiscendum, fit. Nam ἱκανότης sufficientia nostra est à Deo, qui nos ἱκάνωσεν idoneos fecit ministros N. T. 2. Cor. III. 5. 6. Et fidelis est sermo. Si quis ἐπισκοπῆς ὀρέγεται inspectionem desiderat, is bonum opus concupiscit, 1. Tim. III. 1. Ubi duo spectanda sunt, ἐπισκοπῆς opus & bonitas, hoc est, pretium, laudabilitas & pulchritudo operis. Si ita ἐπισκοπὴ inspectio consideratur, recte cognoscitur & appetitur. Si quis autem circa illam spectat dignitatem, occasionem augendæ potentiæ, opum congerendarum, φης, potestatis usurpandæ, dominandi hominibus, & κνεἱως egestatis consolandæ, is ἐπισκο-πὴν nec recte cognoscit, nec recte appetit. Cum enim concupiscentia boni operis charitas quædam sit, ἐπισκοπῆς concupiscentia charitas pariter esse debet. Neque aliud quam charitas esse potest, si revera appetitus curationis, & non appetitus pereuntis boni sub nomine curationis est. Quomodo etiam Christus docuit, non esse in Regno suo hominibus datam ἀρχὴν καὶ ἐξουσίαν principatum & dominium, sed διακονίαν ministerium, ut qui magnus esse voluerit, fit reliquorum διάκονος minister, & qui πρῶτος primus inter illos esse contenderit, fit illorum δοῦλος servus, Matth. XX.26.27. In ministerio ergo nemo magnus, nisi pluribus inserviens, esse potest. Charitas quærit, ut bonum, utile, eximium, & omni laude dignum opus faciat. Nihil autem homine dignius esse potest, quàm Dei gloriæ invigilare, & Ecclesiæ ejusdem inservire. Quia tamen opus est, quod πόνον laborare secum fert, 1. Tim. V.17. & bonum opus est, quod recte & laudabiliter fieri debet, necesse est, ut qui ἐπισκοπὴν curationem & inspectionem illam appetit, tum examinet diligenter, quid ad id opus, quod διακονία Θεοῦ ministerium Dei, cooperatio Dei, 2. Cor. VI. 1. & opus bonum hominis Dei, 2. Tim. III. 17. est, requiratur: tum ut in se ipsum descendat, sinus suos excutiat, & se exploret, quomodo ad id instructus sit, & an virtute ex alto, ad hoc recte agendum, indutus sit; an ἱκανὸς καὶ ἐπιτήδειος idoneus & aptus ad obeundum hoc ministerium sit, atque dotes illas, quas mox Apostolus 1. Tim. III. 2. 3. &c. exigit, possideat; an denique puro gloriæ Dei amore & Ecclesiæ ædificandæ studio, & necessariis ad id charismatis, atque ἀπόστολον profectu, qui φανερῶσθαι idoneè manifestari possint, 1. Tim. IV. 15. non destituatur. Qui conscientiam & ἱκανότητα aptitudinis sufficientiam & charitatis ejusmodi habet, ei conscientia sua sic pro interna vocatione est, ut curationem eam appetere possit, at non sine timore & trepidatione suscipere debeat. Ideo nec passim multi munus illud deposcere debent. Ne multi doctores fiatis, fratres mei, scientes, quòd majus judicium accipiemus, Jac. III. 1. Neque enim tutum est, ut quivis hanc sarcinam suscipiat, vel docere occœptet. Licet enim Ecclesia doctoribus opus habeat, tamen nec plerorumque is captus est, ut docere possint, & recte velint, nec conducit quidvis apud Ecclesiam, quæ institutione indiget, dici. Et prædictum est, fore ut multi parum idonei officium docendi occupent, atque se ipsos ad loquendum & docendum quidvis præcipitent. Erit tempus, quando sanam doctrinam non sustinebunt, sed juxta concupiscentias proprias sibi ipsis coacervabunt doctores, auditu prurientes, 2. Tim. IV. 3. Id quomodo per ineptos doctores in Ecclesia evenerit, & quotidie eveniat, tristis experientia loquitur. Quibus etiam μεῖζον κρίμα majus illud judicium a S. Jacobo intentatum metuendum est, qui suscipiendo munus veluti spondent pro salute animarum, & tamen vadimonium in re tanti momenti deserunt. Quæ causa est, quòd olim inviti multi quorum ministerio Ecclesia indiguit, electi sunt, & vix ullus Episcopus nisi quæsitissimis precibus exoratus, legitimus habitus est. Inventus etiam Ammonius ille Monachus est, qui narrante Sozomeno Hist. Eccl. I. 6. V. 28. invitus ordinandus cum esset, auriculam sibi abscidit, comminatus se etiam linguam sibi præcisurum, nisi coeptis desisterent. Imò introducta tandem est, crescente licet ambitione, formula in ordinationibus adhiberi solita: Visne episcopari? respondente Candidato: Nolo. Quæ Canonistarum ridicula hypocrisis est, non recipientium nisi eum, qui specie saltem renuat, vel trepidè, fœminæ instar admittat, vel callidè, instar Episcopi illius Metinensis, qui interrogatus; Nolens volo; & volens nolo, uti in Gloss. q. 1. c. 8. c. in Script. habetur, respondit, specie recusantis flagrantissimè petat. Cæterum tum is, qui sincerè cum Esaja dicit: Ecce ego, mitte me, Esaj. VI. 8. tum is, qui cum Jeremia expavescens exclamat: Ah, ah, Domine Jehova, en ego nescio loqui, quia puer sum, Jerem. I. 6. bene præesse poterit, ut scitè Gregorius M. loquitur, & is, qui recusat, plenè non resistit, & is, qui mitti vult, antea per altaris calculum purgatum se vidit.
units.tr: XXIV. This divine call is either internal or external. The internal is either extraordinary or ordinary. The former comes through the inspiration alone, a special and extraordinary internal breathing, which serves in place of a call, as God formerly called the prophets. The latter comes through the aptitude for discharging the office which is bestowed, and through love of God and neighbour which desires it. For sufficiency [ἱκανότης] is our sufficiency from God, who has made us fit ministers of the New Testament (2 Cor. 3:5, 6). And this is a faithful saying: If anyone desires the oversight, he desires a good work (1 Tim. 3:1). Here two things must be considered: the work of oversight and its goodness, that is, the worth, praiseworthiness and beauty of the work. If the oversight is considered in this way, it is rightly known and desired. But if anyone looks upon that office as an occasion of increasing his power, of gathering wealth, of reputation [φήμης], of seizing authority, of ruling over men, and of care [κηδεμονίας] for the needy, he neither rightly knows nor rightly desires the oversight. For since the desire for a good work is a kind of love, the desire for oversight must likewise be love. And it can be nothing other than love if it is truly a desire for care, and not a desire for a perishing good under the name of care. Just so Christ taught that in his kingdom there was not given to men rule and authority [ἀρχὴν καὶ ἐξουσίαν], principate and dominion, but ministry [διακονίαν]: whoever wishes to be great becomes the minister [διάκονος] of the rest, and whoever strives to be first [πρῶτος] among them becomes their servant [δοῦλος] (Matt. 20:26, 27). So in the ministry no one can be great unless he serves many. Love seeks to do a good, useful, excellent work, worthy of all praise. Nothing, however, can be more worthy of a man than to watch over the glory of God and to serve his Church. Yet since it is a work which brings with it toil [πόνον] (1 Tim. 5:17), and a good work which must be done rightly and praiseworthily, it is necessary that whoever desires that oversight [ἐπισκοπὴν], that is, the care and inspection, first examine diligently what is required for that work, which is the ministry of God [διακονία Θεοῦ], the cooperation of God (2 Cor. 6:1), and the good work of the man of God (2 Tim. 3:17). Then he should go down into himself, search his heart, and test himself as to how he is equipped for it, and whether he is clothed with power from on high to discharge it rightly; whether he is fit and suitable [ἱκανὸς καὶ ἐπιτήδειος], able and apt, for discharging this ministry, and possesses those qualities which the Apostle immediately requires (1 Tim. 3:2, 3, etc.); and finally whether he is lacking in pure love of the glory of God and zeal for building up the Church, and in the gifts necessary for this, and in progress [ἀπόστολον], by which they may be suitably made manifest [φανερῶσθαι] (1 Tim. 4:15). The man who has such a conscience and such sufficiency [ἱκανότητα] of aptitude and love has in his conscience the internal call, so that he may desire that care, yet he ought to undertake it not without fear and trembling. Therefore not many should demand that office indiscriminately. Let not many of you become teachers, my brethren, knowing that we shall receive the greater judgment (Jas. 3:1). For it is not safe for anyone to take up this burden or to begin to teach. For although the Church has need of teachers, yet the capacity of most men is not such that they can teach and rightly wish to do so, nor is it fitting for anyone to speak carelessly in the Church, which needs instruction. And it has been foretold that many who are little fitted would take up the office of teaching and hurl themselves into speaking and teaching anything at all. There will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own lusts they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears (2 Tim. 4:3). How this has happened through unfit teachers in the Church, and how it happens every day, sad experience tells. Those men too must fear that greater judgment [μεῖζον κρίμα], the judgment threatened by St James, who, in undertaking the office, as it were stand surety for the salvation of souls, and yet abandon their bond in a matter of such great importance. This is the reason why in former times many who were needed by the Church for its ministry were chosen against their will, and scarcely any bishop was regarded as lawfully chosen unless he had been persuaded by the most earnest entreaties. There is also that Ammonius, the monk, who, as Sozomen relates (Hist. Eccl. 1.6; 5.28), when he was to be ordained against his will, cut off his own ear, threatening that he would also cut off his tongue unless they desisted from their undertaking. Indeed, at length, though ambition has grown, there was introduced the formula customarily used at ordinations: Do you wish to be made a bishop? The candidate replying: I do not wish it. This is a ridiculous hypocrisy of the canonists, who admit only the man who at least in appearance refuses, or who admits himself timidly, like a woman, or cunningly, like that Bishop of Metz who, when asked, Unwilling I am willing; and willing I am unwilling, as is found in the Gloss on q. 1, c. 8, c. in Script., replied, and with the appearance of one refusing sought most ardently. Moreover, he who sincerely says with Isaiah: Here I am, send me (Isa. 6:8), and he who, trembling, cries out with Jeremiah: Ah, ah, Lord Jehovah, behold I do not know how to speak, for I am a boy (Jer. 1:6), will be able to preside well, as Gregory the Great wisely says; and he who refuses does not altogether resist, and he who wishes to be sent has first seen himself purged by the coal of the altar.

units.la: XXV. Vocatio externa vel immediata, vel mediata est.
units.tr: XXV. The external calling is either immediate or mediate.

units.la: Immediata, qua Deus sine hominum ministerio & suffragatione vocat. Ita Christus in terris agens Apostolos & LXX. discipulos; & jam glorificatus Saulum vocavit. Illi enim ἐκ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, οὐδὲ δι' ἀνθρώπων nec ab hominibus, nec per homines, uti de se Paulus, vocati sunt, Gal. I. 1. Mediata, qua Deus hominum ministerio, & Ecclesia, ceu instrumento, utens vocat. Qualis vocatio ordinaria est, utpote in qua Ecclesia exploratis legitimo examine donis vocatorum, suffragio suo Divinæ vocationi astipulatur, eámque ratam gratamque habet. Ecclesiæ autem nomine utrumque genus partium integrantium, Pastores & oves, intelligimus. Sunt enim hæ oves λογικαί rationales, non brutæ pecudes; & vocem pastoris à voce alieni, & ululatu lupi internoscunt, Joh. X. 4. 14. Omnino enim cujus authoritate ministerium suscipitur, ejusdem authoritate ministri vocantur. Quocirca cum sacrum ministerium ex Christi & Ecclesiæ, id est, Sponsi & Sponsæ authoritate suscipiatur, utriusque authoritate Ministros vocari necesse est. Ubi Ecclesia plantata & collecta est, nemo illi obtrudi potest, sed Presbyterii & plebis consensus requiritur, salva manente approbatione & confirmatione Magistratus, illius inprimis, qui stipendia pastoribus confert. Unitas enim ἀδελφότητος fraternitatis & conspiratio ad mutuam ædificationem conservanda est. Et Ecclesiæ totidata potestas clavium, jus vocandi Pastores Ecclesiæ, non minimam potestatis illius partem eidem vindicat. Etenim ne ipsi quidem Apostoli, quibus nemo in Ecclesia par dignitate est, soli, & absque populi suffragio ministros elegerunt. In electione enim Matthiæ ad Apostolatum, Petro proponente, discipuli ἔστησαν duos statuerunt, Actor. I. 23. & προσευξάμενοι precantes, v. 24. ἔδωκαν κλήρους αὐτῶν jecerunt fortes eorum, v. 26. Cumque exorto murmure Apostoli Diaconos septem, bono testimonio ornatos, eligi suaderent, placuit sermo coram coram omni multitudine Greek elegerunt Stephanum,&c. quibus demum electis Apostoli manus imposuerunt, ibid. VI. 1-7. In Ecclesia quoque Antiochena Prophetarum & Doctorum luminibus collustrata, Spiritus S. mandatum λειτουργούντων αὐτῶν τῷ Κυρίῳ ἢ νηστευόντων, cum ipsi publice ministrarent Domino & jejunarent, de segregandis Barnaba & Saulo auditum fuit: Tunc cum jejunassent, & parati essent, & imposuissent iis manus, dimiserunt eos, ibid. XIII. 1.2.3. Idem ad ministerium Ecclesiarum ita segregati χειροτονηθέντες αὐτοῖς κατ' ἐκκλησίαν πρεσβυτέρους illis (discipulis) presbyteros per suffragia in singulis Ecclesiis crearunt, ibid. XIV.23. Cum enim χειροτονεῖν; qua voce Lucas ibi utitur; modo proprie porrectis manibus suffragia ferre, modo metaphorice quovis modo aliquid decernere; quo sensu martyres μαρτυρες χειροτονηθέντες testes ante definiti, ibid.X.41. dicuntur, modo synecdochice, sensu apud Patres recepto, & deinceps ab Episcopis supra Presbyteros collocatis, & jus eligendi sibi vendicantibus, detorto, manus imponere, significat; dubitari non potest, quin ibid. XIV.23. primus significatus eligendi per suffragia manibus porrectis obtineat. Hoc enim sensu S. Paulo datus peregrinationis comes χειροτονηθεὶς ὑπὸ τῆς ἐκκλησιῶν per suffragia Ecclesiarum electus, 2.Cor. VIII.19. dicitur. Ubi Chrysostomus habet. Καὶ ψηφῷ τῆς δήμου παντὸς ἐγένετο, Et populi totius calculus factus est. Ubi si in minoris momenti negotio ita Apostoli egerunt, quomodo in majoris longè momenti causa, constitutione Presbyterorum eos acturos fuisse putamus? speciem enim dominantium religiosè vitandam sibi duxerunt, memores etiam, quòd inter doctorem sive Pastorem Ecclesiæ & Ecclesiam ipsam quædam confœderatio sit, Ecclesia stipulante institutionem publicam & privatam in nomine Domini, & Pastore restipulante audientiam & obedientiam in eodem nomine; utrisque verò in hæc consentientibus, & sibi invicem fidem obstringentibus. Et proprie χειροτονεῖν est actus communis & particularis simul, quo unusquisque pro se eligit suffragio suo, & alienis suffragiis eligit. Sicut enim in politica concione, rogante præcone, populus sublatis manibus rogationem vel probabat, quæ καταχειροτονία appellari suevit, vel improbabat, quæ ἀποχειροτονία dicta est: ita S. Paulus, vel alius in Ecclesia quapiam rogationem fecit, & post rogationem etiam Ecclesiam eligentem vidit significatione manus, & ipse significatione sua astipulatus est, proin & rogatione & signo ἐχειροτόνησε. Quæ propria vocis χειροτονίας vis est. Procedente demum tempore, cum plebs suffragari desiisset, vox illa χειροτονίας per abusum pro Episcopali Presbyterorum creatione, ipsaque χειροθεσία usurpata est. Si quis tamen in loco Actor. XIV.23. verbum χειροτονῆσαι synecdochicè accipere malit, ei litem non movebimus. Sic enim verbum hoc ad solos Apostolos Paulum & Barnabam relatum denotabit χειροθεσίαν, quæ χειροτονίαν commu nibus populi suffragiis factam non excludit, sed supponit. Cùm enim duo illi actus individuo nexu cohæreant, aliquando ex consequente antecedens, aliquando ex antecedente consequens colligitur. Praxin veteris Ecclesiæ
units.tr: Immediate calling is that by which God calls without the ministry or suffrage of men. Thus Christ, while on earth, called the Apostles and the seventy disciples, and after his glorification called Saul. For they were called not from men [ἐκ τῶν ἀνθρώπων], nor through men [οὐδὲ δι' ἀνθρώπων], neither by men nor through men, as Paul says of himself (Gal. 1.1). Mediate calling is that by which God calls, using the ministry of men and the Church as his instrument. This is the ordinary calling, since in it the Church, having examined by a lawful inquiry the gifts of those called, adds its vote to the divine calling and approves and accepts it. By the name of the Church we understand both parts that make it up, the pastors and the sheep. For these sheep are rational [λογικαί], not brute beasts, and they know the voice of the shepherd from the voice of a stranger, and the howling of the wolf (John 10.4, 14). For whoever's authority the ministry is undertaken, by the same authority ministers are called. Therefore, since the holy ministry is taken up by the authority of Christ and the Church, that is, of the Bridegroom and the Bride, ministers must be called by the authority of both. Where the Church has been planted and gathered, no one can be forced upon it, but the consent of the elders and the people is required, the approval and confirmation of the magistrate remaining intact, especially of him who pays the stipends to the pastors. For the unity of brotherhood [ἀδελφότητος] and the agreement for mutual edification must be preserved. And the power of the keys, which belongs to the whole Church, claims for it no small part of that power, namely the right of calling the pastors of the Church. For not even the Apostles themselves, to whom no one in the Church is equal in dignity, chose ministers alone and without the vote of the people. In the election of Matthias to the apostolate, with Peter proposing, the disciples set up two [ἔστησαν duos statuerunt] (Acts 1.23), praying [προσευξάμενοι] (v. 24), and they cast their lots [ἔδωκαν κλήρους αὐτῶν] (v. 26). And when a murmur arose and the Apostles urged that seven deacons, adorned with good testimony, be chosen, the saying pleased the whole multitude [placuit sermo coram omni multitudine], and they chose [Greek] Stephen, etc., and when these had been chosen, the Apostles laid their hands on them (ibid. 6.1-7). Likewise in the church of Antioch, enlightened by the lights of prophets and teachers, the command of the Holy Spirit was heard concerning the separation of Barnabas and Saul, while they themselves were ministering to the Lord and fasting: then, after they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away (ibid. 13.1-3). In the same way, for the ministry of the churches, they appointed to them elders in each church by vote (χειροτονηθέντες, ibid. 14.23). For since χειροτονεῖν, the word Luke uses there, sometimes properly means to give votes with outstretched hands, sometimes metaphorically means to decide something in any way (in which sense martyrs are said to be chosen as witnesses beforehand, ibid. 10.41), and sometimes, by synecdoche, in the sense received among the Fathers and afterwards by bishops placed above presbyters and claiming for themselves the right of choosing, means to lay on hands, there can be no doubt that in Acts 14.23 the first meaning, of choosing by votes with hands raised, holds. For in this sense Paul's companion on his journey was chosen by the churches [χειροτονηθεὶς ὑπὸ τῆς ἐκκλησιῶν], that is, elected by the votes of the churches (2 Cor. 8.19). Where Chrysostom has: And it was done by the vote of the whole people [Καὶ ψηφῷ τῆς δήμου παντὸς ἐγένετο]. If the Apostles acted thus in a matter of lesser moment, how can we suppose they would have acted in a matter of far greater importance by the appointment of elders? For they thought the appearance of lording it over others was to be religiously avoided, remembering also that between the teacher or pastor of the Church and the Church itself there is a certain covenant: the Church stipulates for public and private instruction in the name of the Lord, and the pastor restipulates for hearing and obedience in the same name; both agreeing to these things and binding themselves to each other in faith. And properly χειροτονεῖν is an act both common and particular, by which each person chooses for himself with his own vote, and chooses with the votes of others. For just as in a public assembly of the state, when the herald made a proposal, the people, with hands raised, either approved the proposal, which is called καταχειροτονία, or disapproved it, which is called ἀποχειροτονία, so Paul, or some other in a certain church, made a proposal, and after the proposal saw the electing church by the sign of the hand, and himself assented by his own sign; thus he ἐχειροτόνησε by both proposal and sign. This is the proper force of the word χειροτονία. But as time went on, when the people had ceased to vote, that word χειροτονία came to be used by abuse for the episcopal creation of presbyters, and the very laying on of hands (χειροθεσία) was used. If anyone would rather take the word χειροτονῆσαι in Acts 14.23 by synecdoche, we will not quarrel with him. For thus the word, referred to the Apostles Paul and Barnabas alone, will denote the laying on of hands, which does not exclude the choosing made by the common votes of the people but presupposes it. For since those two acts cohere in an inseparable bond, sometimes the antecedent is inferred from the consequent, and sometimes the consequent from the antecedent. The practice of the ancient Church

units.la: luculenter Cyprianus lib.I. epistol.4. ostendit, ubi ita ille: Plebs obsequens præceptis Dominicis, & Deum metuens, à peccatore præposito se separare debet, nec se ad sacrilegi Sacerdotis sacrificia miscere, cùm ipsa maxime potestatem habeat vel eligendi dignos Sacerdotes, vel indignos recusandi, quod & ipsum videmus de Divina authoritate descendere. Aliorum etiam Patrum & Conciliorum consensum post Antonium de Dominis de Repub. Eccl. lib. III.3. & Pammelium Annot. ad Ep.68. Cypr. Polyhistor Blondellus de Episcopis & Presbyteris pag.379-545. luculenter asseruit. In ipso Pontificali veteri Episcopus Ordinator sic loquitur: Non frustra à Patribus institutum, ut de electione eorum, qui ad regimen altaris adhibendi sunt, consulatur, & populus, quia necesse est, ut facilius ei quis obedientiam exhibeat ordinato, cui assensum præbuerit ordinando.
units.tr: Cyprian clearly shows in book 1, letter 4, where he says: The people, obedient to the Lord's precepts and fearing God, ought to separate themselves from a sinful prelate, nor mix themselves into the sacrifices of a sacrilegious priest, since the people itself has especially the power either of choosing worthy priests or of refusing unworthy ones, which we also see to descend from divine authority. The consent of other Fathers and Councils has also been clearly asserted after Antonio de Dominis (On the Commonwealth of the Church, book 3, ch. 3), and by Pamelius (notes on Cyprian's letter 68), and Blondel, Polyhistor, On Bishops and Presbyters, pp. 379-545. In the ancient Pontifical itself, the ordaining bishop speaks thus: It was not in vain that the Fathers instituted that, concerning the election of those who are to be admitted to the service of the altar, the people should be consulted, so that, because it is necessary, the one ordained may more easily be obeyed by the people to whom they have given their assent when he was being ordained.

units.la: XXVI. Præpostera vocationis Aharonis, nullo suffragante populo, & Ministrorum N. T. ordinariorum comparatio est.
units.tr: XXVI. The Ministry of the Old Testament Is Not Comparable to the Ordinary Ministers of the New Testament: Aaron Was Called Without the Suffrage of the People

units.la: Paulus enim docens, neminem sibi sumere honorem, sed qui vocatus est à Deo καθάπερ ὁ Ἀαρὼν sicut Aharon, Hebr. V.4. vocationem, non vocationis modum comparat. Aharon enim immediatè à Deo vocatus, Mose interprete & internuntio, populi suffragatione non indiguit. At ordinarii Ecclesiæ N. T. ministri mediatè vocantur. Ac ne successores quidem Aharonis eo modo vocati sunt, quo Aharon, quia illis carnalis generatio pro vocatione fuit. Particula igitur καθώς similitudinem vocationis quoad rem, non æqualitatem quoad rem & modum significat. Par ratio missionis Christi & Apostolorum est; quæ utraque immediata fuit. Proin verbis illis Christi: Καθὼς sicut me misit Pater, & ego mitto vos; Joh. XX.21. particula καθὼς sicut proportionem, non æqualitatem significat, neque adeò ad omnimodam potestatis paritatem, sed ad Divinam muneris authoritatem, promissionem successus ministerii & defensionis in periculis, aliáque similia, non ad dissimilia referri debet. Nam ne ipsi quidem Apostoli eodem modo vocati sunt, quo Christus. Ille enim, uti non malè Nicetas Choniates Schol. in Orat.42. Nazianz. Christi verba explicat, ut lumen à Sole, sic à Patre missus est, unam atque eandem cum eo habens substantiam: at discipuli ut servi à Domino missi sunt. Ille ceu par à pari, hi tanquam homines à Deo missi sunt. Quòd ovibus non convenire, ut Pastores suos eligant, tricantur, frivolum est. Nam populus Christianus oves propriæ non hominis ullius, sed Ἀρχιποιμένος summi Pastoris Christi sunt. Ideo Christus ad Petrum: Pasce oves meas, Joh. XXI. 15.16. Alia etiam ovium brutarum & proprie talium, alia rationalium & metaphoricè talium ratio est. Illis judicio discretionis carentibus electio Pastorum suorum non convenit, his convenit, tum quia veros Pastores à falsis discernere, illos sequi, hos fugere, ibid. X.3.&c. jubentur: tum quia communis Pastorum ministrantium & ovium sub summo Pastore Christo, conditio est, cùm ejusdem speciei, eorundem beneficiorum participes, ejusdem hæreditatis consortes sint, & qui ob ministerium atque curam fratrum Pastores dicuntur, non absolutè tales, sed respectu Christi etiam
units.tr: Paul, teaching that no one takes this honour to himself but he who is called by God, "as Aaron was" [καθάπερ ὁ Ἀαρών] (Heb. 5.4), compares the manner of calling, not the calling itself. Aaron was called immediately by God, with Moses as interpreter and intermediary, and he did not need the suffrage of the people. But the ordinary ministers of the New Testament Church are called mediately. Nor were Aaron's successors called in the same way as Aaron, since for them carnal descent served as their calling. The particle "as" [καθώς] therefore signifies a likeness in the thing called, not an equality in the thing and the manner. The sending of Christ and of the Apostles is of the same kind, and both were immediate. So in the words of Christ, "As [καθὼς] the Father has sent me, so I send you" (John 20.21), the particle "as" signifies proportion, not equality, and it refers not to a complete equality of power but to the divine authority of the office, the promise of success in the ministry, and protection in dangers, and other similar things, not to dissimilar ones. For the Apostles themselves were not called in the same way as Christ. He, as Nicetas Choniates rightly explains in his scholia on the oration of Gregory Nazianzen, was sent as light is from the sun, having one and the same substance with the Father; but the disciples were sent as servants by their Lord. He was sent as an equal by an equal; they were sent as men by God. That the sheep should not choose their own shepherds, as they object, is trifling. For the Christian people are the sheep not of any man but of Christ, the chief Shepherd [Ἀρχιποιμένος]. Hence Christ says to Peter, "Feed my sheep" (John 21.15–16). The case of brute sheep, which are sheep properly speaking, is one thing, and the case of rational sheep, which are such metaphorically, is another. Electing their own shepherds does not suit the former, who lack the power of judgement; it does suit the latter, both because they are commanded to distinguish true shepherds from false, to follow the one and flee the other (John 10.3 etc.), and because it is the common condition of ministering shepherds and sheep under the supreme Shepherd Christ that they are of the same kind, share the same benefits and are fellow heirs of the same inheritance; and those who are called shepherds on account of the ministry and care of the brethren are so called not absolutely but in respect of Christ.

units.la: Argumentum contrarium occurritur. etiam oves, & seleƈtæ, instrumenta & membra veri atque unici Pastoris eximia, sint. In civili politia subditi Regum oves, sicut ipsi Reges pastores dicuntur. Nil tamen obstat, quò minùs à subditis Reges eligantur. Præterea populi infideles, ad quos Apostoli Evangelistas aliósque miserunt, consiliis & suffragiis suis eosdem non adoptarunt. Sed alia Ecclesiæ plantandæ, alia plantatæ ratio est. Quin & ipsum Evangelistarum munus temporale & extraordinarium fuit. Neque etiam infideles, ad quos illi missi sunt, inviti & coacti, sed libentes volentésque eos vel receperunt, vel repulerunt, non obstantibus illis, vel restitantibus ultra, Matth. X. 23. In Ecclesiis verò plantatis & constitutis Apostoli ipsi suffragia populi minimè omiserunt. Canones verò vetustiores consensum populi ab electione non excludunt, sed hoc tantùm cavent, ne vel populus jure suo abutatur, vel sibi soli excluso Presbyterio potestatem eligendi vendicet, vel modum eligendi insolenter præscribat, vel turbulenter & confusè in negotio hoc agat, uti Concilium Laodicenum can. 13. aliáque fidem faciunt. Et licuisse olim plebi Pastores eligere, Hierarchici diffiteri non audent, diversam tantùm temporum rationem caussati, quòd olim populus moderatus, gravis, publicæ utilitatis studiosus ad suffragia ejusmodi admitti potuerit, at nunc cùm Bestia multorum capitum & seditionibus intenta sit, admitti amplius non posset. Sed perperam discrimen temporum in concessione non humana, sed Divina, adeóque respectu hominum non precaria, sed justa & debita, fingitur. Neque nos cum Fanaticis potestatem eligendi imperitæ plebi, Magistratu & Ministerio Ecclesiæ exclusò, vindicamus, sed omnia κατὰ τάξιν καὶ ἐυσχημόνως secundum ordinem & decenter agenda esse, assignatis suis cuique ordini partibus, pertendimus. Plebs verò Christiana cùm cœtus fidelium Christi ovium sit, petulanti convitio Bestiæ multorum capitum proscinditur. Quin si hodieque fideli populo Pastores ejusmodi præsint, quales olim præfuerunt, & præesse debent, eam piam, moderatam, gravem & publicæ utilitatis studiosam fieri, experientia docet. Quòd si in Papatu plebs adeò degeneravit, ut jam sit Bestia multorum capitum, causa non alia est, quàm quia ejus Pastores veteribus illis & veris Pastoribus dissimiles, & Apocalypticæ Bestiæ capita vel membra sunt.
units.tr: An opposing argument meets us: even the sheep, though chosen, are the excellent instruments and members of the true and only Shepherd. In civil polity the subjects are sheep, just as the kings themselves are called shepherds; yet nothing prevents kings from being chosen by their subjects. Moreover, the unbelieving peoples to whom the Apostles sent evangelists and others did not adopt those men by their counsel and suffrage. But the manner of planting a Church is one thing, and the manner of a planted Church is another. Indeed the very office of the evangelists was temporary and extraordinary. Nor did those unbelievers to whom they were sent receive or reject them unwillingly and under compulsion, but gladly and willingly, unless they resisted or rejected them further (Matt. 10.23). In Churches that were already planted and established, however, the Apostles themselves by no means omitted the suffrage of the people. The older canons do not exclude the consent of the people from election; they only take care that the people do not abuse their right, or claim for themselves alone, to the exclusion of the presbytery, the power of electing, or prescribe the manner of electing insolently, or act in this business in a turbulent and confused way, as the Council of Laodicea, canon 13, and other evidence attest. And the hierarchists dare not deny that in former times the common people were allowed to elect their pastors; they allege only a different state of the times, that in former days the people were moderate, serious, and devoted to the public good, and so could be admitted to such suffrages, but now, since the Beast with many heads is intent on sedition, it could no longer be admitted. But the difference of the times is wrongly invented in a concession that is not human but divine, and so, with respect to men, not revocable but just and due. Nor do we, along with the fanatics, claim the power of electing for an unskilled populace, with the magistracy and the ministry of the Church excluded; we maintain that all things must be done "according to order and decently" [κατὰ τάξιν καὶ ἐυσχημόνως], each order having its own assigned part. The Christian people, however, being the assembly of Christ's faithful sheep, is torn to pieces by the wanton insult of "the Beast with many heads". Indeed, if even today such pastors as formerly presided over the faithful people, and such as ought to preside, were in charge, experience teaches that the people would become pious, moderate, serious and devoted to the public good. But if among the Papists the people have so degenerated that they are now the Beast with many heads, the cause is no other than that their pastors are unlike those old and true pastors, and are the heads or members of the Apocalyptic Beast.

units.la: XXVII. Sed jus tamen vocandi Pastores cum ejusdem exercitio confundi non debet. Jus ipsum totius Ecclesiæ, & singulorum ejus membrorum: at exercitium ordinum Ecclesiæ est. Tres verò in Ecclesia ordines sunt, Magistratus, Pastores & populus, qui idem jus habentes canonicè eligendi Pastores vel per se, vel per Magistratus, Seniores, aliósque à se delegatos, diversimodè tamen jus illud exercent. Unde vocationis totius forma sic variat, ut ὡς ἐν πλάτῃ dici possit, scilicet cum Pastoribus, & delectis Senioribus examen & χειροτονίαν manuum impositionem; Magistratui Christiano & consentienti in doctrina inprimis ei, qui honoraria laborantibus constituit, directionem ordinis, & confirmationem, & subinde etiam nominationem; denique populo consensum, suffragium & approbationem competere. Quæ munerum diversitas illud habet, quòd nec Pastores unà cum Senioribus examen & impositionem manuum, nec Magistratus confirmationem vel abdicare, vel transferre in alios possunt: at singuli jus explorandi, nominandi & per suffragia ad Ecclesiæ particularis ministerium deputandi transferre quidem in alios, at non sic abdicare possunt, ut invitis sibi & prorsus dissentientibus, si graves dissentiendi causæ suppetant, & animarum salus, quæ curam hanc idonei Pastoris providendi deponere prorsus non finit, periclitetur, obtrudi Pastorem patiantur. Et jus ipsum, quoad proprietatem ita in Ecclesia manet, ut non pollit vel auctoritate aliena eripi, vel voluntaria concessione amitti, vel alienæ fidei simpliciter committi. Actus enim Ecclesiæ est causa necessaria ad vocationem Ecclesiasticam requisita.
units.tr: XXVII. Yet the right of calling pastors must not be confused with its exercise. The right itself belongs to the whole Church and to each of its members; the exercise belongs to the orders of the Church. There are three orders in the Church: the magistracy, the pastors, and the people. All of them have the same right of lawfully electing pastors, whether in person or through the magistrates, the elders, and others delegated by them; yet they exercise that right in different ways.
