Hence the form of the whole calling varies, so that it may be said to be "as in a picture" [ὡς ἐν πλάτῃ]: namely, that the examination and the laying on of hands [χειροτονία] belong to the pastors together with the chosen elders; that the Christian magistrate, who is agreed in doctrine, and above all who provides the stipend for those who labour, has the direction of the order, its confirmation, and afterwards also the nomination; and finally that the people have the consent, the suffrage and the approval. The diversity of these offices has this consequence: the pastors together with the elders cannot renounce or transfer to others the examination and the laying on of hands, and the magistrate cannot renounce or transfer the confirmation; but individuals can transfer to others the right of examining, nominating and appointing by suffrage to the ministry of a particular Church, yet they cannot renounce it in such a way that, against their will and in complete dissent, when there are serious grounds for dissent and the salvation of souls is endangered (which does not permit the duty of providing a suitable pastor to be wholly abandoned), they allow a pastor to be thrust upon them. And the right itself, as to its ownership, remains in the Church in such a way that it cannot be taken away by another's authority, nor lost by voluntary concession, nor simply committed to another's trust. For the act of the Church is a necessary cause required for ecclesiastical calling.

units.la: XXVIII. Exercitium vocationis quoad jus eligendi, in quo vocatio essentialiter constitit, modò plenius & perfectius, modò imperfectius est, prout Ecclesia ipsa majore vel minore zelo, pietate, notitia & libertate gaudet.
units.tr: XXVIII. The exercise of the calling, as far as the right of electing is concerned, in which the calling essentially consists, is sometimes fuller and more perfect, sometimes less perfect, according as the Church itself enjoys greater or lesser zeal, piety, knowledge and freedom.

units.la: Est enim ubi fideles paribus votis & suffragiis concurrunt. Alibi familiarum omnium, alibi præcipuarum capita; alibi fideles Magistratus non minimam cœtus partem constituentes, Ecclesiæ Patroni atque Nutritii, & Tabulæ legis utriusque custodes, fideíque defensores, fidelium subditorum personas gerentes, & simul vestigia Regum V. T. piorum prementes, ne lupi gregem invadant, atque ut populus fidei suæ creditus salutariter erudiatur, curantes, denique Pastorum etiam sustentationi providentes; alibi collegia ex personis Ecclesiasticis & politicis vel popularibus etiam mixta, quæ modò suo & Ecclesiæ tantùm, modò etiam magistratus nomine agunt expressam vel tacitam constitutionem ab Ecclesiis habent, atque ea freti nominandi officio non sine fructu defunguntur. Est etiam, ubi Consistoria duos vel tres, quos dignos judicant, Patrono Ecclesiæ, qui sive ut advocatus, œconomus & procurator Ecclesiæ primitus constitutus, sive propter beneficia in Ecclesia extruenda, proventu & stipendio idoneo Pastori sumptibus suis constituendo (neque enim de titulo certò constat) jure Patronatus gaudet, sive is ἰμόπης, sive diversæ religioni addictus sit, ad faciendam ex iis optionem, offerunt. Est, ubi à Patrono oblatus nonnisi unus præsentatur & recipitur. Quod jus Patronatus ex fermento Papatus reliquum tamdiu saltem propter quæsita Patronorum jura, quibus Ecclesia non libenter eosdem defraudat, ne injustitiæ insimulari possit, cum justo moderamine tolerari potest, quandiu nullum ex eo detrimentum Ecclesia patitur, & non planè populi, cui Pastor præficitur, libertas opprimitur, atque is ad audiendos heterodoxos vel aperte scelaratos non adigitur. Alias Ecclesia non libera voluntate se ministris suis subjiceret, quod tamen in ministerio non minùs, quàm in conjugio necessarium est. Ac licèt non raro electionis libertas ab Episcopis, Magistratu, Patronis immi-nuatur, atque tum electio non eo modo libera fit, quo oportet, electio tamen esse non definit; sicut non definit esse conjugium iniquis-ratiorationibus procuratum; Utrobique enim consensus quodammodo voluntarius est. De modis enim eligendi cùm non omnes fideles paribus suffragiis rem promovent, tenendum sic, illos tacito populi consensu firmari, ut tamen Ecclesia jus suum in alios transferre eo, quo diximus, modo, posset. Nam nec Apostoli, Apostolici, & consequens prima Ecclesia forte semper cum tota fraternitate similibus occasionibus consilia miscuit, sed nonnunquam seniorum delectum habuit: nec semper, quando Ecclesia, vel fratres ab Apostolis convocati leguntur, ad unum omnes convocati, vel, ob temporum iniquitatem, congregati sunt: & fraternitate jus plenum constitit, etiam eorum conventui Titius vel Mævius defuerit. Et fuit etiam Ecclesia Christiana prima, utpote coelestis Spiritus luce plenius collustrata, & extraordinariis donis plane insignis ad regiminis Ecclesiastici perfectionem longè aptior, quàm sequentium temporum, quibus singularia illa dona expirarunt, Ecclesia fuit; quæ proin partes quasdam regiminis tutius in aliorum humeros, non abdicata licèt omni cura, devolvit. Quo non obstante apud sic vocatos & doctrinæ puritas, & Divina Christi promittentis, se in medio duorum vel trium in nomine suo congregatorum futurum, Matth. XVIII. 20. & humana publica Ecclesiæ vocantis authoritas sarta & tecta perstat.
units.tr: For in some places the faithful concur with equal votes and suffrages; in others, the heads of all families; in others, the faithful magistrates, who form no small part of the assembly, the patrons and nurturers of the Church, the guardians of both tables of the law and defenders of the faith, who bear the persons of the faithful subjects and at the same time tread in the footsteps of the pious kings of the Old Testament, taking care that wolves do not invade the flock and that the people entrusted to their faith be salutarily instructed, and who also provide for the maintenance of the pastors; in others, colleges composed of ecclesiastical and civil persons, or even mixed with laymen, which act sometimes in their own name and that of the Church only, sometimes also in the name of the magistrate, and have an express or tacit constitution from the Churches, and relying on this discharge the office of nomination not without fruit. In some places too, consistories offer two or three whom they judge worthy to the patron of the Church, who enjoys the right of patronage, whether he was first set up as advocate, steward and procurator of the Church, or on account of benefactions in building the church and providing a suitable income and stipend for the pastor at his own expense (for the title is not certainly established), so that from them he may make a choice, whether he be a layman [ἰδιώτης] or addicted to a different religion. In some places, what the patron offers is presented and received as only one person. This right of patronage, a leaven of the Papacy that remains, may for so long at least, on account of the rights of the patrons already acquired, which the Church does not gladly defraud them of, lest it be accused of injustice, be tolerated with just moderation, as long as the Church suffers no harm from it, and the liberty of the people over whom a pastor is set is not wholly oppressed, and they are not compelled to hear heterodox or openly wicked men. Otherwise the Church would not subject itself to its ministers by free will, which is no less necessary in the ministry than in marriage. And although the freedom of election is not seldom diminished by bishops, magistrates or patrons, and then the election is not made as freely as it ought to be, nevertheless it does not cease to be an election; just as a marriage arranged by unjust reasons does not cease to be a marriage. In each case the consent is in some measure voluntary. Concerning the manners of electing: since not all the faithful advance the matter with equal suffrages, it must be held that those choices are confirmed by the tacit consent of the people, yet in such a way that the Church could transfer its right to others in the manner we have described. For neither the Apostles, nor the Apostolic men, nor, consequently, perhaps the first Church always mingled counsels with the whole brotherhood in similar circumstances; sometimes they had a choice made by the elders. Nor, when the Church or the brethren were summoned by the Apostles, do we read that all were always summoned together, or gathered together because of the wickedness of the times; and the full right of the brotherhood remained intact even if Titius or Maevius was absent from their assembly. The first Christian Church was also, as it were, more fully illuminated by the light of the heavenly Spirit and clearly distinguished by extraordinary gifts, and far better suited to the perfection of ecclesiastical government than the Church of later times, when those singular gifts expired; so it safely handed over certain parts of government to the shoulders of others, though it did not wholly abdicate care. Nevertheless, among those so called both the purity of doctrine and the divine promise of Christ, that he would be "in the midst of two or three gathered in my name" (Matt. 18.20), and the human public authority of the Church calling them, remain whole and intact.

units.la: XXIX. Vocationem ipsam examen & δοκιμασία vocandi præcedit.
units.tr: XXIX. The calling itself is preceded by examination and testing (δοκιμασία) of the one to be called.

units.la: Nam de Diaconis S. Paulus: Δοκιμαζέσθωσαν πρῶτον, εἶτα διακονείτωσαν, Probentur prius, postea ministrent, 1. Tim. III. 10. Et quantò id magis in vocatione Pastorum requiritur? Quos cum judicio accurato, & inquisitione donorum, profectus, vitæ & charitatis legi convenit. Ideo S. Paulus idem: χεῖρας ταχέως μηδενὶ ἐπιτίθει, Manus cito nemini (non invento tali, qualem cap. III. describpsit) impone, neque communica cum peccatis alienis, ib. V. 22. Festinatio enim vel socordiam & contemptum τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς, vel cupiditatem dominandi, suum commodum promovendi, & hominibus placendi arguit, non studium ad gloriam Dei & Regnum ejus propagandum testatur. Qui enim citò manus imponit, quando is, cui manus impositæ sunt, peccat in doctrina vel opere, peccati illius quodammodo reus fit, quia non satis explorato author ministerium suscipiendi fuit.
units.tr: For Paul says of deacons: "Let them first be tested, then let them serve" [Δοκιμαζέσθωσαν πρῶτον, εἶτα διακονείτωσαν], 1 Tim. 3:10. How much more, then, is this required in the calling of ministers? They must be examined with careful judgment and an inquiry into their gifts, progress, life and charity, as the rule of the law requires. So Paul again says: "Lay hands suddenly on no one" [χεῖρας ταχέως μηδενὶ ἐπιτίθει], meaning, if you find no one such as he described in chapter 3, "and do not share in the sins of others", 1 Tim. 5:22. For haste indicates either negligence and contempt of the office [τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς], or a desire to rule, to advance one's own interest and to please men. It does not show zeal for the glory of God and the spreading of his kingdom. For whoever lays on hands hastily, when the man on whom they were laid sins in doctrine or conduct, becomes in some measure guilty of that sin, since he admitted him to the ministry without having tested him sufficiently.

units.la: Nam qui in ministerio agit cum approbatione fratrum, is nomine fratrum ministerio defungi videtur, ut in eosdem administrationis rectitudo vel vitiositas redundet. Si enim nonnisi δόκιμοι & δεδοκιμασμένοι probi & probati admittantur, non facilè fiet, ut in reprehensionem incidant.
units.tr: For one who serves in the ministry with the approval of the brothers seems to act in the name of the brothers, so that the rectitude or the faults of the administration fall back on them. If only men who are proved (δόκιμοι and δεδοκιμασμένοι), upright and tested, are admitted, it will not easily happen that they fall into blame.

units.la: Quia in re à plerisque omnibus minùs circumspectè & religiosè agitur, & quandoque multùm etiam peccatur, atque ex eo innumera & maxima in Ecclesiam mala inundant & inundaverunt hactenus, dum alii minùs probati peccarunt, alii minùs probando authores peccandi fuerunt, alii à præfectis sibi minùs probatis corrupti potiùs quàm ædificati sunt, cùm juxta illud Leonis M. integritas præsidentium sit salus subditorum, & vicissim alii secundum concupiscentias sibi doctores coacervarunt, prurientes auribus, cupientes audire non quod verum est, quod Deus dixit, sed quod vanum, fatuum, sonans histrionicum, vel panegyricum est; imò etiam λοιδορίας convicia εὐλογίας blandiloquentiæ & benedictiones per quas corda minimè malorum seducuntur, Rom. XVI. 18. coll. cum 2. Tim. IV. 3. &c. Elaj. XXX. 10. Mich. II. 6. 11.
units.tr: In this matter most people act with too little care and reverence, and often sin greatly. From this have flowed, and up to now have flowed, countless and very great evils into the Church: some men of little proof have sinned, others by admitting men of little proof have been the cause of sin, and others have been corrupted rather than built up by superiors who were themselves little proved. Yet, according to the saying of Leo the Great, "the integrity of those who preside is the safety of those who are subject." On the other side, some, following their own lusts, "have heaped up teachers for themselves, having itching ears", wanting to hear not what is true, what God has said, but what is empty, foolish, sounding of the stage or of panegyric. Indeed, they welcome abuse [λοιδορίας] in place of praise, and flattering speech and blessings [εὐλογίας] by which the hearts of the wicked are not at all deceived, Rom. 16:18, compared with 2 Tim. 4:3, etc.; Isa. 30:10; Mic. 2:6, 11.

units.la: Neque tamen propterea manus à vulneribus Ecclesiæ abduci debet, sed vigilandum eò diligentiùs est, & præceptum Apostoli de non imponendis citò manibus religiosè servetur, quod reformandæ & ad majorem cognitionem atque pietatem provehendam Ecclesiæ permultùm proderit.
units.tr: Nevertheless, the hand should not for that reason be withdrawn from the wounds of the Church. Rather we must be all the more watchful, and the Apostle's command not to lay on hands hastily should be kept faithfully. This will greatly help to reform the Church and to advance it to greater knowledge and piety.

units.la: XXX. Probatio ministrorum Ecclesiæ in inquisitione & dijudicatione consistit, an illis dotibus, donis & virtutibus, quas in Ecclesiæ ministro Spiritus S. passim requirit, præditi atque ornati sint; verbo, an Ecclesiæ Dei inservire, utilémque operam navare velint & possint. Sicut enim nemo unquam rectè negotium curaverit, si vel nullo, vel non confirmato ejus curandi studio tenetur, & ad illud ritè obeundum non pari & voluntate & facultate præditus est: ita duo sunt, quæ ad ministerium idoneos faciunt, confirmata & ardens voluntas faciendi seriò & ex animo officium, nec non sufficiens & explorata, quæ illud præstare potis sit, facultas. Et voluntatis quidem examen licèt internum & privatum sit, quando interna quadam vocatione, de qua supra diximus, nec non tractu Spiritus S. ad Ecclesiæ ministerium toto animo, & inclinante velut astro se ferri sentit; tamen signis probabilibus etiam innotescere iis, quibus probandi & explorandi negotium datum est, poterit.
units.tr: XXX. The testing of ministers of the Church consists in an inquiry and judgment as to whether they are endowed and adorned with those qualities, gifts and virtues which the Holy Spirit everywhere requires in a minister of the Church; in short, whether they are willing and able to serve the Church of God and to render useful work. For as no one would ever carry out a business properly if he were not bound to it by a settled and sincere desire for it, and were not equipped with a like willingness and ability to discharge it duly, so there are two things which make men fit for the ministry: a firm and ardent will to perform the office seriously and from the heart, and a sufficient and proven ability to perform it. The examination of the will, though it is internal and private, since a man feels himself carried with his whole soul to the ministry of the Church by that inward call of which we have spoken above, and by the drawing of the Holy Spirit, as if by an inclining star, nevertheless can also become known through probable signs to those who have been given the task of testing and examining it.

units.la: Quæ proin in externa vocatione etiam in consilium adhibenda sunt. Ita voluntatem Ecclesiæ inserviendi rectam & seriam hinc æstimare licet, si quis à parentibus, vel iis, qui parentum loco sunt, sacris studiis consecratus, vel propensione propria ad ea inclinans à teneris annis & disciplinæ adhuc subjectus; sacrarum literarum studio & amore flagravit, Theologiæ, & ei ancillantibus studiis operam sedulò navavit, Templa diligenter & libenter adiit, conciones attento, alacri & devoto animo audivit & meditatus est, de rebus sacris colloquendo, scribendo, declamando, disputando se exercuit, modestiam, gravitatem, candorem in quotidiana vitæ consuetudine præ se tulit; & testimoniis non tantùm doctrinæ, sed etiam vitæ sanctè & juxta normam à S. Paulo candidatis præscriptam transactæ eorum, quorum institutioni nomen dedit, & magisterio subfuit luculentis exornatur. De talibus enim confidere licet, quòd non carnali consilio & studio, sed provido Numine, & Deo cor flectente ad Ecclesiæ ministerium cucurrerint. Exemplo sunt David, in quo puero ea dona emicuerunt, ex quibus sperari potuit, eum in magnum virum evasurum; Timotheus, qui sacras literas ἀπὸ βρέφους à pueris didicit, 2. Timoth. III. 15. & Athanasius, qui Rufino Hist. Eccl. lib. I. 14. teste, puer adhuc inter pueros Episcopum egit, confessionem fidei à pueris exigens, & iisdem reddens, baptizans, & cuncta pro Episcopo gerens. Facultatis probatio non puerilis & scholastica, sed gravis inprimis & exacta requiritur. Examen enim de Scriptura & cognitione rerum sacrarum, de instrumentis atque
units.tr: Therefore these signs must also be taken into account in the external call. The will to serve the Church rightly and sincerely may be judged from this: if someone, dedicated to sacred studies by his parents or those in their place, or inclined to them by his own bent from his tender years and still under instruction, has burned with zeal and love for the Holy Scriptures; has diligently pursued theology and the studies that serve it; has gone to the churches diligently and gladly; has heard and pondered sermons with an attentive, eager and devout mind; has exercised himself in talking, writing, declaiming and disputing about sacred things; has shown modesty, gravity and candour in the daily course of his life; and whose conduct, both in teaching and in living holily and according to the rule Paul prescribed for candidates, is commended by splendid testimonies from those under whose instruction he has placed himself and under whose teaching he has been. For we may trust that such men have come to the ministry of the Church not by carnal counsel and desire, but by a providential divine will and by God bending their heart. Examples are David, in whom, as a boy, those gifts shone out from which it could be hoped that he would become a great man; Timothy, who "from infancy had learned the sacred writings" [ἀπὸ βρέφους], 2 Tim. 3:15; and Athanasius, who, according to Rufinus (Hist. Eccl. lib. 1, ch. 14), while still a boy among boys, acted as bishop, demanding the confession of faith from the boys, and giving it back to them, baptizing and doing everything as a bishop. The proof of ability is required to be not boyish and scholastic, but above all serious and exact. For the examination must concern Scripture and knowledge of sacred things, the instruments and means that can bring this knowledge to the Church, all pastoral care, and similar matters.

units.la: {y} Vocandi ad ministerium explorari debent. atque mediis, quæ hanc cognitionem ad Ecclesiam proferre & traducere possunt, de cura Pastorali omni,& id genus aliis instituendum est. Non enim qualiscunque rerum sacrarum cognitio, sed exactior illa, constans Scripturarum penitiore, ex ipsis inprimis fontibus linguarum originalium, quarum ignorantia erudito hoc seculo, quo eas discendi præsentissimæ occasiones sunt, nemini futuro Ecclesiæ ministro condonari debet, petita intelligentia, requiritur. Præterea scientiarum & artium, inprimis illarum, quibus judicium mentis & lingua, ad verbum Dei cum fructu Ecclesiæ annuntiandum, formantur, non vulgaris cognitio requiritur. Opus insuper est dono linguæ, facundia oris, &dexteritate judicii, ut quæ mens invenit, disposuit & ad ædificationem utilia judicavit, cum decoro quodam & suavitate rebus sacris conveniente, in medium proferantur. Denique opus est bona existimatione, gratia & fide apud Ecclesiam, cui operam suam minister navare debet; saltem apud bonos & probatos illius Ecclesiæ, cum omnibus placere vix cuiquam integrum sit.
units.tr: Not just any knowledge of sacred things is required, but the more exact knowledge which rests on a deeper acquaintance with the Scriptures, drawn above all from the original sources of the languages. Ignorance of these languages must not be pardoned in any future minister of the Church in this learned age, when there are the most ready opportunities to learn them. Besides this, a knowledge of the sciences and arts, above all of those by which the judgment of the mind and the tongue are formed for proclaiming the Word of God to the profit of the Church, is required, and it must not be ordinary. Moreover, there is need of a gift of language, eloquence of speech and dexterity of judgment, so that what the mind has discovered, arranged and judged useful for edification may be set forth in a manner that is fitting and gracious and suits sacred things. Finally, there is need of a good reputation, grace and trust with the Church to which the minister must devote his labour; at least with its good and approved members, since it is hardly possible for anyone to please everyone.

units.la: XXXI. Utrasque & voluntatis & facultatis dotes S. Paulus conjunxit, præcipiens Timotheo: Quæ audivisti à me per multos testes, hæc commenda πιστοῖς fidelibus hominibus, qui ἱκανοὶ idonei futuri sunt, ut alios etiam doceant, 2. Tim. II. 2.
units.tr: XXXI. Paul joined both the qualities of will and of ability together, when he charged Timothy: "What you have heard from me through many witnesses, commit to faithful men [πιστοῖς], who will be competent [ἱκανοὶ] to teach others also", 2 Tim. 2:2.

units.la: Fideles quoad voluntatem, non tantum credentes, sed etiam homines constantis propositi, expertæ fidei & sinceritatis, non versatiles, vanos, temerarios: Idoneos ad docendum alios, quoad facultatem, hoc est, præditos ingenio bono, ad percipiendum; judicio ad distinguendum bona à malis, vera à falsis, certa ab incertis, utilia à futilibus; memoria, ad retinendum, & ad ἑτοιμασίαν Εὐαγγελίου τῆς εἰρήνης præparationem Evangelii pacis, Ephes. VI. 15. eloquio bono, profectu in studiis sacris & exoticis necessario; mansuetudine, ad condonandum defectum & culpas eorum, qui erudiri debent; fortitudine ad laborandum in sermone; dexteritate & ἀγχνοίᾳ ad videndum, quid sit ad ἐργάλειον τῆς οἰκοδομῆς usum ædificationis, & ad discernendum spiritus. Easdem dotes, ceu normas judicii probantis copiose idem S. Paulus 1. Tim. III. 1–8. Tit. I. 6–10. persequitur; & suo etiam ipsius, nec non collegarum suorum, Sylvani & Timothei exemplo, & Thessalonicensium Ecclesiæ, & Presbyteris Ephesiis, accurate commendat, Actor. XX. 18–36. 1. Thess. II. 1–13. Quos locos, quia prolixiores sunt, adscribere non libet. Ad voluntatis vero probationem atque trutinam, valde urgentem & gravem illam, Christus S. Petrum revocavit & appendit, tertiò ex ipso, antea quàm ipsi curam ovium commendasset, anquirens. Petre, diligis me? Joh. XXI. 15. &c. Unde liquet, Christi ipsius hoc judicium immutabile esse, eum, qui recte voluerit pascere oves Christi, ceu verus Pastor Christi, non ceu שׁוֹטֶה stultus ille pastor, qui tabescentes non visitat, evagantem ob ruditatem non quærit, fractam non concinnat, confisentem non sustentat, & carnem opimam comedit, & ungulas earum rumpit, Zachar. XI. 16. 17. ipsius Christi amore imbui oportet. Nam qui serio gaudet Christo Salvatore, & ejus amorem amat, & eum cupit habere effectum, & Christum glorificare studet (in quo amor Christi consistit) is non potest non amare & pascere velle oves Christi, quæ ipsi à Patre datæ sunt, & quidem ita, ut Christi τῆς Ἀρχιποίμενος gratia abundantissimè fruantur.
units.tr: Faithful as to will: not merely believers, but men of steady purpose, of tested faith and sincerity, not fickle, vain or rash. Competent to teach others as to ability: that is, endowed with a good mind for apprehending; with judgment to distinguish good from bad, true from false, certain from uncertain, useful from trifling; with a memory for retaining, and for the preparation of the gospel of peace [ἑτοιμασίαν Εὐαγγελίου τῆς εἰρήνης], Eph. 6:15; with a good manner of speaking and the progress in sacred and necessary secular studies that this requires; with gentleness, to pardon the lack and faults of those who must be taught; with fortitude, to labour in preaching; with dexterity and quickness of mind [ἀγχίνοια], to see what is useful for building up [ἐργαλεῖον τῆς οἰκοδομῆς] and to discern spirits. The same Paul sets out these same qualities at length as the norms of a sound judgment in testing, in 1 Tim. 3:1–8 and Titus 1:6–10. He also commends them carefully, by his own example and that of his colleagues Silvanus and Timothy, by the church of the Thessalonians, and by the Ephesian elders, Acts 20:18–36; 1 Thess. 2:1–13. I do not wish to copy out those passages, since they are rather long. But for the proof and weighing of the will, which is very serious and pressing, Christ called Peter back and weighed him, asking him three times, before he had committed the care of his sheep to him: "Peter, do you love me?" John 21:15 etc. From this it is clear that this judgment of Christ himself is unchangeable: whoever rightly wishes to feed the sheep of Christ, as a true shepherd of Christ, and not as that foolish (shoteh) shepherd "who does not visit those who are wasting away, does not seek the wandering because of their ignorance, does not mend the broken, does not sustain the sound, but eats the fat flesh and breaks their hooves", Zech. 11:16–17, must be imbued with the love of Christ himself. For whoever seriously rejoices in Christ the Saviour, loves his love, desires to possess him, and strives to glorify Christ (in which the love of Christ consists), cannot but love and wish to feed the sheep of Christ, which the Father has given to him, and indeed in such a way that they enjoy abundantly the grace of the Chief Shepherd [τῆς Ἀρχιποίμενος].

units.la: XXXII. Exactior ejusmodi probatio inprimis Ecclesiæ prisçæ curæ cordique fuit. Nam ut rectius sanctiusque canon Apostolicus de non citò imponendis manibus servaretur explorati jam & electi nomen in tabella perscriptum loco publico proponere, aut sicubi id integrum non esset, in cœtu Ecclesiastico palam recitare consuevit, ut si quid in eo probri compertum esset, intra constitutum tempus ad Presbyterium deferretur, ne qua labe Ecclesia aspergeretur.
units.tr: XXXII. The ancient Church took especially careful and heartfelt pains over such testing. To observe more correctly and more holily the Apostolic canon against laying on hands hastily, it was customary to post the name of a candidate already tested and chosen in a public place, or, where that was not possible, to read it aloud in the ecclesiastical assembly. This was so that, if anything disgraceful about him came to light, it could be reported to the presbytery within a set time, and the Church would not be stained by any blemish.

units.la: Quem morem etiam Alexandro Severo in delegendis Provinciarum Præsidibus placuisse Lampridius in ejus vita testatur. In examine ipso doctrinæ ne quid prætermitteretur, sicubi idoneis judicibus Presbyterium destitueretur, ex vicinis Ecclesiis Episcopos accersivit, quo sic omnia χωρὶς προκρίσεως & μηδὲν κατὰ τὴν πρόληψιν fine præjudicio, & μηδὲν κατὰ σαρκικὸν nihil secundum propensionem carnalem, 1. Tim. V. 21. peragareturr. Illud quoque rite & ordine factum, quòd Ecclesiastica officia non per saltum, sed per gradus contulit, justo temporis intervallo interposito. Habuit enim suos Ecclesia primitiva clericos, qui peculiari & arctiore disciplina sub Presbyterorum institutione ad ministerium Ecclesiasticum formari debuerunt. Qui ex umbra Scholastica in publicum producti ad minora quædam officia primùm adhibiti, non ante sublimioribus admovebantur, quàm dexteritatis & aptitudinis suæ specimina idonea edidissent. Unde Episcoporum lateri, ceu ἀκόλουθοι acoluthi, & indivulsi comites hærebant, ut eorum recte dicta & facta observarent, & imitationis candore exprimerent. Exacto demum probationis tempore ad publica officia promoti, in ministerio confirmati sunt. Quod factum est, & fieri debet tum exemplo Christi, qui per similes gradus & temporum intervalla ad publici muneris sui administrationem enixus est; & Apostolos suos non saltu, sed gradu ad publicum Ministerium provexit: tum præscriptione S. Pauli, vetantis episcopum deligi νεόφυτον novitium, ne inflatus in judicium Diaboli incidat, 1. Tim. III. 6. Ubi non hoc præscribit, ut deligatur diu ἀκροατὴς ἐπιλησμονῆς auditor obliviosus, & puer centum annorum, in quo vetusto & obliviosō, oscitante & stupido auditore ne fides quidem est, & ex cujus ore frequenter confessio ipsa veritatis exscinditur; sed ut deligatur is, qui διδάσκαλος διὰ χρόνου doctor per tempus esse potest, Hebr. V. 12. saltem qui potens est in Scripturis, in earum mysteria inquisivit, exercitatos in iis sensus habet, spiritualia comparare, habere ζύμην in mysterio pietatis, probare meliora, in promptu habere sermonem σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως sapientiæ & cognitionis potis est; denique qui δόκιμος, probatæ peritiæ & fidelitatis est, 2. Tim. II. 15. Puer enim Episcopus facile τυφῶσθαι inflari, efferri potest, ut fastidiat ministerium, dominetur, leges ferat coli ab aliis velit, atque sic in judicium Diaboli incidit, qui inflatus pariter ministerium hominis fastidivit, atque ideo in veritate non stetit, sed homicida factus, æternam damnationem sibi accersivit. PræPræclarè Gregorius M. ad Synagrium lib. VII. ep. 100. scribens; sicut, inquit, νεόφυτος tunc dicebatur, qui initiò in sanctæ fidei eruditione plantatus fuit: sic modò νεόφυτος dicendus est, qui repente in religionis habitu plantatus, ad ambiendos honores sacros irrepserit. Ordinatè ergo ad ordines accedendum est. Nam casum appetit, qui ad summi loci fastigia, posthabitis gradibus, per abrupta ascensum quærit. Scimus autem, quòd ædificati parietes non priùs tignorum pondus accipiunt, nisi à novitatis suæ humore siccentur, ne, si ante pondera quàm solidentur, accipiant, cunctam simul fabricam deponant.
units.tr: Lampridius testifies in the life of Alexander Severus that this same custom pleased that emperor when he chose the governors of the provinces. In the examination itself, so that nothing of doctrine would be overlooked, whenever the presbytery lacked suitable judges, he summoned bishops from neighbouring Churches, so that everything would be carried out "without prejudgment" [χωρὶς προκρίσεως] and "without preconception" [μηδὲν κατὰ τὴν πρόληψιν], "nothing according to carnal inclination" [μηδὲν κατὰ σαρκικὸν], as in 1 Tim. 5:21. It was also rightly and properly done that the ancient Church did not confer ecclesiastical offices by leaping over steps, but by degrees, with a suitable interval of time between them. The early Church had its own clergy, who, under the instruction of the presbyters, had to be formed for the ecclesiastical ministry by a special and stricter discipline. Brought out of the shadow of the school into public view, they were first employed in certain lesser duties, and were not promoted to higher ones until they had given proof of their skill and aptitude. Hence they stayed close to the sides of the bishops, like "followers" [ἀκόλουθοι] and inseparable companions, so that they might observe what was rightly said and done, and express it in imitation with sincerity. Finally, when the time of testing was over, they were advanced to public offices and confirmed in the ministry. This was done, and ought to be done, both by the example of Christ, who through similar steps and intervals of time strove toward the administration of his public office, and who advanced his Apostles to the public ministry not by a leap but by degrees; and by the prescription of St Paul, who forbids a bishop to be chosen from among the "newly planted" [νεόφυτος], lest, puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the Devil (1 Tim. 3:6). Paul does not here prescribe that one should be chosen who is a long-time "hearer forgetful" [ἀκροατὴς ἐπιλησμονῆς], or a child of a hundred years, in whom, in such an old, forgetful, yawning and dull hearer, there is not even faith, and from whose mouth the very confession of truth is often cut off. Rather, he prescribes that one should be chosen who can be a "teacher through time" [διδάσκαλος διὰ χρόνου] (Heb. 5:12), at least one who is able in the Scriptures, who has searched into their mysteries, has senses exercised in them, is able to procure spiritual things, to have "leaven" [ζύμην] in the mystery of godliness, to prove the better things, and to have ready speech of "wisdom and knowledge" [σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως]; in short, one who is "approved" [δόκιμος] in proven skill and faithfulness (2 Tim. 2:15). For a bishop who is a child can easily be "puffed up" [τυφῶσθαι], inflated and carried away, so that he despises the ministry, lords it over others, wants to make laws and to be honoured by others, and so falls into the judgment of the Devil, who, likewise puffed up, despised the ministry of man, and therefore did not stand in the truth, but became a murderer, and brought eternal damnation upon himself. Gregory the Great writes most admirably to Synagrius in book VII, letter 100: "As, he says, a "newly planted" one was then called he who was first planted in the instruction of the holy faith, so now he should be called "newly planted" who, suddenly planted in the habit of religion, has crept in to seek sacred honours. Therefore one must approach the orders in order. For he seeks a fall who, passing over the steps, seeks to climb by steep ways to the heights of the highest place. We know that walls that have been built do not receive the weight of timbers until they have been dried of the moisture of their newness, lest, if they receive the weights before they are set firm, they bring down the whole structure at once."

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Graduum ejusmodi Ecclesiasticorum observatio postulat, ne vel tyronibus, vel provectioribus quidem, at ea, quæ in Ecclesia geruntur & gerenda sunt, nondum in usu habentibus clavus Ecclesiarum vacantium committatur. Neque adeò peccant Ecclesiæ, quarum in numero Helveticæ sunt, quæ ministerii verbi & Sacramentorum gradum iis etiam, quibus non statim vocantis Ecclesiæ gubernacula traduntur, & disciplinæ ipsius administratio committitur, conferunt. Nam quòd Concilium Chalcedonense Canone VI. vetuit, quemquam ἀπλεῶς χειροτονούμενον absolutè (hoc est, uti Urbanus II. in Concilio Placentino explicat, sine titulo, munere & officio) ordinari, eos demum ferit, qui ordinant eos, qui nunquam munus exercebant in Ecclesia, & quibus Ecclesia, cujus Episcopi creantur, nunquam committitur, vel, rebus sic comparatis, committi potest, cujusmodi illi sunt, qui sequiore ætate Episcopi Titulares, seu potius vitulares dicti sunt, quia ordinati cum titulo licet, hoc est, uti in Lateranensi Concilio can. 5. definitum est, cum reditu, sine titulo tamen, hoc est, officio & munere pascendi quandoque Ecclesiam vacantem (cùm nunquam rebus sic comparatis, vacare possit) ordinati sunt. Sed dispar eorum ratio est, qui statim atque ordinati ad ministerium Ecclesiæ sunt, Evangelium prædicare & Sacramenta administrare possunt, & quibus post temporis nonnullius in Ecclesiæ ministerio, ratione loci, indefinito, exacti spatium Ecclesiæ vacantes, sine nova ordinatione, nisi quòd eò usque manuum impositio & præsentatio differtur, imò in oppidis etiam majoribus ordinatio sine χειροτονία & præsentatione rata & valida est, iis committuntur. Cujusmodi ordinationes propter œconomiam & necessitatem Ecclesiæ, & utilitatem ordinatorum, qui priùs quàm certis Ecclesiis pascendis præsunt, exercitatione muneris crebra, & assectatione eorum, quorum subinde vicibus defunguntur habiliores pascendæ Ecclesiæ reduntur, vitio carent, cùm Ecclesiæ salus suprema lex sit. Licèt enim sine gregis respectu omni nemo minister ordinari possit vel debeat, tamen grege ad tempus destitutus honorem & gradum ministerii certo modo retinere & tueri potest.
units.tr: The observance of such ecclesiastical degrees requires that the helm of vacant Churches not be entrusted to beginners, nor even to those more advanced who are not yet practised in the things that are done and must be done in the Church. Nor, indeed, do those Churches sin, among whom are the Helvetic Churches, which confer the grade of the ministry of the Word and the Sacraments on those also to whom the government of a calling Church is not handed over at once, and to whom the administration of discipline itself is committed. For the Council of Chalcedon, in Canon 6, forbade anyone to be ordained "absolutely" [ἀπλεῶς χειροτονούμενον], that is, as Urban II explains in the Council of Piacenza, "without title, office and duty." That canon strikes only those who ordain persons who never exercised a ministry in the Church, and to whom the Church, whose bishops are created, was never committed, or, the situation being such, could not be committed. Such were those in a later age called "titular bishops," or rather "calf bishops" [vitulares], because they were ordained with a title, that is, as is defined in the Lateran Council, canon 5, "with income, but without a title," that is, without the office and duty of pastoring some vacant Church at some time (since, with things so arranged, it could never be vacant). But the case is different for those who, as soon as they are ordained to the ministry of the Church, can preach the Gospel and administer the Sacraments, and to whom, after a period of some length, indefinite in extent according to place, spent in the ministry of the Church, the vacant Churches are committed without a new ordination, except that the laying on of hands and the presentation are deferred until then; indeed, in even fairly large towns an ordination without election [χειροτονία] and presentation is valid and effective. Such ordinations, on account of the economy and necessity of the Church, and the benefit of those ordained, who before they preside over particular Churches to be fed are made more capable of feeding the Church by frequent exercise of their office and by the company of those for whom they sometimes act in turn, are free from fault, since the safety of the Church is the highest law. For although no one can or ought to be ordained as a minister without regard to a flock at all, yet one who for a time is without a flock can nevertheless keep and maintain the honour and rank of the ministry in a certain manner.

units.la: XXXIV.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: Vocationis ad particularis Ecclesiæ ministerium, & ordinationis ipsius complementum in ejusdem confirmatione seu inauguratione consistit. Per illam enim electus & probatus, adeóque destinatione jam ordinatus, solenni ritu in possessionem muneris immittitur, & Ecclesiæ, cui pascendæ destinatus est, veluti despondetur. Et Apostoli quidem inauguratione seu consecratione hac, quæ ab ultimo actu, adeóque per Synecdochen Ordinationis nomine venit, Ecclesiam ad jejunia & preces vocarunt, & electis per impositionem manuum Ecclesias commiserunt χειροτονήσαντες per suffragia deligentes Presbyteros κατ' ἐκκλησίαν per Ecclesias singulas, cùm precati essent & jejunassent, tradiderunt eos Domino, Actor. XIV. 23. Ne negligas donum, quod tibi datum est per Prophetiam, cum impositione manuum Presbyterii, 1. Tim. IV. 14. Impositio manuum à Judæis doctores suos creantibus usurpari suevit. Eadem ceremonia liberè assumpta Apostoli Evangelii ministros in Ecclesiæ conspectum produxerunt, atque sic productos & approbatos Ecclesiis commendarunt, quò sic in officio faciendo extra ἀνεπιτήδειον exprobrationem invasæ curationis, & non legitimæ vocationis essent. Neque parum χειροθεσία talis & authoritati atque reverentiæ ministerii, & unitati Ecclesiæ inservit, quia per eam minister in collegium cooptatur, & Ecclesiæ jam institutæ solenniter præponitur. Finis enim ritus illius fuit impositis capiti manibus Divinam benedictionem piis precibus in caput ordinandi derivare, atque efficere, ne quisquam privatim coetus colligere, & se ab Ecclesia separare ausus absque suspicione sub nomine Christiani conventus latere, & venenum spargere facilè posset. Simul etiam inaugurationem ejusmodi medium continuandi ministerii & καλήχησις inde ab Apostolis, ad omnes Ecclesias per omnia secula esse voluerunt. Neque tamen iccirco impositio manuum de essentia ordinationis, vel ministerii, sed ejus duntaxat solennis declaratio est. Et minister electus atque verè probatus, & in Ecclesiæ sibi creditæ possessionem immissus verus minister est, licèt solenni ritu ad ministerium sacratus non sit: sicut Rex legitimè electus, & in possessionem Regni immissus verus Rex est etiam ante quàm coronetur: imò etiamsi ob intercedentia impedimenta nunquam coronetur, uti Romanorum Regum inde à longo tempore electorum, at nunquam coronatorum exemplo liquet. Quod etiam Johannes Major in 4. Sent. dist. 24. n. 9. quin & ipse Gregorius IX. Epistola ad Londinensem sentire vili sunt. Saltem à Christo per mandatum expressum instituta non est. Nam & ipsos Apostolos sine impositione manuum vocavit, & iisdem per affla-tum, non impositionem manuum Spiritum S. & potestatem remittendi peccata impertitus est; innuens, & sine ritu ordinationem constare, & ritus liberos & liberè adhiberi posse. Nulla ergo ex inauguratione tali & ipsa manuum impositione specialis consecratio & sanctitas Ministris N. T. adhæret, sicut Ministris V. T. olim adhæsit, quia nulla nunc cultus Divini pars datur, quæ in peculiari ad Deum appropinquatione consistat, quæque non ab unoquoque Christiano, legitimè ad id vocato, administrari possit, imò debeat, omnes enim ἱεράτευμα βασίλειον Regale Sacerdotium sumus, 1. Petr. II. 5.9. Apocal. I. 6. Unde nunc sublato illo discrimine Levitico verè omnis congregatio, omnes illi sancti sunt, Num. XVI. 3. neque aliud inter personam cultu sacro defungentem & alias discrimen quàm ordinis vocationis intercedit, dum ordinis causa cultus publici administratio illis committitur, quae alias unicuique fratrum, requisitis necessariis instructo, pariter quoque imponi posset.
units.tr: The calling to the ministry of a particular church, and the completion of the ordination itself, consist in its confirmation or inauguration. For by this the one elected and approved, and thus already ordained by appointment, is put into possession of the office by a solemn rite, and is as it were betrothed to the Church he is destined to feed. The Apostles, by this inauguration or consecration, which from its last act is called ordination by synecdoche, summoned the Church to fasting and prayer, and committed the churches to the elected by the laying on of hands, having appointed by vote [χειροτονήσαντες] elders church by church [κατ' ἐκκλησίαν], and when they had prayed and fasted, they commended them to the Lord, Acts 14:23. "Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given you through prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery," 1 Tim. 4:14. The laying on of hands was customarily used by the Jews when creating their teachers. The Apostles, freely adopting the same ceremony, presented the ministers of the Gospel to the sight of the Church, and so commended them, presented and approved, to the churches, so that in discharging their office they might be free from the reproach of an unfit [ἀνεπιτήδειον] intrusion into the work, and from the charge of an illegitimate calling. Such a laying on of hands serves no little to the authority, reverence and dignity of the ministry, and to the unity of the Church, because by it the minister is co-opted into the college and solemnly set over the Church already established. For the purpose of that rite was that, by laying hands on the head, the divine blessing might be drawn down upon the one being ordained by pious prayers, and that no one could easily gather a private assembly, and dare to separate himself from the Church, lurking without suspicion under the name of a Christian meeting, and spreading poison. At the same time they willed that such inauguration be the means of continuing the ministry, and of catechizing [κατήχησις] from the Apostles onward, in all churches throughout all ages. Yet the laying on of hands is not on that account of the essence of ordination or of the ministry, but is only its solemn declaration. A minister who has been elected and truly approved, and put into possession of the Church entrusted to him, is a true minister, although he has not been consecrated to the ministry with the solemn rite. Just as a king lawfully elected and put into possession of the kingdom is a true king even before he is crowned; indeed, even if he is never crowned because of intervening hindrances, as the example of the Roman kings, elected for a long time but never crowned, makes clear. John Major in 4 Sent. dist. 24 n. 9 seems to have thought this, and so too Gregory IX himself in his Epistle to the Londoners. At least it was not instituted by Christ by express command. For he called the Apostles themselves without the laying on of hands, and he bestowed on them the Holy Spirit and the power of remitting sins by breathing on them, not by laying on of hands; implying both that ordination can stand without a rite, and that rites are free and may be freely used. Therefore no special consecration and holiness adheres to the ministers of the New Testament from such an inauguration, or from the laying on of hands itself, as once adhered to the ministers of the Old Testament. For no part of divine worship is now given which consists in a special approach to God, and which cannot be administered by every Christian lawfully called to it, indeed which ought to be so administered: for we are all a royal priesthood [ἱεράτευμα βασίλειον], 1 Pet. 2:5, 9; Rev. 1:6. Hence now, with that Levitical distinction removed, truly all the congregation, every one of them is holy, Num. 16:3; nor is there any distinction between the person who performs sacred worship and the others, except that of the order of calling, since the administration of public worship is committed to the former for the sake of their order, which otherwise could equally be laid on any one of the brethren who is furnished with the necessary qualifications.

units.la: XXXV. Manuum impositio primitus a Presbyteris, seu senioribus docentibus facta est. Nam S. Paulus Timotheo charisma datum esse per Prophetiam μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου cum impositione manuum Presbyterii, 1. Tim. IV. 14. Ubi vox πρεσβυτέριον Collegium Seniorum significat. Uti Luc. XXII. 66. Actor. XXII. 5. Alibi 2. Timoth. I. 6. S. Paulus donum Dei in Timotheo esse per impositionem manuum suarum testatur. Potuit enim impositio a Paulo nomine Seniorum, vel a Paulo, negotii illius directore & chorago, accedente Seniorum opera, peragi. Nam quod de uno praedicatur, de caeteris non negatur. Sed postquam humano consilio ex Presbyterorum collegio unus caeteris praepositus fuit, singulari praerogativa Episcopus dictus, mos deinceps obtinuit, ut penes hunc ordinatio esset respectu signi, seu impositionis manuum, Presbyterio suas ei partes concedente, sicut Ecclesia partes suas quasdam in Presbyterium transtulit. Sic ergo ordinationis actus communis fuit Episcopo & Presbyteris, solo ritu ordinandi penes Episcopum manente singulariter. Caeterum actus ille tanto majoris momenti est, quam ritus, quanto id, quod nonnisi mente & judicio perfici potest, doctrinae scilicet & vitae examen potius est eo, quod solis manibus peragitur. At neque ritus ille tam superstitiose semper penes Episcopum mansit, quin eum quandoque Presbyteri etiam usurparent, uti ex Ambrosio in Ephes. IV. & Augustino Quaest. ex utroque Test. lib. IV. q. 101. liquet. Paulatim tamen Episcopi jus illud χειροτονίας, ceu eximium sibi vindicarunt; neque hoc duntaxat, sed etiam plebe suffragandi potestate defraudata, χειροτονίαν cum χειροθεσίας confuderunt, & postquam in Ecclesia dominationem constituerunt, ordinationem ejusmodi in Sacramentum convertentes, ut tremendum illud omnibus facerent, tegendae illegitimae potestatis emplastrum fecerunt, & tandem auctoratos a se libidini suae subjecerunt, neque amplius vel reprehendi se sustinuerunt, vel sanam doctrinam tulerunt, sed δοκίμως probos & rectos ex Ecclesia ejiciendo, se ipsos a vera Ecclesia abscederunt.
units.tr: XXXV. The laying on of hands was at first performed by the presbyters, or elders who taught. For St. Paul says that the gift was given to Timothy through prophecy, with the laying on of hands of the presbytery [μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου], 1 Tim. 4:14, where the word presbyterium signifies the college of elders, as in Luke 22:66 and Acts 22:5. Elsewhere, 2 Tim. 1:6, St. Paul testifies that the gift of God is in Timothy through the laying on of his hands. The imposition could be performed by Paul in the name of the elders, or by Paul as director and leader of the business, with the elders assisting. For what is predicated of one is not denied of the others. But after, by human counsel, one from the college of presbyters was set over the rest with the singular prerogative of being called bishop, the custom gradually prevailed that the ordination rested with him, with respect to the sign or the laying on of hands, the presbytery conceding to him its parts, just as the Church itself transferred certain of its parts to the presbytery. So the act of ordination was common to the bishop and the presbyters, the rite of ordaining alone remaining singularly with the bishop. Moreover, that act is of so much greater importance than the rite, as what can be accomplished only by mind and judgement, namely the examination of doctrine and life, is more than what is done by the hands alone. But that rite did not always remain so superstitiously with the bishop; sometimes presbyters also took it up, as is clear from Ambrose on Ephesians 4 and from Augustine, Questions on both Testaments, book 4, question 101. Gradually, however, the bishops claimed that right of voting [χειροτονίας] as their own special privilege. And not only that: defrauding the people of the power of voting, they confused voting [χειροτονίαν] with laying on of hands [χειροθεσίας]; and once they had established domination in the Church, turning such ordination into a sacrament, so that they might make it awe-inspiring to all, they made a plaster to cover their illegitimate power. Finally, they subjected to their lust those whom they had authorized, and no longer could they bear to be rebuked or to tolerate sound doctrine; by casting out of the Church those who were approved as upright and righteous [δοκίμως], they separated themselves from the true Church.

units.la: XXXVI. Illi ipsi tamen, qui sic ordinationem & vocationem depravarunt, & dominationis suae instrumentum fecerunt, nostrorum ordinationem & vocationem omnem, velut vitio factam, eo quod ab unctis Episcopis, & Papa sacrum ordinem propagante, suspensa non sit, palam traducunt atque sugillant, & una cum ministerio etiam Ecclesiam apud nos periisse impotenter vociferantur. Quae quam impie & falso dicta sint, ex iis, quae diximus, liquet. Legitima utique vocatio & ordinatio est, quaecunque authoritate Christi, qui solus Pastores & Doctores dat, Ephes. IV. 11. & unus solusque verus artifex est τῶν ἀνθρώπων τῆς Θεῷ ἐξαρτίζειν πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν hominem Dei ad omne opus bonum instruendi, 2. Tim. III. 17. coll. cum Cant. VII. 1. & solus operarios suos in messem emittit, Matth. IX. 38. &, ceu Dominus unus, ministeria & charismata distribuit, & omnia in omnibus operatur, 1. Cor. XII. 6. & Christo suffragantis, ejusque characteres impressos fideliter intuentis Ecclesiae, sive totius, singulorumque ejus membrorum, sive ordinum certorum, quibus certae vocationis partes ab Ecclesia commissae sunt, juxta leges a Christo & Apostolis fixas, & ea fide atque diligentia, quae ab iisdem praescripta est, peragitur. Quid enim, quo minus officium boni Pastoris & doctoris sine incommodo gregis & Regni Dei, imo cum utriusque commodo legitime obire possit, deest illi, qui sibi conscius est, saltem mediocris aptitudinis ad officium obeundum, & charitatis Dei & proximi ad illud concupiscendum, atque ad salutem animarum quaerendam, & Ecclesiae atque piorum in ea audientiam & obedientiam in nomine Christi, quasi foedere quodam inito, spondentium votis ad διακονίαν suscipiendam invitatur, & cum consensu Ecclesiae, observato ordine, qui quovis loco secundum generale praeceptum de ordine servando, qui variare potest, recipitur; & denique ab iis, quorum interest, pacis & veritatis vigorem procurare, approbatur, vel saltem non prohibetur? quis homo est, qui alium ad docendum possit ἱκανὸν idoneum facere, vel cujus authoritate & imperio indigeat alius, ne videatur illicitum facere, quando in nomine Christi, & juxta ejusdem leges atque ordinem docet, rogat, hortatur; cum id praeceptum sit omnibus hominibus si occasio & ἀνάγκη necessitas id postulaverit? Quis tam importunus & impudens, ut neget recte fieri, absque nutu suo, opus Domini, & ad fidei obedientiam, invito se neminem adducí posse? Hoc tamen audent illi, qui mittendi munus & potestatem sibi soli, excluso Christo, & iis, qui secundum legem ejus suffragandi ipsi jus habent, arrogant, sed nec probi mittendi artifices, & ad negotium illud parum idonei, ac ne ipsi quidem a Deo missi sunt, cum Divinae missionis tabulis penitus destituantur, & propagando carnali Regno suo per carnalia instrumenta infatiabiliter invigilent.
units.tr: XXXVI. Yet those very men who thus corrupted ordination and calling, and made them an instrument of their domination, openly traduce and revile the whole ordination and calling of ours as if vitiated, because it was not suspended from anointed bishops and from the Pope propagating the sacred order. And they shout impotently that the Church has perished among us together with the ministry. How impiously and falsely these things are said is clear from what we have said. For a calling and ordination is lawful whatever its authority, since Christ, who alone gives pastors and teachers, Eph. 4:11, is the one and only true craftsman of the man of God, to equip him for every good work [τῶν ἀνθρώπων τῆς Θεῷ ἐξαρτίζειν πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν], 2 Tim. 3:17, compared with Cant. 7:1; and he alone sends out his workers into the harvest, Matt. 9:38; and as the one Lord distributes ministries and gifts, and works all in all, 1 Cor. 12:6. The calling is carried out by the Church, which supports Christ and faithfully regards his impressed marks, whether of the whole Church, of each of its members, or of certain orders to which certain parts of the calling have been committed by the Church, according to the laws fixed by Christ and the Apostles, and with that faith and diligence which they prescribed. For what lacks to one who is conscious of at least moderate aptitude for the office, and who desires it out of love of God and neighbour, seeking the salvation of souls, and who is invited by the votes of the Church, pledging, in the name of Christ and as though by entering a kind of covenant, obedience and the hearing of the Church and of the godly in it, so as to undertake the service [διακονίαν], with the consent of the Church, the order being observed (which may vary in any place according to the general precept about keeping order), and who is finally approved, or at least not forbidden, by those concerned to promote the strength of peace and truth? What lacks to him that he should not lawfully discharge the duty of a good pastor and teacher without harm to the flock and the kingdom of God, indeed to the benefit of both? What man is there who could make another fit to teach, or whose authority and command another needs, lest he seem to act unlawfully when, in the name of Christ and according to his laws and order, he teaches, asks, and exhorts? For this is commanded of all men, if occasion and necessity demand it. Who is so importunate and shameless as to deny that the work of the Lord is rightly done without his nod, and that no one can be brought against his will to the obedience of faith? Yet those men dare to claim for themselves alone the office and power of sending, excluding Christ and those who by his law have the right of voting. But neither are such senders skilled and honest craftsmen, nor are they little fit for that business; nor have they been sent by God, since they are utterly destitute of the credentials of divine mission, and tirelessly labour to propagate their carnal kingdom by carnal instruments.

units.la: XXXVII. Haud majore pietatis vel unitatis specie iidem Reformatorum Ecclesiae Evangelicae vocationem exagitant.
units.tr: XXXVII. With no greater show of piety or unity, the same men assail the calling of the Reformers of the Evangelical Church.

units.la: Nulla enim authoritate ad opus illud instructos eos fuisse; & a Monachis, laicis, rudi & seditiosa plebecula tentatum id omne fuisse, nec a talibus Ecclesiae ministros legitimos deinceps pullulare potuisse, exprobrant. Quae praeposttera & insidiosa omnia sunt. Nam Reformatores plurimi in profundo licet Papatus gurgite nati, doctoribus tamen Presbyteris, Scholarum praeceptoribus usi, linguarum artiumque liberalium studiis exculti, praesertim codice sacro Biblico tum temporis ex linguis originalibus per viros eruditos in alias notiores fideliter translato, diligenter lecto, expenso, Spiritu S. efficaciter cooperante, radiis Divinae veritatis magis magisque collucтrati; insuper etiam vocationem Ecclesiasticam ad praedicandum verbum Dei, Sacramenta administranda, & cuncta pro veris pastoribus gerenda in ipso Papatu habuerunt. Quae etiam ordinaria fuit, quatenus ordinarium sumitur non aequivocè, pro eo, quod inveterata consuetudine, qualiscunque ea sit, publicè receptum est; sed proprie pro eo, quod ordine primitus & Divinitus institu-ta to consentaneum est. In ea enim vocatione, quam ex Romana Ecclesia secum attulerunt, tria distinctè consideranda sunt, Deus, quem penes summum vocandi & mittendi jus atque imperium est, & à quo solo vocatio interna per Spiritum S. est: Ecclesia, à qua, ut instrumento vocatio externa est; & Papismus, à quo, ceu adnata struma aut tubere, vitium vocationis profluxit. Triplex igitur in vocatione, qua primi Ecclesiarum Reformatarum Pastores in Ecclesia Romana ordinati sunt, actio concurrit, Dei, Ecclesiæ & Papismi. Porrò Papismi illa labes & tabes vim & veritatem vocationis & institutionis Divinæ in Ecclesia abolere non potuit, quia illa ab hominum vitio non pendet. Actio enim causæ primæ non potest tribui causæ secundæ vel instrumentali, multò minus vitio, quod aliunde adnatum est. Vocatio ergo Reformatorum respectu Dei & Ecclesiæ ordinaria atque legitima fuit, licèt illi heroico in exequendo munere zelo, atque extraordinariis motibus, sed ab ordinario, respectu Dei & Ecclesiæ, munere requisitis, supra communem Pastorum reliquorum, Papismi vitium contrahentium, functionem attolli visi sunt, quatenus duriorem, quàm reliqui, sed necessariam tamen & ordinariam, respectu Dei & Ecclesiæ vocantis, provinciam su ceperunt. Neque ad reformandam Ecclesiam alia iis missione opus fuit, quàm mandato non credendi Pseudo-Prophetis & mendacio, imò vi ordinarii muneris iis ex verbo Dei, cujus prædicatio iis commissa erat, contradicendi, sub spe gubernationis Divinæ Christi, à quo præcipuè vocati sunt, per quam è Babylone educerentur & expellerentur. Ac multò minus miraculis, tanquam extraordinariæ missionis vel veritatis testibus, opus illis fuit, tum quia missio eorum ordinaria fuit eo sensu, quem expositimus: tum quia nova vocatione, adeóque novis testibus ad veterem doctrinam asserendam, Ecclesiæ errores corrigendos, eámque pristinæ luci & nitori restituendam, atque de Babylonis portis educendam, iis opus non fuit, ne tum quidem, postquam ejurarunt Papam cum Papismo, quando sublato vitio & exetta struma in vocatione ipsorum remansit id, quod à Deo & ab Ecclesia est: tum quia eo inprimis tempore, quo Ecclesiæ reformatio successit, miracula Divinæ missionis & veritatis prædonii signa esse non potuerunt, utpote quo Pseudo-prophetas mirabilia & prodigia in nomine Christi facturos, prædictum est, 2. Thess. II. 10. 11. Apoc. XIII. 14. tum quia non novam illi doctrinam, sed æternum Evangelium prædicarunt, ibid. XIV. 6-14. ad quod non miraculis, sed fide principii & fundamenti, satis jam confirmati, opus erat, cui jam confirmato qui non credidit, is ne crediturus quidem fuit, si vel mortuos resurgentes vidisset. Neque illi Ecclesiam sic reformantes juramentum seu votum Episcopo suffraganeo nuncupatum violasse censeri possunt. Tale enim erat: Interrogamus te, sic suffraganeus, vel Episcopus, si omnem prudentiam tuam, quanta tua natura capax est, Divinæ Scripturæ sensibus accommodare volueris; velisne ea, quæ ex Divinis Scripturis intelligis, plebem, cui ordinandus es, & verbis docere & exemplis? Ad quæ futurus Sacerdos respondit:
units.tr: They reproach the Reformers with having been equipped for that work by no authority, with the whole undertaking having been attempted by monks, laymen and a rude, seditious rabble, and with legitimate ministers of the Church being unable to spring up afterwards from such people. All of this is absurd and deceitful. For most of the Reformers, though born in the deep whirlpool of the Papacy, were nonetheless taught by doctors, presbyters and schoolmasters, and were trained in languages and the liberal arts. Especially was this so because at that time the sacred Biblical text had been faithfully translated from the original languages into better-known tongues by learned men. They read it diligently, weighed it carefully, and the Holy Spirit cooperated effectively, so that they were more and more illumined by the rays of divine truth. Moreover, they also held, within the Papacy itself, an ecclesiastical calling to preach the word of God, to administer the sacraments, and to carry out all things as true pastors. This calling was also ordinary, if "ordinary" is taken not equivocally, for what has been publicly received by long-standing custom, whatever that custom may be, but properly for what accords with the order originally and divinely instituted. In the calling which they brought with them from the Roman Church, three things must be distinctly considered: God, who holds the supreme right and authority of calling and sending, and from whom alone the internal calling through the Holy Spirit comes; the Church, from which the external calling comes as through an instrument; and the Papacy, from which the defect of the calling flowed, like a growth or tumour attached to it. Therefore three kinds of action concur in the calling by which the first pastors of the Reformed Churches were ordained in the Roman Church: the action of God, of the Church, and of the Papacy. Further, that stain and corruption of Papism could not abolish the power and truth of the calling and institution by God in the Church, because that calling does not depend on human fault. For the action of the first cause cannot be attributed to a secondary or instrumental cause, much less to a fault which has grown on from elsewhere. Therefore the calling of the Reformers, with respect to God and the Church, was ordinary and lawful. Although in discharging their office they seem to have been raised above the common function of the other pastors, who contracted the fault of Papism, this was by heroic zeal and extraordinary impulses, yet such as an ordinary office requires with respect to God and the Church. They undertook a harder task than the rest, but one which, with respect to God and the Church calling them, was necessary and ordinary. Nor did they need any other mission to reform the Church than the command not to believe false prophets and lies, and indeed the power of their ordinary office, from the word of God whose preaching had been committed to them, to contradict these, under the hope of the divine government of Christ, by whom especially they had been called, so that they might be led out of Babylon and cast out of it. Still less did they need miracles as witnesses of an extraordinary mission or of the truth. This was so because their mission was ordinary in the sense we have explained; and because they had no need of a new calling, and hence of new witnesses, to assert the old doctrine, to correct the errors of the Church, and to restore it to its former light and lustre and lead it out of the gates of Babylon. Nor did they need such witnesses even after they had renounced the Pope together with Papism, when, the defect having been removed and the growth cut away, what is from God and from the Church remained in their calling. Moreover, at the very time when the reformation of the Church took place, miracles could not be signs of divine mission and of the proclamation of the truth, since it was foretold that false prophets would work wonders and signs in the name of Christ (2. Thess. II. 10. 11. Apoc. XIII. 14.). And because they preached not a new doctrine but the eternal Gospel (ibid. XIV. 6-14), for which what was needed was not miracles but faith in the principle and foundation, already sufficiently confirmed; and whoever did not believe that already confirmed truth would not have believed even if he had seen the dead rise. Nor can those reforming the Church in this way be judged to have violated the oath or vow named for the suffragan bishop. For it ran thus: We ask you, suffragan or bishop, whether, if you are willing to adapt all your wisdom, as far as your nature is capable, to the meaning of Holy Scripture, you are willing to teach the people to whom you are to be ordained, both by words and by examples, those things which you understand from the Holy Scriptures? To which the one about to become a priest replied:

units.la: Volo. Cùm ipsi Evangelii liber proponeretur, ipsi dictum fuit: Accipe Evangelia & vade, & prædica populo tibi commissο. Item: Sit doctrina vestra spiritualis medicina populo Dei: Sit odor vitæ vestræ delectamentum Ecclesiæ Christi, ut prædicatione & exemplo ædificetis domum Dei. Tali ergo vocatione præditi, in propagando ordinarie ministerio, partibus suis à Deo & Ecclesia impositis defungi nullo negotio potuerunt, & defuncti strenuè sunt. Sed præterea etiam justum & rectum eo tempore fuit, ut δόκιμοι probi, qui per hæreses oppugnatas, & fermentum Papatus expurgatum manifesti facti sunt, 1. Cor. XL19. & à corrumpentibus Ecclesiam, atque in errore obduratis expulsi sunt, vel soli tres in nomine Christi convenirent. Matth. XVIII. 20. inter quos, à finitimis & jam ordinatis Pastoribus destitutos, qui ministerium susciperet, mandato prædicandi Evangelii, & lege charitatis, nec non verbo ex Babylone evocante, jure conveniendi in nomine Christi, & συμφωνία fratrum instructus, legitimè vocatus censeri debuit, quia & à Christo & ab Ecclesia juxta leges Christi vocatus fuit. Quomodo etiam Matthias accepit Apostolatum partim electione fratrum, partim sorte, præeunte verbo Dei, quo declaratum erat, Judæ curationem alium accepturum. Cujus exempli imitatione A. MCDLXVII. fratres Bohemi, qui à Bokyzano Pragensi Archiepiscopo acceptos ministros fastidire merito cœpissent, & ab Archiepiscopo destituti, imò propterea vexati etiam, tres omnium suffragiis legerunt, & adhibitis precibus atque jejuniis sortitionem instituerunt, quam ita Deus gubernavit, ut cùm fieri potuisset, ut omnes tres sorte præterirentur, nullo excepto approbati sint. Imposterum verò ordinariam in legendis ministris rationem in S. literis depictam secuti sunt. Quæ de laicis (ita enim Magistratus Christianos appellant) aliisque, qui sanctissimo huic operi manum admoverunt, objectant, adeò non obsunt nobis, ut honorifica & ampla nobis, hostibus verò veritatis pudorem incutere apta nata sint. Ita enim deploratæ res erant, ut ab ordine Ecclesiastico Papæ jurato sani nihil expectari potuerit. Frustra enim à lenonum & luparum atque cynœdorum principibus, non ab ædili vel prætore, aliquis lupanaria, & sellas meretricum coërceri expectet. Quod ad alios autem attinet, commune ad Christianos omnes de deferenda Babylone mandatum extabat. Si quid etiam in perturbato adeò Ecclesiæ statu præter ordinem factitatum esset, satis constat, in maxima etiam Reipublicæ civilis perturbatione, multa licere, laudari & probari, quæ statu illius tranquillo & pacato nec licent, nec laudari vel probari possunt. Talem autem in Ecclesia perturbationem fuisse probamus, neque illi Ecclesiæ suæ integritatem & sanitatem vindicare ulla ratione possunt. Atque rebus sic comparatis cui ambiguum esse potest, magis vocationem ad purgandam Ecclesiam à rectoribus suis non tam destitutam, quàm corruptam, necessariam fuisse, quàm vocatio ad extinguendum incendium, lupo, voraci Bestiæ, prædam eripiendam, venenum serpens & integras familias depascens, quacunque ratione abigendum necessaria est, inprimis cùm mandati Divini ad exeundum Babylone incitatio,& conscientiæ instinctus,& fidelium monitus,& dotes extraordinariæ,ultra seculi morem,à Deo collata,& Magistratus pii authoritas non defuerint.
units.tr: I am willing. When the book of the Gospels was presented to him, it was said to him: Take the Gospels and go, and preach to the people committed to you. Likewise: Let your teaching be a spiritual medicine to the people of God; let the fragrance of your life be a delight to the Church of Christ, so that by preaching and by example you may build up the house of God. Endowed with such a calling, they could, in propagating the ministry in the ordinary way, discharge without any difficulty the parts imposed on them by God and the Church, and having discharged them they did so vigorously. But moreover, it was also just and right at that time that approved [δόκιμοι] persons, who were made manifest (1. Cor. XI. 19) through the heresies that were attacked and the leaven of the Papacy that was purged out, and who were expelled by those corrupting the Church and hardened in error, should, if only three gathered in the name of Christ (Matth. XVIII. 20), and destitute of neighbouring and already ordained pastors, take up the ministry. Such a person, equipped by the command to preach the Gospel, by the law of charity, by the word calling them out of Babylon, by the right of meeting in the name of Christ, and by the agreement [συμφωνία] of the brothers, ought to be considered lawfully called, because he was called both by Christ and by the Church according to the laws of Christ. Thus also Matthias received the apostleship partly by the election of the brothers and partly by lot, the word of God going before, by which it had been declared that another would receive Judas's office. Following the example of this, in 1467 the Bohemian brethren, who had rightly begun to loathe the ministers they had received from Rokycana, Archbishop of Prague, and who, being deprived by the Archbishop and indeed harassed for it, chose three by the votes of all. With prayers and fasting they instituted a lot, which God so governed that, although it could have happened that all three were passed over, all were approved, none excepted. Afterwards they followed the ordinary method of choosing ministers depicted in the Holy Scriptures. As for what they object concerning laymen (for so they call the Christian magistrates) and others who laid hands on this most holy work, these objections are so far from harming us that they are fitted to be honourable and ample for us, but to cause shame to the enemies of the truth. For things were so desperate that nothing could be expected from the ecclesiastical order, sworn to the Pope, in its sound state. For in vain would anyone expect brothels and the couches of harlots to be restrained by the princes of pimps, wolves and catamites, rather than by an aedile or a praetor. As for the others, there stood the common command to all Christians to leave Babylon. If something was done beyond the ordinary order in the so disturbed state of the Church, it is quite clear that in the greatest disturbance of the civil commonwealth many things are allowed, praised and approved, which in its tranquil and peaceful state are neither permitted nor can be praised or approved. We prove that there was such a disturbance in the Church, and its rulers can in no way defend its integrity and soundness. With matters so arranged, who can doubt that a calling to cleanse the Church from its rulers, who were not so much destitute as corrupt, was as necessary as a calling to put out a fire, to snatch prey from a wolf, or to drive away by whatever means a serpent, a voracious beast, that poisons and devours whole families? Especially since there were not lacking the command of God to come out of Babylon, the urging of conscience, the admonitions of the faithful, extraordinary gifts conferred by God beyond the custom of the age, and the authority of a pious magistrate.

units.la: XXXVIII. Perpetua successio Pastorum, quam in ordinatione adversarii urgent,dupliciter considerari potest,vel ut successio in corpus,vel ut successio in caput. Illa est,cùm quis in cœtum aliquem, vel collegium cooptatur, tametsi locum,quem occupat, nullius morte vel abdicatione vacuum reperiat. Hæc, cùm quis vivens in mortui vel abdicati locum suffi-citur. Exemplum prioris in Ecclesia Constantinopolitana extat,in qua cùm secunda Synodus œcumenica Patriarcham primum constitueret, non is alicui defuncto vel exauctorato Patriarchæ successit, siquidem nullus ante id temporis Patriarcha ibi fuit; sed cooptabatur ille in commune corpus seu collegium reliquorum Patriarcharum, in quo successio spectabatur. Non absimilis eorum ratio est,quos Pontificii Episcopos suffraganeos appellant, qui commentitio transmarinæ cujuspiam Ecclesiæ titulo & larva ornati ordinandorum Presbyterorum munere vicario plerunque defunguntur. Siquidem isti titulares Episcopi cùm creantur,in nullius defuncti vel depositi locum succedunt. Ipsi igitur ordinatores personali hac successione carentes,ad ordinatos à se eam transmittere non possunt. Inter Reformatores verò primos non desunt,qui utroque successionis genere gloriari potuerunt,qui in Parochorum,seu,uti vocant,curionum,imò etiam alicubi in demortuorum Episcoporum locum personali successione subrogati sunt. Qui verò hac successione in corpus, caruerunt, saltem priore illa successione in corpus per legitimam Ecclesiæ vocationem,non caruerunt.
units.tr: XXXVIII. The perpetual succession of pastors, which our opponents press in ordination, can be considered in two ways: either as succession into a body, or as succession into a head. The first occurs when someone is co-opted into some assembly or college, even though he finds no place vacant through anyone's death or resignation. The second occurs when someone living is substituted into the place of one who has died or resigned. An example of the first is found in the Church of Constantinople. When the second ecumenical Synod established the first Patriarch there, he did not succeed any deceased or deposed Patriarch, since there had been no Patriarch there before that time. Rather, he was co-opted into the common body or college of the other Patriarchs, in which succession was observed. Similar is the case of those whom the Papists call suffragan bishops. Adorned with the empty title and mask of some overseas church, they usually discharge the office of ordaining presbyters on behalf of others. When such titular bishops are created, they succeed no one deceased or deposed. Therefore these ordainers, lacking personal succession, cannot transmit it to those they ordain. Among the first Reformers, however, there were not a few who could boast of both kinds of succession: they were installed by personal succession into the place of parish priests, or as they call them, curates, and in some places even into the place of deceased bishops. Those who lacked this succession into a body, at least did not lack that former succession into a body through lawful call of the Church.

units.la: XXXIX. In electione ministrorum inprimis προσωπολημψία Personarum acceptio & Simonia vitanda est. Personarum acceptio,ne vel indigni vel minùs digni & idonei,solius personæ, & rerum quarundam, quæ ad officii dextram administrationem non pertinent, æstimatione carnali, adeoq; πρὸς προσωπολημψιν, eligantur. Fratres mei μὴ ἐν προσωπολημψίαις ἔχετε τὴν πίστιν ne in personarum acceptione habete fidem Domini nostri Jesu Christi gloriæ,Jac. II. 1. Quod præceptum pertinet tum ad singulos, ut in pretio habeant eos inprimis, qui Deum timent,&c,ceu fratres, eundem Dominum habent,cui vivunt & moriuntur : tum ad cœtum , ne honorentur, vel aliis regendis in cœtu præferantur illi,qui divitiis, splendido vestitu,potentia hujus seculi, nomine & authoritate humana,aliisque rationibus carnalibus se commendant, sed sola fides,charismata,atque ea,quæ Regni cœlorum sunt, in pretio habeantur. Qui enim in nomine Christi conveniunt,& ejus authoritate aliquid gerunt, non ut Reges, potentes,divites; consanguinei, sed ut Christiani id faciunt, & ex fide, atque suadente fide faciunt. In Republica vix tolerabile est, ut indignior dignioris propter inclinationem, cognationem,amicitiam, conspirationem, utilitatem præferatur. Sed minùs id tolerabile est in Ecclesia, in qua non affectibus & concupiscentiis quisque suis indulgere, sed Christo glorificando & Ecclesiæ ædificandæ studere debet. Cùmque ad ministerium multi digni & idonei sunt,dignissimi eligendi sunt , quia aliter facientes personas aspiciunt; sed hoc ita intelligendum,ut comparatio fiat inter illos , qui commodè haberi possunt,& ut ille maximè idoneus & dignissimus censeatur, qui quamvis simpliciter & absolutè inferior sit, in relatione tamen ad illam Ecclesiam, cui Minister quæritur,omnibus expensis circumstantiis aptior invenitur.
units.tr: XXXIX. In the election of ministers, above all, respect of persons (προσωπολημψία) and simony must be avoided. There is respect of persons when men who are unworthy, or less worthy and fit, are chosen by a carnal estimation of the person alone and of certain things that do not pertain to the right administration of the office, and so are chosen with regard to the face of the man. "My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory in respect of persons" [μὴ ἐν προσωπολημψίαις ἔχετε τὴν πίστιν], James 2:1. This precept applies both to individuals, that they esteem above all those who fear God, etc., as brothers who have the same Lord whom they live and die for; and to the assembly, that those are not honoured, nor placed before others in governing the assembly, who commend themselves by riches, splendid clothing, the power of this world, name and human authority, and other carnal considerations; but that faith, spiritual gifts, and those things which belong to the kingdom of heaven alone be held in esteem.
