For those who gather in the name of Christ and act by his authority do so not as kings, the powerful, the rich, or kinsmen, but as Christians, and they act from faith and by the persuasion of faith. In the commonwealth it is scarcely tolerable that the less worthy be preferred to the more worthy on account of inclination, kinship, friendship, conspiracy, or advantage. But this is less tolerable in the Church, in which each person must not indulge his own feelings and lusts, but must strive to glorify Christ and build up the Church. And since many are worthy and fit for the ministry, the most worthy are to be chosen, for those who act otherwise look to persons. But this must be understood thus: comparison is to be made among those who can conveniently be had, and he is to be judged most fit and most worthy who, although he is simply and absolutely inferior, is nevertheless found more suitable, all circumstances considered, in relation to that Church for which a minister is sought.

units.la: XL. Simoniam jam olim Aquinas definivit illam,qua spirituale propter temporale datur. Sed Jesuitæ definitionem virtutum & vitiorum mutandarum miri artifices, duobus modis spirituale propter temporale principaliter, & tanquam propter finem conferri ajunt;uno modo, si temporale æstimet pluris, quàm ipsum spirituale ; altero, si temporale apud eum non fit finis rei spiritualis, quasi temporale pluris ab eo, quàm spirituale æstimetur ; sed tantùm voluntatis, sive applicationis animi ad conferendum spirituale. Priore sensu Simoniam committi asserunt, posteriore negant; hac via Ecclesiæ Romanæ Simoniam subtiliter purgantes & expiantes. Quis enim tam perditus est,qui rem spiritualem pro temporali,vel temporalem pro spirituali offerens,profiteri velit,se majoris rem temporalem, quàm spiritualem facere ; vel pecuniam non potiùs , ceu conferendæ rei spiritualis illecebram,quàm ceu rei spiritualis pretium offerre, vel accipere velit ? Et de interiori sic nundinantium æstimatione quis præter Deum idoneus judex erit? Similis color est,non pro officio, seu cura spirituali,sed pro temporali ei annexo qualemcunque remunerationem dari posse , qualis color ne in Republica quidem rectè instituta ambitum purgaret. Est igitur Simonia vitium electionis,quo quis ad officium ministerii, sicut ad rem emptioni & venditioni subjectam pervenit, adeoque pro spirituali cura pretium exigit & pendit. Quia enim officium curæ animarum spirituale Dei donum est, quod à solo Deo proprie communicatur, iccirco officium illud emere ex natura rei idem cum eo est , quod Simon Magus fecit. Quem graviter sic Petrus increpat : Argentum tuum tecum sit in perditionem , quia donum Dei putasti pretio facultatum comparari,Actor. VIII. 20. Neque Simonia talis committitur tantùm per munus à manu, cùm pecunia ad officium tale procurandum datur,sed etiam per munus ab obsequio, quod in finem illum cuipiam præstatur,nec non per munus à lingua,cùm intercessione & precibus, insuper habita dignitate, procuratur. Si munera sapientum oculos excæcant,necesse est à sic excæcatis ingens Ecclesia cui pretio intercedente æquè lupus atque pastor obtingere potest ; detrimentum patiatur,ut præsentissima hæc Ecclesiæ pestis meritò dicatur. Et studio atque zelo Ecclesiæ ædificandæ , & Dei glorificandi opus ministerii concupiscere , & se ipsum εἰς διακονίαν τοῖς ἁγίοις πιστεὶν ministerio sanctorum destinare,1.Cor.XVI. 15. 1. Tim. III. 1. pium & laudabile est. Neque etiam vel honestati ministerii repugnat, qui se aliorum judicio explorandum & probandum ad ministerium offert : vel peccare censendus est, qui aptitudinis & charitatis suæ conconscientia fretus, Ecclesiæ operam suam defert, quod & Esajas cap. VI. 8. fecisse legitur. Deus enim donorum author & diributor tales Ecclesiis offert. Sed vocationem importunè urgere, malis artibus procurare, ab animo rite ad ministerium comparato alienum : vi vel fraude invitæ Ecclesiæ se obtrudere, Diabolicum: munere à manu, obsequio vel lingua illud nundinari & occupare, Simoniacum est.
units.tr: XL. Long ago Aquinas defined simony as that by which a spiritual thing is given on account of a temporal thing. But the Jesuits, wonderful artificers at redefining virtues and vices, say that a spiritual thing is conferred principally on account of a temporal thing, and as if for an end, in two ways: first, if one values the temporal more than the spiritual itself; second, if the temporal is not the end of the spiritual thing for him, as if the temporal were not valued by him above the spiritual, but there is only the will or application of mind to confer the spiritual. In the first sense they assert that simony is committed; in the second they deny it. By this route they subtly cleanse and expiate simony for the Church of Rome. For who is so abandoned that, offering a spiritual thing for a temporal, or a temporal for a spiritual, would be willing to profess that he values the temporal thing above the spiritual? Or who would wish to offer or accept money not as an enticement to confer the spiritual thing, but as the price of the spiritual thing? And who, apart from God, will be a fit judge of the inward estimation of such hagglers? There is a similar pretext that some kind of remuneration may be given, not for the office or spiritual charge itself, but for the temporal emolument annexed to it; yet that pretext would not cleanse ambition even in a well-ordered commonwealth. Simony, therefore, is a vice of election, by which someone comes to the office of ministry as if to a thing subject to buying and selling, and thus demands and pays a price for a spiritual charge. For since the office of the cure of souls is a spiritual gift of God, which is properly communicated by God alone, to buy that office is by the nature of the thing the same as what Simon Magus did. Peter rebuked him severely: "Your money perish with you, because you thought the gift of God could be purchased with money," Acts 8:20. Nor is such simony committed only through a gift from the hand, when money is given to procure such an office; but also through a gift from service, which is rendered to someone for that end, and through a gift from the tongue, when it is procured by intercession and prayers, over and above the dignity. If gifts blind the eyes of the wise, it is necessary that a vast Church suffer such harm from men so blinded, that, through the intercession of a price, a wolf as readily as a shepherd may attain to it, so that this most present pest of the Church is rightly called such. But to desire the work of the ministry out of zeal to build up the Church and glorify God, and to devote oneself "to the ministry of the saints" [εἰς διακονίαν τοῖς ἁγίοις], 1 Cor. 16:15; 1 Tim. 3:1, is pious and praiseworthy. Nor does he who offers himself to be tested and approved by the judgment of others to the ministry act against the honour of the ministry; nor is he to be judged a sinner who, relying on the consciousness of his own aptitude and love, offers his labour to the Church, as we read Isaiah did, Isa. 6:8. For God, the author and distributor of gifts, offers such men to the Churches. But to press a call importunely, to procure it by bad arts, to foist oneself upon an unwilling Church by force or fraud, a state of mind alien to one rightly prepared for the ministry, is diabolical; to trade in and seize that office by a gift from the hand, by service or by the tongue, is simoniacal.

units.la: XLI. Non tamen Simoniæ ejusdem rea Ecclesia est, cùm Ministris Ecclesiarum & Scholarum æqua stipendia decernit; neque Simoniaci, vel mercenarii sunt, qui illa accipiunt, quod Fanaticorum delirium est. Non enim sic spiritualia pretio addicuntur, sed laborantibus in verbo, & prohibitis se seculi hujus negotiis implicare, vel, neglecto ministerio, aliunde sibi victum comparare, ut ipsi ἀμεριμνοι esse, & hoc agere possint, honesta sustentatio jure meritóque providetur. Nam dignus est operarius alimento suo, Matth.X.10. Quo argumento Christus Apostolis mandavit, ne prædicantes Evangelium sibi providerent de alimentis aliisque necessariis, quamvis illa penes se habere, & secum efferre possent: sed ut suis nummis & obsoniis domi relictis, illorum, ad quos profecturi erant, quadra viverent, quibus etiam obsonia grato animo non præstantibus, valedicere, cum anathematis symbolo, excusso pedibus pulvere jussit, ibid. v.11-15. Cui sic S. Paulus suffragatur: Quis militat propriis stipendiis unquam? Quis plantat vineam, & de fructu ejus non comedit? Quis pascit gregem, & de lacte gregis non edit? An secundum hominem hæc dico? Annon & lex hæc dicit? Nam in lege scriptum est. Bovem triturantem non capistrabis. An boves Deus curat? An propter nos omnino dicit? Propter nos enim scriptum est, quia in spe debet arans arare: & triturans spei suæ particeps esse in spe. Si nos vobis spiritualia seminavimus, magnum quid est, nos vestra carnalia (τὰ ὑφάς καὶ σκηπάσματα), victum & amictum, quibus caro, ut laborare homo possit, conservari & defendi debet) metere? (non tantùm carnalia vestra jure metimus, sed & spiritualia, quia sicut agricolam laborantem oportet primum de fructu percipere, 2. Tim.II.6. & talibus fructibus frui, quales seminat: ita spiritualia seminantes, etiam spiritualia, charitatem, manifestationem profectus, & lætitiam ex eo, expectamus) Si alii potestate utuntur, cur non potiùs nos? An nescitis, quòd qui sacra administrant, ex Sanctuario vivunt? Qui altari affixi sunt, altaris consortes sunt? Sic & Dominus ordinavit iis, qui Evangelium prædicant, ex Evangelio vivere (ἀναλόγως scilicet, quia æquè tales Evangelio ministrant, atque illi altari, atque ideo etiam ex gentibus in Sacerdotes & Levitas, hoc est, διακονίαν λόγῳ καὶ προεστῶσαν ministerium verbi & præsidentiam assumi, Esaj.LXVI.21. coll. cum Rom.XV.16. dicuntur, & diserte etiam Matth. X.10. ubi operarium alimento suo dignum esse declaravit) 1. Cor.IX.7--15. Communicet autem, qui docetur sermonem ei, qui docet, ἐν πᾶσιν ἀγαθοῖς in omnibus bonis, Gal.VI.6. Quid non debemus iis, à quibus verbum salutis accipimus, quibus acceptum referimus, quòd verbum Dei intelligimus, Deum cognoscimus, amamus, sapientes & prudentes evadimus, & salvamur? Imò id ad honorem Dei pertinet, quia ubi honorantur, & bonis nostris mactantur illi, qui sermonem loquuntur, eúmque copiosè in Ecclesia habitare faciunt, ibi Deus & verbum ejus honoratur. Unde bona quæ hoc fine, ut verbum Dei explicetur, & Deus ipse celebretur, erogata sunt, ἀγάπη charitates vocantur, & qui iis abutuntur ἐντρυφῶν τῆς ἀγάπης (sic Codices quidam legunt) luxuriare in agapis fidelium, 2. Petr.II.13. Jud. vers. 12. dicuntur. Denique qui hoc agunt, procurant id, quod sibi & aliis utile. Dicuntur enim σπείρειν εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα seminare in Spiritum, Gal. VI.8. quia quod erogatur & impenditur eo fine, ut verbum Dei copiosè in Ecclesia habitet, id merito in Spiritum seminatum dicitur. Atqui quod iis tribuitur, qui κατηχῆσαι τὸν λόγον, ut iis diligenter & ἀμεριμνως id agere liceat, id erogatur hoc fine, ut verbum Dei copiosè in Ecclesia habitet.
units.tr: XLI. Yet the Church is not guilty of the same simony when it decrees equal stipends to the ministers of the Churches and schools. Nor are those who receive such stipends simoniacal or mercenary; that is the raving of the Fanatics. For spiritual things are not thus sold for a price, but to those labouring in the Word, and forbidden to entangle themselves in the affairs of this world, or, neglecting the ministry, to procure their living elsewhere, so that they may be free from anxiety and be able to devote themselves to this work, an honest maintenance is provided by right and merit. "For the labourer is worthy of his food," Matt. 10:10. By this argument Christ commanded the Apostles, while preaching the Gospel, not to provide for themselves food and other necessities, although they could have them with them and carry them along; but, leaving their money and provisions at home, to live on the means of those to whom they were going, and, when these did not gladly supply provisions, he ordered them to take leave, shaking the dust from their feet with a sign of condemnation, ibid. vv. 11–15. St. Paul supports this: "Who serves as a soldier at his own expense ever? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who feeds a flock and does not eat of the flock's milk? Do I say these things according to man? Does not the law also say this? For it is written in the law: You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain. Does God care for oxen? Or does he say this entirely for our sake? For it was written for our sake, because the ploughman ought to plough in hope, and the thresher to be a partaker in his hope. If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things, the food and clothing by which the flesh must be preserved and defended so that a man can labour? We rightly reap your carnal things, but also spiritual things, since, just as the labouring farmer ought first to receive of the fruit, 2 Tim. 2:6, and enjoy such fruits as he sows, so we, sowing spiritual things, expect even spiritual things in return: love, the manifestation of progress, and joy from it. If others exercise this power over you, why not rather we? Do you not know that those who minister sacred things live from the sanctuary? Those who are attached to the altar share with the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who preach the Gospel should live from the Gospel" (analogously, that is, because such men minister to the Gospel just as the others to the altar; and therefore from the Gentiles men are taken as priests and Levites, that is, they are called "ministry of the word and presidency" [διακονίαν λόγῳ καὶ προεστῶσαν], Isa. 66:21, compared with Rom. 15:16; and it is expressly stated in Matt. 10:10, where he declared that the labourer is worthy of his food), 1 Cor. 9:7–15. "Let him who is taught the word share in all good things [ἐν πᾶσιν ἀγαθοῖς] with him who teaches," Gal. 6:6. What do we not owe to those from whom we receive the word of salvation, to whom we refer it that we understand the word of God, know and love God, become wise and prudent, and are saved? Indeed, this pertains to the honour of God, because where those who speak the word are honoured and supplied with our goods, and cause it to dwell abundantly in the Church, there God and his word are honoured. Hence the goods that are expended for this end, that the word of God may be expounded and God himself celebrated, are called love-feasts [ἀγάπη], and those who abuse them, "revelling in their love-feasts" [ἐντρυφῶν τῆς ἀγάπης] (so some codices read), are said to riot in the love-feasts of the faithful, 2 Pet. 2:13; Jude v. 12. Finally, those who do this procure what is useful both to themselves and to others. For they are said to "sow to the Spirit" [σπείρειν εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα], Gal. 6:8, because what is given and spent for the end that the word of God may dwell richly in the Church is rightly said to be sown to the Spirit. Now what is given to those who "instruct in the word" [κατηχῆσαι τὸν λόγον], so that they may do this diligently and free from anxiety, is given for this end, that the word of God may dwell richly in the Church.

units.la: XLII. Frustra ergo Anabaptistæ gratis Evangelium prædicandum esse vel à ditioribus, qui de suo abundè habent, unde vivant, vel à pauperibus, qui arte aliqua βαναύσῳ & proprio labore victum & necessaria sibi comparare possunt, contendunt. Dixit equidem Christus: Gratis accepistis, gratis date, Matth. X. 8. sed ibidem v. 10. dicit, eos, quos mittebat, ne de calceis quidem curare debere, quia operarius alimento suo dignus sit. Ergo etiam, qui gratis dant, tamen alimenta accipiunt, & iis digni sunt. Et quacunque re dignus aliquis est, eam jure exigit, & jure, non gratis, vel sponte alter reddit. Non ergo ea Christi mens est, quòd ii, qui in verbo laborant, à civitatibus & Ecclesiis liberalitatem & τιμὴν honorem, 1. Tim. V. 17. 18. accipere non debeant, sed quòd non debeant turpi spiritualium nundinatione præmia & lucrum quærere, sed omni occasione, verbo & omnibus donis sibi extra ordinem collatis prodesse, etiamsi nullum fructum ex opere suo percipiant, & homines ingrati sint. Non enim donis & gratiis Dei spiritualibus oportet pretium avaro animo statuere, uti olim Sacerdotes בְּמחִיר יורִי pretio docuerunt, Mich. III.11. & Magi atque Philosophi gentiles merces suas jactarunt, & magno pretio hominibus earum cupidis venditarunt, & hodienum id ipsum fit in Papatu, ubi indulgentiæ, venia les & venales tesserae, venduntur. Neque patrocinatur exemplum Pauli, qui σκηνοποιῶν exercuit; & manibus propriis laboravit, 1. Cor. IV. 12. δωρεάν gratis Evangelium prædicavit, 2. Cor. XI. 7. nihil ab Ecclesiis accipiendo, sed in opere & labore dies noctésque opus faciendo, ne quem gravaret, 2. Thessal. III. 8. quo nomine apud Corinthios gloriatur. Aliud enim jus, aliud juris exercitium est. Jus, seu ἐξουσίαν potestatem accipiendi stipendium ipse sibi asserit. Annon habemus ἐξουσίαν φαγεῖν καὶ πεῖν potestatem edendi & bibendi? (puta impendiis τῶν μισθοφορούντων) An solus ego & Barnabas non habemus potestatem τὸ μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι non operandi? 1. Cor. IX. 4. 6. Ubi potestatem illam ponderosis argumentis sibi vendicat. Non quòd non habeamus potestatem, 2. Thess. III. 9. Sed exercitium juris S. Paulus intermisit, ὑπὲρ τὸ μὴ ἐπιβαρῆσαι ne cuiquam gravis esset, ibid. v. 8. & 2. Cor. XII.16. ne ὑπαρχῶν ὑπὲρ impedimentum alialiquod ponat Evangelio Christi, 1. Cor. IX. 12. non quòd alimenta accipiendo simpliciter Evangelio impedimentum ponatur, cùm id sit debita κοινωνία communicatio bonorum, Gal. VI. 6. & merces competens, Matth. X. 10. & exercitium charitatis atq; justitiæ erga laborantem in verbo Evangelium non impediat, imò per Evangelium ad hoc ipsum homines adducantur; sed quod expedire S. Paulus, qui primus gentibus Evangelium prædicavit, & κατ' ἐξοχὴν Gentium præco fuit, judicavit, ante omnia infidelibus, quibus Evangelium prædicavit, constare debere de prædicantis sincera charitate & missione; quæ nulla re magis liquere poterat, quàm si eum Evangelium prædicare viderent, non quærentem ea, quæ gentes habebant, sed electos gentium, imò totas gentes, ceu lucrum & hæreditatem in Christo, non ὠφελείας χάριν utilitatis gratia, Jud. v. 16. Sed sola spe præmii à Deo potiundi, & nullo cum gentium damno, si Evangelio crederent. Denique abstinuit propter καυχημα gloriationem suam adversus Pseudapostolos, 2. Cor. XI. 10. quam ponit non in prædicatione, sed in prædicatione ἐκούσια voluntaria, sine emolumento & lucro, 1. Cor. IX. 15. 17. ne prædicatio apud gentes moram & suffla men pateretur. Qua in re exemplum suum imitandum proponit, dicens: Non quòd non habeamus potestatem, sed ut nos exemplum demus vobis, εἰς τὸ μιμεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς ad imitandum nos, 2. Thess. III. 9. Unde exemplum ejus imitati fratres illi, qui pro nomine Christi exiverunt, μηδὲν λαμβάνοντες ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν nihil accipientes à gentibus, 3. Joh. v. 7. quos propterea etiam charitati fidelium commendat, jubens eos ἀξίως τοῦ Θεοῦ ad iter instrui, sicut Deo dignum est, ibid. v. 6. hoc est, providere iis non tenuiter & parcè, velut mendicis, sed honorificè, ut oportet eos, qui in ministerio versantur, ut Deus in iis honoretur. Non ergo in universum, sed in simili casu S. Paulus ministerium suum apud gentes ἀδάπανον sine eorum sumptibus exercens, se exemplum aliis imitandum statuit, 2. Thess. III. 9. ut videlicet & alii impeditionem cursus Evangelii omnibus modis caveant, infirmorum & tenuium, ne onerentur, ratio habeatur; studeat quisque bonam habere conscientiam, quòd libens & ex amore Evangelium prædicaverit; denique nemo postulet ali non operans, nempe ea, quæ ministerii cujusque sunt. Licet enim non necesse sit omnibus operari propriis manibus, tamen necesse est operari opus ministerii, ad quod quisque vocatus est, & quod suscepit. Argumentum imitationis non ad omnes casus proferendæ indubitabile est, quòd non semper & ubique Apostolus accipiendo stipendio abstinuit, sed duntaxat in Achaja & Ἐπαδί. Alias, inquit, Ecclesias ἐσυλήσα spoliavi, (non multum, sed à pauperibus accipiendo, 2. Cor. VIII. 1. 2. λαβὼν ὀψώνιον accepto stipendio ad ministrandum vobis; & cùm apud vos essem, & penuria laborarem, nulli gravis fui. Nam defectum meum adimpleverunt fratres, qui ex Macedonia veniebant; ibid. XI. 8. 9. Novistis & vos, Philippenses, quòd in principio annuntiationis, quando exivi Macedonia, nulla mecum Ecclesia communicaverit in rationes expensi & accepti, nisi vos soli, Phil. IV. 15. Quibus verbis declarat, quòd præter rationem instituti sui, initiò prædicationis suscepta cum Philippensibus egerit, ipsorum munera accipiendo. Quod signum erat eximiæ existimationis, quam de ipsis conceperat. Et facto eo se Philippenses arctius quodammodo ei conjunxerant, & cum eo super prædicatione Evangelii, & participandis incommodis quasi societatem contraxerant. Consentaneum igitur erat, ut in finem usque in eodem studio & cura pro Apostolo gerenda, & in communione perseverarent. Ac ne videretur rem suam curare, addit: Non quòd requiram munus (aurum vel argentum vestrum) sed requiro fructum redundantem in rationes vestras, fructum puta verbi Dei, fidei, justitiæ, Regni Dei & Spiritus S. exuberantem, ibid. v. 17. Non ergo S. Paulus stipendio accipiundo prorsus abstinuit, sed juris sui exercitium ita temperavit, uti id saluti Ecclesiæ conducere visum est. Quod faciendum semper est. Neque etiam ministri Ecclesiæ sumptibus sustentati mercenarii sunt similes illis, de quibus Deus: Capita ejus בשחר pro munere judicant, & sacerdotes ejus במחיר pro mercede docent, & Prophetæ ejus בכסף pro argento divinant, Mich. III. 11. His enim verbis avaritia eorum, qui opes quærunt præ Regno Dei, & magis quàm necesse est, & modis non justis, & ad finem malum, qui varius esse potest, & officium faciunt nonnisi in respectu ad quæstum, & pretium exigunt pro iis, quæ gratuita esse debebant, & propter quæstum malè judicant, docent & prophetant. Quæ nihil faciunt ad eos, qui Divino & humano jure freti, ut officio suo fungi ἀπολειτουργήσως possint, alimenta & indumenta ab iis, quorum ministerio se totos addixerunt, accipiunt. Non enim quod sic illi accipiunt, proprie merces dispensationis, sed sustentatio necessitatis est. Nulla enim prædicationem inter & stipendium proportio est. Ac ne quidem stipendium pacisci, non sponte, ultro & gratuito datum accipere, mercenarium est, quia Christus operarium alimento dignum esse diserte pronuntiat, atque Apostoli, domi relictis omnibus, ceu jure τὰ βιωτικὰ accepturos dimisit, Matth. X. 10. &c. Cùm ergo sponte non offeruntur, & charitas Ecclesiæ friget, pacisci æqua ratione, & ex prudentum consilio, atque communi Ecclesiæ, mutuòque consensu, sine Simoniæ vel mercenarii crimine ullo licet. Et qui sic pactum stipendium non ex inopia, sed ingratitudine mera & pertinaciter exsolvere gravantur, næ digni illi sunt, quibus dicatur, quod Christus Apostolos suos iis, qui eos recipere detrectabant, dicere jussit: Ecce pulverem pedum nostrorum in vos excutimus, Matth. X. 14. Luc. X. 11. hoc est, indigni estis, quibus verbum Dei annuntietur. Contempto enim & neglecto præcone verbi Dei, ipsum verbum Dei contemnitur & negligitur.
units.tr: XLII. Therefore the Anabaptists are wrong to contend that the Gospel must be preached free of charge, either by the wealthier, who have enough of their own to live on, or by the poor, who can get their living and necessities by some trade and their own labour. Christ indeed said, Freely you have received, freely give, Matt. 10:8, but in the same place, v. 10, he says that those whom he sent should not even worry about shoes, because the labourer is worthy of his food. So even those who give freely still receive food, and they are worthy of it. Whatever a man is worthy of, he claims by right, and another gives it by right, not as a gift or of his own accord. Christ's meaning, then, is not that those who labour in the Word should not receive the generosity and honour [τιμήν] of cities and churches, 1 Tim. 5:17-18. His meaning is that they must not seek rewards and profit through a shameful trade in spiritual things, but must use every opportunity, by word and by all the gifts conferred on them beyond the ordinary course, to benefit others, even if they receive no return for their work and the people are ungrateful. For one should not, with a greedy mind, set a price on God's spiritual gifts and graces, as the priests once taught for a price [בְּמחִיר], Mic. 3:11, and as pagan magicians and philosophers put their wares on display and sold them at high prices to those eager for them; and the same thing still happens today in Popery, where indulgences, pardons and sale tokens are sold. Nor does the example of Paul support them, for he worked as a tentmaker and laboured with his own hands, 1 Cor. 4:12, and freely [δωρεάν] preached the Gospel, 2 Cor. 11:7, accepting nothing from the churches, but working day and night in labour and toil so as not to burden anyone, 2 Thess. 3:8, and he boasted of this among the Corinthians. For one thing is the right, another the exercise of the right. The right, or authority [ἐξουσίαν], to receive a stipend, he himself claims for himself: Have we not the authority [ἐξουσίαν] to eat and drink? (that is, at the expense of those who serve for pay). Have not I and Barnabas the authority not to work? 1 Cor. 9:4, 6. There he claims that authority with weighty arguments. Not that we do not have the authority, 2 Thess. 3:9. But Paul set aside the exercise of his right, so as not to be a burden [ὑπὲρ τὸ μὴ ἐπιβαρῆσαι] to anyone, ibid. v. 8, and 2 Cor. 12:16, lest he place some hindrance [ἐγκοπήν] in the way of the Gospel of Christ, 1 Cor. 9:12. This is not because receiving food would simply be a hindrance to the Gospel, since it is a due fellowship [κοινωνία], the sharing of goods, Gal. 6:6, and fitting wages, Matt. 10:10, and the exercise of charity and justice towards one who labours in the Word of the Gospel does not hinder it; indeed, through the Gospel people are led to this very thing. Rather, Paul, who first preached the Gospel to the Gentiles and was par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχήν] the herald of the Gentiles, judged that it was expedient that, above all, the unbelievers to whom he preached should be assured of the preacher's sincere charity and mission. Nothing could make this clearer than if they saw him preaching the Gospel without seeking what the Gentiles possessed, but seeking the elect among the Gentiles, indeed whole nations, as gain and inheritance in Christ, not for the sake of advantage [ὠφελείας χάριν], Jude v. 16, but solely in hope of obtaining the reward from God, and with no loss to the Gentiles should they believe the Gospel. Finally, he refrained because of his boasting [καύχημα] against the false apostles, 2 Cor. 11:10, which he places not in his preaching but in voluntary preaching [ἐκούσια], without emolument or gain, 1 Cor. 9:15, 17, so that the preaching among the Gentiles would not suffer delay or suspicion. In this matter he sets forth his own example for imitation, saying: Not that we do not have the authority, but that we might give you an example [εἰς τὸ μιμεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς], to imitate us, 2 Thess. 3:9. Accordingly, those brothers who went out for the name of Christ, receiving nothing from the Gentiles [μηδὲν λαμβάνοντες ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν], imitated his example, 3 John v. 7, and for this reason John commends them to the charity of the faithful, bidding them to be sent on their journey in a manner worthy of God [ἀξίως τοῦ Θεοῦ], as is fitting for God, ibid. v. 6. That is, they should be provided for not meanly and sparingly, as beggars are, but honourably, as those who serve in the ministry ought to be, so that God may be honoured in them. So, then, Paul does not set this down as a universal rule but as an example for others to imitate in a similar case: he exercised his ministry among the Gentiles without expense [ἀδάπανον] to them, 2 Thess. 3:9, so that others too should take care in every way not to hinder the course of the Gospel, and should have regard for the weak and poor so that they are not burdened; each should strive to have a good conscience, in that he has preached the Gospel willingly and out of love; and finally, no one should demand to be fed without working, that is, without doing the things that belong to his ministry. For although it is not necessary for everyone to work with his own hands, it is necessary to do the work of the ministry to which each is called and which he has undertaken. The argument from imitation is not indisputable for all cases, since the Apostle did not always and everywhere refrain from accepting a stipend, but only in Achaia and Macedonia. Other, he says, churches I plundered [ἐσύλησα], not greatly, but by accepting from the poor, 2 Cor. 11:8-9, having received a stipend [λαβὼν ὀψώνιον] for ministering to you; and when I was with you and was in need, I was a burden to no one, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked, ibid. 11:8-9. You yourselves also know, Philippians, that at the beginning of the Gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church shared with me in the account of giving and receiving except you alone, Phil. 4:15. By these words he declares that, contrary to the plan of his mission, at the start of his preaching he dealt with the Philippians by accepting their gifts. This was a sign of the exceptional esteem he had for them. And by this act the Philippians had in some way bound themselves more closely to him, and had entered into a kind of partnership with him in preaching the Gospel and in sharing its hardships. It was therefore fitting that they should persevere in the same zeal and care for the Apostle, and in this fellowship, to the end. And lest he seem to be looking after his own affairs, he adds: Not that I seek the gift (your gold or silver), but I seek the fruit that increases to your account, namely the abundant fruit of the Word of God, of faith, of righteousness, of the Kingdom of God and of the Holy Spirit, ibid. v. 17. So Paul did not altogether refrain from receiving a stipend, but tempered the exercise of his right as seemed conducive to the welfare of the Church. This must always be done. Nor are the ministers of the Church who are supported at the church's expense hired servants like those of whom God says: Her heads judge [בשחר] for a reward, and her priests teach [במחיר] for hire, and her prophets divine [בכסף] for silver, Mic. 3:11. For these words condemn the avarice of those who seek riches before the Kingdom of God, who seek more than is necessary and by unjust means and for an evil end, which can take many forms, who perform their office only with a view to gain, who demand a price for what ought to be given freely, and who for the sake of gain judge, teach and prophesy wrongly. These words have nothing to do with those who, relying on divine and human law so that they may discharge their office without being distracted [ἀπολειτουργήσως], receive food and clothing from those to whose ministry they have devoted themselves wholly. For what they receive in this way is not properly the wage of a transaction but the support of necessity. There is no proportion between preaching and a stipend. Nor is it mercenary to bargain for a stipend, or to receive what is given freely, willingly and gratuitously, because Christ plainly declares that the labourer is worthy of his food, and when the Apostles were sent out, leaving everything at home, he let them know that they would receive the necessities of life [τὰ βιωτικά] as a right, Matt. 10:10 etc. Therefore, when such gifts are not offered voluntarily and the charity of the Church grows cold, it is lawful, on the same principle, and by the counsel of the prudent and by the common agreement and mutual consent of the Church, to agree upon a stipend, without any charge of simony or of being mercenary. And those who grudgingly and stubbornly pay the stipend so agreed, not from poverty but from sheer ingratitude, are indeed worthy of what Christ bade his Apostles say to those who refused to receive them: Behold, we shake off the dust of our feet against you, Matt. 10:14; Luke 10:11. That is, you are unworthy to have the Word of God proclaimed to you. For when the herald of the Word of God is despised and neglected, the Word of God itself is despised and neglected.

units.la: XLIII. Non uno modo τὰ βιωτικὰ verbi Dei ministris providentur. Nam provideri & solvi, vel ex sportulis, uti Veteres vocabant, hoc est, spontaneis oblationibus fidelium, ex Christiana charitate, justitia & liberalitate in communem Ecclesiæ usum de bonis conferentium, uti à primis Christianis & aliquot post seculis factitatum est: vel ex mutuo pacto, & singulorum stipe collatitia: vel à Magistratu Christiano ex ærario publico: vel ex agrorum & prædiorum Ecclesiæ donatorum & legatorum annuis reditibus atque proventu: vel denique ex decimis ; qui modus & ratio maximè conveniens,facilis & æquitati consentanea est; possunt. Quocunque autem horum modorum , vel alio etiam honesto & æquo, id fiat, parum refert, dummodo stipendia sufficientia,certa & tuta sint,atque in iis definiendis servetur modus , ne vel concisa & parca, vel ampla & liberalia nimis, ad luxum & fastum magis, quàm ad usum honestum atque necessarium comparata sint. Utrumque enim extremum vitandum est, ne vel tenuia nimis sint, quia uti non male Panormitanus , non ignorantia tantùm Sacerdotum , sed Sacerdotii ignominia tenuitatem beneficiorum sequitur,& necessariis vitæ honestè transfigendæ subsidiis destituti,facilè Levitarum propter מנוח portiones sibi non datas ad agros suos colendos diverten-tium , atque ita domum Dei destituentium, Nehem. XIII. 10. 11. exemplo,ad indignas artes sordidúmque quæstum occipiendum animum applicant; quod S. Paulus,vetans Episcopum esse αἰσχροκερδῆ turpis lucri cupidum, 1.Tim.III. 3. improbat: nec lauta & opulenta nimis, ne luxui, otio, & inani pompæ se dedant, atque ita, quod veteri adagio vulgatum est , pietas divitias pariat, & filia matrem devoret. His vitatis extremis modus sustentandi Ecclesiæ ministros ejusdem libertati relictus est. Neque enim Canonistæ aliíque assensum impetrant, pertendentes,decimas ex jure Divino Ecclesiæ ministris solvendas esse. Nam quòd ante Christum Israelitæ decimas Levitis solvere jussi sunt,non naturalis vel perpetui,sed positivi & mutabilis juris fuit,manente sola analogia juris,ut ministri Ecclesiæ liberaliter & honestè, quacunque demum honesta ratione,etiam ex decimis, si ita visum fuerit,& pacta, quæ violari nunquam debent,& interceßerint; ab Ecclesia sustentantur. An nescitis , quòd qui sacra administrant, ex sacro vivant ? Qui altari affixi sunt,altaris consortis sunt? Sic & Dominus ordinavit iis, qui Evangelium prædicant, ut ex Evangelio vivant, 1. Cor. IX. 13. 14. Neque illud obstat,quòd etiam ante legem Abrahamus Melchisedeco, ceu Sacerdoti, & sibi benedicenti decimas solvit,Genes. XIV. 20. Hebr. VII. 4. Nam & illud ex ceremoniali , & typico , adeóque mutabili jure non perpetuo & immutabili factum est. Typus autem Melchisedecus fuit Christi,non vel Sacerdotum , vel Ministrorum N. T. Christo autem non decimas , sed nos ὁλοτελῶς totos debemus,quia nos totos corpore & anima redemit,& nobis in spiritualibus & supercœlestibus benedixit. Etiam Jacobus decimas Deo vovit,si feliciter redux foret,Genes. XXVIII. 22. Sed non magis id ex juris naturalis & perpetui instinctu fecit, quam jus naturale ipsi dictavit, ut lapidem quem in titulum posuerat, Deo sic voveret,ut ex eo domum ipsi faceret, ibid. Et Deo, ut absoluto rerum omnium Domino , non magis decimam tantùm bonorum partem , quàm decimam vitæ partem debemus , sed nos totos,vitam & bona, si ad honorem ejus facere constiterit. Aliàs homini dominium in terram , & omnia, quæ in terra sunt, non excepta ulla parte bonorum terræ dedit, ibid. I. 31. Quòd verò ad
units.tr: XLIII. The temporal needs (τὰ βιωτικὰ [ta biotika]) of the ministers of the word are provided for in more than one way. They may be provided for and paid either from sportulae, as the ancients called them, that is, from the voluntary offerings of the faithful, whom Christian love, justice and generosity moved to contribute goods to the common use of the Church, as was done by the first Christians and for some centuries afterwards; or by mutual agreement, through contributions gathered from individuals; or by the Christian magistrate from the public treasury; or from the annual revenues and produce of fields and estates given to or bequeathed to the Church; or finally from tithes, which is the most suitable, convenient and equitable method. Whichever of these methods is used, or any other honourable and fair one, matters little, provided that the stipends are sufficient, certain and secure, and that in fixing them a measure is kept, so that they are neither meagre and scanty nor excessively large and generous, arranged for luxury and display rather than for honest and necessary use. Both extremes must be avoided: the stipends must not be too slender, for, as Panormitanus rightly says, not only ignorance among the priests but also disgrace to the priesthood follows from the poverty of benefices, and when they are deprived of the means needed to live honourably, they easily turn their minds to unworthy arts and sordid gain, since the Levites, not given their portions [מנוח, menuach], turned aside to cultivate their own fields and so abandoned the house of God (Neh. 13:10, 11). Paul forbids a bishop to be greedy of filthy lucre [αἰσχροκερδῆ, aischrokerde], 1 Tim. 3:3, and condemns this. Nor should they be too lavish and rich, lest they give themselves over to luxury, idleness and empty show, and so there comes about what the old proverb says: piety brings forth riches, and the daughter devours the mother. With these extremes avoided, the measure of maintaining the ministers of the Church is left to the Church's own freedom. For the canonists and others do not win assent when they contend that tithes must be paid to the ministers of the Church by divine law. For although the Israelites were commanded to pay tithes to the Levites before Christ, this was a matter of positive and changeable law, not of natural or perpetual law; only the analogy of the law remains, so that the ministers of the Church are supported by the Church generously and honourably, by whatever honourable means seem best, including tithes if so decided, and by agreements, which must never be broken. Do you not know that those who minister in holy things live from the holy things? Those who serve at the altar share the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who preach the gospel should live from the gospel (1 Cor. 9:13, 14). Nor does it stand in the way that even before the law Abraham paid tithes to Melchizedek, as to a priest and one blessing him (Gen. 14:20; Heb. 7:4). For that too was done under ceremonial and typical law, and so under changeable, not perpetual and unchangeable, law. Melchizedek was a type of Christ, not of the priests or ministers of the New Testament. To Christ, however, we owe not tithes but ourselves wholly [ὁλοτελῶς, holoteles], because he redeemed us wholly, body and soul, and has blessed us with spiritual and heavenly blessings. Jacob too vowed tithes to God, if he should return safely (Gen. 28:22); but he did not do so from any impulse of natural and perpetual law, any more than natural law dictated to him that he should vow to God the stone he had set up as a pillar, so that he would build a house from it (ibid.). And to God, as the absolute Lord of all things, we owe not merely a tenth part of our goods, nor a tenth part of our life, but ourselves entire, our life and our goods, if it pleases him to be honoured by them. Otherwise he gave man dominion over the earth and all that is on it, without any exception of any part of the earth's goods (ibid. 1:31). But that God for a time so restricted that dominion as to claim a tenth part for himself belonged to the special ceremonial and political law of the people of the Old Testament. For this was, as it were, a sacred tribute, which God wished to be paid to himself, as to the King and Lord, even the political ruler, of that people, for a special reason. But when the special ceremonial and political law was abolished, this too of the same kind is understood to be abolished, while the analogy of law remains by which the Church is bound to provide sustenance for its ministers, whether from tithes or from some other source. So the payment of tithes, where it has been introduced by consent of the people and is rightly retained, is no longer a matter of special divine or natural law, but of free, human and ecclesiastical law; and it is not so much the payment of tithes as the payment of a stipend, which is owed by divine and natural law. For Seneca wisely said (Epist. 121): What experience teaches is slow and varied. Whatever nature gives is equal for all and immediate. Certainly the law of tithes does not stand thus, either in the sounder judgement of men or in public practice. For the support of workers is commanded by divine and natural law, but its measure is bound by no necessary law, either from Christ, or from the Apostles, or from the universal Church. Rather three things define it best: piety, charity and convenience. It is also absurd to set Paul's words, let him who is taught the word share in all good things with him who teaches [Κοινωνείτω ὁ κατηχούμενος τὸν λόγον ἐν πᾶσιν ἀγαθοῖς τῷ κατηχοῦντι] (Gal. 6:6), beside what Moses said of Abraham, that he gave tithes to Melchizedek of all [כל, kol], Gen. 14:20, or as Paul himself puts it, from all [ἀπὸ πάντων, apo panton] (Heb. 7:2), as if in both places a tenth part of goods were meant by some fixed rule. Certainly to share in all good things is one thing, that is, to hold all goods in common, or to share in the needs of the saints [κοινωνεῖν τῆς χρείας τῶν ἁγίων, koinonein tes chreias ton hagion], which St Paul had said in the former passage; and to give tithes of all is another. For how many people in the Christian world have no fields, estates or cattle from which to pay tithes? How many craftsmen, merchants and others neither know nor can know how much profit they make each year from their labour, industry and work? Finally, if tithes were owed to the ministers of the Church by divine law, St Paul, in 1 Cor. 9:4 and following, and in Gal. 6:6, where he speaks expressly of the stipends of ministers, would surely not have failed to insist on such a right.

units.la: tempus dominium illud sic restrinxit,ut decimam partem sibi vendicaret , ad jus ceremoniale & politicum singulare populi V. T. pertinuit. Erat enim hoc veluti tributum sacrum, quod sibi Deus, ceu Regi & Domino etiam Politico populi illius pendi ex singulari causa voluit. Sublato autem jure ceremoniali & politico singulari, hæc quoque ejusdem speciei sublata intelligitur ; manente analogia juris, quo Ecclesia obstringitur ad alimentum ministris providendum , sive ex decimis , sive aliunde. Ut jam decimarum solutio , ubi illa per consensum populi introducta est, & meritò retinetur,non amplius Divini specialis, vel naturalis,sed liberi,humani & Ecclesiastici juris sit; nec tam decimarum, quàm stipendii jure Divino & naturali debiti solutio sit. Scitè enim Seneca Epist. 121. Tardum, inquit, est & varium,quod usus docet. Quicquid natura tradit, & æquale omnibus est, & statim. Non ita profectò se habet jus decimarum sive saniore judicio hominum , sive in praxi publica. Nam jure Divino & naturali imperata est operariorum sustentatio,sed modus ejus nec à Christo, nec ab Apostolis,nec ab Ecclesia universali ulla lege necessaria circumscriptus est. Sed tria optimè eum definiunt, pietas,charitas & commoditas. Ludicrum & illud est,quòd verba illa Pauli : Κοινωνείτω ὁ κατηχούμενος τὸν λόγον ἐν πᾶσιν ἀγαθοῖς τῷ κατηχοῦντι. Communicet qui docet sermonem ei , qui docet , in omnibus bonis, Gal. VI. 6. cum eo, quod de Abrahamo Moses dixit,eum Melchisedeco decimas dedisse כל ex omnibus,Genes. XIV. 20. seu uti ipse Paulus loquitur, ἀπὸ πάντων de omnibus,Hebr. VII. 2. quasi πεπρωμένα quadam utrobique decima bonorum pars intelligeretur. Aliud certè est communicare in omnibus bonis , hoc est, omnia bona communia habere,seu κοινωνεῖν τῆς χρείας τῶν ἁγίων communicare in necessitatibus sanctorum , quod priore loco S. Paulus dixerat: aliud decimas dare de omnibus. Quot enim in orbe Christiano homines sunt , quibus nulli agri , prædia , pecora sunt , unde decimas solvant ? Quot artifices , mercatores , alii nec sciunt, nec scire possunt, quantum ex suo labore , industria & opera lucri annuatim faciant ? Denique si Divino jure decimæ ministris Ecclesiæ deberentur,S. Paulus 1. Cor.IX. 4. &c. Gal. VI. 6. ubi ex professo de stipendiis ministrorum loquitur,jus ejusmodi inculcare minimè omisisset.
units.tr: That right of ownership was restricted to a tenth part claimed for God's own use. This belonged to the ceremonial and political law peculiar to the people of the Old Testament. For it was, as it were, a sacred tribute, which God wished to be paid to himself for a special reason, as King and also as Lord and political ruler of that people. But when the ceremonial and special political law was abrogated, this too is understood to have been abrogated, as belonging to the same kind. The analogy of law remains, by which the Church is bound to provide maintenance for its ministers, whether from tithes or from some other source. So the payment of tithes, where it has been introduced by the consent of the people and is rightly retained, is no longer a matter of special divine or natural law, but of free, human and ecclesiastical right. It is not so much the payment of tithes as of a stipend owed by divine and natural law. Seneca rightly says in Epist. 121: "What experience teaches is slow and variable. Whatever nature gives is equal for all and immediate." The right of tithes certainly does not stand thus, either in the sounder judgment of men or in public practice. For the support of workers is enjoined by divine and natural law, but its mode has been limited by no necessary law, either by Christ, or by the Apostles, or by the universal Church. Rather, three things define it best: piety, charity and convenience. It is also ridiculous to set alongside what Moses said of Abraham, that he gave tithes to Melchizedek "from all" [כל] (Gen. 14:20), or, as Paul himself puts it, "from all" [ἀπὸ πάντων] (Heb. 7:2), those words of Paul: "Let him who is taught the word communicate to him who teaches in all good things" [Κοινωνείτω ὁ κατηχούμενος τὸν λόγον ἐν πᾶσιν ἀγαθοῖς τῷ κατηχοῦντι] (Gal. 6:6), as if in both places some tenth part of goods were meant by a kind of prescribed measure. Surely to communicate in all good things, that is, to hold all goods in common, or to "communicate in the necessities of the saints" [κοινωνεῖν τῆς χρείας τῶν ἁγίων], which St Paul had said in the former passage, is one thing; to give tithes of all is another. For how many people in the Christian world have no fields, estates or herds from which to pay tithes? How many craftsmen, merchants and others neither know, nor can know, how much profit they make each year from their labour, industry and work? Finally, if by divine right tithes were owed to the ministers of the Church, St Paul would surely not have failed to press such a right in 1 Cor. 9:4 etc., and in Gal. 6:6, where he speaks expressly of the ministers' stipends.

units.la: XLIV. Nihil verò impedit,quò minus Ministris Ecclesiæ Ministri præter stipendia, quibus eos Ecclesia maètat, alia etiam bona , sive ex donatione , sive ex hæreditate paterna , sive ex agnatorum & cognatorum successione,sive ex proprio ære acquisita , possidere & retinere possint. Gratia enim naturam , civitatem, familiam, nec non naturalia, civilia & domestica bona non evertit , sed fovet & conservat. Quisque in vocatione ea , in qua vocatus est, maneat. Vocatus es servus? Ne sit tibi curæ. Sed si liber fieri potes , potiùs utere, &c. 1. Cor. VII. 20. 21. Ecclesia enim in Republica, non Respublica in Ecclesia est,quia etiam sine Ecclesia Respublicas esse constat. Sicut igitur Ecclesia politiam non evertit, neminémque adeò juribus, privilegiis, prærogativis, vel bonis legitimis
units.tr: XLIV. Nothing prevents ministers of the Church from possessing and retaining, besides the stipends with which the Church supports them, other goods as well, whether acquired by gift, by paternal inheritance, by succession from kinsmen on either side, or by their own money. For grace does not overturn nature, the state, the family, or natural, civil and domestic goods, but cherishes and preserves them. "Let each remain in the calling in which he was called. Were you called as a slave? Let it not trouble you. But if you can become free, rather use it," etc. (1 Cor. 7:20-21). For the Church is in the commonwealth, not the commonwealth in the Church, since it is clear that commonwealths exist even without the Church. Therefore, just as the Church does not overturn the polity, and deprives no one of rights, privileges, prerogatives or lawful goods,

units.la: aaaa mis privat : Non aufert terrestria, qui Regna dat coelestia. Potest autem & tenetur Ecclesiæ minister æquè atque alii,imò magis, quia typus esse gregis debet, bonis suis legitimè partis rectè uti. Manifestus eam in rem Canon Apostolicus λεγόμενος quadragesimus est: Ἐγω φανερὸς τὰ ἰδία ἐπισκόπων πράγματα, Manifestum sit, quæ Episcopi facultates propriæ, & quæ Dominicæ (ad Ecclesiam pertinentes) sint, ut Episcopus moriens, quibus vult, & quomodo vult, propria sua relinquere possit, nec intercipiantur sub Ecclesiasticarum obtentu, facultates Episcopi nonnunquam uxorem, cognatos vel servos possidentis. Quòd si ministro, quæ prius possidebat, retinere fas est, eidem propria bona possidenti stipendium accipere nefas non est. Non enim minùs Ecclesia ei alimenta pro labore, quem ei impendit, debet, quàm si inopia laboraret.
units.tr: ...deprives no one of lawful goods at all: it does not take away earthly things from one who gives heavenly ones. Moreover, the minister of the Church, just like others, and indeed more so, both may and ought to use rightly the goods lawfully his own, since he must be a type for the flock. The Apostolic Canon, the fortieth so called, is clear on this point: "Let it be manifest which are the private property of bishops and which are the Lord's (belonging to the Church), so that a bishop, dying, may leave his own property to whom he wishes and as he wishes, and that it may not be intercepted under the pretext of Church property, when a bishop sometimes possesses a wife, relatives or slaves." If, then, it is lawful for a minister to keep what he possessed before, it is not wrong for him, while possessing his own goods, to receive a stipend as well. For the Church owes him maintenance for the labour he gives it no less than if he were suffering want.

units.la: XLV. Nequicquam verò Anabaptistæ & Brownistæ Ecclesiis nostris, stipendia ministrorum ex reditibus & stipendiis, quæ sub Papatus tenebris sacrificuli aliíque clerici Papales, subinde etiam malis artibus quæsita & parta acceperunt, definientibus nescio quam dicam conscribunt. Nam ejusmodi bona sicut abusus polluit, ita & pius & rectus usus sanctificat. Impurum fuit Madianitarum, hominum infidelium aurum & argentum tum, cùm ipsi suo more his uterentur, quia homines impuri & infideles contra verbum Dei iis abutebantur. Impura fuit corona Regis Ammonitarum propter Ammonitas impuros ea utentes. Sed purificatum est aurum & argentum Madianitarum, quando illud ad sanctiorem usum Moses transtulit, Num. XXXI. 22. 50. Et Ammonitica corona sanctificata est, quando David sibi eam imposuit, adeóque ea sanctè usus est, 2. Sam. XII. 30. Quæ exempla pium earum opum, quæ primitus impiè quæsitæ, & abusu maculatæ sunt, usum vindicant. Tum bona illa Ecclesiæ primitus donata cùm sint, satis constat, donationem legitimum modum transferendi dominii esse. Neque adeò exactio decimarum etiam sic Ecclesiæ & ejus ministris donatarum iniqua censeri debet. Ac licèt nonnulli per communem seculi errorem, & circumventionem etiam ad donandum inducti sunt, tamen nec de omnibus id probari potest; & si quid in prima origine vitii intercessit, res ipsa non ideo sic tota vitii labem contraxit, ut effectus juris nullos habere potuerit. Multa enim primò ἀπαξλως fiunt, quæ per sequentem consensum & approbationem convalescunt. Est autem hic consensus communitatis tum politicæ, tum Ecclesiasticæ. Accedit diuturna præscriptio, & consensus primorum & sequentium hæredum, qui donationem ipsam amplius confirmat. Sed manifestum etiam est, collegia & Ecclesias, præsertim vetustiores, institutas esse à Regibus, Principibus & hominibus privatis ad ministerium Ecclesiæ in Sermone & Sacramentis, non autem ullius abusus causa, quæ salva veritate inter ea, quæ idolis immolata sunt, numerari non possunt. Licèt enim temporis progressu propter publicum errorem ad abusum conversæ sint, nunc tamen reformatæ, & antiquo usui restitutæ, errorem & abusum subrepentem exuerunt.
units.tr: XLV. The Anabaptists and Brownists write in vain against our churches, drawing up a kind of rule that the stipends of ministers may not be paid from the revenues and endowments which priests and other Papal clergy received under the darkness of the Papacy, some of them acquired and held by wicked arts. For such goods are polluted by abuse, but are sanctified by a pious and right use. The gold and silver of the Midianites was unclean while those unbelieving men used it in their own way, because those impure and unbelieving men misused it against the Word of God. The crown of the king of the Ammonites was unclean because the impure Ammonites used it. But the gold and silver of the Midianites was purified when Moses turned it to a holier use (Num. 31:22, 50), and the Ammonite crown was sanctified when David placed it upon himself and used it holily (2 Sam. 12:30). These examples vindicate the pious use of those riches which were first acquired impiously and stained by abuse. Since those goods were first given to the Church, it is quite clear that donation is a lawful way of transferring ownership. Nor, for that reason, should the exaction of tithes, which have likewise been given to the Church and its ministers, be judged unjust. And although some were led to give by the common error of the age and by deception, this cannot be proven of all; and if some fault crept in at the first origin, the thing itself has not been so wholly stained by the blot of fault that it could have no legal effect. For many things done at first wrongly are made valid by the subsequent consent and approval. This consent is that of the community, both civil and ecclesiastical. Add long prescription, and the consent of the first and later heirs, which confirms the donation still further. But it is also manifest that colleges and churches, especially the older ones, were established by kings, princes and private persons for the ministry of the Church in preaching and the sacraments, and not for the sake of any abuse, which cannot be counted, with the truth preserved, among those things which were offered to idols. For although in the course of time, through public error, they were turned to abuse, now, reformed and restored to their ancient use, they have cast off the error and the abuse that had crept in.

units.la: Rectè autem Augustinus epistol. 153. ad Publ. observavit, opibus à gentili idololatria ad Dei cultum translatis idem accidere, quod hominibus, qui antea per infidelitatem impuri fide sic sanctificantur, ut immaculati jam & puri sint.
units.tr: Augustine rightly observed in letter 153 to Publicola that when riches are transferred from gentile idolatry to the worship of God, the same thing happens as with men who, once impure through unbelief, are so sanctified by faith that they are now spotless and pure.

units.la: XLVI. Hactenus de Ecclesiæ Pastoribus. Iis in regimine Ecclesiæ πρεσβύτεροι Presbyteri, seu Seniores, à præstantia non tam ætatis, quàm processus in doctrina & vita Christiana sic dicti, adjunguntur. Qui Seniores angustiùs etiam hic dicuntur illi, qui non docent, sed gubernant tamen, & habenas Ecclesiæ tractant. Sunt enim Presbyteri, seu Seniores tales viri pii & graves, ex coetu Ecclesiæ delecti, & Pastoribus adjuncti, ut in regendo populo, parte oneris in se recepta, eos sublevent, & tanquam vigiles in Ecclesiastica specula constituti pro grege & ipsi excubent, singularúmque ovium defectus & profectus notent. Jussit Christus fratrem ὀνομαζόμενον offendentem alium, & correptionem ejus spernentem, corripi secunda vice duobus vel tribus assumptis. Si non audiat te, inquit, assume tecum adhuc unum aut duos, Matth. XVIII. 16. qui scilicet testes fiant tum elenchi, seu demonstrationis factæ, tum inobedientiæ, & per suam quoque ἐλεγξιν proximum convertere studeant. Hic potestas Seniorum, seu Presbyterii fundatur. Nam si unus vel duo prudentiores possunt advocari, possunt etiam rectores constitui ab Ecclesia, & secundum præceptum Christi constituti ad regendam Ecclesiam, adiri & advocari, ut communi elencho disciplinam continuent, & conversionem promoveant. Iisdem Christus injungit, ut, peccatore etiam secundam hanc correptionem spernente, dicant Ecclesiæ v. 17. hoc est, illis, qui Ecclesiæ gubernandæ præsunt, & per eos, si necessitas postulet, universæ fraternitati. De iisdem passim S. Paulus loquitur. Habentes charismata secundum gratiam, &c. sive ministerium in ministrando; sive docens in docendo, sive adhortans in adhortando; qui impertitur in simplicitate; ὁ προϊστάμενος, qui præest in studio, Rom. XII. 7. 8. Ubi voce προϊστάμενος seu ejus, qui præest, ante alios stat, & se pro aliis sistit, aliorum causam defendit tanquam patronus, 1. Tim. III. 4. 5. 12. functio à διακονία ministerio & prophetandi atque docendi munere distincta notatur, de quo alibi. Rogamus vos, fratres, ut cognoscatis eos, qui laborant in vobis καὶ προϊστανμένους ὑμῖν & præsunt vobis in Domino, & vos hortantur, 1. Thess. V. 12. Neque enim Apostolus Magistratuum προστασίαν intelligit, utpote quæ inter charismata non numeratur. Alibi S. Paulus Seniorum hanc functionem κυβερνήσεως gubernationis nomine exprimit. Alios dedit κυβερνήσεις gubernationes, 1. Corinth. XII. 28. quos à διδασκάλοις iis qui docent, distinguit. Cùm enim gubernatio Ecclesiæ perpetuò necessaria sit, & Christus eum in finem Ecclesiæ charismata ordinaria & extraordinaria (perinde uti prophetiæ & doctrinæ) contulerit, necesse est, etiam ordinarium gubernationis munus, huic charismati analogicè respondens institutum fuerit. Sed diserte etiam S. Paulus duo Presbyterorum genera distinguit, sic ad Timotheum scribens: Οἱ καλῶς προεστῶτες πρεσβύτεροι διπλῆς τιμῆς ἀξιούσθωσαν, μάλιστα μάλισα οἱ κοπιῶντες ἐν λόγῳ καὶ διδασκαλίᾳ. Qui bene præsunt, Presbyteri, duplici honore afficiuntur, maxime qui laborant in sermone & doctrina, 1. Tim. V. 17. Alii ergo Presbyteri seu Seniores in sermone & doctrina laborant, alii non. Nam quòd non Seniores, sed laborantes in verbo & doctrina diligentiùs & majore cum studio, à laborantibus in eodem verbo, sed indiligentiùs & minore cum studio, distingui, nonnulli regerunt, dilutum profectò est, quia qui verbum non diligenter & fideliter loquuntur, nec sunt in numero τῶν καλῶς προεστώτων eorum, qui bene præsunt, nec πλεῖ honorem etiam simplicem, nedum duplicem merentur. Neque rectius Remonstrantes per κοπιῶντας laborantes in sermone & doctrina eos, qui docendi provinciam magno cum labore, fatigatione & docendi cura, propter adversarios magnos, & res gravioris momenti, sustinent, interpretantur. Nam non κοπᾶν laborare in universum de ministerio presbyterorum seu ἐπισκόπων usurpari solet, neque ea simpliciter posita gradus ministerii eminentior significatur. Unde S. Paulus eosdem προεστῶτας qui præsunt, & κοπιῶντας laborantes, 1. Thess. V. 12. & συνεργοῦντας cooperantes, & κοπιῶντας laborantes, 1. Cor. XVI. 16. eosdem facit. Non ergo κοπᾶν laborare gradum, modum, vel mensuram, sed rem & laborem specificè notat. Gradus verò aliis vocibus indicatur, velut περισσότερον abundantius, 1. Cor. XV. 10. πλεῖα plus, Rom. XVI. 12. & cum addita voce μόχθῳ fatigationis, 2. Cor. XI. 27. 1. Thess. II. 9. Sed & absurda explicatio ea est, quia sic S. Paulus ministerium eorum Presbyterorum, qui bene præsunt & duplici honore digni sunt, à κόπῳ labore absolveret; cùm tamen ministerio omni labor tam proprius sit, quàm eclipsis lunæ est. Par eorum detorsio est, qui vocem μάλισα negant distinguere Presbyteros; & eam non reddunt inprimis, præsertim, potissimùm, maximè; sed plurimum, multum, valde: sic enim dicendum fuerat, μάλισα κοπιῶντες, seu οἱ μάλισα κοπιῶντες, non μάλισα οἱ κοπιῶντες, uti omnibus liquet. Neque illud obstat, quòd in Presbytero eo, qui bene præest, perinde ut in Episcopo τὸ διδακτικὸν docendi peritia requiritur. Licèt enim Seniores ejusmodi in verbo & doctrina non laborent, officio tamen Seniorum defungi nequeunt, nisi & alios, saltem privatim erudire & de officio admonere possint. Nam ad officium ejus pertinet ἐλέγχειν reprehendere, Matth. XVIII. 16. & ἐπιτιμᾶν corripere, 2. Cor. II. 6. Quæ sine doctrina & demonstratione ex verbo Dei fieri non possunt. Argutior etiam quàm verior adversus Seniores in verbo & doctrina non laborantes Blondelli & aliorum ratiocinatio est, quòd S. Paulus ipse duplicem honorem iis, qui bene præsunt, debitum, de honore stipendii sive salarii explicet, subjiciens, v. 18. Dicit enim Scriptura: Bovem triturantem non capistrabis; & : Dignus est operarius mercede sua. Atqui, inquiunt illi, Senioribus non docentibus stipendia nulla exhibentur. Sed annon saltem illi, qui inopes sunt, & munere seniorum cum dispendio rei familiaris defunguntur, & perpetui sunt, digni sunt, qui stipendiis honorentur? Annon iisdem Apostolorum ætate stipendia ab Ecclesia decerni, imò & solvi potuerunt? Et hodiéque consultò abstinent illi, qui provinciam illam ad breve tempus suscipiunt, & aliorum mox in humeros devolvunt, saltem eam obeuntes nullum rei familiaris detrimentum patiuntur. Accedit, quòd Apostolis etiam Presbyteri conjunguntur. Congregati sunt Apostoli, καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι & Presbyteri, ut viderent de re ista, Actor. XV. 6. Tunc visum est Apostolis & Presbyteris, & toti Ecclesiæ, ibid. v. 22. Tradiderunt iis custodienda decreta Apostolorum & Presbyterorum in Hierusalem, cap. XVI. 4. Nam quòd Presbyteros ejusmodi fuisse docentes, non gubernantes duntaxat, eò quòd ποιμαίνειν pascere, cap. XX. 28. & παρακαλεῖν ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ adhortari in doctrina sana, & contradicentes redarguere, Tit. I. 5. 9. jubentur, contendunt, frivolum certè est. Nam & Seniores gubernantes quodammodo pascunt, imò etiam docent, & errantes redarguunt, licèt verbum non prædicent: & Presbyterorum nomine collegia ex verbi ministris & Senioribus conflata intelligi nihil vetat; licèt non sint προεστῶτες ἐν λόγῳ, seu tales, qui in verbo præsunt, & ministerio verbi adhærent, Act. VI. 4. Quomodo etiam præfecti Regis Josaphati una cum Sacerdotibus & Levitis per civitates Judæ docuisse, 2. Paral. XVII. 7. 9. dicuntur. Sunt tales διδακτικοί ad docendum idonei, at non διδάσκαλοι doctores publici, quia ad publicè docendum vocati non sunt. Denique vetus Ecclesia istum laicorum presbyteratum easdem ob causas constanter, & maximo cum ædificationis fructu retinuit, ut quod de Conciliis nonnemo dixit, de hoc ordine pronuntiari possit, Seniorum saluberrimam semper in Ecclesia authoritatem fuisse, donec eam Antichristus oppressit, quod plurimus Blondellus de jure plebis in Regimine Ecclesiastico.
units.tr: XLVI. So much concerning the pastors of the Church. In the government of the Church, the elders (presbyteroi, or seniors) are joined to them; they are so called from the eminence not so much of age as of advancement in Christian doctrine and life. Those who are more narrowly called seniors here are not those who teach, but who nevertheless govern and hold the reins of the Church. For such elders or seniors are pious and grave men, chosen from the body of the Church and joined to the pastors, so that, having taken on a part of the burden, they may assist them in ruling the people, and, set up as watchmen on the Church's watchtower, keep vigil with them for the flock and mark the faults and progress of the individual sheep. Christ commanded that a brother who offends another, and despises his correction, be corrected a second time with two or three taken along: If he will not hear you, he says, take with you one or two more (Matt. 18:16), who will of course be witnesses both of the reproof, or demonstration, made, and of the disobedience, and who are also to strive to convert the neighbour by their own reproof. Here the power of the seniors, or of the presbytery, is founded. For if one or two wiser men can be called in, there can also be rulers appointed by the Church, and, constituted for governing the Church according to Christ's precept, approached and called upon, so that by a common reproof they may maintain discipline and promote conversion. Christ also enjoins that if the sinner despises even this second correction, they should tell it to the Church (v. 17), that is, to those who preside over the governing of the Church, and through them, if necessity requires, to the whole brotherhood. St Paul speaks of these men in many places: Having gifts differing according to the grace given to us, whether ministry, let us wait on our ministering; or he that teaches, on teaching; or he that exhorts, on exhortation; he that gives, with simplicity; he that rules [ho proistamenos], with diligence (Rom. 12:6–8). Here the word proistamenos, that is, one who stands before others, presents himself on behalf of others, and defends their cause as a patron, denotes (see 1 Tim. 3:4, 5, 12) a function distinct from the ministry of service (diakonia) and from the office of prophesying and teaching, of which elsewhere. We ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who labour among you and rule [proistamenous] over you in the Lord, and admonish you (1 Thess. 5:12). For the Apostle does not mean the presiding (prostasia) of magistrates, since that is not counted among the gifts. Elsewhere St Paul expresses this function of the seniors by the name of governing [kybernēseis]: He has set some in the Church as apostles, prophets, teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helps, governments [kybernēseis] (1 Cor. 12:28), which he distinguishes from those who teach. For since the government of the Church is always necessary, and Christ bestowed the ordinary and extraordinary gifts of the Church for this very end (just as prophecy and doctrine), it is necessary that an ordinary office of government, answering analogously to this gift, also was instituted. But St Paul also expressly distinguishes two kinds of presbyters, writing thus to Timothy: Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in word and doctrine (1 Tim. 5:17). Some elders, then, labour in word and doctrine, and others do not. As for the objection that the words here refer not to seniors but to those labouring in the word and doctrine more diligently and with greater zeal, as distinct from those labouring in the same word but more carelessly and with less zeal, this is plainly weak; for those who do not speak the word diligently and faithfully are neither among those who rule well, nor do they deserve even a simple honour, much less a double one. Nor do the Remonstrants interpret laborantes (labouring) more rightly as meaning those who undertake the office of teaching with great toil, exhaustion and care for teaching, on account of great adversaries and matters of weightier moment. For kopiān (to labour) is not usually applied in general to the ministry of the presbyters or bishops, and when it is put without qualification it does not signify a higher grade of ministry. Hence St Paul makes the same men both proistamenoi, those who rule, and kopiōntes, those who labour (1 Thess. 5:12), and synergountes, those who co-operate, and kopiōntes, those who labour (1 Cor. 16:16). Therefore kopiān does not denote a grade, a mode or a measure, but the thing and the labour itself specifically. Degrees are indicated rather by other words, such as perissoteron, abundantius (1 Cor. 15:10), pleia, plus (Rom. 16:12), and when the word mochthō, fatigation, is added (2 Cor. 11:27; 1 Thess. 2:9). Moreover that explanation is absurd, because it would thus free the ministry of those presbyters who rule well and are worthy of double honour from labour, whereas labour is as proper to every ministry as an eclipse is to the moon. Equally mistaken is the view of those who deny that the word mālista distinguishes the presbyters, and do not render it especially, particularly, chiefly, most of all, but very much, greatly, exceedingly; for it would have had to be said mālista kopiōntes, or hoi mālista kopiōntes, not mālista hoi kopiōntes, as is plain to all. Nor is there any obstacle in the fact that in the presbyter who rules well, just as in the bishop, skill in teaching (to didaktikon) is required. For although such seniors do not labour in word and doctrine, they cannot discharge the office of seniors unless they are also able to instruct others, at least in private, and to admonish them about their duty. For it belongs to their office to reprove (Matt. 18:16) and to rebuke (2 Cor. 2:6), which cannot be done without doctrine and demonstration from the Word of God. The argument of Blondel and others against the seniors who do not labour in word and doctrine is more subtle than true, namely that St Paul himself explains the double honour due to those who rule well as the honour of stipend or salary, adding in v. 18: For the Scripture says: You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the corn; and: The labourer is worthy of his wage. But, they say, no stipends are paid to seniors who do not teach. Yet are not those who are poor, and who discharge the office of seniors at the cost of their own household affairs and are perpetual in it, at least worthy to be honoured with stipends? Could not stipends be decreed, and indeed paid, by the Church in the time of the Apostles itself? And even today those who take up that office for a short time and soon hand it on to the shoulders of others abstain on purpose; and those who discharge it, at least, suffer no harm to their household affairs. Besides, the presbyters are also joined with the Apostles: The apostles and the elders [presbyteroi] gathered together to consider this matter (Acts 15:6). Then it seemed good to the apostles and elders, and to the whole Church (ibid. v. 22). They delivered to them the decrees of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem to keep (Acts 16:4). For the contention that such presbyters taught and did not merely govern, because they are commanded to shepherd (Acts 20:28) and to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict (Tit. 1:5, 9), is certainly frivolous. For seniors who govern also in some measure shepherd, indeed also teach, and refute those who err, although they do not preach the word; and nothing prevents the name of presbyters from being understood as applying to bodies made up of ministers of the Word and seniors, even though they are not proistamenoi en logō, that is, men who preside in the word and devote themselves to the ministry of the word (Acts 6:4). In the same way, the prefects of King Jehoshaphat are said to have taught throughout the cities of Judah together with the priests and Levites (2 Chron. 17:7, 9). Such men are didaktikoi, fit for teaching, but not public teachers (didaskaloi), because they have not been called to teach publicly. Finally, the ancient Church retained this lay presbyterate constantly, for the same reasons and with the greatest fruit of edification; so that what someone has said of the councils may be said of this order: The authority of the seniors has always been most salutary in the Church, until Antichrist oppressed it, as the very learned Blondel says in his work On the right of the people in ecclesiastical government.

units.la: XLVII.
units.tr: XLVII.

units.la: Sed ordo ille Seniorum laicorum una cum Pastoribus docentibus Ecclesiam gubernantium, utpote cum Monarchia Papæ è diametro pugnans, Hierarchicis ἀλγησῶν τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν sudes in oculis est; & à Remonstrantibus etiam præsultore Grotio, aliisque, ceu novitium εὕρημα imò phantasticum Calvini commentum, uti famosus ille, sed infelici catastrophe sua miserandus Cantuariensium Præsul Guil. Laudus appellare non dubitavit: mirè exagitant. Et nominum quidem, Seniorum, Consistorii, Senatus Ecclesiastici novitatem ante omnia exprobrant. Quasi non πρεσβυτέρων & πρεσβυτερίς; quod γερουσίαν seu senatum seniorum notat; nomina passim extent. Sed sufficit nobis rei ipsius institutio ab ipso Christo facta, & ab Apostolis retenta, ut fidem jam fecimus. Neque moramur dicterium, quòd laici sint. Præterquam quod pertinere ad λαὸν Θεοῦ populum Dei, 1. Petr. II. 10. adéoque λαικὸν laicum esse, nemini pudendum est, etiam ipsi Ecclesiastici ex laicis eliguntur, & electi demum laici esse desinunt. Hi verò licèt functioni suæ seculares vocationem conjungant, non ideo tamen personæ publicæ & Ecclesiæ ministri quodammodo esse desinunt magis quàm Diaconi, olim τῆς βιωτικῆς Ecclesiæ præfecti. Etiam Episcopos, Cardinales, Abbates, Canonicos, Sacerdotes, &c. sine ulla necessitate munere cancellarii, consiliarii, notarii, thesaurarii, archithalasii, militiæ ducis, &c. defundefunctos plurimos reperire est. Simile convitium annalium, biennalium, triennalium est. Nam alicubi etiam perpetui sunt; & temporis haec circumstantia singulares ob causas, inprimis dominationis vitationem, delecta rem ipsam mutare non potest. Possunt enim esse חמן ואנש homines per vices sibi succedentes, Ezech. XXXIX. 14. Neque enim etiam Priorum in conventibus legatorum a latere & similium Papismi satellitum munia perpetua sunt. Neque jure ceu simplices, idiotae, ignorantes ab iisdem traducuntur. Aliud enim munus est, ad quod illi vocantur, & quod eos idiotas vel simplices esse non finit; aliud persona, cui munus bene vel male applicatur. Neque desunt plurimi, qui rerum Divinarum cognitione Pontifices ipsos pluribus post se parasangis relinquant. Merum vero seculi typhum, non Evangelii spiritum redolet, quod eos, ceu homines de foece vulgi, sartores, tonsores, nautas laniones, coquos rusticos, quibus vix inter remiges in transtris aut sentina locus esset, ludibrio exponere conantur illi, qui paupertatem vovent, & simplicitatem ubique crepant. Videte vocationem vestram, fratres, quod non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, nobiles; sed stulta mundi elegit Deus, ut sapientes confundat, 1. Cor. I. 26. Neque id honorificum satis animalibus illis gloriae est, quod a vilissimis & infimi subsellii hominibus in rerum Divinarum & spiritualium notitia atque pietate superantur. Sed anarchiam sic in Ecclesiam invehi quiritantur; plane ἀναρχίας, cum nullibi fere magis doctrinae puritas, morum integritas, Evangelii incrementum, disciplinae ἀκρίβεια, schismatum coercitio vigeat, quam ubi ordo & authoritas Presbyteriorum sarta & tecta est. Et impie haec omnia institutioni Divinae Seniorum objiciuntur, quia ex ea nil nisi salutaria & utilia omnia sperari atque expectari possunt. Ecclesia enim Dei non humanis rationibus, vel carnali fastu, sed Divinis consiliis regitur. Denique nec dissimilis quoad Seniores ejusmodi Ecclesiarum Protestantium usus ipsum Seniorum ordinem labefactat. Nam Seniores quidem, seu laicos Ecclesiam una cum Pastoribus regentes omnes illae admittunt: sed aliae ex Magistratu solo, aliae ex populo, vel utroque illos deligunt. Quae diversitas a diversa Ecclesiam reformantium conditione provenit. Quotquot enim Reges, Electores, Principes, Magistratus per Germaniam, Helvetiam, Angliam, Sveciam & Daniam adversus invectas a seculis aliquot in Christianum orbem doctrinae & disciplinae sacrae corruptelas una cum Pastoribus suis protestari coacti sunt, strenuos se tam regiminis quam doctrinae vindices, constitutis ubique Senatibus Ecclesiasticis, praestiterunt, & spartam suam pro virili ornarunt. Nemo tamen eorum, quas in universo Ecclesiae regimine partes reliqua fraternitas obire ex officio teneretur, cogitavit, vel cogitandum putavit. Cum enim illam ab omni consiliorum & potestatis participatione jam pridem depulsam, sui in Christiana societate juris prorsus immemorem, nulla sui cura tangi viderent, de se solis anxii, quid sui proprie officii esset, animo suo volutarunt, & ipso opere exprimere conati sunt, quin & utcunque
units.tr: But that order of lay elders, together with the pastors who teach, governing the Church, since it fights head-on against the monarchy of the Pope, is a thorn in the Hierarchs' eyes [ἀλγησῶν τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν]. The Remonstrants, with Grotius as their leader and others, violently attack it, and the famous but unhappily ended Archbishop of Canterbury, William Laud, did not hesitate to call it a novel discovery [εὕρημα], indeed a fanciful invention of Calvin. Above all they object to the novelty of the names elders, consistory, ecclesiastical senate. As if the terms presbyters and presbytery were not Greek, meaning the senate or gerousia of elders [γερουσίαν]; the names are found everywhere. But for us the institution of the thing itself, made by Christ himself and retained by the Apostles, is sufficient, as we have already shown. Nor do we dwell on the jibe that they are laymen. Apart from the fact that to belong to the people of God [λαὸν Θεοῦ], 1 Peter 2:10, and so to be lay [λαικὸν], is nothing to be ashamed of, even ecclesiastics are chosen from among the laity, and once chosen they cease to be laymen. Although these men combine a secular calling with their office, they no more cease for that reason to be public persons and ministers of the Church than do deacons, who were once in charge of the Church's temporal affairs [τῆς βιωτικῆς Ecclesiæ]. One may also find very many bishops, cardinals, abbots, canons, priests, and so on, who without any necessity have held the offices of chancellor, counsellor, notary, treasurer, archithalassus, commander of an army, and so on. The same objection is made to annual, biennial, and triennial office. For in some places these are even permanent; and this feature of time, which can be chosen for particular reasons, above all to avoid domination, cannot change the thing itself. For there may be men who succeed one another in turn [חמן ואנש], Ezek. 39:14. Nor are the duties of the legates who sit at the side of the Priors in their assemblies, or of similar satellites of Popery, permanent. Nor are they rightly disparaged by these men as simple, unlearned, ignorant. For one thing is the office to which they are called, which does not allow them to be simple or unlearned; another is the person to whom the office is applied, well or badly. Nor are there lacking many men who, in knowledge of divine things, leave the Pontiffs themselves far behind. It is a pure whiff of worldly arrogance, and not the spirit of the Gospel, that those who vow poverty and everywhere boast of simplicity try to expose these men, as if they were dregs of the common people, tailors, barbers, sailors, butchers, rustic cooks, who could scarcely find a place among the oarsmen on the benches or in the bilge. Consider your calling, brethren, that not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble are called; but God has chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, 1 Cor. 1:26. Nor is it much of an honour to those men of glory that they are surpassed in knowledge of divine and spiritual things and in piety by people of the humblest and lowest rank.
