But they complain that anarchy is thus being introduced into the Church; yet it is plainly no anarchy, since nowhere almost does purity of doctrine, integrity of morals, growth of the Gospel, exactness of discipline, and restraint of schisms flourish more than where the order and authority of the presbyteries are preserved intact. And these things are impiously objected against the divine institution of elders, when from it nothing but wholesome and useful results can be hoped for and expected. For the Church of God is governed not by human reasons or carnal pride but by divine counsels. Finally, the practice of the various Protestant Churches regarding such elders is not so different as to weaken the order of the elders itself. For all of them admit elders, that is, laymen who govern the Church together with the pastors; but some choose them from the magistracy alone, others from the people, or from both. This difference arises from the differing condition of the churches that reformed themselves. For all the kings, electors, princes, and magistrates throughout Germany, Helvetia, England, Sweden, and Denmark, who were compelled to protest, together with their pastors, against the corruptions of sacred doctrine and discipline that had crept into the Christian world over several past centuries, showed themselves vigorous defenders both of order and of doctrine, by establishing ecclesiastical senates everywhere, and adorned their Sparta, as far as each could, with their own efforts. Yet none of them thought, or thought it right to think, about those parts in the whole governance of the Church which the rest of the brotherhood was bound by duty to perform. For since they saw that the brotherhood had long since been thrust out from every share in counsel and power, and had quite forgotten its own right in Christian society, and was touched by no concern for itself, they, anxious only about themselves, turned over in their minds what belonged to their own proper office, and tried to express it in action; and even somehow

units.la: seniorum plebis defectum aliis rationibus supleverunt, uti quidem apud nos in urbe judicia matrimonialia, quorum partem etiam Ecclesiastici faciunt, & hinc inde in pagis pastoribus adjuncti plebeji nonnulli defectum illum quodammodo resarciunt. Sed dispar Reformatorum Galliae, Scotiae & Belgii conditio fuit. Illos enim cum Praesulum suorum paterno ductu, nec non Regum & Magistratuum patrocinio destitutos vis major urgeret, & eos, ne causam Dei proderent, contra torrentem niti necesse esset, una iis ex ingruentibus undique malis emergendi spes, restituta in integrum Christiana plebe, residua fuit. Qui proin ad animum sibi Ecclesiae Christianae initia, quibus ipsi etiam Apostoli nihil sine senioribus & Ecclesia consultum duxerunt, &, juxta illud Cypriani Epist. 6. nihil privata sententia sine consensu plebis gesserunt, & singula cum plebe expensa, moderatione librarunt, revocarunt, illis non impeditis, aliunde fraternitatem ad regiminis participationem admittere, & delectorum seniorum plebis dignitatem redintegrare placuit.
units.tr: they made up for the lack of elders from the people by other means, as indeed among us in the city the matrimonial courts, part of which the ecclesiastics also make up, and here and there in the villages some common men joined to the pastors in some way make good that lack. But the condition of the Reformers in France, Scotland, and the Low Countries was different. For when they were deprived of the paternal guidance of their prelates, and likewise of the patronage of kings and magistrates, and superior force pressed them, and it was necessary for them to struggle against the torrent lest they betray the cause of God, the one hope of emerging from the evils that threatened on all sides remained: that the Christian people, restored to its integrity, should be taken back. They therefore thought fit, calling to mind the beginnings of the Christian Church, in which even the Apostles did nothing without the elders and the Church, and, according to Cyprian's saying, Epist. 6, did nothing by private judgement without the consent of the people, and weighed each matter with the people, deciding by moderation, to recall the brotherhood to a share in governance by other means, without hindrance, and to restore the dignity of the chosen elders of the people.

units.la: XLVIII. Habuit etiam Ecclesia Judaica suos Presbyteros, Seniores, qui in cathedra Moisis sedentes populum rexerunt. Tunc egredientur Seniores & Judices tui, &c. Deut. XXI. 2. Exaltent eum in coetu populi & in cathedra senes laudent eum, Psal. CVII. 32. Quorum creberrima in N. T. mentio est, ut & τὰ πρεσβύτερα, Luc. XXII. 66. Actor. XXII. 5. De his supra etiam egimus. Sed aliud Sacerdotum & Seniorum in cathedra Mosis sedentium regimen fuit: aliud Presbyterorum Ecclesiae Christianae regimen est. Illi enim spectabant populum, cui lex Moisis impositia erat, & armati gladio fuerunt, & legibus suis legem instituturum Mosaicorum sapiebant, ut populus hac velut sepe legis a legis Divinae transgressione longius arceretur: denique secundum leges poenas transgressoribus legis irrogabant. Dispar Presbyterorum Christianorum ratio est, qui non spectant nisi eos, qui ipsis per nomen Christianorum, seu confessionem fidei in Christum, se associare volunt, ut ii in fide integri, & in vita irreprehensibiles sint, ut uno humero omnes Deum colant, Dei gloriam narrent, & sancta opera faciant; at de caetero non gladio corporali, sed solo spiritu-ali & oris; non coercitione carnis, sed demonstratione Spiritus; non privatione dominiorum, sed denuntiatione irae Dei, redarguitione & increpatione ad emendandos peccatores instituta aliquando cum supplicatione, 2. Cor. V. 20. & lachrymis Actor. XX. 31. utuntur, neque legibus sibi Ecclesiam subjiciunt. Qui si dominari in Ecclesia, leges conscientias obligantes ferre, Scripturam indemonstrabiliter interpretari, & jurisdictionem, qualem Pontificii exercent, & ipsi exercere, denique ad suum nomen atque authoritatem credentes alligare contenderent, missione, & institutione Dei ad facienda talia destituti, non audiri, sed rejici deberent. Ut vanus sit ille Seniorum, sive ex Magistratu, sive ex plebe delectorum ordinem oppugnantium metus sit, ne ab iis Ecclesia in ser-
units.tr: XLVIII. The Jewish Church also had its presbyters, elders, who ruled the people sitting in the seat of Moses. Then your elders and judges shall go out, etc., Deut. 21:2. Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people and praise him in the seat of the elders, Ps. 107:32. The mention of them in the New Testament is very frequent, and of the elders too, Luke 22:66; Acts 22:5. We have already discussed these above. But the government of the priests and elders sitting in the seat of Moses was one thing; the government of the presbyters of the Christian Church is another. For the former looked to the people upon whom the law of Moses had been imposed, and they were armed with the sword, and, savouring of the Mosaic law, they set up their own laws as a hedge of the law, so that the people might be kept further from transgressing the divine law by this, as it were, hedge of the law; finally, according to their laws they inflicted punishments on transgressors of the law. The method of the Christian presbyters is different: they look only to those who wish to associate themselves with them under the name of Christians, or by confession of faith in Christ, so that they may be sound in faith and blameless in life, that they may worship God with one shoulder, declare the glory of God, and do holy works; and otherwise they use not the corporal sword but only the spiritual sword of the mouth; not coercion of the flesh but demonstration of the Spirit; not deprivation of dominions but the announcement of the wrath of God, rebuke and reproof, instituted to correct sinners, sometimes with entreaty, 2 Cor. 5:20, and with tears, Acts 20:31; and they do not subject the Church to laws. But if they were to seek to rule in the Church, to enact laws binding consciences, to interpret Scripture without proof, and to exercise a jurisdiction such as the Papists exercise and as they themselves exercise, and finally to bind believers to their own name and authority, they would be destitute of the mission and institution of God for doing such things, and so should not be heard but rejected. So that fear is vain, that the Church might be reduced by such men, whether chosen from the magistracy or from the people, who oppose the order of elders, lest it be brought into servitude by them. In doing so, it is clear, the Pope does what he does: he turns the Kingdom of Christ into an earthly one, reduces it to servitude, and changes laws and times.

units.la: Et a Presbyterio Ecclesia Judaica distinguitur. servitutem redigatur. Quod Papam facere, dum Regnum Christi in terrenum convertit, servitutem reducit, legem & tempora mutat, facere manifestum est.
units.tr: And the Jewish Church is distinguished from the presbytery. ...is reduced to servitude. That the Pope does this, when he turns the kingdom of Christ into an earthly one, reduces it to servitude, and changes the law and the times, is plain.

units.la: XLIX. Officium Seniorum fere cum officio Pastorum convenit, nisi quòd in ministerio verbi & Sacramentorum non laborant. De cætero incumbit illis, ut vigilent pro toto cœtu, pro omnibus fratribus, & bonum eorum quærant, malum averruncare satagant. Sunt enim עברים μεταβαίνοντες transeuntes, Ezech. XXXIX. 14. qui per omnes transeunt, observaturi, quomodo quisque ambulet. Tum ipsorum est custodire ordinem, omnémque operam navare, ne is violetur & perturbetur; ut scilicet, qui ministerium acceperunt, eo recte & fideliter fungantur, Ecclesiæ, juventuti, ægrotis, pauperibus nulla in parte desint; & ut discipuli eos audiant, atque iis in nomine Christi loquentibus obediant; Prophetæ Prophetas non turbent, sed admoneri sinant, &, si cui revelatum aliquid fuerit, is revelationem suam in commune bonum sine perturbatione & συμφωνίας publica proferre non impediatur. Etiam vitæ & conversationi singulorum Ecclesiæ membrorum, atque ipsorum etiam Pastorum sic attendere eos par est, ut lapsos moneant, ad meliorem frugem revocare conentur, dissidia componant, & correptionem non tantum ut primores cœtus cum ipso cœtu exerceant, sed etiam eo modo, quo duos vel tres eam privatim exercere possunt, exerceant; denique si quid iis ab Ecclesia commissum sit, id ita faciant, ut fidelitatem suam omnium conscientiæ probent. Quarum functionum instrumenta sunt tum labor à charitate impositus, & cum patientia exantlatus; tum ἔλεγχος, seu admonitio per verbum, qui privatim incipiens definit in judicium Ecclesiæ, quo inobediens pro Ethnico & publicano habetur, Matth. XVIII. 17. &c. Atque talia facientes à nemine impediri possunt, dummodo ἀναγκασμὸς coactio, imperii usurpatio, plagarum inflictio, multarum indictio & ignominiæ atque infamiæ civilis irrogatio abstinent. Incentiva ad officii partes omnes fideliter & strenuè obeundas eadem fere sunt, quibus etiam Pastores docentes ad officium suum stimulari oportere, supra diximus. Denique quæ de Pastorum docentium vocatione & δοκιμασία supra diximus, ἀναλόγως etiam huc revocari possunt. Constitutis Presbyteris penes Pastorem Ecclesiæ & Seniores ipsos jus eos eligendi est; qua in re totius Ecclesiæ vicibus funguntur, cujus etiam & electionem ratam habere, vel irritam reddere. Eligendi sunt tum idonei, religionis Christianæ callentes & studiosi, vitæ inculpatæ testimonio ornati, παρρησίᾳ quadam, citra auræ popularis captationem, prudentia spirituali præditi, non rimarum pleni, nedum impetuosi, vel imperiosi, benefici quoque nec nimium speculatoribus curis districti; denique gravitate verendi: tum charitate & voluntate Deo & Ecclesiæ in negotio salutis animarum inserviendi, abundantes. Qui etiam quoad honorem & obedientiam perpetui esse debent; quoad functionem verò, ut perpetui sint, nec necesse, nec utile est, quia perpetuitas illa facilè in dominatum abit, & non omnibus
units.tr: XLIX. The office of the elders largely coincides with that of the ministers, except that they do not labour in the ministry of the Word and the sacraments. Otherwise it is their task to watch over the whole congregation and all the brothers, to seek their good and to strive to avert their harm. For they are "passers-by" [עברים; μεταβαίνοντες], who pass through among all, to observe how each one walks (Ezek. 39:14). It is therefore their duty to keep good order and to take every care that it is not violated or disturbed, so that those who have received the ministry discharge it rightly and faithfully, and that the Church, the young, the sick and the poor lack nothing on any side; that disciples hear them and obey them when they speak in the name of Christ; and that prophets do not disturb the prophets but allow themselves to be admonished. And if something has been revealed to anyone, he should not be hindered from bringing forward his revelation for the common good, without disorder and without public [συμφωνία] agreement. It is also right that they attend to the life and conduct of each member of the Church, and of the ministers themselves, so that they admonish the fallen, try to recall them to better conduct, settle quarrels, and exercise correction not only as leaders of the congregation before the whole congregation, but also in the way in which two or three can exercise it privately. Finally, whatever has been committed to them by the Church, they should so carry out that they prove their faithfulness to the conscience of all. The instruments of these functions are both the labour imposed by love and borne with patience, and reproof [ἔλεγχος], that is, admonition by the word, which begins privately and ends in the judgment of the Church, by which the disobedient is held as a heathen and a tax collector (Matt. 18:17, etc.). Those who do such things can be hindered by no one, provided they abstain from coercion [ἀναγκασμός], usurpation of authority, the infliction of blows, the imposition of fines, and the bringing of civil disgrace and infamy. The incentives to discharge all parts of the office faithfully and vigorously are almost the same as those by which we said above that the teaching ministers ought to be stirred up to their office. Finally, what we said above about the calling and the testing [δοκιμασία] of teaching ministers can be applied here by analogy. Once the elders have been appointed beside the minister of the Church, they themselves have the right to choose them; in this matter they act in place of the whole Church, and it is for them to ratify its choice or make it void. Those to be chosen are men who are fit, skilled and diligent in the Christian religion, adorned with the testimony of an blameless life, endowed with a certain boldness [παρρησία] without seeking popular favour, endowed with spiritual prudence, not full of cracks, let alone impetuous or domineering, also generous and not too tightly bound by anxious cares; and finally worthy of respect for their seriousness; abounding in love and in the willingness to serve God and the Church in the matter of the salvation of souls. These also ought to be permanent in respect of honour and obedience; but as to the function itself, it is neither necessary nor useful that they be permanent, because such permanence easily turns into domination, and not all

units.la: vacat. Sicut etiam multi ἀνὰ μέρος per vices possunt loqui, vel prophetare: ita multi ἀνὰ μέρος, ceu איש חמיר viri ἐνδελεχισμὸς (in quo stationum vicissitudo est) Ecclesiæ curatione fungi possunt, Ezech. XXXIX. 14. 1. Cor. XIV. 27. 30. 31. Possunt enim fratres unà coram Domino consistentes, sibi invicem per vices esse διάκονοι, διακονοι, ὑγούμενοι, præsides, ministri, ductores, sicut & docentium est non semper loqui, sed vicissim, si quid alii reveletur, audire, ibid.
units.tr: are free. Just as many can speak or prophesy in turn, so also many, in turn [ἀνὰ μέρος], like a "man of vigour" [איש חמיר] (in which there is a rotation of posts), can carry out the care of the Church (Ezek. 39:14; 1 Cor. 14:27, 30, 31). For brothers standing together before the Lord can take turns being deacons [διάκονοι], leaders [ὑγούμενοι], presidents, ministers and guides to one another, just as it is not always the task of teachers to speak, but in turn to listen when something is revealed to another (ibid.).

units.la: L. Sunt etiam in Ecclesia quidam διδάσκαλοι Doctores, qui Ecclesiæ non pascendo, sed docendo tantum ministrant. Dedit Christus quosdam Pastores & διδασκάλους doctores, Ephes. IV. 11. Ubi licet Pastores etiam Doctores esse non obscurè Apostolus innuat, quia pascere non potest, qui docere non potest, & ipsum docendi munus in munere pascendi includitur; tamen doctores quosdam non Pastores esse, non minùs etiam non obscurè innuitur; & rectè Calvinus aliíque sustinent. Pastores enim in Ecclesia, Doctores, non Pastores, in Schola docent. Eandem utrique doctrinam, sed aliter alióque in loco docent. De iisdem alibi S. Paulus. Habentes Prophetiam secundum conformitatem fidei; ὡς ὁ διδάσκων ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ sive docens in docendo hoc agat, doceat tantùm, demonstret, non imperet, nec ἐλεήμων & ἀκολουθοῦντες σκόπος sit, Rom. XII. 7. Suntque illi Doctores, quibus οἰκονομία & quasi villicatio hæc credita est, ut doctrinam sanam, quæ secundum pietatem est, sive prima fidei elementa catechumenis instillando, sive etiam καλὴν χρῆσιν καὶ προκαλοῦντας informatores Ecclesiæ & exhortatores, atque Pastores futuros, per demonstrationem veri Scripturæ sensus, & sermonem sapientiæ, seu expositionem doctrinæ, quæ secundum pietatem est, non sine ἑρμηνείᾳ γλωσσῶν interpretatione linguarum apud eos, quibus Deus loquitur ἐν ἑτερογλώσσοις sermone ipsis peregrino, velut Germanis Hebræo & Græco, 1. Cor. XIV. 21. Esaj. XXVIII. 11. formando & instituendo; sive errores veritati oppositos & mendacia, per demonstrationem veritatis, & convictionem falsitatis, atque ipsorum etiam errantium ἐπισφάλμων, refutando, tradant. Cujusmodi doctores Ecclesiæ apprime necessarii & utiles sunt, quia cùm sunt, qui præeant, & veritatem ad conscientiam proponant, tum facile est assentiri, & in gradu firmum stare, atque etiam in veritatis studio ζηλωτὴν zeloten fieri & proficere: ubi verò illi desunt, multis difficile est, se ex laqueis Sathanæ expedire, & per strophas τῶν ψευδολόγων non labefactari; Signum irae Dei est, si desint ejusmodi doctores, qui habeant ἀποκάλυψιν revelationem Spiritus, ut in bona conscientia & cum demonstratione veritatis loqui possint. Unde nec Christum Judæi receperunt, quia non habuerunt sermonem Dei in se manentem, Johan. cap. V. vers. 38. nescientes quis verborum Mosis & Prophetarum sensus esset.
units.tr: L. There are also in the Church some teachers [διδάσκαλοι], who minister not by feeding but by teaching only. Christ gave some ministers and teachers [διδασκάλους] (Eph. 4:11). Here the Apostle clearly hints that ministers are also teachers, since one who cannot teach cannot feed, and the very office of teaching is included in the office of feeding; yet it is no less clearly hinted that some teachers are not ministers, and Calvin and others rightly maintain this. For ministers teach in the Church as ministers; teachers, who are not ministers, teach in the school. Both teach the same doctrine, but in different ways and in different places. St Paul speaks of the same persons elsewhere: Having prophecy according to the proportion of faith; let the one who teaches [ὡς ὁ διδάσκων] attend to teaching, let him only teach and demonstrate, not command, and let him not be merciful and following the mark (Rom. 12:7). And those are the teachers to whom this stewardship and, as it were, household management has been entrusted: to hand on sound doctrine, which accords with godliness, either by instilling the first elements of the faith into catechumens, or also [καλὴν χρῆσιν καὶ προκαλοῦντας] by forming and instructing those who will be future informants, exhorters and ministers of the Church, through demonstrating the true sense of Scripture and through words of wisdom, that is, the exposition of doctrine which accords with godliness, not without interpretation of tongues [ἑρμηνεία γλωσσῶν] among those to whom God speaks in other tongues [ἐν ἑτερογλώσσοις], in a speech foreign to them, as for the Germans Hebrew and Greek (1 Cor. 14:21; Isa. 28:11); or else to hand on, by demonstrating the truth and convicting falsehood, and by refuting the errors opposed to truth and lies, and even the errors of those who err [ἐπισφάλμων]. Teachers of this kind are especially necessary and useful to the Church, because when there are those who go before and set the truth before the conscience, it is easy to assent, to stand firm in one's rank, and even to become a zealot [ζηλωτής] in the study of truth and to advance; but where they are lacking, it is hard for many to free themselves from the snares of Satan and not to be shaken by the wiles of the liars [ψευδολόγων]. It is a sign of God's wrath if there are no teachers of this kind who have the revelation [ἀποκάλυψις] of the Spirit, so that they can speak in a good conscience and with demonstration of the truth. Hence the Jews did not receive Christ either, because they did not have the word of God abiding in them (John 5:38), not knowing what the sense of the words of Moses and the prophets was.

units.la: LI. Doctorum munus semper in Ecclesia viguit. Nam in V. T. Prophetæ & Prophetarum filii; ac postremis temporibus סופרים Γραμματεῖς Scribæ, Νομικοί dicti munus illud exercuerunt. Qui peculiari etiam ritu creari svesveverunt. Et convenit nomen Διδασκάλων Doctoris cum titulo רבי Rabbi, qui illis peculiariter tribuebatur, qui legis Divinæ periti, eandem docendi alios aptitudinem habuerunt. Quales Doctores illi, in quorum medio Christus adolescens sedit, Luc. II. 46. Nicodemus, Joh. III. 10. Gamaliel, Actor. V. 34. & Antiocheni illi Διδασκαλοι Doctores, ibid. XIII. 1. fuerunt. Quorum munus non abolevit Christus dicens: Vos autem ne vocamini Rabbi, unus enim Doctor vester, Christus est. Neque vocamini καθηγηταὶ ductores, Matth. XXIII. 8. 10. Non enim illis verbis munus & titulus, Rabbi & ductoris atque doctoris magis quàm munus & titulus πατὴρ patris, vers. 9. damnatur: sed magistrale supercilium & fastus, aliaque paedagogorum crimina notantur, nisi quod etiam titulus ille רב quatenus proprie notat majorem, adeóque Dominum fidei, non docentem ex Scripturis, sed dictantem ex cerebro, & velut cum authoritate, sine demonstratione; quo sensu fere Judæi axiomate hoc Rabbi post schismata inter Scholas Schammai & Hillelis exorta, insolescere coeperunt, parùm probi commatis est. Alioquin etiam S. Paulus Διδασκαλὸς ἐθνῶν doctor gentium, 1. Tim. II. 7. cluet. Et Timotheo S. Paulus in mandatis dedit: Quæ à me audivisti per multos testes, hæc commenda fidelibus hominibus, qui ἱκανοὶ ἔσονται ἑτέρας διδάξαι idonei erunt, ut alios etiam doceant, 2. Tim. II. 2. innuens, & nunquam deesse oportere, qui alios doceant, & ad hoc, ut alios doceant, præparentur: & docenda esse non alia, quàm quæ Apostoli tradiderunt, & non aliam Theologiam, quàm quæ, quia non sit publici usus, scholastica dicitur. Celebratur autem inde ab Ecclesiæ Christianæ exordio hoc nomine Ecclesia Alexandrina, quæ Marci Evangelistæ, uti fertur, consilio instituta suos Catechetas & doctores insignes, Pantænum, Clementem, Alexandrinum, Originem, Tryphonem, Hierarcham, Dionysium, Anatolium, Theonem, Athanasium, &c. habuit. Deinceps salutari consilio pallim ab Episcopis, Augustino, Basilio, aliis instituta sunt Monasteria, quæ non aliud quàm Theologica quædam ascéteria, atque doctrinæ multifariæ phrontisteria, quæ docendo vel ipsi Episcopi, vel alii Doctores iis praefecti rexerunt; ex quibus, velut ex equo Trojano Ecclesiarum Pastores & Doctores celeberrimi provenerunt. Sed sic tempore procedente institutum isthoc sanctissimum degeneravit, ut suo tempore Petrus Cluniacensis lib. IV. ep. 2. Monasteria Sathanæ Synagogas appellare non erubuerit. Estque omnis res literaria usque adeò ex Monasteriis profligata, ut Monachorum stupiditas plus quàm asinina proverbio locum dederit: Monacho indoctior, quod in illiteratos & stupidos dici suevit. Factique sunt ex Monasteriis carceres & carnificinæ miserrimæ conscientiarum & omnium errorum, idololatriæ, superstitionis, ventris & scelerum officinæ, in quibus omne religionis, pietatis, veritatis & castitatis studium conculcatum est. Etiam Imperatores Christiani, inprimis Theodosius & Carolus M. Academiis pallim erectis, iisdem doctores praefecerunt. Sed ne Papæ Regno obessent, Pontifices non illas, Juliani apostatæ exemplo clauserunt, sed
units.tr: LI. The office of teacher has always flourished in the Church. For in the Old Testament the prophets and the sons of the prophets, and in later times those called scribes [סופרים; γραμματεῖς] and lawyers [νομικοί], exercised that office. These men were accustomed to be created with a peculiar rite. And the name teacher [διδάσκαλος] agrees with the title rabbi [רבי], which was attributed especially to those who, being skilled in the divine law, had the same aptitude for teaching others. Such were the teachers in whose midst the boy Christ sat (Luke 2:46), Nicodemus (John 3:10), Gamaliel (Acts 5:34), and the teachers [διδάσκαλοι] of Antioch (ibid. 13:1). Christ did not abolish this office when he said: But you, do not be called Rabbi; for one is your teacher, Christ. Nor be called guides [καθηγηταί] (Matt. 23:8, 10). For by those words the office and title of rabbi, of guide and of teacher are not condemned any more than the office and title of father [πατήρ] is condemned (v. 9); rather the magisterial haughtiness and pride, and the other vices of schoolmasters, are marked out. Except that the title rab, insofar as it properly denotes greater, and so a lord of faith, not one who teaches from the Scriptures but one who dictates from his own brain, and as it were with authority and without demonstration, in which sense the Jews, after the schisms between the schools of Shammai and Hillel arose, began to grow proud with this axiom of Rabbi, is of little honest repute. Otherwise, St Paul is also famous as the teacher [διδάσκαλος] of the Gentiles (1 Tim. 2:7). And St Paul gave Timothy this charge: What you have heard from me through many witnesses, commit to faithful men, who will be able [ἱκανοὶ ἔσονται] to teach others also (2 Tim. 2:2), hinting that there ought never to be a lack of those who teach others, and that they should be prepared for this, that they may teach others; and that the things to be taught are none other than those the Apostles handed down, and no other theology than that which, because it is not of public use, is called scholastic. From the beginning of the Christian Church the Church of Alexandria has been celebrated under this name, which, as is said, was founded on the counsel of the evangelist Mark, and which had its catechists and notable teachers: Pantaenus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Tryphon, Hierax, Dionysius, Anatolius, Theonas, Athanasius, etc. Afterwards, by a salutary plan, monasteries were founded almost everywhere by bishops such as Augustine and Basil; these were nothing other than theological schools of asceticism and places of manifold teaching, which were governed by the bishops themselves, or by other teachers set over them as teachers. From these, as from the Trojan horse, the most famous ministers and teachers of the Churches came forth. But as time went on this most holy institution so degenerated that in its time Peter of Cluny (Book 4, Letter 2) did not blush to call the monasteries synagogues of Satan. And all literary learning was so thoroughly driven out of the monasteries that the stupidity of monks gave rise to the proverb, more than asinine, Less learned than a monk, which is customarily said of the unlettered and stupid. And from the monasteries were made prisons and the most wretched torture-chambers of consciences, and workshops of all errors, idolatry, superstition, gluttony and crimes, in which all zeal for religion, piety, truth and chastity was trampled underfoot. Even Christian emperors, especially Theodosius and Charlemagne, set teachers over the academies that were established almost everywhere. But lest they hinder the Pope's kingdom, the Pontiffs did not close these, as the apostate Julian had done, but

units.la: jus illarum deinceps instituendarum sibi arrogarunt, & doctores, ut in verba sua jurarent, adegerunt. Unde falsorum Doctorum turba, torrentis instar, Ecclesiam inundavit & perdidit.
units.tr: They claimed for themselves the right to found such schools from then on, and they compelled the teachers to swear to their words. Hence a crowd of false teachers, like a torrent, flooded the Church and destroyed it.

units.la: LII. Doctoris officium est Διδάσκειν docere, non praecipere, dictare. "Ἐπὶ ὁ διδάσκων, ὁ διδασκαλία sive docens in doctrina, seu docendo, hoc est, non aliud agat, sed doceat tantum, Rom. XII. 7. Docere autem debet non novam revelationem vel Prophetiam offerendo, quia sic nemo amplius docet proximum suum & fratrem suum, dicendo: Cognoscite Jehovam, Jerem. XXXI. 34. Sed revelationem Christi atque Apostolorum narrando, indicando, ad conscientiam demonstrando. Non enim Christus unumquempiam doctorem infallibilem, ex cujus ore reliqui pendeant, & revelationes non demonstratas ex verbo Dei, sed à tali Doctore dictatas obtrudant; constituit: sed dedit Διδασκάλως doctores, adeóque multos, Ephes. IV. 11. Ubi autem multi & sine discrimine sunt, ibi unus non magis, quàm alius doctor est, neque unus accepit verbum, quod alius non acceperit, & quod ad alium non pervenerit, neque unus spiritum independentiæ & dominationis, alius dependentiæ & servitutis habet. Non ergo doctoris est praecipere, vel novam revelationem afferre, sed narrare, indicare, in memoriam revocare, quæ ab omnibus audita sunt, & ex illis veritatem demonstrare. Nemo enim nisi per doctrinam Christi, qui solus מורה לצדקה Doctor ad justitiam, Joel. II. 23. & καθηγητὴς doctor Matth. XXIII. 8. 10. est, & immediatè, non per authoritatem ullius hominis docet, & omnium fratrum, discipulorum suorum doctor æqualiter est, doctor esse potest. Ideo S. Paulus ad Timotheum: Quæ audivisti, à me per multos testes, (multis testibus praesentibus, audientibus, & depositum hoc unà commendantibus) hæc (non alia, nova) commenda fidelibus hominibus, qui idonei futuri sunt, ut alios doceant, 2. Tim. II. 2. Quod audivistis ab initio, id in vobis maneat, 1. Joh. II. 24. ὑπο-τύπωσιν exemplar habe sanorum sermonum, quos (sermones) vel quæ à me audivisti, in fide & charitate, quæ est in Christo Jesu, 2. Tim. I. 13. Sermones suos, seu quæ ille locutus est, exemplar & archetypon sanorum sermonum habeas jubet, quia non alii ὑγιαίνοντες λόγοι sani sermones esse possunt quàm illi, qui à Christo Ecclesiæ per Spiritum ejus dati sunt, & quorum ὑποτυπώσεις exemplar & Archetypon illa sunt, quæ Christus & Apostoli locuti sunt: Si quis ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖ alia, peregrina docet, & non accedit ὑγιαίνουσιν λόγοις sanis sermonibus Domini nostri Jesu Christi, & doctrinæ, quæ secundum pietatem est, τετύφωται, μηδὲν ἐπιστάμενος inflatus est, (vanarum opinionum vento & fumo, φιλαυτίᾳ, & sui admiratione turgens) nihil sciens, 1. Tim. VI. 3. 4. Quid enim ad salutem & justitiam hominis peccatoris spectans sciret is, qui Christi sermones nescit, vel iis non accedit? "Οιηιν opinionem, conjecturam, vanam scientiam talis habere potest; at Divinam ἐπιστήμην scientiam, ἀληροφορίαν, πίστιν certitudinem, fidem habere non potest. Necesse igitur est, doctor sermonum Dei, Christi, Mosis, Prophetarum, Apostolorum θεοπνεύστων, thesaurum apud se habeat,ut prompti sint in ore ejus,apud ipsum reperiantur, neque unquam illorum expers, exsors,rudis & imperitus inveniatur. Hæ voces Spiritus S. sunt, quibus mysterium Dei explicatur,eæque inter se sic compositæ & comparatæ esse debent, ut palam sinceram & solidam veritatem,quæ ab omni errore & mendacio distingui possit,exhibeant; ne verbum Dei in fraude proponatur, & τῇ καπηλείᾳ canpo-natione, 2. Cor. II. 17. qualis illorum est, qui vinum bonum affusa aqua vel vappa corrumpunt,vel aquam & vappam pro vino vendunt; subjiciatur,in quo est תך ומרמה dolus & fraus, Psal. X. 7. quorum illo mixtura alieni,hoc velatio alieni sensus sub verbis Dei significatur. Sed doctorem Dei oportet loqui ex sinceritate, sine ullo dolo vel voluntate loquendi aliud quàm merum Dei verbum, ut ex Deo, ne loquatur vel narret aliud,aut aliter,quàm quod, & sicut Deus dixit, coram Deo,ceu servus & legatus Dei, qui ex ejus ore fideliter sententiam ejus referat,ipsum intueatur,& judicium ejus metuat; denique in Christo, seu in fide Christi, qui sermonem de Deo omnium fundamentum est,& in unione ejus per Spiritum ipsius,2. Cor. II. 17. Et ad hæc quis idoneus est? Magna enim res est, Doctorem & Theologum dici, sed & res ancipitis & plena aleæ, hoc inprimis tempore, quo abundante ἀνομίᾳ charitas,& cum eadem fides & studium veritatis refrixit, & verbum Dei se habet ὡς μαργαρίτης καλὸς καὶ πολύτιμος unio bonus & pretiosus inter multos fucatos, Matth. XIII. 45. & homines secundum concupiscentias proprias sibi doctores coacervant, prurientes auditu ,à veritate auditum avertentes, & ad fabulas exorbitantes,2. Tim. IV. 3. 4. Alibi etiam Christus in parabola sic officium doctoris explicat: Omnis scriba (literarum Sacrarum tractator, Theologus) eruditus ad Regnum Cœlorum similis est homini Patri familias, qui ex thesauro suo καινὰ καὶ παλαιὰ nova & vetera promit, Matth. XIII. 52. Qua cum parabola conveniunt illa Sponsæ Christi: apud ostia nostra sunt כל מגדים חדשים ישנים omnia pretiosa nova etiam & vetera, Cant. VII. 13. Quæ non eum sensum habent, quasi ex agro Domini novale facere, & loqui non audita à Christo & Apostolis liceret, sed quòd sicut Paterfamilias in cellis suis vinum vetus & novum, fructus anni prioris & præsentis recondit,sic Scriba, seu Theologus à Spiritu Dei illuminatus, qui in Regno Cœlorum Christi solius discipulus est, noverit,quæ Patriarchæ, Prophetæ,& qui antegressisseculis fuerunt, noverunt, & in mysteriis regni,quæ per prophetias & parabolas Christi dicta & prædicta sunt, quotidie proficiat,veritatem Evangelii pluribus indies argumentis ex verbo Dei confirmet, plenius explicet,signa temporum investiget, tempus visitationis indicet,consolationem Scripturarum suppeditet, ad certamina imminentia præparet, Deum in operibus suis,ceu veracem laudet,& posteriores fructus prioribus abundantiores proferat. Non ergo novi veteribus omnia debent, sed sic tamen ad nova proficiunt, ut quæ in veteribus solida & permanentia sunt, non rejiciant, sed in thesauris suis conservent, atque ita novis demonstrationibus, experimentis,&
units.tr: LII. The office of a teacher is to teach [Διδάσκειν], not to command or dictate. "He who teaches, let him be in teaching [ὁ διδάσκων ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ], or teaching in doctrine, that is, let him do nothing else but teach," Rom. 12:7. A teacher must not offer a new revelation or prophecy, for then "no one would any longer teach his neighbour and his brother, saying: Know the LORD", Jer. 31:34. He must rather recount and point out the revelation of Christ and the Apostles, and demonstrate it to the conscience. For Christ did not appoint any one infallible teacher, from whose mouth the rest should hang, and who should impose revelations not demonstrated from the Word of God but dictated by such a teacher; instead he gave teachers [διδασκάλους], and therefore many, Eph. 4:11. Where there are many and no distinction among them, no one is more a teacher than another; no one has received a word that the other has not received, and that has not reached the other; no one has the spirit of independence and lordship, while another has the spirit of dependence and servitude. It is therefore not the teacher's office to command or to bring a new revelation, but to narrate, point out, bring to remembrance what has been heard by all, and from these things demonstrate the truth. For no one teaches except through the doctrine of Christ, who alone is the "teacher of righteousness" [מורה לצדקה], Joel 2:23, and the "teacher" [καθηγητής], Matt. 23:8, 10. Whoever teaches immediately, and not by the authority of any man, can be a teacher, and the teacher of all his brothers, his disciples, equally. Hence St. Paul to Timothy: "What you have heard from me among many witnesses" (many witnesses being present, hearing, and jointly commending this deposit), "these things (not other things, new things) commit to faithful men, who will be fit to teach others", 2 Tim. 2:2. "What you have heard from the beginning, let it abide in you", 1 John 2:24. "Hold fast the pattern [ὑποτύπωσιν] of sound words, which you have heard from me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus", 2 Tim. 1:13. He bids them hold his words, or what he said, as the pattern and archetype of sound words, because there can be no other "sound words" [ὑγιαίνοντες λόγοι] than those which Christ gave to his Church through his Spirit, and of which those things that Christ and the Apostles spoke are the patterns and archetype. "If anyone teaches other doctrine [ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖ], teaches strange things, and does not consent to the sound words [ὑγιαίνουσιν λόγοις] of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine which is according to godliness, he is puffed up [τετύφωται], knowing nothing [μηδὲν ἐπιστάμενος]"; he is puffed up (swollen by the wind and smoke of vain opinions, by self-love and self-admiration), knowing nothing, 1 Tim. 6:3, 4. For what could a man know, who is a sinner, that bears on salvation and righteousness, if he does not know the words of Christ or does not agree with them? Such a man can have an opinion, a conjecture, a vain knowledge [δόξα]; but he cannot have Divine knowledge [ἐπιστήμη], full assurance [ἀληροφορία], or faith, which is certainty [πίστις]. It is therefore necessary that the teacher of the words of God, of Christ, of Moses, of the Prophets, and of the Apostles, which are God-breathed [θεόπνευστοι], keep their treasury with him, so that they are ready on his lips, found with him, and that he is never found lacking in them, empty of them, untrained and unskilled. These are the words of the Holy Spirit by which the mystery of God is explained, and they must be so arranged and compared among themselves that they openly present the sincere and solid truth, which can be distinguished from every error and lie; so that the Word of God is not put forward in fraud, nor adulterated by "peddling" [τῇ καπηλείᾳ], 2 Cor. 2:17, like those who spoil good wine by pouring in water or vinegar, or sell water and vinegar for wine; nor is there "deceit and fraud" [תך ומרמה], Ps. 10:7, in which the one is signified by a mixture of what is foreign, the other by a veiling of a foreign sense under the words of God. But the teacher of God must speak with sincerity, without any deceit or intention of speaking anything other than the pure Word of God; he must not speak or relate anything other, or otherwise, than what God has said and as God has said it, standing before God as a servant and ambassador of God, who faithfully reports his sentence from his mouth, and fearing his judgment; and finally in Christ, or in the faith of Christ, which is the foundation of all talk about God, and in union with him through his Spirit, 2 Cor. 2:17. And who is fit for these things? For it is a great thing to be called a teacher and theologian, but it is also a dangerous matter, full of hazard, especially in this time, when, because lawlessness [ἀνομία] abounds, love grows cold, and with it faith and zeal for truth, and the Word of God stands like a "good and precious pearl" [μαργαρίτης καλὸς καὶ πολύτιμος] among many counterfeits, Matt. 13:45; and men heap up for themselves teachers according to their own lusts, "having itching ears, turning their hearing away from the truth and wandering off to fables", 2 Tim. 4:3, 4. Christ also elsewhere explains the office of the teacher in a parable: "Every scribe (a student of the Sacred Letters, a theologian) instructed for the kingdom of heaven is like a householder, who brings out of his treasure things new and old" [καινὰ καὶ παλαιά], Matt. 13:52. The bride of Christ agrees with this parable: "At our gates are all manner of precious things, new and old" [כל מגדים חדשים ישנים], Cant. 7:13. These words do not mean that it is allowed to make new ground in the Lord's field, and to speak things not heard from Christ and the Apostles; rather, just as a householder stores old and new wine, and the fruit of the previous and present year, in his cellars, so the scribe, or theologian, enlightened by the Spirit of God, who is a disciple of Christ alone in the kingdom of heaven, should know what the Patriarchs, Prophets, and those who lived in earlier ages knew, and should daily advance in the mysteries of the kingdom, which were spoken and foretold through the prophecies and parables of Christ; he should confirm the truth of the Gospel more and more each day with arguments from the Word of God, explain it more fully, investigate the signs of the times, point out the time of visitation, supply the consolation of the Scriptures, prepare men for the struggles that threaten, praise God in his works as true, and bring forth later fruits more abundant than the earlier. Therefore the new do not owe everything to the old, yet they so advance to new things that they do not reject what is solid and enduring in the old, but keep it in their treasuries, and so enrich it with new demonstrations, experiences,

units.la: luce nova cumulent, atque ita opportunè ad ædificationem vetera atque nova, tanquam analoga,& inter se similia promant.
units.tr: and new light; and so, aptly, for edification, they bring forth old and new things together, as analogous and similar to one another.

units.la: LIII. In specie oportet doctores linguarum originalium inprimis, quæ Scripturam, Ecclesiæ patrimonium γνῶσις referunt, & voluntatem Dei erudite cognoscere docent; nec non artium,scientiarum & historiarum, ecclesiasticarum inprimis, ad referenda Prophetiarum abdita comparatarum, non mediocriter instructos, sacram Scripturam partim interpretari κατ' ἀνάλυσιν: partim doctrinam in ea comprehensam concinnè proponere κῶς ζυνθέσεν, eámque adversus hæreticorum strophas, & infidelium obtrectationes atque λογισμὸς tueri, operam suam non tam in movendo affectu, pastorum more, quàm in intellectu δυνάμως potenter informando,navantes. Doctorem igitur non solùm διδασκλιγὸν, docendi peritia instructum, sed etiam ἐλεγκτικὸν arte convincendi contradicentes præditum, paratúmque ad differendum de veritate καταφατικῶς, & pro veritate ἀναφατικῶς, esse convenit. Oportet Episcopum (adeóque etiam doctorem in munere docendi cum Episcopo convenientem) ἀντεχόμενον affixum esse sermoni fideli (ut & alium sermonem contemnat, & hunc solum eligat, eíque inhæreat) qui est secundum doctrinam (seu sermonem eum, qui doctrinam præstare,& aptum facere ad docendum, qui idoneus ad discendum est, potest) ut potens sit, & ad exhortandum in doctrina sana, & ad redarguendum contradicentes. Sunt enim multi, iique ἀνυπότακτοι, ματαιολόγοι καὶ φρεναπάται contumaciter repugnantes, vaniloqui, & animorum deceptores, ὡς δεῖ ἐπισπμίζειν, quibus os obthurari oportet, Tit. I. 7. 9. 10. Non tantum igitur verum doceri,sed etiam falsum convinci debet,idque usque ad ἐπισυμισμὸν obthurationem oris illius, qui falsum contumaciter loquitur, cujus os fibulari, & quem ad ἐχεμυθίαν redigi oportet. Licèt enim contumaces & seductores raro eò adducantur, ut sibi ipsis silentium imponant, & contra veritatis stimulum calcitrare desinant: tamen eò adduci vi veritatis demonstratæ possunt, ut cum ratione ampliùs loqui & contradicere desinant, omnésque intelligant, eos non aliud, quàm blaterones, vaniloquos & animorum deceptores esse; neque adeò pii & probi per eos seduci possint. Qui ἐπισυμισμὸς non utique per ματαιολογίαν vaniloquentiam succedit, quia per eam ματαιολόγῳ vaniloquus non convincitur, sed per ἔλεγχον redargutionem, quæ per τὴν κατὰ διδασκαλῶ πίστιν λόγον fidelem sermonem secundum doctrinam, absolvitur. Per demonstrationem enim veritatis anima & conscientia hominis ad credendum & obediendum eidem capitur. Utilissima eam in rem est exercitationum scholasticarum usus, quibus αἰσθήσεσι γεγυμνασμένα sensus exercitati ad discretionem boni & mali comparantur, Hebr. V. 14. Sicut enim ferrum ferro acuitur,& ex duorum silicum attritione ignis latens antea exsuscitatur, elicitur & excutitur; ita illæ disceptationum ζυζητήσεις ingenia vegetiora,magis perspicacia & alacria reddunt, judicia formant, celeritatem & promptitudinem repetendi & explicandi aliorum sententias,nec non elo-
units.tr: LIII. In particular, teachers ought to be well instructed, above all, in the original languages, which bear witness to Scripture as the heritage of the Church and teach us to know the will of God learnedly; likewise in the arts, sciences and histories, especially ecclesiastical ones, which have been acquired for explaining the hidden things of the Prophecies. They should be able partly to interpret Sacred Scripture analytically [κατ' ἀνάλυσιν], and partly to set forth the doctrine contained in it neatly synthetically [κατὰ σύνθεσιν], and to defend it against the cavils of heretics and the objections of unbelievers and reasoning [λογισμός]; exerting themselves not so much in moving the affections, as shepherds do, but in powerfully informing the understanding. It is therefore fitting that the teacher be not only didactic [διδασκαλικός], furnished with teaching skill, but also elenctic [ἐλεγκτικός], endowed with the art of refuting contradicters, and ready to dispute about the truth affirmatively [καταφατικῶς], and to defend the truth negatively [ἀναφατικῶς]. The bishop (and therefore also the teacher in the office of teaching, which belongs with the bishop) ought to be holding fast [ἀντεχόμενον], attached to the faithful word (so that he both despises other words and chooses this one alone, and cleaves to it), which is according to doctrine (that is, the word which is able to furnish doctrine and make one fit for teaching, and which is fit for learning), so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to rebuke those who contradict. For there are many, and they are unruly [ἀνυπότακτοι], idle talkers [ματαιολόγοι] and deceivers of minds [φρεναπάται], obstinately resisting, vain talkers and deceivers of souls, whose mouths must be stopped, as is fitting, Titus 1:7, 9, 10. Therefore it is not enough that truth be taught; falsehood must also be refuted, and that to the point of stopping [ἐπισυμισμός] the mouth of the one who obstinately speaks falsehood, whose mouth must be muzzled, and whom it is necessary to reduce to silence [ἐχεμυθία]. For although obstinate and seducing men are rarely brought to the point of imposing silence on themselves and ceasing to kick against the goad of truth, yet they can be brought by the force of demonstrated truth to the point where they cease to speak and contradict with reason any more, and all understand that they are nothing but babblers, vain talkers and deceivers of souls, and that the pious and honest cannot be seduced by them. This stopping does not indeed come about through vain talk, because by that the vain talker is not convicted; it comes through refutation [ἔλεγχος], which is accomplished through the faithful word according to doctrine [τὴν κατὰ διδασκαλίαν πίστιν λόγον]. For through the demonstration of truth the soul and conscience of a man are captured to believe and obey it. The practice of scholastic exercises is most useful for this, by which senses trained [αἰσθητήρια γεγυμνασμένα] are prepared for discernment of good and evil, Heb. 5:14. For just as iron is sharpened by iron, and fire lying hidden is roused, drawn out and struck from the rubbing of two flints, so those disputations [ζητήσεις] make the minds more lively, more perceptive and more alert; they form judgments, and produce readiness and promptness in repeating and explaining the opinions of others, and also the ability to speak well and fluently, and they strengthen judgment, provided that the lust for wrangling and quarrelling, the childish display of deceiving opponents, and vain-glory [δοχημοσφία] are avoided. This kind of exercise was in use among the Jews, as is clear from history…

units.la: Et requisita, linguarum imprimis originalium & artium peritiae necessitas. eloquendi feliciter gignunt, & judicium confirmant, modò rixandi & vitilitigandi libido, & puerilis adversarios decipiendi ostentatio, & δοχημοσφία vitetur. Quod exercitamenti genus tum apud Judæos in usu fuit, uti ex historia Christi, Luc. II.46. & Stephani, quo cum Libertini, Cyrenæi, &c. ζυζήτιον disquisitionem seu disceptationem instituerunt, Actor. VI.9. tum apud Christianas quoque Ecclesias receptum est, teste S. Paulo, jubente, ut duo vel tres Prophetæ loquantur, & reliqui dijudicent, 1. Cor. XIV. 29. Analytica porro Scripturæ interpretatio veri sensus enarratione & veri ejusdem usus demonstratione constat: de quo pluribus in loco egimus: Synthetica verò docendi ratio in catecheticam institutionem, qua rudiores, lactis potu alendi, informantur: quorum doctores κατηχηταὶ Catechetæ olim dicti fuerunt, & copiosiorem atque sublimiorem, à principio fidei ad perfectionem progredientem locorum Theologicorum tractationem, quo velut solidiore cibo adulti pascuntur, distinguitur.
units.tr: The need for the required skills, above all the original languages and the arts, also gives birth to fluent speaking and strengthens judgment, provided that the lust for quarrelling and wrangling, the display of childish trickery against opponents, and δοχημοσφία [ostentation] are avoided. This kind of exercise was in use among the Jews, as is clear from the history of Christ (Luke 2:46) and of Stephen, with whom the Libertines, Cyrenians, and others instituted a disquisition or debate [ζυζήτιον] (Acts 6:9). It was also received in the Christian churches, as St. Paul attests when he directs that two or three prophets speak, and the rest judge (1 Cor. 14:29). Furthermore, analytical interpretation of Scripture consists in setting out the true sense and demonstrating the true use of it, a matter we have discussed at greater length in its place. Synthetical method of teaching, however, belongs to catechetical instruction, by which the more untutored are formed, nourished on milk. Their teachers were formerly called catechists [κατηχηταὶ], and this is distinguished from the fuller and loftier treatment of the theological commonplaces, which advances from the beginning of faith toward perfection and by which adults are fed, as on more solid food.

units.la: LIV. Doctores æquè atque Pastores vocatione indigent.
units.tr: LIV. Teachers, no less than ministers, need a call.

units.la: Non enim ad docendum circulatores & impostores quivis admitti debent; sed illi, quos Deus & Christus dat, Ephes. IV. 11. & charismatis ab aliis distinguit, & quos nobis ejusmodi insignes Ecclesia, quæ vel ipsa, vel per Pastores, vel per Magistratus, vel per utrosque eos deligit, suffragatione sua ad docendi munus deputat. Nam totius Ecclesiæ non parum refert, idoneos juventuti doctores præfici. Sufficere autem ad vocationem simplex personæ delectus & deputatio potest. Neque aliter primitus doctores creati & vocati videntur. Sed accesserunt procedente tempore, ornamenti & authoritatis docentibus conciliandæ gratia insignia & gradus Academici. Primò quidem legum Civilium Interpretibus, Irnerio, Lotharii Saxonis Cancellario procurante, ac mox etiam Theologis, primò Bononiæ, inde Lutetiæ collati, initium capiendi honoris faciente Lombardo, imitatione, uti videtur, Hebræorum, qui doctores suos traditione clavium & pugillarium in possessionem muneris docendi immiserunt.
units.tr: For not just anyone should be admitted to teach, like itinerant peddlers and impostors. Rather, those whom God and Christ give (Eph. 4:11), and whom He distinguishes from others by their gifts, and whom the Church, which chooses them either by itself, or through the ministers, or through the magistrates, or through both, appoints to the office of teaching by its vote. For it matters not a little to the whole Church that suitable teachers be set over the young. A simple choice and appointment of the person may suffice for the call. Nor does it appear that teachers were created and called in any other way in the early days. But as time went on, academic insignia and degrees were added, to win authority and honour for teachers and to lend them adornment. First these were conferred on the interpreters of civil law, at the instigation of Irnerius, chancellor of Lothar the Saxon, and soon also on theologians, first at Bologna and then at Paris, beginning with the honour bestowed on Lombard. This was done, as it seems, in imitation of the Hebrews, who installed their teachers in the office of teaching by the handing over of keys and writing tablets.

units.la: Quomodo de R. Samuele memorant, post mortem ejus clavim & pugillares ejus in loculo ejus repositos esse, quia non habuerit filium, cui doctoratus insignia relinqueret. Ideo κλεὶς clavis Rabbinis aperire docendo, quia docendo mysteria aperiuntur, appellari solet, usitata iis phrasi: Rabbi hic vel ille sic aperuit, seu explicavit textum: Erat enim iis clavis signum potestatis aperiendi, reserandi & promendi aliis mysteria, ut & ipsis ad necessariam eruditionem innotescerent. Quam quia magno fervore & candore Henochus exeruit, mille claves ei traditas memorant. Eodem allusit Christus legisperitis sic obnuntians: Væ vobis, quia sustulistis τὴν κλεῖδα τῆς γνώσεως clavim cognitionis. Ipsi non intrastis, & intrantes prohibuistis, Luc. XI.52. Cùm enim iis, ceu eximiis per clavis scientiæ traditionem jus docendi, & docendi pœnitentiam & fidem in Filium Dei ad justitiam, quæ ad solvenda omnia Scripturæ ænigmata clavis est, collatum esset, clavi illa sibi solenniter tradita ad populi in doctrina de vera justitia per Christum præstanda institutionem nec usi sunt, nec uti alios siverunt, sed utentes persecuti sunt. Addiderunt iidem imposition-em manuum (unde & promovens & promotus & promotio χειροτονίας nominibus venerunt) nec non Renuntiationem, qua candidatus Rabbi proclamabatur.
units.tr: As they report of Rabbi Samuel, after his death his key and writing tablets were found placed in his chest, because he had no son to whom he could leave the insignia of his teaching office. Hence the rabbis customarily called the key [κλεὶς] "to open," because by teaching, mysteries are opened. The common idiom among them was: "Rabbi so-and-so thus opened, that is, explained, the text." For the key was for them a sign of the power to open, unlock, and bring forth mysteries for others, so that they might also become known to those who needed the necessary learning. Because Enoch practised this with great zeal and sincerity, they record that a thousand keys were given to him. Christ alluded to the same thing when He rebuked the lawyers, saying: Woe to you, for you have taken away the key of knowledge [τὴν κλεῖδα τῆς γνώσεως]. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering (Luke 11:52). For since the right to teach, and to teach repentance and faith in the Son of God unto righteousness, which is the key to unlocking all the enigmas of Scripture, had been conferred on them as though they were eminent men through the handing over of the key of knowledge, they neither used that key, which had been solemnly entrusted to them, for instructing the people in the doctrine of true righteousness through Christ, nor did they allow others to use it; rather, they persecuted those who did. The same rabbis added the laying on of hands (whence both the one who promotes, the one promoted, and the promotion came to be called by the name of ordination [χειροτονία]), and also the proclamation, by which the candidate was announced as Rabbi.

units.la: Cùmque etiam Apostoli Diaconos lecturi populum circumspicere ἀνδρας μαρτυρημένους viros testimonio ornatos jusserint, Actor. VI. 3. & gradus rite collati non aliud quàm testimonia aptitudinis ad docendum publica atque solennia sint, non est quod morem ejusmodi liberè usurpatum, & ornatum atque authoritatem apud eos, qui docentur, conciliantem, quin & stimulum aliis honestissimæ gloriæ & æmulationis subdentem, vel Fanatici & Brovvnistæ fastidiosè nimis rejiciant, vel alii ceu fastus argumentum, ipsi fastum majore fastu calcantes, explodant.
units.tr: Since the Apostles also directed that deacons be chosen from among the people, men attested by testimony [ἄνδρας μαρτυρημένους] (Acts 6:3), and since properly conferred degrees are nothing other than public and solemn testimonies of fitness to teach, there is no reason why the Fanatics and Brownists should disdainfully reject such a custom, which is freely used and which lends ornament and authority among those who are taught, and which even spurs others on to the most honourable glory and emulation. Nor should others, using it as an argument of pride, and trampling pride underfoot with still greater pride, scoff at it.

units.la: Ecclesiæ nostræ primi Reformatores, viri sanctissimi, omnique laude majores, Magisterii in Philosophia gradu ornati licèt, in Theologia tamen similem gradum, quem indignissimis in Papatu conferri svetum vilem merito habuerunt, uti solent dignitates indignis tributæ vilescere, minimè affectarunt, & tantùm non, Papalis abusus, dominatus & superbiæ odio, fastidiverunt, æquè atque alios dignitatis titulos, uti quidem Zvvinglius etiam Professor, Theologus, reverendus appellari renuit. Sed purgatis deinceps à superstitione & fastu Papali ejusmodi gradibus, nulla eos, ubi necessitas vocationis postulat, accipiendi religio incessere quemquam debet, ut frustra nostris contemtum titulorum ejusmodi Eckhardus Fascic. controv. cap. ult. Et ipsis Lutheranis Gresterus in Luthero Academico cap. 3. exprobraverint. Sicut enim nemo cordatus gradus ejusmodi affectat, memor utique, honorem & titulum aliquid habere oneris, & verecundiùs etiam recepti serò quandoque poenitere posse; ne dicam, non magnopere ambiendum esse honorem, quem pro seculi, quo laurigeri multi, pauci Phœbus sunt, & subitò fiunt doctores, sicut in fabulis subitò gigantes nati dicuntur, more digni juxta atque indigni, non virtutis, sed pecuniæ & favoris pretio auferunt, quando, sicut olim Caligula, teste Diogene, equum suum consulem, ita hodie male consulti asinos, Episcopos & doctores faciunt: tamen ubi ordo & mos, atque inprimis vocationis necessitas hoc virtutis & eruditionis testimonium capessere jubent, ordini & mori, qui Ecclesiæ utilis & honorificus esse potest, parere, non refragari morosiùs convenit. Abest modò ambitio, quæ optima quæque polluit, & indignissimos quosque velut pestilens fidus, afflat, & opera religiosè detur, ne claves scientiæ occultentur, sed eæ ad referanda Regni Cœlorum mysteria jugiter in promptu sint.
units.tr: Our Church's first Reformers, most holy men, greater than all praise, though adorned with the degree of Master in Philosophy, nevertheless very much did not seek a similar degree in Theology, which, because it was customarily conferred on the most unworthy in the Papacy, they rightly regarded as worthless, just as honours bestowed on the unworthy usually become cheapened. Indeed, out of hatred for papal abuse, domination, and pride, they almost scorned it, just as they scorned other titles of dignity; Zwingli, for instance, refused even to be called Professor, Theologian, Reverend. But once such degrees had been purged of superstition and papal arrogance, no scruple about accepting them, where the necessity of a call requires it, should trouble anyone. Thus Eckhardt, in his Fascic. controv. (last chapter), reproaches our people for their supposed contempt of such titles, and Gresterus, in Luther the Academic (chapter 3), reproaches even the Lutherans themselves. For just as no sensible person seeks such degrees, mindful that honour and title carry some burden, and that one may sometimes, even when humbly received, regret having accepted them too late, so one should not earnestly seek an honour which, in an age in which many are laurel-crowned and few are Phoebus, and doctors are suddenly made, as giants are said in fables to be suddenly born, is bestowed by the price of money and favour, worthy and unworthy alike, and not by virtue. Just as Caligula once made his horse consul, as Diogenes testifies, so today ill-advised men make donkeys bishops and doctors. Nevertheless, where order and custom, and above all the necessity of a call, require the attainment of this testimony of virtue and learning, it is fitting to submit to the order and custom, which can be useful and honourable to the Church, and not to resist them stubbornly. Only let ambition be absent, which pollutes all the best things and breathes upon the most unworthy like a deadly blight; and let care be taken, in a godly manner, that the keys of knowledge are not hidden, but are always ready for unlocking the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: LV. Sicut Pastorum, ita etiam Doctorum vocationem δοκιμασία præcedat oportet. Nam S. Paulus Timotheum à se audita commendare jussit πιστοῖς ἀνθρώποις fidelibus hominibus, qui & ipsi ἱκανοὶ idonei ad docendum alios existant, 2. Tim. II. 2. Oportet ergo doctores vocandi sint πιστοί fideles, non tantùm credentes, sed etiam homines constantis præpositi, explo-
units.tr: LV. Just as the call of ministers, so also the call of teachers ought to be preceded by examination [δοκιμασία]. For St. Paul ordered Timothy to commend what he had heard from him to faithful men, who themselves are able [ἱκανοὶ] to teach others [πιστοῖς ἀνθρώποις] (2 Tim. 2:2). Teachers to be called must therefore be faithful [πιστοί], not merely believers, but also men of steady disposition, of tested faith and sincerity [εἰλικρινείας].

units.la: Doctorum vocatio & inaugura-tio. exploratæ fidei & εἰλικρινείας sinceritatis; qui sint idonei ad docendum ingenio, judicio, memoria, eloquio pollentes, ac inprimis ἄνδρες λόγοι ϗ δυνατοὶ ἐν γραφαῖς viri facundi & potentes in Scripturis, qualis Apollo Actor. XVIII. 24. laudatur, & potentes etiam ad redarguendum contradicentes, Tit. I. 7. Quod ipsum doctoris officium superius expositum postulat. Sed & peritia linguarum, nativam Spiritus S. sententiam repræsentantium, & artium non mediocris requiritur, ceu quædam ad παιδείαν hanc sacram σωφροσύνην; absque qua est ad docendi alios munus ineptus, imò idiota est. Ideo Apostoli & primi illi Ecclesiæ dati doctores sine linguarum notitia & λόγῳ γνώσεως sermone cognitionis commeatum ad Ecclesiam non habuerunt, Actor. II. 1. 2. &c. 1. Cor. XII. 8. 10. Et quod illis Spiritus S. extra ordinem, singulari afflatu, impertitus est, id deinceps cura, & per charismata ordinaria studio, atque institutione interveniente, impartitur. Quæ impietas, quod scelus est, liceat cum pia illa anima, Phil. Melanchtone, Orat. Tom. I. p. 316 exclamare, donum linguarum, cujus usus tam late patet, aspernari, & Divinitus illatum in has nationes rursus explodere atque ejicere? Leges publicæ atrociter puniunt sacrilegia. At majus sacrilegium est, Ecclesiam spoliare linguarum cognitione, quam aurea & argentea suppellectili. Hæc enim cœlestia dona Evangelio lucem afferunt, & veriùs Ecclesiæ suppellex, quàm ulla ornamenta aurea sint. Neque enim dubium est quin ad hanc utilitatem Deus Evangelio addiderit donum linguarum, ut ad sacras literas explicandas conducant. Itaque sacrilegos ipsos linguarum contemptores putate in ipsas aras ac templa impetum tanti furoris olim facere, & vastitatem atque exitium religioni & omnibus honestis artibus minitari; nec dubitate, quin Deo pœnas daturi sint. Etenim oportet doctorem ὀρθοτομεῖν τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας rite secare verbum veritatis, 2. Tim. II. 15. adeóque recto & vero modo, quo oportet, eum exhibere. Quem in finem non parum etiam artium & linguarum usus conducit. Nam ut ordine, vel verbis aptissimis, & originibus suis proximis, veritas asseratur, & prudenter fundamento inædificetur, atque cum veritatibus aliis conformetur, illæ multum adjuvant. Aptitudinis comes voluntas, seu charitas, fidelitatis in officio nutricula, est, absque qua, qui se ministerio implicat, mercenarius est. Illa instigat ad id faciendum & docendum, quod ædificatio requirit; ut sint tales, quales sint, charitas optat. Illa dominationem, superbiam, inprimis ἔρεις, ζῆλος, θυμός, ἐριθείας, καταλαλιάς, φυσιώσεις, ἀκαταστασίας, controversias, studia partium, iracundias contentiones, obtrectationes, susurros, tumores, conturbationes, 2. Cor. XII. 20. pestes veritatis Ecclesiæ, cohibet. Oportet enim servum Dei non pugnare (in pugnam, equi instar ad prælium semper parati, prurire, & κενοδοξίας ergo, ut gladiatorem, in arena ad duellum comparere, quia ejus, qui Ecclesiæ servit, negotium est, non destruere, fugare, deteriores reddere, sed convertere, & ad Deum adducere) sed ἤπιον mitem esse erga omnes (offensionum pavidum, non temere exulcerantem quenquam, ne aures adversus docentem obthuret & indocilis reddatur) ἀδαχθῆν
units.tr: The call and inauguration of teachers. Those who are fit to teach must excel in intellect, judgment, memory, and eloquence, and above all must be men eloquent and mighty in the Scriptures [ἄνδρες λόγιοι καὶ δυνατοὶ ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς], like Apollos, who is praised in Acts 18:24, and powerful also to refute those who contradict (Titus 1:7). This is precisely what the duty of the teacher, set out above, requires. But also a considerable skill in languages, which represent the native meaning of the Holy Spirit, and in the arts, is required, as certain tools for this sacred instruction and sober wisdom [σωφροσύνη]; without these a man is unfit for the office of teaching others, indeed he is an ignoramus. Therefore the Apostles and the first teachers given to the Church had no access to the Church without knowledge of languages and without the word of knowledge [λόγῳ γνώσεως] (Acts 2:1–2 etc.; 1 Cor. 12:8–10). And what the Holy Spirit bestowed on them outside the ordinary course, by a singular inspiration, is afterwards bestowed through diligent study and instruction, and through the ordinary gifts. What impiety, what crime it is, may one exclaim with that godly soul Philip Melanchthon (Orations, vol. 1, p. 316), to scorn the gift of languages, whose use extends so widely, and to cast out and drive away again among these nations a gift brought from God? Public laws punish sacrilege with severity. Yet it is a greater sacrilege to despoil the Church of knowledge of languages than of gold and silver furnishings. For these heavenly gifts bring light to the Gospel, and they are truly the furnishings of the Church, more than any golden ornaments. Nor is there any doubt that God added the gift of languages to the Gospel for this usefulness, so that they might serve for explaining the sacred writings. Therefore, consider those who despise languages to be sacrilegious men, who in times past made an assault of such fury upon the very altars and temples, and threatened devastation and ruin to religion and to all honourable arts; and do not doubt that they will give account to God. Indeed, the teacher must rightly divide the word of truth [ὀρθοτομεῖν τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας] (2 Tim. 2:15), and so present it in the right and true manner that is fitting. To this end the use of the arts and languages contributes no little. For these greatly help so that truth may be asserted in the proper order, with the most fitting words and their nearest sources, and so that it may be prudently built upon the foundation and brought into harmony with other truths. Accompanying fitness is will, or charity, the nurse of faithfulness in duty, without which the man who entangles himself in the ministry is a hireling. It urges him to do and teach what edification requires, so that men may be what charity wishes them to be. It restrains domination, pride, above all strife, zeal, anger, rivalry, slander, arrogance, disorder (2 Cor. 12:20), factions, party spirit, angry quarrels, contentions, backbiting, whisperings, swellings, tumults, the plagues of the truth of the Church. For the servant of God must not fight (he must not itch for battle like a horse always ready for the fray, nor, for the sake of empty glory, appear in the arena for a duel like a gladiator, because the business of one who serves the Church is not to destroy, put to flight, or make worse, but to convert and lead to God), but must be gentle toward all (fearful of giving offence, not rashly irritating anyone, lest he stop the ears of his hearers against the teacher and make them unteachable) [ἤπιον], apt to teach [ἀδακτικὸν]

units.la: ad dicendum paratum & idoneum, tolerantem malorum (ne convitiis & probris impetitus atque excandescens animum à docendo avertat, & potiùs effreni animo atque dolori suo, quàm veritati & utilitati discentis obsequatur) in manstuetudine castigantem eos, qui se opponunt, (castigantem etiam eos, qui veritati demonstratæ liquidò non parent, sed pertinaciter resistunt, ut eos stultitiæ suæ pudeat; sed ἐν πραΰτητι in manstuetudine, ut species omnis ultionis à verbis, & animi mali à vultu & gestibus absit, & charitatem omnia loquantur, cujus illicio animi facilè devinciuntur, & feri etiam homines cicurantur) 2. Tim. II. 24. 25.
units.tr: ready and fit for teaching, bearing evils patiently (lest, assailed with reproaches and insults and becoming angry, he turn his mind away from teaching, and rather yield to his unbridled spirit and his grief than to the truth and the benefit of the learner), correcting in mansuetude those who oppose themselves (correcting also those who do not plainly yield to the truth once it is demonstrated, but resist obstinately, so that they may be ashamed of their folly; but in mansuetude [ἐν πραΰτητι], so that every appearance of vengeance is absent from his words, and ill temper from his face and gestures, and all things are spoken in charity, by whose allurement minds are easily bound and even wild men are tamed) 2 Tim. 2. 24, 25.

units.la: LVI. Plurima equidem de officio & doctrina docentium præcipi possent. Cæterum sicut gubernator in navi mente portum prospicit, & ad hunc cursum dirigit, atque in alto mari procul extra terræ aspectum avectus notat sidera, Ursam, Orionem, Plejades, aliàsque insigniores stellas, quas tanquam duces sequatur: ita docenti per totam vitam duo principalia præcepta, veritatis & charitatis, quarum ἀρχή ζωή est, curæ cordique esse debent. Vitato ille veritatis studio opiniones, quas ex verbo Dei veris Ecclesiæ judiciis rejectas esse novit: & charitatis minimè simulatæ insidiatu de omnibus rebus temerè & procaciter ne pugnato. Deus enim, qui veritas & charitas est, ἀληθεύειν ἐν ἀγάπῃ verum dicere & sentire seu veritatem sectari, in charitate, atque sic crescere in ipsum quoad omnia, qui caput Christus est, Ephes. IV. 15. jussit. Nam nec fides veritatis sine ejusdem amore vera & viva esse potest; sed similis est fidei Diaboli, mendacii parentis, cui Divinæ veritatis notitia non solatium ullum, vel pacem, sed horrorem & desperationem affert: & veritas, quam fide apprehendimus, quæ in testimonio Dei continetur, & ex fundamento fluit, ad efficiendam charitatem & dilectionem tum Dei & proximi maximè accommodata est; & quod ad charitatem inutile est, ad veritatem non pertinet: & veritas sic asserenda est, ut non deseratur charitas: atque sic charitas colenda est, ut veritas necessaria inprimis ad salutem, detrimentum nullum patiatur. Duæ enim hæ radices sunt, ex quibus incrementum nostrum spirituale in caput nostrum, quod Christus est, exsurgere debet. Sed sic tamen illæ temperantur, ut qui veritatis studio inardescit, charitatem erga errantes ex infirmitate non exuat, sed potiùs ad lucrandum, vel saltem tolerandum infirmum exerceat; & qui verè Deum & proximum amat, veritati sic studeat, ut nunquam eam ejuret, vel mendacio assentiatur. Aliud enim est errantes ex infirmitate in tanta mentium caligine, per charitatem, quæ pietatis arx, & virtutum Christianarum metropolis est, tolerare, infirmitates eorum ferre, iis pro viribus mederi: aliud errantibus suffragari & veritatem agnitam amore errantium abnegare. Illud fas piùmque, hoc nefas est. Licet claudicantem ferre, imò etiam mensa sua dignari, quod à Davide Mephibosetho in gratiam Jonathanis, corculi sui, factum, 2. Sam. IX. 10. 13. legimus; & multò magis nobis circa errantes in fide, & claudicantes in gratiam Christi, fratris nostri primogeniti, cujus illi filii sunt, facto opus
units.tr: LVI. Indeed, very much could be prescribed concerning the office and teaching of teachers. But just as a helmsman on a ship watches the harbour with his mind and steers his course towards it, and, carried out on the open sea far from sight of land, observes the stars, the Bear, Orion, the Pleiades, and other more prominent stars, which he follows as guides, so a teacher throughout his whole life should have at heart and in his care the two principal precepts, of truth and of charity, of which the beginning is life [ἀρχή ζωή]. Let him, by zeal for the truth, avoid opinions which he knows have been rejected from the word of God by the true judgements of the Church; and let him not rashly and boldly fight about all matters, in the snares of a charity that is not wholly sincere. For God, who is truth and charity, has commanded us to speak the truth in love [ἀληθεύειν ἐν ἀγάπῃ], that is, to say and think the truth, or to pursue the truth, in charity, and thus to grow up into him in all things, who is the head, Christ (Eph. 4. 15). For faith in the truth cannot be true and living without love of it; faith of this kind is like the faith of the Devil, the father of lies, for whom the knowledge of divine truth brings no comfort or peace, but horror and despair. And the truth, which we grasp by faith, which is contained in the testimony of God and flows from the foundation, is most suited to producing charity and love both of God and of neighbour; and what is useless for charity does not pertain to truth. Thus truth is to be asserted in such a way that charity is not forsaken, and charity is to be cultivated in such a way that truth, especially that necessary for salvation, suffers no loss. For these are the two roots from which our spiritual growth must rise into our head, who is Christ. Yet they are so tempered that he who burns with zeal for the truth does not strip off charity towards those in error through weakness, but rather exercises it in order to win over, or at least to bear with, the weak; and he who truly loves God and neighbour should so pursue the truth that he never abjures it or assents to a lie. For it is one thing, through charity, which is the citadel of piety and the metropolis of Christian virtues, to bear with those in error because of the great darkness of minds, to put up with their weaknesses and to heal them as far as one can; it is another thing to favour those in error and to deny the truth once recognised out of love for those in error. The former is right and proper, the latter is wrong. It is lawful to bear with one who limps, indeed even to honour him at one's table, as we read David did to Mephibosheth for the sake of Jonathan, his darling (2 Sam. 9. 10, 13); and much more must we deal thus with those who are in error in the faith, and who limp, for the sake of Christ, our firstborn brother, of whom they are the sons.

units.la: {a} Veritatis & charitatis iis præcipua cura esse debet. opus est: at μετὰ χωλὸς χωλαίνων cum claudo claudicare nunquam licet; neque id charitas utcunque illa non nimis lyncea & oculata est, jure exigere ausit. Mandat Apostolus, ut infirmos in fide suscipiamus, Rom. XIV. 1. non ipsi infirmitatem nostro jumento nobis accersamus, vel erroneis opinionibus nos συναπάγειν una abripi, Gal. II. 13. patiamur. Et διδακτικὸν ad docendum idoneum Doctorem, & ἤμερον mitem ergo omnes, imo etiam ἀνεξίκακον tolerantem malorum, & quanto magis ex infirmitate, quæ ἐυπερίστατος facile nos circumstat, nec nisi novissima exuitur, errantium inprimis, si error non deserat fundamentum fidei & salutis, Apostolus 2. Tim. II. 24. jussit. Absint ergo ab Ecclesia Doctores φιλόνικοι, & pestes atque Erynnes istæ, quæ sine justa & necessaria causa rixas movent, concordiam turbant, & quavis dissentiendi occasione ferrum non in hominem, sed in Jesum Christum stringunt. Ille enim, quod dies noctesque animo nostro obversari debet, agonem suum emortualem pro Ecclesia ingressurus, & sanguinem sudans, veritatem & concordiam inprimis in Ecclesia servari à Deo, Patre suo expetiit, his verbis: Sanctifica eos in veritate. Sermo tuus veritas est, Joh. XVII. 17. Concordiam geminis illis: Pater, sanctifica eos, quos mihi dedisti, ut sint unum, sicut nos, v. 11. Ad hujus summi Sacerdotis nostri preces docentes quoque voluntates & vota sua adjungere, & duo illa, veritatem & concordiam insatiabiliter expetere oportet.
units.tr: Veritatis & charitatis iis præcipua cura esse debet. Those who teach should have above all a care for truth and charity. But one who limps must never limp together with the lame [μετὰ χωλὸς χωλαίνων]; nor may a charity which is not very lynx-eyed and clear-sighted presume to demand this in any way. The Apostle commands that we receive those who are weak in faith (Rom. 14. 1); he does not permit us to bring weakness upon ourselves as a burden, nor to be carried away together [συναπάγειν] with erroneous opinions (Gal. 2. 13). And the Apostle (2 Tim. 2. 24) commands that a teacher be apt to teach [διδακτικὸν], gentle [ἤμερον] towards all, and indeed patient of evils [ἀνεξίκακον], and all the more so towards those in error, especially if the error does not abandon the foundation of faith and salvation, given that weakness, which easily surrounds us [ἐυπερίστατος] and is put off only at the last, is our lot. Therefore let teachers who are contentious [φιλόνικοι] be absent from the Church, and those pests and Furies who, without a just and necessary cause, stir up quarrels, disturb concord, and, on any occasion of dissent, direct the sword not against a man but against Jesus Christ. For he, whom we ought to keep before our minds day and night, about to enter upon his deathly struggle for the Church, and sweating blood, sought from God his Father above all that truth and concord be preserved in the Church, in these words: Sanctify them in the truth; thy word is truth (John 17. 17). And concord in these words: Father, sanctify those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we are (v. 11). To the prayers of this our High Priest, teachers ought also to join their wills and desires, and to seek insatiably those two things, truth and concord.

units.la: LVII. Cùm Ecclesia facultatibus ad sustentandos ministros & alendos pauperes, exules, viduas, orphanos & infirmos, carere non posset, etiam corporalium, seu τῶν βιωτικῶν ministros primitus admisit.
units.tr: LVII. Since the Church could not be without resources to support ministers and to feed the poor, exiles, widows, orphans and the sick, it admitted from the first also ministers of bodily things [τῶν βιωτικῶν].

units.la: Statim enim atque fideles in nomine Christi colligi coeperunt, omnia sic communia habuerunt, ut nemo ea, quæ superflua haberet, Ecclesiæ necessitatibus impendere recusaret, Actor. II. 44. 45. IV. 32. 37. Eorum bonorum curatores primò ipsi Apostoli fuerunt; sed deinceps selecti adhibiti sunt, quibus διακόνων Diaconorum, seu ministrorum nomen impositum est.
