Quæ appellatio quamvis promiscuè ad quævis Ecclesiæ ministeria pertineat, tamen aucta jam Ecclesia sacri ærarii custodibus ac administris attributa, & Apostolis ipsis consecrata est, nomine διακονίας καθημερινῆς ministerii quotidiani, & τῶν τραπεζῶν mensarum, ibid. VI. 1. 2. Sunt igitur, ea notione, Diaconi sacri rerum corporearum thesauri custodes & œconomi, à Deo per Ecclesiam ad munus hoc vocati.
units.tr: For as soon as the faithful began to be gathered in the name of Christ, they held all things in common, so that no one refused to devote what he had in excess to the needs of the Church (Acts 2. 44, 45; 4. 32, 37). The first overseers of these goods were the Apostles themselves; but afterwards men were chosen, to whom the name of deacons [διακόνων], that is, ministers, was given. Although this appellation pertains indiscriminately to every ministry of the Church, nevertheless, when the Church had grown, it was assigned to the custodians and administrators of the sacred treasury, and was consecrated by the Apostles themselves under the name of daily ministry [διακονίας καθημερινῆς] and of tables [τῶν τραπεζῶν] (ibid. 6. 1, 2). In that sense, therefore, deacons are the sacred custodians and stewards of the treasure of material things, called to this office by God through the Church.

units.la: Quorum in prisca Ecclesia duo distincta collegia fuerunt, unum virorum, alterum viduarum, quæ Diaconissæ vocabantur. Quarum etiam Plinius junior meminit, Epist. lib. X. 97. eas Ministras vocat. S. Paulo nomine μεταδιδόντων communicantium, seu distribuentium iis, qui opus habent, Rom. XII. 8. veniunt. Propria igitur Diaconorum ejusmodi administratio fuit cura pauperum, quorum usibus vel publicè in Agapis, vel privatim in familiis consulebatur. Agapärum ritus etsi ab ipsis etiam Apostolis aliquandiu usurpatus, 1. Cor. XI. 20. Ubi fideles divites æquè ac pauperes convenisse ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ in unum, hoc est, ad convivia sobria & modesta, sed ex facultatibus divitum instructa crebrò convenisse ἐν ἀγάπαις συνδειπνοῦντες conviventes in agapis 2. Petr. II. 13. Jud. v. 12. dicuntur. Iisdem tamen, uti videtur, authoribus perspectis, quæ inde enascebantur, incommodis, sublatus est; succedentibus earum in locum eleemosynis, & bonis Ecclesiæ, ex quibus stipendia dantur laborantibus in verbo, bona ptochotrophiorum, orphanotrophiorum, xenotrophiorum, & similia. Privatim in familiis omne genus pauperibus per eleemosynas quascunque, spontaneas oblationes, vel ipsis pauperibus factas, vel in commune collatas, consuli svevit.
units.tr: In the ancient Church there were two distinct colleges of these, one of men, the other of widows, who were called deaconesses. Pliny the Younger also mentions them (Epist. bk. 10, no. 97), calling them ministers. St Paul names them as those who share [μεταδιδόντων], that is, distribute to those who have need (Rom. 12. 8). The proper administration of such deacons was therefore the care of the poor, whose needs were attended to either publicly at the agapes or privately in households. Although the rite of the agapes was used for some time even by the Apostles themselves (1 Cor. 11. 20), where the rich and the poor of the faithful gathered together [ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ], that is, to sober and modest banquets, but furnished from the resources of the rich, and where they are often said to have feasted together in agapes [ἐν ἀγάπαις συνδειπνοῦντες] (2 Pet. 2. 13; Jude 12), nevertheless, as appears, the same authorities, having observed the inconveniences that arose from it, abolished it; and in its place came alms and the goods of the Church, from which stipends are given to those labouring in the word, the goods of houses for the poor, orphanages, hospices for strangers, and the like. In private, in households, it was customary to provide for the poor of every kind by whatever alms, voluntary offerings, whether made to the poor themselves or collected in common.

units.la: Eorum, quæ in commune conferebantur, curatores Diaconi fuerunt, quibus ad privatæ administrationis munus Diaconissæ, seu viduæ, quia conjuges maritis obstrictæ rem familiarem curare tenentur; non minores natu sexaginta annis, & nullo probro contaminatæ, & reliqua vita omni virtutum genere ornatæ, 1. Tim. V. 9. 10. adjungebantur, quia certum est, quædam ministeria in vita privata à fœminis quàm à viris commodius & aptiùs præstari. Partes diaconatus ejusmodi duæ sunt, sacri thesauri sancta collectio, & ejusdem justa distributio. Illa, qua ἐυλογία à fidelibus καθὼς ἐαν ἔχῃ ἡς sicut quisque habuit, 2. Cor. VIII. 12. sponte oblatæ summa fide in ærarium inferuntur: ista, qua in pauperum usus eadem fide erogantur, & pro singulorum egestate distribuuntur.
units.tr: The custodians of what was contributed in common were the deacons, and to them, for the office of private administration, were joined deaconesses, or widows, since married women are bound to their husbands and are obliged to look after the household; these were not younger than sixty years, not stained by any disgrace, and adorned in the rest of their life with every kind of virtue (1 Tim. 5. 9, 10), because it is certain that certain ministries in private life are performed more fittingly and suitably by women than by men. The parts of this diaconate are two: the holy collection of the sacred treasury, and its just distribution. The former, by which the bounty [ἐυλογία] offered freely by the faithful, as each has means [καθὼς ἐαν ἔχῃ ἡς] (2 Cor. 8. 12), is brought into the treasury with the greatest good faith; the latter, by which it is spent with the same good faith on the needs of the poor and distributed according to the want of each.

units.la: Sacramentorum verò administratio non magis quàm verbi prædicatio ad ejusmodi Diaconorum primigeniam institutionem pertinuit. Neque ad rem exempla Stephani & Philippi, Diaconi utriusque, faciunt. Nam Stephanus quidem apologetica ad populum oratione usus causam apud judices dixit, Actor. VII. 2. &c. non vel verbum, vel Sacramenta administravit. Philippus verò ex Diacono Evangelista factus, vel extra ordinem à Deo per Angelum vocatus est: quod singularis revelatio, ibid. VIII. 26. testari videtur; vel priùs quàm Hierosolymis digrederetur, ab Apostolis ad hunc ministerii gradum promotus est. Sed crevit tamen sensim eorum dignitas; ac Verbi & Sacramentorum ministerium apud veteres eos obiisse, vix dubitari potest.
units.tr: The administration of the sacraments, no less than the preaching of the Word, did not belong to the original institution of such deacons. Nor do the examples of Stephen and Philip, both deacons, bear on the point. Stephen indeed made a defence before the people and pleaded his cause before the judges, Acts 7:2 etc., but he administered neither the Word nor the sacraments. Philip, who became an evangelist from being a deacon, was called by God through an angel outside the ordinary way, as the singular revelation in Acts 8:26 seems to attest; or else, before he left Jerusalem, he was promoted to this rank of ministry by the Apostles. Yet their dignity gradually grew, and it can scarcely be doubted that the ancients discharged the ministry of Word and sacraments.

units.la: Nam eo sensu passim Diaconi & Diaconnes in historia Ecclesiastica occurrunt. Sicut in Papatu, in Missatico dramate, sacrificulo ministrant, & secundas, mimorum instar, partes tractant. Quæ à prima eorum origine aliena sunt. Tam enim bonorum Ecclesiæ curatores sunt; & munus illorum ad omnes illos, qui sive facultates Ecclesiæ curant, sive pauperibus & ægrotis curandis consecrantur; quocunque illi nomine veniant, transiit.
units.tr: In that sense deacons and deaconesses appear everywhere in ecclesiastical history. Just as in Papacy, in the drama of the Mass, they minister to the little priest and play secondary parts, like mimes. These are foreign to their original character. For they are curators of the Church's goods, and their office has passed to all those who either look after the Church's property or are devoted to the care of the poor and the sick, under whatever name they go.

units.la: LVIII. Diaconi ejusmodi, seu Eleemosynarii curatores quivis bonorum Ecclesiæ & pauperum atque ægrotorum, perinde ut reliqui Ecclesiæ ministri, ad munus illud legitimè sive ab Ecclesia, sive à Magistratu, bonorum Ecclesiæ custode & tutore, sed nomine Ecclesiæ, vocari debent.
units.tr: LVIII. Deacons of this kind, or almoners, that is, any curators of the goods of the Church and of the poor and the sick, ought, just like the other ministers of the Church, to be lawfully called to that office, either by the Church or by the magistrate, the guardian and trustee of the Church's goods, but in the name of the Church.

units.la: Nam etiam primi illi septem Ecclesiæ Diaconi ab Ecclesia electi sunt, & iisdem Apostoli inter precandum manus imposuerunt, Actor. VI. 5. 6. Et de iisdem S. Paulus: Hi verò probentur prius, & postea διακονείτωσαν ministrent, 1. Tim. III. 10. In δοκιμασία hac æquè atque muneris ipsius administratione pe in universum S. Paulus ἁπλότητα simplicitatem exigit. Qui impertitus seu distribuit,in simplicitate distribuat,Rom. XII. 8. Quæ simplicitas fraudi opponitur,atque id postulat,ut qui id facit,nihil aliud spectet,quàm ut egenos adjuvet, non verò id agat, ut eleemosynis piorum ad commodum suum abutatur, sed plura etiam alibi requirit: Diaconos, inquiens,similiter (eligi volo) graves, non bilingues, non ad vinum multum propensos,non turpis lucri studiosos; habentes mysterium fidei in pura conscientia, (non ignaros mysterii fidei, seu verbi, quod Deus ad fidem revelavit,sed fundamentum ejus præ se ferentes, & in ore habentes, ut pateat eos verè Deum, Ecclesiam & fratres in Christo amare; atque id in pura conscientia, ne eam aliquid fingendo, vel temerè falsum dicendo polluant. Nam fieri potest,ut qui ministrant, & quibus ministerium exhibetur, de communi fide colloquantur, & tentati etiam atque errantes corrigendi sint) uxores similiter graves,non calumniatrices (quod fere sexus garruli vitium est,& occasionem ibi habere potest,ubi multorum infirmitates sciri possunt, & cum multis colloqui necesse est) sobrias, fideles in omnibus. Diaconi sint unius uxoris viri, qui liberis,& propriis domibus bene præsint, 1. Tim. III. 8-13. De Diaconissarum requisitis plura cap. V. 4. &c. habet. Manifestum est, absque ejusmodi dotibus ministerium adeò honestum & necessarium, quod vicem Ecclesiæ & fidelium ad charitatem in fratribus tot communionis Sanctorum vinculis conjunctissimis exercendam subit, honestè, decorè & utiliter administrari non posse. Accedit,quòd Diaconi in Ecclesia noscuntur ii, quibus Ecclesia multum confidit & tribuit, qui proin Ecclesiæ pudori probro esse non debent. Neque exiguum ad rite atque fideliter munere hoc defungendum incentivum habet subsequens promissio: Nam qui bene ministraverint βαθμὸν ἑαυτοῖς καλὸν περιποιοῦνται gradum sibi bonum parant,& multam fiduciam in fide,quæ in Christo Jesu est, ibid. v. 13. Qui βαθμὸς gradus potuit esse ad ἐπισκοπὴν Episcopi & curatoris Ecclesiæ munus. Nam ex iis, quorum explorata fides,industria,charitas, & qui mysterium fidei in pura conscientia habent, Episcopi tutissimè sumi potuerunt. Uti etiam Philippus Diaconus fidelitate sua gradum sibi ad Evangelistæ munus munivisse videtur. Licèt enim hic curæ mensarum necessarius ad Episcopatum gradus non sit,tamen, cæteris paribus ad curandam & regendam Ecclesiam idonei illi maximè videri possunt, qui τὰς χρείας necessitatibus fidelium dextrè & religiosè ministrarunt. Ex eodem ministerio fideli & inculpato diaconi magnam fiduciam in fide,quæ in Christo Jesu est,habent; quia quod faciunt, bonum est,in quo δοκιμὴν fidei & charitatis est, quæ παρρησίαν fiduciam multam, in qua fidei perfectio consistit, gignit.
units.tr: For those first seven deacons of the Church were also chosen by the Church, and the Apostles laid their hands on them while praying, Acts 6:5-6. And of these same men St Paul says: "But let them first be proved, and then let them minister" [diakoneitōsan], 1 Tim. 3:10. In this testing, as well as in the administration of the office itself, St Paul generally requires simplicity [haplotēs]. "He who gives, let him give in simplicity", Rom. 12:8. This simplicity is opposed to fraud, and it demands that whoever does this should look to nothing else than helping the needy, and not act so as to turn the alms of the pious to his own advantage. But elsewhere he requires still more: "Deacons, he says, likewise (I wish them to be chosen) grave, not double-tongued, not given much to wine, not greedy for base gain; holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience," (not ignorant of the mystery of the faith, that is, of the Word which God revealed for faith, but bearing its foundation before them and having it on their lips, so that it is plain that they truly love God, the Church and the brethren in Christ; and this in a pure conscience, lest they defile it by feigning anything or rashly saying what is false. For it can happen that those who minister, and those to whom the ministry is given, talk together about the common faith, and those who are tempted and go astray must be corrected) "wives likewise grave, not slanderers" (which is almost the vice of the chattering sex, and can have occasion where the weaknesses of many can be known and it is necessary to converse with many) "sober, faithful in all things. Let deacons be husbands of one wife, who rule well their children and their own houses," 1 Tim. 3:8-13. He has more on the requirements of deaconesses in ch. 5:4 etc. It is plain that without such qualities a ministry so honourable and necessary, which takes the place of the Church and of the faithful in exercising charity towards the brethren through the closest bonds of the communion of saints, cannot be administered honourably, becomingly and usefully. Add to this that deacons are known in the Church as those in whom the Church places great confidence and to whom it entrusts much, and who therefore ought not to be a shame or reproach to the Church. Nor does the following promise give a small incentive to discharge this office rightly and faithfully: "For those who minister well acquire for themselves a good standing [bathmon kalon], and great confidence in the faith which is in Christ Jesus," ibid. v. 13. This standing [bathmos] could be a step to the office of bishop [episkopē] and curator of the Church. For from those whose faith, diligence and charity have been tested, and who hold the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience, bishops could most safely be taken. Just so Philip the deacon seems to have prepared for himself a step to the office of evangelist by his faithfulness. For although the care of tables is not a necessary step to the episcopate, nevertheless, other things being equal, those who have ministered skilfully and devoutly to the needs [tas chreias] of the faithful may seem especially fit to care for and govern the Church. From the same faithful and blameless ministry, deacons have great confidence in the faith which is in Christ Jesus, because what they do is good, and in it there is the proof [dokimēn] of faith and charity, which produces boldness [parrēsian], great confidence, in which the perfection of faith consists.

units.la: LIX.
units.tr: LIX.

units.la: Fuerunt ordines Ministrorum Ecclesiæ, per quos illa in hac vita gubernatur. Gubernatio ipsa in eorum potestate & officio atque utriusque officio consistit. De Officio singulorum in universum, quantum satis est, diximus. Potestas inprimis Pastorum Ecclesiæ in potestate clavium continetur. Dabo tibi claves Regni cælorum. Et quicquid ligaveris in terra,
units.tr: There were orders of ministers of the Church, through whom she is governed in this life. The government itself consists in their power and their office, and in the office of each. We have said enough in general about the office of individuals. The power of the Church's pastors is contained above all in the power of the keys: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you bind on earth,

units.la: ligatum erit in Cœlis. Et quicquid solveris in terra, erit solutum in Cœlis, Matth. XVI. 19. De hac potestate multa operosè disputarunt illi, qui potestati suæ omnia in terris summa subjecerunt, & ex clavibus Ecclesiæ datis enses, lanceas,sceptra & coronas cuderunt, plenámque in maxima Regna, corpora & animas earum obtentu potestatem sibi vendicarunt; idque contra mandatum Domini,qui suis dominium prohibuit,humilitatem autem maximopere commendavit. Nam discipulis quærentibus, quis in Regno Cœlorum seu Ecclesia, major sit, statuto in medio παιδίῳ puerulo respondit: Amen dico vobis: Nisi conversi fiatis instar puerulorum, in Regnum Cœlorum non ingredieminí. Quisquis igitur se humiliaverit instar pueruli illius,is major,vel maximus est in Regno Cœlorum, ibid. XVIII. 1-5. Quæ parabola ex Davide sumpta videtur,sic de se profitente, Jehova,non extulit se cor meum,neque extulerunt se oculi mei, & non ambulavi in magnis & mirabilibus præme. Si non sedavi & compescui animam meam! Ut infantis ablactati apud matrem suam, ut ablactati apud me est anima mea! Psal. CXXXI. 1. 2. Sicut enim infans ablactatus fidit parentibus suis, iisque sui regimen permittit: ita Ecclesiæ est fieri instar infantum, adeóque omnia Deo adscribere,ejusque regimen admittere,non suis viribus quicquam tribuere, vel Regni Dei gubernationem ultra ministerii fidelitatem sibi arrogare. Alibi Christus: Nostis, quòd Principes gentium dominentur iis, & magnates eas in potestatem suam redigant; Non sic erit apud vos. Sed qui voluerit in vobis magnus fieri, erit vester minister. Et qui inter vos primus esse voluerit,erit servus vester. Sicut Filius hominis non venit, ut sibi ministraretur,sed ut ministraret ipse,& daret animam suam vice multorum, Matth. XX. 25-28. Luc. XXII. 25.
units.tr: will be bound in heaven. And whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven, Matt. 16:19. Many who have subjected all things on earth to their own power have argued at length about this power. From the keys given to the Church they have forged swords, lances, sceptres and crowns, and under this pretext they have claimed for themselves power over the bodies and souls of the greatest kingdoms. They did this against the command of the Lord, who forbade his disciples to lord it over others and most strongly commended humility. When the disciples asked who is greater in the kingdom of heaven, that is, in the Church, he set a little child [παιδίῳ] in the midst and answered: Truly I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest [or, is greater] in the kingdom of heaven, ibid. 18:1-5. This parable seems to be taken from David, who professed of himself: LORD, my heart is not lifted up, nor are my eyes raised too high; I do not occupy myself with great matters or things too wonderful for me. Surely I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; my soul is like a weaned child within me, Ps. 131:1, 2. For as a weaned child trusts its parents and leaves its care to them, so the Church ought to become like a little child, ascribing everything to God and admitting his government, attributing nothing to her own strength, and not claiming for herself the governance of the kingdom of God beyond the faithfulness of her ministry. Christ says elsewhere: You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great men exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you. But whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your minister, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant. Just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many, Matt. 20:25-28; Luke 22:25.

units.la: LX. In universum potestas distingui solet. Alia enim est minima, qua quis ita agit, ut vel contineat alium in officio,vel revocet, & non continentis vel revocantis authoritate, sed rei duntaxat veritate nititur, ita ut,qui ea utitur, summisse agat, neque ei liceat eum, qui admonitione utitur, increpare, vel quicquam, quod pœnæ rationem habeat, facere; quali potestate minoris erga majores, filii erga parentes, servi erga heros uti possunt: vel minimæ proximæ, qualis est paris in parem, quæ ἀγαπητικῶς fine authoritate & imperio exercetur,sic tamen, ut recta monenti non obediens, ad incutiendum ei pudorem,vitari possit, quod pœnæ quodammodo rationem habet: vel magna, cùm quis in officio continet,vel ad illud revocat authoritate, sed quæ ejusmodi tamen est,ut nihil habeat,quo vel intellectum vel hominem externum cogere possit, & si res ipsa subsit,magna nihilominus sit;qualis est doctoris in Schola,cui cum viris res est,quíque munere suo fungens, aliquid facere potest, quod pœnæ rationem habet, non objurgando tantùm imparentes authoritate publica,sed etiam, si animum obfirmaverit, summovendo; vel major, quæ tanta est, ut non faciat jus,sed juri tamen facto testimonium infallibile perhibeat, velut cùm olim in Republica Romana prudentes & Juris consulti sic jus interpretati sunt, ut eorum interpretatione ipsimet judices stare debuedebuerint: vel maxima,qua quidem jus aliquis non facit,sed tamen contemptoribus juris poenam irrogare potest: vel denique multò maxima, quæ jus facit, quod alioqui jus non erat, & conjuncta insuper est cum authoritate puniendi eos,qui secus fecerint. Quo discrimine constituto Ecclesiæ potestas non duntaxat vel minima, vel proxima minimæ, sed magna tribui solet,in eo consistens,quòd ejus Ministri cum authoritate verbum Dei prædicare, Sacramenta administrare, &, Ecclesia consentiente,contumaces censuris in verbo Dei præceptis, notare potest. Sed eidem negatur potestas & major, quia non sic jus Divinum interpretari potest, ut conscientia omnium in interpretatione ista acquiescere teneatur: & maxima, quia non potest subjectos censuris & poenis proprie dictis,verae in foro Dei vindictae rationem habentibus, sive lata sententia,sive executione, coercere & in ordinem redigere: & multò maxima, quia nec leges, citra rationem contemptus & scandali, conscientiam obligantes rogare,adeóque nec refractarios poenis proprie dictis,æternis & infernalibus mulctare & afficere potest. Nam posteriores hæ potestatis species soli Christo, Ecclesiæ capiti & Domino competunt.
units.tr: LX. Power is commonly distinguished in general terms. One kind is the least, by which someone so acts that he either restrains another in his duty or calls him back, relying not on the authority of the one restraining or recalling but only on the truth of the matter. The one who uses it must act humbly, and it is not permitted to rebuke the one he admonishes or to do anything that has the character of punishment. Younger people over elders, children over parents, and servants over masters may use this kind of power. Another kind is the least near, such as exists between equals, exercised in a loving manner [ἀγαπητικῶς] without authority or command. Yet if someone refuses to obey correct admonition, he may be avoided so as to bring shame on him, which in some measure has the character of punishment. Another is the great, when someone restrains another in his duty or calls him back to it by authority; but this authority is such that it has nothing by which it can compel either the understanding or the outward person. Even so, if the matter itself supports it, it remains great. Such is the power of a teacher in a school, who deals with men and who, in performing his task, can do something that has the character of punishment: not only by rebuking the disobedient with public authority, but also, if they harden their hearts, by removing them. Another is the greater, which is so great that it does not make law, but nonetheless bears infallible witness to a law already made. So once in the Roman republic the wise men and jurists interpreted the law in such a way that the judges themselves had to abide by their interpretation. Another is the greatest, by which someone does not make law but can still impose punishment on those who despise the law. Finally, there is the far greatest, which makes law, something that otherwise would not be law, and is moreover joined with authority to punish those who act otherwise. With this distinction settled, the power of the Church is usually not ascribed as merely the least or the near least, but as great. It consists in this: that her ministers, with authority, can preach the Word of God, administer the sacraments, and, with the consent of the Church, mark the contumacious with censures prescribed in the Word of God. But the Church is denied the greater, because she cannot interpret the divine law in such a way that the consciences of all are bound to acquiesce in her interpretation. She is denied the greatest, because she cannot restrain and bring into order those under her by censures and penalties properly so called, which carry the character of true vengeance in the court of God, whether by pronouncing sentence or by carrying it out. And she is denied the far greatest, because she cannot impose laws binding the conscience, apart from the matter of contempt and scandal, and therefore cannot punish or afflict the refractory with penalties properly so called, eternal and infernal. For these latter kinds of power belong only to Christ, the head and Lord of the Church.

units.la: LXI. Sed missa hac distinctione potestatis clavium potius potestatem, cujus symbolo ab ipso Christo sancito,quamcunque Ecclesiæ potestatem habet, possidet, discriminemus & explicemus. Eliakimum filium Chilkijæ,in locum Sebnæ promi-condi, & palatio regio Ezechiæ præfecti,subrogatumDeus inter alia,data clavi domus Davidis,investivit. Et dabo clavim domus Davidis in humerum ejus; & aperiet, ac nemo claudet; & claudet,ac nemo aperiet, Esaj. XXII. 22. Qua ratione ei curam palatii, seu domus Davidis, sic Deus commisit,ut nihil in Regia secretum esset,ad quod ille non admitteretur. Nam ministri Regis sub ipsius manu erant, nec cuiquam ad Regem accedere,vel coram eo stare, non admittente ipso liceret. Cùm ergo Rex ejus officio acquiesceret,& id approbaret, ipso aperiente,nemo claudebat & claudente,nemo aperiebat. De Christo dicitur: Hæc dicit ille sanctus, ille verax ὁ ἔχων τὴν κλεῖδα τῆς Δαυείδ, ὁ ἀνοίγων, καὶ οὐδεὶς κλείει· καὶ κλείει, καὶ οὐδεὶς ἀνοίγει, qui habet clavim Davidis: qui aperit, & nemo claudit; claudit, & nemo aperit, Apoc. III. 7. Satis liquet de Christo hæc dici,imitatione phrasewos apud Esajam de Eliakimo, sed cum hoc discrimine, quòd Eliakim minister palatii Regii, Christus Dominus Davidis est. Unde David ipse: Dixit Jehova לאדני Domino meo, CX. 1. Ideo Eliakimo ceu ministro, committebantur claves domus, seu Regiæ Davidis: at Christus dicitur ἔχειν τὴν κλεῖδα τοῦ Δαυείδ habere (ceu Dominus) clavim (non domus, sed simpliciter) Davidis, hoc est, Regni Davidis. Nam Regnum Davidis magnam partem in potestate judicandi in populo Dei consistebat. Sed Christus habet clavim Davidis,hoc est,ceu Rex spiritualis,Regnum Davidis,quia & Davidis Dominus est, & David, quanquam secundum carnem ejus pater, à Christo Regnum illud externum in populo Dei accepit, & Principatus, abolito Regno externo posterorum Davidis, in ipsius humerum transfiit,ita ut populum Dei hactenus etiam externa paedagogia à Regibus, Sacerdotibus & Senioribus gubernatum ipse solus, non in litera & umbris, sed in spiritu & veritate; non in servitute, sed in libertate; non per sceptrum aureum,vel gladium, sed per Spiritum & Verbum suum administraret. Ideo dicitur ὁ ἔχων τὴν κλεῖδα Δαυείδ. Ille qui habet clavim Davidis,nempe βασιλικῶς architectonicè, heriliter & dominicè, atque per repraesentationem seu exhibitionem Regni Coelorum. Has claves Christus sibi reservavit, & iisdem utitur, quando tum dat ostium apertum coram praedicantibus Evangelium, quod nemo claudat, Apoc. III. 8. Actor. XVI. 14. Apoc. XXI. 25. tum parat locum in Coelo,& nos assumit, Joh. XIV. 2. 3. Hebr. VI. 20. tum aditum ad Deum in fiducia concedit, ibid. X. 19. 20. 21. Restant κλεῖδες βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν claves Regni coelorum, à Christo datae Petro, Matth. XVI. 19. Ubi per claves Regni Coelorum metonymicè ἐξουσίαν seu potestatem significari, extra dubitationis aleam est. Nam claudere, solvere opus est, ad quod faciendum potestate concessa opus servo,famulo,oeconomo est. Qua potestate qui gaudent, à nemine juste impediri possunt,quò minùs ea ex praescripto utantur; imò ea legitimè utentes omnes adjuvare tenentur. Cúmque & Petrus,cui haec potestas data est,& omnes quibus in Petri persona potestas haec data est, non ipsi Domini, heri,sed Christi,qui εἰς Κύριον unus & solus Dominus est,1. Corinth. VIII. 6. servi,2. Petr. I. 1. adeóque famuli & oeconomi sint,illorum potestas à Christo, hero ac Domino, iis tributa, non herilis, sed oeconomica & ministerialis sit oportet.
units.tr: LXI. But setting aside this distinction, let us rather define and explain the power of the keys, the power which the Church possesses, under the sign sanctioned by Christ himself. God, among other things, invested Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was appointed in place of Shebna, the steward of the palace and of King Hezekiah, with the key of the house of David: I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David; he shall open, and no one shall shut; he shall shut, and no one shall open, Isa. 22:22. By this arrangement God committed the care of the palace, or house of David, to him in such a way that nothing in the royal household was secret from him, and no one could come to the king or stand before him unless he admitted them. For the king's servants were under his hand, and no one could approach the king or appear before him unless he allowed it. Since the king acquiesced in his office and approved it, when he opened no one shut, and when he shut no one opened. Of Christ it is said: These things says the holy one, the true one, [ὁ ἔχων τὴν κλεῖδα τῆς Δαυείδ, ὁ ἀνοίγων, καὶ οὐδεὶς κλείει· καὶ κλείει, καὶ οὐδεὶς ἀνοίγει] who has the key of David; he opens, and no one shuts; he shuts, and no one opens, Rev. 3:7. It is clear enough that these words are said of Christ in imitation of the phrasing in Isaiah about Eliakim, but with this difference: Eliakim was the minister of the royal palace, while Christ is the Lord of David. Hence David himself says: The LORD said to my Lord [לאדני], Ps. 110:1. Therefore the keys of the house, or royal house of David, were committed to Eliakim as a minister; but Christ is said to have [ἔχειν τὴν κλεῖδα τοῦ Δαυείδ] the key of David (as Lord), not of the house but simply of David, that is, of the kingdom of David. For the kingdom of David consisted largely in the power of judging the people of God. But Christ has the key of David, that is, as spiritual King, the kingdom of David, because he is both Lord of David and, although David was his father according to the flesh, David received that external kingdom over the people of God from Christ. With the external kingdom of David's posterity abolished, the principate passed into Christ's shoulder, so that he alone governs the people of God, who until then were guided by external pedagogy through kings, priests and elders. He governs them not in letter and shadows but in spirit and truth; not in servitude but in liberty; not by a golden sceptre or sword but through his Spirit and his Word. Therefore he is called [ὁ ἔχων τὴν κλεῖδα Δαυείδ] the one who has the key of David, namely, [βασιλικῶς] as a royal master builder, as lord and master, and through the representation or exhibition of the kingdom of heaven. Christ reserved these keys for himself and uses them when he sets an open door before those preaching the gospel, which no one can shut, Rev. 3:8; Acts 16:14; Rev. 21:25; when he prepares a place in heaven and takes us to himself, John 14:2, 3; Heb. 6:20; and when he grants access to God in confidence, ibid. 10:19-21. There remain the keys of the kingdom of heaven [κλεῖδες βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν], given by Christ to Peter, Matt. 16:19. That by the keys of the kingdom of heaven power [ἐξουσίαν] is signified by metonymy is beyond doubt. For to shut and to loose is work that requires a servant, household steward or manager, with the power granted to him. Those who possess this power cannot justly be prevented by anyone from using it according to the rule; indeed, all are bound to help those who use it lawfully. Since Peter, to whom this power was given, and all to whom this power was given in Peter's person, are not masters of their own, but servants of Christ, who alone is one and sole Lord, 1 Cor. 8:6, and servants and stewards, 1 Pet. 1:1, their power must be granted to them by Christ, the master and Lord, not in the manner of a master, but in an economic and ministerial way.

units.la: LXII. Duplex ergo clavium Regni Coelorum potestas,herilis atque dominica,& ministerialis atque oeconomica est. Illa mera & absoluta est, & juris potestas est, atque Christo soli,omnia sibi subjicienti competit. Data,inquit,mihi est omnis potestas in Coelo & in terra, Matth. XXVIII. 18. Ego sum primus & novissimus, & vivens, & fui mortuus, & ecce vivens sum in secula seculorum, Amen. Et habeo claves inferni & mortis, Apoc. I. 17. 18. Sanctus & verax ille, qui habet clavim Davidis,&c. ibid. III. 7. Ille domus suae structor,& Filius super domum suam,cujus domus nos sumus, Hebr. III. 3. 6. Rex, Dominus, Caput Ecclesiae, ceu Corporis sui; de quo supra משרה על שכמו Principatus est super humerum ejus, Esaj. IX. 6. Nam gubernationem non injicit aliis in suos humeros,sed sibi servat,& sua potestat utitur, gubernans omnia. Haec est potestas officii, seu ministerialis, limitata ab eo,qui plena potestate utitur. Ministerio igitur quàm imperio similior est. Concedit enim Dominus aliquis oeconomo suo potestatem in domum suam, quo nomine ei claves dat, quibus in domum intromittat,vel domo excludat,quos Dominus intromitti,vel excludi vult. Juxta hanc potestatem facit minister ex officio,quod à Domino facere jussus est,& Dominus ratum habet, quod ille clave non errante, facit, ipsúmque ministri factum, perinde ut suum,agnosci & aestimari vult. Nisi verò minister atque oeconomus res omnes sic expediverit, uti jussus à Domino est, sed fidei sux suæ limites transfilierit, irritum à Domino habetur,quod ille fecit. Proin potestas Ecclesiastica Ministrorum Ecclesiæ funêtio illa est,qua Ministri Ecclesiam Dei gubernant, cunêta facientes ex præscripto Domini, quæ cùm sic facta sunt , fideles velut ab ipso Domino facta reputare debent.
units.tr: LXII. The twofold power of the keys of the kingdom of heaven is therefore lordly and dominical, and also ministerial and stewardly. The former is pure and absolute, a power of right, and belongs to Christ alone, who subjects all things to himself. All power is given to me, he says, in heaven and on earth, Matt. 28:18. I am the first and the last, and living, and I was dead, and behold I am alive for ever and ever, Amen. And I have the keys of hell and of death, Rev. 1:17-18. He who is holy and true, who has the key of David, etc., ibid. 3:7. He is the builder of his house, and the Son over his own house, whose house we are, Heb. 3:3, 6. He is King, Lord, and Head of the Church, as of his own body, of whom above it is said, the principality is upon his shoulder [משרה על שכמו], Isa. 9:6. For he does not lay the government upon the shoulders of others but keeps it for himself and uses his own power, governing all things. This is the power of office, or ministerial power, limited by him who uses full power. It is therefore more like a ministry than a command. For a lord grants his steward power over his house, and for that purpose gives him keys with which to admit into the house, or shut out of it, whoever the Lord wishes admitted or excluded. By virtue of this power the minister, in his office, does what he has been ordered by the Lord to do, and the Lord wishes to ratify what he does with a key that does not err, and wishes the minister's act to be acknowledged and valued just as if it were his own. But if the minister and steward has not arranged all things as he was ordered by the Lord, and has overstepped the limits of his trust, what he has done is held null by the Lord. Therefore ecclesiastical power is that function of the ministers of the Church by which they govern the Church of God, doing all things according to the Lord's prescription; and when these things have been done in this way, the faithful ought to regard them as done by the Lord himself.

units.la: LXIII. Potestas clavium S. Petro collata in potestate ligandi in terra & solvendi ponitur. Ligare autem Christus ipse retinere peccata, & solvere,remittere peccata explicat. Quorum remiseritis peccata,remissa erunt. Quorum retinueritis, retenta erunt, Joh.XX.23. Quid enim aliud Petro datum, quando ei claves Regni Cœlorum commissæ sunt, Scriptura testatur ? Numquid hoc,ut ipse novas leges pro arbitrio condere,vel ex plenitudine potestatis & motu proprio leges Divinas irritas facere , vel omnino ex Regno CœlorumRegnum humanum,& principatum terrenum facere posset? Sic Papa Petri successor nuncupatus, somniat. Sed sic Regnum Cœlorum,&Regnum solius Dei in Christo non esset, quia ille nec novas leges tulit, nec Regnum ex mundo habuit. Sed accepit S. Petrus verbum ἐμφυλον insitum, quo regeneramur, legem regiam libertatis, Jac. I. 18·21. II. 8. 12. 1. Petr. I. 23. 24. Hoc mediante , & per eundem fideliter prædicato non tantùm Judæi,sed etiam gentes regenerari debuerunt, ut ita participes Regni Cœlorum fierent, atque in illa ipsa rupe , in qua & Petrus, velut jam populo Israelitico data & manifestata ædificarentur, atque in ea ad vitam æternam conservarentur. Tum etiam accepit à Christo potestatem juxta verbum illud sibi commissum, & à se prædicatum judicandi,vel consolandi eos,qui verbo prædicato non obedirent, vel obedirent. Quod maximi momenti est , quia hoc verbum nemini antea datum est. Omnes enim, qui antecesserunt, fuerunt sub νόμῳ ἐνσολῆς Ϛαρκικῆς lege præcepti carnalis , quæ Sacerdotibus & præstitibus populi,ceu patribus carnis data fuit,cum imperio, & ea, qua visum est, παιδείᾳ urgenda, Hebr. XII. 9. 10. Nunc verò lex libertatis ,lex Regis Christi, potentia Spiritus S. ad salutem omni credenti , qua omnes ad Christum cum promissione justitiæ & libertatis à jugo legis, & æternam salutem,traditur; atque traditur non amplius Sacerdotibus , vel principibus seculi prioris, sed Petro, piscatori, uni è multis,imò Galilæo,homini literarum & doctrinæ experti, & ei quidem primo, ut ex Act.X.13.28.34.35. 43.44. patet. Cùm igitur aliunde clarum sit, quid S. Petro noviter datum sit,& quòd id per claves Regni Cœlorum rectè intelligi possit; & quòd verbum & judicium hoc reliquis etiam Apostolis , imò toti Ecclesiæ datum sit, Matth.XVIII.17. 1.Cor. V. 4. dubitari non potest, quin potestas clavium non sit jurisdictio aliqua soli Petro in reliquos Apostolos & totam Ecclesiam , sed potestas prædicandi Evangelium Judæis & Gentibus , adeóque docendi, monendi, redarguendi,consolandi, judicandi consentiente Ecclesia, atque ea denique faciendi, quæ his finibus inserviunt,atque his modis ligandi,seu peccata retinendi, & solvendi,seu peccata remittendi. Si enim quod Patris familias & Domini, Christi solius est, atque cum principali & absoluta potestate conjunêtum est,sequestretur, nihil aliud uspiam Scriptura Ecclesiæ ministris vendicat: & hæc, quæ dixi, passim vendicat.
units.tr: LXIII. The power of the keys given to St. Peter is placed in the power of binding on earth and loosing. Christ himself explains binding as retaining sins, and loosing as remitting sins: Whose sins you remit, they are remitted; whose you retain, they are retained, John 20:23. For what else was given to Peter when the keys of the kingdom of heaven were committed to him, as Scripture testifies? Could he by this power make new laws at his own pleasure, or by the fullness of power and his own motion render the divine laws void, or altogether turn the kingdom of heaven into a human kingdom and an earthly principality? So the Pope, who is named Peter's successor, dreams. But then the kingdom of heaven would not be the kingdom of God alone in Christ, since Christ brought no new laws and had no kingdom from the world. St. Peter received the implanted word [ἔμφυτον λόγον], by which we are regenerated, the royal law of liberty, James 1:18, 21; 2:8, 12; 1 Pet. 1:23-24. Through this word, faithfully preached by him, not only Jews but also Gentiles were to be regenerated, so that they might become partakers of the kingdom of heaven and be built upon that very rock, on which Peter too was to be built, already given and made manifest to the Israelite people, and be preserved in it unto eternal life. Then he also received from Christ the power, according to that word committed to him and preached by him, of judging or comforting those who did or did not obey the preached word. This is of the greatest importance, because this word was given to no one before. For all who went before were under the law of carnal commandment [νόμῳ ἐντολῆς σαρκικῆς], which was given to priests and rulers of the people as to fathers of the flesh, with authority, and with that discipline [παιδεία] to be enforced as seemed fit, Heb. 12:9-10. But now the law of liberty, the law of King Christ, the power of the Holy Spirit unto salvation for every believer, by which all are brought to Christ with the promise of righteousness, liberty from the yoke of the law, and eternal salvation, is handed down; and it is handed down no longer to priests or princes of the former age, but to Peter, a fisherman, one of many, indeed a Galilean, a man versed in letters and teaching, and indeed to him first, as is clear from Acts 10:13, 28, 34-35, 43-44. Since, therefore, it is clear from elsewhere what was newly given to St. Peter, and that this can rightly be understood through the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and since this word and judgment was given also to the other apostles, indeed to the whole Church, Matt. 18:17; 1 Cor. 5:4, it cannot be doubted that the power of the keys is not some jurisdiction of Peter alone over the other apostles and the whole Church, but the power of preaching the Gospel to Jews and Gentiles, and so of teaching, admonishing, rebuking, comforting, and judging with the consent of the Church, and finally doing those things that serve these ends, and in these ways binding, that is retaining sins, and loosing, that is remitting sins. For if what belongs to the Father of the household and to Christ alone, and is joined with principal and absolute power, is set aside, Scripture claims nothing else anywhere for the ministers of the Church; and it claims everywhere the things I have mentioned.

units.la: LXIV. Clavium illa Potestas non uni Petro à Christo data est, sed ei,ut reliquorum Apostolorum & Ecclesiæ ministrorum , imò ipsius etiam Ecclesiæ paradigmati data est. Licèt enim unus Petrus compellatus sit,quia tamen omnes interrogati sunt verbis Christi: Vos autem quem me esse dicitis? Matth. XVI. 15. & unus Petrus pro unitate, seu omnibus Christo respondit, etiam responsum uni,pro unitate seu omnibus perhibitum,ad omnes,quorum nomine locutus est, pertinuit. Proin & symbolum clavium & res symbolo significata non uni illi,sed pluribus à Christo collata est. Amen dico vobis (discipulis, vers. 1. vel fratribus in nomine Christi corripientibus, v. 15. 16. imò etiam Ecclesiæ,& iis, qui immorigerum pro ethnico & publicano habere jubentur,v. 17.) quæcunque ligaveritis in terra, ligata erunt in Cœlo ; & quæcunque solveritis in terra, soluta erunt in Cœlo, Matth. XVIII. 18. Quibus verbis nec solus Petrus,nec Apostoli & eorum successores,vicaria auctoritate Christi,hoc est Papæ, congregati; verùm ministri quivis Ecclesiæ;imò etiam Ecclesia solutioni, vel ligationi consentiens , & cum eadem concurrens, intelligitur , quia potestas habendi aliquem pro ethnico & publicano est non solius Vicarii Christi,imò non est ejus,quia nullus est,sed Ecclesiæ totius; & sublatis Pastoribus Ecclesia , & cum Ecclesia etiam potestas clavium manet; &non soli Pastores,sed Ecclesia universa Christi Sponsa & mater familias est; cui proin clavium potestas collata est. Neque de nihilo est , quòd potestas condonandi peccata,adeóque solvendi cuivis etiam privato, qui priùs elenchum instituit,conceditur,Luc. XVII. 3. 4. Quomodo etiam apud Judæos moris erat etiam privatim denuntiare שמתה, quod reapse aliud non est quàm קללה execratio; dicendo אתה בשמתה Tu es in Schamatah, hoc est, in execrationem incidisti. Et necesse erat quærere remissionem,quæ vocabatur התרה solutio. Ideo claves Petro datas esse,ceu figuram & personam Ecclesiæ gerenti, Augustinus in Joh. tract. so. & 124. dixit,non eo sensu,quo Regno dari dicitur,quod datur Regi regnum repræsentanti, uti Hierarchici explicant, seu,uti Walenburgii fingunt , quo omnibus simul datum esse intelligitur , quod soli Petro datum est, quia omnium bono Petro datum est. Nam quæ sic dantur Regno,quia dantur Regi; iis solus Rex utitur,fruitur,non etiam Regnum ipsum. At sensit pro vero Augustinus, Ecclesiam seorsim etiam persona Petri clavibus uti,frui. S.Petrus igitur figuram personam Ecclesiæ gerendo eandem repræsentavit sociali modo, non ut princeps,sed ut socius Ϲυμπρεσβυτερος consenior, 1.Pet.V.1. & Ϲυνεργος cooperarius eorum,quos repræsentavit , ita ut societatis ejusdem jure beneficii ejusdem particeps esset. Si enim consortes in ædificatione supra Petram habuit,cur in clavibus consortes non etiam habuit ? Neque ullus Apostolus non egit solus , quod solus Petrus agere potuit. Magisterio enim & dominatu omnibus ex æquo interdictum est. Denique ultimus censor, Matth.XVIII. 17.
units.tr: LXIV. That power of the keys was given by Christ not to Peter alone, but to him as a model of the other apostles and ministers of the Church, indeed of the Church itself. For although Peter alone was addressed, yet since all were questioned in Christ's words, But who do you say that I am? Matt. 16:15, and one Peter answered for unity, that is, for all, the answer given by one for unity or for all also pertained to all in whose name he spoke. Hence both the symbol of the keys and the thing signified by the symbol were conferred by Christ not on that one man but on many. Truly I say to you (to the disciples, v. 1; or to brethren rebuking in the name of Christ, vv. 15-16; indeed also to the Church, and to those who are ordered to regard the stubborn as a heathen and a tax collector, v. 17), whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven, Matt. 18:18. By these words it is understood that not Peter alone, nor the apostles and their successors gathered together by the vicarious authority of Christ, that is, of the Pope, but any ministers of the Church are meant; indeed the Church itself is understood, consenting to the loosing or binding and concurring with it. For the power of holding someone as a heathen and a tax collector belongs not to the Vicar of Christ alone, indeed it is not his at all, since there is no such vicar, but to the whole Church. With the pastors removed, the Church remains, and with the Church the power of the keys remains; and not the pastors alone but the whole Church is the Spouse of Christ and the mother of the household, and so it is to her that the power of the keys was given. Nor is it for nothing that the power to forgive sins, and thus to loose, is granted even to a private person, who first undertakes a rebuke, Luke 17:3-4. Among the Jews too it was customary to denounce privately shammatah [שמתה], which in fact is nothing other than qelalah [קללה], execration, saying You are in shammatah [אתה בשמתה], that is, you have fallen into execration. And it was necessary to seek remission, which was called hatarah [התרה], solution. Hence Augustine, in John tractates 50 and 124, said that the keys were given to Peter as one bearing the figure and person of the Church, not in the sense in which a kingdom is said to be given to a king who represents the kingdom, as the Hierarchs explain, or in the sense in which Walenburg imagines, by which it is understood that what was given to Peter alone was given to all together, because it was given to Peter for the good of all. For things given to a kingdom in this way, because they are given to the king, are used and enjoyed by the king alone, not by the kingdom itself. But Augustine rightly thought that the Church also used and enjoyed the keys separately through the person of Peter. St. Peter, therefore, bearing the figure and person of the Church, represented it in a social manner, not as prince but as a fellow elder [συμπρεσβύτερος], 1 Pet. 5:1, and co-worker [συνεργός] with those whom he represented, so that by the right of the same fellowship he was a partaker of the same benefit. For if he had partners in building upon the rock, why should he not also have partners in the keys? Nor did any apostle act alone in what Peter alone could do. For mastery and domination were forbidden to all alike. Finally, the last judge, Matt. 18:17, is set up not Peter or any other, but the Church.

units.la: bbbb non vel Petrus,vel ullus alius,sed Ecclesia statuitur. Cùm porro claves Regni Coelorum potestatem retinendi vel remittendi peccata contulerint , illa ex æquo Apostolis omnibus à Christo collata est. Quorum sic ille ad Apostolos omnes,nullo eorum discrimine, remiseritis peccata remittentur iis; quorum retinueritis, retinebuntur, Joh. XX.23. Etenim cui peccata remittuntur,ei Regnum Coelorum aperitur; cui retinentur,eidem illud clauditur. Ille solvitur peccatorum reatu; hic eidem illigatur. Similia proin loca sunt, & quod apud Matthæum Petro,peculiariter,singularem ob causam, quia os cæterorum fuit, at non ipsi peculiare profsus,dictum est,id ipsum apud Johannem omnibus Apostolis à Christo ipso communicatur. Sed jus clavium in persona Petri toti Ecclesiæ collatum, diversimodè tamen in eadem exercetur. Nam jus pascendi per præconium publicum verbi , & Sacramentorum dispensationem solis præconibus : jus gubernandi solis præconibus & senioribus: jus sic judicandi,ut habeatur refractarius pro Ethnico & Publicano,ita Præconibus & Senioribus competit,ut ab ea consensus fraternitatis & Ecclesiæ totius exulare nec debeat, nec possit. Dixit enim Christus : Sit Tibi velut Ethnicus & publicanus,Matth. XVIII.17. Quæ alias foret , si Seniores judicium exerceant,fratres autem commisceantur iis,qui à Senioribus judicati fuerint. Etsi nullæ ea in re fraternitatis partes sunt,judicium nullum est,& quos Seniores judicaverint, eos simpliciter Ecclesia pro ethnicis habere debet , nullo jure videbimur à Romanis dissentire,qui propterea,quod Episcopis supremum & judicandi jus negamus, pro hæreticis nos habent. Hoc enim modo in Ecclesiam humanum nomen,& Principatus hominum loco , qui per verbum Dei fieri debet , introducitur. Cúmque ea Ministrorum Ecclesiæ vocatio, & non tantùm doctrina & definitio , sed etiam exploratio eorum, quæ præstabiliora docentur, & approbatio eorum,quæ in Synedriis,Synodis & Conciliis circa fidem , & gravioris momenti res, ad conscientiam hominis pertinentes constituuntur, ad jus clavium etiam pertineat , atque tum vocatio Ministrorum, quæ clavis illa,qua functionis publicæ fores reserantur, est; tum , approbatio & consensus doctrinæ decretis religionem & concernentibus testatus Ecclesiæ etiam non gubernantis sit,manifestum est, jus clavium quodammodo ad Ecclesiam etiam universam pertinere. Absque ea enim est,dominatio in Ecclesia inhiberi,& conscientiæ libertas retineri non potest. Tota igitur Ecclesia,sed in distinctis suis ordinibus & actibus nonnullis universæ fraternitati competentibus subjectum potestatis clavium recte Itatuitur.
units.tr: ...not Peter or any other single person, but the Church is established as the subject of the keys. Since the keys signify the power of opening the Kingdom of Heaven and of retaining or remitting sins, that power was conferred by Christ equally on all the Apostles. So he speaks to all of them, with no distinction among them: Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them; whose you retain, they are retained, John 20:23. For he to whom sins are remitted has the Kingdom of Heaven opened to him, and he to whom they are retained has it shut against him. The one is freed from the guilt of sin; the other is bound by it. The passages are therefore alike. What Matthew records as said to Peter in particular, for a special reason, because he was the mouth of the rest, and not as something peculiar to him, the same thing John shows Christ communicating to all the Apostles. The right of the keys was conferred on the whole Church in the person of Peter, but it is exercised in the Church in different ways. The right of feeding the flock, by the public proclamation of the Word and the dispensing of the sacraments, belongs only to the preachers; the right of governing belongs only to the preachers and elders. The right of judging, by which a stubborn person is to be held as a heathen and a tax collector, belongs to the preachers and elders in such a way that it must not and cannot be cut off from the consent of the brotherhood and of the whole Church. For Christ said: Let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector, Matt. 18:17. Otherwise, if the elders exercise judgement while the brothers have no share in it, and those whom the elders have judged are simply to be regarded by the Church as heathens, then, if there is no part for the brotherhood in this matter, there is no proper judgement at all. In that case we would seem to differ from the Romanists in no way, and yet they count us heretics for denying the supreme right of judgement to the bishops. In this way a human name and the rule of men would be introduced into the Church, in place of the rule that must come through the Word of God. Since the calling of the ministers of the Church, and not only their teaching and definition, but also the testing of those things that are taught as more excellent, and the approval of what is established in synods, synods and councils concerning faith and matters of greater weight pertaining to the conscience of men, belong also to the right of the keys, and since the calling of ministers, which is the key by which the doors of public office are unlocked, and the approval and consent of the Church, which witnesses to the decrees concerning religion, belong to the Church even when it is not governing, it is plain that the right of the keys in some measure pertains to the whole Church as well. Without this, domination cannot be restrained in the Church, nor can liberty of conscience be preserved. Therefore the whole Church is rightly set down as the subject of the power of the keys, yet in its distinct orders and in certain acts that belong to the whole brotherhood.

units.la: LXV. Ecclesiæ Ministris omnibus una & æqualis potestas,sive functio à Christo data est.
units.tr: LXV. All the ministers of the Church have one and the same equal power, or function, given by Christ.

units.la: Licèt enim Pastores Ecclesiis particulari- bus præfecti tum supra suos Diaconos , tum supra communem ovium gregem, non minùs quàm doctores supra discipulos suos gradu aliquo honoris emineant,& in communi deliberatione propter ordinem servandum unus ætate, judicio , donorum mensura , laborum gravitate & experientia honoratior, politiæ, ordinis & decori gratia præesse reliquis, ante eos stare,coetum convocare,in coetu res consultandas proponere , sententias aliorum colligere, confusionem averruncare possit , uti in celebri illa Apostolorum Synodo, Actor. XV.7. &c. in qua Jacobus praesidis & antistitis munere functus est, factum fuit ; tamen nemo unus potestate ampliore, quàm cæteri omnes , præditus est. Sive enim Apostolos & extraordinarios illos Pastores,qui à Christo immediatè vocati,eximiis etiam donis ad jacienda Ecclesiæ fundamenta , ornati erant,spectamus,pari omnes, juxta illud Cypriani de Simpl. Præl. consortio honoris & potestatis præditi erant; sive instituta ad perpetuum Ecclesiæ regimen ministeria, tam in doctrinæ & disciplinæ, quæ Pastoribus, Presbyteris & Doctoribus; quàm in pauperum cura,quæ Diaconis commissa est, intuemur, nullibi inaequalia , vel dominationis & elationis speciem ullam reperimus. In singulis Ecclesiis, ut de ministeriis ordinariis agamus , ex instituto Christi & Apostolorum instituta esse Presbyteria,& cuncta communi Presbyterorum consilio gubernata esse satis constat, & Hieronymus Comment. in Tit. I. testatur dicens : Antequam Diaboli institutu studia in religione fierent, & diceretur in populis : Ego sum Pauli , ego Apollo,ego autem Cephæ,communi Presbyterorum consilio Ecclesiæ gubernabantur. Postquam verò unusquisque eos, quos baptizaverat, suos putabat esse,non Christi,in toto orbe decretum est, ut unus de Presbyteris electus præponeretur cæteris , ad quem omnis Ecclesiæ cura pertineret , & semina schismatum tollerentur. Dein pluribus ex Scripturis cùm probavisset , eundem esse Episcopum & Presbyterum his verbis claudit : Hæc propterea, ut ostenderemus, apud veteres eosdem fuisse Presbyteros, quos & Episcopos : paulatim verò ut dissensionum plantaria evellerentur, ad unum omnem sollicitudinem esse delatam. Sicut ergo Presbyteri sciunt , se ex Ecclesiæ consuetudine ei, qui sibi præpositus fuerit,esse subjectos : ita Episcopi noverint, se magis consuetudine,quàm dispositionis Dominicæ veritate, Presbyteris esse majores, & in commune debere Ecclesiam regere,imitantes Mosen, qui cùm haberet in potestate solus præesse populo Israel, septuaginta elegit, cum quibus populum judicaret. Idem Epist. 85. ad Evagrium. Cùm, inquit, Apostolus perspicuè doceat, eosdem esse Presbyteros , quos & Episcopos, quis patiatur,mensarum & viduarum minister, ut super eos se tumidus efferat,ad quorum preces Christi corpus & sanguis conficitur? &c. Quòd autem postea unus electus est, qui cæteris præponeretur,in remedium schismatis factum est,ne unusquisque ad se trahens Ecclesiam Christi rumperet. Nam & Alexandriæ à Marco Evangelista,usque Heraclam & Dionysium Episcopos , Presbyteri semper unum ex se electum excelsiori gradu collocatum Episcopum nominabant ; quomodo si exercitus Imperatorem faciat, aut Diaconi eligant de se, quem industrium noverint , quem Archidiaconum vocent. Quid enim facit, excepta ordinatione, Episcopus, quod Presbyter non faciat? &c. Quòd ergo Episcopi nomen Apostolorum ætate commune omnibus Ecclesiæ Pastoribus & Presbyteris, ris, (fatentibus etiam illis, qui Episcopi & Presbyteri differentiam ex jure Divino derivant, licét rei differentiam sine ulla ratione causentur, cùm tamen Apostolus à nomine ad rei, id est, officii descriptionem, Actor. XX. 28. Tit. I. 7. 1. Pet. V. 1. 2. transeat) seculis sequentibus uni supra Presbyteros cæteros elato, & paulatim etiam potestate majore, jurisdictionis ei arrogatæ titulo, prælato attributum est; non id Divino instituto, sed humana prudentia; nec primitus quidem ad Monarchiæ vel jus, vel gradum ullum, sed ordinis & pacis, non libertatis vel ἰσονομίας opprimendæ gratiâ, constitutum est, parum auspicato, uti procedens tempus docuit, successu. Verùm is, à quo omnis Ecclesiæ regendæ authoritas profluxit, variis institutis ministeriis, & multifariis in homines effusis donis, omnibus Pastoribus, quibus œconomiam verbi tradidit ἴσοις ἴσα ἀequalibus æqualia, adeóque unam & eandem potestatem, non aliud aliis prædicandi verbum, non alia aliis Sacramenta celebranda, non alias aliis claves tradidit. Nemo proin unus aliis potestate major esse potest, licèt zelo, pietate, doctrina, meritis major esse possit, sed tantò etiam animo suo minor, quò opere major est, uti Christus Matth. XVIII. 1. &c. jussit. Affectationem inprimis dominationis ex æquo omnibus interdictam, Christi verbis, ibid. XX. 25. 26. allatis ostendimus. Neque illud de nihilo est, quòd in descriptione Apostolica ordinum Ecclesiasticorum, Ephes. IV. 11. nulli eminentior supra alios potestas adscribitur, sed officii ratione pares omnes æstimantur. Nullus enim Apostolorum, Pastorum, Doctorum princeps; sed alii Apostoli, &c. alii Pastores & Doctores. Ubi autem multi æquali nuncupatione inducuntur, ibi unus multorum princeps & Dominns non intelligitur. Pastores autem, Presbyteri, κυβερνήσεις, ἡγούμενοι, προϊστάμενοι, προηγούμενοι, gubernationes, ductores, præsides, 1. Cor. XII. 28. 1. Tim. V. 17. Hebr. XIII. 7. 17. appellantur non collegarum, συμπρεσβυτέρων, sed gregis sibi commissi respectu; cui tamen ipsi dominari non ausint; utpote non dominantes fidei fidelium, sed lætitiæ eorum cooperantes, 2. Cor. I. 24.
units.tr: For although the pastors set over particular churches, both above their deacons and above the common flock of sheep, rise above others by some degree of honour, just as teachers rise above their disciples; and although, in common deliberation, one of them, who is more honoured by age, judgement, measure of gifts, weight of labours and experience, may for the sake of order, courtesy and decorum preside over the rest, stand before them, convene the assembly, put the matters to be discussed before it, gather the opinions of others, and avert confusion, as was done in that famous synod of the Apostles, Acts 15:7 etc., where James acted in the office of president and chief; yet no one of them is endowed with greater power than all the others. For whether we look at the Apostles and those extraordinary pastors who were called immediately by Christ and adorned with outstanding gifts for laying the foundations of the Church, they all were equal, endowed, according to the saying of Cyprian in On the Simplicity of the Prelates, with a partnership of honour and power; or whether we consider the ministries instituted for the perpetual government of the Church, both those of teaching and discipline, which were committed to pastors, elders and teachers, and those of the care of the poor, which were entrusted to deacons, we find nowhere any inequality or any appearance of domination and haughtiness. In individual churches, to speak of the ordinary ministries, it is quite clear that by the institution of Christ and the practice of the Apostles there were boards of elders, and that everything was governed by the common counsel of the elders. Jerome bears witness to this in his Commentary on Titus, 1, saying: Before the studies in religion were made by the devil's device, and it was said among the people, "I am of Paul, I of Apollos, and I of Cephas," the churches were governed by the common counsel of the elders. But after each man began to regard those whom he had baptized as his own and not Christ's, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the elders should be chosen and set over the rest, to whom the whole care of the Church should pertain, and the seeds of schisms should be removed. Then, having proved from many passages of Scripture that the bishop and the presbyter are the same, he concludes in these words: I have said this so that we may show that among the ancients the presbyters were the same as the bishops; but gradually, so that the seedbeds of dissension might be uprooted, all care was transferred to one. Therefore, just as presbyters know that by the custom of the Church they are subject to the one who is set over them, so let bishops know that they are greater than presbyters by custom rather than by the truth of the Lord's arrangement, and that they ought to rule the Church in common, imitating Moses, who, although he alone had the power to rule the people of Israel, chose seventy with whom he might judge the people. The same, in Epistle 85 to Evagrius, says: Since the Apostle plainly teaches that the presbyters are the same as the bishops, who would tolerate that a minister of tables and widows should puff himself up above those at whose prayers the body and blood of Christ are made? etc. But that one was afterwards chosen to be set over the rest was done as a remedy for schism, lest each man, drawing the Church of Christ to himself, should tear it apart. For at Alexandria, from Mark the Evangelist down to the bishops Heraclas and Dionysius, the presbyters always named one chosen from among themselves, placed in a higher rank, as bishop; just as if an army were to make its emperor, or deacons were to choose from among themselves one whom they knew to be diligent and call him archdeacon. For what does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not do? etc. Therefore, since in the age of the Apostles the name of bishop was common to all the pastors and presbyters of the Church (and even those who derive the difference between bishop and presbyter from divine right admit this, though they allege a difference in the thing without any reason, since the Apostle passes from the name to the description of the thing, that is, of the office, Acts 20:28; Titus 1:7; 1 Peter 5:1-2), in the following centuries the title of bishop was assigned to one man raised above the other presbyters and gradually given greater power, with the title of jurisdiction arrogated to him. This was not done by divine institution but by human prudence; nor was it at first established for the sake of any monarchy, either as a right or as a rank, but for the sake of order and peace, not for the sake of suppressing liberty or [isonomy] equality; and, as the following time showed, it turned out with ill-omened success. Yet He from whom all authority to govern the Church flowed, having given various institutions of ministries and gifts poured out on men in many ways, gave to all the pastors to whom he entrusted the stewardship of the Word [equal things to equals], and therefore one and the same power: he gave to one no different kind of preaching of the Word, to another no different administration of the sacraments, and to another no different keys. Therefore no one of them can be greater than the others in power, though he may be greater in zeal, piety, learning and merit; but he is all the less in his own mind as he is greater in his work, as Christ commanded, Matt. 18:1 etc. We have shown from the words of Christ, Matt. 20:25-26, that the desire for domination in particular is forbidden to all alike. Nor is it without reason that in the apostolic description of the ecclesiastical orders, Eph. 4:11, no power more eminent than the rest is ascribed to any one, but all are regarded as equal in respect of their office. For no one of the Apostles, pastors or teachers is the prince; rather "some apostles, etc., some pastors and teachers." Where many are introduced under the same name, there one is not understood to be the prince and lord of the many. Pastors, however, elders, [governments, leaders, those who preside, those who go before] (gubernationes, ductores, presidents), are called, 1 Cor. 12:28; 1 Tim. 5:17; Heb. 13:7, 17, not in respect of their fellow elders [fellow-elders], but in respect of the flock committed to them; yet they must not dare to lord it over that flock, as those who are not lords over the faith of the faithful, but workers together with their joy, 2 Cor. 1:24.

units.la: LXVI. Ex his de forma Regiminis Ecclesiæ ministerialis proclive judicium est.
units.tr: LXVI. From these points, a judgment about the ministerial form of the government of the Church is easily reached.

units.la: Necque enim illa proprie vel Monarchica, vel Aristocratica, vel Democratica est; quia Ecclesiæ Ministris non competit κυριότης, seu potestas dominans, sed διακονία ministerium merum, sine imperio & dominatione ulla; & gubernatio omnis dominica, quæ tribus illis speciebus continetur & distinguitur, de hoc mundo est. Analogicè tamen Aristocratica dici potest, quatenus certa analogia vel similitudine magis Aristocratiæ, quàm vel Monarchiæ, vel Democratiæ respondet. Christus enim initio collectionem, gubernationem & propagationem Ecclesiæ nec uni alicui absolutè, nec omnibus promiscuè & indifferenter, sed paucis iisque singulariter delectis commisit. Uti ex duodecim Apostolorum & septuaginta discipulorum electione constat. Tum Ecclesia Apostolica & primitiva Apostolorum & Presbyterorum consilio gubernata est, Actor. XV. 6. &c. XX. 28. 1. Petr. V. 1. 1. Timoth. V. 17. De Presbyteris etiam Hieronymum testem supra citavimus; sed proprie loqui, & Scripturæ stylum imitari si amamus, forma gubernationis Ecclesiæ non Aristocratica, sed œconomica dicenda nobis fuerit, quia Ministri Ecclesiam, ceu domum Dei viventis, ut œconomi & dispensatores gubernant. Nam & parabola Christi Matth. XXV. 14. docet, Christum unum patrem familias, peregrè nunc in Cœlum profectum, brevi autem rediturum, tanquam caput unicum, varios sub se ministros & dispensatores mysteriorum, cum suis quemque talentis Ecclesiæ institui-se, & post se reliquisse: & Ecclesia domus Dei viventis, 1. Tim. III. 15. vocatur, cui Christus, ut filius familias præest, & alii, ut fideles ministri, inserviunt: & ministri cujuscunque gradus οἰκονόμοι œconomi 1. Cor. IV. 1. vocantur; atque Scriba ad Regnum Cœlorum edoctus cum homine οἰκοδεσπότῃ Patrefamilias comparatur, Matth. XIII. 52. & potestas Ecclesiæ non gladii vel teli, sed clavium symbolo confertur, cap. XVI. 19. & denique tota œconomia Ecclesiæ lenitate, mansuetudine, censuris, aliisque agendi modis patriam magis quàm politicam potestatem spirat & redolet. Sic verò Regimen Ecclesiæ analogicè Aristocraticum, & proprie œconomicum facimus, ut tamen Christiano populo jus, ipsa vocatione, qua κληροι cleri Dei, 1. Petr. V. 3. vocantur, partum quod sine sacrilegio violari nequit, neutiquam eripiamus. Nam (qua in re Democratiæ vestigium quoddam inesse nonnulli arbitrantur) ipsa Pastorum vocatio, & canonum ad disciplinæ praxin constitutiones invito populo obtrudi non potest; & eidem judicium de doctrina & examen ἐλέγχω competit, nec sine tyrannide abdicari ei potest. Imò ne Pastorum administratio in oligarchiam & tyrannidem degeneret, suæ sunt Magistratui & universo populo partes, quorum est ordine providere, ut verbum Dei purè prædicetur, justus ordo sanctè observetur, & cultus collapsus, uti in Reformatione Ecclesiæ suas sibi partes omnes ordines sibi vindicarunt, instauretur. Omnium denique Ecclesiæ civium & Dei filiorum eo ipso, quòd Christiani sunt, est, totius corporis ædificationem promovere, & ne veritas adulterinis dogmatis, ​ilstertentibus pastoribus, corrumpatur, atque disciplinæ labefactatione perfumdetur, pro vocationis ratione, & doni mensura, vigilare. Quæ vobis dico, omnibus dico; Vigilate, Marc. XIII. 37. Luc. XII. 41. &c.
units.tr: Nor is that form properly monarchical, aristocratic or democratic, because lordship [κυριότης], that is, a ruling power, does not belong to the ministers of the Church. They have only service [διακονία], ministry, without any command or domination whatever. All lordly government, which is contained and distinguished in those three kinds, belongs to this world. Yet it may be called aristocratic by analogy, insofar as by a certain analogy or likeness it corresponds more to aristocracy than to either monarchy or democracy. For at the beginning Christ committed the gathering, government and propagation of the Church neither absolutely to one person, nor indiscriminately and without distinction to all, but to a few, and those individually chosen. This is clear from the election of the twelve Apostles and the seventy disciples. Then the apostolic and primitive Church was governed by the counsel of the Apostles and elders (Acts 15:6 etc.; Acts 20:28; 1 Pet. 5:1; 1 Tim. 5:17). We have already cited Jerome as a witness about the elders. But if we love to speak properly and to imitate the style of Scripture, the form of government of the Church should be called not aristocratic but economic, because the ministers govern the Church, the house of the living God, as stewards and dispensers. For the parable of Christ (Matt. 25:14) teaches that Christ, as one Father of a household who has now gone abroad into heaven but will return shortly, as the sole head, established in the Church various ministers and dispensers of the mysteries under him, each with his own talents, and left them behind after him. The Church is called the house of the living God (1 Tim. 3:15), over which Christ presides as the Son of the household, and others serve as faithful ministers. Ministers of every rank are called stewards [οἰκονόμοι] (1 Cor. 4:1). The scribe instructed for the kingdom of heaven is compared to a householder [οἰκοδεσπότῃ], a father of a family (Matt. 13:52). The power of the Church is conferred not by the symbol of the sword or spear but by that of the keys (ch. 16:19). Finally, the whole economy of the Church breathes and smells of a fatherly rather than a political power, in its gentleness, mildness, censures and other ways of acting. Thus we make the government of the Church analogically aristocratic and properly economic. Yet we in no way take away from the Christian people the right which, by their very calling, by which they are called clergy [κληροι] of God (1 Pet. 5:3), is a right that cannot be violated without sacrilege. For the call of the ministers, and the constitutions of the canons for the practice of discipline, cannot be forced on an unwilling people (in which matter some think there is a certain trace of democracy). The people also has the right of judging doctrine and of examination [ἐλέγχω], and cannot be deprived of it without tyranny. Indeed, so that the administration of the ministers does not degenerate into oligarchy and tyranny, the magistrate and the whole people have their duties, to see to it in good order that the Word of God is purely preached, that a just order is holily observed, and that worship, when fallen, is restored, as in the Reformation all the orders claimed for themselves their parts in restoring the Church. Finally, it is the duty of all the citizens of the Church and sons of God, simply because they are Christians, to promote the building up of the whole body, and to watch, according to their calling and the measure of their gift, that the truth is not corrupted by the adulterous doctrines of ministers who hold them, nor undermined by the weakening of discipline. What I say to you, I say to all: Watch (Mark 13:37; Luke 12:41 etc.).

units.la: LXVII. Gubernatio hæc Ecclesiæ Oeconomica in generalibus, cujusmodi præconium verbi, Sacramentorum administratio, disciplinæ usus & cura pauperum, sunt, uniformis & immutabilis est. Nam & Dei ipsius verbo in perpetuum Ecclesiæ usum hæc sancta sunt, Matth. XXVIII. 19. 20. Ephes. IV. 11. & ad unitatem Ecclesiæ, in communione Sanctorum sitam, impensè faciunt, ibid. v. 4. 5. 6. Quæ ergo Ecclesia externa iis prorsus destituitur, & generalia hæc in regimine suo non admittit, verum Ecclesiæ regimen non habet, adeóque quatenus illa externè congregatur, & sine regimine hoc regitur, vera Christi Ecclesia non est. Sed alia ratio est particularium, cujusmodi sunt ceremoniæ, ordo personis & locis conveniens & peculiaris in Ecclesiis singulis agendi modus, quæ
units.tr: LXVII. This ecclesiastical economic government, in its general aspects, such as the preaching of the Word, the administration of the sacraments, the use of discipline and the care of the poor, is uniform and unchangeable. For these things are holy in the very Word of God, for the perpetual use of the Church (Matt. 28:19-20; Eph. 4:11), and they greatly serve the unity of the Church, which lies in the communion of the saints (ibid. vv. 4-6). Therefore an external Church which is wholly without these, and does not admit these general matters into its government, has no government of the Church at all; and so, insofar as it is externally gathered and is ruled without this government, it is not the true Church of Christ. But the case is different with particular matters, such as ceremonies, an order suited to persons and places, and the particular manner of acting in individual churches, which

units.la: Forma regiminis Ecclesiæ Ministerialis analogicè aristocratica, seu potius œconomica est. quae salvo principali regimine, variare possunt. Licet enim etiam in talibus harmonia exactior optanda sit, tamen nec simpliciter necessaria est, nec morose & contentiose urgeri debet, ne propter paleam triticum ipsum in discrimen adducatur. Nam quae ordinis tantum causa in Ecclesia constituta & sancita sunt, citra opinionem necessitatis & cultus retineri debere, satis Apostolus Rom. XIV. 1.Cor.XIV. Coloss. II. docuit. Etiam Apostolorum aetate non una in omnibus Ecclesiae ex Judaeis & Gentibus collecta ratio fuit; quando circumcisio ab aliis liberè usurpata, ab aliis neglecta est. Neque pauca ejusmodi instituta Apostolorum, sed temporaria illa, procedente tempore in desuetudinem abierunt, velut instituta communionis bonorum, abstinentiae a sanguine & suffocato, interpretationis linguarum, immersionis in Baptismo, quotidianae communionis, pronuntiationis Amen in benedictione Agaparum. In una enim fide Ecclesiae diversam consuetudinem nihil officere, rectè Gregorius M. & nullam religionem eosdem ritus custodire, etiamsi eandem doctrinam complectatur, Socrates dixit. Multa enim verbo Dei non sunt definita, & si definita sunt, controversiam habent, an perpetui usus sint. Aliae etiam Ecclesiae in talibus pro norma solum Dei verbum; aliae praeter verbum Dei etiam Ecclesiam ante & post Concilium Nicaenum habent. Neque Christianus populus sic unus est, ut olim Israeliticus, uni loco affixus, sed varius, ingeniis, moribus & consuetudinibus discretus, quibus proin gubernationis ratio prudenter accommodari debet. Cumque Ecclesia in Politiis, velut hospitiis suis, collocata sit, atque Evangelium politias non aboleat, necesse est earum genium, naturam, conditionem in multis sequatur, adeoque multa, ut Confessionis Helveticae verbis cap. 18. utar, pro conditione temporum, status publici & necessitate moderetur. Ubi, inquit, semper tenenda est regula; omnia fieri debere ad aedificationem, decenter, honeste, sine tyrannide & seditione. Apostolus enim 2. Cor. X.10. testatur, sibi a Deo traditam esse in Ecclesia potestatem ad aedificationem, & non ad destructionem. Nam ipsemet Dominus vetuit, Matth. XIII. 29. lolium in agro Domini eradicari, quando periculum est, ne & triticum evellatur.
units.tr: The ministerial form of government of the Church is analogically aristocratic, or rather economic, and these particulars may vary while the principal government remains safe. For although a more exact harmony is to be desired even in such matters, it is neither simply necessary, nor should it be pressed stubbornly and contentiously, lest the wheat itself be endangered for the sake of the chaff. For the Apostle has sufficiently taught (Rom. 14:1; 1 Cor. 14; Col. 2) that those things which have been established and sanctioned in the Church for the sake of order alone are to be retained, without the opinion of necessity and of worship. Even in the time of the Apostles the practice was not one and the same in all the Churches gathered from Jews and Gentiles; circumcision was freely used by some and neglected by others. Nor did a few such institutions of the Apostles, but those that were temporary, fall into disuse as time went on: such as the community of goods, abstinence from blood and from what is strangled, the interpretation of tongues, immersion in Baptism, daily communion, and the pronouncing of "Amen" at the blessing of the Agapes. Gregory the Great rightly said: that a different custom in one faith does no harm, and that no religion keeps the same rites, even if it embraces the same doctrine; Socrates said the same. For many things are not defined in the Word of God, and where they are defined, there is controversy whether they are perpetual usages.
