Other Churches also have, in such matters, the Word of God alone as their norm; others have, besides the Word of God, also the Church before and after the Council of Nicaea. Nor is the Christian people so one as the Israelite people once was, fixed to one place, but it is various, distinguished by talents, customs and habits, to which accordingly the manner of government ought to be prudently adapted. And since the Church is placed in the commonwealths, as in its inns, and the Gospel does not abolish the commonwealths, it must follow their spirit, nature and condition in many things. Thus, to use the words of the Helvetic Confession (ch. 18), many things must be ordered according to the condition of the times, and the state of public affairs and necessity. Here, it says, the rule must always be kept: that everything should be done for edification, decently, honorably, without tyranny and sedition. For the Apostle testifies (2 Cor. 10:8) that the power given him by God in the Church is for building up and not for destruction. For the Lord himself forbade (Matt. 13:29) that the tares be uprooted in the Lord's field when there is danger that the wheat too be torn up.

units.la: LXVIII. Hoc moderamine & pia cautione adhibita quaestio de Regimine Ecclesiae per Episcopos, an per Presbyteros illud administrari debeat, decidi, & dubidium ea de re natum conciliari potest, absit modo partium studium, quod multos transversos abripit, ut de hoc solo, tanquam aris & focis disputent, perinde ac si in eo religionis prora & puppis sita esset.
units.tr: LXVIII. With this moderation and pious caution applied, the question whether the Church is to be governed by bishops or by elders can be decided, and the doubt arising on this matter can be reconciled, provided only that the zeal of parties, which drags many into unfair disputes, is absent. They dispute about this one point as if it were the hearth and home of religion, as if the prow and stern of religion lay in it.

units.la: Neque enim tanti est, utrum ab Episcopis, an a Presbyteris Ecclesia regatur, dum gnaviter & fideliter omnes, qui ad clavum sedent, munus suum obeant; Diotrephes nulli sint; & qui Ecclesiae praesunt, se non cynosbatos, rubos & infrugiferas spinas, sed vites, oleas & ficus fructiferas praestent, & fructus, pinguedinem & dulcedinem suam haud illibenter communicent, & dominatione omni in cleros, quae Ecclesiae venenum est, abstineant; denique praelatura sua Ecclesiae pacem & unitatem non turbent. De antiquitate ubi sermo est, sentimus cum Hieronymo, Apostolorum aetate Episcopos inter & Presbyteros nihil discriminis fuisse, & communi Presbyterorum consilio primitus Ecclesias administratas esse. Omnino igitur jure Divino Episcopi Presbyteris superiores non sunt.
units.tr: For it does not matter so much whether the Church is governed by bishops or by elders, provided that all who sit at the helm perform their duty diligently and faithfully; that there be no Diotrephes (3 John 9); that those who preside over the Church show themselves not as dog-roses, brambles and unfruitful thorns, but as vines, olives and fruitful figs, and willingly communicate their fruits, fatness and sweetness; that they abstain from all domination over the clergy, which is the poison of the Church; and, finally, that their prelacy does not disturb the peace and unity of the Church. Where the question is about antiquity, we agree with Jerome that in the time of the Apostles there was no difference between bishops and elders, and that the Churches were at first governed by the common counsel of the elders. Therefore, by divine right, bishops are certainly not superior to elders.

units.la: Disceptatio de regimine Ecclesiae per Episcopos, an Presbyteros administrari debeat, conciliari potest. loco amandetur,& ne qui militat, nimium se implicari hujus seculi negotiis,2.Tim. II.4. patiatur. Sicut enim miles non potest simul duci seu exercitum conscribenti placere,simul negotiis civilibus,à munere suo alienis vacare: ita nec Ecclesiæ minister simul Christo, Ecclesiæ principi, qui in eo est,ut Regnum suum occupet,mundum salvet, Diaboli Regnum expugnet, & captivos ipsiùs ex potestate ejus eripiat,vacare,& in iis,quæ ad lucrifaciendum multos, amplificandum Regnum Christi,docendam & patefaciendam veritatem accommodata sunt,semper versari: simul etiam mundo servire, & aliud agere potest. Nemo enim duobus Dominis servire potest. Et quàm malè id Ecclesiæ cesserit, experientia omnium temporum clamat. Ideo S. Paulus: Attendite vobis, & gregi, Actor. XX. 28. Hæc meditare, in his esto, hoc age, non aliud: ibi esto animo, intentione, studio, opera omni, 1. Tim. IV. 15. Quod præcipuum munus cùm pridem Episcopi Papales neglexissent, & in Chorepiscopos, quos hodie Titulares, vel suffraganeos appellant,transtulissent,eos meretricibus similes esse Damasus censuit. Sicut enim hæ infantes in lucem editos, mox aliis nutricibus alendos tradunt, quò citiùs ad Veneris studia redire liceret; sic & illos infantes, id est, populos sibi commissos suffraganeis pascendos tradere,ut libidini & genio licentiùs indulgeant.
units.tr: The dispute over whether the Church should be governed by bishops or by elders can be settled. Let him be removed from his place, and let him not allow himself to be entangled too much in the affairs of this age, who serves as a soldier, 2 Tim. 2:4. For just as a soldier cannot at the same time please his leader or the one enrolling the army and be free for civil affairs that are foreign to his duty, so a minister of the Church cannot at the same time be free for Christ, the Prince of the Church, whose purpose is to take possession of his kingdom, save the world, overthrow the kingdom of the Devil, and snatch his captives from its power, and always be busy with those things that are suited to winning many, extending the kingdom of Christ, and teaching and making the truth known. He cannot also serve the world and pursue other aims. For no one can serve two masters, Matt. 6:24. How badly this has turned out for the Church, the experience of every age cries out. Therefore St Paul says: Take heed to yourselves and to the flock, Acts 20:28; meditate on these things, be in them, do this, and nothing else; be in them with your mind, attention, zeal and all your effort, 1 Tim. 4:15. Since the Papal bishops had long neglected this chief duty and had handed it over to chorepiscopi, whom today they call titular or suffragan bishops, Damasus judged them to be like prostitutes. For just as these women hand over the infants they have brought into the light to other nurses to be fed, so that they may more quickly return to the pursuits of Venus, so these bishops hand over those infants, that is the peoples committed to them, to suffragans to be fed, so that they may indulge their lust and their inclinations more freely.

units.la: LXIX. Regimen Ecclesiæ circa Personas & Res versatur.
units.tr: LXIX. Church government concerns persons and things.

units.la: Personæ,quæ reguntur,omnes Ecclesiæ cives inter se variè distincti,sunt. De iis,qui intus sunt,vos judicatis; De extraneis verò Deus judicat, 1. Cor. V.12. ἐξω foris sunt tum illi, qui Christiani non nominantur; tum,qui baptizati licèt, Christum tamen nondum confitentur,neque aliter agunt, quàm Ethnici,neque ad cœtum Ecclesiasticum accedunt,adeóque semet ipsos foris ponunt: tum denique qui ob indignationem, ἐλεγχον, ἐπιλμίαν Ecclesiæ recedunt & separantur. Nam & ipse Paulus nihil ultra traditionem Sathanæ & ἐξαρον τὸ πονηρὸν ἐκ μέσου ejectionem mali ex medio, ibid. v. 13. habuit; & Christus non audientem dicto Ecclesiæ velut ethnicum, adeóque τὸν ἐξω extraneum haberi jussit,Matth. XVIII.17. Tales verò Deus ipse judicio suo reservat: at eos,qui ἐσω intus sunt,sine ullo discrimine Ecclesiæ subjicit. Omnes enim illi ad τὸ ποίμνιον gregem illum, cui attendere Episcopi, Actor. XX.28. jubentur, pertinent. Ipsorum etiam Prophetarum Spiritus Prophetis subjici, Apostolus 1. Cor. XIV. 32. admonet; quia quisque dona sua aliorum consilio & prudentiæ,ut illis decenter, & in tempore utantur,subjicit. Neque enim unum Spiritus S. donum alteri, velut zelus charitati, mansuetudini refragatur: & Spiritus S. etiam id efficit,ut alii alios libenter audiant & revereantur. Deus enim uni non dat omnia,sed dona sua inter multos sic distribuit, ut alii aliis indigeant, & se ultrò subjiciant. Et quod in ὑπακαλύψει revelatione,quam Spiritus S. impertitur,obtinet,cui nemo se subducere potest. Si quis enim in Ecclesia esset, qui solus loqui, docere, arguere, judicare animum induceret,& audire alios,doceri,argui & judicari renueret, manifesta hæc foret ἀκαταστασία conturbatio Ecclesiæ, cujus Deus author non est, ibid. v. 33. Etiam fidelis Magistratus, qui ἐσω intus est, regimini huic subest, quia doceri, peccans judicari, corripi, & Ecclesiæ elencho subjici potest & debet. Duplex enim Magistratus officium est, alterum commune cum piis omnibus ex vocatione generali: alterum proprium,ex officio seu vocatione Magistratus singulari. Ratione officii communis nullum Magistratum inter & privatum discrimen est. Non enim ille minùs quàm iste Christi jugo collum subdere, verbum ejus audire, peccans adversus legem Divinam, & charitatem Dei & proximi argui,& per verbum,quod Dei est, judicari potest. Quocirca olim pii Imperatores ad Eucharistiam, nonnisi posito diademate, cæterisque Majestatis symbolis,accedebant, ut ostenderent, se intra Ecclesiæ septum nil nisi oves esse,neque ullam supra eam potestatem affectare. Ratione officii singularis sic Ecclesia in functione ejus, seu administratione civitatis, juxta leges civitatis Magistratui subjicitur,ut etiam ipse Ecclesiæ inservire, Regi Regum portas aperire, & Jehovæ scuta sua sacrare vicissim teneatur. Ut plane Ecclesiæ & Magistratus ἀντισπόδ respectus sit. Non tantùm enim Ecclesiæ etiam dictum est: Omnis anima Potestatibus supereminentibus subjecta esto,Rom. XIII. 1. Sed etiam Magistratus Divinitus sic compellatur: Et nunc Reges, animadvertite, erudimini judices terræ. Servite Jehovæ in timore,& gaudete in tremore. Exoscula- mini Filium,ne irascatur,& pereatis,quoad viam, Psal. II. 10. 11. 12. Et quantò magis,qui infra Magistratus authoritatem subsidunt,quocunque demum discrimine,Ecclesiæ subsunt; patres,Ephes.VI.4. filii,ibid. v.1. Domini,ibid. v.9. servi, ibid. v. 5. viri & mulieres, cap. V.22. 25. filioli, patres, pueruli, 1. Joh. II. 12. 13. 14.
units.tr: The persons who are governed are all the citizens of the Church, who are variously distinguished from one another. Those who are inside, you judge; but God judges those who are outside, 1 Cor. 5:12. Outside (ἐξω) are, first, those who are not called Christians; second, those who, though baptized, do not yet confess Christ and do not live otherwise than heathens, nor come to the ecclesiastical assembly, and so put themselves outside; and finally those who withdraw and separate themselves from the Church out of indignation, contention or envy. For Paul himself ordered nothing further than the handing over to Satan and the removal of the evil person from the midst (ἐξαρον τὸ πονηρὸν ἐκ μέσου), ibid. v. 13; and Christ ordered that the one who does not listen to the Church's word be regarded as a heathen and so as an outsider (τὸν ἐξω), Matt. 18:17. Such persons God himself reserves for his own judgment. But those who are inside (ἐσω) he subjects to the Church without any distinction. For all of them belong to the flock (τὸ ποίμνιον) to which the bishops are commanded to attend, Acts 20:28. The Apostle also warns that the spirits of the prophets themselves are to be subject to the prophets, 1 Cor. 14:32, because each one submits his own gifts to the counsel and prudence of others, so that they may be used fittingly and in due time. For one gift of the Holy Spirit does not oppose another, as zeal does not oppose charity or meekness; and the Holy Spirit also brings it about that some gladly hear and reverence others. For God does not give everything to one person, but distributes his gifts among many in such a way that they need one another and willingly submit to one another. The same holds for the revelation (ὑπακάλυψις) that the Holy Spirit imparts, to which no one can refuse to submit. For if there were anyone in the Church who resolved to speak, teach, rebuke and judge alone, and refused to hear others, to be taught, rebuked and judged, this would plainly be disorder (ἀκαταστασία), the author of which is not God, ibid. v. 33. Also a faithful magistrate, who is inside, is subject to this government, because he can and ought to be taught, to be judged and corrected when he sins, and to be subjected to the Church's reproof. For the magistrate has a twofold office: one in common with all the godly by general calling, the other proper to him by the particular office or calling of magistracy. By reason of the common office there is no distinction between magistrate and private person. For he is no less bound than the other to bow his neck under the yoke of Christ, to hear his word, and, when he sins against the divine law and the love of God and neighbour, to be rebuked and judged by the word, which belongs to God. For this reason the godly emperors of old, when they approached the Eucharist, did so only after laying aside the diadem and the other symbols of majesty, to show that within the fold of the Church they were nothing but sheep and aspired to no power above it. By reason of the particular office, the Church, in its function or in the administration of the state, is subject to the magistrate according to the laws of the state, so that the magistrate in turn is bound to serve the Church, to open the gates to the King of kings, and to consecrate his shields to Jehovah. Thus the relation between Church and magistrate is truly reciprocal. For it is said to the Church as well: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, Rom. 13:1. But also the magistrates are thus addressed by God: And now, O kings, be wise; be instructed, you judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish from the way, Ps. 2:10–12. And how much more do those who are placed under the authority of the magistrate, in whatever rank, owe submission to the Church: fathers, Eph. 6:4; sons, ibid. v. 1; masters, ibid. v. 9; servants, ibid. v. 5; husbands and wives, Eph. 5:22, 25; little children, fathers, young men, 1 John 2:12–14.

units.la: LXX. Res circa quas Ecclesiastica gubernatio versatur,Doctrina verbi Dei, Ceremoniæ, Sacramenta, Disciplina & Bona Ecclesiastica, sunt; quæ secundum verbumDei,& congruentes eidem Canones Ecclesiasticos administrari debent In pascendo enim primum est docere. Profecti discipulos facite omnes gentes,&c. docentes eos servare, quæ ego præcepi vobis, Matth. XXVIII. 19. 20. Perseverabant τῇ διδαχῇ in doctrina Apostolorum, Actor. II.42. Oportet Episcopum esse ἀντιχόμενον ἐκ τῆ τῷ διδαχῷ πιστῷ λόγῳ affixum esse sermoni fideli qui est secundum doctrinam,ut potens sit & ad exhortandum in doctrina sana, & ad redarguendum contradicentes, Tit. I. 9. Ubi ἀντιχεῖσθαι affixum esse sermoni fideli secundum doctrinam, cum emphasi notat, ei inhærere unicè, rejecto omni sermone alio, ei attendere,eum scrutari,meditari perpetuò,narrare, repetere, inculcare omni cura & studio. Non igitur satis est præcipere,quid dicendum, vel non dicendum,faciendum vel non faciendum sit. Oportet inprimis διδάσκειν docere,hoc est, veritatem ad conscientiam demonstrare, donec is,qui audit,sapiens & prudens fiat: Sapiens, quoad cognitionem certissimam,plenissimam, maximè claram & distinctam: prudens, quoad δοκιμασίαν τ διαφερόντων explorationem & dijudicationem eorum, quæ meliora & præstabiliora sunt; ut illa in omni vita & conversatione
units.tr: Seventh, the matters with which ecclesiastical government is concerned are: the doctrine of the Word of God, the ceremonies, the sacraments, discipline, and the goods of the Church. These are to be administered according to the Word of God, and by canons agreeing with it. For in feeding the flock the first thing is to teach: Go and make disciples of all nations, etc., teaching them to observe what I have commanded you, Matt. 28:19–20. They continued steadfastly in the teaching (τῇ διδαχῇ) of the apostles, Acts 2:42. A bishop must hold firm to the faithful word that is according to the teaching, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict, Titus 1:9. Here the phrase to hold firm (ἀντιχεῖσθαι) to the faithful word according to the teaching marks, with emphasis, a clinging to it alone, rejecting every other word, attending to it, searching it, meditating on it continually, and recounting, repeating and inculcating it with all care and zeal. It is therefore not enough to command what is to be said or not said, done or not done. Above all one must teach (διδάσκειν), that is, bring the truth home to the conscience, until the hearer becomes wise and prudent: wise as to the most certain, most complete, and especially clear and distinct knowledge; prudent as to the testing and discerning (δοκιμασία) of the things that differ, namely of those that are better and more excellent, so that one may prefer them in all life and conduct.

units.la: cccc satione sua præferat. Ita docere est הבין Σοφίαν sapientem reddere, 2. Tim. III. 15. hoc est, facere, ut quis distinctè intelligat, & possit lucem à tenebris, verum à falso, bonum à malo, utile ab inutili discernere, & למד μαθητεύειν condocefacere, assuefacere, Matth. XXVIII. 19. & אלף familiare atque notum facere. Sed doctrina subniti τῇ ὑπολήψει ἐν πνεύματος demonstratione spiritus fieri διδακτοῖς πνεύματος ἀγίας λόγοις doctis sermonibus Spiritus S. seu vocibus à Spiritu S. doctis, 1. Cor. II. 4. 5. 13. & manifestari ad conscientiam ejus, qui discit, 2. Cor. IV. 2. debet. Neque esse debet ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως propria expositionis, 2. Petr. I. 20. sive procedens ex privilegio non errandi, & alios ad fidem, sine demonstratione ex verbo Dei, obligandi. Nam qui Scripturam habent & tenent, necesse non habent, ut quis eos doceat aliter, quàm unctio ipsos docet, & veritas est, 1. Joh. II. 21. 27. neque indigent κυρίοις τῆς πίστεως Dominis fidei, quales ne ipsi quidem Apostoli esse voluerunt, vel potuerunt, 2. Cor. I. 24. ut recipiat aliquid non per Mosen & Prophetas ante dictum, & per Apostolos praedicatum, quasi propter modum infallibilis alicujus cathedrae, hominis vel multitudinis. Ipsa verò doctrina debet esse ὑγιαίνουσα salubris & sana, 1. Tim. VI. 3. 2. Tim. I. 13. Tit. I. 9. quae sit ut cibus sanus & salubris, qui corpus sanum non corrumpit, ut venenum, sed potiùs ægrotum sanat, ut medicina, & corroborat, ut panis de adipe tritici, denique laetitia & alacritate implet, ut vinum, quibus emblematis Scriptura doctrinam sanam, & sermones sanos comparat. Cum doctrina tali conjuncta esse παράκλησις exhortatio debet, Tit. I. 9. quae ἡθικῶν & πεῖθῳ διδασκαλίᾳ sacri doctoris singularis modus est, consistens non in legali imperio, sed ὡς τῷ δεῖσθαι in rogando. Ideo Apostolus Ὡς Θεὸς παρακαλοῦντος δι' ἡμῶν, δεόμεθα ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ Tanquam Deo per nos adhortante, rogamus pro Christo, seu vice Christi: Reconciliamini Deo, 2. Cor. V. 20. Quapropter vigilate, memores, quòd triennio diem & noctem non cessavi cum lachrymis unumquemque vestrum monere, Actor. XX. 31. Sic Apostoli ad populum & gentes venerant, habiti quidem ut pauperes, sed divites multos facientes, 2. Cor. VI. 10. De quibus dicitur: פנֵיךָ יְחַלּוּ Tibi (Filiae Tyri) supplicant, Psal. XLV. 13. hoc est, illi, quibus thesauri sapientiae & cognitionis commissi sunt, ad vos venient, & rogabunt, ut thesauros eos gratanter accipere velitis. Nam חלות פנים est δυσωπέν, hoc est, tam humiliter & instanter aliquem rogare, ut pudeat eum, qui rogatur, non annuere. Hoc fecisse Apostolos, ex 2. Cor. V. 20. liquet. Hortor vos, fratres, per viscera Dei, ut sistatis corpora vestra hostiam vivam, &c. Rom. XII. 1. &c. Quae exhortatio seu rogatio deinceps tum ad παράκλησιν consolationem, tum ad παροξυσμὸν τῆς ἀγάπης instigationem charitatis & bonorum operum, Hebr. X. 24. facit, quia per eam commendantur illa, quae movere & incitare ad charitatem, ut Divinae consolationis Scripturarum participes fiamus, possunt. Connexum cum docendi munere est contradicentes arguendi munus, Tit. I. 9. Habet enim semper Christi doctrina adversarios, erroris & mendacii patronos; quia Christus positus est εἰς σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον ad signum, cui contradicitur, Luc. II. 34. & בחן אבן lapis probationis, Esaj. VIII. 14. quia dum doctrina Christi proponitur, cogitationes cordium multorum aperiuntur, & aliis quidem εἰς ἀνάστασιν ad resurrectionem, velut gentibus: aliis εἰς πτῶσιν ad casum, velut Judaeis, qui se justitiae Dei non subjiciunt, Luc. II. 34. Christus equidem φῶς τῶν ἀνθρώπων lux hominum Joh. I. 4. est, & tenebrae in illo nullae sunt. Sed cor hominis tenebris, & amore tenebrarum repletum est; quippe quod stultitiam pro sapientia, & sapientiam pro stultitia habet. Ad utrumque ergo Pastor & doctor Ecclesiae, & ad exhortandum in doctrina sana, & ad redarguendum contradicentes, paratus esse debet: & circa hoc primò praecipuè munus pascendi & gubernandi populum versatur.
units.tr: To teach, then, is to make wise (הבין, σοφία), that is, to bring it about that someone understands distinctly and can distinguish light from darkness, truth from falsehood, good from evil, and useful from useless; and it is to make one a disciple (μαθητεύειν), to cause to be learned together, to accustom, Matt. 28:19, and to make familiar (אלף) and known (ידע). But teaching must rest on demonstration of the Spirit (ἀπόδειξις πνεύματος), that is, be carried out in the words taught by the Holy Spirit, that is, words taught by the Spirit, 1 Cor. 2:4–5, 13; and it must be made manifest to the conscience of the learner, 2 Cor. 4:2. Nor ought it to be a private interpretation (ἰδία ἐπίλυσις), 2 Pet. 1:20, that is, one proceeding from a supposed privilege of not erring, and binding others to the faith without demonstration from the Word of God. For those who have and hold the Scriptures have no need that anyone should teach them otherwise than the anointing teaches them, and it is the truth, 1 John 2:21, 27; nor do they need lords of the faith (κυρίοι τῆς πίστεως), such as the apostles themselves neither wished nor were able to be, 2 Cor. 1:24, so that they should accept anything not said before through Moses and the prophets and preached by the apostles, as if on account of some mode of infallibility belonging to a chair, of a man or of a multitude. The doctrine itself must be wholesome and sound (ὑγιαίνουσα), 1 Tim. 6:3; 2 Tim. 1:13; Titus 1:9, like wholesome and healthy food, which does not corrupt a sound body as poison does, but rather heals the sick as medicine does, strengthens as bread made of the fat of wheat does, and finally fills with joy and cheerfulness as wine does; and by such figures Scripture compares sound doctrine and sound words. With such doctrine there must be joined exhortation (παράκλησις), Titus 1:9, which is the singular manner of the holy teacher, both ethical and persuasive, consisting not in legal command but in entreaty (ὡς τῷ δεῖσθαι). Hence the Apostle says: As though God were exhorting through us, we beseech on behalf of Christ, or in Christ's stead: Be reconciled to God, 2 Cor. 5:20. Therefore be watchful, remembering that for three years I did not cease to warn each one of you night and day with tears, Acts 20:31. Thus the apostles came to the people and the nations, regarded indeed as poor, yet making many rich, 2 Cor. 6:10. Of them it is said: The daughters of Tyre (or Tyre) entreat your favour (פָּנֶיךָ יְחַלּוּ), Ps. 45:13; that is, those to whom the treasures of wisdom and knowledge have been committed will come to you and beg you to be willing to receive those treasures gladly. For חלות פנים means to entreat (δυσωπεῖν), that is, to ask someone so humbly and so urgently that the one asked is ashamed not to grant it. That the apostles did this is clear from 2 Cor. 5:20: I beseech you, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, etc., Rom. 12:1 etc. This exhortation or entreaty then serves both for consolation (παράκλησις) and for stirring up of love and good works (παροξυσμὸς τῆς ἀγάπης), Heb. 10:24, because through it are commended those things which can move and incite to love, so that we may become partakers of the divine consolation of the Scriptures. Connected with the office of teaching is the office of refuting those who contradict, Titus 1:9. For Christ's doctrine always has adversaries, patrons of error and falsehood; because Christ is set for a sign that is spoken against (εἰς σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον), Luke 2:34, and a stone of testing (בחן אבן), Isa. 8:14; for while the doctrine of Christ is set forth, the thoughts of many hearts are revealed, and for some it is for the rising (εἰς ἀνάστασιν), as for the Gentiles, and for others for the falling (εἰς πτῶσιν), as for the Jews, who do not submit themselves to the righteousness of God, Luke 2:34. Christ, indeed, is the light of men, John 1:4, and in him there is no darkness. But the human heart is filled with darkness and with love of darkness, since it holds folly for wisdom and wisdom for folly. To both tasks, therefore, the minister and teacher of the Church must be prepared: both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict; and it is chiefly around this first task that the office of feeding and governing the people revolves.

units.la: LXXI. Doctrinae & argumentum & norma est verbum Dei, institutu S.S. per Prophetas & Apostolos in libris V. & N. T. conscriptum, quo ratio universae veritatis secundum pietatem, & consequendae aeternae salutis plenissimè continetur. Haec enim doctrina Ecclesiae anima, pabulum & nutrimentum atque instrumentum, per quod Deus in electorum suorum cordibus gratia & Spiritu suo efficax esse vult. Sicut enim Christus, unicum Regni sui spiritualis, quod Ecclesia est, caput & Salvator est: ita doctrina verbi sui utitur, ceu legitimo & ordinario instrumento atque medio, quo in cordibus electorum suorum per Spiritum S. ut ei, ceu membra capiti suo, uniantur, salutis per ipsum partae conlortes reddantur, adeoque perpetuum & solidum animarum nutrimentum atque pabulum ex eo hauriant, efficaciter operatur. Universae autem doctrinae hujus veluti nucleus & succus in Foedere Gratiae continetur; utpote quo credenti in Jesum Christum & resipiscenti justitia & salus per eundem JesumChristum promittitur. Sed tum de ipso Dei verbo, tum de Foedere Gratiae, & variantibus ejusdem oeconomiis, abundè in loco diximus.
units.tr: LXXI. The word of God is both the content and the rule of doctrine. It was written by the Prophets and Apostles under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, in the books of the Old and New Testament, and in it the whole account of truth according to godliness, and of attaining eternal salvation, is most fully contained. This doctrine is the soul, food, nourishment and instrument of the Church, through which God wills to work effectively by his grace and Spirit in the hearts of his elect. Just as Christ is the head and Saviour of his one spiritual kingdom, which is the Church, so he uses the doctrine of his word as a lawful and ordinary instrument and means. Through it, by the Holy Spirit, he unites his elect in their hearts to himself, as members to their head, makes them partakers of the salvation obtained through him, and so causes them to draw from it a constant and solid nourishment and food for their souls. The kernel and sap of this whole doctrine is contained in the Covenant of Grace, since justice and salvation through the same Jesus Christ are promised in it to the one who believes in Jesus Christ and repents. But we have spoken fully elsewhere both of the Word of God itself and of the Covenant of Grace and its varying dispensations.

units.la: LXXII. Inprimis verbi hujus praedicatio Ecclesiae Pastori incumbit. Κηρύξατε τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον. Praedicate Evangelium omni creaturae, Marc. XVI. 15. Κηρυξ καὶ Ἀπόστολος, διδάσκαλος τῶν ἐθνῶν. Praeco & Apostolus, doctor gentium, 1. Tim. II. 7. 2. Tim. I. 11. Hoc est verbum fidei, quod praedicamus. Quomodo verò praedicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Quemadmodum scriptum est: Quàm speciosi sunt pedes evangelizantium bona! Rom. X. 8. 15. Ipse Christus πρῶτος κήρυξ primus praeco & πρῶτος εὐαγγελιστής primus Evangelista fuit. Unxit me Jehova לבשר ad Evangelium nuntiandum mansuetis לקרא ad praedicandum captivis libertatem לקרא שנת רצון ad praedicandum annum acceptationis Jehovae, Esaj. LXI. 1. 2. Luc. IV. 18. 19. Ex eo tempore Jesus coepit κηρύσσειν praedicare, Matth. IV. 17. Praedicavit Evangelium Regni, ibid. v. 23. Qui etiam discipulos suos ablegans, dixit: Profecti κηρύσσετε praedicate, dicentes: Appropinquavit Regnum Coelorum, ibid. X. 7. Quae in aurem vobis dicuntur, praedicate in tectis, ibid. v. 27. Praedictum etiam est, fore ut praeconium illud duret usque ad finem mundi. Hoc est foedus meum cum ipsis. Spiritus meus, qui est super te, & verba mea, quae posui in ore tuo, non recedent ab ore tuo, & ab ore Seminis tui, & ab ore Seminis Seminis tui, dicit dicit Jehova, à nunc & in seculum, Esai. LIX.21. Κηρυχθήσεται prædicabitur hoc Evangelium Regni in toto orbe habitabili in testimonium gentibus. Et tum veniet finis, hoc est, Συντέλεια & αἰῶνος consummatio seculi, resurrectio mortuorum, & ultimum judicium, quod certaminum & miseriarum Ecclesiæ extremum & finis erit; Matth. XXIV.14. coll. cum v.3.
units.tr: LXXII. First of all, the preaching of this word falls to the minister of the Church. "Preach the Gospel" [Κηρύξατε τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον]: Preach the Gospel to every creature, Mark 16:15. "Herald and apostle, teacher of the Gentiles" [Κῆρυξ καὶ Ἀπόστολος, διδάσκαλος τῶν ἐθνῶν]: herald and apostle, teacher of the Gentiles, 1 Tim. 2:7; 2 Tim. 1:11. This is the word of faith which we preach. But how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news! Rom. 10:8, 15. Christ himself was the first herald [πρῶτος κήρυξ] and the first evangelist [πρῶτος εὐαγγελιστής], the first evangelist. Jehovah has anointed me [לבשר] to bring good news to the meek, [לקרא] to proclaim liberty to the captives, [לקרא שנת רצון] to proclaim the year of the acceptance of Jehovah, Isa. 61:1, 2; Luke 4:18, 19. From that time Jesus began κηρύσσειν to preach, Matt. 4:17. He preached the Gospel of the Kingdom, ibid. v. 23. Sending out his disciples, he said: Go, κηρύσσετε preach, saying: The Kingdom of Heaven is at hand, ibid. 10:7. What is said to you in the ear, preach on the housetops, ibid. v. 27. It was also foretold that this proclamation would last until the end of the world. This is my covenant with them. My Spirit, which is upon you, and my words, which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed, nor from the mouth of your seed's seed, says Jehovah, from now and for ever, Isa. 59:21. Κηρυχθήσεται This Gospel of the Kingdom shall be preached in the whole inhabited world, as a testimony to the nations. And then the end will come, that is, the συντέλεια consummation of the αἰῶνος age, the resurrection of the dead, and the last judgment, which will be the extreme limit and end of the struggles and miseries of the Church; Matt. 24:14, compared with v. 3.

units.la: LXXIII. Prædictio eventum habuit. Nam inde à Christi & Apostolorum temporibus Evangelium in Ecclesia, variante licet methodo, puritate, successu præconiatum est. Extant Patrum, Chrysostomi inprimis & Augustini homiliæ, quibus populo coram prælectis Scripturam illi explicarunt, & ad varios usus applicarunt. Inter opera etiam Gregorii M. liber homiliarum comparet, in quo quadraginta homiliæ recitantur, in totidem particulas textuum Evangelicorum, quæ in Ecclesia Romana statis diebus legi pro more solebant. Beda quoque Homilias æstivas & hybernas de Tempore & de Sanctis in certas lectiones ex Evangelistarum narrationibus depromptas edidit. Post utrumque jussu & authoritate Caroli M. sive Alcuinus, ejus præceptor, sive Paulus Diaconus sive P. Guarenfridus lectiones Dominicales certo ordine distinxit, iisque homilias Patrum, explicationis gratia, accommodavit, quæ Evangeliorum & Epistolarum nominibus venientes, & in mediis Papatus tenebris, non sine superstitioso respectu ad certas quasdam solennitates ab hominibus excogitatæ natæ, hodieque passim, contra praxin Ecclesiæ antiquæ, & Scripturæ regulam, non pericopas duntaxat quasdam, & male dissutas particulas, sed sermonem Christi universum ἀπλώς opulenter in nobis habitare, Col. III.16. atque librum legis lectitari. Deut. XXXI.10.11.12. jubentis; πᾶσαν γραφὴν totam Scripturam ceu Θεόπνευστον Divinitus inspiratam, & utilem ad quosvis usus commendantis, nec sine Divini ordinis & modi Scripturæ, qui populum celari non debet, supino neglectu, usurpantur. Sed prædicandi illud Divinitus injunctum munus temporis ad barbariem præcipitantis progressu magnam eclipsin passum est, quando neglecto Dei verbo Ethicam Aristotelis publice populo prælectam, se ipso Tubingæ in agro Witenbergensi auditore Phil. Melanchton testatus est; & Ti-guri quoque, & passim alibi ex Thoma & Scoto conciones habitæ sunt, jactatúmque à multis est, tametsi S. Literæ intercidissent, ex Platonis, Aristotelis, Senecæ, Plutarchi & aliorum id genus scriptorum monumentis viam ad salutem satis superque erui posse. Consignatissima inprimis de Prædicatorum paulò ante Reformationem inscitia Andreæ Areni Episcopi Cragniensis & Cardinalis querela est. Therfites, sic ille, ignavus arma contrectat Achillis. Prædicatores & Minores ad prædicationis officium tantò improbiùs se ingerunt, quantò minùs ea, quæ loquuntur intelligunt. Sacram Scripturam, cujus fimbriam paucissimi tetigerunt, cùm tanta sit ejus profunditas, ut ab humano intellectu, quantumcunque vigilet, summo otio, & maximo studio nequeat comprehendi; hanc idiotæ illi præsumunt, lacerant, docent, antequam discant, adductóque supercilio grandia verba trutinantes, inter mulierculas de S. Literis philosophantur. Discunt etiam, prohpudor! à fœminis, quod viros doceant, &c. Garrulitatem ipsam summa cum impudentia, rationem, & quicquid dixerint, legem Dei putant.
units.tr: LXXIII. The prediction has had its fulfilment. For from the times of Christ and the Apostles onward the Gospel has been preached in the Church, though the method, purity and success have varied. There survive the homilies of the Fathers, especially of Chrysostom and Augustine, in which they read Scripture aloud before the people, expounded it, and applied it to various uses. Among the works of Gregory the Great there also appears a book of homilies, in which forty homilies are recited on as many passages of the Gospels, which were customarily read on set days in the Roman Church. Bede too published summer and winter homilies on the seasons and on the saints, drawn from the narratives of the Evangelists and arranged into set lessons. After both, by the command and authority of Charlemagne, either Alcuin, his teacher, or Paul the Deacon, or Guarenfrid, arranged the Sunday lessons in a fixed order and adapted to them homilies of the Fathers for the sake of explanation. These, coming under the names of Gospels and Epistles, and born in the midst of the darkness of the Papacy, not without superstitious regard for certain solemnities devised by men, are still used everywhere today, contrary to the practice of the ancient Church and the rule of Scripture. Scripture bids us let the word of Christ dwell in us richly [ἀπλώς opulenter in nobis habitare], Col. 3:16, and commands that the book of the law be read, Deut. 31:10–12, and commends all Scripture [πᾶσαν γραφὴν] as God-breathed [Θεόπνευστον] and useful for every purpose. Yet these are used not merely as certain pericopes and badly stitched fragments, but with a supine neglect, and not without neglect of the divine order and manner of Scripture, which ought not to be hidden from the people. But this office of preaching, enjoined by God, suffered a great eclipse as time sank into barbarism. The word of God was neglected, and Aristotle's Ethics was publicly read to the people. Philip Melanchthon testified that he himself heard this at Tübingen in the Wittenberg region. Sermons were also given from Thomas and Scotus at Zurich and elsewhere. And many boasted that, although the Holy Letters had perished, a way to salvation could be dug out, sufficiently and more than sufficiently, from the monuments of Plato, Aristotle, Seneca, Plutarch and other writers of that sort. Very notable above all is the complaint of Andreas Arenus, Bishop of Cragnia and Cardinal, about the ignorance of the preachers shortly before the Reformation. Thersites, says he, the coward handles the arms of Achilles. Preachers and Minorites thrust themselves into the office of preaching the more shamelessly, the less they understand what they say. Holy Scripture, whose fringe very few have touched, is so deep that it cannot be grasped by the human intellect, however alert, with the greatest leisure and the greatest study. Yet these ignorant men presume to it, mangle it, teach before they learn, and, with raised eyebrows, weighing grand words, philosophize about the Holy Letters among little women. They even learn from women, shame upon them, what they ought to teach men, etc. They think their chatter itself, with the greatest impudence, is reason, and whatever they have said is the law of God.

units.la: Eo usque tenebræ processerunt, donec pulsa per Reformationem densa inscitiæ, barbariei & superstitionis caligine, juxta Divinam prædictionem, serenior lux affulsit, & æternum Evangelium habitantibus super terra, omni genti, tribui, linguæ & populo postliminio evangelizatum iterum est, Apoc. XIV. 6.7. & evangelizabitur ad finem usque mundi.
units.tr: Darkness advanced so far, until, the dense mist of ignorance, barbarism and superstition having been driven away by the Reformation, a clearer light shone forth in accordance with the divine prediction. The eternal Gospel has been preached anew, by right of return, to those who dwell on the earth, to every nation, tribe, tongue and people, Rev. 14:6, 7, and it will be preached until the end of the world.

units.la: LXXIV. Est autem veri præconis & concionatoris officium, Dei voluntatem ex verbo ejus ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem proponere. Qui finis Ecclesiastæ architectonicus esse debet. Nam finis παραγγελίας mandati & annuntiationis est charitas ex mundo corde, conscientia bona, & fide minimè simulata, 1. Tim. I.5. Quo officio defungendum est non tantùm in universum respectu auditorum omnium, sed etiam seorsim respectu ordinis & ætatis cujusque, velut senum, adolescentum, servorum, Tit. II. III. doctorum, αὐτῶν καὶ ἐπιγνωμόνων ἐν τῇ παρούσῃ ἀληθείᾳ scientium & confirmatorum in præsenti (Evangelica) veritate, 2. Petr. I. 12. utpote qui & ipsi indigent commonefactione, vel ut adhuc amplius confirmentur, vel ut confirmatio eorum non vacillet, atque ipsi tententur, Phil. III.1. vel ut adjuvent ipsi quoque commonefacti confirmationem aliorum, & prædicationis propagationem, vel ut ipsi excitentur per commonefactionem, 2. Pet. I.13. Ideo S. Paulus ad Timotheum: Propter quam causam commonefacio Te, ἀναζωπυρεῖν τὸ χάρισμα τῆς Θεοῦ, ut inflammes & vivificare facias donum Dei, quod in te est, 2. Tim. I.6. Etiam Magistratus sceptro, verbo Dei subjici supra diximus. serves ; denique officio isthoc singulorum etiam respectu defungi debet. Scitis, quemadmodum ἑνα ἑκαστον ὑμῶν unumquemque vestrum, velut pater liberos suos,adhortantes (seu rogantes,de quo supra) & consolantes, & contestantes,ut ambularetis digne Deo vocante ad Regnum suum & gloriam fuimus , 1.Thessal.II.11.12. Quod faciendum non publice tantum, sed etiam privatim, exemplo suo S. Paulus docuit. Non subtraxi me, quo minus renuntiarem utilia, & docerem vos δημοσία και κατ' οικας publice & privatim, Actor.XX.20.
units.tr: LXXIV. The office of a true herald and preacher is to set forth the will of God from his word for the edification of the Church. This must be the architectonic aim of the teacher. For the end of the command and of the proclamation is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned, 1 Tim. 1:5. This office must be discharged not only in general, with respect to all the hearers, but also separately, with respect to each rank and age: the old, the young, servants, Titus 2, 3; the learned and the established, αὐτῶν καὶ ἐπιγνωμόνων ἐν τῇ παρούσῃ ἀληθείᾳ, knowing and established in the present (Evangelical) truth, 2 Pet. 1:12. For these too need to be reminded, either that they may be confirmed still further, or that their confirmation may not waver, and that they may be tested themselves, Phil. 3:1; or that they, being reminded, may help the confirmation of others and the spread of preaching; or that they themselves may be stirred up by reminding, 2 Pet. 1:13. Hence St Paul to Timothy: For this cause I remind you to rekindle [ἀναζωπυρεῖν] the gift of God, which is in you, so that you may inflame and make alive the gift of God that is in you, 2 Tim. 1:6. We said above that the magistrate too is subject to the sceptre of God's word; finally, this office must also be discharged with respect to each individual. You know how we, exhorting (or begging, as above) and comforting and testifying, each one of you [ἕνα ἕκαστον ὑμῶν], as a father his own children, that you should walk worthily of God, who calls you to his kingdom and glory, 1 Thess. 2:11, 12. St Paul taught by his own example that this should be done not only publicly but also privately: I did not shrink from declaring to you what was profitable, and teaching you publicly and from house to house [δημοσία καὶ κατ' οἴκους], Acts 20:20.

units.la: LXXV. Hunc aedificationis respectu omnium & singulorum scopum ita semper Ecclesiastes ob oculos habere debet,ut sedulo caveat,ne ab eo divertat εἰς ματαιολογιαν ad vaniloquentiam, 1.Tim.I.6. ad λογομαχίαν vitiligationem de verbis,& rebus nihili,2.Tim.II.14. ad βεβηλους κενοφωνιας profanas vocum inanitates, & oppositiones falso nominatae cognitionis, 1.Tim.VI.20. contra sit ἀντιθέσεις affixus sermoni fideli, qui secundum doctrinam est, Tit.I.9. & υγιης και ακατάγνωστος sanus, & qui condemnari nequit, ibid.II.8. atque id operam gnaviter det,ut sermo Christi copiose in populo habitet ; utque voluntas Dei cum aedificationis fructu proponatur, necesse est, tum ut tota Scriptura paulatim per expositas ejusdem liberaliores pericopas,& continuam librorum integrorum Scripturae seriem, non per concisas praelecti textus particulas,quod cacoethes plerorumque hujus temporis Ecclesiastarum,Scripturas potius vellicantium,quam docentium, & integrum τὸ ὑφος earum explanantium, viam ad ignorantiam Scripturae sternere poterit, populo familiaris reddatur ; tum ut eorum,quae in textu continentur,declaratio fiat; tum ut eorundem applicatio ad auditorum conscientias, prout eorundem conditio postulare videtur,instituatur. In declaratione, quid veri in textu contineatur, ante omnia per genuini sensus ejusdem accuratum ex textus ipsius originalis visceribus, atque totius Scripturae analogia erutam ἐξήγησιν explicandum est; ac demum quid boni ex eo sequatur,consulendum & dispiciendum est. Illa pars in doctrinis, seu documentis; haec in usibus ex doctrinis illis derivatis consistit. Nam tota Scriptura utilis est ad doctrinam, redargutionem, correctionem & disciplinam in justitia, 2.Tim.III.16. Et doctrina quidem est axioma Theologicum,expressis Scripturae verbis propositum,vel per immediatam consequentiam, ex expressis derivatum. Usus vero est axioma Theologicum ex doctrina deductum, quod utilitatem, bonitatem,vel finem ejus ostendit. Applicatio doctrinae ad usum ejus est specialis accommodatio, qua sic veritas generalis acuitur & ingeritur, ut in animos populi cum piorum affectuum commotione influere & penetrare possit. Ubi sic pungendi auditorum animi sunt, ut singuli sentiant, verbum Dei esse vivum & efficax,gladium ancipitem,qui intima usque cogitationum & affectuum configat,& ad ipsam usque medullarum & ossium compagem pervadat. Praedicatio igitur non mortua, sed viva adeo & efficax esse debet, ut infidelis in coetum fidelium ingrediens afficiatur, & verbi Dei auditione sic percellatur, ut Deo gloriam det. Praecipua in his usus & applicationis ratio & cura haberi debet,tum quia usus finis,tum explicationis ordo,tum doctrinae est: tum quia majorem difficultatem & necessitatem in maxima parte auditorum habet. Tanta enim hominum coecitas & perversitas est,ut eorum animi nihil difficilius admittant, neque eorum conditio aliud magis exigat, quam efficacem accommodationem verbi ad conscientias eorum voluntati Divinae in omnibus subjiciendas. Facilius enim verbum Dei in aures & intellectum,quam in cor & voluntatem hominis penetrat. Neque aliter Christus & Apostoli conciones suas instituerunt,utpote qui omnia ad usum & praxin vitae direxerunt, & in praxi illa persuadenda praecipuam operam collocarunt.
units.tr: LXXV. The minister must always keep this aim of building up the whole congregation and each member before his eyes, and he must take careful heed lest he turn aside to idle talk, 1 Tim. 1:6; to a contention of words, a quarrelling over words that profit nothing, 2 Tim. 2:14; to profane babblings and oppositions of falsely named knowledge, 1 Tim. 6:20. Instead he must hold fast to the faithful word, which is according to the doctrine, Tit. 1:9, and speech that is sound and cannot be condemned, Tit. 2:8. He must also take diligent care that the word of Christ dwells richly among the people, and that the will of God is set forth with the fruit of edification. To do this, it is necessary that the whole of Scripture be made familiar to the people gradually, through fuller expositions of its passages and a continuous reading of whole books of Scripture, not through scraps of a chosen text. (The habit of most ministers of this age, who pluck at Scripture rather than teach it and do not explain its whole character, will pave the way to ignorance of Scripture.) The minister must also declare what is contained in the text, and apply it to the consciences of the hearers as their condition seems to require. In the declaration, what truth is contained in the text must first of all be explained, by drawing out the exact genuine sense from the very heart of the original text and from the analogy of all Scripture. Then it must be considered and examined what good follows from it. The first part consists in doctrines or teachings; the second in uses derived from those doctrines. For all Scripture is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction and for instruction in righteousness, 2 Tim. 3:16. A doctrine is a theological axiom, set forth in the express words of Scripture, or derived from them by an immediate consequence. A use is a theological axiom deduced from doctrine, which shows its usefulness, goodness or end. The application of doctrine to its use is a particular adaptation by which the general truth is sharpened and driven home, so that it can flow into and penetrate the minds of the people with a stirring of godly affections. The hearers' minds must be pierced in such a way that each one feels the word of God to be living and powerful, a two-edged sword that pierces even to the division of thoughts and affections, and reaches to the very joints and marrow. Preaching, therefore, must be not dead but so living and effective that an unbeliever who enters the assembly of the faithful is moved, and is so struck by hearing the word of God that he gives glory to God. In these matters the greatest care and attention must be paid to the use and application, both because the use is the end, and the order of explanation and of doctrine points to it, and because it presents the greater difficulty and necessity in most of the hearers. For such is the blindness and perversity of men that their minds admit nothing more difficult, and their condition demands nothing more than an effective adaptation of the word to their consciences, so that they may submit everything to the divine will. For the word of God penetrates more easily into the ears and understanding of a man than into his heart and will. Nor did Christ and the apostles arrange their sermons otherwise, since they directed everything to use and to the practice of life, and bestowed their chief effort on persuading that practice.

units.la: Praecipua in his usus, Aedificatio Ecclesiae, scopus ejus praecipuus esse debet; in declaratione & applicatione Scripturae confisus.
units.tr: The chief aim of these things should be the edification of the Church, relying on the declaration and application of Scripture.

units.la: LXXVI. Neque tamen in publica verbi praedicatione acquiescere verbi Divini praeconibus licet,sed accedere privata singulos instituendi cura debet. Quod S. Paulum & praecepisse ex 1.Thess.II.10. & fecisse ex Actor. XX.20.31. supra ostendimus. Facit huc inprimis parabola Christi, qua perditae unius ovis,quam omnium reliquarum non perditarum enixiorem curam exigit,Luc.XV.4.&c. nec non S. Pauli illa admonitio : Praedica sermonem ἐπίστηθι εὐκαίρως και ἀκαίρως, insta tempestive & intempestive: redargue, increpa,roga in omni longanimitate & doctrina, 2.Tim.IV.2. Non quod molestus praeco esse iis, qui audire nolunt,
units.tr: LXXVI. Yet the heralds of the divine word may not rest content with public preaching; they must also take care to instruct individuals in private. We have shown above that St. Paul both taught this, from 1 Thess. 2:10, and practised it, from Acts 20:20, 31. Above all, the parable of Christ bears on this, in which the one lost sheep calls for a more eager care than all the other sheep that are not lost, Luke 15:4 etc. So too does that admonition of St. Paul: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine, 2 Tim. 4:2. Not that the preacher should be a nuisance to those who are unwilling to hear,

units.la: Privata singulorum institutio praeconi commendata esse debet. nolunt, & sermonem inutiliter jactare debeat, cum tali in casu orandus potius Deus sit, ut aperiat ostium sermoni, hoc est, præbeat aures & animum vacuum, atque auditores adducat; sed quòd loqui debeat omnibus, qui aures habent, neque stato tantùm tempore, sed quavis occasione, in otio, in negotio, inter secunda & adversa, ut sermo Evangelii quàm maximè publicus fiat, & singulis innotescat & applicetur. Per privatam enim institutionem magis verbum Dei ad singulorum conditionem & necessitatem accommodari, quàm per publicam, poterit; & illa ad hanc viam sternit, & eandem multò efficaciorem reddit. Non una autem & simplex privatæ institutionis occasio præconi verbi Dei se offert: velut cùm catechumeni ad mysteriorum sacrorum usum admittendi sunt; cùm neogami conjugii sui denuntiationem Ecclesiasticam petunt; Patres infantum suorum Baptismum flagitant; ægroti, captivi visitantur, & præco cum auditoribus suis iter facit. Inprimis huc visitationes domesticæ faciunt; quarum ad notitiam & directionem singulorum Ecclesiæ membrorum maxima utilitas est. Sicut enim Mithridatem Ponti Regem, duarum & viginti gentium, quæ ejus imperio subjacebant, linguas didicisse ferunt, ut sine interprete suos audire & alloqui posset; & Cyrus numerosissimi exercitus sui militum nomina omnia sic comperta habuisse fertur, ut singulos nominibus suis citare & ad virtutem hortari potuerit: ita Pastoris est, auditores suos omnes & singulos, quos in curam & fidem suam publica & solenni stipulatione, coram S. S. Trinitatis facie suscepit, & de quibus tremendo coram tribunali Christi respondere tenebitur, exactè, & non tam de facie, quàm de animo nosse, hoc est, ipsorum in doctrina profectum, mores, ingenium, conversationem, nævos, fortunam externam, aliàque id genus, curam pastoralem acuentia explorata quàm maximè habere. Nam Pastor bonus exemplo Christi, Pastoris optimi, ovem perditam quærere, depulsam reducere, fractam obligare, ægram confirmare, pinguem & validam profligare, & cum judicio pascere, Ezech. XXXIV. 15. 16. & oves proprias κατ' ὄνομα καλεῖν nominibus suis citare, adeòque etiam nosse, Joh. X. 3. tenetur. Id verò neglectis domesticis visitationibus nunquam præco assequi poterit. Cùmque quævis domus Christiani Patrisfamilias Ecclesia quædam sit, Pastor frugi non minorem ei, quàm publico Ecclesiæ cœtui & corpori curam impendat oportet. Præclarè hoc munere defunctus S. Paulus fuit διδάσκων κατ' οἴκως docens domatim, seu privatim, Actor. XX. 20. Nec non S. Johannes, piæ matronæ gaudium suum testificans, quòd ex liberis ejus invenerit ambulantes in veritate, sicut mandatum accepimus a Patre, 2. Joh. vers. 4. Eundem morem Ecclesiam Christianam post Apostolorum tempora coluisse, Chrysostomus homil. 4. ad Hebr. aliique testantur. Hodiéque Ecclesiæ rectè constitutæ visitationes ejusmodi severis legibus sanciunt, earumque ordinem & modum prudenter præscribunt & exigunt.
units.tr: Private instruction of individuals is to be commended to the preacher. who are unwilling, and should not throw his word away in vain. In such a case he ought rather to pray to God that he would open a door for the word, that is, give ears and an empty mind, and draw the hearers in. Rather, he should speak to all who have ears, and not only at a fixed time but on any occasion, at leisure or at work, in prosperity and in adversity, so that the word of the gospel may be made as public as possible, and become known and applied to each person. For through private instruction the word of God can be adapted to the condition and need of each individual more than through public instruction; and private instruction paves the way for public, and makes it far more effective. Yet a private instruction does not offer itself to the preacher of God's word on one single, simple occasion. For example, when catechumens are to be admitted to the use of the sacred mysteries; when those about to marry ask for the ecclesiastical announcement of their marriage; when parents ask for the baptism of their children; when the sick and the prisoners are visited; and when the preacher goes on his way with his hearers. Above all, domestic visitations serve this purpose, and they are of the greatest use for knowing and guiding each member of the Church. For just as they say Mithridates, king of Pontus, learned the languages of the twenty-two peoples who were subject to his rule, so that he could hear and address his subjects without an interpreter; and as Cyrus is said to have known the names of all the soldiers of his very numerous army, so that he could call each by name and exhort him to virtue: so it is the duty of the minister to know exactly, and not so much by face as by heart, all and each of the hearers whom he has taken into his care and trust by a public and solemn vow before the face of the Holy Trinity, and for whom he will be bound to answer at the dread tribunal of Christ. He should keep as thoroughly as possible in view their progress in doctrine, their morals, character, conduct, blemishes, external fortune, and other such things which sharpen pastoral care. For the good minister, following the example of Christ, the best Shepherd, is bound to seek the lost sheep, bring back the one driven off, bind up the broken, strengthen the sick, destroy the fat and strong, and feed with judgment, Ezek. 34:15, 16; and to call his own sheep by name, John 10:3, that is, to know them. The minister will never attain this if he neglects domestic visitations. And since every Christian household is in a way a church, the faithful minister ought to devote no less care to it than to the public assembly and body of the Church. St. Paul performed this office splendidly, teaching house by house, that is, privately, Acts 20:20. St. John too, bearing witness to his joy in a godly matron that he had found her children walking in the truth as we have received commandment from the Father, 2 John, verse 4. Chrysostom, in homily 4 on Hebrews, and others testify that the Christian Church after the times of the apostles kept this custom. Even today, Churches rightly constituted sanction such visitations by strict laws, and prudently prescribe and require their order and manner.

units.la: LXXVII. Deus in fœdere suo non tantùm nostrum, sed etiam feminis nostri Deum se futurum promisit, Gen. XVII. 7. Actor. II. 39.
units.tr: LXXVII. In his covenant God promised to be God not only to us but also to our seed, Gen. 17:7; Acts 2:39.

units.la: Christus quoque pueros ad se venire jussit, & quò minùs venirent, prohibentes redarguit, Marc. X. 14. Quamobrem & illi doctrina verbi Divini ἀπὸ βρέφους inde à pueritia imbui & pasci necesse est. Hæc institutionis ratio Κατηχήσις Catechisatio à κατηχέω circumsono, quod ex κατὰ & ἠχέω compositum, derivatur ab ἠχῷ & ἠχὼ sono sive simplice, sive exreflexu & repercussione geminato; appellari svevit, quæ institutio seu doctrina facilior & elementaris est, qua rudioribus sive pueris, sive adultis, Christianæ religionis prima elementa, certa methodo comprehensa, viva voce proponitur, & à Catechumenis reposcitur, ut inde ad totius verbi Divini doctrinam accuratius & solidiùs intelligendam gradus & via paretur.
units.tr: Christ also bade the children come to him, and rebuked those who would have kept them from coming, Mark 10:14. Therefore those who are to be taught the doctrine of the Divine Word must be steeped in it and fed on it "from infancy" [ἀπὸ βρέφους], from childhood. This method of instruction is called catechesis [Κατήχησις], from the verb katēcheō, which is compounded of kata and ēcheō and derives from ēchos, a sound, whether simple or doubled by echo and reverberation. The name is given to that instruction or teaching which is easier and elementary, by which the first elements of the Christian religion, set out in a fixed method, are presented by the living voice to the less advanced, whether children or adults, and are required back from the catechumens, so that a step and a way may thereby be prepared towards understanding the whole doctrine of the Divine Word more accurately and solidly.

units.la: Iterum opus habetis doceri, quænam sint στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τοῦ λογίου ἐκ Θεοῦ elementa principii sermonum Dei. Et factì estis χρείαν ἔχοντες γάλακτος, καὶ οὐ στερεᾶς τροφῆς indigi lacte, & non cibi solidi, Hebr. V. 12. Relicto sermone ἀρχῆς τῆς Χριστοῦ principii Christi, ad perfectionem feramur, non rursus θεμέλιον fundamentum ponentes respipiscentiæ ab operibus mortuis, &c. ibid. VI. 1. Quem docebit sapientiam? Quem faciet animadvertere auditionem (verbum auditum?) Amotos à lacte, depulsos ab uberibus? Nam sic apud illos institutio fit: regula ad regulam, litera ad literam, parum hic, parum ibi, Esai. XXVIII. 9. 10. Est illa vel domestica, vel ecclesiastica. Illa à parentibus, vel iis qui parentum vice funguntur; hæc ab Ecclesiæ ministris in publico cœtu Ecclesiæ vel scholæ instituitur. Antiquitus enim κατηχηταὶ Catechetæ seu Catechistæ fuerunt doctores Ecclesiæ, doctrinam catecheticam profitentes, eúmque auditoribus suis tum junioribus, tum adultis, recens ad fidem Christi conversis instillantes. Initiò illi ex reliquis ministerii Ecclesiastici ordinibus promiscuè legebantur. Augescente dein Ecclesia, propter negotiorum varietatem & molem, paulatim, teste Ambrosio in Ephes. IV. à cæteris distingui, & in peculiarem classem redigi cœperunt. De eorum officio fusè Augustinus lib. de Catechizandis rudibus & contr. Faust. Manich. lib. XIII. 7. &c. agit. Viva voce usi sunt non solùm imitatione Patriarcharum, Prophetarum, verùm etiam ut summam sanæ doctrinæ latiùs diffusam in pauciora contrahere, possent; & quòd vocalis traditio habeat quid, ut Hieronymus loquitur, latentis energiæ. Unde sicut efficacior est, & altiùs præcepta auditorum animis infigit, ita attentiores reddit. Ejusmodi Catechetæ Alexandriæ Pantenus, Clemens, Origenes, &c. Hierosolymæ Cyrillus, Carthagine Deogratias, alibi alii, ab Eusebio, Hieronymo, Augustino collaudati, fuerunt. Qui sic à Catechetis institutebantur κατηχούμενοι catechumeni appellari sve-verunt. Ita Apollos dicitur κατηχημένος τὴν ὁδὸν τῆς Κυρίου, instlitutus in via Domini, Actor. XVIII. 25. & Judæi κατηχούμενοι ἐκ τοῦ νόμου instituti ex lege, Rom. II. 18. dicuntur. Patribus ἀκροαταὶ auditores, quòd principia religionis κατὰ τὸν ἦχον viva voce auribus percipe-rent; nec non incipientes, novitiati, illuminandi dicti sunt. Quorum triplex ordo fuit, unus eorum, qui nondum baptizati catechesin discebant, ut Christiani fierent, qui proprie audientes sive auditores fuerunt, alter eorum, qui jam pri-
units.tr: Again you have need to be taught what are the elements [στοιχεῖα] of the beginning of the oracles of God [τοῦ λογίου ἐκ Θεοῦ]. You have come to need milk, and not solid food, Heb. 5:12. Leaving the word of the beginning [ἀρχῆς] of Christ, let us be carried on to perfection, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, etc., ibid. 6:1. Whom will he teach knowledge? Whom will he make to understand the message (the word heard)? Those who are weaned from milk and drawn from the breasts? For among them instruction goes thus: rule upon rule, line upon line, here a little, there a little, Isaiah 28:9, 10. It is either domestic or ecclesiastical. The domestic is given by parents, or by those who take the place of parents; the ecclesiastical is given by the ministers of the Church, in the public assembly of the Church or in a school. For in ancient times the catechists [κατηχηταί] were teachers of the Church, professing catechetical doctrine and instilling it into their hearers, both the younger and the adult, newly converted to the faith of Christ. At first these were chosen without distinction from the other orders of the ecclesiastical ministry. Then, as the Church grew and its business became more varied and burdensome, they gradually began, as Ambrose testifies on Ephesians 4, to be distinguished from the others and placed in a special class. Augustine treats fully of their office in his book On Catechizing the Uninstructed, and in Against Faustus the Manichaean, book 13, chapter 7, etc. They used the living voice not only in imitation of the patriarchs and prophets, but also so that they could reduce into fewer words a wider-spread summary of sound doctrine, and because oral tradition has, as Jerome says, a certain hidden energy. Hence, as it is more effective and fixes the precepts more deeply in the minds of the hearers, so it makes them more attentive. Catechists of this kind were Pantaenus, Clement, Origen, and others at Alexandria; Cyril at Jerusalem; Deogratias at Carthage; and others elsewhere, praised by Eusebius, Jerome and Augustine. Those who were instructed by catechists were called catechumens [κατηχούμενοι]. So Apollos is said to be "instructed [κατηχημένος] in the way of the Lord," Acts 18:25, and the Jews are said to be "instructed [κατηχούμενοι] out of the law," Rom. 2:18. The Fathers called them hearers [ἀκροαταί], because they received the principles of religion by the living voice, through the ear [κατὰ τὸν ἦχον]; they were also called beginners, novices, and those to be enlightened. There were three orders of them. One consisted of those who had not yet been baptized and were learning the catechism so that they might become Christians; these were properly called hearers or auditors. Another consisted of those who had already

units.la: {vel} Ecclesiastica est. pridem accesserant, & in fide instituti Baptismum petebant, competentes dicti; tertius eorum, qui in infantia baptizati, postquam nonnihil adolevissent, in catechesi instituebantur, & manuum impositione confirmati ad sacram communionem admittebantur, qui à Clemente aliisque Incipientes appellantur.
units.tr: {or} It is ecclesiastical. Had already come forward and, being instructed in the faith, were seeking baptism; these were called competentes (the qualified). The third consisted of those who had been baptized in infancy and, once they had grown somewhat, were instructed in the catechism and, confirmed by the laying on of hands, were admitted to holy communion; Clement and others call these Incipientes (beginners).

units.la: LXXVIII. Tanti momenti res catechizatio & domestica & publica est, ut sine illa publica generis humani salus & incolumitas constare non posset, neque generali corruptioni, scelerúmque in mundo cataclysmo alia ratione obviam iri, & remedium inveniri nisi principio à recta puerorum institutione ducto, nequeat. Quo enim est imbuta recens servabit odorem testa diu. Tenera & vacua adhuc aetas citò, quae ei instillantur, imbibit, & audita excipit. Magni certè momenti petra, seu lapis angularis, in cujuslibet aedificii fundamento rectè positus est. Nam ex falsis quidem falsa, at ex veris nonnisi vera sequuntur, Isagoge Porphyrii ad Organon ducit: Prolegomena & vestibulum ad inquisitiones, & domum. Quasi per haec שירי המעלות cantica graduum à lacte ad solidiorem cibum, ab artibus ad professionem, à Catechismis ad sublimiora mysteria gradum promovere necesse est. Henoch illi, qui cum Deo ambulavit חנוך initiantis vel dedicantis & catechizantis nomen inditum est. Similes חנוכים trecenti & octodecim vernae Abrahami, Genes. XIV. 14. fuerunt. Solomon חנך לנער Initia puerum secundum viam suam, etiam cùm senuerit, non recedet ab ea, non fiet apostata, Prov. XXII. 6. Constat sanè, nos optimè loqui eam linguam, quam à pueris didicimus; & de iis commodissimè loqui, quae à pueris vidimus & audivimus; & eas artes optimè facere, quas pueri didicimus; & in iis libentissimè esse, quibus assuevimus, ineptos contrà nos ad eam agendi & vivendi formam esse, quae nobis insolens est. Neque omnino fieri potest, ut quis bene loqui, & salutaria dicere, & honesta dextrè facere possit, qui non multum & prudentis sermonis, & honestarum actionum usum inde à pueris habeat. Talis à gremio aviae Laidos & matris Eunicae prodiit Timotheus, ὅτι βρέφος εἰδὼς τὰ ιερὰ γράμματα ἀ puero doctus sacras literas, 2. Tim. I. 5. III. 13. Neque pauci olim catechumeni ex Schola Origenis, Eusebio teste, martyres facti sunt. Unde maturè in Ecclesia institutiones catecheticae prodierunt, velut Origenis, Clementis Alexandrini Paedagogia, Epiphanii Ancoratus, Lactantii Institutiones, Basilii definitiones, Cyrilli Hierosolymitani Catechesis, Augustini de Doctrina Christiana & Enchiridion ad Laurentium. Quorum imitatione Lutherus, Calvinus aliique Reformationis Ecclesiae per Catechismos sive Dialogi in morem dispositos, sive thesibus aut locis communibus uberius expositos plurimos ex Antichristi faucibus eripuerunt.
units.tr: LXXVIII. Catechizing, both domestic and public, is so important that without it the public welfare and soundness of the human race could not stand, and there could be no other way to meet the general corruption and the cataclysm of wickedness in the world, nor could a remedy be found, unless it began with the right instruction of children. For the jar will keep the smell of what it was first steeped in for a long time. A tender and still empty age quickly soaks up what is poured into it and receives what it hears. Certainly the cornerstone, rightly laid in the foundation of any building, is of great importance. For from false premises only falsehoods follow, but from true premises only truths; Porphyry's Isagoge leads to the Organon, as prolegomena and vestibule to the inquiries and the house. So by these songs of degrees [שירי המעלות] one must advance step by step, from milk to more solid food, from the arts to the profession, from the catechisms to the higher mysteries. Enoch, who walked with God, was given the name Hanokh [חנוך], "initiating" or "dedicating" and catechizing. Similar to these were the trained men [חניכים], the three hundred and eighteen born in Abraham's house, Gen. 14:14. Solomon says: Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it [חנך לנער], Prov. 22:6, so that he does not become an apostate. It is certainly true that we speak best the language we learned as children, speak most easily of what we saw and heard as children, do best those arts we learned as children, and are most delighted with those things to which we were accustomed; and that we are awkward at any way of acting and living that is strange to us. Nor is it at all possible for anyone to speak well, say wholesome things, and act honestly and skilfully, who has not from childhood had much practice in wise speech and honourable conduct. Timothy came forth in this way from the lap of his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, for from infancy [ὅτι βρέφος] he had known the sacred letters, 2 Tim. 1:5; 3:15. Nor were few catechumens from the school of Origen, as Eusebius testifies, made martyrs. Hence early catechetical instructions appeared in the Church, such as the Pedagogue of Origen and Clement of Alexandria, Epiphanius's Anchored Man, Lactantius's Institutes, Basil's Definitions, Cyril of Jerusalem's Catechesis, and Augustine's On Christian Doctrine and the Enchiridion to Laurence. Imitating these, Luther, Calvin and others of the Reformed Church, by catechisms, either arranged in the manner of dialogues or more fully expounded in theses or common places, rescued very many from the jaws of Antichrist.

units.la: LXXIX. Sed ordo & methodus utramque Catecheseos paginam facit. Incipienda enim domi à primis incunabulis, & à lacte quasi materno puerorum institutio est, elementa initii eloquiorum Dei iis instillanda, atque inde ad veram etiam pietatem, vitae integritatem, & morum honestatem formandi sunt. Cujus rei in domestica illa consuetudine, & quotidiano convictu, singulis fere momentis variae & luculentae occasiones ad manum sunt, matribus inprimis, quae prae patribus nunquam non cochlearum instar domi se continent. Qui inprimis saxum hoc domesticae institutionis, à liberis conciones & catechisationes publicè habitas exigendo, & uberius etiam explicando, volvent, quod ruminandarum & repetendarum cum familia & domesticis concionum Patribusfamilias studium Chrysostomus Homil. 5. in Matth. inculcat, acriterque infigit. Multiplex inde usus tum ad liberos, quorum sic prima balbutics Deum & verbum ejus loqui assuescit, & ad salutem aeternam, omnigenámque felicitatem Regia quasi via perducitur: tum ad parentes, qui sic duplici vinculo se exsolvunt, naturali, quo liberos velut propriam carnem, curare tenentur; & supernaturali, sponsione videlicet illa, qua liberos ad Baptismum offerentes huic muneri se obstrinxerunt: tum ad Ecclesiam & Rempublicam, quae ex matura illa liberorum institutione hoc lucrum reportat, quòd nunquam non in promptu fideles operarios habent, qui se ipsos impendant, operam suam pro aris & focis pugnandi praestent, & sibi atque patriae universae ornamento sint. Domesticam institutionem Scholastica sequitur, qua in Scholis, quibus non minùs Ecclesia & Respublica, quàm Sole mundus carere potest, & quarum perpetuus in Ecclesia usus fuit, doctrinae sacrae verbi Divini cognitionem, & ingenii culturam uberiorem juventus percipit. Utramque Ecclesiastica excipit & perficit. In coetibus enim Ecclesiae publicis, quod vel à parentibus domi, vel à praeceptoribus in scholis trivialibus hauserunt, exigi & perfici, atque sermonis sinceri lacte porro ali illi debent, ut per illud magis magisque adolescant, & ad perfectionem ferantur, domestica & scholastica interim institutione non cessante, sed ampliùs etiam promota, imò per Ecclesiasticam quodammodo revivíscente. Neque enim concionatoribus indignum hoc munus est, utpote quorum est florem juventutis maximo studio curare, ut feliciores inde fructus emergant. Ideo Apostolus Corinthios, cum quibus non potuit loqui ut spiritualibus, sed carnalibus, lacte potavit, 1. Cor. III. 1. 2. Modus verò Catecheticae institutionis deligi is debet, qui juventuti in principiis fidei exercendae quàm maximè accommodatus est. Exploratio non memoriae duntaxat, sed etiam judicii maturè instituenda est, non sine prudente ad juventutis captum, nec non cum mansvetudine atque prudentia singulari, ne verborum asperitate vel acrimonia judicium turbetur, & discendi cupiditas sufflaminetur. Non improbandae etiam sunt conciones catecheticae, quibus Dialogismi praecipuo quopiam Scripturae testimonio firmati coram universo populo exponuntur, ut & tyrones in iis, quae didicerunt, confirmentur, & adultiores in memoriam eorum, quae tyrones didicerunt, redeant & corroborentur magis. Quarum concionum extra institutionem catecheticam usus maximus esse potest, ut in votis praecipuis esse debeat, quò illae ubique introducantur, & pari fide, zelo, studio, dexteritate frequententur.
units.tr: LXXIX. But order and method make both pages of catechizing. For the instruction of children must begin at home from the earliest cradle, and from the milk, as it were, of the mother; the elements of the beginning of God's oracles must be instilled into them, and from there they must be formed to true piety, integrity of life and decency of conduct. In that domestic custom and daily intercourse there are almost every moment various and clear opportunities at hand for this, chiefly for mothers, who, compared with fathers, are never anything but snails, always staying at home. Especially let fathers turn over this stone of domestic instruction, by requiring from their children the sermons and catechisings publicly given, and by explaining them more fully; Chrysostom, in Homily 5 on Matthew, urges and sharply impresses upon fathers of families the zeal of chewing over and repeating the sermons with the household and the servants. From this comes a manifold benefit: for the children, whose first stammering is thus accustomed to speak of God and his word, and who are led as by a royal road to eternal salvation and all-round happiness; for the parents, who thereby discharge a twofold bond: the natural, by which they are bound to care for their children as their own flesh; and the supernatural, namely that promise by which, offering their children to baptism, they bound themselves to this duty; and for the Church and the Commonwealth, which from this ripe instruction of children gain this profit: that they always have faithful workers ready at hand, who devote themselves, render their labour in defence of altar and hearth, and are an ornament to themselves and to the whole country. Domestic instruction is followed by scholastic instruction, in which, in schools (without which the Church and Commonwealth can no less do than the world without the sun, and whose constant use has existed in the Church), youth gains a fuller knowledge of the sacred doctrine of the Divine Word and cultivation of mind. The ecclesiastical instruction takes up and completes both. For in the public assemblies of the Church, what they have drawn in at home from their parents or in the common schools from their teachers must be tested and perfected, and they must be nourished further on the milk of sincere preaching, so that by it they may grow more and more and be carried on to perfection; domestic and scholastic instruction meanwhile not ceasing, but even further advanced, and indeed in a way revived through the ecclesiastical. Nor is this duty unworthy of preachers, since it is theirs to care with the greatest zeal for the flower of youth, so that happier fruits may spring from it. For this reason the Apostle, who could not speak to the Corinthians as to spiritual people but as to carnal, gave them milk to drink, 1 Cor. 3:1, 2. The method of catechetical instruction should be chosen to be as well suited as possible to exercising youth in the principles of faith. The examination must be carried out early, not only of memory but also of judgment, with prudence adapted to the capacity of the young, and with singular gentleness and discretion, so that the judgment is not troubled, nor the desire to learn checked, by harshness or sharpness of words. Catechetical sermons are also not to be disapproved, in which dialogues, confirmed by some principal testimony of Scripture, are set out before the whole people, so that novices may be strengthened in what they have learned, and the more advanced may recall and be the more confirmed in what the novices have learned. The greatest use of such sermons may be outside catechetical instruction, and it should be a chief concern that they be introduced everywhere and attended with equal faith, zeal, eagerness and skill.

units.la: LXXX. Post doctrinam Verbi Dei Ecclesiæ ministrorum munus & potestas circa ceremonias versatur.
units.tr: LXXX. After the doctrine of the Word of God, the office and power of the Church's ministers concern ceremonies.

units.la: Homo enim, qua infirmitate est, sive puer, sive adultus, in doctrina verbi Divini commodè erudiri, & in fide Jesu Christi enutriri, ali, foveri, & vivum Regni Christi membrum, nisi certis quibusdam externis & aspectabilibus adminiculis nequit; Scitè enim S. Augustinus contra Faust. Manich. lib. IX. 11. dixit, in nullum nomen religionis sive verum, sive falsum, coagulari posse homines, nisi aliquo signaculorum vel Sacramentorum visibilium consortio colligentur. Hoc nomine in Ecclesia ceremoniis, ceu actionibus, vel gestibus solennibus, quorum subsidio, quæ ad doctrinam verbi Divini & cultum pertinent, non tantùm commodiori ordine, & cum decoro aliquo peragantur, sed etiam oculis quasi subjecta declarentur, imò & obsignentur. Sùntque illæ duplicis generis, Divinitus institutæ, ad quas imprimis Sacramenta referuntur, & τάξεις boni ordinis, quas Scriptores Ecclesiastici modò κανόνας, modò διατυπώσεις, διατάξεις, διατυχάς appellant; sed vetustiores illa distinxerunt, quibus κανόνες dogmata fidei, διατυπώσεις formulas, seu ritus liturgiarum, ὅρισμοι definitiones circa disciplinam Ecclesiæ notant. Nobis de statutis & ceremoniis ab Ecclesia institutis sermo est. De ceremoniis prioris generis Loco XXV. alibique fusius egimus. Posterioris generis illæ vel circa Sacramentorum administrationem, velut tempus, locum, Baptismi petitionem, patrinos & testes Baptismi, lavandi ritum catechumenos communicantes, præparationem ad usum cœnæ, communionem ægrotantium, &c. vel circa externi cultus omnis ordinem & decorum, veluti tempus & locum cultus, dies festos, Templorum ornatum, cantum, denuntiationem publicam matrimonii initi, Neogamorum institutionem, proclamationem, copulationem, benedictionem, & similia versantur. De quibus singulis in loco etiam pluribus egimus.
units.tr: For man, by reason of his weakness, whether child or adult, cannot be suitably taught in the doctrine of the divine Word, nor nourished, fostered and cherished in the faith of Jesus Christ, and made a living member of the kingdom of Christ, unless he is supported by certain external and visible aids. For St. Augustine rightly said contra Faust. Manich. lib. IX. 11. that men cannot be gathered under any name of religion, true or false, unless they are brought together by some fellowship of visible signs or sacraments. In this sense the Church has ceremonies, as solemn actions or gestures, by whose help those things which belong to the doctrine of the divine Word and to worship are carried on not only in a more convenient order and with some decorum, but are also made plain, as it were set before the eyes, and even sealed. These are of two kinds: those divinely instituted, to which the sacraments above all are referred, and the orders of good order [τάξεις], which ecclesiastical writers now call canons [κανόνας], now formulas, arrangements and dispositions [διατυπώσεις, διατάξεις, διατυχάς].
