The older writers, however, distinguished these: canons [κανόνες] denoted the doctrines of faith, formulas [διατυπώσεις] the forms or rites of the liturgies, and definitions [ὅρισμοι] the decisions concerning the discipline of the Church. We are speaking here of the statutes and ceremonies instituted by the Church. We have treated fully the ceremonies of the former kind at Locus XXV and elsewhere. Those of the latter kind concern either the administration of the sacraments, such as the time, the place, the request for baptism, the sponsors and witnesses of baptism, the rite of washing for catechumens who communicate, the preparation for the use of the Supper, the communion of the sick, and so on; or the order and decorum of all external worship, such as the time and place of worship, feast days, the adornment of churches, singing, the public announcement of an intended marriage, the instruction of the newly married, their proclamation, joining, blessing, and the like. We have treated each of these more fully in their places.

units.la: LXXXI. De ceremoniis ejusmodi non Divinitus præceptus, sed humanitus institutis, adeóque legibus merè Ecclesiasticis circa externum ordinem & politiam, in universum tenendum est, nullam Divini cultus necessarii partem in iis consistere, sed eas politici, & quasi humani ordinis partem vel locum, ad commodiorem & decentiorem cultus externi administrationem, obtinere.
units.tr: LXXXI. Concerning ceremonies of this kind, which are not commanded by God but instituted by men, and so are purely ecclesiastical laws concerning external order and polity, we must hold in general that no part of the necessary worship of God consists in them; rather they hold the place of a part of the political and, as it were, human order, serving for a more convenient and decent administration of external worship.

units.la: Neque enim, ceu res in specie adiaphorae, seu indifferentes conscientiam aliter quàm vi mandati generalis ordinem & decorum in Ecclesia sancientis, nec non charitatis fraternæ, quæ scandalum dare vetat, obligant. Ecclesia enim nulla potestate pollet, qua ex re indifferente per se, rem absolutè differentem faciat, & id, quod Deus purificavit, inquinare vel polluere valeat. Ita enim præceptum humanum in Divinum jus, quo fidelibus libertas datur, nec non in præceptum Divinum, quo iidem stare ea libertate, qua Christus ipsos liberavit, & non pati se δογματίζεσθαι placitis hominum obstringi, vel servos hominum fieri, & ἐξαπάζεσθαι in potestatem à quoquam redigi, Gal. V. 1. Col. II. 18. 20. 1. Cor. VII. 23. VI. 12. jubentur. Denique in jus Capitis, & modum, quo in totum corpus suum influere vult, incurreret. Vult enim Christus, ceu caput Ecclesiæ in omnes influere per legem positam in medio omnium, & cordibus omnium, maximorum & minimorum inscriptam, ut conscientia illorum vel per se & sponte, vel per narrationem verbi & demonstrationem ejus, quod ex lege fidei in Christum fluit, judicet, hoc faciendum vel non faciendum esse. Quod ad ea attinet, quæ vi generalis præcepti à singulis agenda sunt, & tamen non uno modo agi possunt, charitatis & prudentiæ est, consilium dare; & ejusdem charitatis ac modestiæ est, bonis consiliis obsequi. Si enim vel inimico tenemur malam præbere, vel tunicam concedere, vel angarianti nos obsecundare, si spes sit eum lucrandi, Matth. V. 39. 40. 41. quantò magis obediendum est ductori, Hebr. XIII. 7. vel fratri, consilium danti, & roganti, ut quod utile nobis est, saltem obesse non potest, faciamus. Neque tamen ad imperanda talia potestas alia, quàm patria, civilis & herilis, competere potest. Sunt etiam, quæ cœtui, vel apud cœtum ex generali præcepto agenda sunt, & non uno modo agi possunt, nec quovis modo semper recte fieri possunt. Illorum determinandorum potestas penes Ecclesiam est. Sicut enim singuli pro se potestatem habent determinandi modum officii sui privati: ita etiam Ecclesia habet potestatem determinandi modum officii communis. Omnia enim decenter & ordine fieri debent, 1. Cor. XIV. 40. Sub illis tamen non continentur, quæ ad actum ipsum mandati nihil faciunt, velut, qua veste præco verbi Dei indui debeat; potest enim quavis indui, quæ & honesta & gravis est, & à moribus in civitate receptis non abhorret. Neque etiam huc pertinent ritus significativi & mystici, quia nec ad ordinem & decorum Ecclesiæ faciunt, & tales ritus atque παλαιά, quæ præcedentibus seculis Ecclesiam obruerunt, ab imitatione gentilium παλαιῶν & gesticulationum originem habent; neque utiles vel necessarii sunt, quia pietas, religio, cultus, ædificatio sine iis consistere potest; & rituum talium instituendorum nec finis nec modus est, atque ne nimis sint, rursus nova moderatione, & delectu & potestate ad faciendam eam moderationem opus erit; & si ritus ejusmodi definiantur, omitti amplius non poterunt. Obediendum equidem ductoribus est, sed ducentibus in via, non καταξεγχεύειν, juri, libertati & fidei præjudicium facientibus. Tales enim non ἡγούμενοι ductores sunt, sed ἀρχοντες principes & Domini esse volunt. Si tamen injungatur id, quod nec contra fidem, nec contra bonos mores est, & ad ordinis custodiam facit, & non ut pars necessaria cultus, sed ut libera observatio præscribitur, præceptum Dei generale servandi ordinis, decori & charitatis, pro eorum, inter quos vivitur, societate servandum esse, pluribus etiam S. Augustinus ad Inquisit. Jan. lib. I. 11. nec non Epist. 109. ad Jan. cap. 18. commonefacit & consulit. Saluberrimam enim hanc regulam sapienter commendat, ut, quæ non sunt contra fidem, neque contra bonos mores, & habent aliquid ad exhortationem melioris vitæ, ubicunque instituì videmus, vel instituta cognoscimus, non solùm non improbemus, sed etiam laudando & imitando sectemur, si aliquorum infirmitas non ita impedit, ut amplius detrimentum sit.
units.tr: For these things, like matters indifferent in themselves, bind the conscience only by virtue of the general command that establishes order and decorum in the Church, and of fraternal charity, which forbids giving offence. For the Church has no power by which it could make absolutely different a thing that is indifferent in itself, or defile and pollute what God has cleansed. A human precept would thereby be set above the divine law that grants liberty to believers, and above the divine precept by which they are commanded to stand in the liberty with which Christ has made them free, and not to suffer themselves to be bound by the decrees of men [δογματίζεσθαι], nor to become servants of men, nor to be brought under the power of anyone [ἐξαπάζεσθαι]: Gal. V. 1; Col. II. 18, 20; 1 Cor. VII. 23; VI. 12. Finally, it would encroach on the right of the Head, and on the manner in which he wishes to flow into his whole body. For Christ, as Head of the Church, wishes to flow into all through the law placed in the midst of all and written on the hearts of all, great and small, so that their conscience may judge, either by itself and spontaneously or through the proclamation of the Word and its demonstration, what flows from the law of faith in Christ, that this is to be done or not to be done. As for those things which, by virtue of a general precept, are to be done by individuals but can be done in more than one way, it belongs to charity and prudence to give counsel, and it belongs to the same charity and modesty to obey good counsel. For if we are bound to offer the other cheek to an enemy, or to give up our tunic, or to go a second mile with one who compels us, if there is hope of winning him, Matt. V. 39–41, how much more must we obey the leader, Heb. XIII. 7, or a brother who gives counsel and asks that we do what is useful to us and cannot at least harm us. Yet no authority other than paternal, civil or master's authority can properly command such things. There are also things which are to be done for the congregation, or before the congregation, by a general precept, which can be done in more than one way and cannot always be done rightly in every way. The power of determining these belongs to the Church. For just as individuals have the power to determine the manner of their private duty, so too the Church has the power to determine the manner of its common duty: "All things must be done decently and in order," 1 Cor. XIV. 40. Yet these do not include things which contribute nothing to the act of the command itself, such as what garment the herald of God's Word ought to wear; for he may wear any garment that is both honourable and dignified and does not offend the customs received in the state. Nor do significant and mystical rites belong here, because they contribute neither to the order nor to the decorum of the Church. Such rites, and the ancient [παλαιά] practices that overwhelmed the Church in earlier centuries, took their origin from the imitation of pagan rites and gestures. Nor are they useful or necessary, since piety, religion, worship and edification can subsist without them; and there is neither end nor measure in instituting such rites, and to keep them from becoming excessive a new moderation, selection and authority would be needed to effect that moderation; and once such rites were prescribed, they could no longer be omitted. We must indeed obey leaders, but leaders who guide us on the way, not those who lord it over us [κατακυριεύειν], doing prejudice to law, liberty and faith. For such men are not leaders [ἡγούμενοι] but wish to be rulers [ἄρχοντες] and lords. If, however, something is enjoined which is neither against faith nor against good morals, which serves the keeping of order, and which is prescribed not as a necessary part of worship but as a free observance, then the general precept of God to keep order, decorum and charity, to be maintained in fellowship with those among whom we live, admonishes and advises us. St. Augustine also admonishes and advises this in several places: ad Inquisit. Jan. lib. I. 11. and Epist. 109 ad Jan. cap. 18. For he wisely commends this most salutary rule: that whatever things are not against faith or against good morals, and have something to encourage a better life, wherever we see them instituted or learn that they have been instituted, we should not only refrain from disapproving them, but also follow and imitate them with praise, provided that the weakness of some does not so hinder them that they become a greater detriment.

units.la: LXXXII. Aliæ
units.tr: LXXXII. Other

units.la: Minis-trorum Eccle-siæ officium circa cere-monias.
units.tr: The office of the ministers of the Church concerning ceremonies.

units.la: In quibus non pars cultus Divini, sed ordinis Ecclesiastici externi exercitium constitit.
units.tr: In these matters the practice of external church order, not a part of the divine worship, is what consists.

units.la: LXXXII. Aliæ quoque circa ceremonias, statuta & leges Ecclesiæ præscriptiones sunt. Nam ante omnia verbo Dei, quantum fieri potest, sic conformari debent, ut ad Ecclesiæ eximiam ædificationem spectent, & utilem declarationem, exercitium & usum ejus doctrinæ, quæ in Scriptura Divinitus patefacta est, contineant, vel ad auditum verbi, usum Sacramentorum & cœtus publicos invitent fideles, vel doctrinæ commodius promovendæ & amplificandæ inserviant. Ubi verò verbo Dei contrariari comperiuntur, repudiandæ planè sunt, quia mandatum Dei per traditiones hominum transgredi non licet; inprimis cùm frustra Deus mandatis humanis colatur, Matth. XV.9. Marc. VII.8.9. Tum nec Ecclesia ceremoniis ejusmodi humanis onerari nimium debet, ne præ earum multitudine fidei ipsius naufragium patiatur. Nam ubi multum ceremoniarum, ibi parum fidei est. Hac in parte, sic præclarè Augustinus ad Inquis. Jan. cap. I. loquitur, Dominus noster Jesus Christus leni nos jugo subdidit & sarcinæ levi. Unde Sacramentis numero paucissimis, observatione facillimis, significatione pvastantissimis, societatem novi populi colligavit. Enixiore cura in id incumbendum, ut doctrina fidei & charitas purè & illibatè tradatur, quàm ut apparatus aliquis, & pompa luxuriosa atque theatrica ceremoniarum in sacris cœtibus videatur; in Novo cumprimis Testamento, quod cultum spiritualem, non carnalem iterum exigit. Præterea hoc ceremoniæ humanæ habent, quòd abusu, superstitione inveterata necessitatis & cultus opinione, & confusionis metu deteriores redditæ abrogari debent, licèt scandalum prætendatur. Nam etiam etiámque cavendum, tum ne probi & rectè credentes offendantur; tum ne hostes veritatis in superstitione sua obfirmentur. Potius est, confessionem veræ fidei semper retinere atque edere, & hac etiam in parte veræ Ecclesiæ se adjungere. Exite è medio eorum, & separamini, dicit Dominus, & impurum ne attingite; & ego suscipiam vos, 2. Cor. VI.17. Exite Babylone populeme mi, & cum peccatis ejus ne communicate, Apoc. XVIII.4. Unde Ezechias æneum serpentem, Divino jussu erectum licèt, confregit, quamprimùm superstitioni eorum, qui ei suffire cœperant inservivit, 1. Reg. XVIII.4. Ac ne quidem rigidè nimis, & cum periculo schismatis, urgeri, vel mordicus etiam retineri debent. Videte, ne quodammodo potestas vestra infirmis offendiculo sit. Et peribit frater infirmus tua ista scientia, propter quem Christus mortuus est, 1. Corinth. VIII.9.11. Neque Ecclesia Dei hanc consuetudinem habet, ut τῇ φιλονεικίᾳ contentioni studeat, ibid. XI.16. Diversitas porro ceremoniarum in diversis Ecclesiis nemini bono offendiculo esse debet; quia quæ-vis Ecclesia libertate sua gaudet, neque ulla alii subjicitur, vel jure Divino se conformare tenetur. Neque omnia omnibus conveniunt; sed alia in alio Regno, vel provincia Christianismi, alia in populosa civitate, alia in angusto oppidulo, vel obscuro vico facienda sunt. Et retinentur alicubi ceremoniæ, quæ nullum adhuc vitium & abusum contraxerunt; quæ alibi, ubi vitium & abusus incessit, piè abolentur. Novas insuper induci, haud raró temporum, personarum, & præsentis status ratio postulat. Neque ullæ à piis Ecclesiarum Reformatoribus ceremoniæ hac lege institutæ sunt, vel institui potuerunt, ne unquam, & nullo in casu mutentur. Quin & utilis subinde ceremoniarum diversitas est, ut libertas Christiana, & discrimen inter dogmata fidei, atque cultum principalem Divinum, & ceremonias humanas rectius intelligatur, & ne ceremoniæ in cultus necessarii partem & opinionem abeant. Nec sine causa Irenæus Victorem Asiaticas Ecclesias & Quartodecimanos in Paschatis celebrandi tempore & jejuniis dissentientes excommunicantem, teste Eusebio Hist. Eccles. lib. V.23. reprehendit eo argumento, quòd dissonantia jejunii fidei concordiam commendet. Denique & illud circa ceremonias & statuta Ecclesiæ animadvertendum, quòd in earum correctione non ab executione, sed à doctrina & institutione populi initium faciendum sit. Abusus enim priùs ex cordibus, quàm externus ceremoniarum usus & aspectus ex oculis abjici debet. Alias non Christiani, sed hypocritæ, vel præfracti, obstinati, rebelles & seditiosi homines fiunt, & infirmi ab agnitione & investigatione veritatis retrahuntur. Sed infirmi docilesque cùm satis instructi sunt, obstinatis & præfractis, qui impias ceremonias mordicus urgentes, institutionem omnem recusant, ne ad momentum quidem per subjectionem cedendum, neque in eorum gratiam veritas Evangelii labefactari, vel Ecclesiæ ædificatio negligi, orthodoxi offendi, vel infirmi in erroribus & superstitione sua confirmari debent.
units.tr: LXXXII. Other statutes, laws and prescriptions of the Church also concern ceremonies. For above all they ought, as far as possible, to be shaped by the Word of God, so that they serve the great edification of the Church and a useful declaration, exercise and practice of the doctrine divinely revealed in Scripture. They should either invite the faithful to hear the Word, to use the sacraments and to public assemblies, or serve to promote and extend doctrine more conveniently. But where they are found to be contrary to the Word of God, they are to be utterly rejected, because it is not lawful to transgress the commandment of God through the traditions of men; especially since God is worshipped in vain with human commandments (Matt. 15:9; Mark 7:8, 9). Nor, again, should the Church be burdened too much with such human ceremonies, lest through their multitude it suffer shipwreck of its faith. For where there are many ceremonies, there is little faith. On this point Augustine speaks admirably in his letter to Januarius, chapter 1: Our Lord Jesus Christ has placed us under a gentle yoke and a light burden. Hence, with sacraments very few in number, very easy to observe, and most excellent in meaning, he has bound together the fellowship of the new people. Far more earnest care must be given to ensuring that the doctrine of faith and charity is handed down purely and undefiled, than that some display, and a luxurious and theatrical pomp of ceremonies, should be seen in sacred assemblies. This applies especially in the New Testament, which again demands a spiritual worship, not a carnal one. Moreover, human ceremonies have this feature: when, through abuse, through superstition grown old, through the opinion of their necessity and worship, and through fear of confusion, they have become worse, they ought to be abolished, even though offence is pretended. For care must be taken on both counts: that the upright and rightly believing are not offended, and that the enemies of the truth are not confirmed in their superstition. It is better always to retain and proclaim the confession of the true faith, and in this matter also to join oneself to the true Church. Come out from among them, and be separate, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; and I will receive you (2 Cor. 6:17). Come out of her, my people, and do not take part in her sins (Rev. 18:4). Hence Hezekiah broke the bronze serpent, although it had been erected by divine command, as soon as it began to serve the superstition of those who burned incense to it (2 Kings 18:4). Nor ought they to be pressed too rigidly, or clung to stubbornly, with the danger of schism. Take heed lest your liberty somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. And through your knowledge the weak brother will perish, for whom Christ died (1 Cor. 8:9, 11). Nor does the Church of God have the custom of being eager for contentiousness [τῇ φιλονεικίᾳ] (ibid. 11:16). Moreover, the diversity of ceremonies in different Churches ought to be an offence to no good person, because every Church rejoices in its own liberty, and is subject to no other, nor is it bound by divine right to conform itself to others. Nor do all things suit all people: some ceremonies must be performed in one kingdom or province of Christendom, others in a populous city, others in a narrow town or an obscure village. Some ceremonies are retained in some places because they have not yet contracted any fault or abuse; those which have in other places, where fault and abuse have crept in, are devoutly abolished. Moreover, the reason of the times, of persons and of the present state often demands that new ones be introduced. Nor have any ceremonies been instituted by the pious Reformers of the Churches under this law, or could be instituted, that they should never and in no case be changed. Indeed, the variety of ceremonies is sometimes useful, so that Christian liberty, and the distinction between the dogmas of faith and the principal divine worship and human ceremonies, may be more rightly understood, and so that ceremonies do not come to be regarded as part of the necessary worship. Nor without cause did Irenaeus rebuke Victor, who excommunicated the Asian Churches and the Quartodecimans for differing in the time of celebrating Easter and in fasts, as Eusebius reports (Hist. Eccl. 5.23), on the ground that disagreement about fasting commends agreement in faith. Finally, this must also be noted concerning ceremonies and the statutes of the Church: in correcting them one must begin not with their enforcement, but with the teaching and instruction of the people. For the abuse must be cast out of the hearts before the outward use and appearance of the ceremonies is removed from the eyes. Otherwise people become not Christians but hypocrites, or stubborn, obstinate, rebellious and seditious men, and the weak are drawn back from acknowledging and searching out the truth. But when the weak and teachable have been sufficiently instructed, the obstinate and stubborn, who clutch impious ceremonies and refuse all instruction, must not be yielded to even for a moment through submission; nor, for their sake, should the truth of the Gospel be weakened, the building up of the Church neglected, the orthodox offended, or the weak confirmed in their errors and superstition.

units.la: LXXXIII. Proxima administrationi Ecclesiæ per ceremonias Divinitus & humanitus institutas est administratio ejusdem per Disciplinam.
units.tr: LXXXIII. The administration of the Church through discipline comes next after its administration through ceremonies, which are instituted both by God and by men.

units.la: Quæ voluntatis Dei in verbo ejus declaratæ, & per Sacramenta obsignatæ personalis quædam per censuras, ad scandala doctrinæ & vitæ sive præcavenda, sive ex Ecclesia averruncanda applicatio est. Disciplina enim πα-δεία, מוסר (quod proprie ςωφρονισμὸν castigationem, cujus Spiritus à Deo datur, 2. Tim. I.7. dixeris) non tantùm vel parentum & patrumfamilias, vel Principum & Magistratuum, sed etiam fratrum inter se, tum rectorum Ecclesiæ, qui κυβερνήσεις, ἡγούμενοι, ποιμένες, ἐπίσκοποι, πρεσβύτεροι, ποιμένες gubernationes, duces, præsides, episcopi, seniores, pastores passim dicuntur, denique totius Ecclesiæ est. Nulla enim sine disciplinæ, legum & poenarum nervis atque fulcris societas: neque disciplina sine ordine eorum, quorum alii corripiunt, judicant, alii corripiuntur & judicantur, stare atque florere potest. Proin nec Ecclesia, domus illa Dei viventis, 1. Timoth. III. 15. ædificata ut civitas שחברה לה יחדיו quæ composita est sibi una (cui nihil deest, cujus nullæ partes hiant, in qua nihil scissum, ruptum & divisum est) Psal. CXXII. 3. disciplina & ordine simili carere potest. Nam in prædicatione quidem verbi Dei voluntas Dei proponitur, & ad fidem & obedientiam gignendam & augendam realiter applicatur. In Sacramentorum dispensatione voluntàs Dei etiam personaliter sigillis, ad fidem & obedientiam confirmandam applicatur. In exercitio verò disciplinæ voluntas Dei personaliter etiam applicatur per censuras, ad removenda da illa vitia, quae cum vera fide & obedientia pugnant. Unde optimi quique Theologi disciplinam inter notas Ecclesiae, post praeconium verbi & Sacramentorum administrationem collocant, quia sine ea Ecclesia statum suum necessarium & completum habere non potest, & nec totum Regnum Christi, nec totum Evangelium recipiunt, qui disciplinam rejiciunt. Licet enim, ubi generalis usus clavium solventium & ligantium per praeconium verbi, & administrationem Sacramentorum apud teneras conscientias, ad gignendam resipiscentiam efficax satis est, singularis usus clavis solventis & ligantis non requiratur; cum disciplina non aliud quam poenitentiam intendat, qua per generale praeconium verbi obtenta disciplinae coercentis usus nullus est: tamen propter duritiem & fraudulentiam cordis, quae in plerisque peccantibus reperitur, personalis eorum, quae ad correctionem peccati, securitatem excutiendam, & seriam curam sanctitatis excitandam faciunt, applicatio requiritur. Ordinatio equidem Christi de personali disciplina exercenda primario & directe ad emendationem lapsi tendit; sed secundario & indirecte eadem ad aliorum etiam aedificationem spectat hactenus, quod tum submovet ea, quae illam impediunt, tum promovet, quae eandem juvant. Iccirco eorum etiam, qui coercendi non sunt, sed hactenus recte currunt, respectu disciplinae exercitium necessarium evadit.
units.tr: Discipline is a personal application of God's will, declared in his Word and sealed by the sacraments, through censures, either to guard against scandals in doctrine and life or to cut them out of the Church. For discipline (παιδεία, מוסר [musar], which one might properly call "correction" [σωφρονισμόν], whose spirit is given by God, 2 Tim. 1.7) belongs not only to parents and heads of households, or to princes and magistrates, but also to brothers among themselves, and to the rulers of the Church, who are commonly called governments, leaders, presidents, bishops, elders and ministers (κυβερνήσεις, ἡγούμενοι, ποιμένες, ἐπίσκοποι, πρεσβύτεροι, ποιμένες), and finally to the whole Church. For no society can stand and flourish without the sinews and props of discipline, laws and penalties, nor without an order in which some reprove and judge while others are reproved and judged. Therefore the Church, that house of the living God (1 Tim. 3.15), built as a city [שחברה לה יחדיו] that is compacted together into one (in which nothing is lacking, no parts gape, nothing is torn, broken or divided; Ps. 122.3), cannot do without discipline and a similar order. For in the preaching of the Word of God the will of God is set forth and really applied to the begetting and increasing of faith and obedience. In the dispensing of the sacraments the will of God is also applied personally, through the seals, to confirm faith and obedience. In the exercise of discipline, however, the will of God is applied personally through censures, to remove those vices which are contrary to true faith and obedience. Hence the best theologians place discipline among the marks of the Church, after the proclamation of the Word and the administration of the sacraments, because without it the Church cannot have its necessary and complete state, and those who reject discipline do not receive the whole kingdom of Christ or the whole Gospel. For although, where the general use of the keys of loosing and binding through the proclamation of the Word and the administration of the sacraments is effective enough among tender consciences to beget repentance, a singular use of the key of loosing and binding is not required, since discipline aims at nothing other than repentance, and where repentance has been obtained through the general proclamation of the Word there is no use of coercive discipline; nevertheless, on account of the hardness and deceitfulness of heart found in most sinners, a personal application of those means is required which serve to correct sin, to shake off security, and to stir up a serious care for holiness. Christ's ordinance concerning the personal exercise of discipline aims primarily and directly at the amendment of the fallen; but secondarily and indirectly it also concerns the edification of others, insofar as it both removes what hinders that edification and promotes what helps it. Hence the exercise of discipline becomes necessary also with respect to those who are not to be coerced, but who are running well so far.

units.la: LXXXIV. Disciplina Ecclesiae Divinitus instituta est.
units.tr: LXXXIV. Discipline has been instituted by God.

units.la: Nam Deus Ecclesiae in Petri persona potestatem clavium, coelum aperientium vel claudentium, & cum eadem potestatem ligandi & solvendi, dedit, Matth. XVI. 19. Quae sine disciplina personali, saltem apud peccatores scandalosos exerceri non potest. Quomodo enim sine disciplina vel coelum homini ἀμετανοήτῳ claudi, vel peccator ligari potest? Tum Christus Ecclesiae & elenchum peccatoris, & ejusdem judicium mandavit. Si peccaverit adversus te frater tuus, vade, ἔλεγξον & reprehende eum, &c. Si Ecclesiam non audiverit, esto tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus. Amen dico vobis, quaecunque ligaveritis in terra, ligata in Coelo erunt; & quaecunque solveritis in terra, soluta in Coelo erunt, ibid. XVIII. 15-20. Incipit enim disciplina ab ἐλέγχῳ redargutione, quae ἀπόδειξιν demonstrationem & applicationem regulae Verbi Dei ad conscientiam necessario continet, & in κρίσει judicio terminatur. Quae passim Scriptura commendat. Domine in arctu visitant te (in tribulatione te quaerunt) fundunt mussitationem מוסר Disciplina tua iis est, Esaj. XXVI. 16. ubi מוסר disciplina Dei appellatur, quia fit per verbum Dei, ut solus Deus in Ecclesia Rex & judex maneat. Jehova enim judex noster est, ibid. XXXIII. 22. Observate judicium & facite justitiam, ibid. LVI. 1. Judicium autem facit, qui verum a falso, bonum a malo, tenebras a luce, fratres a non fratribus discernit, bonum facientibus collaudatur, malum facientibus indolescit, & cum illorum peccatis non communicat, juxta illa: Diligentes Dominum, odio habete malum, Psal. XCVII. 10. Exosi malum, agglutinate vos bono, Rom. XII. 9. Sed missis iis, quae ex V. T. inde ab origine Ecclesiae judicii illius exempla plurima afferri possunt, & sol-
units.tr: For God gave to the Church, in the person of Peter, the power of the keys, of opening or shutting heaven, and with it the power of binding and loosing (Matt. 16.19). This power cannot be exercised without personal discipline, at least toward scandalous sinners. For how can heaven be shut against an unrepentant man, or a sinner be bound, without discipline? Christ also committed to the Church both the reproof of the sinner and its judgement: If your brother sins against you, go and reprove [ἔλεγξον] him, etc. If he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector. Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven (ibid. 18.15–20). For discipline begins with reproof [ἐλέγχῳ], which necessarily contains the demonstration [ἀπόδειξιν] and application of the rule of the Word of God to the conscience, and it ends in judgement [κρίσει]. Scripture commends this everywhere. Lord, in distress they visit you; they pour out a murmuring prayer when your discipline [מוסר] is upon them (Isa. 26.16), where it is called the discipline of God, because it is carried out through the Word of God, so that God alone remains the King and Judge in the Church. For the LORD is our judge (ibid. 33.22). Observe judgement and do justice (ibid. 56.1). He exercises judgement who distinguishes true from false, good from evil, darkness from light, brothers from non-brothers; he is praised by those who do good, he grieves at those who do evil, and he has no fellowship with their sins, according to those words: Love the Lord, hate evil (Ps. 97.10). Hate what is evil; cleave to what is good (Rom. 12.9). But setting these aside, many examples of that judgement, from the Old Testament from the very beginning of the Church, can be cited, and [they] ought to suffice,

units.la: lent, licet non omnia ejusdem generis sint, cum quaedam Divini potius, quam humani judicii exempla sint, velut illud de Adamo & Caino sumptum; multa inprimis in N. T. de judicio eo extant. Rogo vos, fratres, ut animadvertatis eos, qui dissidia & scandala praeter doctrinam, quam vos didicistis, faciunt, & recedite ab eis, Rom. XVI. 17. Nunc autem scribo vobis, ne commisceamini, si quis, qui nominatur frater, sit scortator, aut avarus, aut idololatra, &c. cum tali ne comedatis (ut vel eum invitetis, ceu amicum, vel ab eo invitati honoris causa accedatis) 1. Corinth. V. 11. Qui non diligit Dominum Jesum Christum, sit anathema, Maranatha seu Dominus noster venit, ibid. XVI. 22. Si quis non obedit sermoni nostro, hunc notate, & ne commiscemini ipsi, ut erubescat, 2. Thess. III. 14. 15. Haereticum hominem post unam aut alteram admonitionem rejice, sciens quod talis sit eversus, & peccet a se ipso damnatus, Tit. III. 10. Si quis venit ad vos, & hanc doctrinam non affert, ne suscipite eum domum, & Ave ei ne dicite. Nam qui ipsum jubet salvere, communicat cum operibus ipsius malis, 2. Joh. 10.
units.tr: though not all of them are of the same kind, since some are examples of divine rather than human judgement, such as the one taken from Adam and Cain. But many such examples of that judgement are found especially in the New Testament. I beg you, brothers, to mark those who cause divisions and scandals contrary to the doctrine which you have learned, and turn away from them (Rom. 16.17). But now I write to you not to associate with anyone who is called a brother, if he is a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, etc.; with such a one do not even eat (that is, do not invite him as a friend, nor accept his invitation out of respect) (1 Cor. 5.11). If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema; Maranatha, that is, our Lord comes (ibid. 16.22). If anyone does not obey our word, note him, and do not associate with him, that he may be ashamed (2 Thess. 3.14, 15). Reject a heretical man after one or two admonitions, knowing that such a man is perverted and sins, being condemned by himself (Titus 3.10). If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, and do not say "Hail" to him; for whoever bids him farewell shares in his evil works (2 John 10).

units.la: LXXXV. Manifestum insuper est & gloriae Dei, & salutis Ecclesiae interesse, ut disciplinae hujus exercitium vigeat.
units.tr: LXXXV. It is plainly in the interest both of God's glory and of the salvation of the Church that the exercise of this discipline flourish.

units.la: Cum enim ingens naturae humanae corruptio sit, & sanctissimi quique infirmitate laborent & tententur, disciplina salutare adversus illam remedium & velut froenum quoddam est, quo illa tam in universo Ecclesiae corpore, quam in singulis illius membris cohibetur, ne nimium sibi indulgeant, sed in officio potius suo contineantur, & solidissimo charitatis atque libertatis Christianae vinculo tantum non conglutinentur. Quod igitur in corporis humani compage nervi sunt, id Ecclesiae conservandae disciplina est. Tum Deus ipse contumelia magna afficitur, cum impii, blasphemi, impoenitentes sine justa animadversione feruntur, perinde ac si inter ejus & Diaboli filios nullum discrimen intercederet. Qua ratione Dei & Diaboli regnum turpissime permiscetur & confunditur. Qui gloriaris in lege, per transgressionem legis τὸν Θεόν ἀτιμάζεις Deum contumelia afficis. Nam nomen Dei propter vos blasphematur in gentibus, Rom. II. 23. 24. Praeterea Ecclesia sceleratis & impoenitentibus connivendo, neque illos tam publice, quam privatim castigando, neque per Magistratus tantum gladium externum, qui ad cordis mutationem vim nullam habet, sed per gladium etiam illum Spiritus, quovis gladio ancipiti penetrantiorem, in illos non animadvertendo, damnationis & exitii illorum ipsa quoque coram Divino judicio rea peragitur. Communicat enim cum illorum peccatis & operibus malis, 2. Joh. 10. adeoque etiam cum eorum poenis. Exite Babylone, populme mi, ne communicetis cum peccatis ejus, & plagarum ejus participes fiatis, Apoc. XVIII. 4. Fili hominis, speculatorem dedi te domui Israelis, & audies ex ore meo verbum, & admonebis illos ex me. Cum dixero improbo: Moriendo morieris, & non admonueris illum, & non locutus fueris, ut admonitione abducas improbum a via improba, ad vitam illi conciliandam, ipse improbus in iniquitate sua morietur, & sanguinem ipsius ex manu tua requiram, Ezech. III. 17. 18. XXXIII. 7. 8. Deinde que
units.tr: For human nature is deeply corrupt, and even the most holy labour under weakness and are tempted. Discipline is a salutary remedy against this, and as it were a bridle, by which corruption is restrained both in the whole body of the Church and in its individual members, so that they do not indulge themselves too much but remain rather within their duty, and are bound together, as it were, by the most solid bond of charity and Christian liberty. As the sinews hold together the frame of the human body, so the discipline of the Church holds it together and preserves it. God himself is also greatly dishonoured when the impious, the blasphemers and the unrepentant are suffered to go without due censure, as if there were no difference between them and the children of God and of the Devil. By this means the kingdom of God and that of the Devil are shamefully mixed and confused. You who boast in the law, through transgression you dishonour God, Rom. 2:23-24: for the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you. Moreover, when the Church connives at the wicked and the unrepentant, not rebuking them either publicly or privately, and when it does not punish them, relying only on the external sword of the magistrate, which has no power to change the heart, but not using also that sword of the Spirit, which is sharper than any two-edged sword, then the Church itself is made guilty before the divine judgment of the damnation and ruin of these people. For it shares in their sins and their evil works, 2 John 10, and so also in their punishments. Come out of Babylon, my people, that you may not share in her sins, and that you may not receive of her plagues, Rev. 18:4. Son of man, I have made you a watchman to the house of Israel; you shall hear the word from my mouth and warn them from me. When I say to the wicked, "O wicked man, you shall surely die," and you do not warn him, nor speak to dissuade the wicked from his wicked way, that he may live, the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand, Ezek. 3:17-18; 33:7-8. Next,

units.la: Ejusdem Divina institutio.
units.tr: Its divine institution.

units.la: Rationes disciplinam Ecclesiae confirmantes. que scelerum licentia & grassatione Regnum Christi scandalis impletur. Belialis filii, nec Deum nec homines metuentes, & ipsas etiam humanas potestates contemnentes invalescunt, & infirmi, quorum maximus semper in Ecclesia numerus est, malorum exemplis in transversum abrepti seducuntur. Atqui annitendum potius fuerat, ut qui extra septa Regni Christi constituti adhuc sunt, lucrifiant, & qui adversus nos, ceu maleficos, os aperiunt, opera nostra bona, & conversationem honestam videntes, Deum glorificent, 1.Petr.II.12. quàm ut qui jam oves gregis Christi facti sunt, scandalis, & conniventia Ecclesiæ ad illa perdantur. Ita enim quod crescere debuit Regnum & corpus Christi, indies minuitur & decrescit. Nam & fermenti modicum totam massam corrumpit, 1. Cor. V. 6. Galat. V. 9. & colloquia prava bonos mores corrumpunt, 1.Cor.XV.33. denique morbida facta pecus totum corrumpit ovile. Quanto rectius Christiani veteres, vel ipso Plinio Epist. lib. X. 100. teste, soliti sunt stato die ante lucem convenire, carmen Christo, quasi Deo dicere, seque Sacramento non in scelus aliquod obstringere, sed ut disciplinam custodirent, (seu, uti Tertullianus Apolog. c. 2. legit, confoederarunt) ne furta, ne latrocinia, ne adulteria committerent, ne fidem fallerent.
units.tr: Reasons confirming the discipline of the Church. Through the licence and spread of crimes the kingdom of Christ is filled with scandals. The sons of Belial, fearing neither God nor men, and despising even human authorities, grow strong, and the weak, who have always been the greatest number in the Church, are led astray and carried off by the examples of the wicked. Yet it would have been better to strive that those who still stand outside the fold of Christ's kingdom might be gained, and that those who open their mouths against us as evildoers, seeing our good works and our honest conduct, might glorify God, 1 Pet. 2:12, rather than that those who have already become sheep of Christ's flock should be lost through scandals and through the Church's connivance. For thus the kingdom and body of Christ, which ought to grow, is daily diminished and decreases. For a little leaven leavens the whole lump, 1 Cor. 5:6; Gal. 5:9, and evil communications corrupt good manners, 1 Cor. 15:33. Finally, one diseased animal infects the whole flock. How much more rightly did the early Christians act, as Pliny himself testifies (Epist. lib. X, 100), who were accustomed to meet on a fixed day before dawn, to sing a hymn to Christ as to God, and to bind themselves by a sacrament not to any crime, but to keep discipline (or, as Tertullian reads it in his Apology, ch. 2, they bound themselves by oath), so that they would not commit theft, robbery or adultery, and would not break faith.

units.la: LXXXVI. Non quævis peccata disciplinam postulant.
units.tr: LXXXVI. Not every sin calls for discipline.

units.la: Sunt enim infirmitates quædam, seu παραπτώματα & incursionis quotidianæ peccata, uti Tertullianus appellat, omnibus fere fidelibus communes, quarum singularis curatio & emendatio neque expectari, neque ab iis, quos eadem, vel similes premunt, exigi potest. Neque tantum peccata atrocia, conscientiam & societatem humanam vastantia, quæ civilibus pœnis plecti solent, ferulæ huic subsunt, sed talia etiam, quæ intra scelerum atrocitatem consistunt. Disciplina enim Ecclesiastica est pars administrationis Regni Christi, adeóque spiritualem habet naturam, & perfectionem majorem quærit, quàm quæ in civili honestate collocatur. Atque ea Ecclesiæ sanctitas est, ut non sufficiat intra leges publicas probum esse, cùm aliæ Christi, aliæ Cæsaris leges sint, & aliud Paulus noster, aliud Papinianus loquatur. Neque etiam personales tantùm injuriæ, quæ inter Ecclesiæ membra dissidia faciunt, vel alios à communione ejus avertunt, disciplinæ huic subjiciuntur. Alia etiam peccata sunt, quæ correctionem æquè, vel magis flagitant. Proprium ergo censuræ hujus objectum quodvis scandalum fratri datum, quo ille ad ruinam ædificari potest, est. Si peccaverit in te frater tuus, reprehende eum, &c. Matth. XVIII.15. Fratres, si præoccupetur homo lapsu aliquo, vos spirituales reconcinnate talem in spiritu mansuetudinis, Gal. VI. 1. Finis enim disciplinæ est, tum ne Ecclesiæ communicent cum alieno peccato, 2. Joh. 11. tum ut fratrem lucretur, Matth. XVIII.15. tum ut per correctionem peccantis tollat scandala, quò fideles reliqui inoffenso pede in cursu pietatis pergant, &, offendiculis impedientibus è medio sublatis, alii ad eandem viam alliciantur. Súntque scandala ejusmodi vel manifesta & publica, vel occulta & privata. Quorundam hominum peccata προδηλα manifesta sunt, præcedentia ad judicium, quosdam etiam sequuntur, seu peccantibus adhæscunt, ut, licet ad tempus non appareant, postea tamen apparitura sint, 1.Tim. V. 24. Manifesta & publica sunt, quæ publicè patrata, innotescunt omnibus, & palam Ecclesiæ scandalum præbent.
units.tr: For there are certain weaknesses, or slips, which Tertullian calls daily sins of attack [paraptōmata], common to almost all the faithful. Their individual cure and correction can neither be expected nor demanded of those who are burdened by the same or similar faults. Nor are only the atrocious sins that lay waste to conscience and human society, and which are usually punished by civil penalties, subject to this rod. Discipline also reaches those sins that fall short of atrocious crimes. For ecclesiastical discipline is a part of the administration of the kingdom of Christ, and so it has a spiritual nature and seeks a greater perfection than that which consists in civil decency. Indeed, the holiness of the Church is such that it is not enough to be upright within the public laws, since the laws of Christ are one thing and the laws of Caesar another, and our Paul speaks otherwise than Papinian. Nor are merely personal injuries, which cause quarrels among the members of the Church or turn others away from its fellowship, exempt from this discipline. There are also other sins which call for correction equally or even more. The proper object of this censure is therefore any scandal given to a brother by which he may be built up to his ruin. If your brother sins against you, rebuke him, etc., Matt. 18:15. Brethren, if a man is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, Gal. 6:1. For the end of discipline is that the Church should not share in another's sin, 2 John 11; that the brother may be gained, Matt. 18:15; and that, by correcting the sinner, scandals may be removed, so that the remaining faithful may press on in the course of piety without stumbling, and, with the obstacles that hinder them taken out of the way, others may be drawn to the same path. Scandals of this kind are either manifest and public, or hidden and private. The sins of some men are manifest beforehand, going before to judgment; for some sins follow after, that is, they cling to the sinners, so that although they do not appear for a time, they will afterwards come to light, 1 Tim. 5:24. Manifest and public are those sins which, committed in public, become known to all and openly give scandal to the Church.

units.la: Quæ iterum vel delicta, vel scelera sunt. Delicta sunt, quæ non tam ex προσκαιρως, quàm ex infirmitate & affectuum præoccupatione ab hominibus caeterà non malis, nec impietati addictis, patrantur. Scelera sunt, quæ obfirmato animo & elata manu committuntur. Et quædam publica sunt, ubi nec de scelere, nec de authore dubitatur; quædam quasi publica, quorum, omnibus notorum, author ignotus est, uti sæpe in homicidiis, scortationibus & furtis usu venit. Occulta verò sunt, non quæ nemini prorsus nota sunt, utpote de quibus solus Dominus, non Ecclesia judicat, Rom. II. 16. Sed quæ uni atque alteri, vel paucis tantùm cognita sunt, & ex quibus scandalum publicum nondum emersit. Quæ ipsa tamen etiam manifesta, & ex delictis scelera fieri possunt, quando contemptis privatis admonitionibus scandalum propalari, & Ecclesiæ renuntiari debet. Tum enim non peccati qualitas, sed accedens ei contumacia, & adversus Deum & Ecclesiam rebellio spectatur. Vir, qui fecerit וזד superbe, ut non obediat Sacerdoti, &c. morietur vir ille, &c. Deut. XVII.12. Aliter verò cum peccatis manifestis, aliter cum occultis agendum. In his enim initium ab admonitione privata faciendum est: in illis non item. Τὸς ἁμαρτάνοντας ιλλος, qui palam peccant, redargue coram omnibus, ut & reliqui timorem habeant, 1.Timoth.V.20. Medicina enim ad morbum, cui tollendo inservit, proportionem habere debet. Præterea manifesta judicium subeunt: occulta non subeunt prius quàm manifesta fiant.
units.tr: These again are either faults or crimes. Faults are those committed not so much out of the temporary [ex proskairōs] as out of weakness and the preoccupation of the affections, by men who are otherwise not wicked nor given over to impiety. Crimes are those committed with a hardened mind and a high hand. Some sins are public, where there is no doubt either about the crime or about the author; some are as it were public, where the author is unknown though the deed is known to all, as often happens in murders, fornications and thefts. Hidden sins, however, are not those utterly unknown to anyone, since of these only the Lord judges, not the Church, Rom. 2:16. Rather, they are sins known only to one or two persons, or to a few, and from which public scandal has not yet arisen. Even these hidden sins can, however, become manifest, and faults can become crimes, when, private admonitions having been despised, the scandal must be made known and reported to the Church. For then the issue is not the quality of the sin, but the obstinacy added to it, and the rebellion against God and the Church. The man who acts presumptuously [zed] so as not to obey the priest, etc., that man shall die, etc., Deut. 17:12. The manner of dealing with manifest sins is different from that with hidden ones: in the latter the beginning must be made with private admonition, but not in the former. Those who sin, rebuke [elenche] before all, that the rest also may have fear, 1 Tim. 5:20. For the remedy ought to be proportioned to the disease it is meant to remove. Moreover, manifest sins are subject to judgment; hidden sins are not subject to judgment until they become manifest.

units.la: LXXXVII. Modus cum utrisque agendi spiritualis, non corporalis est.
units.tr: LXXXVII. The manner of exercising both is spiritual, not bodily.

units.la: Arma enim militiæ nostræ non sunt carnalia (qualia sunt illa Pastoris flulti, Zach. XI. 15. oppositia armis Dei, Esaj. LII. 11.) sed δυναμεις τῶ Θεῶ potentia Deo ad destructionem munimentorum, 2.Cor.X.4. Oportet enim ut plantare Regnum Christi, & ei militare velit, attendere, quibus armis utatur, ne, dum Christo se militare putat, Diabolo militet. Sicut enim Christi Regnum non est de hoc mundo, Joh. XVIII. 36. ita in eo non belligerandum est κατὰ σάρκα secundum carnem, 2. Cor. X. 3. Inprimis huc non faciunt vel nomen humanum & autoritas, ut dictum humanum pro ratione dicendi vel agendi reputetur, quia non est fidei, dicere vel facere aliquid propter authoritatem humanam, Esaj. II. 22. vel sapientia humana, quæ apud Deum stultitia est: vel verbum aliquod ἀδηλον, non certò Divinum & Apostolicum, quod propter sentiam hominum tanquam Divinum & Apostolicum recipitur; vel imperium & principatus, & eidem connexæ opes principum, manus & coactio; sed potius arma Dei, & quidem potentia, cujusmodi inprimis verbum Dei, & elenchus ex eodem, spiritus, charitas, mansuetudo, judicium, &c. sunt. Duo inprimis exercendæ disciplinæ media spiritualia sunt ἐλεγχος seu redargutio, & κρίσις judicium. Quæ Christus diserte distinguit, dicens: Si frater in te peccaverit, rit, redargue ipsum,&c. Si Ecclesiam non audiverit, esto tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus, Matth. XVIII. 15-19. Et in occultis quidem scandalis præcedit ἐλεγχος redargutio verbalis: in verè manifestis autem initium à redargutione reali, seu poenis Ecclesiasticis fieri debet, ut hoc quasi cuneo fracta & contusa contumacia atque impietate, censuris salutaribus fenestra aperiatur.
units.tr: For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal (such as those of the foolish shepherd, Zech. 11:15, set against the arms of God, Isa. 52:11), but mighty through God [δυνατὰ τῷ Θεῷ] to the pulling down of strongholds (2 Cor. 10:4). For one who wishes to plant the kingdom of Christ and fight for it must consider what weapons he uses, lest, while he thinks he is fighting for Christ, he is fighting for the Devil. Just as the kingdom of Christ is not of this world (John 18:36), so in it we must not wage war according to the flesh [κατὰ σάρκα] (2 Cor. 10:3). Above all, human name and authority do not help here, so that a human saying is taken as the rule of speaking or acting; for it is not a matter of faith to say or do something on account of human authority (Isa. 2:22), or human wisdom, which is foolishness with God; or some doubtful word, not certainly divine and apostolic, which is received as divine and apostolic because of the opinion of men; or command and princely power, and the wealth, hand and coercion that go with rulers. Rather, these are the arms of God, and indeed mighty ones, of which the chief are the Word of God and reproof drawn from it, the Spirit, love, gentleness, judgement, and so on. Two chief spiritual means of exercising discipline are reproof (elenchus) and judgement (krisis), which Christ plainly distinguishes, saying: If your brother sins against you, rebuke him, and If he refuses to hear the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector (Matt. 18:15-19). In secret scandals, verbal reproof comes first; but in openly manifest sins the beginning must be made with reproof by deed, that is, with ecclesiastical penalties, so that, as with a wedge, stubbornness and impiety, broken and bruised, may have a window opened by wholesome censures.

units.la: LXXXVIII. In occultis peccatis, seu scandalis duos redargutionis seu correptionis gradus Christus distinguit; Prior est, quo unus solus ab uno solo redarguitur & corripitur. Si in te peccaverit frater tuus, vade & redargue eum inter te & ipsum solum, Matth. XVIII. 15. Ubi peccatum adversus fratrem non personalis duntaxat injuria, sed quodvis scandalum, quo quis offendi & deterior reddi potest, intelligitur. Non enim illis tantum peccatis, quibus privatim lædimur, vel damnum accipimus, offendi nos par est, sed iis etiam omnibus, quæ sub conscientia nostra admittuntur, & quorum testes certi esse possumus. Quæ non illico propalanda sunt, nisi Dei gloria & salus Reipublicæ atque Ecclesiæ poscitulet. Vetat enim lex הלך רכיל obtrectare populari, seu nundinari famam ejus, Levit. XIX. 16. Charitas operit multitudinem peccatorum, 1. Petr. IV. 8. Odium excitat lites, & omnia tegit dilectio, Prov. X. 12. Tegit delictum, qui quærit charitatem, ibid. XVII. 9. Qui revelat secretum, obtrectator est, ibid. XX. 19. Obtrectator enim ambulat ab uno ad alterum, & circuit quærens, cui fumos vendat, imò proximum suum & secreta ejus, quæ emphasis phraseωs הלך רכיל est. Charitas verò postulat non ut peccator vel pipulo differatur, vel sibi relinquatur, sed ut corrigatur, si fieri possit, solus à solo, adeóque sine famæ dispendio. Arguendo arguès proximum tuum, & non feres super ipso peccatum, Levit. XIX. 17. Non enim peccatum proximi apud nos odium ejus efficere, sed potiùs charitas fortis & generosa nos instigare debet, ut ipsum redarguamus, & studeamus ipsum à peccato ipsius convertere, ne cum peccato ejus communicemus. Quæ correptio seu redargutio non aliud est, quàm demonstratio veri & boni ad conscientiam, adeóque per verbum Dei, non per authoritatem humanam fieri debet; & quidem privatim, ut sanetur scandalum apud illos, quibus datum est. Tantundem enim minimis in Ecclesia Christus tribuit, quantum maximis; ne putemus elenchum requirere authoritatem vel dominium. Sanatio scandali est, si frater correptus audiat, sive obediat. Ἐὰν ζῳ ἀκούσῃ Si te audiverit, lucratus es fratrem tuum, inquit Christus; hoc est, si conversus dicat fratri redarguenti: Μετανοῶ respicio, Luc. XVII. 4. Nam qui tegit delicta sua, non prosperabitur, sed confitens & desistens misericordia potietur, Prov. XXVIII. 13. Si texi, ut homo, delictum meum, ut abscônderem in sinu meo pravitatem meam. Nam timuissem multitudinem magnam, & ignominia familiarum me consternasset, & continuissem me, non exivissem ostio, Job. XXXI. 33. 34. q. d. Non ea impudentia fuit, ut nihil veritus hominum conscientiam peccatum meum velarem & elevarem. Hoc est, quod S. Jacobus præcipit: Confitemini invicem peccata, Jac. V. 16. Quam resipiscentiam & confessionem sequi condonatio debet. Si adversus te peccaverit frater tuus, corripe ipsum. Et, si respiuerit, ἀφες αὐτῷ remitte ipsi. Et si septies in die adversus te peccaverit, & septies in die erga te converterit, dicendo: pœnitet me; remittes ei, Luc. XVII. 3. 4. Imò & septuagies remittenda ipsi esse peccata poenitenti alibi, Matth. XVIII. 21. 22. Christus Petrum docuit. Multum autem inter condonationem Divinam & nostram interest. Deus condonat ut Dominus, legislator & judex, donans filium & justitiam ejus. Nos condonamus, non ulciscendo, odio habendo, vel malum precibus votisque nostris in caput peccantium vocando, nedum retaliando, quod nefas est, licet alter in peccatis obstinatus sit, sed quærendo salutem proximi per admonitionem, denique, quod inprimis ad disciplinam pertinet, censuram atque ἐπιτιμίαν omittendo, & vice ejus consolando. Estque hæc post exploratam pœnitentiam condonatio & consolatio solutio illa clavium Cœlum aperientium & peccati remissio, ibid. XVI. 19. XVIII. 18. Joh. XX. 23. Unde liquet, singulos fideles habere partem in ea promissione, quam Christus Petro, & in persona Petri toti Ecclesiæ dedit, de quo supra pluribus.
units.tr: LXXXVIII. In secret sins, or scandals, Christ distinguishes two degrees of reproof or correction. The first is when one alone is reproved and corrected by one alone: If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone (Matt. 18:15). Here a sin against a brother is understood not merely as a personal injury but as any scandal by which someone may be offended or made worse. For we ought to be offended not only by those sins by which we are privately harmed or suffer loss, but also by all those committed in our knowledge, of which we can be certain witnesses. These are not to be published at once, unless the glory of God and the welfare of the commonwealth and the Church demand it. For the law forbids to go about as a talebearer, to slander the people or to peddle someone's reputation [הלך רכיל] (Lev. 19:16). Love covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8). Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all things (Prov. 10:12). He who covers an offence seeks love (ibid. 17:9). He who reveals a secret is a slanderer (ibid. 20:19). For the slanderer goes from one to another, looking round for someone to whom he may sell his smoke; indeed, he goes about against his neighbour and his secrets, which is the emphatic sense of the Hebrew phrase [הלך רכיל]. But love does not demand that a sinner be exposed to the crowd or left to himself, but that he be corrected, if it can be done, by one alone, and so without loss of reputation. Reprove your neighbour, and you shall not bear sin on account of him (Lev. 19:17). For our neighbour's sin should not make us hate him; rather, a strong and generous love ought to urge us to reprove him and to strive to turn him from his sin, lest we share in it. This correction or reproof is nothing other than the demonstration of truth and good to the conscience, and so it must be made through the Word of God, not through human authority, and indeed privately, so that the scandal may be healed among those to whom it was given. For Christ grants as much to the least in the Church as to the greatest; so we must not think that reproof requires authority or dominion. The scandal is healed if the brother who is corrected hears, that is, obeys. If he hears you, you have gained your brother, says Christ [ἐὰν σοῦ ἀκούσῃ]; that is, if he is converted and says to the brother reproving him: I repent [μετανοῶ] (Luke 17:4). For he who covers his sins will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy (Prov. 28:13). If I have covered my transgression as a man does, hiding my iniquity in my bosom, because I feared the great multitude and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silent and did not go out of the door (Job 31:33-34); as if to say: I was not so shameless as to cover and excuse my sin, heedless of men's conscience. This is what St James commands: Confess your sins to one another (James 5:16). Forgiveness should follow this repentance and confession: If he sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him [ἄφες αὐτῷ]. And if he sins against you seven times a day, and turns to you seven times, saying, I repent, you shall forgive him (Luke 17:3-4). Elsewhere, indeed, Christ taught Peter that sins must be forgiven to the penitent even seventy times seven (Matt. 18:21-22). There is, however, a great difference between God's forgiveness and ours. God forgives as Lord, lawgiver and judge, granting pardon for the sake of his Son and his righteousness. We forgive not by taking vengeance, nursing hatred, or calling evil down by our prayers and wishes upon the heads of sinners, still less by retaliating, which is wrong even if the other is obstinate in sin; but by seeking our neighbour's salvation through admonition and, most of all, as it belongs to discipline, by omitting censure and penalty [ἐπιτιμία] and consoling in its place. This forgiveness and consolation, once repentance has been tested, is that loosing of the keys which opens heaven, and that remission of sin (Matt. 16:19; 18:18; John 20:23). Hence it is clear that individual believers have a share in that promise which Christ gave to Peter, and through Peter to the whole Church, of which more above.

units.la: LXXXIX. Quòd si frater ὁνομαζόμενος, 1. Cor. V. 11. elenchum privatim, & remotis omnibus arbitris, sic institutum neglexisset, & non audivisset, vel obedivisset corripienti; secundum correptionis gradum Christus his verbis instituit: Si verò non audiverit, assume tecum unum vel duos (fideles & amicos, qui unà docere & testes fieri possint) ut in ore duorum vel trium testium omne verbum stet, Matth. XVIII. 16. Intelligendum id de eo casu est, quo & facti, & admonitionis plures testes fieri possunt. Talium ergo est, elenchum continuare, & pro viribus conversionem promovere. Nam plurium testimonio admonitio illa confirmatur, & firmior, sive apud fratrem corrigendum, sive apud Ecclesiam posthac correcturam efficitur: & magis hac ratione charitati consulitur, quia emendationi fratris cum minima ejus infamia, consulitur. Sicut autem non sufficit semel privatim admonere, sed vel septies in die id faciendum est, Luc. XVII. 3. 4. ita nec semel coram testibus fratrem admonere sufficit. Eo usque enim cum patientia & longanimitate elenchus continuari debet, dum peccator vel poenitentiam, vel contumaciam suam manifestam fecerit. Unde Christus: Si te audiverit: Si te non audiverit: Si te audire neglexerit. Cùm enim tota disciplinæ ratio, & correctionis ordo post Dei gloriam proximi etiam famam, honorem, existimationem, conversionem & salutem sibi finem propositum habeat, non hic ludere, vel subdolè agere, & salutari hac sanctione pro schemate vel velo, sub quo ad nostra contra proximum odia & vindictæ cupiditatem exsatiandam lateamus, uti licet. S. Paulus quoque vetat contra Seniorem κατηγορίαν accusationem suscipere, nisi ubi duo vel tres testes fuerint, 1. Tim. V. 19. non innuens hoc proprium esse accusationi seniorum, cùm Christus de quovis fratre loquatur, sed tum ne seniorem quidem ab hac regula excipi, adeóque convenire, ut etiam ipse juxta regulam hanc judicetur, secus quàm Papæ gnathones nugantur, tur, eum à nemine deferri, vel judicari posse: tum delationem Seniorum ad fidem faciendam ei, qui suscipere debet, præ cæteris niti debere testimonio duorum vel trium fide dignissimorum, quia Presbyterorum tanta, & tam probè circumvallata existimatio & authoritas esse debet, ut non temerè fides habenda iis sit, qui famam eorum appetunt; atque insuper Sathanas iisdem præ cæteris insidiatur, & impii etiam homines ἀναξίως, correptionis impatientes, reperiuntur, qui adversus Seniores corripientes, canum instar insurgunt, ut confictis criminibus eorum correptionem obscurent, & corripientium fidem animumque frangant. Corripiens derisorem sibi ipsi accipit ignominiam, & increpans impium accipit sibi maculam. Ne increpes igitur derisorem, ne odio te habeat: sed increpa sapientem, ut diligat te, Prov. IX. 7. 8.
units.tr: LXXXIX. But if the brother who is named (1 Cor. 5:11) had neglected reproof given privately, with all witnesses removed, and had not heard or obeyed the one correcting him, Christ instituted the second degree of correction in these words: But if he does not hear you, take with you one or two (believers and friends who can teach together and act as witnesses), so that by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established (Matt. 18:16). This must be understood of the case in which there can be several witnesses both to the deed and to the admonition. It is the task of such people, therefore, to continue the reproof and to promote conversion as far as they can. For the admonition is confirmed by the testimony of several, and made firmer, whether it is before the brother to be corrected or before the Church that will correct him afterwards; and in this way charity is better served, because the brother's amendment is promoted with the least possible loss of his reputation. But just as it is not enough to admonish privately once, and it must be done seven times a day (Luke 17:3-4), so it is not enough to admonish the brother once before witnesses. Reproof must be continued with patience and long-suffering until the sinner shows either repentance or manifest obstinacy. Hence Christ says: If he hears you; If he does not hear you; If he neglects to hear you. For since the whole reason of discipline and the order of correction, after the glory of God, has as its aim the neighbour's fame, honour, esteem, conversion and salvation, it is not permitted to play games here, or to act deceitfully, and to use this wholesome sanction as a pretext or veil under which we may hide in order to satisfy our hatred of a neighbour and our desire for vengeance. St Paul also forbids receiving an accusation against an elder except where there are two or three witnesses (1 Tim. 5:19). He does not imply that this is peculiar to accusations against elders, since Christ speaks of any brother whatever; rather, that not even an elder is excepted from this rule, and so it is fitting that he too be judged by it. This is otherwise than the Papal sycophants babble, that he can be accused or judged by no one. Moreover, the accusation of elders, if it is to produce belief in the one who must receive it, ought to rest, above all others, on the testimony of two or three most trustworthy witnesses. For the reputation and authority of presbyters must be so well guarded that no one should readily believe those who seek their ruin; and besides, Satan lies in wait for them above all others, and wicked men are found who, unworthy and impatient of correction, rise up against elders who correct them like dogs, so that by invented crimes they may obscure the correction and break the faith and courage of those who correct. He who corrects a scoffer gets dishonour for himself, and he who rebukes the wicked gets a blot. Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you (Prov. 9:7-8).

units.la: XC. Secundus correptionis gradus, ubi nihil proficit, tertium, quo peccatum jam manifestum redditum corripi debet, Christus præscribit, dicens: Ἐὰν δὲ παρακούσῃ αὐτῶν, si eos non audiverit, iis non obediverit, dic Ecclesiæ, Matth. XVIII. 17. hoc est, da operam, ut peccator jam non coram paucis ampliùs, sed coram Ecclesia, seu coram omnibus, quibus officium illud incumbit, facta, 2. Cor. II. 6. Non ergo Ecclesia vel unus homo singularis est, vel pauciores homines sunt, fraternitatem vel populum sic repræsentantes, ut in eorum sententia & judicio ἀδοκίμαστος non explorato, seu probato continea-tur sententia & judicium illi velut dominanti serviliter obediens totius populi & fraternitatis, quo sensu Princeps populum repræsentat; uti Bellarminus de Concil. lib. I. 1. explicat; quia repræsentatio talis non datur nisi apud Bestiam, coram qua Pseudopropheta & imago Bestiæ omnem potestatem Bestiæ facit, Apoc. XIII. 12. 15. Neque etiam Ecclesia, vel Synedrium Judaicum, vel quæ Erasti opinio insulsa est, Ecclesia Magistratum Christianum fidelem, notat, tum quia nuspiam in N. T. Ecclesia Synedrium notat: tum quia hic Christus conscientiæ legem præscribit, & vult nos esse solicitos non tam de restitutione damni, quæ à Magistratu expectanda est, quàm de emendatione fratris, quam Ecclesia procurare etiam solo ἐλέγχω, si ei peccator obediverit, potest. Alias Christi præceptum mansuetudinem & patientiam christianam non respiet. Fingamus enim, Synedrium summam αὐτονομίαν habuisse, profectò causa apud Synedrium agi non potuisset, nisi frater etiam pœna corporali multaretur. Hoc verò non est dissidia inter fratres componere, sed odia fratrum inflammare. Eadem ratio Magistratus Christiani est, apud quem si noxius deferatur, sine pœna civili absolvi non poterit. Accedit, quòd Christus fratri elenchum admittenti peccatum condonari jubet, quod Magistratus non facit. Neque illud obstat, quòd verba sequentia: Sit tibi velut Ethnicus & publicanus proprie ad Ecclesiam Judaicam referenda videntur, quia Christus locutionibus à consuetudine sui temporis ductis, ad res eas, quæ post ejus in Cœlum ascensionem contingere debuerunt, significandas cerebrò utitur, & S. Paulus eum, qui non diligit Dominum Jesum, locutione Judaica anathema Maranatha, 1. Corinth. XVI. 22. similiter dixit.
units.tr: XC. The second stage of correction, when nothing is gained, is followed by a third, by which a sin that has now become manifest ought to be rebuked. Christ prescribes this, saying: But if he refuses to listen to them [Ἐὰν δὲ παρακούσῃ αὐτῶν], that is, if he does not hear them or obey them, tell it to the Church, Matth. XVIII. 17. That is, take care that the sinner is no longer dealt with before a few, but before the Church, or before all those to whom that duty belongs, 2. Cor. II. 6. Therefore the Church is not a single man, nor a few men who represent the brotherhood or the people in such a way that their opinion and judgment, not yet tested and approved [ἀδοκίμαστος], contain the sentence and judgment of the whole people and brotherhood, which slavishly obeys them as its dominant power. In this sense a prince represents the people, as Bellarmine explains in de Concil. lib. I. 1. But such representation is given only in the Beast, before which the false prophet and the image of the Beast exercise all the Beast's power, Apoc. XIII. 12, 15. Nor does the Church here mean the Jewish Sanhedrin, or a Christian magistrate who is faithful, as Erastus' silly opinion holds. This is so because nowhere in the New Testament does Church denote a Sanhedrin, and because here Christ prescribes a law of conscience, wanting us to be concerned not so much about the restitution of loss, which is to be expected from the magistrate, as about the amendment of our brother, which the Church can bring about even by the mere rebuke [ἐλέγχω], if the sinner obeys it. Otherwise Christ's precept would not regard Christian gentleness and patience. For let us suppose that the Sanhedrin had the highest autonomy [αὐτονομίαν]; certainly the case could not have been brought before the Sanhedrin unless the brother were also punished with bodily penalty. But this is not to settle disputes between brothers, it is to inflame the hatred of brothers. The same reasoning applies to a Christian magistrate: if a guilty man is brought before him, he cannot be acquitted without civil punishment. Add to this that Christ orders that sin be forgiven to a brother who accepts rebuke, which the magistrate does not do. Nor is there any objection in the words that follow, Let him be to you as a Gentile and a publican, which seem properly to refer to the Jewish Church. For Christ, using expressions drawn from the custom of his own time, speaks of things that ought to happen after his ascension into heaven, and St. Paul similarly said of one who does not love the Lord Jesus, in the Jewish phrase, anathema Maranatha, 1. Cor. XVI. 22.

units.la: Ecclesia igitur Christiana talis, qualis illa est, quam supra se, ceu petram, se ædificaturum Christus paulò ante cap. XVI. 18. promiserat, & cui statim v. 19. claves Regni Cœlorum contulerat; eáque non universalis, sed particularis (membrum illius, quam Christus supra se ædificaturum se promisit) cujus etiam membrum individuum peccator ille est, quem Ecclesiæ deferri Christus jussit; intelligitur. Sunt enim in hoc negotio totius Ecclesiæ partes aliquæ, tum quia de fraternitate, nisi fratribus consentientibus, nemo excludi potest: tum quia omnibus de redargutione, rectè illa facta sit, nec ne, judicium relinquitur: tum quia nec Ecclesia, nec ullus fratrum judicium illud, quod vel publicè vel privatim erga peccatorem contumacem exercendum est, abdicare potest. Neque tamen sic & elenchus & judicium promiscuè imperitæ plebi committitur; sed redargutio & demonstratio ex Dei verbo, nec non sententiæ adversus peccatorem contumacem deliberatio & dictio seu definitio senioribus, seu populi πρεσβυτέρους primore loco stantibus, & pro eo, sed non ἀξιοσυνίσως, agentibus; fraternitati verò consensus, & de tota actione judicium discretionis, ne tyrannis Ecclesiam invadere possit, committitur. Si enim, quod Christus ipse Matth. XVIII. 15. 16. 18. innuit, singuli singulos ligare & solvere, hoc est, offensas & scandala iis condonare vel remittere possunt, & debent, universa fraternitas à redargutione & judicio, quod Ecclesiæ tribuitur, penitus excludi, sine defraudatione juris ejus, & tyrannidis usurpatione, nullatenus potest.
units.tr: Therefore the Christian Church is understood to be such as it is: the Church that Christ, shortly before in cap. XVI. 18, had promised he would build upon himself as a rock [supra se, petram], and to which immediately in v. 19 he gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven [claves Regni Cœlorum]; and this is not the universal Church but a particular one, a member of that which Christ promised to build upon himself, of which the sinner whom Christ ordered to be brought before the Church is an individual member. For in this matter there are certain parts of the whole Church. First, because no one can be excluded from the brotherhood without the consent of the brothers. Second, because judgment is left to all as to whether the rebuke was rightly made or not. Third, because neither the Church nor any brother can give up that judgment which must be exercised against an obstinate sinner, whether publicly or privately. Yet in this way neither rebuke nor judgment is committed indiscriminately to the untaught common people. Rather, the rebuke and demonstration from the Word of God, and also the deliberation and pronouncement or definition of the sentence against the obstinate sinner, are entrusted to the elders, or to the presbyters [πρεσβυτέρους] who stand in the first place and act on behalf of the people, but not arbitrarily [ἀξιοσυνίσως]; while consent is entrusted to the brotherhood, and the judgment of discernment over the whole action, so that tyranny cannot invade the Church. For if, as Christ himself hints in Matth. XVIII. 15, 16, 18, individuals can and ought to bind and loose one another, that is, to remit or forgive offences and scandals to one another, then the whole brotherhood cannot in any way be entirely excluded from the rebuke and judgment that is ascribed to the Church, without defrauding its right and usurping tyranny.

units.la: XCI. Delatio peccatoris ad Ecclesiam vel mediata, vel immediata est. Illa mediantibus quibusdam fit; hæc nullis mediantibus, ab eo, adversus quem peccatum est, & sociis ejus testibus, fit. Delatio enim certo ordine progreditur, non per saltum institutitur. Observandus ordo est, ut per illos Ecclesiam adeamus, qui eidem præsunt, & eam suo modo repræsentant: atque adeò ex ordine directionem & administrationem publicorum negotiorum sibi commissam habent. Si igitur is, qui deferri debet, pastor est, mitius utique est, ut uni cuipiam seniori primùm peccator denuntietur: sin vel senior non docens, vel privatus quivis alius est, prudentiæ pariter & charitatis est, Pastori prius quàm toti consessui eorum, qui Ecclesiæ nomine disciplinam moderantur, delictum indicare. Neque obstat, quòd Christus Ecclesiæ dicere jussit. Dici enim aliquid potest vel immediatè Ecclesiæ illi particulari, cujus peccator membrum est; vel mediatè per Synedrium, seu confessum Seniorum; & Synedrio ipsi mediatè per ministrum, vel Seniorem, qui Synedrii illius membrum est. Potest autem vel Pastor, vel Senior alius delicta nondum publicè nota, & privatim sibi hac vel illa ratione innotescentia, tegere, & ad confessum ampliorem non deferre, si post repetitum ex verbo Dei elenchum vera resipiscentia abrumpantur, in futurum non pendeant, & publico non obsint. Ubi verò & hæc correctionis ratio deplorata est, dicendum est Ecclesiæ ordine, hoc est, prius illi consessui, qui Ecclesiæ res & negotia moderatur, & Ecclesiam sano sensu repræsentat; ac demum fraternitati universæ.
units.tr: XCI. The bringing of a sinner before the Church is either mediate or immediate. The former is done through certain intermediaries; the latter, without any intermediaries, by him against whom the sin was committed and his witnesses who accompany him. For accusation proceeds in a fixed order and is not instituted by a leap. The order must be observed, so that we approach the Church through those who preside over it and represent it in their own way, and who therefore hold from that order the direction and administration of public affairs committed to them. If, then, the one who ought to be accused is a minister, it is certainly gentler that the sinner be first denounced to some single elder. But if the one accused is an elder who does not teach, or any other private person, it is equally a matter of prudence and charity to report the offence first to the minister, before the whole assembly of those who govern the discipline in the name of the Church. Nor is there any objection in the fact that Christ told us to speak to the Church. For something can be said either immediately to that particular Church of which the sinner is a member, or mediately through the Sanhedrin, that is, the council of elders; and to the Sanhedrin itself mediately through the minister or elder who is a member of that Sanhedrin. A minister or another elder may, however, cover up offences not yet publicly known, which have become known to him privately in one way or another, and not refer them to the larger council, if after repeated rebuke from the Word of God they are abandoned by true repentance, do not linger for the future, and do not harm the public. But where this method of correction too has been given up as hopeless, it must be said that the case goes in the order of the Church, that is, first to that assembly which governs the affairs and business of the Church and represents the Church in a sound sense, and finally to the whole brotherhood.

units.la: Unde duplex censura distinguenda est; una Presbyterialis, Ecclesiastica altera. Presbyteria-lis coram Senioribus, seu Senatu Ecclesiæ fit. Huc referuntur peccata, quæ vel verè occulta sunt, contemtu tamen admonitionum privata-rum, vel unius tantum, vel duorum aut trium testium, ad Ecclesiæ Presbyterium deferri de-buerunt; vel quæ pluribus etiam, at non toti Ecclesiæ, nec majori ejus parti innotuerunt, neque ad totam Ecclesiam deferuntur, ne ma-jori cum Ecclesiæ scandalo, & delinquentis con-fusione, magis divulgentur. Unde censura hæc quasi publico-privata censeri potest; Publica, quatenus Presbyterium totius Ecclesiæ Senatus est, & eam quodammodo repræsentat, atque aliis etiam extra Presbyterium constitutis peccatum censuræ subjectum innotuit: Privata vero, quatenus peccatores coram toto Ecclesiæ coetu publico ad exomologesin non sistuntur, & Seniores ipsi peccatum non eliminant, sed silentii sigillo obsignatum veluti claudunt. Ecclesiastica vero præsente universa Ecclesia, cujus peccator membrum est, peragitur, tum demum, cùm vel scelus manifestum omnibusque notum est, vel privatarum admonitionum contemptu & sublannationibus ad Ecclesiæ Senatum prolata sunt, illi coram Presbyterio majore gravitate, & rationum pondere admonendi sunt. Si prima vice seria resipiscentia non suc-cesserit, eandem denuo incudem tundere oportet, exaggeratis cum efficaci quadam severitate tum peccato ipso, tum contumacia, qua atrocius illud fiat, tum contemptus ordinis Divini in Ecclesia atrocitate, tum justitia & ira Dei adversus contumaces & impœnitentes, scandalo, famæ & existimationis propriæ jactura, aliisque ad rem pertinentibus. Si verò resipiscentiæ signa indubitata successerint, severius in resipiscentem animadvertendum non est, sed reconciliatio ejus sine dilatione ad populum, instituenda est, nisi forte peccatum non simplex delictum, sed enorme & publicum flagitium fuerit. Tum enim etiam resipiscentes, re ad Ecclesiam delata, eidem per canonicam satisfactionem, uti Veteres appellant, reconciliari debent. Sed peccatore sive ob contumaciam, quæ frangi non potuit, sive ob atrox scelus Ecclesiæ delato, inprimis se exerit studium (quale in vitanda jactura, & lucro quærendo impendi solet) indignatio (justa querela ob peccati inexcusabilitatem) zelus (pro bono adversus malum) vindicatio (consistens in increpatione, & omni eo, quod ad confusionem facit; quæ ipsius judicii inchoatio est) 2. Corinth. VII.11. Qua severitate Ecclesia se sanctam inprimis demonstrat.
units.tr: Hence a twofold censure must be distinguished: one presbyterial, the other ecclesiastical. Presbyterial censure takes place before the elders, or the Senate of the Church.
