To this belong sins that are truly hidden, yet have been brought to the Presbytery of the Church after private admonitions were despised, and that were witnessed by only one, or two or three witnesses; or those that have become known to several people, but not to the whole Church or its greater part, and are not reported to the whole Church, so that they may not be spread more widely to the greater scandal of the Church and the confusion of the offender. Hence this censure can be regarded as public-private. It is public in so far as the Presbytery is the Senate of the whole Church and represents it in some way, and the sin subject to censure has become known also to others outside the Presbytery. It is private in so far as sinners are not brought before the whole public assembly of the Church for public confession, and the elders themselves do not expose the sin but, as it were, shut it up, sealed with the seal of silence. Ecclesiastical censure, however, is carried out in the presence of the whole Church, of which the sinner is a member; this happens only when the crime is manifest and known to all, or when the admonitions have been despised and the offender has answered with mockery, and he has been admonished before the greater Presbytery with great seriousness and weight of argument. If serious repentance does not follow on the first occasion, the same hammer must be struck again, the sin itself being set forth with a certain effective severity, as well as the obstinacy by which the sin becomes more atrocious, the atrocity of contempt for the Divine order in the Church, the justice and anger of God against the obstinate and impenitent, the scandal, the loss of reputation and of one's own good name, and other matters pertinent to the case. But if clear signs of repentance have followed, the repentant man should not be punished more severely; rather his reconciliation to the people is to be carried out without delay, unless perhaps the sin was not a simple offence but a heinous and public disgrace. For then, even penitents, once the matter has been brought to the Church, ought to be reconciled to it by canonical satisfaction, as the ancients call it. But when the sinner, either on account of obstinacy that could not be broken or on account of an atrocious crime, has been reported to the Church, there appears above all zeal (such as is usually expended in avoiding loss and seeking gain); indignation (a just complaint on account of the inexcusability of the sin); zeal (for the good against evil); and vindication (consisting in rebuke and everything that brings confusion, which is the beginning of judgment itself), 2. Cor. VII. 11. By this severity the Church shows itself above all to be holy.

units.la: XCII. Si ad Ecclesiam delatus peccator ferrea fronte ejusdem admonitioni & correptioni obsistat, frænum mordeat, & spes agni lupo eripiendi omnis decollet, Christus peccatorem inobedientem & præfractum pro Ethnico & Publicano haberi jubet, Matth. XVIII. 17. Quod in quovis etiam delicto atroci manifesto obtinet. Atque hoc illud judicium est, in quod omnis causa terminatur. Judicium isthoc cùm in multitudine, nec per diseisionem fieri possit, quia per demonstrationem fieri debet; neque omnium fidelium sermone peragatur, quia quibusdam in Ecclesia ne loqui quidem fas est, 1. Cor. XIV. 34. 1. Tim. II. 12. & pueros atque ἀταζίας strepere indecorum foret; ordine & decenter sic fieri potest, si Seniores Ecclesiæ exponant, quid apud Presbyterium actum fuerit; tum provocent, qui apologiam pro eo, qui scandalum dedisse videri potest, & Seniorum sententiæ non cessit, instituere velit; dein attendant diligenter ad prudentum judicia, quæ Ecclesiæ rectores in omni actu sibi demandato suspicere debent: ac demum Ecclesia locupletem in modum informata, ejus tacito suffragio accedente, sententiam perferant. Ita judicium omnium membrorum Ecclesiæ, ad quæ secundum illud judicium agere pertinet, erit; non propter authoritatem humanam, sed propter timorem Dei & conscientiam. Hoc judicium adversus contumaces & aperte scelera-tos in eo consistit, quòd Ecclesia pro ethnicis & publicanis, hoc est, pro hominibus injustis, qui fidem factis abnegant, cujusmodi publicani erant, Luc. III. 13. XIX. 7. 8. 9. nec non pro ignorantibus Deum & Christum, quales gentiles sunt, tales habeat. Atque ita in gentilis exemplo scandalum doctrinæ, in publicani exemplo scandalum vitæ judicatur. In quo judicio Excommunicatio consistit, quæ scelera-torum & ἀμετανοήτων ab Ecclesiæ communione separatio est. Scitè ad h. l. Bullingerus: Esse Ethnicum & Publicanum est deleri è catalogo Ecclesiastico, & haberi recenseriqe inter facino-rosos, quibus nihil neque officii, neque sinceri tutò committas: ut nos solemus mœchos ἐπ' αὐτοφόρῳ deprehensos honore & trabea exutos publicè dedecorare. Ubi etiam excommunicationem salutare pharmacum appellat, & è cœtu sanctorum Pontificum avaritia eliminatum reduci optat. Quod verò Servator dicit habere ut ethnicum vel publicanum, id alibi nominatur, non miseri, non con-vesci, tollere malum ex medio fratrum, 1. Cor. V. 11. 13. fugere, Joh. X. 5. Atque id in V. T. quandiu potestas gladii penes Seniores fuit, factum est pœna capitali, Deut. XIX. 19. at in N.T. fit vitando, Rom. XVI. 17. Tit. III. 10. Ave non dicendo iis, qui non afferunt doctrinam Christi in Scripturis consignatam, 2. Joh. 10. 11. Quod de ea salutatione, qua fratres cum lætitia excipiuntur, & quæ consolationem & συνδόκιαν beneplacitum in iis, quod faciunt Rom. I. 32. continet, intelligendum est. Nam officia charitatis circa proximum & quosvis homines, sed cum mœstitia super peccatis ipsorum obire non vetantur, sed potius jubentur. Hoc igitur est ligare, seu non dignari consolatione de justitia, & retinere peccatum, seu declarare ex Dei verbo, quòd sic facienti, & in factis ejusmodi animum obfirmanti, & non resipiscenti peccatum non remittatur, sed ad æternam damnationem imputetur. Expressius etiam Apostolus hoc docet, tradere Sathanæ ad interitum carnis, ut spiritus servetur, 1. Cor. V. 5. hoc est, peccati & scandali authorem judicare, non Christianum, non habentem Spiritum Dei, sed in Regno Sathanæ hærentem, & orare super illius afflictione corporali, si aliter converti & servari non possit. Et in universum qui aliud Evangelium docet, Gal. I. 8. & qui Jesum Christum non diligit, 1. Cor. XVI. 22, pronuntiatur ἀνάθεμα, anathema, hoc est מנדה separatus ab Ecclesia Dei, & חרם devotus exitio, nisi resipiscat. Nam vocabula illa non ita apud Hebraeos, uti quidam arbitrantur, in distincto gradu ponuntur, nisi quòd ἀνάθεμα intentatum & corroboratum differunt, de quo Loc. XVI. 29. plura dixmus.
units.tr: XCII. If a sinner who has been reported to the Church stands before its admonition and correction with brazen face, bites the bridle, and cuts off every hope of snatching the lamb from the wolf, Christ orders that the disobedient and stubborn sinner be regarded as a Gentile and a tax collector, Matth. 18:17. This holds in any notorious and manifest offence. And this is the judgment in which every case is finally decided. Since this judgment cannot be made by the multitude, by a show of hands, but must be made by demonstration, and since it cannot be carried out by the voice of all the faithful (because some in the Church are not even allowed to speak, 1 Cor. 14:34, 1 Tim. 2:12, and it would be unseemly for children and disorderly people [ἀταξίας] to make a noise), it can be done in good order and decently in this way: the elders of the Church set out what was done before the eldership; then they call forward anyone who wishes to make a defence for the man who may appear to have given offence and who has not yielded to the opinion of the elders; next they attend carefully to the judgments of prudent people, which the rulers of the Church ought to hold in high regard in every matter entrusted to them; and finally, with the Church fully informed, and its silent assent given, they pronounce the sentence. In this way the judgment will be that of all the members of the Church, to whom it belongs to act in accordance with that judgment; it will rest not on human authority but on the fear of God and a good conscience. This judgment against the obstinate and openly wicked consists in this: that the Church holds such a person as a Gentile and a tax collector, that is, as an unjust man who denies the faith by his deeds, as the tax collectors were, Luke 3:13, 19:7–9, and likewise as one ignorant of God and Christ, as the Gentiles are. Thus a scandal of doctrine is judged by the example of the Gentile, and a scandal of life by the example of the tax collector. Excommunication consists in this judgment; it is the separation of the wicked and the unrepentant [ἀμετανοήτων] from the communion of the Church. Bullinger rightly says on this passage: To be a Gentile and a tax collector is to be struck from the ecclesiastical roll, and to be counted among the criminals, to whom you can entrust nothing of duty or sincere trust, just as we are accustomed to disgrace publicly adulterers caught in the act [ἐπ' αὐτοφόρῳ], stripping them of honour and of the magistrate's robe. There too he calls excommunication a wholesome medicine, and wishes that a man expelled from the company of the saints by the avarice of the Pontiffs might be brought back. What the Saviour calls to hold as a Gentile or a tax collector, is elsewhere described as not to keep company, not to eat with, to remove the evil from among the brethren, 1 Cor. 5:11, 13, to flee from, John 10:5. And in the Old Testament, as long as the power of the sword lay with the elders, this was done with the capital penalty, Deut. 19:19; but in the New Testament it is done by avoiding, Rom. 16:17, Titus 3:10, by not saying hello to those who do not bring the doctrine of Christ recorded in the Scriptures, 2 John 10–11. This must be understood of that greeting by which brethren are received with joy, and which expresses consolation and approval [συνδοκίαν], goodwill towards those who do such things, Rom. 1:32. For the duties of charity towards a neighbour and towards any men are not forbidden, but rather commanded, even if they are discharged with sorrow over their sins. To bind, therefore, or not to deign to console them with regard to righteousness, and to retain sin, is to declare from God's word that sin is not forgiven to one who acts thus, who hardens his mind in such deeds and does not repent, but is imputed to him for eternal damnation. The Apostle teaches this more expressly when he says to deliver to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved, 1 Cor. 5:5; that is, to judge the author of the sin and the scandal not a Christian, not having the Spirit of God, but remaining in the kingdom of Satan, and to pray over his bodily affliction, if he cannot otherwise be converted and saved. And in general, whoever teaches another gospel, Gal. 1:8, and whoever does not love Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 16:22, is pronounced anathema [ἀνάθεμα], that is, separated [מנדה] from the Church of God, and devoted to destruction [חרם], unless he repents. For those words are not, as some think, placed among the Hebrews in distinct degrees, except that anathema differs as something intensified and confirmed; concerning this I have said more at Loc. 16:29.

units.la: XCIII. Et haec quidem disciplinae Ecclesiasticae capitalis ratio est, quae in singulis vigere, non frigere debet. Quam post Brunnerum Ecclesiasten Heidelbergensem Thomas Erastus, Heidelbergensis ibidem Medicus, consentientibus Christophoro Probo, Cancellario Archipalatino, & Adamo Neusero: Pastore ad D. Petri, qui post ad Arianos & Turcas ipsos defecit, adversus Olevianum, institutionem disciplinae ad exemplar Genevensis urgentem, vehementer impugnavit. Censebant enim illi, Ecclesiae nullum regimen, nullam sententiae dictionem, nullum forum, nullam potestatem verbum Dei per censuras, excommunicationem inprimis, applicandi à Christo datam esse; potestatem clavium in solo verbi praeconio consistere; & Ecclesiam magistratui Christiano subjectam, omnem, quam usurpat, disciplinae auctoritatem ex mera Magistratus delegatione usurpare, cum omnis politia externa, omne regimen, & omnis coetuum minorum potestas in Republica à summa Majestate derivari, & in eandem refundi debeat. Proin etiam Magistratuum fasces censuris Ecclesiae obnoxios esse iidem pernegant, & à sententiis Ecclesiasticis ad Magistratuum tribunalia, utpote quibus ultimum & supremum rerum omnium in Republica judicium conveniat, provocationem permittunt. Quorum sententiam in Anglia, gliscentibus Presbyterianos inter & Independentes controversiis, quidam Colemannus, Londinensis Pastor, incrultavit, qui Politicorum instinctu, & vana prurigine motus, in concione Londini Parlamento coram habita, regimen Ecclesiae Magistratui obtulit; cui se G. Gillespius, Minister Edimburgensis, & celeberrimus Samuel Rheterfoordius doctissimis dissertationibus, quibus omnem Erastiani commenti iniquitatem aperuerunt illi, oppugnatum iverunt. In Scripturis certè clavium potestas, & corripiendi, atque pro Ethnicis & Publicanis habendi munus, diserte S. Petro, & in ejus persona Ecclesiae, non civili potestati commissum est.
units.tr: XCIII. And this is indeed the chief principle of ecclesiastical discipline, which ought to flourish in each congregation and not grow cold. After Brunner, a preacher at Heidelberg, Thomas Erastus, a physician of Heidelberg, together with Christoph Probus, Chancellor of the Palatinate, and Adam Neuser, pastor at St Peter's, who later fell away to the Arians and the Turks themselves, vehemently attacked Olevianus, who was urging the institution of discipline on the model of Geneva. For they held that no government of the Church, no pronouncement of sentence, no court, and no power of applying the word of God through censures, and above all excommunication, was given by Christ; that the power of the keys consists solely in the proclamation of the word; and that the Church, being subject to the Christian magistrate, exercises every authority of discipline it claims solely by delegation from the magistrate, since every external polity, every government, and every power of the lesser assemblies ought to be derived from the supreme majesty of the state and referred back to it. Hence they also deny that the magistrates' fasces are liable to the censures of the Church, and they permit appeal from ecclesiastical sentences to the courts of the magistrates, to whom, they say, the final and supreme judgment of all matters in the commonwealth belongs. In England, when the disputes between the Presbyterians and the Independents were flaring up, a certain Coleman, pastor of London, espoused this opinion; moved by the urging of politicians and by vain itching, he offered the government of the Church to the magistrate in a sermon preached in London before Parliament. Against him G. Gillespie, minister of Edinburgh, and the most celebrated Samuel Rutherford, attacked him with most learned dissertations, by which they laid open all the wrong of the Erastian invention. In the Scriptures, certainly, the power of the keys, and the office of rebuking and of holding someone as a Gentile and a tax collector, has been plainly committed to St Peter, and in his person to the Church, not to the civil power.

units.la: Neque clavium potestatem in solo verbi praeconio consistere, Christus injurias & scandala Ecclesiae deferri, & contumaces ab eadem pro ethnicis & publicanis haberi jubens, ostendit. Erasti verò Ecclesiam illam in Synedrium vel Magistratus fidelis convertentis commentum supra convicimus. Neque profectò Christus, vel fideles omnes offensas Hierosolymam ad Synedrium ascendere jussit, vel Judaicam potius quàm Christianam Ecclesiam informare voluit. Accedit mandatum tradendi incestuosum Sathanae, de quo S. Paulus: Vobis & meo Spiritu in nomine Domini nostri Jesu Christi congregatis, cum potestate Domini nostri Jesu Christi, ejusmodi homo tradatur Sathanae, ad exitium carnis, ut Spiritus salvus sit die illo Domini Jesu, 1. Cor. V. 4. Ubi tradere Sathanae non est, uti Erastus finxit, Sathanae occidendum dare, vel miraculosè vitam adimere; tum quia aequivalet ei, quod S. Paulus v. 2. dixerat: Non luxistis, ut tollatur è medio vestri (è coetu fidelium, extra quem vivere datur) qui hoc fecit; tum quia finis traditionis illius est salus spiritus, qualis non contingit, ubi peccator, flagrante peccato suo occiditur.
units.tr: Nor does Christ's command show that the power of the keys consists solely in the proclamation of the word, when he orders that wrongs and scandals be reported to the Church, and that the obstinate be held by it as Gentiles and tax collectors. And I have already refuted the fancy of Erastus that the Church is to be turned into a Sanhedrin or the faithful magistrate. Certainly Christ did not command all the faithful to go up to the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem with their offences, nor did he wish to shape the Jewish Church rather than the Christian. There is also the command to deliver the incestuous man to Satan, of which St Paul says: When you are gathered together, with my spirit, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, let such a man be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus, 1 Cor. 5:4. Here to deliver to Satan does not mean, as Erastus invented, to give him over to be killed by Satan, or to take away his life by a miracle. This is so, first because it amounts to what St Paul had said in v. 2: You have not mourned, so that he who did this might be removed from among you (from the assembly of the faithful, outside which one is permitted to live); and second because the purpose of that delivering is the salvation of the spirit, which does not happen when a sinner is killed while his sin is still burning.

units.la: Sed disciplina efficit, ut spiritus superior fiat carne, hoc est, corrupta natura, atque ita homo in die Domini salvetur. Ideo S. Paulus Hymenaeum & Alexandrum tradidit Sathanae, ut discant non blasphemare, 1. Tim. I. 20. quod de mortuis dici oppido absurdum est. Quid enim illi discunt? Ergo traditio Sathanae est vel ejectio extra Ecclesiam, ubi Sathan Regnum suum habet: vel potestas tradendi peccatorem Sathanae, ut ab eo corpus divexetur, donec peccator resipiscat. Facit huc etiam generale praeceptum Pauli, quod hac occasione eodem capite subjicit: Cum ejusmodi ne conversamini, expurgate vetus fermentum, cum iis ne edite, v. 7. 9. 11. quae de mortuis intelligi non possunt.
units.tr: But discipline brings it about that the spirit becomes superior to the flesh, that is, to corrupt nature, and so the man is saved in the day of the Lord. Therefore St Paul delivered Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan, that they might learn not to blaspheme, 1 Tim. 1:20; which is exceedingly absurd to say of the dead. For what would they learn? Therefore the delivering to Satan is either the expulsion outside the Church, where Satan has his kingdom, or the power of delivering a sinner to Satan so that his body may be harassed by him until the sinner repents. The general precept of Paul also bears on this, which in the same chapter he adds on this occasion: Do not associate with such people; cleanse out the old leaven; do not eat with them, vv. 7, 9, 11; which cannot be understood of the dead.

units.la: Ita enim cum quibus commisceri vetuit, veluti cum scortatoribus, avaris, ebriosis, injustis, convitiatoribus, v. 10. eosdem miraculosè occidere justisset, cum contra pro omnibus non peccantibus ad mortem orandum sit, 1. Joh. V. 16. Et tantum abest, ut Ecclesia disciplina defungens ex delegatione Magistratus in partem exercendae disciplinae, uti alicubi fit, veniens, delegata sibi ab Ecclesia potestate eandem exerceat. Non enim Magistratui, sed Ecclesiae potestas clavium à Christo data est, & longè antiquior Ecclesia, quam Magistratus Christianus est. Magistratus proin actum quempiam potestatis clavium exercens, alieno, Ecclesiae, non proprio nomine exercet.
units.tr: For in this way the Lord commanded that those with whom he forbade association, such as fornicators, covetous persons, drunkards, swindlers, revilers, 1 Cor. 5:10, should be put to death by a miracle, whereas for all who do not sin unto death we must pray, 1 John 5:16. So far is it from being the case that the Church, when it performs discipline, does so by delegation from the magistrate, as sometimes happens, and exercises a power committed to it by the Church. For the power of the keys was given by Christ not to the magistrate but to the Church, and the Church is far older than the Christian magistrate. The magistrate, therefore, when he exercises any act of the power of the keys, exercises it in the name of another, that is, of the Church, and not in his own name.

units.la: Satis enim constat, ea, quae potestati clavium innexa sunt, ad hominem spiritualem & internum, non externum, quem solum Magistratus civili suo imperio regit, pertinere. Atque id tum maximè liquet, cùm Ecclesia non habet Magistratum fidelem & ὁμόπνευον. Tum enim, velut proprio, & à solo Christo sibi concesso jure, utitur; neque omnino Magistratus in regimine merè Ecclesiastico opera utitur, qua tamen nolens volens uti deberet, siquidem illa Magistratui eximia & essentialis esset. Nunquam enim eam sibi civilis potestas eripi pateretur, quae nunquam non sui juris, quandoque etiam supra modum, tenax est.
units.tr: For it is quite clear that the things bound up with the power of the keys pertain to the spiritual and inward man, not to the outward man, whom the magistrate alone governs by his civil authority. This is especially evident where the Church does not have a magistrate who is faithful and [ὁμόπνευον] of one spirit with it. For then the Church uses its own right, granted to it by Christ alone; nor does it at all make use of the magistrate in purely ecclesiastical government, although it would be bound to use him, willing or unwilling, if that government were a remarkable and essential part of his office. For civil power would never suffer that authority to be snatched from it, since it is always jealous of its own rights, and sometimes beyond measure.

units.la: XCIV. An verò à judicio Ecclesiae ad Magistratum politicum, tanquam superiorem judicem provocatio detur, diu anxiè satis quaesitum est. Sunt enim, qui non tantùm cum Erasto & sequacibus, sed etiam cum Celeb. Maccovio, diversis licet argumentis inducto, magno molimine afferant, licere laesis ab Ecclesia ad Magistratum provocare. Alii aliter pronuntiant. Sed res sine distinctionibus definiri non potest. Nam res judiciis Ecclesiasticis obnoxiae, vel merae sunt Ecclesiasticae, vel aliquid politici admixtum habent. Et in rebus merè Ecclesiasticis, quaedam ad internum conscientiarum, quaedam ad externum Ecclesiae regimen pertinent; & in judicio lato ea de re, quae ad hominem internum plane pertinet, judex Ecclesiasticus potest modum excedere, velut si reum carceri addicat, vel aliis poenis corporalibus, quae non sunt juris Ecclesiastici, plectat. Hinc justae causae oriuntur vel declinandi nandi
units.tr: XCIV. Whether an appeal from the judgment of the Church to the political magistrate, as to a higher judge, is permitted has long been anxiously debated. There are those who, not only with Erastus and his followers but also with the celebrated Maccovius, though led there by different arguments, maintain with great effort that those wronged by the Church may appeal to the magistrate. Others judge otherwise. But the matter cannot be settled without distinctions. For matters subject to ecclesiastical judgments are either purely ecclesiastical or have something political mixed into them. In purely ecclesiastical matters, some pertain to the inward conscience and some to the outward government of the Church. In a broad judgment on that matter, which pertains wholly to the inward man, the ecclesiastical judge may exceed his measure, as when he consigns the accused to prison or inflicts other bodily punishments, which do not belong to ecclesiastical law. Hence just grounds arise either for declining ecclesiastical judgment altogether, or for appealing from it to the civil court.

units.la: Erasti, alio-rumque disciplinam Ecclesiae oppugnantium, elenchus. nandi prorsus judicium Ecclesiasticum, vel ab eo ad judicium civile provocandi. Nam si judex Ecclesiasticus potestatis suæ limites transgressus fuerit, vel de re non merè Ecclesiastica, sed politicum aliquid admixtum habente, vel de re ad externum Ecclesiæ regimen pertinente judicaverit, licita ad Magistratum provocatio erit. In cæteris cavendum, ne claves Regni Cælorum, & ligandi ac solvendi potestas, quam Ecclesiæ Christus commisit, temerè cum iis communicetur, qui ad id muneris vel plane inepti, vel certè vocati non sunt. Non quòd omnis potestas Ecclesiastica Magistratui deneganda sit. Sed alia est potestas objectivè solùm, alia formaliter Ecclesiastica est. Illa pio Magistratui competit, quia & res quædam & personæ Ecclesiæ curæ ejusdem objectum sunt: hæc, versans non tantùm circa res & personas Ecclesiæ ratione objecti, sed etiam ratione modi, quatenus circa eas modo non Politico, sed Ecclesiastico & spirituali versatur, non Magistratui, sed soli Ecclesiæ convenit, de quo infra pluribus. Proin duæ hæ potestates, cùm vel diversa objecta habeant, vel circa eadem objecta aliter atque aliter versentur, quandiu intra præscriptos limites manent, non magis sibi mutuo officiunt, quàm planetæ duo, quibus diversum Cœlum assignatum est. Quin alterius altera poscit opem res & conjurat amicè. Ubi verò potestas Ecclesiastica fines suos prætergreditur, ut tyrannidem exerceat, vel de iis, quæ alieni fori sunt, judicet, tum Magistratus officium est, illam evagantem reprimere, & intra limites suos coërcere. Atque id in Gallia appellationibus tanquam ex abusu, uti vocant, quibus ab Ecclesia falcem in alienam messem immittente, ad supremam curiam provocatur, occasionem dedit. Quin & Beza adversus Eraslum non diffitetur, cùm à rectè constituto consistorio possit reis delatis injuria fieri, in angustioribus territoriis citra ullam ordinis Ecclesiastici violationem, Christianum Magistratum, ut tabulas legis utriusque & Ecclesiasticæ ἐνλαξίας custodem & vindicem conquerentibus prospicere posse. Hæc quæstioni accommodata, amplam satis lucem fœnerantur.
units.tr: The refutation of Erastus and of others who attack the discipline of the Church. For if the ecclesiastical judge has transgressed the limits of his power, whether by judging a matter that is not purely ecclesiastical but has something political mixed into it, or a matter pertaining to the outward government of the Church, an appeal to the magistrate will be lawful. In other cases care must be taken that the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and the power of binding and loosing which Christ committed to the Church, are not rashly shared with those who are either wholly unfit for that office or certainly not called to it. This is not to say that all ecclesiastical power is to be denied to the magistrate. But one power is ecclesiastical only objectively, another formally. The former belongs to the godly magistrate, because both certain things and persons are objects of the Church's care; the latter, which is concerned not only with the things and persons of the Church as objects but also in respect of its manner, insofar as it deals with them not in a political but in an ecclesiastical and spiritual manner, belongs not to the magistrate but to the Church alone, as will be discussed more fully below. Therefore these two powers, since they either have different objects or deal with the same objects in different ways, so long as they remain within their prescribed limits, do no more hinder one another than two planets to which different heavens have been assigned. Indeed, each needs the help of the other and joins with it in friendship. But when ecclesiastical power goes beyond its bounds, so as to exercise tyranny or to judge matters belonging to another court, then it is the duty of the magistrate to restrain that wandering power and confine it within its limits. In France, this gave occasion to the appeals as for abuse, as they are called, by which recourse is had to the supreme court when the Church puts its sickle into another's harvest. Indeed, Beza does not deny against Erastus that, when a consistory rightly constituted may do injury to those accused, in smaller territories, without any violation of ecclesiastical order, a Christian magistrate can watch over the complainants as guardian and avenger of the tables of both laws and of [εὐνομία] good order. These points, applied to the question, shed quite enough light.

units.la: XCV. Sed circa Excommunicationem, quæ judicii Ecclesiastici ultima pars est, Ecclesiarum Reformatarum etiam sententia & praxis nonnihil variat.
units.tr: XCV. But concerning excommunication, which is the last stage of ecclesiastical judgment, the opinion and practice of the Reformed Churches also differ somewhat.

units.la: Nam aliæ quidem à sexu excommunicatos & pro ethnicis ac publicanis habitos ab usu Cœnæ Domini, aliisque Ecclesiæ privilegiis suspendunt, vel, si ita contumaciæ & flagitii ratio postulet, graviori obnuntiatione ab omni communione, quæ Sanctorum propria est, arcent. Aliæ verò missa inprimis solenni illa à S. Cœnæ usu remotione, quam Excommunicationem majorem appellant, eosdem ad civilem potestatem, siquidem illa consentiens Ecclesiæ & orthodoxa fuerit, coërcendos, & poenis civilibus ad poenitentiam usque salutarem, vel interitum corporis, frangendos deferunt. Prioribus illis vetus Ecclesia sanctior castiórque adhuc, & inter hostes suos, Judæos & Gentiles vagiens, præivit, quæ in disciplinæ exercitio magnum inprimis vigorem ostendit. Sed dum canonibus & regulis Ecclesiasticas satisfactiones, quibus exantlatis peccator Ecclesiæ reconciliaretur, astrinxerunt, & rursus venias & indulgentias extra earum formulas dispensarunt, occasionem detrahentibus merito Christi, & placamenta propriarum afflictionum vel erogationum, nec non merita humana, αὐτοκεφαλοεἰαν papalem, & authoritatem Sacerdotalem ad absolvendum à peccatis, introducentibus præbuerunt, neque etiam attenderunt ad regulam illam Pauli, qua in disciplina hac κυριαχη τῶν ἀγαπῶν charitatem prævalere, ne poenitens abundantiori tristitia absorbeatur, & ὑπὸ τῆς Σαλανᾶ πλεονεκτήμενοι damno affici possit, seu Sathanas ex eo lucrum captet, jussit, 2. Cor. II. 6-12. Post Reformationem, abusu excommunicationis papalis abolito, non paucis, Oecolampadio, Bucero, Capitoni, Calvino Veteris Ecclesiæ, flagitiosos & contumaces non excommunicantis utcunque, sed sacrorum etiam communione interdicentis, rigor placuit; discipulorum Christi instar dicentibus & quærentibus; Domine, vis ibimus & colligemus zizania? Matth. XIII. 28. Non paucis in Ecclesiis introductus ille rigor est, majore, minore, & alicubi etiam, velut Basileæ, Argentinæ, Constantiæ nullo cum successu. Argumenta illis fuerant, quòd Deus ipse Protoplastos Paradiso pulsos, ab arbore vitæ arcuerit, Genes. III. 23. & Cainum è Sanctorum coetu expulerit, ibid. IV. 14. quòd in lege Mosaica immundi à Sanctuario exclusi sint, Num. XII. 14. 15. XIX. 11. 12. 13. Ezech. XLIV. 23. quòd rigor ille disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ tempore Christi à Judæis observatus fuerit, qui eos, quos pro impiis habuerunt, ἀποσυναγώγυς fecerunt, seu è Synagogis suis exegerunt, Joh. XVI. 2. quòd Christus rotundè monuerit, ne Sanctum demus canibus, nec margaritas porcis objiciamus, Matth. VII. 6. quòd illi, quos Christus pro Ethnicis haberi jussit, non magis quàm ipsi Ethnici ad Sacrorum communionem admitti possint: quòd Sathanæ tradendi, vel traditi, utpote ejus potestati subjecti, participes esse signorum gratiæ non possint: quòd clavis ligantis usus locum habere apud eos, qui Ecclesiæ membra adhuc habentur, & gratiæ sigilla percipiunt, non possit: quòd sigilla gratiæ offerri iis, quibus Evangelium nihil promittit, sine sacrilegio & profanatione sigillorum, nequeant: quòd aliàs ex Ecclesia quoddam veluti Augiæ stabulum fiat, in quo nullum ovium & hircorum, fidelium & infidelium, orthodoxorum & idololatrarum, resipiscentium & impoenitentium discrimen sit; & sententiæ malorum, atque porcorum haræ, quàm sacrato Dei Templo & aræ similior: quin & epulum illud sanctissimum profanorum hominum se invicem velut contagione quadam inficientium, symposium reddatur: quòd denique sic impii foveantur, ut in sua sibi malitia & impietate placeant, & indies magisque indurentur.
units.tr: For some churches suspend those who have been excommunicated, and who are regarded as heathens and tax collectors, from the use of the Lord's Supper and from other privileges of the Church. If the nature of their obstinacy and wickedness requires it, they exclude them, by a heavier sentence, from all fellowship that belongs to the saints. Others, above all by that solemn removal from the Lord's Supper which they call the greater excommunication, refer the same people to the civil power, provided that this power agrees with the Church and is orthodox, so that they may be restrained and broken by civil penalties, either to a salutary repentance or to the destruction of the body. The ancient Church, purer and holier than these, went before in the first of these practices, living still among its enemies, the Jews and Gentiles, and it showed great vigour above all in the exercise of discipline. But when the canons and rules bound the ecclesiastical satisfactions, after which the sinner would be reconciled to the Church, and when they again dispensed pardons and indulgences outside those formulas, they gave occasion to those who detract from the merit of Christ, and to those who introduce the satisfactions of their own afflictions or almsgivings, as well as human merits, papal autocephaly [αὐτοκεφαλοεἰαν], and the priestly authority to absolve from sins. Nor did they attend to that rule of Paul, in which he commanded that in this discipline the sovereignty of love [κυριαχη τῶν ἀγαπῶν] should prevail, lest the penitent be swallowed up by excessive sorrow, and lest, being overreached by Satan [ὑπὸ τῆς Σαλανᾶ πλεονεκτήμενοι], he should suffer loss, or lest Satan should gain advantage from it, 2 Cor. 2.6-12. After the Reformation, when the abuse of papal excommunication had been abolished, the severity of many men pleased not a few, namely Oecolampadius, Bucer, Capito, and Calvin of the ancient Church. They did not excommunicate the wicked and obstinate in any sense, but they forbade them the communion of the sacred things, saying and asking, like the disciples of Christ: Lord, wilt thou that we go and gather up the tares? Matt. 13.28. This severity was introduced in not a few Churches, in the greater and the lesser form, and in some places, as at Basel, Strasbourg, and Constance, with no success. Their arguments were these: that God himself drove our first parents out of Paradise and kept them from the tree of life, Gen. 3.23; that he expelled Cain from the company of the saints, ibid. 4.14; that in the Mosaic law the unclean were excluded from the sanctuary, Num. 12.14-15, 19.11-13, Ezek. 44.23; that this rigour of ecclesiastical discipline was observed by the Jews at the time of Christ, who made those whom they regarded as impious into apostles [ἀποσυναγώγους], that is, drove them out of their synagogues, John 16.2; that Christ plainly warned that we should not give the holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine, Matt. 7.6; that those whom Christ ordered to be regarded as Gentiles cannot be admitted to the communion of the sacred things any more than the Gentiles themselves; that those who are handed over to Satan, or have been handed over, since they are subject to his power, cannot share in the signs of grace; that the use of the key that binds cannot take place among those who are still regarded as members of the Church and receive the seals of grace; that the seals of grace cannot be offered, without sacrilege and profanation of the seals, to those to whom the Gospel promises nothing; that otherwise the Church becomes a kind of Augean stable, in which there is no distinction between the sheep and the goats, the faithful and the unbelieving, the orthodox and the idolaters, the penitent and the impenitent, and an assembly of the wicked and a herd of swine is made more like a sacred temple and altar of God; indeed, that the most holy feast becomes a drinking party of profane men, who infect one another as if by some contagion; and finally, that the impious are so cherished that they take pleasure in their own malice and impiety, and grow harder day by day.

units.la: XCVI. Ab hac sententia & praxi sententia & praxis Ecclesiæ nostræ patriæ, à viris sanctissimis, Huldrico Zwinglio & Henrico Bullingero introducta, & ad nostra usque tempora Tiguri, Bernæ, aliisque Helvetiæ locis, producta, nonnihil dissidet. Nam peccatore Ecclesiam contumaciter spernente, & pro Ethnico jam & publicano declarato, Ecclesiastica disciplina tantùm non ibi cessat & respirat, atque locus datur disciplinæ civili, Christianis tamen legibus, non intra civilem duntaxat honestatem, sed Evangelii etiam Christi πολιτείαν consistentibus instructæ, per quam ἀναθεματισμοί, pestes & carcinomata ejusmodi carcere vel exilio ab Ecclesia, mulctantur, quinimò, si insanabile vulnus appareat, ne pars sincera trahatur, ense etiam reciduntur. Quandiu tamen illa Sathanæ pabula citra pœnitentiæ testificationem in Ecclesia tolerantur, juxta eandem sententiam & praxin, fideles monentur, ut non tantùm lugeant, sed etiam hominum illorum consortium cane pejus & angue vitent, cum operibus eorum infrugiferis commercium nullum habeant, ac ne ave quidem iis dicant, ut ita Salvatoris sententiæ præcipientis: Sit tibi velut ethnicus & publicanus, amplius satisfiat, quin & ipsi contumaces & enormiter scandalosi, quandiu in peccato perfistunt, abstinere ultro à Cœna Domini & symbolis gratiæ severè jubentur (quæ excommunicationis minoris, seu abstentionis à Cœna Domini, sed non violentæ, species quædam est) non neglecta interim, ac ne suspensa quidem admonitione fraterna, cùm ex Evangelio constet, nec de ethnicorum, nec de publicanorum salute desperandum esse. Ministerium enim Ecclesiasticum ædificatio quædam est, quæ in perpetuo actu versatur, neque unquam in hac vita apicem suum attingit.
units.tr: XCVI. The opinion and practice of our own country's Church, introduced by the most holy men Huldrych Zwingli and Heinrich Bullinger, and carried on to our own times at Zurich, Bern, and other places in Helvetia, differs somewhat from this view and practice. For when a sinner obstinately despises the Church and has already been declared a heathen and a tax collector, ecclesiastical discipline there almost ceases and rests, and room is given to civil discipline. This civil discipline, however, is to be governed by Christian laws, which rest not merely on civil decency but also on the commonwealth [πολιτείαν] of the Gospel of Christ. By it, anathemas [ἀναθεματισμοί], plagues, and cancers of this kind are punished by imprisonment or exile from the Church, and indeed, if the wound appears incurable, they are even cut off with the sword, lest the sound part be dragged down with it. Yet, as long as such food of Satan is tolerated in the Church without any testimony of repentance, the faithful are, according to the same opinion and practice, urged not only to mourn but also to avoid the company of such men, worse than a dog or a snake. They are to have no fellowship with their unfruitful works, and they are not even to say hello to them, so that the Saviour's command may be satisfied more fully: Let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector. Moreover, the obstinate themselves, and those who are enormously scandalous, are sternly ordered, as long as they persist in sin, to abstain of their own accord from the Lord's Supper and from the symbols of grace. This is a kind of lesser excommunication, or abstention from the Lord's Supper, though not a violent one. Meanwhile, fraternal admonition is not neglected, nor even suspended, since it is clear from the Gospel that there is no reason to despair either of the salvation of the Gentiles or of the tax collectors. For the ecclesiastical ministry is a kind of building, which is in constant activity, and never in this life reaches its summit.

units.la: XCVII. Habuerunt Ecclesiæ Helveticæ
units.tr: XCVII. The Helvetic Churches

units.la: suæ in revocanda disciplina severiore ad Excommunicationem usque, quam vocant majorem, cunctationis & verecundiæ rationes haud pœnitendas, quas inprimis Benedictus Aretius, Bernensis Theologus, Probl. Loc. 112. cumulavit, quásque ex eodem, aliisque etiam vel per saturam exhibere, non pigebit. Huc autem in universum redeunt, quòd Excommunicatio illa severior, quæ Banni nomine venit, res optima quidem, sed pessimo abusu Pontificio invisa, & tempore Reformationis multis adeò execrabilis visa fuerit, ut ægrè ad Ecclesiam Evangelicam ea retenta transituri fuerint: quòd vix ac ne vix in patria nostra obtineri, & obtenta retineri potuerit, quia ad excommunicationem majorem exercendam requiruntur tum Pastores inprimis cordati, qui præter Deum neminem metuunt, & nihil σπουδαῖον secundum propensionem agant, & parati sint pro salute Ecclesiæ vitam & sanguinem periclitari; tum populus, & in eodem imperantes æquè ac parentes, qui obedire & jugum isthoc pati velint & valeant; Verbo, Ambrosii & Theodosii, rari illi, & velut nantes in gurgite vasto: quòd apud eos, quibus res isthæc committitur, facilè dominandi studium subrepat, & odia privata, atque affectus maligni vincant; quæ res Antichristum peperit: quòd olim res isthæc non consessu paucorum, sed in conventibus Ecclesiasticis, sub conscientia & suffragiis fidelium suscipi conseveverit, quod hodie in Republica libera, cujus populus dissolutior, & major pars corruptissima sit, factu difficilimum foret: quòd, si absque partium studio, & corvorum jure atque columbarum injuria, negotium isthoc procederet, & avari, lascivi, ebriosi, injusti, tyranni, fœnerato-res, Magistratus subditis iniqui, dominantibus obliqui & immorigeri hanc aleam subire debe-rent, paucis impune futurum sit: quòd schismatis in Republica libera periculum subsit, cujus metu olim etiam S. Cyprianus coëpiscopos suos malos toleravit. Irenæus Victorem admonuerit, temperaret sibi ab Excommunicatione Orientalium; & S. Augustinus diu cum Donatistis, Manichæis aliisque conflictatus, & in hoc prælio veteranus miles, passim zizaniorum tolerantiam svaserit: quòd in Scriptura pauca traditorum Sathanæ, dubio traditionis illius sensu, exempla occurrant: quod Scripturæ loca pro excommunicatione majore allegata non adeò clara & diserta sint, ut illam liquidò probent: quòd in locis nonnullis assumptus ille rigor inauspicatò cesserit: quòd denique carentibus rigore illo Ecclesiis non desint ἀναθεματισμοί, quibus rigor ille resarcitur, & peccatores reprimuntur, de quibus mox dicturi sumus.
units.tr: In restoring stricter discipline, the Churches of Helvetia had reasons for caution and hesitation, extending even to excommunication, which they call the greater. These reasons are not to be regretted, and they were set out chiefly by Benedict Aretius, the Bernese theologian, Probl. Loc. 112. I shall not hesitate to present them, even in summary, from him and from others. In general they come to this. That severer excommunication, which goes by the name of ban, is indeed a very good thing, but it was hated for its very bad Papal abuse. At the time of the Reformation it seemed so detestable to many that they would scarcely have passed over to the Evangelical Church had it been retained. It could hardly, or scarcely at all, be established in our country, and once established it could hardly be kept. For exercising the greater excommunication one requires, above all, prudent ministers who fear no one but God, who do nothing out of partisan zeal [σπουδαῖον secundum propensionem], and who are prepared to risk life and blood for the salvation of the Church. One requires a people, and rulers who are as much parents to it, who are willing and able to obey and to bear this yoke. In a word, such men are rare, like Ambrose and Theodosius, and they are as it were swimming in a vast whirlpool. Among those to whom this matter is entrusted, the desire to dominate easily creeps in, and private hatreds and malicious passions prevail; this thing brought forth Antichrist. Formerly this business was undertaken not by the assembly of a few but in ecclesiastical gatherings, under the conscience and votes of the faithful; today, in a free commonwealth whose people is more dissolute and whose greater part is most corrupt, this would be very difficult to do. If the business proceeded without partisan zeal, with the right of crows and the injustice to doves, and if the greedy, the lewd, the drunken, the unjust, the tyrannical, the usurers, those unfair to their subjects and crooked and unruly toward their rulers had to undergo this lottery, then few would go unpunished. In a free commonwealth there is a danger of schism, and for fear of it St Cyprian once tolerated his evil fellow bishops. Irenaeus admonished Victor to refrain from excommunicating the Easterners. St Augustine, long wrestling with the Donatists, the Manichaeans and others, and a veteran soldier in that battle, everywhere urged tolerance of the tares. In Scripture few examples occur of those delivered to Satan, and the sense of that delivery is doubtful. The passages of Scripture alleged for the greater excommunication are not so clear and explicit as to prove it plainly. In some places that assumed rigour has unhappily ceased. Finally, in Churches lacking that rigour there are not lacking anathemas [ἀναθεματισμοί], by which that rigour is made good and sinners are restrained, of which we are about to speak.

units.la: XCVIII. Hoc equidem de quæstione vexatissima multum contendere nec libet, nec juvat, cùm ordo in Ecclesia constitutus, quandiu is salutaris comperitur, & Ecclesiæ ædificationi inservit, temerè vellicari & arrodi non debeat. Etenim is excommunicationis finis est, ut Ecclesiæ mores excolantur ad amussim Evangelii, sancti floreant, profani coërceantur, ne mali porrò impudentia & impietate graf-sentur. Hunc finem quibus per disciplinæ suæ exercitium assequi datur, illis controversia movenda non videtur, licèt labecula & infirmitas aliqua, quam majoris mali metus apud non plane incautos parit, notari possit. Nam omnis ἐξουσία potestas Ecclesiæ data à Domino, non aliter data intelligitur, quàm quatenus εἰς οἰκοδομὴν καὶ οὐκ εἰς καθαίρεσιν ad ædificationem & non ad destructionem facit, 2. Cor. X. 8. Ipse quoque S. Paulus comminatus, quòd incestuosum Sathanæ tradere instituerit, magna cautione & charitate in eo negotio versatus est, malens κυριῶσαι τὴν ἀγάπην prævalere charitatem, 2. Cor. II. 6. 7. &c. quàm ut severitate nimia peccatoris pœnitentia suffl aminetur potiùs quàm promoveatur. Modus enim servandus est, ne nimio rigore perdatur is, quem servatum cupit Dominus, qui arundinem quassatam non confringit, & linum fumigans non extinguit. Ad infirmitatem etiam humanam pertinet, quòd in paucis adeò Ecclesiis Christi disciplina unâ cum ejus doctrina solidè constituitur & exercetur, quia, quæ hujus vitæ imperfectio est, totum Christi Regnum recipere, eíque penitus se tradere plerique etiam eorum, qui videri volunt Christum rectè cognoscere, & in ipsum sperare, detrectant. Tum etiam ubi disciplina Christi rectè constituta est, ἀγωγὴ seu ratio & tenor eam exercendi, & juxta eam vivendi, haud raró deficit. Nam olim quidem, qui ad Ecclesiam venerunt, velut ad militiam, crucem, inopiam veniebant; neque penitus pro fratribus habebantur, nisi in vita & constantia fidei probati. Hinc disciplinæ integritas. Post integræ gentes cum Regibus suis in Ecclesiam intrarunt, non sine vanitatibus & erroribus suis, hinc disciplinæ corruptio. Abundent ergo suo sensu, qui excommunicationis severitatem legibus suis sanxerunt, & id operam navent unicè, ne leges illæ simisimiles sint campanæ sine pistillo, sed ut eo modo, quo salutares judicatæ iis sunt, exerceantur; ne det veniam corvis, vexet censura columbas. Si quid autem hominum consilio & consuetudine accessit, id ne valeat, tanquam lex Christi, sed ut humanum consilium & consuetudo, nempe, quandiu est ad οἰκοδομὴν ædificationem, non ad καταστροφὴν subversionem. Malæ autem consuetudines per admonitiones fraternas, & consensum Ecclesiæ, perinde ut alia peccata, paulatim tollantur. Quòd si contigerit, ut Ecclesia vel judicium negligat, vel in eo turbetur, vel non rectè judicet, tum verò quivis Christianus se ipsum caltum conservare, & suum luctum super peccata palam facere, & quantum fieri potest, plurimos ἐλέγχω, cujus solius telo Ecclesiæ militandum est, ad societatem τῆς πίνθης luctus incitare; & sedulò ea in re cavere, ne vel αὐτάρκειαν fovendo & palliando disciplinam impediat, vel se efferat, & ducem vel sectatorem factionis faciat, vel charitatem, μακροθυμίαν & πεπειτητα lædat. Si Ecclesia non rectè judicet, & tamen à principio & fundamento non discedat, neque aliud fundamentum ponat, charitas similiter retineri, & tristitia atque redargutio continuari debet. Pacatissimè verò & efficacissimè Ecclesia regi & judicium exerceri potest, si nulla arma præter ἐλέγχον luctum & charitatem afferuntur. Tum enim finis disciplinæ, imò consummata disciplina obtinet, cùm Ecclesia ἐν πίνθῃ in luctu communicet, & in nomine Domini Jesu Christi ad ἐπιμέλειαν correctionem congregatur, 1. Cor. V. 2. 4.
units.tr: XCVIII. Indeed, I neither wish nor am glad to contend much on this most troubled question, since an order established in the Church, as long as it is found salutary and serves the building up of the Church, ought not to be rashly plucked at and gnawed. The end of excommunication is this: that the morals of the Church be refined to the rule of the Gospel, that the holy flourish and the profane be restrained, lest the wicked go on in their impudence and impiety. To those to whom it is granted to reach this end through the exercise of their discipline, controversy does not seem to be due, although some weakness and frailty, which the fear of a greater evil produces in not wholly unwary men, may be noted. For all power [ἐξουσία] given to the Church by the Lord is understood to be given only insofar as it serves for building up and not for destruction (ad ædificationem et non ad destructionem), 2 Cor. 10:8. St Paul himself, when he threatened to deliver the incestuous man to Satan, acted with great caution and charity in that business, preferring that charity should prevail [κυριῶσαι τὴν ἀγάπην], 2 Cor. 2:6, 7, etc., rather than that the repentance of the sinner should be hindered rather than advanced by excessive severity. The measure to be kept is that the one whom the Lord desires to save is not destroyed by excessive rigour, for he does not break a bruised reed nor quench a smoking flax. It also belongs to human weakness that in so few Churches the discipline of Christ, together with its doctrine, is solidly established and exercised; for, which is the imperfection of this life, most people, even those who wish to seem to know Christ rightly and to hope in him, shrink from receiving the whole Kingdom of Christ and surrendering themselves wholly to it. Moreover, even where the discipline of Christ is rightly established, the manner [ἀγωγὴ] or the rule and tenor of exercising it, and of living according to it, often fails. For formerly those who came to the Church came as to a warfare, to the cross and to want, and they were not wholly regarded as brothers unless proved in the life and steadfastness of faith. Hence the integrity of discipline. Afterwards whole peoples entered the Church together with their kings, not without their own vanities and errors; hence the corruption of discipline. Let those therefore who have sanctioned the severity of excommunication by their laws abound in their own sense, and let them take pains solely to ensure that those laws are not like a bell without a clapper, but are exercised in the way by which they were judged salutary. Let them not grant pardon to crows, nor let censure vex the doves. If anything has been added by human counsel and custom, let it not have force as the law of Christ, but as human counsel and custom, namely, only as long as it serves building up and not overthrow. Bad customs, however, are to be removed gradually, through brotherly admonitions and the consent of the Church, just like other sins. But if it happens that the Church either neglects judgment, or is disturbed in it, or does not judge rightly, then indeed any Christian should keep himself pure, make his own grief over sins openly known, and, as far as possible, stir up very many to join in mourning by reproof [ἐλέγχω], the only weapon with which the Church must fight; and he should take diligent care in this matter, lest either by fostering and excusing self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκειαν] he hinder discipline, or lift himself up and make himself leader or follower of a faction, or harm charity, longsuffering [μακροθυμίαν] and patience. If the Church does not judge rightly but does not depart from the principle and foundation, nor lay another foundation, charity ought likewise to be retained, and sorrow and rebuke continued. The Church can be governed and judgment exercised most peacefully and most effectively if no weapons are brought except reproof, mourning and charity. For then the end of discipline, indeed discipline in its perfection, is attained, when the Church in mourning [ἐν πένθει] shares in common and is gathered in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ for correction and admonition, 1 Cor. 5:2, 4.

units.la: XCIX. Neque etiam est, cur Patriæ nostræ disciplina legibus circumscripta odiosè nimis exagitetur. Non enim Ecclesia nostra, ejusque σφεσεῶν aliis alium disciplinæ modum servantibus succensent, sed iis potiùs meliori tramite progredi volentibus gratulatur. Nam & Bullingerus, & cum eo Tigurina Ecclesia Genevensem diversam disciplinam servantem hortata est, ut in semel receptis & sanctè quidem ex Scriptura receptis perseveret, uti ex Calvini Epistolis & Responsis pag. 119. liquet. Quantamcunque verò potestatem disciplinæ Ecclesiæ nostræ Magistratus commiscet, eam non ita interpretatur, quasi proprio jure eam, ceu Magistratus civilis, possideat, quæ Erasti prævaricatoris improba sententia fuit, sed quòd eam ab Ecclesia commissam exerceat, non civili duntaxat, sed Ecclesiastica etiam ratione, juxta leges Evangelii, nec seorsim, sed unà cum Ecclesia ejusque Ministris in foro mixto, in peccatores & scandalosos animadvertens. Ubi non ita Ecclesia curam omnem abdicavit, quin Magistratum officio Ecclesiam à scandalis purgandi segniùs fungentem identidem & pro rostris, & per propositiones in curia graviter admoneat, ad animum identidem eidem revocans, quòd non sibi, sed Deo & Ecclesiæ judicium exerceat, & tandiu exercere possit, quandiu legitimè munere eo sibi commisso fungitur, quod non semel esse factum novimus. Non fuit nobis hactenus, fateor, tanta fiducia & animositas, ut famosam illam excommunicationem, quam Majorem appellant, in Ecclesiam nostram Ἱεραρχίας introduceremus: inprimis cùm nobis non liqui-
units.tr: XCIX. Nor is there any reason why the discipline of our country, circumscribed by laws, should be attacked too hatefully. For our Church does not take offence at other Churches keeping a different mode of discipline, but rather rejoices in those who wish to advance by a better path. For both Bullinger and, with him, the Church of Zurich exhorted the Genevan Church, which kept a different discipline, to persevere in what had once been received, and received soundly from Scripture, as is clear from Calvin's Epistles and Responses, p. 119. However great the power of discipline that our Magistrate has mixed into our Church, it is not so interpreted as though he possessed it by his own right, as a civil magistrate; that was the wicked opinion of the prevaricator Erastus. Rather, he exercises it as committed to him by the Church, not only by civil but also by ecclesiastical reckoning, according to the laws of the Gospel, and not separately but together with the Church and its ministers, in a mixed forum, taking action against sinners and scandalous persons. Here the Church has not so abdicated all care that it does not, from time to time, both from the pulpit and by proposals in the council, gravely admonish a Magistrate who performs the duty of purging the Church of scandals too sluggishly, recalling to his mind again and again that he does not exercise judgment for himself but for God and the Church, and that he can exercise it only as long as he lawfully performs the office committed to him; which, as we know, has happened more than once. I confess that we have not hitherto had such confidence and boldness as to introduce into our Church that infamous excommunication which they call the Greater, the hierarchy's invention; especially since it does not clearly appear to us that it was commanded and commended by Christ and the Apostles as perpetual, and as necessary in every condition of the times and public state of the Church; and since the older and still more innocent Church, which exercised it, was driven by a certain necessity, because the Magistrate was unfaithful and...

units.la: dò appareat, illam à Christo & Apostolis ut perpetuò, & in qualibet conditione temporum & status publici Ecclesiæ, ut necessariam, præceptam & commendatam esse: atque vetus & innocentior adhuc Ecclesia, quæ illam exercuit, necessitate quadam compulsa, quia Magistratu infideli & discorde, atque Christianis legibus invisò, vitiosis contra legibus moribúsque Rempublicam gubernante, usa est, hunc disciplinæ rigorem adhibuerit. Confessionis Helveticæ hac de re sententia cap. 17. consignata talis est: Cùm omnino oporteat esse in Ecclesia disciplinam, & apud veteres quondam usitata fuerit excommunicatio, fuerintque judicia Ecclesiastica in populo Dei, Ministrorum quoque fuerit ad ædificationem disciplinam hanc moderari pro conditione temporum, status publici ac necessitate. Ubi semper tenenda est regula: Omnia fieri debere ad ædificationem, decenter, honestè, & sine tyrannide & seditione. Apostolus enim testatur, sibi à Deo in Ecclesia traditam esse potestatem ad ædificationem. Nam ipsemet Dominus vetuit lolium in agro Dominico eradicari, quando periculum sit, ut & triticum evellatur. Non ergo sic adamante fixa Ecclesiæ nostræ sententia & praxis stat, quin disciplinam aliter moderari liceat, si conditio temporum & statuts publici atque necessitas postulet, neque disciplinæ illam ἀπωλείαν, qua in Ecclesia vetustiori ad excommunicationem illam majorem, & diras usque processit, simpliciter Confessio improbat, sed eam pro conditione temporum, statuts publici & necessitate ita moderari jubet, ut ædificationi, non destructioni inserviat. Cujusmodi moderationem pluribus etiam S. Augustinus cont. Parm. Ep. lib. III. 2. commendat; allato eodem argumento, quòd zizanium eradicari non debeat, quando periculum est, ne & triticum evellatur. Poterit autem Ecclesiæ Pastor conscientiæ satisfacere, si hominibus aperte impiis, & impietatem, odia & implacabilitatem profitentibus Sacramentum Cœnæ Domini, ceu sigillum gratiæ Domini, offerre, atque ita Sacramentum sacrilega impietate profanare non obligetur, & vel obligatus etiam recusei. Cui rei etiam legibus publicis sic provisum est, ut qui piè & cordatè agere vult, facilè conscientiam liberare possit. Neque enim ei insignitè malis, & flagrante adhuc delicto Deo & Ecclesiæ palam illudentibus, vel accessum ad mensam Domini suadere, vel symbola gratiæ offerre sine conscientiæ vulnere ausit, quia sic prudens volensque cum alieno peccato indignè manducantis communicaret, 1. Tim. V. 22. profanationis Sacramenti author suasorque exsisteret; sanctum canibus, & margaritas porcis in cœno suo se volutantibus, objiceret, exitii hominum impiorum fabrum architectúmque se gereret; cujus potiùs erat Ecclesiæ Sacramenta illibata, sarta & tecta pro virili sua tueri, & convertendis, non perdendis hominibus religiosè invigilare. Denique carentibus rigore isto Ecclesiis nostris non desunt ἀνλίεα·κόμνα, uti Medici appellant. Nam & Ministri Ecclesiæ, non tantum quotidie illam excommunicationis formulam. Qui talia committunt, non habent partem in Regno Cœlorum, graviter intonant; sed etiam ante Cœnam peccatores præfractos & ἀμετανόητος, indefinitè saltem, severè objurgant, jurgant, & iisdem authores, publica etiam obnuntiatione,sunt,ne impœnitentes & imparati manum ad sacra symbola mittant, mittentibus grave judicium minantur: & consistoria ac fora tum merè Ecclesiastica,tum mixta adhortationibus,comminationibus,instructionibus ex Dei verbo, assiduè calent: Et Magistratus pius omnium ordinum homines in officio suo, juxta leges non civiles duntaxat, sed etiam Divinas , continet ; in sceleratos verò gladio, laqueo, carcere, exilio,infamia aliisque modis severè animadvertit: & pii gemunt atque suspirant propter cunctas abominationes, quæ in populo fiunt: & Deus ipse,quod caput est,suam quotidie excommunicationem exercens, hypocritas prodit, aperte sceleratos malè perdit,solennitérque in extremo judicio à coetu fidelium separatos declarabit. Cui ordini & instituto sic Deus hactenus clementer benedixit, ut Ecclesiam nostram , præfiscine dixero, non major corruptio in doctrina & moribus, quàm alias,quàm majorem disciplinæ austeritatem professas, afflixerit.
units.tr: ...dò appears that it was commanded and recommended by Christ and the Apostles as perpetually necessary, in every condition of the times and state of the public order of the Church. The old and still more innocent Church, which exercised it, was compelled by a certain necessity, because the magistrate was unfaithful and hostile, and was governing the commonwealth with vicious laws and morals contrary to Christian laws, and so it applied this rigour of discipline. The judgment of the Helvetic Confession on this matter is set down in cap. 17. as follows: Since discipline must certainly exist in the Church, and excommunication was once in common use among the ancients, and there were ecclesiastical judgments among the people of God, it has also been the task of the ministers to regulate this discipline for edification, according to the condition of the times, the state of public affairs and necessity. Here the rule must always be kept: that everything should be done for edification, decently, honourably, and without tyranny or sedition. For the Apostle testifies that the power given him by God in the Church was for edification. For the Lord himself forbade the tares to be uprooted in the Lord's field, when there is danger that the wheat would be pulled up as well. Therefore our Church's view and practice do not stand so fixed as adamant that it is not permitted to regulate discipline otherwise, if the condition of the times, the state of public affairs and necessity require it. Nor does the Confession simply disapprove of that severity of discipline by which, in the older Church, things went as far as that great excommunication and its dire consequences; rather it orders that it be regulated according to the condition of the times, the state of public affairs and necessity, so that it serves edification and not destruction. St. Augustine also commends this kind of moderation in many places, in his Contra Parmenianum, Ep. lib. III. 2, citing the same argument, that the tares ought not to be uprooted when there is danger that the wheat too would be torn up. Moreover, the minister of the Church can satisfy his conscience if he is not bound to offer the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper, as the seal of the Lord's grace, to men who are openly impious and who profess impiety, hatred and implacability, and so not to profane the Sacrament with sacrilegious impiety; and even if he were bound, he may refuse. Public laws have also provided for this matter, so that one who wishes to act piously and prudently can easily free his conscience. For he would not dare, with a clear conscience, either to urge to the table of the Lord those who are notoriously wicked and whose sin still blazes, mocking God and the Church, or to offer the symbols of grace to them. For if he did so knowingly and willingly, he would share in another's sin of one eating unworthily, 1 Tim. 5:22, and would become the author and encourager of the profanation of the Sacrament. He would be throwing what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine wallowing in their filth, and would make himself the builder and architect of the destruction of impious men. It is rather his task to guard the Sacraments of the Church undiminished, whole and intact, as far as he can, and to watch over the conversion, not the ruin, of men with devotion. Finally, in churches that lack this rigour there is no shortage of what the physicians call incurable cases [ἀνίατα]. For the ministers of the Church not only thunder daily with that formula of excommunication, Those who commit such things have no part in the kingdom of heaven; they also severely rebuke, reprove and, at least in general terms, censure before the Supper the stubborn and unrepentant [ἀμετανόητοι] sinners, and by public proclamation they warn them not to put their hands to the sacred symbols while unrepentant and unprepared, threatening grave judgment on those who do. Meanwhile the consistories and courts, both purely ecclesiastical and mixed, are constantly active with exhortations, warnings and instructions from the Word of God. A pious magistrate restrains the men of every rank in their duty, according to laws not merely civil but also divine; against the wicked he proceeds severely with the sword, the noose, prison, exile, disgrace and other means. The pious groan and sigh over all the abominations that are done among the people. And God himself, who is the head, daily exercising his own excommunication, exposes hypocrites, plainly destroys the wicked, and will solemnly declare them separated from the assembly of the faithful at the last judgment. So far God has graciously blessed this order and institution, so that, to speak with restraint, our Church has not been afflicted by any greater corruption in doctrine and morals than other churches which profess a greater austerity of discipline.

units.la: C. De cætero nil dissimulamus,Ecclesiæ Reformationem vitæ necessariam videri,ut ab ea perfectior doctrinæ reformatio,de qua merito nobis gratulamur , lucem & splendorem majorem fœneretur. Nam omnino
units.tr: C. Moreover, we do not hide that the reformation of life seems necessary to the Church, so that from it a more perfect reformation of doctrine, for which we rightly rejoice with them, may bring forth a greater light and splendour. For certainly...

units.la: Parva etiam subsunt priscæ vestigia fraudis. Acclamat enim nobis Filius Dei: Vigila & confirma reliqua, quæ mori volunt. Non enim inveni πα ἔργα πεπληρωμένα opera completa in conspectu Dei. Memor igitur esto , quomodo acceperis & audiveris (ex Dei verbo,& juxta illud ex piis doctoribus , qui Spiritu Dei pleni repurgare cœperunt) & serva, & resipisce, Apoc. III.2.3. Regenerationi certè disciplina inservit, ut voluntas & actiones fidelium legibus Divinis & humanis conformes reddantur. Huic jugo quamvis leni ægrè nos subjicimus. Si quid igitur in ipso disciplinæ tenore & exercitio , ob varietatem eorum , quibus eam exercere incumbit, desit , pastorum inprimis & vigilum est , illud omne & doctrinæ & vitæ puritate supplere. Non enim satis est, nos contra Papistas tradere & asserere salutare & præcipuum illud dogma de sola fide, aut,quod eodem redit, gratia & merito Christi justificante ; neque satis est,ejici idola ex Templis, nisi ex animis tetra illa idola avaritiæ,ambitionis,lasciviæ,&c. expellantur, & nisi contra dissolutos profanósque dogma sanctificationis & energiæ fructuumque fidei tueamur,ac solicitè populo Christiano inculcemus , quod à Paulo factum in omnibus Epistolis est. Neque satis est conciones haberi pias & doctas,nisi & vita inculpata sit. Mollissimè enim vitæ exemplo suadetur. Quàm multi Ecclesiastici & Politici disciplinæ præsides, de supplendis inter se mutuò defectibus parum soliciti mensuram peccatorum suorum implent , donec torrentis instar effusa Ecclesiam universam obruant & opprimant ! Quàm multi de ovicula vel tribuli, vel cive interrogati cogitant secum: An custos ego sum fratris mei? Imò Deus & fratri & civi custodem constituit,quem diligere quisque,sicut se ipsum, debet. Ut quisque donum accepit, ita alii etiam illud subministrare tenetur. Quantopere multorum mores ab ore suo diffi-
units.tr: Small traces of the ancient fraud also remain. For the Son of God cries out to us: Watch and strengthen the rest, which are ready to die. For I have not found your works completed [ἔργα πεπληρωμένα] before God. Remember therefore how you have received and heard (from the Word of God, and according to those pious teachers who, filled with the Spirit of God, have begun to purify it) and keep it, and repent, Rev. 3:2-3. Discipline certainly serves regeneration, so that the will and actions of the faithful are made to conform to divine and human laws. We submit to this yoke, though it is gentle, with some reluctance. If anything is lacking in the very course and exercise of discipline, because of the variety of those on whom it is incumbent to exercise it, it is the task of the pastors above all, and of the watchful, to make up for all of it by the purity of doctrine and of life. For it is not enough for us to teach against the Papists and to assert that saving and chief doctrine of faith alone, or, what amounts to the same, justification by the grace and merit of Christ alone. Nor is it enough to cast idols out of the temples, unless those foul idols of avarice, ambition, lust and so on are driven out of the minds of men, and unless we defend the doctrine of sanctification and the energy and fruits of faith against the dissolute and profane, and diligently inculcate into the Christian people what Paul did in all his Epistles. Nor is it enough to hold devout and learned sermons, unless life too is blameless, for people are most gently persuaded by the example of a life. How many officers of church and state, little concerned to make up for each other's defects, fill up the measure of their sins, until, poured out like a torrent, they overwhelm and crush the whole Church! How many, when asked about the sheep or the tribesman or the citizen, think to themselves: Am I my brother's keeper? Indeed God has appointed a keeper for both brother and citizen, whom each ought to love as himself. As each has received a gift, so he is bound to supply it to others. How greatly the morals of many are at odds with their mouths, who offer bread with one hand and a stumbling-stone with the other!

units.la: dent, qui altera manu panem, altera lapidem offensionis proponunt? Nimis imperfecta Reformatio nostra est, nisi disciplina etiam perficiatur & vigeat, atque doctrinæ vita respondeat. Servus enim intelligens voluntatem Domini, & non faciens juxta voluntatem ejus, multùm cœdetur, Luc. XII. 47. Si quis Spiritum Christi non habet, non est ejus, Rom. VIII.9. Vos non ita didicistis Christum. Siquidem eum audivistis, & in ipso edocti estis , sicut veritas in Jesu est, deponere vos, secundum priorem conversationem, veterem hominem corruptum, secundum concupiscentias deceptionis, Ephes. IV. 20. 21. 22. Non enim tantùm idololatræ & hæretici, sed etiam avari, scortatores, ebriosi, maledici, invidi Regno Coelorum excluduntur, 1. Cor. VI.9. 10. Gal. V. 19. Apoc. XXII.15.
units.tr: Our reformation is far too imperfect unless discipline too is brought to completion and flourishes, and unless life corresponds to doctrine. For the servant who knows the will of his lord and does not act according to it shall be beaten severely, Luke 12:47. If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his, Rom. 8:9. But you have not so learned Christ; if indeed you have heard him and have been taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus, to put off, according to your former conduct, the old man which is corrupted according to the lusts of deceit, Eph. 4:20-22. For not only idolaters and heretics, but also the covetous, fornicators, drunkards, slanderers and envious are shut out of the kingdom of heaven, 1 Cor. 6:9-10; Gal. 5:19; Rev. 22:15.

units.la: CI. Sed ut reliqua Reformatio omnis, ita hæc etiam prudentiam Christianam requirit. Ubi enim homines non plane deplorati merum imperium, affectuum regimen,& studium partium vident, difficulter cedunt. Sin & gloriæ Divinæ zelum, & causæ bonitatem, & æqualem in omnes charitatem in Ecclesiæ Ministris animadvertunt, ad omnia se paratos offerunt ; tunc inprimis Deo gloriam daturi, cùm non tantùm facienda dicimus, sed etiam facienda facimus, neque verbi tantùm , sed etiam bonorum operum facem illis præferimus. In omni enim sive doctrinæ,sive disciplinæ reformatione,etsi causa Dei agitur,singularis tamen prudentia requiritur. Non enim valet Ἑρμογένους prætextus ille : Causam Dei ago; mihi ergo,tanquam Dei ministro,omnes obedire tenentur. Si quis se refractarium mihi præbuerit, hunc ego ulciscar, & Christiano nomine indignum judicabo. Thrasonica hæc sunt,non Ministri Christi genium sapiunt. Non enim judicium præcipitandum vel eò devenendum est,nisi plures prudentiæ & mansuetudinis actus præcesserint. Commemorabilis hic est primorum Ecclesiæ rectorum dexteritas & lenitas,qua illi non homines tantùm,sed etiam feras,ut sic dicam,cicurarunt & vicerunt. Palpandæ enim hæ fere lenius sunt,& ad illarum insultum paulisper cedendum,donec patientia nostra, intrepidáque pectoris constantia superatæ cicures reddantur. Dedit enim & Petrus aliquid cùm dixit: Sed nunc scio,quia ignorantes fecistis, sicut & reliqui principes vestri, Actor. III. 17. Dedit & Paulus,cùm Corinthios lacte,non solido cibo aluit, 1. Cor. III.2. Cesserunt omnes Apostoli sævitiæ,dum non pervicaciter Senatui obstrepuerunt,vibicibus etiam lividi,sed à prædicatione non cessarunt, Actor. V. 40. 41. Omnia ergo omnibus fieri oportet, ut omnes lucremur,& ne Christus unâ nobiscum explodatur; 1. Cor. IX. 22. Optata inprimis Mosis & Aharonis,hoc est,utriusque ordinis,concordia populi quoque consensum allicit & conservat. Quomodo etiam Reformationem doctrinæ superiore seculo institutam eandem ob causam tantos omnium civium & subditorum applausus excepit,ut adversariorum paucorum murmura nihil profecerint. Verbi Dei Ministri Reformationem petierunt & docuerunt , Magistratus manens intra officii sui limites,& nihil præter officium faciens, decrevit, & populus obedivit. Quibus igitur arûbus tantum opus perfectum dari potuit: iisdem conservari, & ad posteros propagari, & simul necessarius disciplinæ usus, qui hactenus Reformationi deest, perfici & ipse potest atque debet.
units.tr: CI. But, as with all reformation, this too requires Christian prudence. For where men, not utterly hopeless, see mere domination, the governing of passions and zeal for party, they yield with difficulty. But if they perceive in the ministers of the Church zeal for the glory of God, goodness of cause and equal love toward all, they offer themselves ready for everything. Then, above all, they will give glory to God, when we not only say what is to be done but also do what is to be done, and set before them the torch not only of the word but also of good works. For in any reformation, whether of doctrine or of discipline, although the cause of God is being pursued, singular prudence is nevertheless required. The pretext of Hermogenes does not hold: "I am pursuing the cause of God; therefore everyone is bound to obey me as a minister of God. If anyone shows himself refractory to me, I will take revenge on him and judge him unworthy of the Christian name." These are the boasts of Thrasonides, and they do not savour of the spirit of a minister of Christ. For judgment must not be rushed or reached unless many acts of prudence and gentleness have gone before. Memorable here is the dexterity and mildness of the first rulers of the Church, by which they tamed and conquered not only men but, so to speak, wild beasts. For these are generally soothed more gently, and one must yield for a little while to their assault, until, overcome by our patience and the unshaken constancy of our heart, they become tame. Peter too gave something when he said: But now I know that you did it in ignorance, as did also your rulers, Acts 3:17. Paul too gave something when he fed the Corinthians with milk, not solid food, 1 Cor. 3:2. All the Apostles yielded to cruelty, since they did not shout stubbornly against the Senate, even though they were black and blue with stripes, yet they did not cease from preaching, Acts 5:40-41. So it is necessary to become all things to all men, so that we may gain all, and that Christ may not be driven out along with us, 1 Cor. 9:22. The longed-for concord above all of Moses and Aaron, that is, of both orders, also wins and keeps the consent of the people. In the same way, the reformation of doctrine instituted in the last century was received with such great applause from all citizens and subjects, for this same reason, that the murmurs of a few adversaries achieved nothing. The ministers of the Word of God sought and taught the reformation; the magistrate, remaining within the limits of his office and doing nothing beyond his office, decreed it, and the people obeyed. Therefore, by the same means by which so great a work could be brought to completion, it can be preserved and handed down to posterity; and at the same time the necessary use of discipline, which has so far been lacking in the Reformation, can and must itself be brought to completion.

units.la: CII. Supersunt ex rebus Ecclesiæ Bona ejusdem temporalia; quibus propter sumptus varios in Ministros, pauperes, ædificia erogandos carere non potest. In V. T. lex Divina non tantùm Levitis, sed etiam orphanis, viduis, peregrinis, reliquisque pauperibus ita prospexit, ut agrorum extrema spicilegia, relicti in messe manipuli, racemationes, residua in arboribus poma, viscerationes ac largitiones in festis & anniversariis panegyribus, decimæ tricericæ, fructus insativi, & si quæ præterea ejusmodi, ipsorum usibus cederent. Gazophylacium, quod ab oblationibus קרבן corban vocabant, 2. Reg. XII. 10. Marc. XII. 43. Luc. XXI. 1. ad sacra tecta Templi & legalis cultus usum potissimum institutum erat. Nulla tamen religio aliquid inde pauperibus erogare vetabat. In N. T. Christus nec marsupium, nec pecunias, à piis & locupletibus matronis subministratas aspernatus est, Luc. VIII. 3. quibus non tantùm familiares suos, sed pauperes etiam sustentare consuevit, Joh. XIII. 29. Post Christi in Cœlos ascensionem (ne quid de agapis dicam) prima Christianorum Ecclesia, Hierosolymis collecta, partim charitatis testandæ causa, partim ut hostium injuriis minùs opportuna, & ad fugam capessendam expeditior esset, facultates suas in commune ærarium congessit, ditioribus tenuiorum egestatem, etiam agrorum suorum dispendio subleuantibus, Actor. IV. 34. Non erat hæc bonorum communio talis, qualem Plato instituit, & olim Esseni usurparunt, & fanatici Anabaptistæ inculcant. Non enim à singulis, aut ubique locorum factitatum id est, quod de Hierosolymitanis quibusdam Lucas commemorat. Alioquin nihil attinebat unum Josen ob venditum agrum peculiari elogio ornare, ibid. v. 36. si nemini res suas sibi habere licuisset, quod disertè S. Petrus negat, ibid. V. 4.
