Paulus etiam eleemosynarum & collectarum rationem præscribens, non obscurè docet, quemque facultatum suarum Dominum esse, neque extorquendum cuiquam esse, quod omnes αὐθαιρέτοι voluntarii impertiri debent, 1. Cor. XVI. 1. 2. 2. Cor. VIII. 12. Neque magis communionem bonorum apud Antiochenos, Galatas, Ephesios, Philippenses, Thessalonicenses aliósque quàm apud Corinthios receptam fuisse, ex Actor. XI. 27. &c. Gal. VI. 6. Ephes. IV. 28. Philipp. IV. 18. 1. Thessal. IV. 9. 10. Hebr. X. 34. XIII. 2. 5. liquet. Philemon verò non tantùm opes, sed etiam mancipia possedit, quæ ut in commune conferret, ei ab Apostolo adeò injunctum non est, ut pollicitus etiam fuerit, se ei depensurum, quod ab Onesimo ei interversum fuit, Philem. v. 19. Post Apostolorum tempora singulas Ecclesias æraria sua habuisse, in quæ quisque stipem conjiceret, Justinus & Tertullianus testantur. Quo tempore Ecclesia agros & latifundia possidere cœperit, incertum est. Constat tamen ante Constantinum M. possedisse. Profusæ autem largitiones, quibus immane quantum Ecclesia locupletata intumuit, Constantini demum seculo invaluerunt. Ille enim & à decessoribus suis erepta Ecclesiis restituit, & vectigalium, tributorum, publicique frumenti partem illis admensus est. Tum eorum, qui martyrio coronati sunt, nullis vel incertis hæredibus relictis, bona Ecclesiæ soli idem addixit: eidémque luculentissima, ex conflatis aureis & argenteis idolorum statuis, donaria obtulit, quæ à Juliano deinde adempta, Valentinianus & Gratianus restituerunt. Mox etiam Basilio Epist. 140. teste, privati quandoque facultates suas Ecclesiæ donarunt, quod sub Ethnicis Imperatoribus prohibitum Constantinus M. lege permisit. Sed glisecente superstitione, cujus œstro percitum vulgus, nullum tam atrox scelus, vel turpe flagitium putavit, quin ejusmodi donariis expiari posset; nullis deinceps aggeribus, mole nulla reprimi potuit exundantium largitionum impetus, quo velut decumano fluctu sic Ecclesia obruta & pessumdata fuit, ut à nonnullis patrimoniorum scopulus appellata fuerit, atque spirituale ejus decus in profanæ Monarchiæ splendorem & luxum degeneraverit, & verissimè dictum fuerit: Religionem divitias peperisse, & filiam devorasse matrem. Hieronymus quoque, melioribus adhuc Ecclesiæ temporibus, Epist. ad Nepot. questus est, accrescentibus Ecclesiæ opibus, veras illas opes, pietatem, fidem, charitatem diminui.
units.tr: CII. The Church also has its own temporal goods, and it cannot do without them, since it must meet many costs for its ministers, the poor, and its buildings. Under the Old Testament, the Divine law made provision not only for the Levites but also for orphans, widows, strangers, and the other poor. The gleanings at the edges of the fields, the sheaves left behind at harvest, the grapes left on the vines, the fruit left on the trees, the largesses and gifts at the feasts and annual assemblies, the triennial tithe, the produce of the seventh year, and whatever else of this kind was to go to their use. The offering box, which they called corban [קרבן] from the offerings (2 Kings 12:10; Mark 12:43; Luke 21:1), was set up chiefly for the holy buildings of the Temple and the upkeep of the legal worship. Yet no religion forbade that something from it be given to the poor. In the New Testament, Christ did not reject the purse or the money supplied by pious and wealthy women (Luke 8:3), by which he was accustomed to support not only his own companions but also the poor (John 13:29). After Christ's ascension into heaven, to say nothing of the love feasts, the first Church of the Christians at Jerusalem gathered its resources into a common chest, partly to bear witness to its charity, and partly so that it would be less exposed to the injuries of enemies and more ready to flee. The richer members relieved the want of the poorer, even at the cost of their own fields (Acts 4:34). This communion of goods was not of the kind that Plato set up, that the Essenes once practised, and that the fanatical Anabaptists urge. It was not something done by individuals, or everywhere in the same way, but was what Luke records of certain Jerusalem believers. Otherwise there would have been no point in singling out Joses for a special commendation for selling his field (ibid. v. 36), if no one had been permitted to keep his own possessions, which St Peter expressly denies (ibid. v. 4). Paul, in prescribing the manner of alms and collections, also teaches clearly that each person is lord of his own resources, and that nothing is to be extorted from anyone, since all are to give willingly (1 Cor. 16:1, 2; 2 Cor. 8:12). It is also plain from Acts 11:27 etc., Gal. 6:6, Eph. 4:28, Phil. 4:18, 1 Thess. 4:9, 10, Heb. 10:34, and 13:2, 5 that the communion of goods was not received among the Antiochenes, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Thessalonians, and others any more than among the Corinthians. Philemon possessed not only wealth but also slaves, and the Apostle did not enjoin him to bring these into a common fund. Indeed, he promised to repay what Onesimus had taken from him (Philem. v. 19). Justin and Tertullian testify that after the time of the Apostles, each Church had its own chest into which each person put a contribution. It is uncertain when the Church began to possess fields and great estates, but it is certain that it possessed them before Constantine the Great. Lavish gifts, by which the Church swelled immensely in wealth, came to the fore chiefly in the age of Constantine. He restored to the Churches what had been seized from them by his predecessors, and assigned to them a share of the taxes, tributes, and public grain. Then, when those who had been crowned with martyrdom left no heirs, or only uncertain ones, he assigned their goods to the Church alone. He also offered it very splendid gifts made from the gold and silver of idol statues. Julian later took these away, and Valentinian and Gratian restored them. Soon afterwards, as Basil testifies (Epist. 140), private persons sometimes gave their own goods to the Church, which Constantine the Great permitted by law, though it had been forbidden under the heathen emperors. But as superstition spread, the common people, stirred by its goad, thought that no atrocious crime or shameful disgrace could not be expiated by such gifts. Thereafter no dams, no mass of material could hold back the rush of overflowing gifts. Like a tidal wave, the Church was so overwhelmed and ruined by them that some called it the rock of patrimonies. Its spiritual honour degenerated into the splendour and luxury of a worldly monarchy, and it was said with great truth: Religion brought forth riches, and the daughter devoured the mother. Jerome too, even in the better times of the Church, complained in his letter to Nepotian (Epist. ad Nepot.) that as the resources of the Church increased, those true riches, piety, faith, and charity, were diminished.

units.la: CIII. Bonorum Ecclesiæ pius usus esse debet. Damnantur enim ab Apostolo, qui ἀσπίλοι ἐν ἀγάπαις, ςυνδειπνοῦντες, ἀφόβως ἑαυτοὺς ποιμαίνοντες, maculæ in agapis, convivantur cum fidelibus, & sine metu se ipsos pascunt, Jud. v. 12. Nam qui bona Ecclesiæ ex collationibus piorum hominum, vel etiam à Regibus ei assignata occupant, abliguriunt, & in iis ἀπολυφόμενοι luxuriant, 2. Petr. II. 13. nec faciunt opus ministerii, sed potiùs se ad colendam terram, hoc est, ad politica negotia judicum, principum, Zach. XIII. 5. convertunt, imò principes & Domini Ecclesiæ esse volunt, quid illi aliud quàm maculæ, σπίλοι ἢ μῶμοι maculæ & vitia, 2. Pet. II. 13. Christianæ fidei sunt? Christus certè pecunias à divitibus suppeditatas ad sui, Apostolorum & pauperum sustentationem impendit, Joh. XIII. 29. Idem fecisse Apostolos, ex Actor. XI. 29. 1. Cor. XVI. 1. 2. 2. Cor. VIII. IX. Gal. VI. 6. Phil. IV. 15. liquet. Clarè S. Paulus: Si quis fidelis, mas aut fœmina habet viduas, sustentet eas, & ne gravetur Ecclesia, ut verè viduis sufficiat, 1. Tim. V. 16. Ut Ecclesia verè viduis, hoc est, omnium ope destitutis, liberaliùs succurrere posset, præcipit, ut quæ vidua fideles necessarios habet, ab iis potiùs, quàm ab Ecclesia sublevetur. Tertullianus Apolog. cap. 39. Hæc, inquit, quasi deposita pietatis sunt. Inde non epulis, nec potaculis, nec gratiis voratrinis dispensantur: sed egenis alendis humandisque & pueris, & pupillis, re ac parentibus destitutis, ætatéque domitis senibus, item naufragis, & si qui in metallis, & si qui insulis, vel in custodiis, duntaxat ex causa Dei sectæ, alumni confessionis suæ sunt. Ambrosius de Offic. lib. II. 28. Aurum, inquit, Ecclesia habet, non ut servet, sed ut eroget, & subveniat in necessitatibus. Morem veteris Ecclesiæ ex Gregorii M. instituto introductum his verbis Gratianus C. 12. q. 2. cap. Mos est, breviter describit: Mos est, inquit ille, Apostolicæ sedis Episcopo præcepta tradere, ut de omni stipendio, dio, quod accedit, quatuor fiant portiones, una Episcopo & familiæ ejus propter hospitalitatem atque susceptionem: altera Clero, tertia pauperibus, quarta Ecclesiis. De stipendiis Ministrorum Ecclesiæ supra diximus. Clerici appellati olim sunt, qui se & operam suam Ecclesiæ addixerunt & consecrarunt. Ecclesiæ alumni & beneficiarii, seu, uti Cyprianus eos appellat, sportulantes fratres, quos bonæ spei & indolis compertos illa delegit, & ad Sacrum Ministerium publicis sumptibus præparavit. Tales deligendi, sine prægnante causa non sunt, nisi qui parentum sumptibus propriis tantum tyrocinium posuerunt, ut de eorum indole atque ingenio, & an sumptus, qui in eos fiunt, bene collocentur, judicari queat: Stupidi enim & bardi, ceu canis in præsepi, sunt, & oleum operámque perdunt. Ab his distincti pauperes, proprie eleemosynas accipiunt; cùm nec Ministrorum Ecclesiæ & alumnorum stipendia respectu non dantium, sed accipientium, eleemosynæ sint, sed ceu merces debita pro labore dentur, & Ecclesiæ ministerio hac ratione auctorentur. De eleemosynis talibus Loc. XIV. § 1. V. 37-42. plura etiam diximus. Ultima bonorum portio structuræ & conservationi bonorum Ecclesiæ inservit. Templa equidem Apostolica & subsequens Ecclesia diu nulla habuit, sed in ædibus privatis, cryptis, locis subterraneis & cœmeteriis convenit. Unde Imperatores Gentiles Christianos persecuturi ante omnia à cœmeteriis eos arcere consueverunt, ne conveniendi facultas iis esset. Seculo tertio concessis Ecclesiæ halcyoniis Templa & Oratoria condi atque amplificari cœperunt, quæ mox Diocletianus funditus everti & solo æquari jussit, eadem sævitia utente Galerio Maximino, donec morbo fœtente & desperato correptus edicto restaurationem Templorum Christianis iterum permisit. Demum seculo quarto Constantinus M. ubivis locorum vel gentium Templa in usum suum convertit, vel nova etiam ex fundamentis magnificentissimè extrui curavit. Ejusmodi ædibus sacris, vel extruendis vel conservandis Ecclesiæ ærarium inservit, quo deficiente auditores collatis de suo sumptibus, vel ex Reipublicæ ærario efficere illud tenentur: Ac ne vel Ecclesia, vel Respublica ædificiis talibus exhauriatur, & viva Christi Templa sustentandi impos reddatur, vel contra Christianam religionem, simplicitatem & humilitatem aliquid committatur, modus hic servandus est, ne immodico ornatu & luxu non necessarii sumptus potius prodigantur, quàm in honorem Dei impendantur. Scitè enim Hieronymus Epist. ad Demetr. Alii, inquit, ædificent Ecclesias, vestiant parietes marmorum crustis, columnarum moles advehant, earumque capita deaurent, pretiosum ornatum non sententia, ebore argentóque valvas, & gemmis aurata altaria distinguant. Non reprehendo, non abnuo. Unusquisque in suo sensu abundet: melius que est hoc facere, quàm repositis opibus incubare. Sed tibi aliud propositum est, Christum vestire in pauperibus, visitare in languentibus, pascere in esurientibus, suscipere in his, qui tecto indigent, & maximè in domesticis fidei. Ac sapientius etiam Confessio Helvetica cap. 22. Sicut, inquit, credimus, Deum non habitare in Templis manufactis,
units.tr: CIII. The good things of the Church ought to be put to a holy use. The Apostle condemns those who are spots in your feasts of charity, feasting with you, without fear feeding themselves (ἀσπίλοι ἐν ἀγάπαις, συνδειπνοῦντες, ἀφόβως ἑαυτοὺς ποιμαίνοντες) (Jude v. 12). For those who seize the goods of the Church, which were given by the gifts of pious people or even assigned to it by kings, waste them and, in doing so, live in luxury (ἀπολυφόμενοι) (2 Pet. 2:13). They do not do the work of the ministry, but rather turn themselves to tilling the ground, that is, to the political affairs of judges and princes (Zech. 13:5). Indeed, they want to be princes and lords of the Church. What else are they but spots and blemishes (σπίλοι ἢ μῶμοι), spots and vices (2 Pet. 2:13), to the Christian faith? Christ certainly used the money supplied by the rich to sustain himself, the Apostles, and the poor (John 13:29). That the Apostles did the same is plain from Acts 11:29; 1 Cor. 16:1, 2; 2 Cor. 8, 9; Gal. 6:6; Phil. 4:15. St Paul speaks clearly: If any faithful man or woman has widows, let them relieve them, and let not the Church be burdened, so that it may truly suffice for the widows (1 Tim. 5:16). So that the Church might be more generous to those who are truly widows, that is, those destitute of all help, he commands that a widow who has believing relatives should be supported by them rather than by the Church. Tertullian, in his Apology (Apolog. cap. 39), says: These, as it were, are the deposits of piety. They are not spent on feasts, drinking parties, or the bellies of hangers-on, but on feeding and burying the poor, on boys and orphans, on those destitute of means and parents, on old people confined to the house, likewise on shipwrecked persons, and on those who are in the mines, or on islands, or in prisons, only for the cause of God's sect, are the nurslings of their confession. Ambrose (de Offic. lib. II. 28) says: The Church holds gold, not to keep it, but to give it out and help in necessities. Gratian briefly describes the custom of the ancient Church, introduced by the decree of Gregory the Great, in these words (C. 12. q. 2. cap. Mos est): It is the custom, he says, for the Bishop of the Apostolic See to hand down the rule that, from every stipend that comes in, four portions are to be made: one for the Bishop and his household, because of hospitality and reception; a second for the clergy; a third for the poor; and a fourth for the Churches. We have spoken above about the stipends of the ministers of the Church. Those who devoted themselves and their work to the Church were formerly called clerics. Those chosen by the Church, whom it found to be of good hope and disposition, and whom it prepared for the sacred ministry at public expense, were its nurslings and beneficiaries, or, as Cyprian calls them, fellow brothers receiving the dole. Such persons should not be chosen without a strong reason, unless they have undergone a period of apprenticeship at their parents' own expense, so that their character and ability, and whether the expense laid out on them is well spent, can be judged. For stupid and dull persons are like a dog in a manger: they waste oil and labour. Distinct from these are the poor, who receive alms in the proper sense. The stipends of the Church's ministers and nurslings are not alms with respect to the givers, but are given as a debt owed for labour, and by this arrangement the Church is bound to the ministry. We have also said more about such alms in Loc. XIV. § 1. V. 37-42. The last part of the goods of the Church is devoted to building and maintaining its property. The Apostolic Church and the Church that followed for a long time had no temples of its own, but met in private houses, crypts, underground places, and cemeteries. Hence the heathen emperors, when about to persecute the Christians, usually first kept them from the cemeteries, so that they would have no opportunity to meet. In the third century, when the Church was granted a time of calm, temples and oratories began to be built and enlarged. Soon Diocletian ordered them utterly overthrown and levelled with the ground, and Galerius Maximinus used the same cruelty, until, struck down by a foul and hopeless disease, he granted by edict that the Christians might restore the temples. Finally, in the fourth century, Constantine the Great turned temples to his own use wherever he found them, or took care to have new ones built from the foundations with the greatest magnificence. The treasury of the Church serves to build or maintain such sacred buildings. When the Church's treasury is insufficient, the hearers are bound to supply the cost from their own contributions, or from the public treasury. And so that neither the Church nor the commonwealth is exhausted by such buildings, and the living temples of Christ are not deprived of their means of support, and so that nothing is done contrary to Christian religion, simplicity, and humility, a limit must be observed. Otherwise, necessary expenses are squandered on immoderate ornament and luxury, rather than being spent for the honour of God. Jerome wisely says (Epist. ad Demetr.): Let others build churches, clothe their walls with marble facings, bring in heaps of columns, gild their capitals, decorate their doors with ivory and silver and their altars with gold and jewels. I do not blame it, I do not refuse it. Let each abound in his own sense. It is better to do this than to hoard wealth. But you have another purpose: to clothe Christ in the poor, to visit him in the sick, to feed him in the hungry, to receive him in those who lack shelter, and above all in the members of the household of faith. The Helvetic Confession also speaks more wisely (ch. 22): As we believe that God does not dwell in temples made with hands,

units.la: ita propter verbum Dei & usus sacros scimus, loca Deo cultuique ejus dedicata, non esse profana, sed sacra, & qui in his versantur, reverenter & modestè conversari debere, utpote qui sunt in loco sacro, coram Dei conspectu, & sanctorum Angelorum ejus. Longè itaque à Templis & Oratoriis Christianorum repellendus est omnis vestium luxus, omnis superbia, & omnia, quæ humilitatem, disciplinam & modestiam Christianam dedecent. Ac verus Templorum ornatus non constat ebore, auro & gemmis, sed frugalitate, pietate, virtutibusque eorum, qui in Templo versantur.
units.tr: So too, on account of the Word of God and its holy uses, we know that places dedicated to God and to his worship are not profane but sacred, and that those who spend time in them ought to conduct themselves reverently and modestly, as people who are in a holy place, in the sight of God and of his holy Angels. Far therefore from the temples and oratories of Christians must every extravagance of dress be banished, every pride, and everything that does not befit Christian humility, discipline and modesty. The true adornment of temples consists not in ivory, gold and gems, but in the thrift, piety and virtues of those who worship in them.

units.la: CIV. Bonorum Ecclesiæ administratio, conservatio, & proprium in usum erogatio religiosa esse debet. Profanatio enim illorum, & peregrinos in usus translatio vægrande peccatum & sacrilegium est, cui Deus gravem poenam minatur. Numquid rapere debet homo, quæ sunt Dei? Et vos rapitis mea. Et dixistis: In quo rapimus tua? In decimis & oblationibus. Maledicti estis maledictione, & vos mea rapitis, gens tota, &c. Mal.III.8. Eandem in rem Synodorum & Conciliorum decreta plurima extant. Quibus expensis Christiani etiam Principes & Magistratus æquè Ecclesiæ, quæ Ecclesiæ sunt, dare & relinquere tenentur, atque ipsi Cæsari, quæ Cæsaris sunt, dari & relinqui optant. Nullam verò laudem humanam, vel benedictionem Divinam illi harpagones reportant, qui non tantum sibi optima grana vindicantes, Ecclesiæ paleas & scorias offerunt, sed etiam superfluas Ecclesiæ opes caussati, eas circumcidunt, calentibus digitis attrectant, & non tam Reipublicæ, quàm suo reti per artificiosas ambages, & simoniacas artes, sacrificant; voluntate, ultima & sacro sancta eorum, qui Ecclesiæ donarunt, neque alia lege vel intentione saltem generali donarunt, imò devoverunt, quàm ut cultui Dei & pauperibus inserviant, susque déque habita. Quibus etiam superfluum id omne videtur, quod ipsi desiderant, quasi non propter incerta rerum, futuris etiam necessitatibus prospicere Ecclesia haberet, quæ semel spoliata postliminii jure rarò, uti inprimis mores nunc & tempora sunt, fruitur. Sicut autem Ecclesiæ opes à Magistratu Politico in alios quàm sacros & pios usus converti, fas non est: ita nec Ecclesiæ Ministros præfractè & contumaciter repugnare Principibus, eos in necessitatis extremo casu, vel ob causam non levem repetentibus, licet. Ac minimè vulgari prudentia hic opus est, ut dispiciamus, quando vel Laurentii, thesauros Decio: Ambrosii Basilicam Valentiniano tradere recusantium; vel Augustini tabulas donatorum Ecclesiæ agrorum, repositenti donatori restituentis exempla imitanda sint. Inprimis terrenis opibus pax Ecclesiæ redimi potest & debet: Sicut enim in præclaro fidei depositio laudabilis constantia est: ita in fluxis hujusmodi thesauris mordicus retinendis pervicacia probro non caret.
units.tr: CIV. The administration, preservation and expenditure of the goods of the Church ought to be religious. For to profane them and transfer them to other uses is a very great sin and sacrilege, which God threatens with severe punishment. Will a man rob God? Yet you rob me. But you say, "How have we robbed you?" In tithes and offerings. You are cursed with a curse, for you rob me, the whole nation, etc. (Mal. 3:8). Many decrees of synods and councils exist to the same effect. With these expenses in view, Christian princes and magistrates are bound to give and leave to the Churches what belongs to the Churches, just as they wish what belongs to Caesar to be given and left to Caesar. But those greedy grabbers win no human praise or divine blessing, who not only claim the best grain for themselves and offer the Church chaff and dross, but also, pleading that the Church's wealth is superfluous, cut it down, handle it with grasping fingers, and sacrifice it less to the commonwealth than to their own net, through artful circumlocutions and simoniacal arts. They do this against the final and most sacred will of those who gave to the Church, who gave on no other law or intention, or at least no general intention, than that it should serve the worship of God and the poor; and they hold that will cheap. To them all that they themselves desire seems superfluous, as if the Church ought not to provide for future needs, given the uncertainty of things; yet the Church, once plundered, rarely enjoys the right of postliminy, as the present manners and times in particular show. But just as it is not lawful for the political magistrate to turn the Church's wealth to uses other than sacred and pious ones, so the ministers of the Church may not obstinately and stubbornly resist princes who demand it back in the extreme case of necessity or for no slight cause. Here no ordinary prudence is needed, so that we may discern when the examples of Laurence, who refused to hand over the treasures to Decius, of Ambrose, who refused to surrender the basilica to Valentinian, or of Augustine, who gave back the title-deeds of the Church's fields to the donor who asked for them, are to be imitated. Above all, the peace of the Church can and should be purchased with earthly wealth. For just as steadfast constancy is praiseworthy in the keeping of the glorious deposit of faith, so obstinacy in clinging tenaciously to such fleeting treasures is not free from reproach.

units.la: CV. Non gestit equidem heic animus in prolixiorem de bonis Ecclesiasticis disputationem ingredi. Certus tantum regulis eorum possessionem, usum, administrationem, & abusus vindicationem adstringere libet. Ante omnia quandiu coetus idem manet, tandiu bona collata illius coetus esse propria judicantur, neque ei piè utenti fine gravi injuria eripi possunt.
units.tr: CV. My mind is not eager here to enter into a lengthier discussion of ecclesiastical goods. I am content only to set out the rules that bind their possession, use, administration and the vindication of abuses. Before all else: as long as the same congregation remains, the goods conferred on it are judged to be its own, and they cannot be taken from it while it uses them piously without grave injury.

units.la: Et administratio religiosa. sunt. Ejusdem verò Ecclesiæ,cui bona illa collata sunt,est,deligere, qui maxima fide,cura & studio illa administrant. Tales olim Ecclesiæ Diaconi,deinceps alii bonorum Ecclesiæ curatores & eleemosynarii fuerunt, de quibus supra. Concilii Chalcedonensis canone 26. cautum est, ut Episcopi in idoneos dispensatores rerum istarum administratione rejecta,ipsi ab ea abstinerent, non quòd omnem ejus rei curam deponere debeant. Non tantùm enim illi Diaconis & Oeconomis mandare poterant, quinam ærarii Ecclesiastici alumnorum albo inscribendi sint,sed etiam solicitè iis observandum fuit, qua fide œconomi in munere suo versarentur. Sed hanc quasi servitutem pertæsi Episcopi,liberam facultatum Ecclesiasticarum administrationem , amotis laicis illis administratoribus , à Paschali II. annua pensitatione Sacerdotis imposita, redemerunt, contemptis Chrysostomi reprehensionibus , qui Episcopos hoc pacto in profanos villicos, publicanos,quæstores & caupones converti Homil. 86. in Matth. queritur. Si quando in coetu schisma oboritur, bona manere eorum,qui in eadem fide , veritate & sententia perstant, intelliguntur. De quo judicium Magistratui permittendum videtur , cùm absque eo tuta possessio esse vix posslit. Quando verò in Ecclesia exorta est tyrannis, & Episcopi,& cum iis Presbyteri terrarum Domini facti sunt,volentibus,& juxta prædictionem , quòd Rex ille novus multiplicare honorem, facere, potestatem habere in multos,& terram pro pretio distribuere debeat,Dan. XI. 39. bona sua erogantibus illis, qui diu cum ipsis congregati fuerunt, tum fideles illi,qui sic bona sua erogarunt,vindicandi sibi ea bona jus non habent ; sed altioris potestatis est,ea de re sic statuere,ut,quantum fieri potest,erogantium voluntati decretoriæ satisfiat: ita Christiani facti fideles ex Judæis sibi bona Levitarum , decimas & alias oblationes, quæ secundum legem dabantur, non vindicarunt, sed possidentibus reliquerunt. Denique promisit Deus Ecclesiæ,fore,ut Tyri mercimonium (meretricium) & quæstus fiat Jehovæ, & non ponantur ampliùs in ejus thesauris, neque ab ea possideatur, sed ut יהוה לפני לישבים sedentibus coram Jehova cedat סחרה mercimonium ejus , ut comedant ad satietatem & in vestimentum durabile , Esaj. XXIII. 18. Potest igitur Ecclesia bonis, quibus Antichristus, cujus emblema Tyrum Spiritus S. fecit,& satellites ejus luxuriarunt,uti. Sed non temerè tamen id occupandum,sed expectandum fuit & est, donec Deus ipse id fecerit ; interim pacificè & sine alieni appetitione vivendum. Quomodo etiam Israelitæ noverant,bona Ægyptiorum sua fore,neque tamen ea rapuerunt,verùm operari malentes siverunt Deum efficere , ut justo titulo ipsorum fierent. Tum enim justo titulo Ecclesia bona acquirit,cùm ea vel derelinquuntur, atque sic Ecclesiæ veræ in locum falsæ succedenti ceduntur; vel possidentes ea veram fidem amplectuntur,& usibus verae Ecclesiæ dedicant. Nam idem qui principaliter Ecclesiam per organa certa reformat,Deus,etiam Ecclesiæ bona ad eadem transferre,atque tunc Ecclesia iisdem legitimè utens etiam voluntatem & intentionem causæ primæ,& saltem ge-
units.tr: And the religious administration. It belongs, moreover, to that same Church to which those goods were given, to choose men who administer them with the greatest faith, care and diligence. Formerly the deacons of the Church, and afterwards other stewards and almoners of the Church's goods, were such men, as noted above. Canon 26 of the Council of Chalcedon provides that bishops should withdraw from the administration of these things and hand it over to suitable stewards, not that they should give up all care of the matter. For the bishops could not only assign to the deacons and stewards the task of deciding who should be enrolled on the list of the Church's dependants, but they also had to watch carefully over how faithfully the stewards carried out their office. Yet the bishops, weary of this quasi-servitude, bought back the free administration of Church property from Paschal II, who had imposed an annual payment on the priest, and removed those lay administrators, disregarding the rebukes of Chrysostom, who complains in Homily 86 on Matthew that bishops were in this way turned into worldly stewards, tax collectors, agents and innkeepers. If a schism arises in a congregation, its goods are understood to remain with those who persist in the same faith, truth and opinion. On this question the judgment seems to be left to the magistrate, since without it secure possession can hardly exist. But when a tyranny has arisen in the Church, and the bishops, together with the presbyters, have become lords of the land, and those who have long been gathered with them, the faithful who thus gave away their goods have no right to reclaim those goods for themselves, as the prophecy says that this new king shall multiply honour, make [them] have power over many, and distribute the land for a price (Dan. XI. 39). It belongs to a higher authority to decide such a matter in a way that, as far as possible, satisfies the decisive will of those who gave. So Christians from among the Jews, once converted, did not claim for themselves the goods of the Levites, the tithes and other offerings which were given according to the law, but left them to those who held them. Finally, God promised the Church that the merchandise (or harlotry) of Tyre would become a gain to Jehovah, and that it would no longer be laid up in her treasuries or possessed by her; rather, that her merchandise [סחרה] would go to those who sit before Jehovah [לפני יהוה לישבים], that they may eat to the full and have durable clothing (Isa. XXIII. 18). The Church may therefore use the goods with which Antichrist, whose emblem the Holy Spirit made Tyre, and his satellites lived in luxury. Yet this is not to be seized rashly; it had to be, and still has to be, awaited until God himself does it, and in the meantime we must live peacefully and without coveting what belongs to another. Thus too the Israelites knew that the goods of the Egyptians would be theirs, yet they did not plunder them, but preferred to work and let God bring it about that they became theirs by a just title. For the Church then acquires goods by a just title when they are either abandoned, and so handed over to a true Church succeeding a false one; or when their possessors embrace the true faith and dedicate them to the uses of the true Church. For God himself, who principally reforms the Church through certain instruments, also transfers the Church's goods to the same, and then the Church, using them lawfully, is held to attain by God's special correction of the will and intention of the first cause, and at least of the general, and also of the secondary, cause, the goods which the priests and monks, like robbers of those goods, misused. Yet every faithful magistrate is bound to restore the sacred revenues to the true Churches to which they are due, and to exact punishment from the impious robbers.

units.la: neralem etiam secundæ correcta à Deo ipso ejusdem speciali, qua sacrificuli & Monachi, ceu prædones bonorum illorum , abusi sunt, assequi censentur. Tenetur verò Magistratus fidelis quisque reditus sacros veris Ecclesiis, quibus debentur,restituere,& de impiis prædonibus pœnam sumere. Saltem majori jure & æquitate vera Ecclesia in possessionem eorum bonorum mitti poterunt,quàm olim peregrini, Romani & Itali,locustæ, vulturum & milvorum instar advolantes eadem involarunt,invaserunt, & Ecclesiam non ædificantes, sed corrumpentes,consumpserunt.
units.tr: ...and so the faithful Church is reckoned to obtain that which the priests and monks, who abused those goods as robbers, could not. The faithful magistrate is bound to restore the sacred revenues to the true Churches to which they are owed, and to exact punishment from impious robbers. At the very least, the true Church may be put in possession of those goods by a greater right and equity than the Romans and Italians of old, who swooped down like locusts, or like vultures and kites, and seized, invaded and consumed them, building not the Church but ruining it.

units.la: CVI. Quia ἀδελφότης fraternitas & communio Sanctorum in totum mundum se jam, quando Ecclesia Catholica est, extendit, & qui in diversis locis agunt,æquè alii aliorum membra sunt, Ecclesiæ aliæ aliis, quantum ejus fieri potest,prælucere,communicare,subvenire,opitulari tenentur.
units.tr: CVI. Because the brotherhood (ἀδελφότης) and communion of the saints now extends throughout the whole world, since the Catholic Church is one, and those who act in different places are equally members of one another, the Churches are bound to shine upon one another, as far as this can be done, to communicate with one another, to assist and to help one another.

units.la: Licèt igitur nec unus fidelis ab alio,nec una Ecclesia ab alia sic dependeat, ut ab ea ἐξανιστάω in potestatem & servitutem redigi, atque ita libertate, qua omnes & fideles & Ecclesiæ æqualiter pollent,spoliari possint: cùm omnes sint fratres, unum Dominum,præceptorem & judicem recognoscentes, Matth. XXIII. 8. 9. 10. nihilominus rectum & utile est, ut plurium Ecclesiarum doctores & rectores, & pro re nata,si fieri possit,totius etiam orbis,missi conveniant & de rebus officii sui, & necessitatibus Ecclesiarum deliberent; & ad alias etiam Ecclesias, consilii dandi,vel petendi,vel ὁμοιολογίας testandæ & patefaciendæ causa,ad multorum πληροφορίαν, veniant. Quàm enim bonum & svave est, fratres sedere unà, Psal. CXXXIII. 1. nempe לפני יהוה coram Domino,Esaj. XXIII. 18. ceu magistro & doctore unico, Matth. XXIII. 8. 10. Quorum communio in doctrina & benedictione comparatur cum rore,qui simul cadit in montem Hermon , & in montes Sionis , Psal. CXXXIII. 3. Ubi duo vel tres in nomine meo congregati sunt,ero in medio eorum,Matth.XVIII. 20. Et Ecclesiæ N. T. peculiariter dicitur: Dilata locum tentorii tui,& cortinæ tabernaculorum tuorum extendant se,ne parcas,&c. Esaj.LIV.2. Ideo S. Paulus, ne in vanum curreret,aut cucurrisset, vel prædicatio ejus ullo pacto inutilis redderetur,missus ab Antiochenis, venit Hierosolymam, ut patesceret inde, quòd verbum Dei Hierosolymis egredi debeat, Actor. XV. 1. 2. &c. Gal. II. 1. 2. Esaj. II. 3. Ecclesia verò Hierosolymitana unà cum Apostolis,reliquis Ecclesiis tum præcepta Spiritus S. omnino & semper tenenda, tum fidele consilium suum necessitati temporum accommodatum , fraternè exposuit, Actor. XV. 28. misitque tum ipsa ad Antiochenos, tum hi ad Ecclesias, qui ea observanda traderent. Cujus communicationis is fructus fuit,ut Ecclesiæ fide constabilirentur,ibid. v. 27. 31. 32. 40. XVI. 4. 5. Etiam Paulus Miletum Presbyteros Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ accersivit, ibid. XX. 17. 18. Cúmque is Hierosolymam venisset,apud Jacobum Presbyteri congregati fuerunt,ibid. XXI. 18. Idem S. Paulus in omni perfectione sua secum συνεκδημος peregrinationis suæ comites , Apostolos Ecclesiarum habuit, 2. Cor. VIII. 19. 23. Hæc igitur Synodorum & Conciliorum con-
units.tr: Although no believer depends on another believer, nor one Church on another, so that one could be reduced [ἐξανιστάω] to power and servitude, and so be deprived of the liberty which all believers and Churches equally possess, since they are all brothers, acknowledging one Lord, teacher and judge (Matt. 23:8–10), nevertheless it is right and useful that the teachers and rulers of several Churches, and, as the occasion arises and if possible, of the whole world, should come together as sent men, and deliberate about the duties of their office and the needs of the Churches; and that they should also come to other Churches to give or seek counsel, or to bear witness and make known their agreement [ὁμοιολογίας], for the full assurance [πληροφορίαν] of many. For how good and pleasant it is for brothers to sit together (Ps. 133:1), namely before the LORD (לפני יהוה) (Isa. 23:18), as the one master and teacher (Matt. 23:8, 10). Their communion in doctrine and blessing is compared with the dew that falls together on Mount Hermon and on the mountains of Zion (Ps. 133:3). Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the midst of them (Matt. 18:20). And of the Church of the New Testament it is said in particular: Enlarge the place of your tent, and let the curtains of your tabernacles be stretched out; spare not, etc. (Isa. 54:2). Therefore St Paul, lest he should run, or have run, in vain, or his preaching be rendered useless in any way, sent by the Antiochenes, came to Jerusalem, so that it might be made plain from there that the word of God ought to go out from Jerusalem (Acts 15:1, 2, etc.; Gal. 2:1, 2; Isa. 2:3). The Church of Jerusalem, together with the Apostles, set out fraternally to the other Churches both the precepts of the Holy Spirit, which are wholly and always to be observed, and its own faithful counsel, adapted to the necessity of the times (Acts 15:28). It sent men to the Antiochenes, and they in turn sent men to the Churches to hand on those things to be observed. The fruit of this fellowship was that the Churches were strengthened in the faith (ibid. 27, 31, 32, 40; 16:4, 5). Paul also summoned the elders of the Ephesian Church to Miletus (ibid. 20:17, 18); and when he had come to Jerusalem, the elders were gathered at James's house (ibid. 21:18). The same St Paul, in all his fullness, had as companions of his journey [συνεκδημος] the apostles of the Churches (2 Cor. 8:19, 23). This, therefore, is the assembling of several Churches in synods and councils, which is most useful for arousing unanimous zeal and care among the teachers and rulers of the Church, for restoring what has fallen, for settling disputes, for uncovering the cunning of heretics, for demonstrating the truth, and for the manifestation [φανέρωσιν] of those who are approved (τῶν δοχίμων).

units.la: Ecclesiarum plurium in Synodis & Conciliis congregatio. gregandorum ratio est,utilissima ad excitatio- nem studii unanimis,& curæ doctorum atque rectorumEcclesiæ,ad collapsa redintegrandum, ad componenda dissidia, detegendas hæreti- corum versutias,ad demonstrationem veritatis,& φανέρωσιν τῶν δοχίμων manifestationem eorum qui probi sunt.
units.tr: The gathering of several churches in synods and councils is most useful for stirring up the zeal of all and the care of the teachers and rulers of the Church, for restoring what has fallen into decay, for settling disputes, for uncovering the cunning of heretics, for demonstrating the truth, and for the manifestation of those who are approved [φανέρωσιν τῶν δοκίμων].

units.la: CVII. Metus tyrannidis,an amor licentiæ & libertatis ἀπαιδία prophetandi, maximorum malorum causa,impulerit eos,qui in Anglia superbo Independentium nomine famosi Episcoporum juxta atque Presbyterorum regimini se opposuerunt,ut non tantum particularem quamvis Ecclesiam negarent ampliorem esse oportere, quàm quæ uno ambitu & loco ad celebranda sacra sub uno Pastore convenire queat, sed etiam contenderent, regimen singularum ejusmodi Ecclesiarum, quas congregationales appellant, debere esse independens, & abstractum à communione cum aliis Ecclesiis, ac combinatione mutua in congregationes classicas, Synodales & Conciliares, easque statas & ordinatas,incertum equidem est. Nam posse Ecclesiam particularem constare pluribus membris, quàm quæ uno loco ad publicum cultum ordinarium convenire possunt,satis vel inde liquet,quòd Ecclesiæ particularis definitio non à conditione accidentali loci conventus, sed ab essentiali & formali suo, unione membrorum in eadem doctrina veritatis,sub iisdem rectoribus & eodem regimine sacro peti debeat. Si enim plures Synagogæ in diversis urbibus & tribubus unam Ecclesiam Nationalem sub eodem regimine, iisdem rectoribus obnoxiam in V. T. constituerunt; & plures etiam Ecclesiæ unius Provinciæ, sive gentis unam Ecclesiam Provincialem vel Nationalem coalstituere possunt, imò si omnes per totum terrarum orbem dispersæ Ecclesiæ unum corpus Catholicum, ejusdem fidei & charitatis compage inter se adstrictum constituunt, multò magis plures cœtus ejusdem urbis unam Ecclesiam particularem urbicariam constituere possunt. Hæc enim illa minùs difficilis & operosa est. Ecclesiæ quoque ab Apostolis plantatæ adeò sæpe in urbibus majoribus numerosæ fuerunt,ut uno loco convenire non possent. Neque tamen propterea Ecclesiæ in singulis locis multiplicabantur. Quomodo Ecclesia Hierosolymitana ultra quinque millia virorum excrevit,Actor. IV.4. Et licet κατ' οἶκον domatim Apostoli docuerint, cap. V. 42. totum tamen illud corpus, velut una Ecclesia, cui Diaconi præfecti erant, proponitur, etsi ulterius multiplicatus esset numerus discipulorum, cap. VI. 1. 5. An etiam credibile est, vel totam Ecclesiam Romanam in domo Aquilæ & Priscillæ fuisse coactam, Rom. XVI. 5. vel illam Ecclesiam separatam à fidelibus Romanis aliis constituisse? Etiam Ecclesia Ephesina repræsentatur ut unum πλίον, unus grex, una Ecclesia, ubi tamen plures Episcopi seu Presbyteri, adeòque etiam plura loca conventus fuerunt,Actor. XX. 17.18.28. Neque enim propter rabiem idololatrarum, in urbe ob cultum Dianæ superstitioni addictissima,Christianos eodem loci convenire expediit. At nec verisimile est,in Schola Tyranni convenisse omnes fideles Ephesi coactos, ibid. XIX. 9. 10. cùm tamen tantus eorum,qui Evangelium profitebantur,numerus fuerit,ut publicè in urbe δημοσία libros magicos, περίεργα complexos, comburere ausi fuerint. Et Ecclesiam Philippensium,cui plures Episcopi præfuerant, Phil. I. 1. uno loco convenisse, minùs probabile est. Par ratio Colossæ,Cretæ,&c. est. S. Petrus quoque ex διασπορὰ Ponti,Galatiæ,Cappadociæ,Asiæ & Bithyniæ unum corpus & unum gregem facit,1. Petr. I. 1. V.2. Multò igitur magis ex pluribus cœtibus particularibus unum corpus conflari potest. Accedit,quod Ecclesiæ unius urbis Presbyterium unum duntaxat post tempora Apostolica legitur, & tamen, ubi majores cœtus fuerunt, illi uno loco cogi nec potuerunt, quia in cryptis arenariis sæpenumero iis ob tyrannidem & persecutionem hostium conveniendum fuit; nec debuerunt, ne totam Ecclesiam uno loco exponerent, loco congressus, quod facilè fieri posset,detecto. Præstabat enim Christianos variis & incertis locis, secundum diversas ἐπιζήτησ, ad cultum sacrum congredi,ne à tyrannis, eorumque satellitibus indagine cingi,& cultus eorum turbari posset. Imò Christianos primos ita facere solitos esse, Dionysius Alexandrinus apud Eusebium Hist. Eccles. lib. VII. 19. testis est. Cùmque ex pluribus tribubus & Collegiis civium una eademque urbs, iisdem rectoribus, regimini & legibus subjecta constitui posset, plures cœtus diversis locis coactos unam Ecclesiam,iisdem rectoribus & regimini obnoxiam constituere, quid impedit? Quomodo aliàs Ecclesiæ per gentes varias, imò totum terrarum orbem dispersæ, unam Ecclesiam Catholicam constituent? Et quomodo sic non altare contra altare erigetur, & communio Sanctorum prorsus turbabitur, & Christus ipse dividetur,quando quot locorum pastores, totidem Papæ erunt, & ex una Ecclesia ejecti ad aliam se recipient, atque, quod crebrò fit,mutuis invicem fulminibus percellent,& in suo quisque nido securè dominabitur?
units.tr: CVII. Whether fear of tyranny or a love of licence and of lack of instruction [ἀπαιδία] and of prophesying freely was the cause of the greatest evils, I cannot be sure. Yet it was this that drove those in England who, under the proud name of Independents, became notorious for opposing the government of bishops and presbyters alike. They not only denied that any particular church ought to be larger than one that can assemble in one place under one pastor to celebrate the sacred rites, but they also maintained that the government of each such church, which they call congregational, must be independent and cut off from communion with other churches and from mutual union in classical, synodal and conciliar assemblies, and that these assemblies should be fixed and ordered. That a particular church may consist of more members than can come together in one place for the ordinary public worship is clear enough from this alone: the definition of a particular church is to be taken not from the accidental circumstance of the place of assembly but from its essential and formal basis, namely the union of its members in the same doctrine of truth, under the same rulers and the same sacred government. For if several synagogues in different cities and tribes constituted in the Old Testament one national Church, subject to the same government and the same rulers, and if several churches of one province or people can form one provincial or national Church, indeed if all the churches scattered throughout the whole world form one Catholic body, bound together by the bond of the same faith and love, then much more can several assemblies of the same city form one particular urban Church. For this is the less difficult and laborious task. Also, the churches planted by the Apostles were so often numerous in the larger cities that they could not meet in one place. Yet for that reason the churches were not multiplied in each place. Thus the church of Jerusalem grew to more than five thousand men (Acts 4:4). And although the Apostles taught house by house [κατ' οἶκον] (Acts 5:42), that whole body is nevertheless set forth as one church, over which deacons were placed, even though the number of disciples had increased further (Acts 6:1, 5). Is it credible either that the whole Roman church was gathered into the house of Aquila and Priscilla (Rom. 16:5), or that they formed some other church separate from the faithful at Rome? The church of Ephesus is likewise presented as one fold [ποίμνιον], one flock, one church, although there were several bishops or presbyters there, and so also several places of assembly (Acts 20:17, 18, 28). For it was not expedient for Christians to meet in the same place in the city, because of the fury of the idolaters, in a city most devoted to the superstition of the worship of Diana. Nor is it likely that all the faithful of Ephesus were compelled to meet in the school of Tyrannus (Acts 19:9, 10), since there was so great a number of those who professed the Gospel that they dared to burn publicly in the city the magic books, which were curious [περίεργα]. It is also less probable that the church of the Philippians, over which several bishops presided (Phil. 1:1), met in one place. The same reasoning holds for Colossae, Crete, and so on. St Peter too makes one body and one flock out of the dispersion [διασπορά] of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia (1 Pet. 1:1; 5:2). Much more, then, can one body be formed out of several particular assemblies. Add to this that after the Apostolic times only one presbytery is read of for each church of a city; yet where the assemblies were larger they could not be gathered in one place, because they often had to meet, for fear of tyrants and the persecution of enemies, in sand-pits and caves, and nor should they have done so, lest by meeting in one place they expose the whole church, a meeting which could easily be detected. For it was better for Christians to gather for sacred worship in various and uncertain places, according to different search [ἐπιζήτησις], so that they could not be surrounded by the tyrants and their guards in the hunt and their worship disturbed. Indeed Dionysius of Alexandria bears witness in Eusebius, Hist. Eccles. lib. VII. 19., that the first Christians were accustomed to act in this way. And since one and the same city, made up of several tribes and guilds of citizens, can be constituted under the same rulers, government and laws, what prevents several assemblies gathered in different places from forming one Church subject to the same rulers and government? Otherwise, how would churches scattered among various peoples, indeed throughout the whole world, constitute one Catholic Church? And how would it not thus raise altar against altar, utterly disturb the communion of saints, and divide Christ himself, when there would be as many popes as there are pastors of places, and those expelled from one church would take refuge in another, and, as often happens, would strike each other with mutual thunderbolts, and each would rule securely in his own nest?

units.la: CVIII. Posse etiam plures Ecclesias sub regimine classium & Synodorum sic combinari & contesserari,ut eorundem decreta,sive fidem,sive εὐταξίαν, sive disciplinam concernentia, quatenus illa verbo Dei consentanea, vel ordini vel decoro Ecclesiæ utilia & salutaria sunt, singulas obligent, satis ex iis,quæ de Synodorum & Conciliorum necessitate & utilitate diximus, liquet. Modus verò definiendi controversias qualescunque inConciliis & Synodis non est imperiosus, cum jurisdictione conjunctus, vel αὐθεντικὸς & ἀρχιεπισκοπικὸς principalis & architectonicus, sed talis, qualis omnis Ecclesiastica institutio est, ministerialis nimirum,ὑπηρετικὸς & discretivus,quatenus ii,qui congregati sunt, reliquis, orthodoxam fidem explicando & demonstrando,hæresin verò convincendo & improbando,quasi typi fiunt. Unde fit, ut in Ecclesiis particularibus tum consentientium arctior longè conjunctio, ut quousque pervenerunt, eodem canone ambulent, Phil. III. 16. tum pertinaciter dissentientium secessio & pro re nata exclusio fiat. Duplex enim est δογμάτων κεκρυμμένων dogmatum à Synodis ejusmodi definitorum & dijudicatorum,Actor. XVI. 4. obligatio ; una in foro externo Ecclesiæ, altera in foro interno conscientiæ. In foro externo Ecclesiæ hactenus absolutè obligant, ut qui iis pertinaciter se subjicere detrectant, ab externa Ecclesiæ communione summoveri possint, & summoti, intercedente Potestatis publicæ sanctione, & pactis nullis obstantibus cedere debeant. Alias in externa societate perturbationibus nec finis, nec modus imponi posset. In foro interno conscientiæ nunquam absolutè obligant, sed nonnisi cum conditione veritatis ad conscientiam demonstratæ. Conscientia enim nulli dicto vel placito merè humano, sed soli verbo Dei, eíque ad eam manifestato subjicitur. Neque tamen Concilium & ejusdem actio quoad forum etiam internum & conscientiæ mera inquisitio & consultatio, sed etiam tum inquisitio veri, justi, sancti religiosa communicatione instituta, tum dictio & definitio sententiæ, non judicialis & prætoria, sed ministerialis, & examini & ad Lydium lapidem sacræ Scripturæ subjecta est, quæ tanti est, quanti ratio est, qua nititur, sed facilius tamen rationem & veritatem invenire potest, quia plus oculi sani, quàm oculus sanus, vident, & ardentior flamma ex strue lignorum, quàm uno ligno exit. Judicium autem prætorium est solius Christi, ab iis, qui Concilio adsunt, in Scriptura inquirendum, & ex ea, velut ex tabulis mandati, pronuntiandum, à fidelibus verò per judicium discretionis amplectendum. Cujusmodi judicium est œconomi vel dispensatoris in domo aliqua præsentis Domini, vel medici etiam, quod morbum graviorem non facit, neque ei dat esse.
units.tr: CVIII. It is also clear enough, from what we have said about the necessity and usefulness of synods and councils, that several churches can be so combined and joined together under the government of classes and synods that their decrees, whether concerning faith, good order [εὐταξία], or discipline, bind each single church, insofar as they agree with the Word of God and are useful and salutary for the order and decorum of the Church. But the manner of settling controversies of whatever kind in councils and synods is not domineering, joined with jurisdiction, nor authoritative [αὐθεντικός], archiepiscopal [ἀρχιεπισκοπικός], principal and architectonic, but such as every ecclesiastical institution is, namely ministerial [ὑπηρετικός] and discriminating, insofar as those who are gathered become, as it were, models for the rest, in explaining and demonstrating the orthodox faith and in refuting and condemning heresy. Hence it comes about that in particular churches there is both a much closer union of those who agree, so that they walk by the same rule to which they have attained (Phil. 3:16), and a secession from, and as the case requires exclusion of, those who obstinately dissent. For the obligation of the hidden doctrines [δογμάτων κεκρυμμένων] of the dogmas defined and judged by such synods (Acts 16:4) is twofold: one in the external forum of the Church, the other in the internal forum of conscience. In the external forum of the Church they oblige absolutely to this extent, that those who obstinately refuse to submit to them can be removed from the external communion of the Church, and once removed must give way, with the sanction of public authority intervening, and no agreements standing in the way. Otherwise no end or limit could be put to disturbances in the external society. In the internal forum of conscience they never oblige absolutely, but only on the condition that the truth has been demonstrated to the conscience. For the conscience is subject to no mere human saying or pleasure, but only to the Word of God, and to that as it is made manifest to it. Nor, however, is the council and its action, as far as the internal forum of conscience is concerned, a mere inquiry and consultation, but there is both an inquiry into what is true, just and holy, carried on by religious communication, and a declaration and definition of judgment, not judicial and praetorian, but ministerial, and subject to examination and to the touchstone of Holy Scripture. Its worth is as great as the reasoning on which it rests; yet it can more easily find reason and truth, because more eyes see than one sound eye, and a flame from a pile of wood burns more brightly than one piece of wood gives out. The praetorian judgment, however, belongs to Christ alone, to be sought in Scripture by those who attend the council, and to be pronounced from it as from the tablets of his command, and to be embraced by the faithful through the judgment of discernment. Such a judgment is like that of a steward or dispenser in a house where the Lord is present, or even of a physician, which does not make a more serious illness, nor give it being.

units.la: CIX. Vanus igitur est perdendæ libertatis & tyrannidis metus, quem hoc tempore communionem tum diversi loci cœtuum, eandem Ecclesiam particularem constituentium, tum diversorum, seu pauciorum in Classe vel Synodo, seu plurium in Concilio particularium Ecclesiarum fugientes, ob umbram nescio quam imperii & subjectionis, quam in communione & combinatione cœtuum & Ecclesiarum somniant. Quibus optandum est, ne fiant auctores spargendi ovilis Dominici, & lupos sub specie ovium admittant potius, ut in iis impleatur promissio נוגי ממועד אספתי Angentes sese, ut discedant à cœtu, congregavi, Zeph. III. 18. atque etiam ut Deus sit Rex in monte Sion, & coram senioribus ejus gloria, Esaj. XXIV. 23. Neque profecto hac ratione Ecclesiarum libertas jus & authoritas destruitur, sed cumulatur, conservatur & confirmatur, tum quia in Synodis, vel cœtibus combinatis communia tantùm, & ad universum corpus pertinentia tractantur, relicto singulis cœtibus propriarum rerum arbitrio: tum quia quilibet cœtus in Ecclesia particulari, & quælibet Ecclesia particularis in Classe vel Synodo comparet & suffragium fert, & authoritas cœtuum & Ecclesiarum plurium nihil aliud est, quàm conjuncta plurium cœtuum & Ecclesiarum particularium per delegatos suos comparentium authoritas, quæ, ceu vis unita fortior utique esse debet. Subjectum ergo, quod agit & decidit conjuncti cœtus, Synodus, Concilium est: Principium quo agit, Ecclesiarum particularium deputati sunt. Unde cœtus combinati, & con-
units.tr: CIX. The fear of losing liberty and falling into tyranny is therefore groundless. Those who now shun fellowship with other congregations, whether with the congregations of a different place that together make up one particular Church, or with other particular Churches, whether a few in a classis or synod or many in a council, are afraid of a shadow of rule and subjection which they imagine in the fellowship and combination of congregations and Churches. Such people should be urged not to become the authors of scattering the Lord's flock, and rather not to admit wolves in sheep's clothing. In them may be fulfilled the promise, "I will gather those who grieve for the appointed feast" [נוגי ממועד אספתי], that they may withdraw "from the assembly", "I will gather", Zeph. 3:18; and that "God may be King on Mount Zion, and before his elders glory", Isa. 24:23. Certainly by this arrangement the liberty, right and authority of the Churches is not destroyed but increased, preserved and confirmed. This is so, first, because in synods or combined assemblies only common matters, those that pertain to the whole body, are dealt with, while the decision about their own affairs is left to each assembly. Second, because every congregation in a particular Church, and every particular Church in a classis or synod, appears there through its delegates and casts its vote; and the authority of several congregations and Churches is nothing other than the joined authority of several congregations and particular Churches, exercised through their delegates, which, like a united force, must surely be stronger. The subject, therefore, which acts and decides, is the joined assembly, the synod, the council; the principle by which it acts is the particular Churches that have sent deputies. Hence combined assemblies and synodical gatherings do not use a power extrinsic to the Churches over other Churches, but a power intrinsic to the Churches themselves, and no assembly or particular Church is subjected to an extrinsic power of which it does not itself form a part. Nor do the assemblies and particular Churches lose their right in this way any more than the cities of the Kingdom of England lose theirs when the estates of that realm meet in Parliament, with delegates sent for this purpose from each town, and definitive decrees go forth from it. For precisely because Parliament is composed of delegates from the particular towns, the towns themselves acknowledge this power not as extrinsic but as intrinsic, and they do not think that any part of their authority and power is thereby taken away or lost. Moreover, the decrees of combined assemblies, classes and synods do not of themselves bind the conscience, nor do they bind otherwise than insofar as they are made known to the conscience. To assent or not to assent to such decrees, once they have been made known to the conscience from the Word of God, is free for no one; more on this below.

units.la: ventus Synodici non extrinseca potestate in Ecclesias alias, sed Ecclesiis ipsis intrinseca utuntur, nec ullus cœtus vel Ecclesia particularis potestatis extrinsecæ, cujus ipsa partem non constituat, subjicitur. Nec magis cœtibus & Ecclesiis particularibus jus suum hac ratione perit, quàm perit urbibus Regni Anglicani, cùm ordines ejusdem Regni in Parlamento coëunt, delegatis ad id ex singulis civitatibus missis, & ab eo decreta definitiva promanant. Eo ipso enim quòd Parlamentum ex delegatis urbium particularium componitur, ipsæ urbes hanc potestatem non ut extrinsecam, sed ut intrinsecam agnoscunt, nihilque adeò sibi de authoritate & potestate sua delibari & perire autumant. Accedit, quòd cœtuum combinatorum, classium & Synodorum decreta per se conscientiam non obligant, neque aliter obligant, quàm quatenus ad conscientiam manifestantur. Quibus sic ad conscientiam ex Dei verbo manifestatis, assentiri, vel non assentiri liberum nemini est, de quo pluribus infra.
units.tr: CX. A council is either universal or particular. A universal council consists of the legates of all the Churches of the whole Christian world, who are able to come together. Hence it is also called ecumenical, general or plenary. A particular council is one where the legates of certain Churches meet. It is either national, in which the legates of a whole kingdom or some nation meet, or provincial, in which the legates of some province meet. National councils are also called general in the sense that, although not general simply, they are general within some kingdom or region. A council is either lawful or unlawful. The lawful council agrees with the order consistent with the divine laws; the unlawful one is opposed to them, and the ancients call it a false synod [ψευδοσυνάγμα]. Thus Luke calls one assembly lawful [ἔννομον] and another confused [ξυγκεχυμένην], Acts 19:32, 39.

units.la: CX. Concilium vel universale vel particulare est. Universale ex omnibus totius Christiani orbis Ecclesiarum legatis, quibus convenire licet, constat. Unde & œcumenicum, generale, plenarium appellatur. Particulare est, cùm certarum Ecclesiarum legati conveniunt; Estque vel Nationale, in quo legati totius Regni vel Nationis cujuspiam, vel Provinciale, in quo legati Provinciæ cujuspiam conveniunt. Nationalia etiam generalia καταξεγησικὸς vel καπὰ π appellantur, quia non quidem simpliciter, sed tamen in Regno vel regione aliqua generalia sunt. Rurium Concilium vel legitimum, vel illegitimum est. Illud ordini legibus Divinis consentaneo congruit: hoc eidem adversatur, & ψευδοσυνάγμα non Synodus veteribus appellatur. Ita Lucas Ecclesiam aliam ἔννομον legitimam, aliam ξυγκεχυμένην confusaneam, Actor. XIX. 32. 39. vocat.
units.tr: CXI. A council consists of the men who have the right and duty to take part in it. In general, the men in the Church either feed or are fed, and therefore are either shepherds or sheep. In each order some are superior and some inferior. Neither group is simply excluded from the council. But not all have the same aptitude and capacity for dealing with sacred matters, nor do all have equal power, though power does not always accompany such aptitude. The supreme president of the council is Christ. There are two ministerial presidents: one ecclesiastical, with respect to the business of the council; the other political, with respect to its good order. The former, chosen by the votes of the brethren, sends questions to deliberation, moderates debate and dispute, asks for opinions, settles the question according to the majority of votes, has the decrees recorded in the minutes by the clerks, and attends to anything else of this kind. The latter summons and convenes the council with authority, protects it when assembled, forbids both external violence and internal disorder and unruliness, and by his own authority also ratifies decrees lawfully made and confirmed by the signatures of the legates, establishes them within the territory over which he presides, and restrains those who resist. Hence came those ratifications which confirm the decision of the synod, namely, that the synodal judgment be sanctioned by royal approval.

units.la: CXI. Concilium constat hominibus, quibus illi interesse jus & fas est. In universum verò homines in Ecclesia vel pascunt, vel pascuntur; adeóque pastores, vel oves sunt. In utroque ordine alii superiores, alii inferiores sunt. Neutri simpliciter à Concilio excluduntur. Sed non eadem omnium in tractandis sacris aptitudo & δύναμις, nec par omnium ἐξουσία potestas est; quamvis neque illam semper ista comitetur. Summus Concilii præses Christus est. Ministerialis verò duplex est, alter Ecclesiasticus, quoad Concilii causam; alter Politicus quoad ejusdem ordinem. Ille fratrum suffragiis electus, quæstiones in consilium mittit, disceptationem & altercationem moderatur, sententias rogat, quæstionem juxta plura suffragia definit, decreta per notarios in acta refert, & siquid aliud ejusmodi curat. Hic Concilium cum potestate indicit & cogit, coactum tuetur, ac tum externam vim, tum internam ἀπαξίαν & ἀχημοσύνην prohibet, decreta legitimè facta, & legatorum subscriptionibus confirmata sua quoque authoritate sancit, & in ditione, cui præest, stabilit, reluctantes coërcet. Atque hinc sunt illa Ἰεαπλισματα κυ- ρίντα τῆς ξυνοδικῆς ὑποφάσεως sanctiones sententiarum Synodicarum, nempe ut κείης ξυνοδικῆ τῇ ἐπικελ βασιλικῇ judicium Synodi Regia comprobatione
units.tr: CXI. A Council consists of those men who have the right and duty to take part in it. In general, men in the Church either feed others or are fed, and so they are either ministers or sheep. Within each of these groups some are superior and others inferior. Neither group is wholly excluded from the Council. Yet not all have the same aptitude and capacity [δύναμις] for dealing with sacred matters, nor do all have equal authority [ἐξουσία], although authority does not always go with such capacity. Christ is the supreme president of the Council. There are two kinds of ministerial president: the first is ecclesiastical, with regard to the business of the Council; the second is political, with regard to its order. The ecclesiastical president, chosen by the votes of the brethren, sends questions to the assembly for deliberation, moderates the debate and disputation, calls for opinions, settles each question according to the majority of votes, has the decrees entered into the acts by the notaries, and attends to anything else of this kind. The political president convenes and summons the Council with authority, protects it once assembled, forbids both outward violence and inward unseemliness and disorder [ἀπαξία, ἀχημοσύνη], and by his own authority ratifies the decrees lawfully made and confirmed by the signatures of the delegates, and establishes them throughout the territory over which he rules, restraining those who resist. From this comes the practice by which the synodal decisions are given force [ἐπικύρωσις], that is, the judgement of the Synod is sanctioned by royal approval [βασιλικὴ ἐπικύρωσις].

units.la: Objectio tyrannidis diluitur. probatione sanciatur. Tum in Synodum admittendi sunt, quicunque dono, pietate puta, doctrina & prudentia, nec non vocatione, non ordinaria duntaxat docendi potestate, sed etiam extraordinaria ad Synodum delegatione, instructi sunt. Horum in cognitione causarum Synodicarum praecipuae partes sunt. Neque tamen illi pro judicibus proprie dictis, sed pro Divini Judicii, in verbo Dei comprehensi indicibus, suffragatoribus & interpretibus, non aliter quam quatenus demonstrando sententiam verbi Dei recte indicant & interpretantur, infallibilibus habendi sunt. Et in dicendis sententiis eodem jure Ecclesiarum dissidentium legati utuntur, ex utrovis ordine delecti sint. Absentes autem, & inauditos, nec legitime citatos, adeoque etiam indefensos damnare iniquissimum est. Tertius locus iis dandus est, qui a nulla quidem Ecclesia ablegati, nec publica authoritate instructi, sed in doctrinae vel disciplinae negotio aliquid quod animadversione & Cυζηλήσεσ dignum est, proponere cupiunt, quod quisquis eo, quo par est, ordine & ratione postulat, audiendus est. Nam etiam in Nicaeno Concilio Ethnici Philosophi auditi, & ad disputationes admissi sunt. Denique nec summoveri a Concilio debent, mere privati, si qui aedificandi sui causa coetui illi, in quo omnium Christianorum causa agitur, interesse cupiunt, modo pacate & modeste se gerant, & loco suo se contineant. Sed adesse illi doctrinae tractationi, non offendiculorum cognitioni debent, ne quid adversus charitatem, cujus peplo fraternae offensae tegi debent, delinquatur.
units.tr: The objection of tyranny is answered. Those are to be admitted to the Synod who are endowed with gifts, namely piety, learning and prudence, and also with a calling, not only the ordinary power of teaching but also an extraordinary delegation to the Synod. These men have the chief part in the examination of synodal causes. Yet they are not to be regarded as judges properly so called, but as indicators, advocates and interpreters of the divine judgement contained in the Word of God, and they are to be counted infallible only insofar as they rightly indicate and interpret the sense of God's Word by demonstrating it. In giving their opinions, the delegates of churches that disagree use the same right, whether they are chosen from either order. It is most unjust, however, to condemn those who are absent, or who have not been heard, or who have not been lawfully summoned, and so also those who have not been defended. A third place is to be given to those who have been sent by no church and have no public authority, but who wish to propose something in matters of doctrine or discipline that deserves attention and consideration; whoever demands this in the proper order and manner is to be heard. For even at the Council of Nicaea, heathen philosophers were heard and admitted to the disputations. Finally, purely private persons who wish to attend that assembly, in which the cause of all Christians is treated, for their own edification, must not be removed from the Council, provided they behave peacefully and modestly and keep to their own place. But they ought to be present at the treatment of doctrine, not at the examination of offences, lest anything be done against charity, by which fraternal offences ought to be covered.

units.la: CXII. Ordo Synodorum & Conciliorum arbitrarius, nulla certa lege verbi Dei definitus.
units.tr: CXII. The order of synods and councils is discretionary and not fixed by any definite rule of God's Word.

units.la: Is vero deligi debet, qui controversiis in pace componendis, veritati asserendae, & mendacio convincendo inprimis idoneus & accommodatus est. In Concilio primo Hierosolymitano missi Hierosolymam ad Apostolos & Presbyteros Paulus, Barnabas & alii controversam de lege Mosis, Circumcisione inprimis retinenda, nec ne, quaestionem in medium proposuerunt. Disceptatione de ea mota S. Petrus primus surrexit, & argumentis convicit, quod jugum legis cervicibus discipulorum imponendum non sit. Inde Barnabas & Paulus signa & prodigia Dei apud Gentes patrata commemorarunt. Excepit Jacobus juxta cujus quaestionem communibus suffragiis concludentis sententiam decretum conditum, per Epistolam ad Antiochenos missum, aliisque Ecclesiis oblatum est, Actor. XV. XVI. 4. In veteri Ecclesia initium capiebatur a precibus, praemisso plerunque jejunio. Considentibus Patribus prima de fide tractatio erat; sive ea exponenda, sive vindicanda foret. Tum veterum Synodorum Canones relegebantur, & disciplinam ac regimen spectantia. Ultimo denique loco particulares causae, quae singulas Ecclesias concernebant, tractabantur. Fas etiam fuit cuivis, si quid exponendum haberet, in medium prodire, & desideria sua aperire. Per varias Sessiones Concilium trahebatur, & sequente consessu acta praeterita praelegebantur. Sententiae vel apertis suffragiis, vel χειροτονίαι, porrectis manibus ferebantur. Applausu & acclamatione singulari praeclare dicta & consulta excipi fuerunt. Ubi contradictiones nimium ferverent, Praesidis erat rem componere, & latentem ex isto conflictu veritatem eruere. Denique ex plurium vel omnium suffragatione conclusio formabatur, & decreta juxta atque judicia & disceptatio omnis, Actorum nomine consignata divulgabantur. Finita Synodo acclamationes & gratulationes de asserta fide & triumphato errore percrebrescebant, & vota pro Ecclesiae & Imperii incolumitate nuncupabantur. Conditis a Synodo articulis, & anathematismis subinde ferventius subjectis, omnes subscripserunt, accedente Imperiali confirmatione, per quam fides a Synodo stabilita in legem ibat. Denique sic in Concilio acta & transacta literis encyclicis seu circularibus per Ecclesias vulgabantur, & observanda tradebantur.
units.tr: Those to be chosen should be above all suited and fitted to settle controversies peacefully, to assert the truth, and to refute falsehood. At the first Council of Jerusalem, Paul, Barnabas and others were sent to Jerusalem to the Apostles and elders, and they laid before them the controversial question whether the law of Moses, and above all circumcision, should be retained or not. When the dispute had been raised, St Peter rose first and by argument proved that the yoke of the law should not be placed on the necks of the disciples. Then Barnabas and Paul recounted the signs and wonders God had wrought among the Gentiles. James followed, and on his proposal a decree was drawn up by common vote, sent by letter to the Antiochenes, and offered to the other churches (Acts 15; 16:4). In the ancient Church the proceedings began with prayer, usually preceded by fasting. With the Fathers seated, the first business was the discussion of faith, whether it was to be set forth or defended. Then the canons of earlier synods were read, and those matters that concerned discipline and government were considered. Lastly, particular cases that concerned individual churches were dealt with. Anyone who had something to set forth was allowed to step forward and lay out his wishes. The council proceeded through several sessions, and at the following assembly the acts of the previous session were read aloud. Opinions were delivered either by open vote or by cheirotoniai [χειροτονίαι], that is, by raising the hands. Fine statements and proposals were received with special applause and acclamation. When disagreements grew too heated, it was the president's task to settle the matter and to draw out the truth hidden in the clash. Finally, the conclusion was formed from the votes of many or of all, and the decrees, judgments and whole debate were published under the name of the Acts. When the synod was over, acclamations and congratulations rose up for the faith asserted and the error overcome, and prayers were offered for the safety of the Church and the Empire. After the articles had been drawn up by the synod, and anathemas were subsequently added with greater vehemence, all subscribed, and the imperial confirmation followed, by which the faith established by the synod became law. Finally, what had been done and decided in the council was published through the churches by encyclical or circular letters, and was handed down to be observed.

units.la: CXIII. Fuit Gubernatio Ecclesiae Ecclesiastica. Civilis est, qua Magistratus fidelis gladio Divinitus armatus una cum Republica etiam Ecclesiam curat, & purum Dei cultum, ceu custos utriusque tabulae, promovet & tuetur. Duplex enim Magistratui fideli cura incumbit, una Reipublicae, altera Ecclesiae. De posteriori priusquam dicamus, prior paucis, & velut πυρίργυ οδόν, exponenda nobis est. Tractatio enim curae Reipublicae proprie non ad Theologiam, sed ad eam Philosophiae partem, quae Politices nomine venit, pertinet. Cui etiam relinquenda est: nisi quatenus eam rectior Magistratus constitutio, & Pseudo-Politicorum & haereticorum errores postulant; & regimen politicum populi Dei Divinitus institutum ampliorem explicationem meretur, quo explicationis labore Loc. XVI. ex professo defuncti sumus, reliqua nunc paucis persequi libet.
units.tr: CXIII. The government of the Church is ecclesiastical. It is civil in that the faithful magistrate, armed with the sword by God, takes care of the Church together with the commonwealth, and promotes and protects the pure worship of God, as guardian of both tables of the law. For the faithful magistrate has a twofold care laid upon him: one for the commonwealth, the other for the Church. Before we speak of the latter, the former must be set out briefly and, as it were, in outline [πυρίργυ οδόν]. For the treatment of the care of the commonwealth belongs properly not to theology but to that part of philosophy which goes by the name of politics. It is to be left to that discipline, except insofar as a more correct constitution of the magistracy, and the errors of the pseudo-politicians and heretics, require it, and insofar as the political government of the people of God, instituted by God, deserves fuller explanation. We have already dealt with that task of explanation expressly in Loc. XVI, and it is now our pleasure to go briefly through the remaining matters.

units.la: CXIV. Magistratus Origo Divina est. Non est potestas nisi a Deo. Potestates autem quae sunt, a Deo ordinatae sunt, Rom. XIII. 1. Quomodo & Poeta gentilis cecinit: Ἐκ Διὸς βασιλῆες. A Jove Reges sunt. Deus enim is est, qui gentes erudit, & in disciplina continet, Psal. XCIV. 10. Qui Reges accingit & disciingit, & frenum eorum solvit, Job. XII. 18. Per me, vel in me Reges regnant, & proximi illorum scribunt justitiam. Per me Principes imperium exercent & magnates omnes judices terrae, Prov. VIII. 15.16. Omnis igitur ordo, qui in mundo est, & omnis ejus pulchritudo & jucunditas a Deo provenit: & prudentia atque sapientia omnis civilis, amor ordinis & consensus populorum ad parendum legibus & Principes, sapientiae Divinae donum est. Cum enim omnes homines peccatores & ira digni sint, quod tamen illi nascuntur, & humanum genus, non obstante peccato, propagatur, neque omnes phrenetici, vel moriones nascuntur, sed multi ingeniosi & cordati, valentes rectum a pravo discernere, populos regere, sui reverentiam in illis efficere, in bono & laude omni praire, justa judicare, imo excellentibus virtutibus, generositate, ingenuitate liberalitate, communis utilitatis studio, multorum amorem promereri; quodque homines natura mali, se invicem odio habentes, nihilominus congregantur, societatem ineunt, & acerba multa pati, quam societates illas dissolvi malunt, imo quandoque etiam pro patria & civitate vitam exponunt, Divinae
units.tr: CXIV. The origin of the magistracy is divine. There is no power but of God; the powers that exist are ordained of God (Rom. 13:1). In the same way the heathen poet sang: Ek Dios basileis [Ἐκ Διὸς βασιλῆες], that is, kings are from Jove. For it is God who instructs the nations and keeps them under discipline (Ps. 94:10); who girds kings and loosens their belt, and unbinds the bond of their rule (Job 12:18). By me kings reign, and their counsellors decree justice. By me princes rule, and all the nobles, the judges of the earth (Prov. 8:15–16). Therefore every order that exists in the world, and all its beauty and pleasantness, comes from God; and all civil prudence and wisdom, the love of order, and the agreement of peoples to obey laws and princes, are a gift of divine wisdom. For since all men are sinners and deserving of wrath, yet men are born and the human race is propagated despite sin, and not all are born mad or foolish, but many are clever and sensible, able to distinguish right from wrong, to rule peoples, to win reverence for themselves, to excel in all goodness and praise, to judge justly, and indeed, by outstanding virtues, nobility, good breeding, liberality and zeal for the common good, to earn the love of many; and since men, evil by nature and hating one another, nevertheless gather together, enter into society, and prefer to endure many bitter things rather than see those societies dissolved, and even at times lay down their lives for country and state, all this is the fruit of the divine

units.la: Ordo in Concilis servandus. Divinæ longanimitatis argumentum est. Ideo Daniel: Deus transfert Reges יתנ ⁊ constituit Reges, dat sapientiam sapientibus, & cognitionem cognoscentibus, Dan. II. 21.
units.tr: Order to be observed in councils. It is a proof of divine long-suffering. Hence Daniel says: God transfers kings [יתנ] and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who know (Dan. 2:21).

units.la: CXV. Id ipsum etiam potestatis omnis origo ostendit. Deus enim fecit ex uno sanguine omne genus humanum habitare super omni superficie terræ, Actor. XVII. 26.
