Fecit ergo ut omnes essent ex uno sanguine & velut fratres unâ habitantes, & se invicem diligentes, quod sine ordine & societate ordinata, quæ Reipublicæ instar est, fieri non poterat. Prima igitur Respublica fuit domus Adami; & post diluvium quatuor domus Noachi & trium filiorum ejus. Non possunt homines nati discedere à parentibus suis, sine quibus vivere & subsistere non possunt. Natura enim omnes intelligunt, se parentum esse, & iis amorem, obsequium, reverentiam debere, & in eorundem gratiam etiam fratres suos, ceu eorundem parentum subsistantiam, diligere teneri. Quos vero singulos diligunt, eos conjunctos vivere, & se invicem diligere naturaliter optant, quia nihil fraterno amore suavius, jucundius & utilius est; & φιλαδελφία exemplar amoris amicorum est. Hæc causa est, cur homines, etiam cùm omnia tuta & pacata sunt, unâ vivere & habitare, quàm spargi & dissipari malunt. Sunt enim natura ζῷα πολιτικὰ animalia socialia & conversationi idonea; in quorum corpore & anima cuncta naturaliter ad pacem, concordiam, charitatem spectant. Sed non humano ingenio, verùm Divino nutu fieri, ut homines socientur & in unum coalescant, sibi invicem pacati & officiosi sint, jus & justitiam observent, fraudem & injuriam detestentur, ex Caini mali & corrupti, atque ab integra natura, cum qua homo creatus est, multum degenerantis, parricidio liquet. Cùm igitur in primo fratrum pari humani ingenii perversitas, & amore fraterno, maximisque commodis inde ortis, aversio conspicua sit, dubitari non potest, quin Divinæ bonitatis & longanimitatis singulare argumentum sit, quòd populi coalescunt, pacem & jura inter se colunt, se invicem adversus bestias & homines alienos atque infestantes tuentur. Ideo etiam Cain, parricida licèt, eadem providentia Dei moderante, primus civitatem fossis & septis circumdatam, & excubiis custodiendam instituit, in qua propiùs familiæ plures cohabitarent, & in quam noctu saltem ad tutò quiescendum confugerent, sive ad id metus & conscientiæ pavor, sive ferarum infestantium vis, sive perspecta cohabitationis commoda alia ad id eum compulerunt. Etiam post diluvium homines tandiu conjuncti manserunt, in oriente de loco in locum migrantes, una lingua loquentes, adeóque mirè consentientes, liberi sub parentum disciplina constituti, & parentes consilia in commune, uti ex consilio de condenda turri liquet, conferentes, donec labio eorum confuso, dispergerentur, & passim divisos principatus, regna & gentes constituerent. Animadversione inprimis dignum ad noscendam veram civitatum originem, est, quòd Deus ipse Noacho & filiis ejus præcepta dederit, & judicia commendaverit, ut, qui sanguinem hominis effunderet, ejusdem sanguis per homines effunderetur, quod sine judicio fieri non poterat, ratione addita, quòd homo ad imaginem Dei factus sit, adeóque vita ejus in nullius, nisi Dei potestate sit, pro quo zelare homines debeant, ne invito eo cuiquam vita eriperetur, vel eripienti impunè esset, quò sic homines tutò & tranquillè vivere, & pietatem colere possent; Genes. IX. 6. Deus ergo judicia hominibus dedit, & quosdam potestate, gladio in sceleratos, in vitam, famam & bona aliorum grassantes, pacis, honestatis, pietatis turbatores, animadvertendi instruxit. Neque enim minus in civitate, quàm in domo curari debet, ut homo Dei imago esse, ejúsque privilegio gaudere possit, quod sine judiciis & potestate curari non potest. Sicut igitur à Deo est, ut homo in mundo velut imago, res & servus Dei vivat: ita ab eodem potestas civilis, fini huic inserviens, pariter est. Quæ inprimis necessaria est propter peccatum, quod præter imaginem Dei in mundum intravit; à quo omne pietatis & impietatis, justitiæ & injustitiæ certamen oritur. Necesse enim est, pietatem non nudam malorum omnium violentiæ exponi, sed munitam & armatam clypeo etiam Potestatis publicæ defendi. Finis enim potestatis est securitas, laus operis boni & vindicta adversus malos. Principes non sunt metus bonorum operum. Vis autem non timere Potestatem? Bonum fac, & habebis laudem ex eo; Dei enim minister est tibi in bonum. Si autem malum feceris, time. Non enim frustra gladium portat, Rom. XIII. 3.4.
units.tr: CXV. The very origin of all power shows the same thing. For God made from one blood every nation of men to dwell upon all the face of the earth (Acts 17:26). He therefore made all to be of one blood and, as it were, brothers dwelling together, loving one another; and this could not be done without order and an ordered society, which is like a commonwealth. The first commonwealth, then, was the household of Adam; and after the flood, the households of Noah and his three sons. Men when born cannot leave their parents, without whom they cannot live or subsist. For by nature all understand that they belong to their parents, and that they owe them love, obedience and reverence, and that for their sake they are bound to love their brothers too, as the continuing existence of those same parents. Those whom they love individually they naturally wish to live together and to love one another, because nothing is sweeter, more pleasant or more useful than brotherly love; and philadelphia is the model of friendship. This is why men prefer to live and dwell together, even when all is safe and peaceful, rather than be scattered and dispersed. For by nature they are zōa politika [ζῷα πολιτικὰ], social animals fit for living together; in whose body and soul all things naturally tend towards peace, concord and charity. But it is not by human ingenuity, but by divine nod, that men are brought together and grow into one, are peaceable and dutiful to one another, observe right and justice, and detest fraud and injury; as is clear from the parricide of Cain, who was evil and corrupt and had degenerated far from the integrity of nature in which man was created. Since, then, in the first of brothers there was a conspicuous perversity of the human mind and an aversion to brotherly love and to the very great advantages that arise from it, there can be no doubt that it is a singular proof of divine goodness and long-suffering that peoples coalesce, cultivate peace and rights among themselves, and defend one another against beasts and against hostile and aggressive strangers. Therefore also Cain, though a parricide, under the same providence of God governing him, was the first to establish a city surrounded with ditches and walls and to be guarded by watchmen, in which several families might dwell closer together, and into which at night at least they might flee to rest safely; whether fear and terror of conscience, or the force of savage beasts, or other perceived advantages of living together, drove him to it. Even after the flood men remained together for a long time, migrating from place to place in the east, speaking one language and therefore agreeing wonderfully, free and placed under the discipline of their parents, and the parents conferring counsel in common, as is clear from their counsel about building the tower, until their language was confounded and they were scattered, and set up divided principalities, kingdoms and nations everywhere. The point most worthy of notice for understanding the true origin of cities is that God himself gave precepts to Noah and his sons and commended judgments, so that whoever sheds man's blood, his blood shall be shed by men; which could not be done without judgment, and the reason is added that man was made in the image of God, and therefore his life is in the power of no one but God, for whose sake men ought to be zealous, lest against his will anyone should take away a life or go unpunished in taking it; so that men might live safely and quietly and cultivate godliness (Gen. 9:6). God therefore gave judgments to men, and he equipped some with the power of the sword to punish criminals who rage against the life, reputation and goods of others, and who disturb peace, honesty and godliness. For no less in a city than in a household must care be taken that man, as the image of God, may enjoy that privilege; and this cannot be secured without judgments and power. Just as it is from God that man lives in the world as the image, thing and servant of God, so civil power, serving this end, is likewise from the same God. It is necessary above all because of sin, which entered the world besides the image of God, and from which arises all the conflict between godliness and ungodliness, justice and injustice. For godliness must not be left bare to the violence of all the wicked, but must be defended, fortified and armed with the shield of public power. For the purpose of power is security, the praise of good work, and vengeance against the wicked. Rulers are not a terror to good works, but to evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? Do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same; for he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain (Rom. 13:3–4).

units.la: CXVI. Initiò principalis potestas penes Patres fuit. Illi, multiplicato humano genere, in commune consultarunt; & postulante necessitate, Seniores ex suo numero constituerunt, qui & jura legesque conderent, & jus dicerent. Eorum apud Israelitas in Ægypto degentes, cùm e duodecim Patriarcharum familiis, tanquam totidem fontibus, proximè emersissent, mentio occurrit. Diu post, cùm in gentem redacti, & in Rempublicam compositi essent, istud regiminis subalterni (nam principale ipsius Dei, velut in statu Theocratico, fuit) genus apud eos duravit; donec ejus pertæsi Regem popposcissent, qui adinstar aliorum regum Orientis addictiùs eos regeret. Quod consilium Deo licèt displicuit, non tamen is populum suum ideo deseruit, sed postulantibus Regem dedit, cujus imperium, ne infinita potestas foret, certis legibus circumscriptit, juxta legem Regiam, quam jam ante in deserto, præscius impotentiæ populi, Deut. XVII. 14-20. promulgavit. Sed eam in rem multa satis, Loc. XVI. 4-21. ubi statum regiminis Theocraticum, & Magistratus populi Divini temporarios & perpetuos explicavimus, à nobis dicta sunt, quod compendium heic ponimus.
units.tr: CXVI. At first, supreme power rested with the fathers of families. When the human race had multiplied, they took counsel together, and when necessity demanded it, they appointed elders from among their own number, who were to both make laws and administer justice. Mention is made of these elders among the Israelites while they lived in Egypt, shortly after they had emerged, as it were from twelve springs, from the twelve families of the patriarchs. Long afterwards, when they had been formed into a nation and organised into a commonwealth, this kind of subordinate government (for God's own rule was the principal one, as in a theocratic state) continued among them until, weary of it, they asked for a king who would rule them more firmly, like the other kings of the East. Although God disliked this plan, he did not on that account abandon his people, but gave them a king when they asked, and restricted his authority by fixed laws, so that it would not be unlimited. These were the royal laws which, foreseeing the people's weakness, he had already promulgated in the wilderness (Deut. 17:14–20). But we have said enough on this matter at Loc. 16:4–21, where we explained the theocratic state and the temporary and permanent magistrates of God's people; we set down here only a summary of that discussion.

units.la: CXVII. Tametsi authoritas Magistratuum à Deo est, populi tamen est, reipublicæ formam modúmque, & personas Magistratum gesturas eligere & designare, quibus idoneis rerum ista moles committatur. Non enim populo in regiminis forma & personis constituendis liberum est pro arbitratu agere, sed Divina indicia, & quasi digitum Dei, huic vel illi populo libertatis appetentiori, vel servituti assuetæ magis hanc vel illam formam aptantis, & personas dotibus rectè imperandi & judicandi candi instruentis, sequi. Quae supinè negligere maximorum in Republica malorum causa est. Sicut vero optimum regimen est, in quo Dei verbum summam auctoritatem habet, & caeteroquin ordo & consensus defenditur, quale in populo Dei diu mansit: ita optima regiminis forma illa est, quae indoli populi inprimis congruit, sive illa unius, sive optimatum, sive totius populi sit. Non enim optima forma est, quae simpliciter & in idea talis est, qualis sine dubio Monarchia est, cum & regimen Divinum, perfectissimum utique, Monarchicum sit, sed quae in his vel illis circumstantiis salutis & incolumitati populi conducibilior est.
units.tr: CXVII. Although the authority of magistrates is from God, it belongs to the people to choose and designate the form and manner of the commonwealth, and the persons who are to bear the magistracy, to whom such a weighty charge is to be entrusted. The people are not free to act at their own pleasure in establishing the form of government and its officers, but must follow the divine indications, as it were the finger of God, which fits this or that form to this or that people, according as it is more inclined to liberty or more accustomed to servitude, and which equips persons with the gifts for ruling and judging rightly. To neglect these carelessly is the cause of the greatest evils in a commonwealth. Just as the best government is that in which the word of God holds supreme authority, and in which order and consent are otherwise maintained, as it long remained among the people of God, so the best form of government is that which above all suits the character of the people, whether it be that of one man, of the best men, or of the whole people. For the best form is not that which is simply and in the abstract such, as monarchy undoubtedly is (although the divine government, which is most perfect, is indeed monarchical), but that which in these or those circumstances is more conducive to the safety and welfare of the people.

units.la: CXVIII. Magistratus non debent ἀκεΛ- ται και ἀνυπεύθυνοι judicio nulli obnoxii, constituì.
units.tr: CXVIII. Magistrates ought not to be set up as [ἀκεΛ- ται και ἀνυπεύθυνοι], answerable to no judgment.

units.la: Nam quod Deus & recta ratio ab omnibus curari vult jubetque, id à cura omnium removeri non potest. Et quod hominum bono datum & institutum Divinitus est, adeóque proprie non aliud est, quàm potestas bonum procurandi, & malum coercendi, id in potestatem & licentiam malum impune faciendi, pietatem persequendi, impietatem & injustitiam propagandi, imperandi, & ad eam cogendi, denique Rempublicam & Ecclesiam pervertendi, converti non debet. Qui ergo populus tyrannos sic grassantes, δημιουργος populivoros, & ad impietatem omnem duces, atque pietatis & reipublicae ipsius hostes apertos fert, & potestatem malefaciendi instituit, séque per tales ad impietatem seduci, & rempublicam atque Ecclesiam perdi patitur, is reus fit omnium malorum, quae tyranni faciunt. Ideo Jobo vitio datur, quòd validos brachio, & authoritatem habentes sedendi in terra, leges & mores sibi subjiciendi, tulit, Job. XXII. 8. Peccatum enim ingens, & charitatis communi hominum societati debitae clades est, tacendo, patiendo & mussando admittere, ut tyrannis improborum & blasphemorum ad oppressionem veritatis & pietatis in Ecclesia constituatur, à qua culpa excusari non possunt, quibus Deus donum, jus & locum resistendi dedit, quanquam & cujusvis est, si non ex potestate illis resistere, at certè omni vocis ac vitae renixu se illis opponere, & novissima potius pati, quàm tyrannidem probare. Ubi liberam Rempublicam populus habet, Magistratuum & Ephororum est libertatem tueri, nec novis Dominis eam subjicere, quod haud levius crimen foret, quàm si quis liberum hominem sine culpa sua ἐξανδραποδι- ζειν mancipem facere, & in duram servitutem conjicere instituerit. Si tamen hominum voluntate, delicto vel calamitate effectum sit, ut quidam non sint liberi, sed δεσποτικῶ imperio regantur, sicut & liber homo servus, mercenarius vel mancipium fieri potest, ferenda per humile obsequium, tristis ea conditio est usque ad aras, quandiu Deus offendi non praecipitur. Nam ubi imperia discordant, minor potestas majori, imò maximae & infinitae cedat oportet. In iis verò, quae tristia, non turpia sunt, etiam σχολιοῖς χυρίοις obliquis Dominis, non praestantibus, quae mutuò debent, & quibus se accommodare difficile est, 1. Petr. II. 18. dummodo ne in publicam populi perniciem ceu hostes ejus grassentur, obsecundandum est, quia Dei voluntas est, ut id fiat, & ea re Deus coli-
units.tr: For what God and right reason wish and command to be cared for by all cannot be removed from the care of all. And what has been given and instituted by God for the good of men, and so properly is nothing other than the power to promote good and restrain evil, ought not to be turned into a power and licence to do evil with impunity, to persecute piety, to spread impiety and injustice, to command and compel men to it, and finally to overthrow the commonwealth and the Church. Therefore, if a people endures tyrants who rage in this way, [δημιουργος] devourers of the people, leaders into all impiety, and open enemies of piety and of the commonwealth itself, and if it sets up power to do evil and allows itself to be seduced into impiety by such men, and allows the commonwealth and the Church to be destroyed, that people is guilty of all the evils the tyrants commit. For this reason Job is rebuked because he set up laws and customs for himself, the mighty men of arm, who had authority and dwelt on the earth (Job 22:8). For it is a great sin, and a ruin of the charity owed to the common society of men, to allow this by keeping silent, enduring and muttering, so that the tyranny of wicked and blasphemous men is established for the oppression of truth and piety in the Church. Those to whom God has given the right and the place to resist cannot be excused from this fault; and anyone at all, if he cannot resist them with power, should at least set himself against them with every effort of voice and life, and rather suffer the worst than approve tyranny. Where the people have a free commonwealth, it is the duty of the magistrates and ephors to defend its liberty, and not to subject it to new masters; this would be no less a crime than if someone were to set about enslaving a free man without fault of his own and casting him into harsh servitude. If, however, through the will of men, or through crime or calamity, it has come about that some are not free but are ruled by [δεσποτικῶ] despotic command, just as a free man may become a servant, hired man or slave, then that condition, to be borne by humble obedience, is grievous indeed, as long as God is not commanded to be offended. For where commands conflict, the lesser power must yield to the greater, indeed to the greatest and infinite power. In matters that are grievous but not shameful, submission is required even to [σχολιοῖς χυρίοις] crooked masters who do not give what they owe to each other and with whom it is hard to agree (1 Pet. 2:18), provided they do not rage against the people to its public ruin as its enemies; for it is God's will that this be done, and by this God is honoured.

units.la: tur. Time Jehovam, fili mi, & Regem, &c. ירא את יהוה בני ומלך cum novas res molientibus ne commiscearis, Prov. XXIV. 21. Toleranda enim sunt, quae sine magna pernicie emendari nequeunt: nec evellendum zizanium est cum periculo tritici. Expectanda potius est vel successura emendatio, vel supremi judicis correctio, qui vim & injuriam perpetuam esse non finit. Si tamen populus aliquis justis etiam modis liber fieri potest, Deo ipso libertatis januam aperiente, negligi id non debet, quia potius id est, quàm ut cum discrimine pietatis & vitae serviat. Servus vocatus es? Ne tibi sit cura. Sed si etiam liber fieri poteris, utere potius, 1. Cor. VII. 21. Si autem libero fieri honesta ratione non licet, & ab injustis & duris Dominis iniquum & durum quidpiam perferendum est, patientia opus est, nec recalcitrandum est. Deum timete, Regem honorate. Servi heris in omnibus cum timore subjecti estote; non tantum bonis & aequis, sed etiam obliquis. Hoc enim gratia est, si quis propter conscientiam Dei perferat tristia, patiens injusta, 1. Petr. II. 17. 18. 19. Sunt enim imperia non tantum πολιτικα civilia, sed etiam δεσποτικα herilia à Deo; sed saepenumero ut judice, delicta per ferulam ejusmodi ulciscente & castigante. Qui igitur talibus dura imponentibus resistit, is Deo resistit. Et perinde subditi talium Dominorum imperia, atque filii parentum duriorum etiam iras perferre debent. Æqui enim parentes majorem in modum amandi; iniquiores & amandi, ceu parentes, & ferendi, ceu duri parentes sunt. Sicut autem potestati legitimae resistendum non est: ita ei, qui potestatem legitimam, consentiente populo, vel alio titulo justo, non habet, sed eam sibi arrogat, vel potestatis & jurisdictionis suae limites claré positos transgreditur, impunè potest non pareri, & licitè, justè, imò & debitè, sed modis tamen legitimis, qui minimùm in Republica perturbationis afferant, per Ephoros, qui in bene constitutis imperiis jurium & jurisdictionis atque potestatis uniuscujusque assertores sunt, resistitur.
units.tr: Fear the LORD, my son, and the king [ירא את יהוה בני ומלך] (Prov. 24:21). Do not mix yourself with those who are eager for new things. For what cannot be amended without great ruin must be endured, and the tares must not be uprooted at the risk of the wheat. Rather, one must wait either for a reform that will follow in time, or for the correction of the supreme judge, who does not allow violence and injustice to last for ever. If, however, a people can become free even by lawful means, God himself opening the door of liberty, this must not be neglected, for it is better than to serve at the peril of piety and life. Were you called while a slave? Do not be concerned about it. But if you can also become free, rather use it (1 Cor. 7:21). If, however, it is not lawful to become free by honest means, and some unjust and harsh thing must be endured from unjust and harsh masters, patience is needed, and one must not kick back. Fear God, honour the king. Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward. For this is grace, if for conscience toward God a man endures grief, suffering wrongfully (1 Pet. 2:17–19). For authorities are from God not only as civil, but also as [δεσποτικα] lordly, yet often as a judge, punishing offences through such a rod. Therefore whoever resists those who impose harsh burdens resists God. And in the same way the subjects of such harsh masters must bear their commands, just as children must bear even the anger of rather harsh parents. For parents who are just are to be loved greatly; those who are more unjust are to be loved, as parents are, and endured, as harsh parents are. But just as one must not resist lawful power, so one who does not hold lawful power, either by the consent of the people or by some other just title, but arrogates it to himself, or transgresses the clearly fixed limits of his power and jurisdiction, may with impunity be not obeyed, and lawfully, justly, and even rightly, but still by lawful means that bring the least disturbance to the commonwealth; he is resisted through the ephors, who in well-constituted states are the defenders of the rights, jurisdiction and power of each.

units.la: CXIX. Futuros quandoque in Ecclesia esse, qui dominationem rejiciant, & δόξας gloriae, excellentias, seu eos, qui gloriam & τιμὴν honorem merentur, non reformident, sed blasphement, praedictum est, 2. Petr. II. 10. Jud. vers. 8. dicentes: Quis Dominus nobis? Psal. XII. 5. Rex quid faciet nobis? Hos. X. 3. Blasphemiam id Scripturae vocant, quia magistratus non tantùm à Deo ordinati sunt, sed etiam Dei vicem referunt, & Deo & Christo obedire & servire, atque gloriam suam in civitatem Dei inferre debent. Blasphemant verò non uno modo Pontificii, uti in loco diximus, & dicemus amplius. Blasphemant Anabaptistae, debitum Magistratui Politico subjectionem & obedientiam non parum luxantes hypothesi illa, quòd Christus à populo suo officium Regium, eique annexa, Regnum temporale, gladium, vindictam & bellum abstulerit. Hinc istum conscientiis laqueum injiciunt, quòd nefas Magistratui servire in bello gerendo, aliisque similibus, quia veris discipulis, & veris ovibus, duce inermi agno, quotquot se dederunt ad serviendum Jesu Christo, pacifico Solomoni, non sit retrospiciendum ad serviendum alteri Domino. Fa-tentur Pontificii & Anabaptistae adversus Magistratus blasphemiae. tentur tamen alibi, Magistratibus officio fungentibus, utpote ordinationi Divinæ, obedientiam deberi, ut Dei ministris, etiam propter Dominum. Sed fallunt, sic statim id explicantes, quòd Magistratus officium in se, utpote à Deo ordinatum, non habeat peccatum, vel iniquitatem; attamen functio ejus à Deo Christianis nec mandata, nec permissa sit. Inprimis nullum Magistratui Christiano jus Majestatis circa sacra, quo Christi leges suis legibus & mandatis, ad tuendam Ecclesiæ pacem & tranquillitatem, & compescendos turbatores intus, vel hostes & oppressores foris arcendòs, cumulet, competere pertendunt. Iidem rogati, an Magistratus Christianus in functione Magistratus manens salvari posset; prætextu verborum S. Pauli: De iis, qui extra sunt, Deus judicat, 1. Cor. V. 13. responsionem categoricam detrectant. Forte, ita nostri quærenti ipsi Magistratui responderunt, uni cuipiam salus contingere posset; vernaculis verbis impudenter sic enuntiantes: Es möchte greiter (forte fortuna) einem grathen/ quasi salus aleæ jactu obtingeret. Cùm verò Potestas civilis Divina, uti vidimus, ordinatio, & potestas omnis à Deo sit, saluti hominis Christiani illa obesse neutiquam potest. Quomodo enim obesset id, quod Deus in commune bonum societatis humanæ, & ipsius etiam Ecclesiæ, instituit, probat & imponit? Et in V. T. Magistratus provinciam susceptam & obitam saluti fidelium remoram nullam attulisse, negare non audent. In Novo verò Testamento eandem ordinationem Divinam manere, S. Paulus Rom. XIII. 1. 2. &c. disertè inculcat. Quæ de nuda tantùm permissione illi nequicquam interpretantur. Nam τάξις ordinatio Dei, cui propter conscientiam etiam parendum est, non est nuda rei per se illicitæ permissio, seu non cohibitio. Si enim in N. T. Christiano homini Magistratum gerere illicitum esset, vel inde id proveniret, quia id à Christo & Apostolis expressè vetitum est: vel quia talis religionis Christianæ genius est, ut cum eo munus Magistratus consistere nequeat. Sed neutrum verum est. Non illud, quia nullibi id vetitum est, & in N. T. indicia extant, ex quibus munus hoc non esse illicitum, evidenter colligi potest. Præterquam enim quòd omnis Potestas & à Deo esse & nonnisi à Deo esse, & ordinatio Divina esse dicitur, Rom. XIII. 1. qualia quæ sunt, illicita esse non possunt; etiam jubemur orare pro Regibus, & omnibus in potestate constitutis, ut sub eorum auspiciis tranquillam vitam transfigamus, hac addita ratione, quia Deus vult omnes salvos fieri, & ad cognitionem veritatis pervenire, 1. Tim. II. 1-5. Eum igitur in finem pro Regibus orandum, ut ad cognitionem veritatis pervenientes salventur, & sub Regibus ita conversis vitam tranquillam in omni pietate & honestate degamus. Qui finis obtineri non posset, si Regibus conversis ilico sceptrum deponendum esset. Imò id vitam Christianis duriorem efficeret, si Regibus ad Christum conversis, & sceptra ex vi legis Christi deponentibus, durio-res & sæviores alii succederent. Neque uspiam magistratum abdicasse conversi ad Christum, quales Nicodemus, Josephus Arimatheensis, Cornelius centurio, Paulus Sergius fuerunt,
units.tr: It has been foretold that there will at some time be in the Church people who reject lordship and do not dread to blaspheme the glories (δόξας), the dignitaries, or those who deserve glory and honour (τιμήν): 2 Peter 2:10; Jude, verse 8, "Who is Lord over us?"; Psalm 12:5, "What will the king do to us?"; Hosea 10:3. Scripture calls this blasphemy, because magistrates are not only ordained by God but also bear God's place, and they ought to obey and serve God and Christ and bring their glory into the City of God. The Papists blaspheme in more than one way, as we have said in its place and shall say further. The Anabaptists blaspheme too, greatly weakening the subjection and obedience owed to the civil magistrate by the hypothesis that Christ took from his people the royal office and what is joined to it, namely the temporal kingdom, the sword, vengeance and war. From this they cast a snare on consciences, holding it unlawful for a Christian to serve the magistrate in waging war and in similar tasks, since true disciples and true sheep, following the unarmed Lamb, have given themselves to serve Jesus Christ, the peaceful Solomon, and must not look back to serve another lord. The Papists and Anabaptists admit blasphemy against the magistrates, yet they confess elsewhere that obedience is owed to magistrates in office, as to the ministers of God's ordinance, even for the Lord's sake. But they deceive, explaining it at once in this way: that the office of magistrate in itself, as ordained by God, has no sin or iniquity, yet its exercise has not been commanded or permitted to Christians by God. First, they contend that no right of majesty in sacred matters belongs to a Christian magistrate, by which he would add Christ's laws to his own laws and commands, to preserve the peace and tranquillity of the Church, and to restrain disturbers within or to ward off enemies and oppressors without. When asked whether a Christian magistrate remaining in the function of magistracy could be saved, they refuse to give a plain answer, under the pretext of St Paul's words, "God judges those who are outside," 1 Corinthians 5:13. Our people, when they asked the magistrate himself, have answered thus: "Perhaps (forte) it might be that someone is saved," shamelessly expressing it in the vernacular, "Es möchte greiter (forte fortuna) einem grathen," as if salvation came by the throw of dice. But since civil power is a divine ordinance, as we have seen, and all power is from God, it can by no means hinder a Christian's salvation. For how could that hinder which God has established, approved and imposed for the common good of human society and of the Church itself? And they dare not deny that in the Old Testament the magistrate's office, undertaken and discharged, brought no hindrance to the salvation of the faithful. In the New Testament St Paul expressly insists that the same divine ordinance remains, Romans 13:1, 2, etc. Their attempts to read this as mere permission are in vain. For τάξις, the ordinance of God, which must be obeyed even for conscience's sake, is not a bare permission of a thing unlawful in itself, nor a mere non-prohibition. If it were unlawful for a Christian man in the New Testament to bear the magistracy, this would follow either because Christ and the Apostles expressly forbade it, or because the genius of the Christian religion is such that the office of magistrate cannot consist with it. But neither is true. Not the first, because nowhere is it forbidden, and in the New Testament there are indications from which it can clearly be gathered that this office is not unlawful. For apart from the fact that all power is from God and is said to be from God alone and to be a divine ordinance (Romans 13:1), and such things cannot be unlawful, we are also commanded to pray for kings and for all who are set in authority, that under their protection we may lead a quiet life, with the added reason that God wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:1–5). Therefore we must pray for kings to this end, that those who come to the knowledge of the truth may be saved, and that under such converted kings we may live a tranquil life in all piety and honesty. This end could not be attained if kings, on their conversion, had at once to lay down the sceptre. Indeed it would make life harder for Christians if, when kings became Christian and laid down their sceptres by virtue of Christ's law, harsher and more cruel rulers succeeded them. Nor is it read anywhere that converts to Christ, such as Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, the centurion Cornelius, or Sergius Paulus, laid down the magistracy,

units.la: leguntur, abdicaturi certè vel sponte, vel ex mandato convertentium, si Christus muneris illius functionem prohibuisset. Non enim simplex hoc peccatum fuisset, sed longam peccatorum actuúmque Christi legibus repugnantium catenam post se traxisset. Non hoc, quia cùm munus magistratus legislatione, judiciorum etiam capitalium secundum eas administratione, & subditorum suorum defensione constet, nullum actuum eorum genio religionis Christianæ repugnare mox demonstrabimus. Cùmque sine multarum virtutum stipatu geri non possit, nullis melius quàm Christianis committi potest. Neque leve pro Magistratu argumentum est, quòd sine eo nulla civitas, nulla societas consistere possit, sed omnia confundi & perturbari, bonos impune affligi, atque sceleratissimorum libidini, & rapinis exponi, & malos triumphare semper, & scelerum suorum impunito exemplo alios seducì, & deteriores reddi necesse foret. Quod adeò verum est, ut ne piratarum quidem & latronum societas sine rectoribus vel per exiguum tempus subsistere possit. Sicut denique Evangelium non tollit politiam, sed perficit: ita nec ordinem politicum in officiis civilibus, Actor. X. 1. &c. 1. Petr. II. 13. 14. tributis, Rom. XIII. 6. 7. servitutibus, 1. Cor. VII. 20. &c. contractibus, Actor. IV. 34. abrogat.
units.tr: even though they would certainly have had to lay it down, either of their own accord or by command of those who converted them, if Christ had forbidden the exercise of that office. For this would not have been a simple sin, but would have dragged after it a long chain of sins and acts contrary to the laws of Christ. Nor is it so, because, since the office of magistrate consists in legislation, in the administration of judgements (including capital ones) according to those laws, and in the defence of its subjects, I shall soon show that none of these acts is repugnant to the spirit of the Christian religion. And since it cannot be carried on without the accompaniment of many virtues, it can be committed to no one better than to Christians. Nor is it a slight argument for the magistracy that without it no state and no society can exist, but everything would be thrown into confusion and disorder, good men would be afflicted with impunity and exposed to the lust and plunder of the most wicked, the evil would always triumph, others would be seduced by the unpunished example of their crimes and made worse. This is so true that not even a society of pirates and robbers can subsist for even a short time without rulers. Finally, just as the Gospel does not abolish political order but perfects it, so it does not abrogate the political order in civil offices (Acts 10:1, etc.; 1 Peter 2:13, 14), in tributes (Romans 13:6, 7), in servitudes (1 Corinthians 7:20, etc.), or in contracts (Acts 4:34).

units.la: CXX. Levia hominum imperitorum & ἰχυρογνωμόνων objectamenta sunt. Nimrodo enim, ex impia Chami progenie oriundo, authore Magistratum & politicum imperium omne in mundum incessisse ex Genes. X. 8. 9. ineptè colligunt. Fuit ille Venator imperiorum coram Domino, pietatis & religionis prætextu utens. Sed hoc tyranni & hypocritæ, non verò pii magistratus & imperii est. Venari homines est opprimere homines. Venando venantur me ut aviculam, qui inimicitiam adversus me gerunt sine causa, Thren. III. 52. Non igitur primus Magistratus, sed primus Magistratus tyrannicus, despoticus & hypocriticus ille fuit. Nam Magistratus veri antiquiorem longè originem supra pandimus. Et sprevit Deus Israelem, cùm Regem peteret, 1. Sam. VIII. 7. non spernens magistratum, quia diu ante extitit, sed novam magistratus formam, repugnantem illi, quam primitus instituerat. Cum cujus contemptu impotens postulatio conjuncta fuit. Cæterùm jam ante etiam Deus Regiam potestatem per Mosen certis legibus circumscripserat, Deut. XVII. 14. 15. & Regiam potestatem semel institutam ita probavit, ut ejus contemptores & violatores בני בליעל filii Belialis, 1. Sam. X. 26. appellentur. Præterea Deus dicens: Ipsi constituerunt Reges; at non ex me: præficiunt Principes, quos non agnosco, Hos. VIII. 4. de Jeroboami Regno malis artibus & rebellione, non consulto, sed præterito Deo, quæsito & idololatria novitia sancita, queritur. Et constituendi sic novi Regis modum improbans, Regiam dignitatem in se spectatam non improbavit; imò Israelis etiam Regibus quibusdam benedixit, & Elisæum misit, qui Jehu, Regem Israelis ungeret, 2. Reg. IX. 2. Jothamus verò in parabola non ficum, oleam, vel aliam arborem frugiferam, sed cynosbatum inter arbores ad imperium se offerre, hoc est, AbiAbimelechum, hominem trucem, occisis Jerubahalis liberis, Regnum affectasse ostendens, Jud. IX. 9. non vel Magistratum, vel Regiam dignitatem, sed affectatum per tyrannidem imperium perstrinxit. Quod vero Christus in N. T. & ipse Magistratu abstinuit, Luc. XII. 14. Joh. VI. 15. XVIII. 36. & discipulis suis eodem interdixit, Luc. XXII. 25. 26. non ideo factum, quasi Magistratu fungi Christianus nemo possit: Christus enim fuit Rex regni spiritualis; Christiani omnes sunt Regni hujus subditi; sed alii insuper ministri in eodem regno; alii vero etiam Domini in Regno terreno, pro cujusque vocatione. Conformes quidem Christo fieri Christiani omnes tenentur in spiritualibus, at non in temporalibus, quorum regimen Christus ut Mediator non gerit. Apostolis vero suis Christus discipulatum, alteriusque generis ministerium, non dominatum dederat. Ac licet praedictum sit fore, ut Lapis ille de monte coesus, & sine manibus latus, Christus omnia Regna, Nebucadnezari in colosso exhibita, comminueret, Dan. II. 34. 44. 45. tamen Regnum Christi non adversatur Regnis, Principatibus & civitatibus, quandiu Ecclesia in mundo est, donec aboleat omnem Principatum, & omnem potestatem & potentiam, & Regnum Deo ac Patri tradat, I. Cor. XV. 24. Nam & Reges ei Prophetia assignat curatores, & Reginas nutritias, Esaj. XLIX. 23. & in gratia ac veritate constitui thronos, ibid. XVI. 5. asserit. Vetat quinetiam Apostolus fieri servos hominum, I. Cor. VII. 23. Non obedientiam Potestatibus debitam prohibens, sed caecam hominum servitutem, & vilem servumque animum, quibusvis Dominis obsequi paratum, idque in rebus praesertim Divinis & spiritualibus, in quibus nulli homini serviendum est. Alias idem S. Paulus servis author est, ut Dominis suis fideliter serviant, Ephes. VI. 5. Col. III. 22. 23. Licet etiam Regna civilia sint de hoc mundo, secus ac Regnum Christi est, Joh. XVIII. 36. non ideo tamen Christianis, qui & ipsi, quoad spiritualem statum suum non sunt de hoc mundo, gerere illa nefas est, quia Evangelium & Regnum Christi non tollit politiam, quae de mundo est. Si enim civis Regni Christi maritus, paterfamilias, Dominus esse potest, cur non etiam Magistratus? Aliud igitur est esse de hoc mundo, hoc est, ex hominibus, qui in terra, in mundo vivunt & non Divina, sed humana authoritate, potestate, consilio, praecepto rem gerere; qui sensus hujus loci est; aliud esse de hoc mundo, hoc est, mundi peccatis contaminari, quo sensu phrasis illa, Joh. XVII. 14. 16. intelligitur. Sed & Magistratus sic est ἀνθρωπίνη κτίσις humana creatio, ut tamen eidem obediendum sit propter Dominum, I. Petr. II. 13. Humana enim creatio vocatur, non quod Divinae institutionis non sit, sed merae humanae, cum S. Paulus Divinam ordinationem diserte dixerit, Rom. XIII. 1. sed vel, sive quia est creatio Dei, sed ex hominibus; vel quia ab hominibus creatus, ordinatus est. Denique non ideo Christianus Magistratum gerere non potest, quia vetatur malo resistere, vindictam exercere, & misericors, placabilis, lenis esse, & offensas condonare jubetur, Matth. V. 38--40. Magistratus enim Christianus duplicem personam gerit, unam communem, ex vocatione communi cum aliis Christianis; alteram singularem, ex officio singulari, tanquam Dei minister gladio armatus. Ex vocatione communi, non resistit malo, non indulget vindictae, sed misericors, placabilis est. Ex officio singulari vindictam Dei exercet, & gladium, ceu minister Dei, justissime distringit.
units.tr: CXX. The objections of the unlearned and the obstinate [ἰσχυρογνωμόνων] are trivial. They foolishly infer from Genesis 10:8-9 that Nimrod, sprung from the impious line of Ham, introduced magistracy and every political empire into the world. He was a hunter of kingdoms before the Lord, using the pretext of piety and religion. But this is the mark of tyrants and hypocrites, not of a godly magistrate or empire. To hunt men is to oppress men. They hunt me like a bird, those who are my enemies without cause, Lam. 3:52. So it was not the first magistrate who was Nimrod, but the first tyrannical, despotic and hypocritical magistrate. For we have shown above that the origin of true magistracy is far older. God also rejected Israel when they asked for a king, 1 Sam. 8:7, not rejecting magistracy because it had existed long before, but rejecting a new form of magistracy at odds with the one he had first instituted. Their unbridled demand was joined with contempt for that. Moreover, God had already, through Moses, limited royal power by fixed laws, Deut. 17:14-15, and he so approved royal power once established that its despisers and violators are called sons of Belial [בני בליעל], 1 Sam. 10:26. Again, when God says, They have set up kings, but not by me; they have appointed princes, and I did not acknowledge them, Hos. 8:4, he complains of the kingdom of Jeroboam, established by wicked arts and rebellion, not by consulting God but by passing him over, and sanctioned by a newly invented idolatry. In condemning this manner of setting up a new king, he did not condemn the royal dignity considered in itself. Indeed he blessed some kings of Israel and sent Elisha to anoint Jehu as king of Israel, 2 Kings 9:2. Jotham, in his parable, shows that the bramble, and not the fig, olive or other fruitful tree, offers itself to rule over the trees, that is, that Abimelech, a savage man who had slain the sons of Jerubbaal, aspired to the kingdom, Judg. 9:9. He thereby attacked not magistracy or royal dignity, but power seized by tyranny. As for Christ himself abstaining from magistracy in the New Testament, Luke 12:14, John 6:15, 18:36, and forbidding his disciples the same, Luke 22:25-26, this was not done as though no Christian could hold office. Christ was the King of a spiritual kingdom; all Christians are subjects of this kingdom; but some are also ministers in that kingdom, and others are lords in the earthly kingdom, according to each one's calling. All Christians are bound to be conformed to Christ in spiritual things, but not in temporal things, whose government Christ does not exercise as Mediator. To his apostles Christ gave discipleship and a ministry of another kind, not lordship. Although it was foretold that the stone cut out of the mountain without hands would crush all the kingdoms shown in Nebuchadnezzar's image, Dan. 2:34, 44-45, the kingdom of Christ does not oppose kingdoms, principalities and states for as long as the Church is in the world, until he abolishes every principality, power and might, and delivers the kingdom to God and the Father, 1 Cor. 15:24. For prophecy also assigns kings to him as guardians and queens as nursing mothers, Isa. 49:23, and asserts that thrones are established in grace and truth, ibid. 16:5. Nor does the Apostle forbid becoming servants of men, 1 Cor. 7:23, in order to prohibit the obedience owed to powers, but blind human servitude and a base, servile mind ready to obey any masters, especially in divine and spiritual matters, where no man is to be served. Elsewhere the same Apostle Paul urges servants to serve their masters faithfully, Eph. 6:5, Col. 3:22-23. Although civil kingdoms are of this world, unlike the kingdom of Christ, John 18:36, it is nonetheless not wrong for Christians to hold them, although Christians themselves, as to their spiritual state, are not of this world, because the Gospel and the kingdom of Christ do not abolish the civil order, which is of this world. For if a citizen of Christ's kingdom can be a husband, a father of a family, or a lord, why not also a magistrate? It is one thing to be of this world, that is, of men who live on earth, in the world, and who conduct affairs by human rather than divine authority, power, counsel and command; this is the sense of the present passage. It is another thing to be of this world, that is, to be contaminated by the sins of the world; it is in this sense that the phrase in John 17:14, 16 is understood. Moreover, the magistrate is a human creation [ἀνθρωπίνη κτίσις], yet still to be obeyed for the Lord's sake, 1 Pet. 2:13. He is called a human creation not because he is without divine institution, but because he is purely human, since Paul expressly calls it a divine ordinance, Rom. 13:1; rather, either because it is God's creation but through men, or because it has been created and ordained by men. Finally, a Christian cannot hold the magistracy not because he is forbidden to resist evil, to exercise vengeance, and is commanded to be merciful, placable, gentle, and to forgive offences, Matt. 5:38-40. For a Christian magistrate bears a twofold person: one common, from the calling he shares with other Christians; the other particular, from his singular office, as a minister of God armed with the sword. In his common calling he does not resist evil, does not indulge in vengeance, but is merciful and placable. In his particular office he exercises God's vengeance, and, as God's minister, most justly draws the sword.

units.la: CXXI. Sicut vero Magistratus blasphemantes & rejicientes fidem Christianam abnegant: ita ἐξαπολλύντες Potestatum adoratores, at Purpurae potius quam Dei cultores, qui Magistratus quosvis legibus & judiciis eximunt, & eorum imperia qualiacunque subditos ad caecam & sedentariam assentiendi & obsequendi necessitatem obligare pertendunt, absolutam denique iis potestatem iis arrogant, & subditis in cunctis imperiis eorum nil nisi caeci obsequii gloriam relinquunt, impie Deum ipsum Titanico ausu de solio suo deturbant, & humanae libidini subjiciunt. Horum in censu Machiavellus Florentinus, & Hobbesius Malmesburiensis Anglus, sunt, quos Pseudo-Politicorum turba si non dogmate, at certe praxi quotidiana impie sectatur. De quibus Loc. XIV. § III. 23. nonnihil diximus. Hobbesii certe ξυγίαι δόξαι sunt. Imperantium potestatem esse indefinitam, quia ejus terminus a nemine sciatur: Societatis civilis initium non a Deo, sed a mutuo metu esse: statum naturalem esse statum inimicitiae & belli: Oligarchiam, Anarchiam & Tyrannidem non esse statum civitatis a legitima Aristocratia, Democratia & Monarchia diversum, sed tria duntaxat nomina diversa ab iis impositia, quibus Regimen aliquod displicuit. Nihil injustum a Principe fieri posse. Nullam subdito proprietatem ejusmodi in rebus suis esse, ut ab ejus usu Rex excludi possit: Nihil denique a Rege praecipi posse, quod facto ita improbum fit, ut ipsius mandatum qualescunque subditorum actus indubie non justificet. Fidem a Principe datam non obligare; & si quae alia ejusmodi assertionum imperiosarum prodigia ad absolutae Principum potestatis defensionem aurigantia passim ille protulit.
units.tr: CXXI. Just as magistrates who blaspheme and reject the Christian faith deny it, so the destroyers [ἐξαπολλύντες] who are worshippers of potentates, rather than of God, and who seek to free magistrates from all laws and judgments, to bind their subjects by necessity of blind and passive assent and obedience to whatever commands they issue, and finally to claim for them absolute power, leaving the subjects in every government nothing but the glory of blind obedience, these impiously tear God himself from his throne with Titanic audacity and subject him to human lust. Among these is Machiavelli of Florence, and Hobbes of Malmesbury in England, whom the crowd of pseudo-politicians impiously follows, if not in doctrine, at least in daily practice. We have said something about them in Loc. XIV, § III, 23. Hobbes's opinions are certainly akin [ξυγίαι δόξαι]. The power of rulers is indefinite, because no one knows its limit. The beginning of civil society is not from God but from mutual fear. The natural state is a state of enmity and war. Oligarchy, anarchy and tyranny are not states of the commonwealth different from lawful aristocracy, democracy and monarchy, but merely three different names imposed on them by those who disliked some form of government. Nothing unjust can be done by the prince. No subject has such ownership of his own goods that the king can be excluded from their use. Finally, nothing can be commanded by the king which is so wrongful in fact that the command of the ruler does not indubitably justify whatever acts of the subjects. A promise given by the prince does not bind; and whatever other monstrous imperious assertions of this sort he has everywhere put forward, driving his chariot in defence of the absolute power of princes.

units.la: Pseudo-politicorum, Machiavelli, Hobbesii, tyrannidem & caecam obedientiam propugnantium elenchus. stinguuntur. Si nunquam, tum judicium de tyrannis virorum Ϡεοπνεύςων veritati non erit consentaneum; & recta atq; prava imperandi,& in imperio vel publicam utilitatem, vel animi sui libidinem unicè spectantium ratio non differet. Accedit,quòd hominum affectus præviam de re bona vel mala,regimine recto vel pravo notitiam supponant, adeóque hæc nomina necessariò conceptum eorum, qui iis utuntur, diversum involvunt. Ita non propterea idololatria à vero Dei veri cultu non distinguitur, quia sunt, qui judicant, idololatriam non esse, quod vera idololatria est. Si tyrannus à legitimo Principe non differt,quomodo Deus tyrannos excitasse ad puniendum populum,Esaj. XIX. 4. eorundem sævitiam reprimere in gratiam fidelium,Ezech. XXXIV. 25.26. dicitur? Ac licèt judicium de tyranno affectus comitetur,quia tyrannis res merito invisa & exosa bonis omnibus est; tamen non semper judicium de tyrannide ab affectu,quod Hobbesiani pertendunt, oritur.
units.tr: Refutation of the pseudo-politicians, of Machiavelli and Hobbes, who champion tyranny and blind obedience. Are they to be distinguished? If never, then the judgment about tyrants of men who speak in God's Spirit would not agree with the truth; and the reasoning of those who command rightly and of those who command wrongly, and of those who in government look only to the public good or only to the lust of their own minds, would not differ. Moreover, the affections of men presuppose a prior knowledge of what is good or bad, of right or wrong government, and so these names necessarily involve a concept different for those who use them. Thus idolatry is not distinguished from the true worship of the true God merely because there are those who judge that idolatry is not idolatry. If a tyrant does not differ from a lawful prince, how is it said that God raised up tyrants to punish the people, Isa. 19:4, and restrained their savagery for the sake of the faithful, Ezek. 34:25-26? And although a judgment about a tyrant is accompanied by feeling, because tyranny is rightly hated and detested by all good men, nevertheless judgment about tyranny does not always arise from feeling, as the Hobbesians contend.

units.la: CXXII. Absolutam & infinitam imperantium potestatem, & cæcæ subditorum obedientiæ necessitatem Pseudo-politici rationibus quibusdam suffulcire nequicquam conantur.
units.tr: CXXII. The Pseudo-politicians vainly try to support the absolute and unlimited power of rulers, and the necessity of blind obedience on the part of subjects, with certain arguments.

units.la: Nam jus regium à Samuele, 1. Sam. VIII. 11-19. expositum non morem duntaxat, sed verum etiam jus Regis, qualem Israelitæ postularunt,sed non Divinum,verùm humanum & despoticum fuisse,neque tamen absolutam potestatem continuisse,vel impiis Regibus lenocinari,supra Loc. XVI. 14. ostendimus. Non enim,quod ibidem probavimus,Regis Hebræi infinita nullisque limitibus circumscripta potestas fuit. Filios auscultare parentibus,servos heris obedire ϰαὶ πάντα per omnia Apostolus, Col.III.20.22. & Christus omnia quæ dixerint Scribæ, servare & facere suos,Matth.XXIII.2.3. jussit. Sed vocabulum πάντα omnia non ubique simpliciter universalitatem,sed omnia illa,quæ legitimè & licitè fieri possunt,significat,uti ex Matth.XVIII.19. XXI.22. Marc.XI.24. 1. Cor.II.15. XIII.7. XV.28. Col.I.23. liquet. Contingere enim potest, ut præcepta illa universaliter sumpta observare non liceat. Quid enim si aliud pater,aliud Dominus,aliud Scriba,aliud Nero jusserit? Parendum ergo talibus, quatenus nihil inhonesti & absurdi præcipiunt; atque ita ϰαὶ πάντα per omnia, quæ nec illicita,& parentibus utilia,commoda & decora sunt,sine delectu, cunctatione, vel percunctatione,ac ne opposito quidem voto,Matth.XV. 3. 4. 5. nec exuta in cæteris obedientia, etiam dum injusta parentes & Domini præcipiunt. Ac licèt oris professio,quamMagistratus jubere potest,res tantùm externa sit, non licet tamen Magistratu jubente falsam fidem ore profiteri; uti cæcæ obedientiæ patroni pertendunt; quia Christus id diserte vetuit,dicens: Quisquis me abnegaverit coram hominibus, abnegabo eum coram Patre meo, qui in Cœlis est, Matth. X. 33. Quibus verbis non de solis septuaginta discipulis,qui diu cum Christo conversati jam fuerant, uti Hobbesius detorquet; sed de turba à Christo advocata æquè ac de discipulis, Marc. VIII. 34. 38. Luc. IX. 23. 26. imo de Christianis quibusvis, 2. Tim. II. 11. 12. 14. Ubi præceptum de non abnegando Christo, & seren-
units.tr: For the royal right set out by Samuel (1 Sam. 8:11-19) was not merely the custom but the true right of a king, of the kind the Israelites demanded. It was a human and despotic right, not a divine one, and yet it did not contain absolute power, nor did it flatter wicked kings, as we have shown above at Loc. XVI, §14. For, as we proved in the same place, the power of the Hebrew king was not infinite and bounded by no limits. The Apostle (Col. 3:20-22) and Christ (Matt. 23:2-3) bade children obey their parents and servants obey their masters, "in all things" [καὶ πάντα, "and all things"], "all that the scribes shall say, observe and do." But the word "all" [πάντα, omnia] does not everywhere mean absolute universality; it means all those things which may lawfully and rightfully be done. This is clear from Matt. 18:19; 21:22; Mark 11:24; 1 Cor. 2:15; 13:7; 15:28; Col. 1:23. For it can happen that it is not lawful to observe those precepts taken universally. What if the father commands one thing, the master another, the scribe another, and Nero another? Such commands must be obeyed only so far as they enjoin nothing dishonourable or absurd. Thus obedience "in all things" [καὶ πάντα] extends to whatever is neither unlawful, nor harmful to parents, but is convenient and proper, and it must be given without distinction, hesitation or questioning, and not even with a contrary vow (Matt. 15:3-5); nor should obedience in other matters be laid aside when parents and masters command unjust things. And although the outward profession which a magistrate may order is a merely external matter, it is still not lawful, when the magistrate commands it, to profess a false faith with the mouth, as the advocates of blind obedience contend. Christ expressly forbade this, saying: "Whoever shall deny me before men, I will deny him before my Father who is in heaven" (Matt. 10:33). Hobbes twists these words to refer only to the seventy disciples, who had long been in Christ's company; but they refer equally to the crowd called by Christ and to "the disciples" (Mark 8:34, 38; Luke 9:23, 26), and indeed to all Christians whatsoever (2 Tim. 2:11, 12, 14). Here a general precept is laid down, not to deny Christ, but rather to endure evils, that we may reign with him. [The Latin continues on the next unit.]

units.la: dis potiùs malis,ut cum eo regnemus,generaliter ponitur; sermo est. Neque Naamanis, se incurvantis in ædę Rimmon, & Regem manu sua sustentantis,2. Reg. V. 18. ad rem facit, quia incurvatio illa non erat coram idolo, sed coram Rege,quem se incurvantem manu sua sustentabat. Scitè Tertullianus de Idololat. cap. 16. Utinam, inquit,nec videre possimus,quæ facere nobis nefas est. Sed quoniam malis ita circumsedit seculum idololatria, licebit adesse in quibusdam, quæ nos homini, non idolo officiosos habent. Planè ad Sacerdotium, vel sacrificium vocatus non ibo (proprium enim idoli est officium) sed neque Concilio,neque sumptu.neque alia opera in ejusmodi fungar. Si propter sacrificium vocatus assistam,ergo particeps idololatriæ; si me alia causa conjungit sacrificanti, ero tantùm spectator sacrificantis. Facit huc exemplum Electoris Saxoniæ,cui Lutherus aliíque Theologi, ut Cæsarem ad Missam cumitaretur,Naamanis Syri exemplo allato,non dissuaserunt. Fucum etiam in eo Hobbesiani faciunt, quòd subditum præceptum Principis injustum exequentem à culpa omni absolvunt, eò quòd id respectu habito non ad affectum proprium,sed ad leges Reipublicæ faciat,adeóque hæc non tam subditi,quàm Principis actio sit: neque amplius subditus is sit,qui rebus sic positis Christum abnegat,sed Princeps, & lex civilis. Quæ nimis diluta & fraudulenta sunt. Nam Jeroboamus idololatriæ in vitulis Bethele erectis auctor, 1. Reg. XII. 28. non pro se tantùm peccavit,sed id egit, quo omnis Israelitarum populus, & singuli reos peccati ejusdem se fecerunt. Depulit Jeroboam Israelitas à sequendo Jehovam, & induxit eos ad peccandum peccato magno,& ambulabant filii Israelis in omnibus peccatis Jeroboami, quæ fecerat, donec amoveret Jehova Israelem à facie sua, 2. Reg. XV. 26. XVI. 26. 2.Reg.III.3. Ideo Deus socios Danielis,renuentes coram aurea Nebucadnetzaris statua procumbere,adeóque Regio edicto imparentes, & apertis verbis cultum idoli detrectantes, & propterea in fornacem igneam projectos servavit, & misso Angelo ex incendio eripuit, quia in ipso confisi sunt,& contra edictum Regis prævaricantes exposuerunt corpus suum, ut non colerent, neque adorarent ullum Deum, præter Deum suum,Dan.III.28. Idem Danielem non Regem, ex ejus edicto, sed solum Deum implorantem, & eandem ob causam leonibus objectum, misso Angelo servavit, ne à leonibus læderetur, ibid. VI.22.23. Denique imbellis ille aries Pseudo-politicorum est, cùm voluntatem servi in voluntate Domini contineri, propterea quòd voluntati Domini se subjecit, adeóque jure quidvis ab eo jam exigi posse,objectant. Hæc enim Epicuræorum Dialectica, & nova Monotheletarum hæresis est,quæ voluntates non distinctas duntaxat,sed etiam contrarias in unam compingit. Sed potuit tamen Achabus velle vineam Nabothi: & Nabothus eandem ei negare juste potuit: neque subditi voluntas in voluntate Domini sui continebatur. Quod etiam de voluntate Regum Chaldæorum & Danielis atque Sociorum ejus dici potest. Submiserunt equidem subditi voluntatem suam voluntati imperantium,sed nec omnes eodem gradu æqualiter,nec in omnibus,certè non in rebus fidem & conscientiam spectantibus,nec in libertate residua, pactis conspicuis ab iis,qui principem elegerunt,reservata ; nec eo usque, quin aliquatenus,saltem intrinsecè, vel per suspensionem voluntatis in re dubia,vel per contrariam determinationem voluntatis in re certa ,resistere liceat, sic tamen ut resistentia hæc cum perpetua subditorum,qua privati illi sunt submissione conjungatur, & ad vim imperantibus faciendam non procedat.
units.tr: Nor does the case of Naaman bowing himself in the house of Rimmon and leaning on the king's hand (2 Kings 5:18) bear on the matter, because that bowing was not before the idol but before the king, whom he supported with his hand as he bowed. Tertullian rightly says in De idololatria, ch. 16: "Would that we could not even see what it is unlawful for us to do. But since idolatry so surrounds us in this age, it will be permissible to be present at certain things which oblige us to a man, not to an idol. Certainly, if I am called to the priesthood or to a sacrifice (for that is the proper office of an idol), I will not go; nor will I perform such a duty by giving counsel, or by contributing money, or by any other work of that kind. If I attend a sacrifice because I was summoned to it, then I am a partaker in idolatry; but if some other cause joins me to the one sacrificing, I shall be merely a spectator of the one sacrificing." To this belongs the example of the Elector of Saxony, whom Luther and other theologians did not dissuade from accompanying the emperor Charles to the Mass, citing the example of Naaman the Syrian. The Hobbesians also practise a deception here, in that they absolve from all guilt the subject who carries out an unjust command of the prince, on the ground that in doing so he acts not from his own inclination but in obedience to the laws of the commonwealth, so that it is the act not so much of the subject as of the prince, and the one who in such circumstances denies Christ is no longer the subject but the prince and the civil law. These arguments are too feeble and fraudulent. For Jeroboam, the author of the idolatry in the calves set up at Bethel (1 Kings 12:28), did not sin for himself alone, but acted in such a way that the whole people of Israel, and each individual, became guilty of the same sin. "Jeroboam drove Israel away from following Jehovah, and led them into a great sin, and the children of Israel walked in all the sins of Jeroboam which he had done, until Jehovah removed Israel from his presence" (2 Kings 17:21-23; 2 Kings 3:3 as cited). Therefore God, who preserved the companions of Daniel when they refused to bow down before Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue, and so disobeyed the royal edict and openly refused to worship the idol, and were for that reason cast into the fiery furnace, rescued them by sending an angel out of the fire, "because they trusted in him, and against the king's edict they transgressed and exposed their bodies, so as not to serve or worship any god except their own God" (Dan. 3:28). In the same way he preserved Daniel, who was thrown to the lions for praying to God alone and not to the king by his edict, by sending an angel so that he was not harmed by the lions (ibid. 6:22-23). Finally, the Pseudo-politicians have that feeble battering-ram of objection: that the will of the servant is contained in the will of the master, because he has submitted himself to the will of the master, and therefore they say that anything whatever may now be lawfully demanded of him. But this is the dialectic of the Epicureans and the new heresy of the Monothelites, which crams wills that are not merely distinct but even contrary into one. Yet Ahab could will to have the vineyard of Naboth, and Naboth could justly refuse it to him; nor was the will of the subject contained in the will of his lord. The same can be said of the will of the Chaldean kings and of Daniel and his companions. Subjects indeed submit their will to the will of those who rule, but not all in the same degree or equally, and not in all matters, certainly not in matters touching faith and conscience, nor in the freedom remaining to them, which was reserved by open agreements made by those who chose the prince. Nor may they resist only to such an extent, that is, by inward suspension of the will in a doubtful matter or by a contrary determination of the will in a certain matter, but in such a way that this resistance is joined with the perpetual submission of subjects, by which they are restrained, and does not proceed to the use of force against those in authority.

units.la: CXXIII. Absolutam nullisque finibus circumscriptam Magistratus potestatem adversus Pseudo-politicos oppugnantes,non meremur dicam,quam nobis odio religionis nostræ occæcati Pontificii & Lutherani Doctores nonnulli hoc potissimum tempore, quo Galli per religionis causam profugi apud Principes etiam Lutheranos hospitia quærunt, conscribunt.
units.tr: CXXIII. I do not need to speak of the absolute and unlimited power of the magistrate, which some Papist and Lutheran teachers, blinded by hatred of our religion, write against the Pseudo-politicians who oppose it, especially at this time, when the French who have fled for the sake of religion seek refuge with princes, even Lutheran ones.

units.la: Nam ut illis & religioni universæ nostræ apud Principes suos invidiam conflent, clamant illi,Reformatæ,seu,uti appellant, Calvinisticæ religionis proprium hunc genium esse, quòd obliqua & infida dominantibus sit,& vim Principibus suis religioni suæ adversantibus inferre amet & soleat. Ab hoc genio arcessunt quicquid turbarum civilium à longo tempore in Germania, Gallia, Belgio, Anglia alibique contigit. Addunt Zwinglium exauctorationem Regum Evangelio adversantium suasisse; Mornæum Plessiacum dogma de licitis in Regem pro religione & Ecclesia armis Testamento suo inseruisse ; Paræum in Rom. XIII. 1. disertis verbis statuisse Magistratus inferiores adversus superiores se & Rempublicam & Ecclesiam, seu veram religionem jure defendete posse. De Pontificiis nihil dicam. Quis enim tulerit Gracchos de seditione loquentes? Hi enim sunt,qui coronas & sceptra Principum pridem Papæ pedibus subjecerunt. Lutheranis quibusdam Theologis hoc nomine nobis insultantibus jure occinimus : Parcius ista viris tamen objicienda memento. Non Reformati duntaxat, sed Augustani etiam fuerunt,qui bellum Smalcaldicum,ipsius etiam Lutheri à Jurisconsultis rectiora edocti suffragio probatum,& Germanicum hujus seculi,religionis defendendæ causa susceптum utrumque adversus Cæsares Carolum V. & Ferdinand. II. & III. gesserunt. Restitit urbs Brunsvicensis Duci suo. Dania Christiernum,Svecia Sigismundum Regem expulit ; non Calvini,credo, genio,vel,uti criminantur,turbulento spiritu, ad id adacti omnes. Et de hoc quicquid fiat,non secundum aspectum judicare, sed justum de re ipsa judicium judicare oportet,Joh. VII. 24. Absolutam enim potestatem, qualem Hobbesiani imperantibus asserunt,nemo,credo,pius & cordatus iisdem asseret: potestatem Divinis & naturalibus legibus & pactis circumscriptam nemo pius negabit. Tyrannidem pariter instituere & fovere, & iniqua fidei & conscientiæ repugnantia tyrannorum imperata facere,vel dissimulare nemo nisi impius & irreligiosus sustinuerit. De cætero imperia quoad modum illa habendi diversi generis esse,alia certis legibus concessa, alia merè despotica,& plura his quàm illis adversus subditos impune licere, apertum,& omnium confessione receptum est.
units.tr: For in order to stir up odium against us and our whole religion with their princes, they cry out that it is the peculiar spirit [proprium genium] of the Reformed religion, or, as they call it, the Calvinist religion, to be deceitful and treacherous towards those who rule, and to love and be accustomed to inflict violence on princes who oppose its religion. From this spirit they derive all the civil disturbances that have occurred for a long time in Germany, France, Belgium, England and elsewhere. They add that Zwingli advised the deposing of kings hostile to the Gospel; that Mornay du Plessis inserted into his will the doctrine of lawful arms against a king for religion and the Church; that Paraeus, in Rom. 13:1, stated in plain words that lesser magistrates may defend themselves, the Republic and the Church, or true religion, against their superiors by right. I will say nothing of the Papists. For who could bear the Gracchi speaking of sedition? These are the men who long ago placed the crowns and sceptres of princes beneath the feet of the Pope. When certain Lutheran theologians insult us on this account, we justly reply in the words: Remember, however, that such things are to be thrown at men more sparingly. Not only the Reformed but also the Augsburg Confession men took up arms: they waged the Smalcaldic War, which was approved by the vote of jurists who had been instructed more correctly, even by Luther himself, and both fought the German war of this century, undertaken in defence of religion, against the emperors Charles V and Ferdinand II and III. The city of Brunswick resisted its own duke. Denmark expelled King Christian, and Sweden King Sigismund; not, I believe, all of them impelled to this by the spirit of Calvin, or, as they accuse, by a turbulent spirit. And whatever is done in this matter, it is right not to judge according to appearance, but to judge righteous judgment (John 7:24) about the thing itself. For no pious and sensible person, I believe, will assert the absolute power that the Hobbesians ascribe to rulers; no pious person will deny that power is bounded by divine and natural laws and by covenants. Likewise, no one but an impious and irreligious man will maintain that one should establish and foster tyranny, or carry out, or even conceal, the tyrants' commands that are contrary to faith and conscience. Moreover, it is open and recognised by all that dominions differ in kind according to the manner of holding them: some are granted under fixed laws, others are purely despotic; and that more is allowed with impunity against subjects under the one kind than under the other.

units.la: Sed & inferioribus Magistratibus adversus Superiorem licere potest, quod meris subditis nunquam licet. Sunt enim quidam non absolutè subditi, velut Proceres, Ephori, Ordines, Status Regni,qui & ipsi Magistratus sunt. Quæ distinctio fundatur in verbis S. Petri: Subjecti estote cuivis ordinationi propter Dominum εἴτε βασιλεῖ, ὡς ὑπερέχοντι, εἴτε ἡγεμόσιν ὡς δι' αὐτοῦ πεμπομένοις, sive Regi,ut supereminenti, sive Praesidibus,ut qui per eum mittuntur,1. Pet. II.13.14. Qui ergo fas piumque esse putant, ut Magistratus ejusmodi inferiores superioribus certa cum lege,non despotice regnantibus,& fundamentalia jura evertentibus, atque in subditorum fidem, conscientiam & vitam grassantibus debito modo resistant,illi non singularem quempiam genium, vel tubulentum spiritum sequuntur,sed juri Divino & humano, praxique communi juxta utrumque illud consentanea loquuntur. Hæc Zwinglii sententia fuit, Explanat. art. 42. sic definientis: Quando Magistratus perfide & extra regulam Christi egerint, possunt cum Deo deponi. Id nisi fecerint, quorum illud officium est, graviter eos, & universum populum à Deo puniri, exemplo Manassis impii & tolerati, statim confirmat. Sed de modo exauctorandi Magistratus sic statim loquitur: Non est, ut eum trucidest, nec ut bellum & tumultum quis excitet, sed aliis viis res tentanda, quia in pace vocavit nos Deus. Si communibus suffragiis creatur Rex, & incipit esse flagitiosus, communibus votis rursus ejiciatur, nisi cum eo (uti Israelitæ cum Manasse) puniri velint. Si consensu & electione paucorum Principum electus est, significat populus illis flagitiosam hujus Regis vitam, atque edicat,ferendam hanc haudquaquam esse, ut eum loco moveant, qui inaugurarunt. Hic jam labor est. Nam qui hoc faciunt, in eos pro libidine sua tyrannus grassatur, & quos vult mactat: sed gloriosum est pro justitia & veritate Dei mori. Præstatque pro justitiæ defensione,quam assentiendo injustitiæ, aut dissimulando,postea cum impiis trucidari. Postquam verò is, qui hæreditate Regnum accepit,tyrannus est,non debet per unum aut alterum tolli. (deponi) Nam hoc sine motu fieri non potest. Regnum autem Dei justitia, pax & gaudium in Spiritu S. est. Cùm verò consensu,suffragiis totius , aut certè potioris partis multitudinis tyrannus tollitur, Deo fit auspice. Si non consentiunt,ut tollatur malum,ferant jugum tyranni, & demum cum eo pereant,&c. Eandem fuisse Lutheri à Jurisconsultis sic institui sententiam supra diximus. Paræus quoque,duriter licet, eam ob causam habitus Magistratui inferiori fas esse, ascitis subditis, non quà Ecclesiæ, sed quà politiæ membris adversus summum Magistratum Rempublicam & Ecclesiam defendere, & positiva etiam resistentia tyrannis resistere statuit,his positis conditionibus: Si Rex, aut superior Magistratus degeneret in tyrannum; si ad manifestam idololatriam atque blasphemias ipsas,vel subditos,vel alios fidei suæ commissos cogere tentaverit: si aliter incolumis vita,fortunæ, religio & conscientia esse non possit: servata tamen ubique ἐπιεικείᾳ & moderamine inculpatæ tutelæ,secundum leges. Denique accusationem illam genii proprii Reformatorum ex mero odio religionis nostræ proficisci, vel inde constare potest, quòd ante tempora Reformationis Inferiores seriores titulo Principum,Statuum,Parlamentorum, Ordinum, Civitatum, Episcoporum, Nobilium in Imperio Romano,Bohemia,Anglia, Scotia, Dania, Svecia,Helvetia, Belgio,Superioribus suis, Imperatoribus, Regibus, Principibus injustis & violentis masculè restiterunt,neque imperia injusta & tyrannica,quando Reipublicæ universæ salus concuti & periclitari coepit,toleranda sibi putarunt. Nam iis temporibus Calvini genium prævaluisse accusatores nostri vix affirmaverint.
units.tr: But inferior magistrates may also resist a superior in ways that mere subjects never may. For there are some who are not absolutely subjects, such as nobles, ephors, the estates and orders of the realm, who are themselves magistrates. This distinction rests on the words of St Peter: Submit yourselves to every ordinance for the Lord's sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as those sent by him [εἴτε βασιλεῖ, ὡς ὑπερέχοντι, εἴτε ἡγεμόσιν ὡς δι' αὐτοῦ πεμπομένοις], 1 Pet. 2.13, 14. Therefore those who hold it lawful and right that such inferior magistrates should resist, in the proper manner, superiors who do not rule under fixed law but despotically, who overturn fundamental laws, and who rage against the faith, conscience and lives of the subjects, are not following some singular genius or turbulent spirit. They speak in agreement with divine and human law and with common practice according to both. This was the view of Zwingli in his Explanation of Article 42, where he defines: When magistrates act treacherously and outside the rule of Christ, they can be deposed together with God. If they do not do so, which is their duty, they are severely punished by God, and so is the whole people, as the example of the impious and tolerated Manasseh immediately confirms. But on the manner of removing a magistrate he speaks thus at once: It is not that one should slay him, nor that anyone should stir up war and tumult, but the matter must be attempted by other means, because God has called us to peace. If a king is created by common votes, and begins to be shameless, he should be cast out again by common prayers, unless the people wish to be punished along with him (as the Israelites were with Manasseh). If he was elected by the consent and choice of a few princes, the people should signify to them the shameful life of this king, and declare that it must by no means be borne, so that they remove from office those who installed him. Here indeed is the difficulty. For those who do this, the tyrant rages against them at his pleasure and slaughters whom he wishes; but it is glorious to die for the justice and truth of God. It is better to be slain with the impious later, for defending justice, than to assent to injustice or to connive at it. But once the man who received the kingdom by inheritance has become a tyrant, he should not be removed by one or two men (deposed), for this cannot be done without disturbance. The kingdom of God, however, is justice, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. When a tyrant is removed by the consent and votes of the whole multitude, or certainly of the greater part, it is done under God's auspices. If they do not consent, then, that the evil be removed, they must bear the yoke of the tyrant and at last perish with him, and so on. We have said above that Luther's view was set out in the same way by the jurists. Paraeus too, though harshly treated for this reason, held that it is lawful for an inferior magistrate, having taken subjects to himself, not as members of the Church but as members of the civil polity, to defend the commonwealth and the Church against the supreme magistrate, and to resist tyrants even by positive resistance, under these conditions: If the king, or a superior magistrate, degenerates into a tyrant; if he has attempted to compel either the subjects, or others committed to his faith, to manifest idolatry and blasphemies themselves; if life, fortune, religion and conscience cannot otherwise remain safe: always observing everywhere [ἐπιεικείᾳ] and the moderation of blameless defence, according to the laws. Finally, that accusation of the Reformers' own genius arising from mere hatred of our religion can be seen from this: before the time of the Reformation, inferiors of every sort, under the titles of princes, estates, parliaments, orders, cities, bishops and nobles, in the Roman Empire, Bohemia, England, Scotland, Denmark, Sweden, Switzerland and Belgium, manfully resisted their superiors, emperors, kings and princes when they were unjust and violent, and they did not think that unjust and tyrannical rule was to be tolerated when the safety of the whole commonwealth began to be shaken and endangered. For our accusers can hardly affirm that the genius of Calvin prevailed in those times.

units.la: CXXIV. Potestas Magistratus potissimùm in legislatione, & judiciorum administratione consistit. Cùm enim & pater in familia,& præceptor in schola leges condere possit,quas in familia & schola ordinis conservandi gratia vigere vult, multò magis potestas eminens leges, juxta quas in civitate omnia ordine & decenter fiant, & quibus caveatur, ne cives invicem injuria afficiant, ferre potest. Ordinis enim, non confusionis auctor Deus est. In me Principes צדק decernunt justitiam, seu jus faciunt, juxta quod subditi reguntur,Prov. VIII. 15. Unus quidem est νομοθέτης legislator,qui potest servare & perdere,Jac. IV. 12. Supremus scilicet, authoritate & potestate etiam in conscientiam & animam hominis valens,& leges ferens, juxta quas observatas vel violatas homo æternùm beatus vel miser est. Sed idem unus ille Legislator hominesetiam Legislatores, Genes. XLIX. 10. constituit, potestatem iis impertiens, qua legibus latis civitatem externam in hoc mundo gubernent. Sed potestas illa duabus regulis circumscribitur. Prior est, quòd humana lex circa id,quod Divina lege jussum vel vetitum est,cum effectu versari non possit. Sicut enim homines Deo, ceu supremo Domino, subjiciuntur: ita etiam leges eorum Divinis legibus cedunt, & palmam relinquunt. Posterior est,quòd Magistratui fas sit jubere vel vetare,quicquid lege Divina determinatum non est, & tamen ad societatis humanæ ordinem conservandum facit. Quatenus verò Magistratus ad leges Mosaicas judiciales astringatur, pluribus Loc. XVI. 78. &c. diximus. Quæcunque porro leges Magistratus Divinis legibus non contrariantur; & inhonestum nihil præcipiunt,honestum nihil vetant, obligant eos omnes, quibus à superiore legitimo Domino præscriptæ sunt. Nam qui se coetui cuipiam aggregarunt,aut homini,vel hominibus subjecerunt,ii vel expresse promiserunt,vel ex negotii natura promisisse intelligunter, obsecuturos se iis, quæ à parte majore coetus, vel ea,cui potestas delata est, rite præscripta fuerint. Et subjici inferiores imperiis ejusmodi necesse est, non propter iram tantùm, sed etiam propter conscientiam,Rom. XIII. 5. non quòd conscientia per se humanis legibus subjiciatur, quæ soli Deo subest, sed quia Magistratus Divina ordinatio est, adeóque à Deo ordinante potestatem leges ferendi accepit. Obligant igitur humanæ leges conscientiam per se vi generalis mandati Divini, sive naturæ hominis digito Dei inscripti, sive verbo expresli; non vi specialis mandati humani.
