Conscientia enim hominis nullo etiam extante verbo hominis, docet, bonum & necessarium esse subjici,
units.tr: CXXIV. The power of the magistrate consists chiefly in legislation and in the administration of judgments. For just as a father in the family and a teacher in the school can make laws, which they wish to be in force in the family and school for the sake of keeping order, much more can the supreme power bring forth laws by which all things in the state are done in order and decently, and by which it is provided that citizens do not wrong one another. For God is the author of order, not of confusion. In me princes decree justice [צדק], that is, they make the law by which subjects are governed, Prov. 8.15. There is indeed one legislator [νομοθέτης], who is able to save and to destroy, Jas. 4.12. That is, the supreme one, who has authority and power even over the conscience and soul of man, and who gives laws by which man is eternally blessed or wretched according as they are observed or violated. But this one Legislator also appointed men to be legislators, Gen. 49.10, giving them the power to govern the external state in this world by the laws they enact. This power, however, is limited by two rules. The first is that a human law cannot have effect concerning that which has been commanded or forbidden by divine law. For just as men are subject to God as supreme Lord, so their laws yield to divine laws and leave them the palm. The second is that it is lawful for the magistrate to command or forbid whatever is not determined by divine law, and yet tends to preserve the order of human society. As far as the magistrate is bound to the Mosaic judicial laws, we have said more on this in Loc. 16, 78, etc. Moreover, whatever laws of the magistrate do not conflict with divine laws, and command nothing dishonourable or forbid nothing honourable, bind all those who have been subjected to them by a lawful superior lord. For those who have joined themselves to some assembly, or have subjected themselves to a man or men, have either expressly promised, or are understood from the nature of the matter to have promised, that they will obey those things which have been duly prescribed by the greater part of the assembly, or by the one to whom power has been committed. And inferiors must needs be subject to such authorities, not only for wrath's sake but also for conscience' sake, Rom. 13.5; not because conscience by itself is subject to human laws, since it is subject to God alone, but because the magistrate is a divine ordinance, and so has received from God, who ordains him, the power of making laws. Human laws therefore bind the conscience by the force of the general divine command, whether that command is written in the nature of man by the finger of God or spoken in the express word; not by the force of a special human command. For the conscience of man, even without any human word, teaches that it is good and necessary to be subject,

units.la: & malum esse ἀντισταθῆναι καὶ ἀντικεῖσθαι immorigerum & refractarium esse. Quæ causa est, quòd Reges & Principes plerunque Majestatem aliquam habent. Deus enim conscientiæ dictamen ad timendum, suspiciendum & amandum superiores efficax fecit. Disciplinam Regum solvit,& cingulo adstringit lumbos eorum, Job. XII. 17.
units.tr: and that it is evil to be opposed [ἀντισταθῆναι καὶ ἀντικεῖσθαι] and to be disobedient and refractory. This is why kings and princes generally have a certain majesty. For God has made the dictate of conscience effective, so that we fear, respect and love our superiors. He loosens the discipline of kings and binds a girdle about their loins, Job 12.18.

units.la: CXXV. Judiciorum secundum leges administratio necessaria est. Absque ea enim lex inefficax, & nullius ad conservandum ordinem momenti est. Judices & moderatores constituito tibi in singulis portis, qui populum judicio justo judicent, Deut. XVI. 18. Justitiam justissimam sectare, ut vivas, ibid. v. 20. Si enim non essent judicia,quomodo pauperes, pupillos,viduas,& injustè oppressos patrocinio & suffragio adjuvare possemus? Quamobrem etiam civibus jura à Magistratu petere licet. Neque id Christus in N. T. abrogavit, sed confirmavit potiùs. Esto amicus adversario tuo citò,ne quando te tradat ministro, & in custodiam conjiciaris, Matth. V. 25. 26. Principes non sunt metus bonorum operum. Vis autem non timere potestatem? Bonum fac, & habebis laudem ex ea. Dei enim minister est, tibi in bonum. Si autem malum feceris,time. Non enim frustra gladium gestat, Dei enim minister est,vindex ad iram ei,qui male agit, Rom. XIII. 2. 4. Neque sine judiciis humana societas consistere potest,degeneratura mox in latrocinia,si absque illis fuerit. Cúmque judicia vel civilia vel criminalia sint,utraque à Magistratu Christiano exercenda sunt. Nam etiam de capitalibus Christus legem Dei jubentis sanguinem ejus effundere, qui alterius sanguinem effuderit, Genes. IX. 6. confirmavit, dicens ad Petrum: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit, Matth. XXVI. 52. Quæ generalia verba nonnisi ad Magistratum spectant,cùm non obscurè ibi Christus veterem legem respiciat, quam de novo repetit & sancit. Et apertè S. Paulus Magistratum gladio succingit,quem & stringi ad vindicanda flagitia jubet. Non frustra gladium gerit. Nam Dei minister est, & vindex ad iram ei, qui malum fecerit, Rom. XIII. 4. Et ne quis humani instituti illud esse, vel vitio & nævo laborare,calumnietur,id omne à Divina institutione derivat. Non est, inquit, potestas nisi à Deo, vers. 1. Et in eo Magistratum Dei διάκονον ministrum ad bonorum tutelam, & malorum terrorem,v. 4. facit,addens,eum gladium gestare non εἰκῇ temerè, hoc est, non sine vocationis Divinæ præsidio, quo sensu Col. II. 18. dicitur εἰκῇ temerè turgere carnis suæ sensu, qui se ingerit in ea, quæ Deus non revelavit. Sed & S. Petrus jubet subesse omni humanæ creationi διὰ τὸν Κύριον propter Dominum, sive Regi, sive ejus præfectis missis εἰς ἐκδίκησιν τῶν κακοποιῶν ad ultionem maleficorum,& ad laudem rectè facientium, 1. Petr. II. 13. 14. Accedit,quòd etiam S. Johannes militibus ad Baptismum suum accedentibus & interrogantibus, quid faciemus nos? non interdixit militibus fontes in bello occidere,quod judicii capitalis genus est: quod factum oportebat, si Christianos ejus poenitere debuisset; sed respondit: Neminem (innocentem) concutiatis; neque calumniam faciatis:& stipendiis contenti estote, Luc. III. 14. Nam quod Johannis doctrinam & institutionem legalem,non Evangelicam gelicam fuisse, Anabaptistæ regerunt, in loco confutavimus. Etenim Christus ipse & Apostoli milites in censu fidelium & piorum habuerunt, neque exauctorari à militia petierunt, Matth. VIII. 10. &c. Actor. X. 1. 2. &c. Neque S. Paulus implorare salvum conductum Romanorum militum adversus Judæorum contra se conspirationem veritus est; Actor. XXIII. 23. 24. 25.
units.tr: CXXV. The administration of judgment according to the laws is necessary. For without it law is ineffective and of no weight in preserving order. You shall appoint judges and officers for yourself in all your gates, who shall judge the people with just judgment, Deut. 16.18. Pursue justice most justly, that you may live, ibid. v. 20. For if there were no courts, how could we help the poor, orphans, widows and the unjustly oppressed by protection and support? Wherefore it is also lawful for citizens to seek their rights from the magistrate. Nor did Christ in the New Testament abrogate this, but rather confirmed it. Agree with your adversary quickly, lest at any time he hand you over to the officer, and you be cast into prison, Matt. 5.25, 26. Rulers are not a terror to good works. Do you wish then not to fear the power? Do good, and you shall have praise from it. For he is the minister of God for your good. But if you do evil, fear. For he does not bear the sword in vain; for he is the minister of God, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil, Rom. 13.2, 4. Nor can human society exist without judgments; it would soon degenerate into robbery if it were without them. And since judgments, whether civil or criminal, are of both kinds, both must be exercised by the Christian magistrate. For Christ also confirmed the law of God commanding, concerning capital offences, that whoever sheds man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed, Gen. 9.6, saying to Peter: He who takes the sword shall perish by the sword, Matt. 26.52. These general words refer only to the magistrate, since Christ there clearly regards the old law, which he repeats and sanctions anew. And St Paul plainly girds the magistrate with the sword, and bids him draw it to avenge crimes. He does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the minister of God, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil, Rom. 13.4. And lest anyone should slander this as a human institution, or as blemished by vice and fault, he derives the whole matter from divine institution. There is no power, he says, except from God, v. 1. And in that place he makes the magistrate God's minister [διάκονον] for the protection of good men and the terror of evil men, v. 4, adding that he bears the sword not in vain [εἰκῇ], that is, not without the safeguard of a divine calling; in this sense Col. 2.18 says that a man is puffed up in vain [εἰκῇ] by the sense of his flesh, who intrudes into things which God has not revealed. But St Peter also bids us be subject to every human ordinance for the Lord's sake [διὰ τὸν Κύριον], whether to the king or to his governors sent for the punishment of evildoers [εἰς ἐκδίκησιν τῶν κακοποιῶν] and for the praise of those who do well, 1 Pet. 2.13, 14. Add to this that St John, when soldiers came to his baptism and asked, What shall we do?, did not forbid the soldiers to put men to death in war, which is a kind of capital judgment (something that ought to have been done if Christians had to repent of it); but he answered: Strike no one (innocent), neither accuse anyone falsely, and be content with your wages, Luke 3.14. For the Anabaptists argue that John's teaching and institution was legal, not Gospel; we have refuted this in its place. Indeed Christ himself and the Apostles counted soldiers among the faithful and pious, and did not ask that they be discharged from military service, Matt. 8.10 etc.; Acts 10.1, 2 etc. Nor did St Paul hesitate to seek the protection of Roman soldiers against the plot of the Jews against him, Acts 23.23, 24, 25.

units.la: CXXVI. Judicia Magistratus sive Civilia, sive Criminalia & Capitalia non evertunt, quæ Anabaptistæ iis objiciunt. Christus enim vetans resistere malo, & jubens percutienti dextram maxillam, etiam siniistram percutiendam præbere, eique, qui judicio cum alio contendere, & tunicam ejus tollere voluerit, etiam pallium ei relinquere, Matth. V. 38. 39. 40. non talia ad Magistratus, vel jus à Magistratu petentes fatus est, neque sic judicia omnino sustulit, utpote quæ ibid. vers. 22. confirmavit potius, dicens: Tenebitur judicio : tenebitur consessu : tenebitur Gehenna ignis; sed privatas hominum iras, injurias & odia vetuit, multòque tolerare, & charitatis velo obtegere, nec ad quasvis injurias sic excandescere, ut præcipites vel ad privatam, vel ad publicè implorandam vindictam, ruere velint, jussit. Clarius enim haud dubiè Christus mentem suam expressisset, si judicia qualiacunque in V. T. mandata, & nuspiam alibi distertis verbis abrogata, antiquare voluisset. Imo legem Dei ita solvisset, quod ipse v. 17. diserte inficiatur. Opponit enim se Pharisæis, qui ea, quæ in V. T. judicibus dicta sunt, tanquam dictum omnibus interpretabantur. Ita enim etiam Majmonides alicubi docet, homines plebejos posse de honore suo concedere, sed Rabbinos, Magistros, & omnes jurisdictionem habentes, non posse de honore suo concedere, sed si cui ipsorum injuria & contumelia facta sit, debere esse נקם vindicantem & rancoris retinentem, serpentis instar. Cæterum non tantum uno ore Prophetæ & Apostoli privatam vindictam temerariam, ejusque cupiditatem prohibuerunt, Deut. XXXII. 35. Prov. XXIV. 22. XXV. 21. 22. coll. cum Rom. XII. 17. & Levit. XIX. 18. cum Luc. X. 29. 37. sed etiam in vindictæ publicæ exercitio Deus noluit Magistratum indulgere privato odii vel dedignationis affectui, aut φιλανθρωπίαν exuere, Deut. XXV. 2. 3. jubens etiam ipsa punitione malorum aliorum emendationi, & tranquillitati bonorum consulere, ibid. XIII. 11. XVII. 13. 14. XXI. 21. quod ipsum charitatis officium erga plures est. Neque S. Paulus Corinthios ob jus ab infidelibus petitum objurgans, & dicens: Τολμᾷ τις audet aliquis negotium cum altero habens, litem instituere sub injustis, & non sub sanctis, &c? 1. Cor. VI. 1. in universum judiciorum civilium omnium ordinem tollit, quia saltem litem instituere ἐπὶ τῶν ἁγίων sub sanctis, v. 1. non improbat; sed Corinthios increpat, quòd non haberent eam verecundiam, pudorem & charitatem nominis Christiani, ut lites suas ad Ethnicos deferrent, quod ipsis Ethnicis scandalosum videri poterat, cùm eos, qui resipiscentiam & conversionem ad Deum profitebantur, & amorem Dei & proximi impensè spirabant, injustos, calumniatores, contentiosos, pertinaces, loquaces, ob-
units.tr: CXXVI. Magistrates' judgments, whether civil or criminal and capital, are not overthrown by the objections the Anabaptists raise against them. For Christ, forbidding us to resist evil and bidding us, when someone strikes us on the right cheek, to offer the left as well, and telling one who would contend at law with another and take his tunic that he should also leave him his cloak (Matt. 5:38–40), did not say this to magistrates or to those seeking justice from a magistrate. Nor did he abolish judgments altogether; rather he confirmed them, saying in the same place (v. 22): "He shall be liable to judgment; he shall be liable to the council; he shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna." What he forbade were private human anger, injuries and hatred. He commanded us to bear much and cover it with the veil of charity, and not to flare up at every injury so as to rush headlong into private vengeance or into vengeance sought publicly. Certainly Christ would have stated his mind more clearly if he had wished to annul judgments of any kind commanded in the Old Testament and nowhere else expressly abrogated. Indeed he would thereby have dissolved the law of God, which he expressly denies in v. 17. For he sets himself against the Pharisees, who interpreted what was said to the judges in the Old Testament as said to everyone. So Maimonides also teaches somewhere that common people may remit their honour, but rabbis, masters and all who hold jurisdiction may not remit their honour; and if any of them has suffered injury or insult, he ought to be [נקם, nakam], avenging and retaining rancour like a serpent. Moreover, the prophets and apostles did not forbid rash private vengeance and the desire for it with one voice only (Deut. 32:35; Prov. 24:22; 25:21–22, compared with Rom. 12:17; and Lev. 19:18, compared with Luke 10:29, 37). God also did not wish the magistrate, in the exercise of public vengeance, to indulge a private feeling of hatred or disdain, or to strip off [φιλανθρωπίαν, philanthrōpian]. He commanded (Deut. 25:2–3) that by the very punishment of other evildoers he should provide for the amendment and tranquillity of the good (ibid. 13:11; 17:13–14; 21:21), which is itself a duty of charity towards many. Nor does St Paul, rebuking the Corinthians for seeking justice from unbelievers and saying, "[Τολμᾷ τις, Tolmā tis] Does anyone among you, having a matter against another, dare to go to law before the unjust and not before the saints?" (1 Cor. 6:1), abolish the whole order of civil judgments. For he does not disapprove of bringing suits [ἐπὶ τῶν ἁγίων, epi tōn hagiōn] before the saints (v. 1), but reproaches the Corinthians for lacking that shame, modesty and charity proper to the Christian name, which would have kept them from carrying their suits to the heathen. This could appear scandalous even to the heathen themselves, since these Corinthians professed repentance and conversion to God and breathed love of God and neighbour, while the heathen saw them as unjust, calumnious, contentious, obstinate, talkative and fault-

units.la: Contraria Anabaptistarum argumenta refelluntur.
units.tr: Refutation of the Anabaptists' contrary arguments.

units.la: trectatores viderent. Cogitare enim poterant, homines illos religionis & pietatis prætextu seditiones excitare, & Reipublicæ statum mutare velle; atque ejusmodi religionem hominem non facere meliorem, sed pravam superstitionem alere; neque Christum, quem invocarunt, revera Deum esse, vel Spiritum suum iis impartiri, quia Spiritus Divinus in iis nihil operetur. At nec in universum Apostolus vetat adire Magistratum Ethnicum. Nam & ipse ad Neronem provocavit, & quidem, ne traderetur popularibus suis, & judicio illorum, qui in throno Dei sedere videbantur. Non ergo quascunque lites, sed solùm litigandi pruriginem, & insaniam illam damnat, quæ res levissimas, quæ prudentiorum arbitrio componi poterant, temerè in forum producit, longis ibi nexibus impedit, & prolixo atque inutili labore vix sero ad exitum perducit. Quem fori dementem ambitum apud Ethnicos quoque judices, non sine Christiani nominis opprobrio exercitum merito Apostolus castigat & prohibet. Ac licèt jusserit Christus, Matth. V. 44. inimicos diligere, non tamen judicia criminalia abrogavit. Nam & in V. T. non obstante eodem inimicos diligendi præcepto judicia criminalia viguerunt. Judicia enim publica non ex odio inimicorum, sed scelerum & perturbationis reipublicæ, & ex amore societatis, & proborum, qui in societate sunt, & adversus improbos defendi debent, non sine commiseratione etiam judicantium, & propositio emendandi fontes; proficiscuntur. Magistratus enim proprie ne quidem inimicum habet, quia maleficos puniens, non tam eos punit, à quibus ipse læsus est, quàm eos, à quibus alii læsi sunt, Deus ipse inimicos diligit, Matth. V. 45. neque tamen à judiciis abstinet. Capitalia quoque supplicia licèt pro scopo principali non habeant emendationem fontis, ex amore tamen innocentium, qui defendendi, vel exemplo adversus fontes repræsentato ab impietate revocandi sunt, imò totius societatis, à qua, licèt non sine commiseratione, inutile membrum ense recidendum est, ne pars sincera trahatur, manant. Magistratus enim amputatione membrorum istiusmodi inutilium & noxiorum pro communibus civitatis patribus se gerunt, ejusque salutem procurant; perinde uti homo, qui omnia membra sua amat, membrum gangræna corruptum amputat, ne pars sincera corripiatur. Neque illud obstat, quòd per capitalia supplicia tempus & occasionem emendandæ vitæ præcidi causantur: Non tantùm enim Deus ipse, qui quocunque modo homines sceleratos, quando diu satis patientia ejus abusi sunt, è vita tollere potest, eos in manus Magistratus, vicarii sui, tradit, ut vitæ filo præcisô & ipsi peccare, aliósque contagione sua corrumpere desinant, ipsorumque miseranda mors aliis in exemplum cedat, atque ita discant justitiam moniti, sed etiam in judiciis capitalibus semper mora aliqua reo indulgeri, & Christiano ritu anima ejus ad exitum præparari, atque à maculis & flagitiis si pote, expiari solet & debet. Quo ipsa illa judiciorum severitas non parum conducit; qua peccator domitus felicius quandoque in ferali pegmate, quàm in lectulo, exitiali veterno sopitus, expirat. CXXVII. Ad
units.tr: finders. For they could think that these men, under the pretext of religion and piety, were stirring up sedition and wished to change the state of the commonwealth; that such a religion does not make a man better but nourishes a depraved superstition; and that Christ, whom they invoked, is not really God, or does not impart his Spirit to them, since the Divine Spirit works nothing in them. Yet the Apostle does not forbid in general approaching a heathen magistrate. For he himself appealed to Nero, and indeed so that he would not be handed over to his own countrymen and to the judgment of those who seemed to sit on the throne of God. Therefore he condemns not all lawsuits, but only the itch and madness of litigation, which rashly brings into court trifling matters that could have been settled by the judgment of wiser men, hinders them there with long entanglements, and with prolix and useless labour brings them to an end scarcely and late. The Apostle rightly castigates and forbids this mad ambition of the forum, pursued even before heathen judges, and not without reproach to the Christian name. And although Christ bade us love our enemies (Matt. 5:44), he did not abrogate criminal judgments. For even in the Old Testament, despite the same precept to love enemies, criminal judgments flourished. Public judgments proceed not from hatred of enemies but from concern for crimes and the disturbance of the commonwealth, and from love of society and of the upright who live in it; and the wicked must be restrained, not without compassion even on the part of those who judge, and with the purpose of amending them. For the magistrate properly has no enemy at all; in punishing evildoers he punishes not so much those by whom he himself has been harmed as those by whom others have been harmed. God himself loves enemies (Matt. 5:45), yet he does not abstain from judgments. Capital punishments too, although their principal aim is not the amendment of the offender, nevertheless arise from love of the innocent, who must be defended, or from the example set before others to call them back from impiety; indeed they arise from love of the whole society, from which, though not without compassion, a useless member is to be cut off with the sword, lest the sound part be dragged down. For by amputating such useless and harmful members the magistrate acts as a father of the common state and secures its safety, just as a man who loves all his members cuts off a limb corrupted by gangrene, lest the sound part be seized. Nor is it an objection that by capital punishment the time and opportunity of amending one's life are said to be cut off. For God himself, who can take wicked men out of life in whatever way when they have abused his patience long enough, hands them over into the hands of the magistrate, his vicar, so that with the thread of life cut they may cease to sin and corrupt others by their contagion, and so that their pitiable death may serve others as an example and they may learn justice from the warning. Moreover, in capital judgments some delay is usually granted to the accused, and his soul is prepared for its end in the Christian manner, and is customarily, and ought to be, cleansed as far as possible from stains and crimes. For this very severity of judgments contributes not a little to that end, by which the sinner, subdued, sometimes expires more happily on the scaffold than in bed, lulled to sleep by a deadly lethargy. units.la: CXXVII. Ad judicia Magistratus etiam Bella legitima pertinent. Nam unus vel pauci scelerati supplicio capitales : multi conjurati, etiam non subditi,bello expiantur & vindicantur. Sed de bello plura Loc. XIV. § 57-61. nec non Loc. XVI. 67-74. diximus, quæ heic repetere nihil attinet. De judiciorum etiam ordine Loc. XIV. § IV. 68. 69. 70. egimus. Sed & Fœdera pangere cum aliis, etiam externis, licet. Quatenus verò etiam cum fidelibus pacisci per leges Divinas liceat, alibi Loc. XVI. 65. explicavimus. Denique & officia universa Superiorum erga inferiores,atque inferiorum erga Superiores Loc. XIV. § III. 28. &c. expo-suimus. His ergo amplius edisserendis supersedemus.
units.tr: CXXVII. To the judgments of the magistrate belong also lawful wars. For one or a few criminals are punished by execution, while many conspirators, even if they are not subjects, are expiated and avenged by war. But we have discussed war more fully at Loc. XIV §§57–61 and also at Loc. XVI §§67–74, and there is no need to repeat it here. We have also treated the order of judgments at Loc. XIV §§IV, 68–70. But it is also lawful to make treaties with others, even with foreigners. How far it is lawful to make covenants even with the faithful under divine laws we explained elsewhere, Loc. XVI §65. Finally, we have set out all the duties of superiors towards inferiors, and of inferiors towards superiors, at Loc. XIV §III, 28 and following. We therefore refrain from discussing these further.

units.la: CXXVIII. Fuit cura Reipublicæ Magistratui incumbens. Sed potior, imò principalior ejus cura Ecclesiæ & religionis esse debet. Sive enim infidelis & hostis Ecclesiæ est, religionem veram indagare , amplecti & Filium Dei osculari tenetur. Omnes enim Potestates Supremæ terrestres Regno Christi se subjicere debent. Reges prudenter agite. Erudimini judices terræ. Servite Jehovæ in timore, & exultate in tremore. Osculamini Filium, ne forte irascatur & pereatis in via, Psal. II. 10. 11. 12. Aperite, o Portæ, capita vestra, & aperite vos, Portæ perpetuæ, ut intret Rex gloriæ, ibid. cap. XXIV. vers. 9. Sive jam fideles & orthodoxi sunt, præcipuæ eorum partes sunt, ut Regni Christi, Ecclesiæ pro viribus suis procuratio-nem , Potestati suæ convenientem, suscipiat. Existent Reges nutritii tui, & Principes fœminæ lactatrices, nutrices tuæ. Vultu in terram verso adorabunt te, &c. Esaj. XLIX. 23. Reges ibunt ad splendorem ortus tui, ibid. LX. 3. Reges eorum ministrabunt tibi, ibid. v. 10. Uber Regum suges, ibid. v. 16. Voluntarii populorum congregati sunt, populus Dei Abrahami. Quia Dei sunt clypei terræ, Psal. XLVII. 10. Reges terræ gloriam & honorem suum in eum inferunt, Apoc. XXI. 24. Quam Ecclesiæ & religionis curam strenuè optimi quique Principes , Moses, Josua, Judices, David, Solomon, Josaphat , Hiskias, Josias , Constantinus M. Theodosius,&c. gesserunt. Magistratus enim non armentarii vel opilionis instar ventris duntaxat, cutis & subditorum curam suscipere & gerere debet, sed animæ etiam eorundem, propter quam corpus est; ceu utriusque tabulæ custos, metus non bonorum, sed malorum operum,&c. laudans bonum facientem ; Dei Minister tibi in bonum,Rom. XIII. 3. 4. Finis enim civitatis politicæ est omne bonum civium. Cùm enim subjectio,quæ imperatur omni animæ, sive bono opere versari debeat,finis constitutæ bonitatis alius esse non potest , quàm ut omne opus bonum fieri possit. Ad id enim subjectio introducta est. Accedit,quòd Potestas Civilis suprema constituta est ad laudem boni operis, Rom. XIII. 3. Atqui optimum opus, propter quod Respublica est, pietas est. Orandum enim est pro omnibus in eminentia constitutis , ut quietam & tranquillam vitam transigamus in omni pietate & honestate, 1. Timoth. II. 1. 2. Denique etiam Magistratus gentiles jure &
units.tr: CXXVIII. The care of the commonwealth rests upon the magistrate. But his principal and even more important care should be that of the Church and of religion. For whether he is unbelieving and an enemy of the Church, he is bound to seek out the true religion, embrace it and kiss the Son of God. For all supreme earthly powers ought to submit themselves to the kingdom of Christ: "Be wise now, O kings; be instructed, you judges of the earth. Serve Jehovah in fear, and exult in trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry and you perish on the way" (Ps. 2:10–12). "Lift up your heads, O gates, and be lifted up, you everlasting doors, that the King of glory may come in" (ibid. ch. 24, v. 9). Whether they are already faithful and orthodox, their chief part is to undertake, as far as they can, the care of the kingdom of Christ and of the Church, befitting their power. "Kings shall be your nursing fathers, and princesses your nursing mothers; with their faces to the earth they shall worship you, etc." (Isa. 49:23). "Kings shall walk to the brightness of your rising" (ibid. 60:3). "Their kings shall minister to you" (ibid. v. 10). "You shall suck the milk of kings" (ibid. v. 16). "The willing of the peoples are gathered together, the people of the God of Abraham; for the shields of the earth are God's" (Ps. 47:10). "The kings of the earth bring their glory and honour into it" (Rev. 21:24). The best princes have strenuously exercised this care of the Church and of religion: Moses, Joshua, the judges, David, Solomon, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Josiah, Constantine the Great, Theodosius, and others. For the magistrate, not like a herdsman or shepherd, ought to undertake and carry out the care not merely of the belly, skin and subjects, but also of their souls, for the sake of which the body exists; as guardian of both tables of the law, praising the one doing good; he is God's minister to you for good, not fearing good works but evil works (Rom. 13:3–4). For the end of the political commonwealth is all the good of its citizens. Since subjection, which is enjoined on every soul, ought to be exercised in good work, the end of the constituted goodness can be nothing other than that every good work may be done; for to that end subjection was introduced. Add that supreme civil power is established for the praise of good work (Rom. 13:3). But the best work, for the sake of which the commonwealth exists, is piety. For prayer must be made for all who are placed in eminence, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and honesty (1 Tim. 2:1–2). Finally, the gentile magistrates too, by the right and

units.la: consuetudine gentium religionem curasse, & Philosophorum scripta,& Legislatorum exempla docent.
units.tr: The custom of nations, the writings of the philosophers and the examples of the lawgivers all show that magistrates have cared for religion.

units.la: CXXIX. Cùm ergo certum sit,Potestates Civiles id etiam operam dare debere,ut pietas & religio vera in Republica tuta sit,vigeat, in honore sit,& laudetur,quomodo ea in cura versentur,considerandum est. Nàm æquè indubitatum est , etiam Pastores & doctores à Deo mandatum habere, quid docere & facere debeant, neque ea in re ab hominibus dependere. Officia ergo docentium & regentium, atque ipsiusEcclesiæ à potestatePrincipum distinguere,& Principum potestatem,ne in Christi Regnum arietet,& officii Ministrorum Christi fines audacius ingrediatur,definire,hoc opus,hic labor est. Et in universum quidem,quoad potestatem Magistratus circa religionem & Ecclesiam quadam alii in defectu, in excessu alii peccant. In defectu peccant Pontifici,jus Magistratus circa religionem imaginarii cujusdam privilegii Papæ, & superioritatis ejusdem prætextu,adeò arctantes,ut nec cognitionem,nec judicium ullum,sed solam sententiæ ab Ecclesia latæ executionem , & miseran-dam servitutem erga relinquant,quin & Clerum, magnam Ecclesiæ partem à Magistratus jurisdictione & potestate omni eximant, & emancipent. A' qua culpa Anabaptistæ immunes non sunt , utpote qui & ipsi à libertate Christiana alienum esse clamitant,ut Christiani Magistratui subsint, vel Magistratus Christianus circa religionem quicquam statuat. Iccirco etiam in V. T. unicum tantùm regimen Politicum, non ullum regimen spirituale & ecclesiasticum , à Politico distinctum & independens, institutum fuisse, & expirante regimine Politico V. T. nulli in N. T. regimini Politico,cui religionis cura demandata sit,nugantur. Quæ insulsa nimis sunt. Nam nec abrogatum à Christo regimen Politicum esse, demonstravimus; & distinctio Potestatis Politicæ & Ecclesiasticæ sub V. T. liquet, non tantùm ex concertatione illa, qua Regi Uziæ, ceu alieni muneris usurpatori, Azarias Pontifex , octoginta Sacerdotibus comitatus, sancto zelo se opposuit,quem zelum Deum peccatum in Rege per lepram immissam vindicans, probavit , 2. Chron. XXVI. 16. 17. &c. sed etiam ex distinctione præfecturæ geminæ, ibid. XIX. 11. expressa,quarum altera suum caput in negotiis Regis, seu civilibus, altera in negotiis Jehovæ, seu spiritualibus, in quibus Deo, invitis etiam Regibus, serviendum erat, habuit. Quam distinctionem etiam S. Paulus docens, Deum nihil ad tribum regiam Judæ de Sacerdotio locutum esse, sed vocationem ad Sacerdotium peculiare tribui Levitici fuisse,Heb. VII. 14. confirmat. Neque illud obstat,quòd Divinitus institutum fuit Synedrium, in quo uterque & Sacerdos & judex in Republica Israelis audiri debuit , Deut. XVII. 8. 9. quia non obstante societate ista judicis , & judicii Politici & Ecclesiastici , quam negotia mixti fori,in quibus censuram Ecclesiasticam punitio corporalis lege Dei imperata comitabatur, saepe flagitarunt , distinctio vocationis & gubernationis ac correctionis Ecclesiasticæ spiritualis, à Politica temporali jurisdictione & Regno terreno, mansit. Neque juvant exempla singularia vel Melchisedeci, Eli, Samuelis, qui simul Reges, judices, simul sacerdotes fuerunt, quia ad utrumque illud munus distinctum obeundum specialiter illi vocati fuerunt: vel Mosis simul Principis populi, & Legislatoris Religionis. Fuit enim illud personale privilegium Mosis, faciens per se non ad terreni Regis axioma, quod in populo Israelis sustinebat, sed ad alterum munus Propheticum, in quo ceu Propheta, extra ordinem typum eminentissimi Prophetae Christi gessit. Ad Sacerdotium autem, non Mosi, sed Aharoni & filiis ejus mandatum, spiritualis ordinaria directio & gubernatio populi in religione & cultu institutio ipsius Aharonis in Sacerdotem inauguratio, & Sacerdotii legislatio, spectabat, quam Moses ceu Propheta Dei, ejusdem jussu administravit.
units.tr: CXXIX. Since it is therefore certain that civil powers ought also to take pains that true piety and religion be secure in the commonwealth, flourish, be held in honour and be praised, we must consider how they are to be engaged in this care. For it is equally indubitable that pastors and teachers also have a command from God as to what they ought to teach and do, and that in this matter they do not depend on men. The task, the work and the labour here is therefore to distinguish the duties of teachers and rulers, and of the Church itself, from the power of princes, and to define the power of princes so that it does not butt against the kingdom of Christ, and does not enter too boldly into the bounds of the office of Christ's ministers. In general, as regards the power of the magistrate over religion and the Church, some sin by defect and others by excess. The Papists sin by defect: under the pretext of a certain imaginary privilege of the Pope and of his superiority, they so restrict the right of the magistrate concerning religion that they leave him no cognition or judgment at all, only the execution of the sentence pronounced by the Church, and a wretched servitude. Indeed they also exempt and emancipate the clergy, a great part of the Church, from the jurisdiction and every power of the magistrate. The Anabaptists are not free of this fault, for they too cry out that it is foreign to Christian liberty for Christians to be subject to the magistrate, or for a Christian magistrate to decree anything concerning religion. Hence they also trifle that in the Old Testament only one political government was instituted, and no spiritual and ecclesiastical government distinct from and independent of the political; and that when the political government of the Old Testament expired, there was no political government in the New Testament to which the care of religion was committed. These things are too silly. For we have shown that the political government was not abrogated by Christ, and the distinction between political and ecclesiastical power under the Old Testament is clear, not only from that contest in which Azariah the high priest, accompanied by eighty priests, opposed King Uzziah with holy zeal as a usurper of an alien office, a zeal which God approved by avenging it with the leprosy sent upon the king: 2 Chron. XXVI. 16. 17. etc. It is clear also from the distinction between the two prefectures expressly stated in ibid. XIX. 11, one of which had its head in the affairs of the king, or civil affairs, the other in the affairs of Jehovah, or spiritual affairs, in which God had to be served even against the will of kings. St Paul also confirms this distinction when, teaching that God said nothing about the priesthood to the royal tribe of Judah, but that the calling to the priesthood belonged peculiarly to the tribe of Levi, he cites Heb. VII. 14. Nor is it an obstacle that the Sanhedrin was divinely instituted, in which both priest and judge were to be heard in the commonwealth of Israel, Deut. XVII. 8. 9. For, notwithstanding that association of judge and of political and ecclesiastical judgment, which the matters of mixed courts, in which corporal punishment commanded by the law of God accompanied ecclesiastical censure, often required, the distinction between the calling, governance and spiritual correction of the Church, and the temporal political jurisdiction and earthly kingdom, remained. Nor do the singular examples of Melchizedek, Eli and Samuel help, who were at once kings, judges and priests, since they were specially called to discharge each of those distinct offices; or that of Moses, at once prince of the people and lawgiver of religion. For that was a personal privilege of Moses, which did not pertain to the rule of an earthly king, which he held over the people of Israel, but to his other, prophetic office, in which, as prophet, outside the ordinary order, he bore the type of the most eminent Prophet, Christ. But the priesthood was committed not to Moses but to Aaron and his sons; to it belonged the ordinary spiritual direction and governance of the people in religion and worship, the installation of Aaron himself as priest, and the legislation of the priesthood, which Moses administered as a prophet of God, by God's command.

units.la: CXXX. In excessu adulatores & sycophantae illi sive Politici, sive Ecclesiastici peccant, qui Magistratui in Republica & Ecclesia par jus & aequalem potestatem tribuunt. Quorum antesignanus Thomas Erastus, cum complicibus suis, Ecclesiae potestatem omnem abdicavit, & Politico Magistratui subjecit. Ei in Anglia Colemanniani; in Belgio Grotius & Remonstrantes, quos peculiari libro Utenbogardus defendit, Magistratui architectonicam in Ecclesiam potestatem asserens, secundas fecerunt. Sed Remonstrantes, qui quandiu Magistratum sibi faventem & propitium experti sunt, mire potestatis ejus periStromata dilatarunt, conversa fortuna, velificationem sinuare coeperunt. Nam Episcopius Disputatione de jure Magistratus circa Sacra. A.MDCXVIII. edita, discrimine inter Ecclesias Templares, seu publicas & privatas, seu publico-privatas, quae in propriis aedificiis segreges a Templaribus coetus celebrat, mussitata potius quam constituta, in illa Magistratum jure Divino omni plenissima, in has nulla omnino pollere, obscurius paulo insinuavit; sed mox, detecto arcano omni, Remonstrantes tum in Confessione cap. 25. tum in ejusdem Apologia cap. 24. 25. mussitarunt. Post pugnam cum Remonstrantibus pugnatam, duo Reformati Theologi editis super hac controversia scriptis, pomum in medium projecerunt; unus author Brevis Responsionis ad solutiones datas, &c. cui Petrus Cabeliavius respondit; alter Vedelius vulgato de Episcopatu Constantini M. libro, quem Revius, Triglandius & Apollonius refutarunt. Qui eos secuti, praelium instaurare conati sunt, Ludovicus Molinaeus, Paraenesi ad aedificatores Imperii in Imperio, edita, & Lambertus Velthuysius, qui Ecclesiam spolium dominantium fecit, ab Anonymo, qui Johannes Broun Scoto Britannus est, aliisque ad partes vocatus est, actum egerunt, & operam luserunt.
units.tr: CXXX. In excess sin those flatterers and sycophants, whether political or ecclesiastical, who grant to the magistrate equal right and equal power in the commonwealth and in the Church. Their standard-bearer, Thomas Erastus, with his associates, renounced all power of the Church and subjected it to the political magistrate. In England the Coleman party followed him; in the Netherlands Grotius and the Remonstrants, whom Uytenbogaert defended in a special book, asserting an architectonic power over the Church for the magistrate, took second place. But the Remonstrants, who as long as they found the magistrate favourable and propitious to them, lavishly spread out his power, began, when fortune changed, to trim their sail. For Episcopius, in his Disputation on the right of the magistrate concerning sacred things, published in 1618, lightly hinted, rather muttered than established, a distinction between temple churches, that is public churches, and private churches, or public-private ones, which hold separate assemblies in their own buildings apart from the temple churches: over the former the magistrate has full power by divine right, over the latter none at all. But soon, the secret being revealed, the Remonstrants muttered and backed away from it, both in their Confession, chapter 25, and in its Apology, chapters 24 and 25. After the battle fought with the Remonstrants, two Reformed theologians, by writings published on this controversy, threw the apple into the midst. One, the author of the Brief Reply to the solutions given, etc., was answered by Pierre Cabeliau; the other, Vedelius, by his published book on the episcopate of Constantine the Great, was refuted by Revius, Triglandius and Apollonius. Those who followed them and tried to renew the battle, Louis Molinaeus with his published Exhortation to the builders of an empire within the empire, and Lambertus Velthuysen, who made the Church the spoil of the rulers, summoned to the field by the Anonymous author, who is John Broun, a Scot of Britain, and others, went over old ground and wasted their effort.

units.la: CXXXI. Inter infames hos scopulos Ecclesia Reformata & Doctores ejus orthodoxi medii navigant, neque strictiorem, neque ampliorem erga Ecclesiam potestatem Magistratui vindicantes, quam jure Divino & naturali eidem competit, vel a volentibus etiam, non ut oikeia domestica & propria, sed ut aliena, singulares ob causas, eidem ad tempus, vel, si usus ita ferat, in perpetuum communicatur. Quae priusquam specialius exequamur, nonnulla animadvertenda in antecessum sunt. Primo enim Magistratus hic non spectatur absolute, sed restricte, qua Christianus est. Absolute, qua Magistratus potestatem communem, ut in reliquos subditos, sic in Ecclesiam etiam ditionis suae, ad externae disciplinae conservationem obtinet. Ecclesia enim, quia Ecclesia est, non definit esse societatis civilis pars, adeoque eatenus, perinde ut reliqui subditi, Potestati Civili subest. Restricte, ut Magistratus Christianus, habet potestatem singularem circa regimen, quod propriam Ecclesiae naturam & constitutionem attinet. Secundo Religio tria complectitur, Doctrinam fidei & cultus verbo legis & Evangelii definitam: Oeconomiam Ecclesiasticam generalem de Personis Ecclesiasticis, & earum officiis, & gubernationem Ecclesiae in genere, in verbo Evangelii traditam: denique circa Oeconomiam Ecclesiasticam specialem, personis, locis, temporibus speciatim accommodatam, & in verbo Dei non definitam. Circa quae non eodem modo Potestas Civilis versatur. Tertio Potestas circa Ecclesiam & Religionem non unius generis est. Nam alia objective solum, alia formaliter Ecclesiastica est. Objective talis pro objecto habet res & personas Ecclesiae: Formaliter talis circa res Ecclesiae non ratione objecti duntaxat, sed etiam ratione modi versatur, ecclesiastice puta, non politice. Prioris generis Potestas ei competit, qui Ecclesiam pro viribus tuetur, Pastores bonos fovet, malos coercet, ordinem externum Ecclesiae procurat, tabulam utramque legis Divinae custodit, & pro viribus operam dat, ut nomen Dei per subjectos sanctificetur, & Christi Regnum propagetur. Posterioris generis potestas ei competit, qui Evangelium praedicat, controversias ex verbo Dei dirimit, Sacramenta administrat, Pastores ordinat, disciplinam in sacrum gregem exercet, sacros ritus praescribit, spirituales leges juxta normam legis Divinae condit. Quae duae potestates multum discrepant. Illa enim de hoc mundo est, & Regno Dei universali hunc in mundum subordinatur: haec non de hoc mundo est, & Regno Christi Mediatorio inservit. Illa gladio armata, coactiva est: haec ministerialis, ex imperio alieno agit, & poenis spiritualibus, quae non poenae civiles, sed fraternae correctiones sunt, utitur. Neque tamen hae duae Potestates sibi mutuo officiunt, sed invicem adjuvant. Quarto potestas alia absoluta, alia limitata est. Illa nullis, haec certis legibus circumscribitur. Quinto Potestas alia propria & intrinseca: alia communicata & extrinseca atque delegata est, idque certa conditione legitimi usus.
units.tr: CXXXI. Among these infamous rocks the Reformed Church and its orthodox teachers steer a middle course, attributing to the magistrate neither a stricter nor a wider power over the Church than is due to him by divine and natural right, or than is communicated to him, for a time or, if custom so bears, in perpetuity, for singular reasons, by those willing to do so, not as his own domestic and proper property but as something foreign. Before we treat these matters more particularly, some points must be noted in advance. First, this magistrate is considered not absolutely but restrictedly, as Christian. Absolutely, as magistrate, he holds the common power over his subjects, and so over the Church within his jurisdiction also, for the preservation of external discipline. For the Church, because it is a Church, does not cease to be a part of civil society, and so far, just like the other subjects, it is subject to civil power. Restrictedly, as a Christian magistrate, he has a special power over the governance that concerns the proper nature and constitution of the Church. Second, religion embraces three things: the doctrine of faith and worship, defined by the word of the law and the gospel; the general ecclesiastical economy concerning ecclesiastical persons and their offices, and the government of the Church in general, handed down in the word of the gospel; and finally the special ecclesiastical economy, adapted specifically to persons, places and times, and not defined in the word of God. Civil power does not engage with these in the same way. Third, power concerning the Church and religion is not of one kind. For one power is ecclesiastical only objectively, another formally. Objectively such a power has as its object the things and persons of the Church; formally it concerns the things of the Church not only by reason of the object but also by reason of the manner, that is, ecclesiastically and not politically. The power of the first kind belongs to one who protects the Church as far as he can, fosters good ministers, restrains bad ones, takes care of the external order of the Church, keeps both tables of the divine law, and does what he can so that the name of God is sanctified by his subjects and the kingdom of Christ is propagated. The power of the second kind belongs to one who preaches the gospel, settles controversies from the word of God, administers the sacraments, ordains ministers, exercises discipline over the holy flock, prescribes sacred rites, and enacts spiritual laws according to the norm of the divine law. These two powers differ greatly. The former is of this world and is subordinated to the universal kingdom of God in this world; the latter is not of this world and serves the mediatorial kingdom of Christ. The former, armed with the sword, is coercive; the latter is ministerial, acts by an authority not its own, and uses spiritual penalties, which are not civil punishments but fraternal corrections. Yet these two powers do not hinder each other but help each other. Fourth, one power is absolute and another limited: the former is bound by no laws, the latter by certain laws. Fifth, one power is proper and intrinsic; another is communicated, extrinsic and delegated, and that on a certain condition of lawful use.

units.la: CXXXII. His animadversis de potestate Magistratus circa Ecclesiam & Religionem certum & exploratum aliquid statuendum est. Ante omnia enim firmiter illud tenendum est, quod potestas formaliter ecclesiastica, oikeia & intrinseca, qualem modo explicavimus, Magistratui nullo modo nec formaliter, nec eminenter tribui possit. Cum enim Magistratus, qua talis, non sit Ecclesia, & Magistratus esse possit, licet ne membrum quidem verae Ecclesiae sit, planum est, potestatem Ecclesiae propriam & formalem ei, qua Magistratus est, non competere. Nam potestas Eccle-
units.tr: CXXXII. Having made these observations about the power of the magistrate in relation to the Church and religion, we must lay down something certain and established. Above all, we must hold firmly that the power that is formally ecclesiastical, proper and intrinsic, of the kind we have just explained, can in no way be granted to the magistrate, either formally or eminently. For since the magistrate, as such, is not the Church, and can be a magistrate even though he is not even a member of the true Church, it is plain that the proper and formal power of the Church does not belong to him as magistrate. For ecclesiastical power

units.la: Potestas formaliter & propria Ecclesiastica Magistratui non competit. Ecclesiæ propria & formalis spiritualis tota est, & symbolo clavium, Regnum Cœlorum aperientium & claudentium, adumbratur. Potestas autem spiritualis & clavium Regni Cœlorum Ecclesiæ, non Magistratui, quà tali, à Christo tradita est, Matth. XVI. 19. Neque Ecclesia illa, cui reus ex mandato Christi defertur, ibid. XVIII. 17. Magistratus est. Tum Magistratus potestatem propriè Ecclesiasticam vel quà Magistratus, vel quà Christianus habet. At non quà Magistratus, quia quà talis, ex mundo est, & potestatem corporalem, coërcitivam externam, non spiritualem & internam habet: & Magistratus multi sunt, quibus nihil cum Ecclesia commercii est. Non quà Christianus est, quia aliàs omni Christiano competeret, cùm tamen inter Christianos alii præsint & regant, alii subsint & obediant. Cùmque nec posito Magistratu necessariò Ecclesia ponatur, nec sublato tollatur, non potest Ecclesiæ potestas propria & formalis ei competere, quia proprium à subjecto suo nunquam tolli potest. Neque dici potest, Magistratum, ceu præfectum Ecclesiasticum, & Ecclesiam, ceu subditos, esse relata, & relationem inter subjecta esse potestatem Ecclesiasticam. Ubi enim relatio est, ibi relatum & correlatum sunt, & ubi illa concipiuntur, concipi, ut simul naturâ & tempore existentia, debent. Sed quod correlatum hîc videri potest, Ecclesia sine relato suo, Magistratu, esse potest. Ubi ergo relatio? Nisi forte dicere libet, Magistratum tum Ecclesiæ potestatem concedere. Sed quam ipse Magistratus infidelis non habet, utpote qui non aliam quàm formaliter politicam potestatem habet, eam Ecclesiæ impertiri non potest. Accedit, quòd potestas Magistratus omnis est αρχηλοιτκη, dominans, coactiva, carnalis, armis, carceribus, suppliciis munita. Immediatè à Deo, tanquam Domino mundi, pendens; Ecclesiastica verò formaliter & intrinsecè talis merè spiritualis & ministerialis est. Proin Ministri & præcones Evangelii præcones non amplius Christi, sed hominum servi forent: neque ulla ratione Magistratus clavium potestati, & Ministerium Dei elencho & judicio subsunt. Etiam in V. T. potestatem utramque Regni & Sacerdotii distinctam fuisse, supra adversus Anabaptistas comprobavimus. Nulla verò ratione demonstrari potest, universam eam potestatem, quam distinctam in V. T. Ecclesia habuit, in Novo Magistratui accrevisse, atque ita Magistratum N. T. ampliorem longè potestatem acquisivisse, quàm in V. T. quando Deorum nomine insignitus, & multis prærogativis mactatus est, habuit. Præterea omnis potestas Ecclesiastica immediatè est à Christo, quà Mediatore, & capite Ecclesiæ charismata spiritualia impertiente, & personæ per legitimam missionem, electionem & ordinationem ecclesiasticam applicatur. Sed Magistratui, quà tali, non sic Divinitus potestas confertur; utpote qui non raro potestatem suam per carnalem successionem, jus belli, aliósque ejusmodi modos, planè Ecclesiæ incognitos, acquirit. Insuper potestas Ecclesiastica est formaliter sacra, religiosa, spiritualis, quà homines rogantur, monentur, corripiuntur; iis promissiones & comminationes Divinæ prædicantur, peccata remittuntur,
units.tr: Formal and proper ecclesiastical power does not belong to the magistrate. The proper and formal power of the Church is wholly spiritual, and it is foreshadowed by the symbol of the keys, which open and shut the Kingdom of Heaven. But the spiritual power of the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven was given by Christ to the Church, not to the magistrate as such: Matth. 16. 19. Nor is it to that Church, to which the offender is referred by Christ's command, Matth. 18. 17, that the magistrate belongs. Then, the magistrate has power that is properly ecclesiastical either as magistrate or as Christian. But not as magistrate, because as such he is of the world, and has a bodily, coercive, external power, not a spiritual and internal one; and there are many magistrates who have no fellowship at all with the Church. Nor as Christian, because otherwise it would belong to every Christian, whereas among Christians some preside and rule, while others are subject and obey. And since the Church is not necessarily established when a magistrate is established, nor removed when he is removed, the proper and formal power of the Church cannot belong to him, because a proper attribute can never be taken away from its subject. Nor can it be said that the magistrate, as ecclesiastical overseer, and the Church, as his subjects, are related, and that the relation between the subjects is ecclesiastical power. For where there is a relation, there are a relatum and a correlate, and where these are conceived, they must be conceived as existing together both in nature and in time. But the correlate here, the Church, can exist without its relatum, the magistrate. Where, then, is the relation? Unless one perhaps wishes to say that the magistrate grants ecclesiastical power to the Church. But what the unbelieving magistrate himself does not have, inasmuch as he has only formally political power, he cannot impart to the Church. Add to this that all the power of the magistrate is ruling [ἀρχηλοιτκη], dominating, coercive, carnal, fortified with arms, prisons and punishments, and depends immediately on God as Lord of the world; whereas ecclesiastical power, formally and intrinsically, is purely spiritual and ministerial. Therefore the ministers and heralds of the Gospel would no longer be heralds of Christ but servants of men, and the magistrate would in no way be subject to the power of the keys, and the ministry of God would be subject to the censure and judgment of men. We have already proved against the Anabaptists that under the Old Testament the two powers, of kingdom and of priesthood, were distinct. But it cannot be shown by any argument that all the power which the Church had distinct in the Old Testament has passed over to the magistrate in the New, and that the magistrate of the New Testament has thereby acquired a far greater power than he had in the Old, when he was called by the name of gods and endowed with many prerogatives. Moreover, all ecclesiastical power comes immediately from Christ, as Mediator and Head of the Church, who bestows spiritual gifts, and it is applied to a person through lawful sending, election and ecclesiastical ordination. But power is not conferred by God in this way upon the magistrate as such, since he not infrequently acquires his power by carnal succession, by the right of war and by other such means, entirely unknown to the Church. Furthermore, ecclesiastical power is formally sacred, religious and spiritual, by which men are asked, admonished and rebuked; promises and threats of God are proclaimed to them, sins are forgiven

units.la: vel retinentur, & cuncta etiam pœnæ & judicii rationem habentia ipsaque adeò confusio, objurgatio, separatio ab externo Ecclesiæ corpore, ad eorum ædificationem, conversionem, consolationem & salutem Spiritus diriguntur. Talis non est potestas Magistratus, neque uspiam talia Scripturæ ei vendicant. Denique nihil ita obesit, quò minùs singuli Magistratus in totidem Ecclesiæ capita erigantur, & paulatim totum Ecclesiæ regimen ad particulares status & formas regiminis politici inflectatur, atque Ecclesia, Regnum Cœlorum, in Regnum mundanum & terrestre convertatur, & hominibus hujus seculi, quorum major pars malè Christum didicit, subjiciatur.
units.tr: or retained, and all things that also have the character of punishment and judgment, and indeed confusion itself, rebuke, and separation from the outward body of the Church, are directed by the Spirit to their edification, conversion, consolation and salvation. Such is not the power of the magistrate, nor do the Scriptures anywhere ascribe such things to him. Finally, nothing so hinders individual magistrates from being set up as so many heads of the Church, and gradually bending the whole government of the Church toward particular states and forms of political rule, and converting the Church, the Kingdom of Heaven, into a worldly and earthly kingdom, and subjecting it to the men of this age, most of whom have learned Christ poorly.

units.la: CXXXIII. Nihil ad rem faciunt exempla Melchisedeci, Samuelis, Eli. Una enim persona ex peculiari œconomia geminata potestatem, ex geminata vocatione Divina, suscipiunt. Duplex enim eorum χαρις, una ad Rempublicam, ad Ecclesiam altera tuit. Cæteræ verò Potestates Civiles omnes in V. T. à potestate Ecclesiæ propria exercenda religiosè abstinuerunt. Quod de Mose etiam supra probavimus. Estque potestas à Deo ordinata, & Minister Dei εις το αγαθον ad bonum, Rom. XIII. 1.4. Sed boni illius administer est non quovis modo; certè non propriè & directè ecclesiastico, uti argumentis supra allatis confecimus, sed propriè politico, & indirectè, atque per solam denominationem ecclesiastico, quatenus quodammodo, hoc est, modo sibi conveniente, circa res & personas Ecclesiæ distringitur. Politica quoque potestas architectonica est, cui omnes reliquæ potestates, adeóque etiam spiritualis suo quæque modo subordinantur. Sed spiritualis illa potestas duobus modis architectonicæ subordinari dicitur, vel per se, quà spiritualis est; vel per accidens, quà corporalis, vel secularis, vel corporali & seculari rei conjuncta est. Posteriori illo, non priori modo Ecclesiastica potestas architectonicæ subordinatur. Ita concio Ecclesiastæ pendet à medico, non quà concio est, sed quà actio animalis est, ad quam requiritur sanitas, quam medicus procuravit. Neque Magistratus potestatem quamvis, quæ in Republica, ceu contentum in continente est, in se vel formaliter, vel eminenter continet, vel ejusdem actus liberè exercere potest. Nam & maritalis potestas, & medici ars in Republica continetur; quæ secundum formalem & intrinsecam rationem suam Magistratui non convenit, quia nec eam potestatem propriam & intrinsecam, quam maritus in uxorem habet, Magistratus sibi vendicare; nec medico præscribere, quibus mediis ad valetudinem restituendam uti debeat, ausit. Neque eadem ratio potestatis maritalis est, quæ prætoriæ, militaris, quæstoriæ est. Hanc enim Magistratus exercere etiam potest: illam exercere non potest. Præterea una genere est Potestas civilis, sed genere analogico, quæ inæqualiter ad potestates inferiores sibi directè & per se subordinatas & subjectas, velut prætoriam, militarem, &c. & non directè & per se, sed per accidens subordinatas, velut potestatem spiritualem, maritalem, &c. descendit. Ibi est potestas Cυσχωυς, homogenea, intrinseca, quia non dirigit tantùm, sed etiam exercere potest: hic ratioratione spiritualis objecti extrinseca duntaxat est, & potestatem eam, quippe à se independentem, ratione quadam quoad extrinseca quaedam requisita, & adjuncta, dirigit, sed non exercet. Sed mirè illud adversarii exagitant, quod hac ratione Magistratus ipse quodammodo potestati Ecclesiae subjicitur, & duplex regimen, geminata potestas collateralis, politica & ecclesiastica, statuatur, atque sic imperium in imperio aedificetur, & Papatus, Hierarchia, tyrannis postliminio revocetur. Quae Remonstrantes inprimis non veritatis studio, sed ad invidiam Ministris Ecclesiae apud Superiores conflandam, quasi imperium aliquod, Politico par affectarent; (quam calumniam praxis refutat, & refutare debet) objiciunt. Potestas enim Ecclesiae, à potestate civili jure Divino & naturali distincta in Christo quidem, supremo Ecclesiae Domino, Capite & Rege principalis & verè architectonica: in Ministris vero Ecclesiae & consentiente tota Ecclesia merè ministerialis est, neque adeò in authoritate externa, jurisdictione proprie dicta, vi & coercitione externa, imperio despotico, sed in praeconio verbi, demonstratione veritatis, rogatione hominum, ut Deo reconcilientur, consolatione lugentium, elencho & judicio refractariorum, legum, seu potius διαταξεων, quibus internus Ecclesiae ordo constituitur, formatione, personarum ad ministerium deputatione, & similibus, nihil typhi secularis, authoritatis eminentis & imperii, sed humile ubique ministerium, Divino Christi & Evangelii ejus imperio conformatum & subjectum resipientibus consistit. Subjectio vero Magistratus non ministris Verbi Dei, quà tales illi sunt, sed Verbo Dei, & judicio secundum solum illud administrato debetur. Potestati ejusmodi ministeriali subordinari, imò & subjici personam societatis supremam licet in civitate; at in Ecclesia nil nisi fratrem, & tantò honoratiorem & nobiliorem, quantò fidelior & humilior est, adeóque ratione fraternitatis, & συμβιωσεως spiritualis in corpore & communione matris ejusdem Ecclesiae, nemini verè pio, Deum timenti, & ad verbum ejus trepidanti, absurdum videri debet, quia aliud & toto coelo disparatum potestatis genus est. Clamat enim Deus ipse: Animadvertite Reges, erudimini judices terrae. Servite Jehovae in timore, & gaudete in tremore. Osculamini Filium, ne irascatur, Psal. II. 10. 11. 12. Clamat Christus: Qui vos (verbum meum praedicantes, mihi ex praescripto ministrantes) audit, me audit. Qui vos spernit, me spernit. Qui vero me spernit, eum, qui me misit, spernit, Luc. X. 16. Filius consul, Princeps vel Rex Patri, quoad patriam potestatem: Regina nubens non Regi, marito non Regi, quoad potestatem maritalem: Rex aegrotus medico corporali, & quid ni etiam spirituali, tantò magis audiendo, quantò spiritualis aeterna totius hominis salus corporis in hac vita valetudine praestat, subordinatur & subjicitur. Non ergo collateralem Magistratus & Ecclesiae potestatem facimus, uti Utenbogardus, Grotius, alii Remonstrantes criminantur. Ubi enim est subjectio potestatis Ecclesiasticae, & Superioritas Politicae, ibi non est collateralitas. At in gubernatione externa est subjectio potestatis Ecclesiasticae, & Superioritas Politicae. Caeterum subjectio illa non tantum non est absoluta, verùm limitata, quia Deo magis quàm hominibus obtemperandum, Actor. IV. 19. sed etiam ἀντιπροσωπ & reciproca, qua ita Ecclesiastica Politicae quodammodo subest, ut vicissim Politica Ecclesiasticae, quoad fidem, mores & disciplinam, subsit. Diversi ergo generis potestates, non duplex, politica & architectonica, cùm sint, nulli collateralitati, nulli imperio in imperio locus esse potest. Christus in terris degens fuit Rex, & ad hoc natus est, ut esset Rex, sed non de hoc mundo. In eadem ergo Republica duae potestates supremae disparatae; quarum altera alteri pe se subordinata non fuit: & duae Potestates inferiores disparatae, neutra alteri directè subordinata, puta Ministrorum politicorum & Ecclesiasticorum, Apostolorum & LXX. discipulorum, extitit. Neque tamen sic vel collateralitas potestatum, vel imperium in imperio obtinuit. Et tantum abest, ut potestas propriè Ecclesiastica à Magistratu independens, & à solo Christo dependens, Magistratui verè Christiano gravis & iniqua sit, vel videri debeat, ut potiùs Magistratus munus suum non parùm per illam sublevari, & authoritatem stabiliri sentiat. Nam eatenus revera Magistratui opitulatur. Alterius altera poscit opem res, & conjurat amicè. Denique nec ferit nos id, quòd Reges Angliae post Henricum VIII. Ecclesiae capita dicta sunt. Nam phrasis ipsa in sensu suo emphatico satis quidem insolens foret, quia in Scriptura Caput Ecclesiae solus Christus dicitur, & ejus nomen διαφορώτερον hoc est. Nihilominus impropria, in sensu diminuto, & per καλλιγενην Ecclesiae sic caput Ecclesiae Magistratus dici potest ratione tum eminentiae, quia Ecclesiae nobilissimum & principale membrum est; tum ratione gubernationis, quia Ecclesiae nutritius, & Dei minister in bonum ejus est. Hoc non alio sensu Angli Reformati Regem suum Ecclesiae caput dixerunt.
units.tr: Nothing to the point is achieved by the examples of Melchizedek, Samuel and Eli. For in their case one person, by a special economy, assumed two powers from two divine callings. Each of them had a twofold χάρις, one directed to the commonwealth and the other to the Church. All the other civil powers in the Old Testament refrained religiously from exercising the power proper to the Church, as we have also shown above concerning Moses. The civil power is ordained by God and is "the minister of God for good [εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν]" (Rom. 13:1, 4). But it is the servant of that good not in every way: certainly not directly and properly in an ecclesiastical manner, as we have established by the arguments adduced above, but properly in a political manner and indirectly, and only by a name that is ecclesiastical, insofar as it is in some measure, that is, in a way suited to itself, concerned with the matters and persons of the Church. The political power is also architectonic, and all the other powers, including the spiritual, are subordinated to it in their own way. But that spiritual power is said to be subordinated to the architectonic power in two ways: either in itself, as spiritual, or accidentally, as bodily or secular, or as joined to a bodily and secular matter. The ecclesiastical power is subordinated to the architectonic power in the latter way, not the former. Thus the preaching of the minister depends on the physician, not as preaching, but as an animal action, for which health is required, and which the physician has provided. Nor can the magistrate freely exercise the power of an act of that which is contained in the commonwealth, as the contained in the container, whether formally or eminently. For both the marital power and the physician's art are contained in the commonwealth; but according to their formal and intrinsic nature they do not belong to the magistrate, since the magistrate does not claim for himself the proper and intrinsic power which a husband has over his wife, nor would he dare to prescribe to a physician by what means he ought to restore health. Nor is the marital power the same kind of power as the praetorian, military or quaestorial power: for the magistrate can exercise the latter, but cannot exercise the former. Moreover, civil power is one in genus, but in an analogical genus, which descends unequally to inferior powers that are subordinated and subject to it directly and in themselves, such as the praetorian, military, and so on, and to those that are subordinated not directly and in themselves but accidentally, such as the spiritual, marital, and so on. In the former case the power is univocal [συνώνυμος], homogeneous and intrinsic, because it not only directs but can also exercise; in the latter case it is extrinsic only by reason of the spiritual object, and it directs that power, which is independent of itself, according to certain matters extrinsic and adjoined to it, but does not exercise it. But our opponents strangely harp on this, that by this reasoning the magistrate himself is in some way subjected to the power of the Church, and a twofold government, a twofold collateral power, political and ecclesiastical, is posited, and thus an empire within an empire is built, and Papacy, hierarchy and tyranny are restored again. The Remonstrants object to this, chiefly not out of a zeal for truth but in order to stir up odium against the ministers of the Church before their superiors, as if they were aiming at some kind of power equal to the political (a calumny which practice refutes and ought to refute). For the power of the Church, distinct from the civil power by divine and natural right, is in Christ, the supreme Lord, Head and King of the Church, truly principal and architectonic; but in the ministers of the Church, and with the consent of the whole Church, it is purely ministerial, and it does not consist in external authority, jurisdiction properly so called, force and external coercion, or despotic command, but in the proclamation of the Word, the demonstration of truth, the entreating of men that they be reconciled to God, the consolation of the mourning, the refutation and judgment of the refractory, the laws, or rather the ordinances, by which the internal order of the Church is constituted, the forming and appointing of persons to the ministry, and the like; there is nothing of worldly pride, eminent authority or empire in it, but everywhere a humble ministry, conformed to and subject to the divine command of Christ and of his Gospel, which those who are wise acknowledge. Subjection, however, is owed by the magistrate not to the ministers of the Word of God as such, but to the Word of God and to the judgment administered according to that alone. It is lawful for the highest person of a society in the state to be subordinated, even subjected, to a power of this ministerial kind; but in the Church there is nothing but a brother, and one who is all the more honourable and noble the more faithful and humble he is. Therefore, by reason of brotherhood and spiritual συμβίωσις [συμβίωσις] in the body and communion of the same mother Church, it ought to seem absurd to no one who is truly pious, who fears God and trembles at his word, since it is a different kind of power, wholly disparate. For God himself cries out: Be warned, you kings; be instructed, you judges of the earth. Serve Jehovah in fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry (Ps. 2:10–12). Christ cries out: He who hears you (preaching my word, ministering to me according to what has been prescribed), hears me. He who rejects you, rejects me. And he who rejects me, rejects him who sent me (Luke 10:16). The son, a consul, a prince or a king is subordinated and subjected to his father by paternal power; a queen who marries is subject not to the king, but to her husband, by marital power; a sick king is subordinated and subjected to a bodily physician, and why not also to a spiritual one, the more so by listening the more the eternal spiritual salvation of the whole man surpasses the health of the body in this life. We therefore do not make a collateral power of the magistrate and of the Church, as Uytenbogaert, Grotius and the other Remonstrants accuse us. For where there is subjection of the ecclesiastical power and superiority of the political power, there is no collateralness; but in external government there is subjection of the ecclesiastical power and superiority of the political power. Moreover, that subjection is not only not absolute but limited, because God must be obeyed rather than men (Acts 4:19); and it is also reciprocal and mutual, so that the ecclesiastical power is in some way subject to the political, and conversely the political is subject to the ecclesiastical in matters of faith, morals and discipline. Since, therefore, they are powers of different kinds, and not a twofold power, political and architectonic, there can be no place for collateralness, nor for an empire within an empire. Christ, while dwelling on earth, was a king, and was born to be a king, but not of this world. In the same commonwealth, then, there arose two disparate supreme powers, of which the one was not subordinated to the other in itself; and two disparate inferior powers, neither directly subordinated to the other, namely those of the political and ecclesiastical ministers, of the Apostles and the seventy disciples. Yet neither collateralness of powers nor an empire within an empire has thereby come about. And so far is the power properly ecclesiastical, independent of the magistrate and depending on Christ alone, from being, or from needing to appear, burdensome and unjust to a truly Christian magistrate, that rather the magistrate feels his office not a little relieved by it and his authority strengthened. For insofar as it truly helps the magistrate. One kind of thing asks help of the other and friendly conspires with it. Finally, nor does it trouble us that the kings of England after Henry VIII were called heads of the Church. For the phrase itself, in its emphatic sense, would indeed be rather unusual, since in Scripture Christ alone is called the Head of the Church, and his name is more distinctive [διαφορώτερον]. Nevertheless, in a diminished sense, and improperly, the magistrate can be called head of the Church in this way, both by reason of eminence, since he is the most noble and principal member of the Church, and by reason of government, since he is the nourisher of the Church and a minister of God for its good. It was in no other sense that the English Reformed called their king head of the Church.

units.la: CXXXIV. Potestatem Magistratus erga & circa religionem & Ecclesiam Remonstrantes architectonicam esse, definiunt. Sed vocis ambiguitate ludunt & illudunt. Proprie ἀρχιτεκτονικὸν id est, quod ad architectum, cui reliqui fabri subsunt, pertinet. Graeci Interpretes verba Dei de Bezaleele Divino spiritu impleto לחשוב מחשבות ad cogitandum cogitationes, Exod. XXXI. 4. sic reddunt: διανοεῖσθαι καὶ ἀρχιτεκτονεῖν ad cogitandum & fabrisaciendum, hoc est, uti Vulgatus etiam habet: ad excogitandum, quicquid fabrefieri potest ex auro, &c. Eadem verba ibid. XXXV. 32. reddunt: παντα ἀρχιτεκτονεῖν καὶ παντα τὰ ἔργα τῆς ἀρχιτεκτονίας, ad architectandum cuncta juxta omnia opera architecturae. Architectus is est, qui ingenio & imperio reliquis aedificii fabris praeest. Translata haec vox ab Aristotele aliisque politicis est ad significandam potestatem Magistratus erga subditos. Qualis ergo potestas illa est, tale ἀρχιτεκτονικὸν est. Cùmque singuli etiam fideles & tota Ecclesia in civilibus Magistratui, quoad ordinem & disciplinam externam subsint, eatenus Magistratui erga fideles & Ecclesiam potestas architectonica tribui potest. Par enim hic subditorum omnium, fidelium & infidelium fidelium ratio est. Quoad potestatem verò illam, seu potius curam, quam Magistratui erga Ecclesiam jure Divino singulari ratione competit, illa proprië architectonica dici non potest. Si enim sermo sit de potestate intrinsecè & formaliter Ecclesiastica, illam Magistratui nec formaliter nec eminenter sic competere, ut potestas Ecclesiæ ejus imperio & potestati subordinetur, multis rationibus astruximus. Sin de potestate objectivè & extrinsecè Ecclesiastica, eo sensu, quo suprà illud explicavimus, & amplius explicabimus, illa Magistratui convenit, sed nonnisi improprië & ἀκυρολόγως architectonica dicitur, respectu eorum, quæ aliquid architectonicum, velut jurisdictionem propriè dictam, sanctionem, coercitionem, &c. postulant. Nam potestas Magistratus circa Ecclesiam, velut legislatoria, limitata & multis modis restricta est, non tantùm quia in genere legislatio illa ad ordinem saltem generaliter in verbo Dei præscriptum adstringitur; sed etiam lex nulla inscia, in vita & non consentiente Ecclesia, cujus universæ unâ cum Magistratu, ceu membro Ecclesiæ, est ἐυταξίαν Ecclesiæ definire, constitui, definiri, adeóque nec sigillo architectonicæ potestatis roborari & confirmari potest. Qua in re ingens legislationem inter politicam & Ecclesiasticam discrimen est. Illa enim merè architectonica, ab imperantis arbitrio, non à subditorum voluntate & arbitrio ullatenus pendet: hæc ab Ecclesiæ non minùs quàm Magistratus voluntate & arbitrio pendet. Ideo Magistratus in Republica jus τὸ δοκεῖν intendit & remittit, rogat vel abrogat, nulla voluntatis subditorum habita ratione, quod in Ecclesia circa leges nec Divinas, utpote plane immutabiles, nec ecclesiasticas facere potest. Par reliquorum circa Ecclesiam actuum ratio est. In universum igitur Magistratus circa Ecclesiam, quà talem, potestatem architectonicam propriè dictam nullam habet. Ecclesia enim cùm sit Regnum Dei & Christi, spirituale, consistens in obedientia fidei & confessionis, & omnes subditi ejus sint liberi, ad serviendum soli Deo, imperium humanum nullum patitur. Vos autem ne vocemini Rabbi. Unus enim est doctor vester, Christus. Omnes autem vos fratres estis. Et Patrem vestrum in terra neminem vocetis. Unus enim Pater vester est, qui in Cœlis est. Neque vocemini ductores. Unus enim ductor vester, Christus est. Qui verò inter vos magnus esse vult, esto minister vester, Matth. XXIII. 8-12. Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo, Joh. XVIII. 36. Pretio empti estis, ne fiatis servi hominum, 1. Cor. VII. 23. Christum Deus collocavit ad dextram suam in cœlestibus supra omnem principatum & potestatem, & potentiam & dominatum, Ephes. I. 20. 21. In ipso (Christo) estis completi, qui est caput omnis Principatus & potestatis, Col. II. 10. Solus ergo Deus, Christus architectonicam potestatem in Ecclesiam habet. Unde S. Basilius in cap. 3. Esaj. Τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἀρχιτεκτονεῖν τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν τῆς Θεῦ Spiritum S. architectari seu ædificare Ecclesiam Dei, dixit. Si enim ullus homo eam habet, quid Christo relinquitur? Si enim sub Christo potestas architectonica Magistratui tribuenda est, necessariò efficitur, Ministrorum Ecclesiæ esse potestati illi parére, & servire, quod cum cura iis imposita directè pugnat. Hi enim vigilant pro animabus fidelium, tanquam rationem reddituri, Hebr. XIII. 17. At cui rationem redditumust ri? Certè nulli homini, quia nullius hominis animæ hominum sunt; sed uni Christo, animarum pastori & Episcopo. Quare & jubentur Ministri attendere sibi ipsis, & toti gregi, in quo Spiritus S. ipsos Episcopos constituit ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei, quam ille suo sanguine acquisivit, Actor. XX. 28. Et certè si Magistratui architectonica potestas in externum Ecclesiæ regimen competit, eidem potestas in prædicationem Evangelii & claves Regni Cœlorum competit. Per illa enim externè Ecclesia regitur. Prædicatio autem verbi in animas fidelium penetrat, easque Christo subjicit. Unde sequitur, Magistratui potestatem in animas fidelium competere, quo nihil arrogantius dici potest. Sed architectonicam potestatem regendi Ecclesiam immediatè sub Christo Ecclesiæ competere, illi asserunt. Hinc verò consequens est, supremum & architectonicum judicium de iis, quæ ad externum Ecclesiæ regimen pertinent, immediatè sub Christo Magistratui Christiano competere. Supremum enim regimen sine supremo judicio supremum regimen non est. Qui enim judicium alienum sequi tenetur, is non regit, sed regitur, & mancipium atque servus judicantium est. Hoc posito immediatè sequitur, tum universam authoritatem, inspectionem, curam, directionem, quam Ministris Ecclesiæ Scriptura tribuit, à judicio Christiani Magistratus, tanquam à judicio supremi tribunalis, à quo provocatio non datur, pendere: tum Ministros Ecclesiæ & verbi Dei, non indirectè tantùm, sed etiam directè ubique obligari ad sequendum judicium Magistratus; tum Ministros Ecclesiæ teneri decreta omnia Magistratus, publicum Ecclesiæ regimen concernentia, hominibus prædicare, & iisdem persuadere, ut iis morem gerant: Ecclesiæ membra & fideles non obligari ad parendum Ecclesiæ Ministris, si quid contra qualiacunque decreta Magistratus in rebus ad regimen Ecclesiæ pertinentibus, statuerint: imò obligari ad iis non parendum. Quæ ἀποπήματα Ecclesiam in durissimam hominum servitutem redigentia & Papalis imperii arcanum refodientia, denique & Ecclesiæ & Magistratui ipsi cladem machinantia, narrasse, refutasse est.
