Quid deniquedicemus de Ecclesia, quæ Magistratu fideli destituta, supplet id omne, quod à Magistratus fidelis potestate circa religionem expectari poterat? An Ecclesia in tali statu, in quo in sacris plenissimum jus ex ipsa naturæ lege ad eam devolvi censetur, architectonicam fidelis Magistratus potestatem, velut ad se jam devolutam, exercet? Atque ita geminatam potestatem dominantem & imperium in imperio erigit, vel igitur Magistratus circa Ecclesiam potestas architectonica non est; vel Ecclesia in tali statu potestatem architectonicam Magistratui fideli debitam, sibi arrogat, & imperium in imperio erigit. Posterius quis de Ecclesia sub cruce gemente, inope, præsidio temporali omni destituta dixerit? Prius igitur etiam falsum est.
units.tr: CXXXIV. The Remonstrants define the power of the magistrate over and concerning religion and the Church as architectonic. But they play and trick with the ambiguity of the word. Strictly speaking, ἀρχιτεκτονικόν [architectonikon] means what pertains to the architect, to whom the other craftsmen are subject. In Exodus 31:4 the Greek translators render God's words about Bezaleel, filled with the Divine Spirit, לחשוב מחשבות [lachshov machshavot, to devise designs], as διανοεῖσθαι καὶ ἀρχιτεκτονεῖν [dianoeisthai kai architektonein], "to devise and to fashion", that is, as the Vulgate also has it: to devise whatever can be wrought in gold, &c. In the same chapter, 35:32, they render: παντα ἀρχιτεκτονεῖν καὶ παντα τὰ ἔργα τῆς ἀρχιτεκτονίας [panta architektonein kai panta ta erga tes architektonias], "to architect all things, and all the works of architecture", that is, to architect all things according to all the works of architecture. The architect is the one who presides over the other craftsmen of a building by his skill and command. This word was taken over by Aristotle and other political writers to signify the magistrate's power over his subjects. Therefore, whatever kind of power that is, such is the architectonic power. And since individual believers, and the whole Church, are subject to the civil magistrate in respect of external order and discipline, to that extent an architectonic power over believers and the Church can be attributed to the magistrate. For here the case of all subjects, believers and unbelievers alike, is the same. But as for that power, or rather care, which the magistrate has over the Church by a singular divine right, that cannot properly be called architectonic. For if we speak of power that is intrinsically and formally ecclesiastical, we have shown by many arguments that it does not belong to the magistrate, either formally or eminently, so that the power of the Church would be subordinated to his command and authority. But if we speak of power that is objectively and extrinsically ecclesiastical, in the sense we explained above and shall explain more fully, that belongs to the magistrate; yet it is called architectonic only improperly and catachrestically, with respect to those things which require something architectonic, such as jurisdiction properly so called, sanction, coercion, &c. For the magistrate's power over the Church, as legislative, is limited and restricted in many ways, not only because that legislation is bound, at least in general terms, to the order prescribed in the Word of God, but also because no law may be made without the knowledge and consent of the Church, whose good order it is, together with the magistrate as a member of the Church, to define, establish and be defined; and so it cannot be strengthened or confirmed by the seal of architectonic power. In this matter there is a great difference between civil and ecclesiastical legislation. For civil legislation is purely architectonic and depends wholly on the will of the ruler, not at all on the will and judgment of the subjects; whereas ecclesiastical legislation depends no less on the will and judgment of the Church than of the magistrate. Hence the magistrate in the commonwealth enacts and repeals, proposes and abrogates what seems good to him, with no regard to the will of the subjects; this he cannot do in the Church with regard to laws, which are neither divine, being wholly unchangeable, nor ecclesiastical. The same is true of his other acts concerning the Church. Taken all together, therefore, the magistrate as such has no architectonic power properly so called over the Church. For the Church, since it is the kingdom of God and of Christ, spiritual, consisting in obedience of faith and confession, and all its subjects are free to serve God alone, admits no human command. But you, be not called Rabbi; for one is your Teacher, Christ, and all you are brethren. And call no man your father upon the earth; for one is your Father, who is in heaven. Neither be called masters; for one is your Master, even Christ. But he that is greatest among you shall be your servant, Matt. 23:8-12. My kingdom is not of this world, John 18:36. You are bought with a price; be not made servants of men, 1 Cor. 7:23. God set Christ at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all principality and power, and might, and dominion, Eph. 1:20, 21. In him (Christ) you are complete, who is the head of all principality and power, Col. 2:10. Therefore God alone, Christ, has architectonic power over the Church. Hence St. Basil, on Isaiah chapter 3, said: Τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἀρχιτεκτονεῖν τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν τῆς Θεοῦ [to pneuma to hagion architektonein ten ekklesian tou Theou], that is, the Holy Spirit architects, or builds, the Church of God. For if any man has that power, what is left to Christ? For if under Christ architectonic power must be ascribed to the magistrate, it necessarily follows that the ministers of the Church must obey and serve that power, which directly conflicts with the care laid upon them. For they watch for your souls, as those who must give account, Heb. 13:17. But to whom will they have to give account? Certainly not to any man, since the souls of no man belong to men; but to Christ alone, the shepherd and bishop of souls. Wherefore the ministers are also commanded to take heed to yourselves, and to all the flock, over which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood, Acts 20:28. And certainly, if architectonic power for the external government of the Church belongs to the magistrate, then the power over the preaching of the Gospel and the keys of the kingdom of heaven belongs to him as well. For by these the Church is governed externally. But the preaching of the Word penetrates the souls of believers and subjects them to Christ. From this it follows that power over the souls of believers belongs to the magistrate, than which nothing more arrogant can be said. Yet they assert that architectonic power to govern the Church belongs to the Church immediately under Christ. From this, however, it follows that the supreme and architectonic judgment concerning those things which pertain to the external government of the Church belongs immediately under Christ to the Christian magistrate. For supreme government without supreme judgment is not supreme government. For one who is bound to follow another's judgment does not govern, but is governed, and is the slave and servant of those who judge. Granting this, it follows immediately: first, that the whole authority, oversight, care and direction which Scripture gives to the ministers of the Church depend on the judgment of the Christian magistrate, as on the judgment of a supreme tribunal from which there is no appeal; second, that the ministers of the Church and of the Word of God are bound everywhere, not only indirectly but also directly, to follow the judgment of the magistrate; third, that the ministers of the Church are bound to proclaim to the people all decrees of the magistrate that concern the public government of the Church, and to persuade them to comply with them; fourth, that the members of the Church and the believers are not bound to obey the ministers of the Church if they should set forth anything contrary to whatever decrees the magistrate has made in matters pertaining to the government of the Church; indeed they are bound not to obey them. To relate these absurdities, which reduce the Church to the harshest human servitude, dig up the secret of papal rule, and finally plot the ruin of both the Church and the magistrate himself, is to refute them. What shall we finally say of a Church which, deprived of a believing magistrate, supplies all that could be expected from the power of a believing magistrate over religion? Does a Church in such a state, in which the fullest right in sacred matters is held to devolve upon it by the very law of nature, exercise the architectonic power of a believing magistrate, as if it had already devolved upon itself? And thus does it set up a double dominating power and an empire within an empire? Either therefore the magistrate's power over the Church is not architectonic; or a Church in such a state arrogates to itself the architectonic power owed to a believing magistrate, and sets up an empire within an empire. Who would say the latter of a Church groaning under the cross, poor, and wholly deprived of temporal protection? Therefore the former is also false.

units.la: CXXXV. In specie non pauca sunt, ad quæ Potestas Magistratus se non extendit. Quæ generalia saltem, velut in compendio exhibebimus. bimus. Licèt enim de quavis potestate periculosa, & de Divina & humana suprema periculosissima disceptatio sit,tamen normam verbi Dei, pietatis & justitiæ sequentibus tutò incedere licet.
units.tr: CXXXV. In particular, there are not a few matters to which the power of the magistrate does not extend. We shall set out at least the general ones, in summary form. For although there is dispute about every dangerous power, and about the divine and human supreme power, which is the most dangerous of all, it is nonetheless safe to proceed by the rule of God's Word, of piety and of justice.

units.la: CXXXVI. Primò igitur non potest Magistratus novos fidei articulos condere,vel novum cultum instituere & imperare. Cùm sederit super folium suum, scribet sibi iteratam legem hanc in libro. Eritque apud illum,& leget in eo omnibus diebus vitæ suæ,ut discat timere Jehovam Deum suum, ut custodiat omnia verba legis hujus,& statuta hæc, ut faciat illa. Ne elevetur cor ejus, supra fratres suos, neque declinet à præcepto ad dextram vel sinistram, Deut. XVII. 18. 19.20. Si nos, vel Angelus ex Cœlo aliud Evangelium prædicet, præter id quod nos prædicavimus, anathema sit,Gal. I. 8. Et quàm male id audentibus Jeroboamo,Achabo,Nebucadnetzari cessserit, historia sacra docet. Omnis enim ἐθελοθρησκεία, à quocunque introducta & exercita, damnabilis est, Esaj. XXIX. 13. Matth. XV. 9. Secundò Magistratus Ministris non potest legem docendi & prædicandi præscribere, quia illud solius Christi est. Unus enim καθηγητὴς ductor & doctor est,Matth. XXIII. 8. 10. qui Pastores & Doctores dat, Ephes. IV. 11. & iisdem quid doceant, vel non doceant, in verbo suo præscripsit. Quos proin etiam Magistratus, quò minùs officium suum juxta præsciptum Christi faciant, impedire non potest, Matth. XXVIII.19. Actor. V.29. Tertiò non potest novam regiminis Ecclesiastici formam introducere & cuiquam obtrudere. Nam forma gubernationis Ecclesiæ in genere in Verbo Dei definita est; Matth.XVIII.15.16.17.XXVIII. 18. 19.20. Rom. XII. 1. Cor. XII. inprimis in Epistolis ad Timotheum & Titum. Unus enim Legislator, Deus est, Jac. IV. 12. Quartò non potest ipse jure verbum Dei prædicare & Sacramenta administrare, non tam propter impedimenta,quibus distringi potest,ne huic muneri vacet,quàm inprimis propter Dei & Christi institutionem,qui munera regendi & Ecclesiæ ministrandi in Veteri & Novo Testamento distinxit, & diversis personis,Regi vel Sacerdotibus,mandavit; addito etiam expresso interdicto, ne verbi Dei Ministri dominentur, vel seculi hujus negotiis se implicent. Nôstis,quòd Principes gentium dominentur iis, & Magnates benefici vocentur. Apud vos autem non sic erit. Sed qui magnus esse voluerit, esto vester minister, &c. Matth. XX. 25.26. Tu (Timothee) suscipe molestias, ut bonus miles Jesu Christi. Nemo militans vitæ hujus negotiis implicatur, ut ei, qui exercitum conscripsit, gratum faciat, 2. Timoth. II.2.3. Ad certamina,ad militiam spiritualem præcæteris ministri Jesu Christi vocantur. Ut verò bonum certamen certent, & hoc agant, necesse πεϱιγμαλώσεις ἡ βίω vitæ negotiis & curis abstineant. Quomodo igitur iidem simul dominari, curas seculi hujus volutare, Regnum, quod de hoc mundo est, administrare, simul militiam Jesu Christi, ceu duces & typi ejus, militare & abstinere vitæ,seu mundi negotiis & curis possunt? Provido inprimis Numine id à Deo, ubique functiones has distinguente,factum est,unus vix ad alterutrum satis idoneus est, 2. Cor. II. 16. tum ne iidem, dominio assueti, dominium in Ecclesiam inferant, & sic Ecclesiam perdant : quando vix Ecclesiæ Ministri severè adeò prohibiti, à dominando temperare possunt, & dominium ab iisdem male consultis occupatum, Antichristum peperit. Ideo etiam Sacerdotii invasores Jeroboamum,1. Reg. XIII. 4. &c. & Ufiam,2. Chron. XXVI. 16. &c. gravissimè Deus punivit. Frustra Melchisedeci,Eli & Samuelis exempla obducuntur,quia & pauci illi,& vocatione distincti singulares ob causas, ad utrumque munus vocati,regulam,revelato Dei verbo adversantem non præscribunt,& Christus sic functiones illas & personas disparavit, ut jam; quod scitè Synelius epist. 57. dixit; duas illas administrationes in eodem homine ψυχῶ conjungere, fit συγχωρεῖν connectere, quæ connecti non possunt. Non ergo,uti Grotius pertendit, Magistratus propter solam negotiorum molem sic Ministerio verbi abstinet, ut tamen per verbi Dei Ministros ceu delegatos suos, hoc munus obeat. Nam delegare nonnisi ad politicas functiones, quæ politicæ supremæ subalternari potestati solæ possunt; potest ; & Ministri Ecclesiæ omnes à Christo mittuntur,Johann. XX. 21. & πεπομπευμένοι ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ legatione pro Christo, seu vice Christi funguntur, 2. Cor. V. 20. Quintò Magistratus disciplinam proprie & formaliter Ecclesiasticam, cum authoritate & potestate clavium Regnum Cœlorum aperiendo, vel claudendo, exercere non potest. Clavium enim potestas Ecclesiæ, non Magistratui data est,Matth.XVI.19.XVIII. 18. Joh.XX.23. Cùmque arma Magistratus disciplinam suam exercentis carnalia,Ecclesiæ verò disciplinam suam ab illa diversam exercentis spiritualia in docendo, demonstrando, consolando,corripiendo ex Dei verbo,lugendo,vitando peccatore,&c. consistentia sint, 2. Cor. X.4. non potest ille efficere armis suis carnalibus, quod hæc spiritualibus suis potest. Arma quinetiam carnalia destruunt: spiritualia solvunt. Traduntur enim Sathanæ refractarii & ἀμετανόητοι ad interitum quidem (seu mortificationem) carnis, sed quatenus ille medium est ad salutem spiritus,seu,ut spiritus salvetur in die Domini Jesu Christi,1. Cor.V. 5.Ipsa proin excommunicatio proprie Ecclesiastica, ubi illa in usu est,non consilio,nedum jussu & mandato Magistratus,sed authoritate clavium à Christo,non ulla humana potestate Ecclesiæ, non politiæ datarum, cui fidelis Magistratus imperio suo nihil præscribere potest, vel vult, exerceri debet. Nam si quis Magistratus in excommunicando impœnitente hoc vel illo consilium vel mandatum operiri velit, non minùs inconsultò vel ipsi Magistratui agere videbitur, ac si Medicus vel Chirurgus ex Magistratu quærere vellet,an in gangræna membrum affectum homini resecandum, vel,an & quodnam remedium ægro applicandum sit. Cùmque Magistratus ipse disciplinæ Ecclesiæ, non tantùm in personalibus, sed etiam publicis peccatis, ubi perperam ille contra Dei verbum & principale debitum, officio fungitur, & juramentum Domino factum violat, debita interim cum reverentia & observantia, procul omni maligno affectu & odio,exercendæ subsit,multùm profectò abest,ut ille,si pius, Dei-
units.tr: CXXXVI. First, therefore, the magistrate cannot frame new articles of faith, nor institute and impose a new worship. When he sits upon his throne, he shall write for himself a copy of this law in a book. It shall be with him, and he shall read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, and to do them. That his heart may not be lifted up above his brethren, and that he may not turn aside from the commandment to the right hand or to the left, Deut. 17:18–20. If we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel than that which we have preached, let him be accursed, Gal. 1:8. How badly this turned out for those who dared it, Jeroboam, Ahab and Nebuchadnezzar, sacred history teaches. For every ἐθελοθρησκεία [will-worship], introduced and practised by whomsoever, is condemnable, Isa. 29:13; Matt. 15:9. Secondly, the magistrate cannot prescribe to the ministers the law of teaching and preaching, because that belongs to Christ alone. For one is your καθηγητής [teacher], the Christ, Matt. 23:8, 10, who gives pastors and teachers, Eph. 4:11, and has prescribed in his Word what they are to teach or not to teach. Therefore neither can the magistrate prevent them from doing their office according to Christ's precept, Matt. 28:19; Acts 5:29. Thirdly, he cannot introduce a new form of church government and force it upon anyone. For the form of the government of the Church in general is defined in the Word of God: Matt. 18:15–17; 28:18–20; Rom. 12:1; 1 Cor. 12, and above all in the Epistles to Timothy and Titus. For one is the Lawgiver, God, Jas. 4:12. Fourthly, he cannot himself rightly preach the Word of God and administer the sacraments, not so much because of the hindrances which might distract him from being free for this office, but chiefly because of the institution of God and Christ, who distinguished the offices of ruling and of ministering to the Church in the Old and New Testaments, and entrusted them to different persons, to kings or priests; adding also an express prohibition, that the ministers of the Word should not lord it over others, or entangle themselves in the affairs of this age. You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, and the great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever wishes to be great among you, let him be your minister, etc., Matt. 20:25–26. You, Timothy, endure hardship as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. No one who serves as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of this life, so that he may please the one who enlisted him, 2 Tim. 2:3–4. The ministers of Jesus Christ are called before others to the contests and the spiritual warfare. But in order that they may contend the good contest and do this, they must of necessity abstain from entanglement in the affairs and cares of life [ταῖς τοῦ βίου πραγματείαις]. How then can the same men at once rule, be absorbed in the cares of this age, administer a kingdom which is of this world, and at the same time wage the warfare of Jesus Christ as his leaders and types, and abstain from the affairs and cares of life or of the world? By the wise providence of God, who everywhere distinguishes these functions, it has come about that one is scarcely fit enough for the other, 2 Cor. 2:16. Otherwise those accustomed to rule would bring domination into the Church, and so destroy the Church, since the ministers of the Church, though strictly forbidden, can scarcely refrain from lording it over others; and domination seized by those so ill-advised has brought forth Antichrist. Therefore God also severely punished the usurpers of the priesthood, Jeroboam, 1 Kings 13:4, etc., and Uzziah, 2 Chron. 26:16, etc. The examples of Melchizedek, Eli and Samuel are brought forward in vain, because those few were called to each office for singular reasons, distinct in their calling, and they do not prescribe a rule opposed to the revealed Word of God. Christ also so separated those functions and persons that now, as Synesius rightly said in Epistle 57, to join those two administrations in the same person is to mix together what cannot be mixed [συγχεῖν]. Therefore it is not, as Grotius maintains, that the magistrate abstains from the ministry of the Word only because of the sheer weight of affairs, so that he may still discharge this office through the ministers of the Word as his delegates. For he can delegate only to political functions, which can be subordinate to the supreme political power alone. And all the ministers of the Church are sent by Christ, John 20:21, and act as ambassadors on behalf of Christ [πρεσβεύομεν ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ], that is, they perform the office in the place of Christ, 2 Cor. 5:20. Fifthly, the magistrate cannot exercise discipline properly and formally ecclesiastical, opening or shutting the kingdom of heaven with the authority and power of the keys. For the power of the keys was given to the Church, not to the magistrate, Matt. 16:19; 18:18; John 20:23. And since the weapons of a magistrate who exercises his discipline are carnal, while those of the Church, which exercises its own discipline, distinct from his, are spiritual, consisting in teaching, demonstrating, comforting, rebuking from the Word of God, mourning, and avoiding sinners, etc., 2 Cor. 10:4, he cannot achieve by his carnal weapons what the Church achieves by its spiritual ones. Moreover, carnal weapons destroy, while spiritual ones loosen. For the obstinate and unrepentant are delivered to Satan for the destruction (or mortification) of the flesh, but only so far as that is a means to the salvation of the spirit, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 5:5. Therefore excommunication, properly ecclesiastical, where it is in use, must be exercised not by the counsel, much less the order and command, of the magistrate, but by the authority of the keys given by Christ, and not by any human power given to the Church or to the state, over which a faithful magistrate can prescribe nothing by his command, nor does he wish to. For if any magistrate wished to wait for this or that counsel or command in excommunicating an impenitent person, he would seem to act no less unwisely toward the magistrate himself than if a physician or surgeon wished to ask of the magistrate whether a diseased limb should be cut off a man with gangrene, or what remedy and which should be applied to the sick man. And since the magistrate himself serves the discipline of the Church, not only in personal sins but also in public sins, where he errs against God's Word and his principal duty, and violates the oath made to the Lord, while in the meantime the discipline is to be exercised with due reverence and obedience, far from all malign feeling and hatred, it is far indeed from the case that he, if he is pious and fears God,

units.la: Deíque metuens est, disciplinam Ecclesiæ vel consilio, vel mandato suo moderari possit, vel præsumere velit. Disciplina enim Ecclesiastica necessariò prædicationi verbi & administrationi Sacramentorum adjuncta est. Atqui non Magistratus sed Christi nomine verbum Dei prædicatur, & Sacramenta administrantur. Ergo pari ratione etiam disciplina Ecclesiæ administratur. Accedit, quòd Ecclesia multa peccata sub virgam disciplinæ suæ vocat, quæ Magistratus impune dimittit: & vicissim Magistratus multa peccata atrociter punit, quæ salutaribus lachrymis irrigata, & vera pœnitentia expiata nomine & authoritate Christi condonat. Sextò Magistratus controversias religionis ad suum solius judicium revocare, & de iis pro authoritate sua statuere non potest. Nam ne Apostoli quidem hoc fecerunt, utpote qui in consilium etiam Presbyteros & Ecclesiam adhibuerunt, & cum eorum voluntate & consensu decreta sua condiderunt, Actor. XV. 6.22. Neque id tantùm periculi plenum, cum ἀπολογισμοῦ conjunctum, sed etiam ab ordine Ecclesiæ, & laudatis exemplis alienum est, & totum spiritu Antichristi tumet. Septimò non potest Magistratus subditos ad fidem & religionem veram, nedum falsam amplectendam vi cogere. Hoc enim ejus est, qui conscientiæ & religionis Dominus est; atqui solus Deus conscientiæ & Religionis Dominus est, qui in convertendo homine ne quidem externa vi, sed interna Spiritus S. πνεύματικῇ utitur. Subditi enim Christi voluntarii sunt, Psal. CX. 3. Neque Deus potentiam Spiritus sui per coactionem obscurare vult. Vult distingui fideles ab hypocritis Christo mentientibus: non vult in Ecclesia esse occasionem tyrannidis. Et libertatem conscientiæ, hoc est, judicandi de vero & falso, bono & malo, & credendi id, quod verum est, probandi id quod bonum est, homini eripere homo nullus, ne si velit quidem, potest. At nec libertatem verum profitendi, & bonum sectandi, in quo libertatem exercitii collocare solent, homini ullus homo jure ullo eripere potest, quia verum nolle dici, & bonum nolle ut sectentur homines, eorum est, qui mendacium & veritatem eodem loco habent, & Deum glorificari, ac proximum ædificari nolunt. Ac ne quidem homines vi cogi possunt, ne mendacio credant, & illud profiteantur, quia in talibus doctore, non de sella & tribunali, nedum tortore, Spiritu Dei, non spiritu, qui in naso hominis est; opus est; & quæ Deus coactioni & jurisdictioni humanæ non subjecit, sed suo domino reservavit, ea potestas humana sibi subjicere non debet. Octavò denique Magistratus in bona Ecclesiæ, & peculium ejus, singulariter ipsi & cultui Dei promovendo à piis, ceu anathema quoddam dedicatum, involare pro lubitu, & thesauros Ecclesiæ spoliare non potest. Si enim subditi innocentis bona & fortunas non magis rapere, quàm vitam ejus affligere & perdere potest; quo jure Ecclesiæ bona in sagenam & rete suum pro lubitu pertrahere potest? Et si privato id non licet, quomodo supremæ Potestati id licet, cujus est omnium fortunas adversus rapinam tueri? De quo supra etiam diximus. Nam quoad casum superfluorum, nunquam, vel raro ille contingit: & si-
units.tr: can moderate the discipline of the Church by his counsel or his command, or presume to wish to. For ecclesiastical discipline is necessarily joined to the preaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments. But the Word of God is not preached and the sacraments are not administered in the name of the magistrate but in the name of Christ. Therefore by the same reasoning discipline is also administered in the Church's name. Add to this that the Church calls many sins under the rod of its discipline which the magistrate lets go unpunished, and conversely the magistrate punishes severely many sins which the Church, bathed in salutary tears and expiated by true repentance, forgives in the name and by the authority of Christ. Sixthly, the magistrate cannot call questions of religion to his own judgment alone, nor decide about them by his own authority. For not even the apostles did this, since they took the presbyters and the Church into counsel also, and framed their decrees with their will and consent, Acts 15:6, 22. Nor is this only full of danger, joined with apologetics [ἀπολογισμοῦ], but it is also alien to the order of the Church and to the praised examples, and it swells wholly with the spirit of Antichrist. Seventhly, the magistrate cannot compel his subjects by force to embrace the true faith and religion, much less a false one. For this belongs to him who is Lord of conscience and religion; but God alone is Lord of conscience and religion, who in converting a man uses not even external force, but the internal power of the Holy Spirit [πνεύματικῇ]. For the subjects of Christ are willing, Ps. 110:3. Nor does God wish to obscure the power of his Spirit by coercion. He wishes the faithful to be distinguished from hypocrites who lie to Christ; he does not wish there to be occasion for tyranny in the Church. And no man, even if he wished, can snatch from another man liberty of conscience, that is, the freedom to judge about true and false, good and evil, and to believe what is true and to approve what is good. Nor can any man by any right snatch from a man the liberty of practice, in which they are wont to place it, namely the freedom to profess the truth and to pursue the good; for to be unwilling that the truth be spoken, and unwilling that men pursue the good, belongs to those who count falsehood and truth as the same, and who are unwilling that God be glorified and the neighbour edified. Nor can men be forced by violence not to believe a lie and not to profess it; for in such matters what is needed is a teacher, not a judge's bench or tribunal, much less a torturer; what is needed is the Spirit of God, not a spirit which is in the nose of man. And what God has not subjected to coercion and human jurisdiction, but has reserved to his own Lord, that human power ought not to subject to itself. Eighthly and finally, the magistrate cannot seize at will the goods of the Church and its property, which are dedicated, as a kind of accursed thing, by the pious to the promotion of the worship of God in a special way, nor can he plunder the treasures of the Church. For if he cannot snatch away the goods and fortunes of an innocent subject any more than he can afflict and destroy his life, by what right can he drag the goods of the Church into his net and drag-net at will? And if this is not permitted to a private person, how is it permitted to the supreme power, whose duty it is to guard everyone's fortunes against robbery? Of which we have also spoken above. For as to the case of surpluses, this scarcely or never arises; and if

units.la: mul non de præsenti duntaxat, sed de futuro etiam tempore: nec de nostrâ, sed aliarum etiam Ecclesiarum, quibus subvenire etiam communio Sanctorum jubet, necessitatibus cogitandum est. Quò plura Deo dicata sunt, hoc plura eidem impendere convenit, & licet, cùm nunquam pauperes desint. Quantum verò bonorum Ecclesiæ conservationi & propagationi sufficiat, difficile equidem definitu est, & non sine periculo Politico Magistratui cuivis (nam à-pio nullum periculum est) definiendum relinquitur. Non desunt enim quibus cum Judaa superflua omnia videntur. Neque etiam susque deque habenda voluntas eorum est, qui bona ejusmodi non sine diris adversus raptores Christo dicarunt: quorum intentiones specifica corrigi, generica tolli non potest. Qua in re saniores etiam Jurisconsulti cum Theologis paria sentiunt, vetantes, ne Magistratus eminente potestate sua utatur, nisi in summo periculo, ubi simul Ecclesiæ salus periclitatur. Tum enim in bona Ecclesiæ verecundas manus immitti posse, hac tamen lege, ut quicquid politicos ad usus, urgente acri necessitatis telo sevocatur, id omne sereniore Reipublicæ tempestate affulgente, restituatur, autumant.
units.tr: ...and this must be considered not only for the present time but also for the future, and not only for our own needs but also for those of other churches, since the communion of saints requires us to help them too. The more things are dedicated to God, the more it is fitting, and permitted, to spend on them, since there are never any lack of poor. How much property is sufficient for the preservation and spreading of the Church is indeed hard to define, and it is left to be defined by any political magistrate, not without risk (for there is no risk for the pious). For there are some to whom all surplus seems superfluous, as the Jews thought. Nor should the will of those be treated with contempt who dedicated such goods to Christ, not without curses against robbers. Their specific intentions may be corrected, but their general intention cannot be removed. On this point even the more sensible jurists agree with the theologians, forbidding the magistrate to use his supreme power except in extreme danger, when the safety of the Church is also endangered at the same time. For they maintain that then the Church's goods may be touched with a modest hand, on this condition: whatever is withdrawn for civil uses under the sharp pressure of necessity must be restored when the storm of the commonwealth has calmed into clearer weather.

units.la: CXXXVII. Fuit Potestas Magistratus circa Ecclesiam κατ' ἀρχήν. Nunc qua in re ἡ ἐξουσία consistat, explicandum pariter est. Et in universum Magistratus, quatenus ὁμόπολις, & Ecclesiæ nobilissimum & excellentissimum membrum est, eandem potestatem participat, quæ totius Ecclesiæ est. Nam quod toti homogeneo convenit, etiam convenit parti, quatenus totius illius pars est. Tum Magistratus, quà talis est, in Ecclesiam potestas generaliter in eo consistit, quòd potest, imò non potest tantùm, sed etiam tenetur id omne facere, quo Christo & regno ejus per potestatem sibi à Deo concessam inservire, atque illud amplificare potest. Nam minister Dei est, sicut singulis subditis, ita Ecclesiæ etiam ejus imperio subjectæ εἰς ἀγαθὸν in bonum, Rom. XIII. 4. Ideo etiam ארץ ארץ scuta terræ, potestas omnis Regum & Principum, אלהים Dei esse dicuntur, Psal. XLVII. 10. Cui enim illa majori jure impenderentur, quàm ei, qui illa in manum dedit, sacravit & conservat? Christi igitur & Regni ejus respectu, non tam potestas, quàm διακονία ministerium, officium debitum, & κηδεμονία cura est: quam impendere ei liberum non est. Verecundiùs proin loquuntur, qui non tam de Potestate, imò & Jure Majestatis, circa sacra & Ecclesiam, quæ Christi & Regni ejus, cui omnes Potestates servire & obedire debent, Dan. VII. 27. respectu nimis grave quid sonat, quàm de ejus circa Ecclesiam officio & cura loquuntur. Quamcunque enim Magistratus potestatem habet, per eam Christo & Regno ejus, quod Ecclesia est, servit, non dominatur, quia in Regno Christi solus Christus dominatur. Magna certè beneficia esse possunt, quibus Deus per Magistratum, ministrum suum, Ecclesiam mactare potest. Sed in omnibus beneficiis illis hæc cautio necessaria est, ne putemus Magistratum per ea posse vel debere Ecclesiam, quæ augustior res est, quàm mundus reputat, suam facere, nedum à Christo Rege abalienare. Imò cogitandum ei est, ea de re Deo cultum debitum praestare. Alia plane ratione Princeps in Ecclesia,quam in Republica versatur & agit. Sicut enim in privati domum coenaturus veniens, personam Principis deponit,neque alienis servis imperare praesumit; & cum sociis suis negotium commune habens, id non facit suae potestatis propterea,quia summam in civitate potestatem habet: ita in Ecclesiam,seu societatem Ecclesiasticam veniens, neque patribus familias,& iis,qui ceu patres familias in ea societate sunt vel praesunt,& nil nisi fratres coram uno Patre Deo & Christo sunt, jus suffragii in constituendo ordine eripit,neque coetus libertatem,& Pastorum atque Seniorum authoritatem tollit: neque tributa vel eleemosynas imperat, vel simile quid pro imperio agit: neque Ecclesiam omni voto, quod in Pastore deligendo vel admittendo Divino jure ei competit,defraudat; neque ulla re confoederationem illam, quae inter docentes, regentes, & fratres intercedere debet, turbat. Atque id eo minus facit, quo minus etiam ii, qui potestatem in liberos, uxores, servos habent, pro potestate sua in Ecclesia agunt,sed id potius satagunt, ut omnibus, quod agunt, approbent,memores semper, Ecclesiam fratrum, non imperantium & parentium societatem esse. Cumque pius Magistratus potestatem & paternam & conjugalem,& herilem illibatam relinquat,multo magis Ecclesiae potestatem, a Christo ei datam, illibatam ei,vel propter reverentiam & obedientiam illam, quam Christo debet,relinquit.
units.tr: CXXXVII. The magistrate's power over the Church exists originally [κατ' ἀρχήν]. Now it must equally be explained in what authority [ἡ ἐξουσία] consists. In general, the magistrate, insofar as he is a fellow citizen [ὁμόπολις] and the most noble and excellent member of the Church, shares in the same power that belongs to the whole Church. For what belongs to the whole of a homogeneous body also belongs to a part of it, insofar as it is part of that whole. Then, the magistrate's power over the Church, as such, consists generally in this: he can, indeed he not only can but is bound, to do everything by which he may serve Christ and his kingdom through the power granted him by God, and may advance it. For he is minister of God, for good [εἰς ἀγαθὸν] both to individual subjects and to the Church placed under his rule, Rom. 13:4. Therefore the shields of the earth [ארץ ארץ], that is, all the power of kings and princes, are called gods [אלהים] of God, Ps. 47:10. For to whom should such power be given with greater right than to him who put it into his hand, consecrated it and preserves it? Therefore, with respect to Christ and his kingdom, it is not so much power as service [διακονία], a ministry, a debt of duty, and care [κηδεμονία], a charge, which it is not free for him to withhold. Those speak more modestly who do not speak so much of Power, or even of the Right of Majesty, in matters sacred and concerning the Church, which belong to Christ and his kingdom, to which all powers ought to serve and obey, Dan. 7:27. Such language sounds too heavy with respect to Christ's kingdom, whereas they speak of his duty and care towards the Church. For whatever power the magistrate has, through it he serves Christ and his kingdom, which is the Church; he does not rule over it, because in the kingdom of Christ Christ alone rules. Certainly there can be great benefits by which God may bless the Church through the magistrate, his minister. But in all those benefits this caution is necessary: we must not think that the magistrate can or should make the Church, which is a more august thing than the world reckons, his own through them, much less alienate it from Christ the King. Rather he must consider that in this matter he owes God the due worship. The prince acts in the Church in a quite different way from how he acts in the commonwealth. For just as, coming to dine in a private house, he lays aside the person of a prince and does not presume to command another's servants, and when he has business in common with his companions he does not do so by virtue of his power, even though he holds the highest power in the state; so, coming into the Church, or the ecclesiastical society, he does not take away the right of voting in ordering the community, nor does he abolish the liberty of the congregation and the authority of the ministers and elders, neither does he impose taxes or alms, or do anything similar by way of command, nor does he defraud the Church of any vote which belongs to it by divine right in choosing or admitting a minister, nor does he disturb in any way that fellowship which ought to exist among teachers, rulers and brothers. And he does this the less, since even those who have power over children, wives and servants do not exercise it in the Church by their own authority, but rather take care to approve all that is done, always mindful that the Church is a society of brothers, not of rulers and parents. And since the pious magistrate leaves intact his paternal, marital and domestic power, much more does he leave intact to the Church the power given to it by Christ, both out of reverence and out of that obedience which he owes to Christ.

units.la: CXXXVIII.
units.tr: CXXXVIII.

units.la: Sicut igitur Ecclesiae Ministri,& fideles singuli,Ecclesiae membra,eidem juxta vocationem & charismata, quae a Deo acceperunt,inservire tenentur: ita Magistratus pius & orthodoxus Christo & Regno ejus, quod Ecclesia est, juxta potestatem a Deo sibi datam sic inservire debet,ne quicquam eorum, quae ad curam Ecclesiae pertinent, negligat. Nam Primo sanam doctrinam, & purum Dei cultum,ex verbi Divini praescripto in Republica constituere, constitutum conservare, collapsum restaurare & restituere tenetur. Qua in re potestate sua utitur,non fidem cogendo,sed tum operam dando,ut ea recte doceatur: tum ad media fidei, qualia sunt auditus verbi, institutio sanioris doctrinae,sine violentia tamen in extorquendo assensu & professione,adigendo: tum denique impedimenta removendo, velut cum doctrinas blasphemas, & idololatriam non tantum non tolerat,sed etiam omnibus viribus suis abolet, & religionis purioris hostes ad opprimendam eam violenter grassantes,& Rempublicam perturbantes,coercet, atque ita religionem veram tuetur, idque omne in fide. Est enim constitutus Minister Dei ... vindex ad iram adversus eum, qui malum facit,Rom. XIII. 4. Nam si Paterfamilias blasphemias, idololatriam, violentiam non tolerat, sed pro viribus suis iis resistit, multo magis supremus Reipublicae pater omnibus viribus suis iisdem resistere tenetur. Quomodo ipse etiam Nebucadnezar sub poena capitis edixit,ne quis ... errorem vel sequius aliquid de Deo sociorum Danielis diceret, Dan. III. 29. Accedit, quod religionis purioris exercitium, praeconium ver-
units.tr: Just as the ministers of the Church and each individual believer, as members of the Church, are bound to serve it according to their calling and the gifts they have received from God, so a godly and orthodox magistrate ought to serve Christ and his kingdom, which is the Church, according to the power God has given him, so that he neglects none of the things that belong to the care of the Church. For first, he is bound to establish sound doctrine and the pure worship of God in the commonwealth according to the prescription of the Word of God, to maintain what has been established, and to restore and re-establish what has fallen. In this matter he uses his power not by compelling faith, but by taking care that the true faith is taught correctly; by providing the means of faith, such as the hearing of the Word and instruction in sounder doctrine, yet without violence in extracting assent and profession; and finally by removing obstacles. For he not only does not tolerate blasphemous doctrines and idolatry, but also abolishes them with all his strength, and restrains the enemies of the purer religion who rage violently to oppress it and disturb the commonwealth. In this way he defends the true religion, and all of this in good faith. For he is "God's minister... an avenger to execute wrath on him who does evil," Rom. XIII. 4. For if a father of a household does not tolerate blasphemy, idolatry and violence, but resists them with his strength, much more the supreme father of the commonwealth is bound to resist them with all his strength. So Nebuchadnezzar himself, under penalty of death, decreed that no one should speak "error" or anything amiss about God against the companions of Daniel, Dan. III. 29. In addition, he is bound not only to raise up the exercise of the purer religion, the proclamation of the Word, and the lawful government of the Church within his realm according to the faith and judgment of the whole Church, but also to establish and confirm these by public edicts. In this matter his chief ministry as ruler consists.

units.la: bi, & regimen Ecclesiae legitimum in ditione sua juxta totius Ecclesiae fidem & sententiam non tantum erigere,sed etiam publicis edictis stabilire & confirmare tenetur. Qua in re praecipuum potestatis ejus ministerium consistit. Secundo ad conservationem sanioris doctrinae & cultus inprimis utiles sunt solennes formulae, per quas doctrina & oeconomia Ecclesiae definitur. Cujusmodi sunt Confessio,Catechismus, Liturgia & agenda Ecclesiae. Hae semel juxta normam verbi Dei definitae ab iis, a quibus definiri eas oportet, ne temere a quovis turbone vellicari & impeti possint, ... sanctione indigent, ut publicam authoritatem habeant, & in foro saltem externo, ad vitandam confusionem & ... , vigeant & obligent. Haec sanctio cum ab illo solo, qui potestatem & jurisdictionem in Republica habet,fieri possit,non alii,quam Magistratui,utpote qui solus potestatem & jurisdictionem in Republica externam habet, competit. Tertio sana doctrina & purior cultus sine Ministris Ecclesiae vigere non potest. Tametsi vero Ministri Ecclesiae quoad ministerium & potestatem suam a solo Christo pendent, & deputatio personarum ad ministerium toti Ecclesiae, ipsique etiam Magistratui incumbit. Nam & veris Pastoribus in ditione sua Evangelium praedicandi impertiri, & eosdem praesentare coetui, & obligare coetum ad audiendos eos, ceu legitime ordinatos & vocatos, & avocamenta auditum verbi sufflaminantia impedire, exemplo Nehemiae, qui calcantes torcularia in Sabbatho, & alia cultum turbantia facientes, compescuit, Nehem. XIII. 15. 16. Pastores pios,industrios, probatos fovere, adversus malevolos defendere,desides excitare, malos & scandalosos civilibus etiam poenis coercere,&,si necessitas postulat, exemplo Solomonis, Abiatharem Pontificem, perduellionis reum, deponentis, 1. Reg. II. 22. 26. 27. praevio inprimis Ecclesiae judicio, ob doctrinae & morum labem; exauthorare; deinque iisdem etiam ex fisco stipendia, si aliunde non suppetant, exhibere tenetur. Quarto Ecclesia Scholis, quae ejusdem seminaria sunt,carere non potest. Magistratus igitur officium est, ludos literarios,cultiores inprimis,aperire, peritos & probos ludimagistros, & Professores iisdem praeficere,& una cum Ecclesiae Ministris invigilare,ut in iisdem veritas doceatur,& juventus humili & solida pietate mature imbuatur. Quinto Ecclesia disciplinam propriam, a civili distinctam habet, neque omnino ea carere potest. Habet & hic Magistratus suas partes, non tantum, ut eam non impediat,vel potestate sua turbet, & fontes infamiae praetextu (vix enim ulla castigatio & confusio publica est,quin labeculam quandam,sed,quae nullam in civitate noxam affert,affricet, donec poenitentia expietur) judicio Ecclesiae surripiat: sed inprimis ut,si quando Ecclesiastica potestas fines suos praetergreditur, tyrannidem exercet, & de iis, quae alterius fori sunt, judicat, atque eas ob causas justae querelae moventur, de injuria cognoscat,sive res doctrinam,sive vitam, sive fortunas,sive existimationem tangat. Sic Paulus stans coram tribunali Caesaris, ad Caesarem provocavit,& Judaeorum judicio tradi renuit, Actor. XXIII. 8-11. Manebat interim Judæis integrum judicium suum iis in partibus, quas Deus iis per Romanos non ademerat, ut judicare possent, hominem Christianum debere esse ϭπτουνάγωγον, licèt id judicium falsum & erroneum esset. Non deerat iis potestas ad judicandum; sed scientia & fides ad rectè judicandum deerat. Potest ergo & debet Magistratus omnes turbas & injurias coërcere; sed animum & fidem in sua potestate non habet. Si quid autem ad disciplinam Ecclesiæ pertinens aliunde Magistratui commissum est, tenetur in eo versari, & fidelitatem suam probare, non tam potestate politica utens, quàm œconomica singulari sibi tradita defungens, de qua rationem non Deo duntaxat, sed etiam Ecclesiæ ipsi reddere tenetur. Sextò in Ecclesia, ad conservandam doctrinam, & disciplinæ rigorem, & definiendas controversias obortas, necessarii quandoque conventus ordinarii Pastorum & Seniorum in Consistoriis, & extraordinariis delegatorum à pluribus Ecclesiis in Synodis sunt. Ejusmodi conventus à Magistratu cum authoritate constitui: Synodi Provinciales, vel Nationales, vel Universales, quoties opus fuerit, cogi, earum actiones & judicia prudenti consilio dirigi, ordo externus in iisdem custodiri & contineri; denique acta & decreta, impresso velut publicæ authoritatis sigillo, confirmari, & ut in externo saltem foro valeant, & in leges publicas abeant, edictis ejus sanciri debent. Septimò fieri potest, ut vera religio & cultus omnis depravetur & collabatur penitus. Tum verò Magistratui jus reformandi debito modo incumbit; sed aliter quà membrum Ecclesiæ est, aliter quà Magistratus est. Quà membrum Ecclesiæ est, simul judicare de Ecclesia, an revera Christo obediat, & ei se adjungat: simul unà cum tota Ecclesia, quid in deplorato fidei statu deliberatu factúque opus sit, in medium consulere debet. Quà Magistratus est, rationem & apologiam fidei ab iis, qui Ecclesiæ præsunt, & collapsæ religionis auctores existunt, exigit. Si enim πᾶντὶ αἰτῆσαι omni petenti ratio fidei reddenda est, & parati semper ad apologiam esse debemus, 1. Petr. III. 15. causa dici non potest, cur non potissimum Magistratui rationem fidei & apologiam exigenti, reddi debeat. Inprimis cùm extet lex, secundum quam judicentur omnes, an fideliter agant, quod suarum partium est. Et Magistratus est non tantùm de fide judicare, quod omnium Ecclesiæ membrorum est, sed etiam cognoscere & considerare, quid laudet, Rom. XIII. 3. Hanc Ecclesiæ operam pientissimi quique Reges & Principes, quotiescunque necessitas postulavit, strenuè navarunt; & in Veteri Testamento præ cæteris Ezechias, qui æneum serpentem, quamvis mandato Dei factum, quando organum idololatriæ esse cœpit, confregit, & primo statim Regni sui anno reformationem domus Dei insignem & memorabilem ad omnem posteritatem, unà cum Sacerdotibus & Levitis molitus est, 2. Paralip. XXIX. 3. & Josias, qui & ipse universam idolomaniam sustulit, & librum legis ab Hilkia repertum restituit; denique à solenni Paschate postliminio cultum auspicatus est, ibid. XXXIV. XXXV. In N. T. Constantinus M. & sequentes nonnulli Imperatores fide & pietate præstantes, quin
units.tr: Second, for the preservation of sounder doctrine and worship, solemn formulas by which the doctrine and order of the Church are defined are especially useful. Of this kind are the Confession, the Catechism, and the Liturgy and agenda of the Church. Once these have been defined according to the norm of the Word of God by those who ought to define them, they need sanction, so that they cannot be rashly plucked at and assailed by any troublemaker, but have public authority and are in force and binding at least in the external forum, to avoid confusion. Since this sanction can be given only by him who holds power and jurisdiction in the commonwealth, it belongs to no one but the magistrate, who alone has external power and jurisdiction in the commonwealth. Third, sound doctrine and purer worship cannot flourish without ministers of the Church. Although the ministers of the Church depend for their ministry and power on Christ alone, the appointment of persons to the ministry rests with the whole Church and also with the magistrate himself. For it is his task to grant to true pastors the right to preach the Gospel in his realm, to present them to the congregation, and to oblige the congregation to hear them as lawfully ordained and called, and to hinder distractions that impede the hearing of the Word, after the example of Nehemiah, who restrained those who trod winepresses on the Sabbath and did other things that disturbed worship, Neh. XIII. 15, 16. He must cherish godly, diligent and approved pastors, defend them against the malicious, rouse the idle, and restrain bad and scandalous men even with civil punishments; and, if necessity requires, after the example of Solomon, who deposed Abiathar the high priest, guilty of treason, 1 Kings II. 22, 26, 27, he must remove them from office, chiefly after a prior judgment of the Church on account of the stain on their doctrine or morals. And finally, he is bound to supply stipends to these same ministers from the treasury, if they cannot be had elsewhere. Fourth, the Church cannot do without schools, which are its seminaries. It is therefore the duty of the magistrate to open schools of letters, especially the more advanced ones, to set over them skilled and upright schoolmasters and professors, and, together with the ministers of the Church, to see to it that the truth is taught in them and that the young are early imbued with a humble and solid piety. Fifth, the Church has its own discipline, distinct from the civil, and cannot be entirely without it. Here too the magistrate has his part to play: not merely that he should not hinder it or disturb it by his power, or snatch from the Church's judgment the sources of disgrace under the pretext of infamy (for hardly any punishment or public censure occurs without leaving some small stain which, however, does no harm in the state, until it is cleansed by repentance); but chiefly that, if ever ecclesiastical power exceeds its bounds, exercises tyranny, and judges matters belonging to another forum, and for these reasons just complaints are raised, he may take cognizance of the injury, whether the matter touches doctrine, life, property or reputation. Thus Paul, standing before the tribunal of Caesar, appealed to Caesar and refused to be handed over to the judgment of the Jews, Acts XXIII. 8-11. Meanwhile the Jews retained their judgment entire in those matters which God had not taken from them through the Romans, so that they could judge that a Christian man ought to be put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγον], although that judgment was false and erroneous. They lacked no power to judge; what they lacked was knowledge and faith to judge rightly. The magistrate therefore can and must restrain all disturbances and injuries, but he does not have the spirit and faith in his power. If, however, something pertaining to the discipline of the Church has been committed to the magistrate from elsewhere, he is bound to act in it and prove his faithfulness, not so much using political power as discharging the particular stewardship committed to him, for which he must give an account not only to God but also to the Church itself. Sixth, in the Church, for preserving doctrine and the rigour of discipline and for settling controversies that arise, there are sometimes necessary ordinary gatherings of pastors and elders in consistories, and extraordinary gatherings of delegates from several congregations in synods. Such gatherings must be convened by the magistrate with authority: provincial, national or universal synods, as often as there is need; their proceedings and judgments must be directed by prudent counsel; external order must be kept and maintained in them; and finally their acts and decrees, confirmed with the seal of public authority, must be sanctioned by his edicts, so that they may have force at least in the external forum and pass into public laws. Seventh, it can happen that true religion and all worship are corrupted and utterly fall. Then indeed the magistrate is bound to reform in the proper manner; but he acts one way as a member of the Church and another way as magistrate. As a member of the Church, he must at the same time judge whether the Church really obeys Christ and joins itself to him, and together with the whole Church consider and bring into the open what must be deliberated and done in the despaired-of state of the faith. As magistrate, he demands an account and defence of the faith from those who preside over the Church and are the authors of the fallen religion. For if "to everyone who asks [πᾶντι αἰτοῦντι] a reason for the faith must be given," and we must always be "ready to make a defence," 1 Pet. III. 15, no reason can be given why it should not be given especially to the magistrate who demands it. This is especially so since there is a law by which all are judged as to whether they act faithfully, which is the business of their office. And the magistrate is to judge not only concerning the faith, which is the task of all members of the Church, but also to know and consider what he should praise, Rom. XIII. 3. Pious kings and princes, whenever necessity demanded, have vigorously performed this service for the Church. Among them in the Old Testament Hezekiah stood out, who broke the bronze serpent, though made by God's command, when it began to be an instrument of idolatry, and in the very first year of his reign undertook a remarkable reformation of the house of God, notable for all posterity, together with the priests and Levites, 2 Chron. XXIX. 3. And Josiah, who also himself removed all idolatry and restored the book of the law found by Hilkiah; and finally, by a solemn Passover, he began a restoration of worship, ibid. XXXIV, XXXV. In the New Testament, Constantine the Great and several succeeding emperors, outstanding in faith and piety, [did likewise].

units.la: & horum omnium exemplo superiori seculo religiosissimi quique Reges, Principes & Magistratus. Verbi Dei Ministrorum enim est, demonstrata necessitate & religionis veritate, Reformationem petere: Magistratus eam decernere: Populi ex verbo Dei à Pastoribus demonstratæ necessitati & veritati, & à Magistratu decretæ Reformationi obedire. Octavò cultus Dei sine circumstantiis loci & temporis celebrari non potest. Quæ quatenus in verbo Dei definita non sunt, & definienda prudentiæ Ecclesiæ relicta sunt, sine Magistratus ὁμοπνεύσει arbitrio constitui non possunt, & constituta ejusdem authoritate firmari & sanciri pariter debent, quò ita legitimi conventus Ecclesiastici hoc vel illo tempore & loco instituti à conventiculis distingui possint. Nonò Ecclesia communionem Sanctorum colere debet. Una enim Christi sponsa & Ecclesia est, cujus universæ custodia ac velut Episcopatus, non uni Ecclesiæ sigillatim, sed omnibus singulisque in commune credita est. Eadem enim Ecclesia modò domui, modò navi comparatur. Utriusque salus tam iis, qui in hypogæo, quàm iis, qui in cœnaculo: tam iis, qui in prora, quàm qui in puppi, aut carina versantur, curæ esse debet: ac proin commune incendium communibus viribus restingui, irruens tempestas communi remigio effugi debet. Magistratus igitur est non suæ duntaxat ditionis Ecclesiis providere, sed etiam vexatis oppressisque alibi fratribus ope, consilio, intercessione aliisque modis opitulari. Quò enim majorem, quàm privati, potestatem, quò plura à Deo præsidia acceperit, hoc potiores ejus in Ecclesia afflicta recreanda & erigenda partes sunt. Sic olim Ezechias & Josias non contenti collapsam in Judæa Ecclesiam restaurasse, ad puriorem Dei cultum etiam Israelitas, quamvis Assyrio jam mancipatos, invitarunt: & Christiani Imperatores Ecclesiam adversus Persas & Parthos defenderunt. Non enim iisdem limitibus agros, & Dei gloriam disterminari arbitrabantur. Qui verò montium & munitionum fiducia freti secure agunt, unguentisque delibuti, & luxu diffluentes, fratrum indignis modis oppressorum calamitate parùm afficiuntur, & fractum contritumque Josephum fastidiosè despiciunt, iis justissimam ultionem Deus ipse interminatur. Maledicite urbi Meroz, dixit Angelus Jehovæ. Maledicite maledicendo habitatoribus ejus, quia non adfuerunt ad auxilium Jehovæ, ad auxilium Jehovæ contra fortes, Judic. V. 23. Væ quietis in Tzion, & confidentibus in monte Samariæ, &c. Ecce ego suscito contra vos, domus Israel, dictum Jehovæ Dei exercituum, gentem, & affligent vos inde, quà itur Chamatham, &c. Amos. VI. 1. 14. Quæ diræ utinam Ecclesiæ nostrorum temporum expavescendæ non sint! Decimò Ecclesiam bonis temporalibus ad sustentandos Ministros, pauperes & ædificia sacra extruenda & conservanda carere non posse, supra diximus. Habent & hic fideles Magistratus, qui ἐπιτρόπων Munificorum nomine veniunt, Luc. XXII. 25. partes suas. Eorum enim est, bonorum ejusmodi fideles œconomos & procuratores deligere, qui & debita Ecclesiis urgeant & colligant, & collecta fideliter administrent, & ope supremi Magistratus, adversus hosharpyas defendant. Eorundem est providere, ut Bona illa Ecclesiæ sacrata non parcè,sed largiter ὡς εὐλογία, καὶ μὴ ᾠσπερ πλεονεξία, ut benedictio, non ut avaritia, 2. Cor. IX. 5. sine profusione tamen,dispensentur. Si quid Christo, seu Ecclesiæ hîc deest, compensare & suppeditare Fiscus non gravabitur. Prædictum enim est, fore ut Reges Ecclesiæ מלכים גרולי seu nutritii sint, & Principes Fœminæ ubera ei præbeant,Esaj. XLIX. 23. & ut Reges terræ gloriam & honorem suum in eam inferant,ibid.LXVI.12. Apoc.XXI.24.
units.tr: Following the example of all these, in the last century the most devout kings, princes and magistrates did the same. For it belongs to the ministers of the Word, once the necessity and truth of religion have been demonstrated, to call for reformation; to the magistrate to decree it; and to the people, once the necessity and truth have been shown from the Word of God by their pastors and the reformation has been decreed by the magistrate, to obey it. Eighth, the worship of God cannot be celebrated without the circumstances of place and time. Insofar as these are not defined in the Word of God, and have been left to the prudence of the Church to define, they cannot be settled by the magistrate's decision alone, by common consent [ὁμοπνεύσει]. Once settled, they must likewise be confirmed and sanctioned by the same authority, so that legitimate ecclesiastical assemblies held at this or that time and place can be distinguished from conventicles. Ninth, the Church ought to cultivate the communion of the saints. For there is one spouse of Christ, one Church, whose whole care and, as it were, oversight has been committed in common to all and each, not to one church separately. The same Church is compared now to a house, now to a ship. Her safety must be a concern for those who dwell in the cellar as much as for those in the upper room, for those in the prow as for those in the stern or the keel. Thus a common fire must be put out by common strength, and an approaching storm must be escaped by common rowing. It is therefore the magistrate's duty to provide not only for the churches of his own dominion, but also to help oppressed and persecuted brethren elsewhere with aid, counsel, intercession and other means. For the greater the power he has, beyond that of a private person, and the more defences he has received from God, the more important is his part in restoring and raising up the afflicted Church. So of old Hezekiah and Josiah, not content with having restored the fallen Church in Judah, also invited to a purer worship of God even the Israelites, though they were already in subjection to Assyria. And Christian emperors defended the Church against the Persians and Parthians, for they did not think that the fields and the glory of God were to be bounded by the same limits. But those who, trusting in mountains and fortifications, live securely, anointed with unguents and dissolute in luxury, are little moved by the calamity of brethren oppressed in unworthy ways, and disdainfully despise the broken and crushed Joseph: God himself threatens them with most just vengeance. "Curse Meroz," said the Angel of the LORD, "curse its inhabitants bitterly, because they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty." Judg. 5:23. "Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who trust in the mountain of Samaria," etc. "Behold, I will raise up against you, O house of Israel, says the LORD God of hosts, a nation, and they shall afflict you from the entrance of Hamath," etc. Amos 6:1, 14. Would that these threats were not to be dreaded by the Churches of our own times! Tenthly, we have said above that the Church cannot do without temporal goods to support ministers, the poor, and to build and maintain sacred buildings. Here too the faithful magistrates, who come under the name of stewards [ἐπιτρόπων] of the bounty (Luke 22:25), have their part to play. For it is their office to choose faithful stewards and administrators of such goods, who will both press and collect what is owed to the churches, administer what is collected faithfully, and defend it against these harpies with the help of the supreme magistrate. It is also theirs to see that those sacred goods of the Church are distributed not sparingly but generously, "as a blessing and not as covetousness" [ὡς εὐλογία, καὶ μὴ ὡς πλεονεξία] (2 Cor. 9:5), yet without wastefulness. If anything is lacking here to Christ or to the Church, the treasury will not hesitate to make it up and supply it. For it has been foretold that kings will be the Church's nursing fathers [מלκים גרולי], that is, nurses, and that princesses will offer her their breasts (Isa. 49:23), and that the kings of the earth will bring their glory and honour into her (Isa. 66:12; Rev. 21:24).

units.la: CXXXIX. Quomodo se Magistratus erga subditos heterodoxos, & à vera religione alienos gerere debeat, non plane explicatu facile est, propter personarum & circumstantiarum varietatem. In universum Magistratum violentia abstinere debere,si simplex error, non seditiosus,vel cum blasphemia conjunctus fuerit, supra diximus, & alibi etiam pluribus confirmavimus. Magistratus enim constitutus est ad civium bonum; ad eorum conversionem,non extirpationem. At nec nimia indulgentia infinitæ quidvis docendi & pertendendi licentiæ Magistratum decet. Neque obstat vel libertas prophetandi, quam Dei verbum omnibus concedit,vel libertas conscientiæ, omnibus pariter eximia. Nam quoad libertatem prophetandi, Apostolus sanè adhortatur: Spiritum ne extinguite, Prophetiam ne exinanite, 1. Thess. V. 19.20. Sed idem Prophetiam jubens fieri κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν πίστεως secundum analogiam fidei, Rom. XII.6. libertatem prophetandi extra veram fidem, & fundamentum ejusdem in verbo Dei revelatum evagari non finit. Aliud enim est σωφροσύνη, aliud ψἀδοσοφία: aliud πίστις fides, aliud opinio, & ἴδιον θέλημα, propria voluntas,2. Petr. I. 20.21. Prophetia à Pseudoprophetia, & fides ab opinione, canone conformitatis fidei distinguitur. Qui non affert hanc doctrinam, illi ne quidem Ave dicatis,2. Joh. v. 10. Tenete traditiones,quas docti estis, sive per sermonem, sive per epistolam, 2. Thess. II. 15.16. Vera igitur & laudabilis prophetandi libertas illa est,qua quis id,quod ex verbo Dei demonstrari potest, loquitur, & errantes pro opportunitate, cum modestia & sine conturbatione ordinis, cum demonstratione charitatis per elenchum ex Dei verbo corrigit,& in eo etiam aliorum Prophetarum judicio se subjicit. Prophetæ duo,vel tres loquantur,& alii judicent. Si verò alii revelatur sedenti, primus sileat. Potestis enim per vices omnes prophetare,ut omnes discant, & omnes adhortationem vel consolationem accipiant. Et Spiritus Prophetarum Prophetis subjiciuntur. Non enim est conturbationis Deus, sed pacis, ut in omnibus Ecclesiis sanctorum, 1. Cor. XIV. 29-34. Quibus verbis & licentia prophetandi cohibetur, quia prophetantes singuli aliorum judicio subjiciuntur, iisque, cum alii prophetant, silentium injungitur: & modus liberè prophetandi definitur, ut videlicet non loquatur quis aliud, quàm ὑπακαλυφὴν revelatum, atque dum id loquitur, alii sileant; ne quicquam sibi citra revelationum sermonem ἀφενὶ arroget. Et par ferè libertatis conscientiæ ratio est, quæ non in eo vertitur, ut de rebus Divinis quivis liberè sentire, judicare & loqui ausit,neque etiam in eo,quòd nemo cogi
units.tr: CXXXIX. How a magistrate ought to conduct himself towards subjects who are heterodox and alien to the true religion cannot be explained plainly and easily, because of the variety of persons and circumstances. In general, we have said above, and confirmed at greater length elsewhere, that the magistrate ought to abstain from violence if the error is a simple one, not seditious, and not joined with blasphemy. For the magistrate is set up for the good of the citizens, for their conversion and not their extirpation. Nor does it befit the magistrate to indulge excessively an unlimited licence of teaching and spreading whatever one pleases. Neither the liberty of prophesying, which the Word of God grants to all, nor liberty of conscience, which is equally outstanding in all, stands in the way. For as to liberty of prophesying, the Apostle certainly exhorts: Quench not the Spirit, despise not prophesyings, 1 Thess. 5:19-20. But the same Apostle, while commanding prophesying to be done according to the analogy of faith (κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν πίστεως), Rom. 12:6, does not allow liberty of prophesying to wander outside true faith and the foundation of it revealed in the Word of God. For one thing is σωφροσύνη [soundness of mind], another ψευδοσοφία [false wisdom]; one thing is πίστις [faith], another opinion, and ἴδιον θέλημα, one's own will, 2 Pet. 1:20-21. Prophecy is distinguished from false prophecy, and faith from opinion, by the rule of conformity to the faith. If anyone does not bring this doctrine, do not even say, Greet him, 2 John 10. Hold the traditions which you have been taught, whether by word or by epistle, 2 Thess. 2:15-16. The true and praiseworthy liberty of prophesying, therefore, is that by which someone speaks what can be shown from the Word of God, and corrects those who err, as occasion requires, with modesty and without disturbing order, with a demonstration of love, by proof from the Word of God, and also submits himself to the judgment of other prophets in this matter. Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge. But if something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may receive exhortation or comfort. And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace, as in all the churches of the saints, 1 Cor. 14:29-34. By these words the licence of prophesying is restrained, since each prophet is made subject to the judgment of others, and silence is enjoined on them when others are prophesying; and the manner of prophesying freely is defined, namely that no one should speak anything other than what has been revealed (ὑπακαλυφὴν), and while he speaks that, others should be silent, so that he does not presume to say anything on his own account (ἀφενὶ) apart from the speech of revelation. The reasoning about liberty of conscience is nearly the same. It does not consist in this, that anyone may dare to think, judge and speak freely about divine things; nor yet in this, that no one can be compelled to judge that true which he judges to be false (which is less liberty of conscience than liberty of judgment, or rather the impotence of a man who cannot bring another's mind under his own, and also the nature of the mind itself, which is such that no man can compel it to faith and judgment). It consists rather in this, that no man can justly hinder anyone from saying and doing what God has commanded him to say and do. For conscience is συνείδησις Θεῶ, the conscience of God, 1 Pet. 2:19, and since it has no master but God alone, it ought to be so free that no mortal may justly hinder it from obeying God. Therefore the true liberty of prophesying or of conscience does not demand that the magistrate grant an unlimited licence of thinking, judging, speaking and doing.

units.la: potest,ut judicet hoc verum esse,quod judicat esse falsum (quæ non tam libertas conscientiæ, quàm libertas judicii, seu potius impotentia hominis, non valentis sibi subjicere alterius animum; nec non animi ipsius natura, quæ ejusmodi est, ut ad fidem & judicium à nullo homine cogi possit) sed in eo potius, quòd nemo ab ullo homine justè impediri potest, quò minùs dicat & faciat, quod Deus dicere & facere jussit. Quia enim conscientia est ςυνείδησις Θεῶ conscientia Dei,1.Petr. II.19. adeóque neminem nisi Deum, Dominum habet, ita libera esse debet, ut à nemine Mortalium justè impediatur obsequi Deo. Non ergo vel prophetandi, vel conscientiæ vera libertas infinitam sentiendi, judicandi, loquendi & faciendi licentiam à Magistratu indulgeri postulat.
units.tr: No one can be compelled to judge that what he judges to be false is true. (This is less a freedom of conscience than a freedom of judgment, or rather the helplessness of a man who cannot bring another's mind under his own, and also the nature of the mind itself, which cannot be forced by any man to belief or judgment.) The point is rather that no one can be justly prevented by any man from saying and doing what God has commanded him to say and do. For conscience is conscience of God [συνείδησις Θεοῦ], 1.Petr. II.19, and so has no master but God alone. It must therefore be free, so that no mortal may justly hinder it from obeying God. True freedom of prophesying or of conscience does not require the magistrate to grant an unlimited licence to feel, judge, speak and act as one pleases in matters of God.

units.la: CXL. Alia insuper cautione opus est, ne, quicquid tandem Magistratus adversus errantes statuat,alieno duntaxat judicio & arbitrio statuat, adeóque furoris alieni satellitem se gerat. Licet enim æquissimum sit, ut Doctorum & Pastorum judicia & consilia solerter exploret,& judicium de fide & dogmatibus non solus,sed unà cum tota Ecclesia occupet, nec piè tamen,nec prudenter sic religionis curam aliis, quibuscunque illis, permittet, ut in quoscunque illi suaserint,vel impulerint, gladium stringere, vel severitatem quamcunque exercere,adeóque in incognitos sibi & parùm exploratos errores, cæca credulitate, animadvertere fas piúmque ducat. Quì enim cognoscere possit rectè de religione sentire alios, ut suam iis manum tutò committat & credat,nisi ipsemet ante, quid sentiendum sit,didicerit? Sin autem res tanti momenti eorum tum fidei, tum judicio commiserit,quos intus & in cute non noverit, imò si qualibuscunque commiserit,& ipse alia omnia egerit,qualem administrationis suæ rationem Regi Regum,qui præcipuam religionis curam ei mandavit, reddet? Inprimis si dormitantibus illis, tantàsque res negligentibus, pia doctrina opprimatur,& impia invalescat,multorùmque piorum & innocentium,quorum sanguis Abelici instar,in Cœlum clamat, cædes, & populi Christi perditio inde consequatur. Cujus rei illustre, quo omnes Magistratus moveri, ne alieno judicio considerent, par erat,exemplum est, quòd ipse Filius Dei per hujusmodi ignaviam iniquissimorum hostium suorum non tam judicio, quàm libidini permissus fuit. Accipite eum,inquiebat Pilatus,& judicate eum secundum legem vestram, Joh. XVIII. 31. Neque ideo nunc, quia in clarissima luce Evangelii versamur, omnia tuta sunt: Non enim sic Sathanas stertit, ut nihil novi moliatur, vel Regno suo non ampliùs invigilet.
units.tr: CXL. Furthermore, another caution is needed: whatever the magistrate finally decides against those who err, he must not decide it merely by another's judgment and will, and so make himself a henchman of another's rage. For although it is most right that he carefully examine the judgments and counsels of the teachers and ministers, and take up the judgment about faith and doctrines not alone but together with the whole Church, yet he will neither act piously nor prudently if he so commits the care of religion to others, whoever they are, that he thinks it right and lawful to draw the sword, or to exercise any severity whatever, against whomever they urge or drive him, and so to punish, with blind credulity, errors unknown to him and little examined. For how can he rightly judge that others think rightly about religion, so that he may safely entrust and commit his hand to them, unless he has himself first learned what ought to be thought? But if he commits a matter of such weight, both to their faith and to their judgment, men whom he does not know inside and out, or if he commits it to whomsoever at all and does nothing else himself, what account of his administration will he give to the King of kings, who has entrusted to him the chief care of religion? Especially if, while those men sleep and neglect such great matters, sound doctrine is suppressed and impiety grows strong, and from this follows the slaughter of many pious and innocent people, whose blood cries out to heaven like Abel's, and the ruin of the people of Christ. A notable example of this matter, by which all magistrates ought to be moved not to consider things by another's judgment, is that the Son of God himself was given up, through the cowardice of his most unjust enemies, not so much to their judgment as to their lust. Take him, said Pilate, and judge him according to your law, John 18:31. Nor, because we now live in the clearest light of the Gospel, are all things therefore safe. For Satan does not so slumber that he attempts nothing new, or ceases to watch over his kingdom.

units.la: CXLI. In judicio adversus errantes serendo præcipua Magistratus cura esse debet,ut errantes & errores distinguat. Sunt enim qui leviùs errent; sunt, qui graviùs. Sunt,qui leviùs errantes se dociles præbeant, vel errores sibi retineant; sunt ἑτεροδιδασκαλῆς,qui in errore quovis sic animum obfirmant, ut errores pro idolis habeant, & sectam sibi superstitem moliantur. Graviùs errantes alii capitalia fidei dogmata impetunt, alii fidei Christianæ fundamenta convellunt. Sunt,qui errorem civili vili societati innoxium errent: sunt, qui errorem cum politia ἀσυνδέτῳ foveant. Sunt, quorum error ita in mente residet, ut ad voluntatem & mores, virtutes Christianas & sociales non penetret: sunt, quorum error mentem egreditur, & voluntatem morésque Christianos & sociales inficit. Cujusmodi Gnosticorum, Adamitarum, Priscillianistarum, & superiore seculo Anabaptistarum Monasterienstium, nostróque Libertinorum errores fuerunt. Sunt seductores, qui alios rapidi torrentis instar in errorum regionem inducunt: sunt seducti; qui simplicitate, ignorantia, alióve imbecillioris animi affectu dementati sequuntur, quó ab aliis itur, non quó eundem est. Denique Reipublicæ status liber, vel per factiones turbatus est.
units.tr: In dealing with those who err, the magistrate's chief care should be to distinguish between the erring and their errors. Some err more lightly, others more gravely. Some who err lightly show themselves teachable or keep their error to themselves. Others are teachers of other doctrine [ἑτεροδιδασκαλῆς], who so harden their minds in any error that they treat their error as an idol and build for themselves a surviving sect. Of those who err more gravely, some assail the chief dogmas of the faith, and others overturn the foundations of the Christian faith. Some err in a way that is harmless to the common life of civil society; others cherish their error together with a unconnected [ἀσυνδέτῳ] politics. In some, the error stays in the mind and does not penetrate the will, morals, or Christian and social virtues; in others, the error leaves the mind and infects the will and Christian and social morals. Such were the errors of the Gnostics, the Adamites, the Priscillianists, the Anabaptists of Münster in the last century, and the errors of our own Libertines. There are seducers, who, like a rushing torrent, lead others into the region of error; and there are the seduced, who, dazed by simplicity, ignorance, or some other weakness of mind, follow where they are led, going where others go rather than where they themselves wish. Finally, the state of the commonwealth may be free, or it may be disturbed by factions.

units.la: CXLII.
units.tr: CXLII.

units.la: His sic distinctis in statu Reipublicæ libero & composito nullisque pactis mutuis ligato, pii & fideles Magistratus operam dabunt, ut errantes quivis docendo potius quàm cogendo regiam in veritatis semitam revocentur, delectis eam in rem ad docendum præ cæteris idoneis, mansuetis, & errantibus ipsis non ingratis, ex ordine non Ecclesiastico duntaxat, sed Politico etiam, tum inprimis cùm errantes animum à doctoribus aversum gerunt: ut principiis errorum recta via occurratur, & malum in herba stranguletur, ne in zizanium degenerans sine tritici periculo eradicari amplius non possit; imò juxta Christi institutionem, ne debeat quidem. Si nihil apud errantes institutio profecerit, errores leves, stipulares contra fidem, pietatem & societatem non grassantes, ex infirmitate, non malignitate, vel facturiendi studio defensi; sed non impotenter aliis obtrusi, tolerandi potiùs quàm exagitandi sunt. Non enim gladio ignis ille fodicandus est, ne major flamma excitetur. Fœnum enim & stipulas fundamento salvo superstructas dies & ignis manifestant, hoc est, vel Spiritus Dei & veritatis ex Verbi Dei luce exsplendescentis examen, vel calamitates hujus vitæ; vel ipse mortis articulus sic discutiunt, ut, qui superstruxerunt, salventur tamen velut per ignem, 1. Cor. III. 11-15. Errores graviores, in fidei fundamentum arietantes vel simplices, vel cum blasphemiis & Reipublicæ & societatis humanæ perturbatione conjuncti sunt. Quoad illos, aliter cum seductis, aliter cum seductoribus agendum.
