In seductos, at de cætero quietos & pacificos, & moraliter bonos, nihil civiles poenæ valent, nisi quòd Ecclesiæ communione moti, à privilegiis pariter & honoribus indebitis haud immeritò arcentur: ad media fidei, velut audiendas conciones, dissertationes, institutionem etiam privatam, salvo relicto assentiendi vel dissentiendi arbitrio, coguntur: & cœtus publici atque exercitia religionis erroneæ sive publica, sive privata iisdem interdicuntur: denique si spes conversionis nulla affulgeat, & periculum sit, ne, seductorum licet sermo gangrænæ instar serpat, atque ita seducti in seductores degenerent, in exilium; si errantium numerus, & ex eodem suboriturum Reipublicæ periculum non obstet, mittuntur. Sed gravius seductores, seu hæresiarchæ coërcentur, primò edictis & minis terrendi, ne venenum spargant, vel cœtus faciant: & imparentes, ceu turbatores publici pacis civilis & Ecclesiasticæ, in carceres compingendi, & spe correctionis decollante, in exilium relegandi sunt, quia sano corpori alia ratione consuli non potest. Dispar errorum non simplicium, sed cum blasphemia & perturbatione Reipublicæ conjunctorum ratio est, quorum non levior poena, quàm ipsius blasphemiæ & seditionis esse potest. In statu Reipublicæ turbato, ubi hæresis non amplius in herba est, ut facilè opprimi possit, sed populos, provincias, Regna integra pervasit, & inter multos singuli societate culpæ tutiores sunt, ibi verò de severitate remittere aliquid omnis prudentia sacra & civilis jubet. Neque enim Magistratus aliter quàm ad Reipublicæ salutem & Ecclesiæ conservationem atque ædificationem ex conscientia muneris sui hæreseos licentiam coërcere & impedire tenetur. Et certis etiam calibus tolerantiam religionis falsæ legibus sancire fas est. Veluti cùm vel Magistratui impediendæ legitimis modis hæreseos potestas deest; sive ille potestatem sociam, sive superiorem heterodoxam patitur: vel per temporum iniquitatem tanta errantium frequentia & potentia invaluit, ut iis citra concussionem & perturbationem Reipublicæ Ecclesiæ summum in ordinem redigendis Magistratus planè impar sit: vel potentia supprimendi legitimis mediis falsam religionem non deficit, at periculum ex usu potestatis illius aliis Ecclesiis gravissimum imminet; vel orthodoxa religio alicubi oppressa restitui nequit, nisi ibidem hæresi libertas concedatur. Quibus similibúsque in casibus conditiones ejusmodi in statuenda sanciendáque tolerantia fidelis Magistratus statuet, ne nullis cancellis circumscripta libertas in licentiam & confusionem intolerabilem degeneret. Judicio enim veritatis, charitatis & prudentiæ maximopere opus est; & pacta judicio tali constituta religiosè observanda sunt. Fœdifragum enim illud hominum Punicorum consilium, sublimi omni animo, ac præcipuè Christiano pectore indignum, quòd hæreticis juratò etiam data fides non obliget, quod Concilii Constantiensis parricidæ potiùs quàm Patres sustinuerunt, & hodiéque palam Jesuitæ Hispani & Itali, occulti Germani per interpretationum fraudes sustinent, & praxi omnes confirmant, Romam ablegandum est, ubi loci tam exulat honestas, ut homines perjuri, sicarii, parricidæ, incendiarii, veneficii artifices inter instrumenta Papalis Regni habeantur. Cùm enim infidelibus jurare liceat, Genes. XXI. 23, 24. XXVI. 31. XXXI. 53. Jos. IX. 15, hæreticis, qui infidelibus pejores non sunt, jurare pariter licet. Cui verò jurare licet, eidem fidem juratam servare fas piùmque pariter; & violare impium atque nefas pariter est. Perjurium certè cùm omne, tum illud etiam, quod adversus infideles & hæreticos committitur, gravissimè Deus, Exod. XX. 7. Levit. XIX. 12, vetuit; neque unum vindictæ Divinæ ob violatam fidem, quæ hostibus idololatris etiam data est; imò quæ etiam fraude obtenta fuerat, exemplum, velut Genes. XXXIV. Jos. IX. 2. Sam. XXI. 2. Reg. XXV. &c. Scriptura suppeditat. Ne dicam perjurii doctores istos pessimum in se ipsos exemplum statuere, dum non
units.tr: With these distinctions made, in a free and well-ordered commonwealth, bound by no mutual pacts, pious and faithful magistrates will take care that those who err are brought back by teaching rather than by compulsion onto the royal road of truth. For this purpose they will choose men fitted above others for teaching, gentle, and not unwelcome to the erring themselves, drawn not only from the ecclesiastical order but also from the political order, especially when the erring bear their minds averse to the teachers. The aim is that the beginnings of error be met by the straight way, and the evil be strangled in the blade, lest it grow into tares and can no longer be uprooted without danger to the wheat; indeed, according to Christ's institution, it ought not to be uprooted at all. If instruction has achieved nothing with the erring, minor errors that do not rage against the faith, piety, and society, which are held out of weakness rather than malice or a desire for novelty, but are not forced violently on others, should be tolerated rather than harassed. For the fire is not to be struck with a sword, lest a greater flame be stirred up. For hay and stubble built upon a sound foundation, the day and the fire declare, that is, either the testing of the Spirit of God and of truth shining from the light of the Word of God, or the calamities of this life, or the very moment of death, these things so sift the matter that those who built upon it are nonetheless saved, yet so as through fire, 1 Cor. 3:11-15. Graver errors that strike at the foundation of the faith, whether simple or joined with blasphemies and with the disturbance of the commonwealth and of human society, must be dealt with differently: the seduced differently from the seducers. Against the seduced, who are otherwise quiet and peaceful and morally good, civil penalties avail nothing, except that, moved by the communion of the Church, they are rightly kept from privileges and undue honours; they are compelled to attend the means of faith, such as hearing sermons, lectures, and even private instruction, with the freedom to assent or dissent left intact; and public assemblies and the exercises of false religion, whether public or private, are forbidden to them. Finally, if no hope of conversion shines forth, and there is danger that, although the talk of the seduced creeps like gangrene, the seduced will degenerate into seducers, they are sent into exile; if the number of the erring and the danger to the commonwealth arising from them do not stand in the way. But the more serious seducers, or heresiarchs, are restrained: first by being terrified with edicts and threats, lest they spread their poison or form assemblies; and if they disobey, as disturbers of the public civil and ecclesiastical peace, they are to be thrown into prison and, when hope of correction has failed, relegated into exile, because a healthy body cannot otherwise be cared for. The case is different for errors that are not simple but are joined with blasphemy and disturbance of the commonwealth, for their punishment can be no lighter than that of the blasphemy and sedition itself. In a disturbed commonwealth, where heresy is no longer in the blade and can be easily suppressed, but has spread through whole peoples, provinces, and kingdoms, and where individuals are safer by merging into the crowd of the guilty, all sacred and civil prudence bids us relax the severity somewhat. For the magistrate is bound, out of the conscience of his office, to restrain and impede the license of heresy only for the safety of the commonwealth and the conservation and edification of the Church. And at certain times it is also lawful to sanction by law the toleration of false religion. For example, when the magistrate lacks the power to impede heresy by lawful means, whether he suffers a power beside him or a heterodox one above him; or when, through the wickedness of the times, the number and power of the erring have grown so great that the magistrate is wholly unequal to reducing the Church to order without shaking and disturbing the commonwealth; or when the power to suppress false religion by lawful means is lacking, but great danger to other Churches threatens from the use of that power; or when the orthodox religion, oppressed somewhere, cannot be restored unless freedom is granted to heresy in that same place. In such and similar cases, the faithful magistrate will lay down conditions for establishing and sanctioning toleration, so that liberty, not hemmed in by any barriers, does not degenerate into license and intolerable confusion. For there is great need of the judgment of truth, of charity, and of prudence; and pacts made under such judgment must be religiously observed. That faithless counsel of Punic men, unworthy of every lofty mind and especially of a Christian breast, namely that faith sworn even to heretics does not bind, which the murderers of the Council of Constance, rather than the Fathers, upheld, and which the Spanish and Italian Jesuits openly uphold today, and the German Jesuits secretly uphold through frauds of interpretation, confirming it all in practice, must be sent back to Rome, where honesty is so exiled that perjurers, assassins, murderers, arsonists, and makers of poisons are counted among the instruments of the Papal kingdom. For since it is lawful to swear to unbelievers, Gen. 21:23, 24; 26:31; 31:53; Josh. 9:15, it is equally lawful to swear to heretics, who are no worse than unbelievers. And to whomever it is lawful to swear, it is equally right and pious to keep the sworn faith, and equally impious and wicked to violate it. Certainly God most gravely forbade perjury, Exod. 20:7; Lev. 19:12, in every form, and also that which is committed against unbelievers and heretics; nor does Scripture lack examples of divine vengeance for a violated faith, even one given to idolatrous enemies, or even one obtained by fraud, as in Gen. 34; Josh. 9:2; 2 Sam. 21:2; 1 Kings 25, etc. Not to mention that these teachers of perjury set the worst example for themselves, while they do not

units.la: Alia statu Reipublicæ liberi, alia perturbati est; & utrique judicium Magistratus circa errantes accommodari debet. non modò sibi, ceu hominibus ex professo perfidis, omnem apud Protestantes fidem abrogant, verùm etiam Protestantibus, & quibuscunque aliis non Pontificiis, qui non minùs Pontificios, atque hi illos pro hæreticis habent, idem in se juris, eandémque non servandi pacta facultatem concedunt, atque sic abrogata undique fide, quæ justitiæ fundamentum est, omnem societatem humanam tollunt, nullo foedere vel pace reparandam, cùm nihil, quod altringere valeat, superfit.
units.tr: The state of a free commonwealth is one thing, that of a disturbed one another; and the magistrate's judgment concerning the erring must be adapted to each. They not only deny all faith among Protestants to themselves, as men professedly faithless, but they also grant to Protestants, and to all others who are not Papists, who on their side regard the Papists no less as heretics, the same right over themselves and the same faculty of not keeping pacts; and so, with faith cut off on every side, which is the foundation of justice, they remove all human society, which cannot be restored by any covenant or peace, since nothing remains that could bind.

units.la: CXLIII. Fuit Gubernatio Ecclesiæ civilis.
units.tr: CXLIII. The civil government of the Church.

units.la: Beata Ecclesia est, quæ utraque Ecclesiastica & civili sic potitur, ut non una cum altera conflictetur, sed una alterius opem operiatur & experiatur saluberrimè. Licèt enim utramque gubernationem inter latum discrimen sit, quoad regiminis tum formam, quæ in Ecclesiastica ἐπισκοπική merè ministerialis, in civili Dei quidem respectu etiam ministerialis, Rom. XIII. 4. 6. at subditorum respectu imperio & authoritate instructa est: tum objecti proprii, quòd in illa res spirituales & homo spiritualis versatur, adeóque Magistratus in Ecclesia justum & legitimum ordinem, & ministeria ad internam communionem alendam & provehendam necessariò procurat, externámque idololatriam, corruptelas doctrinæ, blasphemias & scandala tollit: tum finis proximi, qui in illa communio Sanctorum, & ædificatio corporis Christi, in hac conservatio pacis & tranquillitatis externæ, intenditur: tamen non pauca sunt, in quibus amicè conspirant, & non magis quàm anima cum corpore collidi debent. Nullum enim majus & potentius politicæ Magistratus administrationi adjumentum & decus, quàm à Ministerio Ecclesiastico; & vicissim nullum, secundum Deum, fortius præsidium ac munimentum Ecclesiasticæ administrationi, quàm à justa & fideli Magistratus administratione accidere potest. Utriusque status Dei ordinatio est, ibid. XIII. 1. Ephes. IV. 11. Unus idémque utriusque scopus architectonicus, gloria Dei, & salus hominum temporalis & æterna est. Una utriusque procuratio esse debet, ut purum putum Dei Verbum, & cultus ejusdem sincerus atque illibatus in Ecclesia vigeat & obtineat: atque vicissim doctrinæ & cultus corruptelis quibuscunque suppullulantibus medicina adhibeatur. Uterque Decalogi, & tabulæ ejusdem prioris & posterioris custos, tutor, curator & vindex est. Ideo etiam Magistratus Pastorum, Num. XXVII. 16. Psal. LXXVIII. 70. 71. 72. Esaj. XLIV. 28. Deorum, Exod. XXII. 9. 28. Psal. LXXXII. 6. Nutritiorum populi Dei, Esaj. XLIX. 23. nominibus venit, & capita sua portásque aperire, ut Rex gloriæ ingrediatur, Psal. XXIV. 7. jubetur. Utriusque proin ordinis consensus & consiliorum operarúmque in Regni spiritualis gubernatione & conservatione conjunctio obtinere debet. Denique uterque membrum Christi & Ecclesiæ civis est, verbóque Dei subjicitur; & alter quoque alteri certo respectu subjicitur: Ministerium Magistratui civili, non spirituali; Magistratus Ministerio verbi spirituali subjectione, quæ fidei & obedientiæ est, quatenus verbo Dei, quod & quatenus illud Ministri prædicant, morem gerere, & castigationibus atque correptionibus ex verbo Dei, nec non consiliis ex eodem verbi Divini officina deprompti collum subdere tenetur. Quod sic Ambrosius contra Auxent. explicat: Solvimus, quæ Cæsaris sunt, Cæsari; & quæ sunt Dei, Deo. Tributum Cæsaris est: non negatur. Ecclesia Dei est: Cæsari utique non debet addici, quia jus Cæsaris Dei templum esse non potest. Quod cum honorificentia Imperatoris nemo dictum potest negare. Quid enim honorificentius quàm ut Imperator Ecclesiæ filius esse dicatur? Quod cùm dicitur, sine peccato dicitur. Imperator enim bonus intra Ecclesiam, non supra Ecclesiam est. Bonus enim Imperator quærit auxilium Ecclesiæ, non refutat. Hæc ut humiliter dicimus: ita constanter exponimus.
units.tr: The Church is blessed when it holds both the ecclesiastical and the civil government in such a way that they do not fight against each other, but each lends its aid to the other and benefits from it most wholesomely. For although the two governments differ widely: in the form of their rule, since the ecclesiastical is purely episcopal [ἐπισκοπική] and ministerial, while the civil, indeed ministerial in respect to God (Rom. 13.4, 6), is armed with power and authority in respect to its subjects; in their proper object, since the ecclesiastical deals with spiritual things and the spiritual man, so that the magistrate necessarily secures in the Church a just and lawful order and ministries for nourishing and advancing inward communion, and removes outward idolatry, corruptions of doctrine, blasphemies and scandals; and in their proximate end, since the former aims at the communion of the saints and the building up of the body of Christ, the latter at the preservation of external peace and tranquillity: nevertheless there are not a few points on which they agree in friendship, and they ought no more to collide than soul with body. For there is no greater or more powerful help and ornament to the administration of the civil magistrate than the ecclesiastical ministry; and conversely, under God, no stronger defence and bulwark can come to the administration of the Church than a just and faithful administration by the magistrate. Both estates are ordained by God (ibid. 13.1; Eph. 4.11). One and the same architectonic aim belongs to both, the glory of God and the temporal and eternal salvation of men. There should be one care for both, that the pure Word of God and its worship, sincere and unspotted, may flourish and prevail in the Church; and conversely, that a remedy be applied to whatever corruptions of doctrine and worship spring up. Each is the guardian, protector, curator and avenger of both tables of the Decalogue. For this reason the magistrates are also called by the names shepherds (Num. 27.16; Ps. 78.70-72; Isa. 44.28), gods (Exod. 22.9, 28; Ps. 82.6), and nursing fathers of the people of God (Isa. 49.23), and they are commanded to lift up their heads and open the gates, that the King of glory may come in (Ps. 24.7). Therefore the agreement of both orders, and the joining of their counsels and works, ought to hold in the government and preservation of the spiritual kingdom. Finally, each is a member of Christ and a citizen of the Church, and is subject to the Word of God; and each is also in a certain respect subject to the other: the ministry to the civil magistrate, but not in spiritual matters; the magistrate to the spiritual ministry of the Word, by a subjection of faith and obedience, insofar as he is bound to obey the Word of God, and as the ministers preach it, and to submit his neck to the rebukes and corrections drawn from the Word of God, and to the counsels likewise drawn from the workshop of the divine Word. Ambrose explains this thus against Auxentius: We render to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. The tribute is Caesar's: it is not denied. The Church is God's: it certainly ought not to be surrendered to Caesar, because Caesar's right cannot be the temple of God. No one can deny this with the honour due to the Emperor. For what is more honourable than that the Emperor should be called a son of the Church? When this is said, it is said without sin. For a good emperor is within the Church, not above the Church. For a good emperor seeks the help of the Church, he does not refute it. These things we say humbly; we set them out with firmness.

units.la: CXLIV. Sed mutua illa subjectio utrobique cum temperamento quodam exercenda est.
units.tr: CXLIV. But this mutual subjection must be exercised on both sides with a certain moderation.

units.la: Licèt enim Ecclesiæ Ministri, quatenus Reipublicæ membra sunt, Magistratui publico in rebus civilibus, unà cum agris, familia, possessionibus subsint, morúmque etiam censuram subeant, propter verbi tamen Divini, quod prædicant, reverentiam, benigniùs cum iis agit; tum à personalibus quidem, hoc est, quæ industria tantùm, atque opera adhibita obeuntur, & sordidis oneribus atque muneribus eos eximendo, ne à propriis officii functionibus abducantur, & ministerium ipsorum vilescat; quod veteres Imperatores, insignibus de immunitate Ecclesiæ Ministrorum à rebus ejusmodi, constitutionibus editis factitasse constat; tum in exactionibus mitiùs remissiúsque cum iis agendo, tum authoritati eorum, ubicunque licet, consulendo, ne cum eadem officium eorum vilescat. Vicissim Ecclesiæ Ministri Magistratum sic liberè & prudenter officii sui admonere, &, sicubi magna necessitas postulat, Ecclesiasticis censuris ad meliorem mentem revocare possunt, ut tamen enixè caveant, ne eo prætextu Majestatem ejus imminuant, vel in contemptum apud subditos adducant. Alia enim Prophetarum ratio fuit, qui tanquam Regum censores & Ephori à Deo singulari cum afflatu, atque rerum & verborum inspiratione & imperio missi liberiùs acriùsque Reges & Principes impios ferire & perstringere potuerunt. Nihilominus cautè & prudenter Nathan cum Davide, 2. Sam. XII. & Samuel cum Saule, ibid. XV. egerat; & Christus ipse, Dominus rariùs objurgationibus, plerunque instructionibus & commonefactionibus usus est; denique S. Paulus senem, ut patrem, increpare, 1. Timoth. V. 1. jussit. Et quantò major fascibus ipsis reverentia debetur, ne sceptrorum Majestas facilè levitérque lacessatur. Magistratus ne execrator; & Principi in populo tuo ne maledicito, Exod. XXII. 28.
units.tr: For although the ministers of the Church, insofar as they are members of the commonwealth, are subject to the public magistrate in civil matters, together with their fields, households and possessions, and also undergo the censure of their conduct, nevertheless, out of reverence for the divine Word which they preach, he deals more kindly with them: first, in personal matters, that is, those performed by industry and labour alone, by exempting them from base burdens and offices, so that they are not drawn away from the proper functions of their office and their ministry is not made contemptible; which the ancient emperors are known to have done by publishing notable constitutions on the immunity of the ministers of the Church from such duties; and then by dealing more gently and leniently with them in levies and exactions, and by consulting their authority wherever permitted, so that their office is not made contemptible along with it. In turn, the ministers of the Church may freely and prudently remind the magistrate of his duty, and, where great necessity demands it, may recall him to a better mind by ecclesiastical censures; yet they must take earnest care that under this pretext they do not diminish his majesty or bring him into contempt among his subjects. For the prophets had a different manner: sent by God with a unique inspiration, and with the inspiration and command of both matters and words, they could strike and rebuke impious kings and princes more freely and sharply, as censors and ephors of kings. Nevertheless Nathan with David (2 Sam. 12) and Samuel with Saul (ibid. 15) acted cautiously and prudently; and Christ himself, our Lord, used rebukes rarely, and mostly instruction and admonition; finally, St. Paul commanded that an elder be rebuked as a father (1 Tim. 5.1). And the greater the reverence owed to the very rods of office, so that the majesty of the sceptre is not lightly and rashly provoked: You shall not revile the judges, nor curse the ruler of your people (Exod. 22.28).

units.la: LOCI VICESIMI SEPTIMI De REGIMINE ECCLESIÆ SECTIO POSTERIOR. De REGIMINE ECCLESIÆ ANTICHRISTIANO. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: TOPIC TWENTY-SEVEN: ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE CHURCH, SECOND SECTION. ON THE ANTICHRISTIAN GOVERNMENT OF THE CHURCH. SUMMARY.

units.la: Regimen Ecclesiæ Antichristianum Hierarchia Romana exercet. 1. Hierarchiam non Christi, sed Romuli spiritus peperit, & Papæ potestatem ipsemet Papa in Concilio Florentino definivit. 2. Regimen Ecclesiæ externum non est Monarchicum. 3. Capitis Ecclesiæ principalis & ministerialis ; influentis & dirigentis distinctio rejecta. 4. Rationes pro regimine Ecclesiæ Monarchico ex optima forma regiminis: 5. nec non aliunde petitæ expenduntur. 6. Monarchiæ Papalis objectum explicatur. 7. Papa non est universalis Ecclesiæ Episcopus. 8. Potestas Politica Ecclesiasticæ essentialiter non subordinatur. 9. Nec Papa, nec Ecclesia potestatem jure Divino possidet. 10. Argumenta contraria diluuntur. 11. Legislatoria potestas principalis Papæ non competit. 12. Ecclesiæ in ferendis legibus authoritas explicatur. 13. Cum principatu & potestate dominante conjuncta non est. 14. Argumentorum adversantium vanitas. 15. Potestatem etiam judicialem dominantem Papa sibi arrogat. 16. Arrogatæ potestatis illius iniquitas. 17. Argumenta pro eadem ad partes vocantur. 18. Subjectum Monarchiæ Ecclesiasticæ jure Divino nullum est, neque Christus vicarium instituit. 19. Petrus non est institutus vicarius Christi, quia supra Apostolos reliquos non eminuit. 20. Petri Suprematus aliis etiam argumentis convellitur. 21. Objectiones pro Petri supremato discussæ. 22. Nec promissus ille Petro est, vel verbis Christi. Tu es Petrus, &c. 23. vel clavium potestate promissa, quia nec soli illi promissa est. 24. Nec herilis & dominica ei promissa est. 25. Neque etiam Suprematus Petro jusso pascere oves Christi, collatus est. 26. Petrus nunquam Suprematum usurpavit. 27. Nullum proin in Suprematu, nec promissio ei, nec collato, nec exercito successorem habere potuit; neque Papa Petri successor est vel jure. 28. vel facto, quia Petrum Romæ fuisse, incertum est. 29. nec argumentis adversantium confirmatur. 30. Saltem Episcopatu urbis Romæ functus non est. 31. Monarchicorum argumentis contrariis satisfit. 32. Origo Suprematus Papæ Guicciardini verbis contractis panditur. 33. Papa non est Caput Ecclesiæ. 34. Rationes pro Suprematu Papæ eliduntur. 35. Sublato Papa capite, corpus ejus ex clericis & laicis compositum, perit. Cleri appellatio ministris Papæ non convenit. 36. Electionis, ordinationis & missionis ministrorum Ecclesiæ distinctio ficti-tia est. 37. Papa jus ministros Ecclesiæ eligendi & vocandi supremum non habet. 38. Ordinationis Sacramentalis, & Ordinum Papalium vanitas. 39. Rationes pro distinctione ordinum examinantur. 40. Lex cœlibatus ordinibus majoribus annexa est. 41. Quæ tota Antichristiana est. 42. Rationes, quibus illa incrustatur, solutæ. 43. Exemptio Cleri, vi tonsuræ, à potestate seculari, Antichristiana est. 44. Neque argumentis adversantium confirmatur. 45. Clerici gubernantes primi Episcopi sunt. 46. Prærogativas singulares habent in regimine Papali. 47. Episco-
units.tr: The Roman hierarchy exercises the Antichristian government of the Church. 1. The hierarchy was brought forth not by the spirit of Christ but by the spirit of Romulus, and the Pope himself defined the Pope's power in the Council of Florence. 2. The external government of the Church is not monarchical. 3. The distinction between the principal and ministerial head of the Church, and between the influencing and directing head, is rejected. 4. The arguments for monarchical government of the Church, drawn from the best form of government, are weighed. 5. Arguments drawn from elsewhere are likewise examined. 6. The object of Papal monarchy is explained. 7. The Pope is not the bishop of the universal Church. 8. Political power is not essentially subordinate to ecclesiastical power. 9. Neither the Pope nor the Church possesses power by divine right. 10. Contrary arguments are refuted. 11. The chief legislative power does not belong to the Pope. 12. The authority of the Church in enacting laws is explained. 13. It is not joined with principality and dominant power. 14. The vanity of the opposing arguments. 15. The Pope also claims for himself a dominant judicial power. 16. The injustice of that claimed power. 17. Arguments in its favour are called to account. 18. There is no subject of ecclesiastical monarchy by divine right, and Christ did not appoint a vicar. 19. Peter was not appointed Christ's vicar, because he did not stand out above the other Apostles. 20. Peter's supremacy is overturned by other arguments also. 21. Objections raised for Peter's supremacy are discussed. 22. That promise was not made to Peter by the words of Christ, "You are Peter," etc. 23. Nor by the promise of the power of the keys, because it was not promised to him alone. 24. Nor was a lordly and dominical power promised to him. 25. Nor is supremacy conferred on Peter by the command to feed Christ's sheep. 26. Peter never claimed supremacy. 27. Therefore no one could have a successor in the supremacy, neither by promise, nor by conferral, nor by exercise; and the Pope is not Peter's successor, either by right 28. or in fact, since it is uncertain that Peter was ever at Rome. 29. Nor is the matter confirmed by the arguments of the opposing side. 30. At least, he did not hold the episcopate of the city of Rome. 31. The arguments of the monarchists to the contrary are answered. 32. The origin of the Pope's supremacy is set out briefly in the words of Guicciardini. 33. The Pope is not the Head of the Church. 34. The reasons for the Pope's supremacy are refuted. 35. If the Pope as head is removed, his body, made up of clergy and laity, perishes; and the name "clergy" does not belong to the ministers of the Pope. 36. The distinction between the election, ordination and sending of the ministers of the Church is fictitious. 37. The Pope does not have the supreme right to elect and call the ministers of the Church. 38. The vanity of sacramental ordination and of Papal orders. 39. The reasons for the distinction of orders are examined. 40. The law of celibacy is attached to the major orders. 41. This whole thing is Antichristian. 42. The reasons by which it is dressed up are dissolved. 43. The exemption of the clergy from secular power, by virtue of the tonsure, is Antichristian. 44. Nor is it confirmed by the arguments of the opposing side. 45. The clergy who govern are the first bishops. 46. They have singular prerogatives in the Papal government. 47. Episco-

units.la: Episcoporum supra Presbyteros eminentia jure Ecclesiastico introducta est. 48. Jure Divino nulla est. 49. Hierarchicorum argumenta pro eadem ad examen revocantur. 50. Episcopi Pontificii nil cum veteribus commune habent. 51. Archiepiscopi, seu Metropolitani, Patriarchæ, Cardinales. 52. Clerici supererogantes Monachi sunt. 53. Monachatus ex verbo Dei oppugnatur. 54. Argumentis pro eodem occurritur. 55. Monachorum veterum & recentiorum differentia. 56. Clerici adjuvantes, Doctores Theologiæ, Juris Canonici, Catechismi, Prædicatores, Disputatores, Scholastici. 57. Laici, alterum corporis Papalis membrum sunt. 58. Papæ ὑπερέχη supra Concilia. 59. Pro eadem argumenta à Monarchicis allata ventilantur. 60. Papa nec convocandi, nec moderandi, nec confirmandi Concilia jus habet. 61. Argumenta pro hoc jure allata refelluntur. 62. Conciliorum à Papa confirmatorum sententia nec judicialis, nec absolutè infallibilis est. 63. Regiminis Antichristiani author Antichristus est. Vox Antichristi, & synonymæ explicantur. 64. Gemina de Antichristo quæstio est, qualis sit, & quis sit? 65. Qualis sit Antichristus, ejus definitio & vera idea docet. 66. Idea vera Antichristi ex ejusdem characteribus & notis, quæ explicantur, dignoscitur. 67. Idea falsa Antichristi refellitur. 68. Et pro eadem argumenta allata discutiuntur. 69. Papa Romanus, quà Papa, & munus Papæ gerens, Antichristus est. 70. Quod probatur tum ex nomine Antichristi, tum ex eo, quòd negat Jesum esse Christum, & non confitetur, Christum venisse in carne, & se supra id, quod Deus & Augustum dicitur, effert. 71. Tum ex eo, quòd homo peccati, filius perditionis est, sedem Antichristi possidet, & scortatione spirituali & corporali, blasphemiis, tyrannide & crudelitate, magia & avaritia atque nundinatione spirituali maximè pollutus est. 72. Tum ex eo, quòd distinctæ Antichristi in mysterio operantis revelati, spiritu oris Christi consumpti, abolendi denique, periodi aprime ei conveniunt. 73. Tum ex eo, quòd corpus Antichristi Papæ capitis corpus est. 74. Quod miris ille artibus sibi subjecit. 75. Pontificiorum argumenta contraria ad partes vocantur, partim illa, quibus probare conantur, Antichristum nondum venisse; 76. Partim illa, quibus contendunt, Papam non esse Antichristum, petita ex professione Papæ, quòd se famulum Christi, & servum servorum profitetur, Jesum Christum non abnegat, confitetur, quòd Jesus venerit in carne, & se Deum manifestè non facit, sed vicarium Dei; alium præter se Deum patitur, & signa, qualia Apocalypsis Bestiæ tribuit, nunquam patravit. 77.
units.tr: The eminence of bishops above presbyters was introduced by ecclesiastical law. 48. By divine law it is nothing. 49. The arguments of the hierarchists in its favour are brought back to examination. 50. The Papist bishops have nothing in common with the ancients. 51. Archbishops, or Metropolitans, Patriarchs, Cardinals. 52. The clergy who do more than required are monks. 53. Monasticism is assailed from the Word of God. 54. The arguments for it are met. 55. The difference between ancient and more recent monks. 56. Assisting clergy: teachers of theology, of canon law, of the catechism, preachers, disputants, scholastics. 57. The laity are the other member of the Papal body. 58. The Pope's superiority over Councils. 59. The arguments brought by the monarchists in favour of this are weighed. 60. The Pope has no right to convene, to direct, or to confirm Councils. 61. The arguments advanced for this right are refuted. 62. The judgment of Councils confirmed by the Pope is neither judicial nor absolutely infallible. 63. The author of the Antichristian government is Antichrist. The word "Antichrist" and its synonyms are explained. 64. There is a twofold question about Antichrist: what sort of thing he is, and who he is? 65. What sort of thing Antichrist is, his definition and true idea teach. 66. The true idea of Antichrist is recognised from his characters and marks, which are explained. 67. The false idea of Antichrist is refuted. 68. The arguments advanced for that false idea are discussed. 69. The Roman Pope, as Pope, and performing the office of Pope, is Antichrist. 70. This is proved both from the name Antichrist, and from the fact that he denies that Jesus is the Christ, does not confess that Christ has come in the flesh, and exalts himself above what is called God and Augustus. 71. Also from the fact that he is the man of sin, the son of perdition, possesses the seat of Antichrist, and is most defiled by spiritual and bodily whoredom, blasphemies, tyranny and cruelty, magic and avarice, and spiritual simony. 72. Also from the fact that the distinctive marks of Antichrist, the one working in the revealed mystery, consumed by the breath of the mouth of Christ, and finally to be abolished, and the periods, agree with him most fully. 73. Also from the fact that the body of Antichrist is the body of the Papal head. 74. Which he subjected to himself by wonderful arts. 75. The contrary arguments of the Papists are brought to account: partly those by which they try to prove that Antichrist has not yet come; 76. partly those by which they contend that the Pope is not Antichrist, drawn from the Pope's profession that he is the servant of Christ and servant of servants, that he does not deny Jesus Christ, confesses that Jesus came in the flesh, and does not openly make himself God but a vicar of God; that he suffers no other God besides himself, and has never done the signs such as the Apocalypse attributes to the Beast. 77.

units.la: I. REGIMINI Ecclesiæ Christiano opponitur Antichristianum
units.tr: I. The Antichristian government is opposed to the Christian government of the Church

units.la: REGIMINI Ecclesiæ Christiano opponitur Antichristianum, quo Antichristus, vicariam Christi in mundo ἀρχὴν καὶ ἐξουσίαν principatum & potestatem, specie externa spiritualem, revera temporalem & mundanum usurpans, Ecclesiam, perinde ut Regnum aliquod mundanum, gubernat, legibus & judiciis ex plenitudine potestatis latis & exercitis subjicit, & regimini tali universam religionem Christianam accommodat. Sicut enim Regnum Christi non est de hoc mundo, neque visibilis terrestris Monarchiæ instar, terrestri & mundano, sed Cœlesti & spirituali modo, ad salutem inprimis animæ administratur: ita contrà Regnum Antichristi, spirituali licèt assumpta larva, de mundo hoc tamen est, & mundanis atque carnalibus consiliis & rationibus ad salutem corporis, & πληρώσιν σαρκός repletionem carnis, Col. II. 23. qui Regni illius finis atchitectonicus est; administratur. Regnum hoc Hierarchiæ nomine venit, quod nomen Pseudo-Dionysio Areopagitæ, sesquipedalia & ampullata ejusmodi ῥήματα in Ecclesiam invehenti, acceptum referendum est. Cùm enim scriptores sacri eos, qui Ecclesiam pascunt, ᾿Επισκόπων Episcoporum nomine insigniant, Pseudo-Dionysius ne semel quidem Episcopi nomine usus, ἱερ-άρχας Hierarchas, & τῆς τῆς ἱεραρχίας ἐπωνύμως
units.tr: Opposed to the Christian government of the Church is the Antichristian government, by which Antichrist, usurping for himself the principate and power [ἀρχὴν καὶ ἐξουσίαν] that belong to Christ's vicar in the world, rules the Church as if it were some worldly kingdom. Outwardly it has a spiritual appearance, but in reality it is temporal and worldly. He subjects the Church to laws and judgments issued and enforced from the fullness of power, and he adapts the whole Christian religion to this kind of rule. For just as the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, nor is it administered like a visible earthly monarchy, but in a heavenly and spiritual manner, chiefly for the salvation of the soul, so on the contrary the kingdom of Antichrist, though it wears a spiritual mask, is nevertheless of this world. It is administered by worldly and carnal counsels and reasons, for the salvation of the body and for the filling of the flesh [πληρώσιν σαρκός], Col. 2:23, which is the architectonic end of that kingdom. This kingdom came to be called by the name Hierarchy, a name that must be credited to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, who brought such high-flown and bombastic words into the Church. For while the sacred writers mark those who feed the Church with the name of Bishops [Ἐπισκόπων], Pseudo-Dionysius, who never once uses the name of bishop, calls them hierarchs [ἱεράρχας] and those named after the hierarchy [τῆς ἱεραρχίας ἐπωνύμως]

units.la: ab Hierarchia cognominatos, novè, constanter & ubique, planè præter Apostolorum & Apostolicorum hominum morem, dixit. Planè ut hierophantica & recentioris ævi appellatio sit. Sed res ipsa cum Regno Antichristi aprime convenit, utpote quod ἀρχὴ principatu & dominio, & quidem ἱερῷ sacro, rerum quippe sacrarum & religionis, quo nihil in terris ad homines vel impellendos vel retinendos efficacius est, Majestate & fuco quodam ad subjiciendas spiritualium ithac specie dominationi animas, incrustato constat.
units.tr: named from the Hierarchy, new, constant and everywhere, quite contrary to the custom of the Apostles and apostolic men. So the appellation is clearly that of hierophants and of a more recent age. But the thing itself agrees very well with the kingdom of Antichrist, since it consists of a principate and dominion [ἀρχὴ], and indeed a sacred one [ἱερῷ], that is, of sacred things and of religion, than which nothing on earth is more effective for driving or holding men in place. It is encrusted with a certain majesty and gloss, for the purpose of bringing souls under a spiritual domination dressed up in this outward form.

units.la: II. Hierarchiam, qualis hodie est cum imperio & dominatione sacra conjunctam, eámque consummatissimam, non Christi, sed Romuli genius peperit. Forma enim Regiminis Romulæi & Hierarchici exactè quadrat. Translata nempe Imperii ex Occidente in Orientem sede, sicut Imperator Constantinopoli, ita Papa Romanus, omnium Ecclesiarum Monarcha, Romæ sedem affectavit, & Regnum sibi atque suis paulatim & sensim operante mysterio iniquitatis, constituit. Consulibus Romanis Cardinales non duo numero, sed tot, quot Papæ Hierarchiæ Principi visum fuerit: Ducibus Archiepiscopi: Comitibus Episcopi: Præsidibus Imperii & Exarchis Episcoporum Vicarii & Chorepiscopi: Præfectis Imperii Præpositi: Tribunis militum, Archipresbyteri: Tribunis plebis Cancellarii: Prætoribus Archidiaconi: Centurionibus Decani: Duumviris Subdiaconi successerunt & adæquati sunt. Quod jam olim Petrus Messias Pontificius in Sylva variæ lectionis Venetiis edita fusè juxta atque ingeniosè demonstravit; haud diffitentibus Gregorio VII. Papa, Bellarmino, Lipsio, Auberto Miræo, & P. de Marca, quorum testimonia alibi attulimus. Sed operæ pretium inprimis est ipsius Papæ de potestate sibi competente decretum & ψήφισμα repetere. Sic enim Eugenius IV. in Synodo Florentina, seu literis Unionis, ultimæ Sessioni Concilii illius suæ potestatis peristromata dilatat. Ὀρίζομεν Definimus, Sanctam Apostolicam sedem, & Pontificem Romanum in universum orbem terrarum primatum habere: & ipsum Pontificem Romanum successorem esse B. Petri, Principis Apostolorum, & verè (τοῦ ληρητὴν τῶ Χριστῶ) vicarium Christi, totius Ecclesiæ caput, & omnium Christianorum Patrem & doctorem existere: & ipsi in B. Petro pascendi, & regendi, & gubernandi totam Ecclesiam universalem a Domino nostro Jesu Christo (παντὸς ἐξουσίαν) plenam potestatem traditam esse. En παντὸς ἐξουσίαν plenam potestatem, seu potestatis in Ecclesiam universam Christi plenitudinem! Totum verò Regimen Antichristianum Rege, seu Domino, regnantisque actibus & populo regimini parenti, capite & corpore absolvitur.
units.tr: II. The Hierarchy, as it is today, joined with sacred rule and domination, and that in its most complete form, was brought forth not by the genius of Christ but by that of Romulus. For the form of Romulean and Hierarchical government fits exactly. Once the seat of empire had been transferred from the West to the East, the Roman Pope, as monarch of all churches, aspired to the seat at Rome, just as the emperor did at Constantinople, and by the gradual and secret working of the mystery of iniquity he set up a kingdom for himself and his own. In place of the two Roman consuls there are Cardinals, as many as the Prince of the Hierarchy pleases to appoint. For the commanders there are Archbishops; for the counts, Bishops; for the presidents of the empire and the exarchs, the Vicars of Bishops and Chorepiscopi; for the prefects of the empire, Provosts; for the military tribunes, Archpresbyters; for the tribunes of the people, Chancellors; for the praetors, Archdeacons; for the centurions, Deans; and the Subdeacons have taken the place of and are equal to the duumvirs. Petrus Messias, a Papist, has already shown this at length and with ingenuity in his Silva variae lectionis, published at Venice, and Gregory VII, Bellarmine, Lipsius, Aubert Miraeus and P. de Marca do not deny it; I have cited their testimonies elsewhere. But it is especially worth repeating the Pope's own decree and pronouncement on the power that belongs to him. For thus Eugenius IV, in the Council of Florence, in the letters of Union, which were the last session of that council, spreads out the hangings of his own power: "We define that the Holy Apostolic See and the Roman Pontiff hold the primacy over the whole world, and that the Roman Pontiff himself is the successor of Blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, and truly the vicar of Christ [τοῦ ... τῷ Χριστῷ], head of the whole Church, and father and teacher of all Christians; and that to him in Blessed Peter has been handed down by our Lord Jesus Christ the full power [παντὸς ἐξουσίαν] of feeding, ruling and governing the whole universal Church." Behold, the full power [παντὸς ἐξουσίαν], that is, the fullness of power over the universal Church of Christ! The whole Antichristian government is thus completed with a King, or Lord, with royal acts, with a people obedient to the rule, with head and body.

units.la: III. Regem ergo, Dominum & caput Ecclesiæ Hierarchici Papam faciunt. Sed præstruunt illi, ceu κυρίων δόξαν, quòd Ecclesiæ regimen Monarchicum sit, discorde tamen concordia. Nam qui Ecclesiam Papa superiorem agnoscunt, & sine Papa Ecclesiam constare decernunt, statum quidem Ecclesiæ Monarchicum, regimen verò ejus Aristocraticum esse censent, & penes Papam potestatem tantùm ministerialem & executivam esse decernunt. Et internum quidem Ecclesiæ regimen Monarchicum esse, propter Christum Regem & Caput Ecclesiæ unicum, supra probare occupavimus. Externum verò à Christo, Apostolis, Pastoribus & Doctoribus demandatum ἀρχὴν Principatum, vel κράτος Potentiam nullam habet, adeóque proprie nec Monarchicum, nec Aristocraticum, nec Democraticum; sed ἀναλόγως & improprie Aristocraticum est; sic tamen, ut ministerio, quàm regimini similius sit. Aliam verò præter spiritualem Christi Monarchiam superinducere, tyrannicum, Antichristianum & Scripturæ contrarium est. Unicum enim Ecclesiæ Regem & caput illa Christum facit, & honorem illa Divinum alienantem, atque creaturis vendicantem, Antichristi, Adversarii, Bestiæ & Babylonis hieroglyphicis depingit. Dedit autem Christus in Cœlum evectus non unum aliquem Pro-Regem & Dominum, sed alios Apostolos, alios Prophetas, alios Evangelistas, alios Pastores & Doctores, Eph. IV.11. Neq; ulla uspiam Regis & Capitis Ecclesiæ visibilis mentio extat. Qualem si Christo Ecclesiæ præficere cordi fuisset, non minùs authenticis & solennibus tabulis illum instituisset & confirmasset, quàm solenniter & authenticè Deus in V. T. Pontificem instituit & confirmavit; imò solennioribus etiam, quia & Pontifex V. T. Ecclesiæ Minister, non Dominus institutus est; & sub N.T. solus Filius audiri, Luc. IX.35. ceu solus Magister & doctor, Matth. XXIII.8. Unicus Legislator, potens salvare & perdere, Jac. IV, 12.
units.tr: III. So the Hierarchists make the Pope the King, Lord and head of the Church. But they put forward, as it were as a boast of their lords [κυρίων δόξαν], that the government of the Church is monarchical, yet in a discordant harmony. For those who acknowledge that the Pope is above the Church, and who decree that the Church cannot exist without the Pope, judge the state of the Church to be monarchical, but its government to be aristocratic, and they decide that the Pope holds only a ministerial and executive power. That the internal government of the Church is monarchical, because Christ is its only King and Head, we have already taken pains to prove above. But the external government, entrusted by Christ to the Apostles, pastors and teachers, has no principate [ἀρχὴν] or power [κράτος] of its own, and so it is properly neither monarchical, nor aristocratic, nor democratic; it is aristocratic only analogously and improperly, yet in such a way that it resembles a ministry more than a government. To introduce any monarchy other than the spiritual monarchy of Christ is tyrannical, Antichristian and contrary to Scripture. For it makes Christ alone the one King and head of the Church, and it depicts as hieroglyphics of Antichrist, the Adversary, the Beast and Babylon those who take away this divine honour and claim it for creatures. Christ, however, when he was taken up into heaven, did not give one single vice-king and lord, but "some Apostles, some Prophets, some Evangelists, some Pastors and Teachers", Eph. 4:11. Nor is there anywhere any mention of a visible King and Head of the Church. If it had pleased Christ to set such a person over the Church, he would have instituted and confirmed him by records no less authentic and solemn than those by which God in the Old Testament instituted and confirmed the High Priest; indeed by even more solemn ones, since the High Priest of the Old Testament was instituted as a minister of the Church, not as its lord; and under the New Testament the one thing is "Hear the Son", Luke 9:35, as the only "Master and Teacher", Matt. 23:8, "the only Lawgiver, able to save and to destroy", James 4:12.

units.la: debet. Unicum enim Ecclesiæ Caput est; sicut unum corpus est, quod uno isto capite, tanquam unica mente animandum est. Nec magis alterum Ecclesiæ caput, quàm alter Ecclesiæ Sponsus, vir, Dominus, Mediator, Salvator & Rex dari potest. Unde Christus cum articulo ἡ κεφαλὴ τῆς σώματος Illud caput corporis, Col. I. 18. H. 19. ὀρίζεται definitè notatur Ecclesiæ caput. Nam αὐτὸν ipsum, non alium Deus dedit caput super omnia Ecclesiæ, Ephes. I.22. Et in solo Christo reperiuntur proprietates capitis, quales sunt, conjungi cum Ecclesia ἀχωρίστως καὶ ἀδιαιρέτως, diligere Ecclesiam, ejus fundamentum & lapidem angularem esse, σύμ-πνοιαν, & pro ea fieri sacrificium; ἐπιχορηγεῖν suppeditare ei omnem vim & facultatem vivificam, nec non augmentum, ut crescat & educetur Ecclesia in omnem plenitudinem Dei, esse lucem corporis Ecclesiæ & doctorem unicum; quod pluribus supra demonstravimus.
units.tr: For there is one Head of the Church, just as there is one body, which must be animated by that one head as by one single mind. Nor can another head of the Church be given any more than another Bridegroom, husband, Lord, Mediator, Saviour and King of the Church. Hence Christ, with the article, "that Head of the body", Col. 1:18; 2:19, [ἡ κεφαλὴ τῆς σώματος] is definitely designated as the head of the Church. For God gave Himself, and not another, as head over all things to the Church, Eph. 1:22. And the properties of a head are found in Christ alone: to be joined with the Church inseparably and indivisibly [ἀχωρίστως καὶ ἀδιαιρέτως], to love the Church, to be its foundation and cornerstone, to be [σύμ-πνοιαν] of one breath with it, and to be sacrificed for it; to supply [ἐπιχορηγεῖν] to it all life-giving power and ability, and likewise the growth by which the Church grows and is brought up to the full measure of God; to be the light of the body of the Church and its only teacher. We have demonstrated this at greater length above.

units.la: IV. Nec quicquam valent distinctionum latebræ, velut, cùm caput aliud influens, aliud dirigens, velut cùm caput externis sensibus, visu inprimis, corporis actiones dirigit; & vi-sum, vel alium sensum externum in capite radicatum nemo sanus caput ipsum dixerit; aliud principale seu imperiale, aliud ministeriale, aliud absolutum, aliud relatum, & fundamentum Ecclesiæ aliud primarium, aliud secundarium faciunt. Præterquam enim quòd distinctionum ejusmodi præstigias aperté rejecit Papa Bonifacius VIII. qui cap. Unam sanctam. Extravag. de Majorit. & Obed. dicere non erubuit: Christum & Vicarium Christi Petrum, & successorem Petri Papam, unum tantùm omnes esse caput Ecclesiæ; etiam duo illa capita, licèt imperialis & ministerialis, absoluti & relativi, influentis & dirigentis discrimine fucata, non tam capitis officia dividunt, quàm planè disrumpunt, & Monarcham illum visibilem imperiale potiùs & absolutum, quàm ministeriale & relativum constituunt. Nam juxta Stapletonum aliósque capitis imperialis & absoluti officium est, à se tanquam fonte vitam in cæteras corporis partes diffundere; ministerialis verò & relativi corporis externa munia imperio & potestate sua, tum legislativa, tum judiciali, dirigere & administrare. Atqui imperio & potestate sive interna sive externa corporis munia dirigere, præcipua, seu principalis capitis functio est, illo uno digna capite, quod vitæ, sensus & motus potestatem omnem spiritu suo corpori impertitur. Cùmque hoc imperium erga Ecclesiam exercere sit prærogativa Regia, & Regi Regum propria, quisquis eam totam, vel partem ejus cuiquam subditorum, qui εἰς ἔργον διακονίας ad opus ministerii, non imperii constituti sunt, Ephes. IV. 12. tribuit, is læsæ Majestatis Christi reum se facit. Et sanè caput esse in sensu proprio & pleno, non improprio & diminuto, est non tantùm ordine quodam, sed etiam dignitate, imperio & influxu cæteris membris præesse. Qui verò sic præest, is imperio, non ministerio præest. Neque Papam suum aliter Herarchici Ecclesiæ caput facere, quàm meram, infinitam & reapse directam in spiritualibus & temporalibus potestatem ei arrogando,
units.tr: IV. Nor do the hidden corners of distinctions count for anything, such as the distinction that one head is influential and another directive, or that a head directs the bodily actions by the external senses, sight above all, and no sane person would call the sight, or any other external sense rooted in the head, the head itself; or the distinction that one head is principal or imperial, another ministerial; one absolute, another relative; and that the foundation of the Church is one primary, another secondary. For apart from the fact that Pope Boniface VIII openly rejected these sleights of distinction, when he did not blush to say in the chapter Unam sanctam, Extravagantes, On Majority and Obedience: "that Christ and the vicar of Christ, Peter, and the successor of Peter, the Pope, are all one head of the Church"*; even those two heads, though coloured with the distinctions of imperial and ministerial, absolute and relative, influential and directive, do not so much divide the offices of the head as utterly tear them apart, and they make that visible monarch more imperial and absolute than ministerial and relative. For according to Stapleton and others, it is the office of the imperial and absolute head to pour life out from itself, as from a fountain, into the other parts of the body; but the office of the ministerial and relative head is to direct and administer the external duties of the body by its own command and power, both legislative and judicial. Yet to direct the duties of the body by command and power, whether internal or external, is the chief and principal function of the head, the one function worthy of the title head, since it imparts to the body, by its spirit, all the power of life, sense and motion. And since to exercise this command over the Church is a royal prerogative, proper to the King of kings, whoever ascribes all of it, or any part of it, to any of those subjects who are appointed for the work of the ministry [εἰς ἔργον διακονίας], not of command, Eph. 4:12, makes himself guilty of injured majesty against Christ. And indeed to be head in the proper and full sense, not in an improper and diminished one, is to preside over the other members not merely by a certain order, but also by dignity, command and influence. But whoever presides in this way presides by command, not by ministry. Nor do the Hierarchists make their Pope head of the Church in any other way than by arrogating to him mere, infinite and in fact direct power over spiritual and temporal matters,

units.la: Regimen Ecclesiæ externum non est Monarchicum. rogando,eúmque RegemRegum & Dominum dominantium constituendo, potuerunt. Deni- que secundaria ejusmodi nomina non magis rei invidiam minuunt, vel suum Christo im- perium intemeratum relinquunt,quàm si quis secundarium in casto conjugio conjugem in- vehat. Quisquis enim præter Christum Eccle- siæ caput dici amat, is non Ecclesiæ caput & sponsus, sed profanus solii Christi infessor, & castissimi ejus thalami infessor & corruptor est.
units.tr: The external government of the Church is not monarchical. By ascribing to him an unlimited power and making him King of kings and Lord of lords, they could (as they have done). Moreover, such secondary titles do no more to lessen the odium of the thing, or to leave Christ's rule unimpaired, than if someone were to bring a secondary wife into a chaste marriage. For whoever loves to be called head of the Church besides Christ is not the head and bridegroom of the Church, but a profane intruder on Christ's throne, and an intruder and corrupter of his most chaste marriage-bed.

units.la: V. Non paucas tamen Monarchici ratio- nes fabricati sunt, quibus visibilis Monarchæ Ecclesiæ imperium stabilirent. Nam Regimen Monarchicum optimum & præstantissimum, ratione dictante, & Philosophorum omnium, consensu,caussantur. Sed est quidem Ecclesiæ politia Monarchia ab omni parte perfecta, ubi Christus Rex ejus est ; ejus leges, Scripturæ; administri & legati, Episcopi; qui non eum in finem designati sunt, ut uni legato assideant, sed ut ipsi singuli legati sint; Pastores gregis, 1. Petr. V. 2. Duces, Hebr. XIII. 17. & Episcopi, Actor. XX. 28. Si tamen Ecclesiæ politia à re- giis mundanarum Rerumpublicarum formis, de quibus Philosophi loquuntur, nonnihil dis- cedat, uti omnino discedit, mirum id Philoso- phis videri non debet, quia Christus ipse de- nuntiavit; Regnum suum non esse de hoc mundo, Joh. XVIII. 36. Apostoli certè Regnum ejus- modi meditati fuerant. Verùm disertè Chri- stus iis edixit, non ita futurum apud illos, uti apud Principes gentium, Matth. XX. 26. Quæ Christi verba cùm sibi obesse Pontifices vide- rent, & nihil aliud quàm tyrannidem quan- dam Ethnicam Apostolis interdici conjicerent, ne Monarchia Philosophorum testimoniis lau- data iis periret, pro Christi Monarchia visibi- lem Monarchiam excitarunt,& Regnum Chri- sti, quod ex hoc mundo non fuit,in Regnum mundanum, seu, uti Franciscus Torrianus de Eccl. & Ord. Ministr. Eccles. lib. I. 2. loquitur, Regnum Romanorum transmutarunt. Neque se Regni ejusmodi, cujusmodi Principes gentium possederunt,finibus continent,sed se ipsos Prin- cipes super omnes gentes & Regna terrarum, uti Johannes XXII. Extravag. Com. loquitur,con- stituerunt. Quæ grandior Monarchia est,quàm ut Philosophis placeat. Sed liceat cum Ter- tulliano de Præscr. adv. hæret. dicere: Quid A- cademiæ & Ecclesiæ? Christianis enim hoc officium incumbit, ut scrutentur & expendant,in rebus fi- dei,non quid ratio, sed quid religio; non quid Phi- losophi, sed quid Prophetæ & Apostoli ; non quid humanum cerebrum, sed quid Spiritus Dei loqua- tur.
units.tr: V. Nevertheless, they have devised not a few monarchical arguments by which to establish the rule of a visible Monarch of the Church. They allege that monarchical government is the best and most excellent, as dictated by reason and by the agreement of all philosophers. But the polity of the Church is indeed a monarchy in every respect perfect, where Christ is its King; its laws are Scripture; its administrators and legates are bishops, who were not appointed for this end, that they should sit beside one legate, but that each of them should himself be a legate: Pastores gregis (1 Pet. 5:2), Duces (Heb. 13:17), and Episcopi (Acts 20:28). If, however, the polity of the Church departs somewhat from the royal forms of earthly commonwealths, of which the philosophers speak, as it certainly does, this ought not to seem strange to the philosophers, because Christ himself declared it: that his kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). The apostles had certainly meditated a kingdom of this kind. But Christ plainly told them that it would not be non ita among them as among Principes gentium (Matt. 20:26). When the Pontiffs saw that these words of Christ stood in their way, and conjectured that nothing else was forbidden to the apostles than a certain heathen tyranny, lest the monarchy praised by the testimonies of the philosophers should perish for them, they set up a visible monarchy in place of the monarchy of Christ, and transformed the kingdom of Christ, which was not of this world, into a worldly kingdom, or, as Franciscus Torrianus de Eccl. & Ord. Ministr. Eccles. lib. I. 2. puts it, the kingdom of the Romans. Nor do they keep themselves within the limits of such a kingdom as the Principes gentium possessed, but they have made themselves princes over all nations and kingdoms of the earth, as John XXII says in the Extravag. Com. This is a greater monarchy than would please the philosophers. But let us say with Tertullian in de Praescr. adv. haeret.: What has the Academy to do with the Church? For Christians the duty lies in this, that in matters of faith they should examine and weigh not what reason, but what religion; not what the philosophers, but what the prophets and apostles; not what the human brain, but what the Spirit of God speaks.

units.la: VI. Neque saniores reliquæ Monarchi- corum rationes sunt. Prædixit equidem Chri- stus, fore ut sit unus grex, seu ovile,& unus Pa- stor, Joh. X. 16. Sed unus ille Pastor Christus, non visiblis Monarcha est, quod ex scopo to- tius orationis ejus liquet, ubi Christus ossi- cium & authoritatem suam adversus Pharisæo- rum calumnias tutatur,cap. IX. 16. 24. 29. Ego, inquit, sum ille Pastor bonus, & cognosco oves meas, &c. Et alias oves habeo, quæ non sunt ex hoc ovili, illas quoque oportet me adducere, & vocem meam audient, & fiet unus grex, & unus Pastor, ibid. X.14. Unus Pastor, quis præter illum, de quo verba antecedentia & consequentia loquuntur ? Biblia certè à Lovaniensibus casti- gata,& à Plantino Antverpiæ excusa,Pastorem illum unum Christum etiam interpretantur, collato Johanne cum Ezechiele cap. XXXVII. 22.24. ubi Deus promittit, se factypum (ex Is- raele & Juda) unum populum, & servum suum Davidem (Christum, Filium Davidis) Pasto- rem unicum omnibus iis futurum. In Divino ergo jure verbaChristi apudJohannem deChri- sto exponuntur : at in jure Papæ, se Papam iis depingi contendit. Sed non Papa profecto,ve- rùm Christus solus est ille Pastor,qui ex ovibus diversis, à se adductis,hoc est,verbo & Spiritu, ut vocem ejus audirent,vocatis,Judæis & gen- tibus unum ovile fecit. Neque porrò ratio à Pontifice V. T. petita Monarchicum Ecclesiæ regimen confirmat, quia non eadem politiæ Ecclesiæ Judaicæ & Christianæ ratio est. Alias sicut in V. T. Pontifex in rebus Domini & Ze- badias in negotiis Regis præsedit,2. Chron.XIX. 11. ita in N. etiam T. unus religioni,& unus civilibus negotiis omnibus præsidebit. Licèt enim religionis essentialia utrobique constent, forma tamen regiminis æquè atque plura ac- cessoria alia constare non debuerunt. Alia e- nim universi orbis,alia unius populi ratio est. Ille ab uno homine regi non potest ; hic po- test , perinde ut scapham unus homo regere, at non æquè navim onerariam unus gubernare potis est. Alia etiam ratio fuit populi Israeli- tici, in una terra habitantis, qui non tantùm Ecclesiam sed etiam Rempublicam constitue- bat, cujus cultus magnam partem carnalis & externus fuit ; alia populi Christiani, per to- tum terrarum orbem dispersi, nullámque pro- prie Rempublicam , sed corpus spirituale & mysticum constituentis, est. Accedit, quòd Pontifex nec typus fuit Papæ, sed Christi ; & quidem quoad munus ejus non regium , sed sacerdotale ; nec Monarcha fuit,utpote Conci- lio magno subjectus. Mitto similitudines re- giminis Angelici, corporis humani, exercitus, domus , quia regimen Ecclesiæ non ex simili- bus, sed ex Divina institutione æstimari debet. Neque etiam de Angelorum Hierarchia certi quid constat: & satis est, quòd Ecclesia unum Regem & unum caput Christum habet ; sicut corpus unum caput, exercitus unum Impera- torem,& familia unum patremfamilias habet: Sicut verò unus Imperator, plures exercitui duces : & unus paterfamilias familiæ plures œconomos præficere potest : ita Christus Ec- clesiæ non unum Pro-Regem & Dominum, sed varios ministros & œconomos præficere potuit, voluit. Præterea non quia Christus sum in terra agitavit, visibile Ecclesiæ caput fuit , necesse est semper in terra visibile Ec- clesiæ caput existere , tum quia caput licèt visibile Ecclesiæ , in terra degens fuerit , ta- men non conspicuum Majestate & gloria Mo- narcham,sed contemptum præ vilitate servum se gessit : tum quia visibiliter absens, ubique tamen Majestate sua præsens, Ecclesiæ suæ ubi- que terrarum diffusæ præest , nec in Regno suo Regem,vel Proregem alium patitur. Alia enim Regis terrestris, qui Regni sui partibus omnibus nisi per alios principalium curarum parti-
units.tr: VI. Nor are the remaining monarchical arguments any sounder. Christ indeed foretold that there would be one flock, or fold, and one Shepherd (John 10:16). But that one Shepherd is Christ, not a visible Monarch; this is clear from the aim of his whole discourse, where Christ defends his office and authority against the calumnies of the Pharisees (ch. 9:16, 24, 29). I, he says, am that good Shepherd, and I know my sheep, etc. And I have other sheep which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one Shepherd (ibid., 10:14). One Shepherd: who is this besides him of whom the preceding and following words speak? The Bible corrected by the Louvain theologians and printed at Antwerp by Plantin certainly also interprets that one Shepherd as Christ, comparing John with Ezekiel 37:22, 24, where God promises that he would make them one people (out of Israel and Judah) and his servant David (Christ, the Son of David) the sole Shepherd for all those who would be. Thus in the divine law the words of Christ in John are explained of Christ; but in the law of the Pope he contends that he is depicted there. But surely it is not the Pope, but Christ alone, who is that Shepherd, who from the different sheep brought to him, that is, those called by the word and the Spirit so that they would hear his voice, made one fold of Jews and Gentiles. Nor does the argument drawn by the Pontiff from the Old Testament confirm the monarchical government of the Church, because the polity of the Jewish Church and of the Christian Church is not the same. Otherwise, just as in the Old Testament the High Priest presided over the affairs of the Lord, and Zebadiah over the affairs of the king (2 Chron. 19:11), so in the New Testament too one man would preside over all religious and all civil affairs. For although the essentials of religion are the same in both, the form of government and many other accessories ought not to be the same. For the rule of the whole world is one thing, that of a single people another. The one cannot be ruled by one man; the other can, just as one man can steer a small boat, but cannot in the same way manage a freighter. Also, the case of the people of Israel was different, living in one land, who constituted not only a Church but also a commonwealth, whose worship was for the most part carnal and external; the case of the Christian people, scattered throughout the whole world, is different, and constitutes no commonwealth properly so called, but a spiritual and mystical body. Besides, the High Priest was not a type of the Pope but of Christ, and that in respect of his office not as king but as priest; nor was he a monarch, since he was subject to the great Council. I pass over the comparisons with the government of the angels, the human body, an army, or a household, because the government of the Church must be judged not from likenesses but from divine institution. Nor is anything certain known about the hierarchy of the angels; and it is enough that the Church has one King and one head, Christ; just as the body has one head, an army one commander, and a household one father of the family. But just as one Emperor has several commanders of his army, and one father of the family can set several stewards over his household, so Christ could, and did, set over the Church not one vice-king and lord, but various ministers and stewards. Furthermore, because Christ was on earth in the flesh, he was not the visible head of the Church; nor is it necessary that a visible head of the Church always exist on earth: first, because although Christ, the visible head of the Church, lived on earth, he did not conduct himself as a monarch conspicuous in majesty and glory, but as a servant despised for his lowliness; second, because although he is absent in a visible way, he is yet present everywhere in his majesty, presides over his Church spread throughout all the lands of the earth, and does not allow a king or another vice-king in his kingdom. For an earthly king, who cannot preside over all parts of his realm unless through others who share his principal cares and can also discharge those cares themselves, is one thing; but Christ, who though absent in body is most present by his word, grace, Spirit and their operations, and has many sharers in his principal cares, is another.

units.la: Rationes pro regimine Ecclesiæ Monarchico ex optima forma regiminis.
units.tr: Arguments for a monarchical government of the Church drawn from the best form of government.

units.la: Nec non aliunde petita expenduntur. participes, qui & ipsi curas illas obire possunt, præesse non potest : alia Christi, qui corpore absens, verbo, gratia & Spiritu & ejus operationibus præsentissimus est, & curarum suarum principalium consortes multos patitur. Neque etiam absentia illa magis idoneam vicario capiti causam præbet, quàm olim Pontificis typici, in typico sacrario agentis ; aut Mosis in monte cum Domino loquentis mora ejusmodi subrogationem ratam Deóque gratam effecisset. Potest etiam Ecclesia universali visibili Monarcha destituta licet propagari ; sicut & Apostoli plures Ecclesiam longè latéque propagarunt ; & quivis Christianus & minister, quoties occasio datur, Evangelium inter infideles prædicare potest. Cui rei extra ordinem sufficit mislio Divina, quæ ex charismatibus & charitate promovendæ salutis Ecclesiæ cognosci potest. Denique sine opera visibilis Monarchæ unitas fidei servari potest. Nam, qui veritatis author est, Spiritus S. idem unitatis fidei ad salutem necessariæ author est , mediante præconio verbi, quod à pluribus sine συνοδικῶς visibilis Monarchæ obiri potest. Omnium verò sententiarum discrepantia tolli, ad fidei unitatem non requiritur. Neque respectus hactenus talis est, qui omnia schismata, hæreses & errores ex mundo, ac ne ex Ecclesia quidem propria eliminare potis esset. Oportet enim hæreses esse, ut probi manifesti fiant, 1. Corinth. XI. 9.
units.tr: Other arguments drawn from elsewhere are also weighed. Nor does that absence provide a more suitable cause for a vicarious head than that of the typical priest, who acted in the typical sanctuary, or the delay of Moses, who spoke with the Lord on the mountain, would have made such a substitution valid and acceptable to God. Nor is it necessary that the Church, deprived of a universal visible Monarch, cannot be propagated; just as the apostles propagated the Church far and wide, and any Christian or minister, whenever the opportunity is given, can preach the Gospel among unbelievers. For this extraordinary purpose the divine sending suffices, which can be recognised from the gifts and the love for promoting the salvation of the Church. Finally, the unity of faith can be preserved without the work of a visible Monarch. For the Holy Spirit, who is the author of truth, is also the author of the unity of faith necessary for salvation, through the proclamation of the word, which can be carried out by many together synodically [συνοδικῶς] without a visible Monarch. But the removal of all disagreement of opinions is not required for the unity of faith. Nor is it the case that such a reckoning has so far been able to eliminate all schisms, heresies and errors from the world, or even from the Church itself. For there must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest (1 Cor. 11:19).

units.la: VII. Monarchiam suam Hierarchici in totum mundum extendunt ; asserentes cum Bonifacio VIII. pleno ore, de necessitate salutis omni creaturæ esse,ut Papæ, ceu Monarchæ spiritualis Regno subsit. Hic in subditos hos summum sibi imperium & dominium, specie spirituale & Ecclesiasticum, revera autem terrenum merè & temporale vendicat. Sedet enim Babylon illa magna super aquis, seu gentibus multis, ceu domina & rectrix, Apoc. XVII. 1. ϛ. Super Bestia coccinea, septicipite, septimontia & ἑπτάλοφῳ, ibid. v. 3. Et civitas illa magna est, quæ Regnum habet in Reges terræ, ibid. v. 18. Ubi civitatis, seu imperii illius magni nota propria & formalis statuitur imperare Regibus terræ. Cúmque Regnum illud Civitatis Magnæ ita declaretur, ut ei subjiciantur Reges seu Principes Politici ; adeóque illud imperio Politico contradistinguatur, Ecclesiasticum prætextu & externo fuco, sed reapse merè temporale esse debuisse consequitur. Ideo Babylonis fronti nomen inscriptum est, Μυστήριον Mysterium, Apoc. XVII. ϛ. quia per mysterium, seu spiritualium prætextu dominari debuit. Neque aliò collineat Hierarchicorum eorundem dogma, potestatem temporalem Ecclesiasticæ essentialiter subjicientium & subordinantium. Bonifacius certè VIII. Extrav. Una sancta, definit : Spiritualem & materialem gladium esse in potestate Ecclesiæ ; hunc pro Ecclesia, illum ab Ecclesia exercendum : illum Sacerdotis, hunc manu Regum & militum, sed ad nutum & potentiam Sacerdotis. Oportet autem, inquit, gladium esse sub gladio, & temporalem authoritatem spirituali potestati subjici. Potestatem autem subordinantis includere potestatem subordinati, notorium est. Et Romani Pontifices, in propria causa favorabiles sibi judices, similitudine solis & Lunæ subordinationem illam explicant. Sicut Luna, sic Innocentius III. lib. I. Epist. 401. loquitur, lumen suum à Sole sortitur, quo revera minor est illo, quantitate simul & qualitate, situ pariter & effectu : sic Regalis potestas ab auctoritate Pontificali suæ sortitur dignitatis splendorem, cujus conspectu quanto magis inhaeret, tanto minori lumine decoratur ; & quò plus ejus elongatur aspectu, eò plus proficit in splendore. Bellarminus rem spiritus & carnis similitudine adumbrans, Ecclesiasticam potestatem spiritus, temporalem carnis rationem habere pertendit, quasi sicut spiritus vitam corpori & cuilibet ejus parti impartitur : ita spiritualis potestas civili functionem suam præscriberet. Cùm tamen potestas spiritualis dominans solius Christi, temporalis verò Regum & Principum à solo Deo immediatè dependentium sit ; Papa utramque perrumpere aulus, & supremam in spiritualibus potestatem titulo Episcopi universalis, Phoca indulgente, rapuit, cujus tituli Universalis seu Oecumenici nomine quam immensum tyrannidis in Ecclesiam Dei chaos occultetur, Florentini Concilii de potestate summa Papæ in spiritualibus definitio ostendit : Et prætextu ejusdem potestatis in spiritualibus supremæ, supremam etiam in temporalibus, nefariè rapuit ; imò illam propter hanc sibi vendicavit. Unde Innocentius III. in publico sermone, quem de coronatione Papali tertium habuit, in hæc verba prorupit : Ecclesia sponsa non nupsit vacua, sed dotem mihi tribuit absque pretio pretiosam, spiritualem plenitudinem & latitudinem imperialem, magnitudinem & multitudinem utrumque. In signum spiritualium contulit mihi mitram ; in signum temporalium dedit mihi coronam ; Mitram pro sacerdotio, coronam pro Regno ; illius me constituens in vicarium, qui habet in vestimento & femore suo scriptum : Rex Regum & Dominus dominantium. Quadruplex temporalis illa Papæ potestas statuitur, puta in patrimonium Petri, seu Statum Ecclesiasticum ; in Regna homagio Ecclesiæ obstricta, & à Pontifice prætensa ; cujusmodi sunt, Neapolitanum, Siciliæ, Arragoniæ, Sardiniæ, Hierosolymæ, Angliæ, Hiberniæ & Hungariæ : in Clerum universum : denique in omnes reliquos Imperatores, Reges, Principes & populos. Quam postremam potestatem licèt Theologi, invidiam nominis declinaturi, indirectam, ratione potestatis spiritualis temporali dominantis, statuant ; tamen & Canonistæ directam, & Theologi verbis indirectam, re directam tuentur, quia Papæ potestatem supremam legislatoriam & judicialem tribuunt, & personas Regum Principumque Papæ subjiciunt judicio : & Pontifices ipsi in temporalibus etiam summam & directam faciunt. Nam & gnathones cathedram ejus in tantum culmen extollentes æquo animo admittunt ; & indirectam potestatem sibi tribuentibus indignantur ; & Canonistas, aliósque gnathones nullis hactenus censuris notárunt ; & posthabitis distinctionibus rem ipsam definiunt, asserentes, suum esse utriusque gladium ; & denique, quod argumentum omni exceptione majus est, absolutam & directam in temporalibus potestatem exercent. Quod tum ex historia Bonifacii VIII. tum ex actibus variis exercitæ erga Reges varios rios potestatis civilis; tum ex imperio, quo hactenus erga Imperatores, Reges & Principes constituendos, coronandos, juramento iis impositio sibi subjiciendos, imò etiam, per religionis aliásque causas abdicandos, & privatorum etiam quorumvis libidini devovendos, usi sunt, alibi fusiùs & irrefragabiliter ostendimus. Omni quinetiam exceptione major Innocentii IV. vox est, Epistola ad Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum scripta diserté professi, Petro, & in ejus persona Papæ, non solùm universam Ecclesiam, sed totum etiam seculum gubernandum commissum esse; argumento etiam allato, quòd Petrus super aquas ambulaverit, & aquæ populos multos significent, quod ipsi ex Apoc. XVII. 1. 15. ubi Babylon super aquis multis sedere, & aquæ populos, gentes & linguas significare dicuntur, inprimis constare poterat.
units.tr: VII. The Hierarchs extend their monarchy over the whole world, asserting with full voice, with Boniface VIII, that it is necessary for the salvation of every creature to be subject to the Pope, as to the spiritual Monarch. Over these subjects he claims for himself supreme command and dominion, which is spiritual and ecclesiastical in appearance but in reality purely earthly and temporal. For that great Babylon sits upon waters, that is, upon many peoples, as mistress and ruler (Rev. 17:1, ϛ). She sits upon the scarlet beast, seven-headed, [seven-hilled, ἑπτάλοφῳ], ibid. v. 3. And she is that great city which has dominion over the kings of the earth, ibid. v. 18. There the proper and formal mark of that great city or empire is set down as ruling over the kings of the earth. Since that kingdom of the Great City is so described that kings or political princes are subject to it, and so it is set over against political rule, it follows that what is ecclesiastical in pretence and outward show ought in fact to be purely temporal. For this reason the name Mystery [Μυστήριον] is inscribed on Babylon's forehead (Rev. 17:5), because she was to rule under the pretext of a mystery, that is, of spiritual things. Nor does the doctrine of these same Hierarchs aim at anything else, namely that they subject and subordinate temporal power to the ecclesiastical in its very essence. Boniface VIII certainly, in the Extravagant Unam sanctam, defines that the spiritual and the material sword are both in the power of the Church: the one to be wielded for the Church, the other by the Church; the one by the hand of priests, the other by the hand of kings and soldiers, but at the nod and permission of the priest. For, he says, the sword must be under the sword, and temporal authority must be subject to spiritual power. That to have power to subordinate includes power over the subordinate is notorious. And the Roman Pontiffs, being judges favourable to themselves in their own cause, explain that subordination by the likeness of the sun and moon. As the moon, so Innocent III speaks in Book I, Letter 401, receives its light from the sun, by which it is truly less than the sun in quantity and quality, in position and in effect alike: so royal power receives the splendour of its dignity from the Pontifical authority, and the more it clings to its gaze, the less it is adorned with light; and the more it is removed from its sight, the more it gains in brilliance. Bellarmine, shadowing the matter by the likeness of spirit and flesh, contends that ecclesiastical power has the character of spirit and temporal power that of flesh, as if, just as the spirit imparts life to the body and to each of its parts, so spiritual power should prescribe its function to civil power. Yet since spiritual power that rules belongs to Christ alone, and temporal power to kings and princes who depend immediately on God alone, the Pope has dared to break into both, and by the indulgence of Phocas he has seized supreme power in spiritual matters under the title of Universal Bishop. What immense chaos of tyranny against the Church of God is hidden under the name of this title, Universal or Ecumenical, the definition of the Council of Florence on the supreme power of the Pope in spiritual matters shows. And under the pretext of that supreme power in spiritual matters he has also wickedly seized supreme power in temporal matters; indeed he has claimed the former for the sake of the latter. Hence Innocent III, in the public sermon which he gave third on the Papal coronation, burst out in these words: The Church, the bride, did not marry empty-handed, but gave me a dowry without price, precious, spiritual fullness and imperial breadth, greatness and multitude in each. As a sign of spiritual things she gave me a mitre; as a sign of temporal things she gave me a crown: the mitre for the priesthood, the crown for the kingdom; making me vicar of him who has written on his vestment and thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords.
