This fourfold temporal power of the Pope is set out: namely over the patrimony of Peter, or the Ecclesiastical State; over kingdoms bound by homage to the Church and claimed by the Pontiff, such as the kingdoms of Naples, Sicily, Aragon, Sardinia, Jerusalem, England, Ireland and Hungary; over the whole clergy; and finally over all other emperors, kings, princes and peoples. Although the Theologians, to avoid the odium of the name, set down this last power as indirect, by reason of spiritual power ruling over the temporal, yet the Canonists maintain it as direct, and the Theologians, while saying "indirect" in words, maintain it as direct in reality, because they grant the Pope supreme legislative and judicial power and subject the persons of kings and princes to the Pope's judgment. And the Pontiffs themselves also claim supreme and direct power in temporal matters. For flatterers raise his chair to such a height and gladly admit this, and they are indignant at those who attribute to him only indirect power; and hitherto they have marked the Canonists and other flatterers with no censure; and, setting aside distinctions, they define the matter itself, asserting that the sword of both is his; and finally, which is an argument beyond all exception, they exercise absolute and direct power in temporal matters. We have shown this more fully and irrefutably elsewhere: from the history of Boniface VIII, from the various acts of power exercised against various kings and of civil authority, and from the rule by which they have hitherto appointed and crowned emperors, kings and princes, bound them by oath to submit to themselves, and even, for reasons of religion and others, deposed them and devoted them to the lust of any private persons whatsoever. Equally beyond all exception is the voice of Innocent IV, who in his letter to the Patriarch of Constantinople openly professed that not only the whole Church but the whole world has been committed to Peter, and in his person to the Pope, to govern; and he adduced the argument that Peter walked upon the waters, and that waters signify many peoples, which could be grasped especially from Rev. 17:1, 15, where Babylon is said to sit upon many waters, and the waters are said to signify peoples, nations and tongues.

units.la: VIII. Sed Papæ potestas in immensum sic amplificata regimen ejus non Christianum, sed Antichristianum manifestè prodit. Nam Christo, Regi Regum, & Domino dominantium, cui omnis potestas in Cœlo & in terra soli data est, subesse, de necessitate salutis omnium creaturarum rationalium terræ est. Solus enim is Rex Ecclesiæ, & Salvator sui corporis est, Ephes. V. 23. Parem verò potestatem quisquis sibi vendicat, is Majestatis Christi violatæ reus est. Provido certè Numine factum est, quòd in Johanne Jejunatore Constantinopolitano Patriarcha, titulum Universalis Episcopi rapturiente, ipse quoque Bonifacius III. & consequentes eum Pontifices omnes, eodem titulo superbientes, & cum titulo potestatem in spiritualibus supremam sibi vendicantes, à Pontifice Gregorio I. impietatis Antichristianæ crimine arcessiti sunt, idque argumentis ponderosissimis, cujusmodi sunt, quòd si unus Episcopus vel Patriarcha universalis dicatur, cæteris Episcoporum & Patriarcharum nomen derogandum sit: quòd pax & viscera universalis Ecclesiæ superbo hoc nomine turbentur; & libertati Christianæ, à qua est, ut quivis Christianus sit libertus Domini, humanæ cathedræ vel authoritati in spiritualibus nulli mancipatus: quòd S. Paulus 1. Cor. I. 12. membra Domini corporis certis extra Christum quasi capitibus, & particulariter ipsis Apostolis subjici evitaverit: quòd Christus, unum Ecclesiæ caput deseratur, si universalis Episcopus agnoscatur: quòd hæc imitatio sit Diaboli, qui omnibus præesse, nemini subesse voluerit; adeò que titulus ipse Luciferianus sit: quòd elatio illa character Antichristi sit: quòd titulus ille meram superbiam redoleat, & Christi Sanctorúmque humilitati repugnet: quòd Christus etiam Rabbi appellationem prohibuerit: quòd ex nefando hoc elationis vocabulo Ecclesia scindatur & scandalizetur: quòd nec Episcopi Romani antehac, nec Sanctorum quisquam hactenus eo vocabulo usus fuerit. Quid Gregorium M. dicturum putemus, si posteros vidisset Papæ tribuentes πληρη εξουσιαν omnem potestatem, seu plenitudinem potestatis, juxta quam nulli omnino potestati subsit etiam tum, cùm officio suo minimè defungitur; & eidem sic subjecti sint omnes, ut sine ea subjectione nulla creatura salvari possit, & contra ejus ψηφισματα & decreta nemo Mortalium hiscere audeat?
units.tr: VIII. But the Pope's power, so immensely enlarged, plainly shows his rule to be not Christian but Antichristian. For it is of necessity for the salvation of all rational creatures on earth to be subject to Christ, the King of kings and Lord of lords, to whom alone all power in heaven and on earth has been given. For he alone is the King of the Church and Saviour of his body (Eph. 5:23). Whoever claims equal power for himself is guilty of violating the majesty of Christ. Certainly by the providence of God it came about that when John the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople, snatched the title of Universal Bishop, Boniface III himself and all the Popes after him, priding themselves on the same title and claiming with it supreme power in spiritual matters, were charged by Pope Gregory I with the crime of Antichristian impiety; and this on very weighty arguments, such as these: if one bishop or patriarch is called universal, the name of bishop and patriarch must be taken away from the rest; the peace and bowels of the universal Church are disturbed by this proud name; the Christian liberty from which every Christian is a freedman of the Lord, and is subject to no human chair or authority in spiritual matters, is violated; St Paul (1 Cor. 1:12) avoided that the members of the Lord's body should be subject to certain heads outside Christ, and particularly to the Apostles themselves; Christ, the one head of the Church, is abandoned if a universal bishop is acknowledged; this would be an imitation of the Devil, who wished to be over all and subject to none, so that the title itself is Luciferian; that exaltation is the mark of Antichrist; that title smacks of mere pride and is repugnant to the humility of Christ and the saints; Christ also forbade the appellation Rabbi; the Church is torn and scandalised by this wicked word of exaltation; and neither the Roman bishops before this nor any of the saints until now have used that term. What do we suppose Gregory the Great would have said if he had seen his successors attributing to the Pope πληρη εξουσιαν [fullness of power], that is, all power, or plenitude of power, by which he is subject to no power whatever even when he does not discharge his office, and by which all are so subject to him that no creature can be saved without that subjection, and no mortal dare to murmur against his ψηφισματα [decrees] and decisions?

units.la: IX. Potestas porrò Ecclesiastica qualiscunque & Politica sic comparatæ sunt, neutra ut alteri essentialiter subjiciatur, dominetur vel serviat. Distincta quidem sunt Potestas, & subjectum potestatem habens, hactenus, quòd subjectum habens potestatem Politicam Ecclesiæ subjici possit, & vicissim: Potestates verò ipsæ sic discretæ sunt, ut neutra alteri subjici, neutra alterius in fines involare possit. Sicut in rebus ad salutem animæ pertinentibus omnes homines, ne exceptis quidem Regibus, eorum authoritati subsunt, quibus Ecclesia commissa est: ita in rebus seculi omnes animæ, ne exceptis quidem ullis Ecclesiæ Pastoribus, quocunque nomine vel ordine censeantur. Mutua igitur subjectio est personarum potestatem habentium: ipsæ verò Potestates sibi essentialiter non subjiciuntur, quia nec Ecclesiastica in Politica, neque Politica in Ecclesiastica continetur, & neutra ab altera derivatur, quod in omni subordinatione essentiali obtinet. Enimverò si quam Papa potestatem temporalem habet, illam vel jure humano vel Divino habet. At nullam habet jure humano, quia nec per electionem, nec per successionem, nec per vim. Non per electionem, seu consensum eorum, quibus imperat, quia nulli populi, ac multò minùs populorum rectores, de quorum dignitate præcipuè agitur, quicquam ejusmodi decreto suo firmârunt: contrà potiùs omnibus seculis, post inchoatam cumprimis hanc controversiam adversus injustam vim Papæ protestati sunt, uti ex historia Imperatorum Germaniæ, & bellis eam ob rem gestis constat. Non per successionem, uti Bosius contendit, quia nunquam Papa se ullius Imperatoris vel Senatus, sed tantùm Petri successorem dixit. Accedit, quòd Canonistæ dicunt, Papam non per accidens, sed per se, & quatenus Papa est, hoc jus habere. Atqui si hoc jus tantùm ex quo defecerunt Imperatores, vel etiam Senatus, habuit, non illud per se, quatenus Papa, habet, quia aliàs illud commune omnibus Papis esset, haberet; sed per accidens habet. Theologi verò fatentur, jurisdictionem temporalem non directè, sed indirectè ad Papam pertinere. At si pertineret ex successionis jure, directè, non indirectè, ad eum pertineret, quia Imperatores & Senatus directè & per se Rempublicam administrârunt. Non per vim, quia id ne ipsi quidem adversarii affirmare audent: & si per vim potestatem hanc acquisivisset, non habuisset hanc potestatem ab initio; sicut Roma primis suis annis, neque jure, neque facto populis proximis imperare poterat. Utrique autem & Canonistæ & Theologi jus hoc, ceu per se Papæ & Ecclesiæ competens, ab ipsis Ecclesiæ initiis repetunt. Vis quoque externa non tantùm alienior est ab humana natura, sed etiam directè oppositá naturæ Ecclesiæ, quæ alia arma nulla, quàm spiritualia agnoscit. Ac licèt Episcopi Romani tandem propter hanc causam arma adversus Imperatores Occidentis moverint, tamen & ante ipsa arma mota hoc quicquid est juris, prætenderunt, neque adeò arma in omnes populos Christianos moverunt; quinetiam nonnulli populi Christiani armis adversus eam prævaluerunt, atque interdum ipsi etiam Imperatores.
units.tr: IX. Moreover, ecclesiastical and civil power, of whatever kind, are so constituted that neither is essentially subject to the other, nor does either rule over or serve the other. Persons who hold power are indeed distinct from the power itself, in that a person holding civil power can be subject to the Church, and conversely. But the powers themselves are so distinct that neither is subject to the other, and neither can encroach upon the other's domain. Just as in matters pertaining to the salvation of the soul all men, not even kings excepted, are subject to the authority of those to whom the Church has been entrusted, so in matters of this world all souls, not even any ministers of the Church whatever name or rank they bear, are subject to the civil authority. Subjection is therefore mutual between the persons who hold power, but the powers themselves are not essentially subject to one another, because neither ecclesiastical power is contained in civil power nor civil power in ecclesiastical power, and neither is derived from the other, which is true of every essential subordination. Indeed, if the Pope has any temporal power, he has it either by human right or by divine right. He does not have it by human right, since he has it neither by election, nor by succession, nor by force. Not by election, that is, by the consent of those over whom he rules, since no peoples, and still less the rulers of peoples, whose dignity is chiefly at issue, have ever confirmed any such decree of his. On the contrary, in every age, especially since this controversy began, they have protested against the unjust violence of the Pope, as is clear from the history of the Emperors of Germany and the wars waged on that account. Not by succession, as Bosius contends, since the Pope has never called himself the successor of any Emperor or Senate, but only the successor of Peter. Moreover, the Canonists say that the Pope has this right not by accident but per se, and insofar as he is Pope. Yet if he had this right only since the Emperors, or even the Senate, ceased to exercise it, he would not have it per se, insofar as he is Pope, for otherwise it would belong in common to all Popes; he would have it by accident. The theologians, however, admit that temporal jurisdiction pertains to the Pope not directly but indirectly. But if it pertained to him by right of succession, it would pertain to him directly, not indirectly, because the Emperors and the Senate administered the commonwealth directly and per se. Not by force, since not even his opponents themselves dare to assert this; and if he had acquired this power by force, he would not have had it from the beginning, just as Rome in its early years could rule neighbouring peoples neither by right nor in fact. Both the Canonists and the theologians trace this right back to the very beginnings of the Church, as belonging to the Pope and the Church per se. Moreover, external force is not only more alien to human nature, but is directly opposed to the nature of the Church, which acknowledges no weapons other than spiritual ones. And although the Roman bishops at last took up arms against the Emperors of the West on this account, nevertheless even before taking up arms they put forward whatever right this is, nor did they take up arms against all Christian peoples; indeed some Christian peoples prevailed against them by arms, and sometimes even Emperors did.

units.la: X. Mul-
units.tr: X. Much-

units.la: Papa non est universalis Ecclesiæ Episcopus.
units.tr: The Pope is not the bishop of the universal Church.

units.la: Potestas Politica Ecclesiastica essentialiter non subordinatur.
units.tr: Civil power is not essentially subordinated to ecclesiastical power.

units.la: X. Multò verò minùs jure Divino hanc potestatem Papa vel Ecclesia possidet. Nam ejus rei, quæ maximi momenti est, tabulæ nullæ proferri possunt. Et ex jure Divino nullam Ecclesia potestatem habere potest, nisi quam Christus in terra, ut Mediator & Caput Ecclesiæ habuit. Ecclesia enim Regnum Christi est; & Christus ad Apostolos dixit: Sicut Pater misit me; ita ego mitto vos, Joh. XX. 21. Si igitur Apostoli missi sunt ad potestatem secularem habendam, oportet prior Christus ad eam missus fuerit. Atqui Christus ad eam obtinendam non est missus, tum quia non præpositus, sed subditus fuit temporali potestati, judicatus quippe à Pilato, cujus potestatem legitimam fuisse, ipsemet Christus agnovit, dicens: Non haberes potestatem adversus me, nisi tibi data esset superne, Joh. XIX. 11. tum quia litigantes temporales dijudicare noluit, cùm rogatus à quodam: Magister, dic fratri meo, ut partiatur hæreditatem, respondit: Heus tu, quis me vobis judicem aut partitorem præfecit? Luc. XII. 13. 14. tum quia ne quidem habuit, unde suis necessitatibus provideret, quod ipsemet testatus est, dicens: Vulpes lustra habent, & volucres cœli nidos. Filius verò hominis non habet, ubi caput reclinet, Matth. VIII. 20. Regnum enim suum non esse de hoc mundo, ipsemet Johann. XVIII. 36. protestatus est, innuens, non tantùm Regnum ad se non pervenisse humana electione, vel successione; uti Hierarchici nonnulli interpretantur; sed etiam, Regni sui naturam aliam prorsus esse, quàm quæ reliquorum Regnorum est. Subjicit enim: Si Regnum meum ex hoc mundo esset, ministri mei certarent, ne traderer Judæis. Nunc autem Regnum meum non est hinc, ibid. Quod argumentum non ab origine, sed à natura Regnorum hujus mundi manifestè petitum est. Voluit enim obviam ire calumniæ, vel certè suspicioni Pilati, qui dignitatem Cæsaris in Judæa sartam tectam conservare debuit; cui authoritati non poterat bene convenire cum authoritate ullius alterius Regni temporalis. Quæ suspicio refutari non potuisset, si non aliud negasset Christus, quàm quòd non sit factus Rex humana electione vel successione. Necesse ergo fuit, ut negaretur factus Rex eadem Regis definitione, qua Cæsar Rex definitus est. Denique Apostolus: Omnis, inquit, anima potestatibus supereminentibus subjecta est, Rom. XIII. 1. Nam ἐξουσίαι Potestates temporalem potestatem significare, certum est, quia mox Paulus ei tribuit gestare gladium, & eidem tributa persolvi, vers. 4. 6. quorum neutrum ad Ecclesiasticam potestatem pertinet.
units.tr: X. Much less, by divine right, does the Pope or the Church possess this power. For no records of this matter, which is of the greatest importance, can be produced. And by divine right the Church can have no power except that which Christ, as Mediator and Head of the Church, had on earth. For the Church is the kingdom of Christ, and Christ said to the Apostles: As the Father has sent me, so I send you, John 20:21. If therefore the Apostles were sent to hold secular power, Christ must first have been sent to it. But Christ was not sent to obtain it, both because he was not set over the temporal power but subject to it, having been judged by Pilate, whose power Christ himself acknowledged as lawful, saying: You would have no power against me, unless it had been given you from above, John 19:11; and because when a certain man asked him to judge a temporal dispute, saying: Master, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me, he refused, answering: Man, who made me a judge or divider over you? Luke 12:13–14; and also because he did not even have anything from which to provide for his own needs, as he himself testified: Foxes have holes and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head, Matt. 8:20. Christ himself also declared in John 18:36 that his kingdom is not of this world, implying not only that his kingdom had not come to him by human election or succession, as some Hierarchists interpret it, but also that the nature of his kingdom is altogether different from that of other kingdoms. For he adds: If my kingdom were of this world, my ministers would fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here, ibid. This argument is drawn clearly not from the origin but from the nature of the kingdoms of this world. For he wished to forestall the calumny, or at least the suspicion, of Pilate, who had to keep the dignity of Caesar in Judea intact, and whose authority could not well coexist with the authority of any other temporal kingdom. That suspicion could not have been refuted if Christ had denied only that he had become king by human election or succession. It was therefore necessary that he deny having become king by the same definition of king by which Caesar was defined as king. Finally, the Apostle says: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, Rom. 13:1. For that the exousiai [ἐξουσίαι] "powers" signify temporal power is certain, because Paul soon attributes to them the bearing of the sword and the paying of tributes to them, vv. 4, 6, neither of which pertains to ecclesiastical power.

units.la: XI. Frivola Hierarchicorum pro potestate temporali Monarchæ sui argumenta sunt. Non enim qui Regum etiam & Principum spirituali modo Pastor est, is temporalem in eos potestatem habet; sicut nec qui Ecclesiam pascit temporali modo, is spiritualem potestatem obtinet. Christus & Apostoli Ecclesiam spiritualiter paverunt, vel exercuerunt. Si ad pascendum Ecclesiam spiritualiter necessaria potestas temporalis esset, tum minimè omnium floruisset Ecclesia, cùm oppositam sibi potestatem temporalem habuit, velut in persecutionibus pluribus, quas passa est, in quibus tamen mediis veris suis virtutibus tum maximè floruit, tantò marcescens magis, quanto à persecutionibus liberior fuit. Et fuit quidem Christus ex tribu Judæ, quam penes jus Regni fuit; sed non ideo, qua Mediator, Rex temporalis fuit, quia non orti stirpe Regia Reges non sunt; sed ii demum, quorum stirps est in plena possessione Regni. At non ejusmodi stirps Christi tempore; quo sceptrum à tribu Juda ablatum est, fuit. Imò ne nosci quidem Christus debuit, quandiu sceptrum in tribu Juda fuit, Genes. XLIX. 10. At nec tribus Juda potestatem in omnia regna temporalia habuit, qualem tamen Papa sibi vendicat. Christus quoque ceu Filius Regni protestatus est, se liberum esse à solvendo tributo, Matth. XVII. 25. 26. Sed quævis immunitas & libertas Regia potestas est: & solvit Christus tributum, ostendens, se non esse Regem temporalem. Sed hoc Christus voluit, nec se, qui Filius Dei est, obligari ad didrachma solvendum, tanquam ἀντὶ animæ suæ; nec suos discipulos, qui libertatem ab ipso hæreditant, & non argento redimuntur, Esaj. LII. 3. sed pretioso ipsius sanguine, 1. Pet. I. 18. 19. & facti sunt filii Dei vivi, ampliùs ad servitutem figuræ teneri. Intravit Christus Hierosolymam Regio apparatu, cùm ei Apostoli & populus vestimenta sua straverunt, Matth. XXI. 7. 8. &c. Sed honor ille ei delatus est, non ut Regi seculari, cùm plus quàm plebejæ humilitatis fuerit, quòd alieno & commodatitio jumento usus est, & pauperum discipulorum vestimentis, non aureis & propriis insedit, stipatus inermibus comitibus, qui pro hastis & gladiis arborum ramusculos manibus gestarunt, declarans, longè aliam Regni sui, aliam Regnorum mundi rationem esse. Delatus ergo est ut Regi spirituali & cœlesti, Regi Sionis, qualem se jam sufficientibus signis comprobavit, & ampliùs patiendo comprobaturus erat. Quòd verò potestatem spiritualem, ceu superiorem, civili seu inferiori, imperare contendunt, merus vocum ambiguarum lusus est. Nam superiora vel inferiora dicuntur aliàs dignitate; aliàs subjectione. Dignitate, cùm quid præstantius est, quomodo literati mercatoribus illiteratis præferuntur: Subjectione, cùm eodem in ordine alia aliis subjiciuntur; quomodo pater filio, Magistratus subdito superior est. Ecclesiastica porrò potestas civili superior est dignitate, quia finis ei propositus absolutè summus hominis finis est; adeòque cuivis potestati, etiam Christiano Magistratui præferenda hactenus est. Sed non ideo superior est subjectione, sic ut temporalem potestatem sibi subjiciendo, eidem imperet. Non enim quæ dignitate præcellunt, ideo inferioribus imperant. Nam & Medici dignitas supra architecti dignitatem est, neque tamen Medicus architecto imperat. Aliàs quicunque in dignitate quacunque Ecclesiastica est, quibuscunque in authoritate Politica positis imperaret, quod oppidò absurdum est. Frustra enim illi temporalem potestatem spirituali subordinatam asserunt. Nam quæ subordinata sunt, eorum unum sine altero non consistit. Atqui potentissimæ Respublicæ fuerunt inter gentes seorsim, absque potestate spirituali: & Ecclesia non tantùm fuit, sed etiam florentissi-
units.tr: XI. The Hierarchists' arguments for their monarch's temporal power are worthless. For he who is a spiritual shepherd even of kings and princes does not thereby have temporal power over them; just as he who feeds the Church in a temporal manner does not thereby obtain spiritual power. Christ and the Apostles fed and governed the Church spiritually. If temporal power were necessary to feed the Church spiritually, the Church would have flourished least of all at the time when it had temporal power set against it, as in the many persecutions it suffered; yet in those very circumstances it flourished most of all, by its own true virtues, and it withered the more, the freer it was from persecutions. Christ was indeed of the tribe of Judah, in which the right of the kingdom lay; but he was not on that account a temporal king in his capacity as Mediator, since those who are not of royal stock are not kings, but rather those whose stock is in full possession of the kingdom. Yet Christ's stock was not such in the time when the sceptre was taken from the tribe of Judah. Indeed, Christ was not even to be known while the sceptre was in the tribe of Judah, Gen. 49:10. Nor did the tribe of Judah have power over all temporal kingdoms, such as the Pope claims for himself. Christ also, as Son of the kingdom, declared that he was free from paying tribute, Matt. 17:25–26. But every immunity and freedom is a royal power; and Christ paid the tribute, showing that he was not a temporal king. Yet Christ willed this, and did not wish himself, who is the Son of God, to be bound to pay the didrachma as a ransom [ἀντὶ] for his soul, nor his disciples, who inherit freedom from him and are redeemed not with silver but with his precious blood, Isa. 52:3; 1 Pet. 1:18–19, and who have become sons of the living God, to be held any longer in the bondage of a type. Christ entered Jerusalem with royal pomp, when the Apostles and the people spread their garments before him, Matt. 21:7–8, etc. But that honour was paid to him not as to a secular king, since it was more than of lowly humility that he used a borrowed and hired beast, and sat upon the garments of poor disciples, not golden and his own, attended by unarmed companions who carried branches of trees in their hands in place of spears and swords, declaring that the manner of his kingdom is wholly different from the manner of the kingdoms of the world. It was paid to him therefore as to a spiritual and heavenly King, the King of Zion, as he proved himself to be by signs already sufficient, and was to prove himself further by suffering. As for their contention that spiritual power is superior to civil or inferior power, as if it commanded it, this is a mere play on ambiguous words. For things are called superior or inferior sometimes in dignity, sometimes in subjection. In dignity, when one thing is more excellent, as learned men are preferred to unlettered merchants. In subjection, when some things are subject to others in the same order; as a father is superior to a son, or a magistrate to a subject. Ecclesiastical power is indeed superior to civil power in dignity, because the end proposed to it is absolutely the highest end of man; and so it is to be preferred to any power whatever, even a Christian magistrate. But it is not superior in subjection, so that by subjecting temporal power to itself it should command it. For those who excel in dignity do not therefore command their inferiors. For the dignity of the physician is above the dignity of the architect, and yet the physician does not command the architect. Otherwise whoever holds any ecclesiastical dignity whatever would command whoever held civil authority, which is absolutely absurd. For they assert in vain that temporal power is subordinate to spiritual power. For things that are subordinate cannot subsist one without the other. Yet the most powerful commonwealths have existed among the nations separately, without spiritual power; and the Church not only existed but even flourished.

units.la: Argumenta contraria diluuntur.
units.tr: Contrary arguments are refuted.

units.la: Nec Papa, nec Ecclesia potestatem jure Divino possidet. ma fuit, cùm potestatem Politicam sibi non tantùm non subjectam, sed etiam adversariam habuit. Neque etiam finis civilis spirituali subordinatus est, quia ille temporalem, hic spiritualem beatitudinem propositam habet, & beatitudo spiritualis sine temporali, temporalis sine spirituali obtineri potest. Licet enim beatitudo civilis non sit absolutè ultimus finis, tamen nec subordinatus, sed tantùm postponendus est. Possunt etiam Reges & Pastores, clerici & laici unius Ecclesiæ membra esse; & hactenus etiam connexa esse debent, sed non sic, ut unum ab altero pendeat. Nam in humano etiam corpore membra dextra & sinistra, eáque connexa sunt, quatenus partes continuatæ sunt; neque tamen vel dextra à sinistris, vel sinistra à dextris membris dependent. Sic planè in civitate Dei, seu in universitate generis humani potestas Politica & Ecclesiastica ἀνλδιαυρὲν, neque tamen ideo necessaria mutua dependentia est. Accedit, quòd potestas Ecclesiastica & temporalis ejusdem corporis membra sunt non per se, quia una sine altera subsistit, sed per accidens, & adventitia ratione, quia evenire potest, ut civilis potestas, & qui eandem gerit, sit membrum Ecclesiæ. Sed non iccirco Potestas civilis Ecclesiasticæ subjicitur; verùm homo, quà civis, Regi, quà Christianus Ecclesiæ proprie subjicitur. Imò subjectio potest esse mutua, ut possit & civis quatenus Christianus Ecclesiæ & Pastori, & Ecclesia atque Pastor ejus, quatenus civis est, civi, seu Magistratui subjici. Quo sensu Potestates collaterales, non una altera superior vel inferior est. Præterea tenetur quidem Potestas civilis administrationem suam mutare, si Ecclesiæ bonum impediat, sed ex officio videlicet proprio, si meliora docta & planè persuasa ipsa sibi imperet, hoc est, suo motu feratur ad id, quod faciendum est; non alieno motu, non ex alieno imperio, sic, ut nolens volens, nec docta, nec persuasa, externa vi & imperio ad id impellatur. Neque enim, qui alterius commodis se accommodare tenetur, propterea alteri illi subjectus est; quomodo etiam in Rerumpublicarum administratione Reges post pacta inita agnoscunt se teneri alienis commodis, nec tamen subjici; sed is demum alteri subjectus est, qui ex imperio ejus aliquid facere nolens volens tenetur. Unde Constantinus M. Eusebio Histor. Eccl. lib. X. teste, Christianis libertatem Religionis edicto concedens, non tantùm non significavit, se ex alterius imperio id facere, sed etiam testatus est, certa ratione id sibi persuasum esse; Σκοπεῖλες, inquiens, ἡ ἐλεύθερίαν τῆς θρησκείας ἐκ ὀρθῶς ἔχω, ἀλλ' ἐνὸς ἑκάστου τῇ διανοίᾳ τῇ βουλῇ ἐξουσίαν δοῦναι τὰ θεῖα πεῤῥύματα τιμᾶν κατὰ τὸν αὐτῶν τρόπον. Considerantes libertatem pietatis non esse denegandam, sed cujusque voluntati potestatem concedendam, ut res Divinas curet pro arbitrio suo. Denique potestas utendi & disponendi de rebus temporalibus ad obtinendum Ecclesiæ finem, qui animarum salus est, absolutè necessaria non est. Experientia enim docet, finem hunc obtineri posse, etiamsi Ecclesia nullam rerum temporalium administrationem habeat. Alioqui nemo ad salutem perduci potuisset tum, cùm Ecclesia persecutiones publicas impedire non potuit, cùm tamen in mediis furo-
units.tr: Neither the Pope nor the Church possesses power by divine right. It was most flourishing when it had a political power that was not only not subject to it but actually hostile to it. Nor is the civil end subordinate to the spiritual, since the one has temporal happiness in view and the other spiritual happiness, and spiritual happiness can be obtained without temporal, and temporal without spiritual. For although civil happiness is not absolutely the ultimate end, it is not therefore subordinate, but only to be postponed. Kings and ministers, clergy and laity can also be members of one Church, and so far they ought to be connected, but not in such a way that one depends on the other. For in the human body too the right and left members are connected, inasmuch as they are parts of one continuous whole, yet the right members do not depend on the left, nor the left on the right. Thus, plainly, in the city of God, or in the whole human race, political and ecclesiastical power are coordinate [ἀνλδιαυρὲν], and yet there is no necessary mutual dependence. Moreover, ecclesiastical power and temporal power are members of the same body not in themselves, since the one subsists without the other, but accidentally and by an incidental circumstance, because it may happen that the civil power, and the person who holds it, is a member of the Church. But for that reason the civil power is not made subject to the ecclesiastical; rather, a man is subject to the King as a citizen, and to the Church as a Christian. Indeed, subjection can be mutual: a citizen, as a Christian, may be subject to the Church and its minister, and the Church and its minister, as citizens, may be subject to the citizen, that is, to the magistrate. In this sense the powers are collateral, neither one superior or inferior to the other. Furthermore, the civil power is indeed bound to change its administration if it hinders the good of the Church, but this should be by its own duty, if it is itself led to better things by what has been taught and is thoroughly persuaded; that is, it should move of its own accord to what ought to be done, not by another's impulse or another's command, so that, willing or unwilling, untaught and unpersuaded, it is driven to it by external force and command. For one who is bound to accommodate himself to the advantage of another is not on that account subject to him. So too in the government of commonwealths, Kings, after treaties have been made, acknowledge that they are bound to the advantage of others, and yet they are not subject to them; rather, a person is subject to another only when, willing or unwilling, he is bound to do something by that other's command. Hence Constantine the Great, as Eusebius testifies (Hist. Eccl. lib. X.), in granting liberty of religion to the Christians by edict, not only did not signify that he did this by another's command, but also declared that he was persuaded of it on sound grounds; "Σκοπεῖλες," he says, "ἡ ἐλεύθερίαν τῆς θρησκείας ἐκ ὀρθῶς ἔχω, ἀλλ' ἐνὸς ἑκάστου τῇ διανοίᾳ τῇ βουλῇ ἐξουσίαν δοῦναι τὰ θεῖα πεῤῥύματα τιμᾶν κατὰ τὸν αὐτῶν τρόπον" [considering that liberty of piety is not to be denied, but that power should be granted to each person's will, so that each may look after divine matters according to his own judgment]. Finally, the power to use and dispose of temporal things in order to attain the end of the Church, which is the salvation of souls, is not absolutely necessary. For experience teaches that this end can be attained even when the Church has no administration of temporal things. Otherwise, no one could have been brought to salvation at the time when the Church could not prevent public persecutions, when yet in the midst of those furies so great an army of martyrs stormed the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: ribus illis tantus Martyrum exercitus Regno Cœlorum vim fecerit. Est tamen necessaria illa potestas, quatenus fine ea non æquè commodè Ecclesiæ finis obtineri potest. Ideo Apostolus deprecationes fieri pro Principibus jubet, ut tranquillam & quietam vitam degamus, cum omni pietate & honestate, 1.Tim.II.1.2. Sed non quæ sic necessaria sunt, eadem in Ecclesia esse debent. Alioquin etiam in primitiva Ecclesia obtinuissent. Neque enim etiam omnis bene ordinata Respublica penes se habet, quicquid hoc modo necessarium est. Nam extra controversiam est, fuisse Ecclesiam à Christo & Apostolis optimè constitutam, licèt politicæ potestatis administrationem neque actu primo, neque secundo habuerit.
units.tr: Nevertheless that power is necessary, insofar as without it the end of the Church cannot be obtained as conveniently. Therefore the Apostle orders that prayers be made for Princes, so that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life, with all godliness and honesty (1 Tim. II.1.2). But things that are necessary in this way ought not to be the same in the Church. Otherwise they would have prevailed in the primitive Church as well. For not even every well-ordered commonwealth has within itself all that is necessary in this way. For it is beyond dispute that the Church was most excellently constituted by Christ and the Apostles, although it had no administration of political power, neither in the first act nor in the second.

units.la: XII. Cùm duo feré sint, ex quibus τὸ Κυριον, Majestas, seu suprema, nullique obnoxia potestas Reipublicæ cujusvis dominantis à Poliiticis discernitur, puta νομοθετικὴ legislatoria, & διακριτικὴ judicialis potestas summa, utramque Papa non in orbis duntaxat partem aliquam, uti dominantes hujus mundi solent, sed in universum orbem, saltem Christianum, & in spiritualibus minimùm, atque sub spiritualium externa specie, in temporalibus etiam, summam sibi vendicat. Ad legislatoriam infallibilem & supremam quidvis constituendi & definiendi facultatem referunt. Bellarminus enim contendit: In Ecclesia Catholica semper creditum esse, Episcopos in suis Diœcesibus, & Romanum Pontificem in universa Ecclesia, esse veros Principes Ecclesiasticos, qui possint sua authoritate etiam sine plebis consensu, vel Presbyterorum consilio, leges ferre, quæ conscientiam obligent. Et in universum Papalis Monarchia ratum habet, Ecclesiasticis mandatis, etiam extra casum scandali, perinde ut Divinis & Evangelicis, conscientias hominum sub pœna æternæ mortis directè obligari, eò quòd Spiritus S. æquè semper Ecclesiæ, atque olim Prophetis & Apostolis, assistat. Et potestatem eam ad actiones, corpora & bona baptizatorum omnium, etiam Regum & Principum summorum, saltem indirectè, uti loqui amant, extendunt.
units.tr: XII. Since there are almost two things by which the sovereign power [τὸ Κυριον], that is, majesty, subject to none, is distinguished from the political power of any ruling commonwealth, namely the legislative power [νομοθετικὴ] and the supreme judicial power [διακριτικὴ], the Pope claims both for himself: not, as the rulers of this world usually do, over some part of the globe only, but over the whole world, at least the Christian world, and in spiritual matters at least, and under the outward appearance of spiritual things, in temporal matters too. They attribute to himself an infallible and supreme faculty of establishing and defining anything, under the heading legislatoriam. For Bellarmine contends: In the Catholic Church it has always been believed that Bishops in their own dioceses, and the Roman Pontiff in the whole Church, are the true ecclesiastical Princes, who can by their own authority, even without the consent of the people or the counsel of the presbyters, enact laws that bind conscience. And in general, the Papal monarchy holds it established that ecclesiastical commands, even outside the case of scandal, bind men's consciences directly under pain of eternal death, just as divine and evangelical commands do, because the Holy Spirit is equally present with the Church as once with the Prophets and Apostles. And they extend that power, at least indirectly, as they like to put it, to the actions, bodies and goods of all the baptized, even of the highest Kings and Princes.

units.la: XIII. Habet equidem Ecclesia in constituendis legibus authoritatem quandam, neque planè illa ἀναρχῶ est. Constituti enim à Deo sunt Pastores & Doctores, quorum nominum subiata præcipiendi, imperandi, mandandi inanis significatio est. Sed authoritas legum est vel latarum, vel ferendarum. Illa in eo est, ut legibus jam latis perpetuò observandis aliquis invigilet, sicut in Republica subalterni magistratus designantur, non ut singuli leges pro arbitrio condant; quia alias res in immensum abiret; sed ne quæ olim latæ sunt, impunè violentur. Hæc Reipublicæ nunc primùm nascenti vel formam præscribit, vel olim præscriptæ vitia sanat, partim defectibus supplendis, partim exceßibus resecandis. Et res, de quibus leges feruntur, aliæ necessariæ, aliæ adiaphoræ sunt. Necessariæ, quarum in alterutram partem, virtutis vel vitii, certum & constans momentum est, quales sunt ex omnes, quæ legibus à Deo latis imperantur, vel prohibentur, sive illæ ad fidem, sive ad mores pertineant. Adiaphoræ, quæ cùm per se neque in vitiorum, neque in virtutum censu sint, secundum varias circumstantias,
units.tr: XIII. The Church indeed has a certain authority in establishing laws, and it is not altogether without rule [ἀναρχῶ]. For Pastors and Teachers have been appointed by God, and once the power of commanding, ordering and enjoining is removed from their names, the meaning is empty. But the authority over laws is either of laws already enacted or of laws to be enacted. The former consists in this: that someone keeps watch that laws already enacted are constantly observed, just as in a commonwealth subordinate magistrates are appointed, not so that each may frame laws at will (for that would lead to endless confusion), but so that what has been enacted long ago may not be violated with impunity. The latter, for a commonwealth just beginning, either prescribes its form, or, for one already prescribed, cures its faults, partly by supplying deficiencies and partly by cutting away excesses. And the matters on which laws are passed are partly necessary, partly indifferent. Necessary matters are those of which there is a certain and constant weight toward one side or the other, virtue or vice; such are all those things commanded or forbidden by the laws given by God, whether they pertain to faith or to morals. Indifferent matters are those which, since in themselves they are neither in the category of vices nor of virtues, may be variously permitted or forbidden according to various circumstances.

units.la: Legislatoria potestas principalis Papæ non competit.
units.tr: The principal legislative power does not belong to the Pope.

units.la: Ecclesia in ferendis legibus authoritas explicatur. stantias, varie etiam permitti, vel prohiberi possunt. Ecclesiæ igitur authoritas longè maxima est in legibus à Deo latis commendandis, estque ejus perpetua non tantùm cura, sed etiam potestas providendi, ut iis legibus homines debitam obedientiam præstent. Hæc loquere & roga, & redargue μετὰ πάσης ἐπιλαγῆς cum omni imperio, Tit. II. 15. Atque hunc verum & proprium finem authoritatis Ecclesiasticæ esse, S. Paulus docuit, dicens: Per quem accipimus gratiam & Apostolatum ad obedientiam fidei inter omnes gentes, Rom. I. 7. Et Christus: Qui vos audit, me audit; & qui vos rejicit, me rejicit, Luc. X. 16. Si Ecclesiam audire neglexerit, esto tibi velut Ethnicus & Publicanus, Matth. XVIII. 17. Falsi proin & absurdissimi sunt Anabaptistæ, Ecclesiæ non aliam, quàm admonendi potestatem concedentes, quod omnem pœnarum Ecclesiasticarum, quæ sublata authoritate illi nullæ sunt, vim abolere, & ordinem ipsum pessundare est. Cùm enim ipsa charitas omnibus satis legitima causa admonendi, exhortandi, imò & redarguendi proximum sit, quid ultra opus erat Pastores & doctores instituí? Sed alia ferendarum legum ratio est. Nam in necessariis quidem nullæ partes novis legislatoribus sunt, quia nihil ad pietatem absolutè necessarium est, quin à Deo latis disertis legibus constitutum sit. In solis igitur adiaphoris seu indifferentibus legibus circumscribendis Ecclesiæ authoritas distringitur. Non enim illa indifferentia dicuntur, quòd semper & absque discrimine permittantur vel prohibeantur, sed quia pro variis circumstantiis interdum prohiberi, interdum permitti possunt. Cùmque discrimen illud non facilè obvium sit, ideò necessaria est Pastorum prudentia, qui comparatis variis Ecclesiæ partibus & temporibus, quid ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ omitti vel usurpari possit, definiant. Sed legum talium pondus & authoritas longè infra Deum subsistat oportet. Non enim æquè graviter peccat Ecclesiæ, atque Divinarum legum transgressor: & leges ejusmodi non mutant naturam rerum, ut, quæ per se erant indifferentes, subitò necessariæ fiant, adeò ut nullo tempore nullàve causa aliter liceat, quàm constitutum est: Et denique nullæ leges Ecclesiasticæ per se sunt leges, sed propter Divinas, quibus subordinatæ sunt eum in finem, ut earum cognitionem & obedientiam adjuvent. Proin in legum talium violatione peccatum est nonnisi per accidens, non propter rei ipsius usurpationem, quomodo in furto & homicidio, sed propter aliud, nempe tum propter contemptum ordinis & authoritatis legitimæ & à Deo constitutæ, tum propter neglectum fraternæ ædificationis, tum propter impietatem & profanam licentiam: quæ si absint, nullum in transgressione tali peccatum est. Nam si etiam Divinæ de indifferentibus leges, velut illæ de panibus propositionis comedendis, & opere die Sabbati non faciendo, illa à Davide, hæc ab Apostolis casu aliquo bona conscientia omitti potuerunt, quantò magis humanæ? Sed longè aliter Hierarchicis visum est; nempe ejusmodi legum ferendarum in indifferentibus etiam potestatem Papæ competere, ut leges semel ex plenitudine potestatis ejus latæ, perinde ac Divinæ quævis, conscien-
units.tr: The authority of the Church in enacting laws is explained: it may be variously permitted or forbidden according to circumstances. Therefore the Church's authority is by far greatest in commending the laws given by God, and it has not only a perpetual care but also the power of providing that men render due obedience to those laws. "Speak these things and exhort, and rebuke with all authority" [μετὰ πάσης ἐπιταγῆς], Tit. II. 15. And that this is the true and proper end of ecclesiastical authority St. Paul taught, saying: Through whom we have received grace and apostleship, to obedience to the faith among all nations (Rom. I. 7). And Christ: He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me (Luke X. 16). If he neglects to hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector (Matth. XVIII. 17). Therefore the Anabaptists are false and most absurd, who grant the Church no other power than that of admonishing, which, once authority is taken away, leaves them with no power of ecclesiastical penalties at all, and this abolishes the very order itself. For since charity itself is a sufficiently legitimate reason for all to admonish, exhort, and even rebuke a neighbour, what further need was there for Pastors and Teachers to be instituted? But the rationale for enacting laws is different. For in necessary matters there is no part for new legislators, because nothing that is absolutely necessary for godliness is not already established by the plain laws given by God. Therefore the authority of the Church is confined only to laying down laws about indifferent matters. For these are not called indifferent because they are always and without distinction permitted or forbidden, but because they can at one time be forbidden and at another permitted, according to various circumstances. And since that distinction is not easily apparent, the prudence of Pastors is necessary, who, comparing the various parts and times of the Church, define what may be omitted or adopted for the edification of the Church. But the weight and authority of such laws must remain far below God. For a transgressor of the Church's laws does not sin as gravely as a transgressor of divine laws; and such laws do not change the nature of things, so that what was in itself indifferent suddenly becomes necessary, so that at no time and for no cause it is lawful to act otherwise than as has been decreed. And finally, no ecclesiastical laws are laws in themselves, but on account of the divine laws to which they are subordinated, for the purpose of aiding knowledge and obedience to them. Therefore sin in violating such laws is committed only accidentally, not on account of the thing itself being done, as in theft or homicide, but on account of something else: namely, either on account of contempt for an order and authority that is legitimate and established by God, or on account of neglect of brotherly edification, or on account of impiety and profane licence. If these are absent, there is no sin in such a transgression. For if even divine laws about indifferent matters, such as those about eating the bread of the Presence, and not doing work on the Sabbath day, could by some chance be set aside with a good conscience, the one by David and the other by the Apostles, how much more human laws? But the Hierarchs have judged quite otherwise: namely, that the power of enacting such laws about indifferent matters belongs to the Pope, so that laws once enacted by the fullness of his power, just like any divine laws, directly and immutably bind the conscience...

units.la: tiam directè & immutabiliter obligent, integra tamen potestate dispensandi de jure (Divino æquè atque Papali) supra jus, uti Innocentius III. loquitur.
units.tr: ...and yet their laws, once issued from the fullness of his power, bind the conscience directly and unchangeably, as if they were divine, while he keeps full power to dispense from the law (divine as well as papal) above the law, as Innocent III puts it.

units.la: XIV. Cæterùm legislatio talis cum ἀρχῇ & ἐξουσίᾳ principatu & potestate dominante conjuncta, æquè ac Monarchia ipsa Antichristiana tota est. Per Baptismum enim transscribimur in nomen & familiam Dei filius, & in conscientia obligamur ad obedientiam non aliis, quàm Divinis mandatis præstandam. Baptizate eos in nomen Patris & Filii & Spiritus S. docentes eos servare mandata, quæ ego præcepi vobis, Matth. XXVIII. 19. 20. Ubi scitè Cajetanus: Mandavi ego; non mandabitis vos. Mea enim mandata servare necessarium est ad salutem; vestra autem mortifera esse possunt. Nam per Baptismum Christo induimur, & filii ejus evadimus, Gal. III. 26. 27. Quæ cum Christo communio & adoptio nos à servitute hominum, in conscientias nostras dominium sibi arrogantium eximit. Pretio empti estis. Ne fiatis servi hominum, 1. Cor. VII. 23. Complantamur enim per Baptismum similitudini mortis Christi, Rom. VI. 5. adeóque cum Christo mortui censemur. Qui porrò cum Christo mortui sunt, illi ab elementis mundi, decretis & imperio hominum liberantur. Si mortui estis cum Christo elementis mundi, quid tanquam viventes in mundo δογματίζεσθε decretis ex arbitratu & potestate factis, vos onerari finitis, cujusmodi sunt: Ne tangas, ne gustes, ne attrectes, quæ omnia sunt ad corruptionem usu (usu consumuntur & ad hoc facta sunt) secundum mandata & doctrinas hominum, Col. II. 20-23. Ridiculum est, quòd carnalia Philosophorum principia, & dogmata tantùm mundana fidei adversantia elementorum mundi & δογμάτων nomine prohiberi adversarii tricantur. Licèt enim leges Papales Philosophorum carnalibus principiis & doctrinis mundanis præstantiores non sint, cùm carnali ratione & Regno mundano totæ superstruantur; tamen etiam diserte leges Papales notantur. Annon enim Papa legibus & dogmatis, placitis & decretis suis conscientias Clericorum & Monachorum, ne tangant mulieres; omnium, ne gustent certos cibos diebus jejunii: Monachorum, ne opes velut proprias attrectent, constringit? quasi perinde iis homines polluerentur, atque ante mortem Christi tangentes, gustantes, attrectantes quædam elementa mundi polluebantur. Non Philosophorum, vel mundanarum religionum fidei adversantium principia, sed elementa mundi, circa quæ olim Judæi, à Deo decretis onerabantur, & per cacozeliam Christiani à Papa similibus decretis onerati sunt, εἰς ἀπώλειαν τῇ φθορᾷ ad corruptionem usu sunt, vers. 22. consumuntur, & ad hoc ipsum facta sunt; neque proin per se quicquam sanctitatis vel fœditatis habent. Accedit, quòd Deus verbis suis præcipientibus addi, vel detrahi quicquam vetuit. Non addetis ad verbum, quod ego loquor vobis, neque ab eo detrahetis, Deut. IV. 2. Quicquid ego præcipio vobis, custodietis, ut faciatis. Non addes ad illud, neque detrahes ex eo, Deut. XIII. 32. Quæ dicta ad fideles V. T. duntaxat, non ad fideles etiam N. T. pertinere, eò quòd uni genti Israeliticæ necessaria præscribi facilè potuerint, at non æquè facilè
units.tr: XIV. Moreover, such legislation, conjoined with rule and authority [ἀρχῇ and ἐξουσίᾳ] and with a dominating principate and power, is wholly Antichristian, just like the Antichristian monarchy itself. For through Baptism we are transcribed into the name and family of God's sons, and in conscience we are bound to render obedience to no commands except the divine ones. Baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all the things that I have commanded you, Matt. 28:19-20. On this point Cajetan rightly says: I have commanded; you may not command. For it is necessary for salvation to keep my commands, but yours may be deadly. For through Baptism we are clothed with Christ and become his sons, Gal. 3:26-27. This communion and adoption with Christ frees us from the servitude of men, who arrogate to themselves dominion over our consciences. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men, 1 Cor. 7:23. For through Baptism we are planted together in the likeness of Christ's death, Rom. 6:5, and so we are counted as dead with Christ. And those who are dead with Christ are freed from the elements of the world, from the decrees and command of men. If you died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though living in the world, do you subject yourselves to decrees [δογματίζεσθε] made by human judgment and power, such as: Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch; all of which are for destruction in the using (they are consumed by use and were made for this purpose) according to the commandments and teachings of men, Col. 2:20-23. It is absurd that our adversaries pretend that the carnal principles of the philosophers, and mere worldly doctrines opposed to the faith, are forbidden under the name of the elements of the world and of decrees [δογμάτων]. For although the papal laws are not better than the carnal principles and worldly teachings of the philosophers, since they are wholly built on carnal reason and on the kingdom of this world, yet papal laws are plainly marked as well. Does not the Pope, by his laws and dogmas, his opinions and decrees, bind the consciences of clergy and monks that they not touch women; and of all people, that they not taste certain foods on fast days; and that monks not handle riches as though they were their own? As if people were defiled by these things just as, before the death of Christ, those who touched, tasted or handled certain elements of the world were defiled. These are not the principles of philosophers or of worldly religions opposed to the faith, but elements of the world, concerning which the Jews were once burdened by decrees from God, and through the perverse zeal of Christians have been burdened by the Pope with similar decrees; they are unto destruction [εἰς ἀπώλειαν τῇ φθορᾷ] in the using, v. 22, they are consumed, and they were made for this very purpose; and therefore in themselves they have no holiness or foulness at all. Besides, God has forbidden that anything be added to or taken away from his commanding words. You shall not add to the word that I speak to you, nor take anything away from it, Deut. 4:2. Whatever I command you, you shall be careful to do; you shall not add to it nor take away from it, Deut. 13:32 [12:32]. These sayings pertain only to the faithful of the Old Testament, not also to the faithful of the New Testament, because the necessary things could easily be prescribed for the one Israelite nation, but not as easily

units.la: {a} Cum primi-patu & potestate dominante conjuncta non est. facilè ad omnes populos pertinentia necessaria præscribi possint, Bellarminus inscite pertendit, quia non multitudo temporum, aut gentium, sed multitudo duntaxat rerum leges multiplicat. Et quantuscunque personarum vel annorum numerus sit, præscriptum jam olim est, pauciores N. T. observationes esse. Levius enim Novi quàm V. T. jugum est, & resurrectione Christi manifestum indicium libertatis nostrae illuxit. Præterea Dominus Rex noster, Dominus legislator noster, Dominus judex noster est. Ipse servabit nos, Esaj. XXXIII. 22. Unus legislator est, qui servare & perdere potest, Jac. IV. 12. Ubi manifestum est de Ecclesia, non de Republica agi, quia Esajas legislatorem nostrum dicit, & Jacobus legislatorem potentem salvare & perdere, induxit. Futilis verò etiam primarii & secundarii legislatoris distinctio est, quia nemo unquam concessit, legislatoris nomen, hac quidem significatione, ut legem sancire posiit,ulli convenire, nisi ei, quem penes Majestas est. Et sic S. Jacobus unicum legislatorem esse pronuntiat, ut inde nemini fas esse, judicare alterum, concludat. Manifestè igitur legislationem & judicium in conscientias hominum, hominibus universis abrogat. Neque etiam legislator quidem unus est, potens servare & perdere; at plures sunt, qui salvare & perdere tamen non possunt, quia Jacobus manifestè ex eo, quòd nemo servare & perdere nisi unus potest, unitatem legislatoris probat. Quicunque porrò jus habet leges Ecclesiæ imponendi, is Dominus Ecclesiæ est; quia nemo in ulla Republica leges ferre permittitur, excepto eo, quem penes τὸ Κύριον, seu Majestas est. Atqui Pastores non dominari fidei, sed administri lætitiæ esse debent, 2. Cor. I. 24. Pascite gregem Domini, qui penes vos est, non ut dominantes cleris, 1. Petr. V. 2. 3. Et quæ res liberæ à Deo permissæ sunt, iis tanquam necessariis nulla lex conscientias subjicere potest, quia aliàs Divinæ voluntati prævaleret voluntas aliqua alia, & Deo ipsi creatura dominaretur. Atqui res omnes indifferentes liberæ à Deo permissæ sunt. In libertate, in qua Christus nos liberavit, perstate, & ne è contra servitutis jugo implicamini, Gal. V. 1. Ne quis vos damnet ob cibum vel potum, vel respectu diei festi, Novilunii, vel Sabbathorum, Col. II. 16. Libertas enim Christiana est, servire soli Deo viventi. Hinc Ecclesia N. T. passim vocatur Regnum Dei, quia in ea solus Deus regnat. Nam quòd libertatem Christianam in immunitate quidem à servitute peccati, legis Divinæ moralis & ceremonialis, at non ab obedientia Præla-torum consistere, illi regerunt, nugantur potiùs, quàm disputant, quia aliud obedientia Prælatorum, aliud authoritas legis sanciendæ est. Illa enim manente, hæc propterea non ponitur; & Scriptura simul libertatem in rebus indifferentibus constanter conservare, simul obedientiam prælatis deferre jubet. Utrumque proin conservatur, si negetur authoritas Prælatorum eò usque proferri, ut de rebus indifferentibus leges necessarias statuat. Quòd si fideles N. T. ad hominum præcepta, quæ nonnisi in elementa mundi & res terrenas cadere possunt, obligantur, & ex illis judicandi sunt, non parùm minuetur eorum παρρησία libertas
units.tr: {a} Not conjoined with primacy and dominant power. to all peoples, as Bellarmine foolishly contends, since it is not the multitude of times or nations but only the multitude of things that multiplies laws. And however great the number of persons or years may be, it has long since been laid down that the observances of the New Testament are fewer. For the yoke of the New Testament is lighter than that of the Old, and by the resurrection of Christ the clear sign of our liberty has shone forth. Moreover: The Lord is our King, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our judge; he will save us, Isa. 33:22. There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy, Jas. 4:12. It is clear that the Church, not the commonwealth, is being spoken of here, since Isaiah calls him our lawgiver, and James introduces the lawgiver as one able to save and destroy. The distinction between a primary and a secondary lawgiver is also idle, because no one has ever conceded that the name of lawgiver, in the sense of one who can enact law, belongs to anyone except him in whom sovereignty resides. And so St. James pronounces that there is only one lawgiver, so that he concludes that it is right for no one to judge another. Clearly, then, he takes away legislation and judgment over men's consciences from all men. Nor indeed is there only one lawgiver able to save and destroy; yet there are several who nonetheless cannot save and destroy, because James plainly proves the unity of the lawgiver from the fact that only one can save and destroy. Moreover, whoever has the right to impose laws on the Church is the Lord of the Church, since in no commonwealth is anyone permitted to make laws except him who holds the Kyrion, that is, the sovereignty. But ministers ought not to lord it over the faith but to be workers for joy, 2 Cor. 1:24. Feed the flock of the Lord that is among you, not as lording it over the clergy, 1 Pet. 5:2-3. And things that God has left free cannot be made subject to any law as if they were necessary, for otherwise some other will would prevail over the divine will, and a creature would rule over God himself. But all indifferent things have been left free by God. Stand fast in the liberty with which Christ has made us free, and do not be entangled again in the yoke of slavery, Gal. 5:1. Let no one judge you in respect of food or drink, or of a feast day, a new moon, or sabbaths, Col. 2:16. For Christian liberty is to serve the living God alone. Hence the Church of the New Testament is everywhere called the Kingdom of God, because in it God alone reigns. As for their claim that Christian liberty consists in immunity from the servitude of sin and from the divine moral and ceremonial law, but not from obedience to prelates, they are talking nonsense rather than disputing, since obedience to prelates is one thing and the authority to enact law is another. For the former remains, while the latter is not thereby posited. And Scripture at once commands that liberty in indifferent matters be constantly preserved and that obedience be rendered to prelates. Both are therefore preserved if the authority of prelates is denied to extend so far as to enact necessary laws about indifferent matters. But if the faithful of the New Testament are bound to human precepts, which can fall only on the elements of the world and earthly things, and are to be judged by them, their παρρησία liberty will be not a little diminished

units.la: & fiducia loquendi coram Deo, donec ejusmodi δικαιώματα ζαρκὸς impleverint. Præterquam quòd invehitur illa in judicium Ecclesiasticum corruptio, ut qui ea diligentissimè fecerint, nomen & opinionem filiorum Ecclesiæ veris filiis præripiant. Denique cùm ab omnibus ritibus Judaicis Christiani liberi sint, multò magis ab institutis humanis, velut conscientiam obligantibus liberi esse debent, quia ritus Judaici à Deo instituti fuerunt, & longè præstat Deo, quàmulli homini subjici, neque contra voluntatem Divinam religio servili onere premenda est.
units.tr: and their confidence of speech before God, until they have fulfilled such ordinances of the flesh [δικαιώματα σαρκός]. Besides, that corruption is brought into ecclesiastical judgment, so that those who have most diligently done these things snatch away the name and reputation of sons of the Church from the true sons. Finally, since Christians are free from all Jewish rites, they ought much more to be free from human institutions, which would bind their conscience, since Jewish rites were instituted by God, and it is far better to be subject to God than to any man, and religion must not be burdened with a servile yoke contrary to the divine will.

units.la: XV. Diluta Hierarchicorum argumenta adversaria sunt. Nam quod Israelitici Sacerdotis præcepta verè imperia fuisse, & conscientiam obligasse, ex verbis Dei juxta V. Interp. narrantes: Qui superbierit, nolens obtemperare Sacerdotum imperio, qui eo tempore ministrant Domino Deo tuo, ex decreto judicis morietur homo ille; Deut. XVIII. 12. colligunt, frustra sunt, quia mutata est Ecclesiæ gubernandæ ratio, & Sacerdotes Israelitici non tantùm ministri, sed etiam typi Christi fuerunt, neque adeò mirum videri posset, si amplior iis potestas data esset: tum quia minimè constat, Sacerdotibus Judaicis integrum fuisse, novas leges, quibus conscientiæ obstringerentur, condere. Leges enim Divinas, earumque authoritatem tueri poterant, at novis legibus latis conscientiis dominari non poterant. Quod crebra illa Dei prohibitio faciendi quicquam præter ea, quæ Deus ipse præcepit, ostendit. Quod verò de Sacerdotum imperio ex Vulgato Interprete urgent, pro ἀγεφφω & ludicro syllabarum aucupio habendum est, quia Textus Hebraicus simpliciter occidi eos jubet, qui per superbiam Sacerdoti, non Sacerdotis imperio, obedire dedignatus fuerit. Quanquam & imperium circa leges latas, non ferendas, obtinere posse, supra docuimus; & tale omnino Sacerdotum Vet. & Ministrorum N. T. est. Sacerdotes enim imperium habebant, sed circa leges latas, non ferendas, quia diserte על פי התורה juxta os legis docere, & judicium, juxta leges easdem, dicere v. 11. jubentur. Et iidem jus dicere, in judiciis particularibus, inter sanguinem & sanguinem, causam & causam, plagam & plagam, v. 8. poterant. Atqui nulla ejusmodi judicia, veluti inter Titium & Mævium, leges appellari possunt. Et qui jus sic dicendo præcipit, is non actionem ex se indifferentem necessariam efficit, sed actiones ad se delatas cum lege, cujus notitiam habet, confert. Dedit verò etiam Christus Ecclesiæ potestatem ligandi super terra, addita promissione ligationis in Cœlo ratihabendæ, Matth. XVI. 19. Sed ligare non est imponere legem, sed coërcere peccata adversus leges latas, quasi totidem verbis dictum esset; Quicquid puniveritis in terris, ratum erit in Cœlis. Atqui punire peccata eorum etiam judicum est, quibus subalterna authoritas est, & qui ex decreto legum, à summa Potestate jam latarum, jus dicere tenetur. Frustra iidem curam pascendi Ecclesiæ Ministris mandatam in jusRegium, leges ex plenitudine potestatis condendi commutant. Nam vocabulum πομαί-νω sua origine rusticum potiùs, ridiculè Regium vocabulum illi faciunt, cùm de Regibus nonnonnisi per metaphoram, adeóque per acci-dens, usurpetur, quia partes quædam officii Regii similes sunt partibus pastorum. Sed duo Pastorum genera sunt. Alii enim suas, alii alie-nas oves pascunt. Illi Domini, hi ministri me-ri sunt. Utrique ποιμαίνειν pascere cùm dican-tur, manifestum est, hoc verbum non semper Regium esse. Posterioris generis Ecclesiæ Pa-stores sunt, utpote qui nulli suas, sed omnes alienas oves pascunt, teste ipso Christo dicen-te: Pasce oves meas, quasi cùm Labanus Jaco-bo, & Jethro Mosi suas committebat. Rectiùs ergo argumentum sic invertitur: Nullius pa-storis, pascentis oves alienas, est leges ovibus pro arbitrio ponere. At omnes Ecclesiæ Pasto-res oves alienas pascunt. Nulli ergo ovibus suis leges pro arbitrio ponere possunt. Dixit etiam Christus Apostolis suis: Sicut me misit Pater, ita & ego mitto vos, Joh. XX. 21. Cæ-terùm non quicunque mittuntur à Christo, secundum omnem rationem & modum sic mittuntur, uti Christus à Patre missus est; quia Christus missus est ut Mediator, & legislator etiam; Apostoli non eo modo, sed ut ὑπηρέται τῆς λόγῳ ministri sermonis, Luc. I. 2. Authoritas igitur ea ad mittentem, non ad missos perti-net. Tum etiam hæc Apostolis dicta sunt pe-culiariter & primariò; omnibus autem Pasto-ribus secundariò & cum restrictione; quia non omnes Pastores eodem cum Apostolis loco sunt. At si quicunque mittuntur à Christo, parem cum mittente Christo potestatem ha-berent, omnes etiam Apostolis pares forent, quod oppidò absurdum est. Neque etiam A-postolus comminatus: Quid vultis? Cum virga veniam ad vos, an in spiritu mansuetudinis? 1.Cor. IV. 21. Potestatem leges ferendi Ecclesiæ Pa-storibus asserit, tum quia potestas circa leges latas & earum transgressores puniendos, non est potestas ferendi leges; tum quia ῥάβδος seu virga Apostolica peculiare quid Apostolis fuit, non commune omnibus Ecclesiæ Pastori-bus est. Nam ea Apostoli potestas cum mira-culo conjuncta fuit, uti ex Pauli ejusdem Ely-mam verbo solo excæcantis, & Petri verbo eti-am solo Ananiam & Sapphiram occidentis exemplis liquet. Denique obediendum certè est præpositis, Hebr. XIII. 17. Sed non ut legisla-toribus, quia obedientia Pastoribus debita, non est obedientia relata ad ipsorum leges, sed ad leges Christi, quarum præconium illis deman-datum est. Deus enim ministris Ecclesiæ man-datum dedit, ne quid aliud, quàm verbum ipsius loquerentur, cum ἐλέγχω & φανερῶσαι ad conscientias ipsorum. Id qui faciunt, iis obe-diendum certè est. Qui verò omisso Dei ver-bo aliud loquuntur, & in conscientias legibus novis constringendas imperium sibi arrogant, ii non ἡγεμόνοι ductores Ecclesiæ, sed seductores, fures, prædones, hostes sunt, Johann. cap. X. v. 10. 11. &c.
units.tr: XV. The arguments of the hierarchists against this are weak. They argue that the precepts of the Israelite priests were true commands that bound the conscience, citing the words of God in the Vulgate: Whoever acts proudly, refusing to obey the command of the priests who minister to the Lord your God at that time, that man shall die by the decree of the judge (Deut. 17.12). But this proves nothing, because the manner of governing the Church has changed. The Israelite priests were not only ministers but also types of Christ, so it would not be surprising if they had been given greater authority. Moreover, it is by no means clear that the Jewish priests were free to make new laws that would bind consciences. They could enforce God's laws and defend their authority, but they could not lord it over consciences with newly enacted laws. God's repeated prohibition against doing anything beyond what he himself commanded shows this. As for the argument they draw from the Vulgate's command of the priests, this must be regarded as a play on words and a quibble over syllables, since the Hebrew text simply orders the death of those who refused, out of pride, to obey the priest, not the priest's command. Yet we have shown above that a command can apply to laws already given, not laws yet to be made, and this is entirely the case with the priests of the Old Testament and the ministers of the New. For the priests had authority, but only over laws already given, since they were expressly ordered to teach according to the mouth of the law [על פי התורה] and to pronounce judgment according to the same laws (v. 11). They could also pronounce judgment in particular cases, between blood and blood, cause and cause, plague and plague (v. 8). But no such judgments, for example between Titius and Mævius, can be called laws. And one who gives a ruling in this way does not make an action that is indifferent in itself necessary; he simply applies the actions brought before him to a law that he knows. Christ did indeed give the Church the power of binding on earth, with the promise that what is bound will be ratified in heaven (Matt. 16.19). But to bind does not mean to impose a law; it means to restrain sins against laws already given, as if it had been said in so many words: Whatever you punish on earth will be ratified in heaven. And to punish sins belongs also to those judges who hold a subordinate authority and who are bound to pronounce judgment according to the decrees of laws already enacted by the supreme power. In vain, too, do they change the care of feeding the Church, entrusted to its ministers, into a royal right to make laws at will from the fullness of power. For the word poimainō is by origin a rustic term rather than a royal one, and they make it ridiculously royal, since it is used of kings only in a metaphorical sense, and so only incidentally, because certain parts of the royal office resemble the duties of shepherds. But there are two kinds of shepherds. Some feed their own sheep, others feed the sheep of others. The former are lords, the latter are mere ministers. Since both are said poimainein, to feed, it is clear that this verb does not always refer to kingship. The ministers of the Church belong to the second kind, since they feed not their own sheep but the sheep of another, as Christ himself says: Feed my sheep (John 21.16). It is like when Laban committed his flocks to Jacob, and Jethro to Moses. The argument should therefore be reversed, and more correctly: no shepherd who feeds the sheep of another has the right to impose laws on the sheep at his own discretion. But all ministers of the Church feed the sheep of another. Therefore none of them can impose laws on the sheep at his own discretion. Christ also said to his apostles: As the Father sent me, so I send you (John 20.21). But not everyone who is sent by Christ is sent in every respect and manner in which Christ was sent by the Father, because Christ was sent as Mediator and also as lawgiver, while the apostles were not sent in that way, but as hypēretai tou logou, ministers of the word (Luke 1.2). That authority therefore pertains to the one who sends, not to those who are sent. Moreover, these words were spoken to the apostles peculiarly and primarily; to all ministers they apply secondarily and with restriction, since not all ministers hold the same position as the apostles. But if everyone sent by Christ had the same power as Christ who sent them, then all would be equal to the apostles, which is utterly absurd. Nor does the apostle, in threatening, What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness? (1 Cor. 4.21), assert that the ministers of the Church have a power to make laws. For the power to enforce laws already given, and to punish their transgressors, is not the power to enact laws. Also, the apostolic rod was something peculiar to the apostles and not common to all the ministers of the Church. For that apostolic power was joined with miracle, as is clear from the examples of Paul, who blinded Elymas by a word alone, and of Peter, who by a word alone killed Ananias and Sapphira. Finally, the leaders must certainly be obeyed (Heb. 13.17). But they are not to be obeyed as lawgivers, because the obedience owed to ministers is not obedience referred to their own laws, but to the laws of Christ, whose proclamation has been entrusted to them. For God gave the ministers of the Church a command that they should speak nothing but his word, to reprove and make manifest to consciences. Those who do this certainly must be obeyed. But those who, setting aside the word of God, speak other things and arrogate to themselves authority to bind consciences with new laws, these are not guides [ἡγεμόνοι] of the Church but seducers, thieves, robbers, and enemies (John 10.8, 10–11, etc.).

units.la: XVI. Legislationis ἀκαοκρατία seu judi-cialis potestas suprema comes est. Hanc quo-que Monarchici suo Archimystæ Papæ arro-gant. Habet equidem Ecclesia potestatem quan-dam, juxta quam non tantùm cum auctorita-te verbum Dei prædicare, Sacramenta adminis-trare, sed etiam instituto judicio contumaces censuris in verbo Dei præscriptis notare potest.
units.tr: XVI. Legislative autocracy [ἀκρατοκρατία], or judicial power, is the supreme companion of this. The Monarchists also claim this for their archmystagogue, the Pope. The Church does indeed have a certain power by which it can not only preach the word of God with authority and administer the sacraments, but also, through a judgment instituted for this purpose, mark the contumacious with censures prescribed in the word of God.

units.la: Sed illi Ecclesiæ suæ potestatem judicialem ejusmodi arrogant, qua & Magistratus constitu-tere, & judicia suprema, jurisdictionem pro-priè dictam supremam, principalem & αὐτοκρατορικὴν exercere possit, arrogant. De Ma-gistratuum constitutione notissimi sunt Dicta-tus Gregoriani: quòd solus Papa jure dicatur Episcopus universalis: solus possit deponere Episco-pos, vel reconciliare: quòd legatus ejus etiam infe-rioris gradus omnibus Episcopis in Concilio præsit, & adversus eos sententiam depositionis dicere pos-sit: quòd illi soli liceat pro temporis necessitate le-ges condere, novas plebes congregare, de Canonia Abbatiam facere, divitem Episcopatum dividere, inopes unire, Episcopos de sede ad sedem, cogente necessitate, transmutare, absque Synodali conventu Episcopos deponere, & reconciliare, de omni Eccle-sia, quoscunque voluerit, clericos ordinare, &c. Communis omnium sententia stat, quòd om-nes Magistratus Ecclesiastici (tales enim Epi-scopatus, Canonicatus, Abbatias faciunt) quo-ad institutionem & administrationem juris & arbitrii Papalis sint. Etiam in Conciliis Episco-pos nonnisi Magistratuum & consiliariorum vice defungi pertendunt. Etenim Leo X. in Concilio Lateranensi edixit, Solum Pontificem Rom. pro tempore existentem, tanquam authori-tatem super omnia Concilia habentem, Concilio-rum indicendorum, transferendorum ac dissolven-dorum plenum jus & potestatem habere. Sed & judicandi potestatem supremam & αὐτοκρατορικὸν sibi eximiam Papa facit. Nam in Dicta-tibus Gregorianis cautum est, quòd sententia Pa-pæ à nullo debeat retractari, & ipse omnium so-lus retractare possit: quòd à nemine ipse judicari debeat; & nullus audeat Apostolicam sedem ap-pellantem condemnare: quòd majores causæ cujus-cunque Ecclesiæ ad eum referri debeant. Igitur etiam jus absolvendi à peccatis pœnitentes omne uni sibi ac primò competere Papa glo-riatur, eóque nomine partem quidem ejus Presbyteris atque Episcopis, ceu subdelegatis judicibus committit: partem verò, quæ mul-tum Majestatis & quæstus habet, soli sibi & curiæ suæ reservat. Atque illud absolvendi per ministerium clavium jus sic interpretatur, quòd sit potestas & authoritas quædam propria & principalis judicandi, simpliciter absolvendi, vel condemnandi, eo cum effectu, ut clavi non errante (sic dicis causa loquuntur, quia Papa infallibilitatem omnimodam sibi vendicat) ut sententiam semel latam Deus ipse in Cœlis ra-tam semper habeat. Etiam animas ex igne Purgatorio liberare, Papalis arbitrii est, quod fieri non potest, nisi simul etiam Angeli & dæ-mones Papæ imperiis & sententiis obedire co-gantur, hactenus scilicet, ut animas jubente Papa vel Angeli in Cœlum sublevent, vel dæ-mones in tartara detrudant. Nam & Clemens VI. in Bulla Jubilæi disertè Angelis imperavit, ut animam illius, quem ille à peccatis absol-verit, è Purgatorio in Paradisi gloriam intro-ducant.
units.tr: But they claim for their Church a judicial power of such a kind that it can both appoint magistrates and exercise the supreme judicature, the jurisdiction properly so called, supreme, principal, and autocratic. Concerning the appointment of magistrates, the Gregorian Dictates are very well known: that the Pope alone is rightly called universal bishop; that he alone may depose or reinstate bishops; that his legate, even of lower rank, takes precedence over all bishops in a council and may pronounce a sentence of deposition against them; that he alone may, as the needs of the time require, enact laws, gather new peoples, make an abbey out of a canonry, divide a rich bishopric, unite poor ones, transfer bishops from see to see when necessity compels, depose and reinstate bishops without a synodal assembly, and ordain clergy for any church whomever he wishes, etc. The common view of all is that all ecclesiastical magistrates (for that is what bishoprics, canonries, and abbeys are) depend, in their institution and administration of law and discretion, on the Papal will. Even in councils, they maintain, bishops perform only the role of magistrates and counsellors. Indeed, Leo X in the Lateran Council decreed that the Roman Pontiff alone, existing for the time being, as one who has authority over all councils, has full right and power to convene, transfer, and dissolve councils. But the Pope also claims for himself the supreme power of judging and a remarkable autocratic power. For the Gregorian Dictates provide that the sentence of the Pope must not be retracted by anyone, and he alone may retract the sentences of all; that he himself must be judged by no one; and that no one may dare to condemn one who appeals to the Apostolic See; that the greater cases of any church must be referred to him. Therefore the Pope also boasts that the whole right of absolving penitents from sins belongs to himself alone and first of all, and on that ground he commits a part of it to his presbyters and bishops, as subdelegated judges, but reserves the part that carries much majesty and profit for himself and his court alone. And he interprets this right of absolving through the ministry of the keys as a certain proper and principal power of judging: to absolve or condemn simply, with the effect that, with the key not erring (they speak thus figuratively, since the Pope claims for himself complete infallibility), God himself in heaven always holds ratified the sentence once pronounced. Also to free souls from the fire of Purgatory is a matter of Papal discretion, which could not be done unless the angels and demons were also compelled to obey the commands and sentences of the Pope, to this extent: that at the Pope's bidding the angels lift souls up to heaven or the demons thrust them down into hell. For Clement VI, in the Bull of Jubilee, expressly commanded the angels to bring into the glory of Paradise from Purgatory the soul of the one whom he had absolved from sins.
