units.la: XVII. Cæterùm judicialis illa suprema & αὐτοκρατορικὴ potestas æquè ac legislatio Ecclesiæ & ministrorum ejus potestatem planè superat, quia cum dominio conjuncta est, cui omni, non soli illi, cujus finis utilitas propria est, hoc est, tyrannica, interdictum penitus est, Luc.
units.tr: XVII. Moreover, that supreme judicial and autocratic power, like the lawmaking power, plainly exceeds the power of the Church and its ministers, because it is joined with lordship. Lordship is wholly forbidden to everyone except the one whose end is his own advantage, that is, to a tyrant. Luke 22.

units.la: Potestatem etiam judicialem dominantem Papa sibi arrogat.
units.tr: The Pope also claims for himself a judicial power of lordship.

units.la: Arrogate potestatis illius iniquitas. Luc. XXII. 25. 1. Pet. V. 3. Nam ibi τὼ κατα-κυ-ε-ύ-ειν dominari, & τὸ δοῦλον εἶναι, servum esse, è diametro opponuntur. Licèt enim etiam potestas temporalis ministra fit, respectu Dei delegantis, dominans tamen est respectu subditorum. Ministri autem & Christi delegantis, & Ecclesiæ,cui præsunt,respectu meri ministri sunt, procul omni potestate,qua simpliciter iis interdictum est. Solus enim Jehova sicut Legislator & Rex, ita etiam שפטנו judex noster in spiritualibus est,Esaj. XXXIII.22. Neque usquam is potestatem externam & principalem Ecclesiæ delegavit. Ac ne ipse quidem Christus in statu exinanitionis ejusmodi potestatem judicialem externam exercuit, imò Regnum suum de hoc mundo esse,diserte negavit, Joh. XVIII. 36. In Regni enim sui spiritualis occupatione & vindicatione dicitur gentes quassasse בשבט ברזל virgâ ferreâ,Psal. II.9. hoc est, ῥάβδῳ בשבטה virgâ roboris,Psal. CX.2. vi non dominante externa, sed verbi & Spiritus sui,qua superbiam contundit,& mollitiem indurat. Quassat enim corda, & præparat, ut in iis regnare possit. Refractarios verò & persecutores Ecclesiæ ut vas figulinum confringit,Psal. II. 9. Omnipotente scilicet illa virtute,quam, quâ Deus,habet, & in totum mundum exercet. Ac multò minùs Ecclesia, quàm Christus, externa potestate judiciali pollet. Coërcetur enim ejus potestas omnis spirituali objecto,uti præcepta Christi,qualia sunt: Docete,baptizate, ligate, solvite, indicant. In rejectione verò eorum,qui mandatis his & Evangelio sese opponunt,Christus Apostolos non vi externa,ultra animas in temporalia se exerente,armavit,sed in testimonium infidelitatis incurabilis, jussit eos excutere pulverem, Matth. X. 4. habere pro Ethnicis & publicanis, ibidem.XVIII.17. qua in re nullus equidem violentiæ externæ locus est. Ideo S. Paulus jubet obedire præpositis,Hebr. XIII. 7. in iis scilicet,quæ animæ salutem concernunt. Addit enim: Ipsi enim vigilant pro animabus vestris, tanquam rationem reddituri. Neque planè potestas coercendi,puniendi,cogendi externa Ecclesiæ competere potest,quia ea nec in corpus,nec in animam hominum competere potest. Non in animam,cujus regimen & coactio soli Deo subest. Non in corpus,cujus coercitio nusquam Ecclesiæ,ubique civili summæ potestati in verbo Dei vindicatur. Deus enim in verbo suo unicam,supremam, architectonicam & ἀντιπνευ-ον potestatem, eámque jure gladii armatam, instituit, cujus proin solius jurisdictioni externæ πᾶσα ψυχὴ omnis anima subjecta, Rom. XIII. 1. & ad imperata omnia obnoxia esse debet. Ideo etiam sacerdotes V. T. Regibus suis in criminalibus & civilibus subjecti fuerunt: & in N. T. Christus ipse Magistratui vectigal pro se & Petro solvit,Matth. XVII. 27. & Apostoli omnibus sine discrimine civilem obedientiam Magistratibus civilibus præstandam passim injunxerunt. Manstitque civilis jurisdictio omnis uni solíque Magistratui civili, donec,cessantibus persecutionibus Constantini M. tempore Episcopi tribunalia, & judicii formam erexerunt,addita à Constantino M. expressa lege,ut à sententiis Episcoporum provocatio non esset, eásque judices exequerentur. Hæc origo judiciorum forensium in Ecclesia fuit. Cúmque potestate judiciorum talium Episcopi nonnulli abuterentur, Arcadius & Honorius statuerunt,ut abolito foro Ecclesiasticorum religionis solius causas Episcopi dijudicarent, civiles verò non alia conditione, quàm si ita partibus placeret. Quæ Lex A. Christi DLII. ab Imperatore Valentino initaurata est. Sed mox ademptæ hujus potestatis bona pars à sequentibus Principibus iis restituta est; Justiniano etiam forum & Audientiam stabiliente, iisque unâ cum causis religionis, delicta clericorum Ecclesiastica,& adversus laicos jurisdictiones varias assignante. His gradibus potestas, seu potiùs charitas Ecclesiæ in dominationem degeneravit. Separatis posted in Occidente provinciis, paulatim Episcopi à Principibus in consilium adhiberi,mixtum forum institui,laicorum causæ spiritualitatis obtentu ad illud evocari, & ad id Divinum jus, Christiqué institutio allegari cœpit. Tandem ab immenlitate potestatis spiritualis ad tribunal temporale in medio statu cujusque Politici extruendum , & imperium in imperio ædificandum ventum est,& utrumque Ecclesiasticum & politicum imperium Episcopis ademptum Papa super omne ζέλασμα se efferens rapuit.
units.tr: The wickedness of that arrogated power. Luke 22:25; 1 Pet. 5:3. For there to lord it over [κατακυριεύειν] and to be a servant [τὸ δοῦλον εἶναι] are set in direct opposition. Although even temporal power is ministering in relation to God, who delegates it, it is nonetheless lordly in relation to its subjects. Ministers, however, both of Christ who delegates them and of the Church over which they preside, are mere ministers in relation to him, and are altogether without that power, which is simply forbidden to them. For Jehovah alone is Lawgiver and King, and so also is he our judge in spiritual matters, Isa. 33:22. Nowhere has he delegated to the Church external and principal power. Nor did Christ himself, in the state of his humiliation, exercise any such external judicial power. Indeed he plainly denied that his kingdom is of this world, John 18:36. For in the taking up and vindication of his spiritual kingdom, the nations are said to be broken with an iron rod, Ps. 2:9, that is, with a rod of strength [בשבטה], Ps. 110:2, by a power not external and dominating, but by his Word and Spirit, which crushes pride and hardens softness. For he shakes hearts and prepares them, so that he may reign in them. But the refractory and the persecutors of the Church he breaks like a potter's vessel, Ps. 2:9, by that almighty power which he has as God and exercises over the whole world. Much less, then, does the Church possess external judicial power than Christ does. For all its power is confined to a spiritual object, as the precepts of Christ indicate: Teach, baptize, bind, loose. In rejecting those who oppose these commands and the Gospel, Christ did not arm the Apostles with external force reaching beyond souls into temporal things. Rather, as a testimony of incurable unbelief, he ordered them to shake off the dust, Matt. 10:14, and to regard such people as heathens and tax collectors, ibid., 18:17. In this matter there is certainly no room for external violence. So St. Paul bids us obey those who rule over you, Heb. 13:7, that is, in matters that concern the salvation of the soul. For he adds: For they watch over your souls, as those who must give account. Nor can external power to restrain, punish, and compel properly belong to the Church, since it can belong neither to the body nor to the soul of men. Not to the soul, whose governance and constraint lie with God alone. Not to the body, whose restraint is claimed nowhere in the Word of God for the Church, but everywhere for the civil supreme power. For God in his Word has instituted one supreme, architectonic and counter-balancing power, armed with the right of the sword, to whose jurisdiction alone all external things are subject, and to which every soul [πᾶσα ψυχή], Rom. 13:1, must be bound to obey all commands. Hence also the priests of the Old Testament were subject to their kings in criminal and civil matters. In the New Testament Christ himself paid tribute to the magistrate for himself and for Peter, Matt. 17:27, and the Apostles everywhere enjoined on all, without distinction, civil obedience to be rendered to the civil magistrates. All civil jurisdiction remained with the one civil magistrate alone, until, when the persecutions ceased in the time of Constantine the Great, the bishops set up courts and a form of judgment, with an express law added by Constantine the Great that there should be no appeal from the sentences of the bishops, and that the judges should enforce them. This was the origin of ecclesiastical courts in the Church. But since some bishops abused the power of such judgments, Arcadius and Honorius decreed that, with the forum of the clergy abolished, bishops should adjudicate only cases of religion, while civil cases should be decided by them only if the parties so wished. This law was renewed in the year of Christ 452 by the emperor Valentinian. But soon a good part of this power was taken away and restored to the bishops by the following princes, Justinian also establishing a forum and a court, and assigning to the bishops, together with causes of religion, the ecclesiastical offences of clerics and various jurisdictions over laymen. By these steps the power, or rather the charity, of the Church degenerated into lordship. Afterward, when the provinces of the West were separated, the bishops were gradually admitted by the princes into their councils, a mixed forum was set up, the causes of laymen were summoned to it under the pretext of spirituality, and the divine right and the institution of Christ began to be alleged for this. At last, from the immense power of the spiritual realm, they came to erect a temporal tribunal in the midst of each political state, and to build an empire within an empire. Both the ecclesiastical and the political empire were taken from the bishops, and the Pope, lifting himself above every zelasma [ζέλασμα], seized them.

units.la: XVIII. Judicialem potestatem externam principalem Papa potestatis clavium Petro à Christo promissarum prætextu nequiquam sibi arrogat. Quid enim cum clavibus à Christo in persona Petri Ecclesiæ concessis jurisdictio ejusmodi proprie dicta, enses, lanceæ,sceptra,coronæ plena in omnia Regna,animas & corpora potestas,quæ cuncta insani ex clavibus cudunt, commune habent? Claves Christus non uni Monarchæ,sed Ecclesiæ dedit; & dedit claves Regni Cœlorum, non terræ ; & dedit ad solvendum & retinendum peccata, hoc est , declarationem remissorum peccatorum iis, qui credunt & obediunt: retentionem peccatorum iis, qui non credunt & non obediunt. Scitè Bernhardus de Consid. lib. I. 6. clavigeros alloquitur: In criminibus, non possessionibus est potestas vestra, quoniam propter illa, & propter has accepistis claves Regni Cœlorum. Sed de clavium potestate illa, & pascendi munere Petro commisso plura infra. Adversus Presbyterum accusationem suscipere, nisi sub duobus aut tribus testibus, Apostolus I. Tim. V. 19. vetuit. Sed κατηγορίαν accusationem illam intelligit non forensem & streperam,sed ἀγάπῃ charitativam, comparatam ad id,ut accusatus publicè , dum fideles ad Synaxin convenirent,corriperetur,& ad frugem revocaretur. Neque testes examinandi erant, ut Timotheus judicii forma servata ad judiciales forenses actus progredi posset, sed ut tuto modo & legitimè eum corripere posset. Quæ quidem correptio, quia per judicium Ecclesiæ fieri debet, & magna cum confusione conjuncta est, cavendum est , ne temerè & non satis testatò procedat. Licèt enim in omnibus observandum sit, ne accipiatur שם fama ἀδηλος, Exod. XXIII. 1. tamen id vel maximè fieri in Presbyteris Apostolus jubet, quibus Diabolus præ cæteris insidiatur, id satagens unicè,ut eos diffamet. De Virga S. Pauli I. Cor. IV. 21 supra vidimus. Miraculosa ejus per Apostolos adhibi- Argumenta pro eadem ad partes vocantur. adhibitæ operatio fuit ; & adhibita eadem ab omnibus Ecclesiæ Pastoribus ad correptiones, increpationes,& ad extemum ad excommunicationem referri potest. Et habet omnino Ecclesia judicium , quod publicum etiam à correptione ad excommunicationem usque progredi potest,sed citra jurisdictionem coërcitivam & forensem. Licèt enim Ecclesia peccatorem corripere, pœnitentem consolari, & ad reparandum scandalum obligare, contumaces verò vitare , & commercio eorum abstinere possit & debeat,tamen ad pœnitentiam vel reparationem scandali & damni neminem cogere , neque renitenti vim externam opponere potest. Neque excommunicationis gladio obnoxia quævis peccata sunt,sed ea demum,quæ Ecclesiam scandalizant,vel externum ejus statum perturbant, adeò ut si ea non corripiantur vel emendentur, ruinæ spiritualis occasio multis existere possint. Cæterùm non hic vel vis externa, vel vindictæ violentia, vel destructio, sed sola scandali reparatio, pœnitentia,& peccatoris ipsius salus intenditur. Et peccatores scandalosos habere pro Ethnicis & publicanis,eorúmque consortio religioso omni abstinere non ex vi alicujus imperii, sed communis libertatis,licet. Liberum enim cuique est, quem velit, in familiarem secum conversationem recipere; à qua ut excludantur homines perverso ingenio & maleferiati , ipsi quoque sapientes suadent. Merum verò Innocentii III. cavillum & sophistica stropha est, ob rationem solam peccati jurisdictionem in causas civiles acquirere,& supremas potestates,quæ in terris nullum judicem superiorem habent, indirectè subjicere velle ; quia in controversiis publicis quis alteri injuriam faciat , Ecclesiæ constare non potest. Quæstio enim ibi est de jure,quod solius judicis civilis, non Ecclesiæ cognitioni subjacet. Et fieret sic fororum confusio,cùm tamen nemo extra forum suum trahi debeat. Quòd si peccator contumax excommunicatus turbare animum induxerit,non ille per Ecclesiæ,sed per Magistratus civilis imperium in ordinem redigi debet. Inanis quinetiam ratio illa est,quòd causæ fori Episcopalis propriæ,cùm meræ spirituales sint , à laicis dijudicari non possint. Nam verè spiritualia,cujusmodi fides, resipiscentia, justificatio,regeneratio,&c. omnibus fidelibus communia sunt. Sed alia omnia Hierarchicis spiritualia dicuntur. Velut jura Regalia,potestas convocandi Synodos , decretis vim legis imprimendi,hæreticos coërcendi, de decimis, proventibus, prædiis, matrimoniis, gradibus consanguinitatis, repudiis , divortiis, Testamentis , legatis, fabricis Ecclesiarum, Xenodochiis,&c. administrandis decernendi.Quæ spiritualitatis fuco venditata reapse merè temporalia & corporalia sunt; & eos, qui ea occupant & exercent,in Principes mundi commutant, efficiúntque, ut relictis iis, quæ propriè spiritualia sunt, in temporalia involantes,ædilitatem,quod ajunt, sine suffragio gerant.
units.tr: XVIII. The Pope vainly claims for himself principal external judicial power under the pretext of the power of the keys promised to Peter by Christ. For what does jurisdiction of this kind, properly so called, full of swords, lances, sceptres and crowns, a power over all kingdoms, souls and bodies, which madmen forge from the keys, have in common with the keys granted by Christ to the Church in the person of Peter? Christ gave the keys not to a single monarch but to the Church; and he gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven, not of the earth; and he gave them to loose and to retain sins, that is, to declare sins forgiven to those who believe and obey, and to retain sins in the case of those who do not believe and do not obey. Bernhard aptly addresses the key-bearers in his book On Consideration, I, 6: Your power lies in crimes, not in possessions, for it is for those crimes, and for these possessions, that you have received the keys of the kingdom of heaven. But more on that power of the keys, and on the office of feeding committed to Peter, below. The Apostle, 1 Tim. 5:19, forbade receiving an accusation against an elder, except under two or three witnesses. But by that accusation [κατηγορία] he means not a forensic and noisy one, but a charitable accusation, arranged so that the accused might be rebuked publicly, while the faithful were gathered for the Synaxis, and brought back to a good way of life. Nor were witnesses to be examined, so that Timothy, the form of judgment being observed, might proceed to forensic judicial acts; rather, he might rebuke him safely and lawfully. Yet since this rebuke must be made by the judgment of the Church and is attended by great confusion, care must be taken that it does not proceed rashly and without sufficient testimony. For although in all things one must take care not to accept an uncertain report [שם], Exod. 23:1, the Apostle bids this above all be done for elders, against whom the Devil lays snares more than against others, eagerly seeking only to defame them. We have seen above, on the rod of St. Paul, 1 Cor. 4:21, that its miraculous operation was used by the Apostles, and the same power is brought to bear by all the pastors of the Church in corrections, reproofs, and finally in excommunication. And the Church certainly has a judgment, which can proceed in public from correction up to excommunication, but without coercive and forensic jurisdiction. For although the Church can and ought to rebuke a sinner, console a penitent, and oblige him to repair the scandal, and can and ought to avoid the obstinate and abstain from intercourse with them, yet it cannot compel anyone to repentance or to repair scandal and loss, nor can it oppose external force to one who resists. Nor are all sins liable to the sword of excommunication, but only those which scandalize the Church or disturb its external state, so that if they are not rebuked or amended they may become an occasion of spiritual ruin for many. Moreover, here the aim is not external force, nor the violence of vengeance, nor destruction, but only the repair of the scandal, the repentance, and the salvation of the sinner himself. And it is lawful to regard scandalous sinners as heathens and tax collectors, and to abstain from religious fellowship with them, not by the force of any command but by the common liberty of all. For it is free for each to receive into intimate companionship whom he wishes; and wise men themselves advise that people of perverse disposition and bad character be excluded from it. But the sophistry of Innocent III is pure trickery and a clever ruse: that by the reason of sin alone he acquires jurisdiction over civil causes, and wishes to bring supreme powers, which have no higher judge on earth, indirectly under subjection, because the Church cannot know in public controversies who does injury to another. For the question there concerns a right that belongs to the cognizance of the civil judge alone, not of the Church. And in this way there would be a confusion of courts, although no one ought to be drawn outside his own forum. But if a contumacious excommunicated person should decide to disturb the peace, he must be brought into order not by the authority of the Church but by the power of the civil magistrate. Nor is that reason empty, by which it is said that the causes of the proper episcopal forum, since they are purely spiritual, cannot be judged by laymen. For things truly spiritual, such as faith, repentance, justification, regeneration, and so on, are common to all the faithful. But all the other things are called spiritual by the hierarchs. Such are the royal rights, the power of convoking synods, of giving decrees the force of law, of restraining heretics, and of deciding matters concerning tithes, revenues, estates, marriages, degrees of consanguinity, repudiations, divorces, wills, legacies, the building of churches, hospices, and so on. These things, put forward under the cloak of spirituality, are in fact purely temporal and bodily; and they change those who seize and exercise them into princes of the world, so that, leaving behind what is properly spiritual and flying off into temporal things, they conduct, as the saying goes, the office of the aedile without the vote of the people.

units.la: XIX. Cùm Ecclesiæ Regimen externum ministeriale, nec Monarchicum sit, nec populum visibili imperio obnoxium , nec potestatem νομοθετικὴν , vel judicialem externam & principalem obtineat, frustra ejus subjectum quæritur,quod legitimum & Christianum null-lum esse potest. Sed Monarchici tamen Regimini suo Antichristiano incrustando , Divinæ institutionis subjecti colorem invenerunt. Nam regimen Monarchicum à Christo commissum esse B. Petro , velut unico vicario suo, pertendunt. Sed parum à blasphemia & perduellione abest, Christo, qui nunquam ab Ecclesia abest,& verbo, operatione gratiæ, Divinitate & Spiritus S. præsentia ei conjunctissimus & præsentissimus ejusdem negotiis omnibus præesse potest & vult,velut absenti vicarium cum imperio,quale ipsius Christi est,surrogare. Tam enim in regenda Ecclesia nullo indiget, quàm in Regno naturæ nullo indiget, qui vicariam ipsi operam præstet. In Politico verò Regimine temporalibus invigilante , & circa corpora hominum occupato, qui vicarii Dei dicuntur Reges & Principes , non absentis Dei vicarii sunt, & organa potiùs Dei habendi sunt, quibus in regimine eo sic utitur , ut potestatem in corpora iis tradat. Alia verò Ecclesiastici regiminis , quod circa animas & conscientias hominum versatur, ratio est ; utpote in quo vicarius Christi cum dominio & potestate in animas & conscientias dari nullus potest, quia solius Dei id πλεονεξημα est. Proin etiam ad ejusmodi regimen nec corporali præsentia Christi opus est,quia Christus spirituali & interna præsentia omnia præstat. Ecce ego vobiscum sum usque ad consummationem seculi, Matth. XXVIII.20. In solo enim Christo , non in quodam ejus vicario uni sumus. Studentes servare unitatem Spiritus in vinculo pacis. Unum corpus & unus Spiritus. Unus Dominus, una fides : unum baptisma. Unus Deus & Pater omnium, Ephes. IV. 3–6. Et tam non Christi , qui Ecclesiæ caput, & Sponsus est, vicarius datur, quàm non capitis & Sponsi vicarius datur. Præterea Christus Ecclesiam regit , eámque ad se adducit verbo, quod sceptrum roboris ejus est, Psal.CX.2. tum operatione Spiritus ejus. Quatenus verò ille per Spiritum suum operatur, nullus ei vicarius datur , quia ipse aperit cor Lydiæ,Actor. XVI. 14. baptizat Spiritu,Marc. I. 8.& nobiscum est usque ad consummationem seculi, Matth. XXVIII. 20. Quatenus verò homines verbi sui præconio regit & vocat, omnes verbi ministri ejus, nullo discrimine,quodammodo vicarii sunt. Illos enim legat, qui vices ejus gerant , & per quos mortalibus verbum suum annuntiat. Hinc duodecim Apostolos alloquitur: Qui vos recipit,me recipit,&c.Matth. X.40. & Septuaginta discipulos. Qui vos audit, me audit, Luc. X. 16. Ideo S. Paulus de se, Timotheo,Sylvano cæterisque communem in labore Domini operam navantibus testatur: ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ πρεσβεύομεν. Nomine, vice Christi legatione fungimur , tanquam Deo obsecrante per nos,rogamus pro Christo: Reconciliamini Deo, 2. Cor. V.20. Cúmque verbum Dei Spiritus S. ἐνεργὴς efficax reddatur, neque Christo, quatenus per Spiritum suum operatur,quisquam vicarius succedat,manifestum est, Christo Ecclesiæ Regi & Capiti propriè vicarium nullum surrogari posse. Inaniter enim verbum aures pulsat, nisi Dominus Spiritu suo fores cordis referet ; & neque qui plantat, est aliquid, neque qui rigat,sed qui dat incrementum, Deus, 1. Cor. III.7. Et si vicarii Christi propriè essent,quorum
units.tr: XIX. Since the external ministerial government of the Church is neither monarchical, nor subjects the people to a visible empire, nor possesses a legislative or external and principal judicial power, it is vain to seek a subject for such power, since no legitimate and Christian subject for it can exist. Yet the monarchists, to dress up their Antichristian government, have found a colour of divine institution for its subject. For they contend that monarchical government was committed by Christ to St Peter as his sole vicar. But it is hardly far from blasphemy and treason to suppose that Christ, who is never absent from the Church, and who is most closely joined to it and most present with it by his Word, by the working of grace, by his divinity and by the presence of the Holy Spirit, can and wills to preside over all its affairs, and yet needs to appoint a vicar with the authority that belongs to Christ himself, as though he were absent. For he has no more need of a vicar to govern the Church than he has need of anyone to perform a vicarious service in the kingdom of nature. In political government, which watches over temporal affairs and is concerned with men's bodies, those who are called vicars of God, namely kings and princes, are not vicars of an absent God, but are rather to be regarded as instruments of God, whom he uses in government in such a way that he hands over power over bodies to them. The case of ecclesiastical government, however, which is concerned with men's souls and consciences, is different. In it no vicar of Christ can be given dominion and power over souls and consciences, because this prerogative belongs to God alone. Therefore such government does not even need the bodily presence of Christ, since Christ accomplishes everything by his spiritual and inward presence. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world, Matth. XXVIII.20. For we are one in Christ alone, not in some vicar of his. Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one Spirit; one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, Ephes. IV.3–6. Just as no vicar is given to Christ, who is the head and bridegroom of the Church, so no vicar is given to the head and bridegroom. Moreover, Christ governs the Church and draws it to himself by his Word, which is the sceptre of his strength, Psal. CX.2, and also by the working of his Spirit. But insofar as he works through his Spirit, no vicar is given to him, since he himself opens the heart of Lydia, Acts XVI.14, baptizes with the Spirit, Mark I.8, and is with us even to the end of the world, Matth. XXVIII.20. Insofar as he governs and calls men by the proclamation of his Word, all the ministers of his Word, without any distinction, are in a certain sense his vicars. For he sends those who act in his place, and through whom he announces his Word to mortals. Hence he addresses the twelve Apostles: He who receives you receives me, etc., Matth. X.40, and likewise the seventy disciples: He who hears you hears me, Luke X.16. Therefore St Paul testifies of himself, Timothy, Silvanus and the others who share the common labour of the Lord's work: ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ πρεσβεύομεν [we are ambassadors for Christ]. We serve in the name and place of Christ as ambassadors, as though God were entreating through us; we beg on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God, 2 Cor. V.20. And since the Word of God is made ἐνεργὴς [effective] by the Holy Spirit, and since no one succeeds Christ as vicar insofar as he works through his Spirit, it is plain that no vicar can properly be substituted for Christ, the King and Head of the Church. For the Word strikes the ears in vain unless the Lord by his Spirit opens the doors of the heart; neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase, 1 Cor. III.7. And if the vicars of Christ were truly such, through whose work his Word is preached and made known, then not one man alone, such as Peter and his successors, but countless other vicars of Christ would exist. For the Hierarchs talk nonsense when they say that all bishops are vicars of Christ in common, but that Peter alone was, and the Pope is, so by excellence. Their claim is certainly groundless. For the Pope, by that excellence, strips all the bishops of the honour of being vicars of Christ, with which Christ has adorned them, and counts them as vicars not of Christ but of himself; just as Cardinal Turrecremata expressly calls them vicars of the Pope. If they are also vicars of Christ, they will be vicars of the Pope first and directly, and of Christ consequently and secondarily. And since the vicar of Christ is none other than one who preaches the Word of Christ, the Pope certainly cannot be called the vicar of Christ either in common or by excellence, because he does not preach the Word of God. As for their contention that Christ was the visible ruler of the Church on earth, and that therefore a visible ruler of the Church ought never to be lacking, we have already sufficiently refuted it above.

units.la: {a} carium in- stitutionis rum opera verbum ejus prædicatur & innotescit, non unus aliquis, velut Petrus & ejus successores, sed alii innumeri vicarii Christi essent. Nam quòd omnes Episcopos Christi vicarios esse communiter, unum verò Petrum fuisse & Papam esse per excellentiam Hierarchici nugantur, frustra certè sunt. Nam omnes Episcopos Papa per excellentiam illam honore vicariorum Christi, quo à Christo decorati sunt, spoliat, & eos in vicariis non Christi, sed suis numerat, sicut Cardinalis Turrecremata eos diserte Papæ vicarios appellat. Si illi Christi quoque vicarii sunt; primò & directè Papæ, consequenter & secundario Christi vicarii erunt. Cùmque Christi vicarius non alius sit, quàm qui Christi verbum prædicat, Papa certè vicarius Christi nec communiter, nec per excellentiam dici potest, quia verbum Dei non prædicat. Quòd verò illi Christum in terra Ecclesiæ rectorem visibilem fuisse, adeóque nunquam rectorem Ecclesiæ visibilem deesse debere, regerunt, abundè supra diluimus.
units.tr: If they were properly Christ's vicars, through whose ministry of institution his word is preached and made known, then not one man alone, such as Peter and his successors, but countless other vicars of Christ would exist. That all bishops are Christ's vicars in common, but that Peter alone was, and the Pope is, so by pre-eminence, is what the Hierarchists talk nonsense about, and it is certainly in vain. For the Pope, by that pre-eminence, strips all bishops of the honour of Christ's vicars with which Christ has adorned them, and counts them as vicars not of Christ but of his own. Thus Cardinal Turrecremata expressly calls them vicars of the Pope. If they are also Christ's vicars, they will be, first and directly, vicars of the Pope, and consequently and secondarily, vicars of Christ. And since a vicar of Christ is none other than one who preaches Christ's word, the Pope certainly cannot be called a vicar of Christ either in common or by pre-eminence, because he does not preach the word of God. As for their claim that Christ was a visible ruler of the Church on earth, and that a visible ruler of the Church ought therefore never to be lacking, we have already refuted this at sufficient length above.

units.la: XX. Cùm igitur Christus proprie vicarium, cum potestate suprema in Ecclesiam in terris degentem, nullum instituerit, neque talis omnino citra gloriæ ejus detrimentum instituì potuerit, manifestum est, nec B. Petrum vicarium ejusmodi, & visibile Ecclesiæ caput ab eodem institutum esse. Licèt enim B. Petri gloriæ nihil invideamus, vel detrahamus, imò quædam ejus ultro agnoscamus, & Deum in donis, zelo inprimis pro Christi gloria, eximia pietate, animi præsentia & ππαρρησίᾳ, Apostolo huic collatis celebremus: tamen Ecclesiæ caput, Regem & Dominum vicarium eum sine Christi vægrandi injuria agnoscere non possumus. Christus certè Apostolos omnes cum pari potestate misit. Sicut me misit Pater, ita ego mitto vos, Joh. XX. 21. Quæ perperam adversarii sic detorquent, ut asserant, Petrum cum singulari supra Apostolos cæteros ὑπεροχῇ missum esse, quia missus sit ut Ecclesiæ Princeps & rector, ceu figuram gerens Ecclesiæ cum ordine ad perpetuum Ecclesiæ statum super ipso, ceu petra ad finem usque mundi fundandum; & cum potestate regiminis seu præceptiva, relicta Apostolis reliquis, ceu delegatis extra ordinem, & cum potestate gubernationis, hoc est, executiva. Quæ hypocriseos papalis pigmenta Christo, Petro & Apostolis reliquis haud levem injuriam faciunt. Christo, quia ei Principem, Caput & Regem alium conjungentes gloriam potestatis & majestatis ejus promiscuam faciunt, gloriam ejus נכרי alienant, denique cum mundano Rege, vicariis indigo ob impotentiam imperii contendunt. Petro, quia eum sic infra reliquorum Apostolorum dignitatem quodammodo deprimunt. Si enim reliqui Apostoli potestatem delegatam extraordinariam, Petrus ordinariam, acceperunt, illi ergo legati Christi extraordinarii, Petrus ordinarius fuerint. Atqui ministerium extraordinarium majora dona, quàm ordinarium habet. Et si Petrus ordinarius fuit, quid opus at reliquis extraordinariis? Si ordinarius propterea, quia in ejus locum alii succedere debent, atque in eo omnis prærogativa illa constitit, ea ut frueretur, prius mori debuit, nec vivus adhuc quacunque re excelluit. Apostolis reliquis, quia cùm in ministerio Ecclesiæ Apostolica authoritate nulla major sit, Apostoli tamen reliqui infra unius authoritatem, ad facienda hujus imperata sic deprimuntur. Cùmque successores Petri ex eorum sententia, eandem potestatem habeant, majores illi fuissent superstitibus Petro, velut Johanni. Nam ita Linus, vel quisquis Petri successor fuisset, imperii, Johannes Apostolus, Petro superstes, obsequii gloriam habuisset.
units.tr: XX. Since Christ therefore did not institute any vicar in the proper sense, with supreme power over the Church dwelling on earth, and since such a vicar could not have been instituted at all without detriment to his glory, it is plain that neither St Peter was instituted by him as such a vicar and visible head of the Church. For although we begrudge nothing of St Peter's glory and do not detract from it, indeed we gladly acknowledge some of his qualities, and we celebrate God's gifts bestowed on this Apostle: his outstanding piety, zeal above all for the glory of Christ, presence of mind and παρρησία [boldness]: nevertheless we cannot acknowledge him as head of the Church, its king and lord, and as vicar, without injury to the glory of Christ. Christ certainly sent all the Apostles with equal power. As the Father sent me, so I send you, John XX.21. Our opponents twist this words wrongly, asserting that Peter was sent with a singular ὑπεροχή [pre-eminence] above the other Apostles, because he was sent as the Prince and ruler of the Church, bearing the figure of the Church, with reference to the perpetual state of the Church, with the Church built upon him as upon a rock until the end of the world; and with the power of government, that is, a preceptive power, the other Apostles being left as delegates outside the ordinary order, and with the power of administration, that is, executive power. These pigments of papal hypocrisy do no small injury to Christ, to Peter and to the other Apostles. To Christ, because by joining another Prince, Head and King to him they make the glory of his power and majesty common, they alienate his glory [נכרי], and finally they contend with the worldly king, who needs vicars because of the weakness of his rule. To Peter, because they in some measure depress him below the dignity of the other Apostles. For if the other Apostles received an extraordinary delegated power, and Peter an ordinary one, then they would be extraordinary legates of Christ and Peter the ordinary legate. But an extraordinary ministry has greater gifts than an ordinary one. And if Peter was the ordinary one, why is there any need for the others who were extraordinary? If he was ordinary because others ought to succeed him in his place, and because all that prerogative consisted in that, then he ought to have died first, in order to enjoy it, and while still alive he excelled in nothing at all. And the other Apostles are depressed, because in the ministry of the Church no authority is greater than apostolic authority, yet the other Apostles are depressed so as to be below the authority of one man, to carry out his commands. And since, according to their opinion, the successors of Peter have the same power, they would have been greater than Peter while he was still living, as John was. For so Linus, or whoever was Peter's successor, would have had the glory of command, and John the Apostle, who survived Peter, would have had the glory of obedience.

units.la: Petrus non est institutus vicarius Christi, quia supra Apostolos reliquos non eminuit. cum omni Apostolatus jure, cederet; quale quid Papa dictator, officiorum & provinciarum omnium diribitor, ipse,non tam dextram societatis jungere, quàm ad pudenda pedum oscula cunctos adigere suetus,nunquam certè committeret; quodque non dubitavit idem S. Paulus v. 11. Petro in os resistere, quia κα᾽ε-γνωσμένος, non reprehendendus duntaxat,ut Vulgatus perperam reddidit, sed condemnandus etiam,& quidem coram omnibus erat. Ubi S. Petrus correptionis & κατεγνωσμεν illius patiens documentum dedit posteris, posse,ut Augustinus etiam judicavit, priores à posterioribus (talis erat Paulus,ordine posterior,quia posterior vocatus) reprehendi & judicari; non posse superiorem & Principem, ab inferiori subdito, judicari. Imò verò S. Paulus consultò reprehensionem & condemnationem illam Petri commemorat,ut se Petro authoritate & potestate æqualem fuisse contra Pseudapostolos probaret. Neque enim Stapletonus Monarchicorum causam expedit, dicens, Paulum reprehendisse & damnasse Petrum ex humanitate, non authoritate; & Petrum ei cessisse ex modestia, non ex officio. Non enim simpliciter eum reprehendit; quod reverenter aliquis facere posset; sed ei restitit in faciem & coram omnibus,eúmque damnavit,quia subduxit se,metuit circumcisos,simulavit, coëgit judaizare, claudicavit,quæ omnia frontem,constantiam,acrimoniam sonant,neque adeò reverentiæ,humilitatis,modestiæ,qua minor erga majorem utitur, sed authoritatis testificationem habent. Quis, amabò, sic Papæ in faciem restiterit, & coram omnibus, nisi qui vincula & mortem ipsam perpeti prius animum obfirmaverit? Fuisse tamen authoritatem cum modestia,charitate, ὑπακοῆ conjunctam, nulli dubitamus. Sed ut paris in parem. Tum S. Paulus Petro resistens, vel id fecit suo jure, vel contra officium. Hoc quis dicere citra blasphemiam,qualem Hieronymus Porphyrio tribuit,ausit? Si jure resistere potuit, authoritatis igitur, non humanitatis fuit, resistere. Etiam Thomas Aquinas in 4. Sent. Dist. 19. q. 2. art. 2. factum Pauli Petrum reprehendentis excedere modum fraternæ correptionis, quæ Prælatis à subditis debetur,quia id factum coram multitudine fit, ingenuè fatetur. Et cessisse Petrum Paulo ex modestia,non ex officio,jejunum nimis est, quia Paulus Spiritu Dei eum reprehendit, & argumentis convicit. Si igitur cedere dedignatus esset,ipsi Spiritui S.& verbo Dei restitisset.Hoccine præter officium facturum putabimus? Hæc causa est,ob quam Veteres, eodem Thoma in Epist. ad Gal. fatente in fundatione Ecclesiæ Romanæ S. Paulum Petro æquant,& in sigillis plumbeis & cereis Romanensium Pragmaticarum Paulus ad dextram, Petrus ad sinistram collocatur. Fundatione certè Ecclesiæ vix alius illustrior authoritatis actus est.
units.tr: Peter was not instituted as Christ's vicar, because he did not stand out above the other Apostles, but would yield in every right of the apostleship. A thing such as a dictatorial Pope, the distributor of all offices and provinces, would never have done: he is accustomed not so much to extend the right hand of fellowship as to force everyone to kiss his shameful feet. And St Paul did not hesitate, Gal. II.11, to withstand Peter to the face, because he was κατεγνωσμένος [condemned], not merely to be reprehended, as the Vulgate wrongly renders it, but even to be condemned, and indeed before all men. Here St Peter, submitting to correction and to that κατεγνωσμένος [condemnation], gave a lesson to posterity: that, as Augustine also judged, earlier men may be reprehended and judged by later ones (such was Paul, later in order, because called later), but a superior and prince cannot be judged by an inferior subject. Indeed St Paul deliberately records that reprehension and condemnation of Peter, in order to prove against the false apostles that he was equal to Peter in authority and power. Nor does Stapleton help the cause of the monarchists when he says that Paul reprehended and condemned Peter out of humanity, not authority, and that Peter yielded to him out of modesty, not by duty. For Paul did not simply reprehend him, which anyone might do respectfully, but withstood him to the face and before all, and condemned him, because he drew back, feared the circumcised, dissembled, compelled to Judaize, and walked not uprightly. All these words suggest boldness, constancy and sharpness, and do not bear witness to reverence, humility or modesty, with which the lesser uses toward the greater, but to authority. Who, I ask you, would so withstand a Pope to his face, and before all, unless he had first hardened his mind to endure even chains and death itself? Yet we do not doubt that authority was joined with modesty, charity and ὑπακοή [obedience]. But let equal be judged against equal. Then, when St Paul withstood Peter, he either did so by his own right, or against his duty. Who would dare to say this without blasphemy, of the kind that Jerome attributed to Porphyry? If he was able to withstand him by right, then his withstanding was a matter of authority, not of humanity. Thomas Aquinas too frankly admits, in 4 Sent. dist. 19 q. 2 art. 2, that Paul's act in reprehending Peter exceeded the measure of fraternal correction, which is owed to prelates by their subjects, because the act was done before the multitude. And it is too foolish to say that Peter yielded to Paul out of modesty and not by duty, since Paul reprehended him and convinced him with arguments, by the Spirit of God. If Peter had disdained to yield, he would have resisted the Holy Spirit himself and the Word of God. Shall we think that he would have done anything contrary to his duty in this? This is the reason why the Ancients, as Thomas also admits in his Epistle to the Galatians, place St Paul on a level with Peter in the founding of the Church of Rome; and in the lead and wax seals of the Roman pragmatic decrees, Paul is placed on the right and Peter on the left. Certainly there is scarcely any more illustrious act of authority in the founding of the Church.

units.la: XXI. Accedunt alia etiam, fictitiam Petri majestatem non parum minuentia, velut quod pari cum reliquis Apostolis officio & authoritate missus, & Spiritu S. donatus est, Matth. X. 25. quod omnes Apostoli ὁμόθρονοι, ibid. XIX. 28. & fundamenta Ecclesiæ,Ephes. II. 20. Apoc. XXI. 14. dicuntur: quòd Apostolicus gradus summus fuit, neque Apostolo major quisquam in Ecclesia fuit, 1. Cor. XII. 28. Ephes. IV. 11. quòd in certamine Apostolorum de primatu, locus fuisset Petri primatum & prærogativas dominationis ejus aperte declarandi, si Ecclesiæ Pro-Rex & Vicarius is Christo placuisset,cùm tamen omnes pariter,nullo excepto, ob ambitum primatum increpentur, & ad humilitatem revocentur ejusmodi verbis, quibus omnis Monarchia & primatus ex cordibus eorum radicitus evellitur,admonente Christo gravissimè: Nôstis, quòd Principes gentium dominentur iis (non per tyrannidem, quia aliàs omnes tyranni forent) & magnates potestatem in eos exerceant. Non sic autem inter vos erit; sed qui voluerit (non qui jure est) inter vos magnus fieri, esto vester minister: & qui inter vos voluerit esse πρῶτος primus (en primatum omnem non in civilibus duntaxat,qualis Regum est, sed in Ecclesiasticis etiam,quia tota res sine ulla cautione negatur, & Christus non de modo & forma sed de re ipsa dominii loquitur, & Papæ dominatus etiam civilis est, elisum!) esto vester servus, Matth. XX. 25--28. Quòd Christus Apostolis omnibus edixit: Dic Ecclesiæ, adeóque etiam Petrus Ecclesiæ se subjicere debuit, ibid. XVIII. 17. quòd Petrus unà cum Johanne ab Apostolis in Samariam mittitur, ad Evangelium prædicandum, Actor. XI. 2. adeóque Apostolorum curæ æquè ac quivis alius obnoxius fuit: quòd graviter reprehendantur,qui se Cephæ esse dixerint,æquè ac illi,qui sePauli vel Apollinis esse dixerant,1.Cor.I. 12.13.non quòd sequaces Pauli & Apollinis,non sequaces Cephæ reprehendantur,æquè ac reprehendi sequaces Christi non poterant;uti Baroni° finxit, quia aliàs hi concordes fuissent: cùm tamen ceu schismatici cap.III.21.22.reprehendantur, dicente Paulo: Ne quis glorietur in hominibus,&c. Sive Paulus, sive Apollos, sive Cephas,&c. quòd in Concilio Hierosolymitano potiores Jacobi,uti Præsidis Concilii,quàm Petri partes fuerunt, Actor. XV. 13.&c. quòd etiam Johannes in quibusdam Petro major fuerit; velut in eo, quòd in sinu Domini recubuit, & dilectus ille discipulus Christi cluet, Joh. XXI. 20. & Canonem N. T. clausit; & Apostolorum maximè longævus,adventum Domini ad judicium particulare Judææ vidit,ibid. v. 22. quòd nunquam Petrus reliquis Apostolis,ubi de jure & auctoritate agitur, majorem se gessit,vel agnosci voluit, sed potiùs se Apostolum,non aliquid majus, Presbyterum, imò συμπρεσβύτερον conseniorem 1. Petr. V. 1. 2. &c. vocat, & aliorum etiam Apostolorum præcepta fidelibus inculcat, 2. Petr. III. 2. 15. Denique cùm Papatus Oecumenici moderni Majestatis pontificiæ actus ἐξαιρέτοι & characteres γνώρισμα sint, adorari instar Numinis,pedum oscula à summis Monarchis excipere, Scripturæ & legum Divinarum authoritatem arbitrio suo subjicere, fidem ex verbo Dei non probatam,non exploratam à fidelibus conscientiis dictare, & invitis obtrudere: Concilia à nutu suo suspendere; contra leges Divinas dispensare,spiritualium prætextu Regnum merè terrenum in Imperatores, Reges,Principes mundi erigere, atque illud maximo cum splendore in mundo proferre; hos similésque Oecumenici Papatus actus Petrum exercuisse,non priùs Monarchici proprobaverint, quàm Petrum Neronem fuisse iidem probaverint.
units.tr: XXI. There are also other points which greatly diminish the fictitious majesty of Peter. For example, he was sent and endowed with the Holy Spirit (missus, Spiritu S. donatus) with the same office and authority as the other Apostles, Matt. 10:25. All the Apostles are called co-enthroned [ὁμόθρονοι], Matt. 19:28, and the foundations of the Church, Eph. 2:20; Rev. 21:14. The apostolic rank was the highest, and no one in the Church was greater than an Apostle, 1 Cor. 12:28; Eph. 4:11. In the Apostles' dispute about primacy, if Christ had approved of a Vicar and Pro-King of the Church, this would have been the place to declare Peter's primacy and his prerogatives of lordship openly. Yet all alike, none excepted, are rebuked for ambition for primacy and called back to humility by words that tear every monarchy and primacy root and branch from their hearts. Christ warned them most seriously: You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them (not by tyranny, for otherwise all rulers would be tyrants) and the great exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you; but whoever wishes (not whoever has the right) to become great among you, let him be your minister; and whoever among you wishes to be first [πρῶτος], (here is every primacy, not only in civil affairs, as belongs to kings, but in ecclesiastical ones too, since the whole matter is denied without any qualification, and Christ speaks not of the manner and form but of the very thing itself of lordship; and the Pope's lordship is civil as well: refuted!) let him be your servant, Matt. 20:25–28. Christ commanded all the Apostles: Tell it to the Church (Dic Ecclesiæ), Matt. 18:17, and so Peter too ought to have subjected himself to the Church. Peter, together with John, was sent by the Apostles into Samaria to preach the Gospel, Acts 11:2, and so was subject to the care of the Apostles no less than any other. Those who said they were of Cephas are severely rebuked, just as those who said they were of Paul or of Apollos were, 1 Cor. 1:12–13. The reproof was not that the followers of Paul and Apollos were rebuked while the followers of Cephas were not, just as the followers of Christ could not be rebuked; as Baronius imagined, because otherwise these would have been in agreement. Yet they are rebuked as schismatics, 1 Cor. 3:21–22, Paul saying: Let no one glory in men, etc. Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, etc. At the Council of Jerusalem, James, as president of the council, had a greater role than Peter, Acts 15:13 etc. John also was greater than Peter in some respects: for example, in that he reclined in the bosom of the Lord and is celebrated as the beloved disciple of Christ, John 21:20; he closed the canon of the New Testament; and, being the longest-lived of the Apostles, he saw the coming of the Lord to the particular judgment of Judea, ibid. v. 22. Peter never acted or wished to be recognized as greater than the other Apostles when matters of right and authority were at issue. Rather, he calls himself an Apostle, not something greater, but an elder [Presbyterum], indeed a fellow elder [συμπρεσβύτερον] (conseniorem), 1 Pet. 5:1–2 etc., and he impresses upon the faithful the precepts of the other Apostles as well, 2 Pet. 3:2, 15. Finally, since the exceptional acts and marks [ἐξαιρέτοι, γνώρισμα] of the majesty of the modern pontifical Ecumenical Papacy are to be worshipped like a deity, to receive kisses on the feet from the highest monarchs, to subject the authority of Scripture and divine laws to one's own judgment, to dictate and impose on unwilling consciences a faith not proved from the Word of God nor tested by the faithful, to suspend councils at one's nod, to dispense against divine laws, under the pretext of spiritual matters to raise a purely earthly kingdom above emperors, kings and princes of the world, and to display it in the world with the greatest splendour: the Monarchists would not have approved that Peter exercised these and similar acts of the Ecumenical Papacy until they had first approved that Peter was Nero.

units.la: XXII. Ficulnea folia sunt, quibus Petri suprematum illi comprobare & extundere conantur.
units.tr: XXII. They are fig leaves with which they try to prove and force out Peter's supremacy.

units.la: Levia illa sunt, quòd πεῶτον primum illum appellari, Matth. X.2. primo semper loco eum recenseri, primum verba fecisse; à Christo nomen ei mutatum esse; pro solo eo Christum didrachma solvisse, ib.XV II.24. objiciunt. Nam πεῶτων primum vocari solius ordinis velut inter æquales, non potestatis velut inter inæquales, causâ manifestum est, tum quia ibi diserte ordo inter Apostolos initur: tum quia potestas illa Apostolis ordine sic dispositis collata v.5. &c. non uni seorsim, sed omnibus simul, nullo discrimine, collata est. Qualiscunque ergo primatus Petro datus est, ille potestatis primatus esse non potest, quia æquales inter potestate primatus potestatis nulli competere potest, sed vel ordinis est, uti diximus, vel vocationis, uti alii ex, Matth.IV.18. colligunt. Licèt enim Andreas, Petri frater prior Christum Johannis Baptistæ monitu secutus fuerit, tamen uterque post, & prior quidem Petrus vocatus ex Joh.I.42. coll. cum Matth.IV.18. videri potest. Neque etiam primo semper loco Petrus recensetur, postpositus quippe Jacobo, Gal.II.9. Paulo, 1. Cor.III.22. & λοιπῖς Ἀπῳτόλοις reliquis Apostolis, ib.IX.5. Quòd primus ille locutus passim inducitur, ejusdem ordinis & vocationis primatui, imprimis verò singulari zelo & ἑρμότητι fervori, quo prædictum eum fuisse omnis Apostolorum historia docet, non ulli potestatis ὑπερoχῇ ferendum acceptum est. Neque etiam Christus nomen Simonis mutavit, quia constanter illud retinuit, & posteriori Epistolæ suæ capite I.1. ipsemet diserte præscripsit, sed novum duntaxat adjecit. Quod & aliis Apostolis factum est. Velut Jacobo & Johanni fratribus, quoqum nominibus Boanerges nomen Christus adjecit, Marc.III.17. Et pro solo Petro Christus Capernaumi didrachma solvit, quia solus cum Christo Capernaumi habitavit. Ubi autem quis commoratur, ibi etiam vectigal solvit.
units.tr: Those points are slight which they object: that he is called first [πρῶτον], Matt. 10:2, that he is always listed first, that he spoke first, that Christ changed his name, that Christ paid the didrachma for him alone, Matt. 17:24. For that he is called first [πρῶτος] only indicates the order, as among equals, not power, as among unequals. This is clear from the reason that there the order among the Apostles is expressly set out, and because that power, conferred on the Apostles in that order, v. 5 etc., was given not to one separately but to all together, without distinction. Whatever primacy was given to Peter, therefore, cannot be a primacy of power, because a primacy of power cannot belong to one who is equal in power; it is rather of order, as we have said, or of calling, as others gather from Matt. 4:18. For although Andrew, Peter's brother, followed Christ first, at the prompting of John the Baptist, both were called afterwards, and Peter may be seen as called first, from John 1:42 compared with Matt. 4:18. Nor is Peter always listed first; he is placed after James, Gal. 2:9, after Paul, 1 Cor. 3:22, and with the rest of the Apostles [reliquis Apostolis], 1 Cor. 9:5. That he is often introduced as speaking first is to be understood as belonging to the same order and calling as the primacy, and especially to his singular zeal and ardour [ἑρμότητι, fervori], by which the whole history of the Apostles shows him to have been endowed. It should not be taken as any exaltation [ὑπερoχῇ] of power. Nor did Christ change Simon's name, since he constantly retained it, and in his second Epistle, chapter 1 verse 1, he himself expressly wrote it; he merely added something new. This was also done for other Apostles: for James and John, brothers, Christ added to their names the name Boanerges, Mark 3:17. And Christ paid the didrachma at Capernaum for Peter alone because he alone lived with Christ at Capernaum. Wherever someone dwells, there he also pays the tax.

units.la: XXIII. Sed suprematum hunc Petro promissum & præstitum esse Monarchici fortiter asseve rant.
units.tr: XXIII. The Monarchists strongly maintain that this supremacy was promised to Peter and actually conferred on him.

units.la: Promissum enim ajunt à Christo Petro, Filium Dei se confitenti dicente: Ego tibi dico, quòd tu es Petrus. Et super hac Petra ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Et portæ inferorum non prævalebunt ei. Et dabo tibi claves Regni Cœlorum. Et quicquid solveris in terra, solutum erit in Cœlo; &c. Matth.XVI.18. 19. Petrum ergo Ecclesiæ petram, seu fundamentum ædificii spirituålis à Christo proclamatum, & symbolum ejusdem claves Regni Cœlorum, seu plenitudinem potestatis in solvendis & ligandis peccatoribus eidem soli à Christo commissam esse pertendunt. Quæ nimis contorta sunt. Non enim Christus personam Petri πέτρον petram illam, super qua ædificanda erat Ecclesia, intellexit, tum quia Petrus à petra & persona & genere, & ut denominans, quod petra est, & denominatum, quod Petrus est, distinguitur: tum quia ex eo tempore, quo Christus locutus est, eo visibiliter præsente Petrus non fuit petra, seu fundamentum Ecclesiæ, uti ex lapsu ejus constat; tum quia ex usu Scripturæ solus Christus
units.tr: They say that Christ promised this to Peter when he confessed the Son of God, saying: "I tell you that you are Peter. And upon this rock I will build my Church. And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven," etc. Matt. XVI.18, 19. They maintain, therefore, that Peter was proclaimed by Christ as the rock [πέτρα] and foundation of the spiritual building of the Church, and that the keys of the kingdom of heaven, which are its symbol, that is, the fullness of power in loosing and binding sinners, were committed to him alone by Christ. These claims are too strained. For Christ did not mean the person of Peter by that rock [πέτρον] on which the Church was to be built. This is because Peter is distinguished from petra in person and gender, as the one who names from the thing named (what petra is, and what Peter is). It is also because from the time Christ spoke, while he was visibly present, Peter was not the rock or foundation of the Church, as his fall shows. And it is because, by the usage of Scripture, only Christ

units.la: XXIV. Claves Regni Cœlorum, nec soli Petro promissæ sunt, nec potestatem herilem, principalem & dominicam, seu plenitudinem Ecclesiasticæ potestatis, uti Monarchici summam potestatem spiritualem & temporalem intelligentes, loquuntur; promiserunt. Non soli Petro promissæ sunt. Licèt enim ille in clavium ministerio ἐξαίρετον quid habuerit, quatenus ministerio suo & primus & singulari zelo tum Judæis, tum gentilibus Regnum Cœlorum, clavi minimè errante, aperuit, uti supra diximus; atque hæc etiam causa fit, quòd Christus claves eas speciatim Petro tradidit: tamen potestas ipsa clavium à Christo non soli Petro, sed in persona ejus Ecclesiæ universæ distinctis licet ejus muneribus commissa est. Sustinebat enim hic Petrus figuram Ecclesiæ, sive hypotypofin πιστῶν fidelium, ut S. Paulus, qui misericordiam consecutus est, ut Jesus Christus in ipso primò omnium longanimitatem exerceret, ὡς ὑπόντων ... μέλλοντων πιστευειν εις ζωήν ut exemplar esset eorum, qui crediturì erant in ipsum ad vitam æternam, 1.Tim.I.16. Ita plane Augustinus, & ipse Papa Leo I. hunc locum intellexerunt. Et res ipsa loquitur, quia quicquid Christus Petro promisit, id cæteris adpromisit. Sicut enim in illis, cùm omnes interrogarentur: Vos quem me esse dicitis? Matth.XVI.15. Petrus solus respondit. Tu es Christus, Filius Dei viventis, ib.16. ita illi soli Christus dixit: Tibi dabo claves Regni Cœlorum, v.19. quasi solus ligandi solvendique potestatem recepisset; cùm potiùs unus reliquorum omnium vice responsum daret, & hanc cum reliquis omnibus communem potestatem unus obtineret. Nam & illa ligandi & solvendi potestas, qua clavium potestatem ipse Christus explicavit, non uni soliquè Petro competebat, sed Ecclesiæ & fidelibus. Dic Ecclesiæ. Si non audiverit Ecclesiam, esto tibi velut ethnicus & publicanus, Amen dico vobis; ὅσα ἐὰν δήσητε quæcunque ligaveritis (ad plures hoc dictum, sicut cap.XVI.19. ὁ ἐὰν δήσης quicquid ligaveris &c. soli Petro dictum est) in terra, erunt ligata in Cœlo, & quæcunque solveritis in terra, erunt soluta in Cœlo, ib.XVIII.18. Cùmque ligare idem sit quod retinere, & solvere idem quod remittere; Christus potestatem retinendi & remittendi peccata promiscuam Apostolis fecit, dicens ad omnes: Quorum remiseritis peccata, remissa erunt; & quorum retinueritis, retenta erunt, Joh. XX.23. Quicquid ergo potestatis Petro datum est, sive ad jurisdictionem, sive ad ordinem illud retulerint, commune omnibus, non Petro proprium fuit. Perperam enim Bellarminus Apostolos Sacerdotes factos esse in ultima Cœna; clavim jurisdictionis accepisse per verba Christi; Sicut me Pater misit, ita ego mitto vos, ib.XX.21. Clavim verò ordinis verbis sequentibus: Quorum remiseritis peccata, &c. tricatur. Sic enim Sacerdotes fuissent sine clavibus; & Sacerdotium ac jurisdictionem accepisse nondum accepto ordine; & jurisdictionem non unus Petrus, sed aequalem omnes Apostoli accepissent. Quae juxta illos διανεμητικ sunt. Par figmentum eorum est, qui asserunt, clavium plenam potestatem omnibus Apostolis aequaliter collatam esse; sed Petro principaliter, quatenus potestas Apostolis data per Petrum in ea data sit, juxta illud Leonis M. Serm. 3. in ann. die assumpt. quod firmitas, quae per Christum Petro tributa est, per Petrum Apostolis collata sit. Sed aliter Leo ille de tribu Juda, Christus, qui non Apostolos potestatem suam Petro acceptam retulisse, sed cum illis Petrum proxime eam a Christo accepisse, Matth. XXVIII. 19. Joh. XX. 21. docet. Etiam Paulus post ascensionem Christi designatus Apostolus, tamen Apostolus fuit, non ab hominibus (adeoque nec a Petro) neque per homines, sed per Jesum Christum, ac Deum Patrem, qui eum ex mortuis suscitavit, Gal. I. 1. Neque in talibus de Apostolica duntaxat, non etiam Pastorali & Episcopali potestate, quod suppar eorundem figmentum est, sermo est, quia si omnis potestas, qua praediti sunt Episcopi, quatenus Episcopi, est potestas clavium, & Apostolis quatenus Apostoli, omnem potestatem clavium ipsis a Christo delegatam, obtinuerunt, non fuit ulla tam potestas, quam a Petro, quatenus Episcopi, recipere poterant; adeoque nec receperunt ab eo aliquam, nec in ea Petro inferiores fuerunt. Ideo etiam Sixtus Senensis Biblioth. S. lib. VI. Annot. 269. 271. Et Franciscus Victoria Relect. 2. de potest. Ecclesiae has argutias tanquam putridum pharmacum rejecerunt, ostendentes, quod Apostoli omnem suam potestatem immediate a Christo receperint. Qui etiam, ne Papatus rueret, potestati Apostolicae & Episcopali Petri, quam communem cum reliquis habuerit, tertiam addunt, potestatem Regni, qua Petrum omnibus Apostolis antecessisse asserunt, ut ita Papa quoque Episcopis imperaret. Quae potestas, utpote nuspiam Petro tributa, eadem facilitate negatur, qua asseritur.
units.tr: XXIV. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were promised neither to Peter alone, nor with the lordly, principal and dominical power, or the fullness of ecclesiastical authority, as the Monarchists claim when they understand it as supreme spiritual and temporal power. They were not promised to Peter alone. For although he had something outstanding in the ministry of the keys, inasmuch as by his ministry he first and with singular zeal opened the kingdom of heaven to both Jews and Gentiles, with the key never failing, as we said above, and this is also the reason why Christ handed those keys over to Peter by name, nevertheless the power of the keys itself was committed by Christ not to Peter alone but, in his person, to the whole Church, although with its several offices distinguished. For Peter here bore the figure of the Church, or the representation of the faithful [πιστῶν], just as St Paul, who "obtained mercy, that Jesus Christ might first of all show forth all longsuffering in him," [ὡς ὑπόντων ... μέλλοντων πιστευειν εις ζωήν], to be an example to those who would believe on him unto eternal life, 1 Tim. 1.16. Augustine and Pope Leo I himself certainly understood this passage in the same way. The thing itself speaks, because whatever Christ promised to Peter he promised to the others too. For just as, when all were asked, "Whom do you say that I am?" (Matt. 16.15), Peter alone answered, "You are Christ, the Son of the living God" (v. 16), so Christ said to him alone, "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven" (v. 19), as if he alone had received the power of binding and loosing; whereas rather one of them all gave the answer on behalf of all the rest, and one held this power in common with all the others. For that power of binding and loosing, by which Christ himself explained the power of the keys, belonged not to Peter alone but to the Church and the faithful. "Tell it to the Church. If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican" (Matt. 18.17). "Verily I say unto you" (v. 18), "whatsoever you bind" [ὅσα ἐὰν δήσητε] (this saying is addressed to many, just as chap. 16.19, "whatsoever you bind" [ὁ ἐὰν δήσης], was spoken to Peter alone) "on earth, shall be bound in heaven; and whatsoever you loose on earth, shall be loosed in heaven" (ib. 18.18). And since to bind is the same as to retain, and to loose the same as to remit, Christ gave the power of retaining and remitting sins to the apostles in common, saying to all: "Whose sins you remit, they are remitted; and whose sins you retain, they are retained" (John 20.23). Whatever power, therefore, was given to Peter, whether they refer it to jurisdiction or to order, it was common to all and not proper to Peter. For Bellarmine wrongly says that the apostles were made priests at the Last Supper; that they received the key of jurisdiction through the words of Christ, "As the Father has sent me, so I send you" (ib. 20.21); and he maintains that the key of order is given by the following words, "Whose sins you remit," etc. For in that case priests would have existed without keys, and would have received priesthood and jurisdiction before receiving orders, and jurisdiction would not have been received by Peter alone but equally by all the apostles, which by their reckoning is a distribution. Equally fictitious is the view of those who assert that full power of the keys was conferred equally on all the apostles, but on Peter principally, inasmuch as the power given to the apostles was given through Peter, according to that saying of Leo the Great (Sermon 3 on the anniversary of his assumption): that the firmness which was given to Peter through Christ was conferred on the apostles through Peter. But that same Leo, the man of the tribe of Judah, teaches otherwise: that the apostles did not refer to Peter the power they had received, but that Peter, together with them, received it directly from Christ (Matt. 28.19; John 20.21). Paul too, though designated an apostle after the ascension of Christ, was an apostle "not from men" (and so not from Peter), "nor through men, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead" (Gal. 1.1). Nor is the discussion only of apostolic power, but also of pastoral and episcopal power, which is an equally fictitious claim. For if all the power which bishops possess, as bishops, is the power of the keys, and the apostles, as apostles, obtained all the power of the keys delegated to them by Christ, then there was no power which they could receive from Peter as bishops; and so they received nothing from him in that capacity, nor were they inferior to Peter in it. Therefore Sixtus of Siena (Bibliotheca Sancta, bk. 6, annotations 269 and 271) and Francisco Victoria (Relectio 2 de potestate Ecclesiae) also rejected these subtleties as a rotten remedy, showing that the apostles received all their power immediately from Christ. In order that the Papacy should not collapse, these men also add to Peter's apostolic and episcopal power, which he had in common with the others, a third, the power of kingship, by which they assert that Peter surpassed all the apostles, so that the Pope might also command the bishops. That power, since it is nowhere attributed to Peter, is denied with the same ease with which it is asserted.

units.la: XXV. Cum igitur nihil aliud Petro promissum sit, quam quod ei concessum est, concessa vero aequalis cunctis Apostolis potestas sit, promissione illa clavium Petri Suprematus stabiliri non potest, ut vel magis ratae tabulae proferendae sint, vel jus ilthoc omne in nihilum recidat. Quid vero multis? Dicant modo οι ιξ ευαγγελιας Christus Petro claves dederit, ut domino, ad referendos thesauros proprios, an ut ministro, oeconomo; Si prius, ipse dominium una cum jure clavium exuit & abdicavit. Sed id Sanctus & verax ille diserte negavit, dicens; se habere clavim Davidis, & se aperiente nemi-nem claudere, claudente neminem aperire, Apoc. III. 7. Si posterius, cur illi claves Petri in coronam tricipitem, in sceptra, gladios commutant; & cum claves ministrae crucis Christi esse debeant, cur eorum ειδωλον claves Petri dextra, crucem Christi sinistra gerit? Cur claves non Regni Coelorum, sed etiam terrae sibi arrogant? Cur Papa administrat ubique, non ut servus & oeconomus, sed ut herus, Rex regum, & dominus dominantium, qui principali suo, non alienam voluntate fores aperit claudítque, & thesauros velut suos, non alienos referat? Administrat enim verbo, ut minister, sed reapse ut Dominus terrestris, multa praescribens, committens, ordinans & vetans, quae ut committat, praescribat, ordinet & vetet, nuspiam a Christo, supremo domino, ei injunctum est? Par utique ratio est ligationis & solutionis, retentionis & remissionis peccatorum Petro, & reliquis Apostolis, totaque Ecclesiae commissae. Petrus vero, Apostoli, ministri omnes Christi ligant, solvunt, retinent, remittunt peccata, volente, ordinante, praescribente conditionem omnem sententiamque Domino, vel non. Si prius, non aliter utique omni officio eo defunguntur, quam quatenus voluntatem, sententiam, conditionem placitam ex praescripto Domini, praevia vocatione legitima, praedicant & promulgant. Sic ergo ligatio, solutio, retentio & remissio tota erit ministerialis sine potestate principali & judiciali ulla. Si posterius, potestatem Dei involant, qui solus voluntate & sententia propria, atque placita conditione ligat & solvit, peccata retinet & remittit.
units.tr: XXV. Since therefore nothing else was promised to Peter than what was granted to him, and an equal power was granted to all the apostles, the supremacy of Peter cannot be established by that promise of the keys, so that either the more solid charters must be produced or all that right collapses into nothing. But why say more? Let them only say whether Christ gave Peter the keys as a lord, to open his own treasures, or as a minister and steward. If the former, he himself stripped himself of dominion together with the right of the keys and renounced it. But that holy and true one flatly denied this, saying that he has "the key of David, so that when he opens, no one shuts, and when he shuts, no one opens" (Rev. 3.7). If the latter, why do they change the keys of Peter into a three-tiered crown, into sceptres and swords? And since the keys ought to be ministers of the cross of Christ, why does their idol carry the keys of Peter in its right hand and the cross of Christ in its left? Why do they claim the keys not only of the kingdom of heaven but of the earth too? Why does the Pope everywhere govern not as a servant and steward but as a master, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who opens and shuts the doors by his own will and not by another's, and takes up the treasures as if they were his own and not another's? For he administers by the word as a minister, but in fact as a terrestrial lord, prescribing, committing, ordaining and forbidding many things, which he has nowhere been enjoined by Christ, the supreme Lord, to commit, prescribe, ordain and forbid? The rule of binding and loosing, of retaining and remitting sins, is surely the same for Peter, for the other apostles, and for the whole Church committed to them. But Peter, the apostles and all the ministers of Christ bind, loose, retain and remit sins, with the Lord willing, ordaining and prescribing every condition and sentence, or not. If the former, they discharge every office in no other way than by proclaiming and publishing the will, sentence and condition pleasing to the Lord, as prescribed by him, after a prior lawful call. So binding, loosing, retaining and remitting will be wholly ministerial, without any principal or judicial power at all. If the latter, they rob God of his power, who alone binds and looses, retains and remits sins, by his own will and sentence and by his pleasing condition.

units.la: XXVI. Quod Petro a Christo promissum non est, id ei solutum & praestitum esse a Christo, jubente eum praesentibus tribus Apostolis Jacobo, Johanne & Thoma, pascere oves & agnos suos, Joh. XXI. 15-17. nequicquam Monarchici asserunt. Jam enim supra argumento huic nervos elilimus, veritati aperte dantes, quod pascere alienas oves, non sit iis dominari, sed ministrare in gratiam heri. Omni exceptione major interpres ipse Petrus est, Sympresbyter Presbyteros jubens pascere gregem Dei, curando non coacte (ut heri solent) sed sponte, 1. Pet. V. 2. Potest enim etiam ancilla & vile mancipium pascere filium Regis, in quemjus imperii nullum habet. Pascendi enim munus ut plurimum notat ministerium curandi oves alienas, quarum ne lanam quidem pastor diripere, nisi gratiam faciente domino, ausit. Et quoties Regibus illa vox tribuitur, non eorum imperium, sed οικονομιαν curam, seu procurationem subditorum notari Grammatici observant. Si inter oves illas, quas Petrus pascere jussus est, etiam Apostoli fuerunt, ubi Apostolos Petrus pavit? Ubi jura Papatus adversus eos exercuit? Neque soli Petro, sed reliquis etiam Apostolis, imo ministris Ecclesiae omnibus pascendi munus injunctum est, Actor. XX. 28. Ephes.
units.tr: XXVI. What was not promised to Peter by Christ, that the Monarchists vainly assert was resolved and granted to him by Christ, when, with the three apostles James, John and Thomas present, he bade him "feed my sheep and my lambs" (John 21.15–17). For we have already cut the sinews of this argument above, freely granting the truth that to feed another's sheep is not to lord it over them but to minister for the sake of the master. The interpreter above all exception is Peter himself, a fellow elder, who bids the elders "feed the flock of God, taking the oversight not under compulsion, as lords do, but willingly" (1 Pet. 5.2). For even a maidservant or a base slave may feed the son of a king, over whom she has no authority. For the duty of feeding ordinarily denotes the ministry of caring for another's sheep, whose wool even a shepherd dare not tear away except by the lord's favour. And grammarians observe that whenever that word is applied to kings, it denotes not their rule but their oikonomia, that is, their care and management of their subjects. If among those sheep which Peter was bidden to feed the apostles were also included, where did Peter feed the apostles? Where did he exercise the rights of the Papacy against them? And the duty of feeding was enjoined not only on Peter but on the other apostles, and indeed on all the ministers of the Church (Acts 20.28; Eph.).

units.la: Nec herilis & dominica ei promissa est.
units.tr: Nor was a lordly and dominical promise made to him.

units.la: Eph.IV.11. Cujuslibet Pastoris est pascere gregem suum. Si igitur pascendi vocabulum plenitudinem potestatis supremo capiti peculiarem significat, quilibet pastor gregis sui supremum caput erit. Et quid tandem Papæ supererit? Nam quòd Joh.XXI.15.16. soli Petro trina compellatione munus pascendi oves & agnos Christi injungitur, non singulare ejus privilegium, sed potiùs restitutionem in munus Apostolatus, quo per trinam abnegationem excidisse videri poterat, significat. Scitè enim S.Augustinus Tract.123. in Joh. dixit: Ter Petrum Christus de amore interrogat, ut trina responsione trinam abnegationem Christi compenset. Jussus equidem Petrus est pascere oves & agnos Christi indefinitè, non notato ovium & agnorum discrimine. Sed non ideo universos homines, & ipsos etiam Apostolos Petro pastori Christus subjecit; sicut non ideo Christus reliquos Apostolos Petro prædicare Evangelium jussit; quia Evangelium omni creaturæ prædicare, Marc.XVI.15. jussit. Imò minùs etiam omnes oves & agni Petro pastori à Christo subjecti sunt, quia oves & agnos suos, non omnes oves & agnos ei pascendos subjecit. Et oves Christi Sacerdotes atque clerum; agnos verò laicos significare, Christi verbis repugnat, utpote qui de ovibus pascendis, non de pastoribus, quales Apostoli omnes fuerunt, & Ecclesiæ ministri omnes sunt, nec non de ovibus & agnis, ex quibus ovile, à Pastore distinctum constat, loquitur. In Christi certè legatione Apostolis commissa, ut Pastores, non ut oves, illi considerarentur. Ideo cùm commorarentur pariter Hierosolymæ, pascebant omnes Ecclesiam communiter doctrina Apostolorum, Actor. II.42. non illios S.Petrus, & illi cæteros. Et cùm illinc ad alias regiones proficiscerentur, non comitabantur Petrum, ut oves pastorem, sed qui essent ipsi pastores singuli omnium nationum ovibus præpositi. Quatenus verò Apostoli, & cum illidem S.Petrus, etiam oves ovilis Christi fuerunt, provisum iis est à Christo, non unum cæteris pastorem præponendo, sed singulis imperando, ut mutua opera se ipsos adjuvarent. Sicut enim seniores Ephesios S.Paulus alloquitur: Attendite vobis ipsis, & toti gregi, &c. Act. XX.28. præcipiens illis, non ut gregis tantùm, sed sui etiam curam gererent: ita Apostoli provinciam omnium sortiti, quà pastores curandi fuerunt; quà erant oves, admonendi, docendi, pascendi, non singuli à Petro, sed à singulis singuli; etiam vel Petrus ipse, quando illa opus esset. Uti factum ex Gal.II.14. constat. Proin agni Christianos adolescentes & tenellos magis, oves verò maturiores, ætate provectiores, & ad mysteria fidei perdiscenda aptiores significant. Interrogatio porrò Christi ter repetita, an Petrus se diligeret, & magis quàm cæteri diligeret, non dignitatis, sed infirmitatis Petri argumentum fuit. Qui etiam non gavisus est, tanquam collato beneficio, sed contristatus est, quòd ipsi tertium dixisset: Diligis me? v.17. Quia enim Petrus major eorum, quàm cæteri Apostoli amorem Christi professus est, Matth.XXVI.31. & propter temeritatem trina abnegatio ipsi à Christo prædicta est, atque illa etiam successit; ideo Christus dilectionem fortiorem ab eo exigens simul peccatum ejus plus, quàm cæteri promittentis, & minus præstantis reprehendit, simul eum officii promissi admonuit, & stipulanti dilectionem illam pascendi munus ter injunctum restituit; denique eadem opera Petrum condonati peccati sui certiorem reddidit. Qui enim plus diligit, ei plus remittitur, Luc. VII.47. Major proin dilectio remissionis majoris indicium fuit. Denique nec præceptum illud Christi, quo Petrum conversum fratres suos confirmare, ib.XXII.32. jussit, argumento est, quòd Apostolis, ceu fratribus, à Christo præpositus sit. Nam fratres illi confirmandi quivis fideles sunt, quia Petri ipsius judicio cunctis idem pater est, qui ipsi erat, 1.Pet.I.17. & cuncti unà cum Petro cohæredes gratiæ vitæ sunt, ib.III.7. & Petrus eosdem confirmans fratres, 2.Pet.I.10. appellat. Ac licèt eorum in numero etiam Apostoli fuerint, & eosdem Petrus στηρίζειν confirmare etiam debuerit; tamen non iccirco suprematus ex officio hoc confirmandi etiam Apostolos magis, quàm ex munere pascendi eosdem, utpote quod præter confirmationem, stantium etiam lapsorum erectionem involvit, probatur. Sicut enim Petrus officium illud fratribus suis debuit: ita fratres simile officium illi debuerunt, eique S.Paulus illud præstitit, Gal.II.14. Atque idem omnes fideles, singuli fratribus suis, pro gratiæ suæ mensura quisque debent, Actor.XV.41, Rom.I.11. Jud. v.3. &c. utpote qui omnes unius corporis membra sunt, Rom.XII.5.1.Cor.XII.25, ideòque alii alios adjuvare, confirmare & erigere tenentur.
units.tr: Eph. 4.11. It is the task of every pastor to feed his own flock. If, then, the word "feed" signifies a fullness of power peculiar to the supreme head, every pastor of his flock will be a supreme head. And what, finally, will be left for the Pope? For that Christ, in John 21.15-16, enjoined on Peter alone, by a threefold address, the office of feeding the sheep and the lambs, is not a singular privilege of his. It rather signifies his restoration to the office of apostle, from which he might seem to have fallen by his threefold denial. For St Augustine rightly said in Tract. 123 on John: Christ asks Peter three times about love, so that by a threefold answer he may make up for the threefold denial of Christ. Peter was indeed charged to feed the sheep and the lambs of Christ, without any indefinite distinction being drawn between sheep and lambs. But Christ did not therefore subject all men, the Apostles included, to Peter as their pastor, any more than Christ ordered the other Apostles to preach the Gospel through Peter, because he commanded that the Gospel be preached to every creature (Mark 16.15). Indeed, not even all the sheep and lambs were subjected by Christ to Peter as pastor, since he subjected to him for feeding only his own sheep and lambs, not all sheep and lambs. And that sheep signify priests and clergy, and lambs the laity, is contrary to the words of Christ. For he speaks of feeding sheep, not of pastors (and all the Apostles were pastors, as all the ministers of the Church are), and of sheep and lambs, out of which a flock is formed, distinct from the Shepherd. Certainly in the commission of Christ given to the Apostles, they were to be regarded as pastors, not as sheep.
