So when they were together at Jerusalem, they all fed the Church in common with the teaching of the Apostles (Acts 2.42), not Peter feeding them and they the rest. And when they set out from there for other regions, they did not accompany Peter as sheep follow their shepherd, but each was set over the sheep of all nations as their own pastor. Insofar as the Apostles, and St Peter with them, were also sheep of Christ's fold, provision was made for them by Christ, not by setting one of them over the rest as pastor, but by commanding each of them, so that they might help one another by mutual labour. For St Paul addresses the elders of Ephesus thus: Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, etc. (Acts 20.28), charging them to take care not only of the flock but also of themselves. So the Apostles, having divided the whole field among themselves, were as pastors to care for it, and as sheep to be admonished, taught and fed, not each by Peter, but each by each, and even Peter himself by others when there was need. As is clear from Gal. 2.14. Therefore lambs signify Christians who are young and tender, and sheep rather those who are more mature, advanced in age, and better fitted to learn the mysteries of faith thoroughly. Moreover, Christ's question, repeated three times, whether Peter loved him, and more than the others did, was a proof not of Peter's dignity but of his weakness. Nor did he rejoice, as if a benefit had been conferred on him; rather he was grieved that he had said to him the third time: Do you love me? (v. 17). For since Peter had professed a greater love for Christ than the other Apostles (Matt. 26.33), and because of his rashness the threefold denial had been foretold to him by Christ and had indeed followed, Christ, demanding from him a stronger love, at the same time reproved his sin, which was greater than that of the others who promised and performed less; at the same time he reminded him of the office promised, and to Peter's profession of love he restored the charge of feeding, enjoined three times; and finally, by the same act, he assured Peter that his sin had been forgiven. For he who loves more is forgiven more (Luke 7.47). So greater love was a sign of greater forgiveness. Finally, that command of Christ, by which he bade Peter, once converted, strengthen his brethren (Luke 22.32), is no proof that he was set over the Apostles as brethren. For those brethren to be strengthened are all the faithful, since by Peter's own judgment all have the same Father that he has (1 Pet. 1.17), and all together with Peter are fellow heirs of the grace of life (1 Pet. 3.7); and Peter, strengthening them, calls them brethren (2 Pet. 1.10). And although the Apostles were among their number, and Peter ought to strengthen them too [στηρίζειν], it is not therefore proved that supremacy belongs to him by virtue of this office of strengthening, any more than by the duty of feeding them. For that duty includes, besides strengthening, the raising up of those who have fallen as well as the support of those who stand. For just as Peter owed this office to his brethren, so the brethren owed a similar office to him, and St Paul performed it for him (Gal. 2.14). And in the same way all the faithful, each to his brethren, owe it according to the measure of grace given to each (Acts 15.41; Rom. 1.11; Jude 3, etc.), since they are all members of one body (Rom. 12.5; 1 Cor. 12.25), and therefore are bound to help, strengthen and raise up one another.

units.la: XXVII. Denique & praxin suprematus Petro vindicati nequicquam illi tum ex electione Matthiæ, in qua Petrus electionem faciendam propositit, Actor.I.15. tum ex Concilio Hierosolymitano, cui præsidem præfuisse S.Petrum ex Actor.XV.7. contendunt: tum ex suscepto à Paulo itinere ad Petrum videndum, ejúsque apud illum commorratione, Gal.I.18. probare conantur. Nam Petrus quidem Act.I.15. electionem faciendam in locum Judæ propositit ut orator collegii, non ut Princeps ejusdem; quia non ipse electionem authoritate principali suscepit, sed eam, quatenus in ea, quam Deus extraordinaria ratione effecturus erat, aliquid facere licuit, reliquis liberum reliquit, neque quicquam iis præscripsit. Par igitur Petri ratio fuit, quæ est oratoris in comitiis orantis, qui comitiorum dominus non est. In altero verò Concilio Hierosolymitano, cujus Historia Actor.XV. narratur, ne oratorem quidem, nedum Principem egit. Neque enim vel primus locutus est, quod orator is & Præsidis est, quia loqui exorsus est μετὰ τὴν ἀνζήτησιν γνωμῶν post multam disceptationem, ibid.XV.7. & postquam ille locutus tacuisset, Barnabas & Paulus v.12. & Jacobus v.13. locuti sunt, atque ita postremo loquente Jacobo, & secundum verba ejus, v.22. & disertum quoddam orationis caput, quod Petrus non attigerat, Concilium conclusit. Neque igitur Concilii orator, neque præses fuit. Sed fac etiam, præsidem fuisse, nondum ejus suprematus, qualem sibi Papa arrogat constat. Si quod enim præsidendi officium inter Apostolos Petro datum fuit, tamen procul ab illo suprematus fastu, quem Papa inter Episcopos ambit & exer-
units.tr: XXVII. Finally, the practice of the supremacy they try to claim for Peter is in vain. They attempt to prove it from his choice of Matthias, in which Peter proposed that the election be made (Acts 1.15); from the Council of Jerusalem, of which they contend St Peter was president (Acts 15.7); and from Paul's journey undertaken to see Peter and his stay with him (Gal. 1.18). For Peter, indeed, in Acts 1.15, proposed that an election be made to fill Judas's place as spokesman of the college, not as its prince; for he did not himself take up the election by principal authority, but, insofar as something could be done in it, as an act which God was to bring about by an extraordinary means, he left the rest free and prescribed nothing to them. Peter's position was therefore that of a speaker addressing an assembly, not that of the master of the assembly. In the other Council of Jerusalem, whose history is related in Acts 15, he did not act even as spokesman, much less as prince. For he did not speak first, which is the role of a spokesman or president, since he began to speak after much disputation [μετὰ τὴν ἀνζήτησιν γνωμῶν] (Acts 15.7); and after he had spoken and fallen silent, Barnabas and Paul (v. 12) and James (v. 13) spoke; and thus, with James speaking last, and his words being followed (v. 22), and with a distinct point of the address which Peter had not touched upon, the Council concluded. Therefore Peter was neither speaker nor president of the Council. But grant even that he was president: it is still not established that his supremacy is such as the Pope claims for himself. For if any office of presiding was given to Peter among the Apostles, it was so far from that haughty supremacy which the Pope courts and exercises among the bishops, that if we granted Peter all his honours on condition that he accept them and covet nothing more, he would think himself mocked.

units.la: Petrus nunquam suprematum usurpavit. exercet, abest, ut si omnia Petri ornamenta illi largiremur ea conditione, ut ea accipiat, nec quid amplius concupiscat, deridulo is se habere existimaturus sit. Non ille enim in Conciliis oratorem vel praesidem egit, sed quae Francisci Duareni in sua juris Canonici epitome lib.III. 2. verba sunt, id tandem factum est, ut summum in omnes Christianos imperium uni tributum sit; utque legibus omnibus canonibusque Synodalibus, Imperatorum exemplo, legibus solutus sit. Nam, inquit, Paschalis Decretali epistola cautum expressumque est, nulla Concilia Romanae Ecclesiae Legem praescribere posse; & in decretis quibusdam Synodalibus (C. Ideo 25. q.1.) Romani Pontificis excepta reperitur authoritas. Aliter ergo acta Paparum, aliter acta Apostolorum sonant. Et Papa citius triplicem coronam cum omnibus bonis profundet, quam primatui Petri, qualem Scriptura agnoscit, caput suum subjiciat. Denique Paulus post tres annos venit Hierosolymam, visurus Petrum, & apud eundem dies quindecim mansit, Gal. 1.18. Sed venerit ille ad Petrum, ut posterior, adeoque frater ejus minor; & venerit honoris deferendi causa, idque ex officio & jure, ejusdem puta fidei & praedicationis Evangelii declarandi consensus sui gratia, uti Patres nonnulli loquuntur, nihil hoc ad potestatis papalis eminentiam & suprematum facit. Nam & Maria jam ex Spiritu S. gravida in urbem Judaiivit, Elisabetham salutatum, Luc. 1.35. Vir vasi mulieb-ri, inferiori licet, honorem tribuere; & mulier nihilominus viro se subjicere, ceu capiti, 1. Pet. III.1.7. 1.Cor.XI.10. & Timotheus viduas honorare, 1. Tim. V. 3. & omnes alii alios honore praeire, Rom.XII.10. jubentur. Non ergo honor & reverentia quaevis in eo, qui honoratur, potestatis ὑπερόχω, nedum suprematum arguit. Neque etiam S. Paulus quindecim dierum apud Petrum moram traxit, ut ab eo in fidei mysteriis institueretur, quia is Evangelium a nullo homine accepit, neque edoctus est, sed per revelationem Jesu Christi, Gal.I.12. Contulit equidem ille cum Apostolis τῆς δόξης in existimatione positis, ne forte in vacuum curreret, aut cucurrisset, Gal.II.2. quia a Pseudapostolis suggerentibus, non posse Christianos servari nisi servata lege Mosis, traductus erat, quasi id negans seorsim ab Apostolis maximis sentiret. Qua ratione operam suam & oleum se perditurum, & in vacuum curiurum metuebat merito. Cum enim, ceu industrius agricola caperet, ubi sementem jecerat, ibi metere, revellere herbas noxias falsorum Apostolorum, quae frugibus crescentibus aut offecerant, aut officere poterant, necesse habuit. Cumque non cum solo Petro, sed etiam cum Jacobo & Johanne sic contulerit, tam non inde Petri, quam Jacobi & Johannis suprematus probari poterit; inprimis cum, uti Hieronymus observavit, inter conferentes aequitas sit.
units.tr: Peter never usurped supremacy. For he did not act as speaker or president in the Councils; rather, these are the words of Francis Duaren in his epitome of canon law, book 3: It finally came about that the supreme power over all Christians was given to one man, and that, like the emperors, he was freed from all laws and synodal canons. For, he says, it is laid down and expressly stated in the Decretal letter of Paschal that no councils can prescribe law to the Roman Church; and in certain synodal decrees (C. Ideo 25, q. 1) the authority of the Roman Pontiff is found to be an exception. So the acts of the Popes sound different from the acts of the Apostles. And the Pope would sooner pour out his triple crown with all its goods than submit his head to the primacy of Peter as Scripture acknowledges it. Finally, Paul after three years went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days (Gal. 1.18). But even if he came to Peter as the younger, and so as his lesser brother, and came out of respect owed, and that from duty and right, that is, in agreement with him in the same faith and in declaring the preaching of the Gospel, as some of the Fathers put it, this has nothing to do with the eminence and supremacy of papal power. For Mary, already pregnant by the Holy Spirit, went into the city of Judah to greet Elizabeth (Luke 1.35); a vessel of the weaker sex, though inferior, is to be given honour; and a woman is nevertheless to submit herself to her head (1 Pet. 3.1, 7; 1 Cor. 11.10); and Timothy is to honour widows (1 Tim. 5.3); and all are commanded to go before one another in honour (Rom. 12.10). So honour and reverence of any kind shown to one who is honoured do not prove his superiority [ὑπερόχω], much less supremacy. Nor did St Paul delay with Peter for fifteen days in order to be instructed by him in the mysteries of faith, since he received the Gospel from no man, nor was he taught it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ (Gal. 1.12). He did indeed confer with the Apostles who were of repute [τῆς δόξης], lest perhaps he should run, or had run, in vain (Gal. 2.2), because he had been misled by false apostles who suggested that Christians could not be saved unless the law of Moses was kept, as if he, by denying this, held a view separate from the greatest Apostles. For this reason he rightly feared that his labour and oil were being spent to no purpose and that he might run in vain. For, like a diligent farmer, after sowing he had to reap where he had sown, and to pull up the noxious weeds of the false apostles, which had either hindered the growing crops or could hinder them. And since he conferred in this way not only with Peter but also with James and John, the supremacy of Peter cannot be proved from this any more than that of James and John; especially since, as Jerome observed, among those who confer there is equality.

units.la: XXVIII. Sublato Petri suprematu, ejusdem Cathedra, velut successione quadam ad Papam Romanum transmissa, ruit, pari enim insania qua olim Socrate Hist. Eccl. lib.III. 18. narrante Maximus Philosophus Juliano apostatae persuadere laboravit; Alexandri M. animam successione quadam in ipsum immigrare; etiam Monarchici Petri animam in Papis suis successionis quodam jure habitare sinl
units.tr: XXVIII. Once Peter's supremacy is removed, his chair passes, as if by some succession, to the Roman Pope and falls with him. For with the same madness by which, as Socrates relates (Hist. Eccl. lib. III. 18.), the philosopher Maximus laboured to persuade the apostate Julian that the soul of Alexander the Great had passed into him by succession, so the Monarchians hold that the soul of Peter dwells in their Popes by a certain right of succession, or at least strive to make them the full heirs of St Peter.

units.la: gunt, vel certe eos S. Petri haeredes ex asse facere contendunt. Et sicut olim Hortensius eloquentiam suam; ita Papa Petrum in ipsum Coelum tollere gestit, ut cum eo simul ipse ascendat. Sed Petrum non fuisse Ecclesiae Monarcham, abunde jam constat. Ac si maxime fuisset, non iccirco etiam Papa Romanus talis foret, quia successionem in locum Petri nullis tabulis in bona & debita forma, nullis S. Literarum documentis, hactenus probavit. Petrus enim Apostolus non magis quam caeteri Apostoli in munere suo singulari Apostolico successorem habuit. Ad Apostolicum munus inprimis testificatio de resurrectione Christi ex mortuis, in terra visi, nec non universale & infallibile praeconium Evangelii in mundo universo pertinet; in neutro Apostolis successores dati sunt. S. Petrus prae caeteris successore gavisus fuerit. At nulla ratio constat, cur ei potius Linus, Clemens, Cletus vel alius Romanus Papa, quam Johannes dilectus ille Christi Apostolus, diu Petro superstites, successerit. Quis ergo S. Johanni postea successit? Sed Petro nullus Papa Romanus successit sive de jure, sive de facto. Non de jure, fatente ipso Bellarmino, forte de jure Divino non esse, quod Romanus Pontifex, ut talis, Petro succedat. Nihil de fide illud esse contendit: Sicut, inquit, non fuit de jure Divino, ut Paulus haberet penulam, & tamen hoc ipsum de fide fit. Paulum habuisse. Sed penula Pauli longe certior est, successione Papae in Monarchiam Petri, quia penula in Scriptura habetur, de Monarchia vero Petri, vel successione Papae in eandem, altum inibi silentium est. Nuspiam enim scriptum est, vel in Monarchia quapiam succedendum esse Petro vel a Romano Papa, vel alio quocunque. Quam vero illud a sapientia & cura Christi erga Ecclesiam alienum est successorem talem constituere, & nullum tamen de eo verbum cum Apostolis commutare, quo vel obiter saltem, nedum serio admonerentur, successionem illam Papae Romano decretam esse; cum tamen in V. T. diserta adeo Pontificis Judaici mentio facta fuerit? Neque ullo jure Divino successionem illam sibi vendicare Papa poterit, qui nec in munere praedicandi Evangelii, quod supine ille negligit, imo odit & persequitur, nec in testimonio visi Christi ex mortuis resuscitati, Petri imitator est, & in abnegatione potius Christi ejus imitator est. Invalida porro juris Divini successionis hujus ex Conciliis & Patribus attentata demonstratio est, tum quia Conciliorum & Patrum authoritas omnis humana est: tum quia nec Concilia, nec Patres puriores successionem Papae cum omni plenitudine potestatis, quam sequioribus temporibus sibi vendicare re coepit, & hodieque vendicat in locum Petri usurpant tificantur. Neque illud de nihilo est, quod Valerianus Capucinus non ita pridem sepulta traditione, ex sola Scriptura de successione Papae in locum Petri, & Papatu universo, nihil certi constare; nequicquam reclamantibus & ad diras conclamantibus Jesuitis pertendit. Accedit, quod Pontificii doctissimi Scotus in 4. dist. 24. Cordubensis lib.IV. q. 1. Cajetanus de Prim. Papae cap. 23. Bannes in 2.q.1.a.10. contendunt, Episcopatum orbis & urbis per accidens tantum, non jure Divino aut imperio Christi-
units.tr: Just as Hortensius once tried to lift his own eloquence to heaven, so the Pope longs to lift Peter into heaven, so that he may ascend with him. But it is already abundantly clear that Peter was not the monarch of the Church. And even if he had been, the Roman Pope would not on that account be such, since he has so far proved, by no deed drawn up in proper form and by no documents of Holy Scripture, that he succeeded to Peter's place. For the apostle Peter, no more than the other apostles, had a successor in his singular apostolic office. The apostolic office consists chiefly in bearing witness to the resurrection of Christ from the dead, seen on earth, and in the universal and infallible proclamation of the Gospel throughout the whole world; and in neither respect were successors given to the apostles. St Peter may have enjoyed a successor before the others, but there is no reason at all why Linus, Clement, Cletus or some other Roman Pope rather than John, that beloved apostle of Christ, who outlived Peter by many years, should have succeeded him. Who, then, succeeded St John afterwards? But no Roman Pope succeeded Peter, either by right or in fact. Not by right, since Bellarmine himself admits that "perhaps it is not by divine right that the Roman Pontiff, as such, succeeds Peter." He does not contend that this is a matter of faith: "Just as," he says, "it was not by divine right that Paul had a cloak, and yet this very thing is a matter of faith, that Paul had one." But the cloak of Paul is far more certain than the Pope's succession to Peter's monarchy, since the cloak is mentioned in Scripture, whereas concerning Peter's monarchy, or the Pope's succession to it, there is a deep silence there. For nowhere is it written that anyone, whether the Roman Pope or anyone else, is to succeed Peter in any monarchy. How far from the wisdom and care of Christ towards the Church it is to appoint such a successor, and yet to say no word about him to the apostles, not even in passing, let alone seriously warning them that that succession had been decreed for the Roman Pope, when the mention of the Jewish High Priest in the Old Testament is so plain! Nor can the Pope claim that succession by any divine right, since he is no imitator of Peter in the office of preaching the Gospel, which he neglects out of laziness, indeed hates and persecutes; nor is he an imitator of Peter in bearing witness to the risen Christ, but rather of Peter's denial of Christ. Moreover, the attempted proof of this succession by divine right from Councils and Fathers is invalid, both because the authority of all Councils and Fathers is human, and because neither the Councils nor the purer Fathers recognised a succession of the Pope with all the fullness of power, which in later times he began to claim for himself, and still claims today, usurping Peter's place. Nor is it without reason that Valerianus Capucinus, not long ago, after tradition had been buried, maintained that from Scripture alone nothing certain can be established about the Pope's succession to Peter's place and the whole papacy, though the Jesuits protested in vain and cried out curses. Add to this that the most learned Papists, Scotus (in 4 dist. 24), Cordubensis (lib. IV. q. 1.), Cajetan (de Prim. Papae cap. 23.) and Bannes (in 2 q. 1 a. 10.) contend that the episcopate of the city and the world is only by accident, not by divine right or by the command of Christ.

units.la: Nullum proin in suprematu, nec promisso ei, nec collato, nec exercito successorem habere potuit; neque Papa Petri Christi conjungi ita ut jure divino Episcopus Romanus non sit successor Petri, sed Episcopus Parisiensis, aut quivis alius in successorem Petri eligi possit. Quam sententiam esse errorem in fide, aut cum fide pugnare, Azorius Institut. Moral. p. 11. lib. IV. 12. negat.
units.tr: Therefore he could have had no successor in the supremacy, neither promised to him, nor conferred, nor exercised. Nor is the Roman bishop so joined to Peter by divine right that he is Peter's successor, and not the bishop of Paris or any other person might be chosen as Peter's successor. That this opinion is an error in faith, or inconsistent with faith, Azorius denies (Institut. Moral. p. 11, lib. IV. 12.).

units.la: XXIX. Cum igitur successio Papae in locum Petri in jure Divino non fundetur, in facto etiam fundari nequit. Omne enim factum, fidem generans, imo fidei principium constituens, Divino jure, & revelatione Divina nitatur oportet. Atqui factum Petri, successionem ejusmodi fundans, nec in Scripturis ἀνυπολεξίᾳ narratur, uti principia fidei solent, nec ex illis ullo modo probari potest. Fundatur enim in facto tali, quod ne quidem jus humanum, nedum Divinum constituit; & quale vim hujusmodi juris communicandi habere doctissimos Pontificios negare diximus. Factum illud est, quod Petrus Romae fuerit, & ibi mortuus sit: quod Romae Episcopus, proprie loquendo, fuerit, & Pontificem Romanum in eodem munere, quo ibi functus sit, & cum pari authoritate successorem constituerit. Quae partim ἀδηλα, partim salsissima sunt. Ἀδηλον illud est, quod Petrus Romae fuerit. Quod mere humana & incerta traditione Papiae, Hieropolitanae Ecclesiae Episcopi, constat. Cui si in aliis majoris etiam momenti, ob ingenium & morem viri, incerta pro certis venditare sueti, & traditionum rumusculos captantis, ipsi adversarii fidem derogare audent, cur hic, ubi incerta traditione aeque ac in aliis decipi potuit, substringere eam tenemur? Ejusdem Papiae ὑσύρημα est, quod Babylon illa, cujus 1. Pet. V. 13. mentio est, Roma sit. Sed qui illud deinceps sectati sunt, & hodieque sectantur, causam non dicunt, cur Babylon illa mysticam, non veram Seleucienset scilicet iliam, de qua Bochartus Geograph. S. Lib. I. 8. pluribus egit, ubi etiam judaei multi, & Synagogae Æchmalotarcham suum habentes, olim erant, notet. Quorsum enim in plana Epistola ea haec nominis permutatio adhibeatur? Et fuisse Petrum in Asia dubitari nequit. Etiam Methodius, antiquus Episcopus & Historicus, a Mariano Scoto Chron. lib. II. citatus, Petrum Babylone Evangelium praedicasse, retulit. Quin nuper etiam Petrus de Marca, Parisiensis Archiepiscopus de Concord. Imp. & Sacerd. p. II. lib. VI. 1. Babylonem nil minus quam Romam hic notare fassus est. Etiam Paulus & Lucas passim de Roma loquuntur; neque tamen uspiam eam Babylonem appellant. Alia vero libri Apocalypseos ratio est, in qua visiones fatidicae & typicae emblematis ejusmodi locum dare potuerunt. Saltem fide Divina, quod Petrus Romae fuerit, res scilicet tanti momenti, ut sine ea oecumenici Papatus, principii & fundamenti Papalis unici, moles universa corruere debeat, neutiquam constat. Imo conjecturas non contemnendas Scripturae suppeditant, quod vel Romae nunquam fuerit, vel ibi saltem diu non, nedum ut Episcopus ordinarius, substiterit. Cujusmodi praecipuae sunt, quod Romae eum fuisse, & Episcopum egisse, nusquam ullo apice scriptum vel insinuatum est; cum in re tanti momenti, in qua Monarchiae Ecclesiasticae cardo vertitur, testimonium etiam negativum valeat: quod Lucas longe minora pertexens iter Petri momentosum adeo
units.tr: XXIX. Since, then, the succession of the Pope to the place of Peter is not founded in divine law, it cannot be founded in fact either. Every fact that generates faith, indeed every fact that constitutes a principle of faith, must rest on divine law and divine revelation. But the fact of Peter that is supposed to found such a succession is not narrated in the Scriptures [ἀνυπολεξίᾳ] as the principles of faith usually are, nor can it be proved from them in any way. It rests on a fact that does not even establish human law, let alone divine law, and the most learned Papists have said that such a fact has no power to confer this kind of right. The fact in question is that Peter was at Rome and died there, that he was bishop of Rome in the proper sense, and that he appointed the Roman Pontiff as his successor in the same office and with equal authority. Some of these claims are obscure [ἄδηλα], and others are utterly false. It is obscure that Peter was at Rome. This rests only on the purely human and uncertain tradition of Papias, bishop of the church at Hierapolis. If his adversaries dare to deny his authority in other matters of greater importance, because of his temperament and habit of passing off uncertain things as certain and of chasing after little scraps of tradition, why are we bound to accept him here, where he could be deceived by an uncertain tradition just as in other cases? It is also a fabrication of this same Papias that the Babylon mentioned in 1 Pet. 5:13 is Rome. But those who have followed this view since then, and still follow it today, do not explain why that Babylon should be mystical rather than the real one, namely Seleucia, about which Bochart Geograph. S. Lib. I. 8. has written at length, noting that many Jews also once lived there, with their own Exilarch of the synagogue. For why in a plain letter should this change of name be used? Nor can it be doubted that Peter was in Asia. Methodius, an ancient bishop and historian cited by Marianus Scotus Chron. lib. II., also reported that Peter preached the Gospel at Babylon. Indeed, more recently Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, de Concord. Imp. & Sacerd. p. II. lib. VI. 1., admitted that Babylon here means nothing less than Rome. Paul and Luke also speak of Rome throughout, yet nowhere do they call it Babylon. The case of the book of Revelation is different, since in its prophetic and symbolic visions such an emblem could have a place. At any rate, it is by no means established by divine faith that Peter was at Rome. Yet this is a matter of such weight that, without it, the whole structure of an ecumenical papacy, the sole principle and foundation of the Papal claim, ought to collapse. On the contrary, the Scriptures supply conjectures that should not be despised, that he either was never at Rome, or at least did not stay there for long, let alone as the ordinary bishop. The chief of these is that nowhere is it written or even hinted, in the slightest detail, that he was at Rome and acted as bishop there. In a matter of such great weight, on which the hinge of ecclesiastical monarchy turns, even negative testimony carries force. Luke, who relates the journeys of Peter in far less detail, nowhere mentions his important activity and deeds at Rome, not even where the occasion called for mention of him, as in Acts 8, 9, 31, 32; 11:19, 20, etc. Elsewhere, where he recounts Peter's miracles, the same silence holds. When Paul greets the faithful at Rome in Rom. 16, he does not name Peter; and from that entire letter it can be inferred that Peter had neither greeted Rome nor preached the Gospel there, nor founded that church before the letter was written (and it was written late). Moreover, Gal. 2:7–9 shows that Peter was allotted the task of preaching the Gospel to the Jews, yet the Jews were scattered more through the East than through the West, and under Claudius Caesar there were few or no Jews at Rome. For their sake Peter would hardly have left the great harvest of the Eastern Jews, and he would never have returned there except under compulsion of Claudius's edict. Further, in all the other Pauline letters written from Rome there is a deep silence everywhere about Peter, as if he were living at Rome. Again, Clement, who was himself bishop of Rome, in his first letter to the Corinthians, edited by Patricius Junius, speaks of both apostles, Peter and Paul, yet makes no mention of Peter's journey to the West or of the Roman episcopate founded by him. But he does record that Paul, after Peter was taken away, was brought to Rome, the very furthest point of the West [ἐπὶ τὸ πέρας τῆς δύσεως], as the greatest of all in labours and as the teacher of the whole world [μάλα ἐμφαλικῶς]. And it is agreed by all that Paul was not at Rome under Tiberius or under Caligula, unless one departs from the Sicilian and certain Arabic chronicles. Nor was he there under Claudius, as the ancients have handed down, since it is clear from Acts 12 that in the fourth year of Claudius, the last year of Herod Agrippa, Peter was still at Jerusalem; and Valesius himself, Not. ad Eusebius lib. II. 16., was compelled to admit this. It is also clear from Gal. 2:1, 2 that, from the conversion of Paul, which according to Baronius falls in the ninth year of Claudius (or, according to others, in the last year of the same reign), Peter was present at the council at Jerusalem, and from Gal. 2:11, 12 that he afterwards stayed for some time at Antioch. Nor was he at Rome under Nero, for apart from the fact that few years of his episcopate would then have remained, Peter was not at Rome when Paul wrote his letter there in the second or third year of Nero, nor did Paul set foot in Rome in the sixth year of Nero, nor did he send out several letters from Rome.

units.la: & res gestas Romae nusquam attingit, ac ne ibi quidem, ubi occasio ejus mentionem flagitaverat, velut Actor. VIII. IX. 31. 32. XI. 19. 20. &c. Alibi, ubi ejus miracula pertexit: quod S. Paulus Romanos fideles salutans, Rom. XVI. Petrum non nominavit; & ex tota Epistola illa confici potest, Petrum ante scriptam eam (sero autem scripta est) nec Romam salutasse, nec Evangelium praedicasse, nec Ecclesiam eam fundasse, quod S. Petrus, Gal. II. 7. 8. 9. provinciam Evangelium Judaeis praedicandi sortitus est, cum tamen Judaei non tam per Occidentem, quam Orientem dispersi fuerint, & sub Claudio Caesare vel pauci vel nulli Romae Judaei fuerint; quorum in gratiam, tanta relicta Judaeorum Orientalium messe, vix S. Petrus Orientem deseruisset, nunquam scilicet eo, nisi Claudii edicto cogente, rediturus: quod in Paulinis epistolis reliquis omnibus Romae datis altum ubique de Petro, ceu Romae degente silentium est: quod Clemens, Romanus scilicet Episcopus idem, Epistola priore ad Corinthios, a Patricio Junio edita, de Apostolo utroque, Petro & Paulo verba faciens, profectionis Petri in Occidentem, Romanique Episcopatus ab eo fundati non meminit; at S. Paulum post Petrum sublatum, laboribus omnium maximum, ἐπὶ τὸ πέρας τῆς δύσεως ad fines Occidentis Romam delatum, totius orbis doctorem μάλα ἐμφαλικῶς memorat: quod Romae non fuerit vel sub Tiberio, vel sub Cajo, fatentibus cunctis, si a fastis Siculis & Arabibus nonnullis discesseris; vel sub Claudio, uti quidem veteres tradidere, cum anno Claudii IV. qui Herodis Agrippae ultimus fuit, Hierosolymae eum adhuc fuisse ex Actor. XII. constet, & fateri ipse Valesius Not. ad Eusteb. lib. II. 16. coactus fuerit, & Actor. XIV. a conversione Pauli, quae in Claudii annum IX. juxta Baronium, juxta alios vero in ultimum ejusdem annum incidit, Hierosolymis in Concilio eo praesentem fuisse, ex Gal. II. 1. 2. &c. inde aliquandiu eum Antiochiae commoratum esse, ex Gal. II. 11. 12. constet; vel sub Nerone, quia praeterquam, quod sic pauci Episcopatus ejus anni superierunt, Romae non fuit, cum ad eos Paulus Neronis anno II. vel III. Epistolam scripsit, nec cum Neronis A. VI. Romam pedem intulit; nec cum Roma aliquot epistolas expediit.
units.tr: and does not mention his deeds at Rome at all, nor even in the place where the occasion called for mention of him, as in Acts 8, 9, 31, 32; 11, 19, 20, etc. Elsewhere, where Luke recounts Peter's miracles, he does not name him. When St Paul greets the faithful at Rome in Rom. 16, he does not name Peter. And from that whole epistle it can be concluded that Peter, before it was written (and it was written late), had neither greeted Rome, nor preached the Gospel there, nor founded the Church there. St Peter was allotted by lot the province of preaching the Gospel to the Jews (Gal. 2.7, 8, 9), yet the Jews were scattered not so much through the West as through the East, and under Claudius Caesar there were few or no Jews at Rome. For their sake, with so great a harvest of Eastern Jews left behind, St Peter would scarcely have deserted the East, and he would certainly never have gone there, unless compelled by Claudius's edict to return. In all the rest of Paul's epistles written from Rome there is everywhere a deep silence about Peter, as if he were living at Rome. Clement, who was the same man as the Roman bishop, in his first epistle to the Corinthians, published by Patricius Junius, speaks of both apostles, Peter and Paul, but does not mention Peter's departure into the West or the Roman episcopate founded by him. Yet he records that Paul, after Peter was taken away, was brought to Rome, the greatest of all in labours, to the ends of the west [ἐπὶ τὸ πέρας τῆς δύσεως], and the teacher of the whole world, very pointedly [μάλα ἐμφαλικῶς]. It is clear that Peter was not at Rome under Tiberius or under Caligula, as all admit, unless you depart from the Sicilian and some Arabic chronicles; nor under Claudius, as indeed the ancients have handed down, since it is established from Acts 12 that in the fourth year of Claudius, who was the last of Herod Agrippa, he was still at Jerusalem, and Valesius himself was compelled to admit this in Notes on Eusebius, book II, 16; and from Acts 14 (that is, from the conversion of Paul, which falls in the ninth year of Claudius according to Baronius, but according to others in the last year of the same), it is established from Gal. 2.1, 2, etc. that he was present at the council in Jerusalem, and afterwards stayed for some time at Antioch, as is clear from Gal. 2.11, 12. Nor was he at Rome under Nero: apart from the fact that so few years of his episcopate would then have remained, he was not at Rome, since Paul wrote to them in the second or third year of Nero, and did not set foot in Rome in the sixth year of Nero, nor dispatch several epistles from Rome.

units.la: XXX. Inanes porro conjecturae sunt, quibus Petrum Romae fuisse contendunt. Nam Romae Ecclesiam collectam fuisse prius, quam Paulus illuc venerit, adeoque a Petro collectam fuisse statuunt, quae mera ariolatio est. Potuit enim Ecclesia Romae colligi prius quam vel Paulus vel Petrus eo venissent, eodem modo, quo fuit collecta Samariae, atque etiam Antiochiae, quem alterum Petri Episcopatum faciunt, Actor. VIII. 4. 5. XI. 18. 19. Doctrina enim Evangelii multis Romanis antea praedicata Hierosolymis est, ibid. II. 10. Paulus etiam ostendit, Andronicum & Juniam, qui Romae habitabant, in Christo, vel Christianos fuisse ante se, id est, quinque vel sex annis prius quam Petrus Romae fuisse fingitur, Rom. XVI. 7. Quos etiam ἐπισήμως ἐν τοῖς Ἀποστόλοις insignes inter Apostolos fuisse cum testetur ibidem, eorum certe opera, aliqua saltem ex parte, Ecclesia Romana colligi potuit. Ideo S. Paulus Roma-
units.tr: XXX. Equally empty are the conjectures by which they contend that Peter was at Rome. They assert that the church at Rome was gathered before Paul came there, and therefore was gathered by Peter. That is pure guesswork. The church at Rome could have been gathered before either Paul or Peter arrived there, in the same way as the church in Samaria was gathered, and also at Antioch, which they make Peter's second episcopate (Acts 8:4-5; 11:18-19). For the teaching of the gospel had been preached to many Romans earlier, at Jerusalem (ibid. 2:10). Paul also shows that Andronicus and Junias, who lived at Rome, were in Christ, or were Christians, before him, that is, five or six years before Peter is supposed to have been at Rome (Rom. 16:7). Since he also testifies in the same place that they were notable among the Apostles [ἐπισήμως ἐν τοῖς Ἀποστόλοις], the Roman church could certainly have been gathered, at least in part, by their work. Therefore St Paul...

units.la: Nec argumentis adversantium confirmatur. Romanos pertinere ad κανόνα canonem prædicationis suæ, ib. I. 6. 13. 14. 15. XV. 20. &c. 2 Cor. X. 13. innuit. Neque etiam Scriptura narrat, quinam inter Apostolos alias Ecclesias multas collegerint, quæ tamen Petro certò adscribi non possunt. Quæ porrò de certaminibus Petri cum Simone Mago Romæ subitis profecrunt, fide humana, eaque incerta, cùm testes oculati nulli producantur, nituntur. Denique & dilutum illud est, quòd Petrum Romæ mortuum esse, ex ejus sepulchro, quod Romæ ostenditur, peregrinationibus ad illud, atque scriptoribus veteribus, probare conantur. Cadaverosum enim, quod ex sepulchris petitur, in rebus fidei argumentum est: & vagum nimis, quod peregrinationibus nititur. Possunt enim ibi cineres esse, ubi mortuus aliquis non est; nisi dicas Stephanum protomartyrem Romæ & Arelatæ passum, quia Romæ ejus corpus, Arelatæ ejus caput esse fertur. Et innocentum bimulorum ab Herode Bethlehemi cæsorum corpora per universum fere pontificiæ cæcitatis orbem basiantur. Nos verò certiora desideramus etiam testimoniis hominum, præsertim audita & ante acta narrantium, in illo quidem negotio, ex quo Ecclesiæ salus pendet. Veterum quoque Scriptorum de Petro Romæ sedente testimonia omnem vim suam ab authoritate Papæ mutuantur, cujus fidem supra justam in suspicionem adduximus. Usus enim est Evangelio fictitio, quod secundum Hebræos dicitur, Eusebio Hist. Eccl. lib. III. 39. narrante.
units.tr: Nor is it confirmed by the arguments of our opponents. That the Romans belonged to the canon [κανών] of his preaching, Paul hints (ibid. 1:6, 13-15; 15:20, etc.; 2 Cor. 10:13). Nor does Scripture relate which of the Apostles gathered the many other churches, and these cannot certainly be ascribed to Peter. As for what is reported about Peter's contests with Simon Magus at Rome, they rest on human testimony, and uncertain testimony at that, since no eyewitnesses are produced. Finally, that refutation stands: they try to prove that Peter died at Rome from his tomb, which is shown at Rome, from pilgrimages to it, and from ancient writers. But an argument drawn from bones taken from tombs is a weak basis in matters of faith, and an argument that rests on pilgrimages is too vague. For ashes may lie where a man did not die. Unless you say that Stephen the first martyr suffered both at Rome and at Arles, since his body is said to be at Rome and his head at Arles. And the bodies of the innocent boys slaughtered at Bethlehem by Herod are kissed throughout almost the whole world of Papist blindness. But we want more certain evidence, even the testimony of men, especially of those who tell what they heard and what was done before, in a matter on which the salvation of the Church depends. The testimonies of the ancient writers about Peter sitting at Rome also draw all their force from the authority of the Pope, whose faith we have brought under suspicion beyond what is just. For he made use of a fictitious gospel, called according to the Hebrews, as Eusebius relates (Hist. Eccl. 3.39).

units.la: XXXI. Sed adierit Petrus Romam; & Ecclesiam eam præsentia, prædicatione, martyrio suo confirmaverit, ne veterum consensum temerè vellicare videamur. Adierit idem Alexandriam, Antiochiam, Babylonem, urbes alias, & prius quidem, quam Romanos salutasse eum adversarii velint: non tamen adiit, tanquam functurus Episcopatu urbis, tum quia Apostolatus sui gradum reliquisset, & ad unius urbis Episcopatum, longè inferiorem Apostolatu, non sine deminutione capitis, descendisset: tum quia pacta conventa inter ipsum & S. Paulum junctis dextris firmata, etiam post tempus illud, quo Romam profecturus putatur, ut videlicet ille Judæis, hic Gentibus Evangelium prædicaret, notorie violasset, præcipue quippe non Judæis, sed Gentibus, ex quibus Ecclesia Romana ἐξ ἐθνῶν constabat, prædicans. Etiam S. Paulus dicens: Non misit me Christus ad baptizandum, sed ad evangelizandum, 1. Cor. I. 17. manifestè satis discrimen Apostolum inter & Episcopum docet. Episcopus enim non tantum ad prædicandum, sed etiam æquè ad baptizandum: Apostolus magis ad prædicandum missus est. Et si, quod illi asserunt, Antiochiæ per septem annos Episcopus fuit, non potuit simul Romæ esse Episcopus, quia duos Episcopatus particulares & proprios simul retinendo, & simul multas provincias peragrando, perniciosum posteris, ad deferendum gregem, & non residendum, exemplum reliquisset. Accedit, quòd S. Petrus ut plurimùm Hierosolymis commoratus videtur. Ibi enim S. Paulus, annis interjectis quatuordecim, eum quæsivit, Gal. II. 1. Ibi ab Herode in vincula conjectus est, Actor. XII. 6. Inter eos fuit, è quibus Ecclesiæ tubatores egressi sunt, ib. XV. 24. qui tamen v. 1. ex Judæa egressi dicuntur. Si Concilii Hierosolymitani tempore Petrus Romæ Episcopus fuit, tum quæstio illa de necessitate circumcisionis gentium antea necessario Romæ determinata fuisset. Neutiquam verò Petrus circumcisionis gentium curam suscepisset, & provinciam illam alteram Evangelium inter gentes promovendi S. Paulo præcipuè reliquisset. Neque profectò probabile est, uno eodemque anno Petrum fuisse Episcopum Antiochiæ Hierosolymis incarceratum, & Romæ Pontificem. Ideo Irenæus, Tertullianus aliíque Linum primum Episcopum Romanum non respectivè, sed absolutè, distinguentes, quippe Apostolos ab Episcopis, nuncupant. Alii Clementem, alii Cletum primum faciunt. Sed credibile est, Linum, Cletum & Clementem fuisse collegas Episcopos, sive Presbyteros, unumque alio vixisse diutius; atque inde Hierarchicos, πρωτοκαθέδρια somniantes nescire, quo ordine eos censere debeant; fingere etiam ausos, vel Petrum Clementem ordinasse Episcopum viventibus coadjutoribus Lino & Cleto, & illos, ordinatos item à se prætereiisse: vel Clementem detrectasse Episcopatum suscipere, cum judicio delatum: vel Linum & Cletum posthabitos à Petro nihilominus eum suscepisse. Qualia ex sua conjectura scripsit Epiphanius hær. 27. his verbis: Διανοοῦμαι δὲ, καὶ οὐ ζητῶ. Cogito sic, at non definio. Sed origo fabulæ de Petri Episcopatu Romano viginti quinque annos, nempe ab anno II. Claudii ad an. XIX. usque Neronis, durante constat. Diserte enim anni hi memorantur in Chronico Basileensi Eusebii. Verùm ibidem totidem annis in cathedra Antiochena sedisse, ad A. C. XLIV. usque dicitur, ut corruptus procul dubio locus sit. Sed Græcus textus ita habet: Πέτρος ἐπίσκοπος Ἀντιοχείας πρώτην τὴν ἐκκλησίαν εἰς Ῥώμην ἀπῆλθε, κηρύττων τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον, Petrus Antiochiæ prima stabilita Ecclesia, Romam abit, Evangelium prædicans. Additur, eundem primum Antiochenæ & Romanæ Ecclesiæ præfuisse ad mortem usque, præterea nihil. Annos proin illos ab Hieronymo, Eusebium interpretante, adjectos fuisse, vero fit simile. Nec aliter de VII. annis Antiochiæ exactis statuendum videtur; cùm in Græco nulla annorum alterutro in loco exactorum mentio fiat. Denique fuerit etiam Petrus urbis Romanæ Episcopus. Magisne verò Romæ principatum hunc hæsisse, quàm Joppæ & Antiochiæ putabimus? Nam quòd Petrum jus suum in Episcopatum Antiochenum retinuisse, quandiu viveret; sed morientem in Romanum, non Antiochenum Episcopum transtulisse, Bellarminus regerit, fidem certè nullam meretur, nisi jus illud per testamentum Romano legatum demonstraverit.
units.tr: XXXI. But suppose Peter did go to Rome and confirmed that church by his presence, by his preaching, and by his martyrdom; let us not seem to pluck rashly at the consensus of the ancients. He may equally have gone to Alexandria, Antioch, Babylon, and other cities, and indeed earlier than our opponents want him to have greeted the Romans. Yet he did not go there as one about to hold the episcopate of the city, both because he would have left the rank of his apostleship and descended to the episcopate of a single city, far inferior to the apostolate, not without a loss of dignity; and because the agreements made between him and St Paul, confirmed by the joining of right hands, he would then have openly violated, even after the time when he is thought to have set out for Rome, namely that he would preach to the Jews and Paul to the Gentiles. For he would have been preaching not to Jews but chiefly to Gentiles, of whom the Roman church consisted [ἐξ ἐθνῶν]. St Paul also, saying Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel (1 Cor. 1:17), plainly enough teaches the difference between an Apostle and a bishop. For a bishop is sent not only to preach but equally to baptize; an Apostle is sent chiefly to preach. And if, as they assert, Peter was bishop of Antioch for seven years, he could not at the same time have been bishop at Rome, because by holding two particular and proper episcopates at once, and by travelling through many provinces at once, he would have left a harmful example to posterity of deserting the flock and not residing with it. Add to this that St Peter seems to have lived mostly at Jerusalem. For there St Paul sought him, after an interval of fourteen years (Gal. 2:1). There Herod put him in chains (Acts 12:6). He was among those from whom the troublers of the Church went out (ibid. 15:24), although in verse 1 they are said to have come out of Judaea. If Peter was bishop of Rome at the time of the Council of Jerusalem, then the question about the necessity of circumcising the Gentiles would have been decided beforehand at Rome. By no means would Peter have taken up the care of the circumcision of the Gentiles, and left that other province of promoting the gospel among the Gentiles chiefly to St Paul. Nor is it really probable that in one and the same year Peter was bishop of Antioch, imprisoned at Jerusalem, and Pontiff at Rome. Hence Irenaeus, Tertullian and others, who distinguish Linus as the first bishop of Rome not relatively but absolutely, call him so as distinct from the Apostles, as bishops from apostles. Others make Clement the first, others Cletus. But it is credible that Linus, Cletus and Clement were fellow bishops, or presbyters, and that one lived longer than the others; and so the hierarchs, dreaming of primacy of chairs [πρωτοκαθέδρια], do not know in what order they ought to rank them. They have even dared to invent that Peter ordained Clement as bishop while Linus and Cletus were still alive as his coadjutors, and that he passed over them, though also ordained by himself; or that Clement refused to accept the episcopate when it was offered to him by judgement; or that Peter, though he had set Linus and Cletus aside, nevertheless accepted them. Epiphanius wrote things of this kind from his own conjecture, in these words, Διανοοῦμαι δὲ, καὶ οὐ ζητῶ. I think so, but I do not define it. But the origin of the fable about Peter's Roman episcopate lasting twenty-five years, namely from the second year of Claudius to the nineteenth of Nero, is clear. For these years are expressly recorded in the Basel Chronicle of Eusebius. But in the same place it is said that he sat in the Antiochene chair for the same number of years, up to the year 44 of Christ, so that the passage is undoubtedly corrupt. But the Greek text reads: Peter, bishop of Antioch, after first establishing the church there, went to Rome, preaching the gospel. It is added that he presided over the Antiochene and Roman churches, the same man, until his death, and nothing more. It is therefore likely that those years were added by Jerome, who was translating Eusebius. Nor does it seem that anything else should be decided about the seven years spent at Antioch, since in the Greek there is no mention of the number of years spent in either place. Finally, let us grant that Peter was also bishop of the city of Rome. But shall we think that this primacy clung more to Rome than to Joppa and Antioch? For Bellarmine's claim, that Peter kept his right to the Antiochene episcopate as long as he lived, but on dying transferred it to the Roman rather than the Antiochene bishopric, deserves no credit at all, unless he shows that this right was bequeathed to Rome by will.

units.la: XXXII. Nihil Monarchicorum adversariæ rationes proficiunt. Fundatam à Petro Romanam Ecclesiam clamant; sed nullo argumento idoneo freti: Fundaverit tamen ille. At fundavit haud dubiè etiam Paulus; & pridem Christus professores nominis sui Romæ habuit, uti ex Rom. I. 6. constat. Non omnis fundator Ecclesiæ vel ordinarius Ecclesiæ illius Episcopus est, vel potestatis plenitudinem haber,
units.tr: XXXII. The arguments of the monarchists achieve nothing. They cry out that the Roman church was founded by Peter, but they rely on no suitable argument. Yet he may have founded it. But Paul undoubtedly also founded it, and Christ had professors of his name at Rome long before, as is clear from Rom. 1:6. Not every founder of a church is its ordinary bishop, or has the fullness of power,

units.la: Saltem Episcopatu urbis Romæ functus non est. bet, vel eam communicat. Celebrata jam olim cathedra Petri est; Sed pari ratione Cypriani jam ætate Corinthus, Philippi, Thessalonica Ecclesiæ Apostolicæ & Cathedræ Apostolorum dictæ sunt. Et cum cathedra illa Petri tantopere veteribus decantata Antiochena, excelsa illa, uti Durandus Ration. lib. VII. 8. appellat, Cathedra, incidens in 22. Febr. & anniversario festo culta fuit; cum Romana Petri cathedra ante seculum duntaxat, à Paulo IV. instituta, & in 18. Jan. conjecta fuerit, uti Onuphrius Annot. in Plat. vit. Petri, notavit. Ecclesiam porro Romanam in maxima existimatione fuisse olim, nulli diffitemur, sed non propter Episcopatum Petri, verùm alias ob causas, inprimis fidem, Rom. I. 6. decantatam, & amplitudinem urbis. Multis, sic Theodoretus Epist. ad Leonem loquitur, prærogativis sedes vestra ornatur. Alia enim urbes ornat vel magnitudo, vel pulchritudo, vel multitudo incolarum: nonnullas autem iis privatas dona quædam spiritualia illustrant. Vestra autem redundantem bonorum copiam dedit is, qui est bonorum largitor. Ea est omnium maxima & præclarissima, & quæ præest orbi terrarum. & eorum, qui inhabitant, multitudine abundat; &c. Præcipue autem & insigniter eam exornat fides, & fide dignus testis Apostolus, qui clamat; Fides vestra annuntiatur in toto mundo, &c. Omittit ille Episcopatum Petri, in eo totus licet, ut collectis prærogativis Papæ aduletur. Ineptè porro adversarii requirunt, ut exponamus, ubi Petrus Antiochia relicta, nisi Romæ, sederit. Si enim sedere est docere, sedit ille Hierosolymæ, Antiochiæ, Babylone, juxta Scripturas; Alexandriæ & Romæ, juxta traditionem. Potuit autem sic sedere ut Apostolus, Episcopi munere alteri demandato. Sic Paulo cathedram apud Corinthios Tertullianus assignat, non quòd ibi Episcopum egerit, sed quòd Apostolatu ibi defunctus sit. Sin sedere est Episcopum agere, nusquam ille sedit magis quàm Paulus, quia Apostolorum est discurrere in varias orbis partes, & nulli loco alligari. Si qui veterum Petrum Romæ Episcopum appellant, illi Episcopi notione latè, pro functione cum auctoritate regendæ Ecclesiæ, quomodo S. Petrus Christum Episcopum animarum, 1. Pet. II. 25. insignit, & Apostolatus ἐπισκοπῆς Episcopatus nomine venit, Actor. I. 20. non strictè pro certa functione Apostolica infra Apostolos, velut cùm Apostolus dixit: Si quis Ἐπισκοπῆς ὀρέγεται Episcopi munus desiderat, &c. 1. Tim. III. 1. utuntur.
units.tr: At least he did not hold the episcopate of the city of Rome, or he communicates it. The chair of Peter has long been celebrated. But by the same reasoning, already in the time of Cyprian, Corinth, Philippi, Thessalonica were called apostolic churches and chairs of the Apostles. And that chair of Peter, so much sung by the ancients at Antioch, the lofty chair, as Durandus calls it (Ration. 7.8), fell on 22 February and was honoured with an annual feast; whereas the Roman chair of Peter was instituted only a century ago, by Paul IV, and was set on 18 January, as Onuphrius noted (Annot. in Platina's Life of Peter). We do not deny that the Roman church was held in the greatest esteem in former times, but not on account of Peter's episcopate; rather for other reasons, above all the faith celebrated in Rom. 1:6, and the size of the city. Theodoret speaks thus in his Letter to Leo: Your see is adorned with many prerogatives. For other cities are adorned either by greatness, or beauty, or the multitude of their inhabitants; some, lacking these, are illustrated by certain spiritual gifts. But yours has been given an abundance of good things by him who is the giver of good things. It is the greatest and most distinguished of all, and presides over the world, and abounds in the multitude of those who dwell there; etc. But it is especially and notably adorned by faith, and the Apostle, a trustworthy witness, cries out: Your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world, etc. He passes over the episcopate of Peter, though he is wholly intent on flattering the Pope by gathering up his prerogatives. Moreover, our opponents foolishly demand that we explain where Peter sat, if he left Antioch and did not sit at Rome. For if to sit means to teach, he sat at Jerusalem, Antioch and Babylon, according to Scripture; at Alexandria and Rome, according to tradition. But he could have sat in the manner of an Apostle, the office of bishop having been committed to another. So Tertullian assigns Paul a chair among the Corinthians, not because he acted as bishop there, but because he discharged his apostolate there. But if to sit means to act as bishop, then he sat nowhere more than Paul, since it belongs to Apostles to roam through the various parts of the world and to be bound to no place. If some of the ancients call Peter bishop of Rome, they use bishop broadly, for the function of governing the Church with authority, in the way that St Peter calls Christ the Bishop of souls (1 Pet. 2:25), and the apostolate is named episcopate [ἐπισκοπή] (Acts 1:20), and not strictly for a particular apostolic function below the Apostles, as when the Apostle says: If anyone desires the office of a bishop [Ἐπισκοπῆς ὀρέγεται], etc. (1 Tim. 3:1).

units.la: XXXIII. Cùm ergò Ecclesiæ Romanæ suprematus, nec Divino jure, nec facto Divinitus, ac ne humanitus quidem certo nitatur, alia ejus origo pandenda est. Pandemus autem non nostris verbis, quibus abundè eam in Historia Papatus pandimus, sed verbis Scriptoris Pontificii Francisci Guicciardini, Patricii Florentini, qui Leoni X. à secretis consiliis fuit, quæ in Historiarum ejus libri quarti impressis exemplaribus mala fide omissa, ex autographo Florentino alibi repræsentavimus, sed in paucissima contractis. Olim quidem, sic ille, Romani Pontifices omnium humilimi, neque ulla re magis quàm suppliciis & cruciatibus perferendis noscibiles fuerunt ad tempus usque Sylvestri, quo Constantinus M. Christianæ religioni nomen dans, eosdem à periculis & persecutionibus liberavit. Tum verò Christianum nomen propagari, Ecclesia ditari, pietate Episcoporum amplificari vehementer coepit. Cùmque nondum superbia & ambitio in eorum pectoribus iniedisset, facilè iis πρωτεῖα primatus quidam in orbe Christiano cessit, partim quòd ea civitas ob veterem dignitatem, ceu reliquarum caput & princeps, Imperii nomen Majestatemque retineret: partim quòd inde in plerasque Europæ partes religio diffunderetur; partim quòd Constantinus M. à Sylvestro ritu Christiano aquis initiatus ejusmodi auctoritatem in eo & successoribus ejus libenter agnosceret. Sed migravit mox Constantinus M. Byzantium, &, relicta Roma ad Pontificum potentiam viam aperuit. Indies enim, & magis magisque Imperatorum in Italia auctoritate, propter eorum abientiam, & gravissima in Oriente bella, debilitata, populus Romanus ab Imperatorum obedientia desciscens, & Pontifices præsentes tantò magis respiciens, eis non quidem obedientiam, sed voluntarium quoddam obsequium præstare coepit. Sed lentè hæc processerant, ob Gothorum & Vandalorum, aliarumque barbarorum gentium in Italiam effusiones, à quibus capta sæpe & direpta est Roma, & Pontificum nomen, quoad res civiles, in obscuro jacuit, evanescente inprimis Imperatorum in Italia authoritate, quia eam tanta cum ignominia prædæ barbarorum expositam deseruerunt. Aliarum nationum impetus cùm torrentis instar erupisset, Gothorum, qui origine Scythæ & Daci, professione Christiani fuerunt, per annos LXX. potentia permansit. Sed iis tandem Cæsaris armis ex Italia pulsis, per Græcos Magistratus, Exarchos, sedem Ravennæ habentes, Italia iterum gubernari coepit; & mox Episcopi, Constantinopolitanus & Ravennensis, Romanis Pontificibus de primatu controversiam moverunt, quia semper religionis sedes Imperii atque armorum potentiam sequi consuevit. Hac demum occasione, destituti sedis Imperii prærogativa, Divini juris tabulis fingi & prætendi coeperunt, atque eò paulatim perventum, ut Imperatore Phoca indulgente, Romanus titulum universalis Episcopi Ecclesiæ, ante à Gregorio M. in Johanne Constantinopolitano damnatum rapturiret. Paulo post Longobardis Italiam occupantibus, & Roma ab Imperatoribus deserta, per Pontifices gubernari coepit; Pipino Longobardis pulsis partem Imperii ipsorum Ecclesiæ Romanæ donante, & Carolo eandem denuò à Longabardis vindicante, multùmque amplificante, & cultum atque ceremonias Ecclesiæ Romanæ populis sibi subjectis imponente. Sed Pontifices tamen Galliæ Regum beneficio opibus & potentia aucti adhuc Imperatoribus ob eorum potentiam suberant, donec posteris Caroli M. diffidentibus ab iis eligi renuerunt, & inclinante eorundem potentia iis se palam opposuerunt, atque jus in ipsos Imperatores, quasi Christi in terris vices gerentes, usurparunt; adfirmantes eodem praetextu, ad se, multis in rebus Regnorum atque Imperii procurationem pertinere. Qua persuasione freti, Imperatoribus interdum Imperii dignitatem Origo suprematus Papæ Guicciardini verbis contractis pandiuntur. tatem derogarunt; Septemviros Augustales, ut alios in eorum locum surrogarent, incitarunt; vicissim etiam Imperatores aut ipsi novos Pontifices crearunt, aut ut crearentur, procurarunt. Sed successerunt ipsorum Pontificum dissidia; quorum occasione Ecclesiae Romanae oppida proprios dominos, ceu Ecclesiae vicarios, habere coeperunt; Roma vero Magistratibus propriis & suis regebatur. Et quamvis Avenione reduces, tanquam domini agnoscerentur, paulo tamen post Romani creato Magistratu Banderensium nomine, Pontifices suisque deque habuerunt, donec ad incitas fere redacti instante A.MCCCC. Jubilaeo, ex quo magnum sibi quaestum promiserant, Bonifacium IX. Papam demississimis precibus orarunt, Romam redire; id si faceret, Banderensium Magistratum abrogaturos, eique se obsequentes in omnibus futuros promiserunt. His conditionibus in urbem reversus, dum Romani quaestum illius anni unice intenderant, Pontifex occupato omni urbis imperio, Angelicam arcem munivit, eique praesidium imposuit; atque ex eo tempore Pontifices citra ullam controversiam Romae pro sua libidine dominati sunt. His modis & fundamentis ad terrenam potentiam summam enixi, & ad mundana imperia omni cogitatione conversi, animarum salutis & Divinorum praeceptorum penitus obliti, Divina auctoritate quasi telo & instrumento rerum fragilium abusi, Principes potius gentium, imperium suum in totum, qua licet, orbem extendentium, quam rerum sacrarum Pontifices facti sunt. Neque enim aliter religionis Antistites sunt, quam quatenus religiones falsae, imperio eorum terrestri accommodatae velamine & fuco terrestre suum imperium protegunt. De caetero eorum curae & negotia non jam vitae sanctimonia, non religionis Christianae verae incrementa, non erga Deum & homines charitas, sed exercitus, sed bella in Christianos cogitatione & manibus sanguine respersi, sacra tractantes; sed pecuniae immensa cupido, novae leges, artes, insidiae ad pecuniam undique cogendam, homines imperio suo subigendos. Quem in finem arma caelestia audacissime vibrare, profanarum & sacrarum rerum nundinationem impudentissime exercere nulla iis religio fuit. Hinc opes immensum auctae, & in aulam eorum effusae, ex quibus fastus, luxus, mores turpissimi, libidines & voluptates nefandae: nulla Pontificatus solicitudo; sed horum loco cupido anxia & pestifera filios, nepotes, alios conjunctos & necessarios non tantum ad opes immoderatas, verum etiam ad Regna & Imperia evehendi; non honores & emolumenta in merentes & bonos conferendo, sed plerunque auctionando, vel in homines ambitione, avaritia & pudendis voluptatibus perditos effundendo. Tale Regnum tum potestate & authoritate malis quaesita & propagata, tum religionis, qua nihil in terris ad homines impellendos vel retinendos potentius invenitur, nomine & Majestate maxima, qua pollent facultate, sacris beneficiis & honoribus, Principibus atque iis, qui apud illos maxime habentur, conferendis gratificandi adjuta sustentant. Hactenus Guicciardinus, ad compendium positus. Jungi huic potest
units.tr: XXXIII. Since the supremacy of the Roman Church rests on neither divine right, nor a fact divinely established, nor even a certain human foundation, its origin must be laid open. We will lay it open, not in our own words, which we have amply set out in our History of the Papacy, but in the words of the Papist writer Francesco Guicciardini, a Florentine patrician who was Leo X's private secretary. We have shown elsewhere the passages that were dishonestly omitted from the printed copies of the fourth book of his Histories, taken from the Florentine autograph, but here we give them in brief. Formerly, he says, the Roman Pontiffs were the most humble of men, and they were known for nothing so much as for enduring punishments and torments, down to the time of Sylvester, when Constantine the Great, who gave his name to the Christian religion, freed them from dangers and persecutions. Then indeed the Christian name began to spread greatly, the Church to be enriched, and the bishops to be exalted by their piety. Since pride and ambition had not yet crept into their hearts, a certain primacy [πρωτεῖα] over the Christian world was readily yielded to them: partly because that city, on account of its ancient dignity, as the head and prince of the rest, retained the name and majesty of the Empire; partly because religion spread from there into most parts of Europe; and partly because Constantine the Great, having been initiated into the Christian rite by Sylvester, willingly acknowledged such authority in him and his successors. But Constantine the Great soon moved to Byzantium, and by leaving Rome he opened the way to the power of the Pontiffs. For the authority of the Emperors in Italy grew weaker by the day, owing to their absence and to the grievous wars in the East. The Roman people, falling away from obedience to the Emperors and looking more and more to the Pontiffs who were present, began to render them not obedience indeed, but a kind of voluntary deference. Yet these changes came slowly, because of the invasions of Italy by the Goths, Vandals and other barbarian nations, by which Rome was often captured and plundered; and the name of the Pontiffs, so far as civil affairs went, lay in obscurity, the authority of the Emperors in Italy especially fading away, since they abandoned it, exposed as it was to the plunder of the barbarians with such disgrace. When the onslaught of the other nations had burst out like a torrent, the power of the Goths, who were of Scythian and Dacian origin but professed the Christian faith, lasted for seventy years. But when they were at last driven out of Italy by the Emperor's arms, Italy began to be governed again by Greek magistrates, the Exarchs, who had their seat at Ravenna. Soon the bishops of Constantinople and Ravenna raised a dispute with the Roman Pontiffs over primacy, because the seat of religion has always been accustomed to follow the power of the Empire and of arms. At last, on this occasion, deprived of the prerogative of the imperial see, they began to invent and to put forward claims from the tablets of divine law, and so it came gradually about that, with the Emperor Phocas indulging him, the Roman bishop seized the title of universal bishop of the Church, which Gregory the Great had earlier condemned in John of Constantinople. Shortly afterwards, when the Lombards occupied Italy and Rome was deserted by the Emperors, it began to be governed by the Pontiffs. Pepin, having driven out the Lombards, gave a part of their territory to the Roman Church, and Charlemagne again claimed it from the Lombards, greatly enlarged it, and imposed on the peoples subject to him the worship and ceremonies of the Roman Church. Yet the Pontiffs, made richer and more powerful through the favour of the Kings of France, still submitted to the Emperors because of their power, until, when the descendants of Charlemagne came to distrust them, they refused to be chosen by them, and, as the power of those Emperors declined, openly opposed them, and usurped a right over the Emperors themselves, as if they were acting as vicars of Christ on earth, asserting on the same pretext that the government of kingdoms and of the Empire in many matters belonged to them. Relying on this conviction, they sometimes took away from the Emperors the dignity of the Empire; they stirred up the seven Augustal electors to put others in their place; and in turn the Emperors either created new Pontiffs themselves or arranged for them to be created. But disputes among the Pontiffs themselves followed, and on account of them the towns of the Roman Church began to have their own lords, as vicars of the Church; while Rome was governed by its own magistrates. And although, when they were brought back from Avignon, the Pontiffs were recognised as lords, shortly afterwards the Romans, having created a magistracy under the name of the Banderenses, held them in contempt, until, reduced almost to nothing, with the Jubilee of 1400 at hand, from which they had promised themselves a great profit, they most humbly begged Pope Boniface IX to return to Rome, promising that if he did so they would abolish the magistracy of the Banderenses and be wholly obedient to him in everything. On these conditions he returned to the city; and while the Romans were intent only on the profits of that year, the Pontiff, having seized all authority in the city, fortified the Castel Sant'Angelo and placed a garrison in it. From that time on, the Pontiffs have ruled Rome as they pleased without any further dispute. Having striven with these methods and foundations for the greatest earthly power, and having turned all their thoughts to worldly empires, and utterly forgotten the salvation of souls and the commands of God, they abused divine authority as a weapon and instrument for fragile things, and became princes of the nations rather than pontiffs of sacred things, extending their empire over the whole world as far as they could. For they are not servants of religion in any other way than insofar as false religions, adapted to their earthly rule, shelter that rule with the veil and paint of religion. For the rest, their concerns and business are no longer the holiness of life, the growth of the true Christian religion, or love towards God and men; but armies and wars against Christians, hands stained with blood while they handle sacred things; but an immense greed for money, new laws, tricks and snares to extract money from every quarter and to bring men under their rule. To this end they have shown no scruple in hurling heavenly weapons most boldly and in trading in sacred and profane things most shamelessly. Hence their wealth has grown immensely and been poured into their court, and from it come pomp, luxury, the most shameful morals, lusts and unspeakable pleasures; there is no care for the Pontificate, but in its place an anxious and destructive desire to raise sons, nephews and other relatives and dependants not only to immoderate riches but even to kingdoms and empires; and honours and emoluments are conferred not on the deserving and good, but for the most part put up for auction, or lavished on men ruined by ambition, avarice and shameful pleasures. Such a kingdom, sought and propagated by power and authority that are evil, and sustained by the name and very great majesty of religion, than which nothing on earth is more powerful for driving or holding men, and aided by the faculty they possess of gratifying princes and those most highly regarded by them with sacred benefits and honours, has been maintained. Thus far Guicciardini, put briefly. To this may be joined

units.la: Suavis Polani, seu Pauli Servitae narratio valde ἀξιομνημόνευτος de origine & incremento potestatis Papalis, quam ille tum ab exaltatione Episcoporum, tum ab exemptionibus Monasteriorum & Abbatum a potestate Episcoporum derivat, quam Hist. C. T. lib. II. legere est. Quae tum Hieronymi Alcandri orationi in conventu Wormatiensi habitae, & a Pallavicino Hist. C.T. lib.I. 25. repetitae; tum ipsius Pallavicini argutationi, quam Hist. C.T. lib.XII.3. legere est; & qua utrumque Papatus originem ex Coelo derivare contendit, opponi possunt. Quamvis operatio mysterii iniquitatis Divinitus praedicta & impleta utramque demonstrandae terrestris Papatus originis paginam facere potest.
units.tr: The account of Paolo Sarpi, the Servite, called Suave Polano, of the origin and growth of papal power, very worthy of record, which he derives partly from the elevation of bishops and partly from the exemption of monasteries and abbots from the power of bishops, may be read in his History of the Council of Trent, book II. It can be set against the oration of Hieronymus Alcandrus delivered at the Diet of Worms, repeated by Pallavicino in his History of the Council of Trent, book I, 25; and against the subtle argument of Pallavicino himself, which may be read in his History of the Council of Trent, book XII, 3, and in which he contends that both the origin of the Papacy is from heaven. Yet the working of the mystery of iniquity, foretold and fulfilled by God, can furnish both pages for showing the earthly origin of the Papacy.

units.la: XXXIV. Non ergo Papae suprematum Deus, Christus, Petrus, sed caro, & Romuli, uti supra ostendimus, genius peperit.
units.tr: XXXIV. So it was not God, Christ or Peter who gave birth to the supremacy of the Pope, but flesh and the genius of Romulus, as we have shown above.

units.la: Quod plura etiam alia ostendunt. Nullum enim, si a Christo discesseris, Ecclesiae caput esse, supra ostendimus. De Christo, Ecclesiae capite, sententia clarissima extat: Certissime agnoscat omnis domus Israel, quod Dominum & Christum Deus fecerit eum ipsum Jesum, quem vos crucifixistis, Act. II. 36. Hic filius meus dilectus est. Hunc audite, Matth. XVII. 5. Ego sum bonus Pastor. Oves meae audiunt vocem meam, Joh. X. 11. 27. Ipsum (Christum) dedit caput super omnia Ecclesiae, Ephes. I. 22. Haec & similia conscientiam ad obediendum Christo obligant. Ubi vero de Romano Pontifice similis sententia extat? Non allegant Monarchici nisi remota quaedam, incerta & obscura principia, ex quibus conclusio nonnisi per infinitas ambages & consequentiarum trochleas, notitiam rerum vanarum, inprimis historiarum, quam ne centesima quidem pars hominum comparare sibi potest, nedum ut comparet. Neque alia media, vel testimonia rei illius liquido conficiendae suppetunt. Traditio enim res incerta & fallax est. Miracula vero Papa nulla facit. Neque Ecclesia universali consensu eum Caput & dominum elegit, quippe quae se non hominum, sed Christi solius peculium esse novit. Et si quis Ecclesiae caput datus esset, talis haud dubie datus esset, qui Spiritus S. dona copiosiore mensura, quam reliqui omnes, haberet, in fide non erraret, διάκονος, prudens, perspicax, exemplar gregis, & Ecclesiae ὑπογεγραμμένος similimusque Christo foret. Talis certe Romanus Papa non est. Nam eum errare posse in fide, ante Concilium Tridentinum omnibus, & post illud pluribus persuasissimum fuit. Cumque repellere bonam conscientiam, Deum abnegare, in haeresin incidere possit, fatentibus Gratiani decreto, Alberto M. Thoma, Alexandro de Ales, Bonaventura, P. de Tarentasia, Innocentio V. aliisque, quos magno numero ipse Turrecremata citavit, quidni etiam in fide errare possit? Imo erraisse Eleutherii, Felicis, Liberii, Anastasii, Honorii omniumque Pontificum posteriorum, inde a Bonifacio III. exempla comprobant. Posse eundem peccare, & crimina patrare in historiis testatissimum est. Et quam nulla vel exigua rerum divinarum notitia ille polleat, Politices facerrimae & astutissimae, & caussidicorum artis, quam Theologiae fanioris longe peritior sit, historiarum monumentis clarissimum mum est. Neque juvat Papæ & cathedræ privati & publici è cathedra pronuntiantis doctoris diltinctio, in qua haud secus, quàm in Makkedæ spelunca sui olim Amorrhæi, se absondunt, quasi ex eodem ore calidum & frigidum, dulce & amarum manare possit. Atqui etiam Bellarminus de Rom. Pont. lib. IV. §. fatetur, jam olim etiam Nilum, Gersonem, Almainum, Alphonsum à Castro, quin & ipsum Hadrianum VI. (extra Cathedram, an in ea pronuntiârit, ipsi viderint) pronuntiasse; Papam etiam ut Pontificem errare posse. Et privatim errans etiam ut Papa errat, quia ut Papa, etiam privatim docere tenetur. Cùmque ne Moses quidem, habens cathedram in populo Dei, jussu Dei erectam in ea sedens, ex ea judicans infallibilis fuerit, quippe non sanctificans Deum in tali actu, quem maximè publicè & ex cathedræ authoritate peragere debuerat; quantò magis Papa sedens in cathedra, non Divina, sed humana authoritate erecta, & cum Mose nunquam paria faciens, errare potest? In N. T. enim quippe in Regno solius Dei non alia cathedra nisi solius Dei & Christi est. Sià cathedra irrisorum, Psal. I. 1. nequitiæ, quæ fingit ærumnam supra statutum cum Deo insociabilis, ibid. XCIV. 20. diceris. Præterea quid sit ex cathedra, seu doctorem publicum, loqui, nondum hactenus Papa ex cathedra definivit. Atque eò tandem res ipsa redit, ut cathedra illa, seu potestas definiendi infallibilis sit scrinium pectoris Papæ, adeóque Papa ut privus doctor. Denique etiam Papa non unus etiam ex cathedra pronuntians seu publicus doctor pronuntiavit. Ne quid enim de Pontificibus posterioribus Gregorio VII. Bonifacio VIII. Innocentio III. aliis, quorum bullæ, ex imprimis, quibus Concilia Lateranensia, Florentinum & Tridentinum confirmarunt, hæresibus assertis vel confirmatis scatent, dicamus; ipse certè Honorius quondam errorem suum per decretales suos ad Sergium epistolas, quas in publica Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani Bibliotheca asservatum, & à Sergio aliis Patriarchis orientalibus communicatum iri haud ignoraverat, publicè, aperte & obstinatè professus est. Quòd si ex cathedra non fecit, quid publicus doctor ex cathedra facere posset, tandem illorum edocere est. Accedit, quòd Scriptura eum, qui se Ecclesiæ caput, œcumenicum Pastorem, & vicarium Christi cum subjectione Ecclesiæ jactat, sub ænigmatum involucris, puta Bestiæ, Meretricis Babylonis, Pseudoprophetæ, & Antichristi, depingit. Bestia enim est, quæ priori Bestiæ imaginem faciens, repræsentare se Ecclesiam pertendit, Apoc. XIII. 14. Meretrix Babylonica est, quæ ex Ecclesiastico statu in civilem converso Romæ imperitans populis multis, in Regna totius terræ potestatem sibi, mysterii, seu spiritualium prætextu vendicat, ibid. XVII. 3. &c. Antichristus est, qui se super omnia effert, & in Templo Dei sedet, se demonstrans, quòd Deus sit, 2. Thess. II. 4. Neque proin defuerunt omni tempore, qui Papæ potestatem in Ecclesiam rapturienti & usurpanti masculè se opponerent, quod integris voluminibus catalogi testium veritatis, & viri etiam doctissimi, Mornæus in Mysterio iniquitatis, Salmasius, Blondellus, Chamierus, Marc. Ant. de Dominis
units.tr: Many other things also show this. For if you set aside Christ, we have shown above that no one is the head of the Church. The clearest statement about Christ, the head of the Church, stands in Scripture: "Let all the house of Israel know assuredly that God has made him Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified" (Acts 2:36). "This is my beloved Son; hear him" (Matt. 17:5). "I am the good Shepherd; my sheep hear my voice" (John 10:11, 27). "He [Christ] has given him as head over all things to the Church" (Eph. 1:22). Such words as these, and others like them, bind the conscience to obey Christ. But where is any similar statement about the Roman Pontiff? The Monarchists cite nothing but certain remote, uncertain and obscure principles, from which their conclusion follows only through endless detours and the pulleys of consequences, and through knowledge of empty matters, above all of history, which not even a hundredth part of mankind can acquire, let alone acquire it for this purpose. Nor are there any other means or testimonies at hand by which that matter could be clearly established. For tradition is an uncertain and deceptive thing. The Pope, moreover, works no miracles. Nor has the universal Church, by general consent, chosen him as its head and lord, since she knows herself to be the possession not of men but of Christ alone. And if anyone had been given as head of the Church, he would undoubtedly have been given as one who possessed the gifts of the Holy Spirit in a fuller measure than all the rest, who could not err in faith, who was a deacon [διάκονος], prudent, perceptive, the model of the flock, a copy of the Church [ὑπογεγραμμένος], and most like Christ. The Roman Pope is certainly not such a man. For that he can err in faith was held as thoroughly persuaded before the Council of Trent by all, and after it by many. And since he can reject a good conscience, deny God and fall into heresy, as Gratian's Decretum, Albert the Great, Thomas, Alexander of Hales, Bonaventure, Peter of Tarentaise, Innocent V and others confess (whom Turrecremata cited in large numbers), why should he not also be able to err in faith? Indeed, the examples of Eleutherius, Felix, Liberius, Anastasius, Honorius, and of all the later Popes from Boniface III onward, prove that they did err. That the same men can sin and commit crimes is most fully attested in history. And that he possesses little or no knowledge of divine things, but is far more skilled than theology in the most shrewd and cunning arts of politics and of the advocates' craft, is most clearly shown by the records of history. Nor does the distinction between the Pope as a private person and the Pope as a public teacher speaking from the chair help him, by which, no less than in the cave of Makkedah where the Amorites once hid, he conceals himself, as if warm and cold, sweet and bitter could flow from the same mouth. Yet even Bellarmine, in De Romano Pontifice, book IV, §., confesses that Nilus, Gerson, Almain, Alfonso de Castro, and even Hadrian VI long ago pronounced (whether outside the chair or from it, let them themselves decide) that the Pope as Pontiff can err; and one who errs privately also errs as Pope, because as Pope he is bound to teach even privately. And since not even Moses, who had a chair in the people of God, erected by God's command, and who sat in it and judged from it, was infallible, for he did not sanctify God in that act, which he ought above all to have performed publicly and by the authority of the chair, how much more can the Pope, sitting in a chair erected not by divine but by human authority, and never making himself equal to Moses, err? For in the New Testament, in the kingdom of God alone, there is no chair other than that of God and Christ alone.
