You will be called "the chair of scoffers" (Ps. 1:1), "the throne of iniquity, which devises mischief under pretence of statute, and has no fellowship with God" (Ps. 94:20). Furthermore, what it means to speak ex cathedra, that is, as public teacher, the Pope has not yet defined. And the matter itself comes down to this: that the chair, or the power of defining infallibly, is the strongbox of the Pope's breast, and so the Pope is merely a private teacher. Finally, the Pope has not even once pronounced as a public teacher speaking from the chair. To say nothing of later Popes such as Gregory VII, Boniface VIII, Innocent III and others, whose bulls, especially those by which the Lateran, Florentine and Tridentine Councils were confirmed, teem with heresies asserted or confirmed: Honorius himself openly, publicly and obstinately professed his error in his decretal letters to Sergius, which he knew well were kept in the public library of the Patriarch of Constantinople and would be communicated by Sergius to the other eastern patriarchs. If he did not do so from the chair, let them teach us what a public teacher could do from the chair at all. Moreover, Scripture depicts under the veils of enigmas the one who boasts that he is the head of the Church, the ecumenical pastor, and the vicar of Christ with the subjection of the Church: as the beast, the harlot of Babylon, the false prophet, and Antichrist. For he is the beast, who, making an image of the former beast, claims to represent the Church (Rev. 13:14). He is the harlot of Babylon, who, having turned from an ecclesiastical state into a civil one, ruling at Rome over many peoples, claims for himself power over the kingdoms of the whole earth under the pretext of "mystery," that is, of spiritual things (Rev. 17:3, etc.). He is Antichrist, who "exalts himself above all things, and sits in the temple of God, showing himself that he is God" (2 Thess. 2:4). Nor, therefore, has there been any time lacking in which men boldly opposed the Pope's power, which seized and usurped the Church; this has been demonstrated in whole volumes of catalogues of witnesses to the truth, and by very learned men: Mornay in The Mystery of Iniquity, Salmasius, Blondel, Chamier, Marcus Antonius de Dominis,

units.la: aliíque demonstrarunt. In ipso adhuc Concilio Tridentino quotquot definiri postularunt, quòd Episcopatus sit juris Divini, vel Concilium sit supra Papam, authoritati Papali jugulum petierunt. Illi, quia sic Papam in curiam parium redigere conati sunt: hi, quia si Concilium supra Papam est, Papa ab eodem judicari potest, adeóque supremus judex & dominus non est. Atqui prius, exceptis Italis, feré omnes: posterius, Cæsaris, Gallorum legati, inprimis Cardinalis Lotharingus, & Episcopi Lucensis, Imolensis, Conimbricenses, Segovienses, plerique alii saniores definiri petierunt. Sed definitionem miris artibus Papæ in Concilio Legati impediverunt.
units.tr: and others. Even in the Council of Trent itself, all who demanded that the episcopate be declared of divine right, or that the Council be declared above the Pope, aimed their blows at the papal authority. The former did so because they sought in this way to reduce the Pope to the status of one peer among equals; the latter because, if the Council is above the Pope, the Pope can be judged by it, and so he is not the supreme judge and lord. Indeed, the first party, almost all except the Italians, and the second, the legates of the Emperor and of the French, above all Cardinal of Lorraine, and the bishops of Lucca, Imola, Coimbra, Segovia, and many other more sensible men, demanded that these things be defined. But the legates of the Pope, by remarkable tricks, prevented the definition.

units.la: XXXV. Imbelles pro suprematu Papæ Romanensium ratiunculæ sunt. Nam quæ ex Christi ad Petrum dictis illi allegant, neque ad suprematum cujusquam velut Monarchæ Ecclesiastici: neque ad Papam Romanum quicquam attinere, fusius jam demonstravimus. At nec Ecclesiam externam à visibili capite regi debere, abundè etiam veritati dedimus. Reliqua pro Papatu œcumenico Romani Pontificis Ecclesiæ veteris sensui & consensui innituntur. Nam Ecclesiam dubias quæstiones omni tempori Papæ arbitrio & definitioni subjecisse: Concilia, Nicænum, Chalcedonense, Sardicense, ut in controversiis fidei Romanus Pontifex, ceu supremus judex, appelletur, sanxisse: Concilia generalia decretorum suorum confirmationem à Papa expetiisse: Episcoporum toto orbe institutionem & confirmationem à Papa suspensam semper fuisse: aliáque ejusmodi objectant. Sed nullo succeßu. Si qui enim in rebus dubiis Episcopum Romanum consuluerunt, non consuluerunt illi ut Papam œcumenicum, cujus simpliciter arbitrio standum sit. Nam Polycarpus ab Aniceti consilio discessit; & Cyprianus Stephani definitioni se oppositi. Neque etiam vel solum Papam consuluerunt, quia Ambrosius Epist. 2. post Ægyptiorum supputationes, & Alexandrinæ Ecclesiæ definitionem Episcopi quoque Ecclesiæ Romanæ sententiam expectari, scribit: vel semper consuluerunt. Polycarpus enim quæstionem de iterando Baptismo hæreticorum in Concilio Africano, non vocato Romano Episcopo, definivit: & Arius sine authoritate Episcopi Rom. refutatus, convictus & damnatus est. Neque etiam Ecclesiæ Orientales in quæstionibus dubiis quidquam Papæ deferunt. Neque etiam Canones Conciliorum, Nicæni, Chalcedonensis, Sardicensis vel jus Divinum faciunt, vel appellationes in controversiis fidei ad Papam, ceu judicem supremum, uspiam sanxerunt. Nam Concilii Nicæni canon, quem illi eam in rem citant, in eo Concilio non invenitur; sed à Zosimo ex Concilio Sardicensi sub nomine Nicæni obtrusus est. Et Concilium illud Can. VI. diserte Papam Romanum in ordinem parium redigit, definiens, ut Alexandrino Patriarchæ fas sit, gubernare suas provincias, quia ἡ συνήθεια consuetudo eadem Romani sit, uti consuetudo cum consuetudine, non, uti Monarchici pervertunt, causa cum indulgentia comparatur. Ultimus ejusdem Concilii Canon fines etiam Romani, suburbicarias Ecclesias, hoc est, Romæ vicinas, & Urbico præfecto in Piceno & Thuscia subjectos, nominat. Neque etiam in Concilio Chalcedonensi de appellationibus ad Papam quidquam sancitum reperitur; quin potius in eo Can. XXVIII. Romano & Constantinopolitano ἴσα πρεσβεῖα æqualia jura decernuntur. Quam adæquationem adeò ægrè Lucentius, Romani Episcopi Vicarius, tulit, ut contra eam protestari ausus fuerit. Sardicensis Concilii Canon IV. & VII. jus appellandi ad Papam facit. Sed nec Oecumenicum Concilium illud fuit, & appellationem sanxit pro eo tempore, non in perpetuum, provisionaliter, sicut diserte Patres illi loquuntur; quia Ecclesiæ Orientales suspicione partium laborarunt. Quoad appellationum exempla; factæ ex sunt, vel ab æmulis circumcursantibus, uti Cyprianus loquitur, & desperatis; vel à bonis. Illorum exempla non moramur. Hi verò ad Papam appellarunt, non ut supremum judicem, sed subsidium in amica communionis ejusdem societate quærentes. Quoad Conciliorum confirmationem, illa fit vel per edictum, vel per assensum. Edicto soli quondam Imperatores sic Concilia confirmarunt, ut eorum definitione in foro externo eatenus vim legis sortita fuerint. Unde frequentissimæ illæ de Imperatoribus voces βεβαιῶν, ἐπιφέρει, ἐπιφέρειν, κρατῶν, ἐπικυρῶν τὰ πεπραγμένα. Ideo Synodorum etiam quarundam decreta improbata, rejecta, ampliata à quibusdam Imperatoribus, Carolo M. Carolo Calvo, &c. reperias. Assensu verò, sine ulla tamen potestate vel Jurisdictione, etiam Romanus Episcopus confirmavit; sed non solus, verùm unâ cum aliis Episcopis, sine prærogativa ulla. Institutio porrò Episcoporum & Pastorum olim penes Ecclesiam fuit, vel illum, cui Ecclesia consentiens delegavit. Si qui verò Episcopi Romani extra suas provincias ordinarunt, non propria etiam, sed delegata potestate id omne fecerunt. Quomodo etiam Cornelius Papa à plebe sua electus, at à peregrinis Africanis extra dioecesin suam confirmatus est. Denique nulli difficultatem, Ecclesiam Romanam olim in magna veneratione fuisse, tum propter ejus antiquitatem; tum propter depositum nobilissimæ Epistolæ Paulinæ; tum propter urbis nomen, & totius Occidentis ad illam respectum; tum denique propter constantiam fidei & hæresEon detestationem. Quæ ipsæ etiam causæ paulatim, Sathanæ iis abutentis fraude erectionem cathedræ illius, velut authenticæ & fidei dominantis, adjuverunt. Verùm sequiore ætate Ecclesia Romana à fide veteris cùm defecerit, antiquorum Patrum elogiis minimè ampliùs digna est. Et si qui de Episcopo Ramano paulò magnificentius locuti sunt, eos probare non possumus, quia nec verbi Divini authoritate, nec ratione nituntur. Nam proclive & bonis etiam familiare vitium adulatio est. Et quantumvis splendida, œcumenicum tamen Papatum illa non stabiliunt.
units.tr: XXXV. The arguments for the supremacy of the Roman Pontiff are feeble. What they draw from Christ's words to Peter bears neither on the supremacy of anyone as an ecclesiastical monarch nor on the Roman Pope in particular; we have already demonstrated this at greater length. Nor have we denied that the external Church ought to be ruled by a visible head; we have fully conceded that to the truth. The remaining arguments for the oecumenical Papacy of the Roman Pontiff rest on the sense and consensus of the ancient Church. They object that the Church has always submitted doubtful questions to the Pope's judgment and definition; that the Councils of Nicaea, Chalcedon and Sardica decreed that in controversies of faith the Roman Pontiff should be appealed to as supreme judge; that general councils sought the Pope's confirmation of their decrees; that the appointment and confirmation of bishops throughout the whole world was always reserved to the Pope; and other things of this kind. But they succeed in nothing. For if some consulted the Roman Bishop in doubtful matters, they did not consult him as an oecumenical Pope whose judgment must simply be followed. Polycarp departed from the advice of Anicetus, and Cyprian opposed the decision of Stephen. Nor did they always consult the Pope alone: Ambrose, in Epist. 2., after the calculations of the Egyptians and the decision of the Alexandrian Church, writes that the opinion of the bishops of the Roman Church also should be awaited. Nor did they always consult him at all: Polycarp settled the question of rebaptizing heretics in a council in Africa, without summoning the Roman Bishop, and Arius was refuted, convicted and condemned without the authority of the Roman Bishop. Nor do the Eastern Churches refer anything doubtful to the Pope. Nor do the canons of the Councils of Nicaea, Chalcedon and Sardica either establish divine right or anywhere decree appeals in controversies of faith to the Pope as supreme judge. For the canon of Nicaea which they cite for this purpose is not found in that council; it was foisted under the name of Nicaea by Zosimus from the Council of Sardica. And that council, in Can. VI., expressly reduces the Roman Pope to the rank of an equal, defining that the Alexandrian Patriarch may govern his provinces because the custom [ἡ συνήθεια] of Rome is the same: custom is matched with custom, not, as the monarchists distort it, a cause is compared with an indulgence. The last canon of the same council names the territories also of Rome, the suburbicarian churches, that is, those near Rome and subject to the prefect Urbicus in Picenum and Tuscia. Nor is anything decreed about appeals to the Pope in the Council of Chalcedon; rather, in its Can. XXVIII., equal privileges [ἴσα πρεσβεῖα] are decreed to the Roman and Constantinopolitan sees. Lucentius, the vicar of the Roman Bishop, took this equalizing so badly that he dared to protest against it. Canons IV. and VII. of the Council of Sardica do give a right of appeal to the Pope. But that was not an oecumenical council, and it sanctioned appeal for that time only, not in perpetuity, provisionally, as those Fathers expressly say, because the Eastern Churches labored under suspicion of partiality. As to examples of appeals: they were made either by rivals running about, as Cyprian puts it, and by desperate men, or by good men. We do not dwell on the examples of the former. The latter appealed to the Pope not as supreme judge but seeking aid within the fellowship of friendly communion. As to the confirmation of councils, it is effected either by edict or by assent. Only former emperors confirmed councils by edict, so that their definitions acquired the force of law in the external forum to that extent. Hence those very frequent phrases about the emperors: βεβαιῶν, ἐπιφέρει, ἐπιφέρειν, κρατῶν, ἐπικυρῶν τὰ πεπραγμένα. Accordingly you may find that the decrees of certain synods were disapproved, rejected or enlarged by some emperors, Charlemagne, Charles the Bald and others. By assent, however, without any power or jurisdiction, the Roman Bishop too confirmed councils; but not alone, rather together with other bishops, and without any prerogative. Moreover, the institution of bishops and ministers was formerly in the hands of the Church, or of the one whom the consenting Church had delegated. If any Roman Bishops ordained outside their own provinces, they did all that not by their own power but by delegated power. So too Pope Cornelius was chosen by his own people, but was confirmed by African strangers outside his diocese. Finally, no one denies that the Roman Church was once held in great veneration: partly on account of its antiquity; partly on account of the deposit of the most noble Epistle of Paul; partly on account of the name of the city and the regard of the whole West for it; and lastly on account of the constancy of its faith and its detestation of heresies. These very causes, little by little, by Satan's fraud abusing them, helped to raise that chair as though it were authentic and dominant over faith. But in a later age, since the Roman Church has fallen away from the faith of old, it is no longer worthy of the praises of the ancient Fathers. And if some have spoken rather magnificently of the Roman Bishop, we cannot approve them, since they rest on neither the authority of the divine Word nor on reason. For flattery is a prone vice, and one familiar even to good men. However splendid such things are, they do not establish an oecumenical Papacy.

units.la: XXXVI. Sublato Monarchiæ Ecclesiasticæ capite ipsum quoque corpus, cui ille ceu caput spurium, dominatur, perit, hactenus certè, ne Christi corpus habeatur, sed ut Antichristi corpus agnoscatur. Constat illud ex duobus membrorum velut unius corporis generi-
units.tr: XXXVI. When the head of ecclesiastical monarchy is removed, the body itself also perishes, over which he rules like a false head; at least so far that it is not to be regarded as the body of Christ, but recognized as the body of Antichrist. It consists of two kinds of members, as it were of one body, namely clergy and laity.

units.la: bus, puta Clericis & Laicis. Et Cleri quidem appellatio etiam ante revelatum Antichristum, humano consilio Ecclesiæ ministris indita fuit. Occasionem dedit παρεμβολὴ loci, 1.Pet.V.3. ubi οἱ κληροι cleri, & τὸ ποίμνιον grex distinguì videntur. Sed cùm Presbyteri non notent ibi singulos cujusque loci Episcopos præter Scripturæ morem, verisimile est, vocem κληροι positam ceu accommodatiorem verbo καταχυ-ειν, quasi diceret: Non habetis gregem vestrum pro sorte vestra, cui pro lubitu dominemini, cùm sit sors Dei; sed pro grege tantùm vobis commissò, quem ducatis ad Dominum, & cui typo doctrinæ & vitæ præeatis. Neque enim duo pastoris officia ibi ponuntur, pascere laicos & regere clericos; sed commune officium ποιμαίνειν pascendi, & unum commune ejus objectum v.2 Pascite τὸ ἐν ὑμῖν ποίμνιον & Θεοῦ gregem Dei, qui apud vos est. Manifestum verò etiam hoc est ex copulatione modi, qui præscribitur v.3. cum antecedentibus, tanquam ad unum actum pascendi pertinentis: Pascite non coactè, non turpiter, neque ut dominantes. Clerum verò & gregem, unum & eundem cœtum, tanquam objectum illius actus notare, ex eadem copulatione liquet. Sicut etiam ex oppositione illa dominationis & exemplaris institutionis, quæ non sunt oppositæ nisi respectu ejusdem: Non ut dominantes cleris, sed ut exemplaria gregis. Neque etiam Levitæ vocantur sors Domini, cùm tota Ecclesia & populus Dei ubique in V. T. sors, peculium, hæreditas Domini passim appelletur, sed Jehova illorum נחלה hæreditas dicitur, Deut.XVIII.2. & munus ministerii, quod electione iis obtigit, etiam sortis nomine venit. Ideo etiam S.Petrus ipse non Ecclesiæ Ministros, sed Ecclesiam ipsam Sacerdotium & populum, quem sibi Deus ut proprium vendicat, hoc est, sortem Dei, 1.Ep. II.9. appellat. Tertulliani demum ætate usus vocis Cleri de Ministris Ecclesiæ coepit; sicut etiam Sacerdotum, altarium, meritorum, &c. voces præter stylum Scripturæ cum præjudicio veritatis & Ecclesiæ periculo invaluerunt. Denique licèt Ministri Ecclesiæ singulari quadam ratione sint Clerus Dei, tamen nullus inde lenis titulus eorum, sine authoritate Dei, confici potest, neque etiam inde separatio statuum introduci debet, quasi vilis esset λαὸς populus Dei, qui laicorum nomine intra Ministrorum ceu Clericorum dignitatem deprimi meretur. Nam & Ministri Ecclesiæ, Scripturæ stylo, sunt pars κλῆρος, λαός, populi Dei; & populus à Ministris distinctus est pars κλῆρος sortis & hæreditatis Dei. Nulla enim magis propria ratio appellationis sortis, hæreditatis, peculii Dei est, quàm redemptio per sanguinem Christi, quæ ad universam Ecclesiam, pari omnium juie pertinet. Ex quibus liquet, ipsam appellationem Cleri ceu potioris partis corporis Papalis, quæ Papæ uni subjecta, at populo universo præfecta est, non Christianam, sed eo, quo hodie inprimis usurpatur, sensu Antichristianam esse. Nam quod omnium & singulorum, & solorum fidelium atque electorum est, id soli Papæ, in perangendo mysterio iniquitatis mancipiis & satellitibus impiè tribuitur.
units.tr: The name "clergy" was given to the Church's ministers by human counsel, even before Antichrist was revealed. The occasion was the phrase in 1 Peter 5:3, where οἱ κληροι [the clergy] and τὸ ποίμνιον [the flock] seem to be distinguished. But since the elders there do not mean, contrary to Scripture's usage, each single bishop of each place, it is probable that the word κληροι was used as better suited to the verb καταχυ-ειν [to lord it over], as if he said: You do not have your flock as your lot, over which you may lord it at your pleasure, since the lot is God's; but only the flock committed to you, which you should lead to the Lord, and before which you should go as a type in doctrine and life. For Peter does not set two duties of a shepherd there, feeding the laity and ruling the clergy, but one common duty, ποιμαίνειν [to shepherd], of feeding, and one common object of it, in verse 2: "Feed τὸ ἐν ὑμῖν ποίμνιον [the flock among you], the flock of God which is among you." That this is manifest also appears from the mode prescribed in verse 3, joined with what precedes, as belonging to one act of feeding: feed not under compulsion, not for shameful gain, nor as lords. That the clergy and the flock, one and the same assembly, are noted as the object of that act is clear from the same joining. So too from that opposition of lordship and exemplary instruction, which are opposed only with respect to the same thing: not as lords over the clergy, but as examples to the flock. Nor are the Levites called the lot of the Lord, since the whole Church and people of God everywhere in the Old Testament is called everywhere the lot, peculiar possession and inheritance of the Lord; but their Jehovah is said to be their נחלה [inheritance], Deut. 18:2, and the office of ministry which fell to them by choice also came to be called by the name of lot. Therefore Saint Peter himself does not call the ministers of the Church the lot, but calls the Church itself the priesthood and the people which God claims for himself as his own, that is, the lot of God, 1 Peter 2:9. Finally, under Tertullian the use of the word clergy began to be applied to the ministers of the Church; in the same way, the words priests, altars, merits, and so on, beyond the style of Scripture, prevailed with prejudice to the truth and danger to the Church. Lastly, although the ministers of the Church are in a peculiar way the clergy of God, still no soft title for them can be devised from this without the authority of God, nor should a separation of orders be introduced from it, as if the people of God, the λαὸς, were a cheap thing, who deserve to be pressed down under the name of laity beneath the dignity of ministers as clergy. For both the ministers of the Church and the people, in the style of Scripture, are parts of the κλῆρος [clergy/lot] and λαός [people] of God; and the people, distinguished from the ministers, is a part of the κλῆρος [lot], the lot and inheritance of God. For there is no more proper reason for the name of lot, inheritance and peculiar possession of God than redemption through the blood of Christ, which pertains to the whole Church with equal right for all. From these things it is clear that the very name "clergy," as the more powerful part of the Papal body, which is subject to the one Pope but set over the whole people, is not Christian but, in the sense in which it is used today above all, Antichristian. For what belongs to all and each of the faithful and elect alone, that is impiously granted to the Pope alone, the bondsmen and satellites in carrying out the mystery of iniquity.

units.la: XXXVII. Cùm veræ Ecclesiæ veri Ministri,
units.tr: XXXVII. Since the true ministers of the true Church,

units.la: ministri, Pastores & Doctores à tota Ecclesia, vel iis, quibus Ecclesia hanc curam commisit, ad munus suum obeundum deputentur atque ordinentur, & deputati atque ordinati Ecclesiæ ministrent; Hierarchici contra in constitutione Ministrorum Ecclesiæ electionem, ordinationem & vocationem seu missionem distinguunt. Electio enim juxta illos est designatio personæ certæ ad præfecturam Ecclesiasticam. Ordinatio sacra ceremonia, qua certo coetui futurus Ecclesiæ minister consecratur: Vocatio vel missio, quæ jurisdictionem tribuit, & re ipsa pastorem atque præsulem facit. Quorum omnium suprema potestas & arbitrium penes Papam: delegata penes Episcopos, Papæ juratos est; exclusa de cætero Ecclesia & populo fideli omni, utpote cujus est non sibi propter salutem animarum suarum pastorem eligere, eíque lege verbi Dei se subjicere, sed aliena libidine obtrusum recipere, eíque se per cæcam obedientiam subjicere. Sed præterquam quòd tres hæ partes naturam partium constitutionis ministri Ecclesiæ non habent, quia ea proprie in sola vocatione legitima, jus omne, quod Ecclesiæ ministro competit, tribuente, consistit; & electio nihil aliud est, quàm essentialis modus vocationis ordinariæ; Ordinatio vero electionis testificatio & complementum, & post electionem atque ordinationem legitimam nulla vocatio aut missio generaliter expectanda est; neque omnino quid vocationis deest, ministro sic electo & ordinato, intelligi potest; nulla etiam vel jurisdictio, vel præfectura cum dominio conjuncta, vel potestas sacrificandi, cuiquam quacunque sive vocatione, sive missione tribui potest, quia dominandi Ecclesiæ & sacrificandi potestas in ministrum Ecclesiæ N. T. non cadit. Quod ex iis, quæ non semel de statu Ecclesiæ N. T. diximus, liquet.
units.tr: ministers, pastors and teachers, are appointed and ordained to perform their office by the whole Church, or by those to whom the Church has entrusted this care, and since those appointed and ordained minister to the Church, the Hierarchists, by contrast, distinguish three things in the constitution of Church ministers: election, ordination, and vocation or mission. According to them, election is the designation of a certain person to an ecclesiastical office. Ordination is the sacred ceremony by which the future minister of the Church is consecrated to a certain congregation. Vocation or mission confers jurisdiction and actually makes him a pastor and prelate. The supreme power and decision in all of these rests with the Pope; the delegated power rests with the bishops, who are sworn to the Pope. The Church and the faithful people are excluded altogether, since it is not for them to choose a pastor for the salvation of their souls and submit to him under the law of God's Word; rather, they must receive one forced on them by another's lust and submit to him in blind obedience. But apart from the fact that these three parts do not have the nature of the parts that constitute a minister of the Church, since that constitution properly consists in lawful vocation alone, which bestows every right belonging to a minister of the Church, and since election is nothing other than the essential mode of ordinary vocation, while ordination is the attestation and completion of election, and after a lawful election and ordination no further vocation or mission can generally be expected; nor can it be understood what is lacking to a minister so elected and ordained. Nor can any jurisdiction or office joined with dominion, or any power of sacrificing, be granted to anyone by any vocation or mission whatever, because the power of ruling over the Church and of sacrificing does not belong to the minister of the Church of the New Testament. This is clear from what we have said more than once about the state of the Church of the New Testament.

units.la: XXXVIII. Neque etiam eligendi & vocandi Ecclesiæ ministrum jus supremum Papa, delegatum Episcopus, à Presbytero distinctus, & Papæ juratus habet. Neuter enim à Christo institutus est; ullúmque adeò vocandi jus habet; & vocationem Ecclesiæ veræ, ejúsque ordinibus, Magistratui, Pastoribus & populo, sed distincta ratione, convenire, supra Sect. I. § XXV. &c. fusiùs probavimus. Papa verò jus illud Ecclesiæ non pretio, sed vi abstulit, & eo ipso se Antichristum prodit.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Nor does the Pope, who holds the supreme right of electing and calling a minister of the Church, nor the bishop, who holds it by delegation and is distinct from the presbyter and sworn to the Pope, possess that right. For neither was instituted by Christ, and neither therefore has any right of calling; and we have proved at greater length above, in Sect. I. § XXV. etc., that the calling of the true Church and of its orders belongs to the magistrate, the pastors and the people, though on a different basis. The Pope, however, has taken that right from the Church not by agreement but by force, and by this very act he reveals himself as Antichrist.

units.la: XXXIX. Quantum verò ad ordinationem, quatenus illam adversarii ab electione & missione distinguunt, & ritu certo atque ceremoniis, quales sacra unctio, tonsura circularis, aliáque ejusmodi sunt, definiunt, eam in Sacramentorum etiam numerum referre non erubuerunt, haud alium in finem, quàm ut Sacerdotii sui potestatem & dignitatem in immensum velut extollerent, quasi Sacramento tali dedicati sacratiores redderentur, ut dicere possint: Mane apud te, ne appropinques mihi קְדַשְׁתִּיךָ quia sacratior te sum, Esaj. LXV. 5. Sed ex Sacramentorum augustè talium censu ordinationem hanc supra jam summovimus.
units.tr: XXXIX. As for ordination, insofar as our opponents distinguish it from election and mission, and define it by a fixed rite and ceremonies such as sacred anointing, the circular tonsure and things of that sort, they have not been ashamed to count it among the sacraments, for no other purpose than to exalt the power and dignity of their priesthood beyond measure, as if those dedicated by such a sacrament were rendered more sacred, so that they could say: "Stay where you are, do not come near me, for I am holier than you" [קְדַשְׁתִּיךָ], Isa. 65.5. But we have already set aside this ordination from the number of such majestic sacraments above.

units.la: XL. Neque satis illi habent Ordinationem Sacramentum facere. Nam in ordinatissima Ecclesiæ dispositione, sic Tridentini Sess. XXIII.
units.tr: XL. Nor are they content to make ordination a sacrament. For in the most orderly arrangement of the Church, as the Council of Trent speaks in Sess. XXIII.

units.la: Cap. II. Can. 2. loquuntur, diversi ordines sunt, per quos velut supremos gradus quosdam in Sacerdotium tendatur. Quos majores, vel minores faciunt. Majores, Sacerdotium, Diaconatum, Subdiaconatum; Minores, quorum munus qui sustinent, Acoluthi, Lectores, Exorcistæ & Ostiarii dicuntur. Sacerdotis est sacrificare: Diaconi sacrificanti assistere & ministrare, Eucharistiam distribuere, Evangelium legere, baptizare, prædicare. Subdiaconi, Diacono ministrare, patinam, calicem, librum illi porrigere. Acoluthi cum cereo accenso sequi Diaconum, urceolos ac ampullas ad sacrificium, nec non luminaria præparare. Exorcistæ, exorcismos Ecclesiæ supra catechumenos legere: Lectoris extra tempus sacrificii in pulpito Evangelium legere. Ostiarii, templi ostium aperire & claudere. Horum ordinum exercitio & actuum ab illis emanantium vi atque ἐνεργεία Missæ suæ φεκτὴν mysterium & sacrificium confici pertendunt. Sed ordines illi universi inutiles, perniciosi & merè Antichristiani sunt. Tendunt enim ad Sacerdotium, & in eo velut culmine & fastigio suo siltunt; cùm nullum in Nov. Test. Sacerdotium externum certo hominum generi alligatum, nullum sacrificium externum & proprie dictum esse, supra fidem fecerimus. Neque etiam ordines illi uspiam à Christo instituti sunt. Nam Sacerdotes externos & proprie dictos omnes Christi sacerdotium unicum sustulit. Diaconos Apostoli instituerunt, sed mensis, non altari ministrantes. Exorcistarum munus temporale fuit. De cæteris ordinibus altum silentium est. Non igitur institutioni Christi, sed cacozeliæ gentilium & Judæorum ordinum illa distinctio ferenda accepta est. Gentiles enim suos Flamines, Archiflamines, Protoflamines: Judæi Ostiarios, Exorcistas, Cantores habuerunt. Unde Lombardus Dist. 24. singulos ordines diversis verbis ex Judaismo derivat. Et conferunt ordines illi titulos, quibus res nulla subest. Episcopi enim non docent: Sacerdotes non sacrificant, destituti sacrificio: Diaconi non ministrant Ecclesiarum oblationibus, quas satis jam dotatas habent. Acoluthi Sacerdotum & Episcoporum canes venatici, equites, milites prætorii sunt: Exorcistæ nec voce humana, nec potestate Divina dæmonia pellunt: Lectores non legunt, ut intelligantur. Denique his titulis vel nihil subest, vel adulterina officia & pingues tantùm præbendæ subsunt. Fores claudere & aperire, cereos accendere, vasa custodire & mundare, mensam Domini vestire, aquam ad Baptismum, panem ad Eucharistiam afferre, ministeria ejusmodi manualia sunt, quæ æquè validè ordinatus & non ordinatus obire potest; uti hodiéque laici vilissimi, nullis majoribus vel minoribus ordinibus initiati obeunt. Aquinas quoque q. 37. art. 1. ad. 2. in add. rationem Sacramenti Ordinationis totam collocat in Sacerdotio; in aliis nonnisi per attributionem ad illud & participationem quandam, quod est non habere in se formaliter rationem Sacramenti. At nec minores illi ordines ad Sacerdotium ceu supremum gradus dici possunt. Nam etiam Christum Apostolos fecisse Sacerdotes in prima Cœna adversarii affirmant, qui tamen gradatione tione illa usus non est.Neque etiam Matthias cum gradatione tali delectus Apostolus est; & ex septem Diaconis ab Apostolis institutis nullus ad altiorem gradum ascendit. Etiam Petrus Arcudius Corcyraeus ex antiquitate praegnantiffimis argumentis allatis probavit, nunquam veteres minores illos ordines vel inter Sacramenta numerafle, vel necessarios judicaffe. Denique adversariorum circa ordines hos gravis dissensio vanitatem dogmatis probat. De Episcopis cumprimis & Cantoribus, nec non Tonsura prima & Episcopatu ingens Theologos inter & Canonistas disceptatio est; illis negantibus, ad ordines eos pertinere, his strenue afferentibus. Episcopatum quoque & Presbyteratum diversos esse ordines Canonistae & Bellarminus ajunt; Theologi Scholastici plures pernegant.
units.tr: Chap. II, Can. 2, there are "different orders, through which one advances, as through certain supreme grades, to the priesthood," which they divide into greater and lesser. The greater are priesthood, diaconate and subdiaconate; the lesser, whose duty is discharged by those who hold them, are called acolytes, readers, exorcists and doorkeepers. It is the duty of the priest to sacrifice; of the deacon, to assist the one sacrificing, to minister, to distribute the Eucharist, to read the Gospel, to baptize and to preach. The subdeacon is to minister to the deacon, to hand him the paten, the chalice and the book. The acolytes are to follow the deacon with a lighted candle and to prepare the cruets and flasks for the sacrifice, as well as the lights. The exorcists are to read the exorcisms of the Church over the catechumens; the reader is to read the Gospel from the pulpit outside the time of sacrifice. The doorkeepers are to open and close the doors of the temple. By the exercise of these orders and by the efficacy [ἐνεργεία] of the acts that flow from them, they maintain that the mystery and sacrifice of their Mass is accomplished. But all these orders are useless, pernicious, and purely Antichristian. For they aim at the priesthood and come to rest in it as in their culmination and summit, whereas we have shown above that the New Testament knows no external priesthood bound to a certain class of men, and no external sacrifice properly so called. Nor were those orders instituted anywhere by Christ. For Christ's single priesthood abolished all external priests properly so called. The apostles instituted deacons, but to serve at tables, not at the altar. The office of exorcists was temporary. Concerning the other orders there is deep silence. Therefore this distinction is not to be received as an institution of Christ, but as the perverse zeal of the Gentiles and Jews. For the Gentiles had their flamens, archflamens and protoflamens; the Jews had doorkeepers, exorcists and singers. Hence Lombard, Dist. 24., derives the individual orders from Judaism under various names. And these orders confer titles to which no reality corresponds. For bishops do not teach; priests do not sacrifice, having no sacrifice; deacons do not minister to the oblations of the churches, which are already sufficiently endowed. Acolytes are the hunting dogs, horsemen and praetorian soldiers of priests and bishops; exorcists drive out demons neither by human voice nor by divine power; readers do not read so as to be understood. In short, these titles either have no reality behind them or only adulterous offices and fat prebends. To close and open doors, to light candles, to guard and clean vessels, to dress the Lord's table, to bring water for baptism and bread for the Eucharist: these are manual services which an ordained man and an unordained man can equally well perform, just as the lowliest laymen today perform them without being initiated into any greater or lesser order. Aquinas too, q. 37. art. 1. ad 2. in add., places the whole notion of the sacrament of ordination in the priesthood; in the other orders it is only by reference to that and a certain participation in it, so that they do not have in themselves formally the character of a sacrament. But neither can those lesser orders be called the supreme grade leading to the priesthood. For our opponents assert that Christ made the apostles priests at the first Supper, yet he did not use that gradation. Nor was Matthias chosen an apostle by any such gradation, and of the seven deacons instituted by the apostles none rose to a higher grade. Peter Arcudius of Corfu, from the most weighty arguments drawn from antiquity, has also proved that the ancients never counted those lesser orders among the sacraments, nor judged them necessary. Finally, the serious disagreement of our opponents about these orders proves the vanity of the doctrine. Above all there is a vast dispute among theologians and canonists concerning bishops and singers, and likewise concerning the first tonsure and the episcopate; the one side denies that these belong to the orders, the other strenuously affirms it. The canonists and Bellarmine say that the episcopate and the presbyterate are different orders; the Scholastic theologians largely deny it outright.

units.la: XL. Lepidum equidem illud est, quod Christum ordines illos in sua persona geflifle, in Concilio Tridentino Petrus Soto contendit; frigidis conjecturis fretus. Id enim fi verum est, cur non eosdem actus in sua persona Pontifices & Sacerdotes omnes, qui fe Christi substitutos gloriantur, exercent? Non quivis certe actus Ministerii Christi Ordines, & quidem Sacramentales sunt; inprimis non heroici, extraordinarii & miraculofi, cujusmodi fuerunt, offerre fe ipsum, dispensare panem & vinum post coenam, praecincto linteo lavare pedes discipulorum, daemonia ejicere, flagello ementes & vendentes ex templo exturbare, &c. Nec Sacerdotes externi proprie dicti, nec Diaconi, vel subdiaconi altari ministrantes instituti, vel munera sua exercentes uspiam in Scriptura leguntur. Et minores ordines non ex Scriptura, sed ex traditione ipsimet adversarii extundere conantur. Neque difficitemur, gradus quosdam Ministerii fequiore aetate in Ecclesiam introductos esse, at non vel ex Apostolorum institutione, vel ex necessitatis ad oblationem vel confectionem sacrificii opinione, vel cum restrictione ad numerum septenarium, vel ita, ut omnes simul collati sint, sed ad varios Ecclesiae usus & ἐυ&ξίαν, ut majore cum dignitate, gravitate & decentia cultus Dei publicus in frequentioribus coetibus exerceretur, & per varios ordinum diversorum gradus ad ministerium Ecclesiae praeparcarentur. Sed faretur Caffander, minores ordines quinque, praesente tempestate, neglecta omni disciplina & politia Ecclesiastica, prorsus confusos esse, & eorum officia propemodum cessasse. Nam quod ordines illos institutos esse, & retineri debere, ut sancti sacerdotii, inprimis sacrificii Miffatici, ministerium tanto dignius, & majori cum veneratione exerceri posset, Tridentini statuunt, audiendi minime sunt, quia nec ex Scripturae, nec ex Veteris Ecclesiae usu instituti sunt eum in finem; cum Sacrificium Miffaticum utrique aeque incognitum fuerit. Et fi ad sacrificii conficiendi necessitatem ordines illi pertinent, qui fit, quod in singulis paroeciis & sacellis, in quibus Missa quotidie celebratur, unus est sacrificulus, nullique Diaconi, Subdiaconi, Acoluthi, &c. adstant? Nam quod adstare sacrificulum unum, septem illis ordinibus ornatum, atque id sufficere regerunt, cur igitur in Ecclesiis cathedralibus & majoribus numerum illum septenarium diversarum personarum instituunt? Si ad solam ἐυπξίαν, pompam & magnificentiam cultus id pertinere afferunt, fateantur igitur oportet, sacrificii confectionem septenarium illum numerum non requirere, & posse id omne pro locorum, temporum & personarum circumstantiis mutari, omitti vel destitui.
units.tr: XL. Indeed it is a curious thing that Peter Soto contended at the Council of Trent that Christ held those orders in his own person, relying on feeble conjectures. For if this were true, why do all the Pontiffs and priests who boast of being substitutes of Christ not perform the same acts in their own person? Surely not every act of Christ's ministry is an order, and certainly not a sacramental one; above all, those that were not ordinary but heroic, extraordinary and miraculous, such as offering himself, distributing bread and wine after supper, washing the disciples' feet with a towel girded about him, casting out demons, driving out of the temple those who bought and sold with a whip, and so on. Nor are external priests properly so called, nor deacons or subdeacons ministering at the altar, instituted anywhere in Scripture, nor are they read of as performing their duties there. And the lesser orders our opponents themselves strive to extract not from Scripture but from tradition. Nor shall we deny that certain grades of ministry were introduced into the Church in a later age; but they were not introduced by the institution of the apostles, nor on the opinion that they were necessary for the offering or consecration of the sacrifice, nor restricted to the number seven, nor established all together at once; rather, they were introduced for the various uses and decorum [εὐπρέπεια] of the Church, so that the public worship of God in the more frequented assemblies might be carried on with greater dignity, gravity and propriety, and so that men might be prepared for the ministry of the Church through the various grades of different orders. But Cassander confessed that the five lesser orders, in the present age, with all discipline and ecclesiastical polity neglected, have become utterly confused, and their duties have almost ceased. For the claim of the Tridentine fathers, that these orders were instituted and must be retained so that the holy priesthood, above all the ministry of the Mass sacrifice, might be exercised more worthily and with greater reverence, is by no means to be heard, since they were not instituted for that end either by Scripture or by the usage of the ancient Church, the Mass sacrifice being equally unknown to both. And if those orders pertain to the necessity of completing the sacrifice, how is it that in each parish and chapel where Mass is celebrated daily there is one little priest, and no deacon, subdeacon, acolyte and so on stands by him? For as to their reply that one priest, adorned with those seven orders, stands there and that this suffices, why then do they establish in cathedral and greater churches that septenary number of different persons? If they say this pertains only to decorum, pomp and magnificence of worship, they ought then to admit that the completion of the sacrifice does not require that septenary number, and that all of it can be changed, omitted or dispensed with according to the circumstances of places, times and persons.

units.la: XLI. Habent & hoc Ordines majores singulare, quod lex coelibatus iis ex voluntate & arbitrio Papae annexa est.
units.tr: XLI. Major orders also have this peculiarity: the law of celibacy is attached to them by the will and decision of the Pope.

units.la: Nam clericis ommibus, in ordinibus majoribus constitutis, Sacerdotibus, Diaconis & subdiaconis matrimonio Papa interdixit. Nam quod cuiquam prohibere Papam, ne nubat, & eum matrimonium omnium optioni liberae permittere, id unum praecaventem, ne clerici, qui se voto formali & explicito, vel virtuali & implicito ad coelibatum obstrinxerunt, voti sui transgressores fiant, obtendunt, ψεῦδολογία ἐν ὑπο-κρισι mendaciloquium cum hypocrisi conjunctum, quale Apostolus illis ipsis, qui prohibent nubere, 1. Tim. IV. 2. 3. tribuit, est. Prohibet enim, qui author est legis prohibentis; sicut Deus prohibere dicitur id, adversus quod legem dedit; & prohibet clericis omnibus, qui licentiam nubendi implicite iis negat. Neque voti praetextus obstat, quia Sacerdotes initiandos vel initiatos coelibatum vovere, salsissimum est. Votum enim est actus liberrimus, pendens a solo voluntatis arbitrio. Proin qui ordinatur propter opus, quod circa ipsum alius praestat, ordinationis videlicet, non censetur votum emisisse, nisi libere intendat vovere, & intentionem hanc suam diserte profiteatur, cum nihil obstet, etiamsi ordinationem admittat, qui non modo nullam intentionem vovendi, sed etiam contrariam habeat. Ideo Scotus debitum coelibatus exclusa omni ratione voti directe in solum praeceptum Ecclesiae reducit, quae constitutione sua ordinatum inhabilem ad matrimonium reddat. Et si vovent, tenentur volentes nolentes vovere, vel sacerdotio abstinere. Quale hoc votum est? Non cogit Papa ad ordines suscipiendos, inquiunt illi, si quis tamen ordines ultro suscipere voluerit, hunc coelibem vivere vult, jubet. Quod perinde est, ac si dicant latrones, se neminem vi spoliare, qui neminem peregrinari cogant, sed eos demum, qui sponte peregrinantur, se invadere. Imo vero Papa eos in coelibatu vivere cogit, qui charismata & charitatem habentes Ecclesiae inservire volunt: quomodo latrones vere spoliant eos, qui sponte se itineri committunt.
units.tr: For the Pope has forbidden marriage to all clerics in major orders: priests, deacons and subdeacons. As for the claim that the Pope forbids no one to marry and leaves marriage to everyone's free choice, but only takes precaution that clerics who have bound themselves to celibacy by a formal and explicit vow, or by a virtual and implicit one, do not become breakers of their vow, this is lying with hypocrisy [ψεῦδολογία ἐν ὑπο-κρισι], the very thing the Apostle attributes to those who forbid marriage, 1 Tim. 4.2-3. For he forbids who is the author of the law that forbids, just as God is said to forbid what he has given a law against; and he forbids all clerics when he implicitly denies them permission to marry. Nor does the pretext of a vow stand in the way, since it is most absurd to say that men being initiated or already initiated into the priesthood vow celibacy. For a vow is a wholly free act, depending solely on the decision of the will. Therefore one who is ordained for the sake of the work that another performs on him, namely the ordination itself, is not considered to have made a vow unless he freely intends to vow and expressly professes this intention, since nothing prevents a man who not only has no intention of vowing but even has the contrary intention from admitting to ordination. Hence Scotus, excluding every ground of vow, reduces the obligation of celibacy directly to the sole precept of the Church, which by its constitution renders the ordained unfit for marriage. "And if they vow, they are bound to vow whether willing or unwilling, or to abstain from the priesthood." What kind of vow is this? "The Pope does not compel anyone to take orders," they say; "if anyone wishes of his own accord to take orders, he orders that he live as a celibate." This is just as if robbers were to say that they plunder no one by force, since they compel no one to travel abroad, but only attack those who set out of their own accord. Indeed the Pope compels those who have gifts and charity and wish to serve the Church to live in celibacy, just as robbers truly plunder those who willingly entrust themselves to the road.

units.la: XLII. Caeterum lex haec coelibatus non Christum, sed Antichristum authorem habet.
units.tr: XLII. Moreover, this law of celibacy has Antichrist, not Christ, as its author.

units.la: Christus enim matrimonium sine discrimine omnibus continentiae dono carentibus, permisit. Apostolis enim dicentibus, forte non conferre nubere, respondit: Non omnes capiunt hunc sermonem, sed quibus datum est: Qui potest χωρεῖν capere, capiat, Matth. XIX. 10-13. non obscure innuens, χωρεῖν conferre nubere omnibus iis, qui χωρεῖν capere non possunt, & quibus non est datum, seu, qui continentiae donum non habent. At omnes eos, qui ordinantur, continentiae donum habere, vel, si qui habent, durabile illud & perpetuum habere, vel habere
units.tr: For Christ permitted marriage without distinction to all who lack the gift of continence. When the Apostles said that perhaps it is not expedient to marry, he answered: "Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it is given. He who is able to receive it [χωρεῖν], let him receive it" (Matth. 19.10-13), plainly hinting that marriage is expedient for all who cannot receive it and to whom it is not given, that is, who do not have the gift of continence. But that all who are ordained have the gift of continence, or, if some have it, that they have it durable and perpetual, or are able to have it

units.la: Lex caelibatus ordinum majorum annexa est. habere pro arbitrio suo posse, oppido falsum, & testatissimæ experientiæ repugnans est. Nam non omnibus δοθὲν datum esse, collatis scilicet gratiæ viribus,ut capiant, adeóque se propter Regnum Cœlorum eunuchizent, perspicuè Christus ipse contestatus est. Concors Christo Apostolus: Propter fornicationem, inquit, habeat quisque uxorem suam, & quæque virum suum, 1. Cor. VII. 2. Si qui non continent (de dono continentiæ certi non sunt, & tentationem metuunt) nubant. Præstat enim nubere, quàm uri, ibid. v. 9. Sicut enim melius est cibum modicum capere, quàm fame & siti torqueri, atque languidum fieri, & turbari in opere vocationis, uti exemplo Jonathanis patet, 1. Sam. XIV. 29. & melius est parare & acquirere panem suum, quàm mendicare, furari: ita melius, honestius, laudabilius est, habere conjugem cum amore castitatis, procreare atque educare liberos, & domum suam curare, quàm vagis libidinibus se exponere, & ad scortationem atque adulterium tentari. Matrimonium enim honorabile est ἐν πᾶσι in omnibus, seu apud omnes, qui ad nuptias idonei sunt, & nuptias contrahunt, & torus immaculatus est, Hebr. XIII. 4. Neque obstat, quòd conjugia quorundam incesta esse possunt, quia satis est omnium quædam conjugia posse esse τιμια honorabilia, quamvis non quævis, sed Divinis legibus conformata. Omnes nullo discrimine, nubere possunt; verùm nubentes legibus matrimonii Divinis se subjicere tenentur. Apostoli certè Ecclesiæ ministri & sanctissimi & occupatissimi nubere potuerunt: & quidam etiam nupserunt. Annon habemus potestatem sororem uxorem circumducendi, sicut & reliqui Apostoli, & fratres Domini & Cephas? 1. Cor. IX. 5. Ubi genuinæ conjuges, non mulieres Apostolis peregrinantibus inservientes intelligi liquet, tum quia mulieres non conjuges circumducere, suspectum ministerium Apostolorum reddidisset, cùm tales etiam in contubernio habere Synodus Nicæna vetuerit; tum quia ἀδελφὴν circumducere dicitur, non qui secum mulierem habet, sed qui cum authoritate & potestate eam ducit: tum quia non Apostoli potestatem habebant circumducendi mulieres non conjuges, sed illa potestas tota fuit fœminarum, quæ cùm sui juris essent, sponte illos sequi, vel non sequi poterant: tum quia ejusmodi mulieribus Apostoli Ecclesiam non onerassent. Uxorem igitur S. Paulus intellexit, quam ἀδελφὴν sororem appellavit spirituali sensu, nempe in Christo. Licet verò Apostoli à Christo vocati dicantur reliquisse omnia, Matth. XIX. 27. & Christus relinquentibus domus, fratres, sorores, Patrem, matrem, liberos, &c. amplissima quæque ibid. v. 29. promiserit, tamen non sic omnia Apostoli simpliciter reliquerunt, vel nobis relinquenda simpliciter sunt, sed quatenus sequelam Christi impediunt. Sic enim Apostoli officio conjugali renuntiarunt, sicut domestico & filiali. At huic non in universum eos renuntiasse, ex Matth. VIII. 14. Joh. XIX. 27. colligitur. Etiam Christo famulatæ mulieres, quas ille curaverat, Luc. VIII. 3. Sed non illas Christus ad ministerium suum circumduxit; verùm ille potiùs Christum, velut trophæa quædam virtutis ejus Θωμαλεψγυνὴς coluerunt. Multitudo autem obstare poterat suspicioni, & trophæa illa specialem à Christo, quæ in Apostolis non fuit, causam arguit. Grave inprimis illud est, quod S. Paulus interdictum nubendi ceu specimen & characterem eorum, qui in novissimis diebus à fide deficiunt, attendentes spiritibus deceptoribus, & doctrinis dæmoniorum in hypocrisi mendaciloquorum, qui cauteriatam conscientiam habent (qualis hypocrisis illorum est, qui cœlibatum exigunt ob sanctitatem & puritatem suam intrinsecam, nec non ministerii, quod obeunt, puritatem, cùm ipsi tamen impuritate scateant, & impuritatis omnis interdicto eo lato authores sint) 1. Timoth. IV. 1. 2. 3. notantur κωλυοντες γαμεῖν prohibentes nubere, & quidem deficientes à fide in novissimis diebus: proin non illi tantùm, qui in universum nubere omnibus prohibent, & prohibent ob impuritatem matrimonio affictam: quales veteres Encratitæ, Manichæi alii dicuntur, notantur. Hoc enim non Apostolus dixit, sed dicunt illi, qui verba Apostoli detorquent, atque sic conscientiam suam velut cauterias quibusdam obstupefaciunt. Etenim nubere prohibent, & qui absolutè, & qui secundum quid: & qui universis, & qui quibusdam: & qui initiandis: & qui initiatis: & qui voto obstrictis: & qui hanc ob causam, quòd matrimonium per se malum sit, & qui aliam ob causam prohibent. Nam ne Manichæi quidem absolutè, indefinitè & omnibus nubere prohibuerunt; certè non Auditoribus duntaxat, uti appellabant, hoc est, laicis; sed electis duntaxat suis, quales clericos Pontificii appellant; Augustino ipso teste. Et si Manichæi electis matrimonium, ceu rem malam prohibuerunt, at in Auditoribus illud tolerarunt; Pontificii, matrimonium laudantes ut rem bonam, Manichæis deteriores sunt, quòd rem judicio suo bonam & laudandam quibusdam prohibent. Quanquam falsum est, matrimonium ab iis laudari ut rem bonam, quia, si Siricio Papæ ad Himericum scribenti credere fas est, qui in matrimonio vivunt, in carne vivunt, & qui in carne vivunt, Deo placere non possunt, Rom. VIII. 8. Eosdem ergo, uti decet ἐν σαρκὶ ψευδολόγους eos, qui in hypocrisi mendaciloqui sunt, & laudant, & damnant, ex eodem ore & calidum & frigidum, dulce & amarum fundentes. Tum nuptias legitimas, & amorem conjugii dicunt contrariari puritati sacerdotii, & quod verè dæmoniacum est, magis contrariari, quàm scortationem, incestum & sodomiam. Aut si non contrariantur puritati Sacerdotis, quare illos prohibent? Accedit, quòd potestas conjugii contrahendi jure Divino & naturali omnibus competit, juxta verba Dei omnibus dicta: Crescite & multiplicamini, Genes. I. 28. & naturæ ipsius instinctum, insitúmque omnibus appetitum habendi adjutorium se dignum, videndi liberos, semen sanctum, & progenitoribus gratiam referens. Qui igitur conjugium quibusdam prohibet, is se supra Deum & naturam, atque utriusque jus effert, quod nemo nisi Antichristiano spiritu tumens facit. Ac ne ipsos quidem Episcopos excipi, clarissimè S. Paulus docuit, jubens Episcopum eligi, ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς γυναικὸς, si quis est unius mulieris vir, Tit. I. 6. hoc est, non qui fuit digamus; cùm de eo loquatur, qui is est; & iteratae nuptiae nullum ἐγκλημα habeant, nec cuiquam exprobrari possint, dummodo in Domino nupserit; adeò ut Apostolus etiam jusserit viduas juvenes nubere, 1. Tim. V. 9.14. sed qui non est polygamus, vel qui praeter uxorem legitimam pellicem non habeat, neque dimissa legitima uxore, sine causa aliam duxerit. Uxoratus ergo Episcopus esse potest, at non polygamus. Neque etiam obscurè S. Paulus Divino & vaticino spiritu legem coelibatus perstringit, quando illos, qui non tenent caput Christum, sed aliud caput sibi eligunt, se δογματίζειν passuros decretis; inter quae illud etiam est: Μὴ ἅψῃ, ne tangas, uxorem, onerari praedixit, Col. II. 19. 20. 21. Quantae vero illiadis malorum in Ecclesia causa fuerit, & hodieque sit lex coelibatus, nihil dicere attinet. Testes ejus rei gravissimos, & inter eos etiam Pontifices ipsos, Pium II. & Paulum II. quin & Imperatores & Principes, Sigismundum, Maximilianum II. Oratorem Bavari, alios, qui querelas de impuritate Cleri omnigena maximas confignarunt, alibi produximus. Nam quòd legem non luere debere delicta, neque abrogandam esse, quia plures eam violant, regerunt, inane prorsus est. Alia enim ratio est legis Divinae & naturalis, alia tyrannicae, quae prohibet id, quod lex Dei & naturae permittit, & injungit id, quod in hominum potestate non est, & ex qua venenatissimi fructus apud eos, qui charismate continentiae destituuntur, necessario pullulant. Non illa, sed haec lex delicta luere, & vel nunquam ferri, vel lata abrogari debet. Atque licet legem coelibatus nunquam non superstitio Ecclesiae propinaverit, tamen diu in Ecclesia veteri recepta non est. Primi Siricius & Innocentius illam pertulerunt, ingenuè id confitente Petro de Marca, de Concord. Sacerd. & Imp. l. 1. 8. Secuti Pontifices alii citiùs, alii tardius, nec sine gravi virorum piorum & doctissimorum contradictione, legem eam Ecclesiis obtruserunt. Graeci verò nunquam eo jugo a Romanis sese onerari passi sunt. Meritòque lex illa inter arcana dominationis Papalis referitur, quia, uti in ipso Concilio Tridentino multos ita sensisse Svavis Polanus Hist. C. T. lib. VI. testatur, manifestum est; Permisso Presbyterorum conjugio futurum, ut omnes affectum & amorem suum in uxorem & liberos, adeòque familiam & patriam convertant. Inde cessaturam artem illam Ordinis Clericalis cum sede Apostolica conjunctionem, ut matrimonium concedere Episcopis non sit aliud, quàm Hierarchiam de Ecclesia tollere, & Pontificem redigere ad Romae solius Episcopatum. Et Cardinalis Carpensis apud eundem lib. V. ingenuè confessus est, permisso coelibatu, futurum, ut familiam, uxores ac liberos alentes ad Principis quisque sui obedientiam respiciens, Pontificis obsequium detrectet, & intra breve tempus Apostolica sedes Urbis Romanae cancellos non egrediatur. Ante institutum coelibatum Sedem Romanam nullum ex aliis civitatibus ac regionibus fructum percepisse, sublato coelibatu omnium sacerdotiorum dominatum ademptum iri, utpote quae matrimonium exiguo tempore illi eriperet: Tam bellè coelibatus arcana ipsi nobis Hierarchici reserarunt. Denique quo jure, Divino an Ecclesiastico positivo lex coelibatus nitatur, ipsi met Hierarchici vehementer dissident, de quo alibi plura diximus.
units.tr: The law of celibacy is attached to the major orders. The claim that a man may decide this for himself is utterly false and contrary to the most well-attested experience. Christ himself plainly testified that not to all is given [δοθὲν] the gift, that is, the gift of grace bestowed so that they may receive it and so make themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. The Apostle agrees with Christ: Because of fornication, he says, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband, 1 Cor. 7.2. If they cannot contain (they are not sure of the gift of continence and fear temptation), let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn, ibid. v. 9. Just as it is better to take a modest amount of food than to be tormented by hunger and thirst, and to grow weak and disturbed in the work of one's calling, as the example of Jonathan shows (1 Sam. 14.29), and better to earn and acquire one's own bread than to beg or steal, so it is better, more honourable and more praiseworthy to have a wife with a love of chastity, to beget and bring up children, and to look after one's own household, than to expose oneself to wandering lusts and be tempted to whoredom and adultery. For marriage is honourable among all [ἐν πᾶσι], that is, among all who are fit for marriage and enter into it, and the bed undefiled, Heb. 13.4. Nor does it stand in the way that some marriages may be incestuous, since it is enough that some marriages, though not every one, but those conformed to the divine laws, can be honourable [τιμια]. All may marry without distinction, but those who marry are bound to submit to the divine laws of marriage. Certainly the Apostles, ministers of the Church, most holy and most busy, could marry, and some did marry. Have we not power to lead about a sister as wife, as also the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? 1 Cor. 9.5. That genuine wives are meant here, and not women serving the travelling Apostles, is clear: first, because leading about women who were not wives would have made the Apostles' ministry suspect, since the Nicene Synod forbade even keeping such women in one's household; second, because to lead about a sister [ἀδελφὴν] is said not of one who has a woman with him, but of one who leads her with authority and right; third, because the Apostles did not have the power to lead about women who were not wives, for that power belonged wholly to the women, who, being their own masters, could follow them or not as they chose; fourth, because the Apostles would not have burdened the Church with such women. Paul therefore meant a wife, whom he called a sister [ἀδελφὴν], in a spiritual sense, namely in Christ. Although the Apostles called by Christ are said to have left everything (Matt. 19.27), and Christ promised the greatest rewards to those leaving houses, brothers, sisters, father, mother, children, etc. (ibid. v. 29), yet the Apostles did not simply leave everything, nor are we simply to leave everything, but only insofar as it hinders following Christ. Thus the Apostles renounced the conjugal office just as they renounced the domestic and filial. That they renounced this altogether is not inferred from Matt. 8.14 or John 19.27. Women who had been healed by Christ also served him (Luke 8.3), but Christ did not lead them about for his ministry; rather they honoured him as trophies of his power. A crowd, however, could give rise to suspicion, and those trophies point to a special cause from Christ, which was not present in the case of the Apostles. Especially grave is that St Paul marks out a prohibition of marriage as the sign and mark of those who in the last days fall away from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons, in the hypocrisy of liars, who have their conscience seared (such is the hypocrisy of those who demand celibacy on account of their own inward holiness and the purity of the ministry they discharge, while they themselves teem with impurity and are the authors of every impurity once such a prohibition is issued), 1 Tim. 4.1-3. They are branded as forbidding to marry [κωλυοντες γαμεῖν], prohibiting marriage, and indeed as falling away from the faith in the last days. Therefore it is not only those who forbid marriage to all in general, and forbid it on account of the impurity attached to it, such as the ancient Encratites and the Manichaeans are said to be, who are meant. For the Apostle did not say this; those who twist the Apostle's words say it, and so numb their conscience as with cauteries. For they forbid marriage: both those who do so absolutely and those who do so in part; both those who forbid it to all and those who forbid it to some; both to those about to be initiated and to those already initiated; both to those bound by a vow; both those who forbid it because marriage is evil in itself and those who forbid it for some other reason. For not even the Manichaeans forbade marriage absolutely, indefinitely and to all. Certainly they did not forbid it to the Hearers, as they were called, that is, the laity, but only to their own Elect, such as the Papists call clerics; Augustine himself bears witness to this. And if the Manichaeans forbade marriage to the Elect as an evil thing, yet tolerated it in the Hearers, the Papists, who praise marriage as a good thing, are worse than the Manichaeans, since they forbid to some what in their own judgement is good and to be praised. Although it is false that they praise marriage as a good thing, because, if it is right to believe Pope Siricius writing to Himerius, those who live in marriage live in the flesh, and those who live in the flesh cannot please God (Rom. 8.8). These men, then, who are liars in the flesh [ἐν σαρκὶ ψευδολόγους] and liars in hypocrisy, both praise and condemn, pouring forth from the same mouth both hot and cold, sweet and bitter. They say that lawful marriage and love of wedlock are contrary to the purity of the priesthood, and, what is truly demonic, that they are more contrary to it than whoredom, incest and sodomy. Or if they are not contrary to the purity of the priest, why do they forbid them? Moreover, the power of contracting marriage belongs by divine and natural right to all, according to the words of God spoken to all, Increase and multiply (Gen. 1.28), and according to the instinct of nature itself and the appetite implanted in all for having a helper worthy of them, for seeing children, a holy seed, and for returning gratitude to their parents. Whoever forbids marriage to some therefore sets himself above God and nature and the right of both, which no one does except one puffed up with an Antichristian spirit. Nor are even the bishops themselves excepted, as St Paul clearly taught when he bade that a bishop be chosen who is the husband of one wife [ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς γυναικὸς], if he is a man of one wife (Titus 1.6). That is, it means not one who has been married twice, since he speaks of one who is such; and second marriages carry no fault and cannot be reproached against anyone, provided the marriage is in the Lord. So much so that the Apostle even ordered young widows to marry (1 Tim. 5.9, 14). The bishop must be one who is not a polygamist, who has no concubine besides his lawful wife, and who, having not dismissed his lawful wife, has not taken another without cause. A bishop may therefore be married, but not a polygamist. Nor does St Paul, by a divine and prophetic spirit, obscurely strike at the law of celibacy when he foretold that those who do not hold to the head, Christ, but choose another head for themselves, would allow themselves to be burdened with decrees (δογματίζειν), among which is this: Do not touch (Μὴ ἅψῃ) the wife, Col. 2.19-21. But how great a host of evils this law of celibacy has been, and still is, in the Church, there is no need to say. We have elsewhere produced the most weighty witnesses to this, among them the Pontiffs themselves, Pius II and Paul II, and even emperors and princes, Sigismund and Maximilian II, the Bavarian orator, and others, who recorded the greatest complaints about the impurity of the clergy in every form. As for the claim that a law ought not to be blamed for its offences, nor abrogated because many violate it, that is utterly empty. For the divine and natural law is one thing, a tyrannical law another, the latter forbidding what the law of God and nature permits, and enjoining what is not in man's power, and from it the most poisonous fruits necessarily spring up among those who lack the gift of continence. It is not the former but the latter law that ought to bear the offences, and it ought either never to have been enacted or, once enacted, to be abrogated. And although superstition has always promoted the law of celibacy in the Church, nevertheless it was not received in the ancient Church for a long time. Siricius and Innocent were the first to impose it, as Peter de Marca frankly confesses, de Concord. Sacerd. & Imp. l. 1. 8. Later Popes, some sooner and some later, and not without serious opposition from pious and most learned men, forced that law upon the Churches. The Greeks, however, never allowed themselves to be burdened by that yoke from the Romans. And rightly is that law reckoned among the secrets of papal domination, as is clear from the fact that, as Polanus (Svavis) testifies in book VI of his History of the Council of Trent, many at the Council itself thought so: If the marriage of presbyters were permitted, it would come about that everyone would turn his affection and love to wife and children, and so to family and country. The art of joining the clerical order to the Apostolic See would then cease, so that to grant marriage to bishops would be nothing other than to remove the hierarchy from the Church and reduce the Pontiff to the bishopric of Rome alone. And Cardinal Carpensis, also cited by the same author in book V, frankly confessed: If celibacy were permitted, it would come about that each man, supporting a family of wife and children, would look to the obedience of his own prince and refuse obedience to the Pontiff, and within a short time the Apostolic See would not go beyond the walls of the city of Rome. Before celibacy was instituted, the Roman See received no fruit from other cities and regions; with celibacy removed, the dominion of all priesthoods would be taken away, since marriage would snatch that away in a short time. So neatly have the hierarchs themselves unlocked for us the secrets of celibacy. Finally, on which right the law of celibacy rests, whether divine or positive ecclesiastical law, the hierarchs themselves vehemently disagree, on which matter we have said more elsewhere.

units.la: XLIII. Sed non destituitur pigmentis suis lex coelibatus, impia licèt, impura & tyrannica maximè. Nam in V. T. quando res sacra facienda, vel tractanda fuit, abstinentiam ab uxoribus, Exod. XIX. 15. 1. Sam. XXI. 4. praeceptam esse, caussantur. Verùm si qua in V. T. conjugii usui impuritas certo tempore infuit, illa legalis fuit, & communis sacerdotibus & populo fuit, & unà cum ceremoniis expiravit æquè ac impuritas ex contactu mortui. Et si quid exempla illa V. T. efficerent, non illa conjugium Ministrorum Ecclesiae, sed ejus tantùm usum certo tempore tollerent. Nam extra tempus illud toti populo & Sacerdotibus V. T. uxoratis esse utique licuit, tametsi æquè illis incumberet legem diu noctuque meditari. Ἐφημερίαν verò illae Sacerdotum V. T. quingentis post Mosen annis institutae, quibus domo & ab uxoribus aberant, 1. Paralip. XXIV. non ideo institutae sunt, quòd consuetudo conjugalis Sacerdotes ad ministerium indignos redderet, cùm & ipse Pontifex, cujus erat singulis diebus mane atque vesperi Domino sacrificium offerre, Exod. XXIX. 38. conjugatus fuerit; neque lex ulla extiterit, quae sacerdotibus consuetudini conjugali interdiceret, vel tempore ἐφημερίας perpetim domo abesse juberet, vel ex domibus suis venientibus necessitatem purificandi se imponeret. Conjugibus porro edicens Paulus, ne se invicem defraudent, nisi forte ad tempus, ut vacent jejunio & precibus, 1. Cor. VII. 5. neutiquam Ministros nisi coelibes cultui publico vacare non posse, innuit, quia matrimonium honorabile in omnibus, Hebr. XIII. 4. pietatis exercitiis & precibus non obstat; & aequè populus fidelis, qui uxoratus utique esse poterit, verbum Dei audire, Sacramenta percipere, precibus vacare, atque pastores verbum Dei praedicare, Sacramenta dispensare, & orare tenetur. Loquitur ergo S. Paulus de precibus extraordinariis & jejuniis, singularem ob causam suscepti, in quibus sponsus de thalamo suo, & sponsa de cubili suo egredi, Joel. II. 16. jubetur. Neque adeò S. Paulus hoc edixit ex imperio, sed ex concessione: non de abstinentia perpetua, sed ordinaria: non de precibus ordinariis, sed extraordinariis: non de ministris Ecclesiae solis; sed etiam de populo; jubens etiam, ut iterum convenient in unum, ne eos Sathanas tentet. David certè uxoratus frequentior in precibus & exercitiis spiritualibus fuit, quàm sacratorum Papalium quisquam. Vetat verò etiam S. Paulus eum, qui militat, implicari negotiis vitae, 2. Tim. II. 4. nempe immodicis, nimiis, à pietate, sanctitate, obeundo munere avocantibus, quae inter non matrimonium, sed lites forenses, jurisdictio, dominatio temporalis, splendor Persicus, bella referenda sunt. Sanè etiam S. Paulus artem mechanicam exercens, πεϱιγμαλείαν τῆ βίω modicam illam curavit, neque tamen ad obeundum munus Apostolicum ineptior fuit. Idem S. Paulus Episcopum jubet esse σώφρονα & ἐγκρατῆ continentem, Tit. I. 8. sed eundem unius uxoris virum esse jubens conjugio interdicere noluit. Σώφρων verò opponitur vel μαινομένῳ furenti, & cum & tum ad animum refertur, vel ἀνσλάσῳ dissoluto, & tum eum notat, qui in cibo, potu & ἀφροδισίοις modum servat, quod in conjugio etiam licet. Ἐγκρατὴς vero non is duntaxat est, qui à Venere omni temperat, sed qui se à voluptatibus illicitis continet, quod in matrimonio & extra illud locum habere potest. Matrimonio vero tribuere ἀκρατείαν manifesta ejus vituperatio est. Verum est, quòd Apostolus 1. Cor. VII. 9. de iis, qui πυρόυνται uruntur, dicat, eos non ἐγκρατεύεσθαι continere. Et id ipsum v. 5. ἀκρασίαν vocat. Sed hanc ἀκρασίαν idem numerat inter vitia, propter quæ Episcopus non sit ἀνέγκλητος; quia permittit matrimonium, ut remedium πνρώσεως & ἀκρασίας ustionis & intemperantiæ. Si quis in conjugio uxore sua contentus est, is revera jam ἐγκρατὴς castus est. Continet enim se intra ordinem à Deo institutum: in quo si non esset, non contineret se, sed scortaretur. Impium profectò est, non credere pudicitiam et statui, quem Deus instituit, cui benedixit, & quem in remedium ustionis & fornicationis dedit. Quòd vero illi remedium adversus ustiones & fornicationem in precibus ponunt, perperam conjungenda dividunt. Precibus enim jungendum medium est, quod Deus ipse junxit, matrimonium, sine quo preces non fiunt in fide, quippe ordini & institutioni Divinæ repugnantes. Cùmque continentia extra conjugium sit χάρισμα δοθὲν datum seu donum gratuitum singulare quibusdam, non commune omnibus fidelibus, Matth. XIX.11. 1. Cor. VII.7. adeòque ad salutem necessaria non sit, non æquè ac dona fidelium communia & ad salutem necessaria precibus simpliciter impetrari potest. Impedimenta verò illa, quæ matrimonium propter impuritatem & pollutionem suam Sacerdotibus in sacrificando, orando, legendo, prædicando, Sacramenta administrando & similibus objicere pertendunt, ad fucum imperitis faciendum conficta sunt. Cùm enim Bellarminus fateatur, Ecclesiam Romanam à multis jam seculis permisisse Sacerdotibus Græcis matrimonii usum, si impedimenta talia in matrimonio essent, permisisset igitur Ecclesia Romana impuritatem vel pollutionem sacrificandi, orandi, prædicandi, Sacramenta administrandi, &c. muneri adversam. Cùmque matrimonium faciant Sacramentum gratiam sanctificantem conferens, quomodo idem potest esse causa opera gratiæ sic impediens? Si impuritas quævis talia impedimenta objiceret, nemo sacerdotio fungi posset, quia omnes Adami filii, solo excepto Christo, impuritatem quandam secum circumgestant. At nec matrimonio impuritas tribui potest, quod honorabile & impollutum Apostolus Hebr. XIII.4. disertè appellat. Non defuerunt in Concilio Nicæno legis cœlibatus machinatores. Sed insurrexit ibi Paphnutius, testibus Gelasio Cyziceno, Socrate & Sozomeno, inclamans, μὴ βαρὺν ζυγὸν τοῖς ἱερωμένοις ἀνδεγκτὸν ἐπιθεῖναι· τίμιον εἶναι τὸν γάμον λέγων, grave jugum sacratis viris caverent imponere. Honorabile esse cubile, & impollutum matrimonium. Prohibet Concilium illud Can. III. mulierem συνείσακτον subintroductam, non conjugem, quia clericis æquè ac laicis prohibet, & conjux vera non est συνείσακτος subintroducta, & Novella 123. mulier à συνεισάκτῳ muliere distinguitur; sed Focariam, uti Synodus Westmonasteriensis appellat, quam P. Samosathenum habuisse Eusebius Hist. Eccles. lib. VII.24. narrat. Neque ullum aliud Concilium generale pro lege cœlibatus allegare adversarii sustinent. Neocæsariense quidem Concilium can. I. jubet ordine removeri Presbyterum, ἐὰν γάμῃ si uxorem duxerit, post ordinationem, non ante eam. Prohibet nuptias post initum ordinem contrahere, non ante ordinationem contractarum usum. Etiam Carthaginense Concilium II. & V. jubet Episcopos abstinere κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ὄρας secundum propria (non priora) statuta, hoc est, in præstitutis uniuscujusque vicis diebus. Uti Balsamon, & non obscurè ipsum Concilium Trullense Can. XIII. interpretantur. Sed horum aliorumque etiam Conciliorum & Patrum testimonia peculiari libro pridem à me explicata & vindicata, ad compendium hèic ponimus. Non negamus tamen, quosdam larvatæ & imaginariæ sanctitatis laudem & admirationem, perversa quadam æmulatione, quasi aliqua contagione, ab Essæis, Marcionitis, Eucratitis, Origenianis, Montanistis & aliis hæreticis contraxisse. Sed cœlibatus legem ex jure Apostolico pastoribus in Ecclesia primitiva præscriptam, vel universaliter præscriptam fuisse, nunquam fidem misogami facient.
units.tr: XLIII. Yet the law of celibacy is not without its pretexts. They are impious, impure, and above all tyrannical. They argue that in the Old Testament abstinence from wives was commanded when a sacred thing was to be done or handled, Exod. 19:15; 1 Sam. 21:4. But if some impurity attached to the use of marriage in the Old Testament at a set time, it was a legal impurity, shared by the priests and the people alike, and it ended together with the ceremonies, just as the impurity from contact with a dead body did. And if those Old Testament examples proved anything, they would remove not the marriage of the Church's ministers but only its use at certain times. For outside that time it was certainly lawful for the whole people and for the married priests of the Old Testament, although they too were bound to meditate on the law day and night. The priestly courses of the Old Testament, instituted five hundred years after Moses, in which the priests were away from home and from their wives (1 Chron. 24), were not instituted because marital life made priests unfit for ministry, since the high priest himself, whose duty was to offer the sacrifice to the Lord every morning and evening (Exod. 29:38), was married. Nor was there any law forbidding priests marital intercourse, or ordering them to stay away from home continually during their course, or imposing on them the necessity of purifying themselves when they came home. Moreover, when Paul enjoins spouses, "Do not defraud one another, except perhaps for a time, that you may give yourselves to fasting and prayer" (1 Cor. 7:5), he does not imply that only unmarried ministers can be free for public worship. Marriage is "honourable in all" (Heb. 13:4), and it does not hinder the exercises of piety and prayer; the faithful people, who may certainly be married, are likewise bound to hear the Word of God, receive the sacraments, devote themselves to prayer, just as the pastors are to preach the Word of God, dispense the sacraments, and pray. St Paul therefore speaks of extraordinary prayers and fasts undertaken for a particular reason, in which "the bridegroom is to go out of his chamber and the bride out of her closet" (Joel 2:16). Nor did St Paul issue this as a command, but as a concession: not of perpetual abstinence but of ordinary abstinence, not of ordinary prayers but of extraordinary ones, not for the ministers of the Church alone but for the people as well, and he bids them also to come together again into one place, lest Satan tempt them. David, certainly a married man, was more frequent in prayer and spiritual exercises than any of the Papal consecrated men. Paul also forbids the one who "warreth" to be "entangled with the affairs of this life" (2 Tim. 2:4), namely with immoderate and excessive concerns that call away from piety, holiness, and the discharge of the office. Among these are not marriage but lawsuits, temporal jurisdiction and domination, Persian splendour, and wars. Indeed St Paul, while practising a manual trade, looked after that modest livelihood [περιγμαλείαν τῆ βίω], and yet he was no less fit to discharge the apostolic office. The same St Paul orders a bishop to be sober [σώφρονα] and temperate [ἐγκρατῆ], continent (Tit. 1:8), yet in ordering him to be the husband of one wife he did not wish to forbid marriage. Now sober [σώφρων] is opposed either to mad [μαινομένῳ], raging, and is then referred to the mind, or to dissolute [ἀσώτῳ], and then it denotes one who keeps measure in food, drink, and sexual pleasures [ἀφροδισίοις], which is permitted even in marriage. Temperate [ἐγκρατὴς] does not mean only one who abstains entirely from Venus, but one who restrains himself from illicit pleasures, which can take place both within marriage and outside it. To ascribe intemperance [ἀκρατείαν] to marriage is a plain condemnation of it. It is true that the Apostle, 1 Cor. 7:9, says of those who burn [πυρόυνται] that they do not contain themselves [ἐγκρατεύεσθαι], and in verse 5 he calls this incontinence [ἀκρασίαν]. But the same Apostle counts this incontinence among the vices on account of which a bishop is not blameless [ἀνέγκλητος], because he permits marriage as a remedy for burning [πυρώσεως] and incontinence [ἀκρασίας]. If anyone is content with his own wife in marriage, he is in truth already continent [ἐγκρατὴς] and chaste. For he keeps himself within the order instituted by God, and if he were not in it he would not restrain himself but would play the harlot. It is surely impious not to believe that chastity is to be found in the state which God instituted, which He blessed, and which He gave as a remedy for burning and fornication.
