But those who set marriage against prayer, by putting remedies against burning and fornication in prayers, divide what should be joined. For the means which God Himself joined, marriage, must be joined with prayer, since without it prayers are not made in faith, being repugnant to the divine order and institution. And since continence outside marriage is a gift given [χάρισμα δοθὲν], a free and singular gift granted to some and not common to all the faithful (Matt. 19:11; 1 Cor. 7:7), and therefore not necessary to salvation, it cannot be obtained by prayer in the same way as the common gifts of the faithful, which are necessary to salvation. Those hindrances, however, which they strive to put in the way of priests on account of the impurity and pollution of marriage, that it hinders them in sacrificing, praying, reading, preaching, administering the sacraments, and similar tasks, were invented to deceive the unlearned. For since Bellarmine admits that the Roman Church for many centuries has permitted the use of marriage to Greek priests, if such hindrances were in marriage, the Roman Church would have permitted an impurity or pollution opposed to sacrificing, praying, preaching, administering the sacraments, and so on. And since marriage makes a sacrament conferring sanctifying grace, how can the same thing be a cause impeding the works of grace? If any impurity whatever raised such hindrances, no one could hold the priesthood, since all the sons of Adam, Christ alone excepted, carry some impurity about with them. Nor can impurity be ascribed to marriage, which the Apostle in Heb. 13:4 plainly calls honourable and undefiled. At the Council of Nicaea there were not lacking advocates of the law of celibacy. But Paphnutius rose up there, according to the witness of Gelasius of Cyzicus, Socrates, and Sozomen, crying out: "Do not lay a heavy yoke on those in holy orders that they cannot bear; call marriage honourable" [μὴ βαρὺν ζυγὸν τοῖς ἱερωμένοις ἀνδεγκτὸν ἐπιθεῖναι· τίμιον εἶναι τὸν γάμον λέγων]. Let them beware of imposing a grave yoke on consecrated men: the bed is honourable and marriage undefiled. That Council, Can. 3, prohibits a woman subintroduced [συνείσακτον] and not a wife, since it forbids this to clergy and laity alike, and a true wife is not a subintroduced [συνεισάκτος] woman. Novella 123 also distinguishes a woman from a subintroduced [συνεισάκτῳ] woman. Rather she is a concubine, as the Westminster Synod calls her, whom Eusebius, Hist. Eccles. VII.24, relates that Paul of Samosata kept. Nor do the adversaries dare to allege any other general council in favour of the law of celibacy. The Council of Neocaesarea, Can. 1, indeed orders a presbyter removed from his rank if he marries [ἐὰν γάμῃ], that is, if after ordination he takes a wife, not if before it. It forbids contracting marriage after receiving orders, not the use of marriages contracted before ordination. The Councils of Carthage, II and V, also order bishops to abstain according to their own hours [κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ὥρας], that is, according to their own (not previous) regulations, namely on the days set for each one's turn. So Balsamon interprets, and the Council in Trullo, Can. 13, clearly does likewise. But we set down here in brief the testimonies of these and other councils and of the Fathers, which I have already explained and defended at length in a separate book. We do not deny that some, by a perverse rivalry, drew from the Essenes, Marcionites, Eucratites, Origenists, Montanists, and other heretics the praise and admiration of a masked and imaginary sanctity, as if by some contagion. But the law of celibacy, prescribed for pastors in the primitive Church by apostolic law, or prescribed universally, will never be proved by those who hate marriage.

units.la: XLIV. Habet & hoc Ordinatio, quòd vi Tonsuræ, quæ in ea administratur; Ordinati ab omni jurisdictione civili eximuntur; & uni folíque Papæ in temporalibus æquè atque spiritualibus subjiciuntur.
units.tr: XLIV. The ordination also has this effect: by the power of the tonsure administered in it, the ordained are exempt from all civil jurisdiction and are made subject to the Pope alone, in temporal matters as well as spiritual.

units.la: Et Tonsuram quidem primam Canonistæ fere omnes distinctum ordinem constituunt; diserté asserentes, sine ejus divina institutione neque clericatum, neque exemptionem cleri probari posse. Sed & Tonsura tamen illa veruicis, nec non rasura barbæ religiosa non obscurè in verbo Dei damnatur. Non radetis angulum orbem capitis vestri: & non rades extremitatem barbæ tuæ, Levit. XIX. 27. Utraque enim & tonsura capitis & rasura barbæ olim sacrificulis Ægyptiacis & Babyloniis, primam barbæ lanuginem & detonsos capillos Diis suis consecrantibus, in usu fuit. Sed tonsuram tamen illam seriò Tridentini imperarunt, & rasuram barbæ Gregorius VII. Epistola ad Jacobum Calaritanum Episcopum scripta præcepit mandans, ut clericos omnes abradere barbas compelleret. Fuit tamen olim etiam Tonsura poena flagitiorum, & rasura barbæ hominis scelestissimi. Qui capite & supercilio rasus est, inquiebat Cicero pro Roscio, ne unum pilum boni viri habere dicatur. Sed missō hoc, effectus Tonsuræ, exemptio à jurisdictione civili sic à Bellarmino explicatur, quòd exempti sint clerici ab obligatione legum civilium non quidem directiva, quatenus actiones humanas in commerciis temporalibus dirigunt, & sacris canonibus, vel officio clericali non repugnant, sed coactiva tamen, nisi eædem leges ab Ecclesia approbatæ fuerint: quòd non possint clerici à judice seculari judicari, si leges civiles non servant: quòd bona Ecclesiasticorum tam secularia, quàm Ecclesiastica libera sint à tributis secularium: quòd exemptio clericorum
units.tr: Almost all the canonists treat the first tonsure as a distinct order, plainly asserting that without its divine institution neither clerical status nor the exemption of the clergy can be proved. Yet that tonsure of the crown, and the religious shaving of the beard, are not obscurely condemned in the Word of God: "You shall not round off the corners of your head, nor mar the edges of your beard" (Lev. 19:27). For both the tonsure of the head and the shaving of the beard were once practised by Egyptian and Babylonian priests, who dedicated the first down of the beard and the cut hair to their gods. But the Tridentine fathers seriously enjoined that tonsure, and Gregory VII, in a letter to Jacob, bishop of Calaris, ordered that he compel all clerics to shave their beards. Yet the tonsure was once also a punishment for crimes, and the shaving of the beard the mark of the most wicked of men. "He who is shaven on head and eyebrows," Cicero said in the speech for Roscius, "is said not to have a single hair of an honest man." But setting this aside, the effect of the tonsure, exemption from civil jurisdiction, is explained by Bellarmine thus: clerics are exempt from the obligation of civil laws not in their directive force, insofar as they direct human actions in temporal dealings and do not conflict with the sacred canons or clerical office, but in their coercive force, unless those same laws have been approved by the Church; clerics cannot be judged by a secular judge if they do not observe the civil laws; the goods of ecclesiastics, both secular and ecclesiastical, are free from the taxes of laymen; and the exemption of clerics

units.la: Exemptio Cleri, vi tonsuræ, à potestate seculari, Antichristiana est. ricorum in rebus politicis tum quoad personas, tum quoad bona introducta sit jure humano & Divino positivo & naturali, per consequentiam non absolutè necessariam, sed indigam humanæ constitutionis: adeóque ad jus gentium rectè referatur. Sic Bellarminus. Et exemptionem cleri etiam à juramento fidelitatis &Suprematus Principi temporali præstando, à tributis eidem pendendis, denique à supplicijs, quæ civiles Magistratus à sceleratissimis expetere possint, planè apud Hierarchicos ratum est. Atque hoc jus Antichristi est, contrarium juri Christi, juxta quod omnis anima potestatibus supereminentibus (quæ gladium gestant) subjicitur, Rom. XIII.1. In promptu etiam sunt exempla V. & N. T. ipsiúsque etiam Christi & Apostolorum. Nam Christus tributum pendit, Matth. XVII.27. & Pontii Pilati potestatem adversus se agnovit, eíque se subjecit, non de facto duntaxat, sed etiam de jure, eodem scilicet, quo etiam parentibus & legi se subjecit. Etiam S. Paulus Cæsarem appellavit, Act. XXV. II. 12. coactus utique, ut jus Divinum, naturale & gentium, quale adversarii allegant, violaret, aliósque in tali peccato confirmaret; neque de facto duntaxat, sed etiam de jure, eodem videlicet, quo & judicem agnovit. Appellatio enim ad superiorem judicem ab inferiore provocatio est. Ad tribunal Cæsaris sto, inquit, ubi me judicari oportet, ibid. v. 10. Cúmque lex Divina Evangelica & Baptismus à jurisdictione civili neminem eximat, quo jure tonsura, humanum institutum eximit? Tot etiam leges in Codice & Authenticis extant, quæ testantur, clericos olim Imperatorum jurisdictioni obnoxios fuisse. Nihil enim, uti quondam Imperator Antoninus apud Capitolinum in Pio dixit, sordidius, imo crudelius est, quàm si Rempublicam ii arrodant, qui nihil in eam suo labore conferunt: si, quod ferendum esse leges negant, onus subire recusent, qui lucrum amplectuntur: si lac comedant, & lana operiantur, & quod crassum est, occidant. Imo quæ gravior pestis est, quàm in medio sinu habere, non tantùm contra quos, si te injuria affecerint, mutire non ausis, sed etiam, qui alienæ potestati fidem dederint, & teneantur ad nutum alterius; qualis Capitolinus ille Jupiter est; contra te arma sumere, nec quicquam pro salute tua facere possint.
units.tr: The exemption of the clergy, by virtue of the tonsure, from secular power is Antichristian. In political matters, both as to persons and as to goods, it was introduced by human law and by positive divine and natural law; it is consequently not absolutely necessary but depends on human constitution, and so is rightly referred to the law of nations. Thus Bellarmine. And that the clergy are also exempt from swearing the oath of fidelity and supremacy to a temporal prince, from paying taxes to him, and finally from the punishments which civil magistrates may demand against the most wicked, is plainly accepted among the hierarchists. And this right is the right of Antichrist, contrary to the right of Christ, according to which "every soul is subject to the higher powers, which bear the sword" (Rom. 13:1). There are examples at hand from both the Old and New Testaments, and of Christ himself and the Apostles. For Christ paid tribute (Matt. 17:27) and acknowledged the power of Pontius Pilate over himself and submitted to it, not only in fact but also by right, namely by the same right by which he also subjected himself to parents and to the law. St Paul too appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11–12), compelled indeed, and not to violate divine, natural and international law, as our opponents allege, nor to confirm others in such a sin; and he acknowledged the judge not merely in fact but also by right, by the same right. For an appeal is a challenge to a superior judge from an inferior one. "I stand at Caesar's tribunal," he says, "where I ought to be judged" (ibid., v. 10). And since the divine law of the Gospel and baptism exempts no one from civil jurisdiction, by what right does a tonsure, a human institution, exempt anyone? So many laws in the Code and the Authentics survive, attesting that clerics were once subject to the jurisdiction of the emperors. For, as the emperor Antoninus once said in Capitolinus's life of Pius, "nothing is more sordid, nay more cruel, than that those should gnaw at the commonwealth who contribute nothing to it by their labour; if they refuse to bear the burden which, they say, the laws do not allow to be borne, who yet embrace the gain; if they eat milk and are clothed with wool, and slaughter what is fat." Indeed, what is a graver plague than to keep in your bosom not only those against whom, should they wrong you, you dare not murmur, but also those who have pledged their faith to another's power and are bound at his nod, such as that Capitoline Jupiter is, who may take up arms against you and can do nothing for your safety?

units.la: XLV. Sed Josephus, inquiunt illi, Sacerdotum Ægyptiacorum terras liberas reliquit, quia Rex Pharao eas, ceu portionem, iis dederat, Genes. XLVII. 22. 26. Verùm nec exempla jus faciunt, nec certa & extraordinaria privilegia omnimodam exemptionem in realibus & personalibus evincunt; nec probari potest, demensum illud à Rege Sacerdotibus tempore famis concessum perpetuum fuisse; nec Sacerdotum agri ab omni tributo immunes fuerunt, sed tantùm venditi non sunt, quia aliunde habebant, unde vitam sustentarent, adeóque liberi fuerunt à novo tributo quintæ partis, quia nulla erat causa, cur iis imponeretur. Denique eadem ratio fuit præfectorum & procerum aulæ, qui tamen in personalibus & realibus exempti non fuerunt. Nequicquam profin heic Pontificii Sacerdotes fimbrias suas extendunt. Neque etiam Levitæ V. T. soli Pontifici subjecti fuerunt, sed præterea etiam Mosi, ut Principi, Rempublicam vice Dei ordinanti, & Regibus, uti Davidis, Solomonis, Hiskiæ, Josiæ historia clarè testatur. Et filios Regni à tributis pendendis liberos esse, Christus Matth. XVII.26. edixit. Et pertinent etiam ministri Ecclesiæ ad familiam Christi, perinde ut fideles omnes, qui tamen à jurisdictione civili non eximuntur. Ideo ipse etiam Christus, licèt filius Regni, quales non sunt Ecclesiæ ministri, nedum clerici, tamen quia legi subjectus fuit, jubenti tributum dare, cui tributum debetur, Rom. XIII.7. tributum dedit, ne daret scandalum, & ut aliis civilis subjectionis exemplum præiret. Sunt quinetiam Pastores Patres, quoad spiritualem curam, & quatenus tales filiis & ovibus non subsunt. Sed quoad civilem curam Magistratus pariter patres sunt, quibus eatenus omnis anima subesse debet. Qui uno modo præsunt & judicant, alio subesse & judicari possunt, sicut Reges quodammodo à Medicis judicantur. Et flagitiosi quidem Sacerdotes jure & privilegiis piorum excidunt: at possessiones, quæ Ecclesiasticorum sunt, non ideo jure communi excidunt. Neque etiam quia clerici Dei Ministri sunt, iccirco eorum bona sic Deo consecrata sunt, ut nullum homini profano in ea jus esse possit. Quia enim ministri Dei sunt, iccirco ad publicum Dei ministrum pertinet curare, ut officium suum faciant. Neque bona externa ampliùs eo modo Deo consecrari possunt, quo in V. T. consecrata fuerunt. Denique neque Canones Conciliorum Lateranensis, Coloniensis, Tridentini immunitatem hanc sancientes, moramur, quia non sacri, sed sacrilegi sunt.
units.tr: XLV. "But Josephus," they say, "left the lands of the Egyptian priests free, because King Pharaoh had given them to them as a portion" (Gen. 47:22, 26). But examples do not make law, and certain and extraordinary privileges do not establish a complete exemption in property and personal matters. Nor can it be proved that the grain allowance the king granted the priests in time of famine was perpetual. Nor were the priests' fields immune from every tax; they were only not sold, because they had other means of sustaining life, and so they were free from the new tax of a fifth, since there was no cause for imposing it on them. Finally, the same reasoning applied to the prefects and nobles of the court, who nevertheless were not exempt in personal and property matters. The Papist priests here stretch out their fringes in vain. Nor were the Levites of the Old Testament subject to the high priest alone, but also to Moses as prince, ordering the commonwealth in God's place, and to kings, as the histories of David, Solomon, Hezekiah and Josiah clearly testify. And Christ declared (Matt. 17:26) that "the sons of the kingdom" are free from paying tribute. The ministers of the Church also belong to the family of Christ, just as all the faithful do, and yet they are not exempt from civil jurisdiction. Therefore Christ himself, though a son of the kingdom, which the ministers of the Church are not, much less clerics, nevertheless, because he was subject to the law commanding "tribute to whom tribute is due" (Rom. 13:7), paid tribute, lest he give offence, and so that he might go before others as an example of civil subjection. Pastors are also fathers, as regards spiritual care, and insofar as they are not subject to their sons and sheep. But as regards civil care, magistrates are likewise fathers, to whom every soul ought to be subject in that respect. They preside and judge in one way, and in another they can be subject and judged, just as kings are in some sense judged by physicians. Wicked priests indeed fall from the right and privileges of the pious; but the possessions which belong to ecclesiastics do not therefore fall from the common law. Nor, because clerics are ministers of God, are their goods so consecrated to God that no profane man can have any right in them. For since they are ministers of God, it belongs to the public minister of God to see that they perform their office. Nor can external goods now be consecrated to God in the way they were consecrated in the Old Testament. Finally, we need not linger over the canons of the Councils of Lateran, Cologne and Trent, which sanction this immunity, for they are not sacred but sacrilegious.

units.la: XLVI. Sed quatuor clericorum ordines Monarchici faciunt, ministrantium altari, gubernantium, supererogantium & adjuvantium. Ministrantes illi sunt, qui altari & Sacerdoti ad conficiendum sacrificium ministrant. Quorum in censu septem ordines de quibus egimus, sunt. Gubernantes; qui & Dignitatum ab ordinibus distinctarum nomine veniunt; sunt Magistratus Papæ inferiores, per quos is Ecclesiam suam jurisdictione etiam exteriore iis communicata regit. In iis Episcopi, Metropolitani seu Archiepiscopi, Patriarchæ & Cardinales excellunt. Nam inferiorum gentium Dii sunt, quos secundi ordinis gubernantes clericos appellant, Præpositi, Archidiaconi, Vicarii, Archipresbyteri, Canonici, de quibus alibi, sunt.
units.tr: XLVI. But the Monarchists make four orders of clerics: those ministering at the altar, those governing, those supererogating, and those assisting. "Ministering" are those who serve the altar and the priest in the offering of the sacrifice; among these are the seven orders we have discussed. "Governing," which also go by the name of "dignities" distinct from the orders, are the inferior magistrates of the Pope, through whom he rules his Church, with external jurisdiction communicated to them. Among these, bishops, metropolitans or archbishops, patriarchs and cardinals excel. For they are the gods of the lower peoples, whom they call "clerics governing of the second order": provosts, archdeacons, vicars, archpriests and canons, of whom elsewhere.

units.la: XLVII. Episcopos omnes Presbyteris superiores esse Concilium Tridentinum Sess. XXIII. 9. definivit, licèt quo jure immediato-Divino, an Pontificio superiores sint, ob partium in Concilio ea de re conflictantium metum, definire non sustinuit. Superioritatem porro & eminentiam Episcoporum non honorariam duntaxat, nedum imaginariam faciunt, sed in dominatione quadam, & jurisdictione eminente collocant. Et olim quidem Episcopus Presbyterum Ecclesiastico jure sola ordinationis potestate superavit. Quid facit Episcopus, ita Hieronymus ad Evagrium quærit, excepta ordinatione, quod non faciat Presbyter? Quod etiam Chrysostomus in 1. Tim. III. diserte asserit. Sed postea processum ulterius est. Nam in Concilio Hispalensi can. 7. & Leonis Decret. Decret. 83. Episcoporum ἀπλεονεξίμαπα præter jus ordinandi, etiam jus confirmandi, basilicas, altaria erigendi, consecrandi, manus baptizandis, aut conversis ex hæresi, imponendi, publicè pœnitentem conciliandi, firmatos mittendi, &c. recensentur. Prohibitum quinetiam Presbyteris est, præsente Episcopo, infantes tingere, Sacramentum corporis & sanguinis Domini conficere, populum docere, ei benedicere, salutare & exhortari plebem, ut per hoc & discretio graduum & dignitatis fastigium demonstretur. Procedente tempore etiam aucta Episcopalis dignitas & potestas est, eique jam à Canonistis, auctoritas leges condendi & promulgandi, causas in foro externo & ipsius conscientiæ judicandi, in Conciliis suffragandi, judicandi, ordinandi, vocandi, puniendi, visitandi, confirmandi, beneficia conferendi, investiendi: Templa, monasteria, xenodochia erigendi, bona Ecclesiastica administrandi, aliaque ejusmodi, in quibus cumulandis vix Canonistæ sibi satisfaciunt, faciendi, eximia vindicatur.
units.tr: XLVII. The Council of Trent, Session 23, canon 9, defined that all bishops are superior to presbyters. It did not dare to define whether they are superior by immediate divine right or by papal right, for fear of the parties in the Council who disputed this point. Moreover, they make the superiority and eminence of bishops not merely honorary, much less imaginary, but place it in a certain dominion and an eminent jurisdiction. Formerly, indeed, a bishop surpassed a presbyter by ecclesiastical right through the power of ordination alone. "What does a bishop do," Jerome asks in his letter to Evagrius, "apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not do?" Chrysostom also states this plainly in his commentary on 1 Timothy 3. But later the matter went further. In the Council of Seville, canon 7, and in Leo's Decretals, Distinction 83, the bishops' extra privileges [ἀπλεονεξίαι] are listed: besides the right to ordain, also the right to confirm, to erect basilicas and altars, to consecrate, to lay hands on those being baptized or converted from heresy, to reconcile a public penitent, to send out the confirmed, and so on. Moreover, presbyters are forbidden, when the bishop is present, to baptize infants, to consecrate the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, to teach the people, to bless them, or to greet and exhort the people, "so that by this both the distinction of grades and the summit of dignity may be shown." As time went on, the episcopal dignity and power also increased, and canonists now claim for him the authority to enact and promulgate laws, to judge causes in the external forum and in conscience, to vote in councils, to judge, to ordain, to summon, to punish, to visit, to confirm, to confer and invest benefices, to erect temples, monasteries and hospices, to administer ecclesiastical goods, and other such things, in piling up which the canonists can hardly satisfy themselves; all these they claim as his peculiar privileges. ## XLVIII.

units.la: XLVIII.

Eminentiam quampiam Episcopi supra Presbyteros jure Ecclesiastico jam olim introductam esse, nulli diffitemur. Ejus originem sic Hieronymus in Epist. ad Tit. Idem est Presbyter qui & Episcopus. Et antequam Diaboli instinctu studia in religione fierent, & diceretur in populis: Ego sum Pauli, ego Apollinis, ego Cephæ, communi Presbyterorum consilio Ecclesiæ gubernabantur. Postquam vero unusquisque eos, quos baptizaverat, suos putabat esse, non Christi, in toto orbe decretum est, ut unus de Presbyteris electus superponeretur cæteris, ad quem omnis Ecclesiæ cura pertineret, ut schismatum semina tollerentur. Pluribus deinceps Scripturæ testimoniis eam in rem allegatis, addit: Hæc propterea, ut ostenderemus, apud veteres eosdem fuisse Presbyteros, quos & Episcopos; paulatim vero ut dissensionum plantaria evellerentur, ad unum omnem solicitudinem esse delatam. Sicut ergo Presbyteri sciunt, se ex Ecclesiæ consuetudine ei, qui sibi præpositus fuerit, subjectos esse: ita Episcopi noverint, se magis consuetudine, quam dispositionis Dominicæ veritate Presbyteris esse majores, & in commune debere Ecclesiam regere, imitantes Mosen, qui cum haberet solus præesse populo Israel, septuaginta elegit, cum quibus populum regeret. Idem Hieronymus Epist. 85. ad Evagr. narrat; Alexandriæ à Marco Evangelista ad Heraclem & Dionysium Episcopos, Presbyteros semper unum ex se electum in excelsiore gradu collocatum Episcopum nominasse; quomodo, inquit, si exercitus Imperatorem faciat, aut diaconi eligant de se, quem industrium noverint, quem Archidiaconum vocent. Quid enim facit, excepta ordinatione, Episcopus, quod Presbyter non faciat? Hactenus ille.
units.tr: That some eminence of a bishop above presbyters was introduced by ecclesiastical law long ago, we deny to no one. Jerome states its origin thus in his commentary on the Epistle to Titus: "A presbyter is the same as a bishop. And before, at the instigation of the Devil, factions arose in religion, and it was said among the peoples, 'I am of Paul, I of Apollos, I of Cephas,' the churches were governed by the common counsel of the presbyters. But after each one began to regard those whom he had baptized as his own, not Christ's, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be chosen and set over the rest, to whom the whole care of the church would belong, so that the seeds of schisms might be removed." Then, after citing several testimonies of Scripture to this effect, he adds: "I have said these things to show that among the ancients the presbyters were the same as the bishops; but gradually, so that the seedbeds of dissensions might be uprooted, the whole responsibility was transferred to one. Just as presbyters know that by the custom of the Church they are subject to the one who has been placed over them, so bishops should know that they are greater than presbyters more by custom than by the truth of the Lord's arrangement, and that they ought to rule the Church in common, imitating Moses, who, though he alone had to preside over the people of Israel, chose seventy with whom he might rule the people." The same Jerome, in his letter 85 to Evagrius, relates that at Alexandria, from the time of Mark the Evangelist, the presbyters, to Heraclas and Dionysius, always chose one from among themselves, placed him in a higher rank, and named him bishop: "just as if an army should make a general, or deacons should choose from among themselves one whom they know to be diligent and call him archdeacon. For what does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not do?" Thus far he. ## XLIX.

units.la: XLIX.

Verissimè Hieronymus Episcopum idem esse quod Presbyterum, jure scilicet Divino, dixit. S. Paulus enim quos Presbyteros nominavit, eosdem mox Episcopos nominat, & vicissim. Mileto mittens Ephesum convocavit Presbyteros Ecclesiæ, Actor. XX. 17. Quos sic mox alloquitur: Attendite vobis ipsis, & toti gregi, in quo Spiritus S. vos posuit Ἐπισκόπως Episcopos, v. 28. Idem ad Titum: Reliqui te Cretæ, ut constituas oppidatim Presbyteros; Si quis (Presbyter) est irreprehensibilis, &c. Oportet esse Episcopum esse irreprehensibilem, &c. Tit. I. 5. 6. 7. Verè igitur etiam Baronius dixit: Apostolorum ætate Presbyteros Ecclesiarum curæ præfectos etiam Episcoporum nomine venisse. Sed nomina, non etiam officia communia fuisse, falsò idem pertendit, quia distincta officia ex Divina institutione mandata & obita fuisse ab iis, qui iisdem nominibus censebantur, probari nequit.
units.tr: Jerome spoke most truly when he said that a bishop is the same as a presbyter, by divine right of course. For St. Paul, whom he calls presbyters, soon calls the same men bishops, and vice versa. "Sending from Miletus to Ephesus, he called the elders [presbyters] of the church" (Acts 20:17), whom he then immediately addresses thus: "Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops [Ἐπισκόπους]" (v. 28). Likewise to Titus: "I left you in Crete, that you should appoint presbyters in every city... If any (presbyter) is blameless... For a bishop must be blameless" (Titus 1:5–7). Truly, therefore, Baronius also said: "In the age of the Apostles, presbyters placed in charge of the care of the churches were also called by the name of bishops." But that these were names only, and not also common offices, he maintains falsely, since it cannot be proved that distinct offices, mandated and discharged by divine institution, belonged to those who were called by the same names.

units.la: Cùm igitur eo tempore nomina communia fuerint, & nominum communio, cùm verè dicitur, communionem rerum, nominibus iis designatarum importet, & nomina & res nominibus designatas communes fuisse sequitur. Eorum verò, qui idem sunt, qua idem sunt, communis est operatio. Neque enim hodie Episcopum vel Papam promiscuè Episcopum & Presbyterum appellantem, & potestatem nihilominus distinguentem quisquam tulerit. In loco certè ibid. v. 5. 6. &c. & res ipsa, potestas & proprietates Episcopi æquè in commune tribuuntur Presbytero atque nomen. Cui enim aliàs ordini proprie convenirent res, quæ v. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. habentur, Presbyteri an Episcopi? Et inter Ephesinos illos Miletum à S. Paulo accersitos, qui & Presbyteri & Episcopi dicuntur, Episcopus ille Ephesiorum major, cui potestatem eminentiorem tribuunt, vel comparuit, vel non comparuit. Si comparuit, cur seorsim à S. Paulo invitatus non est, vel morem ei invitanti non gessit? quorum utrumque absurdum est, vel nullus fuit. Sed veri nominis Episcopus is est, qui attendit sibi ipsi & gregi, gregem pascendo, Actor. XX. 28. Atqui id omne est, quod Episcopo vero incumbit.
units.tr: Since, then, at that time the names were common, and since the sharing of a name, when it is truly said, implies a sharing of the things designated by those names, it follows that both the names and the things designated by them were common. And of those who are the same, in so far as they are the same, the operation is common. For no one today would tolerate the Pope, who calls himself indiscriminately bishop and presbyter, and yet distinguishes the power. In the same passage (v. 5, 6, etc.) the thing itself, the power and properties of a bishop, is equally attributed in common to the presbyter as the name is. For to what other order would the things mentioned in verses 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 properly belong, presbyters or bishops? And among those Ephesian elders summoned from Miletus by St. Paul, who are called both presbyters and bishops, either that greater bishop of the Ephesians, to whom they assign a more eminent power, was present or was not present. If he was present, why was he not invited separately by St. Paul, or did he not heed the summons? Both of these are absurd; so he was not there at all. But the true bishop is one who "takes heed to himself and to the flock," by feeding the flock (Acts 20:28). Yet that is all that belongs to a true bishop.

units.la: Ideo etiam S. Paulus omnes Ecclesiæ Ministros Episcoporum & Diaconorum nominibus complectitur. Paulus Sanctis, qui sunt Philippis σὺν Ἐπισκόποις καὶ Διακόνοις una cum Episcopis & Diaconis, Phil. I. 1. Et plures ejusdem urbis Episcopos nominat, quod hodie non fit, & Presbyteros omittit, quia idem Presbyter est quod Episcopus. Frivolum planè est, quòd ante schisma illud, de quo S. Paulus 1. Cor. I. 12. loquitur, Presbyteros & Episcopos idem nomen, eandem potestatem habuisse, & unà cum Episcopo proprie dicto Ecclesiam rexisse, post illud verò Episcopos præeminentiam suam tueri certos, Presbyteros communione nominum abusos, ad subsellia inferiora relegasse, regerunt, nulla ratione freti; imò rationi repugnantes, quia prior ad Corinthios post Epistolam ad Philippenses scripta est, & prior illa regiminis per Episcopos & Presbyteros, velut eosdem, forma, si Divinitus instituta est, mutari non debuit; & si mutata est, mutatio humana, non Divina, adeòque ipsa etiam nominum & officiorum distinctio hnmanam originem habet. Neque illud de nihilo est, quòd S. Paulus ordines Ecclesiasticos N. T. nominans & numerans, 1. Cor. XII. 28. Ephes. IV. 11. Episcoporum, qui Pastoribus majores, vel ab iis distincti sint, nullos nominat vel numerat. Nam quòd Episcopos nomine Apostolorum, ceu Pastorum majorum, utpote quibus Episcopi successerint, comprehendi afferunt, ἄλογον planè est; quia Apostoli in munere pastorali proprie Apostolico & extraordinario successores nullos habuerunt, & eatenus etiam à Pastoribus distinguuntur. In iis enim solis Apostolis succeditur, quibus positis ponitur Ecclesia, & sublatis tollitur. Hæc autem non aliud quàm pura Evangelii prædicatio, & Sacramentorum dispensatio sunt, Matth. XXVIII. 19. 20. S. Petrus certè, quo majores nulli Episcopi se esse velint, se Συμ-πρεσβύτερον conséniorem, 1. Pet. V. 1. diserte vocat, non ratione solius ordinis, non regiminis & jurisdictionis, uti Hierarchici moderni somniant, sed eodem sensu, quo seniores erant, quorum ille consenior erat. Illi vero πρεσβύτεροι seniores erant, quatenus munus illorum fuit, pascere gregem Dei, & ἐπισκοπεῖν curare, vers. 2. quod Ecclesiæ regimen, commune omnibus Presbyteris, significat. Eadem ergo ratione etiam S. Petrus consenior erat, quoad potestatem & regimen Ecclesiæ nihil eximium sibi arrogans. Accedit, quòd idem S. Paulus facultatem ordinandi, quam essentialem Episcopi facultatem Hierarchici faciunt, Presbyteris tribuit. Ne neglige donum, quod in te est, quod tibi datum est per Prophetiam μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τῆς πρεσβυτερίου cum impositione manuum Presbyterii, 1. Tim. IV. 14. Ubi Presbyterium non officium, uni cuipiam competens, significat, quia vox illa ex stylo Scripturæ, Luc. XXII. 66. Actor. XXII. 5. plures Presbyteros significat. Ideo Hieronymus hoc etiam loco fretus, Episcopos & Presbyteros eosdem facit, quia Presbyteri Timotheo manus impositerunt, quam ceremoniam in ordinatione Presbyteri Jus Canonicum Dist. 23. c. Presbyt. observari præcipit. Et Græci quidem Patres Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, alii, Presbyteros à Paulo intelligi Episcopos afferentes, interpretationem illam rationi temporum suorum accommodarunt, non perversitati illi, quæ jam regnum in Papatu habet. Et Presbyteros ordinandi potestatem olim apud Scotos, Gallos, aliósque veteres habuisse, pluribus Blondellus Apolog. de Episc. & Presbyt. Sect. III. 309-329. demonstravit. Denique si Episcopatus jure Divino Presbyteratu superior est, & ille jurisdictionem propriam habet, quam hic non habet, diversum ab eo, adeóque etiam proprium ordinem constituet.
units.tr: For this reason too St. Paul embraces all the ministers of the Church under the names of bishops and deacons: "Paul to the saints who are at Philippi, σὺν ἐπισκόποις καὶ διακόνοις, together with the bishops and deacons" (Phil. 1:1). And he names several bishops of that same city, which is not done today, and he omits the presbyters, because the presbyter is the same as the bishop. It is utterly frivolous to argue, relying on no reason, that before that schism of which St. Paul speaks in 1 Corinthians 1:12, presbyters and bishops had the same name and the same power and governed the Church together with the bishop properly so called, but that afterwards the bishops, certain of their preeminence, abused the sharing of names and relegated the presbyters to lower benches; indeed, these arguments are opposed to reason, since the former letter to the Corinthians was written before the Epistle to the Philippians, and that form of government through bishops and presbyters, as if they were the same, if it was instituted by God, ought not to have been changed; and if it has been changed, the change is human, not divine, and so the very distinction of names and offices has a human origin. Nor is it of no account that St. Paul, when naming and numbering the ecclesiastical orders of the New Testament (1 Cor. 12:28; Eph. 4:11), names or numbers no bishops who are superior to, or distinct from, the pastors. For to claim that bishops are included under the name of apostles, as greater pastors, inasmuch as bishops succeeded them, is utterly absurd; for the Apostles, in their properly apostolic and extraordinary pastoral office, had no successors, and to that extent they are also distinguished from pastors. For only those Apostles are succeeded, after whose setting the Church is set up, and when they are removed it is removed. Yet these things are nothing other than the pure preaching of the Gospel and the dispensing of the sacraments (Matt. 28:19–20). St. Peter certainly, who calls himself plainly "συμπρεσβύτερος, a fellow-elder" (1 Pet. 5:1), so that no greater bishops may wish to be his superiors, does so not by reason of order alone, nor of government and jurisdiction, as modern hierarchists dream, but in the same sense in which the elders were elders, of whom he was a fellow-elder. And those were "πρεσβύτεροι, elders," insofar as their office was "to feed the flock" of God and "ἐπισκοπεῖν, to take oversight" (v. 2), which signifies the government of the Church, common to all presbyters. By the same reasoning, then, St. Peter was a fellow-elder, claiming for himself nothing outstanding as to power or government of the Church. Add that the same St. Paul grants to presbyters the power of ordaining, which the hierarchists make the essential power of a bishop: "Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of hands of the presbytery [μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου]" (1 Tim. 4:14). Here "presbytery" signifies not an office belonging to any one man, since that word in the style of Scripture signifies several presbyters (Luke 22:66; Acts 22:5). Therefore Jerome, relying on this passage too, makes bishops and presbyters the same, because presbyters laid hands on Timothy, a ceremony which the Canon Law, Distinction 23, chapter "Presbyter," prescribes be observed in the ordination of a presbyter. And the Greek Fathers, Chrysostom, Theophylact and others, asserting that the "presbyters" of Paul are to be understood as bishops, adapted that interpretation to the circumstances of their own times, not to that corruption which now reigns in the papacy. And that presbyters formerly held the power of ordination among the Scots, the Gauls and other ancient peoples, Blondel has demonstrated at length in his Apology concerning Bishops and Presbyters, section III, pp. 309–329. Finally, if the episcopate is superior to the presbyterate by divine right, and it has its own jurisdiction which the presbyterate does not have, then it constitutes a different order from it, and so also a distinct order of its own.

units.la: L. In V. T. fuisse Principes, Præsules, Præsulatos Sacerdotum, quibus Prælatus Prælatorum, Pontifex præfuit, Num. 111.24.32. adeóque in N. T. analogum regimen esse debere, Hierarchici frustra argutantur. Mutato enim Sacerdotio ipsa lex Sacerdotii mutari debuit, Hebr. VII. 7. 21. Et quod olim Pontifex fuit, nunc Christus est. Imò Principes illi familiarum Gersonis, Cahathi & Merari Levitæ, non alii fuerunt. At his illi non Episcopos, sed Diaconos respondere contendunt. Nec Pontifici veteri Papa, nec Principibus familiarum & Sacerdotibus Episcopi & Sacerdotes novi, nec Levitis ministrantes ordines successerunt. Alia tempora alios mores postulant. Neque nunc lege sacerdotii typici abolita, quando Christus uno sacrificio omnia consummavit, sponte nobis judaizare licet, sed in regimine Ecclesiæ Christi ductus unicè sequendus nobis est. At ne quidem Sacerdotes V. T. alii majores, alii minores jurisdictione etiam distincti fuerunt, ut majoribus illis Episcopi, minoribus Presbyteri congruere non possint. Par congruentiæ & successionis infirmitas est, cùm Episcopos Apostolis, LXX. Discipulis Presbyteros congruere & successisse pertendunt. Non enim ex arbitraria & incerta comparatione cudere licet jus Divinum, quod ex institutione sola Christi arcessendum est. Neque quidquam obstat, quò minùs in communi & ordinario ministrorum N. T. munere Presbyterium & Pastores omnes Apostolis & LXX. Discipulis successisse dicantur; in extraordinario verò, & proprie Apostolico munere iis successisse nemo dicatur. Ac licèt etiam Apostolici muneris gradus eminens fuerit, tamen in missione prima illis & Apostolis ἴσοι, non ἄνισοι paria juxta data sunt, neque jurisdictionem & potestatem prætoriam illi in hos unquam sibi arrogasse leguntur. Si igitur omnino illis Episcopi & Presbyteri successerunt, pari tamen potestate præditi sint oportet. Si qui Patres comparatione ea usi sunt, post factam jam in Ecclesia mutationem usi sunt, imò & abusi sunt, ad palliandam consuetudinem in Ecclesiam introductam, non ad probandum jus Divinum. Antiocheni illi λειτουργοῦντες viri Apostolici Barnabam & Saulum ad opus ad quod vocati sunt à Domino manibus impositis separarunt, Act. XIII. 2. Sed illi nec eminentiorem gradum ministerii, quàm Saulus Apostolus & Barnabas habuerunt, nec manus impo-suerunt velut iis superiores, & Episcopi à Presbyteris distincti, quales illos fuisse minimè constat; vocantur enim προφῆται καὶ διδάσκαλοι Prophetæ & doctores, non vel Apostoli, vel Episcopi, quibus solis χειροτονία Hierarchici vendicant. Potiùs inde colligere est, minores etiam majoribus manus imponere posse. Sed illi Barnabæ & Saulo imponentes, non illos ordinarunt, quia ad ministerium Evangelii Christi jam ordinati erant, & Paulus nec ab hominibus, nec per homines vocatus est, Gal. I. 1. 2. Sed pia vota pro eorum jam ordinatorum ministerio nuncuparunt. Ordinarunt sanè etiam Paulus & Barnabas Presbyteros κατ' ἐκκλησίας per Ecclesias, vel potiùs χειροτονίας suffragio Ecclesiarum eos elegerunt, Act. XIV. 23. Sed tales, qui & ipsi, cùm & nomina illa, & munia communia fuisse Apostolorum tempore constet, veri Episcopi fuerunt; & similes ipsi quoque ordinare potuerunt. Si enim Paulo & Barnabæ propter χειροθεσίαν illam, qua manus iis à Prophetis & doctoribus Antiochenis impositæ sunt, jus competiit alios etiam ordinandi, & eo jure illi alios ibid. v. 23. ordinarunt, quidni pariter ad Presbyteros, quos ipsi oppidatim ordinarunt, jus quoque ordinationum per suam χειροθεσίαν pertinuisse censeri possit? Aut quo indicio constabit, potiùs Timotheo per Paulum χειροτονηθέντα ordinato, quàm aliis Presbyteris, quos itidem Paulus & Barnabas per singulas Ecclesias ordinarunt, jus ordinandi alios eximium fuisse. Ariolatio porro mera est, quòd septem Angelos illos, quibus Johannes Apoc. II. & III. epistolas suas inscripsit, Episcopos à Presbyteris distinctos fuisse afferunt. Epistolæ enim illæ singulæ ad singulos Angelos dirigiuntur, non quòd singuli illi potestate ordinandi & claves exercendi instructi supra alios eminuerint, sed ut ad unum scribendo servaretur illa uniformitas omnibus Ecclesiis communis, quia ut Ecclesiæ singulæ minimum nimùm unum Pastorem habeant, earum recta ratio requirit; ut autem plures habeant, non necessariò postulatur, adeóque illud Ecclesiæ accidentale, non essentiale est: proin illud omnibus commune, hoc quibusdam peculiare est. Christus verò eam scribendi rationem sequi voluit, quæ omnibus communis esset. Aliàs Ecclesiæ illæ non simplices παροικίαι paroeciæ, sed διοικήσεις diœceses seu præfecturæ Ecclesiasticæ certarum provinciarum limitibus comprehensæ fuerint, quales fuisse Johannis tempore, nondum liquet. Nihil etiam obstat, quò minùs Angelus in iis cœtibus, quibus plures ministri præerant, collectivè Angelos, seu Presbyteros plures significet. Quantacunque verò vetustate Episcoporum prælatura se commendet, ab Apostolis tamen eam non manasse, certis jam argumentis demonstravimus. Et successionem Episcoporum ad comprobandum utcunque veritatis traducem Patres, Irenæus, Tertullianus, Epiphanius, alii hæreticis opposuerunt, quia maturè unus supra alium se extollere cœpit. Interim, quòd in nominandis Apostolorum successoribus adeò iidem cæspitarunt & dissenserunt, vix alia causa allegari potest, quàm quia propter illam Presbyterorum in Ecclesiis Apostolicis ἐπισκοπῶν definiri non potuit, cui ex pluribus collegis æqualibus jura πρωτοκαθεδρίας deputarentur. Denique Aerius hæresεos notam apud veteres meruit, non ob simpliciter assertam æqualitatem Ministrorum Ecclesiæ jure Divino, quia aliàs etiam Hieronymus meruissët; sed ob Arianismum; & forte etiam, quia ordinem jam receptum gravi cum scandalo turbare conatus est. Philastrius tamen Brixiensis de hær. cap. 75. agens de hæresi Aerianorum ne quidem hujus dogmatis meminit: non enim cum Aerio de eo disceptatio fuit; an Episcopus jure Divino Presbyteris superior sit; sed an ullo omnino jure superior sit?
units.tr: Hierarchists argue in vain that in the Old Testament there were princes and prelates, a prelacy of priests over which the high priest, the prelate of prelates, presided (Num. 1, 11, 24, 32), and that the New Testament must therefore have an analogous government. When the priesthood was changed, the law of the priesthood itself had to be changed (Heb. 7:7, 21). What the high priest once was, Christ now is. Moreover, those princes were the princes of the families of the Levites Gershon, Kohath and Merari, and none others. Yet the Hierarchists contend that bishops correspond to these, not deacons. Neither did the Papa succeed the old high priest, nor did new bishops and priests succeed the princes of the families and the priests, nor did ministers succeed the Levites who served. Different times demand different customs. Nor, now that the law of the typical priesthood has been abolished, since Christ has completed all things by one sacrifice, are we free to Judaize at will; rather, we must follow solely the guidance of Christ's government of the Church. Furthermore, the priests of the Old Testament were not divided even by jurisdiction into greater and lesser, so that bishops could correspond to the greater and presbyters to the lesser. The argument from correspondence and succession is equally weak, when they maintain that bishops correspond to and succeeded the Apostles, and presbyters the seventy disciples. For divine right may not be forged from an arbitrary and uncertain comparison; it must be drawn from the institution of Christ alone. Nor is there anything to prevent us from saying that, in the common and ordinary office of the ministers of the New Testament, the presbytery and all pastors succeeded the Apostles and the seventy disciples, while no one may be said to have succeeded them in the extraordinary and properly apostolic office. And although the rank of the apostolic office was indeed eminent, yet at the first mission they were given equal (ἴσοι [isoi]), not unequal (ἄνισοι [anisoi]), powers, and we never read that they arrogated to themselves praetorian jurisdiction and power over the others. If therefore bishops and presbyters succeeded them in every respect, they must nonetheless be endowed with equal power. If any Fathers used that comparison, they used it after the change had already taken place in the Church, and indeed they misused it, to excuse a custom introduced into the Church, not to prove divine right. Those Antiochene men, ministering (λειτουργοῦντες [leitourgountes]) apostolic men, laid their hands on Barnabas and Saul for the work to which the Lord had called them (Acts 13:2). But they neither held a higher rank of ministry than Saul the Apostle and Barnabas, nor did they lay on hands as superiors over them, nor were they bishops distinct from presbyters, which it is by no means clear they were; for they are called prophets and teachers (προφῆται καὶ διδάσκαλοι [prophētai kai didaskaloi]), not apostles or bishops, and the Hierarchists claim the laying on of hands (χειροτονία [cheirotonia]) for these alone. It is rather to be inferred from this that those of lower rank could also lay hands on those of higher rank. But those laying hands on Barnabas and Saul did not ordain them, because they had already been ordained to the ministry of the Gospel of Christ, and Paul was called neither by men nor through men (Gal. 1:1, 2). Rather, they uttered pious prayers for the ministry of men who were already ordained. Certainly Paul and Barnabas also ordained presbyters in every church (κατ' ἐκκλησίας [kat' ekklēsias]), or rather they chose them by the vote (χειροτονίας [cheirotonias]) of the churches (Acts 14:23). But such men, since it is established that both those names and those offices were common in the time of the Apostles, were true bishops; and they too could ordain similar men. For if, by reason of that laying on of hands (χειροθεσίαν [cheirothesian]), by which the Antiochene prophets and teachers laid hands on Paul and Barnabas, the right of ordaining others also belonged to them, and by that right they ordained others (ibid. v. 23), why should it not likewise be held that the right of ordination through their own laying on of hands also belonged to the presbyters whom they ordained in the towns? Or by what sign will it be established that Timothy, ordained (χειροτονηθέντα [cheirotonēthenta]) by Paul, had an exceptional right to ordain others, rather than the other presbyters whom Paul and Barnabas likewise ordained in each church? Moreover, it is mere conjecture to say that the seven angels to whom John addressed his epistles (Rev. 2 and 3) were bishops distinct from presbyters. For those letters are each addressed to a single angel, not because those single angels, endowed with the power of ordaining and of exercising the keys, stood out above others, but so that by writing to one a uniformity common to all churches would be preserved. For the correct reasoning concerning the churches requires that each church have at least one pastor; that it have more is not necessarily demanded, and so that is accidental to the church, not essential. Thus the former is common to all, the latter peculiar to some. But Christ willed to follow that manner of writing which would be common to all. Otherwise it is not yet clear whether those churches were not simple parishes (παροικίαι [paroikiai]), but dioceses (διοικήσεις [dioikēseis]), or ecclesiastical prefectures, comprised within the boundaries of certain provinces, as they were at the time of John. Nor is there anything to prevent the angel, in those assemblies over which several ministers presided, from signifying collectively the angels, that is, the several presbyters. However great the antiquity by which the episcopal prelacy commends itself, we have already demonstrated by sure arguments that it did not flow from the Apostles. And the Fathers, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Epiphanius and others, opposed the succession of bishops to the heretics to uphold the truth somehow against the stain of error, because one began early to raise himself above another. Meanwhile, that they stumbled and disagreed so much in naming the successors of the Apostles can hardly be attributed to any other cause than this: because, given the presbyters' equal authority in the apostolic churches, it could not be determined which of several equal colleagues should be assigned the rights of primacy of seat (πρωτοκαθεδρίας [prōtokathedrias]). Finally, Aerius earned the mark of heresy among the ancients, not because he simply asserted the equality of the ministers of the Church by divine right (for on that score Jerome too would have earned it), but because of Arianism, and perhaps also because he tried to disturb an order already received, to grave scandal. Yet Philastrius of Brescia, On Heresies, chapter 75, in treating of the heresy of the Aerians, does not even mention this doctrine. For the dispute with Aerius was not whether a bishop is superior to presbyters by divine right, but whether he is superior by any right at all.

units.la: LI. Sed de jure, quo Episcopi Presbyteris superiores sunt, quicquid fiat, alia planè in veteri Ecclesia Episcoporum ratio fuit, alia Pontificiorum est. Hi enim nil nisi Papæ in Ecclesia dominantis ministri sunt. Tridentini enim Sess. XXIII. cap. 4. & can. 8. in explicando Episcoporum munere & potestate nullam ministerii Verbi & Sacramentorum mentionem faciunt, sed nominata ordinatione & chrismatione, eos alia pleraque peragere posse definiunt. Ambrosius Catharinus, qui & ipse Concilio Tridentino interfuit, de Confid. & jud. temp. lib. 4. inter alia tradit, malorum in Ecclesiam irrumpentium hanc potissimam causam esse, quòd Episcopi pœne omnes facti sint mercenarii vel lupi; additque, Episcopatum non amplius esse superintendentiam & curam gregis; perditam esse cum reipsa vocis significationem. Nunc enim Episcopatus nomine venire honorem & bonorum temporalium proventum, & qui Episcopatum desiderat, non aliud eum desiderare. Et Papæ dominationi promovendæ, ceu γνῆσιοι ejusdem vasalli, toti, quanti sunt, inserviunt. Nam & institutionem, potestatemque suam ἀμέσως, non Christo, sed Papæ acceptam referre coguntur, licèt se in titulis suis Episcopos Dei gratia mentiantur: & juramentum, perinde ut vasalli, Principi præstant, quo summo Pontifici veram obedientiam spondent & jurant: & Archiepiscopi pallium à Pontifice, subjectionis suæ symbolum magno auri pondere redimunt; quale etiam Papa φιλοῖς Episcopis quandoque privilegio singulari concedit. Cùmque ipsi non prædicent Evangelium, quod veri Episcopi munus est, vicarios seu suffraganeos Episcopos titulares; quos veteres Χωρεπισκόπους Chorepiscopos dixerunt; subornant, qui per ludibrium etiam apud vulgus Pontificium portatiles, titulares, imaginarii dicuntur, utpote qui Africanæ vel Asiaticæ cujusdam Ecclesiæ, pridem à Muhammedanis extinctæ titulo à Pontifice ornati, bicornique mitra, & adunco lituo armati, aposcopi Episcopi vices gerunt, ut interim Episcopi alia pleraque, uti Tridentini loquuntur, agere possint. Quod genus hominum jam olim, tanquam tuber, ab Ecclesia excindendum Damasus Papa ipse censuit; Episcopos comparans cum meretricibus, quæ, ut quàm primùm Venerem repetere possint, recentes partus aliis lactandos tradunt.
units.tr: LI. But whatever is the case concerning the right by which bishops are superior to presbyters, the reasoning of bishops in the ancient Church was plainly one thing, and that of the Papists another. For these are nothing but ministers of the Pope, who rules in the Church. Indeed the Tridentine fathers (Session 23, chapter 4 and canon 8), in explaining the office and power of bishops, make no mention of the ministry of the Word and the Sacraments, but, naming ordination and chrismation, define that they can perform many other things. Ambrosius Catharinus, who was himself present at the Council of Trent (On the Confidence and Judgement of Times, book 4), among other things teaches that the chief cause of the evils breaking into the Church is this: that almost all bishops have become hirelings or wolves; and he adds that the episcopate is no longer oversight and care of the flock; the very meaning of the word has been lost. For now by the name of episcopate is understood honour and the income of temporal goods, and whoever desires the episcopate desires nothing else. And, like true vassals of the Pope, they serve with all their might to advance the Pope's domination. For they are also compelled to refer their institution and their power, immediately, not to Christ but to the Pope, although in their titles they falsely call themselves bishops by the grace of God; and, just like vassals, they swear an oath to the prince, by which they pledge and swear true obedience to the supreme Pontiff; and the archbishops redeem the pallium from the Pontiff, a token of their subjection, at a great weight of gold; a privilege such as the Pope sometimes grants to his favourite bishops as a singular favour. And since they themselves do not preach the Gospel, which is the true bishop's office, they appoint vicars or suffragan bishops, titular bishops, whom the ancients called chorepiscopi (Χωρεπισκόπους [Chōrepiskopous]); these, by mockery even among the Papist common people, are called portable, titular, imaginary, inasmuch as they are adorned with the title of some African or Asian church, long since extinguished by the Muhammadans, and armed with a two-horned mitre and a crooked staff, and perform the duties of a bishop of the place, while the bishops themselves can, as the Tridentine fathers put it, perform many other things. Pope Damasus himself judged that this kind of men, like a tumour, should long ago have been cut out of the Church, comparing bishops to prostitutes who hand over their newborn children to others to be nursed, so that they may return to their love-making as soon as possible.

units.la: LII. Sed habent ipsi etiam Episcopi suos Præsules, qui Archiepiscoporum & Metropolitanorum nomine veniunt, & Præsules Episcoporum unius Provinciæ, seu Episcopi Metropoleon, principalium regionum & distinctuum urbium sunt, exceptis iis, quos Papa ab eorum jurisdictione exemptos sibi immediatè subjecit. Quos centum & quinque Miræus recensēt. Eorum olim officium erat, Synodos Provinciales convocare, iis præsidere, & recens electos Episcopos investire. Sed varias jurisdictionis eorum partes Papa rapuit. Ab iis distincti Patriarchæ, Exarchi Diœcesium dicti in Hierarchia Pontificia vel Oecumenici titulares, puta Constantinopolitanus, Alexandrinus, Antiochenus, & Hierosolymitanus, quorum nomina Papa quatuor Basilicis Pauli, Mariæ, Laurentii & Johannis, quæ intra ipsum urbis pomœrium sunt; ut sic tyrannidem, quam frustra in Ecclesias Orientales affectavit, saltem ludicro hoc dramate, orbem urbi includens, tanquam in scena spectandam exhiberet; alii Particulares, qui & Primates dicuntur, quos ex consuetudine, vel privilegio sex Zechius de Repub. Eccl. p. 80. numerat; Aquilejensem, Gradensem, Bituricensem, Cantuariensem, Toletanum & Pisanum; sed duo tantum Aquilejensis & Gradensis Patriarcharum nomen retinuerunt. Supra omnes hos eminent Cardinales, qui ex prima institutione Ecclesiæ Romanæ clerus ordinarius, seu fixus & proprius (velut cardo fixus, unde Cardinalium nomen) fuerunt; quorum proin officium & munus τάξιν idem cum officio clericorum, Presbyterorum inprimis fuit, ut scilicet singuli in suis titulis, seu Ecclesiis, quibus præerant, populum ex verbo Dei erudire, Sacramenta administrare, Romano Episcopo in regimine Ecclesiæ inservire, aliàque ejusmodi munera Ecclesiastica obire. Episcopis subjecti fuerunt usque ad tempora Caroli M. quibus Papatus imperio multarum provinciarum auctus est. Incrementa enim eorum potestas unà cum Pontificiæ potestatis incrementis nacta est. Stephano IV. Pontifice A. DCCLXIX. in Synodo Romana decretum est, ne Papa nisi ex Cardinalibus legeretur. Seculo inprimis undecimo sub Nicolao II. primæ
units.tr: LII. But the bishops themselves also have their own presidents, who come under the name of Archbishops and Metropolitans. The presidents of the bishops of a single province, or the metropolitan bishops, are the heads of the principal regions and distinguished cities, except those whom the Pope has exempted from their jurisdiction and placed directly under himself. Miraeus lists one hundred and five of them. Formerly their office was to convene provincial synods, preside over them, and invest newly elected bishops. But the Pope has seized the various parts of their jurisdiction. Distinct from them are those called Patriarchs, Exarchs of dioceses in the papal hierarchy, or titular Ecumenical ones, namely the Constantinopolitan, Alexandrian, Antiochene and Jerusalem patriarchs. The Pope has honoured their names with four basilicas, those of Paul, Mary, Lawrence and John, which lie within the very boundary of the city. By enclosing the world within the city, he could thus exhibit, as a spectacle on a stage, the tyranny he had vainly aimed at the Eastern Churches, at least through this mock drama. Others are called Particular, and are also named Primates. Zechius (de Repub. Eccl. p. 80) lists six of them by custom or privilege: Aquileia, Grado, Bourges, Canterbury, Toledo and Pisa. But only the patriarchs of Aquileia and Grado have retained the name. Above all these stand the Cardinals, who from the first institution of the Roman Church were the ordinary, or fixed and proper, clergy (called Cardinals from the word cardo, a hinge, because they are fixed). Their office and duty [τάξις] were therefore the same as those of the clergy, especially the presbyters: namely, that each should, in his own titular church over which he presided, instruct the people from the word of God, administer the sacraments, serve the Roman Bishop in governing the Church, and perform other such ecclesiastical duties. They were subject to the bishops until the time of Charlemagne, under whose empire the Papacy was enlarged by many provinces. For their power grew together with the growth of papal power. Under Pope Stephen IV, in the year 769, it was decreed in a Roman synod that the Pope should be chosen only from among the Cardinals. Under Nicholas II, in the eleventh century especially, the first

units.la: Episcopi Pontificii nil cum veteribus commune habent. mæ in eligendo Papa partes eis decretæ sunt; donec exclusò ab ea electione Imperatore & Clero reliquo solis iis hoc jus cessit; atque sic novo quodam eorum principatu paulatim exorto, Cardinales sub appellatione Ecclesiastica seculares Principes facti sunt. Ea ratione Papa, Christi æmulus, Collegium Apostolicum ex Cardinalibus conflatum constituit: multiplicatis non parum eorum prærogativis hodiernum in diem usque, & donato iisdem A. MCCXLII. ab Innocentio IV. galero rubro, Senatus hujus Edomitici tessera, cujus auctoramento principes hujus seculi viri ad partes Pontificias trahuntur. Mira scilicet pudendáque metamorphosi conculcato inprimis à Papa Imperatore, & sede ejus ad maximum in terra fastigium evecta, secularem in typhum toti transierunt, Principes mundi, & Regibus similes ab ipsis Pontificibus proclamati, & facti æmuli summorum Principum; adeò ut Bellarminus in Apologia contra Serenissimi Angliæ Regis Jacobi præfationem, eos Regibus adæquare propudiosis ratiunculis nonnullis haud erubuerit.
units.tr: The Papal bishops have nothing in common with the ancients. part in electing the Pope was assigned to them. Then, with the Emperor and the rest of the clergy excluded from that election, this right passed to them alone. In this way, with a certain new principality of theirs gradually arising, the Cardinals, under an ecclesiastical title, became secular princes. By this method the Pope, the rival of Christ, set up an Apostolic College made up of Cardinals. Their prerogatives have been greatly multiplied down to the present day, and in 1242 Innocent IV gave them the red galero, the badge of this Edomite senate, by whose authority the princes of this age are drawn to the papal side. By a wondrous and shameful metamorphosis, the Emperor, trampled especially by the Pope, and his see raised to the highest height on earth, they have all passed over into secular pride: they are proclaimed by the Pontiffs themselves as princes of the world and similar to kings, and have been made rivals of the highest princes. So much so that Bellarmine, in his Apology against the preface of the most serene James, King of England, did not blush to equate them with kings, on the strength of some shameless little arguments.

units.la: LIII. Clerici Supererogantes sunt Monachi, qui observantia votorum suorum supererogare, hoc est, Deo plus dare ac solvere, quam lex ejus postulat, dicuntur. Monachatum Bellarminus de Monach. c. 2. definit, Statum hominum per paupertatis continentiæ & obedientiæ vota ad perfectionem Christianam tendentium. Azorius contra Instit. lib. IX. s. q. 1. eundem statum perfectorum, non ad perfectionem tendentium, sub certis mandatis & regulis Deo famulantium definit. Sed communis persuasio est, hactenus Monachos ab Episcopis differre, quòd hi perfectionem adepti sint, illi adipisci contendant. Perfectos Pseudo-clericos, & cum veteribus Monachis comparatos Pseudo-Monachos perfectos qui dixit, rectè perfectionem eorum definivit. Status illorum omnino in votis est, quæ duùm illis generum sunt, substantialia & accidentalia. Substantialia tria sunt, obedientiæ, paupertatis & continentiæ. Accidentalia reliqua in vestibus, diæta, exercitiis animæ & corporis, quà noctu, quà interdiu. Hinc multiplicatos ordines distinguunt generaliter in Eremitas & Cœnobitas. Illos, qui in desertis solitariam vitam degunt, procul ab humano commercio, dictos Anachoretas à separatione hac, & Eremitas à loco, quos triplices etiam faciunt; alios, qui Priorem agnoscant, à quo pendeant, singulas cellas singuli habitantes, ut sepulchra; alios antris spelunc​isque inclusos, humanæ societatis extorres; alios amplexos ferale commercium bestiarum. Hos communitatem colentes, qua intra urbium septa, quà in pomœriis, quà in agris; sed vix tamen nisi in locis amœnissimis & commodissimis, qui & sexu, & familiis infinitis, neque tantùm institutis, sed etiam quotidie instituendis, distinguuntur.
units.tr: LIII. Supererogating clergy are the monks, who are said to supererogate by the observance of their vows, that is, to give and pay God more than his law requires. Bellarmine (de Monach. c. 2.) defines monasticism as a state of men tending to Christian perfection through the vows of poverty, continence and obedience. Azorius (contra Instit. lib. IX, s. q. 1.) defines the same as a state of the perfect, not tending to perfection, serving God under certain commands and rules. But the common belief is that hitherto monks have differed from bishops in this: the bishops have attained perfection, while the monks strive to attain it. Whoever called them perfect pseudo-clergy, and, comparing them with the old monks, perfect pseudo-monks, rightly defined their perfection. Their state consists entirely in vows, of which there are two kinds, substantial and accidental. The substantial vows are three: obedience, poverty and continence. The accidental ones are the rest, concerning clothing, diet, exercises of body and soul, by night or by day. Hence they generally divide their many orders into hermits and cenobites. Those who lead a solitary life in the deserts, far from human company, are called anchorites from this separation, and hermits from their place; they also divide these into three kinds: some acknowledge a prior on whom they depend, each living in a single cell like a tomb; others are shut up in caves and grottoes, exiles from human society; others embrace a deadly commerce with beasts. The cenobites cultivate a common life, some within the walls of cities, some in suburbs, some in the fields; yet they are hardly ever found except in the most pleasant and convenient places. They are distinguished by sex and by countless communities, and not only by those already founded but by those founded every day.

units.la: LIV. Cæterùm Monachatum, seu religiosum illum vitæ statum, in quo per observantiam votorum paupertatis, cœlibatus & obedientiæ Evangelica perfectio, supererogatio meritorum, & satisfactio pro peccatis acquiri possit, nuspiam Deus in verbo suo commendavit, vel præcepit. Nam nec vox Monachi, nec res ipsa in Scripturis occurrit. Est autem Scriptura perfectissima credendi & faciendi regula, perfectionis verè Evangelicæ certissima index. Quicquid Deus in religione & cultu sui à se instituto non justit, præcepit, commendavit, mera superstitio & planta illa, quam Cœlestis Pater non plantavit, adeóque eradicanda est, Matth. XV. 13. Tum & Monachatus cum præceptis Divinis è diametro pugnat. Quod de votis, quæ illi nuncupant, & in quibus Monachatus cardo consistit, Loc. XX. 26. fusiùs probavimus: Lex enim Divina inprimis amorem proximi, eique annexam beneficentiam, hospitalitatem, & virtutes homeleticas alias commendat. At Monachi, Anachoretæ inprimis, ex instituto suo, abdicati mundi prætextum præ se ferentes, sibi vivunt, sagenæ suæ sacrificant, neque ullam proximi fovendi, adjuvandi, promovendi, civilibus studiis prosequendi curam suscipiunt: Rempublicam deserunt, civilia onera in alios derivant, nihil pro bonis & honestis civibus faciunt, atque interim civium honestorum sudore & sanguine pascuntur, imò & saginantur. Cùmque regula charitatis sit, ut faciamus aliis, quæ ipsi nobis fieri volumus, Luc. VI. 31. Eremitæ contra nec ab aliis accipiunt, nec aliis communicant quicquam, luporum & aprorum instar; Cœnobitæ verò accipiunt, sed non largiuntur quidquam cuiquam. Taceo ἀπαν​ϑρωπίαν illam, seu affectationem belluinæ feritatis. Quæ licèt non omnes Monachos tangant, omnes tamen Monachorum primos Patres tangunt, quorum nominibus se hodie maximè jactant. Paulus tamen dixit: Nemo unquam odio habuit carnem suam, sed nutrit & palpat carnem suam, sicut & Dominus Ecclesiam, Ephes. V. 29. Illi contra omnes prætexunt odium carnis, non illius, quæ caro nominatur pro corruptione; sed illius, quæ substantia & pars hominis est; & eò referunt βίον ἀνήμερον ex radicibus, in antris, sylvis; nuditatem & ejusmodi alia. Etiam ἐθελο-θρησκείαν cultum electitium omnem inprimis eorum, qui vetant tangere mulierem, contrectare rem, ut propriam, & qui est secundum præcepta & doctrinas hominum, cæcam & obedientiam injungentium, Scripturæ Col. II. 21.22.23. Deut. XII. 32. damnant. Monachi tamen novum & electitium cultum, Dei promerendi causa; instituunt, nullo vocationis Dei intuitu, nullaque ejus approbatione vivendi genus, quale libet, sibi ipsis comminiscuntur, & unà cum cucullo mille superstitionum laqueos sibi induunt. Sed & unitatem Ecclesiæ Monachatus distrahit, tum eam, quæ est cum capite Christo; tum eam, quæ est membrorum inter se. Cum capite Christo, quia se dicunt esse Benedicti, Dominici, Francisci, &c. & superstitionibus suis se à capite Christo separant. Christi fides nos in unum corpus compegit. Et Baptismo in unum corpus baptizamur, ut Christiani dicamur. Si Paulus ne ab Apostolis quidem Christianos denominari voluit, quantò minùs hodie à Pseud-Apostolis, Benedicto, Francisco, Dominico denominari pateretur. Diceret enim, carnales esse, qui id faciunt; Christum dividi, unitatem corporis ejus lacerari, crucem & Baptismum ejus profanari, caput non teneri, 1. Cor. III. 1. 2. &c, Col. I. 19. Neque obstat,
units.tr: LIV. Moreover, God has nowhere in his word commended or commanded that monasticism, or that religious state of life in which Evangelical perfection, the supererogation of merits, and satisfaction for sins can be acquired through the observance of the vows of poverty, celibacy and obedience. For neither the word monk nor the thing itself occurs in the Scriptures. Scripture is the most perfect rule of believing and doing, and the most certain index of truly Evangelical perfection. Whatever God in religion and in his worship has not instituted, commanded or commended is mere superstition, and the plant which the heavenly Father did not plant, and so must be uprooted, Matt. 15:13. Moreover, monasticism fights diametrically against the divine precepts. We have proved this more fully concerning the vows which they call such, and on which the hinge of monasticism rests, Loc. XX. 26. For the divine law above all commends love of neighbour, and with it beneficence, hospitality and other homely virtues. But monks, especially the anchorites, by their own institution, pretend to have renounced the world, and live for themselves, sacrificing to their own nets. They undertake no care to nurture, help or advance their neighbour, or to pursue civic duties. They desert the commonwealth, shift civic burdens onto others, do nothing for good and honest citizens, and meanwhile are fed, and even fattened, on the sweat and blood of honest citizens. Since the rule of charity is that we should do to others what we want done to us, Luke 6:31, the hermits, on the contrary, neither receive anything from others nor share anything with others, like wolves and wild boars. The cenobites indeed receive, but give nothing to anyone. I say nothing of that inhumanity [ἀπανθρωπία], or affectation of bestial savagery. Although this does not touch all monks, it touches all the first fathers of the monks, in whose names they boast most of all today. Paul, however, said: No one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, as the Lord does the Church, Eph. 5:29. They, on the contrary, pretend to hate the flesh: not that which is called flesh for corruption, but that which is the substance and part of man. To this they refer a savage life [βίον ἀνήμερον] of roots, caves and woods, nakedness and other such things. They also condemn self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία], all elective worship, especially that of those who forbid touching a woman, handling a thing as one's own, and who, according to the precepts and doctrines of men, enjoin blind obedience, as Scripture says, Col. 2:21, 22, 23; Deut. 12:32. Yet the monks institute a new and elective worship for the sake of earning God's favour. Without any regard to God's calling, and without his approval, they devise for themselves whatever way of life they please, and along with the cowl they put on a thousand snares of superstition. But monasticism also tears apart the unity of the Church, both that which is with Christ the head and that which is among the members themselves. It tears apart the unity with Christ the head, since they say they are Benedictines, Dominicans, Franciscans and so on, and by their superstitions separate themselves from Christ the head. Faith in Christ has bound us into one body, and by baptism we are baptized into one body, so that we may be called Christians. If Paul would not even have them named after the Apostles, how much less would he suffer them today to be named after the pseudo-apostles Benedict, Francis and Dominic! For he would call those who do this carnal; he would say that Christ is divided, the unity of his body torn, his cross and baptism profaned, and the head not held: 1 Cor. 3:1, 2, etc.; Col. 1:19. Nor does this stand in the way

units.la: Clerici supererogantes Monachi sunt.
units.tr: Clergy who do more than is required are monks.

units.la: Monachatus ex verbo Dei oppugnatur. obstat,quòd nomina non à doctrinæ sed severioris disciplinæ authore desumpta caussantur. Nam etiam in disciplina vivendique modo disceptantes Christum dividunt, quia sic pluris novi fundatoris sectæ suæ, quàm Christi nomen faciunt, & diversam disciplinam, cujus, quatenus diversa est,Christus author esse non potest, eligunt. Etiam unitatem Ecclesiæ cum membris ejus aliis discerpunt. Certè non possunt Eremitæ esse membra aliorum Christianorum, qui de industria quàm possunt longissimè ab humana societate recedunt. Antonium annos viginti; Paulum sexaginta nulla hominis cujusquam familiaritate usum,Legendæ narrant. Hæccine verò communio est ?Omnibus autem, & Eremitis & Cœnobitis persuasio est,se solos esse religiosos,reliquos omnes seculares ; & qui ad se veniunt, à seculo ad religionem converti. Atqui nulla phrasis in Scriptura est,quæ majorem hominum disparationem notet. Nam qui in seculo sunt, negantur esse in Christo,quia in seculo esse, significat eo in statu esse, qui non pertinet ad Christum. Demas me dereliquit.amplexus præsens seculum. 2.Tim.4 V.10. Quin etiam ipsi inter se Cœnobitæ cùm sint variorum institutorum,inter se conjuncti esse non possunt. Nam qui transeunt in varios ordines, tamen ei renuntiant, in quo prius fuerunt; ut mittam supervenientes discordias. Privata ubique sacra, privatæ ædes, privati ritus obtinent. Et Ecclesiæ quidem ea natura est,ut non sit nomen generis sub se continentis speeies differentiis distinctas: sed potiùs speciei continentis sub se individua multa nonnisi numero distincta,Joh. XVII.21. 2. Cor.XIII.11. Phil. III.15.16. At Monachatu instituto factum, ut distinguantur etiam propriis differentiis, planè sicut in sectis & hæresibus factum. Monachismus enim genus est, cujus species sunt Eremitæ, Cœnobitæ, & Cœnobitarum Basiliani,Augustiniani,Benedictini,Franciscani; & hi rursus variis nominibus & institutis discreti. Quid Christum & corpus ejus dividere, & inconsutilem ejus tunicam lacerare est, hoc si non est ? Cùmque Monachatus basis in consiliis Evangelicis perfectionis consistat; Consilia tamen ejusmodi non aliud esse, quàm consilia improborum, supra Loc. XX.25. jam confirmavimus. Per Monachatum certè alia perfectio quàm quæ secundum Verbum Dei est, introducitur. Nam secundum fœdus operum perfectio est diligere Deum ex toto corde, sincerè, summa intentione, constanter, sine omni defectu,Deut. VI.5. Hæc perfectio in solo Christo homine, omnis peccati experte, fuit. Secundum fœdus gratiæ perfectio nostra est abnegare justitiam nostram operum, credere in Christum, perfectè sperare in Deo, & ad sanctificationis perfectionem contendere ; supra hanc nulla est, vel homini possibilis Evangelica perfectio est. Ad illam perfectionem non contendere omni studio,defectus est ; qui tamen fidelibus in voto eam habentibus remittitur. Sed Monachi hac perfectione neglecta aliam,in voluntariis operibus à Deo nec præceptis, nec laudatis, nec probatis uspiam positam sectantur. Verè ut imperfectissimi omnium sint. Præterea Monasticæs professio, status & exercitium hyporiticum & Pharisaicum totum est. Nam supererogationem & observantiam consiliorum , mandatorum tenorem excedentium illi profitentur,qui præcepta ipsa nec perfectè implent,nec perfectè implere possunt,cum Pharisæis omisso Dei mandato tenentes traditionem hominum, Marc. VII.6.7.8. Loco pietatis ceremoniarum larvam deligunt, & in iis, veræ pietatis operibus neglectis, religionis Christianæ summam collocant. Paupertatem vovendo pro incertis opibus stabiliores commutant,& privata bona relinquendo communionem divitiis affluentem ingrediuntur; imò nonnulli eorum etiam Principes salutantur. Qualis enim obsecro Benedictinorum, qualis Jesuitarum paupertas est ? Et nihil minus quàm pauperes eos esse, iners eorum, in quo pinguescunt & computrescunt, otium probat. Neque enim illud colere iis liceret,nisi aliunde de omnibus rebus ipsis provisum esset. Castitatem iidem vovent , incestissimi omnium, immunditiis suis Ecclesiam commaculantes,uti jam olim Petrus de Aliaco de Ref. Eccl. questus est. Cæcam obedientiam homini ascititio vovent,qui Deo,Magistratibus, parentibus,Ecclesiæ eandem negant. In externo habitu,vestitu, & certæ formæ atque coloris affectatione singularem sanctitatem collocant, & histrionicis vestibus suis vim benedictionis,imò & infallibilitatis in fide (uti id jactantes Alph. de Castro adv. hær. lib. I. 9. inducit) non suæ duntaxat professionis hominibus, sed aliis etiam ægris sanisque easdem induentibus conciliandæ inesse, blasphemant. Neque adeò sine causa tres Pontifices , Nicolaus III. Clemens V. & Johannes XXIII. in regula Francisci,de Monachorum habitu , explicanda diu anxiè laborarunt, nec tamen controversiam sic decid…
units.tr: Monasticism is opposed by the Word of God. It is no objection that its names are taken not from the author of a doctrine but from the author of a stricter discipline. For those who dispute even over discipline and manner of life also divide Christ, since they value the name of the new founder of their sect above the name of Christ, and they choose a discipline different from the one Christ taught, and Christ cannot be the author of a discipline insofar as it is different. They also tear the unity of the Church with its members apart. Certainly hermits cannot be members of other Christians, since they deliberately withdraw as far as they can from human society. The legends tell that Anthony went for twenty years, and Paul for sixty, without any human companionship. Is this communion? All, both hermits and cenobites, are persuaded that they alone are religious and that all others are secular, and that those who come to them are converted from the world to religion. Yet no phrase in Scripture marks a greater separation of men. For those who are in the world are said not to be in Christ, because to be in the world means to be in a state that does not belong to Christ. Demas has forsaken me, having embraced the present world. 2 Tim. 4:10. Moreover, the cenobites themselves, since they belong to various institutes, cannot be joined to one another. For those who pass into different orders still renounce the one in which they were before, not to mention the discords that arise. Private sacred rites, private houses and private rituals prevail everywhere.
