The Church is not by nature a generic name containing species distinguished by differences, but rather a species containing many individuals distinguished only by number. John 17:21; 2 Cor. 13:11; Phil. 3:15-16. But monasticism, by its institution, has made them distinguished even by their own differences, just as has happened in sects and heresies. For monasticism is a genus whose species are hermits and cenobites, and among the cenobites the Basilians, Augustinians, Benedictines and Franciscans; and these in turn are separated by various names and institutes. If this is not dividing Christ and his body and tearing his seamless tunic, what is? And since the basis of monasticism rests on the evangelical counsels of perfection, yet we have already shown above (Loc. XX.25) that counsels of this kind are nothing other than counsels of the wicked. Certainly through monasticism another perfection is introduced, one other than that which is according to the Word of God. For according to the covenant of works, perfection is to love God with the whole heart, sincerely, with supreme intention, constantly and without any defect. Deut. 6:5. This perfection was found in Christ the man alone, who was free of all sin. According to the covenant of grace our perfection is to renounce our own righteousness of works, to believe in Christ, to hope perfectly in God, and to strive for the perfection of sanctification. Beyond this there is no perfection, or none possible to man in the Gospel sense. Not to strive for that perfection with all zeal is a defect, which is nevertheless pardoned in the faithful who have it in their vow. But the monks, neglecting this perfection, pursue another, placed in voluntary works which God has commanded nowhere, praised nowhere, nor approved anywhere. So truly they are the most imperfect of all. Moreover, the monastic profession, state and practice are wholly hypocritical and Pharisaic. For they profess supererogation and the observance of counsels that go beyond the tenor of the commands, while they neither fully fulfil the precepts themselves nor are able to. With the Pharisees, setting aside the command of God, they hold to the tradition of men. Mark 7:6-8. In place of piety they choose the mask of ceremonies, and in them, neglecting the works of true piety, they place the sum of the Christian religion. By vowing poverty they exchange uncertain wealth for more secure wealth, and by leaving private goods they enter into a communion overflowing with riches; indeed some of them are even greeted as princes. For what kind of poverty, I ask, do the Benedictines or the Jesuits have? Their idle leisure, in which they grow fat and rot, proves that they are anything but poor. For they could not cultivate that leisure unless provision had been made for everything from elsewhere. The same men vow chastity, though they are the most incestuous of all, defiling the Church with their filthiness, as Peter of Ailly complained long ago in his De Reformatione Ecclesiae. They vow blind obedience to a man made up by themselves, while they deny the same to God, to magistrates, to parents and to the Church. In outward habit, clothing, and the affected form and colour of their dress, they place a singular sanctity, and they blaspheme that their theatrical garments have the power of blessing, and even infallibility in faith (as Alphonsus de Castro introduces them boasting, Adv. haer. I.9), a power that is to be won not only for men of their profession but also for others, sick or healthy, who put them on. Nor without cause did three Popes, Nicholas III, Clement V and John XXII, labour anxiously for a long time over explaining the monks' habit in the rule of Francis, and yet they did not settle the controversy in such a way that they thought it should be abolished.

units.la: abolendos putarunt. Et novissimè Cardinalis Tostatus non unum convitium Monachatui fecit. Denique hodie Monachatus religionis & pietatis speciem mentitus politicum potiùs Papæ vaframentum,quàm religisum institutum est. Exceptis enim paucis viris, quos superstitio dementavit, ut animarum saluti ita consuli posse considerent,plerosque alia omnia,quàm religionis cura, Monachos faciunt. Alii enim vi in Monasteria detruduntur, vel sponte etiam ad ea concedunt, ut vel familiarum dignitas confervetur, & patrimonia ac hæreditates inter paucos distributæ lautiores & opimiores existant: vel facultas sit otio liberiùs indulgendi,& fucorum adinstar paratum & quæsitum mel absumendi. Alios sive scelerum admissorum justam pœnam reveritos,sive honorum, divitiarum,fortunæ spe, magnisque ausis frustratos, desperatio eodem compellit. Sed arcanum Monachatus ipsi in Concilio Tridentino Galli his apud Svavem Polanum Hist. C. T. lib. VIII. p. 470. verbis referarunt: Hoc perpetuum artificium curiæ Romanæ est,bona secularium erepta ad Clerum primò,dein etiam Romam pertrahere. Id scilicet principiò satagit, ut prætextu voti paupertatis Monachi existimationem acquirant, quasi nullam rem temporalem intueantur, sed omnia charitatis causa faciant in populi servitutem. Post existimatione parta curia cum ipsis de voto dispensat, unde facile ditescant. Cùmque bene opulenta facta sunt Monasteria, demandantur in Commendam,& id omne denique in curiam affluit. Taceo aliud etiam arcanum Monachatus, quod cœlibatui inefle supra ostendimus. Non parùm etiam Monachorum multitudinem pœne innumerabilem sustinendo Regno Pontificio conducere,alibi probavimus.
units.tr: Abolished. And most recently Cardinal Tostatus made more than one attack on monasticism. Finally, today monasticism, which feigns the appearance of religion and piety, is more a political trick of the Pope than a religious institution. For, apart from a few men whom superstition has driven mad, who think that the salvation of souls can be cared for in this way, most make themselves monks for reasons other than any concern for religion. Some are forced into monasteries by violence, while others go there willingly, either so that the dignity of their family may be preserved and their patrimonies and inheritances, distributed among a few, may remain more splendid and rich, or so that they may have the opportunity to indulge in leisure more freely and consume the honey that others have prepared and gathered, like the drones. Others, fearing the just punishment for crimes they have committed, or frustrated in their hopes of honours, riches, fortune and great undertakings, are driven to the same by despair. But the secret of monasticism was revealed by the French themselves at the Council of Trent, in these words reported by Soave Polano (History of the Council of Trent, Book VIII, p. 470): This is the perpetual artifice of the Roman court: to draw goods taken from secular people first to the clergy and then also to Rome. Its first concern, of course, is that under the pretext of the vow of poverty the monks may acquire esteem, as if they regarded no temporal thing but did everything out of charity, for the enslavement of the people. After esteem has been gained, the curia dispenses them from the vow, whence they easily grow rich. And when the monasteries have become quite wealthy, they are handed over in commendam, and in the end all of it flows into the curia. I pass over another secret of monasticism, which we have shown above is inherent in celibacy. We have also shown elsewhere that the almost countless multitude of monks is by no means a small support to the Papal kingdom.

units.la: LV. Sed non deest Monachis fucus haud simplex, quo professionem suam incrustant. Audent enim illi Monachatus initia ab initiis feré orbis derivare, & progressum ejus cum progrediente Ecclesia conjungere. Nam ceu & Enoschum, incipientem invocare nomen Domini,Genef. IV. 26. & Nazaræos, seipsos Deo consecrantes,Num. VI. 2. & Eliam, Elisæum, atque filios Prophetarum, 1. Reg. XVII. 1. &c. & Rechabitas, prohibitos domos ædificare,agros serere,vineas plantare,vinum bibere,Jer.XXXV. 14. & Macchabæos, 2.Macchab. V. v. ult. ubi Judas in desertum locum secessisse,ibíque inter feras vitam exegisse dicitur: & Essenos: & Johannem Baptistam, Matth.III. 1. 4. & Apostolos atque primos Christianos, vitam cœnobiticam colentes, Actor. IV. 32. ostentant. Sed ostentant, non demonstrant. In Enoscho enim uxorato & liberos generante quomodo Monachatus adumbrari potuit? Ejus tempore cœpit invocari nomen Domini, Genef. IV. 26. nempe in solenni cœtu,non inter segreges,quales Monachorum greges separati sunt. A' vulgo quidem tum Sancti recesserunt, sed infideli, non fideli; Cainitis non Sethitis. Hi enim ab illis separati, publicè cœperunt invocare nomen Domini. Invocare autem nomen Domini, non utique consilii, sed præcepti Divini est. Nazaræis cum Monachis nihil omnino commune fuit,quia nec fidelium cœtum communem deseruerunt, nec proprios fecerunt; & eorum institutio ad ceremonias Mosaicas & pædagogiam veteris populi pertinuit, & cum iisdem evanescentibus evanuit. Neque vota, qualia Monachi hodie nuncupant, illi nuncuparunt.
units.tr: LV. But the monks have no simple disguise with which to cover their profession. For they dare to derive the beginnings of monasticism from almost the beginning of the world, and to join its progress to the progress of the Church. They display, as if Enos, who began to call upon the name of the Lord, Gen. 4:26; and the Nazirites, consecrating themselves to God, Num. 6:2; and Elijah, Elisha and the sons of the prophets, 1 Kings 17:1 etc.; and the Rechabites, forbidden to build houses, sow fields, plant vineyards or drink wine, Jer. 35:14; and the Maccabees, 2 Macc. 5, last verse, where Judas is said to have withdrawn into a desert place and to have lived there among wild beasts; and the Essenes; and John the Baptist, Matt. 3:1, 4; and the Apostles and the first Christians, living a cenobitic life, Acts 4:32. But they display, they do not demonstrate. For how could monasticism be foreshadowed in Enos, who was married and begot children? In his time men began to call upon the name of the Lord, Gen. 4:26, namely in a solemn assembly, not among separated flocks such as the separated groups of monks are. Indeed the saints then withdrew from the common crowd, but from the unfaithful, not from the faithful; from the Cainites, not the Sethites. For those, separated from these, publicly began to call upon the name of the Lord. But to call upon the name of the Lord is a matter not of counsel but of divine precept. The monks had nothing at all in common with the Nazirites, because the Nazirites neither deserted the common assembly of the faithful nor made one of their own; and their institution belonged to the ceremonies of Moses and the pedagogy of the old people, and with those fading away it faded too. Nor did they make vows such as monks profess today.

units.la: In Elia, Elisæo & Prophetarum filiis ne umbra quidem Monachatus est; utpote quorum instituta non perpetua,sed peculiaria,extra ordinem, ob peculiarem & extraordinariam functionem suscepta fuerunt. Herbis agrestibus usi sunt, compellente fame. Casulas Elias & Elisæus,sed non Prophetarum filii,in Bethel & Jericho habitantes,ædificarunt,non ex voto, sed ob loci, in quo habitabant,angustias. Rechabitæ porrò nec Eremitarum, nec Cœnobitarum figuram gesserunt. Non illorum,quia in desertis nulli oberrarunt. Non horum,quia familias habuerunt & genus propagarunt. Non severunt illi agros, nec vineas plantarunt, neque vinum biberunt. At Monachi plerique & vineas & agros excolendos habent, & vinum genialiter bibunt. Neque etiam domestica sua instituta sic custodiverunt,ut religionem peculiarem, & seorsim à Judæis habuerint. Judæ Macchabæi in desertum secessus ob flagrantem persecutionem tam feliciter Monachatum susfulcit, quàm Davidis exemplum cum armata manu per desertum errarunt. Esseni quales fuerint, Judæi an Christiani, parum refert. Alibi tamen Tumul. C. T. Tom. II. p. 1062. Therapeutas illos non actívos,sed contemplativos,quorum instituta Philo libro de vita contemplativa prosequitur,& Eusebius repetiit,& ad Monachatum adversarii applicant, neque omnino Essenos,neque Christianos,neque Monachos fuisse,fusius comprobavimus. Nam quod à Marco Evangelista ad Christum conversos eos esse, Eusebius Hist. Eccl. lib. II. 17. ex fama prodidit, nullam eum fidem mereri ostendimus. Quanquam ne quidem Monachos eos fuisse, Eusebius scripsit,sed ascetas. Differunt autem ascetæ & Monachi,ut genus & species. Ascetæ enim semper in Ecclesia fuerunt; at non Monachi. Johannis Baptistæ vocatio singularis & extraordinaria notas quoque singulares & extraordinarias conjunctas habuit. Neque tamen ille vel ad cœlibatum, vel ad paupertatem, vel ad obedientiam cæcam ulli homini præstandam voto se obstrinxit, nec in statu suo Evangelicam perfectionem , quàm in Christo ipsum sequente ostendit; vel supererogationem aucupatus est. Ejus victus erant ἀκρίδες, sive herbarum summitates,sive locustæ, quibus fumo & sale duratis in Oriente vesci mos erat, & quales etiam illos in deserto, quos coturnices fuisse, communis persuasio est,fuisse ὁ πάνυ &Jil. Jobus Ludolphus sagacibus conjecturis probare contendit: nec non μέλι ἀγρέιον mel agreste, ab agrestibus apibus confectum , non domesticum,& humana diligentia percolatum,Matth. III. 4. His verò expressis lautitiæ sed non edulliorum genera omnia reliqua negantur. Vestitus fuit è pilis camelorum humilis & rusticus, non singularis & monstrosus,sed agrestibus hominibus usitatus. Habitavit idem in deserto, non absolute, sed comparate tali,in quo ὀφεγή patria urbs Judæ fuit,Luc. I. 39.40. Neque semper in deserto mansit,sed ad dies usque demonstrationis ejus Israeli factæ,ibid. v. 80. Quid hæc singula ad Eremitas, qui non sunt ibi, ubi patria est, nec cibis & vestimentis patriis utuntur, sed è patria in loca simpliciter deserta ἀνα-χωρῆσαι secedunt, & ascitNo, ascititium vivendi genus amplectuntur? Ex uno homine adeò dissimili, & singulari vocatione singulariter fungente tot eremitarum & coenobitarum populos & examina derivabimus? Causæ & circumstantiæ peculiares & privatæ communia effecta gignent? Veteres verò nonnullos, Hieronymum cumprimis, rei à se inventæ, in qua mirè sibi placebant, ex Johannis exemplo colorem quæsivisse, mirum non est. Et par ferè Apostolorum & primorum Christianorum ratio est, qui tam non fuerunt Monachi, quàm non Monachi Apostolis & primis Christianis similes sunt. Licèt enim ex illorum communione veteres coenobitæ instituti sui occasionem forte rapuerint, rationem tamen certam ex ea deprome re non potuerunt, quia communionis illorum & vitæ coenobiticæ ratio δὶς δια πασῶν dissident. Communionis enim finis sustentatio pauperum fuit: in ea familiæ fuerunt, uti ex Anania & Sapphira liquet: nullos Abbates, Archimandritas illa habuit: nullos cæcæ obedientiæ voto obligatos alumnos: in ea omnia omnibus, non certis ordinibus communia fuerunt; non ἰδίων, sed χρῆσιν, non ut nihil cuiquam proprium esset, sed ut proprium non diceretur, hoc est, publicis usibus, si necessitas postularet, non destinaretur: & una omnibus vita fuit: neque omnino Christiani à Christianis distinguebantur; nullus denique votis locus fuit: Votum verò si quod intercessit apud illos, qui sive multa, sive pauca vendiderunt, non illud paupertatis, sed liberalitatis; neque omnium, sed pauciorum sua conferentium in commune, fuit. In vita verò coenobitica diversa omnia sunt. Quæ pro paupertatis, coelibatus & obedientiæ voto, ex Scripturis obtorto collo rapiunt, jam supra Loc. XX. 27. alibíque etiam profligavimus.
units.tr: In Elijah, Elisha and the sons of the prophets there is not even a shadow of monasticism, since their institutions were not perpetual but peculiar, undertaken outside the ordinary order for a special and extraordinary function. They lived on wild herbs, driven by hunger. Elijah and Elisha, though not the sons of the prophets, living at Bethel and Jericho, built small huts, not from a vow but because of the cramped space of the places where they lived. The Rechabites, moreover, bore the likeness neither of hermits nor of cenobites. Not the former, because they never wandered in the deserts. Not the latter, because they had families and propagated their line. They did not sow fields, plant vineyards, or drink wine. But many monks both cultivate fields and vineyards and drink wine freely. Nor did they keep their domestic customs so as to have a distinct religion of their own, separate from the Jews. Judas Maccabeus, withdrawing into the desert because of fierce persecution, was supported in a monastic manner just as happily as the example of David, who wandered through the desert with an armed band. The Essenes, whether they were Jews or Christians, matters little. Elsewhere, however, Tumul. C. T. Tom. II. p. 1062. we have shown at greater length that those Therapeutae were contemplative rather than active, whose way of life Philo follows in his de vita contemplativa, and which Eusebius repeated, and which opponents apply to monasticism; and that they were not Essenes at all, nor Christians, nor monks. For as to Eusebius's report, drawn from hearsay, that they were converted to Christ by Mark the Evangelist (Hist. Eccl. lib. II. 17.), we have shown that it deserves no credit. Yet Eusebius did not write that they were monks, but ascetics. Ascetics and monks, however, differ as genus and species. For ascetics have always existed in the Church, but not monks. The calling of John the Baptist was singular and extraordinary, and it had singular and extraordinary marks joined to it. Nor did he bind himself by a vow to celibacy, poverty, or blind obedience to any man, nor did he display in his own state the evangelical perfection which he showed in Christ following him; nor did he hunt after works of supererogation. His food was ἀκρίδες [ἀκρίδες], either the tops of herbs or locusts, which in the East it was customary to eat dried with smoke and salt; and the common belief is that those in the desert which were quails were of the same kind, a point which ὁ πάνυ [ὁ πάνυ] Job Ludolf, with shrewd conjectures, strives to prove. Likewise μέλι ἀγρέιον [μέλι ἀγρέιον], wild honey, made by wild bees, not domestic, and refined by human diligence (Matt. 3:4). Indeed, by these things every other kind of luxury and dainty is denied. His clothing was of camels' hair, humble and rustic, not strange and monstrous, but such as was common among country people. He lived in the desert, not absolutely, but in a comparative sense, in that hill country in which ὀφεγή [ὀφεγή] was the native city of Judah (Luke 1:39-40). Nor did he always remain in the desert, but until the day of his manifestation to Israel (ibid. v. 80). What has all this to do with hermits, who are not where their homeland is, do not use the food and clothing of their country, but withdraw from their homeland into wholly deserted places, ἀνα-χωρῆσαι [ἀνα-χωρῆσαι], and embrace an adopted, borrowed way of life? Shall we derive from one man, so dissimilar and of a singular calling, fulfilling a singular office, so many peoples and swarms of hermits and cenobites? Shall peculiar and private causes and circumstances bring forth common effects? It is no wonder that some of the ancients, Jerome above all, sought a colouring for their own invention, in which they took special pleasure, from the example of John. And the case of the Apostles and the first Christians is nearly the same: they were no more monks than monks are like the Apostles and the first Christians. For although the ancient cenobites perhaps seized upon the occasion for their institution from the fellowship of those first believers, they could not draw a certain rule from it, because the fellowship of the Apostles and the cenobitic life differ δὶς δια πασῶν [δὶς δια πασῶν], that is, by the octave. For the purpose of the fellowship was the support of the poor; in it there were households, as is clear from Ananias and Sapphira; it had no abbots or archimandrites; it had no pupils bound by a vow of blind obedience; in it all things were common to all, not to certain orders; they were not ἰδίων [ἰδίων] but χρῆσιν [χρῆσιν], not in the sense that nothing belonged to anyone, but that nothing was called one's own, that is, that it was not set aside for private use but made available for common use when necessity required; and there was one way of life for all; nor were Christians at all distinguished from Christians; finally, there was no place for vows. If any vow did pass among them, it was not a vow of poverty but of generosity, and it belonged not to all but to a few who contributed their goods to the common fund, whether they sold much or little. But in the cenobitic life everything is different. The texts which they wrench by force from Scripture in support of the vows of poverty, celibacy, and obedience, we have already overthrown above (Loc. XX. 27.) and elsewhere.

units.la: LVI. Præcipuum adversariorum ex antiquitate petitum scutum est.
units.tr: LVI. The adversaries' chief shield is drawn from antiquity.

units.la: Sed certa ab incertis, & dissimilia à dissimilibus disparanda sunt. Certum enim est, ex humano, non Divino instituto fluxisse, quicquid veteres hac in re suscepterunt & usurparunt. Certum & illud est, Monachatum in virgine adhuc Ecclesia primi & secundi seculi non obtinuisse; & quando obtinere coepit, ne quidem Ecclesiæ totius arbitrio, sed privato quorundam studio, vel secedendi ob flagrantes persecutiones necessitate in Ecclesiam invectum eum esse. Primus Paulus Thebæus A. CCLX. occasione decimæ persecutionis in eremum secessit. Secutus in Ægypto Antonius est. Utrumque illum secuti sunt plures, alii quidem viri præstantes, Hilarion cumprimis, alii verò etiam minùs laudati: Mox etiam coenobia erigi coeperunt, quibus certam formam primus Basilius præscripsit, qui ob novum institutum tum Eusebii, tum Ecclesiæ Neocæsariensis reprehensionem incurrit. In Occidente Monachorum collegia primus Benedictus Narsinus erexit, & tribus etiam votis, velut tribus claustris constrinxit. Cassianus verò Collat. 18. cap. 4. tria in Ægypto Monachorum genera facit, unum coenobitarum, qui in congregatione pariter consistentes unius Senioris arbitrio regebantur: altera rum Anachoretarum, qui priùs in coenobiis instituti, postea solitudinis secreta petierunt; tertium Sarabaitarum, monachalis & anachoreticæ vitæ dedecus, qui Ægyptiaca lingua ita vocati sunt, quòd à coenobiis segreges, terrenis & propriis necessitatibus inhiarent, & nomine Monachorum, absque ulla studiorum æmulatione, censerentur. Tertii generis hodiernos Monachos esse, merito Marc. Ant. de Dominis affirmavit. Si, ita de Rep. Eccl. lib. XI. 12. loquitur, nostri Minoritæ, Dominicani, Carmelitæ, Servitæ, Minimitæ ac similes non sunt ipsissimi Sarabaitæ (bonos, si quis est inter ipsos unus coenobita, excipio) quinam erunt, aut jam diu fuerunt? Etiam Benedictinos quis non videt ferme plenissime jam diu in veros Sarabaitas degenerasse? Ubi summa eorum paupertas etiam in communi? Ubi labor manuum? Ubi austeritas vitus & amictus? Quid Monachis cum clericatu? Quid cum tot deliciis? Hi in curribus & equis; prisci verò in nomine Domini Dei nostri invocarunt. Et lib. IX. cap. 5: 27. hodiernos Monachos cum veteribus comparatos Hermaphroditos Religiosos mendicantes, hoc est, neque veros clericos, neque veros Monachos, sed utrumque imperfecte, ac perfecte Pseudoclericos & Pseudo-Monachos appellat. Monasteriis nempe idem quod Gedeonis Ephod accidit. Nam à bonis bona intentione, sed imprudenter tamen instituta in abusum & superstitionem verterunt. Neque quidquam fere Monachi hodierni cum veteribus commune habent. Veterum enim Monachorum vita privata, & ad poenitentiam agendam secessio fuit; neque illi de cæteris à laicis differebant. Unde olim lapsos clericos Ecclesiastici canones in Monasteria detrusERunt, poenitentiam ibi acturos. Novi clerici esse volunt. Illi completi & perfecti censebantur, antequam externa professione ulli superiori se manciparent, vel ullum votum solenne emitterent: nullam ordinis sui confirmationem à Papa expectabant: nihil cum clericis habebant, neque ordinibus sacris initiabantur: sed initiati Monachi esse desierunt: neque proprias, neque communes facultates & latifundia possederunt, sed singuli manuum suarum labore sibi victum & amictum comparuerunt: unde liber Augustini de Opere Monachorum, qui etiam in Psal. 99. paucis multa complectitur, dicens de Monachis: Cum lectione illis res est; laborant manibus suis; inde se transfigunt; non avare aliquid petunt: nihil in vestitu, victu, aliisque rebus sua natura adiaphoris affectarunt: institutum suum ad exercitia & adjumenta officiorum pietatis, quæ Christianis in universum omnibus commendantur, retulerunt: Episcopis subfuerunt: eorum Monasteria, Scholæ & Seminaria Ecclesiastici Ordinis, & Gymnasia pietatis atque cultorum virtutis, fuerunt: vita verò inculpata, exemplorum bonorum feracissima fuerunt: Vitam monasticam, postulante necessitate reliquerunt. Cuncta hæc à Monachatu hodierno longissimè exulant, verè ut veteris illius cadaver exanime dicatur. Paulatim enim, uti verissimè Cassander Consult. c. 25. queritur: Religio vera & solida in superstitionem & religionis speciem conversa est, & accrescentibus opibus pietas decrevit, & in ejus locum larvæ ceremoniarum successerunt, in quibus vera vera pietatis operibus plane neglectis summa totius religionis constituta est, quarum ceremoniarum inanis observatio adeo veram apud plerosque Monachos religionem imminuit, ut nusquam fere licentior & profanior vita, quàm in nonnullis Monasteriis reperiatur. Teterrimi Monachorum Jesuitæ sunt, quos ultimo patientiæ Dei seculo pater mendacii, tanquam ultimum fœtum suum instaurandis Antichristiani templi parietibus, ex orco emisit, de quibus alibi plura.
units.tr: But certain things must be separated from uncertain, and dissimilar things from dissimilar. It is certain that whatever the ancients undertook and practised in this matter flowed from human, not divine, institution. It is also certain that monasticism did not hold sway in the Church of the first and second centuries. When it began to take hold, it was introduced into the Church not by the decision of the whole Church but by the private zeal of certain people, out of the necessity of withdrawing because of raging persecutions. Paul of Thebes was the first to retire into the desert, in the year 260, on the occasion of the tenth persecution. Antony followed him in Egypt. Many others followed both of them: some were outstanding men, Hilarion above all, while others were less commendable. Soon monastic houses also began to be built, and Basil was the first to prescribe a fixed form for them. He incurred the rebuke of Eusebius and of the Church of Neocaesarea for this new institution. In the West, Benedict of Nursia was the first to establish communities of monks, and he bound them by three vows, as if by three cloisters. Cassian (Collat. 18, cap. 4) distinguishes three kinds of monks in Egypt: first, the cenobites, who lived together in one community and were governed by the decision of a single Senior; second, the anchorites, who were first trained in the monasteries and afterwards sought the secrecy of solitude; third, the Sarabaites, a disgrace to monastic and anchoritic life, so called in the Egyptian tongue, because they kept apart from the monasteries, pursued earthly and private advantages, and were counted as monks without any zeal for study. Marc Antony de Dominis rightly affirmed that today's monks belong to this third kind. He speaks thus (de Rep. Eccl. lib. XI, 12): "Are not our Minorites, Dominicans, Carmelites, Servites, Minims and their like the very Sarabaites (I except any true cenobite among them, if there is one)? Who they will be, or who they have been for a long time?" Who does not see that even the Benedictines have for a long time almost wholly degenerated into true Sarabaites? Where is their extreme poverty, even in common? Where is manual labour? Where is the austerity of food and clothing? What have monks to do with the clerical state? What have they to do with so many delights? These men ride in chariots and on horses; the ancients called upon the name of the Lord our God. And in book IX, cap. 5, §27, he calls the monks of today, compared with the ancients, "religious hermaphrodites, mendicants, that is, neither true clerics nor true monks, but both imperfectly, and perfectly pseudo-clerics and pseudo-monks." Indeed, what happened to Gideon's ephod has happened to the monasteries. Institutions begun by good men with good intention, but imprudently, have been turned into abuse and superstition. Today's monks have almost nothing in common with the ancient ones. For the life of the ancient monks was private, and a withdrawal for the purpose of doing penance; nor did they differ from the laity in other respects. Hence the ecclesiastical canons once thrust fallen clerics into monasteries, there to perform penance. Today's clerics want to be monks. The ancients were regarded as complete and perfect before they bound themselves by external profession to any superior or made any solemn vow. They did not expect confirmation of their order from the Pope; they had nothing to do with the clergy, nor were they initiated into holy orders; but once initiated, they ceased to be monks. They possessed neither private nor common wealth and great estates, but each acquired food and clothing for himself by the labour of his hands. Hence Augustine's book On the Work of Monks, which also, in Psalm 99, embraces much in few words, says of monks: "They are occupied with reading; they labour with their hands; by this they support themselves; they do not ask for anything greedily." They did not covet anything in clothing, food, or other things which are by nature indifferent. They referred their institution to the exercises and aids of the duties of piety, which are commended to all Christians in general. They were subject to the bishops. Their monasteries were schools and seminaries of the ecclesiastical order, and gymnasia of piety and of the cultivation of virtue. Their lives were blameless and most fruitful in good examples. When necessity demanded, they left the monastic life. All these things are far removed from the monkery of today, so that it may truly be said of it that it is the lifeless corpse of that ancient life. For gradually, as Cassander rightly complains (Consult. cap. 25): "True and solid religion has been turned into superstition and a show of religion; and as riches increased, piety declined, and in its place have succeeded the empty masks of ceremonies, in which, with the works of piety plainly neglected, the sum of the whole of religion has been set; and the empty observance of these ceremonies has so diminished true religion among most monks that nowhere is life more licentious and profane than in some monasteries." The most abominable of monks are the Jesuits, whom the father of lies, in the last age of God's patience, sent forth from the pit, as his final offspring, to restore the walls of the Antichristian temple. Of them more elsewhere.

units.la: LVII. Superstunt Clerici Adjuvantes, qui Doctores Theologiæ, Juris Canonici & Catechismi, Prædicatores, Disputatores & Theologi Scholastici vulgò numerantur. Doctores Theologiæ Scholastici de hæresi; Juris Canonici de Jure Pontificio disceptant: Non infimi inter mysterii iniquitatis epoptas, utpote qui cum Divini & Cæsarei juris ac dignitatis à Romano lanista, tanquam retiarii cum mirmillonibus committuntur, ut illorum tridente non solùm Imperatores per horum latus confodiat, sed etiam verbum ipsum Dei, & Regem Regum Christum de solio deturbet, suisque pedibus subjiciat. Doctores Catechismi seu Catechistæ omnes pastores esse debent, si Tridentini Concilii decretis stare voluerint. Prædicatores publici Papalis doctrinæ, moralis potiùs, quàm dogmaticæ præcones sunt. Scholastici vel Ecclesiastici, vel capitulares sunt, qui omnes aut plerique, saltem in pagis, ædituii, cantores, & celebrandæ Missæ administri sunt. Capitulares verò præsunt scholis Capituli, atque olim etiam Theologiam docuerunt. Inter adjuvantes hoscce sunt Doctores illi Seraphici, illuminatissimi, profundissimi, veterani, veteratores, Novatorum flagella, hæreticorum scopuli, quia omnia Babylonici mysterii μιάσματα, & scorti illius ulcera plusquam Chironia, meretricio purpurisso illinere, & crassissimas insipidissimasque fabulas soporifero sophistices fuco, velut adsperso papavere & sesamo condire docti, periti & subacti sunt.
units.tr: LVII. There remain the clerics called Adjutors, who are commonly counted among the teachers of theology, of canon law and of the catechism, preachers, disputants and scholastic theologians. Scholastic teachers of theology dispute about heresy; teachers of canon law dispute about papal law. These are not the least among the initiates of the mystery of iniquity, since they are matched against the gladiators of Rome, like net-men against Thracians, in a contest over the rights and dignity of things divine and imperial. Their trident pierces not only the emperors through their side, but also throws down the Word of God itself and the King of kings, Christ, from his throne and puts him under their feet. Teachers of the catechism, or catechists, ought all to be ministers, if they wish to abide by the decrees of the Council of Trent. Public preachers are heralds of papal doctrine, more of morals than of dogma. Scholastics, or ecclesiastics, are either chapter-men, who, all or most of them, at least in the villages, are sextons, singers and assistants at the celebration of the Mass. Chapter-men, however, preside over the schools of the chapter, and formerly they also taught theology. Among these helpers are those seraphic, most enlightened, most profound, veteran doctors, old campaigners, scourges of innovators, rocks against heretics, who are skilled, learned and trained to smear with harlot's rouge all the pollutions of the Babylonian mystery and the sores of that harlot, worse than Chiron's wounds, and to season the thickest and most insipid fables with the soporific dye of sophistry, as if sprinkled with poppy and sesame.

units.la: LVIII. Fuerunt Clerici. Sed in eodem corpore Papæ etiam Laici sunt, quos non uno nomine obnoxios sibi Papa facit. Præcellunt inter eos devoti quidam seculares hybridæ quodammodo, qui meritis Monachorum inhiantes, sed austerioribus institutis impares, sodalitia & φεγτειᾶς confraternitates certis quidem, sed laxioribus legibus adstrictas, ineunt, atque hoc pacto omnium meritorum Monasticorum participes fiunt; præsertim si φεγτειᾶζοντες illi diebus anniversariis in supplicationum pompa incedentes, obvelata facie, renudatas scapulas flagris conscindant, atque hac ἀντιφαλλικὴ priscos Baalis Sacerdotes gnaviter æmulentur. Tales in urbe illa septicolli à Romulo instituti fuerunt Sodales Titii, & fratrum arvalium collegium. Inde Sodales Augustales apud Suetonium, Antoniani apud Capitolinum. Et confraternitates illas, Rosario-Marianas inprimis tyrannidis & idololatriæ Pontificiæ instrumenta esse, res ipsa docet, quia Pontifici, devotionem talem amplis & magnificis promissis spiritualium & corporalium bonorum locupletanti arctissima fide, propensa charitate & obsequio ita addicti sunt, ut in ejus gratiam nihil non velint nolintque, adeóque etiam eorum, quos Pontificiæ tyran-nidis & idololatriæ adversarios norunt, incendia præsentissima promptissimè procurent, quod experientia, mille testes, comprobat. Cleri inemendabilis, Jesuitarum inprimis, promachos strenuissimos se gerunt, & in militia denique sacra id fere, quod in Turcica Janitzari & Spahy, præstant. Sed præter devotos hoscce seculares Papa, Imperii Ecclesiastici & spiritualis titulo, summum etiam & terrenum in Reges & populos terræ imperium usurpat, omnémque creaturam jurisdictioni suæ, spirituali & temporali subesse contendit, de quo tum supra, tum alibi, Myst. Bab. M. Dissert. VIII. §5. III.37-67. copiosissimè egimus.
units.tr: LVIII. There are clerics. But in the same body there are also laymen whom the Pope binds to himself by more than one tie. Among them especially stand out certain devout secular persons, somewhat hybrid, who, while coveting the merits of monks yet unequal to their stricter rules, enter into sodalities and confraternities of flagellants bound by fixed but looser laws, and in this way become sharers in all the merits of the monks. This is especially so if those flagellants, on their feast days, processing in a solemn procession with veiled faces, lash their bared shoulders with whips, and by this antiphallic [ἀντιφαλλικὴ] rite vigorously imitate the ancient priests of Baal. In that seven-hilled city founded by Romulus there were such companies: the Sodales Titii and the college of the Arval brothers. Hence the Augustales in Suetonius, and the Antonines in Capitolinus. And the fact itself teaches that those confraternities, above all the Rosary-Marian ones, are instruments of Papal tyranny and idolatry. For they are so attached to the Pope, who enriches such devotion with ample and magnificent promises of spiritual and bodily goods, with the firmest faith, ready charity and obedience, that they will do or refuse anything for his sake, and so they most readily and speedily promote the fires of those whom they know to be adversaries of papal tyranny and idolatry, as experience, a thousand witnesses, proves. The unamendable clergy, the Jesuits above all, show themselves most vigorous champions, and in the sacred militia they perform almost what the Janissaries and Spahis do in the Turkish one. But besides these secular devotees, the Pope, under the title of ecclesiastical and spiritual empire, also usurps the supreme and temporal rule over kings and peoples of the earth, and contends that every creature is subject to his jurisdiction, both spiritual and temporal; of which we have treated at length above, and elsewhere (Myst. Bab. M., Dissert. VIII, §5, III.37–67).

units.la: LIX. Ad dominationem Papæ illa etiam referri debet, quam in Concilia usurpat, ὑπερεχὴ supra Concilia. Nam & ipsi Pontifices, Paschalis II. c. significasti de electione; Pius II. Ep. 400. & eorum advocati, Turrecremata de Eccl. lib. III. 46. Sanderus de visib. Mon. Eccl. lib. VII. Torrensis de authorit. S. Pont. supra Concil. Stapletonus Princip. Doctr. Lib. XIII. 15. Scholæ Theologi passim in 4. Sent. dist. 19. & omnes fere Canonistæ in C. signif. de elect. c. si Papa Dist. 40. docent, non generalem Synodum superiorem esse Pontifice, sed Pontificem superiorem esse Synodo. Bellarminus verò Præleet. Controv. III. p. 111. q. 4. Gersonem, Cusanum, Panormitanum, alios id inficiantes his verbis refellit: Qui volunt Pontificem non esse supra Concilium, volunt eum in Ecclesia esse, quod est Dux Venetorum in Republica Veneta; supra singulos Magistratus, & supra singulos Senatores, non tamen supra totum Senatum simul collectum. At verò Pontifex simpliciter & absolutè est supra Ecclesiam universam, & supra Concilium generale, ita ut nullum in terris supra se judicium agnoscat. Pertinet huc, quòd Papa sibi potestatem Concilia indicendi, iisdem præsidendi, suffragandi in iis authoritatem, quibus vult, infulatis, de jure Episcopis, ex privilegio Cardinalibus, Abbatibus & Generalibus Ordinum, exclusis inferioribus, Magistratu & Populo, conferendi, eademque confirmatione sua Papali in legitimorum & infallibilium Conciliorum numerum referendi, arrogat. Quæ cuncta Antichristiana sunt, & vel hoc uno argumento profligantur, quòd Papa ab ipso etiam Concilio judicari potest, eíque villicationis suæ rationem reddere tenetur. Quisquis enim frater in alium peccat, eúmque offendit, is corripi, ab Ecclesia judicari, & refractarius pro ethnico & publicano haberi debet, Matth. XVIII. 1-18. Atqui Papa in alium peccare, alium offendere potest, frequentérque peccat & offendit; corripi ergo idem, ab Ecclesia judicari, & refractarius pro ethnico & publicano haberi debet. Dilutum Bellarmini χρησφύγειον est, nomine Ecclesiæ vel Episcopum, vel fidelium cœtum cum suo capite Episcopo intelligi. Episcopum igitur peccantem ad altiorem deferri debere; at non Papam, quia nulla Ecclesia sit, ad quam is deferri possit. Quod primatui suppositio, at non probato congruit; & prorsus ἄλογον est, quia palam est, intelligi ibi cœtum illum, cujus peccator membrum est. Cùmque verba hæc, Dic Ecclesiæ, etiam Petro dicta sint; possunt ergo Petrus & ejus successores, si quos tamen habet, peccatorem ad Ecclesiam, velut superiorem, deferre. Frustra illi Peli Petrum tum nondum fuisse Papam, regerunt. Nunquam enim Papa fuit. Et regula illa non tantum, neque praecipuè ad praesentem Petri statum, sed ad illum, qui futurus erat, spectabat. Insanum verò est, posse Papam dicere Ecclesiae, id est, sibi & Ecclesiae, cui praeest, excommunicando publicè eum, qui peccavit. Papa enim sic sequetur praeceptum Christi, ut postquam primo gradu solus peccatorem coripuit, & deinde coram testibus, qui est secundus gradus: postea loco tertii gradus, redibit citra primum, dicendo sibimet ipsi, & ultra tertium, excommunicando peccatorem, antequam ab Ecclesia admonitus fuerit. Quis verò unquam fando audivit, Ecclesiam significare unum Episcopum, vel Papam; & dicere Ecclesiae, esse excommunicare; aut lege aliqua praescribi, ut quidquam à quoquam dicatur aliis, & tum sibi ipsi? Scilicet monstrosis ejusmodi propugnaculis Babylonicus Papae primatus muniri debuit, ut operculum simile sit patellae. Accedit, quòd vel Papa Ecclesiae membrum est, vel non est. Si non est, non pertinet ad corpus Christi, quod Ecclesia est. Si est, Ecclesia universa minor est, adeóque ei subjici, & ab ea judicari debet. Pars enim toto minor est. Ecclesia verò accipitur vel cum Papa, & sic est actu totum quid respectu Papae: vel sine Papa, & tum non pars est, magnitudine molis major, at virtutis & auctoritatis minor, uti Bellarminus nugatur; sed totum idem, quod antea fuit, etiam cum relatione ad Papam, non actuali illa, sed potentiali. Et si sine Papa Ecclesia accipitur, non potest esse pars Papae, neque alio aliquo sensu, quàm totum, uno, uti Pontificii putant, membro, uti res est, carcinomate carens. Crudum inprimis & ὑπέρογκον praetumidum est affirmare, unius Episcopi, per se consideranti, majorem esse virtutem & auctoritatem, quàm omnium reliquorum Episcoporum unâ cum Ecclesiis, quibus illi praesunt. Praeterea membrum Ecclesiae putridum fieri potest, adeóque tum, ne totum corpus inficiat, amputari debet. Neque obstat, quòd Papam, utpote authoritatem à Deo habentem, ab eodem solo amputari posse, regerunt, tum quia quilibet etiam Pastor authoritatem à Deo habet: tum quia licet authoritas pastorum à Deo sit, tamen derivatio authoritatis hujus quoad existentiam, quam in hac vel illa persona habet, ab Ecclesiae designatione pendet; adeóque ejusdem authoritatis privatio pendet ab Ecclesia, quae eosdem, quos prius designaverat, justas ob causas postea à functione illa removere potest. Quòd si Papa omnes impune & nemine resistente, vexare & perdere posset, Ecclesia sine remedio ad exitium paulatim praecipitaret. Neque satis est dicere, quòd sic Ecclesia Divinitus protegatur, quia sic omnis medicinae cura non in spiritualibus duntaxat, sed etiam in corporalibus abjici deberet. Salus enim omnis Divina praecipuè protectione nititur. Has similésque ob rationes Concilia etiam Papalia Constantiense, Basileense, Pisanum Papam judicio suo subjecerunt, & decreverunt, quemlibet cujuscunque status, vel dignitatis, etsi Papalis, existat, obedire Concilio teneri in his, quae ad fidem, extirpationem scandali, & reformationem Ecclesiae Dei generalem in capite & membris, quae diserta Concilii Constantiensis Sess. 4. verba, à Papa Martino V. unâ cum aliis Concilii hujus decretis Sess. 45. confirmata sunt. Qui etiam Martinus Bullae ad Inquisitores directae hunc articulum inseruit: Utrum credat, quòd sacrum Concilium Constantiense, universam Ecclesiam repraesentans approbavit, & approbat in favorem fidei, & ad salutem animarum, quòd hoc est ab universis fidelibus approbandum.
units.tr: LIX. To the Pope's domination must also be referred the superiority [ὑπερεχή] he claims over councils. For the Pontiffs themselves, Paschalis II (c. significasti, de electione), Pius II (Ep. 400), and their advocates, Turrecremata (De Ecclesia, lib. III, 46), Sanderus (De visibili monarchia Ecclesiae, lib. VII), Torrensis (De auctoritate S. Pontificis supra concilium), Stapleton (Principiorum doctrinae, lib. XIII, 15), the schoolmen passim in 4 Sent. dist. 19, and almost all the canonists (c. significasti, de elect.; c. si Papa, dist. 40), teach that a general synod is not superior to the Pope, but the Pope is superior to the synod. Bellarmine, in his Praelectiones Controversiarum III, p. 111, q. 4, refutes Gerson, Cusanus, Panormitanus and others who deny this, in these words: "Those who want the Pope not to be above the council want him to be in the Church what the Doge of Venice is in the Venetian Republic: above the single magistrates and the single senators, but not above the whole Senate gathered together. But the Pope is simply and absolutely above the whole Church and above a general council, so that he acknowledges no judgment on earth above himself." To this also belongs the fact that the Pope claims for himself the power of convoking councils, presiding over them, and granting the right to vote in them to whomever he wishes: mitred bishops by right, cardinals, abbots and generals of orders by privilege, while excluding the lower clergy, the magistrates and the people. He also claims the right to count councils as lawful and infallible by his own papal confirmation. All these things are Antichristian, and this one argument alone overthrows them: the Pope can be judged even by the council itself, and is bound to render an account of his stewardship. For whoever is a brother and sins against another and offends him must be corrected, be judged by the Church, and, if he refuses, be regarded as a heathen and a tax collector (Matth. 18:1-18). But the Pope can sin against another and offend another, and he frequently does sin and offend; therefore he too must be corrected, be judged by the Church, and, if he refuses, be regarded as a heathen and a tax collector. Bellarmine's refuge of lies [χρησφύγειον] is that by "Church" is meant either the bishop or the body of the faithful with the bishop as its head. So a sinning bishop must be referred to a higher authority, but not the Pope, since there is no church to which he could be referred. This is a supposition that suits the primacy but is not proved, and it is altogether absurd, for it is plain that the body meant is the one of which the sinner is a member. And since these words, "Tell it to the Church," were also spoken to Peter, Peter and his successors, if indeed he has any, could refer a sinner to the Church as to a superior. It is vain for them to reply that Peter was not yet Pope at that time. For he never was Pope. And that rule looked not chiefly to Peter's present state, but to the one that was to come. Truly it is insane to say that the Pope can tell the Church, that is, himself and the Church he presides over, to excommunicate publicly the one who has sinned. For the Pope would follow Christ's command in such a way that, having first corrected the sinner alone (the first stage), and then before witnesses (the second stage), he would afterwards, in place of the third stage, return to the first, speaking to himself, and go beyond the third, excommunicating the sinner before he has been brought to the Church. But who ever heard it said that the Church means one bishop or the Pope, that "to tell the Church" means to excommunicate, or that some law prescribes that something be said by one person to others and then to himself? Clearly the Babylonian primacy of the Pope had to be fortified with monstrous bulwarks of this sort, so that the lid might fit the pan. Add to this that the Pope either is a member of the Church or is not. If he is not, he does not belong to the body of Christ, which is the Church. If he is, the whole Church is greater, and so he must be subject to it and judged by it, for a part is less than the whole. But the Church is taken either with the Pope, and then it is actually a whole in relation to the Pope, or without the Pope, and then it is not a part (greater in bulk, but less in power and authority, as Bellarmine trifles), but the same whole it was before, even with reference to the Pope, not actually but potentially. And if the Church is taken without the Pope, it cannot be a part of the Pope, nor in any sense other than as a whole with one member lacking, which the Papists think is the cancer, as in fact it is. Above all, it is crude and excessively swollen [ὑπέρογκον] to affirm that the power and authority of a single bishop, considered in himself, is greater than that of all the other bishops together with the churches over which they preside. Besides, a member of the Church can become putrid, and then, lest it infect the whole body, it must be amputated. Nor is it an obstacle that they reply that the Pope, having authority from God, can be cut off by God alone, both because every pastor also has authority from God, and because, although the authority of pastors is from God, the derivation of this authority, as to the existence it has in this or that person, depends on the designation of the Church. So the deprivation of that same authority depends on the Church, which for just causes can afterwards remove from that office those whom it had previously designated. But if the Pope could harass and destroy everyone with impunity and with no one resisting, the Church would gradually be plunged to destruction without remedy. Nor is it enough to say that the Church is thus protected by God, for then all care for medicine would have to be cast aside, not only in spiritual but also in bodily matters. For all salvation rests chiefly on divine protection. For these and similar reasons the councils, even papal ones, of Constance, Basel and Pisa subjected the Pope to their judgment, and decreed that "whoever, of whatever state or dignity, even papal, exists, is bound to obey the council in those things which pertain to faith, the extirpation of scandal, and the general reformation of the Church of God in head and members." These are the explicit words of Constance, Session 4, which Pope Martin V confirmed, together with the other decrees of this council, in Session 45. This same Martin also inserted into the bull addressed to the Inquisitors this article: "Whether he believes that the holy Council of Constance, representing the universal Church, has approved and approves, for the favor of faith and the salvation of souls, that this is to be approved by all the faithful."

units.la: LX. Frivola Monarchicorum pro Papae supra Concilia ὑπερογκ argumenta sunt; & ferè imaginario ejusdem suprematui innituntur. Nam Pastorem & Caput eum esse non solum Ecclesiarum omnium particularium, sed etiam totius Ecclesiae universalis simul congregatae, à Christo immediatè institutum, perperam illos supponere, ex iis, quae supra diximus, liquet. Imò immediatè eum à Christo institutum esse caput totius Ecclesiae universalis, doctissimi Pontificiorum, Thomas VValdensis, Augustinus Triumphus, Scotus, Cordubensis, Bannes teste Azorio Instit. Moral. Lib. IV. 11. ipse etiam Bellarminus de S. Pont. lib. II. 12. scribens, quòd Episcopus Romanus, quà Episcopus Romanus fit Petri successor, ex Petri facto ortum habuerit, non ex prima Christi institutione. Parisienses quinetiam & assectae ad argumentum à primatu Papae petitum respondent; Papam quidem esse caput Ecclesiae ministeriale, quoad statum, sed non quoad regimen Ecclesiae per infallibiles Canonum constitutiones; quoad directionem Concilii, non quoad potestatem coercitivam in totum Concilium. Gratis etiam iidem contendunt, summam potestatem Ecclesiasticam, remoto Papa, non esse in Concilio formaliter vel suppletivè. In neutro enim formaliter est, sed in solo Christo. In Ecclesia verò & ejusdem praefectis ministerium tantum & dispensatio est. Et Ecclesiam non absoluta potestate, sed canone regi, summamque potestatem canones illos constituendi in Concilio generali, etiam remoto Papa, esse, iidem Parisienses asserunt. Denique & illud arrogans, imò Antichristianum est, quòd Papa neque Concilio, neque ulli hominum judicium coactivum, sed tantùm discretivum supra se permittere possit. Non potest igitur sese in Sacramento poenitentiae subjicere potestati clavium, ut peccata ejus solvantur aut ligentur. Confessor enim in Confessione, juxta adversarios jurisdictionem in foro conscientiae supra confitentem exercet. Atque ita nec ad remissionem peccatorum pervenire potest is, qui, ceu ἈΝΟΜΩΣ Exlex, maximè peccatis coopertus est.
units.tr: LX. The arguments of the Monarchists for the Pope's superiority over councils are empty and exaggerated, and rest almost on an imaginary supremacy. That they wrongly suppose the Pastor and Head to be the head not only of all particular churches but also of the whole universal Church gathered together, immediately instituted by Christ, is clear from what we have said above. Indeed, that the Pope was immediately instituted by Christ as head of the whole universal Church is held by the most learned Papists: Thomas Waldensis, Augustinus Triumphus, Scotus, Cordubensis, and Bannes, as cited by Azor (Institutiones Morales, lib. IV, 11). Bellarmine himself (De Summo Pontifice, lib. II, 12) writes that "the Roman bishop, in so far as he is bishop of Rome, has arisen from Peter's deed, not from the first institution by Christ." The Parisians and their followers also reply to the argument drawn from the Pope's primacy: the Pope is indeed the ministerial head of the Church as to its state, but not as to the governing of the Church by the infallible constitutions of the canons; he is head as to the direction of the council, but not as to coercive power over the whole council. The same men also contend, without warrant, that supreme ecclesiastical power, with the Pope removed, is not in the council either formally or supplementarily. For it is formally in neither, but in Christ alone; in the Church and its officers there is only ministry and dispensation. The Parisians also assert that the Church is ruled not by absolute power but by canon, and that the supreme power of making those canons in a general council belongs to it even with the Pope removed. Finally, that claim is arrogant, indeed Antichristian, that the Pope cannot allow a coercive judgment over himself to a council or to any man, but only a discretive one. Therefore he cannot subject himself to the power of the keys in the sacrament of penance, so that his sins may be loosed or bound. For the confessor in confession, according to the adversaries, exercises jurisdiction in the forum of conscience over the one confessing. And thus he cannot attain the remission of sins who, as one lawless [ἀνόμως] and outside the law, is especially covered over with sins.

units.la: LXI. De Ordine in Conciliis convocandis & celebrandis tenendo Sect. I. § III.112. egimus. Sed corrupit eum mirè Papa, qui & convocandi, & iis praesidendi, & suffragatores deligendi & confirmandi illa arbitrium sibi vendicat. Convocandi enim potestas tum ab exteriori jurisdictione, quae jure naturali & Divino summo Magistratui convenit, Rom. XIII. 1.4. pendet: tum humani ordinis opus est; cujus custodi Magistratui pariter civili Ecclesiae nutritio convenit: tum potestatem externam coactivam requirit, quae nulla nisi penes civilem potestatem esse potest. Cùmque Papa ipse
units.tr: LXI. We dealt with the order to be observed in convening and holding Councils in Section I, §III.112. But the Pope has badly corrupted this order, since he claims for himself the right to convene Councils, to preside over them, and to choose and confirm those who vote. The power to convene depends on external jurisdiction, which belongs to the supreme magistrate by natural and divine law (Rom. 13:1, 4). It is also a work of human order, and the care of that order belongs equally to the civil magistrate and to the nursing of the Church. And it requires external coercive power, which can rest with no one but the civil power. Since the Pope himself

units.la: Pro eadem argumenta à Monarchicis allata ventilantur.
units.tr: The same arguments brought forward by the Monarchists are here examined.

units.la: Papa nec convocandi, nec moderandi, nec confirmandi Concilia jus habet. reus, adeóque judicandus, esse possit, ordinarium convocandi & moderandi Concilia jus ei competere non potest. Quid erit remedii, sic Æneas Sylvius in Concilio Basileensi quærebat, si criminosus Papa Ecclesiam perturbabit, si fidei contraria prædicet, & hæreticis dogmatibus subditos imbuat? Neque ullam certè ob causam jus illud sibi arrogat, quàm ne judicari & ex fastigio suo, in quod se efferens super omne Numen, se collocavit, ad subsellia parium, vel reorum redigi possit. Vetera certè Concilia Imperatores coegerunt; Nicænum Constantinus M. Constantinopolitanum I. Theodosius senior: Ephesinum junior; Chalcedonense Martianus, subinde etiam ex sententia seu consilio, non sanctione Episcoporum, Romani, vel aliorum. Neque jus præsidendi Conciliis, sive quoad ordinem externum, sive quoad causam, perpetuum Papa vel lege Divina, vel Ecclesiastica acquisivit. Cùm enim Ecclesiæ particularis Episcopus sit, jus ordinarium præsidendi in disceptatione causæ in Concilio generali habere non potest, quia singulæ Ecclesiæ particulares errare & à fide deficere possunt. At nec in custodia ordinis jus tale arrogare sibi potest. Actus enim ordinis, qui in Concilio servandus est, sunt Pastoribus, doctoribus, aliis legitimè vocatis de necessariis prospicere, authoritatem, ubi necessitas postulaverit, interponere, & efficere, ne in magno cœtu Cyclopum concio habeatur, in qua, ut ait Euripides, ἀκύει decreta publicare cum authoritate; periculis occurrere, conventibus interdicere, contumaces punire, & lupos arcere. Qui similésque actus nisi à summo Magistratu ordini præsidente exerceri non possunt. Quod perpetua etiam Ecclesiæ purioris Conciliorum praxis confirmat. Nam Concilio Hierosolymitano non Petrus, sed Jacobus, Actor. XV. 13. Concilio Niceno I. quoad causam Concilii libera electione Hosius Cordubensis; quoad ordinem Constantinus M. Constantinopolitano I. quoad causam Nectarius Constantinopolitanus; quoad ordinem Theodosius; Ephesino quoad causam Cyrillus Alexandrinus, quoad ordinem Candidianus ab Imperatore missus; Chalcedonensi quoad causam nemo; quoad ordinem Martianus primò per se, postea per judices consulares, præfuerunt. In primis octo Conciliis præsedisse Imperatorem & judices ejus etiam Cusanus de Concord. Cath. lib.II.II.16. fatetur: atque id ipsum pertenderunt Cardinales, Pisanum Concilium celebrantes, quorum, teste Guicciardino lib.IX. libera vox erat; posse Concilium cogere, in quo non præsideat Papa, sed fasces submittat, & villicationis suæ rationem reddat. Par ratio suffragantium in Concilio est, qui non soli Prælati, seu Episcopi, Cardinales, Abbates, Generales Ordinum, Papæ jurati, & ejusdem arbitrio causas disceptantes, definientésque, sed libera Ecclesiarum deputatione electi Ecclesiæ ministri, seniores & laici sunt. Nam Episcopi, Cardinales, Abbates, Generales ordinum, quales Papa sibi obnoxios habet, ne quidem Scripturæ & puriori antiquitati noti sunt. Neque tales in Synodo Hierosolymitana, sed Apostoli, Presbyteri & Ecclesia suffragati sunt. Act. XV. 2. 16. 22. XVI. 4. Singuli enim pastores, Presbyteri, plebeji donum de rebus spiritualibus judicandi habentes ad suffragandum idonei sunt.
units.tr: The Pope has no right to convene, to direct, or to confirm Councils. He may be a guilty party, and so liable to judgment, and therefore the ordinary right to convene and direct Councils cannot belong to him. What remedy will there be, asked Aeneas Sylvius at the Council of Basel, if a criminal Pope disturbs the Church, if he preaches what is contrary to the faith, and imbues the subjects with heretical doctrines? Certainly he claims this right for no other reason than that he may not be judged and be brought down from the height on which he has raised himself, lifting himself above every divinity, to the benches of equals or of defendants. Indeed the ancient Councils were convened by emperors: Nicaea by Constantine the Great; the first Constantinople by Theodosius the Elder; Ephesus by Theodosius the Younger; Chalcedon by Marcian, who sometimes acted on the opinion or advice, not the sanction, of the bishops of Rome or of others. Nor has the Pope acquired a perpetual right to preside over Councils, either as to external order or as to the matter in hand, by divine law or by ecclesiastical law. For since he is only the bishop of a particular Church, he cannot have the ordinary right to preside over the discussion of a matter in a general Council, because individual particular Churches can err and fall away from the faith. Nor can he claim such a right over the keeping of order. For the duties of order to be observed in a Council are to provide, through pastors, teachers and others lawfully called, for what is necessary; to interpose authority where necessity demands it; to see to it that no sermon is held in a great assembly of Cyclopes, in which, as Euripides says, [ἀκύει] decrees are published quickly with authority; to meet dangers; to forbid gatherings; to punish the stubborn; and to keep off wolves. Such acts and similar ones cannot be performed except by the supreme magistrate presiding over the order. The constant practice of the purer Councils of the Church confirms this. For at the Council of Jerusalem it was not Peter but James who presided (Acts 15:13). At the first Council of Nicaea, as to the matter of the Council, Hosius of Cordoba presided by free election; as to order, Constantine the Great. At the first Council of Constantinople, as to the matter, Nectarius of Constantinople; as to order, Theodosius. At Ephesus, as to the matter, Cyril of Alexandria; as to order, Candidianus sent by the emperor. At Chalcedon, as to the matter, no one; as to order, Marcian presided first in person, and afterwards through consular judges. That the emperor and his judges presided at the first eight Councils Cusanus also admits (De concordantia catholica II.16). Cardinals who were celebrating the Council of Pisa likewise asserted this, and according to Guicciardini (Book IX) their voice was free: that a Council could be convened in which the Pope does not preside, but lowers his rods of office and gives an account of his stewardship. The same reasoning applies to those who vote in a Council. These are not only prelates, or bishops, cardinals, abbots, generals of orders, sworn to the Pope and deciding and judging causes at his will, but ministers, elders and laymen chosen by the free deputation of the Churches. For bishops, cardinals, abbots and generals of orders, such as the Pope keeps bound to himself, are not even known to Scripture or to purer antiquity. Nor did such men vote at the Synod of Jerusalem, but the apostles, elders and the Church did (Acts 15:2, 16, 22; 16:4). For individual pastors, elders and ordinary people, who have the gift of judging spiritual matters, are fit to give their votes.

units.la: Et sententiæ in Concilio dicendæ potestas proprie est penes Ecclesiam, cui Christus in persona Petri jus clavium dedit, qui non soli infulati, purpurati, uncti & rasi, sed omnes dono & vocatione instructi esse possunt. Neque alia Ecclesiæ primitivæ praxis fuit. Nam in Concilio Niceno I. etiam Constantinus M. veritatis disceptationem, teste Socrate Hist. Eccl. lib. I. 9. suscepit. In Chalcedonensi Legati Imperatoris, Senatores & Patricii decreverunt suffragiis redditis, Evagrio Lib.II.4. teste. In Concilio adhuc Basileensi Presbyteri Bohemi suffragati sunt. Donum enim Prophetiæ & cognitionis Hierarchiæ Papali alligatum minimè omnium est. Imò unius idiotæ sententiam, testimoniis Scripturæ bene munitam, decretis Papæ & Conciliii in Scriptura non confirmatis prævalere, verissimè Panormitanus pronuntiavit.
units.tr: And the power of giving a sentence in a Council properly belongs to the Church, to which Christ gave the right of the keys in the person of Peter. This right can belong not only to those wearing mitres, purple, anointing and tonsure, but to all who are furnished with the gift and calling. Nor was this the practice of the early Church. For at the first Council of Nicaea even Constantine the Great took up the discussion of the truth, according to Socrates (Ecclesiastical History I.9). At Chalcedon the legates of the emperor, senators and patricians decided, the votes having been given, as Evagrius reports (II.4). At the Council of Basel, still, the Bohemian elders gave their votes. For the gift of prophecy and the knowledge of the hierarchy are by no means bound to the papal hierarchy. Indeed Panormitanus rightly pronounced that the opinion of a single layman, well fortified by the testimonies of Scripture, ought to prevail over decrees of the Pope and the Council that are not confirmed in Scripture.

units.la: LXII. Contraria argumenta Papæ suprematu fere nituntur, quo sublato vim omnem amittunt.
units.tr: LXII. The Pope's opponents' arguments rest almost entirely on his supremacy, and once that is removed they lose all their force.

units.la: Pertinet huc, quòd Papæ, non civili potestati, omnes subesse, adeóque ad Concilium vocari, dirigi posse, argutantur. Non enim Papæ Christiani omnes quoad ecclesiasticas, nedum quoad civiles actiones & potestatem coactivam subsunt. Usurpatio enim hæc juris, non jus legitimum est. In Ecclesias verò ab ipso separatas Orientales & Occidentales nequidem usurpatione imperium habet. Potest verò etiam summus Magistratus civilis, vel unus, vel multi consensione unus, velut Imperator, Reges, Principes, Respublicæ Christianæ omnes consentientes, totum orbem Christianum cogere. Sufficit verò ad generale Concilium, si præsto sint tot Conciliorum membra, quot consentientibus jubentibusque Principibus præsto esse possunt, cùm Christus præsentiam suam duobus vel tribus in nomine ipsius convenientibus promiserit. Neq; etiam solus is Concilium convocare poterit, qui Christianos de rebus fidei instruere potest; quia præter causam, quæ in Concilio agitur, in Concilio cogendo & celebrando etiam ordo servari debeat, qui à civili potestate sola præscribi potest. Pleraque etiam Veterum testimonia, jus convocandi Papæ vendicantia sunt Pontificum, potestatis suæ fimbrias extendentium, qui in propria causa testes audiri non possunt. Frivola eorundem ratiocinatio est, quòd Pastor ovibus, pater filiis, non vicissim, præsidere debeat. Nam sano sensu etiam summus Magistratus Ecclesiæ Pater & Pastor est, Papa verò Ecclesiæ universalis nec Pastor, nec Pater est. Concilia verò Romanum Episcopum subinde Patrem vocant, quia ordinis prærogativa primus erat; & figurato, humili & honorifico loquendi modo, quomodo summo etiam Regi, integra dignitate & auctoritate officii, animus humilimus inesse potest. Non præfuit Concilio Hierosolymitano vel Petrus, sed Jacobus potiùs; vel Imperator aliquis, quia Christianus tunc nullus fuit, ac proin ipsa Ecclesia ordinis custos fuit. Ac licet in Conciliis Christianis de fide deliberatio suscipiatur, non iccirco tamen moderamen eorum, saltem quoad ordinem, à Magi-
units.tr: To this belongs the claim that all are subject to the Pope and not to the civil power, and so can be summoned to a council and directed by him. But not all Christians are subject to the Pope in ecclesiastical matters, still less in civil actions and coercive power. This claim is a usurpation, not a lawful right. Over the Eastern and Western churches that have separated from him, he does not even have authority by usurpation. The supreme civil magistrate, however, whether one alone or many by agreement, such as an emperor, kings, princes, and all the Christian commonwealths agreeing together, can compel the whole Christian world. For a general council it is enough that as many members of the councils are present as the consenting and commanding princes can bring together, since Christ promised his presence to two or three gathered in his name. Nor can the one who is able to instruct Christians in matters of faith alone convene a council, because, besides the business to be transacted in the council, an order must also be observed in convening and holding it, and that order can be prescribed by civil power alone. Moreover, many testimonies of the ancients that claim the right to convene councils for the Pope come from pontiffs who were extending the fringes of their power, and they cannot be heard as witnesses in their own cause. Their reasoning is frivolous, that the shepherd should preside over the sheep and the father over the sons, and not the reverse. For in a sound sense even the supreme magistrate is the Father and Shepherd of the Church, whereas the Pope is neither Shepherd nor Father of the universal Church. Councils sometimes call the Roman bishop "Father" because he held the first place in rank, and this is a figurative, humble and honorific way of speaking, in which even a supreme king, while keeping his full dignity and the authority of his office, can have a most humble spirit. Peter did not preside over the Council of Jerusalem; James did, rather; nor did any emperor, since there was then no Christian emperor, and so the Church itself was the guardian of order. And although deliberation about faith takes place in Christian councils, their direction is nevertheless not on that account taken from the magistrate, at least as regards order.

units.la: Argumenta pro hoc jure allata refellumtur. Magistratu Christiano non pendet, inprimis cùm & ille de fide judicare posset & debeat. Cùmque finis Conciliorum sit, non verbo salutari populo præire, & Sacramenta administrare, quod solius Pastoris utique est, sed hæreticorum erroneas sententias cognoscere, eas ex verbo Dei refellere, damnare, & unitati Ecclesiæ consulere, agenda & credenda definire, nihil obstat, quò minùs talia non solis aut quibusvis Ecclesiæ ministris, sed etiam laicis, consentiente Ecclesia, committantur. Inprimis cùm Papa etiam non pastoribus, puta Cardinalibus, Abbatibus, Generalibus Ordinum talia committat; & Episcopi etiam Pontificii, quibus curam hanc ille demandat, non tam veri pastores, quàm causidici sint, & eorum vicibus non Episcopi, sed Parochi curati defungantur. Qui in Concilio suffragandi potestatem habent, hos Ecclesiam repræsentare fatemur. Sed Ecclesiam non soli Episcopi, vel à Papa designati, sed quivis ab Ecclesia delegati idoneè repræsentant. Veteribus verò Conciliis ut plurimùm Episcopos interfuisse, mirum non est, cùm ex singulis provinciis pauci ablegarentur, & ex singulis Presbyteris Episcopi eligerentur ii, qui doctrina, pietate, peritia præstabant, quod nunc Pontificiorum Episcoporum statuæ, ceu jus quoddam perpetuum, perperam sibi arrogant. Maturè tamen Episcopi latiorem sibi potestatem arrogarunt.
units.tr: The arguments adduced for this right are refuted. The Christian magistrate is not dependent on the Pope in this, especially since he too can and should judge concerning faith. And since the purpose of councils is not to lead the people in the saving Word and administer the sacraments, which belongs to the minister alone, but to examine the erroneous opinions of heretics, to refute and condemn them from the Word of God, to look after the unity of the Church, and to define what is to be done and believed, there is nothing to prevent such tasks from being committed, with the consent of the Church, not only to ministers or to any ministers of the Church, but also to laymen. This is especially so since the Pope himself commits such tasks to non-pastors, such as cardinals, abbots, and generals of orders. And the Papist bishops, to whom he entrusts this care, are less true pastors than advocates, and in their place it is not the bishops but the parish priests who discharge the duties. We acknowledge that those who have the power of voting in a council represent the Church. But the Church is suitably represented not only by bishops, or by those designated by the Pope, but by anyone delegated by the Church. That bishops mostly attended the ancient councils is no wonder, since only a few were sent from each province, and from each group of presbyters those were chosen as bishops who excelled in learning, piety and skill; what the statues of the Papist bishops now arrogate to themselves wrongly, as if it were a perpetual right. Yet the bishops very early arrogated to themselves a wider power.

units.la: LXIII. Tyrannidem Papæ in Concilia ex eo etiam cognoscere est, quòd jus Concilia edicto bullato confirmandi sibi arrogat, & sic confirmatorum sententiam judicialem facit, ut ea lata perinde standum sit, atque in foro civili sententia prætoris statur. Et olim quidem singuli Episcopi Concilia assensu occlamantes suum illud Placet, solus Imperator edicto confirmavit. Unde factum est, ut consentiente Ecclesia deinceps Conciliorum decreta quosvis obligarent in foro externo Ecclesiæ, ne possent se Ecclesiæ aggregare illi, qui ea repudiarent; at non in foro interno conscientiæ; in quo nullus mortalium ulli definitioni hominum, nisi ex verbo Dei ad conscientiam manifestatæ obligatur. Sed Papa & Edicto Bullato Concilia confirmat, & nonnisi sic confirmata legitima esse pertendit, & sic confirmatis cunctos mortales in foro conscientiæ, nullo adhibito definitionum examine, obligari jactat. Quæ mera & Antichristiana tyrannis est. Si enim Conciliorum vis omnis à solo edicto Papæ pendet, certè Præsules nonnisi ad ornandam scenam ad Concilia vocantur. Potest enim Papa vel ex tripode oracula fundere, vel advocatis & auditis Theologis placitam sibi sententiam deligere, &, uti Principes solent, omnibus imperare. Et sanè Præsulum suffragia vel fuerunt à Spiritu S. & decisiva, vel non. Si posterius, non major Concilii generalis, quàm consultationis cujusvis, usus fuit, & frustra Concilium tale, ante Papæ confirmationem, Spiritus S. præsentiam & directionem jactavit. Neque Præsulum aliæ sic partes fuissent, quàm cognoscentium & consultantium, solius Papæ, ut pronuntiantis. Si prius, decreta decisiva, & à Spiritu S. manantia nulla amplius in foro conscientiæ confirmatione principali indiguerunt. Addo, confirmationem illam cum arrogata Concilio infallibilitate pugnare. Si enim infallibilia Concilia fuerunt, confirmatione Papæ non indiguerunt. Neque confirmatio, quæ Concilio posterior & accessoria est, illud reddere infallibile potest, perinde enim hoc esset, ac si quis diceret; hominem mortuum mentiri non posse. Neque ex universa antiquitate bullatum edictum, qualia Pontificum posteriorum fuerunt, depromi possunt. Imperatoribus potius confirmatio, quæ per edictum fit, competebat. Ita enim Constantinus M. Concilium Nicænum Lege confirmavit apud Theodoretum Lib. II. 4. Concilium Constantinopolitanum I. Theodosium rogavit decretorum finem sigillo suo muniret. Has quoque partes posteriorum temporum Pontifices rapuerunt, & quam olim Principes ad exterius forum, conservationem pacis & tranquillitatis publicæ ergo, hi ad conscientiæ tribunal iniquè traxerunt, perinde ac si conscientia hominum decretis Synodi, ceu jam ob confirmationem Papæ infallibilis obligarentur, perinde ut in foro externo sententia judiciali suprema prætoris stare omnes tenentur. Sed non ullum hominem, verùm solum Deum in verbo suo judicialem, prætoriam & principalem sententiam, conscientiæ ipsi imperantem, eámque ad obsequium obligare posse, abundè in loco, ubi de judice fidei egimus, demonstratum dedimus. Sententia porrò conciliaris sive confirmata humano judicio, sive non confirmata, vel verbo Dei conformis est, vel non. Si prius, qui eam tulerunt, non sunt judices prætorii, quia sententia non ab illis, sed à verbo Dei emanat; sed judicii Divini interpretes fideles, jus ipsum non facientes, quod proprie judicis est, sed alibi factum declarantes. Si posterius, audiri non merentur. Ideo errasse in nonnullis, summam fidei non concernentibus Concilia etiam probatissima, historia docet. Nam Nicænum I. optimum illud hæreticos Paulianistas, Arianos, uti nonnulli interpretantur non natos, sed factos omnino rebaptizari, Can. 19. at Concilium Constantinopolitanum I. Can. 7. Græco, Arianos etiam non rebaptizatos recipi jussit. Alterutrum Concilium erraverit, necesse est. Idem Concilium Nicænum I. iis, qui cingulum semel abjecerunt, ad militiam redire prohibuit. De Conciliis Nicæno II. Florentino, Tridentino, Conciliabulis potiùs, & factionis Italicæ catervis, quàm legitimis Conciliis, nihil dicam. Scriptura certè prædixit, fore, ut omnes incolæ terræ Bestiam adorarent, Apoc. XIII. 8. Quo tempore nullum Concilium infallibile futurum erat. Par nempe ratio est Conciliorum omnium, quæ Ecclesiarum particularium, ex quibus illud colligitur, est. Atqui Ecclesias particulares quasvis errare posse, in loco confirmavimus. Nullus porrò mortalium causas propias judicialiter tractare potest; sicut nemo de se testari potest, Joh. V. 31. Atqui causæ fidei & morum omnium hominum propriæ sunt, quia omnium hominum interest veritati credere, & recta facere. Denique Conciliagenerali in quæstionibus facti errare posse nulli diffitentur. Possunt ergo eatenus non habere assistentiam Spiritus S. atque sic dominari in iis, omnia impedimenta instru-ctionis formandæ, & veritatis inquisitionibus etiam fidei cognoscendæ possunt, ut non in nomine & timore Christi conveniant.
units.tr: LXIII. The tyranny of the Pope over councils may also be recognized from the fact that he claims for himself the right to confirm the councils by a bulled edict, and so makes the sentence of the confirmed councils a judicial sentence, so that a decision issued is to be held just as a sentence of the praetor is held in the civil court. Formerly, indeed, the individual bishops, by shouting their "Placet" as an assent, and the emperor alone confirmed the councils by edict. Hence it came about that, with the Church consenting, the decrees of councils later bound everyone in the external forum of the Church, so that those who rejected them could not join themselves to the Church; but not in the internal forum of conscience, in which no mortal is bound to any definition of men except one made manifest to conscience from the Word of God. But the Pope both confirms councils by a bulled edict, and contends that only councils so confirmed are lawful, and boasts that all mortals are bound in the forum of conscience by such confirmed councils, without any examination of the definitions. This is a pure and Antichristian tyranny. For if the whole force of councils depends on the mere edict of the Pope, then certainly the prelates are summoned to councils only to adorn the stage. For the Pope can either pour forth oracles from a tripod, or, after calling in and hearing theologians, choose the opinion that pleases him and command all, as princes are wont to do. And indeed the votes of the prelates were either from the Holy Spirit and decisive, or not. If the latter, there was no more use of a general council than of any consultation whatever, and in vain did such a council, before the Pope's confirmation, boast of the presence and direction of the Holy Spirit. Nor would the parts of the prelates have been other than those of persons examining and consulting, while the part of the Pope alone would have been that of one pronouncing judgment. If the former, the decisive decrees, flowing from the Holy Spirit, needed no principal confirmation in the forum of conscience. I add that this confirmation contradicts the infallibility claimed for councils. For if the councils were infallible, they did not need confirmation by the Pope.
