Novi mundi contemplatio pietatis incentivum esse debet. 103. Status hominum in futuro seculo damnatorum, vel salvandorum est, de illo prius quam de hoc agendum est. 104. Inferni nomina. 105. Infernum existere, probatur tum expressis Scripturæ testimoniis. 106. Tum rationibus à justitia, veracitate & natura Dei, testimonio conscientiæ, & consensu gentium petitis. 107. Infernalium poenarum atrocitas. 108. Poenarum infernalium differentia unde petenda sit? 109. Poenæ infernales privativæ, seu damni. 110. Poenæ inferni positivæ, seu sensus. 111. Ordo poenarum infernalium. 112. Poenarum earundem æternitas. 113. Gradus poenarum infernalium. 114. Elenchus Judæorum, Gentilium, Pseudo-Christianorum infernum, vel saltem æternitatem poenarum infernalium negantium. 115. Argumenta eorundem discutiuntur. 116. Objectio eorum præcipua, quòd infernus justitiæ Dei repugnet, utpote quæ vetet, ne delicta impiorum finita poenis æternis plectantur, proponitur. 117. & fusius diluitur. 118. Inferni locus. 119. Vita æterna æterna definitur: & synonyma ejus colliguntur. 120. Dari vitam æternam, Scripturæ testimoniis, exemplis & rationibus demonstratur. 121. Elenchus eorum, qui vitam æternam negant. 122. Vitam æternam donat communiter Deus Triunus; singulariter Filius. 123. Neque ejus consecutio à viribus naturæ pendet. 124. Vitæ æternæ participes omnes electi, secundum corpus & animam erunt. 125. Æterna beatitudo summa erit. 126. Constans tum carentia malorum omnium; 127. Tum positione Boni Summi; quod non consistit in fruitione creaturæ ullius. 128. Solomonis argumenta, quibus vanitatem rerum omnium extra Deum & timorem ejus demonstrat, colliguntur. 129. Neque in animæ, neque in corporis bonis Summum Bonum consistit. 130. Philosophorum elenchus. 131. Summum Bonum solus Deus O. M. est. 132. Platonis Αυτάγαθον & idea boni. 133. Deus hominis Summum Bonum esse non potest, citra ejus fruitionem, & operationem hominis circa eum, quæ nec increata operatio Dei, nec illapsus essentiæ Divinæ in animam hominis totius optima & sanctissima, qua illa Deo unitur, & fruitur, est. 134. Ejus initium hujus, consummatio alterius vitæ est. 135. Beatitudinis vitæ præsentis & futuræ differentia panditur. 136. Operatio animæ, qua summum Bonum cognoscit & eo fruitur, visionis & cognitionis Dei nomine venit. 137. Quæ nec essentiæ Dei comprehensio, nec arida & sterilis Dei contemplatio est. 138. De visione Dei certiora explicantur. 139. Etiam voluntatis beatæ perfectam renovationem, & cum Divina conformationem includit. 140. Et cum pleno sensu favoris Dei. 141. Acquiescentia in Deo. 142. Ineffabili lætitia. 143. eaque in solo Deo, & spirituali. 144. Denique cum perfecta communione imaginis Divinæ conjuncta est. 145. Beatitudo proin hominis intellectum perfecta sapientia & cognitione perfundet. 146. Et ejusdem voluntatem plena sanctitate & conformatione cum æterna lege Dei, nec non immutabili libertate bene agendi perficiet. 147. Affectus omnes rectæ rationis regimini subjiciet. 148. Denique & potestatem ejusdem consummabit. 149. Corpus etiam hominis beati gloria implebitur. 150. Corporis gloriosi essentia non mutabitur. 151. Ejusdem dotes explicatæ. 152. Beatitudinem hominis mirè augebunt ejusdem habitatio in domicilio cœlesti; 153. Gloriosa societas. 154. Nec non bonorum multitudo, universalitas, æternitas. 155. Beatitudo ejusdem speciei gloriæ gradus recipiet. 156. Quod Scripturæ testimoniis, parabolis, exemplis & rationibus probatur. 157. Joviniani aliorumque argumentis oppositis fit satis. 158. Quorum nam præcipua beatitudo futura sit. 159. Augustini de gloria beatorum sententia commemorabili oratione ejus expósita. 160. Nimiæ circa vitam æternam curiositatis vitium perstringitur. 161. Colophon Loci & totius operis. 162.
units.tr: Glorification is the crown of the benefits of Christ. 1. It belongs either to the soul or to the whole man. The former is defined. 2. And it is illustrated from 2 Cor. 5:2. 3. The separation of the soul from the body in death is described in various ways. 4. The difference between the death of believers and the death of the profane. 5. In what sense death is to be feared is explained. 6. The remedies for procuring [ἀφθαρσία] incorruptibility against death. 7. The process of death is described from Solomon. 8. After death the body and the soul have different states. The body returns to the earth. 9. It ought to be carried out and buried with decency. 10. The relics and bones of the body are to be buried in the ground, not offered to religious veneration and idolatry. 11. The place of burial, and the Papal superstition about it. 12. All men seem to be buried. 13. The funeral rites of the Hebrews, the Papists, and the Evangelicals. 14. After death the soul returns to God. 15. The continuance [διαμονή] of the soul separated from the body in the separate state, which it holds in heaven; opposed to migration into the bodies of men or beasts. 16. Likewise opposed to migration into Purgatory. 17. This is refuted by several weighty arguments. 18. The arguments with which Purgatory is commonly propped up are met. 19. The passage 1 Cor. 3:3, chiefly drawn forward for Purgatory, is vindicated. 20. Neither baptism for the dead, 1 Cor. 15:29, nor the prayers of the ancients for the dead favour Purgatory. 21. The true origin of Purgatory is laid open. 22. The soul, separated from the body, is at once fully sanctified and set free from every sin. 23. And at once it is carried up into heaven, the place of blessedness and glory. 24. The error of those who imagined certain bosoms outside heaven, into which souls are consigned after death, is struck down. 25. The state of the soul separated from the body is glorious. 26. That the souls do not sleep, against the Anabaptists, nor do nothing at all, against the Socinians, is asserted. 27. The arguments of the Psychopannychists to the contrary are refuted. 28. Separated souls do not know what is done on earth by each individual; nor do they know all things in the mirror of the Divine essence. 29. The contrary arguments of the Papists are dissolved. 30. The Papal canonization of saints is refuted. 31. The religious worship of the saints, enjoined by the Pope even under oath, prevails in daily practice. 32. The strong arguments opposed to this are set down. 33. The arguments of the worshippers of saints are discussed. 34. Some souls, while still joined to the body, returned to the earth; what became of them afterwards is uncertain. 35. No souls separated from the body return to the earth and appear to men. 36. Nor did the soul of Samuel appear to Saul. 37. The continuance of the state of separated souls until the coming of Christ. 38. The glorification of the whole man is described. 39. The degrees of this, which Christ will return from heaven to bring about. 40. Prophecies concerning the coming of the Lord to judgment. 41. St Peter answers the contrary arguments of the scoffers. 42. The time of the Lord's coming is not defined in the Word of God. 43. Yet certain signs announcing the same coming are described in the Word of God. 44. Such are especially those which Christ himself indicated in Matt. 24. 45. And revealed to John his beloved, and through him to the Church, by the emblem of seven seals and as many trumpets. 46. The progress of the kingdom of Christ, and of the Church which is to reign with him, is explained. 47. The opinions of the teachers disagree concerning the final state of the Church that is to precede the coming of Christ to judgment. 48. The more probable opinion is that, the polity of Antichrist having been abolished, the gospel is to be preached throughout the whole world, and then the end of the world will follow. How the abolition of Antichrist will be is shown. 49. When he has been abolished, the fullness of the Gentiles will come in. 50. And at last the Jews will be converted. 51. This state of the Church, preceding the coming of Christ to judgment, will be a certain resurrection and quickening. 52. Christ did not cut off the hope of this when he asked: "When the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?" Luke 18:8. 53. That flourishing state of the Church will have peace and security as its companions. 54. The Lord, coming from heaven, will not set up in the world a particular kingdom made up of all the saints, or of the martyrs raised again, to reign in the world for a thousand years. 55. The heretical millenarianism of the Cerinthians is refuted. 56. The dogmatic millenarianism of the ancient and more recent theologians is to be pardoned as a blemish rather than harshly assailed. 57. It is nevertheless refuted, as contrary to the Word of God. 58. The passage Rev. 20:1–8 is wrongly twisted to defend it. 59. The true works of Christ coming from heaven to earth are the resurrection of the dead, the universal judgment, and the glorification of the elect. The resurrection of the dead is defined. 60. It is the foundation of the Christian faith. 61. It is proved by express testimonies of Scripture, by examples, and by types; 62. as well as by arguments from Scripture, 63. and from the light of nature, at least as to its possibility. 64. The history of the Sadducees, the philosophers, and the pseudo-Christians who deny the resurrection. 65. Their arguments are met. 66. God alone raises the dead. 67. Christ is uniquely the cause of the resurrection of the godly and the wicked, but not without distinction. 68. A refutation of those who hold that the dead rise naturally. 69. Properly it is not the whole man but his organic body that rises, and it rises the same in number as that which fell. 70. In those raised from death, body and soul; the organic members, the necessary spirits and humours, and all things pertaining to adornment will be present. 71. Neither will every mass of flesh nor none be raised. 72. The history of those who deny the resurrection of the same flesh in number. 73. Their arguments are brought forward and answered. 74. The dissolution of the same bodily dust, and the consumption of human flesh by cannibals or beasts, is no obstacle to the resurrection of the flesh. 75. The resurrection will be universal, including that of the unjust. 76. The contrary arguments of the Jews and the Socinians are dissolved. 77. The manner in which Christ will use the raising of the dead. 78. The place of those who rise. 79. The change of those still living at the coming of the Lord will be analogous to the resurrection of the dead. 80. The manner of the change of those still living. 81. The end of the resurrection. 82. The second work of Christ coming again will be the universal judgment of the living and the dead. 83. The truth of this future event is demonstrated. 84. And it is vindicated against unbelievers, old and new, above all the Socinians. 85. The Judge will be the triune God. 86. Neither angels nor saints will be judges in the proper sense. 87. The living and the dead will be judged, and so all men in general. 88. Even evil angels will be judged by Christ, and in and with him by the good and holy angels. 89. Preparation for the judgment. 90. The administration of judgment consists in the examination of the cause, the pronouncing of sentence, and its execution. 91. The time and place of the judgment. 92. The last judgment will follow the end of the world and the consummation of the age. 93. Even right reason argues for an end of the world. 94. A refutation of the Jews, the philosophers, and the Eternalists. 95. It is not nature but God who will put an end to the world. 96. This is demonstrated by testimonies of the Old and New Testament. 97. The cause and manner of the conflagration of the world as asserted by Rumetius is examined. 98. The effect of the conflagration of the world will not be its annihilation but its renewal. 99. The disagreement of the ancients and the more recent writers, and the arguments of the dissenters, are sifted. 100. The creatures to be renewed by the conflagration are explained. 101. A refutation of Burnet, who sets holy men as inhabitants of the new world, and who defines more curiously the origin and the endowments and conditions of the new world. 102. The contemplation of the new world ought to be an incentive to piety. 103. The state of men condemned or to be saved in the future age is to be treated; it must be treated before this age. 104. The names of hell. 105. That hell exists is proved by express testimonies of Scripture. 106. And by arguments drawn from the justice, truthfulness, and nature of God, from the testimony of conscience, and from the consent of the nations. 107. The atrocity of the punishments of hell. 108. From what source is the difference of the punishments of hell to be derived? 109. The punishments of hell that are privative, or of loss. 110. The positive punishments of hell, or of sense. 111. The order of the punishments of hell. 112. The eternity of the same punishments. 113. The degrees of the punishments of hell. 114. A refutation of the Jews, the Gentiles, and the pseudo-Christians who deny hell, or at least the eternity of the punishments of hell. 115. Their arguments are discussed. 116. Their chief objection, that hell is repugnant to the justice of God, since it forbids that the finite sins of the wicked be punished with eternal penalties, is set forth. 117. and it is dissolved more fully. 118. The place of hell. 119. Eternal life is defined as eternal, and its synonyms are gathered together. 120. That eternal life is given is demonstrated by testimonies of Scripture, by examples, and by reasons. 121. A refutation of those who deny eternal life. 122. The Triune God in common bestows eternal life; the Son in particular. 123. Its attainment does not depend on the powers of nature. 124. All the elect will partake of eternal life, both in body and in soul. 125. The eternal blessedness will be supreme. 126. It consists both in the absence of all evils; 127. and in the possession of the Supreme Good, which does not consist in the enjoyment of any creature. 128. The arguments of Solomon, by which he shows the vanity of all things apart from God and the fear of him, are gathered. 129. The Supreme Good consists neither in the goods of the soul nor in the goods of the body. 130. A refutation of the philosophers. 131. The Supreme Good is God alone, the best and greatest. 132. Plato's [αὐτάγαθον] the Good-in-itself, and the idea of the good. 133. God cannot be the Supreme Good of man without man's enjoyment of him and his activity about him; which activity is neither the uncreated operation of God nor the most excellent and most holy inflowing of the Divine essence into the whole soul of man, by which the soul is united to God and enjoys him. 134. The beginning of this is in the present life, and its consummation is in the other life. 135. The difference between the blessedness of the present life and of the future life is set forth. 136. The operation of the soul by which it knows the Supreme Good and enjoys it is called by the name of vision and knowledge of God. 137. This is neither a comprehension of the essence of God nor a dry and barren contemplation of God. 138. More certain things are explained concerning the vision of God. 139. It also includes the perfect renewal of the blessed will, and its conformity with the Divine will. 140. And with the full sense of the favour of God. 141. Acquiescence in God. 142. Ineffable joy. 143. And this in God alone, and spiritual. 144. Finally, it is joined with the perfect communion of the divine image. 145. Therefore the blessedness will fill the intellect of man with perfect wisdom and knowledge. 146. And it will perfect his will with full holiness and conformity to the eternal law of God, as well as with an unchangeable freedom of doing well. 147. It will subject all the affections to the rule of right reason. 148. And finally it will complete his power. 149. The body of the blessed man also will be filled with glory. 150. The essence of the glorious body will not be changed. 151. Its endowments are explained. 152. The habitation in the heavenly dwelling will greatly increase the blessedness of man; 153. the glorious fellowship; 154. and likewise the multitude of good things, their universality, and their eternity. 155. The blessedness of man, being of the same kind, will receive degrees of glory. 156. This is proved by testimonies of Scripture, by parables, by examples, and by reasons. 157. Sufficient answer is given to the objections of Jovinian and others. 158. What will be the chief blessedness of those to come. 159. The opinion of Augustine concerning the glory of the blessed, set forth in a memorable speech of his. 160. The vice of excessive curiosity about eternal life is censured. 161. The colophon of the Locus and of the whole work. 162.

units.la: I. BENEFICIORUM Christi ex Fœdere Gratiæ & morte ejusdem mananti- um coronis Glorificatio est.
units.tr: I. Glorification is the crown of the benefits of Christ, which flow from the covenant of grace and from the death of the same Christ.

units.la: Nam quos Deus vocavit, eos justificavit, quos justificavit, eos ὅδοξασεν glorificavit, hoc est, glorificare statuit, & certò glorificabit, Rom. VIII. 30. Nam in ipsa justificatione contineri adjudicationem vitæ, quæ glorificatio est, supra vidimus. Justi enim tum simus, cùm propter Christi justitiam jus petendi & expectandi vitam habemus, quia facienti, vel facta seu justitiam alienam, sed donatam à Deo per fidem habenti, vita promittitur. Quæ vita non hujus duntaxat temporis est, quia illa & fulcris corporis indiget, & ærumnosa est, & cum peccato atque afflictionibus conflictatur, & in morte terminatur, adeóque mortis potius ἀναζωλὴ dilatio quædam, quàm vita est. Vita autem, quæ fructus justitiæ consummatus est, & perpetua, quia simpliciter vita est, sine metu mortis, atque solo Deo & Spiritu ejus vivificante nititur. Deinde in hac vita non videmus Deum, nisi eo modo, quo filius in crepundiis hæreditatem videt. Præterea longè ditior Deus est, quàm ut tantùm panem & aquam hæredibus suis det: & longè appetitus & desiderium hominis, quod rectum Deus nunquam frustratur, majus atque enixius est, quàm ut vita temporali, eáque exercita, & morti quàm vitæ similiori, se exsatiari patiatur. Gloria quinetiam Dei, cujus spe gloriamur in hac vita, Rom. V. 2. revelationem ejusdem requirit, quæ non hujus, sed alterius vitæ est. Nunc Filii Dei sumus, sed nondum revelatum est quid futuri simus: Novimus autem, quòd, cùm id revelatum fuerit; similes ipsi erimus, quoniam ipsum videbimus, sicuti est, in Christo, in quo Deus noster fit omni eo modo, quo fieri potest, 1. Joh. III. 2. Nunc enim ipsum, tanquam per nebulam, & in ænigmate videmus. Tunc verò videbimus & experiemur, quid sit, Jehovam nobis fieri in Deum secundum rem, veritatem & possibilitatem omnem atque expectationem & desiderium creaturæ sapientis. Mortui estis (mox morituri, ut sitis cum Christo) & vita vestra recondita est cum Christo in Deo, decreto & amore ejus, Col. III. 2. 3. quia, quandiu Christus non manifestatur, nec vita nostra manifestatur; quia nondum eum cognoscimus & videmus, sicuti est; & tam verè vita nostra apud Christum est, & nobis manifestanda quandoque τηρᾶται servatur (sicut hieme vita tritici in terra latentis servatur in terra) quàm verè Christus, vita nostra, manifestabitur, & verè ad dextram Dei sedet. det. Sicut Christus in gloria est: ita nos quoque in gloria erimus, quia Deus erit omnia in omnibus, fideles omnes gloria sua, & capitis Christi, implebit, 1. Cor. XV. 28. Ideo etiam S. Petrus ea, quae initii, & quae consummationis sunt, accurate distinguit. De initiis enim dicit: Quem non scientes (qualis jam sit) diligitis, in quem jam, non videntes, credentes autem, exultatis laetitia indicibili & gloriosa, quia laetitia haec digna est operatione Spiritus S. Christo & justitia ejus, Deo & magnitudine ejus, filiis Dei, fide, Evangelio, adeo δεδοξασμένη gloriosa est, 1. Pet. I. 8. De consummatione sic idem loquitur: Regeneravit nos, &c. ad haereditatem incorruptibilem & immarcessibilem, servatam nobis in Coelis, qui potentia Dei custodimur per fidem ad salutem, quae parata est, ut reveletur ultimo tempore, ibid. v. 3. 4. 5. Licet enim Ecclesiae etiam Regnum in mundo promissum sit, & αἱ βασιλεῖαι τῆς κόσμῳ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Regna mundi Domini nostri etiam in mundo fieri debeant, Apoc. XI. 15. tamen Regnum illud non gloriae, credentibus omnibus promissum, & in Coelo adeundum, sed haereditatis gentium est, quae datur partim in afflictione multa & bello, partim in pace, quando omnes gentes populo Dei servient, & Reges gloriam suam in Regnum Christi inferent, ut Ecclesia habeat refrigerium, multorum conversione ad Deum gaudens & cum laetitia ex hac vita ad Christum transiens.
units.tr: For "whom he called, them he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified [ἐδόξασεν]," that is, he decided to glorify them and will certainly glorify them (Rom. 8:30). For we have seen above that the adjudication of life, which is glorification, is contained in justification itself. We are righteous when, on account of Christ's righteousness, we have the right to seek and to expect life. Life is promised to the one who does the works, or to the one who has, through faith, not his own righteousness but the alien righteousness given by God. This life is not only of the present time. The present life needs the props of the body, it is troubled, it struggles with sin and afflictions, and it ends in death; so it is rather a kind of postponement of death than life. But the life that is the fruit of consummated righteousness is perpetual, because it is simply life, free from the fear of death, and it rests on God alone and on his quickening Spirit. Further, in this life we do not see God except in the way that a child in its cradle sees its inheritance. Moreover, God is far richer than to give his heirs only bread and water. And the appetite and desire of man, which God never frustrates when it is right, is greater and more eager than that it should be satisfied with temporal life, and a life that is practised and more like death than life. Indeed, the glory of God, in whose hope we glory in this life (Rom. 5:2), requires a revelation of itself, which belongs not to this life but to another. "Now we are the sons of God, but it is not yet revealed what we shall be. We know, however, that when it is revealed we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is" (1 John 3:2), in Christ, in whom our God becomes, in every way that is possible, ours. For now we see him as through a cloud and in a riddle. But then we shall see and experience what it is for Jehovah to become God to us, in fact, in truth and in all possibility, and beyond all the expectation and desire of a wise creature. "You have died, and are about to die, so that you may be with Christ; and your life is hidden with Christ in God, in his decree and love" (Col. 3:2–3). For as long as Christ is not manifested, our life is not manifested either, because we do not yet know him and see him as he is. Our life is as truly with Christ, and is kept to be made manifest to us at some time (as in winter the life of wheat, hidden in the earth, is kept in the earth), as truly as Christ, our life, will be manifested, and truly sits at the right hand of God. As Christ is in glory, so we too will be in glory, because "God will be all in all," and will fill all the faithful with his glory and with the glory of Christ their head (1 Cor. 15:28). Therefore also St Peter carefully distinguishes what belongs to the beginnings and what to the consummation. Of the beginnings he says: "Whom, not knowing (what he now is) you love; in whom, though you do not see him, yet believing, you rejoice with inexpressible and glorious joy" (1 Pet. 1:8). For this joy is worthy of the work of the Holy Spirit, of Christ and his righteousness, of God and his greatness, of the sons of God, of faith and of the Gospel; it is so glorious [δεδοξασμένη]. Of the consummation the same apostle speaks thus: "He has begotten us again, etc., to an incorruptible and unfading inheritance, reserved for us in heaven, who by the power of God are kept through faith unto salvation, which is ready to be revealed in the last time" (ibid. vv. 3–5). For although the kingdom promised to the Church in the world, and "the kingdoms of the world of our Lord" [αἱ βασιλεῖαι τοῦ κόσμου τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν] "must become the kingdoms of our Lord, even in the world" (Rev. 11:15), nevertheless that kingdom is not the kingdom of glory, promised to all believers and to be entered in heaven; it is the inheritance of the nations, which is given partly in much affliction and war, partly in peace, when all nations will serve the people of God and kings will bring their glory into the kingdom of Christ, so that the Church may have refreshment, rejoicing in the conversion of many to God and passing with gladness from this life to Christ.

units.la: II. Glorificatio, pro subjecti recipientis conditione, vel animae separatim, vel totius hominis est. Illa est, qua electi in fide mortui, statim a morte, secundum animam a corpore separatam plene sanctificantur, ac ministerio Angelorum in Coelum transferuntur, victuri isthic sine corpore usque ad consummationem seculi. De ea S. Paulus loquitur; Scimus, inquiens, si terrestris hujus domus nostrae tabernaculum dissolutum fuerit, nos οἰκοδομὴν ἐκ Θεοῦ aedificium ex Deo habituros, non manufactum αἰώνιον ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς aeternum in Coelis, 2. Cor. V. 1. Soluta proin, non tam domo, quam domus terrestris tabernaculo; quia saepe ejus habitatio mutatur, & tandem relinquitur, deserituer & dissolvitur; succedit spiritui hominis alia domus, non manufacta, quia non indiget labore nostro, & a Deo exstructa est, Hebr. X. 10. eaque ἐπουράνιος coelestis, in qua Christus, Enochus, Moses, Elias, & resuscitati cum Christo etiam corporibus suis habitant, & Angeli atque Sanctorum defunctorum animae a corporibus separatae degunt, & ubi justitia habitat, 2. Pet. III. 13. & αἰώνιος aeterna, quia domus, in qua justitia, vita, laetitia, Deus vita nostra, bonum nostrum, & gloria ejus habitat, finem habere non poterit, quia nec causa destruens, corruptio & vanitas ibi est; & causa conservans potentissima adest.
units.tr: II. Glorification, according to the condition of the subject who receives it, is either of the soul separately or of the whole man. The former is that by which the elect who die in faith are, immediately at death, fully sanctified according to the soul separated from the body, and are carried by the ministry of angels into heaven, there to live without a body until the consummation of the age. Of this St Paul speaks: "We know," he says, "that if the earthly tabernacle of this our house is dissolved, we shall have a building from God [οἰκοδομὴν ἐκ Θεοῦ], a house not made with hands, eternal [αἰώνιον], in the heavens" (2 Cor. 5:1). The house is loosed, then, not so much as a house, but as a tent of the earthly house; because its dwelling is often changed, and at last it is left, deserted and dissolved. In its place succeeds to the spirit of man another "house not made with hands," because it does not need our labour and has been built by God (Heb. 10:10). It is "heavenly" [ἐπουράνιος], in which Christ, Enoch, Moses, Elijah, and those raised up with Christ, even in their bodies, dwell; in which also the angels and the souls of the departed saints, separated from their bodies, live; and where "righteousness dwells" (2 Pet. 3:13). And it is "eternal" [αἰώνιος], because the house in which righteousness, life, joy, God, our life, our good and his glory dwell cannot have an end, since there is no destroying cause there, no corruption and vanity; and a most powerful preserving cause is present.

units.la: III. Idem vero S. Paulus innuit, nos jam induisse habitaculum coeleste, & gestire superinduere. In hoc ingemiscimus τὸ οἰκητήριον ἡμῶν τὸ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἐπενδύσασθαι habitaculum nostrum, quod ex Coelo est, superinduere, 2. Cor. V. 2. Nam Hierosolyma illa, quae terrestri succedit, in qua fideles N. T. omnes sunt, & quae libera est, & mater omnium nostrum, Judaeorum & Gentium in Christum credentium, & eundem induentium, dicitur ἡ ἄνω Ἱερουσαλὴμ Hierosolyma, quae
units.tr: III. St Paul also hints that we have already put on the heavenly habitation, and that we long to put it on over the other. "In this we groan, longing to be clothed upon with our habitation which is from heaven [τὸ οἰκητήριον ἡμῶν τὸ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἐπενδύσασθαι]" (2 Cor. 5:2). For that Jerusalem which succeeds the earthly one, in which all the faithful of the New Testament are, which is "free" and is "the mother of us all," of Jews and of Gentiles believing in Christ and putting him on, is called "the Jerusalem above" [ἡ ἄνω Ἱερουσαλὴμ], "which is from above," set over against the earthly Jerusalem which is in bondage (Gal. 4:26),

units.la: desuper est, oppositia Hierosolymae terrestri servienti, Gal. IV. 26. & quae vocatur καινὴ Ἱερουσαλὴμ nova Hierosolyma, quae descendit ex Coelo a Deo, Apoc. III. 12. XXI. 10. quia ex Coelo in terram extenditur, ita ut David, Prophetae, Sancti V. T. cum patribus suis, & ii, qui in terra sunt, & idem cor habentes, sint una civitas, communem consummationem quandam in justitia, libertate & laetitia habens; cujus Rex est solus Deus in Christo manifestatus. Nam etiam nunc civitas nostra in Coelis est, unde & Salvatorem expectamus Dominum Jesum Christum, Phil. III. 20. quia & solum Coelum patriam, & haereditatem nostram reputamus; & jus civitatis atque communionis habemus cum solis illis, qui in Coelis sunt, & eandem nobiscum spem habent; & in Ecclesia, ceu populus Dei, illa tantum agimus, quae ad spem illam confirmandam & testandam pertinent. Voluit enim Deus ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι confundere, adunare (ut omnes unum sint, sicut Pater in Filio, & Filius in Patre unum sunt, Joh. XVII. 21.) tum quae in terris in ipso, Ephes. I. 10. quia qui in terra nunc sunt, cum Angelis & Spiritibus in Coelo consummatis, ceu συνδοῦλοι conservi, Apoc. XIX. 10. consociantur; & κληρονόμοι consortes fiunt, Ephes. I. 11. In N. T. quippe nulla urbs, domus, patria est, quae nos teneat; Sed domicilium ex Coelo, quod credentes in Christum omnes induunt, ἐπιποθοῦντες ἐνδύσασθαι desiderantes superinduere, 2. Cor. V. 2. hoc est, magis magisque se in illud penetrantes, ita ut ad ejus penitissima & intima cubilia tandem perveniant. Sicut enim in tabernaculo Levitico, quando velum reductum erat, & unum jam velut tabernaculum erat, illi, qui in priori tabernaculo erant, jam communicabant cum iis rebus, quae in secundo tabernaculo fuerunt; sed nondum proxime ad illud accesserant; sed procedentes ad illud accedebant, & sic tabernaculum superinduebant: ita cum caro Christi, quatenus sub Lege erat, & hactenus veli rationem habebat, fracta est, facta est Ecclesia, quae in Coelo & terra est, unum habitaculum. Sed ea, quae in terra est, ad eam, quae in Coelo est, propius magis magisque accedit, atque ita semper aliquid de tabernaculo illo induit, donec totum superinduat. Et ad perfectionem eam magis magisque accedit per πόθον desiderium, quia quod homo desiderat, illud amat, cogitat, & quod quis amat, cogitat, apud illum animus est. Ita per πόθον desiderium ad intima coelestis tabernaculi pervenimus.
units.tr: and which is called "the new Jerusalem, which comes down out of heaven from God" (Rev. 3:12; 21:10). It is extended from heaven to earth, so that David, the prophets and the saints of the Old Testament, together with their fathers, and those who are on earth and have the same heart, are one city, holding a common consummation in righteousness, liberty and joy; whose King is God alone, manifested in Christ. For even now "our citizenship is in heaven, from whence we also await the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ" (Phil. 3:20). We reckon heaven alone as our country and our inheritance, and we have the right of citizenship and fellowship with those alone who are in heaven and have the same hope as ourselves; and in the Church, as the people of God, we do only those things that pertain to confirming and attesting that hope. For God willed "to gather together in one [ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι], to unite (that all may be one, as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father)" (John 17:21), "both the things in the earth in him" (Eph. 1:10), because those who are now on earth are joined with the angels and with the spirits made perfect in heaven, as "fellow-servants" [συνδοῦλοι] (Rev. 19:10), and "become fellow-heirs" [κληρονόμοι] (Eph. 1:11). In the New Testament, indeed, there is no city, house or country that holds us; but there is the dwelling from heaven, which all who believe in Christ put on, "desiring to put it on over" (2 Cor. 5:2) [ἐπιποθοῦντες ἐνδύσασθαι]. That is, we penetrate more and more into it, so that at last we come to its innermost and most secret chambers. For as in the Levitical tabernacle, when the veil was drawn back and it was now as one tabernacle, those who were in the former tabernacle already had fellowship with the things which were in the second tabernacle; but they had not yet come very near to it, and as they advanced they drew nearer to it, and so put on the tabernacle: so, when the flesh of Christ, insofar as it was under the Law and had the character of a veil until then, was broken, the Church which is in heaven and on earth became one dwelling. But that which is on earth comes nearer and nearer to that which is in heaven, and so always puts on something of that tabernacle, until it puts on the whole. And it comes ever nearer to perfection through longing [πόθον], because what a man longs for, that he loves and thinks about; and where a man's love and thought are, there is his mind. So through longing [πόθον] we arrive at the innermost parts of the heavenly tabernacle.

units.la: IV. Animae a corpore separatio in morte est. Per illam enim terrestris domus tabernaculi hujus dissolvitur, 2. Cor. V. 1. Necesse enim & statutum est homini semel mori, post autem judicium, Hebr. IX. 27. Est autem mors proprie & per se privatio vitae, & quidam veluti morsus cruciatusque animae & corporis, per peccatum a Deo avulsi, & judicio ac irae Dei obnoxii acerbissimus. De ea, quatenus poena peccati est, ejusque etiam species abunde supra diximus. Sed a tali morte toto coelo distincta mors fidelium, est quidem privatio vitae corporis & separatio animae a corpore, sed illius in Coelum migrantis; hujus in pulverem redigendi, & ex eo resuscitandi ad immortalitatem, incorruptibilitatem, & gloriam coelestem. Pretiosa enim illa illa est in oculis Domini, Psal.CXVI.15. non utique ζημία ψυχῆς damnum animæ, Matth.XVI. 26. sed κέρδος lucrum, Phil. I.21. Non κόλασις pœna, 1. Joh.IV. 18. ἀντιπτώδομα retributio, Rom.XI. 9. Non ἀνταπόδομα compensatio, Matth. XVI.26. vel ἀντίμισθία retaliatio pro peccato, Rom. I.27. sed καταρργησις τῆς σώματος τῆς ἁμαρτίας abolitio corporis peccati, ibid.VI.6. moriente scilicet corpore propter peccatum deponendum, ibid.VIII.10. non ἀποχώρησις secessio à Christo, Matth.VII.23. vel ἐνδημία ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου peregrinatio à Domino, sed ἐνδημία πρὸς τὸν Κύριον profectio ad Dominum, 2. Cor.V.6.8. & ἄφιξις perventio ad metam, velut currentis, Actor. X X.29. μετάβασις transitus ex morte ad vitam, Joh.V.24. ἀνάλυσις solutio ex corpore & migratio ad Christum, Phil.I.23. 2. Tim.IV.6. שער יהוה Porta Domini, per quam justi in Cœlum intrant, Psal.CXVIII.20. non tam depositio tabernaculi, in quo peregrinamur, quàm ἐπένδυσις superindutio cœlestis domus, 2.Cor. V.4. non κόπος labor, ærumna, calamitas, sed ἀνάπαυσις ἐκ τῶν κόπων requies à laboribus, Apoc. XIV.13. denique non perditio sive corporis, sive animæ, sive utriusque in gehenna, Matth. X.28. sed ζωὴ πνεύματος vita Spiritus, Rom. VIII.10. & σπορὰ seminatio corporis in terram, velut agrum Dei; tanquam משכב cubile, in quo ישנו quiescunt & dormiunt, & in quo corpora piorum, ut grana tritici sata, etsi moriuntur, tamen futuro vere extremi judicii, exoriente & fovente sole justitiæ, nova, incorruptibilia & gloriosa revivisc ent, 1. Cor. XV. 43. Esaj. LVII.2. Quæ cuncta mortem fidelium non pœnam proprie dictam, & satisfactionem pro peccato, sed lætum introitum in patriam & cœleste domicilium, respectu animæ, mox à morte, respectu corporis tempore à Deo præstituto, esse proclamant. Aliæ enim longè fidelibus moriendi causæ sunt; peccati inhabitantis maximè depositio, liberatio ab eo, ceu obsoleto, quod merito fastidimus, scorto, Rom. VI.6. Coloss.II.11. quò sic Christus tandem Templum illud, in quo Spiritu suo æternùm habitare vult, vacuum ab omni macula, ruga, sordibus, servitute, molestia, afflictione; adeoque justitia, gaudio, tranquillitate plenum & exuberans sortiatur. Congruit enim ordini justitiæ & sapientiæ Dei, ut fideles hactenus etiam imagini Christi conformentur. Si enim una fuerimus mortui, etiam una vivemus & regnabimus, 2.Tim.II.11.12. Quæ ergo mors à peccato primo ortum duxit, nunc per Dei gratiam, sublato aculeo peccati, quod sine morte immortale foret, mors & remedium facta est. Per illam enim vetustus homo aboletur, qui nonnisi cum exuviis corporis deponi poterat, Col.II.11.
units.tr: IV. The separation of the soul from the body is death. For through death the earthly house of this tabernacle is dissolved (2 Cor. 5:1). "It is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment" (Heb. 9:27). Death properly and in itself is the privation of life, a kind of bite and torment of soul and body, severed from God through sin, and most bitter, being liable to the judgment and wrath of God. We have already said enough above about this death, insofar as it is the punishment of sin, and about its kinds. But the death of believers is quite distinct from such death, as heaven is from earth. It is indeed a privation of bodily life and a separation of the soul from the body, but the soul migrates into heaven, while the body is reduced to dust, to be raised again from it to immortality, incorruptibility and heavenly glory. Precious indeed is that death in the eyes of the Lord (Ps. 116:15). It is not ζημία ψυχῆς, the loss of the soul (Matt. 16:26), but κέρδος, gain (Phil. 1:21). It is not κόλασις, punishment (1 John 4:18); not ἀνταπόδομα, recompense (Rom. 11:9); not ἀντάλλαγμα, compensation (Matt. 16:26); nor ἀντιμισθία, the requital for sin (Rom. 1:27). It is rather καταργησις τῆς σώματος τῆς ἁμαρτίας, the abolition of the body of sin (Rom. 6:6), the body dying so that sin may be put off (Rom. 8:10). It is not ἀποχώρησις, a departure from Christ (Matt. 7:23), nor ἐνδημία ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου, a sojourn away from the Lord, but ἐκδημία πρὸς τὸν Κύριον, a departure to the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6, 8); and ἄφιξις, an arrival at the goal, as of a runner (Acts 20:29); μετάβασις, a passage from death to life (John 5:24); ἀνάλυσις, a release from the body and a migration to Christ (Phil. 1:23; 2 Tim. 4:6). It is שַׁעַר יְהוָה [sha'ar YHWH], the gate of the Lord, through which the righteous enter heaven (Ps. 118:20). It is not so much the laying aside of the tabernacle in which we sojourn as ἐπένδυσις, the putting on over of the heavenly house (2 Cor. 5:4). It is not κόπος, toil, distress or calamity, but ἀνάπαυσις ἐκ τῶν κόπων, rest from labours (Rev. 14:13). Lastly, it is not perdition of the body, or of the soul, or of both in hell (Matt. 10:28), but ζωὴ πνεύματος, the life of the Spirit (Rom. 8:10); and it is the sowing (σπορά) of the body into the earth, as into the field of God, as a bed, מִשְׁכָּב [mishkav], in which those who sleep, יִשְׁנוּ [yishnu], rest and lie down, and in which the bodies of the pious, like sown grains of wheat, though they die, shall at the coming day of the final judgment, when the sun of righteousness rises and warms them, be raised again new, incorruptible and glorious (1 Cor. 15:43; Isa. 57:2). All these things declare that the death of believers is not punishment properly so called, nor satisfaction for sin, but a joyful entrance into the fatherland and heavenly dwelling: for the soul, immediately after death, and for the body, at the time appointed by God. Indeed, there are far other causes of death for believers: chiefly the putting off of indwelling sin, and deliverance from it as from something worn out, which we rightly loathe, like a harlot (Rom. 6:6; Col. 2:11). Thus Christ may at last possess that temple in which he wishes to dwell by his Spirit for ever, empty of every stain, wrinkle, filth, bondage, trouble and affliction, and so full and overflowing with righteousness, joy and tranquillity. For it accords with the order of God's righteousness and wisdom that believers should be conformed to the image of Christ. "If we have died with him, we shall also live with him and reign" (2 Tim. 2:11–12). So death, which arose from the first sin, has now, by the grace of God, with the sting of sin removed, become a remedy, for sin could have made death immortal. By death the old man is abolished, who could be put off only along with the body's casing (Col. 2:11).

units.la: V. Mors igitur fidelium à מתי חלל mortibus profani, Ezech.XXVIII.8. seu morte infinitè immane quantum differt. Licèt enim utrisque mors sit ultima linea rerum mortalium, & abolitio vitæ naturalis, quam hùc degimus, qua utrique æquè אל עפר in pulverem, Genes.III.19. עד דכא ad contritionem, Psal. XC.3. revertuntur, de cætero tamen δὶς ἀλφὰ πιστῶν, & quantum Cœlum ab orco, lux cœlestis gloriæ à tenebris exterioribus, discrepant. Nam viri integri & recti שלום אחרית novissimum pax est, impiorum verò אחרית נכרתת novissimum est, quod exciditur, Psal.XXXVII.37. 38. Piis mors signum Divini amoris à peccato, anxietate, terrore omni liberantis: impiis verò מלך בלהות Rex terrorum est, Job.XVIII. 14. Piis mors requies à laboribus, Apoc.XIV.13. & consolationis efficacissimæ initium est: impiis contrà laborum, cruciatuum, tormentorum horribile baratrum, Luc.XVI.25. Illis abolitio, depositio peccati, & de eo victoria inclyta & triumphus, Rom.VI.7. 1.Cor.XV.55. his peccati ipsius, sævi tyranni instar, dominantis; & concupiscentiarum immaniter grassantium; de damnatis victoria & triumphus, spiritualisque servitutis apex est. Illis propior & arctior cum Christo conjunctio, Phil.I.23. his à gratia & longanimitate Dei extrema & tristissima exulatio. Piorum mors amisit κέντρον stimulum. Ubi tuus, mors, stimulus? Ubi tua, inferne, victoria? 1. Cor.XV.56. Quia enim mors in Christum, rupem & petram, incurrit, iccirco stimulum suum amisit, & in rupe illa contrivit. Impiorum contrà mors stimulum acerrimum habet, qui in morte & consequente æternitate omni quæsitissimè pungit. Denique piorum mors cum gaudio spirituali & gloriatione spei conjuncta est, Actor.VII.55.56. Rom.V.3.4. Impii contrà moriuntur בנפש מרה in anima amara, Job.XXI.25. & migrantes hinc judicium conscientiæ condemnantis, & מר חמות amaritudinem mortis, ibid.VIII.11. desperabundi persentiscunt, vel indurati saltem in exitium præcipitantur. Et quæcunque supra morti fidelium tribuimus, ceu eximia ejus ἀπολογητήματα apud impios in contrarium versa omnia reperiuntur. Scitè igitur Cyprianus lib. de Mortal. Ad refrigerium, inquit, justi vocantur, ad supplicium rapiuntur injusti: datur velocius tutela fidentibus, perfidis pœna.
units.tr: V. The death of believers therefore differs immensely from the deaths of the profane (מְתֵי חָלָל [metei chalal], Ezek. 28:8), that is, from the death of the uncircumcised. For although death is the final limit of mortal things and the end of the natural life we live here, to which both alike return, אֶל עָפָר [el afar], to dust (Gen. 3:19), עַד דַּכָּא [ad dakka], to crushing (Ps. 90:3), yet in other respects the believer has a δὶς ἀλφά, and they differ as far as heaven from hell, and the heavenly light of glory from outer darkness. For of upright and honest men, שָׁלוֹם אַחֲרִית [shalom acharit], the end is peace, but of the wicked, אַחֲרִית נִכְרָתַת [acharit nikhratat], the end is cut off (Ps. 37:37–38). To the pious, death is a sign of divine love that delivers them from sin, anxiety and all terror; but to the wicked, מֶלֶךְ בַּלָּהוֹת [melekh ballahot], it is the king of terrors (Job 18:14). To the pious, death is rest from labours (Rev. 14:13), and the beginning of most effective consolation; to the wicked, it is the dreadful abyss of toil, torment and torture (Luke 16:25). For the former it is the abolition and laying aside of sin, and a glorious victory and triumph over it (Rom. 6:7; 1 Cor. 15:55); for the latter, sin itself, like a savage tyrant, still reigns, and the lusts rage without restraint; for the condemned it is a victory and triumph over them, and the summit of spiritual bondage. For the former there is a closer and more intimate union with Christ (Phil. 1:23); for the latter, a final and most sorrowful exile from the grace and forbearance of God. The death of the pious has lost its κέντρον, its sting. "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" (1 Cor. 15:55–56). For death, running against Christ the rock and stone, has lost its sting and crushed it upon that rock. But for the wicked, death has a most bitter sting, which pierces most keenly in death and in the eternity that follows. Lastly, the death of the pious is joined with spiritual joy and the boasting of hope (Acts 7:55–56; Rom. 5:3–4). The wicked, on the other hand, die בְּמַר נָפֶשׁ [bemar nafesh], in bitterness of soul (Job 21:25), and as they depart hence they perceive, in despair, the judgment of a condemning conscience, and מַר הַמָּוֶת [mar hamavet], the bitterness of death (Job 8:11 in some readings); or, if hardened, they are at least hurled headlong to destruction. And whatever we attribute above to the death of believers as its excellent defences (ἀπολογητήματα), all of these are found turned to the contrary among the impious. Cyprian therefore rightly says in his book on mortality: "The just are called to refreshment, the unjust are dragged to punishment; protection is given more swiftly to the faithful, and punishment to the faithless."

units.la: VI. Quatenus fidelibus etiam N.T. timenda & quatenus non timenda mors sit, alibi, Differt. Tom.III.Diss.I. §9. fusius exposuimus. Non omnis certè timor mortis ex Christi schola relegat. Non ille, quo & caro naturaliter à morte, ceu destructione corporis, abhorret: & spiritus ipse ex Dei verbo mortem, ceu hostem ultimum, & castigationem Dei paternam, adeoque natura sua terribile quid æstimans, ita reformidat, ut fide tamen & spe timorem leniat, atque intra pietatis cancellos coerceat; quin & ad Dei gloriam, & mortificationem carnis referat: & facinorosus, electus licet, propter scelera terreno judici commeritas pœnas persolvens, graviori utique timore mortis, quàm alius, martyr inprimis, percellitur: Et pius denique cordatùsque quispiam, detrimentum aliquod Ecclesiæ vel Reipublicæ, ex obitu suo metuens συνέχεται constringitur ex duobus, Phil.I.23. & magis propter Dei gloriam & salutem hominum, quàm alius, nulla ejusmodi cura districtus, mortem timet. Et timor ille, subinde ex infirmitate carnis pullulans non tam à Christo anathema facit, quàm majoris minorisve in fide, spe & charitate profectus documentum præbet. Sed non timenda ita mors est, ut abjiciatur fiducia, spes gratiæ & salutis: neque timenda est utilitatis, commodorum, voluptatum terrestrium studio & affectu, sepositá Dei gloria, & affectu mortificationis
units.tr: VI. To what extent death is to be feared, and to what extent not feared, even by believers of the New Testament, we have set out more fully elsewhere (Differt. Tom. III, Diss. I, §9). Certainly the school of Christ does not banish every fear of death. There is that fear by which the flesh naturally shrinks from death, as the destruction of the body; and the spirit itself, judging from the word of God that death is the last enemy and a fatherly chastisement, and so by its nature something terrible, shrinks from it in such a way that, by faith and hope, it nevertheless soothes that fear and restrains it within the bounds of godliness; indeed it refers it to the glory of God and the mortification of the flesh. The criminal, though elect, who pays the penalties he has deserved from an earthly judge for his crimes, is certainly struck with a more grievous fear of death than another, especially a martyr. And lastly, a pious and prudent person who, fearing some harm to the Church or the commonwealth from his death, is πέρι constrained by two things (Phil. 1:23), and who fears death more for the glory of God and the salvation of men than another who is not burdened by any such care, shows that fear, which springs up from the weakness of the flesh, not so much as making one anathema from Christ, but as a proof of greater or lesser progress in faith, hope and love. But death is not to be feared in such a way that confidence, the hope of grace and salvation, is cast aside, nor is it to be feared through zeal and affection for earthly advantages, pleasures and comforts, with the glory of God set aside and the mortification of the flesh and the quickening of the Spirit neglected. Rather, the spirit should not hasten to offer itself when God is to be glorified by death, nor should it fail to look further ahead and, beholding future goods, overwhelm with present joy any fear of death, still less resist it stubbornly. And finally, whenever no more pressing cause urges us to wish for a longer life, the human spirit should not desire to depart hence and be with the Lord. This fearlessness (ἀφοβία) becomes all Christians, and the sayings of the ancients are to be understood of it. Cyprian's words in On Mortality: Let him fear to die who is not reborn of water and the Spirit, who is given over to the fires of hell; let him fear to die who is not counted among those of Christ's cross and passion; let him fear to die who will pass from this death to the second death. Likewise Augustine's words in On the Consolation of Death, chapter 3: He who fears death does not yet believe; and to be unwilling to die is a sign of little progress. Lastly, Bernard's saying in Epistle 105: The just man, though he takes care against death, yet does not dread it.

units.la: Mortis fidelium à mortibus profanorum differentia.
units.tr: Difference between the death of believers and the deaths of the profane.

units.la: Quatenus illa timenda, vel non timenda sit, exponitur. tionis carnis ac vivificationis Spiritus ; ut timori carnis tum naturali & cætera minimè vitioso,tum vitioso etiam à residuo peccato inhabitante,quod mortem æquo terribiliorem reddere, & vanas timendi causas suggerere conatur , exorto non succurrat spiritus ,timorem carnis naturalem mitigando , & pravos ejusdem affectus pro modulo gratiæ cohibendo ; ut cùm morte Deus glorificandus est , non promptè se spiritus offerat, longiúsque prospiciens, & futura bona contuitus, præsente gaudio omnem timorem mortis non obruat , nedum,ut pertinaciter repugnet ; vel denique ut, quoties prægnantior causa optandi vitam longiorem nulla urget,spiritus hominis hinc migrare, & cum Domino esse non appetat. Hæc ἀφοβία omnes Christianos decet ; & de ea intelligenda sunt veterum dicta : Cypriani illud de Mortal. Mori plane timeat, sed qui ex aqua & spiritu non renatus, gehennæ ignibus mancipatur: mori timeat qui non Christi cruce & passione censetur : mori timeat, qui ad secundam mortem de hac morte transibit. Nec non illa Augustini de Consolat. Mort. cap. 3. Qui mortem timet, adhuc non credit : & ; Mori nolle,indicium est parvi profectus. Denique Bernhardi Epist. 105. illud: Justus mortem etsi cavet, tamen non pavet.
units.tr: To what extent that death is to be feared, or not feared, is set out. ...of the flesh and the quickening of the Spirit; so that when the fear of the flesh arises, both natural and otherwise not sinful, and also the fear that springs from indwelling remaining sin, which tries to make death far more terrible and to suggest vain causes for fear, the Spirit may not fail to help, by soothing the natural fear of the flesh and restraining its wicked affections to the measure of grace; so that when God is to be glorified by death, the spirit does not readily offer itself, but, looking further ahead and beholding future goods, does not let present joy be overwhelmed by any fear of death, much less resist it stubbornly; or lastly, so that whenever no more pressing cause urges us to desire a longer life, the human spirit does not long to depart hence and be with the Lord. This ἀφοβία [aphobia, freedom from fear] befits all Christians, and the sayings of the ancients are to be understood of it. Cyprian's words: Let him fear to die plainly who, not reborn of water and the Spirit, is given over to the fires of hell; let him fear to die who is not counted among those of Christ's cross and passion; let him fear to die who will pass from this death to the second death. Likewise that of Augustine, On the Consolation of Death, chapter 3: He who fears death does not yet believe; and to be unwilling to die is a sign of little progress. Lastly, that saying of Bernard, Epistle 105: The just man, though he takes care against death, yet does not dread it.

units.la: VII. Ad procurandam ἀφοβίαν, seu despicientiam mortis illam, sine qua Christianus nemo cluet, Spiritus adoptionis, regenerans ad spem vivam ; fides in Christum, morte sua abolentem cum, qui mortis imperium habet ; spes viva & amor Dei, ceu summi Boni ; abnegatio sui,& contemptus mundi, ac eorum,quæ in mundo sunt , utramque paginam faciunt.
units.tr: VII. To secure that fearlessness of death [ἀφοβίαν], or contempt for death, without which no one can be called a Christian, two things must work together: the Spirit of adoption, regenerating us to a living hope; and faith in Christ, who by his death has destroyed him who holds the power of death. A living hope and the love of God, as the highest Good, and self-denial and contempt for the world and for all that is in the world, also contribute.

units.la: Timorem verò naturalem carnis à destructione sui abhorrentis , & spiritus ipsius , mortem, ceu hostem quendam,& Divinam ferulam,non omnino aspernantis, idem Spiritus efficaci instructione & consolatione ita moderatur , ne saluti & τῆ ευεξιμία moriendi oblúctetur nimium, sed potiùs se ad voluntatis Divinæ præscriptum componat, & in Dei gratia acquiescat. Denique timorem mortis vitiosum,ex residua carne & peccato oriundum , & in hac mortalitate magis magisque obtundendum , eadem Christi Redemptoris, & Spiritus S. gratia vividam fiduciam & spem vegetam, magis magisque ἀναζωπυρῶσα ita componit, ut ad extremum cedat,& victori spiritui palmam relinquat. Sed in omnibus his spiritus hominis cum carne & peccato Divino robore belligerans , argumentorum ponderibus, & vivarum consolationum παρακλήσεις pugnat. Cujusmodi sunt misericordia Dei in Christo, mortis victore & triumphatore: Mortis temporalis læta metamorphosis, quoad ejus tum nomina, tum rem & naturam: Paterna Dei providentia : Auxilii Divini gratiosa præsentia: Dilectionis Christi constantia: Mortis fidelium natura, quod Christi & Spiritus inhabitantis fructus est: Lucto cum peccato & afflictionibus exoptata catastrophe : Reditus ex peregrinatione in patriam cœlestem: Exempla Christi & Sanctorum cœlitum: Immortalitas beata animæ: Futura resurrectio corporis: denique æterna hominis totius gloria & beatitudo. Quæ singula Dissert.T.II.Diss.II. fusissimè expósita, ad compendium heic ponimus.
units.tr: The natural fear of the flesh, which shrinks from its own destruction, and the fear of death itself, which the spirit does not altogether despise as a certain enemy and a divine rod, the same Spirit so tempers by effective instruction and consolation that we do not grieve excessively over our safety and our well-being [εὐεξία] in dying, but rather conform ourselves to the will of God and rest in the grace of God. Finally, the sinful fear of death, arising from the remaining flesh and from sin, and to be more and more blunted in this mortal life, the same grace of Christ the Redeemer and of the Holy Spirit so arranges, by kindling a lively confidence and a vigorous hope and rekindling them more and more [ἀναζωπυρῶσα], that at the last it gives way and leaves the palm to the victorious spirit. But in all these matters the human spirit, fighting with the flesh and sin by the divine strength, contends with the weight of arguments and with living comforts [παρακλήσεις]. Such are: the mercy of God in Christ, the conqueror and triumphant over death; the joyful change of temporal death, both in its names and in its nature; the fatherly providence of God; the gracious presence of divine help; the constancy of Christ's love; the nature of the death of the faithful, which is the fruit of Christ and of the indwelling Spirit; the desired end of the struggle with sin and afflictions; the return from the pilgrimage to the heavenly fatherland; the examples of Christ and of the saints in heaven; the blessed immortality of the soul; the future resurrection of the body; and finally the eternal glory and blessedness of the whole man. Each of these is set out at length in Dissert. T. II, Diss. II, and here we give them in brief.

units.la: VIII. Mors ipsa quemadmodum procedat, Solomon Eccles.XII.5.6.7. explicat. Præmittit enim : Abit homo אל בית עולמו ad domum seculi sui, seu secularem suam. Tum in foro plangentes circumeunt. v. 5. Abit ad domum jeculi sui, & velut æternam. Nunquam enim redit naturæ ordine ad hanc vitam; & mors via est ad æternum domicilium, sive beatitudinis, sive moeroris & tristitiæ. Meminisse igitur, dum in via est, creatoris sui debet, quia non item, ut in hippodromo, licebit κάμψαι τὸν νῦτλον, & à carceribus ad metam iterum procurrere. Cùm eò homo pervenerit, in foro circumeunt plangentes , quia superstites præcedentem lætitiam omnem luctu obsignant. Sed qui rectè vixit, & vitam præsentem miseriarum vallem, qualis est, reputavit; denique creatoris sui in tempore recordatus est, nec dolet ipse in morte, nec ab aliis lugendus plangendúsque est, quasi amissus sit, vel boni quicquam perdiderit, & in conditionem malam pervenerit. Jactura etenim mortui , inprimis dilecti , ex cujus amore & virtutibus ad viventes multum boni redundavit , contemnenda non est, imò plangenda etiam est. Nam & Abrahamus,Saram ,Genef. XXIII.2. & Jacobus Josephum, ib.XXXVII. 34. & Israelitæ Mosen ,Deut.XXXIV.8. acerbè planxerunt ; & Christus ipse Lazaro, amico suo, illachrymatus est, Joh.XI.35. & pii Stephanum deflerunt, Actor.VIII.2. Est enim tempus flendi , & tempus ridendi, Eccles.III.4. Et Apostolus flere cum flentibus, Rom.XII.15. jussit. Absit modò à planctu superstitio & excessus durabilis , qui infidelitatem arguere potest, quasi spes melioris vitæ nec plangenti, nec ei, qui plangitur, superfit. Nolo vos ignorare, fratres, de defunctis ,ne tristemini, ut reliqui, qui spem non habent. Si enim credimus quòd Jesus mortuus fit & resurrexerit , sic etiam Deus, qui obdormiverunt per Jesum Christum, ducet cum ipso, 1.Thess.IV.13.14. Soli enim Christiani habent spem ,seu certam expectationem Rom.VIII.25. boni in vita & morte. Nam Domino vivimus,& Domino morimur, ibid.XIV.8. In Gentilibus & Pontificiis non spes , sed opinio fuit & est. Mortem ipsam corporis, quoad partes interiores , vitæ vegetabili & animali ministrantes, mox Solomon similitudine corruptionis instrumentorum, quibus in re familiari victus parari solet ; & quibus confractis apparatus cibi & potus interturbatur, sapienter adumbrat. Instrumenta ejusmodi sunt funis argenteus , nervorum ,lenticula aurea ,cerebri, hydria hepatis, & rota ad puteum, cordis similitudinem habens. Sicut enim illis fractis vel quassatis cibus & potus parari desinit : ita his conturbatis vita corporis cessat. Laxatur, inquit, חבל הכסף funis argentens ,nervi, qui ab uno principio orti, tanquam funis unius infinita capita, totum corpus permeant,per quos & motus, & sensus omnis perficitur: quorum etiam color argenti formam refert: quassatur הזהב גלת lenticula aurea ,cerebrum, quod & formam lenticulæ in pressa rotunditate, & usum , quia ex cerebro spiritus animales in corpus, sicut ex lenticula oleum, defluunt, & colorem auri à membrana exteriori habet: confringitur כד על המבוע hydria ad fontem salientem, hepar, ex quo in ventre inferiore, velut fonte Procurandæ ἀφοβίας remedia. fonte saliente, post primam concoctionem chylus per venas mesaraicas ascendit & descendit: denique conquassatur הגלגל אל הבור rota ad puteum, totius corporis rotæ similitudinem habens, & in eodem συσπλη̃ καὶ ἁλλαχ̃η, quia sicut rota quassata circumagi desinit: ita corde conquassato spirituum motio, agitatio & circulatio unà cum sanguine omnis desinit; atque ita mors sequitur. v.6.
units.tr: VIII. Solomon, in Ecclesiastes 12:5–7, explains how death itself proceeds. For he first says: man goes to his eternal home [אל בית עולמו], that is, to his age-long dwelling. Then the mourners go about in the marketplace. (v. 5) He goes to his eternal home, as it were forever. For by the order of nature he never returns to this life; and death is the way to an eternal dwelling, whether of blessedness or of sorrow and grief. Therefore, while he is on the way, he ought to remember his Creator, for he will not be permitted, as in the racecourse, to turn the post [κάμψαι τὸν νῦτλον] and run back again from the starting gates to the goal. When a man has arrived there, the mourners go about in the marketplace, because those who survive seal all former joy with grief. But he who has lived rightly, and has considered the present life to be a valley of miseries, such as it is, and who has finally remembered his Creator in time, does not grieve in his death, nor is he to be mourned and lamented by others, as if he had been lost, or had lost some good, and had come into an evil condition. For the loss of the dead, especially of one beloved, from whose love and virtues much good has flowed to the living, is not to be despised, but indeed is to be lamented. For Abraham mourned Sarah bitterly (Gen. 23:2), and Jacob Joseph (Gen. 37:34), and the Israelites Moses (Deut. 34:8); and Christ himself wept over Lazarus, his friend (John 11:35), and pious men mourned Stephen (Acts 8:2). For there is a time to weep, and a time to laugh (Eccles. 3:4). And the Apostle bade us weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:15). Only let superstition and lasting excess be absent from lamentation, for these can betray unbelief, as if the hope of a better life survived neither in the one who mourns nor in the one who is mourned. I would not have you ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep, that you grieve not, as the rest do who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus Christ (1 Thess. 4:13–14). For only Christians have hope, that is, a sure expectation (Rom. 8:25), good in life and in death. For we live to the Lord, and we die to the Lord (Rom. 14:8). Among the Gentiles and the Papists there was and is not hope, but opinion. Solomon wisely shadows forth, by the likeness of the ruin of instruments by which food is commonly prepared in a household, the death of the body in its inner parts, which serve vegetable and animal life; when these instruments are broken, the preparation of food and drink is disturbed. Such instruments are the silver cord, the golden bowl, the pitcher at the fountain, and the wheel at the well, which has the likeness of the heart. For as, when these are broken or shattered, the preparation of food and drink ceases, so, when these are disturbed, the life of the body ceases. The silver cord is loosed, he says, חבל הכסף, the silver cord, that is, the nerves, which, arising from one source, like the many ends of a single cord, pervade the whole body, through which all motion and all sensation are carried on; their colour also resembles silver. The golden bowl is broken [הזהב גלת], the golden bowl, that is, the brain, which has the form of a bowl in its pressed roundness and the use of one, because the animal spirits flow from the brain into the body, as oil from a bowl, and it has its golden colour from its outer membrane. The pitcher is shattered at the fountain [כד על המבוע], that is, the liver, from which, in the lower belly, as from a springing fountain, the chyle, after the first digestion, rises and descends through the mesaraic veins. Finally, the wheel is shattered at the well [הגלגל אל הבור], that is, the wheel of the whole body, which has the likeness of a wheel, and is intertwined and interchanged in the same way [συσπλη̃ καὶ ἁλλαχ̃η]; for as a shattered wheel ceases to turn, so when the heart is shattered the motion, agitation and circulation of the spirits together with the blood all cease, and thus death follows. (v. 6)

units.la: IX. Post mortem alius corporis, alius animæ, separati utriusque, status est. Nam uti idem mox Solomon loquitur, redit pulvis ad terram, sicut fuit, & spiritus redit ad Deum, qui dedit eum, Eccles. XII. 7. Corpus pulvis dicitur, tum quia ex pulvere est, tum quia discedente anima, quæ glutinis instar, pulverem continuit, nihil amplius quàm pulvis est. Licèt enim partes formis similaribus paulisper retentis cohærere & compactæ adhuc esse videantur, tamen vinculo, quo continebantur, destitutæ, non tam corpus unum, quàm pulvis lutulentus sunt, ex quo paulatim humiditate exeunte partes solvuntur; sed in nihilum tamen non rediguntur. Aliud enim est in pulverem reverti, aliud in nihilum redigi. Pulvis quippe non nihil est; & quod in illum revertitur, non esse desinit, sed corrumpitur, amissa priore forma. Diserte enim etiam corpori hominis φθορὰ corruptio tribuitur. Non permittes sanctum tuum videre שחת corruptionem, Psalm. XVI. 10. Seminatur ἐν φθορᾷ in corruptione, 1. Cor. XV. 42. Corpora enim nostra in morte seminantur. Seminatur in ignominia, & resuscitatur in gloria, ib. v. 43. Sicut igitur semen in terra corrumpitur, non annihilatur; imò suo tempore iterum progerminat: ita corpori hominis id ipsum accidit. Ossa nostra graminis instar revirescent, Esai. XXVI. 19. ideo mors cum dormitione, quiete, somno passim comparatur. In somno autem corpus quievit, non annihilatur. Et in morte est ἀνάλυσις dissolutio, Phil. I. 23. 2. Tim. IV. 6. Καταλύσεως τ̃ς ἐπιγείου ἡμῶν οἰκίας ἢ σκηνῆς dissolutio terrestris nostræ domus tabernaculi, 2. Cor. V. 1. Καταθέσεως ἢ σκηνώματος depositio tabernaculi, 2. Pet. I. 14. Deus enim piorum ossa omnia custodit, ne ullum eorum pereat, Psal. XXXIV. 21. Cumque resurrectio corporis sit ἡ παλιγγενεσία ejus quod cecidit, & resuscitatio non sit creatio novi corporis, sed ejusdem corporis, quod per mortem cecidit, consequens est, manere corpus, sed in dissolutis partibus. Neque obstat, quòd mortui non esse, Psal. XXXIX. 14. Jerem. XXXI. 15. XLIX. 10. Matth. II. 18. dicuntur: quia non sunt ratione totius compositi, & in hac vita; non ratione partium componentium, quæ singulæ suo loco ad futuram redintegrationem servantur. Quomodo & Enoch איננו non fuit, in hac vita, quia eum Deus לקח accepit ad se in Cœlum, Genes. V. 24. Hebr. XI. 5. Cujus tamen corpus in nihilum redactum non est. Nec quia resurrectio generationi assimilatur, & παλιγγενεσία regeneratio, Matth. XIX. 28. appellatur, iccirco annihilationem supponit. Generationi enim corruptio, non annihilatio opponitur. Denique Deus ventrem destruit, 1. Cor. VI. 13. non ratione substantiæ, sed usus, quo τὰ βρώματα sunt τῇ κοιλίᾳ cibi ventri, & venter cibus recipiendis, digerendis, concoquendis, & in
units.tr: IX. After death there is one state for the body and another for the soul, each being separated from the other. For, as Solomon himself says soon after: the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it (Eccles. 12:7). The body is called dust, both because it is made of dust and because, when the soul departs, which like glue held the dust together, it is nothing more than dust. For although the parts, while the similar forms are still somewhat retained, seem to cohere and to be still compacted, yet, deprived of the bond by which they were held together, they are rather a muddy dust than one body; from which, as the moisture gradually departs, the parts are dissolved, yet they are not reduced to nothing. For it is one thing to return to dust, and another to be reduced to nothing. Dust is certainly something; and what returns to dust does not cease to exist, but is corrupted, its former form being lost. For even the body of man is expressly called corruption [φθορὰ]: You will not allow your holy one to see corruption [שחת] (Ps. 16:10). It is sown in corruption [ἐν φθορᾷ] (1 Cor. 15:42). For our bodies are sown in death. It is sown in dishonour, and raised in glory (ibid. v. 43). Just as seed sown in the earth is corrupted, not annihilated, but indeed in its season sprouts again, so the same thing happens to the body of man. Our bones will flourish again like grass (Isa. 26:19). Therefore death is everywhere compared to sleep, rest and slumber. But in sleep the body rests; it is not annihilated. And in death there is dissolution [ἀνάλυσις] (Phil. 1:23; 2 Tim. 4:6); the dissolution of our earthly house, the tabernacle [Καταλύσεως τ̃ς ἐπιγείου ἡμῶν οἰκίας ἢ σκηνῆς] (2 Cor. 5:1); the putting off of the tabernacle [Καταθέσεως ἢ σκηνώματος] (2 Pet. 1:14). For God keeps all the bones of the righteous, so that not one of them is broken (Ps. 34:20). And since the resurrection of the body is its regeneration [παλιγγενεσία] of what has fallen, and the raising up is not the creation of a new body but of the same body which has fallen through death, it follows that the body remains, though its parts are dissolved. Nor does it stand in the way that the dead are said not to be (Ps. 39:14; Jer. 31:15; 49:10; Matt. 2:18); for they are not as a whole composite, and in this life; but not as to the component parts, each of which is preserved in its place for the future restoration. So also Enoch was not [איננו], in this life, because God took him [לקח] to himself into heaven (Gen. 5:24; Heb. 11:5). Yet his body was not reduced to nothing. Nor, because the resurrection is compared to generation, and is called regeneration [παλιγγενεσία] (Matt. 19:28), does it therefore imply annihilation. For corruption, not annihilation, is opposed to generation. Finally, God destroys the belly (1 Cor. 6:13), not as to substance, but as to use, by which foods are for the belly and the belly for foods, to be received, digested, and concocted, and converted into the juice and blood of the substance; which use does not obtain in the other life, where the spirit that dwells in the bodies will rule and preserve them, and into

units.la: substantiæ succum & sanguinem convertendis, qui usus in altera vita, ubi corpora spiritus inhabitans reget & conservabit, non obtinet.
units.tr: The substance is converted into juice and blood. This use does not apply in the other life, where the spirit dwelling in the bodies will govern and preserve them.

units.la: X. Corpus defunctorum hominum ab iis, qui potestatem habent, honestè deduci, loco idoneo, decentibusque cum ritibus humi recondi, ad maturandam ejus corruptionem, & testandam ipsem resurrectionis ejus futuræ, debet. Nam quod in hac vita templum Spiritus S. fuit, vel esse debuit, post hanc vitam ludibrio exponi, vel ab animalibus brutis indignis modis dilaniari non debet. Et voluit Deus pulverem in terram reverti כשהיה sicut erat pulvis Eccles. XII. 7. Quòd si cadavera inhumata relinquerentur, bestiis potiùs in alimentum cederent, quàm in pulverem redigerentur. Ideo Deus edixit: Terra es, & in terram reverteris, Genes. III. 19. Quæ verba mandatum sepeliendi implicant, quia cadaver, nisi procurantibus hominibus vivis non semper sine mora in pulverem reverteretur. Et terram μητέρα πάντων matrem omnium Siracides cap. X L. 1. dixit, quia mortuos suo sinu excipit, & pulverem atque ossa nostra complexu suo ad diem usque resurrectionis custodit. Homines enim δισφθεῖς bis sepultos rectè Nanzianzenus dixit, quia homo primùm in utero matris velut sepultus & tectus jacet, donec nascitur; ac demum in alveum terræ receptus delitescit, donec iterum ad vitæ æternitatem nascatur. Hinc adeò antiquissimus & perpetuus usus, ut defunctorum corpora terræ mandentur: ab ipso etiam Deo, jubente servum suum Mosen sepeliri, Deut. XXXIV. 6. confirmatus, obtinuit. Accedit efficacissima ratio, necessitas corruptionis corporis, ut renovetur totum & vivificetur atque resurgat. Demens, quod tu seminas, non vivificatur, nisi moriatur, terræ mandatum, & in ea velut sepultum, 1. Cor. XV. 36. Granum aliquod à fructu, à culmo tollitur; diu post jacet in horreo arens, & vitæ omnis expers. Non enim ibi germinat. Ut verò regeneret, in terram conjicitur, & ibi computrescit, atque sic denique reviviscit. Spiritus enim, quem Deus in semine conservat, à Deo, cùm materia illa diffluxerit, & in saniem conversa fuerit, corpus accipit, quale Deus vult, ex eadem illa materia, quam Deus suppeditatione humoris auget. Sic planè idem corpus, quod ex semine patris in utero matris formatum est, quódque in hac vita in perpetuo fluxu conservatum est, ut idem quodam modo semper manserit, in terram cadere, ibi diffluere & putrefieri, ac demum spiritui suo restitui renovatum debet. Atque præscribunt etiam rationes hæ opinioni Abulensis aliorúmque, quibus videtur, cadaverum etiam combustionem Deo placuisse. Jabesitæ enim Saulis & filiorum ejus corpora ישרפו combusserunt, 1. Sam. XXXI. 12. quia circa corpora eorum aromata combusserunt, quomodo Joramo, Asæ, Zedekiæ, Israelitarum Regibus שרפה combustio facta, 2. Paral. XVI. 14. XXI. 19. Jerem. XXXIV. 5. non ipsi combusti dicuntur. Et de hoc quicquid sit, Jabesitarum, hominum anomalorum factum Divinitus approbatum non legitur, & singularem forte, si omnino cadavera combusserunt, causam habuit, ne corpora ea in manus hostium incidearent. rent. Plus momenti esse videtur in loco, Amos VI. 10. Et tollet quemque eorum patruus ejus, מִסְרְפוֹ & comburet eum; Sic Vulgatus, sed praeter mentem Scriptoris sacri, apud quem מְסְרְפוֹ cremator ejus notat ἐνταφιαστὴν, crematorem non cadaveris, sed thymiamatum inter sepeliendum accensorum.
units.tr: X. The bodies of dead people should be honourably carried out by those who have the power to do so, placed in a suitable place, and buried in the ground with decent rites. This is to hasten their decay and to bear witness to their future resurrection. For the body that was, or ought to have been, the temple of the Holy Spirit in this life must not be exposed to mockery after this life, nor torn apart in shameful ways by brute beasts. God willed that dust return to the earth as it was [כשהיה], "as it was dust" (Eccles. 12:7). If unburied corpses were left, they would become food for beasts rather than being reduced to dust. So God decreed: "You are earth, and to earth you shall return" (Gen. 3:19). These words contain the command to bury, since a corpse would not always turn to dust without delay unless living men attended to it. Siracides (Ecclus. 40:1) called the earth "mother of all" [μητέρα πάντων], because it receives the dead into its bosom and keeps our dust and bones in its embrace until the day of resurrection. Gregory Nazianzen rightly called men "twice buried" [δισφθεῖς], because a man lies first as if buried and covered in his mother's womb until he is born, and then, once received into the hollow of the earth, lies hidden until he is born again to the eternity of life. Hence the very ancient and constant custom that the bodies of the dead be committed to the earth, confirmed even by God himself, who ordered that "his servant Moses be buried" (Deut. 34:6). There is also a most effective reason: the body must decay so that the whole may be renewed, revived and raised. "Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it dies" (1 Cor. 15:36). Committed to the earth and as it were buried in it, a grain is taken from the fruit and the stalk; it lies for a long time dry in the barn, lacking all life, for it does not sprout there. But to be regenerated it is cast into the earth, rots there, and at last comes to life again. For the spirit, which God preserves in the seed, receives from God, once that matter has dissolved and turned to rottenness, a body such as God wills, out of the same matter, which God increases by supplying moisture. So clearly the same body, which was formed from the father's seed in the mother's womb and which in this life has been kept in constant flux, so that in some sense it has always remained the same, ought to fall into the earth, dissolve and putrefy there, and at last be restored renewed to its spirit. These reasons also seem to rule out the opinion of Abulensis and others, who think that God was pleased with the burning of corpses. The men of Jabesh burned the bodies of Saul and his sons (1 Sam. 31:12), but they are not said to have been burned themselves, as the Israelite kings Joram, Asa and Zedekiah were given a "burning" [שרפה] (2 Chron. 16:14; 21:19; Jer. 34:5). Whatever the truth about this, the deed of the men of Jabesh, who were unusual men, is not recorded as having been approved by God. If they did burn the corpses at all, they perhaps had a special reason, namely to keep the bodies from falling into the hands of the enemy. More weight seems to lie in the passage of Amos 6:10: "And his uncle shall take up each of them and burn him" [וּמְסַרְפוֹ]. So the Vulgate renders it, but against the mind of the sacred writer, for among whom מְסְרְפוֹ [mesarpo] denotes "embalmer" [ἐνταφιαστὴν], one who burns spices during burial, not one who burns the corpse.

units.la: XI. Contra institutionem Divinam graviter Pontificii errant, qui non tantum ossa sepultorum e terra effodiunt, & in ossariis, seu aediculis repositá omnium conspectui exponunt; sed etiam Sanctorum, quos Papa tales esse jussit, reliquias & ossa extra alveum terrae recondunt, subinde depromunt, circumferunt, & religiose veneranda ostentant. Nam ossa mortuorum aequè ac carnes ex definito Dei judicio terrae debentur, ut ibi in pulverem redigantur. Nam quòd conspectis ossibus mortalitatis memoriam nobis refricari ajunt, frivolum est; quia pietatis subsidia contra Divinam institutionem deligenda non sunt; & verbi Dei lectione, auditu, quotidianis funerum exemplis efficacius ad mortalitatis nostrae recordationem praesidium est. Quoad reliquias autem Sanctorum tantò perniciosior error est, quantò magis cum idololatria conjunctus est. Medina enim in 3. p. Thomae p.25. art.6. ait: Certum esse de fide, Sanctorum reliquias esse adorandas, de modo autem adorandi non adeo certam & infallibilem fidei definitionem esse. Nempe alii s absolutam, aliis relativam adorationem definientibus. Sed obsecundandum potius fuerat mandato Dei, Genes.III.19. ex quo sancti Patriarchae collegerunt, corpora & ossa Sanctorum humi condenda, non foras proferenda & adoranda esse. Quis Abrahamo, Sara, Isaco, Jacobo, Mose, &c. sanctior fuit? Et tamen illorum corpora terrae mandata sunt. In N. T. Johannes Baptista & Stephanus sepulti sunt. Neque eorum ossa ex terris eruta uspiam legere est. Quin Josias Rex severè prohibuit, ne quisquam ossa sacra viri Dei de ipso prophetantis commoveret, 2.Reg.XXIII.18. Cultus porrò reliquiarum operosus & multiplex satis in verbo Dei, quo solum Deum adorare, & honorem ejus non alienare jubemur, damnatus est: & originem debet gentilium superstitioni, qua factum est, ut praestantiorum virorum ossa ex ignobilioribus in nobiliora loca magna pompa transferrentur, & comiter colerentur; & nascentis crescentisque trium inprimis seculorum Ecclesiae praxi penitus destituitur. Mera ergo haec idololatria est, non quidem talis, qua quis imitetur adulteram desertò marito suo alii adhaerentem, sed adulteram clanculum sui copiam facientem, aut saltem subagitari se ab alio patientem, eíque colludentem.
