units.tr: XI. The Papists gravely err against the divine institution. They not only dig up the bones of the buried from the earth and set them out for all to see in ossuaries or chapels, but also take out the relics and bones of saints, whom the Pope has commanded to be such, from the bosom of the earth, bring them out from time to time, carry them about and display them as things to be venerated with religious devotion. For the bones of the dead, like their flesh, are owed to the earth by God's definite judgment, so that they may be reduced to dust there. As for their claim that the sight of bones refreshes in us the memory of mortality, this is frivolous: aids to piety must not be chosen against the divine institution, and the reading and hearing of the Word of God and the daily examples of funerals are a more effective safeguard for remembering our mortality. As to the relics of saints, the error is all the more pernicious in proportion as it is joined with idolatry. For Medina, in his commentary on the third part of Thomas, question 25, article 6, says: "It is certain from faith that the relics of saints are to be adored, but the mode of adoring is not defined by any very certain and infallible definition of faith." Some define the adoration as absolute, others as relative. But it would have been better to obey the command of God (Gen. 3:19), from which the holy patriarchs gathered that the bodies and bones of saints are to be buried in the ground, not brought out and adored. Who was holier than Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and so on? Yet their bodies were committed to the earth. In the New Testament, John the Baptist and Stephen were buried, and nowhere do we read that their bones were dug out of the earth. Indeed, King Josiah strictly forbade anyone to move the bones of the man of God who prophesied concerning him (2 Kings 23:18). Moreover, the elaborate and manifold cult of relics is condemned in the Word of God, by which we are commanded to adore God alone and not to give his honour to another. It owes its origin to the superstition of the Gentiles, by which the bones of more eminent men were transferred with great pomp from humbler to more noble places and cherished with affection. It is entirely lacking in the practice of the Church in its birth and growth, especially in the first three centuries. This is therefore sheer idolatry, not indeed of the kind in which one imitates the adulterous wife who, having deserted her husband, clings to another, but of the kind in which she secretly gives him access to herself, or at least submits to being driven by another and colludes with him.

units.la: { } Sepeliendi omnes homines videntur.
units.tr: { } All men seem to be buried.

units.la: XII. Sepelienda esse corpora omnium, qui vitam innocuam transegere, in confesso est. Αυτοχειρες vero jam olim honore sepulturae caruisse, etiam apud Hebraeos, Josephus de Bell. Jud. lib. III.25. testis est. Sed latum eorum discrimen est; & qui plane voluntarii sunt, sepeliendi tamen, sed sine honore, videntur; quia in eos, qui mortem pro supplicio non habent, aliud supplicium constitui non potest. Infigniter facinorosos, sacrilegos, parricidas, latrones, fures, leges quaedam civiles jure sepulturae privant. At in Lege Hebraea suspensi ex ligno ante solem occidentem sepeliri debuerunt, Deut.XXI.22.23. Quae lex ita ceremonialis fuit, ut morale quid conjunctum habuerit. Sepultura enim humano generi deltinata est, tam in resurrectionis pignus & symbolum, quàm ut vivorum oculis parcatur, ne rei tam foedae aspectu se contaminent, ad feritatem assuefiant, & ad homicidia inescentur. Saltem laude digna ea politiarum humanitas videtur, quae in re dubia mitiorem sententiam sequitur. At nec haereticos veros, infideles & extra Ecclesiam natos & denatos sepulturae beneficio defraudandos esse judicamus, quia id inhumanum est. Alia tamen ratio Christianarum ceremoniarum est, cum quibus aperti Ecclesiae Christianae hostes, haeretici veri, seductores, blasphemi & persecutores funerandi non sunt, quia id sine nominis Divini abusu, & verè fidelium, quibus ita exaequarentur, manifesta injuria fieri non posset. Sed Papae immanis illa ἀπαντρωπία est, qua eos, qui haeretici non sunt, insepultos abjici, imò jam sepultos ex matris suae gremio exscicari jubet. Non tantum enim viva Christi membra, sed mortuos etiam occidere, atque talibus sacrificiis iis, quos pro idolis erexit, litare, crudelissimus omnium mortalium, audet; operam ei navantibus cornibus Bestiae, uti in parricidali Gallia factum nuper omnis posteritas stupebit. Denique & infantes ἀδαπτισ̀ιδ idem Pontificii sine usitatis ceremoniis, & extra locum communem sepelientes, bellui-nam indolem produnt. Quid enim talibus innocentius esse potest, qui sine culpa sua carentes Baptismo, participes licet foederis gratiae, & promissionum Semini Abrahae & fidelibus parentibus factarum a noverca illa Ecclesia turpiter adeo resurrecturi olim contra eos in judicio, negliguntur.
units.tr: XII. It is agreed that the bodies of all who have lived an innocent life are to be buried. That those who killed themselves [αὐτόχειρες] were already in ancient times denied the honour of burial, even among the Hebrews, is attested by Josephus (Jewish War 3.25). But their case varies widely. Those who are plainly voluntary deaths seem nonetheless to be buried, though without honour, since no other punishment can be imposed on those who do not regard death as a punishment. Certain civil laws deprive notorious criminals, sacrilegious persons, parricides, robbers and thieves of the right of burial. But under the Hebrew law, those hanged on a tree had to be buried before the sun went down (Deut. 21:22-23). This law was so ceremonial that it also had something moral joined to it. For burial was destined for the human race, both as a pledge and symbol of resurrection and so that the eyes of the living might be spared, lest they defile themselves by the sight of so foul a thing, grow accustomed to savagery, and be drawn into murders. At least that humanity of civil governments seems worthy of praise which, in a doubtful matter, follows the milder opinion. Yet we judge that true heretics, unbelievers, and those born and dying outside the Church should not be defrauded of the benefit of burial, because that would be inhumane. There is, however, another rule concerning Christian ceremonies: with these, the open enemies of the Christian Church, true heretics, seducers, blasphemers and persecutors are not to be buried, because this could not be done without abusing the divine name and without manifest injury to the true faithful, to whom they would thus be made equal. But that savage inhumanity of the Pope is of a different kind, by which he commands those who are not heretics to be cast out unburied, and even to be dragged out of their mother's bosom once buried. For the most cruel of all mortals dares not only to slay the living members of Christ but also to slaughter the dead and to sacrifice to those whom he has set up as idols with such offerings, the horns of the Beast serving him in this, as all posterity will marvel at the parricidal France recently. Finally, the Papists, burying infants [ἀβαπτίστους] who are unbaptized, without the customary ceremonies and outside the common burial ground, betray a beast-like nature. For what can be more innocent than such infants, who, lacking Baptism through no fault of their own, although they are partakers of the covenant of grace and of the promises made to the Seed of Abraham and to faithful parents, are neglected by that shameful stepmother, the Church, though they will one day rise again to be judged?

units.la: XIII. Sepulturae Locus in verbo Dei definitus non est. Constat tamen in populo Dei sepulchra omnia extra urbes fuisse. Elati enim mortui ex urbibus, vel collocati in agro dicuntur, quorumcunque sepultura in sacris memoratur, si discesseris tum à Regibus, qui in Civitate Davidis sepeliebantur, in loco tamen extra viventium consortium delecto, puta in hortis, &, quae in iis erant, cryptis & speluncis: tum à Samuele & Joabo, qui singularem ob causam sepeliebantur בביתו domi suae, hoc est, in horto ad domum pertinente, 1.Sam.XXV.1. 1.Reg.II.34. Antiquissimi tamen apud gentiles instituti fuisse, ut intra urbem & domi quoque defunctorum cadavera condererent; atque inde etiam processisse larium & penatum religionem, qui ea de causa domi colerentur, Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus de vario sepeliendi ritu, p.644. notavit; subjiciens mox, eam consuetudinem, ut foedam ac tetram, antiquatam esse; gravem hanc querelam, Pontificius licet, subtexens: Nunc Christiani nostri (Pontificii) (proh majorum nostrorum sancta instituta deperdita!) non intra urbem modò defunctorum corpora condunt, verum etiam, si Deo placeat, in templis, ipsisque delubris & sacellis, in quibus Divorum cineres & reliquias tantùm servare & venerari; majorum nostrorum religio fuit, nefariorum & sceleistissimorum hominum cadavera foedissima condunt, dunt, quod fieri præter majorum leges & instituta, vehementissime doleo. Etiam Stephanus Durantius, lib.I.23. fatetur, eam fuisse veterum patrum religionem, ne intra Ecclesiam corpora defunctorum sepelirentur. Sed eò processum est, ut non tantùm intra urbes, sed intra ipsas etiam Basilicas mortui sepelirentur. Olim enim id Imperatoribus & magnatibus; mox etiam Ecclesiasticis, honoris gratia; demum aliis authoritate præditis; denique omnibus pretio sepulturam talem redimentibus concessum est; nequicquam Conciliis, Triburiensi & Nannetensi, reclamantibus. Gregorius tamen, quisquis ille Dialogorum author est, Dial. lib.IV.10. docuit, hoc prodesse mortuis, quos gravia peccata non deprimunt, si in Ecclesia sepeliantur, quòd eorum proximi, quoties ad eadem sacra loca veniunt, suorum, quorum sepulchra aspiciunt, recordantur, & pro eis Domino preces fundunt. Hoc semel admisso, & crescente indies superstitione, nemo non privilegium hoc ambivit. Unde aucupia testamentorum & donariorum, ac locorum in templis licitationes, pro ratione graduum, & vicinitatis altaris majoris, vel minoris, in immensum creverunt. Omitto superstitionem & δια-χρονεψδίαν, imò & περισωπολη-ψίαν, qua inter nostros etiam divitibus, commune cum pauperibus sepulchrum habere dedignantibus connivetur; alia etiam sunt, quæ intra templa inprimis mortuos sepeliri vetant. Domus enim orationis, Jerem. VII. 11. Marc.XI.17. non communia sepulchra, neque loca דומה silentii, qualia defunctis debentur, Psal.CXV.17. sunt. Et malè etiam sic vivis superstitibus consulitur, quia cùm vivi mortuos sepelire debeant, hic mortui vivos sepeliunt; hoc est, tetro cadaverum odore, non minùs quàm pestilenti aëre eos inficiunt. Denique & consecrationes cœmeteriorum verbi Divini authoritate destituuntur, & superstitione laborant. Nam quòd dæmones sic fugari obtendunt, præterquam quòd is merus lusus est, experientiæ etiam id refragatur; qua teste, nuspiam plures energumeni & dæmoniaci, quàm in ejusmodi locis apparent. Et inefficax hæc consecratio est, quia impii ubicunque sunt, sub dæmonis potestate sunt: piorum verò animæ in Cœlo sunt, & ossa à Deo custodiuntur, neque unquam dæmon efficiet, ut ad resurrectionem inhabilia evadant. Terra ejúsque plenitudo Domini est; neque sanctitatis discrimen ullum recipit.
units.tr: XIII. The place of burial is not defined in the Word of God. Yet it is clear that among the people of God all tombs lay outside the cities. For the dead who were carried out of cities, or laid in the fields, are mentioned in Scripture whenever burials are recorded. The kings who were buried in the City of David were laid in a place set apart outside the company of the living, namely in gardens, and in the vaults and caves within them. Samuel and Joab were buried in a special way, "in his house" [בביתו], that is, in a garden belonging to the house (1 Sam. 25:1; 1 Kings 2:34). Yet Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus, in his work on the varied manner of burial (p. 644), has observed that among the Gentiles the most ancient custom was to bury the dead inside the city and even in the home. From this practice, he says, the worship of the household gods (lares and penates), who were honoured at home for this reason, also arose. He immediately adds that this custom, as foul and loathsome, has been abandoned. Although he is a Papist, he expresses this grave complaint: "Our Christians now (alas, the holy institutions of our ancestors are lost!) do not merely bury the bodies of the dead within the city. If it pleases God, they bury the most foul corpses of wicked and most abominable men in the temples themselves, and in the shrines and chapels, where it was the religion of our ancestors to keep and venerate only the ashes and relics of the saints. I grieve most vehemently that this is done contrary to the laws and institutions of our ancestors." Stephanus Durantius also confesses (bk. 1, ch. 23) that "it was the religion of the ancient Fathers that the bodies of the dead should not be buried within the Church." But matters went so far that the dead were buried not only within the cities but within the very basilicas. At first this was granted to emperors and great men, then also to churchmen as a mark of honour, later to others who held some authority, and finally to all who would purchase such a burial. The councils of Trosly and Nantes protested in vain. Gregory, whoever the author of the Dialogues may be (Dial. bk. 4, ch. 10), taught that this benefits the dead, even those not weighed down by grave sins, if they are buried in the Church, because their kinsfolk, whenever they come to these holy places, remember those whose graves they see and pour out prayers to the Lord on their behalf. Once this was admitted, and superstition grew daily, nobody failed to covet this privilege. Hence the hunting after wills and gifts, and the auctions for places in the temples, graded according to rank and according to proximity to the greater or lesser altar, grew beyond measure. I pass over the superstition and the lasting vanity [διαχρονεψδίαν], and indeed the respect of persons [περισωπολημψίαν], by which among our own people too the rich are indulged, who scorn to share a tomb with the poor. There are other reasons, too, which above all forbid the burial of the dead within churches. For a house of prayer (Jer. 7:11; Mark 11:17) is not a common burial ground, nor is it a place of "silence" [דומה] such as is due to the dead (Ps. 115:17). Moreover, it is also a bad way of caring for the living who remain, because while the living ought to bury the dead, here the dead bury the living. That is, by the foul smell of corpses they infect them no less than with a pestilent air. Finally, the consecrations of cemeteries lack the authority of the divine Word and are tainted with superstition. For the claim that demons are thus driven away is, apart from being pure play, also contradicted by experience, which shows that nowhere do more energumens and demoniacs appear than in such places. This consecration is also ineffective, because the wicked, wherever they are, are under the power of the devil, while the souls of the godly are in heaven, and their bones are kept by God. The demon will never make them unfit for the resurrection. "The earth and its fullness are the Lord's" (Ps. 24:1), and it admits of no distinction of holiness.

units.la: XIV. Sepulturæ Ritus
units.tr: XIV. The Rites of Burial

units.la: ejusmodi seligendi sunt, qui verbo Dei, pietati, humanitati, simplicitati & ordini atque decoro Ecclesiæ maximè consentanei sunt. Quæ generalis cautio si obtinuerit, speciales ritus in Ecclesiis variare possunt. Hebræi veteres lotione & conditura cadaverum, vestitu corporum conditorum, funeris aperta deductione, præficis, quæ Jer. IX. 17.20. Amos V.16. מספדים lamentantes dicuntur, quandoque comitantibus, illatione in sepulchrum, laudatione & convivio funebri, denique epitaphiis, seu honoris perpetui monumenti erectione uti sueverunt. Sed diversi variantésque Christianorum veterum ritus fuerunt. Notiores præparatio corporum, conditura & unctio, vestitus, deductio funeris, preces, orationes funebres, sparsio florum, eleemosynæ fuerunt. Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ ritus Bellarminus de Purg. lib.II.19. recensetcorporum lotionem, comitatum ad sepulchrum, sepulturam in templis & locis sacris, aquæ lustralis usum, hymnorum cantum, lampadum & cereorum accensorum usum, sacrificii altaris pro iis oblationem, orationes pro defuncto, tituli & crucis erectionem, & eleemosynas. In quibus πολλα κολλα, πολλαπε λυγεσι sunt. Nam sacrificii altaris oblatio, preces pro defuncto, sepultura in Basilica vel proximè illam religionis causa instituta, superstitioni deputandæ sunt, & turpi quæstui velificantur. Lampadum & cereorum usus olim etiam receptus mysterium mortui in lucem & locum gloriæ, assumpti complexus, Purgatorii ignem extinguit. Ecclesiæ Evangelicæ ritus consentientes honesta funeris περιπομπη deductio, decora humatio, preces ad Deum eucharisticæ & superstitum ἀφαμυνηπης sunt. In cæteris variant. Epitaphia & monumenta saxis, lapidibus, æneis vel ligneis tabulis inscripta non usque quaque probanda sunt, quia sepulchrorum luxum revocant, & gloriolæ inanis aucupium redolent. Funerum fercula, ferales cœnas, & silicernia jam olim lex Christiana prohibuit. Sermones funebres pium usum habere possunt, quia tum occasione hac mortalitatis, ἀδιναστικ & novissimorum meditatio utiliter instituitur, animis omnium conspicua imagine ob oculos posita ad id præparatis: tum superstitum consolationi sic consulitur: tum auditores ad imitandam fidem & benefacta inflammari possunt. Sed plures etiam rationes eas dissuadent, velut quòd sermonum talium usus nuspiam in Scripturis commemoratur; quòd ex eorum initiis preces pro defunctis fluxerunt: quòd origo eorum gentilibus accepta referri debet: quòd difficile arduúmque est, ad subitos & improvisos casus ita invigilare, ut sermones graves & meditati semper habeantur: quòd res periculosæ plena aleæ est, bene & malè meritos inter discrimen conspicuum statuere: quòd denique experientia, sermones ejusmodi funebres plerunque parasiticos, mercenarios & cum περισωπολη-ψίας semper conjunctos esse testatur. Ubi igitur non obtinent, temerè induci non debent: ubi obtinent, inprimis ubi diversæ religiones exercentur, ceu res ἀδιαφορα per se, abolitis abusibus, ferri possunt, donec sine scandalo abrogare eosdem licet.
units.tr: Such rites are to be chosen as are most in harmony with the Word of God, with piety, humanity, simplicity, and with the order and decorum of the Church. If this general caution prevails, the particular rites may vary among the churches. The ancient Hebrews used to wash and embalm the bodies, clothe the dead, conduct the funeral openly, employ the hired mourning women who are called "lamenters" [מספדים] (Jer. 9:17, 20; Amos 5:16), sometimes accompany the body, lay it in the tomb, deliver a eulogy and hold a funeral feast, and finally erect epitaphs or a lasting monument of honour. The rites of the ancient Christians were diverse and varied. The best known were the preparation and anointing of the bodies, their clothing, the procession of the funeral, prayers, funeral orations, the scattering of flowers, and alms. Bellarmine (De Purgatorio, bk. 2, ch. 19) lists the rites of the Papist Church: washing of the body, accompanying it to the grave, burial in churches and holy places, the use of lustral water, the singing of hymns, the use of lamps and lit candles, the offering of the sacrifice of the altar on their behalf, prayers for the dead, the erection of a title and a cross, and alms. Among these there is much hodgepodge and much that is of many colours [πολλα κολλα, πολλαπε λυγεσι]. For the offering of the sacrifice of the altar, prayers for the dead, and burial in a basilica or next to one, instituted for the sake of religion, must be reckoned superstition, and they are made to serve base profit. The use of lamps and candles, once received as a symbol that the dead man is brought into light and a place of glory, extinguishes the fire of Purgatory. The rites of the Evangelical Church that agree with Scripture are the honourable solemn procession [περιπομπή] of the funeral, a decent interment, prayers of thanksgiving to God, and remembrance [ἀναμνήσεις] of the living and of the departed. In other matters they vary. Epitaphs and monuments inscribed on stones, marble, or bronze or wooden tablets are not altogether to be approved, because they recall the extravagance of tombs and smell of the hunt for empty glory. Christian law has long since forbidden funeral processions with fancy trappings, funeral banquets, and the silicernia (feasts for the dead). Funeral sermons may serve a godly purpose, because on this occasion the meditation on mortality and the last things is usefully undertaken, with a vivid image set before the eyes of all who are prepared for it; the comfort of the survivors is also thus provided for; and the hearers may be kindled to imitate faith and good works. But there are also many reasons that advise against them: for example, that the practice of such sermons is nowhere recorded in Scripture; that from their beginnings prayers for the dead arose; that their origin must be traced to the Gentiles; that it is difficult and hard to be so watchful for sudden and unforeseen deaths that serious and well-considered sermons are always at hand; that to distinguish between the well and ill deserving in a conspicuous way is a dangerous game full of risk; and finally that experience testifies that funeral sermons of this kind are mostly flattering, mercenary, and always joined with respect of persons. Where they are not in use, they ought not to be introduced rashly. Where they are in use, especially where different religions are practised, they may be tolerated as things indifferent in themselves, with the abuses abolished, until it is possible to abrogate them without scandal.

units.la: XV. Fuit status corporis defuncti.
units.tr: XV. The state of the deceased.

units.la: De spiritu separato sic Solomon pergit: Spiritus, anima rationalis, redit ad Deum, qui dedit eum, Eccles. XII.7. Non quòd apud Deum fuerit, ante quàm in corpore extitit, quia aliàs similiter, ut de pulvere, dixisset, כשהיה sicut fuit; sed quia à Deo data est in corpus, & ipsius manu in illo posita, ut ordine non temporis, sed naturæ, priùs esset quasi in manu Dei, quàm in corpore. Proin שובה reditus ille ad Deum significat, quòd non ampliùs in corpore, sed in manu Dei sit. Oportet enim recordari Creatoris, quia statim post mortem anima redibit ad Creatorem suum, ut judicem, ut reportet, quæ sive bona, sive malà in corpore fecit. Sed animæ sic à corpore separatæ in gloriam introitus, statūs, & statūs continuatio distinctè considerari debent.
units.tr: Solomon continues concerning the separated spirit: "The spirit, the rational soul, returns to God who gave it" (Eccles. 12.7). This does not mean that it was with God before it existed in the body, for otherwise he would have said of the spirit, as he did of the dust, "as it was" [כשהיה]. Rather, it was given by God into the body and placed in his hand, so that in the order of nature, though not of time, it was in the hand of God before it was in the body. Therefore that "return" [שובה] to God signifies that the spirit is no longer in the body but in the hand of God. For we ought to remember the Creator, since immediately after death the soul will return to its Creator as its judge, to render an account of whatever it has done in the body, whether good or evil. But the souls separated from the body in this way must be considered distinctly as to their entrance into glory, their state, and the continuation of that state.

units.tr: XVI. Quo-

units.la: Ritus funebres Hebræorum, Pontificiorum, Evangelicorum.
units.tr: The funeral rites of the Hebrews, the Papists and the Evangelicals.

units.la: XVI. Quoad animæ post mortem sepa- rationem, supponimus, eam nec cum corpore mori, neque adeò vel annihilari, vel in partes dividi. Nam & spiritualem, & immortalem esse, Loc. VI. §. 50. 51. 52. probavimus. At nec speciem, facultates, vel aliquid essentiæ amittit, quia id morti simile foret. Neque etiam in animam speciei alterius mutatur, quia spiritus rationalis est, & species creaturæ nulla est, quæ spiritum rationalem cum corpore conjunctum habeat; spiritum verò rationalem sine abolitione ejus commutari in substantiam, quæ rationalis non est, oppidò absurdum est. At nec anima individuationem perdit, vel in animam aliquam universalem ingurgitatur, quia nec anima ejusmodi universalis, ex piis & impiis, salvandis & damnandis animabus conflata datur, nec quidquam obstat, quò minus anima separata individuationem suam retineat. Nam quod principium individuationis materiam Aristoteles constituit, Theologia, quæ Deum, Angelos & animas spirituales, & hos numero differentes ex verbo Dei, imò & ratione sana agnoscit, non recipit. At nec anima in corpus terrestre, brutum vel humanum migrat. Quam μετεμψύχωσιν primi docuerunt Ægyptii, post hos Philosophi in Ægypto peregrinati, Pythagoras, Plato, Stoici; inde Pharisæi, Matth. XI. 14. XVII. 12. & Herodes Antipas, ibid. XIV. 2. Marc. VI. 14. ac demum etiam hæretici, Carpocratiani, Marcionitæ, Manichæi, inter se hactenus divisi, quòd alii eas in ejusdem generis corpora tantum; alii verò etiam in diversa, puta pecudum, migrare contendunt; ne de Pontificiis, affinia nonnulla in Legendis suis statuentibus dicam. Nam Deus singulis hominibus, dum generantur, animas suas creat & infundit, Job. XXXIII. 4. Psal. XXXIII. 15. Eccles. XII. 7. Esaj. XLII. 5. LVII. 16. Zach. XII. 1. eæque ad propria corpora determinatæ sunt, quomodo qui fornicatur, εἰς τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα in proprium corpus peccare dicitur, 1. Cor. VI. 18. & quilibet vir ἴδιον σῶμα proprium corpus habet, ibid. VII. 4. Quisque enim in suo corpore recipiet juxta ea, quæ fecit, bona vel mala, 2. Cor. V. 10. Neque etiam hominis pii vel impii anima corpus brutum ingredi potest, quin illud humanum reddat, & brutum ipsum intellectu & voluntate instructum perficiat. Neque contrarium exempla Nebucadnetzaris, Dan. IV. 16–30. nec non hominum in lupos vel vaccas conversorum probant. Nebucadnetzar enim nec mortuus fuit, cùm habitavit cum bestiis, & fœnum comedit; nec omnino in bestiæ substantiam, amissa humana, transiit, sed sensum duntaxat, intelligentiam & actiones humanas, quoad actum secundum, ad tempus amisit, quæ solæ, non humana substantia ipsi restituta est, ibid. v. 31. Et mutatio ejus in eo constitit, quòd extra societatem humanam conjectus, cum feris conversatus, earundem externum habitum quodammodo induit, non humanam substantiam amisit. Et cor bestiæ ipsi datum est, quia quoad actiones externas nullum ipsum inter & bestias discrimen fuit. Exempla verò transmutationum substantialium vel diabolicæ præstigiæ, vel meræ hominum melancholicorum imaginationes, manente eorum forma substantiali, fuerunt, de quo etiam alibi plura diximus.
units.tr: XVI. As to the separation of the soul after death, we assume that it does not die with the body, nor is it annihilated or divided into parts. For we have proved in Locus VI, §§ 50, 51 and 52 that it is both spiritual and immortal. Nor does it lose its species, faculties or any part of its essence, since that would be like death. Nor is it changed into a soul of another species, since the rational spirit is spirit, and there is no creature of a species that has a rational spirit joined to a body; and it is utterly absurd to think that the rational spirit could be changed without being abolished into a substance that is not rational. Nor does the soul lose its individuality or get swallowed up into some universal soul, since no such universal soul made up of the souls of the pious and the impious, the saved and the damned, is given, and nothing prevents the separated soul from retaining its individuality. For Aristotle made matter the principle of individuation, but theology, which recognises from the Word of God, and indeed from sound reason, God, the angels and spiritual souls, which differ in number, does not accept this. Nor does the soul pass into an earthly body, whether brute or human. This transmigration [μετεμψύχωσις] was first taught by the Egyptians, and after them by philosophers who travelled in Egypt, Pythagoras, Plato and the Stoics; from them came the Pharisees (Matt. 11.14; 17.12) and Herod Antipas (ibid. 14.2; Mark 6.14), and finally also the heretics Carpocratians, Marcionites and Manichaeans, who have hitherto been divided among themselves, some contending that souls migrate only into bodies of the same kind, others into different ones, namely of beasts; not to mention that the Papists, in their Legends, set down some similar notions. For God creates and infuses the souls of individual men when they are generated (Job 33.4; Ps. 33.15; Eccles. 12.7; Isa. 42.5; 57.16; Zech. 12.1), and these souls are determined to their own bodies, just as the one who fornicates is said to sin "against his own body" [εἰς τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα] (1 Cor. 6.18), and every man has "his own body" [ἴδιον σῶμα] (ibid. 7.4). For "each one will receive in his own body according to what he has done, good or evil" (2 Cor. 5.10). Nor can the soul of a pious or impious man enter a brute body without making it human and perfecting the brute itself, endowed with intellect and will. Nor do the examples of Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 4.16–30) or of men turned into wolves or cows prove the contrary. For Nebuchadnezzar did not die when he dwelt with the beasts and ate grass; nor did he pass wholly into the substance of a beast, having lost his human nature, but for a time he lost only sense, understanding and human actions, as to the second act, and these were restored to him, not his human substance (ibid. v. 31). His change consisted in this: being cast out of human society, and living among the wild beasts, he took on in some measure their outward appearance, but did not lose his human substance. "And a beast's heart was given to him" because in external actions there was no difference between him and the beasts. The examples of substantial transformations are either the deceptions of the devil or mere imaginings of melancholic men, their substantial form remaining unchanged; of which we have said more elsewhere.

units.la: XVII. Affinis Pontificiorum de migratione animarum in καθαρτήριον Purgatorium ad obliterandum verum καθαρσμὸν ἁμαρτιῶν veram & unicam purificationem peccatorum per Christum inductum, error est.
units.tr: XVII. The Papists' error of the migration of souls into the Purgatory [καθαρτήριον] is akin to that, and is a way of obliterating the true purgation [καθαρσμός] of sins, the true and only purification of sins brought about by Christ.

units.la: Florentinum enim Concilium definivit, si verè pœnitentes in charitate decesserint, antequam dignis pœnitentiæ fructibus de commissis (post Baptismum) peccatis satisfecerint, & omissis, eorum animas pœnis Purgatoriis purgari. Tridentini etiam Sess. XXX. can. 3. Missam pro vivis & defunctis celebrandam jancientes, Purgatorium supponunt; at Sess. XXV. Decr. de Purgat. Episcopis præcipiunt, ut doctrinam de Purgatorio ubique prædicari studeant, & difficiliores atque incertas de eo quæstiones evulgari non permittant. Suspenso gradu incedebant, neque de loco & foco, aliisque ejusmodi aliquid definiebant, timentes, ne propalata doctrina omni de Purgatorio, populo per falsa de Purgatorio dogmata hactenus inducto, ut omnes fere opes suas in otiosum clerum erogaret, suboleret, Ecclesiæ hactenus per multos errores circa hoc dogma nefarie illusum esse. Iccirco etiam de loco & foco Purgatorii, nec non de remissione culpæ, an pœnæ duntaxat, aliisque permultis nil definire ausi sunt, eò quòd res illa difficultate non careret, nec facile verba invenire possint, quæ omnibus satisfacerent, uti Suave Polanus Hist. C. Trid. lib. VIII. narrat.
units.tr: For the Council of Florence defined that "if those truly repentant die in charity before they have made satisfaction by worthy fruits of repentance for sins committed after baptism, and for omissions, their souls are purged by purgatorial punishments." The Council of Trent also, in Sess. XXX, can. 3, ordering Mass to be celebrated "for the living and the dead," presupposes Purgatory; but in Sess. XXV, Decree on Purgatory, it orders bishops "to take care that the doctrine of Purgatory is preached everywhere, and not to allow the more difficult and uncertain questions about it to be spread abroad." They proceeded with a cautious step, and defined nothing about the place and the fire and similar matters, fearing that if the whole doctrine of Purgatory were openly declared, the people, who had hitherto been led by false dogmas of Purgatory to spend almost all their wealth on an idle clergy, would perceive that the Church had hitherto been wickedly deceived by many errors concerning this dogma. For this reason they dared to define nothing about the place and fire of Purgatory, nor about whether only the guilt or also the punishment is remitted, and many other things, because the matter was not free of difficulty and words could not easily be found that would satisfy everyone, as Suave Polanus relates in his History of the Council of Trent, book VIII.

units.la: XVIII. Locus verò seu Purgatorium, in quo fidelium animæ post mortem, antea quàm ad Regnum Cœlorum aditus iis pateat, à reliquis sive peccatis ipsis, sive peccatorum pœnis purgentur, & fidelium suffragiis, ac potissimum altaris sacrificio adjuventur, non tantùm in Scripturis, sive quoad nomen, sive quoad rem nusquam revelatum est, fatentib⁹ non paucis, Petro Soto, Perefio, Episcopo Roffensi, diligentissimos inquisitores Scripturarum nullum hactenus pro Purgatorio textum invenisse, adeòque ex sola traditione illud probari posse; & Cotono ex Diabolo percontari auso, quis locus Scripturæ apte Purgatorium probet; uti locuples testis Thuanus narrat; Sed etiam Scripturæ in universum repugnat. Non enim medium hominum statum illa prodit, sed duos tantùm hominum ordines, alios credentes, qui salvantur; alios incredulos, qui damnantur, Joh. III. 16. duo loca, consolationis & tormenti, quæ inter grandis hiatus ponitur, Luc. XVI. 25. 26. Credentes enim in judicium pervenire Christus diserte negat, Joh. V. 24. Non ergo pœnam in Purgatorio luunt. Nulla quippe condemnatio, nulla accusatio eorum est, qui in Christo Jesu sunt, Rom. VIII. 1. 33. 34. utpote quorum peccata Christi morte remissa, ne quidem recordationem amplius subeunt, Ezech. XVIII. 22. Quos autem nulla condemnatio manet; & quorum peccatorum, ceu jam remissorum Deus non recordatur amplius, illi nec puniuntur proprie, nec puniri possunt. Animas verò in Purgatorio proprie puniri, ustulari perinde ut in inferno, sola æternitate pœnæ excepta, asserunt. Frustra illi judicium condemnationis, at non punitionis à fidelibus removent, movent,tum quia puniri non potest,qui condemnatus non est. Condemnatio enim sententia, & punitio sententiæ effectus est, qui nunquam à causa sua destituitur. Accedit, quòd Deus in Christo peccata condonat; & Christi sanguis nos purificat ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. I. 7. quia Christus peccatorum purificationem per se ipsum, morte sua peccata tollentem, ne amplius ad noxam imputentur, fecit, Hebr. I. 3. Nam quòd offensam remitti, sed cum restitutione rei ablatæ, excipiunt, hactenus verum est, quod peccatum sine satisfactione propria remitti negant. Justificamur enim gratis, gratia Dei, per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Jesu, Rom. III. 24. Accedit, quòd restitutio rei ablatæ non est pœna, nec pro pœna, qualem in Purgatorio fingunt, quia est opus justitiæ moralis, & pertinet ad privatum quemque ex illo axiomate: Suum cuique reddendum est. Neque etiam conditio hæc ei, qui remittere debet, sed ei, cui remittitur, quia nunquam auditum est, non debere fratrem fratri condonare, nisi postquam satisfactum sibi fuerit. Fieri enim potest, ut satisfactio impossibilis sit. Gemellum & illud sophisma est, quòd peccata remitti, Sacramentum pœnitentiæ plenè recipienti, adeòque etiam satisfacienti, eò quòd satisfactio pœnitentiæ pars sit, pertendunt. Deus enim peccata etiam sine Sacramento ullo condonat, uti exemplo latronis, & eorum, quos adversarii Baptismo Flaminis & Sanguinis, non Fluminis baptizari consentiunt. Præterea satisfactio nulla proprië dicta ad pœnitentiam in foro Dei requiritur, quia pœnitentia, quæ in foro eo requiritur, nihil aliud quàm vitæ mutatio in melius est, quæ pœnæ rationem nullam habet. Præterea post hanc vitam locus pœnitentiam agendi, satisfaciendi, promerendi, bene operandi nullus est. Quærite Deum dum invenitur, invocate eum, dum est propinquus, Esaj. LV. 6. Viventes sciunt, quòd morituri sint. Mortui autem nesciunt quicquam, neque ultra eis, velut promerentibus, merces est, Eccles. IX. 5. Omne, quod invenerit manus tua ad faciendum, secundum vires tuas fac, quia non est opus, vel cogitatio, &c. in sepulchro, proin nec alibi etiam, quia alias ibi saltem facere, promereri liceret, ibid. v. 10. Veniet nox, quando nemo operari poterit, Joh. IX. 4. Tanquam tempus habentes operemur bonum apud omnes, Gal. VI. 10. Imò ne à pœnitentibus quidem Deus ullas pœnas exigit, juxta promissionem Dei: Cùm aversus fuerit ab iniquitate sua, omnium iniquitatum ejus non recordabor, Ezech. XVIII. 22. Sicut Deus peccatorum, quæ punire vult, meminit: ita eorum, quæ punire non vult, obliviscitur. Cùm ergo adversarii in Purgatorio non impœnitentes, sed pœnitentes degere statuant, vel illud nullum elt, vel non pœnale est. Nam quòd Bellarminus regerit, non recordari peccatorum non esse non punire, eò quòd mox vers. 24. Propheta dicat: Si justus se à justitia sua averterit, omnes justitiæ ejus oblivioni tradentur; cùm tamen justitias impiorum Deus præmio aliquo, sed non æterno remuneretur, plane dilutum est. Licèt enim justitiæ impiorum aliquo præmio compensentur in hac vita, in altera tamen, fatentibus adversariis, nullo compensantur. Si ergo cùm, & quatenus Deus ne-
units.tr: XVIII. But the place, or Purgatory, in which the souls of the faithful after death, before the way into the kingdom of heaven is opened to them, are cleansed from the remaining sins themselves or from the punishments of sins, and are helped by the suffrages of the faithful and especially by the sacrifice of the altar, is nowhere revealed in Scripture, either by name or by thing. Not a few confess this: Peter Soto, Perefius, the bishop of Rochester, who say that the most diligent inquirers into the Scriptures have hitherto found no text for Purgatory, and that it can therefore be proved from tradition alone; and Cotton, who asked the devil, when he dared to be questioned, which passage of Scripture aptly proves Purgatory, as the well-informed witness Thuanus relates. But it also runs against Scripture as a whole. For Scripture does not reveal an intermediate state of men, but only two orders of men: some believers, who are saved; others unbelievers, who are damned (John 3.16); and two places, of consolation and of torment, between which a great chasm is set (Luke 16.25–26). For Christ expressly denies that believers "come into judgment" (John 5.24). Therefore they do not suffer punishment in Purgatory. For there is no condemnation and no accusation of those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8.1, 33–34), since their sins, forgiven through the death of Christ, no longer even come to remembrance (Ezek. 18.22). But those whom no condemnation awaits, and whose sins, now forgiven, God no longer remembers, are neither properly punished nor can be punished. Yet our opponents assert that the souls in Purgatory are truly punished, burned just as in hell, except that the punishment is not eternal. In vain do they try to remove from the faithful the judgment of "condemnation" but not of "punishment," since he who is not condemned cannot be punished. For condemnation is a sentence, and punishment is the effect of the sentence, which is never separated from its cause. Add that God forgives sins in Christ, and that the blood of Christ "cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1.7), because Christ "made purification of sins by himself" (Heb. 1.3), by his death taking away sins so that they are no longer imputed to our harm. For the claim that the offence is remitted but with restitution of what was taken away, they maintain, is true only in that they deny that sin is remitted without one's own satisfaction. "For we are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus" (Rom. 3.24). Add that restitution of what was taken away is not a punishment, nor is it in place of a punishment such as they imagine in Purgatory, since it is a work of moral justice and pertains to each private person under that axiom: "to each his own is to be rendered." Nor is this condition imposed on the one who ought to forgive, but on the one to whom forgiveness is granted, since it has never been heard that one brother ought not forgive another unless satisfaction has first been made to him. For satisfaction may be impossible. Equally a sophism is their contention that sins are remitted to one who fully receives the Sacrament of penance, and therefore also to one who makes satisfaction, because satisfaction is a part of penance. For God forgives sins even without any sacrament, as in the example of the thief, and of those whom our opponents agree are baptised with the "Baptism of Blood and of Spirit," not of water. Moreover, no satisfaction properly so called is required for repentance in the court of God, since the repentance required in that court is nothing other than a change of life for the better, which has no character of punishment. Moreover, after this life there is no place for repenting, making satisfaction, meriting or doing good works. "Seek the Lord while he may be found, call upon him while he is near" (Isa. 55.6). "The living know that they will die; but the dead know nothing, nor have they any more a reward," as those who might merit it (Eccles. 9.5). "Whatever your hand finds to do, do it according to your strength, for there is no work or thought," etc., "in the grave" (ibid. v. 10); therefore not elsewhere either, since otherwise there at least it would be lawful to "do" and to merit. "The night comes when no one can work" (John 9.4). "As we have opportunity, let us do good to all" (Gal. 6.10). Indeed God does not even exact any punishments from the penitent, according to God's promise: "When he turns away from his iniquity, I will not remember any of his iniquities" (Ezek. 18.22). As God remembers the sins that he wishes to punish, so he forgets those he does not wish to punish. Therefore, since our opponents hold that those in Purgatory dwell not as the impenitent but as the penitent, either that state is nothing, or it is not penal. For Bellarmine's reply, that not remembering sins is not the same as not punishing, because immediately in verse 24 the prophet says, "If the righteous turns from his righteousness, all his righteousnesses shall be forgotten," is thoroughly refuted, since God rewards the righteousness of the wicked with some reward, though not an eternal one. For although the righteousness of the wicked is compensated with some reward in this life, in the next, as our opponents admit, it is compensated by nothing.

units.la: gat, se memorem futurum justitiarum impii, significat, se nullo præmio affecturum, ergo cum negat, se memorem futurum injustitiarum, oportet intelligi, nullo post mortem supplicio affecturum, quod satis Purgatorium evertit. Illud inprimis Purgatorii flammas omnes extinguit, quòd Scriptura docet, fideles illico post mortem Cœlum ingredi, atque ibi Deo plenos cœlesti gloria frui, quod infra probavimus. Neque minùs firmum illud est, quòd Purgatorium præcipuos fidei articulos evertit, nominatim articulos de misericordia & justitia Dei, sufficientia meriti Christi, Evangelio; quod lætum nuntium est de remissione peccatorum; quòdque salsissimis hypothesibus, non semel à nobis discussis, innititur, cujusmodi tralatitiæ illæ sunt, quòd remittatur culpa, non remissa pœna omni: quòd Christi satisfactio non prosit fidelibus ad perfectam remissionem peccatorum, sed tantùm ad Baptismum usque; post eum autem pœnæ æternæ in temporales convertantur: quòd afflictiones fidelium veræ pœnæ & satisfactiones sint: quòd per merita, satisfactiones, eleemosynas, preces, sacrificium Missæ, aliáque viventium suffragia pœnæ Purgatorii leventur, & finiantur. Cùmque Papæ in ipsum etiam Purgatorium jurisdictionem ejusmodi tribuant, ut juxta sententiam Angeli de Clavasio in Summ. Aug. si velit, posset totum Purgatorium evacuare; & juxta disputationem Jesuitarum A. MDC. de Indulg. habitam, & Petri Stevarti censura laudatam, thes. 52. Papa summa potestate sua utens tot tantasque indulgentias defunctis largiri possit, ut evacuato Purgatorio, omnes animæ ad Cœlum evolent; tyrannum proin Papam esse oportet, qui miseras animas ex eo confestim non liberet. Et tantò tyrannis illa major est, quantò severius Romanenses contendunt, in arbitrio Papæ esse remittere viventibus & morientibus, quibus vult, peccata omnia, quantum ad debitum pœnæ illius residuæ, quòdque remissio ea in foro etiam cœlesti valeat. Efficere ergo Papa debuit, ne animæ in Purgatorium descenderent. Infelix est, in cujus potestate est tot animas à morte defendere, & non est voluntas. Ecclesiæ certè veteri & recentiori Orientali Græcæ Purgatorium incognitum fuit; neque etiam in Conciliis & Symbolis veteribus ullum ejus vestigium extat. Neque etiam veteres loca Scripturæ, quæ adversarii ad Purgatorium detorquent, de eodem interpretantur; & fidei, spei, charitatis operibus & pœnitentiæ ullum post mortem locum relinquunt; quin potius asserunt, homines ibi æternum mansuros, quò morientes ceciderint; negantes etiam, quòd piorum animæ post mortem purgentur, vel discrucientur. Quæ aliáque viri doctissimi, Forbesius Instruct. Hist. Theol. lib. XIII. 11. & Dallæus de Pœnis & satisfact. lib. VI. disertissimis veterum testimoniis confirmarunt. Denique Papatus dogma adeò à Scripturis & antiquitatis sanioris sententia alienum solius quæstus gratia fovet, quia indulgentiarum, & magnæ Missæ partis nundinatio ei, tanquam basi suæ superstructa est. Ideo Concilium Tridentinum Sess. XXV. non tantùm ingenuè confitetur, in materia de Purgatorio quædam turpe lucrum sapere; quæ ita aboabolenda decernit, ut tamen Simoniæ fibras minimè recidat. Statim enim Patres illi subjiciunt, curare debere Episcopos, ut fidelium vivorum suffragia, Missarum orationes, eleemosynæ (lucrosæ collationes) aliáque pietatis opera, quæ à fidelibus pro aliis defunctis fieri consueverunt, secundum Ecclesiæ instituta, piè & devotè fiant; & quæ pro illis ex testatorum fundationibus, vel alia ratione debentur, non perfunctorie, sed à sacerdotibus, & Ecclesiæ ministris, & aliis, qui hoc præstare tenentur, diligenter & accuratè persolvantur. En mercaturam genuinam, contractum ementes inter & vendentes, & persolventes, qui debitum, seu obligationem persolvendi, ob datas scilicet eleemosynas, fundationes, aliásque ejusmodi rationes inducit. Sed malæ fidei contractus hic est, quia ἀνθρακες ὁ Ἡσαυρὸς πλοῦτος carbones pro thesauro, imò Nihil datur, & ærugina-tores illi non tantùm non illam Diomedis in permutando solertiam imitantes, χρύσεα donanti χάλκεα qui dederat, sed hanc potiùs illudentium & jocantium paroemiam sequuntur: Αἶξε μηδὲν, χαῖρε κεῖτε καλῶς Cape nihil, & serva bene, nisi forte aliquid videntur chartæ & plumbea applicandarum indulgentiarum instrumenta, quibus de igne Purgatorio magnopere metuendum est, ne & ipsa in Nihilum redigantur, quia Diaboli calentes candentésque manus habent, quas inter facilè membranæ comburuntur, & plumbum colliquescit.
units.tr: God's refusal to remember the unrighteous deeds of the wicked means that he will impose no punishment after death; it is the same as saying he will not remember their unrighteousness. Since Ezekiel 18:24 goes on to say that if the righteous turns from his righteousness, all his righteous deeds will be forgotten, it is plainly refuted that God rewards the righteousness of the wicked with some reward, though not an eternal one. For although the righteousness of the wicked is recompensed with some reward in this life, our opponents concede that in the next it is recompensed with nothing. If, therefore, God, when and to the extent that he denies that he will remember the righteousness of the wicked, signifies that he will bestow no reward, then when he denies that he will remember their unrighteousness, it must be understood that he will impose no punishment after death, and this overthrows Purgatory well enough. Above all, the Scripture's teaching that the faithful enter heaven immediately after death and there enjoy God, filled with heavenly glory, which we proved below, extinguishes all the flames of Purgatory. No less firm is the point that Purgatory overthrows the chief articles of faith, namely those concerning the mercy and justice of God, the sufficiency of Christ's merit, and the Gospel, which is the joyful message of the remission of sins. Purgatory also rests on the most insipid hypotheses, already discussed by us more than once, such as these commonplaces: that the guilt is remitted while the whole punishment is not; that Christ's satisfaction profits the faithful for full remission of sins only up to baptism, and after that eternal punishments are converted into temporal ones; that the afflictions of the faithful are true punishments and satisfactions; and that the punishments of Purgatory are lightened and brought to an end through the merits, satisfactions, almsgivings, prayers, the sacrifice of the Mass, and other suffrages of the living. Since the Popes assign to themselves such jurisdiction even over Purgatory itself, that according to the opinion of Angelus de Clavasio, in Summ. Aug., he could, if he wished, empty all of Purgatory; and according to the disputation of the Jesuits held in 1600, de Indulg., and the censure of Petrus Stevartus praised there, thes. 52: the Pope, using his supreme power, can grant so many and such great indulgences to the dead that, Purgatory being emptied, all souls fly up to heaven; therefore the Pope must be a tyrant who does not immediately free the wretched souls from it. And that tyranny is all the greater, the more severely the Romanists contend that it is in the Pope's power to remit to the living and the dying, to whomever he wishes, all sins as regards the remaining debt of punishment, and that this remission is valid even in the heavenly court. The Pope ought therefore to have seen to it that souls did not descend into Purgatory. Unhappy is he in whose power it is to save so many souls from death, and yet he is unwilling. Certainly the ancient Church, and the more recent Eastern Greek Church, did not know Purgatory; nor does any trace of it appear in the ancient councils or creeds. Nor do the ancient writers interpret the passages of Scripture which our opponents twist toward Purgatory as referring to it; they leave no place after death for faith, hope, love, works, and repentance; rather they assert that men will remain there forever where they have fallen when dying, and they also deny that the souls of the pious are purged or tormented after death. These and other matters have been confirmed from the most explicit testimonies of the ancients by the most learned men, Forbesius, Instruct. Hist. Theol. lib. XIII, 11, and Dallaeus, de Poenis & satisfact. lib. VI. Finally, the Papacy fosters this dogma, so alien to Scripture and to the sounder opinion of antiquity, for the sake of gain alone, since the trade in indulgences and in a large part of the Mass is built upon it as its foundation. Therefore the Council of Trent, Sess. XXV, not only frankly confesses that in the matter of Purgatory certain things smack of shameful gain, but decrees that these be abolished in such a way that it does not cut back the roots of simony at all. For those Fathers immediately add that the bishops ought to take care that the suffrages of the living faithful, the prayers of the Masses, almsgivings (profitable contributions) and other works of piety, which are customarily performed by the faithful for other dead, be done devoutly and piously according to the institutions of the Church; and that what is owed for them from the foundations of the testators, or in some other way, be paid carefully and accurately, not perfunctorily, by priests, ministers of the Church, and others who are bound to render this. Behold the genuine merchandising, which brings in a contract between buyers and sellers, and those paying, who pay the debt or obligation, namely on account of alms given, foundations, and other such reasons. But this contract is one of bad faith, because [ἄνθρακες ὁ θησαυρός] coals for treasure, indeed nothing is given; and those bronze-merchants not only fail to imitate that cleverness of Diomedes in exchange, gold for bronze [χρύσεα ... χάλκεα], which he gave to the one who had given bronze, but follow rather that jesting proverb of mockers and jokers: [Αἶξε μηδὲν, χαῖρε κεῖτε καλῶς] take nothing, rejoice, lie down well; take nothing and keep it well. Unless perhaps the paper and lead documents for applying indulgences seem to be the instruments, by which one must greatly fear the fire of Purgatory, lest they too be reduced to nothing, since the devil has hot and glowing hands, between which parchments are easily burned and lead melts.

units.la: XIX. Figmentum Purgatorii rationibus falsis adversarii incrustant. Nam animas fidelium defunctorum sacrificiis & precibus vivorum juvari posse, Judæ Macchabæi, duodecim millia drachmarum Hierosolymam, offerendi pro defunctis gratia, mittentis 2. Macchab. XII. 43. exemplo confirmare satagunt. Sed nec liber ille articulo fidei confirmando idoneus est; nec Judas misit sacrificatum pro mortuis, nedum pro his mortuis, tum quia, ceu peritus legis, noverat, Moses nusquam dedisse mandatum sacrificandi mortuis; & exemplum præcedens simile Achanis sacrilegi, pro quo nec oratum, nec sacrificatum est, habuit: tum quia milites illi mortui & cæsi sunt propter furtum ἱερωμάτων ὑπὸ εἰδώλων rerum idolis Jamnienfium consecratarum, à quibus manum ut abstinerent, legem Divinam jussisse, Deut. XIII. 16. ipse author dicit, quale peccatum non veniale certè, suffragiis expiandum, sed mortale, æquè ac Achanis, fuit, & non remissum ante mortem, quia absque poenitentia fuit, & post mortem cum furto deprehensi fuerunt, ut falsò Jason eos μετ' εὐσεβείας κοιμωμένους defunctos in pietate, cùm mortui in flagrante peccato sint, dixerit. Neque proin illud obstat, quod author libri vers. 43. 45. scribit, Judam jussisse sacrificium offerre, de resurrectione cogitantem, & considerantem, iis, qui cum pietate obiissent, καλὸν χαρίσιον optimum gratiæ munus repositum esse. Unde enim scriptori illi libri, Jasoni, Judæ cogitatio innotuit? Et cur non cogitavit de Purgatorio, Limbo? Cur non potiùs cogitasse eum divinavit id, quod legi Divinæ congruens fuit? Ut videlicet, si totus coetus Israel commiserit aliquid per errorem, postquam peccatum innotuerit, tunc offerat congregatio juvencum, filium bovis פר in sacrificium pro peccato, Levit. IV. 13. 14. planè sicut Judas di-
units.tr: XIX. The Papists plaster over the fiction of Purgatory with false arguments. For they strive to confirm that the souls of the faithful dead can be helped by the sacrifices and prayers of the living, by the example of Judas Maccabaeus, who sent twelve thousand drachmas to Jerusalem to be offered for the dead, 2 Maccabees 12:43. But that book is not fit to confirm an article of faith; nor did Judas send money for a sacrifice for the dead, much less for these dead. For, as a learned man of the law, he knew that Moses nowhere gave a command to sacrifice to the dead; and he had before him the similar example of Achan the sacrilegious, for whom there was neither prayer nor sacrifice. Moreover, those soldiers were dead and slain because of theft of things consecrated under the idols [ἱερωμάτων ὑπὸ εἰδώλων] of the Jamnites, consecrated to idols, from which the divine law commanded them to abstain, Deuteronomy 13:16, as the author himself says. Such a sin was certainly not venial, to be expiated by suffrages, but mortal, just like Achan's, and was not remitted before death, because it was without repentance, and after death they were found out with the theft in hand, although Jason falsely called them sleeping in piety [μετ' εὐσεβείας κοιμωμένους], that is, dead in godliness, since they died in the very act of sin. Nor is it an objection that the author of the book, in verses 43 and 45, writes that Judas ordered a sacrifice to be offered, thinking about the resurrection, and considering that for those who had died in piety a fine gift [καλὸν χαρίσιον] had been laid up. For how did that writer of the book, or Jason, or Judas, come to know this thought? And why did he not think of Purgatory or Limbo? Why does he not rather be imagined to have thought what was agreeable to the divine law? Namely, that if the whole congregation of Israel shall commit something through error, and after the sin is made known, then the congregation shall offer a young bullock [פר], the son of a bull, for a sin offering, Leviticus 4:13-14, just as Judas is said to have intended a sacrifice for sin [ἁμαρτίας], that is, on account of the sin committed by the dead, so that it would not be imputed to the living army. And what kind of gift [χαρίσματος] is it to be burned in the flames of Purgatory? What then has a penal thing to do with a gift, which is laid up in heaven, not in a place of punishment? Afterwards indeed...

units.la: citur destinasse sacrificium ἀμαρτίας pro peccato, seu propter peccatum à mortuis scilicet commissum, ne viventi exercitui imputaretur. Et quale χαρίσμεον est, Purgatorii flammis ustulari? Quid itaque poenali cum χαρίσμεῳ, quod in Cœlo, non in loco supplicii reponitur? Post mortem porrò animas fidelium puniri, & à poenis liberari, falsò contendunt. Non enim Christus dicens: Esto amicus adversario tuo citò, dum es in via cum eo; ne quando te tradat adversarius judici, & judex te tradat ministro, & in custodiam conjiciaris; Amen dico tibi, non exibis inde, usque dum reddideris ultimum quadrantem. Matth. V. 25. 26. per φυλακλω carcerem, non Purgatorium, utpote in quo ultimus quadrans solvatur, & peccata venalia puniantur, sed infernum intelligit. Non enim finis futurus carceris illius innuitur, quia, ut finis ille constet, oportet præsupponi ultimum quadrantem periolutum aliquando iri, quod tamen phrasis ipsa non exhibet. Nam etiam in judiciis seculi hujus haud raro fit, ut qui in carcerem detruditur, nunquam solvendo sit. Atque adeò usus communis ita habet, ut ejusmodi minæ sic intelligantur: Si eris solvendo, egressurus eris; sin minùs, nunquam. Cùmque peccati mortalis non remissi, poenæ æternæ sint, hic poenæ sunt & peccati mortalis, quia contra charitatem illud est, quippe inimicitia cum adversario; & peccati nondum remissi, quia nullum peccatum absque poenitentia remittitur, quandoquidem is describitur, qui adversario, fratri suo, in via, seu hac vita non consenserit. Neque adeò ἐκάλεσεν ἡσθέγιλης extremus quadrans peccata venialia notat, tum quia non cumulantur varia peccata, sed unicum, atque mortale illud irreconciliabilitas & pertinacia in odio atque inimicitia: tum quia peccatum illud unicum non secatur in partes minutas, sed agitur de poena, cujus rigidissima exactio, & plenaria solutio urgetur. Dilutum & illud est, quòd liberationem ex poenis Purgatorii ex Zach. IX. 11. ubi Deus sanguine Testamenti vinctos de בור cisterna, sive lacu, in quo non est aqua, eduxisse dicitur, extundere conantur: tum quia Purgatorium non omni aqua consolationis, ex spe salutis æternæ, destitui, ipsimet asserunt: tum quia vincti illi sanguine Testamenti, non propria satisfactione educi dicuntur: tum quia nec de mortuis, nec de animabus, nec de peccatis levioribus sermo est. Verior ille sensus est, quòd vel Christi morte, seu sanguine Testamenti in peccato spiritualiter mortui ex cisterna æternæ mortis, & sub N. T. etiam à timore illo mortis, cui fideles V. T. obnoxii erant, Hebr. II. 15. liberentur: vel captivi Babylone quandoque ex captivitate, quæ cisternæ instar aqua carentis erat, liberandi sint. Christus verò dicens, Peccatum in Spiritum S. nec in hoc, nec in futuro seculo remissum iri, Matth. XII. 32. non peccata quædam in futuro seculo, hoc est, Purgatorio, remitti docet, tum quia remissio cum Purgatorio & satisfactione propria pugnat, cùm in Purgatorio nec peccatum remittatur, quia ibi animæ ustulantur propter peccata, nec poena, quia animæ ibidem poenam subeunt: tum quia, si in altero seculo peccata remittuntur, id fiet in ultimo judicio, in quo peccata fidelium omnia solenni promulgatio-ne ne judicis remittenda sunt; sed peccatum in Spiritum S. in æternum non iri remissum Marc. III.29. declarat. Spem enim omnem tam flagitiosæ nequitiæ præcidit, usitato Hebraismo, quo עולם הזה והבא seculum præsens & futurum æternitatem notat. Futilis etiam consequentia illa est: Si peccatum in Spiritum S. nec in hoc, nec in futuro seculo remittitur, tum peccata alia in hoc, alia in futuro seculo remittuntur. Quidni enim concludamus potius: tum peccatum aliquod,quod non est in Spiritum S. & in hoc, & in altero seculo remittitur? Ea enim natura propositionum disjunctivarum est, ut geminam contradictionem affirmativam; puta copulativam, seu conjunctivam; illam plenam, hanc dimidiatam, admittant. Fatetur Bellarminus, id quod illi ex verbis Christi colligunt, non sequi secundum regulam Dialecticorum; sed tamen sequi secundum regulas prudentiæ. Et Salmeron dicit, collectionem non esse formalem, sed ratione materiæ communis phraseos optime id colligi. Sed potest materia quandoque vera, at forma falsa esse per accidens, ejus vitio, qui argumentatur. Sed quæ consequentia secundum materiam legitima est, eam per se peccare in forma, neque adeo ad ullam formam legitimam redigi posse, monstrosum est. Præterea hortatur Christus, ut faciamus nobis amicos de mammona iniquitatis, ut cum defecerimus, nos in æterna tabernacula recipiant, Luc. XVI.9. Sed perperam verbis illis Purgatorium superstruunt, quasi amici illi Sancti cum Christo regnantes per suffragia sua eos, qui post mortem in Purgatorio sudant, juvare, & ad æternam vitam promovere possint. Non enim hic parabolæ illius scopus est, ex quo solo argumentari licet. Et prius Purgatorium probandum est, quàm ei verba hæc applicentur. Possunt etiam vel pauperes, quorum anima & lumbi nobis benedicunt, Job. XXXI.20. precibus suis in hac vita, & suffragio in extremo Judicio, vel Sancti, qui in Coelo sunt, in æterna tabernacula recipere eos, qui nunquam in Purgatorium descenderunt. Sancti enim deficientes, seu morientes statim in æterna tabernacula recipiuntur, non diu jam mortui ex Purgatorii poenis liberantur. Amici vero illi pauperes hoc hospitalitatis divitibus, quorum eleemosynis juvantur, reddunt, ut precibus & intercessione sua à Deo impetrent, ut à Deo illi in æterna tabernacula recipiantur, vel ab Angelis eò deportentur. Non possunt φίλοι amici meritis, intercessione & potestate sua quemquam in æterna tabernacula recipere. Sed filiis tamen Dei lætantibus, applaudentibus, & in Deo ac Spiritu ipsius volentibus à Deo recipientur ii, qui amici ipsorum esse voluerint, quo sensu amici καταχωνισμὸς in æterna tabernacula recipere dicuntur. Voluntas enim justorum & beatorum efficax est, quia est φρόνημα & πνεῦμα· studium Spiritus, Rom. VIII.27.
units.tr: is sacrificed for sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin [ἀμαρτίας], or on account of sin, namely sin committed by the dead, so that it might not be imputed to the living army. And what sort of gift [χαρίσμα] is it to be burned in the flames of Purgatory? How can something penal be reckoned as a gift [χαρίσματι], which is laid up in heaven and not in a place of punishment? Moreover, they falsely contend that the souls of the faithful are punished after death and freed from their pains. For Christ, when he says, Agree with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way, lest the adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Truly I say to you, you shall not come out from there until you have paid the last farthing (Matt. 5:25, 26), does not mean by prison [φυλακῇ] Purgatory, since in Purgatory the last farthing is paid and venial sins are punished, but he means hell. For the end of that imprisonment is not implied, since for such an end to be established one would have to presuppose that the last farthing will at some time be paid, which the phrase itself does not show. Indeed, even in the courts of this world it often happens that one who is thrown into prison is never able to pay. And so common usage understands such threats in this way: If you are able to pay, you will come out; if not, never. And since the penalties of unforgiven mortal sin are eternal, these are penalties both of mortal sin, because that sin is against charity, being enmity with an adversary, and of sin not yet forgiven, because no sin is forgiven without repentance, since the one described is the man who has not agreed with his adversary, his brother, on the way, that is, in this life. Nor does the last farthing [ἔσχατος κοδράντης] signify venial sins, both because various sins are not piled up here, but one only, and that mortal sin, namely irreconcilability and obstinacy in hatred and enmity; and because that one sin is not cut into small parts, but the discussion concerns a penalty whose most rigorous exaction and full payment is urged. That also is refuted, the attempt to extract the release from the pains of Purgatory from Zech. 9:11, where God is said to have brought out those bound by the blood of the testament from the cistern [בור], or pit, in which there is no water. For, first, they themselves assert that Purgatory is not devoid of all water of consolation, drawn from the hope of eternal salvation; second, those bound by the blood of the testament are not said to be brought out by their own satisfaction; third, the passage speaks neither of the dead, nor of souls, nor of lighter sins. The truer sense is that those spiritually dead in sin are freed, either by the death of Christ, or by the blood of the testament, from the cistern of eternal death, and under the New Testament also from that fear of death to which the faithful of the Old Testament were subject (Heb. 2:15); or that the captives in Babylon were at some time to be freed from their captivity, which, like a cistern lacking water, was such. But when Christ says, that sin against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come (Matt. 12:32), he does not teach that certain sins are forgiven in the age to come, that is, in Purgatory. This is so, first, because forgiveness is at odds with Purgatory and with proper satisfaction: in Purgatory sin is not forgiven, because souls are burned there on account of sins, nor is punishment remitted, because the souls there undergo punishment. Second, if sins are forgiven in the other age, that will happen at the last judgment, at which the sins of all the faithful are to be forgiven by the solemn pronouncement of the Judge; but Mark 3:29 declares that the sin against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven for ever. For he cuts off all hope for such a wicked offence, by the customary Hebraism in which the present and future age [עולם הזה והבא] denotes eternity. That inference is also futile: If sin against the Holy Spirit is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come, then other sins are forgiven, some in this age, others in the age to come. Why should we not rather conclude: then some sin, which is not against the Holy Spirit, is forgiven both in this age and in the age to come? For such is the nature of disjunctive propositions that they admit of two affirmative contradictions, the one complete, the other half-stated, namely the copulative or conjunctive. Bellarmine concedes that what they draw from the words of Christ does not follow according to the rule of the Dialecticians; yet it does follow according to the rules of prudence. And Salmeron says that the inference is not formal, but is very well drawn from the nature of the common phrase. But a matter may sometimes be true while the form is false, accidentally, through the fault of the one who argues. Yet that an inference which is legitimate in its matter should in itself be faulty in form, and so cannot be reduced to any legitimate form, is monstrous. Furthermore, Christ exhorts that we make for ourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when we fail, they may receive us into eternal tabernacles (Luke 16:9). But they wrongly build Purgatory upon those words, as if those holy friends reigning with Christ could by their intercessions help those who after death sweat in Purgatory and advance them to eternal life. For this is not the aim of that parable, and it is from this alone that one may argue. And Purgatory must first be proved before these words are applied to it. Again, either the poor, whose loins and soul bless us (Job 31:20), by their prayers in this life and by their intercession at the last judgment, or the saints who are in heaven, may receive into eternal tabernacles those who never descended into Purgatory. For the saints who fail, that is, who die, are at once received into eternal tabernacles, and are not freed from the pains of Purgatory after being dead for some time. But those poor friends repay the rich for the hospitality they receive from their alms, so that by their prayers and intercession they may obtain from God that they be received by God into eternal tabernacles, or be carried there by angels. Friends [φίλοι] cannot by their merits, intercession and power receive anyone into eternal tabernacles. But by the rejoicing and applause of the sons of God, and by their willing in God and his Spirit, those who have wished to be their friends are received by God; in this sense they are said to receive friends into eternal tabernacles. For the will of the just and blessed is effective, because it is the mind [φρόνημα] and spirit [πνεῦμα]: the striving of the Spirit (Rom. 8:27).

units.la: XX. Achilles inprimis pro Purgatorio λεγόμενον est celebris ille locus S. Pauli, ubi docet, eos, quorum opera malo fundamento superstructa comburentur, salvatum iri ὡς διὰ πυρὸς tanquam per ignem, 1.Cor.III.12. Caeterum per ignem non Purgatorii ignem intelligit, tum quia diserte de igne metaphorico loquitur, quod & particula ὡς tanquam; & series contextus, in quo reliqua, aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosi, lignum, fœnum, stipula, ædificare, fundamentum, omnia metaphorica sunt; & effectus ignis illius, qui est urere opera præterita, cùm proprie dictus nonnisi præsentia ura; tum quia ignis ille & bona & mala opera probat, juxta verba Apostoli: Cujusque opus quale fit, ignis probabit; si cujus opus manebit, mercedem recipiet: si exustum fuerit, damnum faciet, vers. 13.14.15. cùm Purgatorii ignis nonnisi mala probet & purget: tum quia ignis ille agit in opera, uti eadem verba, nec non illud, quòd non operantes, sed opera auro, argento &c. comparantur, probant; at purgatorianus in operantes, utpote qui poenalis est; cùm poena omnis non operibus, sed operantibus infligatur: tum quia ignis Paulinus manifestat opera, ὁποῖα qualia sint, v.13. at purgatorianus non manifestat, quia cùm poena sit, infligitur, non ante, sed postquam opera manifesta sunt: tum denique quia ignis Paulinus constitutus est non propter poenam temporalem pro peccato luendam, uti ignis purgatorianus, sed propter culpam peccatorum Mortalium, cùm in opere malo consideretur tantùm culpa, vel poena, at lignum, fœnum, stipula non poena utique, quia aliter non responderent auro, argento, &c. quæ non ipsæ virtutes, sed virtutum præmia sunt, adeòque peccatum est. Neque illud ferri potest, quòd ignem exploraturum, v.13. ab eo igne, per quem exploratus salvabitur, v.15. sic distinguunt, ut iste metaphoricus ultimi judicii, hic proprie dictus Purgatorii fit, quia de eodem igne Paulus perpetim loquitur, qui videlicet & explorat cujusque opus, tum illius, quod in igne manet, tum illius, quod exuritur; & is est, per quem homo salvatur. Tum etiam Paulus proprie loquitur de ædificantibus Ecclesiam publico ministerio, adeòque in auro, argento, fœno, stipula publicum item ministerium, prout illud rectum & exploratum est, intelligit. Non ergo lignum, fœnum, stipula peccata venialia notat. Sicut enim aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosi ea significant, quæ nunquam, aut difficilime comburuntur: ita lignum, fœnum, stipula ea, in quæ vis ignis facilime exeritur. Si igitur in priore membro sunt justi & fideles, nullus locus venialibus peccatis, utpote quæ non extrema, sed inter extrema sunt, erit. Et hæretici quidem non sunt lignum, fœnum, stipula, tum quia super fundamento ædificant, non ædificantur. Sed hæresin tamen aliquam fundamento superædificari, adeòque fœnum, stipulam esse comburendam, cùm ædificans ipse salvetur, nihil vetat. Nam etiam Cyprianus, nunquam hæreticos inter numeratus, hæresin tamen Anabaptismi docuit. Exceptis etiam hæresibus alia prava etiam superædificari possunt Christo, puta quæcunque disciplinam torquent, ut Quartodecimani, Meletiani, Eustathiani. Proin per fœnum, lignum, stipulam peccata venialia intelligi necesse non est. Et peccata mortalia fidei vitam adimunt potentia, sed non semper actu, alias Petri fides in illa solenni abnegatione periisset. Dies porrò ille, qui cujusque opus manifestabit, v.13. non dies particularis judicii post mortem, in Purgatorio successurus, est, quia nulla opera in particulari tali judicio manifestantur, vel in morte, quia ea, utpote omni-
units.tr: XX. Chief among the passages that are called in support of Purgatory is that famous text of St Paul, where he teaches that those whose works, built on a poor foundation, are burned up will be saved as through fire (1 Cor. 3:12). But by fire he does not mean the fire of Purgatory: first, because he is clearly speaking of a metaphorical fire, as the particle as shows, and the whole sequence of the context, in which the rest, gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, to build, foundation, are all metaphorical; and the effect of that fire, which is to burn up works done in the past, whereas properly speaking fire burns only what is present. Second, that fire tests both good and bad works, according to the Apostle's words: Each man's work will be made manifest; the fire will test it. If anyone's work remains, he will receive a reward; if it is burned up, he will suffer loss (vv. 13–15), whereas the fire of Purgatory tests and purges only evil works. Third, that fire acts upon the works, as these same words show, and also the fact that the works, not the workers, are compared to gold, silver, and so on; but the purgatorial fire acts upon the workers, since it is penal, and all punishment is inflicted not on works but on the workers. Fourth, the Pauline fire makes works manifest, of what sort they are (v. 13), whereas the purgatorial fire does not make them manifest, because, being punishment, it is inflicted not before but after the works are manifest. Lastly, the Pauline fire is appointed not on account of temporal punishment to be paid for sin, as the purgatorial fire is, but on account of the guilt of mortal sins, since in an evil work only the guilt or the punishment is considered; but wood, hay, stubble are surely not punishments, since otherwise they would not correspond to gold, silver, and so on, which are not virtues themselves but rewards of virtues, and so are sin. Nor can it be borne that they distinguish the fire that will test (v. 13) from the fire through which the tested man will be saved (v. 15) in such a way that the former is metaphorical and belongs to the last judgment, the latter properly so called and belongs to Purgatory; for Paul speaks continuously of the same fire, which both tests each man's work, both that which remains in the fire and that which is burned, and is that through which a man is saved. Moreover, Paul properly speaks of those who build up the Church by public ministry, and so by gold, silver, hay and stubble he understands likewise public ministry, insofar as it is right and tested. Therefore wood, hay, stubble do not signify venial sins. For just as gold, silver, precious stones signify those things which are never or most hardly burned, so wood, hay, stubble signify those things to which the force of fire most easily reaches. If, then, in the first member there are just and faithful people, there will be no place for venial sins, since they are not extremes but lie between extremes. Heretics, indeed, are not wood, hay, stubble, since they do not build upon the foundation but are not built upon it. Yet nothing forbids some heresy being built upon the foundation, and so hay and stubble being burned, while the builder himself is saved. For even Cyprian, who is never counted among the heretics, taught the heresy of Anabaptism. Apart from heresies, other wicked things may be built upon Christ, for instance whatever disturbs the discipline, such as the Quartodecimans, Meletians, Eustathians. Therefore it is not necessary to understand venial sins by hay, wood, stubble. And mortal sins take away the life of faith in potency, but not always in act; otherwise Peter's faith would have perished in that solemn denial. Moreover, that day which will make manifest each man's work (v. 13) is not the particular day of judgment after death, to take place in Purgatory, because in such a particular judgment no works are made manifest; nor is it death, because death, being common to all, reveals nothing; nor is it the time following death, because it reveals nothing either to the living or to the dead. Not to the living, because they do not know the state of the dead. Not to the dead, to whom it is not relevant that anything be revealed, because…

units.la: Locus inprimis 1. Cor. III.12. pro Purgatorio obdurat vindicatur. omnibus communis, nihil revelat; vel in tempore mortem consequente, quia neque vivis, neque defunctis aliquid revelat. Non vivis, quia illi statum defuncti ignorant. Non defunctis, quibus non attinet aliquid revelari, quia ex revelatione nec proficere nec deficere possunt. Dies ergo ille praesentis seculi tempus aliquod, quo homo singulariter explorstatur, per tribulationes inprimis, esse potest. Neque obstat, quod tribulationes hujus vitae bonis & malis communes sunt, adeoque opus explorare posse non videntur; tum quia alia etiam sunt, quibus opera explorari possunt: tum quia licet tribulationes bonis & malis communes sint, non eadem tamen in utrisque effecta habent. Si tamen diem aliquem post mortem intelligere libet, uti forte amplissime intelligitur, ille universalis judicii erit. Nam dies extremi judicii vere erit ἡμέρα δηλῶσα dies manifestans, & erit certus dies; & habebit ignem omnia liquefacientem, & erit ut ignis χωνευτὸς fuscoris, Mal. III. 2. adeoque opera salvandorum manifestabit, non vindicando, sed condonando, idque sine pudore. Denique ignem, per quem homo salvatur, non purgatorium esse, sed metaphorice dictum, & eundem, qui opera manifestat, quem metaphorice exactissimum Dei judicium significare adversarii etiam fatentur, jam probavimus. Potius ergo notat ignem vel hujus vitae, de quo loquitur David: Explorasti nos, o Deus, conflasti nos ut conflatur argentum. Venimus in ignem & aquam, & eduxisti nos ad satietatem, Psal.
