LXVI. 10. 12. ad quem ignem afflictiones hujus vitae, angustiae cordis, & omnes amaritudines, quae in hac vita ex nugis nostris sequi solent: vel ignem metaphoricum ultimi judicii, quem illum diem esse, quo opera explorabuntur, & salvabimur velut per ignem, diximus. Non enim obstat, quod non veniemus in judicium; nempe quia salvabimur, sed ut per veniam. Omnes enim nos coram tribunali Christi manifestari decet; ut quisque reportet, secundum ea, quae fecit in corpore, sive bonum, sive malum, 2. Cor. V. 10.
units.tr: The passage 1 Cor. 3.12, which is wrongly used in support of Purgatory, is vindicated. It reveals nothing to all alike, whether in the time following death; for it reveals nothing either to the living or to the dead. Not to the living, because they do not know the state of the dead. Not to the dead, to whom it is no concern to have anything revealed, since by revelation they can neither gain nor lose anything. That day, then, may be some time of the present age in which a man is tested singly, chiefly through tribulations. Nor is it an objection that the tribulations of this life are common to good and bad, and so seem unable to test works; for there are other means by which works can be tested, and although tribulations are common to good and bad, they do not have the same effects in both. If, however, we want to understand some day after death, as perhaps it is most broadly understood, it will be the day of universal judgment. For the day of the last judgment will truly be a day making things manifest [ἡμέρα δηλῶσα], and it will be a certain day; it will have a fire melting all things, and it will be like the refiner's fire [χωνευτὸς fuscoris], Mal. 3.2, and so it will make manifest the works of those who are to be saved, not by punishing them but by pardoning them, and that without shame. Finally, we have already shown that the fire through which a man is saved is not purgatorial but is spoken metaphorically, and that it is the same fire which makes works manifest, which even our adversaries admit is a metaphor for God's most exact judgment. Rather, it signifies either the fire of this life, of which David speaks: "Thou, O God, hast proved us; thou hast tried us as silver is tried. We went into fire and water, and thou broughtest us out into abundance," Ps. 66.10, 12; to which fire belong the afflictions of this life, the anguish of heart, and all the bitterness which usually follow in this life from our follies; or else the metaphorical fire of the last judgment, which we have said is that day on which works will be examined and we shall be saved as if through fire. For it is no objection that we shall not come into judgment; namely, because we shall be saved, but as through pardon. For "we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, that each may receive the things done in the body, whether good or bad," 2 Cor. 5.10.

units.la: XXI. Idem porro Apostolus dicens, baptizari quosdam ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν, 1. Cor. XV. 29. non hoc sibi vult, quod illi baptizentur, baptismo lachrymarum & poenitentiae, orando, jejunando, semetipsos affligendo pro mortuis in Purgatorio aestuantibus, tum quia locus difficilimus est, in quo frustra erroris sui triumphum quaerunt: tum quia Baptismus ille metaphoricus non facit ad spem resurrectionis probandam, sed tantum ad consolationem illorum, quos in Purgatorio agitare supponunt: tum quia nunquam in Scriptura Baptismus afflictionem voluntariam, sed tantum aliunde illatam alicubi notat. Sensum loci supra exposuimus. Et veteres in Ecclesia mature pro mortuis orasse fatemur. Sed illi vel putarunt animas nec dum videre faciem Dei ante ultimum judicium; vel martyres resurrecturos, & per mille annos in terra cum Christo regnaturos; vel animas ultimo die per ignem conflagrationis mundi lustratum iri. Quae a Sibyllis, Diaboli vatibus, Christianos haussisse, viri docti, Blondellus inprimis, & Dallaeus de Poen. & Satisf. lib. V. 7. probarunt. Etenim suffragia pro mortuis Scripturarum authoritate destituuntur, imo & damnantur, utpote in quibus tum solus Christus nobis proponitur Paracletus & ἀντίδωρον πίστεως Redemptor perfectus; tum animas defunctorum fidelium illico beatitudine coelesti frui, neque adeo ejusmodi suffragiis indigere, asseritur. Quos Christus non juvat, quis juvare poterit? Praeterea etiam Veteres orarunt pro defunctis omnibus, non quibusdam: & non, ut mortuos ex Purgatorio liberarent, sed ut iis vel in inferis, & in sinu Abrahae solatium, vel in prima resurrectione fortem, vel ut adversus ultimi diei flammas praesidium, vel in terris ad honestam famam, vel ad beatissimam & ultimam resurrectionem jus, vel denique in judicio supremo misericordiam atque clementiam (quae totidem Patrum verba sunt) quaerent & impetrarent. De Purgatorii vero civibus, ne quidem cogitarunt, qui ante Gregorii M. Bedae Angli, visiones & deliria ne quidem orbi Christiano innotuerunt.
units.tr: XXI. Again, when the same Apostle says that some are "baptized for the dead" [ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν], 1 Cor. 15.29, he does not mean that they are baptized with the baptism of tears and repentance, by praying, fasting, and afflicting themselves on behalf of the dead who burn in Purgatory. This is so, first, because the place is very difficult, and in it they seek in vain a triumph for their error; second, because that metaphorical baptism does not serve to prove the hope of resurrection, but only to console those whom they suppose to be troubled in Purgatory; third, because nowhere in Scripture does baptism denote voluntary affliction, but only affliction inflicted from elsewhere. We have set out the sense of the passage above. We admit that the ancients in the Church early prayed for the dead. But they either thought that souls did not yet see the face of God before the last judgment; or that the martyrs would rise again and reign with Christ on earth for a thousand years; or that souls would be purified on the last day by the fire of the world's conflagration. Learned men, above all Blondel, and Dallaeus in On Penance and Satisfaction, bk. V, ch. 7, have shown that these things were drawn by Christians from the Sibyls, the prophetesses of the Devil. Indeed, prayers for the dead are destitute, and even condemned, by the authority of Scripture, since in Scripture Christ alone is set before us as the Paraclete and the perfect Redeemer [ἀντίδωρον πίστεως]; and it is asserted that the souls of the faithful departed at once enjoy heavenly blessedness and so have no need of such prayers. If Christ does not help them, who will be able to help? Moreover, the ancients prayed for all the dead, not for some; and they sought and obtained for them not that they might free the dead from Purgatory, but that they might have comfort "in hell" and "in Abraham's bosom," or strength "in the first resurrection," or protection "against the flames of the last day," or "honourable fame on earth," or a "right to the most blessed and final resurrection," or finally "mercy and clemency in the supreme judgment" (which are as many words of the Fathers). But they did not even think of the citizens of Purgatory, which were not known even to the Christian world before the visions and delusions of Gregory the Great and of Bede the Englishman.

units.la: XXII. Pandenda hic nobis est Purgatorii genuina origo, ejus femina, conceptio & nativitas.
units.tr: XXII. Here we must lay open the genuine origin of Purgatory, its seed, conception and birth.

units.la: Jam olim enim ex Sacris gentilium & Philosophorum scholis in senescentem jam & inclinatum Judaismum ejus femina invecta sunt. Nam & Bellarminus ipse de Purg. lib. I. 11. Philosophos Platonicos, Judaeos, imo & Muhammedanos Purgatorium agnoscentes imprudenter ad partes advocat, quasi videlicet dogmati ὑγιεῖφω idololatricorum & superborum Philosophorum, excaecatorum Judaeorum, & blasphemorum Muhammedanorum consensus veritatis argumentum suppeditet. Pontificio certe & Platonico Purgatorio bene convenire, Forbesius Instruct. Theol. lib. XIII. 11. fusius demonstravit. Post Apostolorum ἀφιξιν ex iisdem Paganismi & Judaismi reliquiis in Ecclesia scripta apocrypha sub nomine Jacobi, Andreae & Hermae spargi coeperunt, ex quibus ceu semine quodam, Purgatorium tantum non concipi coepit. Ex iis enim, aliisque traditionibus fabulosis Patribus dicta nonnulla exciderunt, cujusmodi sunt illa Clementis Alexandrini; omnem locum sive hic, sive alibi poenitentia agatur, misericordia vacare; Origenis, variis post hanc vitam purgationes fingentis, Lactantii, Ambrosii, Hieronymi, quod Sancti juxta atque impii omnes, nullis, ne quidem B. Virgine Maria, Apostolis & Martyribus exceptis, ejusmodi ignem transituri sint, quali omnes olim pii ardebunt; Augustini, dubitantis, non definientis, an animabus de seculo exeuntibus superesset aliquid rerum, quas impensius in mundo dilexerant, desiderium, arcanusque doloris velut ignis. Accessit usus precum pro mortuis, alio licet fine, uti jam vidimus, receptus; sed procedente tempore nascenti Purgatorio mire inserviens. Nec dum tamen Purgatorii fides incessit, cujus nulla in Symbolis & Conciliis veterum vestigia extant, ne quid de argumentis ponderosissimis, quibus Celeb. Dallaeus de Poenit. & Satisf. lib. VI. primitivae saniori Ecclesiae Purgatorium incognitum fuisse, probatum dedit, dicam. Demum tempore Gregorii I. natum, a Beda aliisque fabularum hamaxariis susceptum, incrementa habuit, diuque titubavit, donec accedentibus fictitiis revelationibus & apparitionibus spectrorum purgatorianorum, quibus aurea LegenLegenda, quam Lombardicam historiam vocant, Jacobi de Voragine, Speculum exemplorum; Brigittæ revelationes, &c. scatent, in Concilio Florentino definitum, & in Tridentino sub anathemate sancitum, eam in formam modumque, quo hodie cœca fide eorum, qui superstitionis, & ejerati amoris veritatis poenas luunt, & æruscatorum fraudibus miserè circumscribuntur, recipitur, redactum est.
units.tr: For long ago, indeed, its seed was brought into Judaism, already aging and declining, from the sacred writings of the Gentiles and the schools of the philosophers. For Bellarmine himself, On Purgatory, bk. I, ch. 11, rashly calls to his side the Platonic philosophers, the Jews, and even the Muslims, who acknowledge Purgatory, as if, forsooth, the consensus of idolatrous and proud philosophers, blinded Jews, and blasphemous Muslims supplied an argument for the truth of the doctrine. That the Papist and Platonic Purgatory agree well together, Forbes has shown at greater length in Instructiones theologicae, bk. XIII, ch. 11. After the departure of the Apostles, apocryphal writings under the names of James, Andrew and Hermas began to be scattered in the Church from the same remnants of paganism and Judaism, and from these, as from a certain seed, Purgatory began almost to be conceived. For from these and other fabulous traditions some sayings fell from the Fathers, such as those of Clement of Alexandria: "every place, whether here or elsewhere, where repentance is done, is void of mercy"; of Origen, who imagined various purgations after this life; of Lactantius, Ambrose and Jerome, that all the saints, as well as the wicked, with no exception, not even the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Apostles and the Martyrs, are to pass through such a fire as all the pious once will burn in; of Augustine, who doubted rather than defined, whether souls leaving this world retain some desire for the things they had loved more eagerly in the world, and a hidden grief like a fire. To these was added the practice of prayers for the dead, received, though for another purpose, as we have already seen; but as time went on it served wonderfully the nascent Purgatory. Yet the belief in Purgatory had not yet taken hold, for no trace of it appears in the creeds and councils of the ancients; I will not speak of the very weighty arguments by which the distinguished Dallaeus, in On Penance and Satisfaction, bk. VI, has shown that Purgatory was unknown to the more sound primitive Church. At last, born in the time of Gregory I, taken up by Bede and other mongers of fables, it gained growth, and wavered for a long time, until, with the addition of fictitious revelations and apparitions of purgatorial spectres, with which the Golden Legend, which they call the Lombard History, Jacobus de Voragine's Mirror of Examples, the Revelations of Bridget, etc., abound, it was defined at the Council of Florence, sanctioned under anathema at Trent, and reduced to that form and manner in which it is now received by the blind faith of those who pay the penalties of superstition and of a depraved love of truth, and are miserably cheated by the frauds of the money-grubbing sellers.

units.la: XXIII. Verè Christiana fides est, quòd electi in fide mortui, statim à morte secundum animam à corpore separatam plenè sanctificentur, & ministerio Angelorum in Coelum transferantur. Nam in ipsa morte plena sanctificatio obtingit. Sanctificatio enim in hac vita inchoatur, & paulatim, certis sæpe etiam lentioribus gradibus provehitur; sed in hac vita perficitur nunquam, quia quantisper heic vivimus, peccatum nobis adhæret, & ad peccandum perpetim allicit & irritat. Sed dum animæ corpora sua deserunt, & ad Dominum migrant, plenè à peccato sic expurgantur, ut nihil sordium superfit. Nam qui mortuus est, δεδικαίωται justificatus est à peccato, Rom. VI. 7. quatenus verum & plenum fructum justificationis à peccato consecutus est. Justificamur enim, cùm Christo per fidem inserimur; magis justificamur, cùm arrhabone Spiritus, & argumento renovationis nostræ de redemptione & justificatione certiores reddimur: magis adhuc, quando peccati lucta finitur, & spiritus in gloria consummatur: consummati, quando etiam corpus in gloriam assumitur. Sed justificatio à peccato in morte perficitur, quia per eam lucta cum peccato finitur. Ideo etiam Sancti mortem expetunt, ut à corpore peccati liberentur. Miser ego homo, quis me eripiet ex corpore hoc mortis? Rom. VII. 24. Nam vere in corpore est captivitas πλαυπωσεις miseria & inquietudinis, cujus causa est corpus hoc mortus, non quatenus est corpus mortis, sed, quatenus est corpus peccatorum carnis, sive quia in membris est lex peccati, quæ hominem captivum reddere nititur, ibid. v. 23. Exitus ex illo corpore mortis, ρυσις liberatio ab ἀνδεσμῶν, sive intentatione captivitatis, à lucta cum peccato, utpote per mortem abolito, molestia & inquietudine omni. Si Christus in vobis est, corpus quidem mortuum est propter peccatum, deponendum, finiendum, ex Regno Christi exturbandum & penitus eliminandum; Spiritus autem est vita, hoc est, vivificatur, quia dum corpus moritur, per novæ vitæ alacritatem pugnat cum peccato & concupiscentiis carnis: corpore autem mortuo est vita, & vita fruitur in pace, idque propter justitiam, quæ in Christo nobis donata est, ibid. VIII. 10. Non enim Paulus simpliciter loquitur de vivificante justitia, quam homo in hac vita habet, quia loquitur de vita, quam habet spiritus, hoc est, anima corpori mortuo opposita, & sic sine morte, propter justitiam, quæ est justitia fidei. Quia enim distinguit corpus à spiritu, & non obstante eo, quòd justitia & vita sit totius hominis, tamen mortem corpori, vitam spiritui tribuit, ideo intelligendum est, quòd vita, quam in corpore accepimus, in spiritu continuetur propter justitiam, & post mortem consummetur. Præterea qui vitæ, idem quoque sanctificatio-
units.tr: XXIII. It is true Christian faith that the elect who die in faith are at once, from death, fully sanctified according to the soul separated from the body, and are carried into heaven by the ministry of angels. For in death itself full sanctification is obtained. For sanctification begins in this life and advances gradually, often through slower steps; but it is never perfected in this life, because as long as we live here sin clings to us and constantly entices and provokes us to sin. But when souls leave their bodies and migrate to the Lord, they are so fully purged from sin that no filth remains. For "he who is dead has been justified from sin" [δεδικαίωται], Rom. 6.7, inasmuch as he has obtained the true and full fruit of justification from sin. For we are justified when we are engrafted into Christ through faith; we are more justified when, by the earnest of the Spirit and the proof of our renewal, we are made more certain of redemption and justification; more still when the struggle with sin is ended and the spirit is consummated in glory; and consummated when the body too is taken up into glory. But justification from sin is perfected in death, because through it the struggle with sin is ended. Therefore the saints also desire death, that they may be freed from the body of sin. "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" Rom. 7.24. For truly in the body there is captivity, misery and restlessness, the cause of which is this mortal body, not inasmuch as it is "the body of death," but inasmuch as it is "the body of the flesh of sins," or because "the law of sin is in my members," which strives to make man a captive, ibid. v. 23. Departure from that body of death, deliverance [ῥύσις] from bonds, that is, from the attack of captivity, from the struggle with sin, since it is abolished through death, from every trouble and restlessness. "If Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin," to be laid down, ended, cast out from the kingdom of Christ and utterly eliminated; "but the Spirit is life," that is, it is quickened, because while the body dies it fights with sin and the lusts of the flesh through the vigour of a new life; but with the body dead, it has life, and it enjoys life in peace, and that "because of righteousness," which is given to us in Christ, ibid. 8.10. For Paul does not speak simply of the righteousness that makes alive which a man has in this life, since he speaks of the "life" which the spirit has, that is, the soul, set over against the dead body, and so without death, "because of righteousness," which is the righteousness of faith. For since he distinguishes the body from the spirit, and although justice and life belong to the whole man, nevertheless attributes death to the body and life to the spirit, it must be understood that the life which we receive in the body is continued in the spirit because of righteousness, and is consummated after death. Moreover, he who is the term of life is also the term of sanctification as regards the purging of sin. "Having therefore these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God," 2 Cor. 7.1. But death is the term of life, and its day is better than the day on which a man was born…

units.la: nis terminus est, quoad peccati expurgationem. Habentes has promissiones, purificemus nos ipsos a pollutione carnis & spiritus, consummantes sanctificationem in timore Dei, 2. Cor. VII. 1. Atqui mors vitæ terminus est, cujus etiam dies melior est eo, quo homo natus est, quia peccatum & miseria in eo exuitur, Eccles. VII. 2. Cùm enim homo moritur, exuit corpus peccatorum carnis, Col. II. 11. Sicut enim corpus hominis est corpus mortis, ita etiam est corpus peccatorum, quia si non esset corpus peccatorum, ne quidem corpus mortis esset. Sed unà cum corpore etiam peccatum in corpore habitans, Rom. VII. 20. exui necesse est. Si enim Coelum nihil κοινὸν impurum capit, Apoc. XXI. 27. & morientes in Coelum ilico recipiuntur, necesse est, in morte omnem impuritatem, peccatum omne deponi. Nam unà cum corpore etiam caro, facta mater omnium peccatorum, deponitur, & Sathanas ad peccandum pellicens, sub pedibus morientium conteritur, Rom. XVI. 20. denique mundus, reliquæque mundi illecebræ, quas morientes relinquimus, cessant. Sed purgatio illa à peccato & consummata sanctificatio in corpore, an extra illud fiat, Scriptura aperte nusquam definit. Satis est, quòd tum fit, cùm vinculum unionis personalis corporis & animæ per mortem dissolvitur, atque ita partes hominis essentiales separantur. Sicut enim homines in generatione naturali peccatores formaliter constituuntur, cùm anima & corpus unitur: ita Sancti, soluta illa unione, peccatores esse desinunt. Neque tamen sanctificatio illa consummata in morte, & per eam fit, morti, ut causæ, tribui potest, quia mors est stipendium peccati, Rom. VI. 23. & ultimus hostis, qui aboleri debet, 1. Cor. XV. 26. & omnibus hominibus communis est, Hebr. IX. 27. cùm Sanctificatio ut inchoata, sic consummata salvandorum propria sit; sed merito mortis Christi, & operationi Spiritus S. accepta referri debet. Christus enim Ecclesiam sibi ipsi sistit gloriosam, non habentem rugam & macnlam, Ephes. V. 26. 27. & Deus pacis sanctificat ὁλοτελῶς totos, 1. Thess. V. 23.
units.tr: ...is the end of sanctification, as far as the cleansing from sin is concerned. Having these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from all defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God, 2 Cor. 7:1. But death is the end of life, and its day is better than the day of one's birth, because sin and misery are put off in it, Eccles. 7:2. For when a man dies, he puts off the body of the sins of the flesh, Col. 2:11. Just as the body of a man is a body of death, so it is also a body of sins, for if it were not a body of sins it would not even be a body of death. But sin dwelling in the body, Rom. 7:20, must be put off together with the body. For if heaven admits nothing unclean [κοινὸν], Rev. 21:27, and those who die are at once received into heaven, then all impurity and all sin must be laid aside in death. For together with the body the flesh is also laid aside, which has become the mother of all sins, and Satan, who entices to sin, is crushed under the feet of the dying, Rom. 16:20. Lastly, the world and the other allurements of the world, which we leave behind when we die, cease. But Scripture nowhere clearly defines whether that purging from sin and that perfected sanctification take place in the body or outside it. It is enough that it happens when the bond of personal union between body and soul is dissolved by death, and so the essential parts of man are separated. For just as men are formally constituted sinners in natural generation, when soul and body are united, so the saints, once that union is dissolved, cease to be sinners. Yet that perfected sanctification in death, and the process by which it comes, cannot be ascribed to death as its cause, because death is the wages of sin, Rom. 6:23, and the last enemy, which must be abolished, 1 Cor. 15:26, and it is common to all men, Heb. 9:27. Sanctification, both as begun and as perfected, belongs properly to the saved, and must be referred to the merit of Christ's death and to the working of the Holy Spirit. For Christ presents the Church to himself glorious, not having spot or wrinkle, Eph. 5:26-27, and the God of peace sanctifies wholly [ὁλοτελῶς] the whole person, 1 Thess. 5:23.

units.la: XXIV. Eadem anima sic consummata & in morte plenè sanctificata sine mora omni in Coelum, locum quietis, beatitudinis & gloriæ transfertur. Nam dissoluta domo tabernaculi terrestri, ædificium habemus ex Deo, domum non manufactam, æternam in Coelis, 2. Cor. V. 1. quem locum supra exposuimus.
units.tr: XXIV. The same soul, thus perfected and fully sanctified in death, is without delay transferred to heaven, the place of rest, blessedness and glory. For when the earthly tabernacle, our house, is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens, 2 Cor. 5:1, which place we have explained above.

units.la: Nam quòd moram interponi, ob conditionem additam: Si tamen vestiti, non nudi, charitate perfecta destituti, inveniamur, ibid. v. 3. Purgatorii assertores regerunt, jejunum nimis est. Lubrica enim nimis & fallacis spei nutricula oratio S. Pauli fuisset, si dicens: Novimus, ἐὰν quando domus terrestris dissoluta fuerit, ædificium ex Deo habituri sumus, moram eamque magis vel minus durabilem imò aliquando usque ad diem judicii extractam, subintellexisset. An hoc est ædificium ex Deo in Christo habere, ἐὰν quando, adeóque statim atque, vel si (ita ut nulla conditio alia intermedia locum habere possit) terrestris domus soluta fuerit, Sed Apostolus v. 8. exitum ex corpore immediate cum ἐνδημῆσαι πρὸς τὸν Κύριον domestica mansione apud Dominum conjungit, dicens: Confidimus mus magis, & beneplacitum habemus potiùs migrare ex corpore & domi manere apud Dominum. Neque planè in verbis: An etiam induti, non nudi reperiemur, vers. 3. conditio talis inest, si discedentes hinc non sint nudi, seu charitate privati, sed perfectè justi reperiantur. Non enim in verbis illis conditio aliqua constituitur, sub qua in fide exeuntes ex corpore cœleste habitaculum subeant; sed causa gemitus, seu desiderii ἐπενδύσεως superindutionis indicatur, solicitudo nempe de communione cum cœlestibus in hac vita habenda. Gemitus enim nostri excitantur ea cogitatione, quæ nunquam nos deserit, an & vestiti Christo & ejus justitia, non nudi reperiamur. Nemo enim superinduet, qui non priùs Christum & justitiam ejus induit; & dum hoc cogitamus, suspiramus. Non ergo nuditas culpæ venia, participatio culpæ venialis, sed Christi, & justitiæ ejus carentia est. Nemo autem sic nudus in fide hinc migrat, & vestitus Christo esse poterit, qui graviora etiam peccata in morte deponenda habet. Sed alia etiam sunt, quæ in fide defunctos recta Cœli ingredi demonstrant. Sic enim David loquitur: In manum tuam commendo spiritum meum. Redemisti me, ô Domine Deus verax, Psal. XXXI. 6. Quæ verba licut emortualia Christi fuerunt, Luc. XXIII. 46. ita omnium in Christo morientium sunt, & esse possunt. Sicut autem Christus spiritum suum Deo Patri commendans, ilico in Paradisum receptus est: ita fideles omnes, Christi capitis membra, & justitiæ ejusdem per fidem participes, suum Deo Patri spiritum vera fide committentes, ilico in paradisum recipiuntur, & in manu Patris, cœlestíque adeò gloria sunt. Certè Christus ipse latroni dixit: Hodie mecum eris in Paradiso, Luc. XXIII. 42. 43. non utique terrestri, in quo Adamus integer fuit, & cujus post Adami exilium mentio nulla in Scripturis extat: & in quo existere animam corpore solutam oppidò absurdum est. Quorsum enim? Aut quomodo illa paradiso fruitura est, cujus deliciæ merè corporales describuntur. Neque etiam introitus ille in Paradisum ad ultimum usque resurrectionis diem differri potest, quia sic nulla vis esset illius σήμερον hodie diserte nominati. Neque enim uspiam hodie significat totum illum temporis tractum, qui à Christo passo ad ultimum usque judicium decurrit; etsi plenitudo temporum tractus ille Gal. IV. 4. dicatur. Neque scitè constituunt, qui sic dictum pertendunt: Hodie dico tibi; non autem: Hodie mecum eris; quia in temporis, quo Christus id locutus est, annuntiatione nullum omnino pondus est. Lazarus certè mortuus ab Angelis in finum Abrahæ deportatus est, Luc. XVI. 22. Qui sinus ibi erat, ubi Abrahamus, qui in Regno Cœlorum, Matth. VIII. 11. ponitur; & locus erat παράκλησις consolationis, post exantlatas hujus vitæ miserias, Luc. XVI. 25. qui nonnisi in Cœlo est. Diserte inprimis S. Paulus spem suæ post mortem in Cœlum receptionis testatus est, dicens: Desiderium habeo εἰς τὸ ἀναλῦσαι ad solvendum, discedendum hinc; (quo modo naves solvere dicuntur, quando discedunt ex portu) & esse cum Christo, Phil. I. 23. conjunguntur enim tanquam connexa. Dissolvi seu solvere ex corpore, & esse cum Christo,
units.tr: As for the claim that a delay is interposed on account of the added condition, If indeed we shall be found clothed, not naked, destitute of perfect charity, ibid. v. 3, the defenders of Purgatory reply that this is far too thin a foundation. The words of St Paul would be a slippery and deceptive comfort if, when he said, "We know that when the earthly house is dissolved we shall have a building from God," he had silently meant an interval, one of greater or lesser length, even sometimes extended to the day of judgment. Is this to have a building from God in Christ, "when" [ἐὰν quando], and so immediately as soon as, or "if" (so that no other intervening condition can apply), the earthly house has been dissolved? But the Apostle in v. 8 joins departure from the body directly with being at home with the Lord [ἐνδημῆσαι πρὸς τὸν Κύριον], saying: We are confident, and we have good pleasure rather to depart from the body and to dwell at home with the Lord. Nor does such a condition lie in the words, "If indeed we shall be found clothed, not naked," v. 3, namely, that those departing hence are not naked, that is, deprived of charity, but are found perfectly righteous. For no condition is laid down in those words under which those who depart in faith enter the heavenly dwelling. Rather, the cause of groaning, or of the desire for superinduction [ἐπενδύσεως], is indicated, namely, anxiety to have communion with heavenly things in this life. For our groanings are stirred by the thought that never leaves us, whether we shall be found clothed with Christ and his righteousness, and not naked. For no one puts on something over, who has not first put on Christ and his righteousness; and while we think on this, we sigh. Nakedness, therefore, is not the pardon of guilt or the participation in venial guilt, but the lack of Christ and of his righteousness. Now no one who departs hence naked in this sense, and in faith, can be clothed with Christ, if he still has graver sins to be laid aside in death. But there are other things too which show that those who die in faith enter straight into heaven. Thus David speaks: Into your hand I commit my spirit. You have redeemed me, O Lord God of truth, Ps. 31:6. As these words were the dying words of Christ, Luke 23:46, so they are and can be the words of all who die in Christ. Just as Christ, committing his spirit to God the Father, was at once received into paradise, so all the faithful, members of Christ the head and sharers through faith in his righteousness, committing their spirit to God the Father in true faith, are at once received into paradise, and are in the Father's hand, and so in heavenly glory. Certainly Christ himself said to the thief: Today you will be with me in Paradise, Luke 23:42-43. This was surely not earthly paradise, in which Adam was whole, and of which there is no mention in Scripture after Adam's exile; and in which it is utterly absurd for a soul to exist when separated from the body. For to what end? Or how would it enjoy a paradise whose delights are described as purely bodily? Nor can that entrance into Paradise be deferred until the last day of resurrection, for then the word today [σήμερον], expressly named, would have no force. For nowhere does today signify that whole stretch of time which runs from Christ's passion to the last judgment, although that stretch is called the fullness of time, Gal. 4:4. Nor do those reason well who press the saying thus, "Today I say to you," and not "Today you will be with me," because the time of the announcement at which Christ spoke it has absolutely no weight. Certainly Lazarus, when he died, was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom, Luke 16:22. That bosom was where Abraham was, who is placed in the kingdom of heaven, Matt. 8:11; and it was a place of consolation [παράκλησις], after the miseries of this life had been endured, Luke 16:25, which exists only in heaven. Above all, St Paul clearly testified to his hope of being received into heaven after death, saying: "I have a desire for to be loosed" (ad solvendum), that is, to depart hence (as ships are said to be loosed when they leave harbour), "and" to be with Christ, Phil. 1:23. For these are joined as connected things: to be dissolved or loosed from the body, and to be with Christ,

units.la: tanquam termini à quo, & ad quem, ideòque immediatè oppositi; velut cùm ægritudini succedit sanitas, imò vitæ mors, & rursus morti vita. Desiderabat ille sicut discedere in præsens, non post multa secula: ita esse cum Christo non post aliquot annorum chiliadas, sed quam primùm. Neque Apostoli verba de solventibus animabus, quæ puræ sunt, non quæ reliquam labem habent, intelligi possunt, nisi dicamus, vel hominem esse posse absque peccato, vel in Christi sanguine non esse propitiationem & purificationem ab omnibus peccatis, 1. Joh. I. 7. Accedit, quòd defunctorum spiritus sunt spiritus consummati. Accessistis πνευμάτα δικαίων τετελειωμένων ad spiritus justorum consummatorum, Hebr. XII. 23. Omnes ergo, qui in terris agere desierunt, secundum spiritum consummati intelliguntur. Spiritus enim non alii intelliguntur, quàm qui liberati sunt à corpore; & sine dubio ii, qui paulò ante etiam à corpore liberati sunt. Qui τετελειωμένοι consummati dicuntur, vocabulo repetito à sacris ritibus; quibus qui profani erant, in ordinem τῶν μυστῶν admittebantur. Hi ergo non amplius exulantes aut separati à commercio cœlesti, sed in illud admilli innuuntur. Denique vox ex ipso Cœlo scribere jussit: Beati sunt mortui in Domino morientes, ἀπάρτι à nunc. Etiam, dicit Spiritus, ut requiescant à laboribus suis, Apoc. XIV. 13. Ubi ἀπάρτι à nunc notat vel illud ipsum temporis instans, quo in Domino moriuntur illi & beati prædicantur; vel certè temporis illius, quo ob instantes gravissimas persecutiones, quibus patientiam Sanctorum perspicuam fore v. 12. prædictum est, satius erat mori, quàm vivere, initium. Qui verò inde ab eo tempore moriebantur, eos Spiritus Dei ipse ἀναπαύεσθαι requiescere à laboribus suis, non amplius laborare, nedum cruciari dixit. Neque etiam Spiritus S. de Martyribus, quos rectà cœlum petere, neque aliquid purgandum habere Pontificii largiuntur, sed de iis potiùs, quibus ob persecutiones instantes, vel præsentes, satius erat mori, quàm vivere, & vivendo certaminum illorum aleam ambiguam subire. Sed & de iis Spiritus S. loquitur, qui in Domino moriuntur, hoc est, quos Deus Pater Christo Domino salvandos dedit, qui morientes à Christo non separantur, sed Christo animas suas vera fide commendant, quod fidelium omnium est, sive illi Martyres sint, sive non.
units.tr: as the terms from which and to which, and therefore immediately opposed, as when sickness gives way to health, or indeed death to life, and again life to death. He desired to depart at once, at present, not after many ages; so too to be with Christ, not after some thousands of years, but as soon as possible. Nor can the Apostle's words about souls being loosed, which are pure and not those that still bear some stain, be understood unless we say either that a man can be without sin, or that in the blood of Christ there is no propitiation and cleansing from all sins, 1 John 1:7. Add that the spirits of the departed are spirits made perfect. You have come to the spirits of just men made perfect [πνευμάτα δικαίων τετελειωμένων], Heb. 12:23. All, therefore, who have ceased to act on earth are understood to be perfected in spirit. For spirits are understood to be none other than those who are freed from the body, and without doubt those too who were freed from the body a little earlier. Those who are called perfected [τετελειωμένοι], a word repeated from sacred rites, into whose order the uninitiated were admitted as initiates [τῶν μυστῶν]. These, then, are indicated as no longer exiles or separated from heavenly fellowship, but as admitted to it. Finally, a voice from heaven itself bade him write: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, from now on" [ἀπάρτι]. "Yes," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labours," Rev. 14:13. Here "from now on" [ἀπάρτι] denotes either that very instant of time in which they die in the Lord and are pronounced blessed, or certainly the beginning of that time, when, because of the imminent and most grievous persecutions by which the patience of the saints would be made manifest (v. 12), it was better to die than to live. But those who died from that time on, the Spirit of God said, rest [ἀναπαύεσθαι] from their labours, no longer labouring, much less tormented. Nor does the Holy Spirit speak of martyrs, whom the Papists grant go straight to heaven with nothing to be purged. He speaks rather of those for whom, because of persecutions impending or present, it was better to die than to live, and by living to undergo the uncertain hazard of those contests. But the Holy Spirit also speaks of those who die in the Lord, that is, whom God the Father has given to Christ the Lord to be saved, who in dying are not separated from Christ, but commit their souls to Christ in true faith. This is the case of all the faithful, whether they are martyrs or not.

units.la: XXV. Improbamus proin Veterum passivum illum errorem, sinus quosdam imaginantium, in quos omnes animæ redemptæ, procul à Cœlis ablegarentur. Quo in numero ipse Stapletonus Def. Ecc. auth. cap. 2. Tertullianum, Irenæum, Originem, Chrysostomum, Theodoretum, Oecumenium, Theophylactum, Ambrosium, Clementem Rom. Bernhardum recensèt. Quibus Augustinum, Lactantium, Justinum Martyrem, Victorium, Euthymium addere licet. Quorum etiam nonnulli animas illas ἐν ἅδῃ apud inferos collocarunt, inferorum nomine intelligentes non locum tormenti, sed communionem, sive animarum separatarum statum: vel locum invisibilem à Deo definitum, quem alii infra, alii intra terram, alii extra mundum, alii hominibus incognitum putant. Quibus sic venia humanæ infirmitatis firmitatis
units.tr: XXV. We therefore reject that old, passive error of imagining certain bosoms into which all redeemed souls are sent away, far from heaven. Stapleton, in Def. Eccl. auth. cap. 2., counts among this number Tertullian, Irenaeus, Origen, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius, Theophylact, Ambrose, Clement of Rome and Bernard. To these we may add Augustine, Lactantius, Justin Martyr, Victorinus and Euthymius. Some of them also placed those souls in Hades [ἐν ἅδῃ] among the dead, understanding by "the underworld" not a place of torment but a fellowship, or the state of separated souls; or else an invisible place appointed by God, which some think lies below the earth, others within the earth, others outside the world, and others unknown to men. To these men some indulgence may be granted on account of human weakness, yet the thing itself is constantly to be rejected.

units.la: Veterum, sinus quosdam extra Cœlum, in quos animæ post mortem relegentur, fingentium, error elidi-tur. firmitatis dari potest, ut tamen res ipsa constanter improbetur. Sed habuerunt illi erroris sui ατεφάσεις quasdam, velut, quòd merces operariis sub vesperam simul omnibus reddita est, Matth. XX. 8. Sed potest vespera esse cuique suus novissimus dies. Nam illud de convocatis operariis circumstantia est parabolæ propria; quia nimirum Paterfamilias soleat simul operarios in vineam mittere; at in Ecclesiam successivè. Si tamen dies resurrectionis intelligatur, non sequetur mercedem ante diem illam nullam omnino dari, quia positio unius non est alterius non oppositi destructio. Et in die mortis singulis animabus merces dari potest; & dari potest simul omnibus, non quoad spiritum duntaxat, sed etiam quoad corpus, in die resurrectionis. Illi porrò, qui non accepisse promissiones dicuntur, Hebr. XI. 39. veteres Patres, promissum Christum in carne non videntes, fuerunt. Qui ipsi tamen debellarunt Regna, exercuerunt justitiam, ἐπιτυχον ἐπαγγελιῶν assecuti sunt promissiones, ibid. vers. 23. eas nempe, quæ limitem hujus vitæ supergressæ sunt. Et similes Christo erimus, cùm apparuerit in secundo adventu, quia videbimus eum sicuti est, 1. Joh. III. 2. non quòd antea quàm apparebit, nullo modo similes ei futuri simus; sicut quod nunc nos esse filios Dei, non obstat, quò minùs etiam tunc futuri simus, & magis id apparituum sit: sed quòd id, quod priùs occultum erat, apparente Christo, futurum manifestius est. Præterea φυλακὴ carcer ille, in quo spiritus ἀπειθῆσαι immorrigeri tempore Petri fuerunt, 1. Petr. III. 19. non locus tertius animarum, inprimis fidelium, quibus carcer ille non deputatur: sed infernus damnatorum est, qui servantur ad pœnam in diem judicii, 2. Petr. II. 9. quomodo de Angelorum, qui peccarunt, custodia, ibid. vers. 4. loquitur. Manifesta justos inter & immorigeros antithesis est. Hi sunt πνεύματα ἐν φυλακῇ spiritus in carcere: illi sunt πνεύματα δικαίων τετελειωμένων spiritus justorum consummatorum, Hebr. XII. 23. & vivunt spiritu propter justitiam, Rom. VIII. 10. Denique nequicquam Calvinus ad partes à Bellarmino aliisque vocatur, quasi & ille animas defunctorum extra Cœlum collocaverit. Quod verbis ejus nonnullis obtorto collo raptus comprobare satagunt. Reprehendit ille Instit. lib. III. cap. 25:6. eos, qui se torquent disputando, quem locum occupent animæ, & an cœlesti gloria jam fruantur, nec ne. Atqui, inquit ille, stultum & temerarium est, de rebus incognitis altiùs inquirere, quàm Deus nobis scire permittat. Scriptura ubi dixit: Christum illis præsentem esse, & eas recipere in paradisum, ut consolationem percipiant, &c. non ultra progreditur. Quis jam doctor & magister, quod Deus celavit, nobis patefaciet? De loco non minùs inepta & futilis est quæstio, quando scimus, non eam animæ esse dimensionem, quæ est corporis. Sed collatis ejus in 2. Cor. V. verbis, quibus animabus fidelium ædificium in Cœlis assignat, satis apparet, noluisse eum præjudicare communi veritati, quòd locus, quò animæ migrant, Cœlum sit: sed proscribere tantùm curiosas quæstiones Scholasticorum, de animarum essentiæ commensuratione ad loci dimensiones corpori convenientes, voluisse.
units.tr: The error of the ancients, who imagined certain bosoms outside heaven into which souls are relegated after death, is refuted. Yet they had some supporting arguments of their error, such as that the wages were paid to the workers in the evening, all of them together, Matt. 20:8. But the evening can be each person's last day. For the calling of the workers together is a detail proper to the parable, since the householder usually sends his workers into the vineyard all at once, whereas the Church receives its members one by one. If, however, the day of resurrection is meant, it does not follow that no wages are given at all before that day, because the positing of one thing is not the destruction of another thing that is not opposed to it. On the day of death wages can be given to individual souls, and they can be given to all together, not only as to spirit but also as to body, on the day of resurrection. Moreover, those who are said not to have received the promises, Heb. 11:39, were the ancient Fathers, who did not see the promised Christ in the flesh. Yet these same men subdued kingdoms, worked righteousness, and obtained promises [ἐπιτυχον ἐπαγγελιῶν], ibid. v. 23, namely those promises that went beyond the limit of this life. And we shall be like Christ, when he shall appear at his second coming, for we shall see him as he is, 1 John 3:2. This does not mean that before he appears we shall in no way be like him, just as our now being sons of God does not prevent us from being so even more then, and the appearing is more clearly to be expected; rather, what was hidden before will be more plainly manifest when Christ appears. Furthermore, the prison [φυλακὴ] in which the spirits were disobedient [ἀπειθῆσαι] in the time of Peter, 1 Pet. 3:19, is not a third place for the souls of the dead, especially of believers, to whom that prison is not assigned. It is the hell of the damned, who are kept unto punishment until the day of judgment, 2 Pet. 2:9, just as the passage speaks of the custody of the angels who sinned, ibid. v. 4. The antithesis between the just and the disobedient is clear. These are spirits in prison [πνεύματα ἐν φυλακῇ]; those are spirits of just men made perfect [πνεύματα δικαίων τετελειωμένων], Heb. 12:23, and live in the Spirit because of righteousness, Rom. 8:10. Finally, it is in vain that Calvin is summoned by Bellarmine and others to their side, as if he too had placed the souls of the dead outside heaven. They try to prove this by twisting some of his words. In Instit. lib. III. cap. 25:6. he rebukes those who torment themselves by disputing which place the souls occupy, and whether they already enjoy heavenly glory or not. But, he says, it is foolish and rash to inquire deeply into unknown things beyond what God permits us to know. Scripture, when it said that Christ is present with them and that they are received into paradise, so that they may receive comfort, etc., goes no further. Who now, as teacher and master, will reveal to us what God has hidden? The question of place is no less foolish and trifling, since we know that the soul does not have the same dimension as the body." But when his words in 2 Cor. 5, in which he assigns a building in the heavens to the souls of believers, are compared, it is clear enough that he did not wish to prejudice the common truth that the place to which souls migrate is heaven; he only wished to banish the curious questions of the Schoolmen about how the essence of souls is measured against the dimensions of place suited to the body.

units.la: XXVI. Fuit introitus animarum separatarum in Cœlum.
units.tr: XXVI. The separated souls entered heaven.

units.la: Status earundem est, quòd gloria cœlesti fruuntur, & eadem fruuntur, qua postliminio cum corpore unitæ in æternum fruentur. Scriptura enim statum animarum mox à funere beatum & gloriosum describit. Ilico enim præteriens levitas afflictionis nostræ, &c. æternum pondus gloriæ nobis operatur, 2.Cor.IV.17. Mors enim, quæ æternitatis veluti janua & vestibulum est, fidelibus in lucrum deputatur. Mihi vivere Christus, & mori lucrum est, Phil. I. 21. Licèt enim lucrum sit, Christo vivere: tamen quæstus & lucrum majoris boni est mori Christo, sive in Christo. Nam qui in Christo, velut Domino suo moriuntur, illi beati sunt, & ab operibus suis ærumnosis quiescunt, Apoc. XIV. 13. Nec leve illud est, quòd Deus, etiam post fata, fidelium Deus & Pater appellari vult, Matth. XXII. 32. Nam id sine eorum felicitate summa intelligi non potest. Potiorem, hoc est, cœlestem civitatem expetunt. Quapropter Deum non pudet eorum, & cognominari Deus eorum. Paraverat enim iis civitatem, Hebr. XI. 16. Unde & apud Christum esse, atque illud κρεῖσσον πολλῷ μᾶλλον multo melius esse, quam in carne vivere, Phil. I. 23. dicitur. Insana fuerit illa optio, si non cum feliciore læti-tia & consolatione solidiori fideles consolationes præsentes, per quas hic in carne habent fomitem gaudii, quo semper gaudentes, Phil. IV. 4. omnem doloris sensum abundè vincunt, Rom. VIII. 37. 1. Pet. I. 8. Jac. I. 2. commutant. Et quanquam mortalis corporis exuvias ponant, non tamen sic nudantur, sed potiori paludamento, cœlesti domicilio superinduuntur, 2. Cor. V. 2. Melior enim est dies mortis die nativitatis, Eccles. VII. 2. Qua porrò in re beatitudo, quies, consolatio & gloria cœlestis animarum separatarum consistat, inferiùs, ubi de vita æterna fusiùs agendum fuerit, dicemus.
units.tr: Their state is that they enjoy heavenly glory, and they enjoy the same glory which, once reunited with the body by a return to life, they will enjoy forever. Scripture describes the state of souls as blessed and glorious straight after death. For the momentary lightness of our affliction, etc., works for us an eternal weight of glory, 2 Cor. 4:17. Death, which is as it were the gate and threshold of eternity, is counted as gain for the faithful. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain, Phil. 1:21. For although to live in Christ is gain, yet the profit and gain of a greater good is to die in Christ, or in Christ. For those who die in Christ, as in the Lord, are blessed, and rest from their labours, Rev. 14:13. It is also no small thing that God, even after death, wishes to be called the God and Father of the faithful, Matt. 22:32, for this cannot be understood without their supreme happiness. They desire a better, that is, a heavenly country. Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city, Heb. 11:16. Hence it is also said that to be with Christ and that it is far better [κρεῖσσον πολλῷ μᾶλλον], as Paul says, to be in the flesh, Phil. 1:23. That would be a mad choice if the faithful did not, with a happier joy and a firmer consolation, exchange the present comforts, through which here in the flesh they have the fuel of joy, by which always rejoicing, Phil. 4:4, they abundantly overcome every sense of pain, Rom. 8:37, 1 Pet. 1:8, Jas. 1:2. And although they lay aside the remains of the mortal body, they are not thus stripped, but clothed upon with a better garment, a heavenly dwelling, 2 Cor. 5:2. For the day of death is better than the day of birth, Eccl. 7:2. In what the blessedness, rest, consolation, and heavenly glory of separated souls consist, we shall say further on, where we must treat of eternal life more fully.

units.la: XXVII. Sed circa statum animæ separatæ errores non unius generis profligandi veniunt.
units.tr: XXVII. But errors about the state of the separated soul are not all of one kind and must be overthrown in different ways.

units.la: Ante omnia enim intolerandus ille Anabaptistarum & Socinianorum est, quo illi quidem animas dormire & quiescere, longo quasi somno sopitas, usque ad resurrectionem corporum, quæ illis ψυχοπαννυχία appellatur: Hi verò non tam dubitant, num sensu aliquo præditæ sint, quàm negant, eas aliquid agere, vel ante conjunctionem suam cum corpore spirituali, cœlesti beatitudine frui. Sed animas fidelium separatas in Cœlo vivere, & non inerti somno sopiri, sed vigilare, aliquid agere, continuis laudibus Deum & Salvatorem suum celebrare, Scriptura manifeste testatur. Disertè enim S. Paulus affirmat, corpore propter peccatum mortuo, spiritum esse vitam propter justitiam, Rom. VIII. 10. & Deum illarum Deum esse, qui tamen non mortuorum sed viventium Deus sit, Matth. XXII. 32. Somnus autem tam longus inprimis, non tam vita quàm mors, saltem lurida mortis imago est. Etenim vivere est ἐνεργεῖν operari; cùm & ipsa corporis, nedum spiritus vita perpetua quædam motio, perpetuus quidam actus sit. Et vita illa, quam facienti Lex promittit, & quam fideles propter Christum facientem, hoc est, Legis justitiam implentem, in Cœlo assequuntur, nihil aliud quàm fruitio & visio Dei beatifica, ad
units.tr: First of all there is the intolerable doctrine of the Anabaptists and Socinians. Those hold that souls sleep and rest, lulled as if by a long sleep until the resurrection of the bodies, which is called psychopannychia [ψυχοπαννυχία]. These do not so much doubt whether the souls have any sense at all as deny that they do anything, or enjoy heavenly blessedness, before they are joined again to a spiritual, heavenly body. But Scripture clearly testifies that the souls of the faithful live in heaven, are not dulled by lifeless sleep, but are awake, active, and ceaselessly praise God and their Saviour. St Paul plainly affirms that, although the body is dead because of sin, the spirit is life because of righteousness (Rom. 8:10), and that God is their God, who is not God of the dead but of the living (Matt. 22:32). Moreover, such a long sleep is above all not so much life as death, or at least a pale image of death. For to live is to be active [ἐνεργεῖν], since even the life of the body, let alone of the spirit, is a kind of continual motion and perpetual activity. And that life which the Law promises to the one who does these things, and which the faithful attain in heaven through Christ, who does them, that is, who fulfils the righteousness of the Law, is nothing other than the blessed enjoyment and vision of God, to which nature itself led man to aspire.

units.la: Status animæ à corpore separatæ gloriosus est.
units.tr: The state of the soul separated from the body is glorious.

units.la: Neque darmire eas, adversus Anabaptistas, neque nihil omnino agere, adversus Socinianos astruitur. ad quam appetendam ipsa natura hominem ducebat, est. Neque certè anima per mortem corporis in deteriorem, sed in meliorem & perfectiorem statum pervenit, quia liberatur à corpore mortis & peccatorum, quæ impedimenta rectè operandi, & Deum perfectè diligendi sunt. Fidelis enim non venit in judicium, sed ex morte transit εἰς τὸν ζωὴν in vitam, laetiorem, beatiorem consummatam, Joh. V.24. Cùmque anima diversæ originis sit à corpore, & non minùs actiones inorganicas extra corpus quàm organicas in corpore, imò in ipso etiam corpore actiones inorganicas, cujusmodi sunt cogitatio de Deo & rebus Divinis, intelligentia principiorum, &c. exerceat, nil planè obstare potest, quò minus extra corpus degens operetur, intelligat, amet, & Deo suo perfectè fruatur. Summa porrò consolationis nostræ, quòd morientes sumus Domini. Sive vivimus, sive morimur, Domini sumus, Rom. XIV.8. Nostra jactura Christi jactura est, & nostra conservatio ipsius divitiæ, sive conservatio hæreditatis ipsius est, quia pro nobis mortuus est, & ad hunc finem resurrexit. Si igitur spiritus noster post mortem corporis iners & ἀέργης est, nec quidquam Christo, eum celebrando & glorificando, prodest; & sibi ipsi etiam deest, quàm hæc vana hæreditas, quàm infrugiferæ hæ divitiæ sunt! ideo Christus dicit: Ego sum resurrectio & vita. Qui credit in me, etiamsi moriatur, vivet in anima donec resurget, & caro nunquam moritura deinceps. Et omnis vivens & credens in me, non morietur in seculum, Joh.XI.25.26. Vita autem animæ non tantùm est superstitatio animæ post mortem in qualicunque statu, sed in statu animæ optabili & felice. Non ergo, cùm dicitur, non morietur, sensus is duntaxat est, non extinguetur, non desinet esse, sed, non perdet laetitiam & charitatem suam. Nam animæ vita charitas, & perfectio ejus vitæ laetitia est. Charitas autem vita est, quia est amor ejus, quod amabile est, & ad quod amandum homo natura factus est; quod cùm obtinuit, nihil est quod desideret amplius. Hæc vita animæ est, quamdiu ea bono suo nondum potitur, sed id quasi eminus videt, & ex parte cognoscit. Ubi verò bono suo potitur, tum charitas est cum laetitia non in spe, sed in specie, Rom. VIII.24. 2.Cor. V.7. Inprimis animarum dormitionem Christus perimit in parabola historica Divitis & Lazari, illum post mortem constituens in inferno, in tormentis, seu cruciatibus; hunc in sinu Abrahæ, in consolatione, Luc. XVI.22.23.25. Licet enim dialogus ille Abrahamum inter & Lazarum parabolicus sit; tamen sermo de statu animarum post mortem corporis, ante diem extremi judicii, necnon loco gemino, altero laetitiae felicis, altero infelicis doloris & cruciat°, historicus est; quia circumstantiae illae de corporis, morte & sepultura, v.22.23. de superstitibus mortui agnatis, v.27.28. de ipsis concessa sufficienti ad conversionis normam & stimulum, Scriptura Mosis & Prophetarum; dum interim dives ille cruciabatur, augente cruciatum etiam anxietate illa de cruciandis quandoque fratribus, v.29.30.31. nullo schemate alio trahi possunt. Eodem Johannis visiones faciunt. Ille enim aperto sigillo quinto sub altari vidit animas martyrum propter sermonem Dei, & propter testimonium, quod habuerunt, clamantes voce magna: Quousque Domine, Sancte & verax, non judicas & vindicas sanguinem nostrum, &c. Apoc. VI.9.10. Similis illa vox Sanctorum coelestium Presbyterorum & animalium applaudentium Babylonis excidio, & adorantium Deum, qui sedet in throno, ibid. XIX.1.4. Cùmque Sancti post mortem ἰσάγγελοι similes Angelis sint, Matth. XXII.30. Luc. XX.35.36. & Angeli Deum sine fine celebrent, Esaj. VI.3. certè inertes nunquam dormient, animabus Sanctorum idem convenire necesse est. Denique somnus corporis; ἀέργεια cadaveris, non spiritus est; & somnus atque ἀναισθησία animæ in morte φιλοψυχῆς, & amantes hujus seculi facit; & beatitudo otiosorum non Christianorum, sed Epicureorum beatitudo est.
units.tr: It is established that souls neither sleep, against the Anabaptists, nor do nothing at all, against the Socinians. Nor does the soul at death pass into a worse state, but into a better and more perfect one, since it is freed from the body of death and from sins, which are the hindrances to acting rightly and loving God perfectly. For the believer does not come into judgment, but passes out of death into life [εἰς τὸν ζωὴν], a happier, more blessed and fulfilled life (John 5:24). Since the soul is of a different origin from the body, and exercises non-bodily acts outside the body no less than bodily acts within it, indeed even within the body exercises non-bodily acts, such as thinking about God and divine things, understanding first principles, and so on, nothing at all can prevent it from acting, understanding, loving, and perfectly enjoying its God while living outside the body. The sum of our comfort is that we are the Lord's when we die; whether we live or die, we are the Lord's (Rom. 14:8). Our loss is Christ's loss, and our preservation is his riches, or the preservation of his inheritance, because he died for us and rose again to this end. If, then, our spirit after the death of the body were idle and inactive, and contributed nothing to Christ by praising and glorifying him, how empty would this inheritance be, how unfruitful these riches! Therefore Christ says: "I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me, even if he dies, will live" in the soul until it rises again, and afterwards in a flesh that will never die again; "and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die" (John 11:25-26). But the life of the soul is not merely the survival of the soul after death in any state whatever, but in a state that is desirable and happy. So when it is said "will never die", the meaning is not merely "will not be extinguished, will not cease to exist", but "will not lose its joy and its love." For love is the life of the soul, and the perfection of that life is joy. Love is life because it is the love of what is lovable, and of that which man was made by nature to love; and once he has obtained it, he has nothing further to desire. This is the life of the soul for as long as it has not yet possessed its good, but sees it, as it were, from afar, and knows in part. But when it possesses its good, then there is love with joy, not in hope but in sight (Rom. 8:24; 2 Cor. 5:7). Above all, Christ destroys the sleep of souls in the historical parable of the rich man and Lazarus, placing the one after death in hell, in torments or agonies, and the other in Abraham's bosom, in comfort (Luke 16:22-23, 25). For although the dialogue between Abraham and Lazarus is parabolic, the account of the state of souls after the death of the body, before the day of the last judgment, and of the two places, one of happy joy and the other of unhappy pain and torment, is historical. This is because those circumstances, of the body's death and burial (vv. 22-23), of the living relatives of the dead man (vv. 27-28), and of the Law and the Prophets given to them as a sufficient rule and goad for conversion (vv. 29-31), while the rich man was tormented, with his anguish increased by the thought of his brothers who might one day be tormented, cannot be drawn into any other figure. John's visions have the same character. When he opened the fifth seal, he saw under the altar the souls of the martyrs, because of the word of God and the testimony they had, crying out with a loud voice: How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood? etc. (Rev. 6:9-10). Similar is the voice of the holy heavenly elders and living creatures applauding Babylon's fall and worshipping God who sits on the throne (ibid. 19:1, 4). And since the saints after death are isangeloi, like the angels (Matt. 22:30; Luke 20:35-36), and the angels praise God without end (Isa. 6:3), the saints' souls must certainly not be inactive, as the idle never would be. Finally, the sleep of the body is the inactivity of a corpse, not of the spirit; and the sleep and insensibility of the soul at death make people philopsychoi [φιλοψυχῆς], lovers of this world; and the blessedness of the idle is the blessedness not of Christians but of Epicureans.

units.la: XXVIII. Tam stultæ Psychopannychitarum rationes sunt, quàm dogma ipsum stultum est.
units.tr: XXVIII. The arguments of the Psychopannychites are as foolish as the dogma itself.

units.la: Non enim quia corpus sine spiritu, hoc est, halitu & spiraculo vitæ mortuum est, Jac.I I.26. iccirco anima rationalis sine corpore mortua est, vel nihil agit, quia vita corporis à spiritu pendet: at vita animæ rationalis à corpore non pendet. Sicut enim anima rationalis non subsistit per corpus, sed se ipsa pro spiritualis naturæ conditione: ita separata à corpore per se operatur. Ideo S. Paulus nescius in corpore, an extra illud in Coelo tertio vidit ἀῤῥήτα ῥήματα res ineffabiles, 2.Cor.XII.2.3. Neque uspiam Scriptura testatur, animas mortuorum dormire, respectu corporis scilicet, testatur. Lazarus, amicus noster, κεκοίμηται obdormivit, Joh.XI.11. His dictis Stephanus ἐκοιμήθη dormivit, Act.VII.60. Si Christus non resurrexit, ergo dormientes in Christo perierunt, 1.Cor. XV.17.18. Omnes non dormiemus, sed mutabimur, ibid. §1. Dormiunt igitur, quia corpus eorum nihil sentit, vel agit, ipsi tamen vivunt, quemadmodum sponsa de se, ut dormiente, in Cantico loquitur: Ego dormiebam, & cor meum vigilabat; Cant.V.2. Et par ratio vocis quiescendi est, quae mortuis tribuitur, Esaj.LVII.2.3. utraque enim dormiendi & quiescendi vox synecdochicè ad corpus refertur, quatenus illud in sepulchro velut molli strato quiescit, & in resurrectione mortuorum à morte haud secus quàm à somno resuscitabitur & evigilabit. Expergiscimini, & laudate habitatores pulveris, Esaj. XXVI.19. Multi dormientium in terra pulveris expergefient, Dan.XII.2. Etiam Gentiles mortem cum somno compararunt. Nobis, inquit Catullus, cùm semel occidit brevis lux, nox est perpetuò una dormienda. Mortui quinetiam non laudabunt Deum, Psal. VI.6. LXXXVIII.11.12.13. eo modo, quo in hac vita consueverunt, videlicet in congregatione aliorum viventium & ad aedificationem eorum. Neque propterea animabus resurrectio corporum, quibus in hac vita unitae fuerunt, optanda non est, quia jam beatitudine & gloria fruuntur. Sunt enim beatitudinis gradus; & quae nunc partis est, tunc erit compositi totius ex anima & corpore; imò totius corporis mystici in Ecclesia triumphante perfectè glorificata. In novissimo verò die plenissimae gloriae manifestatio succedet. Neque etiam, quia animae Sanctorum in Coelo jam gloria fruuntur, & impiorum
units.tr: For the body is dead without spirit, that is, without breath and the breath of life (Jas. II.26), but it does not follow that the rational soul is dead, or does nothing, without the body, because the life of the body depends on the spirit while the life of the rational soul does not depend on the body. For just as the rational soul does not subsist through the body, but by the condition of its spiritual nature, so when separated from the body it still acts of itself. Hence St Paul, whether in the body or out of the body he knew not, he saw in the third heaven unspeakable words, things that cannot be uttered (2 Cor. XII.2–3). Nor does Scripture anywhere testify that the souls of the dead sleep, at least not in respect of the soul itself. Our friend Lazarus sleeps, he is fallen asleep (John XI.11). When he had said this, Stephen fell asleep (Acts VII.60). If Christ is not risen, then those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished (1 Cor. XV.17–18). We shall not all sleep, but we shall be changed (ibid., v. 51). They sleep, then, because their body perceives nothing and does nothing, yet they themselves live, just as the bride speaks of herself as sleeping in the Song: I was sleeping, but my heart was awake (Cant. V.2). The word resting, which is ascribed to the dead, is of the same force (Isa. LVII.2–3); for both the words sleeping and resting refer by synecdoche to the body, inasmuch as it rests in the grave as on a soft bed, and in the resurrection of the dead it will be raised from death no less than from sleep and will wake. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust (Isa. XXVI.19). Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake (Dan. XII.2). Even the Gentiles compared death with sleep. For us, says Catullus, when once the brief light has set, there is one night to be slept through without end. The dead will not praise God (Ps. VI.6; LXXXVIII.11–13), in the way they were accustomed to in this life, namely in the assembly of the living and for their edification. Nor, for this reason, should the resurrection of the bodies, with which the souls were united in this life, be undesired by the souls, because they already enjoy blessedness and glory. For there are degrees of blessedness; and what now is in part will then be in the whole composed of soul and body, indeed of the whole mystical body perfectly glorified in the Church triumphant. But on the last day the manifestation of full glory will follow. Nor, because the souls of the saints already enjoy glory in heaven and the impious are tormented in hell, will there be no need of the last judgment.

units.la: Psychopannychitarum argumenta contraria refelluntur. piorum in inferno cruciantur, judicio ultimo opus non erit, quia animæ corporibus iterum conjungi, & sententia solennis, junctis postliminio utrisque, à judice promulgari debet.
units.tr: The contrary arguments of the Psychopannychites are refuted. The final judgment will still be needed, because the souls must be joined again to their bodies, and the solemn sentence must be pronounced by the judge once both have been restored to each other by right of return.

units.la: XXIX. Succedunt Pontificiorum de statu animæ separatæ errores concatenati.
units.tr: XXIX. The connected errors of the Papists concerning the state of the separated soul follow.

units.la: Nam ante omnia Sanctorum defunctorum religiosæ invocationi fundamenta hæc præstruunt, quòd exactè noverint, quicquid rerum in his terris geritur, ne secretis quidem cordium suspiriis exceptis, ac propterea etiam pro particularibus viventium necessitatibus sigillatim orent: quòd nobis in terra adsint, & nostra contemplentur: quòd cultoribus suis dona spiritualia conferant: quòd denique rebus humanis, Ecclesiæ inprimis præsideant. Nobis certum est, animas separatas rerum Divinarum exacta scientia pollere; neque etiam Ecclesiæ militantis, quam morte sua reliquerunt, statum omnino ignorare; imò eandem precibus suis generatim Deo commendare. Charitas enim in altera vita non excidit, 1.Cor.XIII.8. Et ipse dives epulo in inferno pœnas luens fratrum suorum in terra superstitum meminit, Luc. XVI.27. Sed singula, quæ in terris fiunt, non noverunt, quia ea nosse nec possunt, nisi revelante Deo, quod eum velle non constat, nec beatitudinis eorum interest. Tu, Jehova, es Pater noster; Abraham verò nescivit, & Israel nos non agnovit, Esaj. LXIII.16. notitia non approbationis, seu practica tantùm, sed etiam scientiæ. Loquitur enim Ecclesia pœnitens, conversa, peccata sua serio deplorans, & ab hominibus omnibus ad unum solúmque Deum se convertens; quibuscum etiam Esajas fidelis ipse se conjungit. An tales Abrahamus, Israel non approbasset, dilexisset, sed odisset, contempsisset, si eorum notitiam habuisset, qui pro impia Sodoma & Gomorrha tam enixè vivus intercessit? Et quæ sic peccatorum erga Sanctos fiducia esse potest, si se cognitos licet ab iis non agnosci, id est, odio haberi, non amari, non exaudiri, nedum intercessione eorum adjuvari noverunt. Et non exaudivit Abrahamus populum, nec ejus curam gessit, propter conditionem aliquam vel in Sanctis, vel in Israelitis orantibus hærentem. Prior alia esse non potest, quàm ignorantia, quòd noluit eorum curam gerere, quia quid in particulari illis desit, ignoravit. Posterior verò obtinere non potuit, quia alias Deus propter eandem indignitatem eos repulisset. Gemella Ecclesiæ apud Esajam sunt illa Jobi: Si augeantur filii (mortui) ignorat: sin diminuantur, non animadvertit, Job.XIV.21. nec non Solomonis illa: Viventes sciunt, se morituros esse, mortui autem nesciunt quicquam, Eccles. IX.5. Et Deus ipse ad Regem Josiam: Colligam te ad Patres tuos, & conderis sepulchro in pace, ne videant oculi tui mala, quæ introducturus sum super locum illum, 2. Reg. XXII.20. Inprimis secreta cordium suspiria, & latentes cogitationes ignorant, quia cordis scrutatio, & secretarum cogitationum notitia passim soli Deo, cujus perfectio & proprietas est, vindicatur, Psal.VII.20. 1.Reg.VIII.39. Matth. VI.6. Rom.VIII.27. 1.Cor.II.10. Nam quòd Deum talia nosse proprietate naturæ, Sanctos partim Dei visione, partim revela-
units.tr: For first of all they lay these foundations for the pious invocation of the departed saints: that they know exactly whatever happens in these lands, not excepting even the secret sighs of hearts, and therefore they also pray for the particular needs of the living, one by one; that they are present with us on earth and look upon our affairs; that they bestow spiritual gifts on their worshippers; and finally that they preside over human affairs, especially over the Church. For our part, we hold that separated souls excel in exact knowledge of divine things; nor are they wholly ignorant of the state of the militant Church, which they left at their death; indeed they commend it to God in general by their prayers. For charity does not fall away in the other life (1 Cor. XIII.8). And the rich man in hell, paying the penalty, remembers his brothers still living on earth (Luke XVI.27). But they do not know the individual things that happen on earth, because they cannot know them unless God reveals them, which it is not certain that he wishes to do, nor does it concern their blessedness. You, Jehovah, are our Father; but Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not acknowledge us (Isa. LXIII.16). Here the not-knowing is not merely of approval or of practice, but of knowledge itself. For the penitent Church speaks, converted, seriously lamenting its sins and turning from all men to God alone; with this Church Isaiah the faithful man himself joins himself. Would Abraham not have approved of such people, would he not have loved them, rather than hating and despising them, if he had known them, when he himself, while alive, interceded so earnestly for impious Sodom and Gomorrah? And what confidence in the saints can sinners have, if they know that, though they are recognised by them, they are not acknowledged, that is, are hated, not loved, not heard, and much less helped by their intercession? And Abraham did not hear the people, nor did he take care of them, because of some condition clinging to them, whether in the saints or in the Israelites praying. The former cannot be anything other than ignorance, namely that he was unwilling to care for them because he did not know what was lacking to them in particular. The latter could not hold, because otherwise God would have rejected them for the same unworthiness. Akin to the Church's words in Isaiah are those of Job: If the sons (of the dead) are honoured, he does not know it; if they are brought low, he does not perceive it (Job XIV.21). And there is also that of Solomon: The living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing (Eccles. IX.5). And God himself says to King Josiah: I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be buried in peace, that your eyes may not see the evils which I am about to bring upon that place (2 Kings XXII.20). Above all, the dead do not know the secret sighs and hidden thoughts of hearts, because the searching of hearts and the knowledge of secret thoughts is everywhere claimed for God alone, whose perfection and property it is (Ps. VII.10; 1 Kings VIII.39; Matt. VI.6; Rom. VIII.27; 1 Cor. II.10). As for their claim that God knows such things by the property of his nature, and that the saints know them partly by the vision of God and partly by revelation, this is answered:

units.la: tione, regerunt, dilutum est, tum quia cordis cogitatio cujusvis Sanctis quacunque ratione notas & exploratas esse, nuspiam Scriptura testatur: tum quia visio Dei Sanctorum in Deo solo quiescentium beatitudo, 1.Cor.XIII.8. 12. XV.28. non rerum ad beatitudinem non pertinentium cognitio est; revelatio verò iisdem facta non necessaria, sed libera; neque adeò rerum omnium, sed earum duntaxat, quas ad gloriam Dei & beatitudinem eorum cognoscere refert, est. Et dies ille, quo omnia occulta revelabuntur, novissimus erit. Neque etiam scientiæ ejusmodi catholicæ fundamentum est speculum S. S. Trinitatis, de quo tam multa fabulantur; contradicentibus etiam Scholæ doctoribus non paucis, eò quòd Sancti in Deo plura videre necesse non habeant, quàm quæ ad eorum beatitudinem pertinent. Scitè Thomas Aquinas p.1. q.12. art.8. Aliqua, inquit, videntur in Deo, secundum quod in ipso sunt. Omnia autem alia sunt in Deo, sicut effectus virtute sunt in sua causa. Ille intellectus potest in causa cognoscere omnes effectus, qui causam totaliter comprehendit. Nullus autem intellectus creatus totaliter Deum comprehendere potest. Videns speculum, non est necessarium, quòd omnia in speculo videat, nisi speculum visa comprehendit. Atqui Sancti defuncti Deum non comprehendunt. Non ergo in eo, velut in speculo, omnia vident. Consentiunt Thomistæ, essentiam Divinam nec dici proprie speculum, nec ei per metaphoram rationem speculi commodè accommodari. Speculum autem si habeatur, voluntarium illud tantùm esse, non necessarium, quia plus vel minùs ostendit, non omnia, sed ea duntaxat, quæ repræsentare placuerit. Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate. Ibi autem videbimus à facie ad faciem, 1.Cor. XIII.12. Quomodo ergo essentia Dei prospeculo Sanctis in Cœlo erit, cùm visio in speculo sit hujus vitæ, & velut in ænigmate, atque ex parte. Nam quæ in speculo videntur, ex parte, exteriùs, obliquè, superficialiter, non tota, interiùs, essentialiter & directè videntur. Specularis proin cognitio ne quidem talis est, qualis cognitio gloriæ & Majestatis Dei in Cœlo est, nedum essentiæ Dei, & omnium, quæ Deus necessariò vel liberè vult & efficit. Facilè inferiorum horum omnium, & notitiæ eorum jacturam facient, quibus sublimiora longè, gloriosiora, & Divina omnia contemplanda objicientur. An enim illis omissis beatæ mentes ad crepundia ordinis universi, necessitates Mortalium, quibus Deus fine eorum opera providere potest, redibunt? Sive etiam repræsentationem hujus speculi, sive visionem spectamus, plena difficultatum omnia sunt. Si repræsentationem, quæ repræsentantur? Omnésne, an aliquæ? Actu existentes, an etiam futurae, necessariæ & contingentes; & naturaliter, necessariò an liberè? Si omnes, an ut omnes, etiam contingentes, cognoscantur? Atqui diem ultimi judicii non cognoscunt, Marc. XIII.32. An ut non cognoscantur? Sic frustra erit repræsentatio. Si tantùm aliquæ, quomodo necessariò? Unde res tuas tibi repræsentari constat? Præterea res repræsentatur vel secundum esse eminens, quod in Deo habet: vel secundum formale. Si prius, non ergo secunsecundum esse, quod in se habent. Si posterius, omnes ergo imperfectiones, passiones, peccata ipsa in essentia Divina velut speculo, repraesentabuntur. Si visionem spectamus, pandendum pariter est, omnia, an quaedam videant. Si omnia, quomodo diem ultimi judicii non vident? Si quaedam, incertum est, quae illa sint, & an sint illa ipsa, quae tu illos cognoscere, & in quibus ab ipsis juvari desideras. Has similesque ob causas naturiores Papistae misso Trinitatis speculo, scholasticae speculationis infelice factu, labyrinthum finxerunt, per cujus tortuosos anfractus supplices vivos ducunt & reducunt. Asserunt enim, Deum primo invocantes audire, dein hoc Sanctis invocatis revelare, qui tandem sic edocti impetrent a Deo revelante, quod ab illis insciis ante petitum erat. Ventum ergo ἀγγολαταξία refert, qui circumeundo circumit, & ad circuitus suos revertitur, Eccles. I. 6. Denique Spiritus Dei describens statum animarum beatarum nullo apice vel precum, quas pro superstitum singularibus necessitatibus fundant; vel beneficiorum, quae in homines in terra militantes erogent, vel domini, quod in res hujus seculi exerceant, meminit. Non ergo, qui haec tuentur, Scripturam, sed ingenii vani commenta sequuntur.
units.tr: tion. First, because nowhere does Scripture testify that the thought of any heart is known to the saints by any means at all. Second, because the vision of God, in which the saints rest in God alone, is their blessedness (1 Cor. XIII.8, 12; XV.28), and is not the knowledge of things that do not pertain to blessedness; whereas revelation made to them is not necessary but free, and extends not to all things but only to those which it pleases God to make known for his glory and their blessedness. And that day on which all hidden things will be revealed will be the last. Nor is the mirror of the Holy Trinity, of which they tell so many fables, a catholic foundation for such knowledge; indeed not a few doctors of the Schools contradict it, because the saints have no need to see in God more than what pertains to their blessedness. Thomas Aquinas wisely says (I, q. 12, art. 8): Some things are seen in God as they are in him. But all other things are in God as effects are virtually in their cause. That intellect can know in the cause all the effects which comprehends the cause wholly. But no created intellect can comprehend God wholly. A person looking into a mirror need not see everything in the mirror, unless the mirror comprehends what is seen. But the departed saints do not comprehend God; therefore they do not see all things in him as in a mirror. The Thomists agree that the divine essence is not properly called a mirror, nor can the notion of a mirror be fittingly applied to it by metaphor. But if a mirror is granted, its showing is voluntary, not necessary, since it shows more or less, not everything, but only those things which it pleases to represent. Now we see through a mirror in an enigma; but then we shall see face to face (1 Cor. XIII.12). How, then, will the essence of God be in the mirror to the saints in heaven, since vision in a mirror belongs to this life, and is as in an enigma and in part? For things seen in a mirror are seen in part, outwardly, obliquely, superficially, not wholly, inwardly, essentially and directly. Mirror-knowledge, therefore, is not even of the kind that the knowledge of the glory and majesty of God in heaven is, much less of the essence of God and of all that God wills and effects necessarily or freely. Those blessed minds will easily lose these lower things and the knowledge of them, when far loftier, more glorious and wholly divine things are set before them for contemplation. For would those blessed minds, leaving these aside, return to the trifles of the order of the universe and the needs of mortals, for which God can provide without their work? And whether we look at the representation in this mirror or at the vision, everything is full of difficulties. If we consider representation, what things are represented? All, or some? Those actually existing, or also future, necessary and contingent; and naturally, necessarily or freely? If all, are they known as all, including the contingent? But they do not know the day of the last judgment (Mark XIII.32). Or are they known as not known? Then the representation is in vain. If only some, how is it necessary? How is it established that your affairs are represented to you? Moreover, a thing is represented either according to the eminent being it has in God, or according to its formal being. If the former, it is not represented according to the being it has in itself. If the latter, then all imperfections, passions and sins themselves will be represented in the divine essence as in a mirror. If we consider vision, it must likewise be declared whether they see all things or certain things. If all, how do they not see the day of the last judgment?
