If certain, it is uncertain what those are, and whether they are the very things by which you desire them to know you and by which you wish to be helped by them. For these and similar reasons the Papists, more ingenious than sound, have set aside the mirror of the Trinity, an unhappy product of scholastic speculation, and have contrived a labyrinth through whose winding twists they lead and bring back suppliant living people. For they assert that God hears those who first invoke him, then that he reveals this to the invoked saints, who, thus instructed, obtain from God, who reveals it, what was asked before by those who did not know it. Thus it comes to what the angel-hunter brings, who goes round about going round and returns to his circuits (Eccles. I.6). Finally, the Spirit of God, describing the state of blessed souls, makes no mention of any care for the particular needs of the survivors for which they pour out prayers, nor of the benefits they bestow on men in the militant Church, nor of any rule they exercise over the affairs of this world. Therefore those who defend these things follow not Scripture but the vain inventions of their own minds.

units.la: XXX. Fundamenta isthaec ἀγγολαταξίας caduca maxime argumentis nonnullis, sed aeque caducis suffulcire conantur.
units.tr: XXX. These foundations of angelotaxy [ἀγγολαταξίας], which are very weak, they try to prop up with some arguments, equally weak.

units.la: Nam animas beatas partim clara Dei visione, partim revelatione, partim Angelorum relatione, partim mira naturae glorificatae celeritate & sagacitate, quicquid in mundo geritur, cognoscere delirant. Nam beati quidem omnes Deum a facie ad faciem vident, 1.Cor.XIII.12. neque tamen omnia sciunt magis quam Angeli, qui & ipsi semper vident faciem Dei Patris in Coelis, Matth.XVIII.10. & tamen diem extremi judicii ignorant, ibid.XXIV.36. Marc.XIII.32. Neque enim clarae visionis Dei in altera vita finis est, ut sic videntes Deum omnia cognoscant, sed potius, ut in solo Deo quiescant, & gloria ejus, qui omnia in omnibus erit, 1.Cor.XV.28. fruantur; satientur specie Dei, Psal.XVII.15. similes Deo sint, quantum creatura Deo assimulari potest, & videant Deum uti est, 1. Joh. III.2. denique interprete statim Paulo, cognoscant, ut cogniti sunt, hoc est, sentiant in omni effectu, quomodo a Deo amati sint, 1.Cor. XIII.12. Fictitia etiam Divina revelatio est, quia nuspiam, Deum Sanctis cuncta revelare, Scriptura docet. Et statum superstitum in hac vita Sanctis incognitum esse, supra ostendimus. Par ratio relationis Angelicae est. Mittuntur enim in terram ad ministerium propter eos, qui salutis haeredes erunt, Hebr.I.14. ministrantes illis in terra, non in Coelo Sanctorum suffragia, relatis necessitatibus, procurando. Illi potius preces viventium in terris Angeli piorum referunt, quem & ipsi adorant, qui solus Deus est, Apoc.XIX.10. Ac ne ipsi quidem cordium scrutatores sunt, ut pios animorum affectus cognoscere, & aliis revelare valeant. Et sunt quidem Sancti coelites ἰσάγγελοι Angelis similes, Matth.XXII.30. mira naturae celeritate & animi sagacitate praediti. Sed ἰσότης similitudo illa nec in omnibus obtinet; saltem non in eo, quod aeque ac Angeli nobis in terra ministrent, quod Angeli soli, non animae beatae, faciunt, Heb. I.14. nec omniscientiam illam animarum evincit, quia nec ipsi quidem Angeli omniscii sunt. tatis, quæ aureum altare est, merita Christi ad exauditionem precum efficacia sint. Etiam Seniores XXIV. coram Agno effuderunt phialas aureas plenas thymiamatum, quæ sunt orationes Sanctorum, ibid. v. 8. non eorum, qui in terris degunt, sed ipsorum Sanctorum Coelitum & Seniorum, eaque non ἀιτητικὰ & ἱλαστικὰ petitoriæ & propitiatoriæ, sed ἀχαριστικὰ gratiarum actoriæ; seu canticum illud novum Agno decantatum, quod statim v.9. subjicitur his verbis: Dignus es, qui accipias librum & aperias sigilla ejus, quia mactatus es, & redemisti nos Deo sanguine tuo, &c. Nam quòd adversarii versum 8. à 9. divellentes in illo preces alienas, in hoc proprias Seniorum intelligi pertendunt, seriei verborum aperte repugnant, juxta quam preces Sanctorum, quorum v. 8. mentio est, statim, v. 9. de cantico novo explicantur, ut sensus sit, illos precando canticum novum cecinisse. Denique nec epulonis divitis pro fratribus intercedentis exemplum, Luc.XVI.28. adversariam causam juvat, quia petitio ejus, ut viventes non à Mose & Prophetis, sed à mortuis erudirentur, non recta, sed impia & infidelis, exemplum intercessionis rectæ & fidelis, qualem ipsimet Sanctis tribuunt, esse non potest.
units.tr: For they foolishly imagine that the blessed souls know whatever happens in the world, partly through the clear vision of God, partly through revelation, partly through the report of angels, and partly through the wonderful speed and keenness of their glorified nature. Indeed, all the blessed see God face to face (1 Cor. 13:12), yet they do not know everything any more than the angels, who also always see the face of the Father in heaven (Matt. 18:10), and yet they do not know the day of the last judgment (Matt. 24:36; Mark 13:32). For the end of the clear vision of God in the next life is not that by seeing God they should know all things, but rather that they may rest in God alone and enjoy his glory, he who will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28); that they may be satisfied with the likeness of God (Ps. 17:15), that they may be like God, as far as a creature can be made like God, and see God as he is (1 John 3:2); and finally, Paul himself explaining it at once, that they may know as they are known, that is, feel in every effect how they are loved by God (1 Cor. 13:12). The divine revelation is also a fiction, for Scripture teaches nowhere that God reveals all things to the saints. And we have shown above that the condition of the survivors in this life is unknown to the saints. The same reasoning applies to angelic relation. For they are sent into the earth to minister for the sake of those who will be heirs of salvation (Heb. 1:14), ministering to them on earth; the saints in heaven do not procure intercession by relaying necessities. Rather, the angels report the prayers of the pious living on earth to God, whom they themselves worship, who alone is God (Rev. 19:10). Nor are they themselves searchers of hearts, so as to know the pious affections of souls and reveal them to others. The heavenly saints are indeed equal to angels [ἰσάγγελοι] (Matt. 22:30), endowed with wonderful speed of nature and keenness of mind. But that equality of likeness does not hold in all respects: at least not in this, that they minister to us on earth just as the angels do, which the angels alone do and not the blessed souls (Heb. 1:14); nor does it prove that those souls are omniscient, since not even the angels themselves are omniscient. [Here the text is garbled; the sense is that] the merits of Christ, which are the golden altar, are efficacious for the hearing of prayers. Also, the twenty-four elders poured out before the Lamb golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints (ibid. v. 8). These are not the prayers of those who dwell on earth, but of the saints themselves who are in heaven and of the elders; and these are not petitory and propitiatory [ἀιτητικὰ & ἱλαστικὰ], but thanksgiving [ἀχαριστικὰ], that is, offerings of gratitude. This is confirmed by the new song sung to the Lamb, which immediately follows in v. 9 in these words: You are worthy to take the book and open its seals, because you were slain and have redeemed us to God by your blood, etc. For when the adversaries separate verse 8 from verse 9, and maintain that in the former the prayers of others are meant, and in the latter the elders' own, they plainly contradict the sequence of the words; for according to that sequence the prayers of the saints mentioned in v. 8 are explained at once in v. 9 as the new song, so that the sense is that by praying they sang the new song. Finally, the example of the rich man who interceded for his brothers (Luke 16:28) does not help the adversaries' cause, because his request that the living be instructed not by Moses and the Prophets but by the dead was not right but wicked and unbelieving, and so it cannot be an example of right and faithful intercession, such as they themselves attribute to the saints.

units.la: XXXI. Proximus Pontificiorum error est, quòd quosdam Papa ἀποθεωσιν Deificare per aream Canonizationis scalam non verecundatur, ne videlicet ignorent homines, quibus in Coelo patronis & mediatoribus gaudeant. Canonizationem hanc Bellarminus de S. Beat. lib.I. cap. 7. quòd sit publicum Ecclesiæ testimonium de sanctitate & vera gloria hominis alicujus jam defuncti; nec non sententia, qua ei honores, felix ævum cum Deo degentibus debiti decernuntur. Ejusmodi honores septem faciunt. Velut quòd statuitur, ut ab omnibus pro Sanctis habeantur: quòd in publicis Ecclesiæ precibus invocentur: quòd in eorum memoriam aræ & templa Deo dicantur: quòd sacrificia tam eucharistica, quàm laudum & precum in eorum honorem Deo offeruntur: quòd in eorundem honorem imagines pinguntur, addito certo lumine quodam, in signum gloriæ, qua in Coelis fulgent: quòd denique eorum reliquiæ pretiosis thecis inclusæ publicè religiosè coluntur. Quod impium impiæ gentilitatis & Judaismi imitamentum nec in Scriptura, nec in pia antiquitate ullum fundamentum habet, & terrestrem homuncionem, qui de sua ipse salute dubitare tenetur, coelestium honorum diribitorem se facit. Apostolos certè & Patres non per canonizationem Papalem, sed sanctitate propria coelum conscendisse, & in Calendario locum invenisse, & sanctos veteres coli coepisse non lege aliqua, sed consuetudine Bellarminus loc. cit. cap. 8. fatetur. Primus Nicolaus I. Apollionem canonizavit, si Troilo Malvesio fides est. Sed Bellarminus primatum eum Leoni III. Scribertum Deificanti tribuit. Revera tamen primus Bernhardus, & post eum Franciscus, Dominicus ἀναγέωσιν suam Papæ debent. Scriptura vero Sanctos pronunciat non illos, quos Papæ albo eorum inserere collibitum fuerit, sed illos potiùs, qui Spiritu Dei ducuntur, aspersi sanguine Filii Dei, 1.Pet.I.2. qui sanctificati sunt in Christo Jesu, 1. Cor. I. 2. & in Domino, fide Jesu Christi obdormiverunt, Apoc.XIV.13. Quales soli Deo, nonulli homini, noti sunt. Parum est mihi judicari ab humano die. Neque me ipsum judico. Est qui me judicat Deus, 1.Cor.IV.4,5. Firmum stat Dei fundamentum, habens sigillum hoc: Dominus eos novit, qui sui sunt, 2.Tim.II.19. Solus enim Deus, Christus odoratur timorem Jehova, Esaj. XI.3. Mitto honores, quos Sanctis Papa decernit, & per quos eos in idola, horrenda metamorphosi, convertit, & homines miseros eò adigit, ut quæ solius Dei sunt, creaturis vindicent, atque ita gloriam Dei alienent. Si Deos faciendi potestatem Papa haberet, prius se ipsum Deificaret, quod olim homo natus Thasiis, Agesilaum Deum facientibus, haud insipidè objecit. Cùmque Papam in canonizatione errare posse, ut impium in canonem Sanctorum referat, Thomas Aquinas Quodlib. 2. art. 16. Antoninus Summ. Theol. p.III. tit. 12: 8. Canus, Bellarminus, aliique fateantur, fieri poterit, ut in Divinis officiis pro Sanctis colantur, quorum spiritus cum Diabolo & Angelis ejus in tartaro sepeliuntur. Quorum certè in numero Franciscus, Dominicus, Thomas Beket, homo perduellis, est; aliique forte sunt, ne de Gregoriis, Christophoris, Longinis, & ejusdem deserti, Faunis & Satyris dicam. Neque canonizationum bullæ certitudinem præstant. Innumera enim bullata Paparum edicta à successoribus rescissa sunt; & constat etiam papaliter canonizatos paulò post etiam papaliter excommunicatos & degradatos esse, qualis ille famosus Hermannus de Ferrara fuit. Tales bullæ sunt, qualis Papa bullator est. Neque quisquam bonus vel in Coelo, vel in terra bullatus Papæ Divus haberi velit. Sed quales sint, quos canonizat, parum pensi habent novi Deorum ἀγυροκηποι, dicentes ad Mechanicos suos: Viri, scitis ex hoc quæstu nostras esse copias, Act.XIX.25. Hæc vera & ἐπιτακτικὴ causa est; inanis verò prætextus Bellarmini, quòd id ad imitationem prosit, & nobis viventibus decorum sit, præclaras laudes Sanctorum publicè recitari, ipsósque religiosè venerandos proponi. Nam Scriptura quæ nobis imitandos Sanctos proponit, canonizationem nuspiam commendavit; & eos Sanctos, quorum in Scripturis laudata sanctitas est, & qui in mundo fidem veram charitate ejusque fructibus demonstrare visi, charitatis judicio pro Sanctis haberi possunt, imitari jubet.
units.tr: XXXI. The next error of the Papists is that the Pope is not ashamed to deify certain people [Deificare] by the ladder of canonization [ἀποθεωσιν] in an open court, lest men should fail to know what heavenly patrons and mediators they have. Bellarmine (De sanctorum beatitudine, bk. 1, ch. 7) describes this canonization as the public testimony of the Church concerning the holiness and true glory of a man already deceased, together with the sentence by which the honours due to those who live happily with God are decreed for him. Such honours are seven in number. For instance: it is decreed that he be regarded as a saint by all; that he be invoked in the public prayers of the Church; that altars and temples be dedicated to God in his memory; that sacrifices, both eucharistic and of praise and prayer, be offered to God in his honour; that images be painted in his honour, with a certain light added as a sign of the glory with which he shines in heaven; and finally, that his relics, enclosed in precious cases, be publicly and religiously venerated. This impious imitation of impious heathenism and Judaism has no foundation in Scripture or in pious antiquity; it makes a little earthly man, who is himself bound to doubt his own salvation, the distributor of heavenly honours. Bellarmine himself admits (ibid., ch. 8) that the apostles and Fathers ascended to heaven not by papal canonization but by their own holiness, and found a place in the calendar, and that the ancient saints began to be venerated not by any law but by custom. Nicholas I, if we may trust Troilus Malvesius, was the first to canonize Apollion. But Bellarmine attributes the primacy in this to Leo III, who deified Scribertus. In truth, however, Bernard was the first, and after him Francis and Dominic owe their enrolment [ἀναγραφήν] to the Pope. Scripture, on the other hand, declares those to be saints not whom the Pope has pleased to enter in his roll, but rather those who are led by the Spirit of God, sprinkled with the blood of the Son of God (1 Pet. 1:2), who are sanctified in Christ Jesus (1 Cor. 1:2), and who fell asleep in the Lord by faith in Jesus Christ (Rev. 14:13). Such persons are known to God alone, and to some men. It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by a human day. Neither do I judge myself. He who judges me is God (1 Cor. 4:4–5). The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are his (2 Tim. 2:19). For God alone, and Christ, smells the fear of Jehovah (Isa. 11:3). I pass over the honours which the Pope decrees for the saints, and by which he turns them into idols in a horrible metamorphosis, and drives wretched men to claim for creatures what belongs to God alone, and thus to alienate the glory of God. If the Pope had the power of making gods, he would first deify himself; a man born at Thasos rightly objected this to those who made Agesilaus a god. And since Thomas Aquinas (Quodlibet 2, art. 16), Antoninus (Summa theologica, pt. 3, tit. 12, ch. 8), Cano, Bellarmine and others admit that the Pope can err in canonization, so as to enrol an impious person in the canon of saints, it may happen that people are worshipped in the divine offices as saints whose spirits are buried in Tartarus with the Devil and his angels. Among their number certainly are Francis, Dominic, and Thomas Becket, a traitor; and there are perhaps others, not to mention the Gregories, Christophers, Longinuses, and the Fauns and Satyrs of the same desert. Nor do the papal bulls of canonization give certainty. For countless papal edicts sealed with a bull have been annulled by successors, and it is established that men canonized by the Pope were soon afterwards excommunicated and degraded by the Pope, as was that notorious Hermann of Ferrara. Such are the bulls as the Pope who issues them is. Nor does any good man wish to be regarded as sealed and divine by the Pope, whether in heaven or on earth. But as to what sort of people they are whom he canonizes, the new silversmiths of gods, who care little about it, say to their craftsmen: Men, you know that our wealth comes from this trade (Acts 19:25). This is the true and commanding cause; but Bellarmine's pretext is empty: that it helps imitation, and that it is becoming for us, while we are living, to have the famous praises of the saints publicly recited and the saints themselves proposed for religious veneration. For Scripture, which sets the saints before us for imitation, nowhere commends canonization; and it commands us to imitate those saints whose holiness is praised in the Scriptures, and who have shown the true faith in the world by love and its fruits, and who may be regarded as saints by the judgment of love.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Hisferè fundamentis ἀμολα-τείαν, seu religiosus Divorum in Papatu cultus innititur. Ingens ille συνδεσμὸς ἀδικίας est, quo innodantur Papistæ, calcata conscientia, ad Divorum religiosum cultum juramento etiam se obligantes. Nam Pius IV. in jurata fidei Catholicæ, extra quam nemo salvus esse potest, fidei confessione inter alia hæc præscribit: Ego N. firma fide credo & profiteor, Sanctos verè cum Christo regnantes venerandos atque invocandos esse. Prius etiam Concilium Tridentinum Sess. XXV. mandaverat, de Sanctorum intercessione & invocatione fideles diligenter instrui & doceri debent, quòd bonum atque utile sit, supplicitér eos invocare, & ob beneficia impetranda à Deo per Filium ejus Jesum Christum, D. N. qui solus noster Redemptor & Salvator est, ad eorum opem auxiliumque confugere; illos verò, qui negant, Sanctos {\u03b8}os aeterna felicitate in Coelo fruentes, invocandos esse; aut qui afferunt, eorum, qui pro nobis etiam singulis orent, invocationem esse idololatriam, vel pugnare cum verbo Dei, adversaque honori unius Mediatoris Dei & hominum Jesu Christi, vel stultum esse in Coelo regnantibus voce vel mente supplicare, impie sentire. Caeterum praxis ipsa satis ostendit, quo loco Sanctorum ille cultus habeatur, cum in externo Papatus cultu Sanctorum invocatio & religio utramque fere paginam faciat, & illa quotidie, quae errorum vouλω seu gangraena rationem habentium, indoles est, in pejus vergat.
units.tr: On these foundations almost entirely rests the religious worship of the saints in Popery, that is, saint-worship [ἀγιολατρείαν]. It is that great bond of iniquity [σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας] by which the Papists are bound, binding themselves even by oath, with conscience trampled underfoot, to the religious worship of the saints. For Pius IV, in the sworn profession of the Catholic faith, outside of which no one can be saved, prescribes among other things this formula: I, N., with firm faith believe and profess that the saints, truly reigning with Christ, are to be venerated and invoked. Earlier still, the Council of Trent, Session XXV, had ordered that the faithful ought to be carefully instructed and taught that it is good and useful to invoke the saints in supplication, and to flee to their help and aid for benefits to be obtained from God through his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, who alone is our Redeemer and Saviour; but those who deny that the saints enjoying eternal happiness in heaven are to be invoked, or who maintain that the invocation of those who pray for us individually is idolatry, or that it conflicts with the word of God and is opposed to the honour of the one Mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ, or that it is foolish to make supplication by voice or mind to those reigning in heaven, hold impious opinions. Besides, practice itself shows well enough what place that cult of the saints holds, since in the outward worship of Popery the invocation and religion of the saints makes up nearly both pages, and that daily tendency, which is characteristic of errors with the character of a gangraena (a gangrene that spreads), grows worse.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Sed praeterquam quod fundamenta invocationis hujus jam concussimus, alia etiam ἀγιολατρείαν illam convincunt. Destituitur enim in universum mandato & promissione, neque exempla in Scripturis probata ulla habet; adeoque ad ἐπιλυμα ἀνθρώπων, cultum Dei electitium & excelsa Baalim pertinet. De mandato & promissione expressa fatetur ipse Bellarminus; & aliunde illa supplere posse nequaquam asserit. Nam quod actus religionis, cultus Divini capaces, praecepto expresso non indigere, neque institutione Dei definiri debere, alii regerunt, futile certe est. Supponunt enim, invocationem Sanctorum actum esse religionis Deo probatae, quod falsum esse pronuntiamus. Non enim ad cultum Dei naturalem, vel institutum referri potest. Non ad naturalem, quia natura & sanctitas Dei naturalis cultum Sanctorum, qui creaturae sunt, religiosum non praecipit. Neque enim Sancti Dii sunt; neque in eos credimus, in iis spem nostram defigimus, vel eos supra omnia diligimus. Non ad institutum, quia institutionem voluntatem Dei praecipientem ipsimet adversarii negant. Tum invocatio religiosa est honor soli Deo debitus, Deut. VI. 13. Matth. IV. 10. Si toto corde vestro revertimini ad Jehovam, auferte Deos alienos, ... & servite ei soli, 1.Sam. VII.3. Invoca me in die angustiae. Eruam te, & glorificabis me, Psal. L. 15. Unde idololatriae postulantur, quotquot eum cultum aliis impendunt, Deut. XVII. 3. 2. Reg. XVII.33. Rom. I. 25. Gal. IV.8. Invocatio enim species latriae & sacrificii est, quam in solum Deum competere, in confesso est. Futilem vero duliae, hyperduliae & latriae distinctionem supra excussimus. Certe Samuel populum עבד δουλεύειν servire soli Deo jussit, 1.Sam. VII.3. Et Deus ipse: Jehovam Deum tuum timebis, ואתו תעבוד & illi servies, Deut. VI.13. Qui porro invocat Sanctos pro intercessione apud Deum, & impetratione beneficiorum per eorum opera, merita & auxilium, is Sanctos se inter & Deum Mediatores facit, eosque tum satisfactionis, quia satisfaciendo Mediator est, quisquis interpositis suis operibus temporalia & spiritualia beneficia impetrat; tum intercessionis, quod ipsi adversarii largiuntur. Sed solus Christus Μεσίτης Mediator noster apud Deum est, 1. Tim. II. 5. In eo solo habemus fiduciam & προσαγωγήν accessum in confidentia, per fidem ipsius, Ephes. III. 12. Ipse est ἱλασμὸς propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, 1. Joh. II. 2. Frustra vero Sanctos velut Mediatores Christo Mediatori subordinari, & a merito & μεσιτείᾳ Christi valorem accipere,
units.tr: But apart from the fact that we have already shaken the foundations of this invocation, other arguments also refute that saint-worship [ἀγιολατρείαν]. For it lacks altogether any command and promise, and it has no example approved anywhere in Scripture; and so it belongs to the invention of men [ἐπιλυμα ἀνθρώπων], the elective worship of God, and the high places of Baal. Bellarmine himself admits that there is no express command or promise, and he does not claim that these can be supplied from elsewhere. As for the claim of others that acts of religion, capable of divine worship, need no express precept and need not be defined by the institution of God, that is surely futile. For they assume that the invocation of the saints is an act of religion approved by God, which we declare to be false. It cannot be referred either to natural or to instituted worship of God. Not to natural worship, because the nature and holiness of God do not prescribe religious worship of the saints, who are creatures. For the saints are not gods, nor do we believe in them, nor place our hope in them, nor love them above all. Nor to instituted worship, because the adversaries themselves deny that there is any institution of God commanding it. Moreover, religious invocation is honour due to God alone: Deut. 6:13; Matt. 4:10: If you return to Jehovah with all your heart, put away the strange gods, … and serve him alone, 1 Sam. 7:3; Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me, Ps. 50:15. Hence all who give this worship to others are charged with idolatry, Deut. 17:3; 2 Kings 17:33; Rom. 1:25; Gal. 4:8. For invocation is a form of latria and of sacrifice, which is admittedly due to God alone. We have already shown above the futility of the distinction between dulia, hyperdulia and latria. Certainly Samuel ordered the people to serve [עבד, δουλεύειν] the Lord alone, 1 Sam. 7:3. And God himself says: You shall fear Jehovah your God, and him [ואתו תעבוד] you shall serve [illi servies], Deut. 6:13. Moreover, whoever invokes the saints for intercession with God, and for obtaining benefits through their works, merits and help, makes the saints mediators between himself and God, and mediators both of satisfaction, since whoever obtains temporal and spiritual benefits by interposing his own works is a mediator by satisfying, and of intercession, which the adversaries themselves concede. But Christ alone is our Mediator [Μεσίτης] with God, 1 Tim. 2:5; In him alone we have confidence and access [προσαγωγήν] in confidence through his faith, Eph. 3:12. He is the propitiation [ἱλασμὸς] for our sins, 1 John 2:2. The adversaries vainly contend that the saints, as subordinate mediators, are subordinated to Christ the Mediator, and receive their value from the merit and mediation [μεσιτείᾳ] of Christ,

units.la: pertendunt. In Scriptura enim solus Christus, sine subordinatis aliis, Mediator cluet, εἷς Μεσίτης unus Mediator est; sicut εἷς Θεὸς unus Deus est, qui Deus natura tales sibi subordinatos nullos habet. Mediator enim ille se ipsum dat ἀντίλυτρον redemptionis pretium pro omnibus, 1. Tim. II. 5. 6. sed praeter Christum nemo subordinatus se redemptionis pretium pro nobis dat. Mediatorem enim esse, ἀπολυτρωτής Dei est; quod tam non creaturis subordinatis communicatur, quam non Divinitas ipsa communicari potest. Praeterea illi Sanctos Mediatores subordinatos verbo, at principales reapse faciunt, tum quia Sanctos sic invocant, ut per eorum merita se exaudiri confidant, tum quia quicquid in Psalmis Deo vel Christo assignatur, illi in Psalterio Mariae tribuere Bonaventura non erubuit; tum quia Sanctos Christo & Patri interdum praeferunt; tum quia in libro conformitatum Francisci laborant, uter fit Jesus, Franciscus typicus, an Christus, neque inter eos aliud discrimen agnoscunt, praeter illud, quod a colore & forma vestis petitur. Praeterea intercessio & redemptio, quae fit per Mediatorem proprie dictum, duo actus ita uniti sunt, ut neuter sine altero existere possit. Sunt enim duae partes unius & ejusdem modi: sicut solutio pretii, & ejusdem continuata repraesentatio, ut redemptis applicetur, proprie ad unum modum pertinent. Praeterea nec Christus meruit, ut alii essent subordinati Mediatores & coadjutores, qui merita sua cum meritis Christi, ut partiales salutis causae, conjungerent. Denique omnis Mediator in causis peccatorum verus medius esse Deum inter & homines esse, & pro hominibus mori, atque sic Deum homini, & hominem Deo reconciliare debet, quales Sancti nulli sunt. Accedit, quod religiose invocandus tribus facultatibus ornatus esse debet; puta scientia rerum nostrarum, voluntate eos curandi a quibus invocatur, & viribus atque potentia naturae, quibus eos curare possit. Atqui scientia rerum nostrarum Sanctos destituit, jam probavimus. Voluntas, seu θελήματος Δόξα iisdem deest, quia res ignotas sibi velle non possunt; & voluntas ex vocatione; vocatio ex mandato & conscientia promissionis cognoscitur. Sed Sanctos res nostras ex mandato & conscientia promissionis cognoscere, nusquam dicitur. At nec potestas tanta Sanctis competit, quia jus postulandi a Deo justitiam & vitam peccatoris, habet solus Christus, qui dona in hominibus accipit; & ad tam varia & tam multa aliter quam successive attendere non possent. Infinitae enim virtutis est uno intuitu tam dissita, & tam diffidentia capere & curare. Si vero successive attendunt, quae fiducia praesentium necessitatum nostrarum omnium ab iis procurandarum capi potest? Neque hic Divinae virtutis gratia, & visionis beatificae status defectum potentiae supplet, quia nunquam Divina virtus sic defectum naturae supplet, ut quod suum est, illi largiatur, adeoque Divinam infinitam virtutem & potentiam, quae ad attendendum tam variis, tam dissitis, tam reconditis, requiritur, creaturae communicet. Hinc adeo Scriptura omnipotentiam ei, qui religiose invocatur, semper tribuit, uti conferentibus, Exod. XV.2. Psalm.
units.tr: but in Scripture Christ alone is shown as Mediator, without any subordinate others: one Mediator [εἷς Μεσίτης] is there, just as one God [εἷς Θεὸς] is there, who by nature has no subordinate such beings. For that Mediator gives himself as a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον], the price of redemption for all, 1 Tim. 2:5–6; but apart from Christ no subordinate gives himself as the price of redemption for us. For to be the Mediator is the office of the Redeemer [ἀπολυτρωτής] of God, which is no more communicated to subordinate creatures than the Divinity itself can be communicated. Besides, they make the saints subordinate mediators in name but principal ones in fact: both because they invoke the saints in such a way that they trust to be heard through their merits, and because whatever is ascribed in the Psalms to God or Christ, Bonaventure did not blush to ascribe to Mary in his Psalter; and because they sometimes set the saints above Christ and the Father; and because in the Book of Conformities they labour over which is Jesus and which Francis the type, whether Francis or Christ, and they recognise no other difference between them except that which is taken from the colour and form of the habit. Moreover, intercession and redemption, which are effected through the Mediator properly so called, are two acts so united that neither can exist without the other. For they are two parts of one and the same kind, just as the payment of the price and its continued representation so that it may be applied to the redeemed belong properly to one manner. Furthermore, Christ did not merit that others should be subordinate mediators and co-workers, who would join their merits with the merits of Christ as partial causes of salvation. Finally, every Mediator, to be a true mediator in the causes of sinners, must stand between God and men, die for men, and so reconcile God to man and man to God; and the saints are none of these. In addition, one who is to be religiously invoked must be endowed with three faculties, namely knowledge of our affairs, will to help those who invoke him, and strength and power of nature by which he can help them. But the saints lack knowledge of our affairs, as we have already shown. Will, or will [θελήματος Δόξα], is likewise lacking in them, because they cannot will things unknown to them; and will is known from calling, and calling from command and the awareness of a promise. But that the saints know our affairs from command and the awareness of a promise is nowhere said. Nor does such power belong to the saints, because the right to ask God for righteousness and life for a sinner belongs to Christ alone, who receives gifts for men; and they could not attend to so many and so varied affairs except successively. For to take in and care for things so distant and so diverse at one glance requires infinite power. But if they attend successively, what confidence can be had that all our present needs will be attended to by them? Nor does the grace of divine power, or the state of the beatific vision, here supply the lack of power, because divine power never so supplies the defect of nature as to bestow on it what is its own, and so to communicate to a creature the infinite divine power and might that is required to attend to things so varied, so distant and so hidden. Hence Scripture always ascribes omnipotence to him who is religiously invoked, as is clear from the passages cited: Exod. 15:2; Ps. 18:2, 4, 49; 62:6, 7, 12; 115:3, 4; 146:2.

units.la: XVIII.2.4.49. LXII.6.7.12. CXV.3.4. CXLVI.2. liquet. Ideo nec vetus Ecclesia Apostolica, nec Apostolicæ vicinior, trium inprimis primorum seculorum, Sanctos religiosè invocavit, quod rationibus πολλαπλαῖς Celeb. Dallæus de Relig. cultus objecto, Lib.III. toto, potenter demonstravit. Primus Origenes, bonus interpres, sed malus dogmatistes, uti eum Hieronymus insignit; se à quodam seniore didicisse ajebat, Sanctos συνευχέσθω unà nobiscum Deum precari. Post eum Cyprianus Epist. 57. superstites oravit, si quis illorum prior Divinæ dignationis celeritate præcesserit, ejus pro fratribus & sororibus apud misericordiam Dei Patris ne cesset oratio. Neuter tamen eo adhuc tempore Sanctos religiosè invocandos docuit. Invaluit enim iis temporibus opinio, quòd Sancti clara Dei visione; quæ invocationis Sanctorum basis est; ante extremum Judicium perfruituri non sint. Demum circa An. Chr. CCCLXX. in Græca Ecclesia Basilius, Nyssenus, Nazianzenus: in Latina Ambrosius Mediolanensis ad invocationem Sanctorum præiverunt. Causæ iis fuerunt intercessio Sanctorum maturè satis credita, zelus & imperitia cum cultu Christi Hellenismi reliquias miscens, Poëtarum Christianorum licentia, Oratorum Ecclesiæ rhetoricationes, hyperbolicæ laudationes & apostrophæ ad Sanctos, quas imperitum vulgus malè distinxit; imprudentia Episcoporum, qui Angelorum, Sanctorumque nomine obtento superstitionis gentilitiæ officia sanctificarunt. Post ea tempora etsi paulatim ἀγιολατρεία invaluit, tamen error ille in Concilio Laodicensi cap.35. Carthaginensi III. can.23. damnatus, à privatis etiam doctoribus Vigilantio, Barcinonensi Presbytero, qui tamen modum non custodivit, Epiphanio, hær.97. Augustino, qui etsi intercessionem Sanctorum agnosceret, tamen fundamenta erroris irrumpentis masculè evertit, unumque Deum adorandum & invocandum passim docuit, neque Sanctis alium, quàm societatis & dilectionis cultum tribuit; rejectus est. Ut nunquam Veteri Ecclesiæ toti error ille hæsisse dici potlit. In ipso papatu eruditi viri, Cassander inprimis in Consultatione vulgatos sectæ suæ circa invocationem Sanctorum errores non paucos perstrinxerunt; & durante Tridentino Concilio in Provinciali Synodo Moguntina auspiciis Sebastiani Electoris, A. MDLI. habita cap.45. sancitum est; Cœlites esse quidem honorandos, sed civili & dilectionis cultu, non secus atque vivos sanctos colimus in hac vita; nisi quòd Sanctis beatitudinem adeptis cultum magis religiosum tribuimus, utpote in statu magis tranquillo constitutis. Teste S.Polano Hist. Conc. Trid. p.267. Quin & ipsum Concilium Tridentinum definiens, Sanctos invocare bonum atque utile esse, non obscurè innuit, non necessariò invocandos esse; neque articulum hunc fidei esse, quamvis Pius IV. postea fortiùs nodum adstrinxit: & in cultu hoc Ecclesia Papalis, in deterius indies proficiens, religionis suæ proram & puppim collocat. Conjurant enim indies Papicolæ, Clerus inprimis, cujus quæstui cultus ille insigniter velificatur, ad palmas ad Deum alium extendendas. Quibus dicere possumus: Annon cognoverunt, qui tractant vanitatem? Qui vorant populum meum, comedunt panem, Deum non invocant, Psal.XIV.4.
units.tr: XVIII.2.4.49. LXII.6.7.12. CXV.3.4. CXLVI.2. liquet. Therefore neither the ancient Apostolic Church, nor the age closest to the Apostles, especially the first three centuries, invoked the saints religiously. Celebrated Dallaeus demonstrated this powerfully, throughout Book III of On the Object of Religious Worship, by many-fold [πολλαπλαῖς] arguments. The first to do so was Origen, a good interpreter, but a bad dogmatist, as Jerome labelled him. He said that he had learned from a certain elder that the saints pray together [συνευχέσθω] with us and pray to God. After him, Cyprian in Epistle 57 prayed to the survivors: if any of them has gone before by the swiftness of God's favour, let prayer for his brothers and sisters before the mercy of God the Father never cease. Yet neither of them at that time taught that the saints were to be invoked religiously. For at that time the opinion had gained ground that the saints would not enjoy the clear vision of God, which is the basis of invoking saints, before the last Judgment. Finally, around the year of Christ 370, in the Greek Church Basil, Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory Nazianzen, and in the Latin Church Ambrose of Milan, led the way in invoking the saints. Their causes were: the intercession of the saints, believed too early; zeal and inexperience, mixing the remnants of Hellenism with the worship of Christ; the license of Christian poets; the rhetorical flourishes of Church orators, their hyperbolic eulogies and apostrophes to the saints, which the unlearned crowd badly misunderstood; and the imprudence of bishops who, under the name of angels and saints, sanctified the rites of pagan superstition. After those times, although hagiolatry [ἀγιολατρεία] gradually gained ground, that error was nonetheless condemned at the Council of Laodicea, canon 35, and at the Third Council of Carthage, canon 23; it was rejected by private teachers, by Vigilantius the presbyter of Barcelona, who nevertheless did not keep to due measure, by Epiphanius in heresy 97, and by Augustine, who, although he acknowledged the intercession of the saints, nonetheless manfully overthrew the foundations of the emerging error, and taught everywhere that the one God alone is to be adored and invoked, and granted the saints only the honour of fellowship and love. So it can never be said that that error clung to the whole ancient Church. Among the Papists themselves, learned men, Cassander above all in his Consultatio, laid bare not a few of the common errors of their sect concerning the invocation of saints. And while the Council of Trent was still in session, at the Provincial Synod of Mainz held under the auspices of Elector Sebastian in 1551, it was decreed in chapter 45: The heavenly ones are indeed to be honoured, but with civil and loving reverence, just as we venerate living saints in this life; except that to saints who have obtained blessedness we give a more religious worship, as being placed in a more tranquil state. This is attested by S. Pallavicino? [Polanus] in History of the Council of Trent, p. 267. Indeed, the Council of Trent itself, in defining that it is good and useful to invoke the saints, hints clearly enough that they are not necessarily to be invoked, and that this is not an article of faith, although Pius IV afterwards tightened the knot more firmly. And in this worship the Papal Church, advancing daily for the worse, sets the prow and stern of its religion. For every day the Papists, above all the clergy, whose gain this worship greatly swells, conspire to stretch out their palms to another god than the Lord. To them we may say: Have they not known, those who deal in vanity? Who eat up my people as they eat bread, and do not call upon God, Psalm 14.4.

units.la: XXXIV. Argumenta illa, quibus hagiolatræ impietatem suam tegunt, magnam partem supra discussimus. Ubi objectiones pro eorum scientia, intercessione pro nobis, & regimine mundi atque Ecclesiæ diluimus. At nec exempla ἀγιολατρείας ab iisdem obducta rem conficiunt. Angelus enim ille, qui Jacobum ab omni malo vindicavit, Genes. XLVIII.16. Christus, verus ἀγχιστεύων Redemptor & sanguinis vindex est, quia solus ille ab omni malo, adeòque etiam peccato, judicio & condemnatione liberat; nec si creatus Angelus fuisset, id animarum cœlitum invocationem statuminaret, quia dispar utrumque, propter Angelorum præsentiam, & animarum absentiam, ratio est, & non sic Angelum Jacobus invocasset, sed Deum, ut per Angelum, per quem ipsum à malo liberavit, nepotes suos pariter liberet, & illis benedicat. Sic enim Deus adorationis objectum, Angelus conferendæ benedictionis administer fuisset. Quòd verò ibid. Jacobus nomen suum super nepotes suos invocari petiit, non ie ab illis post obitum suum à nepotibus suis religiosè invocari petiit; ut adversantes Hebraismi illius, cujus vestigia, Esaj. IV.1. occurrunt, imperitia turpiter hallucinantes colligunt, cùm tamen à nepotibus invocatum eum esse non constet, & in limbo positus invocari non potuerit, sed id intendit, ut vocentur de nomine Jacobi, & sint duo capita tribuum inter filios Jacobi. Uti etiam Tostatus, Ribera, Cornelius à Lapide, aliíque interpretantur. Viderint tamen, qui Jacobum invocationem sui petiisse pertendunt, & eo præterito Franciscum, Dominicum, Borrhomæum, & similes larvas invocant, quàm rectè faciant. Moses quoque placando Deo Patriarchas allegans, & dicens: Recordare Abrahami, Isaaci & Israelis, servorum tuorum, Exod.XXXII.13. non Patriarchas illos invocavit, sed commemoravit duntaxat, quia promissa posteros concernentia, veluti quòd multiplicaturus sit semen illorum, sicut stellas Cœli, &c. ib. iisdem facta sunt. Dilertè enim ad juramentum Dei, quo Deus Patriarchis fœdus gratiæ confirmaverat, provocat. Eodem modo populus Dei: Memento, orat, Davidis omnis molestiæ ejus, studii in restituendo cultu, cum molestia conjuncti, Psal.CXXXII.1. Ita quod v.10. subjicitur: Propter Davidem servum tuum, ne avertas faciem Christi tui, statim v.11. sic explicatur: Juravit Jehova ipsi Davidi veritatem. Orat ergo non Davidem, sed Deum, ut propter Davidem, seu promissionem ipsi de Messia factam, à se faciem non avertat. Eliphazus porrò dicens ad Jobum: Clama nunc, & vide, an fit, qui respondeat tibi; & ad quem Sanctorum te convertas? Job.V.1. non de Sanctis defunctis, sed superstitiosis loquitur, quorum neminem sententiæ suæ, quòd Deus innocentes affligat, suffragaturum innuit. Non ergo Sanctos illos invocat, sed dictorum suorum suffragatores & testes citat. Statim enim v.8. subjicit: Certè ego requirerem Deum, & ad Deum eloquium meum ponerem. Deum ergo, non Sanctos invocare instituit. Si de invocatione Sanctorum verba illa intelligenda forent, manifestum
units.tr: XXXIV. We have discussed most of the arguments by which the hagiolaters cover their impiety above. There we answered the objections according to their knowledge, intercession for us, and the government of the world and the Church. But neither do the examples which they bring forward establish hagiolatry [ἀγιολατρείας]. For that angel who delivered Jacob from all evil, Genesis 48.16, was Christ, the true redeemer [ἀγχιστεύων] and avenger of blood, because he alone frees from all evil, and therefore also from sin, judgment and condemnation. Even had the angel been a created one, that would not establish the invocation of the souls of the heavenly ones, because there is a difference between the two cases: the presence of angels and the absence of souls. Nor would Jacob have invoked the angel, but God, so that through the angel, through whom he himself had been freed from evil, God would likewise free his grandsons and bless them. For thus God would have been the object of worship, and the angel the minister of conferring the blessing. But when Jacob asked, in the same place, that his name be called upon over his grandsons, he did not ask that after his death he be religiously invoked by his grandsons. Those who, through the ignorance of that Hebraism whose traces occur at Isaiah 4.1, wretchedly err in their reasoning, gather this, though it is not established that he was invoked by his grandsons, and being placed in limbo he could not be invoked, but the phrase means that they may be called by the name of Jacob, and that they may be two heads of tribes among the sons of Jacob. So also Tostatus, Ribera, Cornelius a Lapide, and others interpret it. Let them see, however, how rightly they act who maintain that Jacob asked to be invoked himself, and, passing him over, invoke Francis, Dominic, Borromeo and similar specters. Moses too, when appeasing God by citing the patriarchs, saying: Remember Abraham, Isaac and Israel, your servants, Exodus 32.13, did not invoke those patriarchs but merely recalled them, because the promises concerning their posterity, such as that he would multiply their seed as the stars of heaven, etc., were made in the same place. For he expressly appeals to the oath of God, by which God had confirmed the covenant of grace with the patriarchs. In the same way the people of God pray: Remember, O Lord, David and all his affliction, the zeal in restoring worship, joined with affliction, Psalm 132.1. So what follows in verse 10: For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your anointed, is immediately explained in verse 11: The Lord has sworn the truth to David himself. So he prays not to David but to God, that for David's sake, that is for the promise made to him concerning the Messiah, he would not turn his face away. Moreover, when Eliphaz says to Job: Cry out now, and see whether there is anyone who will answer you; and to which of the saints will you turn? Job 5.1, he is not speaking of departed saints, but of superstitious people, none of whom he suggests will support his opinion that God afflicts the innocent. So he is not invoking those saints, but summoning supporters and witnesses of his own sayings. For immediately in verse 8 he adds: Surely I would seek God, and set my cause before God. He therefore advises invoking God, not the saints. If those words were to be understood of the invocation of saints, it would be plain that Eliphaz dissuaded Job from it, since that question is equivalent to a negative.

units.la: Hagiolatrarum argumenta dissimuntur. stum esset, eam Jobo ab Eliphazo dissuaderi; quia interrogatio illa negativæ æquipollet. Idem Jobus cap. XIX.21. clamans: Miseremini mei, miseremini mei יד amici mei, quia manus Dei tetigit me; per שמים amicos, vel socios, non vel Angelos, vel Sanctos Coelites, utpote qui eius socii & familiares non fuerunt, sed eos, quos olim socios & amicos habuit, & quos ad συμπάθειαν graphicè invitat, intelligit. De quibus etiam v. 22. ceu de persecutoribus suis queritur. Ille vero מלאך מליץ Angelus advocatus אחד מני אלף unus ex millibus, Job. XXXIII. 23. Angelus fœderis, Christus est, quia ei tribuuntur prædicata, cujusmodi sunt, misereri, orare liberationem, indicare homini rectitudinem, intercedere cum ostensione מישר lytri, & quidem עליו apud eum, hoc est, לפנים coram, apud faciem Patris, soli Christo Mediatori & Sponsori conveniunt. Neque simpliciter propter λύτρον, sed propter λύτρον à se inventum Deo supplicat. Solus vero Christus illud invenit. Denique nec Sancti viventes uspiam à vivis religiosè invocati leguntur. Non enim fideles à vivis petunt, quæ solus Deus dare potest; nec fidunt meritis vivorum, nec quærunt eorum intercessionem, tanquam patronorum & προσκλητῶν; neque invocant Deum in nomine ipsorum, neque loquuntur cum absentibus & quos non vident, tanquam cum præsentibus; nec coram illis, vel eorum imaginibus procumbunt, vel imagines eorum alloquuntur. Etiamsi enim quidam gestus externi, testes honoris, Deo & creaturis communes sint; tamen quod indifferens est ad testandum affectum fraternum, & affectum religionis, id ex circumstantiis, certum affectum significat. Ideo Deus προσκύνησιν adorationem, ingeniculationem, incurvationem, prostrationem corporis sibi soli vendicat, quia quo pacto Deo, eo nulli creaturæ conveniunt. Cum vero fratres in Christo vivi cum, vel pro aliis vivis orant, communionem Sanctorum, & dilectionem proximi exercent, ut per exauditionem precum communium Deus glorificetur, & gratiarum actione afficiatur, tanquam gratia Dei exaudientis redundante in plures, & ad consolationem plurium. Collaborantibus & vobis pro nobis precibus, ut ex multis aspectibus donum in nos per multos gratiarum actionem habeat pro nobis, 2. Cor. I. 11. Neque hic expectant canonizationem, ut judicent, qui sibi, ceu consortes spiritus precum & fidei, compellandi sint.
units.tr: The arguments of the hagiolaters are concealed. The same Job, crying out in chapter 19.21: Have pity on me, have pity on me, my friends [רעים], for the hand of God has touched me, means by friends not angels or heavenly saints, since they were not his companions and intimates, but those whom he once had as companions and friends, and whom he graphically invites to sympathy [συμπάθειαν]. Of these too, as of his persecutors, he complains in verse 22. But that angel-advocate [מלאך מליץ], one among a thousand [אחד מני אלף], Job 33.23, the angel of the covenant, is Christ, because the attributes that belong to him, such as to have mercy, to plead for deliverance, to show a man uprightness, to intercede, along with the showing of a ransom, and indeed with him [עליו], that is before [לפנים] the face of the Father, belong to Christ alone, the Mediator and Surety. Nor does he pray to God simply on account of a ransom, but on account of a ransom which he himself has found. Christ alone found it. Finally, nowhere are living saints read of as being religiously invoked by the living. For the faithful do not ask the living for what only God can give; they do not trust in the merits of the living, nor seek their intercession as patrons and advocates [προσκλητῶν]; they do not invoke God in their name, nor speak to absent persons whom they do not see as if they were present; they do not prostrate themselves before them or their images, nor address their images. For even if certain outward gestures, which are signs of honour, are common to God and creatures, yet what is indifferent for expressing brotherly affection and religious affection is shown to be a definite affection by the circumstances. Therefore God claims for himself alone worship [προσκύνησιν], adoration, genuflection, bowing and prostration of the body, because these cannot belong to any creature in the way they belong to God. But when living brothers in Christ pray with, or for, other living people, they exercise the communion of saints and love of neighbour, so that God may be glorified through the hearing of common prayers, and be moved to thanksgiving, as the grace of God hearing prayers overflows into many, and into the comfort of many. You also helping us by your prayers, so that the gift bestowed on us through many may be thanked by many on our behalf, 2 Corinthians 1.11. Nor here do they await canonization, so that those who are to be addressed as fellow partners in the spirit of prayer and faith may be judged.

units.la: XXXV. Animæ in Cœlum receptæ sic Dei faciem vident, & eo fruuntur, ut à visione & fruitione nunquam abstrahantur; neque etiam ex Cœlo in terram revertantur, ut apparentes hominibus iisdem inserviant, & eos de rebus Divinis instruant.
units.tr: XXXV. Souls received into heaven see the face of God and enjoy it in such a way that they are never drawn away from that vision and enjoyment. Nor do they return from heaven to earth to appear to men, to serve them, and to instruct them in divine matters.

units.la: Quod εὑρημα illorum est, qui Purgatorio novum colorem quæsiverunt. Sic enim illi disputant: Si redeunt animæ, vel ex Paradiso, vel ex gehenna, vel ex Purgatorio redeunt. At non ex Paradiso & gehenna; quia loca hæc æterna sunt. Ergo ex Purgatorio. Sed rationi huic lumbos Pellanus fregit, qui de Purg. c. 10. disertè docet, & ex Paradiso, & ex gehenna animas educi posse. Sed reditus insuper animæ vel separatæ à corpore, vel cum corpore conjunctæ intelligitur. Posteriore sensu animæ, quæ Christo moriente ex monumentis suis prodierunt, & quas Christus & Apostoli revocarunt, reversæ sunt, sed corporibus suis resurgentibus conjunctæ; neque sic reversæ sunt ad docendum homines, sed ad omnipotentiam Dei demonstrandam, & eo ipso resurrectionis suæ miraculo veritatem doctrinæ de resurrectione confirmandam. Curiosum vero nimis est quærere, quid animabus illis postea factum sit, utrum ne bis mortuæ, an aliquo alio modo? Ex silentio enim Scripturæ colligere est, desiisse omnes suscitatos rebus humanis immorari. Neque mortem repetiisse videntur, quia cum mors stipendium peccati sit, iniquum foret jam receptos in beatitudinem peccato iterum subjici. Tum diserte Apostolus pronuntiat. Omnibus semel statutum esse mori, Hebr. IX. 27. Neque exemplo talium resuscitatorum locuples fides resurrectionis fieret, utpote quæ concipitur futura sempiterna, quod in exemplis istis falsum esset. Cumque Enochus & Elias in Cœlum translati sint, nihil obstat, quò minus de reliquis idem judicium sit. Si tamen iterum mortui fuissent, neque ideo spiritus eorum cœlesti beatitudine fruiti essent, potuerunt conservari in manu Dei, & in statu sibi competente, donec corpori restituerentur.
units.tr: This is the invention of those who have sought a new colour for Purgatory. For they argue thus: if souls return, they return either from Paradise, or from hell, or from Purgatory. But not from Paradise or hell, because those places are eternal. Therefore from Purgatory. But Pellanus broke the back of this argument, who clearly teaches in De Purgatorio, chapter 10, that souls can be led out both from Paradise and from hell. Moreover, a return may be understood either of a soul separated from the body or of one joined to the body. In the latter sense, the souls which came out of their tombs when Christ died, and which Christ and the apostles recalled, did return, but joined to their bodies as they rose again; and they did not return to teach men, but to demonstrate the omnipotence of God and, by the very miracle of his resurrection, to confirm the truth of the doctrine of the resurrection. But it is too curious to ask what became of those souls afterwards: whether they died twice, or in some other way? For from the silence of Scripture it can be gathered that all those raised ceased to dwell among human affairs. Nor do they seem to have died again, since death is the wages of sin, and it would be unjust for those already received into blessedness to be subjected to sin once more. Then the Apostle plainly declares: "It is appointed unto all men once to die," Heb. 9.27. Nor would faith in the resurrection be enriched by the example of such raised persons, since it is conceived as a future and everlasting state, which these examples would make false. And since Enoch and Elijah were translated into heaven, nothing prevents the same judgment being made about the rest. Yet even if they had died again, and their spirits had not on that account been enjoying heavenly blessedness, they could have been preserved in the hand of God and in a state suited to them, until they were restored to their bodies.

units.la: XXXVI. Sed animæ sine corpore nullæ in præsentem vitam revertuntur. Nam anima corpore soluta similis est spiritui, seu vento, qui vadit, & non revertitur, Psal. LXXVIII. 39. David quoque de filio suo mortuo: Migrabo ad ipsum, sed non revertetur ad me, 2. Sam. XII. 23. Ideo Abrahamus helluoni supplici, ut mittat Lazarum ad fratres suos, præconem ipsis futurum pœnitentiæ, respondet: Habent Mosen & Prophetas: Eos audiant. Si non audient, non persuadebuntur etiam, si quis ex mortuis resuscitabitur, Luc. XVI. 29. Neque tantùm eo tempore Abrahamus missionem Lazari abnuebat, non negans, quia possit & velit Deus alios mittere, uti Delrio instat, quia de potentia Dei non disputamus, & voluntas ejus patefacta nuspiam est; & obstat ratio Abrahami, quòd viventes habeant Mosen & Prophetas, neque doctoribus aliis indigeant. Sed & disertè Deus prohibuit, ne quisquam mortuos in consilium adhibeat. Ne fit inter vos דרש אל המתים quærens ex mortuis, Deut. XVIII. 11. Et quomodo dicunt ad vos: Consulite engastrimythos & divinos, pipientes & anhelantes? Annon populus Deum suum consulet? vivorum causa mortuos? Ad Legem & Prophetas, Esaj. VIII. 19. 20. Neque vivi mortuorum institutione indigent, neque mortuis in Cœlum receptis redeundi in terram causa ulla esse potest. Cur non enim cum Christo esse, & beatitudine sua perfrui habebunt potius? Scitè Chrysostomus in Matth. homil. 38. Multis, inquit, e locis Scriptura comprobari potest, non errare hic post mortem justorum hominum animas. Nam & Stephanus ait: Suscipe spiritum meum. Et S. Paulus resolvi, ac cum Christo esse desiderabat. De Patriarcha quoque Scriptura dixit: Et appositus est ad Patres suos, e-nutritus in senectute bona. Quod verò nec peccatorum animæ hic commorari possint, divitem audias, qui enixè eam rem petit, nihil tamen impetrat. Quòd si possent animæ hominum hic convertere, venisset ipse, & suos de tormentis inferni certiores
units.tr: XXXVI. But souls without bodies do not return into the present life. For a soul released from the body is like a spirit, or wind, which goes and does not return, Ps. 78.39. David also said of his dead son: "I shall go to him, but he will not return to me," 2 Sam. 12.23. Therefore Abraham, when the rich man in torment asked that he send Lazarus to his brothers to be a herald of repentance to them, answers: "They have Moses and the Prophets: let them hear them. If they do not hear them, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead," Luke 16.29. Nor did Abraham refuse Lazarus's mission only at that time, not denying that God is able and willing to send others, as Delrio insists, since we do not dispute about the power of God, and his will has nowhere been revealed; and Abraham's reasoning stands, namely that the living have Moses and the Prophets and do not need other teachers. But God has also expressly forbidden anyone to consult the dead: "Let there not be found among you one who seeks of the dead" (Hebrew: דרש אל המתים), Deut. 18.11. "And when they say to you: Consult the ventriloquists and the wizards, who chirp and mutter? Should not a people consult its God? Should the living consult the dead? To the Law and to the Prophets," Isa. 8.19, 20. The living do not need instruction from the dead, and there can be no reason for those received into heaven to return to earth. For why should they not rather be with Christ and enjoy their blessedness? Chrysostom wisely says on Matthew, homily 38: "From many places in Scripture it can be proved," he says, "that the souls of righteous men do not wander here after death. For Stephen also says: 'Receive my spirit.' And St Paul desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ. Scripture also said of the patriarch: 'And he was gathered to his fathers, having been nourished in a good old age.' That the souls of sinners also cannot linger here, hear the rich man, who earnestly seeks this, yet obtains nothing. For if the souls of men could return here, he would have come himself and made his brothers more certain of the torments of hell."

units.la: Anima cum corpore conjuncta quædam in terram redierunt; quibus quid factum postea fit, incertum est. tiores reddidisset. Quo ex loco scriptura illud etiam aperte patet, quod post exitum ex corpore in locum certum animae deducuntur, unde redire non possunt, sed terribilem judicii diem ibi expectant. Quae verba Anianus interpres sic corrupit, ut Chrysostomi, negantis, animas ξυ ... potestatem habere redeundi, verbis adderet sponte sua, quasi sponte redire non possent, at possent Deo mandante & veniam concedente. Sed qui mandatum & veniam habet redeundi, etsi sponte sua non redit, ex mandato tamen & venia potestatem redeundi habet. Tum Divina voluntas, ut redeant frequenter animae, nec ex Scriptura, nec ex alia revelatione probari potest; & rationes allatae voluntatem ejusmodi nullam esse, evincunt.
units.tr: Some souls, joined again to their bodies, returned to earth; what became of them afterwards is uncertain. ... From this passage of Scripture it is also plainly clear that after departing from the body souls are led to a certain place, from which they cannot return, but there await the dreadful day of judgment. Anianus the translator so corrupted these words of Chrysostom, who denies that souls have the power of returning, that he added to them "of their own accord", as if souls could not return of their own accord but could return at God's command and with his permission. But one who has command and permission to return, even if he does not return of his own accord, nevertheless has the power of returning by command and permission. Moreover, that it is the divine will that souls often return can be proved neither from Scripture nor from any other revelation; and the reasons adduced show that there is no such will.

units.la: XXXVII. Sed animarum corporibus solutarum ἐπιφάνεια post Philosophos Platonicos, Rabbinos veteres, Muhammedanos & Indos Pontificii severe propugnant.
units.tr: XXXVII. After the Platonic philosophers, the ancient rabbis, the Muhammadans and the Indians, the Papists strenuously defend the appearance [ἐπιφάνεια] of the souls of the departed.

units.la: Samuelis enim mortui animam a Pythonissa excitam Sauli apparuisse, ex 1. Sam. XXVIII. 7. 8. probare contendunt. Caeterum de anima sola excita nihil textus habet. Si verus Samuel apparuit, una cum corpore apparuit, adeoque ex mortuis resurrexit, quales etiam alii Divinitus ex morte resuscitati sunt. At nec γνῶσις Samuel fuit, qui ibi inducitur, sed falsum ejus schema, Diaboli praestigiis excantatum. Verus enim Samuel, omnium-que in pace hinc migrantium animae in Dei manu sunt, minime omnium potestati Sathanae, & incantationibus Pythonicis obnoxiae. Faceret enim id magnopere tum ad minuendum solatium piorum, si post hanc vitam Diaboli imperio subjicerentur: tum ad confirmandam artem magorum, totiusque adeo γοητείας & νεκρομαντείας. Nam quod praeoccupasse Samuelem Pythonissae artes Bellarminus regerit, certe id a Scriptura non habet, quae ejus rei non meminit. Cumque Deus Sauli per Prophetas vivos respondere dedignatus fuerit, vers. 6. multo minus per mortuos in gratiam ejus Divina potentia resuscitatos, qualem Samuelem fingunt, respondere dignatus esset. Neque etiam verus Samuel se adorari a Saule passus esset, uti larvatus ille passus est, ib. v. 14. vel Sauli λοξῶς μαντεύων ambigue vaticinatus respondisset, uti ille, dicens: Cras tu & filii tui mecum erunt, v. 19. fecit. Praeterea petiit Saul a Pythonissa: Divina mihi per Pythonem, ib. v. 8. At verus Samuel non fuit Pytho. Vocat etenim scriptor ille sacer Samuelem, quia nimirum imagines earum rerum, quarum imagines sunt, nominibus appellari solent. Et Saul Samuelem cognovit, ex conjectura & levibus indiciis, qualia erant senectus & pallium, non ex certa scientia; quomodo & Joab reprehendens ludum Davidis super mortem filii Absolonis cognovi, inquit, hodie, quod si Absolon viveret, & nos omnes essemus mortui, bene placeret tibi, 2. Sam. XIX. 6. ubi manifeste conjectura est Joabi, & levis illa. Potuit etiam Diabolus imminens Sauli fatum cognoscere, permittente Deo, & variis quidem modis, quos Augustinus ad Simplic. retulit; nec non ex signis praecedentibus. Quanquam & praedictio illa sic satis leviloqua fuit. Mosis & Eliae cum Christo in monte transfigurato sermones de novissimis ejus, Matth. XVII. 3. Luc. IX. 31. nec non resurgentium cum Christo, Matth. XXVII, 52, 53. exempla ἀναστάσεως sunt, quia Moses & Elias in corporibus propriis apparuerunt, & confestim in Coelum remigrasse videntur; & qui cum Domino resurrexerunt atque Hierosolymis apparuerunt, eorum spiritus cum corporibus resurgentibus etiam uniti sunt, & missi hi sunt plane extra ordinem, singularis oeconomiae gratia, quod in Scriptura Deus testatus est; cum animarum apparitiones jactatae nullum certum testimonium habeant. nem, revelandam in die novissimo; felicitatem æternam, corporis sui resurrectionem & unionem, atque inde ut majorem suppositi perfectionem & aptitudinem, ita felicitatem & lætitiam consummationem. Denique cœlestis illius civitatis, quæ fundamenta habet, perfectionem, per membrorum omnium electorum unionem, & ἀναστέφαλαίωσιν ultimam, redemptionis consummationem, & gloriosum Christi Judicis in terram reditum ad sui ipsius & aliorum justificationem finalem & investituram gloriæ, denique fruitionem magni illius convivii, in quo cum Abrahamo, Isaco & Jacobo multi, maxima multitudo ex Oriente & Occidente in Regno Cœlorum accumbent, Matth. VIII. 11. In specie autem piis Martyribus vindictam Dei adversus persecutores suos implorantibus his verbis: Usque quò Domine, qui sanctus es & verax, non judicas, & vindicas sanguinem nostrum ab iis qui habitant in terra? pro tempore datæ sunt stolæ albæ, symbola sanctæ justæque causæ, quam in mundo pro Christo gesserunt, eisque dictum est, ut quiescerent adhuc parvum tempus, donec etiam πληρωθωσιν impleRent agonem suum, vel plene se associarent eorum fratres, qui similiter atque ipsi interficiendi erant, Apoc. VI. 11.
units.tr: They argue from 1 Sam. 28:7-8 that the soul of the dead Samuel, called up by the witch of Endor, appeared to Saul. But the text says nothing about a soul called up alone. If the real Samuel appeared, he appeared together with his body, and so he rose from the dead, as others also were raised from death by divine power. But the one introduced there was not Samuel in his true γνῶσις [knowledge/true self]; he was a false semblance of him, conjured up by the Devil's tricks. The real Samuel, and the souls of all who depart from here in peace, are in the hand of God, and are least of all subject to the power of Satan and to Pythonic incantations. For if this were so, it would greatly diminish the comfort of the godly, if after this life they were subjected to the Devil's dominion; and it would greatly confirm the art of magicians, and indeed all sorcery [γοητεία] and necromancy [νεκρομαντεία]. As for Bellarmine's claim that Samuel had anticipated the witch's arts, Scripture certainly says nothing of this, since it makes no mention of such a thing. And since God deigned not to answer Saul through the living prophets (v. 6), much less would he have deigned to answer through the dead, raised by divine power for Saul's sake, as the Papists imagine Samuel to have been. Nor would the real Samuel have allowed himself to be worshipped by Saul, as that masked figure did (v. 14), or answered Saul with an ambiguous prophecy [λοξῶς μαντεύων ambigue], as that one did, saying: Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me (v. 19). Moreover, Saul asked the witch: Divine for me by a Python (v. 8). But the real Samuel was not a Python. Indeed, the sacred writer calls him "Samuel" because the images of things are commonly named by the names of the things they represent. And Saul recognised Samuel from conjecture and slight signs, such as old age and the mantle, not from certain knowledge. Likewise Joab, rebuking David's grief over the death of Absalom, says: I know today that if Absalom were alive, and we all were dead, it would please you well (2 Sam. 19:6). There Joab's knowledge is plainly conjecture, and slight conjecture at that. The Devil too could have known Saul's impending fate, by God's permission, and in various ways, which Augustine lists in his ad Simplicianum, and also from preceding signs. Yet even that prediction was rather vague. The words of Moses and Elijah with Christ on the transfigured mountain concerning his departure (Matt. 17:3; Luke 9:31), and of those who rose with Christ (Matt. 27:52-53), are examples of ἀνάστασις [resurrection], because Moses and Elijah appeared in their own bodies, and seem to have returned to heaven at once; and those who rose with the Lord and appeared in Jerusalem had their spirits united again with their rising bodies. These were sent quite outside the ordinary course, by the singular grace of God's economy, as God has testified in Scripture; whereas the boasted appearances of souls have no certain testimony. [...] (the revelation to be made on the last day; eternal happiness; the resurrection and reunion of the body; and from this, as the person's perfection and fitness increase, so too the consummation of happiness and joy. Finally, the perfection of that heavenly city which has foundations; the union of all the elect members, and the final ἀνακεφαλαίωσις [recapitulation]; the consummation of redemption; and the glorious return of Christ the Judge to the earth for the final justification of himself and others and the investiture of glory; and lastly the enjoyment of that great feast, at which with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob many, a great multitude, from East and West shall sit down in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 8:11).) In particular, the godly martyrs, who implore God's vengeance on their persecutors with these words: How long, Lord, who are holy and true, do you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?, were given white robes, the tokens of the holy and just cause which they served in the world for Christ; and it was said to them that they should rest yet a little time, until their fellow servants and brothers, who were to be killed as they were, should be fulfilled [πληρωθῶσιν], or should fully join them (Rev. 6:11).

units.la: XXXIX. Glorificationem animæ excipit Glorificatio Totius Hominis, qua electi in fide mortui, in consummatione seculi, secundum animam & corpus perfectæ beatitudinis & gloriæ consortes reddentur.
units.tr: XXXIX. The glorification of the soul is followed by the glorification of the whole man, in which the elect who have died in faith will, at the consummation of the age, be made partakers of perfect blessedness and glory, in both soul and body.

units.la: De ea loquitur S. Paulus: Oportet, inquiens, Christum regnare donec omnes hostes suos pedibus suis subjecerit. Ultimus hostis aboletur mors. Omnia enim pedibus ejus subjecit, &c. Cum vero omnia ipsi subjecta fuerint, tum & ipse Filius subjicietur ei, qui omnia sibi subjecit, ut Deus sit omnia in omnibus, 1. Cor. XV. 25-29. Nondum enim habetur omnia in omnibus est, quia in hac vita in fidelibus etiam caro, peccatum, corruptio, mortalitas; in altera mors corporis & corruptio ejus extrema in homine est; adeoque non Deus πάντα ἐν πᾶσι omnia in omnibus est. Ultimus hominis hostis mors corporis est. Cum igitur spiritus in morte corporis sit vita propter justitiam, nihil ad completionem hominis, & ut in eo Deus sit omnia in omnibus, restat, nisi ut corpus ex mortuis resurgat. Ideo expectare dicimur ἀπολύτρωσιν redemptionem corporis nostri, Rom. VIII. 23. Expectamus enim, ut cognoscamus plenius, quid sit, à Christo emptum & redemptum esse, & ad quid corpora nostra redempta sint. Spiritu S. obsignati estis εἰς ἡμέραν ἀπολυτρώσεως ad diem redemptionis, hoc est, ad diem perficiendæ liberationis illius, quæ per λύτρον fit, Ephes. IV. 30. coll. cum I. 14. Intelligitur perfecta liberatio nostri, per quam extra periculum constituimur, per lytri dationem paratam. Nam ἀπολύτρωσις consideratur partim ratione meriti, ut est τὸ ἀντάλλαγμα ... dare se ipsum redemptionis pretium pro omnibus, 1. Tim. II. 6. partim ratione efficaciæ τῆς λύτρου. In qua τῆς λύτρου efficacia est primò vocatio per Evangelium sine lege; secundò regeneratio per Spiritum adoptionis: tertiò conservatio usque ad finem: quartò extinctio vetusti hominis per mortem: denique liberatio corporis ex mortem
units.tr: St. Paul speaks of this: "Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. For he has put all things under his feet," etc. "When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to himself, so that God may be all in all." 1 Cor. 15:25-29. For God is not yet "all in all" [πάντα ἐν πᾶσι], because in this life, even in the faithful, there remain flesh, sin, corruption and mortality; in the next life, the death of the body and its final corruption remain in man, and so God is not yet all in all [πάντα ἐν πᾶσι]. The last enemy of man is the death of the body. Since the spirit lives on account of righteousness even in the death of the body, nothing remains for the completion of the man, and for God to be all in all in him, except that the body rise from the dead. Therefore we are said to wait for the redemption [ἀπολύτρωσιν] of our body, Rom. 8:23. For we wait so that we may know more fully what it means to have been bought and redeemed by Christ, and for what purpose our bodies have been redeemed. "You were sealed with the Holy Spirit unto the day of redemption" [εἰς ἡμέραν ἀπολυτρώσεως], that is, to the day of completing that liberation which comes about through a ransom [λύτρον], Eph. 4:30, compared with 1:14. The complete liberation of ourselves is understood, by which we are placed beyond danger, through the giving of the ransom that has been prepared. For redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις] is considered partly with respect to merit, as it is "the exchange" [τὸ ἀντάλλαγμα] ... "to give himself as the redemption price for all", 1 Tim. 2:6, and partly with respect to the efficacy of the ransom [τῆς λύτρου]. The efficacy of this ransom is, first, the calling through the Gospel without the law; second, regeneration through the Spirit of adoption; third, preservation to the end; fourth, the putting to death of the old man; and finally, the liberation of the body from death

units.la: te, quæ illa ἀπολύτρωσις τῆς σωματος, Rom. VIII. 23. est.
units.tr: ...which is that redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις] of the body, Rom. 8:23.

units.la: XL. Glorificationis hujus gradus in Scriptura tres memorantur. Resuscitatio mortuorum, Judicium ultimum & vita æterna. Redibit enim Christus ex Cœlo ad resuscitandos & judicandos vivos & mortuos; & fideles secum in Cœlum assumendos. Ille Jesus, qui sursum receptus est à vobis in Cœlum, sic veniet (redibit) sicut vidistis eum proficiscentem in Cœlum, Actor. I. 11. Ipse Dominus in celeusmate, in voce Archangeli, & in tuba Dei descendet de Cœlo, & mortui in Christo resurgent primò, 1. Thess. IV. 16. Qui descensus Christi de Cœlo, ibid. v. 15. vocatur παρουσία præsentia, hoc est, aspectabilis ejus adventus. Quem Christus ipse describit, respondens discipulis scisciantibus: Quod signum est τῆς παρουσίας adventus & consummationis seculi? Matth. XXIV. 3. Modum enim ejus tradit dicens: Sicut fulgur exit ab Oriente, & lucet usque in Occidentem; ita erit adventus Filii hominis, v. 27. Nihil fulgure ex Oriente in Occidentem exeunte & lucente aspectabilius est. Præstringit enim oculos apertos etiam invitorum & nolentium. Talis Christi in terram reditus erit: neque alius erit invisibilis; quia aliàs Christi ratio, qua dicentibus Pseudo-prophetis: Hic est, in eremo est, in conclavibus est, credere vetat, nullam vim haberet. Et S. Paulus: Contestor coram Deo & Domino Jesu Christo, qui judicaturus est vivos & mortuos κατὰ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν αὐτοῦ cum apparitione sua & Regno, hoc est, cùm apparebit & ceu Rex regnabit, 2. Tim. IV. 1. Nam apparens novissimè Rex esse incipiet modo excellentissimo, quia cùm Pater omnia implebit, & omnia in omnibus erit, tum etiam Filius omnia in omnibus erit. Eo enim fine vivos & mortuos judicabit, ut justos in Regnum suum introducat, & injustos à se ableget. Veniet autem Filius hominis, ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν τῆς οὐρανοῦ, μετὰ δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης πολλῆς super nubibus cœli, cum potentia & gloria multa, Matth. XXIV. 30. Ab hoc tempore videbitis Filium hominis venientem in nubibus Cœli, ibid. XXVI. 64. Nubes enim Christum in Cœlum sustulit, Actor. I. 9. Nubes eundem ex Cœlo in terram feret. Sed nubem illam flamma ignita comitabitur. Nam revelabitur Dominus Jesus ex Cœlo cum Angelis suis ἐν πυρὶ Φλογὸς in flamma ignis, dans ultionem ignorantibus Deum, &c. 2. Thess. I. 7. 8.
units.tr: XL. Three stages of this glorification are recorded in Scripture: the resurrection of the dead, the last judgment, and eternal life. For Christ will return from heaven to raise and judge the living and the dead, and to take the faithful with him into heaven. This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way (will return) as you saw him going into heaven (Acts 1:11). The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will rise first (1 Thess. 4:16). This descent of Christ from heaven, v. 15, is called παρουσία [presence], that is, his visible coming. Christ himself describes it when answering his disciples who asked: What is the sign of your [τῆς παρουσίας] coming and of the consummation of the age? (Matt. 24:3). For he gives its manner, saying: As lightning comes out of the East and shines even to the West, so will be the coming of the Son of man (v. 27). Nothing is more visible than lightning coming out of the East and shining to the West. It dazzles the eyes even of those who are unwilling and unwitting. Such will be Christ's return to the earth; it will not be invisible. Otherwise Christ's rule, by which he forbids us to believe the false prophets when they say: Here he is, in the desert, in the inner rooms, would have no force. And St. Paul: I charge you before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who is to judge the living and the dead, at his appearing [κατὰ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν αὐτοῦ] and his kingdom (2 Tim. 4:1), that is, when he appears and reigns as King. For, appearing at the last, he will begin to be King in a most excellent manner, since when the Father fills all things and is all in all, the Son too will be all in all. For to this end he will judge the living and the dead, that he may bring the just into his kingdom and separate the unjust from himself. The Son of man will come [ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, μετὰ δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης πολλῆς] upon the clouds of heaven, with great power and glory (Matt. 24:30). From this time you will see the Son of man coming on the clouds of heaven (Matt. 26:64). For a cloud took Christ up into heaven (Acts 1:9); a cloud will bring him again from heaven to the earth. But that cloud will be accompanied by a blazing fire. For the Lord Jesus will be revealed from heaven with his angels in flaming fire [ἐν πυρὶ φλογός], giving vengeance to those who do not know God, etc. (2 Thess. 1:7-8).

units.la: XLI. Adventum Domini ad judicium ante diluvium septimus ab Adamo, seu septimæ ætatis vir, Enochus commemorabili prophetia prædixit.
units.tr: XLI. Enoch, the seventh from Adam, or the man of the seventh age, foretold the Lord's coming to judgment before the flood in a memorable prophecy.

units.la: Prophetavit & his septimus ab Adamo Enoch, dicens: Ecce venit Dominus cum Sanctis myriadibus suis, ut faciat judicium de omnibus, & ut redarguat omnes impios eorum de omnibus operibus impietatis eorum, quæ impie egerunt, & de omnibus, quæ locuti sunt contra ipsum peccatores impii, Jud. vers. 14. Quæ Prophetia non ἐγγεγραμμένον, seu totidem verbis scripta fuit, uti Patres multi exiistimarunt, & Judæi etiam fabulati sunt, libro sub nomine Enochi vendito, cujus editio Græca in manus Josephi Scaligeri pervenit, qui ex libro ejus primo fragmentum ... de Egregoris (ficAngelos vocat liber, & ex eo Eusebius & Africanus) notis suis ad Græca Eusebii inseruit, quod nori non dubitaret, quin eo fragmento arcessita sit tum Prophetia Enochi, quæ à Juda citatur: tum ejusdem Judæ de Angelis prævaricatoribus narratio. Sed Judas non scripsisse Enochum Prophetiam, sed simpliciter prophetasse, dicit. Potuit autem oretenus prophetare, quod scripto non mandavit. Et quod ore prophetavit, continetur etiam in potestate verborum, quibus ambulasse coram Deo dicitur, Genes. V. 24. utpote in quibus fundamentum Prophetiæ continetur. Ex eo Judæ facile fuit Divino Spiritu colligere, quod Enoch non tantùm pro se Deum quæsiverit, sed etiam alios propositò metu judicii ad quærendum incitaverit; nec pii viri & prophetæ officio, nisi prænuntiando judicium Dei defungi potuerit. Hactenus igitur prophetia illa in Enochi historia etiam ἐγγεγραμμένον, quod fundamentum, non formulam continet. Quam in rem plura Hist. Patr. Tom. I. Dissert. X. diximus.
