Prophetavit autem Enochus, Juda teste, quod Dominus venerit cum Sanctis myriadibus suis, ut faciat judicium. Venisse ait, qui venturus erat, propter certitudinem adventus. Venit Dominus cum myriadibus sanctitatis, seu sanctorum, prodiens è monte Sinai: venit & apparuit in carne manifestatus in Sion: & veniet in nubibus cum Angelis ad judicandum vivos & mortuos: venit ad judicandum, prodiens è myriadibus sanctitatis, Deut. XXXIII. 2. in monte Sinai, ubi populum Israeliticum propter transgressiones, imponendo ei jugum servitutis, & gentes, quibus non dedit eloquia sua, à fœdere gratiæ eas arcendo, judicavit. Venit in Sionem, ubi effudit Spiritum suum, & eo effuso suos ad myriadas Angelorum, Hebr. XII. 22. adduxit, simul damnans omnes homines & principes, utpote impares præstandæ justitiæ, propter quam Christus è Cœlo venire debuit, factus peccatum, & condemnans peccatum in carne, Rom. VIII. 3. Joh. XVI. 11. & judicans inter populos, Esaj. II. 4. quando gentibus accessum ad Regnum fecit, & Judæos ex Regno suo, ademptis eis prærogativis, ejecit. Denique venturus est in nubibus cum Angelis, ad judicandum vivos & mortuos, Matth. XXIV. 30. XXV. 31. 2. Thess. I. 7. 8. 2. Tim. IV. 1. & quidem μετὰ δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης πολλῆς cum potentia & gloria multa, Luc. XXI. 27. oppositè ad adventum priorem in carnem, qui humilis fuit, & Majestatem latentem habuit. Hic verò erit in potentia aperta, quia ad ejus nutum mortui resuscitabuntur: & in gloria, seu Majestate multa, quia in corpore ejus Majestas relucebit, & veniet stipatus millibus Angelorum, qui honoris gratia, & testes justissimi judicii aderunt. Merito igitur Christianorum symbolum est: Μαρανα θα, quod est, אתא מרן Dominus noster venit; quæ ratio est anathematis, quo percellitur is, qui non diligit Dominum Jesum, 1. Cor. XVI. 22. Qui enim talem Dominum habent, illi anathema ΠΠ ἀποχωρισμὸν separationem habere, seu separare se ab iis, qui non diligunt Dominum Jesum, debent.
units.tr: Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied, saying: Behold, the Lord comes with his holy myriads, to execute judgment upon all, and to convict all the ungodly of all their ungodly deeds which they have committed ungodly, and of all the harsh things which ungodly sinners have spoken against him, Jude v. 14. This prophecy was not written down [ἐγγεγραμμένον], or set down in these very words, as many of the Fathers thought, and as the Jews also invented, in a book sold under Enoch's name. A Greek edition of that book came into the hands of Joseph Scaliger, who, from its first book, inserted into his notes on Eusebius's Greek text a fragment about the Egregores (the book calls them Angels, and Eusebius and Africanus follow it). He did not doubt that from this fragment came both the prophecy of Enoch cited by Jude and Jude's account of the rebellious angels. But Jude says only that Enoch prophesied, not that he wrote a prophecy. He could have prophesied by word of mouth what he did not commit to writing. What he prophesied by mouth is also contained in the force of the words by which he is said to have walked with God, Gen. v. 24, since the foundation of the prophecy is contained in them. From this, Jude could easily gather by the Divine Spirit that Enoch not only sought God for himself, but also deliberately stirred others to seek him by the fear of judgment; and he could discharge the duty of a godly man and prophet only by announcing the judgment of God. So far, then, that prophecy is also written in Enoch's history, in the sense that it contains the foundation, not the formula. On this point we have said more in the Hist. Patr. Tom. I. Dissert. X. Enoch, according to Jude's testimony, prophesied that the Lord would come with his holy myriads, to execute judgment. Jude says that he has come who was to come, because of the certainty of his coming. The Lord came with the myriads of holiness, or of the saints, going out from Mount Sinai; he came and appeared in the flesh, made manifest in Zion; and he will come in the clouds with his angels to judge the living and the dead. He came to judge, going out from the myriads of holiness, Deut. xxxiii. 2, on Mount Sinai, where he judged the Israelite people for their transgressions by laying on them the yoke of slavery, and judged the nations, to whom he had not given his oracles, by shutting them out from the covenant of grace. He came to Zion, where he poured out his Spirit, and by that outpouring brought his people to the myriads of angels, Heb. xii. 22, at the same time condemning all men and rulers, as unequal to the righteousness that had to be supplied, for which Christ had to come from heaven, made sin and condemning sin in the flesh, Rom. viii. 3, John xvi. 11, and judging between the peoples, Isa. ii. 4, when he opened the way into the kingdom for the Gentiles and cast the Jews out of his kingdom, taking away their privileges. Finally, he will come in the clouds with angels to judge the living and the dead, Matt. xxiv. 30, xxv. 31, 2 Thess. i. 7, 8, 2 Tim. iv. 1, and indeed μετὰ δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης πολλῆς [with great power and glory], Luke xxi. 27, in contrast with his earlier coming in the flesh, which was humble and had a hidden majesty. But this coming will be in open power, because at his word the dead will be raised; and in glory, or in much majesty, because his majesty will shine forth in his body, and he will come surrounded by thousands of angels, who will attend for honour and as witnesses of the most just judgment. Rightly, therefore, the watchword of Christians is Μαρανα θα [Maranatha], that is, אתא מרן [Aramaic: "our Lord has come"], Our Lord comes; and this is the reason for the anathema by which he is struck down who does not love the Lord Jesus, 1 Cor. xvi. 22. For those who have such a Lord ought to keep themselves apart, that is, separate themselves, from those who do not love the Lord Jesus, under anathema.

units.la: XLII. Damnandi igitur sunt ἐμπαικταὶ irrisores, qui venient in novissimo dierum, & secundum proprias concupiscentias incedentes, dicent: Ubi est promissio adventus ejus? Ex quo enim Patres obdormiverunt, omnia sic manent ab principio creationis, 2. Petr. III. 3. 4. Quibus verbis gemella illa Manilii sunt.
units.tr: XLII. Those scoffers [ἐμπαικταί] are therefore to be condemned, who will come in the last days, walking according to their own lusts, and will say: "Where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things remain as they were from the beginning of creation," 2 Pet. iii. 3, 4. To these words belong those twin verses of Manilius.

units.la: Idem semper erit, quoniam semper fuit idem. Non alium videre Patres, aliumve nepotes Adspicient.
units.tr: It will always be the same, since it always has been the same. The fathers will not see another world, nor will their grandsons look upon one.

units.la: Irrisores illi haud dubiè athei sunt, qui Scripturam & promissiones in eadem comprehensas vel non intelligunt, vel intellectas explodunt. Quorum ratio, quòd inde à principio creationis cuncta eadem maneant, nimis absurda est. Nam ex prædictionibus, earumque eventu satis constat, Deum mutaturum fuisse tempora, & mutasse etiam secundum ea, quæ prædicta ab eo sunt. Inprimis diluvio mundus judicatus & perditus est. Deus autem non mutatur. Non alio tempore voluntatem judicandi habet, alio non. Quia semel ostendit, se velle venire ad judicandum, & judicare, omnino expectandum judicium, & adventus Domini ad judicium est. Et quia semel mundum totum, hoc est, omnes homines delevit, satis clarè testatus est, se non semper improbos toleraturum, vel velle, ut semper in terra coram oculis suis sint improbi, blasphemantes nomen ejus. Hoc latere irrisores ἐμπαικταὶ volentes dicit, quia non cogitant de argumentis, quibus id judicium fit certissimum; imò contrà disputant. Diluvium autem factum esse, facilè sciri ab eo, qui scire vult, potest. Omitto famam, quæ apud gentes de eo percrebuit etiam antea, quàm libri Mosis in toto mundo legerentur, quod Grotius de Verit. Relig. Christ. aliique collectis gentilium testimoniis, probarunt, & nos quoque Hist. Patr. T. I. Dissert. XVIII. 40. &c. fusius probavimus. Et ipse Moses diluvii testis idoneus est, quia de cætero cognoscitur servus Dei fidelis in tota domo ejus, & ea, quæ hac de re scripsit, à nemine mendacii insimulata sunt. Et quòd homines consilium iniverunt condendæ urbis, cui בבל Babel, confusionis nomen ex eventu hæsit; satis id arguit, quòd diluvium præcesserit. Quòd si autem diluvium verum est, non igitur omnia manent ab initio creationis eodem modo; imò id clarum indicium est futuri adventus Domini ad aliud judicium. In sequentibus etiam Petrus fideles adversus irrisores munit, ostendens, tum apud Deum unum diem esse, ut mille anni, vers. 8. ut ex Divina potentia & omniscientia discant fideles Deo confidere, & curam sui & Ecclesiæ ac Regni Deo permittere: tum Deum non tardare promissa, uti nonnulli interpretantur, imò accelerare καιροῖς ἰδίοις temporibus propriis & definitis; & longanimem eundem esse, nolentem quemquam perire, sed omnes ad resipiscentiam pervenire; v. 9. atque adeò causam dilati adventus & tarditatis, quæ in judiciis ejus esse videtur, esse longanimitatem Dei erga electos, & omnes, qui nondum ad mensuram suam venerunt, & præparari etiam debent, quò & illi omnes noscantur, resipiscant & salventur: tum denique statò quidem die venturum Dominum, sed ut furem in nocte, adeóque die incognito; nihilque adeò opus esse iis scribi de temporibus & opportunitatibus, seu prolixitate & qualitate temporis. Accedit, quòd λόγῳ Θεοῦ verbo Dei olim Cœli fuerunt, & terra ex aqua, & per aquam constitit, utpote quæ super aquas fundata est; ibid. v. 5. Si igitur irrisores illi credere inducunt, quòd Deus solo verbo Cœlum & terram creaverit, atque terram super aquis fundaverit; quin & mundum per aquas deleverit; quomodo de adventu Domini ad judicium vel tantillum ambigent? Tam enim certus est adventus Domini, quàm certa est creatio omnium ex nihilo: fundatio terræ ad genus humanum etiam in peccato ferendum, & subjectio omnis creaturæ in servitutem vanitatis. Sed plura in hanc rem, ubi iterum de necessitate Judicii ultimi mentio incidet.
units.tr: Those scoffers are without doubt atheists, who either do not understand Scripture and the promises contained in it, or, having understood them, reject them. Their argument, that all things remain the same from the beginning of creation, is far too absurd. For from the predictions and their fulfilment it is quite clear that God was going to change the times, and has in fact changed them according to what he had foretold. Above all, the world was judged and destroyed by the flood. God, however, is not changed. He does not have a will to judge at one time and not at another. Because he has once shown that he wills to come and to judge, judgment must certainly be awaited, and the coming of the Lord to judgment is sure. And because he once destroyed the whole world, that is, all men, he has testified quite clearly that he will not always tolerate the wicked, nor wish the wicked to be always before his eyes, blaspheming his name. The scoffers wish this to be hidden, because they do not reflect on the arguments by which that judgment is made most certain; rather they argue the opposite. Moreover, that the flood did happen can easily be known by anyone who wishes to know it. I pass over the report about it that was spread among the nations even before the books of Moses were read throughout the world, which Grotius, in his de Verit. Relig. Christ., and others have proved by gathering the testimonies of the Gentiles; and we too have proved it at greater length in Hist. Patr. T. I. Dissert. XVIII. 40, etc. And Moses himself is a competent witness of the flood, since he is recognised elsewhere as a faithful servant of God in all his house, and no one has accused what he wrote on this matter of falsehood. And that men took counsel to build a city to which the name Babel [בבל], confusion, stuck from the outcome, is sufficient proof that the flood had gone before. But if the flood is true, then not all things remain the same from the beginning of creation; rather that is a clear sign of the future coming of the Lord to another judgment. In what follows, Peter also fortifies the faithful against the scoffers, showing, first, that with God one day is as a thousand years, v. 8, so that the faithful may learn from God's power and omniscience to trust in God and to commit their care of themselves, of the Church and of the kingdom to him; second, that God does not delay his promises, as some interpret, but rather hastens them [καιροῖς ἰδίοις] at their own proper and appointed times; and that he is longsuffering, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance, v. 9; and so the cause of the postponed coming and of the delay, which seems to lie in his judgments, is the longsuffering of God towards the elect and towards all who have not yet come to their measure and must still be prepared, so that all of them may also be known, repent and be saved; and finally, that the Lord will indeed come on an appointed day, but as a thief in the night, and so on a day unknown; and that therefore there is no need to write to them about times and seasons, or about the length and quality of time. Add to this that by the word of God [λόγῳ Θεοῦ] the heavens existed of old, and the earth stood out of the water and through the water, being founded upon the waters, v. 5. If, then, those scoffers are led to believe that God created heaven and earth by word alone, and founded the earth upon the waters, and even destroyed the world by waters, how can they doubt the least thing about the coming of the Lord to judgment? For the coming of the Lord is as certain as the creation of all things out of nothing; as certain as the foundation of the earth to bear the human race even in sin, and the subjection of every creature to the bondage of vanity. But more on this matter will be said where the necessity of the last judgment comes up again.

units.la: XLIII. Tempus adventus Christi ad ultimum Judicium nomine ἡμέρας Κυρίου diei Domini venit, 1. Corinth. I. 8. 2. Petr. III. 10.
units.tr: XLIII. The time of Christ's coming to the last judgment is called the day of the Lord [ἡμέρας Κυρίου], 1. Corinth. I. 8. 2. Petr. III. 10.

units.la: Nam Deus ἡμέραν diem certam statuit, qua vult judicare orbem habitabilem in justitia, Act. XVII. 31. Sed dies ille Deo certus, omnibus tamen hominibus incertus & incompertus est. De die illa & hora, qua Filius hominis veniet in nubibus Cœli, nemo novit, ne quidem Angeli in Cœlo, neque Filius, nisi Pater, Marc. XIII. 32. Hoc noveritis, quòd si paterfamilias novisset, qua custodia fur veniat, vigilasset utique, neque domum suam suffodi sivisset. Propterea & vos estote parati, quia hora, qua non putatis, Filius hominis veniet, Matth. XXIV. 43. 44. Veniet dies Domini tanquam fur in nocte, 2. Petr. III. 10. Audax proin temeritas eorum est, qui vel secretiore Spiritus revelatione, quam spiritus mendax dictat, vel homines sibi fingunt, vel Propheticæ, vel Apostolicæ authoritatis prætextu, vel ratiocinatione tempus adventus Domini definire ausi pridem sunt, & adhuc dum audent. Cùm tamen tempora & opportunitates Deus Pater in potestate sua statuerit, Act. I. 7. Ne citò dimoveamini à mente, neque turbemini, neque per spiritum, neque per sermonem, neque per epistolam, tanquam nobis authoribus, quasi instet dies Christi, 2. Thess. II. 2. Per Spiritum fanatici revelationes jactantes: per sermonem velut Propheticum Judæi, Eliæ Thesbitæ traditionem de mundo sex mille annis duraturo, & Apostolicum, seductores tempore Pauli, instare diem adventus fingentes; per ratiocinationem impostores alii, numerorum supputatione, & mysteriis aliis similibus ludentes & illudentes, seducere conati sunt. Sed Scripturarum disertæ præmonitiones, & confusorum turpiter ariolorum plurium, & curiositatis vitium cohibere debent, ne talibus, qui Divinos se mentiuntur, quisquam fidem habeat. Satis est, quòd & certò Christus veniet, & certum Deo adventus tempus est, & veniet subitò, ut fur, cùm homines dixerint: Pax & securitas, 1. Thess. V. 3. & veniet tempore simili illi tempori, quod in diebus Noæ paulò ante diluvium homines agitarunt, Matth. XXIV. 37. Luc. XXI. 34.
units.tr: For God has appointed a certain day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, Act. XVII. 31. But that day, certain to God, is uncertain and unknown to all men. Of that day and hour on which the Son of man will come in the clouds of heaven, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only, Marc. XIII. 32. Know this, that if the master of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would surely have watched, and would not have allowed his house to be broken into. Therefore be ready also, for the Son of man will come at an hour when you do not think, Matth. XXIV. 43. 44. The day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night, 2. Petr. III. 10. Therefore bold is the rashness of those who, either by a more secret revelation of the Spirit, which a lying spirit dictates, or by inventing things for themselves under the pretext of prophetic or apostolic authority, or by reasoning, have dared, and still dare, to fix the time of the Lord's coming. Yet God the Father has placed the times and seasons in his own power, Act. I. 7. Do not be quickly shaken in mind, nor troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter, as if from us, as though the day of Christ were at hand, 2. Thess. II. 2. By spirit, fanatics boasting of revelations; by word, as if prophetic, the Jews, relying on the tradition of Elijah the Tishbite that the world would last six thousand years; and by apostolic word, the seducers of Paul's time, pretending that the day of coming was at hand; by reasoning, other impostors, playing and deceiving with the calculation of numbers and other similar mysteries, have tried to lead people astray. But the plain warnings of the Scriptures, and the example of many shamefully confused fortune-tellers, and the vice of curiosity ought to restrain us, so that no one gives faith to such men as falsely claim to be divinely inspired. It is enough that Christ will certainly come, and the time of his coming is certain to God, and he will come suddenly, like a thief, when men say: Peace and security, 1. Thess. V. 3, and he will come at a time like that which men were busy with in the days of Noah, shortly before the flood, Matth. XXIV. 37. Luc. XXI. 34.

units.la: XLIV. Præcedent enim omnino diem Domini Signa quædam ὡς προσαγορευόμενα ad præstolationem, fidelibus observanda ab initio ipso, ut in omne momentum parati sint ad excipiendum quodque eorum, quæ ipsius adventum prænuntiant, tanquam adventum quemdam Domini in re quidem evidentem, eo qui operatur, interim non viso. A ficu discite parabolam. Cùm ramus ejus tener fit, & folia germinant, cognoscitis, quòd messis propinqua sit. Sic etiam vos cùm videritis omnia ista, cognoscetis, quòd prope absit ab ostiis, Matth. XXIV. 33. 33. Cùm dixerint, pax & securitas, tunc repentinus ejus interitus superveniet, sicut dolor in utero habenti, & non effugient, 1. Thess. V. 3. Cùm incipient hæc fieri, capita vestra erigite & fustolite, quoniam redemptio vestra approximat, Luc. XXI. 28. Vocantur hæc σημεῖα τῶν καιρῶν signa temporum, qualia non discernere, Christus Pharisæis vitio dedit, Matth. XVI. 3. Sunt res & opera Dei diversis temporum articulis, suo ordine ante adventum Christi primum & secundum patranda. Et S. Petrus, tempora diem novissimum præcedentia vocat χρόνους ἀποκα- τασταστως πάντων tempora repræsentationis & exhibitionis omnium, quæ locutus est Deus per os omnium sanctorum Prophetarum suorum à seculo, Act. III. 21. Tempora enim dicit, quia distinctis temporibus, iisque ordine sequentibus, cuncta impleri debent. In quorum operum suis ἰδίοις καιροῖς propriis temporibus distinctorum singulis, & continua serie quasi appropinquans eminus adventus Christi in nubibus, tanquam totidem tubis ad eum prospiciendum excitantibus, cernitur. Nam ideo etiam insignia & famigerata Dei opera, quæ Deus distinctis temporis articulis facit, σαλπιγγες tubæ, Apoc. VIII. 2. IX. 1. 13. X. 7. XI. 15. appellantur. Quæ vox sumpta videtur vel ex tubis illis, quibus clangentibus mœnia Jerichuntis corruerunt, cùm simili ratione clangentibus mysticis tubis Regnum Diaboli corruat: vel ex Zach. IX. 9. ubi sic Deus: Exulta valde, filia Sion, הריעי clange, jubila, filia Jerusalem. Ecce Rex tuus advenit, &c. Et ultimum Dei opus, adventum Christi ad Judicium proximè instantem prænuntians ἐχάτῃ σαλπιγγὶ ultima tuba, 1. Cor. XV. 52. appellari videtur. Saltem tempus, quo illud molietur Christus, συντελείας τῆς αἰῶνος consummationis seculi, Matth. XXIV. 14. τὸ ἔσχατον τῶν ἡμερῶν ultimum dierum, 2. Petr. III. 3. καιροὶ ἀναψύξεως dies vel tempora refrigerii, Act. III. 19. appellantur. XLV. Signa adventum Christi ad judicium portendentia in universum Cantici Mosis, Deut. XXXII. filum secuti, ahibi libello de Signis Temporum, diversa judicia experto, sed in nonnullis etiam sequentium temporum testimonio comprobato, fusiùs protecuti sumus. Eadem verò dedita opera etiam Christus, Matth. XXIV. 3. &c. nec non Johannes in septem tubarum explicatione descripserunt. Christus enim quærentibus ex se discipulis: Dic nobis, quando hæc fient: & quodnam signum est adventus tui, καὶ τῆς συντελείας τῆς αἰῶνος & consummationis seculi, hoc est, cùm dies seculi finientur, ibid. XXIV. 3. respondet, caveant modò, quia multi venturi sint in nomine suo, dicentes: Ego sum Christus (sive negando Christum, sive vicarium ejus se profitendo) v. 5. 6. fore ut audiant bella & rumores bellorum, bella & propinqua & longinqua, v. 6. ne sibi in Regno Messiæ nil nisi pacem promittant; neque tamen eos turbari debere, quia oporteat hæc fieri, sed nondum instet finis, v. 6. quia & illi terrores & bella, religiosa inprimis, & Draconis & Bestiæ præterire, neque Ecclesiam subjugare debebant: Gentem contra gentem, Regnum contra Regnum excitatum iri, in bello, quod illi tempori proximum fuit, Romanos inter & Judæos; & futura tura esse famem, pestilentiam & terræ motus pas-sim, ordinarias illas plagas, quibus Deus peccatores non resipiscentes afficit, & quæ, ceu virgæ Dei potentes prædicationem Evangelii comitari debuerunt, ut iis moniti homines mature resipiscant; v. 7. sed hæc fore Ἀρχὴ ὠδίνων principium dolorum, seu partitudinum, v. 8. quibus ipes & expectatio Regni Christi, cum doloribus venientis, nec non liberationis, excitanda sit: initio hoc facto fideles traditum in afflictionem, occisum, & omnium gentium propter nomen Christi odio expositum iri, v. 9. quia unà cum bello Judaico, & tumultibus in Judæa persecutio etiam Christianorum incipere debuit, & incepit; atque etiam per Romanos in Judæis persecutio fidelium punita est: tunc, deinde, multos scandalizatum iri, v. 10. hæreticos nomen Christi professos, in gratiam Judæorum & Gentilium doctrinam Christianam ad gustum utrorumque interpolaturos, uti ab Arrianis factum: multos Pseudo-Prophetas suscitatum iri, qui multos seducant, v. 11. quia occasione hæresium condemnandarum quidam tanquam Prophetæ, Spiritum S. veluti sibi promissum & singulariter assistentem jactantes, multos seducturi, & ad obediendum humano nomini & authoritati inducturi erant: multiplicata sic ἀνομία iniquitate fore, ut multorum charitas refrigescat, v. 12. hoc est, Antichristo Ἀνόμῳ illo surgente, & in Ecclesia dominante, minuatur charitas inter fratres, ut alii aliis suspecti fiant, obtrectent, homines inter se rixentur, unus contra alium pro alio intumescat: salvatum tamen iri, qui perseveraverint, v. 13. quia non defuturi sint perseverantes in Christiana fide & charitate, & ἀνόμῳ Exlegi illi se opponentes, quorum certa inter tot pereuntes salus futura, imò & in hac vita quandoque refrigerium aliquod futurum sit: Tunc prædicatum iri Evangelium Regni in toto mundo, in testimonium omnibus gentibus, v. 14. hoc est, Evangelium Regni, quod est annuntiatio Regni Dei, sive Regni Cœlorum, in quo qui sunt, Reges & Sacerdotes sunt, inter omnes gentes, quippe in testimonium illis, quo convincantur omnes, ad quos judicandos veniet Christus, se debere expectare Christum judicem, prædicatum iri: & tum venturum finem, consummationem seculi, non Hierosolymæ, quia & absolute τέλος finis appellatur, & discipuli de συντελείᾳ τῆς αἰῶνος consummatione seculi, seu fine mundi, v. 3. interrogaverunt: & perseverantia ad finem usque ad omnes omnium ætatum homines pertinet: & præcedentia multa post Hierosolymæ excidium contigerunt. Hæc generalia adventus Christi & consummationis seculi signa Christus ipse discipulis suis præivit. Deinceps vero denuo telam eandem orsus eadem signa ad versum usque 32. explicat. Nam Hierosolymæ excidium à v. 15. ad v. 23. usque amplius declarat, & signum fugæ dat. Post finem Hierosolymæ, & destructionem politiæ Judæorum gemina prædictio subjungitur; prior temporis Hierosolymæ excidium subsequentis, v. 23-29. ubi signum dat, quo excitati fideles concludere debeant, Pseudo-Prophetas & Pseudo-Christos venisse, nempe si surrexerint, qui dicant: Hic est Christus, vel hic: posterior de qualitate ultimi temporis, proximè adventum Christi ad judicium præcedentis, v. 29.---32. ubi sic Christus: Statim post afflictionem dierum illorum Sol obtenebrabitur, & luna non dabit splendorem suum, & sidera de Cœlo cadent, & virtutes Cœlorum movebuntur. Et tunc apparebit signum Filii hominis in Cœlo. Et tum plangent omnes tribus terræ, & videbunt Filium hominis venientem in nubibus Cœli, cum potentia & gloria multa. Et mittet Angelos suos cum tuba vocis magnæ, ut colligant electos ex omnibus quatuor ventis, ab extremo Cœlorum usque ad extremum eorum. Sensibilia, an spiritualia hæc signa futura sint, inter Veteres non plane convenit. Non falluntur forte, qui in sermone Christi, ceu Prophetico, parabolica & metaphorica illa esse potius, quàm propria arbitrantur. Si enim Sol adulterinus, lucem & calorem veri Solis justitiæ, Christi mentiens: Luna, Principes hujus seculi; Sidera Cœli, homines, velut in Cœlo sedem suam collocantes & subjectis imperantes; Virtutes Cœlorum, exercitus eorum; Signum Filii hominis, Filium ipsum hominis constitutum in signum gentibus, Esaj. XI. 10. apparitio ejusdem, manifestationem ejus per testimonium verbi Dei, & revelationem ex Cœlo, 2. Thess. I. 7. Κοπετὸς planctus tribuum terræ, pœnitentiam, seu salutarem κατάνυξιν compunctionem populorum, Deo etiam gentibus dante pœnitentiam ad vitam, Actor. XI. 18. significare possunt; nihil prohibebit, quò minus Sol adulterinus obtenebrari, quando princeps Ecclesiæ doctor νομοζόμενος authoritatem doctoris veritatis, recedentibus ab eo piis, amittere: Luna splendorem suum non dare, quando Principes, quos Deus humano generi dedit, ut in miseriis vitæ sint solatio inprimis illis, qui vires non habent, & ab aliis facilè opprimuntur, terribiles, & pro nutriciis Ecclesiæ ejus persecutores fiunt. Sidera de Cœlo cadere, quando homines, qui thronum in Cœlo collocaverunt, tanquam habentes imperium in Ecclesiam, locum & potestatem suam amittunt: Virtutes Cœlorum commoveri, cùm omnis exercitus illius ordinis nutat; Signum Filii hominis in Cœlo, quando Evangelium, seu Christus gentibus in signum propositus, ut ad illud properè concurrant, proponitur: Plangere omnes tribus terræ, omnes populi pœnitentiam agere, quando Deus iis ἴσην δωρεάν æquale donum dat, Actor. XI. 17. dicantur. Ex quibus, indicio Christi ipsius Salvatoris, qualitatem temporis, statum Ecclesiæ, cui adventus Christi ad judicium imminet, adeóque signa adventum illum Christi imminentem portendentia cognoscere est; nimirum, post abolitam Antichristi, Ἀνόμῳ illius, qui Ecclesiæ Solis instar dominatus hactenus est, & Lunam Principes ad persequendum Ecclesiam sibi obnoxios habuit, potestatem, omnémque dominationem in fide eorum, qui fiderum instar Cœli in Ecclesia, velut Cœlo, thronum ad dominandum fidei erexerunt; præconium Εὐαγγελίου τῆς βασιλείας ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ οἰκουμένῃ Evangelii Regni in toto habitabili (non successive, sicut nec successivè intelligendum est, quod v. 30. dicitur: Et tum apparebit signum Filii hominis in Cœlo: & Tunc plangent omnes tribus terræ) in testimonium omnibus gentibus, Judæis & populis reliquis, quòd τότε ἥξει τὸ τέλος tunc veniet finis, v. 14. 29. 30. 31. Sicut enim imminens messis messis ex teneritudine ramorum & germinatione foliorum ficus cognoscetur : ita imminentem adventum suum ex his signis augurari Christus ipse fideles jussit. Neque illud obstat, quod v. 34. dicitur, non transituram generationem hanc, ἕως ἂν πάντα ταῦτα γένηται, donec omnia hæc fiant, quia etiam fieri dicuntur, quæ fieri incipiunt. Sicut enim v. 32. 33. Christus docuit rerum istarum connexionem: ita v. 34. docet, propinquum esse rerum harum initium. Proprie enim γίνεσθαι significat esse incipere. Illa vero quæ tractum habent, & simul esse non possunt, dicuntur esse incipere, quando primum illorum est.
units.tr: XLIV. For certain signs, called ὡς προσαγορευόμενα [as they are called], go before the day of the Lord. Believers are to observe them from the very beginning, so that they are ready at every moment to receive whichever of them foretell his coming. These signs are like a kind of coming of the Lord, plainly visible in fact, while the one who works them is not yet seen. Learn a parable from the fig tree. When its branch becomes tender and puts forth leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see all these things, know that he is near, at the doors, Matt. 24:33. When they say, "Peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labor pains on a pregnant woman, and they will not escape, 1 Thess. 5:3. When these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near, Luke 21:28. These are called σημεῖα τῶν καιρῶν [signs of the times], the kind that Christ rebuked the Pharisees for failing to discern, Matt. 16:3. These are the works and deeds of God, which are to be accomplished in their own order, at distinct junctures of time, before the first and second coming of Christ. And St. Peter calls the times preceding the last day χρόνους ἀποκαταστάσεως πάντων [times of the restoration of all things], the times of the representation and manifestation of all that God has spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets from of old, Acts 3:21. He says "times," because all things must be fulfilled in distinct periods, following one another in order. In each of these works, performed in its own ἰδίοις καιροῖς [proper times], the coming of Christ on the clouds can be discerned as it draws near from afar in an unbroken series, as if by so many trumpets that rouse us to look for him. For this reason the notable and famous works of God, which he performs at distinct junctures of time, are also called σάλπιγγες [trumpets], Rev. 8:2; 9:1, 13; 10:7; 11:15. This word seems to be taken either from those trumpets whose blast brought down the walls of Jericho, since by a similar means the kingdom of the devil will fall at the sound of the mystical trumpets, or from Zech. 9:9, where God says: Exult greatly, daughter of Zion; shout [הריעי], sing for joy, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your King is coming, etc. And the last work of God, which announces the coming of Christ to judgment as the next event, seems to be called ἐσχάτῃ σάλπιγγι [the last trumpet], 1 Cor. 15:52. At least the time in which Christ will bring this about is called συντελείας τῆς αἰῶνος [the consummation of the age], Matt. 24:14, and τὸ ἔσχατον τῶν ἡμερῶν [the last of the days], 2 Pet. 3:3, and καιροὶ ἀναψύξεως [times of refreshing], Acts 3:19. XLV. In following the thread of the whole of Moses' Song, Deut. 32, we have set out more fully the signs that portend the coming of Christ to judgment, in a book on the Signs of the Times, which tests various judgments but also confirms them by the testimony of later times in several cases. Christ himself, Matt. 24:3 and following, and John too, in explaining the seven trumpets, described these same signs deliberately. When his disciples asked him: Tell us, when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age, καὶ τῆς συντελείας τῆς αἰῶνος, that is, when the days of the age will be finished, ibid. 24:3, he answered them. He said only that they should take care, because many would come in his name, saying, I am Christ (either by denying Christ or by professing themselves his vicar), v. 5-6. He said there would be wars and rumors of wars, both near and far, v. 6, so that they would not promise themselves nothing but peace in the kingdom of the Messiah. Yet they should not be troubled, because these things must happen, but the end is not yet at hand, v. 6. For those terrors and wars, especially religious ones, of the Dragon and the Beast, were to pass away and were not to subdue the Church. Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, in the war that was close to that time, between the Romans and the Jews. There would be famine, pestilence and earthquakes in various places, the ordinary plagues with which God afflicts unrepentant sinners, and which, as the rods of God, were to accompany the powerful preaching of the Gospel, so that people warned by them might repent in time, v. 7. But these things would be ἀρχὴ ὠδίνων [the beginning of birth pangs], or of labors, v. 8, by which the hope and expectation of the kingdom of Christ, which comes with pain, and also of deliverance, was to be stirred up. With this beginning made, the faithful would be handed over to affliction, put to death, and hated by all nations on account of the name of Christ, v. 9. For together with the Jewish war and the tumults in Judea, persecution of Christians was bound to begin, and did begin; and also through the Romans, persecution of the faithful among the Jews was punished. Then many will be made to stumble, v. 10: heretics professing the name of Christ would adapt Christian teaching to the taste of both Jews and Gentiles, as the Arians did. Many false prophets will arise and lead many astray, v. 11. For on the occasion of heresies that had to be condemned, some would boast of themselves as prophets, claiming the Holy Spirit as promised to them and assisting them in a unique way, and would lead many astray and bring them to obey human names and authority. Thus, because lawlessness is multiplied, the love of many will grow cold, v. 12. That is, when the lawless Antichrist arises and rules in the Church, love among brothers will diminish, so that they become suspicious of one another, speak ill of one another, quarrel among themselves, and one swells with anger against another on behalf of someone else. But whoever endures to the end will be saved, v. 13, because there would not be lacking those who persevered in Christian faith and love, and who opposed that lawless one, the Ἀνόμῳ [lawless one]. Among so many who perish, their salvation would be certain, and indeed in this life there would sometimes be some refreshment for them. Then this Gospel of the Kingdom will be preached in the whole world, as a testimony to all nations, v. 14. That is, the Gospel of the Kingdom, which is the proclamation of the kingdom of God, or of the kingdom of heaven, in which those who belong to it are kings and priests, will be preached among all nations, as a testimony to them, so that all, before whom Christ is to come as judge, may be convinced that they must await Christ as judge. And then the end will come, the consummation of the age, not of Jerusalem. For τέλος [end] is called absolutely the end, and the disciples asked about the συντελεία τῆς αἰῶνος [consummation of the age], that is, the end of the world, v. 3. Perseverance to the end pertains to all people of all ages, and many of the preceding things have happened after the destruction of Jerusalem. Christ himself laid out these general signs of the coming of Christ and the consummation of the age to his disciples. Then again, taking up the same web, he explains the same signs up to v. 32. For he declares more fully the destruction of Jerusalem from v. 15 to v. 23, and gives the sign of flight. After the end of Jerusalem and the destruction of the Jewish state, a twofold prediction is added. The first concerns the time following the destruction of Jerusalem, v. 23-29, where he gives a sign by which believers, when aroused, ought to conclude that false prophets and false Christs have come, namely if people arise who say, Here is Christ, or here. The second concerns the quality of the last time, immediately preceding the coming of Christ to judgment, v. 29-32, where Christ says: Immediately after the affliction of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven. Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. And he will send his angels with a great trumpet voice, to gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. Whether these signs will be sensible or spiritual has not been plainly agreed upon among the ancients. Perhaps those are not mistaken who think these images in the words of Christ, spoken as prophecy, are parabolic and metaphorical rather than literal. For if the adulterous sun, lying about the light and heat of the true Sun of Righteousness, is Christ's counterfeit; the moon is the princes of this age; the stars of heaven are men who set their seat as if in heaven and rule over their subjects; the powers of the heavens are their armies; the sign of the Son of Man is the Son of Man himself, set up as a sign to the nations, Isa. 11:10, his appearing and manifestation through the testimony of the Word of God and his revelation from heaven, 2 Thess. 1:7; then κοπετός [mourning] of the tribes of the earth can signify repentance, or the saving κατάνυξις [compunction] of the peoples, since God also grants repentance unto life to the Gentiles, Acts 11:18. Nothing will prevent the adulterous sun from being darkened, when the chief teacher of the Church, who is called the authority of the teacher of truth, loses it as the pious withdraw from him. The moon not giving its light means when the princes whom God has given to the human race, to be a comfort in the miseries of life especially to those who lack strength and are easily oppressed by others, become terrible and, instead of nurses of his Church, become its persecutors. The stars falling from heaven means when men who have placed their throne in heaven, as if they held authority over the Church, lose their place and power. The powers of heaven being shaken means when the whole army of that order wavers. The sign of the Son of Man in heaven means when the Gospel, or Christ, is set before the nations as a sign, so that they may hasten together to it. All the tribes of the earth mourning means all peoples repenting, when God gives them ἴσην δωρεάν [an equal gift], Acts 11:17. From these things, by the indication of Christ the Savior himself, it is possible to recognize the quality of the time and the state of the Church, to which the coming of Christ to judgment is imminent, and therefore the signs that portend his coming: namely, after the abolition of the power of that lawless Antichrist, who has hitherto dominated the Church like the sun, and who had the princes as moons, obliged to persecute the Church; and after the abolition of all domination over the faith of those who, like stars in heaven, have set up thrones in the Church to rule over faith. Then comes the proclamation of the Εὐαγγελίου τῆς βασιλείας ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ οἰκουμένῃ [Gospel of the kingdom in the whole inhabited world], not successively (just as what is said in v. 30, Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, is not to be understood successively), as a testimony to all nations, Jews and the remaining peoples, that τότε ἥξει τὸ τέλος [then the end will come], v. 14, 29, 30, 31. For just as the coming harvest is known from the tenderness of the branches and the budding of the leaves of the fig tree, so Christ himself commanded believers to foretell his imminent coming from these signs. Nor does it stand in the way that v. 34 says that this generation will not pass away, ἕως ἂν πάντα ταῦτα γένηται [until all these things come to pass], until all these things happen, because things are also said to happen when they begin to happen. For just as in v. 32-33 Christ taught the connection of these things, so in v. 34 he teaches that the beginning of these things is near. For γίνεσθαι properly means to begin to be. Those things which have a duration, and cannot all exist at once, are said to begin when the first of them does.

units.la: XLVI. Signa temporum adventum
units.tr: XLVI. The signs of the times, indicating from afar and from near the coming of Christ

units.la: Christi ex longinquo & propinquo indicantia, & velut tubis quibusdam præcinentia ipse etiam Filius Dei Johanni dilecto inprimis discipulo suo emblemate sigillorum septem, & totidem tubarum Apoc. V—XII. aperuit. Singula illa à viris doctissimis, Prophetias inter se & cum eventu earum conferentibus, heic non explicabimus. Unum observasse satisfuerit; Si sigillorum & tubarum prophetia illa divinissima ab initio Ecclesiæ Christianæ ad finem ejus usque decurrit, quod nemo sanus forte inficias iverit; Tum ea quæ tuba septima, seu ultima clangit & præcinit, signa proximè adventantis Domini, & imminentis finis mundi intelligi debere. Quando autem Angelus septimus ἕβδομος buccinavit, tum facta dicuntur voces magnæ in Cœlo, dicentes: Facta sunt Regna mundi Domini nostri, & Christi ejus, & regnabit in secula seculorum. Quibus auditis vocibus viginti quatuor Seniores ceciderunt in facies suas, & adorarunt Deum, dicentes: Gratias tibi agimus, Domine, qui est, & qui erat, & qui venit, quia accepisti potentiam tuam, & factus es. Et gentes irata sunt, & venit ira tua, & tempus mortuorum, ut judicentur, & dandi mercedem servis tuis Prophetis & Sanctis, timentibus nomen tuum: parvis & magnis, & corrumpendi corrumpentes terram. Et apertum est templum Dei in Cœlo, & visa est arca Testamenti ipsius in templo ipsius: & facta sunt fulgura, & voces, & tonitrua, & terræ motus, & grando magna; Apoc. XI. 15—f. voces in Cœlo factæ eorum sunt, qui in terra licet agentes, πολίτευμα conversationem suam in Cœlo habent. Eorum voces silentio semihorii, quod sigillo septimo aperto in Cœlo factum est, Cap. VIII. 1. respondent. Voces sunt gratulatoriæ, quòd Regna mundi facta sint Domini nostri & Christi ejus, atque ille regnaturus sit in secula seculorum. Id enim fore prædictum est. Tempore Regum istorum suscitabit Deus Cœli Regnum, quod in æternum non corrumpetur. Et Regnum istud alteri non committetur. Comminuet & consummabit omnia ista Regna, & ipsum stabit in æternum. Dan. II. 44. Illi, Filio hominis, datus est dominatus & dignitas, & Regnum, & omnes populi, nationes & linguæ ipsi servient; dominatus ejus dominatus sæculi, qui non transfertur, & Regnum ejus, quod non corrumpitur. Regnum, potestas, & magnitudo Regni, quod est sub toto Cœlo, dabitur populo sancto Altissimi. Regnum ejus Regnum æternum, & omnes potestates ei servient, ibid. VII. 14—27. Non enim hæc de Regno gloriæ intelligi possunt, quia in eo gentes non serviunt Ecclesiæ, & Ecclesia non obtinet Ma-
units.tr: The Son of God himself, by means of the emblem of seven seals and as many trumpets, opened to his beloved disciple John, above all others, the signs that foretell and herald his coming as with trumpets (Rev. 5–12). We shall not explain each of these here, since learned men have compared the prophecies with one another and with their fulfilment. It will be enough to observe one thing. If that most divine prophecy of the seals and trumpets runs from the beginning of the Christian Church to its end (which no sane person would perhaps deny), then what the seventh, or last, trumpet sounds and announces must be understood as the signs of the Lord's imminent coming and the approaching end of the world. When "the seventh angel [ἕβδομος] sounded the trumpet," it is said that "there were loud voices in heaven, saying: The kingdoms of this world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign for ever and ever. And when they heard these voices, the twenty-four elders fell on their faces and worshipped God, saying: We give you thanks, O Lord God, who are and who were and who are to come, because you have taken your great power and begun to reign. And the nations were angry, and your wrath has come, and the time of the dead, that they should be judged, and that you should give reward to your servants the prophets and the saints, and to those who fear your name, both small and great, and should destroy those who destroy the earth. And the temple of God in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple; and there were lightnings, and voices, and thunders, and an earthquake, and great hail" (Rev. 11:15–19). These voices in heaven belong to those who, though living on earth, have their citizenship [πολίτευμα] in heaven. They answer the "silence of about half an hour" in heaven, which took place when the seventh seal was opened (Rev. 8:1). The voices are songs of joy that the kingdoms of the world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ, and that he is to reign for ever and ever, for this was foretold: "In the days of those kings the God of heaven shall set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed; and that kingdom shall not be left to another people. It shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever" (Dan. 2:44). "To him was given dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed. The kingdom and the dominion and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High; his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him" (Dan. 7:14–27). These words cannot be understood of the kingdom of glory, for in that kingdom the nations do not serve the Church, and the Church does not hold the majesty of the kingdoms of the world, but is in the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

units.la: jestatem Regnorum mundi, sed in gloria Regni cœlestis est. Neque proin judicium illud, quod ibid. v. 26. confessurum dicitur, judicium novissimum, sed illud, quod in terris, per Ecclesiam ex libris Scripturæ peragitur, est. De eodem Regno Christi passim Scriptura loquitur. Compungetur Luna, & pudefiet Sol, cùm Regnum capessiverit Jehova, Deus exercituum, in monte Sion & Hierosolymis, Esaj. XXIV. 23. Regnabit Jehova super eis in monte Sion à nunc in seculum, Mich. IV. 7. Erit Jehova Rex super totam terram, Zach. XIV. 9. Jam satiati estis, jam facti estis divites, sine nobis regnastis. Et utinam regnasfetis, ut & nos vobiscum regnemus, I.Cor.IV.8.
units.tr: Nor is that "judgment" which is said in the same passage (v. 26) to be given the last judgment, but the judgment that is carried out on earth through the Church by means of the books of Scripture. Scripture speaks everywhere of this same kingdom of Christ: "Then the moon shall be confounded and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem" (Isa. 24:23). "The LORD shall reign over them in Mount Zion from now on, even for ever" (Mic. 4:7). "The LORD shall be king over all the earth" (Zech. 14:9). "Now you are full, now you are rich, you have reigned without us; and would that you had reigned, that we also might reign with you" (1 Cor. 4:8).

units.la: XLVII. Regnum Christi, & cum eodem regnantis, seu liberè Christum Regem suum profitentis Ecclesiæ, profectus & coronis Regni Dei in N. T. Nam in N. T. Deus regnat solus sine Principibus seculi prioris. Sed Regnum illud Dei suam βασιλείαν profectum habet. Primo est in iis, qui Evangelio credunt, etiamsi pauci illi sint. Fit deinde Regnum Dei in gentibus, quando Evangelium gentibus prædicatur, & ab iisdem creditur. Amplius regnat, quando hostes suos fugat, qui diversi generis sunt; Reges, Regnum Christi rejicientes; Reges putantes se Christi Regnum erigere, cùm tamen Regnum Bestiæ & Meretricis erigant. Illi enim Christi nomen oppugnant: hi Christi nomen usurpant. Illorum fuga in Imperio Romano primùm facta est. Successerunt, qui nomen Christi usurpantes alii quidem pii & nutritii Ecclesiæ fuerunt, alii ļtructores Babylonis, adorantes Deum Maozim, qui conjuncti fuerunt cum Ecclesia. Quando autem Reges potestatem suam dederunt Meretrici, Apoc. XVII. 13. cum iis Agnus, & qui cum ipso erant, pugnarunt. Regnavit verò Christus etiam in illa pugna. Sed magis adhuc regnavit, quando Sancti ex manu & potestate talium educti in pace Christo inservire coeperunt, quod post Reformationem Ecclesiis omnibus, Evangelium amplexis, contigit. Sed etiamsi Christus in quibusdam sic regnet, nondum tamen omnino regnat, quandiu aliqui, qui ipsius sunt, cum dominatione hominum & persecutione conflictantur. In ipsa quoque Ecclesia Evangelica ex Babylone educta, Regnum Christi eò magis amplificatur & evehitur, quò magis cognitio & pietas abundat, & non authoritas hominum, sed solius Dei reverentia prævalet; & quò liberius Ecclesia facit id, quod Christi jussu facere tenetur; neque quisquam aliquid facit, quod faciendi potestatem non habuit. Quia verò Christus & Ecclesia promissionem habet fore, ut omnes populi ei subjiciantur; quando id ita successerit, ut Ecclesia fratres in omnibus populis habeat, ut ii nutriantur à populis, & pace fruantur, neque supersint, qui per religionis causam eos persequi & occidere tentaverint; tum verò novo, & plenissimo, qui in Ecclesia militante obtinere potest, modo Christus, & cum eodem Ecclesia regnabit. Quandiu enim Ecclesia à persecutoribus liberata non est, & Evangelium in omnibus populis non prædicatur, Christus nondum eo modo regnandi, quem promissio summum in terra portendit, Rex factus est; & habet Ecclesia quod expectet ante adventum Christi, quod ipsum adventum Christi ad judicium praecedens, eundem proximè imminentem, velut buccina quadam, decantet. Est ergo hoc Regnum Christi in terra gerendum κατ' ἐξοχὴν tale, utpote quo, abolito Antichristo, seu politia ejus praedominante, conversis Gentibus & Judæis, pomœria mirè amplificabuntur, & habebit Christus Rex populum spontaneum ubique gentium.
units.tr: XLVII. The kingdom of Christ, and the progress and crowning of God's kingdom in the New Testament, that is, of the Church which freely professes Christ as its King and reigns with him. For in the New Testament God alone reigns, without the princes of the former age. But that kingdom of God has its own progress [βασιλείαν]. First, it is in those who believe the Gospel, even if they are few. Then the kingdom of God is extended among the Gentiles, when the Gospel is preached to the Gentiles and is believed by them. It reigns further when it puts to flight its enemies, who are of various kinds: kings who reject the kingdom of Christ, and kings who think they are setting up the kingdom of Christ while in fact they are setting up the kingdom of the Beast and of the Harlot. The former attack the name of Christ; the latter usurp it. The first of these flights took place in the Roman Empire. There followed those who usurped the name of Christ: some were indeed pious and nurturing to the Church, others were builders of Babylon, worshipping the god Maozim (Dan. 11:38), and these were joined with the Church. But when "the kings gave their power to the Beast" (Rev. 17:13), the Lamb and those who were with him fought against them. Christ also reigned in that battle. But he reigned more fully still when the saints, having been led out from the hand and power of such men, began to serve Christ in peace, which happened after the Reformation, when all churches embraced the Gospel. Yet even though Christ reigns in this way in some places, he does not yet reign altogether, as long as some of his own are struggling under the domination and persecution of men. Moreover, in the evangelical Church itself, brought out of Babylon, the kingdom of Christ is enlarged and advanced all the more as knowledge and piety abound, and as the authority of men gives way to the reverence due to God alone; and the more freely the Church does what it is bound to do at the command of Christ, and no one does anything for which he has no authority. But since Christ and the Church have the promise that all peoples shall be subjected to him, then when this shall have come about, so that the Church has brothers among all peoples, who are nourished by those peoples and enjoy peace, and when no one remains who has tried to persecute and kill them on account of religion, then Christ, together with his Church, shall reign in a new and most complete manner, which can be attained in the militant Church. For as long as the Church has not been freed from its persecutors, and the Gospel is not preached among all peoples, Christ has not yet been made King in that manner of reigning which the promise holds out as supreme on earth; and the Church has something to expect before the coming of Christ to judgment, which it proclaims, as by a trumpet, as imminent. This kingdom of Christ to be carried on upon earth is therefore, above all [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], of such a kind that, when Antichrist, or his polity, which is dominant, has been abolished, and when the Gentiles and the Jews have been converted, the bounds of the Church will be wonderfully enlarged, and Christ the King will have a willing people from all the nations everywhere.

units.la: XLVIII. De hoc Ecclesiæ novissimo statu, adventum Christi ad judicium praecessuro non plane doctorum, cætera piorum, orthodoxorum & cordatorum virorum calculi concordant.
units.tr: XLVIII. On this last state of the Church, which will precede the coming of Christ to judgment, the calculations of not all teachers but of the other pious, orthodox and sound men agree.

units.la: Neque ut concordent non in dogmate fidei, sed in opinione de futuris Ecclesiæ fatis, cui nondum eventus lucem fœneratus est, sed fœnerabitur demum, ulla necessitas postulat. Non desunt igitur, qui Antichristi dominatum abolitum, gentes & Judæos ad Christum Regem conversum iri, vix dici sustineant; & Regnum Christi κατ' ἐξοχὴν tale futurum sub finem mundi, controversiam moveant, & apud populum convitium faciant. Alii, Scripturæ testimoniis convicti Judæorum saltem conversionem haud inviti admittunt. Et Confessiones quidem publicæ rem non decidunt, quia problema hoc est, quod alterutram in partem definitum nec fidem, nec pietatem lædit. Sive enim sub finem mundi pauci, sive multi, sive omnes Christum Regem suum professuri, & fidem Evangelii amplexuri sunt, eadem utique fides & religio paucorum, multorum vel omnium erit; neque adeò ullus fidei articulus periclitabitur. Confessio quidem Helvetica cap. XI. sic de tempore adventus Christi loquitur: Ex Cœlis Christus redibit ad judicium tum, quando summa in mundo erit conscleratio, & Antichristus corrupta religione vera, superstitione impietateque omnia implevit, & sanguine atque flamma Ecclesiam crudeliter vastavit. Redibit autem Christus asserturus suos, & aboliturus adventu suo Antichristum, judicaturus vivos & mortuos. Quæ vera putamus hactenus, quòd Christo adventante propter hypocritas multos, Evangelii luce & libertate abusos, magna in mundo conscelerratio erit, & Antichristus jam ante impietate sua omnia implevit, quia dies Christi ante apostasiam & revelationem τῆ ἀνόμῳ Exlegis non instabat; & Antichristus quoad corpus suum ante adventum Christi ad judicium penitus aboleri non debet, imò in illustri ipso adventu Christi ad judicium sic abolebitur. Quibus si & hoc addiderimus, quòd problema hoc sit, non dogma & articulus fidei, & decidendum illud sit non ex prophetiis ἀδήλοις mundum pervolitantibus, & ad audendum aliquid incitantibus, sed ex prophetiis indubitatis verbi Dei: & status Ecclesiæ, quo Evangelium in toto mundo praedicabitur, Ecclesiæ militantis naturam non exuet, neque hostes debellandi, puta Satanas, caro, peccatum inhabitans, & mundus supererunt: denique status universalis Ecclesiæ non multùm à statu cujuslibet Ecclesiæ particularis hodiernæ, ab Antichristo liberatæ, discrepabit, nisi quatenus numerus credentium major erit, & metus insidiantis Antichristi, utpote in capite suo jam tum extincti & contriti, deerit; nulla causa erit, qua moti vel ajentes negantium, vel negantes ajentium sententiam condemnent, imò erit, qua moti quemque judicio suo abundare sinent, ne videantur in Ecclesia ἐξουσίαζοντι imperio uti, & ipsi Prophetæ Prophetis aliis subjici nolle; imò & temerè μάχεσθαι pugnare, cùm servum Dei non μάχεσθαι pugnare de talibus rixari, contendere, sed mitem esse erga omnes, 2. Tim. II. 24. adeóque docere, demonstrare, non præjudiciis uti, imperare & ἀδήλως incomperta, non demonstrata obtrudere, deceat. Sanè etiam Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ Theologi vetustiores Bibliander, Martyr & Gualtherus Comment. in Rom. XI. sententiæ, quòd abolito Antichristo Judæi & Gentes convertendæ & florentior Ecclesiæ status inducendus sit, calculum addiderunt.
units.tr: There is no necessity that they agree not on a dogma of faith but on an opinion about the future fate of the Church, on which the outcome has not yet shed its light, though it eventually will. So there are those who scarcely dare to say that the dominion of Antichrist will be abolished and the Gentiles and Jews converted to Christ the King, and who raise controversy by denying that the Kingdom of Christ will be in the eminent sense [κατ' ἐξοχὴν] such at the end of the world, and who stir up abuse among the people. Others, convinced by the testimonies of Scripture, at least admit without reluctance the conversion of the Jews. The public Confessions do not settle the matter, because it is a question which, defined in either direction, harms neither faith nor piety. For whether few, many or all will at the end of the world profess Christ as their King and embrace the faith of the Gospel, the same faith and religion will certainly belong to few, many or all, and no article of faith will thereby be endangered. The Helvetic Confession, chapter XI, speaks thus about the time of Christ's coming: Christ will return from heaven to judgment then, when there is the greatest wickedness in the world, and Antichrist, having corrupted true religion, has filled everything with superstition and impiety, and has cruelly laid waste the Church with blood and fire. Christ will return, however, to vindicate his own and by his coming to abolish Antichrist, to judge the living and the dead. We think these things true so far, that at Christ's coming there will be great wickedness in the world, on account of many hypocrites who have abused the light and liberty of the Gospel, and that Antichrist has already filled all things with his impiety, since the day of Christ was not at hand before the apostasy and the revelation of the lawless one [τῆ ἀνόμῳ]. Antichrist as to his body must not be wholly abolished before Christ's coming to judgment; rather, in that illustrious coming to judgment he will be abolished. To these points we may add this: that this is a problem, not a dogma or article of faith, and it is to be decided not from obscure [ἀδήλοις] prophecies flitting through the world and urging men to bold claims, but from the indubitable prophecies of the Word of God. The state of the Church in which the Gospel is preached throughout the whole world will not strip off the nature of the militant Church, nor will the enemies still to be overcome, namely Satan, the flesh, indwelling sin and the world, be gone. Finally, the state of the universal Church will not differ much from the present state of any particular Church freed from Antichrist, except that the number of believers will be greater, and the fear of a lurking Antichrist, already extinguished and crushed in his head, will be absent. There will be no cause for those who are moved to condemn either the assertors of the opposing view or the deniers of the view asserted; rather, they will be moved to let each man abound in his own judgment, lest they seem to exercise lordship [ἐξουσιάζοντι] in the Church, and lest the prophets themselves be unwilling to be subjected to other prophets. Indeed, it is not fitting to fight [μάχεσθαι] rashly, since the servant of God must not fight [μάχεσθαι] or quarrel and contend about such things, but must be gentle towards all, 2 Tim. II. 24. It is fitting to teach and demonstrate, not to use prejudices, to command, or to thrust upon others things uncertain [ἀδήλως] and undemonstrated. Indeed the older theologians of the Church of Zurich, Bibliander, Martyr and Gualther, in their Commentary on Romans XI, also added their vote to the opinion that after Antichrist is abolished the Jews and Gentiles are to be converted and a more flourishing state of the Church is to be introduced.

units.la: XLIX. His animadversis, veriorem Christo Regi gloriosiorem, Ecclesiæ salubriorem, verbo Dei, & Prophetis ejus inprimis, convenientiorem sententiam eorum putamus, qui statum Ecclesiæ adventum Christi ad judicium proximè præcedentem eum tuentur, in quo abolita Antichristi dominatione, Evangelium in toto orbe habitabili prædicetur, & eidem prædicato gentiles & Judæi, maximam saltem partem, & liberè, sine persecutionis religiosæ metu, audientiam plurimi, & obedientiam plures saltem, quàm antehac, præstent. Nam quoad Antichristi abolitionem, illa vel in capite dominante, vel in corpore & ejus reliquiis spectatur. Caput dominans esse Papam & ejus Hierarchiam dominantem, quam Babylonem magnam esse, in loco probavimus, extra controversiam positum est. Atqui Hierarchiæ hujus dominantis excidium cum totius mundi excidio non erit conjunctum, sed illud antecedet, quia Babylonis excidio consummato, superstunt Reges, nautæ, mercatores, Apoc. XVIII. 9. 10. &c. ipsáque etiam Ecclesia, uti ex cap. XIX. 1. 6. 7. 9. 17. 18. non obscurè colligitur. Nam quòd nonnulli testimonio eo commoti, Romam quidem Babylonis metropolin, ante finem mundi incendio consumptum iri, sed Babylonem aliquam ad finem usque mundi perseveraturam, pertendunt, parùm illi verisimilia dicunt. Illa enim Babylon comburetur & destruetur penitus, cujus scortationem, abominationes, dominium in Regna terræ, casum priorem, & ab eadem separationem Ecclesiæ hactenus continua Prophetiæ serie Spiritus S. pertexuit. Hanc porrò Babylonem non urbem solam, mœnibus septam, sed politiam religiosam, & statum Hierarchicum universum figurare, Myst. Bab. M. Diss. III. §13. &c. pluribus comprobavimus. Non ergo Babylonis M. finale excidium, sed universam politiam religiosam Babylonicam involvet, & potestatem cathedræ abolebit. Manebunt tamen ad finem usque mundi apostatæ, seu defectores improbi, Christo occasionem præbituri finiendi tempus patientiæ, celeremque in eos interitum adducendi. Taleserunt superstites Reges, mercatores, nautæ lugentes, aliique non ilico manus victas veritati daturi; sed alii per præconium Evangelii convertendi, alii in impietate sua ad finem usque mundi perstituri, qui ipsi tamen deleti etiam merito censebuntur, quia potestate in Ecclesiam, & authoritate religionis omni, quæ Babylonis anima est, privati, in mundo agent, neque
units.tr: XLIX. Having noted these things, we judge the opinion more true, more glorious to Christ the King, more salutary to the Church, and especially more agreeable to the Word of God and to his Prophets, to be that of those who maintain a state of the Church immediately preceding Christ's coming to judgment, in which, with Antichrist's dominion abolished, the Gospel will be preached throughout the whole habitable world, and to that preaching the Gentiles and Jews, at least the greater part and the many, will give a free hearing, without fear of religious persecution, and will render at least more obedience than before. As to the abolition of Antichrist, it is viewed either in the dominant head or in the body and its remnants. That the dominant head is the Pope and his ruling Hierarchy, which we have proved in its place to be the great Babylon, is beyond dispute. But the destruction of this ruling Hierarchy will not be joined with the destruction of the whole world; it will come before it, because after the fall of Babylon is complete, kings, sailors, merchants survive, Rev. XVIII. 9, 10, etc., and the Church herself survives too, as is clearly gathered from ch. XIX. 1, 6, 7, 9, 17, 18. For some, moved by that testimony, contend that Rome, the metropolis of Babylon, will indeed be consumed by fire before the end of the world, but that some Babylon will persist to the end of the world; they say this is hardly likely. For that Babylon will be burned and utterly destroyed whose whoredom, abominations and dominion over the kingdoms of the earth, whose earlier fall and the separation of the Church from her, the Holy Spirit has woven into a continuous series of prophecy up to now. Moreover, we have proved at length in Myst. Bab. M. Diss. III, §13 etc., that this Babylon figures not merely a city walled about, but the religious polity and the whole Hierarchical state. Therefore it is not the final destruction of the Great Babylon, but the whole Babylonian religious polity that will be involved, and the power of the chair will be abolished. Nevertheless, impious apostates and wicked defectors will remain until the end of the world, giving Christ occasion to end the time of patience and to bring swift destruction upon them. Such are the surviving kings, the mourning merchants and sailors, and others who will not at once yield their hands vanquished to the truth; some are to be converted through the proclamation of the Gospel, others will persist in their impiety to the end of the world. Yet these too will rightly be counted as destroyed, since, deprived of power over the Church and of all religious authority, which is the soul of Babylon, they will act in the world, and neither

units.la: que efficere poterunt, ut non Ecclesia omni in loco colligatur; ipsi vix locum inventuri, in quo tutò religionem suam profiteri audeant. Ita populus Judaicus consumptus & deletus tum censebatur, cùm eorum Politia in toto mundo deleta est, licèt, neque restitui in æternum poterit; licèt Judæi hinc inde palantes, & Christum æternum Regem blasphemantes, non desint. Quòd ergo S. Paulus docet: fore ut Exlegem illum revelatum Dominus consumat Spiritu oris sui, & aboleat τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ affulgentia adventus sui, 2. Thess. II. 8. eum sensum habet; quòd Exlex ille primò Spiritu oris Christi, seu per praeconium Evangelii consumendus; ac dein vel in reliquiis corporis sui in illustri adventu ad judicium; vel in capite etiam suo in adventu Christi ad judicium Antichristi particulare, vel in affulgentia praesentiæ Christi, hoc est, jubare quodam Regni ipsius, praecessuro adventum ejus ad judicandum vivos & mortuos: quomodo Regem advenire dicimus, cùm ejus anteambulones videmus; & aurora solis orientis anteambula ἐπιφάνεια παρουσίας affulgentia praesentiæ seu adventus solis, nondum licèt horizontem ingressi, dici potest; significat. Neque etiam illud obstat, quòd Apoc. XIX. 19.20. post bellum Bestiæ, Regum terræ & exercitus eorum, cum sedente in equo & exercitu ejus, subjicitur: Et prehensa est Bestia, & cum ea Pseudo-Propheta, qui fecerat signa coram ea, quibus seduxerat eos, qui acceperunt Bestiæ signaturam, & adorantes imaginem ejus, vivi conjecti sunt ambo in stagnum ignis, quod ardet sulphure. Ubi Bestia, posterior videlicet, de qua cap. XIII. 14. &c. & Pseudo-propheta distinguuntur ut status, & status caput, ad ostendendam capitis, & simul status una cum capite ruinam. Sicut autem supplicium Corachi, Dathanis & Abirami non ideo cum consummatione seculi conjunctum erat, quia vivi in infernum descenderunt: ita nec Bestiæ & Pseudo-Prophetæ supplicium ideo cum consummatione seculi conjunctum erit, quia vivi in stagnum ignis conjicientur. Poterunt etiam ζῶντες vivi, corporaliter non occisi, in stagnum ignis conjecti dici, quando à judicio & supplicio suo superstites, sed statu & politia sua privati, incipient illa videre & audire, quæ dolorem & infernalem invidiam inconciliabunt, & cum ulcere malæ conscientiæ conflictabuntur, perpetuisque adeò ardoribus æstuabunt. Quomodo plaga populorum, qui contra Hierosolymam belligerati sunt, definitur, quòd stantibus super pedibus suis caro, oculi, & lingua tabescent, Zach. XIV. 12.
units.tr: will be able to bring it about that the Church is not gathered in every place. They will scarcely find a place where they dare to profess their religion safely. Thus the Jewish people were regarded as consumed and destroyed when their polity was destroyed throughout the whole world, although it can never be restored for ever, and although Jews wandering here and there, blaspheming the eternal King Christ, are not lacking. Therefore the sense of what St Paul teaches, that the lawless one will be consumed by the Lord with the Spirit of his mouth and abolished by the brightness of his coming [τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ], 2 Thess. II. 8, is this: that the lawless one is first to be consumed by the Spirit of Christ's mouth, that is, through the proclamation of the Gospel; and then either in the remnants of his body at the illustrious coming to judgment, or in his very head, the particular Antichrist, at Christ's coming to judgment, or in the radiance of Christ's presence, that is, a certain glow of his Kingdom, which will precede his coming to judge the living and the dead. In this sense we say a king is coming when we see his forerunners; and the dawn, the forerunner of the rising sun, can be called the appearing of the presence, the radiance of the sun's coming, even though the sun has not yet entered the horizon. Nor does it stand in the way that Rev. XIX. 19, 20, after the war of the Beast, the kings of the earth and their armies, and the one sitting on the horse and his army, adds: And the Beast was taken, and with it the False Prophet who had done signs before it, by which he deceived those who received the mark of the Beast and worshipped its image; both were cast alive into the lake of fire, which burns with brimstone. Here the Beast, namely the latter one, of whom ch. XIII. 14 etc. speaks, and the False Prophet are distinguished as a state and the head of a state, to show the ruin of the head and, at the same time, of the state together with its head. But just as the punishment of Korah, Dathan and Abiram was not on that account joined with the consummation of the age, because they went down alive into hell, so the punishment of the Beast and the False Prophet will not on that account be joined with the consummation of the age, because they will be cast alive into the lake of fire. Those who are living, not physically killed, may also be said to be cast into the lake of fire when, surviving their judgment and punishment but deprived of their state and polity, they begin to see and hear those things which will stir up pain and infernal envy, and they will be wrestled with by the ulcer of an evil conscience, and so will seethe with perpetual burnings. In this way the plague of the peoples who waged war against Jerusalem is defined: while standing on their feet, their flesh, eyes and tongue will waste away, Zech. XIV. 12.

units.la: L. Sublata Antichristi dominatione multùm Regnum Christi, cui hactenus Antichristus se πανσεγκτικὰ oppositus, proficiet. Nam liberior multò Evangelii cursus erit; & paulatim, juxta praedictionem ipsius Christi, Evangelium in toto mundo praedicabitur, & tum finis erit, Matth. XXIV. 14. Hic autem praeconii illius Evangelii fructus erit, ut paulatim & gentes & Judæi hactenus increduli, ad Christum convertantur. De Gentium conversione praedictiones & promissiones extant. Ei erit obedientia populorum, Genes. XLIX. 10. secundum illud: In te benedicentur omnes gentes, omnes familiæ terræ: In Semine tuo benedicentur omnes Gentes, ibid. XII. 3. XVIII. 18. XXII. 18. Can-
units.tr: L. With the dominion of Antichrist removed, the kingdom of Christ, which Antichrist has hitherto opposed with every means at his disposal [πανσεγκτικά], will greatly advance. For the course of the Gospel will be far freer, and gradually, according to Christ's own prediction, this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world, and then shall the end come, Matth. XXIV. 14. The fruit of this proclamation of the Gospel will be that, little by little, both the nations and the Jews, hitherto unbelieving, will be converted to Christ. There are predictions and promises concerning the conversion of the Gentiles: to him shall the obedience of the peoples be, Gen. XLIX. 10, in accordance with the words in you shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; in your seed shall all the nations be blessed, ibid. XII. 3, XVIII. 18, XXII. 18. Sing,

units.la: tate Gentes, populus ejus; quia sanguinem servorum vindicat, & ultionem reddit hostibus suis, & expiat terram, populum suum, Deut. XXXII. 43. Omnia posuisti sub pedibus ejus, Psal. VIII. 7. Tu hæreditatem cernes in omnibus gentibus, ibid. LXXXII. 8. Omnes gentes, quas fecisti, venient & adorabunt coram te, Domine, & glorificabunt nomen tuum, ibid. LXXXVI. 9. Radicem Jehovæ, quæ stat in signum, gentes adibunt, & erit quies ejus gloria; Et fiet illo die, postea admovebit Jehova iterum manum suam ad requirendum residuum populi sui; & tollet signum gentibus, & colliget populos Israelis, Esai. XI. 11.12.13. In illo die fiet Israel (Ecclesia) tertia Ægyptiis & Assyriis, benedictio in medio terræ, id, quod benedixit Jehova Deus exercituum, dicendo: Benedictus populus meus, Ægyptii, & opus manuum mearum, Assyrii, & hæreditas mea Israel, ibid. XIX. 24.25. Similia capp. LII. 14.15. LIII. 12. LX. LXV. 15-25. LXVI. 18. &c. Ezech. XL-XLVIII. alibíque passim extant. In N. T. praedictionem Christi, Matth. XXIV. 14-31. saepe jam citavimus. Idem Hierosolymam a Gentibus calcandam ἄχρι ἂν πληρωθῶσι καιροὶ ἐθνῶν usque dum implentur tempora Gentium, praedixit, Luc. XXI. 24. Ubi tempora Gentium sunt tempora Regnorum in gentibus, quibus Regnum Christi hactenus oppugnatum est. Quòd igitur Hierosolymam nunc tenent Turcæ, certo argumento est, necdum ei omnia subjecta esse. Tandem verò etiam Hierosolyma fiet Domini Christi cum omnibus Regnis mundi, juxta vaticinium tubæ septimæ, Apoc. XI. 15. Et qualis sit illa impletio temporum gentium, Apostolus explicavit, dicens, indurationem Israelis duraturam, ἄχρις οὗ τὸ πλήρωμα τῶν ἐθνῶν εἰσέλθῃ donec plenitudo gentium intraverit, Rom. XI. 25. ubi plenitudo gentium opponitur τῷ ἡττήματι defectui vel damno, juxta v. 12. Quandiu enim est, & ὑστέρησις, ἀνομία defectus & neglectus legis in gentibus regnant, tandiu ἥττημα damnum non plenitudo est. Nondum plenitudo hæc gentium intravit, quia adhuc ἀνομία & Antichristi dominium durat; & nondum induratio Israelis cessat, & dicere, quòd per Apostolorum praeconium plenitudo gentium intraverit, non licet, quia Prophetæ ostendunt, oriturum fuisse Bestiam, & eam adoraturos omnes incolas terræ, qui nomen quidem dant Christo, sed mendaciter; ac demum, destructa Bestia, Evangelium per totum mundum praedicatum iri. Tum enim demum Regna facta sunt Domini & Christi ejus, Apoc. XI. 15. Quis non timeat Te, Domine, & glorificet nomen tuum, quia gentes venient, & adorabunt coram te, ibid. XV. 4.
units.tr: sing, ye nations, his people; for he avenges the blood of his servants, and takes vengeance on his adversaries, and makes atonement for his land and his people, Deut. XXXII. 43. You have put all things under his feet, Ps. VIII. 7. You shall see your inheritance among all the nations, ibid. LXXXII. 8. All the nations whom you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name, ibid. LXXXVI. 9. The root of Jehovah, which stands as a sign, the nations shall seek, and his rest shall be glory. And it shall come to pass in that day that Jehovah shall again put forth his hand to recover the remnant of his people; and he shall lift up a signal for the nations and gather the outcasts of Israel, Isa. XI. 11, 12, 13. In that day Israel shall be a third with the Egyptians and the Assyrians, a blessing in the midst of the earth, which Jehovah of hosts has blessed, saying: Blessed be my people, Egypt, and the work of my hands, Assyria, and my inheritance, Israel, ibid. XIX. 24, 25. Similar passages are found at Isa. LII. 14, 15, LIII. 12, LX, LXV. 15–25, LXVI. 18, etc., and Ezek. XL–XLVIII, and elsewhere throughout. In the New Testament we have already often cited Christ's prediction, Matth. XXIV. 14–31. He also foretold that Jerusalem would be trodden down by the Gentiles until the times of the nations are fulfilled [ἄχρι ἂν πληρωθῶσι καιροὶ ἐθνῶν], Luke XXI. 24. Here the times of the Gentiles are the times of the kingdoms among the nations, by which the kingdom of Christ has hitherto been assailed. That the Turks now hold Jerusalem is therefore a sure sign that all things are not yet subjected to it. Finally, however, Jerusalem too will become the possession of the Lord Christ together with all the kingdoms of the world, according to the prophecy of the seventh trumpet, Rev. XI. 15. And the Apostle has explained what that fulfilment of the times of the Gentiles will be, saying that the hardening of Israel will last until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in [ἄχρις οὗ τὸ πλήρωμα τῶν ἐθνῶν εἰσέλθῃ], Rom. XI. 25, where the fullness of the Gentiles is set against the loss [τῷ ἡττήματι], that is, the defeat, according to v. 12. For as long as lack [ὑστέρησις] and lawlessness [ἀνομία], the defect and neglect of the law, reign among the Gentiles, so long is there loss [ἥττημα] and not fullness. This fullness of the Gentiles has not yet come in, because lawlessness and the dominion of Antichrist still endure; nor has the hardening of Israel ceased. Nor may one say that the fullness of the Gentiles has come in through the proclamation of the Apostles, since the prophets show that the Beast would arise, that all the inhabitants of the earth, who indeed give their name to Christ but falsely, would worship it, and that at last, when the Beast is destroyed, the Gospel would be preached throughout the whole world. For then at last the kingdoms of the world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ, Rev. XI. 15. Who shall not fear you, O Lord, and glorify your name? For all nations shall come and worship before you, ibid. XV. 4.

units.la: LI. Ubi gentium plenitudo intraverit, cessabit πώρωσις induratio Israelis. Si tu, qui ex naturali oleastro exectus es, & praeter naturam in oleam insertus es, quantò magis ii, qui secundum naturam sunt, inserentur suæ oleæ? Nolo vos ignorare fratres, mysterium hoc, ut non sitis apud vos prudentes, quòd induratio ex parte contigit Israeli, donec plenitudo gentium intret. Et sic omnis Israel salvabitur, quemadmodum scriptum est, Esai. LIX. 20. Veniet ex Sion, qui eripiet, & avertet impietates à Jacob, Rom. XI. 24-27. Cessabit ergo aliquando πώρωσις induratio, quæ Israeli incubuit ἐκ μέρους ex parte illorum, qui Christum & Evangelium ab Apostolis praedicatum rejectarejecerunt; vel in vicem indurationis illius,quæ in V. T. gentilibus obtigit.
