Hence it came about that Antichrist, revealed, was recognised by many and openly exposed, until the eternal Gospel began to be preached again. If that reign is referred to the souls of the martyrs enjoying heavenly glory (which no necessity, however, requires), the determination of the millennial time will pertain to them only in this sense: that they are said to have reigned a thousand years, not that they reigned merely for that time, but that they reign for ever. For the definition of the millennial time is not to be understood absolutely, but must be compared with the binding of Satan. But the rest of the dead did not [ἐζησαν] live, or, as other manuscripts read, did not [ἀνέζησαν] rise again until the thousand years were finished, because they, spiritually dead in sin and in the uncircumcision of the flesh, adoring the beast and hardened in error, were not made alive again from the death of sin by the power of the word and of the Holy Spirit, but remained in their spiritual death until [ἕως] the thousand years were finished. Here the particle ἕως, until, as often elsewhere, denotes a continuation of the action without end. For they constantly rejected the truth and so slept a long night. Moreover, the state of those reigning with Christ is called the first resurrection, that is, quickening from the death of sin (John 5:25; Eph. 2:5; 5:14; Col. 3:1). This resurrection guards them, so that the second death, perdition, which is defection and hardening, has no power over them.

units.la: LX. Vera Domini ex Coelo in terram adventantis opera tria sunt; Resuscitatio mortuorum, Judicium universale, ejusdemque executio per detrusionem damnatorum in infernum, & glorificationem totius hominis in Coelo.
units.tr: LX. The true works of the Lord coming from heaven to earth are three: the resurrection of the dead; the universal judgment, and its execution through the casting of the damned into hell; and the glorification of the whole man in heaven.

units.la: RESUSCITATIO MORTUORUM est, qua Deus verbo suo omnipotente mortuos in vitam revocabit, corpora eorum è terra restituendo, & cum animabus suis rursus conjungendo. Resuscitatorum respectu vocatur ἀνάστασις Resurrectio. Sadducæi dicunt, μὴ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν non esse resurrectionem, Matth.XXII.23. Marc.XII.18. Luc.XX.27. Quomodo dicunt multi, ὅτι ἀνάστασις ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν non fit. 1.Cor.XV.12. Est autem ἀνάστασις resurrectio quædam iterata erectio, & δευτέρᾳ ἢ πρώτης στάσεως secunda velut ejus quod cecidit prius statio, ut Damascenus Orth.fid. lib.IV.28. nomen illud finit. Homo enim ratione corporis & surgere, & ἵστασθαι stare dicitur. Etiam ἔγερσις erectio, seu resurrectio, Matth.XXVII.53. insignitur. Carnis recidivatum Tertullianus de Resurr. c.6.18. dixit. Hebraei קימה stationem & תחיה ἀναζίωσιν iteratam vivificationem appellant. Proprie autem hic resurrectio accipitur pro eo, quod proprie iterum surgere potest; quod solius corporis est; cùm aliàs etiam figuratè tum de anima ex peccati morte vivificata, & velut resurgente, Rom.VI.4.5. tum de mundo, per Evangelii prædicationem quasi renascente, ibid.XI.15. dicatur. Quò ænigmata Apocalyptica de prima & secunda resurrectione, Apoc.XX.5.6. spectant. Prima enim post primum Christi adventum, & primam Evangelii prædicationem: secunda post Antichristi casum, & paulò ante adventum Christi ad judicium illustriùs peracta est, & peragetur. Etiam resurrectio carnis aliquando pro resurrectione justorum ad gloriam æternam duntaxat accipitur. Qui digni censebuntur illo seculo, & resurrectione ex mortuis, Luc.XX.35. Omne quod Pater mihi dederit ἀναστήσω resuscitabo in ultimo die, Joh.VI.39.40. Unde ἀνάστασις κρείττων melior resurrectio, Heb.XI.40. per quam in resurrectione mortuorum datur stare in cœtu justorum, & in sorte bona; quæque adeò est ad vitam, non ad judicium.
units.tr: The resurrection of the dead is that work by which God, through his almighty word, will call the dead back to life, restoring their bodies from the earth and joining them again to their souls. With respect to those who are raised, it is called ἀνάστασις [anastasis], resurrection. The Sadducees say μὴ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν [mē einai anastasin], that there is no resurrection (Matt. 22:23; Mark 12:18; Luke 20:27). Many say ὅτι ἀνάστασις ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν οὐκ ἔστιν [hoti anastasis ek tōn nekrōn ouk estin], that there is no resurrection of the dead (1 Cor. 15:12). Now ἀνάστασις [anastasis] is a kind of repeated erecting, a second standing, as it were, of what has fallen before; Damascene (Orth. fid. lib. IV, c. 28) explains the name in this way, calling it δευτέρᾳ ἢ πρώτης στάσεως [deuteras ē prōtēs staseōs], a second standing after the first. For a man is said to rise up and to ἵστασθαι [histasthai], to stand, by reason of his body. ἔγερσις [egersis], an erection or raising up, is also used for resurrection (Matt. 27:53). Tertullian (de Resurr. cc. 6, 18) called it a recovery of the flesh. The Hebrews call it קימה [qimah], a standing, and תחיה [tehiyah], a renewed vivification, which in Greek is ἀναζίωσιν [anazisin]. Properly, however, resurrection here is taken to mean that which can strictly be a rising again, and this belongs to the body alone. In other places it is also used figuratively, both of the soul made alive again from the death of sin, as if rising (Rom. 6:4, 5), and of the world, which is, as it were, born again through the preaching of the gospel (ibid. 11:15). To this belong the Apocalyptic enigmas about the first and second resurrection (Rev. 20:5, 6). The first was accomplished after Christ's first coming and the first preaching of the gospel; the second, after the fall of Antichrist and shortly before Christ's coming to judgment, has been and will be accomplished more gloriously. Also, the resurrection of the flesh is sometimes taken to mean only the resurrection of the just to eternal glory: "those who are counted worthy to attain that age, and the resurrection from the dead" (Luke 20:35); "all that the Father has given me, I will raise up [ἀναστήσω, anastēsō] on the last day" (John 6:39, 40). Hence ἀνάστασις κρείττων [anastasis kreittōn], a better resurrection (Heb. 11:35), by which, in the resurrection of the dead, one is granted to stand in the assembly of the just and in the good lot; and this resurrection is indeed to life, not to judgment.

units.la: LXI. Doctrinam de resurrectione carnis S. Paulus vocavit θεμέλιον στερεὸν fundamentum firmum, 2.Timoth.II.19. veritas enim illa à Deo decreta & notificata est ut fundamentum, quia ea stante cæteræ quoque partes veritatis, quæ secundum pietatem est, consistunt, & labefactata omnes convelluntur. Si mortui non resuscitantur, neque Christus resurrexit. Si vero Christus non resurrexit, vana est fides nostra, 1.Cor.XV.16.17. Atque id fundamentum firmum stare Apostolus dicit, quia & ipsum per cæteras veritatis salutaris partes confirmatur, & fulcitur. Et habet ea veritas, ut fundamentum à Deo positum, signaturam, per quam cognoscitur esse Divina fundatio, duas nempe veritates certissimas & indubitabiles, quòd Dominus no-vit eos, qui sunt sui, eorum rationem habeat, eos vivificet tanquam suos & peculium suum, tum in anima, tum quandoque etiam in corpore, ne ullam jacturam patiantur: & quòd justum & necessarium sit, ut qui nominat nomen Christi, ab injustitia desistat, hoc est, qui gloriatur Christo, ceu capite suo, ut unctionis ejusdem particeps, & per Spiritum ejus ipsi insertus injustitiam in verbis & factis oderit atque fugiat, & longius longiusque à malo recedat, ib.v.19. Ideo etiam Tertullianus erudithissimum de resurrectione librum ab eleganti hac γνώμη auspicatus est: Fiducia Christianorum resurrectio mortuorum. Non solùm enim doctrina illa adversus metum mortis, & adversa quaeque mundi hujus, ne sub calamitatibus nos undiquaque prementibus fatiscamus, sustinet, munit & consolatur, jubens attollere capita nostra, quia redemptio nostra approximat, Luc.XXI.28. Sed etiam, velut frœnum quodam, à peccato retrahit, gnaros utique, quòd eum in finem resuscitandi simus, ut unusquisque reportet in corpore, secundum quod gessit, bonum vel malum, 2.Cor.V.10. Tantò igitur enixior opera danda nobis est, ut de resurrectione mortuorum πληροφορία & πεισμονή, plena fiducia & persuasio imis animorum omnium medullis infixa hæreat.
units.tr: LXI. The Apostle Paul called the doctrine of the resurrection of the flesh θεμέλιον στερεὸν [themelion stereon], a firm foundation (2 Tim. 2:19). For that truth, decreed and made known by God, is a foundation, because when it stands the other parts of the truth, which accord with godliness, also stand, and when it is shaken they are all overthrown. "If the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen. And if Christ has not risen, then our faith is vain" (1 Cor. 15:16, 17). The Apostle says that this foundation stands firm because it is itself confirmed and supported by the other parts of saving truth. And this truth, as a foundation laid by God, has a seal by which it is known to be a divine foundation, namely two most certain and indubitable truths: that the Lord knows those who are his and takes care of them, and gives them life as his own and his special possession, both in soul and sometimes also in body, so that they suffer no loss; and that it is right and necessary that whoever names the name of Christ should depart from unrighteousness. That is, whoever glories in Christ as his head, as a partaker of the same anointing, and joined to him by his Spirit, must hate and flee unrighteousness in word and deed, and withdraw further and further from evil (ibid. 2:19). Therefore Tertullian also began his very learned book on the resurrection with this elegant maxim: "The confidence of Christians is the resurrection of the dead." For that doctrine not only sustains, fortifies and comforts us against the fear of death and all the adversities of this world, so that we do not faint under calamities pressing upon us on every side, bidding us lift up our heads, because our redemption draws near (Luke 21:28); it also, like a bridle, draws us back from sin, since we know that we are raised up to this end, that each one may receive back in the body, according to what he has done, good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10). Therefore we must apply ourselves all the more earnestly, so that full assurance (πληροφορία [plērophoria]) and persuasion (πεισμονή [peismonē]) about the resurrection of the dead may cling fixed to the innermost marrow of all our souls.

units.la: LXII. Quatuor argumentorum classes sunt, quibus veritas articuli de resurrectione mortuorum in tuta arce collocatur, Scripturæ testimonia, exempla, typi & rationes. Testimonia in V. & N. T. obvia sunt. Licet enim in V. T. vox ipsa תחיה vel תחיה nuspiam occurrat; tamen & Apostolus non obscurè Eleazarum per fidiculas distortum, 2.Macchab.VI.19. 28. 30. cùm posset vitam lucrari simulatione esus porcinæ carnis ἐιδωλοθύτα hanc λύτρωσιν redemptionem non admisisse, hoc pretio vitam redimere dignatum non esse, spe ἀναστάσεως κρείττονος resurrectionis melioris, Heb.XI.35. testatur; & Christus inprimis ipse ἀνάστασιν τῶν νεκρῶν resurrectionem mortuorum, velut ex ῥητῷ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ dicto à Deo, dicente: Ego sum Deus Abrahami, Isaci, & Jacobi, Exod.III.6.16. per cogentem ejusmodi consequentiam demonstravit, quòd cùm Deus non sit Deus mortuorum, sed viventium, necesse sit, Abrahamum, Isacum & Jacobum, omnesque adeò fidei eorumdem consortes mortuos, & secundum spiritum jam viventes, etiam vivere secundum corpus, adeóque ex morte corporis suscitari, quia Deus non partis tantùm hominis, sed totius hominis Deus est, Matth.XXII.32 Luc.XX.37.38. Etenim alicui esse לאלהים in Deum, uti Deus se Abrahamo & Semini ejus in Deum futurum promisit, Gen.XVII.7. significat, cum aliquo, velut Abrahamo & ejus Semine, habere fœdus gratiæ, quale Deus cum Abrahamo pepigit. At fœdus tale non est cum mortuis, hoc est, in morte æternùm manentibus, sed cum illis, qui vel vivi jam sunt, vel saltem ad vitam beatam reviviscent. Aliàs canis vivus mortuo, seu in morte permanente homine, præstat. At nec alia apud Mosen & Prophetas testimonia desunt. Lex enim facienti promisit vitam, Lev.XVIII.5. Ezech.XX.11. Vita illa toti hominis, adeóque etiam corpori, promissa est; & vita vera mortem, saltem perseverantem & dominantem minantem excludit. Sicut enim promissio vitæ vera esse non potest, si homo totus moriatur, vel miser sit: ita non potest perfectè impleri, si pars hominis maneat in morte. Et Deus ipse ... Ego occido, & vivificeo, Deut. XXXII. 39. Ubi vivificatio secundum eam partem, quæ moritur, hoc est, corpus, phrasis ipsa significat. Nam cui omnis vivificatio tribuitur, ei nulla negatur. Idem Moses; Redigis hominem ad minimum, & dicis: Redite filii hominis; Psal. XC. 3. Potente imperio redire jubet, non utique ad pulverem, quia dura hæc ellipsis, & durior phrasis & tautologia foret, & dicendum potius fuisset: abite; sed ex morte ad vitam corporis, judicium & beatitudinem æternam. Ubi etiam Moses fidem resurrectionis ab ejus possibilitate confirmat, tum occurrens dubitationi carnali, quòd possibile non sit carnem hominis, qui per tot mille annos computruit, & in elementa dissipatus est, excitari his verbis: Mille anni in oculis tuis sunt, ut hesternus dies, quando transiit, ut vigilia noctis, v. 4. tum resurrectionem comparans cum lassi & dormientis refocillatione, his verbis, quæ sequuntur, v. 5. Imbre perfundis illos, soporantur mane, ut gramen, recreantur. Etiam Jobus resurrectionis carnis spe mirabiliter in præsentissimis calamitatibus animum sustentavit, dicens: Novi quòd vindex meus vivat, & postremus super pulverem stabit. (cum jam omnia mors occupaverit, ipse solus immortalis, & Dominus vitæ, dominium in mortem, & arcem, vel carcerem mortis, pulverem, exercebit, & stabit super pulverem, ut vindex triumphans, velut spoliato eo mortis carcere, qui & suam carnem, quam is detinebat, vindicabit) Et postquam cutis mea ... Hoc destrinxerint, etiam ex carne mea videbo Deum, Job. XIX. 25. 26. Quem locum supra à falsis interpretum glossis vindicatum dedimus. Etiam Angelus ad Danielem. Et multi, inquit, ex dormientibus pulveris terræ evigilabunt; hi in vitam æternam; isti in probra & nauseam sæculi, Dan. XII. 2. Quæ verba, sive proprie intelliguntur, resurrectionem mortuorum omnium, qui ... multi ob eorum multitudinem ingentem dici possunt, probant; sive allegoricè, quod ex ipsa voce multi, cum multi de omnibus vix dici possint omnes, licèt omnes etiam sint multi, nonnulli colligunt, verba illa de liberatione eorum, qui mortuorum in terra pulveris jacentium instar evigilaturi erant, cùm necesse non sit, etiam illos, qui in probro erunt, evigilaturos dicere, accipientes; saltem typum resurrectionis carnis ex pulvere præbebunt. Eidem tamen Danieli diserte resurrectionem mox Angelus promittit, dicens: Tu autem vi ad finem, & requiesces, & surges ad fortem tuam ad finem dierum, ibid. v. 13. Neque minùs eam in rem disertus David est. Ego in justitia videbo vultum tuum, satiabor cum evigilavero, specie tua, Psal. XVII. 15. Evigilat enim id, quod dormit; at non spiritus, sed corpus dormit. Est etiam spiritualis evigilatio ex morte peccati, sed non conveniens Davidi loquenti, quia ex tali morte is jam evigilaverat. Idem David: Deus ... redimet animam ex manu inferni, cùm assumet me, ibid. XLIX. 16. Quæ illa ... redemptio corporis est, Rom. VIII. 23. quia est effectus ... pretii non pro anima duntaxat, sed etiam pro corpore soluti. Sed diserriores etiam N. T. textus sunt. Clarissimè enim Christus, Joh. V. 28. 29: explicata prius vers. 25. resurrectione spirituali ex morte peccati, resurrectionem corporis explicat: Veniet, inquiens, hora, qua omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus, & prodibunt, qui bona fecerint, ... ad resurrectionem vitæ; qui verò mala fecerint, ad resurrectionem judicii. Quo etiam argumento probat, se verè Filium Dei, Deo æqualem esse, videre, quæ Pater facit, &c. quia ad excitationem mortuorum, & vivificationem illorum æternam, & punitionem æternam omnipotentia, ad judicium omniscientia requiritur; & hanc qui habet, Filius Dei & Patri æqualis est. S. Paulus verò argumentum hoc etiam adversus dicentes quosdam, ... quòd resurrectio mortuorum non sit, disceptavit, 1. Cor. XV. 1–34. argumentis ponderosissimis eam confirmans. Cujusmodi sunt tum resurrectionis Christi & eorum qui sunt Christi, connexio, v. 1–24. quia si Christus resurrexit, etiam illi, qui illius sunt, resurgent; ubi & fundamentum, Christi resurrectionem, v. 1–18. firmiter ponit, & resurrectionis Christi & nostræ nexum indivulsum confirmat, quia alias, qui in Christo obdormiverunt, perient, adeóque Christus iis, qui in ipso sunt, salutem non attulisset, vers. 18. & ne in hac quidem vita salutem ab eo consequeremur, cùm in hac vita persecutionibus obnoxii simus, miserrimique adeò omnium essemus, vers. 19. & Christus factus est primitiæ dormientium, quin & resurrectionis & vivificationis causa & author, sicut Adamus causa mortis fuit; & primitiæ atque manipulus messem post se trahit, vers. 20–24. tum Regnum Christi, quia si Rex est, debet aliquando Regnum suum ... perficere, & tradere Patri, omniáque pedibus ejus subjici debent; atque eundem in finem aboleri principatus, potestas & potentia, ne alius eam præter Christum habeat; & omnes hostes hominis, quos inter ultimus mors est, velut potestatem in hominem habentes, profligari, quò sic Deus omnia in omnibus sit, debent; quod sine resurrectione carnis, mortem pedibus Christi subjiciente fieri non potest, v. 24–28. tum Baptismus, seu lotio propter mortuos contrectatos, quæ in lege injuncta conspicuus resurrectionis mortuorum typus fuit; uti in loco etiam ostendimus, v. 29. tum denique fructus pietatis & patientiæ eorum, qui quotidie periclitantur, qui sine resurrectionis mortuorum spe nulla gliscret, adeò quidem, ut sine ea vix vituperandi videantur, qui Laconicum illud de Schola Epicuri adagium, etiam Esaj. XXII. 13. notatum terunt: Edamus & bibamus, cras enim moriemur; v. 30–34. Denique idem S. Paulus alibi etiam viventes, & morte charissimorum mœstos fide & spe resurrectionis erigit, simúlque ejus mysterium pandit. Si credimus, inquit, quòd Jesus fit mortuus & resurrexerit, sic etiam Deus, qui obdormiverunt per Jesum, ducet cum ipso. Hoc enim dicimus vobis in sermone Domini, quòd nos, qui vivimus, qui superstites erimus ad adventum Domini, non prævertemus eos, qui dormiunt; quia ipse Dominus in celeusmate, in voce Archangeli, & in tuba Dei descendet de de Cœlo, & tunc mortui in Christo resurgent primò,&c. 1.Thess.IV.14–18. Accedunt testimoniis hisce resurgentium Exempla, velut filii viduæ Sareptanæ,ab Elia excitati, 1.Reg.XVII. 22. Filii mulieris Sunamitidis, quem Elisæus resuscitavit, 2.Reg.IV.35. Excitati hominis cujusdam ad contactum ossium Elisæi, in sepulchro jacentis, ibid.XIII.21. Filiæ Jairi, Matth..IX.25. Filii unigeniti viduæ in Nain, Luc.VII.15.16. Lazari Bethaniensis,Joh.XI. 43. Sanctorum quorundam post Christum resurgentem resurgentium,Matth.XXVII.52. 53. Tabithæ Joppensis à Petro,Actor.IX.40. & Eutychi à Paulo,ibid.XX.10. suscitati. Typi quinetiam resurrectionis suppetunt. Velut Enochi & Eliæ,qui in spem resurrectionis unâ cum corporibus translati sunt in Cœlum, ne viderent mortem, Genef.V.24. 2.Reg.II.11. Hebr.XI.5. Isaci,quem Abrahamus ἐν ᾧ ἐκομίσατο in similitudine seu typo, tanquam ex mortuis vivum,exemplar resurgentium ex mortuis,recepit,Gen.XXII.12. &c. Heb.XI.17. 19. Baculi Aharonis virescentis, Num.XVII. 8. Populi Dei ex morte afflictionum liberati, juxta illud Dei : Vivent mortui tui, cadaver meum, surgent. Evigilate & cantate procumbentes in pulvere. Nam ros herbarum est ros tuus. Et terram orcus faciet cadere, seu gignet, Esaj. XXVI.19. Ecce ego aperiam sepulchra vestra,& faciam vos ascendere ex sepulchris vestris,popule mi; & deducam vos ad terram Israel. Et cognoscetis,quòd ego Jehova,cùm aperiam sepulchra vestra, & cùm ascendere vos faciam ex sepulchris vestris,popule mi. Et dabo Spiritum meum in vobis,& vivetis,& constituam vos in terra vestra, &c. Ezech.XXXVII.12.13.14. Et paulò ante : Dixit ad me,fili hominis: An vivent hæc ossa? Et dixi : Domine ,tu nosti: Et dixit ad me : Prophéta de ossibus his, & dic ad illa : Ossa arida audite: Ecce ego insinuabo vobis spiritum,& vivetis, ibid. v.3.4.5. Haud enim insciè Tertullianus de Resurr. carn. cap.30. sic colligit: Hoc ipso, quòd recidivatus Judaici status de recorporatione & readunatione ossium figuratur; id quoque eventurum ossibus probatur. Non enim posset de ossibus figura componi, si non & id ipsum ossibus eventurum esset. Nam etsi figmentum veritatis in imagine est, imago ipsa in veritate est sui, necesse est esse prius sibi, quo alii configuretur. De vacuo similitudo non competit : de nullo parabola non convenit. Ita oportet ossium quoque credi revisce rationem & respirationem, qualis dicitur,de qua possit exprimi Judaicorum reformatio, qualis affingitur. Similia Hieronymi illa in Ezech. cap. 37. sunt : Nemo de rebus non extantibus incerta confirmat. In lege etiam typi resurrectionis extant, purificatio à contactu mortuorum, seu baptismus propter mortuos, Num.XIX.11. 1.Cor.XV.29. & ritus purificationis à lepra, Levit.XIV.4.5.6.7. de quibus in loco diximus.
units.tr: LXII. There are four classes of arguments by which the truth of the article on the resurrection of the dead is set on a secure foundation: the testimonies of Scripture, examples, types, and reasons. The testimonies are plentiful in both Testaments. Although the very word [תחיה] does not occur anywhere in the Old Testament, the Apostle nonetheless bears witness, not obscurely, that Eleazar, stretched on the rack (2 Macc. 6:19, 28, 30), when he could have saved his life by pretending to eat swine's flesh, which is meat offered to idols [εἰδωλόθυτα], refused this redemption and did not deign to buy back his life at that price, in hope of a better resurrection [ἀναστάσεως κρείττονος] (Heb. 11:35). Above all, Christ himself proved the resurrection of the dead [ἀνάστασιν τῶν νεκρῶν] by a compelling inference from a saying of God [ῥητῷ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ], when God says: I am the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Exod. 3:6, 16). His argument was this: since God is not the God of the dead but of the living, it must be that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and indeed all who share their faith, though dead, and already living in the spirit, are also living in the body and so are raised from the death of the body, because God is the God not of a part of a man only but of the whole man (Matt. 22:32; Luke 20:37–38). For to be [לאלהים] God's, as God promised to Abraham and his seed that he would be their God (Gen. 17:7), means to have a covenant of grace with someone, as with Abraham and his seed, such as God made with Abraham. But such a covenant is not with the dead, that is, those who remain in death for ever, but with those who are either already alive or at least will be revived to blessed life. Otherwise a living dog is better than a dead man, or a man who remains in death. Nor are there lacking other testimonies in Moses and the Prophets. The law promised life to the one who does it (Lev. 18:5; Ezek. 20:11). That life is promised to the whole man, and therefore to the body also; and true life excludes death, at least death that persists and threatens to rule. For just as the promise of life cannot be true if the whole man dies or is wretched, so it cannot be perfectly fulfilled if a part of man remains in death. And God himself says: I kill, and I make alive (Deut. 32:39). Here the phrase itself indicates that the making alive is with respect to that part which dies, that is, the body. For to him to whom all making alive is attributed, nothing is denied. Moses again says: You turn man back to dust, and say: Return, you sons of men (Ps. 90:3). He bids them return with a commanding authority, not indeed to dust, for this would be a harsh ellipsis, an harsher phrase, and a tautology, and it would have been better to say: depart; rather, he means a return from death to life of body, to judgement and eternal blessedness. Here Moses also confirms faith in the resurrection from its possibility, meeting carnal doubt, that it is not possible for the flesh of a man, which has rotted over so many thousands of years and been dissolved into the elements, to be raised, with these words: A thousand years are in your eyes as yesterday when it has passed, as a watch in the night (v. 4). Then he compares the resurrection with the refreshing of the weary and sleeping, in the words that follow: You pour rain upon them, they are put to sleep in the morning like grass, they are refreshed (v. 5). Job also, by the hope of the resurrection of the flesh, sustained his spirit wonderfully in the most pressing calamities, saying: I know that my Redeemer lives, and at last he will stand upon the dust. (Although death has already seized everything, he alone is immortal and the Lord of life; he will exercise dominion over death, and the stronghold or prison of death, which is dust, and will stand upon the dust as a triumphant avenger, as if that prison of death has been plundered, and he will claim back his own flesh, which death was holding.) And after my skin has been destroyed ... in my flesh I shall see God (Job 19:25–26). We have already vindicated this passage from the false glosses of interpreters above. The angel also speaks to Daniel: And many, he says, of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake; these to eternal life, those to shame and everlasting contempt (Dan. 12:2). These words, if they are understood literally, prove the resurrection of all the dead, who can be called many because of their huge multitude. Or if they are understood allegorically, some infer from the very word many, since many can hardly be said of all, though all are also many, that these words concern the liberation of those who were to awake from the dead lying like the dust of the earth, since it is not necessary to say that those who will be in shame will also awake. At least they will provide a type of the resurrection of the flesh from dust. Yet to the same Daniel the angel soon promises the resurrection expressly, saying: But you, go to the end, and you shall rest, and you shall rise to your lot at the end of the days (ibid. v. 13). David is no less clear to this purpose: I shall behold your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with your likeness (Ps. 17:15). For what sleeps is what awakes; but it is not the spirit that sleeps, but the body. There is also a spiritual awakening from the death of sin, but this does not suit David speaking, because he had already awoken from such death. The same David says: God ... will redeem my soul from the hand of hell, when he takes me (Ps. 49:16). This is the redemption of the body (Rom. 8:23), since it is the effect of a price paid not for the soul alone but also for the body. But the texts of the New Testament are even clearer. For Christ most plainly explains the resurrection of the body (John 5:28–29), having first explained the spiritual resurrection from the death of sin (v. 25): The hour comes, he says, in which all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice, and shall come forth, those who have done good ... to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgement. By this argument he also proves that he is truly the Son of God, equal to God, and sees what the Father does, etc., because for the raising of the dead, and their eternal making alive, and eternal punishment, omnipotence is required, and for judgement, omniscience; and whoever has these is the Son of God and equal to the Father. St Paul also disputed this argument against certain men who said that there is no resurrection of the dead (1 Cor. 15:1–34), confirming it with very weighty arguments. Such are the connection of the resurrection of Christ and of those who are Christ's (vv. 1–24): for if Christ has risen, those too who belong to him will rise. Here he firmly lays down the foundation, the resurrection of Christ (vv. 1–18), and confirms the indissoluble bond between the resurrection of Christ and ours, since otherwise those who have fallen asleep in Christ would perish, and so Christ would not have brought salvation to those who are in him (v. 18). Nor would we obtain salvation from him even in this life, since in this life we are exposed to persecutions and so would be most miserable of all men (v. 19). And Christ has become the firstfruits of those who sleep, indeed the cause and author of resurrection and making alive, just as Adam was the cause of death; and the firstfruits and the handful draw the harvest after them (vv. 20–24). Then there is the kingdom of Christ, because if he is King, he must at some time bring his kingdom to completion, and deliver it to the Father, and all things must be subjected to his feet; and to this same end the principalities, power and might must be abolished, lest anyone else have it besides Christ; and all the enemies of man, among whom death is the last, as having power over man, must be overthrown, so that God may be all in all. This cannot happen without the resurrection of the flesh, since death is subjected to the feet of Christ (vv. 24–28). Then there is baptism, or washing on account of the dead who had been touched, which in the law was an evident type of the resurrection of the dead, as we have also shown in its place (v. 29). Finally, there is the fruit of piety and patience of those who daily face danger, which cannot flourish without the hope of the resurrection of the dead; indeed, without it, those seem hardly blameworthy who wear out that Laconic saying from the school of Epicurus, also noted in Isa. 22:13: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die (vv. 30–34). Lastly, the same St Paul elsewhere raises up both the living and those saddened by the death of their dearest ones by faith and hope in the resurrection, and at the same time lays open its mystery. If we believe, he says, that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. For this we say to you in the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who sleep; for the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and then the dead in Christ shall rise first, etc. (1 Thess. 4:14–18). To these testimonies are added examples of those who rose: the son of the widow of Sarepta, raised by Elijah (1 Kings 17:22); the son of the Shunammite woman, whom Elisha raised (2 Kings 4:35); a man who was raised by touching the bones of Elisha, lying in the sepulchre (ibid. 13:21); the daughter of Jairus (Matt. 9:25); the only son of the widow at Nain (Luke 7:15–16); Lazarus of Bethany (John 11:43); certain saints who rose after Christ's resurrection (Matt. 27:52–53); Tabitha of Joppa, raised by Peter (Acts 9:40); and Eutychus, raised by Paul (ibid. 20:10). There are also types of the resurrection. Such are Enoch and Elijah, who were taken up into heaven with their bodies in hope of the resurrection, so that they should not see death (Gen. 5:24; 2 Kings 2:11; Heb. 11:5). Isaac, whom Abraham received back, as it were from the dead, in a similitude or type, as a pattern of those raised from the dead [ἐν ᾧ ἐκομίσατο] (Gen. 22:12, etc.; Heb. 11:17, 19). The rod of Aaron putting forth green shoots (Num. 17:8). The people of God, delivered from the death of affliction, according to that word of God: Your dead shall live, my corpse shall rise. Awake and sing, you who lie in the dust. For your dew is the dew of herbs. And the earth will cause the dead to fall, or will bring them forth (Isa. 26:19). Behold, I will open your graves, and cause you to come up out of your graves, my people; and I will bring you into the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I open your graves and cause you to come up out of your graves, my people. And I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will set you in your land, etc. (Ezek. 37:12–14). And a little before: He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? And I said, Lord, you know. And he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and say to them: Dry bones, hear. Behold, I will breathe into you a spirit, and you shall live (ibid. vv. 3–5). Indeed Tertullian (De resurrectione carnis, ch. 30) rightly infers thus: From the very fact that the restored state of the Jews is figured by the re-embodying and re-jointing of the bones, it is also proved that this will happen to the bones. For a figure could not be composed out of bones unless this very thing were also going to happen to the bones. For although the fiction of a truth lies in an image, the image itself must have its own truth, before it can be shaped into something else. A likeness does not fit with nothing; a parable does not agree with nothing. So it must be believed of the bones too that there will be a restoration of their sense and breath, of such a kind that the reformation of the Jews, such as is pictured, can be expressed by it. Similar are Jerome's words on Ezekiel, ch. 37: No one confirms uncertain things about things that do not exist. In the law there are also types of the resurrection: purification from contact with the dead, or baptism on account of the dead (Num. 19:11; 1 Cor. 15:29), and the rite of purification from leprosy (Lev. 14:4–7), of which we have spoken in their place.

units.la: LXIII. Non desunt denique rationes ex Scripturarum & luminis naturæ penetralibus haustæ,quibus fides resurrectionis mortuorum sustentari potest. Nam ne quid de rationibus à S. Paulo 1.Cor.XV.1–34. allatis,&supra expositis, amplius dicam,requirit eam promissio Seminis,caputSerpentis contriturí,Gen.III.15. non conteritur autem caput Serpentis plenè,
units.tr: LXIII. Finally, there are arguments drawn from the inner resources of the Scriptures and of the light of nature, by which faith in the resurrection of the dead can be sustained. I will not say more about the arguments that Saint Paul brings forward in 1 Cor. 15:1–34 and that I have set out above. The promise of the Seed requires it: the head of the Serpent is to be crushed (Gen. 3:15). But the head of the Serpent is not fully crushed

units.la: quandiu corpus hominis in morte jacet,& ex pulvere à Semine mulieris non vindicatur,vel ἀπολυτρώσιν, vi lytri ejus, non redimitur. Mors enim etiam corporis ex colubri illius veneno profluxit,quia Diabolus imperium mortis tam animæ quàm corporis ex peccato habet,& per mortem Christi imperium illud aboleri debuit, Hebr.II.14. Quando mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem,tunc fiet,quod scriptum est,absorpta est mors ad victoriam, 1.Cor.XV.54. Neque adeò Christus, non resuscitatis corporibus, vel perfectus יאל vindex est , vel de morte victa triumphum agitare potest : & retinebit semper partem potestatis Sathanas. Atqui Christus sicut Dominus,ita redemptor etiam corporis est. Empti estis pretio. Glorificate igitur Deum in corpore vestro,& in spiritu vestro, quæ Dei sunt, 1.Cor.VI.20. Nam & caro ad ejus ἀπολύτρωσιν redemptionem pertinet, Rom. VIII.23. Tum fœdus gratiæ homini credenti vitam paciscitur,& quidem etiam corporis. Hæc est voluntas ejus, qui misit me, ut omnis, qui videt Filium,& credit in eum,habeat vitam æternam. Et ego resuscitabo eum in ultimo die, Joh. VI.40. Neque Christus tantùm vita,sed etiam resurrectio nostra est. Ego sum ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωὴ resurrectio & vita, ibid. XI.25. quasi diceret: Ego resuscito ad vitam æternam. Parum enim Christo tribuit, qui ei resuscitationem mortuorum in die ultimo tribuit, nisi & vitam nullo fine terminandam tribuat. Accedit, quòd corpora nostra templa Spiritus S. sunt. An ignoratis,quòd corpus vestrum templum Spiritus S. est, quod habetis à Deo, & non à vobis? Redempti enim estis pretio, 1.Corinth.VI.19.20. Vult enim Spiritus S. in corpore,velut in templo suo,habitare,in eo operari, illud expurgare,in eo cognoscì & reperiri cum majestate & decore. Decor autem Dei sanctitas est. Quòd si autem Spiritus ejus,qui Jesum suscitavit ex mortuis,habitat in vobis,is,qui excitavit Christum ex mortuis,vivificabit etiam mortalia corpora vestra per Spiritum suum in vobis habitantem, Rom. VIII.11. Si enim Spiritus S. est spiritus vitæ, eriget etiam templum suum, in quo condecorari vult,neque illud in pulvere relinquet. Spiritus Dei fecit me, & halitus omnisufficientis vivificabit me, Job.XXXIII.4. qui Spiritus Patris & Filii innuitur. Ideo corpus nostrum vivificatum à Spiritu S. & incorruptibile πνευματικὸν spirituale vocatur, 1.Cor.XV.44. Sed & justitia Dei bonis præmia,& malis supplicia etiam in corpore persolvi jubet. Id verò cùm in hac vita,ubi bonorum & malorum fata confusa sunt, non contingat, post hanc vitam,revocato ex morte corpore,fiat oportet. Justum est apud Deum vicissim reddere iis, qui affligunt vos, affiictionem : Vobis verò, qui affligimini, relaxationem nobiscum , in revelatione Domini Jesu de Cœlo, cum Angelis suis potentibus, 2.Thess.I. 6.7. Cùm porro Christus Ecclesiæ & fidelium omnium caput sit, & singuli membra corporis ejus,ex carne ejus, & ex ossibus ejus sint,Ephes. V.30. fieri non potest , ut Christus corpus, carnem & ossa sua in morte relinquat, & caput ἀσώματον sine corpore in perpetuum maneat. Piè Bernhardus in agone suo timorem mortis hisce verbis discussit : Quid est, cur trepidem, aut desperem , cùm sciam carnem meam & sanguisanguinem meum sedere in Cœlis? Certè is, uti confido, non me aversabitur. Ecclesia enim ipse Christus dicitur, 1. Corinth. XII. 12. Moriente membro Christi, Christus mori, resurgente, Christus resurgere censetur. Cum ipso enim communionem habemus in morte & vita: Semper nos viventes in mortem tradimur propter Jesum, ut & vita Jesu manifestetur in mortali carne nostra, 2. Cor. IV. 11. Transfigurabit corpus nostrum humile, ut sit conforme corpori ejus glorioso, Phil. III. 21. Cum essemus mortui in lapsibus, una cum Christo vivificavit nos, καὶ συνήγειρε & una resuscitavit nos, Ephes. II. 5. 6. Ut nihil de signis & Sacramentis fœderis gratiæ dicam. Nam eorum usu corpora nostra velut consecrantur, & futuræ resurrectioni dedicantur. Consepulti per Baptismum, per quem etiam cum eo suscitati estis, per fidem efficacis illius virtutis Dei, qui suscitavit eum ex mortuis, Col. II. 12. Consepulti sumus ipsi per Baptismum in mortem. Si coaliti facti sumus similitudine mortis ipsius, non tantum, sed etiam resurrectionis erimus, Rom. VI. 4. 5. Poculum gratiarum actionis non ne est communio corporis ejus? 1. Cor. X. 16.
units.tr: as long as the human body lies in death and is not rescued from the dust by the Seed of the woman, or is not redeemed by his ransom-price [ἀπολύτρωσιν], the power of his ransom. For death, even of the body, flowed from the poison of that serpent, since the Devil holds dominion over death, both of soul and of body, through sin, and that dominion had to be abolished through the death of Christ (Heb. 2:14). When this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall come to pass what is written, Death is swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15:54). Nor, indeed, can Christ be a perfect avenger [גּוֹאֵל] unless bodies are raised, nor can he triumph over death conquered; and Satan would always retain some part of his power. Yet Christ is Redeemer of the body as well as its Lord. You were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's (1 Cor. 6:20). For the flesh too belongs to his redemption [ἀπολύτρωσιν] (Rom. 8:23). Moreover, the covenant of grace promises life to the believing man, and indeed life of the body also. This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life. And I will raise him up on the last day (John 6:40). Christ is not only life but also our resurrection. I am the resurrection and the life [ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή] (John 11:25), as if he were saying: I raise up to eternal life. For he gives little to Christ who attributes to him the resurrection of the dead on the last day, but does not also grant him a life that will have no end. Besides, our bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit. Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, which you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought with a price (1 Cor. 6:19–20). For the Holy Spirit wishes to dwell in the body as in his own temple, to work in it, to cleanse it, and to be known and found in it with majesty and glory. But the glory of God is holiness. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you (Rom. 8:11). For if the Holy Spirit is the spirit of life, he will also raise up his temple, in which he wishes to be adorned, and will not leave it in the dust. The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life (Job 33:4), where the Spirit of the Father and the Son is indicated. Therefore our body, quickened by the Holy Spirit and made incorruptible, is called spiritual [πνευματικὸν] (1 Cor. 15:44). Moreover, the justice of God commands that rewards for the good and punishments for the wicked be paid also in the body. But since this does not happen in this life, where the fates of the good and the wicked are confused, it must happen after this life, when the body is restored from death. It is just before God to repay affliction to those who afflict you, and to give relief to you who are afflicted, along with us, at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with his mighty angels (2 Thess. 1:6–7). Since, further, Christ is the head of the Church and of all the faithful, and the individual members of his body are of his flesh and of his bones (Eph. 5:30), it cannot be that Christ should leave his body, flesh and bones, in death, and that his head should remain forever without a body [ἀσώματον]. Bernard, in his last struggle, devoutly dispelled the fear of death with these words: Why should I tremble or despair, when I know that my flesh and my blood are seated in the heavens? Surely he, as I trust, will not turn away from me. For the Church itself is called Christ (1 Cor. 12:12). When a member of Christ dies, Christ is considered to die; when it rises, Christ is considered to rise. For we have fellowship with him in death and in life. We who live are always handed over to death for Jesus' sake, so that the life of Jesus may be made manifest in our mortal flesh (2 Cor. 4:11). He will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Phil. 3:21). When we were dead in our trespasses, he made us alive together with Christ, and raised us up together [συνήγειρεν] (Eph. 2:5–6). I say nothing here of the signs and sacraments of the covenant of grace. For by their use our bodies are, as it were, consecrated and dedicated to the future resurrection. You were buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead (Col. 2:12). We were buried with him by baptism into death. If we have been united with him in the likeness of his death, we shall certainly also be united in the likeness of his resurrection (Rom. 6:4–5). Is not the cup of thanksgiving a participation in his body? (1 Cor. 10:16).

units.la: LXIV. Sanior verò ratio, remota revelatione, equidem possibilitatem resurrectionis agnoscit, utpote quæ & omnipotentiam & justitiam Dei, ejus fulcra, non ignorat. Ipse certè Aristoteles, cur ex materia & forma fiat unum, non alibi quàm in Agente, à quo forma in materiam introducitur, quærendam esse docet, eò quòd manentibus iisdem numero principiis essentialibus rei corruptæ, materia scilicet & forma, eodemque agente, quod eas rursus conjungere potest, nihil obstet, quò minùs res corrupta restituatur. Cùm ergo corrupto homine maneant principia ejus essentialia, anima & corpus; nec non Agens, Deus, qui utrumque antea conjunxit, quid obstat, quò minùs idem homo restitui possit? Ac licet Philosophi plerique facilius Cœlum ruiturum, fractámque orbis molem suo casu cuncta tractuam sibi persuaderi passi sunt, quàm ut corporibus semel ab anima destitutis vitam redituram admitterent; imò etiam Christianos, veluti aniles ejusmodi fabulas, uti Cæcilius apud Minutium Felicem eos traduxit; contendentes, riserint; tamen fuerunt ex Gentibus, qui fidem etiam veritati resurrectionis commodare utcunq; sustinuerint. Velut Persarum magi, qui auctore Theopompo apud Laertium Proœm. p. 6. ἀναβιώσεσθαι ἀνθρώπους, καὶ ἑσεσθαι ἀθανάτους revicturos homines, & immortales futuros dixerunt: Democritus, quem eadem corpora revictura statuisse, Leo Allatius lib. de Engastrimyth. docuit: Pythagoras & Plato, sed corrupta & dimidiata fide, uti Minutius loquitur: Stoici, Clemens Alexandrinus Strom. lib. V. statuere, eum, qui certa qualitate præditus est, ἀναστήσεσθαι resurrecturum, scripsit, quorum etiam de παλιγγενεσία, quam certo annorum spatio confectum iri asseruerunt, sententia notissima est. Facit huc, quòd Æsculapium à diis consecutum, ἀνίστησαι μὴ πεθνεώτας ut mortuos suscitaret, Xenophon de Venat. scripsit. Denique ex multorum Philosophorum sententia Athenagoras Orat. pro Christ. futuram corporum resurrectionem asserit, quam & Germanos priscos credidisse Appianus de Bell. Celt. c. 3. testis est. Taceo quasi exempla, & experimenta resuscitatorum ex mortuis, quæ gentilium quidem opinione jam contigerunt. Nam fabulosæ hujus resurrectionis exempla Alstem, Protesilaum, Theseum & Ulyssem Lucianus de Luct. T. I. p. 785. Erim Armenium, quem Zoroastrum esse Clemens Alex. credit, Plato de Rep. lib. X. Hermolimum Clazomenium Lucianus Musc. Encom. T. I. alios plures Æneas Gazæus de Immort. an. quinetiam Pythagoram Zamolxim, Pythagoræ servum, & Rampsinitum Ægyptium Origenes contra Celf. lib. II. 2. alios alii retulerunt. Sed proclive judicatu tamen est, qualiscunque de veritate resurrectionis cognitio gentilibus contigit, non naturæ & rationis, sed traditionis beneficio eam indeptos esse. Prompserunt quidem etiam Ecclesiæ doctores, ubi cum ethnicis pugnarunt, argumenta quædam ex ipso naturæ penu, quibus rei adeò creditu difficili fidem conciliarent. Sed talia ea esse, quæ ultra rei possibilitatem, ejusdem etiam veritatem probent, & refragantium vim omnem, atque subsannantium risum summoveant, dicere non audemus. Talia apud Tertullianum de resurr. cap. ult. Minutium Felicem, Ambrosium de Resurr. T. III. Epiphanium hær. 42. aliósque legere est, quæ inprimis à creatione rerum omnium, & præmiorum atque pœnarum justitia arcessita, fieri posse, ut mortui resurgant, certò demonstrant; at futurum id, minùs certò arguunt. Nam veritas resurrectionis est mysterium supernaturali verbi luce Ecclesiæ in V. & N. T. patefactum. Estque resurrectio carnis fiducia Christianorum. Et mortuum esse Christum, juxta illud Augustini, Pagani ac inimici ejus credunt. Resurrexisse autem Christum, propria Christianorum fides est. Lumen verò naturæ in hac corruptione plura & speciosiora argumenta, quibus mortuorum resurrectio destruatur, quàm quibus adstruatur, suppeditat, quæ ipsa tamen contrariis instantiis sanior ratio facile enervat.
units.tr: LXIV. A sounder reasoning, setting revelation aside, indeed recognises the possibility of the resurrection, since it does not overlook the omnipotence and justice of God, which are its supports. Aristotle himself teaches that the cause of the union of matter and form into one must be sought nowhere but in the agent by which the form is introduced into the matter; because, when the same essential principles of a corrupted thing remain in number, namely matter and form, and the same agent remains which can again join them, nothing stands in the way of the corrupted thing being restored. Since, then, when a man is corrupted, his essential principles remain, soul and body, and God the agent remains, who joined the two before, what prevents the same man from being restored? And although most philosophers were more willing to be persuaded that the heavens would fall and the broken mass of the world would be dragged down in its ruin, than to admit that bodies once abandoned by the soul would return to life; and although they laughed at Christians, contending for such things as old wives' fables, as Caecilius in Minucius Felix presented them; nevertheless there were among the Gentiles some who managed, in some measure, to accommodate their faith to the truth of the resurrection. Such were the Persian magi, who, according to Theopompus in Laertius (Proem. p. 6), said that men would live again [ἀναβιώσεσθαι] and would become immortal [ἔσεσθαι ἀθανάτους]. Democritus, who, as Leo Allatius showed in his book on the Engastrimythi, held that the same bodies would live again. Pythagoras and Plato, but with a corrupted and half-formed faith, as Minucius puts it. The Stoics, as Clement of Alexandria writes in the fifth book of the Stromata, held that a person endowed with a certain quality would rise again [ἀναστήσεσθαι]; and their doctrine of the palingenesis, which they asserted would be completed at a certain span of years, is very well known. To this belongs what Xenophon wrote in his work on hunting, that Aesculapius received from the gods the power to raise up the dead [ἀνίστησαι μὴ τεθνεῶτας]. Finally, according to the opinion of many philosophers, Athenagoras in his Embassy for the Christians asserts a future resurrection of bodies; and Appian, in his Celtic Wars (c. 3), is a witness that the ancient Germans also believed it. I pass over, as it were, the examples and experiences of those raised from the dead, which indeed have already occurred by the opinion of the Gentiles. For Lucian (On Mourning, vol. 1, p. 785) lists examples of this fabulous resurrection: Alcestis, Protesilaus, Theseus and Ulysses; Plato (Republic, book 10) lists Er the Armenian, whom Clement of Alexandria believes to be Zoroaster; Lucian (Encomium of the Fly, vol. 1) lists Hermotimus of Clazomenae; and many others are listed by Aeneas of Gaza in his work On Immortality. Origen, against Celsus (book 2), relates that Pythagoras' servant Zamolxis and the Egyptian Rhampsinitus were also raised, and others have related others. But it is easily judged that whatever knowledge of the truth of the resurrection came to the Gentiles, they obtained it not by nature and reason but by the benefit of tradition. The doctors of the Church indeed also brought forward, when they contended with the heathen, certain arguments drawn from the very storehouse of nature, by which they might win faith for a thing so hard to believe. But we dare not say that these arguments prove, beyond the possibility of the thing, its very truth, and remove all the force of opponents and the laughter of scoffers. Such arguments may be read in Tertullian (On the Resurrection, last chapter), Minucius Felix, Ambrose (On the Resurrection, vol. 3), Epiphanius (Heresy 42), and others. They are drawn chiefly from the creation of all things and from the justice of rewards and punishments, and they demonstrate with certainty that the dead can rise; but they argue less certainly that they will. For the truth of the resurrection is a mystery revealed in the Old and New Testaments by the supernatural light of the Word of God. And the resurrection of the flesh is the confidence of Christians. That Christ is dead, as Augustine puts it, both pagans and his enemies believe; but that Christ has risen is the particular faith of Christians. The light of nature, in this corrupted state, supplies more and more striking arguments by which the resurrection of the dead is overthrown than by which it is established; and even these a sounder reason readily weakens by contrary instances.

units.la: LXV. Neque adeò mirandum est, quòd nunquam defuerunt Judæi, Gentiles, Pseudochristiani, qui hoc fidei Christianæ Palladium, ceu puerile deliramentum, uti appellare Plinius non erubuit, falsè & albo, quod ajunt, dente irriderent. Ex Judæis Sadducæi jam olim dixerunt, μὴ ἔναι ἀνάστασιν non esse resurrectionem, Matth. XXII. 23. Luc. XX. 27. Actor. XXIII. 8. Qua illi occasione in errorem hunc delapsi sint R. Abraham Davidis filius in Cabbala sua historica, & ex eo juniores, referente Scaligero in El. Trihær. cap. 15. tradidit. Cùm enim Antigonus Sochæus, Alexandro M. coævus, crebrò in ore haberet אלהתיו המשרושין את הרב על מנת לקבל פרס Ne estote, sicut servi, qui servium Domino propter mercedem, ut accipiant præmium; sed estote ut qui ministrant Principi suo, hac conditione, ne accipiant præmium, & sit Dei timor super vos; Discipuli ejus Zadokus, unde Sadducæis nomen, & Baithosus, pio adeò dicto in sententiam impiam detorto, opinionem conceperunt, non esse ἀντιδοτὴν ἔργων, operum mercedem aliquam, vel fructum; atque ideo resurrectionem atque futurum sæculum abnegarunt. Quos etiam dogmatis impietas ad vitæ impietatem transversos avexit, ut nihil ab Epicuræis
units.tr: LXV. Nor is it any wonder that there have never lacked Jews, Gentiles and false Christians who mock this Palladium of the Christian faith, which Pliny did not blush to call a childish delirium, with a false and, as they say, white-toothed sneer. Among the Jews, the Sadducees long ago said that there is no resurrection [μὴ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν], Matt. 22:23; Luke 20:27; Acts 23:8. Abraham ben David, in his historical Cabbalah, and after him the later writers, as Scaliger reports in El. Trihær. ch. 15, have recorded the occasion on which they fell into this error. Antigonus of Sokho, a contemporary of Alexander the Great, was often on his lips the saying: "Be not like servants who serve the master for the sake of reward [אל תהיו כעבדים המשמשין את הרב על מנת לקבל פרס]; but be like those who serve their prince on the condition of receiving no reward, and let the fear of God be upon you." His disciples Zadok, from whom the name Sadducees comes, and Boethus, twisting this pious saying into an impious meaning, conceived the opinion that there is no ἀντιδοτὴν ἔργων, that is, no repayment or fruit of works; and so they denied the resurrection and the future age. The impiety of this doctrine also drove them into an impious life, so that they differed in nothing from the Epicureans.

units.la: Et lumine naturæ, salutem quoad possibilitatem ejus, petitiu. curæis differrent; & שורש למינים radix hæreticorum à Rab. Juda in Cosri appellärentur; & veteres in Sanhed : C. Ohel. s 1. contra eosdem concluderent, non essè partem ei in futuro seculo, qui dixerit, הקמת המתים מן התורה non essè resurrectionem mortuorum in lege traditam. Sadducæis Pharisæi tempore Christi se opposuerunt, Actor. XXIII. 8. sed hactenus eisdem concedentes; quòd incauti imprudentésque asserere non erubuerunt, articuli hujus nullam in lege mentionem בגלוי ובביאור aperte & explicite fieri, quod etiam Abulfeda Arabs Muhammedanus, referente Celeb. Pokoke Miscell. p. 99. &, comparativè saltem, Ahmed Ibn-Edris Cel. Hottingero, de Resurr. Mort. p. 6. asserunt. De Paganis Philosophis jam diximus. Athenienses certè audientes ἀνάστασιν νεκρῶν resurrectionem mortuorum, alii quidem ἐχλευάζον subsannarunt Paulum; alii dixerunt: Denuo hac de re te audiemus, Actor. XVII. 32.
units.tr: And by the light of nature, the possibility of salvation is sought. They were called "the root of heretics" [שורש למינים] by Rabbi Judah in the Cosri; and the ancient writers in the Sanhedrin, in the tractate Ohel ch. 1, concluded against them that they have no part in the future age who say that the resurrection of the dead is not taught in the law [הקמת המתים מן התורה]. The Pharisees opposed the Sadducees in Christ's time, Acts 23:8, yet they conceded this much to them: that the Sadducees, being rash and imprudent, did not blush to assert that this article has no mention in the law openly and explicitly [בגלוי ובביאור]. Abulfeda the Arab Muhammadan, as reported by the learned Pococke, Miscell. p. 99, and Ahmed ibn Idris, at least comparatively, as Hottinger cites him in de Resurr. Mort. p. 6, also assert this. We have already spoken of the pagan philosophers. When the Athenians heard of the resurrection of the dead [ἀνάστασιν νεκρῶν], some mocked Paul, while others said, "We will hear you again about this matter," Acts 17:32.

units.la: Omnis enim post vitam hanc felicitas ad animam ab iis sanioribus translata est, præcipuam ejus partem in eo collocantibus, quòd corporis molem posituri essent, quòd æternum & incorruptibile reddi posse, omnino desperabant. Utrisque Pseudo-christiani non pauci suffragati jam olim sunt, & hodiéque suffragantur. Nam S. Pauli tempore in Ecclesia Corinthiaca quidam dixerunt, ὅτι ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν οὐκ ἔστι, quòd resurrectio mortuorum non sit, 1.Cor. XV. 12. Hymenæus & Philetus resurrectionem jam factam esse asseruerunt, 2. Tim. II. 18. intelligentes resurrectionem mundi per prædicationem Evangelii, quomodo nec injusti, nec corpora justorum resurgerent. Eadem infidelitate proximis post Apostolos temporibus Simon Magus, Basilides Alexandrinus, Carpocrates, Gnosticorum author Valentinus, Marcus, Cajani, Archontici, Marcion, Severus, Hierax, Sejeucus, vel Hermias, similisque notæ hæretici; Manichæos postea & Priscillanistas asseclas adepti, resurrectionem carnis negarunt. Periculose eundem in lapidem Origenem impegisse, Epiphanius & Hieronymus testantur. Haud meliores Sociniani impiorum resurrectionem diserte negant: & fidelium corpora eadem numero resurrectura inficiantes, non obscure horum etiam resurrectionem abnegant. Nostro quoque seculo in Anglia, monitrorum ejusmodi feraci, esse, qui corpora fidelium non resurrectura eadem, sed vel per creationem, vel per productionem ex materia noviter formata; alios, qui infantes non resurrecturos; alios, qui nullam omnino resurrectionem futuram: alios denique, uti stultorum in contraria proclivis lapsus est, qui etiam cum brutis eam communem velint, Cl. Hornius Histor. Eccles. Per. 2. act. 3. pag. 303. 304. testis est.
units.tr: For all the happiness after this life was transferred to the soul by the wiser sort, who placed its chief part in this, that they would lay aside the bulk of the body, since they utterly despaired that it could be made eternal and incorruptible. Not a few false Christians have long since supported both views, and still support them. In Paul's time some in the Corinthian church said that there is no resurrection of the dead [ὅτι ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν οὐκ ἔστι], 1 Cor. 15:12. Hymenaeus and Philetus asserted that the resurrection has already taken place, 2 Tim. 2:18, understanding the resurrection of the world to come through the preaching of the Gospel, so that neither the unjust nor the bodies of the just would rise again. With the same unbelief, in the period soon after the Apostles, Simon Magus, Basilides of Alexandria, Carpocrates, Valentinus the author of the Gnostics, Marcus, the Cainites, the Archontics, Marcion, Severus, Hierax, Sejeucus or Hermias, and heretics of similar note denied the resurrection of the flesh; later, Manicheans and the followers of Priscillian did the same. Epiphanius and Jerome testify that Origen dangerously stumbled on this same stone. The Socinians are no better: they expressly deny the resurrection of the wicked, and by denying that the bodies of the faithful will rise as the same in number, they do not obscurely deny the resurrection of these as well. In our own century, in England, a country fertile in such monsters, there have been some who held that the bodies of the faithful will not rise the same, but either by creation or by production from newly formed matter; others who held that infants will not rise; others who held that there will be no resurrection at all; and finally others who, like fools inclined to the opposite error, wished it to be common to beasts as well. The learned Horn is a witness to this in his Historia Ecclesiastica, Period 2, Book 3, pp. 303–304.

units.la: LXVI. Vanissima verò argumenta sunt, quibus veritatem resurrectionis mortuorum conspirantes in eandem infidelitatem, infringere conantur. Nam quòd impossibile esse, ut idem numero corpus, quod interiit, in integrum restituatur, pertendunt, quàm imbelle sit, infra videbimus. Paucis multa dixit Christus ad infideles Sadducæos: Erratis nescientes Scripturas & potentiam Dei, Matth. XXII. 29. Neque Jobus dicens: Non est arbori, quod expetet. Si exscindatur, repullulascet, & stolo ejus non deficit. Si consenuerit in terra in die ejus,&c. ab odore aquæ florebit. At homo moritur & debilitatur, & ubi expiraverit, ubi est? cap. XIV. 7--12. hominem mortuum simpliciter non esse, sed in hac vita non esse, & in hac vita ejus miseriam cum felicitate non commutari, asseverit; adeóque deteriorem ejus conditionem cæteris esse, quàm arboris, quæ יחליף pullulat, & se ipsam quasi renovat, affirmat. Idem subjiciens v. 12. virum, cùm cubuerit, non resurgere, non simpliciter resurrecturum negat, sed evigilaturum, excitandum à somno suo, adeóque resurrecturum עד בלתי שמים donec non fuerint Cœli hi, quales nunc sunt, & rotant; negat. Cùm igitur Cœli, quales nunc sunt, peribunt, evigilabit. Subjicit verò idem v. 14. Cùm mortuus fuerit homo, an vivet? non dubitans utique de resurrectione mortuorum, sed negans se semel mortuum resurrecturum vel ad hanc vitam, vel quandiu Cœlum est, uti nunc est. Tota enim disputatio Jobi eò collimat, ut probet, in rebus externis non esse signa gratiæ vel iræ, neque in hac vita dari id, quod fideles sperant; ideóque nihil satius esse, quàm ut ad mortem anhelent. Cùm tamen afflictiones habeant nomen & speciem iræ & vindictæ; neque id omnino amici negaverint, iccirco ex hypothesi hac agens ostendit, optabilius esse, vel ut moriatur, & ad alteram vitam transeat, vel ut mortuus alicubi occultetur sub terra, donec tempus gratiæ appetat, siquidem id detur in hoc ævo, quod ille in Cœlo alioquin expectabat. Alias Jobi hypothesis, quòd ira Dei sit abitura, quòd annus gratiæ sit venturus, statio ipsius & militia certis diebus definita sit, quòd spes sit futuræ suæ חליפה mutationis in melius; quòd vocanti Deo, seu resurgere jubenti responsurus sit; & hæc omnia futura sint בלתי שמים quando non amplius erunt cœli in præsenti statu, c. XIV. 13.14.15. resurrectioni mortuorum ingens argumentum suppeditant. Ne quid de cap. XIX. 25. dicam. Ut frustra Hebræi, nominatim R. Solomon Jarchi ad Job. VII. 7. tanquam כפר בתחיית המתים abnegatorem resurrectionis mortuorum eum sugillaverint, quod & Græci nonnulli, Didymus, & Chrysostomus facere videntur. Perspicuè enim etiam Jobus alibi se explicat, dicens: Consumitur nubes & abit. Sic est, qui descendit ad inferos, non ascendit. Non redit in posterum ad domum suam, neque agnoscet eum amplius locus suus, cap. VII. 8.9. Loquitur enim perspicuè de hac vita, in qua mitigationem cruciatus atque terroris, & consolationem petit. Sed & David de impiis dicens: לא יקמו במשפט Psal. I. 5. non eos non resurrecturos, sed non staturos in Judicio, verùm causa casuros, & cum pudore ac confusione à facie judicis sui recessuros. Sùntque homines caro רוח הלך ולא ישוב ventus abiens & non revertens, Psal. LXXVIII. 39. in eum videlicet locum, in quo moribundi erant. Et Deus eorum, qui in sepulchro sunt, & à manu Dei excisi sunt, non amplius recordatur, ibid. LXXXVIII. 6. ut scilicet ad hanc vitam revocatos beneficiis suis mactet, sicut antehac mactavit. Præterea mortui non reviviscunt, cadavera non resurgunt, Esaj. XXVI. 14. sive quia non surgent, quandiu Cœli in hoc statu sunt: sive quia non resurgunt ad vitam præsentem: sive quia afflicti quiquidem & mortuis atque cadaveribus similes, non liberantur; sive denique quia mortui secunda morte, nomen habentes, quod vivant, & mortui tamen, seu per secundam mortem indurati,non revivi\u017ecunt, Apoc. XX. 5. Mox enim subjicitur: Vivent mortui, cadaver meum, surgent. Evigilate & cantate procumbentes in pulvere, v. 19. Etiam is, qui educit currus & equos, copias & robur; pariter occumbunt, non surgunt, extinguuntur, tanquam linum extinguuntur, ib. XLIII. 17. Allusione instituta ad Pharaonem & exercitum, atque \u03c0\u03b1\u03bd\u03c9\u03c0\u03bb\u03b5\u03b8\u03c1\u03af\u03b1 utriusque, non resurgentium ex aquis, quibus semel absorpti sunt, ad vexandum denuo populum Dei. De Babylone quoque Deus: Cum incaluerint, inquit, ponam convivia ipsorum & inebriabo ipsos, ut exultent [Hebrew] et obdormiscent somno perpetuo, & non evigilabunt, Jerem. LI. 39. hoc est, uti Deus ipse v. 64. explicat: Sic demergetur Babylon, & non stabit coram malo, quod ego contra eam adducam, & defetiscent. Sic enim Babylon abolebitur, ut non memoretur amplius. Denique nec corpus animae ad beatitudinem aspiranti obstat, ut vel ideo excitandum non videatur. Non enim corpus animam ratione substantiae, sed ratione concupiscentiae, quam aboleri oportet, impedit.
units.tr: LXVI. The arguments by which those who conspire against the truth of the resurrection of the dead try to overthrow it are most empty. For as to their claim that it is impossible for the same numerical body that has perished to be restored in its entirety, how feeble this is we shall see below. Christ answered the unbelieving Sadducees in few words: You are wrong, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God, Matt. 22:29. Job, too, says: For there is hope for a tree, that if it be cut down, it will sprout again, and its shoot will not fail. Though its root grow old in the earth, and its stock die in the ground, yet at the scent of water it will bud and bring forth boughs like a young plant. But man dies and is brought low; yea, man breathes his last, and where is he? Job 14:7–12. He asserts that a dead man is not simply gone, but is not in this life, and that his misery in this life is not exchanged for happiness; and he affirms that his condition is worse than that of a tree, which yachaliph [יחליף], that is, sprouts again and, as it were, renews itself. Adding in verse 12 that a man, when he lies down, does not rise, he does not simply deny that he will rise, but denies that he will rise to be awakened from his sleep, and therefore that he will rise until the heavens are no more [עד בלתי שמים], that is, until the heavens, as they now are and turn round, are no more. So when the heavens as they now are have perished, he will awake. Verse 14 adds: If a man dies, shall he live again? Certainly he does not doubt the resurrection of the dead, but denies that a man once dead will rise either to this life, or as long as the heaven is as it now is. For the whole argument of Job aims at proving that outward things are no signs of grace or wrath, and that what the faithful hope for is not given in this life; so nothing is better than to long for death. Yet since afflictions have the name and appearance of wrath and vengeance, and his friends have not wholly denied this, he, arguing from this hypothesis, shows that it is more desirable either that he should die and pass into the other life, or that, being dead, he should be hidden somewhere under the earth until the time of grace comes, if indeed that is granted in this age, which he otherwise expected in heaven. Job's other hypotheses, that the wrath of God will pass away, that the year of grace will come, that his station and warfare are fixed for appointed days, that there is hope of his future change [חליפה] for the better, that he will answer God calling, that is, bidding him rise, and that all these things will be when the heavens are no more [בלתי שמים], as they are in the present state, Job 14:13–15, provide a great argument for the resurrection of the dead. I say nothing of Job 19:25. The Hebrews, and especially Rabbi Solomon Jarchi on Job 7:7, vainly reproached him as a denier of the resurrection of the dead [כפר בתחיית המתים], as some Greeks, Didymus and Chrysostom, also seem to do. For Job explains himself plainly elsewhere, saying: The cloud is consumed and vanishes away; so he who goes down to Sheol does not come up. He does not return again to his house, nor shall his place know him any more, Job 7:8–9. For he speaks plainly of this life, in which he seeks relief from torment and terror and consolation. David, too, speaking of the wicked: they will not rise [לא יקמו] in judgment, Ps. 1:5, does not mean that they will not rise at all, but that they will not stand in judgment, but will fall in their cause, and withdraw from the face of their judge in shame and confusion. And men are flesh, a wind that passes and does not return [רוח הלך ולא ישוב], Ps. 78:39, namely into that place in which the dying were. And God no longer remembers those who are in the grave and are cut off from the hand of God, Ps. 88:6, that is, so that he may slay those called back to this life with his blessings, as he slew them before. Moreover, the dead do not live again; the shades do not rise, Isa. 26:14, either because they will not rise as long as the heavens are in this state, or because they do not rise to the present life, or because, though afflicted and like the dead and shades, they are not delivered; or finally because the dead by the second death, having a name that they live, and yet are dead, or hardened by the second death, do not come to life again, Rev. 3:1 (cf. 20:5). For immediately it follows: Your dead shall live, my corpse shall rise. Awake and sing, you who lie in the dust, Isa. 26:19. Also he who brings out chariots and horses, the host and the strength, they lie down together and do not rise; they are extinguished, they are quenched like a wick, Isa. 43:17. This is an allusion to Pharaoh and his army, and to the panoplethria [παναπλεθρία] of both, that is, to those who do not rise from the waters in which they were once swallowed, to trouble God's people again. God also says of Babylon: When they are heated, I will set out their feasts and make them drunk, that they may exult, and sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake [Hebrew], Jer. 51:39. That is, as God himself explains in verse 64: So Babylon shall sink and not rise from the evil that I will bring upon her, and they shall faint. For Babylon will be abolished in such a way that she is not remembered any more. Finally, the body does not hinder the soul aspiring to blessedness, so that it does not seem on that account to need to be raised. For the body hinders the soul not by reason of its substance, but by reason of concupiscence, which must be abolished.

units.la: LXVII. Solus Deus verbo suo omnipotente mortuos ad vitam revocabit. Ego, Ego ille, qui occido & vivifico, Deut. XXXII. 39. Ego aperio sepulchra vestra, & educam vos de sepulchris. Et dabo Spiritum meum in vos, & vivetis, Ezech. XXXVII. 12. 14. Sicut Pater excitat mortuos, ita & Filius, quos vult vivificat, Joh. V. 21. Qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus, Filii, & egredientur, ibid. v. 28. 29. Ubi \u03c6\u03c9\u03bd\u03ae vox vim illam efficacem, qua sibi Deus omnia subjicere potest, Phil. III. 21. notat. Ego in die ultimo resuscitabo id omne, quod Pater mihi dedit, ibid. VI. 39. Ipse Dominus veniet in celeusmate (voce sonora ad attentionem excitante) in voce Archangeli (sua propria, qua se principem Angelorum demonstrabit) & in tuba Dei (potente Divina voce, qua, ut Deus mortuos excitabit) 1. Thess. IV. 16. Revera enim resuscitatio ex mortuis aeque ac creatio omnipotentiae Divinae opus est. Unde & Christus ad Sadducaeos resurrectionem negantes: Erratis, nescientes Scripturas & \u03b4\u03cd\u03bd\u03b1\u03bc\u03b9\u03bd \u0398\u03b5\u03bf\u1f7b potentiam Dei, seu omnipotentiam, Matth. XXII. 29. Ideo Deus Christum ex mortuis resuscitans, operatus dicitur, secundum efficaciam roboris virium suarum, qua \u1f51\u03c0\u03b5\u03c1\u03b2\u03b1\u03bb\u03bb\u03bf\u03bd \u03bc\u03b5\u03b3\u03b5\u03b8\u1f78 \u03b4\u03c5\u03bd\u03ac\u03bc\u03b5\u03c9\u03c2 excellens magnitudo potentiae Dei cognoscitur, Ephes. I. 19. 20. Quin & Christus se Filium Dei, aequalem Patri esse, eo argumento demonstravit, quia, sicut Pater suscitat mortuos & vivificat, ita & Filius quos vult, vivificat, Joh. V. 21. quod de vivificatione & spirituali, ex morte peccati, & corporali ex morte corporis, mox v. 25. 29. explicat. Nam aequalis ad utramque potentia requiritur, ut qui ex morte spirituali vivificare non potest, is nec ex corporali possit; & utriusque connexio est, quia sicut corporis resurrectio ad vitam non est, nisi praecedat resurrectio animae ex morte peccati ad vitam Christi: ita vivificatis per Christum ex morte peccati certa expectatio vivificandae carnis sit, Joh. V. 25. 28-29. VI. 39. Licet enim etiam Prophetae & Apostoli mortuos excitaverint, tamen nec omnis vivificatio mortuorum iis, perinde ut Filio tribuitur; nec quisquam eorum, ut Deus, vivificavit, quia nemo vivificavit, quos voluit; denique ne quidem proprie quisquam eorum mortuos vivificavit. Quid in nobis obtutum defigitis, quasi in ipsa \u1f40\u03c5\u03bd\u03b1\u03bc\u03b9\u03c2 propria potentia & pietate illum ambulare fecerimus. Propter fidem nominis ejus (Jesu) hunc, quem videtis & scitis, firmavit nomen ejus (ipse nominatus & invocatus fecit) & fides, quae per ipsum est in Deum, dedit ipsi incolumitatem hanc coram omnibus vobis, Actor. III. 12. 16. Tam enim non creatura suscitare mortuos, quam non creare potest; quia utrumque opus est a solo nutu & \u1f41\u03bb\u03b7\u03bc\u03bf\u03c5 voluntate, ejusque imperio pendet. Nulla enim creatura voluntatem imperantem, & vocantem id quod non est, habet; vel enim idem vocabit Deus, vel non vocabit. Si vocabit, solius Dei est, quod sic vocatur; & creaturae nonnisi voluntas laudans & approbans relinquetur. Si non vocabit, creatura sine Deo & voluntate ejus erit; & quidem, volente Deo, quia necesse est Deum velle ut creatura creet & resuscitet, erit, quod Deus non vocat, & non vult esse. Vivificabit igitur voluntate \u03b4\u03b5\u03c3\u03c0\u03bf\u03c4\u03b9\u03ba\u1f75 \u03ba\u03b1\u1f76 \u1f00\u03b3\u03c7\u03b9\u03c3\u03c4\u03bf\u03b1\u03bd\u1f77 herili & magistrali, hoc est, verbo imperante, vocatione adducente ea, quae non sunt. Merito ergo etiam Judaei scisc unt. Tres claves non esse dat as ulli legato, [Hebrew] vitae, pluviae & resurrectionis mortuorum.
units.tr: LXVII. Only God, by his almighty word, will call the dead back to life. I, I am he who kills and makes alive, Deut. 32:39. Behold, I will open your graves and bring you up out of your graves. And I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, Ezek. 37:12, 14. As the Father raises the dead, so also the Son gives life to whom he will, John 5:21. Those who are in the tombs shall hear his voice, the Son's, and shall come forth, ibid. vv. 28-29. Here the Greek word [phōnē] denotes that effective power by which God can subject all things to himself, Phil. 3:21. I will raise up on the last day all that the Father has given me, ibid. 6:39. The Lord himself will descend with a shout (a loud voice to arouse attention), with the voice of the archangel (his own, by which he will show himself the prince of angels), and with the trumpet of God (the mighty divine voice by which, as God, he will raise the dead), 1 Thess. 4:16. For the resurrection from the dead, no less than creation, is a work of divine omnipotence. Hence Christ also, to the Sadducees who denied the resurrection: You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God [dynamin tou Theou], that is, the omnipotence of God, Matt. 22:29. Therefore God, raising Christ from the dead, is said to have worked according to the efficacy of the strength of his might [kata tēn energeian tou kratous tēs ischyos autou], by which the exceeding greatness of God's power [hyperballon megethos dynameōs] is known, Eph. 1:19-20. Christ also showed that he is the Son of God, equal to the Father, by this argument: as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will, John 5:21. He explains this, at vv. 25 and 29, of the quickening from the death of sin and of the quickening of the body from bodily death. For equal power is required for both: one who cannot quicken from spiritual death cannot quicken from bodily death either. The two are also linked, because just as the resurrection of the body does not lead to life unless the resurrection of the soul from the death of sin to the life of Christ comes first, so for those quickened through Christ from the death of sin there is a sure expectation that their flesh will be quickened, John 5:25, 28-29; 6:39. For although the prophets and apostles also raised the dead, the quickening of the dead is not ascribed to them as it is to the Son; nor did any of them quicken as God does, since none quickened whom he will; and finally, not one of them quickened the dead in the proper sense. Why do you fix your gaze on us, as if by our own power or piety we had made this man walk? By faith in his name (Jesus), this man whom you see and know, his name has strengthened (the named and invoked one himself did it), and the faith which is through him in God has given him this soundness in the presence of you all, Acts 3:12, 16. A creature can no more raise the dead than it can create, for both works depend solely on the nod and will of God and on his command. No creature has a commanding will that calls into being what does not exist. God will either call a thing or not call it. If he calls it, it belongs to God alone that it is so called, and the creature is left with nothing but a will that praises and approves. If he does not call it, the creature will be without God and without his will; and indeed, since God must will that the creature create and raise, what God does not call and does not will will not exist. Therefore he will quicken by his will, in a lordly and governing manner [despotikō kai archēgikō], that is, by an imperative word, by a calling that brings into being what is not. Rightly, therefore, the Jews also say: Three keys have not been given to any messenger: of life, of rain, and of the resurrection of the dead [Hebrew].

units.la: LXVIII. Tametsi S. S. Trinitas communiter resurrectionis causa sit, tamen singulariter Christus ejus causa est. Nam venit hora, in qua omnes, qui in monumentis erunt, audient vocem ejus, Filii, & exibunt, qui bona fecerint ad resurrectionem vitae, &c. Quam vocem tubam Dei & \u03c6\u03c9\u03bd\u1f30\u03c9 \u1f38\u03c1\u03c7\u03b1\u03b3\u03b3\u03ad\u03bb\u03c9\u03bd vocem Archangeli Apostolus, 1. Thess. IV. 16. appellat, quia, sicut vox naturalis dormientem excitat, ita Christi vox mortuos excitabit, & Angelos ad concilium vocabit. Christus de se Joh. V. 29. Ego suscitabo eum in novissimo die, ibid. VI. 54. Ego sum resurrectio & vita, ibid. XI. 25. Christo enim opus hoc non propter omnipotentiam tantum, sed etiam propter meritum tribuitur. Quia enim merito suo hominem totum sibi acquisivit, & fideles omnes ejus, ceu capitis, corporis membra, caro & ossa sunt, & cum ipso, ceu haereditas, uniri debent; iccirco tanquam [Hebrew] vindex sanguinis sui postremus stat super pulverem, Job. XIX. 25. atque sic corpora nostra, ceu peculium & proprietatem suam, ex pulvere vindicat, & in gloriam asserit. Unde posterior Adamus \u03b5\u1f30\u03c2 \u03c0\u03bd\u03b5\u1fe6\u03bc\u03b1 \u03b6\u1ff7\u03bf\u03c0\u03bf\u03b9\u1ff6\u03bd in spiritum vivificantem factus dicitur, 1. Cor. XV. 45. Et Christus \u1f00\u03c0\u03b1\u03c1\u03c7\u1f74 \u03c4\u03c9\u03bd \u03ba\u03b5\u03ba\u03bf\u03b9\u03bc\u03b7\u03bc\u03ad\u03bd\u03c9\u03bd primitiae obdormientium, ibid. v. 20. dicitur, non quod primus resurrexerit, sed quod per mortem, in qua detineri non potuit, jus primogeniti multorum fratrum adeptus est, & in primitiis talibus massa sanctificatur. Resuscitabit vero Christus etiam impios, sed non ut [Hebrew] eorum vindex, verum ut judex, hostes suos de latibulis suis eruturus, & redivivos ad supplicium productu-rus. Estque opus hoc resuscitationis \u1f14\u03c0\u03c0\u03b9\u03b1\u03c3\u03bc\u03b1.
