units.tr: LXVIII. Although the Holy Trinity is in common the cause of the resurrection, Christ alone is its cause in a singular way. For the hour comes in which all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice, the Son's, and shall come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, etc. The Apostle calls this voice the trumpet of God and the voice of the archangel, 1 Thess. 4:16, because just as a natural voice wakes a sleeper, so Christ's voice will raise the dead and summon the angels to the assembly. Christ says of himself: I will raise him up at the last day, John 5:29; I am the resurrection and the life, ibid. 6:54 and 11:25. This work is ascribed to Christ not only on account of omnipotence but also on account of merit. For by his merit he has acquired the whole man for himself, and all the faithful are, as members of his head, the limbs of his body, flesh and bones, and must be united with him as an inheritance. Therefore, as the avenger of his blood [go'el], he shall stand last upon the dust, Job 19:25, and so claims our bodies from the dust, as his own possession and property, and asserts them to glory. Hence the last Adam was made a life-giving spirit [eis pneuma zōopoioun], 1 Cor. 15:45. And Christ is called the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep [aparchē tōn kekoimēmenōn], ibid. v. 20, not because he rose first, but because through death, in which he could not be held, he obtained the right of the firstborn among many brothers, and in such firstfruits the whole lump is sanctified. Christ will raise the impious too, but not as their avenger; he will raise them as judge, to drag his enemies from their hiding places and to bring the revived to punishment. And this work of raising is his epiphany [epiphaneia].

units.la: Singulariter Christus causa resurrectionis omnium & impiorum causa est; sed non sunt discrimine. ἀναστασις Christi totius personæ, secundum utramque naturam conjunctim, non secundum alterutram separatim. Nam & naturæ Christi humanæ opus isthoc convenit, & modus operationis ejus tum merito, tum efficacia constat. Merito, quia sicut alia beneficia, ita etiam resurrectionem ex morte, obedientia & passione sua nobis acquisivit & promeruit. Qui comedit carnem meam, & bibit sanguinem meum, habet vitam æternam, Joh. VI. 54. Efficacia, quia si in statu exinanitionis in hoc opere ministerium humanæ naturæ intervenit, multò magis in statu exaltationis interveniet. Nam & secundum naturam humanam resuscitationem hanc efficaciter volet, juxta verba ejus: Pater, quos mihi dedisti, volo, ut ubi ego sum, etiam mei mecum sint, ibid. XVII. 24. Et descendet de Cœlo, voce sua, tanquam celeusmate mortuos è monumentis suis evocaturus, ibid. V. 28. Matth. XXIV. 31. 1. Thess. IV. 16. adeóque ceu Ecclesiæ & mundi Dominus aëreo in gyro, cœlesti satellitio suffultus & armatus, apparebit, & natura humana est ὁμοούσιον ἐνυπόστατον, per quod in una persona natura Divina resuscitationem illam operabitur; ipsa operante, quod suum est, hoc est, quod humanæ & finitæ potentiæ est: Divina autem natura operante id, quod omnipotentiæ est. Accedit, quòd quà homo, etiam resurrectionis exemplar, primitiæ, & specimen factus est, 1. Cor. XV. 13. &c. Veniet ergo Christi natura humana in partes hujus operis, licèt immensa Deitatis virtute, seu omnipotentia sibi communicata mortuos resuscitatura non sit, neque unquam resuscitare possit.
units.tr: Christ is the singular cause of the resurrection of all, and of the impious too, but not without distinction. Christ's resurrection [anastasis] belongs to the whole person, according to both natures together, not to either nature separately. For this work befits the human nature of Christ, and the manner of his operation is established both by merit and by efficacy. By merit, because just as he acquired other benefits for us, so also he acquired and merited the resurrection from death by his obedience and passion. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, John 6:54. By efficacy, because if in the state of humiliation the human nature had a ministerial part in this work, much more will it take part in the state of exaltation. For according to his human nature also he will effectively will this resurrection, in accordance with his words: Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, ibid. 17:24. And he will descend from heaven with his voice, as with a shout about to call the dead out of their tombs, John 5:28; Matt. 24:31; 1 Thess. 4:16. Thus, as Lord of the Church and of the world, he will appear in an aerial circuit, supported and armed by a heavenly host. The human nature is consubstantial and enhypostatic [homoousion enhypostaton], through which the divine nature will in one person accomplish that resurrection, the human nature acting in what is its own, that is, in what belongs to human and finite power, and the divine nature acting in what belongs to omnipotence. Add that, as man, he has been made also the pattern, the firstfruits and the specimen of the resurrection, 1 Cor. 15:13 etc. Christ's human nature will therefore take a part in this work, although by the immense virtue of the Deity, that is, by the omnipotence communicated to it, it will not itself raise the dead, and could never do so.

units.la: LXIX. Sed occurrunt, qui in resurrectione nihil supra naturam agnoscant, prolato simili naturali grani, quo cum S. Paulus 1. Cor. XV. 36. resurrectionem comparat. Addunt simile ignis, radiis Solis accensi, inque aëra paulatim conversi, posteaque denuo Solis radiis accensi, & in ignem commutati. Sic planè Richardus & ejusdem assecla Scotus in 4. Sent. Dist. 43. q. 3. Cùmque ex resoluti corporis humani pulveribus alia animalia gigni Physici scribant, iidem majorem in iis aptitudinem ad gignendum corpus humanum existere autumant. Denique cùm appetitus animæ utique naturalis sit, & anima reditum ad corpus naturaliter appetat, à natura reditum illum promoveri posse argutantur. Sed levia nimis eorum argumenta sunt. S. Paulus enim non medullam & seminarium interius, seu ἀσπέρμα in cadavere hominis, quale in grano seminato est, principium futurum resurrectionis, latere innuit; sed comparatione à minori ad majus instituta resurrectionem declarat; nempe si natura creata vitam dat rei mortuæ, & exiguum semen ita vegetat, ut magna ex eo moles nascatur; multo facilius esse creatori colligit, resuscitare mortuos. Ingens verò animalcula inter imperfecta, quæ ex putrefactione nascuntur, & animalia perfecta, quorum organa nonnisi ex semine, quod idoneo loco suscipitur, peculiari vi formantur, discrimen est. Quoad appetitum, illud scire oportet, ut aliquid naturaliter fiat, non sufficere, ut illud appeti possit, nisi etiam producti possit. Resurrectio autem naturali potentiæ non subjicitur. Tum & appetitus hic in anima sola, non in pulveribus, obtinet.
units.tr: LXIX. But there are those who acknowledge nothing above nature in the resurrection, and they bring forward the natural comparison of a grain, which St Paul uses when comparing the resurrection, 1 Cor. 15:36. They add the comparison of fire, kindled by the rays of the sun, gradually turned into air, and afterwards kindled again by the sun's rays and changed into fire. So plainly Richard and his follower Scotus, in 4 Sent. dist. 43, q. 3. And since the natural philosophers write that other animals are generated from the dust of a dissolved human body, these men likewise think there is in that dust a greater aptitude for generating a human body. Finally, since the appetite of the soul is surely natural, and the soul naturally seeks a return to the body, they argue that this return can be promoted by nature. But their arguments are far too slight. For St Paul does not hint that some marrow or inner seed, or aspermon [ἀσπέρμα], lies hidden in a human corpse, like the seed in a sown grain, to be the principle of the future resurrection. Rather, by an argument from the lesser to the greater, he sets out the resurrection: if created nature gives life to a dead thing, and so nourishes a tiny seed that a great mass grows from it, then it is much easier, he infers, for the Creator to raise the dead. There is a difference between the vast swarms of tiny creatures that arise from putrefaction, which are imperfect, and perfect animals, whose organs are formed by a peculiar power only from seed received in a suitable place. As to appetite, one must know that for something to come about naturally it is not enough that it can be desired, unless it can also be produced. But resurrection is not subject to natural power. Moreover, this appetite is found in the soul alone, not in the dust.

units.la: Elenchus eorum, qui mortuos naturaliter resurgere statuunt.
units.tr: Refutation of those who hold that the dead rise naturally.

units.la: quidlibet etiam potest; vel intellectus sapientia pollens quidlibet scit; vel desiderans vehementer desiderio ipse suo satisfacere potest. Neque Apostolus similitudine Seminis tritici utens, 1. Cor. XV. 36. tale quid insinuat. Si enim non granum in terram projectum sibi corpus dare potest, sed Deus ipsi dat corpus, ut ipse vult, v. 37. quanto magis id de corpore humano humi condito, & nondum cum anima spiritu suo, unita, dicendum est. Nam in grano manet spiritus, neque semen, qua semen, proprie mortuum dici potest, quia alias nunquam planta inde germinaret; sed νεκρὸν mortuum dicitur, quia sepultum adeoque quasi mortuum est, & ejus appendices quaedam moriuntur, & mutatio seminis in materiam germinis & radicis est quasi corruptio, & ita mors unius, dum inde est alterius generatio. At in corpore humano mortuo non manet spiritus, utpote ab eo separatus, & reversus ad eum, qui eum dedit.
units.tr: anyone can do anything at all; or an intellect strong in wisdom knows anything; or one who desires intensely can satisfy his desire by his own power. Nor does the Apostle, in using the likeness of the grain of wheat, 1 Cor. XV. 36, suggest anything of the kind. For if the grain cast into the earth cannot give itself a body, but God gives it a body as he wills, v. 37, how much more must this be said of the human body laid in the ground, which is not yet joined again to its soul, its spirit. For the spirit remains in the grain, and the seed, as seed, cannot properly be called dead, since otherwise a plant could never sprout from it. Yet it is called νεκρὸν [dead], because it is buried and so is in a sense dead, and certain of its parts die, and the change of the seed into the matter of the shoot and root is a kind of corruption; thus the death of one thing is the generation of another. But in a dead human body no spirit remains, since it has been separated from the body and has returned to him who gave it.

units.la: LXX. Quanquam totus homo resurgit, non tamen κυρίως totum hominis resurgit. Anima enim non resurgit, nisi per accidens: proprie vero & per se resurgit corpus organicum qua tale; seu idem numero corpus, eadem numero caro. Quod ipsa ἀνάστασις vox resurrectionis evincit, quia finitore Damasceno orth. fid. lib. IV. 28. est τῆς πεπωκότος δἰ ἀποκατάστασις ejus quod cecidit iterata statio. Ex hypothesi vero adversantium prima, non iterata statio erit. Unde Aquilejensis Ecclesia in symbolo dicebat: Credo resurrectionem carnis Hujus, teste Rufino in Symbolo. Disertissime Jobus: Novi, quod vindex meus vivat, & postremus super pulverem stabit. Et postquam cutis mea destrinxerint hoc, etiam ex carne mea videbo Deum. Quem ego videbo mihi. Et oculi mei videbunt, & non alius, Job. XIX. 25. 26. Non opus erit, ut stet Christus super pulverem nostrum, si corpus in pulvere latens non resuscitabit: & videbit Goelem suum non Jobi oculus, sed pro ipso alius; nec ex carne sua videbit Deum. Vita enim Christi in corpore nostro, in mortali carne nostra manifestari debet, 2. Cor. IV. 10. 11. Si Spiritus ejus, qui excitavit Jesum ex mortuis in nobis habitat, qui excitavit Christum ex mortuis, vivificabit etiam mortalia corpora nostra per Spiritum suum, qui in nobis habitat, Rom. VIII. 11. Etiam ipsi primitias Spiritus habentes, etiam ipsi, in nobismet ipsis ingemiscimus, adoptionem filiorum expectantes, redemptionem corporis nostri, ibid. v. 23. Oportet φθαρτὸν τοῦτο corruptibile Hoc induat incorruptionem, & mortale Hoc induat immortalitatem, 1. Cor. XV. 53. 54. Corpora enim nostra membra Christi sunt, & templum Spiritus S. & quae habemus a Deo, & quae non sunt nostra. Redempti estis pretio. Glorificate igitur Deum in corpore vestro, & in spiritu vestro, ut quae Dei sunt, ibid. VI. 15. 19. 20. Christus transfigurabit corpus humiliationis nostrum, ut fiat conforme corpori gloriae ejus, Phil. III. 21. Ideo idem corpus quandiu in hac vita est, caro, sanguis, corpus animale, pulvereum, corruptibile, mortale; receptum vero ex morte & in Coelum translatum spirituale, incorruptibile, immortale, coeleste dicitur, 1. Cor. XV. 44. 47. 48. 50. 53. Neque profecto indigna caro nostra est, quae resuscitata & vindicata ex morte coelesti gloria superinduatur. Nam caro nostra aeque ac Spiritus singulari consilio totius S. S. Trinitatis creata est. Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram, Genes. I. 26. Deus enim ipse hominem plasmavit de luto, ibid. II. 7. Si terram & limum despicimus, at cogitandum nobis est, Deum ei admovisse manum, effinxisse in carnem, oblitera-to limo, transmutasse, organis plusquam phrygionico artificio instruxisse, animae, quae Deo proxima est, univisse, conjunctione arctissima, qualis nullas inter creaturas unitas & conjunctio apparet. Cumque nulla anima servetur, nisi quae credidit in carne; & caro in hac vita privilegiis Christianismi fruatur, & una cum anima pugnet & conflictetur, causa reddi non potest, cur non caro aeque atque anima salvetur, coronata privilegiis aeternae vitae atque beatitudinis fruatur. Caro in Baptismo abluitur, ut anima purgetur: ungitur, ut anima consecretur: manuum impositione afficitur, ut benedictio in animam veniat; corpore & sanguine Christi vescitur atque potatur, ut anima spirituali cibo saginetur. Quomodo ergo in mercede separabuntur, quae iunguntur in opere? Nam & sacrificia Deo grata, conflictationes animae, jejunia, feras & aridas escas, similiaque caro de suo instaurat, Rom. XII. 1. & pro fide & testimonio veritatis Evangelii patitur, in carceribus maceratur, terrimo lucis exilio, penuria, squalore, pedore, contumelia, morte subinde atrocissima multatur. Cur hic anima sola coronaretur, & caro eadem, quae id fecit atque passa est, καταβεβλημένη brabeo suo defraudaretur? Praeterea talis caro nostra resurget, qualis caro Christi resurrexit, quia conformari corpori Christi glorioso debet, Phil. III. 21. & Christi resurrectio exemplar nostrae est, 1. Cor. XV. 20. At caro Christi eadem numero resurrexit: quia nec corruptionem videre, Psal. XVI. 10. debuit, & carnem & ossa habuit, Luc. XXIV. 39. & manus ac pedes ostendit Thomae, eum jubens immittere digitum lateri suo, ut vulneris vestigia cognosceret. Accedit, quod caro aeque ac Spiritus judicari debet. Oportet enim omnes manifestari coram tribunali Christi, ut reportet quisque quod in corpore suo fecit, convenienter iis, quae egit, sive bonum, sive malum, 2. Cor. V. 10. Nam πράξεις primo & praecipue sunt animae, deinde & membrorum, nominatim linguae & manus, quin & oculorum, aurium & palati. Sicut igitur eadem numero anima secundum πράξεις actiones suas judicari debet: ita etiam carnem eandem numero juxta actiones etiam suas judicari aequillimum est. Scite Ambrosius de Fide & resurr. Haec, inquit, est series & causa justitiae, ut quoniam corporis & animae communis actus est; quae animus cogitavit, corpus effecit; utrumque in judicium veniat; utrumque aut poenae dedatur, aut gloriae reservetur. Neque vel cogitatione fingi potest aliud hominis mortui τὸ πεπωκός quod cecidit, cujus expectetur resurrectio, quam illud ipsum, quod Graecis σῶμα, Hebraeis גוף Latinis cadaver una a cadendo analogia dicitur. Denique & resurrectio ex morte peccati, quae corpus idem numero spiritualiter mortuum non excludit: & exempla resuscitatorum ex mortuis; & immutatio mutatio eorum, quos superstites Christus adventans reperiet; qui aliud & novum corpus non recipient; & typi resurrectionis supra expositi identitatem corporis resuscitandi manifestè demonstrant.
units.tr: Although the whole man rises, the whole of man does not rise κυρίως [properly]. For the soul does not rise except accidentally. Properly and in itself, the organic body rises as such, that is, the same body in number, the same flesh in number. The very word ἀνάστασις [resurrection] proves this, since, as Damascene says in his Orthodox Faith IV. 28, it is τῆς πεπωκότος δἰ ἀποκατάστασις ejus quod cecidit iterata statio [the restoring of what has fallen, a second standing]. But on the hypothesis of our opponents, the first standing will not be a second one. Hence the Church of Aquileia in its creed used to say, I believe the resurrection of this flesh, as Rufinus witnesses in his commentary on the Creed. Job speaks most clearly: I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth. And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God; whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another, Job XIX. 25, 26. There would be no need for Christ to stand upon our dust if the body lying hidden in the dust were not to be raised; and Job's eyes will see his Redeemer, not another in his place, and he will not see God from without his flesh. For the life of Christ must be made manifest in our body, in our mortal flesh, 2 Cor. IV. 10, 11. If the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you, Rom. VIII. 11. Even we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, the redemption of our body, ibid. v. 23. This corruptible must put on incorruption [φθαρτὸν τοῦτο], and this mortal must put on immortality, 1 Cor. XV. 53, 54. For your bodies are the members of Christ, and the temple of the Holy Spirit, which you have from God, and you are not your own. You are bought with a price. Glorify God therefore in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's, ibid. VI. 15, 19, 20. Christ shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, Phil. III. 21. Therefore the same body, as long as it is in this life, is called flesh, blood, animal body, dusty, corruptible, mortal; but once it is taken up out of death and carried into heaven, it is called spiritual, incorruptible, immortal, heavenly, 1 Cor. XV. 44, 47, 48, 50, 53. Nor is our flesh indeed unworthy, since, once raised and rescued from death, it is clothed with heavenly glory. For our flesh, no less than the spirit, was created by the singular counsel of the whole Holy Trinity. Let us make man in our image and likeness, Gen. I. 26. For God himself formed man of dust, ibid. II. 7. If we look down on earth and clay, we must consider that God laid his hand upon it, shaped it into flesh, changed the clay that had been mixed in, furnished the organs with more than Phrygian craftsmanship, and united it to the soul, which is nearest to God, in a most close conjunction, such as no union or conjunction among creatures appears to be. And since no soul is saved except one that believed in the flesh, and since the flesh in this life enjoys the privileges of Christianity and fights and struggles together with the soul, no reason can be given why the flesh should not also be saved, crowned with the privileges of eternal life and blessedness. In Baptism the flesh is washed so that the soul may be cleansed; it is anointed so that the soul may be consecrated; it is subjected to the laying on of hands so that the blessing may come to the soul; it eats and drinks the body and blood of Christ so that the soul may be fed with spiritual food. How then will they be separated in reward when they are joined in the work? For the flesh too offers sacrifices pleasing to God, the struggles of the soul, fasts, dry and rough food and the like, Rom. XII. 1; and for the faith and testimony of the truth of the Gospel it suffers, is worn down in prisons, is punished with the most dreadful exile from the light, with want, squalor, filth, reproach, and often with the most atrocious death. Why then should the soul alone be crowned, and the same flesh, which did and suffered these things, be defrauded of its καταβεβλημένη brabeo suo [prize]? Moreover, our flesh will rise as the flesh of Christ rose, since it must be conformed to the glorious body of Christ, Phil. III. 21, and Christ's resurrection is the pattern of ours, 1 Cor. XV. 20. But the flesh of Christ rose the same in number: for it ought not to see corruption, Ps. XVI. 10, and it had flesh and bones, Luke XXIV. 39, and it showed his hands and feet to Thomas, bidding him put his finger into his side, so that he might recognise the traces of the wound. Add to this that the flesh, no less than the spirit, must be judged. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad, 2 Cor. V. 10. For πράξεις [deeds] belong first and chiefly to the soul, and then also to the members, especially the tongue and hand, and indeed the eyes, ears and palate. Just as the soul, the same in number, must be judged according to its πράξεις [actions], so it is most just that the flesh, the same in number, should also be judged according to its actions. Ambrose says well in his book on the Faith and the Resurrection: This is the order and the ground of justice, that since the act is common to body and soul, what the mind has thought the body has carried out; both must come to judgment, and both must be given over to punishment or kept for glory. Nor can we imagine, even in thought, any other τὸ πεπωκός [fallen thing] of the dead man, whose resurrection is to be awaited, than that very thing which the Greeks call σῶμα [body], the Hebrews גוף [guf], and the Latins cadaver, by analogy with falling [cadere]. Finally, the resurrection from the death of sin, which does not exclude the body, the same in number, that is spiritually dead; the examples of those raised from the dead; and the change of those whom Christ will find alive at his coming, who will not receive another and new body, and the types of the resurrection set out above, all clearly demonstrate the identity of the body that is to be raised.

units.la: LXXI. Cùm tamen quatuor fere sint, quæ ὁλοκληρίαν, seu integritatem hominis constituunt; puta corpus & anima: ea, quæ ad naturam hominis constituendam sic referuntur, ut tamen simpliciter necessaria non sint, vel oculus, manus, pes & similia membra, quæ præter essentiam hominis certam quantitatem & figuram denotant: spiritus & humores, absque quibus secundum consuetum naturæ ordinem corpus non subsisteret: denique quæ ad ornatum pertinent, capilli, formæ venustas, & similia τυχόντα, dubitari non potest, quin singula hæc resuscitatis piis & impiis constitura sint. Utrique enim corpore & anima constabunt. Membra organica omnia ne exceptis quidem illis, quibus heic caruerunt, piis restituentur. Cùm enim beati non desinant esse homines, integritatem illam concupiscent; neque in cupiditate illa ἀπαξία fit; atque gloria naturam non mutilet, sed perficiat, piè credi potest, Deum in παλιγγενεσία ista non minùs benignè cum filiis suis acturum, quàm in πεω-ποκλησία egit; ac proin quicquid in hac accepit, in illa recuperaturum. Non enim in altera vita ζημία damnum ullum, sed κέρδ lucrum obtinebit. Alia forte impiorum ratio est, qui recipient membra, quæ cadentes habuerunt, at non ea, quibus caruerunt, ad augendam eorum miseriam & ignominiam. Cùmque organorum corporis duplex sit σχέσις, seu relatio; prior materiæ ad formam, secundum quam finis membri non ejus operatio, sed speciei perfectio est; posterior organi ad principium activum, secundum quam finis membri est operatio, qua tamen deficiente non frustra est organon; quia agens organis instruitur non ad exequendam tantùm potentiam; priore respectu organa necessaria, posteriore non supervacanea erunt. Æquum etiam est, ut quibus quis membris in hac vita bene vel malè usus est, eadem præmium vel pœnam in altera reportent. Etiam juxta illud Tertulliani de Resurr. c. 60. carina, prora & puppis, omnisque propago pristina necessaria est navis salvi, licet vacatura. Sed & spiritus atque humores naturæ corporis necessarii neutris deerunt. Alia humorum supervacaneorum & excrementitiorum ratio erit, eorum inprimis, quæ generationi & nutritioni inserviunt, uti lac & semen sunt. Denique & ornamenta corporis non deerunt corporibus piorum: at deerunt corporibus impiorum. Quoad deformitates verò impiorum, quibus in hac vita corpora eorum laborarunt, præstat cum Augustino ἐπι-χεῖν, quia, uti Enchirid. cap. 92. loquitur, incerta habitudo eorum, quorum certa & sempiterna damnatio erit, nos fatigare non debet. Forte pili & ungues corpori gloriosò restituentur, non obstante fœditate originis, quæ si spectatur, pari jure etiam corporis ipsius resurrectio in dubium vocabitur. Et quid de statura resuscitatorum etiam infantum sentiendum sit, πεωτοκλησίας analogia ostendere potest. Nam quod infantibus tardius in tempore ac-
units.tr: LXXI. Although there are about four things that make up the ὁλοκληρίαν [wholeness], or integrity, of man, namely body and soul; those things which relate to the constitution of human nature in such a way that they are yet not simply necessary, such as the eye, hand, foot and similar limbs, which besides the essence of man denote a certain quantity and shape; the spirits and humours, without which the body would not subsist according to the customary order of nature; and finally those things which pertain to adornment, hair, beauty of form and the like τυχόντα [chance additions]: there can be no doubt that each of these will belong to the raised, both pious and impious. For both will consist of body and soul. All organic members, not excepting even those which they lacked here, will be restored to the pious. For since the blessed do not cease to be men, they will desire that wholeness; nor does that desire come to nothing ἀπαξία [in vain]; and since glory does not maim nature but perfects it, it may be piously believed that God in this παλιγγενεσία [regeneration] will deal no less kindly with his sons than he dealt in the first creation [πρωτοκλησία]; and therefore he will restore in that life whatever they received in this one. For in the next life no ζημία [loss] will be incurred, but κέρδος [gain]. The case of the impious is perhaps different: they will receive the members which they had when they fell, but not those which they lacked, so that their misery and shame may be increased. And since the organs of the body have a twofold σχέσις [relation], or relationship: the first of matter to form, according to which the end of a member is not its operation but the perfection of the species; the second of the organ to the active principle, according to which the end of a member is its operation, yet an organ is not in vain even if the operation fails, because the agent is equipped with organs not only for exercising its power: with respect to the first, the organs will be necessary; with respect to the second, they will not be superfluous. It is also fair that whatever members a man has used well or badly in this life should bring him reward or punishment for them in the next. This too agrees with the saying of Tertullian, On the Resurrection, chapter 60: The keel, the prow and the stern, and all the original fittings, are necessary for the saved ship, even though they will be idle. Moreover the spirits and humours necessary to the nature of the body will be lacking to neither. Superfluous and excrementitious humours will have a different account, especially those which serve generation and nourishment, such as milk and seed. Finally, the ornamenta [ornaments] of the body will not be lacking to the bodies of the pious, but they will be lacking to the bodies of the impious. As for the deformities of the impious, with which their bodies were afflicted in this life, it is better to suspend judgment ἐπιχεῖν [to withhold assent], with Augustine, because, as he says in the Enchiridion, chapter 92, the uncertain condition of those whose damnation is certain and everlasting ought not to trouble us. Perhaps hair and nails will be restored to the glorified body, notwithstanding the foulness of their origin, which, if one looks at it, would equally cast doubt on the resurrection of the body itself. And what should be thought of the stature of the raised, even of infants, the analogy of the πρωτοκλησία [first creation] can show. For what infants would have come to only later in time,

units.la: cessurum erat, hoc celerrimo & miro Dei opere recipient facilè. Interea verum putamus illud Augustini de Civit. Dei lib. XXII. 20. Nihil obeerit, etiamsi erit infantilis vel senilis corporis forma; ubi nec mentis, nec ipsius corporis ulla infirmitas manebit. Unde etiamsi quis in eodem corporis modo, in quo defunctus est, resurrecturum unumquemque contendit, non est cum illo laboriosa contradictione pugnandum. Et si idem numero corpus resurget, etiam affectiones ejus, non derogantes gloriæ, remanebunt, in quibus præcipuè sexus est. Erit, uti Julianus Toletanus Προγνως. lib. II. 24. verbis præceptoris sui Eugenii laudatis sapienter loquitur: tanta ac talis (fœminei) pulchritudo, ut oblectet intuitum, & cor nullatenus inflectat ad vitium. Nec illud obstat, quòd fœmineus sexus virili vilior habetur, quia vilitas illa ratione subjectionis, non sexus censetur. Et Christus negans fore, ut in resurrectione uxores ducant, vel nuptum dentur, Matth. XXII. 30. non affectionem ipsam, sed sexus usum sustulit.
units.tr: will receive it easily by God's swift and wonderful work. Meanwhile we hold to be true that saying of Augustine, De Civitate Dei XXII.20: "Nothing will be harmed, even if the form of the body is that of infancy or old age, where no weakness of mind or of the body itself will remain. Hence even if someone contends that each one will rise in the same bodily state in which he died, we need not contend with him in laborious argument." And if the same body rises in number, its affections also will remain, not detracting from its glory, and chief among these is sex. It will be, as Julian of Toledo wisely says in his Prognosticon II.24, using the words of his teacher Eugenius, which he praises: such and so great a beauty of the female sex, that it delights the eye and in no way turns the heart to vice. Nor does it count against this that the female sex is held to be inferior to the male, since that inferiority is reckoned by reason of subjection, not of sex. And Christ, in denying that in the resurrection men will take wives or women be given in marriage, Matt. 22:30, removed the use of sex, not the affection itself.

units.la: LXXII. Neque omnis moles seu materia ejusdem carnis, neque nulla resurget. Non omnis, quia materia corporis antea, quàm moritur, & seminatur, in perpetua ῥεῦσι fluxu est: & sicut, uti Heraclitus dixit, non licet bis in eundem fluvium descendere; ita non licet bis eundem hominem tangere, vel videre. Materia vetus avolat, & in auras evanescit; & ex aëre, potu & cibis concoctis nova quotidie accedit & oritur, mox iterum avolatura. Dum enim spiritus ignei continuò in materiam agunt, & fomitem suum dissipant, vel vorant, materia corporea parum sibi constare potest. Et qui in juventute in hac materia corporea peccavit, non tantùm in senectute, sed forte paucos intra annos, ne dicam mensès, exiguam ejusdem materiæ sanguineæ, vel carneæ partem retinet. Non nulla, quia aliàs non resurgeret corpus, cujus vocem cum voce carnis Apostolus 1. Cor. XV. 39. 40. alternat, & sicut in semine, quo cum S. Paulus corpus comparat, 1. Cor. XV. 36. &c. aliquid est ejus, quod satum est; ita etiam in corpore nostro aliquid ejus, quod vivens habuit, & mortuum habet, remanet. Alioquin dicendum esset de superstitibus, etiam eorum corpus penitus abolitum iri, & eos aliud corpus accepturos. Apostolus enim dicens: Quod seminas non corpus, quod renascetur, seminas, sed nudum granum, ut contigerit, tritici, ibid. v. 37. hoc unum innuit, corpus, quod seminatur, non vivificari sine mutatione. Omnes quidem non moriemur, sed omnes ἀλλαγησόμεθα mutabimur, ibid. v. 51. Sed non omnis mutatio substantiæ, vel integritatis substantiæ, mutatio est. Quomodo nec semen in terram projectum, quoad substantiam integram, mutatur. Nam κόκκος granum cadit in terram, & quidem aridum, sed non tale, vel tantum renascitur, verùm σπάχυς spica, vel etiam plures spicæ plenis aristis nascuntur. Deus enim dat corpus, ut ipse vult, v. 38. quia ex uno grano alias centum, alias quinquaginta, alias triginta grana nascuntur; & dat unicuique proprium, ibid. nempe לזרעו secundum speciem suam. Ita resurgere idem multiplicatum videtur, quia aliquid habet ex eo quod cecidit. Est enim זרע מזריע semen sementans, seu semen faciens, uuuu Genef.
units.tr: LXXII. Neither will every mass or matter of this same flesh rise, nor will none of it rise. Not every, because the bodily matter, before a man dies and is sown, is in constant flux [ῥεῦσις]; and just as Heraclitus said, one may not step twice into the same river, so one may not touch or see the same man twice. The old matter flies away and vanishes into the air, and new matter daily comes in and arises from air, drink and digested food, soon to fly away again. For while the fiery spirits constantly act upon the matter and dissipate or consume its fuel, bodily matter can hardly keep itself constant. And one who in youth has sinned in this bodily matter, retains not only in old age but perhaps within a few years, not to say months, only a small part of the same blood or flesh. Not some, because otherwise the body would not rise, whose voice the Apostle, 1 Cor. 15:39–40, sets alongside the voice of flesh; and just as in the seed, to which Paul compares the body, 1 Cor. 15:36 etc., something of what was sown remains, so also in our body something of what it had while living and has in death remains. Otherwise we would have to say of those who are still alive that their body will be utterly abolished and that they will receive another body. For the Apostle, saying: You sow not the body that shall be, but bare grain, as it may chance, of wheat, ibid. v. 37, means only this: the body that is sown is not made alive without change. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed [ἀλλαγησόμεθα], ibid. v. 51. But not every change is a change of substance, or of the integrity of the substance. Just as the seed thrown into the earth is not changed as to its whole substance. For the grain [κόκκος] falls into the earth, indeed dry, but it does not rise again as such, or only as such; rather a spike [σπάχυς] is born, or even several ears with full awns. For God gives it a body as he pleases, v. 38, since from one grain there arise sometimes a hundred, sometimes fifty, sometimes thirty grains; and to each seed its own body, ibid., namely according to its kind [לזרעו]. So it seems that what rises is the same thing, multiplied, because it has something of what fell. For it is a seed that sows seed [זרע מזריע], that is, a seed-producing seed, Gen. uuuu

units.la: Genef. uuuu
units.tr: Gen. uuuu

units.la: Genef. I. 11. 12. Mutationem verò illam corporis resuscitandi Apostolus vers. 42. &c. perspicuè sic explicat, ut ad abolitionem materiæ, seu substantiæ integræ nullo modo referri possit. Non ergo Apostolus in corpore resuscitato vel identitatem speciei, vel numericam materiæ, quia neutra Apostoli scopum ferit, sed vel solam materiæ integritatem, vel accidentium identitatem negat. Quænam tamen, qualis & quanta materiæ ejusdem pars, quam corpus hominis inde à conceptione ejus usque ad mortem habuit, resurrectura sit, difficultas forte homini ἀνλ/Θ-, & à solo Deo explicabilis est. Nugantur enim, qui partes spermaticas, velut à sanguineis distinctas corporis stamina durantia, non mutata, ideóque resurrectura, statuunt. Nam etiam nervi, omnes venarum & arteriarum tunicæ, ligamenta, membranæ, fibræ, cartilagines inter partes spermaticas numerantur, quæ tamen augmentum recipiunt, & nutritione indigent. Neque etiam consentaneum rationi est, ut solæ materiæ corporeæ particulæ, quæ morienti adsunt, resuscitatæ vel præmio mactentur, vel pœnas dent, cæteris, quæ avolarunt, & quibuscum optima & pessima vitæ negotia transacta sunt, omnibus insuper habitis. Haud saniores puto, qui animam sensitivam animæ rationali conjunctam superstitem manere, & animam vegetativam, ceu purum putum ignem cadaveribus, quin & ipsi pulveri atque ossibus adhærentem, durare perpetim, adeóque in resurrectione corporeæ moli restitui arbitrantur. Cúm enim sensus & vegetatio omnis corporis vita sit, quemadmodum viventibus illis, & corpori inhærentibus corpus mortuum dici possit, parum liquet. Verissimiliora loquuntur, quibus videtur, spiritus illos igneos, quibus corpus animatur, & cum quibus anima à juventute ad mortem usque bene vel male se gessit, quoad substantiam feré solos, licet aliquando magis, aliquando minùs suscitatos; manere, & fomitem quidem materialem ab igne illo absumi, & dissipari, ignem verò ipsum non dissolvi, nec consumi, sed suo tamen loco, à Deo creatore ei destinato, ad tempus usque resurrectionis, quiescere, & primò resuscitatum iri. Quid verò, quantum & quale materiæ passivæ terrestris, aquææ & aereæ præterea resurrecturum, & gloria cœlesti donandum, vel in inferno puniendum sit, nemini mortalium constat. Deus novit. Et satis est, quòd is, ceu bonus & justus, nec præmia nec pœnas nisi corpori bonum vel malum facienti repræsentaturus, nec corpus, quod vel quatenus ἀγαθὸν ἢ κακὸν ἐπεργάξε bonum vel malum fecit, 2. Cor. V. 10. in morte relicturus; & vel præmio defraudaturus, vel impunitate donaturus sit. Non injustus Deus est, ut oblivisca- tur operis vestri, & laboris charitatis vestræ, Heb. VI. 10. Justum apud Deum est, reddere afflictionem affligentibus vos, & vobis afflictis relaxationem, 2. Thess. I. 6. 7.
units.tr: Gen. 1:11, 12. The Apostle, at v. 42 etc., explains that change of the body in the resurrection so plainly that it cannot in any way refer to the abolition of the matter or of the whole substance. The Apostle therefore denies in the raised body either identity of species or numerical identity of the matter, since neither reaches the Apostle's aim; he denies only the integrity of the matter, or the identity of the accidents. What precise, what kind and how much of this same matter, which the body of a man had from his conception to his death, will rise, is perhaps a difficulty beyond man and explicable by God alone. Those are trifling who hold that the seminal parts, as distinct from the blood, are the enduring framework of the body, unchanged and therefore destined to rise. For the nerves, all the coats of the veins and arteries, the ligaments, membranes, fibres and cartilages are also counted among the seminal parts, and yet these receive growth and need nourishment. Nor is it consistent with reason that only those particles of bodily matter which are present at death should be raised and either be rewarded or pay penalties, while all the others which have flown away, and with which the best and worst deeds of life were done, are passed over entirely. I think no saner are those who hold that the sensitive soul, joined to the rational soul, remains surviving, and that the vegetative soul, like pure fire, clings to corpses, even to the dust and bones themselves, and endures forever, and so is restored to the bodily mass at the resurrection. For since sense and all vegetation is the life of the body, it is scarcely clear how a dead body could be said to be in such living things, cleaving to the body. More probable are those who think that those fiery spirits by which the body is animated, and with which the soul has behaved well or ill from youth to death, remain, substantially almost alone, though sometimes raised more and sometimes less; that the material fuel is consumed and dissipated by that fire, but the fire itself is not dissolved or consumed, but rests in its own place, assigned to it by God the Creator, until the time of the resurrection, and is first raised again. But what, how much and of what kind of passive matter, earthly, watery and airy, will rise besides, and be granted heavenly glory or be punished in hell, is known to no mortal. God knows. And it is enough that he, as good and just, will bring forward neither rewards nor punishments except for the body, as it has done good or evil, and will not leave behind in death the body which has done good or evil [ἐπεργάσατο], 2 Cor. 5:10; and he will either defraud it of reward or grant it impunity. God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the labour of your love, Heb. 6:10. It is just with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you, and relief to you who are afflicted, 2 Thess. 1:6–7.

units.la: LXXIII. Pie Concilium Toletanum A. DCLXXV. celebratum can. 7. sanxit: Exemplo capitis nostri confitemur vera fide resurrectionem carnis, omnium mortuorum: nec in aere, vel qualibet alia carne, ut quidam delirant, resurrecturos nos credimus, sed in ISTA, qua vivimus, consistimus & movemur. Per delirantes intelligit Origenistas, qui Origene, cui errorem hunc Epi-
units.tr: LXXIII. The Council of Toledo, celebrated in the year A.D. DCLXXV, piously decreed in canon 7: Following the example of our Head, we confess with true faith the resurrection of the flesh of all the dead. Nor do we believe that we shall rise in air, or in any other flesh, as some rave, but in THIS flesh in which we live, stand and move. By those who rave it means the Origenists, who impute this error to Origen, which Epiphanius, Methodius and Nicetas Choniates [attack], and which Jerome, sharply censuring it in his letter to Pammachius, vigorously refutes; for the authors of it taught that the body to rise would not be fleshly but aerial or some other body finer than wind, and they dismissed those who disagreed as if they were philosophizing.

units.la: phanius, Methodius, Nicetas Choniates impingunt, & quem in eodem graviter perstringens Hieronymus Epist. ad Pammach. acriter refellit; authore, non carneum, sed aereum, aliudve corpus vento subtilius resurrecturum tradiderunt, & dissentientes ceu φιλοσόφως traduxerunt. Origenistarum errorem pœne ad mortem usque secutus est Eutychius, Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus, Romanæ Ecclesiæ Diaconus apocrisiarius, uti Gregorius, qui cum eo hac de re disputavit Moral. lib. XIV. 29. testis est. Eodem errore infectus fuit Stephanus Tritheita, cognomento Gobarus, uti Photius in Bibliotheca sua testatur; nec non Johannes Hierosolymitanus Hieronymo Epist. ad Pammach. teste. Secuti errorem Sociniani sunt; uti ex Ostorodi & Vaidovii Compend. doctr. cap. 8. liquet. Negant, inquiunt illi, Socinianî resurrectionem carnis, hoc est, hujus ipsius corporis, quod carne & sanguine præditum est. Nam corpus quidem illos habituros, at non carnem nugantur, secuti in eo Origenem, quem fusè Hieronymus Epist. cit. refutavit, urgens inprimis illa Jobi, sperantis, ex carne sua suisque ipsius oculis Deum visurum, Job. XIX. 26. Paulus σὰρξ καὶ σῶμα pro eodem sumens, 1. Cor. XV. 39. imò vitam Jesu ἐν σωμᾷ σαρκὶ ἡμῶν in mortua carne nostra manifestari debere, 2. Cor. IV. 11. asserit. Quos secuti Anabaptistæ induci non possunt, ut credant, mortuos cum suis manibus, pedibus, pelle, carne & ossibus resurrecturos esse. Et quàm facilè hic error incautis surrepat, argumento est ipse summi ingenii Vir, Calvinus, cui hic aqua aliquando hæsit; Sed ut dies diem docet, sive argumentis Farelli Epistola ad eum hac de re data compulsus, sive aliunde veritatem persuasus, prodigiosum hunc errorem, sic ipse appellat, Institit. lib. III. 25: 7. solidè refutavit; fassus etiam, nullius doctrinæ clariorem vel certiorem probationem desiderari posse. Neque à sententia hac Scholastici illi abluderre videntur, qui identitatem formæ ad ejusdem individui resurrectionem sufficere docent, ut licet diversum corpus sit, tamen propter eandem animam unus numero homo dicatur.
units.tr: Eutychius, Patriarch of Constantinople, who was apocrisiary deacon of the Roman Church, followed the error of the Origenists almost to his death, as Gregory attests, who disputed with him on this matter, Moralia XIV.29. Stephen the Tritheite, surnamed Gobarus, was infected with the same error, as Photius testifies in his Bibliotheca; and so was John of Jerusalem, as Jerome attests in his letter to Pammachius. The Socinians followed the error, as is clear from the Compendium of Doctrine of Ostorod and Vaidovius, chapter 8. The Socinians deny, they say, the resurrection of the flesh, that is, of this very body which is endowed with flesh and blood. For they babble that they will have a body indeed, but not flesh, following Origen in this, whom Jerome refuted at length in the letter cited, pressing especially those words of Job, hoping that in his flesh he would see God with his own eyes, Job 19:26. Paul, taking flesh and body [σὰρξ καὶ σῶμα] as the same thing, 1 Cor. 15:39, asserts that the life of Jesus ought to be made manifest in our mortal flesh [ἐν τῇ θνητῇ σαρκὶ ἡμῶν], 2 Cor. 4:11. The Anabaptists, followers of these, cannot be induced to believe that the dead will rise with their own hands, feet, skin, flesh and bones. And how easily this error creeps upon the unwary is shown by that man of the highest genius, Calvin, who at one time was himself stuck here; but as day teaches day, whether compelled by the arguments of Farel's letter written to him on this matter, or persuaded of the truth from elsewhere, he solidly refuted this monstrous error, as he himself calls it, Institutes III.25.7, confessing also that no doctrine could require a clearer or surer proof. Nor do those Scholastics seem to differ from this view, who teach that identity of form suffices for the resurrection of the same individual, so that although the body is different, one man in number is still said to be the same because of the same soul.

units.la: LXXIV. Infirma horum omnium pro capitali errore argumenta sunt. Nam resuscitatos ἰσαγγέλως Angelis similes futuros Christus, Matth. XXII. 30. Luc. XX. 36. dixit non in omnibus, sed in iis, quæ expressit, quòd ἔτε γαμίσιν, ἔτε ἐκγαμίσκονται, neque nubunt, neque nuptum dantur, ἔτε ἀποθνῄσκειν δύνανται, neque amplius mori possunt. Assimilatio igitur intelligitur non in novo corpore cœlesti, quale nec vetus, nec novum Angeli habent, qui etiam non sunt υἱοὶ ἀναστάσεως filii resurrectionis, sed in eo, quòd nec nubent, nec nuptum dabuntur, & immortales erunt, & υἱοὶ ἀναστάσεως resurrectionis filii, participes, consortes (usitato Hebraismo) erunt, filii Dei, sicut Angeli sunt, perfecta sanctitate, justitia, immortalitate præditi. Et caro & sanguis Regnum Dei non possunt hæreditare, 1. Cor. XV. 50. non simpliciter, quia reclamant argumenta supra allata; sed quatenus caro & sanguis est ψυχικὸς animalis, statum suum animalem habet, cibo atque potu in hac vita sustentatur, fluxum suum habet, & indies mutatur, tandemque corrumpitur. Ipse enim S. Paulus se explicat subjiciens: Corruptio non hæredi- Historia resurrectionem carnis ejusdem numero negantium. Eorundem argumenta ad partes vocata. hæreditabit incorruptibilitatem. Caro nempe in hac vita est à sanguine, sanguis à cibo & potu, & in sanguine est illa ψυχὴ anima à qua corpus ψυχικὸν animale appellatur. Alia enim est ψυχὴ anima à qua corpus animale; alia, à qua homo ψυχικὸς animalis, 1.Cor. II.14. Jud. v.19. appellatur. In Regno autem Dei corpus, caro & sanguis ejusmodi animalis non obtinebit, quia ad substantiam corporis sustentandam,& ψυχὴν animam, quæ nos ita tenuiter vivificat, restituendam & reparandam, atque ita vitam conservandam non indigebimus cibo & potu, sed Deus erit omnia in omnibus, 1. Cor. XV.28. si alterius causæ vitæ, sive alterius rei vivificantis indigeremus. Eodem etiam sensu corpora nostra non ψυχικὰ animalia, sed πνευματικὰ spiritualia erunt, ibid. v. 44. Non enim corpus nostrum substantiam spiritualem habebit, quia hoc contradictionem involveret, sed quia habebit πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν spiritum vivificantem, ibid. v. 45. Nam si Spiritus ejus, qui Jesum ex mortuis resuscitavit, in vobis habitat, qui Christum ex mortuis suscitavit, vivificabit etiam mortua corpora vestra, διὰ τὸ ἐνοικοῦν ... ἐν ὑμῖν, per Spiritum ejus in vobis habitantem, Rom. VIII.11. Sicut enim corpus animale non illud est, quod mera anima est, sed quod solam animam vegetabilem vivendi principium vel causam habet; uti nec homo ψυχικὸς animalis, 1. Cor. II.14. is homo est, qui nil nisi anima est, sed qui ad sapiendum non Spiritu Dei, sed sola anima rationali regitur: ita corpus spirituale non illud est, quod est spiritus, aut per modum spiritus existit, sed quod à Spiritu Dei vivificatur, & vivificatum ab eodem solo, seu à Deo, qui omnia in omnibus est, sustentatur & conservatur. Non ergo corpus spirituale erit corpus tenue instar aëris, venti, vel spiritus Chymicorum. Tale enim erit corpus nostrum, quale Christi est, quod conspicabile est, utpote visum à S. Paulo, & videndum ab oculis eorum, qui eum confixerunt, imò à πᾶντι ὀφθαλμῷ omni oculo, Apoc. I. 7. Et fuit primus homo εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν in animam viventem, animal vivens, seu corpus ψυχικὸν animam habens, quæ in sanguine est, & vegetabilis dicitur, in quam hominis spiritus non æquè ut in motum organorum potestatem habet: at postremus Adam, Christus, factus est εἰς πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν in spiritum vivificantem, 1. Cor. XV. 45. hoc est, persona spiritualis, Divina, causa omnis vitæ, qui ceu verus Deus operatus est in carne propria, 1. Petr. III. 18. & operatur, & operabitur in suis, vivificando. Sicut enim Christus non aliud corpus nunc habet, quam quod resuscitavit, & nunc etiam vivificat, & in quo Deo Patri ἐμφανίζεται apparet: ita nos non alia corpora habebimus, mutata solum quoad πιστωτα qualitatem, juxta verba Pauli: Dicet quis; quomodo resuscitantur mortui? Ποίῳ δὲ σώματι ἔρχονται quali autem in corpore veniunt? 1.Corinth. XV. 35. Neque proin etiam Christus est spiritus ζωοποιῶν, hoc est, spiritualis substantia, quæ non vitam efficit in se vel aliis, sed vitam suam tuetur & conservat: quomodo ζωογονῶν & ζωοποιῶν, חיה & חיה notet etiam in vita esse permittere, uti Socinani pervertunt, quia Apostolus non dicit ἑαυτὸν ζωοποιῶν seipsum vivere faciens, & ζῆν & ζωοποιῶν v. 45. diserte opponit, & quia Christus est spiritus vivificans, ideo & nos corpora spiritualia habebimus; sed non nos ipsi πνεῦματα ζωοποιοῦντα spiritus vivificantes sumus; & qui ab alio vivificatur, non vivificat seipsum; denique nunquam חיה & חיה vivificare seipsum significat; uti etiam nullum exemplum proferri potest nominis aut participii compositi, per mixtionem thematis intransitivi cum verbo πoιέω facio, quod significationem intransitivam habeat. Talis ergo Adami primi & secundi oppositio est, quod ille fuerit ψυχὴ ἄνθρωπος, creatus & factus à Deo anima, hoc est, animal in carne vivens; qui proin, quando fœdere spirituali cum Deo excidit, posteros tantum vitæ animalis ex ipso hæredes habuit: hic vero, quamvis caro factus in similitudine carnis nostræ peccato obnoxiæ, tamen idem verus, vivens & vivificans Deus est. Nam πνεῦμα ζωοποιῶν Spiritus vivificans solius veri & viventis Dei indigetamentum est. Præterea S. Paulus corpus mortuum contendit cum grano, quod seminatur, & granum, quod seminatur, non esse ζῶμα τὸ γινόμενον corpus illud, quod renascitur; quia Deus ipsi dat corpus, ut ipse vult, 1. Corinth. cap. XV. v. 37. 38. dicit; non quod aliud substantia corpus resurrecturum sit, quam quod cecidit, sed quia corpus quod cecidit, debet μεταχηματίζεσθαι transfigurari, ex humili in gloriosum commutari, Rom. VIII. 11. Phil. III.21. Nam & ipse Christus se moriturum & terræ mandandum comparavit cum grano tritici, quod in terram cadens nisi mortuum solum manet; at mortuum fructum multum fert, Joh. XII.24. qui tamen resurrexit in eodem corpore, in quo mortuus est; Templum quippe resuscitans illud ipsum, quod solutum erat; ibid. II.19. & quod carnem & ossa habuit, Luc. XXIV. 39. Neque planè granum tritici in terram projectum substantiam suam amittit, sed mutatam licet quoad qualitates retinet, & in eadem, sed per potentiam Dei mirè aucta resurgit. Dat enim Deus corpus, ut ipse vult, non substantiam abolendo, sed augendo. Spiritus enim grani ex eadem materia suppeditatione humoris aucta, quæ seminata est, accipit corpus, quale Deus vult. Ac licet Apostolus dicat: Cibi ventri, & venter cibis; sed Deus hunc & illos abolebit, 1. Cor. VI. 13. tamen non ventrem etiam quoad substantiam abolendum innuit, sed quoad solum usum, qui est recipere cibos. Nam & cibi ad hoc facti sunt, ut recipiantur à ventre, & in succum & sanguinem hominis convertantur: & venter ad hoc factus est, ut in hac vita cibos recipiat. Cibi enim & ventris mutua relatio, sed temporaria, est, qua cessante ventris substantia, non ilico cessabit, sed manebit, ut præmio vel pœna afficiatur, & corpori sua perfectio & integritas constet. In ipsa enim etiam vita hac animali contingere quandoque in singularibus potest, ut partis alicujus usus partis illius proprius & characteristicus cessetet, & nunquam exerceatur; cujus tamen partis abolitionem corporis universi perfectio & integritas abhorret. Abdicatis igitur usibus partium, qui ad vitam hanc animalem pertinent, eædem partes vitæ spirituali & cœlesti dedicabuntur; ut in iis Deus laudetur; Omne genu se in nomine Jesu Jesu flectat, & omnis lingua Deum confiteatur, Phil. II. 9. 10. Distinguit enim S. Paulus ipse inter corpus, prout illud Domino, vel cibis destinatum est, dicens: Venter escis, corpus vero non fornicationi, sed domino, & dominus corpori. Deus autem & Dominum resuscitavit, & vos resuscitabit, 1. Cor. VI. 13. 14. Antithesis porro illa inter tabernaculum terrestre & domicilium coeleste, 2. Cor. V. 1. non corporis abolitionem, sed ex tabernaculo carnis terrestri in domicilium coeleste μεταχηματισμὸν probat. Desideramus enim non ἐκδύσασθαι sed ἐπενδύσασθαι exuere, sed superinduere, ut absorbeatur corruptibile a vita, ibid. v. 4.
units.tr: LXXIV. The arguments these men bring against the whole of this doctrine are weak, and the basic error rests on them. Christ said that the risen will be like the angels (Matth. 22:30; Luke 20:36) [ἰσαγγέλως], but he did not mean this in every respect, only in the points he went on to name: they neither marry nor are given in marriage [ἔτε γαμίσιν, ἔτε ἐκγαμίσκονται], and they can no longer die [ἔτε ἀποθνῄσκειν δύνανται]. The likeness therefore lies not in a new heavenly body, which the angels have neither in their old nor in a new form, and angels are not even sons of the resurrection [υἱοὶ ἀναστάσεως]. It lies in this: the risen will neither marry nor be given in marriage, they will be immortal, and as sons of the resurrection they will be partakers and companions (by a common Hebraism) of the sons of God, as the angels are, endowed with perfect holiness, righteousness and immortality. And flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 15:50). This does not mean flatly that they cannot, since the arguments adduced above stand against that reading. It means that flesh and blood, insofar as it is animal [ψυχικός], has an animal state of its own: it is sustained by food and drink in this life, it has a constant flow and changes day by day, and at last it decays. St Paul himself explains this by adding: corruption does not inherit incorruption. The flesh in this life is sustained by blood, the blood by food and drink, and within the blood is that soul [ψυχή] from which the body is called animal [ψυχικόν]. For one soul makes the body animal, and another makes a man animal [ψυχικός], as in 1 Cor. 2:14 and Jude 19. In the kingdom of God the body, flesh and blood of this animal kind, will not persist, because we shall not need food and drink to sustain the substance of the body and to restore and repair the soul [ψυχή], which gives us life in so slender a way, and so to keep life going. Instead God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28), since we shall have no need of any other cause of life or any other thing that gives life. In the same sense our bodies will not be animal [ψυχικά] but spiritual [πνευματικά] (ibid. v. 44). Our body will not have a spiritual substance, for that would be a contradiction, but it will have a life-giving spirit [πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν] (ibid. v. 45). For if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also quicken your mortal bodies [διὰ τὸ ἐνοικοῦν ... ἐν ὑμῖν], through his Spirit dwelling in you (Rom. 8:11). Just as an animal body is not one that is mere soul, but one that has only the vegetative soul as the principle or cause of its living, and just as an animal man [ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος] (1 Cor. 2:14) is not one who is nothing but soul, but one who for wisdom is governed not by the Spirit of God but by his rational soul alone, so a spiritual body is not one that is spirit or exists in the manner of a spirit, but one that is quickened by the Spirit of God and is sustained and preserved by him alone, or by God, who is all in all. The spiritual body therefore will not be a thin body like air, wind, or the spirit of the chemists. Our body will be like Christ's, which is visible, since it was seen by St Paul and will be seen by the eyes of those who pierced him, indeed by every eye [πᾶν ὀφθαλμός] (Rev. 1:7). The first man became a living soul [εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν], a living animal, that is, a body having the animal soul that is in the blood and is called vegetative, over which the spirit of man does not have the same power as over the motion of the organs. But the last Adam, Christ, was made a life-giving spirit [εἰς πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν] (1 Cor. 15:45), that is, a spiritual, divine person, the cause of all life, who as true God acted in his own flesh (1 Pet. 3:18), and who acts and will act in his own by giving them life. For just as Christ now has no other body than the one he raised, and in which he now also gives life, and in which he appears [ἐμφανίζεται] before God the Father, so we shall have no other bodies, only changed in quality, according to Paul's words: someone will say, how are the dead raised? And with what body do they come? [Ποίῳ δὲ σώματι ἔρχονται] (1 Cor. 15:35). Nor, for the same reason, is Christ a life-giving spirit [ζωοποιῶν] in the sense of a spiritual substance which does not produce life in itself or in others but keeps and preserves its own life, as the Socinians distort the words ζωογονῶν and ζωοποιῶν and the Hebrew [חיה] and [חיה], taking them to mean only permitting something to be in life. The Apostol does not say making himself alive [ἑαυτὸν ζωοποιῶν], and he explicitly opposes ζῆν and ζωοποιῶν in v. 45. And because Christ is a life-giving spirit, we too shall have spiritual bodies, but we ourselves are not life-giving spirits. Whoever is given life by another does not give life to himself. Finally, [חיה] and [חיה] never mean to make oneself alive. Nor can any example be produced of a compound noun or participle formed by joining an intransitive stem to the verb ποιέω, I make, which has an intransitive sense. So the contrast between the first and the second Adam is this: the first was a living soul [ψυχὴ ἄνθρωπος], created and made by God as a soul, that is, an animal living in flesh, and so when he fell from the spiritual covenant with God he had handed on to his posterity only an animal life. The second, though made flesh in the likeness of our sinful flesh, is nonetheless the same true, living and life-giving God. For life-giving spirit is the attribute of the true and living God alone. Moreover, St Paul compares the dead body with a grain that is sown, and says that the grain sown is not the body that is to be [ζῶμα τὸ γινόμενον] that is raised, because God gives it a body as he wills (1 Cor. 15:37–38). He does not mean that the body to rise will be a different substance from the one that fell, but that the body that fell must be transfigured [μεταχηματίζεσθαι], changed from lowly to glorious (Rom. 8:11; Phil. 3:21). Christ himself compared his own death and burial to a grain of wheat, which falling into the earth, unless it dies, remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). Yet he rose in the same body in which he died, for he raised up the temple itself, which had been destroyed (ibid. 2:19), and which had flesh and bones (Luke 24:39). Nor does the grain of wheat thrown into the earth lose its substance altogether. It keeps its substance, though changed in qualities, and rises in the same substance, but wonderfully increased by the power of God. For God gives a body as he wills, not by destroying the substance but by enlarging it. The spirit of the grain, by the moisture supplied from the same matter that was sown, receives a body such as God wills. And although the Apostle says: Food is for the stomach, and the stomach for food; but God will destroy both (1 Cor. 6:13), he does not mean that the stomach is to be abolished as to its substance, but only as to its use, which is to receive food. Foods were made so that they might be received by the stomach and converted into the juice and blood of the man; and the stomach was made so that in this life it might receive food. The mutual relation of food and stomach is a temporary one, and when it ceases the substance of the stomach does not cease at once, but remains, to be rewarded or punished, and so that the body may have its perfection and integrity. Indeed even in this animal life it can happen in individual cases that the particular use of some part, the use peculiar to that part and characteristic of it, ceases and is never exercised; yet the abolition of that part is something the perfection and integrity of the whole body cannot bear. So when the uses of the parts that belong to this animal life are laid aside, the same parts will be dedicated to the spiritual and heavenly life, so that God may be praised in them: at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, and every tongue should confess God (Phil. 2:9–10). For St Paul himself distinguishes the body as destined for the Lord from the body as destined for food, saying: Food for the stomach and the stomach for food, but the body is not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. And God raised up the Lord and will raise us up (1 Cor. 6:13–14). Moreover, that contrast between the earthly tabernacle and the heavenly dwelling (2 Cor. 5:1) proves not the abolition of the body but its change [μεταχηματισμόν], from the earthly tabernacle of the flesh into the heavenly dwelling. For we desire not to be unclothed [ἐκδύσασθαι] but to be clothed upon [ἐπενδύσασθαι], so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life (ibid. v. 4).

units.la: Maximus adversus resurrectionem ejusdem numero corporis aries τῶν χλαζῶν irrisorum resurrectionis infidelitatem prodit. Turbat illos inprimis pulveris corporei quaquaversum dissipati, collectio. Ejusdem numero corporis de suis cineribus exsuscitatio & reconcinnatio: denique difficultas illa, quam ab humanis aut inhumanis ἀνθρωποφάγων cibis, & foeda gula, qua integrae nationes, Canibales inprimis, coeforum hominum reliquias turpi in alvo condere & digerere solent. Sed novis his Sadducaeis Christus ipse jugulum incidit, paucis eos increpans: Erratis, nescientes Scripturas & potentiam Dei, Matth. XXII. 29. Alibi idem: Omnes, qui in sepulchris sunt, audient vocem ejus, Joh. V. 28. Dedit mare mortuos, quos continebat; & mors & infernus mortuos, quos continebant, Apoc. XX. 13. non utique nova corpora, sed mortuos. Gemellum etiam locum Tertullianus de Resurr. c. 63. citat, qui tamen nusquam reperitur. Et mandabo piscibus maris & eructabunt ossa, quae sunt comesta, & faciam compaginem ad compaginem, & os ad os. Idem cap. 63. Nominantur bestiae; & pisces in redhibitione carnis & sanguinis, quo magis exprimatur resurrectio etiam devoratorum corporum, cum de ipsis devoratoribus exactio edicitur. Etenim si diligens & solers paterfamilias quantumvis madida subinde ejus memoria sit, probe novit, ubi quidque repositum & reconditum sit in aedibus suis, quamvis amplissimis; quidni אל־ידעת Deus ille scientiarum, 1. Sam. II. 3. cujus infinita tum sapientia, tum potentia est, noverit, ubi corporum nostrorum materia latet, cum ipsi longe minor sit orbis universi longe amplissima domus, quam cuivis homini angustissima theca, vel capsula est. Potest igitur omnipotentia Dei solo nutu revocare quicquid usquam a bestiis absumptum, vel in cineres conversum, vel in humorem solutum, vel in auras exhalatum est; neque ullus sinus, specus vel latibulum usquam est, quod creatoris vel notitiam fugiat, vel potentiam frustretur. Denique quoad ἀνθρωποφάγως, facilimum erit Deo, quod ex aliena carne hominivoro accessit, ceu aes alienum injusto possessori ereptum restituere priori, & aliunde posteriori supplere. Si enim maxime omnibus devorantis membris aliquid ex devorato accesserit, quidni facilius Deus inde illud eximat, integro manente devorante, quam forte bibliopegus aliquis libri marginem quadantenus resecando cunctis quidem ejus foliis aliquid detrahit, librum tamen ipsum nulla parte mutilat. Quinimo contingere potest, ut margo libri in folio tantae capacitatis sit, ut abscissa charta novi libri in octavo materia fiat, cujus extremitates denuo resecentur ad libellum in decimo sexto conficiendum. Plane sicut in propagatione hominum avus, pater, filius, nepos ipse consequuntur; ubi tamen generantis corpori, prius quam generet, praeter eam, quam accepit a parentibus, multum materiae aliunde accedit, perinde ut chartae a margine desumptae, antequam novus liber inde formetur, nonnihil chartae aliunde acceptae adjungi potest. Licet ergo posset etiam substantia devorati hominis in corpore devorantis ex parte abire in semen, ex quo alius homo generari incipiat, poterunt tamen priores homines, devoratus & devorans, propter istam materiae detractionem, ex quibus tertii hominis corpus originem habet, in resurrectione Divinae virtutis efficacia essentialia membra sua recipere. Facit huc medicorum illa observatio, quod planta purgans a capra devorata in ventriculo ejus coquitur, & chylo permiscetur; chylus ille in sanguinem, sanguis in mammis caprae in lac mutatur, lac a nutrice bibitur, & rursus tot in corpore ejus mutationes subit, quot prius in capra subierat; denique enatum inde lac nutricis infans haurit, qui eo purgatur. Si post tot mutationes materiae purgantes illius plantae particulas natura discernit, earumque vires integras conservat; quidni Deus potentissimus totius naturae Dominus & auctor particulas devorati hominis ad essentiam ejus pertinentes conservare & secernere queat, licet etiam cum semine devorantis partes aliquae ad novae sobolis procreationem transiverint; quas tamen ipsas ad essentiam devorati pertinere, nondum liquido constat? Praeterquam quod ad illud parentis semen & foetum in utero formandum aliunde quotidie materia advenit, & admirabili Dei Providentiae pro humana gente excubanti id omne committendum est, quae facillime impedire potest, ne devorati hominis substantia, vel pars aliqua ad integritatem ejus necessaria in semen, unde alterius hominis corpus effingatur, abeat, uti etiam bibliopegus novi libelli faciendi gratia a libri craßioris margine chartam resecans facile cavet, ne literas vel syllabas vocum inscriptarum abradat; Quinetiam facile Deus cavere potest, ne de humana ista sagina ferorum hominum caro nimium augescat, cum exiguum etiam sit, quod de alimento in substantiam nostram transit.
units.tr: Against the resurrection of the same numerical body, Maximus exposes the unbelief of the mockers [τῶν χλευαζόντων]. Chiefly they are troubled by the gathering of bodily dust scattered in every direction, by the raising up and reassembling from their ashes of the same numerical body, and finally by the difficulty arising from the food of [ἀνθρωποφάγων] man-eaters, whether human or inhuman, and from the foul gluttony by which whole nations, Cannibals above all, are accustomed to store and digest the remains of their fellow men in a shameful belly. But Christ himself cut the throat of these new Sadducees, rebuking them briefly: You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God, Matt. 22:29. Elsewhere the same: All who are in the graves shall hear his voice, John 5:28. The sea gave up the dead which were in it; and death and hell gave up the dead which were in them, Rev. 20:13: not new bodies, certainly, but the dead. Tertullian, in his book on the resurrection, ch. 63, also cites a twin passage, which nowhere however is found: And I will command the fishes of the sea, and they shall bring up the bones which have been eaten, and I will make joint to joint and bone to bone. In the same chapter 63 he says: Beasts are named; and fishes, in the restoration of flesh and blood, so that the resurrection of bodies, even of those devoured, may be more clearly expressed, since the demand is made upon the devourers themselves. For if a diligent and skilful householder, however much his memory may from time to time grow hazy, knows well where each thing is stored and hidden in his house, however spacious it is, why should that God of knowledges [אל דעות], 1 Sam. 2:3, whose wisdom and power are infinite, not know where the matter of our bodies lies hidden, since the whole universe, the most spacious of houses, is to him far smaller than the narrowest box or casket is to any man? Therefore the power of God can, by a mere nod, recall whatever has been consumed by beasts anywhere, or turned to ashes, or dissolved into moisture, or exhaled into the air; and there is no bosom, cave or hiding place anywhere that can escape the Creator's knowledge or frustrate his power. Finally, as to man-eaters, it will be most easy for God to restore to the former owner what has come from another's flesh into the flesh of the one who devoured him, as a debt wrongly taken from its rightful possessor and supplied from elsewhere to the later one. For even if something from the devoured man has passed into all the members of the devourer, why should God not more easily extract it from them, while the devourer remains whole, than a bookbinder who trims a little from the margin of a book, taking something from all its leaves, yet mutilates the book itself in no part? Indeed it may happen that the margin of a book in a folio of such size is cut off to make material for a new book in octavo, whose edges are again trimmed to make a little book in sixteenmo. Just so in the propagation of men, grandfather, father, son and grandson follow one another; yet before the begetting parent's body begins to generate, much matter from elsewhere, beyond that which he received from his parents, is added, just as, before a new book is formed from the margin, some paper received from elsewhere may be added to it. Therefore, although the substance of the devoured man may in part pass, in the body of the devourer, into the seed from which another man begins to be generated, the earlier men, the devoured and the devourer, will nevertheless be able, in the resurrection, by the efficacy of divine power, to recover their essential members, despite the removal of that matter out of which the body of the third man takes its origin. To this belongs the observation of physicians, that a purgative plant eaten by a goat is cooked in its stomach and mixed with its chyle; that chyle is changed into blood, the blood in the goat's udders into milk; the milk is drunk by a nurse, and undergoes in her body as many changes as it had undergone in the goat; finally, the infant drinks the milk the nurse has produced and is purged by it. If, after so many changes of matter, nature distinguishes the purgative particles of that plant and keeps their powers intact, why should not God, the most powerful Lord and author of all nature, be able to preserve and separate the particles of the devoured man that belong to his essence, even though some parts of the devourer have also passed with his seed into the production of a new offspring? Yet whether those parts belong to the essence of the devoured man has not yet been clearly established. Besides, for the parent's seed and for the formation of the foetus in the womb, fresh matter arrives every day from elsewhere, and all of this must be committed to the wonderful providence of God, who watches over the human race and can most easily prevent the substance of the devoured man, or any part of it necessary for his integrity, from passing into the seed from which the body of another man is fashioned; just as the bookbinder making a new little book, cutting paper from the margin of a thicker book, carefully takes care not to scrape away the letters or syllables of the words written there. Moreover, God can easily take care that the flesh of savage men does not grow too much from this human fattening, since even what passes from food into our substance is small.

units.la: LXXVI.
units.tr: LXXVI.

units.la: Resuscitatio erit universalis mortuorum omnium, justorum & injustorum. Non enim tantum ii, quorum Christus primitiae est, in ipso vivificabuntur, 1. Cor. XV. 22. sed etiam injusti, quod distertis verbis sic Christus docuit: Venit hora, qua omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus: & prodibunt, qui bona fecerunt, ad resurrectionem vitae, qui mala patrarunt, ad resurrectionem judicii, Johann. V. 28. 29. Ubi non de instante vocatione Gentium, sed de resurrectione omnium hominum Christus diserte loquitur, quia vocatio Gentium nec immediate a Christo, sed ab Apostolis peracta est, & Gentes nondum conversae non fecerunt bona, per quae ex monumentis suis prodirent ad resurrectionem vitae, v. 29. sed fuerunt ἀμαρτωλοί peccatores, ahei in mundo, Ephes. II. 12. Qualem resurrectionem etiam sic credere S. Paulus profitetur dicens: Spem habeo in Deum, quam etiam illi expectant, resurrectionem futuram mortuorum δικαίων τε ἡ ἀδίκων justorum & injustorum, Actor. XXIV. 15. Ubi per justos fideles Christianos in hac vita justificatos, per injustos fideles Christianos nondum conversos, & in altera demum vita perfectè justificandos, in hac vero vita adhuc injustos; utpote qui ante conversionem injusti fuerint; Christus justus passus pro injustis, 1. Pet. III. 18. & Deus ἀσεβῆ impium justificare, Rom. IV. 5. dicatur; intelligi, nequicquam Socciniani pertendunt. Monstrosa enim haec fidelium Christianorum distributio est, cum in illa antithesi Scriptura non fideles fidelibus usquam opponat, sed semper impios. Deus solem suum oriri facit super bonos & malos, pluit ἐπὶ δικαίους καὶ ἀδίκους super justos & injustos, Matth. V. 45. Audet quis judicari ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδίκων, καὶ οὐκ ἐπὶ τῶν ἁγίων ab injustis, & non à sanctis? 1. Cor. VI. 1. Novit Deus εὐσεβεῖς pios eruere ex tentatione, ἀδίκους δὲ injustos vero servare in diem judicii, 2. Petr. II. 9. Eadem antithesis inter צדיקים justos, & רשעים injustos, Psal. I. 6. & alibi extat. Cum vero Christus justus pro injustis passus, 1. Petr. III. 18. & Deus impium justificare, Rom. IV. 5. dicitur, illa non est unius vel alterius, seu publicani, seu latronis in cruce, sed communis omnium fidelium in justificationis primo objecto nomenclatura, utpote in quo οὐκ ἔτι δίκαιος, ἀδὲ ἡς non est justus, ne unus quidem, ibid. III. 10. & credens, velut ex se injustus & impius, opponitur justitiam operanti, ibid. IV. 4. 5. Cumque in hoc seculo justificatio fidelium à peccatis perac-ta sit, nulla erit Christianorum fidelium injustorum resurrectio, qui tum demum justificentur, justificatione priori ex causis; quae Socinianae doctrinae, justificationem demum peragi, cum à morte liberati in aeternam vitam traducimur, afferentis, gangraena est; sed omnes partem & sortem habebunt ἐν ἀναστάσει τῶν δικαίων in resurrectione justorum, Luc. XIV. 14. Neque minor illa anonymi authoris libri de statu mortuorum, Belgicè editi, & à Camphusio Remonstrante conversi, interpretatio dicti Paulini, quo resurrectionem justorum & injustorum profitetur; quod nimirum Paulus sibi ipsi maximè intenderit, quia crebrò professus sit, se peccatorem esse. Nam id eo loco & tempore alienissimum fuit, quia non tractavit mysterium justificationis coram Deo ex causis, sed potius contestatus est, se quod ad justitiam, quae ex lege est, ἐξ ἰδίων ... extitisse irreprehensibilem, 1. Cor. IV. 4. Phil. III. 6. Nam cum ad judicium traheretur, praefatus est; se omni bona conscientia servivisse Deo usque ad diem illum, Actor. XXIII. 1. & post fidei suae de resurrectione justorum & injustorum confessionem cap. XXIV. 15. editam, mox v. 16. pietatis illam praxin profitetur, qua se ipsum in hoc exercebat, ut conscientiam haberet sine offendiculo apud Deum & apud homines semper; provocans insuper v. 20. ad conscientiam accusatorum, εἰ τι εὑρον ἀδίκημα numquid in ipso injustum invenerint? Etiam in V. T. resurrectio impiorum fundamentum habet. Nuspiam enim ad solos justos restringitur. Imò Daniel inter resurgentes ex terra pulveris etiam illos, qui לחרפות ולדראון עולם ad opprobria & fastidium aeternum resurgent, numerat, Dan. XII. 2. Denique injusti non resurgentes judicari non possunt. At judicabuntur omnes. Coram tribunali enim Christi manifestari oportet πάντας omnes, ut quisque reportet τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος quae per corpus fecit, 2. Cor. V. 10. Cogentur coram eo omnes gentes, & separabit eas, alteras ab alteris, Matth. XXV. 32. Qualia inepte ad solos, qui ultimo die vivi deprehendentur, torquent; quia nihil hoc ad terrendos praecedentium aetatum homines faceret; nec ratio constat, cur soli illi injusti, quos dies Domini deprehendet, ad judicium resuscitentur. Ideo etiam Sodomaorum & Gomorrhaeorum, Tyri & Sidonis, Reginae Austri & Ninevitarum in judiciali illo die mentio habetur, ibid. X. 15. XI. 21. 22. Luc. XI. 31. 32. ubi etiam Sodomaeis & Gomorrhaeis in die illo judicii ultimi futurum, non fuisse, ἀνεκτότερον tolerabilius, Matth. XI. 22. dicitur; ne Judaeae excidium cum Sodomae excidio tantum comparari videri posset.
units.tr: The resurrection will be universal, of all the dead, both the just and the unjust. For it is not only those whose firstfruits Christ is who shall be made alive in him (1 Cor. 15:22), but also the unjust, as Christ taught in plain words: "The hour is coming, in which all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice, and shall come forth, those who have done good, to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment" (John 5:28–29). Here Christ speaks plainly not of the impending calling of the Gentiles, but of the resurrection of all men. The calling of the Gentiles was accomplished not immediately by Christ but by the Apostles, and the Gentiles, not yet converted, had not done good works by which they could come forth from their tombs to the resurrection of life (v. 29). They were rather sinners [ἁμαρτωλοί], without God in the world (Eph. 2:12). St. Paul professes that he believes in this kind of resurrection too, when he says: "I have hope in God, which these also themselves allow, that there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and of the unjust" [δικαίων τε καὶ ἀδίκων] (Acts 24:15). Here by the just are meant Christian believers who are justified in this life, and by the unjust Christian believers not yet converted, who are to be fully justified only in the next life, while in this life they are still unjust, since before their conversion they were unjust. Christ, the just one, suffered for the unjust (1 Pet. 3:18), and God is said to justify the ungodly (Rom. 4:5).
