The Socinians contend in vain that this is to be understood of one or another particular person, whether a tax collector or the thief on the cross. It is rather the common term for all believers in the first object of justification, since in that case there is none righteous, no, not one (ibid. 3:10). And the believer, regarded as unjust and ungodly in himself, is set over against him who works righteousness (ibid. 4:4–5). And since in this age the justification of believers from their sins has been completed, there will be no resurrection of the unjust Christian believers, who would then at last be justified by a prior justification of causes. The doctrine of the Socinians, who assert that justification is only completed when we are freed from death and led into eternal life, is a gangrene. Rather, all will have their part and lot in the resurrection of the just (Luke 14:14). Nor is the interpretation of the Pauline saying, by which he professes the resurrection of the just and the unjust, any less mistaken in the anonymous author of the book On the State of the Dead, published in Dutch and translated by the Remonstrant Camphuysen, who holds that Paul meant it of himself, since he often professed that he was a sinner. For that interpretation is most alien to that place and time, since he did not treat of the mystery of justification before God by causes, but rather testified that as to the righteousness which is of the law he had been blameless [ἐξ ἰδίων] (1 Cor. 4:4; Phil. 3:6). When he was brought before the judgment seat, he declared that he had served God with a good conscience up to that day (Acts 23:1). And after the confession of his faith concerning the resurrection of the just and the unjust, published in chapter 24:15, he immediately, at v. 16, professes that practice of piety by which he exercised himself to have a conscience without offense toward God and toward men always. Moreover, at v. 20 he appeals to the conscience of his accusers: whether they had found any wrong [εἴ τι εὗρον ἀδίκημα] in him. Even in the Old Testament the resurrection of the wicked has its foundation. For nowhere is it restricted to the just alone. Indeed Daniel, among those who awake from the dust of the earth, also numbers those who will rise to shame and everlasting contempt [לחרפות ולדראון עולם] (Dan. 12:2). Finally, the unjust who do not rise cannot be judged, yet all shall be judged. For before the judgment seat of Christ all must be made manifest, so that each may receive what he did through the body (2 Cor. 5:10). All nations shall be gathered before him, and he shall separate them one from another (Matt. 25:32). Those who twist these texts so as to apply them only to those who will be found alive on the last day do so foolishly, since this would not be a terror to the men of earlier ages, nor is there any reason why only those unjust whom the Day of the Lord finds should be raised for judgment. For this reason also the Sodomites and Gomorrhites, Tyre and Sidon, the Queen of the South and the Ninevites are mentioned in that day of judgment (Matt. 10:15; 11:21–22; Luke 11:31–32), where it is also said that it will be more tolerable [ἀνεκτότερον] for Sodom and Gomorrah in that day (Matt. 11:22), which would not be the case if they were not to rise at the last judgment. This was said so that the destruction of Judea might not seem to be compared only with the destruction of Sodom.

units.la: LXXVII. De resurrectione hac impiorum non concors Judaeorum sententia est. Non desunt enim, qui eam fortiter asserant; in Thalmude Roscb hasschanah cap. I. tres classes eorum, qui ad diem judicii futuri se sistent, recensentur, nimirum צדיקים גמורים perfectè justorum, רשעים גמורים imperfectè justorum, & בינים intermediorum, quorum iniquitates & justitiae pares sunt.
units.tr: LXXVII. The opinion of the Jews is not in agreement about this resurrection of the wicked. For there are not lacking those who assert it strongly. In the Talmud, tractate Rosh Hashanah, chapter 1, three classes of those who will stand before the judgment to come are recounted, namely perfectly righteous [צדיקים גמורים], perfectly wicked [רשעים גמורים], and intermediates [בינים], whose iniquities and righteousnesses are equal.

units.la: In Pirke Abboth R. Eleazar à Kafar inquit הילודים למות והמתים לחיות והחיים לידין Qui nati sunt, nati sunt, ut moriantur: qui mortui, ut vivificentur, qui vivunt ut judicentur. Consentit Abarbanel, & Menasse Ben Israel, qui etiam refutant sententiam oppositam Judaeorum, velut Majmonidis, Chasdai, Saadiae, afferentium, non esse resurrecturos כי אם צדיקים מבני ישראל nisi justos ex filiis Israel. Et Josephus Albo in Ikkar. c. 35. allegat illud veterum: Beneficium pluviae ad omnes spectat: Resurrectio mortuorum ad solos justos. De Kimchii sententia docti certant. Judaeorum horum sententiae Socinian astipulantur, qui universalem omnium hominum resurrectionem albis dentibus rident, & solos fideles resurrecturos scisicunt. Nullus vero errori utrorumque color esse potest in verbis Davidis: Improbi לא יקימו במשפט non stabunt in judicio, Psal. I. 5. Aliud enim est, non stare in judicio, hoc est, in judicio causa cadere, aliud non resurgere. Nam qui in judicio ultimo cadent causa, prius illi resurrexerint oportet. Et sanè impii in judicio non resurgent, quia jam de illis praejudicatum est. Qui non credit, ἤδη κέκριται, jam judicatus est, Joh. III. 18. Etiam mortui non resurgent, Esaj. XXVI. 14. puta vel spiritualiter mortui & indurati ad vitam spiritualem: vel tyranni, qui praeter Deum dominati sunt, sive ad praesentem vitam & tyrannidem denuo exercendam; sive ad vitam beatam. Sed & רבים multi resurgent, Dan. XII. 2. & inter eos etiam impii, ad opprobria aeterna, ibid. & omnes pii & impii, quia maxima eorum multitudo erit; vel multi ad vitam, & (ὑπὸ κοινῶν) multi ad opprobria. Praeterea Christus dicens: Retribuetur ei ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει τῶν δικαίων in resurrectione justorum, Luc. XIV. 14. non injustos non resurrecturos, sed justos in resurrectione justorum sortem & ἀντιμισθίαν retributionem butionem accepturos, innuit. Revera enim alia justorum, alia injustorum resurrectio erit; illa in emphasi talis, quia erit ad vitam, & post-quam resuscitati verè ϰαθισταντες statuentur & stabunt; & meriti Christi iis applicati conse-ctaria: hæc, quia erit ad mortem, minùs emphaticè talis; & ex decreti Divini mortem peccatori destinantis necessitate, & judiciaria potestate Christi, qua non pro illis, sed adversus illos utetur, oriunda. Proin etiam soli fideles & electi υἱοὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως filii (consortes) resurrectionis dicuntur, quia soli ad vitam, statum & gloriam resuscitabuntur. Ego credentem ἀναστήσω iterum stare faciam, plenè erigam, ab omni casu liberabo, & faciam, ut sine pudore, cum παῤῥησίᾳ ad Deum accedat. Per unum hominem erit ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν resurrectio mortuorum, 1. Cor. XV. 21. Denique Deus eos, qui obdormiverunt, per Jesum ἀξεῖ σὺν αὐτῷ ducet cum ipso, 1. Thess. IV. 14. quia sibi datos post mortem quoad spiritum, & in ultimo die etiam quoad corpus per Christum, & efficacia meriti ad se ducet. Sed non iccirco Deus impios non resuscitabit, & non ducet ad suppliciùm in inferno.
units.tr: In Pirke Avot, R. Eleazar of Kafar says: "Those who are born are born to die; the dead, to be made alive; and the living, to be judged" [הילודים למות והמתים לחיות והחיים לידין]. Abarbanel agrees, and Menasseh ben Israel, who also refute the opposing opinion of the Jews, such as that of Maimonides, Chasdai, and Saadiah, who assert that they will not rise except the just from the sons of Israel [כי אם צדיקים מבני ישראל]. And Joseph Albo, in Ikkarim, chapter 35, cites the saying of the ancients: "The benefit of rain extends to all; the resurrection of the dead to the just alone." Learned men dispute about the opinion of Kimchi. The Socinians support the opinion of these Jews: they laugh with white teeth at the universal resurrection of all men, and cut it down to the believers alone who will rise. But there can be no colour of error for either side in the words of David: the wicked shall not stand [לא יקימו] in judgment (Ps. 1:5). For it is one thing not to stand in judgment, that is, to lose one's cause in judgment, and another not to rise. For those who will lose their cause in the last judgment must first have risen. And indeed the wicked will not rise in the judgment, because they have already been prejudged. He who does not believe is already judged [ἤδη κέκριται] (John 3:18). Likewise the dead shall not rise (Isa. 26:14), that is, either those spiritually dead and hardened against spiritual life, or tyrants who ruled apart from God, whether to exercise their tyranny again in the present life, or to the blessed life. But many shall rise [רבים] (Dan. 12:2), and among them also the wicked, to everlasting shame (ibid.), and all the godly and the ungodly, since their greatest multitude will be there; or many to life and (by a common ellipsis) many to shame. Moreover, when Christ says, you shall be repaid in the resurrection of the just [ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει τῶν δικαίων] (Luke 14:14), he does not mean that the unjust will not rise, but that the just will receive their lot and recompense in the resurrection of the just. For there will indeed be a different resurrection of the just and a different one of the unjust. The former is emphatically of such a kind, because it will be to life, and after they have been raised they will truly be set up and will stand, and the consequences of Christ's merit applied to them; the latter, because it will be to death, is less emphatically of that kind, and arises from the necessity of the divine decree destining the sinner to death, and from the judicial power of Christ, which he will use not for them but against them. Therefore also only believers and the elect are called sons of the resurrection (fellow heirs of the resurrection), because only they will be raised to life, state, and glory. I will raise up the believer and make him stand again, fully set him upright, free him from every fall, and make it so that he may approach God without shame, with boldness [παῤῥησίᾳ]. By one man will come the resurrection of the dead [ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν] (1 Cor. 15:21). Finally, God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep, with him [ἄξει σὺν αὐτῷ] (1 Thess. 4:14), because he will lead to himself, through Christ and the efficacy of his merit, those given to him after death as to spirit, and at the last day also as to body. But this does not mean that God will not raise the wicked, nor will he not lead them to punishment in hell.

units.la: LXXVIII. Modum refuscitationis futuræ subtiliùs scrutari non licet.
units.tr: LXXVIII. It is not permitted to inquire too closely into the manner of the future resurrection.

units.la: Satis est illud nosse, quòd Christus ex Cœlo venturus Φωνῇ voce sua, quæ erit instar κελευσματι celeusmatis, clamoris excitantis, jubentis, vocantis ad vitam, & φωνῆς Ἀρχαγγέλου vocis Archangeli, Angelorum; quos adventans comites & stipatores habebit; Principis, Christi Θεανθρώπου, cui vox competit; & in tuba Dei seu potentissima ipsius Dei voce, & imperio, quo vocare potest, quæ non sunt, mortuos resuscitabit, 1. Thess. IV. 16. Eodem verbo, quo omnia creavit, etiam mortuos resuscitabit. Credidit Abraham Deo vivificanti mortuos, & vocanti ea, quæ non sunt, tanquam si essent. Rom. IV. 17. Redigis hominem ad minimum, & dicis: Redite filii hominis, Psal. XC. 3. Qui subtiliùs rem putant, tria in resurrectione considerant, quemadmodum & triplicem in morte casum, quem resurrectio præsupponit, distinguunt, puta compositi, per separationem animæ à corpore, corporis, quod dissolvitur in elementa, & materiæ, in quam corpus in elementa dispersum postremò resolvitur. In resurrectione igitur ex mortuis, primo casui colleƈtionem pulverum ac cinerum dissipatorum: secundo formationem corporis: tertio ejusdem animationem oppo-nunt; & primum ministerio Angelorum, non sine tractu temporis & motu locali; reliqua duo sola virtute Dei immediata, & momento successura statuunt. Sed nobis ista vel Angelorum ministeria, vel temporum momenta ἐξουνχίζεσθαι, & ad calculos revocare, curiosum satis, & à sobrietate alienum videtur. Sed resuscitationem tamen illam futuram ἐν ἀτόμῳ, ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ in momento, in ictu oculi, 1. Cor. XV. 52. Illud rem subitam, hoc brevitatem moræ & temporis notat. Momentaneum oculi motum, Tertullianus interpretatur. Neque tam instans, quàm tempus brevissimum & ἀκαταλήπτως Apostolus indicat. Nihil enim oculi agitatione velocius & agilius est. Ingens opus est, mortuos resuscitare; majus est in propriis corporibus in pulverem redactis eos resuscitare; maximum in momento temporis resuscitare. De cætero circa modum refuscitationis corporum prudenter sic S. Augustinus de Civ. Dei lib. XX. 20. loquitur: Resurrectionem mortuorum futuram esse, oportet, si Christiani esse volumus, ut credamus; sed non ideo inanis est fides nostra, si, quemadmodum futura sit, comprehendere non valemus.
units.tr: It is enough to know this: that Christ, coming from heaven, will raise the dead with his voice (Φωνῇ), which will be like a κελευσμα (celeusma), a shout that stirs up, commands and calls to life; and with the voice of the Archangel (φωνῆς Ἀρχαγγέλου) of the angels, whom he will have as companions and attendants as he comes. He is the Prince, the God-man Christ (Θεανθρώπου), to whom the voice belongs; and he will raise the dead with the trumpet of God, that is, by the most powerful voice and command of God himself, by which he can call into being things that are not, 1 Thess. 4:16. By the same word by which he created all things, he will also raise the dead. Abraham believed God, who gives life to the dead, and calls those things which be not as though they were, Rom. 4:17. You turn man to destruction, and say, Return, ye children of men, Ps. 90:3. Those who think about the matter more subtly consider three things in the resurrection, and likewise distinguish a threefold fall in death, which the resurrection presupposes: namely, the fall of the compound, through the separation of the soul from the body; of the body, which is dissolved into its elements; and of the matter, into which the body, scattered into the elements, is at last resolved. In the resurrection from the dead, therefore, they set against the first fall the gathering together of the scattered dust and ashes; against the second, the forming of the body; and against the third, its animation. They hold that the first is effected by the ministry of angels, not without a lapse of time and local motion, while the other two will follow by the immediate power of God alone and in a moment. But it seems rather curious, and foreign to sobriety, for us to dissect these angelic ministries or moments of time and reduce them to calculation. Yet that future resurrection will take place in an atom, in a twinkling of the eye, in a moment, in the blink of an eye, 1 Cor. 15:52. The one word denotes a sudden event, the other the brevity of delay and time. Tertullian interprets it as a momentary motion of the eye. And the Apostle indicates not so much an instant as a very short time, incomprehensibly. For nothing is swifter or more nimble than the movement of the eye. It is a great work to raise the dead; greater to raise them in their own bodies reduced to dust; greatest to raise them in a moment of time. As to the rest, concerning the manner of the resurrection of bodies, St. Augustine speaks prudently thus, City of God book 20, chapter 20: It must be that the resurrection of the dead will come, if we wish to be Christians, and we must believe it; but our faith is not therefore empty, if we are not able to grasp how it will come about.

units.la: LXXIX. Locus resurgentium corporum cujusque monumentum erit.
units.tr: LXXIX. The place of the rising bodies will be each one's own tomb.

units.la: Nam audient omnes vocem Dei ἐν τῆς μνημείοις, Joh. V. 28. & ubi audient, ibi surgent. Cujusque ergo monumentum & κοιμητήριον etiam χωρίον ἀναστάσιμον ejusdem erit. Superstitionem enim & ἀνυπόδεται Judæorum sapit, quòd terram sanctam hac prærogativa donant, quòd sola illa locus resurrectionis futura sit. Cùm tamen extra terram sanctam longè maxima hominum pars moriatur; iidem in tenebris suis micantes, otiosè disputent, qua ratione limina illius terræ mortui subituri sint; statuentibus aliis, quod extra terram ex sepulchris suis in eam ascensuri sint: aliis verò, quòd ex sepulchris suis ascensuri sint per גלגל המחים & המחלות revolutionem mortuorum & viam cavernarum. Qnam etiam causam esse, quòd Patriarchæ in terra sancta sepeliri maluerint, iidem perhibent: quia extra terram sanctam non nisi per dolorem volutationis resuscitari possent. Sed fabulas has ipse Abarbanel in Dan. sol. 50. explodit; & R. Menasse ben-Israel de Resurr. lib. II. 3. verecundatur, hoc unum pertendens, quòd terra Canaan hac prærogativa gavisura sit, quòd primò ejus cadavera resuscitanda sint, & momento postreliquarum gentium; consultò sic contradicens S. Paulo, afferenti, quòd mortui in momento & ictu oculi resuscitandi sint. Ridiculum verò ridiculæ & momentaneæ hujus prærogativæ rauonem ex verbis Davidis: Ambulabo coram Domino in terra viventium, Psal. CXVI. 9. affert; quasi terra Canaan ideo terræ viventium nomenclaturam habeat, quia in ea sepulti momento uno prius quàm cæteri resuscitandi sunt. Credat hoc Judæus Apella. Nos, uti universum genus humanum de ruina sua resuscitatum iri credimus; ita toto, qua patet, orbe, de monumentis suis prodituros; & mare, tellurem, cunctaque elementa, quibus cineris nostri custodia est, fidem servatura, & de thecis suis depositum redditura; & redditura simul, quia uni voci illi: Redite, filii hominis; Psal. XC. 3. sine mora obsequentur omnes, nulli dubitamus.
units.tr: For all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of God, John 5:28, and where they hear, there they will rise. The tomb of each, therefore, and his cemetery, and even his place of rising, will be the same. For it savours of the superstition and ἀνυπόδεται of the Jews to grant the holy land this privilege, that it alone shall be the place of the resurrection. Since, however, by far the greater part of mankind dies outside the holy land, these same men, glimmering in their darkness, idly dispute by what route the dead of that land are to get out: some maintaining that those outside the land will ascend from their sepulchres into it; others that they will ascend from their sepulchres through גלגל המחים and המחלות, the rolling of the dead and the way of the caverns. These same men also assert that this is the reason why the patriarchs preferred to be buried in the holy land: because outside the holy land they could be raised only through the pain of rolling. But Abarbanel himself explodes these fables in his commentary on Daniel, p. 50; and R. Menasseh ben Israel, On the Resurrection book 2, chapter 3, is ashamed of them, maintaining this one point only, that the land of Canaan will enjoy this privilege, that its corpses are to be raised first, and a moment before the rest of the nations; thus contradicting St. Paul knowingly, who asserts that the dead are to be raised in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye. Moreover, he gives a ridiculous reason for this ridiculous and momentary privilege from the words of David: I will walk before the Lord in the land of the living, Ps. 116:9; as if the land of Canaan therefore bore the name land of the living because those buried in it are to be raised one moment before the others. Let the Jew Apella believe that. We, as we believe the whole human race will be restored from its ruin, so we believe that, throughout the whole extent of the world, the dead will come forth from their tombs; and that the sea, the earth, and all the elements, in whose keeping our ashes lie, will keep faith and return the deposit from their coffers; and they will return it at once, because all of them, at that one voice, Return, ye children of men, Ps. 90:3, will obey without delay; of this we have no doubt.

units.la: LXXX. Mortuorum refuscitationem mutatio illorum, quos Dominus vivos offendet, excipiet.
units.tr: LXXX. The change of those whom the Lord finds alive will follow the resurrection of the dead.

units.la: Nam Dominus vivorum & mortuorum judex cluet, Actor. X. 42. & in Symbolo venturus ad judicandum vivos & mortuos dicitur. Sed quod unus nos, & quidem tanquam mysterium, utpote non naturali ratione, sed ἐν λόγῳ Κυρίου verbo, revelatione Domini, 1. Thess. IV. 15. S. Paulo forte in Paradiso facta noviter patefactum, docuit Apostolus: Πάντες ου κοιμηθησόμεθα omnes non obdormiemus, sed omnes mutabimur; & in momento vel temporis puncto & ictu oculi non tantùm mortui resuscitabuntur, sed etiam ἡμεῖς nos vivi & superstites ἀλλαγησόμεθα mutabimur, 1. Cor. XV. 51. 52. Ubi veteres quidam ante Hieronymum & Augustinum gustinum Latinos codices corruperunt, legentes : Omnes quidem resurgemus, sed non omnes mutabimur : vel, omnes quidem dormiemus, non omnes mutabimur. Unde Augustinus (qui tamen sententiam Retract. lib. II. 33. retractavit) & secuti eundem Pontificii omnes homines morituros & resurrecturos, solos vero electos ad gloriam commutandos esse opinantur. Sed legendum omnino est : Non omnes quidem obdormiemus, sed omnes immutabimur, prout in Codicibus aliquibus inveniri Augustinus ipse aliique testantur; & Tertullianus de Resurr. cap. 42. legit; e Graecis quinetiam Origenes contra Celf. lib. II. Theodorus Heracleotes, Chrysostomus, Theodoretus aliique, quin & Versio Syriaca & Arabica legerant; ut Codices Graecos corruptos esse, impie & imprudenter Stapletonus scribit. Suffragatur inprimis Apostolus alibi, scribens : Hoc dicimus vobis in sermone Domini, quod nos viventes, qui superstites erimus ad adventum Domini, non praevertemus eos, qui dormiunt, quia ipse Dominus in celeusmate, in voce Archangeli, & in tuba Dei descendet de Coelo, & mortui in Christo resurgent primo, deinde nos vivi, qui relinquemur, una cum ipsis rapiemur in nubibus obviam Domino : & sic semper cum ipso erimus, 1. Thess. IV. 15. 16. 17. Ubi Paulus se viventibus includit, non determinans, vel πχαζόμενος, quam longa vel brevis mora sit, vel quid ipse de se conjiciat; uti etiam Thessalonicenses verba ejus interpretati videntur, quorum proin παρεμμένειν, 2. Thess. II. 2. 3. &c. refellit; sed hypothetice loquens, & vivestes tunc, ut exemplum viventium tempore ultimo commemorans. Quomodo in Scripturis saepe cum de posteaa futuris sermo est, praesentes compellantur. Ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi, Matth. XXVIII. 20. Loquitur in persona eorum, qui superstites erunt, ut eorum animos in expectatione adventus Domini erectos teneat. Et cui bono exhortationes ad sobrietatem, vigilantiam & preces, nec non dehortationes a securitate carnali, quia Christi adventus inopinos opprimet, ibid. XXIV. 44. XXV. 13. Luc. XII. 39. 40. XXI. 34. 1. Thess. V. 2. si superstites Christus nullos offendet, & ante adventum ejus omnes morientur? Praeterea quae ratio est particularis resuscitationis quorundam mortuorum, in V. & N. T. eadem est particularis transmutationis Enochi & Eliae. Sicut igitur illa fuit praeludium universalis resuscitationis mortuorum : ita haec universalis mutationis superstitum praeludium fuit. Denique viventium aeque ac mortuorum corpora spiritualia ex animalibus fieri debent, nec sine mutatione talia fieri possunt. Neque illud obstat, quod S. Paulus dixit. Omnibus hominibus statutum est semel mori, Hebr. IX. 27. quia id ex 1. Cor. XV. 52. restringi debet ad mortalitatis conditionem, quae vel mortem, vel ejus vicariam immutationem inducit. Singularis igitur haec exemptio & privilegium superstitum in fine mundi erit. Et sicut manet lex illa semel moriendi, etiamsi pauci aliqui miraculo resuscitati bis mortui sint : ita mutatio superstitum illam non tollit vel abolet, praesertim cum mutatio illa instar mortis, eique analoga futura sit. Denique caro & sanguis non haereditabunt Regnum Coelorum, ibid. vers. 50. citra mutationem puta; quae vel per resuscitationem mortuorum, vel per transformationem superstitum viventium fieri debet.
units.tr: For the Lord of the living and the dead is declared, Acts 10:42, and in the Creed he is said to be coming to judge the living and the dead. But the Apostle taught us this as a mystery, not by natural reasoning but by the word of the Lord [ἐν λόγῳ Κυρίου], that is, by a revelation of the Lord, 1 Thess. 4:15, perhaps newly disclosed to St. Paul in Paradise: we shall not all sleep [Πάντες οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα], but we shall all be changed. In a moment, in a point of time and the twinkling of an eye, not only will the dead be raised, but we who are alive and remain [ἡμεῖς] will be changed [ἀλλαγησόμεθα], 1 Cor. 15:51, 52. Here some ancient writers before Jerome and Augustine corrupted the Latin manuscripts, reading: We shall indeed all rise, but not all be changed, or we shall indeed all sleep, but not all be changed. Hence Augustine (who nevertheless retracted this opinion, Retract. lib. II. 33) and all the Papists who followed him think that all men are to die and rise again, but only the elect are to be changed into glory. But the text must surely be read: We shall not indeed all sleep, but we shall all be changed, as Augustine himself and others testify is found in some manuscripts. Tertullian, de Resurr. cap. 42, reads it so; and among the Greeks Origen, contra Celsum lib. II, Theodore of Heraclea, Chrysostom, Theodoret and others; indeed the Syriac and Arabic versions also had read it. So Stapleton impiously and imprudently writes that the Greek manuscripts are corrupt. The Apostle supports this above all elsewhere, writing: This we say to you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who sleep, because the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord; and so we shall always be with him, 1 Thess. 4:15, 16, 17. Here Paul includes himself among the living, without determining how long or short the delay will be, or what he himself conjectures about it; as the Thessalonians also seem to have understood his words, which is why he refutes their notion that the day of the Lord was already present, 2 Thess. 2:2, 3, etc. He speaks hypothetically, and as one who would be alive at that time, offering himself as an example of the living at the last time. This is how Scripture often speaks of future events, addressing the present generation as though it were there: I am with you always, even to the end of the age, Matt. 28:20. He speaks in the person of those who will be alive, to keep their minds lifted up in expectation of the Lord's coming. And to what purpose are the exhortations to sobriety, watchfulness and prayer, and the warnings against carnal security, because the coming of Christ will overtake men unawares, ibid. 24:44; 25:13; Luke 12:39, 40; 21:34; 1 Thess. 5:2, if Christ will meet no survivors and all will have died before his coming? Moreover, the reason for the particular resurrection of certain dead persons, in the Old and New Testaments, is the same as for the particular translation of Enoch and Elijah. Just as the latter was a prelude to the universal resurrection of the dead, so the former was a prelude to the universal change of the survivors. Finally, the bodies of the living, no less than those of the dead, must be made spiritual out of animal bodies, and such bodies cannot be made without change. Nor does it stand in the way that St. Paul said, It is appointed for all men once to die, Heb. 9:27, because that must be restricted, by 1 Cor. 15:52, to the condition of mortality, which brings about either death or its equivalent change. This singular exemption and privilege of the survivors will therefore belong to the end of the world. And just as that law of dying once remains, even if a few who were raised by miracle die a second time, so that change of the survivors does not remove or abolish the law, especially since that change will be like death and analogous to it. Finally, flesh and blood shall not inherit the kingdom of heaven, ibid. v. 50, unless there is a change; which must come about either through the resurrection of the dead or through the transformation of the living survivors.

units.la: LXXXI. Modus mutationis hujus superstitum in mysterio cubat.
units.tr: LXXXI. The manner of this change of the survivors lies hidden in mystery.

units.la: Mysterium vobis dico, 1. Cor. XV. 51. Hoc dicimus vobis in sermone Domini, 1. Thess. IV. 15. Revelavit tamen de eo nonnulla S. Paulus. Velut, quod sic mutandi sint viventes, superstites in die Domini sine discrimine, pii & impii, quorum sub adventum Christi amplior quam illorum, numerus erit, ibid. 15. 16. quod principium mutationis illius aeque ac resuscitationis futurum sit Dominus, seu vox Archangeli, qua & mortui resuscitabuntur, & vivi mutabuntur, ibid. v. 16. quod mutatio illa constituta sit in depositione mortalitatis, & assumptione immortalitatis, quia & ipse Paulus sic explicat, dicens; Mortui resuscitabuntur incorruptibiles, & nos mutabimur. Oportet enim corruptibile hoc induere incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc induere immortalitatem, 1. Cor. XV. 52. 53. quia nec opus Dei in imperfecto consistere, nec creatura subjecta vanitati, cui invita subjicitur, nec Regnum Dei in luctu manere semper, & auxiliatrice manu indigere potest : & id ipsum analogia mortis & resuscitationis, cui mutatio illa vivorum respondet, docet : quod illa continget in terra, utpote in qua superstites degunt, & ex qua pii jam mutati & resuscitati in nubibus, in aera in occursum Domini rapientur, 1. Thess. IV. 17. quod denique resuscitatione mortuorum futura posterior sit. Nos viventes ... neutiquam anticipabimus eos, qui dormiunt, ibid. v. 15. hoc est, non consummabimur, non intrabimus in gloriam sine illis, quasi Deus mortuos neglecturus, & Christus ad glorificandos solos superstites venturus sit. Sed optabilior tamen illa transmutatio, quam resuscitatio ex mortuis, erit, quia citra dolorem & corruptionem continget; & Christi sepulti conditio melior fuit, quia corruptionem non vidit, Psal. XVI. 10. adeoque melior etiam eorum erit, qui mortem ne quidem experientur.
units.tr: I tell you a mystery, 1 Cor. 15:51. This we say to you by the word of the Lord, 1 Thess. 4:15. Yet St. Paul did reveal some things about it. For instance, that the living, who survive until the day of the Lord, are to be changed without distinction between the pious and the impious, of whom there will be a greater number at the coming of Christ than of the others, ibid. 15, 16. That the beginning of that change, as of the resurrection, will be the Lord, or the voice of the archangel, by which both the dead will be raised and the living changed, ibid. v. 16. That the change consists in putting off mortality and putting on immortality, as Paul himself explains: The dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality, 1 Cor. 15:52, 53. For the work of God cannot remain in an imperfect state, nor can creation, subjected to vanity against its will, nor the kingdom of God remain forever in mourning and in need of a helping hand. The analogy of death and resurrection, to which the change of the living corresponds, teaches the same thing: that it will happen on earth, since that is where the survivors live, and from which the pious, now changed and raised, will be caught up in the clouds, in the air, to meet the Lord, 1 Thess. 4:17. Finally, that it will take place after the resurrection of the dead. We who are alive ... shall by no means precede those who sleep, ibid. v. 15; that is, we shall not be made perfect, we shall not enter into glory without them, as if God were going to neglect the dead and Christ were coming only to glorify the survivors. Yet that transmutation will be more desirable than resurrection from the dead, because it will happen without pain and corruption. The condition of Christ in the tomb was better, since he did not see corruption, Ps. 16:10, and so the condition of those who will not even experience death will be better still.

units.la: LXXXII. Resurrectionis finis alius respectu Dei, alius respectu hominis.
units.tr: LXXXII. The end of the resurrection is one thing with respect to God and another with respect to man.

units.la: Respectu Dei gloria bonitatis, potentiae, justitiae & sapientiae ejus. Nam resuscitando mortuos sapientiam & potentiam & bonitatem eandem declarat, quam creando declaravit, Rom. IV. 17. Ephes. I. 18. 19. & justitiam, ceu justus futurus judex, propalat; & omnia in omnibus fiet, 1. Cor. XV. 28. Respectu hominis est vita & felicitas aeterna fidelium, a qua resurrectio ad vitam, Joh. V. 29. denominatur. Respectu utriusque est judicium, quod iccirco de resurrectione, tanquam causa sua, καθ' αυτο enuntiatur. Ideo enim Deus homines suscitabit, ut judicet de universis, grana a paleis, oves ab haedis, pios ab impiis discernat, & omnia denique ad liquidum, finemque ultimum perducat. Quam rem plenius Christus Matth. XXV. 32. &c. explicat. Fatentur etiam Hebraei nonnulli, velut R. Saadias, Nachmanides, Chasdai, & plures alii, resurrectionis finem esse, ut omnes sistantur judicio, ultimam mercedem accepturi, quæ בעולם הנשמות in mundo animarum non recipitur, cùm non permittat justitia Dei, ut cùm anima & corpus conjunctim Deo servive-rint, soli animæ, & non etiam corpori merces rependatur. Sed Abarbanel Præfat. ad Esaj. finem resurrectionis duplicem facit, unum Israeli proprium, alterum omnibus communem. Illum, ut pii Israelitæ, qui in captivitate & exilio tristitia oppressi & mortui fuerint, salutis Domini in liberatione futura participes fiant: hunc, ut Gentibus idola colentibus, & à fine creationis aberrantibus via recta patefiat, quando pios ad vitam, impios ad supplicia resuscitatos visuri, resurrectionis hoc miraculo exciti, non amplius idola culturi, sed ad finem creationis obtinendum omnibus viribus connixuri sint. Quasi resurrectionis miraculum post eandem superstitibus impiis convertendis infervitu-rum sit, quod delirium recitasse, refutasse est.
units.tr: With respect to God, it is the glory of his goodness, power, justice and wisdom. For by raising the dead he displays the same wisdom, power and goodness that he displayed in creating, Rom. IV. 17. Eph. I. 18. 19., and as the judge who is to come he makes known his justice; and God will be all in all, 1 Cor. XV. 28. With respect to man, it is the eternal life and happiness of the faithful, from which the resurrection to life, John V. 29., takes its name. With respect to both, there is the judgment, which for that reason is attributed to the resurrection as its cause [καθ' αὐτό]. For God will raise men up in order to judge all, to separate the grain from the chaff, the sheep from the goats, the pious from the impious, and finally to bring everything to clarity and to its ultimate end. Christ explains this more fully, Matt. XXV. 32 etc. Some Hebrew writers also admit this, such as R. Saadia, Nachmanides, Chasdai and many others: the end of the resurrection is that all may be brought before judgment to receive their final reward, which is not received in the world of souls [בעולם הנשמות], since the justice of God does not permit that, when soul and body have served God together, the reward should be paid to the soul alone and not also to the body. But Abarbanel, in his preface to Isaiah, makes the end of the resurrection twofold: one proper to Israel, the other common to all. The first is that pious Israelites who died oppressed by sorrow in captivity and exile may share in the Lord's salvation in the future deliverance; the second is that for the Gentiles who worship idols and have strayed from the end of creation, the straight way may be opened, when, seeing the pious raised to life and the impious raised to punishment, roused by this miracle of resurrection, they will no longer worship idols but will strive with all their strength to attain the end of creation. As if the miracle of resurrection would afterwards serve to convert the impious who survive! To recite this delirium is to refute it.

units.la: LXXXIII. Alterum adventantis Domini opus erit Judicium universale & ultimum, augustissimum ille actus, quo Christus judex universorum electos resuscitatos per Angelos suos ex toto mundo colliget, eosdemque à reprobis infidelibus separabit, & publica ac solenni sententia vitæ æternæ mox adeundæ, hæredes declarabit; reprobos vero morti æternæ mox etiam adeundæ mancipabit.
units.tr: LXXXIII. The second work of the coming Lord will be the Judgment, universal and final, that most august act by which Christ, the judge of all, will gather the raised elect from the whole world through his angels, separate them from the reprobate unbelievers, and by a public and solemn sentence declare them heirs of eternal life, which they are soon to enter; but the reprobate he will consign to eternal death, which they too are soon to undergo.

units.la: Differt enim à judicio particulari quovis, etiam privato illo, quod quisque statim post mortem subit; quando anima à corpore soluta Christo judici sistitur, & vel fidelis in Paradisum ilico transfertur: requiem à laboribus, refrigerium, πλέωσιν, gloriam, honorem & pacem experitur; vel infidelis in infernum detrusa excandescentiam, iram, oppressionem & angustiam patitur, Rom. II. 7. 8. 9. de quo judice agit S. Paulus, dicens: Fixum est homini semel mori, μετὰ δὲ τοῦτο κρίσις postea autem judicium, Hebr. IX. 27. Judicari enim debet, ut abeat in locum, & ad eum statum, in quo anima semper mansura est. Quale judicium etiam Gentiles agnoverunt, sed in inferno, judice Rhadamanto, instituendum. Unde Tertullianus Apol. c. ult. Ridemur, Deum prædicantes judicaturum. Sic enim & Poetæ & Philosophi tribunal apud inferos ponunt. Cùm tamen judicium illud sit particulare, occultum, in cujusque conscientia ilico post mortem peragendum, neque sit de toto homine, sed de ejus parte, anima; neque simul de omnibus, sed de singulis procedente tempore; convenit, ut huic judicium universale, publicum, manifestum, peremptorium, finale & consummatum, in novissimo die post corporum resurrectionem in publico totius orbis comitio & conspectu de toto homine, & singulis hominibus simul omnibus instituendum, succedat. Scitè enim Durandus in 4. Sent. Dist. 47. q. 1. observavit, hominem considerari ut personam singularem, & ut partem universitatis, ut personæ singulari judicium particulare in die mortis, occultum, ut personæ universitatis universale novissimo die palam exercendum imminere. Dies ille censorius, quo judicium isthoc instituetur, vocatur ἡμέρα κρίσεως dies judicii, Matth. X. 15. XII. 36. à Paraphraste Chaldæo in Psal. L. דינא רבא dies judicii magni; κρίσις μεγάλης ἡμέρας judicium magni diei, Jud. v. 6. Dies Dei, 2. Petr. III. 12. ἀποκατάστασις πάντων restitutio omnium, Act. III. 21.
units.tr: For it differs from any particular judgment, even that private one which each person undergoes immediately after death, when the soul, loosed from the body, is presented to Christ the judge, and the faithful is at once carried into Paradise, where he experiences rest from his labours, refreshment, fullness [πλέωσιν], glory, honour and peace, Rom. II. 7. 8. 9.; or the unbeliever, thrust down into hell, suffers wrath, anger, oppression and distress. Of this judge St. Paul speaks, saying: It is appointed for men once to die, but after this [μετὰ δὲ τοῦτο] judgment, Heb. IX. 27. For judgment must be passed so that one may go to a place and into that state in which the soul will remain for ever. The Gentiles too recognised such a judgment, but one to be held in hell, with Rhadamanthus as judge. Hence Tertullian, Apol. last chapter: We are laughed at, for proclaiming that God will judge. For thus the poets and the philosophers set a tribunal among the dead. Since, however, that judgment is particular and hidden, to be carried out in each one's conscience immediately after death, and concerns not the whole man but a part of him, the soul; and is not held for all together but for each one as time goes on; it is fitting that there should follow upon it the universal judgment, public, manifest, decisive, final and complete, to be held on the last day after the resurrection of the bodies, in the public assembly and sight of the whole world, concerning the whole man and all men together. For Durand, in 4 Sent. dist. 47 q. 1., rightly observed that man is considered both as a single person and as part of the universe: for the single person a particular judgment, hidden, impends on the day of death; for the person as part of the universe a universal judgment, to be exercised openly on the last day. That day of censure on which this judgment will be held is called ἡμέρα κρίσεως [day of judgment] dies judicii, Matt. X. 15, XII. 36; by the Chaldee paraphrast in Psal. L. דינא רבא [the great day of judgment] dies judicii magni; κρίσις μεγάλης ἡμέρας [judgment of the great day] judicium magni diei, Jude v. 6; Dies Dei [the day of God], 2 Pet. III. 12; ἀποκατάστασις πάντων [restitution of all things] restitutio omnium, Acts III. 21.

units.la: ἡμέρα ἐκείνη dies illa, Matth. VII. 22. XXIV. 36. 2. Thess. I. 10. κατ' ἐξοχὴν & ἐξαίρετως, quia magna illa, & ab omnibus accurate observanda dies est, quæ omnibus vitæ hujus diebus finem imponet; denique simpliciter ἡ ἡμέρα illa dies, 1. Cor. III. 13. 1. Thess. V. 4. quia nulla intercipietur nocte, neque ulla vespera eum limite circumscribet.
units.tr: ἡμέρα ἐκείνη [that day] dies illa, Matt. VII. 22, XXIV. 36, 2 Thess. I. 10; by pre-eminence and above all others, because it is that great day, to be carefully observed by all, which will put an end to all the days of this life; and finally simply ἡ ἡμέρα [the day] illa dies, 1 Cor. III. 13, 1 Thess. V. 4, because no night will intervene and no evening will bound it with its limit.

units.la: LXXXIV. Futurum quandoque esse ejusmodi judicium universale in Scripturis tes-tatissimum est.
units.tr: LXXXIV. That there will one day be such a universal judgment is most abundantly attested in Scripture.

units.la: Nam mox ab initio mundi Caino Deus illud insinuavit, dicens: Si non bene feceris לפתח חטאת רבץ peccatum ad fores cubat, tibi adhærescit, puniendum, judicandum quandoque, nisi respueris, Genes. IV. 7. Tum & septimus ab Adamo, Enochus prophetavit, dicens: Ecce venit Dominus cum Sanctis millibus, ut faciat judicium de omnibus, & ut redarguat omnes impios de omnibus operibus ipsorum, quæ impiè egerunt, & de omnibus duris, quæ locuti sunt contra ipsum peccatores impii, Jud. v. 14. 15. de qua Prophetia suprà, alibique etiam pluscula diximus. Abrahamus quinetiam ad Angelum Jehovam, Filium Dei: An judex totius terræ non faciet judicium? Genes. XVIII. 25. Deus ipse in Cantico celebri Mosis: Illud pugno conclusum est apud me, obsignatum in thesauris meis. Mea est vindicta & retributio ad tempus, quo nutabit pes eorum. Judicabit Jehova populum suum. Videte, quòd ego is, & non est Deus mecum. Ego interficio & vivifica, & nemo eripiet ex manu mea, Deut. XXXII. 34. 35. 36. 39. Quibus verbis & judicium particulare urbis Sodomæ proprie dictæ, & spiritualis, id est, Romæ Antichristianæ ceu pignus & prodromus universalis; & universale, vivificationi mortuorum succedaneum, ex quo nemo impios eripiet, describitur. David: Dominus paravit ad judicium solium suum. Ipse judicabit orbem in justitia; judicabit populos in rectitudine, Psal. IX. 8. 9. Veniet Deus, & non silebit. Ignis coram eo vorabit. Advocabit Cœlos & terram, ut judicet populum suum, ibid. L. 3. &c. Ubi sub particularis judicii Judæorum Evangelium rejicientium schemate non obscurè universale involvitur. Veniet Dominus ad judicandum terram, judicabit orbem in justitia, & populos in rectitudine, ibid. XCVIII. 9. Anna in Cantico: Conterentur adversarii Domini, quia super eos è Cœlis tonabit: Judicabit Dominus fines terræ, 1. Sam. II. 10. Solomon: Justum & impium judicabit Dominus, Eccles. III. 17. Scito, quòd propter omnia hæc Deus te in judicium adducet, ibid. XI. 9. Omne opus vocabit Deus in judicium super omni habendum, sitne bonum vel malum, ibid. XII. 14. Pleni Prophetæ testimoniis judiciorum particularium, universalis prodromorum. Apud Esajam inprimis Dominus: Per me ipsum juravi, & exiit de ore meo verbum justitiæ, & non revertetur, quòd curvabitur mihi omne genu, Esaj. XLV. 23. Quæ verba ad extremum judicium S. Paulus trahit, dicens: Omnes sistemur ante tribunal Christi: scriptum est enim. Vivo ego, ait Dominus, mihi omne genu curvabitur, Rom. XIV. 10. 11. In Novo inprimis Testamento Spiritus S. oracula & numero plurima & pondere gravissima, & claritate disertissima habentur. Extantiora pauca delibemus. Multi dicent mihi in illa die, Domine, Domine, &c. Matth. VII. 22. Tolerabilius erit terræ Sodomæ & Gomorrhæ & Gommorrha in die judicii, quàm vobis, ibid. XI. 22. Ninevitæ surgent in judicio. Regina Austri surget in judicio, &c. ibid. XII. 41. 42. Integer judicii processus, Matth. XXV. 31. &c. describitur. Judicii dies repentina superveniet, tanquam laqueus in omnes, qui sedent in superficie terræ, Luc. XXI. 34. Pater omne judicium dedit Filio, &c. Joh. V. 22. Præcepit nobis Deus testificari, quòd ipse, Jesus Nazarenus, constitutus est à Deo judex vivorum & mortuorum, Actor. X. 42. Ideo etiam Apostolus coram Felice de judicio futuro disseruit, sed parum ad palatum ejus, ibid. XXIV. 25. Idem: An putas, quòd effugies judicium Dei? Secundum duritiem tuam & cor impœnitens thesaurizas tibi iram in die iræ & revelationis justi judicii Dei, Rom. II. 3. 5. Omnes nos manifestari oportet coram tribunali Christi, ut referat unusquisque secundum ea, quæ per corpus gessit, sive bonum, sive malum, 2. Cor. V. 10. Justum est apud Deum, retribuere afflictionem iis, qui vos affligunt; vobis verò, qui affligimini, relaxationem nobiscum, cùm patefiet Dominus Jesus de Cœlo, cum flamma ignis, infligens ultionem iis, qui Deum non nôrunt, &c. 2. Thess. I. 6. &c. Testificor coram Deo & Domino Jesu Christo, qui judicaturus est vivos & mortuos, per adventum & Regnum ejus, &c. 2. IV. 1. Meritò igitur judicium æternum, tot quippe oraculis, quot vix aliud dogma in V. & N. T. testatum, idem S. Paulus inter fundamenta religionis, Hebr. VI. 1. posuit; & Symbola, Apostolicum & Nicænum illud apertis verbis confitentur. Suffragantur enim eidem etiam prægnantes rationes petitæ tum à justitia Dei, quia justum est apud Deum affligentes reddere iis, qui affligunt, & relaxationem iis, qui affliguntur, 2. Thess. I. 6. quòd cùm nec in hac vita, in qua mali bona capiunt, & boni malis affliguntur: nec statim post mortem in judicio particulari plenè & perfectè fiat, corpore in pulvere jacente, necesse est fieri in judicio novissimo, quando anima cum corpore postliminio conjungetur: tum à veritate & immutabilitate Dei, quia, uti scite Augustinus Epist. 42. loquitur: Omnia alia, quæ futura prædixerat Spiritus S. in Scripturis, evenerunt, etiam illa, quæ de adventu Christi ad judicium prædixit, evenient: Tum à conscientiæ testimonio, utpote quæ attestatur, cogitationibus invicem accusantibus & defendentibus; quale testimonium sine judicio Dei, quo in die illo judicabit occulta hominum, invalidum esset, Rom. II. 15. 16. & cujus testimonii magna in utramque partem vis est, ut neque timeant, qui nihil commiserint, & poenam atque judicium semper ante oculos versari putent, qui peccarunt: tum ab universitatis natura, quæ multò minus quàm domus vel civitas judicio carere potest: tum à nexu resurrectionis & judicii, quia resurgent mortui, ut judicentur, & resurrectio vel vitæ, vel judicii, Joh. V. 29. tum ab anxia universali expectatione piorum omnium, clamantium: Veni Domine Jesu, Apoc. XXII. 17. cujusmodi suspiria tenues in auras non evanescunt, sed Christi ad judicium adventum provocant & maturant; cùm etiam illi, qui primitias Spiritus S. acceperunt, in se ipsis suspirent, expectantes adoptionem, redemptionem corporis plenariam, Rom. VIII. 23. tum denique à Legis promulgatione, utpote quam Deus non tantùm in creatione tabulis cordis humani inscripsit, sed etiam in monte Sinai solenniter promulgavit, & præmiorum promissione, poenarum comminatione sanxit. Quæ promulgatio sine ejusdem executione judiciali vanissima foret. Quicunque sine lege peccarunt, sine lege peribunt. Qui in lege peccarunt, per legem judicabuntur, ibid. II. 12. Taceo non Poëtarum duntaxat gentilium carmina, sed etiam Philosophorum quorundam libros, quibus de judicio ultimo sententiæ consignatæ reperiuntur: ad quas passim Patres, Justinus Paræn. I. ad Gent. Theophilus Antiochenus lib. II. ad Autol. Athenagoras Legat. pro Christ. aliique provocant. Qui etiam pro judice vivorum & mortuorum Christo, suos divos judices, Æacas, Minoas, Rhadamantos, & Divam Rhamnusiam, fandi atque nefandi ultricem, substituerunt. Ac licèt ex sacris Scripturis de hac re per qualemcunque traditionem Gentiles audivisse aliquid inficiandum non sit; illud tamen etiam constat, præcipuo argumento hoc illos fuisse usos, quòd bona malis, & mala bonis in hac vita plerunque obtingant, neque Divinæ justitiæ ratio constare posiit, si post mortem aliud & supremum judicium nullum superfit. Sed plura ejusmodi traditionis & rationis de judicio ultimo apud Gentiles post Augustinum Steuchum de perenni Philosoph. lib. IX. 19. &c. Doctiss. Pfannerus Syst. Theol. Gent. cap. 20. collegit.
units.tr: For right from the beginning of the world God gave Cain this intimation, saying: If you do not do well, sin lies crouching at the door [לפתח חטאת רבץ], it will cling to you, to be punished and judged at some time, unless you reject it, Gen. IV. 7. Then Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying: Behold, the Lord comes with thousands of his saints, to execute judgment on all, and to convict all the ungodly of all their works, which they have done ungodly, and of all the harsh things which ungodly sinners have spoken against him, Jude v. 14, 15. We have spoken of this prophecy above and elsewhere in more detail. Abraham too said to the Angel Jehovah, the Son of God: Will not the judge of all the earth do right? Gen. XVIII. 25. God himself, in the famous song of Moses: This is laid up with me, sealed among my treasures. Vengeance and recompense are mine, for the time when their foot shall slip. Jehovah will judge his people. See that I am he, and there is no God with me. I kill and I make alive, and no one shall snatch out of my hand, Deut. XXXII. 34, 35, 36, 39. In these words both the particular judgment of the city of Sodom properly so called, and the spiritual Sodom, that is, Antichristian Rome, as a pledge and forerunner of the universal judgment, are described; and the universal judgment, which takes the place of the resurrection of the dead, from which no one will snatch the wicked away. David: The Lord has prepared his throne for judgment. He himself will judge the world in righteousness; he will judge the peoples in uprightness, Ps. IX. 8, 9. God will come and will not keep silent. Fire will devour before him. He will call heaven and earth to judge his people, ibid. L. 3, etc. Here the universal judgment is not obscurely wrapped within the figure of the particular judgment of the Jews who rejected the Gospel. The Lord will come to judge the earth; he will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in uprightness, ibid. XCVIII. 9. Hannah in her song: The adversaries of the Lord shall be broken, for he will thunder against them from heaven; the Lord will judge the ends of the earth, 1 Sam. II. 10. Solomon: God will judge the righteous and the wicked, Eccles. III. 17. Know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment, ibid. XI. 9. God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it be good or evil, ibid. XII. 14. The Prophets are full of testimonies to particular judgments, which are forerunners of the universal. Above all in Isaiah the Lord himself: I have sworn by myself, and the word of righteousness has gone out of my mouth and shall not return, that to me every knee shall bow, Isa. XLV. 23. St. Paul applies these words to the last judgment, saying: For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ; for it is written, As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, Rom. XIV. 10, 11. In the New Testament especially the oracles of the Holy Spirit are found in great number, of the greatest weight and most explicit clarity. Let us consider a few of the more prominent. Many will say to me on that day, Lord, Lord, etc., Matt. VII. 22. It will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for you, ibid. XI. 22. The men of Nineveh will rise up in the judgment. The queen of the South will rise up in the judgment, etc., ibid. XII. 41, 42. The whole course of judgment is described in Matt. XXV. 31, etc. The day of judgment will come suddenly, like a snare on all who dwell on the face of the earth, Luke XXI. 34. The Father has given all judgment to the Son, etc., John V. 22. God commanded us to testify that he, Jesus of Nazareth, has been appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead, Acts X. 42. For this reason the Apostle also, before Felix, discoursed of the future judgment, though it was little to his taste, ibid. XXIV. 25. Again: Do you suppose that you will escape the judgment of God? Because of your hardness and your impenitent heart, you store up for yourself wrath on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, Rom. II. 3, 5. We must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil, 2 Cor. V. 10. It is righteous with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you, and to give relief to you who are afflicted, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with the flame of fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God, etc., 2 Thess. I. 6, etc. I charge you before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who is to judge the living and the dead, by his appearing and his kingdom, etc., 2 Tim. IV. 1. Rightly, therefore, the same St. Paul has placed eternal judgment among the foundations of religion, Heb. VI. 1, since it is attested by as many oracles as almost any other doctrine in the Old and New Testaments; and the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds confess it in plain words. Weighty reasons drawn from several sources also support the same doctrine: from the justice of God, since it is righteous with God to repay affliction to those who afflict, and relief to those who are afflicted, 2 Thess. I. 6. Since this is not fully and perfectly done in this life, in which the wicked obtain good things and the good are afflicted with evils, nor immediately after death in the particular judgment, while the body lies in the dust, it must necessarily be done in the final judgment, when the soul will be restored to the body by resurrection. From the truth and immutability of God, because, as Augustine rightly says in Epistle 42: All the other things which the Holy Spirit had foretold in the Scriptures have come to pass; so also those things which he foretold about the coming of Christ to judgment will come to pass. From the testimony of conscience, since it bears witness, as thoughts accuse and defend one another; such testimony would be powerless without the judgment of God, by which on that day he will judge the secrets of men, Rom. II. 15, 16. Its force is great in both directions, so that those who have done nothing wrong need not fear, and those who have sinned must think that punishment and judgment are always before their eyes. From the nature of the universe, which can much less than a household or a city be without judgment. From the connection between resurrection and judgment, because the dead will rise to be judged, and the resurrection is either of life or of judgment, John V. 29. From the anxious universal expectation of all the godly, crying out: Come, Lord Jesus, Rev. XXII. 17. Such sighs do not vanish into thin air, but call forth and hasten the coming of Christ to judgment; since even those who have received the firstfruits of the Spirit groan within themselves, waiting for adoption, the full redemption of the body, Rom. VIII. 23. Finally, from the promulgation of the Law, since God not only wrote it on the tables of the human heart in creation, but also solemnly promulgated it on Mount Sinai, and confirmed it with the promise of rewards and the threat of punishments. Such a promulgation would be utterly vain without its judicial execution. Whoever has sinned without law will perish without law; and whoever has sinned under law will be judged by law, ibid. II. 12. I pass over the poems not only of the Gentile poets, but also the books of certain philosophers, in which sentences concerning the final judgment are found. The Fathers, Justin in Exhortation I to the Greeks, Theophilus of Antioch in Book II to Autolycus, Athenagoras in Embassy for the Christians, and others, appeal to these everywhere. The Gentiles also set up their own divine judges, Aeacus, Minos, Rhadamanthus, and the goddess Rhamnusia, avenger of right and wrong, in place of Christ as judge of the living and the dead. And although one must not deny that the Gentiles heard something on this matter from the sacred Scriptures by some kind of tradition, it is also certain that they used this as their chief argument: that in this life good things commonly fall to the wicked and evil things to the good, and that the order of divine justice cannot stand if there is no other and final judgment after death. Steuchus, in On the Perennial Philosophy, Book IX, 19, etc., after Augustine, and the most learned Pfanner, in System of Theology of the Gentiles, chapter 20, have gathered many more instances of such tradition and reasoning about the last judgment among the Gentiles.

units.la: LXXXV. Sed obstrepunt tamen veritati huic captali non pauci, Philosophi inprimis Epicurei & Stoici, Actor. XVII. 18. 31. 32. aliique Æternales dicti; & hæretici veteres & recentiores. Inter veteres Dositheani, Samaritani, Prodianitæ, Seleuciano-rum & Hermenitarum soboles, Manichæi, Borboriani, Gnostici, Floriani, similisque farinæ alii, testibus Philastrio, Augustino, aliisque judicium ultimum assa voce abnegarunt, ut carni fibulas licentius laxarent. Recentiores veteribus suffragantes Sociniani inprimis sunt, qui licèt judicium ultimum verbis profiteantur, reapse tamen illud tollunt. Nam animam, cùm homo desierit vivere, fortasse per vicariam animam, & corpus per vicarium corpus glorificari, aut judicari: impios verò solos in adventu Christi superstites, annihilatis reliquis omnibus, cùm judicati fuerint, esse desinere, inter illorum est. Quale verò sine poena & noxa caput ipsum sequente, judicium est? Atqui horrenda illa expectatio judicii,& fervor ignis, qui devoraturus est adversarios, Hebr. X. 27. & ultio infligenda in patefactione Domini Jesu è Cœlo cum flammante igne, 2. Thess. I. 6. 7. 8. denuntiatur, quantisper hodiernus dies nominatur, non solis in judicio superstitibus, sed hodie viventibus, & contra verbum prædicatum cor obdurantibus, Hebr. III. 7–15. ea lege, ut soli verè resipiscentes iram venturam effugiant, Matth. III. 7. 1. Thess. I. 10. Novit enim Dominus injustos in diem judicii puniendos servare, 2. Petr. II. 9. Ludibrium aliàs Thessalonicensibus debuisset Apostolus, quando, cum tanto zelo tunc viventibus impiis (à quibus persecutiones & afflictiones pii sustinebant) expectationem
units.tr: LXXXV. Yet not a few oppose this truth, chiefly the philosophers, the Epicureans and Stoics (Acts 17:18, 31, 32), and others called Eternalists, along with heretics both ancient and modern. Among the ancients, the Dositheans, Samaritans, Prodianites, the offspring of the Seleucians and Hermenians, Manichaeans, Borborians, Gnostics, Florians and others of the same stripe, according to the testimony of Philastrius, Augustine and others, openly denied the last judgment, so that they might loosen the reins on the flesh more freely. Among the more recent, the Socinians chiefly support the ancients: although they profess the last judgment in words, in fact they remove it. For they hold that when a man has ceased to live, the soul is perhaps glorified or judged through a vicarious soul, and the body through a vicarious body, and that the wicked alone, who survive until the coming of Christ, cease to exist once all the rest have been annihilated and they have been judged. But what kind of judgment is it, without punishment or harm to the one being judged? Yet that dreadful expectation of judgment, and the fervour of fire that is to devour the adversaries (Heb. 10:27), and the vengeance to be inflicted at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with flaming fire (2 Thess. 1:6-8), are proclaimed as applying to the present day, not only to those who will survive to the judgment but to those living today who harden their hearts against the word preached (Heb. 3:7-15), on the condition that only those who truly repent escape the wrath to come (Matt. 3:7; 1 Thess. 1:10). For the Lord knows how to keep the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment (2 Pet. 2:9). The Apostle would have made a mockery of the Thessalonians if, while the impious were then living with such zeal (by whom the godly endured persecutions and afflictions), he had held out to them the expectation

units.la: Et adversus infideles veteres & novos, Socinianos inprimis, vindicatur. nem ultionis in die illo novissimo, 2. Thess. I. 6. 7. intonuit, & mox eosdem ὑπερ τῆς παρουσίας Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, καὶ ἡμῶν ἐπισυναγωγῆς ἐπ' αὐτὸν per adventum Domini Jesu Christi, & nostri ad eum aggregationem obsecrat, ne seducи se patiantur ullo modo à quoquam, ut opinentur, propediem instare diem illum Christi, 2. Thess. II. 1. 2. Neque etiam obstat, quòd Christus dixit; Nunc est judicium mundi, Joh. XII. 31. quia sermo est de judicio particulari Judæorum obduratorum, quos post longam patientiam & frustra expectatos tandiu pœnitentiæ fructus, Esaj. V. 3. 4. judicare constituit. Revelatur ira Dei è Cœlo in omnem impietatem & injustitiam hominum, veritatem in injustitia detinentium, Rom. I. 18. Severum certè judicium fuit, quando Deus decrevit, ut qui justitiam propriam volunt constituere, & se ipsos adversus Evangelium obfirmant, non amplius ferant nomen populi Dei, & omnis materia gloriationis eorum dissipetur & profligetur. Infidelitate sua effractisunt, ibid. XI. 20. Qui porrò credit non judicatur; qui non credit, is ἤδη κέκριται jam judicatus est, quod non credidit in nomen unigeniti Filii Dei, Joh. III. 18. quia credens non condemnatur, sed Regni Christi, vitæ & cœlestis gloriæ hæres efficitur; & qui non credit, jam positus est ad iram & judicium, non ad salutem, 1. Petr. II. 8. 1. Thess. V. 9. & seipsum condemnat, quatenus se vita æterna non dignum judicat, Act. XIII. 46. Sed hæc anticipatio quædam erit judicii, quod in ultimo die pronuntiabitur. Cùm enim credere in nomen Filii Dei, sit fidem ei, ceu testi fideli & mentiri nescio, habere, & confidere ipsius merito & potentiæ ad sperandum vitam æternam, qui non credit, neutrum facit, adeoque se indignum salute judicat, se condemnat, & αὐτοκατάκριτος ἐστί; talisque etiam in ultimo judicio promulgabitur.
units.tr: Also vindicated against the unbelievers, both old and new, the Socinians above all. ...of vengeance on that last day (2 Thess. 1:6-7), and soon after he begs the same people, "for the coming [ὑπὲρ τῆς παρουσίας] of our Lord Jesus Christ, and our gathering together to him" (2 Thess. 2:1-2), that they should not allow themselves to be led astray in any way by anyone, as if that day of Christ were imminent. Nor does it stand in the way that Christ said, "Now is the judgment of this world" (John 12:31), because the reference is to the particular judgment of the hardened Jews, whom God determined to judge after a long patience and after the fruit of repentance had been looked for in vain for so long (Isa. 5:3-4). "The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness" (Rom. 1:18). It was certainly a severe judgment when God decreed that those who wish to establish their own righteousness and harden themselves against the gospel should no longer bear the name of the people of God, and all the material of their boasting should be scattered and destroyed. "They were broken off through unbelief" (ibid. 11:20). "He who believes is not condemned; but he who does not believe is already judged [ἤδη κέκριται], because he has not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God" (John 3:18). For the one who believes is not condemned, but becomes an heir of the kingdom of Christ, of life and of heavenly glory; and he who does not believe is already "appointed to wrath and judgment, not to salvation" (1 Pet. 2:8; 1 Thess. 5:9), and condemns himself, inasmuch as he judges himself "unworthy of eternal life" (Acts 13:46). Yet this is a certain anticipation of the judgment that will be pronounced on the last day. For to believe in the name of the Son of God is to have faith in him as a faithful witness who cannot lie, and to trust in his merit and power in hoping for eternal life. He who does not believe does neither, and so judges himself unworthy of salvation, condemns himself, and is "self-condemned" [αὐτοκατάκριτος]; and such a one will also be pronounced so at the last judgment.

units.la: LXXXVI. Judex erit universa S. Trinitas, auctoritate & potestate, speciatim Christus, non ut testis duntaxat, uti Muhammed Alcor. Sur. 49. blasphemat; sed exercitio, visibili judicatura & imperio; quia illi omnis potestas, & omne judicium à Patre datum est; & judicandi potestas pars muneris ejus Regii est, quæ respectu fidelium à gratia Mediatoris; respectu infidelium à dominio à Patre ipsi concessō provenit. Pater non judicat quemquam, sed omne judicium dedit Filio, Joh. V. 22. Potestatem dedit ei judicandi, ὅτι υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ἐστί, quia filius hominis est, ib. v. 27. Statuit Deus diem, quo juste judicaturus est orbem habitabilem in justitia, per virum eum, quem definivit, fide palam omnibus facta, quando ex mortuis eum resuscitavit, Act. XVII. 31. Dei Patris nempe voluntas est, ut secundum Filii voluntatem vivant & salventur, quos ipse vivere & salvari vult; & judicentur, quibus ipse satisfactionem suam non dat; utque ii, qui justitiæ ejus participes sunt, vivant, qui ea vacant, moriantur. Quo sensu Pater neminem judicat, nempe absque Filio. Consilium enim hoc Pacis est, quod est inter ambos, nempe Jehovam & virum Germen, Zach. VI. 13. Et dedit sic Pater Filio τῷ κρίσιν πᾶσαν judicium omne, non abdicando quicquam, quia voluntate & nutu Patris judicabit Filius, & utriusque una voluntas & nutus est, sed dando, seu communicando non partem judicii, vel judicandos quosdam, sed judicium totum, ὀλικῶς, πολεῖς & in universum, idque, quia Filius hominis est, Joh. V. 27. Nam nisi Θεάνθρωπω judicium tale dari non poterat. Voluntas enim Dei est consentanea ipsius gratiæ; qua Filium nobis Sponsorem & Mediatorem Testamenti, Sacerdotem, Intercessorem, Dominum, Fratrem, Sponsum & Caput dedit, qui habet δικαίωμα τῆς νόμου ad nos justificandum. Quæ gratia non aliud postulat, quàm ut idem suos intercessione sua salvet, & hostes suos condemnet. Manifestum ita est, judicandi potestatem talem Christo secundum utramque naturam competere, neque sine alterutra competere posse; quia nisi Deus nec jus in omnes habere, nec cœlesti authoritate & imperio & sapientia ad cordium secreta & tenebras perrimandas, sententiámque de genere humano pronuntiandam, & sine provocatione exequendam defungi: nisi homo nec peccatum condemnare; nec morte sua peculium aliquod sibi acquirere, in quod vindicandum ab interitu jus haberet; nec visibili Majestate, in nubibus, tanquam in tribunali, comparere posset. Non tamen Christus judicabit, ut judex delegatus, sicut Jovem filiis suis Minoi & Rhadamanto vices istas delegasse, Plato in Gorgia finxit; quæ Socinianorum blasphemia est; sed ut principalis, quia ut Θεάνθρωπος. Licet enim visibilis manifestatio, & sententiæ dictio secundum humanam naturam futura sit; tamen robur & vis sententiæ & potestas ἀνθρωπολογικὴ omnis principaliter non ab humana, sed à Divina natura erit. LXXXVII. Solus Christus judicium & sententiam feret, non cum ipso vel Angeli, vel Sancti, puta Patriarchæ, Prophetæ, Apostoli, vel Deipara Virgo. Nam Angelis quidem Christus utetur, velut satellitibus & apparitoribus, qui operam suam in congregatione judicandorum, & segregatione judicatorum navabunt. Matth. XXIV. 31. XXV. 32. Sancti vero Apostoli sedebunt super duodecim thronos, judicantes duodecim tribus Israelis, ibid. XIX. 28. non quoad personas, sed quoad doctrinam ipsorum, qua etiam post ascensionem Christi terram Israelis velut anathemate percusserunt, & in ultimo judicio impios omnes ferient & percellent. Sancti vero omnes mundum judicaturi, 1. Cor. VI. 2. 3. putantur, tum quatenus in & cum Christo capite, tanquam corporis ejus membra, sententiam ferent: tum quatenus sententiam Christi, & judicium omne, ceu justum prædicabunt & approbabunt; tum quatenus comparatione vitæ ipsorum cum vita injustorum, justitia judicis magis manifestabitur, quomodo Regina Austri, & Ninevitæ Judæos infideles damnabunt. Matth. XII. 41. 42. Addit Thomas, judicaturos eosdem mundum, quatenus judicium Christi iis, qui judicabuntur, manifestabunt, quod plane ἀδηλον est. Cùmque etiam judicium, quod Sanctis vulgò tribuitur, admodum ἀχυρόλογον fit, & sancti non judices sessuri, sed inter oves apparituri, & coram tribunali Christi omnes staturi sint, rectius forte alii hæc non de judicio extremo, sed de judicio & regno populo Sanctorum excelsorum in hoc seculo promisso, Dan. VII. 18. 27. interpretantur. Nam & illud præterea scopo Apostoli aprime quadrat. Et tum maximè mundus {y} Judex Deus triunus erit. dus à Sanctis judicatur, quando à profanitate, injustitia, infidelitate, malis moribus & idololatria ad Deum convertitur, quod per תוכחת seu ἔλεγχον demonstrationem & correptionem factum est, & amplius fiet, Efaj. II.4. Joh. XVI. 7-12. Eodem modo etiam Angelos Sancti judicant, 1.Cor. VI.3. quando Diabolum sanguine & verbo suo vincunt, Apoc. XII.10.11. & de spiritu, per quem Antichristus loquitur, judicant, spiritus probant, 1.Joh. IV.1. Etiam Sanctorum sermo, fides, charitas & sincera resipiscentia Diaboli damnatio in ultimo judicio erit: sicut Ninevitarum resipiscentia, & Reginæ Austri zelus infidelium, quibus Christus prædicatus est, generationem pravam ἐν τῇ κρίσει in judicio κατακρινῦσι condemnabunt, Matth. XII.41.42.
units.tr: LXXXVI. The judge will be the whole Holy Trinity, with authority and power; in particular Christ, not merely as a witness, as Muhammad blasphemes in the Qur'an (Sura 49), but in the exercise of a visible judging and rule, because "all authority and all judgment have been given to him by the Father" and the power of judging is part of his kingly office, which with respect to believers arises from the grace of the Mediator, and with respect to unbelievers from the dominion conferred on him by the Father. "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son" (John 5:22). "He gave him authority to judge, ὅτι υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ἐστί [because he is the Son of Man]" (ibid. v. 27). "God has appointed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, by the man whom he has appointed, having given assurance of this to all by raising him from the dead" (Acts 17:31). It is indeed the will of the Father that those whom he wills to live and be saved should live and be saved according to the will of the Son, and that those to whom he does not give his satisfaction should be judged, and that those who share in his righteousness should live, while those who lack it should die. In this sense "the Father judges no one", namely apart from the Son. "For the counsel of peace is between the two", namely "Jehovah and the Man, the Branch" (Zech. 6:13). Thus the Father has given to the Son "all judgment" [τῷ κρίσιν πᾶσαν], not by abdicating anything, since the Son judges by the will and nod of the Father, and their will and nod are one; but by giving, or communicating, not a part of the judgment or certain persons to be judged, but the whole judgment, "wholly, entirely and in universal terms" [ὀλικῶς], and this because he is the Son of Man (John 5:27). For such judgment could not be given to a God-man [Θεάνθρωπω] otherwise. For the will of God is consistent with his grace, by which he has given us the Son as Surety and Mediator of the covenant, Priest, Intercessor, Lord, Brother, Bridegroom and Head, who has "the right of the law" [δικαίωμα τῆς νόμου] to justify us. This grace asks nothing more than that he should save his own by his intercession and condemn his enemies. It is therefore evident that this power of judging belongs to Christ according to both natures, and cannot belong to him without either: for unless he were God, he could not have right over all, nor discharge the office, with heavenly authority, power and wisdom, of searching the secrets and darkness of hearts, pronouncing sentence on the human race, and executing it without appeal; and unless he were man, he could not condemn sin, nor acquire for himself by his death any possession over which he would have a right to claim deliverance from destruction, nor appear in visible majesty, in the clouds, as on a tribunal. Yet Christ will not judge as a delegated judge, as Plato in the Gorgias fancied that Jove had delegated these duties to his sons Minos and Rhadamanthus; that is the blasphemy of the Socinians. He will judge as the principal judge, because he is God-man [ὡς Θεάνθρωπος]. For although the visible manifestation and the pronouncing of the sentence will be according to the human nature, nevertheless the strength and force of the sentence, and all the power [ἀνθρωπολογικὴ] of it, will principally come not from the human but from the divine nature. LXXXVII. Christ alone will pass judgment and sentence; neither angels nor saints, such as patriarchs, prophets, apostles, or the Virgin Mother of God, will sit with him. For Christ will indeed use the angels as attendants and officers, who will labour in gathering those to be judged and separating those judged (Matt. 24:31; 25:32). The saints, the apostles, will sit "on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel" (ibid. 19:28); this refers not to persons but to their doctrine, by which, even after the ascension of Christ, they struck the land of Israel as with a curse, and in the last judgment they will strike and smite all the impious. Moreover, "all the saints will judge the world" (1 Cor. 6:2-3) is held to mean, first, that they will pronounce sentence in and with Christ the Head, as members of his body; second, that they will proclaim and approve the sentence and all the judgment of Christ as just; and third, that by comparing their lives with the lives of the unrighteous, the justice of the judge will be made more manifest, just as the Queen of the South and the Ninevites will condemn the unbelieving Jews (Matt. 12:41-42). Thomas adds that they will judge the world insofar as they will make manifest the judgment of Christ to those who are to be judged, which is plainly obscure. And since the judgment commonly attributed to the saints is quite inaccurate, and the saints will not sit as judges but will appear among the sheep and all stand before the tribunal of Christ, others perhaps more rightly interpret these words not of the last judgment but of the judgment and kingdom "promised to the people of the saints of the Most High in this age" (Dan. 7:18, 27). For that also fits the aim of the Apostle very well. And then the world will be judged by the saints when it is converted to God from profanity, injustice, unbelief, evil morals and idolatry; this was done through תוכחת, that is ἔλεγχος [demonstration and reproof], and will be done more fully (Isa. 2:4; John 16:7-12). In the same way the saints also judge the angels (1 Cor. 6:3), when they conquer the devil by their blood and their word (Rev. 12:10-11), and judge the spirit by which the Antichrist speaks, "testing the spirits" (1 John 4:1). The preaching, faith, love and sincere repentance of the saints will also be the condemnation of the devil at the last judgment, just as the repentance of the Ninevites and the zeal of the Queen of the South, the faith of those to whom Christ was preached, will condemn that evil generation "in judgment" [ἐν τῇ κρίσει] (Matt. 12:41-42).

units.la: LXXXVIII. Judicabit Christus vivos & mortuos: uti in Symbolo profitemur, hoc est, qui eo adventante, vel mortui jam, & ex morte resuscitati fuerint, vel in vivis erunt. Est enim Christus κριτὴς ζώντων καὶ νεκρῶν judex vivorum & mortuorum, Actor. X.42. ubi per vivos non vel animæ solæ, vel justi; nec per mortuos vel corpora sola & peccatores, quæ veterum quorundam, Diodori Tharsensis, Isidori Pelusiotæ, παραμονή est, sed mortui & superstites omnes intelliguntur. Omnes enim stabimus coram tribunali Christi, Rom. XIV.10. Unusquisque nostrum pro se rationem reddet, ibid. v.12. Omnes nos comparere oportet coram tribunali Christi, ut unusquisque reportet, quæ in corpore fecerit, sive bonum, sive malum, 2.Cor. V.10. Et judicium subibunt omnium bonorum æque atque malorum hominum actus tum boni, tum mali: Omne enim opus Deus adducet in judicium habendum de omni occulto sitne bonum, sive malum, Eccles. XII.14. Quod etiam processus judicii, Matth. XXV.32. &c. amplius confirmat. Etsi enim particularia judicia de singulis præcesserint, omnia tamen omnium in universali hoc judicio manifestentur oportet. In particularibus enim judiciis quisque judicatur ut privatus: in universali vero judicabitur, quatenus est civis cœlestis Hierosolymæ, vel civitatis Diaboli; & utriusque civitatis multitudo per generale hoc judicium tota simul in sedes sibi paratas mittetur. Et executio sententiæ per particulare judicium inchoatur, per universale consummabitur. Neque etiam recipienda est sententia Patrum, Lactantii, Hieronymi, Augustini, Gregorii, à judicio hoc infideles, Paganos, Judæos, hæreticos; nec non justos perfectos eximentium. Nam quoad infideles, non favere iis locum, Joh. III.18. Qui non credit, jam judicatus est; quo solo nituntur; supra vidimus. Addo, μὴ πιστεύοντα non credentem ne quidem solum infidelem, qui de Christo nihil audivit, sed omnes illos, qui non credunt in nomen Unigeniti Filii Dei, vel plane eum non cognoscunt, vel ei cognito ad salutem & vitam non confidunt, significare; & κρίνεσθαι judicari synecdochice politum videri pro condemnari. Inter perfectos vero Scholastici B. Mariam, quæ nunquam peccaverit, familiam ducere ajunt; adeoque approbationis duntaxat, non discussionis judicio judicari debeat. Sed id Scripturis & antiquitatis primævæ judicio repugnat. Et si in Maria eos ratio fugit, quanto magis decipiuntur in cæteris? Ne veni, in judicium cum servo tuo, (extra Christum) quia apud te non justificatur vivens ullus, Psal. CXLIII. 2. Neque illud, quoad peccata etiam fidelium judicium ilthoc subitura, obstat, quod per justificationem tecta sunt; quia sententia illa justificationis & absolutionis in judicio ilthoc non retractabit, sed publice ac solenniter confirmabitur; & peccata eorum vel plane non, vel saltem non ad pudorem eorum, vulgabuntur, sed ita memorabuntur, conscizque mentes ferient, ut de adepta venia, publicaque absolutionis sententia immensum quantum gavisuri, & sibi æternum gratulaturi sint.
