Sed potissimum in judicio hoc erit, quod fidei & charitatis eorum fructus, ceu absolutionis testimonia, publice & propensissimè laudabuntur, & iis laudatis in possessionem æternæ vitæ immittentur, Matth. XXV.34. &c. LXXXIX. Neque homines duntaxat, sed etiam Angeli mali à Christo, & in ac cum eo à Sanctis in novissimo die judicabuntur. Si Deus Angelis, qui peccaverunt, non pepercit, sed in tartarum detrusos catenis caliginis (immutabili & ineluctabili tenebrarum statu) tradidit servatos ad judicium, 2.Pet. II.4. Angelos ad judicium magnæ diei vinculis æternis sub caligine servavit, Jud. v.6. Licet enim Angeli peccatores semper in pœna sint, nihilominus gravissima eorum pœna ad diem judicii usque differtur. Fallun-tur enim haud dubie Patres nonnulli, quibus visum est, dæmones hoc tempore plane à pœna immunes esse. Si enim animæ impiorum jam dum infernales cruciatus experiuntur, Angeli hominis seductores & homicidæ ab initio, à similibus pœnis immunes censeri non debent. Gradus pœnæ minores pœnam, ejusque gradus majores non tollunt. Et habet etiam Sathanas ante finem mundi abyssum, in quam subinde detruditur, Apoc. XX.3. Pœna saltem est, exulare à facie Dei, qui summum bonum est. Si igitur metus etiam κόλασιν tormentum habet, 1.Joh. IV.18. privatio rei optimæ tormento carere non potest. Amor enim deliciatur, & timor cruciat, atque torquet. Sed non propterea Angelorum malorum pœnæ ante judicium ultimum consummantur, quia ipsi ad judicium magnæ diei servantur. Vincula & catenæ, quibus ante judicium captivi attinentur, nunc sunt illis ad custodiam, tum erunt ad supplicium & pœnam, nunc laxiora sunt, tum strictiora longe, & manifestiora etiam erunt. Quæ ad consolationem piorum inprimis faciunt, quia etsi nunc à Sathana & Angelis ejus vexantur, tamen tempus veniet, cum ipsi etiam à Deo & Sanctis omnibus judicabuntur, & æternæ damnationi mancipabuntur. XC. De judicii totius ratione & forma sapienter Augustinus de Civ. D. Lib. XX.3. judicavit. Quo modo atque ordine illud fit futurum, magis tunc docebit rerum experientia, quam nunc valet consequi ad perfectum hominem intelligentia. In Scriptura tamen sub idea judicii augustissimi conspicabiliter & magnificè exercendi describitur. Distinctè autem solennis ad judicium præparatio, & judicii ipsius administratio in ea describitur. Solennis ad judicium præparatio in eo consistet, quod & Christus judex sedebit super thronum Majestatis, sive gloriæ suæ, Matth. XIX. xxxx 2 28.
units.tr: LXXXVIII. Christ will judge the living and the dead, as we profess in the Creed. That is, those who are alive when he comes, and those who have already died and been raised from death, will all be judged. For Christ is κριτὴς ζώντων καὶ νεκρῶν [judge of the living and the dead], Acts 10.42, where by "the living" are meant not the souls alone or the righteous alone, and by "the dead" not the bodies alone or sinners alone (which is the view of certain older writers, Diodorus of Tarsus and Isidore of Pelusium, who take it as παραμονή [those who remain]). Rather, all the dead and all the survivors are meant. For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, Rom. 14.10. Each of us shall give account of himself, ibid. v.12. We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil, 2 Cor. 5.10. The deeds of all men, good and bad alike, will come under judgment: for God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good or evil, Eccl. 12.14. The course of the judgment in Matt. 25.32 and following confirms this further. For although particular judgments of individuals have gone before, nevertheless all men's deeds must be made manifest in this universal judgment. In particular judgments each is judged as a private person; but in the universal judgment he will be judged insofar as he is a citizen either of the heavenly Jerusalem or of the city of the Devil. The multitude of each city will be sent all together, by this general judgment, into the seats prepared for them. The execution of the sentence, begun in the particular judgment, will be completed in the universal one. Nor is the opinion of the Fathers, Lactantius, Jerome, Augustine and Gregory, acceptable, that unbelievers, pagans, Jews and heretics, and also the perfectly righteous, are exempt from this judgment. As for unbelievers, John 3.18 does not support them: He who does not believe is already judged; this is the only text on which they rely, as we saw above. I add that μὴ πιστεύοντα [not believing] signifies not only the unbeliever who has heard nothing of Christ, but all those who do not believe in the name of the only Son of God, either because they do not know him at all or, knowing him, do not trust in him for salvation and life. And κρίνεσθαι [to be judged] seems to be used by synecdoche in the sense of to be condemned. As for the perfectly righteous, the Scholastics say that the Blessed Virgin Mary, who never sinned, leads their company, and so she ought to be judged only by approval, not by examination. But this contradicts Scripture and the judgment of earliest antiquity. And if reason fails them in the case of Mary, how much more are they mistaken about the rest? Enter not into judgment with your servant (outside Christ), for in your sight no living man is justified, Ps. 143.2. Nor does it stand in the way, with regard to the sins even of the faithful who will undergo that judgment, that they have been covered by justification. For that sentence of justification and absolution will not be reversed in that judgment, but will be publicly and solemnly confirmed; and their sins will either not be published at all, or at least not to their shame. Rather, they will be recalled in such a way as to strike their consciences, so that they will rejoice immensely at the pardon obtained and the public sentence of absolution, and will eternally congratulate themselves. Yet chiefly in this judgment the fruits of their faith and love will be publicly and most warmly praised, as evidence of their absolution; and, so praised, they will be put into possession of eternal life, Matt. 25.34 and following. LXXXIX. Not only men but also evil angels will be judged by Christ on the last day, and by the saints together with him and in him. If God did not spare the angels who sinned, but cast them down into hell and delivered them into chains of darkness (in an unchangeable and inescapable state of gloom), to be kept until the judgment, 2 Pet. 2.4. He has kept the angels who did not keep their first estate, in everlasting chains under darkness, for the judgment of the great day, Jude v.6. For although sinful angels are always under punishment, their most grievous punishment is nevertheless deferred until the day of judgment. Certainly some Fathers are mistaken, who thought that demons at this time are wholly free from punishment. For if the souls of the wicked already suffer infernal torments, the angels, who were seducers and murderers of man from the beginning, ought not to be considered exempt from similar punishments. Lesser degrees of punishment do not remove punishment, nor do its greater degrees. Satan also has, before the end of the world, the abyss into which he is from time to time thrust, Rev. 20.3. At the very least it is a punishment to be exiled from the face of God, who is the highest good. If therefore fear has torment (κόλασιν), 1 John 4.18, then the deprivation of the best thing cannot be without torment. For love delights, while fear tortures and racks. But the punishments of the evil angels are not for this reason completed before the final judgment, though they themselves are kept for the judgment of the great day. The chains and bonds by which the captives are held before judgment are now for their custody; then they will be for punishment and torment. Now they are looser; then they will be far tighter, and they will also be more evident. These things especially serve the comfort of the godly: although now they are harassed by Satan and his angels, yet the time will come when those angels themselves will be judged by God and all the saints, and handed over to eternal damnation. XC. Augustine, in De Civitate Dei book 20, chapter 3, has wisely judged the manner and form of the whole judgment: In what manner and order this will happen will then be taught more by the experience of the facts than the intelligence of the perfect man can now grasp. Nevertheless, Scripture describes the judgment under the idea of a most august judgment, carried out in a visible and magnificent way. It describes distinctly both the solemn preparation for judgment and the administration of the judgment itself. The solemn preparation for judgment will consist in this: that Christ the judge will sit upon the throne of his majesty or glory, Matt. 19.28.

units.la: 28. XXV.31. qui thronus erit βῆμα tribunal illud, quo coram omnes manifestari oportet, 2.Cor. V.10. Rex enim & supremus judex cùm sit, throno & tribunali suo carere non potest, sive illud est dextra Dei, ad quam evectus est, quæ δεξιὰ τῆς μεγαλωσύνης ἐν ὑψηλοῖς dextra Majestatis in excelsis, Heb.I.3. appellatur; vel visibilis etiam, splendida & augusta illa nubes, in qua ex cœlo veniet. Coram hoc tribunali omnes homines congregabuntur, & quidem ministerio Angelorum, qui colligent electos ex omnibus quatuor ventis, ab extremo cœli usque ad extremum eorum, Matth.XXIV.31. A qua congregatione dies ille tempus ἐπισυναγωγῆς collectionis ad Christum, 2.Thess.II.1. appellatur. Ita omnes παραστήσονται) sistentur coram tribunali hoc, Rom. XIV.10. nempe tanquam judicandi, quomodo Pauli hostes eum παρεστῶτα stiterunt præsefto, Act.XXIII.32. imò & manifestabuntur, 2.Cor. V.10. quia nec occultationi, nec ὑποστολῇ fugæ locus erit. Tum impii montibus & petris dicent: Cadite super nos. & abscondite nos à facie sedentis supra thronum, & ab ira Agni, quoniam venit dies magnus iræ ipsius, & quis stare poterit? Apoc.VI.16.17. Sed fruitra, quia montes & petræ instar ceræ coram tali judice colliquescent, Psal. XCVII.5. Cùmque Majestas judicis permissura non sit, ut sine ullo reverentiæ signo totum hoc hominum omnium Concilium coram se compareat, omnes etiam statuendi ante hoc tribunal genu incurvabunt, Esaj. XLV.23. Rom. XIV.11. Congregati sic duas in partes separabuntur, altera ovium ad dextram, altera hædorum ad sinistram stante, Matth.XXV.32.33. Judicabit enim inter pecudem & pecudem, arietes & hircos, Ezech.XXXIV.17. Sicut enim in die, cùm in campum greges mittuntur, oves hoedis permixtæ συναγεται compascuæ sunt; at vespera separantur: ita hac in vita pii & impii in latissimo mundi campo commixti, in fine seculi separabuntur, & tam facili negotio separabuntur, quàm facilè pastor quivis oves suas ab hoedis separat. Et ipsa hæc collocatio, omniscientiæ & omnipotentiæ Christi testis omni exceptione major, sententiæ mox ferendæ præjudicium & præludium erit. Certum jam enim & irrefragabile causæ stantis & cadentis judicium Christus omniscius secus ac mortalis aliquis judex, animo suo præfinivit.
units.tr: 28. Matt. 25.31. This throne will be the βῆμα [judgment seat], that tribunal before which all must be made manifest, 2 Cor. 5.10. For since he is king and supreme judge, he cannot be without a throne and tribunal. This is either the right hand of God, to which he has been exalted, which is called the right hand of the Majesty on high (δεξιὰ τῆς μεγαλωσύνης ἐν ὑψηλοῖς), Heb. 1.3; or else the visible, bright and majestic cloud in which he will come from heaven. Before this tribunal all men will be gathered, and indeed by the ministry of angels, who will gather the elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other, Matt. 24.31. From this gathering that day is called the time of the ἐπισυναγωγὴ [gathering together] to Christ, 2 Thess. 2.1. So all will be set (παραστήσονται) before this tribunal, Rom. 14.10: namely as those to be judged, just as Paul's enemies set him (παρεστῶτα) before the governor, Acts 23.32. Indeed they will be made manifest, 2 Cor. 5.10, since there will be no room for concealment or for ὑποστολὴ [shrinking back] in flight. Then the wicked will say to the mountains and rocks: Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him who sits on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb; for the great day of their wrath has come, and who shall be able to stand? Rev. 6.16-17. But in vain, because mountains and rocks will melt like wax before such a judge, Ps. 97.5. And since the majesty of the judge will not permit this whole assembly of all men to appear before him without any sign of reverence, all who are to stand before this tribunal will also bow the knee, Isa. 45.23; Rom. 14.11. Thus gathered, they will be divided into two parts, the sheep on the right hand and the goats standing on the left, Matt. 25.32-33. For he will judge between cattle and cattle, rams and he-goats, Ezek. 34.17. Just as on a day when flocks are sent out into the field, the sheep and goats mixed together feed in the same pasture, but in the evening they are separated, so in this life the godly and the wicked, mingled together in the wide field of the world, will be separated at the end of the age, and separated as easily as any shepherd divides his sheep from the goats. And this very arrangement, a witness of the omniscience and omnipotence of Christ beyond all exception, will be the prejudgment and prelude of the sentence about to be pronounced. For Christ, being omniscient and unlike any mortal judge, has already settled in his mind the certain and irrefutable judgment on the cause of standing or falling.

units.la: XCI. Ad judicii administrationem causæ cognitio, sententiæ dictio & ejusdem executio pertinet. Causæ cognitio in revelatione omnium, quæ quisque per vitam universam cogitavit, dixit, fecit, confiteret. Cùmque Christus noverit omne quod in homine est, nec opus sit, ut quis testimonium de homine perhibeat, Joh.II.25. & coram eo omnia nuda, & oculis ejus resupinata sint, Heb.IV.13. nec testibus aliis, nec testium examine ullo, nec examine reis extorquendo opus erit. Sicut enim lux omnia, quæ hactenus in tenebris delituerant, revelat: ita multò magis lux Divinæ Majestatis & gloriæ, in qua Christus ad judicium veniet, conscientiæ hominis admota φωτισμὸς τὰ κρυπτὰ & σκότος καὶ φανερωσει τὰς βουλὰς τῶν καρδιῶν illustrabit occulta tenebrarum, & manifesta faciet consilia cordium; & tum laus erit unicuique a Deo, 1.Cor.IV.5. Nam odoratus timorem Domini, & non secundum auditam aurium suarum arguit, Esaj.XI.3. Oculi ejus
units.tr: XCI. The administration of judgment involves the examination of the case, the pronouncing of the sentence, and its execution. The examination of the case consists in the disclosure of everything that each person has thought, said, done, or confessed throughout his whole life. Since Christ knows all that is in a man, and there is no need for anyone to bear witness about a man (John 2:25), and all things are naked and laid open before his eyes (Heb. 4:13), there will be no need for other witnesses, for any examination of witnesses, or for extracting an admission from the accused. Just as light reveals all things that have hitherto lain hidden in darkness, so much more will the light of the divine majesty and glory, in which Christ will come to judgment, brought to bear upon the human conscience, "bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of the hearts" [φωτίσει τὰ κρυπτὰ τοῦ σκότους καὶ φανερώσει τὰς βουλὰς τῶν καρδιῶν]; and then each one will receive his praise from God (1 Cor. 4:5). For he will sense the fear of the Lord, and will not reprove according to what his ears have heard (Esaj.XI.3.). His eyes

units.la: sunt ut flamma ignis, Apoc. I.14. Et judicat secundum ea, quæ in homine sunt, Rom.II.16.28.29. Quædam enim vis erit Divina, qua fiet, ut cuique opera sua, bona vel mala, cuncta in memoriam revocentur, & mentis intuitu conscientia συμμαρτυροῦσα una testificante, mira celeritate cernantur. Accusabit vel excusabit scientia conscientiam, atque ita simul & singuli, & omnes judicabuntur. Quæ citri succo scribuntur, eorum nisi igni admotorum nulla notitia, vestigium nullum est. Sic plane dies manifestabit, quia in igne revelatur, & cujusque opus, quale fit, ignis (judicii) probabit, 1.Cor.III.13. Quatenus verò etiam peccata fidelium judicium hoc subitura sint, supra diximus. An verò ipsi peccatorum & malorum suorum in judicio recordaturi sint, piè & sapienter sic Augustinus, de Civ. D.Lib.XX.30. arbitratus est: Voluntas beatorum oblita culparum, oblita pœnarum, nec tamen ideo suæ liberationis oblita, ut liberatori suo sit ingrata. Quantum ergo attinet ad scientiam rationalem, memor præteritorum etiam malorum suorum, quantum autem ad experientis sensum, prorsus immemor. Nam & peritissimus medicus, sicut arte sciuntur, omnes fere morbos corporis novit, sicut autem corpore sentiuntur, plurimos nescit, quos ipse passus non est. Neque minùs elegānter Gregorius M. Enarrat. in Psal.88. Quomodo in æternum misericordias Dei canit, qui miseriæ non meminit? Quomodo autem plena beatitudo, si memoria reatus mentem tangit? sed sæpe læti tristium meminimus, & sani dolorum meminimus sine dolore, & inde amplius læti & grati sumus. Causæ cognitionem sententiæ dictio excipiet. Nam piis eam his verbis lætissimis dicet Christus: Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis à jactis mundi fundamentis, Matth. XXV.34. Impiis verò sævis & tristissimis his obnuntiabit. Ite maledicti in ignem æternum, qui paratus est Diabolo & Angelis ejus, ib.v.41. Quibus in verbis tergemina ἀντίθεσις est. Nam justis dicitur: Venite; injustis, discedite à me. illis: benedicti, his, maledicti: illis: Possidete Regnum: his, ite in ignem æternum. Non tamen sicut illi benedicti Patris. ita maledicti Patris vocantur, quia benedictionis Pater, maledictionis sibi quisque author est: neque sicuti illi possidere paratum Regnum; ita hi ire in ignem sibi, sed Diabolo & Angelis ejus paratum jubentur; quia atrocitatis pœnæ, quippe ipsi Diabolo decretæ, obnuntiatione impios, Diaboli semen, severus judex percellet. Sententia dicetur secundum normam, quæ verbum Dei, & Evangelium inprimis est. Sermo, quem ego locutus sum, ille judicabit eum in ultimo die, Joh. XII.48. Sermo puta ille, quem locutus est de justitia & salute, secundum id, quod antea dictum à Patre, & à Spiritu Dei Patriarchis & Prophetis revelatum est. Ille enim sermo est κεῖνος ἐνθυμήσεων καὶ ἐννοιῶν καρδίας judicans cogitationum & intentionum cordis, Heb.IV.12. In die ultimo judicabit Deus occulta hominum κατὰ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιόν μου secundum Evangelium meum, per Jesum Christum, Rom.II.16. Ubi Evangelium sive latiùs notat omnem doctrinam Christi & Apostolorum, adeóque etiam legalem, norma erit judicii adversos quoscunque etiam impios infideles, qui opus legis à Christo etiam & Apostolis explicatum, in cordibus suis scriptum habent: sive strictius
units.tr: They are like a flame of fire (Rev. 1:14). And he judges according to what is in a man (Rom. 2:16, 28, 29). For there will be a divine power by which everything that each person has done, good or evil, is called back to memory, and the conscience, bearing witness together with the mind's gaze [συμμαρτυροῦσα], will perceive it with remarkable speed. Knowledge will accuse or excuse conscience, and so all will be judged together and individually. Things written with citron juice are unknown and leave no trace unless they are held to the fire; so plainly the day will reveal them, because it is disclosed by fire, and the fire of judgment will test what sort of work each person's work is (1 Cor. 3:13). How far the sins of believers too will undergo this judgment, we have said above. Whether they themselves will remember their sins and evils at the judgment, Augustine has reasoned piously and wisely, in De Civitate Dei, book 20, chapter 30: "The will of the blessed forgets their faults and forgets their punishments, yet they are not therefore forgetful of their deliverance, so as to be ungrateful to their deliverer." So far as rational knowledge goes, they remember even their past evils; but so far as the sense of experience goes, they are altogether forgetful. For the most skilled physician, although he knows by his art nearly all the diseases of the body, does not know many of those which he himself has not suffered from in his body. Gregory the Great also says no less elegantly in his Enarrationes on Psalm 88: "How can one who does not remember misery sing of the mercies of God for ever? How can happiness be full if the memory of guilt touches the mind? But often we who are glad remember sad things, and we who are healthy remember our pains without pain, and so we become all the more glad and grateful." The pronouncement of the sentence follows the examination of the case. For Christ will say to the pious, in these most joyful words: "Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world" (Matt. 25:34). But to the impious he will announce these harsh and most sorrowful words: "Depart, cursed, into everlasting fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels" (ibid., v. 41). In these words there is a threefold antithesis. For to the righteous it is said, "Come"; to the unrighteous, "Depart from me"; to the former, "blessed"; to the latter, "cursed"; to the former, "Possess the kingdom"; to the latter, "Go into everlasting fire." Yet the blessed are not called blessed of the Father in the same way as the cursed are called cursed of the Father, because the Father is the author of blessing, while each person is the author of his own curse; nor, as the former are told to possess the kingdom prepared, are the latter told to go into fire for themselves, but they are ordered into the fire prepared for the devil and his angels; because the severe judge will strike down the wicked, the seed of the devil, with the pronouncement of the punishment of atrocity decreed for the devil himself. The sentence will be pronounced according to the norm, which is above all the Word of God and the Gospel. "The word that I have spoken," he says, "will judge him on the last day" (John 12:48). That is, the word which he spoke about righteousness and salvation, in accordance with what was previously spoken by the Father and revealed by the Spirit of God to the patriarchs and prophets. For that word is "a judge of the thoughts and intentions of the heart" [κριτικὸς ἐνθυμήσεων καὶ ἐννοιῶν καρδίας] (Heb. 4:12). On the last day God will judge the secrets of men "according to my Gospel, through Jesus Christ" (Rom. 2:16). Here the Gospel, taken more broadly, denotes all the teaching of Christ and the apostles, and so also the law, and will be the norm of judgment against all, even the impious and unbelieving, who have the work of the law, as explained by Christ and also by the apostles, written in their hearts; or, taken more strictly, the doctrine of faith and repentance will be the norm of judgment, both of absolving the faithful in Christ and of condemning the unbelievers, to whom Christ was preached and for whose judgment also he came into the world, so that those who see...

units.la: Judicii administratio cognitione causæ, sententiæ dictione, & executione ejusdem constabit. strictiùs doctrinam fidei & pœnitentiæ, norma erit judicii tum absolventis fideles in Christo, tum condemnantis infideles, quibus Christus prædicatus est, & ad quorum etiam judicium in mundum venit, ut videntes cæci fierent, Joh. IX. 39. quíque, si Christus non venisset, & iis non dixisset, peccatum non haberent (consummatum, quale erat Amorrhæorum, Gen. XV. 16. & infesti odii: non quodvis, velut stuporis, ἀπαθίας & ignorantiæ) & προφάσιν prætextum peccati sui haberent, non quo à toto, sed quanto illud defenderent, adeóque non absolutè, sed comparativè; Joh. XV.22. Ex verbo hoc Dei, ceu libro, attestante eidem conscientia, & libro vitæ, in quo scripti sunt, judicabantur mortui & spiritualiter & corporaliter, κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν secundum opera sua, Apoc. XX. 12. Qualia opera disertè commemorantur à Christo, tum laudante opera electorum, tanquam testimonia & effecta fidei de veris causis suis testificantis: tum vituperante opera reproborum, tanquam causas sententiæ condemnantis. Illos enim sic alloquitur: Venite, benedicti Patri mei, &c. esurivi enim, & dedistis mihi comedere: Sitivi & potastis me: Peregrinus eram, & congregastis me, &c. v.34.35.36. Hos verò sic: Abite à me, maledicti, &c. esurivi enim & non dedistis mihi edere: Sitivi & non potastis me, &c. v.41. &c. Opera illa in benedictis laudata, opera charitatis & misericordiæ erga membra Christi, imò ipsum Christum, cujus illi corpus & membra sunt, velut signa occulti hominis, & fidei ἀνυπόκριτος, ex quibus constet, eos pertinere ad benedictos Dei, ad quos hæreditas ab æterno parata pertineat; allegantur. Christus enim ponens id, quod facilimum est, subintelligi voluit, quibus datum est à Christo pati, non habere minorem πεπίστιν, & opera charitatis laudabit convenienter ipsi rationi judicii, quod exercebitur. Cùm enim Mortales omnes judicis misericordiam & charitatem ex æquo imploraturi sint; justissimum erit judicium, quod secundum misericordiam ab ipsis factam, vel negleētam exercebitur. Nam condemnatio absque misericordia erit ei, qui non præstiterit misericordiam, & gloriabitur misericordia adversus judicium, Jac. II.13. Nam qui diligit, & studiosè diligit, & miseretur, habet καύχημα gloriationem, quæ confusionem & condemnationem in judicio non metuit. Ideo precatur Paulus: Det Dominus misericordiam Onesiphori domui, quia sæpius me recreavit, & vinculorum meorum eum non puduit. Det ei Dominus misericordiam invenire apud Dominum in die illa, 2.Tim.I.16.18. Cùmque bonorum corporalium ex sincera charitate profecta communicatio tantopere laudetur, spiritualium communicatio laude sua multò minùs defraudabitur. Et magna illa Christi judicis ἐπιμέλεια est, qua testatur, se charitatem & studium, si modò absit superbia, & adsit confessio defectus in suas rationes referre, & amplissimè remunerari velle. Mala porrò reproborum opera, negleētus inprimis Christi in membris suis patientis, (qui si justè punietur, quid fiet seduētoribus & persecutoribus, Antichristo inprimis) nec non arrogantia meriti, objicientium Christo, quòd nunquam non ipsi famelico, sitienti, nudo, peregrino, infirmo, captivo ministraverint, v. 44. & signum & causa maledictionis & condemnationis justissimæ, ab eodem judice Christo acerrimè perstringentur. Et generalis quidem sententia sensibili quadam voce forte pronunciabitur: sed ea, qua particulatim omnes scient, quantum præmium & quanta pœna quoad rem & gradus quemque maneat, & quæ utriusque causa sit, cujusque menti repræsentabitur. Nam φωτίσει illustrabit Christus occulta tenebrarum, 1.Cor.IV.5. Administrationem judicii sententiæ executio, efficaciam judicii ostendens, confestim consequetur, quam Christus his verbis ponit. Et abibunt isti (maledicti) in ignem æternum, justi verò in vitam æternam, v. 46. Sicut autem in dicenda sententia à piis initium faciet, quos coram universo mundo absolvet, non sine multo verborum honore, ad præsentissimam impiorum ignominiam: ita in ea exequenda ab impiis, ad piorum uberiorem lætitiam & consolationem, auspicabitur. Lætabitur enim justus, cùm ultionem videbit, Psal. LVIII.11.
units.tr: The administration of judgment will consist in the examination of the case, the pronouncing of the sentence, and its execution. Taken more strictly as the doctrine of faith and repentance, the rule of judgment will serve both to absolve the faithful in Christ and to condemn the unbelievers to whom Christ has been preached, and for whose judgment he came into the world, that those who see might become blind, John 9:39. These are the ones who would have no sin, if Christ had not come and had not spoken to them (sin in its full extent, such as that of the Amorites, Gen. 15:16, and of open and bitter hatred, not any sin such as stupor [apatheias], insensibility and ignorance), and who would have a pretext [prophasin] for their sin. This does not mean that they would defend it entirely, but only to some extent; so the statement is comparative, not absolute, John 15:22. By this word of God, as by a book, with conscience bearing witness to it, and by the book of life in which they are written, the dead were judged both spiritually and bodily, according to their works [kata ta erga autōn], according to their works, Rev. 20:12. These works are expressly named by Christ: he praises the works of the elect as testimonies and effects of faith, which bear witness to its true causes, and he censures the works of the reprobate as the causes of the condemning sentence. To the former he says: Come, blessed of my Father, etc., for I was hungry and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger and you took me in, etc., vv. 34, 35, 36. To the latter he says: Depart from me, you cursed, etc., for I was hungry and you gave me no food; I was thirsty and you gave me no drink, etc., v. 41, etc. The works praised in the blessed, works of love and mercy toward the members of Christ, and indeed toward Christ himself, whose body and members they are, are cited as signs of the hidden man and of unfeigned [anypokriton] faith, by which it is evident that they belong to the blessed of God, for whom the inheritance prepared from eternity belongs. Christ, stating what is most easy, wished it to be understood that those to whom it was given by Christ to suffer should not have less faith [pistin], and he will praise works of love in a way that agrees with the very nature of the judgment to be exercised. For since all mortals will equally need to implore the mercy and love of the judge, the judgment exercised according to the mercy shown or neglected by them will be most just. For judgment will be without mercy to him who has shown no mercy, and mercy will triumph over judgment, James 2:13. For he who loves, and loves earnestly, and shows mercy, has boasting [kauchēma], which does not fear shame and condemnation in judgment. So Paul prays: May the Lord grant mercy to the house of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chains. May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day, 2 Tim. 1:16, 18. And since the sharing of bodily goods, flowing from sincere love, is so greatly praised, the sharing of spiritual goods will much less be deprived of its praise. That great care [epimeleia] of Christ the judge is also there, by which he testifies that he wishes to refer love and zeal, provided pride is absent and a confession of defect is present, to his own account and to reward them most abundantly. Moreover, the evil works of the reprobate, above all their neglect of Christ suffering in his members (if he will justly punish this, what will happen to the seducers and persecutors, above all Antichrist?), and also the arrogance of merit, which objects to Christ that they have always ministered to him when he was hungry, thirsty, naked, a stranger, sick, or in prison, v. 44, will be most severely censured by the same judge Christ, as both the sign and the cause of the curse and of the most just condemnation. The general sentence will perhaps be pronounced with a certain audible voice, but each person will know individually how great a reward and how great a punishment awaits him, both in substance and in degree, and what is the cause of each, and this will be presented to each one's mind. For Christ will illumine [phōtisei], the hidden things of darkness, 1 Cor. 4:5. The execution of the sentence will immediately follow the administration of judgment, showing the efficacy of the judgment, as Christ states in these words: And these [the cursed] will go away into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life, v. 46. Just as he will begin the pronouncing of the sentence with the pious, whom he will absolve before the whole world, with no small honor of words, to the most present shame of the impious, so he will begin its execution with the impious, to the fuller joy and consolation of the pious. For the righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance, Ps. 58:11.

units.la: XCII. Judicio huic certus à Deo dies constitutus est, sed omnibus creaturis incertus & ignotus. De die & hora illa nemo novit, neque Angeli, qui in cœlo sunt, neque Filius, nisi Pater, Marc. XIII.32. Sed præcedent tamen signa quædam εἰς σύγκλησιν ad præstolationem, Matth. XXIV.30.31.32.Luc.XXI.27.28. revelata, & inde ab initio observanda, ut omni momento parati simus ad excipiendum quodque eorum, quæ Christi adventum ad judicium prænunciant. De quibus pluribus supra. Certos de judicio nos esse Christus voluit, ad consolationem nostri in adversis; at incertos de tempore, ad excutiendam securitatem. Vigilate, quia nescitis, qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit, Matth.XXIV.42. Etiam Hieronymus hoc documentum tradidisse fertur: sive bibas, sive comedas, sive vigiles, sive dormias, hæc tibi tuba insonet: SURGITE MORTUI, VENITE AD JUDICIUM. Quod quidam non inepte his versibus expressit:
units.tr: 92. God has fixed the day of this judgment, but it is unknown and uncertain to all creatures. Of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels who are in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father (Mark 13:32). Yet certain signs go before it, revealed for the gathering, that is, the waiting [εἰς σύγκλησιν], as Matthew 24:30-32 and Luke 21:27-28 show, and from the beginning they are to be observed, so that at every moment we may be ready to receive whatever announces Christ's coming to judgment. I have said more about these above. Christ willed that we should be certain of the judgment, for our comfort in adversity, but uncertain of the time, to shake off complacency: Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come (Matt. 24:42). Jerome is also said to have handed down this lesson: whether you drink or eat, whether you watch or sleep, let this trumpet sound in your ears: ARISE, YOU DEAD, COME TO JUDGMENT. One man has expressed this, not unhappily, in these verses:

units.la: Seu vigilo intentus studiis, seu dormio, semper
units.tr: Whether I wake, intent on my studies, or sleep, always

units.la: Judicis extremi nostras tuba personat aures.
units.tr: the trumpet of the final Judge sounds in my ears.

units.la: Hodie tamen gnome illa in operibus Hieronymi non reperitur; sed superior ordinis Hieronymiani in regula Monachorum, quæ operum Hieronymi, Tom. IV. extat, eam ex operibus Hieronymi collectam posuit. Locus porrò, unde venturus est, cœlum est; ad quem venturus est, aër & nubes sunt. Localis enim planè Christi ad judicium adventus erit, quia erit motus corporis ex cœlo in aërem per loca subordinata, Cœlum æthereum, sive orbes cœlestes, per quos etiam in Cœlum ascendit, Ephef.IV.10. Sicut ascendit, ita ἐλεύσεται veniet, Actor.I.11. At ascendisse eum localiter, supra ostendimus. Neque obstat, quòd dies ejus venturus est ut fur in nocte, Matth. XXIV. 43. Luc.XII.39. instar laquei, quo capiuntur aves, ibid.XXI.35. sicut fulgur, Matth. XXIV.27, quia non sic ejus adventus illocalis & successionis expers, sed subitaneus, inopinatus, & quasi momentaneus describitur. Locus verò Judicii speciatim non magis, quàm tempus definitur. Christus de eo sciscitantibus respondit: Ubi fuerit cadaver, ibi congregabuntur aquilæ, Luc.XVII.37. In universum tamen dici potest, locum illum respectu electorum futurum esse aëra, in quem occurcursuri Christo rapientur,' 1.Thess.I V.17. respectu reproborum terram, in qua, ceu humiliore loco relinquentur, ibique à sinistris Christi subsistent, donec damnati in gehennam ignis conjiciantur. Sed fabulis deputamus, quae Judaei, & ex iisdem nasutiores Pontificii de loco judicii, Valle Josaphati, cujus sub nomine פמק ברכה vallis benedictionis, mentio est, 2.Chron. XX. 26. propinant. Nam quòd Joel. III. 12. Deus se gentes congregaturum in vallem Josaphati, & ibi cum iis propter populum suum disceptaturum minatur, huc trahi neutiquam potest, quia de ultimo judicio ibi sermonem non esse, vel inde liquet, quia peracto hoc judicio demum vers,17.18.20. Hierosolymae libertas, aedificatio, abundantia doctrinae & benedictio promittitur. Sicut enim Apoc.XVI.16. gentes congregandae dicuntur in locum dictum Harmagedon: ita hic in vallem Josaphati propter analogiam & consilii atque conspirationis gentium, & judicii Dei, & praecedentis prophetiae, & actionum Ecclesiae atque spoliationis. Latet enim causa in nomine יהושפט Josaphat, quod sonat, Dominus judicat. Sicut Deus dicit: שפטי עמים contendam, vel disceptabo ibi cum gentibus. Sicut igitur olim Deus Moabitas & Ammonitas, hostes populi Judaici, terram Judaeorum ingressos, in conspectum ipsius congregavit ante urbem Hierosolyman, atque in valle Josaphati prostravit, 2.Chron. XX.26. ita simile quid facturum se quandoque cum hostibus Ecclesiae, terminum Ecclesiae ingressuris, eo animo, ut Ecclesiam vastent, & depopulentur, comminatur. Neque enim exiguum adeò spatium vallis hujus populorum omnium judicandorum, tótque myriadum hominum receptaculum idoneum foret. Neque etiam ratio ulla est, ut dicamus, Christum, quia in Coelum ascendit ex monte oliveti, qui imminet valli Josaphati, proximè Hierosolymam in eundem locum ad judicium descensurum & mundum judicaturum esse. Nam Angelus dicens: Jesus ille sublatus in Coelum sic revertetur, sicut eum vidistis migrantem in Coelum, Act I.11. non locum judicii, sed modum adventus ejus, qui visibilis erit, definit.
units.tr: Today, however, that saying is not found in the works of Jerome; but the author of the rule of the monks, a superior of the Hieronymian order, which is in the works of Jerome, vol. IV, collected it from Jerome's writings and set it down. The place, moreover, from which he is to come is heaven; the place to which he is to come is the air and the clouds. For Christ's coming to judgment will be truly local, since there will be a movement of his body from heaven into the air, through the lower regions, the ethereal heaven, or the heavenly spheres, through which he also ascended into heaven (Eph. 4:10). He will come [ἐλεύσεται] in the same way as he ascended (Acts 1:11). That he ascended locally we have shown above. Nor is it an objection that his day will come like a thief in the night (Matt. 24:43; Luke 12:39), like a snare, in which birds are caught (ibid. 21:35), or like lightning (Matt. 24:27), because his coming is not described as unplaced and without succession, but as sudden, unexpected and, as it were, momentary. The place of judgment, however, is no more defined in particular than the time is. When those who asked him about it, Christ answered: Where the carcass is, there the eagles will be gathered together (Luke 17:37). Still, it may be said in general that for the elect that place will be the air, into which they will be caught up to meet Christ (1 Thess. 4:17); for the reprobate it will be the earth, in which, as in a lower place, they will be left, and there they will stand at Christ's left hand, until the damned are cast into the fire of Gehenna. But we count as fables what the Jews, and the more keen-nosed Papists after them, put forward about the place of judgment: the Valley of Jehoshaphat, mentioned under the name emek berakah [עמק ברכה], the valley of blessing (2 Chron. 20:26). For that Joel 3:12 threatens that God will gather the nations into the valley of Jehoshaphat and there contend with them on account of his people cannot be drawn to this at all, since it is clear, even from this, that the last judgment is not being discussed there: after this judgment is over, verses 17, 18 and 20 promise Jerusalem freedom, building, abundance of teaching and blessing. For just as Revelation 16:16 says the nations are to be gathered into the place called Armageddon, so here they are gathered into the valley of Jehoshaphat, by analogy with the counsel, conspiracy and judgment of God, with the preceding prophecy, and with the actions of the Church and its plundering. For the reason lies in the name Jehoshaphat [יהושפט], which means the Lord judges, just as God says: I will contend, or I will dispute there with the nations [שפטי עמים]. Therefore, just as God once gathered the Moabites and Ammonites, enemies of the Jewish people, who had entered the land of the Jews, before his face outside the city of Jerusalem, and struck them down in the valley of Jehoshaphat (2 Chron. 20:26), so he threatens that he will one day do something similar to the enemies of the Church, who will enter the borders of the Church with the intent of laying waste and plundering it. Nor, indeed, would that small valley be a suitable receptacle for all the peoples to be judged, and so many myriads of men. Nor is there any reason for us to say that Christ, because he ascended into heaven from the Mount of Olives, which overhangs the Valley of Jehoshaphat, very near Jerusalem, will descend to that same place for judgment and judge the world. For the angel, saying: This Jesus, taken up into heaven, will return in the same way as you saw him going into heaven (Acts 1:11), defines not the place of judgment but the manner of his coming, which will be visible.

units.la: XCIII. Finito Judicio & impiis ad Tartara ablegatis, piis à Christo in Coelum sic assumptis mundo finis imponetur. Sicut enim initium habuit, ita finem habiturum eundem esse, Scriptura dubitare non sinit. Nam cùm primam cataströphen suam mundus in diluvio subiisset, foedus cum Noacho iniens Deus dixit: עד כל ימי הארץ Adhuc omnibus diebus terrae, sementis & messis, frigus & calor, aestas & hiems, dies & nox non cessabunt, Gen. VIII.22. Quae verba significant, Deum definivisse dies terrae, quibus homines & animalia in terra viverent, cibum comederent, & generarent. Mose antiquior Jobus negat, resurrecturum virum, qui cubuit עד בלתי שמים donec non erunt amplius Coeli, nempe illi, qui vanitati serviunt, Job.XIV.12. Clarius David de Coelo & terra simul: Terram fundasti, & opus manuum tuarum Coelum est. Ipsa peritura sunt. Tu autem permanes. Ipsa, inquam, omnia ut vestimentum veterascent: ut indumentum mutabis ea, & mutabuntur, Psal.CII.26. 27.28. Quae non mysticè duntaxat de mutatione oeconomiarum Ecclesiae, sed phy sicè etiam intelligimus de mutatione mundi, aeternitati Dei immutabili opposita; quae mysticè etiam mutationi substernitur. Deus ipse apud Esajam: Contabescent omnes exercitus Coelorum, ... convolventur sicut liber, Coeli, & omnis exercitus illorum marcescet, quemadmodum marcescens pampinus defluit a vite, & ut marcida de ficu, Esaj.XXXIV.4.
units.tr: 93. When the judgment is finished and the wicked have been sent away to Tartarus, and the godly have been taken up into heaven by Christ, an end will be put to the world. For just as it had a beginning, Scripture does not allow us to doubt that it will have the same end. For when the world had undergone its first catastrophe in the flood, God, making a covenant with Noah, said: As long as the earth endures [עד כל ימי הארץ], seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will not cease (Gen. 8:22). These words mean that God has determined the days of the earth, during which men and animals live on the earth, eat food and beget offspring. Job, older than Moses, says that a man who has lain down will not rise again until the heavens are no more [עד בלתי שמים], that is, those who serve vanity (Job 14:12). David speaks more clearly of heaven and earth together: You founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you remain. Indeed, all of them will grow old like a garment; like a robe you will change them, and they will be changed (Ps. 102:26-28). We understand this not only mystically, of the change of the economies of the Church, but also physically, of the change of the world, set against the immutable eternity of God, which is also mystically laid under change. God himself says through Isaiah: All the host of heaven will waste away, ... the heavens will be rolled up like a scroll, and all their host will wither, as a withered vine sheds its leaves, and as a withered fig (Isa. 34:4).

units.la: XCIV. Etiam recta ratio finem mundi arguit. Deus enim, qui coelum & terram creavit, & in iis hominem ad imaginem suam fecit, postquam ille peccato inquinatus est, mundum vanitati velut invitum subjecit ad tempus, ut scilicet ipse suo tempore a servitute
units.tr: 94. Even right reason proves that the world will end. For God, who created heaven and earth, and in them made man in his own image, after man was defiled by sin, subjected the world to vanity, as it were against its will, for a time, so that at his appointed time he himself might free it from the bondage

units.la: Judicium ultimum finis mundi & consummatio seculi excipiet. te vanitatis liberaretur, & gloria filiorum Dei illustraretur. Quæ illa mutatio Cœli & terræ est, ut pro ministris vanitatis justitiæ & gloriæ domicilium fiant. Nam & ipsæ creaturæ à servitute corruptionis in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei asseri debent, Rom. VIII. 20.21. Naturaliter etiam cognoscimus justitiam Dei, cujus caput est, pios præmiis afficere, malos pœnis plectere. Cùmque nec pietatis præmium, nec impietatis pœna idonea in mundo repræsentari possit, & homine ex mundo exempto novam mundi formam & faciem exoriri necesse sit, mutatum mundum iri, manifestè sequitur. Vidit insuper natura originem mundi, vidit prodeuntem lucem ex tenebris; & quem sic orientem vidit, occidentem non mirabitur; neque resolvi posse negabit, quod coalescere vidit. Ideo S. Petrus eo argumento, quòd cœlum Dei sermone creatum extitit, & terra ex aqua & per aquam constitit, conficit, fore ut mundus iterum aboleatur, 2. Pet. III. 5.6.7. Præludia hujus abolitionis tum diluvium universale, quo mundus aqua inundatus periit, ibid. v.6. unde S. Petrus etiam colligit Cœlos servari igni in diem judicii, ibid. v.7. tum inundationes particulares & terræ motus, quibus terræ & urbes concussæ funditus eversæ sunt; tum quotidianæ in mundo generationum & corruptionum vicissitudines, & antipathiarum mirabiles formæ. Mitto consensum Judæorum duo secula, præsens & futurum constituentium. Sibyllarum Orac. Lib. II. Poëtarum Ovidii, Lucretii, Lucani & Philosophorum, qui ante Aristotelem plerique omnes, ipso Aristotele de Cœlo Lib. I. 10. fatente, statuerunt, mundum esse genitum; sed alii genitum esse corruptibilem, uti Plato, ajens in Timæo; non esse Ipsius-Boni ad fœtus sui optimi perniciem impelli. Optime equidem, si non interit, ut resurgat pulchrior. Quotquot verò in Græcis cum Stoicis ipsòque Platone rerum periodos, Annos Magnos, & temporum docuerunt, ii omnes hodiernum mundum interiturum esse suppo-suerunt. Alii etiam Strabone Lib. IV. teste ita mundum esse incorruptibilem, ut aliquando ignis & aqua invalescant. Locum sic vicissitudinibus cedentes asseruerunt. Taceo Plinium aliósque, quibus est, mundum fatiscere, senescere, tandemque conteri & corruere penitus.
units.tr: The last judgment will follow the end of the world and the consummation of the age, so that it may be freed from vanity, and the glory of the sons of God may be displayed. That change of heaven and earth will be such that they become a dwelling for justice and glory instead of servants of vanity. For the creatures themselves must be set free from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God (Rom. 8:20-21). We also know by nature the justice of God, whose chief part is to reward the godly with prizes and to punish the wicked with penalties. And since neither a fitting reward for piety nor a fitting punishment for impiety can be shown in the world, and since, once man has been removed from the world, a new form and face of the world must arise, it plainly follows that the world will be changed. Moreover, nature has seen the origin of the world; it has seen light coming forth out of darkness; and one who has seen it rise will not be surprised that it sets, nor will he deny that what he has seen come together can be dissolved. Therefore St Peter concludes, from the argument that the heavens existed by the word of God, and the earth was made out of water and through water, that the world will again be destroyed (2 Pet. 3:5-7). Forerunners of this destruction are the universal flood, by which the world perished, flooded with water (ibid. v. 6), from which St Peter also infers that the heavens are kept for fire until the day of judgment (ibid. v. 7); then the particular floods and earthquakes, by which lands and cities were shaken and utterly overthrown; then the daily alternations of generation and corruption in the world, and the wonderful forms of antipathies. I pass over the agreement of the Jews, who posit two ages, the present and the future; the Sibyls in Oracles, Book II; the poets Ovid, Lucretius and Lucan; and the philosophers, who, nearly all before Aristotle, held that the world had been generated, Aristotle himself admitting this in On the Heavens, Book I, ch. 10; but some held that what was generated is corruptible, as Plato does, saying in the Timaeus that it is not for the Good Itself to bring about the ruin of its best offspring. Indeed, it is best, if it does not perish, that it should rise again more beautiful. As for all those among the Greeks who, with the Stoics and Plato himself, taught periods of things, Great Years, and cycles of time, they all supposed that the present world would perish. Others, as Strabo testifies in Book IV, held that the world is so incorruptible that at times fire and water prevail, yielding in this way to vicissitudes. I say nothing of Pliny and others, who hold that the world decays, grows old, and at last is worn away, and collapses altogether.

units.la: XCV.
units.tr: XCV.

units.la: Neque tamen defuerunt in Ecclesia, & extra eam, qui mundi æternitatem & immutabilitatem propugnarent. Nam & Judæi nonnulli, Philo inprimis, scripto de Incorruptibilitate Mundi libro, mundi finem aperte negat; & Philosophi Chaldæi teste Diodoro Siculo Bibl. Lib. II. Pythagorici, Epicuræi, Peripatetici inprimis, Aristotele duce, semper fuisse mundum, sempérque sine fine & renovatione futurum, pertenderunt. Licèt enim Scaliger Exercit. III. Aristotelis sententiam sic explicare conatus fuerit, ut diceret, mortem ejus fuisse, quòd ingenitus sit, & non interiturus mundus sit naturaliter; non paucos tamen Aristotelis textus, ingenitum & incorruptibilem mundum simpliciter asserentes, Tau-
units.tr: Yet there were not lacking, within the Church and outside it, those who defended the eternity and immutability of the world. Some Jews also, above all Philo in his book On the Incorruptibility of the World, plainly deny that the world will end. The Chaldean philosophers, according to Diodorus Siculus, Bibl. Book II, and the Pythagoreans, Epicureans and, above all, the Peripatetics, following Aristotle, contended that the world has always existed and will always exist without end or renewal. Scaliger, in Exercitation III, tried to explain Aristotle's view as meaning only that the world is unbegotten and will not perish naturally. Nevertheless, Tau-

units.la: rellus de Rer. et. Lib. II. citavit. Sed & Porphyrius Christianos finem mundi astruentes acriter exagitat. In ipsis Ecclesiæ visceribus hæserunt Cerinthus, qui Cœli & terræ destructionem Hierosolymæ excidium interpretatus est. Innominati hæretici & Æternales, mundi æternitatem asserentes; quibus Origenes succesfivam mundorum creationem asserens, consensit. Sed longè plures sub finem seculi irrisores erunt dicturi: Ubi est promissio adventus ejus? Ex quo enim Patres nostri dormiverunt, omnia sic permanent, inde à principio creationis, 2. Pet. III. 3. Quibus nullatenus Scriptura patrocinatur. Nam locum Gen. VIII. 22. obtorto collo Æternales rapuerunt, quia manifestè ibi omnes dies terræ, quibus tempestatum vicissitudines erunt, certum & definitum vicissitudinum illarum tempus constituitur. Neque etiam montes æterni, & colles seculi, Deuter. XXXIII. 15. montes & colles simpliciter æterni & antiquissimæ durationis intelliguntur. Et Sol, Luna, Stellæ, Cœli dicuntur stare in perpetuum, in seculum, Psal. CXLVIII. 6. sed non absolutè, quia Deus iis dedisse dicitur statutum, quod non transgrediantur. Præscripsit enim Deus certum motum & ordinem, quem usque ad diem novissimum homines in terra degentes observabunt. Omnia enim in ipso consistunt, Col. I. 17. Omnia fert verbo potentiæ suæ, Heb. I. 3. Omnia denique certa lege & ordine immutabili ad finem usque suum reguntur. At nec Solomon dicens: Ætas abit, & ætas venit, & terra in seculum stat, Eccles. I. 4. convenienter illis Davidis: Fundasti terram super basin suam, non commovebitur in seculum seculi, Psal. CIV. 5. terræ immobilitatem & immutabilitatem absolutè astruit; sed quòd non sic oriatur & intereat, sicut homines & animalia intereunt, adeóque eorum respectu fiet, non occidat, quandiu erit domicilium hominis, qui ex terra alitur & sustentatur; innuit. Uti ipsa antithesis docet. Deniq; omnia sic permaneant à principio creationis, 2. Pet. III. 4. supra perstrinximus: & S. Petrus efficacissimis argumentis discussit.
units.tr: rellus, De Rer. et. Book II, cited not a few passages of Aristotle which simply assert that the world is unbegotten and incorruptible. Porphyry also attacks fiercely those Christians who maintain the end of the world. Within the very bosom of the Church there arose Cerinthus, who interpreted the destruction of heaven and earth as the destruction of Jerusalem; the heretics called Innominati and Aeternales, who asserted the eternity of the world; and Origen, who, asserting a successive creation of worlds, agreed with them. But far more scoffers will arise at the end of the age, saying: "Where is the promise of his coming? For since our fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation" (2 Pet. 3:4). Scripture lends them no support. For the Aeternales wrested Gen. 8:22 by the neck, since there the "days of the earth" are plainly stated, during which the changes of the seasons will occur, and a fixed and definite time for those changes is appointed. Nor are the "everlasting mountains" and "perpetual hills" of Deut. 33:15 understood as simply eternal, of the most ancient duration. The sun, moon, stars and heavens are said to "stand fast for ever and ever" (Ps. 148:6), but not absolutely, since God is said to have given them a decree that they should not transgress. God has prescribed a fixed motion and order, which men living on the earth will observe until the last day. For in him all things "consist" (Col. 1:17), and he "upholds all things by the word of his power" (Heb. 1:3). In short, all things are governed by a fixed law and an unchanging order until their end. Nor does Solomon, when he says, "One generation passes away, and another comes, but the earth abides for ever" (Eccl. 1:4), absolutely assert the immobility and immutability of the earth in agreement with David's words, "You founded the earth upon its base; it shall not be moved for ever and ever" (Ps. 104:5). He means rather that it does not arise and perish as men and animals do, and so, with respect to them, it will not perish as long as it is the dwelling place of man, who is nourished and sustained by the earth. The antithesis itself shows this. Finally, "all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation" (2 Pet. 3:4) has been touched on above, and St Peter refuted it with very effective arguments.

units.la: XCVI. Mundo finem Deus imponet.
units.tr: XCVI. God will put an end to the world.

units.la: Sicut indumentum mutabis eos (cœlos) & immutabuntur, Psal. CII. 27. Heb. I. 11. In igne Dominus judicabit, Esaj. LXVI. 16. Nam cœli & terræ creator idem ejusdem consummator & renovator erit. Perperam enim Plinius, aliíque naturam vigore amisso mori, & Stoici, humore consumpto nec terram ali, nec aëra subsistere, nec ea, quæ in terra & aëre sunt, durare amplius posse delirant. Retinebit enim Cœlum & terra vigorem, donec Christus adventans vim suam ei inferet; & Cœli cum fragore transfibunt, qui non est infirmorum, & virib naturalibus exhaustorum, sed iisdem pollentium, 2. Pet. III. 10. De quo suprà. Utetur nihilominus Deus ad finalem hanc prætereuntium abolitionem igne: Sicut ad deletionem prioris mundi aqua usus est. Mundus, qui tunc fuit, aqua inundatus periit. Cœli autem, qui nunc sunt, & terra eodem verbo repositi sunt, qui igni servantur in diem judicii, 2. Pet. III. 6, 7. Magnas enim mundi clades per aquam & ignem succcessuras, & per has purgandas, veteres etiam Ægyptii, Druidæ, aliique crediderunt. Quæ proin elementa in purgationum ritibus apud Græcos & Barbaros ferè semper usitata fuerunt. Quomodo etiam Spiritus S. qui in purgandis animabus nostris occupatur, aquæ & igni confertur, Matth.III.11. Luc.III.16. Et S. Paulus opera quædam igni extremæ diei purganda, 1. Cor.III.13. docet. Priorem purgationem mundus in cataclysmo subiit: posteriorem in conflagratione mundi subibit. Juxta Stoicos etiam, Scripturis consentientes; nisi quòd Heraclitus in vita Zenonis, mundum ex igne genitum esse, κπάλιν πυρὸς ὅτι κατὰ πινας αἰῶνας (non semel duntaxat, sed) secundum periodos certas accendi & conflagrare asseruit, & cum eodem alii, teste Laërtio, mundum per vices ἐξαναχωρεῖσθαι καὶ ἐξυδατοῦσθαι exustionibus & eluvionibus subjici statuerunt. Idem asseruit Cicero Somn. Scip. ubi perituri mundi contemptum Africani sui animo ingesturus: Propter eluviones, inquit, exustionésque terrarum, quas accidere tempore certo necesse est, non modo non æternam, sed ne diuturnam quidem gloriam assequi possumus. Proximas autem esse vices in hoc fatorum ordine, omnes consentiunt. Sed addunt Stoici, exusto hoc mundo, renasciturum alium, eadem forma & facie; nihilque, uti Cicero de Nat. Deor. Lib.II. loquitur: relinqui præter ignem, à quo rursus animante, ac Deo, renovatio mundi fieret, atque idem ornatus interiret. Consentiunt igitur Scripturis, quòd igne periturus mundus & renovandus sit: at in eo dissentiunt, quòd & indefinitam, & nunquam desituram incendiorum & diluviorum seriem supponunt, & mundum post conflagrationem cum tota sua suppellectile in ipsissimam eandem formam, quam ultimò habuit, renovandum; atque eandem rerum temporúmque seriem restitui & inchoari denuo, iterúmque iterúmque repetendam, scisçunt, quo nihil absurdius, aut à ratione alienum magis videtur. Quid enim hic labor actus in orbem proderit? ut crambe hæc non cocta bis, sed iterum iterúmque, Diis hominibúsque apponatur? Fabula, quæ haud placuit prima vice, cum fastidio repetitur: nec feret cœlum, ut renoventur ea hominum scelera, quæ incendio purgari vel puniri voluit. Neque mundum naturalem, forma & suppellectile eundem, sed pulchriorem & præstantiorem habituri sumus. Sed de hoc quicquid sit, manifesta gentilium væsania est, propter assertum mundi per ignem excidium Christianos supplicio afficientium, cùm hæc domestica Philosophorum gentilium plurium sententia fuerit.
units.tr: "As a garment you will change them (the heavens), and they shall be changed" (Ps. 102:27; Heb. 1:11). "By fire the Lord will judge" (Isa. 66:16). For the same one who created heaven and earth will also be their consummator and renewer. Pliny and others wrongly rave that nature dies once its vigour is lost, and the Stoics wrongly rave that once moisture is consumed the earth is no longer nourished, the air cannot subsist, and the things in earth and air can no longer endure. For heaven and earth will retain their vigour until Christ, coming, inflicts his power upon them, and the heavens "shall pass away with a great noise" (2 Pet. 3:10). That is not the work of those who are weak and exhausted in their natural powers, but of those who are mighty in them; of this we have spoken above. Nevertheless, God will use fire for this final abolition of the things that pass away, just as he used water for the destruction of the former world: "The world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished. But the heavens that now are, and the earth, by the same word are kept in store, reserved for fire until the day of judgment" (2 Pet. 3:6–7). For the ancient Egyptians, the Druids and others also believed that great calamities would come upon the world through water and fire, and that by these it would be purged. Hence these elements were almost always used in the rites of purification among the Greeks and barbarians alike. In the same way the Holy Spirit, who is at work in purging our souls, is compared to water and fire (Matt. 3:11; Luke 3:16). And St Paul teaches that certain works are to be tested by fire on the last day (1 Cor. 3:13). The world underwent the former purging in the cataclysm; it will undergo the latter in the conflagration. The Stoics also agree with Scripture, except that Heraclitus, in the Life of Zeno, asserted that the world was generated from fire and was set alight again "according to certain ages" [κατὰ τινας αἰῶνας], that is, not once only but according to certain periods; and others with him, as Laertius reports, held that the world is by turns "turned into fire and turned into water" [ἐξαναχωρεῖσθαι καὶ ἐξυδατοῦσθαι], and so subject to conflagrations and floods. Cicero asserted the same in the Somnium Scipionis, where, wishing to impress upon his Africanus contempt for a world destined to perish, he says: "Because of the floods and burnings of the lands, which must necessarily happen at a certain time, we can attain not only no eternal glory, but not even a lasting one." All agree that the next of these cycles in this order of fates is near. But the Stoics add that, once this world has been burned, another will be born again, of the same form and appearance; and, as Cicero says in De Natura Deorum Book II, nothing remains except the fire, from which the renewal of the world is made again, a living and divine being, and the same adornment perishes. They therefore agree with Scripture that the world is to perish by fire and be renewed. But they differ in this: they suppose an indefinite series of conflagrations and floods that will never cease, and they hold that after the conflagration the world, with all its furniture, will be renewed into exactly the same form it last had, and that the same series of things and times is restored and begun anew, and is to be repeated again and again. Nothing seems more absurd or more alien to reason. For what would this labour, going round in a circle, profit? Would this cabbage be served up to gods and men not once cooked but again and again? A fable that did not please the first time is repeated with disgust. Nor will heaven allow those human crimes to be renewed which it willed to be purged or punished by fire. Nor shall we have a natural world the same in form and furniture, but one more beautiful and more excellent. Whatever the truth of this may be, it is a manifest madness of the Gentiles, who, on account of the asserted destruction of the world by fire, inflict punishment on Christians, when this has been a common opinion among many of the Gentile philosophers themselves.

units.la: XCVII. Ab authoritate igitur sacra vis maxima certitudinis exoritur, inprimis, cùm ea in re, quòd mundus igni finiendus sit, Prophetarum & Apostolorum calculi consentiant.
units.tr: XCVII. The greatest certainty therefore arises from sacred authority, above all because, on this point, that the world is to be ended by fire, the reckonings of the Prophets and Apostles agree.

units.la: Nam incendii hujus præludium in conflagratione Sodomæ & Gomorrhæ fuit. Et de eodem David prædixit: Veniet Dominus noster. Ignis coram eo vorabit, Psal.L. 3. Ignis coram eo ambulat, ibid.XCVII.3. Esajas; Ecce Jehova cum igne venturus est, & curribus suis similibus turbini ad reddendum cum excandescentia iram suam, cap. LXVI.15. Igne zeli ipsius comedetur tota terra, Zeph.I.18. III.8. Ecce dies ille adveniet, ardens tanquam fornax, &c. Mal.IV.1. Quæ
units.tr: For the prelude to this conflagration was the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah. And David foretold the same: "Our God will come; a fire will devour before him" (Ps. L.3), "A fire goes before him" (ibid., XCVII.3). Isaiah says: "Behold, the LORD comes with fire, and with his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his anger with fury" (Isa. LXVI.15). "The whole earth will be consumed by the fire of his jealousy" (Zeph. I.18, III.8). "Behold, that day comes, burning like a furnace," etc. (Mal. IV.1). Which

units.la: ad secundum etiam adventum Christi referenda sunt. Ante utrumque Moses: Ignis exarsit in naso meo, & ardet usque in orcum inferiorem; & comedit terram & proventum ejus, & inflammat fundamenta montium, Deut.XXXII.22. Quæ verba sic ad excidium populi Judaici referenda sunt, ut tamen judicium Dei, quod in Judæis incepit, ad reliquos Dei hostes transfire, & tandem in mundi combustione terminari debeat. De qua proin ἐκπυρώσει etiam Justinus Martyr, Apolog. 2. rectè hunc locum explicavit. Nihil dicam de Sethitarum columnis duabus, lapidea & lateritia, eo consilio erectis, ut si lateritia in diluvio periret, lapidea, & inscripta eidem à Setho mysteria superarent, quam suo ævo superstitem Josephus prodidit. Licèt enim à Setho erectas esse parum constet, tamen Isaci Vossii de Æter. M.p.271. conjectura est, columnas illas esse סמליים גלυφὰ sculpturas, quas Ehud transivisse, evadentem השעירה in Seiratah, Judic.III.26. dicitur. Nam locus columnarum apud Eustathium in Hexaemeron, qui ex Josepho eandem historiam narrat; Locus ille Γῇ Σηιρεαδὶ terra Seireiath appellatur. Illic erat cippus lapideus ille, quem Judæi à Setho erectum crediderunt. Sed clarissimè S.Petrus in verbis supra laudatis, qui v.10. amplius sic rem declarat: Veniet dies Domini, ut fur in nocte, in qua Cœli ῥοιζηδὸν cum fragore (qualis ῥοιζῶ tribuitur vento, Sap.V.11. & stridori currus, 2. Macchab.IX.7.) præteribunt, & elementa κωνσιμένα candefacta solventur, (pro quo v.12. dicitur τήκεται liquefient) & terra, & quæ in illa erunt opera, concremabuntur. Hac nempe ratione placuit Deo creaturam liberare à servitute vanitatis, peccati & miseriæ, cui invita, hoc est, præter naturæ suæ institutum, propter voluntatem Dei, in longanimitate sibi parantis populum peculii sive thesauri, subjecta est, Rom. VIII.19.20.21. Appetet verò ignis iste S.Petri in die illa Cœlos & elementa, aquam & terram, & terræ, hoc est, hominum in terra, opera, ib. v.10.12. Omnia enim sicut vestimentum veterascent, Psal.CII.27. Nam quòd Barradius aliíque Pontificii, & novissimè etiam Doctiss. Burnetius ab incendio hoc Cœlos sidereos excipiunt, non adeò certi videntur; cùm simpliciter ἐξωνοὶ cœli nominentur; & Esajas cœlos & omnem exercitum eorum defluxurum prædixerit, cap.XXXIV.4. Exercitus autem Cœlorum stellæ sunt. Nam πᾶσα κτίσις συστενάζει omnis creatura unâ suspirat, Rom.VIII.22. Sol quoque & Luna peccatori ministrarunt, adeòque vanitatem contraxerunt. Quod ex idololatria Persarum, Ægyptiorum, aliorum, cœlestia corpora religiosè colentium inprimis perspicuum est. Haud probabiliori ratione Valentia ignem, idem Barradius etiam aëra, Ribera, à Lapide paradisum terrestrem, idem à Lapide Lignum crucis Christi ab hoc incendio eximunt. Nam ἀδηλα sunt. Et si aër & ignis variè elementis permixtus lustrationem hanc effugient, qui igitur Cœli, quæ elementa lustrabuntur? Restat, ut soli homini nullum ab igne lustratore periculum imminere dicatur. Nam qui ex mortuis jam tum resurrexerunt, corpora incorruptibilia, cœlestia, immortalia, gloriosa, spiritualia habebunt, neque lustratione ulla indigebunt. Superstitum verò corpora mutabuntur quiquidem, sed ante incendium tamen fatale unâ cum resuscitatis Christo obviam in aëra rapientur, Coelúmque ingredientur, 1. Thess. IV. 15. 17. Neque quicquam illis, sanguine Christi plane purificatis, purgandum aderit, ut ignem hunc conflagrationis ingredi, & eo purgari necesse habeant. Licet veteribus nonnullis Lactantio, Theodoreto, Hieronymo, aliis, verba S. Pauli 1. Cor. III. 15. eò detorquentibus, aliter visum fuerit. Neque enim igni conflagrationis ea vis suppetit, ut vel minimi peccati reatum expungat. Denique forte nec igne isto impii damnati amburentur; utpote jam ante incendium in tartara rapti. Multò minùs illis ignis iste conflagrationis infernus suus, & aeternus ille ignis, Diabolo & Angelis ejus, ipsisque paratus erit, quae impia Socini & asseclarum sententia est, quam infra jugulabimus.
units.tr: are also to be referred to the second coming of Christ. Before both, Moses said: "A fire is kindled in my nostril, and burns to the lowest hell; and it devours the earth and its produce, and sets fire to the foundations of the mountains" (Deut. XXXII.22). These words must be referred to the destruction of the Jewish people in such a way that the judgment of God, which began among the Jews, passes on to the remaining enemies of God, and at last ends in the burning of the world. Justin Martyr, in his Apology 2, rightly explained this passage of this ekpyrosis [ἐκπύρωσις]. I say nothing of the two pillars of the Sethites, one of stone and one of brick, set up with the purpose that if the brick one perished in the flood, the stone one, inscribed with mysteries by Seth, would survive; Josephus reports that it was still standing in his own age. For although it is hardly certain that they were erected by Seth, yet Isaac Vossius, in De Aetern. Mundi, p. 271, conjectures that those pillars were the pesilim [סמליים], carved images [γλυφά], which Ehud is said to have passed, escaping from ha-Se'irah [השעירה] into Seirath (Judg. III.26). For the place of the pillars in Eustathius on the Hexaemeron, who relates the same story from Josephus, is called "the land of Seireiath" [Γῆ Σηιρεαδί]. There was that stone pillar which the Jews believed had been erected by Seth. But St. Peter most clearly declares the matter in the words cited above, where he explains it further at v. 10: "The day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night, in which the heavens will pass away with a rushing noise [ῥοιζηδόν] (the word rhoizō is applied to the wind, Wisd. V.11, and to the noise of chariots, 2 Macc. IX.7), and the elements, burning [καυσούμενα], will be dissolved," (for which in v. 12 it says "will melt" [τήκεται]), "and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up." It was surely in this way that God pleased to free the creature from the bondage of vanity, sin and misery, to which it was subjected against its will, that is, beyond the order of its nature, on account of the will of God, who in his long-suffering was preparing for himself a people as his own treasure (Rom. VIII.19–21). Now that fire of St. Peter will appear on that day to consume the heavens and the elements, water and earth, and the works of the earth, that is, of men on the earth (ibid., vv. 10, 12). "For all of them will wear out like a garment" (Ps. CII.27). For that Barradius and other Papists, and most recently the most learned Burnet, exclude the starry heavens from this burning, does not seem very certain; since they are simply called "the heavens" [οὐρανοί], and Isaiah foretold that "the heavens and all their host will melt away" (Isa. XXXIV.4). Now the host of heaven is the stars. For "all creation groans together" (Rom. VIII.22). The sun and moon too served the sinner, and so were made subject to vanity. This is especially clear from the idolatry of the Persians, the Egyptians and others, who worshipped the heavenly bodies religiously. On no more probable ground do Valentia exempt fire, and the same Barradius even the air, Ribera and à Lapide exempt the earthly paradise from this burning, and the same à Lapide the wood of the cross of Christ. For these things are unknown. And if air and fire, variously mixed with the elements, escape this purging, then which heavens, which elements, will be purged? It remains that it is said that no danger from this purging fire threatens man alone. For those who have already risen from the dead will have incorruptible, heavenly, immortal, glorious, spiritual bodies, and will need no purging at all. But the bodies of those who survive will indeed be changed, yet before the fatal burning they will be caught up together with those raised by Christ, to meet him in the air, and will enter heaven (1 Thess. IV.15, 17). Nor will they have anything to be purged, since they are wholly purified by the blood of Christ, so that they need to enter that fire of the conflagration and be purged by it. Although some of the ancients, Lactantius, Theodoret, Jerome and others, twisting the words of St. Paul (1 Cor. III.15) in that direction, thought otherwise. For the fire of the conflagration does not have the power to wipe out the guilt of even the smallest sin. Finally, perhaps the wicked who are damned will not even be burned by that fire, since they have already been carried off to hell before the burning. Much less will that fire of the conflagration be their hell, and that eternal fire prepared for the Devil and his angels and for them, which is the impious opinion of Socinus and his followers, and which I shall overthrow below.

units.la: XCVIII. Caeterum causae & modus hujus conflagrationis mundi in recessibus sapientiae Divinae latent, neque deficiente revelatione indagari in solidum possunt.
units.tr: XCVIII. Moreover, the causes and manner of this conflagration of the world lie hidden in the recesses of divine wisdom, and cannot be fully investigated where revelation is lacking.

units.la: Nulla quidem orbis nostri materia est, praeter aquam, quae non posset suo modo ignescere. Ipsa quoque aqua marina, si vincatur ab igne, eundem auget & intendit. Sed quoad regiones interpolares, suo situ igni inaccessas, gelida & diuturna hieme contra omnes ignis impetus armatas, & illud contingere poterit, ut vastata terra habitabili, & sublato ex terris humano genere, in caeteris lentior flammarum progressus obtinere possit. Cùmque tantus futurus sit Atmosphaerae fervor, omnis regio zona torrida esse poterit; & venti tam in ductibus subterraneis, quàm in aperto aëre in omnes partes, subter & supra terram flammas cum impetu cogere & impellere poterunt. Montes quoque igni vomi, lacus sulphurei & bituminosi, omnes terrae pingues & glebae sulphureae facile ignem concipientes; omnes foci totius terrae; mineralia & fossilia subterranea ignifera, halitus ignei, fumi, & quaecunque thermarum & calidorum fontium causae, vel fomenta sunt, aliáque ejusmodi operam navabunt. Nihil dicam de meteoris igneis, & reversò igne eo, qui ex Coelo delabi potest. Sed succumbent tamen ignis hodierni in natura latentis & se exerentis universi vires, nisi Deus Ἀπὸ μηχανῆς, quod ipse molitus est opus, sua potentia infinita resolverit. Non enim ad interitum sua sponte natura ruet, sed Deo volente, jubente, operante. Quomodo etiam in Sodomae incendio pluit Jehova super Sodomam sulphur & ignem מאת יהוה מן השמים à Jehova è Coelis, Gen. XIX. 24. Poterit enim Deus ignem undecunque sufficere, vel novum creare, vel ignis naturalis vires mirè intendere. Nam quod Deus potest, & quod futurum revelavit, de eo, an futurum sit, dubitatio Mortalium nemini incessere debet.
units.tr: Indeed, there is no material in our world, except water, that could not in its own way catch fire. Even sea water, if it is overcome by fire, feeds and intensifies it. But as for the polar regions, which by their position are inaccessible to fire and are armed against every assault of flame by their cold and long winter, it may happen that, once the habitable earth has been laid waste and the human race removed from the earth, the progress of the flames will be slower in the remaining regions. And since the heat of the atmosphere will be so great, every region may become a torrid zone. Winds too, both in subterranean channels and in the open air, will be able to drive and force flames with violence in every direction, beneath and above the earth. Mountains will also vomit fire; sulphurous and bituminous lakes, all fat lands and sulphurous clods, which easily catch fire; all the hearths of the whole earth; subterranean minerals and fossils that bear fire; fiery exhalations, smokes, and whatever are the causes or fuel of hot springs and thermal waters; and other things of this kind will lend their assistance. I say nothing of fiery meteors, or of that fire which may fall again from heaven. Yet the forces of the fire that now lies hidden in nature and breaks forth in the universe would nonetheless be overcome, unless God, deus ex machina [Ἀπὸ μηχανῆς], dissolves by his infinite power the work he himself has set in motion. For nature will not rush to destruction of its own accord, but by the will, command and working of God. So also in the burning of Sodom, Jehovah rained sulphur and fire upon Sodom from Jehovah out of heaven [מאת יהוה מן השמים], Gen. 19:24. For God will be able to supply fire from any source, or create new fire, or wonderfully intensify the powers of natural fire. For concerning what God can do, and what he has revealed will come to pass, no doubt of mortals ought to trouble anyone as to whether it will come to pass.

units.la: Neque adeò necessitas urget, ut vel Solis ad terram approximationem, vel ignis, qui in terrae centro sit, eruptionem, vel dispositiones materiae novas, ut idoneum igni fomitem praebeat. Licèt enim Sol & ignis centralis suis in hoc incendio partibus defungi possint, non tamen sedibus suis excuti, & universi ordinem sic perturbari necesse erit. Disparès etiam Astronomorum de Solis & terrae distantia calculi sunt; & mo-derni etiam Solem à terra remotiorem statuunt, & ab ejus incendio periculi metum minuunt. Multa etiam sunt, quae eruptionem ignis centralis impediunt, velut quòd ignea illa massa involucro aliquo tegitur, & velut circumquaque munitur, sine quo facilè exsiliret & dissiparetur, neque adeò nisi sensim & minutim per angustas vias & meatus eluctando, exire posset: quòd tenuis ille & subtilis ignis, qui in corde terrae latet, depraedandis corporibus terrae exterioris crassioribus vix idoneus sit: quòdque solidae terrae & ignis centralis nimia distantia celerem illam eruptionem mirè impediat.
units.tr: Nor does any necessity press us to posit either a approach of the sun to the earth, or an eruption of the central fire that lies in the centre of the earth, or new arrangements of matter to supply fuel suited to the fire. For although the Sun and the central fire may discharge their parts in this burning, they will not necessarily be shaken from their seats, and the order of the universe thus disturbed. The calculations of astronomers concerning the distance between the Sun and the earth also differ; and modern writers too place the Sun more remote from the earth, and thereby lessen the fear of danger from its burning. There are also many things that hinder an eruption of the central fire: for instance, that this fiery mass is covered by some envelope and fortified on all sides as with a wall, without which it would easily leap out and be scattered, and could not escape except gradually and little by little, struggling through narrow passages and channels; that the thin and subtle fire which lies hidden in the heart of the earth is scarcely fit to lay waste the thicker bodies of the outer earth; and that the great distance between the solid earth and the central fire wonderfully hinders that swift eruption.

units.la: Neque denique dispositiones illae, quas sub finem mundi rerum naturae ad incendium superventuras, quoad materiam, formam & situm telluris Doctiss. Burnetius Tell. Th. S. Lib. VIII. 8. prodidit, omnes dubitatione carent.
