Inprimis novus terrae situs, & recta ad solem conversio, quam unicam pro causa incendii Plato agnovit, & ex eodem Burnetius mutuatus est, omni ratione carere videtur, & nescio quam exorbitationem terrae à Sole, praeter ordinem Divinitus constitutum, qui statutum aeternum, Jer. V. 22. appellatur, supponit.
units.tr: Finally, those dispositions which, according to the most learned Burnet, will come upon the natural world at the end of the age, leading to the burning, with regard to the matter, form and position of the earth [Tell. Th. S. Lib. VIII. 8.], are not beyond all doubt. In particular, the new position of the earth and its direct turning towards the sun, which Plato alone recognised as the cause of the burning and which Burnet borrowed from him, seems to lack all reason, and supposes some strange deviation of the earth from the sun apart from the order established by God, which is called an eternal statute, Jer. 5:22.

units.la: XCIX. Sed de effectu conflagrationis mundi quaesitum est. Alii enim cum conflagratione ab agnata impuritate & vanitate purgandum & renovandum: alii in nihilum redigendum statuunt. Utrum credamus, nihil ad fidei summam refert, quia homines fideles salvi, infideles miseri & damnati erunt, sive coeli & elementa in substantia sua renovata, sublatis vitiosis qualitatibus durent; sive in nihilum redigantur. Sed prior tamen sententia Scripturis explicandis aptior est. Nam primum quidem Coelum, & prima terra tulit hominem χοῦικὸν pulvereum, ex pulvere factum, & corpus ψυχικὸν animale, sanguinem & carnem. Intervenit peccatum, & δουλεία τῆς ματαιότητος & corruptionis, Rom. VIII. 20.21. In tali statu Coeli & terra fuerunt, cùm Apostoli de fine mundi scriberent. Cùmque Coelos novos & terram novam promiserint iidem, & quidem juxta ἐπαγγελμα promissum Dei, 2. Pet. III. 13 Esaj. LXV. 17. LXVI 22. Hagg. II. 6. planum esse videtur, Coelum & terram purgatum à vanitate & corruptione, quae peccato hominis cunabula debet, adeóque renovatum, non in nihilum redactum iri.
units.tr: XCIX. But the question has been raised about the outcome of the conflagration of the world. For some hold that by the conflagration it is to be purged of its inherent impurity and vanity and renewed; others that it is to be reduced to nothing. Whichever we believe makes little difference to the sum of the faith, since believers will be saved and unbelievers will be wretched and damned, whether the heavens and the elements endure in their substance renewed, with their faulty qualities removed, or are reduced to nothing. Yet the former opinion is better suited to the interpretation of Scripture. For the first heaven and the first earth bore man earthly, of dust [χοῦικὸν], made from dust, and a body natural, of blood and flesh [ψυχικὸν]. Sin came in, and the bondage of vanity [δουλεία τῆς ματαιότητος] and corruption, Rom. 8:20, 21. In such a state the heavens and the earth were when the Apostles wrote about the end of the world. And since the same Apostles promised new heavens and a new earth, and indeed according to the promise [ἐπαγγελμα] of God, 2 Pet. 3:13; Isa. 65:17; 66:22; Hag. 2:6, it seems plain that the heaven and the earth will be cleansed from the vanity and corruption which owe their cradle to the sin of man, and so will be renewed, not reduced to nothing.

units.la: Et sanè ignis operatio non est in nihilum redigere, sed resolvere, purgare, renovare. Ad annihilationem enim aequè ac ad creationem infinita virtus, nulli creatae, ut causae inferiori vel instrumento sociata, requiritur. Ac licèt Coeli novi & terra nova promissa aliquid etiam continent, quod praesentis saeculi est, & diem judicii praecedit, quia Apoc. XXI. 1. ubi Coelo priore & terra priore praetereunte, sic coelum novum & terra nova facta dicuntur, ut tamen Hierosolyma illa nova de Coelo descendisse, & gentes in ejus loco ambulare, & in eam gloriam suam inferre, ib. v. 2. 24. 26. dicantur: tamen nihil obstat, quo minùs novitatis illius consummationem & perfectionem ad tempus judicium consequens referamus. Nam Christo mortuo, & justitiam saeculorum adducente coeperunt novi coeli, & nova terra, in quibus justitia habitat,
units.tr: And indeed the work of fire is not to reduce to nothing, but to dissolve, purge and renew. For annihilation, as much as creation, requires an infinite power, not joined to any created cause or instrument, as an inferior cause or tool. And although the promised new heavens and new earth also contain something that belongs to the present age and precedes the day of judgment, since in Rev. 21:1, where the first heaven and the first earth pass away, the new heaven and new earth are said to be made, yet that new Jerusalem is said to have come down out of heaven, and the nations to walk in its light, and to bring their glory into it, ib. vv. 2, 24, 26; nothing stands in the way of our referring the consummation and perfection of that newness to the time following the judgment. For with the death of Christ, who brought in everlasting righteousness, the new heavens and the new earth began, in which righteousness dwells,

units.la: quia justitiæ consummatio per authorem ejusdem consummatum cœpit: Antichristo, quoad vim seducendi & nocendi abolito, & Evangelio in toto mundo prædicato, Cœli, terræ, in quibus justitia habitat, novitas progressa amplius manifestabitur. Peccato & luctu carnis per mortem abolita, quin & abolito ultimo hoste, morte, eadem Cœli & terræ, in qua justitia habitat, novitas sic consummabitur & perficietur, ut Cœli & terra ab omni vanitate & corruptione penitus liberentur. Nullus hic locus est expositionibus allegoricis, nisi mundi conflagrationem, cui novi Cœli & nova terra opponuntur, in allegoriam convertere pariter liceat. Idem enim Cœli, eadem terra renovabuntur, qui conflagratione dissolvuntur. Uterque ergo mundus, qui peribit & renovabitur, vel neuter metaphoricus, sed naturalis uterque est. Neque dici potest, fore illos novos creatione, non instauratione. Quorsum enim in nihilum sic Deus rediget, & reficiet, si eadem materia, aut ejusdem molis reliquiæ sufficerent? Sed inprimis ῥητῶς καὶ ἐνεργῶς S. Paulus rem explicat, scribens: Solicita expectatio creaturæ revelationem filiorum Dei expectat, vanitati enim creatura subjecta est non sua sponte, sed propter eum, qui subjecit; ob spem, quòd & ipsa creatura, liberabitur à servitute corruptionis in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei. Novimus enim, quòd omnis creatura unà gemit, & unà parturit hactenus, Rom. VIII.19--23. Ubi κτίσις creatura totum mundum, quem velut personam Apostolus inducit; non Christianos, ceu novam creaturam significat. Aliud enim est creatura simpliciter, aliud nova creatura. De Christianis primitias Spiritus habentibus demum v.23. sermo est. Neque etiam corpora Christianorum intelliguntur, quia v.22. πᾶσα κτίσις omnis creatura nominatur. Omnes ergo res conditæ, præter filios Dei, intelliguntur, quia omnes illas Deus propter peccatum hominis, vanitati, per quam in tolerantia Dei peccato hominis, rebus Dei non rectè utentis, inserviunt, & servituti corruptionis, tormento hominis & morti subjecit. Nam & terræ Deus propter hominem maledixit, Gen.III.17. Sed non sic vanitati Deus creaturas subjecit, ut in perpetuum ei subjectæ maneant, sed ut suo tempore filii Dei, qui in illa colluvie, quæ in terra est, vix dignoscuntur, revelentur, & gloria Dei in ipsis patefiat; atque ita non ipsi soli liberentur, sed etiam unà cum iis creaturæ à servitute vanitatis & corruptionis, hoc est, omni dolore & morte, quæ jam regnat, liberentur. Ideo creaturæ unà gemunt, imò συνωδίνουσι unà parturiunt, & velut Deum admonent, ut filii Dei liberentur, quò simul & ipsæ à servitute corruptionis in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei liberentur. Qualis verò in annihilatione ἐλευθερία libertas esse potest? Quidlibet enim sui conservationem, non destructionem appetit. Neque ὑπομονὴ δοξία solicita expectatio illa, qualem Apostolus v.23. etiam filiis Dei tribuit, alia quàm mutationis ad meliorem statum esse potest. Nam vox illa Senecæ: Non potest esse miser, qui nullus est, hominis Epicuræi potiùs, quàm probi & sapientis esse potest. Et quomodo tum liberatio εἰς ἐλευθερίαν ad libertatem constat? Nam quòd eas εἰς ἐλευθερίαν non ad, sed per vel propter libertatem fi-
units.tr: because the consummation of righteousness began to be accomplished through its author. When Antichrist has been abolished as to his power of seducing and harming, and the Gospel has been preached in the whole world, the newness of the heavens and the earth in which righteousness dwells will be shown further and more fully. When sin and the mourning of the flesh have been abolished by death, and even the last enemy, death, has been done away, the newness of the same heavens and earth in which righteousness dwells will be so completed and perfected that the heavens and the earth are wholly freed from all vanity and corruption. There is no place here for allegorical expositions, unless it is equally permissible to turn into allegory the conflagration of the world, to which the new heavens and the new earth are opposed. For the same heavens and the same earth which are dissolved by the conflagration will be renewed. Therefore each world, that which will perish and that which will be renewed, is either metaphorical, or each is natural. Nor can it be said that they will be new by creation, not by restoration. For why would God reduce things to nothing and then remake them, if the same matter, or remnants of the same mass, would suffice? But above all St. Paul explains the matter expressly and forcefully, writing: The earnest expectation of the creature waits for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who subjected it, in hope that the creature itself also will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groans together and labours together until now, Rom. 8:19–23. Here creature [κτίσις] signifies the whole world, which the Apostle introduces as if it were a person; it does not mean Christians as a new creature. For creature simply is one thing, new creature another. Only in v. 23 does he speak of Christians having the firstfruits of the Spirit. Nor are the bodies of Christians meant here, since in v. 22 the whole creation [πᾶσα κτίσις] is named. Therefore all created things, apart from the sons of God, are meant, because God subjected all of them, on account of the sin of man, to vanity, by which they serve, while God tolerates the sin of man, who does not rightly use the things of God, and to the bondage of corruption, the torment and death of man. For God also cursed the earth for man's sake, Gen. 3:17. But God did not subject the creatures to vanity in such a way that they remain subject to it forever; rather, in due time the sons of God, who can scarcely be distinguished in that filth which is on the earth, will be revealed, and the glory of God will be made manifest in them; and thus not they alone will be freed, but the creatures together with them will be freed from the bondage of vanity and corruption, that is, from all pain and death, which now reigns. Therefore the creatures groan together, indeed labour together [συνωδίνουσι] in travail, and as it were remind God that the sons of God should be freed, so that at the same time they themselves may be freed from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. But what liberty [ἐλευθερία] can there be in annihilation? For anything seeks its own preservation, not its destruction. Nor can that earnest expectation [ὑπομονὴ δοξία], which the Apostle in v. 23 also attributes to the sons of God, be anything other than expectation of change to a better state. For that saying of Seneca, He cannot be wretched who does not exist, belongs rather to an Epicurean man than to an upright and wise one. And how then is deliverance into liberty [εἰς ἐλευθερίαν] established? For the claim that they are freed not into liberty but through or on account of the liberty of the sons of God, according to Chrysostom's interpretation, cannot be accepted.

units.la: liorum Dei liberatum iri ex Chrysostomi interpretatione pertendunt, recipi non potest. Neque εἰς ἐλευθερίαν ita converti potest, quia insolens est εἰς convertere in ᾱᾱ. Quanquam ne sic quidem non liberabuntur, sed per & propter libertatem filiorum Dei ipsæ quoque liberabuntur; sicut nutrix, quæ infantem Regium alit, illo ad Regnum evecto & ipsa ampliorem gradum honoris adipisci potest. Accedunt emphatica illa Davidis: Ante terram fundasti, & opus manuum tuarum Cœlum est. Illa תאבד peribunt: at tu permanebis. Et omnia illa ut vestimentum veterascent; instar indumenti mutabis illa, & mutabuntur, & tanquam amictum convolves ipsos, & mutabuntur, Psal.CII.26.27. Heb.I.11. Ubi אבד perire non significare nihil esse, sed desinere esse hoc quod fuit, hoc est, non amplius vanitati & corruptioni subjici, ipsa comparatio vestimenti veterascentis & mutandi evincit. Non enim vestimentum, quod veterascens mutatur, & convolvitur, esse desinit, sed esse id, quod ante erat, desinit. Quomodo etiam Angeli hactenus mutantur, quòd orbis futurus habitabilis iis non subjicitur, Heb.II.5. non ideo, quia sic mutantur, esse desinunt. Mutatio igitur Cœli & terræ talis erit, qualis est vestimenti veterascentis, vel mutatio in conversum & renovatum idem; vel permutatio cum veste splendidiore, qualis est חלופה שמלה permutatoria vestis, seu nova toga, quæ loco quotidianæ vestis, diebus inprimis festis, assumitur, Genes. XLV.22. Alludere enim ad id verbum Davidis, תחליפם permutabis ea, videtur. Nam & חליפה passim ἀδοχλω successionem, vel decessionem velut ex statione sua, succedente alio, uti in militia fieri solet, significat. Job.XIV.14. Psal.LV.20. Ideo S. Paulus non ὑσίαν essentiam vel substantiam, nec φύσιν naturam, sed σχῆμα figuram, statum externum mundi transfire, 1.Cor. VII.31. dixit. Denique cur propter crimina hominis Cœli & terra abolebuntur, postquam hominis crimina in mundo cessabunt, & subjectionis suæ, qua Deo volenti, nolens, hoc est, præter naturam suam obsecundavit, præmio, non pœna affici debuit? Si Sanctos in Cœlos subvehas, ubi extra cœlum damnati Tartarum, infernum, carcerem habebunt, si corpora omnia in nihilum reciderunt? Ubi illa πολυσεινία & ὑποταπόσις mundi, cujus Scriptura Matth. XIX.28.29. Act.III.21. meminit, in futuro seculo erit, si tot nobiles creaturæ in nihilum redgentur? Ubi dominium hominis in creaturas plenum, quale Psal. VIII.6. &c. promissum, in hac vita nunquam præstatur? Præterea neque satis constat, an ἀποκατάστασις sit, creaturam ullam conditam annihilare, cùm id cum pœnitudine Dei conjunctum, & bonitati atque sapientiæ ejus repugnans videri possit.
units.tr: Nor can the view be accepted that the creature will be freed from corruption along with the sons of God, as in Chrysostom's interpretation. Nor can εἰς ἐλευθερίαν be rendered in that way, since it is unusual to translate εἰς as though it meant in. Even so, they will not be freed in that way; rather, the creatures themselves will also be freed through and because of the liberty of the sons of God. Just as a nurse who suckles a royal infant may herself attain a higher rank of honour when the child is raised to the kingdom, so too the creature may gain a greater dignity. There is also David's emphatic language: Of old hast thou laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of thy hands. They shall perish [תאבד], but thou shalt endure; and they all shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed, and thou shalt fold them up, Ps. 102.26-27; Heb. 1.11. That אבד [to perish] does not mean to be nothing, but to cease to be what it was, that is, no longer to be subject to vanity and corruption, is shown by the very comparison with a garment that wears out and is changed. For a garment that is worn out and folded up does not cease to exist; what ceases is its former condition. So too the angels are, until now, changed in the sense that the world to come is not put in subjection to them, Heb. 2.5; but they do not cease to exist because they are thus changed. The change of heaven and earth, therefore, will be like that of a worn-out garment, or a change into the same thing renewed; or an exchange for a more splendid garment, such as the חלופה שמלה [changing of garments], that is, a new robe, which is put on in place of everyday clothing, especially on festal days, Gen. 45.22. For David's word תחליפם [thou shalt change them] seems to allude to this, since חליפה generally signifies succession, or the departure of one from his post as another takes his place, as commonly happens in war, Job 14.14; Ps. 55.20. Hence St Paul said that the σχῆμα [fashion], the external state of this world, passes away, 1 Cor. 7.31, not its οὐσία [substance] or φύσις [nature]. Finally, why should heaven and earth be abolished on account of man's sins, once the sins of men have ceased in the world; and why should they not rather be rewarded than punished for their subjection, by which they obeyed God, though against their will, that is, beyond their nature? If you carry the saints up into heaven, where the damned will have Tartarus, hell and prison outside heaven, what becomes of it if all bodies have been reduced to nothing? Where will the [πολυσεινία] and the [ὑποταπόσις] of the world be, which Scripture mentions in Matt. 19.28-29 and Acts 3.21, in the age to come, if so many noble creatures are reduced to nothing? Where will the full dominion of man over the creatures, promised in Ps. 8.6 and elsewhere, be found, since it is never granted in this life? Moreover, it is by no means certain whether it is a restoration (ἀποκατάστασις) to annihilate any created thing, since this may seem to be joined with the repentance of God and to conflict with his goodness and wisdom.

units.la: C. Non desunt tamen veteres & recentiores, qui onere explicandi futurum mundi statum, si ille permanserit, se levantes, mundum in conflagratione penitus abolendum statuant. Et veterum quidem, quæ allegari solent, dicta, sic satis ambigua sunt, nisi quòd Arnobius Junior de Deo Trino & uno diserte satis, mundum ad nihilum redigendum esse, sicut ex nihilo factus est, profitetur; & Ambrosius Hexaëm. lib. I. 6. Cœli substantiam mansuram negare videtur. Diser-tior Johannes Chassanio Loc. comm. lib. III. 22. rationibus quibusdam tueri,quòd mundus annihilandus fit, satagit. Recentiores Lutherani nonnulli, inprimis Sociniani, ne inferno locus fit,id ipsum asserunt. Neque nostrorum etiam nonnullorum Tileni,Prideaux,& aliorum suffragia desunt. Sed leviora eorundem argumenta sunt. Nam testimonia Psal. CII. 27. 2. Petr. III. 7.10.12. quibus hypothesin suam firmare coguntur, sententiæ nostræ favere, jam ostendimus. Neque magis iis favet, quòd cœlum evaniturum, ut fumus, Esaj. ς 1. 6. dicitur, quia fumus non annihilatur,sed tenues in auras evanescit. Et non resurgent mortui ... usque dum non erunt Cœli, Job. XIV. 12. puta in præsenti hoc statu, quo vanitati serviunt,adeóque qui nunc sunt cœli, 2. Petr. III. 7. 10. quales cœli & terra praeteribunt, Matth. V. 18. XXIV. 35. quoad caducam conditionem suam & mutationem, Psal. CII. 27. non abolitione plenaria. David enim ibid. perire per mutari vel permutari explicat. Quanquam Christi verba Cœli & terra præteribunt, verba verò mea non præteribunt, Matth. cap. XXIV. vers. 35. sensum comparativum habent, quòd citiùs illi, quàm hi (sermones) præteriturí sint. Usitato enim Hebraismo ponitur pro praeterirent potiùs, quia Hebraei non habent ... sive ..., & pro eo futurum modi indicativi usurpant, quos Hellenistæ sæpius sequuntur. Comparatione igitur rei, quæ videatur maximè impossibilis, utitur Christus, ut ostendat multò ... esse, ut sua oracula non impleantur, quàm ut cœlum & terra prætereat. Et primo Cœlo & prima terra prætereunte, non erit mare, Apoc. XXI. 1. Sed non ideo non erit novum Cœlum & nova terra, ibid. Mare verò mysticum gentes Christo sese opponentes, non erunt amplius. Neque opus habebunt lucerna, & luce solis homines novæ Hierosolymæ, novi Cœli & novæ terræ, ibid. XXII. 5. non in altero duntaxat, sed præsente etiam seculo, in quo nova Hierosolyma incipit. Ubi Dominus Deus eos illuminat, ita ut doctore & illuminatore alio non indigeant. Omnes filii tui docti à Deo, Esaj. LIV. 13. Præterea etiam sublato naturalium luminum usu, quali in hoc seculo homines indigent, non deerunt usus alii. Neque enim nullus omnino finis vel usus renovati mundi erit, licèt finis ille & usus, quem in hoc seculo hominis sustinendi & alendi respectu, habuit, cessaturus sit. Unius enim rei eodem & diverso tempore multi fines esse possunt. Dei nempe sapientiam, omnipotentiam, bonitatem & æternitatem magnopere commendabit: & spiritualis beatorum hominum contemplationis & oblectationis secundaria quædam incitamenta & exercitamenta erunt,ne de aliis finibus nobis ignotis dicam; qui facilè efficient, ne sit vagina sine gladio, uti Tilenus timebat. Sapienter Calvinus Instit. lib. III. 25: 11. In ipso inquit, aspectu tanta erit amœnitas,tanta sine usu suavitas in sola notitia, ut hæc felicitas omnia, quibus nunc juvamur, adminicula longè exuperet. Fingamus in opulentissima, & ubi nulla nos voluptas deficiat,mundi plaga esse positos: quem non sui morbi ab usu beneficiorum Dei subinde impediunt, ac prohibent; Cui non sua intemperies cur-
units.tr: C. Nevertheless, there are not lacking ancient and more recent writers who, relieving themselves of the burden of explaining the future state of the world if it were to endure, hold that the world must be utterly abolished in a conflagration. Among the ancients, the passages usually cited are rather ambiguous, except that Arnobius the Younger, On the Triune and One God, professes quite plainly that the world is to be reduced to nothing, just as it was made out of nothing; and Ambrose, Hexaemeron I.6, seems to deny that the substance of heaven will remain. John Chassanion, Loci communes III.22, is more explicit and strives to defend, by certain arguments, that the world is to be annihilated. Some of the more recent Lutherans, and above all the Socinians, assert the same thing, so that there may be no place for hell. Nor are the votes of some of our own people wanting: Tilenus, Prideaux and others. But their arguments are weaker. For we have already shown that the testimonies of Ps. 102.27 and 2 Pet. 3.7, 10, 12, by which they are compelled to support their hypothesis, favour our view. Nor does it help them that heaven is said to vanish like smoke, Isa. 51.6, since smoke is not annihilated but dissolves into thin air. Nor does the dead will not rise ... until the heavens are no more, Job 14.12, help them; this refers to the present state, in which creatures serve vanity; and so the heavens that now are, 2 Pet. 3.7, 10, such as heaven and earth will pass away, Matt. 5.18; 24.35, refer to their frail condition and change, Ps. 102.27, not to complete abolition. For David himself explains perish as be changed or be exchanged. Although Christ's words, heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away, Matt. 24.35, have a comparative sense, namely that heaven and earth will pass away more quickly than these words. For by a common Hebraism it stands for would rather pass away, since the Hebrews do not have the comparative form, and in its place they use the future of the indicative mood, which the Hellenists often follow. Christ therefore uses the comparison of a thing that seems most impossible, to show that it would be far more impossible for his oracles to go unfulfilled than for heaven and earth to pass away. And the first heaven and the first earth having passed away, there was no more sea, Rev. 21.1. But this does not mean there will be no new heaven and new earth, ibid. The sea, however, is the mystical nations opposing Christ, which will be no more. Nor will the men of the new Jerusalem, the new heaven and the new earth, have need of a lamp or the light of the sun, Rev. 22.5, not only in the age to come but also in the present age, in which the new Jerusalem begins. There the Lord God gives them light, so that they need no other teacher or illuminator: all your sons will be taught by God, Isa. 54.13. Moreover, even when the use of natural light, such as men need in this age, has been removed, other uses will not be lacking. For there will be no end or use whatever of the renewed world, although that end and use which it had in this age, with respect to sustaining and nourishing man, will cease. For one thing can have many ends, both at the same time and at different times. It will greatly commend the wisdom, omnipotence, goodness and eternity of God; and there will be certain secondary incitements and exercises of the spiritual contemplation and delight of the blessed men, not to mention other ends unknown to us, which will readily ensure that it is not a sheath without a sword, as Tilenus feared. Calvin wisely says, Institutes III.25.11: In the very sight, he says, there will be such loveliness, and such sweetness without use in the knowledge alone, that this happiness will far surpass all the aids by which we are now helped. Let us imagine that we are placed in the most opulent region of the world, where no pleasure fails us; a man whom the sicknesses of his body do not from time to time impede and prevent from using the benefits of God; a man whose own bodily weakness does not often break off his course.

units.la: sum sæpe abrumpit? Unde consequitur, liquidam & puram ab omni vitio fruitionem,quamvis nullus sit vitæ corruptibilis usus, felicitatis esse cumulum. Neque etiam Cœli & terra, aliæque creaturæ non intelligentes, quia elementares & corruptibiles sunt,iccirco perennitatis & felicitatis capaces non sunt. Licèt enim capaces non sint per naturam, uti nec corpus humanum sic capax est: capaces tamen sunt per eudoxiam beneplacitum Dei & gloriam. Neque par perennitatis, seu & felicitatis ratio est: quia Apostolus Rom. VIII. 27. illam simpliciter, hanc secundum quid creaturis tribuit. Estque omnino tempus adjunctum mundi, & rerum naturalium hujus seculi oppositè ad Deum & spiritus,& quia hujus seculi tempus quædam mensura est; non futuri seculi. Quid enim aliàs de homine,& corpore ejus elementari fieret? Denique neque mundus, quia ex nihilo creatus est,in nihilum etiam dilabetur, quia, uti illi arguunt,contrariorum eadem ratio est. Ita enim etiam Cœlum beatorum & spiritus annihilari deberent. Non ergo hactenus opponuntur, quia creaturarum annihilatio ex Scripturis apodicticè probari non potest.
units.tr: Hence it follows that a clear and pure enjoyment, free from every fault, is an abundance of happiness even though there be no use of corruptible life. Nor do heaven and earth and the other creatures, not understanding this, because they are elemental and corruptible, for that reason fail to be capable of permanence and happiness. For although they are not capable by nature, just as the human body is not capable in that way either, they are nevertheless capable through the good pleasure [εὐδοκία] of God and his glory. Nor is the ground of permanence the same as that of happiness, since the Apostle, Rom. 8.21, ascribes the former to creatures simply, and the latter in a certain respect. And time is wholly attached to the world and to natural things of this age, as opposed to God and spirits; and since the time of this age is a certain measure, it is not that of the age to come. For what would otherwise become of man and his elemental body? Finally, the world, since it was created out of nothing, will not also dissolve into nothing, because, as they argue, contraries have the same reason. For in that case the heaven of the blessed and the spirits would also have to be annihilated. Therefore these are not opposed so far, because the annihilation of creatures cannot be proved from Scripture by apodictic argument.

units.la: CI. Cùm igitur certa,vel valde probabilis saltem sit vindicatio,instauratio & παλιγγενεσία creaturarum, quibus ea non obventura, vel obventura sit, obscurum esse non poterit. Apostolus equidem πᾶσαν κτίσιν omnem creaturam suspirare dixit, Rom. VIII. 22. sed omnes tamen à filiis Dei, ibid. v. 23. disparavit. Non ergo simpliciter omnes sic instaurabuntur, ut renovatæ in mundo existant, sicut ante exiterunt. Non enim instaurabuntur vel Angeli,licèt ita visum nonnullis sit, ob cessaturum eorundem ministerium hac in vita electis navatum; quia non obstante eo ministerio, ceu beati, semper faciem Patris gloriosam vident, Matth. XVIII. 10. & durum foret dicere,quòd propter ministerium illud vanitati subjecti sint: vel homines sive electi, quia eorum glorificatio à creaturæ liberatione diserte distinguitur, v. 22.23. vel reprobi, quia nulla iis instaurationis spes proposita est,sed æterna eosdem damnatio manet,ibid. XXV. 41. Vel Cœlum beatorum & Tartarus, quia utraque sedes à jacto mundi fundamento glorificandis & damnandis parata est, ibid. v. 34. 41. & immutabiliter servatur, ibid. v. 46. & Cœlum illud expers corruptionis: Infernus verò non magis,quàm ipsi Diaboli instaurationis capax est. Deerunt etiam novo huic mundo, tum spinæ, tribuli, sentes, cardui,&c. utpote quæ ex justa mundi maledictione propter peccatum hominis provenerunt, Genes. III. 18. tum creaturæ ex putrefactione & corruptione natæ, velut bufones, ranæ, mures &c. nec non ex confusa generatione producte, quia à prima creatione non extiterunt,nec ante lapsum hominis obtinuerunt: tum omne genus plantarum & animalium,quæ ante consummationem seculi interierunt & dissolutæ sunt,quia iis nusquam resuscitatio, vel παλιγγενεσία promittitur, imò totalis interitus obnuntiatur,Psal. XLIX. 13.21. Eccl. III. 19. tum opera artificialia, urbes, arces, domus, fabricæ, quia terræ opera unà cum terra comburentur, 2. Petr. III. 10. & illa terrenæ vitæ vitæ solius usum, cum hoc seculo desituru m, spectabant. Instaurabuntur verò tum Cœlum æreum & æthereum & terra,quia Cœli novi & terra nova promittuntur ibid. v. 13. &c. tum Cœlorum exercitus, Sol,luna,sidera reliqua,quia inde à lapsu Adami nunquam suos gemitus, suspiria, parturitiones intermiserunt,adeóque etiam libertatem recuperabunt, Rom. VIII. 19.22. & passim perpetuitas spiritualis Regni Christi ex continuatione Solis & Lunæ adumbratur,Psal. LXXXIX. 30. 37. 38. & alibi; & usus eorum licèt non ad illuminationem & vegetationem mundi inferioris,vel ad distinctionem temporum : tamen ad glorificationem Dei & Beatorum ἀνακτιν inservire poterunt: tum denique plantarum omne genus,quarum semina terra non prorsus perdet: tum & animalium omnis generis non extinctorum individua,sed species,quia nomine omnis creaturæ vanitati obnoxiæ, & saltem quoad eorum speciem à servitute vanitatis & corruptionis liberandæ continentur,Rom.VIII.20.22. & homini plenum dominium in creaturas peccato amissum,restituetur,quod nos in medio relinquimus. Id enim si continget, vel animalium species miraculosè ab igne conflagrationis præservabuntur,vel novæ creabuntur,sed neutrum eorum liquet. Hæc probabiliter edisserruisse sufficiat. Plura & certiora in Schola coelesti,cùm in ἀνπεκλαν instaurationis hujus perducti fuerimus, discere erit.
units.tr: CI. Since the vindication, restoration and palingenesia [παλιγγενεσία] of creatures is certain, or at least highly probable, it cannot be unclear which creatures will or will not share in it. The Apostle indeed said that every creature [πᾶσαν κτίσιν] groans, Rom. 8:22, but he set apart those who are not sons of God, ibid. v. 23, from the others. So not all creatures will be restored in such a way as to exist in the world renewed as they existed before. Angels will not be restored, although some have thought so, on the ground that their ministry, given to the elect in this life, will cease. For even without that ministry, as blessed beings they always behold the glorious face of the Father, Matt. 18:10. And it would be harsh to say that they were made subject to vanity because of that ministry. Nor will human beings, that is, the elect, be restored in that way, since their glorification is explicitly distinguished from the liberation of creation, vv. 22–23. Nor will the reprobate, for no hope of restoration is held out to them, but eternal damnation remains for them, ibid. 25:41. Nor will the heaven of the blessed and Tartarus, since both abodes were prepared from the foundation of the world for those to be glorified and those to be damned, ibid. vv. 34, 41, and are kept unchangeably, ibid. v. 46. That heaven is free from corruption; hell is no more capable of restoration than the devil himself. There will also be missing from this new world: thorns, thistles, brambles, thistledown, and so on, since they arose from the just curse on the world because of human sin, Gen. 3:18. Also those creatures born from putrefaction and corruption, such as toads, frogs, mice and so on, and those produced by confused generation, since they did not exist from the first creation and were not there before the fall of man. Also every kind of plants and animals that perished and were dissolved before the end of the age, since no resurrection or palingenesia is promised to them, but total destruction is announced, Ps. 49:13, 21; Eccl. 3:19. Also artificial works, cities, citadels, houses, buildings, since the works of the earth will be burned together with the earth, 2 Pet. 3:10, and those works looked only to the use of earthly life, which will cease with this age. But the heaven of air and ether and the earth will be restored, since new heavens and a new earth are promised, ibid. v. 13, etc. Also the host of heaven, the sun, the moon and the other stars, since from the fall of Adam they have never ceased their groaning, sighing and travailing, and so they too will recover their liberty, Rom. 8:19–22. And the perpetuity of the spiritual kingdom of Christ is everywhere foreshadowed by the continuance of the sun and moon, Ps. 89:30, 37–38, and elsewhere. Their use, though not for illuminating and nourishing the lower world, nor for marking the times, may nevertheless serve for the glorification of God and the blessed. Lastly, every kind of plants, whose seeds the earth will not utterly lose; and also the species of animals of every kind, not the individuals that have died, since under the name every creature subject to vanity they are included, and at least as to their species they are to be freed from the bondage of vanity and corruption, Rom. 8:20–22. And the full dominion over creatures that man lost through sin will be restored to him. We leave this open. For if it happens, either the species of animals will be miraculously preserved from the fire of the conflagration, or new ones will be created; but neither is clear. It is enough to have set this out as a probable account. More and more certain things we shall learn in the heavenly School, when we have been brought to the ἀνπεκλαν of this restoration.

units.la: CII. Nimis enim curiosè Cl. Burnetius novum hunc mundum metatus est. Nam ante omnia novos incolas, novam hominum progeniem eidem destinare ausus est, quam ex Cœlo ipso repetit; homines videlicet perfectè justos & sanctos. Cùm enim Deus terram creaverit לא תהו non in vanum, sed לשבת ad habitandam eam,Esaj. XLV. 18. & in terra illa nova habitare justitia dicatur,2. Pet. III. 13. iccirco Divam Astræam cum cœlitum Sanctorum comitatu in terram rediturram adRegnum mille annorum, seu beatum illud seculum in corporibus terrestribus & sui generis, transigendum,continxit. Sed nos Regnum illud suprà verbi Dei mucrone confiximus: Habitabit certè in nova illa terra justitia,habitabunt justi tum ante judicium, propter possessionem justitiæ Christi; tum post judicium, propter consummatam juitorum gloriam, uti suprà explicavimus. Sed non sic post judicium in terra perfectè Sancti & justi habitabunt,ut in ea cum Christo regnent. Christi enim, capitis illorum Regia Cœlum, & in Cœlo dextra Dei Patris est. Ibi cum Christo capite suo plenè uniti plenè regnabunt. Habitabunt nihilominus in terra,quia in capite suo Christo terram scabellum pedum suorum habebunt, & creaturis omnibus dominabuntur. Nam & in Regno habitare Rex dicitur,qui in Regia sua considens, à Regni partibus reliquis corpore suo divulsus,easdem voluntate & imperio suo regit & moderatur. Neque etiam præsentis seculi est dijudicare,annon pii quoque terras,& habitatas olim sedes revisuri, novámque rerum faciem admiraturi sint: cognoscemus id tum,cùm & ipsi cogniti erimus. Sed & ortum novi mundi ex reliquiis antiqui; nec non novi Cœli & novæ terræ dotes & conditiones sub-tilius æquo,& insistens hypothesi suæ de prioris mundi ex Chao productione, & consecuta mutatione idem Clar. Vir pensavit. In incendio enim mundi quicquid fusum & liquefactum erat ab igne imum petiturum,atque interiorem solidamque terram non combustam ambiturum; quicquid autem in fumos & halitus resolutum abiit,partes superiores occupaturum, atque ita portionem terræ exustam duas in massas,craßiorem,instar materiæ fusæ, vel ex fusione concretæ, & levem atque volatilem priori superincumbentem, abituram, ac demum partem massæ exustæ in aëre fluitantem novos Cœlos & novam terram composituram,arbitratur. Quoad ejusdem mundi conditiones & qualitates, eum futurum Paradisiacum seu primigenium, cujus forma integra, levis, æquabilis, sine montibus & mari, & litus ad solem rectus & æquilibris, atque inde ver perenne; Cœlúmque perpetuò placidum & serenum,solum fertile,rerum omnium ubertas, fructus nullo non tempore maturi, lenes amnes, patulæ arbores, molles auræ ad repellendum solis æstum,vegeta & longæva,sine morbis & ægritudine natura, procul venenis vel venenatis herbis, metallis & mineralibus, ex quorum mixturis veneni origo sit; nullæ bestiæ immites vel rapaces, sed propter mutatum temperamentum sanguinis & succorum acrium mites & cicuratæ omnes, extituræ sint, statuit. Quæ singula excutere hujus loci non est. Vereor id unum,ne vir ingenii cætera vastissimi,non tantùm Prophetias quasdam,quibus ad probandas illas novæ terræ conditiones & qualitates usus est, nimis liberales fecerit; sed inprimis etiam,ne ad probandam duplicem terram, Paradisiacam,cum qua novam illam aurei seculi sui terram comparat, & hodiernam,abusus sitS.Petri verbis,scribentis contra illusores novissimi temporis,quòd ἐκπυλαι ab olim fuerint Cœli & terra, quæ ex aqua & per aquam constitit, Dei verbo, per quæ mundus, qui tunc fuit, aqua inundatus periit: Cœli autem, qui nunc sunt, & terra eodem verbo repositi, igni servantur in diem judicii,2. Pet. III. 5.6.7. Non enim aliam terram fuisse initio,aliam nunc esse docet. Nam etiam,quæ nunc est,illa est,quæ fuit ἐκπυλαι ab olim, quia ex aqua & per aquam Dei verbo utroque consistit. Ex aquis enim constitit,quia terra super aquas inferiores,quæ eam non operiunt, fundata est, Psal. XXIV. 2. & in creatione ipsa, quando terra & aqua separatæ sunt, ab increpatione Dei, hoc est, uti S. Petrus dicit, Dei verbo,Genef. I. 9. 10. fugerant aquæ in locum suum, & ascenderunt montes ac descenderunt valles, Psal. CIV. 5-9. adeóque mare ex utero terræ exiit, Job. XXXVIII. 8. Qui status terræ hodiernæ etiam est. Etiam per aquam terra prima constitit, quia Deus non tantùm verbo suo fecit, ut terra ab aquis separaretur, & supra aquas extaret,sed etiam terram aquis circumdedit. Sunt enim cava patentia, in quibus est aqua: sunt cavernæ subterraneæ aquæ plenæ,sunt venæ aquæ exuberantes; ita ut humore mediante pulvis cohæreat,& ab eo, quæ nascuntur,alimenta trahant,& ubique sint putei aquis scatentes. Præterea sunt aquæ superiores, non tantùm quæ ex inferioribus per partes ascendunt, & in terram recidunt; sed etiam humor subtilis, qui totum aëra implet, absque quo esset, vivere animalia non possent. Pertinet huc moderatio aquæ in periodis lunaribus, de quibus Jobus: Modum circinavit super faciem aquarum (quem æstu suo & incremento non egrederetur) usque ad finem lucis cum tenebris (plenilunium, quando lux non tantum interdiu, sed etiam noctu est) Job. XXVI. 10. & fluxus ac refluxus quotidianus. Deus enim mari limitem posuit, quem non transgrediatur, ibid. XXXVIII. 10. 11. Psal. CIV. 9. Cùm ergo & prima terra ex aqua, & per aquam constiterit, & hodierna sic consistat, telluris illius Paradisiacæ & hodiernæ discrimen, nec non futuræ terræ novæ cum Paradisiaca comparationem fundamento destitui, & hiare multum, necesse est.
units.tr: CII. For the illustrious Burnet measured this new world too minutely. For above all he dared to assign to it new inhabitants, a new race of men, which he fetches from heaven itself, namely men perfectly just and holy. For since God created the earth not in vain [לא תהו] but to be inhabited [לשבת], Isa. 45:18, and it is said that righteousness dwells in that new earth, 2 Pet. 3:13, he therefore imagined that the divine Astraea with the company of the holy inhabitants of heaven would return to earth for the kingdom of a thousand years, or that blessed age, to be spent in earthly bodies of their own kind. But we have already transfixed that kingdom with the sword of God's word. Righteousness will certainly dwell in that new earth, and the just will dwell there both before judgment, by the possession of Christ's righteousness, and after judgment, by the perfected glory of the righteous, as we explained above. But after judgment the perfectly holy and just will not dwell on the earth in such a way as to reign there with Christ. For the royal seat of Christ, the head of them, is heaven, and at the right hand of God the Father in heaven. There, fully united with Christ their head, they will reign fully. Nevertheless they will also dwell on the earth, because in their head Christ they will have the earth as the footstool of their feet, and will rule over all creatures. For a king is also said to dwell in his kingdom when, sitting on his throne, though his body is separated from the other parts of the kingdom, he governs and directs them by his will and command. Nor is it for the present age to judge whether the godly too will revisit the lands and the seats once inhabited, and marvel at the new face of things. We shall know that when we too shall be known. But this illustrious man has weighed in too subtle a way, beyond what is right, both the origin of the new world from the remains of the old, and the endowments and conditions of the new heaven and new earth, relying on his hypothesis of the production of the former world out of chaos and the subsequent change. For in the burning of the world, he thinks, whatever was melted and liquefied by the fire would sink to the bottom and surround the inner and solid earth, which was not burned; whatever dissolved into smoke and vapour would occupy the upper parts; and thus the burned portion of the earth would split into two masses, the denser, like melted matter or matter concreted by fusion, which would sink, and the light and volatile mass lying above it; and at last the part of the burned mass floating in the air would compose the new heavens and the new earth. As to the conditions and qualities of that same world, he lays down that it will be paradisiacal or original, its form entire, smooth, even, without mountains or sea, its shore level with the sun and balanced, and hence an everlasting spring; the heaven perpetually calm and serene; the soil fertile, abundance of all things, fruits ripe at every season, gentle streams, spreading trees, soft breezes to repel the heat of the sun; a nature vigorous and long-lived, without disease and sickness; far from poisons and poisonous herbs, metals and minerals from whose mixtures poison arises; no savage or ravening beasts, but all gentle and tame, because of the changed temper of the blood and the sharp juices. Each of these points it is not the place here to examine. I fear this one thing: that a man of otherwise most vast talent has been too free not only with certain prophecies, by which he used to prove those conditions and qualities of the new earth, but above all that he has abused the words of St Peter, writing against the scoffers of the last times, in order to prove a double earth, the paradisiacal one, with which he compares his new earth of the golden age, and the present one. For he wrote that the heavens and the earth were of old, which consisted out of water and through water by the word of God, through which the world that then was perished, being overflowed with water; but the heavens which now are, and the earth, by the same word are stored up, reserved for fire unto the day of judgment, 2 Pet. 3:5–7. For he does not teach that the earth was one thing at the beginning and another now. For even the earth that now is, is the one that was of old, since it consists out of water and through water by the word of God. For it consisted out of waters, because the earth was founded upon the waters beneath, which do not cover it, Ps. 24:2; and at creation itself, when the earth and water were separated, at the rebuke of God, that is, as St Peter says, by the word of God, Gen. 1:9–10, the waters fled to their place, and the mountains rose and the valleys sank, Ps. 104:5–9; and thus the sea issued from the womb of the earth, Job 38:8. This is also the present state of the earth. The first earth also stood through water, because God did not only by his word make the earth to be separated from the waters and to stand above them, but also surrounded the earth with waters. For there are hollow open places in which there is water; there are subterranean caverns full of water; there are abundant veins of water, so that by the mediation of moisture the dust holds together, and things that spring up draw their nourishment from it, and everywhere there are wells bubbling with water. Besides these there are upper waters, not only those that rise from below in parts and fall back on the earth, but also the fine moisture that fills the whole air, without which living animals could not exist. To this belongs the regulation of the water in the lunar periods, of which Job speaks: He has compassed the waters with bounds (so that they should not go beyond their swell and increase) until the day and night are ended (the full moon, when there is light not only by day but also by night), Job 26:10; and the daily ebb and flow. For God set a bound for the sea which it does not pass, ibid. 38:10–11; Ps. 104:9. Since, then, the first earth both stood out of water and through water, and the present earth so stands, it must be that the distinction between that paradisiacal earth and the present one, and also the comparison of the future new earth with the paradisiacal one, lack foundation and gape wide.

units.la: CIII. Potius nobis esse debet, non de rebus incompertis, & nec per revelationem, nec per naturam cognitis ἀδηλα dicere, quàm Cœli & terræ conflagrationis & renovationis contemplatione uti ad pietatis incrementum & exercitium, monitore eodem Apostolo: Cùm igitur hæc omnia solvantur, quales nos esse oportet in sanctis conversationibus & pietatis exercitiis? Expectantes & accelerantes præsentiam diei Dei (operam dantes, ut parati simus ad præsentiam diei Domini, & quantum in nobis est, ejus adventui remoram & obstaculum non ponere, sed ea, quæ interim fieri oportet, cujusmodi sunt Gentium vocatio, & earum cum Judæis introductio, studio nostro accelerare) propter quam cœli æstuantes solventur, & elementa candefacta liquescent. Novos autem Cœlos, & novam terram, secundum promissum ejus expectamus, in quibus justitia habitat. Quapropter hæc expectantes studete immaculati & inculpati ipsi inveniri in pace, 2. Petr. III. 11–16. Nam qui præsentia solvenda norunt, & novos Cœlos, novámque terram, in qua justitia habitat, expectant, eos missis caducis præsentibus, animum ad cœlestia intendere, & omnibus votis & desideriis præsentiam diei Domini, & novos Cœlos novámque terram accelerare convenit. Non enim acquiescendum est in Cœlis & in terra illa, in qua si maximè justitia habitat, tamen cum eadem etiam ματαιότης & φθορὰ vanitas & corruptio habitat. Neque aliter efficere poterimus, ut ea novitas appropinquet, & ejus quandoque participes fiamus, quàm sancta conversatione, & omni pietate, quia Deus injustos & impuros novorum Cœlorum, & novæ terræ hæreditate neutiquam dignabitur; & pietate atque sancta conversatione plurimos ad justitiam adducere, Regnum Cœlorum, Cœlos novos & terram novam, in quibus justitia habitat, accelerare oportet.
units.tr: CIII. Rather than speak of matters that are unknown, known neither through revelation nor through nature, [ἀδηλα: unseen things], we ought to use the contemplation of the burning and renewal of heaven and earth to grow and exercise our piety, the Apostle himself advising us: Since therefore all these things are to be dissolved, what manner of persons ought you to be in holy conversation and exercises of piety? Looking for and hastening the presence of the day of God (taking care to be ready for the presence of the day of the Lord, and, so far as lies in us, not to place any delay or obstacle in the way of his coming, but to hasten by our zeal those things which must meanwhile come to pass, such as the calling of the Gentiles and their introduction along with the Jews) because of which the heavens, being set on fire, will be dissolved, and the elements, melted by heat, will be liquefied. But we look for new heavens and a new earth according to his promise, in which righteousness dwells. Wherefore, looking for these things, be diligent that you may be found by him without spot and blameless in peace, 2 Pet. 3.11–16. For those who know that present things are to be dissolved, and who look for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells, ought to let go of transitory present things and direct their minds to heavenly things, and with all their prayers and desires hasten the presence of the day of the Lord and the new heavens and new earth. For we must not rest in those heavens and in that earth, since in them, however much righteousness may dwell, there also dwell [ματαιότης: vanity] and [φθορὰ: corruption]. Nor can we bring it about that this newness draws near and that we one day become partakers of it, except by holy conversation and all piety, because God will by no means deign to make the unrighteous and impure heirs of the new heavens and the new earth. And by piety and holy conversation, bringing very many to righteousness, we ought to hasten the kingdom of heaven, the new heavens and the new earth in which righteousness dwells.

units.la: CIV. Superest, ut de statu hominum in futuro seculo dicamus. Qui vel damnatorum vel salvandorum est. Ille pœna in inferno æternùm sustinenda: hic vita æterna est. De illo quàm de hoc prius agendum est; quia Christus Matth. XXV. 34. sic processum judicii descripsit, ut sententiam quidem absolventem prius, condemnantem posteriùs dixerit & pronuntiaverit, at executionem sententiæ à damnatione impiorum cœptam in glorificatione piorum terminaverit. Faciet enim non parum ad augendam beatitudinem electorum, quòd
units.tr: CIV. It remains for us to speak of the state of men in the future age, which is either of the damned or of the saved. The former is punishment to be endured in hell for ever; the latter is eternal life. The former must be treated before the latter, because Christ, in Matt. 25.34, so described the course of judgment that he spoke and pronounced first the sentence absolving, and afterwards the sentence condemning, and he ended the execution of the sentence, begun in the damnation of the impious, in the glorification of the pious. For it will contribute not a little to increasing the blessedness of the elect that

units.la: impios ad supplicium rapi coram videbunt, ut ex comparatione beatitudinis suæ cum miseria damnatorum magis Dei erga se gratiam agnoscant & prædicent. Eundem ordinem secutus Augustinus de Civ. D. lib. XXI. 1. hanc methodi rationem reddit: Incredibile videtur esse in æternis corpora durare cruciatibus, quàm sine dolore ullo in æterna beatitudine permanere. Ac per hoc cùm illam pœnam non debere esse incredibilem demonstravero, adjuvabit, ut multò facilius omni carens molestia immortalitas corporum in Sanctis futura credatur. At nec minùs sapienter idem Augustinus ibid. lib. XX. 30. de ordine hoc scripsit: Quibus modis, inquiens, & quo ordine veniant Christus venturus ad judicium, mortuorum, resurrectio, bonorum & malorum diremtio, mundi conflagratio, ejusdemque renovatio, magis tum docebit rerum experientia, quàm nunc valet consequi ad perfectum hominem intelligentia.
units.tr: they will see the impious dragged off to punishment before their eyes, so that from the comparison of their own blessedness with the misery of the damned they may the more acknowledge and proclaim God's grace towards them. Following the same order, Augustine (de Civ. Dei, bk. 21, ch. 1) gives the reason for this method: It seems incredible that bodies should endure in eternal torments, when it is less incredible that they should remain in eternal blessedness without any pain. And so, when I have shown that that punishment ought not to be incredible, it will help to make it much easier to believe that the immortality of the bodies of the saints, free from all discomfort, is to come. But no less wisely Augustine wrote about this order in the same work, bk. 20, ch. 30: In what manner, he says, and in what order Christ will come to judgment, the resurrection of the dead, the separation of good and bad, the burning of the world and its renewal, will then be taught more by experience of the facts than human understanding, in its perfection, can now attain.

units.la: CV. Terribilis natura sua mors est: terribilius judicium: maximè terribilis Infernus, seu in interno κλαυθμὸς καὶ ὀδόντων supplicium æternum, ad quod Christus damnatos facessere, Matth. XXV. 46. jubilit. Voces, quibus ille in Scriptura describitur, inprimis שאול & ἅδης sunt, quæ perinde ut infernus, proprie sepulchrum, in quod corpora inferuntur, & in quibus homo sepultus est velut in שאול in loco, in quo, ceu abiens, in שאלה quæstione est; & ἅδης, hoc est, ἀιδὴς τόπος loco invisibili: impropriè autem locum damnatorum significant. שאול עריה יהמכו Orcum gressus ejus (adulteræ) tenent, Prov. V. 5. hoc est, non ad vitam, quæ verè vita est, sed ad locum tristitiæ æternæ gressus ejus tendunt. דרכי שאול ביתה Viæ inferni, tristitiæ æternæ viæ domus ejus, ibid. VII. 27. למען סור מטאול מטה ad recedendum ab orco infra, ibid. XV. 24. שאול עם Cum inferno, Diabolo, morte inducias fecimus, Esai. XXVIII. 15. Redeunt improbi לשאולה ad infernum, ad Regnum Diaboli, tenebrarum, Psal. IX. 18. Etiam ἅδης in N. T. locum damnatorum notat. πύλαι ἅδου Portæ inferorum non prævalebunt ei, Matth. XVI. 18. Helluo ἐν τῷ ᾅδῃ in inferno sustulit oculos, Luc. XVI. 23. Ubi tua ô mors, victoria, ubi tuus, ἅδη inferne stimulus? 1. Cor. XV. 55. Habeo claves τὰς ἀδὸς καὶ τὸ θανάτου inferni & mortis, Apoc. I. 18. Aliis quinetiam locus ille nominibus venit, velut אבדון perditionis, Job. XXVI. 6. XXVIII. 22. Prov. XV. 11. גיא הנם Ge-Hinnom, Vallis Hinnom seu Γέεννα & Γεέννη, gehenna, quæ proprie vallis urbi Hierosolymæ vicina, amœna, & Cedronis aquis irrigua, in qua erat תפת Thophet, ubi filios & filias inter תופת tympana strepentia Molocho offerebant, 2. Reg. XVI. 3. 2. Paralip. XXXIII. 6. Jerem. VII. 31. quámque Thophet, Rex Josias abolevit, 2. Reg. XXIII. 10. impropriè etiam locus ignominiæ, cruciatus, ejulatus, horroris & ignis ἀσβέστῳ damnatorum est. Qui dixerit; Stulte, reus est gehennæ ignis, Matth. V. 22. Timete eum, qui animam & corpus perdere potest in gehenna, ibid. X. 28. Etiam Ἀδύσσος profunditatis nomine, Luc. VIII. 31. Apoc. IX. 1. XI. 7. XX. 1. 3. venit. Occurrunt & aliæ inferni descriptiones paraphrasticæ, velut, quòd appellatur φυλακὴ carcer, Matth. V. 26. 1. Pet. III. 19. Κάμινος τῆς πυρὸς caminus ignis, Matth. XIII. 42. XIII. 42. Τόπος βασανισμῶ locus tormenti, Luc. XVI. 28. Λίμνη πυρὸς καὶ θεῖου stagnum ignis & sulphuris, Apoc. XX. 10. 14. XXI. 8. Σκότος ἐξώτερον tenebrae exteriores, Matth. XXII. 13. ignis æternus paratus Diabolo & Angelis ejus, ibid. XXV. 41. Jud. v. 7. Κόλασις αἰώνιος supplicium æternum, Matth. XXV. 46. mors secunda & æterna, Apoc. II. 11. XX. 6. XXI. 8.
units.tr: CV. Death is terrible by its nature, judgment more terrible, and hell most terrible of all: the eternal punishment, in the inner part, of [κλαυθμὸς καὶ ὀδόντων: weeping and gnashing of teeth], to which Christ bids the damned depart, Matt. 25.46. The words by which hell is described in Scripture are chiefly שאול [sheol] and ἅδης [hades], which, like infernus, properly mean the grave into which bodies are carried and in which a man is buried, as if in שאול, the place into which one goes away, and so is in שאלה [she'elah], a question. And ἅδης, that is [ἀιδὴς τόπος: an unseen place], a place invisible; but improperly they signify the place of the damned. שאול עריה יהמכו [sheol 'aryah yehemku]: her steps take hold of Orcus (of the adulteress), Prov. 5.5; that is, her steps tend not to life, which is truly life, but to a place of eternal sorrow. דרכי שאול ביתה [darkhei sheol betah]: the ways of hell, the paths of eternal sorrow, are her house, ibid. 7.27. למען סור מטאול מטה [lema'an sur me-sheol mattah]: to depart from the grave below, ibid. 15.24. שאול עם [sheol 'im]: with hell we have made a covenant, with the Devil and death, Isa. 28.15. The wicked return לשאולה [lisheolah]: to hell, to the kingdom of the Devil and of darkness, Ps. 9.18. ἅδης also in the New Testament denotes the place of the damned. [πύλαι ἅδου: the gates of hell] shall not prevail against him, Matt. 16.18. The glutton, [ἐν τῷ ᾅδῃ: in hell], lifted up his eyes, Luke 16.23. O death, where is your victory? O hell [ἅδη], where is your sting? 1 Cor. 15.55. I have the keys of [τὰς ἀδὸς καὶ τὸ θανάτου: hell and of death], Rev. 1.18. That place also has other names, such as אבדון [abaddon], destruction, Job 26.6, 28.22, Prov. 15.11; גיא הנם [ge hinnom], the valley of Hinnom, or Γέεννα and Γεέννη, Gehenna, which was properly a valley near the city of Jerusalem, pleasant and watered by the waters of Kidron, in which was תפת [tophet], where they offered their sons and daughters to Moloch amid the sounding drums (תופת), 2 Kings 16.3, 2 Chron. 33.6, Jer. 7.31; and King Josiah abolished this Tophet, 2 Kings 23.10. Improperly, it is also the place of ignominy, torment, wailing, horror and the unquenchable fire of the damned. Whoever says, "Fool," is liable to the fire of Gehenna, Matt. 5.22. Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna, ibid. 10.28. Ἀδύσσος [abyssos], the name of the deep, also occurs, Luke 8.31, Rev. 9.1, 11.7, 20.1, 3. There occur also other paraphrastic descriptions of hell: it is called prison, φυλακὴ, Matt. 5.26, 1 Pet. 3.19; [κάμινος τῆς πυρὸς: the furnace of fire], Matt. 13.42; [τόπος βασανισμῶ: a place of torment], Luke 16.28; [λίμνη πυρὸς καὶ θεῖου: a lake of fire and sulphur], Rev. 20.10, 14, 21.8; [σκότος ἐξώτερον: outer darkness], Matt. 22.13; the eternal fire prepared for the Devil and his angels, ibid. 25.41, Jude 7; [κόλασις αἰώνιος: eternal punishment], Matt. 25.46; the second and eternal death, Rev. 2.11, 20.6, 21.8.

units.la: CVI. Existere igitur Infernum, hoc est, locum damnatorum, in quo Diabolus, Angeli ejus, & homines damnati omnes æternam damni & sensus seu cruciatus per ignem, poenam subibunt; ipsa hæc nomina satis superque demonstrant. Omnis enim Prophetarum & Apostolorum chorus id ipsum clamat. Deus ipse apud Moses: Ignis succensus est in furore meo & ardebit usque ad infernum inferiorem, Deut. XXXII. 22. Licet enim judicium particulare Hierosolymæ & populi Judaici verbis iis declaratur; tamen judicium inferni damnatorum omnium, in quo Dei ira & furor terminatur, excludi non debet. David: Redibunt improbi ad infernum, omnes gentes oblitæ Dei, Psal. IX. 18. Pudejant improbi, pereant ad infernum, ibid. XXXI. 18. Instar ovium in infernum se ponunt. Mors ipsos depascet, & dominantur in eos recti matutino; & petra illorum in nebulas inferni abit, ibid. XLIX. 15. Ex Solomone textus nonnullos supra citavimus. Esajas: Vermis eorum non morietur, & ignis eorum non extinguetur, & erunt nausea omni carni, cap. LXVI. 24. Quod vaticinium de gehenna πυρὸς ἀσβέστου ignis, qui non extinguitur, ipse Christus Marc. IX. 43. 44. citat, æternum illum ignem iterato ignem inextinguibilem appellans, & ultra, ter confirmationem illam adjiciens: πῦρ ἃ ζέννυται ignis non extinguitur; vers. 44. 46. 48. addens etiam πᾶς γὰρ πυρὶ ἁλισθήσεται Totus enim igne salietur, v. 49. ut ita ignis ille inextinguibilis damnandis pro sale sit, ne penitus consumi possint; qui victima velut nil miserantis Orci sunt; nisi forte sensus est, ut vermem non morientem averruncemus, necesse esse, ut nosmet ipsos, tanquam hostiam vivam spirituali igni & sale, quo pravi affectus purgantur & excoquuntur, condiamus. Respexit enim Christus typicum ignem, quo olim sacrificiorum ἐμπυρισμὸς fiebat, & cum oblatione igniaria salem, quo eadem ante ἐμπυρισμὸν saliebantur, conjunxisse videtur. Quamvis alii aliter. Porro etiam vermis non moriturus victurum perpetuum conscientiæ morsum arguit. Ideo Christus, paleam comburendam esse πυρὶ ἀσβέστῳ igne inextinguibili, Luc. III. 17. dixit. Clarissimè etiam Christus: Discedite à me maledicti εἰς πῦρ αἰώνιον in ignem æternum, qui paratus est Diabolo & Angelis ejus, Matth. XXV. 41. Ibunt hi in supplicium æternum, ibid. v. 46. Impii enim omnes dabunt poenas ὄλεθρον αἰώνιον interitum æternum à facie Domini, & à gloria roboris ejus, 2. Thess. I. 9. Neque aliam ob causam χρῖμα αἰώνιον judicium æternum appellatur, Hebr. VI. 2. quam quia ejus effectus in damnatis æternus erit. Nam iis, æquè atque Diabolo ζόφος τῆς σκότους εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετήρηται caligo tenebrarum in æternum servatur, Jud. v. 13. Faciunt huc etiam exempla tum Diaboli & Angelorum ejus, Matth. XXV. 41. 2. Petr. II. 4. Jud. v. 6. Apoc. XII. 9. tum Sodomæ & Gomorrhæ & incolarum earum, jam jam memoratum: tum Core, Dathan & Abiram, qui viventes, flagrante crimine ab ira Divina absorpti, in infernum descenderunt, Num. XVI. 33. tum divitis Epulonis qui εἰς ᾅδου in infernum conjectus ὑπῆρξεν ἐν βασάνοις extitit in cruciatibus, & in flamma cruciatus est, Luc. XVI. 23. 24. Licet enim quandantenus parabola ibi narretur, tamen scopus ejus praecipuus est, ut de statu fidelium & infidelium post hanc vitam certi quid nobis constet.
units.tr: CVI. Hell therefore exists, that is, the place of the damned, in which the Devil, his angels, and all damned men will undergo eternal loss and punishment of sense, or torment, by fire; these very names abundantly demonstrate it. For the whole chorus of the Prophets and Apostles cries out the same thing. God himself says through Moses: A fire is kindled in my wrath, and shall burn to the lowest hell, Deut. 32.22. For although a particular judgment on Jerusalem and the Jewish people is declared in those words, yet the judgment of hell on all the damned, in which God's wrath and fury are finished, ought not to be excluded. David: The wicked shall return to hell, all the nations that forget God, Ps. 9.18. Let the wicked be ashamed, let them perish in hell, ibid. 31.18. Like sheep they lay themselves in hell; death shall feed upon them, and the upright shall have dominion over them in the morning; and their rock shall pass away into the clouds of hell, ibid. 49.15. We have cited some texts from Solomon above. Isaiah: Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abhorring to all flesh, ch. 66.24. Christ himself cites this prophecy of the Gehenna of fire that is not quenched, Mark 9.43, 44, calling that eternal fire again unquenchable fire, and adding a threefold repetition of the same: [πῦρ οὐ σβέννυται: the fire is not quenched], vv. 44, 46, 48; and he adds also, [πᾶς γὰρ πυρὶ ἁλισθήσεται: for everyone shall be salted with fire], v. 49, so that that unquenchable fire is salt to the damned, lest they can be wholly consumed; they are victims, as it were, of a Hell that spares nothing. Unless perhaps the sense is that, in order to ward off the worm that does not die, it is necessary for us to season ourselves, as a living sacrifice, with spiritual fire and salt, by which depraved affections are purged and refined. For Christ seems to have had regard to the typical fire by which the burnt offering of sacrifices was once made, and to have joined with the offering of fire the salt by which the same offerings were salted before the burning; though others explain it otherwise. Moreover, the worm that will not die indicates an everlasting gnawing of conscience. Therefore Christ said that the chaff is to be burned with [πυρὶ ἀσβέστῳ: unquenchable fire], Luke 3.17. Christ also speaks most clearly: Depart from me, you accursed, [εἰς πῦρ αἰώνιον: into eternal fire], into the eternal fire which is prepared for the Devil and his angels, Matt. 25.41. These shall go away into eternal punishment, ibid. v. 46. For all the wicked shall pay the penalty of [ὄλεθρον αἰώνιον: eternal destruction] from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power, 2 Thess. 1.9. Nor is [χρῖμα αἰώνιον: eternal judgment] called eternal judgment for any other reason, Heb. 6.2, than that its effect on the damned will be eternal. For for them, just as for the Devil, [ζόφος τῆς σκότους εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετήρηται: the blackness of darkness is reserved for ever], Jude 13. To this point also belong examples: both of the Devil and his angels, Matt. 25.41, 2 Pet. 2.4, Jude 6, Rev. 12.9; and of Sodom and Gomorrah and their inhabitants, already mentioned; and of Korah, Dathan and Abiram, who, while living, were swallowed up by divine wrath when their crime blazed, and went down into hell, Num. 16.33; and of the rich man Dives, who, cast [εἰς ᾅδου: into hell], was [ὑπῆρξεν ἐν βασάνοις: in torments] and was tormented in the flame, Luke 16.23, 24. For although a parable is related there to some extent, its chief aim is that some certainty about the state of believers and unbelievers after this life should be known to us.

units.la: CVII. Expressis testimoniis Scripturæ justitia & veracitas Divina, peccati natura, judicium conscientiæ, impiorum resurrectio, daemonum & spectrorum apparitiones, & consensus Gentium suffragantur. Etenim δίκαιον justum est apud Deum retribuere tribulationem illis, qui pios in hac vita affligunt, 2. Thess. I. 6. Id vero cum raro in hac vita contingat, necesse est, ut in altera contingat. Cumque peccator creatura rationalis sit, & peccatum ejus adversus infinitam Majestatem Dei arietet, adeoque infinitum reatum contrahat, nec poena sine ejus sensu ei decerni potest, quia impossibile est non sentire poenam eum, qui ratione utitur; nec nisi infinita duratione adeoque æterna ei decerni potest; quia infinitam Majestatem laesit, & poenam inter & delictum ini-quitas æqualitas intercedere debet. Id ipsum veracitas Dei, transgressori legis suae maledictionem comminantis, Deut. XXVII. 26. consistere etiam in morte æterna, non in solo dolore hujus vitæ, & perpetua damnatorum dissolutione; uti Socini schola definit, non semel, veluti Loc. IX. 62. 63. X. 27. ostendimus. Peccati quoque ea natura & indoles est, ut peccatum adhaereat, neque is, postquam tempus liberationis praeterit, ab eo, ceu morbo & miseria liberari non possit. Peccatorem autem, cujus anima immortalis est, & corpus resuscitatur, manere & non esse miserum, impossibile est. Etiam conscientiæ judicium eo augutur, quia satis constat, impios, quamvis properis in hac vita rebus fruantur, gravissimis tamen conscientiæ angoribus discruciari, & futuri judicii, poenarumque consequentium metu immaniter percelli. Sua quemque fraus, ita Cicero, Orat. pro Rosc. loquitur, suus terror maxime vexat. Suum quemque scelus agitat, amentiaque afficit, sua mala cogitationes, conscientiæque animi terrent. Hæ sunt impiis assiduæ domesticæque furiæ, quæ dies noctesque parentum poenas a conscelleratis filiis repetunt. Sicut enim cruciarii Romano ritu ferebant suam crucem, ipsi ab ea mox ferendi: sic impiis hanc conscientiæ crucem Deus impositum, in qua poenas luant, priusquam luant. Atqui illud ἐντὸν τὸ βῆμα interim tribunal testimonium futuri judicii, & damnationis in inferno sustinendæ, est. Neque impii duntaxat, sed etiam pii in hac vita quandam infernalium cruciatuum experiuntur. Sed hoc interest, quod pii dolores & terrores eos fide vincunt, atque ex iis eluctantur: impii iis succumbunt: illis probationis & tentationis causa immittuntur; his certum αἰῶνος χρῖμα & ὀργαὶ ὠδίνων principium æternorum cruciatuum & dolorum sunt. Sed & impiorum resurrectio, superius certissimis argumentis confirmata, inferni poenas probat. Non alio enim fini resurgent, quam ut luant mala, quae in corpore pore patrarunt. Prodibunt ad resurrectionem judicii, seu damnationis, Joh. V.29. Etiam Daemonum & spectrorum apparitiones, quas nemo sanus negare potest, infernum jam aestuare,& sibi similes in eodem torqueri clamant. Denique & Gentium saniorum consentiens judicium stipulatur. Nam & Judæi & Gentiles, & Muhammedani, & hæretici plerique infernum se agnoscere, saltem ore profitentur, licet de ejus poenis & puniendis non idem sentiant. Inter Gentiles equidem Cæsar apud Sallustium de Bell. Catil. increpitus quidem ideo à Catone; Mortem ærumnarum requiem, non cruciatuum esse censet; eam cuncta Mortalium mala dissolvere, ultra neque curæ, neque gaudio locum esse, ajens. Et Seneca Consol. ad Marc. c.19. mœstitiam Marciæ ob excessum filii solaturus, ad Stoicæ doctrinæ formam: Cogita, nullis defunctum malis affici. Illa, quæ nobis Inferos facit terribiles, fabula est. Nullas scimus imminere mortuis tenebras, nec carcerem, nec flumina flagrantia, nec oblivionis amnem, nec tribunalia, nec reos ullos in libertatem laxa, nullos iterum tyrannos. Luserunt ista Poëtæ, & vanis nos agitavere tortoribus. Mors omnium dolorum & solutio & finis est. Polybius quoque Histor. lib. VI.54. commentum id hominum prudentum putat, qui coercendo vulgo istos hominum animis vanos quidem, at utiles Reipublicæ terrores injecerint. Sed expleroramque tamen sententia supplicia hominibus post mortem exanthlanda supererunt. Ut enim Poëtas, levioris quippe authoritatis, praetereamus, Plato de Leg. lib. IX. negat, mortem esse ἐσχάλον ultimam. Οἱ δὲ, inquit, ἐν ᾅδῃ τὰ τῶν ... Sed extrema magis sunt inferorum supplicia. Cato quoque Cæsarem, supplicia post mortem ridentem, perstrinxit: Et Stoici ipsi malorum animabus loca, ubi post mortem luant, assignarunt, non rem ipsam negantes, sed fabulas Poëtarum ridentes. Protagoras quoque Laertio in Prot. teste, περὶ τῶν ἐν ᾅδῃ de iis, qui in inferno sunt, librum scripsit. Euripidem gentilium de inferni igne, tenebris, abysso, carcere, ejulatu & stridore, varietate & diversitate supplicio-rum, æternitate, diversis gradibus & tortoribus consonas sententias fusius Cl. Pfannerus Theol. Gent. cap. XXI.8–19. tradidit. Quin & barbaris incultissimisque populis eam opinionem insedisse Richardus Waitbornius Descript. Nov. Angl. part. I. c.4. auctor est. Taceo Poëtarum de Plutone, inferorum Rege, Rhadamanto judice, Charonte, infernali nauclero, Styge, Cocyto, Phlegetonte, Acheronte, & aliis infernalibus fluviis lusus, qui mentem tamen eorum hac de re obscuram esse non sinunt. Licet nempe poenarum infernalium modi & circumstantiae ex sola revelatione innotescant, & existentiae earum futuræ certitudo & clara notitia aliunde sperari non possit, tamen lumine naturæ constat, animas hominum omnium immortales esse, & malorum animas miseras, adeóque immortaliter miseras fore, nisi aliquod remedium sit, naturæ ignotum; ideóque spem liberationis nullam affulgere, quamvis eventus certitudo naturæ dubia sit. Hæc Ethnicis sapientioribus minimè ignota fuerunt.
units.tr: CVII. The justice and truthfulness of God, the nature of sin, the judgment of conscience, the resurrection of the wicked, the appearances of demons and ghosts, and the agreement of the Gentiles all confirm this by clear testimonies of Scripture. For it is just [δίκαιον] with God to repay tribulation to those who afflict the godly in this life (2 Thess. 1:6). But since this rarely happens in this life, it must happen in the next. And since the sinner is a rational creature, and his sin strikes against the infinite Majesty of God and so incurs infinite guilt, no punishment can be decreed for him without his feeling it, because it is impossible for one who uses reason not to feel punishment; and it can be decreed for him only with infinite duration, and so eternally, because he has offended the infinite Majesty, and there must be an equality between the punishment and the offence. The truthfulness of God, who threatens the curse of his law on the transgressor (Deut. 27:26), likewise implies that the curse consists in eternal death, and not merely in the pain of this life and a perpetual dissolution of the damned, as the school of Socinus defines it. We have shown this more than once, for example at Loc. 9:62–63 and 10:27. The nature and character of sin is also such that sin clings to the sinner, and once the time of deliverance has passed, he cannot be freed from it as from a disease or a misery. But it is impossible for a sinner, whose soul is immortal and whose body is raised again, to remain and not be wretched. The judgment of conscience also confirms this, since it is well established that the wicked, although they enjoy prosperity in this life, are nonetheless tormented by the gravest anguish of conscience and are terribly struck with fear of the coming judgment and of the punishments that follow. Each man's own treachery, so Cicero speaks in the pro Roscio, his own terror torments him most. Each man's own crime stirs him up and drives him mad; his own evil thoughts and the reproaches of his conscience terrify him. These are the constant and domestic furies of the wicked, who day and night demand from their criminal sons the penalties owed to their parents. For just as condemned men in the Roman manner carried their own cross, to be soon nailed to it, so God lays on the wicked this cross of conscience, in which they pay their penalties before they pay them. And indeed that tribunal within [ἐντὸς τὸ βῆμα] meanwhile is a testimony of the future judgment and of the damnation to be endured in hell. Not only the wicked but also the godly in this life experience something of the infernal torments. But this is the difference: the godly overcome these pains and terrors by faith and struggle out of them, while the wicked succumb to them; for the godly they are sent as a trial and temptation, but for the wicked they are the certain judgment of the age [αἰῶνος χρῖμα] and the beginning of eternal torments and pains [ὀργαὶ ὠδίνων]. Moreover the resurrection of the wicked, already confirmed by the most certain arguments above, also proves the punishments of hell. For they will rise for no other end than to pay for the evils they committed in the body. They will come forth to the resurrection of judgment, that is, of damnation (John 5:29). The appearances of demons and ghosts, which no sane person can deny, also cry out that hell is already seething and that their like are tormented in it. Finally, the agreed judgment of the saner Gentiles supports this. For Jews and Gentiles, Muslims, and most heretics, at least with their mouths, profess that they acknowledge hell, although they do not all think alike about its penalties and what is to be punished there. Among the Gentiles, Caesar, as he is reproached by Cato in Sallust's de Bello Catilinae, judges death to be the rest from troubles, not from torments, saying that it dissolves all the evils of mortals, and that there is then no place either for care or for joy. And Seneca, to console Marcia for the death of her son in the manner of the Stoic doctrine, says in Consol. ad Marc. c.19: Consider that the dead man suffers from no evils. That fable which makes the underworld terrible to us is a story. We know that no darkness hangs over the dead, nor a prison, nor blazing rivers, nor the river of forgetfulness, nor tribunals, nor any accused persons set free by a loose hand, nor any tyrants again. The poets have played with these things and have frightened us with empty torturers. Death is the release and end of all pains. Polybius too, in Histor. lib. VI.54, thinks that story was invented by prudent men who, to restrain the common people, instilled in their minds such terrors, empty indeed, but useful to the state. Yet, whatever the opinion of these men, punishments to be endured by human beings after death remain. For, to pass over the poets, whose authority is indeed of lesser weight, Plato in de Legibus lib. IX. says that death is not the last [ἔσχατον] evil. But, he says, the extreme punishments are in Hades [Οἱ δὲ ... ἐν ᾅδῃ]. Cato also rebuked Caesar, who scoffed at punishments after death. And the Stoics themselves assigned places where the souls of the wicked pay for their evils after death, not denying the thing itself but mocking the fables of the poets. Protagoras too, according to Laertius in Prot., wrote a book On those in Hades [περὶ τῶν ἐν ᾅδῃ], concerning those who are in the underworld. The consonant opinions of the Gentiles about the fire of hell, its darkness, its abyss, its prison, wailing and gnashing, the variety and diversity of punishments, their eternity, and the different grades and torturers, have been set out at greater length by the illustrious Pfanner in Theologia Gentilium, chap. 21.8–19. Richard Waitbornius, in Descriptio Novae Angliae part I, chap. 4, vouches that this opinion has also settled among barbarous and most uncultivated peoples. I pass over the poets' playful tales of Pluto, king of the underworld, Rhadamanthus the judge, Charon the infernal ferryman, the Styx, Cocytus, Phlegethon, Acheron, and other infernal rivers, which nonetheless do not allow their mind on this matter to be unclear. For although the modes and circumstances of the infernal punishments are known from revelation alone, and the certainty and clear knowledge of their future existence cannot be hoped for from elsewhere, yet it is established by the light of nature that the souls of all human beings are immortal, and that the souls of the wicked are miserable and so will be miserable immortally, unless there is some remedy unknown to nature; and therefore no hope of deliverance shines forth, although the certainty of the outcome is doubtful to nature. These things were by no means unknown to the wiser Gentiles.

units.la: CVIII. Infernii essentia ex poenis gravissimis, quas in eo damnati sustinebunt, co-
units.tr: CVIII. The essence of hell is known from the most grievous punishments that the damned will suffer there.

units.la: gnoscitur. Quæ gravitas nec mente comprehendi, nec verbis plenè explicari potest magis, quàm beatitudinis æternæ perfectio potest. Nihil enim in rebus corruptibilibus est, quod cum incorruptibilibus sive bonis, sive malis comparari possit. Sed utcunque tamen gravitas illa ex malorum multiplicium atrocitate & æternitate earum cognoscitur. Malorum multiplicium atrocitas in universum inde cognoscitur, quòd in Scriptura אבדון ἀπωλείας perditionis, θάνατος mortis passim, & ὀλέθρος interitus, Matth. X.28. 1.Thess. V.3. 2.Thess. I.9. nominibus venit; non quòd sit absoluta ἀνυπαρξία seu reductio in nihilum, sed quia perditur, moritur, interit in homine quicquid boni est, & ejus loco omne malum, & miseriarum ξυνασθροϊσμὸς atque colluvies subit.
