Licèt enim anima cum corpore unita existat, tamen mors infernalis etiam cum morte temporali convenit ratione tum originis, quia est poena & consequens peccati: tum horroris, quia maximè terribilis est: tum ratione doloris & angoris, quia perpetua anxietate laborat: tum ratione effectus & consequentis, quia sicut per mortem temporalem cadaver anima destitutum, ponderosum, fœdum, abominabile, vermibus scatens & putrescens redditur: ita damnatorum corpora cum anima unita licèt, ponderosa, fœtida, abominabilia erunt, & à vermibus rodentibus in æternum lancinabuntur. Accedet mors spiritualis & æterna, quia à Deo sanctificante & laetificante separati, deficiente omni gratia & bono, quo in hac vita adhuc propter Dei longanimitatem maclabantur, impietati & impuritati miseriæque ineffabili mancipabuntur. Scite Augustinus de Civ. D. lib. XI.11. Secunda mors, inquit, est pessima omnium, quæ non fit separatione animæ & corporis, sed in æternam poenam potius utriusque complexu. Ibi non erunt homines ante mortem, & post mortem, sed semper in morte, ac posthac nunquam viventes, nunquam mortui, sed sine fine morientes. Nunquam enim erit homini pejus in morte, quàm ubi erit mors ipsa sine morte. Tota illa malorum congeries, quæ damnatos premet, ὀργὴς iræ Dei nomine ἐπιθυμικῶς exprimitur. Qui non obedit Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super ipsum, Joh. III.36. Thesaurizas tibi iram in diem iræ, Rom. II.5. Totam igitur iram & θυμὸν excandescentiam suam Deus in damnatos effundet. Nam bibent ex vino excandescentiæ Dei, in poculo τὸ κεκερασμένον ἀκρατος quod infusum, temperatum & meracum, iræ ipsius, hoc est, per oxymoron, meram iram, Apoc. XIV.10. Bibent enim improbi terræ מסך שמרים cramatis fœces, Psal. LXXV.9. Erit enim iræ hoc poculum ἄκρατον merum, non temperatum ulla dulcedine gratiæ, misericordiæ, bonitatis Dei; sed κεκερασμένον temperatum tamen turbidis variarum & diversarum poenarum fœcibus permixtum. Et manebit ira Dei super ipsos, Joh. III.36. quia gravissimi ponderis instar in æternum, sine ulla ab eo liberatione, vel mitigatione, iis incumbet. Erit enim ira illa τελεία & ἀπογνωστική perfecta & plane separatoria, uti Damascenus Orth. fid. lib. II.29. appellat.
units.tr: This gravity can be grasped neither by the mind nor fully expressed in words, any more than the perfection of eternal blessedness can. For nothing in corruptible things can be compared with incorruptible things, whether good or evil. Yet that gravity is nonetheless known from the atrocity and eternity of the manifold evils. The atrocity of the manifold evils is known in general from the fact that Scripture everywhere calls it by the names of perdition [אבדון], destruction [ἀπωλείας], death [θάνατος], and ruin [ὀλέθρος] (Matt. 10:28; 1 Thess. 5:3; 2 Thess. 1:9). This is not because it is an absolute non-existence or a reduction to nothing, but because whatever is good in a man is lost, dies, and perishes, and in its place every evil enters, along with a heap and sewer of miseries [ξυνασθροϊσμὸς]. For although the soul exists united with the body, infernal death nevertheless agrees with temporal death in several respects: in its origin, because it is a punishment and consequence of sin; in its horror, because it is most terrible; in respect of pain and anguish, because it labours under perpetual anxiety; and in respect of its effect and consequence, because just as through temporal death the corpse, deprived of the soul, becomes heavy, foul, abominable, swarming with worms and rotting, so the bodies of the damned, though united with the soul, will be heavy, stinking, and abominable, and will be torn to pieces forever by gnawing worms. Spiritual and eternal death will be added to this, because, separated from God who sanctifies and gladdens, and lacking all the grace and good by which they were still sustained in this life through God's long-suffering, they will be given over to impiety, impurity, and unspeakable misery. Augustine says well in De Civitate Dei, book 11, ch. 11: The second death, he says, is the worst of all. It comes not by the separation of soul and body but rather by the joining of both in eternal punishment. There men will not be living before death and after death, but always in death; afterwards never living, never dead, but dying without end. For it will never be worse for a man in death than when death itself is without death. The whole mass of evils that will press upon the damned is expressed by the name of the wrath of God [ὀργὴ], in a passionate manner. He who does not obey the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him (John 3:36). You are storing up wrath for yourself for the day of wrath (Rom. 2:5). Therefore God will pour out his entire wrath and fury [θυμὸν] upon the damned. For they will drink of the wine of the anger of God, in the cup of what is mixed [τὸ κεκερασμένον] unmixed [ἄκρατος], which, poured in, tempered, and undiluted, is his wrath, that is, by oxymoron, pure wrath (Rev. 14:10). For the wicked of the earth shall drink the dregs of the cup [מסך שמרים] (Psalm 75:9). This cup of wrath will be unmixed, pure [ἄκρατον], not tempered with any sweetness of God's grace, mercy, or goodness; but mixed [κεκερασμένον], tempered yet mingled with the turbid dregs of various and diverse punishments. And the wrath of God will remain upon them (John 3:36), because it will lie upon them forever like a weight of the greatest heaviness, with no release or mitigation from him. For that wrath will be perfect and wholly separating [ἀπογνωστική], as Damascene calls it (Orth. fid., book 2, ch. 29).

units.la: CIX. In specie poenæ damnatorum differentiam à subjecto, mediis & ordine recipiunt. Quoad subjectum erunt animi & corporis.
units.tr: CIX. In particular, the punishments of the damned differ in respect of their subject, their means, and their order. As to the subject, there will be punishments of the soul and of the body.

units.la: Animi poenae intellectum, memoriam, cogitationes,ceu poenarum januam & thesaurum, voluntatem & affectiones, ceu principem earum sedem, & potentiam vitalem, quam passiones & cruciatus vehementer acuieret,afficient. Corporis poenae inprimis animam sensitivam ejus afficient. Sicut enim impii per sensus peccarunt, ita per sensus poenas dabunt. Visus,auditus,gustus, tactus & olfactus, imaginatio & passiones interiores poenarum velut januae & organa erunt. Quoad media, poenae & mala damnatorum alia στερητικά privativa, alia θετικά positiva sunt. Illa damni, haec sensus appellantur. Sicut enim visio beatifica στερησις πάντων κακῶν, καὶ θέσις πάντων καλῶν privatio omnium malorum, & positio omnium bonorum est: ita contra alienatio a conspectu Dei στερησις πάντων καλῶν, καὶ θέσις πάντων κακῶν, privatio omnium bonorum, & positio omnium malorum est. Nam dari in creatura rationali poenam damni sine poena sensus,fabula est,quia idem id foret, ac si quis diceret,dari animam sine sensu. Ubi vero sensus est, si jucundus est, poena damni non est,si injucundus est, poena sensus non est. Et anima ad amandum Deum facta, cum a Dei amore aberraverit, impossibile est, ut non sentiat,quid perdiderit, & quantum bonum sprevrit,& quam sanctum & zelotypum Deum offenderit, & provocaverit. Non ergo re, sed sola ratione haec poenarum genera differunt.
units.tr: The punishments of the soul will affect the understanding, the memory, and the thoughts, as the gateway and treasury of the punishments; and the will and the affections, as their chief seat; and the vital power, which the sufferings and torments will vehemently sharpen. The punishments of the body will chiefly affect its sensitive soul. For just as the wicked sinned through the senses, so through the senses they will suffer punishment. Sight, hearing, taste, touch, and smell, together with imagination and the inner passions, will serve as the gateways and organs of the punishments. As to the means, the punishments and evils of the damned are partly privative [στερητικά] and partly positive [θετικά]. The former are called of loss, the latter of sense. For just as the beatific vision is a privation of all evils and a positing of all goods, so on the contrary, alienation from the sight of God is a privation of all goods [στέρησις πάντων καλῶν] and a positing of all evils [θέσις πάντων κακῶν]. For to say that there is a punishment of loss in a rational creature without a punishment of sense is a fable, since it would be the same as saying that a soul exists without sense. Where there is sense, if it is pleasant, there is no punishment of loss; if it is unpleasant, there is no punishment of sense. And the soul, made to love God, when it has strayed from the love of God, cannot fail to feel what it has lost, how great a good it has spurned, and how holy and jealous a God it has offended and provoked. Therefore these kinds of punishment differ not in reality but only in our reasoning about them.

units.la: CX. Mala damnatorum στερητικά privativa seu damni erunt multiplicia. Privabuntur enim innocentia & sanctitate per se ipsos; Complacentia Divina, quia nauseam & fastidium Deo toti creabunt; auxilio & gratia Spiritus S. quia non ejus, sed Diaboli templa erunt, a sanctitate & puritate omni, quae sola Spiritum S. retinent & oblectant, deserti: Pace & gaudio, cujus solus Spiritus S. author esse potest,nec author esse potest, nisi in iis,qui Christi sunt, & ad Regnum ejus pertinent, Rom. XIV. 17. Cum damnati sint in Regno tenebrarum projecti in terram obscuritatis,tenebras horribiles & absconditas,Job. X. 22. XX. 26. caliginem tenebrarum, 2.Petr.II.17. Remissione peccatorum,adoptione & unione cum Christo,quia peccata iis retinentur, & semen non Dei, sed Serpentis,Diaboli sunt: denique avulsi a capite Christo,justi ab ipso facessere,Matth.VII.23. XXV.41. & relicti,Luc. XVII. 34. ita ut nulla spes assumptionis & insitionis eorum in corpus Christi mysticum superfit; Gloria sempiterna Sanctorum in beatifica Dei visione & amore, quia a Deo & Filio ejus Jesu Christo, facie & conspectu Dei separati,in perpetuum exilium ablegabuntur,& Deus contra illos ponet & obfirmabit faciem suam, Levit. XVII. 10. XX. 5. XXVI.17. & contra a facie Dei exibit ignis ardens usque ad novissima inferni, Psal. XVIII. 9. nec poterunt tamen a facie Dei effugere, ibid. CXXXIX. 7. poenas dabunt a facie Dei, 2. Thess. I. 9. denique jacturam irreparabilem sapientiae, justitiae, vitae, gloriae, laetitiae & beatitudinis vitae aeternae, in qua Deus erit omnia in omnibus,1. Cor. XV. 28. patientur, & longe gravius illam faciei Dei defraudationem ferent, quam Absolom tulit jacturam conspectus paterni, qui iccirco Joabum urgebat, ut se in conspectum Regis iterum produceret,vel occideret, 2. Sam. XIV. 32. Coelesti Angelorum & hominum sanctorum consortio, quia ubi non habet locum Dei gratia,ibi nec gratiola Angelorum praesentia obtinet, & sicut fumus apes, & foetor columbas abigit, ita peccatum pertinax Angelos; neque ibi Angeli & Sancti esse possunt,nisi ubi Deus & Christus gratia & gloria sua habitat, atque magnum nimis χάσμα, hiatus ingens sinum inter Abrahae & infernum firmatus est, Luc. XVI. 26. Amore & miseratione amicorum & beatorum, quia Deus ipse in interitu eorum ridebit, Prov. I. 26. & videbunt justi atque ridebunt super eos, dicentes: Ecce vir, qui non posuit Deum adjutorem suum, Psal. LII. 8. Laetabitur justus, cum videbit vindictam,ibid. LVIII. 11. imo damnati nauseae erunt omni carni, Esaj. LXVI. 24. Denique in conspectu S. Angelorum, & in conspectu Agni cruciabuntur,Apoc. XIV. 10. adeoque miserrimi, at non miserabiles erunt. Necessariis omnibus ad levamentum mali, quia gratiae Dei & Christi exsortes,& Sanctorum amore atque consortio privati,nullum uspiam solatium,vel praesidium minuendorum malorum reperient:Spe omni futurae liberationis, quia Salvatore & hostia pro peccato destitutos non aliud,quam terribilis expectatio judicii,& zelus ignis devoraturi adversarios Dei, manere potest,Hebr. X.26.27. Consortio eorum, qui Deum laudant,quia jubilantium & Deo psallentium choro non intererunt,qui blasphemabunt Deum Coeli pra doloribus & vulneribus suis, Apoc. XVI. 11. denique deliciis sensibilibus & oblectatione in contemplatione novorum coelorum & novae terrae,quia ex terra viventium exterminati,nullum eorum sensum experientur.
units.tr: CX. The evils of the damned that are privative [στερητικά], or of loss, will be many. They will be deprived of innocence and holiness in themselves; of the complacency of God, since they will create nausea and loathing in God altogether; of the help and grace of the Holy Spirit, since they will be temples not of the Spirit but of the Devil, deserted by all holiness and purity, which alone the Holy Spirit retains and delights in; of the peace and joy whose sole author is the Holy Spirit, and who can be the author only in those who are Christ's and belong to his kingdom (Rom. 14:17). Since they are cast out into the kingdom of darkness, into the land of obscurity, horrible and hidden darkness (Job 10:22; 20:26), the blackness of darkness (2 Pet. 2:17), they will be deprived of the remission of sins, adoption, and union with Christ, because their sins are retained in them, and they are the seed not of God but of the Serpent, of the Devil. Finally, having been torn away from Christ the head, and being just [justi] departing from him (Matt. 7:23; 25:41), and left behind (Luke 17:34), there is no hope left of their being taken up and grafted into the mystical body of Christ. They will be deprived of the eternal glory of the saints in the blessed vision and love of God, because, separated from God and from his Son Jesus Christ, from the face and sight of God, they will be sent away into perpetual exile; and God will set his face against them and make it firm (Lev. 17:10; 20:5; 26:17), and a burning fire will go out from the face of God to the lowest depths of hell (Psalm 18:9), yet they will not be able to escape from the face of God (ibid., 139:7); they will suffer punishment away from the face of God (2 Thess. 1:9). Finally, they will suffer the irreparable loss of wisdom, justice, life, glory, joy, and the blessedness of eternal life, in which God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28), and they will bear the deprivation of the face of God far more heavily than Absalom bore the loss of his father's sight, who therefore urged Joab to bring him again into the king's presence, or else to kill him (2 Sam. 14:32). They will be deprived of the heavenly fellowship of the angels and holy men, because where God's grace has no place, not even the gentle presence of the angels is obtained; and just as smoke drives away bees and a stench drives away doves, so stubborn sin drives away the angels; nor can angels and saints be there, except where God and Christ dwell in their grace and glory, and a very great chasm, a vast gulf, has been fixed between Abraham's bosom and hell (Luke 16:26). They will be deprived of the love and compassion of friends and of the blessed, because God himself will laugh at their destruction (Prov. 1:26), and the righteous will see and laugh at them, saying, Behold the man who did not make God his strength (Psalm 52:8); the righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance (ibid., 58:11); indeed, the damned will be a loathing to all flesh (Isa. 66:24). Finally, they will be tormented in the sight of the holy angels and in the sight of the Lamb (Rev. 14:10), and so they will be most wretched, yet they will not be pitied. They will be deprived of all the necessary means of relief from evil, because, being strangers to the grace of God and Christ, and cut off from the love and fellowship of the saints, they will find nowhere any comfort or protection to lessen their evils. They will be deprived of all hope of future deliverance, because, being left without a Saviour and without a sacrifice for sin, nothing remains for them but a terrible expectation of judgment and the zeal of a fire that will devour the adversaries of God (Heb. 10:26–27). They will be deprived of the company of those who praise God, because they will not take part in the choir of those who rejoice and sing to God, but will blaspheme the God of heaven because of their pains and wounds (Rev. 16:11). Finally, they will be deprived of sensible delights and pleasure in contemplating the new heavens and the new earth, because, having been cut off from the land of the living, they will experience none of these pleasures.

units.la: CXI. Poenae θετικά positivae seu sensus damnatorum non minus horrendae & terribiles erunt, exeque vel exteriores, vel interiores. Exteriores erunt poenae corporeae,quae accident vel ex privatione bonorum,quales erunt sensus famis, sitis, & plurimarum calamitatum; vel ex positivis applicatis; cujusmodi inprimis erit ignis inextinguibilis, Esaj. LXVI.24. Marc. IX. 43. 44. Quem ignem ad animam relatum fore metaphoricum,consistentem in irae Divinae & reatus quaesitissimo sensu: ad corpus vero relatum fore proprium & materialem, corpora damnatorum & propter corporis & animae conjunctionem arctissimam quodammodo etiam animam cruciaturum, sic satis probabile est. Sapientis autem & pii est ignis illius cruciatus omni cura & studio vitare,& fidei scuto extinguere, quam de natura ejus inaniter disputare, & nescio quo contentionis gladio,ultra quam fas est,fodere. Ex Scriptura tamen tenendum est,ignem illum esse ignem Gehennae,Matth.V.22. XVIII.9. κάμινον πυρὸς fornacem ignis, ibid.XIII.42. תנור האש clibanum ignis, Psal. XXI.10. Mal. IV. 1. propter ignis in urendo vehementiam & perpetuitatem: Stagnum ignis,Apoc. XIX.20. XX.10.14. propter stagnantem & inexplicabilem ejus copiam; Picem,Esaj. XXXIV.9. & sulphur,Psal. XI.6. Apoc. XIV.10. XIX.20. & quidem גפרית torrentem sulphuris, Esaj. XXX.33. stagnum sulphuris, Apoc. XX.10. propter ignis tum aeternitatem,qui ignis,cui quotidie torrens sulphuris allabitur,nunquam extinguitur; cum efficaefficaciam,quia ignis in pice & sulphure magis, quàm in alia quavis materia, urit & saevit; tum fœtoris vehementiam, qualem pix & sulphur excitare solet. Φλόγα flammam ignis,Luc. XVI. 24. 2. Thess. I. 8. quia non leviter, & in superficie corporis allambendo uret, sed intima quæque immeabit & penetrabit. Unde eidem ζῆλος zelus tribuitur,Hebr. X. 27. quia instrumentum erit Divinæ justitiæ & zeli justissimi,quo Deus in peccatores animadvertit. Interiores pœnæ positivæ in Scripturis comparative & effectivè describuntur. Comparativè, quia comparantur cum doloribus parturientium, juxta illud helluonis: ὠδῦνῶμαι ἐν τῇ φλογὶ, Luc. XVI. 24. 25. & Pauli illud: Repentinus interitus eis superveniet, sicut ὠδὶν τῇ ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχούσῃ dolor parturienti, 1. Thess. V. 3. acutissimos autem dolores parturientium esse constat,quia in iis multiplicando multiplicatur dolor,Gen. III. 16. ut merito apud Euripidem Hecuba dixerit: malle se decies in acie stare, quàm semel parere: cum βασάνοις tormentis,quibus facinorosi subjiciuntur, Luc. XVI. 23. unde infernus τόπος τῶν βασάνων locus tormentorum,Matth. VIII. 29. dicitur, tantò diriorum & vehementiorum, quia nec qui torquet, fatigatur; nec qui torquetur, moritur: cum δεσμοῖς vinculis & laqueis, Psal. XI. 6. Matth. XIII. 30. XXII. 13. 2. Pet. II. 4. ad exprimendum damnatorum captivitatem,captivitatis & tormentorum in ea æternitatem, dolorum acerbitatem, quia vinculis constricti exquisitissimos dolores sentiunt; bene operandi ἀδυναμίαν, quia vincula illa peccati & miseriæ sunt: tum denique damnatorum societatem,quia in fasciculum constricti sui similibus jungentur: tum cum plagis & flagellis,Prov. XIX. 29. Luc. XII. 48. Apoc. XXII. 18. quia graves nimis Diaboli scutica, firmi & infracti ungues, perdura flagella sunt. Effectivè autem describuntur, per clamorem & ululatum, juxta illud Dei: Servi mei ovabunt præ jucunditate, & vos clamabitis præ dolore cordis, & præ contritione spiritus ululabitis, Esaj. LXV. 14. per fletum & stridorem dentium, Matth. VIII. 12. XIII. 42. 50. XXII. 13. XXIV. 51. XXV. 30. fletum, ob dolorem ex sensu malorum propriorum,stridorem, propter livorem, seu sensum boni alieni: per vermem,qui non moritur,Esaj. LXVI. 24. Marc. IX. 44. 46. hoc est, morsum conscientiæ perpetuum & continuum ex peccatorum recordatione ortum, rapidam displicentiam,infructuosam pœnitentiam, maximos & nunquam interrumpendos angores cordis: sicut enim vermes continuo morsu corpora arrodunt; ita conscientiæ vermis damnatorum animas lancinare non desinet. Quod tineæ vestimento,& vermis ligno, id mala conscientia animæ est. Et pertinent ad eundem vermem θλῖψις καὶ στενοχωρία affliction & angustia, Rom. II. 9. seu coarctatio, pressura, Esaj. VIII. 22. qualis in acutis morbis & subitis terroribus est,multò uberantior illa piorum,qui infernalis anxietatis gustum sentientes clamant: Sagittæ tuæ infixæ sunt mihi,confirmasti super me manum tuam, &c. Psal. XXXVIII. 3. 4. &c. quia pii iræ Divinæ guttulam libant, damnati totum iræ Divinæ poculum ad fæces usque imas absorbere habebunt: Ὀνειδισμὸς καὶ αἰσχύνη opprobrium, pudor,confusio & ignominia,
units.tr: CXI. The positive punishments, or the sensations, of the damned will be no less dreadful and terrible, and they will be either external or internal. The external punishments will be bodily, arising either from the privation of goods, such as the sensations of hunger, thirst and many calamities, or from positive things applied to them. Chief among the latter will be unquenchable fire (Isa. 66:24; Mark 9:43-44). That this fire, as it relates to the soul, will be metaphorical, consisting in the wrath of God and in the most exquisite sense of guilt, while as it relates to the body it will be proper and material, and will torment the bodies of the damned and, because of the very close union of body and soul, will in some way torment the soul also, is quite probable. But it is the mark of a wise and godly person to avoid that torment by every care and effort and to quench it with the shield of faith, rather than to dispute vainly about its nature and, with some sword of contention, to pierce it beyond what is right. Nevertheless, from Scripture we must hold that this fire is the fire of Gehenna (Matt. 5:22; 18:9); a furnace of fire [κάμινον πυρός] (ibid. 13:42); a oven of fire [תנור האש] (Ps. 21:10; Mal. 4:1), because of the vehemence and perpetuity of the burning; a lake of fire (Rev. 19:20; 20:10, 14), because of the stagnant and boundless abundance of it; pitch (Isa. 34:9) and sulphur (Ps. 11:6; Rev. 14:10; 19:20). Indeed there is a torrent of sulphur [גפרית] (Isa. 30:33) and a lake of sulphur (Rev. 20:10): because of the eternity of the fire, which is fed daily by a torrent of sulphur and is never extinguished; because of its efficacy, since fire burns and rages more in pitch and sulphur than in any other material; and because of the vehemence of stench which pitch and sulphur are wont to produce. There is a flame of fire [φλόγα] (Luke 16:24; 2 Thess. 1:8), because it will not merely lick the surface of the body lightly, but will burn and penetrate every inner part. Hence the same fire is ascribed zeal [ζῆλος] (Heb. 10:27), because it will be the instrument of divine justice and of the most just zeal by which God takes vengeance on sinners. The internal positive punishments are described in Scripture comparatively and effectively. Comparatively, because they are compared with the pains of a woman in labour, after the manner of the glutton's words: "I am tormented [ὠδῦνῶμαι] in this flame" (Luke 16:24-25); and Paul's words: "sudden destruction shall come upon them, as travail [ὠδὶν] upon a woman with child" (1 Thess. 5:3). The pains of women in labour are very acute, since in them "I will greatly multiply your sorrow" (Gen. 3:16); so rightly in Euripides Hecuba says that she would rather stand ten times in battle than give birth once. They are also compared with torments [βασάνοις], such as wrongdoers are subjected to (Luke 16:23), whence hell is called "the place of torment" [τόπος τῶν βασάνων] (Matt. 8:29), so much the more dreadful and violent because the one who torments is not wearied, nor the one tormented put to death. They are compared with bonds [δεσμοῖς] and snares (Ps. 11:6; Matt. 13:30; 22:13; 2 Pet. 2:4), to express the captivity of the damned, the eternity of their captivity and torments, and the bitterness of their pains, since being bound fast they feel the most exquisite pains; their inability [ἀδυναμίαν] to do good, since those bonds are of sin and misery; and finally the fellowship of the damned, since bound together in a bundle they will be joined to their like. They are compared with stripes and scourges (Prov. 19:29; Luke 12:48; Rev. 22:18), since the Devil's whips are very heavy, his claws firm and unbroken, and the scourges lasting. The pains are described effectively by clamour and wailing, after the words of God: "My servants shall sing for joy of heart, but you shall cry for sorrow of heart, and shall howl for vexation of spirit" (Isa. 65:14); by weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30): weeping on account of the pain arising from the sense of one's own evils, gnashing on account of spite, or the sense of another's good. They are described by the worm that does not die (Isa. 66:24; Mark 9:44, 46), that is, the perpetual and continual gnawing of conscience arising from the recollection of sins, swift displeasure, fruitless repentance, and the greatest anguish of heart that is never to be interrupted. For just as worms gnaw bodies with continual biting, so the worm of conscience will never cease to tear the souls of the damned. What the moth is to a garment and the worm to wood, an evil conscience is to the soul. To the same worm belong affliction and distress [θλῖψις καὶ στενοχωρία] (Rom. 2:9), or constriction and pressure (Isa. 8:22), such as occur in acute diseases and sudden terrors; far more abundant is that of the godly, who, tasting a foretaste of infernal anguish, cry out: "Your arrows stick fast in me, and your hand presses me down" (Ps. 38:2-3, etc.), because the godly only sip a drop of the wrath of God, whereas the damned will have to drain the whole cup of divine wrath down to its lowest dregs. Reproach and shame [Ὀνειδισμὸς καὶ αἰσχύνη], opprobrium, disgrace, confusion and ignominy,

units.la: Esaj. LXVI. v. ult. Dan. XII. 2. oriunda ex manifestatione peccatorum omnium, occultissimorum etiam,& horrore,qui illa cogitantibus subibit: nec non ex animæ & corporis deformitate horrenda; inprimis cùm stupor ille,qui in hac vita obstat,ne miseriam suam,& peccati atrocitatem multi videant & sentiant, auferetur: Φθόνος livor & tabescens invidia, quia peccator videbit,& irascetur,dentibus suis fremet & tabescet,Psal. CXII. 10. cujus comes stridor dentium continuus erit, quem vehementia ipsa tabescentis ob felicitatem piorum,suppliciorum inæqualitatem & odium mutuum,invidia,& obstinata malignitas extorquebit: Φόβος ἢ ἔκπληξις timor, tremor,horror perpetuus, & desperatio plena,quæ ex loci conditione,daemonum societate, æternitatis pœnarum conscientia, peccatorum recordatione μανία & furore horribili, quo adversus Deum, creaturas omnes,& se ipsos immaniter æstuabunt. Ex quibus, similibúsque aliis de damnatorum pœnis positivis & sensus judicium Scripturis conformatum, proclive erit.
units.tr: (Isa. 66:24, last verse; Dan. 12:2) arise from the manifestation of all sins, even the most hidden, and from the horror that will strike those who think upon them; and also from the dreadful deformity of soul and body; above all, when that stupor which in this life prevents many from seeing and feeling their misery and the atrocity of sin is taken away. Envy [Φθόνος], spite and a wasting jealousy, because "the wicked shall see it and be angry; he shall gnash with his teeth and waste away" (Ps. 112:10). Its companion will be a continual gnashing of teeth, which the very violence of wasting away, from the happiness of the godly, the unequal distribution of punishments and mutual hatred, will wring out of envy and obstinate malice. Fear or terror [Φόβος ἢ ἔκπληξις], trembling, perpetual horror and full despair, which arise from the condition of the place, the company of demons, the consciousness of the eternity of punishments and the recollection of sins; madness [μανία] and dreadful fury, by which they will rage monstrously against God, against all creatures and against themselves. From these and similar other things, a judgment about the positive and sensible punishments of the damned, conformed to Scripture, will readily follow.

units.la: CXII. Ordo pœnarum harum infernalium quidam etiam obtinet. Prima enim gehennæ pœna est peccatum ipsum, uti est miseria peccatoris, & mors spiritualis. Pœna hæc erit, Deum non cognoscere salutariter & sine tremore,Jac. II. 19. non amare,in eo,ceu judice & vindice peccati ἀπροσδιαγήτῳ inexorabili nullam fiduciam ponere; ei non servire; in eo non deliciari; sanctitate & bono spirituali non oblectari; sed contra Deum,sanctitatem & sanctos omnes odio internecino prosequi; voluptates illicitas & nefarias, negatas licet, appetere,esurire & sitire; privationem bonorum summo cum angore & impatienter ferre; & si qui alii cruciatus similes peccato ipsi insunt. Consequuntur pœnæ peccati relativæ, quæ ei, ut causæ & fundamento innituntur, cujusmodi sunt complacentiæ Divinæ, & amoris omnium beatorum omnimoda incapacitas & privatio: amissio finalis juris & capacitatis bonorum omnium,quæ felices reddere apta nata sunt; nec non mediorum omnium salutis, liberationis à miseria horribili, consolationis, spei status melioris,& Spiritus S. operationis salutaris consequendæ; unà cum aptitudine, σωτηρίας & velut jure ad displicentiam, nec non miserias positivas animæ & corporis. Subit negatio miserationis Divinæ omnis: puta negatio Christi,& hostiæ pro peccatis ipsorum. Spiritus sanctificantis, qui sine Christo nemini datur; Divinæ εὐδοκίας seu complacentiæ; solatii spiritualis & corporalis; non tantùm Regni Cœlorum,sed etiam inferiorum omnium,quæ vel delectare,vel dolores mitigare possunt; denique gratiæ omnis & gloriæ,& cum iis etiam bonorum naturalium, quæ desiderant. Connectuntur negationi huic cruciatus tum ex conscientia peccati, quod stultitia & obstinata contumacia mirè aggravabitur: tum ex sensu æternæ felicitatis penitus conclamatæ & amissæ; & miseriæ tantæ proprio jumento, spretis Dei & hominum suasionibus, accersitæ; unde pudor, tristitia, timor & angor incredibilis miseras damnatorum mentes discruciabit: tum ex justa permissione illa Divina,qua Diaboli & damnati adversus se ipsos malitiam suam omnem exercebunt,& qui nunc blandus tentator,ibi sævissimus tortor & cruciator erit: tum ex Divina applicatione illa, qua ignis & alia justitiæ instrumenta Divinam vindictam promptissimè exequentur; quin & Angeli atque Sancti cœlites super ipsos regnabunt, lætum de iis triumphum canendo; & voluntatem Divinam adversus illos exequendo, uti custodes rebellibus incarceratis, & homines canibus,asinis & anguibus facere solent. Plura etiam experientur damnati, quæ in hac vita ignorantur.
units.tr: CXII. There is also a certain order among these infernal punishments. For the first punishment of Gehenna is sin itself, as it is the misery of the sinner and spiritual death. This punishment will consist in not knowing God savingly and without trembling (James 2:19); in not loving him, who as judge and avenger of sin is inexorable [ἀπροσδιηγήτῳ], in putting no trust in him, in not serving him, in taking no delight in him; in not being gladdened by holiness and spiritual good, but on the contrary in pursuing God, holiness and all the saints with deadly hatred; in craving, hungering and thirsting after unlawful and wicked pleasures, even though they are denied; and in bearing the privation of goods with the greatest anguish and impatience; and whatever other torments are similar and inherent in sin itself. There follow the relative punishments of sin, which rest on it as on their cause and foundation: such as the displeasure of God, and the complete incapacity and privation of love for all the blessed; the final loss of the right and capacity for all good things, which are by nature fit to make them happy; and likewise of all the means of salvation, of liberation from horrible misery, of consolation, of the hope of a better state, and of the saving operation of the Holy Spirit to be obtained; together with an aptitude for displeasure, and as it were a right to it, [and the loss of] salvation [σωτηρίας], and positive miseries of soul and body. There comes the denial of all divine mercy: namely, the denial of Christ and of the sacrifice for their sins; of the sanctifying Spirit, who without Christ is given to no one; of divine good pleasure [εὐδοκίας] or complacency; of spiritual and bodily comfort; not only of the Kingdom of Heaven, but of all the lower things which can either delight or mitigate pains; and finally of all grace and glory, and with them also of the natural goods which they desire. Connected with this denial are the torments: partly from the consciousness of sin, which through folly and obstinate contumacy will be wonderfully aggravated; partly from the sense of eternal happiness utterly lost and forfeited, and of misery so great brought upon themselves, by their own folly, after the counsels of God and men were spurned; whence shame, sadness, fear and incredible anguish will torment the wretched minds of the damned; partly from that just permission of God by which the Devil and the damned will exercise all their malice against themselves, and he who is now a gentle tempter will there be a most savage torturer and tormentor; partly from that divine application by which fire and other instruments of justice will most promptly carry out divine vengeance. Indeed, the angels and the holy inhabitants of heaven will reign over them, singing a joyful triumph over them and carrying out the will of God against them, just as jailers do with rebellious prisoners, and as men do with dogs, asses and snakes. The damned will also experience many things which are unknown in this life.

units.la: CXIII. Augebit miseriam malorum omnium æternitas: quam passim Scriptura asserit,& supra ex testimoniis nonnullis probavimus. Quis habitabit ex nobis cum igne devorante? Quis habitabit ex nobis מוקדי עולם cum ardoribus sempiternis, Esaj. XXXIII.14. Quidam expergiscentur ad opprobria & contemptum sempiternum, Dan. XII.2. Vermis eorum non moritur, & ignis non extinguetur, Esaj. LXVI.24. Marc. IX.44. Neque semel duntaxat πῦρ αἰώνιον ignis æternus & ἄσβεστον inextinguibilis dicitur,velut Matth. III.12. XVIII.8. XXV.41. Marc. IX.43. Luc.III.17. Jud. v. 7. κόλασις αἰωνιος supplicium æternum, Matth. XXV.46. mors æterna, Joh. VIII.51. XI.26. ὀλεθρος αἰωνιος interitus æternus, 2.Thess.I.9. Vincula æterna, quibus caligo tenebrarum in æternum reservata est, Jud. v.13. Facit huc fumus ille tormentorum ascendens in secula, Apoc. XIV.11. & quòd cruciandi dicuntur die ac nocte in secula seculorum, ibid. XX.10. Nam quòd ignem, supplicium, interitum æternum dici,quia impii semel isto igne absumendi, ex eo in æternum liberandi non sint,& in eo perpetuò mansuri sint, Socini asseclæ pertendunt,nimis profectò violentum est. Qualis enim διαμονη permanfio perpetua esse potest apud illos quibus ignis ille διαμονω permanentem existentiam in rerum natura auferet? Et quidnì censeamus illam ex ignis supplicio liberationem fore,quando supplicium finietur,& Dei ira sævire desinet? Neque sanius illud, quod Hobbesius ignem illum æternum & inextinguibilem esse posse, licet homines urendi esse desinant,nugatur. Quorsum enim post consumptos impios æternus ille & inextinguibilis ignis? Quorsum vermis rodens,si desit,quod roditur? Neque etiam ignis tantùm ille æternus dicitur, sed etiam κόλασις supplicium ipsum damnatorum αἰωνιω æternum,Matth. XXV.46. dicitur. Facit huc inprimis, quòd civitates Sodoma & Gomorrha πυρὸς αἰωνίου δίκην ὑπέχειν ignis æterni supplicium sustinere, atque ita ὑποδειγμα proflare exemplum Jud. v.7. dicuntur. Igne conflagrasse eas civitates, extra dubium est. Quomodo autem is ignis æternus dicitur? An quia sic civitates eæ consumptæ sunt, ut nec restitutæ sint,nec restitui potuerint,etiamnum ignis ille ardere videtur? Sed quid tum de hominibus, qui ibi extincti sunt, dicemus? In ignem sine dubio æternum inciderunt,non quòd in æternum esse desierint, sed quia spiritus illorum in æternum dolorem & βασανισμὸν velut uno momento præcipites dati sunt. Urbes igitur ipsæ habent ὑπόδειγμα vel ἀντίτυπον ignis æterni, quia semel combustæ nunquam iterum extructæ sunt. Sed impii homines pœnam æterni ignis sustinent, atque ita facti sunt δίγμα exemplum eorum,qui in æternum ignem conjiciuntur. Argumentum ab igne æterno petitum sic jam olim Tertullianum de Res. car. prementem audiamus: Si quis, inquit, occasionem carnis atque animæ in gehenna,ad interitum & finem utriusque substantiæ arripiet,non ad supplicium, quasi consumendarum, non quasi puniendarum, recordetur, ignem gehennæ æternum prædicari,in pœnam æternam,& inde æternitatem occisionis agnoscat, propterea humanæ, ut temporali pratimendam. Tum & æternas substantias cie-det, quarum æterna sit occisio in pœnam. Certè cùm post resurrectionem corpus cum anima occidi debeat à Deo in gehenna,satis de utraque constabit, & de carnali resurrectione, & de æterna occisione. Absurdissimum alioqui, si iccirco resuscitata caro occidatur in gehennam, uti finiatur; quod & non resuscitata pateretur. In hoc scilicet reficietur, ne sit, cui non esse jam evenit. Denique & pœnarum infernalium æternitatem potenter confirmant tum animæ peccatricis etiam immortalitas, quia si non moritur,nec bene ei esse potest,cùm peccatori non liberatio à peccato, adeóque peccatum ἐνοικοῦν retinenti bene esse non potest, juxta illa Dei: Dicite justo, כי טוב quòd bonus, beatus sit,quia fructum studiorum suorum comedet; Væ improbo, malo כי גמול ידיו יעשה לו quia retributio, seu prærogatum manuum ipsius fiet ipsi, & opera ejus talionem justam habebunt, Esaj. III.10.11. tum peccati non remissi,sed imputati reatus,qui infinitus est propter infinitatem Majestatis,quæ læditur, adeóque ut æqualitas peccati & pœnæ servetur, infinitam etiam pœnam non intensivè,quia finitus actus intensionis ejus capax non foret, sed extensivè, quoad durationem interminabilem, exigit: tum peccati & reatus ejus atque justitiæ Dei perpetuitas, quia peccator in peccato mortuus, & per gratiam Dei in Christo non vivificatus, peccare non definit,& peccare ei in naturam vertit; neque adeò justitia Dei, quam abnegare non magis quàm seipsum potest, patitur, ut peccatum continuatum continuè non puniatur, & super inobediente non maneat ira Dei, Joh. III.36. tum defectus remedii & causæ liberantis, quia post mortem hominis fores gratiæ claudentur, Matth. XXV.10. Luc. XIII.25. & frater fratrem redimere non poterit, Psal. XLIX.8. at nec Deus redimit,nisi per λύτρον Christi,& hostiam pro peccato, qualis nulla superest voluntarie peccantibus,Hebr. X.26. tum comes pœnarum desperatio, quia nulla ex inferno redemptio est, neque qui ibi, in inferno,sunt, ad nos, Abrahamum & socios, transeunt,Luc. XVI.26. & nulla in inferno pœnitentia vel sanctificatio est, in quo qui sunt, à severo judice Deo,sic traduntur in manum peccati, ut in perpetuum peccent, propter legem peccati, quæ non potest non vim legis mortis prorogare, & regnum ejus interminabile reddere: tum veritas legis & sententia judicis ac prædictionis Divinæ, quia lex æternam mortem, uti in Loco probavimus, comminata est transgressori, sicut æternam vitam obedienti promisit; & tam comminationi veritas, quàm promissioni sua constabit: tum denique voluntas Dei potentissimi, sanctissimi, sapientissimi, cujus interest, sanctitatis & justitiæ suæ gloriam in æternum patefacere. Deus enim omnia fecit propter propter se ipsum, etiam improbum ad diem mali, Prov.XVI. 4.
units.tr: CXIII. Eternity will add to the misery of all the wicked. Scripture asserts this everywhere, as we have already proved from several testimonies above. "Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? Who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings [מוקדי עולם]?" (Isa. 33.14). "Some shall awake to shame and everlasting contempt" (Dan. 12.2). "Their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched" (Isa. 66.24; Mark 9.44). Nor is it only once that the fire is called eternal [πῦρ αἰώνιον] and unquenchable [ἄσβεστον], as in Matt. 3.12; 18.8; 25.41; Mark 9.43; Luke 3.17; Jude 7. It is called eternal punishment [κόλασις αἰώνιος] (Matt. 25.46), eternal death (John 8.51; 11.26), eternal destruction [ὄλεθρος αἰώνιος] (2 Thess. 1.9), and everlasting chains in which the blackness of darkness is reserved for ever (Jude 13). To this belongs the smoke of their torment, which ascends for ever and ever (Rev. 14.11), and the fact that they are said to be tormented day and night for ever and ever (Rev. 20.10). That the fire, the punishment and the destruction are called eternal because the wicked are to be consumed once by that fire and are never to be freed from it, and will remain in it for ever, is what the followers of Socinus contend; but this is surely far too forced. For what perpetual continuance [διαμονή] could there be for those whose existence in the nature of things that very fire would take away? And why should we not think that they will be freed from the punishment of the fire, once the punishment has ended and God's wrath ceases to rage? Nor is the claim of Hobbes any more sound, that the fire may be eternal and unquenchable even though men have ceased to be burned in it; for to what end is that eternal and unquenchable fire once the wicked are consumed? And what is the gnawing worm for, if there is nothing left to be gnawed? Nor is it only the fire that is called eternal; the punishment itself of the damned is called eternal [αἰώνιος] (Matt. 25.46). Chiefly to the point is that the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah are said to undergo the punishment of eternal fire [πυρὸς αἰωνίου δίκην ὑπέχειν] and so to set forth an example [ὑπόδειγμα] (Jude 7). That those cities were burned with fire is beyond doubt. But in what sense is that fire called eternal? Is it because those cities were so consumed that they were neither restored nor could be restored, and that fire still seems to burn? But what shall we say then of the men who were destroyed there? Without doubt they fell into an eternal fire, not because they ceased to exist for ever, but because their spirits were cast down, as if in a single moment, into eternal pain and torment [βασανισμός]. The cities themselves, therefore, are an example or antitype [ἀντίτυπον] of eternal fire, because once burned they were never built again. But wicked men suffer the punishment of eternal fire, and so have become an example [δεῖγμα] of those who are cast into eternal fire. Let us hear Tertullian, who long ago pressed this argument from eternal fire in his work on the Resurrection of the Flesh: "If anyone, he says, seizes upon the opportunity, in gehenna, of the flesh and soul's destruction and end of both substances, let him not think of a punishment, as if they were to be consumed rather than punished; let him recognise that the fire of gehenna is proclaimed as eternal, for an eternal punishment, and from this let him acknowledge the eternity of the killing, which, being human, is to be dreaded as temporal." Then too he would summon eternal substances, whose killing is eternal as punishment. Certainly, since after the resurrection the body together with the soul ought to be killed by God in gehenna, both will be established sufficiently: the resurrection of the flesh and the eternal killing. Otherwise it would be most absurd if the raised flesh were killed in gehenna in order that it might cease to exist, which it would have suffered even had it not been raised. Its restoration would be for this purpose only, that there should be no one to whom it has already happened not to exist. Finally, the eternity of infernal punishments is powerfully confirmed both by the immortality of the sinful soul itself, since if it does not die it cannot be well with it (for a sinner who is not freed from sin, and who therefore retains sin dwelling within him, cannot be well), according to those words of God: "Tell the righteous that it is well [כי טוב] with him, for he shall eat the fruit of his doings; woe to the wicked, it shall be ill with him [כי רע], for the reward [גמול] of his hands shall be done to him, and his works shall have their just recompense" (Isa. 3.10, 11). It is also confirmed by the guilt of sin, not remitted but imputed, which is infinite on account of the infinity of the Majesty that is offended; and so, in order that the equality of sin and punishment may be kept, it demands an infinite punishment, not intensively, since a finite act would not be capable of such intensity, but extensively, as to an unending duration. It is confirmed too by the perpetuity of sin and of its guilt, and of the justice of God*: since the sinner, dead in sin and not made alive through the grace of God in Christ, does not cease to sin, and sinning has become his nature; and thus the justice of God, which he can no more deny than he can deny himself, does not allow a continuing sin to go on being unpunished, and wrath does not remain on the disobedient (John 3.36). It is confirmed by the lack of a remedy and of a cause of deliverance, since after a man's death the doors of grace are shut (Matt. 25.10; Luke 13.25), and a brother cannot redeem (Ps. 49.8); nor does God redeem except through the ransom of Christ and the sacrifice for sin, of which no remnant remains for those who sin wilfully (Heb. 10.26). It is confirmed by despair, the companion of punishments, since there is no redemption from hell, nor do those who are there pass over to us, to Abraham and his company (Luke 16.26); and there is no repentance or sanctification in hell. Those who are there are so handed over by the severe judge God into the hand of sin that they sin for ever, on account of the law of sin, which cannot but extend the power of the law of death and make its reign interminable. It is confirmed by the truth of the law, and the sentence of the judge, and of the Divine prediction: for the law has threatened eternal death to the transgressor, as we have proved in its place, just as it has promised eternal life to the obedient; and the truth of the threat will stand as surely as that of the promise. Finally, it is confirmed by the will of God, most powerful, most holy, most wise, whose concern it is to reveal for ever the glory of his holiness and justice. For God made all things for himself, even the wicked for the day of evil (Prov. 16.4).

units.la: CXIV. Erunt tamen in his poenarum infernalium generibus gradus. Servus enim, qui noverit voluntatem heri sui, & non fecerit, neque fecerit secundum voluntatem ejus, δαρήσεται πληγὰς vapulabit multis. Et qui non cognoverit, fecerit autem digna plagis, δαρήσεται ὀλίγας vapulabit paucis, Luc.XII.47.48. Tolerabilius erit terrae Sodomae & Gomorrhae in die judicii, quam urbi illi, quae vos non audiverit, Matth.X.15. Tyro & Sidoni ἀνεκτότερον tolerabilius erit in die judicii, quam vobis, ibid.XI.22. Dico vobis, quod terrae Sodomaeorum tolerabilius erit, quam tibi, ib. v.24. Ideo Christus distinguit poenam judicii, Synedrii, gehennae, ibid. V.22. alludens ad Judaeorum judicia etiam capitalia, quae gravitatis gradibus variarunt; nec non comparans poenas cum peccatis, quia levius est irasci sine causa, quod judicium; gravius dicere fratri Racab, quod Synedrium; gravissimum dicere stulte, quod ignem gehennae mereri Christus declarat. Ad Pharisaeos etiam Christus: Vae vobis, &c. Propterea accipietis περισσότερον κρίμα judicium abundantius, ibid.XXIII.14. Facietis proselytum filium gehennae διπλότερον duplo majorem vobis, ibid. v.15. S. Paulus: Thesaurizas tibi iram in diem irae, & revelationis justi judicii Dei, qui reddet unicuique secundum opera sua, Rom. II.4.5. Cum enim peccata damnatorum in hac vita admissa inaequalia sint, supplicia etiam inaequalia sint oportet, quia poena proportione respondet culpae. Venio cito, & merces mea mecum est, ut reddam unicuique secundum opera sua, Apoc.II.23. XXII.12. Sicut in domo Patris mansiones multae & diversae sunt: ita in gehenna diversae mansiones, & suppliciorum differentiae sunt. Sed non obstantibus gradibus hisce recte Augustinus contra Donat. Lib.IV.13. scripsit, ad non possidendum Regnum Dei tantundem valere ex vitiis illis, quod elegeris mitius, quantum plura vel unum, quod perspexeris gravius. Omnes poenae infernales aeternae, & quoad speciem eadem, gradibus solis differunt.
units.tr: CXIV. There will nevertheless be degrees within these kinds of infernal punishment. For the servant who knew his lord's will, and did not do it, nor did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes; and he who did not know it, but did things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes (Luke 12.47, 48). It shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city which does not hear you (Matt. 10.15). It shall be more tolerable [ἀνεκτότερον] for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for you (ibid. 11.22). I tell you that it shall be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites than for you (ibid. v. 24). Thus Christ distinguishes the punishment of judgment, of the council, and of gehenna (ibid. v. 22), alluding to the Jewish judgments, even capital ones, which varied in degrees of gravity; and also comparing the punishments with the sins: it is a lesser thing to be angry without cause, which is liable to the judgment; graver to say to a brother Raca, which is liable to the council; gravest of all to say fool, which Christ declares deserves the fire of gehenna. Christ also speaks to the Pharisees: "Woe to you," etc. For this reason you shall receive greater judgment [περισσότερον κρίμα] (ibid. 23.14). You make a proselyte a child of gehenna [διπλότερον], twice as great as yourselves (ibid. v. 15). St Paul: "You treasure up for yourself wrath against the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to every man according to his works" (Rom. 2.4, 5). For since the sins of the damned committed in this life are unequal, their punishments must also be unequal, because punishment corresponds in proportion to guilt. "Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to every one according to his works" (Rev. 2.23; 22.12). Just as in my Father's house there are many mansions, and they are diverse, so in gehenna there are diverse mansions and differences of punishments. But notwithstanding these degrees, Augustine rightly wrote against the Donatists (Book 4, ch. 13): "For not possessing the kingdom of God, the choice of milder vices is worth just as much as the choice of many, or of one that you have perceived to be more grave." All infernal punishments are eternal, and in kind they are the same; they differ only in degree.

units.la: CXV. Haec cum ita habeant, gravissime errant, qui Infernum, & cruciatuum aeternitatem inficiantur, imo albis dentibus rident. Quorum voces sic μιμητικῶς repraesentantur: pepigimus foedus cum morte, & cum inferno fecimus ṁ visionem, tractationem de pace, induciās, Esaj. XXVIII.15. Edamus, bibamus, nam cras moriemur, ibid.XXII.13. Exigua & cum tædio est vita nostra, & non est remedium in fine hominis; & non est agnitus, qui ex inferno redierit, Sap.II.1. Gentilium nonnullorum vox fuit; Fabulae sunt manes; nec non juxta Poëtae illud: Esse aliquos manes & subterranea Regna, vix pueri credunt. De Epicuro sic Tertullianus Apol. 45. Epicurus omnem cruciatum doloremque depretiat, modicum quidem contemptibilem pronuntiando, magnum vero non diuturnum. Sed variasse tamen Gentilium sententias, supra vidimus. Judaei inferos agnoscunt, sed impios non quosvis, sed insignite tales in illis torquendos in aeternum, reliquos ad tempus, quo finito, liberandi sint, asserunt. Alii etiam sine discrimine impios liberatum iri affirmant; eo quod per cruciatus enecandi, & bestiae instar perituri sint; uti diserte Maimonides Halach. Thefchubab c.8. & in Tract. Maddah. ubi etiam mortem seu interitum illum in inferno excidium toties intentatum interpretantur. Neque aliter Nachmanides aliique, quorum sententiam Abarbanel ad Num.XV.30. exponit. Judaeorum veterum etiam vestigiis insistens Origenes poenarum infernalium aeternitatem negavit. Nam hunc ei errorem Theophilus Alexandrinus Lib. II. Epiphanius Epist. ad Joh Hierosol. Hieronymus Epist. ad Avit. aliique impingunt; & ipse passim, imprimis Lib. I. 6. prodidisse videtur. Ab errore tamen illo eum Sixtus Senensis Biblioth. Lib V. Annot. 141. nec non Jacobus Merlinus Apol. pro Orig. absolvunt. Notavit vero etiam Augustinus de Civit. D. Lib. XXI.17. quosdam misericordium nomine insignes, qui damnatos post certi temporis metas pro cujusque peccati quantitate liberandos docuerunt. Sed & Armenii Infernum abnegare feruntur, eo quod Christus eum destruxerit, dum in illum descendit: asserentes nihilominus, infideles & perfecte malos in Oceano sulphuris cruciari. Omnem vero pudorem deposuit, de quo ὁμολογοῦσι eidem Theod. Raph. Camphuysen Epist. de abolit. injustorum, profiteri ausus est; se arbitrari, Socinum nullibi plus praestitisse, quam quod spissas & communes tenebras perrumperet fabulosi inferni, & infinitae damnationis; & in re ista reddiderit hominibus lucem oppido excellentem. Qui etiam infernum modo fabulam, modo puerile terriculamentum, modo Papisticum, Ethnicum, Poeticum commentum impuro & tartareo ore proclamat. Sic autem Socinus statuit, impios defunctos in morte manere, & in statu ἀνυπαρξίας non existentia, qui illorum infernus sit, esse; superstites vero tempore adventus Christi ad judicium, peracto eo, in ignem conflagrationis mundi, una cum Diabolo detrusum, & semel omnes illo igne absumptum iri: qui tamen aeternus propterea dicatur, quia nulla unquam liberatio ex eo contingat. Aestipulatur Socinianis Hobbesius, uti habent similes labra lactucas. Nam & ille negata animae immortalitate, simul passim impios post mortem aeternos cruciatus manere negare necesse habuit. Denique etiam Remonstrantes Sarmaticis his portentis abblandiri sueti, ne hic quidem ab illorum impietate plane absunt. Adamo enim posterisque ejus, quibus nulla vitae aeternae promissio facta sit, nec aeternas in morte poenas timendas esse asserunt, exceptis iis solis, quibus Evangelii praeconium factum sit. Episcopius vero poenam damni aeternam admittit, poenam vero sensus partim dum ignis ille urit, partim, igne illo extincto, in aeterna scelerum conscientia & desperatione ponit. Socinianorum porro impietatem non semel jam perstrinximus. Nam & immortalitatem animae Loc.VI.86.87. &c. vindicavimus: & impios resurrecturos, supra § LXXVI. demonstravimus, & eosdem omnes, non solos, qui Christo adventante superstites erunt, judicandos esse, § LXXXIV. evicimus; & denique poenarum infernalium aeternitatem §. CXI. argumentis irrefragabilibus astruximus. Quae capitalia dogmata haereticorum impietatem penitus confodiunt.
units.tr: CXV. Since these things stand as they do, those grievously err who deny hell and the eternity of torments, and even laugh at them with white teeth. Their voices are represented mimetically [μιμητικῶς] thus: we have made a covenant with death, and with hell have we made an agreement, a vision, a treaty about peace, a truce (Isa. 28.15); let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die (ibid. 22.13); our life is short and wearisome, and there is no remedy at the end of a man's life, and no one has been known to return from hell (Wisd. 2.1). This was the saying of some Gentiles: the shades are fables. So too the line of the poet: that there are shades and kingdoms under the earth, scarcely children believe. Of Epicurus Tertullian says thus (Apol. 45): Epicurus belittles all torment and pain, pronouncing the small to be contemptible and the great to be not lasting. But we have seen above that the opinions of the Gentiles varied. The Jews acknowledge hell, but they maintain that not all the wicked but only those who are notably such are to be tormented there for ever, while the rest are to be freed after a time, when it has ended. Others affirm that the wicked without distinction will be set free, because they will be destroyed by torments and will perish like beasts; so Maimonides expressly (Halach. Thefchubab c. 8, and in Tract. Maddah), where he also interprets that death or perishing in hell, the destruction so often threatened, in this way. Nachmanides and others hold no different view, whose opinion Abarbanel sets out on Num. 15.30. Following also the footsteps of the ancient Jews, Origen denied the eternity of infernal punishments. Theophilus of Alexandria (Lib. II), Epiphanius (Epist. to John of Jerusalem), Jerome (Epist. to Avitus) and others charge him with this error, and he himself seems to have set it forth in many places, especially Lib. I. 6. Yet Sixtus of Siena (Bibl. Lib. V, Annot. 141) and also Jacob Merlin (Apol. pro Orig.) acquit him of that error. Augustine, however, in de Civitate Dei Lib. XXI. 17, noted that certain men distinguished by the name of mercy taught that the damned, after the limits of a certain time, in proportion to the amount of each one's sin, were to be set free. But the Armenians are also said to deny hell, on the ground that Christ destroyed it when he descended into it, while nevertheless asserting that unbelievers and the thoroughly wicked are tormented in a sea of sulphur. Theodore Raphael Camphuysen, in his letter on the abolition of the unjust, [ὁμολογοῦσι] as they confess of him, laid aside all shame and dared to profess that he considered Socinus nowhere to have done more than that he broke through the thick and common darkness of the fabled hell and infinite damnation, and in this matter gave to men a most excellent light. He also loudly proclaims hell, with a foul and infernal mouth, now a fable, now a childish bugbear, now a Papal, Pagan, poetic invention. Socinus, moreover, laid down that the wicked, when they die, remain in death, in a state of non-existence, and that this is their hell; but those who survive until the time of Christ's coming to judgment, when that is over, will be cast into the fire of the world's conflagration together with the Devil, and all will be consumed once for all by that fire, which is nevertheless called eternal because no deliverance from it ever takes place. Hobbes agrees with the Socinians, as lips suit lettuce, as the saying goes. For he too, having denied the immortality of the soul, was obliged to deny that the wicked remain after death in eternal torments. Finally, the Remonstrants, who are accustomed to flatter these Sarmatian monsters, are not wholly free from their impiety. For they assert that Adam and his posterity, to whom no promise of eternal life was made, need not fear eternal punishments after death, except for those alone to whom the proclamation of the Gospel has come. Episcopius, however, admits the eternal punishment of loss, but places the punishment of sense partly in the time while that fire burns, and partly, once that fire has been extinguished, in the eternal conscience and despair of sins. Nor have we merely touched upon the impiety of the Socinians once already. For we have defended the immortality of the soul (Loc. VI. 86, 87, etc.); we have shown above (§ LXXVI) that the wicked will rise again; we have proved (§ LXXXIV) that all of them, not only those who survive until Christ's coming, will be judged; and finally we have established (§ CXI) the eternity of infernal punishments by unanswerable arguments. These principal dogmas utterly overthrow the impiety of the heretics.

units.la: CXVI. Neque contraria infidelium horum in impietate argumenta quicquam roboris ris habent. Nam quòd pœnam peccati mortem esse & mortem perditionem atque interitum peccatoris esse objectant, jejunum planè est. Sicut enim non vivere, sed bene vivere vita est: ita mors est, non quæ vitam, sed quæ vitam rectam & beatam tollit. Nam & in peccatis mortui dicuntur, Ephes.II.1. quibus naturalis vita non adimitur. Est enim quædam mors separatio non ab omni eo, quod vivit, sed ab eo, quod sancte & gloriose vivit & regnat, quod Deus est, & occisio non transitoria & perpetua, in qua qui moritur, non sic moritur, ut extinguatur, sed ut continuè & in æternum puniatur. Pessimum enim mortis & perditionis genus est, cùm quis, juxta ferale illud Tiberii, sic perit, ut se perire sentiat & æternùm sentiat. Unde τὸ ἀπολέσαι perdere opponitur τῷ σῶσαι salvare, Matth. XV.25. & pro βασανίσαι cruciare, ibid. VIII.29. coll. cum Luc.IV.34. disserè ponitur; & mundus diluvio inundatus ἀπώλετο perditus est, 2.Pet.III.6. qui tamen annihilatus non est; & κόλασις αἰώνιος supplicium æternum, Matth. XXV.46. appellatur. Immortalitas verò illa, quam morte sua nobis Christus peperit, 2.Tim. I.10. non quævis immortalitas, sed beata immortalitas est. Scitè enim Rufinus in Symb. Dabitur, inquit, & peccatoribus & incorruptionis & immortalitatis de resurrectione conditio: ut sicut justis ministrat ad perpetuitatem gloriæ, ita peccatoribus (pœnitere nesciis) ad prolixitatem confusionis & pœnæ. Frustra etiam magnitudinem Divinæ commiserationis ad extinguendum infernum, prædicant. Non enim ejusdem objectum peccatores ἀμετανόητοι & damnati, sed fideles & salvandi sunt. Judicium enim sine misericordia erit illi, qui misericordiam non exercuerit, Jac.II.13. Et tempus misericordiæ & pœnitentiæ præsens seculum est, non futurum, in quo claudetur janua, Matth.XXV.10. Ecce nunc καιρὸς εὐπρόσδεκτος & tempus acceptabile, nunc dies salutis est, 2.Cor.VI.2. Neque etiam major Dei misericordia, quàm justitia est, quia utraque infinita est, licèt objecta ejus, quæ velit, statuere plura vel pauciora, liberum eidem sit. Nam & libertas in statuendo Dei perfectio est. Poenæ porrò infernales non erunt effectus crudelitatis, quæ misericordiæ & bonitati opponitur, sed severitatis & justitiæ, neque ex iis quicquam colligendum est, quod Dei bonitatem & amabilitatem suspectam homini reddere possit vel debeat. Nihil enim miseriæ damnatis obtinget, quod Dei misericordiam & essentialem amorem dedeceat, vel Angelis & hominibus beatis, quorum sanum & rectum judicium erit, displicere possit. Qui potiùs justitiæ Divinæ executionem probabunt vehementer & laudabunt. Non decet igitur eos, qui in hac vita tenebris involvuntur; sepositá etiam Scriptura, in qua voluntas Dei justa & sancta est, ob pœnas damnatorum bonitatem Dei accusare. Sicut enim verè fideles Dei castigationibus in hac vita exerciti Deo sanctitatem & justitiam non ideo criminantur, sed potiùs laudant, & bonitatem ejus confitentur: ita multò magis glorificati Deum sanctissimum peccatores damnantem glorificabunt. Neque etiam damnatorum numerus Divinam bonitatem & amabilitatem obscurabit, quasi severitas ejus amorem & bonitatem ejusdem minueret vel vinceret. Licèt enim globi hujus terrestris pars major futura misera est, id tamen de totius universitatis incolis dici non potest. Innumerabilis enim etiam Angelorum bonorum multitudo est; Etiam magnitudo & dignitas vicem multitudinis supplere poterit. Sicut Sol unus multis astris minoribus præstat, & Rex ac palatium ejus innumeris plebejis & casis eorum splendorem præripit. Si igitur maximè omnes orbis hujus habitatores perditi essent, non magis tamen inde bonitas Dei gloriam suam amitteret, quàm Regis clementissimi bonitas, & Regni ejus gloria ex tugurioli vel carceris squalore detrimentum patitur. Accedit, quòd infinita Dei bonitas & clementia in unico etiam, qui salvatur, homine distringitur: & quod infinitum est, superari & vinci non potest. Qui porrò voluntatem Dei ignorat, is vapulabit paucis, Luc.XII.48. comparate, & quoad pœnarum gradus, non absolutè, & quoad speciem; non pauxillo tempore, sed in æternum. Non enim illud ὀλίγοις paucis, finem, sed supplicii sine fine diversitatem declarat. Etiam omnium Deus miseretur, Rom.XI.32. sine distinctione populorum, & in hoc seculo, non in altero. Quòd verò mors & infernus in stagnum ignis conjici, & hoc mortem secundam esse, Apoc. XX.14. dicuntur, non eum sensum habere potest, quòd in stagno illo ignis omnia consumenda & annihilanda brevi sint, cùm v.10. præcesserint illa: Torquebuntur in illo stagno die & nocte in secula seculorum; & quæ igni committantur, dissolvi possint, at annihilari non possint. Sive igitur mors illa secunda mors spiritualis & induratio in peccato τῶν ἀμετανοήτων in hac vita intelligitur; stagnum ignis conscientiæ cruciatus erit, qui ita mortuos in hac vita torquet: sive mors temporalem consequens, sensus erit, eam non alibi futuram, quàm in stagno ignis, in quo impii dies noctésque in secula seculorum torquebuntur. Impium verò illud Hobbesii est, quòd Deum æterna supplicia comminatum, non ideo injustum esse, quia non infligit, cùm is demum injustus sit, qui bona promissa non servat, objiciunt. Nam & veracitas Dei sic periclitatur, & justitia puniens, quæ Deo essentialis est, abnegatur. Non enim Deus minùs infinitè justus, quàm infinitè misericors est. Qui justificat improbum, & condemnat justum, abominatio Jehovæ uterque est, Prov.XVII.15. Stultum quinetiam est, pœnas infernales non credere, quia de earum ratione universa liquidò non constat. Nam & gloriæ cœlestis universa ratio & magnitudo nemini mortalium innotescit. Ad timorem verò debitum incutiendum satis est, quòd terribilia & tremenda maximè sunt, quæ Scripturæ de pœnis damnatorum revelant. Ac licèt plerique ea credere non videantur, victuri alioqui, sicut qui de leone, urso vel lupo in insidiis latente, & ex iis erupturo ab homine fide digno audit, fugam ilico capessit; tamen non iccirco infernus non est, quia hominum incredulitas Dei fidem & veracitatem non abolet, Rom. III.3. & frustra etiam esse potest quòd expanditur rete in oculis omnis alitis, Prov.I.17. Sicut igitur capitur avis reti, quod illa videnté expansum est, ita ut frustra sit oculos habuisse buisse ad videndam laquei expansionem : ita damnati videntes & prævidentes εἰς πέδηλον ὀλεθρον in exitium prævisum, prævisámque pestem ruunt. Quomodo nec fata prædicta multi evitare possunt; & qui meliora vident probántque multi, deteriora sequuntur. Obstare enim potest fatalis & lethalis illa impietatis arundo nullo dictamno sanabilis; nec non durites illa cordis, qua constricti sibi benedicunt, in corde suo, dicendo; Pax erit mihi, cum in duritie cordis mei ambulavero, Deut. XXIX. 19. Praeterea neque opus esse, ut ex inferno aliquis revertatur, & poenarum infernalium rationem exponat, Abrahamus cœles heluonem, & in ejus persona impios omnes docuit ad Mosen & Prophetas eos amandans. Habent Mosen & Prophetas. Illos audiant. Si Mosen & Prophetas non audient, neque, si quis ex mortuis resurrexerit, persuadebuntur. Luc. XVI. 29. 31. Annon populus Deum suum consulet? Vivos pro mortuis? Ad legem & testimonium, Esaj. VIII. 19. 20.
units.tr: CXVI. Nor do the opposing arguments of these unbelievers in their impiety have any real force. For when they object that the punishment of sin is death, and that death means the ruin and annihilation of the sinner, they are plainly talking nonsense. Just as living is not life but living well is, so death is not the thing that takes away life in general, but the thing that takes away right and blessed life. For men are also said to be dead in sins, Eph. 2.1, though natural life is not taken from them. There is indeed a kind of death that is a separation not from everything that lives, but from that which lives holily and gloriously and reigns, namely God; and it is a killing that is not transient but perpetual, in which the one who dies does not die so as to be extinguished, but so as to be punished continually and for ever. For the worst kind of death and destruction is when someone, in the dreadful words of Tiberius, perishes in such a way that he feels himself perishing and feels it for ever. Hence to destroy [τὸ ἀπολέσαι] is set against to save, Matt. 15.25, and is plainly placed for to torment [βασανίσαι], Matt. 8.29, compared with Luke 4.34; and the world overwhelmed by the flood is said to have perished [ἀπώλετο], 2 Pet. 3.6, though it was not annihilated; and it is called eternal punishment [κόλασις αἰώνιος], Matt. 25.46. But that immortality which Christ obtained for us by his death, 2 Tim. 1.10, is not any immortality whatever, but a blessed immortality. Rufinus rightly says in his commentary on the Creed: There will be given to sinners also, as the condition of resurrection, incorruption and immortality; so that, just as it ministers to the just the perpetuity of glory, so it ministers to sinners, who know not how to repent, the length of confusion and punishment. In vain also do they proclaim the greatness of divine compassion as a means of abolishing hell. For the object of that compassion is not the impenitent and the damned [ἀμετανόητοι], but the faithful and those to be saved. For judgment will be without mercy to the one who has not shown mercy, James 2.13. And the time of mercy and repentance is the present age, not the age to come, in which the door will be shut, Matt. 25.10. Behold, now is the acceptable time [καιρὸς εὐπρόσδεκτος], now is the day of salvation, 2 Cor. 6.2. Nor is God's mercy greater than his justice, since each is infinite, although it is open to him to appoint more or fewer objects for each, as he pleases. For freedom in determining is itself a perfection of God. Moreover, the infernal punishments will not be the effect of cruelty, which is opposed to mercy and goodness, but of severity and justice; and nothing should be inferred from them which could or ought to make the goodness and lovableness of God suspect to a man. For nothing of misery will befall the damned that would be unworthy of God's mercy and essential love, or that could displease the angels and the blessed men, whose sound and right judgment it will be. Rather, they will vigorously approve and praise the execution of divine justice. Therefore it is not fitting for those who in this life are wrapped in darkness, even setting aside Scripture, in which the will of God is just and holy, to accuse God's goodness on account of the punishments of the damned. For just as true believers, exercised in this life by God's chastisements, do not therefore accuse God of holiness and justice, but rather praise him and confess his goodness, so much more will the glorified praise the most holy God who condemns sinners. Nor will the number of the damned obscure the divine goodness and lovableness, as though his severity lessened or overcame his love and goodness. For although the greater part of this terrestrial globe is destined to be miserable, that cannot be said of the inhabitants of the whole universe. For the multitude of the good angels too is countless; and greatness and dignity can take the place of multitude. Just as one sun surpasses many smaller stars, and a king and his palace outshine countless commoners and their huts, so, if all the inhabitants of this world were utterly lost, the goodness of God would not lose its glory any more than the goodness of the most merciful king, or the glory of his kingdom, suffers loss from the squalor of a hut or a prison. Moreover, the infinite goodness and mercy of God is displayed even in one man who is saved; and what is infinite cannot be overcome or conquered. Furthermore, the one who is ignorant of the will of God will be beaten with few stripes, Luke 12.48, comparatively speaking, and as regards degrees of punishment, not absolutely, and as regards the kind; not for a short time, but for ever. For that word [ὀλίγοις] few does not denote an end, but a difference in punishment that has no end. God has mercy on all, Rom. 11.32, without distinction of peoples, and in this age, not in another. But as for the statement that death and hell are cast into the lake of fire, and this is the second death, Rev. 20.14, it cannot have the sense that all things are to be consumed and annihilated in that lake of fire in a short time, since verse 10 has already said: They will be tormented in that lake day and night for ever and ever; and things committed to fire can be dissolved, but cannot be annihilated. Therefore, whether that second death is understood as a spiritual death and hardening in sin of the impenitent [τῶν ἀμετανοήτων] in this life, the lake of fire will be the torment of conscience which so torments the dead in this life; or whether it means the temporal death that follows, the sense will be that it will be nowhere else than in the lake of fire, in which the wicked will be tormented day and night for ever and ever. As for the impious saying of Hobbes, that God, having threatened eternal punishments, is not unjust for not inflicting them, since only the one is unjust who does not keep his promised good things, they object wrongly. For thereby the truthfulness of God is endangered, and his punishing justice, which is essential to God, is denied. For God is no less infinitely just than he is infinitely merciful. He who justifies the wicked and condemns the just, both are an abomination to Jehovah, Prov. 17.15. It is also foolish to disbelieve in infernal punishments because the whole manner of them is not clearly known. For the whole manner and greatness of heavenly glory is known to no mortal either. To strike fear as is due, it is enough that what Scripture reveals about the punishments of the damned is most terrible and dreadful. And although many do not seem to believe it, they would otherwise be alive; just as one who hears from a trustworthy man of a lion, a bear or a wolf lying in ambush, and about to burst out from it, at once takes to flight; yet hell does not therefore not exist, because the unbelief of men does not abolish the faith and truthfulness of God, Rom. 3.3; and it is in vain that the net is spread in the sight of every bird, Prov. 1.17. Just as a bird is caught in a net which was spread out while it was looking on, so that it is in vain to have had eyes to see the spreading of the snare, so the damned, seeing and foreseeing, rush into the foreseen destruction [εἰς πέδηλον ὀλεθρον] and the foreseen plague. So too many cannot escape the foretold fates; and many see and approve the better course yet follow the worse. For that deadly and fatal arrow of impiety, curable by no dittany, can stand in the way; and so too that hardness of heart, by which men bound up bless themselves in their heart, saying: I shall have peace, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart, Deut. 29.19. Moreover, there is no need for anyone to return from hell and explain the nature of infernal punishments; Abraham, in the person of the rich glutton, taught all the impious and sent them to Moses and the Prophets. They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them. If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be persuaded if one rises from the dead, Luke 16.29, 31. Will not a people consult its God? For the living on behalf of the dead? To the law and to the testimony, Isa. 8.19, 20.

units.la: CXVII. Sed aries præcipuus, quo Sociniani infernum debellare conantur, justitiæ Dei ratio est, utpote qua cum hostiliter pugnet, delicta impiorum finita supplicis æternis punire. Proportionem enim delictum inter & poenam, quam justus judex respicere debeat, desiderant, utpote quæ finitum inter & infinitum intercedere nulla possit. Delicta porro impiorum infinita esse negant, quia vim infinitam nec ex se ipsis, neque in vel à delinquente, neque ab eo, in quem, & contra quem delinquitur; neque ab horum aliquibus, neque ab omnibus simul, habeant. Non ex se ipsis, quia nec duratione sint infinita, cum omnes creaturarum actiones sint transeuntes & tempore finitæ; nec gravitate intensiva, quia creatura omnis, omnesque ejus actus infiniti sint. Non à delinquente, ob easdem causas. Non à Deo, adversus quem delinquitur, tum quia alias omnia delicta forent æqualia, cum pariter omnia in Deum desinant, & infinita nulla inæqualitatis differentia fit: tum quia nec singula delicta, nec omnia, nec quædam infinita sint; Non singula, quia non tantum sic justitiæ Divinæ nunquam satisfieret, cum si unum puniatur poena in temporis æternitatem producta, alterum eidem puniri nequiret, quia prius delictum poena sua æternitatem præoccupavit, adeóque hujus poena non alia quàm intensiva esse posset: sed etiam passio Christi justitiæ divinæ non satisfecisset, quia saltem extensive infinita non fuit, nec ullam cum æterna passione proportionem habuerit; & si unum delictum poena luet intensione propter dignitatem patientis, alterum poena extensione infinita, quomodo tum satisfacturum Christum fuisse pro tertio, quarto, centesimo, millesimo delicto, cum præter intensam & extensam infinitatem nulla superfit; & si utraq; uni delicto debeatur, quem pro cæteris satisfacturum, quando primum jam omnem infinitatem ex justitia sibi vindicet? Ut porro diversæ poenæ diversis delictis irrogentur, & toties detur infinitas, quot dantur poenæ, ut quolibet tempore, & forte etiam intensione, seu gravitate infinita sit; impossibile esse clamant, quia nec omnes poenæ simul tempore & gravitate infinitæ esse possint, cùm nec specie, sed gradu differre putentur, atque ita non omnes poenæ intensivè infinitæ esse possint, quia remissior gradus minor infinito sit. Addunt & illud, si uni delicto una species poenæ gravitate & intensivè infinita debeatur, foresic, ut peccata reliqua inulta maneant. Quòd si poenæ extensione & intensione infinitæ propterea sint, quia in Deum commissa delicta sunt, tanti ponderis futuram esse hanc infinitatem gravitatis peccati simpliciter, colligunt, quanti est dignitas & majestas personæ læsæ; cum verò hæc infinita sit simpliciter, ut nihil ulla ex parte neque idem, neque diversum specie ei possit accedere, quod majorem faciat; quem sustinere posse delictum tanti esse ponderis, & poenam talem & tantam fore, quantum vel potest majestas Divina imponere, vel puniendus suscipere, ita ut nulla ex parte in eadem specie ei quicquam accedere possit? Alioquin enim infinitatem delicti non exæquare infinitatem læsi, cujus rei causa exponenda sit ei, qui gravitatem delicti oriri ex dignitate personæ læsæ asserit. Concessô enim hoc, sequi, Christum non potuisse nisi pro uniu hominis unico delicto satisfacere. Præterea cum ipsi Dei offensi ratione delicta sint inæqualia, majora & minora, infinita esse non posse, argutantur, quia infinitorum nullum altero majus, vel minus esse possit. Cúmque delicta, quatenus sunt actiones creaturarum, inter se proportionem habeant, apud Deum etiam, quem offendunt, habitura, colligunt. Cùm igitur inter ipsa per se considerata intervallum sit gravitatis; etiam illud quod inter situm & majus est, habiturum finitam rationem apud Deum ad alterum apud eundem Deum; adeóque omnia finita, & consequenter etiam poenas justas finitas fore. Denique sicut se habet delinquens ad delictum, ita se habere debere læsum ad poenam, ratiocinantur. Cùm igitur delinquentem inter & culpam, seu delictum certum intervallum sit, inde læsum inter & poenam tolli rationem intervalli rationalis, si utrumque, vel alterutrum infinitum statuatur, conficiunt. Denique delicta vim infinitam non habere à delinquentium aliquibus, vel omnibus simul, eo argumento, quòd ex multis numero & virtute per se finitis infinitum fieri non posset, sed oporteat saltem unum esse infinitum per se, ut constituatur ex iis infinitum, atque ita reliqua frustra sint, confirmare satagunt; & justitiam Dei ex æternis impiorum supplicis nullo modo elucere, sed injustitiam potius, concludunt. Hæc illa subtilis argumentorum, quibus supplicium æternitatem peculiari scripto, cui titulum fecerunt: Demonstratio, quòd æterna impiorum supplicia non justitiam, sed injustitiam Dei arguunt; cum justitia Dei non convenire asserunt, acies: hic: Ἀχαῖον est.
