units.tr: CXVII. But the chief battering-ram with which the Socinians try to demolish hell is the reasoning about God's justice: since it fights against this, that sinners who are finite should be punished with eternal punishments. For they require a proportion between the sin and the punishment, which a just judge ought to observe, and they hold that no proportion can exist between the finite and the infinite. They deny that the sins of the wicked are infinite, because they have no infinite force either in themselves, or from the sinner, or from the one against whom and in whom the sin is committed, or from some of these, or from all of them together. Not in themselves, because they are not infinite in duration, since all the actions of creatures are transitory and finite in time; nor in intensive gravity, since every creature and all its acts are finite. Not from the sinner, for the same reasons. Not from God, against whom the sin is committed: first, because then all sins would be equal, since they all terminate in God alike, and no difference of inequality would arise among infinites; second, because neither single sins, nor all sins, nor some of them, are infinite. Not single sins: for not only would divine justice never be satisfied in this way, since if one sin were punished with a punishment extended over the eternity of time, another could not be punished with the same, because the earlier sin would have already occupied the eternity of time with its punishment, so that the punishment of the latter could be only intensive; but also the passion of Christ would not have satisfied divine justice, since it was not infinite at least in extent and had no proportion to eternal suffering. And if one sin is paid for by an intensive punishment, on account of the dignity of the one who suffers, and another by a punishment infinite in extent, how would Christ then have made satisfaction for the third, fourth, hundredth, or thousandth sin, since nothing remains beyond the intensive and extensive infinity? And if both kinds are owed to one sin, for whom would he make satisfaction for the rest, when the first has already claimed all the infinity from justice? Again, they cry out that it is impossible for different punishments to be inflicted for different sins, and for infinity to be given as many times as there are punishments, so that each is infinite in duration and perhaps also in intensity or gravity; for not all punishments can be infinite at once in time and gravity, since they are thought to differ not in kind but in degree, and so not all punishments can be intensively infinite, because a milder degree is less than infinite. They add this as well: if one kind of punishment that is infinite in gravity and intensity were owed to one sin, the remaining sins would thereby remain unpunished. But if punishments are infinite in extent and intensity because the sins were committed against God, they infer that this infinity of gravity in the sin is simply as great as the dignity and majesty of the person offended; and since that majesty is simply infinite, so that nothing can be added to it in any part, whether of the same kind or of a different kind, that would make it greater, how could one sin be able to bear such a weight, and the punishment be of such a size and magnitude as the divine majesty can either impose or the one to be punished can undergo, so that nothing of the same kind could be added to it in any way? Otherwise, they say, the infinity of the sin does not equal the infinity of the one offended, and whoever asserts that the gravity of the sin arises from the dignity of the person offended must explain how this is so. For if this is granted, it follows that Christ could have made satisfaction only for one sin of one man. Moreover, since the sins are unequal in relation to God whom they offend, greater and lesser, they argue that they cannot be infinite, because none of the infinites can be greater or less than another. And since sins, insofar as they are actions of creatures, have a proportion to one another, they conclude that they will also have one in relation to God whom they offend. Therefore, since among these, considered in themselves, there is a difference in gravity, and what lies between the lesser and the greater will also have a finite relation before God to the other, and so all things will be finite and consequently also the just punishments will be finite. Finally, they reason that just as the offender stands to the offence, so the one wronged ought to stand to the punishment. Therefore, since there is a certain interval between the offender and the fault or sin, they conclude that if either or both are posited as infinite, the rational proportion of the interval between the one wronged and the punishment is removed. Finally, they strive to confirm that sins do not have infinite force from some or all of the sinners together, on the argument that from many things finite in number and power in themselves, an infinite cannot be made; rather at least one must be infinite in itself, so that an infinite may be constituted from them, and thus the rest would be in vain; and they conclude that the justice of God does not shine forth in any way from the eternal punishments of the wicked, but rather injustice. These are the subtle arguments by which, in a special writing with the title Demonstration, that the eternal punishments of the wicked prove the injustice, not the justice, of God, they sharpen their battle, asserting that the justice of God does not agree with them; here is the crux: [Ἀχαῖον] is.

units.la: CXVIII. Nihil tamen hîc præter λογικὰς ratiocinationes, & ὕψωμα ὑπεροχὴν ... γνῶσιν Θεοῦ altitudinem oppositam cognitioni Dei, 2. Cor. X. 5. qualia Sociniani religionis suæ principium venditant, & homines carnales, ad indurandos se ipsos, in deliciis habent, cernere est. Siccine verò voluntatem Dei, clarè adeò revelatam, eludere & explodere, atque ἀντιμανηεύεσθαι respondere Deo pium illi & fas ducunt? Quasi scilicet non Dei, sed hominis sit inter peccata & poenas peccatis suis debitas propor-tio- Objectio eorum præcipua, quòd infernus justitiæ Dei repugnet, utpote quæ vetet, ne delicta impiorum finita pœnis æternis plectantur, proponitur. & fusius diluitur. tionem definire, & Dei actiones & verba ad alienum rationis humanæ bacchantis forum trahere, integrum esset. Nos verò satis Deum & justitiam ejus, voluntate ejus, quæ injustitia semper vacat, ostensa tuemur; tutóque ei adversus serpentinas haíce technas nos involvimus; memores etiam, judicia Dei esse abyssum magnam, Psal. XXXVI.7. & ἀνεξερεύνητα imperscrutabilia, Rom.XI.33. Ipse etiam eventus homines impios docebit, quòd frustra ratiociniis suis contra stimulum calcitraverint. Cúmque Deum inter & hominem delinquentem nulla proportio sit, vanum est, punientem inter & delinquentem proportionem quærere, vel illam, quæ pœnam inter & delictum est, impotentius vexare. In proportione enim illa, qualiscunque à Deo, pœnam inter & delictum constituta, & sapienter constituta est, spectanda inprimis infinita illa Deum inter & hominem distantia est; secundum quam etiam varias delictorum formas & gradus respexit, & in pœnis ipsis gradus dispares pro peccatorum diversitate constituit. Tum etiam illum finiti ad infinitum proportionis defectum, quem disputationis hujus basin facient, ipsimet alibi lancinant, Christo finito scientiam & potentiam infinitam tribuentes. Qualis etiam proportio delicti & pœnæ à Deo servabitur, si, quod illi tuentur, impii ante ultimum judicium mortui non puniuntur, sed non exi-stunt; at superstites soli & simul omnes eadem pœna incendii affecti pariter delebuntur & extinguentur? Præterea pœnam peccatorum cum Scripturis potiùs æternam, quàm infinitam dicimus, quia æternitatis vox minùs quàm infinitatis μαλον μᾶλλον est. Argutiæ verò omnes, quas cæca ratio nectit, ex conceptu infinitatis potiùs, quàm æternitatis nectuntur. Nullam autem delictum inter & pœnam æternam proportionem esse vix illi dicere sustinebunt; quia ne apud homines quidem pœnarum justitia in proportione durationis constat, ut non diuturnior sit pœna, quàm delictum fuit. In confesso porrò illud est, delicta ex se ipsis non esse infinita, quia omnino actiones transeuntes sunt. Infinita tamen sunt metonymicè propter objectum infinitum, Majestatem Dei, in quam incurrunt. Neque ideo delicta omnia æqualia in se sunt, sed tantùm ex æquo in infinitam Majestatem Dei arietant, atque ita reatum infinitum æqualiter trahunt. Nam res ipsa loquitur, peccata ex dignitate ejus, qui offenditur, æstimari oportere. Ex personæ dignitate pœnæ species; ex peccantis verò, & beneficiorum, quæ accepit, ratione ejusdem gradus proveniunt. Porrò & singula peccata, & quædam, & omnia infinita esse, denominatione ab objecto petita, nihil prohibet. Possunt enim in se finita esse numero, duratione & tempore, quæ alio sensu infinita omnia sunt. Sed quomodo, sic inquiunt, justitiæ Dei satis fiet, quia si unius delicti pœna in æternitatem protrahetur, alterum delictum eadem infinitate puniri nequit, adeóque necessario alteri huic infinitas intensiva erit. Quæ sic satis stulta sunt. Nam si & homo uno crimine capitali mortem commeritus, decem & plura ejusdem, vel alterius generis crimina superaddiderit, primum illud mortis pœnam præoccupabit, nec minus tamen reliqua pariter mortifera erunt, licèt pro rerum conditione pœnam, vel pœnæ gradus in intensione augere possint. Neque dispar infinitæ pœnæ ratio est, quia omnia equidem & singula peccata illam merentur; sed gradus tamen inæqualitatis, in mortis varia intensione & gravitate variabunt. Neque quia singula peccata Deum infinitum offendunt, ideo etiam singula pœnam intensivè & extensivè infinitam requirunt. Sufficit enim ad reparandam offensam pœna, quæ respectu durationis in æternum exeat, respectu verò intensionis gradus à Deo definiendos & mensurandos recipiat. Neque obstat, quòd peccatum pœnam infinitam meretur, quia, quoad intensionem, illa infinita physicè esse non potest, cùm sicut actus, ita etiam passio semper finita sit; Sed moraliter tamen infinita, hoc est, indefinita, & nullo homine definienda & limitanda, in qua gradus & varia inæqualitas constitui poterit, esse queat. Quærgo de duplici infinitate intensiva & extensiva illi garriunt, ulterius examen non merentur. Alia enim prorsus ratio passionis & obedientiæ Christi fuit, quæ propter dignitatem personæ patientis infinita intensivè esse potuit, & fuit: at infinita extensivè esse nec potuit, nec debuit, quia alias mortem superare, hæreditatem sibi promissam acquirere, & sibi datis vitam æternam donare non potuisset. Venit Christus, uti scitè Augustinus in Psal.95. loquitur, & dedit pretium, fudit sanguinem suum, & emit orbem terrarum. Quæritis quid emerit? Videte, quid dederit, & videte, quid emerit. Sanguis Christi pretium est. Tanti quid valet? Quid nisi totus orbis? Quid nisi omnes gentes? Licet etiam argumentum adversariorum in ipsosmet sic retorquere. Esto, peccatum omne pœnam temporalem & finitam duntaxat requirat; si igitur propter unum peccatum illam fert, quomodo satisfiet justitiæ Divinæ pro secundo, tertio, decimo, centesimo, millesimo? Nulla enim pœna præter temporalem superest, qua exanthlata pro uno, quam pœnam cætera omnia subibunt? Ubi igitur justitiæ Divinæ ratio? Ac licèt etiam delicta, quatenus actiones creaturarum sunt, inter se proportionem habeant, & habere ab ipso Deo, cujus judicium secundum veritatem est, Rom.II.2. judicentur, adeóque finita eatenus sint, non tamen relata ad Deum offensum denominari infinita, & æternam pœnam non mereri possunt; quia diversus planè respectus est, ut priore illo proportionem habere, posteriore non habere censeri possint. Denique nec simpliciter id verum est, ut se habet delinquens ad delictum, ita se habere læsum ad pœnam. Dissimilima enim ratio læsi Dei, & lædentis peccatoris est, ac proin etiam Dei ad hujus pœnam. Licèt proin delinquentem inter & culpam intervallum sit, non propterea etiam delinquentem inter & læsum esse debet. Et si maximè foret, non propterea par cum illo, quod hominem inter & actionem ejus est, foret. Pœna etiam spectatur, vel ut à Deo infligitur, vel ut ab homine excipitur. Observat verò Deus in puniendo proportionem vel intervallum inter peccatum hominis & ejus pœnam, sed sibi ab actione hominis proportionem vel intervallum non accipit. Levissimum sæpe hominem inter & peccatum intervallum est, quod tamen Deum inter atque pœnam, quam infligit, & peccator ab ipso excipit, non est. Sed ad justitiam Dei vindicandam unum hoc adversus γογσυρμὸν obmurmurationem cæcæ rationis sufficiat, quòd Deus ipse proportionem delictum inter & pœnam ejusmodi constituit, ut supplicia impiorum æterna sint. Quod quisquis negat, convincendus in ipso demum inferno rerum documentis tristissimis, qui Scripturæ testimoniis, & Divinis comminationibus confignatissimis convinci non potuit. Quomodocunque verò suppliciorum ista æternitas explicetur, manebit semper proportio delictum inter & pœnam, qualem ipse Deus constituit. Quam si homo obduritiem cordis sui, vel ingenii tarditatem & imbecillitatem ignorat, at non ignorat Deus; cujus & scientia infinita est, & omnia judicia justa sunt.
units.tr: CXVIII. Yet there is nothing here but logical reasonings and a height raised up against the knowledge of God [λογικὰς ratiocinationes, ὕψωμα ὑπεροχὴν ... γνῶσιν Θεοῦ], 2 Cor. 10:5, of the kind the Socinians peddle as the principle of their religion, and of the kind carnal men take pleasure in to harden themselves. Is it really thought pious and right to mock and explode the will of God, so clearly revealed, and to answer back to God antimanteuesthai [ἀντιμανηεύεσθαι]? As if it were not God's but man's place to fix the proportion between sins and the punishments owed to them, and as if it were a whole matter to drag the actions and words of God before the alien tribunal of a raving human reason. Their chief objection, that hell is at odds with the justice of God, since it would forbid that the sins of the wicked, being finite, be punished with eternal punishments, is put forward and more fully refuted. We, however, sufficiently defend God and his justice by showing his will, which is always free of injustice, and we wrap ourselves safely in that will against these serpentine snares. We remember too that the judgments of God are a great abyss, Ps. 36:7, and unsearchable [ἀνεξερεύνητα], inscrutable, Rom. 11:33. The outcome itself will teach impious men that they have kicked against the goad in vain with their reasonings. And since there is no proportion between God and a sinning man, it is pointless to seek a proportion between the one who punishes and the one who sins, or to harass with greater force that proportion which lies between the punishment and the sin. For in that proportion, whatever it is, which God has established between punishment and sin, and has established wisely, one must chiefly consider that infinite distance between God and man, according to which he has also taken account of the various forms and degrees of sins, and in the punishments themselves has set unequal degrees to match the diversity of sins. Then too, they themselves elsewhere tear apart that deficiency of the finite in relation to the infinite, which they make the basis of this dispute, when they attribute infinite knowledge and power to the finite Christ. What proportion of sin and punishment will God keep, if, as they maintain, the wicked who die before the last judgment are not punished but cease to exist, while only the survivors, all together, are destroyed and extinguished at once by the same punishment of fire? Moreover, we call the punishment of sinners eternal rather than infinite, following the Scriptures, because the word eternity is less than infinity, the lesser the greater [μαλον μᾶλλον]. All the subtleties that blind reason weaves are woven from the concept of infinity rather than of eternity. Yet they will hardly dare to say that there is no proportion between sin and eternal punishment, since even among men the justice of punishments does not consist in proportion of duration, so that a punishment is not to last longer than the offence did. It is admitted that sins are not infinite in themselves [ex se ipsis], since their actions are altogether transitory. Yet they are infinite metonymically [metonymicè], on account of the infinite object [objectum] against which they run, the Majesty of God. Nor are all sins therefore equal in themselves, but they strike equally against the infinite Majesty of God, and so equally incur an infinite guilt. For the matter itself speaks: sins must be valued by the dignity of the one offended. The kind of punishment arises from the dignity of the person, but from the rank of the sinner and of the benefits he has received it arises by the same measure. Moreover, nothing prevents single sins, some sins, and all sins from being called infinite, by a denomination taken from the object. For in themselves they can be finite in number, duration and time, while in another sense they are all infinite. But, they say, how will justice be satisfied to God, since, if the punishment of one sin is to be extended into eternity, another sin cannot be punished with the same infinity, and so of necessity this second one will have an intensive infinity? These arguments are foolish enough. For if a man, having deserved death by one capital crime, adds ten or more crimes of the same or another kind, the first will anticipate the punishment of death, yet the rest will be equally deadly, although, according to the condition of the things, they can increase the punishment or the degrees of punishment in intensity. Nor is the reasoning about infinite punishment different: all and each sin indeed deserves it, but still the degrees of inequality will vary in the different intensity and gravity of death. Nor, because individual sins offend the infinite God, do individual sins therefore require a punishment infinite in intensity and extent. For to repair the offence a punishment suffices which, as to duration, goes on into eternity, and as to intensity receives degrees to be defined and measured by God. Nor is it an obstacle that sin deserves an infinite punishment, because, as to intensity, that punishment cannot be physically infinite, since, as the act is finite, so too the suffering is always finite; yet it can be morally infinite, that is, indefinite, and of such a kind that it cannot be defined or limited by any man, in which degrees and varied inequality can be established. Therefore those who prattle about a twofold infinity, intensive and extensive, do not deserve further examination. For the passion and obedience of Christ was of an altogether different nature: on account of the dignity of the person who suffered, it could be, and was, infinite in intensity; but it could be neither infinite in extent nor ought it to have been, since otherwise he could not have overcome death, acquired the inheritance promised to him, and given eternal life to those given to him. Christ came, as Augustine rightly says on Psalm 95, and gave a price, he poured out his blood, and he bought the world. You ask what he bought? See what he gave, and see what he bought. The blood of Christ is the price. What is it worth so much? What but the whole world? What but all nations? It is also possible to turn the adversaries' argument back on themselves. Grant that every sin requires only a temporal and finite punishment; if then he bears it for one sin, how will the justice of God be satisfied for the second, third, tenth, hundredth, thousandth? For no punishment remains beyond the temporal, and once that has been undergone for one sin, what punishment will all the others undergo? Where then is the reason of the justice of God? And although sins, insofar as they are the actions of creatures, do have a proportion among themselves, and are judged by God himself, whose judgment is according to truth, Rom. 2:2, and so are finite in that respect, yet in relation to the God who has been offended they cannot be called infinite and do not deserve eternal punishment, because the respects are entirely different, so that they can be judged to have a proportion in the former sense and not in the latter. Finally, it is not simply true that as the offender stands to the offence, so the injured party stands to the punishment. For the position of the injured God and of the sinning offender is most dissimilar, and therefore so is that of God to the punishment of the sinner. Although there is an interval between the offender and the fault, it does not follow that there must be one between the offender and the injured party; and even if there were, it would not for that reason be on a par with what lies between the man and his action. The punishment is considered either as inflicted by God or as received by man. God, in punishing, observes a proportion or interval between the sin of man and his punishment, but he does not take a proportion or interval for himself from the action of man. The interval between a man and his sin is often very slight, yet the interval between God and the punishment he inflicts, which the sinner receives from him, is not slight. But to vindicate the justice of God, it is enough to set against the murmuring [γογσυρμὸν] grumbling of blind reason this one point: that God himself has established such a proportion between the offence and the punishment that the punishments of the wicked are eternal. Whoever denies this must be convinced by the most miserable evidence of hell itself, since he could not be convinced by the testimonies of Scripture and the most firmly sealed divine threats. However this eternity of punishments is explained, there will always remain the proportion between the offence and the punishment that God himself has established. If man is ignorant of this, through the hardness of his heart, or the slowness and weakness of his wit, God is not ignorant; his knowledge is infinite, and all his judgments are just.

units.la: CXIX. De Loco inferni curiosa quàm utilior disputatio est.
units.tr: CXIX. On the place of hell: how much more useful a curious disputation about it is.

units.la: De rebus nec necessariis, nec revelatis disceptare, si non periculosum, saltem inane est. Probamus sobrietatem Augustini, de Civ. D. Lib. XX. 16. scribentis: Ille ignis, in qua mundi vel rerum parte fit, hominem scire arbitror neminem, nisi forte, cui Spiritus Divinus ostendit; Nec non Chrysostomi Homil. 31. in Ep. ad Rom. suadentis: Μὴ ζητῶμεν πῦ εἴην, ἀλλὰ πῶς ἐκφύγωμεν. Non quaeramus ubi fit, sed quomodo illam effugiamus. Sathanas jam dicitur princeps potestatis aëris, & operari in filiis contumaciæ, Ephef. II. 2. An verò pœnarum locus post ultimum judicium ei immutandus fit, Scriptura non revelavit. Impii autem damnati cum Diabolis manebunt. Certum interim est, infernum alicubi esse. Cùm enim damnati nec nullibi, nec ubique futuri sint, alicubi erunt. Et si alicuibi erunt, etiam infernus, in quo erunt, alicubi erit. Ideo etiam τὸπος βασανισμοῦ locus tormenti, Luc. XVI. 28. appellatur. Sicut enim beati locum peculiarem habent: ita etiam damnati habebunt. Sed locus in hoc mundo aspectabilis non est; quia ἀιδὴς ἀιδὴς invisibilis præsenti mundo vocatur. Neque plane, ubi fit, revelatum est. An revelatæ tibi sunt portæ mortis, an portas umbræ lethalis vidisti? Job. XXXVIII. 17. Audaciter igitur satis Pontificii, in terræ eum esse centro definiunt. Licet enim Coreh, Dathan, & Abiram viventes absorpti à terra in infernum descendisse, Num. XVI. 33. dicantur: non tamen sic locus damnatorum definitur. In eo enim miraculum conspicuum fuit, quòd terra os suum aperiens vivos eos absorpsit, & sic absorpti in infernum descenderunt. In centrum certè terræ descendisse non dicuntur; nec quò iverint absorpti à terra, constat. Cœlo quoque infernus cùm opponitur, tanquam supremo infimum, Esaj. XIV. 13. Matth. XI. 23. non tam locus inferni, quàm status damnatorum innui videtur. Neque etiam καταχθόνιοι subterranei illi, Phil. II. 10. Christo exaltato genua flectentes impii soli, sed etiam pii, omnésque adeò mortui, secundum corpora infra terram, & secundum spiritus in Cœlo, vel inferno existentes, intelliguntur. Neque minùs audaciter alii eum in aëre, vel in mari, vel in terra collocant. Idem certè locus diversis voluptatis & doloris locus esse potest, sicut in eodem lecto alius morbo cruciatur, alius suaviter dormit. Status enim sunt, ibid.XIII.14. Ratione Status appellatur vita simpliciter, quia nil nisi vita est, procul omni metu mortis: יהוה אל חי עולמים vita aeterna, Dan.XII.2. & passim alibi, propter rationem supra expositam: Regnum Dei, coelorum, coeleste, Patris, Christi, &c. passim, propter singularem regiminis in altera vita rationem, cum ineffabili gloria debellatis omnibus hostibus Regni, altissima cum pace regnantium: Hereditas, quia aeterna dispositione & testamento quibusdam maximorum bonorum haeredibus in Christo destinata est; eaque ἀφθαρτος incorruptibilis, quia nec peccato corrumpitur, nec finem, quo corrumpatur, nec corruptores habebit, utpote non caduca vel fluxa, sed constans & aeterna: ἀμίαντος incontaminata, quia nulli erunt, qui eam contaminent, uti olim fuerunt, qui haereditatem terrae Canaan polluerent; nec pravo affectu cujusquam attaminabitur, sicut terrestria attaminantur: ἀμάραντος immarcessibilis, quia non aeque ac terrae Canaan haereditas hiemem patietur, enervabitur & languescet, sed constante ubertate & amoenitate possessores suos oblectabit, 1.Pet.I.4. Gaudium piorum, Joh. XVI.22 Domini, Matth.XXV.23. Satietas gaudiorum, Psal.XVI.11. in Spiritu S. Rom.XIV.17. quia ibi vera & incorrupta laetitia spiritualis, coelestis & aeterna, sine ulla doloris & perturbationis vicissitudine vigebit; Pax, Rom. XIV.17. Luc.I.79. Requies, 2.Thess.I.7. Sabbathum ex Sabbatho, Esaj.LXVI.23. Heb.IV.9. καταπαυσις requies, ibid.v.11. Salus, Beatitudo, passim: Corona justitiae, 2.Tim.IV.8. Vita, Jac.I.12. gloriae, Psal.VIII.6. 1.Pet.V.4. Gloria filiorum Dei, Rom. V.2. VIII.21. coelestis, 2.Tim.II.10. aeterna, 1. Pet. V.10. Adoptio in filios, quoad omnem ejus efficaciam, adeoque consummata, Rom. VIII.23.
units.tr: To dispute about things that are neither necessary nor revealed is, if not dangerous, at least empty. We commend the sobriety of Augustine, who writes in de Civ. D. Lib. XX. 16.: That fire, in what part of the world or of things it is, I think no man knows, unless perhaps the one to whom the Divine Spirit shows it. We also commend Chrysostom, who urges in Homil. 31. in Ep. ad Rom.: Let us not seek where it is, but how we may escape it. [Μὴ ζητῶμεν πῦ εἴην, ἀλλὰ πῶς ἐκφύγωμεν.] Satan is already called the prince of the power of the air, and the one who works in the sons of disobedience, Eph. 2.2. Whether the place of punishment is to be changed for him after the last judgment, Scripture has not revealed. The wicked who are damned, however, will remain with the devils. It is certain, meanwhile, that hell exists somewhere. For since the damned will be neither nowhere nor everywhere, they will be somewhere. And if they will be somewhere, the hell in which they are will also be somewhere. Hence it is also called τόπος βασανισμοῦ, the place of torment, Luke 16.28 [τόπος βασανισμοῦ]. For just as the blessed have a particular place, so also the damned will have one. But the place is not visible in this world, since it is called ἀιδής, invisible [ἀιδής] in relation to the present world. Nor has it been plainly revealed where it is: Have the gates of death been revealed to you? Or have you seen the gates of the shadow of death? Job 38.17. The Papists therefore rashly define that it is at the centre of the earth. For although Korah, Dathan and Abiram are said to have gone down into hell alive, having been swallowed up by the earth, Num. 16.33, the place of the damned is not defined in that way. For in that event the visible miracle was that the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them alive, and so, having been swallowed, they went down into hell. They are certainly not said to have gone down to the centre of the earth, nor is it established where those swallowed up by the earth went. Likewise, when hell is set over against heaven as the lowest over against the highest, Isa. 14.13, Matt. 11.23, it seems to signify not so much the place of hell as the state of the damned. Nor are those καταχθόνιοι, subterranean beings [καταχθόνιοι], Phil. 2.10, who bend the knee to the exalted Christ, only the wicked; the pious too are understood, and indeed all the dead, who according to their bodies are below the earth, and according to their spirits exist in heaven or in hell. Others no less rashly place hell in the air, or in the sea, or in the earth. Certainly the same place can be a place of both pleasure and pain for different people, just as in the same bed one man is racked by sickness while another sleeps sweetly. For these are states, Rev. 13.14. By reason of the state, life in general is called simply life, since it is nothing but life, far from all fear of death: Jehovah, the living God of ages [יהוה אל חי עולמים], eternal life, Dan. 12.2, and in many other places, for the reason set out above. The kingdom of God, of heaven, heavenly, of the Father, of Christ, and so on, passim, on account of the singular manner of ruling in the other life, with ineffable glory, all enemies of the kingdom having been subdued, and the reigning ones reigning in the highest peace. Inheritance, because by an eternal disposition and testament it is destined in Christ for certain heirs of the greatest goods; and it is ἄφθαρτος, incorruptible [ἄφθαρτος], because it is not corrupted by sin, nor will it have an end by which it may be corrupted, nor any corrupters, being not perishable or fleeting but constant and eternal; ἀμίαντος, undefiled [ἀμίαντος], because there will be none to defile it, as there once were those who polluted the inheritance of the land of Canaan; nor will it be tainted by the evil affection of anyone, as earthly things are tainted; ἀμάραντος, unfading [ἀμάραντος], because it will not, as the inheritance of the land of Canaan did, suffer winter, be weakened and languish, but with constant fertility and pleasantness it will delight its possessors, 1 Pet. 1.4. The joy of the pious, John 16.22; the joy of the Lord, Matt. 25.23; the fullness of joys, Ps. 16.11; in the Holy Spirit, Rom. 14.17, because there true and incorruptible spiritual joy, heavenly and eternal, will flourish without any alternation of pain and disturbance. Peace, Rom. 14.17, Luke 1.79. Rest, 2 Thess. 1.7. Sabbath from Sabbath, Isa. 66.23, Heb. 4.9. Rest [καταπαυσις], ibid. v. 11. Salvation, blessedness, passim. The crown of righteousness, 2 Tim. 4.8. Life, Jas. 1.12. Of glory, Ps. 8.6, 1 Pet. 5.4. The glory of the sons of God, Rom. 5.2, 8.21. Heavenly, 2 Tim. 2.10. Eternal, 1 Pet. 5.10. Adoption as sons, as to its whole efficacy, and thus consummated, Rom. 8.23.

units.la: Dari igitur vitam aeternam, ipsa haec nomina abundè probant; & tota Scriptura ejus rei testis est, merito ut Symbolum fidei confessione vitae aeternae claudamus, & velut obsignemus. Nam etiam in Paradiso symbolo arboris vitae ea confirmata est, Gen.II.17. & benedictio Abrahamo promissa fuit spiritualis in τοις επουρανιοις in supercoelestibus, ibid.XII.2.3. XVIII.18. XXII.18. Ephes.I.3. & Jacobus Patriarcha expectavit ישועה salutare Domini, Gen.XLIX.18. & Deus se Deum Abrahami, Isaaci & Jacobi confessus, Exod.III.6. promisit vitam post mortem, Matth.XXII.32. & Lex, quam Christus pro nobis implevit, habet promissionem vitae, factam illi, qui Legem impleverit, vel pro quo alius impleverit, Levit. XVIII.5. Luc. X.25. 28. cujus proin verba sunt λογιαζωντα verba viva, Actor.VII.38. Omitto de eadem vita aeterna & salute fidelium testimonia Davidis, Prophetarum, Christi & Apostolorum, quibus Scriptura adeo scatet, ut vix ullum caput sit, in quo non explicita, vel implicita, ejus mentio fiat. Nam & foedus operum,& foedusGratiae in quavis oeconomia promissionem aeternae vitae continuisse in loco amplissimè probavimus. Accedunt exempla Enochi, candidati illius aeternitatis, nec non obsidis & testis aeternae vitae, Gen.V.24. Heb.XI.5. Eliae, 2.Reg.II.11. units.tr: That eternal life is given is proved abundantly by these very names, and all of Scripture bears witness to the thing. It is fitting that we close the confession of faith with the confession of eternal life and, as it were, seal it. Even in Paradise the promise of it was confirmed by the symbol of the tree of life, Gen. 2:17. The blessing promised to Abraham was spiritual, in the heavenly places [τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις], Gen. 12:2-3; 18:18; 22:18; Eph. 1:3. The patriarch Jacob waited for the salvation [yeshu'ah, ישועה] of the Lord, Gen. 49:18. God, confessing himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Exod. 3:6, promised life after death, Matt. 22:32. The Law, which Christ fulfilled for us, holds a promise of life made to the one who fulfils the Law, or for whom another fulfils it, Lev. 18:5; Luke 10:25, 28. Its words are therefore "living oracles" [λόγια ζῶντα], Acts 7:38. I pass over the testimonies of David, the prophets, Christ and the apostles to the same eternal life and salvation of believers, with which Scripture so abounds that there is hardly a chapter in which some explicit or implicit mention of it is not made. Indeed, we have shown at length elsewhere that both the covenant of works and the covenant of grace, in every economy, contained the promise of eternal life. To these come the examples of Enoch, the candidate of that eternity and the pledge and witness of eternal life, Gen. 5:24; Heb. 11:5; of Elijah, 2 Kings 2:11; of Christ raised from the dead into life, and of the saints raised together with him,

units.la: ctorum, Matth.XXVII.52. Pauli, tertium in coelum rapti, 2.Cor.XII.4. & post coelestis vitae promulsidem perceptam magna spiritus contentione pronuntiantis: Existimo, quòd passiones non sunt dignae futura gloria, Rom.VIII.18. Omnium piorum, qui in hac vita ex doloribus inferni Dei beneficio eluctantur, Psal. XXX.4. XLIX.16. LXXXVI.13. & vitae aeternae quendam in cordibus suis sentiunt. Gustate, & videte quàm bonus est Dominus, Psal.XXXIV.9. Vix quisquam enim pius est, quin aliquando strictuFam vitae aeternae haud leviter ferientem, in articulo inprimis suae sentiat. Eandem aeternae vitae certitudinem alia etiam confirmant, velut Dei Bonitas, qui, ceu fons omnis boni, & Bonum summum atque infinitum, non potest noa se creaturis imagine sua praeditis communicare, & in eos se totum effundere: Desiderium beatitudinis omnibus innatum, quod alio quàm Deo authore ingenerari non potuit, & quod Deus frustrari non potest, quoties ab homine, eodem auxiliante, recta consequendae ejus viainitur, quia frustra quaeri non potest: Justitiae Divinae ratio, utpote quae id requirit, ut obedientibus, vel conjunctis cum Christo, qui eorum vice Legi perfectè obedivit, praemia reddantur, & quidem perfecta in altera vita, utpote quae in hac vita nonnisi affecta redduntur, & cum multiplice tribulatione conjuncta sunt. Promissionum Divinarum veracitas, quia Deus, qui vitam aeternam promisit, ἀψευδὴς mentiri nescius est, Tit.I.2. Et hac est promissio illa, quam promisit nobis, vita aeterna, 1.Joh.II.25. quam, ceu ἀληθινὸς καὶ πιστὸς verax & fidelis, destituere nullo modo vult, & ceu potens servare depositum usque ad diem illum, 2.Tim.I.12. implere poterit. Meriti Christi dignitas & efficacia, quia cùm infiniti ponderis, valoris & pretii sit, infinita etiam bona commeruit, & Christus morte sua sibi aeternum populum, peculium & haereditatem comparavit, denique Rex, Sponsus, Salvator aeternus, populo, sponsa, salvatis aeternùm carere non potest: Animae hominis immortalitas, quia si animae piorum post hanc vitam exsistunt, malè iis esse non potest, adeòque bene erit, cùm medium non detur: Piorum in hac vita conditio plurimis malis exercita, ut miserrimi omnium sint, si tantùm in hac vita in Christum spea erunt, 1.Cor.XV.19. Conscientiae vis, magna in utramque partem, ut qui Deum amant, eique obediunt, spe maxima futurae felicitatis, adversissimis etiam rebus, animum sustentent; cujus rei etiam umbram Gentiles, confictis campis Elysiis, sectati sunt: Beneficia spiritualia hujus vitae, justificatio, regeneratio, primitiae Spiritus S. ejusque in cordibus nostris habitatio & testimonium, quòd sumus filii Dei, adeòque etiam haeredes & cohaeredes Christi, ut, si unà patimur, etiam unà glorificemur, Rom.VIII.17. Fidei Christianae finis, qui σωτηρία ψυχῶν salus animarum, 1.Pet.I.9. sive ibi finis exitum, sive perfectionem, sive mercedem gratuitam, quae etiam אחרית finis, quia in fine operis datur, insignitur; significat: Piorum resurrectio, cujus alius finis esse, quàm eorum aeterna felicitas & gloria non poterit; cùm aliàs in morte eos relinqui praestaret: denique consensus etiam plurium Philosophorum gentilium, qui naturae lumilumine paratam bonis vitæ melioris felicitatem prospexerunt. Nam Pythagorei, antiquissimæ sectæ Philosophi, Clemente Alexandrino Strom. lib. IV. laudante, iis, qui philosophabantur, spem in fine denuntiabant. Et melioris vitæ fiducia elatus Socrates, morti jam proximus, tanquam ad Deos illius beneficio profecturus, se mortem haud moleste ferre, sed se bona spe duci professus est, sperans multò melius fore bonis, quàm malis, uti apud Platonem in Phædo legere est. Plutarchus quoque de Consol. ad Apoll. Apollonii mœrorem ex filii morte conceptum mitigavit eo argumento, quòd Diviniorem quandam vitam adeptus sit. Quo etiam argumento uxorem suam filiolæ morte mœstam erexit, Consol. ad uxor. Neque adversati Stoici animas sapientum & bonorum vita hac defunctorum meliorem, si non sempiternam, at diuturnam tamen naturos putarunt. Non uno enim loco spem cœlestis beatitudinis Seneca testatur. Quomodo etiam Aquilejenses duces apud Herodianum lib. VIII. 6: 6. Gordianos vita functos in cœlum ad Deum migrasse, dixit. Quos similesque alios, si spes sua fefellit, at opinio vitæ melioris bonos manentes non fefellit. Tametsi etiam opinio illa & notitia Gentilium imperfecta & obscura satis fuit, quia modum ad vitam æternam pervenien-di ignorarunt. Unde Plato in Phædone. clarè aliquid cognoscere de vita futura vel impossibile, vel difficile admodum dixit.
units.tr: Matt. 27:52; of Paul, caught up into the third heaven, 2 Cor. 12:4, who, after he had received a foretaste of the heavenly life, declared with great earnestness of spirit: "I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to come," Rom. 8:18. There is also the testimony of all the godly who, in this life, by God's kindness struggle out of the pains of hell, Ps. 30:4; 49:16; 86:13, and who feel in their hearts something of eternal life: "Taste and see that the Lord is good," Ps. 34:9. For hardly any believer exists who does not at some time, especially at the point of death, feel the sharp stroke of the thought of eternal life. Other considerations also confirm this same certainty of eternal life: the goodness of God, who, as the fountain of all good and the supreme and infinite Good, cannot refrain from communicating himself to creatures endowed with his own image and pouring himself out wholly upon them; the desire for blessedness, implanted in all, which could not have been instilled by any author other than God, and which God cannot frustrate whenever a man, with God's help, sets out on the right way to attain it, since it cannot be sought in vain; the reason of divine justice, since justice requires that rewards be given to the obedient, or to those united with Christ, who perfectly obeyed the Law in their place, and indeed perfect rewards in the other life, since in this life rewards are given only in part and are joined with manifold tribulation; the truthfulness of the divine promises, since God, who promised eternal life, is "not able to lie" [ἀψευδής], Titus 1:2, and this is the promise which he has promised us, "eternal life," 1 John 2:25, which, as he is "true and faithful" [ἀληθινὸς καὶ πιστός], 2 Tim. 1:12, he by no means wishes to fail, and as he is able to keep what has been entrusted to him until that day, he will be able to fulfil it; the worth and efficacy of Christ's merit, since, being of infinite weight, value and price, it has merited infinite goods, and since Christ by his death has acquired for himself an eternal people, a special possession and an inheritance, and finally since he is the eternal King, Bridegroom and Saviour, he cannot be without an eternal people, bride and saved ones; the immortality of the human soul, since if the souls of the godly exist after this life, it cannot go ill with them, and so it will go well, there being no middle state; the condition of the godly in this life, exercised by so many evils that they are most miserable of all, if they have hope in Christ only in this life, 1 Cor. 15:19; the power of conscience, great in either direction, since those who love God and obey him sustain their spirits, even in the most adverse circumstances, by the greatest hope of future happiness, a shadow of which the Gentiles also pursued in their invented Elysian Fields; the spiritual benefits of this life, justification, regeneration, the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit and his indwelling in our hearts and his testimony that we are sons of God, and therefore also heirs and co-heirs of Christ, so that if we suffer with him we shall also be glorified with him, Rom. 8:17; the end of the Christian faith, which is "the salvation of souls" [σωτηρία ψυχῶν], 1 Pet. 1:9, whether that end signifies outcome, perfection or the free reward, which is also marked by the Hebrew word for end, [אחרית], because it is given at the end of the work; the resurrection of the godly, whose end cannot be anything other than their eternal happiness and glory, since otherwise it would be better to leave them in death; and finally the agreement of many gentile philosophers, who, by the light of nature, foresaw a happiness for the good in a better life. For the Pythagoreans, philosophers of a very ancient sect, as Clement of Alexandria praises them in Stromata book IV, announced hope for those who philosophised at the end. And Socrates, elated by the confidence of a better life, now close to death, professed that he did not bear death grievously, but that he was led by good hope, as if about to depart to the gods for his benefit, hoping that it would go much better for the good than for the bad, as one may read in Plato's Phaedo. Plutarch too, in On Consolation to Apollonius, eased Apollonius's grief conceived at his son's death by this argument, that the son had attained a more divine life. By the same argument he raised up his own wife, saddened by the death of their little daughter, in Consolation to His Wife. Nor did the Stoics, who opposed this, think that the souls of wise and good men who had departed this life would have a better, if not everlasting, yet at least lasting, nature. For Seneca bears witness to the hope of heavenly blessedness in more than one place. Likewise the Aquileian generals, in Herodian book VIII, said that the Gordians, having departed this life, had migrated to heaven, to God. Such hopes, and others like them, if they failed, yet the opinion of a better life did not fail the good who remained. Although that opinion and knowledge of the Gentiles was indeed imperfect and obscure, because they did not know the way of attaining eternal life. Hence Plato said, in the Phaedo, that to know anything clearly about the future life was either impossible or very difficult.

units.la: CXXII. Non desunt tamen, nec defuerunt olim Sadducæi, Epicuræi, alii, qui hanc piorum omnium vitæ melioris futuræ fiduciam & spei anchoram unicam convellerent. Quotquot enim animæ immortalitatem & resurrectionem hominum unquam negarunt, iidem sicut infernum, ita etiam vitam æternam sustulerunt. Quomodo etiam Plinius Hist. Nat. lib. II. 7. quæstionem de vita æterna cæcæ mortalitatis argumentum dixit. Et Aristoteles Beatitudinem vitæ præsentis cancellis omnem includit, & boni quicquam cuiquam post mortem superesse negavit. Verba ejus extant Ethic. Nicom. lib. III. 6. Maximum terribilium est mors. Extremum enim est; nihilque mortuo superesse videtur, neque bonum, neque malum. Eandem disputationem Ethic. Nicom. lib. I. 10. verbosè agitat. Inter Christianos ipsos Michael Ballius Amorhæus, Zonara in Michaele teste, circa A. DCCCXX. doctrinam de bonis æternis exfibilavit. Ipse quoque Johannes XXIII. Papa, Concilio Basileensi Sess. 11. memorante, vitam æternam non esse dogmatizavit, adeóque Papaliter asseruit. Ex Philosophorum veterum lacunis hausta etiam illa quorundam Scholasticorum sententia est, quòd Beatitudo quædam naturalis sit, quam ut & media eam acquirendi naturæ connaturaliter, uti loquuntur, debeantur, cùm supernaturalis liberè negari possit. Sed post peccatum beatitudo naturalis homini connaturaliter debita gehenna & interminabile exitium est. Ejusmodi igitur beatitudinem naturalem impossibilem esse, neque ad eam naturam puram ordinari posse, Jansenius August. de statu pura Nat. lib. II. 5. 6. 7. ex Augustino, qui ad beatitudinem tria, nempe non falli, non mori, non offendi, cum statu purae naturæ requirit, fusè demonstrat. Placuit verò ita Scholasticis impiè nugari, ne ipsis cœlum Philosophorum, Aristotelis inprimis, uti scitè Verulamius appellat, periret. Mitto Socini hæresin, negantis, quòd vita æterna in V. T. homini promissa sit, quam in loco refutavimus.
units.tr: CXXII. Yet there are, and there have long been, Sadducees, Epicureans and others who would undermine this confidence of all the godly in a better life to come and this sole anchor of hope. For whoever has ever denied the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the dead has likewise done away with hell and with eternal life. So Pliny, Hist. Nat. lib. II. 7., called the question of eternal life an argument of blind mortality. Aristotle also confines blessedness to the bounds of the present life and denied that anything good remains for anyone after death. His words are in the Nicomachean Ethics, book III, ch. 6: Death is the most terrible of terrible things. For it is the end, and nothing seems to remain for the dead, neither good nor evil. He discusses the same question at length in the Nicomachean Ethics, book I, ch. 10. Among Christians themselves, Michael Ballius of Amorium, according to Zonaras' witness on Michael, around the year 820, hissed down the doctrine of the eternal goods. Pope John XXIII too, as the Council of Basel records in its eleventh session, asserted that eternal life is not a dogma, and in this he spoke like a Pope. That opinion of certain Scholastics also, that there is a certain natural blessedness, which is due by nature, as they put it, to human nature and to the means of acquiring it, while the supernatural may be freely denied, is drawn from the dregs of the old philosophers. But after sin, the natural blessedness that is due to man by nature is hell and endless ruin. That such natural blessedness is therefore impossible, and cannot be ordained for pure nature, Jansenius demonstrates at length from Augustine, August. de statu pura Nat. lib. II. 5, 6, 7., who requires three things for blessedness in the state of pure nature: not to be deceived, not to die, not to be offended. But the Scholastics have pleased themselves in talking such impious nonsense, lest the heaven of the philosophers, especially that of Aristotle, as Verulam aptly calls it, should perish. I pass over the heresy of the Socinians, who deny that eternal life was promised to man in the Old Testament; we have refuted this in its place.

units.la: CXXIII. Vitam æternam Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. operatur, & solus immediata virtute omnibus beatis confert & donat. Is, qui nos paravit ad hoc (ut non exuamus, sed superinduamus gloriam) Deus est, 2. Cor. V. 5. Vitam æternam dedit nobis Deus. Et hæc vita in Filio ejus est, 1. Joh. V. 11. Dedit eam testamento hæredibus omnibus; quoad oblationem & propositionem vocatis omnibus. Et dedit in Filio, quia solus is, & non alius salutis æternæ causa est, Heb. V. 9. Ne time parve grex, quia placuit Patri vestro vobis dare Regnum, Luc. XII. 32. Datio enim Regni & vitæ æternæ ab beneplacito Patris, ab æterno ponentis nos ad acquisitionem salutis per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, 1. Thess. V. 9. est. Sicut verò Pater causa vitæ hujus est æterno testamento & propositio: ita Filius ejusdem causa est voluntate sponsionis & meriti. Nam Filius, quos vult, vivificat, Joh. V. 21. Habet enim voluntatem herilem & magistralem, verbum imperans, & vocationem, quoad vitam spiritualem & æternam adducit quoscunque vult, tanquam munerum Divinorum, quæ ipse morte sua promeruit, dominus & diributor liberrimus. In ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux hominum, Joh. I. 4. Unde & arbor vitæ, Gen. II. 9. Apoc. II. 7. Quia enim voluntatem Patris fecit, ideo jus accepit potestulandi hæreditatem, Psal. II. 8. Semen, Esaj. LIII. 10. Corpus & membra, in quibus viveret, Eph. V. 23.30. Ego vitam æternam do iis, Joh. X. 28. quæ in hac vita inchoatur, in Cœlo consummatur. Dicit Jesus: Ego sum resurrectio & vita, Joh. XI. 25. Parum enim est resuscitari à Christo, nisi & sic ab eodem vivificemur, ut non amplius moriamur, sed æternùm bene vivamus. Ego sum via, veritas & vita, Joh. XIV. 6. quia & vitam in se habet, ibid. V. 26. & vivit propter Patrem, utpote Filius Dei Patris, cujus vita est, habere filium, ibid. VI. 57. Et habet potentiam vitæ indissolubilis, Heb. VII. 16. & princeps vitæ, Actor. III 15. est. Denique & Spiritus S. causa æternæ vitæ est, quia est Spiritus vitæ, Rom. VIII. 2. quem qui non habet, non est Christi, ib. v. 9. adeóque à Christo vivificari non potest. Nam si Spiritus ejus, qui suscitavit Jesum à mortuis, habitat in vobis, is qui excitavit Christum ex mortuis, vivificabit etiam mortalia corpora vestra per Spiritum suum in vobis habitantem, ibid. v. 11. Nam ut Spiritus vitæ eriget templum suum, ut totus homo Deo vivat, & ipse in templo suo in æternum habitet. Est enim Spiritus vivificans, 1. Cor. XV. 45. Vitam ergo æternam Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. conferunt atque donant, & sic donant, ut immediata virtute sua vivamus.
units.tr: CXXIII. God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit work eternal life, and God alone bestows and gives it to all the blessed by his immediate power. He who has prepared us for this (so that we may not be stripped, but clothed upon with glory) is God, 2 Cor. 5:5. God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son, 1 John 5:11. He has given it to all the heirs by testament, since all are called to the offer and proposal of it. And he has given it in the Son, because he alone, and no other, is the cause of eternal salvation, Heb. 5:9. Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom, Luke 12:32. For the giving of the kingdom and of eternal life depends on the Father's good pleasure, which from eternity appointed us to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Thess. 5:9. Just as the Father is the cause of this life by the eternal testament and its proposal, so the Son is its cause by the will of his undertaking and by his merit. For the Son quickens whom he will, John 5:21. He has a lordly and authoritative will, commanding by his word, and he leads to spiritual and eternal life whomever he wishes, as the most free lord and distributor of the divine gifts which he has merited by his death. In him was life, and the life was the light of men, John 1:4. Hence also the tree of life, Gen. 2:9; Rev. 2:7. For because he did the will of the Father, he therefore received the right to possess the inheritance, Ps. 2:8; the seed, Isa. 53:10; the body and the members in which he lives, Eph. 5:23, 30. I give eternal life to them, John 10:28, a life which begins in this life and is brought to completion in heaven. Jesus said: I am the resurrection and the life, John 11:25. For it would be little to be raised by Christ unless we were also quickened by him in such a way that we no longer die, but live well forever. I am the way, the truth and the life, John 14:6, because he has life in himself, ibid. 5:26, and lives because of the Father, as the Son of God the Father, whose life it is to have a Son, ibid. 6:57. He has the power of an indissoluble life, Heb. 7:16, and is the prince of life, Acts 3:15. Finally, the Holy Spirit is also the cause of eternal life, because he is the Spirit of life, Rom. 8:2; whoever does not have him is not of Christ, ibid. v. 9, and so cannot be quickened by Christ. For if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also quicken your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you, ibid. v. 11. For as the Spirit of life raises up his temple, so that the whole man may live to God, and he himself may dwell in his temple forever. For he is the life-giving Spirit, 1 Cor. 15:45. Therefore God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit confer and give eternal life, and give it in such a way that we live by their immediate power.

units.la: Elenchus eorum, qui vitam æternam negant.
units.tr: Refutation of those who deny eternal life.

units.la: Vitam æternam donat communiter Deus Trinus; singulariter Filius. Non enim iterum vita illa vel corporalis alimentis sustentabitur, vel spiritualis, per ea adminicula, quibus in hac vita utitur, qualia verbum, ejus praeconium, Sacramenta, aliaque ejusmodi sunt, suffulcietur, vel aliunde distrahetur, sed Deus erit omnia in omnibus, 1.Cor. XV.28. tum quia nihil in Sanctis erit, quod non sit immediatè à Deo, sicut nunc in Sanctis est, tum peccatum, miseria & mors, quae plane non sunt à Deo: tum cognitio Dei, fides, quae à Deo est, sed mediante natura, verbo & utriusque ministerio multiplice: tum quia illi, qui Dei sunt, ad τελειωσιν & consummationem suam adducentur, ut Deus non sit tantum aliquid in ipsis, sicut nunc est in iis, qui per Evangelium quodammodo consummantur, sed ut in iis sic πάντα omnia sit, ut abolito omni eo, quod ἐκ μέρους ex parte est, illis plenitudinem sui largiatur, & iis perfectissimè se in Deum faciat, quod est videre Deum uti est, τὸ εὖ Φ-conspicere, satiari, cognoscere quemadmodum cogniti sumus. Praeclarè sic Augustinus de Civ. D. lib XXII. 30. Apostoli verba illa explicat. Quanta erit illa felicitas, ubi nullum erit malum, nullum latebit bonum, vacabitur Dei laudibus, qui erit omnia in omnibus, &c. Praemium virtutis erit ipse, qui dedit virtutem, eique se ipsum, quo nihil melius & majus posset esse, promisit. Quid est enim aliud, quod per Prophetam dicit: Ero illorum Deus; & illi erunt mihi populus, nisi Ego ero, unde satientur; ego ero, unde satientur. ego ero, quaecunque ab iis honestè desiderentur, & vita, & salus, & victus, & copia, & gloria, & honor, & pax, & omnia bona. Sic enim & illud rectè intelligitur, quod ait Apostolus; ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus. Alibi: Omnia, inquit, ipse nobis erit, quando ipso sufficiente nihil deerit. Aliter verò etiam in hac vita sub N.T. τὰ πάντα καὶ ἐν πᾶσι omnia & in omnibus Christus esse, Coloss.III.11. dicitur, quatenus in iis est, qui novus homo sunt, & in novo homine, quà novo, omnia est, quia omnium novorum causa est, omnisque novitas in ejus cognitione, fide, amore, & imitatione obedientiae ejus consistit; & omnia in omnibus, qui ipsius sunt, est, non obstante defectu & profectu multiplice.
units.tr: God the Trinity gives eternal life in common, and the Son in particular. For that life will not again be sustained by bodily food, nor by spiritual food through those aids which we use in this life, such as the word, its preaching, the sacraments and other such things, nor will it be propped up or drawn away from elsewhere. Rather God will be all in all, 1 Cor. 15:28; first, because nothing will be in the saints that is not immediately from God, as now is the case in the saints; second, because sin, misery and death, which are plainly not from God, will be gone; third, because the knowledge of God and faith, which are from God, but which now come through nature, the word and the manifold ministry of both, will cease. Third, because those who belong to God will be brought to their [τελείωσιν] completion and consummation, so that God will not merely be something in them, as he now is in those who are in some measure perfected through the Gospel, but will be [πάντα] all things in them, so that, with everything that is [ἐκ μέρους] in part abolished, he will bestow his fullness upon them and will make them most perfectly like God, which means to see God as he is, to gaze upon him, to be satisfied, to know him as we have been known. Augustine explains those words of the Apostle admirably in de Civ. D., lib. XXII, 30.: How great will that happiness be, where there will be no evil, no good will be hidden, the praises of God will be unceasing, who will be all in all, etc. The reward of virtue will be he himself who gave virtue, and he promised himself to them, than whom nothing better or greater could be. For what else is it that he says through the prophet: I will be their God, and they will be my people, except: I will be that from which they are satisfied; I will be that from which they are satisfied; I will be whatever they may honestly desire, both life and health, and sustenance and abundance, and glory and honour and peace and all good things. For this is rightly understood also in what the Apostle says: that God may be all in all. Elsewhere he says: All things, he says, he himself will be to us, when, with him sufficient, nothing will be lacking. But in another way, even in this life under the New Testament, Christ is said to be [τὰ πάντα καὶ ἐν πᾶσι] all things and in all, Col. 3:11, insofar as he is in those who are the new man, and in the new man, as new, he is all things, because he is the cause of all the new, and all newness consists in the knowledge, faith, love and imitation of obedience to him; and he is all in all who belong to him, notwithstanding a manifold defect and progress.

units.la: CXXIV. Arrogantissima igitur Philosophorum Stoicorum sententia est; Beatitudinis consecutionem humanis viribus acceptam ferentium. Ex quorum mente Cicero Parad. 2. Nemo non potest beatissimus esse, qui est totus aptus ex se, quique in se uno sua ponit omnia. Neque aliter Seneca Epist. 31. Unum, inquiens, bonum est, quod beatae vitae causa & firmamentum est, sibi fidere. Qui etiam Numinis ipsius opem diserte excludit, addens: Turpe est etiamnum Deos fatigare. Quid votis opus est? Fac te ipsum felicem. Et rursus: Hoc est summum Bonum, quod si occupas, incipis Deorum esse socius, non supplex. Quomodo, inquis, isto pervenitur? Tutum iter est, jucundum est, ad quod natura te instruxit. Dedit tibi illa, quae si non deseruEris, par Deo surges. Et Epist. 41. impie: Stultum est, bonam mentem à Deo optare, cum possis à te impetrare? Non sunt ad Coelum elevandae manus. Quae & Aristotelis mens fuit, Deum à commercio & bonitate hominis summoventis penitus. A quibus Scholastici beatitudinem suam naturalem, naturae & arbitrii viribus parabilem, haud ferunt, de quo supra. Ita illi hominem liberum & independentem, fortunaeque suae fabrum unicum facientes, sacrilegum simul faciunt, & Deum boni omnis fontem, imò Oceanum, abnegant. Quantò rectius Plutarchus de Stoic. Contrad. ex fundamentis à Stoico etiam dogmate desumptis, sic argumentatur: Deus si non virtutem hominibus largiatur, sed eam sibi tribuunt mortales, opes vero corporisque valetudinem citra virtutem largiatur, ne ille hominibus nihil quicquam prodest. Et sui penitus oblitus Seneca ipse Epist. 41. Bonus vir sine Deo nemo est. An potest aliquis nisi ab illo adjutus exurgere? Ille dat consilia magnifica & erecta. In unoquoque virorum bonorum quis Deus incertus est, habitat tamen Deus.
units.tr: Therefore the Stoic philosophers' opinion is most arrogant, since they ascribe the attainment of blessedness to human powers. In their view Cicero says: Parad. 2. Everyone can be most blessed who is wholly fit in himself and who places all his good in himself alone. Seneca likewise says, Epist. 31. "There is one good, which is the cause and foundation of a happy life: to trust in oneself." He also plainly excludes the help of the Deity itself, adding: "It is shameful to still weary the gods. What need is there for prayers? Make yourself happy." And again: "This is the highest good; if you lay hold of it, you begin to be a companion of the gods, not a suppliant. How, you ask, is it reached? The road is safe and pleasant, the one to which nature has equipped you. She gave you those things which, if you do not desert them, will make you rise up equal to God." And in Epist. 41 he says impiously: "Is it foolish to ask God for a good mind, when you can obtain it from yourself? Hands must not be raised to heaven." This was also the mind of Aristotle, who wholly removes God from intercourse with man and from his goodness. From these men the Scholastics do not shrink, as I said above, in holding that their natural blessedness can be obtained by the powers of nature and of the will. So by making man free and independent, the sole maker of his own fortune, they are at the same time guilty of sacrilege, and they deny God, the fountain, indeed the ocean, of all good. How much more rightly Plutarch, in De Stoicorum repugnantiis, argues from principles drawn from the Stoic doctrine itself: "If God does not grant virtue to men, but mortals attribute it to themselves, while he grants wealth and bodily health apart from virtue, then he is of no use to men at all." And Seneca himself, quite forgetful of himself, says in Epist. 41: "No one is a good man without God. Can anyone rise up unless he is helped by him? He gives noble and lofty counsels. In every good man there is a god, uncertain who he is, yet God dwells in him."

units.la: CXXV. Vitae aeternae participes erunt electi omnes resuscitati, & ad vitam iemel admissi; idque secundum animam & corpus omnésque illius potentias, hujus partes & membra. Nam vita aeterna & Regnum coeleste dabitur iis, οἷς ἡτοίμασται ὑπὸ τοῦ πατρός, quibus à Patre praeparatum est à jacto mundi fundamento, Matth. XXV. 34. Ephes. I. 3.4. Participes verò illi erunt secundum animam & corpus. Secundum animam, quia reportabunt finem seu mercedem fidei, σωτηρίαν ψυχῶν salutem animarum, 1.Pet.I.9. Non enim sumus filii subductionis ad exitium, sed fidei ad acquisitionem (lucrifactionem, conservationem, ut sit pro spolio, Jerem. XLV. 5.) animae, Hebr. X. 39. Secundum corpus, quia Christus μετασχηματίσει transfigurabit corpus humiliationis nostrae, ut fiat conforme corpori suo glorioso, Phil. III. 21. Seminatur enim corpus ignominiosum, excitatur gloriosum: seminatur infirmum, excitatur potens, &c. 1.Cor. XV.43. 44. Novimus, si terrestris hujus domus nostrae tabernaculum dissolutum fuerit, nos habituros aedificium ex Deo, domicilium non manufactum, aeternum in Coelis, 2.Cor. V.1. Coronabitur enim & anima & corpus, quia utrumque certavit. Ὁ ἀθλῶν νομίμως ἀφανήσει Qui legitimè certaverit, coronabitur, 2.Tim. II. 5. Denique secundum animae potentias & corporis partes atque membra. Precatur enim S. Paulus: Integer vester spiritus (judicium animi, quo is verum à falsò discernit) & anima (voluntas, qua bonum appetit, malum fugit) & corpus (unà cum organis ejus) irreprehensibiliter in adventu Domini nostri Jesu Christi servetur, 1.Thess.V.23. Sistite membra vestra arma justitiae ad sanctificationem, & quantò magis etiam ad glorificationem Dei, Rom. VI.19. Nam etiam ἐν τῷ ςῷ-μαῖ in corpore & membris ejus, quae aequè Dei sunt, atque spiritus est, Deus glorificari debet, 1.Cor. VI.20.
units.tr: Those elect who are raised up and admitted once for all to life will all share in eternal life, and this according to soul and body and all their powers, parts and members. For eternal life and the heavenly kingdom will be given to those "for whom it has been prepared by the Father" [ὑπὸ τοῦ πατρός: οἷς ἡτοίμασται], that is, "from the foundation of the world", Matt. 25:34; Eph. 1:3–4. They will share in it according to the soul and the body. According to the soul, because they will receive the end or reward of faith, "the salvation of souls" [σωτηρίαν ψυχῶν], 1 Pet. 1:9. "For we are not of those who shrink back to destruction, but of faith to the gaining of the soul" (that is, to its acquisition and preservation, so that it is as booty, cf. Jer. 45:5), Heb. 10:39. According to the body, because Christ "will transform [μετασχηματίσει] the body of our humiliation, that it may be conformed to his glorious body", Phil. 3:21. "For the body is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power," etc., 1 Cor. 15:43–44. "We know that if the tabernacle of this earthly house of ours is dissolved, we shall have a building from God, a dwelling not made with hands, eternal in the heavens", 2 Cor. 5:1. For both soul and body will be crowned, because both have striven. "He who strives lawfully [Ὁ ἀθλῶν νομίμως] will be crowned," 2 Tim. 2:5. Finally, according to the powers of the soul and the parts and members of the body. For St Paul prays: "May your whole spirit (the judgement of the mind by which it distinguishes true from false) and soul (the will, by which it seeks good and flees evil) and body (together with its organs) be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ," 1 Thess. 5:23. "Present your members as weapons of righteousness for sanctification," and how much more for the glorification of God, Rom. 6:19. For God must be glorified also in the body and its members [ἐν τῷ σῷ-μαῖ], which are as much God's as the spirit is, 1 Cor. 6:20.

units.la: CXXVI. Totus sic homo, anima & corpore constans, in aeterna vita beatitudine & felicitate summa fruetur. Licèt enim ea, quae paravit Deus electis in coelo fruenda, talia sint, ut multò minùs oculus mortalis ullus ea viderit, vel auris audiverit, vel in cor hominis ullius ascenderint, quàm olim fidelium ante Christum oculi bona eximia sub Evangelio revelanda viderunt, aures audiverunt, vel in corda eorum ascenderunt, Esaj. LXIV. 4. 1.Cor. II. 9. tamen, ut cum Augustino de Civ. D. lib. XXII.2. loquamur, Spei nostrae gandium non est tacendum & de
units.tr: In this way the whole man, consisting of soul and body, will enjoy the highest blessedness and happiness in eternal life. For although the things God has prepared for the elect to enjoy in heaven are such that no mortal eye has seen them much less, nor ear heard them, nor have they entered into the heart of any man, nevertheless the good things of the gospel, which the eyes of the faithful before Christ did not see, the ears did not hear, nor did they enter into their hearts (cf. Isa. 64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9), yet, to speak with Augustine in De civitate Dei book XXII, "the joy of our hope must not be left unspoken" and

units.la: Neque ejus consecutio à viribus natura pendet. & de intimis ardentis sancti amoris medullis dictum est: Domine, dilexi decorem domus tuae. Si non cominus, at eminus saltem, velut in speculo & aenigmate ex Dei verbo felicitatem aeternae vitae intueri licet. Nam summam illam fore appellationes supra collectas, inprimis voces Beatitudinis, Pacis & Vitae aeternae, quae procul dubio malum omne excludunt, & bonum omne, quale in hominem beatum cadere potest, includunt: tum opposita felicitati illi poenarum infernalium aeternitas, atrocitas supra a nobis delineata: quia sicut color candidus nigro oppositus pulchrior: ita Sanctorum requies damnationi malorum opposita gloriosior evadit: tum comparatio bonorum hujus vitae, quae a bonis coelestibus tantum, quantum Coelum a terra, distant: tum gaudii gustus & promulsis illa coelestis vitae, quam pii in hac quandoque vita percipiunt: tum parabolicae descriptiones in Scripturis occurrentes variae, velut quando cum nuptiis, convivio, pascuis uberrimis, Regno, aliisque ejusmodi comparantur passim: tum denique bonorum species, quas ex Dei verbo enumeravimus, evincunt. Multa paucis S. Augustinus de Civit. D. lib. XX. 30. dixit: Quanta, inquiens, erit illa felicitas, ubi nullum erit malum, nullum latebit bonum; vacabitur Dei laudibus, qui erit omnia in omnibus. Vera ibi gloria erit, ubi laudatus nec errore quisquam, nec adulatione laudabitur. Verus honor, qui nulli negabitur digno, nulli deferetur indigno, sed nec eum ambiet ullus indignus, ubi nullus permittetur esse nisi dignus. Vera pax ibi est, ubi nihil est adversi, nec a se ipso, nec ab alio quicquam patietur. Premium virtutis erit ipse, qui virtutem dedit, eique se ipsum, quo melius & majus nihil possit esse, promisit. Quid est enim aliud, quod per Prophetam dixit: Ero illorum Deus, & illi erunt mihi plebs, nisi: Ego ero unde satientur, &c. Ipse finis erit desideriorum, qui sine fine videbitur, sine fastidio amabitur, sine defatigatione laudabitur.
units.tr: nor is its attainment dependent on the powers of nature. "Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house," has been said from the innermost marrow of holy and burning love. If not face to face, at least from afar, as in a mirror and in a riddle, it is possible to behold the happiness of eternal life from God's word. For the chief things will be the names gathered above, above all the words Blessedness, Peace and Eternal life, which without doubt exclude every evil and include every good that can fall to a blessed man. Then there is the eternity of the infernal punishments, opposed to that happiness, whose atrocity we have described above: for as white is more beautiful when set against black, so the rest of the saints becomes more glorious when set against the damnation of the wicked. Then there is the comparison of the goods of this life, which are as far from the heavenly goods as heaven is from earth. Then there is the foretaste and first-fruits of that heavenly life, which the godly sometimes perceive in this life. Then there are the various parabolic descriptions occurring in the Scriptures, as when it is everywhere compared to marriage, a feast, rich pastures, a kingdom and other such things. Finally, the kinds of good things which we have listed from God's word make this plain. St Augustine, in De civitate Dei book XX chapter 30, said much in few words: "How great, he says, will that happiness be, where there will be no evil and no good will be hidden; there will be leisure for praising God, who will be all in all. There true glory will be, where no one will be praised either through error or through flattery. True honour, which will be denied to no one who is worthy and given to no one who is unworthy, nor will any unworthy person seek it, where none will be allowed to be present except the worthy. There true peace is, where there is nothing adverse, and no one will suffer anything from himself or from another. The reward of virtue will be he who gave virtue, and he promised himself to them, than whom nothing better or greater can exist." For what else did he say through the prophet: "I will be their God, and they will be my people", except: "I will be that by which they are satisfied," etc. He will be the end of desires, who will be seen without end, loved without weariness, and praised without fatigue.

units.la: CXXVII. Sicut Inferni mala in privatione bonorum, & positione malorum: ita Vitae aeternae bona in carentia malorum, & positione bonorum consistunt.
units.tr: CXXVII. As the evils of hell consist in the privation of goods and the presence of evils, so the goods of eternal life consist in the absence of evils and the presence of goods.

units.la: Prima enim pars felicitatis est carere malis. Et facilius est dicere in vita aeterna, quid ibi non sit, quam quid ibi sit. Quicquid igitur mali nomen & omen habet, illud omne a vita aeterna aberit longissime. Cumque malum vel culpae vel poenae sit; malum culpae, malorum omnium scaturigo, & calamitas fundi, peccatum aberit. Nam hominis corpus mortuum est di' amartian propter peccatum deponendum, Rom. VIII. 10. quod semel depositum non revivisci. Exuitur enim corpus peccatorum carnis in circumcisione Christi, Col. II. 11. de quo plura supra. Non intrabit in civitatem illam pan koinon omne, quod ceu impurum, polluit, Apoc. XXI. 27. Aberunt peccati causae & fomes, puta tum carnis corruptio & concupiscentia, quia caro talis & sanguis non ingredientur Regnum Coelorum, & corruptio incorruptibilitatem non hereditabit, 1. Cor. XV. 50. tum Diaboli insidiae, quia Deus pacis eum conteret sub pedibus nostris, Rom. XVI. 20. & Diabolus, qui seducebat, mittetur in stagnum ignis & sulphuris, Apoc. XX. 10. quin & Sancti ipsi Angelos malos judicabunt, 1. Cor. VI. 3. tum Mundus, & quae in mundo est concupiscentia car-
units.tr: The first part of happiness is to be free from evils, and it is easier to say what is not in eternal life than what is there. Therefore whatever bears the name and mark of evil will be far absent from eternal life. Since evil is either of guilt or of punishment, the evil of guilt, the fountain of all evils and the source of calamity, will be absent: sin. For the body of man is dead because of sin, Rom. 8.10, to be laid aside, and having once been laid aside it does not come back to life. For the body of the sins of the flesh is put off in the circumcision of Christ, Col. 2.11, of which more above. Nothing that defiles, and makes unclean [κοινὸν], will enter that city, Rev. 21.27. The causes and tinder of sin will be absent: both the corruption of the flesh and concupiscence, because flesh and blood will not enter the kingdom of heaven, and corruption will not inherit incorruption, 1 Cor. 15.50; and the snares of the devil, because the God of peace will crush him under our feet, Rom. 16.20, and the Devil who seduced them will be cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, Rev. 20.10. Indeed the saints themselves will judge the evil angels, 1 Cor. 6.3. Then the world, and the lust of the flesh,

units.la: nis, oculorum & superbia vitae, 1. Joh. II. 16. quia mundus una cum ēmthumia concupiscentia & illecebris ejus transit, ibid. v. 17. Victores horum omnium, imo & triumphatores erunt, qui in Coelo erunt. Praeclare enim Fulgentius Epist. IV. 8. Tunc, inquit, erit in nobis vera, perfecta & excelsa humilitas, cum & in carne & in mente nostra nulla remanserit prava cupiditas, nec cogitationibus fatigabitur spiritus, nec laboribus macerabitur corpus; nulla erit solicitudo certaminis; sed perfecta erit securitas pacis; nulla erit justitiae indigentia, sed cum delectatione saturitas plena. Et tantum abest, ut in coelo peccata vel peccatores sint, ut qui in eo sunt, ne quidem peccare possint. Sunt enim isangeloi similes Angelis, Luc XX. 36. Atqui Angelos bonos in sanctitate confirmatos & impeccabiles esse, supra ostendimus. Sed & peccatorum poenae omnes tum metaphoricae, tum proprie dictae, calamitates, dolores, morbi, lachrymae, infamia, paupertas, fames, sitis, errores, tentationes, angustiae spiritus, mors ipsa quaevis a sancto domicilio illo aeternum exulabunt. Convertere anima mea in requiem tuam, quia benefecit tibi Dominus, quia eripuit animam meam a morte, oculos meos a lachrymis, pedes meos a lapsu, Psal. CXVI. 7. 8. Auferet Deus omnem lachrymam ab omni facie, & opprobrium populi sui auferet, Esaj. XXV. 8. Fugiet dolor & gemitus, ibid. XXXV. 10. Non esurient, nec sitient, & non percutient eos aestus aut Sol, ibid. XLIX. 10. Absorbebit mortem in sempiternum, ibid. XXV. 8. Ero pestilentia tua, o mors, Hos. XIII. 14. Novissimus hostis destruetur, mors, 1. Cor. XV. 26. Absorpta est mors in victoriam. Ubi tuus, mors, stimulus? Ubi tua, inferne, victoria? ibid. 54. 55. Infernus & mors missi sunt in stagnum ignis, Apoc. XX. 14. Neque etiam ob causam piorum felicitas aeterna vitae nomine venit, quam quia mortalitas, mors, & causae mortis omnes aberunt. Quantum ergo illud erit, quod juxta Senecae etiam ad Polyb. c. 20. illud, non ira beatos torquebit, non morbus affliget, non suspicio lacesset, non edax & inimica semper alienis processibus invidia consectabitur; non metus solicitabit, non levitas fortunae cito munera sua transferentis inquietabit. Et quanta felicitas futura sit, carere peccato & concupiscentia, reputare potest, quem hac in vita oyk pondus, & amarti peccatum facile circumstans, Hebr. XII. 1. ita premit, ut cum Apostolo ut cere necesse habeat. Misfer ego homo, quis me liberabit ex corpore istius mortis? Rom. cap. VII. vers. 24.
units.tr: the lust of the eyes and the pride of life, 1 John 2.16, because the world passes away together with its lust and allurements, ibid. v. 17. Those who are in heaven will be conquerors, indeed triumphers, over all of these. For Fulgentius excellently says, Epist. 4.8: Then there will be in us true, perfect and lofty humility, when no wicked desire remains either in our flesh or in our mind, when the spirit will not be wearied by thoughts, nor the body worn down by labours; there will be no anxiety about the contest, but a perfect security of peace; there will be no lack of righteousness, but a full satisfaction with delight. And so far is it from being the case that sins or sinners are in heaven, that those who are there cannot even sin. For they are equal to the angels, Luke 20.36. Yet we have shown above that the good angels have been confirmed in holiness and are impeccable. Moreover all the punishments of sinners, both metaphorical and properly so called, calamities, pains, diseases, tears, infamy, poverty, hunger, thirst, errors, temptations, anguish of spirit, and death itself in any form, will be banished for ever from that holy dwelling. Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you; for he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from falling, Ps. 116.7–8. God will wipe away every tear from every face, and will take away the reproach of his people, Isa. 25.8. Sorrow and sighing will flee away, ibid. 35.10. They will not hunger nor thirst, and neither heat nor sun will strike them, ibid. 49.10. He will swallow up death for ever, ibid. 25.8. O death, I will be your plague, Hos. 13.14. The last enemy, death, will be destroyed, 1 Cor. 15.26. Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your sting? O grave, where is your victory? ibid. 54–55. Death and hell were cast into the lake of fire, Rev. 20.14. Nor is the eternal happiness of the pious called by the name of life for any other reason than that mortality, death, and all the causes of death will be absent. How great, then, must that be which, according to Seneca also, To Polybius, c. 20, anger will not torment the blessed, disease will not afflict them, suspicion will not vex them, envy, greedy and always hostile to the success of others, will not pursue them; fear will not disturb them, nor the fickleness of fortune, quickly transferring its gifts, will unsettle them. And how great the happiness of being free from sin and concupiscence will be, one can judge from the person whom, in this life, the sin which easily entangles [ἡ εὐπερίστατος ἁμαρτία], Heb. 12.1, so presses down that with the Apostle he must groan: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? Rom. 7.24.

units.la: CXXVIII. Verum cum peccato carere, & dolore non affici istarum etiam rerum sit, quae sensu destituuntur; quanquam id magnum satis sit iis, qui sentiendi & intelligendi facultate pollent; alia praeterea esse debent, non tantum non mala, sed & Bona, imo Optima, quae summam istam felicitatem conficiant. Licet enim, quod apud Ciceronem de Fin. lib. II. Ennius dixit, nimium boni est, cui nihil est mali, attamen, uti ibidem Cicero ait, non, si malum dolor est, carere eo malo satis est ad bene vivendum.
