Quamobrem & Bona vitae aeternae Jxa positiva prosequenda sunt. Vel in aeterna igitur vita Beatitudo vera, Summum Bonum, ejusque fruitio obtinet. Sed quodnam Summum Bonum, quae ejus fruitio sit, videndum. Nam Constans tum carentia malorum omnium; Nam illud vel Deus, vel creatura est. Medium nihil intervenit. Atqui nulla creatura Summum hominis Bonum est. Cùm enim Summum Bonum propter se amandum & expetendum sit, nulla creatura propter se amari & expeti potest, quia aliàs creatura principium primum & finis ultimus alterius creaturæ esse posset. Atqui ex solo Deo, per ipsum, & εἰς αὐτὸν in ipsum omnia sunt, Rom. XI. 36. Ex ipso sunt omnia, & nos in ipsum, 1. Cor. VIII. 6. Et amor, quo supra, vel ultra Deum aliquis propter se ipsum amatur, meretricius & idololatricus est, & talis etiam, qualis Adamo causa lapsus extitit, cui universum genus humanum implicitum est. Tum Deus omnes creaturas, exceptis Angelis, dominio hominis subjecit, & hominem medium se inter & creaturas illas collocavit. Amoris autem hæc natura est, ut amantem rebus amatis subjiciat, quia quod amatur, animo velut dominatur, & amantem perturbat. Si igitur ulla creatura, ceu Summum Bonum hominis, amaretur & expeteretur, jam homo ordinem & gradum suum perderet, & qui creaturis inferioribus dominari debuit, iisdem se subjiceret. Atque ita, qui creaturam, ut bonum suum amat, atque ea, ceu bono suo fruitur, is libertatem suam perdit, saltem duobus Dominis servit, & se ipsum creaturis inferioribus, ipsique mundo συγκαταθ configurat, animum velut glutine quodam, rebus terrenis alligat & illaqueat, quò minùs humeros excutere, & casto sanctóque amore ad Deum eniti possit: carendi difficultatem, & quotidianos cruciatus excitat, inquietudinem propter crebras vicissitudines & mutationes auget; hominem polluit, & pristina dignitate sua exuit; denique omnem rectum creaturarum usum tollit, in eo consistentem, ut sic mundo utamur, ut parati simus eo, si necesse sit, non uti, sed ei valedicere. Ne amate mundum, & quæ in eo sunt. Siquis amat mundum, in eo Patris amor non est, 1. Joh. II. 15. Maledictus vir, qui fidit homini, & facit carnem brachium suum, Jer. XVII. 5. Qui habent, sint, sicut qui non habent; Præterit enim schema hujus mundi, 1. Cor. VII. 29. 31. Qualis fiducia hominis est, talis ejus status, solidus vel caducus & arundineus est. Præterea qui in creaturis suis bonum suum quærit, & iis exsatiari expetit, is Christo meliora promittenti credere non potest; quia Christus paupertatem, crucem, humilitatem, abnegationem sui pro magnis bonis commendans mundo ridiculus videtur. Quin & fiducia in creaturis, ceu bono propter se amando, omne obsequium Christo debitum tollit. Quis enim jubenti ei animam pro fratribus ponere, 1. Johann. III. 16. obediet, qui persuasum non habuerit, quòd qui animam perdit, eam inventurus, qui servaverit, perditurus sit? Quis porrò hac fide imbuetur, qui vitam præsentem aliquid esse statuerit, & pro bono suo reputaverit? Denique nunquam lætitia spiritualis ad maturitatem perveniet, quandiu animus præsentibus affixus & devinctus manet. Quæ autem hominis pii & Christiani mica in eo esse potest, in quo nec fiducia in Deum, nec æternorum & solidorum bonorum desiderium, nec fides, nec spes, nec obsequium, nec lætitia stabilis & solida reperitur?
units.tr: CXXVIII. But since to be free from sin and not to be affected by pain belongs also to things that lack sensation, though that is enough for those who are endowed with the faculty of feeling and understanding, there must be other things besides, not merely not evils but goods, indeed the best goods, which make up that supreme happiness. For although, as Ennius said in Cicero's On Ends, book 2, he has too much of good who has no evil, nevertheless, as Cicero says in the same place, if pain is an evil, it is not enough for living well to be free from that evil. Therefore the goods of eternal life must also be pursued as positive goods. Therefore in eternal life true blessedness, the Supreme Good, and the enjoyment of it are obtained. But what the Supreme Good is, and what its enjoyment is, must be considered. For there are only two possibilities: either God or a creature. There is no middle ground. Now no creature is the Supreme Good of man. For since the Supreme Good is to be loved and desired for its own sake, no creature can be loved and desired for its own sake, since otherwise a creature could be the first principle and last end of another creature. But from God alone, through him, and unto him [εἰς αὐτὸν] are all things, Rom. 11.36; from him are all things, and we are for him, 1 Cor. 8.6. And the love by which someone loves anyone above or beyond God for his own sake is harlot-like and idolatrous, and of the same kind as that which was the cause of Adam's fall, in which the whole human race is involved. Moreover God subjected all creatures, except the angels, to the dominion of man, and placed man as mediator between himself and those creatures. Now it is the nature of love to subject the lover to the things loved, because what is loved in a sense rules the mind and disturbs the lover. If therefore any creature were loved and desired as man's Supreme Good, man would already have lost his order and rank, and he who ought to have ruled over the lower creatures would submit himself to them. And so the one who loves a creature as his good, and enjoys it as his good, loses his freedom, at least serves two masters, and conforms himself to the lower creatures and to the world itself, binding and ensnaring the mind with a kind of glue to earthly things, so that it cannot shake off its shoulders and strive upward toward God with chaste and holy love. It stirs up the difficulty of being deprived and daily torments, increases restlessness on account of the frequent changes and vicissitudes; it defiles man and strips him of his former dignity; finally, it removes all right use of creatures, which consists in using the world in such a way that we are ready, if necessary, not to use it but to bid it farewell. Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, 1 John 2.15. Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, Jer. 17.5. Let those who have be as though they had not; for the form of this world is passing away, 1 Cor. 7.29, 31. The condition of a man is such as his trust is, solid or fragile like a reed. Furthermore, one who seeks his own good in his creatures and wishes to be satisfied by them cannot believe Christ, who promises better things; for Christ, commending poverty, the cross, humility and self-denial for great goods, seems ridiculous to the world. Indeed trust in creatures, as a good to be loved for its own sake, takes away all the obedience owed to Christ. For who will obey him when he commands him to lay down his life for the brothers, 1 John 3.16, if he has not been persuaded that whoever loses his life will find it, and whoever saves it will lose it? Who, moreover, will be imbued with this faith, if he has judged the present life to be something and has counted it as his good? Finally, spiritual joy will never come to maturity as long as the mind remains fixed and bound to present things. And what crumb of a pious and Christian man can there be in the one in whom neither trust in God, nor desire for eternal and solid goods, nor faith, nor hope, nor obedience, nor stable and solid joy is found?

units.la: CXXIX. Veritatem hanc præprimis Salomon, mortalium Regum sapientissimus & opulentissimus post multiplicia vanitatis rerum omnium experimenta, scripto eam in rem de industria Ecclesiastæ libro, confirmavit. Ibi enim in universum hanc thesin fixit, quòd in rebus creatis, quæ fluxæ sunt, & pereunt, si vel maximè ex iis omnibus unum quasi corpus & systema colligatur, atque id etiam geminetur, & iterum iterumque collapsum instauretur, nihil solidi, quo quis beatior vel melior reddi possit, insit. Hoc sibi volunt verba, quæ totius scripti nobile compendium fecit: Vanitas vanitatum, dixit Ecclesiastes, vanitas vanitatum, & omnia vanitas, Eccles. I. 1. Atque id absoluta demonstratione sua repetit, & velut concludit, ibid. XII. 8. Qua in thesi μυκη-ερισμὸς quidam est. Non enim sine mordaci sale & derisione hæc dixit. Perinde ac dubitabundus & hæsitans quærit: Vanitas vanitatum? atque ita vel sedens & meditabundus diu, recte probè probéque expensa, & ad omnes calculos revocata, in hæc tandem verba categorica & rotunda erumpit: Imò verò, vanitas vanitatum, & omnia vanitas. Ubi הבל vanitas id notat, quod nullam stabilitatem & essentiam habet, qua quis tanquam bono suo uti frui possit, cui opponi videtur תושיה res, essentia talis, qua quis beatior & melior redditur. Licet enim nihil eorum, quæ à Deo creata sunt, natura sua vanum vel malum sit, tamen vana omnia sunt, quando extra Deum sic appetuntur, ut in iis desiderium hominis, velut summo bono acquiescat; & vana consilia, studia & actiones hominum sunt, quibus ipsi suæ beatitudinis extra Deum fabri esse contendunt. Thesin hanc Solomon ponderosissimis argumentis confirmat: cujusmodi sunt, quòd hominis יתרון εὐθυμία emolumentum ex omni labore suo sub Sole nullum sit; atque id ostendit tum rerum aspectabilium in statu suo zquabilis & immutabilis tenor, qui cura & labore humano non mutatur: cap. I. 2-7. tum rerum omnium ingens difficultas & imperfectio ad satiandum appetitum hominis, vel consolandum eum spe futurę gloriæ, ibid. 8-11. tum species humanorum operum, quæ nil nisi רעות רוח depasio spiritus sint, v. 12-f. & capp. II. III. quod ipsa εὐθυμία, seu lætitia bonæ conscientiæ, quam bonum hominis esse, cap. III. 12. 22. concluserat, variè in hac vita labefactetur, puta vel per aliorum violentiam, injustitiam, & defectum consolationis, cap. IV. 1-4. vel per proprium affectum, invidiam, avaritiam, ibid. v. 4-16. quòd bonorum operum patrationi multiplex periculum peccati subsit, cujus evitandi solicitudo lætitiam minuat, efficiátque, ne pro bono hominis haberi possit: quòd datis circa cultum Dei externum frequentandum, preces, vota, tentationem dubitationis circa Providentiam Dei præceptus ostendit, ibid. v. 16-f. & cap. V. 1-8. quòd ipsa seculi hujus bona, quæ vulgus appetit, dignitas & exis-timatio, pecunia, copia, proventus, otium & satietas, thesauri, πλούτος, πλυνμεσία, vana sint, ibid. v. 8-f. & cap. VI. 1-7. quòd finis proximus omnis laboris, etiam cùm is acquiritur & obtinetur, ob naturæ humanæ infirmitatem durabilis non fit, ibid. v. 7. 8. quòd anima, seu concupiscentia sua longius vagetur, nec solidam delectationem afferat, & molestiam atque anxietatem plurimam creet, adeóque mera vanitas & depaßtio spiritus sit, quod argumentorum prægnantium inductione reliquo libro demonstrat.
units.tr: CXXIX. Solomon, the wisest and wealthiest of mortal kings, confirmed this truth above all others after many experiences of the vanity of all things, and he did so deliberately in writing, in the book of Ecclesiastes. There he laid down this thesis in general: among created things, which are fleeting and perish, nothing solid is to be found by which anyone could be made happier or better, even if all of them were gathered into one body and system, even if that system were doubled, and even if it collapsed and was restored again and again. The words that make up the noble summary of the whole work express this: Vanity of vanities, said the Preacher, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, Eccles. 1. 1. He repeats this in his complete demonstration and, as it were, concludes with it, ibid. 12. 8. In this thesis there is a certain sneering [μυκτηρισμός]. For he did not say these things without biting irony and mockery. He asks, as if doubtful and hesitant, Vanity of vanities? and then, sitting and meditating for a long time, having weighed everything carefully and properly and submitted it to every test, he finally breaks out in these flat and categorical words: Indeed, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. Here the Hebrew הבל [hebel] (vanity) means that which has no stability or substance by which a person can use or enjoy it as his good, and it seems to be opposed to תושיה [tushiyyah], a thing, a substance by which someone is made happier and better. For although none of the things created by God is vain or evil in its own nature, all of them are nevertheless vain when they are sought apart from God in such a way that human desire rests in them as the highest good. Vain too are the counsels, pursuits and actions of men by which they strive to be the makers of their own happiness apart from God. Solomon confirms this thesis with very weighty arguments. Such are these: that a person's יתרון [yitron], that is, his gain (εὐθυμία [euthymia], cheerfulness), from all his labour under the sun is nothing. He shows this both from the constant and unchanging course of visible things in their own state, which is not altered by human care and toil (ch. 1. 2–7), and from the immense difficulty and imperfection of all things in satisfying the human appetite or comforting it with hope of future glory (ibid. 8–11). He shows it also from the kinds of human works, which are nothing but רעות רוח [re'ut ruach], a pasturing of the spirit (v. 12 ff.; chs. 2–3). Further, the cheerfulness itself, that is, the joy of a good conscience, which he had concluded to be the good of man (ch. 3. 12, 22), is variously weakened in this life, whether by the violence and injustice of others and the lack of comfort (ch. 4. 1–4), or by one's own feelings, envy and avarice (ibid. 4–16). There is a manifold danger of sin in performing good works, and the anxiety to avoid it diminishes joy and so prevents it from being counted as the good of man. He shows that the temptation of doubting God's providence arises when we are commanded to attend to the external worship of God with prayers and vows (ibid. 16 ff.; ch. 5. 1–8). The goods of this age that the crowd desires, namely dignity and reputation, money, plenty, produce, leisure and satiety, treasures, πλούτος [ploutos] and πολυμεσία [polymesia] (abundance), are all vain (ibid. 8 ff.; ch. 6. 1–7). The nearest end of all labour, even when it is acquired and obtained, is not lasting because of the weakness of human nature (ibid. 7, 8). The soul, or its desire, wanders farther and does not bring solid delight but creates much trouble and anxiety; it is therefore pure vanity and a pasturing of the spirit. He demonstrates this by the weighty arguments that he brings forward through the rest of the book.

units.la: CXXX. Bona universa extra Deum vel animæ vel corporis, vel fortunæ sunt. In nullis horum veræ & solidæ bonitatis & beatitudinis ratio consistit. Inter animæ bona Sapientia humana principem locum obtinet. In illa tamen vera felicitas non consistit, tum quia maximis laboribus quæritur & augetur, Eccles. I. 13. 17. &c. tum quia nunquam finem & perfectionem suam assequitur; tum quia homini ad salutem æternam nihil prodest, cùm Deus non per talem sapientiam, sed per stultitiam prædicationis credentes salvare velit, 1. Cor. I. 21. Inter bona corporis ευεξια ejus, valetudo, robur, pulchritudo, agilitas, longevitas censentur, quæ cuncta cùm per se homi nibus & brutis communia sint, imò quædam brutis magis quàm hominibus conveniant; quin & pro conditione vitæ hujus variis casibus exposita sint, & tandem morte ipsa amittantur, denique nisi ad animam relata, & verbi Dei imperio subjecta, eximium nihil habeant, verorum honorum pretio destituuntur. Inter Bona Fortunæ potissimum voluptates, divitiæ, decus, potentia, gratia & gloria apud homines referuntur. Atqui omnibus his mali & corrupti operam impensam, præbonis, navant, neque unquam propositum finem consequuntur. Voluptates corporis brutis magis, quam homini ad imaginem Dei condito conveniunt, & extremum earum dolor, saltem satietas est, quia vana ejusmodi non possumus ferre diu; & juxta Tertulliani illud, nocet oblectabile longum. Adeò ut Bonum Scyllæum, quippe ex humana & belluina natura compactum rectè Augustinus appellaverit: Non enim voluptates hominis appetitum explere queunt, ut ne ipsi quidem Reges iis circumfluentes beati censeri possint, Eccles. cap. VI. v. 7. 8. &c. Quærimus enim fluvium vanitatis & rerum præterecuntium, ut semper nova cupiditate caro nostra titilletur, quæ mors, & velut verminatio quædam in cadaveribus est. Divitiarum haud dispar ratio est, utpote quæ plerunque cum labore & molestia acquiruntur, nonnisi summa cum cura & anxietate custodiuntur, atque suavitatem possessoribus adimunt, Eccl. V. 9. 10. &c. amissionis periculo obnoxiæ sunt, quandoque veram felicitatem impediunt, 1. Tim. VI. 9. 10. & ferè semper apud malos potiùs quàm bonos sint. Potentia quoque piis & impiis, sapientibus & stultis ex æquo convenit, & alienis injuriis facilè lacessitur, quia pauci gubernationis suæ calculos ita exactè instituunt, ut legi justitiæ cuncta ad amussim respondeant. Ne de vicissitudinibus imperiorum dicam. Gloria denique apud homines vana, incerta, fugax est, & raro à recto judicio, crebrò ab imperitorum vel adulatorum applausu provenit.
units.tr: CXXX. All goods outside God, whether of the soul, of the body or of fortune, are such that the reason for true and solid goodness and happiness does not rest in any of them. Among the goods of the soul, human wisdom holds the chief place. Yet true happiness does not consist in it: first, because it is sought and increased with the greatest labour (Eccles. 1. 13, 17, etc.); second, because it never reaches its end and perfection; third, because it profits nothing for eternal salvation, since God wishes to save believers not through such wisdom but through the foolishness of preaching (1 Cor. 1. 21). Among the goods of the body are counted good health, strength, beauty, agility and long life. All these are common in themselves to men and beasts, and some of them even suit beasts better than men. Moreover, they are exposed to various accidents under the conditions of this life, and they are finally lost in death itself. In short, unless they are referred to the soul and made subject to the command of God's word, they have nothing outstanding and are deprived of the worth of true goods. Among the goods of fortune, the chief are pleasures, riches, honour, power, favour and glory among men. But the wicked and corrupt labour in vain for all these things, and even the good are harmed by them, and they never attain the end proposed. Pleasures of the body suit beasts more than man, who was made in the image of God, and their extreme is pain, or at least satiety, because we cannot bear such vanities for long; and, as Tertullian has it, what delights does harm when it lasts. So Augustine rightly called this the Scyllaean good, since it is compounded of human and bestial nature. For pleasures cannot satisfy the appetite of man, so that not even kings who abound in them can be counted happy (Eccles. 6. 7, 8, etc.). We pursue a stream of vanity and of things that pass away, so that our flesh may be tickled by constant new desire; this is death, and a kind of worm-eating in corpses. The case of riches is not different: they are usually acquired with labour and trouble, kept only with the greatest care and anxiety, and they rob their possessors of sweetness (Eccles. 5. 9, 10, etc.). They are exposed to the danger of loss, they sometimes hinder true happiness (1 Tim. 6. 9, 10), and they are almost always found more among the wicked than among the good. Power also falls equally to the pious and the impious, the wise and the foolish, and it is easily assailed by the injuries of others, because few people calculate the reckoning of their government so exactly that everything answers to the rule of justice. I say nothing of the changes of empires. Finally, glory among men is vain, uncertain and fleeting, and it rarely comes from right judgement, but often from the applause of the unskilled or of flatterers.

units.la: CXXXI. Hinc quid de Philosophorum circa Summum Bonum opinionibus censendum sit, judicatu proclive est. Pleræque enim hunc in lapidem impingunt, ut in creaturis ul-
units.tr: CXXXI. From this it is easy to judge what should be thought of the opinions of the philosophers concerning the highest good. For most of them stumble on this stone, seeking and fixing their end in creatures,

units.la: lud quærant, & defigant: & ἐκ τῶν βίων ex diversis vivendi generibus, uti sagaciter Aristoteles Eth. Nicom. lib. I. 5. conjectavit, illud constituant. Ipsius Aristotelis de Summo Bono sententia, quam Christiani Philosophi nonnulli laudare non verecundantur, rectæ rationi & sapientiæ Christianæ è diametro repugnat. Distinguit enim in Summo Bono τὸ κυριον, τὰ ἐπιχωρούντα, καὶ τὰ ὑπηρετικά principale, accessoria & ministrantia. In illo Summi Boni essentiam, in iis adjunctum, in his integritatem: Essentiam porrò in virtute & ejus actionibus: Adjunctum in voluptate animi & conscientia recte factorum ex virtute oriunda: Integritatem in bonis saltem mediocribus tum naturæ, qualia pulchritudo, nobilitas, εὐλεξία: tum fortunæ, qualia divitiæ, potentia, amici, honor sunt, collocat. Quæ excutere omnia hîc nihil attinet. Id solum animadvertimus, quòd Beatitudo hæc Aristotelica nos & amorem nostrum affigat creaturis, quales sumus nos, actiones nostræ & animæ nostræ tranquillitas, nec non bona illa naturæ & fortunæ sunt. Ipsa animi tranquillitas, quam ex virtute oriundam magnificè Aristoteles prædicat, & acribus tibiis Stoici inflant, solida & vera non hujus, sed alterius vitæ bonum est. Et erit opus justitiæ pax, & opus justitiæ tranquillitas & securitas usque in seculum, Esaj. XXXII. 17. Oritur autem non ex conscientia propriæ virtutis & justitiæ, sed ex gratuita justificatione, quam in Christo habemus. Justificati habemus pacem apud Deum, Rom. V. 1. Ahoquin animi voluptas & tranquillitas, quæ sive securitas, sive gaudium quoddam est, hac in vita omnibus communis esse potest.
units.tr: and they define it, as Aristotle shrewdly conjectured from the diverse ways of life (Nicomachean Ethics, bk. 1, ch. 5). Aristotle's own opinion about the highest good, which some Christian philosophers are not ashamed to praise, is diametrically opposed to right reason and Christian wisdom. For he distinguishes in the highest good τὸ κυριον, τὰ ἐπιχωρούντα and τὰ ὑπηρετικά [the principal, the accessory and the subservient]. In the principal part he places the essence of the highest good, in the accessory part its adjunct, and in the subservient part its completeness. The essence he places in virtue and its actions; the adjunct in the pleasure of the mind and in the consciousness of right deeds arising from virtue; and the completeness in goods of nature, at least of moderate kind, such as beauty, nobility and good health, and in goods of fortune, such as riches, power, friends and honour. There is no need to examine all these points here. We note only this: this Aristotelian happiness binds us and our love to creatures, as we ourselves are, and to our actions, the tranquillity of our souls, and those goods of nature and fortune. The tranquillity of mind itself, which Aristotle magnificently proclaims as arising from virtue, and which the Stoics puff up with their shrill pipes, is not a solid and true good of this life but of another. "And the work of justice shall be peace, and the effect of justice quietness and assurance for ever" (Isa. 32. 17). This tranquillity arises not from the consciousness of one's own virtue and justice, but from the free justification that we have in Christ. "Being justified, we have peace with God" (Rom. 5. 1). Otherwise, the pleasure and tranquillity of the mind, which is either security or a certain joy, can be common to all in this life.

units.la: CXXXII. Cùm Summum Bonum in creaturis nullis constitui possit, in Deo Creatore constituendum est. Vera enim beatitudo est, potiri Bono suo, quod semel possessum hominis desiderium nullum relinquit. Hoc Deus solus est. Ne timeas, Abraham, ego scutum tuum: Ego merces tua magna valde, Genes. XV. 1. Ero tibi, & Semini tuo post te in Deum, ibid. XVII. 7. Multi dicunt: מי יראנו טוב Quis faciet nos videre bonum? Attolle super nos lucem faciei tuæ, Jehova, 1 Psal. IV. 7. Bonum igitur hominis est Deus, lux faciei Jehovæ, qua is cum omnibus bonis & thesauris suis, solis adinstar fulgidissimi, fidelibus in vita æterna pleno jubare illucescit, & iisdem communione sui vitam, beatitudinem & lætitiam impertitur. Beatus est populus, quorum Jehova est Deus, quem sibi in hæreditatem elegit, ibid. XXXIII. 12. Dic animæ meæ ישועתך Salus tua ego sum, ibid. XXXV. 3. Anima mea gaudebit in Jehova, lætabitur in salute ejus, ibid. v. 9. Hoc novi, כי אלהים לי quòd Deus meus sit, ibid. LVI. 10. Quis est mihi in Cœlo? Et tecum (præter te) nulla res mihi voluptati est in terra. Defecit caro mea, & cor meum. Rupes cordis mei & portio mea est Deus in seculum, ibid. LXXIII. 26. 27. Ego sum Dilecti mei, & Dilectus meus, meus est, Cant. cap. VI. 2. Nemo bonus est, nisi unus Deus, Matth. XIX. 17. Deus erit omnia in omnibus, 1. Cor. XV. 28. Soli enim Deo conveniunt proprietates Summi Boni, cujusmodi sunt, quòd appetitum hominis satiat, quippe ἀκρότατον καὶ πανότατον summum & perfectissimum, uti etiam Aristo-
units.tr: CXXXII. Since the Highest Good cannot be placed in any creature, it must be placed in God the Creator. For true blessedness is to possess one's Good, which, once possessed, leaves no desire in a person. God alone is this Good: "Fear not, Abraham, I am your shield; I am your exceedingly great reward" (Gen. 15:1). "I will be a God to you and to your seed after you" (ibid. 17:7). Many say, "Who will show us any good?" [מי יראנו טוב]. "Lift up the light of your face upon us, O Jehovah" (Ps. 4:7). Therefore man's good is God, the light of Jehovah's face, which, with all his goods and treasures, shines upon the faithful in eternal life like the most brilliant sun, in full radiance, and by fellowship with himself imparts life, blessedness and joy. "Blessed is the people whose God is Jehovah, the people he has chosen for his inheritance" (ibid. 33:12). "Say to my soul, I am your salvation" [ישועתך] (ibid. 35:3). "My soul shall rejoice in Jehovah; it shall delight in his salvation" (ibid. 35:9). "This I know, that God is mine" [כי אלהים לי] (ibid. 56:10). "Whom have I in heaven? And there is none upon earth I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart fail; but God is the rock of my heart and my portion for ever" (ibid. 73:25–26). "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine" (Song 6:2). "There is none good but one, that is, God" (Matt. 19:17). "God shall be all in all" (1 Cor. 15:28). For the properties of the Highest Good belong to God alone: it satisfies the desire of man, being supreme and most perfect [ἀκρότατον καὶ πανότατον], as Aristotle also says.

units.la: Aristoteles Ethic. Nicom. I. 7. docet : quòd propter se ultimò expetendum est : quòd independens est, cùm illi, qui ab alio dependet, & sui arbitrii non est, tutò confidi non possit: quòd cum ipso communio haberi potest: quòd se omnibus & singulis Beatitudinis hæredibus simul communicare potest: quòd denique hominem meliorem perfectioremque tum se ipso,tum rebus ipso inferioribus, reddere potest. Solus autem Deus hasce Summi Boni perfectiones possidet, quia tum apud ejus solius faciem est satietas lætitiarum,Psal.XVI.11. & ipse se summo hoc elogio ornat בחמדים כלו desiderabilis totus,Cant.V.16. & αὐτὸς ἐστι τὸ πᾶν Ipse est omnia, Syrach. XLIII.29. Causa Ϛυνεχὴ complexa omnia bona, uti de idea sua & αὐτοαγάθῳ Plato dixit: tum solus propter se & ultimò,ex toto corde,ex tota anima & omnibus viribus amandus & expetendus est: tum solus à nemine alio dependet : tum communionem & commercium cum homine habere potest, & habet, utpote Deus, Pater,Dominus, Salvator noster communionem habens nobiscum, ita ut nostra communio sit cum Patre & Filio, 1. Joh. I. 3. tum se omnibus & singulis beatitudinis hæredibus simul communicare potest,quia solus essentia & virtute infinitus est; tum denique solus hominem meliorem & perfectiorem se ipso, & rebus ipsi subjacentibus efficit; Fieri enim, uti scitè Augustinus in Psal. XXXIII. argumentatur, non potest, ut res deterior te meliorem faciat. Homo es. Deterius te est quicquid cupis,quo beatus esse desideras. Aurum, argentum, quælibet corpora,quibus inhias acquirendis, possidendis, fruendis, te inferiora sunt. Tu melior es: tu fortior es : & utique vis melior esse, quàm es, cùm beatus esse vis,quia miser es. Vis esse melior te, & quæris, perquiris, per quæ id fiat, deteriora te. Quicquid est in terra, deterius est quàm tu. Jam ergo superest, ut quæras, quid melius sit te. Quid erit objecro, nisi DEUS tuus? Ipse,qui fecit, ut esses, qui his, qui tecum sunt, etiam malis, præstat Solem, præstat pluviam, præstat fructus, fontes, vitam, salutem, tantas consolationes, servat tibi aliquid,quod non det nisi tibi. Quid est autem, quod tibi servat nisi Se? Avare,quid inhias Cœlo? Melior est, qui fecit cœlum & terram. Ipsum vi-surus, ipsam habiturus es. O verè Divina!
units.tr: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.7, teaches that the Highest Good is that which is desired ultimately for its own sake; that it is self-sufficient, since no one who depends on another and is not his own master can safely trust in it; that fellowship with it can be had; that it can share itself with all and each of the heirs of blessedness at once; and that finally it can make a man better and more perfect, both in himself and in the things beneath him. But God alone possesses these perfections of the Highest Good, because in his presence there is "fullness of joy" (Ps. 16:11); and he adorns himself with this supreme praise, "altogether lovely" [בחמדים כלו] (Song 5:16), and "he himself is all things" [αὐτὸς ἐστι τὸ πᾶν] (Sirach 43:29). He is the continuous cause [συνεχὴς αἰτία] embracing all good things, as Plato said of his idea and of the Good itself. He alone is to be loved and desired ultimately and for his own sake, with the whole heart, the whole soul and all the strength. He alone depends on no other. He can have fellowship and intercourse with man, and does have it, as God, Father, Lord and our Saviour, "having fellowship with us," so that "our fellowship is with the Father and the Son" (1 John 1:3). He can share himself with all and each of the heirs of blessedness at once, because he alone is infinite in essence and power. Finally, he alone makes man better and more perfect than himself and than the things subject to him. For, as Augustine skilfully argues on Psalm 33, it cannot be that a lesser thing makes you better. You are a man. Whatever you desire, by which you wish to be blessed, is lower than you. Gold, silver, any bodies at all, which you crave to acquire, possess and enjoy, are beneath you. You are better; you are stronger; and surely you wish to be better than you are, since you wish to be blessed, because you are wretched. You wish to be better than yourself, and you seek and search for the things by which this may happen, things lower than yourself. Whatever is on earth is lower than you. So there remains only for you to seek what is better than you. What can it be, I beg you, but your God? He who made you that you might exist, who gives, to you and to those with you, even to the evil, the sun, rain, fruits, springs, life, salvation, and such great comforts, keeps for you something he will give to none but you. And what is it he keeps for you but himself? Covetous one, why do you crave heaven? He is better who made heaven and earth. You will see him, you will have him himself. O truly divine!

units.la: CXXXIII. Accedit:quòd & ipsi Philosophi nonnulli gentiles, solo naturæ lumine ducti,Beatitudinem in solius Dei participatione sitam esse, nulli dubitarunt. Nam Plato in Idea,hoc est, ταγάθῳ, 'Αυλαγάθω Ipso Bono,Deo, summum Bonum constituit. De quo sic Augustinus; de Civ. D. lib. VIII.9. Ipsum verum ac summum Bonum Plato dixit Deum. Unde vult Philosophum esse amatorem Dei, ut quoniam Philosophia ad beatam vitam tendit, fruens Deo sit beatus, qui Deum amaverit. Diserta ipsius Platonis de Legg. lib. IV. verba sunt: Ἀπάντων κάλλιστον καὶ ἀληθέστατον οἴμαι λόγων ... Omnium pulcherrimam & verissimam arbitror esse orationem, ut Bono immolent, & adhæreant Diis votis,donariis & universa eorum religione. Nam hoc pulcherrimum & optimum, & commodissimum ad vitam beatam
units.tr: CXXXIII. Moreover, some of the pagan philosophers themselves, guided by the light of nature alone, never doubted that blessedness lies in the participation of God alone. For Plato, in his Idea, that is, in the Good itself [αὐτοαγάθῳ], set up God, the Good itself, as the Highest Good. Of him Augustine speaks thus in De Civitate Dei VIII.9: Plato called the true and highest Good God. Hence he wishes the philosopher to be a lover of God, so that, since philosophy tends toward the blessed life, he who has loved God may be blessed by enjoying him. The explicit words of Plato himself in Laws IV are these: "I think the most beautiful and truest of all discourses is that one should offer sacrifice to the Good and cleave to the gods with vows, gifts and all their worship [Ἀπάντων κάλλιστον καὶ ἀληθέστατον οἴμαι λόγων]. For this is the most beautiful, best and most suitable for the blessed life."

units.la: Platonis 'Αυτοαγάθον & idea boni.
units.tr: Plato's Autoagathon [αὐτοαγάθον] and the idea of the good.

units.la: est. Et Aristoteles Ethic. Nicom. lib. I.4. Platonis sententiam ita explicat, quòd exillimaverit, præter singularia hæc bona aliud quoddam esse, καθ' αὑτὸ per se bonum, τοῖς πᾶσιν αἴτιον ... omnibus causa, quòd bona sint, & cujus participatione bona sint. Unde Deum 'Αυτοαγάθον & ideam boni eum intellexisse, etiam Alcinous de Doctr. Plat. testatur. Sed hanc Platonis sententiam idem Aristoteles mirè detorsit,& Ethic Nicom. lib. I. 6. futilibus argumentis convellere aggressus est. Τὸ χωριστόν, inquit, αὐτὸ καθ' αὑτὸ, ὑπὸ περιέχον ὑπὸ κληλον ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ. Id quod ab alio separatum est,ac per se subsistit,non cadit sub actionem humanam, neque ab homine comparari potest. Quasi Deus αὐτοαγάθον, summi idea boni,ita ab homine abstractus esset,ut eum communione & bonitate sua implere non posset; quomodo nec Deus,nec bonus esset. Perperam etiam περιέχον & κληλον conjungit, quia Deus quidem in se περιέχος non est, ita ut sub actionem hominis cadat,at κληλος tamen & ὑπλωσις est, qualis is, qui summum Bonum est, esse debet. Quomodo omnis labor est propter cessationem,inquietudo propter quietem, dies laboriosi propter festum; non vicissim. Quidni autem Deus sit κληλος? Ejus enim fideles domus & templum sunt, in quo habitat. Venit enim ad eos, & μονὴν mansionem apud eos facit, Joh. XIV. 23. Et Deus noster est,Genes. XVII. 7. Dilutum & illud est, quòd cum Bonum ἰσχὼς λέγεται τῷ ὄντι æquè patet atque id quod est, & in omnibus categoriis sit καθόλου καὶ ἐν commune, universale & unum quid esse non possit. Nam verum bonum, cujus participatio beatum reddit, nullam categoriam subit. Id omne,quod bonum facit,solus Deus continet; & cum Angelis & hominibus,quos beatos reddere vult, communicat. Neque etiam absurdum illi videri debuit, Bonum esse ἀφ' ἑνὸς, ἢ πρὸς ἓν ab uno & ad unum, sicut enim omnes aquæ ex oceano fluunt,& ad eum redeunt,Eccles. I. 7. ita à Deo,ceu oceano Bonitatis,omne bonum est, & ad eundem omne bonum redit, quia omnia sunt ἐξ αὐτοῦ ... ex ipso & in ipsum, 1. Cor. VIII. 6. Ita dies,qui claritas solis est, à sole est, & ad solem redit: neque potest diei particula rescindi, ut maneat disiecta à claritate solis, & à continentia caterarum lucis; semper enim dies solem suum sequitur. Si igitur id in natura fieri potest,cur non idem privilegium habeat naturæ author, ut ipse & sol & mare quoddam Bonitatis universæ sit? Denique insciter Aristoteles Platoni ideam boni summum Bonum facienti opponit, quòd παράδειγμα aliquod unum atque immutabile, quod semper in actionibus nostris imitemur, dari non possit, quia quotquot bonum expetunt,ejus cognitionem praetermittant,neque vel textor,vel faber,vel medicus, vel dux aliquis ad artis suæ exercitium ideam illam respicere pensi habeat. Sed Deus tum in verbo, tum in natura sua ubique se imitandum proponit. An enim faber,textor, medicus,dux ideam illam negligeret,cui probè constare debet omne bonum Dei donum esse, & in omnibus Deo gratias agendas esse: denique cuncta ornamenta nostra ad ejusdem donantis gloriam referenda esse.
units.tr: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.4, also explains Plato's opinion as follows: he thought that, apart from these particular goods, there is something else, the good in itself [καθ' αὑτὸ], the cause for all things [τοῖς πᾶσιν αἴτιον], by whose participation things are good. Hence Alcinous, in De doctrina Platonis, testifies that Plato understood God to be the Autoagathon and the idea of the good. But Aristotle himself twisted this opinion of Plato in a remarkable way, and in Nicomachean Ethics I.6 he set about refuting it with frivolous arguments. "What is separate," he says, "which is good in itself and subsists by itself [τὸ χωριστόν, αὐτὸ καθ' αὑτὸ], does not fall under human action, nor can it be obtained by man." As if God, the Autoagathon, the idea of the highest good, were so cut off from man that he could not fill him with his fellowship and goodness; in which case God would not be good either. He also wrongly joins "containing" [περιέχον] and "contained" [κληλον], since God is indeed not "containing" in himself so as to fall under human action, but he is nevertheless the "contained" [κληλος] and the [ὑπλωσις], as he who is the Highest Good ought to be. Just as all labour is for the sake of rest, and unrest for the sake of quiet, and working days for the sake of the feast, and not the reverse. And why should God not be the "contained"? For his faithful are his house and temple, in which he dwells. "For he comes to them and makes his abode [μονὴν] with them" (John 14:23). And he is "our God" (Gen. 17:7). That also is weak, that when the Good is said in the strict sense [ἰσχὼς λέγεται τῷ ὄντι], it is as clearly the same as that which is, and since it is found in all the categories [καθόλου καὶ ἐν], it cannot be something common, universal and one. For the true good, whose participation makes one blessed, falls under no category. God alone contains all that makes a thing good, and he communicates it to the angels and men whom he wishes to make blessed. Nor should it have seemed absurd to him that the Good is "from one and to one" [ἀφ' ἑνὸς, ἢ πρὸς ἓν]. For just as all waters flow from the ocean and return to it (Eccles. 1:7), so all good comes from God, as from the ocean of goodness, and all good returns to the same God, because all things are "from him and to him" [ἐξ αὐτοῦ ... ex ipso] (1 Cor. 8:6). So day, which is the brightness of the sun, comes from the sun and returns to the sun; nor can a particle of day be cut off so as to remain separated from the brightness of the sun and from the continuity of the other light, for day always follows its sun. If this can happen in nature, why should the Author of nature not have the same privilege, that he himself should be both the sun and a kind of sea of universal goodness? Finally, Aristotle rightly opposes Plato, who made the idea of the good the Highest Good, on the ground that some one unchanging pattern, which we should always imitate in our actions, cannot be given, since all who desire the good neglect its knowledge, and neither the weaver, nor the smith, nor the physician, nor any leader has a concern to look to that idea in the exercise of his art. But God, both in his Word and in his own nature, sets himself forth everywhere to be imitated. For would not the smith, the weaver, the physician or the leader neglect that idea, which ought to be clearly known to him: that every good is a gift of God, and that thanks are to be given to God in all things; and finally, that all our adornments are to be referred to the glory of the same giver?

units.la: CXXXIV. DEUS,
units.tr: CXXXIV. GOD,

units.la: CXXXIV. DEUS, Summum Bonum, homini se communicat, & fruendum offert. Sicut enim Summum Bonum in universum λόγον καὶ ὑπόλαυστον tale est, ut ab homine poslideri, & is eo frui possit, absque quo esset; ne bonum quidem, nedum summum bonum esset: ita talem etiam se Deus praebet. Nam is se homini communicat in Christo. Ero Deus tuus & Seminis tui post te, Genes. XVII. 7. Ego sum Deus Abrahami, Isaci & Jacobi, Exod. III. 6. 16. Dic animae meae: Salus tua ego sum, Psal. XXXV. 3. Erit omnia in omnibus, 1. Cor. XV. 28. Neque etiam Deus homini summum bonum sine operatione aliqua hominis circa ipsum est. Licet enim operatio illa circa Deum, Summum Bonum, quae beatum efficit, sit a Deo, & per lumen gratiae vel gloriae efficiatur: tamen formalis ratio beatitudinis nostrae non est ipsa operatio increata Dei, qua se ipsum videt, & se ipso fruitur; neque adeo beatitudo hominis increatum aliquid est, uti nonnulli olim Parisienses, quibus e Scholasticis Johanne de Ripa annumeratur, censuisse dicuntur.
units.tr: CXXXIV. God, the Supreme Good, communicates himself to man and offers himself to be enjoyed. For just as the Supreme Good is, in the universal sense, something enjoyable [ὑπόλαυστον] that can be possessed by a man, who can enjoy it, and without which he would not even have a good, let alone a supreme good, so God presents himself in the same way. For he communicates himself to man in Christ: "I will be your God and the God of your seed after you" (Gen. 17:7); "I am the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob" (Exod. 3:6, 16); "Say to my soul: I am your salvation" (Ps. 35:3); "God will be all in all" (1 Cor. 15:28). Nor is God the supreme good for man without some activity of man directed toward him. For although that activity directed toward God, the Supreme Good, which makes a man blessed, comes from God and is brought about through the light of grace or of glory, the formal ground of our blessedness is not God's uncreated activity by which he sees himself and enjoys himself. Nor, for that matter, is the blessedness of man something uncreated, as some of the Parisians of old are said to have held, among whom John of Rippa is counted among the Scholastics.

units.la: Creatura enim formaliter vitae increatae capax non est. Actus quinetiam beatificus, quo Deum, Summum Bonum suum attingit, illi quodammodo proprius & peculiaris esse debet. Neque immerito olim damnatus est error Monothe-letarum, afferentium, quod humanitas in Christo nihil formaliter velit, nisi voluntate Divinitatis. Et quanto minus hominis operatio vel voluntas formaliter operatio vel voluntas Divina esse poterit? Neque minus solemnia insanivit Henricus Gandavensis, eumque secuti Mystici, statuentes, illapsu essentiae Divinae in animas beatorum, eas formaliter beatas constitui. Qui merus enthusiasmus, & quaedam ἐνθουσιασμός est. Illapsus enim ille in animam intelligi non poterit, nisi Deus intelligatur novo modo inesse illi, cui illabitur. Proinde fiet per mutationem. Atqui in Deo nulla mutatio est. Erit igitur in anima hominis recipiente, quod ante non habuit. Atqui anima hominis, cum beatur, novam substantiam nullam recipit; neque essentiam Divinam sine ἐνθεώσει recipere poterit. Nam quod recipere illam unionem substantialem cum essentia Dei, atque ita per Divinitatem, quasi ignem quendam, igniri, regerunt, nimis illud crassum est, quia sic per essentiam Dei & animam una substantia composita fieret, quae vel una natura, vel una persona foret. Atqui non potest fieri una natura, quia Deus simplicissimus in compositionem naturae tertiae venire non potest. Neque etiam fieri potest una persona, quia alioquin illapsus ille & unio mystica foret unio hypostatica, qualis duarum naturarum in Christo est. Imo unio talis mystica praestantior foret, quam hypostatica & incarnatio Christi, quia esset unio immediate & praecise cum essentia, qua essentia est. Essentiae vero conceptus excellentior est, quam conceptus substantiae seu personalitatis, quam unio hypostatica respicit. Superest igitur, ut formalis beatitudo consistat in ἐνεργεία operatione quadam hominis totius, animae & sensuum gloriae capacium optima, sanctissima, integerrima, jucundissima, circa Deum, tanquam Summum Bonum, per quam illi arctissimè unitur, & ἀδιαλείπτως adhaerescit.
units.tr: For a creature is not formally capable of uncreated life. Moreover, the beatifying act by which one attains God, one's Supreme Good, must in some way be proper and peculiar to the creature. Nor was the error of the Monothelites rightly condemned long ago, when they asserted that the humanity in Christ formally wills nothing except by the will of the Divinity. And how much less can the operation or will of man formally be the divine operation or will? Henry of Ghent raved no less solemnly, and the Mystics who followed him, holding that by the inflowing of the divine essence into the souls of the blessed, those souls are formally made blessed. This is sheer enthusiasm, a kind of ἐνθουσιασμός [enthusiasm]. For that inflowing into the soul cannot be understood unless God is understood to be present in a new way in the one into whom he flows. Hence it would come about through a change. But there is no change in God. Therefore the soul of the man who receives him would receive what it did not have before. But the soul of a man, when it is blessed, receives no new substance; nor can it receive the divine essence without ἐνθέωσις [deification]. For to say that it receives that substantial union with the essence of God, and so is set aglow by the Divinity as by a kind of fire, is too crude, because in that case the essence of God and the soul would become one composite substance, which would be either one nature or one person. But it cannot become one nature, because the most simple God cannot enter into the composition of a third nature. Nor can it become one person, because otherwise that inflowing and mystical union would be a hypostatic union, such as that of the two natures in Christ. Indeed, such a mystical union would be more excellent than the hypostatic union and the incarnation of Christ, because it would be a union immediately and precisely with the essence as essence. But the concept of essence is more excellent than the concept of substance or personality, which the hypostatic union regards. It remains, therefore, that formal blessedness consists in a certain ἐνέργεια [activity], an operation of the whole man, soul and senses, both capable of glory, the best, most holy, most upright, and most delightful, directed toward God as the Supreme Good, by which man is most closely united to him and cleaves to him ἀδιαλείπτως [without intermission].

units.la: CXXXV. Vitae aeternae in participatione Dei, Summi Boni, & operationis hominis beatifica circa illud consistentis initium in hac vita fit. Aliud enim beatitudinis & Summi Boni essentia, aliud ejusdem integritas & consummatio est. Illa in omnes electos justificatos per Christum, & filios Dei, adeoque etiam in viatores cadit. Nam & Christus ipse beatos praedicat lugentes, esurientes & sitientes justitiam, persecutionem propter justitiam patientes, Matth. V. 4. 6. 10. & S. Paulus μακαρισμόν beatitudinem in remissione peccatorum collocat, Rom. IV. 6. & justificatos a charitate Dei separari negat, cap. VIII. 35 & S. Johannes, Dilecti, inquit, nunc filii Dei sumus, sed nondum manifestatum est, quid futuri simus. Novimus autem quando manifestabimur, nos ipsi similes futuros esse, 1. Joh. III. 2. Et de vita aeterna sic Christus loquitur: Haec est vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te solum illum verum Deum, & quem misisti, Jesum Christum, Joh. XVII. 3. ubi explicatur, in quo consistat vita aeterna, nempe in cognitione Dei & Christi, hoc est, in sapientia & prudentia. Nam cognoscere ibi significat active cognitionem exercere, intueri, quaerere faciem Dei, eum ante oculos habere, curare, quod Esaj. LV. 6. dicitur דרשׁ יהוה quaerere Dominum. Et passim pietas per cognitionem Dei describitur. Etiam Deus dicitur nos cognoscere, hoc est, amare, curare, custodire, oculos super nos ponere, Psal. XXXIV. 16. Et sicut cognitio Dei vita nostra est, ita contraria ei Dei ignoratio, oblivio, & aversio cogitationis ad aliud, mors est. Vita enim actio jucunda ejus, quod vivit; & non amare, quod amandum est, amare autem, quod bonum non est, & quod praeterit, actio non jucunda, sed cum pudore & poenitentia conjuncta, adeoque non vita, sed mors est. Cum igitur fideles etiam in hac vita Deum Patrem & Filium ejus cognoscant, vere utique vivere incipiunt, & beatitudinem suam in hac vita inchoant. Nam primitias Spiritus S. etiam in hac vita accipimus, Rom. VIII. 23. & ipse salvati sumus, ibid. v. 24. Sed perfecta beatitudo post hanc corporis hujus vitam differtur cum Christo in Deo occultata, Col. III. 3. In hac enim vita non contingit perfectio novitatis, nedum gloriae & beatitudinis; sed in altera demum. Deus enim in operibus suis semper procedit ad perfectius & gloriosius, secundum illam potentiam, qua potest longe supra id, quod petimus aut cogitamus, facere, Ephes. III. 20.
units.tr: CXXXV. The beatific life of eternity, consisting in the participation in God, the Supreme Good, and in the activity of man directed toward him, begins in this life. For the essence of blessedness and of the Supreme Good is one thing; its integrity and consummation is another. The former falls upon all the elect who are justified through Christ and are sons of God, and so also upon those who are still on the way. For Christ himself pronounces blessed those who mourn, who hunger and thirst after righteousness, and who suffer persecution for righteousness (Matt. 5:4, 6, 10); and St. Paul places the blessedness [μακαρισμός] in the forgiveness of sins (Rom. 4:6), and denies that the justified are separated from the love of God (Rom. 8:35). And St. John says: "Beloved, we are now the sons of God, but it has not yet been made manifest what we shall be. We know, however, that when he is manifested we shall be like him" (1 John 3:2). And Christ speaks thus of eternal life: "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17:3), where it is explained in what eternal life consists, namely in the knowledge of God and of Christ, that is, in wisdom and prudence. For "to know" here means actively exercising knowledge, looking upon, seeking the face of God, keeping him before one's eyes, taking care, which is what Isaiah 55:6 calls דרשׁ יהוה [to seek the Lord]. And everywhere piety is described by the knowledge of God. God too is said to know us, that is, to love, care for, guard us, and set his eyes upon us (Ps. 34:16). And just as the knowledge of God is our life, so the ignorance of God, forgetfulness, and the turning of thought to other things, which are the opposite of it, are death. For life is the pleasant activity of that which lives; and not to love what is to be loved, but to love what is not good, and what passes away, is an activity that is not pleasant but joined with shame and repentance, and so is not life but death. Since, therefore, the faithful, even in this life, know God the Father and his Son, they truly begin to live, and they begin their blessedness in this life. For we receive the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit even in this life (Rom. 8:23), and "we have been saved" (ibid. v. 24). But perfect blessedness is deferred until after this bodily life, when "our life is hidden with Christ in God" (Col. 3:3). For in this life no perfection of newness is attained, much less of glory and blessedness, but only in the other. For God always proceeds in his works toward what is more perfect and more glorious, according to that power by which he is able to do far above all that we ask or think (Eph. 3:20).

units.la: CXXXVI. Non aliud igitur alterius vitae bonum, quod postremò habituri sumus, est, quam quod & in hac vita habemus. Gradum tantum & perfectionis discrimen intercedit. Sapiens, uti scite Ambrosius de Jac. cap. 7. loquitur, non frangitur doloribus corporis, nec vexatur incommodis, sed etiam in aerumnis beatus est. Nam & Stoici dicere ausi sunt: Sapientem in tormentis beatum esse. Et Seneca de Benef. lib. IV. 22. Si corpus, inquit, plenum bona conscientia sit, placebit illi ignis, per quem bona fides collncollucebit. Beatitudo igitur hujus & alterius vitæ non re,sed gradu perfectionis differt. Nititur enim fœdere gratiæ, in quo æterna vita credenti promittitur. Sicut autem Fœdus Gratiæ in hac vita variantem œconomiam recipit, & alia sub promissione, alia sub lege, alia sub Evangelio obtinuit & obtinet: ita diversam œconomiam in altera vita habebit ab ea, quam in hac vita habuit & habet. Quicquid in promissionibus ejus imperfectum est,hujus vitæ est: quicquid perfectum,alterius est. Nolumus enim exuere (id quod per regenerationem & fidem induimus,& τὸ καλοικητήριον domicilium ex Cœlis) sed superinduere (gloriam, incorruptibilitatem, perfectionem cognitionis, amoris,sanctitatis,lætitiæ,domum,quæ in Cœlo est) ut absorbeatur corruptibile a vita (ut in nobis sit vita mera,sine corruptione, pravitate, carne,pugna & lucta,& luctu, lachrymis & ἀδενίᾳ omni) 2.Cor.V.4. Ex parte cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus. Cum autem venerit, quod τὸ τέλειον perfectum est, tunc quod ex parte est,abolebitur,&c. 1.Corinth.XIII.9.10. Certa proin bonorum alterius vitæ æternæ inveniendorum,&,quantum in mortalitatis hac umbra licet,reputandorum,ratio est,bonorum spiritualium hujus vitæ, per quæ Deus, ceu Summum Bonum nostrum, se ipsum & bonitatem suam fidelibus in hac vita communicat, imperfectionem demere, & perfectionem ex Dei verbo,quatenus in illo describitur,meditari: Quò pertinet scitum illud Bernhardi: Quicquid olim præparavit & inchoavit gratia, tunc absolvet & perficiet gloria. Cúmque in hac vita salus & beatitudo fidelium,Dei,ceu Summi Boni nostri, cognitione & amore, atque inde manante lætitia spirituali,ex sensu favoris Dei,conjuncta cum acquiescentia in ipso: denique communione imaginis Dei, pro subjecti modo, constet: planum erit,vitam æternam , & consummatam salutem atque Beatitudinem nostram,Dei,ceu Summi Boni nostri, omnem Summi Boni vim & efficaciam exerentis , perfecta cognitione & amore , atque inde manante lætitia ineffabili ex pleno sensu favoris Dei, conjuncta cum omni acquiescentia in ipso , constare. Ex quibus etiam cœlestis gloria beatorum quoad animam & corpus refulgebit. De quibus nunc αὐτὰ μέρῳ agendum.
units.tr: CXXXVI. The good of the other life, which we shall finally possess, is therefore no different from what we have in this life. Only a difference of degree and of perfection lies between them. The wise man, as Ambrose rightly says in On Jacob, chapter 7, is not broken by the pains of the body nor troubled by its discomforts, but is blessed even in his distress. For even the Stoics ventured to say that the wise man is blessed in torments. And Seneca, On Benefits, book IV, 22: "If the body is full of a good conscience, it will be pleased by the fire through which good faith shines." The blessedness of this life and of the other therefore differs not in substance but in degree of perfection. For it rests on the covenant of grace, in which eternal life is promised to the believer. But just as the covenant of grace in this life takes on a changing economy, and has obtained and still obtains one form under promise, another under law, another under the Gospel, so it will have in the other life an economy different from the one it has had and has in this life. Whatever is imperfect in its promises belongs to this life; whatever is perfect belongs to the other. For we do not wish to be stripped (that which we have put on through regeneration and faith, and the "habitation from heaven," the house which is in heaven), but to be clothed upon (with glory, incorruptibility, perfection of knowledge, love, holiness, joy, the house that is in heaven), so that "what is mortal may be swallowed up by life" (so that in us there may be pure life, without corruption, depravity, flesh, fight and struggle, and mourning, tears and every sorrow) (2 Cor. 5:4). "We know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be done away" (1 Cor. 13:9–10). There is therefore a sure method of finding and, so far as the shadow of mortality permits, of reckoning the good things of the eternal other life: to remove imperfection from the spiritual goods of this life, through which God, as our Supreme Good, communicates himself and his goodness to the faithful in this life, and to meditate on perfection from the Word of God, so far as it is described there. To this pertains that saying of Bernard: "What grace has formerly prepared and begun, glory will then complete and perfect." And since in this life the salvation and blessedness of the faithful consist in the knowledge and love of God, our Supreme Good, and in the spiritual joy flowing from this, arising from the sense of God's favor, joined with acquiescence in him, and finally in the communion of the image of God, according to the measure of the subject; it will be plain that eternal life, and our consummated salvation and blessedness, consist in God, our Supreme Good, exercising all the power and efficacy of the Supreme Good, in perfect knowledge and love, and in the ineffable joy flowing from this, arising from the full sense of God's favor, joined with complete acquiescence in him. From these things the heavenly glory of the blessed will also shine forth, both as to soul and body. Concerning these we must now treat in their own part.

units.la: CXXXVII. De perfectione cognitionis, imò & amoris Dei, ceu Summi Boni nostri, passim Scriptura phrasibus videndi Deum, faciem ejus aspiciendi, cognoscendi utens loquitur.
units.tr: CXXXVII. On the perfection of knowledge, and indeed of love, of God as our Supreme Good: Scripture everywhere speaks in the language of seeing God, beholding his face, and knowing him.

units.la: Deus ipse ad Moisen: Non poteris videre faciem meam: quia non videbit me homo,& vivet,Exod. XXXIII.20. non negans,visum iri Deum & faciem ejus,sed afferens,impossibile esse,ut homo in corpore peccati & mortis ad plenitudinem videndæ faciei & gloriæ Dei perveniat. In altera igitur vita, mortalitate hac exutos, Deum & faciem ejus visuros innuit. Etiam Jobus: Ex carne inquit,mea videbo Deum; quem ego videbo mihi, cap.XIX.25.26. David: Ego in justitia videbo faciem tuam. Satiabor,cum expergefiam,specie tua, Psal.XVII.15. Credo,me visurum bona Domini in terra viventium, ibid. XXVII.13. Tecum vena vitæ; & in lumine tuo videbimus lumen, ibid.XXXVI.10. Christus ipse: Beati mundi corde quia ipsi videbunt Deum, Matth.V.8. S. Paulus: Videmus nunc in speculo, in ænigmate; tunc a facie ad faciem. Nunc cognosco ex parte. Tunc vero cognoscam, ut & cognitus sum, 1.Cor.XIII.12. Secundum fidem ambulamus,& non κατ' εἶδος- secundum aspectum, vel speciem,2.Cor.V.7. Denique S. Johannes. Nunc filii Dei sumus, & nondum manifestum est, quid futuri simus. Novimus autem, quòd,cum id manifestabitur,similes ei erimus. Quoniam videbimus eum sicuti est, 1.Joh.III.2. Videbunt faciem ejus,& nomen ejus super faciebus suis,Apoc. XXII.4. Etiam Gentiles visionem Dei meliori vitæ reservatam esse,agnoscunt; & causam,cur animus non semper in conspectu Dei, quo & hic certo quodam modo quandoque fruitur,defixus maneat,hanc Plotinus Enn.VI.9.10. reddit; Erit autem & quando dabitur continuitas videndi,cùm scilicet corpus nullo modo intuitum perturbabit.
units.tr: God himself said to Moses: "You cannot see my face, for no man shall see me and live" (Exod. 33:20). He does not deny that God and his face will be seen, but asserts that it is impossible for a man in a body of sin and death to attain the fullness of seeing the face and glory of God. He therefore indicates that in the other life, freed from mortality, we shall see God and his face. Job also says: "In my flesh I shall see God; whom I shall see for myself" (Job 19:25–26). David says: "As for me, in righteousness I shall behold your face; I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with your likeness" (Ps. 17:15). "I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living" (ibid. 27:13). "With you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light" (ibid. 36:10). Christ himself said: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" (Matt. 5:8). St Paul: "Now we see in a mirror, in a riddle; then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am known" (1 Cor. 13:12). "We walk by faith, and not [κατ' εἶδος] by sight, or appearance" (2 Cor. 5:7). Lastly, St John: "Now we are the children of God, and it has not yet been made manifest what we shall be. But we know that, when it is made manifest, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is" (1 John 3:2). "They shall see his face, and his name shall be on their foreheads" (Rev. 22:4). Even the Gentiles acknowledge that the vision of God is reserved for a better life; and Plotinus (Enn. 6.9.10) gives the reason why the mind does not remain always fixed on the sight of God, though even here it sometimes enjoys this in a certain way: there will be a time when the continuous seeing will be granted, namely when the body will in no way disturb the gaze.

units.la: CXXXVIII. Qualis futura sit visio Dei, nemini adhuc revelatum est. Id verò certum est,non ita Deum à nobis comprehensum iri, ut ejus essentia videatur oculis vel corporis, vel animæ beatæ. Deus enim est & manet mirabilis,Esaj.IX.6. & habitat lucem inaccessam,quem nemo hominum vidit, vel videre potest, 1.Tim.VI.16. De quo Loc.III.36.37. plura diximus. Tum & illud æquè certum est, visionem illam non futuram esse aridam contemplationem quandam,dilectioni & fruitioni Dei contradistinctam,vel saltem ei præviam, per quam nudè objectum voluntati proponatur,quò hæc in illud ferri possit,quam sententiam Scholasticis nonnullis Jansenius tribuit, meritóque refellit,eò quòd visio Dei tantopere in Scripturis prædicata partim ex luminosissimo Dei amore jam fruente nascatur, partim amorem quodammodo sequatur,dum qui ita videt,illuminatam mentis aciem in Deum figat, quò ejus contemplatione irretorte perfruatur. Ideo Apostolus dicit: Nunc cognosco ex parte: Tum autem cognoscam,ut & cognitus sum, 1.Cor.XIII.12. Deus autem cognoscit amando. Proin & ipsi Deum cognoscemus amando, sentiendo in omni effectu, quomodo Deus nos amaverit. Præclarè Augustinus Quæst. lib.LXXXIII.35. sic rem explicat: Fieri potest, ut habeat quis aliquid, quod habere hoc fit, quod nôsse; nequé amet tamen. Verbi gratia,numeros arithmeticos. Quanquam bonum, quod non amatur, nemo potest perfectè habere vel nôsse. Quis enim potest nôsse, quantum sit bonum, quo non fruitur? Non autem fruitur, si non amat. Nec habet igitur, quod amandum est,qui non amat; etiam ji amare possit, qui non habet. Nemo igitur vitam beatam novit & miser est,quoniam si amanda est, sicuti est, hoc est eam nôsse, quod habere. Quæ cùm ita sint, quid est aliud beatè vivere,nisi æternum aliquid cognoscendo habere? Æternum est enim,de quo solo rectè siditur, quod amanti auferri non potest: idque ipsum est, quòd nihil sit aliud habere, quàm nôsse. Omnium enim rerum præstantissimum est,quod æternum est:& propterea id habere non possumus, nisi ea re, qua præstantiores sumus, id est, mente. Quicquid autem mente habetur, noscendo habetur, nullúmque bonum perfectè noscitur, quod non perfectè amatur. CXXXIX. Ne-
units.tr: CXXXVIII. What the vision of God will be like has not yet been revealed to anyone. This much is certain: God will not be comprehended by us in such a way that his essence is seen with the eyes either of the body or of the blessed soul. For God is and remains wonderful (Isa. 9:6), and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen or can see (1 Tim. 6:16). We have said more about this at Loc. 3.36–37. It is equally certain that this vision will not be some dry contemplation, set apart from the love and enjoyment of God, or at least preceding them, through which the object is merely presented to the will so that the will may be carried towards it. Jansenius attributes this opinion to some of the Scholastics, and rightly refutes it, because the vision of God, so highly praised in the Scriptures, arises partly from the most luminous love of God already enjoyed, and partly follows love in a certain way, since the one who thus sees fixes the illuminated edge of his mind upon God, so that he may enjoy him in a contemplation that does not let him go. Therefore the Apostle says: "Now I know in part; then I shall know, even as I am known" (1 Cor. 13:12). But God knows by loving. Thus we too shall know God by loving, by feeling in every effect how God has loved us. Augustine explains the matter admirably (Quaest. 83, q. 35): "It can happen that someone has something which to have is to know, and yet does not love it; for example, arithmetical numbers. Yet no one can perfectly have or know a good which is not loved. For who can know how great is the good that he does not enjoy? But he does not enjoy it if he does not love it. So the one who does not love does not have what is to be loved, even if he could love what he does not have. No one therefore knows the blessed life and is miserable; for if it is to be loved as it is, to know it is to have it. Since these things are so, what is it to live blessedly except to have something eternal by knowing it? For that is eternal of which alone one rightly speaks, which cannot be taken from the one who loves; and this is precisely that to have is nothing other than to know. For what is eternal is the most excellent of all things, and so we cannot possess it except by that by which we are more excellent, that is, by the mind. Whatever is had by the mind is had by knowing, and no good is perfectly known which is not perfectly loved."

units.la: CXXXIX. Neque igitur essentiæ Dei hæc visio erit; neque arida & sterilis contemplatio rei; velut ad contemplantem non pertinentis, & quam videndo non amet, amando non fruitione suam faciat, erit. Sed qualis tamen illa futura sit, varii varie explicant. Nobis placet Augustini ejusdem moderatio, sic de Civ. D. lib. XXII. 29. loquentis: Et illa quidem actio, vel potius quies atque otium, quale futurum sit, si verum velim dicere, nescio. Non enim hoc unquam per sensus corporis vidi. Si autem hoc mente, id est, intelligentia vidisse me dicam, quantum est, aut quid est, intelligentia nostra ad illam excellentissimam? Ibi est amor, pax, quæ sicut Apostolus inquit, superat omnem intellectum. Sed nonnulla tamen certiora de visione illa videmur asserere posse. Ante omnia Deus iis, qui eum videbunt, præsentissimus erit. Videbitur enim à facie ad faciem, 1. Cor. XIII. 12. Κατ' εἰδῶ- secundum speciem, 2. Cor. V. 7. Satiabimur etiam בתמונה specie Dei, Psal. XVII. 15. Non igitur per speciem mediam intelligibilem abstractam videbitur, quia alias rursum foret ænigma & speculum. Deus enim longè intimius sese animabus nostris infundere poterit, quam anima nostra, & animæ nostræ habitus se corpori nostro infundunt. Tum ad visionem illam perficiendam donabitur nobis lumen aliquod gloriæ. Penes Te est vena vitæ, בְּאוֹרְךָ in lumine tuo videbimus lumen, Psal. XXXVI. 10. Illo affulgente animabus nostris, discussa omni nube & obscuritate, Deum in omni sua pulchritudine videbunt, gloriam ejus videbunt, neque morientur tamen; & denique plenam pacem, justitiam, gaudium sentient. Si enim hac in vita lumine Spiritus S. opus est, ut per fidem Deum agnoscamus, in altera ad videndum Deum à facie ad faciem lucidiore ejusdem lumine opus erit. Erit insuper visio hæc bonum totius hominis, quoad animam & corpus. Habebunt enim oculi corporis, quod vident, Christum, Salvatorem, Caput & Regem suum. Novimus, quod cum (in secundo adventu gloriioso) revelatus fuerit, (sicut in primo adventu revelatus est ad tollenda peccata,) similes ei erimus. Videbimus enim eum, sicut est, 1. Joh. III. 2. ς. Omnis enim gloria Dei, quam videbimus, sicut nunc cum Christo occultatur, Col. III. 3. ita cum eodem, & in eodem gloriosè manifestabitur. Quomodo etiam videbunt faciem ejus, Apoc. XXII. 4. nempe gloriosi corporis Christi τὸ Ἀρνίον Agni. Videbimus autem non tantum oculis mentis, cum cognoscemus, sicut ipse cognitus est; sed etiam oculis corporis. Sed inprimis oculi animæ quod videant, habebunt. Videbunt enim illi Deum in Christo, quemadmodum nos dilexerit in Christo, ut Deus noster fieret. Et videbimus Deum in Christo, non quoad essentiam Dei, sed quoad vitales actiones, opera & effecta. Non enim tam visio essentiæ, quàm infinitarum ejus virtutum, sapientiæ, bonitatis, misericordiæ, justitiæ, quæ Numini πυρὴν καὶ ἐπαινέσαν conciliant, ad beatitudinem conferunt. Similes enim erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est. Id igitur videbimus, in quo similes erimus. At qui non erimus similes Deo in essentia, qua coram etiam Angeli faciem suam velant, Esaj. VI. 2. sed in bonitate, sapientia, amore, sancti-
units.tr: CXXXIX. Therefore this vision will be neither the essence of God, nor a dry and barren contemplation of a thing, as if it did not belong to the one contemplating, which would not make it his own by enjoyment through loving it in seeing it. But writers explain variously what it will be like. We prefer the moderation of the same Augustine, speaking thus in De Civ. Dei 22.29: "Indeed, what that action, or rather rest and leisure, will be like, I do not know, if I am to speak the truth. For I have never seen this through the senses of the body. But if I should say that I have seen it with the mind, that is, with understanding, how great, or what, is our understanding in comparison with that most excellent thing? There is love there, and peace, which, as the Apostle says, surpasses all understanding." Yet we seem able to assert some things about that vision with more certainty. Above all, God will be most present to those who see him. For he will be seen face to face (1 Cor. 13:12), [κατ' εἶδος] according to appearance (2 Cor. 5:7). We shall also be satisfied with the [בתמונה] likeness of God (Ps. 17:15). Therefore he will not be seen through an intermediate, intelligible, abstract species, for otherwise it would again be a riddle and a mirror. For God will be able to pour himself into our souls far more intimately than our soul pours itself into our body, and the habits of our soul into our body. Then, for the completion of that vision, some light of glory will be given to us. With you is the fountain of life; [בְּאוֹרְךָ] in your light we shall see light (Ps. 36:10). When that light shines on our souls, every cloud and darkness being dispelled, they will see God in all his beauty, they will see his glory, and yet they will not die; and at last they will feel full peace, righteousness and joy. For if in this life we need the light of the Holy Spirit to know God by faith, in the other life we shall need his light, which will be clearer, to see God face to face. Moreover, this vision will be the good of the whole man, as to soul and body. For the eyes of the body will also have what they see: Christ, their Saviour, Head and King. We know that when he is revealed (at his glorious second coming, just as at his first coming he was revealed to take away sins), we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). For all the glory of God which we shall see, now hidden with Christ (Col. 3:3), will then be manifested gloriously with him and in him, just as they shall see his face (Rev. 22:4), namely the glorified body of Christ, [τὸ Ἀρνίον] the Lamb. We shall see not only with the eyes of the mind, when we know as we are known, but also with the eyes of the body. But above all, the eyes of the soul will have what they see. For they will see God in Christ, how he loved us in Christ so as to become our God. And we shall see God in Christ, not as to the essence of God, but as to his living actions, works and effects. For it is not so much the vision of the essence as of his infinite virtues, wisdom, goodness, mercy, justice, which [πυρὴν καὶ ἐπαινέσαν] make him worthy and praiseworthy, that contributes to blessedness. For we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. Therefore we shall see that in which we shall be like him. But we shall not be like God in essence, in which even the angels veil their faces (Isa. 6:2), but in goodness, wisdom, love, holiness

units.la: tate & beatitudine. Accuratè intelligemus, Deum esse Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S. Divina attributa, naturarum in Christo ἐνωσιν, ituprenda naturæ & gratiæ opera, jam fere ignota, noscemus rectius. Et cognitio hæc, quia Deus infinitus est, & nos finiti semper manebimus, augebitur semper atque in æternum. Et quò magis sic Deum videbimus, hoc amabimus, gaudebimus magis.
units.tr: holiness and blessedness. We shall understand accurately that God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and we shall come to know more rightly the divine attributes, the union of the natures in Christ [ἕνωσιν], and the works of nature and grace, which are now almost unknown. And since God is infinite, and we shall always remain finite, this knowledge will grow always and for eternity. The more we thus see God, the more we shall love him and the more we shall rejoice.

units.la: CXL. Cùm enim visio hæc Dei non nudæ contemplationis, sed affectus visio sit similis illi, qua Deus hominem videre, cognoscere, intueri dicitur, in quem amore suo fertur, etiam voluntatis beatorum consummationem, renovationem ejus, & plenissimam cum Divina conformationem, quæ non tam sanctificatio, quàm plena sanctitas erit, includit. Nos autem detecta facie Domini, quasi in speculo intuentes secundum eandem imaginem transformamur ex gloria in gloriam, sicut a Spiritu Domini, 2. Cor. III. 18. Consistit autem in purissimo & perfectissimo amore Dei, ex immenso illo lumine, cœlestíque intuitu oriundo. Nam ἡ ἀγάπη Charitas nunquam excidit, 1. Cor. XIII. 8. Naturalis enim ratio dictat, beatum neminem esse posse, quin adeptus sit bonum, quod diligat, & quo delecto fruatur. Quis enim beatum se existimet, nisi fruendo? Quis frui potest, nisi diligendo? Scitè Augustinus de Morib. Eccl. cap. 3. Quid aliud est, inquit, quod dicitur frui, nisi præsto habere, quod diligis? Imò non diligere verum bonum, quo creatura rationalis, ut beata sit, frui debet, explorata miseria est. Languor enim animi est, qui non aliunde, quàm ex rei alterius dilectione proficiscitur. Unde ibid. Augustinus: Beatus, inquit, quantum existimo, neque ille dici potest, qui non habet, quod amat, qualecunque fit: neque qui habet, quod amat, si noxium fit: neque qui non habet, quod amat, etiamsi optimum fit. Nam qui appetit, quod adipisci non potest, cruciatur: qui adeptus est, quod appetendum non est, fallitur: qui non appetit, quod adipiscendum esset, ægrotat. Etiam Plotinus, supra fere gentilitatis captum, amorem illum descripsit. Indicat, sic inter alia Enn. lib. IX. 9. loquitur, illic bonum nostrum consistere, amor ipse ingenitus animo nostro, prout amor conjugatus animis. Nempe quoniam animus est ex illo, necessario amat illum. Jam verò cùm ibi vivit, cœlestem habet amorem: hic autem fit communis & vulgaris. Cœlestis enim illic regnat Venus, hic autem vulgaris, quasi adulterata. Est autem omnis amor Venus, quod indicant natalia Veneris, amórque simul cum Venere genitus. Animus ergo in naturali habitu constitutus amat Deum, Deo commiscerì desiderans, quasi pulchram virginitatem honesto amore affectans, &c.
units.tr: CXL. For this sight of God is not a bare contemplation but a sight of affection, like that by which God is said to see, know and regard a man, on whom he sets his love. It therefore includes the fulfilment of the blessed's will, its renewal, and its most complete conformity with the divine will, which will be not so much sanctification as perfect holiness. But we all, with unveiled face beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord, 2 Cor. III. 18. This consists in the purest and most perfect love of God, arising from that immense light and heavenly vision. For charity never faileth [ἡ ἀγάπη οὐδέποτε ἐκπίπτει], 1 Cor. XIII. 8. For natural reason dictates that no one can be blessed unless he has obtained the good which he loves and in which he delights and enjoys. For who thinks himself blessed unless he enjoys? And who can enjoy unless he loves? Augustine rightly says in De moribus Ecclesiae, chapter 3: "What else is it," he says, "to enjoy, than to have present what you love?" Indeed, not to love the true good, which a rational creature must enjoy in order to be blessed, is a plainly proven misery. For it is a languor of the soul, which arises from nothing else than from the love of some other thing. Hence Augustine says in the same place: "Blessed, as I judge, cannot be called the one who does not have what he loves, whatever it may be; nor the one who has what he loves, if it is harmful; nor the one who does not have what he loves, even if it is the best. For he who desires what he cannot obtain is tormented; he who has obtained what ought not to be desired is deceived; he who does not desire what ought to be obtained is sick." Plotinus also, almost beyond the grasp of the Gentiles, described that love. He indicates, speaking thus among other things in Enn. lib. IX. 9, that our good consists there, namely the love implanted in our soul, just as love joins souls together. Since the soul is from that good, it necessarily loves it. Now, when it lives there, it has heavenly love; but here it becomes common and vulgar. For there Venus reigns heavenly, but here vulgar, as if adulterated. Every love is Venus, as the birthday of Venus indicates, and love is born together with Venus. The soul, therefore, established in its natural condition, loves God, desiring to be mingled with God, aspiring to a fair virginity with honourable love, etc.

units.la: CXLI. Visio Dei cum pleno favoris Dei sensu conjuncta est. Penes Te est vena vitæ: In lumine tuo videmus lumen, Psal. XXXVI. 10. Inebriabuntur ab ubertate domus tuæ, & de torrente deliciarum tuarum, potabis eos, ibid. v. 9. Nam quos Deus in gloriam suam introducit, illos longè magis, quàm terrestris hospes & evergetes, ut amicos, imò filios lautè excipit, neque quomodocunque nutrit, sed quod sapidissimum est, domi suæ in penoribus suis, id non modò gustandum præbet, sed eo etiam imbuit & irrigat, & omne deliciarum suarum flumen in eos effundit. Id vero quale futurum sit, in hac vita non magis nosse, quam Deum videre datur. Quod si in hac vita charitas Dei effunditur in cordibus nostris, per Spiritum S. qui nobis datus est, Rom. V. 5. quia objectum fidei nostrae, amor Dei effusissimus totum cor nostrum implet, & ad Deum, ac quicquid in Deo est, tanquam unicum solum & cibum & gaudium rapit, & convertit, eumque amorem tam certum habemus & sentimus, ac si eum in corde Dei cerneremus; quem non sensum amoris & favoris aspectus ipse, ejusque objectum, facies Dei, quam cum sua bonorum omnium plenitudine visuri sumus, pariet? Non enim amplius per fidem ambulavimus, sed per aspectum, 2. Cor. V. 7. & videbimus a facie ad faciem, 1. Cor. XIII. 12. Facies equidem Dei aliquando ejus iram atque furorem, Levit. XVII. 10. XXVI. 17. 2. Thess. I. 9. aliquando favorem & gratiam notat. Cumque in lumine Dei lumen Dei visuri simus, Psal. XXXVI. 10. & faciem Dei simul visuri simus, erit igitur illhoc lumen אור פנים lumen faciei Dei, quod semper singularem favorem & gratiam Dei, ejusque sensum plenum signis favoris & gratiae notat. Lucere faciat Jehova faciem suam super te, & misereatur tui, Num. VI. 25. Eleva super nos lucem faciei tuae, Jehova, Psal. IV. 7. hoc est, benignitatem tuam ostende, demonstrando bonum iis, qui te quaerunt. Fac lucere faciem tuam super servum tuum, ibid. XXXI. 17.
