Sicut nempe in hac vita signum favoris & gratiae eximiae est, si quem Rex vel Princeps in secretius conclave ad faciem suam admiserit, laeto, sereno & lucido vultu eundem intuitus fuerit, juxta illud Solomonis: באור פני מלך חיים In lumine faciei Regis vita est, Prov. XVI. 15. ita visio Divinae faciei arguit, Deum beatos summo amore complecti, cum iis familiarissime & suavissime consuescere & conversari, ut sint populus ejus, & ipse Deus eorum, Apoc. XXI. 3. Atque eundem favoris Dei inusitati & plenissimi sensum Christus pluribus verbis promisit dicens: Beati pauperes Spiritu quia eorum est Regnum Coelorum. Beati lugentes, quia consolationem accipient. Beati esurientes & sitientes justitiam, quia saturabuntur. Beati mundi corde, quia videbunt Deum, &c. Matth. V. 3. &c.
units.tr: CXLI. The sight of God is joined with the full sense of God's favour. With thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light, Ps. XXXVI. 10. They shall be abundantly satisfied with the fatness of thy house; and thou shalt make them drink of the river of thy pleasures, ibid. v. 9. For those whom God brings into his glory, he receives far more lavishly than an earthly host and benefactor receives his friends, or rather his sons: he feeds them not in any ordinary way, but with what is most savoury, from his own store-rooms; and he not only offers it to be tasted but also steeps and waters them with it, pouring out upon them the whole river of his delights. What this will be like in the future, we are no more permitted to know in this life than to see God. But if in this life the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit which is given unto us, Rom. V. 5, because the object of our faith, the most abundant love of God, fills our whole heart and draws and turns it to God, and to whatever is in God, as its only treasure, food and joy; and if we hold and feel that love as certainly as if we beheld it in the heart of God: what sense of love and favour will the very sight of the face of God, and its object, produce, when we shall see it with the fullness of all good things? For we walk by faith, not by sight, 2 Cor. V. 7, and we shall see face to face, 1 Cor. XIII. 12. Indeed the face of God sometimes denotes his wrath and fury, Lev. XVII. 10, XXVI. 17, 2 Thess. I. 9, and sometimes his favour and grace. And since we shall see the light of God in the light of God, Ps. XXXVI. 10, and shall see the face of God at the same time, this light will therefore be אור פנים [or panim] "the light of the face of God", which always denotes the singular favour and grace of God, and his sense of it, full of signs of favour and grace. The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee, Num. VI. 25. Lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us, O LORD, Ps. IV. 7, that is, show your kindness, by showing good to those who seek you. Make thy face to shine upon thy servant, ibid. XXXI. 17. Just as in this life it is clearly a sign of great favour, if a king or prince admits someone into his more private chamber and looks upon him with a joyful, serene and bright countenance, according to that saying of Solomon: באור פני מלך חיים [In the light of the king's face is life], Prov. XVI. 15, so the sight of the divine face proves that God embraces the blessed with the highest love, and lives with them most intimately and sweetly, so that they are his people and he himself is their God, Rev. XXI. 3. And Christ promised this same sense of the unusual and most full favour of God in several words, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God, etc., Matt. V. 3, etc.

units.la: CXLII. Plenus ille favoris Dei sensus ἐξαναπαυσιν acquiescentiam in Deo comitem habebit. Acquiescentiam in Summo Bono hac etiam in vita testatus est Asaphus, dicens: Quis mihi est in Coelo? Et praeter Te לא חפצתי nulla re delectior in terra. Defecit caro mea, & cor meum. Rupes cordis mei, & pars mea est Deus in seculum, Psal. LXXIII. 26. 27. Testatus est Petrus, dicens ad Christum: Domine, ad quem abibimus? Tu verba vitae aeterna habes, Joh. VI. 68. Major sic exclamandi, sic interrogandi fiducia erit in altera vita, ubi haec mera, non mixta, sicut in hac vita, erunt. Non enim ibi delectationis perturbatio & frigus a peccato, carne, tentatione & miseria, quae in hac vita reliqua est, erit: non nausea & fastidium rerum discruciantium, quae יהפ voluptatem & delectationem in Deo minuat. Ego in justitia tua videbo vultum tuum: Satiabor, cum evigilavero, specie tua, Psal. XVII. 15. Videbimus enim sine obscuritate & nube, illuminatis oculis mentis nostrae, ut Deum & gloriam ejus ferant; & voluntas nostra depositia fame, siti, mutabilitate, bono sic viso satiabitur, & in eo penitus acquiescet, neque aliud praeterea ad vitam & laetitiam desiderabit.
units.tr: CXLII. That full sense of God's favour will have as its companion a resting [ἀνάπαυσις] in God. Asaph bore witness to this resting in the Supreme Good even in this life, saying: Whom have I in heaven but thee? And there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever, Ps. LXXIII. 25, 26. Peter bore witness, saying to Christ: Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life, John VI. 68. Such confidence in crying out and asking will be greater in the other life, where these things will be pure, not mixed as they are in this life. For there will be no disturbance of delight and no chill from sin, flesh, temptation and the misery that remains in this life; no nausea and disgust at things that torment, which would diminish the pleasure and delight in God. As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness, Ps. XVII. 15. For we shall see without obscurity and cloud, our mind's eyes being enlightened, so that they may bear God and his glory; and our will, freed from hunger, thirst and mutability, will be satisfied by the good seen in this way, and will rest fully in it, and will desire nothing else besides for life and happiness.

units.la: CXLIII. Etiam ineffabilem laetitiam sic David, vel Christus potius expressit: שבע satietas laetitiarum (non unius vel simplicis laetitiae) apud faciem tuam, נעמות amoenitatem, quae sunt in dextra tua perpetuo, Psal. XVI. 11. Alibi: Accedam אל אל שמחה גילי ad Deum fortem, omnipotentem, laetitiam gaudii mei, ibid. XLIII. 4. Crescit enim laetitia ad gaudium, quia שמחה laetitia est suavitas, quae sentitur ex perceptione rei jucundae praesentis גיל gaudium vel ἀγαλλίασις exultatio motus ad bonum praesens vel absens. Id amplius etiam explicat alibi: Multi dicunt, inquiens, o quis faciet nos videre bonum! Attolle super nos lucem vultus tui, Jehova. Dedisti laetitiam in cor meum ex tempore, quo frumentum eorum & mustum abundarunt. In pace simul cubabo & dormiam. Nam tu, Jehova, solus tuto me habitare fecisti, Psal. IV. 7. 8. 9. Laetitiam enim, quam in hac vita percipimus ex propriis & alienis benedictionibus infinitis parasangis minorem esse illa, quam in altera vita, Deo lucem vultus sui super nos attollente, percepturi sumus, ostendit. Quid enim gaudii temporalis, seu potius absinthii guttulae ad mellis oceanum, immensum, optimum, maximum bonum? Si igitur in hac vita Deum, quem non videmus, amamus, & in eum nunc non videntes, credentes tamen, exultamus χαρᾷ ἀνεκλαλήτῳ καὶ δεδοξασμένῃ laetitia ineffabili & gloriosa (superante omnem opinionem hominum, per totam vitam se extendente, omnes vitae casus edulcante, sensum sui in maxima varietate perpetuum afferente, gloriosa inprimis & digna operatione Spiritus S. Christo, justitia ejus, Deo, sanctitate & magnitudine ejus, filiis Dei, fide, veritate & spe, quae nunquam pudefacit) 1. Petr. I. 8. quanto magis, cum Deum visuri sumus laetitia ἀνεκλάλητῳ καὶ δεδοξασμένῃ ineffabilis & glorificata erit? Nam justi laetabuntur ילי לפני אלהים exultabunt coram Deo, & bilaescent in laetitia, Psal. LXVIII. 4. Quod cum in hac vita per consolationem & pacem animi, charitatem, in qua motus est, & patientiam crucis contingat; multo enixius continget in altera, ubi adversa & laetitiam infestantia omnia procul aberunt; Delebit enim Deus omnem lachrymam ab omni facie, Esaj. XXV. 8. Redempti Domini revertentur, & venient in Sion cum laude: & laetitia sempiterna erit super caput eorum, gaudium & laetitia apprehendet eos, & fugient dolor ac gemitus, ibid. XXXV. 10. Ecce servi mei edent, & vos esurietis. Ecce servi mei bibent, & vos sitietis. Ecce servi mei laetabuntur, & vos pudefietis. Ecce servi mei cantabunt prae bono, & vos clamabitis prae dolore cordis. שמח גילו עדי עד Exultate & gaudete in seculum, in eo, quod ego creo, Esaj. LXV. 13. 14. 18. Serve bone & fidelis, intra in gaudium Domini tui, Matth. XXV. 21. 23. Ubi scite Thomas: Tum gaudet homo ut Dominus, cum fruitur ut Dominus. Quo sensu etiam super mensam Domini edere & bibere dicuntur, Luc. XXII. 30. χαίρωμεν ἡ ἀγαλλιώμεθα laetemur. mur & exultemus,& dewus gloriam ipsi,quoniam venerunt nuptiæ Agni, & uxor ejus se præparavit,Apoc XIX. 7. Deus potens est vos statuere in conspectu gloriæ suæ incontaminatos, ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει in exultatione,Jud. v. 24. Quæ causa est, quòd etiam Philosophi Beatitudinem voluptate, gaudio,suavitate definiverunt. Nam Aristoteles Magn. Moral. lib. II. 7. Τὴν εὐδαιμονίαν, inquit, οἴονται πάντες ἡδονὴν εἶναι, καὶ τὸ ἡδέως ζῆν, ἢ ἁπλῶς ἀνάγε ἡδονῆς. Beatitudinem omnes putant voluptatem esse, & suaviter, vel saltem non sine voluptate vivere. Et Eudæm. lib. VII. 15. Ὁ ἀληθῶς εὐδαίμων ἡδέως ζῇ, καὶ τοῦτο ἀμάτλω ἀνθρωπος ἀξιῶσι. Qui revera beatus est, jucundissimè vivit. Et hoc non sine causa homines arbitrantur. Denique Rhetor. lib. I. 5. beatitudinem definit τὸν βίον μετ' ἀσφαλείας ἡδὺν vitam cum securitate suavissimam. Verùm illi plerunque voluptatem & gaudium in nescio qua umbratili καταγαθία collocantes, tanquam Polyphemi miseri in caliginoso antro oberrarunt, & pro vera voluptate misererimam ejus umbram prensarunt.
units.tr: CXLIII. David, or rather Christ, also expressed this inexpressible joy in these words: a satiety of joys (not of one simple joy) [שבע] before your face, pleasures [נעמות] which are at your right hand forever, Psal. XVI. 11. Elsewhere: I will go to God, the mighty God [אל אל], the joy of my gladness [שמחה גילי], ibid. XLIII. 4. Joy [laetitia] grows into gladness [gaudium], since שמחה [simcha] is the sweetness felt from the perception of a pleasant thing that is present, and גיל [gil], or ἀγαλλίασις [exultation], is the movement toward a good that is present or absent. He explains this more fully elsewhere: Many say, "Oh, who will show us good things!" Lift up over us the light of your face, Jehovah. You have put gladness in my heart, from the time when their grain and wine abounded. In peace I will both lie down and sleep, for you alone, Jehovah, have made me dwell safely, Psal. IV. 7, 8, 9. For he shows that the joy we perceive in this life, from our own and others' blessings, is less by infinite parasangs than that which we shall receive in the other life, when God lifts up the light of his face over us. For what is temporal joy, or rather a few drops of wormwood compared with the ocean of honey, the immense, best and greatest good? If therefore in this life we love God, whom we do not see, and in him, though now not seeing but believing, we exult with joy ineffable and full of glory (χαρᾷ ἀνεκλαλήτῳ καὶ δεδοξασμένῃ), surpassing all human opinion, extending through the whole of life, sweetening every event of life, bringing a sense of himself that lasts through the greatest variety, glorious above all and worthy of the work of the Holy Spirit; to Christ, to his righteousness, to God, to his holiness and greatness, to the sons of God, through faith, truth and hope, which never puts to shame, 1 Pet. I. 8. How much more, when we shall see God, will the joy be ineffable and glorified (ἀνεκλάλητῳ καὶ δεδοξασμένῃ)? For the just shall rejoice: they shall exult before God and be glad with joy [ילי לפני אלהים; ביל], Psal. LXVIII. 4. Since this happens in this life through the consolation and peace of mind, through charity, in which the emotion moves, and through patience in the cross, it will happen much more eagerly in the other life, where adversities and everything that disturbs joy will be far away. For God will wipe away every tear from every face, Isa. XXV. 8. The redeemed of the Lord shall return and come to Zion with praise, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away, ibid. XXXV. 10. Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry. Behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty. Behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame. Behold, my servants shall sing for good, but you shall cry out from heartache, Isa. LXV. 13, 14. Exult and rejoice forever in what I create [שמח גילו עדי עד], ibid. 18. Good and faithful servant, enter into the joy of your Lord, Matth. XXV. 21, 23. Where Thomas rightly says: Then a man rejoices as the Lord, when he enjoys as the Lord. In this sense also they are said to eat and drink at the table of the Lord, Luke XXII. 30. Let us rejoice and exult (χαίρωμεν ἡ ἀγαλλιώμεθα), and give glory to him, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself, Apoc. XIX. 7. God is able to set you before his presence, without blemish, in exultation (ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει), Jude v. 24. This is why philosophers also defined blessedness in terms of pleasure, joy and sweetness. For Aristotle, Magna Moralia II. 7, says: "All men think blessedness is pleasure, and living pleasantly, or at least living not without pleasure." And Eudemian Ethics VII. 15: "He who is truly blessed lives most pleasantly, and men think this is not without reason." Finally, Rhetoric I. 5 defines blessedness as life most sweet with security (τὸν βίον μετ' ἀσφαλείας ἡδύν). Yet they, for the most part placing pleasure and joy in some shadowy good-state (καταγαθία), wandered like wretched Polyphemus in his dark cave, and grasped at his most miserable shadow instead of true pleasure.

units.la: CXLIV. Enimverò gaudium illud gaudiosissimum in solo Deo erit,utpote qui erit omnia in omnibus, 1. Corinth. XV. 28. & se una cum omnibus ἁγίοις suis fidelibus omnibus penitus atque intimè tractandum, gustandum, fruendum præbebit. Et gaudium erit hominis totius, secundum animam & corpus, sed pro objecti ratione, spirituale totum. Nam & ipso Christo oculis corporis videndo gaudium spirituale & inexplicabile occupabitur.
units.tr: CXLIV. Indeed that most joyful joy will be in God alone, since he will be all in all, 1 Cor. XV. 28, and will offer himself, together with all his saints and faithful, to be handled, tasted and enjoyed fully and most intimately by all. The joy will belong to the whole man, body and soul, but, according to the nature of its object, it will be wholly spiritual. For even in seeing Christ himself with bodily eyes, the mind will be occupied with a spiritual and inexplicable joy.

units.la: Licèt enim Scriptura gaudium illud rerum corporearum, velut deliciarum Paradisi, Luc. XXIII. 43. nuptiarum solennium, Apoc. XIX. 9. lætitiæ convivialis, Matth. VIII. 11. figura commendet, & esum ac potum, Apoc. II. 7. citharæ cantum, ib. V. 8. 9. omniúmque deliciarum cumulum, Psal. XXXVI. 9. Matth. V. 4. 12. Luc. XVI. 25. Joh. XVI. 22. in æterna vita promittat,non tamen hæc & similia corporaliter, uti Judæi & Muhammedani somniant, sed spiritualiter intelligi debent. Omnes enim suavitates mundi hujus immundi serperastra sunt, quibus ad consiberationem, æstimationem, & desiderium fruitionis Dei ipsius, ut boni nostri summi & unici, erigimur. Non enim voluptates corporis propter ipsas voluptates in hac, nedum in altera æterna vita, appetere licet, quem errorem verè belluinum Jansenius de statu Nat. lapsæ lib. II. 15. Scholasticis nonnullis, quos Catholicos nullo jure vocat, impingit.
units.tr: For although Scripture uses bodily things to set forth that joy as figures of the delights of Paradise, Luke XXIII. 43; of solemn weddings, Apoc. XIX. 9; of festive gladness, Matth. VIII. 11; and promises in eternal life eating and drinking, Apoc. II. 7, the singing of the harp, ibid. V. 8, 9, and a heap of all delights, Psal. XXXVI. 9; Matth. V. 4, 12; Luke XVI. 25; John XVI. 22; these and similar things must not be understood bodily, as the Jews and Muhammadans dream, but spiritually. For all the sweetnesses of this unclean world are shadows by which we are raised to the contemplation, esteem and desire of enjoying God himself, as our highest and only good. For it is not lawful to desire bodily pleasures for their own sake in this life, much less in the other, eternal life. That is a truly bestial error, which Jansenius, in De statu naturae lapsae II. 15, charges upon some Scholastics, whom he calls Catholics without any right.

units.la: Nam quod propter se expetitur, summum hominis Bonum est. Neque errorem minuit, quòd voluptates moderatas propter se appetendas esse definiant, quia, uti recte Jansenius, cupiditas moderationem non recipit, sed tollenda atque extirpanda est radicitus, in quo omnis labor, omne certamen, omnis gemitus spiritualium virorum occupatur. Perversa Philosophia, vel potius Theologia est, quæ non interitum affert pravitatis, sed moderatione vitiorum contenta est. Nec video, qui differat sententia ista ab opinione Epicuri, nisi quod ille solam voluptatem, hi honestatem simul cum voluptate per se expeti posse fateantur. Sed Epicuri dogma fugiendo, in Calliphonis ac Dicomachi errorem, quem etiam Pelagianorum antesignanus, Julianus, amplexus est, incidunt. Hominem, inquit Tullius, jungunt cum bellua, ut Calliphon, qui honestatem cum voluptate conjungunt. Verissimè ita Jansenii adversus Catholicos suos. Addimus Augustini regulam, utriusq; Testamenti literis confirmatam: Jubet æterna Lex avertere amorem a temporalibus, & eum mandatum ad æterna convertere.
units.tr: For what is desired for its own sake is man's highest good. Nor does it lessen the error that they define moderate pleasures as to be desired for their own sake, since, as Jansenius rightly says, desire does not admit of moderation but must be removed and uprooted entirely; this is where all the labour, struggle and groaning of spiritual men are spent. It is a perverse philosophy, or rather theology, which does not aim at the destruction of wickedness but is content with the moderation of vices. Nor do I see how this opinion differs from that of Epicurus, except that he admits only pleasure to be desired for its own sake, while they admit honesty together with pleasure. But in fleeing the doctrine of Epicurus they fall into the error of Callipho and Dicomachus, which Julian, the forerunner of the Pelagians, also embraced. Tully says: "They join man with a beast, as Callipho does, who joins honesty with pleasure." Very truly so does Jansenius speak against his own Catholics. We add Augustine's rule, confirmed by the letters of both Testaments: the eternal law commands us to turn love away from temporal things and to direct it toward eternal ones.

units.la: CXLV. Ex visione beatifica Dei etiam perfecta imaginis Divinæ communio sequitur.
units.tr: CXLV. The full communion with the divine image also follows from the beatific vision of God.

units.la: Nam similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est, 1. Joh. III. 2. Sicut enim puritas & mundities speculi requiritur, ut imago in eo fulgeat, & plena conspiciatur; ita animæ & corporis perfecta mundities in beatis erit, ut Deum videre, ejúsque imaginem perfectè repræsentare possint. Beati mundi corde, quia Deum videbunt, Matth. V. 8. Nam quos præscivit, eos etiam prædestinavit συμμόρφους τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ Υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ, ut conformes sint imagini Filii sui, ut sit primogenitus inter multos fratres, Rom. VIII. 29. Ubi præscitos etiam ante destinatos esse, ut sint conformes imagini Filii Dei in gloria, quia interest gloriæ Filii Dei, ut sint sicut ipse est, ut ipse glorificetur in iis, ut caput ipsorum; cujus Spiritum acceperunt, docet. Filio ergo Dei conformabimur in gloria, ut quod ipse in anima & corpore habet, etiam nos tanquam corpus & membra ejus habeamus.
units.tr: For we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Just as the purity and cleanness of a mirror is required for an image to shine in it and be seen whole, so in the blessed there will be a perfect cleanness of soul and body, so that they can see God and perfectly represent his image. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt. 5:8). For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed [συμμόρφους] to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers (Rom. 8:29). Here he teaches that those whom he foreknew were also predestined beforehand to be conformed to the image of the Son of God in glory. This is because it concerns the glory of the Son of God that they should be as he is, and that he should be glorified in them as their head, whose Spirit they have received. We shall therefore be conformed to the Son of God in glory, so that we too, as his body and members, shall have what he himself has in soul and body.

units.la: Debemus enim per maxima & pretiosa promissa nobis donata fieri κοινωνοὶ θείας φύσεως participes Divinæ naturæ. 2. Pet. I. 4. hoc est, assimilari ei, imago ejus perfecta fieri, quatenus corruptionem concupiscentiæ, quæ in mundo est, perfectè effugimus, & amorem incorruptibilem & corpus incorruptibile habemus. Et in hac quidem vita imago Dei peccato perdita per regenerationis gratiam restituitur, sed manente carne & peccato, veteris hominis λείμματι: in altera verò restituitur in solidum, non tantùm qualem Adamus habuit instatu integro, sed etiam qualem in statu cœlesti & gloriosò adepturus erat.
units.tr: For through the very great and precious promises given to us we are to become sharers [κοινωνοὶ] in the divine nature (2 Pet. 1:4). That is, we are to be made like him and to become his perfect image, in so far as we fully escape the corruption of desire that is in the world, and have an incorruptible love and an incorruptible body. In this life, indeed, the image of God, lost through sin, is restored by the grace of regeneration; but while the flesh and sin remain, there is only a remnant [λεῖμμα] of the old man. In the other life, however, the image is restored entirely, not merely as Adam had it in his state of integrity, but as he was to attain it in the heavenly and glorious state.

units.la: Nam revelata facie τὴν δόξαν τοῦ Κυρίου κατοπτριζόμενοι gloriam Domini intuentes, vel tanquam speculum accipientes ad eandem imaginem transformamur à gloria in gloriam, tanquam à Spiritu Domini, 2. Cor. III. 18. Renovatio enim nostri magis magisque, donec ad imaginem Christi perveniamus, & gloria Christi in nobis plenè perfectèque relucet. Transformamur à gloria hujus vitæ ad gloriam alterius. Una alteram præcedit & pollicetur atque asportat. Sicut primitiæ futuræ messis: ita imaginis Divinæ renovatio in hac vita secuturæ in vita æterna renovationis & ἀποκαταστάσεως restitutionis plenariæ, testimonium est. Tum enim demum filii Dei gloriosiore modo erimus, quando sic imago Dei perfectè fulgebit. Quò enim perfectior Patris in Filio imago est, hoc perfectior filiatio est. Nos ipsi, qui primitias Spiritus S. habemus, & intra nos gemimus, expectantes υἱοθεσίαν filiationem, redemptionem corporis nostri, Rom. VIII. 23.
units.tr: For with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord [τὴν δόξαν τοῦ Κυρίου κατοπτριζόμενοι], as in a mirror, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18). Our renewal goes on more and more until we attain to the image of Christ, and the glory of Christ shines fully and perfectly in us. We are transformed from the glory of this life to the glory of the other. One goes before the other, promises it, and carries us toward it. As the firstfruits are a pledge of the coming harvest, so the renewal of the divine image that begins in this life is a witness to the full restoration [ἀποκατάστασις] of renewal in eternal life. For then at last we shall be the sons of God in a more glorious way, when the image of God shines perfectly. The more perfect the image of the Father in the Son, the more perfect the sonship. We ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit and groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption [υἱοθεσία], the redemption of our body (Rom. 8:23).

units.la: CXLVI. Divinæ imaginis illius perfectio in anima æquè atque in corpore fulgebit.
units.tr: CXLVI. That perfection of the divine image will shine as much in the soul as in the body.

units.la: Nam animæ potentiæ omnes intellectus, voluntas & potestas Deo similimæ erunt, quantum id, quod creatum est, Deo assimilari potest. Intellectum perfecta sapientia & cognitio Dei atque mysteriorum ejus perficiet. Abolebuntur enim omnes cogitationes pueriles, & viriles atque maturæ succedent. Ex parte cognoscimus & ex parte prophetamus, cùm autem venerit,
units.tr: For all the powers of the soul, understanding, will and capacity, will be most like God, as far as what is created can be made like God. Perfect wisdom and the knowledge of God and of his mysteries will perfect the understanding. For all childish thoughts will be abolished, and mature and manly ones will take their place. We know in part and we prophesy in part, but when that which is perfect comes,

units.la: bbbbb 2 nerit, quod perfectum est, tum, quod ex parte est, abolebitur. Cum essem infans, loquebar ut infans, ut infans cogitabam, ut infans sentiebam. Postquam autem vir factus sum, abolevi, quae sunt infantis, 1.Cor.XIII.9.10.11. Virilis illius perfectionis ᾐκμή & eminentia in altera vita obtinebit: Unde statim subjicitur: Videmus nunc in speculo (per radios reflexos, saepe a speculo inquinatos & coloratos, non recte redditos, & in parte non redditos, ut dextra videantur, quae sinistra sunt, & vicissim) in aenigmate (obscure & per ambages atque anfractus) Tunc vero a facie ad faciem, &c. v.12. Tam ergo plene & perfecte intelligemus illa, ad quorum intelligentiam stupor nolter in hac vita pertingere potis non est; Veluti, quomodo tres personae in unitate essentiae sint. Filius ab aeterno a Patre genitus sit; Filius & Spiritus S. a Patre procedant; Naturae in Christo unitae sint: Deus omnia ex nihilo condiderit; ab aeterno hos elegerit, alios reprobaverit. Etiam novos Coelos & novam terram, omniumque creaturarum penetralia, & intimos recessus cognoscere dabitur. Etiam invicem beati se dignoscent. Licet enim carnales & terreni affectus in Coeli municipibus locum habituri non sint, & affectus ejusmodi omnes unius Dei, in quo solo deliciabimur, & in cujus solius beneplacito suavissime, sine ulla querela recumbemus, studium & amor absorpturus sit, & coelicolas omnes, atque universum beatorum chorum ex aequo culturi & dilecturi simus, tamen notos olim, ac in Ecclesia Dei cognitos, praesertim majoris dignitatis viros, Apostolos, Martyres, aliosque Ecclesiae antesignanos, quin & parentes, liberos, propinquos & amicos multo certius agnituri & discreturi sumus, quam vel Adamus Evam, ex costa sua creatam, licet nunquam visam hactenus, sic cognovit, ut sine ullius indicio statim haec in verba eruperit: Hac vice est os ex ossibus meis, & caro de carne mea, Gen.II.23 vel Apostoli Moses & Eliam in monte cum Christo colloquentes, Matth.XVII.3.4. Et si damnati videbunt Abrahamum, Isacum & Jacobum, omnesque Prophetas in Regno Dei, Luc.XIII.28. quanto magis beati videbunt; in eadem mensa cum iisdem accubituri? Matth.VIII.11.12. Rerum porro ad vitam temporalem spectantium, aliarumque artium & studiorum inanium & futilium jacturam facile & eleganter ferent; uti etiam in hac vita homines aetatis provectioris puerilium nugarum aequo animo oblivescuntur, & quae juvenes didicere, senes perdenda fatentur. Caeteroquin ratio non apparet, cur memoria rerum hominumque, quos in terris superstites reliquerunt, quatenus illa tristitiae exsors esse potest, & ad Deum laudandum ac glorificandum facit, abolenda sit. Spiritualium inprimis rerum notitia non peribit, sed multiplice luce augebitur, & consummabitur. Denique nec Ecclesiae in terra militantis conditionis statusque ejus universi, pugnarum atque certaminum memoria eos fugiet: Clamabunt voce magna dicentes: Quousque o qui es Dominus sanctus & verax, non vindicas sanguinem nostrum ab iis, qui habitant in terra? Apoc.VI.10. Sed personarum & rerum singularum nullam conscientiam habebunt. Neque his omnibus obstat illud, quod Apostolus dixit; H' γνώσις κατρι-
units.tr: then what is in part will be abolished (1 Cor. 13:9–11). When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child, I felt as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things. The strength and eminence of that manly perfection will hold good in the other life. Hence it is immediately added: We now see in a mirror (through reflected rays, often dimmed and coloured by the mirror, not rightly returned, and in part not returned, so that the right hand appears as the left and vice versa) in a riddle (obscurely and through circumlocutions and windings). But then face to face, etc. (v. 12). So we shall understand fully and perfectly those things to whose understanding our dullness cannot attain in this life: for example, how three persons are in the unity of the essence; that the Son was begotten by the Father from eternity; that the Son and the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father; how the natures are united in Christ; that God created all things out of nothing; that he chose some from eternity and rejected others. We shall also be given to know the new heavens and new earth, and the innermost parts and secret recesses of all creatures. The blessed will also know one another. For although carnal and earthly affections will have no place among the citizens of heaven, and all such affections will be swallowed up in the study and love of the one God alone, in whom alone we shall delight and in whose good pleasure alone we shall rest most sweetly without any complaint, and though we shall equally worship and love all the inhabitants of heaven and the whole company of the blessed, nevertheless we shall recognise and distinguish far more certainly those once known and acknowledged in the Church of God, especially men of greater dignity, the apostles, martyrs and other leaders of the Church, and indeed our parents, children, relatives and friends. Adam knew Eve, created from his rib, though he had never seen her before, so well that without any prompting he burst out at once with these words: This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh (Gen. 2:23). Or the apostles Moses and Elijah talking with Christ on the mountain (Matt. 17:3–4). And if the damned see Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God (Luke 13:28), how much more will the blessed see them, and recline at the same table with them (Matt. 8:11–12)? Moreover, they will easily and gracefully bear the loss of things belonging to temporal life, and of other arts and studies that are vain and trifling; just as in this life men of advanced age forget childish trifles with equanimity, and admit that what they learned as young men must be lost in old age. Otherwise there is no apparent reason why the memory of things and men they left behind as survivors on earth should be abolished, since, so far as it can be free of sorrow and serves to praise and glorify God, it may remain. Above all, the knowledge of spiritual things will not perish, but will be increased and perfected by a manifold light. Finally, the memory of the Church militant on earth, of her condition and state as a whole, and of her battles and struggles, will not escape them. They will cry with a loud voice, saying: How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? (Rev. 6:10). But they will have no awareness of individual persons and particular events. Nor does that saying of the Apostle stand in the way of all this: knowledge [ἡ γνῶσις]

units.la: γνώσις Cognotio abolebitur, 1.Cor.XIII.8.quia id non de universa cognitione, sed de ea, quae est εκ μέρος ex parte, & quae multiplice cura, studio & scientia ratiocinante, difficile ex facili, obscurum ex clariore colligente; non de ea, quae rei praesentis, quam coram intuebimur, est, intelligi debet. Sicut enim majus lumen obscurat minus: ita perfecta vitae alterius cognitio imperfectam hujus vitae abolebit. Praeclare de cognitione isthac beatorum Augustinus de tripl. habit. cap.6. In Dei visione trina scientia nascitur, hoc est, homo, qui cernit, Deus, qui cernitur, & caeteri omnes omnia videbunt & intelligent. Sicut enim per speculum vitreum trina nobis visio administratur, quia nos ipsos, & ipsum speculum, & quicquid praesens adest, videmus: Sic per speculum Divinae claritatis & ipsum Deum, uti est, videbimus, quantum possibile est creatura, & nos ipsos, & caeteros vera & certa scientia comprehendemus. Tunc abdita creaturarum & ipsius inferni videndo Deum videbimus. Tunc justis manifestum erit, quomodo Deus est invisibilis, incomparabilis, sine initio & fine, ante omnia; quid interfit inter nasci, quod ad Filium pertinet, & inter procedere, quod ad Spiritum S. quomodo Pater non praecesit Filium tempore, sed origine, nec Spiritum S. quomodo omnia Dei unum sint ex Deo, excepto, quod ad relationem pertinet: quomodo Deus ubique totus sine loco, magnus sine quantitate, bonus sine qualitate: & quomodo omnia penetrat munda & immunda sine sui pollutione. Hic nempe nox est: ibi dies erit. Hic in visione veritatis caligamus, ibi Deus ipse, tota veritas mentibus illucescet.
units.tr: knowledge will be abolished (1 Cor. 13:8). This must not be understood of all knowledge, but of that which is partial [ἐκ μέρους], which, by manifold care, study and reasoning, works out the difficult from the easy and the obscure from the clearer; it must not be understood of that knowledge which concerns a present thing that we shall see face to face. For just as a greater light obscures a lesser, so the perfect knowledge of the other life will abolish the imperfect knowledge of this one. Augustine speaks admirably of this knowledge of the blessed in De tripl. habit., ch. 6: In the vision of God a threefold knowledge arises, that is, the man who sees, God who is seen, and all the others, who will see and understand everything. For just as a threefold vision is given us through a glass window, because we see ourselves, the glass itself, and whatever is present before it, so through the mirror of the divine brightness we shall see God himself as he is, as far as a creature can, and we shall comprehend ourselves and others with true and certain knowledge. Then, by seeing God, we shall see the hidden things of creatures and of hell itself. Then it will be plain to the just how God is invisible and incomparable, without beginning and end, before all things; what the difference is between being begotten, which pertains to the Son, and proceeding, which pertains to the Holy Spirit; how the Father did not precede the Son in time but in origin, nor the Holy Spirit; how all the things of God are one from God, except what pertains to relation; how God is wholly everywhere without place, great without quantity, good without quality; and how he penetrates all things, clean and unclean, without being polluted. Here indeed it is night; there it will be day. Here we grope in the vision of truth; there God himself, the whole truth, will shine upon our minds.

units.la: CXLVII. Sicut beatitudo intellectum perfecta scientia: ita voluntatem sanitate & sanctitate, exactissima rectitudine & conformitate cum norma aeternae Legis & justitiae Dei, & perfecta atque immutabili bene agendi libertate, ab omni quippe peccati servitute & corruptione liberata, imbuet. Nam Summo Bono perfecte cognito voluntas inseparabiliter, sine ullo taedio & cum immutabili cursu, aeterno quippe, adhaerebit. In Deo enim, ceu bono infinito, omnia bona eminentissime continentur, & tota objecti voluntatis amplitudo & peripheria, in quam voluntas fertur, reperitur, ut nihil melius ab homine cogitari vel appeti possit. Proin beati per suam voluntatem se a Deo, quem jugiter videbunt, avertere non poterunt, neque aliud nisi in ordine ad objectum illud, in quo summa hominis perfectio, desiderii omnis complementum & finis ultimus continetur, & quo semel obtento, voluntas acquiescet, appetent. Nam ex natura status sui, visione beatifica & charitate atque amore delicatissimo, qui nihil peregrini vel fucati habebit; non ex Lege quapiam extrinseca, uti Scholastici opinantur, in bono immutabiliter confirmabuntur. Quomodo etiam Angeli semper videntes faciem Patris, qui in coelis est, Matth.XVIII.10. in bono confirmati, & ab omni peccandi periculo liberati intelliguntur. In statu integro poterat homo liber non peccare: in statu restituto & a peccato sanato idem liber non sic peccare poterit, ut irregenitus peccabat, poterit tamen ex residua infirmitate carnis: in vita aeterna idem liberrimus nullo modo peccare poterit. Neque enim immutabilitas illa & confir-
units.tr: CXLVII. Just as blessedness perfects the intellect with full knowledge, so it will imbue the will with soundness and holiness, with the most exact rectitude and conformity to the norm of the eternal Law and the justice of God, and with a perfect and unchangeable freedom to act well, since the will will be freed from all slavery and corruption of sin. For once the Highest Good is perfectly known, the will will cling to it inseparably, without any weariness, and with an unchanging course that is eternal. In God, as infinite good, all goods are contained in the most eminent way, and the whole breadth and circumference of the object toward which the will is carried is found there, so that nothing better can be thought or desired by a human being. Therefore the blessed, by their own will, will not be able to turn away from God, whom they will continually see, and they will desire nothing except in relation to that object, in which the highest perfection of man, the completion of every desire and the final end, is contained, and once it is obtained the will will find rest. For from the nature of their state, from the beatific vision and from charity and most refined love, which will have nothing foreign or feigned in it, they will be confirmed in good immutably; not by some external Law, as the Scholastics suppose. So too the Angels, who always see the face of the Father who is in heaven (Matth. XVIII.10), are understood to be confirmed in good and freed from every danger of sinning. In the state of integrity man was able, being free, not to sin; in the restored state, healed from sin, the same man, being free, will not be able to sin in the way he sinned while unregenerate, though he may still sin from the residual weakness of the flesh; in eternal life the same most free man will be unable to sin in any way. For that immutability and confirmation

units.la: Et ejusdem voluntatem plena sanitate & conformatione cum aeterna lege Dei, nec non immutabili libertate agendi perfecta. confirmatio in bono libertati bene agendi detrahet magis, quàm immutabilitas sanctitatis libertati Dei summæ, nec non Angelorum, detrahet. Quò enim voluntas bono suo arctiùs & immutabiliùs adhæret, hoc liberior est. Deus sibi sistet Ecclesiam gloriosam, maculis & rugis carentem, sanctam & inculpatam, Ephes. V.27. cujus salus erit æterna, & hereditas ejusmodi, ut nec corrumpi, nec inquinari, nec marcescere possit, 1.Pet.I.4. Deus statuet, præsentabit nos sibi ἁγίους sanctos, ἀμώμους sine vitio (ut ne Momus quidem quod carpat, inveniat) & ἀνεγκλήτους irreprehensibiles (ut ne hostes quidem ἔγκλημα quicquam accusatione dignum reperturi sint), Col.I.22. Hæ illæ stolæ albæ erunt, quibus coram throno Dei amicti comparebimus, Apoc.III.5. IV.4. VI.11. VII.9.13. Neque par ratio cognitionis & charitatis erit. Illa abolebitur, hæc δὲ ἐκπίπτει nunquam excidit, 1.Cor.XIII.8. non quòd charitas hujus vitæ non etiam habeat defectum, qui abolebitur & excidet; sed quidem non sicut cognitio ratione objecti cujusdam & modi abolebitur: ita etiam charitas ratione objecti & modi abolebitur. Retinebit enim semper idem objectum, Deum in Christo, qui solus per & propter se semper amandus est, & amabitur; & retinebit eundem amandi modum, qui nobiscum ex corpore discedit.
units.tr: and the full soundness of the same will, and its conformity with the eternal law of God, along with its perfect and unchangeable freedom to act, will take nothing away from the freedom to act well any more than the unchangeability of holiness takes away from the freedom of the supreme God and of the Angels. For the more closely and unchangeably the will clings to its good, the freer it is. God will present to himself a glorious Church, without spot or wrinkle, holy and blameless (Eph. V.27). Its salvation will be eternal, and its inheritance is of such a kind that it can neither be corrupted, nor defiled, nor fade (1 Pet. I.4). God will establish us and present us to himself as holy (ἁγίους), without blemish (ἀμώμους) (so that not even Momus could find anything to carp at), and irreproachable (ἀνεγκλήτους) (so that not even enemies could find any charge (ἔγκλημα) worthy of accusation) (Col. I.22). These are the white robes in which we shall appear before the throne of God, clothed in them (Apoc. III.5; IV.4; VI.11; VII.9, 13). Nor will knowledge and charity be of the same kind. The former will be abolished, while the latter never falls away [οὐδέποτε ἐκπίπτει] (1 Cor. XIII.8). This is not because the charity of this life also has no defect, which will be abolished and will fall away; but knowledge will not be abolished in the same way, with respect to a certain object and mode, as charity will be abolished with respect to object and mode. For charity will always retain the same object, God in Christ, who alone is, and will be, always to be loved for his own sake and through himself; and it will retain the same mode of loving, which departs with us from the body.

units.la: CXLVIII.
units.tr: CXLVIII.

units.la: Perfectæ sanitatis & sanctitatis, quæ in voluntate obtinebit, affectuum ejusdem sanitas & sanctitas comes erit. Omnes enim affectus & appetitus cum recta ratione Divino lumine collustrata πανταρμόσως convenient, & amicissimè conspirabunt. Nam in summo gradu amoris finiti Deum propter se, Angelos & beatos omnes, quin & se ipsos propter Deum amabunt, & malum omnne, malosque omnes perfectissimo & flagrantissimo odio prosequentur. Non ampliùs affectus & voluntates Dei & hominum discordabunt, sed conspirabunt in omnibus. Nullus enim, ut scitè Anselmus Epist.2. ad Hug. loquitur, ibi volet, nisi quod Deus, & quod volet unus, hoc volent omnes; & quod unus vel omnes, hoc Deus volet. Quapropter quicquid unusquisque volet, hoc erit de se ipso, & de omnibus aliis, & de tota creatura, & de ipso Deo. Et sic singuli erunt perfecti Reges, quia quod singuli volent, hoc erit; & omnes, simul cum Deo unus Rex, & quasi unus homo, quia omnes unum volent, & quod omnes volent, erit. Cùm enim intellectus plenitudine Divinæ lucis collustratus, & voluntas in omni bono confirmata Deo, Bono suo, ἀδιαστάτως adhærebit & erit ὁ κολλώμενος τῷ Κυρίῳ ἓν πνεῦμα agglutinatus Domino perfectissimè unus spiritus, propter unitatem Spiritus Christi & fidelium, 1. Cor. VI.17. affectus cordis pariter purissimi, castissimi, & ab omni ἀτάξια remotissimi erunt. Constabit, imò perficietur Divinus ille ordo, quo Deus voluntatem omnésque ejus affectus rationi ejúsque νόμος & dictamini subjecit, quem solum peccatum turbare potuit. Dilectio ipsa jucundissima, quietissima, pacatissima erit. Non metus, periculum, tristitia, terror ullus amantes percellet: ac ne spes quidem boni, velut absentis, vel boni præsentis anxia, ceu conjuncta cum periculo amittendi, vel expectatione solicita, obtinebit. Fructu entur enim bono suo beati jugiter & insatiabiliter.
units.tr: Together with the perfect soundness and holiness that the will will obtain, the soundness and holiness of the affections will accompany it. For all affections and appetites, illumined by the Divine light, will agree with right reason in perfect harmony [πανταρμόσως], and will work together most amicably. For at the highest degree of love they will love God for his own sake, and the Angels and all the blessed, and indeed themselves for God's sake; and they will pursue every evil and all evil people with the most perfect and burning hatred. The affections and wills of God and of men will no longer disagree, but will agree in everything. For, as Anselm rightly says in Epistle 2 to Hugh, no one there will will anything except what God wills, and what the one wills, all will will; and what the one or all will, God will will. Therefore whatever each one wills will be so, both concerning himself and concerning all others, and concerning the whole creation, and concerning God himself. And so each will be a perfect king, because whatever each wills will be; and all together, with God as the one King, and as if one man, because all will one thing, and what all will will be. For when the intellect, illumined by the fullness of Divine light, and the will, confirmed in every good, cling to God, their Good, without separation [ἀδιαστάτως], and become perfectly one spirit [ὁ κολλώμενος τῷ Κυρίῳ ἓν πνεῦμα], joined to the Lord, because of the unity of the Spirit of Christ and of the faithful (1 Cor. VI.17), the affections of the heart will likewise be most pure and chaste, and far removed from all disorder [ἀτάξια]. That divine order will stand, indeed it will be made perfect, by which God subjected the will and all its affections to reason and its law [νόμος] and dictate, an order which only sin could disturb. Love itself will be most joyful, most tranquil and most peaceful. No fear, danger, sadness or terror will strike those who love; nor will even hope for a good, as for a good absent or present, anxious because it is joined with the danger of losing it, or troubled by uncertain expectation, have any place. For the blessed will enjoy their good continually and without satiety.

units.la: CXLIX.
units.tr: CXLIX.

units.la: Neque etiam intellectus sapiens & voluntas sancta potestate, hoc est, intelligentiæ & voluntatis vi & efficacia destituetur. Imò & in hac Deo & Christo quodammodo assimilabitur. Qui vincit, dabo ei sedere in throno meo mecum; quemadmodum ego vici, & consedi cum Patre meo in throno ipsius, Apoc.III.21. Fidus sermo est, si cum ipso mortui fuerimus, etiam cum ipso regnabimus, 2.Tim.II.12. Cúmque beati futuri sint ἰσάγγελοι similes Angelis, non minor illorum, quàm horum potestas erit. Reges enim erunt, & cum Christo regnabunt, quod quomodo futurum sit, modò ex Anselmo exposuimus. Sed quantacunque tamen Regia illa potestas erit, finita erit, & Deo subjicietur. Etiam obedire Deo regnare est, quia sola obedientia Deo præstita liberos; sola libertas nulli creaturæ subjecta, & soli Deo, ceu summo bono, serviens, dominos Regéque facit. Neque adeò potestas Beatorum sic amplificanda est, ac si Mediatoriæ potestatis participes generis humani in Cœlo advocatione fungerentur: de quo supra pluribus.
units.tr: Nor will the wise understanding and the holy will be deprived of power, that is, of the force and efficacy of understanding and will. Indeed, in this respect they will to some extent be made like God and Christ: "He that overcometh, will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne" (Rev. 3:21). "It is a faithful saying: For if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him" (2 Tim. 2:11–12), and "we shall also reign with him." Since the blessed are to be made [ἰσάγγελοι] "equal unto the angels" (Luke 20:36), their power will be no less than the angels', for they will be kings and will reign with Christ. How this is to be, we have already explained for now from Anselm. Yet however great that royal power will be, it will be limited and subject to God. Even reigning is obeying God, because only obedience rendered to God makes free, and only freedom, subject to no creature and serving God alone as the supreme good, makes lords and kings. Nor is the power of the blessed to be enlarged in such a way as if the partakers of the mediatorial power, the human race, were to act as advocates in heaven, a point discussed above at length.

units.la: CL. Neque anima duntaxat, sed etiam corpus hominis Beati gloria implebitur, & imagini corporis Christi assimilabitur. Jesus Christus transfigurabit corpus nostrum humile, ut fiat conforme corpori gloriæ suæ, juxta efficaciam, qua potest sibi subjicere omnia, Phil.III.21. Ubi συμμορφον γενέσθαι τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης conforme, ejusdem formæ & conditionis fieri corpori gloriæ Christi, seu corpori Christi glorioso, brabeon cœlestis vocationis (v.14.) ponitur. Sicut enim gestavimus imaginem pulverei, ita gestabimus imaginem cœlestis Adami secundi, 1.Cor.XV.49. Expectamus ἀπολύτρωσιν adoptionem, τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν σώματος ἡμῶν redemptionem corporis nostri, Rom.VIII.23. Redemptio igitur corporis adoptionis nostræ, quam per regenerationem Spiritus S. consecuti sumus, & redemptionis, quæ in Christo est, plenus fructus est. Pendet enim à morte Christi, ceu pretio, quo Christus & animam & corpus nostrum sibi emit, 1.Cor. VI.19.20. Estque illa redemptio liberatio à miseria & corruptione corporis omni, & ejusdem cum incorruptibilitate & felicitate permutatio, in qua μεταχρηματισμὸς transfiguratio corporis consistet. Manente enim substantia corporis mutabuntur ejusdem qualitates, ut ignobilitati gloria succedat. Id ipsum etiam ostendit analogia oppositi, nempe miseriæ, cui totus homo mancipatur. Alioquin enim resurrectio carnis supervacanea foret. Hoc namque etiam pertinet ad munus Christi, ut sicut corpus suum immune præstitit à corruptione, & illud in æternam vitam vivificavit, atque in cœlo collocavit, ceu Spiritus vivificans: ita nostro corpori, quod ei conformari, & cum ipso esse debet, idem faciet. Ipse enim est structor templi Dei, quod corpus ejus & nostrum est, Zach.VI.12.13. In templo Dei non debet esse mors, corruptio, iniquitas, potestas & potentia aliena, defectus vel indigentia. Ubi Deus omnia in omnibus est, 1.Cor.XV.28. ibi ipse quoque vita in corporibus est.
units.tr: CL. The blessed glory will fill not only the soul but also the body of man, and it will be made like the image of Christ's body. Jesus Christ "shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself" (Phil. 3:21). There, to be conformed [συμμορφον γενέσθαι τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης] to the glorious body, that is, to be of the same form and condition as the glorious body of Christ, is set forth as "the prize of the high calling" (v. 14). "As we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly" Adam, the second Adam (1 Cor. 15:49). "We wait for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body" [τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν σώματος ἡμῶν] (Rom. 8:23). Therefore the redemption of the body is the full fruit of the adoption which we have obtained through the regeneration of the Holy Spirit, and of the redemption which is in Christ. For it depends on the death of Christ as the price by which Christ bought both our soul and our body for himself (1 Cor. 6:19–20). This redemption is a deliverance from all misery and corruption of the body, and an exchange of it for incorruptibility and happiness, and in it the [μεταχρηματισμὸς] transfiguration of the body will consist. For while the substance of the body remains, its qualities will be changed, so that glory succeeds to baseness. The analogy of the opposite confirms this, namely misery, to which the whole man is enslaved. Otherwise the resurrection of the flesh would be pointless. For it also belongs to the office of Christ that, just as he presented his own body free from corruption, and quickened it to eternal life and placed it in heaven, as the quickening Spirit, so he will do the same for our body, which ought to be conformed to his and to be with him. For he is the builder of the temple of God, which is both his body and ours (Zech. 6:12–13). In the temple of God there ought to be no death, corruption, iniquity, alien power or might, defect or want. Where "God is all in all" (1 Cor. 15:28), there life itself is also in the bodies.

units.la: CLI. Dotes corporis gloriosi S. Paulus diserte, 1.Cor.XV.37–50. explicat. In universum ver-
units.tr: CLI. The Apostle Paul explains expressly the endowments of the glorious body in 1 Cor. 15:37–50. Speaking generally, in the verse

units.la: Affectus omnes rectæ rationis regimini subjiciet.
units.tr: He will subject all the affections to the rule of right reason.

units.la: Denique & potestatem ejusdem consummabit.
units.tr: Finally, he will also perfect its power.

units.la: Corpus etiam hominis beati gloria implebitur.
units.tr: The blessed glory will also fill the body of man.

units.la: Corporis gloriosi essentia.
units.tr: The essence of the glorious body.

units.la: versum enim sic loquitur: Dicet quis: In quali corpore venient? Demens, &c. Quod seminas, non corpus, quod renascetur seminas, sed nudum granum, prout contigerit, tritici, aut alicujus reliquorum, Deus autem ipsi dat corpus, ut ipse vult, & unicuique suum proprium corpus, v.35–39. Quae scite sic Tertullianus de Resurr. c. 52. illustrat: Seritur solummodo granum sine folliculi veste, sine fundamento spicae, sine munimento aristae, sine superbia culmi. Exurgit autem copia faeneratum, compagine aedificatum, ordine structum, munitum, cultum, & usquequaque vestitum. Haec sunt ei corpus a Deo aliud, in quod non abolitione, sed ampliatione mutatur. Nempe similem in modum Deus mortuis & putredine absumptis carnem largietur, & eandem & diversam: eandem per naturam, diversam per gloriam: eandem per veritatem, & diversam per potentiam, uti scite Gregorius in Job. Lib.XIV.33. loquitur.
units.tr: For he speaks thus in the verse: "But some man will say, How are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come? Thou fool..." What thou sowest is not the body that shall be, but bare grain, it may chance of wheat, or of some other grain. But God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body (vv. 35–39). Tertullian illustrates this aptly in On the Resurrection, chapter 52: "The grain alone is sown, without the husk's covering, without the foundation of the ear, without the protection of the awn, without the pride of the stalk. But it rises up abundantly increased, built up in structure, arranged in order, fortified, adorned, and clothed on every side. These are its body, given by God, into which it is changed not by destruction but by enlargement. In like manner God will bestow on the dead, consumed by putrefaction, flesh that is both the same and different: the same by nature, different by glory; the same in truth, and different in power," as Gregory speaks well in his Commentary on Job, Book 14, chapter 33.

units.la: CLII. Sed distincte id Apostolus explicat per quadruplicem antithesin corporis ejus, quod seminatur, & quod excitabitur: Prima est ratione durationis. Nam φθορᾷ in corruptione, seminatur in corruptione, excitatur in incorruptione, v.42. Oportet enim φθαρτὸν corruptibile hoc induere ἀφθαρσίαν incorruptibilitatem, ib.v.53. Corpus hujus vitae fluxum est; & postquam cecidit, computrescit, & in cineres resolvitur. Idem vero resuscitatum prodit incorruptibile, non fluxum, non labascens, non iterum vitium faciens. Non enim corpus iterum corrumpetur, dissolvetur, morietur, quia Deus in eo vim suam totam exeret, & mortem expellet. Licet enim natura corporis semper ex contrariis constet, tamen dissolutio metuenda non est, quia contraria illa non habebunt appetitus contrarios indeterminatos, & invicem infestantes & vastantes; qualis ratio contrariorum in natura hujus seculi est. Facit ergo huc etiam tum ἀπάθεια impassibilitas corporis, quia nihil vel extra vel intra corpus erit, a quo patiatur, & nec luctus, nec clamor, nec dolor ultra erit, Apoc.XXI.4. & corpus perfecte spiritui subjicietur: tum ἀθανασία immortalitas, eandem ob causam, & quia mors, ultimus hostis, per resurrectionem abolebitur, 1. Cor. XV.26. Ne quidem mori amplius poterunt, quia similes Angelis erunt, Luc.XX.36. quod & peccati, quae causa mortis est, absentia: & conformitas cum Christo, & perfecta Dei imago, & domicilii habitatio, & vitae aeternae appellatio evincit. Secunda antithesis est ratione decoris & gloriae. Nam seminatur in vilitate, excitatur in gloria, v.43. Corpus enim hujus vitae non uni vitio obnoxium esse potest; & mortuum foedum, putidum, nausea est, sed resuscitatum omnem ἀτιμίαν exuit, amabilitatis, decoris, majestatis, gloriae copiam omnem induit. Cujus specimen in vultu Mosis candicante, Exod.XXXIV.29. item in Christo coram tribus discipulis transfigurato, cujus membra Solis fulgore rutilantia Apostolorum oculos praestrinxerunt, Matth. XVII.2. fuit. Transformatus enim Christus est in eadem gloria & claritate, in qua post in Regno suo venturus, & cujus fulgorem mortales oculi non tulissent, est. Et corpori gloriae ejus conformabimur, Phil. III.21. Tunc justi fulgebunt sicut Sol in Regno Patris ipsorum, Matth. XIII.43. Deus enim qui ipsa lux est, beatos, quibus se videndum praebebit, collucтrabit totos, ut non minus auro mundo, similis vitro mundo similes sint, quam ipsa caelestis Hierosolyma erit, Apoc.XXI.18. Non quod futura sint pellucida, aerea vel aetherea, uti Origeni placuit, quia mutatio haec colorem illorum non abolebit; vel non solida, sed fluxa, quia carnem & ossa non deponent; sed quia caelesti fulgore micabunt; licut facies Mosis & Christi transformata eadem fuit, sed radios caelestis gloriae induit. Quam in rem plura Hieronymus adversus errores Johannis Hierosolymitani & Origenis Epist.61. ad Pammach, dixit. Accedet sanitas & pulchritudo, quae ex congruente ordine, mensura & ratione partium exurget. Nulla oris deformitas, cutis fuscedo vel imparitas, pedum claudicatio, narium, oris distorsio, nil truncum, morbidum nil erit. Neque senectus vitium conflabit: & fulgor atque claritas pulchritudinem maximam conciliabit. Tertia antithesis est ratione potentiae. Nam seminatur in ἀσθενείᾳ in imbecillitate, excitatur in δυνάμει in potentia, ib.v.43. Corpus enim hujus vitae infirmum est, cibi & potus, lomni, vestitus fulturis indiget, aegre & tarde movetur ob molem & medii renixum; & mortuum nihil in se habet, unde vel subsistat, vel vivat; nec idoneum animae habitaculum est; & nulla pars ejus organi usum habet. Sed resurget idem δυνατὸν potens, nullique infirmitati vel defectui obnoxium, neque pristino pondere suo gravatum. Pertinet igitur huc ejusdem agilitas & subtilitas. Agilitas, qua potens erit se, ad nutum spiritus, expedite quaquaversum movendi, quorum proin motus volatui, quam motui progressivo similior erit. Nam obviam in nubibus rapiemur Domino in aera, 1.Thess.IV.17. Ubi volet spiritus, ita Augustinus de Civ.D. Lib.XXII.30. loquitur: ibi protinus erit corpus, nec volet aliquid spiritus, quod nec spiritum, nec corpus decere possit. Macarius quoque Homil.34. Cum, inquit, Deus conderet Adam, non aptavit ei corporeas alas, sicut volatilibus: nempe praeparans ei alas Spiritus S. quas illi in resurrectione donaturus erat, quae ipsum allevarent & raperent, quod spiritui bonum videretur. Quas quidem alas etiamnum animae Sanctorum (κατ' ἐξιν) obtinent, quae mente ad cogitationes caelestes evolant. Aberunt enim tardioris motus causae, δυσχέρεια & infirmitates hujus vitae, moles corporis, defatigatio; & aderit velocitatis causa spiritus, quo agitante calebit. Ita pullus ovo inclusus aegre movetur; sed exclusus paulatim volat, & avolante, agitante spiritu, quem ei Deus dedit. TalE corpus Christus post resurrectionem habuit, utpote qui modo circa sepulchrum stetit, modo se discipulis in via associavit, modo Hierosolymae discipulis astitit. Neque tamen sic agile corpus erit, ut motus localis expers abuno extremo ad alterum sine transitu per medium penetret, quia id naturae corporis repugnat, & soli spiritui, qui localiter non movetur: convenit. Satis erit ad explenda eorum desideria, quod per medium movebuntur celerrimé, quia corpori δυναμῶ potenti, quale beati habebunt, non resistet medium, sicut resistit ἀσθενεῖ imbecilli, quale in hac vita habemus. Deus enim, uti scite Augustinus de Civ.D. lib. XIII. XIII.18. naturam relinquet, congruentiam figuræ membrorúmque detinebit, ponderis tarditatem detrahet. Alibi de Civ. D. Lib. XXII.11. Si Deo minor vel Angelus, vel dæmon potuit pondus humidi elementi (in cribro Virginis vestalis) sic suspendere, ut aquarum videretur mutata fuisse natura, itáne Deus omnipotens, qui ipsa creavit elementa, terreno corpori grave pondus auferre non poterit, ut in eodem elemento habitet vivificatum corpus, in quo voluerit spiritus vivificans? Quæ tamen cum grano salis sic accipienda sunt, ne putemus spiritum vivificantem velle id, quod naturæ corporis, quà tale est, repugnet, quia, uti eundem Augustinum loquentem videmus, non volet spiritus, quod nec spiritum, nec corpus decere possit. Agilitatem hanc comitabitur subtilitas, qua à corpore non corporeitatem, sed celeritatem removebit, efficiétque, non ut dimensiones corporum penetrare, quæ quorundam hallucinatio est, sed ut eas facilius transire possit, quomodo acus, & visus subtilis non corporum objectorum dimensiones penetrat, sed facilius per corporis partes transit. Non enim subtilitas illa vel figuram, vel quantitatem corporis destruet, qua naturam corporis humani relinquet, neque ex corpore spiritum faciet. Cùm enim agile, potens, radiis solaribus fulgidius corpus futurum sit, per dimensiones corporum facilius velociúsque transibit; sed non spiritus instar, penetrabit, vel illocaliter movebitur. Neque enim corpus gloriosum, uti nonnulli somniant, erit vel illocale, quia erit in cœlo, quod locus proprie dictus est: vel invisibile, quia carnem & ossa habens, figura non carebit: vel impalpabile, quia Christus corpus suum resuscitatum palpandum obtulit, & quod carnem & ossa, aliáque organa retinet, palpari utique potest. Quarta denique antithesis est ratione spiritualitatis. Nam seminatur σῶμα ψυχικὸν corpus animale & resuscitatur πνεῦμα πνευματικὸν spirituale, ib. v.44. Ubi nec corpus animale dicitur, quod mera anima est; nec spirituale, quod merus spiritus est; sed animale, quod solam animam vegetabilem vivendi principium & causam; Spirituale, quod à Spiritu Dei vivificatur, & non externa adminicula, qualia hujus vitæ sunt, sed spiritum vivificantem, vitæ suæ conservandæ principium habet, quam in rem plura s. LXXIV. diximus. Cùmque corpus gloriosum ab eodem spiritu vivificante suam ἀφθαρσίαν incorruptibilitatem, δόξαν gloriam, & δύναμιν potentiam habeat, merito præcedentium illarum dotum corporis gloriosi basis spiritus vivificans statuitur. Ab eo enim est, quòd corpus incorruptibile, gloriosum & potens erit, neque vel basi quadam indigebit, uti hac in vita indiget; vel cibo, potu, somno, aliísque infirmitatis sustentandæ mediis indigebit.
units.tr: CLII. But the Apostle explains this distinctly through a fourfold contrast between the body that is sown and the body that will be raised. The first is in respect of duration. For it is sown in corruption [φθορᾷ], and raised in incorruption, v. 42. "For this corruptible must put on incorruptibility," ib. v. 53. The body of this life is perishable; once it has fallen, it rots and is reduced to ashes. But the same body, raised again, appears incorruptible: not perishable, not failing, no longer subject to defect. For the body will not be corrupted, dissolved or die again, because God will put forth all his power in it and expel death. Although the nature of the body always consists of contraries, dissolution is nonetheless not to be feared, because those contraries will not have indeterminate appetites that attack and lay waste to one another, which is the condition of contraries in the nature of this age. Here also belongs impassibility [ἀπάθεια], since nothing will exist either outside or inside the body by which it could be made to suffer; there will be no mourning, no crying, no pain any more, Rev. 21.4; and the body will be wholly subject to the spirit. Here also belongs immortality [ἀθανασία], for the same reason, and because death, the last enemy, will be abolished by the resurrection, 1 Cor. 15.26. They will not be able to die any more at all, because they will be like the angels, Luke 20.36. This is shown both by the absence of sin, which is the cause of death, and by conformity to Christ, the perfect image of God, the dwelling place of the household, and the name of eternal life. The second contrast is in respect of comeliness and glory. For it is sown in dishonour, raised in glory, v. 43. The body of this life cannot be free from every defect, and a dead body is foul, putrid and loathsome; but raised again it puts off all dishonour [ἀτιμίαν] and clothes itself in a full measure of loveliness, comeliness, majesty and glory. A specimen of this was the shining face of Moses, Exod. 34.29, and likewise Christ transfigured before three disciples, whose limbs, glowing with the brightness of the sun, dazzled the eyes of the apostles, Matt. 17.2. For Christ was transformed into the same glory and brightness in which he is to come afterwards in his kingdom, and whose radiance mortal eyes could not bear. "We shall be conformed to the body of his glory," Phil. 3.21. "Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father," Matt. 13.43. For God, who is light itself, will illumine the blessed, to whom he will show himself to be seen, through and through, so that they will be as pure as gold, and as clear as glass, just as the heavenly Jerusalem itself will be, Rev. 21.18. This is not because they will be transparent, airy or ethereal, as Origen thought, since this change will not take away their colour; nor because they will be non-solid but fluid, since they will not lay aside flesh and bones; but because they will sparkle with heavenly radiance, just as the face of Moses and Christ, though transformed, remained the same, but put on the rays of heavenly glory. Jerome has said a great deal on this matter against the errors of John of Jerusalem and Origen, Epist. 61 to Pammachius. Health and beauty will also be added, which will arise from a harmonious order, measure and proportion of the parts. There will be no deformity of face, no darkness or unevenness of skin, no lameness of feet, no distortion of nostrils or mouth, nothing mutilated, nothing diseased. Nor will old age bring its defects; and brightness and radiance will bestow the greatest beauty. The third contrast is in respect of power. For it is sown in weakness [ἀσθενείᾳ], raised in power [δυνάμει], ib. v. 43. For the body of this life is feeble; it needs props of food, drink, sleep and clothing; it moves with difficulty and slowly because of its mass and the resistance of the medium; and a dead body has nothing in itself by which it might either subsist or live, nor is it a fit dwelling for the soul, and no part of its organs has any use. But the same body will rise powerful [δυνατὸν], subject to no weakness or defect, and no longer weighed down by its former heaviness. To this belong its agility and subtlety. Agility, by which it will be able, at the nod of the spirit, to move swiftly in any direction, so that its motion will be more like flight than progressive motion. For "we shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air," 1 Thess. 4.17. "Where the spirit wills," Augustine speaks thus in De Civitate Dei 22.30: "there the body will at once be, and the spirit will will nothing that could not befit either spirit or body." Macarius too, Homily 34: "When God created Adam, he did not fit him with bodily wings, as with birds; rather, he prepared for him the wings of the Holy Spirit, which he was to bestow on him in the resurrection, which would lift him up and carry him away wherever it seemed good to the spirit. These wings the souls of the saints already possess by habit (κατ' ἕξιν), and they fly up by the mind to heavenly thoughts." For the causes of slower motion will be gone: difficulty [δυσχέρεια] and the infirmities of this life, the mass of the body, and fatigue; and the cause of speed, the spirit, will be present, warming the body as it moves it. So a chick enclosed in the egg moves with difficulty; but once hatched, it gradually flies, and as it flies, the spirit which God has given it moves it. Such was the body Christ had after the resurrection, since he at one time stood by the tomb, at another joined the disciples on the road, and at another stood among the disciples in Jerusalem. Yet the body will not be so agile that, free of local motion, it passes from one extremity to the other without traversing the middle, for that is contrary to the nature of a body and belongs only to the spirit, which is not moved locally. It will be enough to satisfy their desires that they move through the medium most swiftly, since the medium will not resist a body that is powerful [δυναμῶ], such as the blessed will have, as it resists a body that is weak [ἀσθενεῖ], such as we have in this life. For God, as Augustine rightly says in De Civitate Dei 13.18, "will leave the nature, will preserve the congruity of figure and of the limbs, and will remove the slowness of weight." Elsewhere, De Civitate Dei 22.11: "If a lesser god, or an angel, or a demon could so suspend the weight of the watery element (in the sieve of the Vestal Virgin) that the nature of the waters seemed to have been changed, can not almighty God, who created the elements themselves, remove the heavy weight from an earthly body, so that the quickened body may dwell in the same element, in which the quickening spirit has willed it to be?" Yet these words are to be taken with a grain of salt, so that we do not think the quickening spirit wills what is contrary to the nature of a body as such, since, as we see the same Augustine saying, "the spirit will not will what could befit neither spirit nor body." This agility will be accompanied by subtlety, by which it will remove from the body not its corporeality but its sluggishness, and will make it possible for it to pass through the dimensions of bodies more easily, not to penetrate them (which is the delusion of some), just as a needle or a keen sight does not penetrate the dimensions of the objects they meet, but passes more easily through the parts of the body. For that subtlety will not destroy the figure or quantity of the body, by which it keeps the nature of the human body, nor will it make the body into spirit. For since the body will be agile, powerful and brighter than the rays of the sun, it will pass through the dimensions of bodies more easily and swiftly; but it will not penetrate them like a spirit, nor will it move without place. For the glorious body will not be, as some dream, without place [illocale], because it will be in heaven, which is properly called a place; nor invisible, because, having flesh and bones, it will not lack figure; nor impalpable, because Christ offered his raised body to be touched, and what retains flesh and bones and other organs can certainly be felt. Lastly, the fourth contrast is in respect of spirituality. For it is sown as a natural body [σῶμα ψυχικὸν] and raised as a spiritual body [πνεῦμα πνευματικὸν], ib. v. 44. Here the body is not called "animal" because it is pure soul, nor "spiritual" because it is pure spirit; rather, it is called animal, because it has only the vegetative soul as the principle and cause of life; spiritual, because it is quickened by the Spirit of God, and has as the principle of preserving its life not external aids, such as belong to this life, but the quickening Spirit; on which matter we have said more at Locus 74. And since the glorious body has from the same quickening Spirit its incorruptibility [ἀφθαρσίαν], glory [δόξαν] and power [δύναμιν], the quickening Spirit is rightly set as the foundation of these earlier endowments of the glorious body. For it is from him that the body will be incorruptible, glorious and powerful, and will need neither some support, as it needs in this life, nor food, drink, sleep, or other means of sustaining weakness.

units.la: CLIII. Beatitudinem totius hominis, & seorsim etiam animæ & corporis, ejusdem habitatio, societas, bonorum multitudo, universalitas, continuitas & æternitas mirè augebunt. Habitatio enim erit in Cœlo supremo, quod & Paradisi Luc.XXIII.43. 2.Cor.XII.4. Apoc.II.7. quippe per terrestrem Paradisum adumbrati, & tertii Cœli, 2.Cor.XII.2. quia supra aspectabiles cœlos est, & domus Patris cœlestis, Joh.XIV.2. ob singularem gloriæ Patris in eo manifestationem, & domus ἀχειροποίητος μὴ ἐν χερσὶν ποιήτος aeternæ in Cœlis, 2.Cor.V.1. oppositè ad domum Dei Hierosolymæ à Solomone & Zorobabele extructam, aliusque nominibus venit. De ejus natura & gloria plusculà Loc.VI.42. diximus. Ejus typus nova Hierosolyma ex Cœlo descendens, Apoc.XXI.2. &c. illustri modo describitur. Cùmque Fulgentius gloriam Curiæ Romanæ contemplatus alta voce exclamaverit. Quàm speciosa est cœlestis Hierosolyma, si sic fulget Roma terrestris? merito nos exclamamus: Quàm gloriosa Hierosolyma cœlestis est, si talis est, quam ex cœlo in terram descendentem Johannes celebravit? Cœlum enim est, in quod impurum nihil ingredietur, Apocal. XXI.27. in quo consummata justitia habitat, 2.Pet.III.13. Cujus etiam incredibilis amplitudo est. In domo Patris mei mansiones multæ sunt, Joh. XIV.2. Singuli enim cœlites mansionem, imò & Regnum suum ibi habent. Ibi erit κληρος ἁγίων ἐν τῷ φωτί, hereditas Sanctorum in luce, cujus quisque μερίδα portionem habebit, Col.I.12. Civitas enim illa multò minùs, quàm nova Hierosolyma opus habebit Sole vel Luna, quia gloria Dei eam collustrabit, & lucerna ejus Agnus erit, Apoc.XXI.23. Quicquid de urbe illa regia dixerit homo, quasi stilla de mari, vel scintilla de foco est. Civitatis illius, sic pulchrè Bernhardus, de Medit. cap.4. scribit, cives sunt Angeli, Deus Pater Templum, Filius ejus splendor, Spiritus S. charitas. O Civitas cœlestis, mansio secura, patria fertilis & ampla, tutum continens, quod delectat, populus sine murmure, incolæ quieti, homines nullam indigentiam habentes.
units.tr: CLIII. The blessedness of the whole man, and of soul and body separately, will be wonderfully increased by its dwelling, its fellowship, the multitude of its goods, their universality, continuity and eternity. The dwelling will be in the highest heaven, which is also called Paradise (Luke 23:43; 2 Cor. 12:4; Rev. 2:7), since the earthly Paradise foreshadowed it, and the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2), since it lies above the visible heavens, and the house of the heavenly Father (John 14:2), because of the singular manifestation of the Father's glory there, and the house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens [ἀχειροποίητος μὴ ἐν χερσὶν ποιήτος] (2 Cor. 5:1), in contrast to the house of God at Jerusalem built by Solomon and Zerubbabel. It has other names too. I have said more about its nature and glory at Loc. VI, §42. Its type, the new Jerusalem coming down out of heaven (Rev. 21:2, etc.), is described in a splendid way. When Fulgentius, contemplating the glory of the Roman Curia, exclaimed aloud, How splendid is the heavenly Jerusalem, if earthly Rome shines so brightly? we rightly exclaim, How glorious is the heavenly Jerusalem, if it is such as John celebrated, coming down from heaven to earth? For heaven is that place into which nothing unclean will enter (Rev. 21:27), and in which righteousness dwells in its fullness (2 Pet. 3:13). Its vastness is also incredible: In my Father's house there are many mansions (John 14:2). Each of the heavenly inhabitants has a mansion there, indeed his own kingdom. There will be the inheritance of the saints in light [κληρος ἁγίων ἐν τῷ φωτί], and each will have his own portion [μερίδα] (Col. 1:12). That city will need the sun or moon much less than the new Jerusalem does, because the glory of God will light it, and its lamp is the Lamb (Rev. 21:23). Whatever a man says of that royal city is like a drop from the sea or a spark from a fire. Bernard, in his Meditations, chapter 4, writes beautifully of that city: its citizens are angels, God the Father its temple, his Son its splendour, the Holy Spirit its love. O heavenly city, secure dwelling, fruitful and spacious homeland, holding all that delights, a people without complaint, inhabitants at rest, men with no want.

units.la: CLIV. Hæc vero beata illa societas est, reputa cum Deo & Christo, cum Angelis & beatis Sanctis. Cum DEO enim & Christo erimus. Hodie mecum eris in paradiso, Luc.XXIII.43. Ubi ego sum, illic & minister meus erit, Joh.XII.28. Ubi ego sum, ibi et vos sitis; ib. XIV.3. Volo, ut ubi ego sum, & illi, quos dedisti mihi, sint mecum, ut videant claritatem, &c. ibid.XVII.24. Desideramus præsentes esse apud Dominum, 2.Cor.V.8. Cupio dissolvi, & esse cum Christo, Phil.I.23. Ecce tabernaculum Dei cum hominibus, & habitabit cum eis, & ipsi populus ejus erunt, & ipse Deus erit eorum Deus, Apoc. XXI.3. Cùm in cœlo Deum à facie ad faciem visuri simus, & ipse omnia in omnibus futurus sit; necesse est, ut Deo arctissimè ibi conjungamur. Non tantùm enim Deus nobiscum, sed etiam in nobis habitabit. Neque cum Deo duntaxat, sed etiam cum Angelis habitabimus, utpote qui unà nobiscum semper intuentur faciem Patris in cœlo, Matth.XVIII.10. Denique & cum omnibus beatis hominibus arctissima societate & necessitudine conjungemur. Multi ab Oriente & Occidente venient, & cum Abrahamo, Isaco, & Jacobo in Regno cœlorum accumbent. Matth.VIII.11. Luc.XIII.28.29. Accessistis ad panegyrin & Ecclesiam primogenitorum in cœlis descriptorum, Heb.XII.23. Semper cum Domino erimus, 1.Thess.IV.17. Atque ex beatissima hac societate orientur, & sociatos inter illibata vigebunt tum ἐρως καὶ ἀντιφιλία mutuus amor, quia ibi charitas perfectissima, snavissima, castissima, qua quisque Deum super omnia, ipsum, & proximum sicut se ipsum diliget in ἀφθαρσίᾳ incorruptibilitate, sine ejus φθορᾷ corcorruptione quæ per concupiscentiam fit, Ephes. IV.24.obtinebit:tum mutuus honor subjectionis, qui Deo, & societatis, qui angelis & hominibus debetur, quia omnes erimus Reges & Sacerdotes coram Deo, Apoc.I.6. & ipse Pater Christi honorabit eos, qui ipsi ministrant, Joh.XII.26. tum gaudium ineffabile, quia ubi livoris omnis affectus exulabit, quisque de bono alterius, velut de suo lætabitur; & videre summa cum delectatione Deum, Angelos, Patriarchas, Prophetas, Apostolos, heroas illos, Martyres, Parentes, liberos, necessitudines, inprimis Christum Regem & ἐξαρχον, omnibus illis præsidentem, cum diademate, quo coronavit illum mater in die desponsationis illius, & in die lætitiæ cordis ejus, Cant.III.11. incredibiles delicias faciet: tum denique Colloquium suavissimum, quia beati non erunt κωφοὶ θεασταὶ, muti spectatores, sed suavissimos gravissimosque de magnalibus Dei sermones coædent, quomodo etiam Moses & Elias ὀφθέντες ἐν δόξῃ apparentes in gloria cum Christo de ejus exitu, quem Hierosolymis impleturus erat, collocuti sunt, Matth.XVII.3. Luc.IX.30.31. Neque forte mentale duntaxat, sed etiam vocale Sanctorum colloquium erit. Non enim omnes corporis functiones cessabunt; & functio præcipua glorificatio Dei per linguam erit.
