Omnia enim membra & viscera, uti scite Augustinus de Civ. D. Lib. XXII. 30. loquitur, incorruptibilis corporis in laudibus Dei proficient. Neque obstat, quòd linguæ cessaturæ dicuntur, 1.Cor. XIII.8. quia id non de usu linguarum, sed de necessitate linguas studio, arte & usu discendi, intelligi debet. Non enim ut beati inter se colloquantur, & Deum etiam voce celebrent, cura & labore opus erit; neque miraculum erit pluribus linguis loqui. Una enim lingua communis omnium, & qualis illa, Heberis, an alia, an plures obtenturæ sint, nemini Mortalium revelatum est.
units.tr: CLIV. This blessed fellowship consists in being with God and Christ, with the angels and the blessed saints. For we shall be with God and with Christ. Today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). Where I am, there my servant will be also (John 12:26). Where I am, there you also may be (John 14:3). Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may be with me where I am, so that they may see my glory (John 17:24), etc. We desire to be present with the Lord (2 Cor. 5:8). I long to depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1:23). Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be their God (Rev. 21:3). Since we shall see God face to face in heaven, and he himself will be all in all, we must be most closely joined to God there. For God will dwell not only with us but also in us. We shall live not only with God but also with the angels, who together with us always behold the face of the Father in heaven (Matt. 18:10). Finally, we shall be joined in the closest fellowship and kinship with all the blessed. Many will come from east and west and will recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 8:11; Luke 13:28-29). You have come to the festal assembly and the church of the firstborn written in heaven (Heb. 12:23). We shall always be with the Lord (1 Thess. 4:17). From this most blessed fellowship will arise, and among the associated saints will flourish unspoiled, the mutual love [ἐρως καὶ ἀντιφιλία], because there will be a most perfect, sweetest and purest charity, by which each will love God above all and his neighbour as himself, and will possess it in incorruptibility [ἀφθαρσίᾳ], without any corruption [φθορᾷ] that comes through lust (Eph. 4:24). There will also be a mutual honour: of subjection, owed to God, and of fellowship, owed to angels and men, because we shall all be kings and priests before God (Rev. 1:6); and the Father himself will honour those who serve him (John 12:26). There will be an inexpressible joy, because where every feeling of envy is banished, each will rejoice in another's good as if it were his own. There will be the delight of seeing with the greatest pleasure God, the angels, the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, those heroes, the martyrs, parents, children, and kinsfolk, and above all Christ the King and leader [ἐξαρχον], presiding over all of them, wearing the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousal, and on the day of the gladness of his heart (Song 3:11). Finally there will be the sweetest conversation, because the blessed will not be silent spectators [κωφοὶ θεασταὶ], but will exchange the sweetest and weightiest words about the great works of God, just as Moses and Elijah, appearing in glory [ὀφθέντες ἐν δόξῃ], spoke with Christ about his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem (Matt. 17:3; Luke 9:30-31). Perhaps the fellowship of the saints will be not merely mental but also vocal. For not all bodily functions will cease, and the chief function will be the glorifying of God by the tongue. As Augustine wisely says in The City of God, book 22, ch. 30, all the members and organs of the incorruptible body will contribute to the praises of God. Nor is it an objection that tongues will cease (1 Cor. 13:8), since this must be understood not of the use of tongues but of the necessity of learning languages by study, art and practice. For the blessed will have no need of toil and effort to converse with one another and to praise God aloud, nor will it be a miracle to speak in many tongues. Whether there will be one common language for all, such as Hebrew, or others, or several, no mortal has been told.

units.la: CLV. Denique etiam Bona vitæ æternæ multa, universalia, continua & æterna erunt. Multa & Universalia, quia & in universis beatis, & in singulorum animæ potentiis & corporis membris locum habebunt, uti supra ostendimus. Hæreditas enim illa nec copia possessorum minuitur, nec angustia ex numero cohæredum evadet. Sicut non minuitur felicitas eorum, qui Solem intuentur, si maximè innumeri alii eundem intueantur; ita nec beatitudo illorum, qui Deum videbunt, minuetur, si plurimi alii juxta viderint.
units.tr: CLV. Finally, the good things of eternal life will be many, universal, continuous and eternal. They will be many and universal, because they will have their place in all the blessed and in the powers of each soul and the members of each body, as we have shown above. That inheritance is not diminished by the number of its possessors, nor does it become narrow by the number of co-heirs. Just as the happiness of those who look at the sun is not lessened even if countless others look at it too, so the blessedness of those who see God will not be diminished if very many others also see him at the same time.

units.la: Mirus amor Christi, quem si quis diligit, omnes Is corrivales velit habere sibi.
units.tr: Christ's love is wonderful: whoever loves him would wish to have all his rivals for himself.

units.la: Erit Deus plenitudo luminis intellectui, multitudo pacis & gaudii voluntati, speculum visui, mel gustui, cithara auditui, balsamum odoratui, flos tactui. Sanabit Christus ὅλον ἄνθρωπον totum hominem, Joh.VII.23. Continua etiam bona illa erunt, quia bona & gaudia vitæ æternæ nullum intervallum & incisionem, nullam bonorum & malorum vicissitudinem patientur. Non enim sicut in hac vita rara bora, brevis mora est, ita in æterna etiam erit. Nam πάντοτε semper cum Domino erimus, 1.Thess.IV.17. Sancti requiem non habebunt ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτὸς diu noctuque vociferando ἁγιος Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Dominus, Deus omnipotens, Apoc. IV.8. Nunquam enim Deus iis faciem suam lætabilem subtrahet. Sicut fons perennis jugiter aquas fundit: ita ex Deo, apud quem vena vitæ est, Psal.XXXVI.10. nunquam interrupta, perpetuáque adeò flumina bonitatis scaturient. Hæreditas enim illa ἀμάραντος: immarcessibilis erit, non florum caducorum & fugacium instar flaccescet, sed similis erit flori, cui nomen semper viventis est. Lignum vitæ affert fructus duodecim per singulos menses (perpetuoque adeò) reddens fructum suum, Apoc.XXII.2. Denique æterna erunt. Nam ipsa cœlestis vita, vita æterna, Dan.XII.2. Matth.XXV.46. Joh.III.16. XVII.3. domus æterna in cœlis, 2.Cor.V.1. Tabernacula æterna, Luc.XVI.9. Regnum æternum, 2.Pet.I.11. Hæreditas æterna, Heb.IX.15. Salus æterna, Heb.V.9. gloria æterna, 1.Pet.V.10. æternum pondus gloriæ, 2.Cor.IV.17. diserte appellatur. Qui sermonem meum servaverit, non morietur in æternum, Joh.VIII.51. Gaudium vestrum nemo tollet à vobis, ibid.XVI.22. Mors ultra non erit, Apoc.XXI.4. Rationem appellationis vitæ æternæ supra §.CXX. expressimus. Neque non poterit non in æternum durare vita electorum, qui in bono confirmabuntur, peccare, mori amplius non poterunt; quorum vita & beatitudo omnibus numeris perfecta erit; & quibus Deus omnia in omnibus erit. Vera enim beatitudo quietum reddere appetitum, & omne malum excludere debet. Sed beatus maximè appetit beatitudinis suæ perpetuitatem, & nisi de hoc certus foret, timore amittendi affligeretur, atque ita perfectè beatus non esset. Sapienter sic Augustinus de Trin. lib. XIII.8. ratiocinatur; Ut homo beatè vivat, oportet ut vivat. Quem porrò morientem vita ipsa deserit, beata vita cum illo manere quomodo potest? Cùm autem deserit, aut nolentem deserit, aut volentem, aut neutrum. Si nolentem, quomodo beata vita est, quæ ita est in voluntate, ut non sit in potestate? Non potest vita beata esse, & nolentem deserre, quia beatus nolens nemo fit, ac per hoc quanto magis nolentem deserendo miserum facit, quæ si nolenti præstò esset, miserum faceret. Si autem volentem deserit, etiam sic quomodo beata erat, quam perire voluit, qui habebat? Restat, ut dicatur, neutrum esse in animo beati, id est, cum deseri, a beata vita, cùm per mortem deserit tota vita, nec nolle, nec velle, ad utrumque enim paratò & æquo animo consistere. Sed nec ista beata est vita, quia talis est, ut quem beatum facit, amore ejus sit indigna. Quomodo enim est beata vita, quam non amat beatus? Aut quomodo amatur, quod utrum vigeat an pereat, indifferenter accipitur?
units.tr: God will be the fullness of light to the intellect, the abundance of peace and joy to the will, a mirror to sight, honey to taste, a harp to hearing, balm to smell, a flower to touch. Christ will make whole the whole man [ὅλον ἄνθρωπον] (John 7:23). Those good things will also be continuous, because the goods and joys of eternal life will suffer no interval or interruption, no alternation of good and evil. For it is not as in this life, where the hour is rare and the delay brief, so it will not be in eternal life. For we shall be with the Lord always [πάντοτε] (1 Thess. 4:17). The saints will have no rest, but day and night [ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτὸς] they will cry out, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty [ἁγιος] (Rev. 4:8). For God will never withdraw his joyful face from them. As a perennial spring pours out water without ceasing, so from God, with whom is the fountain of life (Ps. 36:10), rivers of goodness will flow forth, never interrupted and perpetual. That inheritance will be unfading [ἀμάραντος], unwithering; it will not wilt like fallen and fleeting flowers, but will be like the flower whose name is ever-living. The tree of life bears twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit every month (Rev. 22:2), and so perpetually. Finally, these goods will be eternal. Heavenly life itself is expressly called eternal life (Dan. 12:2; Matt. 25:46; John 3:16, 17:3), an eternal house in the heavens (2 Cor. 5:1), eternal tabernacles (Luke 16:9), an eternal kingdom (2 Pet. 1:11), an eternal inheritance (Heb. 9:15), eternal salvation (Heb. 5:9), eternal glory (1 Pet. 5:10), and an eternal weight of glory (2 Cor. 4:17). Whoever keeps my word will never die (John 8:51). No one will take your joy from you (John 16:22). There will be no more death (Rev. 21:4). I have explained the reason for the name of eternal life above, §120. Nor can the life of the elect fail to last forever: they will be confirmed in good, they will be unable to sin, and they will be unable to die any more. Their life and blessedness will be perfect in every respect, and God will be all in all to them. For true blessedness must quiet the appetite and exclude every evil. But the blessed man most of all desires the perpetuity of his blessedness, and unless he were sure of it, he would be troubled by the fear of losing it, and so would not be perfectly blessed. Augustine reasons wisely in this way, On the Trinity, book 13, ch. 8: For a man to live blessedly, he must live. But how can a blessed life remain with a man whom life itself forsakes when he dies? When it forsakes him, it forsakes him either unwilling or willing or neither. If unwilling, how is it a blessed life, which is so in the will that it is not in its power? A blessed life cannot forsake one who is unwilling, for no one becomes blessed against his will; and therefore the more it forsakes him unwilling, the more it makes him wretched, since if it were present to him unwilling, it would make him wretched. But if it forsakes him willing, how was it blessed, when he who had it wished to lose it? It remains to say that neither is in the mind of the blessed, that is, that when the whole of life forsakes him through death, he neither wills nor is unwilling, but stands ready and calm for either. But this is not a blessed life either, since it is such that the one whom it makes blessed is unworthy of its love. For how is that a blessed life which the blessed man does not love? Or how is that loved which is received with indifference whether it flourishes or perishes?

units.la: CLVI. Par, an impar & inæqualis omnium beatorum in Cœlis gloria futura sit, Hieronymum inter & Jovinianum olim disceptatum est. Hic enim futuram æqualem, ille inæqualem, contendit. Hieronymi sententiam ita Pontificii amplectuntur, ut inæqualitatem gloriæ meritorum inæqualitati superstruant, & quibusdam doctoribus, Martyribus Monachis, Divis inprimis, altiorem gradum occupaturis aureolas & coronulas supra sortem vulgi Sanctorum, promittant. Sed meritorum jactantiam supra in loco retudimus. Evangelicorum alii Martyr, Tilenus, Camero, &c. graduum æqualitatem; alii, iique plures longè cum Hieronymo, Augustino & Patribus plerisque omnibus, inæqualitatem propugnant. Posterioribus adstipulamur, sic tamen, ut
units.tr: CLVI. Whether the glory of all the blessed in heaven will be equal or unequal and uneven was once disputed between Jerome and Jovinian. The one held that it would be equal, the other that it would be unequal. The Papists embrace Jerome's view so far as to build the inequality of glory upon the inequality of merits, and they promise certain teachers, martyrs, monks and, above all, saints who will occupy a higher rank little golden crowns and wreaths above the lot of the common saints. But we have already refuted the boasting of merits in its proper place. Some evangelical writers, Martyr, Tilenus, Camero and others, defend the equality of degrees; others, and far more of them, together with Jerome, Augustine and almost all the Fathers, defend inequality. We side with the latter, yet in such a way that

units.la: {x} Beatitudo et judicium ipsa gloria gradus recipiat. ut occupemus illud, Beatitudinis essentiam omnibus eandem affulsuram, & gradus ejus discrepaturos, atque ita discrepaturos esse, ut nemini quicquam ad beatitudinem desit, omnésque adeò, sive angustiora, sive ampliora & angustiora vasa sint, cœlesti gloria impleantur. Singulis enim sua laus erit à Deo, & multi multorum operum jacturam facient, sed sine invidia & frendore dentium. Cùm enim omnibus beatis Deus futurus sit אל למושעות Deus ad salutes, seu salutem omnimodam, Psal.LXVIII. 21. & futurus omnia in omnibus fit, 1.Cor.XV. 28. adeóque omnia, quæ ad plenam felicitatem pertinebunt, in omnibus electis immediatè operaturus sit; nemini quicquam ad perfectam felicitatem deesse, nemini adesse invidendum quicquam poterit. Quomodo luminaria multa, singula in suo ordine perfecta, alia tamen aliis decore & gloria sic præstabunt, ut tamen suum cuique decus, sua pulchritudo sufficiat. Propter communionem enim capitis & membrorum, quæ singulorum sunt, in totum corpus redundabunt. Tum inæqualitas illa justificationis actívæ discrepantiam non arguet, sed obtinget secundum gratiam Dei, qua Christo datum est corpus, in quo Deus πολυποίκιλον σοφίαν multifariam sapientiam, Ephes. III.20. servato discrimine capitis & membrorum singulorum, manifestet.
units.tr: {x} Blessedness itself, and glory, admit of degrees. We maintain this: the essence of blessedness will shine equally upon all, and its degrees will differ, and they will differ in such a way that nothing is lacking to anyone's blessedness, and all of them, whether their vessels are smaller or larger and narrower, will be filled with heavenly glory. For each will have his own praise from God, and many will suffer the loss of many works, but without envy and gnashing of teeth. For since God will be for all the blessed God unto salvations [אל למושעות], that is, complete salvation (Ps. 68:21), and will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28), and will work immediately in all the elect everything that pertains to full happiness, no one can lack anything for perfect happiness, and no one can envy anything. Just as many lights, each perfect in its own order, nevertheless surpass one another in beauty and glory, yet each has its own splendour and its own beauty sufficient for it, so because of the communion of the Head and the members, which belongs to each, the good will overflow into the whole body. Then that inequality of active justification will not indicate any discord, but will hold according to the grace of God, by which the body has been given to Christ, in which God will display manifold wisdom (Eph. 3:10), the distinction between the Head and each of the members being preserved.

units.la: CLVII.
units.tr: CLVII.

units.la: Inæqualitatem graduum gloriæ Scripturæ testimonia, parabolæ, exempla & rationes comprobant. Scripturæ testimonia aperтiora quædam sunt. Erudientes alios splendebunt כזהר הרקיע instar splendoris firmamenti, & justificantes multos ככוכבים ut stellæ in secula, Dan. XII.3. Ubi de erudientibus & justificantibus, hoc est, de iis, qui verbo & exemplo faciendi ac patiendi alios ad fidem justificantem adducent, adeóque & se ipsos, & alios salvabunt, 1.Tim.IV. 16. amplius quid dicitur, quam de singulis justis, qui v.2. לחיי עולם ad vitam æternam resuscitandi dicuntur; quia ibidem de omnibus resuscitandis ad vitam æternam, at v.3. de quibusdam in vita æterna eadem majorem gloriam & splendorem habituris sermo est. S. Paulus clarius: Alia gloria Solis, alia gloria Lunæ, & alia gloria stellarum. Sidus enim à sidere in gloria differt: Ita erit in resurrectione mortuorum, 1.Corinth.XV.41.42. Quibus verbis sic declaratur diversitas inter corpus, quod in morte deponitur, & corpus, quod in resurrectione instauratur, ut corpora cœlestia δόξη gloria & decore non solùm à terrestribus, quod principaliter ad institutum faciebat, sed etiam inter se, distinguat. Quæ disparitas corporum cœlestium etiam inter se non fine causa asseritur, licèt eo loco ad institutum non accommodatur. Idem S.Paulus: Hoc autem dico; qui serit parcè, parcè etiam metet: & qui serit in benedictionibus, etiam in benedictionibus metet, 2.Cor.IX.6. Quæ verba sic idem Apostolus declarat: Qui seminat in spiritum, ex spiritu ille metet vitam æternam, Gal. VI.8. Atqui quisquis eleemosynas sincero corde erogat, is seminat spiritui, cujus etiam fructus ἀγαθωσύνη beneficentia est, ibid.V.22. Parabola talentorum; Matth. XXV.14. &c. Luc. XIX.12. idem confirmat. Sicut enim ibi disparitas præmii, juxta disparitatem laboris fœnebris, v.21.23. innuitur: ita in cœlis gloriæ disparitas innuitur. Non enim Christus de donorum Dei augmento & amplificatione duntaxat in hac vita, sed etiam de remuneratione æternæ vitæ loquitur, tum quia sermo est de homine nobili peregrè abeunte, & post longum tempus reduce, ibid.v.14 19. hoc est, de Christo in cœlum ascendente, & ad judicium rediturō: tum quia servi frugi mittuntur in gaudium Domini, v.21.22. tum quia id ipsum ex parabola antecedente de virginibus, & consequenter de extremo judicio amplius colliquescit. Sed & Exempla rem confirmant. Nam & Patriarchæ Abraham, Isac & Jacob, velut duces fidelium cum iis in regno cœlorum accubiturorum in cœlesti gloria, Matth.VIII.11. statuuntur, & singulariter Abraham, pater credentium, Rom.IV.11.12. insignitur, eique proximus, velut in sinu ejus discumbens Lazarus, Luc. XVI.23. describitur; & Mosi & Eliæ in transfiguratione, Matth.XVII.3. &c. Apostolis, velut in regeneratione super duodecim thronis sedentes, & duodecim tribus Israelis judicaturis, ibid.XIX.28. singularis prærogativa in cœlesti gloria defertur: & fideles omnes sub nominibus viginti quatuor seniorum, Apoc. IV.4. censentur: & Apostolorum duodecim in inscriptione fundamentorum cœlestis Hierosolymæ mentio singularis, ibid.XXI.14. fit, quæ prærogativam gloriæ & honoris non obscurè loquuntur. Licèt enim quod Apostolis promissum est, alibi, 1.Cor.VI.2.3. Apoc.II.26.27. III.21. ad omnes fideles traducatur, id tamen suo ordine & gradu fit. Denique illam ἀναξίαν rationes aliæ statuminant, velut quod gradus charismatum in hac vita distincti, Rom. XII.6. 1.Cor.XII.4.5.6. & opera ipsa fidelium distincta, etiam gradus præmiorum & gloriæ in altera vita distinguere videntur, quia Deus sua in nobis dona coronat, & reddet unicuique secundum opera ipsius, Rom.II.6. & mulieri Christum inungenti in hac etiam vita majus præmium collatum est, ut, ubicunque Evangelium in mundo prædicatur, id quod fecit, commemoretur ad memoriam ejus, Matth.XXVI.13. quòd pœnarum infernalium gradus cœlestium etiam præmiorum gradus arguere videntur, quia Deus retribuet unicuique secundum opera ipsius, bona vel mala; adeóque sicut in inferno pœnarum disparitas propter disparia peccatorum merita erit; ita in cœlo disparitas præmiorum secundum gratuitam Dei benignitatem obtinebit: quòd etiam ordo resurrectionis, quo mortui resuscitandi vivos immutandos præverent, 1.Cor.XV.5. 1.Thess.IV.16. 17. id ipsum postulare videtur, quia ubi ordinis & temporis differentia obtinet, ibi etiam graduum differentia obtinere potest, tum quòd Deus etiam in hac vita laborantibus inæqualiter vitæ hujus præmia inæqualia promittit, juxta illa S.Pauli: Qui bene præsunt Presbyteri, duplici honore digni habeantur, 1.Tim.V.17. tum denique quòd & ipsum hoc gentiles nonnulli agnoverunt. Nam Plotinus, Enn. V.8.4. Ἀπειρος, inquit, ἡ ἀιγλὴ ἑκάστην δὲ αὐτῶν μέγα· ἐπὶ τὸ μικρὸν μέγα· καὶ ἡλιος ἐκεῖ πάντα ἀσφαλὲς, καὶ ἑκάστην ἡλιος αὖ, καὶ πάντα· ἐξῆς ἡ ἐν ἑκάσῳ ἄλλο. Splendor ibi immensus micat. Quod libet enim ibi magnum est. Ibi Sol, stellæ omnes. Unaquæque stella Sol est, & stellæ similes militer omnes. Præcellit autem in quolibet aliud. Etiam Plato in Phæd, eos, qui satis per Philosophiam purgati fuerint, οἰκίας καλλίους habitationes pulchriores naCturos, & de Republ. lib. X. eos qui erga Deos & parentes pii fuerint, μειζόνως μισθὸς majora præmia accepturos asserit.
units.tr: The testimonies of Scripture, parables, examples and reasons confirm the inequality of degrees of glory. The testimonies of Scripture are some of the plainer ones. Those who teach others shall shine [כזהר הרקיע] like the brightness of the firmament, and those who justify many [ככוכבים] like the stars for ever (Dan. 12:3). Here, by those who teach and justify, that is, those who by word and example bring others to justifying faith, and so save both themselves and others (1 Tim. 4:16), more is said than about individual righteous men who are said to be raised to eternal life (v. 2). For in the same place, of all who are to be raised to eternal life, one speaks in general; but in v. 3 it speaks of certain persons who, in eternal life, will have greater glory and splendour. St Paul speaks more clearly: Another glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars. For star differs from star in glory. So shall it be in the resurrection of the dead (1 Cor. 15:41-42). By these words the difference is so declared between the body that is laid down in death and the body that is restored in the resurrection, that the heavenly bodies are distinguished in glory and splendour not only from earthly ones, which was the main purpose of the passage, but also from one another. This disparity among the heavenly bodies is asserted not without reason, although in that place it is not adapted to the present purpose. The same St Paul says: But this I say: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings will also reap in blessings (2 Cor. 9:6). The same Apostle explains these words thus: He who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life (Gal. 6:8). Now whoever gives alms with a sincere heart sows to the Spirit, whose fruit is also goodness and beneficence (ibid. 5:22). The parable of the talents (Matt. 25:14, etc.; Luke 19:12) confirms the same. For just as there the disparity of reward is indicated according to the disparity of labour in trading (vv. 21, 23), so in heaven a disparity of glory is indicated. For Christ speaks not only of an increase and enlargement of God's gifts in this life, but also of the reward of eternal life, both because the matter concerns a nobleman going away to a far country and returning after a long time (vv. 14, 19), that is, Christ ascending into heaven and about to return to judgment, and because good and faithful servants are sent into the joy of their lord (vv. 21-22), and because the same thing becomes clearer still from the preceding parable of the virgins, and consequently from the last judgment. Examples also confirm the matter. For the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, as leaders of the faithful who are to recline with them in the kingdom of heaven, are set forth in heavenly glory (Matt. 8:11); and Abraham is singled out as the father of believers (Rom. 4:11-12), and Lazarus, reclining next to him as if in his bosom, is described (Luke 16:23). Moses and Elijah appear at the transfiguration (Matt. 17:3, etc.). A singular prerogative in heavenly glory is conferred on the Apostles, as those who in the regeneration, sitting upon twelve thrones, and judging the twelve tribes of Israel (ibid. 19:28). All the faithful are counted under the name of the twenty-four elders (Rev. 4:4). And the singular mention of the twelve apostles in the inscription of the foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem (ibid. 21:14) speaks plainly of a prerogative of glory and honour. For although what was promised to the Apostles is elsewhere extended to all the faithful (1 Cor. 6:2-3; Rev. 2:26-27; 3:21), it is nevertheless done in its own order and degree. Finally, other reasons support that view: the degrees of gifts distinguished in this life (Rom. 12:6; 1 Cor. 12:4-6), and the works of the faithful themselves, distinguished in the same way, seem also to distinguish degrees of reward and glory in the other life, because God crowns his own gifts in us and will render to each according to his works (Rom. 2:6). And to the woman who anointed Christ, a greater reward was given even in this life, so that wherever the Gospel is preached in the world, what she did is recalled in memory of her (Matt. 26:13). The degrees of infernal punishments seem also to indicate degrees of heavenly rewards, because God will render to each according to his works, good or evil; and therefore, just as in hell the disparity of punishments will correspond to the unequal merits of sinners, so in heaven the disparity of rewards will hold according to God's free goodness. The order of the resurrection, by which the dead who are to be raised will go before the living who are to be changed (1 Cor. 15:51; 1 Thess. 4:16-17), also seems to require this same thing, because where a difference of order and time holds, a difference of degrees can also hold there. Moreover, God promises unequal rewards in this life to those who labour unequally, according to that saying of St Paul: Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honour (1 Tim. 5:17). Finally, some of the Gentiles also recognised this very thing. For Plotinus (Enn. V.8.4) says: Splendour there shines immense. For whatever is there is great. There the sun is all the stars. Each star is a sun, and all the stars are alike in the same way. Yet each excels in something else. Plato too, in Phaedo, asserts that those who have been sufficiently purified by philosophy will obtain more beautiful dwellings [οἰκίας καλλίους], and in the Republic, book X, he says that those who have been pious towards the gods and parents will receive greater rewards [μειζόνως μισθὸς].

units.la: CLVIII. Haud æquè ponderosa sunt, quæ dissentientes pro ἰσοκαδμία afferunt, argumenta. Licèt enim in parabola operariorum in vinea omnibus & toto die,& nonnisi una diei hora laborantibus ex æquo denarius solutus fuerit, Matth. XX. 8. &c. tamen id nihil ad scopum parabolæ attinet, qui in eo vertitur,quòd multi primi ultimi & ultimi primi futuri sint,ibid. XIX. 30. Aliàs etiam murmuratoribus & hypocritis, quibus æquè atque reliquis denarius datus est, æterna vita promitteretur. Si tamen extra scopum argumentum validum foret, id unum consequens foret, quòd singulis unum idémque præmium, vita æterna expectandum sit; quod graduum inæqualitati non contrariatur. Erit quoque Deus omnia in omnibus, 1. Cor. XV. 28. atque adeò in omnibus veram, solidam, perfectam salutem immediatè operabitur, sed suo ordine & gradu in singulis, uti v. 41. innuitur. Etiam justi omnes fulgebunt sicut Sol, Matth. XIII. 43. & nulla major lux est ea, qua Sol præditus est. Licèt tamen omnes absolutè & indefinitè splendorem Solis habituri sint, comparatè tamen & relatè ad alios, alii splendorem Solis, alii lunæ, alii siderum, majore vel minore luce radiantium habebunt, 1. Cor. XV. 41. Etiam Solis splendor gradus admittit. Et erit lux lunæ ut lux Solis & lux Solis erit septupla, tanquam lux septem dierum, Esaj. XXX. 26. Solet quinetiam Scriptura fideles comparare rei cuipiam, cujus gradus non omnes & æqualiter habent; velut cùm eos argento, ibid. I. 22. comparat. Præterea tolletur in altera vita caro, quæ hac in vita regenerationis profectum distinguit. Sed non ideo par gloriæ gradus omnibus continget, quia sicut in hac vita dispar gratiæ dispensatio, & in regeneratione inæqualis profectus, juxta ejusdem gratiæ mensuram, obtinet: ita juxta eandem in altera gloria inæqualiter dispensabitur. Non ergo caro magis vel minus spiritui resistens, sed gratiosa Dei voluntas causa illa est, quæ gloriam illam distinguet, juxta ea,quæ homo in hac vita fecit,non quæ in altera faciet. Invalidum porrò ex justificationis activæ æqualitate petitum argumentum est, quia ea non obstante inæqualis & justificatio passiva, seu applicatio activæ; & sanctificatio est, & glorificatio etiam esse poterit. Illis enim,quibus Divina gratia majorem in hac vita justificationis applicatæ sensum quæsitiorem, & sanctitatis copiam majorem largitus est, ampliorem etiam gloriam largiri poterit. Ideo Deus sacrificium pro peccati analogia majus vel minus instituit, Levit. IV. 3. 13. innuens, sacrificium Christi analogicè applicari, prout alii plus, alii minus, iidémque nunc plus,nunc minus, pro peccatorum differentia,eadem indigent. Cùm ergo non sanctificatio duntaxat, sed etiam justificatio passiva per sacrificium Christi, in qua justificationis activæ applicatio consistit, inæqualis sit, gloriam inæqualem esse,nihil prohibebit. Qualis enim sementis est,talis messis erit. Deus enim dona sua in piis vario fine & modo coronabit, sic tamen, ut beatas mentes nulla invidia, æmulatio, luctus afflicturus sit, & mensura desideriorum omnium ex æquo implenda sit. Et par etiam ratio est sanguinis Christi, quem Christus pro sibi datis omnibus ex æquo effudit. Sicut enim ex communi medicina plus huic, minus illi vulneri sanando impenditur: ita in Christi sanguine,quando iis, pro quibus fusus est,applicatur,usu venit. Omnes præterea filii, omnes hæredes Dei in altera vita erimus. Neque iccirco æqualis omnium gloria erit; quia & primogeniti prærogativa esse potest; & filii magis vel minus parentibus chari esse possunt; & in hac etiam vita potestatem nacti credentes,ut fiant filii Dei, Joh. I. 12. nihilominus donis gratiæ distinguuntur. Reliqua, quæ afferunt, argumenta,velut, quòd in Cœlo omnes æquè sancti futuri, Deum à facie ad faciem visuri,eum æquè dilecturi sint,nec fieri possit,ut juxta gradus sanctitatis hujus vitæ in Cœlo distinguantur, quia aliàs primi ab ultimis nimium distarent; tam non præmiorum inCœlo,quàm non poenarum in inferno æqualitatem,quam omnes ferè negant,evincit. Nam in inferno etiam omnes ex æquo impuri erunt, à facie Dei exulabunt, Deum odio habebunt, & primi ab ultimis distabunt. Præterea vitæ æternæ inæqualis quoad gradus gloria non à sanctitate, visione & dilectione alterius vitæ; sed à vitæ præsentis sanctitate, cognitione & amore inæquali dependebit. Neque immane adeò primos inter & ultimos in cœlesti gloria discrimen est; quia nec immane primos inter & ultimos sanctificatos in hac vita discrimen elt. Omnes enim Spiritum Dei & semen regenerationis habent, licèt fructus utriusque,non immensum tamen differant.
units.tr: Far less weighty are the arguments that dissenters bring forward for ἰσοκαδμία [equal reward]. For although in the parable of the labourers in the vineyard the same denarius was paid to all, both to those who laboured the whole day and to those who worked only one hour, Matt. 20:8 etc., this has nothing to do with the purpose of the parable, which turns on the saying that many first will be last and last first, ibid. 19:30. Otherwise eternal life would also be promised to the murmurers and hypocrites, who received the same denarius as the rest. Yet even if the argument were to the point, it would only follow that each person is to expect one and the same eternal life as his reward, and this does not contradict inequality of degrees. God will also be all in all, 1 Cor. 15:28, and so he will work true, solid and perfect salvation immediately in all, but in each one in his own order and degree, as v. 41 indicates. Likewise all the righteous will shine like the sun, Matt. 13:43, and no greater light exists than that which the sun possesses. Although all will absolutely and without limit have the splendour of the sun, yet compared and related to one another, some will have the splendour of the sun, others that of the moon, others that of the stars, shining with greater or lesser light, 1 Cor. 15:41. Even the splendour of the sun admits of degrees: And the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, Isa. 30:26. Scripture also customarily compares the faithful to something of which not all have the same degrees and in equal measure, as when it compares them to silver, ibid. 1:22. Moreover, in the other life the flesh will be removed, which in this life marks the progress of regeneration. But this does not mean that all will receive an equal degree of glory, for just as in this life the dispensing of grace is unequal and the progress in regeneration is uneven, according to the measure of that same grace, so in the other glory it will be dispensed unequally according to the same measure. It is therefore not the flesh, resisting the spirit more or less, but the gracious will of God that is the cause which will distinguish that glory, according to what a man has done in this life, not according to what he will do in the other. The argument drawn from the equality of active justification is also weak, because despite that equality, passive justification, that is, the application of the active, is unequal; and it can also be sanctification and glorification. For to those to whom God in this life has given a greater and more exquisite sense of the applied justification and a greater abundance of holiness, he can also bestow a larger glory. Thus God appointed a sacrifice for sin of greater or lesser size according to the analogy of the sin, Lev. 4:3, 13, indicating that the sacrifice of Christ is applied analogously, so that some need more and others less of it, and the same persons now need more and now less, according to the difference of their sins. Since therefore not only sanctification but also passive justification, in which the application of active justification consists, through the sacrifice of Christ is unequal, nothing will prevent glory from being unequal. For as the sowing is, so will the harvest be. God will crown his gifts in the pious with varied purpose and manner, yet in such a way that no envy, rivalry or grief will trouble the blessed minds, and the measure of all desires will be fulfilled equally. The same reasoning holds for the blood of Christ, which Christ shed equally for all who were given to him. For just as from a common medicine more is applied to heal one wound and less to another, so in the blood of Christ it comes about when it is applied to those for whom it was shed. Moreover, we shall all be sons and all heirs of God in the other life. Nor for this reason will the glory of all be equal, since the privilege of the firstborn can exist, and sons can be more or less dear to their parents, and even in this life believers who have received power to become sons of God, John 1:12, are nonetheless distinguished by the gifts of grace. The remaining arguments they bring forward, such as that in heaven all will be equally holy, will see God face to face, and will love him equally, and that it cannot happen that in heaven they are distinguished according to the degrees of holiness of this life, because otherwise the first would be too far removed from the last, are refuted by the equality, which almost everyone denies, not of rewards in heaven but of punishments in hell. For in hell too all will be equally impure, will be exiled from the face of God, will hate God, and the first will be as far from the last. Moreover, the glory of eternal life, unequal in degrees, will depend not on the holiness, vision and love of another life, but on the holiness, knowledge and unequal love of the present life. Nor is the difference between the first and the last in heavenly glory so immense, since the difference between the first and last sanctified in this life is not immense either. For all have the Spirit of God and the seed of regeneration, although the fruits of both do not differ immensely.

units.la: CLIX. Sed quorum ex genere humano præcipua gloria futura sit, solus novit is, qui eam servis suis paravit; & discemus nos,quan- do in Regno Cœlorum cum Abrahamo, Isaco & Jacobo discumbemus, Matth. VIII. 11. & ampliore gloria coronatos admirabimur eos, quos hac in vita velut posteriore loco amandatos mundus despexit: sicut etiam in judicio ultimo ad sinistram stantes mirabimur plures, quos hac in vita nimium suspeximus. Id tamen ex Scripturis affirmare licet, præcellentiam quandam gloriæ Patriarchis, Prophetis, Apostolis, Ecclesiæ doctoribus multos erudientibus & justificantibus,denique Martyribus, qui sanguinem suum pro testimonio Jesu effuderunt donatum iri. Nam cum Patriarchis, Abrahamo, Isaco & Jacobo,ceu primore loco in Regno Cœlorum (in hac vita inchoando, in altera consummando) sedentibus reliqui ex Oriente & Occidente venturi accumbent, Matth. VIII. 11. Quod fieri citra ἐξοχῶν quandam Patriarcharum non poterit. Etiam Apostoli in παλιγγενεσία regeneratione (quæ in hac vita inchoata,in altera terminabitur) sedebunt super duodecim thronos, judicantes duodecim tribus Israelis, ibid. XIX. 28. Ubi Apostolis amplius aliquid tribuitur, quàm reliquis, ab iis v. 29. distinctis, qui propter Christum omnia sua in mundo reliquerunt, quibus propterea ζωὴ αἰώνιος vita æterna promittitur. Fideles enim hi non sedebunt bunt & judicabunt praeter Apostolos, licèt judicaturi sint, quatenus idem cum Apostolis loquentur. Quod cùm in hac vita factum & futurum sit, in altera praerogativam Apostolorum post se etiam trahet. Si enim novæ Hierosolymæ duodecim fundamentis inscripta præ cæteris nomina duodecim Apostolorum Agni fuerunt, Apoc. XXI. 14. in cœlesti Hierololyma prærogativa quadam non defraudabuntur. De Doctoribus Ecclesiæ erudientibus & justificantibus multos, diserte Daniel: Fulgebunt instar splendoris firmamenti, & ut stellæ in seculum, cap. XII. 3. Denique de Martyribus Johannes: Vidi stantes coram throno Agni, & amictos stolis albis, & palmæ in manibus ipsorum. Et interrogavit unus ex Senioribus dicens: Illi induti stolis albis, quinam sunt, & unde venerunt? Et dixit ipsi: Domine tu nosti. Et dixit mihi: Hi sunt, qui venerunt ex tribulatione magna; & laverunt stolas suas, & dealbarunt stolas suas in sanguine Agni, Apoc. VII. 9.-15. Sed præter hos in altiore gloriæ gradu collocabuntur heroes, quotquot in hac vita fidei, amoris, patientiæ, humilitatis facem cæteris prætulerunt.
units.tr: CLIX. But who from the human race will have the chief glory, only he knows who has prepared it for his servants; and we shall learn this when we recline in the kingdom of heaven with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Matt. 8:11, and we shall marvel, crowned with greater glory, at those whom the world despised in this life as though sent to a lower place; just as, too, at the last judgment, standing on the left, we shall marvel at many whom in this life we too highly esteemed. Yet from the Scriptures it may be affirmed that a certain pre-eminence of glory will be given to the Patriarchs, the Prophets, the Apostles, the teachers of the Church who taught and justified many, and finally to the Martyrs, who shed their blood for the testimony of Jesus. For together with the Patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who sit as the first in the kingdom of heaven (begun in this life, to be completed in the other), the rest coming from east and west will recline, Matt. 8:11. This cannot happen without a certain eminence of the Patriarchs. The Apostles too will sit in the regeneration [παλιγγενεσία] (begun in this life, to be finished in the other), sitting on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel, ibid. 19:28. Here the Apostles are given something more than the rest, distinguished from those in v. 29 who for Christ's sake have left all their things in the world, to whom therefore eternal life [ζωὴ αἰώνιος] is promised. For these faithful will not sit and judge in place of the Apostles, although they will be judges in so far as they speak the same things as the Apostles. Since this is done and will be done in this life, it will also draw the Apostles' prerogative after it into the other. For if the names of the twelve Apostles of the Lamb were written on the twelve foundations of the new Jerusalem above the others, Rev. 21:14, they will not be deprived of a certain prerogative in the heavenly Jerusalem. Concerning the teachers of the Church, who instruct and justify many, Daniel speaks plainly: They shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and like the stars for ever, ch. 12:3. Finally, concerning the Martyrs, John: I saw standing before the throne of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands. And one of the Elders asked, saying: Those clothed in white robes, who are they, and whence have they come? And he said to me: Lord, you know. And he said to me: These are they who have come out of great tribulation; and they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb, Rev. 7:9-15. But besides these, heroes, as many as in this life have set the torch of faith, love, patience and humility before others, will be placed in a higher degree of glory.

units.la: CLX. Æternam Beatorum felicitatem luculenter S. Augustinus depinxit. Lubet ejus verbis memoratu dignissimis, ceu quodam eorum, quæ hactenus de æterna Beatitudine diximus, compendio rem tanti momenti, cujus jugis & pia meditatio in hoc mortalitatis curriculo mirè certantium fidem corroborat, & spem inflammat, complecti. Ita autem ille de Civ. Dei lib. XXII. 29. admirabili & efficacissimo sermone Beatitudinem describit: Quanta erit illa felicitas, ubi nullum erit malum, nullum latebit bonum, vacabitur Dei laudibus, qui erit omnia in omnibus. Nam quid aliud agetur, ubi neque ulla desidia cessabitur, neque ulla indigentia laborabitur, nescio. Admoneor etiam sancto Cantico, ubi lego, vel audio: Beati, qui habitant in domo tua Domine, in secula seculorum laudabunt te. Omnia membra & viscera incorruptibilis corporis, quæ nunc videmus per usus necessitatis varios & motus distributa, quoniam tunc non erit ipsa necessitas, sed plena, certa, secura, sempiterna felicitas, proficient in laudibus Dei. Omnes quippe illi, de quibus jam sum locutus, qui nunc latent harmoniæ corporalis numeri, non latebunt, intrinsecus & extrinsecus per corporis cuncta dispositi, & cum cæteris rebus, quæ ibi magnæ atque mirabiles videbuntur, rationales mentes in tanti artificis laudem rationabilis pulchritudinis delectatione succedent. Qui motus illic talium corporum sint futuri, temere definire non audeo, quod excogitare non valeo. Tamen & motus & status sicut ipsa species decens erit, quicunque erit, ubi, quod non decebit, non erit. Certè ubi volet spiritus, ibi protinus erit corpus, nec volet aliquid spiritus, quod nec spiritum possit decere, nec corpus. Vera ibi gloria erit, ubi laudantis nec errore quisquam, nec adulatione laudabitur. Verus honor, qui nulli negabitur digno, nulli deferetur indigno, sed nec ad eum ambiet ullus indignus, ubi nullus permittetur esse, nisi dignus. Vera pax ibi est, ubi nihil adversi, nec à se ipso, nec ab alio quisquam patietur. Præmium virtutis erit ipse, qui virtutem dedit, & qui se ipsum, quo melius & majus nihil esse possit, promisit. Quid est enim aliud, quod per Prophetam dixit: Ero illorum Deus, & ipsi mihi erunt plebs: nisi. Ego ero, unde satientur: Ego ero quæcunque ab omnibus honestè desiderantur, & vita, & salus, & virtus, & copia, & gloria, & honor, & pax, & omnia bona? Sic enim & illud rectè intelligitur, quod ait Apostolus, ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus. Ipse finis erit desideriorum nostrorum, qui sine fine videbitur, sine fastidio amabitur, sine fatigatione laudabitur. Hoc munus, hic affectus, hic actus profectò erit omnibus, sicut ipsa vita æterna, communis. Cæterum qui futuri sint pro meritis præmiorum etiam gradus honorum atque gloriarum, quis est idoneus cogitare, quantò magis dicere? Quòd tamen futuri sint, non est ambigendum. Atque id etiam beata civitas illa magnum in se bonum videbit, quòd nulli superiori ullus inferior invidebit; sicut nunc non invident Archangelis Angeli cæteri: tanquam nolit esse unusquisque quod non accepit, quamvis sit pacatissimo concordiæ vinculo ei, qui accepit, obstrictus, quàm nec in corpore vult oculus esse, qui est digitus, cùm membrum utrumque contineat totius carnis pacata compago. Sic itaque habebit donum alius alio minus, ut hoc quoque donum habeat, ne velit amplius. Nec ideo liberum arbitrium non habebunt, quia peccata eos delectare non poterunt. Magis quippe erit liberum à delectatione peccandi usque ad delectationem non peccandi indeclinabilem libertatem. Nam primum liberum arbitrium, quod homini datum est, quando primùm creatus est rectus, potuit non peccare, sed potuit & peccare: Hoc autem novissimum eò potentius erit, quo peccare non poterit. Verùm hoc quoque Dei munere, non suæ possibilitate naturæ. Aliud est enim esse Deum, aliud participem Dei. Deus natura peccare non potest; particeps verò Dei ab illo accipit, ut non possit peccare. Servandi autem gradus erant Divini muneris, ut primum daretur liberum arbitrium, quo non peccare posset, novissimum, quo peccare non posset: atque illud ad comparandum meritum; hoc ad recipiendum præmium pertineret. Sed quia peccavit ista natura, cùm non peccare potuit, largiore gratia liberatur, ut ad eam perducatur libertatem, in qua peccare non possit. Sicut enim prima immortalitas fuit, quam peccando Adam perdidit, posse non mori, novissima erit, non posse mori: ita primum liberum arbitrium posse non peccare, novissimum, non posse peccare. Sic enim erit inamissibilis voluntas pietatis & æquitatis, quo modo est felicitatis. Nam utique peccando nec pietatem, nec felicitatem tenuimus, voluntatem verò felicitatis, nec perdita felicitate perdidimus. Certè Deus ipse numquid, quia peccare non potest, ideo liberum arbitrium habere negandus est? Erit ergo illius civitatis, & una in omnibus, & inseparabilis in singulis voluntas libera, ab omni malo liberata, & impleta omni bono, fluens indeficienter æternorum jucunditate gaudiorum, oblita culparum, oblita pœnarum, nec tamen ideo suæ liberationis oblita, ut liberatori suo sit ingrata. Quantum ergo attinet ad scientiam rationalem, memor præteritorum etiam malorum suorum; quantum autem ad experientiæ sensum, prorsus immemor. Nam & peritissimus medicus, sicut arte sciuntur, omnes fere morbos corporis novit; sicut autem corpore sentiuntur, plurimos nescit, quos ipse non passus est. Ut ergo scientiæ malorum duæ sunt, una qua potentiam mentis non latent, altera, qua experientis sensibus inhærent. Aliter quippe sciuntur omnia vitia per sapientiæ doctridoctrinam, aliter per insipientis pessimam vitam: ita & obliviones malorum duæ sunt. Aliter ea namque obliviscitur eruditus & doctus, aliter expertus & passus. Ille si peritiam negligat, iste si miseria careat. Secundum hanc oblivionem, quam posteriore loco posui, non erunt memores sancti praeteritorum malorum. Carebunt enim omnibus malis, ita ut penitus deleantur de sensibus eorum. Ea tamen potentia scientiæ, quæ magna in eis erit, non solum sua praeterita, sed etiam damnatorum eos sempiterna miseria non latebit. Alioquin si se fuisse miseros nesciturí sunt, quomodo sicut ait Psalmus: Misericordias Domini in æternum cantabunt? Quo cantico in gloriam gratiæ Christi, cujus sanguine liberati sumus, nihil erit profecto illi jucundius civitati. Ibi perficietur: Vacate & videte, quoniam ego sum Deus. Quod erit ibi verè maximum Sabbathum, non habens vesperam. Quod commendavit Dominus in primis operibus mundi, ubi legitur: Et requievit Deus die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis, quæ fecit: & benedixit Deus diem septimum, & sanctificavit eum; quia in eo requievit ab omnibus operibus suis, quæ inchoavit Deus facere. Dies enim septimus etiam nos ipsi erimus, quando ejus fuerimus benedictione & sanctificatione pleni atque refecti. Ibi vacantes videbimus, quoniam ipse est Deus, quod nobis nos ipsi esse voluimus, quando ab illo cecidimus, audientes à seductore: Eritis sicut dii; & recedentes à vero Deo, quo faciente dii essemus ejus participatione, non desertione. Quid enim sine illo fecimus, nisi in ira ejus defecimus? A quo refecti, & gratia majore perfecti, vacabimus in æternum, videntes, quia ipse est Deus, quo pleni erimus, quando ipse erit omnia in omnibus. Nam & ipsa bona opera nostra, quando ipsius potius intelliguntur esse, quam nostra, tunc nobis ad hoc Sabbathum adipiscendum imputantur, quia si nobis ea tribuerimus, servilia erunt, cum de Sabbatho dicatur: omne opus servile in eo non facietis. Propter quod & per Ezechielem Prophetam dicitur: Et Sabbatha mea dedi eis in signum inter me & inter eos, ut scirent, quia ego Dominus, qui sanctifico eos. Hoc perfectè tunc sciemus, quando perfectè vacabimus, & perfectè videbimus, quia ipse est Deus. Ipse etiam numerus ætatum veluti dierum, si secundum eos articulos temporis computentur, qui in Scripturis sanctis videntur expressi; iste sabbathismus evidentius apparebit, quoniam septimus invenitur, ut prima ætas tanquam dies primus sit ab Adam usque ad diluvium: secunda inde usque ad Abraham, non æqualitate temporum, sed numero generationum. Denas quippe habere reperiuntur. Hinc jam sicuti Matthæus Evangelista determinat, tres ætates usque ad Christi subsequutum adventum, quæ singulæ denis & quaternis generationibus explicantur. Ab Abraham usque ad David una; altera inde ad transmigrationem usque in Babyloniam: tertia inde usque ad Christi carnalem nativitatem. Fiunt itaque omnes quinque. Sexta nunc agitur, nullo generationum numero metienda, propter id quod dictum est: Non est vestrum scire tempora, quæ Pater posuit in sua potestate. Post hanc tanquam in die septimo requiescet Deus, cum eundem septimum diem, quod nos erimus, in se ipso Deus faciet requiescere. De istis porro ætatibus singulis diligenter longum est disputare. Hæc tamen septima erit Sabbathum nostrum, cujus finis non erit vespera, sed Dominicus dies velut octavus, æternus, qui Christi resurrectione sacratus est, æternam non solum spiritus, verùm etiam corporis requiem præfigurans. Ibi vacabimus & videbimus: Videbimus: Videbimus & amabimus: amabimus & laudabimus. Ecce quod erit in fine sine fine. Nam quis alius noster est finis, nisi pervenire ad regnum, cujus nullus est finis?
units.tr: CLX. Augustine has described the eternal happiness of the blessed in a striking way. It is worth while to take in, as a kind of summary of what we have said so far about eternal blessedness, a matter of such great weight. Constant and devout meditation on it wonderfully strengthens the faith of those who struggle in this course of mortality and kindles their hope. He describes that blessedness in these words, in a wonderful and most effective passage, De Civitate Dei book XXII, chapter 29: How great will that happiness be, where there will be no evil, where no good will be hidden, and where there will be leisure for the praises of God, who will be all in all. For I do not know what else will be done where no idleness will be allowed and no want will be felt. I am reminded also of the holy canticle, where I read or hear: Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you for ever and ever. All the members and organs of the incorruptible body, which we now see distributed to various uses and movements for the needs of life, will then, since there will be no such need, but a full, certain, secure and everlasting happiness, be devoted to the praise of God. Indeed all those proportions of the bodily frame which now lie hidden will not be hidden then, but will be arranged within and without throughout the whole body. And along with the other things which will then appear great and wonderful, rational minds will be brought, by the delight of a reasonable beauty, to praise the great Artificer. What movements such bodies will then have I dare not define rashly, because I cannot think it out. Yet both their movements and their state will be as fitting as their form will be, whatever it is, and where there is nothing unfitting there will be nothing unfitting. Certainly wherever the spirit wills, there at once the body will be, and the spirit will will nothing that could be unfitting either for spirit or for body. There will be true glory where no one is praised through error or flattery. There will be true honour, which will be denied to no one worthy and given to no one unworthy, and no unworthy person will even seek it, since none will be permitted to be there except the worthy. There will be true peace, where no one will suffer anything adverse either from himself or from another. The reward of virtue will be he who gave the virtue, and who promised himself, than whom nothing better or greater can exist. For what else is it that he said through the Prophet: I will be their God, and they will be my people; yes, I will be the one from whom they are satisfied; I will be whatever is honestly desired by all, both life and health and virtue and abundance and glory and honour and peace and all good things? For thus that also is rightly understood which the Apostle says, that God may be all in all. He himself will be the end of our desires, to be seen without end, to be loved without weariness, to be praised without fatigue. This gift, this affection, this activity will certainly be common to all, just as eternal life itself will be. But as to what degrees of honours and glories there will be, according to the merits of the rewards, who is fit to think, much less to say? Yet that there will be such degrees is not to be doubted. And that blessed city will see this as a great good in itself, that no lesser one will envy any greater one; just as now the other Angels do not envy the Archangels; as if no one wished to be what he has not received, although each is bound to him who has received by the most peaceful bond of concord. In the same way the eye does not wish to be in the body what the finger is, since the peaceful framework of the whole flesh contains both members. So each will have a gift less than another's, yet he will have this gift too, that he does not want more. Nor on that account will they not have free will, because sins will be unable to delight them. Rather, freedom will be greater, from the delight of sinning to the unchangeable freedom of delight in not sinning. For the first free will, which was given to man when he was first created upright, could not sin but could also sin; but that last will be the more powerful, in that it will be unable to sin. Yet this too is a gift of God, not the possibility of its own nature. For it is one thing to be God, another to be a partaker of God. God by nature cannot sin; but the partaker of God receives from him that he cannot sin. The degrees of the divine gift were to be kept, so that first free will was given, by which he could not sin, and last, by which he could not sin; the former pertaining to the earning of merit, the latter to the receiving of reward. But because that nature sinned when it could not sin, it is freed by a more abundant grace, so that it may be brought to that freedom in which it cannot sin. For just as the first immortality was that Adam lost by sinning, being able not to die, while the last will be not being able to die, so the first free will was being able not to sin, the last, not being able to sin. For thus the will of piety and justice will be unlosable, just as it is with happiness. For certainly by sinning we kept neither piety nor happiness; but the will for happiness we did not lose, even when happiness was lost. Surely God himself is not to be denied free will because he cannot sin? So there will be in that city one free will in all and inseparable in each, freed from every evil and filled with every good, flowing without failure with the sweetness of eternal joys, forgetful of faults, forgetful of punishments, yet not therefore forgetful of its own liberation, so as to be ungrateful to its liberator. So, as far as rational knowledge goes, they will remember even their own past evils; but as far as the sense of experience goes, they will be wholly unmindful. For the most skilled physician, though he knows by his art almost all the diseases of the body, does not know very many which he himself has not suffered, as they are known through the bodily senses. So there are two kinds of knowledge of evils: one by which they are not hidden from the power of the mind, the other by which they cling to the senses of experience. For all vices are known one way through the teaching of wisdom, and another way through the worst life of the foolish. So too there are two kinds of forgetting of evils. The learned and instructed man forgets one way, the one who has experienced and suffered forgets another. The former forgets if he neglects his skill, the latter if he is free from misery. According to this second forgetting, which I put in the later place, the saints will not remember their past evils. For they will be without all evils, so that they are wholly erased from their senses. Yet that power of knowledge, which will be great in them, will not hide from them not only their own past, but also the everlasting misery of the damned. Otherwise, if they did not know that they had been wretched, how would they, as the Psalm says, sing of the mercies of the Lord for ever? In that canticle to the glory of the grace of Christ, by whose blood we have been freed, nothing will certainly be more pleasing to that city. There will be fulfilled: Be still and see that I am God. This will truly be the greatest Sabbath there, having no evening, which the Lord commended in the first works of the world, where it is read: And God rested on the seventh day from all his works which he had made; and God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he rested from all his works which God had begun to make. For we ourselves will be the seventh day, when we have been filled and refreshed with his blessing and sanctification. There, at leisure, we shall see that he himself is God, while we wanted to be ourselves what we were when we fell from him, hearing from the seducer: You will be as gods; and receding from the true God, by whose making we would have been gods through participation in him, not through desertion of him. For what have we done without him, except fail in his anger? Refreshed by him and made perfect by a greater grace, we shall rest for ever, seeing that he himself is God, and we shall be filled with him when he himself will be all in all. For even our good works, when they are understood to be his rather than ours, are then imputed to us for obtaining this Sabbath; since if we attributed them to ourselves they would be servile, when it is said of the Sabbath: You shall do no servile work in it. On account of this it is also said through the Prophet Ezekiel: And I gave them my Sabbaths as a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them. We shall know this perfectly then, when we rest perfectly and see perfectly that he is God. And the very number of the ages, as if of days, if they are reckoned by those periods of time which are set forth in the holy Scriptures, will make this Sabbath rest more evident, since the seventh is found: so that the first age is like the first day, from Adam to the flood; the second from there to Abraham, not by equal lengths of time but by the number of generations, for these are found to be ten. From there, as the Evangelist Matthew determines, there are three ages up to the coming of Christ, each of which is set out in fourteen generations: from Abraham to David one; the second from there to the transmigration into Babylon; the third from there to the carnal birth of Christ. So all five are made. The sixth is now going on, not to be measured by any number of generations, on account of what was said: It is not for you to know the times which the Father has put in his own power. After this, as on the seventh day, God will rest, when God will make that seventh day, which we ourselves shall be, rest in himself. Now it would be long to dispute carefully about each of these ages. Yet this seventh will be our Sabbath, whose end will not be evening, but the Lord's day as if an eighth, eternal, which was consecrated by the resurrection of Christ, foreshadowing an eternal rest not only of the spirit but also of the body. There we shall rest and see: we shall see, we shall see and love, we shall love and praise. Behold what will be, without end, at the end. For what other end is ours, except to attain to the kingdom, which has no end?

units.la: Dici de vita æterna innumera poterant; sed de re tam sacro-sancta nihil pronuntiandum temerè putavimus; neque omnino fas duximus ad quæstiunculas humanas revocare, quod Deus arcanissimum esse justit, & nec oculis ostendit, nec vocibus elocutus est, nec in cogitationes mentésque Mortalium immisit. Non igitur, liceat Ludovici Vivis ad August. de Civ. D. lib. XXII. 30. verba mea facere, curiosius inquirimus cum Scholasticis: Sitne beatitudo nostra futura intellectus, an voluntatis? Sitne mens nostra in Deo omnia intuitura, an aliquibus arcenda? Ne si contentiosè nimium hæc quæsiverimus, nec voluntatis sit, nec intellectus felicitas, nec aliquid videamus in Deo. Placet Divinum illud Scaligeri, quod non hic duntaxat, sed universa in hac tractatione nostra, in qua non semel in malè curiosorum tricas incidimus, ad mentem nobis revocatum curiositatem cohibuit: Nescire velle, quæ Magister Maximus docere non vult, erudita inscitia est.
units.tr: Countless things could be said about eternal life; but we have thought it rash to pronounce anything on so sacred a matter, and we have judged it wrong altogether to bring down to human trifles what God has willed to be most hidden, and what he has neither shown to our eyes, nor declared in words, nor placed in the thoughts and minds of mortals. Therefore, let me not, in the words of Ludovicus Vives on Augustine's De Civitate Dei book XXII, chapter 30, inquire too curiously with the Scholastics: Will our future blessedness be of the intellect or of the will? Will our mind see all things in God, or will some things be withheld from it? For if we ask these questions too contentiously, our happiness will be neither of the will nor of the intellect, and we shall see nothing in God. That divine saying of Scaliger pleases me, which has recalled to my mind, not only here but throughout this whole treatment, in which I have more than once fallen into the snares of those who are too curious, a restraint upon curiosity: to wish not to know what the great Teacher does not wish to teach is learned ignorance.

units.la: Quod superest, Deo immortales gratias agamus, qui tot inter miserias errorum humanorum, tamen veri summique Boni nostri, DEI T.O.M. desiderium conservavit in natura nostra; & ejus, omniúmque ad consecutionem illius pertinentium mediorum, quæ longo opere, pro modulo infirmitatis nostræ, prosecuti sumus, cognitionem aperuit in verbo suo; & possessionem æternam promisit in CHRISTO, qui ἀρχηγὸς dux vitæ & salutis nostræ est. Faxit idem, Beatus & Immortalis, ut Bonum nostrum, & vitam nunc cum Christo in Deo occultatam, studiosè quæramus, quæsitam inveniamus, inventam in æternum amplexemur! Ei verò, qui potest nos custodire inoffensos, & sistere coram gloria sua inculpatos in exultatione, SOLI SAPIENTI DEO SALVATORI NOSTRO, SIT GLORIA ET MAGNITUDO, IMPERIUM ET POTESTAS, ET NUNC ET IN OMNIA SECULA AMEN!
units.tr: For the rest, let us give immortal thanks to God, who, amid so many miseries of human error, has nevertheless preserved in our nature the desire for the true and highest Good, namely God the best and greatest; who has opened in his Word the knowledge of this Good and of all the means pertaining to its attainment, which we have pursued in this long work, according to the measure of our weakness; and who has promised eternal possession in Christ, who is the ἀρχηγὸς [author] of our life and salvation. May the same blessed and immortal God grant that we seek eagerly our Good and the life now hidden with Christ in God, that having sought it we find it, and having found it embrace it forever! To him who is able to keep us from stumbling and to present us blameless before his glory with exceeding joy, to the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and for all ages. Amen!

units.tr: The love of God: a perfect love of God is impossible for a sinful man. I.317.a. It must be sincere, as toward the highest good. 519.b. It is either of union or of benevolence; the mystical love of the Scholastics is opposed to it. 520.a. What kind of love the Law requires: 502. It is a requisite of a good work: 329.a.

units.la: Amor Dei erga electos. I. 96. b. amore Dei, vel odio dignum esse quid sit? II.412. a. amoris nostri erga Deum indoles salutis certitudinem confirmat. I. 416. a. proximi amori Dei innexus est. I. 314. a.
units.tr: The love of God towards the elect. I.96.b. What it is to be worthy of love or hatred by God: II.412.a. The character of our love towards God confirms the certainty of salvation. I.416.a. The love of neighbour is bound up with the love of God. I.314.a.

units.la: Amor sui ipsius quis licitus sit. I.505. b. rectus amicitiae fons est. 506. b. societatis in civitatibus. 507. a. ejus characteres. 508. a. cum amore proximi similitudo. ibid. b.
units.tr: Self-love: which kind is lawful. I.505.b. It is the right source of friendship. 506.b. Of society in states: 507.a. Its marks: 508.a. Its similarity with love of neighbour: ibid.b.

units.la: Amor conjugalis in quo consistat. I.570, a.
units.tr: Conjugal love: in what does it consist? I.570.a.

units.la: Amyraldus de promissione foederis operum notatur. I.172. ejusdem de ea promissione error. 474. a. refellitur, ibid. b. 475. opinio de spiritu servitutis refutatur. 476. de bonis terrestribus Paradisi refelli tur. 319. a. Legem Moisis operum legem facit. 462. b.
units.tr: Amyraut is criticised on the promise of the covenant of works. I.172. His error about that promise: 474.a. It is refuted, ibid.b. 475. His opinion on the spirit of bondage is refuted: 476. His view on the earthly goods of Paradise is refuted: 319.a. He makes the Law of Moses a law of works: 462.b.

units.la: Amplitudo non est nota Ecclesiae. II.452. a.
units.tr: Extent is not a mark of the Church. II.452.a.

units.la: Anabaptistae, eorum error, dum Christum assumta carne mutatum Filium Dei asserunt. I. 79. b. Sacramenta negant esse sigilla gratiae ad remissionem peccatorum. 393. a. Sabbathi praeceptum mere ceremoniale faciunt. 552. b. Leges Mosaicas quasvis sine discrimine in N. T. abrogatas esse contendunt. 739. b. Eorum argumenta contra Paedobaptismum refutantur. I I.450. 451. argumenta contra stipendia ministrorum Ecclesiae refelluntur. 575. b. fusius. 578. a. adversus Magistratus Christianos blasphemiae proponuntur. 618. b. refelluntur. 620. a. Magistratuum potestas adversus eorum cavillamenta vindicatur. 624. Christianum subesse Magistratui libertati Christianae adversari docent. 526. a. a causa religionis magistratus prorsus removent, ibid. b. animas a corpore separatas ad resurrectionem usque dormire nugantur. 707. b. Monasterienses Cerinthi in dogmate de Chiliasmo affectae fuerunt. 726. a. eandem numero carnem resurecturam esse negant. 738. b. jurandum esse negant. I.543. b.
units.tr: The Anabaptists: their error, in asserting that the Son of God was changed by assuming flesh. I.79.b. They deny that the sacraments are seals of grace for the remission of sins. 393.a. They make the command about the Sabbath merely ceremonial. 552.b. They contend that all the Mosaic laws without distinction were abrogated in the New Testament. 739.b. Their arguments against infant baptism are refuted: II.450, 451. Their arguments against the stipends of Church ministers are refuted: 575.b; more fully 578.a. Blasphemies are brought against Christian magistrates: 618.b. They are refuted: 620.a. The power of the magistrate is vindicated against their cavils: 624. They teach that for a Christian to be subject to the magistrate is contrary to Christian liberty: 526.a. They remove the magistrate altogether from the cause of religion: ibid.b. They babble that souls separated from the body sleep until the resurrection: 707.b. The Münsterites were affected by the dogma of Chiliasm held by Cerinthus: 726.a. They deny that the same flesh will rise in number: 738.b. They deny that oaths are to be sworn: I.543.b.

units.la: ᾿Ανάληψις ascensio est jure meriti quaesita. I I. 65. b. Filio tribuitur, sicut ἀνάληψις Patri. ib. b.
units.tr: Analēpsis [ἀνάληψις]: an ascension obtained by right of merit. II.65.b. It is attributed to the Son, just as analēpsis is to the Father. Ibid.b.

units.la: Anachoretarum origo. I I. 675. b.
units.tr: The anchorites: their origin. II.675.b.

units.la: ᾿Ανάληψις Christi fuit ejus in coelum ascensio. I I,65. b, est argumentum justificationis ejus, ibid,
units.tr: The analēpsis [ἀνάληψις] of Christ was his ascension into heaven. II.65.b. It is an argument for his justification. Ibid.

I. 456. b.
units.tr: The angels. Their theology: I.187.b. Predestination: 155.a. Creation: 201.a; 273.a. They are pure, incorporeal spirits: 272.a. How they are called sons of God: 273.a; see the Breviary. Their power: 275.b. Their number is unknown to us: 276. Their duration: 278.a. Their distinction: ibid.b. The fictitious hierarchy: 280.b. Are they guardian angels? 281.b. They are not to be worshipped religiously: 283.b. Nor are they to be adored: 526.b. They are the armies of Jehovah: 273.b; 280.a. Their names: 278.a; see Brev. What was the sin of the evil angels: 286.b. Angels served Christ at his resurrection: II.58.b. They do not need a Mediator for salvation: 83.b; 84.a, because they have been confirmed by God, ibid. Christ did not die for them: 122.a. Whether and how they belong to the Church: 508.b. They are not searchers of hearts: 710.a. Nor will they be the joint cause of the resurrection of the dead: 735.b. The evil angels will be judged on the last day: 747.b. See Devil. The ministry of good angels in the giving of the Law: I.456.b.

units.la: Angelus cum Mose in monte Sinai loquens fuit Christus. I, 456. a. eidem nomen Jehovae in medio fuit, 115. a. idem est angelus foederis, vindex, &c. ibid.
units.tr: The angel who spoke with Moses on Mount Sinai was Christ. I.456.a. The name of Jehovah was in the midst of him: 115.a. He is the same as the angel of the covenant, the avenger, etc. Ibid.

units.la: Anglorum Directoria quid? II.430. b.
units.tr: The Directories of the English: what are they? II.430.b.

units.la: Anima, Christi non ejus Divinitatem notat. II.8. b. a Deo sancta creata est, 17. b. eidem sanctum corpus junctum est, ibid. Christo in cruce mortuo in coelum recepta est. 586. infernales passiones sustinuit. 53, b. 54. a.
units.tr: The soul of Christ: this does not signify his divinity. II.8.b. It was created holy by God: 17.b. The holy body was joined to it: ibid. When Christ died on the cross it was received into heaven: 586. It underwent infernal sufferings: 53.b; 54.a.

units.la: Anima hominis. Ejus creatio a Mose prodita. I. 217. est spiritualis & diversae a corpore essentiae. ibid. b. adeoque immaterialis. 218. a. immortalis. ibid. 218. b. 219. a. non est forma hominis. 222. a. ejus vita a corporis vita realiter distincta est. ibid. b. nonnisi una in homine est. 223. a. non est ex traduce. 233. a. non ante corpus creatum extitit. 234. a. nec statim in conceptione corporis inditur. ibid. ejus creatio peccati originalis propagationi non obstat. I. 351. a. pii post mortem est in manu Dei, I I.699. b. non migrat in alia corpora. 700. a. nec in purgatorium. ibid. b. non revertitur in terram nisi corpori unita. 714. a. animae proin defunctorum non apparent in terris. ibid. exemplum animae Samuelis nihil probat. 715. a. piorum a corpore separatae ilico a peccato liberantur, sanctificantur & in locum beatitudinis transferuntur. 705. b. 706. a. earum status gloriosus est. 707. a. 708. b. non dormiunt, aut nihil agunt, sed absque corpore vivunt & operantur. 708. b. Pontificii heic errantes refutantur. 709. 710. anima a corpore separata ad resuscitandum corpus nullas habet vires. 735. non resurget, sed corpori denuo unietur. 736. a.
units.tr: The soul of man. Its creation is related by Moses: I.217. It is spiritual and of a different essence from the body: ibid.b. And so it is immaterial: 218.a. Immortal: ibid.; 218.b; 219.a. It is not the form of man: 222.a. Its life is really distinct from the life of the body: ibid.b. There is only one in a man: 223.a. It is not by traduction: 233.a. It did not exist before the body was created: 234.a. Nor is it infused at the very moment of the body's conception: ibid. Its creation does not hinder the propagation of original sin: I.351.a. The soul of the pious after death is in the hand of God: II.699.b. It does not migrate into other bodies: 700.a. Nor into purgatory: ibid.b. It does not return to earth unless united with the body: 714.a. Therefore the souls of the dead do not appear on earth: ibid. The example of Samuel's soul proves nothing: 715.a. The souls of the pious, separated from the body, are at once freed from sin, sanctified and transferred into a place of blessedness: 705.b; 706.a. Their state is glorious: 707.a; 708.b. They do not sleep or do nothing, but live and act without a body: 708.b. The Papists, erring here, are refuted: 709, 710. A soul separated from the body has no power to raise the body: 735. It will not rise, but will be joined again to the body: 736.a.

units.tr: Why is the Antichrist so called? II.680. a. What and who is he? ibid. His marks and characteristics. ibid. b. They are the same marks which the Papists say belong to the Church. 552. b. 683. a. How he sat in the Church itself. 524. a. He was to sit in the temple of God. 540. a. Sanctificationem in sola actuum emendatione collocant. 317. b. Perseverantiam sanctorum habitum moralem faciunt. 379. a. Prævisionem eorum, qui gratiam Dei amplexuri erant, electionem factam esse. 390. a. Perseverantiam sanctorum dubiam reddunt. 402. b. eam impugnant. 421. b. Magistratui architectonicam in Ecclesiam potestatem tribuunt. 626. a. pœnarum infernalium æternitatem negant. 763. b.
units.tr: The Arminians. See Remonstrants. Their error on the decree of predestination. I. 165. b. They teach that Christ ascended into heaven before he descended. I. 3. b. In Christ the Mediator they separate his merit from its efficacy. 85. b. They attack the merit and satisfaction of Christ. 121. 122. a. They hold that Christ's satisfaction cannot stand together with faith and repentance. 217. a. They are Semipelagians, ibid. a. They teach that faith is an acquired habit, not an infused one. 243. 244. Their error concerning the object of saving faith. 246. b. They hold that a sinner's own righteousness is imputed to him. 280. b. They hold that imperfect faith is obedience to God's commands. 296. b. They place sanctification solely in the amendment of acts. 317. b. They make the perseverance of the saints a moral habit. 379. a. They hold that the election was made by foreseeing those who would embrace God's grace. 390. a. They render the perseverance of the saints doubtful. 402. b. They attack it. 421. b. They grant the magistrate architectonic power over the Church. 626. a. They deny the eternity of infernal punishments. 763. b.
